Orach Chaim: It is written (Proverbs 15:24): "The path of life leads upward for the wise, that he may keep away from Sheol below." And its explanation seems to be: For the angels were created on the second day as explained in the Midrash, and it is also explained in the Psalm "Bless the Lord, O my soul": "He makes the clouds His chariot... He makes His angels spirits." And the separation of the waters was on the second day, and the animals were created on the fifth day. The angels serve their Creator and do not have an evil inclination, while the animals have an evil inclination but do not have understanding. Consequently, the angels do not receive a reward for their service, since they do not have an evil inclination, and the animals are not subject to punishment since they do not have understanding.

And for this reason, the Holy One, blessed be He, created man on the sixth day. And He created him from two extremes: He gave him a soul that enlightens a person to know the Creator, blessed be He, like an angel, as it is said: "The soul of man is the candle of the Lord." And He formed him with a body which is coarse matter like an animal, to eat and drink and sleep. And for this reason, great battles arise within a person all his life, for the animalistic soul incites him to the desires of this world like an animal, and the pure soul fights against it and shows him that he was not created for this, but rather to serve the Creator like an angel. And even the physical things that he must do, such as eating, drinking, and sleeping, should be intended so that he can serve his Creator. And about this it is said: "I have set the Lord always before me." And after a person's death, it is shown to him that all his deeds are written in a book, and the hand of man signs it. And if he walked in the way of the Torah and the commandment, he inherits the Garden of Eden, which is an infinite and timeless pleasure. And about them it is said: "They are abundantly satisfied with the fatness of Your house; and You give them drink from the river of Your pleasures. For with You is the fountain of life; in Your light we see light." And if, God forbid, the opposite – he inherits Gehinnom, where all the sufferings of this world are as nothing compared to it. And about them it is said: "And they shall go forth and look upon the carcasses of the men that have transgressed against Me; for their worm shall not die, neither shall their fire be quenched; and they shall be an abhorring unto all flesh." And Gehinnom has seven names, and these are: "Sheol," and "Abaddon," and "Pit of Destruction," and "Pit of Tumult," and "Miry Clay," and "Shadow of Death," and "Lower Earth" (Eruvin 19a). And anyone who is enticed by his inclination falls there, and therefore it is also called "Tophet," as it is written: "For Tophet is ordained of old" (Isaiah 30:33).

And this is what Solomon said: "The path of life leads upward for the wise, so that he may turn away from Sheol below." This means: You, the wise person, have two paths before you—either to lift your eyes and heart upward to the Blessed Creator, which is the path of life, or to look downward at base desires. Therefore, I command you that your path of life should always be upward, so that you may turn away from Sheol below. This means: if you look downward, you will fall into Sheol, which is the first level of Gehenna, and from there you will fall further and further down.

And every sensible person should understand: Just as if one sees a mortal king building a precious structure composed of two opposites, within which he places precious stones like onyx and jasper and all kinds of precious stones, as well as clay and dirt, would anyone imagine that the king's ultimate purpose is for the clay and dirt? Certainly, the purpose of the building is the precious stones, and the clay and dirt are merely to strengthen the building. Similarly, the King of kings, the Holy One, blessed be He, created man composed of a pure soul, which is a part of God above, and it will return to God after his death, and also of a coarse body, which is clay and dirt. Could it be thought that the purpose is the clay and dirt? Anyone who thinks so is merely a fool and insane. And this is what Akavya ben Mahalalel said: "Consider three things and you will not come to sin: Know from where you came, and where you are going..." Meaning: the soul is a part of God above and will return to its source. In contrast, the body: from where did you come? From a putrid drop. And where are you going? To a place of dust, worms, and maggots. This clarifies that the purpose is the divine soul. Therefore, first and foremost, a person must know the fundamentals of our holy and pure Torah.

The foundation of the Torah and the pillar of worship is to know that there is one unique God, and He created all the worlds, and He oversees them at every moment and every instant. If, God forbid, His supervision were to be removed even for a moment, all the worlds would revert to chaos and void. This is what is meant by: "Hear, O Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is One." And it is stated: "Know today... that the Lord is God in heaven above and on the earth below, there is no other." This means that there is no power besides Him, blessed be He, and He brings all the worlds into existence, He enlivens all the worlds, and He sustains them. At the giving of the Torah, we saw this with our own eyes, as it is written: "You were shown to know that the Lord is God, there is none else besides Him." This means that the Lord who created all the worlds is the one who oversees and governs them forever and ever. And "Elohim" means supervision and governance, and there is no power, great or small, besides Him, blessed be He.

We are obligated to love this God with complete and absolute love, to the extent that all other loves, like the love of oneself, the love of one's wife, the love of one's sons and daughters, the love of wealth – are nullified in comparison to the love of the Blessed One, and they are as nothing at all. This is what the scripture says: "And you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your might." The term "might" means: everything that is very, very dear to you – nullify it in comparison to the love of the Blessed One. "With all your heart," our sages of blessed memory interpreted: with both your inclinations, the good inclination and the evil inclination. This means: do not say that since the evil inclination incites you to transgress His will, why then was it created? The truth is that the evil inclination's intent is also that you should not desire it nor heed it. However, the Blessed Creator decreed that it should incite you to transgress His will, so that through your choice, you will serve God and not as if compelled. This is the primary purpose of human creation, and in this power, one is greater than an angel, as I wrote in section 1 (and this is also explained in the Zohar).

And in the Sifrei it is taught: Rabbi Meir says: It states, "And you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart" — love Him with all your heart like our forefather Abraham, as it is said, "Abraham, who loved Me." And it says, "And You found his heart faithful before You." "And with all your soul" — like Isaac, who offered himself on the altar. "And with all your might" — be grateful to Him like Jacob, as it is said, "I am unworthy of all the kindness..." It also says there: "And you shall love..." — love Him in front of all creatures like your father Abraham, as it is said, "And the souls that they made in Haran." Meaning: just as Abraham, because he loved Him with his heart and soul, called upon people to believe in His divinity, so too should you love Him before all creatures and bring them closer to His service, blessed be He. We also learn in the Sifrei: Since it states "And you shall love," I do not know how to love Him? Therefore, it teaches: "And these words which I command you today shall be upon your heart," meaning that through this you will recognize the One who spoke and the world came into being. In other words: through contemplation in the Torah, love will necessarily be established in the heart (Chinuch).

And so we are commanded to fear Him, blessed be He, as it is written: "You shall fear the Lord your God." This is the language of the Rambam in the Book of Commandments, Commandment 4: He commanded us to believe in His exalted fear and to be afraid of Him. And we should not be like heretics who walk in the stubbornness of their hearts and casually, but we should fear His punishment at all times. And this is what is said: "You shall fear the Lord your God." Thus far his words. And in his great composition, at the beginning of the second chapter of the Foundations of the Torah, he wrote: And how is the way to love and fear Him? When a person contemplates His deeds and His wondrous and great creations, and sees from them His wisdom, which has no measure and no end, immediately he loves, praises, and glorifies, and desires with a great desire to know the great name, as David said: "My soul thirsts for God, for the living God." And when he thinks about these same things, immediately he recoils, and he fears and is afraid, and knows that he is a small, lowly, and obscure creature, standing with a slight and small understanding before the Perfect Knowledge. As David said: "When I see Your heavens, the work of Your fingers, what is man that You are mindful of him?" Thus far his words. And in the Book of Commandments, he explained "simple fear," which is the fear of punishment, and here he explained "awe of exaltation." And regarding this, we have learned in the Sifrei: There is no love in the place of fear, and no fear in the place of love, except in the attribute of the Holy One, blessed be He, alone. See there. Meaning: Fear and love are two opposites, but in the awe of exaltation, both can indeed exist, for through the greatness of His exaltedness, blessed be He, one fears Him with awe of exaltation, and loves Him with all one's heart and all one's soul.

And we are commanded to follow His good and upright ways, as it is said: "And you shall walk in His ways." And it is said: "After the Lord your God you shall walk." And it is said: "To walk in all His ways" – just as He is gracious, so you too be gracious; just as He is merciful, so you too be merciful (a similar idea is found in Sotah 14a), and to emulate His good actions and upright attributes to the best of our ability. And it is a positive commandment to cleave to the sages and their disciples in order to learn from their deeds, as it is said: "And to Him you shall cleave." Can a person possibly cleave to the Divine Presence, which is a consuming fire? Rather, cleave to the sages and their disciples (Ketubot 111b). And be covered in the dust of their feet, and drink their words thirstily. And it is said: "He who walks with the wise will become wise." And it is said: "Happy is the man who does not walk in the counsel of the wicked..."

The Sefer Mitzvot Gadol (SeMaG) writes in the positive commandments, commandment 17: It is a positive commandment to justify God's judgment in all occurrences, as it is stated: "And you shall know in your heart, that just as a man disciplines his son, so the Lord your God disciplines you..." (Deuteronomy 8:5). Until here is his language. And we, the children of Israel, weary from time, without rest for nearly two thousand years - we must understand that all of this is for our benefit to purify us, as the prophet Zechariah said: "And I will refine them as silver is refined, and I will test them as gold is tested. He will call on My name, and I will answer him. I said, 'They are My people,' and they will say, 'The Lord is my God'" (Zechariah 13:9). The explanation of the verse: to believe with complete faith that all our troubles and all our wanderings are not in the way of revenge, God forbid, but to purify us. For if it were not so, we would have ceased to exist long ago over these many centuries, and there is no greater sign and wonder than our long existence, which is only because His providence, blessed be He, is upon us, not ceasing and will not cease even for a moment, like a father watching over his only son and disciplining him for his benefit. And proof of this: for in all times of exile "he will call on My name, and I will answer him." Meaning: when we pray to Him, blessed be He, He answers us in every time of trouble and distress. "I said, 'They are My people,' and they will say..." Meaning: that we see that throughout this long time, the people of Israel follow the way of the Torah and the commandments, and He, blessed be He, calls us "My people," and we call Him "the God of Israel."

It is a fundamental principle of the faith to believe that our holy Torah, as it is, was given to us from Sinai through Moses our teacher. If even one letter is missing, it is invalid. There is no difference in sanctity between the verse "Shema Yisrael" and the verse "And Timna was a concubine." Just as the Holy One, blessed be He, lives and exists forever and ever, so too the Torah is eternal, as we say in "Emet Veyatziv": "He exists, and His name exists..., and His words are living and enduring, faithful and delightful forever and to all eternity..." Therefore, Malachi, who was the last prophet, said: "Remember the Torah of Moses My servant..."

And it is a fundamental principle of our faith to believe in the Oral Torah, as it is stated: "According to the instruction that they will teach you…" (Deuteronomy 17:11). The Holy One, blessed be He, made a covenant with Israel only because of the Oral Torah, as it is stated: "For according to these words I have made a covenant with you and with Israel" (Gittin 60b). The Oral Torah gives life to the Written Torah, for there is not a single commandment in the Written Torah that is explained in detail; the Oral Torah elucidates it. This is the Mishnah and the Gemara, which clarify all the details of the commandments. Anyone who does not acknowledge the Oral Torah has no portion in the God of Israel.

One of the fundamentals of the faith is to believe in the reward of the World to Come, the punishment of Gehenna, the coming of the Messiah, and the resurrection of the dead. Another fundamental of the faith is to perform all the commandments not because reason dictates so, such as in the commandments between a person and another, but because the Holy One, blessed be He, commanded us to do so. Therefore, it is stated in the latter set of the Ten Commandments regarding the Sabbath and honoring one's parents: "As the Lord your God has commanded you." This is because it is universally agreed upon in every nation and language that a person needs to rest one day a week to strengthen their abilities, and it is also universally agreed upon in every nation and language to honor one's parents. Hence, the Torah states: "Keep the Sabbath day to sanctify it as the Lord your God has commanded you," "Honor your father and your mother as the Lord your God has commanded you," meaning not because reason dictates so. In the first set of the Ten Commandments, before the sin of the Golden Calf, there was no need for this warning, since they were all on the level of angels, as it is written: "I said, 'You are gods, and all of you are children of the Most High.'" There are other fundamentals of the faith, and Maimonides included them in thirteen principles, which are printed in prayer books and known to all. However, the truth is that every commandment among the 613 commandments is a fundamental principle of the faith, and every letter of the Torah is a fundamental principle of the faith. The proof is that if one letter is missing, it is invalid. Similarly, in the Oral Torah, anyone who denies even one matter is considered a heretic, as Maimonides wrote at the beginning of the third chapter of "Mamrim," and this is his language: "Anyone who does not acknowledge the Oral Torah is included among the heretics." There is no difference whether one denies it all or denies just a part of it, just as with the Written Torah. There is no need to elaborate on this, for it is known to those who study our holy Torah.

And these are the words of the Ra'ah in Sefer HaChinuch (in the introduction): Six commandments are obligatory at all times, they do not cease even for a single moment all the days of a person's life. And every moment that one thinks about them, he fulfills a positive commandment. And these are they: The first: to believe that there is one God in the world, who created this great creation. He was, He is, and He will be forever. And He brought us out of Egypt, and gave us the Torah. This is included in the verse "I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt..." The second: to believe that there is no god other than Him, as it is said: "You shall have no other gods before Me." Meaning, that there is no power other than Him. The third: to unify Him, as it is said: "The Lord is one." The fourth: to love Him, as it is said: "And you shall love..." The fifth: to fear Him, as it is said: "You shall fear the Lord your God." The sixth: not to stray after the heart and after the eyes, as it is written: "And you shall not stray after your heart and after your eyes..." "After your heart" - this refers to heresy. "After your eyes" - this refers to promiscuity (end of the first chapter of Berachot). Until here are his words, and the intention is not to entertain thoughts of heresy. And if such thoughts come to the heart by themselves, he should divert them from his mind, and strengthen himself with Torah and fear of God, and keep his eyes away from matters of promiscuity. And if by chance such matters come before his eyes, he should divert his mind and strengthen himself...

It is taught in Avot, Chapter Four: Rabbi Yaakov says: This world is like a corridor before the World to Come. Prepare yourself in the corridor so that you may enter the banquet hall. This is a fundamental principle in the life of a Jewish person, to know that this world is a world of action, and the World to Come is a world of reward. This world is the gateway to enter the World to Come. Therefore, one should be careful not to waste time in vain, for time is more precious than all material possessions, and a day that has passed will never return. It is sufficient that necessities take up a large portion of time, and the days of a person's life are short. When a person reaches old age, they see that everything is vanity. This is why Solomon said: "And remember your Creator in the days of your youth, before the evil days come, and the years draw near when you will say, 'I have no pleasure in them'" (Ecclesiastes 12:1). The "evil days" are the days of old age. At that time, you will say, "I have no pleasure in them," meaning in all worldly matters. Then you will recognize the truth on your own, but your strength will be weakened. Therefore, "Remember your Creator in the days of your youth," and dedicate your life to the sanctification of God's name. This will be explained at length in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 157, with the help of Heaven.

In the fifth chapter of Avot, it is taught: Yehuda ben Tema says: Be bold as a leopard, light as an eagle, run like a deer, and strong as a lion to do the will of your Father in Heaven. The commentary of the Ra'avad explains: "Bold as a leopard" – do not be ashamed to ask your teacher about what you did not understand, for a bashful person does not learn. "Light as an eagle" – to review your studies without weariness, as it is written: "They will mount up with wings as eagles, they shall run and not be weary." "Run like a deer" – to pursue mitzvot. "Strong as a lion" – to conquer your inclination towards sin. Thus far his words. The Tur explains: "Bold as a leopard" – to stand firm against those who mock, and do not refrain from performing a mitzvah because of the mockers. "Light as an eagle" – that flies in the heavens, and close your eyes from seeing evil, for the eye is the beginning of sin. "Run like a deer" – that your feet run towards good. "Strong as a lion" – against the heart, to strengthen your heart in His service, see there. (And in my humble opinion, it seems that because a person is composed of four primary elements: fire, wind, water, earth. He said "bold as a leopard" corresponding to the element of fire which is very bold, "light as an eagle" corresponding to the element of wind which is very light, "run like a deer" corresponding to the element of water which moves back and forth, "strong as a lion" corresponding to the element of earth which is strong and tough. The intention is that one should use all the elements of the body only for matters of the Creator, may He be blessed, and not for matters of this world.)

Our teacher, the Rema, wrote: "I have set the Lord always before me" – this is a great principle in the Torah and in the virtues of the righteous who walk before God. For a person's sitting, movements, and activities when he is alone in his house are not the same as his sitting, movements, and activities when he is before a great king. Nor is his speech and the way he freely expresses himself as he wishes when he is with his household and relatives the same as his speech in the presence of a king. All the more so when a person sets in his heart that the great King, the Holy One, blessed be He, whose glory fills the whole earth, stands over him and sees his deeds, as it is said: "If a man hides in secret places, do I not see him? says the Lord" – immediately, fear and humility will come upon him with the awe of the Blessed One and his shame before Him will always be present. Even in private, and when he lies on his bed – he should know before whom he lies. And as soon as he wakes from his sleep, he should rise with alacrity to serve his Creator, blessed and exalted be He. He should not be ashamed before people who mock him in his service of the Blessed One (this is the correct way to say it). Thus far is his language, and he says two things: Because the Holy One, blessed be He, stands over him always, therefore even in private, meaning even when he is alone or with his wife and children – he should conduct himself with fear and humility as if standing before a king. And it is also explained in the Guide for the Perplexed (Part III, Chapter 52) from where these things are sourced, see there. And he further says that the fear and shame before the Blessed One should always be upon him. Therefore, even when he is among people – he should do what is incumbent upon him in the service of the Blessed One, and not be ashamed before those who mock if there are mockers, because the shame before the Blessed One should outweigh the shame before people. And he should also not quarrel with them (Magen Avraham), for quarreling is a bad trait and leads to brazenness. One should distance oneself from it even when quarreling for the sake of a mitzvah, rather he should perform his actions for the sake of the Blessed One, and not worry about their mockery. (And what David said: "I will quarrel with those who rise up against You" – this is in the context of disputing matters of religion, or when they prevent the performance of commandments, for it cannot be otherwise. But for mere mockery, there is no need to quarrel.)

In the words of Ben Teima, it is explained that one must be "mighty as a lion." Therefore, every morning when rising from his bed, he should strengthen himself like a lion to stand up to serve his Creator. And even if his inclination persuades him in the winter, saying: "How can you get up in the morning when the cold is severe?" or persuades him in the summer, saying: "How can you get up from your bed when you have not yet had enough sleep?"—he should overcome it and rise, so that he awakens the dawn and the dawn does not awaken him. As David said: "Awake, my glory; awake, harp and lyre; I will awaken the dawn"—I awaken the dawn, and the dawn does not awaken me. All the more so if he rises before the dawn to beseech his Creator—how good and how beautiful (Tur). And if he cannot rise before the dawn, at least the prayer which is the time for all living beings—he should not delay it (he should pray with the congregation). And he should think in his heart: If he were in the service of a mortal king, and the king commanded him to rise at dawn for his service, he would be careful and diligent to stand and serve as commanded. All the more so and certainly before the King of kings, the Holy One, blessed be He (ibid.). And this is what our teacher, the Rema, wrote—that in any case, he should not delay the time of prayer that the congregation prays, see there.

David said: "But as for me, let my prayer be unto You, O Lord, in an acceptable time...". Similarly, Isaiah said: "In an acceptable time have I answered you". From this we learn that "an acceptable time" is a significant concept (Yevamot 72a). And the Gemara explains: When is "an acceptable time"? When the community is praying (Berachot 8a). And so it is in the Zohar Terumah (page 156a), and this is its language: "We have learned, when is it called 'an acceptable time'? At the time when the community is praying...," see there. However, in Yevamot it is explained that midnight is "an acceptable time," see there. And in Yoma (69b) it is explained that there is "an acceptable time" even without a fixed time and without a community. And it is also explained in Ta'anit (24b) that through a dream it was revealed to Rava that presently is an acceptable time, see there. And all is true, for certainly there are fixed times for "an acceptable time," and there are also non-fixed times according to the decree of the King of the Universe.

The Tur and the Shulchan Aruch wrote in section 2: One who rises early to plead before his Creator should aim for the times when the guards change, which are at a third of the night, at the end of two-thirds of the night, and at the end of the night. For the prayer that one prays at those times about the destruction and the exile is desirable. Thus far is his language. And this matter is explained by what is stated at the beginning of Berachot, that at each guard shift, it is as if, so to speak, He roars like a lion, as it is written: "The Lord roars from on high... He roars mightily over His dwelling." Now, according to the first explanation in the Gemara (3a) which considers the middle of the middle guard, it works out well, as it also includes midnight among them. But according to the second explanation which considers the end of the guards, the reason it does not include midnight among them is because midnight is a time of favor for all matters, and these three are only for the destruction of the Temple. Therefore, what the Kabbalistic sages elaborated that midnight is a favorable time to seek mercy for the destruction and for the congregation of Israel also fits well according to the Gemara, that midnight is a time of favor for everything. (And the commentators labored in vain. And see Magen Avraham, small section 4, who wrote that according to the second explanation the Gemara disagrees with this, see there. In my humble opinion, it is not so. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

And our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 3: It is proper for every God-fearing person to feel distressed and concerned about the destruction of the Holy Temple. These are his words, and it seems that this refers to the three watches mentioned earlier. This is derived from the language of the Rosh, who wrote about the three watches as follows: It is proper for every God-fearing person to feel distressed and concerned at that time, and to pour out supplications over the destruction of the Holy Temple, as it is said: "Arise, cry out in the night at the beginning of the watches; pour out your heart like water..." These are his words. Also, what he wrote afterward in section 4: A few heartfelt supplications are better than many without intention. These are also his words, referring to the same matter, the destruction of the Holy Temple. This is from the words of the Tur, who wrote about the three watches as follows: The prayer offered at that time for the destruction is desirable... whether one prays much or little, as long as one's heart is directed in one's supplications. For a little with intention is better than much without intention. These are his words, meaning: If one has time to say supplications but no more, it is better to say a few with intention than many without intention. This applies to all matters, such as Torah study, reciting Psalms, and the like: a little with intention is better than much without intention. According to the Kabbalistic sages, the main rectification is at midnight, as printed in the prayer books. This is also according to the Gemara, as I wrote in the previous section. Midnight is the middle of the night, twelve hours after noon, whether in summer or winter. Most of the great sages of Israel agreed on this, and this is the main practice. (But the Beit Yosef’s intention is not to remind us to remember the destruction of the Holy Temple, which is obvious, for in the Amidah there are three fixed blessings for this: "And to Jerusalem," "The offspring of Your servant," "Be favorable...". Also in the Grace after Meals, there is a fixed blessing for this. Before Grace after Meals, it is customary to say "By the rivers of Babylon," and on Shabbat, Yom Tov, and Rosh Chodesh, "A song of ascents." We have many remembrances for the destruction of the Holy Temple, especially during the Three Weeks. Who among the people of Israel would forget it? Rather, his intention is about the time of the watches, as I have written. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

The Tur and Shulchan Aruch write in Section 5: It is good to recite the passage of the Binding of Isaac, the passage of the Manna, the Ten Commandments, the passage of the Burnt Offering, the Meal Offering, the Peace Offering, the Sin Offering, and the Guilt Offering. This is their language. And in Section 9, our teacher the Beit Yosef wrote: Some have the custom to recite the passage of the Basin and the passage of the Removal of the Ashes. And afterward, the passage of the Daily Offering. And afterward, the passage of the Altar of Incense and the passage of the Ingredients of the Incense and its Preparation. This is his language. And in Section 8, he wrote: One should say with the passage of the sacrifices: "And he shall slaughter it on the side of the altar, northward before the Lord." This is his language, because it is stated in the Midrash that at the time when the Israelites say this verse, the Holy One, blessed be He, remembers the Binding of Isaac. And we say it after the passage of the Daily Offering.

Our custom, as printed in the prayer books, is to recite the passage of the Binding of Isaac, followed by the passage of the Laver and the removal of the ashes, and the passage of the daily offering and the incense, including both what is written in the Torah and all the teachings of our Sages of blessed memory at the beginning of Tractate Keritot (6a), which mention that there were eleven ingredients in it, and these are: the balsam, the onycha..., and all the detailed laws concerning them. After this, we recite: "Abaye would arrange the order of the arrangement," which is from the third chapter of Yoma; see there. However, we do not recite the passage of the manna, nor the Ten Commandments, nor the passages of the burnt offering, the meal offering, the peace offering, the sin offering, and the guilt offering. Instead, we recite the entire fifth chapter of Zevachim: "What is the location of their offering...". This is not contrary to the words of Rabbeinu the Beit Yosef, as it seems to me that what he wrote in paragraph 9, "There are those who have the custom...", also means this. In other words, there are those who have the custom not to recite as I wrote in paragraph 5, but only the passage of the Laver...

And the reason appears to me that a prayer which is established for the congregation, meaning that all of Israel says it, consists only of matters for the congregation and not for an individual. And why is it that we recite the sections of the burnt offering, meal offering, peace offering, sin offering, and guilt offering, since these are not for the congregation and also not obligatory for an individual? The reason we say the chapter "Eizehu Mekoman" is to study a chapter of Mishnah every day, which is the Oral Torah, and they chose this chapter that deals with the matters of sacrifices, and it is stated without dispute. But to establish these sacrifices from the Torah portions is unnecessary. And if it is because of the study of the Written Torah, there is already much in the prayer: the three sections of the Shema, the Song of the Sea, the section of the daily offering… and certainly, we say the section of the Akedah (Binding of Isaac), since it is a merit for all of Israel and to remember the merit of our holy ancestors. Therefore, it was established afterward to say "Ribono Shel Olam" (Master of the World), and its essence is from the Midrash regarding the Akedah, see there. Also, the Ten Commandments cannot be established for the congregation, since they were abolished because of the complaints of the heretics, who would say: there is no Torah except this, as it is stated at the end of the first chapter of Berachot. Indeed, they challenged what is written in paragraph 5, which says to recite the Ten Commandments, and they answered that it is permitted for an individual. And this is what Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote there, and this is his language: "And it is specifically permitted for an individual to recite the Ten Commandments every day. But it is forbidden to say them in public." Until here is his language. And if so, it is impossible to establish this as a fixed text. But regarding the section of the manna, which was omitted – I do not know the reason. However, in truth, the section of the manna is not mentioned in the Talmud. Some bring it from the Jerusalem Talmud Berachot (Pri Megadim, section 14), and I did not find this in the Jerusalem Talmud. The reason appears to me: because this section includes many complaints against God, as it is written there: "for I have heard your complaints," "I have heard the complaints of the children of Israel," and more, see there. And they also spoke ill of the manna, saying: "and now our souls are dried up, there is nothing at all except this manna to look at." And it is also stated in the Midrash Shemot (section 25): "I was found by those who did not seek me" – they should have sought mercy from before Me, but instead, they stood and poured out complaints towards Heaven. Until here is his language. And further, we say there: And why did they not sing a song about the manna… because they spoke trivial words about the manna. The Holy One, blessed be He, said: I do not seek neither your complaints nor your praises, see there. Therefore, it was not established for the congregation (so it appears according to my humble opinion).

The section of the Tamid and the Ketoret should not be recited at night, as the offering of the Tamid and the burning of the Ketoret are only performed during the day. However, the section of the Kiyor (laver) and the removal of the ashes (Terumat HaDeshen) may be recited even before dawn. Indeed, the primary removal of the ashes took place at night, as it is taught in Yoma (20a): "Every day they would remove the ashes from the altar at the call of the rooster or close to it... but on Yom Kippur from midnight, and on the festivals from the first watch," see there. Similarly, the burning of the limbs, which is mentioned in this section, occurred throughout the night, so they needed to first sanctify their hands and feet from the Kiyor. Therefore, we recite the section of the Kiyor before the section of the Terumat HaDeshen. Afterward, for the Tamid, the priests did not need to sanctify from the Kiyor. Although we hold like Rabbi in Zevachim (19b) that overnight invalidates the sanctification of hands and feet, nevertheless, we hold like Rabbi Yochanan there (20a) who says: "If one sanctified his hands and feet for the removal of ashes for the next day, he does not need to sanctify again, because it is the beginning of the service," see there. And so ruled Rambam in the fifth chapter of Beit HaMikdash, see there. According to this, it seems that even before midnight one can recite the section of the Kiyor and the Terumat HaDeshen, as on the festivals they would separate from the first watch, but this is not the custom. Perhaps because throughout the year they would separate before the call of the rooster or after the call of the rooster, we also mention this only before dawn after midnight.

And there are those who wrote that these passages must be recited specifically while standing, because sitting is invalid for the service (Magen Avraham, beginning of Siman 48). And many disagree with this (Shaarei Teshuvah there in the name of the Tvuot Shor, the Chacham Tzvi, and the Mor Uketzi'ah). And in truth, were all of Israel offering sacrifices? The priests were the ones who offered, and we say "as if we offered" because the sacrifice was on behalf of all Israel, from the funds of the Temple treasury. The priests are our agents, and agents of Heaven. And if it is because of the "Ma'amadot" (standing groups) which was an obligation on all Israel as it is taught in the fourth chapter of Taanit, were they obligated to stand specifically? And in my humble opinion, it seems that a Kohen needs to stand, as he should think: if it were in the time of the Temple, he himself would be offering and burning [the sacrifices]. But a Levite and an Israelite do not need to stand. (And it needs investigation why they did not institute saying the daily song after the Tamid and the incense, since the song was during the wine libation, as it is taught in Tamid. And in the portion of the Tamid we said "and its libation of wine…", so why did they institute it after the prayer? And perhaps because we hold: their meal offerings and libations [can be brought] even at night, therefore they did not worry about this. Additionally, the priests themselves would recite the Shema and pray a bit immediately after the slaughter of the Tamid, as it is taught in the fifth chapter of Tamid, and the song was a long time after that, and therefore we also do so. And be precise and you will find a light.)

The Tur wrote: When one finishes the section of the burnt offering, he should say: "Master of the Universe! May it be Your will that this be considered and accepted before You as if I had offered a burnt offering in its proper time." Similarly, he should say this in the sections of the meal offering, the peace offerings, and the guilt offering. However, after the section of the sin offering, he should not say this, because it is not brought voluntarily. Thus far his words. But our master, the Beit Yosef, did not mention the guilt offering either, because it is also not brought voluntarily, as he wrote in his major work. The Tur holds that a contingent guilt offering can also be brought voluntarily, as is clear from his words in Yoreh De'ah, section 5 (where he ruled according to Rabbi Eliezer in Kritut 25a that one may voluntarily bring a contingent guilt offering every day). The Rambam did not rule this way. Therefore, we must say: even though the Tur did not specify a contingent guilt offering, nevertheless, his intention is so, because the general term "guilt offering" refers to a contingent guilt offering. Some say it is because one can vow to become a nazirite and defile himself and bring a guilt offering (see Magen Avraham, subsection 11). This is not understood at all, for who would vow to become a nazirite? There are several other difficulties with this, and therefore, it seems as I wrote previously that his intention is a contingent guilt offering. (In my humble opinion, the Tur's words follow the opinion of Rabbeinu Tam in Pesachim 73a, s.v. "guilt offering," see there. Examine this and you will find it clear.)

And now we say the "Yehi Ratzon" in the Mishnayot of "Eizehu Mekoman" concerning the Olah, Todah, and Shelamim offerings. The Maharshal wrote that conditionally, one can also say it concerning the Chattat and Asham offerings: "If I were obligated to bring a Chattat offering, it should be as if I offered a Chattat," and similarly for the Asham. Meaning: and if not, it should be as if he is reading from the Torah (thus resolving the Taz's question at the end of sub-section 7). Some are puzzled by this, as it is established that a Chattat requires awareness at the beginning (Magen Avraham there). However, this is not puzzling, as he says: "as if I offered a Chattat," meaning: "as if I offered it with awareness" (according to some). And also, the Asham, according to the Rambam, requires awareness at the beginning, and there is no need to elaborate further on this.

In the Jerusalem Talmud, at the beginning of the chapter "Tefillat HaShachar," it says: From where did they derive the three prayers? Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani says: Corresponding to the three times the day changes for people. In the morning, one should say: "I give thanks before You... for You have brought me out of darkness into light." In the afternoon, one should say: "I give thanks... just as You have allowed me to see the sun in the east, so too have You allowed me to see the sun in the west." In the evening, one should say: "May it be Your will... just as I was in darkness and You brought me out of darkness into light, so too bring me out of darkness into light." See there, and none of the decisors have brought this. (And perhaps it is because Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani says this is in relation to the prayers, while Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi and Rabbi Yose say there that we derive it from the Patriarchs and the daily offerings, see there. And in our Talmud only the words of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi and Rabbi Yose are brought, and not the words of Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani, therefore the decisors omitted this.)

It has already been explained that even in the innermost chambers, a person must conduct themselves with modesty, for the Holy One, blessed be He, fills the whole earth with His glory. Therefore, if one sleeps naked, they should not rise naked from their bed but should put on their robe while still lying down. And one should not even put on their robe while sitting, because half of their body would be exposed. Rather, they should take their robe, insert their head and arms into it while still lying down, so that when they rise, they will be covered. Similarly, when going to sleep and removing their robe, they should not remove it standing or sitting but while lying down and covered with a blanket over their body. They should place the robe next to them so that when they rise, they will not need to sit naked. This is a measure of modesty. And one should not say: "Who sees me?" – for the whole earth is filled with His glory, blessed be He. (And there is no strictness regarding the feet, nor in the bathhouse.)

One should be particular with their garment to wear it in the proper manner, ensuring not to turn it inside out, so that the seams and the hems of the garment are not visible, which would cause disgrace among people. This applies even to a garment where there is not much difference between the inner and outer sides, and certainly to other clothes. Just as a person needs to avoid causing people to speak ill of them, so too must they avoid being disgraced in the eyes of people. It is stated in Shabbat (Shabbat 114a): Who is a Torah scholar? It is one who is particular to turn their garment right-side out. This means that even if they accidentally wore it inside out, they trouble themselves to take it off, turn it right-side out, and put it back on. One who is not a Torah scholar would not trouble themselves so much. Initially, everyone should be meticulous about this (Taz, subparagraph 2). If this is true for a garment, it is certainly true for other clothes. In Bava Batra (57b), it is stated: What is the garment of a Torah scholar? It is one where their flesh is not visible beneath it and it reaches the ground when they walk barefoot (Rashbam). Consequently, in our times, there is no concern. However, Rambam in the fifth chapter of De'ot explains that it should not be so thin that their flesh is visible through it. It is further stated there: What is the tallit of a Torah scholar? It is one where their garment does not show beneath it by a handbreadth. The tallit is the outer garment, and the intention is that the lower garment should not be longer than the outer one. Any student who is found with a stain on their garment, such as milk or fat or any repulsive thing, is liable to death because they bring the Torah into disrepute in the eyes of people (Shabbat, ibid.). Rather, their clothes should be clean from dirt. It is forbidden for a student to walk in patched shoes, with patch upon patch (ibid.), in a manner that would cause disgrace, unless it is in mud and mire during the rainy season, in which case there is no concern.

This is the language of the Rambam there, Law 9: The dress of a Torah scholar should be pleasant and clean, and it is forbidden for him to have a stain or grease or similar on his garment. He should not wear garments of purple that everyone looks at, nor should he wear garments of the poor that disgrace the wearer, but rather moderate, nice clothes. His flesh should not be visible under his clothing, like the light linen garments made in Egypt. His clothes should not drag on the ground like those of the arrogant, but rather reach his ankles, and the sleeve should reach the tips of his fingers... He should not go out perfumed to the market, nor in perfumed clothes, nor should he put perfume in his hair. However, if he anoints his body to remove dirt, it is permitted. Also, he should not go out alone at night unless he has a fixed time to go out for his studies. All these are due to suspicion. So far his words. (See Berachot 43b and Chullin 91a where it explains due to harm, and it requires investigation.)

Further, it is written there in law 7: A Torah scholar should not shout and scream while speaking. He should not raise his voice excessively, but rather speak gently with all people. And when he speaks gently, he should ensure not to appear overly distant, like an arrogant person. He should greet every person first and judge everyone favorably. He speaks of the praise of his friend and not of his disgrace at all. He loves peace and pursues peace. If he sees that his words are effective and heard, he speaks; if not, he remains silent... He only speaks words of wisdom and acts of kindness, and the like. He should not converse with a woman in the marketplace, even if she is his wife, sister, or daughter. Up to here is his wording. All the more so, he should not be accustomed to oaths and vows. He should not frequent banquets everywhere. He should distance himself from gatherings of scoffers and from unworthy people.

It is stated at the end of Horayot: There are five things that cause one to forget their learning: One who eats from what a mouse has eaten, and from what a cat has eaten; one who eats the heart of an animal; one who regularly eats olives; one who drinks the water from leftover washing; and one who washes his feet one atop the other. And some say: Also, one who places his garments, meaning his clothes, under his head. And there are five things that restore one's learning: Bread baked on coals, and all the more so, the coals themselves; one who eats an egg that is slightly roasted without salt, and "slightly roasted" means it is somewhat cooked (see Rashi on Shabbat 38b, "because"); one who regularly consumes olive oil; one who regularly drinks wine and spices; and one who drinks the water from leftover dough. And some say: Also, one who dips his finger in salt and eats.

It is further stated there: Ten things are difficult for learning (to understand what one studies): One who passes under the camel’s yoke, and certainly under the camel itself; and one who passes between two camels; and one who passes between two women; and a woman who passes between two men; and one who passes under the foul smell of a carcass; and one who passes under a bridge that water has not flowed under it for forty days; and one who eats bread that has not been fully baked; and one who eats meat that has been stirred with a stirrer (this is the spoon used to stir the pot); and one who drinks from a water conduit that passes through a cemetery; and one who looks at the face of a dead person. And some say: Even one who reads the writing on a grave, see there. And some have written that wearing two garments together is also difficult for memory (Magen Avraham, subsection 3, in the name of Kavanot). And it appears that with shoes, there is no concern.

Our Rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, wrote in Section 4: One should put on the right shoe first and not tie it. Then put on the left shoe and tie it, and then go back and tie the right shoe. And with our shoes, which do not have laces, one should put on the right shoe first. And when taking off one's shoes, one should remove the left shoe first. So far is his language. The same applies to socks: when putting them on, one should put the right one on first, and when taking them off, one should remove the left one first (Shulchan Aruch HaRav). There are those who disagree with this (Ozrot HaChaim), but this is not the main opinion. And even with tying them, just as we tie our socks around the foot which we call "paduska," the same rule applies: one should put on the right sock and not tie it, then put on the left sock and tie it, and then go back and tie the right one. This is also our practice, and one should not deviate from the words of our Rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch. The Tur ruled similarly; see there.

And the explanation of the matter is as follows: Behold, in every place the Torah gives honor to the right side, as in the service of the Temple where only the right side is fit for service. Similarly, in the sprinklings on the thumb of the hand and the big toe in the portion of "Metzora" it is written: "the right." And in all human actions – the right is primary. Therefore, one should dress it first. Hence, in the case of removing shoes, the left should be removed first, so that the right remains dressed, for the honor of the limb is when it is dressed. However, in the tying of tefillin, we find that the Torah gives honor to the left, as the tefillin are tied on the left hand. Therefore, anything related to tying – honor is given to the left. And anything related to wearing and dressing – honor is given to the right first, and this is according to the words of the Tur and Shulchan Aruch. And so it is in the Gemara Shabbat (61a), where Rav Nachman Bar Yitzchak said that this is how Mar, the son of Ravina, acted. And all our early authorities – the Rif, the Rambam, the Rosh, the Mordechai, and the SeMaG – omitted this entirely and did not mention this matter at all. Their reasoning is clear, for later it says there: Rav Ashi said: I saw Rav Kahana who was not particular about this. See there, and Rav Ashi is the later authority. (And in Eretz Hachaim, it is written that Mar, the son of Ravina, is a later authority like Rav Ashi, see there. But this is not so, for here it is Mar, the son of "Ravna" and not "Ravina." And about him, Rav Ashi said in Yevamot (22a): Is it not Mar, the son of Ravna, who signed this? And he was an earlier authority. Nevertheless, the Tur and Shulchan Aruch were concerned with this, since Rav Nachman Bar Yitzchak said: "A God-fearing person should act this way..." and we must uphold the words of the Tur and Shulchan Aruch.)

It is forbidden for a person to walk four cubits with an upright posture, as it is stated: "The whole earth is filled with His glory" (Kiddushin 31a). And anyone who walks with an upright posture – it is as if he is pushing away the feet of the Divine Presence (Berachot 43b). The intention is not that one should walk bent over, but rather that one should not walk overly erect with an extended neck like the manner of the arrogant. And this is the language of the Rambam in the fifth chapter of De'ot, law 8: A Torah scholar should not walk with an upright posture and an extended neck, as it is stated: "And they walk with outstretched necks." He should not walk heel-to-toe leisurely, like women and the haughty, as it is stated: "Walking and mincing as they go." He should not run in the public domain like the manner of lunatics, nor should he bend his back like those with hunched backs, but rather he should look downward as if he is standing in prayer. And he should walk in the marketplace as a person who is occupied with his business. Even from a person's manner of walking, it is discernible whether he is wise and understanding or foolish and senseless. So too, Solomon said in his wisdom: "Even when the fool walks on the road, his heart lacks sense, and he says to everyone that he is a fool" – he informs everyone about himself that he is a fool. Thus far is his language.

It is stated in Kiddushin there: Rav Huna the son of Rav Yehoshua would not walk four cubits with his head uncovered. He said: "The Divine Presence is above my head." And he himself said in Shabbat (118b): "May it be a merit for me that I do not walk four cubits with my head uncovered." And there (156b) it is stated: "Cover your head so that the fear of Heaven will be upon you." And it brings there a story that uncovering the head led a person to transgress. And it is stated in Tractate Kallah: Once the elders were sitting at the gate and two children passed by them. One covered his head and the other uncovered his head. They investigated the one who uncovered his head and found that he was a mamzer (illegitimate child) and the son of a menstruant woman, see there. 

The matter is that the head, which contains the brain, the source of wisdom and reverence, should not be exposed before the Blessed One, whose glory fills the whole earth, just as one should not stand in a holy place with an uncovered head. And if one does not do so, the brazenness of his inclination will overpower him even without him realizing it. 

Now, there are some great authorities who hold that, by strict law, there is a prohibition in this, and there are those who hold that this is merely a pious practice. However, whether one way or the other, experience testifies to this. (And in cases of necessity, such as in the courts of the king where the law of the kingdom requires not to cover the head by name — it is permitted. But where there is no necessity, whoever wants to merit the fear of Heaven should guard himself from this. And it is sufficient for the understanding. Pay attention and you will find it light.)

And one should check their bodily needs before prayer, as Rabbi Yochanan said (Berachot 15a): Whoever wishes to accept upon himself the yoke of the Kingdom of Heaven completely should relieve himself, wash his hands, put on tefillin, recite the Shema, and pray. A person should make it a practice to relieve himself in the morning and evening, which is a matter of vigilance, alacrity, and cleanliness. He only needs to check himself. However, if he has checked and nothing comes out, even if he thinks he needs to, he is still considered to have a "clean body" and is obligated to pray. God forbid he misses the time of the Shema because of this, as the Torah was not given to ministering angels. What can he do? Many make this mistake, so it is necessary to warn them. And he should not walk with part of his body exposed, nor should he walk barefoot, for there is nothing more disgraceful than someone who walks barefoot.

It is written: "For He will command His angels concerning you, to guard you in all your ways." And in Shabbat (119b), we say: Two ministering angels accompany a person, see there. And in Chagigah (16a), it is stated: Two angels accompany a person and testify about him, see there. Therefore, our sages of blessed memory instructed in Berakhot (60b) that when one needs to enter the bathroom, he should say before entering: "Be honored, honored holy ones, servants of the Most High, guard me, guard me! Help me, help me! [...] Wait for me until I enter and exit, for this is the way of human beings." Its explanation is that he asks the angels, since they are holy and will not enter there, to wait for him until he exits. And he asks them to guard him from harmful entities, as this is the intention of the verse: "For He will command His angels concerning you, to guard you in all your ways." Meaning, in any way you must go, even in a place where they cannot enter. And the guarding is from harmful entities, as it is written earlier: "You will not fear the terror of night... nor the destruction that lays waste at noon..." And he says "Help me, help me" regarding cleanliness, since the removal of waste is crucial for health – therefore, he says so. And he concludes "for this is the way of human beings," meaning: what can be done after a person is compelled to this.

And now we do not have the custom of saying it. For only the early pious ones, whose thoughts were always attached to God, and about whom it is said, "He who dwells in the secret place of the Most High shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty," and they would feel the sanctity of the angels accompanying them – it was fitting for them to say it. But for us, although certainly we also have the matter of the accompaniment of the angels, as explained from the words of our sages of blessed memory that we have brought, we do not feel it at all – saying this would be arrogance and haughtiness, and it would appear as pride. And certainly the holy person who sits in Torah study with sanctity and purity should say it, but not us, ordinary people. And so is the essence, and so is the custom. (And in the "Land of the Living" this was a difficulty, but according to what I have written, it is well explained. Be precise and you will find ease.)

And one should conduct oneself in the bathroom with modesty, and the term "modest" is only applied to one who is modest in the bathroom (Berachot 62a). This means that even there he should behave with modesty, and all the more so in other places. And this is the language of the Rambam in the fifth chapter of De'ot, law 6: Great modesty is practiced by Torah scholars: they do not disgrace themselves, nor expose their heads or bodies. Even when they enter the bathroom, they should be modest and not uncover their clothes until they sit down. They should not clean themselves with their right hand. They should distance themselves from everyone, enter a room within a room, a cave within a cave, and relieve themselves. If they relieve themselves behind a wall, they should distance themselves so that their friend does not hear their sound if they sneeze. If they relieve themselves in a valley, they should distance themselves so that their friend does not see their exposure. They should not speak while relieving themselves, even for a great need. And just as they behave with modesty during the day in the bathroom, so they should behave at night. A person should always train himself to relieve himself only in the morning and evening, so that he does not have to distance himself. Until here is his language, and he omitted several laws that will be explained. And I do not know his reason.

He should close the door behind him, and two people should not go together. Regarding women, it was said in Sanhedrin (19a): They decreed that women should talk to each other in the bathroom because of seclusion, see there. This applies to a bathroom in the fields and not in the city. Therefore, nowadays, women also should not enter together (Magen Avraham). And if one wants to stimulate the rectum with a stone or a stick to open his bowels, he should stimulate and then sit, but not stimulate after he has sat. Thus our Sages commanded in Berachot, see there. And they said at the end of the eighth chapter of Shabbat: One who needs to relieve himself but cannot should stand and sit, stand and sit. Or he should move to the sides, for perhaps this place is not suitable. Or he should stimulate the area with a stone, or divert his mind from other matters and think only about this, for the thought process is effective. And they said there: One who enters a regular meal, and if he needs to relieve himself in the middle of the meal it is disgraceful for him, should walk ten times four cubits or four times ten cubits and then relieve himself, and then return to his place and he will not need to go out. And one who needs to relieve himself and does not do so is afflicted by a spirit of impurity. And one who needs to relieve himself and eats is like an oven that was heated on top of its ashes. This is the beginning of the impure smell.

It is stated in the Sifrei (Parashat "Ki Teitzei") that one should not relieve themselves while standing. The reason seems to be so that one's body does not become weak. And one should not expose oneself excessively, but only a handbreadth from behind and two handbreadths from the front, because for the stream of urine, more exposure is needed. And even if one currently needs only for large excretions, the small ones will come out naturally when one strains for the large ones. And for a woman, a handbreadth from behind and nothing from the front, because her stream goes only downward. And one should not strain oneself excessively, lest the teeth of the rectum become dislocated. Rather, one should strain little by little, and the excesses that are ready to come out will come out, and for those that are not ready, straining will not help. And when one enters, one should not sit down immediately (Shabbat there). Meaning: quickly and forcefully, because the orifice opens forcefully, and the teeth of the rectum can become dislocated, see there.

One should not wipe with pottery shards or with dry grass. And one who wipes with something that fire can burn – his lower teeth will fall out. Nor with a clod of earth that someone else wiped with, because it brings a person to hemorrhoids. But with a clod of earth that he himself wiped with – we have no issue. In the time of the Talmud, they would wipe with soft stones. They would use three stones for wiping: one very small to remove the excrement sticking to the anus, the second somewhat larger to wipe the area, and the third larger than that to completely clean the area and its surroundings (Shabbat 81a). All this was for them, as the latrines were in the field. Now, we wipe with pottery shards, with the primary wiping done with paper. And although fire can burn it – we cannot use anything else, and "The Lord protects the simple" since many are accustomed to it, and observe what the people do. Additionally, in the time of the Talmud they were concerned about sorcery, and nowadays sorcery is not common. Therefore, we are not concerned about it (Magen Avraham, section 11), as the main concern for these things was due to sorcery.

It has already been explained that one should not wipe [themselves] with the right hand, but rather with the left. This is because one eats and writes with the right hand, demonstrates the reasons of the Torah with it, and ties tefillin with it. It is also close to the mouth, as one uses the right hand to bring all food and drink to the mouth. Moreover, the Torah was given by the right hand of the Holy One, blessed be He, as it is said, "From His right hand, a fiery law for them" (Deuteronomy 33:2). Therefore, it is not respectful to use it for wiping (Berakhot 62a). 

And a left-handed person, who does everything with their left hand, should wipe with their right hand, which is the left hand of everyone else. Although according to the last reason, we should not follow his actions, nevertheless, for him, it is reversed. And thus have agreed the great authorities (Taz, subsection 9, and Magen Avraham, subsection 8).

And know: If this left-handed person does some things with the right hand as everyone does, and some things with his left hand – the great authorities have different opinions on this matter, making various distinctions (see Magen Avraham there, Shaarei Teshuvah sub-paragraph 9, and Pri Megadim and Elya Rabbah). In my humble opinion, it is clear that if he uses both hands, the last reason, because the Torah was given with the right hand of the Holy One, blessed be He, determines that he should clean himself with the left hand of everyone, as this reason is sufficient to be decisive. There are those who distinguish whether this hand is used for writing or not for writing, but it seems to me as I have written. And a woman also needs to be cautious about this, as several reasons apply to her as well. Some have written that one should be cautious not to clean with the middle finger of the left hand, because the strap is wound around it (there in the name of the Shlah). And certainly, if he can be careful about this, how good. But if without this finger he cannot clean himself properly – he should clean himself as usual (so it seems to me).

It has already been explained that one should comport oneself modestly at night just as during the day. However, this pertains to modesty but not to distance, as at night one does not need to distance oneself as during the day. And know that all this applies to adults. But for children, it is permitted to urinate even during the day and in public if necessary, because there is a danger if they hold it in too long, as stated in Bechorot (44a). And a woman should not stand before a child to urinate. This applies directly in front, but from the side, there is no issue (ibid.).

One should not urinate while standing, because of the splashes that rebound onto his feet, and people might say that he is a "petzua daka" (one with crushed testicles) since he does not urinate in a stream but rather dribbles, and thus he cannot father children, causing people to cast aspersions on his offspring. This does not apply if he stands in a high place where the splashes will not fall on his feet, or if he urinates into soft earth where there are also no splashes. And even though it is a mitzvah to clean off the splashes, in the case of many splashes, cleaning is not sufficient (Magen Avraham in the name of Tosafot). If it is not possible for him to urinate from a high place, nor into soft earth, he can urinate normally, but he should assist by lifting his testicles slightly to direct the urine further away. If only a small amount falls on his feet, he should clean it off. He should be careful not to hold the organ itself while urinating, except from the corona and below, because this can lead to emission of semen in vain, unless he is married and has his wife available to him. However, it is a measure of piety to be careful even if one is married. But assisting by holding the testicles is permitted for anyone. Even a married man is only permitted to hold the organ itself for urination and not for other purposes. Using a thick cloth is allowed. One who delays relieving himself transgresses the prohibition of "do not make yourselves abominable," and for children, he also transgresses "there shall not be a barren man among you." However, until he finds a suitable place to urinate or defecate, he does not transgress. Delaying flatulence when necessary is not a transgression. One should be careful to thoroughly clean the anal area because if there is feces in place, it is forbidden to recite the Shema. This will be explained further in section 76.

We learn in Berachot (61b): One who relieves himself in Judea should not direct his back to the east and his face to the west, nor his back to the west and his face to the east, but rather north and south. This is because Jerusalem is in Judea, and Judea runs from east to west along the length of the Land of Israel. In the Galilee, north and south are forbidden, but east and west are permitted. This is because the Galilee is in the north of the Land of Israel, and when one faces north or south, it would be toward Jerusalem. Rabbi Yossi permits. Rabbi Yehuda permits when the Temple is not standing. Rabbi Akiva prohibits in all places, even outside the Land of Israel, to relieve oneself between east and west. The halachic authorities ruled in accordance with Rabbi Akiva because Raba did so in the Gemara; see there.

And this is the language of the Tur: When one sits, he should ensure that his face is towards the south and his back towards the north, or vice versa, but he should not sit between east and west. However, this is specifically when relieving oneself in an open place, but in a place with partitions, such as a bathroom within a house, one does not need to be meticulous. This is his language, as it is explained in the Jerusalem Talmud that the prohibition is only in an open place. And this is the language of the Jerusalem Talmud: "Provided it is a place without a wall." It implies that even one wall permits, meaning the partition should be behind him (Magen Avraham, subsection 5). And the Tur wrote "such as a bathroom within a house" – he did not elaborate, and his main intention is that the prohibition is only when one is exposed from all sides, like in a valley or a field. But in a courtyard surrounded by partitions – it is permitted. And the enclosure of a city does not help for this (ibid.), because the partitions are not recognized at all. And the Tur did not differentiate between a country situated to the east and west of the Land of Israel or to its north and south like the Galilee, because the Tur holds that Rabbi Akiva holds that in any place, east and west is forbidden, and in any place, north and south is permitted, because the prohibition is due to the Shechinah (Divine Presence) being in the west (Beit Yosef). And this is also explained from the words of the Rambam in the seventh chapter of Beit HaBechirah, and he wrote: because the Sanctuary is in the west, see there. And the Rambam did not mention any permission with partitions at all, because he holds that our Talmud does not differentiate in this matter. And our teacher, the Beit Yosef, in subsection 5 ruled like the Tur, see there. And some are concerned even with one's back to the south, but it is only permitted with one's back to the north (see Magen Avraham, subsection 6). And from all the poskim it does not imply this, but rather there is no meticulousness. And so too, our teacher, the Rema, in his book Darkei Moshe, wanted to establish that in countries situated to the north and south of the Land of Israel, it is like in the Galilee, and the Tur did not mention this because all our country is to the west of the Land of Israel, see there. However, in the Shulchan Aruch he did not mention this, and he did well, for it is also evident from the Rambam, and he was in Egypt, which is to the south of the Land of Israel. And to urinate – it is permitted in any manner. And only from the Tzofim and inward, meaning from a place where they can see the Temple – one should not urinate with his face towards the holy place. Rather, to the north or south or turn the holy place to the sides.

And know that the Rambam wrote there that it is also forbidden to sleep from east to west, but rather one should sleep from north to south. See there. And this is based on what we say at the beginning of Berakhot: "All my days I was troubled... and on my bed that it should be placed between north and south. And one who places his bed between north and south will have male children." And the Tur did not mention this, because he holds that this is merely a matter of diligence. And the Tosafot wrote there that this is only when his wife is with him, see there. But from the Rambam it is clear that even when he is alone—it is forbidden. And our Rabbi the Beit Yosef in section 6 ruled like the Tosafot and wrote that it is proper to be cautious like the Rambam, see there. And we are not cautious about this, and we follow the Tur in practice. Moreover, there is a disagreement among the authorities whether between north and south means the head and feet or the width of the bed. Accordingly, this law has fallen into disuse. (See Magen Avraham subsection 7 and Levush, that partitions do not help here because there is no recognition, see there. And in my humble opinion, this is not necessary, because the source is from the Rambam, and according to the Rambam even in the bathroom partitions do not help. Examine and you will find it easy.)

In Berachot (6b), it is stated that one should think between the morning blessings upon rising from bed, including the blessing "Al Netilat Yadayim." It says there: When one raises their hands, they should say: "Blessed are You... Who has sanctified us... concerning the washing of the hands." This is also found in Rambam, Chapter 7 of Tefillah, and in Tur and Shulchan Aruch, Siman 47. However, the nature of this blessing is not explained.

We find in the Gemara two reasons for washing in the morning: one in Shabbat (108b) which says that an evil spirit rests on the hands in the morning before washing, and one should not touch their mouth, ears, or eyes before washing. This evil spirit does not leave until one washes their hands three times, pouring water over their hands three times (Rashi). Therefore, we can say that this blessing is related to this matter.

Additionally, we find in Berachot (14a) that for reciting the Shema and prayer, one needs to wash their hands, as it is written: "I will wash my hands in cleanliness, and I will encircle Your altar, Hashem." If one does not have water, they can clean their hands with dirt or anything that cleans, and this will be explained in Siman 92. Therefore, we can say that this blessing is related to the morning prayer.

From the words of the Rambam, there is no definitive ruling. In Chapter Seven of the Laws of Prayer, he considers it among the morning blessings, and in Chapter Four of the Laws of Prayer, he writes that the purification of the hands is essential for prayer. And this is his language: "How does one purify the hands? He washes with water up to the wrist and then prays... And if he did not have water... – he wipes his hands with a cloth or with earth... In what case does this apply? To all prayers except the morning prayer. But in the morning, he washes his face, hands, and feet and then prays." This is the end of his language. And in Chapter Six of the Laws of Blessings, he writes: "Anyone who washes his hands, whether for eating, or for reciting the Shema, or for prayer, recites the blessing: 'Who has sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us concerning the washing of hands.' For this is a commandment of the Sages, whom we are commanded by the Torah to obey..." See there, where he equates all the laws of washing hands for eating with washing hands for prayer in all details. If so, what he considers among the morning blessings – it is not clear if it is the same as for prayer, or if it is something else because of an evil spirit. It seems more likely that it is for prayer, since he did not mention at all that three times are required, nor did he mention the issue of an evil spirit at all. This also seems likely, as he mentioned there the washing of the face as well. See there. And according to him, in the morning, this is essential for prayer as I have written.

And from the Tur, it is clarified that this applies to both. And this is the language of the Tur: "And he should wash with clean hands and bless: 'Blessed are You, Hashem, our God, King of the universe, who has sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us concerning the washing of hands.' And he should be meticulous to pour over them three times, because an evil spirit rests upon the hands before washing, and it does not leave until he pours over them three times. Therefore, he must avoid touching his mouth, nose, ears, or eyes before washing, because an evil spirit rests upon them. And if he does not have water, he should clean his hands with a rock or any cleaning medium and bless 'concerning the cleanliness of hands.' Thus far is his language."

It is clearly explained that this blessing is for both the evil spirit and for prayer. It is impossible to say it is only for the evil spirit, for if so, what benefit is there in cleaning his hands with a rock? Rather, it certainly means this: if he does not have water, and there is no remedy for the evil spirit at this time, nevertheless, for prayer he can suffice with the cleaning of a rock. But he should not bless 'concerning the washing of hands' because there is no washing here, but rather 'concerning the cleanliness of hands.' According to this, it seems clear to me that according to the Tur, this blessing applies to both: for the evil spirit and for prayer.

However, the Rosh in the chapter "HaRo'eh" (Siman 23) explained that it is only for prayer, and this is his language: When one washes his hands, he blesses "Al Netilat Yadayim" (upon the washing of the hands). Since a person's hands are busy, and it is impossible that he will not touch... during the night, they instituted a blessing before he recites the Shema and prays... Until here is his language. It is explicitly explained that this blessing is only for the purpose of prayer. And it is necessary to explain his reasoning: he holds that for the reason of an evil spirit, a blessing is not instituted, because since it is due to danger, a blessing is not relevant for this. Just as they did not institute a blessing for the washing of hands after a meal for this reason, because it is due to danger, as the Rambam wrote in the sixth chapter of Berachot, see there. And the Rosh further added that according to the law, one should bless "Al Nikyut Yadayim" (upon the cleanliness of the hands), but since for a meal washing is required, they also established here the blessing "Al Netilat Yadayim". And therefore, when he does not have water and wipes his hands with a stone, he blesses "Al Nikyut Yadayim", see there.

I have seen that the great authorities hold that according to the Rosh, it is necessary to specifically recite this blessing adjacent to the prayer, since it was instituted because of the prayer. However, in my humble opinion, it is evident from the Rosh himself that this is not the case, as he wrote in Responsa, General Rule 4, which is brought by the Tur later at the end of Siman 47, and this is his language: "One who rises early to study before dawn should recite 'Al Netilat Yadayim' and 'Asher Yatzar'... until here is his language." And it is still not the time for prayer, and he sits to study, and nonetheless he recites "Al Netilat Yadayim"! Rather, it is certain that the institution of the blessing was because of the prayer, but they established it to be recited immediately upon rising from his bed. And so it is evident from the Rambam and from the Gemara, that they instituted it among the morning blessings. And so it is the primary halacha. (See Chayei Adam, General Rule 7, and Maaseh Rav. And in my humble opinion, it appears as I have written.)

And also, the Rashba in his responsa (siman 191) wrote that the blessing is due to prayer, but explained it differently.
