And this is his language: I did not find a clear matter that requires washing hands in the morning, for if it is because of a harmful spirit or a demon's daughter – it is sufficient with washing (and this requires investigation), and if it is because of prayer, it is sufficient either with washing or with cleaning with earth... However, there is some proof... And we say: one who washes his hands and recites the Shema... – it slightly implies that one must wash his hands with a vessel. And if you ask what is the difference between the morning prayer and the afternoon and evening prayers, it can be said that in the morning one becomes like a new creation, as it is written: "They are new every morning..." Therefore, we need to sanctify ourselves with His sanctity, and wash our hands from a vessel like a priest who sanctifies his hands from the basin... until here is his language. However, he also holds that the washing is for prayer. But the Rosh says the reason is because the hands are not clean, and the Rashba says it is because of being a new creation. (And it seems in my humble opinion that there is no practical difference at all: what does it matter if they instituted it for this reason or for that reason? Ultimately, since they instituted it – it is instituted. And for both, it is like washing hands for eating as equated by the Rambam, as I have written. And the great poskim made a dispute among them as will be explained, but in my opinion, it is not so. And this is also implied by the Bach, see there. And be precise and you will find it easy.)

In the Zohar, Parashat Vayeshev, it is explained that because of the reason of an impure spirit, one must wash their hands in the same manner as all hand washings, specifically with a vessel. And this is its language: Rabbi Shimon opened: "I will wash my hands in innocence..." – for there is no person in the world who does not taste the taste of death at night, and an impure spirit rests upon this body... and it has been said that the hands of a person retain impurity... until they are washed. And when they are washed properly – then one becomes sanctified... One needs one vessel below and one vessel above... until here is its language. And there are more sayings about this (see Beit Yosef). Therefore, according to this, for all reasons, the obligation to wash the hands in the morning is specifically with a vessel. (And the Rashba in his responsa there wrote that it is sufficient to immerse one’s hands in a vessel. And the Beit Yosef rejected this based on the words of the Zohar, see there.)

Our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch wrote in Section 1: Water that is invalid for washing hands for a meal, as discussed later in Siman 160, is valid for washing hands for prayer. However, there is an opinion that one should not recite a blessing over it. This is their language. 

The explanation of their words: In Siman 160, it is explained that water whose appearance has changed, or that has been used for work, or is salty, or foul-smelling to the extent that a dog cannot drink from it, is invalid for washing hands for eating. However, for prayer, it is valid, as here only cleanliness is required. Nevertheless, there is an opinion that one should not recite a blessing over it, since it was not established in such a manner (this is the original ruling in Beit Yosef in the name of the Ra'ah).

And I am very astonished by these statements, for what relevance is there to say that they are fit for prayer? Certainly, the primary enactment was that this washing should be exactly similar to the washing for a meal, as the Rambam wrote in the sixth chapter of Berachot that we have cited. Similarly, the Rosh wrote that they instituted the blessing just like for the washing of hands for eating. And also, the Rashba in that responsum equated it to eating, where he wrote there: “And he immerses his hands in a vessel both in the morning and at the time of eating...” until here is his language. And they only said in the Gemara that when there is no water, one does not cancel prayer because of this, and cleans with a pebble or some other item. And indeed, in such a manner, the Rosh wrote that one does not bless “al netilat yadayim” but “al nekiyot yadayim,” and there are those who disagree with this as will be explained. But if one can obtain water that is fit for eating – one is obligated to obtain it. And if it is impossible to obtain – even a pebble is acceptable. But what relevance is there to say that it is fit for prayer? Certainly, they are not fit initially unless he does not have [water]. And also what they wrote that one does not bless on it, I am astonished: Should he bless “al nekiyot yadayim”? And is it worse than a pebble? And in my humble opinion, it appears that the fundamental halacha is that one must obtain water that is completely fit for eating. And if it is impossible – one fulfills the requirement with whatever he has. And according to the Rosh, he should bless “al nekiyot yadayim,” and according to those who disagree, he should bless “al netilat yadayim.” (The source of the ruling is from the Ra’ah, as written in the Beit Yosef. And his words are not understood: he began by saying that even initially it is effective, and concluded that one does not bless, see there. And if so, how is it effective initially? Behold, they instituted to bless, and he does not bless? It requires investigation. Be precise and you will find it light.)

In Section 6, they wrote: One does not need a quarter-log (revi'it) of water for washing hands for prayer. And in Section 7, they wrote: It is good to be careful with morning hand washing regarding all the things that are essential for hand washing before a meal. However, it is not essential to use a vessel, nor human force, nor the other matters that invalidate hand washing before a meal. So far their words, and these matters also seem puzzling to me: for behold, the Rambam (Maimonides) completely equated this washing to the hand washing before a meal, and we have not seen anyone who disagrees with him. And also the Rosh there explicitly wrote: because one needs to wash from a vessel, they also instituted to bless "on the washing of hands." So far his words. And likewise, the Rashba explicitly wrote that one needs to wash his hands with a vessel in the morning, see there. And that which he permitted by dipping into the vessel – this is because he holds this likewise for a meal, and this is his language: and he dips his hands into the vessel whether in the morning or at the time of eating, see there. And this will be further clarified. Only the Ran in the chapter "Kol HaBasar" wrote that a vessel is not needed. Similarly, the Mordechai in the chapter "Elu Devarim" wrote that they did not institute a blessing for this washing, see there. But the Rambam, Rashba, and Rosh equated it to all the laws of hand washing before a meal, and from where do we say that a quarter-log is not needed? And what does "it is not essential" mean, for if he does not have it, it is obvious that even a pebble suffices, and if he has it, it is certainly essential? This requires investigation. (Especially since the Zohar clearly ruled this way, as I wrote.)

In section 12, our master the Beit Yosef wrote: If one immersed his hands into a vessel of water, it counts as washing for the purposes of reciting the Shema and prayer, but not for removing the evil spirit upon them. And if he immersed his hands into three different bodies of water, it is questionable whether it counts for removing the evil spirit upon them. Until here are his words. And in this, I am also astonished: It is true that the Rashba ruled this way, but he also held that even for a meal it is effective in this manner, as we brought his words in the previous section. But for us, who hold in Siman 159 that for a meal it is invalid in this manner, certainly it is the same for the morning unless he has no vessel, as we explained that they are the same. And also, regarding his doubt about three different bodies of water, whether it is effective for removing the evil spirit, I am astonished: Since according to the Zohar it is ineffective as he wrote in his great book, why did he not decide accordingly? This needs great study. (And a river is considered like three different bodies of water; Magen Avraham, small section 10.)

They also wrote in paragraph 13: If one was awake all night, there is a doubt whether he needs to wash his hands in the morning to pray and to remove the impure spirit from his hands. And he should wash without a blessing. This is the end of his words. The reason for the doubt is that, according to the Rosh, the enactment was made because the hands are not clean, and if one was awake all night, they are indeed clean. Also, according to the Rashba, the reason is because of becoming a new creature – this applies when one was sleeping and entrusted his soul to the Holy One, blessed be He, which is not the case if he was awake all night (Beit Yosef). And some say that he certainly needs to bless, because once the Rabbis enacted it – they did not differentiate, and it is a fixed enactment (Bach). And there is someone who wrote that this reasoning applies only according to the Rosh, because he holds that one needs to wash his hands also for Mincha, but not according to the Rashba (Magen Avraham, section 12). And I do not know what the connection is between these matters, and on the contrary, our master, the Beit Yosef, in his great book wrote that according to the Rashba, it is even more logical to say that they did not differentiate than according to the Rosh, see there (and similarly wrote the Taz, section 9). And so it seems correct to bless if one was awake all night. And there are great ones who wrote not to bless, as ruled by our master, the Rema. (And I wonder: since the Magen Avraham agreed that according to the Rosh one should bless like the Bach, and regarding the Rashba it was clarified that they did not differentiate, why should they not bless? And it is obvious to the Rema who ruled later in section 46 that all the morning blessings are recited even if one is not obligated in them, see there. And examine and you will find leniency.)

They further wrote in section 14: If one arose before dawn and washed his hands, there is a doubt whether he needs to wash his hands again when the day breaks to remove the impure spirit that rests on the hands. He should wash them without a blessing. Thus are his words. And the doubt is that perhaps before the light of day, the impure spirit returns and rests. This is also implied in the Zohar (Beit Yosef), and even if he slept before dawn, he washes without a blessing. And for prayer, certainly, we do not need to make a blessing again for the reason of the Rashba (Magen Avraham, section 13). Similarly, if one slept during the day, there is a doubt whether he needs to pour water over his hands three times because there is a doubt whether the night causes it or sleep causes it. And specifically if he slept sixty breaths. Therefore, he should wash them three times and without a blessing.

Therefore, one who rises from his bed, whether it is already daylight or before dawn, and washes his hands – recites the blessing "Al Netilat Yadayim." However, the blessing "Asher Yatzar" should not be recited if he has not yet relieved himself. There are those who say that even if he has not relieved himself, he should still recite "Asher Yatzar," the reason being that before washing, it is forbidden to touch his eyes, mouth, or ears. Additionally, because he has become like a new creation (Magen Avraham, Section 2). These reasons are not sufficient, and therefore, it is better to relieve oneself first. Certainly, if he needs to relieve himself, it is forbidden to recite the blessing (ibid., Section 1). This is also the prevalent custom and should not be changed. Especially since most people, when they rise from their beds, need to relieve themselves either major or minor needs. Therefore, one should wash without a blessing, relieve himself, wash his hands again, and then recite "Al Netilat Yadayim" and "Asher Yatzar." It is forbidden to go relieve oneself without washing unless it is very close to the bed, because there are those who are stringent and caution based on the Zohar that it is forbidden to walk four cubits without washing hands. Also, the Talmud implies this, as it includes it among the morning blessings that are recited near the bed (Berachot 6b). Refer to what I have written at the beginning of Section 6.

And this is the order of the washing: One takes the vessel of water in their right hand and gives it to their left hand in order to pour it on the right hand first, for in all places, honor is given to the right. One should pour on them three times alternately, to remove the evil spirit that is upon them. Some have the custom to wash their mouth in the morning because of the saliva in the mouth, and it is also beneficial for several things. One should wash their face and be careful to dry it well, for one who washes their face and does not dry it well – their face cracks or boils appear on it. The remedy is to wash frequently with beet water (Shabbat 133b). And beet water is spinach broth (Rashi), but it is not clear to us what this is. The blessings should be recited before drying. One should not touch their mouth, nose, ears, or eyes before washing. Even one who has washed their hands should not make a habit of touching the anus frequently, as it brings about hemorrhoids. One should not touch a place of bloodletting, and similarly any place of a wound, for the touching of the hand harms the wound. Similarly, one should not touch a beer barrel, and certainly not before washing, as it brings an evil spirit into the beer. It is also forbidden to touch any food or drink before washing. In retrospect, this does not prohibit consumption. (Some have written that when washing the right hand, one should say "the great hand," and for the left hand, "the strong hand," and when rubbing them together, say "the exalted." When washing the face, say "his head is pure gold…" When washing the eyes, say "his eyes are like doves…" For the cheeks, say "his cheeks are like beds of spices." For the lips, say "his lips are lilies…" For the mouth, say "his mouth is most sweet…" There is a wonderful charm in this, as man was created in the image of God. Be precise and you will find ease.)

Washing the hands in the morning – one should not wash them over the ground, nor over trees or sticks, but rather into a vessel. And the water from washing the hands in the morning – it is forbidden to derive benefit from it. Even giving it to an animal is forbidden, because an evil spirit rests upon it, and the animal can be harmed by this. One should not pour it out in the house, nor in a place where people walk. Rather, it should be poured out in a place where people do not walk. One should not wash with water from someone who has not yet washed their hands in the morning, meaning: such a person should not pour water over the hands of another. However, bringing him water [to wash] is not a concern. One should be careful to prepare a vessel with water near his bed. Some were also stringent with this water because of exposure, but we do not worry about this, because we are not cautious about exposure since snakes are not common among us, as explained in Yoreh De'ah, section 116.

King David did not sleep for more than "sixty breaths" in one stretch; rather, he would wake up every "sixty breaths." And in Sukkah (26b) it is explained that some were only careful about this during the day and not at night (see Magen Avraham section 16). The measure of "sixty breaths" has not been clarified for us. Some say it is approximately half an hour, and others say it is about two hours (see Rashi on Sukkah there). We do not observe this practice, as it is not according to our level, and there is no prohibition in this; rather, it is considered a way of holiness.

Every person must be careful during prayer and eating not to touch the thigh, hip, or other covered parts of the body, because there are sweat secretions there, which are greatly unclean. Similarly, one should not scratch their head. However, in the exposed parts of the head and body, one does not need to be particular. Even scratching or mere touching of the head is not an issue (as it seems to me). Likewise, one can touch the exposed part of their arms, which is up to the joint called the elbow. And one can touch the neck up to the chest. If one touched the covered parts or took a louse in their hands, they must wash with water. If one is in the midst of prayer and cannot wash, they should rub their hands on a wall or beam or something similar. A wise person should foresee this and avoid it. (If one touched a flea, known as a "flea," they do not need to wash their hands.)

If he does not have water for washing hands in the morning, he should wipe his hands with a rock, or with dirt, or with a beam, or with anything that cleans, and he should recite the blessing "on the cleanliness of hands." This will suffice for prayer, but not to remove the evil spirit that rests upon them. Therefore, when he later finds water, he should wash his hands three times without a blessing. Now, it would have been possible to recite the blessing "on washing the hands," for the Sages did not differentiate, and this appears from the words of the Rashba. However, the Rosh and the Tur explicitly ruled to bless "on the cleanliness of hands," and how can we go against their words? (See Magen Avraham, section 25. His words require investigation.)

And this applies when he wants to pray now or when the time for reciting the Shema will pass. But if he is not yet praying, he should seek to obtain water until the time of prayer. All the morning blessings can be recited even before washing, for they did not institute washing except for the Shema and prayer. And ordinary hands are not disqualified for blessings, as we bless on fruits without washing. If he knows that his hands are not clean, such as when he rises from his bed and he lay there without clothes, and the like, he should not delay the blessings due to the absence of water, and he should clean his hands with a cloth... and recite the blessings. For it is forbidden to mention the Name when his hands are not clean. And it is customary to say: "I give thanks before You, living and eternal King, for You have returned my soul within me..." immediately upon rising from his bed, even though his hands are not clean, because this does not contain the Name or a designation.

Besides the washing of hands in the morning, there are other instances that require washing specifically with water, although they do not require washing three times (Magen Avraham, section 17). And these are: one who exits the bathroom, and he should wash immediately. And one who exits the bathhouse. And one who cuts his nails. And one who removes his shoes with his hands. However, one who removes his socks from his feet does not need washing, as they are like other garments. And one who touches his feet or his shoes. And one who combs his head, whether with his hands or with a comb. And some say: even one who walks among the dead in the cemetery. And he should wash his hands before praying there, and wash upon exiting. And one who touches a corpse. And our custom is that even those who accompany the deceased and stand within four cubits of the bier wash their hands. And one who delouses his clothes, even if he did not touch the louse. And one who touches a louse. And one who touches covered parts of his body. And one who engages in marital relations. 

And one who does any of these and does not wash his hands, if he is a Torah scholar, his learning is forgotten. And if he is not a Torah scholar, his mind becomes confused. And our Sages of blessed memory said in Pesachim (112b) that one who lets blood from his shoulders and does not wash his hands will be fearful for seven days. One who shaves and does not wash his hands will be fearful for three days. One who cuts his nails and does not wash his hands will be fearful for one day. And he will not know what he fears, see there.

What we say in all blessings, "Blessed are You" – it is not that He, blessed be He, needs our blessings, Heaven forbid. Rather, it is like a reflective light that causes His blessing to impact us, as David said: "And from Your blessing may the house of Your servant be blessed forever" (II Samuel 7:29). The matter that we need to arouse this is as it is written: "Ascribe strength to God." That is to say, since all matters depend on our actions, it is therefore upon us to add strength to the celestial entourage, and then the blessing will descend to us. And this is what is written: "He rides the heavens to your aid."

In all the blessings and prayers, we speak to the Blessed One in the second person: "Blessed are You." And in psalms and praises, there are some instances where we say "You are" – using both second and third person. The matter is understood thus: His essence, may He be blessed, is hidden and concealed from all. Even the Seraphim and the Ofanim do not know it; it is only through His actions that we and they recognize Him. This is what we mean when we say: "Blessed be the glory of the Lord from His place," meaning that we perceive His glory, which is His actions, in every place, but not His essence. This is why we say "You are," meaning "You" through Your actions, "He" through His essence. Therefore, in prayers where we ask Him to do certain things, we are speaking in terms of His actions, and thus we say "You." Similarly, in all types of blessings, such as blessings over enjoyment when we bless for creating a particular fruit or bread – we are speaking of His actions. Likewise, in the blessings of the commandments, we speak of His actions, as He commanded us in such and such a manner. And in all types of blessings, such as blessings over seeing seas and rivers, or thunder and lightning, and similar instances – we bless Him, may He be blessed, for His actions. Therefore, we say "You" in the second person.

The primary name of the Blessed One is the Tetragrammaton. This is the "Explicit Name," and it is forbidden for us at this time to pronounce it as it is written; instead, we use the name "Adonai," because the world is not currently worthy to articulate it (end of the third chapter of Pesachim). And here is the language of the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch: One should have in mind the meaning of the words he utters in his blessings. When mentioning the Name, he should intend the meaning of its pronunciation as "Adonai," which signifies "Master," as He is the Master of all. Additionally, he should intend the meaning of its written form as "Yud-Hei," signifying "He was, He is, and He will be." When mentioning "Elohim," he should intend that it means He is strong, mighty, and has the power over the upper and lower realms, for "El" connotes power and strength, as in "the mighty ones of the earth…" (Tur).

According to this, when saying "Baruch Atah Hashem" – one should intend both the meaning of "Master" and the concept of "He was, He is, and He will be." However, in places where "Adonai" is written, such as "Adonai, open my lips" – one should intend only that He is the Master of all. Some say that even with the Tetragrammaton (YHVH), one should intend only "Master of all," for in all places we follow the pronunciation (the Gra). The vocalization of the name: when "Adonai" is written, it is pronounced with a chataf-patach. When the Tetragrammaton is written, some pronounce the aleph with a sheva as the vowelization of the yod in YHVH, and some pronounce it with a chataf-patach as the vowelization of the aleph in "Adonai" (the GraZ). The simple custom among us is to pronounce the aleph with a chataf-patach. (These are basic intentions, and those who are privy to the secrets of Hashem have profound intentions. Some great Kabbalists mention that if one intends the name by combining the Tetragrammaton with "Adonai" – it is a significant matter. There is no need to elaborate on this.)

The blessing "Asher Yatzar" is unique among all blessings. All other blessings are short and specific to the matter at hand. For example, in blessings over enjoyment, when one eats bread, one says: "Hamotzi lechem...," and similarly for all other blessings. The morning blessings are also like this. However, this blessing is lengthy, and the primary matter for which it is recited is not mentioned at all. In my humble opinion, the truth is that the sages did not find it appropriate in this blessing to mention the excretion of waste. Firstly, because it is not a matter of honor. Additionally, if we compare this to blessings over enjoyment, it is impossible, because even though a person benefits from the removal of waste, all blessings over enjoyment are recited before the act. Furthermore, all blessings over enjoyment are dependent on the person's choice to enjoy or not, whereas this act is necessary. If we compare this blessing to the morning blessings, which are about the natural order, one recitation a day would suffice. Therefore, our sages of blessed memory established it based on the creation of man, from which the matter of cleanliness is implicitly understood in a respectful manner. This is the rationale of the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, who explained the intention of this blessing, which is not their usual practice since they are not commentators. However, this matter touches upon the essence of the blessing. (Similarly, the Rosh and Ran wrote at the beginning of Ketubot regarding the blessing of betrothal. It also seems to me that this is the reason behind the Rema's ruling at the beginning of Siman 6 to recite "Asher Yatzar" in the morning even without having relieved oneself, see there. Many were puzzled by this, but according to what I have written, that it is about the creation of man, it makes sense. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

"Who formed man with wisdom" – Rashi explains (Berachot 60b) that He created many openings in him, and nevertheless, the spirit remains within him all the days of his life, and this is a wonder and wisdom. Until here is his wording. According to this, "with wisdom" refers to the aforementioned, to "and created many openings in him…". And Tosafot explained according to the Midrash that He prepared man's sustenance first and then created him. And there are those who explain "who formed man with wisdom" to mean: that man possesses wisdom (Maharsha), and this is relevant to this matter because an animal has no shame and excretes waste in front of everyone, which is not the case with man. And there are those who explain "with wisdom" – that He created within him the power to nourish, which includes four forces: the force that attracts food, the force that holds the food, the force that digests, and the force that expels the waste. And without these forces – it would not be possible to live (Levush).

"And created within it many openings" – the mouth opening to intake food and drink, which is the beginning of the digestive power, and the openings of the intestines and bladder to expel them. The phrase is repeated to also hint at other openings like the nose and ears, but the main intention is regarding those pertinent to the matter. "Hollow cavities" – these are the stomach, intestines, and the esophagus, which are large cavities so that food can enter them and they can hold it until it is digested. The phrase is repeated to hint at other cavities, "if one of them were to open or be sealed..." – meaning: all these were created by the Blessed G-d in measure and in weight according to the needs of a person for these four powers. If one of them were to open, meaning the cavity would be larger than it is now, or one of them were to be sealed, meaning the cavity would be smaller than it is now, and similarly the openings of the mouth and intestines, if they were larger or smaller than their measure – "it would be impossible to exist and stand before You" for many days. And it concludes "Healer of all flesh," meaning: through creating the four powers in their measure, You are the "Healer of all flesh," preventing them from coming to illness. "And does wondrous deeds" – that man is like a pouch full of air, and in a pouch, if there is a small opening, the air escapes. And man is full of openings and still exists (Levush).

There are those who have the version "if it is blocked" before "if it is opened." And there are those who have the version "it is impossible to exist even for one hour." According to this interpretation: "if one of them is opened or one of them is blocked" refers to the time of creation. This means that there is one of the openings, which is the mouth, that in the mother's womb it is closed, and when [the baby] comes out into the air of the world, it opens. If the mouth were to open in the mother's womb, or if it were to remain closed when coming into the air of the world, [the baby] would not be able to exist even for one hour. Likewise, the hollow organs, if they were to open completely immediately, [the baby] would die (Shulchan Aruch). "Who performs wondrously" refers to the good from the food remaining in the human body, and the bad being expelled as waste, because the exit of the openings is the waste from the food (there).

And our teacher, the Rema, explained: "Who acts wondrously" – in that He preserves the spirit of man within him, binding a spiritual entity, the soul, to a physical entity, the body. And all this is through Him being the "Healer of all flesh," for then a person is in good health and his soul is preserved within him. Thus far his words. And this matter also pertains to the topic, for the primary wonder is that the soul is sustained through eating and drinking, and if a person does not eat for many days, the soul will depart from him. What connection does the soul have with eating and drinking? Indeed, in every food and drink there is also a spiritual element, meaning the word of God who created and sustains them, and the soul is nourished by the spiritual while the body is nourished by the physical. (And this is the intention of the Magen Avraham in subparagraph 4, see there.)

Our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, wrote in section 2: There are those who have the custom to wait to recite the blessing "Al Netilat Yadayim" (upon washing the hands) until they arrive at the synagogue, and they arrange it with the other blessings. However, the Sefardim (Jews of Spanish descent) did not have this custom. In any case, one should not recite the blessing twice; one who recites it at home should not recite it again in the synagogue, and one who recites it in the synagogue should not recite it again at home. Someone who studies before entering the synagogue or prays some prayers (such as Selichot and Psalms) should recite the blessings at home and not in the synagogue. Even in such a case, some have the custom to arrange the blessings with the other blessings in the synagogue and do not recite them at home. This is the end of their wording. Even if they study at home before or say Psalms, Selichot, and supplications, they should not recite "Al Netilat Yadayim," "Asher Yatzar," and "Elokai Neshama" until they arrive at the synagogue. This custom has no basis or root. Nowadays, we all follow the custom of the Sefardim, that in the morning upon rising from bed or after using the restroom, we immediately recite the blessings "Al Netilat Yadayim," "Asher Yatzar," and "Elokai Neshama." If one studies at home, they also recite the blessing on the Torah, as it is forbidden to study without it. We also recite all the morning blessings at home, although some leave the morning blessings until they arrive at the synagogue. But "Al Netilat Yadayim," "Asher Yatzar," and "Elokai Neshama" – everyone recites them at home. Even on the days of Selichot, they should recite them at home. Since they have already become obligated in these blessings, how can they delay them until later? We have not heard of anyone who follows a different practice. Maybe there are some who do not follow this and wait until they arrive at the synagogue; they should be taught to bless at home. Except for someone who lives in a single room and the room is not clean from filth, in which case they must go to the synagogue and bless there.

And the prayer leader (Shaliach Tzibbur) also recites these three blessings at home. In the synagogue, he begins with the morning blessings, starting from "Who gives the rooster understanding..." before the prayer stand. We have never heard of a prayer leader starting from the blessing "on washing the hands" because this must be recited at home. However, the morning blessings are recited in the synagogue because the congregation wishes to respond with many "Amens." Therefore, they are arranged before the prayer stand. If it happens that the prayer leader recited them at home, he should not repeat them in the synagogue. This is the simple custom and should not be changed. There is an opinion that the prayer leader can repeat them again to fulfill the obligation for those who are not knowledgeable, similar to the prayers. But this is not comparable, as the prayers were specifically instituted to be recited in the synagogue, also due to the sanctity. However, these blessings and all the morning blessings, according to the Talmudic law, should specifically be recited at home. It is just that some have the custom to arrange them in the synagogue, but the sages do not approve of this. How can we say that the prayer leader should recite them twice? This would be considered blessings in vain (Magen Avraham, Section 7).

The Tur writes that there are those who say that after one recites the blessings "Al Netilat Yadayim" and "Asher Yatzar," one should immediately recite the blessing "E-lohai Neshamah" until "Who restores souls to dead corpses," because it is adjacent to the blessing "Asher Yatzar," and therefore it does not begin with "Baruch." And there are those who say that it is not necessary to say it immediately afterward, and the reason it does not begin with "Baruch" is because it is a blessing of thanks, which does not begin with "Baruch." And this seems logical, as it is proven in the chapter "HaRo'eh" where it says: When one awakens from sleep, one should say "E-lohai Neshamah." And after that, it says: And when one washes his hands, one should say "Al Netilat Yadayim." And this is also the order arranged by the Rambam, of blessed memory. Thus far is his language. And similarly, it is written in Shulchan Aruch, Section 3. And the later authorities wrote that, in any case, it is good to say it adjacent to the blessing "Asher Yatzar" (Bach and Magen Avraham).

And I say that according to the law, it is necessary to place it adjacent to "Asher Yatzar," as the Rosh wrote in a responsum at the beginning of section 4 that it is adjacent to "Asher Yatzar." Nonetheless, there is no difficulty from the Talmud, as the Rosh already wrote there in the Talmud that the reason the Talmud arranged the blessing "Al Netilat Yadayim" after the morning blessings is when one's hands are clean and he has not removed his clothing, see there. And this is also written by all the early authorities. We brought this in section 4, paragraph 14, that we always precede the blessing "Al Netilat Yadayim" and "Asher Yatzar," and therefore for us, it is certainly a blessing adjacent to its companion. And this is also indicated by the language of Tosafot in Pesachim (104b, s.v. "Kol"), who wrote that originally it was not adjacent to its companion, see there – it clearly implies that now it is adjacent to its companion. And it is understood that even in the time of the Talmud, not everyone was so holy as to rise from their bed with clean hands. Therefore, for the majority of people, it is adjacent to its companion. And this is what the Rosh says, that it is adjacent to its companion, meaning: that what the Talmud initially thought – this was according to the custom of the holy ones themselves. But the ordinance of the sages is according to the majority of the world, and as ruled by the Rosh, of blessed memory. And the Rambam arranged according to the language of the Talmud, and indeed the Rosh also arranged it thus in his rulings. And so we practice to place it adjacent to "Asher Yatzar." And I have also seen great authorities who did so, and it is proper to print it thus in the prayer books (this seems according to my humble opinion).

Some require that immediately after washing hands and reciting "Asher Yatzar," one should recite all the morning blessings up to "Who bestows kindness upon His people Israel," reasoning that the washing of hands was instituted for the sake of prayer, and there is a bit of prayer in the blessing "Who removes sleep from my eyes" with the phrase "accustom us to Your Torah" (Magen Avraham, subsection 8, in the name of A"H). However, we do not see the elder rabbis doing so. In fact, in the Talmud, the blessing "Al Netilat Yadayim" is recited last, implying that one does not pray immediately (Magen Avraham there). And indeed, this is true. As we have clarified in Siman 4, subsection 5, from the words of the Rosh and the Tur in Siman 47, although the blessing "Al Netilat Yadayim" was instituted because of prayer, the enactment was to recite the blessing immediately upon rising from bed even though one may pray later, see there. Nevertheless, I have seen great rabbis who recite all the morning blessings immediately. And this is our practice, provided there is no hindrance due to cleanliness as required. This is not for the reason previously stated but because the closer we can connect the blessings to the time of rising from bed, the better it is according to the Talmudic law, as explained from the order of blessings in the Talmud (Berachot 60b). And this should be the practice as long as one's body is completely clean. More will be explained in Siman 46, with the help of Heaven, see there in subsection 11.

There are those who say that if one wakes up early to study or to say Tikkun Chatzot, and knows that he will need to sleep again, what should he do? He should say the blessing "Elohai Neshamah" without the concluding Divine Name. Similarly, before sleeping a second time, he should say the blessing "Hamapil" without the Divine Name and sovereignty. And when he wakes up a second time, he should say "Elohai Neshamah" with the blessing (Magen Avraham, subsection 8, in the name of Seder HaYom). 

It seems that this applies if he wakes up after midnight. But before midnight, he does not need to say it at all. And there are those who wrote that if he knows he will need to sleep again, he does not need to say the blessing "Elohai Neshamah" at all until the second awakening (Pri Chadash in siman 46), because Rambam wrote in the seventh chapter of Tefillah that "Elohai Neshamah" was instituted only at the end of sleep – see there. This is not a proof, for Rambam's intention was not every time one wakes up, but rather when one wakes up completely (Shaarei Teshuvah, subsection 7). 

However, it seems more reasonable that since it was only instituted once a day, it suffices to say it the second time, and it seems that this is the custom. Certainly, for those who hold that even for a daytime sleep one must say "Elohai Neshamah," it is appropriate to say it even the first time, but we do not hold this way. 

And it is certain that the blessing "Al Netilat Yadayim" and the blessing on the Torah should only be said the first time if it is after midnight, and not at all the second time. Similarly, for the blessing "Elohai Neshamah," if it was said the first time, it should not be said again the second time, for it was instituted only once a day. See what I wrote in siman 46, subsection 13.

Some say that if one forgets to recite the blessing "Elokai Neshama" until after the prayer service, he should not recite it anymore. Since he has already recited "Mechayei HaMeitim" (He who revives the dead), he has fulfilled this blessing as well, as it is implied in the Jerusalem Talmud that saying "Mechayei HaMeitim" in place of "Elokai Neshama" is sufficient. Although they are two different concepts—"Mechayei HaMeitim" referring to the future resurrection of the dead, and "HaMachazir Neshamot" referring to the daily return of souls to bodies—nonetheless, the greater (Mechayei HaMeitim) includes the lesser (HaMachazir Neshamot). Therefore, once one has said "Mechayei HaMeitim," it is not appropriate to say the lesser blessing. (This also resolves the question posed by the Shaarei Teshuva there; see there. Be precise and you will find it easy.) The text of "Elokai Neshama" is as follows: "My God, the soul that You have placed within me is pure. You created it, You formed it, You breathed it into me..."—corresponding to the natural soul, the vital spirit, and the intellectual soul, as it is written: "And He breathed into his nostrils the breath of life" (Maharam).

Rabbeinu the Beit Yosef wrote in section 4: There are those who have the custom that after one person recites the morning blessings and others respond "Amen," another one of those who responded "Amen" then recites the blessings, and the others respond "Amen" after him. And in this manner, all those who initially answered "Amen" take turns reciting the blessings. One should not object to them and say that they have already fulfilled their obligation with the initial "Amen" they answered, because the one reciting the blessing does not intend to fulfill the obligation for others. And even if the one reciting the blessing intended to fulfill the obligation for others, they intend not to fulfill their obligation with his blessing. This is the end of his words. 

The reason for those who perform this practice is to increase the number of "Amens" recited. Some of the great scholars have objected to this, arguing that since one responded "Amen," he has already fulfilled his obligation and does not need to recite the blessing afterward, and if he does, it is a blessing in vain. In response, it is written that there is no concern in this practice because they do not intend to fulfill their obligation. Nevertheless, there are those who have raised significant objections to this practice, reasoning that intention to fulfill the obligation is irrelevant here, as it merely follows the custom of the world, and once someone has responded "Amen," it suffices.

There is someone who wrote that when there are not ten people in the synagogue, the prayer leader does not fulfill the obligation for others (Levush). However, this is not relevant to the prayer leader, as it is not part of the prayer service. (This is the intention of the Magen Avraham in subsection 10, who wrote: "See Siman 59. Examine and you will find it easy to understand.") Rather, it appears to me that when one says "Blessed is He and blessed is His name," he has not fulfilled the obligation, as this constitutes an interruption in the blessing. Therefore, it is good if one has not yet recited the morning blessings, and hears them from the prayer leader who recites the blessings before the lectern according to our custom, to say "Blessed is He and blessed is His name." And it is even better for him to first recite the morning blessings himself, and this is our custom.

Our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, wrote: Throughout the day, when one relieves oneself, whether for minor or major needs, one recites the blessing "Asher Yatzar" and not "Al Netilat Yadayim," even if one wishes to study or pray immediately. If one’s hands are dirty from rubbing them, even then, one does not recite "Al Netilat Yadayim." Thus far are their words. The explanation of their words is that they are teaching us two things: First, regarding the blessing "Asher Yatzar," they are informing us that it is not only recited in the morning like all the morning blessings, since it does not explicitly mention the act of relieving oneself, as I wrote at the beginning of the previous section. They inform us that this is not the case, and each time one relieves oneself, one is obligated to recite "Asher Yatzar." Secondly, to counter the opinion of an early authority mentioned by the Sefer Mitzvot Gadol in Positive Commandment 27, who held that for minor needs one should not recite a blessing at all, they inform us that one is obligated to recite a blessing even for minor needs.

And the second case teaches us: The Raavad holds that one must also recite the blessing "Al Netilat Yadayim" after relieving oneself (see Responsa Ramban, Siman 193 in his name). His reasoning is that since one is obligated to recite the blessing "Asher Yatzar," and it is forbidden to bless without washing hands, therefore one recites this blessing. However, many disagree with this, and some have written that for major needs one must recite the blessing "Al Netilat Yadayim" (see Beit Yosef). Thus, it teaches us that in every situation, one does not need to recite the blessing "Al Netilat Yadayim." It is written, "even if he wants to learn or pray immediately," to exclude the opinion of the Rosh that we brought in Siman 4, that even for the Mincha prayer, if one relieved oneself beforehand, one must recite "Al Netilat Yadayim" and "Asher Yatzar." This teaches us that it is not so, and only for Shacharit was it established as I wrote there, and as I wrote in Siman 233 that for Mincha one does not need the blessing "Al Netilat Yadayim." It is written, "his hands were dirty…" because there are those who differentiate between dirty and clean hands regarding the blessing (see Beit Yosef). Thus, it is said that there is no difference, for certainly one must wash hands for Mincha and Maariv prayers, and nevertheless, one does not recite "Al Netilat Yadayim," and here too it is the same. The rule is that the blessing "Al Netilat Yadayim" was instituted once a day only in Shacharit, unless at the time of a meal. (And in the Aretzot HaChaim, it is elaborated that many Poskim hold that for Mincha, if one relieved oneself beforehand, one should recite "Al Netilat Yadayim," see there. But one should not instruct others to do so. If a great individual wants to do so himself, he may, but not as an instruction to others. We only follow the words of the Shulchan Aruch. And the Pri Megadim was uncertain if another doubt was added to the blessing, such as if one wants to eat something dipped in liquid after relieving oneself and then pray Mincha afterwards, should one bless? See there. There is no doubt that certainly, one should not bless. And so it is written in Aretzot HaChaim.)

It has already been explained that after relieving oneself, whether for minor or major needs, one washes their hands and recites the blessing "Asher Yatzar." If one did not wipe after minor needs or did not clean after major needs, such that their hands are not dirty and did not touch covered areas, they do not need to wash their hands but should still recite "Asher Yatzar" without washing. If one wiped with one hand, they wash that hand (Yoma 30a). Nevertheless, the common custom is to wash hands in all cases. This is also written by Rabbeinu the Beit Yosef in section 2, and this is his language: "If one urinated and did not wipe… they do not need to wash hands except for reasons of cleanliness or preparation." This is his language. Meaning, since one relieved themselves, in any case, personal cleanliness requires washing hands in all situations, or because of "Prepare to meet your God, O Israel," meaning that even the honor of God demands this. And even though it will be explained later in section 91 that we are only concerned with "Prepare" in the context of prayer, this refers to the "Prepare" of a belt, as there is nothing repulsive here. But cleanliness without washing hands is considered repulsive and the concept of "Prepare" applies to all blessings. And know that some require washing hands three times when exiting the bathroom, and some are meticulous about doing this. However, Rabbeinu the Beit Yosef at the end of section 4 did not rule this way, as we have explained there; see there (and so wrote the Magen Avraham).

Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote in paragraph 3: If one urinated, then diverted his attention from urinating, and afterward decided and urinated again, he needs to recite the blessing "Asher Yatzar" twice. This is his language, and his reasoning is that he already became obligated the first time. This is not similar to a meal, where even if one diverted his attention from eating and then ate again, he only recites the blessing once, because there it depends on one's will, which is not the case with bodily needs. This is more similar to prayer, where if one forgot to pray, he prays the missed prayer twice (Taz, small paragraph 2). However, many great scholars have rejected this ruling and ruled that one should only recite the blessing once, and this is the common custom (Bach, Shlah, Magen Avraham, Gra, Shagat Aryeh). Furthermore, if one forgot to bless "Asher Yatzar" and remembered, and at that moment he had the urge to relieve himself, he should not bless, but should relieve himself and afterward recite one blessing for both (Shaarei Teshuva). And someone who takes a laxative and relieved himself, even though he knows that within a certain period he will need to relieve himself again, he should bless each time. However, if it seems to him that he will need to relieve himself immediately again, he should wait with the blessing until he has finished completely. This matter depends on one's understanding (see Shaarei Teshuva).

There is no specific measure for urination, and similarly for defecation. Even for a single drop, if it exits from him, he is obligated to bless, for if, Heaven forbid, the opening were sealed and prevented that drop from exiting, it would be difficult for him; therefore, he must bless. And if he is in doubt whether he blessed or not, he should not bless, because in cases of doubt regarding blessings, we are lenient. And if he urinated twice and is uncertain whether he blessed, in this case, one could say that he should bless out of doubt, for even if he blessed once, perhaps we rule like Rabbeinu the Beit Yosef that one must bless twice. This would be akin to a double doubt in favor of stringency. However, some are hesitant in this situation as well and say not to bless (Birkei Yosef). If someone ate something that requires an after-blessing and then went to relieve himself, he should wash his hands and bless "Asher Yatzar," and afterward bless the after-blessing (Maharshal, Siman 97), because "Asher Yatzar" is considered frequent, and what is frequent takes precedence.

Some have written in the name of the Zohar that one who recites the Shema without tzitzit bears false witness against himself (the Gra and Magen Avraham at the end of Siman 24). However, in the Gemara in Berachot (14b) it is stated that this applies to tefillin and not to tzitzit. For it is understandable regarding tefillin, where one says "and you shall bind them..." and does not have the binding on him. But tzitzit, even if one recites the paragraph about tzitzit and does not have tzitzit on, nevertheless the obligation only exists when one wears a garment with four corners, as stated in Siman 19. And indeed, it appears that the Zohar's intention is the same: when one wears a garment with four corners without tzitzit, besides transgressing a positive commandment, it is also bearing false witness by wearing a four-cornered garment without tzitzit. This is also implied by the language of the Zohar in Parashat "Shelach" (page 175), which states: "For they recite the Shema without tzitzit, and they bear false witness. And these are traitors..., and the garment of traitors they have betrayed, their clothing without tzitzit is called the garment of traitors." Thus far the language. It is clearly stated as I wrote: when their clothing is without tzitzit.

Even though according to the basic law this is sufficient, nevertheless, every Jewish person should be careful to wear a small tallit with tzitzit all day. For the mitzvah of tzitzit is equivalent to all the other mitzvot, as it is written, "And you shall see it, and you shall remember all the commandments" (Menachot 43b). And in a time of divine anger, there is punishment from Heaven for neglecting this (ibid. 41a). And whoever is diligent in this mitzvah merits to receive the Divine Presence (ibid.). In the future, he will be served by two thousand eight hundred servants (Shabbat 32b). All of Israel wear a small tallit all day, and a large tallit during prayer.

Immediately in the morning after washing his hands, one should don the tzitzit while standing (Tur). The blessing should be recited while standing, similar to several other mitzvah blessings that the Rabbis derived from the counting of the Omer, which is blessed while standing, as will be explained in its place. Therefore, the wrapping (in the tallit) should also be done while standing, as the blessing needs to be immediately adjacent to the wrapping, meaning just before wearing it. This is the primary halachic ruling.

Be aware that "wrapping" applies only to a large tallit, hence the blessing recited over it is "to wrap oneself in tzitzit," with the "b" in "b'tzitzit" pronounced with a patach. However, a small tallit does not involve wrapping, and the blessing recited over it is "concerning the mitzvah of tzitzit." The small tallit should be worn immediately upon rising after washing hands, even if it is before dawn. When dawn breaks, one should touch it and then recite the blessing.

It is obvious that the requirement to bless while standing is not indispensable. This is not mentioned in the Talmud but was inferred by the early authorities. Therefore, in a pressing situation, one can recite the blessing while sitting. (The Magen Avraham in subsection 2 raises a difficulty from the case of a sick person; see there. According to what I have written, it is understandable, but his words require further examination. Is it really indispensable? The Jerusalem Talmud is cited as stating that all blessings should be recited while standing; see Beit Yosef and Bach. This is also ideally. I do not know the source of this in the Jerusalem Talmud, and in Berachot chapter 9, halacha 3, where the primary discussion of blessings is found, this is not mentioned.)

The Nimukei Yosef writes in the name of the Ritva (in his commentary on the Rif, Hilchot Tzitzit), and this is his language: "And now we are left to explain whether the wrapping is essential or not... For there are some of the early authorities who said that the mitzvah of the tallit is not fulfilled except by wrapping the head, to cover both the head and the body or most of it, as it is written: 'which you cover with.' According to their words, the mitzvah of tzitzit is not fulfilled with these small tallitot that are customarily worn in most kingdoms. And this does not seem so, and the fact that they used to bless 'to enwrap'—this is for the most preferable way of performing the mitzvah. And it is possible that the Talmud speaks according to their custom, as they were not accustomed to wear anything but a large tallit. But according to the strict letter of the law, any garment with four corners is obligated in tzitzit, and one fulfills the mitzvah of tzitzit even though it does not cover or enwrap. For the Merciful One says 'their garments' and 'your covering,' and it implies all clothing and coverings, provided that it has four corners. And if because of 'which you cover with...'—this includes the covering of a blind person or one that has five... And thus the custom has spread throughout Israel... And so ruled the Rabbi, author of Halachot... And with these small tallitot, they do not bless 'to enwrap' but rather 'on the mitzvah of tzitzit...'" Thus far his language, and most of the great authorities agreed with this, as did the Maharik and the Maharil (as written in Beit Yosef). And see what I wrote in Siman 10, Se'if 20, and it requires further study.

And this is what the Tur wrote: The order of wrapping it was explained by the Geonim as the wrapping of Ishmaelites, which is a complete wrapping. And Ba'al Ha'itur wrote that we do not require all that, but rather as people cover themselves with their garments and are engaged in their work, sometimes covering their heads and sometimes uncovering their heads. End quote. The intention is not that according to the Geonim there is no obligation of tzitzit in another manner, but rather this is its explanation: that a large tallit, upon which we recite the blessing "to wrap," requires the wrapping of the Ishmaelites specifically, which is the wrapping of most of the body and the entire head, and to cover the mouth with the tallit. And the Ba'al Ha'itur holds that wrapping the head is not a requirement. But regarding the obligation of a small tallit, it is not discussed, as is evident from the words of the Tur throughout this entire section, see there.

And this is what our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 2: The order of wrapping it is like the way people cover themselves with their garment and engage in their work, sometimes with their head covered and sometimes with their head uncovered. And it is proper to cover one's head with the tallit. Until here are his words. Meaning: the main point of the law is like the Atur that we only require the covering of the body, and we do not concern ourselves with covering the head with the tallit. And when he wrote "with the head uncovered" – his intention is not literally with the head uncovered, because it has already been explained in section 2 that it is forbidden. Rather, his intention is that the tallit should not cover his head. And for this he wrote "and it is proper to cover one's head with the tallit" – in order to fulfill the opinion of the Geonim. And so is the custom. And the Ari, of blessed memory, would cover the tallit over the tefillin on the head but not completely (Magen Avraham, small section 3), because we require that part of the tefillin on the head be visible to all. And this will be explained in section 27.

Afterwards, our master the Beit Yosef wrote in section 3: Our small tallitot, which we customarily wear even though they do not involve envelopment – we still fulfill the obligation of tzitzit with them. This is his wording. Meaning: This is as we have explained, that the Geonim and the Eitur refer to large tallitot, but in any case, they agree that one also fulfills the obligation of tzitzit with a small tallit. However, one does not bless "to wrap oneself in tzitzit," since there is no envelopment here. Therefore, our master the Beit Yosef further wrote, and this is his wording: It is good to place it on one's head, the width of it corresponding to one’s height, and wrap oneself in it, and stand thus wrapped for at least the time it takes to walk four cubits. Then, one should take it off from one's head and wear it. This is his wording.

Explanation of the matter: Because the Geonim said that we require the wrapping of the head similar to the wrapping of the Ishmaelites, which means covering the mouth, our custom when we wear the tallit is to throw one end of the tallit over the opposite shoulder, thus covering the mouth and lips, and we stand like this for the duration of walking four cubits. One must be careful not to wrap the entire tallit only over the shoulder, as the main point is to cover the body, but rather as I have written. After walking four cubits, the length of the body is covered by the tallit, and also part of the head is covered (see Magen Avraham, subsection 2). Therefore, our teacher the Beit Yosef said that one can also fulfill the opinion of the Geonim with a small tallit, meaning that at the time of donning it, place it on the head, the width of the tallit over the person’s stature, and wrap it around the face and mouth, and stand like this for the duration of walking four cubits. Afterwards, move it from the head and wear it, because the main requirement is only at the time of donning. (Some have written that in this case one should bless "to wrap" [the Gra and Sha'arei Teshuvah, subsection 3]. However, from the Magen Avraham at the end of subsection 4, it does not seem so, according to the opinion of the Rema that for a small tallit the blessing is "on the mitzvah of tzitzit." This also seems to be the main opinion, and this is the common custom.)

And what has been explained about also performing "Atifah" (wrapping) with a small tallit (tallit katan) – this applies to a small tallit that is not sewn side to side in part of it. Rather, it is a long piece with a neck hole in the middle, like the small woolen tallitot that are customary among us. But a small tallit that is sewn side to side in part of it cannot be wrapped, for if so, all four tzitzit would be on one side, and we require two in front and two in back (Magen Avraham, section 4). There is no strictness in this since it is not essential, and most people do not practice this wrapping. And we recite the blessing "to enwrap in tzitzit" (ibid.).

There are some who are particular that the tzitzit in front of them should never be behind them. This is because the main mitzvah of tzitzit is to have two tzitzit in the front and two in the back, so that one is surrounded by the mitzvah (Tur). It seems that this is essential, for it is written "on the four corners of your garment," and the corners are two in the front and two in the back. Therefore, some are particular that those in the front should never be in the back, because the front is considered more important. This is similar to the principle of ascending in holiness and not descending. Hence, they place a piece of silk or some other material on the upper side of the tallit. Among us, we do this by sewing a piece under the head of the tallit so it does not get ruined by sweat, and thus there is a distinction between the upper and lower sides. It seems that in ancient times they did not do this, for it is written about the Ari (Magen Avraham, section 6) that he did not insist on always placing the tallit on one side. That is, sometimes one side would be worn facing inward and sometimes the other side. If he had a piece sewn under the head of the tallit, it would not have been possible to do this, since the sewn piece would be on the outside. Some have written that he was not particular about the upper and lower sides either, and therefore sometimes what was in front would be in the back. Some have the custom to place the right side of the tallit on the left shoulder so that it is properly wrapped, but this is not the custom. Some also place a silver crown at the head of the tallit that rests on the head. This is not advisable, as this implies that the main part is what is on the head, while in truth the main part is what is on the body. Therefore, some have the custom for this reason to place a silver crown in the middle of the tallit (see Be'erot HaChaim). But this too is not advisable, and many great people refrain from this. It is proper that the tallit be made only of wool, and what do silver and gold have to do with a tallit? (And the Ari certainly did not do this, for if he did, he would not have been able to reverse it.)

One recites the blessing "to wrap oneself with tzitzit." According to the fundamental law, another person can also recite the blessing on his behalf, as is the rule with blessings over commandments. However, some are cautious about this unless the person himself is unable to recite the blessing. Nevertheless, if two or three people each wrap themselves in their tallit at the same moment, even ideally, one person can recite the blessing, and the others listen to the blessing, respond "Amen," and wrap themselves, as this is also the case with blessings over enjoyment. They can also each recite the blessing on their own. And although it is preferable for one person to recite the blessing and everyone else respond "Amen," with the intent of fulfilling the obligation and they with the intent to fulfill their obligation, because "in a multitude of people is the King's glory," as I have written later in Siman 298, nevertheless, this is not the custom because it is difficult to ensure that everyone wraps themselves at the same moment. It is better for each person to recite the blessing for himself. And when wearing new tallitot and needing to recite "Shehecheyanu," each one certainly recites the blessing for himself (Pri Megadim).

Our master, the Beit Yosef, in section 6 ruled that one may also recite the blessing "to wrap oneself" on a small tallit, even though one does not wrap oneself in it but rather wears it, because the wording of the blessing is thus as explained in the Talmud and the Tosefta. Just as we bless "upon the washing of hands" even when immersing hands in a river, as mentioned at the end of section 159. Therefore, our master the Rema, who ruled there that one should bless "upon the immersion of hands," also ruled here that one should bless "upon the mitzvah of tzitzit." And so is the custom, and it should not be changed. One should not be puzzled by the wording "upon," which implies past tense. However, in truth, according to the conclusion in Pesachim (7a), it also implies future tense, see there. It seems to me that "upon" is better, for in most cases one wears it before the blessing, such as in winter when one wears it before dawn or when one's body is not clean, and one blesses afterward when handling it. Therefore, "upon," which implies even past tense, is better. (See Taz, section 7, who wrote: And with this resolved... – which is not understood, see there. Examine and you will find it easy.) (And the custom mentioned by the Magen Avraham in section 9 is not practiced by us.)

The Sages taught: "Tzitzit" refers only to a branch. And so it says: "And he took me by the tzitzit of my head." And Abaye said: One must separate them... (Menachot 42a). And this is what the Tur and Shulchan Aruch wrote in Section 7, that one must separate the threads of the tzitzit from each other. This is their language. They are called "tzitzit" because of the threads that are separated from it (Tur), like branches that are distinct from each other. Therefore, before the blessing, one should separate them if they are tangled together. However, if by doing so one will miss praying with the congregation, it does not prevent the mitzvah, since they are always essentially separated from each other and the tangling is insignificant. But if there is time, one should separate them. The intention of the Gemara was during the making process, they should not be attached to each other. Therefore, if the tzitzit are of good quality and smooth, and they never get tangled, one does not need to separate them with his hands before the blessing, as they are already separated. And one should have the intention, when wrapping in the tzitzit, that the Holy One, blessed be He, commanded us to wrap in it in order to remember all His commandments to perform them, as it is written: "And you shall see it and remember all the commandments of Hashem and do them."

The Tur and the Shulchan Aruch wrote in section 9: Before one blesses, one should inspect the threads of the tzitzit to ensure they are valid, so that one does not recite a blessing in vain. Thus are their words. They were not concerned about the possibility of wearing a four-cornered garment without tzitzit, because we establish the presumption (chazakah) that they are intact as they were previously. They were only concerned about the blessing, to ensure it is not in vain, and to avoid transgressing the prohibition of "You shall not take the name [of the Lord your God in vain]" (Taz, subsection 8). This means that the prohibition of taking God's name in vain is very severe. 

Some say that according to the law, inspection is necessary, because whenever it is possible to verify, we do not rely on presumption, similar to the ruling in Yoreh De'ah, section 1, regarding the majority of those who are present at a slaughter being experts; we do not rely on the majority when verification is possible, as I wrote there. And here, the same applies to presumption (Magen Avraham, subsection 11). However, this is not so, for we only say this when there is a presumption of prohibition, as in Yoreh De'ah there. But here, there is no presumption of prohibition. Some want to say that this applies to a majority, but even without a presumption of prohibition, verification is necessary (Machatzit HaShekel). This is also not so, for it is clearly proven in section 337 that this applies even to a presumption (Magen Avraham, there, subsection 4). 

Others want to say that a presumption of obligation is like a presumption of prohibition (Aroch HaShulchan), but this is mere speculation. Additionally, another reason given for the presumption is that it might become invalid at any moment (Magen Avraham, there). This is also questionable, for we see that this is not the case. And if the argument is that over time it will certainly become invalid, then all presumptions of life in the Talmud would be nullified, for ultimately, a person will die. Therefore, it is certain that as long as there is no necessity to remove from the presumption, we maintain the presumption.

And it is clear that according to the letter of the law, there is no concern in this matter. Its source is from the Rosh, and he wrote in this language at the end of the laws of Tzitzit: "And one who is fearful of the word of God should check beforehand, so that he does not make a blessing in vain." Thus are his words, and in a responsum, section 2, he wrote that the world is not accustomed to checking it because we rely on a presumption of validity, see there. And this is only an act of piety, and therefore he wrote about the concern of a blessing in vain. And it is not because it is very severe as I wrote earlier, but regarding a tallit without tzitzit, even if it is found invalid – he will immediately remove it, and beforehand he did not commit a transgression because according to the law it was permitted to wear it due to the presumption of validity. But regarding a blessing in vain, even though he is not punished for it, because it was permitted for him to bless based on the presumption of validity, nevertheless, in the end, he uttered a blessing in vain from his mouth, and therefore as an act of piety he should check. Therefore, if the congregation is praying – he should not check at all, and this checking is only when he has time. And all the more so if the tallit was placed in a stored place, and he stored it with valid tzitzit, there is no need to check in any case. (And in this, also the Magen Avraham agreed at the end of subsection 11, see there.)

If one wears a small tallit (tzitzit) while his hands are not clean, or if he wears it before dawn in a manner that makes it impossible to bless it at that time, and similarly if he needs to relieve himself — he should wear it without a blessing. When he washes his hands, or when it is daylight, or after he relieves himself and washes his hands — he should handle the tzitzit and recite the blessing. Although this is not "before performing the mitzvah" (over la'asiyatan), since it is not possible in any other way, it is still considered as such because he is wearing it afterward (see Beit Yosef and Taz, subsection 9). Alternatively, when he puts on the large tallit and blesses it, he should intend to exempt the small tallit as well, and he does not need to handle the tzitzit of the small tallit. Many prominent people follow this practice because it is often difficult to bless the small tallit at the time it is worn. (In this way, we also satisfy the opinions of the early authorities that we mentioned in paragraph 4, although the law is not like them, see there. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

Some say that the main mitzvah of the small tallit is to wear it over one's clothes, so that one will always see it and remember the commandments. However, this is not the custom. Additionally, in the name of the Ari z"l, it is written that, on the contrary, it should be worn under one's clothes (Magen Avraham, subsection 13, in the name of the writings, and so it is in Pri Etz Chaim). There are those who say that one should not tuck the fringes in, as we say in Menachot (41b): "Tzitzit is only valid when it is visible." This is not a proof at all, as there the explanation is about the primary making of it, see there. Nevertheless, even though according to the law it does not invalidate: why should we be ashamed of the mitzvot of Hashem? Similarly, those who tuck the small tallit into their pants – the sages are not pleased with them. Unless one is walking among dignitaries and knows they will mock him, in which case he may do so. (See Magen Avraham, subsection 13. His proof is questionable as Rashi wrote there. Pay attention and you will find it easy.)

If one has several garments with four corners and wears them, all of them are obligated in tzitzit. If he wears them all without a significant interruption and initially had in mind for all of them, he only recites one blessing on the first garment, which covers all of them. However, if there was a significant interruption, even if he had intention for all of them, or if he spoke a lot about matters not related to wearing the garments, he needs to recite the blessing again. Similarly, if he did not explicitly have in mind for all of them but just wore them without specific intention, he needs to recite the blessing again. From this, one can learn that if someone wears a tallit and recites the blessing on it, and immediately afterward wears a large tallit and recites the blessing on it, the sages do not approve of this, as he could have exempted both with one blessing, and one should not increase blessings unnecessarily. This applies only when he prays at home and immediately after wearing the small tallit. But if he goes to the synagogue or there is a significant interruption, this does not apply. Similarly, if he did not initially intend to wear the large tallit immediately and then decided to wear it, it requires its own blessing. (See Taz, Section 11, who challenges the Beit Yosef's opinion that going to the synagogue constitutes an interruption, from Tosafot Sotah 39a. The Beit Yosef's words are correct, as the Tosafot refers to the Temple. Also, in the case of washing hands, it is all one matter and must be done, so it does not constitute an interruption, which is not the case here where they are two different matters, and it is indeed an interruption. Examine and you will find this clear.)

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote in section 12 that if the first garment was removed before the second garment was worn, one must recite the blessing again. These are his words. Many have objected, arguing that it is certainly referring to a case where one had the intention, at the time of the blessing, for the second garment, for if not, it would require a blessing regardless. And since he had intention for it, why should it matter that he removed the first garment? What is this comparable to? To one who slaughters with the intention to slaughter two birds—does he need a blessing for the second one even though he already slaughtered the first? (Levush, Magen Avraham, section 16, Gra, and Eliyah Rabbah). 

And it seems to me that the opinion of our teacher, the Rema, is that we see that in the obligation of a blessing, whenever one changes his mind to do differently than what he intended at the time of the blessing, another blessing is required. And here too, it is the same, for at the time of the blessing, his intention was to wear both garments, and afterward, he changed his mind to remove the first. And every change of mind requires another blessing. And it is not comparable to slaughtering, for there, it is not considered a change of mind. 

Nevertheless, in practice, the law follows the majority opinion, and one does not recite a blessing in such a case for the second garment.

Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote in Section 14: If one removed his tallit, even if he intended to wrap himself in it again immediately, he must recite a blessing when he wraps himself in it again. End of his words. And they were astonished at him: for indeed it is obvious that if he intended to wrap himself in it again, he does not need to recite a blessing, as he himself ruled later in Siman 639 that if one leaves the sukkah with the intention to return, he does not need to recite a blessing (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 18). And what he compared this in his great book to what is stated in Sukkah (46a), that for tefillin, when one removes them to enter the bathroom and then puts them back on, he recites a blessing – this is not a valid comparison because it is necessary to remove tefillin, as it is forbidden to enter the bathroom with them (Taz, subparagraph 12, and Bach and Drisha). And it appears, in my humble opinion, that his words are correct, for the reason he removed his tallit is that he does not want to do something while wearing the tallit even though it is permissible by law, such as attending to his needs, etc. If so, it is an active deferral of the tallit and is not comparable to the sukkah, where one is compelled to leave the sukkah. Therefore, if his intention is to return immediately, he does not need to recite a blessing. But here, where he could have kept the tallit on and chose to remove it, it is indeed considered an active deferral and interruption, and he must recite a blessing. And indeed, it is worse than tefillin, where one is compelled to remove them. And in several matters, we find that an active deferral is worse than a passive one. (And the Gra agreed with Beit Yosef, see there. And perhaps for the reason we have explained.)

But our teacher, the Rema, wrote that some say one does not recite a blessing if it was his intention to return and wrap himself in it. And some say this is specifically when he remains wearing a small tallit, and this is the practice. So far his words. And many have already labored over this: what logic is there to distinguish between when he remains wearing a small tallit or not? And what relevance does a small tallit have to the removal of the large one? And they interpreted his intention as follows: that if it was explicitly his intention to wear it again immediately in any situation, he does not need to recite a blessing again. And if it was his intention not to wear it immediately, and afterward he decided to wear it in any situation, he needs to recite a blessing again. However, if he removed it without any specific intention, then if he remains wearing a small tallit, it is as if he intended to wear it immediately, and he does not need to recite a blessing. And if he does not remain wearing a small tallit, it is as if he intended not to wear it immediately, and he needs to recite a blessing again (this is the intention of the Bach and the Magen Avraham, section 19). And regarding the practical law: in cases of doubt concerning blessings, one should be lenient. In any situation, one does not need to recite a blessing when wearing it immediately, even if he does not remain wearing a small tallit (Taz, end of section 13), and even in a general case.
