And this is the simple custom, and it should not be changed. And changing places does not constitute an interruption, since he wore the same tallit.

If one's tallit fell off his body unintentionally, whether it fell to the ground or he caught it in his hand, and he then rewraps himself – he must recite a blessing according to all opinions. Since it fell off without his intention, the mitzvah has departed, similar to tefillin that have slipped from their place, as I wrote in Siman 25. This applies specifically when the entire tallit fell off. But if only part of it fell, even if most of it fell and a minority remained on his body, he does not need to recite a blessing. If the entire tallit fell off during the middle of prayer and others returned it to him, there is an opinion that after the prayer he should touch it and recite a blessing (Shiyarei Knesset HaGedolah). In my humble opinion, if he himself returned it and was in the middle of a section where interruption is forbidden, it is proper for him to recite a blessing afterward. But if he was praying the Shemoneh Esrei and others returned it to him, he does not need to recite a blessing. (As proof of this, see the Mishnah at the beginning of the fourth chapter of Eruvin. Examine it and you will find clarity.) Be aware that some say even if most of it fell off, he needs to recite a blessing (Taz, subsection 14). And in cases of doubt regarding blessings, we are lenient.

The Tur wrote: One who sleeps in his tallit does not need to recite a blessing on it in the morning. Thus are his words, and his reasoning is simple: since according to the Rosh, as will be explained in Siman 18, a garment designated for daytime use is also obligated at night, it follows that the night does not constitute an interruption. But according to the Rambam there, at night all garments are exempt from tzitzit, certainly one must recite a blessing. And our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 16: One who sleeps in his tallit at night must recite a blessing on it in the morning even if he did not remove it. And it is good to handle it at the time of the blessing. Thus are his words, and he follows his own reasoning in his great book: that the Rosh himself ruled so in response in Klal 2. And there are those who wrote that the Rosh ruled thus according to the opinion of the questioner, who held like the Rambam (Drisha), or that at the time he wrote the response, this law was not yet settled, that a daytime garment is obligated even at night (Taz section 15). And all these explanations are strained, as is evident. And in my humble opinion, it seems that the Rosh holds that sleeping is different. For although a daytime garment is obligated even at night, nevertheless it constitutes a significant distraction. And this also seems evident from the words of the Levush; see there. According to this, the ruling of our teacher, the Beit Yosef, makes sense, but in any case, in cases of doubt regarding blessings, we are lenient. And know that what he wrote, "and it is good to handle it..." which implies that it is not strictly necessary, is certainly correct. For specifically with tefillin, handling them is essential, as it is a mitzvah to handle them, and there is also an obligation (Shabbat 12a). But with tzitzit, handling them neither adds nor detracts, for with tefillin, it is forbidden to be distracted from them. Therefore, one is obligated to handle them but not with tzitzit (Bach). And our teacher, the Rema, wrote that one should do so if he dons his tallit before dawn. Thus are his words, and it is simple. (And see Taz section 17. Be precise and you will find leniency.) And anyone who dons a garment or covers himself with a garment that is obligated in tzitzit and did not attach tzitzit to it has nullified the mitzvah of tzitzit and transgresses every moment a positive commandment, even if he is wearing another garment with tzitzit. (And one who sleeps in his tallit – it is good to exempt it with a large tallit.)

Know that in the Gemara there is a dispute among the Tannaim and Amoraim, and similarly among the poskim (decisors), whether garments other than wool and linen are obligated in tzitzit by Torah law; or if they are exempt by Torah law, and only obligated in tzitzit by Rabbinic decree in order to be cautious with the mitzvah of tzitzit (Rambam, beginning of Chapter 3). The reason for the dispute is that those who obligate (other garments) say that it is written "and they shall make for themselves tzitzit on the corners of their garments" – implying all garments. Those who exempt (other garments) say that since the Torah revealed in the context of afflictions (negaim) a garment of wool or linen, and similarly in the context of shaatnez it is written "wool and linen" – we learn from this that all garments mentioned in the Torah are only wool and linen. And this is the language of the Talmud in Menachot (39b): Since garments are mentioned in the Torah generally, and the text specified for you in one of them wool and linen – so too, all (garments mentioned in the Torah are) wool and linen, see there. And one of them is negaim where "garment" is written, but regarding shaatnez, "garment" is not written. (The words of Rashi there need further examination, and perhaps there is a printing error there. Examine it carefully, and you will find it easy to understand.) The Rif and the Rambam ruled that the obligation for other garments is Rabbinic. Rashi, Tosafot, the Rosh, and the Sefer Mitzvot Gadol (SMaG) ruled that it is a Torah obligation, and so ruled Rabbeinu the Rema in Section 1. (And in the book "Eretz Hachaim" he brings proof for this from the Mishnah at the beginning of Chapter 9 of Kilayim, which counts matters of wool and linen, and did not count this of tzitzit. And perhaps because all those mentioned there also from Rabbinic law – there is no obligation. But it is not so with tzitzit.)

The tzitzit must be of two kinds, from white threads and from blue threads, as it is written: "And they shall put upon the fringe of the corner a thread of blue." Rashi and Tosafot wrote at the beginning of the chapter "The Blue Thread" that we require two white threads and two blue threads. And Maimonides at the beginning of the laws of tzitzit wrote: one thread of blue and three of white. And the Sefer Mitzvot Gadol in Mitzvah 27 wrote both opinions, and this is his wording: two of white and two of blue or three of white and one of blue. Until here is his wording, and it implies that there is no strict requirement in this matter. But from Tosafot there it implies that two are essential. And we say there in the Gemara: it is a commandment to precede the white to the blue, and if one preceded the blue to the white – he has fulfilled the obligation, only that he has omitted performing the commandment in the best manner.

And this is not two commandments, but one commandment. And this is the language of the Rambam there: The sages said: "And it shall be for you as fringes" – teaches that they are both one commandment. And we learned in the Mishnah there: the blue thread does not prevent the white thread, and the white thread does not prevent the blue thread. For if he made all four threads blue or all four threads white – he has fulfilled his obligation (Rashi). And according to the Rambam, the white thread is indeed essential, for if he made blue without white – he has not fulfilled his obligation, but white without blue – he has fulfilled his obligation. And only in this regard, the white thread is not essential: that if he made white and blue, and the white thread was cut and only the blue thread remained – it is valid, see there.

And what is "Techelet"? The Rambam writes at the beginning of the second chapter of Tzitzit: "Techelet" mentioned in the Torah everywhere is wool dyed with a specific dye that is blue, and this resembles the appearance of the sky as seen in the sunlight in the purity of the sky. And the Techelet mentioned in Tzitzit must be dyed with a known dye, which retains its beauty and does not change. Any wool that is not dyed with this dye is invalid for Tzitzit, even if it resembles the color of the sky. For example, if it is dyed with indigo, or with black, or with other darkening agents – it is invalid for Tzitzit. Wool from a Rachel goat is invalid for Tzitzit. (And what is the known dye? It is the blood of the Chilazon, as will be explained.)

How does one dye the techelet for tzitzit? One takes the wool and soaks it in lime, and then washes it until it is clean. Then, they boil it in gallnut or something similar, as dyers do, so that it will absorb the eye. Afterwards, they bring the blood of the chilazon, which is a fish whose eye is similar to the color of techelet, and its blood is black like ink, and it is found in the Dead Sea (see Megillah 6a, further inquiry is needed). They put the blood into a pot, and they add to it ingredients like cumin or similar substances, as dyers do. They boil it, and then they put the wool into it until it becomes like the color of the sky. This is the techelet for tzitzit.

The tekhelet (blue dye) of the tzitzit needs to be dyed with specific intent, "for the sake of tzitzit." If it is dyed without this intent, it is invalid, because all aspects of tzitzit require specific intent. The person must explicitly state that he is dyeing it for the sake of tzitzit, similar to the requirement for shechita (slaughtering) with specific intent, as will be explained in Siman 11. However, if it is done with a general intention, it is invalid, because a general intention does not suffice for specific intent. It is possible that even if one merely thinks in his heart that it is for the sake of tzitzit, it is valid. And the halacha is that taste-testing invalidates it (Menachot 42b). This means: just as in cooking, when one takes a little to taste to see if it is good, similarly, if one takes a little dye from the pot to dye something else and test if it is good, it is invalid. The reason is that since specific intent is required, what is taken for testing is not for the sake of tzitzit (Gemara). Moreover, if a bit of the test sample falls back into the pot, the entire pot becomes invalid. It appears that nullification does not help, and I do not know the reason.

Even when one performed the test on the tekhelet and intended it for the sake of tzitzit, it is still invalid (Tosafot, there, s.v. "Ma"). Since it was also done for the sake of testing, it is considered as being done both for its intended purpose and not for its intended purpose, which is invalid in such cases (there). So how should one act when they want to test it? They should take some dye from the vat in a small vessel, place wool in it to test, burn the wool that was tested since it was dyed for testing, and pour out the dye from the vessel that was used for testing since it has been tasted and invalidated. Then, they should dye the tekhelet with the remaining dye in the vat that has not been compromised.

The techelet (blue dye) should only be obtained from an expert (as stated there), lest it be dyed improperly or dyed with an experimental dye. This matter cannot be checked, obviously, and therefore an expert is needed, meaning someone who knows the law and is trustworthy. Additionally, our sages of blessed memory have said that an expert is required because there is another dye that resembles techelet and is called "kala ilan." If the person is not trustworthy, there is a concern that he dyed with kala ilan and not with techelet. And our sages of blessed memory said (Menachot 61b) that this is why it is written in the section on tzitzit, "I am the Lord"—the Holy One, blessed be He, said: I am destined to punish one who places kala ilan on his garment and says "it is techelet."

However, if it is only due to the concern of "Kala Ilan" (indigo) alone, we would not be concerned, because there is a test for this. How do we test it? We bring "Magvia Gili" and "Maya Deshavilta." Rashi explains: "Magvia Gili" is alum, and "Maya Deshavilta" is water that comes from fenugreek. The Rambam wrote: straw and snail slime. Additionally, we bring urine that has fermented for forty days and soak the tekhelet in it for twenty-four hours. If it remains unchanged and does not fade, it is valid. If it fades, we take barley dough that has been fermented to make murias, place the discolored tekhelet in it, bake the dough in the oven, and then take the tekhelet out from the bread and examine it. If it has faded from its previous state, it is invalid. If its color has intensified and it has become darker than it was before baking, it is valid. Therefore, even if it was obtained from an expert, if this test is performed and it does not pass successfully, it is invalid.

A courtyard where blue dye is sold, and it is established to be kosher – one may buy from it without inspection. It retains its presumption of being kosher until it is suspected otherwise. It appears to me that this is specifically when the people in the courtyard have not changed, but rather the same people who were established to be kosher, they and their household members, are still there. If one deposits blue dye with a non-Jew – it is invalid, as we suspect that it may have been switched. However, if it was in a vessel and sealed with two seals, a seal within a seal – it is valid. With only one seal – it is invalid, for anything that is Biblically mandated requires a seal within a seal, as explained in Yoreh De'ah, siman 118. The same applies if it was deposited with a Jew who is suspect – it requires two seals as explained there.

The one who finds tekhelet (blue-dyed threads) in the market, even if they are cut and it appears that they were intended for use as tzitzit, they are nonetheless invalid, because who can say they were made in a kosher manner? Therefore, if they are both cut and spun, meaning that they were twisted in a kosher manner, since so much effort was invested, it is certain that they were made for the purpose of tzitzit. But if they are spun and not cut, there is no proof of their validity, as it is possible they were spun for a garment. However, if they are cut, they are not suitable for a garment (as is proven in Eruvin 96b). The Rambam in the second chapter, law 7, is brief in his language; see there. But his intention is also the same, as it is proven in the Gemara, see there. And even though tekhelet is only purchased from an expert, nevertheless, if one finds them spun and cut, it can be assumed they fell from an expert. For if he is not an expert, he would not normally deal in this, since he knows they would not be purchased from him, and why would he go to such trouble (Tosafot there, s.v. "the one who finds")? And all this applies only to tekhelet. But one who buys a tallit with tzitzit from the market from a Jew—it is kosher (Menachot 43a), even from any Jew, since the tallit was made with tzitzit—it is certainly made in a kosher manner. Not only that, but even if one bought it from a Samaritan, if he is a merchant, it is kosher, because he certainly bought it from a Jew, as a merchant would not ruin his reputation. But from a common person, it is invalid.

Rabbi Meir used to say (Menachot 43b): The penalty for neglecting the white (threads of tzitzit) is greater than the penalty for neglecting the blue (threads of tzitzit), because white is readily available everywhere and easy to obtain, and yet he did not do it. Therefore, his penalty is greater. This is not the case with the blue, which is expensive and difficult to obtain, therefore its penalty is not as great as the absence of the white. Due to our sins, since the time we were dispersed, we do not have the blue. We do not know about it at all, and all our tzitzit are white. Nevertheless, we are fulfilling the mitzvah properly, as it has already been explained that the blue does not invalidate the white. Therefore, one who neglects this mitzvah has a greater penalty. Know that a few years ago, someone boasted that he found the chilazon (the source of the blue dye) and made blue from it, and he attracted some people after him. However, he did not have the approval of the great sages of the generation or the community of Israel, and the matter was nullified until the righteous redeemer will come speedily in our days. Amen.

Know that the Torah permits [the use of] kilayim (a forbidden mixture of wool and linen) in tzitzit, as it is written: "You shall not wear shaatnez (a mixture of wool and linen), wool and linen together," and immediately following it says: "You shall make twisted cords on the four corners of your garment…" (Deuteronomy 22:11-12), to indicate that in tzitzit, shaatnez is permitted (beginning of Yevamot). This is also evident from the verses concerning tzitzit, as the Torah requires placing techelet (blue dye), and techelet is dyed wool. Garments of wool and linen are certainly obligated in tzitzit, and therefore techelet on linen would constitute kilayim (ibid.).

And we say there that Rava posed a contradiction between verses: here it is written "Wool and linen... make for yourself twisted cords," implying that tzitzit must be only from wool or linen. And it is written: "And they shall put on the tzitzit of the corner..." and this word "corner" is extra, for it should have written "And they shall put on the tzitzit a thread of blue." Rather, certainly, "corner" refers to the type of the corner, meaning to make the tzitzit from the same type as the garment. How so? Wool and linen exempt whether they are the same type or not the same type, but other types only exempt if they are of the same type, meaning: if the garment is silk, one can make tzitzit from silk, and similarly. And this is what is written in the Tur and Shulchan Aruch that tzitzit of wool or linen exempts all types, but other types such as silk or cotton only exempt if the tzitzit are of the same type as the garment. This is their language. And this is according to the opinion that all garments are biblically obligated in tzitzit, and Rava holds this way. But according to the Rif and the Rambam who ruled not like Rava, seemingly none of this applies, obviously, and according to them, certainly tzitzit must only be from wool or linen. And according to them, this derivation does not apply. And I found in the responsa of the Rashba (Third Volume, Siman 280) that according to this opinion, "the corner" refers to the type of the corner, to begin with white because of the corner being of the same type, and ends with white because we ascend in holiness and do not descend as stated in Menachot (39a). And indeed the Rif brought this, and so did the Rambam in the first chapter, law 7, see there. And consequently, regarding the type of the corner as Rava, they do not hold this way.

And based on this, we can understand the words of the Rambam in the third chapter, law 5, where he wrote that for other garments, one makes their white threads from their own kind, such as silk threads for a silk garment, and feather threads for a feather garment. But if one wants to make the white threads for other kinds of garments from wool or linen, he can, because wool and linen exempt both their own kind and other kinds, whereas other kinds only exempt their own kind and do not exempt other kinds. This is his language. It is not understood: for he ruled not like Rava, so how could he bring Rava's teaching? However, his words are correct, and he did not intend Rava's teaching but rather because in the Gemara (39b), it says this explicitly, that on the contrary, according to the one who says that the obligation of other garments is Rabbinic – certainly they are exempt with their own kind of tzitzit. And this is the language of the Gemara: If you say it is Rabbinic, then it makes sense that they are exempt with their own kind, but if it is Biblical, then we require wool and linen? And it answers like Rava, see there. It is explicitly stated that if it is Rabbinic – it is obvious that they are exempt with their own kind. And this is the intention of the Rambam, and not because of Rava's teaching. Therefore, also our master the Beit Yosef wrote this, even though he follows the method of the Rambam. And based on this, this law is applicable according to all opinions.

And since the Torah permitted the mixing of wool and linen (kilayim) in tzitzit, we should therefore permit making tzitzit of linen, meaning the white (threads) in a garment of wool and wool tzitzit in a linen garment. The answer to this is written by the Rambam in the third chapter, law 6, and this is his wording: "By law, it should be permitted... And why don't they do this? Because it is possible to make the white threads from its own kind. And whenever you find a positive commandment and a negative commandment, if you can fulfill both, it is better... And here you can fulfill both." Until here is his wording. There is a question on this: it is understandable in a time when there is no tekhelet (blue thread), like in our time – it is good to fulfill both. But in the time of tekhelet – it is impossible to fulfill both in linen garments, for it is necessary to insert the tekhelet. The answer to this: Firstly, it is indeed said that this applies to wool garments and linen garments in a time when there is no tekhelet. Additionally, even when there is tekhelet, in any case, the white can be from its own kind. Furthermore, in linen garments, it will be explained that tekhelet is not inserted at all due to a decree, as we will explain with the help of Heaven.

And this is the language of the Rambam there: A linen garment – one does not place tekhelet (blue dye) in it, but rather makes only the white threads of linen. And it is not because the tzitzit is set aside due to sha'atnez (the prohibition of mixing wool and linen), but rather a decree from the sages lest one cover himself with it at night... for the obligation of tzitzit is during the day and not at night... thus far his language. And according to the opinion of the Rosh that we brought, that a daytime garment is obligated even at night, it can be said the decree is due to a garment specifically designated for night. And according to this, according to the Rambam's method, one can make a four-cornered linen garment and place linen tzitzit on it, and thereby fulfill the commandment from the Torah. And this is also the opinion of Rashi and the Rif, of blessed memory.

However, according to the opinion of Rabbeinu Tam in Menachot (41a), the Maor in the second chapter of Shabbat, and several other Geonim, a linen garment with tzitzit is prohibited, even if the tzitzit themselves are made of linen. In other words, the Sages prohibited making any tzitzit on a linen garment, even tzitzit made of linen. The explanation is as follows: the primary prohibition is due to the concern about techelet (blue dye), so that one does not come to place techelet on a night garment and thereby transgress the prohibition of wearing a mixture of wool and linen (shatnez). There are further decrees in the Talmud related to this, all pertaining to techelet and not to white threads. However, since the commandments of techelet and white threads are interdependent, and even though they do not invalidate each other, nevertheless they are both considered tzitzit and should not be separated from one another. Since techelet was prohibited, the white threads were also consequently prohibited. It is impossible to obligate the use of white linen and prohibit techelet, for how can one mitzvah be partially obligatory and partially forbidden? Such an idea is not reasonable (Maor, ibid). Therefore, the Sages completely prohibited any type of tzitzit on a linen garment.

And if one questions this approach: How can the Rabbis nullify a positive commandment from the Torah by allowing one to wear a four-cornered garment without any tzitzit at all? Indeed, this question is asked in the Talmud, Yevamot 90b, and they answer that in a situation of "sit and do not do" (passive non-fulfillment), they have the authority to nullify it. And even though this is not a "sit and do not do" since one is actively wearing the garment, the Tosafot answer there that at the moment of donning the garment, one is not yet obligated until after it is fully worn. And after it is fully worn, it becomes a "sit and do not do," see there. On the contrary, according to the first approach, I have a stronger question: Why does the Talmud there consider wearing a linen garment with tzitzit as nullifying a Torah commandment? Since one is making tzitzit from linen, one is fulfilling the mitzvah, as the Rambam explicitly writes in the first chapter, halacha 5, that if one wears a tallit that has white or tekhelet or both, one has fulfilled the positive commandment. Thus he writes. And since one attaches white tzitzit made of linen, one fulfills the positive commandment, and there is no nullification of a Torah commandment at all. This requires further investigation.

However, even according to Rabbeinu Tam's opinion, it can be said that nowadays it is permissible to make linen tzitzit on a linen garment. When did the sages prohibit it? When there was tekhelet, which in a nighttime garment could lead to the prohibition of shaatnez. But nowadays, when there is no tekhelet - there is no possibility of coming to a prohibition. And if one worries that someone might come to insert woolen tzitzit, it has already been clarified that in our times shaatnez is prohibited wherever it is possible to fulfill both commandments, the prohibition is not overridden, as I wrote in paragraph 16 in the name of the Rambam. And I found this reasoning in the responsa of the Rosh, section 2; see there. And so he wrote at the end of the laws of tzitzit.

According to these two opinions, for a woolen tallit, one makes tzitzit of wool. For a linen tallit, according to Rashi, the Rif, and the Rambam, one makes tzitzit of linen. However, according to Rabbeinu Tam and the Meor, in the time of techelet, it is forbidden to make them of linen, but nowadays it might be permissible. For other garments, such as those made of cotton, silk, camel hair, or goat hair, one can make the tzitzit from whatever material they desire, whether the same type as the garment or from wool or linen.

And there is another opinion among some of the early authorities, that what Rava said, that wool and linen exempt even when not of their kind, refers specifically to wool and linen together, two threads of wool and two threads of linen. Consequently, in other garments, it is not possible to use tzitzit except from its own kind. This opinion is brought by the Terumat HaDeshen in Siman 44 in the name of Maharam, and so it is in the Hagahot Maimoniot (Chapter 3, Note 6). And there is also an opinion among some of the Geonim, brought by the Rif, that tzitzit made of linen alone does not exempt in any case. And the Rif rejected their words. However, in other types of garments, it is proper not to place linen threads except from its own kind or wool. And this is what the Tur wrote in the name of the SeMaK, that it is proper to be careful not to make tzitzit of linen for a silk garment. Until here is his language. That is to say: for a linen garment, other tzitzit are not possible, and we follow the opinion of Rashi, the Rif, and the Rambam. But for silk or other kinds, why should we enter into controversy? Let us make it from its own kind of wool (see Bach and Taz, subsection 4, who explained similarly). And he used the term "of silk," and the same applies to other kinds (Bach).

And some have explained the words of the Tur with a completely different reason: that it is only with a silk garment that one should not make tzitzit of linen, because there is wool that appears like silk; and they might come to attach linen tzitzit to a woolen garment, thinking it is silk (Beit Yosef and Magen Avraham, subsection 2). Therefore, even on a hemp garment, one should not attach woolen tzitzit, because there is not much of a distinction between hemp and linen, and they might come to attach woolen tzitzit to a linen garment (Beit Yosef). Some say that in this case, we are not concerned, because people are well-versed between hemp and linen, and they only use it through investigation, as I wrote in Yoreh De'ah, section 302. However, wool that comes from overseas resembles silk and could lead to mistakes (Magen Avraham there). Based on this, they explained also the words of our master, the Rema, in section 2, who wrote: "Some say not to make tzitzit out of linen at all, even with other types of materials. And that is the custom." Until here is his language, indicating the reason that was explained. These matters are perplexing, and it is clear that he intended the opinions we have explained. And what he wrote "even with other types of materials," this is its explanation: not only with a linen garment, which according to Rabbeinu Tam is completely forbidden as explained, but even with other types of materials one must be concerned for the opinion that it requires specifically together.

Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote in section 4: If one attached to a garment of other materials some fringes of the same material, and some of wool or linen, there is a doubt concerning it. Thus far is his language. And the doubt is that there is neither the "corner of the same material as the corner," nor wool or linen. And some have questioned: this doubt applies if the obligation of other garments is from the Torah, but Rabbeinu Beit Yosef ruled that they are rabbinic (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 5). However, this is not difficult at all, for besides the fact that it can be said that whatever the rabbis instituted, they did so in the manner of the Torah, and I have seen someone who explained it this way (the Gaon Rabbi Yitzchak of Bialystok), nevertheless, there is no need for this, as we have already explained in section 15 that in the Gemara it is more straightforward if other garments are rabbinic, that they are exempt either with their own kind or with wool and linen. See there. Consequently, with both together, the matter is not as simple.

And the conclusion of the law is written by our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch in Section 6: There are those who say that one should not make a tallit of linen. And even though the law is not like this, a God-fearing person fulfills all opinions and makes a tallit of wool, which is certainly obligated in tzitzit from the Torah without any doubt. However, if it is only possible to have a tallit of linen – it is better to make a tallit of linen and tzitzit of linen than to nullify the mitzvah of tzitzit. Thus far their language. And if one makes a tallit from other materials – he should make tzitzit of wool. And if he only has tzitzit of linen – he should make them of linen. And even with a silk tallit, the concern explained in Section 23 does not apply to us, as we do not have wool that resembles silk. (The Magen Avraham in Subsection 8 wrote that with a linen tallit – one should make corners of leather and put wool tzitzit on them, see there. However, this is a heavy ordinance, and it is possible to come to complications, and it is not the custom. Also, the Elyah Rabbah and the Tvuat Shor dismissed this, see there, as written in Shaarei Teshuvah.)

Rambam, of blessed memory, ruled that the white threads of tzitzit, and according to our custom where they are all white, must match the appearance of the tallit. And this is his wording at the end of Chapter 2: "A tallit that is entirely red, or green, or any other color – its white threads should be of the same color. If it is green, the threads should be green; if it is red, the threads should be red. If it is entirely sky-blue, the white threads should be of other colors except black, because it looks like sky-blue..." until here is his wording. And this is explained in Menachot (41b). And the Tosafot there are puzzled by this, as Rava questions at the beginning of the chapter "Techelet": Does color matter? And they answered that this is a rabbinic decree because of "This is my God and I will beautify Him" (Exodus 15:2), see there. And the Raavad explained it differently. In my humble opinion, it appears that specifically Rava, who holds that the obligation for other garments is from the Torah, and derives "of the same kind as the wing" regarding the essence of the tzitzit as explained – properly questions: Does color matter? But Rambam ruled not like Rava, and properly derives "of the same kind as the wing" regarding the color. And so the Gemara there holds, requiring the color to be the same as the tallit. And the Tur brought that Rabbi Yitzchak disagrees with this. And so wrote the Rashba in a responsum that the custom is not in accordance with Rambam (Part Three, Siman 280), and so wrote the Terumat HaDeshen in Siman 46. And this is what our teacher the Rema wrote on the words of our teacher the Beit Yosef in Section 5, who wrote: Some say that the tzitzit must be made of the same color as the tallit. And the meticulous ones practice this way. Until here is his wording. He wrote that the Ashkenazim are not accustomed to make the tzitzit except white even for colored garments, and there is no need to change. Until here is his wording, and so is the simple custom. However, certainly it is better that the tallit also be white to fulfill the opinion of Rambam, of blessed memory, and so many of the righteous and complete practice. (And what we make at the edge of the tallit the appearance of the sky and call it "Techelet" – it is only for adornment. And its essence is white as is known.)

Only wool from sheep and rams is called "wool." But not wool from camels, rabbits, goat hair, or similar materials. If sheep's wool is mixed with other types, we follow the majority, as I have written in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 298 (Magen Avraham, section 1). It has already been clarified that wool from a sheep that is the offspring of a goat is invalid for tzitzit, and therefore it only exempts its own kind (ibid.). A garment where the warp is wool and the weft is silk, or vice versa, cannot be rectified according to those who hold that for other materials, the tzitzit must be both wool and linen together, as I have written in section 22. In this case, it is not applicable to follow the majority since each material is distinct and not nullified. This is not similar to mixing them together (ibid., section 4). It is written that in Ashkenaz, they are stringent about this (ibid.), but according to most of our Rabbis, it is permissible to make tzitzit from wool since this fulfills the requirement even for other garments, as has been clarified. If the composition is linen with other materials, it is necessary to make tzitzit from linen, relying on the opinion of Rashi, the Rif, and the Rambam, as has been clarified.

And behold, we have explained with the help of Heaven all the opinions. The preferred way is to make a tallit and tzitzit of wool. At the very least, if they are made of other materials, they should be white and not of another color. Also, the stitching should be with white threads, and the atarah (decorative collar) should be of white silk. This is what Maharshal wrote, and this is the practice that should be followed. However, after the fact, one can rely on the opinions of our sages that were explained and not be exempt from the mitzvah of tzitzit, which is equivalent to all the commandments. Its reward is very great, whether with a large tallit or a small tallit, and one should not cast off the yoke of the Kingdom of Heaven from his neck all day long. May it be pleasant for the listener, and may a good blessing come upon him. Amen.

It is written: "You shall make tassels on the four corners of your garment with which you cover yourself" – four corners and not three. Or perhaps it means four and not five? The Talmud teaches: "with which you cover yourself" (Zevachim 18b). This is an inclusion to include a garment with five corners, as a three-cornered garment is not suitable for covering the body, because any triangular shape is pointed. To exclude, anything more than four is considered as four, since it has four corners and is suitable for covering the body. And the same applies to a garment with six corners or more. And even though there is another Baraita that excludes a garment with five corners, and it also appears that way in the Sifrei, nevertheless, most of our Rabbis have ruled that a garment with five corners is obligated. Their reasoning seems to me to be because in Menachot (43b), where the main laws of tzitzit are discussed, only this Baraita is brought, see there. And this is how we rule, and so it is ruled in the Tur and Shulchan Aruch. (And Rabbi Eliezer of Metz and the Rash ruled according to the other Baraita, see Beit Yosef and Bach. And it is proper to also fulfill their opinion.)

Even though a tallit with five corners is obligated in tzitzit, nevertheless, it is forbidden to make more than four tzitzit, and one should place them on the most distant corners. If one makes five tzitzit, they violate the prohibition of "bal tosif" (adding to the commandments). The reason is that since all four tzitzit are considered one commandment, the Holy One, Blessed be He, commanded that this is the mitzvah: four tzitzit, no more. This reason is explicitly stated at the end of the chapter "Hakomets Rabba" (Menachot 37b), where it says: "A garment with five (corners) is the subject of their dispute." Rashi explains that according to Rabbi Yehuda, since there are four separate mitzvot, one would put five tzitzit, but according to the Rabbis, only four. And we follow the opinion of the Rabbis.

I am astonished at the Taz in Subsection 1, who provided a reason from his own understanding, which has no basis, see there. I am puzzled by him: Why did he not mention the words of the Rosh, which are brought in the Beit Yosef, that this is the intention of the Sifrei—to not make more than four tzitzit? However, we have written the reason that is in the Gemara. Pay attention and you will find it easy to understand.

If it has four corners, and one corner is cut diagonally and made into two, it becomes a garment with five corners and is obligated [in tzitzit]. Similarly, if two corners are cut, it becomes a garment with six corners and is obligated [in tzitzit]. We do not say that since his intention was to nullify it from being a four-cornered garment by cutting the corner, his intention should be effective. This is not so, because in the end, it is a garment with five corners. (This is what should be said, for if not, what significance is there in this? And this is implied in Rashi at the end of the chapter "HaKometz Rabba," beginning with "Lo," see there. Analyze this and you will find it easy.)

It is a simple matter that when we said that if one cuts one corner diagonally, it becomes a five-cornered garment and is obligated in tzitzit – this applies when part of the corner is cut. But if one cuts half of the garment diagonally, each of the halves becomes three-cornered, as is evident. For in any rectangle, when it is cut into two equal parts diagonally, each part will have three projections. However, when part of the corner is cut, the remaining part becomes five-cornered. The same law applies if the garment initially had three corners, and part of one corner is cut diagonally – it becomes four-cornered and is obligated in tzitzit. Yet, in this case, some distance is required, for it is not reasonable to say that cutting a small part diagonally near the corner makes it considered as two corners. It seems to me that one must cut at least a tefach (handbreadth). Or it is possible that three fingerbreadths might suffice, because in the context of impurity, three by three is considered significant. This requires further examination. And it is clear that this applies specifically when the corner is cut equally diagonally. But if it is cut in a circular manner, making the corner rounded – it is exempt from tzitzit, as Rabbeinu the Beit Yosef wrote in section 9: the corners need to be squared and not rounded. This is his language. And it seems to me also that some length is required, for it is not reasonable to say that a small circular cut exempts from tzitzit. It appears to me that in this case, three tefachim are required, meaning that the circumference of the circle should be three tefachim. (And simply tearing is not like cutting, see Pri Megadim. And cutting in a manner of four is like diagonally, as the Mishnah Berurah wrote. And see in Mordechai, who wrote that there needs to be a separation between the corners, which is as I have written.)

The Rambam wrote in the first chapter, law 17: "One does not fold the tallit in two and place tzitzit on its four corners while it is folded, unless it is sewn together when folded, even on one side." Thus is his language. The Tur wrote regarding this that from the language of the Rosh, it seems that it is obligated [to have tzitzit] even if it is not sewn at all. Thus is his language. His intention is that it is obligated in the four corners as it is when spread out (as the Rabbis say in Menachot 41a, disagreeing with Rabbi Shimon who exempts). And even though from the words of the Rambam it is not clarified except that one does not make [tzitzit] on the fold, nevertheless it implies to the Tur that if the Rambam held like the Rosh, he should have clarified this. Therefore, it seems to him that the Rambam rules like Rabbi Shimon there, who exempts because the tallit is not suitable for him when it is spread out. And so wrote the Nimukei Yosef, see there. And our master the Beit Yosef in his great work holds that even according to Rabbi Shimon, it is obligated in the four spread corners, and also the Rosh holds this, see there. But our master the Rema in his work Darkei Moshe refuted him, because the language "Rabbi Shimon exempts" implies a complete exemption. And see there that his words are not entirely clear. Nevertheless, he agreed in practice as well, that on its spread corners it is obligated in tzitzit, see there.

The words in Shulchan Aruch, Section 6, follow a different path. Our master, the Beit Yosef, copied the words of the Rambam, and he wrote on this that one must attach tzitzit to the four plain corners. Afterwards, he wrote: "And there are those who say that one is obligated even without sewing. It is good to make tzitzit for it, but not to recite a blessing on it." Thus far his words, and his intention is that according to the "some say," it is obligated on its four folded corners. They interpret according to the Rabbis that this is their intention and they ruled according to the Rabbis. They hold that what the Tur wrote, that the Rosh would obligate even without sewing, refers to its folded corners, not as we explained in the previous section. But this is strange, because since it is explicitly mentioned in the Gemara there that the Amoraim hold that one should not make tzitzit on the four folded corners, see there – if so, even though the plain meaning of the Baraita implies that the Rabbis obligate on the folded [corners], nevertheless, since the Amoraim rejected it, how can one rule like this? The Rif and the Rosh quoted the words of the Baraita and the words of the Amoraim without writing anything, see there. And the Nimukei Yosef ruled explicitly to the contrary, as did the Rambam. If so, where do we get that the Rosh disagrees on this? And if it is because of the words of the Tur, it is better to strain his words a bit and say that his intention is on the plain corners, as I wrote in the previous section. He holds that according to the Rambam even the plain corners are exempt, as the Nimukei Yosef wrote. But to say something against the ruling of the Amoraim is a surprising matter. It requires great examination. (Furthermore: the main point is missing, and he should have explained that the obligation is on the folded corners. Also, the Magen Avraham, Section 7, questioned: how can one satisfy all opinions, since according to the Rambam the obligation is on the plain corners, and according to the Rosh on the folded ones? See there. Therefore, it appears in my humble opinion that there is an error here, and the first gloss was printed in error. This also seems from the Levush, who did not bring it. The intention of the "some say" is on the plain corners, and this is also implied by the Taz, Section 8, for if not, his words are not understandable? See there. According to this, everything fits well, as I wrote in the previous section. And what the Taz and the Magen Avraham differentiated between the interpretation of the Nimukei Yosef and that of Rashi, see Taz, Section 7. The Magen Avraham there is not conclusive, see there well. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

And that which they wrote "unless one sews it entirely, even from one side," it seems that the explanation is: sewing it entirely from the top of the garment to its bottom, but all only on one side, that is, corresponding to the side of the fold, for in this manner it will not spread further, obviously. And I have seen someone who explained that the sewing is on all sides, and that what they wrote "from one side" means a weak sewing (Mishnah Berurah). This is not clear at all, and the language does not imply this. (And so it is explained in the Beit Yosef in his major work, see there.)

Our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in paragraph 3: "If one folded the corners of his tallit and tied or sewed them, making it appear as if they were cut off and the garment has no corners – nevertheless, it is not exempt." This is his exact wording, meaning that if one raised the corners and folded them in a circular manner to nullify them as corners, and if he had cut them in this way – he would certainly be exempt, as I wrote in paragraph 4. However, tying or even sewing them does not help. Even though it has been clarified that folding it into two and sewing it is effective – it is not similar, because there it is customary to fold it into two. But folding the edges is not customary, and therefore we consider it as if it is not folded (as Mordechai wrote). Therefore, in this case, one makes the tzitzit as before because eventually he will return the corners to their original state. According to this, even if he folded them not in a circle but diagonally – the same law applies, and he makes the tzitzit in the original place. But Tosafot (Menachot 37b, s.v. "Hai") wrote that in this manner, sewing is effective, and one places the tzitzit on the fold, see there. And we must say according to their words that in a circular fold, sewing is not effective, and it is not similar to folding it in two because sewing does not help to nullify the mitzvah of tzitzit. Therefore, in a case where the mitzvah is not nullified, such as folding them diagonally, leaving the corners intact – sewing is effective. (This is the intention of the Magen Avraham, paragraph 4, as explained in Machatzit Hashekel. And the criticism of the Arzot HaChaim on him is unnecessary. This law is disputed between Tosafot and Mordechai, and in folding it into two, certainly tying does not help, only sewing. The Mishnah Berurah wrote that if one tucked the edge of the garment inside and sewed it so that the fold is not visible at all, as tailors do – it is certainly effective, see there. And this is correct. Nevertheless, it seems to me that doing so in a circular manner to exempt it from tzitzit – is not effective according to the Tosafot that we explained. Be precise and you will find clarity.)

Leather is not considered a garment, as it is written concerning impurities: "or garment or leather." Therefore, even if it is sewn like a garment, it is still nothing. And our Sages of blessed memory said (Menachot 40a): If the main part is of fabric and its corners are of leather, it is obligated [in tzitzit]. If the main part is of leather and its corners are of fabric, it is exempt. For we follow the main part of the garment and not the corners, even though the tzitzit are attached to the corners, as it is written: "with which you cover yourself" – and the main covering is with the main part of the garment, not with the corners. Similarly, if the main part of the garment is mostly fabric and minority leather, it is obligated in tzitzit. If the main part is mostly leather and minority fabric, it is exempt. And if the leather is the lower part of the garment that is called "undershirt" – we do not follow it, as we always follow the upper part of the garment which is the main part (Magen Avraham, subsection 5). However, when leather is used for reinforcement, such as sewing leather around the holes or at the edges – this is not an issue at all. Not only because it is a minority of the garment, but because anything used for reinforcement is considered like fabric. (And therefore Rashi wrote there: and its corners are of leather which means he cut the corners, see there. And he should have said that the leather is on top, but in this manner it is for reinforcement. And even those who follow the corner in the Gemara, it is nothing. And so wrote the Beit Yosef at the end of Siman 11. And this is the intention of the Magen Avraham at the end of subsection 5, and see Machatzit HaShekel. Be precise and you will find light.)

It is written: "And they shall make for themselves fringes on the corners of their garments." Therefore, when one begins to attach the tzitzit, all four corners of the garment must be complete. However, if they are not complete, such as if the garment has three corners and one attaches three tzitzit, and afterward adds a fourth corner and attaches the fourth tzitzit, all the tzitzit are invalid. They must be undone, and the tzitzit must be removed, and then reattached. This invalidation is referred to in the Gemara as "ta'aseh veloh min ha'asuy" (make, and not from what is already made). This means that the tzitzit should be made when the garment has all four corners, which makes it obligated in tzitzit, and not that the tzitzit be made in an invalid state when the garment was not yet obligated. Similarly, any tzitzit made in an invalid state when attached to the garment, regardless of the type of invalidation, cannot be made valid afterward, since they were made in an invalid state. Many laws regarding this invalidation will be further explained, and the intent is as I have written.

The general principle is: if even one tzitzit was attached improperly, even if only the upper knot was tied improperly and afterwards the four corners were completed, or if the improper element was later removed and this tzitzit and the other three tzitzit were completed – all are invalid. This remains the case until the improperly made tzitzit is removed and remade properly. However, if this was corrected, even if it was corrected after the other three were attached – it is acceptable, as the three were made properly. There are those who invalidate in such a case, but there is no reason for this (Magen Avraham, subsection 6).

If one attaches tzitzit to tzitzit, meaning a garment had valid tzitzit, and he added another four tzitzit to the four corners, Rambam writes in Chapter 1, Law 15: If one attaches tzitzit to tzitzit, if his intention was to nullify the first set, he should untie the first set or cut them off, and it is valid. But if his intention was to add, even if he cuts off one of the two, it is invalid. For when he added, he invalidated them all, and when he untied or cut the additional ones, the remainder was made from what was already done, and its initial making was invalid. Thus far his words. (This ruling is based on his interpretation in Menachot 42b regarding Rabbi Zeira, Rava, and Rav Pappa, as noted by the Beit Yosef and Taz in subsection 9, see there.)

However, the core issue is perplexing: How can the initial tzitzit, which were made properly, be invalidated by adding more tzitzit and thereby transgressing "bal tosif" (the prohibition against adding to the Torah's commandments)? The original tzitzit stand on their own, and this one stands by itself and that one stands by itself, as it is said at the end of the chapter "Hanekhinakin" (Sanhedrin 88b). This is the intention of the Ra'avad in his criticisms, and the commentators did not respond to this at all. But the truth is that the Rambam follows his own reasoning in the seventh chapter of Lulav, that if one adds another etrog or lulav, it is invalid. And there too, the Ra'avad objected for the reason explained. We must say that the Rambam holds that "this one stands alone..." is only in the case of adding a different species, because since it is not of its kind, it does not spoil it when it stands on its own, but not with its own kind. This reasoning is written by the Ran there, and the Mordechai in the name of the Rash in Hilchot Tzitzit (as also written in "Artzot HaChaim"). But indeed, in the case of the lulav, it is written that the Rambam retracted at the end of his life, and held that even with its own kind we say "this one stands alone..." and he commanded to correct there that if one adds, it is not invalid (Kesef Mishneh there). Here, however, we do not find that he retracted. It seems to me in my humble opinion that here he did not retract, because here, in this garment that has two kinds of tzitzit, it is indeed "bal tosif" and they are invalidated. The reasoning of "this one stands alone" is only in the case of a lulav if there is no need for binding, as they do not relate to each other. Similarly, with tzitzit if there is no need for an upper knot according to the Torah, as this reasoning is stated in the Gemara there. But according to what we hold, that an upper knot is needed, and in this garment, he made two kinds of tzitzit, and the Torah said one tzitzit and not two tzitzit, thus the garment is invalid and it is forbidden to wear it. (And "Artzot HaChaim" labored over this in a distant way, see there. To me, it seems as I have written. And I think this is the intention of the Mordechai, see there. Examine carefully and you will find the light.)

However, the Tur wrote: If it had four tzitzit on its four corners, and he made additional ones and cut off the original ones – it is valid with the latter ones. Thus is his language. And even if he intended to add, and all the more so if he cut the latter ones, it is valid with the original ones. And from Rashi there it seems that the original ones are always valid even if he did not cut the latter ones, but nevertheless, they did not rule this way. And these are the words of our Rabbi the Rema in section 6, where our Rabbi the Beit Yosef ruled according to Rambam, and wrote that there are those who permit in all cases and this is the main ruling. And before he cut the original ones – it is invalid in all cases. Thus is his language. And this is the opinion of the Tur, and this is its explanation: And there are those who permit in all cases, whether he cut the original ones and the latter ones remained, or he cut the latter ones and the original ones remained. And whether he intended to nullify or intended to add, there is no difference, for if he only cut one of them – the others are rendered valid. And before he cut one of them – it is invalid in all cases. And that he mentioned "the original ones" because he was referring to cutting these, but there is no practical difference, as I wrote, there is no reason to distinguish between them. (And so wrote the Magen Avraham in subsection 9. And according to Rambam, the original ones are always invalid because they were invalidated by the making of the latter ones, as the Magen Avraham wrote in subsection 8. And the words of the Taz in subsection 9 require further examination.)

And know that the ancients raised significant questions regarding the garments we wear, such as why we do not attach tzitzit to them, for example, our outer garment which has four corners. However, all [corners] are on one side; that is, two corners are near the neck and two are lower down. And it is true that when there is a piece of cloth attached behind it called a collar, even though its ends are squared, nonetheless, since these two corners of the collar do not align with the two corners in front which are lower near the ground, and the collar is higher up – this is not considered a four-cornered garment, as the corners need to be opposite each other (Beit Yosef and Magen Avraham at the end of this section). But without a collar – it would seemingly be obligated in tzitzit. However, our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, wrote at the end of this section, and this is their language: The garments in Egypt called jochas, even though they have four corners, are exempt. And the same applies to the garments of the regions of Ashkenaz and Sefarad, since their corners are not made so that two are in the front and two in the back, aligned opposite each other – they are exempt. This is their language. And even though in the Torah it is written simply "the corners of their garments," nonetheless, their garments were like our tallit, which is called "sudar" in the language of the Gemara, and they would wrap themselves in it. And so it is in the Midrash, that Gabriel proclaimed at the splitting of the Red Sea: Beware of those who carry two tzitzit behind them (see Taz section 10). And even though the Torah had not yet been given, the forefathers observed the Torah before it was given and passed it on to their descendants after them.

And this is an answer regarding the outer garments. But the undergarment called a surdot or frock, which are open in the front and back, and have four corners aligned with each other—why don’t we make tzitzit on them? And they already asked the Rashba about this in his responsa, Siman 434, and this is his language: "What you asked about the garment called a gonilla which is cut in the front and back… it is not called a four-cornered garment unless it is entirely open… but garments that are sewn and connected at the top are not considered a four-cornered garment." And this was the custom… until here is his language. And from its simple meaning, it appears that any garment connected at the top is not considered a four-cornered garment. And so many great authorities have ruled in the days of the Maharik. And the Maharik in Shoresh 149 disagreed with them, saying his intention was specifically when most of the garment is connected. But when most of it is open and a minority is closed—it is obligated in tzitzit. And he wrote that similarly, Rabbi Meir of Rothenburg and the Rash said so, see there.

Based on this, our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in Section 7: Garments that are open at the sides at the bottom and have four corners at the bottom but are closed at the top, if most of it is closed, it is exempt [from the obligation of tzitzit]. If most of it is open, it is obligated [to have tzitzit]. If half is closed and half is open, we rule stringently, and it is obligated in tzitzit, but one does not go out with it on Shabbat. This is his language. And even in a karmelit [a rabbinic public domain], one does not go out with it, for initially, it is forbidden in a case of doubt, even in a rabbinic prohibition (Magen Avraham, subsection 11). And it is obvious that one does not recite a blessing on it (ibid.). And if most of it was closed and one made tzitzit on it, and then he opened it until most of it [became open], the tzitzit are invalid because of "make [the tzitzit] and not from what is made" (ibid., subsection 10). Based on this, one must be careful with those who wear a small tallit that has sleeves, meaning that it is closed at the sides at the top but leaves a space to insert the arms, that most of it should be open, meaning most of the length of the tallit. And the place where the arms are inserted is not counted.

According to this, our modern cloaks, when they are a bit long, are mostly open, and yet we do not attach tzitzit to them. Those who are meticulous sew them at the back. It seems to me that people rely on the straightforward words of the Rashba, which we brought in paragraph 16, that as long as they are connected at the top, it is not considered a garment of four corners. Indeed, the interpretation of the Maharik is puzzling; if he meant specifically when most of it is closed, how did he not mention the main point? It also seems to me that even according to the Beit Yosef, since our garments are completely open in the front, and when the garment is spread out, the four corners are all at the upper and lower edges in the front, and these are exempt because the top is rounded as is known. And these four corners that are in the front and back, when worn, are in the middle of the garment when it is spread out. Thus, it is not considered four corners that require tzitzit, and it follows the law explained in paragraph 5.

It also seems to me to permit based on what is written in the responsa of Maharam of Rothenburg (Siman 287), and this is his language: "And those tallitot that are made in the fashion of a cape, I have heard that these are the tallitot of the pious ones of Ashkenaz. They have four corners, and when one removes it from himself, he spreads it out and covers himself with it. And some say that it is not called ‘tallitot’ except for those like ours, which are made to wrap oneself in and cover oneself, as it is written ‘your covering,’ and we bless ‘to wrap oneself.’ And I am careful not to wear them, to extricate myself from doubt. But those coats that have sleeves are not similar at all, and there is no concern here, for their ‘corner’ is not a corner." This is his language (part of which the Magen Avraham brings in Section 12). He explicitly writes that those that have sleeves, meaning that the hands are dressed in what is called a coat, are certainly exempt from tzitzit. And if so, our modern coats indeed have sleeves. (And according to the ‘some say,’ there is no obligation of tzitzit in a garment worn on the body unless it wraps the body and covers it. Therefore, it is written ‘your covering’ and not ‘your garment.’ And this is only with our tallitot.)

It was taught in the Sifrei, in the section on "Tetzaveh" (Pisqa 234): "Your garment" excludes a sheet. "You shall cover" excludes a rough garment. "With it" excludes a cloak that does not cover the head and the majority of the body. Thus far its wording. And it seems to me that the explanation is as follows: excluding a sheet that is on the bed or used to cover oneself while sleeping, even if one sleeps during the day, because the Torah only obligated [the mitzvah of tzitzit] with regard to an envelopment. Therefore, our quilts which cover the body during sleep are exempt for two reasons: one, because it is a night garment, and second, because it is not a manner of envelopment. And excluding a rough garment because it is a thick garment, as is taught in the fifteenth chapter of Oholot: a rough garment is thick. And it is not considered a garment. And excluding a cloak – there is a cloak that one wraps around the head, as is taught in the twenty-ninth chapter of Kelim. And the Ra'avad explained: a scarf that one wraps around the head, see there. And in Shabbat (9b) it is stated: when he removes his cloak from him. And Rashi explained: his scarf is the first of his garments to be removed. Thus far his wording, implying that it is an outer garment. In any case, we learn from the Sifrei that anything that does not cover the head and the majority of the body is exempt from tzitzit. According to this, our garments are exempt for another reason, since they do not cover the head. This is in line with the opinion of the poskim that without covering the head one is not obligated in tzitzit, as I wrote in Siman 8, section 4, see there. And there we brought in the name of the Nimukei Yosef that it is not so, see there. But from this Sifrei, it seems so, and it requires investigation. However, according to these opinions, another exemption is added to our garments.

Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in paragraph 8: If a cape that is open in a manner that it has four corners, and they attach a string (ashtringa) to make it closed in order to exempt it from tzitzit - this correction does not help unless it is fixed from half its length and below at least, and also that it is fixed below the belt so that most of the closed part is visible to the eyes. For if not, it will be forbidden due to the appearance (of being a four-cornered garment requiring tzitzit). These are his words. 

And it appears that the "ashtringa" is a permanent connection that connects side to side always, because if it is just loops that they tie and untie always - this is not considered closure. And this that he wrote "from half its length and below" - is not precise, and his intention is: a little more, for we need the majority closed. However, what he wrote that it should be fixed below the belt - is not understood, because since it is fixed from half its length and below, by itself it is below the belt. Therefore, one must say that his intention "from half its length and below" means from above until a bit below half its length, so that the majority is closed. And for this he said that if the belt is below this measure - you need to extend the astringa below the belt, so that everyone sees the closure. 

(The connection of hooks is not considered a connection unless they are very bent. And even though the Magen Avraham in paragraph 12 was concerned about the appearance, even with just hooks the later authorities disagreed with him. And it appears that even when it is connected securely by sewing - it needs to extend also below the belt. Some are uncertain about this, but it appears to me as I have written.)

He also wrote: A mitznefet (turban) is exempt. Even those from the western countries, whose two ends are thrown over their shoulders and bodies, even though it covers the head and most of the body, it is exempt because its primary purpose is to cover the head. For the Torah said "your garment," and not a head covering. And a sudar that is placed on the neck in the Kingdom of Israel, which is called in Arabic 'shayd,' and also a 'boka' that was placed on the shoulders in Spain—they are exempt. So far his words. Because their primary use is not for the benefit of covering but for usage, such as to wrap money in (Beit Yosef). And silk scarves that are folded and carried on the neck are exempt, even if they have four corners, since they serve only for the neck and not for the body. However, if one wraps their body in a large scarf and goes out to the market with it—they are obligated in tzitzit. Therefore, one should make one corner rounded, as it has already been explained that the corners need to be squared and not rounded. But there needs to be some extension in the rounding of at least three handbreadths in the circumference of the round part, for it is unreasonable to say that a slight rounding at its edge would nullify its status as a corner, as I have written at the end of section 4.

The threads of the tzitzit need to be spun and twisted, meaning that several fine threads are twisted together to form a single thread. As it is stated in the Sifrei: "A thread of tekhelet that is spun and twisted"—I only know this for tekhelet; how do I know this for white? You derive it thus: Since the Torah says to give tekhelet and to give white, just as tekhelet is spun and twisted, so too white must be spun and twisted. This is the language of the Sifrei. The term "thread" implies that several threads are twisted together, as it is a term of connection, as it is written: "Wrestlings of God have I wrestled with my sister." There is no fixed measure for the twisting; some twist four together, and some do eight for beautification. However, two are essential, and two suffice since they are twisted. (And in the priestly garments, their thread was sixfold in six and twisted eightfold, as mentioned at the end of the seventh chapter of Yoma. Perhaps because of this, they hold eightfold for beautification, due to the term "twisted" in the Sifrei. Be precise and you will find ease.)

It appears from the language of the Sifrei that twisted and spun threads have the same law. If so, just as spun threads require oiling (as will be explained), and if not, they are invalid — so too with twisted threads. Some of the poskim (halachic authorities) have written this (Nimukei Yosef and Magen Avraham section 3). However, Rambam did not require twisted threads at all in tzitzit. This is his language in the first chapter, law 10: Whether white threads or blue threads, if one wishes to make them twisted — he may. Even if the thread is doubled into eight threads, and twisted until it becomes a single cord — it is still considered just one thread. End of his language. It appears to me from his language that he interprets the Sifrei as permitting even twisted threads. Meaning: do not say there are many more threads than the required measure, as this is not so, for they are all considered one thread. And although in Eruvin (96b) it is clearly implied that tzitzit threads are twisted, see there — indeed this is so, they would do this for enhancement but not out of obligation (see Beit Yosef). It seems to me that there is evidence for his words from Yoma (72a), where it is expounded: "And cut cords," a cord is one, cords are two — altogether four. Meaning: "cord" — one, "cords" — two, and when they are cut — they make four. It is implied that a cord is just one and not twisted, for regarding this, it is said there, see there. (And the Raavad challenged him. His response to the sages of Lunel, brought by the Kesef Mishneh, is not satisfactory at all, and therefore his words were rejected. But according to what I have written, it fits well. Be precise and you will find ease.)

Most of the authorities disagree with him and hold that twisting the threads is essential. However, regarding the requirement of "for its sake," it also appears from the language of the Tur that only the spinning must be done for the sake of the mitzvah and not the twisting, as he wrote: "And they should be spun for the sake of tzitzit. But if they were not spun for its sake – they are invalid. And they must be twisted." This is his language. It is explicitly implied that twisting does not invalidate if not done for the sake of the mitzvah. Moreover, it seems more logical that since twisting comes after spinning, and since he spun each thread for the sake of the mitzvah, the twisting is automatically considered as "for its sake," since it is done with the original intent in mind. Some later authorities are lenient after the fact even if there was no twisting at all (Pri Megadim in the name of N"TZ, Eliyah Rabbah, and Shaarei Teshuva, subsection 2). This requires further study, as most authorities disagree on this matter. However, it is certain that if they were not twisted for the sake of the mitzvah, one can definitely rely on the reasoning mentioned above.

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote in Section 1 that there are those who are stringent even regarding combing the wool for its sake (i.e., with intent for the mitzvah). And the custom is to be lenient regarding combing. Thus far his words. And certainly, even those who are stringent do not intend this as an essential law, as is evident from the words of the Mordechai, who wrote: Mahar"m wrote that one should be stringent to comb the wool for tzitzit for its sake, see there – thus he wrote it as a mere stringency. For by law it is certainly not required, since combing is only to remove the impurities. And the Maharal of Prague said that since it is written "You shall make twisted cords for yourself" next to "You shall not wear Shaatnez" (a mixture of wool and linen), and Shaatnez is combed, spun, and woven – therefore, also in combing, it must be done "for its sake" (for the sake of the mitzvah) (Drisha). And therefore, it is certainly proper to be cautious about this.

How is the spinning for the sake of the mitzvah performed? One should state at the beginning of the spinning that it is for the sake of tzitzit. If a woman is spinning, he should say to her: "Spin for me tzitzit for a tallit." All the more so if she herself states this. If one said this, even if the spinning was not completed at that moment but was left for the next day, we say that the completion is based on the initial intention. However, if it was only said at the end or the middle of the spinning, it is invalid. We do not say in this case that the end proves the beginning, because there is no distinctive act here, only spinning as usual, so how can we say that his intention was for the sake of tzitzit without any expression of intent at the time of the act? We have already explained in Yoreh De'ah, Chapter 271, Paragraph 11, that for matters of spirituality such as designating for holiness, the primary requirement is at the beginning of the act. Refer there. And it has been explained there that one of the early authorities was uncertain whether in all matters requiring intent, verbal declaration is specifically needed or if mere thought suffices. From the language of the Rosh there, it is clearly implied that it is effective, as he wrote: "It is good to express it with one's lips." Refer there.

Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote in paragraph 2: "A gentile weaver, with a Jew standing over him and instructing him to weave for the sake of the mitzvah – according to the Rambam, it is invalid; according to the Rosh, it is valid." These are his words. And Rabbeinu Ramah wrote: "And the custom is that the Jew assists a little, as it is stated later in Siman 32 and in Yoreh De'ah Siman 271 regarding tefillin and a Torah scroll." These are his words. 

But I am puzzled by this: what similarity is there to processing leather for the sake of the mitzvah? For with leather, when the Jew assists a little in the processing and says he is doing it for the sake of the mitzvah – then this leather is considered processed for the sake of the mitzvah. But in the weaving of tzitzit, how does a little assistance help for what will be woven afterwards? Since, according to the Rambam, the gentile works with his own intention, what he weaves afterward is not for the sake of the mitzvah. Even according to the Rosh, there is no proof from processing, which takes a short time and is done with the Jew’s intention, to weaving, which takes a long time. Therefore, in my humble opinion, it is difficult to rely on this ruling, and I have also found that great authorities questioned this ruling. 

And if a deaf-mute, an imbecile, or a minor wove – it is invalid. But if a Jew stands over them and instructs them to do it for the sake of the mitzvah – it is valid. (The Magen Avraham in small paragraph 2 wrote that it depends on the dispute in Siman 600, and there we are lenient as the Gra wrote in his annotations. And so it is ruled there in the Shulchan Aruch.)

And since tzitzit must specifically be made for their own sake, therefore, if one finds threads in the market, even if they are spun and cut off, they are invalid. We do not say that they were certainly made for the sake of tzitzit, for perhaps they were made just as general threads. This is how Rambam ruled in the second chapter regarding techelet. However, he later retracted and ruled that spun and cut threads are valid, as I have written above in Siman 9, Se'if 11, see there. Nevertheless, regarding white threads, they should not be validated. Specifically for techelet, we can say that one would not go to great lengths unless it was for the sake of tzitzit, but for white, it is forbidden. So wrote Rabbeinu Beit Yosef in his great book at the end of Siman 20, see there. (And this is the intention of the Magen Avraham in Se'if Katan 1. He was brief as usual, see there.)

It has already been explained that twisting is required. Therefore, if the threads unravel from their twisting, if they were originally twisted such that each thread was made of two thin threads and all eight threads unraveled and became sixteen, they are invalid because the twisting is nullified. This is unless we rely on the Rambam, who holds that twisting is not essential. If there remains enough of the original twisting to form a knot, they are certainly valid. And even though it will be explained in Siman 12 that if all the threads were cut, some say that having enough for a knot is not effective, in this case we can rely on the Rambam's opinion that twisting is not essential (Magen Avraham, subsection 4). Similarly, if only one thread unraveled from its twisting, it is not a concern. Also, if they were twisted from three or four thin threads or more, and they unraveled a bit, there is also no concern, for in any case, there will still remain twisted threads. There is no issue of "adding to the mitzvah" by increasing the number of threads, as this was not done intentionally, and even now there is no intention for this. I have seen someone write that if one retwists them, it constitutes "making, and not from what was made" and they are invalid (Mishnah Berurah). However, I say that in this case we can certainly rely on the Rambam that they are not invalid at all for this. And our teacher, the Rema, wrote that initially it is good to tie the threads below. This is his language: "And with this, they will not unravel from their twisting." This does not add to the knots, for it is evident that his intention is not for the sake of a knot but to prevent them from unraveling. See Section 18.

The mitzvah of tzitzit involves taking four long threads and inserting them into the corner of the tallit. When they are pulled through the hole in the corner, there will be eight threads, and they should be tied with two knots near the corner. After that, one of the eight threads, which is made longer than the others, is wound around the remaining seven threads for a portion of its length. This winding is called "gedil," which means that they are bundled together. The rest of the threads from the gedil downwards are called "ptil," as ptil refers to when each thread is separate, as Onkelos translated "ptil techelet" as "a thread of blue." The length of the gedil and the ptil will be clarified later. This procedure is done for each of the four corners. When there was techelet, there were two white threads, either of wool or linen, and two threads of techelet. According to the Rambam, there were three white threads and one techelet thread, which were wound together. Now that we do not have techelet, all four threads are white. This is the essence of tzitzit.

And all this is explained in the Torah, as it is written: "You shall make twisted cords for yourself, on the four corners of your garment..." "Gedil" (twisted cord) - two, "Gedilim" (twisted cords) - four. Make a twisted cord and intertwine it from within (Yevamot 5b), for less than two cannot be called "Gedil," as there is no connection with less than two. And it is written: "Gedilim" - thus, there are four threads. And it is written: "On the four corners of your garment" - thus, on each corner, there are four threads. And when they are folded, it becomes eight. And the Torah said: make a twisted cord and intertwine it from within, so that they should hang as threads, meaning cords. One should not make the entire thing a twisted cord, but part twisted cord and part free-hanging (Rashi). This is the thread mentioned in the section of Tzitzit. From this, it is clear that part of the threads should be twisted and part should be free-hanging.
