According to Torah law, there is no requirement for how much should be twisted and how much should be free-hanging. And so our Sages said in Menachot (39a): If the majority is twisted, it is valid. Conversely, even if only one section is twisted, it is valid. However, the beauty of the Tzitzit is that one-third should be twisted and two-thirds should be free-hanging. (And the Gemara said: the beauty of the Techelet, see there. And now it is the beauty of the white, of course.)

And what is the length of the threads when they are doubled? Our Sages, of blessed memory, said in Menachot (41b): Four fingerbreadths in the thumb. That is, four thumb-widths. And in width: the space of the thumb. Rashi explained that this refers to the hanging branch, meaning the thread. And since the braid is a third, the braid must be two thumb-widths, making a total of six thumb-widths. The Rambam explained in the first chapter that this refers to the total, with the braid and the branch together being only four thumb-widths, of which two-thirds are the branch and one-third is the braid. But Rabbeinu Tam explained that it refers to the braid, which should be four thumb-widths and the branch eight, making a total of twelve thumb-widths. Many of the halachic authorities agreed with his interpretation, and so is the custom. 

Know that all this measurement is aside from the part that lies on the corner, but below the corner, this measurement is required. It is permitted to be longer than this measurement. There is no mitzvah in this, and it is permissible to cut the excess even after the tzitzit have been made, as there is no issue of "You shall make and not from what is already made" because there is no invalidation in this. Thus, our Sages, of blessed memory, said there: There is no upper limit for them. But there is a minimum limit, and that is the measurement explained. (And what is said there: tzitzit is only a little – needs some examination. Even though the Tosafot wrote in Shabbat 63b, beginning with "Weaving" that even a little has some minimum measure, see there – nevertheless, how can one say a little about a length of many thumb-widths? And Rashi explained that it refers to remnants, and it needs examination – for this too has a measure for tying. Moreover, if so, why did the Gemara offer another explanation? The thumb is measured by an average person. Examine and you will find it easy.) (And this is like the length of two barley grains.)

And it has already been explained that one should make one long thread to wrap around the "gedil" (braid). If he does not have a long thread, he should wrap a little from one thread, and then from another thread, and so on. He should not wrap from one thread alone, because if so, this thread will be greatly shortened. In the time when the techelet (blue dye) was used, they would wrap some wrappings with techelet and some with white, as explained in the Rambam. (And note that in all of our printed Shulchan Aruch, in section 4 after the word "gedil," there is a gloss, which reads: this refers to the part of the tzitzit that is not woven. End of quote. This has no meaning. The truth is that a mistake occurred, and it should be stated: that it is made like a weave. Meaning: the "gedil" is made like a weave through the wrapping of the thread around it. And because in the Shulchan Aruch the term "gedil" has not yet been explained, and also in section 11 "gedil" is used with a different intention, see there – therefore it was explained.)

It is written, "You shall make twisted cords for yourself on the four corners..." and it is also written, "And they shall put on the fringe of each corner." From this, it is clear that the tzitzit must be attached to the corner of the garment and not in the middle of the garment. And "corner" does not refer to anything above three thumb-breadths from the edge of the garment. Therefore, care must be taken not to make the holes through which the tzitzit threads are inserted higher than three thumb-breadths. This requirement must be adhered to even post facto, because it would not be considered a "corner." If, after making them above this measurement, one were to cut the edge of the garment from below until they fall within the three-thumb-breadth range, they are invalid due to the principle of "you shall make, and not from what is already made" (Magen Avraham, Subsection 15). Even if only one tzitzit is made above the three-thumb-breadth limit, it is invalid. One must untie the tzitzit and make the hole below the three-thumb-breadth limit, and then attach the tzitzit.

Just as it is forbidden to make [the tzitzit] higher than three [fingerbreadths], similarly, one should not place them at the very edge of the corner, as it is written "on" the corner and not "below" the corner. And "on" the corner is defined as the measure from the thumb joint, which is the middle until the end of the entire nail. And this too is essential even after the fact (b'dieved), except that there is a leniency if at the time of making [the tzitzit] it was above the thumb joint as I have written, and afterward it tore within the hole until the tzitzit hangs below the thumb joint – it is valid (Gemara Menachot 42a). For the Torah only insists on the time of making, as it is written: "And they shall make for themselves fringes on the corners..." and "You shall make twisted cords for yourself on the four corners...". After the making – we are not concerned. And this law is not applicable except for below the thumb joint and not above three fingerbreadths, as the tzitzit does not rise higher, obviously. Likewise, if it was made above the thumb joint, and the warp threads of the garment were torn until it is now below the thumb joint – it is also valid for the same reason explained, that the requirement is only at the time of making. Therefore, it is customary to make a hem around the hole, that is, to sew the edge nicely so that it does not tear there and become less than the required measure. And although there is no invalidity in this as I have written, nonetheless, it is not an enhancement. Similarly, it is customary to make a hem at the edge of the garment below so that the warp threads do not tear. And know that the three fingerbreadths and the thumb joint are measured from the edge of the garment straightforwardly, not from the corner diagonally.

The opinion of the Tur is that this measurement applies only to the length of the tallit and not to its width, for in the width of the garment, one can place the tzitzit even close to its edge. However, there are great authorities who wrote that these measurements are also required for the width (see Beit Yosef), and so our teacher the Beit Yosef ruled in section 10, see there. The length refers to the width of a person, as this is the wrapping around the body. This is the length, and the width corresponds to a person’s height (Magen Avraham, subsection 16). It appears to me that this applies to a large tallit, which is used for wrapping, but for a small tallit, the length would be according to a person's height and the width according to their width. However, in terms of the law, there is no difference since this measurement applies both to the length and the width, and the measure of a thumb's knot is close to two thumbs (Gra”z).

The custom of those who make tallitot (prayer shawls) is to leave on its edge a border without warp, which in our language is called shlyak, and in the language of the ancients is called orilayu. This is not considered part of the garment, and even if it is very wide, one should not attach the tzitzit (fringes) to it. If one did attach the tzitzit to it, the tallit is invalid, as it is written, "on the corners of their garments," and this is not part of the garment. Nevertheless, since it is the way of weavers to do so, it is considered for this purpose as part of the garment to be included in the calculation of the three thumb-widths and the tying of a thumb-width, as long as the hole is within the garment. There is no clear permission in this matter, and therefore it is better that the tying of a thumb-width be done without it, and it should also be considered in the calculation of the three thumb-widths. If it is very wide, it should be completely cut off at the corners. This is indeed our custom, and in this way, we avoid all doubt. Similarly, where there are protrusions from the tallit, whether warp without weft or weft without warp, these should be completely cut off at the corners. (See Magen Avraham, subsection 17, and Taz, subsection 12. In Shulchan Aruch, subsection 11, this is called a "fringe," see there. I do not know the reason.)

It has already been explained that the number of threads in each corner of the tzitzit is four doubled, which makes eight. If additional threads are added, it is invalid. If the threads are not yet cut into four, one should be careful to initially cut them into four threads before inserting them into the hole of the corner, and then insert them into the corner and fold them to make eight. However, if they were inserted before being cut, it is not invalid, since there is not yet a completed act of tzitzit. Nevertheless, one should be careful that if they were inserted into the hole without being cut, they should be cut into eight before making the knot and before the wrappings. If even one section of the wrappings, which is the part of the wrappings between one knot and another, was wrapped and tied even with one knot, they become invalid even if they are cut afterward, because of "you shall make and not from what is made," since they were made in an invalid state. Also, if they were not wrapped at all but were tied with two knots, they are invalid because of "you shall make and not from what is made." (For those who make two holes, as will be explained, it is invalid even with one knot that can hold.)

The eight strings should be divided by hand into four on this side and four on that side, and then tied twice, one knot on top of the other. Afterward, the long string should be wound around the seven strings with a few windings, and tied twice, one knot on top of the other. This process of winding and tying should be repeated until five double knots and four sections in between are completed, with the sections filled with windings. By law, there is no fixed measure for the windings and knots. Even if most of the strings were wound, or only one section was wound, it is valid. However, if the entire string is wound, it is invalid because it lacks a tassel. For beautification and enhancement of the mitzvah, it should be one-third wound and two-thirds tassel, meaning the wound part should be four thumb-breadths and the tassel part eight thumb-breadths, according to the opinion of Rabbeinu Tam as explained in section 11. The custom is to wind seven complete windings in the first section, eight in the second, eleven in the third, and thirteen in the fourth, corresponding to the numerical value of "Hashem Echad" (the Lord is One). It is proper that the space between each knot should be the width of a thumb, and that all the sections should be equal. Therefore, in the first section, the windings should be spaced slightly apart, and in the fourth section, they should be closely spaced to make them equal. It has already been explained that some people tie each string at its end to prevent the twist from unraveling. This is not considered adding to the knots. However, some are particular about not adding and do not do this (Levush and Magen Avraham, subsection 23). This is also our custom, as our strings are well twisted and do not unravel.

The tzitzit should not be hung down towards the ground, but rather on the side of the corner, as it is stated: "on the corners of their garments" – that it should hang on the corner (and this is the intention of the Shulchan Aruch in section 15). Therefore, it is proper when tying the upper knot – to tie it close to the side of the corner, so that it will hold there and not fall down. And even though by doing so the corner may shrink a little and will not have the length of a thumb's width – it does not matter, because the shrinking is insignificant, as long as when it is spread out it has the required measurement, as we consider it based on its spread-out state. And similarly, if it is above three thumb-widths – it is invalid even though it is shrunk and does not have three thumb-widths, but since when it is spread out it is invalid. And know that some say not to put anything in the holes of the tallit where the tzitzit are inserted, so that it should not be "above and above." And some permit it, and this is the custom. And even sewing them with leather – is permitted, since this is done only for reinforcement. And there should be no doubt about this at all.

The common custom is to make one hole in the tallit, as is explained by all the decisors. Some make two holes side by side like the letter "Yud," inserting through one and exiting through the other. This is the opinion of the Itur. The reason is that otherwise, it might appear as though there are eight fringes, since the fringes appear on both sides. Rabbi Yosef Karo wrote in his major work that one who wishes to be stringent with himself and do so is not among those who are stringent but rather among those who are perplexing, and it appears as arrogance. Thus far his words. This means that, according to all the decisors, there is no concern for this issue, as what does it matter if they appear as eight since that is how they are made? Furthermore, it appears as arrogance to fulfill the obligation according to a singular opinion. In truth, this opinion is wondrous, for the Gemara (Menachot 42b) states that it should hang over the corner, and with two holes, it would not hang over the corner, obviously. And one is forced to interpret that it does not mean at the edge of the corner but rather that it should be raised above the end of the corner by a thumb's breadth. The language clearly implies "at the edge of the corner," for if not, it should have said it should be raised above the end of the corner. Additionally, some have questioned that according to Rambam regarding mixtures (kilayim), it would be obligatory even without a knot in such a manner, as he wrote in the tenth chapter of Kilayim. And the Gemara (Menachot 39a) clearly explains that there is no issue of mixtures in tzitzit until it is doubled twice, meaning two knots. Even according to the Tur in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 300, who disagrees with Rambam, he still agrees that with one doubling, it is obligatory in such a manner (Magen Avraham, Siman 13). Nevertheless, some say that for a small tallit, which is worn under the clothes and has no issue of arrogance, it is proper to do so (Bach). Similarly, the Pri Etz Chaim, Shaar HaTzitzit, Chapter 1, writes that the Ari z"l practiced this way, see there. However, one of the great Sephardic sages (the Chida in Birkei Yosef) testified in the name of Rabbi Chaim Vital, who was a prominent student of the Ari z"l, that he did not practice this way. Especially since it is not only because of the concern of arrogance but there is an essential halachic concern. Therefore, we have never practiced this way. There are individual people who do so, and it requires further investigation. (The Pri Etz Chaim there also writes that when dividing the winding of the four strings from the other four, they should remain that way until the end of their making: these four on this side and those four on that side, see there. It is proper to be cautious about this.)

It is a mitzvah to make tzitzit from good and choice wool, due to the principle of "This is my God and I will glorify Him." However, if they are made from completely inferior materials, from which no garment is typically made, they are entirely invalid, as this is not considered the same type as the wing (garment). Therefore, the sages stated (Menachot 42a) that tzitzit should not be made from wool caught on thorns when the sheep lie down among them, nor from fibers plucked from the animal. Additionally, this constitutes a disgrace to the mitzvah (see Magen Avraham, section 9). Similarly, it is forbidden to make them from the leftover threads that the weaver leaves at the end of the garment, due to the disgrace to the mitzvah. Even if they are spun specifically for tzitzit and afterward one decides to make a garment from them, they are invalid due to the reason that they were not spun for the sake of the mitzvah (Taz, section 4). All of this applies even after the fact (ibid.).

If one stole wool and made from it tzitzit, they are invalid, for it is written: "And they shall make for themselves"—from their own property. Similarly, if one stole a tallit and attached tzitzit to it—even if the tzitzit are his own—it is invalid, for the Torah says "your garment" (as explained by the Pri Megadim) and not the garment of others. Likewise, if one bought a tallit or tzitzit, and the seller is coming and going with the money in a manner that it is still not considered his as I wrote in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 190, he also cannot recite a blessing over it (as explained by the Mishnah Berurah). However, if it is known that the seller will not retract and will wait for the money for a period of time as is customary among merchants, then it is permitted. If one stole the tzitzit and attached them to his garment, and afterward compensated the owner or received them as a gift, it is permitted. In this case, the principle of "you shall make and not from the already made" does not apply to invalidate them, because the invalidation was not due to the tzitzit themselves but because they were not his own, and now they are his. (The Mishnah Berurah is uncertain about this, but there is no doubt in this matter.)

Regarding the case where one stole wool and made it into tzitzit, they are invalid. Our teacher, the Rema, wrote in Section 6 that this specifically applies when one steals the threads. But if one stole wool and made it into threads, they are valid. However, initially, it is forbidden to make them. Concerning the blessing, see the beginning of Section 689. These are his words: Meaning, when one steals threads and makes them into tzitzit, one does not acquire them even after despair, for there is neither a change of name nor a change of action. There is no action here because the wrapping and tying are not considered an action since they can be easily undone, and there is no change of name because even now, they are still called "tzitzit threads." But if one stole wool and made it into threads, it is considered a complete action and a complete change of name. Therefore, even before despair, one acquires them as the law of change of action. And if it is a change that can revert to its original form, it requires despair, for one acquires through despair and change of name, for originally it was wool and now it is threads. The main laws of this matter are explained in Choshen Mishpat Sections 360 and 361, see there. All this is regarding wearing, but reciting a blessing on it is forbidden, even if one acquired it through change, for this is not blessing but cursing.

And the Rambam wrote in the first chapter, law 11: "One should not make them (tzitzit) from stolen wool, nor from the wool of a city that has been led astray, nor from consecrated items. And if one did – it is invalid." This is his language, and it is clear from his wording that even if one stole wool and made tzitzit from it – they are invalid. Our master, the Beit Yosef, in his great book, wrote that this applies before despair (of the owner), see there. And certainly, it is possible to say so. (And the Taz, in subsection 5, questioned him: if so, why do I need a verse, see there. And his words are perplexing. And in the Korban, the Talmud asked similarly, that it is impossible to consecrate it. Examine it and you will find it easy.) He also wrote that it could be said that he (the Rambam) holds that it is a change that reverts to its original state, and if so, even after despair it does not help, see there. And this cannot be said, for it has already been explained in Choshen Mishpat, section 361, that despair with a change for the worse – acquires (Derech HaDrisha and see Taz there). There are those who wanted to say that the Rambam holds that in matters of mitzvah, despair and change do not help (Taz there). But the Maggid Mishneh, in the sixth chapter of Chametz, wrote explicitly to the contrary, see there. And in my humble opinion, it seems there is another reason in the Rambam, if he means also after despair as his language implies. Because the beginning of the spinning must be for its sake, as explained, and despair alone does not acquire. And if so, even though after spinning he acquires it due to despair and change, nevertheless, how can "for its sake" occur when it is not yet his? And "for its sake" cannot occur at all without the owner's intent. (However, in any case, practically it is difficult to be lenient against the Rambam's opinion, as the Taz wrote there.)

Strings that are borrowed – it is considered a loan because they do not return in their original state, and it is as if they are his own. Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in paragraph 7, meaning: even though the term "borrowing" typically applies to an item that is returned in its original form, and a loan refers to something that is not returned in its original form but rather something else in its place, such as a monetary loan which is repaid with other money, nevertheless, if one borrowed the strings of tzitzit, it is certainly intended as a loan. For if they were to be returned in their original state, why would he borrow them, and what would he do with them? If we were to say that he borrowed them to attach them to his tallit for a certain period of time and then would remove them from the tallit and return them, that is not the usual practice. Therefore, if he explicitly stipulated that they be returned to him, he may attach them to his tallit but does not bless upon them, because they are not his. 

And even though in Siman 14 it will be explained that according to the Rosh, one who borrows a tallit with tzitzit on it blesses upon it immediately, nevertheless, it can be said that here he does not bless. For there, we assess the intention of the lender, that if he did not intend it as a gift on condition that it be returned so that he could bless upon it, why would he lend it? But here we say that he lent it to attach to his tallit because it is forbidden to wear a four-cornered garment without tzitzit. Therefore, he lent them until he obtains his own tzitzit, but he did not intend for him to fulfill his obligation of tzitzit with them, only to remove the prohibition. For certainly, even though tzitzit need to be one's own, this is for the fulfillment of the mitzvah. But the prohibition is removed from him. 

Accordingly, it seems to me that even in the case of borrowing, he can attach them to his tallit even if he explicitly said he would return them. And some say that in such a case it is forbidden to attach them to his tallit. They distinguish between tzitzit strings and prepared tzitzit, that prepared tzitzit may be attached, but tzitzit strings may not (Magen Avraham, subsection 11). These are puzzling matters, for if so, why would he lend them? (And the Magen Avraham also holds that if he lent them to attach to his tallit, he blesses, see there. And in my humble opinion, it seems as I have written, that even in such a case it is not similar to borrowing a tallit with tzitzit. Be precise and you will find the truth.)

Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote in section 8: If one bows to an animal, its wool is invalid for [use in] tzitzit. If one bows to planted flax, it is valid for [use in] tzitzit, since it has changed. This is his language, and it is derived from the words of the Rambam. And the explanation is: Even though we hold that a change acquires [ownership]—this applies to other transgressions, like theft and similar cases. But wool or flax that is prohibited for benefit, and certainly if they were bowed to—no change in the world helps. Anything made from them is forbidden for benefit (Rashi on Avodah Zarah 46a, beginning of the commentary "Or"). However, it is known that if one bows to a living being or to something attached to the ground—it is not forbidden for ordinary use, only for sacred use, as it is written: "Their gods on the mountains"—but not the mountains their gods (ibid. 45a). Also, living beings are only forbidden for sacred use and not for ordinary use (beginning of chapter six of Temurah). According to this, by the letter of the law, whether one bows to an animal or to planted flax which is attached [to the ground]—the wool and flax are permitted for [use in] tzitzit, since they have changed. However, despite this, they invalidated the wool, because it is obvious to everyone that it is wool and there is a denigration of the mitzvah. But flax is not recognizable at all, for when it is attached, it is like a regular tree, and now they are threads (Magen Avraham, section 12). Nevertheless, in retrospect, it could be that even wool is valid (ibid. in section 686, end of section 6). All this is according to the Rambam. But according to what appears from the words of Tosafot in Avodah Zarah (beginning of the commentary "Hainu"), they have one law and even flax is invalid, refer there. And perhaps it is invalid even in retrospect, and this requires further study.

It has already been explained that the measurement of the length of the threads is twelve thumb-lengths according to the opinion of Rabbeinu Tam, which we hold as the main ruling. Of this, one-third is braided and two-thirds are threads. This applies at the time of making [the tzitzit], but if they were cut afterward, our sages of blessed memory said: Shortened [threads] are valid, as long as enough remains to tie a knot (beginning of the chapter "Techelet"). The reason can be explained: The Torah was only particular about the length at the time of making, as I wrote in the previous section regarding the thumb knot. Some have written that the reason is because, according to the Torah, it is valid even with any amount, and it is the Rabbis who required this measurement. Therefore, they were not stringent when they were cut (Levush). In my humble opinion, it seems that this depends on the dispute among the authorities, as will be explained.

In the Gemara there, it was asked: regarding tying a knot, does it mean that each thread individually? That is to say, to tie each thread by itself, which is a smaller measure, or to tie them all together, which requires a larger measure because it is thicker, as is clear? And it remains unresolved, see there. The Rif and the Rambam in the first chapter ruled leniently, that it suffices for each one individually. The Rosh, the Tur, and the Shulchan Aruch ruled stringently. Therefore, it is proven from this that the Rif and the Rambam hold that it is a rabbinic doubt and thus ruled leniently, while the Rosh, the Tur, and the Shulchan Aruch hold that it is a biblical doubt and thus ruled stringently. Therefore, according to them, one must say the reason that we have explained. (And it is clear with the help of Heaven. And this is also implied by the Kesef Mishneh, see there. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

And this is the language of the Tur: If all the threads are cut, and there remains enough to tie – it is valid, provided that there remains enough to tie all of them together, which is more than the amount needed to tie each one individually... And if there is not enough left to tie, even if only one thread is cut – the entire thing is invalid. Therefore, since each one is doubled into two, if two ends are cut – it is invalid, for perhaps one thread is entirely cut. But if only one end is cut – it is valid. This is the end of the Tur’s language, and similarly wrote Rabbeinu the Beit Yosef in section 1. He concludes that according to what we are accustomed to be meticulous about when making tzitzit, to place a mark on the four ends in such a way that the four ends are always on one side of the knot and the four ends on the other side, if two ends on one side are cut – it is valid. For certainly, they are from two different threads, and there remains from each the second end, which is more than the amount needed to tie. This is the end of his language, and the matters are clarified.

It is straightforward that each of the threads needs to be long enough to tie around the others. If some of the threads are broken, it is sufficient that each remaining thread is long enough to tie around the broken ones. If all of them are broken, each of the threads needs to be long enough to tie around all seven of the others. There is an opinion that requires each thread to be long enough to tie around each and every one of the broken threads individually, based on the Mordechai (as cited by the Magen Avraham, Section 2). However, this opinion has been rejected, as even if the Mordechai holds this view, all the early authorities disagree with him. Additionally, it is evident from the Rif and the Rambam that they do not hold this view. Particularly since they ruled leniently on this matter, how can we be stringent to rule according to the stringent opinion, especially when it is a lone stringent opinion? (And particularly since the Beit Yosef did not interpret the Mordechai in this way. Similarly, this is the view of the Maharam Benet, and it is also written in the Sidur Derech Chaim and the Mishnah Berurah.) There is also an opinion that the length needed for tying is four fingerbreadths (Chayei Adam). I am astonished: according to the Rambam, the entire length of the tzitzit is just four fingerbreadths, so at most, we should not be stricter than two fingerbreadths (as also written in the Mishnah Berurah).

The words of the Rambam on this matter are very perplexing. For in the first chapter, Halacha 4, he wrote: "Similarly, if one made [the tzitzit] with white and blue threads, and the white thread was torn and shortened to the corner, and only the blue thread remained - it is valid." Thus far his words. And there at the end of the chapter, he wrote: "Similarly, if the threads of the tzitzit were shortened, even if only enough remained to tie - it is valid. But if a thread was torn from its base - even one thread invalidates if it was torn from its base." And this has been questioned (see Kesef Mishneh).

Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, explained his words in his large work and in the Kesef Mishneh in three ways: The first way is that when it is written "and if the thread is completely severed," it means that if the threads of one type are completely severed, and also one thread of the other type is severed from its root, it is invalid. But without this, it is valid. See there. The second way is that when it is written at the beginning of the chapter "if the white thread is severed until the wing..." it means that if a sufficient length for tying remains, he did not bother to explain because he relied on what he wrote at the end. And when it is written "and similarly if the tzitzit threads are reduced, even if only a sufficient length for tying remains, it is valid," this is when only one type is severed, and the other type remains intact. He relied on what he wrote at the beginning of the chapter. But if the thread is completely severed from its root, even in one, it is invalid. The third way is that when it was previously written that if the white thread is severed and reduced until the wing, it means "until but not including," that a bit less than the length for tying remains. And at the end, he says that if all are reduced, a sufficient length for tying is needed, and if completely severed, even one thread invalidates it. See there. And it is understood by all that all these explanations are forced.

In my humble opinion, there is another intention here, and his words are straightforward. Our master, the Beit Yosef, held that "the thread is cut from its root" means up to the corner. Therefore, it was difficult for him. But in truth, it is not so, for "from its root" was explained by Rashi in Menachot (39a): This means the end connected to the tallit. Until here are his words, and so wrote the Nimukei Yosef. And this is above the braid. According to this, his words are clear: when one type of thread is cut, when it is reduced up to the corner – it is kosher. But the end connected to the tallit, meaning above the braid which is on the corner, still remains. But if it is cut from its root, meaning that even the end connected to the tallit is cut – even one thread makes it invalid. This means it is completely cut off from the hole in the corner. And if all are cut, and there remains from all of them enough for a bow – it is kosher. According to this, the method of the Rambam is as the previous method, which is the method of the Rosh and most of the poskim. However, in this, the Rambam is more lenient, meaning that according to the previous method, if one thread is completely cut off, and from the eight threads (when they are one thread) there does not remain enough for a bow – it is invalid. According to the Rambam, it is not invalid in such a case until it is cut from the end connected to the tallit. However, it is certain that according to the previous opinion, even if in one there is not enough for a bow but combined with the other two threads it is also kosher. In any case, our master the Beit Yosef in his great book is uncertain about this in practice, see there. However, it is clear that one does not need enough for a bow in both threads, and it is enough in one of them, for they are from one thread, and why would we need two "enough for bows" (Beit Yosef, and Ma'adanei Yom Tov, Siman 6, end of Ot 100, see there). And I am astonished that the Tur and Shulchan Aruch did not bring the words of the Rambam at all.

And it emerges that according to the law, per the previous opinion and according to the Rambam, if he was meticulous at the time of making (the tzitzit) to divide (the strands) four here and four there, even if all four threads on one side are completely severed up to the knot – it is valid. Since, as long as all four threads on the other side remain, there is enough thread left for a knot. This is according to the Rambam and the majority of the poskim (decisors). However, there is one of our great rabbis who has a completely different opinion about this, as will be explained, and this is the opinion of Rabbeinu Tam. And although the Rosh rejected this opinion, nonetheless, the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch brought it. Certainly, one should be concerned about this opinion when possible. The primary halacha, however, follows the first opinion.

Rabbeinu Tam's opinion is that when the Gemara states "remnants of tekhelet are valid" – it means that enough remains for tying in each one. All our rabbis explained that "tekhelet" refers to the entirety of the tzitzit. Rabbeinu Tam holds that "tekhelet" specifically means when the two white threads are completely intact. Thus, if the two tekhelet threads are severed, and enough remains for tying – it is valid. According to this, for us, where all four threads are white, with two designated as white and two designated as tekhelet – it is only valid if two threads remain completely intact, which means twelve thumb-lengths. Then, if the other two threads are severed and enough remains for tying – it is valid. However, if three threads are severed, even if enough for tying remains – it is invalid.

Based on this, according to this opinion, when three out of the eight strands are cut, even if enough remains to tie a knot, it is invalid, because we are concerned that perhaps they are from three different strands, and therefore, two complete strands do not remain. There is no difference whether he was meticulous in dividing four strands here and four strands there, or whether he was not meticulous. Indeed, if he was meticulous, it is worse when the three ends are from one side, as they are certainly from three different strands. However, even if he was not meticulous, or if two were cut from one side and one from the other side, we are still concerned that they are from three different strands, and out of doubt, it is invalid. But when two ends are cut, if they are from two sides, one of them must have enough to tie a knot. Similarly, if they are from one side and he was not meticulous in dividing four here and four there. But from one side and he was meticulous in dividing them, it is valid even if enough to tie a knot does not remain, like the previous opinion. (And we have explained all the opinions with Heaven's help. Only when a strand is cut from its root, according to Tosafot and the Rosh, it is considered invalid if enough to tie a knot does not remain. According to Rashi and the Rambam, it is when the end connected to the tallit is cut. And I do not know why we assume that Rabbeinu Tam does not hold this opinion. It requires further investigation that the words of Rashi and the Rambam are not brought at all. And perhaps in a pressing situation, one can rely on them, but it needs further investigation for the final ruling. Analyze this well, and you will find it easy.)

It is obvious that "sufficient for tying" depends on the quantity and thinness of the threads. If they are thin, less is sufficient, and if they are thick, more is needed. However, even if they are thick and do not have enough for tying, we measure as if they were medium threads, and if then they would have enough for tying, it is valid. But with thin threads, there is no need to measure with medium ones. And it is an initial mitzvah to make the threads medium because of "This is my God, and I will glorify Him." And there is one who wrote that it should be measured to be sufficient to wrap around eight hairs (Magen Avraham, small section 6).

And know that what has been explained that it is required to have a remainder for tying means that from the branch there should remain this measure. This is the opinion of Rashi. But Rabbeinu Yitzchak wrote that even if the entire branch is cut off, as long as from the braid there remains enough for tying, it is valid. And the world follows Rashi, except in a case where it is impossible to obtain other tzitzit, then one can rely in a pressing situation on the opinion of Rabbeinu Yitzchak. And according to Rabbeinu Tam, one should be very cautious wherever it is easy to find other tzitzit. But there is no need to seek after them (there, subsection 7). And one who relies on the opinion of Rabbeinu Yitzchak in a pressing situation should not recite a blessing on the tzitzit, and should also not wear them on Shabbat (there). And it is proper for every person when checking the tzitzit to also examine the base of the tzitzit, from the hole and below, because there if it is torn, the thread is torn from its base and it is invalid (Taz, subsection 3). And when the tzitzit are torn in a manner that they are invalid, it does not help to tie the torn part to the remaining part, because even if tying would help, it is only before they are made. But afterwards, since they become invalid, it is impossible to make them valid through tying, as it is considered "something made" and not "something made properly" (there). And in this, the commentators of the Shulchan Aruch agreed that at the beginning, before attaching them to the garment, tying helps (there and Magen Avraham, section 15, subsection 1). According to this, when one has short threads, he can tie them to each other and attach them to the tallit.

Tzitzit are not like tefillin, which are two separate commandments: one for the arm and one for the head, and they do not impede one another. If one puts on one of them, he fulfills a commandment. But tzitzit – all four tzitzit are considered one commandment. They impede one another, such that if one of the tzitzit is missing or invalidated, they are all nullified. If one wears a tallit with three tzitzit, not only does he not fulfill the commandment, but he also commits a transgression by wearing a four-cornered garment without tzitzit. And if one goes out with such a tallit on Shabbat into the public domain, he is liable for a sin offering because the remaining tzitzit are considered a burden. They are not nullified to the garment like other attachments hanging from the garment, which are nullified as I wrote in Siman 301, as tzitzit are significant and not nullified (Shabbat 139b), since his intention is to complete and fix them. Therefore, if all of them are completely invalidated in a manner that his intention is to make all new ones – they are nullified to the garment. He is not liable for a sin offering, but he does transgress by wearing a four-cornered garment without tzitzit. However, regarding Shabbat, he does not transgress, as will be explained in Siman 301. (Rashi there explained that the significance is due to the techelet, see there. According to this, in our time, when we do not have techelet – they are nullified. But Tosafot and Rambam explained as I wrote, due to his intention to complete them, see there.)

But a tallit (prayer shawl) that is properly adorned with tzitzit (ritual fringes) is permitted to be worn in the public domain on Shabbat, whether it is a small tallit or a large tallit. This applies even at night, when the obligation of tzitzit does not apply, because they are considered an adornment of the garment. All the more so according to the opinion that a daytime garment is obligated in tzitzit even at night, as I have written in Siman 15. Therefore, in the winter, one can wear the large tallit before the break of dawn without a blessing and go to the synagogue with it. Even in these times when we do not have the blue thread (techelet), we do not say that the mitzvah is not fulfilled properly, as this is not the case; the mitzvah is fulfilled properly. For we hold (as Magen Avraham, subsection 3 states) that the absence of techelet does not invalidate the white threads. However, one must be careful when going out into the public domain that the sides of the tallit should not rest only on the shoulders, as this is not the usual manner of wearing a garment, as will be explained in Siman 301. See there that this applies when it does not cover most of the body, but if it covers most of the body, it is permitted even if the sides rest only on the shoulders. This applies specifically to a tallit that is definitely obligated in tzitzit, whether its obligation is from the Torah or from Rabbinic law, like a silk garment according to those who hold that its obligation is not from the Torah. But if its obligation is due to doubt, such as a garment that is half open and half closed, or does not have the required measure of obligation as will be explained in Siman 16, it is certainly forbidden to go out with it on Shabbat into the public domain. Since it does not require tzitzit, it is not nullified to the garment, as I have written. According to this, very small tallitot, which do not have the required measure, are forbidden to be worn on Shabbat in the public domain. However, people customarily permit it, and perhaps they hold that since this garment does not require tzitzit at all, the tzitzit have no significance on this garment and are nullified. (In Be'er Heitev, it is written that in the Responsa of the Rema, Siman 110, he discusses this matter, but it is not presently in my possession to examine it.)

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote that we establish a presumption that the tallit is properly tied according to the law, and there is no need to check it before wearing it. Thus are his words. Meaning: Although in Siman 8 he ruled that one must check it before the blessing, and according to this I would say that certainly when going out with it on Shabbat into the public domain one must check it – he informs us that this is not the case. And the reason is simple: In truth, it should have been established by presumption also in the aforementioned case, but because if that were so, one would never check it, they therefore required checking it once a day. Hence, there is no need to check it here, because according to the law we establish a presumption. Therefore, even when sitting in the synagogue, if he removes the tallit and there is a significant interruption such that when he puts it on again he needs to recite a blessing, nevertheless, checking is not required for the reason explained (Magen Avraham, subsection 5). And earlier in Siman 8, we explained that there is room to question the necessity of the check itself, see there.

Our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, wrote in Section 3: If it becomes known to a person on Shabbat while he is in a karmelit that the tallit he is wearing is invalid, he should not remove it until he reaches his home, because of the principle of human dignity (kevod habriyot). Even a small tallit worn under his clothes need not be removed. The same applies if one of the tzitzit strings breaks, and he is embarrassed to sit without a tallit; he may wear it without a blessing due to the principle of human dignity. This specifically applies on Shabbat when it is forbidden to make tzitzit, but on a weekday, in such a case, it is forbidden. Thus far his words.

Explanation of their words: It is established for us that the dignity of human beings is so significant that it overrides a negative commandment in the Torah, specifically the negative commandment of "do not deviate" which is of rabbinic origin (Berachot 19b). That is to say, the dignity of human beings certainly does not override a definite negative commandment from the Torah, for "There is no wisdom, no understanding, and no counsel against the Lord" (ibid.). Rather, regarding the negative commandment of "do not deviate," which the Torah commanded us to listen to the words of the sages — in this case, the dignity of human beings overrides it. And even though this too is of Torah origin, since it stems from the mitzvah of the sages — the sages waived their honor for the sake of human dignity (Rashi there).

According to this, if one is walking in a public domain on Shabbat and finds that his tallit is invalid, he should remove it even in the marketplace. But in a karmelit, which is a rabbinic prohibition, he should not remove it until he reaches his home. According to this, since we hold that we do not have a public domain in our times, he should not remove it anywhere. Even a small tallit under his clothes, where there is no disgrace in walking without it as it is not noticeable, nevertheless, removing it in the middle of the street is a disgrace. Similarly, even a large tallit of ours, where there is no disgrace in removing it as it is not made as a garment, nevertheless, he does not need to remove it since the rabbis did not decree so (Beit Yosef and Magen Avraham, subsection 7).

They further permitted that even to wear it initially in the synagogue at the time of prayer, if he finds on Shabbat that it is invalid, and there is disgrace in sitting without a tallit — he may wear it without a blessing for the sake of human dignity. This is only on Shabbat, but on weekdays, since he can fix it, it is forbidden to wear it. This is the way of the Shulchan Aruch.

But these two rulings are perplexing, for after all, they only permitted it out of respect, meaning that there is disgrace in removing it. But if there is no disgrace – they did not permit it. If so, why should we allow our large tallit, where there is no disgrace in removing it? Also, the second ruling, to wear it initially due to disgrace, from where do we derive such a leniency? Our sages permitted only to not remove it due to disgrace, but not to wear it initially. The first question I found someone else also raised (the genius Rabbi Akiva Eiger). Moreover, regarding the essence of these rulings, there is a significant question: although concerning the prohibition of Shabbat by rabbinic law – we are lenient out of respect for human dignity, in addition to this, there is a Torah prohibition to wear a four-cornered garment without tzitzit. And indeed, it is written that at the time of wearing, there is no prohibition, for the Torah did not say not to wear it without tzitzit, but rather that when wearing it, one is obligated to attach tzitzit, and then it is a case of "sit and do not act," which is overridden by respect for human dignity. But if so, it should also be permissible on weekdays (Magen Avraham, Siman 108)?

And it appears to my humble opinion that the main point is as follows: Certainly, to override any Torah prohibition for this reason is untenable. This is not comparable to other cases of human dignity where they permitted passive non-action in matters involving significant disgrace, and the case of removing one's tallit is not similar, as is evident. Therefore, on weekdays, there is no allowance, but on Shabbat, there is another allowance that seems clear to my humble opinion: From the Torah, there is no prohibition at all to wear a four-cornered garment without tzitzit on Shabbat, for the Torah commanded to make tzitzit on this garment when you wear it, and on Shabbat, the Torah prohibited all work, and consequently, this is like the prohibition to make tzitzit on it today. We do not find that the Torah prohibits wearing it when it does not have tzitzit if the Torah itself forbade making tzitzit on it today. Because if it were due to the possibility of making it yesterday – it is not the way of the Torah to prohibit for this reason, and the sages can forbid it. Certainly, in the case of tzitzit that were torn on Shabbat – it is obvious that, from the Torah, it is completely permissible. It follows that concerning the prohibition of tzitzit, there is no Torah prohibition on Shabbat at all, and therefore they permitted wearing it on Shabbat for the sake of human dignity, since from the Torah it is completely permissible – the sages did not uphold their words, since it is impossible to make tzitzit today, and from the Torah, it is a complete allowance. Similarly, one should not remove the large tallit for this reason, since it is a complete allowance from the Torah. All this applies on Shabbat. But on weekdays, there is a Torah prohibition, and it is forbidden in any manner, and one is obligated to remove the tallit from oneself. And thus, the words of our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, are stringent. (And it seems to me that this is the intention of the Mordechai. The Magen Avraham there elaborated in questioning him, and according to what I have written, his words are clear to the understanding. Examine and you will find it easy.) According to what we have explained, on weekdays it is also forbidden with a small tallit, and one is obligated to remove one's clothes and take it off. There are those who permitted a small tallit even on weekdays (Magen Avraham). And it seems to me that it is forbidden, and only on Shabbat is it allowed in any manner, and similarly on Yom Tov. (And with our words, the question of the Magen Avraham in the name of his brother is also resolved, for he can give it as a gift, see there. And according to our words, on Shabbat it is a complete allowance. Examine and you will find it easy.)

The Rambam wrote in Chapter 1, Law 11: "The threads of the tzitzit require spinning for the sake of tzitzit…". So far his language. And this law has already been explained in Siman 11. And in Sukkah (9a) they learned this from what is written: "You shall make twisted cords for yourself" – for the sake of your obligation. Meaning: for its sake. And afterward, he wrote in Law 12: "Tzitzit made by a non-Jew is invalid, as it is stated: 'Speak to the children of Israel… and they shall make for themselves tzitzit.' But if a Jew made them without intention – they are valid." So far his language. And this making refers to attaching them to the garment and making two knots with part of the twisting, which is required by Torah law. The Rambam holds that this making does not need to be for its sake, and therefore it is valid even without intention. And only concerning a non-Jew, the Torah decreed, and not due to the reason of "for its sake", for this does not require a verse, as a non-Jew acts with his own intention even if a Jew supervises him according to the Rambam, as I wrote in Siman 11. And from this itself, the Rambam deduces that there is no need for it to be for its sake, since a verse is needed to exclude a non-Jew. And one should not ask: How do we know that "You shall make twisted cords for yourself" refers to spinning which requires intention, and the verse "and they shall make for themselves tzitzit" refers to attaching them to the garment? Perhaps it is the opposite? It is impossible to say so, for in that verse it is written (there) "and they shall make for themselves tzitzit on the corners of their garments" – it is clearly referring to the time of attaching them to the garment, and consequently, the other verse refers to spinning (so it appears to me).

The Rosh in Siman 14 wrote that we require hanging [the tzitzit] with intent for the sake of the mitzvah, see there. And it must be said: that which the verse needed to disqualify a non-Jew [from making tzitzit] is even when he stands over him and instructs him to do it for the sake of the mitzvah, for according to the Rosh, in such a situation, it is valid in the spinning, as I wrote in Siman 11. And the reason of the Rosh seems to be because he holds that the requirement of "You shall make twisted cords for yourself" with intent for the sake of the mitzvah applies to all actions, both to the spinning and to the hanging. And the verse "The children of Israel shall make for themselves tzitzit on the corners of their garments" comes to disqualify a non-Jew in any manner, even if he stands over him. And this verse refers only to the hanging, as it is written: "on the corners of their garments," as I have written. Therefore, in the spinning, it is valid with the non-Jew standing over him, according to the Rosh. The Tur did not mention "for the sake of the mitzvah" at all, which requires investigation. And perhaps it is because his opinion leans more towards the Rambam, and he did not want to explicitly rule against his father's opinion, and therefore he omitted it entirely.

And this is the language of our teacher [the Beit Yosef] in paragraph 2: If an Israelite attached tzitzit to a garment without intention, if other tzitzit are not readily available to make it kosher – one can rely on the Rambam who permits it. However, one should not recite a blessing over it. Thus far is his language. And it appears that he fundamentally holds according to the Rambam. However, concerning blessings, since they are not indispensable, he was concerned for the opinion of the Rosh. And regarding wearing such a tallit in the public domain on Shabbat, it seems to me that in any case it is permitted: According to the Rambam, it is obvious, and even according to the Rosh, who considers them invalid – they are nullified in regard to the garment, for the reason that "tzitzit are not nullified" is due to their importance, as I wrote in the previous section. And according to the Rosh, who considers them invalid – their importance is removed. (See Levushei Serad. This does not seem correct to me.)

However, the words of our master, the Beit Yosef, who wrote: "If other tzitzit are not available...", from his language it is clear that when other tzitzit are available, one is obligated to untie them and attach the others—if so, should one untie those same tzitzit and reattach them with the proper intention? Some have explained it as being close to Shabbat, where there is time to attach but not to untie and reattach (Magen Avraham, subsection 4, and as explained by the Machatzit HaShekel). Alternatively: if one of the heads has been cut, so that if they are untied, they cannot be reattached (ibid.). And some have explained it as being thin and worn out, so that if they are untied, they will be completely ruined (Sha'arei Teshuvah, subsection 5). And it appears to me that he did not mean this at all. Rather, he intended to teach us that this is not comparable to other invalidations which are forbidden to wear—he intended to teach us that one may rely on the Rambam and wear them. And so it is explained in the Levush, see there. And this too is obvious: that ostensibly this invalidation is more severe than other invalidations since it can be corrected, so why should we rely gratuitously on the Rambam's opinion? If so, this law would not be found at all. Therefore, I say that indeed it is so, but in any case, if at this moment it is impossible to correct them, such as if he himself is unable to attach them or has no time or some other reason, where others are not available. Meaning: that it is impossible to correct them, that when they are corrected, they are also considered as others. And know that the main aspect of "for its sake" is in the upper knot and the first segment. But from then on there is no concern at all. And even if a gentile finished it—it is valid, as this does not invalidate it after the fact.

It is obvious that when Maimonides (Rambam) permits hanging (the tzitzit) without specific intention, his meaning is that one hangs them without any specific intention for the sake of tzitzit. According to the Rosh, intention is necessary because it requires the specific intention of "for its sake," similar to the requirement in spinning (the threads). Maimonides, however, does not see intention as a requirement. But if one explicitly hung them not for the sake of tzitzit, even according to Maimonides it is invalid, as this would nullify them from being tzitzit. This was also written by one of the great authorities (Mashkanot Yaakov, Siman 20). The Mishnah Berurah writes that from the language of the Beit Yosef it is proven that even if one explicitly hung them not for their sake, it is still valid. Refer there and you will see. God forbid to say this. Also, the Prisha does not intend this. Besides, his words are puzzling. Refer there and you will see. It is also obvious that hanging with the intention for its sake is sufficient, as the act of hanging itself demonstrates the "for its sake" intention, as the Mishnah Berurah also writes. Examine this and you will find it easy.

The Tur and the Shulchan Aruch wrote that women are permitted to attach the tzitzit to the garment and make them, for the Talmud in Menachot (42a) only excluded a Samaritan from "Bnei Yisrael" (the children of Israel) and not a woman. In all of Torah, when it is written "Bnei Yisrael," women are also included. Only concerning sacrifices, since the Temple service is only for the male priests, as it is written "the sons of Aaron" and not the daughters of Aaron, for only the males are included in the sanctity of priesthood. Therefore, in matters of sacrifices, when it is written "Bnei Yisrael," women are excluded, as in laying hands (semicha) and other services (Kiddushin 36a). Similarly, in Menachot (61b) regarding waving, both a Samaritan and a woman are excluded from "Bnei Yisrael" because in matters of sacrifices, only males perform the service. (This resolves the difficulty of the Magen Avraham, section 2, and the response of the Eliyah Rabbah is strained, see there). A clear proof that women are included in "Bnei Yisrael" is written: "Therefore, the children of Israel do not eat the sinew of the thigh, because it touched the hollow of Jacob's thigh" – and are not women also descendants of Jacob? Therefore, the Talmud only excluded a Samaritan.

Even though women are not obligated in the mitzvah of tzitzit, what of it? It is specifically regarding tefillin that the Torah decrees "and you shall bind... and you shall write" – anyone who is obligated in binding is also obligated in writing, but not regarding tzitzit. Moreover, it is not applicable to say that "anyone who is exempt from a matter cannot exempt others," as this applies to a mitzvah where one fulfills it through performance, such as Kiddush and Havdalah and similar cases. But regarding tzitzit, the mitzvah is the wearing. Nonetheless, some of the great early authorities were concerned with these reasons and disqualified a woman from affixing tzitzit to a tallit. This is why our teacher, the Rema, wrote that some are stringent and require men to do it. It is preferable to do so from the outset. These are his words: that it is merely a stringency, and the main ruling is that it is permitted. A minor has the same status as a woman. However, since it must be done with proper intent, it follows that a minor is not capable unless he is taught. Therefore, a minor should be distanced from affixing tzitzit. But regarding his own tallit, there is no concern. A deaf-mute and an imbecile are certainly disqualified, as they do not have the understanding to do it with proper intent. A blind person is certainly permitted to do it. And know that it is clear that one can affix tzitzit to a tallit either by day or by night. Although night is not the time for tzitzit, this is not relevant to their making. And indeed, even women are valid to make them, and even those who are concerned about women – it is because they are not obligated in this mitzvah at all.

It is written: "You shall make tassels on the four corners of your garment…" It is explained that you are only obligated to place tzitzit on your own garment when you wear it, and not on someone else's garment. Therefore, according to Torah law, if one borrows a tallit from another that does not have tzitzit, he is exempt from placing tzitzit on it forever. It is only by rabbinic decree that after thirty days, he is obligated to place tzitzit on it (Chullin 110b), because it appears as if it is his own. And this is specifically when it has been with him for thirty consecutive days, but if he returned it in the middle, the previous days are not counted together. Nevertheless, if he wants to place tzitzit on it, he may do so. Regarding the blessing, it is better not to recite it. And although there are those who say that he can recite the blessing, like women who recite the blessing on the sukkah and lulav even though they are exempt, nonetheless, the Rosh wrote there that it is better not to recite the blessing. However, if one does recite the blessing, it is not considered a blessing in vain. (And this is the intention of the Magen Avraham, section 5. And this is also implied by the Machatzit HaShekel, see there.)

It appears to me that this only applied during the time of the Talmudic sages, who would wear garments with four corners all day. This is also implied in the original source of the law in Chullin. But with us, who only wear tallitot for the purpose of fulfilling the mitzvah, if someone borrows a non-fringed tallit from his friend for a period of time – he is obligated to immediately attach tzitzit and recite a blessing over it. For we can assume that it was lent in order to fulfill the mitzvah of tzitzit, and if so, the lender's intention is for the borrower to attach tzitzit, and he has given it to him as a gift on the condition that it be returned. Otherwise, why would he lend it, as it is not considered a garment at all among us? And if one might argue that it was lent out of embarrassment to be without a tallit and not to fulfill the mitzvah of tzitzit, it is known that among us it is even more embarrassing to sit with a tallit without tzitzit, for not everyone is knowledgeable in the law that a borrowed tallit is exempt [from tzitzit]? Certainly, it was lent to fulfill the mitzvah, and therefore, it is treated like borrowed threads as explained in Siman 11, Seif 25, see there. And the same applies to a small tallit, as we only wear it to fulfill the mitzvah of tzitzit. (And the later authorities did not speak of this at all. In my humble opinion, it is clear as I have written.)

And also, according to the law of the Gemara, this applies only when one borrows a tallit that is not fringed. However, if one borrows it when it is fringed, the Rosh rules there that one blesses it immediately, and so ruled the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch in section 3. Certainly, the lender had in mind that the borrower would bless it immediately, and if the method of borrowing does not suffice, it should be considered as a gift on condition to return (there, and this also serves as proof for what we have written). It is obvious that this applies only to a tallit designated for the mitzvah of tzitzit, and not to just any four-cornered garment (Taz, small section 4). This also applies only when one borrows it for prayer, but if one borrows it momentarily, such as to go up to the Torah or similar cases, one does not bless it, for it was not lent for the sake of the mitzvah but rather for politeness. The great authorities have ruled this way as well (Yam Shel Shlomo in Chullin there, and Magen Avraham, small section 6). Similarly, if one borrows a tallit from a friend to serve as a mohel or a sandak, one does not bless it. But if one borrows it to lead the prayers as a cantor, one blesses it. Likewise, a Kohen who ascends the platform (for the priestly blessing) is as if he is praying (there). And a community tallit is considered like one's own, as everyone has a share in it.

The Tur and Shulchan Aruch wrote in section 4 that it is permissible to take one's friend's tallit and recite a blessing over it, provided that it is folded if found folded. This is the end of their words. This is because it is certainly pleasing to a person that a mitzvah be performed with his property (Tur), and the owner of the tallit desires this and does not object. Therefore, if we know that the person is particular about it, it is forbidden to take it without his knowledge. In my humble opinion, even though our Rabbis ruled this law, that generally it is permitted to take a friend’s tallit without his knowledge and pray with it on the grounds that he surely finds it agreeable, we see that many are very particular about this, especially when the tallit is new and clean. Additionally, there are people who cannot tolerate at all someone else wearing their garment due to reasons of sweat and cleanliness. In my humble opinion, this law requires much deliberation.

And also in the source of the law, it is not so clear-cut to permit in all cases. For the SeMaK wrote this permission regarding a tallit that is not folded and placed in a concealed location, but if it is folded, one needs to get permission (as brought in Beit Yosef). And the Mordechai wrote about this that if one folds it as initially done, it is permitted. Or perhaps because the owner folded it, it reveals his intention that he is particular about lending it. Thus far his words (there), indicating that even regarding folding he is uncertain, and all the more so when it is placed in a concealed location. And the Nimukei Yosef wrote as follows: "And in a place where it is customary to leave their tallitot in the synagogue, if a person comes to wrap himself in it briefly and return it to its place, it is permitted... And the Ri wrote: And those who take a tzitzit they find in the synagogue without the knowledge of their owners, it is permitted... thus far his words." It is explicitly stated that even those who permit, only permit when the tallitot are placed in the synagogue, and not when each person conceals his tallit in a hidden place, for in such a case we do not find anyone who permits it. And it seems clear to me that also the Tur and Shulchan Aruch refer to such a case. But in our situation, where each person folds his tallit and conceals it in a box, or gives it to the shamash to conceal it in a box, it is certainly forbidden without the owner's knowledge unless it is clearly known that the owner does not mind. And now the custom is that the shamash takes the tallit of one of the householders that is concealed in his box and gives it to a guest to pray with. In my opinion, it is forbidden to do so without the knowledge of the owners. And one should not be lenient in this matter because there is a concern of theft, for borrowing without the owner's knowledge is considered theft. And regarding this it is said: "And the robber blesses, he despises the Lord," and it is better to pray without a tallit.

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote that it is permissible to take tefillin without the owner's knowledge. However, it is forbidden to study from someone else's books without their knowledge, for we are concerned that he might tear them during his study. Thus are his words. Even occasionally it is forbidden, for he might examine it extensively until it tears from much handling. Nevertheless, it is customary to permit a cursory glance, and similarly to take a siddur or machzor without the owner's knowledge, for most people do not mind this. And see what I wrote in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 292, Section 34. (And see Taz, Section 7, and Magen Avraham, Section 10.)

A tallit (prayer shawl) owned by partners is obligated in tzitzit, as it is written: "on the corners of their garments" (Chullin 136b). Who will wear it – that depends on their agreement. If they did not set an agreement, each one will wear it for a designated time. It is clear that one of them can claim the argument of "take or give" (partition). A garment that has four corners and has a partnership with a woman or a non-Jew is exempt from tzitzit. This requires further examination.

It is permitted to remove tzitzit from one garment and place them on another garment. There is no concern of disrespecting the mitzvah since the tzitzit are being placed on another garment. And why would one do this? Either because the first garment is old and the second one is new, or because one prefers the second garment and is displeased with the first. There is no halachic difference in this regard. However, to remove tzitzit from a garment and not place them on another garment is forbidden, just as it is forbidden to remove a mezuzah from a house, as there is no greater disrespect than this. The exception is if one intends to make the garment have fewer than four corners, or if one intends to sell it to a non-Jew, in which case it is permitted to remove the tzitzit in any manner (Magen Avraham, Section 2). But if one sells it to another Jew, it is forbidden to remove the tzitzit unless one intends to place them on another garment (ibid.). If one wants to replace the tzitzit with nicer ones, it is also permitted to remove them in any manner (ibid.). Likewise, if the first set of tzitzit is torn, even if they are still technically valid, if one wants to replace them with whole tzitzit, it is also permitted in any manner (ibid.). Similarly, it is permitted to remove tzitzit from the garments of the deceased, as they are not subject to the obligation.

There is an opinion that a thread that remains with enough length for a knot is valid, as I have written in Siman 12. Nevertheless, to affix it initially to a garment is forbidden, as ideally, a whole thread of twelve thumb-lengths is required (there, subsection 1). However, if one wishes to tie another thread to this one to complete the required length, it is permitted, as tying is considered a complete connection as if it were one thread (there). And when does tying help? Before it is affixed to the tallit. But to validate by tying after they are already affixed to the tallit does not help. For example, if the threads were torn and did not remain with enough length for a knot, and one wishes to validate them by tying – it does not help, as this is "you shall make and not from what is already made," which is invalid (there). And we have already explained this at the end of Siman 12, see there.

It is stated in the Gemara (41a): A tallit that was torn outside of three [fingerbreadths] — one may sew it. Within three — one may not sew it. A Baraita also teaches this: A tallit that was torn... Rabbi Meir says... and the Sages say... And they agree that one should not bring even a square cubit from another place with tekhelet and attach it to it. And they agree that one may bring tekhelet from another place and attach it to it. And Rashi explained: "Outside of three" — more than three fingerbreadths from the edge of the corner. "One may sew" — and we are not concerned that perhaps something from the sewing thread will remain, and he will leave it and add to it up to four threads for the sake of the tzitzit, and it will be "make and not from what is made." For outside of three it is not fit to attach tzitzit. But "within three" — which is fit to place tzitzit there, "one may not sew" — for here we are concerned as we have explained. This is the end of his words. And regarding "and they agree..." Rashi explained that one brings from another tallit which has tekhelet and attaches it to it, because "on the corners of their garments" is written, and this "corner" was not from this garment at the time of making. And they agree that one brings tekhelet, unravels the tzitzit from another tallit and attaches it to it, for here there is no "and not from what is made," for he needs to re-twist and fix it here as at the beginning. This is the end of his words.

It is explained from his words that the concern within three [fingerbreadths] not to sew is because one might join a thread of sewing to the tzitzit, and there would be an issue of "you shall make, and not from what is made." This means: even if the sewing threads are from threads spun for the sake of tzitzit, nonetheless there is an issue of "and not from what is made," for they were inserted into the garment for the sake of sewing and not for the sake of tzitzit. Therefore, it is made invalidly. And according to Rashi, there is no difference whether the piece was completely torn from the garment or still attached to the garment, since the concern is about the sewing thread. However, against this there is a leniency, that this concern is only when one sews with threads of the type used for making tzitzit. But if one sews with silk threads or something similar, this concern does not exist, for we do not make tzitzit from silk. And the fact that we do not bring a piece, even a large one, from another place when it has tzitzit on the piece and sew it onto this tallit, even though there is no concern of leftover sewing since it is above three [fingerbreadths]. But in this there is no need to be concerned that it is invalid from the essence of the law, for it is written "and they shall make for themselves tzitzit on the corners of their garments" – and this corner was not on this garment at the time of making. This means, even though it later became part of this garment, it was made invalidly, and there is an issue of "and not from what is made." Therefore, when one unties tzitzit from another garment, one is permitted to attach them here, for he is making anew and there is no issue of "from what is made."

And also in the Rambam, in the first chapter, law 13, it is explicitly stated that the invalidation of bringing a piece with tzitzit from another place is because of "not from what is made." And this is the wording of the Rambam: Tzitzit that were made from what was already made beforehand are invalid. How so? He brought a corner that has tzitzit and sewed it onto the garment, even if that corner has a dimension of one cubit by one cubit, it is invalid, as it is stated: "And they shall make for themselves tzitzit" — not from what is already made... until here is his wording. And the law of being torn within three [fingerbreadths], he wrote there in law 18 and this is his wording: If the corner that has tzitzit is torn outside of three fingerbreadths, he may sew it in its place. Within three, he should not sew it. Until here is his wording. And he did not explain the reason. However, in any case, the first law is because of "not from what is made," as Rashi explains.

The words of the Tur are completely obscure, as he wrote the two laws without providing any reasoning for them, see there. And certainly, if he had disagreed with the first law based on the reasoning of Rashi and the Rambam, he would have explained this. And undoubtedly, he also holds that the reason is due to "not from the [already] made." The Nimukei Yosef also wrote that the reason is due to "not from the [already] made." And even regarding the law of "within three," he wrote this reason, as will be explained with the help of Heaven. And also the Rosh (Siman 11) who wrote regarding the first law, and this is his language: because we require "on the corners of their garments," and this "corner" was not on this garment at the time of its making. Thus far his language. His intention is also the same, as he copied the language of Rashi. (And Rashi concludes in the second "and they agree" that here there is no "not from the [already] made." Thus far his language. It is explicitly explained that in the first "and they agree" there is "not from the [already] made" as the Rambam explicitly states, and there is no doubt about this at all. And also the intention of the Shulchan Aruch in section 2 is the same, see there.)

And there is a question about this: If so, why, when it is completely torn outside of three [fingerbreadths], should it be sewn? Since this corner has been torn from the garment, how can it be sewn with the tzitzit? Is it not invalid due to "not from what is made"? One could say that this is not a comparison, for ultimately this corner is from this garment and not from another garment, and when it is reattached, it returns to its original state. For in this garment, it was initially made in a valid manner, and we do not call it "made" in an invalid manner, for it was not made invalidly. But when it is brought from another place, it was made invalid in regard to this garment. (And this is the intent of the Magen Avraham, subsection 3. And the great Acharonim have debated this, and the matter is clear as I have written. Examine and you will find it light.)

And know that there are those who wish to say that when the corner (of a garment) has the measure of a tallit that is obligated in tzitzit, it is permissible to sew it onto another tallit. And we do not consider the tzitzit on the corner to be invalid due to "not from that which is made" since it itself has the measure of tzitzit. According to their words, it must be said: that which the Gemara states even one cubit by one cubit is because in one cubit by one cubit there is not yet the measure of a tallit. But in my humble opinion, this is not so, for it is implied from the Gemara that it is stating this for emphasis: even if it is much larger. And it appears to me that as long as it has the designation "corner" upon it, its tzitzit are invalidated when it is attached to another garment. And this is when a minority is attached to a majority, meaning the corner has less than what is in the garment to which it is attached. For the garment is named after the majority, and consequently, the minority is called "corner" and there is no "on the corners of their garments." However, when it is the majority and the minority is attached to it, it is valid, since this is not a corner but the main part of the garment. And the minority should not have tzitzit (this appears according to my humble opinion).
