Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote in Section 3: A properly made tallit with tzitzit, which is divided into two, and each part has the measure to be used for wrapping, and each part retains one or two tzitzit – there is no issue of "you shall make, and not from what is already made." So are his words, and this is from the responsa of the Rashba, Siman 217, see there. The explanation of his words: Do not say that since it is forbidden to attach a corner with tzitzit to a garment, therefore the tzitzit in the corner are invalid forever. This is not so, for when are they invalidated? When attached to another. But when it stands alone – the tzitzit are valid, and one makes another two tzitzit on its corners where it was divided. Some say that therefore, when sewing it with another – it is invalid (Bach). And some say it is valid. And initially, it is permitted to sew it with another (Magen Avraham, subsection 4). According to my humble opinion, both are true: if one attaches it to a piece larger than it – the tzitzit are invalid, because it becomes a "corner" on it. If one attaches it to a smaller piece – it is valid as I wrote in the previous section, because it is considered a "garment" upon it and not a "corner." (See Magen Avraham subsection 4, where it implies that the Bach also forbids attaching the two halves together afterward. On this, he disagrees from being torn outside the three. This needs examination, for in the Bach it is explicitly stated when attaching another piece to each part, see there. And if the Magen Avraham also disagrees with this, then what is the proof from being torn outside the three? Nonetheless, the main law is as I wrote. Be precise and you will find it easy. And the words of the Taz in subsection 3, who forbids attaching them together – are puzzling.)

And regarding a tear within three [fingerbreadths], as we explained that according to Rashi the reason is because of the sewing thread, as I have written, and Rabbeinu the Beit Yosef wrote in section 4 that for this reason, even if it is torn any amount – one should not sew it, see there. And we have already explained this. He further wrote that according to this, a woolen tallit that is torn within three [fingerbreadths] – it is permissible to sew it nowadays, because it is not customary to sew with woolen threads. Thus are his words. That is to say: on a woolen tallit, the tzitzit are also made of wool, and consequently with other threads it is permissible. (And this is also the conclusion of the Magen Avraham in subparagraph 6. And what he wrote in subparagraph 5 that the sewing was not spun for its sake – is puzzling, for if so, why does Rashi need the reason of "and not from what is made"? Therefore, it seems to me as I have written in section 4. And it seems to me that for us, since the tzitzit are always of wool, and it is not customary to sew with woolen threads, according to Rashi's opinion this is entirely permitted. Be precise and you will find leniency.)

But there are some of our rabbis who did not agree with Rashi's interpretation but with that of Rav Amram Gaon, who explained that within three [fingerbreadths] the tzitzit becomes invalid immediately, as it no longer retains the measure of a "corner." And when one re-attaches it, it becomes "made and not from what is made" (Nimukei Yosef). It is understood that the invalidation only occurs if it is completely torn from the garment. However, if it is still slightly attached, it is permitted. Additionally, even if it is completely torn, the invalidation applies only to the tzitzit that was hanging from the torn part. But to make new tzitzit after reattaching it is permitted, as there is no concern of "and not from what is made."

And so it is explained from the words of the Rambam that we brought, as he wrote: If the corner (of the garment) with the tzitzit is torn... within three (fingerbreadths) - it should not be sewn. Thus far is his language. Therefore, the disqualification is only on the tzitzit that is currently on it, and not on what will be made afterward. And hence he was precise to say "the corner is torn," meaning it is completely torn. But if it is somewhat attached - it is permitted. However, the language of the Tur, who wrote: If the tallit is torn within three (fingerbreadths) of the corner - one cannot sew it. Outside of three (fingerbreadths) - one can sew it. Thus far is his language. And since he did not mention "tzitzit" and also did not write "torn," it implies like the explanation of Rashi (and so wrote the Bach). And even though the Rosh brought both explanations, he did not decide between them. Therefore, the Tur agreed with Rashi's explanation. And also the Mordechai wrote according to Rashi's explanation, see there.

However, the language of the Rosh in the explanation of Rav Amram is peculiar, as he writes the following: And Rav Amram explained: “Outside of three [fingerbreadths] – one should sew; since it has three by three [fingerbreadths] – it has the status of a ‘garment.’ Within three – it does not have the status of a ‘garment,’ and it is as if it does not exist. And even though it is sewn, it is considered as if it is cut, and we do not place tzitzit on it. And if one makes tzitzit on it – it does not exempt the tallit.” End of his words. From the straightforward reading of his words, it implies that even if tzitzit are placed on it after sewing – it does not help. And so held our Rabbi the Beit Yosef in his intention in Section 4. However, these words are very puzzling, for all the decisors agreed that sewing is considered a complete connection, as I wrote in Section 2. It seems more reasonable to slightly push his language and say that the Rosh also intended regarding the tzitzit that were on it. When he wrote "and if one makes tzitzit on it," his intention was regarding the piece of the tear before sewing. And when he wrote "and even though it is sewn it is considered as if it is cut," his intention was also before the sewing, and his intention was only that the sewing does not help regarding the previous [state]. (And so wrote the Taz in Section 4, and this is also necessary from the Talmudic discussion there, and so ruled the Bach. And the Beit Yosef concluded that a God-fearing person should fulfill [everything] wherever possible, see there. And according to what I wrote, this is only the opinion of Rashi, Rav Amram, and as explained by the Nimukei Yosef, and as clarified, it is not completely ruled out. And with us who do not sew with wool, and tzitzit are only of wool – it is permitted according to all opinions. And be precise and you will find ease.)

And our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 5: If it tore from the hole where the tzitzit is hanging and downwards, if the placement of the tzitzit preceded the tear, and the tzitzit was there at the time of the tear – it is valid. And if it tore and any amount of it remained and it was sewn, and afterward the tzitzit was placed on it, if it is made of wool – it is valid according to all opinions. But if it is made of other materials where it is customary to sew with threads of that same material – it should not be sewn according to Rashi. And if it tore and it was sewn, and afterward the tzitzit was placed on it – there is room for doubt. Thus far his words, and his words need clarification.

And this is its explanation: It has already been explained in Siman 11 that the tzitzit must be placed above the distance of a thumb's width from the edge of the tallit. Only if, after making the tzitzit, it tears from the hole downward and the tzitzit hang below the thumb's width, is it kosher. The Torah only insists on this at the time of making, see there. And this is what he says: "If it tore from the hole... if it preceded... it is kosher." And afterwards, he says, "If it tore and a part remained..." meaning: if it tore before the tzitzit were attached, one must sew it even if a small piece remains, because it needs the thumb's width. The same applies if it tore completely, leaving no part. And when he wrote "a part remained," it does not refer to tearing from the hole downward but rather the entire edge of the corner of the tallit being cut off, in which case some part must remain according to the opinion of Rav Amram, as I have written. The concern is only according to Rashi due to the thread of sewing. Thus, he says, "if it is of wool," meaning if the tallit is of wool, it is kosher according to all opinions. For according to Rav Amram, some part remains connected. And according to Rashi, there is no way to sew with wool threads. However, if the tallit is of other materials that are typically sewn, meaning that the tzitzit are also kosher from them, it should not be sewn according to Rashi due to the thread of sewing. According to what I have written, since we only make tzitzit from wool, there is no concern according to Rashi even with other materials. For extra stringency, it should be sewn with colored threads, thus eliminating any concern according to Rashi, as all our tzitzit are white. All the more so according to Rav Amram’s opinion, there is no concern because part remains connected. And he says further: "If it tore and he sewed it, and afterwards he attached tzitzit, there is a doubt." Meaning: if it tore completely from the tallit, there is a doubt according to Rav Amram’s opinion. According to the Nimukei Yosef, it is permissible to attach tzitzit afterwards, and according to the Rosh, it is invalid. And this is according to the opinion of the Beit Yosef in the words of the Rosh. But according to what I have written, the Rosh also holds this way. (And the Gra wrote that there is a doubt according to Rashi’s opinion: whether it is a hindrance even after the fact or not, see there.)

He further wrote: One who sews a piece of fabric to the corners of the tallit, and similarly, the practice of sewing around the hole where the tzitzit is placed—if the tallit is made of silk and one sews it with white silk thread—one should be concerned according to Rashi's opinion that there should not be any sewing below three fingerbreadths or above the thumb joint. The same applies to any place where one sews with a thread that is from the tzitzit, as we are concerned that he might take that thread for the tzitzit thread. So far his words, and his statements are clear. Similarly, there is a concern according to Rashi's opinion regarding sewing around the hole, but for woolen tallitot there is no concern as explained. And for other types of tallitot as well, according to our custom where the tzitzit are only made of wool as I have written. And if indeed they make tzitzit from other types of materials, one should sew with a colored thread. (And in retrospect, one could perhaps rely on the opinion of Rav Amram, as the great authorities have written that most of the decisors follow his view. And see the Magen Avraham, subsection 14, who wrote that therefore the world customarily sews a piece of fabric to the corners of the tallit on the opposite side, because most garments, even new ones, have sewing within three fingerbreadths. And according to Rav Amram, it is invalid... see there. It is not understood, as it is not commonly completely torn. Rather, it is more reasonable to say to follow Rashi's opinion, so that it will be strong and will not require sewing within three fingerbreadths. Examine and you will find it easy.)

It was taught in Menachot (40b): A tallit that a minor can cover his head and most of his body with, and an adult can wear it temporarily, is obligated in tzitzit. If the minor cannot cover his head and most of his body with it, even though an adult can wear it temporarily, it is exempt. See there. And certainly, there is a specific age for this minor, as it is unreasonable to refer to a child of one or two years old or slightly older. Indeed, Rambam writes at the beginning of the third chapter: a minor who can walk alone in the market and does not need another to guard him. This is his language. However, even this measurement is not clear, as it cannot be said that this is a minor who does not need his mother, which is around the age of four or five as stated at the beginning of the eighth chapter of Eruvin, for if that were the case, Rambam would have used that language. Therefore, it is certain he means older than this. The Tur writes nine years old, see there. Perhaps this measurement comes because we find in the Talmud (Yevamot 96b) that a nine-year-old is considered capable of intercourse – indicating that at this age, he has reached some level of maturity. Nimukei Yosef writes: a minor who is embarrassed to go outside without a covering. See there. And it appears to me that since the Tur provided a measurement and they did not, we hold by the Tur. And perhaps they also agree, as if we tried to measure by their standard, we still would not know exactly how much. (The Taz brings up the case of minors, and it requires investigation. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

The Rambam did not mention at all the condition that an adult can wear it temporarily, only that a child can cover his head and most of his body with it. But the Tur wrote that the size of a tallit to be obligated in tzitzit is: any tallit that a nine-year-old child can cover his head and most of his body with, and an adult would not be embarrassed to go out to the market with it occasionally. However, if the child cannot cover his head and most of his body with it, even though an adult can go out with it occasionally to the market, it is exempt. Thus is his wording. And many have taken it that the Rambam and the Tur disagree: that the Rambam holds that it is sufficient if the child can cover…, and the Tur holds that both conditions are required. Based on this, our master the Rema wrote regarding the words of our master the Beit Yosef, which are in the style of the Rambam. He wrote, and this is his wording: specifically when the adult wears it occasionally and goes out with it to the market. Thus is his wording. And they also examined: why did the Tanna not mention the second case, if the child can cover himself but the adult does not go out with it occasionally. Each one elaborated according to his method (see Beit Yosef, Bach, Drisha, Taz, and Magen Avraham). They also examined what the law is when an adult goes out with it regularly and the child cannot cover himself with it, and they agreed that it is obligated in tzitzit (Bach, Magen Avraham, and Eliyah Rabbah). And certainly, this is so, for a garment that an adult regularly goes out with, why should it be exempt?

However, in my humble opinion, all this effort is unnecessary. It is certain that all these laws apply to adults, as minors are not obligated in mitzvot. Therefore, the Rambam did not need to clarify except regarding an item for a minor that serves as a sign, and there was no need to mention adults since the default is that we are discussing adults. The baraita states: A garment in which a minor can cover his head and most of his body is obligated in tzitzit. This is puzzling: the Torah says "with which you cover yourself," and it is directed at adults. It is obvious that a garment in which a minor can cover his head and most of his body will not suffice for an adult, as it is not customary for an adult to go out in such a short garment, and if he does, his opinion is disregarded. This is what the baraita resolves: and an adult can go out with it temporarily, meaning that although it is certainly not suitable for regular use, it can be used temporarily. The Torah obligates even when one goes out with it temporarily. The Rabbis have determined that any garment in which a minor can cover his head and most of his body is suitable for an adult temporarily. However, according to this logic, one might argue that even less than this measure might be suitable temporarily; therefore, it states that if a minor cannot cover his head and most of his body, even if an adult goes out with it temporarily, it is exempt. But the reverse is not possible, as it is inconceivable that if only a minor can cover his head and most of his body, it would be suitable for an adult temporarily. Thus, the entire law depends on the minor, which is why the Rambam did not mention more. The Tur copied the language of the Gemara, and we interpret it as in the Gemara. However, in any case, the Rambam and the Tur do not disagree at all. Also, the inquiries of the great scholars about an adult going out with it regularly are impossible according to our explanation. If someone does so, his opinion is disregarded. (This seems to be my humble opinion. It appears to me that this is the opinion of Rabbi Yitzchak Aboab as brought in the Beit Yosef, though he was very brief. According to what I have written, everything they questioned is resolved. Also, what the Magen Avraham wrote in subparagraph 2, that if the adult is embarrassed, he is exempt—this is incorrect, because since the Sages measured that with this measure an adult can go out temporarily, who can dispute this? Whoever is embarrassed, his opinion is disregarded, and all measurements of the Sages are like this.)

The great sages have also investigated and protested against the custom of wearing very small tallitot (prayer shawls) and making tzitzit (fringes) on them, and wearing them in the public domain on Shabbat. They have protested vehemently and written that at the very least, the length of the tallit should be one and a half cubits, three-quarters of a cubit in front and three-quarters behind. If we consider according to the cubits of the Talmud, three-quarters of a cubit is nine vershoks according to the measurement of our country, Russia. According to them, those who wear smaller than this do not fulfill the obligation of tzitzit, meaning it is as if they are walking without a garment that requires tzitzit. Consequently, it is forbidden to go out with them on Shabbat, as the tzitzit are considered significant and are not nullified. Therefore, I am puzzled by those who wrote that it is better to wear it than to go without tzitzit at all (Magen Avraham in the name of the Rema), but isn’t it considered a burden on Shabbat? They wrote to warn the public not to do this (Taz and Bach, etc.). At the very least, it should be three-quarters of a cubit in length on each side and half a cubit in width. The shoulders should be wide, meaning it is open in the middle, and if they are not wide, it appears as if the entire thing is open. (What the Magen Avraham wrote about not bringing air from one side... it is obvious that this is not relevant here, and only applies to partitions and places considered sealed. But his intention is as we have written, and so wrote the Machatzit Hashekel.)

In my humble opinion, all this investigation is unnecessary, and people fulfill the mitzvah of tzitzit with small tallitot. As we have already explained at the beginning of Siman 8 from the Nimukei Yosef and the Ritva, some of the early authorities said that tzitzit is only applicable to a garment that covers the head and most of the body. According to this, all our small tallitot would not be obligated in tzitzit. However, their words were rejected, and according to Torah law, any four-cornered garment worn on the body is obligated in tzitzit, see there. And this is also the opinion of Rabbi Yosef Karo, as I wrote there. The requirement to cover most of the body pertains to the outer tallit, which is like the cloak in the time of the Gemara, which was their manner of dress as is known. Therefore, we bless on it "to wrap in tzitzit." For this, we need a specific size since it is worn over the clothes. But a small tallit worn under the clothes does not need any specific size at all; as long as it has four corners, it is obligated in tzitzit. This is also explicitly explained in the words of the Ritva and the Nimukei Yosef that we brought in paragraph 4, see there.

Women are exempt from the obligation of tzitzit because it is a positive time-bound commandment, as it applies only during the day and not at night. We derive this exemption through a comparison to tefillin, from which women are also exempt (Kiddushin 35a). Therefore, even though women are obligated in the prohibition of mixing wool and linen (kilayim), and the verse places tzitzit next to the prohibition of kilayim as it is written, "You shall not wear shatnez... you shall make tassels for yourself" – we do not say that anyone obligated in shatnez is also obligated in tzitzit. This is similar to the derivation regarding matzah: anyone who is included in the prohibition of "you shall not eat chametz" is included in the obligation to "eat matzah," and women are obligated (Pesachim 43a). The comparison to tefillin takes precedence over the juxtaposition in the verses (Tosafot Yevamot 4a). Additionally, the juxtaposition of shatnez to tzitzit is only to permit the wearing of kilayim in tzitzit (Ramban, second chapter of Shabbat in Milchamot). This is also clarified by the language of the Rambam in the tenth chapter of Kilayim, law 4, see there. (And even though in Menachot 43a it appears that we derive the juxtaposition also for the obligation and exemption of tzitzit, see there – there is no need to be concerned about it. The Tanna informs us so as not to make a mistake, that even according to a mistaken view, it is not so, see there. Examine it closely, and you will find it straightforward.)

And since women are exempt, slaves are also exempt, for they are only obligated in commandments like a woman. And the Rambam wrote in the third chapter, law 9, that women and slaves who want to wrap themselves [in a tallit] can do so without a blessing. And similarly, with other positive commandments from which women are exempt, if they want to perform them without a blessing, we do not protest against them. Thus are his words. But our women do recite a blessing on the Sukkah and the Lulav, and we follow the opinion of Rabbeinu Tam in Tosafot on Rosh Hashanah (Rosh Hashanah 33a, s.v. "ha") that they can recite a blessing even though they are exempt. According to this, it would seem that with tzitzit as well, they can wrap themselves and recite a blessing.

But in truth, we have not heard of this. And we do not allow them (women) to wear a tallit, and certainly not to recite a blessing. It is not analogous to the shofar, sukkah, or lulav, which are once a year and the mitzvah is momentary, but tzitzit is a mitzvah for the entire year and it is not appropriate for women. Additionally, all mitzvot are obligatory for men, and therefore women can also perform them. But tzitzit is not obligatory, as I wrote in Siman 19, so how can we allow women to perform it? This is the intention of our master, the Rema, who wrote: "Nevertheless, if they want... however, it appears as arrogance." Therefore, women should not wear tzitzit, since it is not an obligatory mitzvah for an individual. Until here is his language, meaning: it appears as arrogance because it is constant, and also because it is not obligatory for a man unless he has a four-cornered garment. Therefore, we do not allow this mitzvah to be practiced. This is the custom and it should not be changed.

A tumtum and an androgynous person, the Rambam ruled there that they are obligated in tzitzit out of doubt, but they should not recite a blessing. However, according to what we hold like Rabbeinu Tam – they can also recite a blessing. And so ruled Rabbeinu the Rema. And one should not say: how is it appropriate to say "and commanded us" for women in commandments that they are not obligated in? For "and commanded us" refers to men, meaning: to the entirety of Israel. However, they also receive reward like one who is not commanded but performs (Magen Avraham, small section 1). And a blind person is obligated in tzitzit, for although it is written "and you shall see it" – this excludes a night garment. And a blind person is included from "with which you cover yourself" which is redundant. And a blind person is preferable to night, for he is subject to being seen by others (Magen Avraham 3).

Maimonides wrote there: "It is a rabbinic decree that any minor who knows how to wrap himself [in a tallit] is obligated in tzitzit in order to train him in the mitzvot." This means that his father is obligated to obtain a tallit for him (Beit Yosef and Magen Avraham). This is also stated in the Mordechai according to the Jerusalem Talmud there. This is puzzling: even the father himself is not obligated to obtain a tallit, so how can we be stricter regarding the training of his son than on himself? I did not find this in the Jerusalem Talmud at all, but rather the language of our Talmud: "obligated in tzitzit," meaning if he wears a garment with four corners. This requires further investigation. Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote that this is specifically when the child knows how to wrap two tzitzit in front of him and two tzitzit behind him, and knows how to hold the tzitzit in his hand during the recitation of Shema. These are his exact words. And our custom is that when the child is three years old, we dress him in tzitzit. And the sign for you is: "For three years it shall be considered uncircumcised to you," and "Man is like the tree of the field." And we accustom him to the letters of the Torah, as written in the books of the pious (Sha'arei Teshuvah, subsection 4).

It has already been explained that nighttime is not the time for tzitzit. However, there is a dispute among the authorities regarding this: According to the Rambam, it depends on the time and not on the garment, whereas according to the Rosh, it depends on the garment and not on the time. That is to say, according to the Rambam, even a garment designated for daytime is exempt at night, and a garment designated for nighttime is obligated during the day. According to the Rosh, it is the opposite: a garment designated for daytime is obligated even at night, and a garment designated for nighttime is exempt even during the day. The reason it is called "a positive commandment that is time-bound" is because the night causes the garment designated for it to be exempt – thus it is indeed a positive commandment that is time-bound, and women are exempt (Rosh, beginning of Hilchot Tzitzit). A garment designated for both day and night, it is taught in the Sifrei in the section of Tzitzit that it is obligated in tzitzit (there). This is also explicitly stated in the Jerusalem Talmud, the first chapter of Kiddushin (Halacha 7).

And ostensibly, this presents a significant refutation of the Rambam. The Rosh brought proof for his viewpoint, from the fact that throughout the Talmud it says "to exclude nighttime garments" – thus it is dependent on the garment. In my humble opinion, it appears that the Rambam's approach is necessary according to our Talmud, and the approach of the Sifri follows the Jerusalem Talmud, which clearly demonstrates that it disagrees with our Talmud. For behold, in Menachot (43a), Rabbi Shimon expounds "and you shall see it" – excluding nighttime garments. And "with which you cover yourself" – to include the garment of a blind person, and women are exempt. And we hold according to Rabbi Shimon as written by the Rif, Tosafot, and all the early authorities (see Beit Yosef). And it raises a question against the Rabbis: what do they do with "with which you cover yourself"? And Rashi explains: that to exclude the garment of a blind person is unnecessary, for now that nighttime garments are obligated – all the more so the garment of a blind person, since it is visible to others. Thus far his words. And he resolves that it is necessary to include a garment with five corners that is obligated in tzitzit, and Rabbi Shimon includes it from "with which", see there.

In the Jerusalem Talmud, it is stated that there is a dispute between Rabbi Shimon and the Rabbis. Rabbi Shimon said to them: "Do you not agree with me that it is a positive time-bound commandment? For a night garment is exempt from tzitzit." Rabbi Hila explained the reasoning of the Rabbis, that if it is designated for both day and night, it is obligated in tzitzit. According to this, even the Rabbis agree that a night garment is exempt from tzitzit. However, they consider it a non-time-bound positive commandment because a garment designated for both day and night is obligated in tzitzit. If you think that our Talmud holds this view, what would the Rabbis derive from "which you cover yourself with"? This is necessary for the covering of a blind person, as they also believe that a night garment is exempt. Additionally, throughout the Talmud, it is clear that only Rabbi Shimon holds that a night garment is exempt. Therefore, it is certain that the Jerusalem Talmud follows the opinion of the Rosh, while our Talmud follows the Rambam. This is why the Sifrei is not cited in our Talmud or the Rambam. When the Talmud says "night garment," it simply means that night is exempt from tzitzit, and consequently, a garment designated for night does not require tzitzit. Rashi explicitly interpreted it this way. In Menachot, he explained: "It is a time-bound commandment, as night is not the time for tzitzit according to Rabbi Shimon, and day is its time. The Rabbis hold that night is the time for tzitzit." In Shabbat (25b), he explained: "However, the Rabbis decreed concerning it because of a night garment, lest one have a garment designated for nights..." According to the Rambam, the exemption depends on the time, yet he wrote "night garment," meaning that typically a garment designated for night is worn at night. But the main point depends on the time.

This is the wording of our teacher, the Beit Yosef, in Section 1: Night is not a time for tzitzit, as it is excluded by "and you shall see it." According to the Rambam, anything worn at night is exempt, even if it is designated for daytime use, and anything worn during the day is obligated, even if it is designated for nighttime use. According to the Rosh, a garment designated for night use is exempt even when worn during the day, and a garment designated for day or both day and night use is obligated even when worn at night. That is his wording. According to the Rosh, one recites a blessing at night when wearing a daytime garment, as he wrote in his rulings there, even though Rabbeinu Tam, of blessed memory, holds in one explanation that one does not recite a blessing at night. Also, if the tzitzit become damaged at night, they do not need to be repaired until daylight, which aligns somewhat with the approach of the Rambam, of blessed memory. Consequently, according to this view, when kilayim (a mixture of wool and linen) is permitted in tzitzit, it is not permitted at night, even in a daytime garment. Nevertheless, the Rosh ruled according to the other explanation that one recites a blessing at night and is obligated to repair them if they become damaged. And when kilayim is permitted, it is permitted even at night. The decree regarding a linen garment with tzitzit, because of a night garment, means a garment designated for night use. According to the Rambam, it means that one might wrap oneself in it at night.

And this is the language of the Rambam in Chapter Three, Law 7: A linen garment – one does not place blue dye (tekhelet) in it…, a rabbinic decree lest he cover himself with it at night when it is not the time of the obligation of tzitzit, and he transgresses a negative commandment… It is permissible for a person to wear tzitzit at night, whether on a weekday or on Shabbat. And even though it is not its time, provided that he does not recite a blessing. This is his language, meaning: do not say that since night is not the time for tzitzit – it is forbidden to go with them at night, as it would be "adding to the commandment" (bal tosif), just as it is forbidden to wear tefillin at night and one is required to remove them. And certainly on Shabbat night to go out with them into the public domain. This is not so, for it is an adornment to the garment since it has the obligation of tzitzit during the day. And according to the Rosh, regarding a garment designated for night – it is certainly forbidden to place tzitzit on it, as it would be "adding to the commandment", and all the more so it is forbidden to go out with it on Shabbat into the public domain. However, even according to the Rambam, it is only permissible with tzitzit that are not of mixed fabric (shaatnez), but those of mixed fabric – are forbidden at night on a weekday, and all the more so on Shabbat. (This is what the Beit Yosef wrote. And the Bach exerted himself to say that according to the Rambam even those of mixed fabric are permissible, and he does not disagree with Rabbeinu Tam. And they only prohibited those of linen and not of wool, see there. All his words are strained, and the main ruling is like the Beit Yosef. And so wrote the Derisha.)

However, it is necessary to understand the opinion of the Rambam, that mixed fabrics (kilayim) in tzitzit are only permitted during the day and prohibited at night. How can it be said that the Torah commanded such a thing? After all, the Torah was not given to ministering angels. For this reason, it is stated in Kiddushin (54a) that the priests are permitted to wear their priestly garments even after the service, despite the fact that they contain mixed fabrics, because the Torah was not given to ministering angels who would immediately remove their garments after the service. See there. Now, by a fortiori reasoning, if the priests, who are diligent, cannot adhere to this requirement of immediately removing their garments after the service, how much more so for the general populace of Israel. And if they do not remove them at twilight, there is a potential prohibition. Therefore, it appears to me that this is why the Rambam was precise in saying "lest he cover himself with it at night," and not "lest he wear it at night." For surely there is no prohibition if he does not remove it at night, due to the reason we stated, that the Torah was not given [to ministering angels]. Rather, "lest he cover himself with it at night" means after he removes it, he puts it back on, which would certainly be a transgression. Thus, according to this, even according to the Rambam, if one wears a tzitzit of mixed fabrics during the day, he may also wear it at night. Only when he removes it is he not permitted to wear it again. (And if we scrutinize, we can align it with the second explanation of Rabbeinu Tam brought by the Rosh there, which he rejected. See there. And examine carefully and you will find it easy.)

According to this, in practice, we must be concerned with both approaches, as our master the Rema wrote in paragraph 1, and this is his language: "In cases of doubt regarding blessings, we are lenient; therefore, one should not recite the blessing on it unless they wear it during the day and it is designated for daytime use. After the evening prayer, even though it is still day, one should not recite the blessing on it. On the eve of Yom Kippur, one should wrap themselves in it while it is still day and recite the blessing on it." This is his language. The reason is that on Yom Kippur we are likened to angels (Bach). Also, one should not recite the Thirteen Attributes without being wrapped (Magen Avraham), because on Rosh Hashanah (17b) it is stated that the Holy One, blessed be He, wrapped Himself like a prayer leader when He told Moses the Thirteen Attributes; see there. From this, we learn that every prayer leader who stands before the ark must be wrapped in a tallit. Some have written that even the one reciting the mourner's kaddish should be wrapped out of respect for the congregation (there). However, this is not the custom. Certainly, the sage who delivers a sermon must be wrapped out of respect for the congregation, and this is the custom. Also, the sandek (the one holding the baby during the circumcision) and the mohels should be wrapped in a tallit out of respect for the Angel of the Covenant. (See Magen Avraham, subsection 1, who wrote in the name of the Bach that immediately after "Barchu" he should remove the tallit. According to what we have written, there is no need, as the Torah was not given... However, in Shaarei Teshuva, it is mentioned that the Ari, of blessed memory, was careful not to go wrapped in a tallit and tefillin after sunset; see there.)

Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in Section 2: "Bed sheets, even though a person sleeps in them in the morning, do not require tzitzit." Thus are his words, meaning: because they are primarily intended for nighttime use. And it seems that without this reasoning, they would be obligated in tzitzit, even though one does not wear and wrap in them, but rather uses them to cover the body while sleeping. According to this, there is a question about the common custom not to put tzitzit on them, because according to the Rambam, a nighttime garment used during the day is obligated in tzitzit. And indeed, many times one covers their body while sleeping during the day (see Beit Yosef). However, some say that this is what is stated in the Sifrei: "A garment" – to exclude a sheet, see there. Meaning: the Torah only obligates tzitzit on a garment that one wears on their body or wraps themselves in, like in the time of the Gemara when they used to wrap themselves in sheets (Shabbat 25b). But a sheet on one's bed, which one uses to cover their body, is not considered a garment at all and is exempt from tzitzit (Magen Avraham, Section 3). And "with which you cover yourself" means in the manner of a garment, which wraps and covers the body when worn. And this is the main halachic ruling. (And the Magen Avraham there deduced from Tosafot Menachot 41a, who wrote that regarding tzitzit, there is no distinction between spreading and wearing, implying that even when spreading it out, it is obligated in tzitzit, see there. And I am puzzled, for the Tosafot wrote this about a garment that one wears, that then even when it is spread out, it is obligated in tzitzit and the prohibition of mixed fabrics is permitted, see there carefully. And similarly, the matter from the Sifrei that they bring. But a sheet that is only for spreading out is exempt from tzitzit. Be precise and you will find the truth.)

From when does one bless on the tzitzit in the morning? From when one can distinguish between the blue [threads] and the white [threads]. And now that we do not have blue threads, we should estimate the difference in colors between blue and white, if one can distinguish, he should bless on it. Nevertheless, some say that if one wears it from dawn, he should bless on it. And the same applies in the evening until the stars come out - if one wears it, he blesses on it (Magen Avraham, small section 4). And it seems to me the reason: that there are several commandments whose ideal time is from sunrise, but after the fact, it is valid from dawn, as it is taught at the end of the second chapter of Megillah. And even though here it is written "and you shall see it," it is still day and a time of seeing. Therefore, if one wears it at dawn, he blesses on it, as it is considered after the fact. And if he wears it before dawn, such as during the days of Selichot or in the winter when he rises before the light of day, he wears it without a blessing, and when the day becomes light, he should touch it and bless. Or for us, he fulfills it with the blessing on the large tallit, as I wrote in Siman 8, section 16, see there. However, after sunset, it seems that one should not bless on it (Rabbi Akiva Eiger).

It has already been explained that the commandment of tzitzit is not an obligation like tefillin and mezuzah, for if one does not have a garment with four corners, he is exempt from this commandment unless he has such a garment. Also, there is a debate in Menachot (42b) whether it is an obligation of the garment, meaning that when he has a garment with four corners, even if it is placed in a box, he is obligated in tzitzit, or if it is specifically an obligation of the person, meaning when he wears it, then he is obligated in tzitzit, but when he does not wear it, he is exempt. There is also a practical difference regarding the blessing, as we hold that every blessing on a commandment must be recited at the time of the completion of the commandment. Therefore, if it is an obligation of the garment, he must say the blessing "Who sanctified us... to make tzitzit," as this is the completion of the commandment. But if it is an obligation of the person, then the commandment is at the time of wearing it, and he blesses then "on the commandment of tzitzit" or "to wrap in tzitzit." And this is the ruling we follow, that it is an obligation of the person, and the blessing is at the time of wearing and wrapping (there). (And it seems to me that if it were an obligation of the garment, one would only need to bless once.)

There is a question in this: Mezuzah is also an obligation associated with dwelling, and if a person does not live in the house, they are exempt from the mezuzah. Yet, we hold in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 289, that one recites a blessing at the time of affixing it to the doorpost, not when moving in to live there (Magen Avraham, section 1). We must say that with a mezuzah, it is assumed that one will live there immediately, which is not the case with a tallit (there). Even if one is not yet living there, it is still assumed that they will bring some household items into the house, and it is therefore obligated in a mezuzah, as explained there in Siman 286. Following this reasoning, one might say that if someone is wearing a tallit and its tzitzit become invalid, when they make the tzitzit and immediately wear the tallit, they should bless "to make tzitzit" just like with a mezuzah, "to affix a mezuzah" (there). However, this is not truly comparable, because with a tallit, when the tzitzit become invalid, one must immediately remove the tallit, unlike with a mezuzah, where if it becomes invalid, one is not required to vacate the dwelling (there). Additionally, fundamentally it is not comparable. Certainly, if the blessing on tzitzit were only once at the time of starting the mitzvah and not more, like with a mezuzah, then we could properly bless at the conclusion of making them, and it would not matter if one wears it immediately or not. But with tzitzit, one must bless each time they put it on, since it is an obligation on the individual and not on the tallit. Therefore, it is not possible to change the blessing from the first time to subsequent times. (And as stated in Menachot there, where it is said to bless at the conclusion of making them, this is according to the opinion that it is an obligation on the tallit. See there. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

If one made a tallit (prayer shawl) for the purpose of being used as burial shrouds, even though he may occasionally wear it during his lifetime, it is exempt from tzitzit (fringes). This is because it is like a nighttime garment, which is exempt even during the day according to the opinion of the Rosh. Even according to the Rambam, it is not considered "your garment" at all since it is not a garment for the living (Beit Yosef). There are those who question this and suggest that according to the Rambam, when it is worn, it is obligated in tzitzit (Magen Avraham, subsection 2). In the Gemara, this was only stated according to the opinion that holds the obligation of the tallit itself; see there (Menachot 41a).

We learn in Menachot (43a): The Rabbis taught: One who purchases a fringed garment (tallit) from the market from a Jew – it retains its presumed status. From a Samaritan or from a merchant – it is valid. From an ordinary person – it is invalid. And even though they said a person is not permitted to sell a fringed garment to a Samaritan until he unties its fringes, see there (for further details). And when purchasing from a Jew, there is no particular novelty, as all Jews are trustworthy when they are not suspected, as explained in Yoreh De'ah, section 119. And it seems to me that the innovation is that even though tekhelet (blue dye) is only to be obtained from an expert, as it is stated there earlier and as I wrote in section 8 – this applies only to tekhelet alone. But a fringed garment can be purchased from anyone, and it retains its presumed status that the one who made this garment bought the tekhelet from an expert (see Bayit Chadash, but his words require further examination). And the Tur and Shulchan Aruch who wrote this law, even though now we do not have tekhelet and there is no innovation in this, nevertheless they copied the law from the Gemara as is their holy custom.

And for a Samaritan merchant, it is valid, as a merchant would not harm his reputation, and certainly, he bought it from a Jew, making it valid (Rashi). But from an ordinary person – it is invalid, as perhaps it was made without the proper intention (ibid.). And it is not specifically that he is a merchant in prayer shawls, but even if he is a merchant in other items – he is also believed. Some have questioned: What relevance is there to "not harming his reputation" in matters of prohibition, as "harming his reputation" pertains to merchandise that is inherently problematic, like fish brine mixed with vinegar, and not to the issue of improper intention, which makes no physical difference? Otherwise, we would permit buying meat from a Samaritan when he claims he bought it from a Jew. Therefore, it is written that only for a prayer shawl do we permit, because it is not their usual practice to make fringes on garments. But buying the fringes themselves – it is forbidden to purchase even from a merchant (Magen Avraham, subsection 1). And some prohibit for another reason to buy fringes from a merchant: only when he sells a prayer shawl with fringes, as the main profit is from the prayer shawl – he is believed regarding the fringes due to "not harming his reputation." But not when he sells the fringes alone, as the profit is from the fringes, in which case he is not believed due to "not harming his reputation" (Taz, subsection 1). (And some say that when buying from a merchant – one must untie the fringes. This is not conclusive.)

In my humble opinion, from the language of the Baraita it is clearly implied that it specifically mentions a tallit (prayer shawl) to emphasize a point. Even though it is said that a person is not permitted to sell a tallit with tzitzit (fringes) to a non-Jew, nevertheless, he is believed (and this is also written by the Eliyah Rabbah). Therefore, our teacher, the Rema, was precise in saying that if the merchant claims he bought it from a Jew, he is believed. This is his language. His intention is also this: if not, he would not harm his reputation at all, as he could say, "How should I know that it needs to be made ‘for its own sake'?" and the merchandise is good. Therefore, it is necessary to say that if a merchant claims he bought it from a Jew, he is believed, meaning that it was spun, twisted, and attached for the sake of the mitzvah. And since he is a merchant, he would not harm his reputation by lying in his statement. The reason why meat is not bought from a merchant is for a different reason: because the Sages forbade meat that was out of sight. But certainly, this law also applies solely to tzitzit. Nevertheless, in practice, it is difficult to disagree with the great authorities of the later generations.

And this is why one should not sell a tallit with tzitzit to a non-Jew: the reason is that he might accompany a Jew on the way and kill him, or give it to a prostitute as payment, and people will say: "A Jew gave it to her" (Gemara Menachot there). And even to a merchant, it is forbidden to sell, contrary to those who are lenient in this matter (Magen Avraham, subsection 2). And know that it is said in the chapter "Ein Ma'amidin" (39a) that one should not send tekhelet by the hand of a non-Jew except with two seals, as with meat and milk. And some have written: specifically tekhelet, which is expensive, but for our tzitzit, one seal suffices. And some say: since it is a biblical prohibition, two seals are required (Magen Avraham, subsection 1). And this is specifically when there is concern that he will benefit in exchange. But otherwise, there is no concern, as he is not suspected of causing stumbling. And the same law applies to a Jew who is suspected, and similarly when depositing with them, and the details of these laws are explained in Yoreh De'ah, section 118. And some say that if they are twisted and separated, it is permissible (there), as it is evident that they are tzitzit. And just as one should not sell a tallit with tzitzit to a non-Jew, similarly one should not lend a tallit to him when it has tzitzit, and likewise, one should not deposit it with him. Unless it is deposited for a short time, as there is no concern for these aforementioned suspicions.

It is stated in Megillah (26b): Items used for a mitzvah may be discarded. Items used for holiness must be put in genizah (a designated storage area for sacred items). These are the items used for a mitzvah: a sukkah, a lulav, a shofar, and tzitzit. And items used for holiness... a Torah scroll cover, and a tefillin pouch... At first glance, "items used for a mitzvah" would also seem to be similar to "items used for holiness," in that it does not refer to the holiness itself but to something that served for holiness, like a cover or a pouch. Here too, items used for a mitzvah do not refer to the mitzvah itself, but something that served the mitzvah. However, it is impossible to say this, for since the mitzvah does not have intrinsic holiness, how could the items that served the mitzvah become sanctified? What is the teaching here? And none of the halachic authorities explained it this way, as is evident from their words.

It appears to me that from this the Sheiltot cited by the Tur derived, where it is written in the portion "Shelach": It is forbidden for the children of Israel to use items that are designated for fulfilling a commandment, such as threads fixed in a tallit... that we learn from the blood... that we say one should not cover it with his feet, so that the commandments should not be degraded. Specifically, items used for a commandment after the commandment has been performed with them – are discarded. Thus is his language. And the Tur objected to this, saying it is not comparable to blood, because when covering with the feet it is a manner of disgrace, which is not the case here... thus is his language. In my humble opinion, it seems that the Sheiltot did not derive this from the blood, but rather from calling it "items used for a commandment" – hence it is understood that it does not refer to the time when they are fit for the commandment, because if so, they are the commandment itself and not items used for a commandment. Instead, it refers to after the commandment has been performed with them, meaning they are no longer fit for the commandment, such as when they become invalid. And it is rightly called "items used for a commandment," meaning: it served the commandment, and when it was valid, it was the commandment itself. And after it became invalid, it is called that it served the commandment. And also the tallit is called "items used for a commandment," having served the tzitzit. (And what he wrote that we learn from the blood – it is not derived from that but rather stated as a reason. But the essence of his ruling is from the language, and this is also implied from Rashi there. Study it and you will find it light.)

And this is the language of the Rambam in the third chapter, law 9: It is permitted to enter the bathroom and the bathhouse with tzitzit. If the white or blue threads are torn, they should be thrown into the garbage, because it is a commandment item that does not have inherent sanctity. End of his words, meaning: Therefore, it is permitted to enter the bathroom and the bathhouse with them, because they do not have sanctity. And this is not a disgrace to the commandment, for this is the way of people and he is not doing anything with them. Nevertheless, using the tzitzit for any other purpose is forbidden as per the words of the Sheiltot. However, if they are torn, they are now just items used for a commandment and should be thrown into the garbage because they do not have sanctity, only items used for a commandment and are discarded. (See Beit Yosef and Taz. And according to what we have written, the words of the Sheiltot emerge from the body of the Talmud in Megillah.)

And so wrote our Rabbi, the Beit Yosef, in Section 1, that when the tzitzit are torn off, one can throw them into the trash. As long as they are attached to the tallit, it is forbidden to use them for any other purpose, such as tying something with them or similar uses, due to the disrespect for the mitzvah. This is his wording. Our Rabbi the Rema wrote on this: There are those who say that even after they are torn off, one should not treat them disrespectfully by throwing them in a disgraceful place, but they do not require burial. There are those who are meticulous to bury them, and one who is stringent and meticulous in mitzvot will be blessed. This is his wording. To me, it seems his intention is that from the fundamental law, he wrote this. For though our sages said that accessories of a mitzvah can be discarded, it does not mean to treat them with actual disrespect, like throwing them into a bathroom or using them for wiping, Heaven forbid. This is not logical at all. Rather, the intention is that they do not require honorable burial like sacred accessories, but they can be disposed of without honor, yet also not in a disrespectful manner. And in this, no one disagrees. Afterward, he wrote: "There are those who are meticulous to bury them" because perhaps they interpret the words of the Gemara regarding accessories of mitzvah similarly to accessories of holiness, meaning the bag in which the tallit was placed or the tallit itself, but not the invalidated tzitzit. Therefore, he wrote "one who is stringent…" meaning to fulfill the opinion of an individual, since most authorities did not interpret it this way. And thus, it was brought from the Mahari"v to place the tzitzit in a book as a sign (Magen Avraham), meaning he was concerned about this.

A proof to our words: that everyone agrees with the ruling of our teacher, the Rema, from the words of our teacher, the Beit Yosef, in section 2 where he wrote: "Garments used for the mitzvah that have worn out — a person distances himself from them. It is not permitted to use them for wiping oneself, nor to designate them for a disgraceful use. Rather, one throws them away and they are discarded." Until here is his language. And if you thought that the "some say" of our teacher, the Rema, disagrees with the preceding opinion, then the Beit Yosef contradicts himself. Rather, certainly it is according to our words. And in section 2, it teaches us something significant: not only should one not use the tzitzit themselves for a disgraceful use, but even the garments, as I have written.

They wrote in Paragraph 3: It is permitted to enter a bathroom with tzitzit, and all the more so to lie down with them, which is allowed. And there are those who wrote that the custom is not to lie down with a tallit that has tzitzit, nor to give it to a non-Jewish laundress to wash. And all this is so that the commandments should not be disgraced. However, the custom is to be lenient and to lie down with them. So far his words. The reason for those who prohibit lying down with a tallit is not understood: Is lying down worse than a bathhouse or a bathroom? And it appears to me that their reason is: We have already clarified that everyone agrees that anything disgraceful is forbidden even when the tzitzit are invalid, and all the more so when they are valid. And seemingly, entering a bathroom or bathhouse is disgraceful. And we must say the reason, as I wrote, because this is the way of people and it is impossible otherwise except with great effort. Therefore, lying down, since it is the way of people to remove their clothes – if so, it is a disgrace when lying down with a tallit. However, our teacher the Rema ruled that the custom is to be lenient and to lie down with them. And the reason: We do not consider this a disgrace at all. (And on the contrary, the Ari of blessed memory lay down with a small tallit, as the Magen Avraham wrote in Subsection 2.) And there are those who wrote that all this is with a small tallit. But with a large tallit, which is made only for prayer, one should not enter a bathroom with it (Taz, Subsection 3). And certainly this is so, for there is no difficulty in removing it, and if so, it is considered a disgrace to go with it into a bathroom or bathhouse. And it is proper to be careful to remove the tallit even when going out for a minor need. And this is our custom, and all for the reason we have explained.

One must be careful when wearing a tallit not to drag its tzitzit. Regarding this, it is said: "And I will sweep it with the broom of destruction." So wrote our master the Beit Yosef in section 4. There are contradictions in the Gemara (see Magen Avraham section 3). It is possible that the concern is only at the time of wearing, when one makes the blessing, and not afterward. This also seems evident from the phrase "when a person wears a tallit," which implies only at the time of wearing (see Magen Avraham there, who also wrote this from another reason). Some have written that dragging in a disrespectful manner is forbidden (Arotzot HaChaim). This is also implied in the Rokeach, who wrote that one should not step on the tzitzit, see there. It clearly implies that dragging is allowed. How could it not be so, as one is preoccupied with prayer or Torah? Some tuck the corners of the tallit into their belt for this reason. I have not seen great ones do so, and there is no concern if they are occasionally dragged on the ground. (The Ba'er Heitev brought in the name of some who say to differentiate between a large tallit..., see there. This does not seem clear at all.)

The Tur wrote: One who makes tzitzit for himself recites "Shehecheyanu." Thus are his words. And Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote in his great book that it should not be said that his intention is because of the mitzvah, and according to the opinion of Rambam in the eleventh chapter of Blessings, that on tzitzit and tefillin one recites "Shehecheyanu." For if so, why did the Tur write only about tzitzit and not about tefillin? Rather, his intention is that it is not less than a new garment, and the tallit is also like new vessels on which one recites "Shehecheyanu," as I have written in Siman 223.

Based on this, the Shulchan Aruch writes: "If one buys a tallit and makes tzitzit on it, one recites the 'Shehecheyanu' blessing, as it is no less significant than new garments." This is the end of his words. And even though for new garments one recites the blessing at the time of purchase, this applies to utensils that are immediately usable. However, a garment, as long as it is not ready for wearing, one does not recite the blessing. And tzitzit on a tallit, as long as their making is not completed, it is not ready for wearing. (And one must examine the Magen Avraham in section 1 who elaborates on this. It is clear as I have written. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

There are those who have endeavored to prove that the intention of the Tur is due to the mitzvah, and therefore, even with an old garment when one makes tzitzit, one blesses. And the reason he did not write this by tefillin is because in the Tosefta of Berachot, Chapter Six, it is regarding tzitzit (Bach). And this is puzzling: for in the Tosefta it is also explicitly mentioned regarding tefillin, see there. And some have written that the Tur wrote regarding tzitzit, and the same applies to tefillin (Taz). And this is even more puzzling. Therefore, the primary opinion is like that of Rabbeinu Beit Yosef. And it appears to me more likely that the intention of the Rambam is not due to the mitzvah but because of acquiring the object, for he wrote: "And so with every mitzvah that is an acquisition for him, such as tzitzit and tefillin..." thus far his language. And he holds that tefillin is also an acquisition. And the Tur does not hold this for tefillin because it is only for the mitzvah. However, a tallit, even though it is for the mitzvah, is still called a "garment." And Rabbeinu Rema wrote that if one did not bless at the time of making, he blesses at the first wrapping. Thus far his language, and it is clear. (And the Gra in subsection 1 came to differentiate between if one makes it himself and if others make it for him. And I did not understand his reasoning, for what difference does it make? And in the Gemara where they said "for himself," it means: not for others. And Rashi explained so. And the main opinion is like the Beit Yosef. And the Rema in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 28, ruled to bless "Shehecheyanu" for the covering of the blood. If so, why did he not rule so for tefillin? This requires investigation. And the Magen Avraham wrote: because it is not so common, see there. And this is reasonable for circumcision and redemption of the firstborn, but not for covering. And we have already written there not to bless on covering, as that is the conclusion of the Shach there, see what I wrote there, section 10. And when blessing at the time of wrapping, one should first bless "to wrap" and then "Shehecheyanu.")

It is permitted to enter a cemetery while wearing tzitzit, provided that they are not dragging on the graves. However, if they are dragging on the graves, it is forbidden because of "mocking the poor." This is evidenced in Berakhot (18a). And although it is forbidden to enter with exposed tefillin, as will be explained in Siman 45, and there is no issue of dragging with tefillin, tefillin are different because their primary purpose is for a mitzvah, and thus there is an issue of "mocking the poor." But a tallit is just a regular garment, and the Torah requires placing tzitzit on it. Therefore, there is no issue of "mocking the poor" unless the tzitzit are dragging on the graves. But otherwise, it is permitted.

Therefore, the early authorities wrote that this applies specifically in the time of the Talmud, when they would attach tzitzit to garments that they wore for their own use. But our tallitot, which are only for the purpose of the mitzvah, their law reverts to being like that of tefillin. And even if they do not drag [on the ground] – it is forbidden. And specifically when they are exposed it is forbidden with tefillin, and similarly with a tallit when it is covered – it is permitted. Therefore, it is not necessary to remove the tallit katan when going to a cemetery, since it is under one's clothes. Similarly, with a tallit, when one wears an outer garment over it – there is no concern. And just as the law is in a cemetery, so too when one enters within four cubits of a dead person or a grave – the law is the same as in a cemetery. And this law has already been explained in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 367. (And there is a need for further inquiry regarding a small grave or a small dead person, and some say there is no difference. To me, this requires further investigation.)

There are those who have the custom to tie together the two tzitzit from the corners when entering a cemetery. However, this practice is ineffective, as it does not nullify the tzitzit. This is because the knot is not meant to be permanent, as it will be untied immediately. Additionally, according to their reasoning, they would be walking without tzitzit. Furthermore, according to their reasoning, there is a concern of "make, and not from what is already made" (see Magen Avraham, small section 1).

And our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 4 that in a place where it is customary to remove the tzitzit from a garment of a deceased person, if the shoulders are wearing tzitzit, there is concern due to "mocking the poor." Thus are his words. And it implies that in a place where it is not customary to remove [the tzitzit], there is no concern of "mocking the poor," for due to the difference that this one is alive and that one is dead, there is no "mocking the poor." And it is not comparable to a cemetery, where there is concern of "mocking the poor" even in places where they do not remove the tzitzit from the garments of the dead, as explained in his words in Yoreh De'ah, section 351, that since this one has recently died, there is not as much mockery as in a cemetery. Nevertheless, the consensus of the great [authorities] is that even when they do not remove the tzitzit, the shoulders should not go with tzitzit exposed. And there are more laws regarding this, which are explained in Yoreh De'ah there.

It was taught in Menachot (43b): "And you shall see it and remember [...] and do them"—seeing leads to remembering, and remembering leads to doing. And Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai says: Anyone who is diligent in this mitzvah will be rewarded by receiving the Divine Presence. And beloved are the Israelites, whom the Holy One, blessed be He, surrounded with mitzvot: tefillin on their heads and arms, tzitzit on their garments, and mezuzah on their doorways. And regarding them, David said: "Seven times a day I praise You." Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov says: Anyone who has tefillin on his head and arm, tzitzit on his garment, and a mezuzah on his doorway is assured that he will not sin, as it is said: "A threefold cord is not quickly broken." And it says: "The angel of the Lord encamps around those who fear Him and delivers them."

And conversely, it is stated there (Menachot 41a): Anyone who does not have tzitzit on his garment transgresses five positive commandments. And in Pesachim (113b), there are seven who are distanced, and one of them is someone who does not have tzitzit on his garment, see there. And even though this applies when one wears a garment without tzitzit, and the garment is obligated in tzitzit, nevertheless, it is good and proper for every person to be careful with this mitzvah to wear a small tallit (tallit katan) all day, so that he will remember the commandments at every moment. Therefore, it has five knots corresponding to the Five Books of the Torah, and four corners so that whichever direction he turns, he will remember. And also a large tallit (tallit gadol) during the time of prayer, which is over all the garments, so that he will see them.

It is a mitzvah to hold the tzitzit between the ring finger and the little finger of the left hand, opposite the heart, during the recitation of the Shema. And when one reaches the section of tzitzit, he should take them also in the right hand, look at them, and hold them in his hand until he reaches "faithful and pleasant forever." Then he should kiss them and remove them from his hand. Similarly, one should be careful to make a beautiful tallit, because of "This is my God, and I will glorify Him." It is good to look at the tzitzit while wrapping oneself and when making the blessing. Some have the custom to look at the tzitzit when they reach "and you shall see it" and to place them on the eyes. This is an expression of love for the mitzvah. It is also customary to kiss the tzitzit at certain times during the recitation of the tzitzit section. All of this is an expression of love for the mitzvah.

And there are those who hold the two front tzitzit during the recitation of Shema, for the two tzitzit have ten knots, alluding to the ten sefirot which are interconnected and unified with one another, and they are all tied to His great light, blessed be He, which are connected like a flame to a coal. Additionally, they have sixteen strings and ten knots, which together total twenty-six, corresponding to the numerical value of the divine name, YHVH, blessed be He. And there is an allusion to holding them opposite the heart as it is stated in Shocher Tov: "And these words that I command you today shall be upon your heart." And great is the punishment for one who neglects the mitzvah of tzitzit. Concerning him it is said: "To grasp the corners of the earth, and the wicked shall be shaken out of it" (Job 38:13). And one who is careful with the mitzvah of tzitzit merits and sees the Divine Presence. (And it is forbidden to embroider verses on a tallit.)

Rabbi Yosef Karo wrote: After one dons a fringed tallit, he should put on tefillin, as we ascend in matters of holiness. End of quote. And they objected to him: On the contrary, since tefillin are holier, we have the principle that whatever is holier takes precedence, and thus tefillin should precede tzitzit (Shagat Aryeh, Siman 28 and Dagul Mervava). But the words of Rabbi Yosef Karo are correct. For, behold, in Menachot (49b) we conclude that when something is frequent and something is holy, they are equal in rank, and one may precede whichever he wishes. And so ruled the Rambam at the end of Chapter Eight of Tamidin; see there. And tzitzit in relation to tefillin is frequent, as it is practiced even on Shabbat and festivals. And this is what he says: Since they are equal in rank, therefore, due to "ascending in holiness," meaning to elevate one's body, the tallit is donned before the tefillin. And so it is in the Zohar at the end of Parashat Bamidbar, that tzitzit should be worn before tefillin; see there.

Nevertheless, it is written in Section 2 that one who is meticulous with a small tallit should wear it and put on tefillin in his home, and go dressed in a tallit and adorned with tefillin to the synagogue, and there he should wrap himself in a large tallit. Thus are his words. That is to say, the Zohar warns to come to the synagogue adorned with a tallit and tefillin, and it is not customary to go with a large tallit from one's home to the synagogue. And what should one do, since he needs to put on the tallit before the tefillin as I have written? To this, he says that since he has a small tallit on, he can put on the tefillin without the large tallit, and go to the synagogue where he should put on the large tallit, thereby fulfilling everything. And our master the Rema wrote about this: "And the custom of the world is to wrap even in the large tallit first and bless on it, and afterwards put on the tefillin and go to the synagogue." Thus are his words. And he does not disagree with our master the Beit Yosef. Rather, in his time, Jews lived among themselves and could go even with a large tallit to the synagogue. Therefore, they did not need to fulfill the words of the Zohar with the small tallit, which is not primary, but would wear the large tallit and the tefillin and go to the synagogue. And in our times, due to our many sins, it is not possible to do this at all. And we put on the tallit and tefillin in the synagogue.

Since it has been explained in Section 1 that one should put on the tzitzit before the tefillin, therefore, those who place the tefillin bag together with the tallit into one bag, according to our custom, should be careful not to place the tefillin bag on top and closer to the opening of the bag than the tallit, so that they do not encounter the tefillin first and be required to put them on before the tallit. For one does not pass over the commandments. And even though the tefillin are still in their bag and the principle of not passing over the commandments may not apply so strongly in this case (as explained by Magen Avraham, subparagraph 1), nevertheless, since the reason for putting on the tallit before the tefillin is also not entirely clear, and especially according to what we have explained that they are equal in importance according to the basic law—the tallit is more frequent, and the tefillin are more sacred—therefore, if one encounters the tefillin in any manner, they should be put on first. And even though with tefillin, if one encounters the tefillin of the head first, we are not concerned with the principle of not passing over the commandments, as will be explained, there it is different because it is a scriptural decree to put on the tefillin of the hand first, as will be explained, which is not the case with tallit and tefillin (as explained by Taz, subparagraph 1).

However, in the scenario outlined in section 2, where one leaves their tefillin at home and their tallit in the synagogue, there is certainly no concern even if they encounter the tallit first. Nonetheless, one does not need to wrap themselves in it at home, since their intention is not to wear it there, and therefore the rule of precedence does not apply. This is similar to the law in Siman 168, which states that one must prioritize the blessing over wheat bread before barley bread. This applies when one wants to eat wheat bread, but if one does not want to eat it, it does not matter. The same principle applies here (Magen Avraham, subsection 4). Be aware that all of this is relevant when both the tallit and tefillin are prepared in front of the person, and we are considering which to prioritize. However, if the tefillin are ready in front of the person and the tallit is not prepared, one should not wait until the tallit is brought. Rather, one should put on the tefillin, and when the tallit arrives, they can wrap themselves in it.

It has already been explained that according to the Zohar, it is a significant matter to go to the synagogue wrapped in a tallit and adorned with tefillin. And even if one needs to go through filthy alleyways, one can still go, provided one covers the "head tefillin." This matter is so important that there was a ruling by one of the great authorities regarding a person who had committed himself with a penalty to go to the synagogue before dawn to recite Psalms in a group, and now wants to retract because he cannot go wrapped in a tallit and tefillin before dawn, that he can retract and is exempt from the penalty. And the vow does not apply to him because it is considered a vow made in error (Magen Avraham, subsection 3, in the name of Maharam of Lublin, Siman 37). For this reason, the Ari of blessed memory was not one of the first ten in the synagogue, because many came before dawn, and he did not want to go without being wrapped and adorned with the tallit and tefillin (ibid). Nevertheless, several great authorities have disagreed with this, arguing that before dawn, when it is not yet the time for tzitzit and tefillin, there is no issue. And the Zohar's warning does not apply in this case (Eliyah Rabbah, Nehar Shalom, and Ma'amar Mordechai). In any case, the annulment of the vow is certainly required (Magen Avraham, ibid). The reason for the Ari's practice was not only this but also because he had an intestinal illness and needed to relieve himself, and he could not come earlier (Machatzit Hashekel. This is also written by the Magen Avraham in Siman 90, subsection 28, see there).

And this was the custom of the Rosh, of blessed memory: He would wrap himself in a tallit and arrange the blessings until "[He] crowns Israel with glory" and then put on tefillin. He would recite this blessing because the tefillin are called "glory," and it is fitting to bless immediately after putting on the tefillin. This is what the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch wrote in his name. However, this is not the law, for in the Gemara, the morning blessings are arranged for other matters (Berachot 6b), and this blessing is for putting on the hat, as I wrote in Siman 46. But because we are not capable of arranging the blessings each in its proper place, we arrange them either at home or in the synagogue, as will be explained there. Nonetheless, it teaches us that since a great person like the Rosh, of blessed memory, did so, certainly whoever is able, according to his body and custom, to do so should do so. However, this is not the law.

Every Jewish man is obligated to ensure that he has tefillin on during the recitation of the Shema and prayer. Anyone who recites the Shema without tefillin is as if he is bearing false witness against himself, and it is as if he is offering a sacrifice without the accompanying libations (Berachot 14b). This means that the false testimony is in saying "And you shall bind them as a sign upon your hand..." – and he has not bound them. Furthermore, the recitation of the Shema that he has done is only like half a mitzvah, similar to someone who offers a sacrifice without the libations. Until when should the tefillin remain on him? This will be explained at the end of this section, that they should remain on him until after "Aleinu," see there.

Know that even according to the poskim (halachic authorities) who hold that mitzvot do not require intention, it is certain that one must know the essence and nature of the mitzvah. And with tefillin, if one does not pay attention to its significance at all, he has not fulfilled the mitzvah, and it is like a mere act of a monkey. Therefore, one should have in mind when putting them on that the Holy One, blessed be He, commanded us to place these four sections, which contain the unification of His name and the exodus from Egypt, on the arm opposite the heart and on the head opposite the brain, so that we remember the miracles and wonders He performed for us. These indicate His unification and that He has power and dominion over the upper and lower worlds. Through this, one's faith in Him, blessed be He, will be strengthened, and he will trust in Him in all matters. And he will dedicate to the Holy One, blessed be He, the soul that is in the brain, and also the heart, which is the source of desires and thoughts. In this way, he will remember the Creator, reduce his pleasures, and understand that he was created for this ultimate purpose, to do His blessed will. He will cast his burden and all his needs upon Hashem.

Know that from these four sections we are commanded to read only two sections: "Shema" and "Vehaya Im Shamoa." But "Kadesh" and "Vehaya Ki Yeviacha" do not need to be read. And so they expounded in the Sifrei on the verse "You shall teach them diligently to your children": "Shema" and "Vehaya Im Shamoa"—with diligence, but not "Kadesh" and "Vehaya Ki Yeviacha" with diligence. And what you find by the great ones who wrote to say these sections as well (see Magen Avraham, subsection 6)—it is neither obligatory nor a mitzvah, but rather an additional love like the measure of the righteous. They only came to indicate that the intention was not to forbid reading them, but that there was no obligation to read them. And if one wishes, he can read them as well, and no one should prevent him.

He should first put on the hand tefillin, and afterward the head tefillin. Even if he encounters the head tefillin first, he is required to pass over it, even though one should not pass over mitzvot, and take the hand tefillin and place it on the hand, and afterward take the head tefillin and place it on the head. The reason is because it is written: "And they shall be as frontlets between your eyes," and we interpret (Menachot 36a) from the term "they shall be" which is in the plural form (Rashi), that as long as it is "between your eyes," there should be two. And even though if he does not have the hand tefillin, or is unable to put it on the hand, he places the head tefillin alone as I wrote in Siman 26 – this is because they are two separate mitzvot, and therefore he is required to fulfill the one he has.
