But when he has both, the Torah decreed to place the head tefillin after the hand tefillin, and therefore we do not pay attention to the rule of "do not pass over mitzvot." Therefore, our sages of blessed memory said (Yoma 33a) that a person should be careful not to encounter the head tefillin first, so he does not have to pass over the mitzvah.

With regard to the blessings, there is a dispute among the Rabbis. Some of our Rabbis ruled to recite one blessing for both [tefillin of the arm and the head], and some ruled to recite two blessings: for the arm "to place tefillin" and for the head "concerning the mitzvah of tefillin." The Ashkenazim follow the latter opinion, while the Sephardim recite one blessing according to the first opinion. The simple reading of the Gemara in Menachot (36a) that states: if one did not interrupt between the tefillin of the arm and the tefillin of the head, one makes one blessing; if one interrupted, one makes two blessings, implies one blessing for both, as Rashi explains. However, the simple reading of the Gemara in Berachot (60b) that states: when placing the tefillin on the arm, say "Blessed... to place..."; when placing on the head, say "Blessed... concerning the mitzvah...", indicates that two blessings are required. This is also stated in the Jerusalem Talmud and in Midrash Tanchuma at the end of Parashat "Bo," see there. And Rabbeinu Tam ruled this way, explaining that the Gemara in Menachot referring to "if interrupted, make two blessings" applies to the head tefillin alone. Rashi would interpret the Gemara in Berachot as referring to an interruption. The Rif, Rambam, and Rashba ruled according to Rashi, while the Rosh and Tur ruled according to Rabbeinu Tam.

(It is not understandable according to Rabbeinu Tam, that "if interrupted, make two blessings" applies to the head tefillin alone, as how can one make two blessings on one mitzvah? The Maharal of Prague, as brought by the Bach, already addressed this, writing that one should handle the arm tefillin and consider one blessing as related to the arm tefillin. According to this, if one only has the head tefillin, one should only make one blessing, see there. However, this does not seem to be the opinion of Tosafot and the Rosh, and it also appears from the Magen Avraham, section 15. Additionally, I found in the Or Zarua HaGadol, section 682, in the name of the Geonim, that originally, each tefillin required two blessings: "to place" and "concerning the mitzvah," see there. It seems to me that "to place" is the blessing of the mitzvah, and "concerning the mitzvah" is a blessing of thanks that God has granted us to perform a sign between Him and us. This relates to the head tefillin, as derived (Menachot 35b) from the verse "and all the peoples of the earth will see that the name of the Lord is called upon you, and they will fear you" – these are the head tefillin. According to this, it fits well. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote that this is indeed the custom among the Ashkenazim to recite two blessings. And it is good to always say after the second blessing, "Blessed be the name of His glorious kingdom forever and ever." This is his exact wording. This is due to the concern of a possible blessing in vain, as I have written in Siman 206 that when one utters God's name in vain, he should say "Blessed be the name of His glorious kingdom forever and ever," see there. However, this is entirely unclear. For, whatever the case may be: if the matter is uncertain for us, such that one should say "Blessed be the name of His glorious kingdom forever and ever," then why should we bless twice? We should bless once, as is the rule in all cases of doubtful blessings. And if the law is clear to us, then why should we say "Blessed be the name of His glorious kingdom forever and ever"?

In truth, the Levush omitted this. (And also the Bach questioned this, and the Ma'adanei Yom Tov wrote that it is for additional measure. It requires further study.) Simply, we can say that for the Ashkenazim it is clear that two blessings are necessary, and only our teacher, the Rema, had doubts. But it is impossible to change the custom, and therefore he ruled accordingly. Therefore, one whose heart troubles him may recite a single blessing. And we have heard that some great individuals were meticulous to answer "Amen" between the blessings for the arm tefillin and the head tefillin, considering this an interruption so that they could bless over the head tefillin according to all opinions. (And in Beit Yosef, he indeed wondered about Mahari ben Chaviv who practiced this way, questioning why he would enter into the doubt of a blessing in vain and save himself by saying "Blessed be the name of His glorious kingdom forever and ever"? See there.)

In my humble opinion, it seems that the recitation of "Blessed be the name of His glorious kingdom forever and ever" is not due to a doubt concerning the blessing but for another reason. Even though the poskim (decisors of Jewish law) have written that it is due to this reason, nevertheless, the custom appears to me to be for a different reason. For we have already examined how it is possible to recite two blessings for one thing? Additionally, there are those who question the fundamental approach of Rabbeinu Tam, for it is taught in the Tosefta in the sixth chapter of Berachot, and similarly written by the Rambam in the first chapter of Maaserot, that if one separates terumah, terumat maaser, and maaser sheni simultaneously, one recites a single blessing for all of them. If so, how can two blessings be established for the two tefillin? (The Gra, section 17. And the answer given by the Arot HaChaim is puzzling; see there.)

Therefore, it seems to me that the blessing "on the commandment of tefillin" is a blessing of gratitude, as I wrote earlier, since this commandment is the great bond that binds Israel to their Father in Heaven. For this, we recite a blessing of gratitude, to thank the Blessed Name for this goodness. And since the primary bond is in the verse "Hear O Israel," we therefore say "Blessed be the name of His glorious kingdom forever and ever," just as our father Jacob responded when the tribes said "Hear O Israel," as it is stated in Pesachim (56a). And there is evidence for this from the very term "tefillin," which the Tur explains as a term of "plilah" (judgment), that they are a sign and testimony to all who see us that the Divine Presence dwells upon us... until here is his language. 

And this is its explanation: that for the commandment of tefillin, meaning for the fact that the Blessed Name connects to us – we give Him, blessed be He, praise and thanks for this. (See Beit Yosef who brings from the Zohar "Pinchas": Rabbi Shimon said: Tefillin... one blessing for both... until here is his language. And he wrote that it means the blessing "to place" applies to both, but in any case, two are required, see there. And in my humble opinion, this is certainly so. For in the Tikkunei Zohar Chadash (Vilna edition, page 46b) it says on the verse "One thing God has spoken, two things have I heard" and this is his language: and because from the side of the right and left "two things have I heard" (so it should be said) – one must bless two blessings on them, one "to place" on the hand and one "on the commandment" on the head. And if he speaks in between – he blesses on the head two blessings. But from the side of the central column it is said "One thing God has spoken" (so it should be said), and only one blessing is needed... until here is his language. And it seems that this is the explanation: that from the essence of the blessing on the commandment – one is sufficient. And this is the "central column," Tiferet, which is the Torah as we say in Berachot 58a, and Tiferet is the giving of the Torah. And only from the right and left, which are Chesed and Gevurah, are two blessings needed: the first being the decree of the king which is "Gevurah," and the second being gratitude for the connection which is the right "Chesed." Pay attention and you will find it easy.)

Tefillin is pronounced with a dagesh in the lamed, because its root is PLL, as I have written in the name of the Tur. It should technically have two lameds, but the dagesh compensates for the missing letter, as is known. Therefore, when saying "to put on tefillin," as well as "on the commandment of tefillin," the lamed should be pronounced with the emphasis of a dagesh. And one should say "lehaniach" with a kamatz under the hei, indicating placement on the hand, like "to place a blessing upon your house," and not with a patach, which means abandonment, as in "one of your brothers leave with me." And "on the commandment" should have a patach under the vav, because it only refers to the head tefillin, and thus should be in singular form. Even if one were to say it refers to both, isn't it written: "the commandment of the Lord is pure, enlightening the eyes," referring to all commandments? Yet it uses the singular form with a patach (Magen Avraham, section 9), as all commandments are one commandment, meaning that the Holy One, Blessed be He, commanded us. Some say to bless "on the commandment" with a cholam, and only if one has the head tefillin alone, to bless with a patach (Taz, section 6, in the name of his brother). The custom follows the first opinion, as confirmed by the great latter authorities (Eliyah Rabbah, the Gra, Levushei Serad, and Darchai Chaim).

It is well known that for all commandments, one must recite a blessing "prior to performing them," meaning before performing them and immediately adjacent to the action. Therefore, one should not recite the blessing on the arm tefillin before placing it on the bicep, which is the place where the tefillin is placed as I have written in Siman 27, because it is not immediately before the binding, which is the performance of the commandment, nor after the binding, because we require "prior to performing them." Rather, one should place it on the bicep, hold the strap with the right hand, recite the blessing, and immediately tighten it, which completes the commandment. Similarly, for the head tefillin, one should recite the blessing before tightening it on the head, that is, after placing it on the head and before tightening (Magen Avraham, Siman 13). According to this, one must be careful not to uncover the head (Pri Megadim), and should cover the head with the tallit. This is difficult, especially for young men who do not have a tallit, as is obvious. Therefore, some have the custom to hold the head tefillin near the head and recite the blessing, and immediately place it on the head, which is also adjacent to performing them. Know that all this is initially. But if one did not recite the blessing beforehand, one recites it afterward, since the tefillin remains on for a long time afterward (Pri Megadim). This is similar to someone who did not recite the "Hamotzi" blessing before starting to eat; one recites it in the middle of the meal. The same applies here, but one should touch the tefillin when reciting the blessing, as touching is somewhat like placing.

Initially, it is forbidden to interrupt with any speech between the arm tefillin and the head tefillin. If one did speak between the two tefillin, they must repeat the blessing on the head tefillin, "upon the commandment of tefillin." This applies to those who recite one blessing for both. For those who recite two blessings, they should recite two blessings on the head tefillin as previously explained. This is what should be done: touch the arm tefillin and tighten the strap, then recite both blessings on the head tefillin, as it is considered as one on the arm tefillin due to the touching, and one on the head tefillin (Magen Avraham, subsection 15, in the name of the Ran, see there). This is because it is surprising to recite two blessings on one item. This has already been explained with the help of Heaven.

The fact that speaking constitutes an interruption applies when one speaks about matters unrelated to the tefillin. However, if one speaks for the sake of the tefillin, although it is preferable to avoid this unless absolutely necessary, one does not need to recite another blessing, because any speech related to the mitzvah being performed is not considered an interruption. If one hears Kaddish or Kedushah between donning the arm tefillin and the head tefillin, Rabbeinu the Beit Yosef wrote in section 10 that one should not interrupt to respond. Rather, one should remain silent, listen, and focus on what is being said. This is due to the principle that listening is considered as responding, and thus for the purposes of interruption, it is not deemed an interruption. If one did respond to Kaddish..., some say that another blessing must be recited on the head tefillin (Magen Avraham, subsection 17). Others say that another blessing is not required, since responding to such obligatory matters is no worse than speaking for the sake of the tefillin (Taz, subsection 8). This latter opinion seems to be the main one. (From the language of the Shulchan Aruch, it appears that for responding "Amen," an interruption is not necessary, even in the form of merely listening. Perhaps he did not mention this explicitly, as he also did not mention "Barechu." Investigate and you will find this to be clear.)

It is understood by all that the blessing "to place" also pertains to the head tefillin, and not only for those who recite only one blessing, but even for those who recite two blessings, the blessing "to place" also pertains to the head tefillin. Therefore, one should minimize interruption as much as possible. Therefore, our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 11 that after tying the arm tefillin on the arm, one should place the head tefillin before wrapping the strap around the arm. So far are his words. And the Tur wrote that this was the practice of the Rosh, of blessed memory, even though he held that two blessings are recited. Nonetheless, we do not follow this practice. They wrote that the Ari Zal would wrap the wraps and then place the head tefillin, even though he, of blessed memory, would recite only one blessing. Simply put, the reason is: since the wraps are to be done, they are also part of the placing of the tefillin and this is not an interruption. Additionally, it is known that if the wraps are not done, the tie of the arm tefillin will loosen, and it will turn out that the head tefillin will be tied before the arm tefillin. However, besides this, they wrote that there are hidden reasons for this (see Taz, section 9, and Magen Avraham, section 18). And so is the custom, and it should not be changed.

And likewise, one should not take the head tefillin out of the bag until they have put on the hand tefillin. Even if both are in front of them outside of the bag, one should not prepare the head tefillin before putting on the hand tefillin. If not, since they are engaged with the head tefillin and will put it down and then put on the hand tefillin first, they will be transgressing the mitzvah, as we do not pass over mitzvot, as I have written. Therefore, our custom is to place both in one bag, with the head tefillin on the right side of the bag and the hand tefillin on the left side. We always do so. Hence, one opens the bag and turns to their left for the hand tefillin and puts it on, and afterward takes the head tefillin from the bag and puts it on. This meticulousness applies specifically to the individual themselves. But if another person takes the head tefillin from the bag and prepares it for the one putting it on, there is no concern.

And know that it is written, based on the Zohar, to place the tefillin of the arm while seated, and the tefillin of the head while standing. And our Rabbi, the Rema, wrote in section 11 that we do not practice this, but rather both are placed while standing, see there. There are those who wrote that the placement should be seated, and the blessing and binding while standing (Magen Avraham section 2). And the Maharshal (Siman 98) ruled that even the placement should be while standing. And many great authorities wrote this, and this is the common practice. And the truth is that according to the Talmudic law, there is no strict requirement in this matter, and it is only because we perform all blessings over commandments while standing. But it is not an absolute requirement. Based on this, it is not understood why we do not follow the opinion of the Zohar. However, in any case, all the great sages of Israel in previous generations did not follow this practice. (And it seems to me that their reasoning is that there is no conclusive proof from the Zohar for this. And this is its wording at the end of Parashat "Bamidbar": "The prayer while seated corresponds to the tefillin of the arm, afterward the prayer while standing which corresponds to the tefillin of the head. And this is similar to the practice and similar to the speech…" until here is its wording. And the explanation is not to place the tefillin of the arm while seated, but this is its interpretation: the prayer while seated, which is "Yotzer Or," is much lower in level than the Amidah prayer as is known. And similarly, the tefillin of the arm is lower in level than the tefillin of the head, as explained in the Zohar "Chayei Sarah" in the Midrash HaNe'elam. And this is its wording: "Upper fervor… these are the tefillin of the head, tefillin of the arm… similar to the lower fervor…" until here is its wording. And therefore, the tefillin of the arm symbolizes the prayer while seated and the tefillin of the head symbolizes the prayer while standing. And "the practice similar to the speech" means: just as in speech there are two levels, so too in practice. And analyze this, and you will find it light.)

The Tur wrote that any time one puts them on during the day, he must make a blessing. And even if they slipped from their place and he adjusts them to return them to their place, he must make a blessing. These are his words. This means: not only when he completely removes them and puts them back on after some time does he make a blessing, but even if they merely slipped from their place by themselves and he adjusts them to return them to their place immediately, he must make a blessing. And this is not because of the short interruption, for it was explained above in Siman 8 that if they are moved from their place with the intention of returning them immediately, he does not make a blessing, see there. Rather, it is because they slipped unintentionally, and therefore he must make a blessing even immediately. And the obligation to make a blessing every time he puts them on is when he removed them with the intention of not wearing them, or to wear them after some time. And when it says "even," it is because regarding a long time, when he removes them by himself, it is significant even for a short time, even when they slipped by themselves.

According to this, in the opinion of the Tur, one who removes his tefillin to go urinate or defecate with the intention of putting them back on immediately upon returning does not need to recite a blessing. However, our master, the Beit Yosef, disagrees in Section 12, where he writes: If they slipped from their place... one must recite a blessing. If one moved them from their place with the intention to put them back immediately, one must recite a blessing. Thus are his words. He holds that in any case where they have been removed from their place, whether intentionally or unintentionally, whether with the intention to put them back immediately or not, one must recite a blessing. And on this, our master the Rema writes: Some say not to recite a blessing, and this is the custom. Thus are his words, and this applies to moving them from their place with the intention to put them back immediately, in accordance with the opinion of the Tur as we have explained. And this is our custom. Moreover, even if they slipped from their place on their own, we do not customarily recite a blessing. I do not know the reason for this, as in this case everyone agrees that one should recite a blessing. Some have written that the reason is because during prayer, one is presumably not distracted from them, and it is as if he removed them with the intention to put them back (Magen Avraham, Section 21, in the name of Shelah). This reasoning is very weak because even if we compare it to this, our master the Beit Yosef still holds that one should recite a blessing in such a case. Furthermore, the earlier authorities did not adopt this view, as in the case where they slipped, everyone agrees that one must recite a blessing, even those who hold that if one removes them with the intention to put them back, one does not need to recite a blessing. It must be said that the intention of the earlier authorities was not during the time of prayer when they slipped, and this is clearly forced. (In my humble opinion, it seems that the source is from the Rabbis of the house of Rav Ashi, who say that whenever one touches them, one recites a blessing. The Rosh explains this as referring to when they slipped. The Rambam in the fourth chapter of the Laws of Tefillin omits this. The Kesef Mishneh writes that this is a clear matter, see there. It requires further study, for if so, why did the Rambam omit an explicit ruling from the Gemara? Rather, the Rambam explains that they disagree on the earlier matter, and the halacha does not follow the Rabbis of the house of Rav Ashi in several places in the Talmud, as I have written in Yoreh De'ah, Section 293. Investigate and you will find it simple.)

And know that the leading authorities among the later scholars have agreed that even though we follow the ruling of the Tur that one does not recite a blessing when removing [tefillin] with the intention of putting them back on immediately, nevertheless, if one removes them to go to the bathroom, one must recite a blessing when he comes back and puts them on again. Because since he is not permitted to go to the bathroom with them, he has dismissed them, and therefore must recite a blessing (Taz, subsection 11, and Magen Avraham, subsection 22). This is clearly proven in the Talmud (Sukkah 46a). And even though there are those who wanted to say that this only applied to them, since their bathrooms were outside the city and it was a significant interruption, which is not the case with us (ibid.), nevertheless, it does not appear so. And this is indeed our practice. Similarly, if one removes them with the intention of not putting them back on immediately, even if he changes his mind and puts them back on immediately, he is required to recite a blessing (ibid.). And likewise, the opposite: if one removes them with the intention of putting them back on immediately, but delays for a long time, he is required to recite a blessing. Similarly, if one removes them because he needed to pass gas, even if his intention is to put them back on immediately, it is possible that he needs to recite a blessing, and this requires further consideration. However, if one removes them to urinate or to eat a temporary meal, and his intention was to put them back on immediately, and he does so, he does not need to recite a blessing. If he removes them without any specific intention, it seems that it is like removing them with the intention of not putting them back on, because if it were not so, why did he remove them? Therefore, when he decides to put them back on, he recites the blessing again. But this is when he removes both. However, if he removes only the head tefillin and then decides to put it back on, he does not recite a blessing, because as long as the arm tefillin is still on, it is not considered a complete removal, even according to those who recite two blessings. And even though regarding them slipping out of place, Rabbi Rema wrote that if one puts one of them back on, it is as if he put both on, as will be explained in Siman 26, until here is his language – this is when it slipped off by itself. But if he removed them, as long as he has not removed both, it is not considered a removal. And he does not need to recite a blessing when he puts back on the one he removed, even if his intention was not to put it back on again. (So it appears to me in my humble opinion. And see in Arzot HaChaim and Mishnah Berurah. Be precise and you will find clarity.)

Our Rabbi, the Beit Yosef, wrote in Section 12: If someone places the hand tefillin and recites the blessing, and at the beginning of the tightening the knot of the hand tefillin breaks and he needs to make another knot, but he did not divert his attention – he does not need to recite the blessing again. These are his words. This is not considered an interruption. Even if he asked another person to make the knot and spoke – it is not an interruption, since this is for the need of the tefillin. From his language, it implies that specifically when the knot breaks at the beginning of the tightening, the blessing has not yet taken effect on the mitzvah, and therefore he does not need to bless again. But if it breaks after the tightening – he needs to bless again, even if it broke before placing the head tefillin.

And they questioned him from what he himself wrote later: If the arm [tefillin] became loose before placing the head [tefillin] – he tightens it, and does not need to recite another blessing. But if he placed the head [tefillin], and afterwards the arm [tefillin] became loose – he tightens it and recites a blessing. Thus far his words. And they resolved that if the knot became undone, which is a significant interruption in making the knot – he recites a blessing even before placing the head [tefillin] if it became undone after tightening. But if it merely became loose, which only requires tightening – he only recites a blessing if it became loose after placing the head [tefillin] (Magen Avraham, subsection 24). And there are those who ruled that even if the knot became undone, if it became undone before placing the head [tefillin], even if it became undone after tightening – he does not recite a blessing (Taz, subsection 13). And it seems to me that this is also the intention of our master, the Beit Yosef. And it is the usual way of the matter, that the knot can become undone even after tightening. But if it becomes undone, which is due to the weakening of the strap – it usually does not become undone only at the beginning of tightening when pulling it, and not afterwards.

And know that there are those who say that since it has been explained in paragraph 22 that we customarily do not recite a blessing when the tefillin slips from its place, then similarly, if the knot becomes untied or the knot breaks, one does not need to recite a blessing (Magen Avraham, subsection 23). However, it appears that there is no proof from there except in the case of the knot becoming untied, which is a common occurrence like slipping from its place. But if it breaks, that is not its usual manner. Furthermore, the reason for the custom not to recite a blessing when it slips from its place is not entirely clear, and it is best not to add to it. Therefore, it seems that in this case, one should be instructed to recite a blessing, and this also appears to be the opinion of the great later authorities (and this is also implied by the Gra who did not mention this, see there. But in Eretz HaChaim, it is written like the Magen Avraham. And see the Mishnah Berurah who wrote as we have. And it is obvious that if one puts on another's tefillin, he should recite a blessing. But another strap does not necessitate a blessing, for the blessing is on the box and not on the strap).

It is permitted to recite a blessing over borrowed tefillin. This is not similar to the case of tzitzit, as explained in Siman 14, where one does not recite a blessing over a borrowed tallit, because it is written "your garment," meaning it must be your own, but this does not apply to tefillin. Furthermore, it is explained there that it is permitted to take someone's tefillin without their knowledge to pray with them, because it is generally assumed that a person is pleased to fulfill a mitzvah with their possessions in a way that does not cause them loss; unless we know that the person is particular about it, in which case it should not be taken without their consent. One does not recite a blessing over stolen tefillin, and regarding this, it is said: "The robber blesses..." When there is despair of recovery and a change of ownership, one may recite a blessing. Some are still uncertain about this because a blessing is different. (See Taz section 14, and see what I have written in Siman 14 on this matter.)

In the time of the Talmud, people would wear tefillin all day. Nowadays, it is not possible to do so because of our many distractions and the great care required for them. Therefore, we put on tefillin from before the prayer until after the prayer. It is customary not to remove the tefillin until after the Kedusha of "Uva Letzion." Some have written, based on the wisdom of the Kabbalah, not to remove them until after reciting and hearing three Kedushot, which are the Kedusha of the morning, the Kedusha of the Shemoneh Esrei, and the Kedusha of "Uva Letzion," and four Kaddishes, which are the Kaddish before "Barechu," the Kaddish after the Shemoneh Esrei, the full Kaddish after "Uva Letzion," and the mourner's Kaddish after "Aleinu." These are fundamental parts of the prayer and hint at lofty matters. It is obvious that on a day when the Torah is read, one should not remove them until after the Torah reading. Consequently, this is so because one needs to remove them after "Aleinu," as I have written, and the Torah has already been read. Even in places where the Torah is read afterward, one should not remove them until after the reading. One should be careful not to remove them in front of the Torah scroll, as it is disrespectful to bare one's head in front of the Torah scroll; rather, one should move aside. On Rosh Chodesh, tefillin are removed before Musaf, even in places where "Keter" is not said in Kedusha. Although some significant authorities have protested this, nevertheless, this is the custom in all Jewish communities. It must not be changed for it is based on the wisdom of Kabbalah. On Chol HaMoed, tefillin are removed before Hallel. The prayer leader should also remove them before Hallel on Chol HaMoed Sukkot. Some do so even on Chol HaMoed Pesach, and each river follows its course. (See Magen Avraham, Section 28, where it is written that there should be three Kaddishes and four Kedushot, which requires further study. Note carefully and you will find it easy.)

And know that regarding the matters of tefillin, as well as other commandments, there are practices based on the wisdom of Kabbalah. The decisors have written a general rule about this: when the Talmud and the decisors are in disagreement with the Zohar, we follow the Talmud and the decisors. If the Zohar is stricter, one who wishes may act stringently according to the Zohar. And in a matter not mentioned in the Talmud, it is certainly proper to follow the Zohar, but one is not compelled to do so. (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 20, in the name of Radbaz; see there. However, I have accepted that it is impossible for the Zohar to be in disagreement with the Talmud unless there is also a disagreement in the Talmud itself. And in places where the law is decided in the Talmud, the Zohar also agrees with it. And perhaps in places where it seems that the Zohar does not explain it this way, they did not intend the truth, and it is necessary to interpret it in a manner that aligns with the Talmud. Examine carefully and you will find it easy.)

The tefillin of the arm and the tefillin of the head are two separate commandments. The Rambam and all those who enumerate the commandments count them as two positive commandments. And so it is taught at the beginning of the chapter "HaTechelet": The tefillin of the arm does not prevent the tefillin of the head, and the tefillin of the head does not prevent the tefillin of the arm. And even though with tzitzit, the blue thread does not prevent the white thread, and the white thread does not prevent the blue thread, and yet it is considered one commandment – this is because they are considered one action (Rivash, Siman 137). That is to say, it is considered one commandment that has parts, and the commandment is tzitzit, and the parts of the commandment are the blue and the white threads. But with tefillin, they are two actions, each one on its own.

Therefore, the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch wrote that if one has only one tefillin – he puts on the one he has and blesses over it, because each is a separate commandment. And the same applies if he has both, but due to some unavoidable circumstance, he can only put on one – he should put on the one he can. This is their language. The Tur further explains: such as if he needs to embark on a journey and cannot delay – he may put on one of them... this is his language. And it seems that it teaches us a significant point: not only when he has a wound on his hand or head, preventing him from putting on one of them, should he put on the one he can; but even if he can put on both, but the urgency of the journey prevents him, and I would think that in such a case it is not permitted; especially if he puts on the head tefillin alone, as the Torah says that as long as "between your eyes" there should be two – it teaches us that it is not strict, since he cannot now put on the hand tefillin – he can put on the head tefillin alone. And if there is not enough time to put on both but he can choose which one to put on – he should put on the hand tefillin alone so as not to change the order in the Torah (Artzos HaChaim). And there is someone who does not say so, but this is not the main opinion. And know that all this is when on the way he will put on the other. But if he will not put it on at all – surely they did not permit him, due to the urgency of the journey, to neglect the mitzvah of tefillin properly. Unless he is going for the saving of lives or a similar case, as one engaged in a mitzvah is exempt from another mitzvah. But otherwise, they did not permit it. (And this is also implied by Magen Avraham, subsection 1, see there. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

If one puts on the arm tefillin alone, he should say the blessing "to place." And if he puts on the head tefillin alone, he should say the blessing "for the commandment." Our teacher, the Rema, wrote that for us, who are accustomed every day to recite two blessings, one should recite both blessings on the head tefillin alone. And if one puts on the arm tefillin alone, he should recite only "to place." Thus far are his words. And likewise, the Tur wrote, see there. There are those who hold that even on the arm tefillin one should recite two blessings. But the main opinion is as I have written, and so have agreed the great later authorities.

It is clear that if one needs to pray and only has one set of tefillin, he should keep the one he has in order to pray with the congregation, especially if the time for reciting the Shema will pass. He should not wait for the second set, as there is no false testimony here since he does not have it. Furthermore, it seems to me that if the time for reciting the Shema will pass and he does not have tefillin now, or he cannot put them on because he is on the road and it is very cold, he should recite the Shema without tefillin since he is compelled, and later put them on and recite the Shema again after the time has passed. Similarly, it seems to me that he can pray with the congregation if the time for prayer will pass and then put them on afterward.

One who erred and placed the head tefillin before the hand tefillin, it is written in the name of the Abudraham that he should remove it from his head, place the hand tefillin, and then the head tefillin (Artzot HaChaim). However, if he already recited the blessing on the head tefillin, he should not recite the blessing again. And one who does not have a hand at all, in a manner that he will never place the hand tefillin, nonetheless he is obligated to place the head tefillin alone and recite the blessing on it (Shagat Aryeh, Siman 34).

The place for placing the tefillin of the arm is on the left arm, as it is written: "And it shall be for a sign upon your hand" — the weaker hand, meaning the one that is weaker in strength. Additionally, it is written: "Even My hand has laid the foundation of the earth, and My right hand has spread out the heavens" — thereby implying that "hand" refers to the left hand (Menachot 37a), as whenever "hand" is written without specification, it refers to the left (ibid.). Not all of the hand is suitable, but specifically the bone between the elbow (what is called the 'al-len-bow') and the armpit, which is the end of the hand connected to the body. Thus, our Sages explained there: "Your hand" — this refers to the upper arm, meaning the place of a gathering of flesh, for this bone has much more flesh than the bone after the palm of the hand until the elbow. We derive this from the placement of the tefillin of the head being at the height of the head, as will be explained — similarly, the tefillin of the arm should be at the height of the arm. Additionally, it is written: "And it shall be for a sign unto you upon your hand" — to you as a sign and not to others as a sign. This means in a place where others do not see clearly, and this is the upper part of the arm, for its lower part is visible to all. Additionally, it is written: "And you shall put these words of Mine upon your heart [...], and you shall bind them" — such that the placement is opposite the heart. Therefore, one needs to tilt the tefillin slightly towards the body, so that when he bends his arm downward, it will be opposite his heart. And this is all in the upper part of the arm, for in its lower part it will not be opposite the heart.

And know that from the general language of the Talmud and the poskim (Jewish legal decisors), it is explicitly implied that the entire bone between the elbow and the armpit is suitable for placing tefillin. This is also clarified from the language of the Tur, who wrote: "On the highest part of the flesh in the joint between the neck and the shoulder." These are his words. However, our teacher the Beit Yosef, in his major work, brought from the Sefer Mitzvot Katan (SeMaK) that not all of this bone is suitable, but only the half towards the elbow. And even this is not in the entire half, but only in the place where it is fleshy. Based on this, he wrote in the Shulchan Aruch: "On the fleshy part of the bone between the elbow and the armpit." These are his words. And he explains the language of the Tur "on the highest part of the flesh in the joint," meaning: that on this bone there is a place where the flesh is higher, and that is the place for placing them.

And so it is explained in the Rambam, Chapter Four, where he wrote: "The flesh that swells at the elbow...," see there. This is what our Rabbi the Rema wrote, that one must place [the tefillin] at the top of the bone adjacent to the cubit, but not on the half of the bone that is adjacent to the armpit. Thus far his words. Meaning: specifically on its half where the flesh swells, and not on its entire half (Magen Avraham, subsection 2). This is what our Rabbi the Beit Yosef wrote in section 7, that the bone adjacent to the armpit from its midpoint to the cubit is the place to place the tefillin. Thus far his words – he did not mean on its entire half but relied on what he wrote previously, that it is specifically on the swelling flesh. (See Magen Avraham there. And this is his intention to also resolve the words of the Beit Yosef, as the Pri Megadim wrote there. And the Machtzit HaShekel held that his intention was only to resolve the words of the Smak, and on the Beit Yosef he remained with a difficulty, see there. But the main opinion is like the Pri Megadim. And so is the practice of the world to place it not at the beginning of this bone, but rather slightly higher. And in that place itself, there is room to place two tefillin, as this is explicitly stated in the Talmud. Be precise and you will find relief.)

However, one of our later rabbis extensively disagreed with all of this and brings clear proofs that the entire area between the elbow and the armpit is permissible for placing tefillin. The proof brought from the Shimusha Rabbah, which states "half of the arm," is certainly correct, as the entire arm is considered half (the Gra, small section 5). According to this, we must say that when our sages mentioned "kiboret," meaning the muscle mass, it is certainly true that throughout this entire bone there is a considerable amount of flesh against the bone, from the wrist to the elbow, as is evident. And according to our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, we must say that in that specific area there is a place with more muscle mass than in any other part of this section, which is slightly after the beginning of this section. And thus is the custom of the world. (And Rashi there clearly implies like the Gra, where he wrote: "the height of the kiboret which is near the shoulder." End of his words. And the language of the Talmud there also implies this, that the entire bone is called "the height of the arm," and it is entirely opposite the heart. And similarly, the language of Rabbeinu Tam in Tosafot and the Rosh implies this, see there. And it appears clear to my humble opinion that one who has a wound in the place of tefillin according to the words of the Shulchan Aruch can simply rely on this opinion and place them above the middle of this bone. And this is how it should be instructed. Investigate and you will find ease. And it is explicitly implied in the Or Zarua HaGadol, section 576, like the Gra, see there.)

We learn in Menachot (37b): "Your hand" with a "hey" – this refers to the left hand ("a weak hand"). Others say: "Your hand" – this includes someone who is maimed, as "your hand" implies a crushed and damaged hand (Rashi). Another Baraita teaches: If he has no arm, he is exempt from tefillin. Others say: "Your hand" – this includes someone who is maimed, see there. And it is not understood: why did our Rabbis omit this whole matter, as the Rif, Rambam, Semag, Rosh, and Tur did not mention any of this at all? And they should have ruled the halacha one way or the other? And I have not found anyone who addressed this.

And what appears to me in the opinion of our Rabbis, when we scrutinize the reasoning of the first Tanna who said: if he does not have an arm, he is exempt from tefillin. For he does not derive this from a verse, but rather states it as a logical deduction. And what logic is there in this? On the contrary, we say in Arakhin (19b) that in regard to Torah law, the entire bicep is called "hand." And we are forced to say that it deals with a case where the bicep remains and only the arm is missing, for if not, it would not be appropriate to say he is exempt since he has no place to put it. And also, the language "does not have an arm" explicitly implies that the bicep remains. If so, why is he exempt? He has a hand, and we call it "and it shall be for you a sign on your hand." And from the tefillin itself, they deduced in the Gemara there that it is placed on the bicep, and the Torah said "on your hand" – we learn from this that the bicep is called a hand. And this is also proven from the verses about Samson, as it is written: "And the cords that were upon his arms," and it concludes: "And the bindings dissolved from upon his hands." If so, it is difficult: from where does the first Tanna derive that if one does not have an arm, he is exempt? And also for others, it is difficult: why do they need a derivation to include the amputee for obligation, since logically we know this, as we call the bicep "your hand?"

And it is necessary to state the reason: Certainly, the primary part of the hand is the palm of the hand, as it is clearly stated throughout the entire Tanach (Bible): "and he placed in his hand," "and she placed in her hand," "and he took from his hand," and with what do people take and give if not with the palm of the hand? Rather, the term "hand" is used to refer to the entire arm up to the shoulder, for in general, the arm is called a hand. Therefore, in the case of valuations, when the primary part of the hand exists, it is called a "hand" up to the shoulder. Similarly, in the case of Samson, when he had the strength of his hand, the arm is also called "hand." But when the primary part of the hand is missing, meaning when the palm of the hand is cut off, and he cannot take or give with it, it is not called a hand at all. Therefore, the first Tanna maintains that if one does not have an arm, he is exempt from tefillin because we do not call it "a sign upon your hand." And it is not specifically that he does not have an arm, for the same applies if he does not have a palm. It is just that he mentioned "if he does not have an arm" to imply that even if the upper arm (kiborit) remains, nonetheless, without the primary part of the hand, it is not called a "hand." The same applies when the palm of the hand is cut off. This is the reason why our rabbis omitted all this because these Tannaim did not derive "yadcha" – "your weak hand," but rather to include one who is missing a hand. The law is not like them, for Rav Ashi, who is the final authority, ruled earlier that we derive "yadcha" – "your weak hand." And since there is no verse for this, it is known to all that when one does not have a hand, there is no obligation, just as if one does not have a sukkah, there is no need to say, "You are exempt from the sukkah," as it is understood automatically. The same applies here. And the Baraita that states "if he does not have an arm, he is exempt from tefillin" was not necessary at all. But because others have a derivation that one who is missing a hand is obligated from the verse "yadcha," it informs us that it is not so. And since the poskim (decisors) wrote about "your weak hand," it is understood automatically that if one does not have a hand, he is exempt. And this is an obvious matter.

However, this is not the approach of our rabbis, the Tosafists, who wrote regarding the Baraita "If he does not have an arm, he is exempt": Others say "Your hand" to include someone with a maimed hand, as one says one thing and another says another thing, but they do not disagree. This is their language. Meaning: The first Tanna says when there is no arm, which means it is amputated up to the shoulder – exempt. And others said to include the maimed, meaning: the hand is amputated up to the arm, and the arm remains. Therefore, this is the law. However, also from this there is no proof, as we will explain with the help of Heaven. And our teacher, the Rema, wrote in section 1: A maimed person who has no hand, only an arm – should put on [tefillin] without a blessing. This is his language. And he explained his reasoning in his book "Darkei Moshe" because the Tosafists ruled for obligation. And the Or Zarua ruled for exemption, therefore he ruled thus. And the later authorities struggled with the words of the Or Zarua as to why he exempts, and they wrote that he had a different version of the Gemara. And they struggled greatly with his words (see Magen Avraham section 3 and other later authorities). And this caused them to do so because they did not have before them the great book of Or Zarua. And now we have merited this and his reasoning has been revealed.

And this is the language of the Or Zarua (Siman 577): "Yad'cha" – this is the left hand. Others say... it is taught elsewhere... And Rabbeinu Elikim explained in the Baraita: The first Baraita includes the one who is maimed, who does not have a hand but has an arm... and in the second Baraita... And Mory Rabbeinu Simcha explains in this manner that they disagree, and he ruled according to the first Tanna who exempts. Since the first Tanna derives to the left hand, if so, he exempts the maimed. This is his language, and according to this, his reasoning is clear: that he explains that the others are dealing with one who has an arm, and even so, the first Tanna exempts. And the law follows the first Tanna. And according to this, I say that also from Tosafot there is no proof. Although in the second Baraita they do not disagree, and one who has an arm is obligated, nevertheless, perhaps in the first Baraita they explain like the Or Zarua and the law follows the first Tanna. And behold, Tosafot did not rule the law in this matter. And according to this, it seems more correct in law that if his hand was cut off, even though he has an arm, he is exempt. However, since it comes from the mouth of Rabbeinu the Rema, it is difficult to go against his words. (And all the words of the Magen Avraham are not clarified. For what he questioned on Tosafot from Sifrei, on the contrary, if the others are Rabbi Yehuda from Sifrei, certainly their words were rejected. For Rabbi Yehuda the hoarder also in our Gemara there says that the right hand is called "hand," and the Talmud rejected this. And even if this is not Rabbi Yehuda from our Talmud, nevertheless, the words of Rabbi Yehuda from Sifrei were rejected by the strength of our Talmud that the right hand is not called "hand." Also what he questioned that if he has an arm he should place it on the left, and hinted to that of Arakhin, we have already explained that it is not called "hand." And from Arakhin it is not difficult at all, as we wrote. And be precise and you will find ease.)

Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote in paragraph 2: The proper custom is that the yud of the knot of the hand tefillin should be towards the heart, and the tefillin itself should be outward. One should be careful that the yud of the knot does not move away from the tefillin. This is his language, meaning: We do not have clear evidence that the knot should be towards the heart. The requirement by our sages that it be placed opposite the heart refers to the tefillin itself. Nevertheless, it is appropriate and seems correct to do so, since the yud is one of the letters of "Shaddai," and it is a halacha transmitted to Moses at Sinai that it should be opposite the heart. Also, regarding the knot not moving away from the tefillin – there is no clear proof from the Gemara. One could say that just as the dalet of the head tefillin is distant from the tefillin itself, so too the yud of the hand tefillin. However, it appears correct, and according to the wisdom of Kabbalah it is essential. Therefore, it is better that the wrappings on the arm should be wrapped from the arm outward, as per the Sephardic custom, for in this way the knot will be tightened to the tefillin. According to the Ashkenazic custom, where they wrap from outside the arm inward, the knot will be distanced, obviously.

He also wrote that the proper custom is to arrange that the loop through which the strap passes should be placed towards the shoulder, and the box towards the hand. Thus are his words. And so do all of Israel practice, even though there is no clear proof for this, as I have written. And because in his great book he brought from the Terumat HaDeshen that some do not act this way, therefore he warned about this. (And according to some commentators, these laws can be derived from the Talmud in Menachot 35b, which states that the knot of the tefillin must be above and inward. See Nimukei Yosef and Beit Yosef. Examine and you will find clarity.)

One must place the tefillin directly on the arm, not on any garment on the arm. Rashi, in Megillah (24b), explained the reason: because we require "for you as a sign" – and not for others as a sign. According to this reason, this applies only to the arm tefillin. However, the Rosh explained the reason to be similar to the priestly garments, as expounded in Zevachim (19a): "and he shall wear it on his flesh" – meaning there should not be anything interposing between the garment and his flesh; the same applies to tefillin, as it is written: "on your hand" – there should not be anything interposing between it and the hand. The same applies to the head tefillin, as it is written: "between your eyes" – at the height of the head corresponding to between the eyes, as will be explained, there should not be anything interposing. The Rashba, in his responsa, is uncertain about this, but there is no doubt that an interposition invalidates both the arm tefillin and the head tefillin according to the Rosh.

Therefore, I am astonished at those who wish to be lenient with the arm tefillin when they have a wound on the bicep and place rags on the wound, so they can put the tefillin on them, arguing that in this case, the issue of "and not for others as a sign" does not apply because he is wearing another garment over it (Magen Avraham, subsection 6). This follows the reasoning of Rashi, of blessed memory, and for this reason, the Rashba is uncertain regarding the head tefillin. But we, who follow the opinion of the Rosh, that there should be nothing interposing between the tefillin and the arm, it is certainly forbidden. It seems more appropriate to permit him to place it above the middle of the bicep bone, as I wrote at the end of subsection 4. And regarding what our master, the Rema, ruled that it applies specifically to the tefillin, but with the straps one need not be particular, thus his words end – the great ones disagree. They hold that even with the straps on the arm and on the head, it is forbidden to have an interposition (Levush and Taz, subsection 4, and Magen Avraham, subsection 5). And such is the custom, and one should not change it.

Nevertheless, our master the Beit Yosef wrote in Section 5 that a person who is prone to nasal congestion, meaning he has a headache and cannot uncover his head, and if he needs to place the head tefillin directly on his head, he will not put them on at all – it is permissible for him to place the head tefillin on a thin cap close to the head. And he should cover it from public view. Those who do it this way – should not recite a blessing on the head tefillin, only recite the blessing on the hand tefillin "to place." Thus far are his words. This permission is based on the words of the Rashba, who is uncertain about this, as I have written. But according to the Rosh, there is no permission for this at all, and it requires further investigation. And perhaps since otherwise, he would not put them on at all – it is better to put them on in any manner. But it is difficult to permit such a thing. And know that a dead louse creates a barrier. Similarly, if there is dirt on the head – it creates a barrier. One must clean the area where the head tefillin are placed, and it is proper to comb the area so that it is clean. Some wish to be stringent even when the hair is very long. I see no reason for this, for what limit can you set for the hair? The hair of the head is like the head itself. And perhaps if he has a lock of hair that surrounds the sides of the head from another place to the place where the tefillin are placed – in this case, it certainly creates a barrier, but not the natural hair that grows in that place. And so the custom is simple, and there is no need to question it at all.

And know that even though regarding the arm tefillin, our Sages of blessed memory said, "For you as a sign," and not for others as a sign – it does not mean that one is obligated to cover the arm tefillin. The intention is only in the place of "for you as a sign." And so it is explicitly stated in Menachot (37b). And likewise, conversely: the head tefillin needs to be visible to all, as it is written: "And all the peoples of the earth shall see that the name of the Lord is called upon you." And we expound: these are the tefillin of the head. This does not mean that it is forbidden to cover them, for it is permitted to cover them with a tallit or another object, as the Torah only insisted on the place. Therefore, one who has an issue with their head can put on the head tefillin and cover it along with their head with some covering. And so the great authorities have ruled.

A left-handed person who performs all his tasks with his left hand should place [the tefillin] on his left hand, which is the right hand for most people, because for him this hand is "weakened." If he is ambidextrous, meaning he performs tasks with both hands equally, without one hand having any advantage over the other, he should place [the tefillin] on his left hand, like everyone else. However, if his left hand has an advantage over his right hand, he should place [the tefillin] on his right hand, which is weakened for him. If he writes with his right hand and performs all other tasks with his left hand, or writes with his left hand and performs all other tasks with his right hand, some say that we follow his primary activities, and he should place [the tefillin] on the hand that is weaker in strength for him, which is weakened for him. Others say that we follow his writing hand, because it is written: "And you shall bind them... and you shall write them," and the hand with which he writes is considered the right hand, and he should place [the tefillin] on the other hand. The primary ruling follows the first opinion (as stated by the Gra in subsection 17). The derivation of "weakened hand" is the halachic ruling, unlike the derivation of "and you shall bind them... and you shall write them," which clearly in the Talmud does not serve as a halachic ruling. (For indeed, Rav Ashi on page 37a holds the opinion of "weakened hand." Furthermore, in the Baraita, there is a dispute between the first Tanna, Rabbi Yossi the Chorem, and Rabbi Natan, who derives "and you shall bind them... and you shall write them." And it is mentioned there that Rabbi Yossi the Chorem holds like Rabbi Natan, and the opinion of Rabbi Yossi the Chorem was rejected. Moreover, the halacha certainly follows the first Tanna, who does not hold like Rabbi Natan.)

A left-handed person who placed [the tefillin] on the left hand of a right-handed person has not fulfilled his obligation. There are those who disagree, but their opinion is not the main one. If a left-handed person needs to borrow tefillin from a right-handed person, he should turn the loop (ma'avarta) outward, so that the knot will face his body. For if he places it in the usual manner, the knot will not face his body, which is absolutely unacceptable. However, regarding the loop itself, there is not much concern. Similarly, a right-handed person borrowing tefillin from a left-handed person should do the same. 

Know that a "left-handed person" typically refers to someone born that way. However, if a person has trained himself to be left-handed, there is a dispute whether his status is the same as a naturally left-handed person. (See Magen Avraham, subsection 9, who cites Mordechai with two opinions. The opinion of the Rema in Darkei Moshe appears to treat him as left-handed. All the more so if a person’s right hand was weakened by divine decree, everyone agrees he is considered left-handed. Some say the same applies if his hand was amputated, but this is not correct, as there is no comparison between the cases. Investigate and you will find it clear.)

Even though a person has a wound in the place where the tefillin are placed, he should still put on tefillin, because there is enough space on the bicep to place two tefillin. From the bone near the armpit halfway to the elbow, in the area where it swells, is the place for the tefillin. And if the wound reaches halfway, he can place it on the half towards the body, as we explained at the end of section 4. (And one should not be surprised at what is said at the beginning of the chapter "One who finds tefillin": There is enough space on the head to place two tefillin, as there is even more if it is valid on the whole bone? For indeed it is so, but it is said similarly to the head, as Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai said: There is enough space on the head... – here too, there is enough space on the arm, see there. And be precise and you will find light.)

The length of the strap for the hand tefillin should be sufficient to encircle the arm, make a knot, and extend to the middle finger, where it should be wrapped three times: twice on the lower joint and once on the middle joint (see Magen Avraham, Section 12, who writes "upper," but it's not precise). And it should be secured, meaning the strap should be inserted in a way that it stays in place. It is customary to also wrap the strap seven times around the arm, corresponding to the seven words in the verse "You open Your hand..." Rabbi Moshe Isserles (the Rema) writes in Section 8 that one should not wrap the strap around the base of the tefillin to secure it to the hand. This is because the base of the tefillin is holier than the strap, and how can one place a lesser holiness on a greater holiness? This is the custom of the Ashkenazim. However, the Sephardim wrap the strap three times around the base, forming the shape of the letter "Shin." This is indeed written in the Kavanot and Pri Etz Chaim of the Arizal. But one of his greatest disciples disagrees with this. (Rabbi Chaim Vital appeared in a dream to his son and told him not to do so, as written in Sha'arei Teshuvah, Section 15, citing several great Sephardic authorities. He said that what is written there is not from the Arizal but from his associates. There are several such matters there; see there.) (What the Magen Avraham writes in Section 14, that while putting on the tefillin one should place the strap over it so that it does not move until the head tefillin is placed, see there. This is according to the custom where the head tefillin is put on before the wrappings, not according to our custom, as I wrote in Section 25, Section 18, see there.)

The placement of the head tefillin is from the beginning of the roots of the hair on the forehead until the end of the place where a child's brain is soft, meaning it is soft when he is one year old (Rashi, Menachot 37a). The fact that it is written "between your eyes," we learn from the law of making a bald spot, as it is written: "You shall not make a bald spot between your eyes for the dead." And "bald spot" does not refer to between the eyes literally, because there is no hair there at all. Rather, it refers to the place of the roots of the hair. The intention is that it should be placed on the brain opposite between the eyes. It is necessary to warn the masses about this, as we have seen with our own eyes that many wear the head tefillin with half of it on the forehead. Woe to that shame, for they have never fulfilled the mitzvah of tefillin, and they bless in vain, and their punishment is great. The reason for this is due to large tefillin and loose straps. Also, many mistakenly think that the place for the tefillin is where the hair stops growing. This is not so; rather, it is at the place where the hair begins to grow. I have seen several God-fearing individuals who go and inspect many people to see if the head tefillin is placed correctly. If it is not, they correct it to be proper. Fortunate is their portion, and their reward is very great.

The knot should be positioned at the back of the head, at the upper part of the nape, which is the end of the skull and opposite the face. One must ensure that the head tefillin is centered on the head so that it is opposite the area between the eyes. Additionally, the knot should be in the middle of the nape and should not tilt to either side. The part of the knot that is visible should appear like a "dalet" (the Hebrew letter ד) facing outward, and not like those who make it appear as two dalets. Care should be taken that the knot does not become inverted. Similarly, with the hand tefillin, care should be taken that it does not become inverted, and the black side of the straps should face outward, both for the hand tefillin and the head tefillin. The primary concern is with the area where the straps encircle the head and the arm. In the Gemara, we find that one of the Amoraim fasted because the black side of his strap once turned inward. It is said that he fasted forty fasts for this (Moed Katan 25a).

One should let the straps of the tefillin shel rosh (head tefillin) hang down in front of him, reaching to the navel or slightly above it. Some have written that the right strap should reach the navel, and the left one should reach the chest. According to the Talmudic law, there is no specific measurement for this, just that it should hang down a bit in front. The width of the strap of the arm tefillin and the head tefillin should be at least the length of a barley grain without its husk. If the straps are shorter or narrower than this measurement, if he cannot find others, he should use them as they are until he finds others, as this is not an absolute requirement but rather an enhancement of the mitzvah. Whether it is permissible to sew the strap if it tears will be clarified in section 33. It is good for the tefillin shel rosh to be visible, but it is not an absolute requirement, as I wrote in section 15. A student in front of his teacher should not expose his tefillin in front of his teacher, as it is not respectful. (This is also implied at the beginning of the chapter "Ein Omdin" where Rabba did not notice Abaye's tefillin. Similarly, Rabbi Zeira with Rabbi Yirmiya; see there and analyze it well.) Rabbi Rema wrote that for the tefillin shel yad (arm tefillin), there is no need to be particular whether they are exposed or covered. Likewise, for a student with his teacher, since nowadays tefillin are worn only during the recitation of the Shema and prayer, even a student in front of his teacher can expose even the tefillin shel rosh. This is also the custom, not to be particular. Thus ends his wording. Since it is obligatory to wear them at that time, it is not considered arrogance before his teacher. It is only during study time, when it is not as obligatory, that there is an issue of respect.

We learn in Menachot (36b): A person is obligated to touch their tefillin at all times, all the more so from the tzitz (forehead plate of the High Priest). If the Torah says about the tzitz, which has only one mention of God's name, "It shall be on his forehead always"—so that he does not divert his attention from it—how much more so with tefillin, which have many mentions of God's name. The Rosh and the students of Rabbeinu Yonah have already written in his name in the third chapter of Berachot (Siman 28), and the Tur later in Siman 44, that distracting one's mind is only considered when one is engaged in frivolity and light-headedness. But it does not mean that one must think about the tefillin every moment, for that is impossible: when one is praying or studying, their thoughts are on that and not on the tefillin. Therefore, the Sages permitted in Sukkah (26b) to sleep a temporary sleep in tefillin, and there is no greater distraction of the mind than this. Rather, as long as one is not engaged in frivolity, it is acceptable.

One must say, according to this, that the obligation to check the tefillin at every moment is explained as follows: At every moment one remembers them, one is obligated to check them, so as not to come to a state of distraction (Bach and Magen Avraham, subsection 1). That is to say, if even at the moment one remembers he does not check them, he might completely forget about them and come to a state of frivolity, flatulence, or deep sleep. Similarly, I found in the book "Or Zarua HaGadol" (siman 285) the following: A person is obligated to check... Thus, a person must remember that he is wearing tefillin and not become distracted from them, so that he does not sleep in them or release gas in them. Because by remembering that he carries the holy name upon him, he does not come to frivolity, and he maintains fear of Heaven in his heart... Therefore, when a person focuses his heart in prayer or in study of Halacha, this is not considered distraction, for certainly there is fear of Heaven. And it was concluded in the chapter "HaYashen" that one may sleep a temporary sleep in them... until here is his wording. Thus, the main intention is to bring about fear of Heaven and not frivolity. And a temporary sleep is permitted, as it is necessary for a person. (And this answers the difficulty of the "Shagath Aryeh" siman 39, for frivolity and light-headedness are prohibited in any case, see there. And according to what I have written, it is clear, for one leads to the other. And that which we say in Shabbat 12a: a person may go out wearing tefillin on Friday evening at dusk, since he is obligated to check them, he will surely remember them and check them, and remove them before darkness. Examine and you will find it precise.)

However, if so, it is puzzling what the Tur and Shulchan Aruch wrote in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 388, and this is their language: "An mourner must compose his mind to focus his heart on the tefillin, so that he does not divert his attention from them. But during the eulogy and weeping, he does not wear them." Until here is their language, and this is from the words of the Ramban in Torat HaAdam; see there. And if diversion of attention is only frivolity, behold, on the contrary, the mourner's heart is broken within him and far from frivolity. What kind of diversion of attention applies here (Sha’agat Aryeh there)? But in truth, it is not difficult at all: for we do not say that diversion of attention is frivolity but rather actual diversion of attention, so as not to come to frivolity. Rather, we mean this: that the intent is not to think every moment specifically about the tefillin but when he remembers, he should touch them, and thereby remember, and this will prevent frivolity. However, it is also obvious that when one wears tefillin, he must be in awe and joy, in the manner of "rejoice with trembling." And this is also proven from the beginning of the chapter "Ein Omdin," that one must be in joy. And this is what Abaye responded there: "I am wearing tefillin," meaning: and from this, I am joyful. But when his heart is broken and he is in sadness, this too is called diversion of attention. Meaning: he diverts his attention from the joy of the mitzvah. And this is what our Rabbis said: that a mourner must compose his mind..., meaning: to compose his mind so that he is not in excessive sadness, in order to focus his heart on the tefillin so that there will be the joy of the mitzvah. Therefore, during the eulogy and weeping, he does not wear them, for it is impossible to have the joy of the mitzvah at that moment.

And the Rambam wrote in the fourth chapter: One who is distressed or whose mind is not settled is exempt from wearing tefillin, because one who wears tefillin is prohibited from diverting his attention from them. So far his language, and similarly, it is written by the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch later in Siman 38. And this is its explanation: Since he is distressed or his mind is not settled, he will certainly forget about them entirely and come to act with levity. This means he might pass gas while wearing them or sleep a fixed sleep. Besides, one must be in a state of joy for the mitzvah. Hence, from this, there is no proof that the Rambam disagrees with what has been explained. And see what I have written in Siman 38, section 14.

However, it is further written there: A person is obligated to touch his tefillin at all times while they are upon him, so that he does not divert his attention from them even for a single moment. For their sanctity is greater than the sanctity of the tzitz (the headplate of the High Priest), for the tzitz contains only one name of God, whereas these contain twenty-one names of the Tetragrammaton (Yod-Heh) in the head-tefillin, and an equal number in the hand-tefillin. Thus far is his language, and he wrote "so that he does not divert his attention even for a single moment." 

However, if so, it is not understood what he wrote afterwards that one may sleep in them a temporary sleep; see there. For there are many moments when one diverts his attention from them. And there is one who says that there is a specific measure of time during which it is forbidden to divert one's attention from them, which is approximately the time it takes to walk one hundred cubits, and a temporary sleep is less than this measure, and therefore it is permitted (Sha'agat Aryeh, ibid.). 

But it is impossible to say this, for Rambam wrote "even for a moment." And there is one who says that since one covers the tefillin, as explained there, there is no prohibition of diverting one's attention (Artzos Hachaim). And this explanation does not hold any reasoning for praise, as is evident.

In my opinion, casual sleep is not problematic at all, for a person is compelled to sleep and is then exempt from all the commandments. What relevance does distraction have at that time? The sages did not trouble him to remove [the tefillin] from his head because they estimated that in such a short time, he would not come to flatulence. But at that time, there is no obligation upon him. Indeed, during sleep, we are like the dead, and therefore we bless "He who restores souls to dead bodies," and what obligation applies to a person then? However, the main difficulty lies with the Rambam's opinion: how is it possible not to be distracted even for a moment? If so, how can one think about prayer and Torah, since all his thoughts are on the tefillin? Therefore, it appears to me, in my humble opinion, that the Rambam only spoke about times when one is idle or engaged in worldly matters. But during prayer and study, even the Rambam would agree with this. Nevertheless, this does not seem to be indicated by their words. (And according to the Rambam, the case in Shabbat 12a, which we wrote about at the end of paragraph 2, fits perfectly, see there. Examine carefully and you will find it easy.)

When one touches the tefillin to check their placement – he first touches the tefillin of the arm, and then the tefillin of the head. Just as he does when putting them on, so too when touching them. As it is written: "And you shall bind them as a sign upon your hand," and afterwards: "And they shall be as frontlets between your eyes." When he says "And you shall bind them" – he touches the tefillin of the arm, and when he says "And they shall be" – he touches the tefillin of the head. But when removing the tefillin – he removes the tefillin of the head first and then the tefillin of the arm, because it is written: "And they shall be as frontlets between your eyes" – that as long as the tefillin are between your eyes, there should be two. Before removing the tefillin of the head, he should remove the strap of the arm tefillin from the middle finger. And he should remove them while standing, just as he puts them on while standing, so too should he remove them. Therefore, those who put on the arm tefillin while sitting – should remove it also while sitting, and only the head tefillin should be removed while standing. It is the custom of the scholars to kiss the tefillin when putting them on and when removing them, as a sign of love for the mitzvah.

Our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in Section 2 that one should place the tefillin of the head in the bag first and then the tefillin of the hand on top of it, so that when one comes to put them on, one will encounter the tefillin of the hand first. This is his wording. And although the tefillin of the head has greater sanctity than the tefillin of the hand, there is no concern with the tefillin of the hand being placed on top of the tefillin of the head. Only in the case of the Torah and the Prophets, where the difference is very great, is it forbidden to place the Prophets on top of the Torah, as I wrote in Yoreh De'ah, Section 282. But regarding the difference between the tefillin of the hand and the tefillin of the head, there is no concern. And the proof is that it is permitted to place the Prophets on top of the Writings, and the Writings on top of the Prophets, even though their sanctity is certainly not the same. But since the difference is not that great, there is no concern (Magen Avraham, Small Section 4). Some have the custom to make two separate pouches (ibid.). And our custom is to place the tefillin of the head on the right side, and the tefillin of the hand on the left side. We have already mentioned this in Section 25, Subsection 19. 

Some are particular about not wrapping the straps around the tefillin, since the tefillin's sanctity is much greater than that of the straps. Therefore, they wrap the straps separately like wings. But there is no concern in this matter because this is the customary manner of use, just as one wraps a cloth around a Torah scroll. Similarly, wrapping the straps around the tefillin keeps them well-preserved. This is also our custom. Additionally, some have the custom to place the dalet of the knot of the head tefillin on the ma'avarta (the part of the strap that goes around the head) and not under it, since, being part of the name "Shaddai," it is not appropriate to place it at the bottom. They wrap the straps around the ends (see Magen Avraham, Small Section 4). And one removes the head tefillin with the left hand to show that parting from them is difficult (ibid., Small Section 3).

The Tur wrote: One should not recite "Who has sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us to observe His statutes" when removing [the tefillin]. For the law does not follow the custom of the people of the West (Berachot 44b) who would recite "to observe His statutes" at the time of their removal, because they believe that the night is not a time for tefillin. They derive this from "And you shall observe this statute..." which they interpret as applying to days and not nights (like Rabbi Yossi HaGalili in Menachot 36b). However, we hold that the night is a time for tefillin... (like Rabbi Akiva there). Even on the eve of Shabbat during twilight, when one must remove them, one should not bless, for we do not learn this from "And you shall observe" but rather from "as a sign...". And I have seen in the name of Rav Hai Gaon that it is permissible: if one wishes to bless, he may bless. And I am puzzled: since he is not obligated, wouldn't this be a blessing in vain? Until here is his language. (See Beit Yosef and Bach, who exerted themselves to explain the words of the Gaon with forced explanations. See there.)

I am astonished by the people of the West: Granted, the Torah decreed "and you shall observe" that one should not leave them [tefillin] on at night. And wherever it says "observe," "lest," or "do not" – it is only a negative commandment, as it is stated in Menachot there. Nevertheless, the Rosh, the Ran, and all the early authorities wrote at the beginning of Ketubot that it is not appropriate to recite a blessing over a prohibition, see there. And in my humble opinion, it appears explicitly from Berachot there and Nidda (51b) that this blessing is an after-blessing for the tefillin, similar to the after-blessings for eating and drinking, and like the blessing over the Torah. For it is stated explicitly there, see there.
