However, this blessing is only relevant if nighttime is not a time for tefillin, from the derived interpretation – in this case, it is appropriate to recite the blessing "who has sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us to observe His statutes," which is the blessing after the tefillin. But if nighttime is a time for tefillin – this blessing is not relevant even on the eve of Shabbat, for "as a sign" a blessing is not relevant, obviously, for only "to observe" which He commanded us to observe, is a blessing relevant (as also written by the Beit Yosef). And this is also the intention of the Jerusalem Talmud in the third chapter of Berachot (halacha 3), see there, and not that the blessing is for the prohibition of wearing them at night. Therefore, the opinion of the Gaon is that just as the blessing "Borei Nefashot" is mentioned in the Gemara: one who blessed over the water and one who did not bless, see there – here too with tefillin it is the same. And he ruled according to Rabbi Yosei HaGlili that nighttime is not a time for tefillin. And indeed, the opinion of Maimonides is also like this, as will be explained in Siman 30, and with all this he did not write this blessing because we hold that one does not recite an after-blessing for a mitzvah, as explained in the Gemara there. And the Gaon said that one who wishes to – may bless, and there is no concern with this. (And also the words of the Tosafot there can be explained in this manner, see there well. However, from the words of the Tur, the Beit Yosef, and the Bach, it is clear that they did not explain it this way. And also what we have written answers the questions of the Taz and the Magen Avraham, see there well, because we hold that a mitzvah does not require a blessing after it. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

There are those who have the custom, when they reach the phrase "May it be Your will that we keep Your statutes…" in the "Uva Letzion" prayer, to remove the strap from the finger as a remembrance of "keeping His statutes" according to the custom of the Westerners (Jews of the Land of Israel). I do not know if we should do this, since we do not follow the practice of the Westerners. Moreover, the Westerners only used to bless if they removed the straps in the evening. On the other hand, what concern is there in doing this? Nonetheless, I do not know if we should make a remembrance for something that is not established according to the law. This requires further investigation.

The time to put them on in the morning is when one can see their friend from a distance of four cubits and recognize them. This is because it is written concerning tefillin: "And all the peoples of the earth shall see that the name of the Lord is called upon you..." Therefore, it depends on sight. And it is stated in the Jerusalem Talmud, the first chapter of Berakhot, that this friend should be someone whom he recognizes somewhat. For if he recognizes him well, he would recognize him even from a distance. This is what the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch wrote: a friend who is somewhat familiar with him..., see there.

It is taught in Menachot (36b): "And you shall observe this statute in its appointed time from year to year." "Days" – and not nights; "from days" – and not all days, excluding Sabbaths and Festivals, these are the words of Rabbi Yossi the Galilean. Rabbi Akiva says: This statute is only stated regarding Passover. And in another Baraita it is taught: Rabbi Akiva says: Could a person wear Tefillin on Sabbaths and Festivals? The verse states: "And it shall be a sign..." – for those who need a sign, excluding Sabbaths and Festivals which are themselves a sign. And Rabbi Yochanan said there: Anyone who wears Tefillin after sunset transgresses a negative commandment, and this follows Rabbi Yossi the Galilean. And it was said there that even according to Rabbi Yossi the Galilean, if one’s intention is to guard them, it is permitted to wear them at night so they are not lost. And we say there that Rav Ashi holds like Rabbi Akiva that night is a time for Tefillin. However, we do not rule this way, lest one falls asleep in them and comes to a state of disrespect. Therefore, by rabbinic decree, one should not wear them at night.

The Rambam in Chapter Four, Law 10, rules according to Rabbi Yosi HaGlili, who wrote: "The time for laying tefillin is during the day and not at night, as it says: 'from days to days.' This statute is the mitzvah of tefillin. Similarly, Shabbat and holidays are not the time for tefillin, as it says: 'and it shall be a sign,' and Shabbat and holidays are themselves a sign... And anyone who lays tefillin initially after sunset transgresses a negative commandment, as it says 'and you shall observe...' up to here is his wording."

And even though he ruled according to Rabbi Yosi HaGlili, nevertheless, regarding Shabbat and holidays, he takes the verse from Rabbi Akiva of 'for a sign.' And it seems that he holds like the Tosafot in Eruvin (96a) that Rabbi Yosi HaGlili himself relies on the verse of Rabbi Akiva, see there. And their reasoning is clear: for if not so, how would we know to exclude 'from days' and not all days for Shabbat and holidays (Maharshal)? Perhaps it refers to other days? Rather, it is certainly that he relies on the verse of 'for a sign.' And even though it ostensibly seems that even on Shabbat and holidays there is a difference between Rabbi Yosi HaGlili and Rabbi Akiva: for Rabbi Yosi HaGlili, one transgresses a negative commandment because it comes from 'and you shall observe,' like at night; and for Rabbi Akiva, one only does not need to lay them on Shabbat and holidays, but does not transgress a negative commandment (and so wrote the Sha'agat Aryeh, Siman 41) – the Rambam does not seem to hold this way. And proof for this is from Rabbi Yochanan, who holds like Rabbi Yosi HaGlili, why did he not say that anyone who lays tefillin at night or on Shabbat and holidays transgresses a negative commandment? Rather, surely on Shabbat and holidays, even according to Rabbi Yosi HaGlili, one does not transgress a negative commandment, and the reason is because the primary verse of 'and you shall observe' applies to the night. But for Shabbat and holidays, the primary verse is 'for a sign,' as I have written. Therefore, the Rambam did not bother to bring the verse of 'and you shall observe' for Shabbat and holidays.

However, our Rabbis, the Ba'alei HaTosafot, the Rif, the Rosh, and the SeMaG ruled according to Rabbi Akiva, because Rav Ashi holds this view. And nighttime, according to the Torah, is a time for Tefillin; it is only by rabbinic decree that they prohibited wearing them at night, lest one falls asleep in them. This is also the ruling of the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch. Here are the words of Rabbi Yosef Caro in Section 2: It is forbidden to put on Tefillin at night, lest one forgets and sleeps in them. However, if one put them on before sunset and it became dark while they were on, it is permitted even if they remain on all night. But this is not instructed as a common practice (and in public, one should remove them). If one did not remove their Tefillin after sunset because they had no place to safeguard them, and they remained on to guard them, it is permitted and this is indeed instructed. Thus far are his words. And he needs to state that he is doing this to safeguard them (Magen Avraham). And also Rambam wrote these laws. Now, if it is explicitly stated in the Gemara that it is permitted to keep them on to safeguard them, even if nighttime is not a time for Tefillin as I wrote. But the first law, that if it became dark while they were on it is permitted but not instructed, why was this written? In the Gemara, this was only for those who hold that nighttime is a time for Tefillin. It appears clearly that Rambam interprets a different explanation in the Gemara, in a way that this applies even to those who say that nighttime is not a time for Tefillin. (And this is its explanation: I was sitting before Rav Ashi and it became dark and he put on Tefillin, meaning: he did not remove them… – it is the law but not instructed as a common practice. Meaning: the law is that from the Torah it is forbidden to put them on at night, but there is no Torah obligation to remove them, but it is not instructed unless it is to safeguard them. According to this, the reason of Rambam is revealed why he ruled according to Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, because he interprets that Rav Ashi also holds like Rabbi Yosei HaGelili. According to this, it can be said that also the Rif holds this way, as he wrote: and the law is according to Rav Ashi. And according to Rambam’s explanation, it does not contradict Rabbi Yochanan. According to this, it is well understood why the Rif also brought the words of Rabbi Yochanan. The great later authorities labored much on their words, and in my humble opinion, their reasoning is clear that this is so. Be precise and you will find it easy (to understand).

If one wishes to set out on a journey early in the morning, he should put on the tefillin without a blessing, even according to those who say that night is a time for tefillin according to the Torah. Nevertheless, since the Rabbis prohibited it, even though they permitted it for someone setting out on a journey because in such a case there is no concern that he will fall asleep while wearing them, for how can he sleep while walking on the way? Nonetheless, it is impossible to recite a blessing, for how can he say "and commanded us"? Did not the Sages prohibit it at night? Therefore, he should put them on without a blessing, and when the proper time arrives, he should touch them and recite the blessing. 

Know that this permission was only granted to one who is walking on foot. But if he is sitting in a wagon, they did not permit him to put them on before daybreak, for one sitting in a wagon has the same concern of sleeping as in his own home (Taz and Magen Avraham, subsection 5). Similarly, one riding on a horse or donkey is prohibited from putting them on before daybreak (ibid.). And even though it would seem that a rider cannot sleep, for he would fall, nevertheless, those accustomed to riding can sleep while the horse or donkey is not running fast, and therefore it is prohibited. However, there is an opinion that permits it for a rider (Eliyah Rabbah), and this seems to be the primary opinion.

Here is the translation of the passage:

"Behold, the Tur and Shulchan Aruch wrote this law, but the Rambam did not write it. They were puzzled by this, as this is a Baraita at the end of the chapter 'HaKometz' (36a). They wrote that he (the Rambam) holds that this goes according to the one who says that nighttime is a time for Tefillin (Beit Yosef). I am puzzled by them: On the contrary, the Baraita explicitly supports the Rambam. And this is the language of the Baraita: 'If one rises early to go on a journey and fears that they might be lost – he puts them on, and when the time comes – he touches them…', see there – thus, they only permitted it if there is a fear they might be lost, which is for safeguarding them, and this is indeed what the Rambam wrote. Moreover, I am astonished at the Tur and Shulchan Aruch for omitting this 'fears they might be lost', and how do we know that it is permitted even without this concern? We must say that they hold that the Baraita 'and fears they might be lost' – this is according to the one who says that nighttime is not a time for Tefillin. And since they ruled that nighttime is a time for Tefillin – it is permitted even without this concern. But how do we know to say this? In any case, the words of the Rambam are necessary from the Baraita itself. And perhaps the Tur and Shulchan Aruch did not have the text 'and fears they might be lost' in the Baraita. And I saw that indeed the Rif and Rosh (Siman 16) had this version, see there. But the Mordechai brought it and had the text 'and fears they might be lost', and this was also the Rambam's version. According to this, all the words of our Rabbis are explained well."

If one was on the way with tefillin on his head, and the sun set upon him – he does not remove them. However, he should place his hand over the tefillin on his head until he reaches home, so that an observer does not think he is wearing them at night. But if he was sitting in his home or in the study hall – he does not need to cover them with his hand, because those present there saw that he put them on before nightfall. However, on Friday evening during twilight when he was sitting in the study hall, and he cannot leave them there due to fear of theft or loss, and he cannot carry them in his hand because of Shabbat – he should go home, placing his hand over them until he reaches his house. If there is a house closer to his own where they can be safeguarded – he is obligated to remove them and place them there.

And our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote: There are those who say that if one prayed the evening prayer while it was still daytime, before having put on tefillin, he should not put them on afterward. Thus is his language. Because he already made it night, and it would be two leniencies that contradict each other. Therefore, if he did not pray, even though the congregation prayed, it is permitted to put on tefillin. And there are those who say that if one thought it was day and made the blessing, but it was actually night, he is not required to make the blessing during the day, because we hold according to most of the authorities that night is a time for tefillin (Birkhei Yosef). And know that the Kabbalists warned not to have tefillin on at night, and also not to pray the evening prayer with them. And perhaps they hold like the Rambam, that according to the Torah, night is not a time for tefillin.

Shabbat and Yom Tov are not times for Tefillin, as we derive from "and it shall be for a sign"—excluding Shabbatot and Yomim Tovim, as they themselves are a sign. And we have already written in the previous section, paragraph 3, that even according to the Rambam, who rules like Rabbi Yosi HaGlili that nighttime is not a time for Tefillin based on the verse "and you shall observe," and according to him, one transgresses a prohibition if he puts them on at night, and he also derives from this verse for Shabbat and Yom Tov. Nevertheless, one who puts them on during Shabbat and Yom Tov does not transgress a prohibition, for the reason we explained there. In any case, our master the Beit Yosef wrote that on Shabbat and Yom Tov it is forbidden to put on Tefillin because they themselves are a sign, and if one puts another sign on them, it would be a disrespect to their sign. Thus are his words. And the intention is not a Torah prohibition, but a prohibition due to the disrespect of Shabbat and Yom Tov.

And so it is written in the Mekhilta at the end of Parashat 17: Rabbi Yitzchak says: Since Shabbat is called "a sign" and Tefillin are called "a sign" – one should not place one sign within another sign. Or should one place a sign within a sign? You say: Let Shabbat, for which one is liable for karet (excision) and death by the court, override Tefillin, for which one is not liable for karet and death by the court. Thus far his words. This means: Shabbat overrides Tefillin, and it is a disgrace to Shabbat to need another sign. And in the Yalkut, there is another statement in different language: Let Shabbat, which is called "a sign," and the covenant of Tefillin, which is called only "a sign," be overridden? The intention is that it is forbidden to add one sign to the sign of Shabbat. And Yom Tov is also like Shabbat, for it is written about them "a rest day": "On the first day a rest day," "and on the eighth day a rest day." And even the second day of Yom Tov, which is rabbinic, is forbidden for Tefillin, for the sages have the power to uproot a matter from the Torah by "sit and do not act," like shofar and lulav when it falls on Shabbat, as we say in Yevamot (90b). And it is obvious that if one puts on Tefillin on Shabbat and Yom Tov for the sake of the commandment, he transgresses "do not add." And whether it is permitted to handle Tefillin on Shabbat and Yom Tov will be explained in Siman 38 with the help of Heaven.

And what is the sign? Rashi explains that the essence of Shabbat itself is the sign. This is Rashi's wording: "They themselves are a sign between the Holy One, blessed be He, and Israel, as it is written: 'For it is a sign between Me and you.' And it is said: 'Between Me and the children of Israel it is a sign forever,' that the essence of the day is the sign." And in the Or Zarua HaGadol (siman 589) it is written: "Shabbatot and Yomim Tovim are excluded, as they themselves are the sign." Rabbi Eliezer explains that it is written: "Between Me and the children of Israel it is a sign," meaning that they themselves are the sign, as the Sambatyon River and the manna from heaven prove they rest on them. So far his wording. And similarly, it is explained in the wording of the Rif, who wrote that they themselves are the sign, as it is written: "For it is a sign between Me and the children of Israel." So far his wording. And Shabbat and Yom Tov are one, as Yom Tov is also called "Shabbaton," as I have written. Similarly, "the day after Shabbat" refers to the first day of Pesach. And Tosafot and the Rosh wrote that one could say: either the prohibition of work is called the "sign," or matzah on Pesach and sukkah on Sukkot. The practical difference pertains to Chol HaMoed, as will be explained with the help of Heaven. And the Rokeach (siman 30) wrote that the sign of the Exodus from Egypt is a sign, and this is in Shabbat and tefillin. (Therefore, even though circumcision is a sign, it does not fulfill this sign, because it is not a sign of the Exodus from Egypt, see there. Some of the early authorities wrote that the sign of circumcision is a sign, but every person must have two signs upon him, as it is said: "By the word of two witnesses a matter shall be established." Therefore, on weekdays it is circumcision and tefillin, and on Shabbat and Yom Tov it is circumcision and the sign of Shabbat and Yom Tov.)

Regarding the law of wearing Tefillin on Chol HaMoed: In the Talmud, Rif, and Rambam, it is not explicitly mentioned whether one is obligated to wear Tefillin or not. The Rosh ruled that one is obligated to wear Tefillin because the sign is the prohibition of work, and work on Chol HaMoed is permitted by Torah law. Similarly, the Mordechai ruled, and he wrote that also Maharam of Rothenburg ruled thus. Likewise, Rabbi Yitzchak of the Tosafists, the Sefer Mitzvot Katan, and the Sefer HaTerumah ruled to wear them without a blessing. In several places in the Tosafot, they seem to be uncertain about this, and in Eruvin (96a), they wrote that one is obligated according to the Jerusalem Talmud in the third chapter of Moed Katan. They wrote that this is the custom, see there. The Rashba in a responsum (Siman 690) ruled that one is exempt because work on Chol HaMoed is forbidden by Torah law. He wrote that also the Raavad holds this view. Indeed, it is found in the Raavad's Sefer Temim Deim (Siman 40), and he also wrote this in the name of the Tosafot, see there. However, in the Tosafot before us, this is not found. Also, the Tosafot wrote that the Baal Halachot Gedolot forbids wearing them on Chol HaMoed, see there. In the Baal Halachot Gedolot before us, this is not found. According to the Zohar, the poskim wrote that it is forbidden to wear them. Our master, the Beit Yosef, ruled not to wear them. Our master, the Rema, ruled to wear them and to recite the blessing quietly. All Sephardim do not wear them, and all Ashkenazim wear them. However, now they wear them without a blessing, and this is appropriate. Many of the great Acharonim have already elaborated on this, some saying this and some saying that, and therefore everyone should follow their own custom. Nowadays, many Ashkenazim also do not wear them, and there is no need to elaborate on this. However, in any case, in one Beit Midrash, one should not do so and another do otherwise, because of "lo titgodedu" (do not form factions).

(If the sign is the prohibition of work, it depends on whether the prohibition of work on Chol HaMoed is Torah law or Rabbinic law. If the sign is matzah and Sukkah – one is exempt. If the sign is, according to Rashi, the Rif, and the Or Zarua, the essence of the day, it seems one is obligated, and this is also written in Mishkenot Yaakov Siman 37. Nevertheless, it is possible to say that just as on Yom Tov we do not find the expression "sign" explicitly but that they are like Shabbat, perhaps the same applies to Chol HaMoed because all these days are days of sanctity. Also, according to the Rokeach, who holds that the sign is the Exodus from Egypt – certainly this applies to Chol HaMoed, as we say in the Musaf prayer "a remembrance of the Exodus from Egypt". It is not possible to decisively rule on this as it stands in the heights of the world, and both these and those are the words of the living God.)

The mitzvah of tefillin is to write these four sections: "Sanctify to Me every firstborn" until "from year to year," "And it shall be when the Lord brings you" until "with a strong hand the Lord brought us out of Egypt," the section of "Shema" until "and on your gates," and "And it shall be if you listen" until "upon the earth." In the head tefillin, each section is written on a separate parchment, and in the hand tefillin, all are written on one parchment. It is taught in the Mekhilta at the end of the section "Bo": If they were written out of order, they should be buried. This "out of order" includes three things: the first is the placement, meaning that in the hand tefillin, "Shema" was placed next to "Sanctify" or similar. Similarly, in the head tefillin, "Shema" was placed next to "Sanctify." The second is the writing of the sections, meaning if "And it shall be when the Lord brings you" was written before "Sanctify," it is invalid because it needs to be written in the order we explained. Therefore, if the last section becomes invalid, it must be rewritten. But if the first section becomes invalid, all are invalid, meaning not invalid itself, but there is no one to join it unless there is another first section that was written before the other three sections, then it can be joined and they are valid. The third is in the letters, if a mistake was made in one letter and it needs to be erased or corrected, all the letters after it until the end of the section are invalid. The writing must be in order, the earlier first and the later later. This is what is said in the Jerusalem Talmud, first chapter of Megillah (halacha 9): One does not hang [letters or words] in tefillin and mezuzot. Meaning, in a Torah scroll, if one letter is missing, it can be hung between the lines. In tefillin and mezuzah, it is not so because it would be out of order. In these laws, they are stricter than the Torah scroll, because it is written: "And they shall be" – they shall be as they are, meaning in the order written in the Torah.

According to this, if one letter in a Torah scroll is erased or damaged, it is invalid. This applies specifically when the letter is completely erased; however, if its outline is still recognizable, it is valid, and one can go over it with a quill. This will be further explained. If the damage is minor, meaning the letter is damaged but its shape is still discernible, such as if the yuds of the alefs are broken but the alef shape remains – one can fix them and they are valid. If there is a small break in the roof of a bet or similar, if the break is small enough that the shape of the bet remains – one can fix it and it is valid, as this is not considered "out of order." This will be further explained with Divine assistance. Likewise, "out of order" only applies to missing letters, not extra ones. The Rambam wrote this in Chapter 2, Law 3, and this is his wording: One must be careful about full and deficient spellings... for if a deficient word is written fully, it is invalid until the extra letter is erased. If a full word is written deficiently, it is invalid and cannot be corrected. This is his wording, and the reason is simple: every extra letter is as if it is nonexistent, and "out of order" does not apply to it, so one erases it and it is valid. However, one must be careful that if the extra letter is in the middle of the word, there should not be a large gap in the middle of the word, and one should draw the previous or following letter as much as possible (as the Magen Avraham wrote at the end of subsection 33, see there). Likewise, if an extra word is written – one erases it and it is valid, provided that a space of nine small letters does not remain, for then it is invalid because it constitutes a section break. (And although Rabbeinu Tam holds that a section break is three letters – we do not follow this, as the Magen Avraham wrote there.)

In writing the sections of the tefillin for the arm and the head, which should be done first – it is not an impediment, for in this matter, the order does not matter, as both are equal. However, some say that since the head tefillin is of a higher sanctity than the arm tefillin, one should write the head tefillin first. But our teacher, the Rema, ruled the opposite, that ideally, one should write the arm tefillin before the head tefillin. His reasoning seems to be that the arm tefillin is written first in the Torah. Additionally, it appears to me that since all the sections are written on one parchment for the arm tefillin, as I have written, because the Torah decreed "And you shall bind them as a sign on your hand" – it must be one sign (Menachot 34b). Therefore, this parchment, at the time of its writing, is more sanctified than any parchment of the head tefillin, which has no more than one section on each parchment. Furthermore, the writing of the tefillin is not explicitly stated and is included in the binding, making it as if it is written "And you shall bind them and write them." If so, just as in the placement, the arm tefillin comes first, so too in the writing. Nevertheless, it is not an impediment, and perhaps this is why the Torah did not specify the order of writing because it is not an impediment.

And similarly with the writing of the letters, for each letter individually, the requirement of "in order" does not apply. That is to say: within each letter itself, there is an order of earlier and later parts, such as the letter "Hei" which should be written first with the "Dalet" and afterward the "Yud," and so it is with all the letters. Nevertheless, if one writes the later part first, it does not matter, for as long as the letter is not completed, it is considered as nothing (Pri Megadim). Similarly, if one wrote part of a letter and afterward wrote the preceding letter, and then returned and completed the following letter, it is not considered "out of order" for the reason explained (there). And it appears to me that if one did not add the crowns to the letters that require them and wrote the subsequent letters afterward, this is not considered "out of order," and one may add the crowns afterward. The same applies to the small lines extending from the letters; one can add them afterward, for since the main parts of the letters were written in order, it does not matter. (And the Magen Avraham writes in Section 1 that the "Dalet" of "Echad" should be larger, like four very small Dalets, but not like the Dalets of the parshiyot. Pri Megadim.)

Some have written to be careful to write all the sections of the tefillin (both for the arm and the head) consecutively, without any interruption in speech at all. At the very least, there should be no interruption between the first and second sections, and similarly between the third and fourth sections. If one did interrupt between the second and third sections, when beginning to write the third section, he should pass the quill over the first word of the first and second sections, and then write the third section (Sha'arei Teshuvah, section 4, in the name of Kavanot). However, this is not a strict requirement by law, but rather an enhancement of the mitzvah. Certainly, it is appropriate to enhance such a significant mitzvah. Additionally, one should write them in purity, meaning one should immerse in a mikveh to purify from the impurity of seminal emission. He should write the sections consecutively for both the arm and the head tefillin. But as for an interruption between the arm and head tefillin, I do not know of any stringent requirement, as they are two separate commandments. None of this is an absolute requirement, as I have written.

The writing must be specifically with ink. And what is "ink"? We have explained this in Yoreh De'ah, section 271, from paragraph 26 to paragraph 35, and the words of our Rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, which seemingly contradict themselves there, section 3. And we explained there that the essential law depends on three things: it must be black, it must endure, and its source must be from a tree. Therefore, in the time of the Talmud, they would make it from the smoke of oils of fruits that are from a tree. And now we are not knowledgeable in this, therefore we make it from gallnuts which are from the tree, and gum and copperas water, and this is kankantom (verdigris).

And this is what our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, wrote in section 3: they should be written in black ink, whether it contains gallnut water or not. Ideally, one should be stringent to write with ink made from the smoke of trees, or oils soaked in gallnut water. Up to here is their language, meaning: initially, they wrote that the main requirement is the blackness, as in the opinion of the Rambam, this alone is essential, as I wrote there. However, in truth, something derived from a tree is essential, even though the Rambam did not mention this. And it is explicitly stated in the Zohar Terumah (page 159), and this is its language: “And all matters of ink are from trees.” And more: "Black ink," see there. And this is why they wrote that ideally one should be stringent to make it from smoke soaked in gallnut water, as both are from trees. But we are not experts in this, and therefore in Yoreh De'ah it is explained that it should only be from a tree. And this is like what we do with gallnuts and gum arabic, as both are from a tree: gum arabic is also from a tree, as it is the resin that drips from a tree, and vitriol for blackness, which is copperas. (And with this, everything that the Magen Avraham found difficult in section 2, and the Pri Megadim, see there, is resolved. Examine and you will find it easy.)

If one writes even a single letter with other types of colors or with gold, where gold dust is mixed with water and written with – it is completely invalid. This is because correction does not help since it requires "in order," and this letter that was not written with ink is considered as if it was not written at all. If one sprinkled gold dust on the letters to beautify them – he should remove the gold, and the underlying writing will remain, and it is valid. As long as the gold is not removed – it is invalid. Therefore, if he sprinkled gold even on a single letter of the names [of God] – there is no remedy, because it is forbidden to remove the gold since it is like erasing the name, and while the gold is on it, the letter is invalid. Therefore, they require genizah (burial). (Nonetheless, "not in order" does not apply when removing.)

It is necessary that no letter should touch its neighboring letter. Rather, each letter should be surrounded by parchment on all four sides (Gemara 29a). Even the final letter must be surrounded by parchment on all sides. The reason for this is not explicitly stated, but it appears to me that this is a law given to Moses at Sinai. There is someone who wrote that this is due to "complete writing" (the opinion of the Gr"a). However, it seems to me that "complete writing" pertains only to the body of the letter. Additionally, in the Mordechai at the beginning of the laws of Torah scrolls, he brings opinions that in a Torah scroll there is no need for the surrounding of parchment, and this also seems to be the view of the Nimukei Yosef at the beginning of the laws of mezuzah. Also, the Rif did not bring this in the context of a Torah scroll. If it were due to "complete writing," then it should also apply to a Torah scroll, shouldn't it? Therefore, it is certain that this is a law given to Moses at Sinai, and it is believed that it was not said regarding a Torah scroll. However, we hold that even in a Torah scroll this is a requirement, as I have written in Yoreh De'ah, siman 271. This is also the ruling of the Rambam in the first chapter, law 19, see there. (From the language of the Tur, it seemingly implies like the Gr"a, and so wrote the Taz and the Perisha. But the Bach wrote like our words, and he wrote that the Tur relates different matters without bringing proofs. It is clear that his reasoning is based on the proofs we have brought.)

And in the Jerusalem Talmud Berakhot (Chapter 2, end of Halacha 3) it is stated: If one joined the letters together – some teach it is valid, and some teach it is invalid. Rabbi Idi... (meaning, they do not disagree): if it is joined at the bottom, it is valid; if it is joined at the top, it is invalid. For example, "ארצינו תפארתינו" – "ארצך" requires, "תפארתך" requires, see there. And its explanation is as follows: Regarding letters that are of equal length, the law is clear that if the joining is at the top, it is invalid, and if at the bottom, it is valid; because even without the joining, the shape of the letter remains. However, for letters that are not equal in length, like "ארצך", "תפארתך", where the final letter extends below the other letters, and the joining is at the bottom of the other letters, and in the middle of the final letter – it requires a question. Meaning: it is a doubt and we rule stringently, and so wrote the Rashba in a response (Siman 511). And his version in the Jerusalem Talmud was not like ours, and he explained that joining at the top does not help by scraping, because it is considered "chiseling from the inside" since the letter is not yet complete. But joining at the bottom by scraping does help, see there. And from the words of all the poskim it is clearly implied that scraping helps in all cases, as this is not comparable to "chiseling from the inside" since one is only scraping between the letters. And so it is explicitly written in the Hagahot Maimoniot (Chapter 1, letter 80) and in the Mordechai at the beginning of the chapter "Hakometz Rabbah", that when dealing with separating the letters – it is not considered "chiseling from the inside", see there. And only the Mordechai is stringent even at the bottom until one scrapes, because our Talmud does not make such a distinction, see there (and so wrote the Taz, section 3).

In terms of the law, it appears that erasure is certainly effective, as explained by the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch in sections 25 and 26, that even if letters of the Divine Name are attached, it is permissible to erase them. This is also the opinion of most poskim. However, regarding attachment from below, if one is obligated to erase it—certainly, during the weekdays, one should erase it. But on Shabbat and Yom Tov, when erasing is prohibited, one can rely straightforwardly on the Jerusalem Talmud and not act otherwise to avoid disgracing this Torah. (See Magen Avraham, subsection 3, who tends to be stringent, and in the name of Radak, he brings a lenient view; see there. Therefore, when it is impossible to erase, one can rely on this. And if the crowns [of letters] touch each other, one should erase, but it does not invalidate it. And what is written that according to Rambam it is invalid, I am astonished: for Rambam wrote in the second and seventh chapters that the crowns do not hinder at all; see there. And Meiri explicitly permits, as Magen Avraham wrote. Be precise and you will find leniency.)

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote in section 4: One should write with a complete and proper script, not omitting even the smallest part of the letter yud, and ensuring that it is crowned according to the halacha. Ideally, one should write in a slightly thick script so that it does not get erased quickly. It is also a mitzvah to beautify them both inside and outside. This is the end of his words. And even though in Shabbat (103b) it is said: "And you shall write" – a complete writing, not to write the letter aleph like an ayin... Nevertheless, even the omission of the smallest part of the yud does not constitute a complete writing, because a complete writing is when the letter is written in its entirety. Furthermore, even in the name [of God], it is not necessarily intended to literally mean alephs like ayins, for if that were the case, the verse "And you shall write" would not be necessary, as that is not the letter that needs to be written. Rather, the intention is that it should look somewhat like an ayin, for example, if the lower yud of the aleph extends very high upwards, or the upper yud of the aleph goes very low downwards, and it appears somewhat like an ayin, although in reality it is an aleph but not in its completeness. Therefore, even with the omission of a small part, it is not in its completeness. This will be further clarified in section 36, paragraph 6, see there.

And know that there are three strokes on the letter Yud: the first one is slightly curved on its right side, and it is the main one; the second is opposite it on the left side, much smaller, and it is not curved; and the third is a small stroke on the upper left side, as will be explained in Siman 36. These two also seem to be essential, but it is possible to correct them even after the tefillin has been written, since there is no issue of "out of order" because the main part of the letter exists (as the Pri Megadim wrote in Taz, Siman 3). However, if the right stroke is completely missing, it seems that it is not effective to write it afterward, since without it, the letter does not have the form of a Yud (Beit Yosef, and Taz, Siman 36, Siman 1). The scribes are not careful about the left stroke, and they should be reprimanded because, according to Rabbeinu Tam in Tosafot Menachot (29a), this is the stroke of the Yud that is essential, see there.

And know that from his wording, which combines the law of the crowns with the law of the thorns, it appears that both are essential. This follows the position of the Tur in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 273. However, in Tur, Siman 36, our master the Beit Yosef rules according to the Rambam that the crowns are not essential, and he did not comment on it. And we have already written in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 274, Section 14, that we follow the Rambam. See there. It must be said that he did not intend to equate them completely, and this is why he did not write that this is only preferable, as he wrote regarding large writing—because it is not comparable: there, it is only an enhancement, like beautifying the writing, and not a fundamental law. But the crowns are essential according to the Rambam, as it is a law from the Talmud, and one is obligated to correct them. We just do not invalidate [the writing] without the crowns. And this law is only addressed here in Siman 36.

The Tur wrote: "One must write with the right hand even if one is ambidextrous. And a left-handed person – his left hand is considered his right." So is his language, and the reason: "perfect writing" can only be achieved with the right hand (Levush). Additionally, it is written "and you shall bind […] and you shall write" – just as binding is done with the right hand, so too is writing (ibid). This is explained in Menachot (37a). And Rabbi Yosef Karo wrote in his major work that even post facto, it is invalid if written with the left hand if one is not ambidextrous, and so was ruled in the Hagahot Maimoniot (Chapter Two) in the name of the Sefer Mitzvot Katan. And so ruled the Bach, see there.

And according to this, it seems clear that what our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in paragraph 5: One must write with his right hand even if he is ambidextrous. If he wrote with his left hand—it is invalid if it is possible to find others written with the right... until here is his language, which implies that if it is not possible to find others—they are valid post facto. And it is clear that his intention is only regarding someone who is ambidextrous. But if he is not ambidextrous—it is invalid, for otherwise, he contradicts himself. Furthermore: From where do we say this, since the glosses of Maimonides and the SeMaK invalidate it, and this is explained in the Gemara? Therefore, I am astonished at the commentators of the Shulchan Aruch (Levush, and similarly implied by Magen Avraham, paragraph 4) who interpret it also for someone who is not ambidextrous. There are those who wrote not to recite a blessing over them, but nevertheless to place them (Pri Megadim, and Beit Shmuel in Even HaEzer, Siman 123, paragraph 4). And in my humble opinion, they are completely invalid. And also regarding Shabbat, one is not liable when writing with his left hand, as explained in Shabbat (103a), see there. And similarly, a left-handed person who wrote with the right hand of everyone—it is invalid, as implied there in Shabbat, see there. And know that there is someone who says that one who does his work with his right hand and writes with his left, or vice versa—should not be a scribe, since there is doubt about what is considered "his right hand," as explained in Siman 27 where there is a dispute regarding the placement of tefillin, and therefore it is a Torah doubt with which hand he writes (Pri Megadim in Eshel, paragraph 5). And these are reasonable words. And one who writes with his mouth—it is completely invalid (Magen Avraham, paragraph 5).

The law given to Moses at Sinai is that a mezuzah requires ruled lines for every line written. Tefillin do not require ruled lines for every line, only for the top line, because it is forbidden to write without ruled lines. One should rule the top line, the bottom line, and the lines on the sides, so that when writing all the lines, they will be written evenly. In the Jerusalem Talmud, the first chapter of Shabbat is strict about not ruling lines, saying: "Anyone who is exempt from something and does it is called a 'hediot' (an unlearned person)," and it says this regarding another matter, and consequently, the same applies to this law (Tosafot 32b). However, this is when one does it out of stringency. But if one knows that they cannot write the lines evenly without ruling, they may rule all the lines. They just need to be careful not to rule with lead, because the place where the lines are ruled remains colored. And so it is taught in the Jerusalem Talmud Megillah (first chapter, ninth law): "They measure with a reed, and this is ruling lines." And our Rabbi the Rema writes in section 6: "There are those who say that one should always rule the top, bottom, and side lines, even if they know how to write without ruling." And this is the practice. Until here is his language, and it is not understood: is it not that even according to the first opinion the top line is necessary as I have written? And if because of the other three lines, everyone agrees to this, as clarified by the Sefer Mitzvot Gadol and Sefer HaTerumah (see Beit Yosef). And one must say that since from the language of our Rabbi Beit Yosef there it seems he only required the top line, therefore he says in the language "there are those who say." (See Magen Avraham, section 8, who deduced: are there not many stringencies we are stringent about and yet are called 'hediot'? See there. And it seems to me that certainly, where there is no opinion to be stringent, or any safeguard, certainly one should not be stringent. And most stringencies are because of opinions. Be precise and you will find it light and forget it. And so it seems from the Pri Megadim, see there.)

And know that the Rambam wrote in the first chapter, law 12: "It is a law given to Moses at Sinai that one may not write a Torah scroll or a mezuzah without scoring lines. But tefillin do not require scoring because they are covered." Thus his wording, meaning: they are not visible to the reader's eye, as a Torah scroll and a mezuzah are inspected periodically, and if written crookedly, everyone would see. But tefillin are not visible, and we do not worry if they are written crookedly. According to his view, even the first line does not require scoring, as he holds that what our sages said, that it is forbidden to write without scoring, applies to something visible to everyone. What we wrote earlier is the opinion of Rabbenu Tam and most of the poskim. It seems to me that they follow their reasoning, as Rabbenu Tam holds that even a Torah scroll does not require scoring, as the Tur wrote in Yoreh De'ah, section 271. Therefore, it is impossible to explain like the Rambam regarding tefillin because they are covered, for the same applies to a Torah scroll. The Rambam, according to his reasoning, holds that a Torah scroll requires scoring; therefore, he explained that tefillin do not because they are covered. Rabbenu Tam explained that the first line requires scoring. According to this, if one wrote the tefillin passages without scoring at all, including not scoring the uppermost line and writing the lines crookedly, one may rely on the opinion of the Rambam and use them until other tefillin are obtained. Rabbenu Beit Yosef here and in Yoreh De'ah there was stringent according to both opinions, requiring scoring for the uppermost line here and scoring for the Torah scroll in accordance with all opinions there. This is the primary ruling, as I wrote there in section 25.

A law given to Moses at Sinai: Tefillin on parchment, not on duxustus nor on gevil. And they write on the parchment on the flesh side. If one changes and writes on the hair side, and all the more so if he writes on duxustus or gevil, it is invalid. And what is "parchment," what is "duxustus," and what is "gevil"? It is explained in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 271, that "gevil" is called when the hide has not yet been split at all in its thickness, but they scrape off the hair and prepare it a bit there, and on the flesh side, they do not prepare at all. "Parchment" is called when the hide is split in its thickness; the outer part towards the hair is called "parchment," and the inner part attached to the flesh is called "duxustus." Therefore, when we say "they write on the parchment on the flesh side," it means on the side closer to the flesh, which is the part that was split, and before it was split, it was attached to the duxustus. And this was their custom in the time of the Talmud, that they used to split the hides.

However, our parchments, where the hide is not split but rather heavily scraped in the area attached to the flesh, consequently causing the duchsustos part to fall off and leaving only the parchment. And they write on this heavily scraped area, for on the hair side, where they scrape off the top layer, it is only to the extent needed to prepare and smooth it. All our parchments have the status of parchment because the scribes are skilled in recognizing if any part of the duchsustos remains. This means that it is heavily scraped, and the parchment is not as smooth. And if perhaps a thin layer remains, they scrape it off with a knife, and this is known to the scribes. They must be careful not to scrape too much on the hair side so that only the duchsustos remains, for in such a case, it would be invalid, as I wrote.

The parchment must be processed with gallnuts or lime. It must be processed for its intended purpose, and one must verbally declare that it is being processed "for the sake of tefillin." This declaration should be made at the beginning of the processing, or it can be processed for the sake of a Torah scroll. However, if it was processed for the sake of a mezuzah, it is invalid for tefillin because the sanctity of tefillin is greater than that of a mezuzah. Nonetheless, parchment processed for a Torah scroll is valid for tefillin, even though the sanctity of a Torah scroll is greater than that of tefillin, because anything that is merely designated but not yet used can have its designation changed from a higher sanctity to a lower sanctity. If a non-Jew processed it and a Jew stood over him — according to the Rambam, it is invalid even if the Jew instructed the non-Jew to process it for the intended purpose. According to the Rosh, it is valid if a Jew stood over him and assisted somewhat in the work. This is the common practice. These detailed laws are explained in Yoreh De'ah, section 271, paragraphs 5-12; see there. It is also explained there whether a verbal declaration is strictly necessary or if intention alone suffices, and if it was processed not for its intended purpose, whether it can be corrected by reprocessing it with the proper intention. It is also explained that the declaration "for its intended purpose" must be made specifically at the beginning of the processing; see there.

Our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in Section 10: When marking holes with an awl in the form of letters, even though it is easy for the non-Jew to forge – we are not concerned. Because he is fearful that a Jew might recognize it with a discerning eye. This is the end of his words, meaning: the practice of scribes when leaving the skins during the tanning process under the non-Jew's supervision is to make marks on the skins to prevent them from being switched. Random holes are meaningless until holes are made in the form of letters. And even though it is easy to forge this as well by placing one skin over another and making the same holes on this skin, nevertheless, he is fearful that they may not align perfectly. And we have already explained in Yoreh De'ah there, Section 9, that this applies in a case where the non-Jew benefits from the exchange. For if not, he is not suspected of causing a stumbling block. (And this answers the question raised by the Eliyah Rabbah in subsection 18 about scribes who make smaller marks than this, see there. And see Magen Avraham subsection 13 who raised a difficulty from Yoreh De'ah, Section 118, Subsection 3. And I did not understand, because even here he surely recognizes the writing. And what he wrote in the name of the glosses of the Maimonides that if it was initially given for tanning for the sake of holiness, it does not need anything further, we have explained in Yoreh De'ah there).

The parchment (klaf) must be from the hide of a kosher animal, beast, or bird, as it is written: "so that the law of the Lord will be in your mouth" — from that which is permitted in your mouth. Even other books that contain divine names are forbidden to be written on impure materials (Magen Avraham, subsection 11). In my humble opinion, it seems that even without divine names, it is forbidden to write words of Torah on impure materials. Who can bring purity from impurity? However, it is permitted to write on hides of kosher animals, even if they were from a carcass or a tereifah (an animal with a defect that would cause it to die within a year) (Shabbat 108a), because it is of a type that is permitted "in your mouth." But from the hide of a fish, it is forbidden even if they are kosher, because their filth is abundant (ibid.). The parchment must be intact, without holes that the ink cannot pass over, meaning that the letter should not appear split into two. However, what appears divided when held against the sun is not an issue (Beit Yosef and Magen Avraham, subsection 15). Some have graded the parchments: the best of all is the hide of a fetus, and that of a beast is better than that of an animal, and kosher ones are preferred over tereifah. But I do not know where this innovation came from, as our sages did not say so. We have already written about this in Yoreh De'ah, section 271.

The meticulous scribes make three types of parchment: a thicker one to write the "Shema" section, which is small; a thinner one for the "Vehaya Ki Yeviacha" section, which is larger; and for the "Kadesh" and "Vehaya Im Shamoa" sections, which are longer, they make a very thin parchment. This way, the compartments of the head tefillin will be filled evenly, which is an enhancement for the tefillin. (In the Shulchan Aruch, section 14, there is a printing error, see there. There is also the same error in the Beit Yosef.) Some place larger margins in the smaller sections than in the larger sections, and they make the thickness of the parchments equal.

Maimonides, at the end of the first chapter, after writing the law that every letter must be surrounded by parchment on all its sides, and that every letter must be properly formed so that a child can read it and the reader can read it smoothly, wrote as follows: A parchment that was perforated – one should not write on the perforation. Any perforation over which the ink passes – is not considered a perforation… If the parchment was perforated after it was written, if it was perforated within the letter, such as within the "hei" or within the "mem" and similarly in other letters – it is valid. If it was perforated in the leg of the letter to the extent that it was severed, if there remains from it the size of a small letter – it is valid, provided it does not resemble another letter. And if there does not remain from it the size of a small letter – it is invalid. Until here is his language.

(And it is explained in Menachot 29a: if the inside of the "hei" was perforated according to one version of Rashi's interpretation, "inside" means the part that is inside it. And the Rosh in the laws of the Torah scroll, Siman 15, ruled according to the first version of Rashi, that "inside" means the left leg of the "hei". And he questioned the other version because of what is written, that it mentions the letter "hei", see there. And it seems to me that it mentions it because of its leg, as this is only in the "hei". And similarly in the Jerusalem Talmud, Megillah, first chapter, Halacha 9, it mentions the "hei" in its leg, and the "bet" in its inside, see there. And in Menachot, as it is one statement, it mentions the "hei" because of its leg.)

From the words of the Rambam, it is explicitly understood that with regard to the requirement of being surrounded by parchment, there is a distinction between before the letter is written and if it was punctured afterward. This reasoning was written by our teacher, the Beit Yosef, in his great book in the name of "Seder Get Ashkenazi," and he wrote that this is explicitly seen from the Rambam. See there. Likewise, it is written in the Shulchan Aruch at the end of section 16, and this is his language: "The matter of validating when a letter is interrupted - specifically [when it is written] (when it is interrupted) validly and afterward it was interrupted. But if initially when it was written there was a hole there and it was interrupted in it, or if the leg of the final 'kaf' or the like reaches the end of the parchment without being surrounded by parchment from its beginning - it is invalid." End of his language.

And one should not ask: If so, why did he write in Shulchan Aruch Orach Chaim section 4 that a letter should not be attached to its neighbor, but each letter should be surrounded by parchment? End of his language. And similarly, in sections 25 and 26, he wrote that letters that are attached can be separated. See there. He should have explained that this is only at the time of writing, but if they were attached afterward - it is not necessary to separate them because being surrounded by parchment is only required at the time of writing and not if they were attached afterward, as with a hole. One could say that it is not comparable: One, because with attachment it can be corrected, which is not the case with a hole. Additionally, the attachment of one letter to another is more severe because they appear as one letter, and this is invalid even if they became attached afterward. And you should know that this is the case, for the Rambam in the tenth chapter, in the twenty invalidations he counted there, included the touching of letters to one another. And why did he not count the requirement of being surrounded by parchment? Rather, certainly because being surrounded by parchment invalidates only at the beginning of writing, and touching invalidates even afterward.

(And with this, the difficulty raised by Maharal Ben Chaviv, which the Beit Yosef brought, why the Rambam did not count the requirement of being surrounded by parchment, is resolved. See there. And according to what I have written, it is well explained. Pay attention and you will find it easy.)

However, it is clear that the Tur, Sefer HaTerumah, SeMaG, Mordechai, and Hagahot Maimoniyot do not make this distinction between before writing and after writing. For the Tur wrote: "And if after it is written, a hole is made within the letter, it is valid. And some say even if a hole is made through the entire interior." And in the Yerushalmi, it implies that it also needs to be surrounded by parchment on the inside. Thus is his language, and so wrote the poskim that we have mentioned. And if one would think that they distinguish between before writing and after writing, he would not have said that the Yerushalmi requires being surrounded by parchment from the inside, as our Talmud also holds this. Rather, they believe that after writing it does not need this, and he would have said that the Yerushalmi requires it even after writing. Moreover, why should we create a dispute between the Bavli and the Yerushalmi? Let us say that the Yerushalmi refers to the time of writing, and indeed this is said according to the Rambam. And if because it seems to them that the Yerushalmi also refers to after writing, he would have said so, since this is the main point of dispute. Rather, it is certain that they do not hold this distinction at all.

And one should not ask: If so, how did the Tur and the poskim (decisors of Jewish law) write that if the inner leg of the letter "hei" is punctured and any part remains, it is kosher, and if the right leg is punctured and a small part remains, it is kosher—there is no "surrounding margin" (hekef gevil)? It is for this reason that our master, the Beit Yosef, and the Ashkenazi Gett arrangement specifically differentiate between before the writing and after, as explained in his great work. However, in my humble opinion, this distinction is unnecessary, because in matters of surrounding margin, we also consider part of the letter that is after the puncture. A clear proof for this is that Rashi, of blessed memory, in Menachot 29b explained regarding the severed leg of the letter "vav" in "vayehareg," that the "vav" coincided with the location of the puncture—see there. According to him, there was a puncture at the time of writing (and similarly, the Drisha wrote this in letter "hei" and left it as a question, see there). Rather, it is certainly not difficult at all: we require the size of a small letter without the interruption of the puncture, otherwise, it does not have the status of a "letter." But in any case, we also consider what is beyond the puncture and it is surrounded by a margin. …

And according to this, the words of our master, the Beit Yosef, in the Shulchan Aruch are very puzzling. For in Section 15, he wrote in the language of the Tur, and at the end of Section 16, he wrote according to the words of the Rambam. And these contradict each other, and indeed, they have already wondered about this (Taz, subparagraph 14, and Eliyah Rabbah, subparagraph 27). And it seems to me that he always holds like the Rambam. And that which he wrote in the language of the Tur is because, according to the opinion of the Tur, our Talmud holds that from the inside it does not require an encircling of parchment, and in order not to rule this way, he copied his language. For even according to the Tur, the law is not so, since it is explicitly stated in the Jerusalem Talmud that it is required. And all the more so according to the words of the Rambam, everyone agrees with this. And since there is no practical halachic difference in this matter, he copied his language in order to be concise, as is his way. (And that which the Taz wrote that the Tur holds like the first answer of the Beit Yosef to differentiate between attachment and a hole is puzzling. For if so, even if it is pierced from the outside, it does not invalidate, all the more so from the inside. And the Pri Megadim also wondered about this. And the rest of the words of the Pri Megadim in subparagraph 14 and subparagraph 8 I do not understand; see there, for his language is convoluted.)

It has already been explained that according to the opinion of the Tur, if the right leg of the letter "hei" (ה) is pierced, there needs to remain the equivalent of a small letter. But for the inner leg, it is valid even with any amount remaining. This is also the opinion of the Rosh. However, other authorities require even in this case the equivalent of a small letter, which is the letter "yud" (י). And if it is severed in its thickness, if a thin thread remains, it is valid. And this is the halacha (Magen Avraham, subsection 16).

Our masters, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, wrote in paragraph 16: If one of the simple letters, such as a Vav, Zayin, or the like, is broken, if a child who is neither clever nor foolish can read it – it is kosher. If not – it is invalid. There is no need to cover the other letters as is commonly practiced. However, if we see that the form of the letter is not maintained properly, or if the leg of the Aleph is broken – it is invalid even if the child reads it correctly. Thus ends their words. (This is how it should be stated according to the emendation of the Taz at the end of sub-paragraph 9, see there. The words of the Magen Avraham in sub-paragraph 18 are strained. And the correct interpretation is as written by the Yad Ephraim, that what the AChD [Aleph, Chet, Dalet] wrote refers to the letters Heh, Chet, Dalet, see there.)

The explanation of the matter is as written by the Rivash (Responsa 120), and this is his language: The reading of a child is only effective when the disqualification is because this letter resembles another letter. But when the disqualification is because its form is interrupted, it does not help... Similarly, one should not validate an Aleph whose left leg does not touch the middle line just because a child reads it as an Aleph, for due to the separation, he would not mistake it for another letter... Thus far is his language. Similarly, the Maharik wrote (Root 69) regarding Alephs whose Yuds do not touch each other, and similarly, the dot of the Peh that does not touch its roof, and this is his language: It is obvious that one should not validate it through the reading of a child, as this was only said when the letter is broken and lacks its required measure, such as a cut Vav where we are unsure if it reaches the length of a Vav or is the size of a Yud. In this case, the reading of the child helps when he reads it as a Vav, since he did not call it a Yud. But when it is clear that the letter has not retained its form, what benefit is the reading of the child, as our eyes see that the letter has not retained its form? Thus far is his language (and it is brought by the Taz in subsection 9). And with this, the words of the Shulchan Aruch are elucidated.

And according to this, with a short Vav that resembles a Yod, or a long Yod that resembles a Vav, or a short Zayin that resembles a Yod, or a long Zayin that resembles a final Nun, or a round Bet that resembles a curved Kaf, or a square Kaf that resembles a Bet, or a Dalet with a short head that resembles a Vav, or a Vav with a broad head that resembles a Dalet, or a Dalet whose side extends and resembles a final Kaf, or a final Kaf whose side is short and resembles a Dalet, or a Gimel whose bottom head is connected and resembles a curved Nun, or a curved Nun whose bottom head is not connected and resembles a Gimel, or a He whose left leg is connected and resembles a Chet, or a Chet whose left leg is not connected and resembles a He, or a He whose left leg is not clearly visible and resembles a Dalet, or a Vav whose line is in the middle and resembles a Zayin, or a Zayin whose line is on the side and resembles a Vav – in all these and similar cases, the reading of a child is effective. But with Alephs, Shins, Ayins, and Tzadis where the heads are not connected to the lines – the reading of a child is not effective. And similarly with all letters like these. (See Sha’arei Teshuvah subsection 23 in the name of Ginat Veradim, that a final Kaf at the end of a line where the roof extends so that it resembles a Dalet or a Resh, there is leniency in pressing circumstances because it is clear that it was extended to complete the line, see there. However, there is no reason for this, and even in pressing circumstances it is invalid if the child reads it as a Dalet or a Resh. The rest of his words will be explained in Siman 36.)

What is a child who is not wise? One who does not understand the matter, for when he understands, he will indicate because of the context and not because of the shape of the letter. And not foolish, meaning he knows well the shapes of the letters. And what is written that it is not necessary to cover for him from before and after, the reason is simple: since he does not understand the continuation of the matter, why should we cover for him? Nevertheless, there are those who say that before him it is necessary to cover but not after (Magen Avraham, subsection 19). And the reason: we are concerned that he might understand a little of the matter, for otherwise there is no concern in this. And so the custom is to cover what is before him. And know that this reliance on a short vav for the reading of a child, this is in a completely short case. But if it is interrupted in the middle - we do not rely on him if he says it is a vav, because his saying it is due to the combination. Therefore, it is necessary to cover the lower part for him (Taz, subsection 10). And although there are those who disagree with this, and believe that we are not concerned that he will say it because of the combination (see Eliyah Rabbah), nevertheless the main opinion is as I have written. And know that in all this there is no difference whether the letter was corrupted after writing, or the scribe wrote it this way, for in all cases we rely on the reading of the child (Taz, ibid.). This is not like there are those who disagree, and believe that we rely on the reading of the child only for a letter that was corrupted and not for what the scribe initially wrote (see Bach), for there is no reason to differentiate in this.

If a drop of ink fell onto a letter and ruined the letter, whether it fell during the writing or after the writing, and whether it ruined it by losing the shape of the letter or by making it look like a different letter—such as if a drop fell into the letter dalet and it now looks like a he or into the space of the leg of the he and it now looks like a chet, or anything similar—the letter is invalid. Even if the drop only removed the small stroke (tag) of a yud, it is invalid. However, if it removed the crowns (tagin), we do not concern ourselves with it, and we rely on the Rambam that the crowns do not invalidate, as I wrote in section 14. Similarly, other small strokes of the letters, if a drop fell on them, we do not concern ourselves with it as long as the main body of the letter remains. If there is doubt whether the form of the letter was lost or if it resembles another letter, we rely on a child who is neither particularly wise nor foolish, and as he says, so it shall be.

And know that there is no difference between ink and paint, as any type of paint that falls and ruins the letter invalidates it. Except for wax, when it falls on a letter, it does not invalidate it, as it is merely a covering, and one can scrape it off and it is valid. Whether it is permissible to scrape it off on Shabbat will be explained in section 340, that it is forbidden, as regarding the prohibition of stoning, it is considered erasing. Nevertheless, for reading the Torah on Shabbat, if this happens, one can read from it as it is considered merely a covering. But ink and paint, even if they are still wet and the letter is dry, it is still not considered a covering, because once it spilled and ruined it, it is considered as if the letter were erased, and it requires correction as will be explained. And before it is corrected, it is completely invalid. Therefore, in tefillin and mezuzot, when ink falls on a letter and ruins it, and many letters have already been written after this letter, they are invalid. The correction does not help because it would be out of order unless he can erase all the letters written after this letter, such as if there are no other letters in between.

And what is the remedy? Dragging the ink to the place where it fell and returning the letter to its original form does not help. This is considered "erasing from within," meaning, the Torah said "and you shall write" and not "and you shall engrave." "Engraving" is called when one engraves around the letter and the letter is formed automatically. And this applies to a drop of ink that damaged the letter, and now one corrects it by dragging the ink around the letter – this is "erasing from within" and is invalid according to the Torah. Instead, one must completely scrape off the entire letter and rewrite it. Similarly, if the drop made it into another letter, such as extending the leg of a "hei" to its roof – dragging the drop does not help, as it is "erasing from within". Instead, one must scrape off the entire leg and rewrite it. Similarly, if the drop turned a "bet" into a "pe" – erasing the drop does not help. Instead, one must scrape off the entire roof with the drop, and then redo the roof. However, if a drop turned a "dalet" into a "hei", it seems that erasing the drop does help, as it stands on its own and did not damage the "dalet", but merely altered it into a "hei". Now one removes it, and the "dalet" returns to its original form. This needs further examination, but according to my humble opinion, the ruling is as I have written.

If one needed to write a letter and a drop of ink fell and formed a shape resembling half a letter, one should not complete the letter by incorporating the drop, as this is not considered proper writing. Instead, the drop should be erased, for the entire letter must be written properly (Magen Avraham, subsection 23). And although there are those who are lenient in such a case regarding a divorce document (get), as I have written in Even HaEzer, section 125, it is not comparable. In the case of a get, there is no requirement for holiness, only "for its sake" (l'shma), and the primary element of the get is from the Torah as explained there, and therefore we do not worry about this. This is not the case with Torah scrolls, tefillin, and mezuzot, where each letter and part of a letter require holiness, and missing even part of a letter renders them completely invalid. It is obvious that in such a case it is invalid, as part of the letter was not written, and it is clear that it lacks holiness. (This is how it appears to me. Further examination is required regarding the Magen Avraham at the end of subsection 23; see there. The ruling is clear as I have written.)

And similarly, if one made a mistake and wrote a "Dalet" instead of a "Reish," or a "Beit" instead of a "Kaf" – there is no remedy by erasing the tag to correct the letter to make it rounded, as this is considered "chiseling out." Rather, one should add ink to the tag and make it rounded, as this is considered actual writing. And similarly, if he wrote a "Reish" instead of a "Dalet," or a "Kaf" instead of a "Beit" – there is no remedy by chiseling out the rounded part to make it a tag, as this is "chiseling out." Rather, one should add ink to the rounded part and make it a tag, and similarly for other letters. And this is when he did not write after it, because if he wrote after it, no correction is effective, as it would be "out of order." Unless he also erases them if there is no name between them (all this is explained from Taz, subsection 16, and from Magen Avraham, subsection 24). And know that when the invalidation is due to "chiseling out" – passing a quill over the letter does not help.

A final mem (ם) that has been closed up because its opening stuck together, our master the Beit Yosef ruled in section 18 that it is not effective to scrape off the adhesion and open it, because this would be considered "chiseling out" (chak tokhot), since no action is being performed on the body of the remaining letter. This is unlike the opinion of "some say" that this is not considered "chiseling out" since it is like two letters that are stuck together, where scraping between them is effective (see Magen Avraham, subsection 25 in the name of the Ra’am). This is not so, because in the end it is one letter. However, it is also not necessary to scrape off the entire mem, as some hold (Ram Alshakar and Radach, see Beit Yosef). Rather, it suffices to scrape off the "chisel" of the mem, that is, the vav of the mem, to scrape it off entirely, for the mem is as if it consists of a bent nun with a vav. Therefore, since the nun was written properly, it remains in its place. The vav should be scraped off and another vav written. Even if it was closed after the entire writing, and thus the vav was also made properly, nevertheless, it is necessary to perform an action on the body of the letter as I have written, and it suffices with the vav alone. But this is only with a mem, because its creation involves two writings: a nun and a vav, as I have written. However, if a resh was made like a dalet, and one comes to scrape it, one must scrape the entire letter. It is not sufficient to scrape only the roof or only the leg, because since the entire letter was made as one and it was entirely made invalid, therefore, both must be scraped. Similarly with other letters. Therefore, if initially a resh was written properly, and afterward one erred and made a crown on it, it suffices to scrape off the roof with the crown or the leg with the crown, since it was made properly and is similar to the mem (Magen Avraham there). Some are stringent even in this, and one who is stringent shall receive a blessing. But the main ruling is as I have written (see what I wrote in section 36, subsection 17).

And since it has been explained regarding the letter mem, that because its formation is not completed in one stroke, it is not necessary to erase it entirely. Therefore, it is obvious that for the legs of the letters heh and kuf that touched the roof, it suffices to erase only the leg and then rewrite it. It is not necessary to erase the entire letter since the roof was written correctly, and they are considered two separate entities. Similarly, the yuds in the aleph, which need to be connected only by thin lines to the long line; if they are connected more than necessary, meaning the entire width of the yuds is connected, the aleph becomes invalid. Erasing just the connection does not help, as this is considered "erasing from within" (chak tochot). Instead, one must erase the yuds and correct them, and it is not necessary to erase the long line since they are not made in one stroke. The same rule applies to the yuds of the shin, ayin, tzadik, peh, and the legs of the tav; if they are connected more than necessary, they should be erased and corrected. It has already been explained that connecting one letter to another, whether during or after writing, invalidates the letter. However, in this case, separation is effective, as it is not considered "erasing from within" since each letter is recognizable in its correct form. Therefore, separating them makes it valid. Similarly, if the leg of the final kaf or other long letters reaches the end of the parchment without any margin of parchment around it, one may erase part of it, as this is not considered "erasing from within." This rule that erasing is effective in the case of connecting letters applies when the letters themselves are not damaged. But if they are damaged, only erasing the body of the letters helps. Some say that even if the connection extends along the entire length of the letters, only erasing the body of the letters helps. This is not the case (Magen Avraham, section 27). Similarly, if the leg of the heh is connected only by a hair's breadth, and a child recognizes it as a heh, it is permitted to erase the connection (ibid.). The same applies to the fine points of the yuds in the aleph when they touch; we are not concerned about it. This principle applies to all letters. (What the Magen Avraham wrote in section 26 in the name of R. Moses Galanti, and the rest of his words will be explained with Divine assistance in section 36, for that is their proper place.)

Regarding the recognition of the child concerning the letters as explained, it has happened several times that they show the letters to a child and he says one thing, and then they show them to another child and he does not say the same as the first. It appears in my humble opinion that we should not pay attention to the second child. Since our sages of blessed memory commanded to show it to a child, we should follow what the first child says. Otherwise, the matter will never be clarified, as just as there are differences of opinion among adults, so too among children according to their understanding. And similarly, our sages of blessed memory said: "In any place where the Torah trusts a single witness, he is considered as two." However, if two children say the opposite of the first, it seems that we follow them. And if we ask many children, and one says this way and another that way, we follow the majority. And if it is split evenly, we follow the stricter opinion (this is how it appears to me in these laws).

At the beginning of writing the parshiyot (scrolls), he should say aloud: "I am writing for the sake of the sanctity of tefillin, and all the divine names in it for the sake of the sanctity of the name" (Pri Megadim). Besides this, each time he writes a divine name, he must say for each name that he writes it for the sake of the sanctity of the name. If he writes two or more divine names at once without interruption, one sanctification suffices. Some say it is sufficient if he intends in his mind that he writes the divine name for its sanctity, since he verbalized it at the beginning of the writing, and that suffices. This leniency applies after the fact, but initially, he should verbalize it explicitly. If he feels sleepy, he should not write, because then he writes without intention. Before writing the name, he should examine the quill to ensure it is not overly filled with ink, to avoid erasure. Therefore, when he dips the quill, he should write one letter before the name, and then write the name, thus sanctifying the ink with that letter.
