If he did not leave a letter before the name, he should still examine whether there is a letter or a tag (decorative stroke) that needs correction and make the correction before writing the name. (There are profound and awesome secrets in writing the divine name, as explained in Ataret Zekenim and Pri Etz Chaim. Not every mind can grasp this, and fortunate is the scribe who merits this. Therefore, it is proper that every scribe ensures he is ritually pure and writes in solitude. The main thing is to be mindful that he is writing tefillin. Unfortunately, many errors have increased among scribes, and every God-fearing person is obligated to ensure that his tefillin are not written by young boys, but by an experienced and God-fearing man.)

The scribe must be meticulous about missing and extra letters, for if a single letter is missing or extra, the tefillin are invalid. Consequently, those who wear them are reciting a blessing in vain every day and are every day without the mitzvah of tefillin. The scribe's punishment is very severe. Therefore, one who engages in writing tefillin must be God-fearing and reverent of the word of God. After writing each section, he should read it thoroughly with intention and precision two or three times, and read it again before placing it in its case to ensure that no section is mixed up with another. It is good to test the quill before beginning to write, to ensure that it does not have too much ink, which could cause damage. Additionally, he should be careful before writing any divine name to review all that he has written to ensure there is no error, so that the divine name does not come to be stored away due to his error. It is a great enhancement if he can seclude himself and write all the sections without interruption, with proper and desirable thoughts before God.

If it is found that a letter is missing, it cannot be corrected, because fixing it is not effective due to it being "out of order," which renders it invalid, as it is written: "and they shall be" — they must remain as they are. However, if there is an extra letter, it can be corrected by scraping it off. This applies when the extra letter is at the end or beginning of the word, but if it is in the middle of the word, scraping it off will leave a gap, making it appear as two words. Unless it is possible to extend the preceding or following letter, such as if the preceding letter is one of the letters with a wide roof — extend them a bit more, and similarly if it is the following letter. 

The poskim (halachic authorities) are uncertain if after scraping off, one can extend the preceding letter downward and not upward, for example, if "mitzvot" is written fully and it is necessary to erase the vav, and the tzadi is extended downward and it appears as one writing, but upward it appears as two words. Similarly, if the preceding letter was a bent nun, it can extend its lower leg and not the upper one, for if the upper one is also extended, it will appear as a bet (Taz section 20 and Magen Avraham section 33). And since there is doubt, we are stringent. It seems to me that this depends on the visual perception, or they should ask a child who knows how to combine the letters into a complete word if they are two words or one word. 

Also, at the beginning of writing, one should be careful not to extend the lower leg of the nun and the tzadi more than the upper leg, so that the following letter will not be separated from the preceding one and appear as two words. If this happens and the following letter is inserted into it, such as needing to write nun yod or tzadi yod, and extending the lower leg and inserting the yod into the lower leg, meaning it is adjacent to the upper leg and naturally within the lower leg — it is kosher, as they clearly appear as two letters (ibid.).

If an extra word is found, it should be erased even if an empty space remains, since there is not the measure of nine letters, which is the measure of a paragraph as I wrote in Yoreh De'ah section 274 — we do not care (ibid.). There are those who permit double words even without erasing, and it is surprising to say so (ibid.). When erasing, one should erase the second word, as the first was written according to the law. In hindsight, if the first word was erased, it is kosher. (What the Magen Avraham wrote there that one can extend the roof of the hei even if its leg will not be at its end, see there — it requires further examination. Be precise and you will find it easy.) (From this it is clarified that with an extra letter there is no issue of "out of order." A reason is needed, and it can be said that it is similar to a connection between the letters. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

It is permitted to write even Divine Names on a place that has been erased or scraped. "Erased" refers to when it was erased while dry, and "scraped" refers to when it was scraped while wet. Nevertheless, it is preferable initially not to scrape it while wet, but rather to wait until it has dried and then scrape it. Because then it can be easily scraped without leaving any trace, unlike when it is wet. And it is forbidden to suspend any letter between the lines in tefillin, even if it would be in the correct order. And this is what we say in the Jerusalem Talmud, Megillah, Chapter One (Halacha 9): One does not suspend in tefillin and mezuzot. (Even though the main reason, according to what the poskim have written, is because it is out of order, nevertheless, the plain meaning of the words should not be dismissed. And so it is written in Shaarei Teshuva, Section 36, quoting several responsa, see there.)

A fundamental principle must be understood regarding the correction of letters in the passages of tefillin: when it is permissible to correct them without considering it "out of order" (she-lo ke-sidran) and when the correction is ineffective because it constitutes "out of order." The detailed laws are as follows: If the form of the letter has completely changed, it is considered "out of order" and invalid. Even if the form has not changed, but due to the defect, part of the letter needs to be scraped off, such as if the leg of the aleph touches the face of the aleph in a complete adhesion, necessitating the scraping of the entire leg, or if the face of the aleph is touched—that is, if the upper yud is entirely attached to the roof below it and needs to be scraped off, or if the legs of the hei or the kuf touch the roof—in all these cases, it is necessary to scrape the leg, and therefore they are invalid. For although at present their form is correct, nevertheless, after scraping, they will lose their form, and when corrected afterward, it is considered "out of order" and thus invalid.

And a letter that is split, whether it is one of the simple letters like a vav, zayin, or similar, if the form of the vav or zayin remains even without the bottom part according to the recognition of a child – it is obvious that one can fix it and it is valid. But if its form does not remain without the bottom connection, if the separation is significant enough that its form is lost – the child's reading does not help, and it is considered "out of order" and invalid. However, when the separation is minor to the extent that its form still remains, although it is invalid as it currently is, nonetheless, one can fix it and it is valid, and this is not considered "out of order." (I learned this from yuds that are not touching, as mentioned in Shulchan Aruch, section 25, as we will explain.)

And so too, if some of the yuds on the alephs, shins, and ayins are not touching the body of the letter, but are not so distant that the letters do not appear as they should, and a child also identifies them correctly, although they are invalid as they presently are and much has already been written after them – in any case, they can be corrected, and this does not constitute "out of order." Similarly, separating letters that are stuck together also does not fall under "out of order," since the letters retain their form. Unless, through the adhesion, the form of the letters has changed, then it would be "out of order" and invalid. And we have already explained this.

And similarly with the division of a letter into two letters, such as a *tzadi* that was written as a *yud* and a *nun*, and it is apparent to the observer that it is a *yud* and a *nun*, such as when they are separated from each other like two distinct letters, and even a child says so, and similarly with a *shin* that was written as an *ayin* and a *yud*, or a *chet* that was written as two *zayins* – this is considered "not in their proper order" and is invalid. However, if it appears to be a *tzadi*, meaning that the *yud* and the *nun* are very close to each other but there is a slight separation between them, yet it does not look like two distinct letters, and similarly with a *shin* and a *chet* in such a manner, and even if a child says so, although they are invalid as they are now – nonetheless, they can be corrected and are valid, for this is not considered "not in their proper order." (This seems to me to be the explanation of what is written in the Shulchan Aruch, section 25, regarding a letter divided into two letters. See there. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

And this is what is written in the Shulchan Aruch at the end of paragraph 25: there is an opinion that if the stems of the letter "Chet" above do not touch each other, but their separation is not clearly visible, even though a child would read it as two "Zayin" letters, it is permitted to connect them. So far his words. The explanation of the matter is as follows: According to the rules that have been explained, as long as the form of the letter is present, meaning that the separation is very close, even though the letter is currently invalid, with respect to "not in their order" it is not invalid. And it is understood from this that a child would read such a letter correctly. But if the child does not read it correctly, it is invalid, because according to the Talmudic law, the primary factor is the child's reading. According to this, when the stems of the "Chet" do not touch each other, the same law applies, depending on whether the form of the letter is recognizable. Consequently, if the child reads it as two "Zayin" letters, this is a sign that the form of the letter is not present. And even if in our eyes it seems that the form of the letter is present, it is meaningless. Therefore, it is said that there is an opinion that with the stems of the "Chet" it does not depend on the child's reading but only on our visual assessment, because the fact that the child reads it as two "Zayin" letters is due to not being accustomed to such a "Chet" (and this is the intention of the Magen Avraham in paragraph 37). And this is the established law, that in this case, if their separation is not so noticeable, it is valid and can be corrected.

It has already been explained that letters that are stuck to each other can be separated. This applies even to the letters of the Divine Name when they are stuck together—they can be separated. This is not considered erasing the Divine Name, since one is not erasing the body of the letter but rather what is between one letter and another. Therefore, one must be very careful not to erase even a small part of the letter itself, so as not to transgress the prohibition of erasing the Divine Name.

And just as in the law of "out of order" there is an issue with the letters being corrupted from the beginning of the writing, so too this law applies if the letters were erased after the writing, even after a long time. If even a single letter is completely erased, the entire section is invalid, because it cannot be corrected, as that would be "out of order." However, this applies only if it is completely erased. But if it is partially erased, meaning the main part of the ink has been removed, but the form of the letter is still recognizable with faint ink such that a child reads it as usual, it is permissible to pass a quill over the letter and correct it to improve the writing. This is not considered "out of order" since the form of the ink is recognizable on the letter, and in such a case, the letter is already valid, but it is being fixed to prevent further deterioration. It is obvious that this is only when the form of the ink is recognizable on the letter. But if the ink has completely faded, and only the mark of the letter remains from the rust of the ink, meaning from what the ink has eaten into the parchment, leaving a mark, this is nothing and is invalid. It is forbidden to correct it, as this would be "out of order." Great expertise is required to understand if it is ink or merely rust (see Magen Avraham, section 39). This is when the ink deteriorated afterward. But if at the time of writing the ink was not black, but somewhat white or somewhat red, making its appearance dull, it is invalid. Passing a quill over it does not help if the ink is not black, and this is considered "out of order." However, if it is black and one wants to darken it further, there is no issue, and it is permissible. It seems to me that if the entire section is written not in black, one can pass a quill over the entire section, as there is no "out of order" since the entire section is like this. (And what the Magen Avraham wrote in section 38 is when there are good letters.) Know that in "out of order" there is no difference between one letter and many letters.

Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in paragraph 28: One must be careful that the head of the letter Lamed does not enter the space of the letter Hei or Chet, even without touching. Thus far his language, and from his wording, it seems that this is merely a precaution. However, some invalidate it even post facto (Bach, Taz, paragraph 22, and Eliyah Rabbah). But in truth, his words are correct, for certainly if the shape of the letter has changed to the extent that a child cannot recognize it, it is invalid. However, this is only common when it enters the letter Dalet, making it appear as a Hei. Therefore, our teacher, the Rema, wrote in Even HaEzer, section 125, paragraph 18 at the end, and this is his language: And if the shape of the letter has changed, that the head of the Lamed extends into the space of the Dalet, making it appear as a Hei, it is invalid. Thus far his language. But when it enters the Hei or Chet, it is uncommon for it to completely change, as it does not take on the form of another letter upon entering, and it is only invalid if it completely eliminates the letter, which is uncommon. Therefore, he wrote here only the language of precaution. (And so wrote the Beit Shmuel, paragraph 34, and the Chelkat Mechokek, paragraph 38. And so wrote the Magen Avraham, paragraph 40, and this is the main ruling. And even the Ramban, brought by the Ran in the second chapter of Gittin, who invalidates, did not disagree with Tosafot there 2b who validate it. For the Ran refers to when the letter's shape has changed and it has lost its form, and Tosafot do not refer to such a case. And one can say the same about the Taz, and there is no necessity that they disagree. Analyze and you will find it simple.)

We learned in Masechet Soferim (Chapter 1, Halacha 12) that one is not permitted to write unless he knows how to read. And it is stated in Menachot (32b) that tefillin and mezuzot can be written without a written text in front of them. This means that for a Torah scroll, one should not write from memory lest he make a mistake. Rather, another book should be placed before him, and he should look at it and write. But tefillin and mezuzot can be written from memory because one is accustomed to them and will not make a mistake. Therefore, if one knows that he is not accustomed, he should not write except from a written text. And if he is accustomed to some parts and not to others, he should write from memory what he is accustomed to, and what he is not accustomed to, he should write from a written text (Magen Avraham, Subsection 41). And regarding a Torah scroll, it is established that one must read each word before writing it, and it is possible that the same applies to tefillin and mezuzot even when writing from memory. And it is possible that since one is accustomed to them, it is not necessary (see there, Subsection 42). However, if one is not accustomed and writes from a written text, he certainly needs to read each word, as it is like a Torah scroll as explained in Yoreh De'ah, beginning of Siman 274. And it is more reasonable to require it for them as well, even if one is accustomed. And our master the Beit Yosef wrote in Subsection 31 that if one does not write from a written text, he should not write from memory while someone else reads to him, unless he himself first reads it aloud. Until here is his language. And it is questionable whether his intention is specifically regarding someone who does not know them by heart. But if one is accustomed to them, he does not need to read beforehand. Or even if one is accustomed, he still teaches us that even if he is accustomed and someone else reads it to him, he should still read it himself. Therefore, in practice, one should be stringent in all cases to read before writing (see Beit Yosef, and there is no clear conclusion from there. Delve and you will find it easy.) And in Yoreh De'ah, there in Subsection 6, we explained further on this matter, see there.

One must leave a blank space at the top equivalent to the height of the roof of a "ל" (lamed), and a little more space to ensure that it is surrounded by parchment. Some require a space above the roof equivalent to half a fingernail, which is referred to as "אטבא דספרא" in the Talmud (Menachot 32a) in reference to a mezuzah, see there. The same applies to tefillin, and this is agreed upon by the major authorities (Bach, Taz, and Magen Avraham, subsection 43). At the bottom, one must leave a space equivalent to the size of the final forms of the letters "כ" (kaf) and "נ" (nun), and a little more space to ensure it is surrounded by parchment. Some require a space equivalent to half a fingernail, just like at the top, and this is the proper practice. However, from the sides, no space is required by law. Nevertheless, scribes customarily leave some space also on the sides, and it is a good practice because it adds beauty.

It is necessary to leave between each word the space of one letter, and between each letter the space of a hair's breadth, and between each line the space of a line, as in a Torah scroll according to Yoreh De'ah, Chapter 274. Some say that the space of a line is only required for a Torah scroll, which is made for reading, but not for tefillin and mezuzot, and so the scribes customarily do not insist on this (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 44). Furthermore, even with a Torah scroll, it is explained there that all of this is only ideally required, see there (Taz, subparagraph 24). Our Rabbi, the Rema, wrote at the end of paragraph 32 that it is also necessary to leave a slight space between verses. This is his language. And they were astonished at him: for it is explained in the Rivash that if one did so, it does not invalidate, but to require this - certainly not (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 45). However, in the book "Baruch She'amar," it is required to leave some space between verses, see there. And certainly, this was his intention (Eliyah Rabbah, subparagraph 51). And this is ideally required, and similarly, it is not the custom to do so. (And even in Yoreh De'ah in the laws of a Torah scroll, this is not mentioned.)

Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 33: One should make the lines even, so that one should not be indented and another protruding. At the very least, one should be careful not to write three letters outside the line. And if he wrote them, it does not invalidate [the writing]. And two letters that are one word should not be written outside the line. And the letters of the Divine Name should all be within the page and none should go outside the page at all. Until here are his words.

We have already written in Yoreh De'ah, section 273, paragraph 19, that our teacher the Beit Yosef was brief here and relied on what he wrote in Yoreh De'ah there. And this is the principal law: two letters, even when they are the majority of a word, are permitted unless they constitute the entire word. And three letters, when they are the majority of a word, are forbidden, but when they are not the majority of a word, they are permitted.

And in section 18, we explained there that after the fact, it is not invalid even if an entire word is outside the line. See there. However, concerning the letters of the Divine Name, we are uncertain: perhaps even after the fact, it is invalid even if part of it is outside, since it resembles hanging [letters], which are invalid. See there. And there in section 276, paragraph 2, we concluded that after the fact, even the Divine Name is valid. But it is obvious that this is not considered an enhancement [of the mitzvah]. (And this is also implied by the Magen Avraham, subsection 47. And what he wrote there in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua of Pozna to correct with erasures of the upper lines does not apply to tefillin, as it would be considered "out of order." And the Machatzit HaShekel wrote similarly, see there.)

Rambam writes at the beginning of the second chapter: How are the tefillin of the head written? The four sections are written on four separate parchments... and the one for the arm is written on one parchment... One must be careful with the sections, for if one makes a closed section open or an open section closed, they are invalid. The first three sections are all open, and the last section is closed. This is his wording. 

Now, this law is not explicitly stated in the Gemara regarding tefillin but rather concerning a Torah scroll. We must say that the Rambam's intention is as follows: It is known that one must be careful with the sections of the Torah, for if one makes a closed section open or vice versa, it is invalid. And since this is the law for a Torah scroll, and these three sections "Kadesh," "Vehaya Ki Yeviacha," and "Shema" are all open in the Torah, it follows that they must also be made open in the tefillin. The fourth section, "Vehaya Im Shamoa," which is closed in the Torah, must also be made closed in the tefillin.

According to this, the Rambam did not decree that any variation in tefillin renders them invalid. It can be said, as is stated in Menachot (32a) regarding mezuzah, that it is a mitzvah to make the two sections "Shema" and "Vehaya im shamoa" closed, as they are written in the Torah. Therefore, if they are made open, it is acceptable, because in the Torah they are not adjacent to each other; "Shema" is in "Va'etchanan" and "Vehaya im shamoa" is in "Ekev". Therefore, there is no impediment in this matter. According to this, the first two sections "Kadesh" and "Vehaya ki yeviacha", which are adjacent in the Torah, and are open, indeed have an impediment even in tefillin, even post facto. But between "Vehaya ki yeviacha" and "Shema", and between "Shema" and "Vehaya im shamoa", which are not adjacent in the Torah, it is certainly a mitzvah to make them as in the Torah. That is, between "Vehaya" and "Shema" it should be open, and between "Shema" and "Vehaya im shamoa" it should be closed. However, post facto, it is valid even with a variation, since they are not adjacent in the Torah. Many great scholars interpret that the Rambam's intention when he wrote that if one changes them they are invalid, refers to tefillin. But in my humble opinion, this is not so, as this is not clarified in the Gemara. Moreover, if this were the case, he should have first written that these need to be open and the last one closed, and if changed, it is invalid. How could he write the invalidation before stating the law? Therefore, certainly as I have written, that this refers to the law explained in the Gemara regarding a Sefer Torah. (And with this, the difficulties raised by the Beit Yosef and the Bach regarding mezuzah are resolved, as it is not an impediment because they are not adjacent in the Torah, and they struggled greatly, see there. According to what I have written, it is straightforward. It seems that this is the opinion of Maharamp in his response in Rosh Siman 37. The Taz in section 25 tried to differentiate between tefillin and mezuzah, and I don't understand why we need to strain this way, and to cause an uproar about the customs of variations in tefillin. According to what I have written, this is not an impediment. Therefore, all customs are valid post facto. The Tur also did not write that it is an impediment post facto, see there. Blessed is the Lord who has taught us to find merit for the entire Jewish people. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

And this is the language of our teacher the Beit Yosef in section 36: One should make all its sections open, except for the last section written in the Torah, which is "Vehaya Im Shamoa" (And it shall come to pass if you listen), which should be made closed. And if one changes this, it is invalid. Thus far his language, and he follows his method in his great book that this is indeed the intention of the Rambam. However, according to what I have written, even the Rambam's intention is not to make it an absolute requirement. And I did not find among the early authorities anyone who explicitly states that if one changes it, it is invalid.

And our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote there that therefore it is customary that the sections "Kadesh Li," "Vehaya Ki Yeviacha," and the section "Shema" – start at the beginning of a line. And at the end of "Kadesh" and at the end of "Vehaya Ki Yeviacha" – they leave a space sufficient to write nine letters. And at the end of "Shema" they do not leave a space, and if they do, it is less than sufficient to write nine letters. And the section "Vehaya Im Shamoa" starts in the middle of the upper line, and they leave a space before it sufficient to write nine letters. Therefore, three sections are open according to both Rambam and the Rosh, and the last section is closed according to Rambam. So far his words. And these laws of open and closed sections are explained in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 274. And it is explained there that according to the Rosh, this form that starts in the middle of the line is considered open. And how is it considered closed according to the Rosh if it is impossible to leave a space of nine letters and write the other section at the end of the line, which is considered closed according to all opinions? One should leave an entire line empty and then start at the beginning of the line. And according to Rambam, this form is considered open, see there. And this is what our teacher, the Beit Yosef, says, that since in Tefillin it is impossible to satisfy both opinions regarding the closed section of "Vehaya Im Shamoa," they follow the Rambam, since the main halacha follows his view, as I have written in Yoreh De'ah there.

And our master, the Rema, wrote that some permit all of them to be open. And in these regions, the custom is that even the paragraph "Vehaya Im Shamoa" is at the beginning of the line like the other paragraphs. Until here is his wording. And there has already been astonishment at this: How can we initially make "Vehaya Im Shamoa" open, which is invalid according to the Rambam? And even according to what we have explained that even according to him it is not invalid, nonetheless all the poskim wrote that it should be closed, so how can we initially make it open? And while we may not be able to make it closed according to everyone, at least we should make it closed according to the Rambam. And therefore, the way of our master the Beit Yosef is much clearer.

And one of the commentators on the Shulchan Aruch devised a method that would be acceptable according to all opinions: that is, to leave less than the space of nine letters at the end of "Shema," and to leave a blank space at the beginning of "Vehaya Im Shamoa" also less than nine letters, and to start "Vehaya Im Shamoa" there (Taz, small section 26). Most of the great sages of Israel agreed with this, and this is the practice in most Jewish communities. The reason is that this format is considered sealed according to everyone. We combine these spaces, and it is as if the break is in one line, and the second section begins at the end of that line, which is considered sealed according to everyone, as I have written. We have already written in Yoreh De'ah there that what the Rambam wrote there that a sealed section is from the middle of the line is not precise, but rather as long as it does not start from the beginning of the line. See there. According to the Rosh, it is also explained there that as long as it ends in the middle of the line and starts in the middle of the line in the row below, it is sealed. And we explained there in section 6 that according to the Jerusalem Talmud (Megillah, Chapter 1, Halacha 9), any space at the end of one line and the beginning of the next line is considered sealed. This is also explicitly stated in the Sefer Mitzvot Gadol, Mitzvah 23, and this is his wording: "And in the Jerusalem Talmud in Megillah... open on both sides is sealed." And I received this interpretation: it should not be completely open from its beginning the measure of nine letters..., and it should not be completely open from its end... but rather divide the measure of the opening here and there, less than nine letters at the end of "Uvishe'arecha" and less than nine letters at the beginning of "Vehaya Im Shamoa"... and this is a completely sealed section, since there is no measure of opening neither at the beginning nor at the end. This is his wording regarding mezuzah, and the same applies to tefillin. (And the scribes of Reissin followed the custom based on the Gra that they leave the measure of nine letters at the end of "Shema" and the measure of nine letters at the beginning of "Vehaya Im Shamoa." However, in all other regions, the custom is as per the opinion of the Taz, as I have written. And the Gra in his Shulchan Aruch did not mention this at all. He wrote like the Taz, see there.)

And know that there are those who wrote that regarding the laws of open and closed sections in tefillin – one only needs to be careful with the arm tefillin, as all the sections are written on one parchment. But with the head tefillin, this does not apply, because each section is on its own parchment and in its own compartment (Magen Avraham, section 49, in the name of the Sefer Mitzvot Katan, and see Beit Yosef). However, from the words of the Rambam, it is clear that this also applies to the head tefillin, for he started with the head tefillin as well. And he wrote: "One must be careful...," and as I wrote in section 58 – it is clear that this applies to both. This is also implied by the language of the Rosh and the Tur and all the poskim, who wrote simply that it also applies to the head tefillin. And this is the common practice, and it should not be changed. And know that the section "Kadesh" which starts at the beginning of the line with nothing before it, is still considered an open section since it is the first one. This is similar to the Torah, where the first section "Bereshit" starts at the beginning of the line (Beit Yosef, in the name of Rabbi Yosef Abuhav).

And with regard to the Tefillin of Rabbeinu Tam, where "Vehaya Im Shamoa" is the last [parsha], in its writing it is written before "Vehaya Im Shamoa," as will be explained in Siman 34. How should this be done? It is straightforward: according to the Beit Yosef, "Kadesh" and "Vehaya Ki Yeviacha" are at the top of the line, and at the end of "Kadesh" one should leave a space equivalent to nine letters, and at the end of "Vehaya Ki Yeviacha" one should not leave any space or leave less than nine letters. The parsha "Vehaya Im Shamoa" should start in the middle of the line or leave a space equivalent to nine letters, and at its end leave a space equivalent to nine letters. The parsha "Shema" should begin at the top of the line, and as explained in section 63 (according to the Taz), one should leave at the end of "Vehaya Ki Yeviacha" less than nine letters, and at the beginning of "Vehaya Im Shamoa" less than nine letters (B'er Heitev, small section 53), for "Vehaya Im Shamoa" needs to be closed as it is in the Torah. There is one who says that since it is written before "Shema" it does not need this, but all of them should be open (Nodah B'Yehuda, Siman 5). This is not the main opinion. Rather, as I have written, and so the scribes have practiced, and it should not be changed.

The leather of the compartments must be made from the skins of a kosher animal, beast, or bird, even from their carcasses and those that are non-kosher due to health issues. However, it should not be from non-kosher animals, as it must be from a species permitted "in your mouth" similar to the requirements for the parchments. Additionally, one is permitted to make them from parchment, as this is also considered leather. Similarly, one can make them from the skin of a fetus. The straps have the same laws as the compartments. The general rule is: everything involved in the making of tefillin, the parchments, the skins, and the sinews must all be from kosher species. If they are made from non-kosher species, they are invalid. There is an opinion that the compartments should not be made from parchment unless the parchment is placed in a solution of tree bark called "lo'a," used for tanning leather, and it is good to be stringent from the outset (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 50). All our scribes make them from leather because it is difficult to make them from parchment, as is known.

And if it is necessary to perform tanning "for its sake" for the compartments, there are different opinions: For the Rambam in the third chapter, law 15, wrote: The leather that covers the tefillin and that from which the straps are made, they are from... pure... animals. And if he made it from impure animals, or covered the tefillin with gold – they are invalid. And the leather of the strap requires tanning for its sake. But the leather that covers it – does not require any tanning at all. Even if he made it from rawhide (this is leather as it is) – it is valid. And in many places, it is customary to make them from rawhide. Thus far his words. And the Tur, in the name of the Rosh, ruled that it requires tanning for its sake, and thus ruled Rav Cohen Tzedek. And thus ruled in the Sefer HaTerumah and the SeMaG, and the law follows the majority. Therefore, our master the Beit Yosef wrote in section 37: It must be tanned for its sake where possible. Thus far his words, meaning: And where it is not possible – it is better to rely on the opinion of the Rambam and not exempt oneself from tefillin entirely, and put them on without a blessing. (The BaCH and Eliyah Rabbah, not like the Magen Avraham in sub-section 51, since many disagree with him.) And even though we do not find in the Rambam that he explicitly does not require tanning for its sake, nonetheless you can infer from him that since he does not require tanning at all – it follows that even when tanning, it does not need to be for its sake, for it is no worse than not tanning at all (and in any case, there is room to distinguish).

The Rambam wrote at the beginning of the third chapter: There are eight laws regarding the making of tefillin, and all of them are an oral tradition from Moses at Sinai. Therefore, they are all indispensable, and if one deviates in any of them, it is invalid. And these are they: They must be square, and so must their stitching be in a square and their diagonals in a square, so that they have four equal angles. And there must be a form of the letter "Shin" on the leather of the head tefillin, on the right and on the left. And the scrolls must be wrapped in a cloth. And they must also be wrapped in hair above the cloth, and afterward inserted into their compartments. And they must be sewn with sinews. And there must be a passageway made from the leather covering, through which the strap passes until it goes through its hole. And the straps must be black. And their knot must be in a known form of the letter "Dalet."

How are the head tefillin made? They take a square piece of wood, its length equal to its width and its height. If its height is more than its length or less than it, it does not matter. The only precision required is that its length be equal to its width. Grooves are carved into it to make four compartments. They take leather and soak it in water, place the wood inside, and insert the leather into each groove. While it is still wet, they press it from both sides until they form the shape of a Shin with three heads on the right side of the person wearing the tefillin and a Shin with four heads on the left side. The leather is left on the wood until it dries, and then the leather is removed from the wooden mold. As a result, the leather has four empty compartments, and a scroll is inserted into each compartment. They fold back some of the leather at the bottom and sew it at the four corners. They leave some leather at the bottom to form a place where the strap can be inserted, which is called the “ma'avarta” (passage).

And how does one make the tefillin of the arm? They take a squared piece of wood, its length equal to its width, and its height approximately the width of a finger, either a bit more or a bit less. They cover it with wet leather and place the leather on the mold until it dries. Then they remove the leather and place the four sections of scripture in the space of the wood. They fold some of the leather from the bottom and sew it at its four corners. They leave a part of the leather as a passage for the straps, which is called the ma'avarta. All of this is according to the Rambam in the third chapter; see there.

From his words, it is clear that all the tefillin, including the base (titora), which is the lower covering, and the passageway (ma'abarta), whether of the head or the arm, are all made from one piece of leather. This is also evident from Rashi's language in Menachot (35a, s.v. "titora", see there). This is explicitly indicated in the Shimusha Rabba, see there. However, the Rosh (Siman 7) wrote, and this is his language: From Rashi's language, it seems that the compartments and the base are from one piece of leather. But the world does not practice this way, because the leather of the compartments is thin and the leather of the base is thick... until here is his language. And how is it done? The Tur wrote, and this is his language: Some take thick and strong leather and fold it in two, and cut a square hole in the upper fold according to the square of the compartments, and insert the compartments into it. The remaining thin leather of the compartments on all four sides is spread here and there between the two folds of thick leather and sewn together with them. This is called the "titora". And from this thick leather, they also make the "ma'abarta". It is good to do so because, as it is thick and strong, the base of the tefillin is maintained, and its sewing and squareness are preserved. Until here is his language.

And from the words of our teacher, the Beit Yosef, it also seems so, as in section 38 he wrote: One should make four compartments from one piece of leather for the head tefillin, and one compartment for the arm tefillin. Thus far his words, and he only wrote about the actual compartments and not about the base. And in section 44 he wrote: The base (titora) of the tefillin is a law given to Moses at Sinai. This means that one should place leather underneath to cover the opening of the compartments, and it should appear like a kind of bridge board called "titora." And the passageway (ma'avarta) of the tefillin is a law given to Moses at Sinai, and this means that the leather of the base should be extended on one side, and the passageway should be made from it. How so? One should cut it on both sides so that it is not as wide as the base, in order that the squareness of the base be recognizable. And through this passageway the strap passes, and it is called "ma'avarta" because of this. And also for the arm tefillin, one should make a base and a passageway. Thus far his words, hence he wrote to place leather underneath, implying a separate piece of leather. For if not, he would have said to leave some of the leather below to cover the opening of the compartments, as Rambam wrote in such language. And nevertheless, he did not write this explicitly because Rambam did not write it that way. Rather, the custom of the world is as the Rosh wrote, and therefore he left the matter in general terms. And certainly, one who wants more beautiful tefillin should make them all from one piece of leather. And thus the meticulous do in all our lands.

And know that there are those who say that even the boxes themselves can be made from several pieces of leather and sewn together, as sewing is considered a connection (Magen Avraham, subsection 52, in the name of Agudah and Sefer HaTerumah, see there). And they wrote that this is what is implied in Tosafot Menachot (32a, beginning of "Dilma"), where they wrote that even the parchments can be glued according to Rashi's opinion, see there – and certainly with the boxes. And they wrote that even though it is said in the Jerusalem Talmud that tefillin and mezuzot are only written on one piece of leather – this is when the pieces are not sewn together, see there. According to this, we must say that what Rashi explained regarding the base (titora) being from one piece of leather, as I wrote in section 71 – this is not a requirement. If so, we can say that the opinion of the Rambam is also not a requirement. Nevertheless, the custom of the world is that the boxes are made from one piece of leather, and only the base is a separate piece of leather. And those who are meticulous also make the base from one piece of leather, as I wrote.

The length and width of the houses and their height do not have a set measure according to the law. However, the Geonim have said that the base (titora) should not be less than two fingers in length, width, and height. This is also clarified in Shimusha Rabba, where it is explained that this is not an absolute requirement. It states: "Bring a good piece of clay, two fingers by two fingers. If it is more, it is acceptable. If it is less, it is not invalid." This is the end of the quote. Similarly, the Tosafot at the beginning of the tenth chapter of Eruvin cite the Midrash stating this. There is a support for this idea from the fact that the width of the Tzitz (frontlet) was two fingers, as it is mentioned at the beginning of Sukkah and at the beginning of Arakhin. This implies somewhat that the measure of Tefillin is like the measure of the Tzitz. (Refer to Beit Yosef and Magen Avraham, Section 56, where it is written that the sages and the head of the court should make the head Tefillin higher than three fingers so that everyone can see. A Torah scholar and a student before his teacher should wear Tefillin that are as small as one and a half fingers and cover them under the turban so as not to equate themselves with their teachers. This is not our custom. Additionally, it appears from the Tosafot there that the width and length of the base of the head Tefillin should not exceed four fingers, as the place for Tefillin is not more than four fingers. According to this, it is appropriate to protest against those who make large Tefillin that do not sit in the place of Tefillin on the head, and do not fulfill the mitzvah of Tefillin.)

It has already been explained that the base (titura) must be square, both on the top and bottom. This is the language of our Rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, in section 39: Tefillin, whether of the head or the hand, is a law given to Moses at Sinai that they must be square in their stitching and their diagonal. This means that their squareness must be precise, their length equal to their width, so that they have the correct diagonal. As our Sages said: any square cubit has a diagonal of one cubit and two-fifths. And it is necessary to square the place where they rest and also the compartments. But for the height of the compartments, it does not matter if it is more than their width and length. This is their language. And even though the calculation of one cubit and two-fifths for the diagonal is not completely precise according to the mathematicians' calculations, as is known, nevertheless the Torah decreed that it be measured according to this calculation, as I have written in Yoreh De'ah section 30, paragraph 13, see there. (And this resolves the question of the Tosafot in Eruvin 14a.) And know that even if we say that it is impossible for a person to achieve perfect precision to make an exact square, nevertheless the Torah said: Do as best as you can to be precise, and with this you fulfill the commandment. And so our Sages said in Bechorot (17b) regarding the measurements of the altar and the vessels of the Temple that the Torah specified a measure, and this is the language of the Gemara: The Merciful One said to do, and in any way that you can do it is acceptable to Him, see there. And here too with the tefillin, it is the same.

And it turns out that the tefillin must be square both on the top and the bottom, in the base and in the stitching. This means that one should not pull the sewing thread too tightly, so that it does not shrink and ruin the squareness (Rashi, Menachot 35a). And our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 39: If they were made square and afterward their squareness was ruined, there is an opinion that they need to be squared again. This is his language: This means that even though in the case of tzitzit we say in Siman 11 that if the warp threads are torn until less than a thumb's width remains from the corner, they are valid, see there – this is because the Torah only insisted on tzitzit at the time of making, as it is written: "And they shall make for themselves tzitzit," see there. But the squareness of tefillin is a law given to Moses at Sinai, and they need to be square at all times. Ideally, one should ensure that all the compartments of the head tefillin are equal, but this is not essential.

And what is considered a distortion of the square? It appears to me that it is when there is some contraction in the length or width, or a slight deficiency, and the like. Some want to say that when the edges are slightly damaged in their sharpness, and they appear somewhat rounded at the corners, it is called "distortion of the square." In my humble opinion, this does not seem correct. Firstly, the square is not distorted by this, as the sharpness is removed equally from both the length and the width. And if you say that this makes them round tefillin and not square ones—surely, it is even more surprising that the tefillin remain square as before, for if the sharpness of the corners is not as it should be, do we lose the name "square"? This is astonishing. In my opinion, this is what our Sages of blessed memory said regarding the square and its diagonal, as explained, and it is in Menachot (35a). And it is difficult: since it is made square, will its diagonal not naturally be correct? And indeed, Rashi explained there that its length should not be greater than its width, see there. But Maimonides at the beginning of the third chapter wrote: "and its diagonal should be squared, so that it has four equal angles." Thus far his words, and his intention is clear: that the main point is that the angles should be equal. If so, even if the sharpness of the corners is slightly damaged, what of it? The angles remain equal. Furthermore: the Torah was not given to ministering angels, and some distortion of the angles is inevitable. And indeed, there are great experts in their craft who make tefillin boxes that do not get distorted, but the majority are not capable of doing so. Moreover, they charge a lot of money for their boxes, which not everyone can afford. And in the end, I have also seen that over time they get slightly damaged, because it is inevitable. Therefore, I say that Heaven forbid to declare this invalid, and the Holy One, Blessed be He, does not come with excessive demands upon His creatures. This is like what they said in Bechorot (17b) regarding a square: "Do whatever you can," as I wrote in section 75. And those who seek excessive stringencies—the opinion of the Sages does not approve of them.

The groove between each compartment in the tefillin shel rosh must reach all the way down to where the base (titora) is sewn. However, if it does not reach all the way down, it is still kosher. This is only if the groove is noticeable to everyone, so that the four compartments are visible to all; otherwise, the tefillin are invalid. Each compartment must stand independently, meaning they should not be so attached to each other that they cannot be easily separated; otherwise, it would be considered as one compartment. Scribes who attach the compartments too closely should be reprimanded. It should not be claimed that the lack of attachment will ruin the squareness, as this is not the case; the squareness is considered based on their actual attachment to each other, and this matter is not relevant here (see Chayei Adam and Chasam Sofer, section 5). In Menachos (34b), it is explicitly stated that if the grooves are not noticeable, the tefillin are invalid—see there. Likewise, it is explicitly stated by Rambam that there must be a distinction between each compartment—see there.

In regard to the blackening of the tefillin boxes, we do not find this mentioned in the Gemara. It is only regarding the straps that it is said to be a law given to Moses at Sinai that they should be black (Menachot 35a). We do not find this regarding the boxes. Therefore, Rambam writes in Hilchot Tefillin 3:14 that the tefillin box can be green or white. Nonetheless, he writes that it is preferable for tefillin that everything should be black, the box and the straps entirely, see there. This is what our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in Orach Chaim 32:40, and this is his language: "The leather of the boxes – it is a mitzvah to make them black." Until here is his language. His intention by saying "mitzvah" is that it is for the enhancement of the mitzvah, and it is a mitzvah but not an obligation. And so the simple custom is to blacken them. Therefore, if they become somewhat whitened over time, we are not concerned. Thus, if there is a scribe in one's locality, one should give him the tefillin to blacken, but it is not essential. There are scribes who apply a thick coating to make them shine, and one should reprimand them if there is any real substance to the coating. The great ones of the generations have already protested against this. And now we do not see people doing this. (And from Tosfot on Shabbat 28b it is explained that they hold that blackening is required by law, see there. And see Beit Chadash.)

It has already been explained that the Shin on the tefillin is a law given to Moses at Sinai. On the head tefillin, the leather is creased, one on the right and one on the left. The Gaonim received that the right one of the wearer has three heads, and the left one has four heads. If they are reversed, it does not invalidate them. Similarly, if both are made with three heads or both with four heads, since the Talmud simply states Shin, and both are included in Shin. Even though I did not find this explicitly stated, it still appears to me to be so. Many reasons have been given for these Shins, as explained in the Zohar Pinchas (page 228b), that they correspond to the seven thousand years. More reasons are found in the commentators (see Beit Yosef, Taz paragraph 35, and Magen Avraham paragraph 59). The heads of the Shins – some make them rounded, and some make them squared. The Yuds of the Shins need to touch the bottom edges of the Shins, not like those who say that on the Shin with four heads, the Yuds do not touch the bottom (see Magen Avraham there). The groove of the Shin, meaning the point at the bottom, should reach the place of the stitching. The Shin should not extend below the stitching, but also, the bottom edges of the Shin should be visible on the stitching.

The Tur and Shulchan Aruch in section 42 wrote that the Shin (ש) should be made from folds of the leather, meaning that the leather should be folded to form the shape of the letter Shin (ש). But if it is made like a printed form, it is considered "chiseling out from within." And even though the Shin is protruding, pressing the print against the letters themselves and not around the letters, which is considered "chiseling around" and is valid as explained in Gittin (20a), nevertheless, the leather, being soft, also presses around the protrusion of the Shin and it is considered "chiseling out from within." However, some say that "chiseling out from within" is not invalid for this Shin, because it is specifically something that requires "writing" that this is not considered writing. But these Shins do not require "writing," rather it is a law given to Moses at Sinai that it should have the form of a Shin. Therefore, even "chiseling out from within" is considered the form of a Shin. And this is the language of our teacher, the Rema, in his book Darkei Moshe: One should not change from the custom of the elders, who made it with a fold in the leather. However, if they made it in print or wrote it with ink on the white of the house, we do not have the authority to invalidate them. Thus far his language.

When the construction of the houses is finished, he should roll each section from its end to its beginning. Similarly, for the tefillin of the arm, which is on one parchment, he should roll it from its end to its beginning, so that when it is opened, it can be read in order. He wraps them in a small piece of parchment and in kosher parchment. It is a law given to Moses at Sinai that he should wrap it with the hair of a pure animal or beast, and this is indispensable even post facto. However, wrapping with parchment is not indispensable post facto if he has no other tefillin (Bach and Magen Avraham, subsection 60). Likewise, if he wrapped them from the beginning to the end, it is not indispensable post facto. And in this case, he can fix it and wrap them correctly. Our custom is to wrap hair directly on the section itself, and afterward wrap it with kosher parchment, and then wrap hair again. The reason seems to me: because wrapping with hair is a law given to Moses at Sinai, and wrapping with parchment is not explicitly mentioned, and perhaps the hair needs to be specifically on the parchment of the section itself. However, since according to the tradition of the Geonim, parchment is required on the sections and hair on the parchment, as stated in Shimusha Rabba, we therefore do both.

And the hair should be from a calf, to atone for the sin of the Golden Calf. However, if calf hair is not found, one may use hair from a cow or an ox. The hair should be washed thoroughly at first until it is clean. Tradition has it that part of this hair must be visible outside the compartments, at the location of the "Vehaya Im Shamo'a" section, on the side facing the "Kadesh" section. Consequently, in the tefillin of Rashi, the hair comes out not far from the edge, and in the tefillin of Rabbeinu Tam, it comes out in the middle. According to the Zohar, the hair should not extend more than the length of a barley grain but less than that. (See Magen Avraham, subsection 61, who questioned: the hair does not transmit impurity. It seems to me that the Zohar's intention is the same. The explanation is: hair does not transmit impurity unless it is connected to something else, like here where it is wrapped around the parchment and serves the parchment. If the parchment becomes impure, the hair also becomes impure. As we learn in the thirteenth chapter of Keilim, Mishnah 6: wood that serves metal – becomes impure, see there. And if it does not reach the length of a barley grain even when connected, it does not transmit impurity, because impurity does not apply to less than a barley grain. Examine and you will find it correct.)

Place each section in its proper compartment, ensuring it stands upright within its compartment and not lying down. Although according to Rabbeinu Tam, it must specifically be lying down, as explained in the Tosafot on Menachot 33a ("Ha"), we hold according to Rashi's opinion there that it must specifically be upright. And although with regard to the order of the sections, we are cautious according to Rabbeinu Tam's opinion because many early Geonim hold this way, as will be explained in Siman 34, this is not the case regarding the law of being upright. 

How should they be positioned upright? The upper row should be at the top, and the lower row towards the opening of the compartments. The beginning of the section should be placed towards the right of the reader, so that when he comes to open and read them, they will be positioned properly before him, and he can open and read them in order. It appears that all this is essential, especially since it is possible to arrange it this way. (See Magen Avraham, Siman 32, subparagraph 62).

And similarly, for the arm-tefillin, one writes the four sections on one piece of parchment, rolls them from end to beginning, wraps parchment around them, and ties hair around it. According to our custom, we also wrap hair around the parchment of the sections. We place them in their compartment upright, just like the head-tefillin. It is taught in Menachot (34b) that if, after the fact, one wrote them on four separate pieces of parchment and placed them in one compartment, he has fulfilled his obligation, and there is no need to glue the sections together. Moreover, even if he placed them in four compartments like the head-tefillin, if he placed a piece of leather over the four compartments so that it appears as a single piece from the outside, he has fulfilled his obligation. The Mishnah there also teaches that if one does not have arm-tefillin but has two head-tefillin, he can place a piece of leather over one of them and wear it as arm-tefillin. This is also ruled by the Rambam in the third chapter of Hilchot Tefillin, Mezuzah, and Sefer Torah, and by the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch, section 47. Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote that the custom is to glue them together so that they appear as one piece of parchment, and one should ensure to use kosher glue. His exact words are: "And the custom is to glue them with glue so that it all appears as one piece of parchment. And one should be careful to use kosher glue." However, I do not understand: since he places them in four compartments, how can he glue all four sections together? Rabbeinu Beit Yosef only mentioned four sections in one compartment, not in four compartments. How can he glue them? It must be said that he is not referring directly to the previous law. Rather, he wrote that if it happens that the sections are written on four pieces of parchment, one should glue them together and not place them in the compartments separately. The reason for this law is that the Torah's insistence that the arm-tefillin be a single unit refers to its external appearance as a single unit, and we are not concerned about the inside. Note that this ruling permitting the use of head-tefillin for arm-tefillin applies to new ones that have not yet been worn. However, if they have been worn, it is forbidden to change them from a higher level of sanctity (head-tefillin) to a lower level (arm-tefillin). For unworn ones, designation alone does not constitute a significant act (as taught in the Gemara there).

And similarly, the opposite applies to the tefillin of the head. It is taught there that if one wrote the passages on one piece of parchment and placed them in four compartments, it is valid. There is no need for a large space between them; one can place a thread or string between each passage, as mentioned there. This is also stated in the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, section 47. The requirement for no space between them refers to a large space between each passage, but a small space is necessary because each passage needs to be placed in its own compartment (Nimukei Yosef). The thread or string serves as a marker of the separation. 

Some of the early authorities inferred from this that the standing of the passages is not an absolute requirement after the fact, since here, by necessity, they would be lying down, as is evident (see Beit Yosef). However, in truth, there is no proof for this, and therefore Rashi explained there that after writing them on one piece of parchment, one should cut the top of the parchment into fingers, leaving the parchment connected at the bottom. This means that one should insert each passage into its own compartment under the compartment while they stand upright, so that they are separated at the top and connected at the bottom. Some interpret further that the cutting should be above the writing, where there is a large margin above the writing, and all the writing is on one piece of parchment. Otherwise, it wouldn't be considered one piece of parchment (Taz, section 36). In any case, according to this, they can be upright. Maimonides does not mention this law at all, which requires further investigation.

It appears to me from what the Rambam wrote there in Halachah 11: And if the separation is not discernible, they are invalid. And one must pass a thread or cord through each and every groove on the surface of the leather, to distinguish between each compartment. And the simple custom is to pass a sinew from the sewing sinews through each and every groove of all three. Until here are his words, meaning: that in all the tefillin they do so at the time of their making, and afterwards they remove it. Just like all the crafts that require separation – they do so at the time of the craft, and after completing the craft they remove it, like the wood in the tefillin that they remove afterwards, as I wrote in section 69, see there; and like the work of the altar in Zevachim (54b), see there. According to this, the separation mentioned in the Baraita there is in all the tefillin, as well as the thread or cord. This is not like all the poskim (decisors of Jewish law) who explain this as when all the sections were on one piece of parchment. And what we learned there: And if he wrote them on one piece of leather and placed them in four compartments, he has fulfilled his obligation, the Rambam would explain it as follows: Do not say that it is necessary to write on four separate pieces of leather. Rather, even if he wrote them on one piece of parchment and then completely cut them apart, section by section, he has fulfilled his obligation, since when placing them in the compartments, each one stands by itself. Thus, there is no novelty here at all (so it appears to me clearly with the help of Heaven).

The Tur and Shulchan Aruch wrote in Section 48: If the compartments (batim) are coated with gold or the skin of an impure animal, they are invalid. This is the end of their statement, and it is a baraita in Sanhedrin (48b). The commentators explain: "Coated with gold" means on the compartments, and not that the compartments themselves are made of gold. However, Rashi in Menachot (42b) explained regarding the skin of an impure animal that the compartments are made from the skin of an impure animal, see there. Consequently, the interpretation regarding gold is the same. And there is evidence that Rashi explained regarding gold that the reason is that a pouch made of leather is required, see there. Thus, Rashi also interpreted regarding gold that the compartments are made from gold, and not merely coated with gold. One of the great authorities has already addressed this (Nodah BiYehudah, Section 1). Nevertheless, it appears to me that it is clear to the Tur and Shulchan Aruch that both matters are included in the intention of the baraita: one is making the compartments themselves from gold or from an impure material, and the second is coating the compartments with gold or an impure material. Evidence for this is from the language of Rashi in Gittin (45b), where he wrote: made a coating for their pouch, see there. It is one reasoning: that when the compartments are coated with gold or an impure material, the underlying material is nullified because the outer layer is not visible at all. Additionally, the outer compartments do not see the air. Furthermore, regarding impurity, the coating nullifies the essence of the vessel, as Rambam wrote in the Laws of Vessels, Chapter Four, Law 4, see there. (And it is obvious that this is when they are attached to the compartments. But the cases made for the compartments, which are taken off from the compartments, are nothing. Even if they were on the tefillin at the time of their placement, it does not nullify the tefillin. However, it is not appropriate and not fitting to do so. There are those who do not remove the case of the hand tefillin even during prayer, and it is not proper to do so. Examine and you will find clarity.)

It is a law given to Moses at Sinai that tefillin should be sewn with the sinews of a kosher animal or beast. However, one should not sew with the sinews of a bird because they are weak, and it is also not clear to distinguish between the sinews and the flesh. It is good to sew with the sinews of an ox. The sinews are taken from the heel of the animal where they are white. If they are hard, they are softened with stones until they become like flax, then they are spun and twisted, and they become very strong (Magen Avraham, section 65). One should not take sinews from a Samaritan because we are concerned that they might be from an impure animal. Rabbi Yosef Karo wrote in Section 50 that in a place where sinews are not available, they sew with talidros, which are made from parchment, until they can obtain sinews. This is his language. But it is not understood: since the law was stated to sew with sinews, how can we permit using parchment (Noda B'Yehuda, Part 2, Section 2)? We need to say that it is considered that the law was stated this way, that even the stitches must specifically be from kosher animals, and thus it is usual to sew with sinews. However, the sinews are not indispensable, and therefore in cases of pressing need, one can rely on the words of Rabbi Yosef Karo and sew with thin, dry intestines. Some prohibit this, saying it is not sinews (Sha'arei Teshuva, section 69, in the name of Noda B'Yehuda), and one should be stringent because perhaps the law was stated specifically for sinews, and so the decisors have ruled. (See Magen Avraham, section 66, that one should not buy sinews from a Samaritan even if it is known that they are from a kosher animal, because since this is a law given to Moses at Sinai, they must be made "for its sake," and a Samaritan does not have the concept of "for its sake.")

He should sew three stitches on each side. The sewing thread should go around from both directions, from above and below. The stitches should be right next to the compartment itself and not on the base, and he should pass the sewing thread between each compartment. (See Taz, subsection 38, and see what I wrote in subsection 87.) There must be twelve stitches on the arm tefillin, and likewise on the head tefillin. However, if he made only ten stitches or less, it is not invalidated. There is an opinion that these twelve stitches must all be with one thread and the thread should not be cut, and if it is cut, it is invalid, meaning until he reties it (Taz, subsection 39). Nevertheless, if the thread is short and he cannot complete all the stitches with it, he may complete the sewing with another thread (Magen Avraham, subsection 68). It seems to me that if he sees that the thread will not suffice, he should tie another thread to its end. And this should not be altered.

Insert the strap through the loop (ma'avarta), and make a knot in the shape of a Dalet for the head tefillin and in the shape of a Yud for the hand tefillin, to complete the letters of Shaddai with the Shin that is on the head tefillin. And thus they said in Shabbat (62a) that the Shin, Dalet, and Yud of the tefillin are a halacha given to Moses at Sinai (see Tosafot there). Therefore, one should ensure to make this name in order: first the Shin, then the Dalet, and then the Yud. If one changes the order, it is not invalid, but ideally, one should be careful with this. (And what the Magen Avraham wrote in subsection 69 to make the Dalet on both sides - this is not the custom. Similarly, what the Rema wrote in subsection 52 that the custom is to pass a strip of leather over the hand tefillin widthwise across the arm, and that its width should be the same as the width of the tefillin box, this is not understood at all what he means. And in the Tur, there is also something similar, and there he explained to pass the strap over the hand tefillin box, meaning over the loop during tying to strengthen it, as the Sephardim do. It is also apparent that this is the intention of the Rema. However, his wording is puzzling, what is meant by "and its width should be...?" And perhaps there is a printing error here.)

It is stated in Menachot (35a) that if two compartments of the tefillin shel rosh (head tefillin) are damaged, and these compartments are adjacent to each other—meaning that the leather between the compartments has been slightly torn, but the sides and the top are intact—if the tefillin are old, they are invalid because they have already deteriorated due to their age. However, if they are new, they are valid as long as the leather base of the compartments, which is the titura, is intact, and the main part of the compartments is also intact, though they are slightly torn, as I have described. This is according to the version of the Rambam in the Gemara there. According to Rashi’s version, the opposite is true: new tefillin are invalid, and old tefillin are valid. The reason is that new tefillin are still soft and flexible, and thus they can easily become damaged (Levush). Additionally, it is revealed that the leather is defective since it deteriorated in a short time, whereas old tefillin have already become sturdy, indicating that the leather was good from the start. It seems to me that each opinion follows its own reasoning properly: Rashi explains that it refers to the leather, as I have written, hence new tefillin are worse because this is a sign that the leather is rotten. But Rambam, who explains that it refers to the sinews, as will be clarified—certainly, old tefillin are worse because they have rotted due to their age, whereas new tefillin are mostly strong, as is commonly observed.

However, if the two houses are not adjacent to each other, such as the first and the third, even if they are old, they are valid. According to Rashi's opinion, even if they are new, they are valid. And if three houses are damaged, in any case, they are invalid even if they are new, and according to Rashi's opinion, even if they are old. And know that what was explained in the previous section that if they are adjacent to each other, they are invalid — there is no difference whether the damage is on one side, such that the damage is opposite each other, or whether one side is damaged from one direction and the other from another direction. In all cases, they are invalid (Taz, subsection 3).

And what is considered "new" and what is "old"? "New" is considered any time that if they were to be pulled by the straps, the compartment would stretch and open – it is called "new." If it does not open – it is called "old." However, this applies to those who make the compartment and the passageway from one piece of leather. But those who make the passageway from a separate piece of leather – it is not applicable as is obvious (see there, subsection 2). It seems to me that for us there is another sign, as the Gemara there states two signs: the first is the sign we explained; the second is when one holds the leather and stretches it, and when released it contracts – this is old, and the other is new, see there. However, in truth, with the way our compartments are made, which are very hard – we are not at all proficient with these signs. And it appears that the compartments in the time of the Talmud were not hard at all. And know that all these distinctions apply to the head tefillin which have four compartments. But with the hand tefillin, as soon as one of the walls is damaged – they are entirely invalid (Responsa Pnei Yehoshua).

And the Rambam, may his memory be blessed, in Chapter 3, Law 18, has a different approach to this, and he holds that the defect is not in the boxes (batim) but in the sewing threads. And this is his wording: Tefillin whose stitches have torn, if two stitches next to each other have torn or three stitches have torn even if not adjacent (and according to the Rambam, this means they are truly next to each other, examine and you will find it easy) – these are invalid. In what case is this said? In old ones. But in new ones, as long as the surface of the tablet (this is the titura) is intact – they are valid. And these are the new ones: any that, when a part of the torn leather is held and sewn, they can support the tefillin and it is strong and not detached – these are new. But if it is not fit to support and it is detached – these are old. Until here is his wording, and our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, brought both approaches. And in both they were stringent in every matter, because according to Rashi the old ones are preferable and according to the Rambam the new ones are preferable. However, according to what I wrote, there is no need to say this, as I wrote in section 1. And in practice, one should not be lenient at all, and only in the defect of the stitches there is a way to correct with new threads and to sew them. But in the defect of the boxes, no correction helps at all, because the tears testify that they are completely ruined, and new boxes need to be made (this seems according to my humble opinion).

The leather of the straps must be from the skins of pure animals, beasts, or birds. They must be processed for their specific purpose, meaning: for the sake of tefillin straps, as this is a law given to Moses at Sinai. They must also be black, which is a law given to Moses at Sinai. Therefore, both the processing and the blackening must be done for their specific purpose, and by an adult Jew specifically. However, if a Samaritan did it, it is invalid. This is not the case with the blackening of the boxes (batim), for according to the Rambam, the Tur, and the Shulchan Aruch, they do not need to be black. Therefore, if a Samaritan blackened them, it is valid. However, according to those who hold that even the boxes need to be black according to the law, their status is like the straps. The blackening of the straps only needs to be on the outer side. However, on the inner side, any color is valid. Nevertheless, the sages said that they should not be red on the inner side, lest people say that they were dyed and reddened from the blood of sores, and they will spread a bad rumor that he has sores (Gemara 35a). Note that straps are valid whether made from leather or from parchment. The custom is to make them from calf or sheep skins, and those from calves are better and stronger. (The Magen Avraham wrote in subsection 7 that if a Samaritan blackened them and then a Jew blackened them again for their specific purpose, it is valid, see there. If processed not for their specific purpose, it is entirely invalid. They should not be smeared with the fat of impure fish. See Sha'arei Teshuvah subsection 5.)

The Tur wrote: If the strap that encircles the head or the arm breaks, it cannot be fixed, neither by tying nor by sewing. However, the part that hangs from it and the part that wraps around the arm, tying does not invalidate it. Thus are his words. Meaning: all the more so with sewing. For in the Gemara (35b) it says that tying is certainly forbidden, as it is written: "And you shall bind them" – we require a complete binding, meaning that the binding of the strap must be intact, entirely a whole strap and not tied. They also inquired there about sewing, and said: Go out and see what the people practice. Rashi explained this as a prohibition, because it also is not a complete binding. Rabbeinu Tam in Tosafot there explained it as a leniency, since the sewing is inside and from the outside it appears whole – it is called a "complete binding." The Tur ruled according to Rashi. However, this is only for the strap required by Torah law, meaning what encircles the head and the arm. But what is longer than that according to our custom, if it breaks there – one can even tie it, and all the more so sew it. Also, Rambam at the end of the third chapter holds the same opinion as the Tur, see there.

And there are some of the early authorities who were even more stringent in this matter, as our teacher the Beit Yosef wrote in Section 5, and this is his language: "If the strap has been severed, some permit sewing it from the inside (Rabbeinu Tam's opinion). And there are those who say: what encircles the head, and for the hand, enough to encircle the arm to tie the tefillin with the arm, and enough to extend to the middle finger and to wind it three times around that finger and tie it – there is no remedy for them, neither in tying nor in sewing. But any extra length that is for winding the strap several times around the arm, and for the head what hangs from it – sewing and tying do not invalidate it. And in a pressing situation, one can rely on those who permit it so that the mitzvah of tefillin is not nullified." Thus far is his language. Meaning: to rely on Rabbeinu Tam who permits sewing even for the main part of the strap. And it is good to sew with sinew and not with thread, but if he does not have sinew – he may sew with thread. And he should sew in such a way that the seam is on the inside, towards the body, so it is not visible on the outside. And when relying on the lenient opinion, there is one who says not to recite a blessing, for blessings are not essential (Taz, Section 7).

And know that there is another stringent opinion even regarding the head tefillin, that if the strap hanging on the right reaches the navel and on the left reaches the chest, stitching does not help (see Beit Yosef and Taz, subsection 6). But our master, the Beit Yosef, did not consider this at all, for although this was the tradition of the ancients from the Shimusha Rabba as I wrote in Siman 27, nevertheless, it is clear that this is not a law given to Moses at Sinai, as is evident from Menachot (35b) and Tosafot there. If so, how can we be more stringent in this matter, to prohibit stitching which is permitted by Rabbeinu Tam and many of the early authorities even regarding the main strap? And so we practice according to the words of our master, the Beit Yosef. (And the Taz there was puzzled by his words, see there. And the matter is clear as I have written.)

The order of writing the [tefillin] passages has already been explained to be as they appear in the Torah: "Kadesh," "Vehaya Ki Yeviacha," "Shema," and "Vehaya Im Shamoa."
