It is taught in the Mekhilta: If one wrote them out of order, they must be buried. However, regarding the order of placing them in the compartments [of the tefillin], there is significant disagreement among the great sages. According to Rashi in Menachot (34b) and the Rambam in the third chapter, the placement in the compartments is the same as the writing order. In the head tefillin, "Kadesh" is placed in the outer compartment to the left of the person putting on the tefillin, which is to the right of the reader facing him. Following it in the second compartment is "Vehaya Ki Yeviacha," then "Shema" in the third compartment, and "Vehaya Im Shamoa" in the fourth compartment, which is the outer compartment to the right of the person putting on the tefillin and to the left of the reader. The reader reads them in the order they appear in the Torah. The same applies to the hand tefillin.

However, Rabbeinu Tam holds that when placing [the parchments] in the compartments, "Vehaya Im Shamoa" comes before "Shema." Their order is as follows: "Kadesh," "Vehaya Ki Yeviacha," "Vehaya Im Shamoa," "Shema." And when writing them, "Shema" is written before "Vehaya Im Shamoa." Similarly, for the arm [tefillin], "Kadesh," "Vehaya Ki Yeviacha" are written, leaving a space for the writing of "Vehaya Im Shamoa," and "Shema" is written at the edge of the parchment. Afterwards, on the empty space, "Vehaya Im Shamoa" is written. Their dispute is based on the Talmudic discussion there. The Rosh and the Tur write that the Geonim, Rav Sherira and Rav Hai Gaon, hold like Rabbeinu Tam. They provide a mnemonic: the "Vehaya" sections are together, and the "Shin" sections are on the outside. That is to say, the "Vehaya" sections are adjacent to each other, "Vehaya Im Shamoa" next to "Vehaya Ki Yeviacha," and the "Shin" sections of "Kadesh" and "Shema" are on the outside next to the "Shin" sections of the tefillin. They also write that Rabbeinu Chananel holds this way, and this is also the opinion of the Raavad in his glosses there. The Barcelonian attributed a mistake to the Shimusha Rabba, which wrote the order of placement according to Rashi and the Rambam. He writes: "We also find an error in this Shimusha, which should not be relied upon at all, as it writes and places the 'Kadesh' section… and 'Shema' in the third compartment, and 'Vehaya Im Shamoa' in the fourth. This is a great error, as this is the order for writing them, but when placing them in their cases, 'Shema' is in the first compartment to the right of the wearer, 'Vehaya Im Shamoa' in the second, 'Vehaya Ki Yeviacha' in the third, 'Kadesh' in the fourth…" End of his words (at the end of Rif on the laws of tefillin; see there).

In the responsa of the Rambam (brought in Kesef Mishneh), the scholars of Lunel wrote to the Rambam expressing their astonishment at his arrangement, as they had a tradition from the Geonim, led by Rav Hai Gaon, that the sequences were in the middle. The Rambam replied to them as follows: "What you thought regarding the arrangement of the sections... I also thought the same initially. The tefillin I had in the West were likewise. Thus it was written..., and that composition misled me and all the people of the West... Many Geonim disagreed with this, and all the people of the East and the ancient people of the Land of Israel disagreed with this. They said the Geonim opened Rav Hai's tefillin, and they were arranged as I wrote in my composition. And Rabbi Moshe Drai, when he came from the West to the Land of Israel, had his tefillin like those of your place, but when he was shown the words of the ancient Geonim and their proofs, he discarded his tefillin and made them in the proper order. The clear proof in this matter is what they said in 'Hakometz Rabba': 'And the reader reads them in their order,' meaning... in the order of the Torah. This version was not in our books, but I found it in the old manuscripts... until here is his wording. 

It is astonishing that the Rosh and the Tur, and several other early authorities, held that Rav Hai ruled according to Rabbeinu Tam, while the Rambam wrote that they opened Rav Hai's tefillin and it was not so. In Mordechai and other early authorities, it is written that the bima (platform) upon the grave of Ezekiel the Prophet fell, and they found his tefillin and opened them, and they were in the order of Rashi and the Rambam. In any case, it seems that among the early ancients there was a dispute regarding this, and the entire world has adopted this as the halacha. Even those who put on Rabbeinu Tam's tefillin only recite the blessing on Rashi and Rambam's tefillin and pray with them, as if a divine voice declared that this is the law.

The Rosh and the Tur wrote: Since the great sages of the world disagreed about it, and the tefillin of one are invalid for the other. As it is taught (Menachot 34b): If one switched their passages, meaning that he put the passage of one house into another – they are invalid. And the sages said (beginning of the tenth chapter of Eruvin): There is enough space on the head to place two tefillin, and similarly on the arm. Therefore, a God-fearing person should fulfill the obligation according to both opinions. He should make two pairs of tefillin and put on both, intending when putting them on: "With those that are made correctly according to the law – with them I fulfill my obligation. The others – they are merely like straps." And there is no concern here for "adding to the commandment," as this is only an issue if he makes five compartments. He should not place the two pairs in one pouch, since one of them is ordinary and it is forbidden to place it in a tefillin pouch. Rather, he should make two pouches, marking each pouch so as not to mix them. This was the practice of my lord father, may his memory be blessed, and his teacher, our master Rabbi Meir, may his memory be blessed. Thus far is his wording. Now, this is only possible with very small tefillin. But with our tefillin, it is impossible to put on two at once.

Our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote after he cited the words of the Tur, and this is his language: "And if one does not know how to position them correctly and place both together, he should place according to the opinion of one [Rashi or Rabbeinu Tam] for the arm and head and remove them immediately, then place the others relying on the initial blessing." And there are those who say that if he cannot place them together, he should place Rashi's and recite the blessing over them, and they should be on him during the recitation of the Shema and the prayer. After the prayer, he should place Rabbeinu Tam's without a blessing and recite with them "Shema" and "Vehaya Im Shamoa." However, only someone who is known and reputable in piety should do so. This is the end of his language. That is to say: Initially, he said that if he cannot place them both at once, he should place them one after the other immediately and can bless over whichever he wants. To this, he says "and there are those who say," meaning that he should bless only on Rashi's. He should not remove them immediately to place Rabbeinu Tam's but after the prayer, and the reason is that the main halacha follows Rashi and the Rambam. (And similarly, the Taz explained in subsection 3. And see Magen Avraham subsection 4 and 5, who struggled with his words. It seems he had a different version in the Shulchan Aruch. He wrote in subsection 6 that what they wrote that one should not place them in the same bag is when he did not initially intend to place both. But if he intended from the start, it is permitted, see there. And also what the Beit Yosef wrote that only someone known and reputable in piety should do so, nowadays it has spread in many countries to place Rabbeinu Tam’s tefillin, and there is no arrogance in this. Anyone can do so, and he will be blessed.)

Do not be astonished that since the tefillin according to Rashi are invalid according to Rabbeinu Tam, and the tefillin of Rabbeinu Tam are invalid according to Rashi, how it is possible that the great sages of the world, the pious of the generations, and the entirety of Israel at various times did not fulfill the mitzvah of tefillin, and their blessings were in vain, God forbid? Therefore, even though it is not appropriate in works of laws and statutes to write things that are whispered, and the hidden matters are for the Lord our God, and especially in our sins we have no knowledge of this; nevertheless, so that it does not seem astonishing to you, we will explain a little of the much, according to our understanding with the help of Heaven.

Know that the author of "Migdal Oz," who resolves the critiques of the Raavad on the Rambam, wrote on this matter, and these are his words: The Raavad of blessed memory wrote: "Rav Hai Gaon does not say this… And I say, the esteemed author interprets as he received from his teachers… And I found that the sages of Lunel asked…, and he answered them… And one who knows the secret… will understand that all opinions have a root and a branch, and these and those are the words of the living God… And a spirit from above has already enlightened us, and we found a hidden and concealed Midrash, and we were compelled to change what we had been accustomed to and upheld as their order. And so did our latter sages practice… Thus far his words, meaning: initially they acted according to Rabbeinu Tam, and after they found the hidden Midrash – they were compelled to change and follow the order according to the opinion of Rashi and the Rambam of blessed memory.

In my humble opinion, this hidden Midrash is found in the Zohar, Parashat Pinchas (page 258a). For behold, at the end of Zohar Parashat Bo, it explicitly states: the first section is "Kadesh"..., the second is "Vehaya Ki Yeviacha"..., the third section is "Shema"..., and because of this "Shema" is adjacent to "Vehaya".... The fourth section is the secret of the harsh judgment "Hishameru Lachem..." until here is its language. This is clearly in line with Rashi. And I have seen someone who rejected this, saying that its intention is regarding the writing. But in truth, this is not the case, as it is evident from the entire context there that it refers to the order of placement. And indeed, this is the truth, and based on the Zohar in Parashat Pinchas, the matters will be clarified.

And this is the language of the Zohar there: His tefillin are arranged in the order of the Tetragrammaton, which is "Sanctify to me," "And it shall be when the Lord brings you," "Hear," "And it shall be if you diligently obey." But in the world to come, the Tetragrammatons are in the middle, which are HaShem HaShem... until here is his language. And he elaborated on this, see there. And in my humble opinion in his explanation: Behold, at the end of the third chapter of Pesachim our Sages of blessed memory said that in the future to come, the name of the Tetragrammaton will be said as it is written. And this is what is written: "On that day, the Lord will be one and His name one." Because then the evil inclination will be nullified, as it is written: "They shall not harm nor destroy," and consequently, the troubles will also cease, as is known. Therefore, now the last "And it shall be if you diligently obey," in which it is written "Beware, lest your heart be deceived... and you will quickly perish..." This is not the case in the future to come – "Hear" will be last, in which only the love of God is written, and there is no punishment in it. And this is what the Zohar says in Parashat "Bo" the fourth section: The secret of the difficult judgment, as explained to those who understand. And in "Pinchas" it says that in the future to come, the Tetragrammatons will be together, meaning: the two "And it shall be" will be adjacent to each other, because in the letters of "And it shall be" there is the whole name of the Tetragrammaton. And in the future to come, they will be next to each other, which are HaShem HaShem, meaning the Tetragrammaton will be read as it is written. And there is a hint to this in the shin(s) of the head tefillin, as "Sanctify" and "Hear" are next to the shins of the head, and together they have thirteen heads, the numerical value of "one," as it is written: "On that day, the Lord will be one and His name one." And it turns out that according to this, both are true according to the intention of the Torah. But in this time, it is more correct according to Rashi, because of the reasons we have said. Therefore, the Baraita said "Hear" "And it shall be" – "Hear" on the left, because now it is interpreted first "Hear" and then "And it shall be if you diligently obey." And in the future to come, it will be interpreted "Hear" "And it shall be if you diligently obey" on the left, meaning: on the left will be "Hear" and then "And it shall be if you diligently obey." And that is that "Hear" will be at the end and the Tetragrammatons in the middle.

According to ancient tradition, it is customary to write seven lines in each section of the arm tefillin, and four lines in the head tefillin. If one deviates from this, it does not invalidate the tefillin, since this is not explicitly stated in the Talmud. Additionally, the reason for this custom has not been revealed to us, and therefore it is not essential. Nevertheless, a scribe who does not follow this custom is not considered praiseworthy and should be checked. (In my humble opinion, the reason seems to be: The arm tefillin is opposite the heart, and the heart is under the influence of time, containing both good and bad, and time is encompassed in seven days. The head tefillin is opposite the brain, which is entirely holy, and the four lines correspond to the letters of the Divine Name. For further exploration of this, see the Zohar, Pinchas 257a: "The sixth commandment...", see there. Investigate, and you will find it easy.)

There are those who have written that our scribes are meticulous about the number of lines and not the beginnings of the lines. They do not extend or shorten the letters because of the beginnings of the lines. However, they can extend the letters slightly on the second line to align the ends of the lines. They only prohibited extending them in such a way that it is visibly apparent that they are larger than the other letters, making the writing appear spotted, as I wrote in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 273 and Even Ha'Ezer (the Gra"z). The expert scribes of our region do not extend or shorten the letters. They align the beginnings of the lines, for certainly we must be cautious in all that the ancients commanded us, to whom the secrets of wisdom were revealed.

The scribe must be exceedingly meticulous in writing the letters so that none of them changes form and appears as if it is not a letter at all, such as if the yuds in the aleph completely stick together in all their thickness, and similar issues. Also, it must not resemble another letter, for example, the heh—if there is not a noticeable space in its left leg, it will appear like a chet, and conversely, with a chet, if it is not completely joined, it will appear like a heh. And all similar cases. Even the holy Tannaim warned each other when one was a scribe to be careful. As we say in Eruvin (13a), Rabbi Yishmael warned Rabbi Meir, who was a scribe, and said to him: "Be careful, my son, because your work is heavenly work." See there. And how much more so for us, who are like ants compared to them, we must be careful. The careful scribe—his reward is endless, and conversely, his punishment is endless. (It is prohibited to make a letter with a break in the middle, like "<>").

Each letter must be one complete entity, except for the letters "hei" (ה) and "kuf" (ק). Therefore, care must be taken with the dot on the "aleph" (א), that it should be similar to a "yud" (י), and with the dot beneath it. The "yud" on it should be upright, as it is stated in "Otios deRabbi Akiva": Why is the "yud" of the "aleph" upright on its side? Because it testifies and looks towards the Holy One, Blessed be He, that He is true (Hagahot Maimoniyot, Chapter 1). One must ensure that the "yud"s touch the "aleph" with thin lines, and similarly with the "yud"s on the "shin" (ש) and the "ayin" (ע) and the back of the "tzadi" (צ), that they touch the letter. If one of them does not touch, it is invalid. In this case, the reading of a child does not help, as I have written in Siman 32. One must complete the letter entirely before starting another, for otherwise, it is considered "not in order" (Taz, Section 1). However, the small protrusions on the letters do not prevent it from being considered "in order" (ibid.), as long as the entire letter is complete. Similarly, with other letters, one must ensure that each letter is a complete entity, except for "hei" and "kuf" where the leg should not touch the roof. If it does touch, it is invalid. Some permit it, but this is not the primary view. This is also the practical ruling. There must be a clear separation in the "hei" and "kuf," such that an average person can recognize it when standing by the Torah scroll (Magen Avraham, Section 1).

It is necessary to place crowns (tagin) on the letters שעטנ"ז ג"ץ. Scribes have the custom to place crowns on other letters as well. If one did not place crowns even on שעטנ"ז ג"ץ, it does not invalidate [the writing]. The crowns need to touch the body of the letters, and each crown should be separate from the other. There are those who invalidate [the writing] if the letters שעטנ"ז ג"ץ are not crowned, but this is not the primary opinion, as I have written in Siman 32. However, they should be corrected. (See Magen Avraham, subparagraph 3, who wrote that if the crowns do not touch the body of the letter or if they touch each other, it is invalid. See there. This is surprising, as it should not invalidate at all, as I have written. This requires further investigation.)

And our master, the Rema, wrote in section 1 that ideally one should write in a clear script, as explained in the Tur and other decisors. This is known among the scribes. Nevertheless, if one changed the form of the script, it is not invalid. Thus are his words. The explanation of his words: He refers to "clear script" as the manner in which we write in Torah scrolls, tefillin, and mezuzot. If one changed to another script, such as the Veilish script, it is valid. However, certainly in any script we require "clear script," and this is essential even after the fact. As it is stated in Menachot (34a) and Shabbat (103b) that "clear script" is defined as having the form of a letter, not resembling another, and being a single entity, except for the letters He and Kuf, as I have written. And it is obvious that this requirement is essential even after the fact, as I have written.

Regarding the form of the letters – our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, did not mention it at all, because it is known to the scribes. But the Tur and the Beit Yosef in his great book explained them, and therefore we will also explain a little. However, first, we need to explain what is taught in Shabbat there: "And you shall write them" – that the writing should be perfect, that one should not write an Aleph as an Ayin..., a Mem as a Samech, a Vav as a Yud..., see there. And one needs to understand: that it makes sense for a Mem and a Samech as they resemble each other, except that the Samech has rounded corners and the Mem has pointed ones. Similarly, a Vav and a Yud which have the same form, except that the Vav is long and the Yud is short. But an Aleph and an Ayin – do they have any resemblance to each other? And even if it is because they are similar in their pronunciation as Rashi explains, see there – in any case, why is a verse needed for this? They are completely different letters.

And I found in the Hagahot Maimoniot, the first chapter, it is written as follows: One should not make Alephs look like Ayins, one should not make a real indent on the right side like an Ayin on the left side. Thus far his words, and this is similar to what we explained in Siman 32, Se'if 12: for example, if one extends the upper Yud of the Aleph all the way down, and the lower Yud all the way up, it resembles an Ayin, see there. Therefore, even if it is truly an Aleph but it appears like an Ayin, it is invalid, for this is not "complete writing." According to this, I say that the difference between a Bet and a Kaf K'fufa is that the Bet's corners are squared and the Kaf's are rounded, and the squaring and rounding are on both their upper and lower sides. If the Bet is squared on top and rounded on the bottom or vice versa, and similarly the Kaf in such a manner, they are invalid, because if on one side it resembles another letter, it is not "complete writing." Perhaps even the reading of a child will not help in this case, because we see that its form is incorrect on one side, and it is not intact. "Complete writing" seems to be essential even post facto, as proven in Menachot (34a), and similarly implied in Shabbat there, for it is listed there with several things that are certainly essential post facto, see there. However, if we are unsure whether the corners are rounded or squared, that they are neither rounded nor squared, we should ask a child who is neither clever nor foolish (so it seems in my humble opinion). And see what I wrote in Se'if 15.

Alef: The upper point should be like a small yud with a small thorn on it, and its face with the thorn should be turned upwards. The leg of the yud should be attached to the middle of the roof of the body, and the end of the roof should be slightly bent upwards behind it. The lower point should be at a distance from the head of the body equivalent to the thickness of a quill and a half. The lower point should have a small thorn on its bottom right side. The left thorn of the upper point should be aligned with the right thorn of the lower point (Beit Yosef in the name of Baruch She'amar). Some have written, according to the teachings of the Ari, that in tefillin the lower yuds of the alefs should be like a small inverted dalet (the Gra. And see there where it is written sometimes: its form is like an inverted dalet, and similarly in tefillin... It seems that sometimes this is also the case in a Torah scroll, but it does not clarify for us when its form should be like this. This requires further examination).

The letter "Beit" should be squared at the top and bottom. It should have a sharp thorn on the top right side, leaning towards the letter "Aleph," and a thick heel at the bottom, and a small stick on the top left side of its face (Beit Yosef). The length and width of the "Beit" should be about three quills, and the width of its hollow should be the thickness of a quill (Rema in Darkei Moshe). The measure of a quill is the width of the line that comes out of the quill when writing. See what I wrote in Section 6.

The letter Gimel should look like the letter Zayin: its head is thick, and its right leg extends slightly lower than the left thigh. The thigh should be thick and somewhat slanted and a bit low, with three crowns on its head (Beit Yosef in the name of Baruch She'amar). Care should be taken that the left thigh extends forward and not downward (Darkei Moshe in the name of Hagahot Maimoniyot). The explanation is as follows: the head and body resemble a Zayin, meaning that the long line of the Gimel does not start at the edge of the thick head to the right like a Vav, but in the middle like a Zayin. The "left thigh" refers to the lower part which is distant from the line and connected by a thin stem. This is what it means when it says the line goes down slightly from the thigh. It is called "left" because it is on the left side of the line. This thigh should be thick and extend forward in width. It is wider than the thick upper head and somewhat slanted and somewhat low. The Ari Zal disagreed that it should resemble a Zayin, but rather that the line should start at its right edge like a Vav (HaGra Zal).

The dalet's roof is long and its leg is short, so it does not resemble a final kaf. Ideally, one should make sure that the leg is straight but slanted slightly to the right, and that there is a small crown on the left side of its roof. The main caution is with the crown at the back of the dalet, to square it off, so it has an angle and does not appear like a reish. Some say that it is not enough for it to have a sharp angle, but it should have a proper heel. Meaning: the leg should not start at the edge of the roof, but a point of the roof should remain behind the leg, thus making it considerably different from a reish. At the edge of the roof on the right side, there should also be a small thorn. It appears that this is not critical after the fact.

The "hei" should have the roof and the right leg like a "dalet," with only a point resembling a suspended "yud" on its left side. This point should be quite distant from the roof so that someone standing near the Torah scroll can recognize it as a "hei." It should not be aligned with the middle of the roof but rather at its end on the left. The point should be thin at the top and slightly thicker at the bottom, curved downward to the right like a "yud," because the shape of the "hei" is composed of a "dalet" and a "yud." If the "yud" is placed in the middle of the roof, it is invalid (according to the Gra"Z). However, there is an opinion that validates it (Magen Avraham, Siman 32, end of Subsection 33). In my humble opinion, the first view seems correct. Similarly, if the "yud" touches the roof even slightly, it is invalid. Scratching it out does not help, as it would be considered "erasing from within." Instead, the "yud" should be completely removed. We have already explained this in Siman 32.

The top of the letter "vav" should be short so that it does not resemble the letter "reish," and its leg should be long so that it does not resemble the letter "yud." It is preferable that it be rounded on the right side so that it does not resemble the letter "zayin." Although the "zayin" has another distinguishing mark, namely that the leg is in the middle of the head, nevertheless, care should be taken that it does not resemble the "zayin." The leg should be straight without any curvature. The thickness of the leg should gradually diminish until it becomes sharp at the bottom. According to the kabbalistic tradition of the Ari, tefillin should have a small thorn on the left side of the head of each "vav." This is only for tefillin and not for a Torah scroll or mezuzah. The "zayin" should have a square head, and its leg should be in the middle of its head, such that the head extends on both sides so it does not resemble the "vav." It should not be made too long so that it does not resemble a final "nun." There should be three crowns on its head.

Chet: According to Rashi, the chet resembles the chet found in print, but at the top left side, it has a small stroke. According to Rabbeinu Tam, it consists of two zayins with crowns on them. The custom follows Rabbeinu Tam. Additionally, a small crown should be placed on the top of the left leg. The right leg should have a rounded head towards the right initially. The two legs should resemble zayins. According to the Kabbalistic tradition of the Ari, in tefillin, the right leg should resemble a vav, and the line of the crowns on the right leg should be thick, while the one on the left leg should be thin. If the chet is made according to Rashi, it is still kosher, as any letter that has the form of a chet is kosher after the fact. This applies to all letters.

The right side of the letter Tet should be slightly longer, and its head should be slightly inclined. The top should be round and not evenly straight. The left leg should extend downward, and the head on the left side should resemble a Zayin. The leg should extend evenly downward, and at the top left, there should be three tagin (crowns). According to the Ari, the left head resembles a Vav (as noted by the Gra). The Yod should ideally have a small tag (crown) on top. Its head should be bent downwards on the left side, resembling a small downward extension. This should be very short so as not to resemble a small Chet. The right leg should ideally be slightly bent to enhance its form. The leg should not be too large so as not to resemble a Resh, and it should be short and not long so as not to resemble a Vav. If the right leg is missing, it is invalid, and fixing it is not allowed because it would be considered "out of order." However, if the left extension is missing, it can be fixed, as this issue does not fall under "out of order," as I have written in Siman 32.

A bent "kaf" should be round on all sides, and it should not have any angles. Its top and bottom should be equal. Some have written that the primary part that should be round is the bottom, but the top is also valid if it has an angle (see Beit Yosef, section 40, and Shulchan Aruch HaRav). In my humble opinion, this requires further investigation, as I wrote in section 6; see there. An extended "kaf" has a short roof and a long leg. When bent, it should be round. The length should be such that if it is bent, it would be a bent "kaf." Therefore, the length is twice the size of the roof. Some say that if it has an angle at the top, it is invalid (Shulchan Aruch HaRav). Others permit it (Magen Avraham, section 32, sub-section 26, in the name of Galanti). This also appears to be the main opinion in my humble view.

According to some, the letter "Mem" is composed of a bent "Kaf" with a "Vav." Therefore, its neck must be long like a "Vav," its head round on the right side, and on the left side, an angle at its head like the head of a "Vav." Its tail should be thick and curved forward, and rounded behind like a "Kaf." However, the place where its body and neck connect should have an angle between the end of the "Vav," which descends thinly like a "Vav," and the "Kaf." All this is ideally. According to Kabbalah, it should have two crowns on the head of its neck, the right one large and the left one small (according to the GR"A). There is a disagreement about whether the lower line of the "Kaf" should be level with the upper line. Some say it should be level (according to the Radbaz), and some say it should not be level (Kohelet Yaakov in the name of the GR"A). The scribes' custom is to shorten it from the upper line and extend it to the middle of the upper line.

An open "Mem," some say it is like a "Nun" with a "Vav" (Taz, Siman 32, Se'if Katan 17). This also appears to be the opinion of Rabbeinu Beit Yosef there in Se'if 18, and we have written similarly there in Se'if 39 (as well as the Pri Megadim). This is like the "Mem" found in print, and I believe this is also the case in Vellish script. However, in this Siman, Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote in his major work that the "Mem" is like a "Kaf" and "Vav," meaning it is made like a "Kaf" and connected to a "Vav," with the "Vav" extending evenly. If it were a "Nun" and "Vav," the "Vav" would necessarily extend diagonally somewhat, as is understood. Both forms are valid. However, most of the great authorities have agreed that ideally, it should be written like a "Kaf" and "Vav," and such is the common practice, and it should not be changed.

And know that the open Mem and the closed Mem need to be equal, as much as they can be equal. For both are Mems, except that one is open and the other is closed. Therefore, one should not make an open Mem rounded on the top and bottom on the right side like a Kaf, because if one does so with the closed Mem, there is a concern that it will resemble a Samekh. Rather, ideally, one should make a corner on the bottom right side. However, on the top, some make it rounded initially, so that it somewhat resembles a bent Kaf with a Vav. Therefore, the roof should not be made rounded; rather, it should be extended until it reaches the bottom edge like a Kaf. The nose should reach opposite the bottom seat, and it should be connected from above with a fine thorn. The shape of the closed Mem is also as follows: a Kaf and a Vav, except that the Vav closes it (according to the Gra, Rabbi Zalman). One should make it rounded on the top right side initially, but not on the bottom, so that it does not resemble a Samekh (according to the same source). And there are those who say that it is better if it is squared on all sides (Pri Megadim).

A bent Nun should have its head like a Zayin. The head should be short, and its lower part should extend slightly to the left more than the upper part, so that it does not resemble a Bet. The bottom head should be rounded. If it is made in the shape of a Vav, meaning that the line is extended from its end, it is valid post facto, as it is not mistaken for a Vav due to the bottom head. Three tagin (crowns) should be made on it. 

A straight Nun also has its head like a Zayin and is longer than a Zayin. Its length should be such that if it were bent, it would become a bent Nun. In this case, if it is made like a Vav, it is certainly invalid, as it appears like a long Vav. Vavs are commonly long, so there is a possibility of confusion with a Vav. This is not the case with a Zayin, as long Zayins are not written. It requires investigation if correction helps, due to the concern of "not in their order." It seems to me that one should ask a child: if the child says it is a Vav, correction does not help; if the child says it is a Nun, correction helps. Three tagin should be made on it.

The letter Samech should have its roof extended above, and its base should be short. The top should be rounded on the right side, and the bottom should be rounded on both sides, right and left. It should be completely closed. Thus, it is rounded on three sides, except for the upper left side which is not rounded, and there the roof should slightly extend beyond the closure initially. 

The letter Ayin should have the right head shaped like a Yud, with its face slightly upward, as all the Yuds on the right side of Ayin, Tzadi, and Shin face upward. Therefore, crowns are not placed on them, only on their left side. Then, the body is extended slightly upright, not completely curved like a printed Ayin. The left head is like a Zayin standing, connecting to the body. According to the Kabbalistic tradition of the Ari, the two lines of the Ayin in the Tefillin should be like two straight Vavs (according to the Gra), and it should have three crowns.

A bent Pe (פ"א כפופה) on the right side: From the inside, it should have an angle at the top and bottom, and from the outside at the bottom, it should be rounded. All the bends are rounded at the bottom from the outside. However, on the top from the outside, the author of "Baruch She'amar" wrote that it should be rounded like the bottom, but our master the Beit Yosef brought in the name of Rabbi Yehuda HaChassid that at the top it should have an angle from the outside like from the inside. In the whiteness inside, it should have the form of a Bet (ב), and it should be wide enough, a quill and a half, to hang the dot inside it, so it does not touch the body. And it should have a thorn on its face to the left side initially, descending down to the dot inside it. The dot and the extension of its thorn should be in the form of a Vav (ו) when the Pe is reversed. An open Pe (פ"א פשוטה): Some say it should initially be rounded at the top on the right side, but the Chassid's tradition is to make it squared at the top. It should be long enough to form a bent Pe if it is bent. Its dot and thorn are like those in the bent Pe. One should be careful that the dot does not extend outwards, so it does not resemble a Tav (ת).

The right head of the bent Tzaddi should be slightly bent upwards, as I wrote regarding the Ayin; see there. Its leg should be attached to the middle of its neck and not below, so that it does not resemble an Ayin. The left head should be like a Zayin, and its neck somewhat long. Its base should be well extended to the left, and its form should be like a bent Nun with a Yud upon it. Ideally, it should be rounded at the bottom on the right side, like all the bent letters, as I wrote. According to the Kabbalah of the Ari, all the Tzaddis in Tefillin should have the right head like an inverted Yud, and its left side like a bent Nun (there). It has three crowns. The straight Tzaddi should have its head like the bent one, and its leg should extend downward from the connection of the heads to each other. Its proper measure is such that when it is bent, it forms a bent Tzaddi.

The kuf should have its roof even. Its back leg should be well curved. It should have a small tag on its roof on the left side, and there should be a leg hanging that does not touch the body. If it touches, it is invalid, similar to the letter heh. However, it should not be distanced from the roof more than the thickness of a quill. The leg should be somewhat thick at the top and gradually become thinner. The reish should be completely rounded at the back, so it does not resemble the dalet. Its leg should be short so it does not resemble the final kaf.

The right and middle heads of the letter "Shin" should be like a "Yud" facing upwards, as I have written about the "Ayin," see there. The third head on the left should be like a "Zayin." According to the tradition of the AriZal, all the "Shins" in the tefillin should have three lines like three straight "Vavs" (ibid). It is necessary to attach the middle head to the left side below. Its base below should not be wide but sharp towards the left, so that all the heads stand on one leg like the "Kuf" and the "Resh." There should be three crowns on its head, and the heads should not touch each other. It has already been explained that all the crowns are on the left leg, and the "Tav" according to the tradition from the early authorities should have its roof with the right leg like a "Dalet." The left leg, some make it like an inverted "Vav," and some make it like a small inverted "Dalet." This is the custom of the scribes, as this form is from the Rokeach (see Beit Yosef). The form of the inverted "Vav" is from the book of forms. Therefore, in places where this form is customary, one should not protest. The left leg should touch above, and the right leg should not be very long so that it does not resemble a final "Pe." One should make the protrusion on the left leg below towards the outside, and be careful that the roof does not protrude beyond the protrusion of the leg. Thus, we have explained all the letters of the alphabet. Some aspects are critical post facto, and some are not. The general rule is: if the letter retains its form and does not resemble another letter, it is kosher as explained several times.

It is necessary to put crowns on the letters שעטנ"ז ג"ץ. However, if one did not put the crowns, it does not invalidate [the writing]. There are those who invalidate it (Bach). One should be careful to correct them, as this does not fall under the prohibition of "out of order." The crowns should be very small like the letter zayin. There should be three crowns on top of the left head, as I have written. The Rambam rules it valid even if the crowns were not made. There are other crowns that scribes customarily add to tefillin based on the tradition of the ancients, and it is proper to be careful about this. Certainly, if one did not make these crowns, it does not invalidate [the writing]. The Rambam in the second chapter lists the letters that require crowns in the four portions of tefillin, and they are:

In the first section, there is one letter: the closed Mem of "miyamim," upon which there are three Zayins. In the second section, there are five letters, all of which are Hei, and upon each one, there are four Zayins. These are: the Hei of "venatna," and the Heis of "hikshe Pharaoh": the first Hei and the last Hei of "hikshe," the Hei of "veyaharog," and the Hei of "yadcha." In the third section of "Shema," there are five letters: the Kuf of "uvkumecha" with three Zayins, the Kuf of "ukshartam" with three Zayins, and the Tet of "totafot," each letter of which has four Zayins. In the fourth section, there are five letters: the Pe of "veasafta" with three Zayins, the Tav of "veasafta" with one Zayin, and the Tet of "totafot," each of which has four Zayins. All the letters with crowns amount to sixteen. If they are not crowned, they are not disqualified. This is in accordance with the Rambam's acceptance. However, in Shimusha Rabba, as brought by the Tur, it is stated and these are his words: "All the alphabet of letters with crowns are found in the tefillin, and these are: Chet, Tzaddi, Vav, Samech, Shin, Lamed, Mem, Ayin, Tet in the section 'Kadesh.' Pe, Resh, Hei, Zayin, Aleph, Chaf, Dalet, Kuf, Chaf, Tet in the section 'Vehaya ki yeviacha.' Shin, Ayin, Tet, Nun, Zayin, Gimmel, Tzaddi in the sections 'Shema' and 'Vehaya im shamoa.'" And this is its explanation: Chet of "chametz" has one crown, Tzaddi has five crowns. Vav and Samech of "hayevusi" each have three crowns (and be careful with the crowns of Vav to make them very fine, and also on the Yodim so that they do not spoil the form of the letters). The Shin of "asher" has two crowns. The Yod of "li" has three crowns. Lamed of "lemaan" has four crowns. The Tav of "torah" has three crowns (it needs examination as to which Tav). The Bet of "yeviacha," the Pe and Resh of "peter" each have three crowns. Hei, Zayin, Mem of "hazechurim" each have three crowns. Aleph, Chaf of "yishalcha" each have four crowns. Dalet of "yad," Kuf of "hikshe," Chet of "leshalachno," Chaf of "yadcha" each have three crowns. Tet of "totafot" has five crowns. Shin, Ayin, Tet, Nun, Zayin, Gimmel, Tzaddi, Shin with three crowns. Shin, Ayin of "shema," Tet of "totafot," Nun of "nafshecha," Zayin of "mezuzot," Gimmel of "degancha," Tzaddi of "haaretz" each have three crowns. Thus far are his words. The Tur wrote that he should not have mentioned the acronym Shatnez Gatz; see there. In truth, he mentioned them only to complete the alphabet.

The mitzvah of tefillin is great, for anyone who dons them will have a prolonged life, as it is stated: "Hashem upon them shall live" (Menachot 44a) – those who carry the name of Hashem upon them, which are the tefillin, shall live (Rashi). And it is stated in the Shimusha Rabba that anyone who puts on tefillin, wraps in tzitzit, recites the Shema, and prays – it is assured that he is destined for the World to Come. The fire of Gehinnom does not control him, and his sins are forgiven (Tur). And in Berachot (15a), it is said: Anyone who relieves himself, washes his hands, dons tefillin, recites the Shema, and prays – it is as if he built an altar and offered a sacrifice upon it, see there. And anyone who does not don tefillin transgresses eight positive commandments (Menachot there). For in the four sections of the tefillin, both hand and head tefillin are written, and each one is a separate positive commandment. And anyone who does not don tefillin is called "a transgressor of Israel with his body" (Rosh Hashanah 16a). Therefore, every Jewish man must be careful with this great mitzvah. He should seek a God-fearing scribe, and beautiful and meticulous tefillin. And he should remember that tefillin are not bought every day or every year, but for many years. So why would he skimp on a small amount of money for such a great mitzvah that lasts for many years?

And there is someone who divides this sin into three categories. First, someone who does not put them on because they are contemptible to him is considered a "willful transgressor of Israel with their body," and about them it is said in Rosh Hashanah (17a): they are judged for generations in Gehinnom. Second, someone who does not put them on because he does not want to interrupt his work is also considered a "willful transgressor of Israel with their body," and is judged in Gehinnom for twelve months. However, someone who does not put them on because he is concerned that his body is not clean is not included in the category of "willful transgressor of Israel." But still, he has a sin in his hand, as every person can take care for a brief time during the recitation of the Shema and prayer. So wrote the Rosh, of blessed memory (Bach).

The Tur and Shulchan Aruch wrote: "The commandment is to wear them all day. However, because they require a clean body, so that one will not pass gas or become distracted from them, and not everyone can be careful with them, the practice developed not to wear them all day. Every person must be careful to wear them during the recitation of the Shema and the prayer. This is their language, meaning: Certainly, the obligation of the commandment from the Torah is fulfilled by wearing them for one hour a day, during the recitation of the Shema and the prayer. Only if one did not wear them at all, even once a day, has he nullified a positive commandment. But there is no obligation to wear them all day. However, since it is a great mitzvah, one of the greatest, as it includes the unification of God, His fear and love, blessed be He, and the acceptance of the yoke of the commandments, it is proper to wear them all day. Our Sages of the Mishnah and Gemara, and the Rabbanan Savoraim and Geonim, practiced this. And thus our Rabbis say that nowadays this is not practiced. Some imply that if one wants to wear them all day now, trusting that he will not pass gas or become distracted, nevertheless, he should not wear them all day (see Magen Avraham, small section 2). In my humble opinion, this does not seem correct. We have also heard that there are unique individuals, especially in previous generations, who wore them all day. Now, certain individuals also practice learning a little while wearing them after the prayer (see there in Magen Avraham, who cites the responsa of the Rama of Pano, who instituted wearing them again at Mincha. Fortunate is their lot)."

A minor who knows how to guard the tefillin in purity, so that he will neither pass gas in them nor sleep in them, and will not enter a bathroom with them – his father is obligated to buy him tefillin to educate him. But before this stage, it is prohibited to give him tefillin. And some say that this minor is specifically when he is thirteen years and one day old. And this is the custom and should not be changed (Rema), and before this time, they do not put on tefillin. Nowadays, the custom is to begin two or three months before the time (Magen Avraham, subsection 4). And now they start one month before. And there are those who do not start at all before. Many have rejected the opinion of "some say," arguing that if he is thirteen years and one day old – it is obvious, since he is obligated in all the commandments. Also, the obligation is incumbent upon him (Bach, Eliyah Rabbah, Pri Megadim, and the Gaon Rabbi Akiva Eiger). Some have explained that this applies even if he has not brought forth two hairs (the Gaon Rabbi Akiva Eiger and this also seems to be the opinion in Pri Megadim, see there). In truth, this is the solitary opinion of the Itur, and Rabbeinu the Beit Yosef in his major work rejected this, as is evident from all the primary authorities that the minor in question is actually a young child, see there. In my humble opinion, it seems that according to the fundamental law, this indeed aligns with the opinion of all the primary authorities. However, this was in the time of the Talmud when they were meticulous and diligent, but nowadays, it is not customary to act this way. Therefore, it is written that this is the custom and should not be changed, meaning: nowadays, it is impossible to rely on any minor before he is thirteen years old, and we hope they will be careful with the sanctity of tefillin when they are thirteen. Note that it is commonly said among the masses that an orphan should start a year earlier to put on tefillin. I do not know any reason for this, and it is not proper to practice this for the reasons we have explained. As for a deaf-mute or a fool – certainly, they should not be given tefillin, as they will undoubtedly not be careful with their sanctity.

The Tur and the Shulchan Aruch wrote: One who has bowel illness is exempt from tefillin. Similarly, the Rambam wrote in the fourth chapter: Those with bowel illness, and anyone who cannot control their bodily functions without distress, are exempt from tefillin. See there. This law is explicitly stated in Chullin (101a) regarding one who was brought before Rabbi Chanina. He saw that the person was not wearing tefillin. He asked him: Why are you not wearing tefillin? He replied: I have bowel illness. And Rav Yehuda said: One who has bowel illness is exempt from tefillin. And even though in Ketubot (104a) it says regarding Rabbeinu Hakadosh (Rabbi Judah the Prince) that he suffered from this illness and still wore tefillin, it is different for Rabbeinu Hakadosh, who conducted himself with extraordinary sanctity (Tosafot there).

It is certainly clear that for this reason, one cannot completely exempt oneself from wearing tefillin during the recitation of Shema and prayer, as one can be cautious for a short time. (And so wrote the Magen Avraham in subsection 1; see there where he wrote that it is permissible, but seemingly it is obligatory.) And a clear proof for this: In the source of this law in Chullin there, it was not during the recitation of Shema and prayer, for he conversed with him as explained there. But because their custom was to wear tefillin all day, they asked, and he answered that he had an intestinal illness. If so, I have a difficulty with the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, why did they bring this law at all? Since they wrote in the previous section that we do not wear tefillin all day, only during the recitation of Shema and prayer, if so, even without an intestinal illness one is exempt? And one cannot say that with an intestinal illness there is also a prohibition to wear tefillin all day. It is impossible to say so, for they did not write a prohibition but an exemption. Moreover, our holy Rabbi wore them all day, as explained in Ketubot there. And although we do not learn from him, as I wrote, nevertheless, there is no prohibition in this matter for one who wishes to act with extra sanctity. Furthermore, I have a difficulty with the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, for if so, why did they leave the matter ambiguous? They should have explained that an intestinal illness exempts one from tefillin all day, except during the recitation of Shema and prayer. Regarding the Rambam, it is not difficult since his style is to write in the language of the Talmud, and he also did not mention the law in the previous section. But the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, who wrote the previous law – they should have explained.

And furthermore, I am puzzled: Behold, our master the Beit Yosef in his great book brought what the Mordechai wrote, that a sick person is exempt from tefillin. And he raised a difficulty: If so, why did Rav Yehuda say in Chullin that one with intestinal illness is exempt? For any sick person is exempt. And he answered: That any sick person is exempt only when he is in distress, and one with intestinal illness is exempt even when he is not in distress. See there. And based on this, our master the Rema wrote in section 1 regarding this that one with intestinal illness is exempt, and these are his words: "Even if he has no distress. But any other sick person, if he is in distress due to his illness and his mind is not settled upon him – he is exempt. And if not – he is obligated." Until here are his words. And I do not understand at all: What is the relevance of a sick person to illness, for certainly a sick person confined to bed is obviously exempt also during the time of recitation of the Shema and prayer. And this is explicitly proven in the Jerusalem Talmud Berachot (Chapter 2, Halacha 3) where it says: Rabbi Yannai would wear them three days after his illness. See there. And until that time, he would not put them on at all. And now if one with intestinal illness is obligated during the time of recitation of the Shema and prayer? What is the relevance of this, and what was the difficulty and what was the answer? This requires further investigation.

Therefore, it seems to me that our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, hold that one who has intestinal illness is completely exempt, even at the time of reading the Shema and praying. They derived this from the language of the Gemara, which states simply that one with an intestinal illness is exempt from tefillin. The reason is that since he is prone to flatulence and diarrhea, it is considered as distress which he cannot remove from himself, and thus he is exempt from tefillin, as will be explained. The term "prohibition" could not be used because of the story of our holy teacher (Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi). Therefore, the Mordechai's difficulty was justified, as it was obvious that it does not refer to someone severely ill and bedridden, who has no strength or awareness, for in such a case, the concepts of obligation and exemption do not apply. Rather, it refers to a sick person who, if he wishes to strengthen himself, can put on tefillin, yet he is still exempt as explained in the Jerusalem Talmud. And therefore, they correctly questioned the case of one with an intestinal illness, and they explained that one with an intestinal illness is exempt even if he is not distressed. Meaning: even if he does not suffer from the act of putting them on, because this illness exempts him due to cleanliness concerns. But for other illnesses, it is obvious that if he does not suffer from putting them on, why should he exempt himself? He is only exempt when he suffers from putting them on due to his weakness, and his mind is not settled because of this, then he is exempt. (Therefore, one with an intestinal illness is completely exempt, unlike the later authorities who did not write this. Examine and you will find it easy.)

Nevertheless, it is impossible to give a general rule in this matter, as it depends on the individual's digestive condition and his natural constitution, whether strong or weak. It seems to me that this is what our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 2: that someone who is certain that he cannot pray without passing gas—it is better that he miss the time for prayer than to pray without a clean body. And if it appears to him that he can maintain a clean body during the recitation of the Shema—he should put on tefillin between "Ahava" and the recitation of the Shema and make the blessing. This is his language. This pertains to digestive illness, and therefore it depends on his condition and nature. However, after the prayer, he certainly should not put them on, even if he estimates that he will not pass gas, for why should he put himself into a doubtful situation? (And this is also implied by the Magen Avraham in subsection 1, who wrote that it is forbidden to be stringent with oneself, see there. And he further wrote: that if one estimates that he cannot hold himself back from passing gas except to the extent that he can remove the head tefillin, nevertheless he should put on both, see there. Because the main concern is with the head tefillin, see there.)

Women and slaves are exempt from the obligation of tefillin because it is a positive commandment that is time-bound, as tefillin are not worn on Shabbat and Yom Tov. If they wish to be stringent upon themselves and wear tefillin, they are prevented from doing so. This is not similar to the exemptions from sukkah and lulav, where women are exempt but may still recite the blessings upon them, because tefillin require extra care to maintain bodily cleanliness, as it is stated in Shabbat (49a): "Tefillin require a clean body like Elisha the Winged." And in the Jerusalem Talmud, Berachot, it is said: "There they say, anyone who is not like Elisha the Winged should not wear tefillin." However, men who are obligated must take care during the recitation of the Shema and prayer. Therefore, tefillin are not worn all day, as I wrote in the previous section. Since women are exempt, why should they assume such a significant concern? For them, the time of the Shema and prayer is like all day for men, therefore, they are not allowed to wear tefillin. And even though it is taught in Eruvin (96a) that Michal, the daughter of Saul, wore tefillin and the Sages did not protest, one cannot derive from this, as it is presumed they knew she was entirely righteous and knew how to be careful. Similarly, this applies to slaves in such a manner. (See Magen Avraham, small section 3, and Beit Yosef. According to what I have written, this is understandable.)

One who puts on tefillin must be careful not to have lustful thoughts about a woman. If he cannot avoid such thoughts, it is better for him not to put them on. This is the ruling of our Rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, in section 4. And even though in Sukkah (26b) it seems that there is no prohibition based solely on thoughts, this applies in cases of doubt. But when one is certain to have such thoughts, it is forbidden (Magen Avraham, subsection 4). However, from Rashi there, it explicitly implies that there is no prohibition due to thoughts alone (see there in the comment starting with "customarily" and in the comment starting with "perhaps," scrutinize and you will find it easy to understand). Some have cited from the Jerusalem Talmud that it says one must have a clean body and a pure mind (Beit Yosef in the name of Orach Chaim). I did not find this statement in the Jerusalem Talmud. The reason for the prohibition is that it is no less of a distraction than diverting one's mind. Even according to what I wrote in section 28, that diverting one's mind is considered frivolity—there is no greater frivolity than such thoughts. This is also the ruling. And a blind person is obligated to wear tefillin (Beit Yosef in the name of the Rosh, contrary to Sefer Ha'itim, see there).

A mourner on the first day is forbidden to put on tefillin for the entire day, even after the burial, as it is written, "And its end is as a bitter day." Tefillin are called "glory," and they should not be worn on a bitter day, as the first day is the main force of mourning. However, on the second day, one should put them on after sunrise, as I have written in Yoreh De'ah, section 388 (see Magen Avraham, subsection 5). Even if new faces (people) come, he does not remove them once he has put them on. If he has not put them on, he does not put them on while they are sitting with him until they leave (ibid.). And even though he is distressed in his mourning and one who is distressed is exempt, as will be explained, this applies to an involuntary distress. But in this distress, he is obligated to strengthen himself and divert his distress when putting them on (Sukkah 25b). On Tisha B'Av, one is obligated to wear tefillin, as it is an old mourning. However, our custom is not to wear them in the morning, as there is no day more bitter than this. And in the afternoon, when the distress has somewhat subsided, we wear them. This will be explained later in section 555, see there.

A groom and his attendants, and all members of the wedding party, are exempt from wearing tefillin during the time of the feast because intoxication and frivolity are commonly found (Sukkah 25b). This is when the feast extends until the morning. They are also exempt from prayer since they will not be able to concentrate. However, they are obligated to recite the Shema because the primary intention is in the first verse, which they can manage to focus on in a minimal way. This was according to their time. But nowadays, since we generally do not concentrate so well anyway, they are obligated in prayer as well. One should not question how they can recite the Shema and pray without tefillin, as it is not an issue: since they are exempt from tefillin due to intoxication and frivolity, it is similar to Shabbat and Yom Tov (see Magen Avraham, small section 7). Even though with regard to the Shema and prayer, such intoxication does not exempt them, as they are not truly intoxicated but rather very joyous, nevertheless, with regard to tefillin, it is considered frivolity and is forbidden.

And this is according to the law. But our Rabbi, the Rema, already wrote in a responsum (Siman 132) that we customarily interrupt the feast when the time for prayer arrives. We put on tefillin, because since we interrupt to pray, there is no frivolity involved. We recite the Shema and pray as on all other days, and even the groom puts on tefillin and prays. There is an opinion among the early authorities that the exemption given by our sages to the groom, his attendants, and the wedding guests is not due to drunkenness or lack of intention, but because of the principle that "one who is engaged in a mitzvah is exempt from another mitzvah," and the joy of the groom and bride is considered a mitzvah. Therefore, they are exempt from other mitzvot. According to this reasoning, there is no difference between our generations and previous generations, and whoever wishes to rely on this reason may do so. This applies in the summer when sometimes the feast extends several hours into the morning—they can eat and drink, provided that the groom is with them, for if the groom has left them, there is no mitzvah. However, the common custom follows the first opinion. And see what I wrote at the end of Siman 70.

And so our Sages of blessed memory said there that those who write tefillin and mezuzot, while they are engaged in their work, since their intention is not for livelihood but for the sake of the mitzvah, and similarly their merchants and the merchants' merchants, and all who are engaged in sacred work solely for the sake of the mitzvah – are exempt from laying tefillin all day, except during the recitation of the Shema and prayer. According to this, for us, this law does not apply, as in any case, we do not wear tefillin all day as I wrote in the previous section. However, when they are engaged in their work and the time for the recitation of the Shema and prayer arrives – they should not interrupt even if the time will pass, for one engaged in a mitzvah is exempt from a mitzvah. According to this, this law applies even to us. Nevertheless, initially, one should be careful not to start when the time for the recitation of the Shema arrives. But if they have started – they do not interrupt, and certainly not if they started before this time. And our scribes, who do it for livelihood – are obligated to interrupt in every matter.

And know that what we said, that one does not need to interrupt even if the time passes, is because one who is engaged in a mitzvah is exempt from another mitzvah – this applies even if he can finish the writing after he prays, and it turns out that the recitation of the Shema and the prayer is a passing mitzvah and this is not a passing mitzvah. Nevertheless, he does not need to interrupt, for the Torah decreed that anyone engaged in a mitzvah is exempt, at the time of the act, from other mitzvot. Therefore, we hold that one who guards the dead is exempt from the recitation of the Shema, prayer, and tefillin, even though he can fulfill them while guarding (the Gra). Similarly, one who digs a grave for the dead is exempt; even though he may rest a bit between digging, it is to strengthen his powers. And so with all similar cases (there).

However, one is not called "engaged in a mitzvah" with regard to being exempt from other mitzvot except at the time of performing the mitzvah, and not when the mitzvah is already upon him. That is to say: when one lays tefillin, he is called "engaged in a mitzvah." But when he has already laid them, even though the tefillin are on him and he is performing a mitzvah, in any case, he is not called "engaged in a mitzvah." Similarly, when one finds a lost object and attends to it, he is called "engaged in a mitzvah," but when he places it in his house, even though he is performing a mitzvah by guarding it, he is not called "engaged in a mitzvah" to be exempt from another mitzvah. This is not similar to guarding a deceased, for in that case, every moment he is considered to be performing an active deed since he needs to watch it from mice and the like. And it is proper that even in a case of being truly "engaged" and another mitzvah presents itself, and he can perform both without difficulty, "do not refrain from doing good" and he should do both (ibid). It is also possible that according to the law, this is so, that they did not say "one engaged in a mitzvah is exempt from another mitzvah" except when the second mitzvah requires an additional effort beyond the first, but not when one effort suffices for both. This requires further study.

The one who is distressed: even if he is distressed due to the cold, and similarly anyone whose mind is not settled because of bodily pain or toothache, and any similar case where the distress comes on its own and he cannot distract himself from it, unlike distress from business or mourning, where he can exert himself to distract his mind from it, as I wrote in section 8. But such distresses that cannot be distracted from – he is exempt from tefillin, as this is like a distraction and as I wrote in Siman 28. Therefore, if he can settle his mind and put them on, he is obligated to do so. And we have never heard of one exempting himself from tefillin because of this. Furthermore, the essence of this law is not understood: its source is from the Rambam, and he holds that distraction is to be taken literally, and therefore during distress, he indeed distracts his mind. But the Tur and Shulchan Aruch hold that distraction only refers to lightheadedness, and in a distressed state, there is no lightheadedness. However, in Siman 28, section 4, we struggled to reconcile these views by saying that through this, one may come to lightheadedness, see there. But in any case, this is not so clear according to their view, and therefore one should not be lenient in this matter. Further study is needed.

Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote in Section 10: One who reads from the Torah is exempt from putting on tefillin all day, except during the recitation of the Shema and prayer. This is his language, and it is based on the Mekhilta in the portion of "Bo" which states: Anyone engaged in Torah study is exempt from tefillin. See there. And Rabbi Yitzchak explained that this exemption applies to the entire day, not to the recitation of the Shema and prayer (see Beit Yosef). According to this, for us, who in any case do not put on tefillin all day as I wrote in the previous section, he would not have needed to bring this ruling. However, in order to avoid misunderstanding the Mekhilta as providing a complete exemption, he brought it and explained that it applies to the entire day. (And in Or Zarua, Section 594, there was a different version in the Mekhilta, that one puts on tefillin while engaged in Torah study, as it is written: "So that the law of the Lord will be in your mouth." See there.)

One should not remove their tefillin in front of their teacher, as it is disrespectful to uncover one's head in their presence. Rather, one should turn to another side and remove the tefillin not in front of them, as there should be an aura of reverence towards one's teacher. Similarly, one should not remove tefillin in front of a Torah scroll, but should turn to another side. This is our custom. Based on this reasoning, one should also not remove tefillin in front of their father. However, this is not the common practice, and it is not mentioned by the halachic authorities (see Tur and Magen Avraham subparagraph 14). If one needs both tefillin and a mezuzah and cannot afford both, tefillin takes precedence because it is a personal obligation. But if one can borrow tefillin from someone else, then mezuzah takes precedence (Magen Avraham subparagraph 15). A person who is excommunicated or a leper is prohibited from wearing tefillin.

Tefillin written by a slave, or a woman, or a minor even if he has reached the age of education, or even if he has reached the age but has not shown signs of puberty, or a Samaritan, or a habitual transgressor of the entire Torah, or a star-worshiper, or a Sabbath desecrator; or even a transgressor of a single sin, provided he does it defiantly and even if it is a rabbinic commandment; or an informer to a tyrant – all these are invalid. For it is written: "And you shall bind them […] and you shall write them" (Deuteronomy 6:8-9), anyone who is included in binding and believes in it – is included in writing. And anyone who is not included in binding, such as a woman, or a slave, or a minor, or a deaf-mute, or a mentally incompetent person, or does not believe in it as all those we mentioned – is not included in writing. And a minor, as long as it has not been proven that he has grown two hairs – is invalid, even if he has reached the appropriate age. For in matters of Torah law we do not presume that he has shown signs of puberty (Magen Avraham, section 1). And it seems to me that a transgressor only with regard to tefillin, even if not defiantly – is invalid. And even though in the case of slaughtering he is valid – that is when another checks his knife, as I wrote in Yoreh De'ah, siman 2. And if so, in the case of tefillin he is not believed to say that he wrote them according to the law, since it requires effort. And there are those who say that if it is out of desire – he is valid, for he is considered someone who is included in binding, like in slaughtering he is included in slaughtering (Magen Avraham, section 3). And I am astonished: even though he is considered someone who is included in binding, doesn't he refuse to put in the effort? And this is similar to slaughtering when there is no Israelite to check the knife, for it is forbidden to eat from his slaughter. And someone whose left hand is amputated – is valid in writing, for he is considered someone who is included in binding, only he has no hand to bind it on. (there, section 5. And see Taz, section 1 for the reason regarding an informer. Delve and you will find clarity.)

And all these, just as they are invalid for writing the parchments, so too they are invalid for making the compartments and straps and for sewing them. However, for tanning – they are valid. And similarly, if one scraped between one letter and another – we do not worry about this. Similarly, for sewing a Torah scroll, there are those who permit it (there, subsection 6). And see Yoreh De'ah, Siman 278, subsection 11, where we brought someone who prohibits the sewing of women, and we explained there to permit it. According to what we explained there, also for sewing and straps they are valid. And only for the compartments they are invalid, because they have the letter "shin" which is like writing; see there.

A convert (in ancient times) who reverted to his religion out of fear, the Rosh, the Tur, and the Shulchan Aruch ruled that he is fit to write. However, from Tosafot in Gittin (45b) it does not appear so, and similarly, the Rif and the Rambam did not bring this. Therefore, one should not be lenient (there, subsection 7). And tefillin written by a heretic – they should be burned. Some say they should be buried. And if written by a Samaritan – the same law applies. And tefillin found in the possession of a heretic, and it is not known who wrote them – they should be buried. If found in the possession of an idol worshiper – they are kosher, for certainly a Jew wrote them, as they are not skilled in writing. A mamzer (a person born from certain forbidden relationships) – is fit to write tefillin. And see Yoreh De'ah, Siman 281 (see Magen Avraham, subsection 9).

One should not purchase books, tefillin, and mezuzot from non-Jews for more than their worth by a significant amount, due to societal rectification, so that they do not become accustomed to stealing and robbing. However, adding a small amount over their worth is permitted. It is a mitzvah to redeem them from their hands. Tefillin should only be purchased from an expert scribe who is knowledgeable in the matters of missing and extra letters, and proficient in the laws of tefillin. If one bought them from someone who is not an expert, they need to be checked. And if, upon checking, they are found to be written correctly regarding missing and extra letters, we say that the writer was certainly proficient in the other laws as well. It seems to me that if the lines are not aligned properly, as explained in Siman 35, their validity is diminished. They should not be relied upon unless it is confirmed that an expert wrote them, for although this is not a disqualification after the fact, it is still a deficiency.

Our Sages of blessed memory said (Eruvin 97a) that if one purchased many pairs of tefillin from someone who is not known to be an expert, he should check three of them: two arm-tefillin and one head-tefillin, or two head-tefillin and one arm-tefillin. If he finds them to be kosher, all of them are presumed to be kosher, and the rest do not need to be checked. This applies when it is apparent that they were all written by the same scribe, thereby establishing the scribe's reliability. However, if they are in several bundles, indicating that they are from different scribes, he should check three from each bundle: two arm-tefillin and one head-tefillin, or vice versa. A seller who states that the tefillin are "from a reputable person" is trusted, because a single witness is believed in matters of prohibition, and they do not need to be checked, provided that the seller himself is known to be trustworthy.

Tefillin that have been established as kosher do not need to be checked ever. However, if one only puts them on occasionally, they must be checked twice a week, as we are concerned that they may have decayed. The same applies if they have come into contact with water—they need to be checked. But if there is no one available to sew them back together afterward, it is better not to open them for inspection and to leave them as they are without checking. And know that this is the law. However, in our times, it is known that our ink tends to peel off the parchment after several years. Therefore, nowadays, it seems to me that by law, they need to be checked from time to time, and this is how one should conduct oneself.

It is forbidden to hang tefillin, whether the boxes are placed and the straps are hanging, or the straps are placed and the boxes are hanging, as it is a disgrace when they are hanging in the air. This does not include when, during the placement of the head tefillin, one holds the strap and the head tefillin is hanging in the air while placing it on the head, as this is necessary for putting them on. Similarly, during their removal, when the straps are hanging, this is also the typical way of removing them. One should only ensure that the straps do not drag on the ground. Occasionally, when one holds the tefillin and the straps are hanging, this is not an issue since this is their manner. However, to hold the straps and have the tefillin hanging is forbidden even occasionally (see Magen Avraham, subsection 1). It is also forbidden to hang them on a peg, whether the tefillin are placed on the peg and the straps are hanging, or the straps are placed and the tefillin are hanging. As it is said in Berachot (24a): "He who hangs his tefillin – his life will be hung." The interpreters of hints said: "And your life shall hang in doubt before you" – this refers to one who hangs his tefillin. However, if one places them in a pouch and hangs the pouch, this is permitted, as there is no disgrace here. With a Torah scroll, even in such a manner it is forbidden. A Torah scroll must only be placed in an ark or a box (Gemara there). Similarly, it is forbidden to hang prayer books with a silver chain (Magen Avraham, subsection 1). This applies when the chain is attached to the prayer book, but placing it in a pouch and hanging the pouch is permitted, just like with tefillin. The same rule applies to other holy books.

A room that contains tefillin – it is forbidden to engage in marital relations there until they are removed or placed in a double covering. This is only if the second covering is not designated specifically for them, for if it is designated, even a hundred coverings are considered as one. If a garment is spread over them, even if it is not spread underneath them, it is permitted (Shulchan Aruch, Orach Chaim 40:2). A tallit is not considered a "covering." Those who always place a tefillin bag within a tallit bag, the tallit bag is considered as a "covering" and does not suffice. An additional covering is required. If neither of the coverings is designated specifically for them, it is obviously permitted. The same law applies if the inner covering is not designated and the outer covering is designated – it is also permitted. (Regarding what the Magen Avraham wrote there about a mezuzah, I have already explained my humble opinion on the matter of mezuzah in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 286, see there.)

Even to place them (tefillin) in a double vessel is forbidden to place them under one's feet, as this is a great disrespect to the tefillin. Similarly, it is forbidden to place them even at the head of the bed, and even in a double vessel if they are placed directly against his head, because since his head is resting on them, it is considered disrespectful, even if his wife is not with him. Rather, he should place them at the head of the bed but not directly against his head, and then if his wife is not with him, it is permitted even in a single vessel (Taz and Magen Avraham, subsection 3). And if his wife is with him, a double vessel is required. And the pillow at the head of the bed is considered a vessel (ibid.). Know that "with his wife" means when he intends to engage in marital relations. Otherwise, even if she is in bed with him, it is considered "without his wife." And to place them on the bed against his side is forbidden like placing them under his feet, for at his side is also a disrespect to the tefillin. Some have written that placing a tallit on the tefillin is a disrespect to the tefillin (Sha'arei Teshuvah, subsection 4). However, this only applies when placing them in a bag. But when placing the tallit for covering the tefillin or to guard them, it is certainly permitted (ibid.). There is a doubt whether the straps also require a double vessel or not. The practical difference would be if there is a case where there is a bag for the tefillin, and the straps are outside the bag as is customary. Therefore, when covering them with an additional vessel, it counts as a double vessel for the tefillin but not for the straps. It seems that the main stringency is with the tefillin and not with the straps. In any case, practically, one should be careful, but according to the law, this appears correct. (See Taz, subsection 4, who writes that "with his wife" is considered even if he does not intend to engage in marital relations.)

And know that what we have written, that placing [tefillin] under one's head is permitted if not directly under one's head, this is all when they are being protected only in one's bed from mice. But if they are protected elsewhere, it is not proper conduct to place them in one's bed, even under one's head, unless it is in a place three handbreadths higher or three handbreadths lower than one's head (Magen Avraham, small section 4).
