For even sitting on the same level as tefillin on a bench is considered a disgrace, as I have written in Yoreh De'ah, section 282. And when placing the tefillin in a box in the synagogue, and the box is the bench that people sit on, there must also be a space of three handbreadths from the top of the box to the tefillin, and at least a space of one handbreadth. For if not, it is as if one is sitting on the tefillin (Sha'arei Teshuvah, small section 5). And similarly with prayer books and other books in the box, this is required as well. This is the custom and should not be changed.

If one forgot and engaged in marital relations while wearing tefillin, he should not grasp the straps, and certainly not the tefillin themselves, until he washes his hands. This is because hands are generally busy and have surely touched a place that requires washing. When he washes his hands, he should remove the tefillin until he cleans the seminal emission, and afterwards it is permissible to wear them, as one who has had a seminal emission is permitted to wear tefillin (Sukkah 26b). If he slept in tefillin and experienced a seminal emission, he should not grasp the boxes. Rather, he should grasp the straps and remove them until he cleans the seminal emission from himself and washes his hands. 

Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 8: One who enters a fixed meal should remove them and place them on the table until the time of the blessing (Birkat Hamazon), and then put them back on. But for a casual meal, it is not necessary to remove them. Thus far his words, indicating that it is permissible to eat a casual meal while wearing tefillin. This was according to their custom of wearing tefillin all day, but not according to our practice. It seems to me that according to our practice, even a casual meal is not appropriate while wearing tefillin.

We learn in Bava Metzia (102b): It was taught: If one was carrying a load on his head, if the tefillin press down – it is forbidden. If not – it is permitted. Regarding what load did they say this? A load of four kav. Rabbi Chiyya taught: One who carries manure on his head, and has tefillin on his head – should not move them to the side, nor should he tie them in his hand, because he would be treating them disrespectfully. Rather, he should tie them on his arm, in the place of the tefillin. The school of Shila said: Even a cloth of theirs (some say "a cloth of bread") – it is forbidden to place on the head where the tefillin are. How much? Abaye said: A quarter of a quarter of a Pumbedita measure. Thus far is the language of the Gemara.

And it implies that Rav Shela disagrees with the previous opinion. That is, even a light load like a cloth is prohibited. And since Abaye explains his words, we follow this ruling. This is also the opinion of the Rambam in the fourth chapter, where he writes: "One who carries a load on his head must remove the head tefillin until he removes the load. And even a cloth is prohibited to place on a head that has tefillin. But he may wrap his turban over the tefillin." This is the end of his words. In other words, the turban that he always wears on his head is not considered disrespectful if a part of the turban rests on the tefillin, because it is his garment. And this is our custom. Moreover, in this way, the head tefillin are secured in their place and do not move. And our teacher, the Beit Yosef, copied his words into the Shulchan Aruch and concluded: "But something that is customarily placed on the head, such as a hat or a turban, is permitted." This is the end of his words.

However, the Rif and the Rosh also recorded the Baraitot and the words of Rav Shila. The early authorities deduced that they do not disagree at all and divided their statements into different distinctions. There are those who say that the Baraita refers to a case after the fact where one is already carrying the load, or for someone whose livelihood depends on it, in which case the measure is four kavs. And Rav Shila refers to the initial stage, where it is forbidden even to carry a handkerchief, since his livelihood does not depend on it (Beit Yosef in the name of R. Yosef Abuhav). But in any case, carrying dung is forbidden due to disrespect, and this is the Baraita of Rabbi Chiya. Others differentiate that the Baraita refers to a situation where the load is already on his head and he wants to put on tefillin, then less than four kavs is permitted, and only dung is forbidden. And Rav Shila refers to when the tefillin are already on his head and he wants to place a load on them, then even a handkerchief is forbidden (Beit Yosef). And there are those who explain that the Baraita does not refer at all to a load on his head, but the load is slung over his back and tied with a rope on his head, and the rope presses the tefillin when the load is heavy, four kavs (there in the name of R. Yosef Aschkenazi). And it seems more reasonable like the first explanation to differentiate between initial and after the fact (and so wrote the Bach and the Derisha, see there).

But our master, the Rema, wrote in the Shulchan Aruch, and this is his language: "But an item that is customarily placed on the head, such as a hat or turban, is permitted. However, if it is a heavy burden of four kavim, and it presses on the tefillin, one must remove them." Until here is his language. His intention is: that which requires four kavim is referring to an item that is customarily placed on the head. And what prohibits a turban is an item that is not customarily placed on the head. The pressure is evident, for it is not customary to have something of four kavim on the head. There are those who interpret to differentiate between things that press on the tefillin and things that do not press, that if they press on the tefillin, even a cloth is prohibited, and if they do not press, it is permitted up to four kavim (Taz, subsection 1). This is more strained, for how is it applicable for a turban to press? Some have written to differentiate between places where it is customary to carry a burden on the head, where it is then permitted up to four kavim, and places where it is not customary, where even a cloth is prohibited (see Magen Avraham at the beginning of this section). In my humble opinion, it seems that certainly when he is sitting in his house, even a cloth is prohibited, for who compels him to do so? This is the opinion of Rabbi Shela. And the Baraita refers to when he is walking on the road, as the language "carrying a burden on his head" proves. Then it is permitted up to four kavim, but manure is prohibited because of disrespect.

It is forbidden to change the tefillin of the head to make it a tefillin of the hand, because the sanctity of the head tefillin is greater than that of the hand. For in the head tefillin, there is the letter "Shin" on the body of the box, which is not the case with the hand tefillin. Additionally, the name "Shaddai" is mostly present in the head tefillin: the "Shin" and the "Dalet," whereas in the hand tefillin, there is only the "Yud." It is forbidden to change from a higher level of sanctity to a lower level of sanctity. Even to take a strap from the head tefillin and place it on the hand tefillin is forbidden for this reason. However, it is permitted to make the hand tefillin into head tefillin, because we ascend in sanctity. One should then make four compartments, as I have written in Siman 32.

And this is specifically when they have already been worn. But new ones that have not yet been worn - it is permissible to make from those designated for the head (tefillin shel rosh) for the arm (tefillin shel yad), for it is established that "designation is not a significant act." And how should one do this? Cover them with one leather cover so that they appear as one unit, as I have written there. Similarly, if one inserts a new strap into an old head tefillin, and the strap has not yet been worn - it is permissible to remove it and place it in the arm tefillin. Also, if one initially stipulated that they could change them - it is permitted to change them, even from the head tefillin to the arm tefillin. Such a stipulation is effective for everything, such as parchment intended for a Torah scroll, tefillin, or mezuzot; if one stipulates on them, they can be used for mundane matters, like writing divorce documents or the like. All of this is when it is explicitly stated. But in an unstated case, it is not considered a stipulation (Taz, subsection 1). Nevertheless, if it appears from the context that this was his intention, it is considered as if he explicitly stipulated (ibid.). Indeed, it is not necessary to verbally declare the condition, and it suffices if one has this intention in mind. Therefore, the custom among scribes to use some of the parchment for secular purposes is considered as if they stipulated (ibid.).

There are those who are uncertain whether, when the strap near the knot breaks, it is permissible to reverse it and use the other end to make the knot, with the place of the knot being below in the windings on the hand and the finger (Magen Avraham, subsection 3). And there are those who permit it (Eliyah Rabbah). In my humble opinion, it seems that the main place of the knot — the dalet and the yud — certainly should not be changed. This is an a fortiori argument from the tefillin of the head, which should not be made for the hand because of the shin in it. All the more so, the actual letter of the name should not be changed into a plain strap. However, aside from the place of the knot, it seems to me that there is no concern whether it is above or below, since it is all one holiness. There is no above or below in this matter, as it all wraps around the hand or hangs from the head tefillin. What difference does it make if it is close to the box or not? (It is not similar to the boards of the Tabernacle mentioned by Magen Avraham in subsection 3, where one side is near the ground and it is not respectful compared to the upper side, which is not the case here. It seems to me that Magen Avraham's main doubt is only about the place of the knot. See there and in Sha'arei Teshuvah. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

The Rambam wrote in Chapter 4, Halacha 9: A vessel that was designated to place tefillin in it, and tefillin were placed in it – it becomes sanctified, and it is forbidden to use it for mundane purposes. If it was designated but tefillin were not placed in it, or if tefillin were placed in it temporarily and it was not designated – it does not become sanctified and it remains mundane as it was. This is his exact wording. And it seems to me from the precision of his wording that only with temporary placement does it not become sanctified without designation, but with permanent placement – it becomes sanctified even without designation, because permanent usage itself serves as designation. And the Gemara (Berachot 23b) explains that which it says that if he placed tefillin in it without designating it – it is not sanctified, but this is only with temporary placement. And there is a doubt to what extent "temporary" is considered. And it seems to me that three days is considered "permanent." And it seems to me that if he stated at the time of usage that he is not doing so permanently, even if he used it for many days it does not become sanctified, for a condition is effective as I have written. And this is like a condition that does not sanctify it completely.

Our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 3: "A scarf that was designated forever to wrap tefillin in it, and he wrapped tefillin in it once – it is forbidden to wrap money in it." Thus are his words. And he was precise in saying "forever," meaning: certainly if he designated it simply to wrap tefillin, it is considered as forever. However, if he explicitly stated that he is not dedicating it for this purpose forever – it is considered as a condition and it is permitted. Therefore, our master the Rema wrote that if he conditioned from the beginning in any manner – it is permitted. Thus are his words. Meaning: it requires an explicit statement that it is not forever, and then even if he used it many times – it is not sanctified. There is a question if he designated it and another person placed tefillin in it, if it becomes sanctified. In my humble opinion, from the language of the Talmud and the decisors, it appears that it is specifically when he himself used it and not another. And it will be explained further in section 10.

It is questionable whether the designation must specifically be through an action, meaning that one sews a pouch specifically for tefillin, or if taking a pouch and saying "I designate this for tefillin" is sufficient, unless something is modified in it. Alternatively, perhaps mere verbal designation is sufficient. I have found that there is a disagreement among the early authorities on this matter: Riaz and his grandfather, Rabbi Isaiah the Elder, as written by the Shiltei Giborim in the third chapter of Berachot in the Rif (folio 17a, letter 5), and this is his wording: "My grandfather, the Rabbi, differentiates in designation between land and movable items, that land cannot be designated by mere speech..., but movable items can be designated by speech... Similarly, if one says about a scarf, 'This scarf shall be for tefillin,' this is a designation even by speech alone. And if he ties tefillin in it, even temporarily, it is forbidden to tie his money in it... And it seems to me that there is no difference in this between land and movable items. Rather, even movable items cannot be designated by speech alone but only through an action... Similarly, a scarf for tefillin, if any modification is made in it for the purpose of tefillin, this is a designation. And if he ties tefillin in it, even temporarily, it is forbidden. But if he designated it by speech alone, this is not a designation, and if he ties tefillin in it temporarily, it is permitted. However, if he permanently designated it to place tefillin in it, and placed tefillin in it, there is no greater designation than this... Thus far are his words."

It follows that even according to the opinion of the Riaz, speech is effective if one designates it to permanently place tefillin in it. According to him, if there is designation through an action, even if it is not designated permanently, it is still considered designated. This is very puzzling: if it is not designated permanently, what kind of designation is it? And our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote explicitly that it must be "permanent," as I wrote in section 5. It is forced to say that his intention is when the designation was through speech alone, for if so, he should have clarified, and certainly, he meant in any type of designation. And logically, this makes sense, for without "permanence," it is considered a mere condition. It must be said that the Riaz holds that a condition is ineffective. It requires investigation because in Menachot (34b) regarding changing from the head tefillin to the arm tefillin, if one initially conditioned it, it is permitted, see there. It is possible that he holds that a condition is only effective for a lesser sanctity, but not to completely secularize. None of the authorities made this distinction.

And behold, our teachers, the Ba'alei Tosafot, in Sanhedrin (48a, s.v. "Natnu") wrote in the opinion of Rabbeinu Yeshaya the First that verbal designation is effective if he took it in his hand and designated it for this purpose. And this is their language there: "It is necessary to say that mere verbal designation is not effective, unless he took it and said: 'This will be for the dead and for a book.' And the fact that it mentions the weaver – it is not specifically, but because of the greater novelty of Rava, that even so it is permitted." Thus is their language. According to this, in practice, we certainly hold according to the opinion of our teachers, the Ba'alei Tosafot.

And know that there is someone who wrote that if one made a bag for the sake of tefillin, even if he intended to use it temporarily, it is forbidden. The same rule applies if there was already a bag and he added something to it for the sake of tefillin, and he intended to use it temporarily, it is forbidden until he removes what he added. And if he used it once with the intention to use it forever, even if he did not designate it, it is forbidden (Magen Avraham, subsection 5), as explained in Yoreh De'ah, section 364 regarding a corpse. And the Talmud in Sanhedrin (48a) compares this to that, see there. There is a doubt whether even with verbal designation, when he said, "This will be to store tefillin," the law is the same that even if he intended to use it temporarily it is forbidden? Or perhaps this only applies to designation through an act, and does not apply to verbal designation? This doubt also exists regarding a corpse in Yoreh De'ah, there. From the language of the Tur and Shulchan Aruch there it seems somewhat that we only say this through an act. This requires further examination for the practical law.

It is stated in Chullin (13a) that a minor has the capacity to perform actions but does not have the capacity for intention. Therefore, something that is prohibited by designation alone, such as an object of sanctity as will be explained – the designation of a minor is insignificant. However, if a minor designates something for sanctity and places sanctity upon it – it is prohibited, because he has the capacity to perform actions (ibid, subsection 4). Based on this, a minor also has the ability to designate through action. It is clear that a person cannot prohibit something that does not belong to him (ibid). Therefore, if Reuven designates something, and Shimon comes and places sanctity upon it – it is not prohibited, as I wrote in subsection 5. All the more so, the designation of another person is insignificant. Nevertheless, it seems that if another person designates it, and the owner agrees to his designation and places sanctity upon it, even if the other person places it with the owner's consent – it is also prohibited, as it is considered as his agent. And if someone stole a garment and made it into a tefillin bag – he acquires it through a change in form and prohibits it (ibid).

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote in section 3 that parchment processed for the sake of tefillin is forbidden to be used for secular writing, for such preparation for an item of holiness is significant. Thus are his words. Meaning: that which we say "preparation is not significant" applies only to items not of intrinsic holiness but to items that serve holiness, like a tefillin bag and the like. But for items of intrinsic holiness, preparation is significant, as we derive from the calf for the atonement ritual which was forbidden by mere preparation because it is of intrinsic holiness. And this matter is explained in Sanhedrin there.

However, according to this, there is a major question: If so, how did we rule that it is permitted to make the hand tefillin from the head tefillin when they are new, because designation alone is not significant? After all, the boxes themselves are inherently holy, and this law is explicitly stated in Menachot (34b). It must be said that regarding changing from a more stringent holiness to a lesser holiness, designation alone is enough even for something inherently holy. But to remove it from holiness completely, it is forbidden even with mere designation for something inherently holy. They wrote that straps are not called "inherently holy" but rather "accessories for holiness" (as stated there in subsection 6). However, some say that even for something inherently holy, designation does not prohibit until an action is done to it, such as starting to write on a parchment, and then it is forbidden to write mundane matters on it, even if one made a condition about it. For a condition does not help for something inherently holy to use it for mundane purposes while it is in its sanctity (according to the Gra”z). But for accessories for holiness, a condition helps according to all opinions even while they are in their sanctity, as will be explained in Siman 154, provided that one does not use it for a disgraceful purpose as I wrote in Siman 151. And the law seems to follow the first opinion since Rabbeinu the Rema ruled so. (And the Gra”z wrote that the main opinion is like the "some say".)

All that has been explained pertains to items used for sanctity. However, for items used for a mitzvah, such as tzitzit, shofar, etrog, lulav, Chanukah candle, and the like, which are for a mitzvah and not for sanctity, even though during the time of the mitzvah they are considered to have sanctity – this is not actual sanctity but rather they are set aside due to the mitzvah, and it is forbidden to use them during the time of the mitzvah. But after the mitzvah has been performed, one may use them for mundane purposes, even if the mitzvah was performed with them many times, and no condition is needed at all. Therefore, a vessel designated for an etrog may be used for mundane purposes after Sukkot, and similarly for all such cases. (Magen Avraham, subsection 6. And what he wrote that even for an item of sanctity a condition is effective to use it for mundane purposes, see there – this is when there was no designation, as I wrote in subsection 4. But when there was designation, a condition is not effective, as he himself wrote in subsection 5, and as he wrote in subsection 9, see there thoroughly. Examine carefully and you will find it easy to understand.)

It has already been explained that tefillin require a clean body. Even passing gas is forbidden, and certainly so for relieving oneself. Even if one merely needs to relieve oneself, it is forbidden to wear them, and all the more so for actually relieving oneself. In the Gemara and the Rambam, no distinction is mentioned between the head-tefillin and the hand-tefillin. On the contrary, it is clearly proven that even the hand-tefillin are forbidden, as it says in Shabbat (49a): "Tefillin require a clean body so that one does not pass gas in them," see there – thus, it uses the plural form. Furthermore, the term "tefillah" refers to one in the Talmudic language, not "tefillin." Even the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch in section 1, which state: "It is forbidden to enter a bathroom... with the tefillin on one's head," are not excluding the hand-tefillin, as some say (see Ma'adanei Yom Tov). Rather, they are excluding when one is not wearing them in the place of the tefillin, but they are placed in his hand or bosom. But the same law applies to the hand-tefillin. (And so wrote the Magen Avraham in section 1, and he ruled this way in practice. See also Eliyah Rabbah and Be'er Heitev in the name of Beit Yaakov, their words are perplexing. And so agreed the Yad Ephraim and the Bnei Chayiah, as Be'er Heitev wrote. Even though Tosafot in Menachot 32b were uncertain about this, and the Rosh in the laws of Tefillin section 12 brought this, nonetheless, according to them it would be a doubt concerning a Torah prohibition. Certainly, the Rambam did not mention this at all. From the language of the Gemara, it is clearly explained this way. And if because of the Shabbat 62a passage, see there – it is concerning the removal of four cubits beforehand, see there. Be precise and you will find leniency.)

And know that all our rabbis agreed that it is only forbidden for adults to wear tefillin in the bathroom by law, but for children, it is permitted by the fundamental law. However, there are distinctions between a permanent bathroom, where we are concerned that one might defecate there, and a temporary bathroom, which means standing in some place to urinate – it is permitted to urinate even when they are on his head. And only when they are in his hand, not in the place of the tefillin – it is forbidden for another reason as will be explained. And the opinion of Rambam is that even when they are on his head it is forbidden to urinate as will be explained. And they wrote the reason: because we decree that he might pass gas with them (Kesef Mishneh and Magen Avraham, subsection 5). And it seems that it is necessary to say this, as in Berachot (23a) there is a question: Is it permissible for a person to enter a permanent bathroom with tefillin to urinate? Ravina permits. Rav Adda forbids, we are concerned that he might defecate with them or pass gas with them, see there. Therefore, even the one who forbids it does so only because of a decree. But in my humble opinion, this does not seem to be the case according to the words of Rambam, as we will explain with the help of Heaven in subsection 6.

This is the wording of the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch, Section 1: It is forbidden to enter a permanent bathroom to urinate with tefillin on one's head, due to a decree lest one defecates while wearing them. However, if one holds them in one's hand, it is permissible to urinate in a permanent bathroom. In a temporary bathroom, it is permissible to urinate while they are on one's head. But if one holds them in one's hand, it is forbidden to urinate while standing, even if one holds them in one's garment, because one needs to wipe the drops from one's feet with one's hand. Therefore, one should remove them at a distance of four cubits and give them to a friend. Thus ends the text.

According to this, the main distinction between permanent and temporary is that in a permanent situation, one urinates while sitting and there are no splashes, whereas in a temporary situation, one urinates while standing and there are splashes. This is what our teacher, the Rema, wrote there, and this is his language: "This is specifically when one urinates while sitting, since there is no concern for splashes. But if one urinates while standing, it is certainly forbidden, as it is not better than a temporary bathroom. The same applies if one urinates while sitting or in loose soil where there are no splashes in a temporary bathroom – it is also permitted. There is no difference between permanent and temporary in this matter. However, in a permanent situation, one presumably relieves oneself while sitting, and in a temporary situation, one presumably does so while standing since one does not relieve oneself for defecation." Until here is his language.

And I am astonished by this: for we are concerned lest one defecate or pass gas, as I wrote in section 2. If so, even though in a temporary situation there is no concern lest one defecate, but lest one pass gas, this concern exists also in a temporary situation? It must be said that in a temporary situation, this concern also does not exist. This is not understood and requires further investigation. (Also, in the Gemara itself, it is difficult according to the opinion of our teachers, for the concern lest one pass gas exists also when urinating in any place, and the issue is only in a permanent situation. Indeed, the Kesef Mishneh and the Magen Avraham explained that this is the reason of the Rambam, meaning: according to the conclusion, it is forbidden to urinate wherever they are above him, see there in the Kesef Mishneh. This is not the way of the Talmud. But according to what we will explain in the intention of the Rambam, it fits well.)

Our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote that from the words of the Rambam it appears that it is forbidden to urinate while wearing tefillin, whether in a permanent bathroom or a temporary one. And one should be concerned about his words. This is his language. And this is the language of the Rambam in the fourth chapter, law 17: If one was wearing tefillin and needed to go to the bathroom, he should not place the tefillin in holes adjacent to the public domain and enter, lest passersby take them. What should he do? Even if he needs to urinate, he should remove his tefillin at a distance of four cubits, wrap them in his garment like a Torah scroll, and hold them in his right hand opposite his heart. He should be careful that no strap extends a handbreadth from his hand. He then enters and relieves himself. When he exits, he should distance himself four cubits from the bathroom and then put them back on. In what case are these words said? In a permanent bathroom where there are no splashes. But in a temporary bathroom, he should not enter with them wrapped, but rather remove them and give them to his friend to guard. And urine ceases only when sitting, or on loose earth, or in a sloped place. This is his language. And we have already written that the great authorities explained that the reason he forbade even in a temporary bathroom when urinating while wearing them is due to the concern of flatulence, and not because there is an intrinsic prohibition to urinate with tefillin as there is with major bodily functions. But in my humble opinion, it does not appear so from his words there, as he wrote: If one forgot and entered the bathroom while wearing tefillin, he should place his hand on them until he finishes the first stream, exit and remove them, and then re-enter and relieve himself. For if he interrupts during the first stream, whether for major or minor bodily functions, he will come to illnesses that pose great danger. This is his language, hence he wrote this law also regarding minor bodily functions. And if you would think that there is no intrinsic prohibition, only due to the concern of flatulence, why didn't they permit him to finish? Rather, it is certain that he holds that it is intrinsically forbidden to urinate with tefillin.

In truth, I do not understand the opinion of our Rabbis: Why should it be permitted to urinate while wearing tefillin? After all, this does not constitute a clean body. Therefore, it seems that according to the Rambam, urinating while the tefillin are on one's head and arm in the place where tefillin are worn is certainly forbidden in any case due to the disgrace to the tefillin, just as it is for defecating. And regarding the question raised in the Gemara there: "May a person enter a fixed bathroom to urinate while wearing tefillin?" – it does not refer to when they are on his head. Rather, the explanation is as follows: Prior to this, the Rabbis taught: "One who enters a bathroom should remove his tefillin at a distance of four cubits and then enter." Rav Sheshet said: "This was only taught regarding a fixed bathroom, but for a temporary bathroom, he removes the tefillin and immediately relieves himself. And when he exits, he should distance himself four cubits and then put them on, because he has made it a fixed bathroom." The question was raised: "May a person enter a fixed bathroom to urinate while wearing tefillin?" Ravina permitted it, Rav Adda and Rava forbade it... And this is the explanation: What is the ruling when he enters holding them in his hands? Does he need to distance himself four cubits since he is entering a fixed place? Or does he not need to distance himself four cubits since he is only entering to urinate? And it concludes that it is forbidden, meaning: he needs to distance himself four cubits, because he might defecate or pass gas. And it is as if he defecates, and he needs to distance himself four cubits. And if you ask: is it not forbidden to urinate while holding them because of the splashes? However, this is according to the conclusion there, where the Gemara disputes Rav Sheshet and Rava, and they were refuted. But Rav Sheshet and Rava did not consider the concern of splashes, as they wondered: "Now, in a fixed place it is permitted, in a temporary place is it even necessary to ask?" And the Gemara rejects their opinion, see there. And indeed, the Rambam ruled this way, as I have written. Moreover, according to the conclusion of the Gemara, is there no situation where it is permitted? Indeed, while sitting or on loose soil or on a slope, it is permitted. Nonetheless, in any case, this question pertains only to the distancing of four cubits, but when they are placed in their designated place, it is fundamentally forbidden to urinate.

And know that what we wrote in Section 3 in the name of the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch, that when one enters a permanent bathroom it is permitted to urinate while holding the tefillin in his hand – this is indeed what Rabbi Yosef Karo wrote in the Shulchan Aruch. However, the Tur wrote: "in his garment and in his hand," meaning he wraps them in his garment and holds them in his hand. Rambam also wrote this. Therefore, some have written that Rabbi Yosef Karo caused a stumbling block for those who study this, as certainly he also intended this, as he wrote himself in Section 5 (Taz, Section 1, and see Eliyah Rabbah). But in truth, it seems that he wrote this intentionally, as Rashi also explained there that he only holds them in his hand, see there. And indeed there is a dispute among the Tannaim there, as Beit Hillel holds only in his hand, and Rabbi Akiva holds in his garment and in his hand. Some of the great ones have written that wherever Beit Hillel and Rabbi Akiva disagree – the halacha follows Beit Hillel, as in the end of the chapter "HaMafkid" and in Ohalot chapter five, and in several other places (Pnei Yehoshua in his novelties there). And this is the reasoning of Rashi, of blessed memory. And in Section 5 where Rabbi Yosef Karo was stringent – this is regarding defecation as explained there, and as we will quote his words in Section 11, and if so there is no stumbling block here. Nonetheless, in practice, certainly we require "in his garment and in his hand," since Rambam ruled this explicitly.

However, what the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch have written – that, in a temporary situation, it is permissible to urinate while they [tefillin] are on one's head, but if one is holding them in his hand it is forbidden, and one must remove them at a distance of four cubits and give them to his companion – this is certainly perplexing. For why is there a need for a distance of four cubits, since the prohibition is only due to the concern of splashes? And indeed, the Rambam did not write about a distance of four cubits, see there. Therefore, it has been written that this applies only to a fixed situation, but in a temporary situation, there is no need for a distance of four cubits (Magen Avraham, subsection 4, and Taz, subsection 3). However, this does not seem to be the case from their language. And perhaps they hold that even in a temporary situation, a distance of four cubits is required, for what Rav Sheshet said in the Gemara there – that in a temporary situation one removes them and relieves oneself immediately – was omitted by the Rif and the Rambam. Their reasoning seems to be because we do not hold according to Rav Sheshet at the end of the discussion regarding holding them in his hand in a temporary situation, as I have written. Therefore, we do not hold according to Rav Sheshet in this matter either (and so wrote the Pnei Yehoshua).

Our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote: A permanent bathroom is one that contains excrement and is in an open field without a pit. A temporary bathroom is, for example, a place used for urination, where a person does not usually go to a bathroom for this purpose, and this time the place has become a bathroom for the first time. So far his words. And it seems to me that its explanation is as follows: Earlier, he wrote two laws regarding a permanent bathroom: if the excrement is on his head, it is forbidden to urinate because he might defecate, but if it is in his hand, it is permissible to urinate. Regarding a temporary bathroom, he wrote that it is permissible to urinate if the excrement is on his head, but if he holds it in his hand, it is forbidden. Therefore, he says that a permanent bathroom, where I permitted you if the excrement is in his hand, this applies even if it is without a pit. Do not say that because it is without a pit, it is very disgusting and it is forbidden even to hold it in his hand. He comes to inform us that it is not so. And afterward, he says that regarding a temporary bathroom, where I permitted you if the excrement is on his head, do not say that there was a temporary bathroom there until now, for in such a case I did not permit you, but this time the place has become a bathroom. The commentators explained his intention that when it is covered, one does not need to distance four cubits. Only when the excrement is in the open field does one need to distance four cubits (Magen Avraham, section 6, and Pri Megadim and the Gra). Consequently, they were pressed, see there. In my humble opinion, it is not so, and its explanation is as I wrote. (Also, what Magen Avraham wrote from Rashi there is not a proof, and Rashi's intention is also as I wrote. And proof can be seen from what he wrote regarding a temporary bathroom, see there. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

Additionally, it is written in section 4: If [the tefillin] are in his lap and he is wearing a belt, or if they are in his garment in his hand—it is permitted both to urinate and to defecate. Thus far his language. Meaning: in a temporary restroom, there is no concern of splashes, because when they are in his lap—he will not touch them with his hands. And regarding what is written "in his garment in his hand," the explanation is: they are wrapped in the garment and he holds the garment in his hand, so even if he wipes the splashes and touches them, he will touch the garment and not the tefillin themselves. This is not comparable to what was written previously that it is forbidden even if he holds them in his garment, for there the intention is that he holds them in his garment, and we are concerned that he might touch them directly since they are exposed. But here the explanation is that they are wrapped in his garment. (See Magen Avraham, subsection 8, and Taz, subsection 4, who struggled and wrote distant explanations. The Magen Avraham explained that they are tied in his garment, and the Taz explained that the tefillin are under his garment, and he holds his hand on the garment. See there. And it is astonishing: why should we not be concerned that he might move his hand and they might fall? According to what I have written, it is simple and straightforward. Examine it and you will find it clear.)

Additionally, it is written in paragraph 5: If one wishes to enter a fixed bathroom to relieve himself, he should remove them (tefillin) at a distance of four cubits, roll them up with their straps, and hold them in his right hand and in his garment opposite his heart. He should be careful that no strap extends from under his hand by a handbreadth. When he exits, he should distance himself four cubits and then put them on. Thus far are his words, and this is from the words of the Rambam that we brought in paragraph 5. Know that regarding what is written, that when he enters a fixed bathroom to relieve himself, he should remove them at a distance of four cubits, our Rabbi the Rema wrote that some say even without relieving oneself. And it is good to be stringent. Thus far are his words. It seems to me that his intention is not about the entrance, for in this matter there is no one who disputes that it is forbidden to enter with tefillin into a bathroom or a bathhouse. And in this matter, "it is good to be stringent" is not relevant, for it is a complete prohibition. Rather, his intention is about the distancing of four cubits. (And with this, the difficulty of the Magen Avraham in paragraph 9 is resolved, see there. Be precise and you will find it easy.) And what he wrote that "he should hold them in his right hand" is because the left hand is needed for cleaning, as I wrote in Siman 3.

It is permitted to enter with tefillin into dirty alleyways, even if there is a place that is explicitly dirty. It is preferable to cover them with a hat. And if one wishes to remove them and then put them back on, that is also acceptable (Magen Avraham, Siman 11, citing Maamar Mordechai). This means that even though one would need to make a new blessing upon putting them back on, nevertheless, if one wishes to do so, it is acceptable. It seems to me that it is only permitted to walk through such a place, but to stand there is forbidden. (See Magen Avraham there, who brings a proof for this law from Berakhot 24b; however, it is not a proof, as it might be referring to the recitation of the evening Shema. Examine and you will find this to be correct.)

All the permissions clarified regarding tefillin in the context of a bathroom apply when one intends to put them back on afterward. However, if one was wearing tefillin at night or close to dusk, such that there is no time to put them on again after leaving the bathroom, and one needs to relieve oneself, one should not enter the bathroom with them even if they are wrapped in a garment, and even if one only intends to urinate while seated, where there is no concern of splashing. Rather, what should one do? One should remove them and place them in a container if it has a space of a handbreadth, or in a container that is not typically used for tefillin even if it does not have a space of a handbreadth. One holds the container in one's hand and enters. In what case is this said? In an outdoor bathroom. But in an indoor bathroom, one should not bring them in at all, since one can leave them in a secure place. Similarly, travelers who have a secure place to leave them on the wagon or can give them to a companion should not bring them into the bathroom at all (Ataret Zekenim). Rambam wrote in the tenth chapter: Amulets containing Torah passages should not be brought into a bathroom unless they are covered with leather. One should not hold a Torah scroll in one's arm and enter a bathroom, even if it is wrapped in a cloth... up to here is his wording (see Magen Avraham, subsection 13 and subsection 14). Also, placing tefillin on the ground requires a container with a space of a handbreadth, as it is considered a barrier between them and the ground (there).

If one forgets that he has tefillin on his head and attends to his bodily needs, whether large or small, he should place his hand over them until he finishes the first segment, then exit and remove them, and then return to finish his needs. For the returning segment can lead to intestinal illness, and the returning flow of urine can lead to jaundice. And it is permissible for a doctor to hold a urine container in his hand while having tefillin on his head, but a meticulous individual should be stringent with himself. And know that from everything explained, it is not proper to urinate while wearing tefillin, even the hand tefillin, for as we have clarified, there is no difference between the hand tefillin and the head tefillin. And according to what we have explained in the view of the Rambam, there is no difference between large and small needs. Besides this, there is a desecration of God's name (chilul Hashem) in front of the masses, and one who does so should be reprimanded.

Since tefillin require a clean body so that one does not pass gas while wearing them, it is therefore forbidden to sleep in them, as during sleep one is likely to pass gas (Shabbat 49a). We learn in Sukkah (26a): One teaching states: A person may sleep a temporary sleep in tefillin but not a permanent sleep. Another teaching states: Whether permanent or temporary sleep. And another teaching states: Neither permanent nor temporary sleep? It is not difficult: The teaching that even temporary sleep is forbidden refers to when one is holding them in his hand, as we are concerned that they might fall from his hand. The teaching that temporary sleep is permitted but permanent sleep is forbidden refers to when they are placed on his head, as for temporary sleep we are not concerned about passing gas, but for permanent sleep we are concerned. The teaching that even permanent sleep is permitted refers to when he spreads a cloth over them. Rashi explains that he placed them next to his head and spread a cloth over them; see there. According to this, the teaching in Berakhot (23b): A person should not hold tefillin in his hand and pray... and should not sleep in them, neither a permanent nor a temporary sleep, see there – the reason is lest they fall from his hand. (And it is surprising about Rashi who explained there: lest he pass gas, see there. This requires further study.)

But the Rambam wrote in Chapter Four, Law 15: "Tefillin require a clean body... Therefore, it is forbidden to sleep in them, whether a regular sleep or a short sleep. But if one places a cloth over them and there is no woman with him, he may sleep a short sleep in them. And how does he do this? He places his head between his knees, sits, and sleeps. If his tefillin are wrapped around his hand, it is permitted to sleep in them even a regular sleep." So far his words. He explains that the statement "spreads a cloth over them" means that they are placed on his head, and without a cloth it is forbidden even for a short sleep, as we are concerned that he might sink into a deep sleep even when he places his head between his knees. However, when he spreads a cloth over them, he will certainly wake up shortly. But this reasoning is not logical; therefore, it must be said that without a cloth we are concerned that he might forget he is wearing tefillin, and with the cloth he will remember (Kesef Mishneh) and will not come to pass gas. Therefore, a short sleep is permitted but not a regular sleep. And that which is taught that a regular sleep is also permitted – this is when they are wrapped around his hand, not in the place of the tefillin, and wrapped tightly so they will not fall. And why is it not forbidden due to distraction when wearing them on his head? They wrote that the reason is that distraction only refers to frivolity and light-headedness, as I wrote in Siman 28. And we further explained there that during sleep, the prohibition of distraction does not apply, as he is not in the world at all then, see there. And this is also implied in the Levush, see there.

Our master, the Beit Yosef, copied the words of the Rambam and added that if one holds them in his hand but they are not wrapped around his hand, it is forbidden to sleep with them even a temporary sleep. These are his words. The Rambam did not mention this because it is self-evident. Since he wrote that if they are wrapped it is permitted, it follows that holding them without wrapping is completely forbidden. The main concern is obvious: lest they fall. Our master, the Rema, wrote that this is specifically when holding them without their case. But with their case, it is permitted in any situation. These are his words. Meaning: we are not concerned that they might fall to the ground, for even if they do fall, there is no prohibition since they are in their case. According to this, the common practice that when tefillin fall to the ground due to some reason, people fast or give something to charity, does not apply when they fall in their case and nothing is required. (Magen Avraham, subsection 5. I am puzzled by what he wrote in subsection 3 regarding the measure of temporary sleep according to the Shulchan Aruch. For the Shulchan Aruch follows the Rambam’s view that placing one's head between his knees is considered temporary sleep, as the Rambam ruled according to Rabbi Yochanan in Sukkah. This should have been written about the Tur, who did not mention the measure of temporary sleep at all. As the Taz wrote in subsection 1, see there.)

It is forbidden to enter a cemetery or come within four cubits of a corpse while wearing tefillin on one's head, as this would be considered "mocking the poor." If the tefillin are covered, it is permitted. Even within four cubits of a cemetery is forbidden (Magen Avraham, Small Paragraph 1). If there is a partition for the cemetery, it is permitted up to the partition. When entering a cemetery, it is forbidden even beyond the four cubits of the graves. This is implied by the language of the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, who wrote: It is forbidden to enter a cemetery or come within four cubits of a corpse. See there, and it implies that in the cemetery it is forbidden even beyond four cubits. And in Berachot (18a) it is explicitly stated that outside of four cubits is permitted in the cemetery, see there. We must say that they wrote the language of the Talmud but meant only within four cubits of the graves. Some say that although this is the basic law, they made a fence to prevent someone from mistakenly entering within four cubits, and therefore they forbade even beyond four cubits (Taz, Small Paragraph 1). It is forced to say so, that they added to the words of the Talmud. And know that it has been explained that if the tefillin are covered, it is permitted, but the straps also need to be covered, and this is obvious (there, Small Paragraph 2). One should remove the strap from the finger and hide it under one's garment.

In the outer room of the bathhouse, where everyone is clothed, one may put on tefillin and recite blessings from the outset. In the middle room, where some people are clothed and some are naked, one should not put on tefillin from the outset. However, if one already has them on, he does not need to remove them. In the innermost room, where everyone is naked, even if one already has tefillin on, he must remove them. From the language of the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch, it seems that the concern is only with the head tefillin, but for the hand tefillin, which is covered, we are not concerned. The prohibition of tefillin in the bathhouse applies even if there is no one else there, due to the significant filth. However, in a mikvah when no one is present, it is permitted, as there is not significant filth (Magen Avraham, subsection 2). Any sacred item is forbidden to bring into a bathhouse unless it is well covered. Therefore, the Rambam, of blessed memory, rebuked those who embroidered verses on their garments, because they would go to the bathhouse in them (ibid).

It is taught in Menachot (43b) that a person is obligated to recite one hundred blessings every day. They based this on the verse "And now, Israel, what does the Lord your God ask of you?" (Deuteronomy 10:12), see there. And the Tur wrote in the name of the Geonim that David instituted this because one hundred people from Israel were dying every day, and they did not know why. He stood up with his divine inspiration and understood, and he instituted one hundred blessings, and the plague stopped. And therefore David said: "The declaration of the man who was raised on high" (2 Samuel 23:1), for the word "on high" (על) in Gematria equals "one hundred." 

And the reason why every blessing has the formula "Blessed are You," and the hidden "Who has sanctified us," is because the Holy One, blessed be He, is both revealed and hidden, as I wrote in Siman 5, see there. (And the sanctity is hidden without physical sensation, therefore we say "Who has sanctified us" in the hidden form. And the reason for the one hundred blessings, it appears to me, is because within every ten there is sanctity, and the tithe of the tithe is the Holy of Holies. And all the blessings are the returning light to draw down from above an abundance of blessing, as I wrote in Siman 5. Therefore, we draw from the depths of the heights, from the Holy of Holies. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

In the counting of one hundred blessings exactly, the poskim (decisors of Jewish law) have made efforts: some have calculated one hundred and five blessings every day (Beit Yosef), and some have calculated one hundred only on a fast day (Magen Avraham, subsection 8). In my humble opinion, it seems that there are one hundred blessings exactly every day, according to the necessity for a person to eat one meal in a 24-hour period, as it cannot be otherwise. And this is: upon arising from bed, one recites "Al Netilat Yadayim" and "Asher Yatzar" and "Elokai Neshamah," and a blessing on the small tallit, and fifteen morning blessings, and the blessing of "Who sanctifies His name in public," and three blessings of the blessings of the Torah, and a blessing on the large tallit, and two blessings for the tefillin—these are twenty-six blessings. "Baruch She'amar," "Yishtabach," "Yotzer Or," "Ahavah Rabbah," "Ga'al Yisrael," and nineteen blessings of the Amidah—these are twenty-four, totaling fifty. Nineteen in the Amidah of Mincha, and nineteen in the Amidah of Maariv, and the blessing of "Ma'ariv Aravim," and "Ohev Amo Yisrael," and "Ga'al Yisrael," and "Hashkiveinu," and "Yiru Eineinu," and the blessing of "Hamapil"—these are forty-four. And eating a meal involves six blessings: four of Birkat Hamazon, and "Al Netilat Yadayim" and "Hamotzi"—these are fifty. And with the previous fifty—these are exactly one hundred according to the Ashkenazi custom. However, according to the Sephardic custom, four blessings are missing, namely: the blessing "Who gives strength to the weary," the blessing "Who sanctifies His name in public," "Yiru Eineinu," and one blessing from the tefillin. And it seems to me that they hold that the blessings of the Torah are two blessings according to the opinion of Tosafot and the Rosh, which will be explained in Siman 47, and not three blessings according to the opinion of the Rambam. Also, they do not bless on the small tallit because they fulfill it with the large tallit, as I wrote in Siman 8, subsection 16, see there. Therefore, they are missing six blessings. And they count two meals, one during the day and one at night, and also this way it is exactly one hundred. However, on Shabbat and Yom Tov, many are missing: on weekdays, in three prayers there are fifty-seven blessings, and on Shabbat and Yom Tov in four prayers there are twenty-eight blessings, excluding the blessings of the tefillin. Thus, thirty are missing for Sephardim and thirty-one for Ashkenazim. Correspondingly, on Shabbat, three meals are added, and on weekdays we only counted one meal for Ashkenazim and two for Sephardim, so it turns out that on Shabbat six blessings are added for Sephardim and twelve for Ashkenazim. Additionally, two blessings of Kiddush at night are added, and one blessing of daytime Kiddush—nine are added for Sephardim and fifteen for Ashkenazim. Thus, twenty-one blessings are missing for Sephardim and sixteen for Ashkenazim. And in Menachot there it is said that on Shabbat and Yom Tov we fill in with fruits and spices, see there. But we do not have fruits or spices. Some wrote that one should hear the blessings from those who are called to the Torah and answer "Amen," and the one who answers "Amen" is greater than the one who blesses (Beit Yosef in the name of a Gaon, see there). And some say that even if the one blessing whispers the blessing so that it cannot be heard, since one knows what is being blessed, one answers "Amen" and fulfills it (Beit Yosef). See Siman 124.

In the Gemara, all the morning blessings are arranged each in its proper place. How so? When one awakens from sleep to rise from his bed, he says "Elohai Neshamah... until... who restores souls...". When he hears the rooster’s crow, he blesses "who gives the rooster understanding", for "sechvi" means "heart" in the holy tongue, and in Arabic it is "rooster". The understanding is in the heart, and through this, one discerns between day and night. Because even the rooster perceives this, they established this blessing at the time of the rooster's crow. The reason for this blessing is that it is forbidden to benefit from this world without a blessing, and all the morning blessings are of benefit to a person. The primary enjoyment of a person is during the day when there is light, and he can do all his activities. Therefore, one must bless for this. In the Gemara (Berachot 60b), the version is: "who has given the rooster understanding", see there. In the Rambam, Tur, and Shulchan Aruch, the version is: "who gives the rooster understanding". This also seems primary, as all the blessings are formulated in the present tense and not the past, like "who forms light", "who gives the Torah", "who creates the fruit of the ground", and so on. The reason is that the Holy One, Blessed be He, acts at all times and every moment, not like a human craftsman who only does the work and afterward it stands by itself, and his supervision ceases. But the Holy One, Blessed be He, His actions and supervision do not cease at any time or moment, as it is written: "who makes great lights". (And the reason "Asher Yatzar" begins in the past tense is because it blesses on an action that has already happened. Therefore, in its conclusion, it says: "heals all flesh" in the present tense. Examine and you will find it correct.)

In the Gemara there, after the blessing "Who gives the rooster understanding," it is stated: When one opens his eyes, he should say "Who gives sight to the blind." When he sits up, he should say "Who releases the bound." When he dresses, he should say "Who clothes the naked." When he stands upright, he should say "Blessed is He who straightens the bent." When he steps on the ground, he should say "Who spreads the earth upon the waters." This means that naturally, the earth should sink into the water, as any heavy object sinks into water, so that man would have a place to stand and walk. Therefore, we bless the Holy One, Blessed be He, for this. When he walks, he should say "Blessed is He who prepares the steps of man." For man is tall in stature compared to animals, which walk on all fours, while man walks on his legs alone, looks upwards, and gives praise and thanks to the Holy One, Blessed be He, for this. When he puts on his shoes, he should say "Blessed is He who has provided me with all my needs." The letter "kaf" in "tzorki" has a chirik (vowel indicating 'ee' sound) and not a kamatz (vowel indicating 'ah' sound), as it does not refer to all of man's needs but only to shoes. The reason is that there is nothing more disgraceful than walking naked and barefoot. Therefore, first one blesses "Who clothes the naked," and now he blesses "Who has provided me with all my needs," meaning that with shoes, all my clothing needs are complete. When he girds himself with a belt, he should say "Blessed is He who girds Israel with strength," for the belt strengthens a person. When he covers his head with a head covering, he should say "Blessed is He who crowns Israel with glory," for it is a glory when the head is covered. These two blessings mention "Israel" because the intention of the Israelite man in them is for the sake of holiness: the belt so that his heart does not see his nakedness, and the head covering so that he does not walk with an uncovered head (Bach). When he washes his face, he should say "Blessed is He who removes sleep from my eyes..."

In the Rambam, Chapter 7 of "Tefillah," there is a different order for these blessings, namely: "Who gives the rooster understanding," "Who clothes the naked," "Who crowns Israel with glory," "Who gives sight to the blind," "Who releases the bound," "Who spreads the earth upon the waters," "Who straightens the bent," "Who removes the bonds of sleep...," "Who girds Israel with strength," "Who has provided me with all my needs," "Who sets firm the steps of man"—see there. And his version is like that of the Rif. However, in the Rif, the blessing "Who crowns Israel with glory" is not found at all, and instead he wrote: When covering oneself with a sheet, one says "to wrap in tzitzit"—see there. And it seems to me that there is no disagreement, and the matter is as follows: If one wraps the sheet around both his body and head together, he blesses "to wrap in tzitzit" and does not bless "Who crowns...," because we do not find two blessings for one thing, and this is what the Rif refers to. But in the Gemara and Rambam, the intention is that the sheet is only on his head alone.

The Rosh and the Tur have the same version as the Gemara. However, there is one difference: in the Gemara, the blessing "Who clothes the naked" comes after "Who gives sight to the blind" and "Who releases the bound," while they place "Who clothes the naked" earlier, see there. Additionally, in the Rosh, there is another change where "Who has provided me with all my needs" precedes "Who prepares the steps of man," see there. And our master the Beit Yosef in Section 1 wrote according to the version of the Rosh. In our prayer books, the text is: "Who gives sight to the blind," "Who clothes the naked," "Who releases the bound," "Who straightens the bent," "Who…," "Who has provided me with all my needs," "Who prepares the steps of man," and some have "Who has prepared," "Who girds…," "Who crowns…." And in the Sephardic version: "Who gives sight to the blind," "Who releases the bound," "Who straightens the bent," "Who clothes the naked," "Who…," "Who prepares…," "Who has provided me with all my needs," "Who girds," "Who crowns." It is impossible to give accurate reasons for the differing versions. (See Magen Avraham, sub-section 2, who wrote that everything depends on the time and place. This means that some bring forward the matter they bless on first, and others delay it. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

Another blessing that we have is "He who gives strength to the weary." This blessing is not found in the Talmud, and our master the Beit Yosef in paragraph 6 complained about this. However, it is common in all regions to recite it, and so wrote our master the Rema. The Ashkenazim say it last, before "Who removes sleep from my eyes." In the Sephardic version, it is said after "Who clothes the naked." Perhaps this blessing was in their version of the Talmud (Bach). The Tur wrote that this blessing is based on the Midrash: "They are new every morning; great is Your faithfulness." A human being deposits a pledge with his friend, and he returns it worn out and ruined. But a person deposits his soul with the Holy One, blessed be He, every evening when it is tired, and He returns it to him new and refreshed. Thus far his words. Additionally, we are weary from the passage of time, and without divine providence, we would not be able to stand even for one day. Therefore, we bless that the Holy One, blessed be He, gives us strength, and the prophet said this verse regarding this matter.

And know that the blessing "Who removes sleep" is one blessing until "Who bestows good kindnesses upon His people Israel." There are those who say all the "May it be Your will" in the singular form: "that You accustom me to Your Torah, and attach me to Your commandments, and do not bring me...". And there are those who say that it is better to say it in the plural form: "that You accustom us..., and attach us..., and do not bring us..." as in the Traveler's Prayer in Siman 110 (Magen Avraham, small section 4, in the name of Orach Chayim). But in the Tur the version is in the singular form and this is the main version, since it is a singular blessing, and the beginning of the blessing is in the singular form: "Who removes sleep from my eyes." And likewise all the morning blessings, like "Who has provided me with all my needs." It is not similar to the Traveler's Prayer, which was established in the plural form (the Gra). And in the siddurim it is printed in the plural form, and this is the practice among the people. And in truth, we cannot understand the reasoning behind why there are blessings in the singular form like "Who has provided me with all my needs," "Who removes sleep from my eyes," and there are blessings in the plural form like "Who gives sight to the blind," "Who clothes the naked," "Who girds Israel," which are said about the community and not about oneself in particular. However, in any case, in the Gemara, Rambam, and Tur this blessing is entirely in the singular form, and it requires investigation as to why it is printed in the siddurim in the plural form. And know that one must say "May it be Your will" with a vav of connection, as it refers to the preceding.

In the time of the Talmud, each person would recite the morning blessings in his own place, because they were holy and careful that even in their sleep their hands would not touch covered parts of their bodies. But now it is impossible for each person to bless in his own place, as our hands are not clean. Although it is possible to clean them against a wall or some other item immediately upon rising, nevertheless, because there are many unlearned individuals who do not know this, and do not know these blessings at all, it has become customary to arrange them in the synagogue and answer "Amen" after them, thereby fulfilling their obligation. We ourselves each recite these blessings at home after washing hands, and also after cleansing when necessary. It is impossible for us to bless each one in its place for several reasons.

In Menachot (43b) it is taught: A person is obligated to recite three blessings every day: "Who has not made me a gentile," "Who has not made me a slave," "Who has not made me a woman." This is because a woman is exempt from Torah study and from positive commandments that are time-bound. Even a convert in ancient times could recite these two blessings: "Who has not made me a slave," and "Who has not made me a woman." But the first blessing he could not recite, since he was indeed a gentile. Some disagree even regarding the other two blessings (Bach), because he did not become an Israelite from his creation but through his choice. Some reconcile this (Taz, section 5 and Magen Avraham, section 10, see there). These blessings were instituted in a negative form to indicate that all are necessary in the world, but one's portion is better (Taz, section 4). If he were to bless "Who has made me an Israelite," it would imply that the making of others is not a making at all. Furthermore, since it is preferable for a person not to have been created than to have been created, it is impossible to bless on the creation except in a negative form (ibid.).

And know that in the Ashkenazic prayer books, these three blessings are printed at the beginning of the blessings, after the blessing of "Who gives the rooster understanding." In the Sephardic prayer books, they are printed at the end of the blessings. It seems to me that certainly according to the main law of the Gemara, where each blessing is recited at its appropriate time, these blessings remain for the end, because no action is contingent upon them. However, nowadays, when all blessings are arranged together, it is certainly proper to precede these three, as they pertain mainly to creation. And behold, our teacher wrote in Section 4 that women recite "Who has made me according to His will," and so it is printed in some prayer books. This is somewhat like justifying the judgment that she was created this way. However, this blessing is not mentioned in the Gemara, and to my knowledge, it is not customary to recite it nowadays. There are those who customarily recite additional blessings such as "Blessed is He who raises the lowly" and "Who supports the fallen," but they are mistaken, and one should protest against them. Therefore, one should reprimand those who print at the end of the prayer "Blessed are You, Lord" (the GRa"Z).

All these blessings, if one recited the second blessing before the first – he should still recite the first afterward. There are those who say that for two specific blessings it is not so: if one recited "who has not made me a woman" before "who has not made me a servant" – he should not afterward recite "who has not made me a servant." The reason is that a woman has a higher status, and since he already recited this blessing – how can he afterward bless for something of lesser status (Magen Avraham, end of subsection 9)? Similarly, if he recited "who straightens the bent" before reciting "who releases the bound" – he should not recite it afterward. The reason is that "who releases the bound" is said when one sits on his bed and stretches his limbs that were bound all night, and "who straightens the bent" is said when he stands up completely, and since he already blessed for his complete standing – how can he bless for something of lesser status? There are those who say there is no need to be concerned about this, for since the sages instituted these blessings – one should recite them even afterward (Rashal and Bach). Nevertheless, in case of doubt regarding blessings, one should be lenient (Magen Avraham, subsection 11). Know that also a blind person is obligated to recite these blessings, as well as a mamzer (child of forbidden relations), a tumtum (a person with indeterminate gender), and an androgynous person. However, they should not recite "who has not made me a woman," obviously. Some say that a blind person should not recite "who gives sight to the blind" (Magen Avraham, subsection 14). It seems that the custom is not to follow this opinion, and they bless according to the custom of the world, as will be explained later according to the opinion of our teacher, the Rema.

Our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 8: All these blessings, if one does not become obligated in one of them, such as not hearing the rooster's crow, or not walking, or not dressing, or not girding – one should recite that blessing without mentioning the Name. This is his language. And our master, the Rema, wrote: There are those who say that even if one is not obligated in them, one still recites them. For the blessing is not specifically about oneself but rather we bless that the Holy One, Blessed be He, created the needs of the world. And this is the custom and it should not be changed. This is his language. And this is not similar to the case where we do not recite on the Ninth of Av and Yom Kippur "who has provided me with all my needs," because all of Israel is forbidden to wear shoes then. Therefore, it appears clear to me that, according to our master the Rema, even if one did not sleep all night, one should still say the blessing "My God, the soul" and the blessing "Who removes sleep from my eyes." And I have seen one who wrote that if awake all night, one should not say these two blessings (Eliyah Rabbah section 12). But it does not seem so to me, for certainly according to the Beit Yosef, one should not say them. But according to our master the Rema, since we bless according to the general custom of the world, then here too it is the same. Therefore, the poskim did not speak about this. And when should one bless "Who gives the rooster understanding," whether specifically when the day begins to lighten or even before the light of day – it will be explained at the end of section 47, see there. And all the morning blessings can be recited simply even before the light of day. (And I have seen in Sha'arei Teshuvah section 12 that the opinion of the Ari, of blessed memory, is also to recite them even when awake all night. And likewise, a mourner can recite "who has provided me with all my needs" because one blesses according to the general custom of the world.)

Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote in paragraph 9: One should not recite verses before the blessing of the Torah, even if he says them as supplications. And there are those who say that there is no concern, since he is only saying them as supplications. And it is proper to be concerned with the first opinion. Thus far his words. And it is clear from his words that his opinion is lenient, that the prohibition is only to study before the blessing of the Torah, but not prayers and supplications. Therefore, even verses are meant only for supplications. And so Rabbeinu the Rema wrote that the custom follows the latter opinion, for during the days of Selichot, we pray the Selichot and afterwards make the blessing on the Torah along with the order of the other blessings. And similarly, every day when entering the synagogue, we say several verses and supplications, and afterwards bless on the Torah. It is customary to arrange the blessing of the Torah immediately after the blessing of "Asher Yatzar," and this should not be changed. Thus far his words. But we have the custom to say "Elokai Neshamah" after "Asher Yatzar," and then the blessing of the Torah. And if the body is completely clean, we say all the morning blessings up to "Gomel Chasadim..." and then the blessing of the Torah, as I wrote in Siman 6, paragraph 10, see there. Although this is not printed in the Siddurim, and the masses say as it is printed, nevertheless the main practice is as I have written.

It is also written that it is good to say after "Shema Yisrael" in the morning, "Blessed be the name of His glorious kingdom forever and ever." Because sometimes one delays with the recitation of Shema and recites it out of its proper time and fulfills the obligation with this. Thus is his wording. And one should intend conditionally: if the congregation will pass the time of the recitation of Shema, he fulfills the obligation with this. And if not, he does not fulfill the obligation with this, for it needs to be recited with its blessings. And after "Blessed be the name of His glorious kingdom forever and ever," one should recite the first paragraph (Magen Avraham, section 16). And on weekdays, this is not effective without tefillin (Dagul Mervavah). However, there are those who are not pleased with this, as how can we initially rely on reciting it without the blessings and also without connecting redemption to prayer (the Gra, section 19)? And many of the poskim (decisors of Jewish law) hold that it is necessary to recite specifically three paragraphs. But the truth is that this is good in the case where the congregation passes the time of the recitation of Shema, and there are people who initially rely on this every day, to put on tefillin and recite all three paragraphs of the Shema, and then pray after the time of the recitation of Shema. And this is certainly not correct to nullify the ordinance of the sages, for the sages established for us the order of the blessings, the recitation of Shema, and the prayer, and how can we say to do this after the time of the Shema regularly? And our teachers, when they permitted this, permitted it only in a case of necessity, and not regularly.

The text of the prayer that precedes "Baruch She'amar" is printed in the prayer books: When one enters the synagogue, one should say "Ma Tovu Ohalecha Yaakov..." "Adon Olam," "Yigdal." The Kabbalists are not pleased with the hymn "Yigdal," and the reason is explained in Section 1, Paragraph 13; see there. Afterward, all the morning blessings and the blessings of the Torah. Then the passage of the Akedah and "Master of the Universe... as our father Abraham subdued..." "A person should always be God-fearing in private and in public" (this should be said) "and admit the truth... therefore... fortunate are we... You are He before the world was created." One should not say "before You created the world" (Magen Avraham, end of subsection 16). And it concludes "Blessed are You, Lord, who sanctifies His name among the many." Some say: "who sanctifies Your name among the many." In the Sephardic rite, it is without the name, as this blessing is not found in the Talmud but is found in Tana Devei Eliyahu. Some have written that it is found in the Jerusalem Talmud, but I do not know its place. Afterwards, they say: "You are the Lord our God...," the passage of the Laver and the Terumat HaDeshen, the passage of the Tamid and the Ketoret, "Eizehu Mekoman," and "Psalm of the Song of the Dedication." In Section 51, the difference between the Ashkenazi and Sephardic rites will be explained.

The Ramban wrote in the Sefer HaMitzvot at the end of the positive commandments, and this is his wording: We are commanded to give thanks to His blessed name every time we are called to the Torah, for the great goodness He has done for us by giving His Torah to us, and informing us of the actions that are desirable before Him, by which we shall inherit the life of the World to Come... And in Berachot (21a) we say: From where do we derive the blessing over the Torah before it from the Torah itself? As it is written: "For the name of the Lord I will proclaim, ascribe greatness to our God." For the Torah is the name of the Lord, and the blessing over the Torah after it we learn from the blessing after meals, see there. And the Ramban wrote that from all this it is explained that this blessing is from the Torah. And it is not appropriate to count it as one commandment along with the reading, just as the recitation of the first fruits is not counted as one commandment with their bringing, and the retelling of the Exodus from Egypt with the eating of the Passover sacrifice. Thus far his wording.

All the great authorities agreed with his opinion that this blessing is of Torah origin (Pri Chadash, Magen Avraham, and Sha'agat Aryeh, Siman 24). They were puzzled by the Rambam for not listing this mitzvah, and certainly, he holds that this blessing is rabbinic like all blessings, and they struggled to explain his view. In my humble opinion, this is not the case, and Rambam also holds that it is of Torah origin, as is evident from the Talmud that we brought, and so it is in the Jerusalem Talmud at the beginning of Chapter Seven of Berachot. Rather, he holds that this is a part of the mitzvah of Torah study, and it is one mitzvah. And what the Ramban brought as proof from the verses about the bringing of the first fruits and their recitation that they are two mitzvot, and similarly the recounting of the Exodus with the eating of the Passover sacrifice, I am puzzled: there they are at two different times and there is an interruption between them, which is not the case with the blessing of the Torah where one must study a little immediately after the blessing as will be explained, and if so it is one mitzvah. And that Birkat HaMazon is considered a separate mitzvah even though its obligation is immediately after eating, this is because the eating is not a mitzvah but a necessity. But the study of Torah, which is a mitzvah – the blessing is part of the mitzvah. And see at the end of Section 21 that there is no interruption between them.

And there are some great authorities who inferred from the Jerusalem Talmud there, that for public Torah study, the blessing is of biblical origin, but for individual study, the blessing is rabbinic (Mishkenot Yaakov, Siman 60). For the Jerusalem Talmud, after expounding that the blessing before study is from the Torah based on the verse "For there..." and the blessing after study is derived from the Grace after Meals as in our Talmud, Rabbi Zeira says: "There is a question about these three readings that are read at Mincha on Shabbat and on Monday and Thursday, what should be done with them? Are they like three who ate together, and one blesses for all of them, or like three who ate separately, and each one blesses for himself, even the middle one blesses before and after?" Rabbi Shmuel said: "They did not learn the blessing of the Torah from the blessing of the invitation except for the public. And if for the public, even when alone, one should not bless." Rabbi Abba said: "They made it like all other commandments of the Torah; just as other commandments require a blessing, so too this requires a blessing." Thus far is the language of the Jerusalem Talmud, clearly indicating that the obligation for an individual is only rabbinic, like the blessings for all other commandments.

In my humble opinion, this is not so, and there is a different intention in the Jerusalem Talmud.
