Otherwise, how could it state that we learn the blessing over the Torah from the blessing of the zimmun? For it is not so, as we learn the first blessing from "When I call out the name of the Lord" and the last blessing from the Grace after Meals. And is an individual not obligated in the Grace after Meals from the Torah? However, the explanation of the matter is as follows: when we understand what the blessing after it is, in the Gemara and the Jerusalem Talmud, do we bless after it? Furthermore, what relevance does it have to the Torah afterwards, for one is obligated to always study day and night if it is within their ability? And if we say that the intention is regarding the public reading of the Torah, we cannot say this, for it lists there two or three blessings: "to engage in words of Torah," "and make the words of Your Torah sweet," and "Who has chosen us," and do we bless this in public? We only bless "Who has chosen us." Moreover, it is a clear halacha that what we bless in the Torah reading is only a rabbinic enactment and not because of the blessing of the Torah, as the Tosafot wrote in Rosh Hashanah (33a, beginning of "ha"), and this is their language: "And Rabbeinu Tam said that the blessing over the Torah before it and after it is not because of Torah study..., see there." And similarly, the Tur and Shulchan Aruch wrote later in Siman 139, see there.

It seems to me, upon careful consideration, why they established two blessings over the Torah, for where do we find two blessings for one matter? While it is reasonable that "V'haarev Na" is considered a blessing on its own according to Rambam's view, as will be explained, it is fitting to say it because it is a prayer that the sweetness of Torah be in our mouths and that we engage in it for its own sake. However, the blessing "Who has chosen us" seems entirely superfluous. While it is true that it will be explained that the three blessings correspond to Scripture, Mishnah, and Talmud, this is still not sufficient. It seems clear that this is in place of the final blessing, for during the reading of the Torah and when an individual is studying, a final blessing is not applicable, as there is no end to the study of Torah, as I have written. Therefore, they established it at the beginning (a similar idea is written by the Levush, see there). In the Gemara, they derived the final blessing through a kal v'chomer from Birkat Hamazon, and similarly, there is someone in the Jerusalem Talmud who says this. But first, it says there that we learned it through a gezeirah shavah of "Hashem-Hashem," see there. And in the Tosefta of Berachot, chapter six, and in the Gemara (48b), the Rabbis taught: From where do we derive Birkat Hamazon?... "And you shall bless" – this is the blessing of "Who sustains." "The Lord your God" – this is the blessing of the invitation. If so, the Jerusalem Talmud rightly says that they did not derive Birkat HaTorah from Birkat HaZimun except for the public, for since we derive it from a gezeirah shavah of "Hashem-Hashem" – this is Birkat HaZimun. And this is for the final blessing of "Who has chosen us" and not for the preceding ones, and this is only according to the Jerusalem Talmud's method that we derive this blessing from a gezeirah shavah. But according to our Gemara – this too is from the Torah. And it turns out that the first blessings are certainly from the Torah according to all opinions, only the final one can be said according to the Jerusalem Talmud to be Rabbinic for an individual.

And based on this, it is clear that if one is uncertain whether they have recited the blessings over the Torah or not, they must recite them again due to the principle of doubtful cases concerning Torah commandments. There are those who say that one should recite all the blessings (Pri Chadash), and there are those who say that one should only recite one blessing, as from the Torah, certainly, one is sufficient. Therefore, one should recite "Who has chosen us" because the Talmud refers to it as the most excellent of the blessings (Sha'agat Aryeh). However, based on what we have clarified, it seems that according to our Talmud, all the blessings are from the Torah. Nevertheless, it is preferable to be lenient like this opinion, as reducing the number of blessings is better. This is also the case if one remembers before "Ahava Rabba," for if one remembers afterward, "Ahava Rabba" exempts them, as will be explained. Certainly, if it is a day of Torah reading, it is advisable to have an aliyah to the Torah, thereby fulfilling the obligation in any case.

The blessing over the Torah is exceedingly great. Our sages of blessed memory said in Nedarim (81a) that due to this sin (not reciting the blessing over the Torah), the Land of Israel was destroyed. This showed that the sanctity of the Torah was not cherished by them, and they learned it only as if it were other wisdoms (see the Ran there). Indeed, it is the precious vessel of the Holy One, blessed be He, and with it, He rejoiced even before the creation of heaven and earth. And we, the people of Israel, have nothing in the world of greater importance than it. The entire Torah consists of His blessed names, as it is written: "Your name is like purified oil." Through it, we merit the life of the World to Come and the life of this world. For its sake, the world was created, as it is written: "Were it not for My covenant day and night, I would not have established the laws of heaven and earth." Therefore, one must be exceedingly careful with it. One may recite the blessing over the Torah either standing or sitting.

One must recite a blessing whether for the Torah, the Mishnah, the Talmud, or the Midrash, referring to the interpretation of the Scriptures in Mekhilta, Sifra, and Sifrei (Rashi, Berakhot 11b). And know that there is a doubt regarding one who studies Aggadah, such as Midrash Rabbah or the wisdom of Kabbalah, if he is obligated to recite the blessing of the Torah. For in the Gemara there, there is a dispute: Rav Huna said that only for the Torah is a blessing required, and Rabbi Yochanan said that also for the Mishnah a blessing is required (according to the Rif's version). And the students of Rabbeinu Yonah explained: because the Mishnah explains the reasons for the mitzvot. And Rabbi Elazar said that also for the Talmud a blessing is required, because the Talmud explains the fundamentals of the verses (students of Rabbeinu Yonah). And the conclusion is that also for the Midrash a blessing is required, because in the Midrash one also learns from the legal principles like "kal vachomer," "gezera shava," and the hermeneutical rules by which the Torah is expounded (there). According to this, it seems that the obligation is only for things that explain the laws of the Torah. But the words of Aggadah or Kabbalah, whose main purpose is not laws and halachot – do not require a blessing. However, if we say the reason is because everything was given to Moses at Sinai (Gra"z), or because all of it is called Torah (Levush) – it is obvious that also Aggadah and Kabbalah were given to Moses at Sinai and are called "Torah." But from the language of the students of Rabbeinu Yonah, it does not seem so, and it requires further investigation for the halacha.

Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote in Section 3: "One who writes words of Torah, even though he is not reading, must recite a blessing." Thus is his wording. And in Section 4 he wrote: "One who contemplates words of Torah does not need to recite a blessing." Thus is his wording. And Rabbeinu the Rema wrote: "And the same applies, that one can render a legal ruling without providing a reason for his words." Thus is his wording. And it has already been questioned that his words contradict each other, for since in contemplation one does not need to recite a blessing because we hold that "contemplation is not equivalent to speech," if so, why does one who writes need to recite a blessing? For there is only contemplation here (Taz, subsection 2, and the Gra, subsection 1). And there are those who have disputed the fundamental ruling, and hold that there is also a mitzvah in contemplation, as it is written: "You shall meditate on it day and night." And "meditation" is in the heart, as it is written: "And the meditation of my heart." Therefore, one must recite a blessing in contemplation (the Gra, subsection 2). And in truth, the Beit Yosef himself in his great work "Bedek HaBayit" felt this, for at the beginning of the section he brought from Rabbeinu David Abudraham that one who writes must recite a blessing, and at the end of the section he brings in the name of the Agur that in contemplation one does not need to recite a blessing. And he noted at the beginning of the section regarding the ruling of Rabbeinu David Abudraham, and this is his wording: "And see what I will write later in the name of the Agur." Thus is his wording, indicating that he felt they contradict each other. If so, why did he establish both rulings in the Shulchan Aruch? This requires further study.

And it appears to me, in my humble opinion, that our master the Beit Yosef holds that these two laws do not contradict each other. For although there certainly is a mitzvah in contemplating Torah, nonetheless the primary mitzvah of Torah study is learning verbally. For many times we find in the Tanach that "Hegayon" refers to verbal speech, such as "And my tongue shall utter Thy righteousness," "The mouth of the righteous utters wisdom," "They do not utter with their throats," "For my palate shall utter truth." And where the intention is about the heart, it is written there with the term "heart," such as: "And the meditation of my heart," "And the meditations of my heart are understanding." And in Proverbs: "The heart of the righteous meditates to answer," "For their heart meditates violence." And if so, in the Torah where it is written: "And you shall meditate on it day and night," and similarly: "And in His Torah he meditates day and night" – it means verbally, since it does not mention "heart." And the blessing on the Torah itself proves it, as we say "Make the words of Your Torah pleasant … in our mouths and in the mouths of Your people …" And similarly "to engage in words of Torah" – means verbal speech. And in Eruvin (54a), they were strict even on one who learns quietly, and they expounded "arranged in all and preserved" – that it should be arranged in all your 248 limbs, see there. Therefore, the blessing on the Torah was not instituted for contemplation of Torah, only for verbal study. However, writing is different, for this is the main fulfillment of the Torah. Not only the Written Torah, but even the Oral Torah after they permitted writing it – it is like teaching Torah to many, for the main fulfillment of the Torah is through writing, and without writing, the Torah would have already been forgotten from Israel. Therefore, since during writing one contemplates in his heart and brings it out through writing – it is like speech, and one is obligated to bless. And so it appears to me, in my humble opinion, to be the main law. (And so it is implied in the Mechilta and the Midrash at the beginning of "Yitro," that writing is like speech.)

And it is obvious that this only applies to someone who writes as part of their study. However, a scribe who copies words of Torah without paying attention to understand them does not need to recite a blessing, as this is not considered learning at all. Similarly, someone who writes secular matters, even if they include verses or some teachings of our sages in the middle of their writing, does not need to recite a blessing because the main purpose of their writing is for secular matters (Magen Avraham, section 1). Likewise, when someone responds to a question with "forbidden," "permitted," "kosher," or "invalid," since they do not explain the reason, it is considered like mere contemplation, and they do not recite a blessing, even though it is a great mitzvah. And this is the custom.

The first blessing is: "Who has sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us regarding the words of Torah." Meaning: to speak and learn in Torah. The Ashkenazim have the version "to engage in the words of Torah," and "engage" refers to toil in it. There are those who wrote that there is a difference in the interpretation of the blessing between the versions, that when one blesses "regarding the words of Torah," it also refers to the practice of the commandments. And "to engage in the words of Torah" refers only to Torah study (as mentioned in subsection 3). And I am puzzled: for regarding the practice of the commandments, there is a separate blessing for each commandment. Moreover, the early authorities did not write that there is a difference in intention between them, and certainly "regarding the words of Torah" also refers only to Torah study, as is evident from what we say afterward, "and make the words of Your Torah sweet in our mouths," which is only about Torah study.

Afterwards, we say: "And please, Hashem, our God, make the words of Your Torah sweet in our mouths and in the mouths of Your people, the House of Israel. May we and our descendants, all of us, know Your Name and study Your Torah for its own sake. Blessed are You, Hashem, Who teaches Torah to His people Israel." Some have the version: "our descendants and the descendants of our descendants." There is no need for this, as "our descendants" already implies our progeny for many generations (there). According to Tosafot and the Rosh, this is one blessing together with "to engage in the words of Torah," and with the blessing we pray that we will study with sweetness and for its own sake. Since it contains many elements, it begins with "Blessed" and ends with "Blessed." They phrase "and please make" with a conjunctive vav because it refers to the previous part. However, Maimonides holds that it is a separate blessing and phrases "please make" without a vav. Afterwards, we bless: "Who chose us from all the nations and gave us His Torah. Blessed are You, Hashem, Who gives the Torah." We say "Who gives" in the present tense because at every moment the Holy One, blessed be He, grants and gives a person understanding to comprehend His Torah, especially since there are new insights in Torah every day. According to Maimonides, there are three blessings corresponding to Scripture, Mishnah, and Gemara. According to Tosafot and the Rosh, there are two blessings corresponding to the Written Torah and the Oral Torah. Rabbi Moshe Isserles wrote that it is better to say "and please make" with a vav, but in any case, we can answer "Amen" after "to engage in the words of Torah." This is also the practice of the Ari z"l (see Magen Avraham and Taz, small section 5).

The matter of these blessings that we recite beforehand is similar to the blessings recited before performing any mitzvah. Afterwards, we bless that He should grant us wisdom, understanding, sweetness, and a pure heart "for its own sake." This is because in this regard, the study of Torah is not like other mitzvot. In all other mitzvot, their performance is with physical organs, while this mitzvah originates in the heart and mind. If one does not understand what he learns, his learning is meaningless. If his intention is not "for its own sake," his learning is meaningless. Therefore, one must bless in the manner of a request, asking that God help us to know His Torah and study it properly. Afterwards, we recite a blessing of thanks, for having chosen us and given us His holy and pure Torah. We have also written that this blessing takes the place of the blessing that follows, as I wrote in section 5. And in the public reading of the Torah, we bless first "Who has chosen us..." and then "Who has given us...," which is not because of the study of Torah but because of a specific ordinance they instituted, as I wrote in section 4. They instituted these blessings, which are blessings of thanks, as the Tur wrote, that one should intend in this blessing regarding the standing at Mount Sinai, when He made us hear His words out of the fire and gave us His precious instrument, which is the most exalted of blessings. After the reading, we say “and eternal life He implanted within us,” for eternal life is only for the Torah and mitzvot that the Blessed God has granted us, which is the Oral Torah along with the Written Torah.

I have a major question regarding these two blessings: these are short blessings, so why do they conclude with "Blessed"? I haven't found anyone who addressed this. It seems to me that even though "Who gives the Torah" is similar to the opening, it has a different intention. The opening refers to the fact that He gave us the Torah at the event of Mount Sinai, which is a blessing on the past, but the conclusion "Who gives the Torah" refers to His giving it to us every day, as I wrote in paragraph 13. Therefore, it is a different blessing, but they established them together as a kind of opening and conclusion.

It is stated in Berachot (11b) that if one has not studied until after reciting the Shema, he does not need to recite the blessing for the Torah, as he has already fulfilled it with "Ahava Rabbah," which contains an element of the blessing for the Torah: "And instill in our hearts to study and to teach..." (Rashi). And even though the main aspect of the blessing is its beginning and conclusion, it seems to me that both references to the giving of the Torah are mentioned here. Since we say "With great love have You loved us" or "With eternal love," and conclude with "Who chooses His people Israel with love," this is indeed the blessing for the Torah itself, as there is no greater love and eternal love than the giving of the Torah.

Our rabbis, the Tosafists, wrote, and this is their language: In the Jerusalem Talmud, there is the statement that one has already fulfilled their obligation with the "Ahavah Rabbah" blessing, provided they immediately engage in study at that place. Explanation: immediately, meaning learning right at that spot. And Rabbi Yitzchak was asked: For us, who do not learn immediately after the morning prayer, as we are busy and go without learning until midday or later, why do we not recite the blessing over the Torah again when we start learning? And Rabbi Yitzchak answered... that specifically "Ahavah Rabbah," which is not primarily a blessing for the study of Torah, does not exempt one from the blessing over the Torah unless they study immediately and also do not have a distraction of thought. But the blessings "Who has chosen us" and "to engage in the words of Torah," which are primarily blessings for the study of Torah, exempt for the entire day... as one does not despair in their mind. For every hour a person is obligated to study, and it is as if they are sitting the whole day without interruption... And the French have the custom to say verses, the Priestly Blessing, and also the Mishna of "These are the things..." because of the Jerusalem Talmud that requires study immediately... until here is their language, and so wrote the Rosh and the Tur, see there.

And our teacher, the Beit Yosef, in his great book, and all the prominent authorities hold the same intention of the Tosafot, that the blessing "Ahava Rabba" only exempts one (from the obligation to say the blessing for Torah study) if one learns immediately after the blessing, and then it exempts. But with the blessing of the Torah – one does not need to learn immediately after the blessing, and it exempts for the entire day. And even though for all other commandments the act of the commandment needs to be close to the blessing, and if there is an interruption between the blessing and the commandment one has to bless again, the blessing of the Torah is different. Since one is obligated to engage in it always – an interruption is not considered an interruption, as one is obligated to learn then (Beit Yosef). Meaning: in Torah study, there is no concept of distraction of thought, that one would be obligated to bless again if there was an interruption between the blessing and the learning (Magen Avraham, subsection 7, and Taz, subsection 6).

Based on this, our teacher the Beit Yosef wrote in Section 9: Some say that if one interrupts between the blessing on the Torah and his learning, it doesn't matter. However, it is proper not to interrupt between them. Therefore, it is customary to recite the passage of the Priestly Blessing immediately after the blessing on the Torah. This is the end of his words. This means: even though according to the law it is not necessary, nevertheless, it is proper not to interrupt. And one can recite the Priestly Blessing even before dawn. And even though the Priestly Blessing is not recited at night, nevertheless, he is not saying it because of the Priestly Blessing but because of Torah study (there in subsection 8), unlike those who require saying it specifically at dawn. And our teacher the Beit Yosef further wrote according to this interpretation in Section 7 that the blessing "Ahavat Olam" exempts the blessing on the Torah if one learns immediately without pause. This is the end of his words. And then it exempts the learning for the whole day (there in subsection 6).

However, they themselves raised a significant question regarding this: How does the Jerusalem Talmud state "and that is when he reviewed it on the spot," implying that it is possible he did not study on the spot? For it is necessarily studied immediately after "Ahavat Olam," when one recites the three paragraphs of the Shema? And is it because these also contain the mitzvah of reciting the Shema that it does not count as Torah study? This is puzzling. And he answered that the recitation of the Shema and prayer are not considered study for this purpose, as supplication and prayer are one thing, and Torah study is another (Beit Yosef and Taz, subsection 7). Additionally, he answered that it is possible he did not recite the Shema after "Ahavat Olam," as was the case in the Temple at the end of the first chapter of Berakhot (Beit Yosef). Based on this, he wrote in subsection 8 that one should be uncertain whether it suffices to recite the Shema immediately afterward without interruption. Therefore, one should be careful to bless the blessing of the Torah before "Ahavat Olam." Thus far is his language.

In truth, all these explanations are forced, as is clear to the one who delves into it. Were it not for their words, it would seem that our Rabbis of the Tosafists were not referring to the interruption between the blessing and the study. For it is an obvious matter that one must study a bit immediately after the blessing of the Torah, just as with all commandments that need to follow the blessing without interruption. And if one interrupts, one must go back and bless again. The difference between "Ahava Rabba" and the blessing of the Torah is only that the blessing of the Torah exempts one for the entire day, while "Ahava Rabba" exempts only what is studied immediately. This is what the Jerusalem Talmud says: "And that is if he studies immediately," meaning that it exempts only what is studied immediately after the prayer. But if one interrupted, even if he studied immediately, he must bless the blessing of the Torah when he sits to study. This is what they asked Rabbi Yitzchak: if so, every time one sits to study, one must bless the blessing of the Torah, since they thought there is no difference between "Ahava Rabba" and the blessing of the Torah. He responded that this applies only to "Ahava Rabba" and not to the blessing of the Torah itself. (And what they wrote, "and the French... and also these things... because of the Jerusalem Talmud..." their intention is: they also study Mishnah immediately, because they hold that only what is studied immediately is exempted by the blessing of the Torah. And I think that the Tosafists also explained it this way, see there. However, the language of the Rosh implies according to both explanations, see there. And similarly, the Gaon "Even HaOzer" wrote in a different manner, see there. Therefore, what we say some words of Torah after the blessing of the Torah, this is the main law. And so it is explained in the words of the Rambam in the seventh chapter, halacha 11, see there. According to "Even HaOzer," one needs Scripture, Mishnah, and Gemara or halacha. See the Gra, small paragraph 7).

The Tur wrote: If one recited the blessing for the Torah and began to study but then interrupted, he does not need to recite the blessing again all day if he is accustomed to always engage in Torah study... until here is his language. This implies that if he is not accustomed, he needs to recite the blessing. And similarly, it is implied from the words of Rabbeinu Beit Yosef in paragraph 10, who wrote: If he stopped studying and engaged in his business, since his intention is to return to study, it is not considered an interruption. The same applies to sleep, the bathhouse, and the bathroom, which are not considered interruptions. Until here is his language. This also implies that only if his intention is to return to study does he not need to recite the blessing (Magen Avraham, small paragraph 9). And so wrote the Rosh in his response, general 4 (paragraph 62). And there are those who wrote that one does not need to intend to study further (Taz, small paragraph 8). However, this is not according to the opinion of the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, although the custom is indeed so. Nevertheless, since the custom is so, everyone behaves as if they had this intention at the time of the blessing, covering all "from time to time." But regarding the interruptions of sleep, the bathhouse, and the bathroom, which are not considered interruptions, it needs examination, because since one cannot study then, the intention does not help, as with the phylacteries (Gra, small paragraph 9). And there are those who wrote that there are several laws concerning the bathhouse and the bathroom (Agur), and this is not related to the blessing of the Torah, which does not need a blessing (Gra, there). And it must be said that Torah study is not similar in this regard to all other commandments, because in all other commandments, since there is no obligation on one the entire day, the place where one cannot fulfill the commandment is considered an interruption. But this is not the case with Torah study, for which there is an obligation all day and all night when one has the time to study—nothing interrupts.

And this is what our Rabbi, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 11: "A fixed sleep during the day on one's bed is considered an interruption. Some say it is not considered an interruption, and this is the custom." Until here are his words. Seemingly, the primary opinion is the first one. However, according to the reason we have explained, it makes sense, since he is compelled to study, nothing constitutes an interruption. And anyone who recites the blessing over the Torah has in mind a 24-hour period, similar to the morning blessings. And this is what he wrote in section 12: "Even if one studied at night, the night follows the past day, and there is no need to bless again as long as one has not slept." Until here are his words. Meaning, that every 24-hour period requires reciting the blessing over the Torah, and only when one goes to sleep at night does the 24-hour period end. That is, when one wakes from sleep at night, even if the 24-hour period from the previous blessing has not yet completely ended, nevertheless, upon rising to study, one must recite the blessing over the Torah, as one's intention is up to the time of waking, like all the morning blessings. And if one does not sleep all night, one does not bless until the morning light. There are those who interpret his words to mean that if one does not sleep at all, one does not need to bless at all. They are puzzled by this (see Magen Avraham, section 11, who wrote this and questioned it). But indeed, this is not his intention, rather as I have written. One does not meticulously count the 24-hour period as less or more, rather that every day one blesses the blessing over the Torah, or when one rises from bed, whether at night or in the morning light. And this is the simple custom and should not be changed. And if one rises from bed with the intention to sleep again, it seems to me that if one rises before midnight, one should not bless, and bless the second time upon rising. And if after midnight, one should bless. And it seems that this is the opinion of the Kabbalists, that after midnight is considered as day (see Sha'arei Teshuvah, section 12). But if one does not intend to sleep again, then one blesses even upon rising before midnight.

And this is what our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in paragraph 13: One who rises before dawn to study must recite the blessing for Torah study. He does not need to recite the blessing again when he goes to the synagogue. So are his words. And this is as I have written, that anyone who rises from his bed – the "twenty-four-hour period" is completed and he must recite the blessing. He further wrote that one who rises before dawn recites the entire order of blessings, except for the blessing "Who gives the rooster understanding" and the section of the Tamid offering, which he should wait to say until daybreak. So are his words. For the Tamid offering is not brought at night, and this is also written by the Tur. And if he hears the rooster's crow – he blesses after midnight the blessing "Who gives the rooster...". According to the Kabbalah, even without hearing the rooster's crow, one can recite this blessing after midnight upon rising from his bed (see Magen Avraham and Sha'arei Teshuvah, subsection 13). And some follow this practice.

Women recite the blessings over the Torah. Even though they are not commanded to engage in Torah study, and are exempt from its recitation, nevertheless, since they are obligated in prayer, and it has been established as an obligation for them to recite the Shema, the verses of praise, and the Song of the Sea, and there are those who maintain that they are obligated to learn the laws applicable to them (Sefer Mitzvot Gadol). Similarly, they customarily recite blessings over all positive time-bound commandments. Likewise, in the Grace after Meals, they say "and for Your Torah which You have taught us." Therefore, for all these reasons, they are permitted to recite the blessings. (And it must be said that this is the intention of the Shulchan Aruch, Section 14, and the Magen Avraham, Subsection 14. Additionally, in ancient times, a convert would also recite the blessings over the Torah. Examine this and you will find it clear.)

After he has finished the morning blessings, the blessing over the Torah, the passage of the Binding of Isaac, the passage of the removal of the ashes, the passage of the laver, and the blessing "Who sanctifies His name in public," all of which can be recited even before the light of day, when the day begins to shine – he should recite the passage of the daily offering: "My offering, My food..." At the end of this, he should say the verse "And he shall slaughter it on the side..." After this, he should say "You are He... the incense of spices...", the passage of the incense, the eleven spices... and the related Baraitot, and the order of the arrangement, which means "Abaye would arrange...", and "Ana Bekoach", and also "Master of the Universe, You commanded us...", as printed in the siddurim. This is based on what is said at the end of tractate Megillah (31b) regarding the verse "By what shall I know?", where the Holy One, blessed be He, said to Abraham that even when the Temple is destroyed, He has arranged for them the order of the sacrifices. As long as they read them, He considers it as if they are offering a sacrifice before Him, and He forgives all their sins, see there. After this, they recite the Mishnah "What is the location", and the Baraita of Rabbi Yishmael, because it includes all the principles of the Oral Torah. And "What is the location" is the essence of the sacrifices. There are those who require standing during the recitation of the sacrifices, since the offering of a sacrifice is only done while standing (Magen Avraham). And we have already written in section 1, paragraph 26 that many disagree with this, see there.

On Shabbat, after the incense, one recites the verses of the Musaf offering: "And on the Shabbat day, two lambs..." because the incense precedes the additional offerings. However, the section "B'zichin" (about the frankincense) is not customary to recite, and none of the poskim (decisors of Jewish law) mentioned this. It appears to me that the reason is because at the beginning of the chapter "Tamid Nishchat" it states that the frankincense is offered after midday, see there. Therefore, it was not established in the prayer at all.

But on Rosh Chodesh (the New Moon), we do not say "U'veroshei Chodsheichem" (the verse about the New Moon offerings), because it is read in the Torah. However, in Ashkenaz (Germany), they do recite it on Rosh Chodesh (Tur), and the reason is to publicize that it is Rosh Chodesh. Similarly, it is mentioned at the end of Shekalim that they would place the parts of the Rosh Chodesh offering on top of the altar to publicize that it is Rosh Chodesh, see there.

And the matter appears to me that Shabbat and Yom Tov (festival days) do not need publicity, as preparation is done on the eve of Shabbat and the eve of Yom Tov, and there is a prohibition of work on them. This is not the case with Rosh Chodesh – it requires publicity.

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (the Rema) wrote that those who are meticulous have the custom to sway when they read the Torah, similar to the Torah that was given with trembling. Similarly, when they pray, based on the verse "All my bones shall say...". This is his exact wording. The Torah is called "fire," and fire is always in motion. During the Shemoneh Esrei prayer, some sway and some do not sway. It depends on the person's nature; if swaying helps one to concentrate better, it is proper to sway. There are people who concentrate better when they stand completely still and do not sway. All is done for the sake of Heaven. In the Zohar, there is a reason given for why Jews sway; see there in Pinchas, page 218b, for an important reason on this matter.

It is stated in Gittin (60a) that matters written in the Torah – you are not permitted to say them by heart. And it is derived from a verse, see there. Now, we pray by heart, and indeed, in the prayers, there are many Psalms, the Shema, the Song of the Sea, the Binding of Isaac, and the sacrifices. How can we recite them by heart? However, in contrast to this, we find in Yoma (70a) that the High Priest would recite "On the tenth" from the Book of Numbers by heart on Yom Kippur. And in Ta'anit (28a) regarding the Ma'amadot, the members of the Ma'amadot would recite the sections of "Genesis", we say that in Shacharit and Mussaf they enter the synagogue and read (from a scroll), but in Mincha, an individual would recite it by heart (and the Ra'av writes because of the burden of the fast). Rabbi Yose said: Can an individual recite Torah matters by heart in public? Rather, they all enter and recite it by heart as they recite the Shema, see there.

And it is explained from the language of Rabbi Yossi that the prohibition is only when an individual reads by heart in public. But each person reading for themselves – it is permitted. According to this, in our case where each person says it for themselves – there is no prohibition at all. And it appears that this is the intention of the Tosafot in Temurah (14b) where they wrote: "And if you say: How do we recite psalms by heart? One could say that it is only stringent regarding what is written in the Chumash. However, it is difficult to understand how we recite 'Vayosha' and the Shema?" One could say that it is only stringent in a context where one is fulfilling the obligation for others. This is their language. And the same intent is with the matter in Ta'anit, that an individual cannot read by heart in public, meaning: because they are fulfilling the obligation for others. And regarding the fact that the High Priest used to read by heart, one could say that there it was not to fulfill their obligation, as they were not obligated in it at all. And this is also explained in the Zohar Vayakhel (folio 106b) that it is only forbidden in public when reading from the Torah.

In the Jerusalem Talmud, Yoma, it is stated that the order of the day may be recited by heart, see there. The Tosafot Yeshanim in Yoma also wrote this based on the Jerusalem Talmud, see there. Additionally, they wrote that it is merely a preferred mitzvah not to recite by heart things that are written, and there is no prohibition in the matter. They further wrote that it is only forbidden to recite by heart in order to fulfill the obligation for others, as the Tosafot wrote in Temurah which we have cited. They also wrote: How then does the prayer leader say Hallel and fulfill the obligation for others? And they answered: Since it is only praise and thanksgiving, it is not a concern, see there. This means that the main concern is with the Torah, which is the primary study. This is also the intention of the Tosafot in Temurah, who wrote that one should only be concerned with what is written in the Chumash, because this is the primary Torah study. The Mordechai in Gittin wrote in the name of Rabbeinu Tam that anything commonly spoken by everyone is permitted. The Tur also wrote this reasoning, and in the name of the Rosh, he wrote the opinion of the Tosafot that it is only forbidden to fulfill the obligation for others, see there. Rabbeinu Beit Yosef did not write anything except the opinion of the Mordechai in the Shulchan Aruch, see there. Some have written that anything obligatory is permitted to say by heart (Turei Zahav brought in Beit Yosef). This is not found in the Rambam at all. Perhaps he holds that just as it is forbidden to write oral matters, but it was permitted because of "It is time to act for the Lord," similarly with written matters that are forbidden to recite by heart, it is also permitted because it is impossible for everyone to have a book during prayers and hymns. We have written all the words of our Rabbis on this matter. According to this, there is not much concern in this matter, as we have great authorities to rely on. I do not understand why some have been stringent in this matter (see Magen Avraham and Shaarei Teshuva). A blind person is permitted to recite by heart due to "It is time to act for the Lord" (there). Some have written that when reciting the passage by heart while the prayer leader is reading, I am careful but do not object to others (there in the name of Radbaz). According to the Tosafot and the Rosh, who said that it is only forbidden to fulfill the obligation for many, I do not see any concern in this matter, as he is reciting for himself.

After the section of the Tamid and the Ketoret, they established the chapter "Eizehu Mekoman" and the Baraita of Rabbi Yishmael due to what is stated in Kiddushin (30a) that a person must study scripture, Mishnah, and Talmud every day. Scripture is abundant in the prayer, and for the Mishnah, they established "Eizehu Mekoman" because it is written, "In every place incense is offered to My name" (Malachi 1:11). Is incense offered in every place? Rather, these are the Torah scholars who are engaged in the (Temple) service everywhere—I consider it as if they are offering and presenting to My name (Menachot 110a). And in this chapter, all the sacrifices are included, and it is without dispute. And the Baraita of the Thirteen Principles, because this is the fundamental generality of the Oral Torah. And it is repeated at the beginning of "Torat Kohanim" at the head of all the sacrifices. And the Midrash of the Torah is considered like the Talmud, and therefore they established it after "Eizehu Mekoman." And one must understand what they are learning, for if not, it is not considered learning. And it has already been explained in Siman 1 that for the Olah, Todah, and Shelamim offerings, one should say "May it be Your will as if I had offered (them)," see there.

There are those who say that in the house of a mourner, this (prayer) is not recited because it is considered a study, and the mourner is prohibited from studying Torah. But this is not so, for anything that is part of the daily order is permitted. And since it has been established as part of the daily order, it is like the entire prayer service, as I have written in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 384.

And know that the prayer until after the Amidah (the Eighteen Benedictions) is divided into four sections: the first until "Baruch She'amar", the second until "Yotzer Or" which includes the Verses of Song (Pesukei Dezimra), the third from "Yotzer Or" until "Ga'al Yisrael" and the fourth is the Amidah. These divisions allude to lofty and hidden matters. There is a difference between the Ashkenazi and Sephardi nusach (prayer rite): in the Ashkenazi nusach, after the Baraita of Rabbi Yishmael, they say "Mizmor Shir Chanukat" and then "Baruch She'amar", followed by "Hodu" until "Romemu" and other selected verses such as "V'hu Rachum", "Hashem Tzvaot", and "Mizmor L'Todah". Then they recite eighteen selected verses from "Yehi Chavod" until "Ashrei", and "Ashrei" until the end of the Verses of Song. Thus, "Hodu" and all these verses are also included in the Verses of Song, since they are also words of praise. The Sephardim say all of this except for "Mizmor L'Todah" before "Baruch She'amar", as they hold that the main part of the Verses of Song starts from "Tehillah L'David". They additionally include verses of "Hashem Malach..." and "Lamenatzeach B'Nigginot". Both are the words of the living God, and each place follows its custom. One should not change to avoid dispute, and it is also like "Do not cut yourselves" (a prohibition against causing divisions).

And the reason for reciting these verses: "A Psalm of Song for the Dedication" was said by Solomon at the time he brought the Ark into the Holy of Holies, and he was not answered until he mentioned the merit of David, as it is stated in Shabbat (30a). And since all the verses of praise are the verses of King David, therefore, they precede this psalm wherein his righteousness is revealed. And therefore, they did not include it within the verses of praise (this seems to me). And the verses "Give thanks to the Lord, call upon His name" are mentioned in Seder Olam, that all the years the Ark was under a curtain, David instituted the recitation of this psalm. And the verses "The Lord of Hosts," we say in the Jerusalem Talmud, chapter "One does not stand," that these verses should never depart from your mouth, see there. And the eighteen verses of "May the glory" correspond to the eighteen blessings of the Amidah. Therefore, even according to the Sephardic custom, they included them within the verses of praise.

It is stated in Berachot (32a): A person should always arrange the praise of the Omnipresent, and then pray. From where do we derive this? From Moses, as it is written: “And I implored the Lord… O Lord God, You have begun to show Your servant Your greatness and Your mighty hand… Let me, I pray, cross over” (Deuteronomy 3:23-25). Therefore, before the recitation of Shema and the prayer, we arrange the praise of the Omnipresent in the Psalms of Praise (Pesukei Dezimra) which King David, peace be upon him, said at the end of the Book of Psalms, from “A Psalm of David” (Psalm 145) to “Let every soul praise the Lord” (Psalm 150), for there are many praises there. It is said in Shabbat (118b): May my portion be with those who complete the Psalms of Praise every day. And it is said: Whoever says “A Psalm of David” three times every day is assured that he is a son of the World to Come (Berachot 4b), because it is arranged according to the alphabet and contains the verse “You open Your hand.” Preceding it are two verses of “Ashrei”: “Happy are those who dwell in Your house” and “Happy is the people for whom this is so.” And even in the time of the Talmud it was so, as they said there: Why is the letter Nun not included in “Ashrei”? See there, and they did not say “in A Psalm of David.” The reason is that from the verse “Happy are those who dwell in Your house” we learn that one must pause a little before prayer (Berachot 32a). And this is its interpretation: “Happy are those who dwell in Your house” and afterwards “they will still praise You, Selah.” Incidentally, they also added “Happy is the people…” because it is a great praise for Israel, as is evident. At the end of “A Psalm of David,” they added the verse “And we will bless… Hallelujah,” in order to connect “Hallelujah” after “Hallelujah” (Tur), because all these psalms end with “Hallelujah” and begin with “Hallelujah,” and “A Psalm of David” does not end with “Hallelujah.” Therefore, they appended this verse so that it too would end with “Hallelujah.” (And the expression “to connect” which the Tur wrote in the name of Rabbi Akiva Gaon clarifies that they should be said together, the “Hallelujah” at the end with the “Hallelujah” at the beginning without interruption. Some have this custom. There are ten “Hallelujahs,” and they hint at lofty matters as known to the understanding. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

They instituted a blessing before the Verses of Praise (Pesukei D'Zimra) and after them. The preceding blessing is "Baruch She'amar," and it must be said with melody and pleasantness because it is a beautiful and delightful song. It is written in the Book of Heichalot that it contains eighty-seven words, and a mnemonic for this is "His head is refined gold" (Tur). It also contains the word "Baruch" (blessed) thirteen times, corresponding to the thirteen attributes, to draw a blessing from each attribute. Additionally, there are thirteen aspects of praise in the Verses of Praise, which are: "Hodu," "Mizmor LeTodah," the verses of "Yehi Kavod," "Ashrei," five psalms of "Hallelujah," "Baruch Hashem LeOlam Amen VeAmen," "Vayevarech David," "V'Choret," and the Song at the Sea – totaling thirteen. Correspondingly, they instituted the word "Baruch" to be said thirteen times (this is my opinion). "Baruch She'amar" is said standing, even when alone. They say "B'feh Amo" and not "B'fi." The closing is "B'tishbachot," with a chirik under the letter Tav (Magen Avraham, section 1). They say "V'nagdilcha V'nashabchacha V'nifarcha V'namalicha, V'nazkir Shimcha Malkeinu Eloheinu." In the prayer books, it is printed "V'nazkir Shimcha V'namalicha Malkeinu," but this is incorrect. This was edited by someone who thought to connect "V'namalicha" with "Malkeinu," and they erred in this, as the original texts had it as I have written (Ma'adanei Yom Tov in the fifth chapter of Brachot, section 17). This is also the Sephardic version, and this is the correct version. It is customary to hold two fringes (tzitzit).

This blessing of "Baruch She'amar" is different from all other blessings. For all blessings that open with "Baruch" and conclude with "Baruch" – we start the blessing with "Blessed are You, Hashem, our God, King of the universe," whereas "Baruch She'amar" is said in the middle of the blessing at "the merciful Father who is praised by the mouth of His people." Why was it not established at the beginning like all other blessings? Therefore, it appears to me in my humble opinion that indeed the main blessing of "Pesukei Dezimra" starts from "the merciful Father who is praised." It is necessary to say so, for every blessing relates to the matter that we are blessing for. And indeed, from "Baruch She'amar" until "praised by the mouth of His people," there is no mention at all of praise and hymns. According to this, the blessing indeed starts in the middle, and they only attached "Baruch She'amar" until "Baruch Shemo" because the Men of the Great Assembly wanted to mention at the beginning of the prayer how the world was created by the word of the Holy One, blessed be He, and how in His goodness He renews the act of Creation every day continually, and this is "Blessed is He who makes the beginning." In the Sephardic version, it is after "Blessed is He who speaks and acts, Blessed is He who decrees and fulfills," because these two refer to the moment of creation, and "who makes the beginning" refers to every day. And they wanted to mention that He is merciful to the earth and its creatures, and rewards those who do His will, and that He is living and enduring, therefore they attached these. But the essence of the blessing is from "praised, glorified, and exalted with the songs of David we shall praise You…" which is in the spirit of "Pesukei Dezimra." According to this, it can be said that it is permissible to interrupt when necessary from "Baruch She'amar" until "Baruch Ata…" but in practice, one should deliberate.

Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote: If one finishes "Baruch She'amar" before the chazzan (cantor) finishes – he should respond "Amen" after him. These are his words. Meaning: But if he finishes together with the chazzan – he should not respond "Amen," because it would be responding "Amen" to his own blessings, which is forbidden, as I have written in Siman 215. And Rabbeinu Beit Yosef's opinion is that even though he is responding to the chazzan's blessing, nevertheless, since he also finished the blessing – it is like responding to his own blessing. This reasoning does not agree with this, but the Elder (Magen Avraham, Siman 2) has already ruled. And he further wrote that after "Yishtabach" one can respond "Amen" to his own blessing. These are his words. Because there it will be explained that at the end of the blessings one can respond "Amen" even to his own blessing. However, it will be explained there that this is not the custom, and only after "Boneh Yerushalayim" in Birkat Hamazon do they respond "Amen." However, it is certain that after "Yishtabach" when he finishes with the chazzan – he can respond "Amen" (there). And similarly, if the chazzan finishes a different blessing from the one he finished, even according to Rabbeinu Beit Yosef, he can respond "Amen." And this is the simple custom (there).

One must be careful not to interrupt with speech from "Baruch She'amar" until the end of the Shemoneh Esrei. Even for the sake of a mitzvah, one should not interrupt between "Baruch She'amar" and "Yishtabach." Similarly, one should not interrupt between "Yishtabach" and "Yotzer," and this will be explained in Siman 54. Our Rabbi, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 5: Between these psalms, one may ask out of respect and respond with a greeting to any person. In the middle of a psalm, one may ask out of fear and respond out of respect. This is his language, and so wrote the Tur. The explanation of "out of fear" and "out of respect" will be clarified in Siman 66. They compared the Pesukei Dezimra to the blessings of the Shema, and if so, it is also forbidden to answer "Amen" in the middle of a section. However, according to the intentions of the Ari z"l, it is permitted to answer "Amen" (Magen Avraham, Small Section 3), and even in the middle of the blessing of "Baruch She'amar" it is permitted to answer "Amen" (there). It seems to me that the Tur and Shulchan Aruch also agree with answering "Amen," for "Amen" is no less than any of the songs and praises. They only spoke about interrupting with mundane words, likening it to the blessings of the Shema, and not about answering "Amen." This is also our practice. However, responding "Baruch Hu u'Varuch Shemo" is forbidden, as this is not required by law at all.

And similarly, it is permissible to interrupt in the middle of Pesukei Dezimra to recite the blessing "Asher Yatzar," and also to respond with "Modim D'Rabbanan," and similarly to respond to a necessary blessing that cannot be delayed, such as hearing thunder and the like – it is permissible to respond in the middle of Pesukei Dezimra. However, one should try to complete the verse, as this is always possible, of course. And certainly, if one did not have a tallit and tefillin – one can put them on in the middle of Pesukei Dezimra and recite the blessings over them. And similarly, it is permissible to respond with "Shema Yisrael" with the congregation in the middle of Pesukei Dezimra, and all the more so to be called up to the Torah. And what the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch equated Pesukei Dezimra to the blessings of Kriyat Shema – this is concerning optional matters.

And what is considered "between the sections" in the Pesukei Dezimra? From "Hodu" until "Amen and Hallel to Hashem" is considered the middle of the section, and after "Hallel to Hashem" is considered between the sections. Similarly, from "Tenu Oz" until "Baruch Elokim" is like the middle of the section. Similarly, from "El Nekamot" until "Al Ge'im," and from "Nafshenu Chikta" until "Yachalnu Lach," and from "Yehi Shem" until "Al Hashamayim Kevodo," and afterwards until "Tehillah L'David" – between each verse is like between the sections. And from "Tehillah L'David" until "Yishtabach" it is clear that in the middle of each psalm it is the middle of the section, and at the end of each psalm it is "between the sections." And in the verses "Baruch Hashem L'Olam Amen V'Amen" these four verses are considered one section. And in "Vayevarech David" the matter concludes at "L'Shem Tifartecha," and from there until "B'Mayim Azim" it is one matter. And from "Vayoshea" until "Hashem Yimloch" it is one matter. And from "Ki LaHashem Hamelucha" each verse is its own matter.

It is proper to pause between "elilim" and "ve'Hashem shamayim asah" for a moment or slightly longer, as well as between "ki kol" because there is a separation between them. The "kaf" in "kol" should be pronounced with a dagesh. Similarly, one should pause between "ha'amim" and "elilim" and between "shamayim" and "asah" so that the mems are not swallowed. 

Anyone who recites "Tehillah leDavid" (Psalm 145) three times is assured of being a child of the World to Come, meaning that this merit will tip the scales in favor of their virtues (Beit Yosef). It is understood that this applies specifically to one who recites it with intention. Therefore, one should be careful to have intention while reciting it, and at the very least, one is obligated to have intention during the verse "You open Your hand." If one did not have intention, they must repeat the verse. 

It has already been explained that one should complete the verse with "va'anachnu nevarech…". The verse "Kol haneshamah tehallel…" is repeated because it is the end of the praises. Similarly, in the Song of the Sea, "Hashem yimloch" is repeated because it is the end of the song. One does not need to say the verses "For the horse of Pharaoh…" but instead says "For to Hashem belongs the kingship…" (according to the Gra). Some have written that one should say the verse "For the horse…" (according to Nagid and Mitzvah in the name of the Ari z"l).

When one reaches "And now, Hashem our God, we thank You" and in "Nishmat" to "And all that stand before You shall bow," one should not bow at all, as one should only bow where the Sages instituted. Some have the custom to stand during "Va'yivarech David," the Song of the Sea, and "Yishtabach." There are those who wrote that this is specifically in a sitting position according to the Kabbalah (Bach in Siman 53, see there). According to the strict law, there is no particular insistence except that during the Amidah, Kedushah, Kaddish, and "Barchu," one must stand. According to the Zohar, from "Yotzer Or" until "Tehillot leEl Elyon," one should specifically be seated, and this is called in the Zohar "Tefillah de'MeYushav" as explained there in Parashat Terumah, page 132 at the top and end of the page, see there.

One should not recite the hymns hastily, but rather word by word. If the congregation is rushing, and he wants to pray with them, it is better to skip parts than to say them hastily. Concerning this, it is said, "Better a little with intent than much without intent," as I wrote in Siman 1. Especially "Mizmor LeTodah" should be sung, because all the songs are destined to be nullified except for "Mizmor LeTodah." "Mizmor LeTodah" is not recited on Shabbat, Yom Tov, all days of Pesach, and Erev Pesach, because it contains chametz, and the Thanksgiving offering is not brought on those days. Similarly, on Erev Yom Kippur, there are places where it is not said because it is eaten for a day and a night, and on Erev Yom Kippur one cannot eat at night, which would lead the sacrifices to become invalid. Likewise, on Tisha B'Av, there are places that say it and places that do not. The verses "V'Hu Rachum" in "Hodu" and "Yehi Chavod" – some skip them on Shabbat and Yom Tov. And some do not skip them, and this is our custom. (See Magen Avraham, Siman Katan 9, who is puzzled by the custom for the mohel to divide verses: for any verse that Moses did not divide, we do not divide? And see his explanation there. Indeed, our sages of blessed memory in Taanit (27b) said this regarding Torah reading, that it should not end in the middle of a verse and not read further. Besides, it is a great interruption until the second one stands and reads. What is the relevance to all who say together, one the beginning of the verse and one the end? Similarly, in "Yhallelu," the chazan starts, and the congregation responds "Hodu al eretz v'shamayim," and there is no interruption. In the Kedusha, when they say "Kadosh," did they not say previously "V'kara zeh el zeh v'amar"? Or the chazan said, and the congregation responds immediately "Kadosh..."? But at the end of the first chapter of Berachot (12b), it says any passage that was not divided... – and there are many readings on Monday and Thursday that end in the middle of a passage? We need to say that since on Shabbat it ends – we have no issue. But in the name of permanence forever, see there. Be precise and you will find ease.)

And a great question arises: Why did they establish the Song of the Sea in Pesukei Dezimra after the Psalms? After all, the Torah precedes the Prophets and certainly the Writings, as we say at the end of Rosh Hashanah regarding the verses of "Kingship," "Remembrances," and "Shofarot." Perhaps for this reason, the Rambam wrote in Chapter 7 of Tefillah, Law 13, that the Song of the Sea is recited after "Yishtabach," and he similarly wrote at the end of the prayer's text—see there. The explanation of his words might be that the Song of the Sea is not part of Pesukei Dezimra at all, but rather they established it before the blessing of "Yotzer Or" for some hidden reason. However, according to our custom, this is difficult. I found that the Zohar in Parashat Terumah (page 131b) raises this difficulty, and this is its language: "Then the praise of the Song of the Sea... And if you say... Why is it in the order after the praise of David? Behold, the Written Torah... and it precedes the Writings... Rather, from within... and this praise is superior..., and for this reason, it is adjacent to the 'sitting prayer'... until here is its language." Meaning: On the contrary, due to its great significance, they placed it next to the recitation of the Shema and its blessings, which the Zohar calls "the sitting prayer," as I wrote in the previous section at the end of paragraph 8—see there.

The main components of Pesukei Dezimra, according to Rashi in Shabbat (118b), are two psalms: "Halleluyah! Praise the Lord from the heavens" and "Halleluyah! Praise God in His sanctuary," see there. This is also the opinion of the Sefer Mitzvot Gadol and the Hagahot Maimoniyot. Some have written that the essential part is only the last psalm "Halleluyah! Praise God in His sanctuary," and this is the opinion of Rav Natronai, as brought by the Tur. The Rif and the Rambam wrote from "A psalm of praise, of David" until "Let every soul praise the Lord," implying that according to them, all are equal. Nevertheless, it can be said that they also agree that in a situation where it is impossible to say all of them, as will be explained, some take precedence over others.

And this is the language of Rabbeinu the Beit Yosef: If one comes to the synagogue and finds the congregation at the end of Pesukei DeZimra, he should say "Baruch She'amar" until "Mehulal Batishbachot," and then "Tehillah L'David" until "Me'atah V'ad Olam Halleluyah," and then "Hallelu Et Hashem Min Hashamayim" until "L'vnei Yisrael Am Kerovo Halleluyah," and then "Hallelu Kel B'kodsho" until "Kol Haneshamah...," and then "Yishtabach," and then "Yotzer" and the Shema and its blessings, and pray with the congregation. If there is not enough time, he should also skip the psalm "Hallelu Et Hashem Min Hashamayim." If the congregation has already started "Yotzer" and there is no time to say Pesukei DeZimra even with skipping, he should recite the Shema and its blessings with the congregation, pray with them, and afterward recite all of Pesukei DeZimra without the blessing before them or after them. Until here is his language. Because these blessings were only instituted before the prayer to arrange the praise of the Omnipresent and then to pray, as I wrote at the beginning of Siman 51. But once he has already prayed, there is no place to bless over the praise.

And from this, it is clarified how great is the power of communal prayer: not only do we shorten the praises and hymns of Pesukei Dezimra, but we even cancel them entirely, for anything without a blessing is considered nothing. And what is written that afterward one should recite all of Pesukei Dezimra – this is not obligatory, for Rav Natronai Gaon, as quoted by the Tur, wrote that one should not recite them afterward at all. However, our teacher the Beit Yosef, in his great work, wrote that certainly, his intention is with a blessing, for without a blessing, it would be desirable to recite them all day long, see there. Thus, it is evident that it is not stated as an obligation but merely as a recital of psalms. According to this, even one who shortens Pesukei Dezimra, as explained above – may recite them after the prayer as a mere recital of psalms.

Indeed, the words of our master, the Beit Yosef, are perplexing: How is it possible to say that the Gaon intended this regarding the blessings? He (the Gaon) is discussing someone who recited "Baruch She'amar" and "Yishtabach," but shortened the Pesukei Dezimra. And on this he wrote: "And do not say them at all after the prayer," as explained in the Tur. It is clear that he does not refer to the blessings, since they were already said, but he refers to the psalms themselves, which should not be recited after the prayer because they were only instituted to be said before the prayer. And I have seen someone who ruled this way: Even if one began from "Yotzer Or" and did not say any Pesukei Dezimra before the prayer, he should not say them afterward, even without the blessings. And certainly, if he said "Baruch She'amar" and "Yishtabach" and shortened the Pesukei Dezimra, he should not complete them after the prayer at all (Bach), for after the prayer it is not proper to say the psalms. And it is true that in the name of Rabbeinu Yonah, the Tur brought that if one did not say the Pesukei Dezimra at all, he should say them after the prayer with their blessings, "Baruch She'amar" and "Yishtabach" as before the prayer. See there. However, this is not our standing (halacha). And there are those who want to differentiate between not saying them at all, in which case he says them with their blessings after the prayer, and saying part of them with their blessings, in which case he does not complete them after the prayer at all, even without the blessings (Agur, and to the Prisha this is also the opinion of the Tur, see there). But these words have already been refuted (as written by the Beit Yosef and the Bach). And in practical halacha, it appears that "sitting and not doing is preferable." Especially since some say it is a great prohibition to say them after the prayer, as several of the Rishonim have written. (See Bach who wrote this in the name of the Semag and Ramban and Likutei Pardes, see there. And this also seems to be the opinion of the Kabbalists. Be precise and you will find light.)

And behold, it has already been explained that one should say "Baruch She'amar," the two Hallelujahs, "Tehillah L'David," and "Yishtabach." If time is short, he should only say the last "Hallelujah." Our teacher, the Rema, wrote that if there is not enough time even for this, he should only say "Baruch She'amar," "Ashrei," and "Yishtabach," see there. For in a pressing situation, one fulfills the obligation of Pesukei D'Zimra with "Ashrei" alone. And so it is in the Tur in the name of Rav Amram Gaon, see there. They did not mention "Mizmor L'Todah" at all. However, our custom is to say it, since it does not take much time, as it can be said in a few moments. Similarly, we say the psalm "Hallelu El B'Kodsho" because it is short, and it is not applicable to say "there is no time for this."

If there is still ample time, one should recite all the Halleluyahs. If there is still time, one should also recite the Song of the Sea. If there is still time, one should also recite "Blessed be the Lord forever, Amen and Amen." If there is still time, one should also recite "And David blessed." If there is still time, one should recite from "Give thanks" until "Exalt," and then skip and begin from "Ashrei." And the words of our master the Rema who wrote: If he has more time, he should recite "Give thanks to the Lord, call upon His name" until "And He is merciful," and skip to "And He is merciful" before Ashrei, because in between these are just collected verses. Up to here are his words. His intention is not that if one has more time beyond two of these Halleluyahs, for according to this, "Give thanks" would precede the other Halleluyahs, and this cannot be said. Rather, his intention is: if one has more time after reciting all the Halleluyahs (Magen Avraham). His wording is strained, and also the Smak explicitly wrote that "Give thanks" comes first. However, the primary ruling is as I have written, because this is agreed upon by most of the poskim (as explained in Maadanei Yom Tov and Eliyah Rabbah). And know that it is straightforward that if one comes to the synagogue and finds the congregation in the middle of Pesukei Dezimra, and by the time he dons his tallit and tefillin they will already be past "Yotzer Or," and it will be difficult for him to catch up even if he starts from "Yotzer Or" – he is exempt and should pray by himself in the complete order of the prayer. However, if he can only start from "Yotzer Or," he is obligated to start, because the power of public prayer is great, as I have written.

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote: "Nevertheless, one should say all the blessings that one is obligated to recite in the morning." Thus are his words. Meaning: if someone arrives in the middle of Pesukei D'Zimra and prays with the congregation as has been explained, and has not yet recited the morning blessings, he should say all the morning blessings after the prayer. However, there is an opinion that if he did not say the blessing "Who restores souls..." he should not say it after the prayer, for he has already fulfilled it with the blessing "Who revives the dead" (Pri Chadash). Similarly, there is another opinion that if he did not recite the blessing over the Torah, he should not recite it after the prayer, for he has already fulfilled it with "Ahava Rabba." But this matter has already been explained in Siman 47; see there. Also, in my humble opinion, one should not recite "Who gives the rooster understanding" after having recited "Who forms the luminaries." Also, I do not understand how one would recite "Who releases the bound" as it is mentioned in "Who sustains the living," and this requires further study. Therefore, one should be careful not to come to such a situation. If one does come to such a situation, it seems to me that in cases of doubt regarding blessings, we are lenient, and one should not recite those blessings we considered after the prayer.

Know that in ancient times, the prayer leader (Shaliach Tzibur) did not go down before the lectern at the very beginning of the prayer as is our custom. Rather, "Baruch She'amar" and all the verses of praise (Pesukei Dezimra) were recited by each individual in their place, and the entire congregation would say "Yishtabach" up to "Chai HaOlamim" together. Then, the prayer leader would go down before the lectern and begin "Yishtabach." Therefore, the Tur and Shulchan Aruch established the laws of the prayer leader in this section after the laws of Pesukei Dezimra. 

And all the fifteen words in "Yishtabach" from "Shir U’Shvacha" to "Berachot VeHodaot" should ideally be said in one breath (Magen Avraham) if one is able to do so, as it is not appropriate to interrupt the praises of the Blessed Name even with a breath. The prayer leader goes down before the lectern and recites "Yishtabach" standing. The standing is not because of "Yishtabach" but because of Kaddish (Bach, Taz, and Magen Avraham, subsection 1). 

It is clear that the prayer leader should not say "Yishtabach" unless he has said "Baruch She'amar" and part of the Pesukei Dezimra, for otherwise, it is forbidden for him to say "Yishtabach," as it is the concluding blessing of the Pesukei Dezimra. 

Therefore, if the prayer leader arrives at the synagogue and needs to say "Yishtabach" at the lectern, he is obligated to say "Baruch She'amar" and "Ashrei" at the very least, even if the congregation has to wait a bit.

It is forbidden to interrupt between the verses of praise (Pesukei Dezimra) and "Yishtabach" even for the sake of a mitzvah, except to answer "Amen," which is permitted as I wrote in Siman 51, Section 5. For "Amen" is also a form of praise and is similar to the verses of praise. But for other mitzvah matters, it is forbidden. Therefore, if they brought him the tallit and tefillin during "Yishtabach," he should finish "Yishtabach" and then put on the tallit and tefillin with a blessing. For this, it is permitted to interrupt between "Yishtabach" and "Yotzer" as will be explained in Siman 54. And know that this applies to an individual. But if they brought the tallit or tefillin to the prayer leader during "Yishtabach," he must put them on before "Yishtabach," because afterwards he needs to say Kaddish and "Barchu," and it is obviously impossible to interrupt in public. Therefore, he must interrupt between Pesukei Dezimra and "Yishtabach." He should bless over them, and it is considered like "due to fear," which is permitted to interrupt even in the middle of a chapter, as I wrote in Siman 66.

If there is no quorum (minyan) in the synagogue and it is not possible to recite the Kaddish, the prayer leader should not say "Yishtabach" until a minyan arrives. He should then recite "Yishtabach" followed by Kaddish, because every Kaddish must be preceded by some text. He may wait even for half an hour, for it is established that if one waited the amount of time it takes to complete the entire prayer and the interruption was not due to necessity, he does not need to start from the beginning, as I have written in Siman 65. Here, however, the interruption was not necessary, as he could have recited "Yishtabach" but chose not to until a minyan arrived. According to this, if the place was not clean and he was therefore compelled to pause, and he waited the amount of time it takes to complete the entire prayer, he must start from the beginning, as I wrote there. However, in the case of Pesukei Dezimra, which are of rabbinic origin, one can rely on the lenient opinions there even in cases of compulsion.

And this applies to the prayer leader. But each individual on their own should not pause in silence and should say "Yishtabach" immediately after the Verses of Praise (Pesukei Dezimra). Similarly, on Shabbat, when the prayer leader extends "Nishmat" or "Shochein Ad" – each individual should also complete the blessing of "Yishtabach" without pausing in silence, as ideally, there should be no interruption at all. However, the prayer leader is compelled to pause when necessary, but this does not apply to each and every individual. Between "Yishtabach" and Kaddish, neither the prayer leader nor any individual should interrupt. It appears to me that if the prayer leader extends the melodies and the individual has finished the blessing of "Yishtabach" – they may look into a book and study until the prayer leader reaches Kaddish.

In this section, the Tur and Shulchan Aruch wrote the laws of the prayer leader (Shaliach Tzibur). In the times of the ancients, there used to be a fixed prayer leader for weekdays, Sabbaths, and holidays. This was very good because he knew the order of the prayers well, did not prolong them, and did not rush through them. He was a God-fearing man. But now, due to our many sins, in all our regions there is no fixed prayer leader for weekdays at all. Rather, anyone who wants to leads the prayers. Moreover, the custom has spread that someone who is mourning for his father or mother or on a yahrzeit (anniversary of death) leads the prayers, even if he is an ignoramus, does not know his right hand from his left, does not understand the meaning of the words, and is not fit to lead the prayers. As a result, the prayers become confused, with one person rushing and another skipping parts. It becomes a shadow of death with no order. However, this custom has persisted for generations before us, and we cannot protest against it. Yet, because of the essence of the prayer, we do not rely on the prayer leader, as we are all proficient, and we do not need the prayer leader to fulfill our obligation. We each pray individually.

It is written: "She has lifted up her voice against me, therefore I have hated her." And our sages of blessed memory expounded in Taanit (17b): This refers to an unworthy prayer leader who leads the congregation. And who is a worthy prayer leader? One who is free from transgressions, has no bad reputation even from his youth, is humble, accepted by the people, has a pleasant voice, and is accustomed to reading Torah, Prophets, and Writings. If one cannot find someone with all these qualities, they should choose the best among the congregation in wisdom and good deeds. If there is an elderly unlearned person with a pleasant voice whom the people desire, and a thirteen-year-old who understands what he is saying but does not have a pleasant voice – the younger one takes precedence. However, due to our many sins, in these times the power of the masses is strong, especially in matters of cantorship, and it is difficult to oppose them. "And He, being merciful..."

It has been explained that if no bad reputation has emerged about him, this is in regard to appointing him initially. However, if a bad reputation has emerged about a prayer leader, he is not removed from his position, for we do not remove a person from his appointment because of mere rumors. Unless it is a persistent rumor, and we know that enemies did not spread the rumor, in a manner similar to the type of rumor we would be concerned about regarding a married woman, as explained in Even HaEzer, Siman 11, then he is removed. And even a single individual can object and have him removed if we know that his intention is for the sake of Heaven (Magen Avraham, subsection 7. And it must be said that his intention is as I have written. Pay close attention and you will find it easy to understand.) And in any case where he has already been removed and has remained so for a long time, and now they want to reinstate him, his status is as if he is being appointed anew (ibid.). And if there are leaders in the city on whom all matters of the city rely, they are also the primary decision-makers regarding the appointment of the prayer leader (ibid.).

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote: Someone who committed a sin inadvertently, such as killing a person unintentionally, and repented – it is permissible for him to be a prayer leader. However, if he sinned intentionally – it is not permissible, because in any case, he had a bad reputation before his repentance. This is the end of his words. From this language, it appears that for an intentional sin, even once, repentance does not help regarding his appointment as a prayer leader, but for an inadvertent sin, it does help for one instance. And it is surprising: why should someone be disqualified for inadvertent sins even if they happened multiple times? For an inadvertent sin does not naturally lead to a bad reputation. It should be said that his intention is not about one instance, for in one instance, even if intentional, since he repented – it is permissible for him to be a prayer leader, because once he repents, the bad reputation is immediately nullified. His disqualification for intentional sins applies only when he sinned multiple times, and for inadvertent sins, even in such a case, he is still fit, as seems to be implied from his words in his book Darchei Moshe, see there. And what he wrote, "because in any case, he had a bad reputation before his repentance," means: since he sinned multiple times, even though he repented each time, nevertheless before the repentance, he had a bad reputation each time. Some have written that the disqualification of "a bad reputation" applies only to fast days and not to the rest of the year. To me, it seems that a regular prayer leader for the whole year is preferable to one for fast days. (See Magen Avraham, subsection 8. Analyze and you will find it light.) And know that what he wrote "killed a person" is not specific, and the same applies to other sins (Eliyah Rabbah). There is a question regarding rabbinic transgressions when someone repents, whether they are also considered to have "a bad reputation" or not. It seems that there is no difference between Torah and rabbinic transgressions.

Someone who transgressed a sin under duress—there is certainly no concern in the matter (Magen Avraham there). And a prayer leader who was also a ritual slaughterer and inspector, and a non-kosher animal was found from his hand—he is forbidden to be a prayer leader. The details of this law are elucidated in Yoreh De'ah, Chapter 2, where there is a distinction between one time and many times. The prayer of a righteous person who is the son of a righteous person is more effective than the prayer of a righteous person who is the son of a wicked person. It should be ensured that the prayer leader is not a fool and understands community matters (there). A prayer leader who has physical defects, such as whose arms have fallen or is lame in his legs, and the like, Maharshal wrote that he can be a prayer leader. On the contrary, the Holy One, Blessed be He, uses broken vessels. However, in the Zohar "Emor," it is forbidden, and "broken vessels" means that he should be humble and contrite in spirit, and not an actual physical defect, see there. (There. And in the Sh'lah it is permitted in the name of Maharam of Rothenburg, that "A broken heart, O God, You will not despise." And so wrote the Elyah Rabbah.)

One should only appoint as a permanent prayer leader (Shaliach Tzibur) someone who has a full beard, meaning he has a beard, which classifies him as "a man of years."
