But not someone younger, as it is not respectful to the congregation. Meaning: it is not respectful to Heaven for the congregation's representative to be a youth and tender in years. Therefore, even if the congregation desires it, he cannot be a permanent prayer leader (Beit Yosef, Taz subsection 2, and see Magen Avraham subsection 9). On a public fast day, he must actually be an elder (ibid.). However, throughout the year, we are not particular about the beard, only that he has reached the strength of a man. Therefore, even if he does not have a beard, for example, if by nature he does not grow a beard, since he has reached the age where others like him have a full beard – he may be appointed as a permanent prayer leader. And even if there is another prayer leader, but he is appointed by the congregation or by the prayer leader to assist at specific times in leading the prayers, since he is appointed to a fixed role – he must specifically have a full beard (see Taz subsection 4).

And this is regarding a permanent appointment. But for a temporary occasion to lead the prayers – it is permitted as soon as he has brought two pubic hairs. And once he is thirteen years old and one day – he is permitted to lead the prayers on a temporary basis because we assume he has brought hairs, unless we know that he has not yet brought hairs, in which case he is considered a minor. Before thirteen years of age, he should not be allowed to lead the prayers at all. And on a public fast day, we require "his beard has filled out" even when he is praying temporarily (there). And a twenty-year-old, even if he does not have a beard, is counted, because it is the way of the beard to fill out when he is twenty. And if he has even a small amount of a beard, if he is eighteen years or older – we consider "his beard has filled out." But if he is younger than eighteen, we require that he has many hairs in his beard. And a eunuch who shows signs of being a eunuch, some say it is permitted to appoint him when he is twenty. And there are those who are particular about appointing a eunuch as a permanent prayer leader (Magen Avraham, subsection 11, in the name of Rashal).

All this applies when it is possible to appoint a cantor who has a fully grown beard. However, if there is no one suitable to be a cantor except a boy of thirteen years and one day, it is necessary to appoint him. Otherwise, everyone will miss out on hearing the Kedusha and Kaddish. Nowadays, it is unlikely that such a situation will occur. It has already been clarified that a minor is not to lead the prayers. Nevertheless, our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 10 that one should find merit for those places where minors do lead the prayers for the Maariv service on Saturday nights. This is because Maariv does not include the repetition of the Amidah. This practice was instituted for orphans, as it is explained in Yoreh De'ah, section 376, that it is beneficial for the soul to pray at the amud on Saturday nights. However, the elders objected to this practice, as our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in his larger work. One can see this there. Also, nowadays we do not see this practice. This is the language of our master, the Rema: In places where this is not the practice, a minor should not lead the prayers, even for Maariv. Even if he turns thirteen on Shabbat, he should not lead Maariv of Shabbat, because he is not yet thirteen years old. This is his language: the Maariv of Shabbat is prayed while it is still daytime, and he becomes Bar Mitzvah at nightfall. But when praying after the appearance of the stars, it is permitted. When we say generally "thirteen years and one day," it means thirteen full years, i.e., immediately after thirteen, he becomes an adult (Magen Avraham, section 3, and Taz, section 6).

Anyone whom the Holy One, blessed be He, has graced with a pleasant voice should sing to the Holy One, blessed be He, with the joy of a mitzvah and not with secular matters, and certainly not to sing licentious songs. His sin is too great to bear. A prayer leader who prolongs his prayer so that people will hear his pleasant voice—if it is because he is joyful in his heart for giving thanks to the blessed Name with melody, a blessing shall come upon him. This is provided that he prays with solemnity and stands with awe and reverence. But if his intention is to make his voice heard, and he rejoices in his voice, this is disgraceful. In any case, anyone who prolongs his prayer is not doing well because it burdens the congregation. There is much to say about the conduct of cantors in our time due to our many sins, but just as it is a mitzvah to say... and it is forbidden to repeat words.

One should not appoint as a prayer leader someone who pronounces alephs as ayins and ayins as alephs, as the pronunciation of an ayin is stronger and deeper than that of an aleph. However, in our country, people are not proficient in this. Similarly, one should not pronounce chet as he, and he as chet, and in our country, their pronunciations are not the same at all. A person who is poorly dressed, meaning someone whose clothes are torn and whose arms are exposed, should not lead the prayers. Similarly, if his legs are exposed, he should not lead the prayers. It is appropriate that the prayer leader have long clothes and be the first to enter the synagogue and the last to leave (Magen Avraham at the end of sub-section 7 in the name of the Rema). Rabbi Yosef Karo wrote in section 14: A blind person may lead the prayers, provided that he does not read from the Torah, because one is not permitted to recite written things by heart. According to the words of the Zohar that we mentioned in section 9, it is not proper for a blind person to lead the prayers. Whether a blind person is permitted to be called to the Torah will be explained in section 141. A deaf person has difficulty being a prayer leader.

A regular cantor (prayer leader) descends before the ark on his own and does not wait until he is told. But a cantor who is not regular must initially refuse a little before descending before the ark. However, he should not refuse too much, for that is not respectful to the congregation. Rather, the first time he should refuse, when they ask him a second time, he should prepare himself as though he wants to stand, and the third time he should stand. If the one who asks him to descend is a great person, he should not refuse at all and should descend immediately, for one does not refuse a great person. However, in a matter that involves authority, he should refuse a little even if a great person asks him, for the refusal is to show that perhaps he is not worthy, and this is proper etiquette (see Tosafot, Pesachim, end of the seventh chapter). Sometimes even a cantor who is not regular should not refuse, such as when the regular cantor makes a mistake or becomes silent, and it is necessary to appoint another in his place – the one who is appointed in his place should not refuse at all, since it is in the middle of the prayer and it is not proper to interrupt much (the Gaon of Vilna in section 24 raised a difficulty from Arakhin 11b, where it says: just as a cantor who seeks permission, see there – it is explicitly stated that even a regular cantor needs permission. In my humble opinion, it seems there is no difficulty, for Rashi explained: he seeks permission if he should pray. This means: if they do not tell him to pray, he needs to seek permission, for perhaps the congregation does not want to pray yet. But when they tell him "Descend and pray" – he should not refuse at all. A proof for this: for it is compared there to "Hezekiah said," see there. And he initiated it himself, not from others, and it is clear. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

The Sages taught in the Mishnah of Megillah (24b): One who says, "I do not pass before the ark in colored garments" – even in white garments he should not pass. [If he says,] "I do not pass wearing sandals" – even barefoot he should not pass. The reason is that we are concerned that perhaps heresy has entered him (as explained in the Gemara), for the heretics were particular about this. Therefore, even if it is possible that he said this for another reason, we are still concerned. And not only when he retracts and says, "I will descend in colored garments" or "in sandals," do we suspect that initially he spoke out of heresy and then retracted out of fear of people. Rather, even if he does not retract and it can be said that his intention was for reasons of modesty or cleanliness, nevertheless, he should not pass (Taz, section 8). And since it is merely a suspicion, we only worry about it for that specific prayer. Even if he subsequently gives a reason for his words, explaining why he said so, he should still not descend for that prayer. However, if he gives the reason at the same time as he says, "I do not pass in colored garments" or "in sandals," there is no concern, and he may descend for that prayer. (And see Magen Avraham, section 18, who writes: "Nevertheless, since the congregation requests...," these are his words. It requires examination why the request of the congregation is needed, since even without this, giving a reason afterward does not help. Examine and you will find it clear.)

A convert (in ancient times) is permitted to be a prayer leader. There are those who prevent him from doing so because he cannot say "the God of our fathers." Their words were rejected, for Abraham is a father to converts, as it is written, "for I have made you the father of a multitude of nations." It is also explicitly stated in the Jerusalem Talmud, Bikkurim, Chapter One, that this is the law (see there). A mamzer (illegitimate child) is not fit to be a prayer leader. It also seems to me that a chalal (a descendant of priests who violated certain prohibitions) should not be a prayer leader, for anyone born from a prohibited union is not suitable to be an advocate, obviously. All the more so if the prayer leader himself is a habitual sinner, it is forbidden to appoint him to lead the prayers. Anyone who supports such a prayer leader is a sinner and causes others to sin, and his punishment is great in this world and the next. An accuser cannot become an advocate (Or Zarua, Siman 112).

Every prayer leader (shaliach tzibbur) must stand before the lectern as one stands before a king, with the tallit over his head and not merely on his shoulders. He should not make unusual movements, nor should he look to the sides, and certainly not behind him. He should not belch, yawn, or spit, neither from his mouth nor certainly from his nose. If it is absolutely necessary for him to do so, he should do it discreetly and under his tallit, and clean his mouth and nose before praying. He should ensure that he does not need to relieve himself in the middle of the prayer, as this would be disrespectful to the congregation. He should prepare himself beforehand to avoid this. However, if despite all this he is compelled to leave, he should appoint another to take his place and then leave. The same rules apply when reading the Torah.

Our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, wrote in section 19 that even a single individual can object and say, "I do not want so-and-so to be the chazzan," unless he has already been agreed upon from the beginning. And this is specifically if that individual has a valid reason according to the seven leading citizens of the city. But otherwise, he cannot protest against the chazzan. And if he hates him, he can protest before he has been agreed upon. And someone who hates the chazzan should not be called up to the Torah when the rebuke is being read. So far their language. Their words need clarification: where do we find that one person can object? And why can even a minority object? For in all of Torah law, we follow the majority.

And I found a response to this in the Or Zarua HaGadol (Siman 114), which writes: My teacher, Rabbi Shmuel, ruled that an individual can object to a chazzan. And it is clear in all our communities that the minority can prevent the majority from appointing a chazzan… for anyone appointed as a chazzan who is not from the same group – the Sages are not pleased with him… and how can he fulfill their obligation when they do not agree with his prayer…? And even though he possesses all good qualities, we require that the people agree… You should know that if an Israelite separated his obligatory offering and a priest came and sacrificed it for him, and the owner of the offering did not want him, would you think he has achieved atonement…? Similarly here, the chazzan should pray only with the consent of all… until here are his words. And from this, it is clarified that this was in ancient times when the congregation did not pray at all, and the chazzan would fulfill their obligation. Therefore, it was compared to an offering, and according to this, one could rightfully object and say, "I do not want him to be my chazzan." However, one must still provide a valid reason, for otherwise, there would be no end to it, and one would have to accept him against his will. Similarly, if one already agreed to him, he cannot retract for the same reason, for otherwise, there would be no end to it. And if one hates him, he can object initially but not afterward. The chazzan is obligated to include him in his prayer and remove the hatred from his heart. Nevertheless, when it comes to reading the rebuke, if he wishes, he may abstain. This is the explanation of the words of our Rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch.

However, in these times when each individual prays on their own, and on weekdays the community's prayer leader does not lead the prayers at all, and even on Shabbat, the prayer leader only occasionally leads the service, and it is only on Rosh Hashanah, Yom Kippur, and the festivals that the prayer leader leads the service, primarily for the sake of the melody; and many members of the community do not pray at the synagogue where the prayer leader leads; and the cantor is obligated to sing for the bride and groom before the wedding, and to sing "Romemos" for a circumcision, and other similar duties – it is obvious that an individual cannot object, and even a minority of the community cannot object. And when the majority of the city wants to appoint a particular prayer leader – the minority cannot protest against them. His salary is paid from the communal funds, and even those individuals are obligated to bear the expense unless the minority proves that the prayer leader is unfit, in which case the law is with them. (And with this, you can understand the words of the Magen Avraham in subsection 20. And what he wrote at the beginning of this subsection: "and also regarding all appointments, one can protest," see there – this is not according to his conclusion, and it is not taught as such. This is also the opinion of the Levush. And what he wrote in subsection 21 that the majority of the community can protest even after they have agreed, see there – it is clear that this is only when a fault is found in him, or they have not yet written an agreement with him, or it is after the time of the agreement, or they want to remove him before his time, as the Machatzit HaShekel wrote there. And an individual cannot protest in any case. Examine and you will find clarity.)

One should not appoint a prayer leader (shaliach tzibbur) based on the influence of powerful people in the city, even if the majority of the congregation desires him (see Beit Yosef regarding an incident on this matter). It is forbidden for a person to lead prayers without the congregation’s consent. Anyone who leads prayers forcefully and through coercion – one should not respond "Amen" to his blessings. If he possesses fear of Heaven, he should flee from the prayer stand if he sees even a few individuals who do not want him. Any mitzvah that involves dispute is not a mitzvah. One should not quarrel to perform a mitzvah that is not obligatory upon him, for certainly, eating the holy offerings is a great mitzvah, and nonetheless, we learned regarding the showbread that the modest ones would withdraw their hands from the division if there was quarreling over it, as stated in Yoma (39a). And on this, they said (Moed Katan 5a): Whoever sets their ways properly will merit and see the salvation of God.

If there is an option to hire a prayer leader for a fee, and there is another who would do it for free – it is better to hire for a fee rather than for free, because every mitzvah is better when money is spent on it. Additionally, when someone is paid, they will take their job more seriously. Furthermore, when there is a fee, another person who is not fit to pray will not dare to step forward to lead the prayers, whereas for free, it is not as clear that the role belongs solely to him. The payment for the prayer leader is made from the community fund. Although the fund contains much more from the wealthy than from the poor, and the prayer leader serves both equally, and therefore it would be appropriate to pay equally, nonetheless, the poor person cannot afford as much as the wealthy person, so necessarily this one will pay more and that one less. Our master, the Rema, wrote in section 23: Some say that they collect half according to wealth and half according to the number of people. This is also the custom of the communities. This is his language, and this is a compromise approach. In our case, we do not have this custom, and we always pay permanent salaries from the public fund, and the income is naturally according to wealth, as is known (see Magen Avraham, small section 27). This is also our practice for all appointments of rabbis, judges, and sextons – we pay salaries from the fund, and the contributions are according to the means of each individual.

In a place where there is no chazzan, or in our diaspora communities where there is no designated chazzan and anyone who wishes can pray, only someone who is acceptable to the congregation should lead the prayers. Therefore, even though regarding Kaddish the precedence is given to one whose parent has passed away, in terms of leading the prayers, although mourners and those observing a yahrzeit customarily lead the prayers and it is a significant merit for the soul of the deceased when the prayer is conducted properly, nonetheless, they do not have precedence in this matter. This is what our master the Beit Yosef wrote in section 20: If one person wants to lead the prayer for his father and another for someone else, whoever the congregation prefers to lead the prayer should do so. Thus, if in certain places the mohel (circumciser) displaces the mourner from leading the prayers, if the congregation prefers the mourner, the mourner should lead. A yahrzeit observer takes precedence over a mohel if both are equally acceptable to the congregation (Magen Avraham, sub-section 24). In our communities, it is not customary for the mohel to lead the prayers; rather, he chants "And You shall cut" verse by verse.

A congregation that cannot pray by themselves, and must necessarily hire a prayer leader to pray every day to fulfill their obligation—they are obligated to hire one. They compel one another to hire a prayer leader, and even a minority compels the majority. Similarly, they compel one another to hire a rabbi to instruct them on matters of prohibition and permission and other issues. If they need both, but can only afford one, if the rabbi is great in Torah, distinguished, and expert in teaching—then the rabbi takes precedence. If not, the prayer leader takes precedence, since they cannot pray by themselves. They hire a prayer leader to pray for them every day. In our situation, this law does not apply at all, and the rabbi always takes precedence (this is the intention of the Shulchan Aruch in section 24).

A prayer leader is not removed from his position unless a disqualification is found in him. Then he is disqualified until he repents, and it is evident to all that he has repented. He is not removed due to mere rumors, such as a rumor that he informed on someone or was caught with a non-Jewish woman. Such rumors are not taken into account until witnesses come and testify. If the rumor is very strong, a court should be convened to investigate the source of the rumor (see Magen Avraham, Siman 29). A prayer leader who is also a slaughterer and examiner should not pray in dirty and foul-smelling clothes as is customary for slaughterers. If he refuses to change his clothes during prayer, he should be removed. He should also not walk among people in dirty clothes. Similarly, a prayer leader who speaks vulgarly or sings licentious songs should be rebuked not to do so, and if he does not listen, he should be removed.

Our master, the Rema, wrote in paragraph 25: "A prayer leader who has aged and wants to appoint his son to assist him occasionally, even if his son's voice is not as pleasant as his own, if the son can fulfill the other duties, he takes precedence over any other person, and the community cannot object to him." Thus are his words. And it is stated in the Sifrei in the portion "Shoftim": "So that he may prolong his days... he and his children among Israel" – "he and his children" implies that if he dies, his son takes his place. And I only know this for him, but how do I know it for all the leaders of Israel that their sons take their place? The text states: "among Israel," meaning anyone "among Israel" – his son takes his place. Thus are the words. And the intention is: when his son can fulfill his place. Now, this ruling of our master, the Rema, is derived from the responsa of the Rashba (Siman 300), and he brought at the end of his words the Sifrei that we cited to support this. And the essence of his responsa was according to the custom in those places that the son would fill his father's place. And they agreed with him on this specific question there, that whoever he wants he can take to assist him, and they accepted him as the prayer leader for all the days of his life, see there. And our master, the Rema, did not mention this at all, and a reason is needed.

It appears to me that, in truth, the words of the Sifrei are not at all related to the hiring of a prayer leader or a rabbi, for the Sifrei only spoke of those leaders who are appointed merely for honor. But when the community hires a prayer leader for a salary, what relevance is there to say that his son should take precedence? They can indeed say: "We want to give money to you and not to your son." And is there any established right for money? For in the case of one who allocated money for his son-in-law, and his son-in-law died and fell to levirate marriage, where the Torah decreed so, nevertheless, we learn at the beginning of the sixth chapter of Ketubot that he can say, "I wanted to give to your brother, but I do not wish to give to you"? All the more so for those who make a contract with a prayer leader or a rabbi to pay him such and such for a year, how can we compel them to pay his son, even if he fills his father's place? And all the more so if the contract is for a specific number of years. Therefore, the Rashba only granted this prayer leader due to their custom, as I have written. And he brought support from the Sifrei only as a supplementary aid.

Therefore, our teacher the Rema did not write this law, that the son precedes when the father dies. He only ruled in this matter: when he was appointed for all his life, or even if he was appointed for a term but the custom of the world is that they do not remove him when the term ends, it is considered as if he was hired permanently. Consequently, it is considered as if they stipulated that when he would need assistance, as people usually do when they age or occasionally fall ill, he could take an assistant according to his desire. And now, automatically, the son precedes if he is fit for the position. However, when he dies, certainly the community is not obligated to accept the son, unless they wish and choose him now, and not because of inheritance. (See Magen Avraham, subsection 33. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

In the appointment of rabbinic positions, aside from the reason already explained, inheritance does not apply in matters of Torah. Therefore, we find among our sages of blessed memory that whoever was the head of the exile did not have his son inherit the position, as we find with the pairs in the first chapter of Avot. Similarly, among the sages of the Gemara, such as Rav Huna who was the head of the exile, and after him was Rav Chisda, even though Rav Huna had a son named Rabbah bar Rav Huna, and there are many similar examples. The fact that from Hillel and onward the presidency was inherited was a special enactment to uphold the Torah due to Herod and his supporters (see Magen Avraham there). However, if the son truly fills his father’s place, it is fitting for the people of the city to appoint him in his father’s position, and this is also fitting for the descendants of Abraham.

Our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in Section 26: A community that has the custom to appoint individuals for public needs for a set time, and when the time arrives, these individuals leave and others take their place; whether it is for a cantor, for the charity fund, or for other positions necessary for the community; whether they receive payment or not; even if no set time was established for them – their general practice is considered as their specific expression, since this is their custom. This is his language, and it is clear. And our master, the Rema, wrote that there are those who say that the prayer leader should pray from a book designated for the community, as it was certainly written for that purpose. This is his language. And now, since they pray from printed prayer books – this is not applicable.

Know that the "Shaliach Tzibur" mentioned in the Talmud was appointed for all the needs of the city, as Rashi wrote in Chullin (24b). He would pray every day Shacharit, Mincha, and Maariv to fulfill the obligations of the community. The term "Chazan" is found in the Mishnah for several matters: In the first chapter of Shabbat (Mishnah 3), the Ra'av (Rav Ovadiah of Bartenura) explains "Chazan" to mean a teacher of children. In the third chapter of Makkot (Mishnah 12), he explains it to mean a servant, a messenger of the court. In Tamid, the fifth chapter (Mishnah 3), he also explains it as a servant, see there. The Aruch in the entry "Chazan" explains that "Chazan" means "Shaliach Tzibur," which is related to the term "Chozeh" (seer), as he needs to see how to read from the Torah. Nowadays, the terms "Chazan" and "Shaliach Tzibur" are one and the same, and he is only appointed to pray and chant on certain Sabbaths and holidays, Rosh Hashanah, and Yom Kippur. Everyone prays individually, and we do not need them to fulfill our obligations. Therefore, the precision in their selection is not so stringent. Nevertheless, it is obligatory that he be God-fearing, and if not, his prayer is an abomination and provokes accusations, Heaven forbid.

"'Yishtabach' does not begin with 'Baruch' because it is adjacent to the blessing 'Baruch She'amar.' This means that 'Baruch She'amar' is the blessing before the Pesukei Dezimra, and 'Yishtabach' is the blessing after the Pesukei Dezimra. Therefore, one should not say 'Yishtabach' unless 'Baruch She'amar' and some of the Pesukei Dezimra have been recited. The conclusion of the blessing is 'Chai HaOlamim.' At that point, one must respond 'Amen,' and not after 'Gadol Umehulal B'tishbachot' as per the Sephardic custom. Even though in Hallel we conclude with 'Mehulal B'tishbachot,' in 'Yishtabach' it continues until 'Chai HaOlamim.' One must pronounce 'Chai' with a tzeirei and not with a patach. It has already been explained in Siman 51, Se'if 4, that although Rabbi Yosef Karo holds that after 'Yishtabach' one may respond 'Amen' to his own blessing, just as after 'Boneh Yerushalayim' in Birkat Hamazon, we do not follow this opinion, nor is it the custom. However, regarding this matter, it is preferable that when concluding simultaneously with the chazan, one may respond 'Amen,' see there."

Even though "Pesukei Dezimra" and "Yotzer Or" are two different sections, and we recite Kaddish between them, it is nevertheless forbidden to interrupt with speech between "Yishtabach" and "Yotzer" because they are all part of the order of prayer and are considered as one matter. The decisors have brought from the Jerusalem Talmud that one who speaks between "Yishtabach" and "Yotzer" commits a transgression, and he must return from the battle formations so that this transgression does not accuse him. This is not related to the custom that some have of reciting "Shir Hama'alot Mima'amakim" after "Yishtabach" during the Ten Days of Repentance, as this is considered part of the order of prayer, similar to the Rambam's ruling that "Az Yashir" is recited after "Yishtabach" as I have written in Siman 51. An interruption is only called secular words. (And the Magen Avraham, subparagraph 2, remains in "needs investigation," and I do not know why.)

Nevertheless, since these are two different matters, they are not entirely comparable to an interruption in the middle of Pesukei Dezimra. This is what our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, wrote in paragraph 3, and this is their language: "There are those who say that for communal needs, or to allocate charity to someone who comes to seek sustenance from charity, it is permitted to interrupt." And from this, it has become customary in many places to bless a sick person or to make a complaint in the synagogue to have justice done for him between "Yishtabach" and "Yotzer," for all this is considered "for the sake of a mitzvah." And afterwards, when they return to pray, the prayer leader should recite some of the Pesukei Dezimra and say Kaddish over them, for there is never a Kaddish without a preceding praise. Therefore, we begin the evening prayer without Kaddish. Similarly, if one did not have a tallit or tefillin and they brought it to him between "Yishtabach" and Kaddish, he may put them on and bless over them. But between Kaddish and "Barchu," he should not interrupt for anything. Certainly, he should not interrupt after the prayer leader has said "Barchu" before beginning the blessing of "Yotzer." Until here is their language.

Explanation of the matter: Due to the fact that these are two distinct matters, it is customary to interrupt them for a mitzvah-related matter. Ideally, the interruption should occur after the recitation of Kaddish because the Kaddish refers to the verses of praise (Pesukei Dezimra), as there can be no Kaddish without a preceding prayer. Therefore, how can it be possible to interrupt before Kaddish and then recite Kaddish without an adjacent prayer? Nonetheless, the custom is to interrupt before Kaddish, based on the Kabbalistic principle that it is forbidden to completely interrupt between Kaddish and "Barchu" and between "Barchu" and "Yotzer." Thus, it is necessary to interrupt before Kaddish. And if you wonder about what the Kaddish will be recited over, the response is that the prayer leader will subsequently recite a portion of the verses of praise. This, however, was in their time. But in our time, we have never heard of making an interruption between "Yishtabach" and Kaddish. Any delays in prayer for us or any act of charity are done before the Torah reading. Regarding the ruling that when one is brought a tallit and tefillin, he should put them on between "Yishtabach" and Kaddish, we have already clarified in Siman 53, Section 2, that this applies to an individual. But the prayer leader should put them on before "Yishtabach," as noted there. (And what the Magen Avraham wrote concerning the recitation of Shema after the Amidah and after the final Kaddish—we have not heard of this custom in our time. And in places where this custom exists, it is obvious that two Kaddishes should not be recited in close succession without a break of psalms in between. He instructed to shorten the Kaddishes, as will be explained at the beginning of Siman 55.)

Kaddish is a great and awesome praise that was instituted by the Men of the Great Assembly after the destruction of the First Temple. It is a prayer concerning the desecration of His blessed name due to the destruction of the Holy Temple, the devastation of the Holy Land, and the dispersion of Israel to the four corners of the earth. We pray that His blessed name be magnified and sanctified, as the prophet said: "And I will be magnified and sanctified, and I will be known in the eyes of many nations, and they shall know that I am the Lord." Rabbi Yose said at the beginning of Berachot that once he heard a Divine Voice cooing like a dove and saying: "Woe to the children, that due to their sins I have destroyed My house, burned My sanctuary, and exiled them...". And Elijah the Prophet told him that such a Divine Voice goes out three times a day. Moreover, when the Israelites enter synagogues and study halls and respond "Amen! May His great name be blessed...", the Holy One, Blessed be He, shakes His head and says: "Happy is the king who is thus praised in his house. What is it to a father who has exiled his children, and woe to the children who have been exiled from their father's table." Due to its great importance, it was instituted in the Aramaic language because this was the spoken language in Babylonia. Therefore, in order for everyone to understand, it was established in the common language. There are also hidden reasons for this.

Our Sages, of blessed memory, said in Shabbat (119b): Anyone who responds "Amen! May His great name be blessed" with all his might – his decree is torn, and the gates of the Garden of Eden are opened for him. And in the Pesikta, in the story of Rabbi Yishmael ben Elisha, it says: When the Israelites enter synagogues and say "May His great name be blessed" in a loud voice – severe decrees are annulled (as explained in the Tosafot there). And at the end of Sotah, it is stated that "Amen! May His great name be blessed" is one of the pillars of the world, see there. Therefore, one must be very careful about this, to respond with intention and in a loud voice.

There are many among the Jewish people who believe that it is a mitzvah to increase the number of Kaddish recitations. How mistaken they are! I say about them, "The holy stones are poured out...". We do not use the scepter of the King of Kings, the Holy One, blessed be He, except as He has permitted us, and one who increases them disrespects the sanctity. One of the great decisors has already written in this section that just as it is good to minimize blessings, so too it is good to minimize Kaddish recitations (Knesset HaGedolah). And one distinguished among the great pious ones cried bitterly about this (the pious one Devar Shmuel in Responsa, section 183, brought in Be'er Hetev, small section 1), and this is his language: those who increase the recitations of Kaddish... and weaken the power of the great and awesome sanctity of God... thus far is his language. Therefore, we will explain how many Kaddish recitations should be said in the prayers. The explanation of Kaddish will be clarified in section 56 with the help of Heaven.

The early authorities only established seven Kaddishes throughout the day: three in Shacharit: one after "Yishtabach," the second after Tachanun, and the third after "Uva Letzion Goel." Two in Mincha: one after "Ashrei," and the second after Tachanun. And two in Arvit: one before the Amidah, and the second after the Amidah. This is based on the verse "Seven times a day I praise You" (Rokeach). Subsequently, they added three more, one in each prayer after "Aleinu." It is written that every person should fulfill the letters of "Tzadi-Kuf" every day, which stands for "Tzadi-Kuf Amnin": four Kedushot, ten Kaddishes, and one hundred blessings (Magen Avraham, siman ?). They established a Kaddish after "Aleinu" for the orphans who cannot lead the prayers, and this is called the "Orphan's Kaddish." On days of Torah reading, an additional Kaddish is recited after the Torah reading. Beyond this, there is no place for additional Kaddishes. Despite this, they added one more after the "Shir Shel Yom" because of the many orphans, but adding more than this is forbidden. In this way, they uphold the banner of the holy Shechinah. It is forbidden to recite Kaddish hastily and without proper intention; this is the way of the ignorant. Rather, it should be recited with intention and contemplation, and with sorrow for the exile of the holy Shechinah.

Maimonides wrote in the order of prayers in the text of Kaddish: "Any group of ten or more Jews who are engaged in the study of the Oral Torah, even in midrash or aggadah, when they finish, one of them says Kaddish in this form... This is called 'Kaddish deRabbanan.'" So are his words. It is clear from his words that only a group of ten studying together has the permission to say this Kaddish, excluding if fewer than ten are studying, and certainly excluding a single individual when studying. According to this, one should rebuke people who, when they have a yahrzeit, study some chapters of Mishnah by themselves and say Kaddish. This is forbidden. Some have written that Kaddish should only be said over words of aggadah, and therefore it is customary to say some aggadic teaching after the study in order to say Kaddish deRabbanan (see Magen Avraham, section 54, subsection 3). Although it seems from Maimonides' words in his commentary on the Mishnah at the end of Avot that this is also the case, upon examining his words that we have cited explicitly, it does not appear so. On the contrary, he wrote "even" regarding aggadah, meaning: and certainly halachot. See section 9.

Any matter of sanctity cannot be performed with fewer than ten Jews: males, adults who have brought two pubic hairs, and freemen, to the exclusion of slaves. Therefore, for Kaddish, Kedushah, and Barchu, if there are not ten present, they should not be recited, for the Divine Presence rests upon ten. The Gemara derives this from a verse in Berachot (21b), from "I will be sanctified among the children of Israel" (Leviticus 22:32), see there. Nevertheless, if they began to recite Kaddish or Kedushah with ten and some of them left in the middle, they may complete that Kaddish or Kedushah that was started. This is provided that six remain, which is the majority of ten. Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) writes in section 2 that, in any case, it is a transgression to leave, and about them it is said: "Those who forsake the Lord will perish" (Isaiah 1:28). However, if ten remain, it is permissible to leave. This is his language. Meaning, if ten remain, it is permissible to leave when there is a compelling reason to do so, such as needing to relieve oneself or similar. For without such a necessity, it is obvious that even if ten remain, it is forbidden to leave. However, if fewer than ten remain, it is under all circumstances forbidden to leave (this seems to be the humble opinion of the author).

A fundamental rule in this law is: when there were ten [people] and some of them left in the middle, they complete that section with the Kaddish associated with it, but no more. For example, if in the middle of Pesukei Dezimra some left – they complete [it] until "Yishtabach" and say Kaddish, but no more because "Yotzer Or" is a different matter. If some left during "Yotzer Or" – they complete until the Amidah but no more. If some left before the Shaliach Tzibbur began the repetition of the Amidah – the Shaliach Tzibbur does not repeat the prayer. If some left after the Shaliach Tzibbur began the repetition of the Amidah – they complete the Kedusha and the entire repetition of the Amidah with the Kaddish after the Amidah, but "Ashrei"-"Uva Letzion" – each one should say it individually. If some left after they began "Ashrei"-"Uva Letzion" – they say the full Kaddish. However, with "Aleinu," even if some left after they began "Aleinu" – they do not say the Kaddish after "Aleinu," because it is only a custom. The same rule applies to Mincha and Maariv. Hallel and Musaf and the reading of the Torah are separate matters. (The Rema in paragraph 3 wrote: And if they left after he began aloud... – they can complete... and say the full Kaddish... thus far his words. This is puzzling, for the full Kaddish is after "Uva Letzion." The Pri Chadash and the Knesses Hagedolah objected to this. And it seems to me that his intention is on the half Kaddish after the Amidah, but nonetheless, it should be said in full because the full Kaddish won't be said again, so it is better to conclude with "Tiskabel" in this Kaddish. Look closely and you will find that this is correct.)

It appears to me that this is also the law regarding the reading of the Torah: if some of the congregation leave, they can fulfill the obligation of the day with those who were called up. The one who reads the Haftarah should not recite the blessings, as the Haftarah is a different matter. Consequently, he should also not recite the blessings over the Torah. However, at Mincha on a public fast day, the one who reads the Haftarah should be the third person called up to the Torah, because he is one of those called up. But the Haftarah and its blessings should not be recited, as it is a separate matter (this is how it appears to me in my humble opinion). See the Magen Avraham at the beginning of Siman 143. This requires further study; see also the Eliyah Rabbah there.

Just as when some of them leave, they complete the prayer with the Kaddish associated with it, so too if they start without ten and in the middle ten arrive, for example, if they started "Baruch She'amar" without ten and by "Yishtabach" ten are present—they say Kaddish as I wrote in Siman 53, and similarly in the evening prayer. There are those who apply this also to learning: that if they started learning without ten and in the middle ten arrived, they should say Kaddish (Taz, Siman 3). Behold, if they learned together for some time—certainly this is the case. But if they came after they had learned— they should not say Kaddish (Magen Avraham, Siman 69, Siman 4). There are those whose words imply that even in such a case they say Kaddish (Taz, ibid), but this is not so. It is not similar to "Yishtabach" because there, the main prayer was established to be prayed with ten and to say Kaddish, but not in learning. There are also those who wanted to say that if there were ten in the synagogue, even though not all learned, they say Kaddish (ibid in the name of Levush, and this seems to be implied by Taz). From the words of the Rambam, it is clearly not so, because even though Kedusha is done also for an individual, as I wrote in Siman 69—this is because every individual is obligated daily in this, as it is a fundamental ordinance of prayer. This is not the case for Kaddish on learning, which is not an obligation, but if ten learn together, the sages permitted saying the Rabbi's Kaddish and not in any other manner, as I wrote in section 5 in the name of the Rambam.

Our Rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, wrote in Section 4: "Some permit saying matters of sanctity with nine and including a minor younger than six who knows to whom one prays. However, the leading decisors do not agree with their words. Similarly, a servant and a woman are not included. And even with a Chumash in his hand, he is not to be included. Nevertheless, there are those who are lenient in a pressing situation." This is the end of their words.

And behold, regarding this matter, it is a dispute among the authorities, with some wanting to permit including him in the ten. Nevertheless, even those who permit it did not resort to doing so in practice (Tosafot Berachot 48a, s.v. "Ve'leit," wrote this about Rabbeinu Tam, see there). And the opinion of the Rambam in the eighth chapter of Berachot is also like this, see there. And this is the wording of our Rabbis, the Tosafot, there: "The conclusion of the matter is: one does not make a minor an addition to the ten for a quorum for blessings and prayer until he brings two pubic hairs." This is the end of their words, and so wrote the Rosh, and so it is in the Jerusalem Talmud there, and so it is in Midrash Rabba "Bereshit" (section 91, see there).

And regarding what they wrote that "some are lenient in a pressing situation," the Levush wrote that he did not see anyone being lenient even in a pressing situation. And so we rule in practical halacha. (See Magen Avraham, subsection 5. And the Eliyah Rabbah and Shevut Yaakov already disagreed with him, as written in Machatzit HaShekel.)

A minor who has reached the age of thirteen years and one day is considered an adult for all matters. We assume that he has brought forth two pubic hairs, as this is the presumption for rabbinic matters, though not for Torah-mandated matters, as explained in several places. However, if we know that he has not brought forth two pubic hairs, he is not considered an adult until he does. But if he is a eunuch, showing signs of being a eunuch, he is considered an adult at twenty years old. If he does not show signs of being a eunuch, he is considered an adult only when the majority of his years have passed, i.e., at thirty-six years old, and not before. (In the Shulchan Aruch, Section 5, it is written: "If he shows signs of being a eunuch earlier, he is considered an adult." This is the end of his words. I am puzzled: Why did he not mention twenty years old? As it is explicitly stated in Yevamot 80a and Niddah 47a. Similarly, the Rambam wrote in the second chapter of Ishut, and the Tur and Shulchan Aruch Even HaEzer, Siman 155.)

A person who is definitely a fool does not count [towards a minyan]. Similarly, a deaf-mute who neither hears nor speaks is considered like a fool. However, if he speaks but does not hear, or hears but does not speak, he is considered competent in all matters and counts [towards a minyan]. One should not ask: since he does not hear what the prayer leader says, or does not speak himself, how can he be included for the recitation of Kaddish and Kedusha? This is not a question at all, for it does not prevent [the recitation] if not everyone answers and hears, as will be explained that even someone who is asleep counts towards the minyan. Similarly, one who is in the middle of the prayer counts, even though he cannot interrupt to respond. The reason is that we need ten [people], for the Divine Presence dwells where there are ten. And when the Divine Presence is here, it is possible to say any matter of sanctity, even if not everyone responds.

This is the language of our teacher, the Beit Yosef, in section 6: If one of the ten started praying alone and cannot respond with them, or he is asleep – even so, he is counted with them. This is his language, and the reason is as we explained. There is one who disagrees regarding the one who is asleep and holds that he is not counted. It is not the same as one who is standing in prayer, for he can be silent and listen to the Kaddish and Kedusha, which is not the case for one who is asleep (Taz, subsection 4). Furthermore, the one who is praying is engaged in the needs of Heaven, but the one who is asleep is at that moment like a dead person, which is why we bless "Who restores souls to dead bodies," so how can he be counted? Nonetheless, there are those who support his words (Magen Avraham, subsection 8, and Eliyah Rabbah, subsection 7). However, more than one should not be counted (Magen Avraham there). But those who are standing in prayer can be counted up to four. However, for one who is asleep, it is certainly preferable to wake him. Also, regarding one who is still standing in prayer, our teacher the Beit Yosef wrote in section 7, and this is his language: When one is praying alone – it is proper for others to wait from saying Kaddish until he finishes, so that he too can merit. This is his language. But if he takes a long time – they should not wait for him. And a sick person who is conscious – they count him if he is lying in the room where they are praying. If he is not conscious, it seems to me that he is not counted. And even according to those who hold that one who is asleep is counted – it is not the same as a sick person, for the one who is asleep can be awakened, which is not the case for the sick person. (There is evidence for this from Gittin 72b, see there. Study it well and you will find clarity.)

A person is always considered a "minor" until he is thirteen years old and one day. It is not necessarily one full day; even one hour after thirteen years, he is considered an adult. He must also have grown two pubic hairs, and we assume he has grown these hairs as I wrote in section 11. A leap year is counted as thirteen months. Therefore, if someone was born in Adar and becomes bar mitzvah in Adar of the thirteenth year, and that year is a leap year, he does not become bar mitzvah until the second Adar. Even though the general rule is that an unspecified Adar refers to the first Adar, this applies to vows and similar matters. But in counting years, it does not conclude in a leap year until thirteen months. Nevertheless, if he was born in a leap year in the first Adar, and the thirteenth year is also a leap year, he becomes bar mitzvah in the first Adar. This is the agreement of most authorities (Eliyah Rabbah section 9, Pri Chadash, Responsa of Rabbi Yaakov ben Meir, and Shvus Yaakov section 9, and the Gaon Rabbi David Oppenheim). Even though there are those who disagree (Magen Avraham section 10 and others), the main ruling follows the majority of authorities. This is also the ruling of the Levush in section 625 (and it is also evident from the words of the Shulchan Aruch in section 10).

Sometimes, two children are born one before the other, yet the one who was born later becomes Bar Mitzvah first. For example, one boy is born in a leap year on the 29th of the first Adar, and the second is born at the beginning of the second Adar. In a non-leap year, the Bar Mitzvah for the second boy occurs at the beginning of Adar, while the first boy becomes Bar Mitzvah on the 29th of Adar. If the year were a leap year, the first boy would become Bar Mitzvah on the 29th of the first Adar, as I wrote in the previous section. However, in a regular year, the boy born at the beginning of the second Adar becomes Bar Mitzvah at the beginning of Adar, and the boy born on the 29th of the first Adar becomes Bar Mitzvah on the 29th of Adar. A boy born on Rosh Chodesh (the first day of the month) becomes Bar Mitzvah on Rosh Chodesh, regardless of whether the Rosh Chodesh was the same in birth and Bar Mitzvah, or whether it was different — such as one day being Rosh Chodesh and now it’s two days; or vice versa, like Kislev and Tevet, which sometimes have one day and sometimes two days. This is also agreed upon by the great authorities (Magen Avraham there, and Sha'arei Teshuva Section 13 in the name of the responsa of the Bach).

A transgressor of the entire Torah is not counted toward a quorum of ten. However, a transgressor of a single sin, or one who violated a communal decree, is counted. However, if he has been excommunicated, as explained in Yoreh De'ah, section 334, he is not counted, for it has been clarified there that one who is distanced is not included in any matter requiring ten. Nevertheless, it is permissible to pray in the synagogue where he is present. One does not need to distance oneself from him unless it has been explicitly decreed to do so, as explained there.

The statement in Pesachim (85b) that even an iron partition does not separate between Israel and their Father in Heaven, means that one who is passing by a synagogue and hears the congregation saying Kaddish, Kedusha, or Barchu must respond with them, provided there is no filthy object or idolatry between them. However, this is only when there are ten people in one place, meaning in one room. But to combine ten people from two different places – they do not combine. It is necessary to say so, for wherever there are ten, the Divine Presence dwells, and this only applies when they are gathered in one place. Otherwise, there are always ten people in a city, so what difference does it make if they are in two places or ten places? Rather, the joining of the ten requires that they all be in one room. Also, the prayer leader must be with them in the same room, and there are detailed laws regarding this, which will be explained with Divine assistance.

And our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 13: One who stands within the entrance from the doorpost and outward, meaning when the door is closed from the point of the inner edge of the door's thickness outward, is considered as being outside. These are his words. This means: the place of the doorframe up to the inner edge of the door is considered inside, since it is always outside the door. But that piece of the doorframe that the door covers is always considered outside, even when the door is open. However, regarding Shabbat, in the discussion of the threshold (Shabbat 9a), it is said: An open door is considered inside. And in truth, there are those who disagree with this, and even our teacher the Beit Yosef himself in his larger work holds this way. However, he found that the Ravyah did not write this, and therefore he ruled stringently. But the later authorities have noted that the great poskim disagree on this (Magen Avraham section 11 and Eliyah Rabbah). Therefore, one may be lenient in this matter if it is needed for those standing under the doorframe when the door is open.

Roofs and upper stories are not considered part of the house, and someone standing on them does not count towards the quorum with those in the house. The Tur and the Shulchan Aruch ruled in section 15 that if some are outside and some are inside, and the prayer leader stands in the doorway, he joins them together. This is their language. This is like in the Grace After Meals later in section 195, where the prayer leader joins them as if they were all in one room, even if they cannot see each other, because both sides follow the prayer leader.

Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in Section 14: Someone who is standing behind the synagogue, and there is a window between them even if it is several stories high, even if it is not four handbreadths wide, and he shows them his face from there - he joins them to make a quorum of ten. Thus was his wording. He also brought this in his great book in the name of a Gaon, see there. He holds that seeing the face in this manner is considered as if the whole body is present. And it could be that since the Shechinah (Divine Presence) resides where there are ten people, and the primary resting of the Shechinah is on the face, as it is written: "the skin of his face shone." And some have written that although upper-levels do not join those standing in the main part of the synagogue, nevertheless, if the upper levels are not complete partitions but rather with poles, in a way that those below can see those above, and it is difficult for them to come down - they join together. Some are hesitant about this (see Eliyah Rabbah Section 12, and Sha'arei Teshuvah Section 15). And perhaps in a pressing situation, one can rely and permit it. However, it is certain that those standing in the women's section do not join with those standing in the synagogue, even if there are windows from the women's section to the synagogue, and they can see each other's faces, because they are complete partitions - they are considered two separate domains. And it is not similar to someone standing behind the synagogue who joins by showing their face, because there he is not in a separate house but in a courtyard or street, and therefore we consider him as if he is standing in the synagogue. But not someone standing in a separate house. (This seems to be my humble opinion. And also, someone standing behind the synagogue - only one person joins, not more, as this seems to be the implication of the language of the Shulchan Aruch, and let's not add to it. This seems to be my humble opinion on these laws.)

It is stated in Eruvin (92a) that if a small courtyard is breached into a larger one, meaning that the wall of the small courtyard is entirely breached into the larger one, and there are no remnants of the wall for the small courtyard while the larger courtyard retains remnants of the wall, and for someone standing in the small courtyard it appears as if they are one courtyard, these two courtyards are considered as one. The residents of the larger courtyard dominate the smaller one, but the residents of the smaller courtyard do not dominate the larger one. In other words, the residents of the larger courtyard have authority over the smaller one, drawing it to be considered as one courtyard with them. However, the smaller courtyard does not draw the larger one after it. The reason is that since on one side they appear as one and on the other side they appear as two, the smaller courtyard is nullified in relation to the larger one for all the laws in the Torah, as explained there.

Therefore, the same law applies to the combining of a quorum of ten. That is, if the congregation is in a large room and the prayer leader is in a small room, they combine to form a quorum and fulfill their obligation, as it is considered as if the prayer leader is also in the large room. However, if the congregation is in a small room and the prayer leader is in a large room, they do not fulfill their obligation, because the congregation cannot draw the prayer leader after them, since the prayer leader is in the large room. And the prayer leader cannot draw the congregation, because the congregation does not follow an individual as an individual follows the congregation. Certainly, if there are nine in the large room and one in the small room, they combine; but if one is in the large room and nine in the small room, they do not combine, for the reason explained. And it seems to me that they mentioned the case of the prayer leader, and similarly, more than one individual up to four individuals. If there are four in the small room and six in the large room, they combine. Conversely, they do not combine, as the majority does not follow the minority. Likewise, if it is half and half, they do not combine. If the prayer leader or individuals are on the threshold of the large room and the majority are in the small room, they combine (Perisha and Eliyah Rabbah).

However, if the smaller room does not fully open into the larger room, they do not combine at all. Therefore, people in two different rooms cannot be counted together for a minyan (prayer quorum). In a synagogue, everyone needs to be in the synagogue itself. If someone stands in the entryway, which is the room leading into or adjacent to the synagogue, even if there is a doorway from that room to the synagogue, they do not combine to form a minyan. It has already been clarified that all of this applies to forming a minyan. But if there is already a minyan in one place, then those standing in other places can respond "Amen," and participate in Kaddish, Kedusha, and "Barchu." And if they are praying with the congregation, they are considered as praying with the community.

The platform (bimah), even though it is ten handbreadths high and four handbreadths wide, and it has partitions and constitutes its own domain, nevertheless, regarding the joining for a minyan (quorum of ten), since it is an accessory of the synagogue, one who stands there joins the minyan, for in this respect it is considered as one place with the synagogue. And it seems to me that even if nine are on the platform and one is in the synagogue, they join together. It is not comparable to a large and small room, as it has been explained that the platform and the synagogue are considered as one entity for the purpose of joining. And even though regarding standing before a Torah scroll it is considered a separate domain, as I wrote in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 242, it is not comparable, for there the standing is due to the honor of the Torah scroll, and when the division of the domain is apparent, the reason for the honor is nullified. But for joining, they are one. Nevertheless, there is an opinion that if the partitions reach the ceiling, they constitute a separate domain. One should be concerned for this opinion. However, this is not common at all, and even if from one side or both sides they reach the ceiling, since from the other sides they do not reach, they are considered one.

A city that has only ten [men] and one of them wants to leave for the entire year – they cannot prevent him [from leaving]. But during the High Holy Days, they can prevent him, either not to leave or to appoint another in his place. However, if there are ten without him – they cannot prevent him. Even though it can be argued that perhaps one of them will need to relieve himself, or might become ill and the quorum will not be maintained, for if so, there would be no end to the matter (see Taz). And if there are eleven men, and two want to leave – they hire someone to replace them to complete the minyan. They pay half according to wealth and half according to individuals. And there are those who say that in this case, the payment is only according to individuals, since each one is obligated to appoint someone in his place. Only when there are eight and they need to hire two for the minyan – in this case, the eight pay half according to wealth and half according to individuals, because the poor can say that from their side they can go to pray elsewhere, but not so the wealthy who fear leaving their property – they need to pay more. But when two are leaving from here – the poor and rich are equal (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 16). And those who leave from here need to pay their share also for hiring the chazan. There is no difference whether they want to leave before the High Holy Days or much earlier, for as long as they do not return by the High Holy Days – they are obligated to appoint someone in their place and to bear the burden with those who remain. And one who is forced to flee – is completely exempt if he is not negligent in his fleeing. (See Magen Avraham, subparagraph 16, and Eliyah Rabbah, subparagraph 20, that "negligence" is called if he injured his fellow or damaged his property, see there. Examine and you will find it easy.)

It is not obligatory to force someone to rent in order to complete a quorum except during the High Holy Days, and only if lacking one or two people. Unless there is a well-established and publicized custom in the city to compel renting even if lacking three or four or more, according to the custom. And when there is a quorum in the city, but none of them can serve as a prayer leader, they compel each other to hire a cantor. Similarly, in a place where there is not always a quorum in the synagogue, and not everyone comes to pray, they can compel each other with fines to always have a quorum in the synagogue so that the regular prayers are not disrupted. However, if there is another synagogue in the city, they cannot compel attendance specifically at this synagogue.

The Mahari"l responded regarding settlements that need to hire a quorum and a cantor, and there are surroundings where people are accustomed to come to these settlements to pray; nevertheless, the settlements cannot compel the people from the surroundings to share the burden with them, because they can say, "We can travel to another place" (Magen Avraham, subsection 17). Nevertheless, it seems to me that this is not a general rule, and everything depends on the circumstances. And with us, the simple custom is that all the people from the surroundings share the burden of the expense.

It has already been explained the great importance and sanctity of the Kaddish at the beginning of the previous section. This is our hope for the future, as the prophet said: "And I will be exalted and sanctified and known... and they will know that I am the Lord" – this is the ultimate purpose of creation. This verse is said regarding the war of Gog and Magog, when, up until now, His blessed name has been profaned among idol worshippers, but then His great name will be exalted and sanctified. And this is its explanation: "Y'hei Sh'mei Rabba" in Aramaic, this is like in Hebrew "His great name" and it refers to the Tetragrammaton. Some say that "Sh'mei" consists of two words: "Shem" (name) Yud-Hei, because from the day the Temple was destroyed, it is sufficient for the world to use the two letters of the name Yud-Hei. The name is not complete and the throne is not complete until the seed of Amalek is obliterated, as it is written: "For there is a hand on the throne of Y'[H], the Lord will wage war against Amalek." And this is what we plead for, that the name Yud-Hei be exalted and sanctified, and that the entire Tetragrammaton be complete, as it is written: "On that day, the Lord will be One and His name One," as stated at the end of the third chapter of Pesachim. And this is the great name Yud-Hei, which will further increase: the Vav and the second Hei.

"In the world that He created according to His will" – in the world that He created according to His desire. The "kaf" of "kir'utey" is soft, as per the rule of Beged Kefet when following a vowel. Some say that the "kaf" is hard, as "kir'utey" refers to "may He be magnified and sanctified," implying that this will be according to His will, and does not refer to "that He created." And it is hard as per the rule of interruption, as known to grammarians (the Gra). A proof for this interpretation is from the phrase "on everything may He be magnified and sanctified" which is recited on Shabbat and Yom Tov during the Torah reading, where it says "according to His will and the will of all who fear Him," and it refers to "may He be magnified and sanctified." Here as well it is the same (ibid.). "And may He establish His kingdom" – this is a prayer as it is written: "The Lord will be king over the whole earth." In the Sephardic version, they add "may His salvation sprout and may His anointed one draw near," and some versions have "the end of His anointed one." However, by saying "and may He establish His kingdom," it implicitly refers to the coming of the Messiah, as is evident.

"In your lifetime… speedily and soon" – This is a prayer that we merit to see this in our lifetime, and that it should happen quickly. Because the pains of the Messiah are difficult to endure, we therefore pray that it should happen quickly. The Aramaic term "speedily" is equivalent to the Hebrew term "soon," as stated in Berachot (18b). "And soon," meaning: it should be quickly and in the near future. "And say Amen. May His great name…" – The prayer leader commands that the congregation respond "Amen," and they respond "Amen." Meaning: it should indeed be so that His great name be blessed forever and ever, meaning: after we merit that His great name be magnified and sanctified, it should remain blessed forever and ever. Unlike the first and second Temples, after which His blessed name was again desecrated, but now His great name should remain blessed forever. Some versions have "and blessed." This follows the opinion that "His name" consists of two words, but the primary interpretation is the first one. This is what our teacher the Ramah wrote in section 1, that one should not pause between "May His great name" and "blessed," as is proven in Sukkah (39a). It appears to me that his intention is not to say it in one breath, for it is explicitly stated there that we do not hold by this. Rather, his intention is that there should not be a break in the topic, and then say "blessed" afterward, but rather to say it together (and this resolves the question of the Magen Avraham in subsection 2). It has already been explained at the beginning of chapter 55 that one must respond "Amen, May His great name" with intention and in a loud voice. "Magnified" the dalet has a tzeirei, and also the dalet of "and sanctified." "His name" is without a mappiq hey. "Blessed" with a kamatz under the bet and a patach under the resh. "Forever" with a kamatz under the ayin. "And forever and ever," and some say "forever" without a vav. The primary custom is to say it with a vav, and this is the custom of the world.

Until where should one answer "Amen. Yehei Shmei Rabbah"? There are differing opinions regarding this. Some say to answer only until "Almaya," and this is the opinion of the Tur. This also appears to be the understanding of the Rambam; see there. The opinion of the Kabbalists is to answer "Yitbarach" as well, and this is the opinion of our teacher, the Beit Yosef, who wrote in section 3: Those who answer only until "Le'almaya" are mistaken, for it is forbidden to separate between "Almaya" and "Yitbarach." Until here are his words, and his source is from the Midrash (see Beit Yosef). There, the intention is regarding interrupting speech, as is clear to the one who examines there. Nevertheless, it seems that even in the response, one should not interrupt (Beit Yosef). Similarly, Rabbeinu Bachya wrote in Parashat "Shemot" on the verse "And their cry went up to God," and these are his words: One must connect the word "Almaya" to "Yitbarach," and one should not interrupt them at all just as... until here are his words. Some answer until "De'amiran Be'alma" (Beit Yosef in the name of Rabbeinu David Abudarham). Most of the world holds according to the opinion of our teacher, the Beit Yosef, who answers until "Yitbarach," and this is the custom (and the Gra wrote "until Almaya"). However, all this applies if the prayer leader says word by word slowly. But when he says it quickly, and by the time the responder answers until "Yitbarach," the prayer leader is already at the end of Kaddish – the individual should answer until "De'amiran Be'alma." This is also what I have seen practiced.

Maimonides wrote that after the Chazzan (prayer leader) says "Yitbarach," the congregation responds "Amen." The Tur wrote that this is not the custom, see there. All the more so according to our custom, where we respond until "Yitbarach," it is certainly not relevant to respond "Amen." And we say "Yitbarach v'yishtabach... v'yit'aleh v'yithalal." Some say not to say "v'yithalal," as there is no need to say more than seven praises corresponding to the seven heavens. From "Yitbarach" to "v'yit'aleh" there are seven words, and those who say this count from "v'yishtabach." The simple custom is to say it. Our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote that one must have intention when responding to the Kaddish, meaning that Kaddish requires intention to understand what is being said and to pay attention to this holy prayer. Without intention, it is nothing, and it is better not to say it. He also wrote that one should respond in a loud voice and make an effort to hear Kaddish, see there.

When the prayer leader says "Yitgadal v'yitkadash sh'mei rabba" (May His great name be exalted and sanctified), the congregation responds "Amen." Similarly, after "v'yikarov meshichei" (and may His Messiah draw near) according to the Sephardic custom, the congregation responds "Amen." Likewise, after "b'reich hu" (blessed is He), the congregation responds "Amen." The Ashkenazi custom is to respond "b'reich hu." After "v'imru amen" (and say Amen), the congregation responds "Amen."

Rabbeinu the Rema wrote that one should not pause between "hu" and "l'eila min kol birchata" (above all the blessings), see there. For he holds that "b'reich hu" refers to the lower part, meaning: "b'reich hu l'eila min kol birchata" (blessed is He above all the blessings). However, there are those who object to this, claiming that "b'reich hu" refers to the earlier phrase "Kudsha Brich Hu" (the Holy One, blessed be He), as in the Hebrew phrase "Hakadosh Baruch Hu" (the Holy One, blessed be He). And so it is explained by the Rambam, who wrote that "Amen" is said after "b'reich hu." And such is the widespread custom. "L'eila" (above) refers to "yitbarach v'yishtabach" (may He be blessed and praised), meaning He should be blessed above all the blessings, songs, and praises that have ever been uttered.

The phrase "v'nechemata" (and the consolations) needs clarification. It seems to me that the intention is that the consolations foretold by the prophets are also great, and therefore we say that He should be above the consolations of the prophets. Moreover, our Sages of blessed memory also said this, that all the prophets prophesied only for the days of the Messiah. But for the World to Come – no eye has seen...

And during the Ten Days of Repentance, we say "l'eila ul'eila" (above and above). Then we say "mikol birchata" (from all the blessings), not "min kol birchata" (from all the blessings). The reason is that there is a specific number of words in the Kaddish, and therefore when one word is added, another word must be subtracted.

The Tur and Shulchan Aruch wrote that there are five bowings in the Kaddish: when saying "Yitgadal" one bows, similarly at "Yehei Shemei Rabba," at "Yitbarach," at "Brich Hu," and when saying "Amen." The Tur wrote in the name of Rav Natrunai Gaon that four bowings are obligatory and one is optional. However, he considers the fifth bowing to be at "Oseh Shalom," see there. Some are hesitant about these bowings (Gra), because one should not add to the bowings prescribed by the Sages. In my humble opinion, these are not actual bowings like those of the Shemoneh Esrei, but rather a slight bend, and so it should be done. After completing the Kaddish, one takes three steps back, and then says "Oseh Shalom...". The custom is to bow slightly, as per the words of Rav Natrunai that we mentioned.

And know that people customarily refer to "Half Kaddish" and "Full Kaddish." There are some among the masses who believe that this is truly "Half Kaddish." This is a mistake, as the real end of the Kaddish is only up to "da'amiran b'alma." However, at the end of the prayer, we add the prayer "Tiskabel" and "Yehei Shlama Rabba," since peace is the pillar of the world. Therefore, after the conclusion of the prayer and when we need to go out into the world, we ask the Blessed Name that there be peace among us. We also add "Oseh Shalom Bimromav…" even though it is a single matter with "Yehei Shlama Rabba," it seems to me that this is a different prayer. Initially, we ask that there be peace among us, and afterwards, we ask that even if, God forbid, some dispute arises, the Holy Blessed One will help us make peace as He makes peace in His heights between two opposites, as the Tur wrote: "Oseh Shalom Bimromav" refers to the angels who are fire and water, and one does not extinguish the other. See there. Therefore, we say that even if a dispute arises with differing opinions to two extremes, nonetheless, He will help us make peace. And the term "Half Kaddish" is just a name.

Our teacher, the Rema, wrote that one should stand when answering Kaddish and any matter of sanctity. Thus is his language. However, the Maharil does not hold this way. And it is similarly written in the Kavanot and writings of the Ari, of blessed memory, that any Kaddish that one encounters while standing – one should stand until after "Amen, Yehei Shmei Rabbah." And when he is sitting – he does not need to stand (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 4). Nevertheless, since we find that Eglon, king of Moab, stood when he heard the word of God – all the more so should we stand (ibid.). And it seems to me that the custom is that for the obligatory Kaddishes within the prayer, one should stand, and for other Kaddishes, there is no need to stand. 

He further wrote that one who comes to the synagogue and hears the congregation answering Kaddish, should answer with them even though he did not hear the chazzan say "Yitgadal." Thus is his language. Meaning: when he arrives at the moment the congregation is answering "Amen, Yehei Shmei Rabbah" – he should answer with them. And this is obvious.

He also wrote that when beginning "Yitgadal," one should say "And now, may the power...". Thus is his language. And this is not the custom. Similarly, some say verses at "Titkabbal" and "Yehei Shlama Rabbah," and this is not the custom. And the Ari, of blessed memory, commanded not to say them (as the Magen Avraham wrote in subparagraph 7, see there).

After the Kaddish, the prayer leader (Shaliach Tzibbur) says: "Bless the Lord who is to be blessed!" and the congregation responds: "Blessed is the Lord who is to be blessed forever and ever!" The prayer leader also repeats: "Blessed is the Lord who is to be blessed forever and ever!" (According to the Rambam in Chapter Twelve of the Laws of Prayer, he does not repeat "Blessed...". This is also the opinion of Maharam of Rothenburg.) This is in order to include himself in the blessing, as he initially said "Bless!" meaning that the congregation should bless. Therefore, he also blesses the Holy One, Blessed be He, as I have written below in Siman 139. One does not respond "Amen" after the prayer leader repeats "Blessed...". There are those who do respond, but they are mistaken.

Rabbeinu the Rema wrote that it is customary for the prayer leader to extend the word "Barchu," and the congregation says "May He be blessed and praised..." while he extends "Barchu" — thus far his words. This applies when the prayer leader extends the melody. However, when he is saying the words, nothing should be said. Therefore, we do not have this custom, as in our practice, the prayer leader does not extend the melody of "Barchu".

Know that it is customary to bow slightly when saying "Barchu," though not with the full bowing as in the Shemoneh Esrei. This is proper. Even according to what will be explained in Siman 139, that during the Torah reading one should not bow, nonetheless, during prayer, one bows. This is the prevalent custom. There are those who wrote not to turn their face from the east until they say "Blessed..." (Shaarei Teshuva). I do not know the reason for this: for during the Torah reading, we do not turn our faces to the east, so what is the difference here? Rather, it happens naturally, since one is facing east, why should he turn his face? But according to the law, it seems to me that there is no hindrance in this. (And what the Magen Avraham wrote in subparagraph 1 will be explained in Siman 124, that it is not so, see there.)

It is forbidden to interrupt between Kaddish and "Barchu" and between "Barchu" and "Yotzer Or". The same applies for Maariv. Even for the sake of a mitzvah, it is forbidden to interrupt. In places where it is customary to delay the prayer for some reason, the delay should occur before Kaddish, as I wrote in Siman 54. Nonetheless, even in this case, our custom is not to delay as I wrote there. See there.

Maimonides wrote in the first chapter of the Laws of Reading the Shema, Law 11: What is its proper time during the day? The mitzvah is to begin reciting it before sunrise so that one finishes the Shema and blesses the final blessing with the sunrise. This timing is about one-tenth of an hour before the sun rises. If he delayed and read the Shema after the sun rises, he has fulfilled his obligation, as its time extends until the end of the third hour of the day for one who delayed.
