And if one read the Shema after dawn, even if he finished before the sunrise, he has fulfilled his obligation. In pressing circumstances, such as when one needs to leave early on a journey, one may initially read the Shema from the time of dawn. Thus far are his words. According to his opinion, the primary time for reciting the Shema from the Torah is a bit before sunrise, so that he finishes the final blessing of the Shema, which is the blessing "Who redeemed Israel," exactly at sunrise, allowing him to start the Amidah prayer immediately after sunrise, as it is written: "They shall fear You with the sun," referring to the prayer. This was the practice of the pious ones, as explained in Berakhot (9b). Although others say there that the time for reciting the Shema is when one can recognize his friend from a distance of four cubits, and Rav Huna said the law follows the others, nonetheless, Abaye later said for tefillin like the others, for reciting the Shema like the pious ones..., see there. The law follows Abaye, and this is also the opinion of the Rif.

The approach of Rabbeinu Tam and Rabbeinu Chananel, as presented in Tosafot Yoma (37b), is that the primary time for reciting the Shema according to Torah law is after sunrise (netz hachamah), as proved from Yoma there. The verse "They shall fear You with the sun" refers to the recitation of the Shema, since the Shema also signifies "fear". The pious ones (vatikin) would indeed recite it slightly before the time, because they wanted to begin the Amidah prayer immediately after sunrise, and Abaye also held this view. When it is said "like the vatikin" regarding the recitation of the Shema, it is merely a signifier that the appropriate time is at sunrise, though the vatikin would start a little earlier. There is no concern in doing so, as one can fulfill the obligation of Shema immediately after dawn (amud hashachar) in extenuating circumstances. Thus, according to this approach and that of the Rambam, the time for reciting the Shema according to others is completely dismissed. However, this is not the opinion of most of the poskim, as will be explained.

This is the language of the Tur: From when is its time? From when one can see his acquaintance who is somewhat familiar to him from a distance of four cubits and recognize him. And it extends until the end of three hours. And the preferred mitzvah is to recite it like the "vatikin" (those who are scrupulous in their observance), who would aim to recite it a little before sunrise, so that they would finish it and its blessings with sunrise, and immediately follow it with the prayer at sunrise. And so wrote the Rambam... And whoever can do so – his reward is very great, and it is assured for him that he is a son of the World to Come, and he will not be harmed all day. Thus far his words. And this is the opinion of the Tosafot and the Rosh and most of the poskim (decisors of Jewish law), that the time is from when one can see his acquaintance who is somewhat familiar to him from a distance of four cubits and recognize him. For if he is very familiar with him, he would recognize him even at night, and if he is not familiar with him at all, surely he would not recognize him even later. But one who is somewhat familiar, and so it is stated in the Jerusalem Talmud. And this time is much before sunrise. And that which is written "and so wrote the Rambam," does not refer to the entire matter but rather to the mitzvah of the vatikin (Kesef Mishneh). And our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, ruled according to the opinion of the Tur, because most of the poskim hold this way.

And we need to understand what all these opinions are arguing about. Since, after the fact, one fulfills their obligation from dawn, because after dawn it is considered day for all matters in the Torah. If so, where do we derive other measures? According to the view of Rabbeinu Tam and Rabbeinu Chananel, it is satisfactory, as it is taught at the end of the second chapter of Megillah that all daytime commandments are ideally performed from sunrise, and if they are performed from dawn, they are valid, because the main strength of the day is at sunrise. And even according to the Rambam, it is not so difficult, since the main prayer time is from sunrise, as it is written, "They shall fear You with the sun," and it is a great mitzvah to connect redemption to prayer. Therefore, we begin before sunrise so that one finishes with sunrise, as I have written. But according to the Tur and most of the poskim who hold that the measure is when one can recognize his friend..., and likewise all the measures of the Tannaim in the Mishnah there, which are between dawn and sunrise, from where do we derive this?

The explanation of the matter is as follows: The positive commandment of reciting the Shema is not comparable to other commandments. For all commandments that apply during the day are applicable throughout the entire day, and all commandments that apply at night are applicable throughout the entire night and no more. However, the recitation of the Shema is different, as the daytime Shema is only applicable until three hours into the day and no further. Moreover, the nighttime Shema is not only applicable throughout the entire night but also extends into the day. This is why the Sages stated that sometimes, if one recites the Shema after dawn, they fulfill the obligation of the nighttime Shema (Berachot 9b), as I have written later in Siman 235.

The reason for this is that since the Torah states regarding the Shema, "when you lie down and when you rise" (Deuteronomy 6:7), it emphasizes the times of lying down and rising. And since there are people who sleep even after dawn, it is still considered night for this purpose, even though dawn generally marks the beginning of the day in all other matters. Similarly, the Gemara there explains that this is because there are people who sleep at that hour (Berachot 9a). The daytime Shema is also considered valid because there are people who rise from their beds at that hour (Berachot 9b). However, after three hours into the day, it is not common for anyone to still be sleeping, and even princes rise from their beds by the end of the third hour, so it can no longer be called "when you rise." Therefore, the nighttime Shema extends even after night until sunrise, as everyone rises from their beds by then. But until sunrise, there are still some who remain in bed. The daytime Shema, however, is only until three hours into the day, as by then everyone has risen from their beds.

The Tannaim (Mishnaic sages) disagree about the initial time: when is the time that most people rise from their beds, so that it can be called "when you rise"? One says this, and another says that. And we follow the opinion of the "Acharim" (others), that this is the time when most people rise from their beds.

And with this, it is understood what is in the mitzvah of the recitation of the Shema, ideally and after the fact. Ideally, one should recite it from the time he can see his friend at a distance of four cubits or another measurement, and after the fact, until the end of the third hour. Because certainly, ideally, one should fulfill "when you lie down" for most of the world, but after the fact, if there are only some people who are now getting up like princes – he has fulfilled it. And there is no question: why do we not say that the entire day is "when you lie down" just as the entire night is "when you lie down,” as indeed our teacher, the Beit Yosef, asked in his great book? It is not similar: lying down can properly be called so as long as one is lying down, but rising is only recognized when one gets up. After that, it is not called "rising" but "standing," "sitting," or "walking" (Magen Avraham, small section 7, and Taz, end of small section 4). And for this, our teacher the Beit Yosef wrote in section 2 that if one did not recite the Shema before sunrise, he should hasten to recite it as soon as possible. Until here is his language. And the reason is that then, at any rate, more people rise from their beds in the world compared to later.

There are those who asked: Just as one fulfills the obligation of reciting the nighttime Shema after dawn because there are people who are still lying in their beds and it is considered "when you lie down," so too should one fulfill the obligation of reciting the nighttime Shema until three hours into the day, for there are princes who are still lying in their beds? There are those who answered that they are lying down but not sleeping, and therefore "when you rise" applies to them and not "when you lie down" (Magen Avraham, section 6, in the name of Milchamot). And there are those who answered that, indeed, for the daytime Shema, we follow "when you rise" of the princes even though they are a minority, since it is completely day. But for the nighttime Shema, reciting it during the day does not follow the minority of the princes (ibid., in the name of Rashba). However, after dawn, many are still sleeping in their beds, and the day has not yet fully broken – it is properly considered "when you lie down."

In my humble opinion, this question does not even begin, for it is clear that if one recites the nighttime Shema after dawn, one does not fulfill the obligation of the daytime Shema, as our master the Beit Yosef wrote in section 5. His words are as follows: "If one was coerced and did not recite the evening Shema until dawn rose, since the sun has not yet risen, one recites the Shema and fulfills the obligation of the evening Shema. And if at that moment one was compelled to leave on a journey due to the danger of wild animals or bandits, one should not recite the Shema again to fulfill the obligation of the daytime Shema, because once that time has been designated as night, it cannot be reconsidered as day." This is his language. And now, consequently, it is absolutely impossible to recite the Shema after sunrise for the obligation of the night, for if so, it would not be possible to recite the morning Shema. For once you have designated it as night, how can you now designate it as day? And the entire time after sunrise is in the same status. All the more so, if one recites the evening Shema within the three hours, there would be no time left for the morning Shema, because after three hours the time has passed. And if we say that one should then recite the morning Shema before sunrise and the evening Shema after sunrise, it is certainly impossible to advance the time of the morning Shema before the evening Shema of the previous day. Therefore, this question has no place at all. (See Magen Avraham, subsection 6, who wrote in the name of the Milchamot as follows: "Regarding the morning Shema, although we require it to be in the morning and not all day, since it is written 'when you rise'... Moreover, because they fixed the paragraph of Tzitzit, where it is written 'and you shall see it,' therefore they fixed its time from when one can distinguish between blue... until here is his language. I do not understand: is it written morning for the Shema? Moreover, we hold like the others, not from when one can distinguish between blue... This requires further study. And according to what we have explained in section 7, it comes out simply and clearly. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

One who is compelled, such as someone who needs to go on a journey in a place with bands of wild animals and robbers, and will not be able to stand and concentrate even for the first paragraph, and even up to "upon your heart." And even according to what will be explained in Siman 63 that the main intention is in the first verse, nonetheless, it is explained there that a temporary journey is forbidden to read. According to the opinion of the Ba’al HaMaor in the Tur there, one needs intention up to "upon your heart." If so, in such a dangerous place when he goes, it will certainly be a temporary journey (see Magen Avraham Section 4). And similarly, if the caravan is moving quickly and they will not wait for him at all – he may read it with its blessings from the time the dawn rises, and he can also say the blessing of "Yotzer Or." Some say he should not say "Yotzer Or" at that time (there, Section 5). However, if he is not going to a place with bands of wild animals and robbers, and the members of the caravan are not in such a hurry, even if he leaves for the journey after dawn has risen – he does not read until its designated time. Nonetheless, in retrospect, if he has already read it from when dawn has risen, even though he was not compelled – he has fulfilled his obligation. If he read it without the blessings – he should read it again at its proper time with the blessings, and see further in Siman 60. Also, if there is something urgent in the city that necessitates reading the Shema as early as possible, such as there is a deceased, or a circumcision, or on Hoshana Rabbah when they increase supplications – they may read it immediately after dawn. Similarly, those who pray at the break of dawn on the first day of Shavuot (there, Section 3).

Three hours constitute a quarter of the day when the day and night are equal. At all times, we estimate based on a quarter of the day. When the day is sixteen hours long, the time for reciting the Shema extends until four hours. In winter, when the day is eight hours long, the time for reciting the Shema is only two hours into the day. According to this, in our countries, which are in the northern part of the world, the time for reciting the Shema in summer ends at the middle of the eighth hour, even if we calculate from sunrise, as explained in the tables. Therefore, in summer, one must be careful to begin prayer no later than a quarter past the seventh hour, so that they reach the recitation of the Shema before the middle of the eighth hour. However, in winter, the time for reciting the Shema extends until the tenth hour and a bit more, as explained in the tables. (And the Taz in subsection 1 brings from the Beit Yosef that in winter, when the day is short, one should hasten, see there. This is in their countries. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

This that we have written, that at all times we measure a quarter of the day, and this is called "proportional hours" (sha'ot zemaniot), meaning that the day is always twelve hours and the night is twelve hours, but the hours are not equal except on days when the day and night are equal. However, when the day is longer than the night, the hour of the day is longer than that of the night, and when the night is longer than the day, the hour of the night is longer than that of the day. So wrote the Rambam in his commentary on the Mishnah in the first chapter of Berakhot, see there. And what is said in the Zohar Vayakhel (page 195b) that if an hour is added to the night, those hours that are added are from the day, see there – this refers to the Garden of Eden, where the Holy One, blessed be He, delights there with the righteous as explained there. And there, the day and night are equal in hours, but not concerning our Torah laws. Otherwise, we would say in the winter on Friday evening that it is permissible to do work until after the sixth hour after midday, and on Saturday night we would forbid doing work until after the sixth hour? Ridiculous. And heaven forbid to say so. (And so it appears in the Magen Avraham, Siman 1, subsection 4. And so wrote in the Yad Ephraim there in the name of the Kabbalist Rabbi Shalom Sharabi.)

However, there is a question regarding this: Although certainly for all the laws of the Torah this is the case, nevertheless, concerning the recitation of the Shema, where it is written "when you lie down and when you rise," isn't it true that lying down and rising do not change whether the day is lengthened or shortened? That is to say, when the day and night are equal, the time for reciting the Shema is until the end of the third hour of the day, because princes sleep until the third hour. If so, does it mean that during the summer solstice, when a quarter of the day is at half of the eighth hour, will princes then rise? They sleep until after the ninth hour. Therefore, the time for reciting the Shema should always be until the end of the ninth hour, since it is still considered "when you rise." I have seen one of the great authorities who thought to say so (Mishkenot Yaakov, Siman 76, and he wrote "if I were not afraid," see there).

However, in truth, this is not a question at all, and the laws of the Torah will never change, meaning to consider the custom of the place. The Torah commanded us regarding matters dependent on day and night that each person, wherever they are, should follow the laws of the day when it is day for them, even if it is night elsewhere, and follow the laws of the night when it is night for them, even if it is day elsewhere. About this, it is said: "It is a Sabbath to the Lord in all your dwellings." This means: you should accept the Sabbath wherever you are dwelling, such that when it is night on Friday in your place, it is Sabbath for you, even if it is still Friday elsewhere. Conversely, on Saturday evening, when it is night, it is a weekday for you, even if it is still Sabbath elsewhere. The same applies to the recitation of Shema, about which the Torah said "when you lie down and when you rise up" – it does not depend on each individual’s time to lie down and rise up, but rather on the time of lying down for most of the world and the time of rising up for most of the world. Our sages of blessed memory estimated that at the time of sunrise most of the world rises from their beds, some rise at dawn, and princes sleep until three hours into the day, which is a quarter of the day. We do not consider the fact that in some cities at sunrise everyone is still sleeping and similar cases. Accordingly, it is as if the Torah said that you should recite Shema at sunrise, and the time for reciting Shema extends until the quarter of the day. Therefore, in every place according to its position on the globe, when the sun rises there, it is the time for reciting Shema. When a quarter of the day passes there, the time for reciting Shema has passed, just like the Sabbath. We do not consider whether the people there have already risen or are still sleeping, for the Torah was not given according to human customs, but it is a decree: such and such you shall do by day and by night. Consequently, whenever it is day for someone, the commandments of the day apply to him, and at night, the commandments of the night apply to him.

There is an opinion that a quarter of the day is calculated from dawn (Magen Avraham, subsection 1). According to this, in our country during the summer, the time for reciting the Shema would pass after the middle of the seventh hour, because here in the summer, the time from dawn until sunrise is long. However, the great scholars of the generation have extensively refuted this, bringing clear evidence that we calculate from sunrise (the Gra in Siman 459, and the Grash in his Siddur). Similarly, the Levush wrote later in Siman 233, and this is the primary opinion we follow in practice. Thus, the time for reciting the Shema is printed in the schedules according to the calculation from sunrise, and may we adhere to this calculation. Yet, due to our many sins, it has become as if permitted to pass the time for reciting the Shema, especially in the summer. In any case, if one sees that the time will pass, one should recite the Shema even without the blessings. Although this is not entirely in accordance with the rabbinic enactment, which specifically instituted it with the blessings, nonetheless, from the Torah, he fulfills his obligation. Even if he does not have his tefillin available at that moment, he should recite it without the tefillin. For our sages did not say, "Anyone who recites the Shema without tefillin is as if he bears false witness against himself" (Berachot 14b) except when he has tefillin available; but not that the time for reciting the Shema should pass because of this. Several great authorities have also written this (Levush and Ma'adanei Yom Tov, and see Taz). They have also written that one should recite it with its blessings, see there.

The recitation of the Shema is a positive commandment from the Torah, to be recited twice every day, once in the morning and once in the evening. Rambam includes it in the enumeration of the commandments, and this is the opinion of most of our Rabbis. Even those who hold that the recitation of the Shema is of rabbinic origin agree that there is an obligation and a positive commandment from the Torah to recite "when you lie down and when you rise up." However, they believe that according to the Torah, one fulfills the obligation with other sections of the Torah as well (Tosafot Yom Tov in the third chapter, and Sha'agat Aryeh, section 1), and the Rabbis instituted the recitation of these three sections. Nonetheless, we hold that the actual recitation of the Shema is of Torah origin. Some say that only the first verse is from the Torah (Kesef Mishneh and Magen Avraham at the beginning of section 67). Others say that the first section is from the Torah (Sha'agat Aryeh, section 2). Still others say that "Vehaya Im Shamoa" is also from the Torah (Pri Chadash at the beginning of section 67). From Rashi at the beginning of Berachot, it seems that only the first section is from the Torah, but from Tosafot and Rosh there, it seems that all of them are from the Torah. (In any case, regarding a doubt whether one has recited it, one recites all the sections according to all opinions. This will be explained in section 67 with the help of Heaven.)

From the words of Maimonides at the beginning of the laws of Kriyat Shema, it appears to me that he holds that all three paragraphs are of Torah origin. For he first writes: "It is a positive commandment to recite the Shema twice daily." And afterwards he writes: "And what is [to be recited]? One recites these three paragraphs… We precede the recitation of the paragraph 'Shema' because it contains the unity of God and the love of Him and the study of His Torah, which is the great principle upon which everything depends. After it [comes] 'Vehaya im shamoa' because it contains the command to observe all the other commandments. And after it [comes] the paragraph of Tzitzit, because it also contains the remembrance of all the commandments… These three paragraphs in this order—this is what is called 'Kriyat Shema.'" Up to here is his wording. Besides that the plain wording suggests that all of them are of Torah origin, there is also this: If we were to say that only the first paragraph is of Torah origin, or only the first verse, why does he need to give a reason for the precedence of the first over the second? Let him say because the first is of Torah origin. And also, regarding the second, which precedes Tzitzit, let him say because the third is rabbinic. Furthermore, it is known that his method in his entire great composition is to explain what is of Torah origin and what is rabbinic. And if he held that not all of them are of Torah origin, he would have explained that this one is of Torah origin and this one is rabbinic. Rather, it is certain that he holds that all of them are of Torah origin. And the reason that Rabbi Judah the Prince only recited "Shema Yisrael" (Berachot 13b) was because, according to the law, he was entirely exempt. For even one who is engaged in communal needs is exempt, as I wrote in Siman 70, all the more so Rabbi Judah the Prince who was teaching Torah to the students, as Rashi writes there. Nevertheless, he would recite the first verse because it does not interrupt Torah study. And the reason that one stands for only the first verse is because it requires greater intention, as is evident.

And this is what our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in Siman 63, Seif 6: "One who recites the Shema should not signal with his eyes... in the first paragraph, which is the primary acceptance of the yoke of Heaven." Until here is his language. There is no proof that the rest are of rabbinic origin, for he explained the reason as being because it is the primary acceptance of the yoke of Heaven. That is to say, this is disgraceful in it, and not in the others. Furthermore, in truth, the Rambam did not write "first paragraph"; see there (as the Magen Avraham wrote there in Seif Katan 10). And it is explained there that craftsmen read at the top of a tree and do not need to come down. And if it were to enter your mind that there are paragraphs of rabbinic origin, why did they not ease for craftsmen that they should not read them, just as they eased the blessing "HaTov VeHaMeitiv" in Birkat HaMazon, as I wrote in Siman 191? Rather, certainly, in the recitation of the Shema, all are from the Torah. However, this can be refuted, for since it is permissible to engage in work during the second paragraph, there is no nullification of work in this. And another proof: from the fact that the sages required meticulousness in the words of all the paragraphs, as I wrote in Siman 61. And if it were of rabbinic origin, they would not have been so meticulous, just like the entire reading of the Torah, which is of rabbinic origin, and they were not so meticulous as with the Shema. And it is more puzzling to me: how is it possible to say that not all of them are from the Torah? For if so, at the beginning of the second chapter where it is taught: Why did "Shema" precede..., and if only "Shema" or the first paragraph is from the Torah, why is a reason needed for this? And as I wrote about the Rambam, it is obvious that the one from the Torah needs to precede. And similarly, according to the one who holds that two paragraphs are from the Torah and not the paragraph of Tzitzit, why is a reason needed there for the precedence of "Vehaya Im Shamoa" over "Vayomer"? See there. Rather, certainly, all of them are from the Torah.

The sages taught in the Mishnah (9b): "One who reads from this point onward has not lost out, as if he were reading from the Torah." For it is as if he is reading any of the portions from the Torah. And although he has not fulfilled the obligation of reading the Shema, he receives the reward as one who engages in Torah study (Rashi). The Gemara explains: What does "has not lost out" mean? He has not lost out on the blessings. This means that he can still, after the appropriate time, recite the blessings of "Yotzer Or" and "Ahava Rabba" before the Shema, and "Ga'al Yisrael" after the Shema. However, the Rashba and the Rosh write in the name of Rav Hai Gaon that this is only until the fourth hour, a third of the day, which is the time for prayer. But after the time for prayer, it is forbidden to say the blessings. And if he recited them, it would be a blessing in vain, and he would transgress "Do not take [the name of the Lord your God in vain]." This is also the ruling of the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch, section 6. However, the Rambam writes at the end of the first chapter that one can recite the blessings all day, see there. This is not understood: since "has not lost out" refers to the blessings, what does "as if he were reading from the Torah" mean? What is the connection between the blessings and the Torah? According to the Gaon, it is satisfactory, as this refers to after the third of the day. But according to the Rambam, it is difficult and requires further study. And one who reads it in its proper time is better than one who reads from the Torah (Gemara there). And be aware that Tosafot R"i raised a question regarding the phrase "has not lost out" and explained it in terms of being able to recite it by heart, see there. This requires significant further study, as the Gemara questions and resolves matters regarding the blessings.

And know that the language of the Tur is as follows: Despite the fact that its time extends until the third hour, if one was forced and did not recite it, he can recite it with its blessings throughout the fourth hour... thus far his language. It implies that the Sages only permitted him to recite the blessings if he was forced. But if he willingly missed the time for reciting the Shema, he should not recite the blessings. And our master, the Beit Yosef, in his great book, wrote that it is not specifically restricted to this, see there. And I am astonished: for the Rambam in his commentary on the Mishnah also wrote similarly, and this is his language: "He has not lost the blessings... and this is for one who forgot..." thus far his language. And it also implies from his language in his composition at the end of the first chapter, where he wrote: "One who recites after the third hour of the day, even if he was forced, has not fulfilled his obligation of reciting the Shema in its proper time..." thus far his language. And what the master Beit Yosef questioned there about the Tur, regarding from where we derive this distinction, see there—I do not know. For certainly, all the enactments of the Sages are such, and all the more so with a positive commandment from the Torah for which the Sages enacted the blessings. And although the blessings are not intrinsically connected to the recitation of the Shema as will be explained, nevertheless, ultimately, this is how they enacted it. And certainly, they only enacted it if it was fulfilled according to the Torah law, and not if the time for reciting the Shema had passed. And only if one was forced did the Sages permit him to recite it later with its blessings, but not if he missed it willfully. And this requires further investigation.

And know that in the Jerusalem Talmud, the first chapter of Berachot (Halachot 5), it is explained that in a public setting, one should not recite the Shema at all after the prescribed time for reciting Shema. And this is what it says there: Rabbi Yossi and Rabbi Acha went out for a fast. The congregation came and recited the Shema after three hours. Rabbi Acha wanted to object to them. Rabbi Yossi said to him: Have they not already recited it at its proper time? Do they recite it now except to stand in prayer from words of Torah? He said to him: Because of the common people, so they do not say they are reciting it at its proper time. Thus far his words. Thus, it is clear that in a public setting, it is forbidden to recite the Shema after its prescribed time.

And I found that our teacher, the Beit Yosef, in his great book, Siman 46, brought this and wrote: From the fact that it says "he wanted to object," we learn that he did not object. See there, this is a clear and simple deduction. And he further wrote that they would not listen to us even if we objected to them. See there. And this is certainly true, as is known. And there is a slight proof to his first explanation, for there he first brought the Jerusalem Talmud that in the days of Rabbi Yochanan they would do so and he did not object to them. See there. However, even if we say so, it is explicitly understood that this is only when they have already recited it at its proper time, as Rabbi Yochanan responded to him. And how do we find our hands and feet in all our communities during the summer days? May He, who is merciful, forgive sin. This requires great investigation.

Later in Siman 108, it will be explained that in prayer, if one was forced and did not pray, they should pray twice in the subsequent prayer. Therefore, some say that also with the recitation of Shema, if one did not recite it during the day, it is effective to compensate by reciting it in the evening, and they should recite the first one as an obligation and the second one as compensation if they were forced during the day. Similarly, if one did not recite it in the evening, they can compensate by reciting it during the day. However, some disagree, saying it is not similar to prayer, which is a plea for mercy and can be done at any time, unlike the recitation of Shema, which requires lying down and rising. How can one recite it for rising at the time of lying down, and for lying down at the time of rising? Regarding this, it is said: "A crooked thing cannot be straightened." It is obvious that the blessings should not be recited (according to the Gra). And we have never heard of a ruling according to the first opinion.

The Men of the Great Assembly instituted that two blessings should be recited before the Shema, which are "Yotzer Or" and "Ahava Rabba," and one after the Shema: "Ga'al Yisrael." And in the evening, two before it and two after it, for in the evening an additional blessing, "Hashkiveinu," is included, which is not relevant in the morning. And this is what we have learned in the Mishnah (Berakhot 1:4): In the morning, one recites two blessings before it and one after it. And in the evening, two before it and two after it. And it is said in the Jerusalem Talmud: based on the verse, "Seven times a day I praise You" (Rashi).

The Rashba wrote in a responsum (Siman 47) that the blessings of the Shema are not considered blessings of the Shema in the same manner as the blessings of the Torah or the blessings of the commandments. For if they were, we would need to bless "to read the Shema," just as we bless on reading the Torah and reading the Megillah. Rather, their blessings were instituted independently, but it was ordained to recite them before and after the Shema. And this is also the consensus of the Geonim. Therefore, one who recited the Shema without its blessings must go back and say its blessings independently... Thus far are his words. However, one who recited the Shema without its blessings should afterward recite the Shema again with its blessings, as explained in the Jerusalem Talmud that we brought in the previous Siman, paragraph 20. And this is the simple custom, and it is also evident from what I wrote at the end of Siman 46, see there.

First blessing: "Who forms light and creates darkness, Who makes peace and creates everything." This is written in Isaiah (45:7). The end of the verse states "and creates evil," but they did not want to mention something negative, so instead used the positive expression "everything" (Gemara 11b). The intention is the same, and this is the explanation: to refute the belief of dualists who think there are two separate powers – one that does good and one that does evil. The prophet therefore said it is not so, for the Holy One, blessed be He, created both light and darkness. Hence, He makes peace between them, meaning: light keeps its appointed time and darkness keeps its appointed time, and they do not encroach upon one another. If, according to the dualists' view, Heaven forbid, how could the ruler of light not encroach upon the domain of the ruler of darkness, and vice versa? Rather, He, blessed be He, also created evil. And for what purpose did He create it? So that choice would be in the hands of man, as we explained in Siman 1, see there. This is also the intention when we say "and creates everything," that He, blessed be He, created everything.

And why did they not change the term "darkness," which is also not praiseworthy? On the contrary, this is in order to mention the attribute of day at night, and the attribute of night during the day (Gemara there). That is to say, this is the main point: to teach that one God created them, the day and the night, the light and the darkness. Therefore, in the morning, we mention "darkness" of the night, and in the evening, we say "He rolls away light before darkness, and darkness before light." And all of this is for the purpose that we have explained.

The second blessing is "Ahava Rabba" or "Ahavat Olam." The blessing that follows it is "Emet Veyatziv" until "Ga'al Yisrael." In the evening, the first blessing is "Asher Bidvaro Ma'ariv Aravim," and the second is "Ahavat Olam." The one that follows it is "Emet Vemunah" until "Ga'al Yisrael," and the second is "Hashkiveinu," which will be explained in Siman 236. The first blessing before the recitation of the Shema, both in the morning and the evening, begins with "Baruch" and concludes with "Baruch." The second blessings do not begin with "Baruch" because they are adjacent to the first ones. Although the order of the blessings is not obligatory, the primary enactment was to arrange them in this order. Similarly, the blessings after the recitation of the Shema do not begin with "Baruch" because they are adjacent to the first blessings, as any blessing adjacent to another concludes with "Baruch" and does not begin with "Baruch." This applies to long blessings. However, short blessings begin with "Baruch" and do not conclude with "Baruch." Therefore, in the morning blessings, and in Kiddush and Havdalah, and the seven blessings of the wedding – all begin with "Baruch." Only some conclude with "Baruch" and do not begin with "Baruch," such as "Sos Tasis" and "Sameach Tesamach." This is explained in Even Ha'ezer Siman 62.

And the Rambam wrote in the first chapter, law 7: All these blessings, along with all other blessings that are arranged in the mouths of all Israel, were instituted by Ezra and his court. And no person is permitted to diminish from them or to add to them. In a place where they instituted to conclude with "Blessed" – one is not permitted not to conclude. And in a place where they instituted not to conclude – one is not permitted to conclude. In a place where they instituted not to begin with "Blessed" – one is not permitted to begin. In a place where they instituted to begin – one is not permitted not to begin. In general: one who deviates from the format that the sages established for a blessing – is in error, and must repeat the blessing in the correct format. And anyone who did not say "Emet Veyatziv" in the morning and "Emet Ve'emunah" in the evening – has not fulfilled his obligation. Thus far his words. And what he wrote "one who deviates from the format... and must repeat..." – this is when he deviated in the opening and closing, not when he deviated in the middle with some words that are not critical (see Kesef Mishneh, first chapter of Berachot, law 6). Nevertheless, it is forbidden to do so. And any variations in words that exist between different versions – are not considered a change. Both versions have a place, and both are the words of the living God. And indeed, in the openings and closings, no variations are found between the versions.

And this is what is written: Anyone who did not say "Emet Veyatziv" in the morning… – so it is in the Gemara (Berachot 12a). They derived from the verse: "To declare Your lovingkindness in the morning and Your faithfulness every night" (Psalms 92:3). The blessing "Emet Veyatziv" is entirely about the kindness that He performed with our forefathers, bringing them out of Egypt, splitting the sea for them, and leading them through it. The blessing "Emet Ve'emunah" speaks of future events, that we hope He will fulfill His promise and faith with us… and to keep our souls alive, and to guide us on high places… all these are the continuous miracles (Rashi). And because the exile is likened to the night, we mention this in the evening. Nevertheless, we also mention the Exodus from Egypt in "Emet Ve'emunah" in order to juxtapose it to the conclusion "Who redeemed Israel" (Kesef Mishneh). Additionally, the reason we say "Emet Ve'emunah" in the evening is because we entrust our souls into His hand every night, and He returns them to us rested and pure (Tosafot R”Y). This is what is said in Midrash Eicha: "They are new every morning; great is Your faithfulness" (Lamentations 3:23), that a person believes and entrusts his spirit into His hand and He returns it without toil (Tosafot there). And this is what our Sages of blessed memory said, that if one did not say it, he has not fulfilled his obligation, meaning: even if he recited the entire blessing but did not begin with "Emet Veyatziv" in the morning or "Emet Ve'emunah" in the evening, or if he switched to say "Ve'emunah" in the morning and "Veyatziv" in the evening – he has not fulfilled the obligation of the blessings (Kesef Mishneh).

The Rambam writes there: In the morning, if one began with "Yotzer Or" and concluded with "Ma'ariv Aravim" – he has not fulfilled his obligation. If he began with "Ma'ariv Aravim" and concluded with "Yotzer Or" – he has fulfilled his obligation. And in the evening, if one began with "Ma'ariv Aravim" and concluded with "Yotzer Or" – he has not fulfilled his obligation. If he began with "Yotzer Or" and concluded with "Ma'ariv Aravim" – he has fulfilled his obligation. For all blessings are determined by their conclusion. (And it explains what is written in the Gemara 12a: In the morning, if one began with "Yotzer…" as it is straightforwardly understood.)

However, the Tur wrote: If one made a mistake and said, "Blessed are You, Lord our God, King of the Universe, Who speaks and brings on the evening," and immediately remembered and said "Creator of light," and also concluded properly with "Blessed are You, Lord, Creator of the luminaries" – he has fulfilled his obligation. But if he did not conclude properly, or if he said "Blessed… Creator of light and Maker of darkness, Who speaks and brings on the evening" and concluded with "Who brings on the evening" – he has not fulfilled his obligation. However, if he concluded with "Blessed are You, Lord, Creator of the luminaries" – he has fulfilled his obligation. Thus far his words.

The Tur's opinion is that, although it is said that everything follows the conclusion, nevertheless, if he did not mention at all in the opening anything similar to the conclusion – this is not a blessing at all, and he has not fulfilled his obligation. Therefore, in the morning, if he began with "Who brings on the evening" and concluded with "Creator of the luminaries" – he has not fulfilled his obligation. And this that they said that in such a case he has fulfilled his obligation – it means that he also mentioned "Creator of light," such as if he began and said: "Blessed are You, Lord our God, King of the Universe, Who speaks and brings on the evening, Creator of light and Maker of darkness," and concluded with "Creator of the luminaries." Or if he began: "Blessed are You, Lord our God, King of the Universe, Creator of light and Maker of darkness, Who speaks and brings on the evening," and concluded with "Creator of the luminaries" – he has fulfilled his obligation, even though he interrupted in the middle. But if he did not conclude with "Creator of the luminaries," even though he began only with "Creator of light" – he has not fulfilled his obligation. The same applies in the evening in reverse. 

Now, the Tur's wording requires correction and explanation, and the commentators have already labored over it. However, for the practical ruling, this is his intention. And this is the way of the Rosh and many of the early authorities, that we require a proper conclusion and also an opening similar to the conclusion. However, we do not worry if there was an interruption with words not related to the opening and the conclusion, whether this interruption was right at the beginning or whether he started properly and interrupted in the middle, as the main point is that if he mentioned the matter in the opening and the conclusion – he has fulfilled his obligation. And if he did not mention it in one of them, either in the opening or the conclusion – he has not fulfilled his obligation. And so wrote our teachers, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch in paragraph 2.

And this law applies only to long blessings and not to short ones, and it will be explained in Siman 209, see there. And if he did not say "Creator of light" properly in a manner that requires him to repeat the blessing, and he remembered while reciting "Ahava Rabba" – he should not interrupt, but rather say "Creator of light" after the Amidah. For the order of blessings does not prevent the fulfillment (Magen Avraham, subsection 1).

The reason we say "Creator of ministering angels, and whose ministering angels" is because it is stated in Chagigah (13b) that every day new angels are created from the River Dinur. This is "Creator of ministering angels" – those who are created every day. "And whose ministering angels" are like Michael and Gabriel, who always serve before Him, blessed be He (Tur and Tosafot there). "In clear speech and in holy melody..." – some versions have the letter dalet with a cholam vowel, referring to the earlier part, meaning "in holy melody." Others have it with a melupum vowel, referring to the latter part, meaning that they respond with holy awe (see Beit Yosef). Similarly, "they respond and say with awe, 'Holy.'" Some versions have "they respond with fear and say with awe." The Pri Etz Chaim writes that this is the main version; see there.

In the Kedusha of "Yotzer," there is a disagreement among the authorities. The Rambam wrote that an individual skips it because Kedusha is only recited in a congregation. However, the Rosh and several other Rishonim (early authorities) hold that it is recited because it is merely recounting what the angels say. The Rambam's son testified in a responsum that the Rambam retracted his opinion later in life and ruled that an individual should recite it. This is also the prevalent custom in all Jewish communities. The proof for this is that we say it while seated, and according to the Zohar, it should specifically be said while seated and not standing, and it is called the "seated prayer" as is known. If it were a Kedusha like that in the Amidah, how could we say it while seated? Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote that it is proper for an individual to recite it with the cantillation and melody as if reading from the Torah; see there. However, this is not the custom. Rabbeinu Rema wrote: When responding to this Kedusha, it should be said out loud. This is his language: Even though it is a recounting of events, nevertheless, it is said out loud. And when saying "For He alone performs mighty deeds," some add and say, "For He alone is exalted and holy, performing mighty deeds." (This is proper, for there are ten Sefirot in it. Pay attention and you will find it easy.) "To the Almighty blessed," the "lamed" has a kamatz, and similarly "to the King" (Pri Etz Chaim).

In Ashkenaz, the custom is to conclude with "A new light shall shine upon Zion…", but this is not the custom in Sepharad. Similarly, Rashi wrote that one should not conclude with the future light because it is not in line with the essence of the blessing, as the blessing is about the light that is renewed every day and not about the future light. However, the Rosh wrote that it is indeed fitting and in line with both the opening and the conclusion, because "He who forms light" refers to the light that the Holy One, Blessed be He, created during the six days of creation, which the world was not worthy to use, and He reserved it for the righteous in the future. This is as it is written: "Nations shall walk by your light", as explained in the Midrash on Genesis. This is also the new light that the Holy One, Blessed be He, will return to us in the future (Tur). And it is fitting to say "He who forms light" and "He who forms the luminaries" about it, since it has already been created. The Tur wrote that Rav Sherira Gaon also wrote that it should be said, see there.

The blessing of "Yotzer" should be recited quietly with the chazan (prayer leader), and one should not rely on hearing it from the chazan and merely responding "Amen" for two reasons: First, at the end of Rosh Hashanah, we say that the chazan only fulfills the obligation for those who are not proficient, but not for those who are proficient. Second, even if we say that the chazan can fulfill the obligation for those who are proficient, as will be explained, perhaps one will not hear it clearly, missing words in the hearing and not fulfilling the obligation. Therefore, it is better to recite it oneself along with the chazan. The chazan should say it aloud, while the individual should say it quietly, not aloud; because if the individual also says it aloud, the chazan's voice will not be heard, as two voices cannot be heard simultaneously. And this is impossible, for the chazan must fulfill the obligation for those who are not proficient. One should aim to finish the blessing before the chazan so that they can respond "Amen" to the chazan's blessing, as it is forbidden to interrupt in the middle. It appears to me that this applies when the chazan recites the blessing slowly. But if the chazan rushes, it is better to recite it slowly and not respond "Amen," since for him "Amen" is not essential as he is reciting it alone and not fulfilling the obligation through the chazan's blessing. The same applies to other blessings in the morning and evening prayers. This is also implied in the Tur, see there. (And this is the explanation of the Shulchan Aruch in section 4, see there. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

And our master, the Rema, wrote in section 4: "However, if one did not recite it but only heard it from the Shaliach Tzibur (prayer leader) – they have fulfilled their obligation. For these blessings, the Shaliach Tzibur can fulfill the obligation for an individual, even if the individual is knowledgeable. However, the Shaliach Tzibur cannot fulfill the individual's obligation with less than ten people present." End of his words.

Explanation of his words: Even though we say at the end of Rosh Hashanah that the Shaliach Tzibur does not fulfill the obligation of someone who is knowledgeable to pray on their own, this applies to prayer, which is a plea for mercy. Therefore, everyone is obligated to request mercy on their own when they can, and the Shaliach Tzibur only fulfills the obligation for those who are ignorant and do not know how to pray on their own. But for these blessings, the Shaliach Tzibur can fulfill the obligation even for a knowledgeable person, just like any blessing over enjoyment or mitzvot, where if two people are required to bless, one blesses, and the other listens and responds "Amen," thus fulfilling their obligation.

However, in this case, it is preferable to other blessings because it specifically requires ten people, as these blessings follow Kaddish and also contain Kedusha, and they are part of the prayer order. Therefore, with fewer than ten people, the Shaliach Tzibur cannot fulfill their obligation. (See Magen Avraham, sub-section 5, who wrote from the Tosafot of Rabbi Yitzchak about those in the fields, and wrote that this applies to those who are not knowledgeable. This requires further study, for even those in the fields who are knowledgeable are exempt, as is explicitly proven from Rashi at the end of Rosh Hashanah. And this is implied by the entire discussion there. Furthermore, the Rambam, the Tur, and the Ran in Megillah omitted the entire rule about those in the fields, as they do not agree with this distinction between prayer and these blessings. See there. However, many early authorities hold this view, as the Beit Yosef wrote in his great work. Therefore, the main halachic decision follows the Rema. And what the Beit Yosef wrote about not answering "Amen" after "Who chooses His people Israel with love" because of an interruption between the blessing and the Shema – we do not hold this view, since the blessings do not pertain to the Shema, as I wrote in the name of the Rashba. And this is what the Rema referenced to look at in Siman 61, where it is explained that one answers "Amen." And so is the custom. Be precise and you will find clarity.)

It is well-known that if the prayer leader becomes silent in the middle of the blessing, when another one takes his place, he begins from the start of the blessing. This is also true for the blessing of "Yotzer." However, in the Jerusalem Talmud, it is stated that this applies before the Kedusha, but if he becomes silent after saying "Kadosh..." – the next one does not begin from the start of "Yotzer" but from "Veha'ofanim v'Chayot Hakodesh." The same applies if he errs in the Ofanim. And if he errs after concluding "Baruch Kevod..." – he begins from "Le'el Baruch," since the Kedusha is considered the end of the blessing. It is forbidden to start from the beginning of "Yotzer," because it is unnecessary and would be considered a blessing in vain (Magen Avraham, subsection 6).

The second blessing is "Ahava Rabba" according to the Ashkenazic rite, and "Ahavat Olam" according to the Sephardic rite. In the Gemara (Berachot 11b) there is a dispute about this. Our Rabbis, the Tosafists, wrote that therefore it was established to say "Ahava Rabba" in the morning and "Ahavat Olam" in the evening, see there. This follows the Ashkenazic rite. And the Rif ruled "Ahavat Olam." And one who examines the Gemara and the Rif will see that there is a difference in the text from the Gemara to the Rif, for in the Gemara it is written: "It was also taught: They do not say 'Ahavat Olam' but 'Ahava Rabba.'" And in the Rif's text: "It was also taught: They do not say 'Ahava Rabba' but 'Ahavat Olam.'" See there. And the Tur wrote in the name of the Geonim "Ahava Rabba." And I am puzzled that the poskim did not bring the version of the Gemara at all. (And I do not understand the version of the Rif: why does the Baraita need to say: they do not say 'Ahava Rabba' but 'Ahavat Olam'? It should have said: say 'Ahavat Olam.' And according to our version it is understandable, because in the verse we find "Ahavat Olam" in Jeremiah 31, therefore it says not to say as the wording of the verse. But for the Rif it is difficult, because in the verse we do not find the wording "Ahava Rabba." And it can be said according to what is explained in Pri Etz Chaim, that "Ahava Rabba" is a higher level than "Ahavat Olam," but in this time it is not possible to say so. This is what it says: even though it is a higher level, in any case, it should not be said. Pay attention and you will find it easy.)

If the blessing "Ahavat Rabbah" exempts the blessing of the Torah, it is explained in Siman 47. The order of the blessings is not critical, so if one recited "Ahavat Rabbah" before "Yotzer Or", he should afterwards recite "Yotzer Or" and does not need to say "Ahavat Rabbah" again. Nevertheless, this blessing does not begin with "Baruch" because its primary institution is after "Yotzer" and it is considered adjacent to its companion. Similarly, the recitation of Shema is not related to the blessings, for if one recited Shema without the blessings, he has fulfilled his obligation of reciting Shema from the Torah, and he returns to recite the blessings without Shema. Nevertheless, our master the Beit Yosef wrote in section 2 that it is better to return and recite Shema with the blessings; see there. And it is obvious that this is so, for the primary Rabbinic institution is to recite Shema in the order of the blessings, and if so, he has not fulfilled the obligation of Shema in its proper institution (Machtzit Hashekel, section 1, and it is also evident in Beit Yosef. Analyze and you will find it easy.) Specifically, the order of the blessings is not critical. But the blessings themselves are critical, whether in private or in public. And not like those who hold that in private they are not critical at all, for this is not so. (See Beit Yosef and Taz. Analyze and you will find it easy.)

It is appropriate that when one says "and You chose us..." to remember the event of Mount Sinai, when He chose us, as it is written: "Lest you forget the things... the day you stood before Hashem your God at Horeb." And when one says "for Your great name" he should remember the act of Amalek, for the name is not complete until the seed of Amalek is erased, as it is written: "Remember what Amalek did to you..." And when one says "to thank You" he should remember that the mouth was created to thank Him, blessed be He, and not to speak lashon hara (evil speech). And he should remember the act of Miriam, as it is written: "Remember what Hashem your God did to Miriam..." And when one says "with love" he should remember what is written: "Remember how you angered Hashem your God in the wilderness." And when one says "and you shall remember all the commandments of Hashem" he should remember Shabbat, which is equivalent to all the commandments, as it is written: "Remember the day of Shabbat." Meaning: that you should always remember the day of Shabbat. And as our Sages, of blessed memory, said: from one Shabbat to the next Shabbat. Therefore, in the song of the day, we say: "Today is the first day of Shabbat..." And when one says "from the four corners of the earth" – he should let the corners of the tallit on his shoulders fall down. (Magen Avraham, section 2. And we do not concern ourselves with this. And see Pri Etz Chaim, Gate of the Shema, chapter three, and you will understand why we do not practice this. Be precise and you will find it light.)

And know that these remembrances, some say them after the prayer, and they have been printed in the prayer books as six remembrances: the remembrance of the Exodus from Egypt, the remembrance of the Giving of the Torah, the remembrance of Amalek, the remembrance of the Provocation, the remembrance of Miriam, and the remembrance of Shabbat. However, this is only a beautification of the mitzvah, for we do not find in the Gemara and the legal decisors an obligation to remember these. Only the remembrance of the Exodus from Egypt is an obligation every day, evening, and morning, from the Torah. And the remembrance of Amalek is a Torah obligation to recite once a year. Therefore, we hold that the portion "Remember" is from the Torah, as will be explained in Siman 685. And the remembrance of Shabbat is an obligation every Shabbat to remember in the prayer and in the Kiddush, as we expound: "Remember the Shabbat day" – remember it over wine. But the other three remembrances we do not find any obligation at all to mention them. (See Magen Avraham at the end of subparagraph 2. And it is difficult, for if the Torah obligated us to remember them, we should not look at the disgrace. And furthermore: why is the remembrance of the Exodus from Egypt twice every day, the remembrance of Amalek once a year, and the remembrance of Shabbat every Shabbat?)

It appears to me that the matter is as follows: The Torah wrote about the remembrance of the Exodus from Egypt: "so that you may remember the day you came out of the land of Egypt all the days of your life." This is like it is written that you should remember every day. And from "all," we include the nights, as it is stated at the end of the first chapter of Berachot. Therefore, the Torah explicitly commanded to remember every day. And with the remembrance of Amalek, it is written: "And it shall be, when the Lord your God gives you rest... you shall blot out the memory..." – and the Torah revealed that the purpose of this remembrance is to fulfill "you shall blot out." This is for the future, of course, and therefore it is sufficient to recall it once a year, for every year we anticipate our ultimate purpose in the month of Nissan, as our Sages said: in Nissan they were redeemed, and in Nissan they are destined... Therefore, we juxtapose the remembrance of Amalek before Purim, which is adjacent to Nissan. And the remembrance of Shabbat, since it is written "Remember the Sabbath day to keep it holy" – it is clear that the remembrance is only on the Sabbath day, for Kiddush is only on the Sabbath. But regarding the Giving of the Torah, it does not use the language of "remembrance" at all. And the Torah writes: "Only be careful... lest you forget... the day you stood before the Lord your God at Horeb." This is guarding in the heart, for "remember" our Sages expounded in Megillah (18a) and in Sifra that it is with the mouth, and here it does not say "remembrance." And guarding in the heart we fulfill at all times and at every moment, by keeping the Torah and the commandments. And the remembrance of the provocation, it seems clear that it was said only to the generation of the wilderness. This is evident from the verses in the portion of "Eikev" which began: "Hear, Israel! You are crossing the Jordan today... not because of your righteousness... you are coming to possess their land... and you shall know that not because of your righteousness... for you are a stiff-necked people. Remember, do not forget how you provoked..." – it is explicitly stated that it was said to the generation of the wilderness. And similarly with the remembrance of Miriam, the beginning of the verse "Take heed concerning the plague of leprosy," and it does not apply in this time and not outside the Land. And in Sifrei, this is linked to the prohibition of lashon hara (evil speech), which is a prohibition like all other prohibitions and does not require remembrance. And the remembrance is about the plague of leprosy to act according to its law (such is my humble opinion).

Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote in Section 4: There are those who say that mitzvot do not require intent. And there are those who say that they require intent to fulfill the obligation of performing that mitzvah. And this is the law. Until here are his words. And in Section 5 he wrote: One who recites the Shema and did not have intent during the first verse, which is "Shema Yisrael" – has not fulfilled his obligation. For the rest, if he did not have intent, even if he was reading in the Torah or correcting these sections during the time of the recitation of the Shema – he has fulfilled it, provided he had intent during the first verse. Until here are his words. The explanation of his words: There is a dispute among the poskim whether anyone who performs a mitzvah needs to have intent to fulfill the obligation of the mitzvah with this action, or whether one does not need to have intent to fulfill the obligation of the mitzvah, and even if he did not have intent – he has fulfilled the obligation of the mitzvah. This will be explained in Siman 429. And there are those among the Rishonim who said that even according to the opinion that mitzvot do not require intent – this applies to practical mitzvot, where the action itself serves as the intent for the mitzvah. But a mitzvah that depends on speech – certainly requires intent, for without intent it is as if he has done nothing (Tosafot Ri, end of the first chapter of Berachot).

And behold, our master, the Beit Yosef, ruled that mitzvot (commandments) require intention, as this is the opinion of most authorities. And what is written in Section 5 is not about the intention of the mitzvah but another matter, which is to pay attention to what one is saying. Therefore, the verse "Shema Yisrael," which is the primary acceptance of the yoke of the Kingdom of Heaven, requires one to pay attention, for if not, it is not considered an acceptance of the Kingdom of Heaven at all, and it is like prayer without intention (Magen Avraham, Siman 63, Subsection 7). Therefore, if one did not have intention, he must go back and say it with intention, as I have written in Siman 63, see there. But for the rest (of the Shema), even if one did not have intention, as long as he said all the words, he has fulfilled his obligation. And even in prayer, if one did not have intention, he does not need to go back, even for the first blessing, as I have written later in Siman 101. And prayer is supplication, which certainly requires intention, all the more so for the recitation of the Shema. (See Magen Avraham, Subsection 4, who wrote in the name of the Kesef Mishneh that even if one did not have intention to fulfill the obligation except for the first verse, he has fulfilled his obligation. And they follow their reasoning that from the Torah, one fulfills the obligation of reciting the Shema with the first verse, as written in Siman 63, Subsection 8, see there. And a rabbinic mitzvah does not require intention, as written in Subsection 3. And this is not the opinion of the later authorities, as I have written in Siman 58, Section 15. And according to us, there in Section 16, all of them are from the Torah, see there. Be precise and you will find it clear.)

According to the principle that mitzvot (commandments) require intention, one must be careful with every mitzvah to have the proper intention for the sake of the mitzvah. It is not necessary to have the specific intention for this particular mitzvah, but rather a general intention for the sake of performing a mitzvah, as is explained in Rashi at the beginning of the second chapter of Berachot, where he writes: “Mitzvot require intention – that one intends for the sake of the mitzvah,” see there. The intention is in the heart and does not require verbal articulation. 

And even though regarding sacrificial offerings we say at the end of the fourth chapter of Zevachim: “For the sake of six things the offering is slaughtered...,” and it is implied at the beginning of Zevachim that it requires verbal articulation, see there – this is because there are various types of offerings, therefore it is necessary to specify for the sake of which type one is slaughtering. However, there we say that even a general intention is valid, as a general intention is considered to be for its specified type, see there.

One should not ask: if so, why do mitzvot require intention? Are mitzvot superior to sacrificial offerings, where even a general intention is valid? This is not a valid comparison, because in the case of sacrificial offerings, the animal has already been consecrated, therefore even a general intention maintains its sanctity. This is not the case with other matters where they need to be consecrated now with the sanctity of the mitzvah, and if one does not intend now for the sake of the mitzvah – it is meaningless. This is also proven from the language of Rashi there, who writes: “In general, they are considered to be for their specified purpose, therefore as long as one does not explicitly change their designation – they remain for their specified purpose.” Thus far his language. It is clear that he wrote “does not change their designation,” meaning the previous sanctity. (And the difficulty he raised there regarding a woman is because he thought to compare a woman to consecration, as we say at the beginning of Kiddushin that she is prohibited to everyone like consecration. Nevertheless, he answered that she is not designated for divorce.)

And it is customary to gather the tzitzit when saying "and bring us in peace from the four corners of the earth." Some have the custom to take only the two tzitzit in front of them. When reaching the phrase "and you shall see it," it is customary to look at the tzitzit. It is also customary to kiss the tzitzit. All these practices are for the love of the mitzvah and are not obligatory according to the law.

One must recite the Shema with intention, in awe and fear, with trembling and quaking. For behold, an earthly king, when he sends his words to a province and they read his words, everyone hears his words with awe and fear. All the more so before the King of Kings, the Holy One, blessed be He. And each day it should be in his eyes as new, as something he has not yet heard, for the love is exceedingly great. And he should intend at the time he recites the Shema to accept upon himself the yoke of the Kingdom of Heaven, to give over his body and soul in self-sacrifice for the sanctification of the Name. And this is "with all your soul" – even if He takes your soul (Beit Yosef). And he should imagine to himself that even if they inflict upon him great suffering, it should be insignificant in his eyes because of his love for the Blessed One, like Rabbi Akiva, who had his flesh combed with iron combs and recited the Shema. And how many holy individuals, at the time of their execution and burning, cried out in a loud voice: "Shema Yisrael!" (And it is written in the responsa of Maharam of Rothenburg, Siman 517: Once a person has resolved in his mind to give his life for the recitation of the Shema, he feels no pain from any death they inflict upon him. And the proof… and another proof from the Sefer Heichalot… and know that this is so, for there is no person in the world who, if he touched fire, would not cry out… and we see holy individuals who do not cry out at all. Thus far his words).

"The commandment that I am commanding you today shall be upon your heart" – and the word "today" is connected to the preceding words, meaning: "I am commanding you today" – that every day it should be in your eyes as if new, as if I commanded you today. It should not be connected to the following words to say "today upon your heart," which would imply "today" – and not tomorrow. Rather, one should pause briefly between "today" and "upon your heart." And so the cantillation marks indicate, as "today" is marked with a tipcha, which is one of the disjunctive accents. Just as one must pause between "today" and "upon your heart," similarly, at the beginning of "And it will be if you listen," one must pause between "today" and "to love" for the reason explained.

The custom in all Jewish communities is to recite "Shema Yisrael" out loud in order to awaken intention. It is recited with enthusiasm. The practice is to place one's hands over one's face when reciting the verse "Shema Yisrael." There is a proof for this in the Talmud (Berachot 13b), which says the same about Rabbi Judah the Prince—see there. This is done so that one does not look at anything else that might distract him from focusing. The right hand is placed over the face. The aleph of "Echad" should be pronounced very briefly. The chet should be extended slightly, to proclaim that the Holy One, blessed be He, rules in the heavens and on the earth. The protrusions on the roof of the chet hint at this, meaning: He lives in the heights of the world (Menachot 29b). There are seven heavens and with the earth, they are eight, which is hinted at by the chet. The dalet should be extended longer, to the extent that one should think that the Holy One, blessed be He, is unique in His world and rules over the four directions of the world. One should not extend it longer than this measure. One should be careful to enunciate the dalet properly, so that it does not sound like a reish, God forbid. One should ensure that the dalet is pronounced softly, not like those who seem to pronounce it with a shva. Some have the custom to tilt their head according to their thoughts: up and down and to the four directions. Whoever finds this distracting should not do so.

Certainly, here is the translation of the provided passage:

"Surely, there are profound intentions in the verse 'Shema Yisrael,' but in its simplicity, it is as Rashi explained: 'Hear, O Israel, the Lord is our God,' meaning: He is our God now. 'The Lord is one' – in the future, the Lord will be one, as it is said: 'For then I will turn to the peoples a pure language, that they may all call upon the name of the Lord' (Zephaniah 3:9). And it is said: 'On that day, the Lord will be one and His name one' (Zechariah 14:9). And this is our entire hope, that His blessed name will then be magnified and sanctified. Therefore, immediately after this verse, we say: 'Blessed be the name of His glorious kingdom forever and ever.' Meaning: that then the glory of His kingdom will be revealed openly. Therefore, it is recited quietly, because now it is not revealed due to our sins, except on Yom Kippur when we are like angels and say it aloud. But throughout the year, the world is not worthy to say it aloud. And in Pesachim (56a), our sages said that we recite it quietly because Moses did not say it, but Jacob did, see there. (And in my humble opinion, this also means that in the days of Jacob, they were all righteous and said it aloud. But not in the days of Moses, when they made the golden calf and other sins. Delve into this, and you will find it easy to understand.)"

This is the wording of the Rambam in the first chapter, law 4: When one recites the Shema and finishes the first verse, he says in a whisper, "Blessed be the name of His glorious kingdom forever and ever." ...And why do we say this? It is a tradition in our hands that when Jacob our father gathered his sons in Egypt before his death, he commanded and urged them regarding the unity of God and the way of the Lord that Abraham and Isaac walked in. And he asked them and said to them: "My sons! Perhaps there is some defect among you, someone who does not stand with me in the unity of God...?" They all answered and said: "Hear, O Israel...", meaning: Hear from us, our father Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is one! The elder opened and said: "Blessed be the name of His glorious kingdom forever and ever." Therefore, all of Israel has the custom to say the praise with which the elder praised after this verse. Thus far his words.

And know that there is one who wrote in this language: If one did not say "Blessed be the name of His glorious kingdom forever and ever," he is not required to repeat it (Bach, Shiltei Giborim). And the Levush wrote that even if one said it but did not say it with intention, he must repeat it. Thus far is his language (Magen Avraham, small section 11). And it seems to me that they are not in disagreement at all. For certainly, if one did not say it and has already started the "V'ahavta" section, he is not required to go back, since it is not mentioned in the Torah. And even if he wishes to say it between sections, it has no relevance there, obviously. And the Levush says that if he said it and did not say it with intention, and has not yet started "V'ahavta," he must go back and say it again with intention. And so it seems to me is the main ruling in practice. (And it is astonishing that I did not find this in the Levush at all, see there.)

One should pause in the verse "Shema Yisrael" between "Yisrael" and "the Lord," and between "our God" and "the Lord" the second time, so that it is heard that the Lord, who is our God, is one Lord, as I have written in section 4. Without pausing, this meaning is not evident, of course. One should also properly pronounce the yod in "Yisrael," so that it is not swallowed entirely and does not sound like an aleph. Similarly, the yod in "vehayu" should not sound like an aleph, i.e., "veha'u." Additionally, one should emphasize the mem in "Shema" so that the ayin is felt. One should pause slightly between "echad" and "Baruch Shem...," because the primary acceptance of the yoke of Heaven is in "Shema," and since in "Baruch Shem..." there is also an acceptance of the yoke of Heaven upon ourselves, one should pause slightly between "le'olam va'ed" and "ve'ahavta." Although "ve'ahavta" is also about the yoke of Heaven, it is through commandment, whereas "Shema" and "Baruch Shem" are from ourselves, as we are aroused to this (Taz, subsection 6).

One must leave a space between "וחרה" (Vechara) and "אף" (Af), so it does not sound like "וחרף" (Vecharaf). Similarly, one must leave a space in every word that ends with the same letter as the beginning of the next word, such as "בכל לבבך" (Bechol Levavecha), "על לבבך" (Al Levavecha), "בכל לבבכם" (Bechol Levavchem), "עשב בשדך" (Esev Besadcha), "ואבדתם מהרה" (Va'avadtem Mehera), "על לבבכם" (Al Levavchem), "הכנף פתיל" (HaKanaf Petil), "אתכם מארץ" (Etchem Me'eretz). Similarly, every Aleph following a Mem requires a pause, such as "ולמדתם אותם" (Ulemadtem Otam), "וקשרתם אותם" (Ukeshartem Otam), "ושמתם את" (Usamtem Et), "וראיתם אותו" (Ureittem Oto), "וזכרתם את" (Uzchartem Et), "ועשיתם את" (Va'asitem Et) – so that the Aleph is not swallowed entirely. One must pronounce the Zayin of "תזכרו" (Tizkeru) clearly so it does not sound like "תשקרו" (Tishkeru), God forbid, or "תשכרו" (Tishkeru), which would imply serving the master for a reward. Similarly, one must pronounce the Zayin of "וזכרתם" (Uzchartem) clearly. One should also be precise with the Ayin in the recitation of the Shema, as in our pronunciation, Ayin and Aleph sound the same, and in the Shema, they should be distinguished from one another. Similarly, one should be careful between a left Shin and a soft Tav. Therefore, in the word "ועשיתם" (Va'asitem), one should be very careful to articulate the Ayin and distinguish between the Shin and the Tav. Similarly, the Samech should not resemble a soft Tav. In the case of a soft Bet, one should articulate it so that it does not appear as a soft Pe, such as in "ואהבת" (Ve'ahavta), "לבבך" (Levavecha), "ובכל" (Uvechol), and many others. One should articulate the Ayin in "אשר נשבע" (Asher Nishba).

One must also be careful with the dagesh (dot) and rafeh (absence of dot) in the letters bet, kaf, peh, and tav, not to soften a letter with a dagesh or to harden a letter without it. Similarly, with sheva vowels, there are resting and moving shevas. At the end of a word, a sheva is always resting, and in the middle of a word after a short vowel, it is also resting. At the beginning of a word, a sheva is always moving, and in the middle of a word after a long vowel, it is moving as well. When there are two consecutive shevas, the first one is resting and the second one is moving. There are many rules in the science of grammar, so one must be careful not to say a moving sheva as resting, or a resting sheva as moving. Every Torah scholar must have some knowledge of grammar. Indeed, even in the verses of praise and in prayer, one must be meticulous to pronounce the words correctly. Similarly, one who reads from the Torah, the Prophets, and the Writings must be careful with all these rules, but unfortunately, we are not accustomed to this in all matters. However, with the recitation of the Shema, one must certainly be very meticulous to pronounce the letters and words accurately and correctly. As our sages said in Berachot (15b): Anyone who recites the Shema and is meticulous with its letters, Gehenna (purgatory) is cooled for him, for because he takes care to be meticulous, therefore Gehenna, which is very hot, is cooled for him.

One must recite the Shema with the cantillation marks, as it is read in the Torah, but this is not the custom in these regions. It seems the reason is that many people, when they read with the cantillation marks, become confused and do not understand the meaning of the words, as the melody for those not accustomed to it disrupts concentration. Nevertheless, those who are meticulous are stringent with this, provided they also understand the meaning of the words. When saying "ukshartam le'ot al yadecha" ("and you shall bind them as a sign on your hand"), one should touch the tefillin on the arm. And when saying "vehayu letotafot bein einecha" ("and they shall be as frontlets between your eyes"), one should touch the tefillin on the head. There are those who kiss their hand at this point, but this is not essential. Some have the custom to recite the Shema out loud, while others recite it quietly, depending on personal nature. Some concentrate better when reciting out loud, while others concentrate better when reciting quietly. However, "Shema Yisrael" is said out loud by everyone. This is the widespread custom and should not be changed. When reaching the paragraph about the tzitzit, one should take the tzitzit in the right hand and kiss them several times as a sign of affection for the mitzvah.

In the recitation of the Shema, there are 245 words.
