To complete 248 words corresponding to the limbs of a person, the prayer leader concludes with "Hashem Elokeichem Emet" ("The Lord your God is true") and then repeats aloud "Hashem Elokeichem Emet." In this manner, everyone fulfills the requirement since they hear these three words from the prayer leader. If an individual wishes to recite them along with the prayer leader, they are not prevented from doing so.

There is no need to question why, since there are 245 words in the Shema, and with the word "Emet" it becomes 246. Thus, when the prayer leader repeats "Hashem Elokeichem Emet," it becomes 249 words. One can explain that the second "Emet" is not counted as it pertains to "V'yatziv V'nachon" (the next section of the prayer). Additionally, there is no issue with saying "Emet" twice, even though the Talmud (Berachot 14b) criticizes this practice, as this applies only when said consecutively without any intervening words. With an intervening word, there is no issue.

However, some prominent authorities actually hold that the first time, the prayer leader does not conclude with "Emet," but rather "Ani Hashem Elokeichem" ("I am the Lord your God"). Afterwards, he says "Hashem Elokeichem Emet." According to this opinion, there are exactly 248 words, and "Emet" is not said twice (this is the opinion of Rabbi Menachem Azariah of Fano in his work Asarah Maamarot). This is also the custom of some communities.

Our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, wrote that if one is reciting alone, one should focus on the fifteen "vavs" in "Emet Veyatziv" which add up to ninety. These correspond to three instances of the Divine Name (each name equals 26, and the four letters of each name total 30). There is another reason for this: the fifteen "vavs" add up to ninety, and the recitation itself counts as one, thus making ninety-one, which equals the numerical value of the Divine Name in its reading and writing, as if one said, "Hashem Adonai Emet." 

Some have written that anyone reciting the Shema alone should say "El Melech Ne'eman, Shema Yisrael..." because these three words complete the count of 248, and it serves in place of saying "Amen" after "who chooses His people Israel with love," which is the custom. However, when one recites with the congregation, one should not say "El Melech Ne'eman," but rather say "Amen" after the prayer leader finishes the blessing. This is the custom and it is proper. 

Some of the great authorities have very much questioned the interruption of saying "El Melech Ne'eman" even when alone (Magen Avraham, sub-section 4 in the name of Maharshal). We do not have the custom of saying this. Some also repeat "Hashem Elokeichem Emet" even when alone, but I do not know the basis for this. It is better to repeat these three words: "etchem meeretz Mitzrayim" since they do not contain the Divine Name. I have seen this practiced.

It is forbidden to say "Shema Shema" twice, as it appears as if acknowledging two authorities, Heaven forbid, whether one says the word twice "Shema Shema" or repeats the verse twice. According to Rashi (Berachot 33b), repeating the verse is more severe, and one should be silenced. Repeating the word is only considered improper, but one is not silenced. According to Tosafot, it is the opposite: one is silenced for repeating the word, and repeating the verse is only considered improper. Therefore, in practice, one is silenced in both cases. Hence, even to recite the entire passage twice is not advisable. Only in the case of reciting the Shema before sleep is it permitted to read the entire passage and then repeat it, as the intention is to fall asleep while reciting Shema. Some say that even in this case, one should avoid saying the first verse twice; therefore, one should start from "Ve'ahavta" the second time.

Therefore, those who say "Shema Yisrael" during the Selichot in the pre-dawn hours and after the Ne'ilah prayer should be careful not to say the Shema twice. For even in a congregation, it is forbidden, contrary to those who are lenient in a congregation (see Magen Avraham, subsection 9, who disputes with the Bach on this matter). Nevertheless, if one did not recite the verse "Shema Yisrael" with proper intention, he should repeat it quietly, since he is doing so for the sake of intention (Taz, subsection 3). And regarding the practice of saying "Blessed be the name of His glorious kingdom forever and ever" three times, and "The Lord is God" seven times, there is no concern about this. On the contrary, it is an appropriate custom to indicate that in the seven heavens "The Lord is God." In Scripture, we find "The Lord is God" twice, with Elijah when he defeated the prophets of Baal. This is not similar to "Shema Yisrael," which is the essential acceptance of the yoke of Heaven's sovereignty, and it is forbidden to repeat it, as it appears to imply two authorities, Heaven forbid. Some say one should also be careful not to respond "Amen" twice to a blessing. Others disagree, for in Scripture it is written: "And the woman shall say, 'Amen, Amen'" and David said: "Amen and Amen" (see Magen Avraham, subsection 10). And from Maimonides, chapter two, it is clear that not only "Shema" but any words or verses should not be repeated. See there for further details.

Even though it has been explained that one must be meticulous with its letters, nevertheless, if one read it and was not meticulous with the exact pronunciations as explained – he has fulfilled his obligation, and he does not need to read it again. And so the Sages taught in the Mishnah (15a): If one read but was not meticulous with its letters – he has fulfilled his obligation. And Rashi explained: That he was not meticulous to pronounce them well with his lips. This is the end of his wording. The intention is not that he did not pronounce the words and letters at all, such as saying half words and the like. For certainly, in such a case, he has not fulfilled his obligation, for this is not considered reading at all. Rather, the intention is as explained by the Rambam and the Ra'avad in their commentary on the Mishnah: That he was not meticulous in separating similar letters, or he confused a moving letter with a stationary one, and similar cases. In such instances – he has fulfilled his obligation. It is obvious that someone who has a speech impediment, like some people who cannot properly pronounce the letter "resh," or cannot say the right "shin," or say "gimel" like "dalet" and the like – he has fulfilled his obligation, since he speaks according to his manner of speech. And more than this is stated in the Midrash Chazit on the verse "And his banner over me was love": Rabbi Acha said: An unlearned person who reads "ahavah" (love) as "eivah" (enmity), such as "ve'ahavta" (and you shall love) as "ve'ivata" (and you shall hate), the Holy One, blessed be He, says: "And his distortion is love for Me."

And for this reason, I say that according to our pronunciation, where there is no distinction between an aleph and an ayin, between a chet and a chaf, between a samech and a soft tav, and between a tet and a hard tav, they have fulfilled their obligation since that is their language. And we see that those who are meticulous about this find it very difficult to make the distinction, and still, the distinction is not proper. Especially between an aleph and an ayin, there are instances where they are like opposites, and it can be like blasphemy, God forbid. For example, in the Amidah prayer, "and purify our hearts to serve you in truth," and in the Shema, "beware… and you will turn away and serve…," if one says it like with an aleph, it is actually the opposite, God forbid. Nevertheless, since this is our pronunciation, there is no concern about the matter. And the Merciful One desires the heart, but one who is meticulous in mitzvot should strive to be very precise in this. And similarly, throughout the Torah, with the word "service" (avodah), which according to our pronunciation appears like "loss" (aveidah), his reward is great if he is meticulous about this.

One may recite it in any language, as it is written: "Shema" – in any language that you understand. One must be careful about errors in that language and be precise with it just as in the Holy Tongue. This applies specifically when one understands the language. The same rule applies to prayer and Grace After Meals, as it is taught in the seventh chapter of Sotah. The same applies to Kiddush, blessings over fruits, blessings over commandments, and Hallel. There is an opinion that for these, even if one does not understand the language, one fulfills the obligation (Magen Avraham, subsection 1), but many disagree with this (see Mishnah Berurah). In the Holy Tongue, one fulfills the obligation of reciting the Shema even if one does not understand the language, since one knows the essential meaning of the Shema. There is no ignoramus who does not know the meaning of "Hear, O Israel," and every Jew is obligated to sacrifice their life for the sanctification of the Name. And in Siman 185, we will further explain this with the help of Heaven, see there.

And know that the recitation of Shema and prayer can be said in any language, and certainly this is when one translates all three paragraphs of the Shema and all eighteen blessings of the Amidah into another language exactly. For if not, it is not considered the recitation of Shema and prayer. According to this, this rule only applied during the time of the Mishnah and the Gemara, when they knew our language well and could translate it. But now it is known that we have many doubts about the interpretation of the words and the commentators have disagreed about them. For example, how would we translate "totafot"? Similarly, the verse "Shema Yisrael," which even in its simplicity has many interpretations. The word "tzitzit" has been explained by some to mean "looking" and by others to mean "protruding." Likewise, the word "petil" and many similar examples. Indeed, we do not know how to translate the essential name of God (the Tetragrammaton) properly, as some translate it as "eternal" and others as "all-powerful." There is no accurate translation for "He was, He is, and He will be," which is the essence of the Tetragrammaton, and in translation, the name of God is equivalent to the name "Elohim." Similarly, "and His anger burned" in translation both mean anger, whereas in the Holy Tongue there is a significant difference between them. Therefore, at this time it is forbidden to recite Shema and prayer and all blessings except in the Holy Tongue. And thus the great sages of the world have ruled for about eighty years, and this is the main ruling in practice.

One should not recite the Shema quietly, for one must make audible to one's ear what is being uttered by the mouth, as suggested by the straightforward meaning of "Shema Yisrael" which implies hearing. However, if one did not make it audible to one's ear after the fact, one has fulfilled the obligation, though it is not the ideal way. The primary interpretation of "Shema" is an expression of understanding, as there are instances of "Shema Yisrael" in the Torah that imply understanding, such as "Hear, O Israel, you are crossing the Jordan today," and similar expressions. Therefore, although hearing is also included in the term "Shema," our sages of blessed memory have stated that it does not invalidate the recitation after the fact. This is how the law is decided in the Babylonian Talmud (Berachot 15b) and in the Jerusalem Talmud in the second chapter of Berachot (Halacha 4), see there. (From this, they derive there: "in any language that you understand," because "Shema" is an expression of understanding.)

Our Rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, wrote in section 4: If due to illness or another unavoidable circumstance, one recited the Shema in his heart, he has fulfilled his obligation. And even initially, one should do so if he is in a place that is not completely clean and cannot clean it due to an unavoidable circumstance—he should contemplate it in his heart. However, the place should not be completely filthy, as it is forbidden to contemplate words of Torah in a filthy place. Thus far his words. 

The explanation of these matters seems to me to be as follows: It is certainly established in Halacha that contemplation is not considered the same as speech. This is the ruling of the Tosafot and the Rosh in Berakhot (20b) according to Rav Chisda, that contemplation is not considered the same as speech. Similarly, the students of Rabbeinu Yonah there, in the name of the Geonim, and also the Maor and the Raavad in Sefer Tamim De'im, Siman 240, ruled this way (except for the Ri’az in Shiltei HaGiborim there, which is a solitary opinion). Even the Rambam, who ruled in the first chapter of Berakhot that blessings can be fulfilled through contemplation, nevertheless, in the case of the Shema, it seems clear that he agrees that one does not fulfill the obligation this way. The proof is that in the context of blessings, he wrote: “If he did not make it audible to his ears, he has fulfilled [his obligation], whether he articulated it with his lips or blessed in his heart.” Thus far his words. But regarding the Shema, which precedes the blessings, he wrote: “If he did not make it audible to his ear, he has fulfilled [his obligation].” See there. He did not conclude with “whether he blessed in his heart,” from which we can infer that in the case of the Shema, one does not fulfill the obligation. The reason seems to be that regarding the Shema, it is written, “and you shall speak of them.” Nonetheless, in any case, all our Rabbis agree that one does not fulfill the obligation of the Shema through contemplation. And this is the primary ruling in Halacha.

And this is the intention of our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch: if due to illness or a pressing circumstance... - one fulfills his obligation. That is to say, even though mental contemplation is not considered equivalent to verbal speech, nevertheless, when it is not possible in any other manner, one fulfills his obligation in this way. Meaning, it is better than not reciting at all. For we say regarding Rav Chisda that a person who has had a seminal emission contemplates in his heart, so that the whole world is engaged in it [the recitation], while he sits idly by. Certainly, if the pressing circumstance or illness passes within the time of the recitation of the Shema, he should recite it verbally, but this is uncommon. And this is why they wrote afterward: even initially, one should do so if he is in a place that is not completely clean... Meaning, because they previously said "fulfills his obligation" in a post-facto (bedi'avad) sense, they now say there is no distinction between initially (lekhatchila) and post-facto, for certainly even post-facto one does not fulfill his obligation with contemplation if he can speak. Rather, those who cannot speak fulfill their obligation in this manner, and for them, even initially, it is permissible because it is not possible in any other way. Therefore, even in a place that is not completely clean, it is forbidden to speak aloud due to the doubt, but contemplation is permitted. And similarly, one who is thirsty at night in his bed and it is not possible for him to wash his hands and get out of bed—he is immersed in sleep and it is considered as if it is not possible, and he contemplates the blessing in his heart (Taz, subparagraph 1). But in a completely filthy place, even contemplation is forbidden. (So it seems in my humble opinion, and this resolves the questions of the Eliyah Rabbah, subparagraph 2).

One who hears the recitation of the Shema from his fellow has not fulfilled his obligation, even if the other intended to fulfill it for him (Rabbi Moses Alashkar). For the mitzvah of the Shema is the recitation and not the hearing, as it is written: "And you shall speak of them" (Deuteronomy). And even if he is not proficient, the other cannot fulfill it for him. However, in a minyan when the prayer leader recites it, he fulfills it for one who is not proficient, as it is stated at the end of Rosh Hashanah. And there are those who say that for the blessings of the Shema, the prayer leader fulfills it for one who is not proficient, but not for the Shema itself (Eliyah Rabbah in the name of Abudraham). But this does not seem correct (Eliyah Rabbah). The prayer leader must make his voice heard in "Shema Yisrael" so that the congregation hears and declares the sovereignty of Heaven together.

It was taught in the first chapter of Berachot (10b): Beit Shammai say: In the evening, every person should recline and recite [the Shema], and in the morning, they should stand, as it is said: "When you lie down and when you rise." Meaning, in the manner of lying down and in the manner of rising. But Beit Hillel say: Every person recites in their own way, as it is said: "When you walk on the way." If so, why is it said "When you lie down and when you rise"? At the time when people lie down, and at the time when people rise. This means it refers to the time of the recitation of the Shema. Rabbi Tarfon said: I was once on the way, and I reclined to recite [the Shema] according to the words of Beit Shammai, and I endangered myself because of bandits. They said to me: You deserved to be harmed, for you transgressed the words of Beit Hillel.

Based on this, the Tur and Shulchan Aruch ruled that one may recite it while walking, standing, lying down, riding on an animal, or sitting... And one who wishes to be stringent and stand while he is sitting and recite it standing is called a "transgressor." Thus is their language. And even though in several disputes between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel, where Beit Shammai is stringent and Beit Hillel is lenient, in any case, one who wishes to be stringent like Beit Shammai is not reprimanded. However, this dispute is not similar to all other disputes, for in all other disputes, even Beit Hillel admits that there is a stringency in the words of Beit Shammai, and therefore, one who wishes to be stringent, why shouldn't he be stringent? But here, there is no stringency according to Beit Hillel in the words of Beit Shammai, for according to Beit Hillel, it is all the same whether one stands or sits. And since he is stringent, it appears as though he rules according to Beit Shammai. Moreover, since according to Beit Hillel, the interpretation of "when you lie down and when you rise" refers to the time of reciting the Shema, if so, when one is stringent like Beit Shammai, who interpret it as lying down specifically in the evening and standing specifically in the morning, the time for reciting the Shema would be nullified. Therefore, Rabbi Tarfon was also punished.

Based on this, it appears that whether one is standing, it is prohibited to sit, and whether one is sitting, it is prohibited to stand. The Tur and the Shulchan Aruch only mention that one should not stand when sitting. I have seen it written that in truth, one who is standing is permitted to sit, as this does not appear to be a stringency but rather a desire to sit, for sitting is better for a person than standing (Eliyah Rabbah in the name of Magen Avraham). It is difficult: if so, why was Rabbi Tarfon punished? After all, reclining is also better for a person than sitting. The truth seems to be that in the morning according to Beit Shammai, specifically standing – in this case, it is forbidden to stand when sitting. And in the evening according to Beit Shammai, specifically sitting – in this case, it is forbidden when standing to sit, as it appears like one is acting according to Beit Shammai. However, conversely, in the morning when standing – it is permitted to sit, and in the evening when sitting – it is permitted to stand. In this case, it is not possible to suspect that one is acting according to Beit Shammai, for on the contrary, this is the opposite of Beit Shammai. Therefore, the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, which refer to the morning, wrote that when sitting it is forbidden to stand. This also seems to be the primary ruling (and so it implies in the Bach). It also appears that specifically when one acts according to the law to fulfill the requirement of Beit Shammai, there is a prohibition, like Rabbi Tarfon who said, "I reclined to read according to the words of Beit Shammai." But when one acts without intention, like those people who are not at ease and keep rising and sitting, and then rising again, and sitting again – there is no concern. According to the Zohar, the recitation of the Shema in the morning and its blessings should specifically be done while sitting until "Praises to the Most High God," at which point one should stand. This is also explained in Pri Etz Chaim and in the Kavanot, and it is called "the prayer of sitting."

And behold, even though one recites [the Shema] in his usual manner, whether standing, sitting, or walking, nevertheless, when he is traveling on the road and wants to recite the Shema, he should stand for the first verse. This is done so that he can concentrate, as the main concentration is on the first verse. And there are those who require standing for the entire first paragraph, so that it does not appear as if he is reading it casually. And there are those who wish to say that standing for the entire paragraph is forbidden, as it appears like he is following the opinion of Beit Shammai (Bach). Others disagree, arguing that since he already stands for the first verse, it no longer appears like he is following Beit Shammai (Taz, subsection 2 and Magen Avraham, subsection 4). And it is obvious that for "Blessed be the name of His glorious kingdom" he needs to stand (there). Also, one riding on a donkey needs to stand, but one sitting in a carriage does not need to stand, as he is sitting comfortably and can concentrate well (there). However, one riding cannot concentrate well while the donkey is moving.

It is stated in the Gemara (13b): One who lies on his back should not recite the Shema. Rashi explains: lying on his back with his face upward. And the Rambam in the second chapter (Halachot 2) wrote: whether his face is upward or lying on his face with his back upward. The reason is that this is not the way of propriety. But when lying on his side, it is permitted to recite [the Shema] from the outset, and he does not need to stand up even if he has no difficulty standing up. And this is the opinion of most of the poskim. But some say that specifically when he is already lying down and it is difficult for him to stand up, such as needing to put on his clothes. But if he has no difficulty in this, such as lying in his clothes and can easily stand – he is obligated to stand. And this is the inclination of our teacher the Rema, although most of the poskim do not hold this way (and so wrote the Magen Avraham and the Taz in subsection 1). And someone who is very corpulent and cannot turn on his side and is compelled to lie on his back, or he is sick – he should lean a bit to his side and recite. And if he cannot lean at all – he is permitted to recite in this manner. And a healthy person should not lie on his back even without reciting the Shema, only he should lean a bit (Gemara). And it appears that lying with his face upward is worse than lying with his face downward, for with his face upward there is a concern that he might become warm and see a seminal emission. For this is implied there in the Gemara and Rashi, see there.

The primary intention is in the first verse, as I have written several times. "Blessed be the name of His glorious kingdom forever and ever" is included in this. Therefore, if one recited and did not intend his heart in the first verse, he has not fulfilled his obligation, and he must go back and recite it again. Even according to the opinion that commandments do not require intention, they agree with this, as this is the very intention of the commandment. However, one must have intention of the heart, as I have written in Siman 60, section 7; see there. This is not like one who says "Shema, Shema," whom we silence, since he does this because he did not intend the first time. Furthermore, he should actually say it the second time in a whisper. Additionally, he can wait a bit (Taz, section 3). If he remembered that he did not intend in Shema until he finished "V'ahavta," he must go back to the beginning and recite the first portion completely (Magen Avraham, section 6). Similarly, if he did not remember until after "Vehaya im shamoa," he also goes back to the beginning and recites the first portion but not the second. For after the fact, it does not prevent fulfillment if the second was recited before the first, as I have written in Siman 64. If he did not intend in "Blessed be the name of His glorious kingdom," if he remembers before starting "V'ahavta," he should go back and say it with intention. If he remembers afterward, he does not need to go back, as we have already explained in Siman 61, section 6; see there. (Magen Avraham, section 6, wrote in the name of Sefer Chasidim: if one did not intend in the first verse, he should read the portion twice; see there. It implies even if he has not yet read the portion. This requires further study.)

And since the primary intention (kavanah) is in the first verse, therefore if someone is dozing, they should be disturbed and woken up until they read the first verse while fully awake. But from then on, they should not be disturbed until they read while fully awake, and even if they read while dozing, they have fulfilled their obligation. Similarly, if they had another compulsion preventing them from reading with intention, they have fulfilled their obligation, except for the first verse. And we have already written in Siman 58, Section 16 that even if all three paragraphs are obligations from the Torah, nevertheless, there is a difference in intention between the first verse and the rest of the paragraphs, and between the first paragraph and the second. See there in Section 17.

Just as there is a difference between the first verse and the rest of the Shema in terms of intent, so too there is a difference between the first and second paragraphs regarding casual recitation, because it is written: "And you shall speak of them." And we derive in Yoma (19a): make them fixed. Therefore, one who reads the Shema should not signal with his eyes, nor move his lips, nor gesture with his fingers during the first paragraph, which is the acceptance of the yoke of Heaven, because it appears as if he is reading casually. And even for the sake of a mitzvah, he should not signal... And from Maimonides, it is implied that this is also forbidden in the second paragraph, see there. Therefore, if he was engaged in work and wants to read the Shema, he should stop his work until he reads the first paragraph. According to Maimonides, this could also apply to the second paragraph, as I have written. All this is to ensure that it does not appear as if he is reading casually.

And it is specifically the performance of labor that is forbidden. However, descending from the place of labor is not obligatory, and one can recite [the Shema] there. Therefore, craftsmen who are working at the top of a tree, or on a building, or in another place – they do not need to descend but recite [the Shema] while standing there. Even a homeowner engaged in his own labor – he does not need to descend. And although for prayer one must descend as I wrote in Siman 90 – this is because the prayer is long and requires concentration throughout, which is not the case with the recitation of the Shema. And a porter who is carrying a load on his shoulders – he can recite the Shema in that state, as it does not disturb him. But he should not start while he is lifting the load onto his shoulders or while he is taking it down, because at those times he is somewhat preoccupied and cannot concentrate, as his mind is not settled. And if he started beforehand, it seems that he should neither load nor unload until he completes the entire Shema, for who compels him to do so? Regarding prayer, it seems that even when the load is on his shoulders – he should not pray until he has unloaded his burden. The status of one who is tipsy or drunk with respect to the Shema is like that of prayer, and this will be explained in Siman 99.

We learned in the Mishnah (15a): If one recites [the Shema] out of order, he has not fulfilled his obligation. This means that if he read the second verse before the first, as it is written: "And they shall be" – they must be in their proper order (Megillah 17b). This applies specifically to the verses themselves. However, if he recited [the paragraph starting with] "And it will be if you listen" before [the paragraph starting with] "Hear, O Israel," or "And he said" before "Hear, O Israel" or "And it will be if you listen" – he has fulfilled his obligation, since they are not arranged consecutively in the Torah. Therefore, even though the Sages ordained to recite "Hear, O Israel" first, followed by "And it will be if you listen," and then "And he said," nevertheless, this is not critical after the fact.

There is a question regarding this: Since the reason is because of the term "vehayu" (they shall be), as I have written, this makes sense in the case of "Shema" and "Vehaya im shamoa," where "vehayu" is written. But in the section of Tzitzit, where "vehayu" is not written, from where do we know that reading out of order is not allowed? And if you say that indeed it is allowed, then the poskim should have clarified this, and from their silence, it implies that this applies to all three sections. Additionally, there is another question: According to those who hold that one fulfills their obligation of reciting the Shema with just the first verse or the first section, what prohibition is there if one reads out of order? And if we say that rabbinically one does not fulfill their obligation, then it should also invalidate the sections if read out of order. However, this actually serves as proof for what we wrote in Siman 58, Section 16, that all the sections are mandated by the Torah, see there. Also, there is no question: why is it that in the writing of Tefillin and Mezuzot, it is invalid if not in order even within sections, as I wrote at the beginning of Siman 32, but in their reading, we are not particular about the order of sections? Some of the great commentators (Pri Megadim) have raised this difficulty. However, in truth, it is not comparable, because in the writing of Tefillin and Mezuzot, it is all one mitzvah, as one without the other is nothing. Therefore, we are particular about the order written in the Torah, even though they are not adjacent to each other in the Torah. But in their reading, each section is its own matter: the first for accepting the yoke of Heaven, and the second for the yoke of commandments – we are not concerned if one precedes the other. Only within a single section should one not precede a later verse to an earlier one, because it says "vehayu." But in the section of Tzitzit, why should it invalidate? And perhaps because the two sections are mandated by the Torah, the Rabbis also established this for the third section. This requires further study.

If one recited a section and made an error in it: if he knows where he made the error, for example, he recited the entire section but skipped one verse in the middle – he returns to the beginning of that verse. Even if the skip was in the middle of the verse, nevertheless, he returns to the beginning of the verse, and recites from there until the end of the section. And if he does not know where he made the error – he returns to the beginning of the section. And if he does not know if he also said "Shema Yisrael" – he returns to "Shema Yisrael." And if he knows that he said "Shema Yisrael," and the doubt is from there onwards – he begins from "Ve'ahavta," or from "Baruch Shem Kevod Malchuto Le'olam Va'ed" if he is in doubt whether he said it. And even though it has already been explained that in the case of doubt regarding "Baruch Shem Kevod Malchuto Le'olam Va'ed" one does not need to return – this is when it is certain that "Ve'ahavta" was said. But when one needs to return to "Ve'ahavta" due to a doubt – consequently, he also returns to "Baruch Shem Kevod Malchuto Le'olam Va'ed" if there is also a doubt about it.

And similarly, if he made a mistake between one section and another, knowing that he finished a section but not knowing whether it was the first or the second one, he returns to the first section and starts from "Vehaya im shamoa." If he was standing at words that are similar in both sections, such as "u'k'tavtam," "u'k'shartam," or "u'v'shivtecha b'veitecha," and he does not know if he is in the first or the second section, he returns to the one in the first section. This is specifically when he has not yet started "lema'an yirbu." But if he has started "lema'an yirbu," it is certainly from the second section, as it is assumed he follows his usual habit. All the more so if he knows he has started the section of Tzitzit, it is certainly from the second section. And similarly, if he clearly knows which word he said, it is assumed that he said everything above it, and he only returns to the beginning of the verse of that word.

Not only in the recitation of the Shema, if one errs, must they repeat it; but even in its blessings, if one deviates from the text established by the Sages in any of the blessings, they must go back to the beginning of the blessing (Rambam, Chapter One). However, this is specifically if one changed the opening or closing. But if one added some words in the middle of the blessing, or omitted some words – we do not concern ourselves with it, since the opening and closing were as they should be. And we have already explained this in Siman 59.

Know that when a person performs a mitzvah, such as reciting the Shema, praying, blowing the shofar, or reading the Megillah, and he pauses in the middle and the interruption lasts long enough to complete the entire mitzvah, it is explained in Rosh Hashanah regarding the shofar blasts that if one hears nine shofar blasts on Rosh Hashanah over nine hours of the day, he fulfills his obligation (Rosh Hashanah 34b). Similarly, in Megillah (11b) regarding an interruption during the reading of the Megillah and in Berachot (22b) regarding someone who is praying and begins to urinate, and the interruption is long enough to complete the entire prayer, there is a dispute there, and the Rif rules in the name of the Gaon that he must start from the beginning. However, later on in the same place regarding the Shema, it is ruled that he does not need to start from the beginning, and similarly with the Megillah and the shofar, he does not need to start from the beginning. It is held that only in prayer, which is stringent and one is forbidden to interrupt even if a king inquires about his welfare, must he start from the beginning, but not in other matters. The Rambam also ruled similarly, in the second chapter of the laws of Shema that one does not need to start from the beginning, and in the fourth chapter of the laws of prayer that one must start from the beginning. Look there for more details.

However, our Rabbis, the authors of the Tosafot, wrote that all the laws are equal. The practical difference is in what manner the interruption occurred: if he interrupted willingly and could have finished if he wanted to — he does not return to the beginning, because it is not called an "interruption" since he could have finished. But if he was forced to interrupt according to the law, such as when he began to urinate or walk in filthy alleyways and similar cases — he returns to the beginning if he delayed long enough to finish it all, because this is certainly considered an interruption since he was forced to stop. Many of our Rabbis agreed with this opinion. And this is what the Tur wrote: if one recites in intervals, meaning with interruptions, even if he delayed long enough to finish it all — he fulfills his obligation, provided that the delay was not due to compulsion that prevented him from reciting. But if the delay was due to compulsion, such that the place was not suitable for reciting or some other compulsion, if he interrupted and delayed long enough to finish it all, when he resumes reciting, he must start from the beginning. This is his language, and this follows the opinion of the Tosafot. And so ruled our Rabbi, the Rema, in Section 1, and wrote that this is the custom. The duration of the delay is assessed according to the reader and not according to the majority of people. This is his language. And any compulsion is considered "compulsion," even if robbers fell upon him. And there are those who disagree, as will be explained in Section 4.

But our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote: If one recited [the Shema] intermittently, meaning he began reciting and then paused, whether in silence or in speech, and then resumed and completed it, even if the pause was long enough to complete the entire Shema – he has fulfilled his obligation, even if the interruption was due to unavoidable circumstances. Thus are his words. And later in Siman 104 regarding prayer, he ruled that one must start from the beginning, see there. Because he follows the opinion of the Rif and the Rambam that it is specifically in prayer that one must start from the beginning, but not in the recitation of the Shema and other commandments. And they did not differentiate between an interruption caused by unavoidable circumstances and one made willingly, but rather between prayer and other matters, for the reason that we have explained.

And certainly, in practice, we follow the opinion of the majority of our rabbis, distinguishing between cases of coercion and cases without coercion. We have explained that even robbers are considered "coercion." Specifically, when the delay was due to one's own actions, such as wanting to stop or stopping due to an argument, which he could have avoided, this is not considered "coercion." However, any delay caused by others is considered "coercion." Nevertheless, the opinion of the Raavad and the Meor is that "coercion" is only considered if it was impossible to pray according to the law, such as when urinating or if the place is not clean. But other types of coercion are not considered coercion at all in this matter. Therefore, in practice, regarding prayer, one can rely on the previous opinion that even robbers are considered coercion, because according to the Rif and the Rambam, even without this, one must start the prayer from the beginning. But in other matters, we follow the Raavad and the Meor. And it also appears this way in the Tosafot (and so wrote the Magen Avraham, subsection 2).

Based on what has been explained, there is no concern when the congregation lengthens the recitation of piyutim (liturgical poems) before the Shemoneh Esrei, and the cantors sing and extend their melodies in the middle of "Yotzer Or" and in the middle of the last blessing after the Shema, when they sing in "Ezrat." Even if there is an interruption in the middle of the blessing longer than the time required to complete it, nevertheless, one does not need to return to the beginning. This is not only according to the Rif and the Rambam, but even according to the majority of our Rabbis who say it depends on duress – here it is not considered duress, since one can complete the blessings. Certainly, ideally, one should not interrupt in any manner, but if one does so to pray with the congregation – it is considered as if it was done after the fact, and it is not called "duress" as I have written. (The Tosafot and Mordechai at the end of Rosh Hashanah who were critical of this did so because they did not differentiate between duress and willingness, see there. And the Magen Avraham, section 1, wrote that their intention was regarding ideally, see there. But this does not seem to be their intention. Additionally: since one needs to pray with the congregation, and if it was regarding the primary issue that piyutim are an interruption – this is certainly considered after the fact since they have already been established. But the main point is as I have written. They have difficulty with the primary piyutim: that it is an interruption and one returns to the beginning, as well as those who wait? However, based on what I have written in Berachot to differentiate between duress and willingness, there is no difficulty at all. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

When one enters a synagogue and hears the congregation reciting the Shema, even if he has already recited it, he is still obligated to say the verse "Shema Yisrael" with the congregation, so that it does not appear as if he does not wish to accept the yoke of Heaven together with his peers. Similarly, if he is in the synagogue studying, or saying supplications, or engaged in other activities that he is permitted to interrupt, when the congregation reaches "Shema Yisrael" he should respond together with them. However, if he is engaged in an activity where interruption is not allowed, such as from "Baruch She'amar" onward, our master the Beit Yosef ruled in section 2 that he should not interrupt. Instead, when the congregation recites "Shema Yisrael," he should sing the tune on the words where he is standing, so it appears as if he is reading with them. This is the end of his words. And some say that one should interrupt even in the middle of the blessings of the Shema to respond "Shema Yisrael" with the congregation (Bach and Magen Avraham, subsection 4). However, we do not follow this practice. Nevertheless, during Pesukei Dezimra (verses of praise), it is certainly appropriate to interrupt. Our master the Beit Yosef maintains his position in Siman 51 that one should not interrupt during Pesukei Dezimra to respond "Amen." However, we have already explained there that we do respond "Amen" according to the Ari, of blessed memory. Therefore, responding "Shema Yisrael" is no less than responding "Amen." And be aware that some wish to say that for any matter that the congregation says, like "Tehillah L'David," one should respond with them (Magen Avraham, subsection 3). However, we do not follow this practice, only for "Shema Yisrael" and "Aleinu" when they say "And we bow," one must bow with them, just as with "Modim," so that it does not appear that the entire congregation is bowing while he is not. And some have the custom to also recite "Aleinu" with the congregation.

Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 3: If one recited the Shema and then entered the synagogue and found the congregation reciting the Shema, it is good to recite the entire Shema with them and he will receive a reward as if he were reading from the Torah. His words end here, meaning: although according to the law he only needs to say the verse "Shema Yisrael" with them, as I wrote earlier, nevertheless it is good to recite the entire Shema in full. And why should he not do so, since he is considered as if he were reading from the Torah? This is what our teacher, the Rema, wrote there: But he is only obligated to say the first verse, as has been explained. His words end here, and this is as I wrote. However, our custom is not so, and we only respond "Shema Yisrael."

It is taught at the beginning of the second chapter of Berachot that in the middle of a section, one may ask [after someone's welfare] out of fear and respond out of respect, and between sections, one may ask out of respect and greet anyone. This means that when one is in the middle of the blessing of "Yotzer" or "Ahava Rabba," or in the middle of a paragraph of the Shema, or in the middle of a blessing after the Shema, and a person who he is obligated to honor passes by, he should not initiate a greeting. However, if this person greets him first, he should respond. But if a person whom he must have fear of passes by, then it is permitted even to initiate a greeting, and certainly to respond. Yet between sections, such as between "Yotzer" and "Ahava Rabba," between "Ahava" and the Shema, between "Shema" and "Vehaya im Shamoa," and between "Vehaya" and "Vayomer"—one may ask after the welfare of even someone he is obligated to honor, but to respond is permitted to anyone. There is a dispute as to who is considered "out of respect" and who is "out of fear."

Rashi explained that "because of honor" refers to an important person who deserves to be greeted first, and "because of fear" refers to a person one fears might kill him. The Rambam, in his commentary on the Mishnah and in his Code, interpreted "because of fear" like Rashi. However, for "because of honor," he explained it as referring to a person whom one is obligated to honor, such as his father or his teacher. The Rosh and the Rashba challenged their interpretation of "because of fear," arguing that if there is a fear of being killed, it is obvious, and what is being taught? For there is nothing that stands before the preservation of life. Therefore, they interpreted "because of fear" as referring to one's father or teacher whom he is obligated to fear, and "because of honor" as referring to an important person, like Rashi. The Tur and the Shulchan Aruch, section 1, also wrote this, see there. And Rabbeinu Beit Yosef added to include in "because of fear" someone who is greater than him in wisdom, see there. This is puzzling, for the Rashba explicitly wrote that this is included in "because of honor," unless he means the greatest sage of the generation. For the Terumat HaDeshen (Siman 135) wrote that one must fear someone who is exceedingly great in wisdom (see Magen Avraham, sub-section 2).

Some of the great authorities agreed specifically with Rashi and Rambam in their interpretation of "due to fear." The intention is not that he will certainly kill him, and on the contrary, it is unlikely that he would kill him because of this. As we find an incident with a certain pious person and the bishop (Berakhot 32b), see there. Rather, there is a slight remote concern, and therefore they indeed permitted him even to interrupt in the middle of a chapter and even to inquire about his well-being. But for one's father or teacher, it is surprising to interrupt in the middle of a chapter, as we find in the Midrash that Jacob did not interrupt when he encountered Joseph because he was reciting the Shema, and Joseph was a king. Only to respond with a greeting is permitted (Beit Yosef and Taz, Section 1). And in the interpretation of "due to honor," everyone agreed with Rashi's interpretation. (I am puzzled that the commentators did not notice the difference between Rashi and Rambam in "due to honor." Only the Eliyah Rabbah noticed this, see there. However, everyone agreed with Rashi's interpretation.)

And know that this allowance to interrupt even in the middle of a section to inquire out of fear or to respond out of respect, however, in the middle of "Shema Yisrael" or in the middle of "Baruch Shem..." – one should not interrupt under any circumstances unless fearing a danger to life. And some say further that one should not interrupt in the middle of any verse, for it is easy to complete it without interruption. And if he does interrupt – he returns to the beginning of the verse (see Magen Avraham, small section 3). And it is also known that where it is permitted to interrupt – it is allowed even in secular language. And where it is forbidden – even in holy language (ibid., small section 1). And some of the great authorities have written further that nowadays we do not see anyone being particular about this at all, and therefore we do not even return greetings. It is not our custom to interrupt even for one's father or teacher, and even between sections one should not interrupt (ibid. in the name of the Chinuch), and on the contrary, now it is considered irreverent to interrupt. And indeed we see even a minister, when he comes to a Jew's house and finds him praying, he will not speak to him and will wait until he finishes his prayer. Therefore, now any form of interruption is forbidden until the end of the prayer, and such is the simple custom and it should not be changed. And when asking questions of prohibition and permission to the teacher – he can answer between sections. But when the questioner is a person of understanding – he waits until the prayer is finished. And this is the correct way to act unless the matter is urgent, then it is a mitzvah to ask even in the middle of the prayer, and the teacher interrupts between sections and responds to the questioner.

If he did not have a tallit and tefillin when he began to pray, or he forgot to put them on, and in the middle of the prayer the tallit and tefillin came to him or he remembered them, our teacher the Beit Yosef ruled in paragraph 2 that he can interrupt between the sections to put them on, and he should bless upon them. The reason is simple: since he is obligated to put them on, he must naturally bless upon them. It is no less than one who inquires out of respect, and the blessing is an honor to the mitzvah. And our teacher the Rema wrote: "And there are those who say that he should not bless upon them until after the prayer, and this is the custom regarding the tallit." Thus far his words, meaning: there are those who hold that since he can bless afterward, why should he interrupt? But this is not a correct reason, and the author of this opinion himself retracted (see Beit Yosef in the Bedek Habayit) for the reason we explained. And only regarding the tallit should this opinion be upheld, since the tallit is not an obligation for prayer – it is not appropriate that its blessing should override the prohibition of interruption. But tefillin, which are an obligation – certainly their blessing overrides, as it is comparable to out of respect. (See Magen Avraham paragraph 4. Observe and you will find it easy.)

For Kaddish, Kedusha, and "Barchu," one interrupts even in the middle of a verse. For if one interrupts out of respect for human honor, how much more so for the honor of Heaven. This is akin to responding rather than initiating, for since everyone responds to the prayer leader, praising the Holy One, Blessed be He, he too is compelled to respond. Therefore, even if one hears thunder or sees lightning, he is obligated to bless even in the middle of a verse, as explained (Magen Avraham, subsection 5), because this is also considered responding and not initiating. Similarly, one interrupts for "Modim," but should only say "Modim anachnu lach" and no more, since the rest is merely supplications and one should not interrupt for them. Similarly, in Kaddish, one should respond "Amen! Yehei shmei rabbah" only up to "yitbarach," and not to other "Amens" in Kaddish, as they are not essential to Kaddish. However, one does respond to the "Amen" after "da'amiran b'alma," as it is essential to Kaddish. 

Regarding Kedusha, some say one should only respond "Kadosh" and "Baruch," but not "Yimloch," as it is not essential to Kedusha. This is also implied in the Tosefta. Others say one should also respond "Yimloch." There is no definitive ruling on this, so one may follow his preference. However, it is certain that one should not say "Nekadesh" or "Nakdishach" or "Keter" at all, but should start from "Kadosh." Similarly, on Shabbat and holidays when additional phrases like "Az b'kol," "Mimkomcha," and in Musaf "Kevodo malei olam," "Mimkomo...," and "Shema Yisrael" are added, one should not respond to these as they are not essential to Kedusha. However, it seems to me that one should respond to "Shema Yisrael," since everyone is accepting the yoke of Heaven's sovereignty, and he should respond up to "Echad." Nevertheless, according to Rabbeinu the Beit Yosef, whom we cited in Siman 65, subsection 6, one should not interrupt; see there.

Similarly, during the Torah reading, when the person called up says "Barchu," one should respond "Blessed is the Lord, who is blessed forever and ever," but should not respond with "Amen." Likewise, it is forbidden to respond with any form of "Amen." Although it is a matter of honoring Heaven to respond with "Amen," nevertheless, he is also engaged in honoring Heaven. Only for matters that involve the sanctification of God's name, which are only said with a quorum of ten, such as Kaddish, Kedusha, "Barchu," and "Modim," is one obligated to interrupt and sanctify Him with everyone, but not with "Amen." Nevertheless, our teacher the Rema wrote in section 3, and this is his language: "Similarly, for 'Barchu,' one should not say 'May He be blessed and praised...'" Some say that the "Amen" said after the blessing "the holy God" and after "He who hears prayer" has the status of Kedusha, and one may respond to them during the recitation of the Shema. This is the primary ruling. For all these matters, one interrupts even more so when saying supplications. Thus far his words, meaning: supplications after the Amidah.

And we do not know why these two "Amens" are different. Some say it is because they are the conclusion of a matter: the end of the first three blessings and the end of the intermediate blessings (Magen Avraham and Taz). And indeed, one should also respond "Amen" to "He who blesses His people..." (ibid.). But it is not understood: What of it? This is not something that requires a minyan (quorum of ten). Even though the "Amen" after "the holy God" could be considered included in the sanctity, the "Amen" after "who hears prayer" certainly has no connection to sanctity. And this is what is brought from the Jerusalem Talmud in the chapter "The Morning Prayer," that these two "Amens" have a greater obligation to be answered, yet it has no bearing on making an interruption in a place where interruptions are forbidden. And from the words of our teacher Rema, it is understood that these have the status of sanctity, which is not understood at all. And indeed, our teacher the Beit Yosef in his great book disagrees with this; see there. And it appears that his reasoning is because this is a general praise—that He is holy and hears the prayer of every mouth—which somewhat resembles the sanctity of God's name, and is not comparable to all the "Amens" of individual blessings. (And know that the Magen Avraham in subsection 6 wrote: And on the blessing of the Torah, one responds "Blessed is the Lord..." and also "Amen." These are his words. And the Levushei Serad explained that this is on the "Amen" after "Blessed is the Lord...". I am puzzled: it is not explained anywhere that one should respond "Amen" after "Blessed is the Lord who is blessed." And I recall seeing this explicitly in some early authority, and we do not respond with this "Amen" at all. Therefore, it seems that the intention of Magen Avraham is the "Amen" after "who gives the Torah." And the reason is: since an interruption was made for "Blessed is the Lord who is blessed"—one can also interrupt for this "Amen." And there is a support for this from Zevachim 32b: since it was permitted for his affliction, it was permitted for his covering; see there. Nonetheless, this also requires further examination.)

A Kohen who was reciting the Shema and was called up to the Torah, there are those who say that he should interrupt and go up. And there are those who say that he should not interrupt, and someone else should go up in his place. Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, ruled in paragraph 4 in accordance with this opinion, which is the opinion of the Rashba, that he should not interrupt. However, the great later authorities have written that the custom is to interrupt (Levush and Magen Avraham, subsection 8). But he should not read along with the reader, and certainly should not say the "Mi Sheberach" prayer (there). Some have ruled that during the Shema he should not go up, but during the blessings of the Shema he may go up (Taz, subsection 5). And know that this does not apply only to a Kohen, for the same law applies to a Levite and an Israelite (see Eliyah Rabbah, subsection 7). It seems to me that if there is no other Kohen in the synagogue, he certainly should go up, and similarly for a Levite if there is no other Levite. It is obvious that all this applies when he is in the middle of a section, but between sections, he certainly should go up. Therefore, if he can finish the section while walking, he should do so. And between "Geulah" and "Tefillah," he should not go up under any circumstances. We customarily interrupt and go up in accordance with the opinion of the great later authorities. He should try to descend immediately after the second blessing. Even though the one who goes up customarily waits until after the reading of the one who follows him, here, where he is in the middle of a section, he should descend immediately. It has already been explained in Siman 65 that even if he made a long interruption during which he could have finished the entire Shema, he does not go back to the beginning but to the place where he stopped, for this is not considered "unavoidable circumstances" (see Magen Avraham there).

We have already explained what constitutes "between the sections" (beyn haprakim). These are: between the blessing of "Yotzer" and "Ahava," between "Ahava" and "Shema," between "Shema" and "Vehaya im Shamo'a," and between "Vehaya" and "Vayomer." However, between "Vayomer" and "Emet Veyatziv," one should not interrupt, so as not to interrupt between "Hashem [Elokeichem]" and "Emet," as it is written: "Hashem Elokim Emet." Rather, one should conclude with "Emet," and then it will be considered as in the middle of a section. 

We are puzzled why the poskim did not mention that in "Yotzer," after Kedusha, it is like the beginning of the blessing, as I wrote at the end of Siman 59 regarding the matter that the second one only begins from there, based on the Yerushalmi that here it is considered the beginning of the blessing. If so, it should be treated as between one section and another. We must say that only regarding the law there it is considered the beginning of the blessing, but not regarding interruption. The proof is that in the Mishnah it is stated: "And these are between the sections: between the first blessing and the second" – it implies clearly that before this, there is no "between the sections." However, from the language of the Yerushalmi in the chapter "Ein Omdin," it is clear that from "Le'el Baruch" it is indeed considered the beginning of the blessing; see there. This requires further investigation.

When an individual finishes saying "emet" and waits for the chazzan to finish, even if a considerable amount of time has passed, he should not begin again from "emet" but rather from "v'yatziv." Similarly, if he interrupts after "emet" for matters that warrant interruption in the middle of a section, as explained earlier, he should not start again from "emet" but from "v'yatziv." Saying "emet" twice consecutively is forbidden. There are those who suggest that one should also say "v'yatziv" along with "emet," because "v'yatziv" also means "true" in Aramaic. However, this is not the custom. (See Magen Avraham, subsection 9. Note that in the "Ezrat" blessing, we do say "emet" twice: "emet ata hu Adon..." and "emet ata hu rishon...". This is not considered saying "emet" twice consecutively because there are other words in between. According to the Zohar, Vayakhel 217a, one should say "emet" four times, and this is the custom of the Sephardim. The chazzanim who chant "emet emet" several times are committing a grave sin.)

It is stated in Pesachim (117b): In the recitation of the Shema, "Who has redeemed Israel" refers to the past, and in the Amidah, "Who redeems Israel" refers to the future. The great authorities have already wondered why the prayer leader concludes the evening service of a festival with "King, Rock of Israel and its Redeemer," which goes against the Gemara (Taz, subsection 6, and Bach and Magen Avraham at the beginning of section 236). Some have explained that specifically the redemption in the morning refers only to the past, but the evening redemption also refers to the future (Magen Avraham there). Some have explained that even "redeems" is in the present tense, and the present tense can also refer to the past (Taz there). Some say it is preferable to say "and its Redeemer" without a "vav" after the "gimel," which is in the past tense (Bach there). All these explanations are strained. Some of the great authorities have established that the prayer leader concludes with "Who has redeemed Israel" as throughout the year, and so we practice. Why should we enter into strained interpretations?

Our rabbis, the authors of the Tosafot, wrote at the beginning of the second chapter of Berachot that Rabbeinu Tam was accustomed to wait at "Oseh Pele" in order to respond to Kaddish and Kedusha with the congregation; see there. It is explained that he holds that between Geulah and Tefillah is more severe than in the middle of a section, and it is considered just like Tefillah itself, for which one should not interrupt for anything. Similarly, the Mordechai wrote there in the name of the Ra'avyah that it is forbidden to interrupt for Kaddish and Kedusha after "Ga'al Yisrael" of Shacharit; see there. The Maharik (Shoresh 42) and the author of Terumat HaDeshen (Siman 12) wrote similarly. Our master, the Beit Yosef, also ruled this way in his great book; see there. Although the Rokeach wrote that one should respond to Kaddish, Kedusha, and "Barechu" after "Ga'al Yisrael" (Rokeach Siman 321), nevertheless, the halacha follows the majority. Hence, one who is standing there in prayer and sees that the congregation will soon say Kaddish, Kedusha, or "Barechu," should wait at "Shira Chadasha" or "Tzur Yisrael." It is even better to wait at "Tehillot Le-El Elyon," as according to the Zohar, one pauses there. And know that one should say "LaMelech El Chai V'kayam" with a Kamatz, and similarly "Tehillot La-El Elyon," the Lamed with a Kamatz (Pri Etz Chaim).

Regarding the matter of responding "Amen" to the blessing of "Ga'al Yisrael," there is a dispute: The Tur wrote that even when praying individually, one responds "Amen," see there. He holds that one must respond "Amen" after one's own blessing when it concludes a section. However, our custom is not so, except after the blessing of "Boneh Yerushalayim" in the Grace After Meals. Accordingly, it would seem that one should not respond "Amen" after the Chazan concludes "Ga'al Yisrael." This is certainly derived from Kedusha, where interruptions are not made, as I have written. This is also the opinion of the Zohar, which advises not to respond "Amen," and so ruled our master, the Beit Yosef, in section 7. But our master, the Rema, wrote there that some say one should respond "Amen" after the Chazan but not after one's own blessing. This opinion must hold that this is preferable to Kedusha because it pertains to the obligation of the blessing itself. Just as one recites the blessing, so too does one respond "Amen" to the Chazan's blessing, as with all blessings, and this is not considered an interruption. Nevertheless, our custom is not so. (And the Eliyah Rabbah wrote in subsection 10 that the Re'em disagrees on this matter. Similarly, the Shelah wrote that one should not respond "Amen" after the Chazan. The Maggid warned the Beit Yosef not to respond.)

And know that there is one who wrote in this language: "And those who are meticulous wait at 'Tzur Yisrael' in order to answer 'Amen.'" And in paragraph 9 it implies that one should wait at 'Shirah Chadasha.' And it seems to me that if one wishes, they can intend to finish with the Chazzan, and then they are not obligated to answer 'Amen.' Thus far is his language (Magen Avraham, subsection 11). And behold, this idea of finishing with the Chazzan is correct, for even though in Siman 59 there are those who disagree and hold that if one finishes with the Chazzan, they must answer 'Amen,' nevertheless, regarding the 'Amen' of 'Ga'al Yisrael,' it is certainly not required to answer. And this is the ruling for all 'Amens,' as I have written there. However, what was written about waiting at 'Tzur Yisrael' or 'Shirah Chadasha' in order to answer 'Amen' – these are perplexing words, for in the middle of a section it is forbidden to answer 'Amen' except for 'Amen' of 'Ha-Kel Ha-Kadosh' and 'Shomea Tefillah,' as has been explained. And what was brought from paragraph 9 – this pertains to Kaddish and Kedusha as explained in the Shulchan Aruch there, and not to answering 'Amen.' Therefore, this ruling does not apply. (And also the Eliyah Rabbah, subsection 13, and the Pri Megadim were amazed by this, see there.) And perhaps on Shabbat and Yom Tov, where there is an opinion that one does not need to juxtapose redemption to prayer, as I wrote later in Siman 111, it might be permissible to answer 'Amen' after 'Ga'al Yisrael' if one finishes the blessing before the Chazzan. But in the middle, it is certainly forbidden. And know that there are those who say that the waiting to answer Kedusha is only before 'Shirah Chadasha' and not afterwards (Eliyah Rabbah). And I do not understand the difference in this. And perhaps, according to the Sephardic rite where they do not say 'Tzur Yisrael' but 'Vene'emar Goaleinu...' it is correct, because afterwards there is no continuation, obviously. But according to the Ashkenazic rite, where they say 'Tzur Yisrael,' there is still a prayer, and there is no difference between before 'Shirah Chadasha' and after it.

Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote in section 8: One must connect the blessing of redemption ("Ga'al Yisrael") to the Amidah prayer. One should not interrupt after saying "Ga'al Yisrael," except in a case of necessity, such as if one did not put on tefillin and they became available between the blessing of redemption and the Amidah prayer – then one should put them on but should not recite the blessing over them until after the Amidah prayer. However, one should not put on a tallit at that time. If the tallit and tefillin became available before saying "Ga'al Yisrael," one should put them on but should not recite the blessing over them until after the Amidah prayer. Thus far are his words. And Rabbeinu Rema wrote about this: And some say that before "Ga'al Yisrael," one should recite the blessing over the tefillin, and this is the prevailing custom. Thus far are his words. But his words are puzzling: for in section 2, regarding "between the sections," he brought the opinion that one should not recite the blessing over the tefillin. And here, in the middle of the section before "Ga'al Yisrael," he brought the opinion that one should recite the blessing. And the Levush indeed omitted this gloss. However, the custom he wrote is acceptable to me, for there he wrote the custom that one should not recite the blessing over the tallit, but one should recite the blessing over the tefillin, and here it concerns tefillin. It seems that he holds that any absolute obligation that arises during the act, like the "Amen" of "Ga'al Yisrael," and the blessing of tefillin that comes at its time – one is permitted to interrupt. However, in any case, our custom is not so, and we do not recite the blessing over the tefillin, nor the "Amen" of "Ga'al Yisrael."

And how could it happen that one would pray without tefillin? For example, if an unavoidable circumstance occurs and the time for reciting the Shema will pass, one is compelled to recite it without tefillin. And if he sees that the time for prayer will pass, he should pray also without tefillin (Magen Avraham, subsection 12). And if one does not have tefillin at the time the community prays, it is better to pray alone when he has tefillin, for praying with tefillin is preferable to praying with the community (ibid.), provided that the time does not pass. However, for a tallit, one should not wait at all, and he should pray with the community without a tallit. And it has already been explained in Siman 62 that anyone who did not say "Emet Veyatziv" in the morning and "Emet Ve'emuna" in the evening has not fulfilled the obligation of the blessings. And the recitation of the Shema is also not in the optimal manner as instituted by the Sages, see there. The Tur wrote in the name of the Yerushalmi: It is necessary to mention in "Emet Veyatziv" the Exodus from Egypt, the kingship, the splitting of the Red Sea, and the plague of the firstborn. And it appears that this is essential, and so it seems from the Rashba (section 11, see there). And also in the evening, all this is mentioned. And there is room to consider whether all these are essential after the fact.

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote in section 10: If someone is compelled and pressured, and does not have the time to pray immediately after reciting the Shema, he should recite the Shema until "Emet" (True) and wait to say the rest of the blessing until he prays, at which point he will say "Veyatziv Venachon..." and then pray, in order to juxtapose the redemption to the prayer. This is his wording. The explanation of his words: For instance, if someone began to pray intending to complete the entire prayer, but when he reached the Shema, an unavoidable circumstance occurred that forced him to stop, he should stop at "Veyatziv" and not afterward. However, if he knows in advance that he will not be able to complete the entire prayer, and fears that the time for reciting the Shema will pass, he should recite the Shema without the blessings, and afterward, recite the Shema with the blessings and then pray. (And with this, the difficulty raised by the Magen Avraham in section 15 is resolved, as the Pri Megadim also wrote.)

The Rambam in the second chapter, as well as the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch, wrote: If one is uncertain whether he has recited the Shema, he should recite it again, with the blessings before and after it. However, if he knows he has recited it but is unsure whether he recited the blessings before and after it, he does not repeat the blessings. Thus are their words. The explanation is as follows: The recitation of the Shema is of Torah origin, and therefore, in a case of doubt, he recites it again, in accordance with the principle that a doubt concerning a Torah commandment is treated stringently. Therefore, even according to those who hold that from the Torah obligation only the first verse or the first section is required, as I wrote at the beginning of Siman 58, and certainly regarding the blessings which are entirely rabbinic, nevertheless, since he is obligated in the primary obligation, he is obligated in all, as that was the enactment (Rashba in Teshuvot Siman 320). Additionally, whenever there is a Torah obligation in doubt, one must recite a blessing, like the second day of Yom Tov in the Diaspora. And even though in several cases of doubt concerning Torah obligations we do not recite a blessing, such as in the case of a doubt regarding circumcision on an androgynous or the sounding of the shofar, and similar cases, this is because there the doubt is in the primary obligation itself. But here, the obligation is clear, only there is a doubt whether it has already been fulfilled, and therefore, in doubt, he recites the Shema again with its blessings. However, when the doubt is only concerning the blessings, he does not recite the blessings, as the principle of doubt concerning rabbinic obligations is lenient, and there is also a slight concern of a blessing in vain. But when the doubt also concerns the recitation of the Shema, there is no concern of a blessing in vain, as this is the law as I have written.

It is obvious that this refers to a case where there is doubt about everything: about the recitation of the Shema and about the blessings. But if the doubt is only about the recitation of the Shema, and the blessings were certainly recited – it is clear that he should say the Shema and not the blessings, because the blessings are not intrinsically connected to the Shema, as I wrote in Siman 59. However, one could argue that if it is certain to him that he said "Emet Veyatziv" – he should also not go back and recite the Shema, because it is certain that he also recited the Shema, as he follows his usual pattern. As I wrote in Siman 64, when he begins with "Lema'an Yirbu," we say that he certainly said "Vehaya Im Shamoa" because he follows his pattern, see there. The same applies here. And if it is clear to him that he said the blessings before the Shema, and the doubt is about the Shema and the blessings after it – he recites the Shema and the blessings after it.

And behold, from what has been explained, any Torah doubt for which one is obligated due to the doubt, one is also obligated to recite a blessing. According to this, if one is uncertain about taking the lulav during Sukkot or sounding the shofar on Rosh Hashanah, and he takes the lulav again or sounds the shofar again, he must recite the blessing. However, it is established that he does not recite the blessing (Magen Avraham, Siman 588, subsection 3, in the name of the Rivash). The same law applies to any doubtful Torah commandment: due to the doubt, one must perform it, but does not recite a blessing. One cannot learn from the case of the second day of Yom Tov in the Diaspora, which is a constant obligation, and thus the Sages instituted it, and not from a doubtful case, which is not a constant obligation. We have already brought this reasoning in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 28, subsection 11, in the name of the Rosh at the beginning of the chapter on the covering of the blood, see there. And I have seen that the greats have also wondered about this reasoning (the Gra and the Pri Megadim). Rather, certainly, one cannot derive from this rule for all matters.

In truth, in the responsa of the Rashba there, he wrote only that this was the enactment regarding the recitation of Shema. He further wrote that even if it is certain to him that he recited the first verse, he fulfills the biblical obligation of the recitation of Shema according to his opinion; nevertheless, he repeats it with its blessings because this was the enactment, see there. However, we do not know from where this enactment originated, as it is not clarified in the Gemara. This requires investigation. (And perhaps it is derived from "one who reads from here onward").

We have already written in Siman 58 that there is a dispute regarding the Torah obligation of reading the Shema: some say it is one verse, some say it is the first paragraph, and some say it is two paragraphs. In our opinion, according to the Rambam, all of them are from the Torah, see there. And I saw one of the greats who wrote that both are true: that from the Torah one is obligated to read all three paragraphs, but conversely, one fulfills the Torah obligation with the first verse, similar to the obligation of Torah study which is required by the Torah, and if one studies a little during the day and a little during the night, one fulfills "and you shall meditate on it day and night." And if one studies all day and all night, one also fulfills "and you shall meditate on it day and night" (Lechem Mishneh, Chapter 2, Halacha 13, in the name of Kiryat Sefer, see there). And it is a great reasoning, that just as in Torah study, the more one studies, the more reward one receives, so too in the reading of the Shema: all are from the Torah, yet one fulfills the obligation with any one of them (and this resolves Rashi at the beginning of Berakhot).

It is clear that everything that has been explained regarding the doubt whether one has recited the Shema, that they should recite it again with its blessings – this is only while it is still the time for the recitation of the Shema. But if the time for the recitation of the Shema has already passed – they do not recite it with its blessings. For what was said, "One who recites [the Shema] from this point onward has not lost [the opportunity to recite the blessings]," is only when it is certain that they did not recite it, and not in a case of doubt. And this is clear.

Remembering the exodus from Egypt every day, as well as every night, is a Torah commandment, as explained in the Talmud (Berakhot 21a). It is clear that one must mention it verbally and does not fulfill the obligation by merely thinking about it, for it is established that thinking is not equivalent to speaking. Furthermore, in every instance where "remember" is mentioned in the Torah, the implication is verbal, and the same applies here. The reason why the enumerators of the commandments did not count the remembrance of the exodus from Egypt among the general commandments, it seems to me, is because the Torah states: "so that you will remember the day of your departure…" and does not use the imperative "remember the day…". Rather, the remembrance is due to the preceding matters mentioned in that verse, and therefore, although it is a Torah obligation, it is not included in the count of the commandments. It appears to me that this is the difference between the night of Passover and all other nights. Seemingly, since there is also an obligation to remember the exodus from Egypt at night, what difference is there? However, according to what I have written, the difference is that on that night, it is an intrinsic obligation and a complete positive commandment, and it is counted among the commandments. There are also other differences, explained elsewhere. (The obligation of the daytime remembrance of the exodus extends throughout the entire day. If one remembers during twilight, it is still valid. The obligation of the nighttime remembrance lasts until dawn. See Sha'agat Aryeh, who elaborates on this.)

Regarding the piyutim (liturgical poems) that have become customary to recite in the blessings of "Yotzer Or" and in the blessings following the Shema, although some of the great authorities were not pleased with this practice, nonetheless, many of the great sages of the world and exceedingly holy individuals have ruled to permit it. There was already a dispute on this matter between Rabbeinu Yosef Tov Elem and Rabbeinu Eliyahu, and they concluded that it is permitted (Hagahot Ashri at the end of the first chapter). This is not included in what we have learned (Berachot 11a): "In a place where they said to lengthen [the blessing] – one is not permitted to shorten [it]; to shorten – one is not permitted to lengthen [it]." This refers to short blessings without a concluding blessing and long blessings with a concluding blessing, as it continues there: "In a place where they said to conclude..." see there. On the contrary, it is taught there: "One [blessing] long and one short." Rabbeinu Tam explained that the meaning is: whether long or short, meaning if one wishes to lengthen in the middle, he may lengthen, and if he wishes to shorten in the middle, he may shorten. The only condition is not to change a blessing with a conclusion to one without a conclusion, or vice versa. This is also explained in the Tosefta in the first chapter of Berachot, and this is the wording of the Tosefta: "And why did they say 'one long and one short'? In a place where they said to lengthen..., to conclude...," thus far is its language.

And this is what our sages of blessed memory said (Berakhot 34a) that one should not ask for their needs in the first three blessings nor in the last three blessings [of the Amidah prayer].
