It has already been written there by our rabbis, the authors of the Tosafot, in the name of Rav Hai Gaon and Rabbeinu Chananel that this applies to an individual but not to the community. Therefore, during the Ten Days of Repentance, we say "Remember us for life," "Who is like You," "Write," and "In the book of life." Their authors were the geniuses of the world and supreme holy ones, like Rabbi Eliezer HaKalir and Rabbeinu Shimon the Great, and the Holy Spirit rested upon them. The early authorities wrote that when Rabbi Eliezer HaKalir composed [his piyut] "and life…" – a fire blazed around him. And who would not see that holiness rests upon all their words, and awe and the outpouring of the soul? Let the spirit of those fools who say that their language is stammering expire. Do we not see the prayers of HaKalir on Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, and for dew and rain – they are easy and simple to understand, and holiness and purity hover over them. And those who composed several piyutim in sharp and hidden languages did so intentionally, in my opinion, because they revealed in them awesome secrets. Therefore, they concealed their holy words in their sacred manner.

The Arizal, of blessed memory, did not recite liturgical poems and hymns except those composed by the early ones, such as the Kalir, which were instituted with the true intention. The customs practiced in the prayer versions should not be changed from the local custom, for there are twelve gates in the heavens corresponding to the twelve tribes, and each tribe has its gate and custom, aside from what is mentioned in the Talmud as common to all (Magen Avraham). And this is the language of the Jerusalem Talmud in the third chapter of Eruvin: Even though we have sent you the order of the prayer, do not change from the customs of your ancestors (there). And truly, in the fundamental matters, all the versions are equal, in the number of blessings, their openings, and their conclusions. And even in the middle parts of the blessings, there is no difference except in words that do not make a difference either way, like in the blessing "You graciously endow" where in Ashkenaz they say "knowledge, understanding, and wisdom" and in Sepharad they say "wisdom, understanding, and knowledge," and similarly in all the blessings in such manner. What does it matter? For we all have one Torah, one judgment, and one prayer, and who is like Your people Israel, one nation on earth. Heaven forbid to cause division or to say, God forbid, that there is any division among Israel. And one who says so is a fool and ignorant.

And these are the words of our master, the Rema, regarding what our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote: There are places where they interrupt the blessings of the Shema to say piyyutim (liturgical poems). It is proper to refrain from saying them. And he wrote on this: And some say that there is no prohibition in this matter, and so it is customary in all places to say them. And one who is lenient and does not say them does not lose out. Nevertheless, one should not engage in any other activity, and even discussing words of Torah is forbidden as an interruption, as long as the congregation is saying piyyutim. All the more so, it is forbidden to engage in idle chatter. However, one who learns by contemplating, by looking in a book and reflecting – this is not considered an interruption, for contemplation is not like speech. But from this, one might come to speak and thus to an interruption. Therefore, a person should not separate himself from the congregation in a place where it is customary to say them, and he should say them with them. So far his words. And there are those who customarily do not say those that are before the Amidah, but the piyyut in the repetition of the Shaliach Tzibbur (prayer leader) they do say. And it is proper to do so, and to be careful not to nullify any piyyut from the congregation, for heaven forbid, one could be punished. And the Bach wrote that one of the greats in his days began to abolish saying Kerovetz, and he did not live out the year, see there. And Kerovetz is an acronym for "Kol Rina V'Yeshuah B'Ohalei Tzadikim" (A voice of rejoicing and salvation in the tents of the righteous). (The Magen Avraham in subsection 1 brought from our master Moshe Peretz that it is proper to say piyyutim before the blessing of "Yotzer Or" and then to bless, see there. And it seems to me that this is proper. And what the Magen Avraham wrote from section 54 needs examination, as how can this be considered an interruption? See there. Be precise and you will find light.)

It is taught in the Megillah (23b): "One does not recite 'Barchu' and one does not pass before the ark with less than ten." According to Rashi's explanation as clarified by the Ran, the meaning is as follows: If there were ten individuals who each prayed by themselves, privately, and did not hear Kaddish or Kedusha, one of them stands up and says Kaddish and "Barchu," and the first blessing of "Yotzer." The term "Poresin" (recite half) is like "a piece," meaning half of the blessings. And if you ask: Why do they need this blessing, since they already said it individually? One could say: Either because of the sanctity of "Yotzer," if we say it is not recited alone as some hold, as I wrote in Siman 59, or because once the prayer leader says "Barchu" to them, they are compelled to bless some blessing. Otherwise, they would appear as deniers, Heaven forbid, since he tells them to bless and they do not bless. Therefore, they bless "Yotzer Or" (Beit Yosef). And it is not understood: They responded "Blessed be He who is blessed forever and ever," so how does it relate to being deniers? For it is the same in the reading of the Torah (Rema in Darkei Moshe).

And this is what our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in Section 1: If there are people who have prayed... individually... – one of them stands and says Kaddish, and "Barchu," and the first blessing... until here is his language. And our master, the Rema, wrote about it: And now the custom is not to say the entire blessing of "Yotzer Or." Rather, they say Kaddish and "Barchu," and they answer after him "Baruch...". Until here is his language, and this is for the reason we explained. And know that before Kaddish one needs to say some Psalm, for it has already been explained in Siman 56 that Kaddish is not said unless something has been said beforehand.

The Mishnah's statement: "and one does not pass before the ark" refers to this matter as well. Those who prayed individually and say Kaddish, and "Barchu," and "Yotzer," one of them stands and says the blessings of Avot (Patriarchs), Gevurot (Powers), Kedusha (Sanctification), and "You are Holy." Why do they do this? In order to say Kedusha, which they have not yet heard because they prayed individually. This is what our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote: After completing the blessing of "Yotzer Or," one says the blessings of Avot, Gevurot, Kedusha, and "You are Holy," and this is called "passing before the ark." This is his exact wording. The one who performs Kedusha completes the entire eighteen blessings, as our teacher the Rema wrote there, and this is his wording: One who passes before the ark and says the first three blessings should complete the entire prayer and not stop, even though he has already prayed. But others can stop afterward. And certainly, if the one who leads has not prayed yet. The one who passes before the ark initially should complete it, even though he will then need to recite the Shema, and he will not link redemption directly to prayer. This is his exact wording. That is to say: Even if he has not yet prayed, he should lead the Shema and then pray the eighteen blessings, and afterward, he should say "Ahava Rabba" and the Shema, and "Ezrat" until "Ga'al Yisrael." This is puzzling: Why should he do this? He should pray in order, and they should wait until he reaches the eighteen blessings, pray aloud, and say Kedusha (and so wrote the Magen Avraham, Section 6).

And one should not ask, according to this explanation, why the Mishnah divided it into two sections: "One does not recite the Shema" and "One does not go down before the ark"? For it is one matter: that he goes down before the ark, recites the Shema, and says the first three blessings with the Kedushah. However, in truth, the Jerusalem Talmud asked this and answered that it teaches us that they are two separate matters in regard to if they started with ten and some left, that they complete this matter, as this law is explained in Siman 55. Therefore, it divided it into two to teach us that if they started with ten in the recitation of the Shema, and some left—they complete the recitation even without ten. But they do not say the Kedushah, as it is another matter.

And behold, although this interpretation is brought by the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch as halacha, it has never been practiced this way. Some of the great authorities have objected to this, arguing that once one has already prayed individually, the obligation for Kaddish and Kedusha has lapsed, just as the obligation for Zimun in Birkat Hamazon lapses when each person recites Birkat Hamazon individually (Radbaz, First Volume, Siman 241). However, I do not see any comparison between the two: there, Zimun does not exist without Birkat Hamazon, and therefore without Birkat Hamazon, there is no Zimun. But Kaddish and "Barechu" exist even without prayer, as in the blessings of the Torah. And also Kedusha, if one hears multiple Kedushot, one is obligated to respond. If so, why shouldn't they do this? In truth, even now, it is done in part, meaning that in some places, before the repetition of the Shaliach Tzibbur, someone stands and recites Kaddish and "Barechu." This is for those who come after "Barechu" (as the Taz writes in Section 1). On Mondays and Thursdays, there is no need to do this since they will hear "Barechu" during the Torah reading, and they will also hear many Kaddish recitations. But to perform Kedusha when everyone has already prayed is not the custom in our times. And I say the reason: not because the obligation has already lapsed, but because the Rambam and the Geonim interpret this Mishnah completely differently, as will be explained. According to their interpretation, this ruling was never mentioned in the Mishnah at all, and therefore it is not practiced (so it appears in my humble opinion).

The Ran wrote that the Geonim explained this Mishnah in a completely different manner, and "porasin" is not a term for "piece" but rather a term for "beginning." And this is its explanation: One does not begin with the blessings of Shema, where one person would bless and others would fulfill their obligation through his blessing, except with ten [people]. This is not the case with other blessings, such as Kiddush and Havdalah and similar ones, where an individual says it and another individual hears it and fulfills his obligation, for hearing is like responding. But here, specifically ten are required, whether for the Shema and its blessings or for prayer. The Ran questioned them, for at the end of Rosh Hashanah it is said that one does not fulfill the obligation of another except for someone who is not proficient. But for someone who is proficient, even with ten, one does not fulfill the obligation [for another], see there. However, this is not a difficulty, for the Geonim hold, as our teacher the Rema wrote at the end of Siman 59, that this applies only to prayer and not to the Shema and its blessings. And we have already explained this there.

And it appears clearly that also Maimonides in the eighth chapter of Prayer, law 4 and law 5 follows the method of the Geonim. And this is his language: "And how is the prayer of the congregation conducted? One person prays aloud and everyone listens. And this is not done with less than ten adults and freemen, and the prayer leader is one of them. And even if some of them have already prayed and fulfilled their obligation, they complete the count to ten, provided that the majority have not prayed... Similarly, one does not recite the blessing of Shema, with everyone listening and answering 'Amen', except with ten. And this is called 'Porais al Shema'." Thus far is his language, which is clearly in accordance with the interpretation of the Geonim. (And the Raavad there in his critique follows the method of Rashi, see there.)

Behold, this that is written that we require a majority who have not prayed, there are differing opinions on this. As the Tur wrote, Rabbeinu Tam holds that seven who have not heard are necessary, and the students of Rashi wrote in his name that even for one who has not heard—it is permitted, see there. And this is the opinion of Rabbeinu Beit Yosef, who wrote: One must seek out six who have not heard, which means the majority of the ten. And if they are not found, even for one who has not heard, they say it. And even one who has heard can recite the Shema and lead the prayers for the one who has not heard. Nevertheless, if the one who has not heard is proficient in reciting the Shema and leading the prayers, it is preferable that he recite and lead the prayers himself rather than having someone who has already heard do so. Thus far his words.

And behold, our current custom is that if someone comes to the synagogue after the prayer, when they reach "Yotzer Or," if they wish, they may say Kaddish and "Barchu," and everyone responds "Baruch…" and no more. Afterwards, when they reach the Amidah, they say the Avot and Gevurot blessings out loud, and say Kedusha, and everyone responds after them "Kadosh" and "Baruch" and "Yimloch." Then they say "Atah Kadosh" and everyone responds "Amen," and then they continue praying the rest of the prayer silently. This custom is appropriate according to all opinions, for even those who require a majority of those who did not hear specifically, this is when they also say the "Yotzer Or" blessing. And in the Amidah, they complete the Amidah even if they have already prayed, as I have written. But Kaddish and "Barchu" alone, as well as the Kedusha – it is permitted for this person who is now praying according to all opinions. And it appears to me that this person who says Kedusha as I have written – should not say "L’dor Va’dor Nagid Godlecha" according to the Ashkenazic custom, as this is only established for the prayer leader and not for an individual. Rather, they should say "Atah Kadosh" (so it seems clear to me).

It is a straightforward matter that someone who was in the synagogue during the recitation of "Barchu" and "Kedusha," even if they have not yet prayed or are still in the middle of the Pesukei Dezimra, nevertheless, we do not recite the "Barchu" for them. There are places that have the custom that when they reach "Barchu," they recite the "Barchu" for them, or the individual themselves says "Kaddish" and "Barchu" when they reach "Yotzer Or." This is not a proper custom, and we have never heard of such a custom in our times. (This is the extended discussion of the Magen Avraham in the name of the Rama, and what he wrote in the name of the Beit Yosef and the Darkei Moshe has already been clarified. See there and examine it closely.)

Rabbeinu the Rema wrote: Some say that one may recite "Barchu" during the recitation of the Shema in the evening just as in the morning. However, the custom is not to do so, because there is no Kaddish in the evening as there is in the morning. Thus far his words. Meaning: in the evening, there is only "Barchu." And they did not deem "Barchu" alone sufficient to warrant reciting the Shema in this manner. However, it seems to me that this pertains to the recitation that includes the first blessing as well. But to merely recite "Barchu" alone, one can also do so in the evening. Why should the evening be inferior to the morning? And this is indeed the common custom: if someone has not yet prayed the evening service, and there are ten who have already prayed, he stands and says "Barchu," and everyone responds "Baruch…". According to the Sephardic custom, where they also say Kaddish before "Barchu" in the evening and recite verses beforehand, they should not say Kaddish unless there are ten people reciting the verses with him. We have explained this above in Siman 55, Section 9; see there. (And the Magen Avraham in sub-section 4 requires ten during the study. And there we explained that ten must specifically be studying. This is not analogous to reciting "Barchu" during the Shema in the morning where Kaddish is recited, because there it was an ordinance of the sages. Examine and you will find it light.)

It is also written that it is forbidden to interrupt with these matters between the redemption (blessing) and the prayer, or during the recitation of the Shema and its blessings. Therefore, it is forbidden for the prayer leader to interrupt between the recitation of the Shema and the prayer, or during the recitation of the Shema and its blessings, in order to recite the Shema for those who come to the synagogue after the congregation has prayed the Kaddish and "Barchu" and has begun the blessing of "Yotzer Or." However, in the evening blessing, which is optional, one may interrupt to fulfill the obligation for others. Until here is his language. And this is all according to their custom of reciting the Shema. But according to our custom, this is not relevant at all, as is evident.

Moreover, it is written: Nevertheless, another person can recite the Shema or pray with a quorum (minyan) the entire prayer, even in the same synagogue where they have already prayed, to fulfill the obligation for others. However, the second cantor should not stand in the place where the first one stood, as this seems demeaning to the first group, as if the first ones did not fulfill their obligation. It seems to me that this applies specifically when the first group is still in the synagogue but has completed their service. But if the first group has left, the cantor may stand even in the place where the first one stood. This is the end of his words.

The explanation of the matter is that because some wanted to say in the explanation of the Mishnah "One does not recite the Shema" that this means: when ten people come who have not yet prayed, they only recite the Shema and not the entire prayer. And also, from the language of Rashi, it seems to imply this. See there. Therefore, it is said that if there is a quorum, why should they not pray the entire prayer like the first group, and only that the cantor should not stand in the place of the first? In our country, we do not adhere to this, and even if several groups pray one after the other, the cantor of each group stands in the same place before the lectern. And among us, there is no concern that people will say the first group did not fulfill their obligation, because it is known that many groups pray, some earlier and some later. And since this is the custom, there is no dishonor or concern, and there is no need to question this at all.

And know that there is an opinion which states that if the first group took out the Torah scroll and read from it, the second group should not take out the Torah scroll again and read from it. So writes the Magen Avraham in the name of Mishpetei Shmuel. And there is no understanding of this. There are those who explain that the intention is perhaps people will say that the first Torah scroll was defective (Pri Megadim). But these are astonishing matters to create new decrees. And perhaps the word "again" is a mistake, and it should be said "another Torah scroll" in order not to cast aspersion on the first one. It seems to me, in my humble opinion, that the explanation is as follows: Behold, the "Barchu" and Kedusha are said even for six who did not hear, and even for a single individual as has been explained. But concerning the reading of the Torah, it seems clear to me that if there are not ten who did not hear the Torah reading, there is no need to read the Torah. And specifically concerning matters of prayer, which every individual is obligated in, therefore "Barchu" and Kedusha are done on their behalf, as these are matters of prayer. But the primary obligation of the Torah reading is only with ten. According to this, the explanation is as follows: If the first group took out the Torah scroll and read from it, meaning the second group was present at the time but had not yet prayed. Therefore, the second group should not take out the Torah scroll again when they pray, since they heard the Torah reading, and its obligation is not specifically after the prayer. And so it seems to me to rule in practice, even if there are some who did not hear, until there are ten who did not hear.

A blind person, even though he has never seen the lights in his life, may recite the Shema and bless "the Creator of the lights," because even though he does not see, nevertheless he benefits from the lights that others see, and they show him the way he should go. However, a minor should not recite the Shema (Pri Chadash).

Women and slaves are exempt from the recitation of the Shema, because it is a positive time-bound commandment. For the recitation of the Shema during the day is only until three hours; and although the nighttime recitation is valid for the entire night, nevertheless, the nighttime recitation is not valid during the day, and thus it is time-bound. Similarly, they are exempt from the blessings of the Shema, as these are also time-bound. Even though they are obligated in prayer as I have written in Siman 106, prayer is different because it is a plea for mercy. Likewise, women are exempt from the blessing of the moon (Kiddush Levana) (Magen Avraham, Section 1). Nevertheless, if they wish, they may bless and recite the Shema, just as they are exempt from Sukkah and Lulav but may bless over them. Our women do so, and they are blessed for it. They are obligated by law in the morning blessings, as they fall under the category for which all the morning blessings were instituted. "Baruch She'amar" and "Yishtabach" are not obligatory for them, but they may recite them. And why shouldn't they be able to sing to God, as Miriam and all the women of Israel did at the splitting of the Red Sea?

Indeed, it is certain that regarding the unification of God's name and love for Him, women are obligated just as men are. In truth, our teacher, the Beit Yosef, in his great book, cited the Sefer Ohel Moed, which states that women are obligated in the first verse of the Shema's unification of God's name. See there. Therefore, according to the authorities who hold that the obligation of reciting the Shema is only the first verse, what then is the reason that they are exempt from reciting the Shema? Furthermore, our teachers, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, wrote that it is proper to teach them to accept upon themselves the yoke of the Kingdom of Heaven and to at least recite the first verse. This is their language. The difficulty is: what does "proper" mean, isn't it an obligation? However, this is not a difficulty, as although they are obligated in this, nevertheless, they are not commanded to recite these verses. Rather, they are commanded to love and to sacrifice their lives for the sanctification of His blessed name. Additionally, even if they need to recite these verses, is the obligation at the time of the recitation of the Shema? But the truth is that they are not obligated to recite these verses, and therefore it is correct that our teachers, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, said "it is proper to teach them." But there is no obligation.

And minors are also exempt according to Rabbeinu Tam, specifically if they have not yet reached the age of education. According to Rashi, even if they have reached the age of education, because they are not commonly available at the time of the evening Shema and are asleep in the morning. Therefore, the sages did not impose upon the father to educate them as with other commandments. However, it is proper to follow the opinion of Rabbeinu Tam. Therefore, we guide the minors to pray every day.

There are those who say that women are obligated in the remembrance of the exodus from Egypt, and therefore they are required to say "Emet Veyatziv" and to connect redemption to prayer (Magen Avraham, Section 1). For the obligation to mention the exodus from Egypt exists throughout the whole day and the entire night, and if so, it is not a "time-bound positive commandment" and women are obligated. However, there are those who disagree, arguing that there are two separate obligations: one by day and one by night. And the daytime obligation does not apply at night, for if one forgets to mention it by day, mentioning it at night does not fulfill the daytime obligation, and similarly, the nighttime obligation does not apply by day. Therefore, it still remains a time-bound positive commandment, and women are exempt (Sha'agat Aryeh, Section 13). And necessarily, one must say so, for according to the Rabbis who follow Ben Zoma at the end of the first chapter of Berakhot, there is no obligation to mention the exodus from Egypt at night, and according to them, women are certainly exempt. And if one were to think that according to Ben Zoma women are obligated, the Talmud should have mentioned this distinction. In truth, the obligation of mentioning the exodus from Egypt is not counted among the positive commandments, as I wrote at the end of Section 67, see there. And this obligation was not imposed on women, for the remembrance of the exodus from Egypt is included in the section of tzitzit, and women are exempt from tzitzit. Therefore, when the Mishnah, Gemara, and Poskim said that women are exempt from the recitation of Shema, and the exodus from Egypt is included in the Shema, if one were to think that in this they are obligated, it should have been specified. And since their words were general, we learn from this that women are exempt.

A groom who marries a virgin is exempt from reciting the Shema on the first night, because his mind is preoccupied with the concern that he may not find her to be a virgin. This is considered an obligation-related preoccupation, and he is therefore exempt. However, one who marries a widow is obligated, because there is no preoccupation concerning virginity. A non-obligatory preoccupation, such as if his ship sank at sea, does not exempt him, as he should calm his mind. A groom who has not consummated the marriage on the first night is exempt for up to three nights, but after that, his mind becomes familiar with her, and he is required to recite the Shema. Some say he is exempt for four nights (Tur), such as if he married before reciting the morning Shema, as the exemption lasts for three days excluding the day of the wedding (Magen Avraham, subsection 2). It is also possible that even if he did not marry before the preparation for the wedding, it is considered a mitzvah and exempts him from another mitzvah (Beit Yosef and Taz, subsection 1). If he wishes to be stringent with himself and recite it, the Rosh ruled in the second chapter that he is not allowed, as it appears arrogant. However, the Rif and the Rambam ruled that he is allowed. There is also a disagreement about whether he is exempt from the morning Shema or only the evening Shema (see Tosafot Yom Tov, second chapter). However, all this was in their days when they had a lot of intention. Nowadays, when even other people do not have so much intention, the groom is also required to recite the Shema. He is forbidden to be stringent and not recite it, as it appears arrogant, as if he always has a lot of intention and now cannot have so much intention. This is the simple custom and should not be changed.

The Rambam wrote in the second chapter, law 5: If one is engaged in the study of Torah and the time for the recitation of the Shema arrives, one should stop and recite it, including the blessings before and after it. If one is engaged in public needs, one should not stop but rather complete the task and read the Shema if there is still time remaining to recite it. The reasoning is that we hold the principle that one who is engaged in a mitzvah is exempt from another mitzvah, and there is no greater mitzvah than being engaged in public needs. And even though Torah study is greater than all the mitzvot, and why should one interrupt it, this is because, otherwise, one would never perform any mitzvah. The Torah was given to be studied and to be performed. Additionally, when one recites the Shema, is that not also considered Torah study (see Jerusalem Talmud, Shabbat, chapter 1, halacha 2)? However, for other mitzvot, this does not apply. Even if there is still time to perform the mitzvah afterward, since one is engaged in it, one must complete it, even if the time for the Shema will pass. Similarly, a teacher who is teaching Torah to students and the time for the Shema arrives should not interrupt, because the Torah study of the many is a mitzvah in its own right. We also find with Rabbeinu HaKadosh (Rabbi Judah the Prince) that he did not interrupt but merely passed his hands over his eyes and recited the verse "Shema Yisrael," as explained in Berachot (13b), see there.

However, the poskim have written regarding the exemption of those engaged in communal needs, that this applies to the earlier generations who were involved in communal needs entirely for the sake of Heaven, and not in our times. Nevertheless, it is not an absolute rule. For even nowadays, if one is engaged with them, even for the sake of saving their property, and there is no one else to take care of it except him – he is exempt from reciting the Shema, even if the time passes (Kesef Mishneh and Magen Avraham, subsection 4). Therefore, our master the Beit Yosef did not bring this in the Shulchan Aruch, subsection 4, as nowadays one is obligated, because even nowadays sometimes one is exempt. It must be understood according to the context.

The Rambam further wrote: If one was engaged in eating, or was in a bathhouse, or getting a haircut, or handling hides, or engaged in judgment – he should complete [what he is doing] and then recite the Shema. However, if he was concerned that the time for reciting the Shema might pass, and he stopped and recited it – this is praiseworthy. Thus are his words. The Raavad disagrees with him, and these are his words: Not so, rather, one interrupts and recites it even if there is still time to recite, because it is a Torah obligation. And if there isn’t enough time, he interrupts even for a rabbinic prayer. Thus are his words. The commentators have elaborated on the reason for their disagreement. However, it appears more that they do not disagree at all. The Rambam is referring to a case where one began permissibly before the time for reciting the Shema arrived, and therefore he does not need to interrupt unless the time for reciting the Shema would pass. The Raavad is referring to a case where one began impermissibly, and therefore he is obligated to interrupt (Bach). You should know that this is the case, as the Rambam wrote: If one was engaged in eating… And if you would think that he began after the time for reciting the Shema arrived, how did he begin to eat? For it is wicked to eat before prayer. Rather, certainly he began eating at night and continued into the day, such as at weddings and the like. And it seems to me that this is the intention of the Tur later in Siman 89, who wrote: And if he began to eat before dawn broke, the Rambam wrote that he does not need to interrupt, see there. And the commentators wrote that an erroneous version came to the Tur in the words of the Rambam, for this is not found in the Rambam but in Mincha (see there in Beit Yosef and in Bach). And it seems that his intention is on these words. And the Raavad thought that the Rambam referred to a case where one began impermissibly, and therefore he disagreed with him. But in truth, they do not disagree, and this is the main ruling (as the Magen Avraham wrote at the end of subsection 6). And see what I wrote above in Siman 38, subsection 10.

Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote: Someone who has a deceased relative, for whom he is obligated to mourn, even if he is not responsible for burying him, is exempt from reciting the Shema and from prayer. And even if he wants to be stringent upon himself and recite, he is not permitted. However, if there is someone else who will take care of the burial needs for him, and he wants to be stringent upon himself and recite, we do not prevent him. This is his language. And Rabbeinu the Rema wrote: Refer to Yoreh De'ah, section 341. This is his language. Meaning: there it is explained that we do prevent him, and it is forbidden to be stringent. And so have determined the great later authorities (Taz, small section 3, Levush, Bach, and see Taz). And we have already explained this in Yoreh De'ah there, section 10, and we brought it from the Jerusalem Talmud. And so is the practical halachic ruling. And in Yoreh De'ah there, many laws regarding a mourner (onen) are explained, see there.

And immediately when they begin to throw earth on the deceased, one should recite the Shema and pray. This is also the practice of the Maharil (Magen Avraham, subsection 1). This applies until midday, but after midday, one should not pray. Regarding the morning blessings, one is always exempt, since at the time of their obligation, one was exempt (ibid.). However, one is obligated in the blessing of the Torah. On the first day, one should not put on tefillin, as a mourner is forbidden to wear tefillin on the first day, as I have written in Siman 38. The three blessings "Who has not made me a non-Jew," "Who has not made me a slave," and "Who has not made me a woman" should also be recited throughout the day. One should not recite Kaddish until after the burial. There are those who say that a son for his father should recite Kaddish during his period of aninut (deep mourning) before the burial (Taz, end of subsection 2). There are those who disagree, arguing that before the burial, one should not recite Kaddish for him (Nekudot HaKesef on Yoreh De'ah, Siman 376). See what I have written in Siman 106, subsection 3.

In what case are these words stated? On a weekday. But on Shabbat, one is obligated the entire day until evening if he is engaged in the needs of burial. However, if he is not engaged in the needs of burial after Shabbat - he is also obligated in the evening. This is the language of our teacher, the Beit Yosef, in section 2. And it seems clear that this is its meaning: if he is engaged in the needs of burial - he is exempt from all commandments, even though it is still day and he is in a state of mourning. But if he is not engaged - he is obligated in all commandments until night. And this is not referring to the evening prayer of Motza'ei Shabbat, for he is always exempt even if he is not engaged in the needs of burial. This is also explained in his major work, and it is implied in the Drisha. And I am very puzzled by the commentators who wanted to explain the matter also regarding the evening prayer, that if he is not engaged, he needs to pray the evening prayer. And they struggled with this (see Bach, Magen Avraham section 3, and Taz section 4). And they interpret similarly in the words of the Tur. And I am puzzled and this requires further study. And the second day of Yom Tov has the same law as a weekday. And on the first day of Yom Tov, if he wants to bury through a non-Jew - he observes mourning, and if not - he does not observe mourning. And in Yoreh De'ah there, we elaborated on this.

One who guards a deceased person, even if it is not his own deceased relative, is exempt. If there are two people guarding, one guards while the other recites (Shema), and then they switch, with the other guarding and the first one reciting. Similarly, one who digs a grave for the deceased is exempt. If there are two or more people digging, all those who are necessary for the digging at the same time are exempt. If there are additional people who are not essential for the digging, they withdraw and recite (Shema), and then those who were reciting return to the task while the others withdraw and recite. More details on this are explained in Yoreh De'ah, section 365. 

It is prohibited to recite the Shema within four cubits of a deceased person or in a cemetery. If one recites it, he has not fulfilled his obligation, since the Sages penalized him for transgressing their words, even if it was done inadvertently (Kesef Mishneh and Magen Avraham, subsection 5). This specifically applies within four cubits of a grave. However, outside of four cubits in a cemetery, although it is initially prohibited, if one recites it there, he does not need to repeat it (Taz, subsection 5). Refer to what I wrote in Yoreh De'ah, section 341, at the end of subsection 24.

The pallbearers, their replacements, and the replacements of their replacements, whether they are before the bier or after the bier, those who are necessary for the bier, such as when there is a group of pallbearers, and all of them are from the society and are among the pallbearers (see Magen Avraham, subsection 1) – are exempt from the recitation of the Shema. And the other escorts of the deceased, who are not necessary for the bier – are obligated [in the recitation of the Shema]. And even though escorting the deceased is a mitzvah, nonetheless they are not exempt from the recitation of the Shema because of this. And it appears to me that even the pallbearers, if it is not necessary for all of them to carry at the same time – these will carry and these will recite [the Shema] and then they will switch, as with the digging of the grave mentioned in the previous section.

One does not take out the deceased close to the time of the recitation of the Shema when there is not enough time to take him out and bury him before the time of the Shema arrives. But if they have already begun to take him out, they do not interrupt in order to recite the Shema. And it appears that even if the time for reciting the Shema will pass, they do not interrupt, for one who is engaged in a mitzvah is exempt from another mitzvah. And the Rambam in the fourth chapter wrote that an important person is permitted to be taken out close to the time of the Shema, as it is explained in Berachot (19a). The Tur and the Shulchan Aruch omitted this because in our times there is no such important person for whom it would be worthwhile to take him out close to the time of the Shema (Beit Yosef). And whatever was explained in the Gemara regarding the rule of an important person, if it leads to leniency, it does not apply in our times (Taz, small section 1). There is no difference between the time for the Shema of the morning and that of the evening. Some are lenient regarding the evening Shema, and we have explained this in Yoreh De'ah, section 358, paragraph 2. (And see the Magen Avraham, small section 2, who wrote that if it is after "plag hamincha," one should recite the Shema first; see there. However, this is not the custom, for we bury first since the entire night is its time.)

People who are involved in delivering a eulogy, when the deceased is lying before them – should withdraw one by one to read and pray. However, not everyone should do this simultaneously, as it would not honor the deceased. But when the deceased is not lying before them, they read and pray, and the onenim (those in immediate mourning) sit in silence. And in the Tur it is written that the eulogizing cantors are exempt, see there. This is the explanation: if the entire congregation has already prayed, even if the cantors have not yet prayed – they should not interrupt the eulogy out of respect for the congregation and the deceased. And this applies only on the first day, but from the second day onward – they should interrupt (Taz, subsection 2).

After they have buried the deceased, the mourners return to receive condolences, and all the people follow them from the place of the burial to the place where the mourners stand to form a line to receive condolences. If the people can start and complete even one verse before reaching the line, they should start and read as much as they can. If they can complete the entire verse, they should complete it (see Magen Avraham, subsection 3). And even though they will read the first verse while walking, and it was explained in Siman 63 that the first verse must certainly be recited while standing, nevertheless, in this case, out of respect for the mourners and the mitzvah of consoling them, they are lenient to read even while walking (this is what seems to me). If they cannot complete even the first verse, they should not start. This is specifically if there is enough time in the day to read it afterward, without missing its prescribed time. But if the time will pass, they should read first and then console the mourners. Those standing in the line to console, the inner ones who see the face of the mourner are exempt, and the outer ones who do not see the face of the mourner are obligated. Some say that even the line surrounding the first line is considered "seeing the face of the mourner" (see Taz, subsection 3). All this applies when it happened that they brought out the deceased close to the time of the Shema reading, or when the time for Shema has already arrived. But ideally, one should not bring out the deceased close to the time for Shema reading as has been explained, and certainly not when the time has already arrived. All this pertains to the morning. But if they brought him out close to the evening, and upon their return, it becomes night, they do not need to concern themselves with this; they should read the Shema and pray afterward, since the entire night is its time. And it seems to me that this is the custom (this is what seems according to my humble opinion).

Two people who are sleeping under one garment, with their bodies touching each other, meaning they are sleeping naked and covered by one garment – it is forbidden for them to recite the Shema or speak words of Torah, because their bodies are touching and this leads to improper thoughts. Whether they are lying face to face or back to back, as long as their bodies are touching, it is forbidden. What is their solution? They should place a garment between them, from their waist down to the end of their bodies. But from their waist up, there is no concern, because in that area, touching does not lead to improper thoughts. When they make this separation, it is permitted, even if they are lying face to face. One should not ask: are they not forbidden anyway, since they are naked and their hearts see their nakedness? One can say: it is a case where they are covering their hearts with the garment, which is permitted as will be explained in Siman 74. It seems clear that all this applies when their bodies are touching each other, because if they are not touching, there is no need for a separation of a garment. There are those who say that if they are lying face to face, even if they are not touching, a garment separation is required when they are lying close to each other (Pri Megadim). I do not know the reason for this stringency. And if they are lying clothed, it is permitted in any manner.

If one sleeps with his wife, he does not need a separation of a garment, because his wife is like his own body and he is accustomed to her, so there is no improper thought. Nevertheless, face-to-face is forbidden without a separation of a garment, because in such a situation there is improper thought. Instead, they should turn their faces away, and even though their backs touch each other, there is no issue with this. And so our Sages said (Berachot 24a): "Buttocks do not constitute nakedness," and "buttocks" refers to the touching of their backs to each other. If one of them turns their face away while the other does not, the one who turns their face away is permitted, and the one who does not is forbidden. Some say that the law concerning his wife is like that concerning another person, and it is forbidden without a separation of a garment even if they turn their faces away. It is proper to be concerned with this opinion. It is also clear that in this case, there should be a separation of a garment over the heart, so that the heart does not see the nakedness. The woman does not need this, because for them, their heart does not see the nakedness, as will be explained in Siman 74.

There are those who say that after the fact, if one recited the Shema even without a separation of a garment and face to face, and even if it was someone not with his wife – they have fulfilled their obligation (Pri Chadash). And there are those who question this (Pri Megadim). It seems the main opinion is the first one, for we do not find that one needs to go back and recite except in the case of needing to relieve oneself, as "the sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination," or in a place where there was filth, as I wrote in Siman 76, which is more of a disgrace. But in this case, which is merely a concern of thought – surely one does not need to go back and recite. It also seems to me that even if in his heart he sees the nakedness – he does not need to go back and recite. Therefore, we do not find any indication of these laws in the Gemara and the Poskim that one needs to go back and recite or pray. And a proof for this: for here contemplation is permitted in matters of Torah, and likewise if in his heart he sees the nakedness, as written by the great Acharonim (Magen Avraham Siman 85, subsection 2, and Pri Chadash at the end of Siman 75). This is not the case in dirty places, and certainly when one needs to relieve himself. And since contemplation is permitted, it follows that after the fact if one recited the Shema or prayed – they do not need to go back (so it seems according to my humble opinion).

If he was sleeping with his children while they were still small, it is permitted to recite the Shema with his back turned without separating with a garment. If they are older, a garment is required for separation. Turning one's back is also necessary with small children, as otherwise, there is a concern of improper thoughts due to their private parts touching each other. This also seems to be implied by the Rambam at the end of Chapter 3, see there. However, in the Hagahot Ashri in the third chapter, it is written in the name of the Or Zarua that even if their private parts touch each other, it is permitted, see there. And ostensibly, the Gemara (Berachot 24a) also implies this clearly, as it does not mention at all the need to turn one's back when it comes to his children, see there. However, since the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch ruled that turning one's back is necessary, and it also seems to be implied by the Rambam, this is our established ruling. Nonetheless, it appears to me that this is specifically when the children are somewhat older, like three or four years old. But if they are younger than this, there is no concern.

Up to what age are children considered minors? A boy until he is twelve years old, and a girl until she is eleven years old. Even if they have grown two hairs, it is permitted, as hairs that appear before the time of maturity are considered insignificant. In the thirteenth year for a boy and the twelfth year for a girl, if they have grown two hairs – it is forbidden without interruption. If they have not grown two hairs – it is permitted. From the age of thirteen onward, meaning when the thirteenth year is fully completed, and similarly when the twelfth year for a girl is completed, even if they have not grown two hairs – it is forbidden. This is the ruling of the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch. It seems that for a girl of twelve years, if she has not grown hairs, it is permitted only with her mother; with her father, it is forbidden for him to lie with her in close proximity, as explained in Even HaEzer, Siman 21. For a boy with his father or mother – it is forbidden. Here we are only discussing the matter of the recitation of the Shema, whether they are considered as nakedness (ervah) for the purpose of reciting the Shema or not. These laws apply equally to two males or two females. (Eliyahu Rabbah. This also resolves the question of the Magen Avraham, Siman Katan 2, see there for more details.)

It is written, "When you go out as a camp... for the Lord your God walks in the midst of your camp... therefore your camp shall be holy, and He shall not see in you any unclean thing...". It is explained that in any place where there is sanctity of the Name, such as a military camp where the Ark and the Name placed there was within the camp, as explained in the Tosefta of Sotah, chapter seven, on the verse "for the Lord your God walks in the midst of your camp"—this refers to the Name in the Ark. This is also explained in Sotah (42b). They were commanded about two things: that the camp should be holy, and anyone who needed to relieve himself was required to go outside the camp, as explicitly stated in the Torah there. Hence, it is prohibited for excrement to be seen in a holy place. The second is that no nakedness should be seen in a holy place. And even if we interpret "any unclean thing" as referring to transgressions, as Onkelos translates, nevertheless, since the scripture equates a transgression with "nakedness," it is certainly forbidden for nakedness to be seen.

And since the Torah even prohibited these things in the camp, how much more so for a person who is standing and praying, or reciting the Shema, or making a blessing, where he mentions the holy Name several times and directs his heart to God, that the place around him must be clean from two things: excrement and nakedness. For all around him is certainly like the camp of the Divine Presence at that time. And our Rabbis, of blessed memory, in Shabbat (150a) deduced from the language of the Torah that in one aspect excrement is more stringent than nakedness: for regarding excrement the Torah says "and your camp shall be holy," which implies that even thinking about Torah is forbidden. But regarding nakedness it says "thing," from which we understand that speech is forbidden, but thought is permitted, see there. And this is the foundation for many laws that will be explained in this matter. And any type of Torah learning, whether Written or Oral, whether Midrash or Zohar, or other holy books, it is forbidden to study them in the presence of either of these two things. For all words of Torah are His holy Names, as is known, and we apply to them "and your camp shall be holy, and He shall not see any indecent thing among you."

We learn from this that when one is reciting the Shema, praying, blessing, or studying Torah, it is forbidden to have any kind of exposed nakedness in front of one's eyes, whether of a male or female. This is the meaning of "and He shall see no unseemly thing among you" (Deuteronomy 23:15), meaning "among you"—in your camp of the Divine Presence, no nakedness should be seen. All the more so if one's own nakedness is exposed, even if one does not see it. Similarly, if one closes one's eyes so as not to see the nakedness of another, it does not help, for this reason it is written "He shall see no unseemly thing among you" and not "you shall not see any unseemly thing." Its interpretation is: the onlooker shall not see any unseemly thing among you when the Lord your God walks in the midst of your camp. (Rashba Berachot 24a in the name of the Raavad.)

This prohibition is from the Torah. However, one does not receive lashes for it because it is a prohibition that does not involve an action (Pri Megadim at the beginning of this section). Regarding excrement, there is a positive commandment of "your camp shall be holy" (ibid). These prohibitions are more severe than other prohibitions because they involve a disgrace to Heaven, as is evident. His prayer is an abomination and he must repeat his prayer, and similarly with the recitation of the Shema. There are specific details regarding these laws which will be explained in section 76.

Concerning the issue of "the heart seeing the nakedness," there is a dispute in the Gemara (Berachot 24b), and most of the poskim rule that it is forbidden. The explanation is as follows: For example, he is clothed and his nakedness is not exposed, so there is no issue of "there shall not be a naked matter seen among you." However, if there is no separation between the heart and the nakedness, it is considered that the heart sees the nakedness, and it is also forbidden. The reason is that since the Torah is particular that in the camp of the Divine Presence, nakedness should not be seen, and the heart is the primary camp of the Divine Presence in a person when he is praying and reciting the Shema, as the sacred thoughts are in the heart, there must therefore be a separation between it and the nakedness. This is a Rabbinic decree, and post facto, he has fulfilled his obligation since there is truly no actual exposure of nakedness. It appears to me that regarding Torah study, there is no concern for "the heart seeing the nakedness," and we do not find in the Gemara and the poskim that this law applies except for the recitation of the Shema and prayer. It seems that this stringency also applies to all blessings because mentioning the explicit Name of God is similar to the Shema and prayer. I have seen someone write that for the Shema, one should repeat it if the heart saw the nakedness (Siddur Derech HaChaim). In my humble opinion, this is not so, as we do not find that repetition is required except for excrement and exposed nakedness. This is also implied by the early authorities who did not mention this. (See Pri Megadim, Orach Chaim 71:5, who connects this to the dispute about whether if one acts it does not help. I do not understand what the connection is.)

We learn from this that one who lies naked, even if he covers himself with a tallit over his entire body and head, it is forbidden due to the visibility of the nakedness. Meaning, there is no separation between his eyes and his nakedness. And even if he covers himself up to his neck, where there would then be a separation between his eyes and his nakedness, it is still forbidden because "his heart sees the nakedness," and there must be a separation between his heart and his nakedness. This is what our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in paragraph 1: if one is sleeping naked with his tallit, he needs to place a separation with the tallit over his heart and then he can read, because if his heart sees the nakedness it is forbidden. These are his words. Consequently, the same law applies when one lies in his robe and his body is covered; there must be a separation between his heart and his nakedness. (And the Beit Yosef uses the term "naked" because the Gemara there discusses in such a manner; see the Tur and Beit Yosef for more details.)

It is simple that when one is lying naked, even if he covers his heart, it does not help if his entire body is naked from the heart downwards, for this is considered seeing actual "nakedness." However, if one is covered from the heart downwards to the end of the body, even if he is naked from the heart upwards, we do not concern ourselves with this regarding the recitation of Shema and other blessings, for there is no exposure of nakedness from the heart upwards. Only for prayer does one need to cover from the heart upwards as well, for this is like standing before a king and it is not respectful behavior. And this is what our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 6: If his tallit is girded around his waist, covering him from the waist downwards, even though he is naked from the waist upwards, it is permitted to recite Shema. But to pray is forbidden until he covers his heart. Thus far his words. Also, behind him opposite his heart needs to be covered for the reason we explained (and so wrote the Taz in subsection 5).

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote in paragraph one that if one's heart sees the nakedness of another, it is forbidden. So are his words, and the Tur wrote similarly. This requires explanation. There are those who explain that this refers to two people standing in water, and the heart of one does not see his own nakedness because it is covered by clothing. However, he sees the nakedness of his fellow who is not covered, and it is forbidden to recite [Shema]. And even though his eyes are outside the water and looking outward, and they do not see the nakedness but only his heart sees the nakedness of his fellow—it is also forbidden (Bayit Chadash). However, this explanation does not fit well according to what the authors of the Shulchan Aruch decided later at the end of Siman 75, that closing one's eyes helps regarding the nakedness of another, see there. And all the more so in such a case where his eyes are outside the water and looking outward. And indeed it is true that there are those who disagree with this ruling there, as will be explained there. Nevertheless, in any case, it is impossible to interpret the intention of Rabbi Moshe Isserles in this manner according to their view there.

There is an opinion that explains it as when there is no separation between his heart and his fellow’s nakedness (Magen Avraham, subsection 1). For example, if they are sleeping under one blanket naked and are not touching each other, and his own nakedness is covered by a garment and his head is outside the garment (Pri Megadim), and only his heart sees his fellow’s nakedness. But this primary law is puzzling: From where do we derive to be stringent about his heart seeing his fellow’s nakedness? After all, this prohibition is rabbinic. And it is explicitly understood from Rashi (Kiddushin 24a, s.v. "Even") and Tosafot (s.v. "Two") that there is no concern about this, see there. (And the words of the Ateret Zekeinim – there is no reason in his words, see there.)

In my humble opinion, it seems there is another intention in their words. In truth, in the words of the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch, these matters are not explained in detail. This means that "one's eye seeing nakedness" is a Torah prohibition, and his heart [seeing nakedness] is a Rabbinic prohibition. However, they were concise and said that "his heart sees nakedness" is forbidden, and in this they included everything, as is clear to one who studies it in depth. And regarding seeing the nakedness of another, they did not mention it at all in this section, but only in section 75 where they wrote that it is forbidden to read opposite another's nakedness. Therefore, here they included this matter briefly and said that it is forbidden if his heart sees his fellow's nakedness. Their intention is not specifically about the heart, but rather that if his heart is opposite his fellow's nakedness, meaning that they are lying face to face naked, even if there is a separation in his heart, nevertheless, his fellow's nakedness is exposed in front of him. This is similar to the law explained in section 73 that there needs to be a garment separating them. See there. However, their intention is not that it should be exactly the same as when one's heart sees his own nakedness compared to seeing another's nakedness.

It is stated in Sukkah (10a): One who is standing in a house naked should not stick his head out of the window to recite the Shema. Since the house is a fixed place, his head is considered part of his body, and it is as if his head is in the house and sees the nakedness. This is not similar to someone who sticks his head out of his garment. Similarly, the law applies when one is lying naked in a canopy, which refers to curtains spread around the bed. He should not stick his head out of the canopy and recite the Shema if the canopy is ten handbreadths high, as it is considered a significant place like a house, and his head is considered to be inside the canopy. However, if it is not ten handbreadths high, it is like a garment, and he can stick his head out of the canopy and recite the Shema. This is stated in the Gemara there. The Talmud does not concern itself here with "his heart seeing his nakedness" (Tosafot there). That is to say, it does not deal with this matter, and he can make a separation between his heart and his nakedness. It is surprising that the poskim (decisors of Jewish law) did not mention this law at all. (The Magen Avraham wrote that it is because we hold that "if his heart sees his nakedness" it is forbidden, see there. It requires further investigation as to what this has to do with the matter. And in the Jerusalem Talmud "The Seer" chapter 2, this law is required regarding a house and a tower concerning blessings, see there. Since in our Talmud it is clear it is forbidden, there is no need to be concerned with the Jerusalem Talmud. And the Eliyah Rabbah wrote that perhaps there is a distinction between blessings and Shema, see there. It is not understood. A great investigation is required regarding the Rosh in "The Seer" who brought the Jerusalem Talmud, while our Talmud disagrees with him, in addition to the precision of the Magen Avraham. The Magen Avraham only brought from the Jerusalem Talmud a tower made of wood. But in truth, the Jerusalem Talmud there also requires it regarding a house, and it requires investigation. Pay close attention and you will find it easy.)

One who bathes naked in clear water and wishes to drink is not considered to be exposing their nakedness, because the water covering their nakedness is considered as a covering. However, their head must be covered with some sort of covering, because it is forbidden to make a blessing with an uncovered head. Covering with a hand does not suffice for making a blessing. Regarding "his heart seeing his nakedness," if his heart is above the water, the water serves as a separation between his heart and his nakedness. If his heart is below the water, he needs a garment as a separation on his heart, because both his heart and nakedness are within the water, and his heart sees his nakedness. And so did Rabbeinu Tam practice, covering with a garment from his heart and below when he would bathe (Beit Yosef). And specifically with a garment, but covering with his hands does not suffice. All this applies in clear water. But if the water is murky to the extent that his limbs are not visible, it is permitted to recite while he is in it, as the water itself serves as a separation between his heart and his nakedness. Provided that the water is not foul, for in foul water it is forbidden to recite any blessing. And when one is sitting in a spring with an earthen bottom, he can make clear water murky by stirring it with his feet. This does not apply in a vessel, obviously. It seems to me that if one bathes with soap in the water, and the water becomes whitened from the soap, it is considered as murky. There is one who disagrees and says that even if his heart is above the water, it does not suffice, and he needs a tallit as a separation on his heart (Pri Chadash). This is not necessarily correct. (I have examined his words and did not find them fundamentally convincing, see there.)

Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote in Section 2 that this is specifically regarding a garment, but covering with hands does not constitute a covering. Thus his words, and as we have explained. And in Section 3, he wrote that if a person hugs his body with his arms, it is considered an interruption. Thus his words. Meaning: even though covering with his hands is not considered a covering, this is because covering with the same type does not apply. But in terms of interruption, it is effective even with the same type. Therefore, hugging the body with the arms is called an "interruption" between the heart and the nakedness (Magen Avraham, subsection 6, and Beit Yosef). And some disagree with this, as covering is certainly preferable to interruption. And since covering does not help, all the more so interruption would not help (Pri Chadash and Ba’er Heitev, subsection 8, in the name of Mahar”m Tayvil). And the first opinion holds that interruption is preferable to covering. Therefore: since there is something interrupting, whatever it may be, the heart does not see the nakedness. But covering is not an interruption but rather covers below the heart, and how can one cover flesh with flesh? (And it seems to me that this is the intention of the Taz, subsection 3; see there.)

A barrier between the heart and the nakedness does not need to be something tied like a belt. Rather, if the garment ends below the heart, it serves as a separation. Similarly, if the garment starts below the heart, like pants, it serves as a separation, as will be explained in Siman 91. The garment just needs to be placed on his flesh or on his shirt.

We are only particular about "his heart seeing the nakedness," for the reason explained in section 5. But for other limbs that see the nakedness, we are not concerned, because aside from the eye and the heart, they do not have significance, as is understood. However, if any of his limbs touches his own nakedness or the nakedness of another person, it is forbidden to recite the Shema or to pray. Even his thighs, upon which the nakedness lies when he is reclining, must be separated by a garment or distanced so that the organ does not touch them. There are those who permit this with small children when touching their nakedness, but there are those who forbid it, and this is the main opinion. This is agreed upon by the great authorities (Beit Yosef, and Magen Avraham, subsection 9).

And know that for a woman, there is no law of "her heart sees her nakedness," because her nakedness is below. Therefore, when they wear a robe, they are permitted to recite blessings and pray even though there is no separation between their heart and their nakedness, for their heart does not see their nakedness. However, there is someone who disagrees with this (Bach), but his opinion is not the main one (Taz, sub-paragraph 4). But when they are completely naked, it is forbidden for them to recite blessings and pray unless their nakedness is pressed against the ground or they are sitting on something soft, as then their nakedness is concealed and not visible. This does not help for a man, because his nakedness protrudes. But when they are completely naked, they have a revelation of nakedness like a man.

Even though regarding a man, the term "ervah" (nakedness) only applies to the actual genital area and there is no issue if other parts of his body are exposed, with a woman it is not so. As Maimonides writes in Chapter 3, Law 16, and this is his language: "The entire body of a woman is considered 'ervah'." Therefore, one should not look at a woman's body while reciting the Shema, even if it is his own wife. And if a tefach (handbreadth) of her body is uncovered, one should not recite the Shema in front of her. This is the end of his language, and it seems this is the explanation: that looking at her body is forbidden for reciting the Shema even if the exposure is less than a tefach, but without looking, it is permitted. However, if a tefach is uncovered, it is forbidden to recite the Shema in front of her even without looking at her. In all this, there is no difference between his wife and another woman. (And so it appears from the Gemara 24a that looking is forbidden even for a small amount, and consequently, in such a situation, it is forbidden to recite the Shema, even with his wife.)

I have seen someone write concerning Maimonides' intention that specifically with one's wife does it require a handbreadth [to be considered an issue], but with another woman, even less than a handbreadth is forbidden, and so it is written in the Baal Halachot Gedolot (according to the Lechem Mishneh). And I am astonished: for it is true that it is written so in the Hagahot Maimoniot there. And this is what Rabbi Moses Isserles (Rema) wrote in paragraph 1, that some say specifically with one's wife, but with another woman even less than a handbreadth is considered ervah (nakedness). So far his words. But Maimonides' opinion is not like this. And also, the Baal Halachot Gedolot does not hold this opinion, and this is the wording of the Baal Halachot Gedolot: even one's wife, when a handbreadth of her is revealed, it is forbidden to recite the Shema opposite her. So far his words, meaning: how much more so with another woman. However, in any case, we require a handbreadth.

This is the language of the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch, section 1: "A handbreadth of exposed skin on a woman in a place where it is customary to cover, even if she is his wife, it is forbidden to recite the Shema opposite her." Thus are their words. And indeed, it is certain that the opinion of the Rambam is also that it refers to a place where it is customary to cover. However, upon examination, it seems obvious that even in places that are usually exposed, it is forbidden [to recite the Shema]. And it is also apparent from their words that less than a handbreadth is not forbidden even if she is not his wife, according to the Rambam. Our master, the Rema, wrote that some say that for another woman, even less than a handbreadth constitutes ervah (nudity), and we have already explained this matter. And know that the Tur wrote: "Similarly, if her thigh is exposed, it is forbidden to recite opposite her." Thus are his words. And some interpret his words to mean that regarding the thigh, it is forbidden even if less than a handbreadth is exposed, and even if she is his wife, because that is a place that incites more contemplation (Bach and Taz, subsection 1). It is puzzling to explain it this way, for if so, he should not have left this ambiguous. It seems more likely, as the Rashba wrote in the name of the Raavad regarding this ruling in the Gemara, that it teaches us that the exposure of the thigh is also considered ervah, meaning that even though there are places where women go barefoot, and there is no issue of ervah with their feet, nevertheless, the upper part of the leg has the status of ervah. Therefore, our master the Beit Yosef did not bring this from the Tur, because this is also included in the category of covered places. (And this is also written by the Beit Yosef and the Derisha, see there.)

And our master the Rema wrote: It appears from the words of the Rosh that a handbreadth on a woman is considered nakedness even for another woman, except that she herself can recite [the Shema] even though she is naked, as mentioned earlier in Siman 74. Thus are his words. However, the Rashba explicitly wrote the opposite, that it is considered nakedness only for men due to thoughts [of impropriety], but not for women. And why should another woman be worse than she herself? And from the Rosh who wrote "specifically for another woman, but for herself…"—thus are his words—there is no proof, because it must be a printing error, as previously he did not speak about another woman at all. And it should be said: "specifically for others" (the Gra, Section 3). And also the Levush did not copy this, see there. And proof for this is from the Tur, who did not mention this matter. And it is also clear from his words in the hints, see there. And there are those who interpret the words of our master the Rema differently, that his intention was to disagree with what he himself wrote earlier, that there are those who say that for another woman who is not his wife, it is forbidden even less than a handbreadth. To this he says that from the Rosh it appears that a handbreadth on a woman is considered nakedness even for another woman, meaning that even for another woman, there is no prohibition less than a handbreadth (Eliyah Rabbah, Section 101). And indeed, this is clarified from the words of the Rosh, see there. Therefore, the practical ruling is to be lenient in this matter like the Rashba.

It is questionable whether a woman is permitted to recite the Shema and bless in the presence of a man with an exposed handbreadth in a concealed place. Just as it is forbidden for a man regarding a woman, so too it is forbidden for a woman regarding a man. Or perhaps: it is more relevant for a man to have inappropriate thoughts than for a woman, and so it appears from the poskim who did not mention this law. This also seems to be the implication in Ketubot 64b, see there.

Our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, wrote in Section 2: The hair of a woman that she usually covers - it is forbidden to recite [the Shema] in front of it, even if it is one's own wife. However, unmarried women who usually go with uncovered heads - it is permitted. The same applies to the hair of women that generally protrudes from their braids, and all the more so to the hair of a non-Jewish woman, even if it is usually covered. Thus far his language. And what has been explained in Even HaEzer, Siman 21, that even unmarried women should not go with uncovered heads - this refers to those who have been married, such as widows and divorcees, and not to virgins (Chelkat Mechokeik and Beit Shmuel there). There are those who wrote that even a virgin should not go with her hair unkempt and unbraided (Magen Avraham, Section 3). And some say that in a courtyard, all women, even married ones, are permitted to go with uncovered heads. See Even HaEzer, Siman 115, and in Zohar "Naso" it is strongly warned about this (there, Section 4). And women who come from places where their custom is not to cover their hair to a place where the custom is to cover it, and they do not intend to return - they are permitted to uncover their hair (there, in the name of Alshich).

And now let us cry out about the breaches of our generation, due to our many sins, for many years the daughters of Israel have been lax in this matter and go with uncovered heads. And despite all the protests about this – it has neither helped nor availed. And now the plague has spread, with married women going with their hair uncovered like maidens. Woe to us that it has come to this in our days! Nevertheless, it appears that according to the law, we are permitted to pray and bless in front of their uncovered heads, since now most of them go this way, and it is considered like the exposed parts of their body. As Mordechai wrote in the name of Ra'avya at the end of the third chapter, and these are his words: All the things we mentioned regarding nakedness – specifically refer to something that is not usually revealed. But a maiden who regularly reveals her hair – we are not concerned, for there is no lustful thought. Thus far his words. And since among us even the married women do so, by extension, there is no lustful thought. (And the Rif and Rambam omitted entirely the law regarding hair and voice, because they held that it was not stated in regard to the recitation of Shema. See Beit Yosef.)

One must be careful not to hear a woman's singing voice during the recitation of the Shema, even if it is his wife. For if it is not his wife – it is forbidden even when not during the recitation of the Shema. As our sages of blessed memory said there: "A woman's voice is considered an ervah (intimate part)." However, the sound of her speaking voice is permitted, and similarly, a voice he is accustomed to, such as his wife's, is permitted even during the recitation of the Shema. And this is the language of the Mordechai there in the name of Rabbi Eliezer of Metz: "Therefore, it is forbidden to say matters of holiness while hearing a woman's singing voice, and in our sins… we are not careful to avoid studying while hearing the singing voice of non-Jewish women." Thus far his language. And it appears that specifically when they are singing with their mouths it is forbidden, but not when they are playing an instrument, as this does not lead to improper thoughts and ervah.

It has already been explained that it is forbidden to recite the Shema in the presence of nakedness, even in the presence of the nakedness of a non-Jew, and even in the presence of the nakedness of a minor. Some permit it in the presence of the nakedness of a minor as long as he is not of age for sexual relations, which means a boy under nine years and one day. And this is the primary ruling. See Yoreh De'ah, section 265, where it is noted that some do not hold the nakedness of the infant during the blessing of the circumcision. And some do hold it, as in this case, nakedness is not relevant, since he is engaged in sanctifying him with the sanctity of the circumcision.

Nakedness behind a glass partition, meaning in a glass vessel, even though the nakedness is covered—and in the case of excrement, it is permitted in such a manner—nevertheless, regarding nakedness, it is forbidden, since it is visible. Concerning nakedness, it is written: "and no nakedness of a thing shall be seen among you"—and indeed, it is seen. Similarly, when one is dressed in a thin garment through which the nakedness is visible, or a woman who wears a thin garment through which her flesh is visible—it is considered as exposed nakedness.

Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote in section six: If there is nakedness opposite him, and he turns his face away from it, or he closes his eyes, or it is at night, or he is blind—it is permissible to recite, for the sight is what the Torah depends on, and he does not see it. This is his language. And many disagree with him, and they hold that nothing helps except turning the face, for the interpretation of "he shall not see" is not that he does not see, but that it should not be visible to be seen. And if so, what benefit is there in closing the eyes, or it being night, or being blind, since others standing in his place can see? And this is the main ruling (Bach and Taz section 2, and Magen Avraham section 9), and this is also proven in the Jerusalem Talmud. Also, turning the face only helps when he turns his whole body to the other side (Taz there). And we have already explained at the beginning of section 74 that thoughts are permitted even opposite nakedness, see there.

It has already been explained that excrement is like nakedness. It is forbidden to recite the Shema, to pray, to say blessings, and to study in a place where there is excrement opposite oneself. Excrement is more severe than nakedness, as with excrement even contemplation is forbidden, as I wrote at the beginning of Siman 74. However, in this matter, excrement is lighter than nakedness: regarding nakedness behind glass, it is forbidden to recite [the Shema] opposite it, as I wrote in the previous Siman. But excrement behind glass is permitted even though it is visible, because the Torah depends on covering, as it is written: "And you shall turn and cover your excrement." And it is considered covered, and therefore, even though one sees it through its walls, it is permitted.

And similarly, if there is excrement in a hole, one may place his sandal over it and recite the Shema, as it is considered covered. If the bad smell does not reach him, it is permitted. However, if there is a bad smell, it is forbidden, even according to the opinion in Siman 79 that a partition is effective even for a bad smell (see there). This is referring to a partition and not merely a covering. Additionally, it is only allowed if the sandal does not touch the excrement. Since the sandal is on the person's body, if the sandal touches the excrement, it is as if the excrement is on his body.
