Therefore, those who come out of the bathroom or from unclean places must be very careful to thoroughly clean their shoes before entering the study hall to pray.

If excrement is moved in front of him, meaning he is reciting the Shema and excrement is carried in front of him, even though the excrement is passing by, it is still forbidden, since ultimately, "your camp is not holy." Therefore, when the excrement passes in front of his eyes, it is forbidden to recite even if the excrement is four cubits away from him, and he must distance it from his sight. If the excrement is behind him, it is sufficient to distance himself four cubits from it, provided he does not smell it. When the excrement is to his side, it is also sufficient to distance four cubits, as if it were behind him. Therefore, when a person stands by water and excrement floats on the water, the law is as explained (Beit Yosef and Taz, Section 1). There are those who wish to be lenient in front of him with four cubits, but this is not the primary opinion (Magen Avraham in the name of Bach, see Taz there. However, Eliyah Rabbah, Section 4, agrees with Bach that even in front of him, four cubits is sufficient).

Excrement in water is not nullified unless the water is murky so that the excrement is not recognizable (Shiltei Giborim). And this is specifically when there is no bad odor present. The mouth of a pig is considered like passing excrement (Gemara 25a). Even if it comes up from the river, washing does not help it, as it is like a chamber pot of excrement. Therefore, one should be careful not to pray in a house where pigs are found. It is forbidden to make any blessing there, and it is forbidden to put on tefillin there. Travelers must be very cautious about this.

If there is excrement on his flesh and it is covered by his clothes, or if he inserted his hand into a latrine through a hole, and no foul odor reaches him, the Gemara (25a) presents a dispute. Rav Huna says: It is permissible to recite the Shema, as it is written: "Let every soul praise the Lord" – the organs of respiration, the mouth and the nose, praise, but not the other organs. And we are not concerned with their cleanliness, as the excrement is covered. Rav Chisda says: It is forbidden to recite, as it is written: "All my bones shall say: 'Lord, who is like You?'" Therefore, all the organs are included in the praise and need to be clean. The Rif and the Rosh ruled in accordance with Rav Huna, that it is permissible to recite the Shema. This is also clarified by the Rambam in Chapter Three, Law 11, see there. However, Rabbeinu Chananel ruled in accordance with Rav Chisda that it is forbidden. Seemingly, the law follows the majority, and it is permissible to recite.

However, our master the Beit Yosef wrote in section 4, after bringing the two opinions, that there are those who say that the permissive ruling regarding excrement on one's body only applies to a place where it is naturally covered without clothing, such as the armpits. And it is proper to follow the stringent opinion. Thus far are his words. The reason for this opinion is that it is entirely unreasonable to permit actual excrement on one's body, as it is obvious that in such a case there is no "your camp shall be holy," even if it is covered by clothes. Nevertheless, it is still on his body, and the body is certainly no less significant than the camp itself, and covering it with clothes does not help. Therefore, they interpret this to mean a place where it cannot be revealed at all, like between the armpits. Thus, it is called "your camp shall be holy."

Additionally, the Rambam of blessed memory safeguarded against this question, as he wrote there: "If there was a residue of excrement on his flesh, or his hands were soiled from the bathroom, and there was no foul smell at all due to their smallness or dryness – it is permitted to recite [the Shema]…". These are his words. Thus, he explained "a residue of excrement," meaning not actual excrement but traces of excrement. Similarly, he did not write "he inserted his hands into the bathroom" but rather "his hands were soiled from the bathroom," meaning that he wiped himself with something and there remained some traces of filth on his hand. And one must say that it is discussing a situation where he does not have water, and he cleans his hands with a rock or a wall, as I wrote in Siman 4, see there. However, in any case, even the Rambam only permitted this in such a scenario. And regarding this very point, he wrote afterward that many Geonim ruled that it is forbidden to recite [the Shema] if his hands were soiled, and this is how it should be done. These are his words.

According to this, if there is actual excrement on his body, it is certainly forbidden. However, with traces of excrement or in a covered area, like between his arms or similar places, and he does not have water, he may rely on the opinion of our Rabbis who permit it. If there is excrement on his clothes, such as his robe or pants and it is covered by another garment, it is permitted according to all opinions (Magen Avraham, subsection 6). This is not comparable to excrement stuck to his sandal, which is forbidden, even if it only touches briefly as I wrote in subsection 2, because with a sandal, one walks and the excrement can be slightly exposed through walking. This is not the case with other garments (there, in the name of the Maor and Tury). Additionally, the sandal is more attached to the body than other garments. Furthermore, the sandal is considered like a "chamber pot" (Eliya Rabba, subsection 5). Rabbi Rema writes that semen on his body has the same status as excrement. Hence, if there is actual semen on his body, it is forbidden to recite until it is removed. If there are traces of semen on his body, or even actual semen, but it is between his thighs where it is never exposed, and he does not have water, he may recite the Shema and pray as he is. If there is semen on his robe and it is covered, he is permitted to recite the Shema, pray, and study. This is the law. However, it is certainly meritorious if he can easily wash the area and completely remove the semen, for he will receive great reward and it is an honor to Heaven. But according to the strict law, it is not required, as this is the consensus of the great authorities as explained with divine assistance. (And the Sefer Chasidim speaks of pious conduct.)

Feces in its place, which means at the anus — it is forbidden to recite the Shema (Yoma 30a). However, if it is not visible externally — it is permitted, as the Torah was not given to the ministering angels (ibid.). For there are people who strain their bowels, and the feces stands at the anus, and they cannot expel it. However, if part of it is visible externally when they are sitting, even though it is not visible when they are standing — it is forbidden (ibid.). This is not similar to feces on the flesh, which is permitted according to most authorities, as I wrote in paragraph 5, because in its place its filth is greater (Gemara ibid.).

Therefore, one who has hemorrhoidal disease, which is called "gildernem" or "adar," and blood always flows from it, and along with the blood, foul and putrid discharge comes out, and it has a bad smell – it is forbidden for him to engage in any matter of sanctity as long as this discharge is dripping from him (Magen Avraham, subsection 8). And even if the time for reciting Shema or prayer passes – he should neither recite Shema, pray, nor bless. However, if there is no bad smell, if the blood or discharge comes out intermittently by external pressure – he has a remedy by washing the unclean area. But if it drips and flows continuously on its own from the anus, there is no remedy for it (ibid.). And he is forbidden to mention any matter of sanctity until the dripping stops.

If there is a small amount of excrement in front of him, he can nullify it with saliva by spitting on it, and then he may recite [prayers] opposite it. This is specifically when the saliva is thick. Adding water on the excrement does not help unless the water is murky, so that the excrement cannot be seen through it. This is not similar to a glass lantern, which is a proper cover (as explained there in subparagraph 9). Even thick saliva only nullifies the excrement temporarily. Over time, the saliva dissolves and is absorbed into the excrement, and it no longer helps, reverting to its prohibited status.

Our Sages of blessed memory said (Berachot 25a): In a case of uncertain presence of excrement in a house, it is permitted [to pray]; in a garbage dump, it is forbidden. One must say that this applies even if there is a reason to believe that excrement was present in the house, such as knowing that children go there to relieve themselves, but there is uncertainty whether the excrement was removed or not—it is permitted, because a house generally has a presumption that it is cleaned. And necessarily, one must say this, for if excrement was not presumed to be in the house, what relevance would there be to the case of uncertain excrement in the house? Alternatively, it is possible that one should not be so lenient, and if it is known that children go there, one must be certain that the excrement was removed. If not, it is forbidden to read [the Shema], pray, or bless. However, if there are children and it is not known that they go there, in such a case it is called "uncertain excrement in a house", and it is permitted.

However, from the words of the students of Rabbeinu Yonah in the third chapter, it is clear that even in such a case it is forbidden. For they wrote regarding what is said, "he prayed and found excrement in his place" – since he sinned, even though he prayed, his prayer is not considered a prayer, and he needs to pray again. And they wrote that this refers to a place where children are commonly found, and he had an obligation to check the place, see there. It is explicitly stated that if there are children in the house, it is considered a doubtful case of excrement which is forbidden. According to their words, it is necessary to say that the case where doubtful excrement in the house is permitted refers to a situation where there are no children at all. If so, it is not understood what relevance there is to the doubtful excrement, and further investigation is required.

The words of the Tur and Shulchan Aruch are unclear in this matter, as they wrote in the language of the Talmud: "If there is a doubt whether there is excrement in the house, it is permitted to recite [Shema], as the presumption is that the house does not have excrement." This is their language. And afterwards, they wrote: "If one recited [Shema] in a place where it is reasonable to suspect there might be excrement, and later found excrement — one must repeat the recitation. But if it is not a place where it is reasonable to suspect, one does not need to repeat the recitation." This is their language. And they did not explain the criteria of the place, how and what.

However, in the words of the Rambam, I see a significant change from the language of the Talmud. He wrote in Chapter 3, Law 15: If one was reading the Shema at home and was uncertain whether there was excrement there... – it is permissible to read. Thus are his words. And the second law, that if one prayed and found excrement in his place, he needs to pray again – is not found in it at all. Only at the beginning of the chapter, when he wrote that one should not read in a bathhouse or a bathroom, he wrote that anyone who read in a place where one should not read – must read again, see there. But in this specific case, when one finds excrement in his place – he did not mention anything.

And it appears to me that even according to the Rambam, the point we emphasized is also a kal vachomer (an a fortiori argument). How is it possible to have a doubt about excrement in a house if there are no children there? And if so, since it is permitted to read (the Shema), how could they say that if one found excrement in his place, he needs to repeat the prayer? Therefore, it is interpreted as follows. And this is the arrangement of the teaching: Certainly, if before reciting the Shema and the prayer, it occurred to him that there might be a doubt of excrement, such as if there are children or the like, he is forbidden to begin until he checks the place. And if he did not check and found excrement, he is negligent and must repeat the reading and the prayer. This matter does not need to be explained in detail, as it is included in what was written at the beginning of the chapter, that in filthy places it is forbidden to read, and if he read, he must repeat the reading. Consequently, if there is a doubt of filth, it is like any doubt concerning a Torah law, and we are stringent. And there is no novelty in this.

And this that they said, "If there is a doubt about excrement in the house, it is permitted" – this is a different matter. And this means that before the recitation of the Shema and the prayer, it did not occur to him at all that there might be any doubt about excrement there, and he began to recite. And in the middle of the recitation, the doubt arose in his heart, because there are children there or something similar. However, since he began to recite with permission, and the presumption of the house is that there is no excrement there, and when the children leave, they take it out from there, as indeed is the way of most people. Therefore, they permitted him to finish. And even if he finds excrement afterwards – he is considered coerced, since the doubt did not occur to him at all beforehand. And the Torah was not given to the ministering angels, and regarding this, they did not say that he needs to go back and recite. And this is what the Rambam precisely meant in his words: "He was reciting and then became doubtful," meaning the doubt arose after he began to recite. And so it appears to me in my humble opinion to be the main ruling.

A doubtful situation of excrement in a garbage heap is forbidden because of the presumption that there is excrement in the garbage heap. Therefore, one is prohibited from reciting Shema, praying, or making blessings opposite the garbage heap until it has been checked. This applies even if the garbage heap itself does not have a bad smell, for if it had a bad smell, it would be prohibited regardless.

I have seen someone write that a garbage heap is forbidden even if it is in the house (the Gra"Z), but in my humble opinion, this is not so. In Chullin (12a), there is a dispute about whether carcasses are placed in a garbage heap in the house. We hold by Yoreh De'ah, Siman 1, that they are not placed there. Rashi explains that a person would not place his carcass in a garbage heap in the house because it would become foul and have a bad smell. Thus, it stands to reason that human excrement would certainly not be placed there, as there is no worse smell than human excrement.

Therefore, it seems to me that the garbage heap discussed in the Gemara and poskim refers specifically to a garbage heap in the courtyard, not in the house.

And similarly, if it is known that there is excrement in the house, but it is not known whether it is human excrement or dog excrement, some say that in the house it is permitted, but in a garbage heap, it is forbidden (Magen Avraham, subsection 10, in the name of the Riaz). And some say that we follow what is common, that we assume based on what is common, whether to be lenient or stringent, as I have written in Yoreh De’ah, Siman 57 (Magen Avraham). And when children are more common than dogs, it is also forbidden in the house. And when dogs are more common, it is also permitted in the garbage heap (ibid.). And some are stringent regarding the garbage heap in any case (Pri Chadash). And similarly, when it is known that there is excrement in the house, it is forbidden in any case (ibid.), for in a place that is known to have excrement, it is certainly forbidden to recite [prayers] until it is clearly known that it is dog excrement. And so is the ruling. And it is obvious that if it is later clarified that it is human excrement, one is required to repeat [the prayers].

Urine is not treated the same way, for even in a place where there is doubt whether there might be urine, it is permitted, even in a trash heap. The reason is that according to Torah law, it is only forbidden to pray opposite someone urinating in the usual manner at the time they are urinating. But once the urine has fallen to the ground, it is permitted according to Torah law, and the reason for this will be explained in Siman 77. It is only rabbinically forbidden, and in cases of doubt, the rabbis did not decree a prohibition. Therefore, with urine, even if it is found in a place where there was reason to doubt, one does not need to repeat the reading or the prayer. (And see Magen Avraham, subsection 11, that even if it is trickling, it is permitted according to Torah law; see there.)

It appears to me that just as it is rabbinically prohibited to read and pray in the presence of urine, so too it is prohibited in the presence of anything repulsive, such as vomit, excessive nasal mucus, or phlegm and saliva that are disgusting, for they are no less repulsive than urine. And it is written, "Prepare to meet your God, O Israel." There are those who are lenient about this, but it does not seem correct to me. Additionally, it seems that if one read near a garbage heap and then moved away without checking it, even though he acted improperly, he does not need to repeat the reading unless it is confirmed that there is definitely excrement there. (There are those who did not write this way; see Biur Halacha. But it seems to me as I have written. Analyze and you will find it to be lenient.)

According to the Torah, there is no prohibition against reciting the Shema, praying, or making blessings in the presence of urine, except opposite someone who is urinating at that moment, as I have written in the previous section. Our sages of blessed memory (Berakhot 25a) derived this from scriptural verses, as it is written: "You shall have a place outside the camp, and you shall go out there" (Deuteronomy 23:13), and it does not say: "That you shall cover what comes out of you." And it is written: "You shall have a spade among your tools, and when you sit down outside, you shall dig with it and cover up your excrement" (Deuteronomy 23:14) – here for urine, it does not require covering, but here for excrement, it does require covering. By rabbinic decree, they also prohibited it after it has fallen to the ground if there is enough moisture to make another object wet upon contact. In other words, if you place something on the urine, it will get so moist that it can dampen another object upon touching it.

A vessel containing urine – it is forbidden to recite the Shema in front of it, unless water is added to the vessel. It makes no difference whether the water preceded the urine or the reverse. We do not say that the latter addition nullifies the earlier one. This is provided that the vessel is not designated specifically for urine. For an earthenware pot designated for urine is considered as the urine itself, and it is forbidden to recite or pray in front of it, as will be explained in Siman 87. It is obvious that this pertains to a case where there is no foul odor from the urine, for if there is a foul odor, it is forbidden in any case, even if water is added to it.

And what is the measure of water? A quarter-log for one instance of urine, and for two instances, two quarter-logs, and so on indefinitely. There is no distinction whether the urine is in large or small amounts (Kesef Mishneh and Magen Avraham). Some say that if the urine is less than a quarter-log, one does not need a quarter-log of water but rather the majority of water (Chacham Tzvi). Others say that even the majority is not required, only the measure of the urine (Shiltei Giborim). One may be lenient in a rabbinic prohibition (ibid). And if the urine is on the ground, one should pour water over the entire area until it is sufficiently wet, and a quarter-log is also required.

And know that the Rashba wrote that a quarter-log of water suffices even for multiple times. And there is one who says that according to the Rambam, a quarter-log is needed only if he urinated and then urinated again and thus requires new water. But if he has not yet poured water, even if he urinated several times, one quarter-log suffices. (Mishnah Berurah in the name of Magen Giborim. And the Gra agreed with the Rashba's opinion, see there. One can rely on this in a time of need.)

We learned in Berachot (22b): The Sages taught: If one was standing in prayer, and water was dripping on his knees, meaning he was urinating – he stops until the water ceases, and then he resumes praying. If he did not delay long enough to finish the entire prayer, he returns to the place where he stopped. If he delayed long enough to finish the entire prayer, he returns to the beginning. We have already explained in Siman 65 that according to the Rif and the Rambam, this rule applies only to prayer, that one returns to the beginning. However, for the recitation of the Shema, even if he delayed long enough to finish the entire recitation, he does not return to the beginning. Tosafot and the Rosh disagree with this and hold that there is no difference between prayer and the recitation of the Shema, and if the interruption was due to a necessity that prevented him from reciting, he returns to the beginning even for the recitation of the Shema. Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, ruled according to the Rif and the Rambam. The Tur and our teacher, the Rema, ruled according to Tosafot and the Rosh, see there.

Therefore, the Tur writes here: If one was reading, and his urine started to drip onto his knees, he stops until the urine ceases... And if he delayed for the amount of time it would take to complete the entire reading, he must start from the beginning. If not, he returns to the place where he stopped. Thus is his language. But Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote that even if he delayed for the amount of time it would take to complete the entire reading, he does not need to return but only to the place where he stopped. Thus is his language. And Rabbeinu Rema wrote on this: There are those who say that if he delayed for the amount of time it would take to complete the entire reading, he must start from the beginning. And this is the main ruling, as I wrote above in Siman 65. And the time is estimated according to the reader. Thus is his language.

The urine, when one has urinated, if he is walking without pants and it falls on the ground – he should distance himself from it by four cubits or go into another room, whether during the recitation of the Shema or during prayer. And although one should not walk from place to place in the middle of prayer, nevertheless in this case it is necessary. And even though it is inevitable that some drops also fell on his knees, we do not worry about this, even if his knees are still wet from the urine (Pri Megadim and A.Z.). If the place is soft ground, which can absorb it quickly so that it will not be wet enough to make something else wet – he is allowed to wait until it is absorbed. We do not worry that he may delay in waiting until it is absorbed to the extent that he could finish the entire Shema, and would need to start over according to Tosafot and the Rosh. What of it? For even if he recites it twice, it is only like reading from the Torah. Therefore, in prayer, he should not wait until it is absorbed, as he might delay significantly and need to start over, causing unnecessary blessings. Therefore, in prayer, in any case, he should distance himself by four cubits and pray immediately. And also in the recitation of the Shema, it is better to do so. All the more so if he is standing in the blessings of the Shema, which is like prayer, and he is obligated to distance himself by four cubits or go into another room. (See Magen Avraham, small section 2, and the matters are tight. It is also better in the recitation of the Shema to distance. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

And all this applies when the urine did not fall on his clothes. But if it fell on his clothes, such as his shirt and pants, and they are damp to the extent that they can make something else wet, the law is as follows: If they are covered by clean clothes, for example, if the outer garment he is wearing is clean from the urine, he can recite [the Shema] in this state. For even with excrement on his clothes, we hold that if it is covered there is no issue, as I wrote in Siman 76, section 8. All the more so with urine. But if they are not covered, such as when he is not wearing an outer garment, or if the outer garment itself is also soiled with urine, he must remove his clothes. This applies to the recitation of the Shema. However, during prayer, where it is not possible to interrupt so much to remove one's clothes, he can pray as he is, even if they are uncovered, since from the Torah it is permitted, as I wrote in the previous Siman, and the prohibition is Rabbinic. And during prayer, they permitted it because it is not possible to manage otherwise (Beit Yosef and Magen Avraham, small section 1).

One who has an illness that causes a constant involuntary dripping of urine, and therefore he would never be able to pray, our teacher, the Rema, wrote in a responsum (Siman 98) that it is permissible to make a garment around the organ. Consequently, his outer clothes will remain clean, and he will be able to go to the synagogue to pray. During the dripping, he should pause and then continue praying. He may start praying when there is no dripping, even though he knows he will have to pause, since it is impossible otherwise. See there.

Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote: If there is human excrement behind him, he needs to distance himself four cubits from the place where the smell ends. Even if he has an illness that prevents him from smelling, he still needs to distance himself four cubits from the place where the smell ends for someone who can smell. And in front of him, he needs to distance himself as far as his eyes can see. Even at night, or if he is blind and cannot see it, he must distance himself to the point where it cannot be seen during the day. And if it is to his side, it has the same rule as if it were behind him. Thus far his words. And the opinion of the Rambam in the third chapter is that he only needs to distance himself behind four cubits and until the smell ends. However, four cubits from the place where the smell ends is not necessary. Most of the decisors disagree with him. (And the Rambam's intention in Halacha 12 is about behind him, as for in front of him – he ruled in Halacha 8 to the extent of his sight. Examine and you will find this to be lenient.)

In regard to the ruling that the sides are considered as behind, this is also the ruling of the Rambam there in Law 8, and so wrote the SeMaG. However, there is someone who disagrees, saying that the sides are considered as in front, as we find regarding a bent lulav in Sukkah (32a). He says that the Rambam is referring to a case where it is impossible to place it behind, then it is considered as behind. But in a place where it is possible, it is considered as in front, as I have written later in Siman 81 (Kesef Mishneh in the name of Rabbeinu Manoach). And there is someone who wrote that the sides in front are considered as in front, and those behind are considered as behind, like with the priests later in Siman 128 (Magen Avraham, Small Paragraph 2).

And these comparisons seem strange to me: for with the lulav, the reason is "hadar" (beauty), and with the priests, the reason is that their blessing is not considered important to him, see there. But here the reason is because of visibility, for from the front one necessarily sees, but from the sides one does not necessarily see. Additionally, concerning matters of prayer, we find regarding passing in front of someone praying that the sides are treated like behind, as I wrote later in Siman 102. It is not comparable to Siman 81 where we distinguish between possible and impossible, for there, when one finds excrement in front of him and is forced to move away from that place, certainly it is better to move behind, and why shouldn't he do so? But here we are discussing seeing excrement from the sides, and there is no need to move from this place. Therefore, we maintain its status, that it is like behind. (And also the Pri Chadash and the Eliyah Rabbah disagree with them, see there. Therefore, it seems in my humble opinion that the main ruling is as I have written.)

And know that these measurements—four cubits and the full range of one's sight as explained—make no distinction whether the excrement is in a courtyard, on the street, in a field and one is reading there, or if one is reading in a house and the excrement is in the same room. These distances are sufficient. We do not say that since the person and the excrement are in the same room, the entire room is considered as four cubits. This was a disputed matter among the Tannaim at the end of the third chapter of Berachot, and the Rif, the Rambam, the Tur, and the Shulchan Aruch in Siman 87 ruled that we do not consider the entire room as four cubits. Refer there. And even though the Ri"tz Giyyot ruled there that it is considered as four cubits, as Rabbeinu Yonah wrote in his name—it is a singular opinion. Refer there. And indeed, one who wishes to be stringent for himself according to this opinion must either leave the room entirely or remove the excrement from there.

And this is what our teacher, the Rema, wrote in paragraph 1: If a prayer leader (chazzan) is praying in a synagogue or a house and there is excrement there, even if it is behind him and far from him, he needs to be silent until it is removed, since he is fulfilling the obligation for many, and it is impossible that none of the congregation is within four cubits of the excrement. Thus are his words. Meaning: even if the excrement is behind all the congregation, nevertheless, certainly some of them are within four cubits. He only considered the congregation, but for the prayer leader himself there is no concern even though they are in the same room, and this is due to the reason explained. And what he wrote: the measure of four cubits – this is from the place where the smell ends. And if the excrement separates between the congregation and the prayer leader – it is prohibited in any case, as I wrote above in Siman 55 regarding the response of "Amen," see there (Magen Avraham, small paragraph 3). And even though now each individual prays by himself, nevertheless he needs to respond "Amen" to the blessings of the prayer leader (Eliyah Rabbah, small paragraph 6). Therefore, in the verses of praise (Pesukei Dezimra) where he does not fulfill their obligation, and there is no "Amen" here – it is permitted for the prayer leader to say them when the excrement is behind him at the distance explained (there, and Magen Avraham there). And if there is urine in the synagogue, and the entire congregation is far from it by four cubits – it is permitted for the prayer leader to pray (Taz, small paragraph 2).

It appears to me that according to what will be explained in Siman 82, even dry excrement that is like earthenware and does not have a bad odor is prohibited. If so, regarding being behind or to the sides, one only needs to distance oneself four cubits. However, in front of oneself, there is no distinction, since the prohibition is as far as the eye can see. Because one sees it, there is no difference whether it has an odor or not. Similarly, for a prayer leader in a synagogue, if for the entire congregation it is behind them and they are distanced by four cubits, it is permissible for him to pray, just as we explained regarding urine.

Even if there is excrement in the house, but it is in a place that is considered a separate domain by itself, such as if it is in a place that is ten handbreadths high and four handbreadths wide, which is the definition of a private domain, or it is in a place that is ten handbreadths deep, and no bad odor reaches from there – it is permitted to recite [prayers]. There are those who permit it even if it is not four handbreadths wide, as long as it is ten handbreadths high – that is sufficient (Taz, Section 3). However, this is not the main opinion. Most of the major authorities agree that it must specifically be ten handbreadths high and four handbreadths wide (Bach, Magen Avraham, and Eliyah Rabbah). Similarly, if the excrement is in another room, even if one is sitting by the door and the smell does not reach him – he may recite [prayers] even if there are not four cubits between him and the excrement. Since the excrement is in a different domain, we apply the verse “and your camp shall be holy.”

According to the Rosh, when excrement is in a different domain, it is permitted even if one can see it. This is also written by the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch in section 3. The reason is that with excrement, there is no prohibition of "and no unseemly thing shall be seen in you," only the positive commandment of "your camp shall be holy." And here, the camp is holy. However, the Rashba holds that if one can see it, it is forbidden, as he believes that there is also a prohibition of "and no unseemly thing shall be seen in you" with excrement. The primary ruling follows the Rosh (Beit Yosef), as I have written in Siman 74, section 4, see there. Nevertheless, one should be concerned with the opinion of the Rashba, which means to close one's eyes or turn one's face away, as in this case even the Rashba agrees that closing the eyes or at night is effective, since it is in a different domain (Magen Avraham, subsection 8). There are those who wrote that according to the Rashba, closing the eyes or night does not help (Eliyah Rabbah, subsection 8). Therefore, it is best to turn one's face away.

In this matter that we have written that a bad smell should not reach, this is also the ruling of the Rambam and the Tur that for a smell, an intervening domain does not help. But some of our rabbis ruled that it does help, just as it helps for the excrement itself, it likewise helps for its bad smell (Rosh and Tosafot R”I in the name of the French rabbis). At first glance, this opinion is not understood: after all, there is still a bad smell? It seems to me that their intention is that its law is like a bad smell that has no substance, which will be explained that it is permitted in the study of Torah (see Prisha who also raised this difficulty, and his solution is strained). And it seems that even according to the first opinion, one does not need to distance oneself four cubits from the place where the smell ends (there). And if the excrement was in this room and they removed it from there, and it is still possible to smell it – it is forbidden according to all opinions until the smell ceases, because the excrement was in this room (Magen Avraham, subsection 9). And one who does not smell – it is permitted (there), since the excrement itself is not present. All the more so when it is in another domain, it is permitted for one who does not smell. (And the words of the Levush require examination, as the Prisha wrote.)

A small courtyard that is completely open to a larger one, and the larger one extends beyond it on the sides – the small courtyard is not considered as a separate entity since it is completely open to the larger one. However, the larger one, since its walls extend beyond those of the small one on both sides, is considered as a separate entity, as I have written in Siman 55 regarding the inclusion in a minyan; see there. Therefore, if there is excrement in the larger courtyard, it is forbidden to read [the Shema] in the smaller one until one distances oneself according to the measures that have been clarified, as it is considered as if the excrement is with the person in the same room. But if the excrement is in the smaller courtyard, it is permissible to read in the larger one without distancing, provided the bad smell does not reach him, as long as people are generally troubled by that smell. And we do not say that the person in the larger courtyard will draw the excrement after him, because since the prohibition is due to the excrement, we follow the excrement and not the person, just as in Siman 55 we follow the majority and not the minority. (The Magen Avraham in subsection 10 wrote that according to the "yesh omrim" (some say) – it is permitted in any case; see there. But according to what I have written in subsection 9 – the permission is only for Torah study; see there. Be precise and you will find leniency.)

And know that even though it ostensibly appears in Eruvin (92b) that any small area is considered as part of the entrance of the larger area, and if so, distancing four cubits would not help, as it pertains to other laws discussed there. And I have seen someone who raised this difficulty against Rabbeinu the Beit Yosef, who wrote in section 3 that distancing does help in the smaller area when the excrement is in the larger area, as I wrote in the previous section. However, in truth, the words of Rabbeinu the Beit Yosef are correct, for certainly the plain meaning of the sugya in Eruvin is indeed so. But that applies to the opinion at the end of the third chapter of Berachot that the entire house is considered as four cubits. But we hold that it is not considered within four cubits, as I wrote in section 4. And according to this opinion, the sugya there is interpreted regarding distancing. (See Mishnah Berurah who remains in wonder, but it is not difficult at all. They did not bother to mention it there because it depends on a dispute. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

And know that according to what has been explained, in a different domain, distancing is not necessary. Therefore, if one is standing in prayer opposite an open window, and a pig passes by in front of the window, distancing is not required. One should simply close their eyes so as not to see it, and also ensure that no foul odor reaches them. Similarly, when performing the sanctification of the moon (Kiddush Levana) and a pig passes in front of them, one must turn their face away or distance themselves as far as their eyesight reaches. Even when turning their face, a distance of four cubits is required, because the appearance of a pig is considered equivalent to passing excrement, as I have written in Siman 76.

Dog and pig excrement—if skins have been placed within them, one must distance oneself from them as from human excrement, for when skins are present, their smell is very foul. If there are no skins within them, their status is the same as that of excrement from other animals, beasts, and birds, where one does not need to distance oneself if they do not have a foul smell due to accumulation and aging, like manure that has been left in one place for a long time, which becomes putrid. If they do have a foul smell, their status is like that of human excrement in all the detailed laws that have been explained.

The soft droppings of a donkey after it comes from the road, and the droppings of a cat and a weasel, and a rotting carcass—all have the same status as human excrement. For typically, their smell is bad. Therefore, even if by chance their smell is not bad, they are forbidden as human excrement (Magen Avraham, section 12). And it appears that for all laws, their status is like human excrement, meaning: behind him, he must distance himself four cubits from the place where the smell ends, and in front of him, as far as his eyes can see. And someone walking on the road, even if he sees the form of an animal in front of him, our master the Beit Yosef wrote in section 5 that if he does not smell it, he need not be concerned about the minority and attribute it to a donkey. And near a city, some say one should be concerned, because most of the animals found there are donkeys, in a place where donkeys are common. This is his wording.

There are those who explain that what is written, "if the smell does not reach him, he need not worry," means that even if there is a smell, but it does not reach him, it is permitted. The question arises: for it is required to distance oneself four cubits from the place where the smell dissipates (Magen Avraham, Section 13). However, the truth is that the intention is that one does not need to worry that there might be a smell (there). This is evident from what is written that one does not need to suspect that it might be from a donkey. However, the Tur wrote that one only needs to distance oneself to the place where the smell dissipates, see there. According to this, indeed, it is not treated like human excrement, which requires distancing four cubits from where the smell dissipates. Therefore, if the smell does not reach him, even though there is a smell, we do not worry about it (there). Nevertheless, in practice, it is difficult to contradict the words of our teacher, the Beit Yosef (see Eliyah Rabbah, Section 14).

In the Jerusalem Talmud, it is forbidden to recite [the Shema] opposite donkey urine that is on the road, and opposite red chicken feces, meaning: when the feces are red. Some say that the red chickens are called "angilas han." Others say that it refers to chickens from the land of Edom, who eat barley and their feces smell bad (Magen Avraham, subsection 14). And some say that any animal, beast, or bird whose feces have a bad smell – it is forbidden to recite [the Shema] opposite them. And some say that any animal that eats bread – it is forbidden to recite [the Shema] opposite its feces, such as dogs and pigs. And any animal that does not generally eat bread – it is permitted (see Taz). The "angilas han" we mentioned is called "indik" in our language, and we do not have a clear ruling on this matter. Certainly, it is proper to be stringent if the smell is foul.

And our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in Section 7: The excrement of chickens that walk in the house has the same status as the excrement of domestic and wild animals and birds (and it is permitted). But their coop has a foul odor and is similar to human excrement. Until here is his language. The same law applies to a cattle pen — it is forbidden to read [the Shema] there when there is a lot of animal excrement (Chayei Adam). Some want to be lenient in this matter, but this is not the main opinion. For it is even forbidden to read opposite a garbage heap if it has a bad smell, as stated in the Gemara (Berachot 25a), and in the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, Section 8. And necessarily, this is when there is no excrement there, for if there is excrement there, it would be forbidden due to the excrement itself. If so, a cattle pen is no less stringent than a garbage heap (and so wrote the Mishnah Berurah).

The smell of excrement is considered a "bad odor that has a substance." The smell from flatulence is considered a "bad odor that does not have a substance," and it is stated in the Gemara there that it is less severe than a bad odor that has a substance. This means that if the flatulence came from another person and it has a bad odor, one is prohibited from reciting the Shema, praying, or reciting blessings until the odor dissipates. However, one is not required to distance oneself four cubits from the place where the odor dissipates, as with excrement. But it is permitted to study Torah even if the odor has not yet dissipated. Only if one himself emitted the flatulence and there is a bad odor is he prohibited from studying Torah until the odor dissipates. The reason is that since a bad odor that does not have a substance is a rabbinic prohibition, leniency is allowed to avoid the neglect of Torah study when the odor comes from another person, as is common in yeshivas where some sleep while others study (Gemara).

Someone who cannot prevent themselves from passing gas and is unable to complete the recitation of the Shema and the prayer without doing so— it is better for the time of the recitation of the Shema and the prayer to pass rather than to pray without a clean body. If the time for prayer has passed, they are considered compelled by circumstances and should pray the afternoon prayer (Mincha) twice. If it seems possible for them to control themselves during the recitation of the Shema, they should put on tefillin between the blessing of "Ahava" and the recitation of the Shema and bless upon them. This is the ruling of the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch, and its source is from the responsa of the Rosh (beginning of Klal 4, see there).

There are those who wrote that this does not seem correct according to the law (the Gra). And there are those who wrote in this language: Even though in the Gemara it only says that one who needs to relieve himself should not pray, this is because it wants to say: And if he prayed, his prayer is an abomination. But here too, it is better not to pray now, than to pray with an unclean body... And all this is when an incident occurred due to stomach upset from some food, in such a way that by the evening he will certainly be able to pray with a clean body. But if he has an illness that causes him to pass gas at all times – he should pray, and when the gas comes, he should remain silent and wait until the odor dissipates. And if he delays to the extent that he can finish the entire prayer – he should start from the beginning (Pri Chadash).

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote in a responsum (Siman 98): Since he did not say there is a prohibition in the matter, but rather it is better for him to wait, since he has the option to pray the Mincha prayer twice. However, someone who is accustomed to this, and if he does not pray, he will be exempt from the prayer forever – it is permissible for him to pray without a clean body. For a rabbinic prohibition does not come and override a Torah obligation, or a prayer which is a communal mitzvah. Thus far his words. And this is similar to what I wrote in the previous section. And indeed, the words of the Tur and Shulchan Aruch are not understood: for even though a makeup prayer is effective for prayer, regarding the recitation of Shema there are opinions whether a makeup is effective, as I wrote at the end of Siman 58, see there (Eliyah Rabbah). And it is more puzzling that in the responsa of the Rosh he did not mention the recitation of Shema at all, only prayer, see there (ibid.).

Therefore, there are some of the great authorities who ruled that in truth, one should not pray the Amidah. Similarly, one should not say the verses of praise (Pesukei Dezimra), as they were instituted because of the prayer. But the Shema should be recited even without a clean body, for prayer is akin to standing before the King, which is not the case with the Shema. And even if he is unable to wear tefillin, he should recite the Shema without tefillin (according to the Gra). He can also say the blessings of the Shema. If he is able to put on tefillin between "Ahavah" and the Shema, he should put them on with a blessing. As for the tallit, it is obvious that he can put it on with a blessing, for it is permitted to enter the bathroom with a tallit (according to the Taz). This is the proper way to instruct. Also, it has been clarified that if someone has an illness causing flatulence, he should definitely pray — this is a clear ruling and the law. (And also the Tur and Shulchan Aruch wrote: It is better to let the time for reading the Shema and prayer pass than to pray... – their intention was only regarding prayer, for they did not write "not recite nor pray" but "not pray." And what they wrote about the time for reading the Shema and prayer means: not to pray to the extent that the time for reading the Shema will pass, even if the time for prayer passes. Examine and you will find it easy. And the morning blessings must be recited.)

We learn at the end of the third chapter of Sukkah (42b): A minor who can eat an olive's bulk of grain – we distance from his excrement and his urine four cubits. This is when he can eat an olive's bulk within the time it takes to eat half a loaf (kedei achilat pras). For an adult, even if he cannot eat within the time it takes to eat half a loaf. And Rashi explained: All five species are called "grain": wheat, barley, spelt, oats, and rye – we distance from his excrement from when he ate an olive's bulk of these, in any manner of eating… until here are his words. Meaning: whether he ate them dry, or he ate them moist or soaked and cooked, as in the food made for an infant called pap (Magen Avraham). And the measure that he eats an olive's bulk of them within the time it takes to eat half a loaf: for an average person, it is four eggs, and according to Rambam, three eggs. But if the minor needs to delay more than this measure – it is like eating half an olive's bulk today and half an olive's bulk tomorrow, as this is a law given to Moses at Sinai that eating does not combine over a long duration (Rashi).

Some say that even if this child is naturally weak and unable to eat an olive's bulk of grain, but has reached the stage where others like him can eat an olive's bulk of grain within the time it takes to eat half a loaf ("k'dei achilat pras"), one must distance oneself from his excrement and urine. This is the opinion of Rabbeinu the Beit Yosef in Section 1, see there. In his major work, he explains that Rashi's opinion is not like this, and according to Rashi, it is required that the child himself be able to eat specifically, see there. And there are those who say that Rashi's opinion is indeed like this (Taz). However, many of the great authorities have ruled according to Rashi and have written that all the poskim agree that it is required that the child himself be able to eat an olive's bulk of grain within the time it takes to eat half a loaf. They have also written that even if he can eat, if it has been several days since he has eaten an olive's bulk of grain, one does not need to distance oneself from his excrement and urine, even though for an adult this is not the case (Bach, Magen Avraham, Eliyah Rabbah, Pri Chadash). For with an adult, there is certainly no difference whether he has eaten or not, or whether he can eat or cannot eat, as one must distance oneself from all of them as explained in the Gemara there.

And know that from the Jerusalem Talmud, Chapter Three (Halacha 5), there is proof for our master, the Beit Yosef. For it says there: It was taught: A child who can eat an olive's bulk of grain – one must distance from his excrement… They asked Rabbi Abbahu: Why must one distance from his excrement…? He said to them: Because his thoughts are evil. They said to him: But isn’t he a child? He said to them: Doesn’t it say: "For the inclination of man's heart is evil from his youth"? It says "from his youth"… Thus far his language. And it is not understood why they asked, "Why must one distance from his excrement," did he not explain earlier because he can eat an olive’s bulk of grain? Rather, it is certainly as our master the Beit Yosef says, that only if he can eat, even though he has not eaten. Consequently, if he reached an age where others can eat, even if he cannot eat – one must distance from his excrement. And thus they asked correctly: Why must one distance from his excrement, if he has not eaten or cannot eat? And he answered them: Because his thoughts are evil. And this is similar to what our sages of blessed memory said in Sukkah there: "He who increases knowledge increases pain." Meaning: that when he reaches this stage – everything he eats becomes putrid (and see Pri Chadash).

There are those who have written that in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 265, Se'if 8, it implies that it is good and proper to distance oneself from the excrement of an infant, even one who is eight days old (Magen Avraham, Se'if Katan 1). His intention is regarding what I wrote there, that one should clean the infant of his excrement before blessing on the circumcision, see there. However, this is not proof: For there, since he is involved with the infant himself to bring him into holiness, it is certainly a beautification of the mitzvah that he should be clean and presentable. This is no less than the beautification of any mitzvah. But what relevance is it to someone who is praying at home or reading the Shema and there is an infant present? And thus it explicitly implies in the large book of our Rabbi, the Beit Yosef, there, see there. There are those who have written that it is not proper to read the Shema near an infant, for an infant typically soils in waste (there, in the name of the Rema). Additionally, they do not wipe themselves. And excrement at the anus, even if it is covered, is forbidden, as I have written in Siman 76 (there). For this reason, if he is wearing a shirt, it is permitted, similar to covered excrement. Therefore, if he is wearing a shirt and it is seen that his hands are clean, there is no concern in this.

The Tur and the Shulchan Aruch wrote in Section 2: If one is reading and sees excrement in front of him, he should walk enough to put it behind him by four cubits. And if this is not possible, for example, if there is a river or something else obstructing him, he should walk enough to put it to the side by four cubits. This is the end of their words. And we have already explained in Section 79, Paragraph 3, that even though the sides have the same law as behind, nevertheless, here where he is compelled to leave the place where he stands because the excrement is in front of him, it is better to put it behind him than to the side if possible.

And know that there is one who questioned: What does it mean "it is impossible to cast it behind him," let him turn his face around (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 3)? And he struggled with this. But in truth, according to what we have explained, there is no difficulty at all, for the sages did not impose any burden on him in this matter. And this is the explanation: if he was reciting the Shema and walking on the way, and he sees excrement in front of him - he should continue on his way until it is cast behind him. And if it is impossible - he should walk so that it is placed to the sides. Meaning to say: that he should not be required to turn his face and stop walking. Rather, he should continue on his way and estimate when it will be placed to the sides.

If he interrupts until it is cast behind him or to the sides, he does not need to return except to the place where he stopped. Because since it was not within his four cubits, he did not need to check. But if he delayed long enough to finish the entire prayer, he returns to the beginning. Rabbeinu Yonah wrote: If he was in a place where he should have considered that there might be excrement, he needs to return to the beginning. Thus far is his language. And the Rashba disagrees with this. The main opinion is that of the Rashba (Beit Yosef), that in front of him, they were not so stringent. Therefore, they did not say his prayer is an abomination (there).

Regarding excrement, how moist must it be to be considered excrement? The Gemara concludes (25a) that Rava said: The halacha is that excrement as hard as pottery is prohibited, and urine is prohibited as long as it is still damp. And what is the case of excrement as hard as pottery? The conclusion is that even if it is so dry that if it were thrown, it would crumble, it is still prohibited until it crumbles by rolling, as it crumbles more easily by being thrown than by being rolled. However, when it crumbles by rolling, it is like dust and permitted. This is the ruling of the Tur. 

And Rambam wrote in the third chapter that if it is drier than pottery, such that if it were thrown it would crumble, it is like dust and one may read the Shema opposite it. Thus are his words. And according to Rabbeinu Yonah, it crumbles more easily by rolling than by being thrown. And Rabbeinu Beit Yosef ruled according to Rambam, and Rabbeinu Rema wrote that the main opinion follows the Tur. (And Magen Avraham wrote that Rambam also holds the stringent opinion, but he agrees with Rabbeinu Yonah that it crumbles more easily by rolling than by being thrown. See there.)

Specifically, crumbling is effective. But if it is broken into two pieces—it is not effective (Magen Avraham). And even if it has no smell, as long as it does not crumble—it is forbidden (ibid. and Beit Yosef). And we have already explained that there is a distinction between it and excrement that has a smell, in that one does not need to distance oneself from it more than four cubits, as I wrote in Siman 79, Section 6. And in cold weather when the excrement has frozen like a stone, since it will return to its original state after the cold—it is forbidden like fresh excrement (ibid., Small Section 2).

And this that they said regarding urine, "as long as it moistens," means that even if it has been greatly absorbed into the ground, if it would dampen a hand, it is forbidden to recite [the Shema] opposite it. Some say that it is only forbidden if it is "moist enough to dampen something else." That is to say, when another object is placed upon it, that object becomes moist and can dampen others. If it does not have so much moisture, it is permitted to recite [the Shema] opposite it. One can rely on this, since it is only a rabbinic prohibition.

Just as it is forbidden to recite [Shema or other sacred texts] opposite excrement, so too it is forbidden to recite opposite a bathroom. And even if the excrement has been removed from it, because it once contained excrement – it is repulsive and remains forbidden, and we do not fulfill with it the verse "and your camp shall be holy." However, regarding a new bathroom, there is a question in the Gemara (Berachot 26a) whether designating it as a bathroom is effective or not. In other words: in all matters, we hold that “designation is not significant.” But concerning a bathroom, perhaps because it is something repulsive, we are concerned even with its designation. And it is stated in the Gemara there that the doubt is only whether it is permissible to read and pray inside it. But opposite it – it is certainly permissible if it is new and has not yet contained excrement. And so have ruled the Rambam in the third chapter, the Rosh there, the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch, section 2. The opinion of the Raavad is that it is also permissible inside, since it is a rabbinic doubt, and in all of the Torah we hold that “designation is not significant.” And this also seems to be the opinion of the Rif. In any case, we hold it to be prohibited, as this is the opinion of the majority of the authorities. And even contemplating [sacred matters] is forbidden. There are those who are lenient regarding contemplation (Atret Zekenim, and see Beit Yosef).

And it is explicitly understood in the Gemara there that facing a bathroom is forbidden even as far as the eye can see, just like facing excrement, and from behind it, four cubits from the place where the smell ends. And so the later authorities have written. According to this, for the opinion that will be explained that partitions do not help for a bathroom, even in a large and clean courtyard, when there is a bathroom at the end of the courtyard – one should not make any blessing when facing the bathroom. And closing one's eyes does not help, as I wrote at the beginning of Siman 79. Likewise, night does not help, as I wrote there. However, regarding the primary law of partitions, we have another way, as will be explained with Heaven’s help in paragraph 6.

And know that there is no difference in the designation of a place as a bathroom, whether his intention was to designate it temporarily or permanently. Similarly, a bathroom that was made temporarily is treated the same as one made permanently. However, it is certain that if one happened to relieve himself in a certain place without the intention of making it a bathroom, it does not acquire the status of "bathroom." And when the excrement is removed, everything is permitted. Similarly, even an old bathroom that was dismantled and all its structure nullified, and the place was cleaned and the soil leveled so that it no longer appears as a bathroom, is also permitted. For even in matters of impurity, a change in the act can nullify its previous impurity, and all the more so in this case (so it seems according to my humble opinion).

He said, "This house is for a bathroom," and he said about another house, "And also this one" – the second house has the same status as the first one, and it is designated for a bathroom. Opposite it – it is permitted, inside it – it is forbidden, as I wrote in section 1. And we do not say: since the designation itself is only doubtful, and according to the Raavad it is entirely permitted as I wrote there; and if so, although we are stringent regarding its interior, this applies to the first designation where he mentioned "bathroom." But the other house that is dependent on the first one and he did not mention about it the term "bathroom" – it is entirely permitted. We do not say this, and its status is the same as the first. However, if he did not say about the second house "and also this" but "and this house," even though it is more likely to interpret that his intention is also that this house should also be for a bathroom, because if his intention was for another use, why did he associate it with the matter of the bathroom? Nevertheless, since it can be interpreted with difficulty in this manner – it is doubtful whether he designated it for this or not. Therefore, one should not read in it initially, but if one read – he has fulfilled his obligation, because the primary nature of the designation is very lenient. (This seems to me the explanation of the Sugya in Nedarim 7b, and the words of the Tur Shulchan Aruch section 3. Investigate and you will find leniency.)

And know that our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section A that the prohibition to read (Shema or other sacred texts) opposite a bathroom applies only when it has no partitions. But if it has partitions, even if there is excrement inside, one may read opposite it nearby without concern, as long as there is no foul smell reaching him. Thus are his words. And many poskim (halachic decisors) agree with him (the Levush, the Bach, and the Ma'adanei Yom Tov), but they require that the partitions be ten tefachim high. However, the commentators on the Shulchan Aruch disagreed with him and wrote that certainly all bathrooms in the time of the Talmud had partitions, as the Tosafot wrote in Sukkah (36b). And if so, when it was said that it is forbidden opposite a bathroom, this means even if it has partitions. The reason is that partitions made for the sake of a bathroom have the same status as the bathroom itself. And there must be another partition outside the partitions of the bathroom, or the partition must be made for the sake of a house, but the bathroom is adjacent to it on the other side. In that case, it is permitted to read and pray opposite this partition (Taz, and the Magen Avraham is somewhat uncertain about this, see there). And behold, even according to this opinion, on the railways where one sits in the wagons, and in front of him there is a bathroom where one of the walls of the wagon serves also as the bathroom wall, it is plainly permitted to pray and read and bless opposite it. (For even the Taz permits in this manner, and the Magen Avraham is also uncertain about the primary ruling of the Beit Yosef, for he wrote: and one who is lenient should ensure that at least the partitions are ten tefachim high. Thus are his words, see there.)

In my humble opinion, it seems that the words of our master, the Beit Yosef, are correct. Even according to what Tosafot wrote that they had partitions, it is still clearly proven at the beginning of Tamid (27b) that they did not have a door that could be opened. For it says there: "Rav Safra was sitting in the bathroom. Rabbi Abba came and coughed...," and Rashi explains that there was no door to open. Rather, this was the custom: a person who wanted to enter would cough, and if there was someone inside, they would cough in response... Thus far his words. And this explanation is necessary: a bathroom that had a door was called a "dignified bathroom," as it is taught in the Mishnah at the beginning of Tamid that this was the case in the Temple. And this is the language of the Mishnah: "And there was a fire there, and a dignified bathroom. And this was its honor: if it was found locked, it was known that there was someone inside. If open, it was known that there was no one inside." See there. Therefore, among us, some call the bathroom "the dignified house" because it has a door. But a plain "bathroom" did not have a door, and therefore it is correctly stated in the Gemara at the end of the third chapter of Berachot that it is forbidden to recite [the Shema] opposite it, meaning opposite the opening, because excrement is visible there. But in our case – it is indeed a complete partition.

"And there is further clear evidence that there are latrines without any partitions at all. For it is stated at the end of Berachot: Rabbi Akiva said, 'Once I followed Rabbi Yehoshua into the latrine, and I learned three things from him: that one should not defecate facing east and west, but only north and south...' (see there). And it is certain that if Rabbi Yehoshua had been sitting in a latrine with partitions, Rabbi Akiva would not have been able to see him. For it is obvious that he was not inside the partitions with him. Furthermore, if there were complete partitions, one could see the seating place even when it is unoccupied, like in our latrines, where one must sit in only one place. Rather, it is certain that it was without partitions, and he could sit in any direction he wished. And Rabbi Akiva stood behind him and saw how he sat. And it cannot be said that there were partitions without an entrance, for in such a case, the seating place would still be evident in any direction. Moreover, if this were the case, Rabbi Akiva would have had to stand facing him, which is certainly something he would not have done. Rather, it is certain that he stood behind him, and even for this, they said to him: 'To this extent, you have been brazen before your teacher?' And he replied, 'It is Torah, and I need to learn,' (see there)."

And even according to the language of the Tosafot that there were partitions there, and let us say that they were on all four sides, it is possible to say that these were low partitions, just slightly above the seating area. And the main matter is as follows: Certainly there are partitions for the bathroom itself, meaning the partitions of the seating area, which are considered like the excrement itself. But the partitions built around the seating area – their status is like the partitions of a house in regard to “opposite it.” And the law that was explained regarding one who says “this house is for a bathroom” also applies to the inside of the house. And furthermore, I ask: even those who disagree agree that if a partition is made before the partition of the bathroom, it is effective. If so, these partitions are also considered as prior to the partition of the bathroom, because the main partitions of the bathroom are the partitions of the seating area. Therefore, it appears in my humble opinion that one can rely on the words of Rabbeinu Beit Yosef and the decisors who agreed with his words, that a bathroom which has partitions around it on all four sides, one can read opposite the partitions as long as the bad odor does not reach him. (And with what we have explained, all the proofs of the Taz and the Magen Avraham are removed – see there carefully. And be precise and you will find it easy.)

Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote in Section 4: A latrine that is dug into the ground, with its opening four cubits away from the pit, and it is made on a slope in such a way that the feces roll and immediately fall far away, and similarly, the urine immediately flows into the pit – it is considered as if it were sealed and it is permissible to recite [the Shema] there if there is no foul odor, and also if people do not urinate outside the pit. However, if they sometimes urinate there – it is forbidden to contemplate Torah thoughts there, all the more so to recite the Shema. Until here his words. Nevertheless, it is permissible opposite it, as is the law regarding urine. (Taz, Section 2. And see Taz, Section 1, where he is certain there are partitions here. There is no proof, see there. Be precise and you will find an easy solution.)

It is further written in Section 5: People who have a bench with a hole and defecate on it – it is permissible to recite the Shema in front of it, since the excrement is not on the hole, and there is no vessel underneath the hole. Additionally, the hole is always covered by a board. Thus far his language. However, there are those who disagree with this, and they hold that this bench has the status of a full-fledged bathroom, and one is obligated to remove it or cover it all around. Similarly, in houses that have small chairs for children, if their excrement is prohibited as explained in Siman 81 – these chairs also have the status of a bathroom, and they must be removed or covered (Magen Avraham, subsection 5). And this is how one should rule.

The Rambam wrote at the beginning of the third chapter: One should not read (Torah) in a bathhouse, nor in a bathroom even if there is no excrement there, nor in a cemetery, nor beside a corpse itself... And anyone who reads in a place where one should not read – must reread. End of his words. And the Raavad disagrees on the matter of "reading beside a corpse," see there. And Rabbeinu Beit Yosef above at the end of Siman 71 ruled like the Rambam, and wrote the reason that the Sages penalized him, see there.

It is stated in Shabbat (10a): One who enters a bathhouse, in a place where people stand clothed – there one may recite the Shema and pray, and it goes without saying that one may greet with "Shalom." One may also wear tefillin, and it goes without saying that one does not remove them. In a place where people stand both naked and clothed – there one may greet with "Shalom," but one may not recite the Shema or pray, and one does not remove tefillin, though one does not put them on initially. In a place where people stand naked – there one may not greet with "Shalom," and it goes without saying that one may not recite the Shema or pray, and one should remove tefillin, and it goes without saying that one does not put them on. See there. For they had three sections in the bathhouse: the innermost section where they would wash, the middle section where they would dress and undress, and the outer section where, after dressing, they would sit to rest a bit. Therefore, part of the middle section is considered like a bathhouse, and part is not. The outer section is entirely not like a bathhouse even though it is named after the bathhouse. The innermost section is treated like a bathroom. Greeting with "Shalom" involves using G-d's name. Some are particular not to call a man whose name is "Shalom" by his name in the bathhouse, because "Shalom" is one of the names of the Holy One, blessed be He, as stated there. But in a foreign language like "Salaam" or something similar – it is permitted (Magen Avraham and Bach). Some permit it entirely, because one does not intend anything other than the man's name (Taz). It is obvious that in filthy alleyways it is also forbidden to greet with "Shalom."

A new bathhouse that has not yet been used for bathing – it is permissible to pray within it. In this regard, it is more lenient than a bathroom, because a bathhouse is not as repulsive as a bathroom. However, an old bathhouse, even if no one is currently using it – it is forbidden (Gemara there). There is an opinion that the same applies to the ritual baths where women immerse – that it is forbidden to recite blessings there. But this is not the case, and this has already been clarified in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 200; see there. The Rambam wrote that it is permissible to say "Rachum" (Merciful) in a bathhouse. The Ra'avad disagreed with this. The primary ruling follows the Rambam, since this term can also be used for a person, unlike "Shalom" (Peace) (Kesef Mishneh and Taz). If one wants to drink in the bathhouse – one should make the blessing in the outer room with the intention of drinking in the inner room (see Taz).

If a person asks a question about a halachic matter in a bathhouse, it is forbidden to answer him. Even to tell him "we do not answer halachic questions in a bathhouse" is also forbidden. Only in the middle room is it permitted to tell him that we do not answer halachic questions in a bathhouse. In the outer room, one may give him the ruling. However, to prevent someone from committing a transgression, it is permitted even in the bathhouse (Shabbat 40b), for example, if one sees someone intending to do something prohibited, one must tell him that it is forbidden to do so. There is no difference whether one speaks in secular language or in Hebrew (ibid). It is forbidden to contemplate matters of Torah in a bathhouse. However, if his learning is fluent in his mouth and he involuntarily thinks about it, there is no prohibition (Zevachim 102b). The same applies in a restroom (ibid. and see Beit Yosef in Siman 85).

It was taught (24b): If one was walking in filthy alleyways, he should not recite the Shema. Moreover, if he was already reciting it, he must stop. If he did not stop, Scripture says about him...: "For he has despised the word of the Lord." And if he did stop, what is his reward? Scripture says about him: "And through this thing you will prolong your days." And when he exits from there, he completes the recitation of the Shema. Even if he waited long enough to finish the entire Shema, our master, the Beit Yosef, ruled that he only needs to resume from where he stopped. This is the approach of the Rif and the Rambam, who hold that only in prayer does one need to return to the beginning, as I wrote in Siman 65. Our master the Rema wrote that there are those who say one should return to the beginning, following the opinion of the Tosafot and the Rosh, as explained there.

Even to contemplate words of Torah is forbidden in filthy places, in the bathhouse, and in the bathroom. The term "filthy place" refers to places where there is excrement or urine. Even the laws of the bathhouse should not be contemplated in the bathhouse, and similarly, the laws of the bathroom should not be contemplated in the bathroom. Therefore, one should think of their financial accounts there, to avoid coming to contemplate Torah (Magen Avraham). Mundane matters are permitted to be spoken there in Hebrew, though it is a measure of piety to be stringent (ibid). Similarly, terms such as "Merciful," "Faithful," and the like may be spoken there. But names that cannot be erased must not be mentioned or contemplated. Additionally, it is forbidden to greet someone there. It has already been clarified that to prevent a transgression, it is permitted even in Hebrew and regarding sacred matters. Similarly, if one has a lewd thought, it is permitted to contemplate words of Torah, as it is like preventing a transgression (ibid). It has already been clarified in Siman 74 that opposite nakedness, it is permitted to contemplate (ibid). Our master the Rema wrote that in a place where it is permitted to contemplate words of Torah, it is permitted to issue a ruling, provided the reasoning is not stated. These are his words. When not speaking in a manner of instruction, but rather saying, "Do this and that for me," it is permitted, even though a ruling can be derived from it (ibid). Someone who is naked may not hear a blessing from another, nor may they answer "Amen." See Yoreh De'ah, Siman 1 (ibid).

Just as one must distance themselves from excrement and urine, so too must one distance themselves from putrid waters and from soaking water used for soaking flax or hemp, as well as the soaking water of washers in which they wash children's clothes that have excrement on them. Similarly, from vomit that has a foul odor or putrid phlegm, and likewise in a place where wastewater is collected in a vessel for a long time and it becomes foul-smelling – one must distance themselves from this. Also, from putrid mikvahs – a woman is prohibited from reciting a blessing in them. And if someone has caused a foul matter to be near a synagogue, they are obligated to remove it from there, even if it preceded the synagogue, because it is a matter of prohibition (see Sha'arei Teshuvah).

The measure for distancing oneself from these things: The Tur wrote that it is like excrement, in front of him as far as his eyes can see, and behind him four cubits from where the smell ends, see there. This is also implied in the Mishnah (22b), where it is taught: "One should not cover oneself with foul water and soaking water… And how far should one distance oneself from them and from the excrement? Four cubits." This shows they are equated with excrement. But Rashi explained there: "And how far should one distance oneself from them – from urine?" see there. Similarly, Rambam wrote in his commentary on the Mishnah, see there, and he also wrote in his code, Chapter Three, Law 8, see there. Furthermore, in Chapter Two of the Laws of the Recitation of the Shema, Law 7, he wrote this law concerning foul water and soaking water without mentioning any distancing at all, see there. This requires further analysis regarding the law.

And know that the Rambam in the fourth chapter of Hilchot Tefillah, Law 9, wrote that the great sages would not pray in a house that had beer, nor in a house that had fish brine at the time of its fermentation, because its smell is foul... until here is his wording. And the meaning is not that its smell is as foul as filth, for if so, it would be prohibited by law. Rather, the meaning is that the intensity of the smell for someone unaccustomed to it is difficult to tolerate, similar to the smell of intoxication. And so wrote Rashi in Eruvin (65a), see there. And this is not similar to all the foul smells that have been explained.

It was taught at the end of the third chapter (Berakhot 25b): A chamber pot (geraf) of excrement and a urinal (avit) of urine – it is forbidden to recite the Shema opposite them, even if they are empty. The geraf and avit are both earthenware vessels, but the one for excrement is called "geraf" and the one for urine is called "avit" (Rashi). As for the urine itself – until water is poured into it. Our rabbis deduced: From the fact that the remedy of pouring water is not taught for the geraf and avit – we learn that it does not help. And if you ask: How is it possible that the vessel for urine is more severe than the urine itself? Indeed, this is the case, because when the urine itself is mixed with water, it is nullified. But the vessels in which the filth is absorbed – the filth is not mixed with the water, and the filth remains fully intact. Therefore, their law is exactly like excrement, that in front of them one must distance as far as the eye can see, and behind them four cubits from where the odor ends (Tur).
