And even if they do not have a bad smell – it is forbidden, as this is like a bathroom that does not contain excrement (Magen Avraham, subsection 1, in the name of the Rosh). The distancing is also from in front of them as far as the eye can see, and from behind them four cubits from the vessel.

Specifically, when they are made of earthenware, the grime is significant in them when feces and urine have been placed in them several times, because they absorb a lot. But metal, glass, and glazed earthenware, which is called "glaze," and this is our "poliva" – it is permitted if they are well washed and have no bad smell, because these do not absorb much, and the grime is not significant in them. There are those who say that since it will be explained later in Siman 551 that for glass vessels, boiling does not help – the same law applies here that glass is treated like earthenware (Taz, subsection 2). And I am astonished: what does this have to do with that? For our eyes see that they are as clean as metal vessels when they are washed, and if so, what prohibition applies here? In boiling, the reason is different, for we say that the absorption of the prohibition is not expelled. And in this matter, many disagree as explained there. But regarding grime – we see that it does not have it. (And so it is written in Ba'er Heitev and Sha'arei Teshuvah, that Yad Aharon and Birkei Yosef disagree with him, and also the Eliyah Rabbah disagrees with him, see there. And therefore, it is simply permitted. Additionally, the Taz wrote in subsection 3 that Tosafot permits other vessels by placing water in them, see there. And I did not find this in Tosafot. And know that the coating of earthenware vessels must be inside and outside.)

A wooden pot and chamber pot appear to have the same status as earthenware vessels. Those made of stone have the status of metal vessels; similarly, those made of bone, as our eyes see that they are clean and do not absorb much filth. Those made of plaster and gypsum have the status of earthenware vessels. Additionally, there are many white earthenware vessels that are smooth, yet their status remains that of earthenware vessels (this seems to be the case according to my humble opinion).

A pottery or wooden chamber pot that has been turned upside down – some permit it because it functions like a cover. Others prohibit it because since the filth is absorbed inside it, the entire vessel is like excrement and requires covering with another item. However, if it is made of metal, even if it is not washed inside, turning it over is effective because its prohibition is only from its interior, and turning it over is like covering it. Similarly, for all vessels that have the same status as metal vessels, covering is effective. This also applies to glass vessels, even though the filth is visible – covering is effective for excrement even if it is visible, as I wrote in Siman 76. If one covered the chamber pot, and a foul smell emanates from it, whether it is earthenware and washed, or metal and not washed – one must distance oneself four cubits from the point where the smell ends. But if it is metal and washed – it is sufficient to distance oneself only until the point where the smell ends (Derech HaChaim).

One of the great scholars wrote that it is proper for a person to accustom himself to have a metal or glass container, which should be washed and clean, and to pour a quarter-log of water into it when urinating in it. Then, it is permitted for him to recite the blessing "Asher Yatzar" and to study beside it. If it is clean and does not emit a foul odor, it is sufficient to wash it from one Sabbath eve to the next (Eliyah Rabbah in the name of the Shnei Luchot HaBrit).

It is permissible to recite the Shema in a house that contains excrement and urine, or a chamber pot and a bedpan, as long as one distances oneself from them according to the measurements that have been elucidated. We do not say that the whole house is like four cubits, as this is the halachic ruling at the end of the third chapter of Berachot, as I have written in Siman 79. Similarly, if one covers them with a vessel, even though they are in the house with him, they are considered as if they are buried, and it is permitted to recite and pray opposite them.

If there is in the house a bed that is ten handbreadths high, and its partitions reach the ground on the sides facing the house, and even if they do not reach the ground but are within three handbreadths of the ground, which is considered as if they do (lavud), and excrement or a bedpan is placed behind the bed, the bed is considered a "partition," and it is permitted to recite [prayers] in front of the bed as long as the bad smell does not reach him, and he does not see it with his eyes. Some require that the bed reach from wall to wall, otherwise it is not considered a partition (Magen Avraham, subsection 4). This is puzzling: why should this matter to us? Others disagree with this (see Mishnah Berurah). If the bedpan is under the bed, and its partitions reach the ground or are within less than three handbreadths from the ground, even if the bed is not ten handbreadths high, it is considered covered, and it is permitted to recite [prayers] opposite it, as long as no smell reaches him. Specifically, if the bedpan is placed behind the bed, the permission is due to the partition, so it needs to be ten handbreadths high. But if it is under the bed, it is considered covered and does not need to be ten handbreadths high. However, a bed whose sides are three handbreadths high from the ground, as well as our tables and chairs whose partitions do not reach within three handbreadths of the ground, are neither considered a partition nor a cover, and are treated as if they are standing in the house. Most of our beds are more than three handbreadths high from the ground. Therefore, it is not effective until it is removed or covered according to the laws explained.

Maimonides wrote at the end of the Laws of Reading the Shema: All those who are impure are obligated in the recitation of the Shema and bless before and after it, even while in their state of impurity, even though they can purify themselves from their impurity on that very day, such as those who touch a creeping creature or a menstruating woman or a woman with a discharge and similar cases. Ezra and his court decreed that only those who experienced a seminal emission should not read words of Torah until they immerse themselves. This decree did not spread among all of Israel, and the majority of the public could not uphold it, therefore it was nullified. And all of Israel is accustomed to reading from the Torah and reciting the Shema even when they have had a seminal emission, since words of Torah do not become impure, as it is stated: "Are not My words like fire, says the Lord" – just as fire does not become impure, so too the words of Torah do not become impure. Up to here is his wording.

The reason Ezra instituted immersion for those who had a seminal emission is because it came from lightheadedness (Tur). Additionally, so that Torah scholars would not be constantly with their wives like roosters (Talmud 22a). From the words of Rambam, it appears that it was not the sages who annulled it, but rather it was annulled on its own because people could not uphold this ordinance. This is also implied by the language of the Talmud there, which says: "The world has adopted..." And even though it says there "they annulled the immersion," it can be interpreted that after it became customary, the sages reinforced this practice. Therefore, we find in the Mishnah that they adhered to this ordinance, as it had not yet been annulled. Even now, there are those who are meticulous and observe immersion for those with a seminal emission, and this is not considered as going against the ordinance of the sages who commanded its annulment. In truth, it was not the sages who decreed its annulment; rather, the people themselves adopted this practice, and the sages agreed to it due to the neglect of Torah study and procreation. Therefore, even now one can be stringent with this immersion, as long as it does not cause the missing of the time for reciting Shema or communal prayer. And Rambam testified in a responsum that he never in his life neglected this immersion.

Our rabbis, the authors of the Tosafot, wrote there that there are those who interpret that the annulment was only for Torah study and not for prayer. However, Rabbi Yitzchak (R"i) interpreted that there is no distinction, see there. Similarly, this was written by the Rambam, the Rosh, and all the legal decisors. Some of the Geonim said that although they annulled the requirement for immersion, nevertheless, washing with nine kavim of water is required. However, our legal decisors disputed this, as the Tur wrote that neither immersion nor washing with nine kavim is required. This immersion can even be with drawn water, as it is stated in the eighth chapter of Mikvaot. And even according to the enactment of Ezra, it is only required for a full seminal emission that shoots like an arrow. But if he saw fragmented emissions, immersion is not required even according to the enactment (Magen Avraham, subsection 1). And the nine kavim must be specifically from three vessels, no more. And there should be no interruption from the pouring of the first until he begins with the second, and similarly from the second to the third (Taz, subsection 1).

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote: "There are those who write that a menstruating woman should not enter the synagogue during her days of menstruation, nor pray, nor mention God's name, nor touch a holy book. And there are those who say she is permitted to do all these things, and this is the main opinion. However, the custom in these regions follows the first opinion, while during the days of purification, they have practiced leniency. Even in places where they have the custom to be stringent, nevertheless, on the High Holy Days and similar occasions when many gather to go to the synagogue, they are permitted to go to the synagogue like other women, because it is a great sadness for them if everyone gathers and they must stand outside." Thus is his language. "And from the first day of Selichot, it is considered 'High Holy Days' (Magen Avraham, subsection 3). And when they go, they may also pray. Similarly, after childbirth, when women customarily go to the synagogue, or at the wedding of their son or daughter, they may go and pray (ibid). Even during her menstruation, she is obligated to recite the Grace After Meals, which is a Torah obligation, provided they are clean from blood and filth (see there in Magen Avraham). And she should not look at the Torah scroll during its elevation (Taz)."

The Rambam writes at the beginning of the Laws of Prayer: It is a positive commandment to pray every day, as it is said: "And you shall serve the Lord, your God." From tradition, they learned that this service is prayer, as it is said: "And to serve Him with all your heart." The sages said: What is the service of the heart? This is prayer. The number of prayers is not from the Torah, nor is the formula of the prayer from the Torah, nor is there a fixed time for prayer from the Torah. Therefore, women and slaves are obligated to pray because it is a positive commandment that is not time-bound. Rather, the obligation of this commandment is as follows: A person should supplicate and pray every day, and recount the praises of the Holy One, blessed be He, and then ask for his needs that he requires in a request and supplication, and afterward give praise and thanks to God for the goodness that He has bestowed upon him. Each according to his ability. This is the language of the Rambam.

And behold, according to the opinion of the Rambam, prayer every day is a positive commandment, as he explained in the Book of Commandments, Commandment 5. And in the Sifrei, they said likewise. The Ramban disputes him there, and holds that prayer is of rabbinic origin, as is well-known throughout the Shulchan Aruch that prayer is rabbinic. According to the Rambam, it pertains to the formulation and times of prayer. And what they said, if one is in doubt whether he prayed or not, he does not repeat the prayer (Berakhot 21a) – this also refers to the fixed prayer. Additionally, since the doubt concerns one prayer, if he prayed two prayers, he fulfills his obligation from the Torah. Similarly, regarding a person who had a seminal emission, they said there that he should not pray, this refers to the fixed prayer. However, he should supplicate before God for his needs without mentioning the Name of God, and he fulfills his obligation from the Torah. Likewise, when they said that women are obligated in prayer – it does not refer to the fixed prayer but rather that they are obligated to supplicate before God in prayer and supplications. This will be further clarified with the help of Heaven in Siman 106.

However, one might ask: From where does the Rambam derive that the obligation of prayer from the Torah includes first proclaiming the praise of the Holy One, blessed be He, then asking for one's needs, and afterwards giving praise and thanks? From where does he derive this? We have only learned this from "And you shall serve…" (Exodus 23:25). It seems to me that it is derived from what we say (Berachot 32a): A person should always arrange the praise of the Omnipresent first, and then pray. And we learned this from Moses our teacher, see there. Hence, when the Torah commanded us to pray, it implicitly commanded us to first arrange the praise of the Holy One, blessed be He. And from what we say there (Berachot 34a): The first blessings are like a servant arranging the praise of his master…, the middle blessings are like a servant requesting a reward from his master, the last blessings are like a servant who has received a reward and takes his leave. Meaning: he gives thanks to his master. And since it is an obligation to do so before a human king, it is all the more so before the King of Kings, the Holy One, blessed be He. For this reason, the Men of the Great Assembly also established it this way, and therefore when the Torah obligated us in prayer, it implicitly obligated us in this manner as well.

And it appears to me in my humble opinion that even according to the Ramban, it does not mean that the primary obligation is Rabbinic and that from the Torah there is no obligation at all to pray. For this is not a logical position at all. Rather, he says that it is not counted in the enumeration of the commandments, and its law is like all Rabbinic laws, where in cases of doubt, we are lenient. And this is similar to what the Ramban himself wrote regarding the prohibitions of Shabbat, where it is established that buying and selling on Shabbat is Rabbinic. This does not mean that from the Torah it is permitted to sit in a shop on Shabbat, for if so, it would not be Shabbat at all. And Nehemiah indeed cried out about this, that they were desecrating the Shabbat. Rather, the intention is certainly that the prohibition is from the Torah, but it does not fall under the categories of labors for which one would be liable for stoning. However, the prohibition is from the Torah. So wrote the Ritva in the name of the Ramban.

And so I say: How is it possible to say that we should not pray at all to our Father in Heaven? For indeed, worship is one of the three pillars of the world. And now, due to our many sins, we no longer have the Temple, and we are left only with prayer. And we, like the eyes of servants upon the hand of their master, how is it possible that we should not plead before Him, blessed be He, every day? Moreover, I bring proof from the Ramban himself, who wrote there, and this is his language: "And the essence of the verse 'to serve Him with all your heart' - a positive commandment that our service to the Almighty should be with all our heart, meaning: with the proper intention... as in the matter of 'and you shall love...' that the commandment is to love Hashem with all one's heart..." Until here is his language. If so, it follows that prayer is included in this, as this is service with the proper intention. And how can we depict love of Hashem if we do not pray to Him at all? Additionally, it is known that the Ramban's opinion is that the blessing on the Torah before studying it is a positive commandment from the Torah, as I wrote at the beginning of Siman 47; see there. And this is the language of the Ramban there: "We are commanded to give thanks to His Name for the great goodness He has done for us by giving us His Torah..." Until here is his language. If so, how is it possible to say that we are not obligated to give thanks to His Name, blessed be He, for the kindnesses and miracles He does for us at every moment and every hour? And how shall we not seek His mercy every day for our creation and our sustenance? Is there a greater obligation than this? Rather, it is certain, as I wrote, that there is an obligation from the Torah to pray every day, except that it is not included in the count of the mitzvot.

It appears to me, in my humble opinion, that according to the Ramban, it is not considered among the specific commandments because it is of a higher nature. Prayer is akin to standing before the king and speaking with him face to face, as it were. Therefore, it should be done while standing, in awe and reverence. During the repetition of the prayer by the leader of the congregation, we sanctify His holiness like the angels above. Our sages, of blessed memory, called it "matters that stand at the pinnacle of the world," and from the prayers, crowns of glory are made for Him, as explained in the Midrashim. It encompasses all the commandments, like the spine that supports the entire body of a person. It does not fall under the category of the 248 limbs and 365 sinews because it is not specific but rather general. Similarly, prayer does not fall under specific commandments because it is a general matter. This is also in accordance with the wisdom of the esoteric teachings (as well as the brain, heart, and liver).

King David, peace be upon him, said, "Evening, morning, and noon I will speak and moan, and He will hear my voice." And he also said, "Let my prayer be set forth as incense before You" – thus, prayer is as significant as incense. The righteous Daniel, even when he was in a position of greatness, prayed three times a day, as it is written: "And three times a day he kneeled upon his knees, and prayed, and gave thanks before his God." He risked his life for prayer, and for this, he was thrown into the lions' den. The Men of the Great Assembly, among whom there were several prophets and 120 elders, did not labor in vain. They arranged the order of prayer for us with their holy spirit, and every single word stands at the height of the world. Heaven forbid that we should change even the slightest part of their formula, even as small as the tip of a yod. Certainly, those heretics who changed the wording of the prayer from the Holy Tongue to a foreign language have no share in the God of Israel and His holy Torah. Their arrogance is as their folly, for how can one dare in our generations to change what the ancestors of the world, 120 elders, including several prophets like Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi, Ezra and Nehemiah, Zerubbabel, and Joshua the son of Jehozadak the high priest, established? As the Sefer Mitzvot Gadol (SmaG) wrote in Mitzvah 19, see there, and likewise the Rambam there. The minor differences between the Ashkenazi and Sephardi rites are not considered changes, for both have been accepted from the earliest times. They are all equal in the number of blessings and the main elements, and both are the words of the living God. We have already written about this in Siman 68, see there.

They instituted the first three blessings as praise to God, and the last three as thanksgiving, while the middle blessings contain requests for all the needs of the world. As the Rambam wrote there: they are like the archetypes for all the desires of each individual and for the needs of the entire community. Thus far his words. And anyone who examines those holy prayers meticulously will find in them wonderful matters even according to the plain meaning, and certainly, they hinted in each blessing at matters that reach the heights of the universe. It is not for nothing that the sages said that prayer is a divine need.

And they established that the number of prayers should correspond to the number of sacrifices: two prayers each day corresponding to the two daily offerings, the morning offering and the afternoon offering. And every day that has an additional offering, like Shabbat, Yom Tov, and Rosh Chodesh, they established a third prayer called the Musaf prayer. The morning prayer corresponds to the morning offering, and the Mincha prayer corresponds to the afternoon offering. They also established that a person should pray one prayer at night, called the Maariv prayer, corresponding to the limbs of the afternoon offering that would burn and consume throughout the night, as it is said: "It is the burnt offering on the hearth... all night." As David said: "Evening, morning, and noon I will speak..." and like Daniel who prayed three times a day as I wrote. The Maariv prayer is not obligatory like the Shacharit and Mincha prayers, since it does not correspond to an independent offering. Nevertheless, all of Israel in all their places of dwelling have the custom to pray Maariv and have accepted it upon themselves as obligatory.

And so they instituted a prayer after the Mincha prayer on a public fast day close to sunset, in order to add supplication and request because of the fast. This prayer is called "Ne'ilah," meaning: the gates of heaven are locked before the sun and it sets (Rambam). And we only pray it on Yom Kippur alone, because we hold (Pesachim 54b): there is no public fast day outside the Land of Israel. And even Tisha B'Av is not considered a public fast day regarding Ne'ilah (ibid). Therefore, on every day there are three prayers, and on Shabbat, Yom Tov, and Rosh Chodesh there are four, and on Yom Kippur there are five. And it is also said in the Gemara (Berachot 26b) that Avraham instituted the Shacharit prayer, Yitzchak instituted the Mincha prayer, and Yaakov instituted the Ma'ariv prayer. And we derive this from the verses, see there. And so it is in the Jerusalem Talmud at the beginning of the chapter "Tefillat Hashachar." And it also implies there that prayer is an obligation from the Torah, from the verse "and to serve Him" according to the opinion of the Rambam, see there.

Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote in Section 1: The time for the morning prayer ideally begins with the sunrise, as it is written: "They shall fear You with the sun." However, if one prayed from the break of dawn when the eastern sky lights up, they have fulfilled their obligation. Its time extends until the end of the fourth hour, which is one-third of the day. This is his language, and so is the language of the Tur, who wrote: The time for the morning prayer begins from the break of dawn when the eastern sky lights up... see there. Similarly, the language of the Rosh at the beginning of the chapter "Morning Prayer" is: The beginning of its time appears from the break of dawn when the eastern sky lights up. See there. It is evident from their words that the break of dawn is when the eastern sky lights up, and before this, it is night. So also wrote Rashi at the beginning of the third chapter of Yoma. Similarly, one of the great commentators wrote in his commentary on the Mishnah at the beginning of Berachot (the Gra in Shnot Eliyahu), and this is his language there: Rabban Gamliel says: Until the break of dawn – this is when the eastern sky lights up. This is his language. And what is explained at the beginning of the third chapter of Yoma that the entire eastern sky lighting up is after the break of dawn, this is the entire eastern sky lighting up, which is the spreading of the full day. But the eastern sky lighting up simply is the break of dawn. (And the words of the Magen Avraham in Subsection 3 are very puzzling. According to his opinion, the passage in Yoma refers to the eastern sky lighting up, see there. But it is not so, because due to the moonlight, they continued there until the entire eastern sky lit up, which is not relevant here. Also, what he challenged in Subsection 2 on the Rambam – the Gra answered there, see there. Delve and you will find correctly.)

However, in Midrash Rabbah Bereshit (Parsha 50) it is stated: Rabbi Chanina said: From the rise of the morning pillar until the east is illuminated - four mils. And from the illumination of the east until the sun rises - four mils. See there. And this saying is also found in the Jerusalem Talmud at the beginning of the third chapter of Yoma and at the beginning of the first chapter of Berachot. And in the Jerusalem Talmud, they use the term "Ayelet HaShachar" (the morning star), see there. (And the Gra in Shnot Eliyahu there wrote that "Amud HaShachar" is not "Ayelet HaShachar", and he refers to the Jerusalem Talmud. But I am puzzled: Isn't it stated in the Midrash "Amud HaShachar"? And so the Matnot Kehuna wrote there that they are the same, see there. And perhaps he believes so because it is stated in our Talmud in Pesachim 94a that from Amud HaShachar until the sunrise is four mils, and according to the Jerusalem Talmud and the Midrash, it is eight mils - we can infer that our Talmud does not agree with this. But in my humble opinion, it is not so, and we have resolved this according to Rabbeinu Tam's opinion which will be explained in Siman 261 in our work "Or LeYesharim" on the Sefer HaYashar by Rabbeinu Tam, Siman 181, see there. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

The Sages taught in the Mishnah (beginning of the fourth chapter): The morning prayer [can be recited] until midday. Rabbi Yehuda says until four hours [into the day]. And the halacha is decided in the Gemara according to Rabbi Yehuda. The Rif wrote: And even though the opinion of the Rabbis who say "until midday" is not accepted, if one erred and prayed after four hours, he is given the reward for praying, but he is not given the reward for praying on time. This is his language, and so wrote the Rambam in the third chapter of Prayer. The language of the Tur is as follows: And if one passed and did not pray until four hours, he should pray until midday. Even though he does not receive the reward as for praying on time, he still receives the reward for praying. This is his language, and so is the language of Rabbeinu the Beit Yosef in Section 1. However, he wrote: And if he erred or intentionally missed…, see there. Rabbeinu the Rema wrote: And after midday it is forbidden to pray the morning prayer. This is his language. (And the language of the Rambam is like the Beit Yosef, see there.)

And even though the Rif and the Rambam did not mention "until midnight," their intention is indeed this, since they derived it from the reasoning of the Rabbis, and they only said "until midnight." And after midnight, the law is thus: if one intentionally missed it, there is no compensation. But if one erred or was prevented, one prays the afternoon prayer twice, as will be explained in Siman 108. And the Rif did not mention this because he was not yet dealing with this law. Therefore, the Rambam and Shulchan Aruch added: "erred or missed," because in the case of "missed," this law does not apply. And our teacher, the Rema, who wrote that after midnight one should not pray, his intention was regarding "missed" and not "erred," and he relied on what is stated later. Additionally, because one prays the afternoon prayer beforehand, as I have written there. And this is also the conclusion of the great authorities (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 5, and Taz, subparagraph 1), and this is how one should rule.

Once the time for prayer arrives, which is from dawn (as stated in Siman 6), it is forbidden for a person to go to his friend's door to greet him with "Shalom," because the name of the Holy One, blessed be He, is "Shalom." Thus it is said in Berachot (14a): Whoever greets his friend with "Shalom" before he prays – it is as if he made a private altar. This means: since prayer is in place of a sacrifice, greeting a friend before greeting the Divine Presence in prayer is akin to sacrificing on a private altar and neglecting the Temple of G-d (Maharsha). The Tur wrote that this applies specifically when one goes to his friend's door early in the morning. However, if he encounters him by chance, he may greet him with "Shalom." Thus are his words.

And the language of our teacher, the Beit Yosef, in section 2 is as follows: Once the time has arrived... However, it is permitted to say to him: "Good morning." And even this is only permitted if he needed to go to attend to some matter. But if he is not going except to greet him before prayer, even this language is forbidden. Similarly, it is forbidden to bow to him when one rises early to his door. And some say that bowing is forbidden even without rising early to his door. And if he has begun to recite the blessings afterwards – it is not of great concern. And if he is not rising early to his door but merely encounters him on the way – it is permitted to greet him. And some say that even if he meets his friend in the market – he should only say "Good morning," so that he may be mindful that it is forbidden to engage in other matters at all until he has prayed. Thus far is his language.

And his words are not understood in what he wrote earlier: "And even this is not permitted except... but...". It is difficult: even if one is not going to greet him, even "Shalom" is permitted, as he himself concludes. And it cannot be said that he wrote this according to the opinion of "some say," because if so, it is entirely superfluous, and he should have stated briefly that it is forbidden to go to his door even to say "Good morning." And if he meets him on the way, some say it is permitted to say even "Shalom," and some say only "Good morning." And I have seen someone who explained that this is what he meant: that even this is not permitted except when he is going to see some business, and in passing goes to his friend's door, then it is permitted to say "Good morning." But "Shalom" in such a case is forbidden (there, subparagraph 7). Meaning: that even according to the opinion that permits giving "Shalom" when meeting on the way, in such a case it is forbidden. And in my humble opinion, this is not implied, for if so, the main point of his words is missing from the text. Furthermore, since in the end, he is going to his door, what difference does it make if he went for this or for business? Moreover, I am astonished: how is it permitted to go for business before prayer, for it will be explained later that it is forbidden to engage in any business before prayer. And this requires great investigation.

In my humble opinion, it appears that this is the explanation: At first glance, according to the language of the Talmud, it seems that the prohibition is only due to "peace," but there is no prohibition to go to the entrance of one's friend. Indeed, there are those who hold this view, that one can go to the entrance of one's friend and say to him: "Good morning" (Tosafot Yeshanim in the name of the Rabbis of Provence). And our teacher, the Beit Yosef, holds that going to the entrance is prohibited even without any speech. For so ruled the Rosh (see Beit Yosef), that what is written there that it is forbidden to go even with the saying of "Good morning" – does not mean that without saying it is permitted. For it is impossible to say this, as the saying of "Good morning" is nothing, but this is the usual manner of speech. But the main prohibition is to go to the entrance of one's friend. And the measure of the words of our teacher, the Beit Yosef, is as follows: And even this is only permitted when one needs to go to see some business, meaning some matter. And it is a matter of mitzvah, and his intention is not for business itself. And so it is explained from the source of the law (see Beit Yosef). But if he is only going to greet him, even this language is forbidden. Meaning: even this language that is nothing is nevertheless forbidden because the visit itself is forbidden. And if he goes for some business and meets him – it is permitted even to say "peace" according to the first opinion afterward. But this is not what it is referring to, nor is it coming to teach us this. The main point it is coming to teach us is that there is a prohibition in the greeting itself. And so should be taught.

And know that what our master, Rabbi Yosef Karo, wrote—that after the blessings one need not be so concerned—his intention was not referring to the saying of "Shalom" but rather to the matter of bowing (Taz, subparagraph 2), or to the saying of "Shalom" when one does not initiate with greeting. But if one explicitly initiates with greeting, it is proven in the Gemara there that it is forbidden to say "Shalom" (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 8). Similarly, if one only initiates with greeting and says "Tzafra Demarei Tav" (good morning) – this too is permitted. And this is why he precisely said "need not be so concerned", meaning: if both conditions are not met—initiation and the saying of "Shalom"—then saying "Shalom" is permitted. But if both conditions are met, it is forbidden. And know that in all cases where saying "Shalom" is forbidden, it is forbidden even for someone who is accustomed to initiate with "Shalom". Moreover, it seems to me that even according to the "some say" opinion that it is also forbidden in the marketplace to say "Shalom", this applies when one initiates with "Shalom". But if his friend said "Shalom" to him, for example, after he prayed, he is allowed to respond with "Shalom". For responding is less severe than initiating, as is proven in the Gemara, see there.

It is stated in the Gemara (14a): It is forbidden for a person to attend to his affairs before he prays, as it is said: "Righteousness shall go before him and shall set his steps on the way." Rashi explains: "Righteousness" means prayer, which justifies him before his Creator. Only afterward does he set his steps on the way to his affairs. This is his language. Moreover, it is stated there that anyone who prays and only then sets out on his journey, the Holy One, blessed be He, attends to his affairs, as it is said: "Righteousness shall go before him...". The version of the Rif and the Rosh in the first statement is: "It is forbidden for a person to set out on a journey before he prays," look there. The Tur and the Shulchan Aruch, in Section 3, write both matters, and this is their language: It is forbidden for a person to attend to his needs or to set out on a journey until he prays the Shemoneh Esrei prayer. Look there. And certainly, this is correct, for even according to our version, a journey is included in his affairs. The plain meaning of the verse "and shall set his steps on the way" refers to a journey. And the language of the Rambam in Chapter 6, Law 4 is the same: It is forbidden for a person to taste anything or to do any work after dawn until he prays the Shacharit prayer... and he should not set out on a journey before he prays. This is his language. And it appears that his version in the Gemara is like that of the Rif, but he learned the prohibition of work from the verse "And Me you have cast behind your back," from which we derive the prohibition of tasting, as will be explained. And work is also included, for one casts aside the work of Heaven behind his back and attends to his own work. It is also explained in the Gemara (5b) that prayer should be close to his bed. The Tosafot explain that it is forbidden to do work before prayer, look there. And it is obvious that not only work is forbidden, but the same applies to any type of engagement, for what difference is there between this and that?

In the book Terumat HaDeshen (Siman 18), a question was posed about people who pray up to "Baruch She'amar" and then go to their business and pray later. Is it permissible to do so? He responded that it is forbidden, as the intention of the Gemara is regarding the Shemoneh Esreh prayer, as the Rambam, Tur, and Shulchan Aruch have written. He concluded his response by noting that he has seen people doing this, but it is not in accordance with the law of the Talmud. Based on this, our teacher, the Rema, wrote that some are lenient after saying some blessings before "Baruch She'amar." However, it is good to be stringent in this matter. These are his words. It is not understood who the "some are lenient" refers to. If he means some people who are lenient on this matter, then he should not have said "it is good to be stringent," which implies that it is merely a stringency, whereas according to the fundamental law, it is as the Terumat HaDeshen wrote. Therefore, he should have said, "and some are lenient... but one should not be lenient in this." This requires further investigation. In fact, the Levush wrote this way. Refer there. And this is the main ruling.

It is obvious that only one's personal affairs are forbidden, but matters concerning Heaven are permitted. And not only collecting charity or other mitzvah, but even preparing for Shabbat on Friday and preparing for a festival on the festival itself. For this reason, it is said in Megillah (23a) that on a festival, people come to the synagogue later. And it is explicitly stated in Masechet Sofrim (Chapter 18), and similarly written by the great later authorities (Pri Chadash and Shulchan Aruch HaRav). Similarly, going on a journey for the purpose of a mitzvah is permitted even before prayer. Some permit this even for personal matters if the caravan is not willing to wait (Magen Avraham, subsection 10). All the more so, if one leaves before dawn, it is permitted in any case (see Taz, subsection 3).

It is forbidden to eat or drink before prayer. Thus, our Sages of blessed memory said (Berakhot 10b): "You shall not eat on the blood" – you shall not eat before you pray for your blood. And anyone who eats and drinks and then prays, the scripture says about him: "And you have cast Me behind your back" – do not read "your back" (גויך) but "your pride" (גאיך). The Holy One, blessed be He, said: After this one has acted arrogantly, he accepts upon himself the kingdom of heaven. The Tur and the Shulchan Aruch wrote that water is permitted to drink before the prayer, as water does not involve arrogance. It is permitted both on weekdays and on Shabbat and Yom Tov, for even though tasting is forbidden before Kiddush, before the prayer the obligation of Kiddush has not yet taken effect. And so the Rosh acted in practice as the Tur wrote, and so it is written in the Hagahot Maimoniyot and other great authorities. Their reasoning: since our Sages derived "your pride" (גאיך) – this does not apply to water, as there is no arrogance here. But from the words of the Rambam who wrote "it is forbidden to taste" – it seems that no tasting is permitted. However, most of our Rabbis do not agree with this. And so the common custom is to drink hot water with the herb called "tea" before the prayer. And generally, it is beneficial for cleanliness as is known. Some have prohibited drinking with sugar, and I do not know the reason, because is there really a name of "eating" in this? It is merely to flavor the hot water a bit. Some have permitted drinking with sugar when the sugar is in the mouth, but to put it in the hot water and make sweet water – this is forbidden (see Be'er Heitev, small section 11, and Mishnah Berurah). This is not the main opinion. But with milk, it seems to me it is forbidden, because milk is satisfying. Additionally, it comes from blood, as blood is transformed and becomes milk, so it relates to "before you pray for your blood." However, the world customarily permits even with milk, because it only serves to flavor the water. And also coffee is permitted to drink, even though it appears that coffee is satisfying, yet the great authorities wrote that it is permitted (see there in Be'er Heitev). There is doubt if it is permitted to drink seltzer water or lemonade when one is not drinking for medicinal purposes, for medicinal purposes it is certainly permitted as will be explained. And it seems there is no difference between plain water and these waters.

Our Master the Beit Yosef wrote that eating and drinking for medicinal purposes is permitted. Thus far his words. And his intention is not regarding a seriously ill person, for that is an obvious matter even if there is no danger. Rather, the intention is that one takes it for medicinal purposes, and he is not ill but merely has discomforts. Or even if he has no discomfort at all but takes it to strengthen himself, like in the springtime when people take medicines to strengthen the body and muscles. And if these medicines include even complete types of food and drink, it is permitted, for since he is doing this for medicinal purposes, there is no issue of arrogance. And even if he can do it after the prayer, it is permitted. Therefore, someone who has a heart weakness may eat before praying, for it is for medicinal purposes. (See Magen Avraham, subparagraph 12, Chayei Adam, and Mishnah Berurah.)

Maimonides wrote in the fifth chapter: "The thirsty and the hungry are considered among the sick. If they have the ability to concentrate their mind, they should pray. If not, they should not pray until they eat and drink." Thus far his words. It implies that it is forbidden for them to pray until they eat and drink. However, Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote in section 4: "If one wishes, they should not pray until they eat and drink." See there. And he explained his reasoning in his larger work: Because in any case, we do not concentrate so well, therefore, we do not object if one wishes to pray before eating and drinking. See there. And it is obvious that this is in a manner that does not harm their health by not eating immediately. But if there is a concern for bodily harm, it is obvious that it is forbidden to pray until they eat and drink, as it is written: "And you shall guard your lives."

The Tur wrote: "If one began eating before dawn, the Rambam of blessed memory wrote that one does not need to stop. And my master and father of blessed memory wrote in the name of the R"i that one needs to stop." Thus far his words. Based on this, Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote in paragraph 5 that if one began eating before dawn, one needs to stop. And there are those who say that one does not need to stop. Thus far his words. His main opinion is that one needs to stop, for he wrote in his larger work that what the Tur wrote in the name of the Rambam that one does not need to stop is a mistake, for he only wrote this regarding Mincha, not Shacharit. Only the opinion of the Rashba is that one does not need to stop, see there. And all the commentators on the Tur wrote similarly. But in my humble opinion, it is not so, and his intention is based on what the Rambam wrote in the second chapter of the laws of Kriyat Shema: "If one was engaged in eating... he finishes, and then recites Kriyat Shema." And the Ra'avad objected to this, saying that since Kriyat Shema is a Torah obligation, one must stop even if there is time to recite it afterward. And for the prayer, which is Rabbinic, one should not stop unless there will not be time to pray, see there. And we already wrote at the end of Siman 70 that they do not disagree at all. The Ra'avad is referring to when one began eating in a forbidden manner, and the Rambam is referring to when one began eating permissibly before dawn (and so wrote the Bach there). Therefore, it is correct what the Tur said that if one began before dawn, according to the Rambam, one does not need to stop, since even regarding Kriyat Shema his opinion is that one does not need to stop, and certainly for prayer. And so is the opinion of the Ra'avad and the Rashba, thus the majority opinion is lenient. And so is the custom at summer weddings where they eat into the day, and according to the Rosh, in any case, one must stop. This is not similar to Mincha, where one does not stop, because for Shacharit they relied on the verse "Do not eat on the blood." According to this opinion, at weddings, one should not begin the feast if they cannot finish it before dawn. And it is possible that for a mitzvah meal one need not be concerned. (And perhaps this is the intention of the Magen Avraham in paragraph 14, who wrote that it is not conclusive, see there. Be precise and you will find it easy.) And so is the simple custom. According to the "some say," even if one began after dawn, one does not need to stop for prayer, only for Kriyat Shema, and he recites Kriyat Shema and eats. And if he began before dawn, he does not need to stop even for Kriyat Shema. (See Magen Avraham paragraph 14 and paragraph 15. And what he wrote in the name of Rabbi Chaim Vital that even at midnight one should not taste anything before praying, see there – this is for the pious ones and not by law. And even in this, there are those who disagree, as written in Shaarei Teshuva paragraph 11 in the name of Shevut Yaakov. Some differentiate that eating is forbidden, but drinking is permitted, as written by the Be'er Heitev paragraph 15. And the main ruling is as I wrote.)

According to Rashi in Berachot (5b), it is forbidden to learn once the time for prayer has arrived. However, Tosafot and the Rosh disagree with him on this matter. The Rosh writes that even according to Rashi, the prohibition only applies when one is learning in his study hall and prays there, without going to the synagogue to pray. In this situation, there is a concern that he might become engrossed in his studies and miss the time for Shema and prayer. But when one goes to pray in the synagogue or in a study hall that is not the place where he usually learns, it is permitted. Similarly, if one is teaching others, even if he prays there, it is permitted, as communal Torah study is preferable. Especially when the time is passing, if they do not study now, they will miss their learning opportunity, for the merit of the public is significant. And indeed, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi would teach his students, and when the time for Shema arrived, he would pass his hands over his eyes and recite only the verse "Shema Yisrael" (13b). And be aware that the Beit Yosef in section 6 wrote that teaching others is permitted since the time is passing, and if they do not study now, they will miss it. See there. It appears to me in my humble opinion that this is not specific. The general assumption is that this is the case, but certainly, in any situation, it is permitted, as Tosafot and the Rosh completely disagree. (And I find the whole matter difficult: from where does he derive that Rashi holds this view? Perhaps Abba Benjamin was stringent upon himself, and it is possible that if it were permitted according to the law, he would not have been stringent to avoid learning? And also, the Tosafot of Rabbi Yehuda wrote that Rashi of blessed memory acted in this manner. And one cannot object to Rashi from the fact that one should not stand to pray except from a clear halacha as it states (there 31a), for that is a brief matter and there is no concern of prolongation, unlike with long study. And now the custom is to learn in any case according to the opinion of Tosafot and the Rosh. And also, Rambam did not mention anything about this.)

Even though it is taught in Shabbat (9b): A person should not sit before a barber close to Mincha until he has prayed, and should not enter a bathhouse... – nevertheless, Rambam writes in Chapter Six and the Shulchan Aruch in Section 7 that it is permissible to get a haircut and enter a bathhouse close to Shacharit, as they only decreed this close to Mincha, which is a common occurrence. This is their language. Consequently, everything we learned there: not to a tanner, not to eat, and not to judge – except for eating, these are permitted.

Even though the primary time for the mitzvah is at sunrise, nevertheless, someone who is in a pressing circumstance, such as needing to leave on a journey early, can pray from the time dawn breaks. He should wait to recite the Shema until its proper time, which is when one can recognize a familiar acquaintance at a distance of four cubits, as I wrote in Siman 58. If he cannot stay home until this time, so that he would recite the Shema and pray, but is compelled to leave earlier, he should pray at home immediately after dawn and then leave. When the time for Shema arrives, he can recite it on the way, ensuring he can stand still for the first verse and concentrate on it, as I wrote there. Even though in this way he will not be able to connect the redemption blessing to the prayer, it is still preferable to pray standing at home and not join the redemption blessing to the prayer, rather than praying at its proper time while walking and joining the redemption blessing to the prayer. This is the ruling of the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch at the end of this Siman.

And even though it was clarified in Siman 58 that in a time of need one can recite the Shema from dawn, and if so, one could recite it and pray before setting out on a journey—this applies only when on the journey it will be impossible to recite even one verse with proper intention while standing, such as when one is going to a place with dangerous animals and bandits. But here, he is setting out on a journey that is not dangerous, and therefore it is preferable to recite the Shema on the way at its proper time and to stand for the first verse. However, for the prayer (the Amidah), which must be recited entirely while standing, and this is not possible on the way—they permitted him to pray not at the primary time, but on the condition that he prays standing at home, even though he will not connect the redemption blessing to the prayer (Beit Yosef and Bach).

The translation of the passage:

And our custom is not like this (Magen Avraham, Section 16). And it is possible because there is a dispute in the Gemara (Berachot 30a), and also in the Gemara there it says that we do not see people acting this way. And we hold like the other Tanna that one should go on his way, and on the way, he should recite the Shema and pray, and connect the redemption to the prayer. And even though he prays while walking, in this situation it is better to connect the redemption to the prayer. Furthermore, Rashi explained the reason that praying while standing is preferable: so that one can have proper intention. And nowadays, we do not have proper intention, and therefore it is better to pray on the way (there). And know that one who is sitting in a carriage, and the carriage is moving – it is considered as if he is walking in this matter (Gemara), and similarly in a boat. And it is obvious that if he will delay in his house until he can recognize his friend from a distance of four cubits – he should recite the Shema and pray (there). And one should not ask: it has been explained in Section 20 that it is forbidden to go on the way before praying. However, it has already been explained in Section 22 that for a mitzvah matter it is permitted, or if the caravan does not want to wait, or if he has another compulsion that forces him to go. And furthermore, it is obvious: if he is on the way and sees that the time for Shema will pass – he should recite the Shema while walking, and stand for the first verse. And even without tefillin if he cannot put on tefillin. And when he reaches the inn, he should recite the Shema with its blessings and pray. And even though one should not recite the Shema without tefillin, in a situation where it is impossible, it is different.

It is stated in the Gemara there that Rav Ashi, on the Shabbat of the festival, would deliver the sermon at daybreak and would pray during the sermon while seated, and all the people would slip away and pray one by one. He would not delay the sermon until after the prayer, see there. And this was in their days, when the main laws were taught on the Shabbat of the festival, and they would reprove the people, and all their actions were for the sake of Heaven. But nowadays, this law does not apply (Magen Avraham there).

Maimonides wrote at the beginning of the fifth chapter: There are eight things a person praying must be careful with and do. If he was pressured or forced, or if he transgressed and did not do them - they do not invalidate the prayer. These are: standing, facing the direction of the Temple, preparing the body, preparing the clothes, preparing the place, adjusting the voice, bowing, and prostration. End of quote. From his words, we learn that all these laws do not invalidate the prayer after the fact. Even if one prayed sitting intentionally and was able to stand, and not facing east, in any case, he does not need to repeat the prayer. In this section, the preparation of the place and the preparation of the body will be explained.

Fixing the place, how is it done? Thus the sages said (Berachot 10b): A person should not stand on a chair, nor on a stool, nor in a high place and pray. Because there is no haughtiness before the Omnipresent, as it is said: "Out of the depths I call to You, O Lord" (Psalms 130:1). And it is written: "A prayer of the afflicted when he is faint" (Psalms 102:1). And it is taught in the Tosefta of Berachot (Chapter 3) that if one was elderly or ill, it is permitted. And similarly, if one needs to be heard by the congregation, and if he stands in a low place they will not hear him, it is permitted for him to stand in a high place. And the Rambam wrote that the measure of "height" is three handbreadths, for less than this is not considered "height," as anything less than three handbreadths is regarded as ground level. And there is one who says that on an object like a bed, chair, or bench, it is forbidden even if it is not three handbreadths high for another reason: because the place is narrow and he is afraid he might fall and will not be able to concentrate. And this is the opinion of our teacher the Rema who wrote so, see there. And there are those who disagree (Bach and Taz, and this also seems to be the opinion of the Magen Avraham). And now in some synagogues, the place where the prayer leader stands is lower than the floor of the synagogue, based on "Out of the depths I call to You, O Lord." And perhaps this is the meaning of "descending before the Ark" found throughout the Talmud. (Magen Avraham, section 3. But the Beit Yosef in Siman 150 explained in the name of Rabbi Yosef ben Chaviv that "descending before the Ark" means descending from his place to go before the Ark, see there.)

A high place that is prohibited – this is when it is not its own domain, such as when it does not have four cubits by four cubits. But when it has four cubits by four cubits, it is considered its own domain, even if it does not have walls around it, and it is like an upper story and it is permitted to stand on it. Similarly, if it is surrounded by walls, even if it does not have four cubits by four cubits, it is considered its own domain and it is permitted to pray on it, since its height is not noticeable because it is a separate domain. Therefore, if one praying is standing on the bimah – it is permitted, as it is considered its own domain. This is specifically when it is surrounded by walls, or it has four cubits by four cubits, but otherwise – it is forbidden. And it seems that even if it is only surrounded by walls on two sides – it is also permitted, since it appears as its own place.

Artisans who perform work for a homeowner are permitted to pray at the top of an olive tree or a fig tree, and this does not violate the prohibition against standing in a high place. They may pray there because, since they climbed up to perform their work, it is as if they ascended to an upper story. However, for other types of trees, they must descend to pray. The reason olive and fig trees are different from other trees is that they have many more branches than other trees, making it very laborious to climb up and down, which would cause a significant interruption in their work. Therefore, the Sages said they may pray there. But for other trees where such interruption is not an issue, they must descend.

The homeowner, however, must descend even from the top of an olive or fig tree, as he is not obligated to others and is in his own domain. The leniency given to workers was only due to the potential interruption of someone else's work, which does not apply to a homeowner. Similarly, our artisans who work on roofs or other high places that do not have a distinct domain of their own, if there is labor involved in descending and ascending, if he is a worker, he is permitted to stand there and pray. If he is the homeowner, he must descend. However, if the area has its own domain, such as if it is four cubits by four cubits or surrounded by partitions, it is permitted in any case. The measure of four cubits is three "arshin" of our country, Russia, which is a known measurement called a "sazhen."

Our Sages of blessed memory said at the end of the chapter "Ein Omdin" (Berachot 31a): A person should only pray in a house that has windows, as it is said: "And his windows were open in his upper chamber towards Jerusalem" (Daniel 6:11). Rashi explained that windows cause him to focus his heart, as he looks towards the heavens and his heart becomes humble. So far his words. And even though the one who prays must have his eyes downwards, as I wrote in Siman 95, nevertheless, in passing, if he looks towards the heavens, his heart will become humble (Beit Yosef there). According to this, the windows need to be in the direction one is praying. Therefore, he brought proof from the verse about Daniel, whose windows were open towards Jerusalem, because he prayed facing Jerusalem.

According to Rashi, we must say that when it is written "towards Jerusalem" – it does not only mean that one should remember Jerusalem but also that one should look towards the heavens. However, from the language of the Rambam, it does not seem so, as he wrote in the fifth chapter, law six: One needs to open windows or doors towards Jerusalem in order to pray towards them, as it is said: "and his windows were open...". This is his language. It is explained that the intention is solely because of Jerusalem. And perhaps it is all one, that when one looks towards the heavens in the direction of Jerusalem – one will concentrate more and his heart will be humbled. And this is also implied by the words of the students of Rabbeinu Yona, who wrote the following: One can say that the reason is that by seeing the light, his mind will be more settled, and he will be able to concentrate properly. Alternatively: it means that the windows should be open towards the east, as it says in the verse "towards Jerusalem", because through this orientation he will concentrate more in his prayer towards the place, and his prayer will be more acceptable and welcomed. This is their language.

Nevertheless, it seems that according to all interpretations, one should pray specifically opposite the windows. However, we have not seen anyone being particular about this. On the contrary, most often people choose to pray by a wall that is not opposite a window, and the place of the rabbi is usually by the Ark where there is no window, because praying opposite a window can be distracting due to people passing by. In my humble opinion, it appears that people interpret the Talmud's lack of explicit instruction to pray "opposite the window" as implying that the main concern is merely that there be windows in the house, but not necessarily that one prays directly opposite a window. The words of our Sages, who said it is so one can look, can be understood even if one is not standing directly opposite the window. This is also evident from the language of the Zohar in "Pekudei" (page 251), which states: "And for this reason, any synagogue that does not have windows is not a place to pray in, for the earthly synagogue corresponds to the heavenly synagogue, which has twelve upper windows. And here, too, below..." Thus, it is clear that the requirement is only that there be windows, specifically twelve windows. And the custom is to ensure twelve windows when possible, and it is a mitzvah to heed the words of the Zohar. Similarly, our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 4 that it is good to have twelve windows, see there. (See Magen Avraham, subsection 4. And I do not know why he did not mention the words of the Beit Yosef that we brought.)

One should only pray inside a house, and not in an open place like a field or a valley, unless he is traveling. If there are trees there, it is good to stand among the trees. A house without windows is better than an open place. Similarly, one should not pray in a courtyard. The reason is that when one is in a private place, the awe of the King falls upon him, and his heart is broken. If there is filth or pigs in the house, he should pray in a clean place in the courtyard. According to one explanation in Tosafos at the end of the chapter "Ein Omdin," there is no prohibition unless there is a concern that passersby might interrupt him. (And even though the Beis Yosef rejected their explanation, the Taz in subsection 2 and the Magen Avraham in subsection 6 have explained it well. See there. However, from the Zohar it seems not so. See there.)

When one is traveling on the road, he should not enter a ruin to pray, due to three concerns: suspicion (lest people say he has a prostitute there), collapse (lest it fall and he be harmed), and demons. However, if the ruin is in a field, there is no suspicion, as a prostitute is not commonly found in a field. If the ruin is sturdy and strong, there is no concern of collapse. And if two people enter it, there is no concern for demons, for it is established that to one person, the demon appears and harms; to two people, it appears but does not harm; and to three people, it does not appear at all, unless it is a place known to be frequented by demons. Similarly, with two people, there is also no suspicion, unless they are known to be promiscuous individuals (Gemara, beginning of Berachot). If he has a torch, he is considered as two people. If the moon is shining, it is considered as three people. Therefore, in a field with a sturdy ruin, and with two people or a torch, it is permissible to enter. It is better to pray there than on the road, even though it is not roofed, for we do not worry about the lack of a roof. If he fears being interrupted by passersby, he should pray the "Havinenu" prayer, which will be explained in Siman 110.

Our Sages of blessed memory said (Berachot 6b): Anyone who prays behind a synagogue is called "wicked," as it is stated: "The wicked walk around on every side" (Psalms 12:9). However, this only applies if he does not turn his face towards the synagogue. But if he turns his face towards the synagogue, there is no issue. Some explain that "behind the synagogue" refers to the western side where the entrance is. Therefore, if he does not turn his face towards the synagogue and his back is to the synagogue, he is called "wicked" because it appears as if he is denying [God]. For the entire congregation bows to the east, and he bows to the west, which seems like there are two authorities, God forbid. But if he turns his face towards the synagogue, he is also bowing towards the east. And if he is behind the eastern wall, he should specifically turn his back to the synagogue in order to bow to the east. There is no concern about turning his back to the synagogue because it is not a Torah scroll.

But there are those who specifically interpret it this way: that one stands behind the eastern wall, and it is forbidden for him to turn his back to the synagogue even if he bows to the east like the rest of the congregation. Rather, he should face the synagogue and bow to the west, for the primary concern is about turning his back to the synagogue. However, regarding bowing to the west – there is no concern, since he is bowing towards the wall of the synagogue. According to this, it is forbidden in any manner to stand to the east, for if he turns his face to the east – it is forbidden according to the second interpretation. And if he turns his face to the west – it is forbidden according to the first interpretation. To satisfy both opinions, the only permissible way is to stand on the western side and face the synagogue. And on the north and south sides, there is certainly no concern, as he faces east and his back is to the west like the rest of the congregation. And even when standing outside, it is considered as if he is praying with the congregation. However, it is a superior mitzvah to pray inside the synagogue itself. And know that standing to the east, which is forbidden according to the second interpretation because his back is to the synagogue, applies when he is in the street. But when there is a building in front of the eastern wall, and the eastern wall also serves the building, even according to this interpretation, one standing in the building should bow to the east, even though his back is to the eastern wall of the synagogue. For it is not apparent that he is turning his back to the synagogue, since he is standing in a separate domain.

It is forbidden to pass by the entrance of a synagogue at the time when the congregation is praying and the entrance is open. This appears like one is rejecting the yoke of Heaven, as he passes by the entrance during the time of prayer and does not enter. This specifically applies when there is no other synagogue in the city, but if there is another synagogue, there is no concern, as the observer will say he is going to the other synagogue. This does not only apply to another synagogue; if there is any other place where the congregation is praying, one may pass by. Similarly, it seems to me that if there are two or more prayer services in the synagogue, one after another, it is also permitted, as the observer will say that he has already prayed or will pray later. Also, if one is carrying a load on his head or body, or riding a horse, or traveling in a wagon, and the like, it is permitted, as everyone sees that he is preoccupied with this. Similarly, if one is walking with a non-Jew, people see that he is preoccupied with him. Also, if one is wearing tefillin, it is permitted, for there is no suspicion of rejecting the yoke of Heaven since he is wearing tefillin. It seems to me that the same applies to a tallit. Furthermore, it seems that even if he is merely carrying a tallit and tefillin in his hand, it is permitted, for it is evident that he is not rejecting the yoke of Heaven. Additionally, if there are two entrances to the synagogue, it is permitted, as people will say that he will enter through the other entrance. It seems to me that this specifically applies when they are on different sides, but if they are on the same side, it is evident that he is not entering through the other entrance. (There is proof for this from Shabbat 23a, see there. Examine and you will find it easy.) And they said (61a): Behind a non-Jew, but not behind a synagogue...

The most accepted prayer and the greatest mitzvah is to pray in the synagogue with the community, as it is written: "Indeed, God does not despise the mighty." The merit of the community is very great, and there is not as much scrutiny from above on the prayer of the community as there is on the prayer of an individual. And if it is not possible for him to go to the synagogue, if it is easily possible to gather a minyan in his home, where there is not much effort involved for him and not much effort for the people (see Magen Avraham, small section 17 in the name of Sefer Mitzvot Gadol) – he should do so. And if this involves effort and he prays alone in his home, in any case, he should strive to pray at the same time that the community is praying. And similarly, people who live in settlements and do not have a minyan – it is proper that they should pray at the time the community in the city is praying. Unless the community is very delayed – it is better not to consider this and to pray at his own time alone. And if he can pray at sunrise – how good and pleasant it is. And it is obvious that when the community prays the evening prayer before nightfall and he prays at home, he should not pay attention to the community and should pray at his own time, and similarly in all such cases. And it is also a mitzvah to pray in the synagogue, even if he missed the communal prayer and prays alone, for the prayer in the synagogue is more heard than at home, for there is great sanctity there. (See Jerusalem Talmud beginning of the fifth chapter, and it requires further study.) And what we have said, that he should strive to pray at the time the community is praying – this is only when praying that specific prayer, this is also called "praying with the community." But if he is praying Shacharit (morning prayer) and the community is praying Mussaf (additional prayer) or vice versa – this is not called praying with the community. (There. And what Magen Avraham was uncertain about regarding the words of the Tosafot – I do not know why. For it is obvious that one who prays at home at the time of the community's prayer is not equivalent to one who prays with the community, as he is not joining them at all. And what compelled Magen Avraham to establish this only in a time of anger? Further study is required.)

When one stands with the congregation, it is forbidden to pray earlier than the congregation. This applies even if one wishes to leave the synagogue, unless the time for prayer is passing and the congregation is not praying because they are lengthening the recitations of liturgical poems (piyyutim) or for another reason. In such a case, it is better to go home and pray unless the time is so pressing that by the time one reaches home, the time for prayer will have passed. In that case, one should pray in the synagogue by oneself before the congregation (Bach). Some say that even if there is time to go home, one may pray in the synagogue (Magen Avraham, Section 21, in the name of Tosafot R"i), for the prohibition against praying in the synagogue before the congregation only applies when they are praying at the appropriate time for the Shema and the prayer, and not when they are delaying the time.

Know that a person who is weak-hearted may always pray at home before the congregation, even when they are praying at the proper time, because he cannot wait as he needs to eat. However, in the synagogue, he is not allowed to pray before the congregation even in such a case. If he is ill or under another form of compulsion, he may pray earlier even in the synagogue (ibid.). The reason is that his illness proves why he is praying early, and similarly, his compulsion is evident, unlike with a weak heart, which is not apparent to everyone.

Maimonides wrote at the beginning of the eighth chapter: "The prayer of the community is always heard. And even if there are sinners among them, the Holy One, blessed be He, does not reject the prayer of the many. Therefore, a person should include themselves with the community and not pray alone as long as they can pray with the community. And a person should always rise early and come late to the synagogue, for their prayer is only heard at all times in the synagogue. And anyone who has a synagogue in their city and does not go in to pray is called a 'bad neighbor,' as it is written: 'Thus says the Lord about all My evil neighbors... behold, I will uproot them from their land, and I will uproot the house of Judah from among them.' This is what our sages of blessed memory said in Berachot (5a), and it is measure for measure: he did not want to go on a short walk, so he will go on a long walk. And if there are two synagogues in the city, there is more reward for going to the further one, for they pay him the reward for his steps (Sotah 22a). And in a place where there are more people, it is a greater mitzvah, for 'in the multitude of the people is the King's glory.' However, if they talk there during the prayer, it is better to pray in a small minyan where they do not talk." (See Be'er Heitev, subparagraph 11, in the name of the Radbaz, that one who is in prison and is given permission once to pray with the community should not miss the opportunity and should pray immediately. See there, and this is the main point. And the Chacham Tzvi raised an objection against him, but it is not a difficulty. See there, and scrutinize and you will find leniency.)

It is a mitzvah to run to the synagogue, as this demonstrates that one performs the mitzvah with enthusiasm and eagerness. This applies to any mitzvah, as it is stated: "Let us pursue knowledge of the Lord." However, one should only run until the entrance of the synagogue. Once inside, one should not run, as it is not respectful; rather, one should walk with awe and reverence, as if walking before a king. Even on Shabbat and Yom Tov, it is a mitzvah to run when going to the synagogue. Although it is forbidden to take long strides on Shabbat—and even on weekdays, it diminishes one five-hundredth of one's vision—nevertheless, for the sake of a mitzvah, it is permitted. "One who observes a mitzvah will not know any evil." Conversely, upon leaving the synagogue, one should not run, nor should one take long strides, as it appears as though one is happy to leave, and that one's time in the synagogue was burdensome. Rather, one should walk slowly to show that it is difficult to part from the synagogue. If one is leaving with the intention to return to the synagogue, one may run, as it is evident to all that one is running in order to return quickly. Similarly, when going from the synagogue to the study hall, it is a mitzvah to run, as the sanctity of the study hall is greater than that of the synagogue (Megillah 27a).

It is permitted to spit in the synagogue. Even though it is forbidden to spit in the Temple, even nowadays, nevertheless, it is permitted in the synagogue. Just as shoes are forbidden in the Temple, as it is written: "Remove your shoes…", but are permitted in the synagogue (Berachot 62b). However, this is specifically not during prayer. But during prayer, one should not spit. And how one should act if spitting becomes necessary will be explained in Siman 97. There are those who say that just as it is explained there that spitting to the right or in front is forbidden, but to the left or behind is permitted, so too here, not during prayer (Magen Avraham, Small Section 27 in the name of Or Zarua). However, this does not seem to be implied by the straightforward language of the Talmud and poskim. Nevertheless, it is certain that one should spit gently, not far away in a prideful manner. And the spittle should be trampled with the foot, or covered with sand or straw. This is a significant obligation everywhere, so that others do not find it disgusting, as we say in Chagigah (5a): "For God will bring every deed into judgment—even that which is hidden"—this refers to one who spits in front of his fellow and it is disgusting to him, see there. And they wrote a remedy not to spit: to chew licorice before going to the synagogue. And on the eve of Yom Kippur and the eve of Tisha B'Av, it is forbidden so that the sweetness does not remain in the mouth, and when swallowing the spittle, the sweetness is swallowed on Yom Kippur and Tisha B'Av. (And swallowing spittle is permitted on Tisha B'Av and Yom Kippur, as Magen Avraham wrote at the end of Siman 606, not like the Bach, see there.)

A person should always rise early to come to the synagogue so that he will be among the first ten. Even if a hundred people come afterward, he receives a reward equivalent to all of them (Berachot 47b). The reason is that since the Divine Presence rests wherever there are ten, and the Divine Presence arrives first (Berachot 6a), and since it is through him that the Divine Presence comes, he is worthy of receiving a reward equal to all those who come after him. This is specifically if he prays with them. And in the Zohar, it implies that all ten should come at once. And even one who is unable to be among the first ten due to the burden of cleanliness and similar reasons should still strive to come as early as possible, for anyone who comes earlier is closer to receiving the holiness than those who come later (see also Taz).

If a person remains alone in the synagogue after the prayer, whether in the evening or even in the morning when the synagogue is outside the city, and if he remains alone he will be afraid and confused in his prayer – there is an obligation on the other person present not to leave the synagogue until after this person has finished his prayer, even if he has already completed his own prayer. Just as a person is obligated to perform acts of kindness with his money, so too is he obligated to perform acts of kindness with his body. There is no greater act of kindness than ensuring that his fellow is not afraid and confused in his prayer. And if he waits, our sages of blessed memory (Berachot 6a) said that it will be fulfilled in him what is written in Isaiah: "Your peace would have been like a river, and your righteousness like the waves of the sea, and your offspring like the sand..." Therefore, the one who is praying should not prolong his supplications, but should pray only the fixed prayer. If he prolongs his supplications, the other is not obligated to wait for him. Some are stringent even in a synagogue within the city and in the morning, because a person's heart is distressed when he remains alone. And some wrote that all this applies when the person praying came together with the congregation but was compelled by circumstance to pray after the congregation. In that case, there is an obligation to wait. But if he came at a time when the congregation is about to finish their prayer – there is no obligation to wait for him, as he has revealed his intention that he is not afraid to remain alone (Magen Avraham, section 29, in the name of Tosafot R"I). And this is also implied by the language of the Talmud there, which says: "Two who entered to pray," see there. In any case, the R"I of blessed memory would wait even in such a situation (there), as it is no less than other acts of kindness.

One who is traveling and arrives at an inn while it is still daytime and wants to stay there overnight, if there is a place along the way within a distance of four mil where people pray in a minyan (with ten men), and he can reach there while it is still daytime without having to travel alone at night, he must go there to pray with the congregation. However, more than four mil, the Sages did not obligate him, even if he needs to travel on that route. But if he needs to go back or to the side, he is only obligated to go up to one mil, and not more. Similarly, if one lives within a mil of a place where they pray with a minyan, he is obligated to go there every day, morning and evening, to pray with the congregation. The measure of a mil is a Russian verst, which they call a "verst."
