And it is obvious that a person should not depart on a journey for a non-essential purpose from a city where there is a synagogue, even if he leaves before dawn. The reason we are not cautious about this is that we travel for our livelihood, and this is considered a mitzvah (commandment), for it is a mitzvah to provide for one's wife and children. Providing for one's wife is a duty; and regarding children, our Sages of blessed memory said that this is what is meant by "performing righteousness at all times" (Ketubot 50a, and similarly implied in Moed Katan, beginning of the third chapter, see there). Additionally, this applies only when one can reach his destination during the day, as written in the Shulchan Aruch, section 17.

The reason for this is: Prayer with a congregation, even though it is of rabbinic origin, is a great mitzvah. For in addition to communal prayer, it also includes the recitation of Kedusha, Kaddish, and "Barchu." It is permitted to free a slave in order to pray with ten people, as explained in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 267. However, this applies to a person who is not constantly engaged in Torah study, but merely sets fixed times for Torah study. But a Torah scholar who is always learning—Torah study is greater than all the mitzvot. And if this will cause him to lose much time from Torah study, he should pray alone and continue his Torah study. Nevertheless, a Torah scholar should not make this a habit, so that the matter of communal prayer does not become insignificant in the eyes of the common people. Therefore, a Torah scholar should not engage in Torah study at the time when the congregation is reciting Selichot and supplications. And a Torah scholar who can gather ten people in his home to pray with a congregation—it is better for him to do so rather than go to the synagogue, if going would cause some loss of Torah study. But he should not pray alone in the city, even if it would cause a slight loss of Torah study, for if he does so, it will weaken the importance of this mitzvah in the eyes of the people.

If there is in the city a synagogue and a study hall where one learns, and he is a Torah scholar and learns in the study hall, it is more meritorious for him to pray in the study hall where he learns than to pray in the synagogue, even though there are more people in the synagogue. As it is written: "The Lord loves the gates of Zion more than all the dwellings of Jacob" (Psalms 87:2). And the "gates of Zion" refer to the gates distinguished by Halacha. And we hold that the sanctity of the study hall is greater than the sanctity of the synagogue, and therefore this is preferable to the virtue of "with a multitude of people." And this applies to a Torah scholar. But one who is not a Torah scholar – it is better for him to pray in the synagogue. Firstly, because of "with a multitude of people." Additionally, because it is the designated place for prayer, and the virtue of the study hall is only for a Torah scholar (so it seems to me).

A person should always establish a fixed place for their prayer, meaning they should consistently pray in one place. That is to say, whether regarding the house, they should always pray in this synagogue or this study hall, and not sometimes in this one and sometimes in that one. Similarly, in the specific place within that house where they pray—they should always pray in a particular spot, and not sometimes in the east and sometimes in the south, and so forth. Even when praying in their home—they should always pray in one place. And any four cubits is considered as one place, as it is impossible to be exact. And our forefather Abraham established a place for his prayer, as it is written: "To the place where he had stood before..." Therefore, one should not change their place except for a significant reason or if they are compelled to do so. Some of the early authorities said that in a synagogue, it does not matter which place, since the entire synagogue is a place of prayer (Tosafot of Rabbi Yehudah, first chapter). However, it is explained differently in the Jerusalem Talmud, fourth chapter of Berakhot, where it is stated: Rabbi Tanchum said: A person must designate a place for themselves in the synagogue, as it is written: "And David came to the head, where he would bow there." It does not say "where he bowed" but "where he would bow," meaning he regularly bowed there. This is also the ruling of the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, section 19.

It is stated in Berakhot (8a): A person should always enter the distance of two doorways, and then pray. And Rashi explained: When one enters the synagogue, one should not sit near the entrance, as it appears as a burden to him, and he will be ready to leave. Thus far his words. And the measure of two doorways is eight cubits. And in the Jerusalem Talmud, in the chapter "One Does Not Stand," it is derived from the verse: "To watch at my doors" – two doors. And for this reason, if one has a designated place near the entrance, there is no issue, as it is evident to everyone that he is sitting in his designated place. Nevertheless, according to the reason of the Jerusalem Talmud, it implies that there must always be two doors (see Beit Yosef and Magen Avraham, subsection 35). And it seems that for this reason, it has become customary to make a house before the synagogue which they call a foyer, and it is like a gatehouse so that one enters through two doors.

There are those who explain that this applies only when the entrance is open to the public domain, as the reason is that one should not gaze outside and thus be unable to concentrate during their prayer (Tur in the name of the Ra'am). According to this, if it is not open to the public domain, there is no issue. And there are those who explain that it refers to the waiting time, meaning: one should not rush to pray immediately upon entering but should wait the time it takes to pass through two entrances. This explanation is written by the Rosh. It is proper to be concerned for all interpretations. Therefore, if there is a house before the synagogue, as I have written, and its place is designated near the entrance, and it is not open to the public domain, and one waits the time it takes to pass through two entrances – it is permissible according to all opinions.

One must ensure that there is nothing intervening between oneself and the wall, as it is stated: "Hezekiah turned his face to the wall and prayed" (Isaiah 38:2). An "intervening object" is defined as something that is ten handbreadths high and four handbreadths wide. Anything less than this is not considered an obstruction. Living creatures are also not considered obstructions, nor is a person considered an obstruction. However, our teacher, the Rema, ruled that while a person is not an obstruction, living creatures are. Nevertheless, some say that one should not pray behind any person. It is good to be concerned about this opinion, as it appears as though one is bowing to the person. The same applies to living creatures. In a synagogue, people pray one behind the other because it is not possible otherwise, and it is evident to all that this is the customary manner of praying.

And similarly, something that stands permanently, like a closet or a cabinet, does not create a partition, as they are considered like the wall itself. However, a bed does create a partition (Tosafot there). Some say that our beds, which are used for lying down, do not create a partition because they always stand in one place (Beit Yosef). Others say that they do create a partition (Bach), but this is not necessarily the case (see Magen Avraham, subsection 36). Anything that is needed for prayer does not create a partition. Therefore, a stand on which one places the prayer book does not create a partition (Taz, subsection 5). However, some have reservations about this (Magen Avraham there). It appears, according to what the Rambam wrote in a responsum, that the reason is so that one does not look around, and for this reason, he prohibited having colorful clothes hanging on the wall so that one would not look at them and become distracted in prayer (see Beit Yosef) – there is no concern regarding the stand. Moreover, is this matter truly a strict requirement? It is merely an optimal practice (Taz there). The advice for this is to close one's eyes (there) and not look around. Therefore, with the stand, there is no concern. Also, in the responsum of the Rashba (Siman 96), it implies that anything needed for prayer and the synagogue does not create a partition, see there.

The garments that have illustrations, even though they are not protruding, it is not proper to pray opposite them, so that he will not be distracted. And if it happens that he prays opposite a garment or wall with illustrations, he should avert his eyes. Similarly, it is forbidden to draw illustrations on the walls of the synagogue opposite the faces of the worshippers. Rather, they should be above the height of a person, which is above three cubits, as this is the height of a man. Likewise, there should not be illustrations in the prayer books that are used for prayer, so that concentration is not disturbed. And items upon which indecent images are illustrated – it is forbidden even to sit on them in the synagogue, and even in his home, he should distance himself from them. In general, it is proper to eliminate all illustrations of animals and birds, and all the more so illustrations of people, that are made on the walls of synagogues. In general, it is advisable to avoid all illustrations even in the home. Indeed, the most appropriate prayer is that which is against a plain wall, and there should be nothing large or small opposite him. And they honor at the entrance of the synagogue by allowing the elder to enter first (Berachot 47a).

A person should never pray beside his teacher, as this appears as if he is equal to his teacher. Nor behind his teacher, as this also seems arrogant (Rashi 27b). Additionally, it appears as if he is bowing to his teacher (Tosafot there). Nor in front of his teacher, as this is certainly disrespectful, turning his back to his teacher. Rather, he should distance himself four cubits, as this is considered a different domain, and even praying in front of him is permissible. Some say that behind him requires four cubits and three steps (Pri Megadim), because some say the reason praying behind him is prohibited is so that the teacher does not suffer when he finishes his prayer and the student has not yet finished, preventing the teacher from taking the three steps back, since it is forbidden to pass in front of someone praying. This reasoning is found in the Jerusalem Talmud. Therefore, a distance of four cubits and three steps is required.

And all of this applies to one's primary teacher or the greatest sage of the generation, who is considered like one's primary teacher, as I have written in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 242. But regarding a teacher who is not one's primary teacher or a fellow student, it is permissible to pray beside him, in front of him, or behind him. There are those who forbid praying in front of him (Magen Avraham, subsection 39), and this is the primary ruling since it is more disrespectful. Rabbi Rema wrote in section 24 that some say this applies only to someone praying alone. But in a congregation, if that is the arrangement of the seating, there is no concern if one prays in front of or behind him. And although it is good to be stringent, the custom is to be lenient. This is the end of his words. It is proper to be stringent in practice (see Levush and Eliyah Rabbah). And on the bimah it is allowed.

Every place where one does not recite the Shema, one does not pray. Just as we distance ourselves from excrement, urine, foul odors, a corpse, and the sight of nakedness for the Shema, so too we distance ourselves for prayer. And similarly, for any sacred matter and Torah study, one must distance oneself. If one was standing in prayer and a child urinated in the synagogue, one should remain silent until water is brought to pour over the urine, and even on Shabbat it is permitted to pour the water. Alternatively, one should move four cubits in front of oneself or to the sides, or leave the synagogue and finish one's prayer. It is better to leave the synagogue to another place rather than to interrupt with silence, for perhaps one will delay long enough to finish the entire prayer and then have to start over. But under no circumstances should one interrupt with speech. If it is impossible to go to another place and there is no water, one can rely on the opinion of the Rashba, who permits praying in the presence of urine if one is already standing in prayer, for urine is a rabbinic prohibition. However, with excrement, which is a Torah prohibition, one must follow the aforementioned procedures. There are those who permit interrupting with speech in the case of excrement, but this does not seem correct to me. Rather, one should go to another place and signal to the congregation to leave or remove the excrement, and wait until the odor dissipates. These laws have already been explained in the laws of the Shema.

We have already written at the beginning of Siman 90 in the name of the Rambam that among the eight things one must be careful about during prayer is the proper arrangement of clothing. Refer there. Meaning: we are not speaking about matters that are also forbidden during the recitation of the Shema, such as if one's heart sees the nakedness, and certainly if one is naked. Rather, even something that is permitted during the recitation of the Shema, nevertheless, during prayer it is forbidden because in prayer it is as if one is standing before the King – one must be dressed properly. For this reason, it was said in Shabbat (10a) that Rabbah bar Rav Huna would put on fine socks and pray. And Rashi explained: he would put on important shoes on his feet because it is said: "Prepare to meet your God, O Israel."

They also said there: Rav Ashi stated: I saw Rav Kahana, when there was distress in the world, he would remove his cloak. Meaning: he would throw off his robe so as not to appear important (Rashi). When there was peace in the world, he would wear it, cover himself, wrap himself, and pray. He would say: "Prepare to meet your God, Israel." And in times of distress, he would cast off his robe and clasp his hands with his fingers as a person in pain from the fear of his master (there). Therefore, there are those who are meticulous now when there is distress in the world, not to pray Mincha and Maariv on weekdays with an outer garment. But on Shabbat and Yom Tov, they pray with an outer garment, for it is not proper to mention distress on Shabbat and Yom Tov. And the prayer leader also wears an outer garment on weekdays, or he wears a tallit. This is the common practice in these regions. Also, when going up to the Torah, they wear an outer garment out of respect for the Torah, and similarly when lifting the Torah.

Therefore, even though he had a garment wrapped around his waist to cover himself from the waist down, such that his heart does not see the nakedness, which in this manner for the recitation of Shema is permissible even though he is naked above the waist, as I wrote in Siman 74, nevertheless, in prayer it is forbidden until he covers his heart and his entire body from the front and from the back. However, after the fact, if he did not cover his heart, or he was compelled and has nothing with which to cover himself, since he covered his nakedness and prayed – he has fulfilled his obligation, as the Rambam already wrote there that these matters do not invalidate after the fact. And even if his heart sees the nakedness, we clarified in Siman 74 that he does not need to repeat the prayer, since this is only a rabbinic prohibition. But if his nakedness was exposed – he must repeat the prayer, as this is a biblical requirement. There are those who want to say that even if his heart sees the nakedness, he must repeat the prayer (see Chayei Adam and Mishnah Berurah), but this does not seem correct to me. And it is explicitly clear from the language of the Rambam in the fourth chapter and from the language of the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, Siman 1, that they wrote: since he covered his nakedness – he has fulfilled his obligation. This is their language. It is explicitly understood that the covering of nakedness alone is essential.

And it is also a mitzvah to gird oneself with a belt, referred to as a gartel (belt), during prayer, even if one is wearing pants with a waistband and his heart does not see the nakedness. Nevertheless, one should gird with a belt because of "prepare yourself...". However, someone who goes all day without a belt does not need to gird with a belt during prayer either (Magen Avraham, section 1). There are those who are meticulous and gird with a belt during prayer even if they go all day without a belt, but this is only for the Shemoneh Esrei prayer. For the recitation of the Shema and all blessings, it is permissible from the outset to do so without a belt, as long as he is wearing pants and his heart does not see the nakedness. Even if he does not have pants, if his clothes are placed directly on his stomach, forming a separation between his heart and the nakedness, it is permissible, as I have written in Siman 74. And know that I have seen it written that if one has nothing to cover his heart from the outset, he should not pray at all. I am astonished by this, for we have a rule that anything permissible after the fact (bedi'eved) is considered as if it were permissible from the outset (lechat'chilah) if one does not have the means. We rule this way in many laws, so why should the law change here? Therefore, it seems clear to me as I have written. (The Mishnah Berurah wrote that one should not pray [without covering the heart]. To me, it seems as I have written.)

Maimonides wrote in Chapter 5, Law 5: How should one prepare their clothing? First, they prepare their clothing, adorn themselves, and enhance their appearance, as it is said: "Worship the Lord in the beauty of holiness." One should not stand in prayer wearing an apron (a hollow belt in which money is placed), nor with a bare head, nor with bare feet if it is the custom of the people of that place not to stand before dignitaries except with shoes. Until here are his words. And in a place where it is customary to stand before dignitaries without shoes, it is permitted according to Maimonides. However, some forbid even in such a case, as it is stated in Chagigah that it is not proper etiquette to reveal one's feet before one's master; see there. It appears to me that they do not disagree: Certainly, barefoot is forbidden even according to Maimonides, but he speaks of leaving one's socks on the feet, which are called zaki"n. However, regarding a bare head, it is explicitly clear from his words that it is not dependent on the custom of the place. Even in a place where it is customary to stand before dignitaries with a bare head, it is forbidden during prayer. And although it is forbidden throughout the day, as I wrote in Siman 2, this is a matter of piety. Here it is by law (Magen Avraham, Small Section 3).

In our countries, one should not pray even with the head covered by a small covering, but rather a hat is required, similar to what is worn in the street. Also, one should not pray in a short garment called a kapote, because one does not go out into the street in it. And for uncovering the head, it does not help even if he covers it with his hands, unless he extends the sleeve of his shirt or garment over his hand and covers with it, for this helps. Likewise, if another person places his hand on this one's head, it also helps. And hats woven from straw are considered a covering. It is forbidden to mention God's name with an uncovered head. Concerning garments: the general rule is that one needs to pray in garments that one would wear in the street. Therefore, in a house garment called a "house coat," if it is not suitable to go out into the street in it, one should not pray in it. (The Magen Avraham mentioned a distinction between woolen and linen house coats. Among us, no difference is known between them.) And in felt boots in the winter, it seems to me that one can pray, for people do go out into the street in them.

And our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, wrote in paragraph six: The way of the wise and their students is to only pray when they are wrapped (in a tallit). And in times of distress, one should clasp their hands during prayer like a servant before their master. And in times of peace, one should adorn themselves with nice clothes to pray. So far his words, and we have already written about this. And "clasping hands" means interlacing the fingers of one's hands together, like a person who breaks their fingers when in distress. Some of the sages would do this even in times of peace (Rava in Shabbat 10a). Nevertheless, one should be careful not to clasp their fingers in times of peace, because this brings judgment upon oneself. Rather, one should place their hands one on top of the other, bound together (according to the Vilna Gaon). Not all people's natures are the same in this regard. Some find it difficult to pray in this manner and instead place their hands on the stand or on the sheet attached to the wall. There is no fixed rule in this, and each person should do as is best for them to pray in this manner. And one should not pray with gloves on (according to the Chaye Adam).

Preparing the body—how so? If one needs to relieve oneself, whether for urination or defecation, one should not pray, as it is stated: "Prepare to meet your God, O Israel" (Amos 4:12); and it is stated: "Guard your steps when you go to the house of God" (Ecclesiastes 5:1)—guard your bodily needs when you stand in prayer before Him. If one prayed while needing to relieve oneself, the prayer is considered an abomination when one needed to defecate, and one must pray again. But if it was for urination, the prayer is still considered a prayer (Magen Avraham, subsection 1), as urination does not cause as much impurity. Even if the time for reciting the Shema would pass, one is forbidden to pray when needing to defecate. For urination, the passing of time does not apply, as it only takes a few moments. However, for defecation, the process is difficult for many people, and it necessitates waiting.

When did they say that one needs to go back and pray again? When one could not hold himself for the duration of a parsah, which is one hour and twelve minutes, for until this time he was compelled to release waste and prayed in his complete impurity. However, if he could hold himself for this duration – after the fact, his prayer is considered a prayer. But initially, one should not pray until he examines himself thoroughly beforehand. This is written by the Rambam in the fourth chapter, and by the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch, Section 1. However, Rashi and the Rif wrote there that if he can hold himself for a parsah – it is permitted for him to pray initially. And the poskim (Rosh and Tosafot Yom Tov and Beit Yosef) dismissed their words, as it is explicitly taught: One who needs to relieve himself should not pray. There are those who differentiate between when the time will pass and when it will not (Bach). And there are those who wrote that if the time will pass – one can rely on the Rif and Rashi (Magen Avraham, Section 1). And although it is possible that halachically one should rule this way, nevertheless, it appears to me in my humble opinion that they do not disagree in practice at all.

This is something that is obvious: if, when he checks himself now, waste would come out, he is obligated to check himself even though he can hold it in for the length of a parasang (a Persian mile, approximately 4 kilometers) or more. Regarding this, it was taught: "One who needs to relieve himself should not pray," meaning until he checks himself. And this is what they concluded: "until he checks..." And even Rashi and the Rif would be compelled to agree with this. How could it be said otherwise? However, Rashi and the Rif refer to a different case: it is known that some people have difficulty with bowel movements, and no checking helps. In such a case, they rightly said that if he cannot hold it in for the length of a parasang, meaning he knows that during this time he will inevitably need to relieve himself, even though he cannot do so now – he should not pray. And if he prayed, his prayer is an abomination, and he must pray again. But if he can hold it in for the length of a parasang, he can initially pray now, since he cannot relieve himself at this moment. And if you ask: how does he know this? This is not a question at all, for every person recognizes this in themselves, and in this, even the Rambam, the Tur, and the Shulchan Aruch would agree. This seems to me to be the primary ruling in this matter.

Anyone who needs to relieve themselves is forbidden to engage even in words of Torah as long as their body is repulsive due to the need to relieve themselves. One is obligated to remove phlegm and mucus before prayer, as well as any other distractions, before praying. Similarly, if one’s face and hands are dirty, the dirt must be removed before prayer. One should also clean their nose and eyes, and their ears. Additionally, if the hair on their head is disheveled, they should smooth it with their hands so that it is orderly, as if standing before a king.

And if in the middle of prayer he feels a desire for his needs, our master the Beit Yosef rules in section 2 that he should stand firm until he finishes and not interrupt. And if during the recitation of the Shema and its blessings he feels the urge, whether for minor or major needs — he should continue as usual. If he wishes to distance himself and urinate, he may do so. Thus far his words. And our master the Rema writes that this is only if the urge is not so strong that it involves "Bal Teshaktzu" (do not make yourselves abominable). But otherwise, it is better to interrupt. Thus far his words. And he explains his reasoning in his book Darkei Moshe: because in the responsa of the Rashba (Siman 131) he rules that one does not need to interrupt, and in the Terumat HaDeshen (Siman 16) he rules that it is forbidden. And this distinction must be made, see there. And there is one who wrote that they certainly disagree. And in public, it is certainly permissible to rely on the Rashba because of the great honor of human dignity, and even the Terumat HaDeshen agrees with this. But even when praying individually, it is permissible to rely on the Rashba (Magen Avraham, subsection 2), because since he began permissibly, he does not need to interrupt. (And what the Magen Avraham wrote that it is a Rabbinic prohibition, see there — it requires further analysis. For though "Bal Teshaktzu" is Rabbinic, nevertheless, to pray or to read seems to me to be forbidden from the Torah. And it seems to me that what he wrote about urinating applies also to major needs, and it is even more so.)

And I am astonished by all these things, for in the Terumat HaDeshen it is a different matter regarding what they said, that if one wishes to sneeze from below, he should distance himself four cubits and sneeze, and wait until the smell dissipates, as will be explained in Siman 103. And the Terumat HaDeshen wrote that he did not see this practice being observed. He wrote the reason: that in public it is disgraceful to do so, and the honor of people is great and it overrides the prohibition of "do not make yourself repulsive." And what relevance does this have to one who needs to relieve himself and must leave the synagogue entirely? For this reason, the Rashba permitted him to finish his prayer because he started it permissibly. And our teacher, the Rema, in Siman 103 brought these words of the Terumat HaDeshen, but it has no connection to one who needs to relieve himself and must leave the synagogue entirely. This requires great scrutiny, and see in the next section.

Additionally, it is perplexing regarding the Rashba: for it is understandable that one should not interrupt in prayer, but why should one not interrupt in the recitation of Shema and its blessings? Is it worse than "responding out of respect"? It must be said that he holds it is entirely permissible since he began permissibly. And it is not comparable to sneezing mentioned in Siman 103, where one must interrupt even in prayer, for this is not called an "interruption" but rather moving a bit from his place. However, when one needs to relieve himself and must go to the bathroom – that is considered a complete interruption. And from this, there is clear evidence for what we wrote in the previous section, that the ruling of the Terumat HaDeshen is not relevant here at all.

One must wash their hands with water before prayer if they have water available. If they do not have water, they must go search for it up to a distance of a parasang (approximately four kilometers). This applies when they are traveling and there is water ahead on their path within a parasang. However, if they need to go back for water up to a distance of a mile, they should go back; beyond a mile, they are not required to return. Similarly, if one is at home, they must make an effort to obtain water within a mile. All this is required as long as it does not cause them to miss the time for prayer. But if they fear that the time for prayer will pass, they are not required to search for water under any circumstances. Instead, they should clean their hands with a cloth, dust, or anything else that cleans. According to the Rif, even in such a case, one must seek water for prayer, and only for the Shema is it sufficient to use a cloth. (Taz, section 1)

And when did they require him to use water? When his hands are dirty from things that require washing or if they touched something unclean. But if he does not know of any dirt on them and in the morning he washed his hands, even though he was distracted since then, he does not need to wash his hands or clean them, as hands are generally considered fit for prayer just as they are fit for other blessings. Similarly, for Mincha, if he washed his hands for a meal and does not know of any dirt, he does not need to wash or clean his hands for Mincha. This is the opinion of the Tur in the name of "some say," and it is also the opinion of the Ran. However, some say that distraction invalidates for prayer because hands are generally busy and certainly touched something unclean. This is the opinion of the Rambam and the Rosh, and this is the main opinion (the Gra). And even though for other blessings we are not concerned about hands being generally busy, it is not comparable to prayer which has many blessings and is like standing before the king. However, even according to this opinion, he is not obligated to go out of his way to find water if he does not have it in his place, since he does not know of any dirt on them. Rather, he should clean them with a cloth, dust, or on a beam or wall, and this suffices for distraction, as the reason for distraction is that perhaps there is some sweat or filth stuck to them, and when he rubs them with these things they get cleaned. And similarly, if he is standing in prayer and remembers that he touched something unclean and it is impossible to leave his place during prayer, he should clean with these things. This applies when standing in the Amidah. But during Pesukei Dezimra or the Shema and its blessings, he can go to wash his hands with water if there is water in the synagogue. But to go elsewhere, even for these, it suffices to clean with these things. (This seems to me, and see Magen Avraham, subparagraph 3). And for someone engaged in Torah study, it always suffices to clean with these things (ibid., subparagraph 5).

A "filthy place" refers to places covered by the body. The hand up to the elbow is considered "exposed," and from the neck to the chest and onwards is considered "covered." When one touches there, they need to wash their hands, and all the more so in places on the body that are completely covered. Touching the hair on the head does not require washing, but if one scratches their head, washing is necessary. If one removes a louse with their hands, washing is necessary. However, for a flea, it seems to me that washing is not necessary, as it is not as repulsive as a louse unless it is killed. However, a bedbug, which is called a "wanze," is considered repulsive, and washing is necessary. Scratching one's beard or sideburns is not considered anything (i.e., does not require washing).

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote in paragraph 7 that therefore it is forbidden to touch these places while standing in prayer or engaged in Torah study, as well as the earwax and nasal mucus, except through a garment. These are his words. And it implies from his words that for nasal mucus, one needs to wash hands if touched with them, but I have not seen people being careful with this. And it appears to me that for nasal mucus and earwax, water is not needed but rather cleaning with a wall or beam, and all that has been explained. And it seems to me that this is the custom. And there are those who completely disagree with this (the Gra in subsection 16 and Mor U'Ketzia). And contemplation is permitted if one touched unclean places (Rabbi Akiva Eiger). (From the language of the Shulchan Aruch, it implies that only in a place where there is sweat or remnants of sweat one needs washing, see there in paragraph 7.)

It is stated in the Megillah (27b): One who urinates should not pray until he waits the distance of four cubits because of the droplets. And so it is in the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, section 8. Rashi explains "because of the droplets" – so that his clothes do not become soiled by the droplets from his organ. Until here is his language. And it appears that the explanation is as follows: that after one finishes urinating, he should not yet walk away from the place where he urinated for the time it takes to walk four cubits, because the droplets are still dripping within this measure of time. According to this, even without considering prayer, one should be concerned, as he needs to recite the blessing of "Asher Yatzar." And perhaps for the sake of one blessing, they were not so concerned, and this is also implied by the language of the Levush, who wrote that it is as if he is praying opposite the droplets, see there. Consequently, even if he did not do so, he is obligated to wait this measure of time until the droplets are absorbed into his clothing (so it appears to me).

One who prays should not urinate until he has waited the amount of time it takes to walk four cubits, because during this entire time his prayer is still fluent in his mouth and he will think about it while urinating. The same applies to one engaged in Torah study. From the language of the Talmud and the legal decisors who wrote that during the four cubits his prayer is fluent in his mouth and his lips are still moving, it implies that the concern is only with speech. If so, it is possible that with Torah study, there is no need to be stringent, as the words of Torah are not as fluent in his mouth as prayer. This requires further study as to why they did not also consider the issue of thinking about it. It is permitted to urinate in the place where one prayed if he prayed in a courtyard or in a field. However, it is an act of piety not to urinate there (as stated in the Gemara). Similarly, one who spits should not pray until he has waited four cubits, so that it does not appear as though he spat on what he will say afterward. Certainly, if he prayed, he should not spit until he has waited four cubits. This specifically applies if he spits willingly. But if saliva happens to come up and he is compelled to spit, such as with phlegm or mucus, it is permitted, as everyone sees that he is compelled to spit. It is good to give charity before praying. Some wrote to give it when reaching "And David blessed...". (It is written in Sefer Chasidim that one should not urinate or spit in a place where he covered the blood of a bird, while the blood is still visible. And it is stated in Shabbat 50b: A person washes his face and hands in honor of his Creator.)

Maimonides wrote in Chapter 4, Halacha 15: What is the meaning of concentration of the heart? Any prayer that is not with concentration is not considered prayer. If one prayed without concentration, he must go back and pray again with concentration. If he finds his mind confused and his heart troubled, it is forbidden for him to pray until his mind settles. Therefore, if one comes from the road and is tired or distressed, it is forbidden for him to pray until his mind settles. The sages said: He should wait three days until he rests and his mind cools down, and then he may pray. Thus far is his language. And this is in Eruvin (65a), see there. And what he did not bring from there: Shmuel would not pray in a house where there was beer. Rav Pappa would not pray in a house where there were fish brine. See there – for he understood that this was their personal stringency, and it is not a fixed law for the public. To exclude, regarding one coming from the road, it is said there: Rabbi Eliezer said: One who comes from the road should not pray for three days. And this is a decided law for all people.

The Tur brings this later in Siman 98, and writes in the name of the RaM that nowadays we are not careful about all this, because we do not have so much intention in prayer. Thus are his words. And likewise, Rabbeinu the Beit Yosef writes there in Se'if 2. And also Rabbeinu the Rema in Siman 101 Se'if 1 writes that nowadays we do not repeat because of lack of intention, for even in the repetition it is likely that one will not have intention. So why should he repeat? See there. And likewise, the Tur writes there, see there.

The Rambam also wrote there: How should one have proper intention? One should clear their mind of all thoughts and see oneself as if standing before the Divine Presence. Therefore, one should sit quietly for a short time before praying in order to direct one's heart, and then pray calmly and with supplication. One should not treat their prayer as if they are carrying a burden and throwing it off and then leaving. Therefore, one should sit quietly for a short time after praying, and then depart. The early pious ones would wait for one hour before praying, one hour after praying, and extend their prayer for one hour. Thus far his words. And this is its explanation: Even though they extended their waiting time to a full hour before prayer, which is one twenty-fourth of a day, and also did so after prayer, nevertheless, it is not necessary to impose this on everyone. Therefore, a short time before prayer and a short time after prayer suffices. It appears that the time it takes to walk eight cubits is sufficient, as this is the explanation of "two entrances" in Siman 90, section 25 according to the latter interpretation, see there. And we do not find anyone who disagrees with this.

And also, the Tur wrote, and this is his language: "And when he comes to pray, he should wait a little..." But our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 1: "He should wait one hour before he rises to pray, so that he can direct his heart to Heaven, and one hour after the prayer..." Until here is his language. And this is against the Rambam and the Tur, who did not require us to wait an hour. However, it seems to me that his intention is because the term "hour" includes both a little and a lot, therefore he did not worry about it and his way is to be brief. But his intention is not for an actual hour. (See Magen Avraham, small section 1. And according to what I wrote, it fits well.) And there are those who specifically require that he sit and wait, because by sitting, one settles more into the intention of the prayer. And one should not ask: Since this law is for the sake of intention, and according to the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, nowadays we do not have such intention, why do we need to wait? This is not a question, for we are certainly commanded to do everything possible to come to a state of intention. And if it does not help, it certainly does not harm, and we cannot absolve ourselves from this. And know that here the intention is not about the Amidah prayer, since we wait a lot until the Amidah through the verses of praise, and through the Shema and its blessings. Rather, the intention is about the entire order of prayer, for the matter of "waiting" is silence and contemplation in the heart, to understand before whom he prepares himself to pray. And it is written in the Seder Hayom that after the prayer, when one needs to leave, if he can wait until there are no less than ten people in the synagogue, it is good, so that he will not be among those who cause the departure of the Shechinah. For he waited until the point that there was no longer the presence of the Shechinah, as the Shechinah does not rest with less than ten, see there. And behold, this certainly not everyone can do. However, certainly one must be careful in this: if there are exactly ten people, he should not be the first to leave from the ten, for this certainly nullifies the resting of the Shechinah.

The Sages taught in the Mishnah (Berachot 30b): One should not stand to pray except in a state of seriousness. This means: with humility and awe. Therefore, it is beneficial to pause before praying, to contemplate the greatness of the Holy One, Blessed be He, and one's own lowliness. One should not stand to pray from a state of frivolity or levity, nor from idle talk, nor from anger, but rather from the joy of a mitzvah. This means: even if one cannot stand with seriousness, at the very least one should not stand from a state of frivolity or levity, or from idle talk or anger.

This is the language of our master, the Beit Yosef, in section 2: One should not stand to pray... except with joy, such as words of consolation, of Torah, like adjacent to the redemption from Egypt, or adjacent to "Tehilla LeDavid" in which it is written: "He fulfills the desire of those who fear Him... He watches over all who love Him." This is its language, and here the intention is about the Amidah prayer. Therefore, in Shacharit (the morning prayer) where the redemption is adjacent to the prayer – there is the joy of the redemption from Egypt. And in Mincha (the afternoon prayer) where they say "Ashrei" beforehand – there is the joy of "He fulfills the desire of those who fear Him." And so it is explained from the language of the Tur who wrote: One does not stand... except with joy. Therefore, it became customary to say "Ashrei" and the verses of praise before the prayer, in order to stand in prayer with words of joy of a commandment... This is its language. And so our sages of blessed memory said: One should not stand to pray from judgment, nor from halacha lest his heart be preoccupied with it. Rather, from a decided halacha. And our master the Rema wrote that this also means like "with joy," because "The precepts of the Lord are right, rejoicing the heart." This is its language. And this does not contradict the previous, for here the intention is about the entire prayer service and not about the Amidah. Nonetheless, if one was involved in dialectical reasoning before the prayer – he should not refrain from praying with the congregation or when the time of prayer arrives, for it is merely a concern and especially nowadays when in any case there is not so much intention (Magen Avraham, subsection 3).

Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote in section 4: One who is engaged in public needs is considered as if he is engaged in Torah study. This means regarding standing to pray from within it, for this too is a joy for him as he is engaged in public needs. And some explain that this means he does not need to interrupt to pray. Until here are his words, because one who is engaged in a mitzvah is exempt from another mitzvah, and so it appears in the Jerusalem Talmud. And specifically public needs that do not involve disturbance. But when there is disturbance – one does not stand to pray from within it, like from within a matter of law that is not decided (there, subsection 4). And when one is engaged in public needs and the time for prayer has passed – he does not need to pray the afternoon prayer twice, because he was not obligated at the time of the act, for one who is engaged in a mitzvah is exempt from another mitzvah. (there, subsection 5. And see there, and in Yoreh De'ah, section 341, and in Eliyah Rabbah. And not like the Taz there and later at the beginning of section 108).

Upon entering the synagogue, one should say: "But I, in the abundance of Your loving kindness, will enter Your house" (Zohar). However, "I will bow down toward Your holy temple in fear of You" should only be said if one is wrapped in tefillin (ibid). Some pray from a prayer book to enhance their concentration, as written in the Book of Intentions. But in truth, it depends on the individual (Magen Avraham, subsection 2), for some people do not have concentration when praying from a prayer book, yet have concentration when praying by heart. Fortunate is he whose eyes are closed throughout the entire prayer, from "Blessed is He Who spoke" until "Aleinu," for closing the eyes significantly aids concentration. Some have this custom, and the main thing is that one's intention be for the sake of Heaven. As for those who stand in prayer and appear fatigued, regarding them, the scripture says: "But you have not called upon Me, O Jacob, for you have been weary of Me, O Israel" (Eliyah Rabbah in the name of Shiyarei Knesset HaGedolah).

In the eight matters we considered at the beginning of Siman 98, we considered "facing the Temple." And so the Sages taught (Berachot 30a): If one is standing outside the Land of Israel, they should direct their heart towards the Land of Israel, as it is said: "And they shall pray to You by way of their land" (I Kings 8:48). If one is standing in the Land of Israel, they should direct their heart towards Jerusalem, as it is said: "And they shall pray to the Lord by way of the city" (I Kings 8:44). If one is standing in Jerusalem, they should direct their heart towards the Temple, as it is said: "And they shall pray to this house" (II Chronicles 6:32). If one is standing in the Temple, they should direct their heart towards the Holy of Holies, as it is said: "And they shall pray towards this place" (I Kings 8:30). It therefore follows that one standing in the east should turn their face to the west, in the west - they should turn their face to the east, in the south - they should turn their face to the north, in the north - they should turn their face to the south. Thus, all Israel direct their hearts to one place. And this is what is written: "Your neck is like the tower of David, built for an armory" (Song of Songs 4:4) - "a mound to which all mouths turn." And a blind person or one who cannot determine the directions should direct their heart to their Father in Heaven, for it is not an absolute requirement to pray facing Jerusalem. Similarly, one who is sitting in a wagon or on a ship, and it is not possible for them to pray facing Jerusalem when the wagon or ship do not move in that direction, should direct their heart to their Father in Heaven. More will be explained on this matter.

We need to understand what is meant by the term "direct his heart." One must turn his face towards the name, as it says later: "It turns out that one who stands in the east should turn his face to the west...". We must say that it means it is not sufficient to just turn one's face, but one must also direct his heart to that holy place. From this, it seems to me that Rabbi Yosef Karo, the author of the Shulchan Aruch, derived his ruling in section 1: If one is standing outside of the Land of Israel, he should turn his face towards the Land of Israel and also direct his heart towards Jerusalem, the Temple, and the Holy of Holies. Similarly, if one is standing in the Land of Israel, he should turn his face towards Jerusalem and also direct his heart towards the Temple and the Holy of Holies. And if one is standing in Jerusalem, he should turn his face towards the Temple and also direct his heart towards the Holy of Holies. See there, he is a disciple of Rabbeinu Yonah. And at first glance, from where do we know to say this? However, they derived it from the term "directing the heart," implying that since one must direct to the holy place, consequently, one must direct to the holiest places. Additionally, it is stated there that if one was standing behind the Ark Covering, meaning to the west of the Temple behind the Holy of Holies, he should turn his face to the Ark Covering. (And in section 5, another reason for the term "direct his heart" will be explained.)

And our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 2: If one prays facing a direction other than east, he should turn his face towards the Land of Israel if he is outside the Land, towards Jerusalem if he is in the Land of Israel, and towards the Temple if he is in Jerusalem. These are his words. He explained his words in his larger work: there are places where people pray facing north or south. By law, we should pray facing east because we are to the west of the Land of Israel, as will be explained, but they do not want to change their custom. He wrote the counsel that one should turn his face towards the Land of Israel to the east. The proof is from what our sages said (Bava Batra 25b): one who wants to become wise should face south; one who wants to become rich should face north. And what do those who pray facing east or west do? They turn their faces slightly to the south or north. Thus, turning slightly is effective, and here too it is the same (see Beit Yosef). And when he wrote "facing a direction other than east," he did not mean all directions, for one standing to the west cannot turn his head to the east, nor from east to west, as this is not turning slightly but rather completely turning one's face. His intention was specifically about north and south, as he wrote in his larger work (Taz section 1). And know that if one prays in a direction other than what is required, and remembers in the middle of the prayer, he should not interrupt and move himself to the proper place, but rather he should turn his face to that direction if he can do so, as I have written (ibid.).

Tosafot, the Rosh, the Mordechai (there), and the Tur wrote that we pray facing east because we are to the west of the Land of Israel. Similarly, our teacher, the Rema, wrote in paragraph 2, and this is his language: "And we who turn our faces to the east, because we are situated to the west of the Land of Israel. Thus, our faces are toward the Land of Israel." Until here are his words. And behold, our early rabbis who were in France and Germany, it makes sense, as these countries are directly west of the Land of Israel. But our teacher, the Rema, who was in Poland, and similarly our country, Russia, which are situated to the north of the world, if so, we are to the northwest of the Land of Israel. And when we stand facing east—it is not directly toward the Land of Israel. And the great ones have already addressed this (Levush and Ma'adanei Yom Tov there, and Taz and Magen Avraham). And they wrote that indeed, when building a synagogue, the eastern wall where the Holy Ark is should be inclined towards the southeast, so that it will be directed toward the Land of Israel and Jerusalem. However, we do not have the ability to build as we wish, because the buildings are constructed according to the permissions of the government.

According to this, the most appropriate place for this is in the southeastern corner. Similarly, all those standing on the side of the Holy Ark facing the northern wall can stand facing east and slightly turn towards the south. But those standing on the side of the Holy Ark facing the southern wall cannot turn towards the south, for if they do, their backs will be towards the Holy Ark, and they must stand directly facing east. However, during the bowing, they should turn their heads towards the south. This was also the practice of one of the great sages (Ma'adanei Yom Tov in that place).

And behold, the entirety of Israel does not do so, but builds towards the east and stands completely facing east as is known. And it seems to me to justify their practice as correct. For in Bava Batra (25a), it is said that Rabbi Akiva holds that the Divine Presence is in the west, and so does Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, and one must pray only towards the west. Similarly, Rabbi Abahu holds this view, see there. And Rabbi Oshaya, Rabbi Yishmael, and Rav Sheshet hold that the Divine Presence is everywhere, and one can pray in any direction he wishes, see there. And our Rabbis, the Tosafot, wrote there and in Berakhot (30a), as well as the Rosh there and the Tur in this siman, that all these Tannaim and Amoraim do not hold by that Baraita which obligates one to pray facing Jerusalem, see there. If so, the matter is perplexing: since all these authorities dispute it, how do we rule according to that Baraita? And they wrote that there in Bava Batra, Rabbi Chanina holds like that Baraita, as he said to Rabbi Yashia: "You who sit in the north of the Land of Israel, turn southward," see there. And this too is perplexing, to rule like an individual against many. And even more perplexing: how can it be that all these Tannaim and Amoraim do not hold thus? Did not Solomon in his prayer say, "And they shall pray toward their land, toward the city which You have chosen, and they shall pray toward this house"? And Daniel prayed facing Jerusalem.

It appears that the matter is as follows: In Bava Batra, there is a discussion regarding Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's statement that the Divine Presence is in the West, and he himself said that one should always face south. It is explained there that he means to turn partially. Rashi explains that this means standing in the west and turning slightly towards the south. The Sefer Mitzvot Gadol (Positive Commandment 19) explains the opposite; see there for further details. From this, it is clear that when it is said to pray in a certain direction or towards a certain place, it suffices to turn slightly, and it is not necessary for one's entire body and face to be directed there.

Accordingly, I say that all the Tannaim and Amoraim in Bava Batra do not disagree with the principle in Berachot, and they all agree that one must direct oneself towards the Land of Israel and towards Jerusalem. Those who hold that the Divine Presence is in the West also agree that one can turn slightly. This means that countries situated to the east, south, or north of the Land of Israel can pray towards the west. Those in the south or north should pray towards the west and turn slightly to the south or north, or alternatively, they may pray towards the south or north and turn slightly towards the west.

Countries situated to the west, like ours, necessarily cannot face west, as this would mean their backs would be towards the Land of Israel. They agree that it is impossible to pray towards the west in such cases, and they were speaking about the majority of the world. Those who hold that the Divine Presence is everywhere and that one can pray in any direction they wish, also agree that one is obligated to turn their face towards the Land of Israel or pray towards the Land of Israel, and they can turn their face in any direction they wish.

According to this, standing toward the direction of the Land of Israel and Jerusalem does not mean facing precisely in that direction, but rather inclining slightly toward it. I say that for this reason it is taught in the Baraita: "One should direct his heart toward the Land of Israel and toward Jerusalem." Why does it not say "stand facing the Land of Israel"? Because this is not possible in every place, and it suffices to incline slightly, as it concludes: "he should turn his face." Meaning: turning one's face is sufficient. When we scrutinize Solomon's prayer: "They shall pray to You toward their land" and "they shall pray toward the city which You have chosen," and also it is written: "they shall pray toward this place" as explained in Kings. Why does it not say here "toward this place" as it says "toward their land" and "toward the city"? The reason seems to me that "they shall pray toward this place" refers to when one is standing in Jerusalem and can precisely direct himself toward the location of the Temple. But "toward their land" refers to those who are in exile, and "toward the city" refers to those praying anywhere in the Land of Israel. The matter is clear that throughout the world it is impossible to pray directly toward the Land of Israel, as the breadth of the world is much larger than the Land of Israel, and similarly, all of the Land of Israel is much larger than Jerusalem. Therefore, it says "toward their land," meaning any inclination toward it, and one should direct his heart. (This is an additional reason to what I wrote in Section B.)

Based on this, that it is not necessary to stand directly facing the Land of Israel, our custom of standing towards the east aligns well. Even though we are in the northwestern region, there is still a slight inclination towards the west, as is evident. This is not less effective than turning one's face, since the main thing is the intention of the heart towards the Land of Israel. And since we stand to the east and direct our hearts towards the Land of Israel, there is also an inclination towards the Land of Israel, for we are not standing at the northernmost edge, but rather in the north adjacent to the west. Consequently, when we stand towards the east, there is an inclination towards the west of the world, where the Land of Israel is situated.

Rabbi Moses Isserles (Rema) writes: One should not place the Ark and the direction of prayer directly facing the sunrise, for this is the custom of the heretics. Rather, align it facing midday. And one who wishes to fulfill the statement (Bava Batra there): "One who wants to become wealthy should face north, and one who wants to become wise should face south," should still direct his face towards the east. This is his language. There are those who explain it thus: Since our country leans towards the northern part of the world, and the sun never rises precisely in the east for us but leans towards the south, if we position the Ark and the eastern wall directly facing the sunrise, the prayer will be directed towards the south, not the east. Rather, it should be aligned according to the sun's path at midday, when it is between the south and the north, in the middle, and the wall will be directly east (Ma'adanei Yom Tov there, section 28). According to this, it is the opposite of what I wrote in section 4, that we need to align it towards the southeastern side. Indeed, there are those who disagreed with this. (See Taz, subsection 2; Magen Avraham, subsection 4; Ma'adanei Yom Tov there; and Eliyah Rabbah, subsection 3, all agreeing with the Levush to align it towards the southeastern side.)

And I am astonished by this: Did our teacher, the Rema, not know this? And who is as wise in wisdom as he, as we see in his book "Torat HaOlah"? Furthermore, if so, why did he say it is because this is the way of the heretics? Rather, it seems clear to me that on the contrary, he was teaching us that even though according to the tendency of our country we should face towards the sunrise, which would be southeast, nevertheless, since the heretics are meticulous in this to bow towards the sunrise – we should not do so, and we should face towards the middle of the east even if it is not exactly towards the Land of Israel. And this supports our words in section 9. Therefore, he concludes that one who wants to be meticulous should turn his face to the east. That is to say: it is enough to turn one's face. Therefore, we do not need to be meticulous to stand directly towards the Land of Israel, as we stated in section 9. (The genius Rabbi Yeshaya Pick disputed this, as from Rashi it is clear that the turning should be to the south, see there. But the SeMaG wrote that the turning is to the east. And the Rema intentionally wrote so, meaning: that we do not need to stand directly to the east but just a general turning. Therefore, our custom is proper. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

The Holy Ark is placed in the east. Even if it was placed on another side, nonetheless, one should pray facing east (Magen Avraham, subsection 3, in the name of Knesset HaGedolah). Therefore, one should be careful not to place it on the west, for in that case, their backs would be towards the sanctuary. According to what the great authorities have written to incline towards the south, as I have written in subsection 4 – it should not be placed in the north for this reason, but only in the south. However, we have never seen this done, and the Holy Ark is always placed on the eastern wall. (See Beit Yosef, from whose words it appears that the Rama's words are like those of the Levush. This is also implied in the Machatzit HaShekel, subsection 4, see there. This is puzzling, as explained in Ma'adanei Yom Tov. This is also implied in Taz, subsection 2.)

If the Holy Ark stands to the north or to the south, and the entire congregation prays in that direction, and one person wants to pray facing the east – he should not do so, because then they will not all bow in the same direction, and it will appear as if there are two authorities. Rather, he should pray in the direction that the congregation is praying, and slightly turn himself towards the east (and this is also implied in the Beit Yosef). However, if he is praying there alone, not at the time when the congregation is praying – he may pray facing the eastern wall, because then it will not appear as if there are two authorities.

And know that according to the words of the great ones in section 4, that in our case, we need to position the eastern wall in the southeastern direction because we are in the northwestern part of the Land of Israel — not all places are equal in this placement. This depends on the inclination of the central eastern point of this location towards Jerusalem. This point is the place where the sun rises for this location during the seasons of Nisan and Tishrei, and it is the place where the equatorial circle meets the horizon at this location, at which time the day and night are equal. In the more northern countries — even during these seasons, the day and night are not equal. Therefore, one needs to know when the day and night are equal in this location, and accordingly, position the eastern wall and the Holy Ark (see Shulchan Aruch of the Alter Rebbe, section 3).

If one is riding on a donkey, he does not need to dismount to pray, even if he has someone who can hold his donkey. Rather, he should pray while riding, because if he dismounts, his mind will not be settled. However, if he can turn his face towards the Land of Israel, it is good, as this he can do even while riding on the donkey. Similarly, if he feels inclined to dismount from the donkey and pray, and knows that his mind will be settled, a blessing shall come upon him. The same law applies to one riding a horse, even though the horse runs a lot and this could cause a lack of concentration. Nonetheless, he is not required by law to dismount. He should pray while riding.

And similarly, if one is sitting in a carriage or a boat, if he can stand within the carriage or the boat, such as when the carriage or boat is moving slowly, and he stands while they are moving – he must stand, for even though they are moving, in regard to prayer it is considered as standing (see Taz, subparagraph 4). But if he cannot stand, such as when they are moving quickly and he will fall if he stands – he sits in his place and prays, and he should turn his face towards the Land of Israel if he is able. The sages did not trouble him to stop the carriage or the boat, even though they are within his control and he could stop them. If he wishes to stop them himself – a blessing shall come upon him.

And similarly, if one is walking on the road on foot – he prays while walking, even if his face is not directed towards the Land of Israel, even if it is not a place of danger. The sages did not burden him to stand and pray, because it would be difficult for him to delay his journey, and his heart would be troubled, and he would not be able to concentrate. And it appears that in this situation it is impossible for him to turn his face towards the Land of Israel, for one who is walking must have his eyes in front of him. However, everything depends on the road, his fear (of God), and his presence of mind, and one who is stringent in this matter will be blessed. And there are those who say that one is obligated to stand during the blessing of the Patriarchs, and it is proper to take this opinion into consideration if it is not a place of danger. Similarly, if one is riding on an animal – he should stop the animal during the blessing of the Patriarchs, and he does not need to dismount. Likewise, if one is traveling in a wagon when possible. However, the custom is not to do so because it is a great inconvenience.

How should one perform the bowings? If one is walking on foot, they can bow, and upon reaching the end of the Shemoneh Esrei, they should take three steps backward. When seated in a carriage or a boat, if they can stand at the time of the bowings, they should stand and bow. For although one is permitted to pray while seated, it is certainly fitting to stand on one's feet during the bowings if possible, as well as for the three steps backward at the conclusion of the prayer. If it is not possible, one should bow while seated, and the three steps cannot be performed. If one is riding an animal and cannot stand, they are not required to. As for the three steps, they should make the animal take three steps backward, and it will be as if they themselves did so, and it will count as if they stepped back themselves. Alternatively, if possible, one may move themselves backward on the animal, and if not, they are not required to (see Magen Avraham, section 9).

A sick person may pray even while lying on his side, provided he can concentrate his mind. Even if he is unable to put on tefillin, he should still recite the Shema and pray when he is able. If he cannot concentrate his mind, he should not pray. Nevertheless, he should meditate in his heart if he can, as it is written: "Speak in your hearts upon your beds." Even though we hold that meditation is not equivalent to speech, a sick person is different. This is the explanation of the verse: when you are on your beds, speech through meditation is acceptable. The general principle is that a sick person who is mentally sound should do as much as he can. Even if he can only say one verse, he should say "Shema Yisrael" and the rest in meditation. If he can say the blessing of the fathers (Avot) with his mouth, he should say it, and the rest in meditation. And so on with similar cases. A wise person has his eyes in his head to understand himself how much he is able to do.

There are times when one is sitting at home, and he is healthy, and it is permitted for him to pray while seated. For example, if non-Jews are sitting next to him on either side, and he is afraid that if he stands up to pray, they will steal his belongings or interrupt his prayer—it is better for him to pray while seated rather than standing, because his mind will not be at ease. He should bow while seated. And although one must take three steps back after praying—here he is exempt, since it is impossible, as is evident. Therefore, one who is traveling on a train, even though it is possible to stand there, nevertheless, if there are people sitting next to him who are not respectable, and he fears they might take his belongings—it is permitted for him to pray while seated.

Care should be taken not to lean on a pillar, or on a friend, or on the stand during prayer. For standing that is supported by leaning is not called "standing" but rather "sitting," and the Amidah prayer requires standing. Therefore, slight leaning, where even if the object were removed one could still stand, is permitted. There is an opinion that the reason is because one must stand with fear and reverence. According to this, even in such a case it is forbidden, unless one is weak and compelled to lean, in which case it is permitted in all circumstances. In Choshen Mishpat, section 17, it implies that standing by leaning is not considered "sitting," and similarly, it implies in the Jerusalem Talmud, at the end of the seventh chapter of Sotah. There is an opinion that for all rabbinic matters, leaning is considered as standing, and since prayer is of rabbinic origin, it could be said that leaning is permitted. (Chacham Tzvi in his glosses on Taz in Choshen Mishpat there, and similarly implied in the responsa of the Rivash, section 266. See also below, section 141 and in Magen Avraham there, subsection 2, who did not write so, and this requires further study. Investigate and you will find clarity.)

Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote in Section 9: If one was compelled to pray while seated, when able, he should repeat the prayer while standing. He need not add anything to it. Thus are his words. However, we have never heard of such a practice, that those who pray while traveling seated should repeat the prayer while standing. And the prominent authorities agreed that one should not do this, unless he wishes to pray it as a voluntary prayer (Taz, subsection 5, and Magen Avraham, subsection 11). And nowadays, it is not appropriate to pray a voluntary prayer (Pri Megadim), as we do not have the proper intention.

If someone is traveling and near an inn where there are idols, if he can leave the road and pray standing in a place where passersby will not interrupt him, it is better for him to pray there than to pray in such a house. For Moses, our teacher, peace be upon him, said, "When I leave the city, I will spread out my hands…" – and he did not want to pray in Egypt because it was full of idols. If he cannot do so, he should pray in a corner of the house where the household will not disturb him, and there is no concern about the idols. If he cannot leave the road, and he also cannot find a corner in the house where the household will not disturb him, it is better for him to pray on the road while walking, since he can then concentrate better. Nevertheless, if he knows that in the inn he will find a place to pray in the courtyard or garden or similar, it is better for him to pray there standing than to pray on the road while walking (Magen Avraham, subsection 14).

It is stated in Berachot (10b): One who prays must align their feet one next to the other, as it is said: "And their feet were a straight foot" – implying that both feet are referred to as a single "foot" (Tosafot R"Y). And since this is how it is with the angels, therefore in prayer, when we are as if speaking before the King, we must do the same. Similarly, during Kedusha, when we sanctify like the angels, we must also align our feet. Some also have the custom to do so during "Barchu".

The Tur brings the Jerusalem Talmud that one who stands in prayer must align their feet. Rabbi Levi and Rabbi Simon: one says like the ministering angels, as it is written: "and their feet were a straight foot." And one says like the priests, as it is written: "you shall not ascend with steps," for the priests would walk heel-to-toe, as if their feet were even with each other. This is the end of his words. The commentators are perplexed as to why he brought this Jerusalem Talmud, since in our Talmud it says like the angels (see Beit Yosef, Bach, Prisha, and Taz)? In my humble opinion, it seems that the Tur's intention is as follows: Firstly, when entering the synagogue, one should walk heel-to-toe, like the priests when they went up to the platform, for prayer is in place of the sacrifice. Secondly, one who cannot place their feet together due to some pain or other reason, should at least place the heel of one foot next to the big toe of the other. For while we hold to the reason of resembling the angels, nevertheless, when this is not possible, one should resemble the priests. This also seems to me to be the primary ruling in this matter.

Rabbeinu the Rema wrote in the name of the Rokeach that when one stands to pray, one should take three steps forward as a way of drawing near and presenting oneself for the matter that needs to be done. Thus are his words, and this is the custom. And a hint to this is that we find in the Tanach three instances of approaching for prayer: "And Abraham approached," "And Judah approached," "And Elijah approached" (Rokeach). And there are those who wrote that when one stands in their place, they do not need to step back three steps in order to go forward (Eliyah Rabbah). This is not the custom. And it is proper to do so, for every matter of holiness requires preparation and readiness. And the Maharil, when he reached "Tehillot l'El Elyon" would customarily stand, and at Mincha when the chazzan begins Kaddish, as well as at Ma'ariv.

Our Sages, of blessed memory, stated in Yevamot (105b): When one prays, one should direct his eyes downward and his heart upward. His eyes downward, as it is written: "My eyes and My heart shall be there all the days" (I Kings 9:3). Rashi explained: This refers to the Land of Israel, because the Divine Presence resides there. This is his language. In other words, this verse was said by Solomon after he built the Holy Temple, and it should not be said that after the destruction, the Divine Presence was removed to the heavens. This is not so, as it is stated in the Jerusalem Talmud on this verse: Even after the destruction, the Divine Presence did not move from its place (Maharam). And one's heart should be directed upwards to the heavenly Temple, which corresponds to the earthly Temple (ibid.). This is what was explained in the previous section, that one should direct his heart towards the Land of Israel, Jerusalem, and the Holy Temple, and turn his face in that direction. This is what the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch wrote: One should bend his head slightly, so that his eyes are downward to the ground. And he should consider as if he is standing in the Holy Temple, and in his heart, he should direct himself upwards to the heavens. This is their language. And this is the language of Rabbeinu Yonah: His eyes should be downward and his heart upward, meaning he should think in his heart as if he is standing in the heavens, and remove from his heart all the pleasures of this world... And after he reaches this thought, he should also think as if he is standing in the earthly Temple, for through this, his prayer will be more favorable before the Omnipresent (Tosafot R”Y in the fifth chapter of Berachot). And fortunate is the person who reaches this level, and one should close his eyes during the Amidah prayer. Then he will merit to see the Divine Presence before his death (Knesset HaGedolah).

And the Rambam wrote in Chapter 5: He places his hands on his heart, bound (tied), the right on top of the left. And he stands like a servant before his master, in awe, fear, and dread. And he should not place his hands on his hips, because it is a haughty manner. Thus far his words, and similarly wrote the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch. And this is not related to what I wrote in Siman 91 that when there is suffering in the world, one should clasp his hands, but not so in times of peace, see there. For there it is a different matter, like a person who breaks his fingers, but here it is merely the placement of the right on the left, as one stands before a king in humility, to hint at the submission of the evil inclination which is on the left side (Taz, small section 3). However, all of this is according to the custom of the places, how servants stand before their masters (Magen Avraham, small section 2). And some have written that when placing the right on the left, the middle joint of both arms should face the worshiper (there in the name of the Ari, of blessed memory). And some have written to bend the thumb inside the palm (there in the name of the Ramak). And one should think in his heart of the exaltedness of the Blessed One and the lowliness of man, and think in his heart: Who am I, poor and despicable, to come and ask from the King of kings, the Holy One, blessed be He? And during prayer, he should lower his eyes, and before the Amidah, he should direct his eyes to the windows in the wall (Bach). And during the seated prayer, he should also sit with humility and respect. And it is good to align his feet also when saying the Kedusha with the chazzan, and it is proper to stand this way until after the blessing of "the holy God" (Eliyah Rabbah). And he should not raise his head and look upwards as if looking at the ceiling, and one who does so, the angels mock him (Magen Avraham, small section 8, in the name of Sefer Chassidim).

It states in Berachot (23b): A person should not hold tefillin in his hand or a Torah scroll in his arm and pray, because his mind would not be settled in prayer, as his heart would constantly be on them to ensure they do not fall from his hand (Rashi). And it further states there that it is also forbidden to hold a knife, money, a bowl, or a loaf of bread during prayer, because he would worry that the knife might fall and injure him, the money might be lost, the bowl might spill, and the loaf might become dirty (there). 

It implies that specifically an item which, if it falls, constitutes a transgression, like a Torah scroll or tefillin, or an item which could cause bodily harm if it falls, like a knife, or financial harm like money, a bowl, or a loaf, it is forbidden. But an item with no concern if it falls, like threads or handkerchiefs, it is permitted. However, there are those who say that ideally, one should not hold anything in his hand during the Amidah prayer (Bach). And certainly, this is true, but the Gemara considered items that have a definite prohibition due to the significant distraction they cause. Ideally, one should not hold anything in his hand.

There are those who say that for all these items mentioned by the Talmud, if one held them in his hand, he needs to repeat the prayer (Bach). These statements are puzzling, even according to the time of the Talmud when they would repeat the prayer due to a lack of proper intention (Taz, sub-paragraph 1, and Eliyah Rabbah). This is also evident from the words of the Rambam, except if he said that he did not focus because of this, then according to their time he would repeat. We do not repeat the prayer due to a lack of intention, as I wrote in Siman 93, paragraph 2, see there.

It is stated in the Talmud, Sukkah (41a), that it is permitted to hold the lulav during the festival of Sukkot while praying. And although if it were to fall, it could become invalid and one might be concerned about this, nevertheless, since holding it in one's hand is a mitzvah at its proper time, one is not troubled by it.
