From this, we learn that it is permitted to hold a siddur or machzor in one's hand during the Amidah to pray from it, because since one holds it for the purpose of this prayer, it is certainly no less significant than the lulav. Just as holding the lulav, which is a mitzvah, does not cause distraction, all the more so, a mitzvah related to the very essence of prayer for one who is accustomed to praying only from the siddur. One should hold it before starting the Amidah. However, during the Amidah, one should not turn back to retrieve it. But if it was placed beforehand in the place where one is praying, it is permissible to take it even in the middle of the Amidah. And we have already explained at the end of Siman 93 that whether to pray from the siddur or by heart depends on the nature of individuals; see there.

Since one must stand in prayer as if standing before a king, it is therefore forbidden to belch or yawn in the middle of prayer. A "belch" is defined as emitting a sound from the mouth along with the smell of the food or drink consumed. In our language, this is called "greptzen." A "yawn" is when one opens the mouth widely and emits a slight breath, similar to a person who is waking up from sleep. This is called "genetzen." The prohibition applies when one does this willingly, but not when it happens involuntarily. However, in the case of a belch, involuntariness does not apply, as one can hold it back, as is well known. But a yawn must be done when it occurs, and therefore one should place a hand over the mouth so that the opening of the mouth is not visible. This is due to necessity, but when not necessary, one should not place a hand near the mouth, meaning on the chin or lower jaw during prayer, as this is a sign of arrogance. Some cantors do this not out of arrogance but to enhance their voice. Therefore, they also tend to spread their hands upwards, downwards, and to the sides, as is the custom in singing. Hence, they also open their mouths widely and make various movements, as it is impossible for them to do otherwise.

And know that regarding what we wrote that there is no compulsion in belching, so I have deduced from the language of our teacher, the Beit Yosef, in Section 1, where he wrote: "One should not belch, nor yawn. And if he needs to yawn out of compulsion...see there." And from the fact that he did not mention "belching" as well, it implies that there is no compulsion in belching. However, from the language of the Rambam in the fourth chapter and from the language of the Tur, it does not imply this. And it is also explained from the language of the Gemara (Berachot 24b) that for both of them it says that compulsion is permissible, see there. Nevertheless, the sense experience testifies like our teacher, the Beit Yosef, that in belching a person can compel himself. Therefore, it appears to me that for practical law, certainly it is so that one needs to compel himself, as we see when sitting at a party and needing to belch – he compels himself not to belch, because it is not proper behavior. And the Talmud and the poskim who said that it is permitted under compulsion – certainly it is so, that if the compulsion is great and he is forced to belch – he should place his hand over his mouth and belch. And our teacher, the Beit Yosef, did not mention this because generally one can compel himself. And so it should be instructed.

And just as one standing before a king would not dare to spit, similarly it is forbidden to spit during the Amidah. One should swallow the saliva in his mouth. If it is impossible for him not to spit, such as in the case of phlegm or mucus, if it is possible for him to swallow the saliva into his garment, such as his undergarment, or if he has a handkerchief that he uses to wipe his nose and saliva—he should spit into it. But into an outer garment where the saliva will be visible—he should not swallow it. If he is fastidious, and it is repugnant to him to do so—he should spit the saliva behind him. And the Rambam wrote: he should throw it with his hand behind him, which implies that he should spit into his hand and then throw it behind him, and not turn his head backward. But the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, in Section 2, wrote: he should throw it behind him, meaning that he should turn his head and spit. And in his large book, he challenged the Rambam’s interpretation: since he is fastidious and cannot swallow it into his garment, how will it be acceptable to put it into his hand? Therefore, he wrote that the Rambam's intention is also through a handkerchief, and when he does not have a handkerchief—he should spit it out as is, see there. I do not understand: for certainly, taking the saliva in his hand for a moment and then throwing it—there is no fastidiousness in this. Whereas swallowing it into a garment where the saliva will certainly be—this is unbearable for a fastidious person, and common sense confirms this. This requires further study. Therefore, it seems in my humble opinion to adhere to the words of the Rambam, to spit into the hand and then throw it behind him. And it is obvious that just as the rule is for saliva—so it is for nasal mucus. And even though it was explained in Siman 92 that one who touches nasal mucus needs to wash, we clarified there that it is sufficient to wipe it on a wall, see there. And the reason they permitted him to spit when necessary is because it is better that he prays cleanly rather than be distressed and have his prayer disturbed (Tosafot R”Y). This is also explained in the Jerusalem Talmud. And know that the supplications after the prayer are considered like the prayer in regard to spitting, as long as he has not taken the three steps back. For as long as he has not taken the steps—it is as if he is still standing before the king (Magen Avraham, Section 2).

In the Tur it is written: "He should spit behind him or to his left, but not in front of him nor to his right." This implies that behind and to the left are equal. However, our teacher, the Rema, wrote that if it is not possible to spit behind him, he should spit to his left but not to his right, and certainly not in front of him, which is forbidden. This concludes his words. Thus wrote the students of the R"I, that the left is preferable to behind. They asked about this: How could they write here that the right is preferable to the left, when later in Siman 123 it is written regarding the three steps back that one first gives peace to his left, which is the right of the Holy One, blessed be He, and afterwards to his right – hence the left is preferable. And they answered that there, when one stands before the Divine Presence, certainly the left is preferable, because it corresponds to the right of the Holy One, blessed be He. But here, when spitting, one should not consider it as standing before the Divine Presence, as one does not spit in front of the Divine Presence. Therefore, the right is preferable (Rema in Darkei Moshe). And some explain because the Divine Presence never descended below ten handbreadths, and therefore when standing in prayer, we do not consider his left as the right of the Divine Presence, for the Divine Presence is above him. Therefore, his right is preferable, unlike the case when distancing himself from his place of prayer and bowing towards the Divine Presence – there, certainly, one gives peace first to the right of the Divine Presence, which is his left (Beit Yosef in the name of his father).

And know that the Rambam only mentioned "throwing it behind him" alone. And our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in his great book that it implies from his words that they only permitted [throwing] it behind him, and so is the halacha, see there. Therefore, he also did not write in the Shulchan Aruch except "throwing it behind him." And I do not understand: what should he do if it is impossible for him to throw it behind him, such as if people are standing behind him? Furthermore, in the Jerusalem Talmud, Chapter 3, it is explicitly explained like the words of the Tur, see there. Rather, it is certain that the Rambam also does not disagree on this, and he did not bother to elaborate on this because most of the time he can throw it behind him.

If a louse bites him during prayer, he is permitted to remove it with a garment so that he is not distracted by the pain. If it is on the garment, he should not touch it. Specifically, during prayer he should not remove it with his hand, but outside of prayer, he may remove it with his hand and throw it away in the synagogue. Even though this requires washing the hands, he can clean his hand on the wall (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 7). Therefore, if it happens that he removed it with his hand during prayer, he should clean his hand on the wall. 

If his tallit falls off during prayer, if it slips from its place but does not fall completely, even if most of it falls, he can adjust it and return it to its place. However, if it falls completely, he cannot pick it up and wrap himself in it again because this would be an interruption; rather, he should finish the prayer without the tallit. It seems to me that the same rule applies if his tefillin fall from his head or his arm—he should not interrupt and should finish the prayer without them, as it is forbidden to interrupt during prayer. Therefore, if the tefillin merely become loose, he can tighten them as with the tallit when it does not fall completely, since this kind of adjustment is not very noticeable as an interruption.

If one is carrying a burden on his shoulders that is less than four kavs, he may shift it behind him and pray. For four kavs, he must place it on the ground and then pray. It appears to me that this applies when he is afraid to place it on the ground due to a concern of theft, or when he must pray while walking, as I wrote in Siman 94. In such a case, they permitted him to shift a burden of less than four kavs behind him. However, if he can place it on the ground or in any place, and he can pray standing without the burden, he is obligated to do so even for a burden of less than four kavs. Similarly, it seems to me that holding a staff in his hand during prayer is forbidden. If he is concerned about theft, he should place it in front of him and keep an eye on it. In places where it is safe, he can pray when they are properly placed.

One must prepare the intention of his heart for prayer, as it is written: "You will prepare their heart, You will cause Your ear to listen" – that he should direct the meaning of the words that he utters with his lips, and think as if the Divine Presence is opposite him, removing all distracting thoughts from himself until his thought remains pure and his intention clear in his prayer. And he should think in his heart: If he had to arrange his words before a mortal king, how much would he arrange his words and be very careful not to stumble in his words. And he would forcibly remove all other thoughts so as not to think of them at all. All the more so when standing before the King of kings, the Holy One, blessed be He, who investigates all thoughts, and examines the heart and tests the kidneys. And so did the pious and men of deeds do, who would seclude themselves and direct their intention in their prayer until they would reach a state of detachment from physicality and strengthening of the intellectual power, until they were close to the level of prophecy. And now, due to our many sins, may it be that we direct the meaning of the words, and pour out our soul before our Creator in our prayers.

Some have written a segulah (spiritual remedy) to remove foreign thoughts during prayer: Before praying, one should pass his right hand three times over his forehead and say each time: "Create in me a pure heart, O God, and renew a steadfast spirit within me." If a thought intrudes during prayer, he should pause for a moment and reflect on this verse (Eliyah Rabbah). He should remain silent until the thought dissipates, and think about things that humble the heart and direct it towards his Father in Heaven. He should not think about frivolous matters. Before praying, he should contemplate the exaltedness of God and the lowliness of man, and remove all worldly pleasures from his heart. It is forbidden for a person to kiss his young children in the synagogue in order to instill in his heart that there is no love like the love for the Blessed One. (What the Magen Avraham wrote in the name of the Sefer HaGan – he himself wrote that it constitutes an interruption.)

It is known to those who understand grace that there are lofty and exalted intentions in prayer. The Men of the Great Assembly, who were all righteous pillars of the world and great sages, and among them several prophets, hinted in the prayer at matters of the utmost significance and fearsome unifications, but not every mind can grasp this. One who is not entirely righteous and separated from the vanities of this world, or who is not a great sage in both the revealed and the hidden aspects [of Torah] – it is better that he only intends the simple meaning of the words and understands the matters with the intention of the heart (Magen Avraham). And it says in the Zohar "Beshalach": Any person who comes to unify the Holy Name, and does not intend with his heart, will, and awe so that blessings may flow from it above and below – his prayer is cast outside... and the Holy One, blessed be He, says: "When you come to appear before Me, who has required this at your hand?" Thus are his words. Therefore, one should be cautious about this (ibid.).

One should not pray in a place where there is something that distracts their concentration, nor at a time that distracts their concentration. And thus it is said in Eruvin (65a): Anyone whose mind is not settled should not pray. Rabbi Chanina, on a day when he was angry, would not pray. And someone who has come from a journey should not pray for three days. Rabbi Eliezer says: Even someone who is distressed, meaning someone who is suffering. Shmuel would not pray in a house that had beer, because of the smell that distracted him. Rav Pappa would not pray in a house that had "harsana" (fish fried in flour, with brine and their fat), because of its strong smell. However, the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch wrote that we do not take care now with all this, because we do not concentrate so much. And one should only be careful to pray with supplication like a poor person begging at the door, and gently, and it should not appear as a burden that he wants to get rid of. This means: Even though he says it in the language of supplication, if he does not think properly as one should when coming to ask before the king, but only prays because of the obligation to fulfill his duty and get it over with – it is not an accepted prayer (see Magen Avraham, subsection 4).

Prayer is in place of the sacrificial offering. Therefore, one must be careful that it resembles the offering in intention, and should not mix in any other thoughts, just as improper thoughts invalidate sacred offerings. It should be done standing, similar to the service, as all sacrificial services are performed standing, as it is written: "to stand to serve" (Zevachim 23b). The feet should be positioned together, like the priests during the service (Tur). Additionally, this is akin to the angels, as I wrote in Siman 95, see there. There should be a designated place, similar to the sacrifices, where each type of sacrifice has a set place for its slaughter and for the sprinkling of its blood on the altar. There should be no barrier between the person and the wall, similar to the sacrifice where any barrier invalidates it between it and the vessel used in the service. Also, a barrier between the person and the ground invalidates when they are not standing directly on the floor (see Taz, section 2). Just as one who stands in the Temple stands with awe and reverence, so too with prayer, which is in place of the sacrificial offering. It is fitting to have nice clothing for prayer, like the priestly garments. However, not everyone can afford this, and one who can and is wealthy – certainly should strive for this. Nonetheless, it is good to have special pants for prayer for cleanliness if one's regular pants are dirty. Clean shoes are also appropriate for prayer. "Prepare to meet your God, O Israel."

And after all the intentions, a person should not think in his mind that he is worthy for the Holy One, blessed be He, to fulfill his request, because he had proper intentions in his prayer. On the contrary, through this, a person’s sins are recalled, as they scrutinize his actions, saying: This one relies on his merits. For the obligations of the Holy One, blessed be He, upon a person cannot be counted due to their abundance. Rather, one should think that the Holy One, blessed be He, will act out of His kindness. And he should say in his heart: Who am I, poor and despicable, to come and request from the King of kings, the Holy One, blessed be He, if not for His abundant kindness that He, blessed be He, conducts with His creations? And then his prayer will be accepted.

Our sages of blessed memory said (Berachot 34a): The first three blessings are like a servant who arranges praise for his master. The middle blessings are like a servant who requests a reward from his master. The last three blessings are like a servant who has received a reward from his master and takes his leave. One should present himself as a pauper. And King David, peace be upon him, said: "A prayer of the afflicted when he is overwhelmed" (Psalms 102:1). When one reaches the phrase "Helper of the poor," he should join in the suffering of the Shechinah, which is impoverished and afflicted in these times. When he reaches "Praises to the Supreme God," he should stand to prepare himself for prayer. Before "Rock of Israel," he should take three steps backward, return to his place, and pray with closed eyes in concentration.

Maimonides wrote in Chapter Four, Law 17: A drunk person should not pray, because he lacks intention. And if he prays – his prayer is an abomination. Therefore, he must repeat his prayer when he becomes sober. A tipsy person should not pray, but if he prays – his prayer is still considered a prayer. Who is considered drunk? One who cannot speak before a king. A tipsy person is one who can speak before a king without becoming confused. Nevertheless, since he drank a quarter log of wine – he should not pray until the wine has left him. Thus far is his wording.

One must scrutinize his words: if the main reason that a drunk person is forbidden to pray is that he lacks intention, why is his prayer considered an abomination? Is it that one who prays without intention has his prayer considered an abomination, God forbid? And behold, for us, we do not repeat the prayer for lack of intention, as I wrote in the previous section. Moreover, in Berachot (31b) it is said that a drunk person who prays is like one who serves idolatry, see there. And is it that one who prays without intention stands on such a level, God forbid? And indeed, the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch did not write this language, and according to them, the reason is that it is considered something disgusting like excrement. Therefore, his prayer is an abomination and as if... and therefore, even for us, it is necessary to repeat the prayer. This is not the case according to the reasoning of the Rambam, we would not need to repeat the prayer, for we do not repeat it for lack of intention, as I wrote.

It seems to me, in my humble opinion, that the Rambam has conveyed something significant regarding prayer. For in Eruvin (65a) it is explained that it addresses someone who is drunk but has not reached the drunkenness of Lot. Because of this, it is said there that a drunk person's transactions are valid, and their purchases and sales are effective. They are only prohibited from praying, which means they have some sense. For this reason, it is said there: "I can exempt the entire world from the judgment of prayer because we are 'drunk but not from wine.'" According to this, why indeed is their prayer an abomination? Moreover, it is difficult: if so, it should be forbidden for us to pray in our times, since we are like drunkards. Furthermore, why did the codifiers not bring this statement? Rather, it is certainly due to the lack of intention, as the Rambam says, and if so, why indeed is their prayer an abomination?

The matter, however, is as follows: It has already been explained that prayer is akin to standing before a king. Accordingly, one must prepare oneself with the proper intention to stand before the King of Kings, the Holy One, blessed be He. Nevertheless, if one's intention becomes confused while standing in prayer – the Torah was not given to ministering angels. What can one do? Therefore, one does not repeat the prayer due to a lack of intention. However, if one initially stands to pray without any intention – there is no greater audacity than this. There is nothing more repugnant than entering the palace of a king with a confused mind. Therefore, his prayer is an abomination, and he must repeat the prayer. This is why it was said that in our times we could be exempt from the obligation of prayer, meaning due to our inability to have the proper intention, because we are like drunkards. Perhaps from this, it emerged for the decisors that we do not repeat the prayer due to a lack of intention, since we are like drunkards. All this applies during the time of prayer, but prior preparation must be done properly. Hence, it was said that a drunkard is anyone who cannot speak before a king: How can you enter the palace of a king, and this is great audacity and repugnant in the eyes of the king? Therefore, one must repeat the prayer. This is why it was said: It is as if he worships stars. Meaning: It shows that his service before the Blessed One is not important to him at all, as if...

From this, we learn a great moral lesson for those people who come from the street into the synagogue without any decorum and without any preparation for even a few moments, and they hastily pray, not knowing their right from their left. Rather, every person is obligated to contemplate for a few moments, each according to their level. Therefore, we take three steps backward before the prayer and return, as if preparing oneself to enter the palace of the King. And if afterward, one's intention becomes confused – the Holy One, blessed be He, does not come with excessive demands upon His creations. Therefore, the legal authorities did not bring the statement that nowadays one could be exempt from the duty of prayer: because the implication is not to completely refrain from praying, God forbid, but rather from the "duty of prayer" in that we do not have the proper intention. And this is indeed what they brought, that we do not repeat the prayer due to a lack of intention. (And with this, it is understood in the Gemara that they said if one does not pray in his drunkenness – his reward is very great and troubles are closed off from him, see there. And it is difficult: why is this so? Rather, it is because in this itself, it shows that one needs to stand as if standing before the King, and now, in his drunkenness, he cannot, and therefore his reward is great.)

If one was drunk and the time for prayer passed before his drunkenness wore off, he should pray twice in the next prayer. Even though this only applies if it was unintentional or due to circumstances beyond his control, and not intentional as will be explained in Siman 108, here we treat him as if it were unintentional since he did not take proper care. And even if he started drinking after the time for this prayer arrived, if he thought he would have time afterwards, he is considered "compelled" (Magen Avraham, subsection 3). There are those who say that if he started drinking after the time for prayer arrived, he is considered "intentional" (see Taz). In my humble opinion, it seems to me to rule that in the case of drinking for a mitzvah, such as a mitzvah meal and the like, as in the case of the pairs of Rabbis in the Talmud (Berachot 19a), then even if they started after the time arrived, and it was voluntary drinking, he is not called "unintentional" but "compelled" only if they started before the time arrived. And know that the law of the Shema is like the law of prayer. But other blessings, as well as the Grace after Meals, can be recited even when one is drunk (and this will be further explained in Siman 108).

The Tur and Shulchan Aruch wrote in Section 2: A journey of a mile and any amount of sleep dispels the effects of wine. This applies when one drank a quarter-log, but if one drank more, even a little sleep intoxicates him and a journey distracts him. This applies when walking on foot, but if riding, certainly the journey dispels the effects of the wine. Thus far are his words, and the Tur brought this from the Bahag (Ba'al Halachot Gedolot). And all the great sages questioned this, as it is clearly necessary in Eruvin (64b) that when riding, one needs three miles. Many things have been said about this. Regarding the law, for a quarter-log, a mile suffices, and for more than a quarter-log, three miles are required (Eliyah Rabbah, and this is also implied in Magen Avraham, subsection 5). The Rif and the Rosh did not mention at all the distinction between riding and walking. It appears to me that they hold that according to the conclusion of the Talmud in Eruvin there, there is no need to differentiate between riding and walking, see there. (And so wrote the Korban Netanel there. And the words of the Taz, subsection 2, who wrote that he holds that riding a mile does not help, are puzzling, for if so, it is obvious they should have explained this. And similarly, Rambam in the first chapter of Beit HaMikdash did not mention this distinction. It is surprising that Rambam did not write this law at all in the laws of prayer. And perhaps he holds that specifically regarding entering the Temple, which desecrates the service and incurs a death penalty, one must be precise about this. But concerning prayer, as long as it appears to him that the wine has left him, he is permitted to pray. Examine and you will find it easy.)

Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote in Section 3: Anyone who is inebriated – it suffices for him according to what he feels within himself that his wine has dissipated. This is his language, and in his great book, he brought this in the name of the Geonim. And it is not understood: What is he teaching us? And it seems clear to me that their intention here is that we do not differentiate between whether one drank a quarter-log or more, whether one slept a little or a lot, or whether one walked a mile or more or less. And what our Sages of blessed memory said – this is specifically concerning the annulment of vows in Eruvin there, which is not a Torah prohibition, and also concerning entering the Temple, which carries the penalty of death. But with prayer, one does not need to be meticulous about this; rather, as long as it seems to him that his wine has dissipated – he is permitted to pray. And according to this, the opinion of the Rambam in the fourth chapter of Prayer is understood, as he omitted all of this, as I wrote in the previous section. (And the Shulchan Aruch, which wrote both laws – requires examination.)

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote that therefore we are not strict with our wines that are not strong, and one can pray even though he drank a revi'it (a specific measure) or more. All the more so when he prays from a siddur that he holds in his hand, as there is no concern for a slight intoxication. So far his words. Additionally: most of our wines are diluted with a lot of water. Furthermore: it is required that one drink the revi'it all at once (Magen Avraham, small section 1), which is not so common. Moreover: if he drank during the meal – wine during the meal does not intoxicate. And some say that even before the meal it does not intoxicate (see Beit Yosef, Siman 473). Nevertheless, regarding ruling, one should not give a ruling even if he drank during the meal (there). And on Yom Tov, one can pray Mincha even though he drank a little, as it is impossible to wait until the wine wears off. All the more so nowadays when, in any case, we do not concentrate so much (there, small section 6). And it is obvious that all intoxicating drinks have the same ruling as wine. And it is clear that distilled wine intoxicates greatly, and one must be careful with it.

Maimonides wrote at the end of the fourth chapter: Prayers that are recited periodically, such as the Musaf prayer for Rosh Chodesh and for the festivals, one must arrange his prayer and then stand and pray, so that he does not make a mistake in it. Until here is his language, and it is at the end of Rosh Hashanah. And the Tur wrote that according to the opinion of the Rosh, it is not necessary on Rosh Chodesh, only on festivals. See there. And the commentators wrote that there is no proof (see Beit Yosef and Bach). However, from Rashi there it implies like the Tur, see there. And our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote: "Prayers of the festivals and of Rosh Hashanah...". And it seems that this is a printing error, and it should say "and of Rosh Chodesh". And so it is in the Levush.

According to this, there is also a "prayer of sections" in the morning, which is "Ya'aleh Veyavo." So why did they write only about the Musaf prayer? It can be said: because it is a short prayer. Additionally, because he says it many times on Rosh Chodesh in the three prayers and in Birkat Hamazon. And our master, the Rema, wrote that some say it is only when one prays by heart. But when one prays from the siddur, it is permitted, for he sees what he is praying. And this is the custom. Thus far is his language. And there are those who question this, but it is not the main opinion (see Taz).

However, in truth, our custom is not like this. Even though we pray by heart, we do not arrange [the prayers] beforehand, and even during the High Holy Days, we are not accustomed to arrange [the prayers] beforehand. Perhaps the intention of the Gemara is only regarding the prayer leader (Shaliach Tzibbur) who prays for the congregation, and not regarding the prayer of each individual. However, this is not implied in the Gemara; see there. Many great authorities have already struggled with this issue, but have not provided any satisfactory answer (see Sha'arei Teshuvah). It appears to me that the Rif wrote there that even though the prayer leader only exempts those who are not proficient, nevertheless, if one listens to the prayer leader from beginning to end, the proficient one also fulfills his obligation; see there. Based on this, we can say that this is why we pray by heart even on Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, as well as on festivals and Rosh Chodesh, because in any event: if we make a mistake in the prayer, we will hear it from the prayer leader. And on Rosh Chodesh, those who are traveling and praying individually rely on the opinion of the Tur and Rashi that we wrote in section 1. This requires further investigation.

One who prays must have intention (kavanah) in all the blessings. If he is unable to have intention in all of them, he should at least have intention in the Avot (Patriarchs) blessing (end of the fifth chapter), because this blessing begins with "Blessed" and ends with "Blessed"; and several names of God are mentioned in it: "Our God and the God of our forefathers"; and it is adjacent to the blessing of the Redeemer of Israel (Maharam Shif). Also, within it, redemption is mentioned: "and brings a redeemer...". This is what the Gemara (30a) says: One should always evaluate himself: if he can have intention, he should pray. If not, he should not pray – this also applies to the Avot blessing (Tur). If one estimates that he can have intention in the Avot blessing, even if he cannot in the others, he should pray. If he cannot have intention even in the Avot blessing, he should not pray. (Additionally, the merit of the three forefathers is included in this blessing.)

And since the primary intention is in the "Avot" (the first blessing of the Amidah), therefore the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch wrote that if one did not have intention during the "Avot," even if they had intention for the rest of the prayer, they need to go back and pray again. And our teacher, the Rema, wrote that nowadays we do not repeat the prayer due to lack of intention, because even in the repetition it is likely that one will not have intention. Therefore, why should one repeat it? Thus are his words. And what they ruled in Siman 63 that if one did not have intention in "Shema Yisrael" they must repeat it – that is because it is only one verse and it is easy to have intention, as I wrote there. Nonetheless, it seems to me that if one assesses themselves beforehand and knows that they will not be able to have intention in the "Avot" – even nowadays they should not pray. However, I am puzzled: why did they not bring this law at all in the Shulchan Aruch? And with the Rambam who did not bring this – it is understandable, because he already ruled in the fourth chapter according to the law of the Gemara in Eruvin that we brought in Siman 98; thus this matter is also included. But the Shulchan Aruch who ruled there that nowadays we are not careful about all this as I wrote there, why did they not bring this? Rather, one must say that they hold that even in this matter we cannot be precise. And according to this, nowadays this law does not apply, and we rely on their statement that "I can exempt…" And this requires further investigation.

One must be very careful with intention during "Modim" (the prayer of thanks), for it is an expression of gratitude to the Holy One, blessed be He. It is even more important to be careful with the praises and thanksgivings to the Holy One, blessed be He, than with the rest of the prayers (Bach in the name of Sefer Mitzvot Katan). The Tur wrote in the name of Rabbeinu Eliezer that a person should accustom themselves to have intention during the conclusions of all the blessings, which contain one hundred and thirteen words, similar to the prayer of Hannah. And similarly, in the Torah, the word "heart" appears one hundred and thirteen times, hinting that one needs to have the intention of the heart in them. And furthermore: the conclusions of the blessings are the main parts of the thanksgivings.

In the Gemara (Berachot 31a), it is learned from the verses about the prayer of Hannah, as it is written: "And Hannah was speaking in her heart, only her lips moved, but her voice was not heard" – from here we learn that one who prays must articulate with their lips. That is to say: one must pronounce the words properly. "But her voice was not heard" – from here we learn that one should not raise their voice in prayer. And it is taught: one who makes their voice heard in prayer – this is of the small-minded, as if, Heaven forbid, the Holy One, Blessed be He, does not hear in a whisper. One who raises their voice in prayer – this is like the false prophets, as it is written about them: "Cry aloud." And from the verse "speaking in her heart," we learn that one who prays must direct their heart, as it is written: "You will prepare their heart, You will cause Your ear to hear." But one who prays with mere thought of the heart – has not fulfilled their obligation, because we hold that thought is not equivalent to speech. And that which we permitted in Siman 94 for a sick person to pray with their heart – this is because they are unable to speak. And even though we learn prayer from "to serve Him with all your heart" – this refers to the requirement of intent of the heart. But with mere thought of the heart alone, one has not fulfilled their obligation at all. (See Magen Avraham, Section 2, and Eliyah Rabbah.)

Regarding the matter of not making one's voice heard to one's own ears, there is a dispute: Some say that one should not make it heard even to one's own ears. This is explicitly stated in the Tosefta (Chapter Three), where it says: "Could it be that one should make his voice heard to his own ears? Chana explained: 'She was speaking to her heart, and her voice was not heard.'" This is the end of its wording. But the Rambam wrote in Chapter Five: "He articulates the words with his lips and makes them heard to his ears in a whisper, but does not make his voice heard." This is the end of his wording. Similarly, the Tur and the Rashba wrote. And so it is in the Jerusalem Talmud (Chapter Two), where it says: "If one prays and does not make it heard to his ears – he has fulfilled his obligation." This is the end of its wording; thus, only ex post facto has he fulfilled his obligation. And so our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, ruled in Section 2 that one must make it heard to his own ears, and this is the main ruling. (And regarding the Tosefta, one can say, as the Bach wrote, that the interpretation is: It could be that without making it heard, he has not fulfilled his obligation. See there. Additionally, one can say that the intention is not to make it heard to his ears in a loud voice but only in a whisper, as the Rambam wrote. And in Bedek HaBayit, he brought from the Zohar that it implies like the Tosefta, and it is in "Vayakhel," where it says: "If that prayer is heard to a person's ears – no one listens to it above." This is the end of its wording. And the Magen Avraham already wrote in subsection 3 that the intention is that another person should not hear it, see there. And even if it refers to oneself, the intention is that one should not hear it in a loud voice, but only in a whisper, as I have written. Examine this, and you will find it easy.)

All of this applies when one can concentrate on the meaning of the prayer even when reciting it quietly. However, if one cannot concentrate quietly, as there are people who when they speak quietly, the words do not enter their hearts – it is permissible for such a person to raise their voice a little, since it is not possible for them otherwise. This is only when they are alone. But in a congregation, it is forbidden, as it would disturb the congregation, meaning: it would confuse others with their voice. Therefore, if they raise their voice a little such that it does not disturb the congregation – it is permissible even in a congregation. And sometimes, even if one can concentrate quietly, it is permissible to raise their voice, such as when praying at home and the household members do not know the order of the prayer themselves – it is permissible to raise one’s voice a little so that the household members can learn from them how to pray. Since this is for the sake of a mitzvah – we do not object. This is how it is stated in the Jerusalem Talmud (at the beginning of the fourth chapter) and brought in the Tur, see there. (And the Taz, section 1, wants to say that at home, even if one can concentrate quietly, if they can concentrate better with a raised voice – it is permissible even if not for the sake of the household members, see there.)

Our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, wrote in section 3: Some say that on Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, it is permissible to raise one's voice during prayer even in public. And so is the custom, but nevertheless, one should be careful not to raise their voice too much. Thus is their wording. And behold, the Mordechai in Yoma explained the reason: that they do so in order to teach one another. And we do not worry about causing errors, for they have machzorim and siddurim in their hands, see there. And now, it is no longer relevant for them to teach one another since everyone knows, and therefore, we should not pray loudly. However, there is another reason: because these are days of repentance, they raise their voices to concentrate more. And further: since they are not proficient in them, if they pray silently, they will not be able to concentrate properly (see Beit Yosef). Nevertheless, many great ones were not content with this practice. And also according to the Zohar, it is not proper to do so. It is better to pray silently if one can concentrate (Magen Avraham, subsection 4), and this is the practice of many great ones. And the Ari of blessed memory would not raise his voice even during the verses of praise, and only on Shabbat would he raise his voice a little (there).

The fact that people recite Selichot and liturgical poems out loud – there is no issue with it. The concern is specifically during the Amidah prayer, as it is akin to standing before the king. However, for other prayers and supplications – there is no issue. On the contrary: in order to awaken the hearts, it is better, as the Ramban wrote in his commentary on the Torah at the end of Parashat Bo, and these are his words: "The intention of raising voices in prayers… as our Rabbis of blessed memory wrote: 'And they cried out to God with strength' – from here you learn that prayer requires a voice. See there. And all the more so for songs and praises that are said aloud due to joy, it is certainly permissible. And Psalms should also be said aloud, as at the end of Megillah (32a): Whoever reads without melody and studies without song, upon him the verse says…, see there."

In the beginning of the seventh chapter of Sotah, it is taught that prayer can be recited in any language. This means that one who comes to ask for mercy and requests from the Blessed One can do so in any language he wishes. The reason for this is also given in the Gemara there (Sotah 33a): prayer is a plea for mercy, and one can pray in any language he desires, see there. And behold, after Solomon built the Temple, he said in his prayer: "Moreover, concerning the foreigner who is not of Your people Israel and comes from a distant land... when he prays toward this house, hear..." – and certainly, he did not pray in the Holy Tongue. However, the Rif wrote at the beginning of the second chapter of Berachot that this applies to communal prayer. But an individual should only pray in the Holy Tongue, see there. And it is explicitly stated in Sotah there, where it questions: "And can prayer be in any language?" For Rabbi Yohanan said: one should never request his needs in the Aramaic language, for the angels do not attend to him. And it answers: here it refers to an individual, here to the community, see there. And some say that even an individual can ask in any language, only the angels do not attend to the Aramaic language. And one who examines the Gemara there will clearly see that this does not refer to the fixed prayers established by the Men of the Great Assembly, for who would dare to change words that stand at the pinnacle of the world into a foreign language? And one who does so is merely acting wickedly and foolishly. As we explained in Siman 62, section 4, it is impossible to translate them properly at all, see there. The Talmud is referring to supplications, prayers, and entreaties that are sometimes said in public, such as Selichot and Piyutim and the like. And this is what our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 4: "And some say that this applies when one is asking for his needs, such as praying for a sick person or for some distress in his house. But for the fixed prayer of the community, even an individual can say it in any language." Until here are his words – he does not refer to the Amidah prayer but to Selichot and similar prayers that have become customary to say in public. But the fixed prayers for weekdays, Sabbaths, festivals, Rosh Hashanah, and Yom Kippur – Heaven forbid to change them even a slight change. And this is the main ruling according to the law, and so ruled the great ones of previous generations (as explained in the book "Eleh Divrei HaBrit"). And in Siman 185, we will explain more on this with the help of Heaven.

Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote: It is forbidden to sit within four cubits of someone who is praying. Whether in front of him or to the sides – one must distance oneself four cubits. Thus far his words. It is explained that behind him is permitted, and so wrote the Levush, see there. But Rabbeinu Rema wrote: Whether behind him, see there. And know that there are many printing errors in this matter. For behold, before us it is written in the Tur "whether in front of him or behind him," see there. And Rabbeinu Rema in his book Darkei Moshe questioned this: Why did he not write "behind him," as the Rosh wrote in the fifth chapter (Siman 8) where he wrote "behind him"? From this, he concluded that behind him is also forbidden. And all the commentators on the Tur and Shulchan Aruch wrote that the Tur did not forbid behind him (Bach, Perisha, and Taz subsection 2), and all their reliance is on the Rosh.

And it is a perplexing matter: It is clear that this error also occurred in the Rosh as it did in the Tur according to the version before us, for in the Kitzur Piskei HaRosh it does not mention "behind him," see there. Also, the Ma'adanei Yom Tov wrote there that in the Rosh the version does not have "behind him," see there. Furthermore, if the version in the Rosh had "behind him," our master the Beit Yosef would not have refrained from mentioning it in his book as is his usual practice. On the contrary, he wrote that the words of the Tur are like the words of the Tosafot, the Rosh, and the Mordechai, see there. From this, it is understood that in all of them before him it did not say "behind him." (And also in the Beit Yosef there was a printing error, where it is written "behind him," which certainly is not so as I have written. Pay close attention and you will find it easy.) In the Tosafot (not in [the version we have]) it was written "behind him" and was erased, see there. And our master the Rema himself there brought in the name of "some say" that the version in the Rosh does not have "behind him," see there. For indeed, the matter of the Shechinah seems to be relevant only in front of the one praying and not behind him, for this reason when taking three steps back one goes backward out of respect for the Shechinah. And if one happens to have saliva, one should spit behind him. (And it is even more perplexing what they themselves questioned, that the Rosh gave a sign for this that it totals twelve, and if also behind him – it totals sixteen. The answers given for this are far from convincing in a practical sense. See Darchei Moshe, Bach, Taz, and Magen Avraham. And it seems to my humble opinion that one who relies on the Beit Yosef and the Levush in this matter has not lost. And what is written in the Darchei Moshe in the name of the Zohar – will be explained later with Divine assistance in section 12. Pay close attention and you will find it easy.)

And all our rabbis have written in the name of the Geonim that it is specifically when one sits idle that it is prohibited. But if one is engaged in matters that pertain to the rectification of prayers, even in the chapter "Eizehu Mekoman," one does not need to distance oneself, for since it has become customary to recite it, it is considered part of the rectification of prayers, and it is permitted for him to sit. The Tur wrote that if one is engaged in Torah study, it is prohibited. And even though Torah is more stringent than prayer, in this matter it is not so. The reason it is prohibited to sit within four cubits is because it appears as though his fellow is accepting the yoke of the kingdom of heaven and he is not. Therefore, when one is engaged in matters of prayer, it is as if he too is accepting the yoke of the kingdom of heaven, but not in the case of Torah study. Refer there. And our master, the Beit Yosef, in his great book, wrote that Torah is preferable, and this too is considered the yoke of the kingdom of heaven. Therefore, he wrote in the Shulchan Aruch that there are those who say that even when engaged in Torah study, it is permitted. Refer there. And it is specifically when he learns verbally and not in thought (Taz and Magen Avraham).

However, the primary reasoning of the Tur is puzzling: for if so, during the recitation of Shema, which is the essential acceptance of the yoke of Heaven, it should be forbidden for another to sit within four cubits of him. Furthermore, if so, what benefit is there beyond four cubits (Taz, small section 3)? Additionally, this is relevant in a communal setting and not for an individual. In truth, it appears the reason is that this place is sacred as long as he is praying. A person's space is four cubits, and one must show it respect. Therefore, when he is sitting idle, it is forbidden. However, when he is praying or studying, he is engaged in holy matters (there). Similarly, the Levush ruled that one engaged in Torah matters is permitted to sit, see there (and see Eliyah Rabbah, small section 2).

Our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in Section 1 that there is an opinion that permits only from the side, but directly in front, even at a full view's distance, it is forbidden (to sit), even if one is engaged in reciting the Shema. Thus are his words. In my humble opinion, this is not understood: for the Tosafot, the Rosh, the Tosafot of Rabbi Yitzchak, the Mordechai, the Sefer Mitzvot Gadol, and the Rashba all wrote in the name of the Geonim that when engaged in prayer (and Torah study), it is permitted. And if it were to be thought that in front is forbidden, how did they not clarify this, thereby placing a stumbling block before the learners? And the Tur did not clarify this either. In his major work, he brought this in the name of the Sefer Ohel Moed; see there. And seemingly, this is a singular opinion. It appears to me that this is the intention of the Levush, who wrote about this: because it appears like bowing to him. Thus are his words. His intention is: certainly there is no difference between in front of him and from the sides. Rather, directly in front is certainly disgraceful because it appears like bowing to a person. This does not need clarification. But anything that is not directly in front of his face is permitted, even before him. And this seems to be the primary ruling. (And what is written in the Perisha requires great examination, for what relevance is standing to one passing before him? And already the Eliyah Rabbah was astounded in Section 3).

Regarding the sides: Certainly, the sides in front of him are considered like in front of him, and the sides behind him are considered like behind him. If it is forbidden behind him, then the sides behind him are also forbidden. If it is permitted behind him, then the sides behind him are also permitted. If he is sitting diagonally, we measure the four cubits diagonally, and there is no need for four cubits and a diagonal (see Pri Chadash and Magen Avraham, subsection 1).

There are those who say that if the person sitting next to the one praying is a weak person, it is permitted, because everyone sees that due to his weakness he is compelled to sit. And if you ask: who compels him to sit within four cubits of the one praying? This is not a difficulty at all, for example, if there is no other place to sit, and he is unable to move the chair or bench outside of the four cubits. It is obvious that if he is able to move it outside of the four cubits of the one praying, he is obligated to do so. (And in this way, the difficulty of the Taz, section 4, is resolved. As for what he wrote that he was an old man, his words are puzzling: for the incident with Hannah was forty years earlier. And indeed, many have wondered about this.)

And the language of the Talmud (Berachot 31b) states: It is forbidden to sit within four cubits of someone who is praying. From this, the Tur and Shulchan Aruch deduced that this prohibition applies specifically when someone comes to sit after the first person has already begun to pray. However, if the person was already sitting and then someone else comes to pray beside him, he does not need to get up, since the second person has entered his space. It does not appear as if he is unwilling to accept the yoke of Heaven, according to the reasoning of the Tur. Additionally, it is not considered disrespectful, based on the explanation we provided in section 4. On the contrary, the one who came to pray is acting somewhat improperly by choosing to pray next to someone who is sitting. Therefore, it is considered an act of piety to stand up even in this situation, in order to remove any stumbling block caused by the person who acted improperly (according to the Gra). But according to the strict law, it is permitted.

And there are those who say that this applies specifically in one's home. But in places designated for prayer, such as a synagogue, even if someone is already sitting – they are obligated to stand (Bach and Magen Avraham, subsection 4). Since these are places designated for prayer – it is not appropriate to say that one acted improperly by standing to pray next to someone who is sitting, because it is not within the sitter's rights to prevent the other from praying in that place. Consequently, the person is obligated to stand. And even if they have a designated place in the synagogue and are sitting there – they need to stand. However, this is certainly when one is studying, as they do not need to stand according to the Tur, because Torah study does not exempt one from standing, in any case in such a situation where they preceded in sitting, they do not need to stand. And even the attribute of piety does not require it.

It is questionable if Reuven is standing during Pesukei D'Zimra, and Shimon is sitting next to him, so that when Reuven stands in prayer, Shimon is already sitting. Is this considered that the one sitting was first and is permissible? Or perhaps the one praying was first, since the one sitting knew that he would soon pray the Shemoneh Esrei, and this is considered "the one praying was first" and he must stand? From a logical perspective, it seems permissible, since there is no lack of respect here. And it also does not appear as a lack of acceptance of the yoke of Heaven, since he was sitting before he began praying the Shemoneh Esrei.

Our sages of blessed memory said (Berachot 27a) that it is forbidden to pass in front of someone who is praying within four cubits directly in front of him. The language of the Gemara is: It is forbidden to pass in front of those who are praying. From this, our rabbis deduced that it is specifically in front of him that it is forbidden, but to pass by their sides is permitted. The reason is that by passing in front of him, his concentration will be disturbed (Eliyah Rabbah), but at the sides, his concentration will not be disturbed. Similarly, at a distance of four cubits, even in front of him, his concentration will not be disturbed. It is obvious that merely standing does not constitute a prohibition, as this does not disturb concentration. However, this is if he was already standing there. But to come and stand there – he will inevitably pass slightly in front of him and disturb his concentration. (And so wrote the Eliyah Rabbah, small section 8. And from the Magen Avraham, small section 6, it is explained that passing by his side should not go beyond the place of his standing in prayer, as long as he sees him, it is considered in front of him, see there. But this is not the custom. And also the Eliyah Rabbah objected to this, for certainly if it is not directly in front of him, there is no disturbance of concentration. And what is written in the Shulchan Aruch "to pass and stand" – the intention is not that it is forbidden to stand in front of him, but to pass and stand is forbidden. But one who was already standing there – it is permitted. And the Eliyah Rabbah forced this interpretation, and it seems as I have written. Consider and you will find it light.) (And also when he says "Shema Yisrael" – one should not pass in front of him.)

And know that it is written in the name of the Zohar in the portion "Chayei Sarah" (page 133a) that it is forbidden to pass in all directions. And this is the language of the Zohar: "And one who prays – it is forbidden to pass within four cubits of him. And they established these four cubits in all directions except in front of him... until here is its language." And from this, they wrote (Magen Avraham, subsection 5, and Eliyah Rabbah, subsection 8) that the Zohar forbids in all directions. It is difficult for me to say that the Zohar would disagree with the Gemara where there is no dispute in the Gemara. Furthermore: why would it say "except in front of him"? According to their words, its meaning is: "except in front of him" yet it is still forbidden in all directions. And this is forced. Additionally, it is difficult: if so, is it also forbidden behind him? This is clear, there is no reasoning at all, for even sitting is permitted according to the Tur and Beit Yosef, as I have written. Furthermore: everywhere that the Zohar says "and they established," we find this in some place. Therefore, it seems to me that on the contrary, even the Zohar permits to the sides. And thus it says "and they established," meaning: that the sages of the Talmud said so. And this is its explanation: "and they established these four cubits," meaning: they established that within four cubits in all directions it is permitted, except in front of him – it is forbidden. And this is a concise expression in the manner of the Jerusalem Talmud.

If someone has finished his prayer and another person is praying behind him, he is not allowed to take three steps back until the person behind him finishes his prayer. This is because if he steps back, it is as if he is crossing in front of someone who is praying. One must be meticulous about this: even if the latter started praying after him, since he has already begun. It seems to me that if the person praying has already finished the Amidah but is extending his supplications, there is no prohibition to pass in front of him, as this does not disturb his prayer. Especially if it is necessary, such as to take the steps back. Additionally, it seems to me that if a rabbi has finished his prayer and the chazzan is waiting for him as is customary, he is allowed to take steps back even if someone is praying behind him, because of the burden on the congregation. There are those who want to say that since the reason is due to disturbing the prayer of the one praying, if he covers his face with his tallit, it is permissible to pass in front of him. However, this does not seem correct to me at all. If there is an object in front of the person praying that is ten handbreadths high and four handbreadths wide, it is considered a separation.

It is stated in the Gemara (24b): If one was standing in prayer and sneezed, expelling wind from below, he should wait until the odor dissipates and then resume praying. To where does he return? If he did not pause for the amount of time it would take to finish the entire prayer from beginning to end, he returns to the place where he stopped. If he paused for the amount of time it would take to finish the entire prayer, according to the Rif and the Rambam, he always returns to the beginning, as I wrote in Siman 65. Refer there. According to the Tosafot, the Rosh, the Tur, and the Shulchan Aruch, if the odor did not dissipate within that amount of time, he returns to the beginning. If the odor dissipated earlier, which in truth it is uncommon for the odor to persist for so long (and this is the intent of the Magen Avraham in subsection 1; analyze and you will find it easy), but he delayed willingly for the amount of time it would take to finish the entire prayer, he does not return to the beginning, as I wrote there. For any delay that was necessary due to the law, he returns to the beginning. If he delayed willingly, he returns to the place where he stopped. (Bach. And the Magen Avraham does not disagree on this, as written by the Machatzit HaShekel. See also Pri Megadim.)

If one feels in the middle of prayer that he needs to pass gas, he must force himself not to do so until after the prayer. This does not fall under the prohibition of "do not make yourselves abominable," as this only applies to holding in one's needs and not to holding in gas (Beit Yosef in the name of Terumat HaDeshen). Furthermore, even if it were considered "do not make yourselves abominable," it would only be a rabbinic prohibition, and they did not decree in such a case where there would be an interruption in prayer and a disgrace (see Magen Avraham, subparagraph 4). All the more so when wearing tefillin, as there is a great prohibition against passing gas while wearing tefillin. This is applicable when one can force himself and hold it in.

However, if one cannot control himself and delay, and is compelled to pass gas, our sages of blessed memory said (Berachot 24b) that he should move back four cubits and release the gas. Specifically, he should move back, to distance himself from the Divine Presence standing before him (Levush). Even to the sides appears to be forbidden, because the distancing is not as noticeable. It is also obvious that if this occurs during the morning prayer, he must first remove his tefillin. After he has passed gas, he should stand in his place and wait until the odor dissipates. He should then recite: "Master of the Universe! You created us with many openings and many cavities. It is revealed and known before You our disgrace and our shame, disgrace and shame in our lives, maggots and worms in our deaths" (Rif). He then returns to his place and resumes from where he stopped. If he delayed long enough to finish the entire prayer, this is explained in Section 1. He specifically returns to his place, but he should not finish his prayer in the place where he passed gas, since the Divine Presence has already established its place there (Levush). It seems to me that if he removed his tefillin, he should complete the prayer without them, and not interrupt in the middle of the prayer to put them back on. (In the case of urine that splashed on his knees in Siman 78, they did not require him to recite the "Master of the Universe" prayer, because in that case he was at fault for not checking before the prayer. This is not the case with passing gas, where he is compelled. So wrote the Tosafot R"I. Additionally, perhaps in this case it is more disgraceful due to the bad odor. Examine this carefully and you will find it easy to understand.)

The early authorities wrote that the custom nowadays is not to act in this manner, because perhaps this requirement was only for someone praying at home. However, in a synagogue, it would be a great disgrace to distance oneself from one's place, and therefore one stands in their place and passes wind. Consequently, the prayer "Ribono shel Olam" (Master of the Universe) is also not recited, for when one does not distance themselves, their shame and embarrassment are not evident (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 5). One waits until the odor dissipates, and this is the common practice. It seems to me that one must remove their tefillin, as it is impossible to permit passing wind while wearing them. Our sages of blessed memory said (Berakhot 24b): "If one sneezes during their prayer from below, it is a bad sign for them. If they sneeze from above, which is called 'Nisin', it is a good sign for them, as just as they are given satisfaction from below, they are given satisfaction from above." Sneezing from above is a pleasure for a person. Know that with sneezing from below, there is no difference whether it is loud or not (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 6 and Eliyah Rabbah, subparagraph 7). The sign from below is bad because it distances the person from their prayer. But sneezing from above does not interrupt, and it is pleasurable. See above in Siman 80.

Even though it is permitted to interrupt in the middle of the recitation of the Shema due to fear and respect, as I wrote in Siman 66, nevertheless, this is not the case with the Amidah prayer. Since one is considered as if standing before the King, it is forbidden to interrupt even due to loss of money. All the more so for fear and respect, because one who stands before a human king and interrupts in the middle of speaking with the king would be liable to the monarchy. All the more so when standing before the King of Kings, the Holy One, blessed be He. Interruption is only permitted in a situation of life-threatening danger, as nothing takes precedence over saving a life. The law of the prayer is like the law of the verse "Shema Yisrael," as explained there, that interruption is only permitted in a situation of life-threatening danger.

And this is what the Sages taught in the Mishnah: even if a king inquires about his well-being, he should not interrupt; even if a snake is coiled around his heel, he should not interrupt. And it is stated in the Gemara (Berakhot 32b): this was only taught regarding the kings of Israel, but for the kings of other nations, he should interrupt, lest they kill him. Similarly, if a robber comes upon him in the middle of prayer, he should interrupt for this reason. And he is obligated to interrupt, as it is written: "And you shall guard your souls" (Deuteronomy 4:15). And this is what we find in the Gemara there: an incident involving a pious man who was asked by a governor in the middle of prayer and did not interrupt, even though the governor had the power to kill him as explained there — this was because he was confident that the governor would accept his response and not kill him, as indeed happened (see Magen Avraham, sub-paragraph 1). And we find even more than this with Rabbi Yochanan in the Jerusalem Talmud there, who was engaged in Torah study and did not interrupt, and they wanted to harm him but did not harm him, see there. And there is room for doubt if there is no danger of death but only a fear of suffering, such as being beaten, whether it is permissible for him to interrupt. This requires further investigation.

And even in a situation where one is compelled to interrupt, as I have written, nevertheless if it is possible for him to shorten – he should shorten. This means that he should say the beginning of the blessing and its end before it reaches him, and he should shorten in this manner for all the blessings. Alternatively, if it is possible for him to deviate from the path – he should deviate and not interrupt with speech. Walking is not considered an interruption like speech. If none of these are possible, and there is a concern of danger – he should interrupt with speech.

Not only is it forbidden to interrupt one's prayer by speaking or walking, but even mere gesturing is prohibited during prayer. There are those who permit gesturing when a baby is crying and disturbing one's prayer, allowing one to signal with their hands to stop the baby from crying. If this does not help, one should distance oneself from the baby. Similarly, if one is praying and feels that the prayer leader is waiting for them, it is permissible to signal with one's hand to indicate not to wait due to the burden on the congregation (Sha'arei Teshuvah). I am very puzzled by this, as it is forbidden to gesture even in the first section of the Shema, as I wrote in Siman 63, and certainly during the verse "Shema Yisrael." All the more so during the Amidah, even if we say it is for the necessity of the prayer or the burden on the congregation, it cannot be permitted, and certainly not walking. Therefore, it seems to me that all these actions are prohibited. When a baby cries and disturbs the prayer, one should strengthen their prayer, and Heaven will assist them. Due to the burden on the congregation, one should shorten the prayer and not prolong it, but not interrupt with gestures, and certainly not with walking.

Even if a snake is coiled around his heel, he should not interrupt, because it does not bite in most cases (Rambam in his commentary on the Mishnah). But if it is a scorpion, he interrupts, because it bites in most cases, and it is more likely to cause harm than a snake. And if the snake appears angry and ready to harm – he interrupts. And our master the Rema wrote in Section 3 that even in the case of an ordinary snake, one can walk to another place so that the snake will fall off his leg. These are his words. Meaning: he should not interrupt by speaking to ask someone else to remove it from him, or by himself engaging to lift his leg and remove it, for this is a major interruption. But slight walking so that it falls off – is permitted. And there is an opinion that walking is not considered an interruption (Magen Avraham, Subsection 3, citing Tosafot R”Y). And the intention is not that it is not considered an interruption, for certainly walking is an interruption (as the Taz writes in Subsection 1). Rather, the intention is that it is not the same kind of interruption as speaking or acting. And they permitted this kind of interruption because although in most cases it does not harm, nonetheless there is some concern of danger, and therefore they permitted the interruption of walking. And it seems to me that this applies specifically to his heel. But if the snake is on his body – he can remove it with his hands. But if it is on his heel – he must necessarily lift his leg, and this involves a major interruption. And it is uncertain whether this applies only when his heel is covered, and when his heel is bare, it is permitted because the danger is closer. Or perhaps even in such a case, there is no danger. And this requires investigation. And in our country, snakes and scorpions are not common at all. And there are places where snakes are common, and they say they do not harm at all. And in any case where there is doubt – doubt concerning life is to be lenient.

If one was praying on the way and saw an animal or a wagon approaching him, and he was praying while standing and not walking, he is nevertheless required to move aside from the path and should not interrupt his prayer with speech. Our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 2: "But in other matters, one should not leave his place until he finishes his prayer, unless he is in the midst of supplications after the prayer." Thus are his words. It is necessary to understand what is meant by "other matters." If it is regarding a discretionary matter, then even in the midst of supplications, one should not move from his place until he has taken three steps back, as I wrote in Siman 123. And if he is compelled to move from his place, such as if a bad odor developed in that place, then even in the middle of the prayer, he should move from his place, as I wrote at the end of Siman 90; see there.

However, the explanation of his words is as follows: In the Gemara (31a) it is stated: They said about Rabbi Akiva that when he prayed with the congregation, he would shorten [his prayers], but when he prayed alone, a person would find him in one corner and then in another corner, due to the many bowings and prostrations. Meaning: when he would bow with outstretched hands and feet, it was inevitable that he would move from his place (Tosafot Yeshanim). And our Rabbis raised a question: Isn't it forbidden to add in bowings? And they answered that this was done in the supplications after the prayer, because otherwise, it is indeed forbidden to move from one's place (Rosh and Tosafot Yeshanim). And the Tosafot there explained that in the middle of a blessing, it is permitted to increase bowings, see there. And it must be said, the reason they were not concerned about his moving from his place is because this is not really considered moving in the manner of walking but rather in the manner of prostrating – therefore it is not considered moving from his place.

And these are the words of our teacher, the Beit Yosef: In any other matter, even for the sake of a mitzvah, one should not leave his place in the middle of prayer, except during the supplications after the prayer. But for a voluntary matter, it is forbidden before the three steps back. And it seems to me that this applies specifically to a complete mitzvah. However, if one is honored with opening the Ark or something similar, or even if he is called to the Torah, he should not go without taking the three steps back, and he should shorten the supplications and ascend after taking the three steps. For there is no delay in this, and even for any mitzvah, he may do so. And our teacher, the Beit Yosef, only stated that there is no prohibition in this as in the case of Rabbi Akiva and the like. He does not agree with the Tosafot that Rabbi Akiva did this in the middle of the blessings but rather with the Rosh and the Tosafot of Rabbi Yitzchak. But for other mitzvot, where he can immediately take the steps and shorten the supplications, he is obligated to do so. This seems to be my humble opinion. (See Magen Avraham, subsection 2, and Eliyah Rabbah, subsection 3. Delve and you will find it easy.) And the cantors on Yom Kippur who move from their place to "kneel" – it is not proper to do so. (And perhaps according to Tosafot it is permitted, as I wrote in the previous section. Delve and you will find it easy.)

If one sees an ox approaching him, the law is that one must keep a distance of fifty cubits from a tame ox and as far as one can see from a goring ox. If the oxen in that place are known not to cause harm, then this law does not apply. Similarly, if any harmful animal approaches him, the law applies, and all the more so for a mad dog or similar. The application of the law should be understood according to the situation.

Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote in Section 5: In every case where one interrupts, if the pause was long enough to finish the entire prayer, he must start over from the beginning. If not, he returns to the beginning of the blessing where he interrupted. If he interrupted during the first three blessings, he starts over from the beginning. If during the last blessings, he returns to "Retzeh." This is his language. It has already been explained in Siman 65 that Rabbeinu Beit Yosef agrees with the Rif and the Rambam that in prayer, one always starts over from the beginning if the pause was long enough to finish the entire prayer. Rabbeinu Rema agrees with Tosafot and the Rosh that if the pause was voluntary, he does not start over from the beginning, but if the pause was involuntary, he starts over from the beginning. Therefore, he did not correct anything here, because here the pause was involuntary, as one was forced to pause due to an oppressor, a scorpion, or an ox, as explained. And the ruling that he returns to the beginning of the blessing where he erred is because the middle of a blessing is not significant. Similarly, the first three blessings are considered as one blessing, and the last three as well. And indeed, in the blessings of the Shema, he returns to the beginning of the blessing, as I wrote in Siman 59, see there. (And so wrote the Taz in Section 2, not like the Bach who held that according to Tosafot here, he does not return to the beginning, see there.)

He also wrote: The statement "if one delayed enough to complete the entire prayer" is measured by the one praying. This means that if, according to his own prayer, the interruption was long enough for him to be able to pray from the beginning to the end, it is called "delayed enough to complete the entire prayer." And likewise, conversely: if, according to his prayer, he did not delay enough to complete the entire prayer, even though according to the prayer of others it would be enough to complete the entire prayer, he does not go back to the beginning. For we measure only by him and not by others, as with the recitation of the Shema above in Siman 65. And this is why he used the phrase "measured by the one praying," because this law originates from the Rashba at the beginning of the second chapter, and he is speaking about the recitation of the Shema. Therefore, the same phraseology is used here. And know that there are those who say that the statement that one returns to the beginning of the blessing applies specifically when there was an interruption by speaking. But without speaking, one returns to the place where he stopped (Derech HaChaim). This does not seem correct to me. (And regarding what he wrote about urine, I do not know from where we derive this. And the Beit Yosef equates this to returning to the beginning, and certainly, this is the case as I have written. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

He also wrote: If one speaks during prayer, the law regarding repetition is the same as the interruptions mentioned in this section. Thus is his language, meaning: if one engages in a brief conversation, one returns to the beginning of the blessing, even if the interruption was only for a moment. If the interruption lasted long enough to finish the entire prayer, one returns to the beginning of the prayer. The first three blessings are considered as one, and so too the last three. This applies if one spoke inadvertently or under duress. If one spoke intentionally, some say it is treated the same as inadvertent or forced interruptions, and they have the same law (Levush, Taz 3, and Gra in the name of Rashba). This is the opinion of our teacher, the Beit Yosef. Some say that if one spoke intentionally in any case, one returns to the beginning (Bach, Magen Avraham 6; and regarding the Shema, there is doubt, see there). If one spoke between blessings and did not delay long enough to complete the entire prayer, there is no correction needed, and one should continue their prayer. If one interrupted in the middle of a blessing and started from where they left off or delayed enough to complete the entire blessing, and did not return to the beginning but completed their prayer, what was done is done, and one does not need to pray again. This is not similar to one who forgot "Ya'aleh Veyavo" and completed the prayer, where they are required to repeat the prayer, because in that case, they did not pray what they were obligated to pray. But here, one prayed everything required, only they interrupted; and since they finished, they finished (Elya Rabbah 8). Some say it is the same as "Ya'aleh Veyavo" and one must return and pray again (Taz end of 3). The primary view seems to be the first opinion.

It is forbidden to interrupt in the middle of the prayer, even for Kaddish, Kedusha, or "Barchu." Rather, one should remain silent until the prayer leader says "Yitbarach" in Kaddish, in Kedusha until "Yimloch," and in "Barchu" until the congregation responds "Baruch Hashem...". This is the language of Rashi, of blessed memory, in Sukkah (38b): If one heard and intended to listen, even though he did not respond, he has fulfilled his obligation. Similarly, for those praying in a congregation and the prayer leader says Kedusha or "Yehei Shmei Rabbah," they should remain silent in their prayer and listen attentively, and it is as if they responded. Once the Kedusha is finished, they should return to their prayer. This is also established by the Behag. This is the end of his language.

One should not ask: If so, why did they say that if one enters a synagogue and finds the congregation praying, if he can start and finish before the prayer leader reaches Kedusha or "Modim," he should pray, and if not, he should not pray, as will be explained in Siman 109?
