Why should he not pray? Can't he remain silent and listen? Indeed, if he were to remain silent, his listening would interrupt his prayer. However, perhaps even though "hearing is like responding," responding is preferable and a more optimal mitzvah. This is what our rabbis, the Tosafists, wrote there. In Berachot (21b), they wrote that Rabbeinu Tam and the Ri dispute this, arguing that since hearing is like responding, it constitutes an interruption when one is silent. Nevertheless, the custom among the people is to remain silent and listen, and great is the custom. This is the end of their language.

The Rosh also investigated this and agreed with Rashi and the Behag. The Tur brought both opinions and did not decide. Rabbeinu Yonah wrote there that since this matter depends on the pillars of the world, we do not have the power to decide between them. Whoever acts according to one master has acted, and whoever acts according to another master has acted, provided that he directs his heart to heaven. This is the end of his language. Rabbeinu Beit Yosef in section 7 ruled straightforwardly according to Rashi, and this is the simple custom.

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote: If one is standing in prayer and they call him to go up to the Torah, he should not interrupt. Thus is his language. And there is no novelty in this, for even in the recitation of the Shema he does not interrupt, as I have written in Siman 135, all the more so in prayer. However, his intent is: because earlier in Siman 66 he brought two opinions regarding the recitation of the Shema, and some say that he does interrupt, for this he says that in prayer everyone agrees that he should not interrupt. And know that if he interrupted for Kedusha, Kaddish, or "Barchu" and responded verbally, it is considered an interruption, and it is treated as if he interrupted for mundane speech. And according to those who hold that if one interrupts intentionally he must return to the beginning, here too it is the same (see Magen Avraham, Siman 8). And after he finishes the eighteen blessings, he can interrupt for all these matters, and he should say "Yehi Ratzon" and take the three steps back, and then go up to the Torah. But for responding to Kedusha, Kaddish, and "Barchu" he does not need to take the steps back. And he can also answer all the "Amens".

The Gemara states (30b): How long should one wait between prayers? Meaning, sometimes one needs to pray two prayers consecutively, such as when a person made a mistake and wants to pray again. Also, between the Shacharit prayer and the Musaf prayer (Tosafot), when one does not say "Ashrei" in between (Tosafot Ri), or when one forgot to pray and makes it up during the next prayer time, praying two prayers consecutively (Tur). How long should one wait between these prayers? One opinion says: Enough time for one's mind to become composed, so that one's mind is settled enough to arrange one's words in a supplicatory manner (Rashi), as it is written: "And I pleaded with the Lord" (Gemara). Another opinion says: Enough time for one's mind to become fervent, using the language of "fervor" as it is written: "And Moses pleaded" (see there).

And the Rambam in Chapter 10, Halacha 15 ruled that [one must wait] in order to compose one's mind, see there. However, Rashi of blessed memory explained that they do not disagree, and it is merely a difference in language, see there. And Tosafot wrote: "Regarding in order to compose" - it is explained in the Jerusalem Talmud, which means when one walks four cubits. This is their language. And in the Jerusalem Talmud, these terms "to compose" and "to compose" are not mentioned at all. And this is what is stated there (Chapter 4, Halacha 6), that Rabbi Yochanan said: I saw Rabbi Yannai standing and praying... and he walked four cubits and prayed the Musaf prayer, see there. And from this language, it implies that one must specifically walk four cubits. However, the Tur and Shulchan Aruch wrote: One who prays two prayers consecutively must wait between them the time it takes to walk four cubits. This is their language. And the law aligns with them, as it is stated later in the Jerusalem Talmud. And not that one must actually walk four cubits, but even if one waited the time it takes to walk four cubits, see there. Therefore, it is necessary to question Tosafot for not writing according to the conclusion of the Jerusalem Talmud. (And it is also difficult: why did they reference this "in order to compose"? And perhaps they do not agree with Rashi that there is no disagreement? And they indeed disagree on this point: according to the one who says "in order to compose" - it suffices to wait the time it takes to walk four cubits. And according to the one who says "to compose" - one must actually walk. And so wrote the Pnei Moshe there. According to this, since the Rambam ruled "in order to compose" - the rulings of the Tur and Shulchan Aruch stand. Be precise and you will find clarity.)

It is obvious that the waiting period is after taking three steps backward. One should not ask: if so, then even without this, one would be required to wait the time it takes to walk four cubits before returning to his place, as will be explained in Siman 123. Here, we are discussing a case where he wants to pray in the place where he stepped back to and does not want to return to his original place (Magen Avraham). This concern is only for the Shemoneh Esrei prayers. However, for other prayers, one can pray one after the other immediately, even several prayers (ibid.). Nevertheless, according to our custom to say "Ashrei" between Shacharit and Mussaf and the Torah reading, there is already a considerable interruption. Even the recitation of "Ashrei" alone is more than the time it takes to walk four cubits.

All those who are exempt from reciting the Shema, because they are engaged in a mitzvah or are preoccupied with a mitzvah, and those who are occupied with a deceased person – are exempt from prayer. And there is one particular aspect in which prayer has more exemptions than the recitation of the Shema, as the sages taught in the Mishnah at the beginning of the third chapter: Those who carry the bier... those in front of the bier who are needed – are exempt. Those who are behind the bier who are not needed – are obligated. But all of them are exempt from prayer. The reason: according to those who hold that prayer is of rabbinic origin, the reason is simple, as the recitation of the Shema is of Torah origin and prayer is of rabbinic origin. And according to those who hold that prayer is of Torah origin, it is because prayer requires standing and they do not have the time for this, which is not the case with the recitation of the Shema: they can say the first verse while walking (Tosafot R”Y).

And know: From the language of the Tur, it implies that specifically those who have no need for the bier [are exempt]. Nevertheless, they are related to the bearers of the bier. However, those who escort the deceased, who have no connection at all to the carrying of the bier, are obligated in prayer (Beit Yosef). But the Rambam wrote at the end of the sixth chapter that all those who escort the deceased are exempt from prayer; see there. And so ruled Rabbeinu [the Beit Yosef] in section 1. And he holds that those who have no need for the bier are included among the escorts. And perhaps the Tur also follows the language of the Talmud, but in practice agrees that all the escorts are exempt. And so wrote the students of Rabbeinu Yonah in the name of the Jerusalem Talmud, that those who are behind the bier are never needed for the bier; see there. If so, they are merely escorts. (But I have not found this in the Jerusalem Talmud.)

And it is clear that those who are exempt from prayer are exempt even if the time for prayer passes. Also, for the subsequent prayer, they do not need to pray twice, since they were exempt at the time of the first obligation. It seems to me further: that even if it is still before midday, if a third of the day has passed, they should no longer pray. And even though it was explained in Siman 89 that one receives the reward for prayer until midday, see there – this is when one acts on their own, either by mistake or intentionally not praying in its proper time as explained there. But here, since they are exempt by law at its proper time, how can we impose upon them to pray after the time? However, if they pray until midday, it is possible that they will receive a reward similar to prayer beyond its time. Or it is possible that it is forbidden to pray because they were exempt at the time of obligation, and it is not similar to the recitation of Shema, which is like reading Torah. But there are some decisors who wrote simply that one is obligated to pray until midday. (Magen Avraham in Siman 71, subsection 1. And we also wrote there in subsection 2. This requires further investigation.)

And there is a question according to the second reason mentioned in section A: Why do we not permit him to pray while he is walking, just as we permitted one who is walking on the way in Siman 94? There are those who answer that while he is walking, he is engaged in a mitzvah and therefore exempt. Nevertheless, he is obligated in the recitation of the Shema, because he can easily recite it (Magen Avraham, subsection 1). And this is obviously not sufficient. It appears to me that, in truth, prayer is only valid while standing, and only on the way did the sages permit it for the reason explained there. And this is all for one who is obligated in it and not for one who is exempt from it, and we cannot correct the prayer for him in a manner that contradicts the fundamental law of prayer, which is specifically while standing.

Women and slaves, although they are exempt from the recitation of Shema, are obligated in prayer. The Rambam wrote at the beginning of the first chapter that the reason is because it is a positive commandment not bound by time. Meaning, he holds that prayer is a Torah-level positive commandment, and from the Torah, it does not have a fixed time, therefore it is a positive commandment not bound by time. And therefore, even though the Rabbis established specific times for prayer and based it on the verse "Evening, morning, and afternoon, I pray" as I wrote at the beginning of Siman 89, nevertheless, it is obvious that they did not intend to lessen the obligation of the Torah by exempting women and slaves from this commandment. And this is what is stated in the Mishnah (Berakhot 20b) that women and slaves are obligated in prayer. The Gemara asks: Isn't it obvious? And it answers: You might have thought that since it is written "Evening and morning..." it would be considered a positive commandment bound by time? It teaches us otherwise. Meaning, it teaches us that since by Torah law it does not have a fixed time, they are obligated. And the Rif wrote similarly, see there. (And Rashi, of blessed memory, deleted this version, writing: This is our version "Because it is [a matter of] mercy," and did not write "Isn't it obvious?" because it is not a Torah-level commandment. So far his words. He holds like the Ramban that we explained at the beginning of Siman 89 that prayer is rabbinic. But the Rif and the Rambam have the version "Isn't it obvious?" and do not have the version "Because it is [a matter of] mercy." And this is clear with the help of Heaven. And I have seen great commentators who struggled to explain the Rambam's version "Because it is [a matter of] mercy," but it is clear that they did not have this version at all. Examine and you will find it simple.)

According to the approach of Rashi, Tosafot, and the Ramban that prayer is of Rabbinic origin, it would seem that since its essence is Rabbinic and they established it at specific times, it should be considered a time-bound positive commandment. This is why the Gemara states that it is because "it is an act of mercy." According to Rashi's explanation there, it does not apply at all to Rabbinic commandments to distinguish between "time-bound" and "not time-bound." The Tosafot there wrote that even with Rabbinic commandments, there is a distinction, as they exempted women from Hallel because it is time-bound, even though it is Rabbinic (Sukkah 38a). However, because prayer is an act of mercy, they instituted it even for women.

Certainly. Here is the translation:

And behold, it is certain that according to Rashi, women are obligated in three prayers a day just like men, for according to him, there is no distinction in Rabbinic obligations between "time-bound" and "not time-bound." And similarly, according to Tosafot, the Gemara explicitly states this: that even though it is time-bound, nevertheless, since it is a matter of mercy, the Rabbis obligated them even in time-bound commandments, and consequently, they are obligated just like men. However, according to the Rif and Rambam, who do not include the reasoning of "because it is mercy," but rather base their obligation from the Torah because it is not time-bound, it follows that their obligation is only once a day and in any form. It cannot be said that after the Sages instituted three times a day and at their specific times, this obligation also applies to them, for if so, what is the Gemara's question "it is obvious," as it teaches us a lot? Rather, it is certain as I have written. (And the Magen Avraham in subsection 2 is brief in this matter. For certainly, according to the Rambam, it is so, but according to Rashi and Tosafot, women are certainly obligated in all prayers just like men and at their specific times. And the students of Rabbeinu Yonah wrote: even though it has a fixed time, nevertheless, since they said that ideally a person should pray all day long, it is considered as if it is not time-bound, and therefore women are obligated. Alternatively, because it is a matter of mercy. Thus far their language. And I do not understand the need for the first reason, for according to Rashi and Tosafot, it is explicitly stated that the reason is because it is a matter of mercy, and according to the Rif and Rambam, there is no difficulty at all. It must be said that they hold that it is Rabbinic, and they did not have the version "because it is mercy," and it was difficult for them: is it not time-bound? And they hold like Tosafot that even in Rabbinic matters, time-bound applies. Therefore, they offered two answers: and for the first answer, it can be said that women are only obligated once a day, like the Rambam. And the Levush wrote a completely different reason, see there. And this is certainly surprising: for he saw the version of Rashi and Tosafot "because it is mercy," and also in the Bahag there is this reason, and similarly in the Jerusalem Talmud, see there. And according to this, it is difficult to reconcile why our women are not careful with all three prayers according to the opinion of Rashi and Tosafot, whereas according to the Rif and Rambam, it makes sense. Be precise and you will find leniency.

Children are required to be educated in prayer if they have reached the age of education. According to the Rambam, since prayer is a Torah obligation, it is obvious that it is like all other commandments where there is an obligation to educate them, and the responsibility lies on the father. Even according to those who say that prayer is of rabbinic origin, nevertheless, since it is about requesting mercy, the sages imposed on the father to accustom them as adults. However, regarding the prohibition of eating before prayer, this is not practiced with them, and one may feed them before prayer, lest they become weak and come into danger. Additionally, something that is not an intrinsic prohibition but rather dependent on time is not relevant to education. Therefore, they are also permitted to eat before Kiddush as will be explained in Siman 269, and he should feed them by hand.

The Sages taught in the Mishnah (Shabbat 9b): One interrupts [their study] for the recitation of the Shema, but does not interrupt for the prayer. And the Gemara establishes that this refers to one who is constantly engaged in Torah study. The difference between the recitation of the Shema and the prayer is explained there in the Jerusalem Talmud with three reasons: The first reason: the recitation of the Shema is a Torah obligation, while prayer is a rabbinic obligation. And the one who says this holds like the Ramban that prayer is rabbinic. The second reason: because the time for the recitation of the Shema is fixed by Torah law, while the time for prayer is not fixed. And the one who says this holds like the Rambam that prayer is from the Torah, except that its time is not fixed. And it is necessary to say this: because if he holds that it is rabbinic, behold, from a rabbinic perspective, its time is fixed. The third reason: the recitation of the Shema does not require intention except for the first verse, whereas prayer requires intention, see there. And he also holds that it is from the Torah. It turns out that there is a disagreement among our Rabbis in the Jerusalem Talmud. (And the Shagat Aryeh in siman 14 challenged the Rambam based on this Mishnah, see there. And he did not see this Jerusalem Talmud, which necessitates interpreting it as I have written. Examine it, and you will find it easy.)

It states in the Gemara there that the ruling that those engaged in Torah study do not interrupt for prayer applies only to individuals like Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai and his colleagues, whose Torah study was their profession and who did not interrupt even for a moment. But for people like us, we interrupt both for the recitation of Shema and for prayer when the time for prayer is about to pass. If the time is not about to pass, we too are permitted to continue studying (Beit Yosef in the name of the Ran and the Maor). And Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai and his colleagues, even when the time is about to pass, are forbidden to interrupt (there).

Regarding the recitation of Shema, one is obligated to also recite the blessings before and after it (Magen Avraham, subsection 4), because even though they are of rabbinic origin, since one is obligated in the recitation of Shema, one is also obligated in its blessings. Afterward, one interrupts and studies and does not pray (there). And what we wrote that if the time is not about to pass, we too are permitted to study, this is according to the opinion of most poskim who disagree with Rashi, who forbids studying before prayer, as I wrote in Siman 89, subsection 27; see there. And it is explained there that when one is teaching others, one does not need to interrupt either for the recitation of Shema or for prayer, for the Torah study of the public is very great. And so did our holy teacher, who would pass his hand over his eyes and recite only the verse "Shema Yisrael," and he was diligent to teach a halacha that includes the exodus from Egypt (Yoma 19b), and after the lesson, he would complete the recitation of Shema (Magen Avraham, subsection 8). And know that even according to Rashi's opinion, if one began to study, one should not interrupt if the time is not passing, and there will still be time to recite Shema and pray (there, subsection 9).

Know that the words of the Rambam on this matter are very perplexing. For he wrote in Chapter 6, Law 8: "One who is engaged in the study of Torah and the time for prayer arrives – he interrupts and prays. But if his Torah study is his occupation and he does not engage in any work at all, and he was studying Torah at the time of prayer – he does not interrupt, for the mitzvah of Torah study is greater than the mitzvah of prayer." Thus far his words. And this is perplexing, for in the Gemara Rabbi Yochanan said: "They only taught this regarding someone like Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai and his colleagues, but we interrupt...," as the Tur and Shulchan Aruch have written. And since Rabbi Yochanan interrupted, all the more so should we. And it is certain that Rabbi Yochanan's Torah study was his occupation, so how could the Rambam write that one whose Torah study is his occupation does not interrupt? Are we greater than Rabbi Yochanan? This requires great investigation.

It appears that the Rambam interprets what is said about Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai and his colleagues—not due to their great stature and diligence, but rather because they did not engage in any work to earn a livelihood. And since they did not interrupt for livelihood, they also did not interrupt for prayer. However, other Tannaim and Amoraim had some form of livelihood as is well-known in the Talmud, and therefore they would interrupt. According to this, even nowadays, one who has no livelihood should also not interrupt. And know that from his words it is implied that only when the time for prayer arrives does one interrupt, and this aligns with Rashi's view that we wrote that it is forbidden to study before prayer. And it is possible that his intention is that the time for prayer will pass, and this requires further investigation. (A blessing was not instituted for prayer, see Magen Avraham at the end of subparagraph 4.)

It is already known that the Men of the Great Assembly instituted for us three prayers each day. And they said (Berachot 21a): "Could a person pray all day long? The verse comes to teach us from Daniel: 'And he had windows open in his upper chamber toward Jerusalem, and he kneeled upon his knees three times a day, and prayed, and gave thanks before his God, as he did aforetime' (Daniel 6:10)." This implies three times, and therefore they said (Berachot 21a): "If one was standing in prayer and remembered that he already prayed, he should stop, even in the middle of a blessing." They also said there: "If one is uncertain whether he prayed or not, he does not go back and pray." The reason is that prayer is a rabbinic obligation, and in cases of doubt regarding rabbinic obligations, we are lenient. Even according to Maimonides, who holds that prayer is a Torah obligation, it still does not have a set text or fixed time and is only once a day. All of this is rabbinic, as I wrote at the beginning of Siman 89. However, Rabbi Yochanan said there: "Would that a person could pray all day long." Rashi, Tosafot, and Bahag explained that the law follows Rabbi Yochanan in cases of doubt whether one has prayed, but if it is certain that one has prayed, the law is to stop even in the middle of a blessing. This is also the opinion of several other authorities. Even though regarding Rabbi Yochanan it was not mentioned at all about doubt concerning prayer, they wrote that since the Talmud fixed his words regarding doubt whether one prayed, it is presumably in such a case. Additionally, it seems to me that since it is explicitly stated in the Jerusalem Talmud (Chapter 4, Halacha 4), where it says: "They asked Rabbi Yochanan: If one is uncertain whether he prayed or not? He answered them: 'Would that people would pray all day long, for prayer is never harmful.' This is his language, clearly indicating he was referring to doubt. (And this is its explanation: Would that we could pray all day. But we are forbidden more than three times, as it was said: Could a person pray all day…, and if so, do not add to it. This applies in cases of certainty that one prayed, but in cases of doubt, one is permitted to pray. So wrote the Bach, see there.)

And know that the statement concerning the one who prayed and then stopped was said by Shmuel. And he said another statement there in the Gemara: If one prayed and then entered a synagogue and found the congregation praying, if he can introduce something new in his prayer, he may pray again. If not, he should not pray again. The Gemara explains that even an individual in relation to the congregation is not allowed to pray twice without introducing something new. Whether an individual alone is permitted to pray a second time by introducing something new is not clarified in the Gemara. The explanation there that a congregation is not better than an individual means that without introducing something new, it is also forbidden for the congregation. But to say that it is permitted for an individual without introducing something new, we have not heard. From the language of the Ba'al Halachot Gedolot (Behag), it explicitly implies that only in a congregation is it permitted by introducing something new, see there. However, this is not the opinion of our Rabbis, as will be explained. And it also seems from Tosafot there that by introducing something new, even an individual is permitted to pray again even if he certainly already prayed, see there.

And this is the opinion of Rav Hai Gaon, as brought by the Rosh. And the Tosafot of Rabbi Yitzchak there and the Tur, who hold that what Rabbi Yochanan said, "Would that one could pray all day long," refers to doing so with a new element introduced. And that which they prohibited praying more than three times a day is without a new element, and there is no distinction between public prayer and individual prayer. And this certainly requires a new element when one prays, but in the case of doubt whether one has prayed, it does not require a new element, because since one needs to pray again due to doubt – there is no greater new element than this (Tosafot of Rabbi Yitzchak). And it turns out that regarding the doubt whether one has prayed, the opinion of the Gaon aligns with that of Rashi and the Baal Halachot Gedolot. However, in the case of certainty that one has prayed, if it is permitted to pray more with a new element individually – Rashi's opinion is not clear to us. (And also in the Baal Halachot Gedolot, it is possible to interpret in accordance with the words of the Gaon, that he did not mean specifically in public. But this is a strained interpretation, see there.) And see in section 5.

And the Rambam, of blessed memory, his opinion aligns with the previous opinions that if one is certain they prayed, they may indeed pray again if they introduce something new [in their prayer]. However, in the case of doubt whether one prayed, he disagrees with the previous opinions, and for him, certainty is equivalent to doubt, as will be explained. And this is his wording in the first chapter, law 9: "These prayers are not diminished, but one may add to them. If a person wishes to pray all day, they have the permission to do so, and all those additional prayers are like bringing voluntary offerings. Therefore, one must introduce something new in each of the middle blessings, related to the blessings, and if one introduces even in one blessing – it is sufficient to indicate that it is a voluntary prayer and not obligatory. The first three and the last three blessings are never added to, nor reduced, nor is anything changed in them." Thus far his wording.

In the tenth chapter, law 6, it is written: If one is uncertain whether they have prayed or not, they do not repeat the prayer. However, if they prayed this prayer with the intention of it being a voluntary prayer, then if an individual wishes to pray a voluntary prayer all day, they may do so. Thus far his words. His intention is that one must introduce something new in it, as stated in the first chapter, for he wrote "with the intention of it being a voluntary prayer," and in the first chapter, it is explained that a voluntary prayer requires something new. He did not bother to explain this here and relied on what was written there. He follows the approach of the Rif, that Rabbi Yochanan, who said "if only one would pray..." – was not referring exclusively to a definite or doubtful situation, but in any case, this is so. Indeed, this is not clarified in the words of the Gaon, but Rabbeinu Yonah ruled that in a case of doubt, no novelty is required. They do not agree with this, but rather in any case, a novelty and the intention of it being voluntary are required.

The Rambam further wrote there in the tenth chapter: "One who was standing in prayer and remembered that he had already prayed – he stops, even in the middle of a blessing." Thus is his language. And one should not question: Why should he stop, let him finish it as a voluntary prayer and innovate something within it? For the Rif has already explained there the reason is that he already began it as an obligatory prayer, and it is as if he is offering two daily offerings, see there. And this is what the Rambam concluded there: "If it was the evening prayer – he does not stop, because he did not initially pray with the intention that it was obligatory." Thus is his language. Meaning: for we hold that the evening prayer is optional. And the Raavad was not satisfied with this, and wrote: "There is no satisfaction here." Thus is his language. His intention is: for we have accepted upon ourselves the evening prayer as obligatory (Kesef Mishneh). And this is not a challenge, for the Rambam himself did not differentiate in all the laws explained between the evening prayer and other prayers because we have accepted it as obligatory. However, regarding this matter of stopping in the middle of the prayer, we establish it according to the original law. And it appears to me that his intention is that in any case, he should innovate something within it. For although both are optional, nevertheless, in the second prayer, he needs to innovate something so that the prayers are not identical. (So it appears in my humble opinion. And although there might be a distinction, nevertheless, this seems correct. Consider it well and you will find it easy.)

And know that the Rif, of blessed memory, did not mention at all that one needs to innovate something [in the prayer], and he holds that even without innovation, one can pray an optional prayer. And even though the Rif later brings the case of one who finds a congregation praying and whether he can innovate..., nevertheless, it does not seem that this applies to the previous laws. And the proof for this is from the words of the Tur, who wrote: "And if he does not know how to innovate something, and it is clear to him that he has prayed, and he wants to pray with the intention of an optional prayer — according to the Rif, he can pray... And according to the Gaon, one cannot pray an optional prayer without innovation." And he also wrote: "It is impossible... until here are his words." And the opinion of the Rambam on this is like that of the Gaon, as we have explained. And the opinion of the Ra'avad in the first chapter is like that of the Rif, that one does not need innovation, see there.

Maimonides wrote there in the first chapter: The community does not pray a voluntary prayer, for the community does not bring a voluntary offering. An individual should not pray the Musaf prayer twice, one as an obligation of the day and one as a voluntary prayer, for a voluntary Musaf offering is not brought. Some of the Geonim have ruled that it is forbidden to pray a voluntary prayer on Sabbaths and festivals, for only obligatory offerings are brought on those days. Thus far his words. The Raavad wrote that for a different reason one should not pray two prayers on the Sabbath and festivals: because any additional prayer is only to request mercy and supplication, and the prayers of the Sabbath and festivals consist only of praise and thanks, and any such addition would be a blessing in vain. Similarly, the blessings of "Yotzer" and of the evening, the blessings over fruit, and the blessings over commandments — it is forbidden to repeat them. See there. And what Maimonides wrote, that the community does not bring a voluntary offering, even though they bring voluntary burnt offerings when the altar is idle, and this is called "maintenance of the altar" — this is not so common, for most of the time the altar was not idle (Magen Avraham, subsection 5). Additionally, the verses about voluntary offerings are written concerning individuals, not the community. Nevertheless, an individual praying a voluntary prayer may pray it in a community (Elya Rabba).

And I have a question about this: If the second prayer is in place of a voluntary offering, then how do we pray a voluntary prayer during Mincha? After one has prayed the obligatory Mincha, it is like having offered the obligatory Mincha offering, which corresponds to the evening Tamid (continual offering). And after the evening Tamid, it is forbidden to offer another sacrifice, as it completes all the sacrifices (Pesachim 58b). It seems to me to resolve this: since the prohibition after the evening Tamid is only in relation to slaughtering and sprinkling, but burning (of the sacrifices) is permitted, as they burn all night, therefore, in correspondence to this, one may pray a voluntary prayer. And indeed, the evening prayer was instituted corresponding to the burning of limbs and fats, as it is taught at the beginning of the fourth chapter, see there.

Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, ruled in accordance with the Rambam, except in the case of doubt whether one has prayed, where he rules differently. This is his wording in Section 1: "If one is uncertain whether he has prayed, he must pray again and does not need to innovate anything new...". This is the end of his wording. According to the Rambam, however, one must pray as a voluntary prayer and introduce something new. The Rashba wrote that one must stipulate: if I have not prayed, this will be my obligatory prayer, and if I have prayed, this will be my voluntary prayer (Magen Avraham, Subsection 1, and Beit Yosef). I am puzzled: if so, one must introduce something new, for according to the Rambam, there is no voluntary prayer without innovation? And many of the poskim as I have written. It is possible that the Rashba holds like the Rif and the Raavad that do not require innovation, as I have written in Section 7. This requires further study. And know that there are those who say that for Ma’ariv, one does not need to pray if there is doubt whether one has prayed, since the Ma’ariv prayer is optional (Derech HaChaim). This does not seem to be the case according to all the poskim. On the contrary, the Rambam is more lenient with Ma’ariv, as I have written in Section 6.

And regarding the matter of introducing something new in one's prayer, we have already cited from the Rambam that, ideally, one should introduce something new in each blessing, and if not, it suffices in one blessing. Similarly, the Tur wrote this, but he mentioned that in the blessing of "Shome'a Tefillah" (Who hears prayer), introducing something new does not suffice because it is a general blessing, and one can ask for anything he wishes, so it does not appear as something new. See there. None of the other halachic authorities mentioned this. The Rosh, of blessed memory, questioned: What does it mean that one cannot introduce something new? Who is it that cannot introduce something new? Therefore, he explained that one must introduce a new request, whether in matters of livelihood or other concerns. And our master the Rema brought this in section 2, see there. And our master the Beit Yosef, in his great work, questioned this, for there are many who cannot introduce something new, as they are simple people. And it is even more astonishing, as it is explicitly clarified in Berachot (29b) that the interpretation of "cannot introduce something new" means that he is not capable of adding, see there (Magen Avraham, subsection 4).

It appears to me that the words of the Rosh are correct. For the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, in Section 4, wrote: "One who wishes to pray a voluntary prayer must recognize himself as being careful, diligent, and possessing a clear mind, so that he can concentrate in his prayer from beginning to end. But if he cannot concentrate well, it is said of him, 'Why do I need your numerous sacrifices?' And it would be fortunate if he could concentrate during the three fixed prayers of the day." This is their language, and it is from the response of the Rosh, see there. Therefore, such a person is obviously not a simple person but a learned scholar who is careful and diligent. And such a person can obviously innovate something, unlike the blessings there that pertain to the general Jewish populace—obviously, there are many unlearned people who do not know how to innovate anything. Nevertheless, from what has been clarified, one should distance himself in this time from praying a voluntary prayer, for we are not careful and diligent. And indeed, we have never seen anyone who does so.

In any case of doubt whether one has prayed or not, even nowadays, one must repeat the prayer. For according to most authorities, by the letter of the law, one must repeat the prayer, and not as a voluntary prayer, since one does not need to introduce something new in it, as ruled by Rabbeinu the Beit Yosef, as I wrote in section 10. And even though we wrote there that according to the Rashba one must make a condition, it appears that this is not the opinion of most authorities. And this is how one should rule. (And the Chayei Adam ruled in this case as well that one should not pray, but this does not seem correct.)

Maimonides wrote in Chapter Three, Law 8: Anyone who missed the time for prayer and did not pray intentionally has no remedy and does not compensate. But if it was accidental, or he was coerced or preoccupied, he compensates for that prayer in the time of the next adjacent prayer, and he first prays the prayer for its time and afterwards prays the compensatory prayer. How does this work? If he erred and did not pray the morning prayer, and half the day has passed, he should pray the afternoon prayer twice: the first is the afternoon prayer, and the second is the compensatory prayer for the morning. If he erred and did not pray the afternoon prayer until the sun set, he should pray the evening prayer twice: the first is the evening prayer, and the second is the compensatory prayer for the afternoon. If he erred and did not pray the evening prayer until dawn arose, he should pray the morning prayer twice: the first is the morning prayer, and the second is the compensatory prayer for the evening. If he erred and did not pray either this prayer or the adjacent one, he only compensates for the last one. How does this work? If he erred and did not pray either the morning or the afternoon prayer, he prays the evening prayer twice: the first is the evening prayer, and the second is the compensatory prayer for the afternoon. But the morning prayer has no compensatory prayer because its time has already passed. And so it is with other prayers. Thus far is his wording (and all this is at the beginning of Chapter Four).

Behold, regarding what is written that one who intentionally misses a prayer has no rectification, this is stated by the Rosh and the Rashba in the name of the Gaon, and this is his wording: One who intentionally misses a prayer — "A crooked thing that cannot be made straight." He has no rectification except for seeking mercy, which is merely voluntary. But he has no reward for a mitzvah. They wrote that from the words of the Gaon it is evident that if one wishes to pray twice in the next prayer, the first as the obligatory prayer and the second as compensation for the missed prayer — he is permitted, and he has the reward of a voluntary prayer seeking mercy, see there. This is also the ruling of the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch, Section 7. The difference between this case and one who made an error is that in the case of an error, compensation is obligatory, and he receives the reward for a mitzvah, whereas for intentional omission it is merely voluntary. Therefore, the Talmud there calls it "A crooked thing that cannot be made straight," meaning that the mitzvah is lost to him. They also wrote that there is no need to innovate anything in it. Although it is merely voluntary, it is still not comparable to a voluntary prayer which requires an innovation, as I wrote in the previous section. Since here one prays it in the adjacent prayer time, and in the case of an error, it would be proper to pray without innovation in such a scenario, therefore even in the case of intention, it is similar to an error in this particular detail (Beit Yosef and Taz, Subsection 5).

But their words are perplexing. For behold, the Rambam, the Tur, and the Shulchan Aruch ruled that compensatory prayers only work for the immediately subsequent prayer. And this is the language of the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, Section 4: "There is no compensation except for the immediately subsequent prayer. For if one erred and did not pray Shacharit and also not Minchah, he prays Maariv twice, the second as compensation for Minchah. But Shacharit has no compensation, and similarly with other prayers." This is their language. And even though the Ba'al HaMaor wrote that compensatory prayers are effective for two prayers, as the Tur wrote in his name, nevertheless, they decided the law is not according to him. However, in any case, there are those who disagree with this ruling. And on all of this, our teacher the Beit Yosef wrote in Section 5 that even though there is no compensation except for the immediately subsequent prayer, and other missed prayers have no compensation, nevertheless, if one wishes to pray it as a voluntary prayer and add something new in it – he is permitted to do so, and it is proper to do so. This is his language. And now, all the more so: if it is by mistake, and according to the Ba'al HaMaor compensatory prayers are effective, with all this he ruled that it requires something new – certainly, in the case of intentional omission, it requires something new. And this has already been challenged (by the Bach and the Gra, Section 8).

It appears to me that according to the view of Rabbeinu Beit Yosef, if we scrutinize, from where does the Gaon derive that one can pray a voluntary prayer intentionally, and some have questioned him on this (Bach, Siman 234). It seems that the Gaon deduced this from the language of the Talmud there, which states: "A crooked thing cannot be made straight" – this refers to one who missed the recitation of the morning Shema or the evening Shema, or prayer… see there. And he compares prayer to the recitation of the Shema, and regarding the Shema it is obvious that one can recite it as a voluntary reading, as it would be no worse than reading from the Torah. If so, the same applies here to prayer. And since it is explicitly stated in the Gemara that one can pray a voluntary prayer, it is therefore not comparable to a voluntary prayer that requires innovation. This is not the case with a prayer that is not adjacent [to its proper time] and is not mentioned at all in the Gemara according to his opinion, and is only considered a voluntary prayer, therefore it requires innovation.

And what is called "unavoidable circumstance"? It does not mean only a complete compulsion. Rather, even if one did not pray while there was still time to pray because he thought there would still be time left after the matter he was engaged in, and in the meantime the time passed. Similarly, someone who was preoccupied with his financial needs to prevent loss, and because of this missed praying, such as if he was with a master to claim what was due to him and was engaged in conversation until the time passed, thinking that the time had not yet passed, or if he was busy with his business placing goods in their place, thinking that he would have time to pray after he finished. And even more: even if he was idle and the time for prayer arrived, and he could have prayed but was lazy, saying "there is still time to pray," and then forgot that he needed to pray – this is also called "unavoidable circumstance" because forgetfulness is considered unavoidable (Magen Avraham, subsection 11). Likewise, if he sat to drink, thinking he would not get drunk, and then got drunk and the time passed – this is considered unavoidable. In summary: except for a deliberate transgression, it is considered either inadvertent or unavoidable or mistaken, and he compensates with the adjacent prayer as I have written.

And our master, the Rema, wrote in Section 8: However, ideally, one should not miss the time of prayer due to financial loss. These are his words. At first glance, it appears that his intention is that even in the case of a definite loss, one should not miss the time of prayer. However, it is impossible to say this, for even with a positive commandment from the Torah whose time can pass, such as an etrog on Sukkot, where one is obligated to spend money on it, nevertheless, one is not obligated to spend a large amount of money (Tosafot Bava Kama 9b), as will be explained in Section 656. And our master, the Beit Yosef, in his great book, was astonished at those who said that one must spend ten percent of their assets on this, see there. All the more so with prayer, that even according to the Rambam, from the Torah, it is only required once a day, as I wrote at the beginning of Section 89, one is not obligated to lose a significant amount of money for it. And especially since there is a possibility of making up the prayer in the next adjacent prayer. And although it is a pious practice, and one would be called "holy" for it, according to the basic law, it is impossible to say this.

Therefore, it appears to me clearly that his intention refers to the concern of potential monetary loss and not an actual, definite loss. This is also evident from the source of this ruling in Terumat HaDeshen (Siman 5), regarding someone who went to the officials to help him collect his debts and had to speak with them at length; see there. In this context, it is written that initially, one should not neglect [Torah study or prayer] and should not be concerned about monetary loss, because even with Torah, there is a distinct time for Torah study and a distinct time for prayer. And it is taught: "Consider the reward of a mitzvah against its loss..." Thus far his words. And this refers to the concern of potential monetary loss, not an actual, definite loss (so it appears according to my humble opinion).

It is known that in ancient times they would pray the evening prayer (Maariv) while it was still broad daylight. There is an incident of someone who had not yet prayed the afternoon prayer (Mincha), and he came to the synagogue close to the time for Maariv, and he led the prayer service and prayed Maariv. At first glance, it appears as if he intentionally did not pray Mincha. Nonetheless, this is not so, for the day had not yet passed and it was still the time for Mincha. Even though, as soon as he made it night, he could no longer pray Mincha, as I wrote in Siman 30, that one should not put on tefillin after Maariv even though it is still daytime, because he has already made it night and it would be a contradiction – it is not comparable. For tefillin are not worn at night at all, and it would indeed be a contradiction. But the Mincha prayer can be made up at night, and therefore it is not a contradiction. Hence, it is not similar to someone who intentionally skips a prayer (as explained in Magen Avraham, subsection 10, and this is his intention). It is obvious that if he thought it was permissible to pray Maariv before Mincha, he is certainly considered inadvertent, and therefore he should pray again to make up for Mincha. And if he said "Ya'aleh V'yavo" in Maariv because the next day is Rosh Chodesh – he should also say it in the second prayer to make up (as mentioned there), even though he prays it while it is still day, as he has already made it night.

And this that it is written that one prays the first prayer as an obligation and the second as a make-up, our master the Beit Yosef wrote in Section 1 that if one reversed them – he has not fulfilled the obligation of the make-up prayer, and he needs to go back and pray it again. And the same law applies wherever one needs to pray a make-up prayer. So far his words. And there are those who say the reason is because the obligation is regular and takes precedence over the make-up which is not regular (Levush). And it is impossible to say this, as regularity is not a requirement (Ma'adanei Yom Tov) as is proven in Menachot (49a). And there are those who say they established this rule to prevent one from initially coming to pray out of its proper time. Therefore, they made this a requirement to pray the obligatory prayer first, and consequently, one will not come to this negligence (ibid.). And this also is not understandable, for where is this decree found? And further: this explanation is satisfactory in the case of intentional negligence, but if one did this inadvertently, this decree does not apply. And our master the Beit Yosef did not make this distinction (and so wrote the Pri Megadim). Rather, it is certain that the make-up prayer does not precede the obligatory prayer. And it appears to me the reason is: since prayer is like standing before the king, it is indeed necessary to fulfill one's current obligation immediately, and if not, it is as if he rebels against the kingdom. And afterward, he may request for not having stood before Him blessed be He earlier. And how can he ask forgiveness for the past while rebelling now as he stands before Him? (And see the Eliyah Rabbah who also gave a reason. And what appears in my humble opinion I have written).

Our teacher, the Rema, wrote in his book Darkei Moshe that one only fulfills the obligation if he intended the first prayer as a makeup and the second prayer for his obligation. If not, he has not fulfilled his obligation and must pray the makeup prayer afterward. There is an opinion that intention in the heart is not sufficient unless there is a verbal declaration. For example, if he prayed the first prayer without "Ashrei" and the second prayer with "Ashrei," it is evident that the second is for Mincha. Or it could be that we require a verbal declaration in the prayer itself, as will be explained regarding Havdalah on Motzei Shabbat (Magen Avraham, subsection 2). 

In my opinion, the primary halacha follows our teacher, the Rema. Otherwise, this law would only apply in rare cases, such as on Motzei Shabbat and similar situations, which is not the impression given by the poskim. Indeed, according to the reason we have explained, that it is as if one is standing before the king, this makes sense, for the Holy One, blessed be He, knows thoughts, and automatically, if one does not intend for his obligation, it is as if he is rebelling against the kingdom according to the reasoning we have written. 

(And what the Magen Avraham wrote as a proof from Terumat HaDeshen, that if one recited Havdalah in both prayers he has fulfilled his obligation even if he intended otherwise, is not a proof at all. There, it is clear that he intended the first prayer for the obligation since he recited Havdalah in it, and the mistake was in the second prayer where he also intended it for the obligation, as is evident from his language. If not, why did Terumat HaDeshen not write this law regarding two identical weekday prayers? Examine it well and you will find it clear.)

When one did not pray Mincha and prays Ma'ariv twice, he should pray Ma'ariv as usual: the recitation of the Shema and its blessings, followed by the Shemoneh Esrei. Afterward, he should wait the time it takes to walk four cubits and then pray the makeup prayer for Mincha. Our teacher, the Rema, wrote in section 2 that one should say "Ashrei" before the second [prayer]. However, there are those who caution against saying "Ashrei" at Ma'ariv, and even after Mincha, the Kabbalistic sages are not pleased with saying "Ashrei," as is explained in the Zohar. On Yom Kippur, when "Ashrei" is recited at "Ne'ilah," it is because Yom Kippur is a time of favor throughout the entire day (Magen Avraham, section 5). Therefore, one should recite a different psalm. This does not hinder [the prayer] at all, as I have written that only after waiting the time it takes to walk four cubits can one pray. It is obvious that if one first prayed the Shemoneh Esrei, and afterward prayed the Shema and its blessings and then the Shemoneh Esrei again, he has revealed his intention to prioritize the makeup prayer over the obligatory prayer, and he must pray another [prayer] as the makeup. It seems to me that he is not believed when he claims that he intended the first [prayer] as obligatory, because if so, why did he recite the Shema and its blessings for the second [prayer]?

If one did not pray Maariv and prays Shacharit twice, it is obvious that after the first Amidah and after Tachanun, he should pray the second one as a compensation. If he wishes, he can pray it after "Ashrei" and "Uva L'Tzion". If one prays the Amidah before the prayer service, and then prays the entire order of the prayer service including the Amidah, he has revealed his intention that he prayed the compensatory prayer first, and he must pray again, as I have written. If one did not pray Shacharit and prays Mincha twice, he should say "Ashrei" before the first Amidah, and afterwards say Tachanun or another psalm, or wait the time it takes to walk four cubits. It is better to say some psalm in order to begin the prayer from words of Torah. It seems to me that if in Mincha one prays the first Amidah without "Ashrei" and the second Amidah with "Ashrei", there is no necessity to say that he intended the first Amidah as compensatory. If he says that he intended it as the obligatory prayer, he is believed, because from "Ashrei" there is not such a strong indication. This is not similar to what I wrote earlier.

And it has already been explained that there is no make-up prayer except for the adjacent prayer. And our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 3: The fact that one makes up the prayer that was missed is specifically during the time of prayer. But at a time when it is not the time of prayer – no. Thus are his words. And I do not know when "it is not the time of prayer," for until midday one can pray Shacharit, and from midday until night it is the time for Mincha, and all night is the time for Maariv. And it is strained to say that his intention is for the half-hour from midday when one cannot yet pray Mincha. And indeed, the source of this law is from the Rashba, as he wrote in his great book. And he holds according to the opinion of the Bahag, that even for many prayers, make-up is effective. And therefore, he says that these prayers should be prayed during the time of prayer, meaning that one should pray the obligatory prayer first and then make them up, see there. And as is evident from his words that he wrote: And indeed, specifically during the time of prayer, since it is the time of prayer and he is engaged in his prayer – he returns and makes up what he missed in his prayers. For if not so, what is "pray twice" that he said? Let him say: He missed and did not pray Shacharit before midday – he returns and prays after midday. He missed and did not pray Mincha – he prays all night... thus are his words. And if so, our master, the Beit Yosef, who has already ruled that one must pray the obligatory prayer first – all this law is but redundant. And it requires investigation.

And it appears that if one remembers after their obligatory prayer that they forgot the previous prayer, they can pray a second prayer as a make-up. According to this, there is a doubt when one prays Shacharit (the morning prayer) and after a third of the day remembers that they did not pray Maariv (the evening prayer), if they can make it up, for it is not the time for Shacharit? And if we say so, we can easily explain the words of Rabbeinu the Beit Yosef, that this is his intention when he wrote "specifically during the time of prayer...", meaning: it is not effective to make up Maariv only until a third of the day. But this does not seem to be the case according to all the poskim (decisors of Jewish law). And it clearly appears that for this matter, the time for Shacharit is considered until midday. And practically, this law needs further examination. And I have seen that for the great ones it is clear that after a third of the day there is no make-up for Maariv (Pri Megadim and Derech HaChaim). And there is someone who wants to say that the make-up for Mincha (the afternoon prayer) is also only until midnight. All these things are perplexing in my eyes, for it has already been clarified at the beginning of Siman 89 that even though we hold according to Rabbi Yehuda that the time for prayer is until four hours, nevertheless, since according to the Rabbis it is ideally until midday, therefore even according to Rabbi Yehuda, if one did not pray intentionally until four hours, they may still pray until midday. And we have explained this there in paragraph 13, see there. And if so, for a make-up prayer it is effective until midday. And all the more so for Maariv, whose main time is all night, but in order to distance from transgression it is ideally until midnight, as it is taught at the beginning of Berachot and will be explained in Siman 235. And all the more so for a make-up. (And the words of the Gaon Rabbi Zalman in his Shulchan Aruch, paragraph 7, are even more perplexing, where he takes the words of the Beit Yosef that if one did not pray immediately after the obligatory prayer, they are forbidden to pray the make-up, see there. And where did he get this from? For the source of the law is from the Rashba, and he wrote this regarding praying the obligatory prayer first as I have written. And the Atarat Zekeinim holds that his intention is regarding the half-hour after midnight, see there. This too is perplexing as I have written. And in my humble opinion, it seems clear in law as I have written. Be precise and you will find clarity.)

There is no make-up prayer for the Musaf prayer if the day has passed and it was not prayed. How can one recite the offerings when the time for Musaf has already passed? And once its time has passed, its offering is nullified. However, other prayers are supplications for mercy (Magen Avraham, subsection 9). And even though when one prays at night as a make-up, it will be a weekday prayer as will be explained, and one will not mention the offerings at all, nonetheless, it does not relate to a make-up for an offering whose time has already passed (Taz, subsection 4). And it seems that even the Musaf of Rosh Hashanah, which contains many supplications, such as the Kingship, Remembrances, and Shofar sections—nonetheless, it cannot be made up, for the main aspect of Musaf is for the offerings. Moreover, the main parts of these prayers are relevant only to Rosh Hashanah, and they are similar to the Musaf offering, which, once its time has passed, its offering is nullified.

The prayer leader can fulfill the obligation of a missed prayer with the repetition of the prayer leader. For example, if one did not pray Maariv and in the morning prays in a whisper and aloud, he fulfills the obligation of the missed prayer. Not only that, but even if someone is obligated to make up a prayer and hears it from the prayer leader from beginning to end, he fulfills his obligation. Even though the prayer leader intends it for Shacharit and he intends it for the make-up prayer, it is still acceptable (see Magen Avraham, section 1, and in Shaarei Teshuvah, section 1, in the name of Birkei Yosef).

And know that just as there is no make-up for the Musaf prayer, similarly, the Musaf prayer cannot serve as a make-up prayer. And if someone forgot to pray Shacharit and prayed Musaf, he should pray Shacharit after Musaf if it is still before midday. And if someone did not pray Shacharit and Musaf and remembers after midday, he should pray Mincha and then Musaf, since both are obligations of the time, and then pray Shacharit as a make-up. If he prayed Musaf before Mincha, he fulfills his obligation (ibid.). But if he prayed Shacharit before Mincha, he does not fulfill his obligation because he performed the make-up before the obligatory prayer. However, if he prayed Shacharit before Musaf, it seems to me that he fulfills his obligation even though Musaf is an obligatory prayer, because it is not related at all to Shacharit.

Sometimes, the compensatory prayer is different from the prayer for which it is compensating, and it is effective. How so? Our Sages of blessed memory said (at the beginning of the fourth chapter): If one made a mistake and did not pray the Mincha prayer on Friday afternoon, he should pray twice on Shabbat, with both prayers being Shabbat prayers. The first is for the obligatory prayer, and the second is for the compensatory prayer. The reason is that this is the fundamental principle of the law: for missing this prayer, one is obligated to pray two prayers during the next appropriate time. Therefore, since the sanctity of Shabbat has arrived, one must mention Shabbat in all his prayers. However, it is possible that if he did not mention Shabbat in the second prayer, he has still fulfilled his obligation, since ultimately it is compensatory for a weekday prayer (Magen Avraham, Subsection 12). But there are those who disagree (Taz), and the primary opinion follows the first view (Eliyah Rabbah and Knesset HaGedolah).

And similarly, if one did not pray Mincha on the eve of Rosh Chodesh, he should pray Maariv twice and mention "Ya'aleh Veyavo" in both. If he did not mention it in either, he has fulfilled his obligation, since in the Maariv of Rosh Chodesh one does not need to repeat the prayer if "Ya'aleh Veyavo" was forgotten. This is also the case if he mentioned it in the first prayer but not in the second. However, if he mentioned it in the second and not in the first, he must repeat the prayer, because in this case, it shows that he prayed the first as a make-up and prioritized the obligatory prayer, and he has not fulfilled his obligation. There is a question regarding someone who did not pray Maariv on Rosh Chodesh and prayed Shacharit twice but did not mention "Ya'aleh Veyavo" in the second. Do we say that since at Maariv if one did not say "Ya'aleh Veyavo" he is not required to repeat the prayer, the same rule applies here? Or perhaps, since the reason for not repeating the prayer at Maariv is because the new month is not sanctified at night, and now it is daytime and he is required to repeat the prayer. The primary ruling is the latter (Magen Avraham). However, there are those who disagree with these rulings and hold that Shabbat is not comparable to Rosh Chodesh (Levush). There are also those who disagree and hold that if one did not pray Maariv on Rosh Chodesh and prayed Shacharit twice and did not mention "Ya'aleh Veyavo" in the second, he is not required to repeat the prayer (Knesset Hagedolah). Nevertheless, the primary ruling is as I have written.

If one made a mistake and did not pray the Mincha (afternoon) prayer on Shabbat, he should pray the weekday Amidah twice on Saturday night. He should include Havdalah in the first Amidah but not in the second. This is not similar to Shabbat and Rosh Chodesh when one is obligated to mention them in all the prayers of the day, unlike Havdalah in "Ata Chonen" which is only mentioned once. Therefore, in the second Amidah, which is for compensation, why should he mention it? However, if he mentioned Havdalah in both Amidot or did not mention it in either, he has fulfilled his obligation. But if he did not include Havdalah in the first and included it in the second, the second Amidah counts for his obligation, and the first does not count. Since he did not include Havdalah in the first but did in the second, it reveals his intention to prioritize the compensation prayer over the obligatory one, which is not valid. However, if he explicitly states that his intention in the first Amidah was for the obligation but he mistakenly did not include Havdalah, he is believed and does not need to pray again. (This is how it appears to me. Refer to Magen Avraham, subsection 14, and Taz, subsection 10. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

And since one needs to pray the compensatory prayer in the same manner as the obligatory prayer, even though it is not in the same format as the prayer he is obliged to make up, one might question the reverse: in a case where he gains nothing from the compensatory prayer. For example, if he did not say "Ya'aleh V'yavo" on Rosh Chodesh during Mincha, and needs to pray Ma'ariv twice without "Ya'aleh V'yavo," what benefit does he gain, since he already prayed without "Ya'aleh V'yavo"? Or, for example, if he made a mistake during Mincha on Shabbat and prayed the weekday eighteen blessings, the law is that he needs to repeat the Shabbat prayer, and he remembered on Motzei Shabbat and needs to pray twice of weekday. What does he gain, since he already prayed this prayer? Therefore, some of our Rabbis hold that in such a case he does not need to repeat the prayer (Tosafot in the name of R"Y at the beginning of the fourth chapter). However, some of our Rabbis ruled that he needs to repeat the prayer, because what he prayed is considered as if he did not pray at all since he did not pray correctly, and if he prays now, it is considered correct (ibid.). And thus ruled the major poskim, the Tur, and the Shulchan Aruch, section 11, see there. It is clear that if he gains from his prayer, such as if it is still Rosh Chodesh at night, or if he made a mistake during Mincha on the first day of Yom Tov, or forgot "Tal Umatar" or "Mashiv Haruach," even according to the first opinion, he should repeat the prayer. And know that even though the law follows the latter opinion, they still ruled that he should intend the prayer as a voluntary offering. There is no loss in this to fulfill the first opinion, but he does not need to innovate anything in it, since the main law follows the latter opinion.

Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 12: One who makes a mistake and mentions the event of other days in prayer out of its proper time – it is not considered an interruption. Thus are his words. And our teacher, the Rema, wrote: However, if he realizes that he made a mistake – he stops even in the middle of the blessing. Thus are his words. Meaning: for example, if he made a mistake and prayed a weekday prayer on Shabbat or Yom Tov – he stops in the middle of the blessing. 

Many of the great authorities disagreed with this ruling of our teacher, the Beit Yosef, as he learned this from what we say: if one made Havdalah in both [the Amidah and over a cup] – he has fulfilled his obligation. Even though he should not have mentioned Havdalah in the second [instance], nevertheless, he has fulfilled his obligation – we see from here that it is not considered an interruption. But this is not similar: there, it is the time for Havdalah, unlike mentioning something that is not relevant to that day – it is certainly considered an interruption, similar to idle conversation, and he must repeat his prayer (Taz, Pri Chadash, the Gra, and Knesset Hagedolah). 

Furthermore, it is worse than idle conversation, which is merely an interruption, whereas here he makes this day like another day. (In this, you will understand the words of the Gra. Be precise and you will find it easy.) It is good for him to repeat the prayer as a voluntary offering. He does not need to add anything new to it (according to the Gra”z), as I wrote in the previous section.

The Tur wrote: One who enters a synagogue and finds the congregation praying, if he can start and finish before the prayer leader reaches the Kedushah, he should pray. If not, he should not pray, because he needs to recite the Kedushah with the congregation. If he enters after the Kedushah, if he can start and finish before the prayer leader reaches Modim, he should pray. If not, he should not pray, because he needs to bow with the congregation at Modim, so that it does not appear as if he is denying the one to whom the congregation is bowing. This is the end of his words, and it is also stated in the Shulchan Aruch, Section 1. These are two sayings in Berachot (21b), one regarding Kedushah and one regarding Modim. And in the Gemara, even regarding Modim it says: one who enters a synagogue and finds the congregation praying, see there. The Tur changed the language regarding Modim to say when he enters after the Kedushah. The commentators struggled greatly with his intention, and wrote that this is not necessarily precise (see Beit Yosef and Perisha).

In my humble opinion, it seems that the Tur was compelled to this. For ostensibly, this saying of "Modim" is puzzling: for in the case of Kedusha, it is forbidden for him to pray so that he does not miss the Kedusha, since an individual is not permitted to recite Kedusha. And although he can remain silent and listen as I wrote in Siman 104, nevertheless, this is not the same as saying it. Furthermore, not everyone agrees with this permission as I wrote there. But regarding "Modim," what difference does it make? If he prays, he can bow along with the congregation at the place where he is in prayer, as indeed Rabbeinu Tam used to do this as explained in the Tosafot there. And if it is because of "Modim deRabbanan" – we do not find a basis for this that he should not pray because of it, as the Tosafot there wrote that we do not find a basis in the Gemara for "Modim deRabbanan," see there.

Indeed, the explanation of the matter is as follows: One who enters a synagogue and finds the congregation praying regarding Kedusha, even if the congregation is praying silently, and it is a great mitzvah to pray with the congregation, nevertheless, if he cannot finish before Kedusha – he is obligated to wait and respond to Kedusha, even though afterwards he will pray alone. But for "Modim" – Heaven forbid to forgo praying with the congregation for this reason, for praying with the congregation is preferable to "Modim". However, regarding "Modim", the explanation is that the congregation is praying, meaning they are engaged in prayer, but he comes to the synagogue after Kedusha. Therefore, since now he will also pray alone – it is better for him to wait until after "Modim". And what will he lose by this? For indeed its time does not pass, for if the time were to pass also for Kedusha – he would not need to wait. And this is what the Tur precisely said regarding "Modim" that it comes after Kedusha.

And know that the Rambam at the end of the tenth chapter only wrote the law regarding Kedusha (the sanctification), and did not mention the law of "Modim" (the thanksgiving prayer) at all, see there. And it seems that he holds that these two sayings are in disagreement with each other, and the one who says Kedusha does not agree with "Modim", and he ruled accordingly (and so wrote the Lechem Mishneh). And it appears to me that this is the reasoning of the Mahari"l who used to begin even if he did not finish before "Modim", as our teacher the Rema wrote in his book Darkei Moshe, see there. And he struggled to explain that perhaps the time was passing, see there. And who would not see the difficulty in this explanation? And it is known that the ancients used to pray in the morning. But it is clear to me that he adhered to the opinion of the Rambam as the primary one, and I am astonished at the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch for not bringing the opinion of the Rambam at all. And behold, the great later authorities accepted the law of "Modim" as the same as Kedusha. And in my humble opinion, it is clear that this is not so even according to the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch, and certainly according to the Rambam. And it seems to me that Rabbeinu Tam also holds like the Rambam, for the Tosafot wrote there in this language: And Rabbeinu Tam was accustomed when he prayed alone, when the chazan (cantor) reached "Modim" he would bow with the congregation without saying anything at all. Thus far their language. And it is difficult: how did he begin to pray before "Modim"? Rather, it is certain that he holds like the Rambam that the law is not according to the saying of "Modim". And it seems to me that this is also the current custom.

According to what has been explained, that Kedusha (the sanctification prayer) overrides praying with a congregation, if so, those individuals who extend their Shemoneh Esrei (the Amidah prayer) in a manner that even if they start with the congregation, they will not finish before Kedusha—how can they justify their actions? For this is against the Gemara, and they should wait until after Kedusha. Moreover, we have never heard or seen anyone who does this, and many great individuals extend their prayers until after Kedusha. Perhaps this is why the custom in most Jewish communities is to wait for the rabbi during the repetition of the Shaliach Tzibbur (the prayer leader), so that they do not stumble in this matter. However, this is not sufficient. It appears to me that our sages only said this regarding a person who does not usually extend their prayer, but who arrives after the congregation has already begun praying. Such a person should wait until after Kedusha and pray individually. But one who habitually extends their prayer and always prays with the congregation—it is not reasonable to say that they should always be deprived of communal prayer. Rather, they should pray with the congregation, and if the congregation responds with Kedusha, they should remain silent, as explained in Siman 104.

In the Gemara there, it is explained that "Amen, Yehei Shmei Rabba" is greater than Kedusha, see there. And since it is clarified that one should not begin praying if he will not finish before Kedusha, all the more so he should not stand to pray if he will not finish before Kaddish, meaning before "Amen, Yehei Shmei Rabba." And this is what our master the Beit Yosef wrote in section 1: before the chazzan reaches Kedusha or Kaddish, see there. And there are those who wrote that this applies only to Ma'ariv (Magen Avraham, section 1). His intention was regarding the ruling in the Shulchan Aruch: one who enters the synagogue and finds the congregation praying, meaning praying the Amidah — it follows that in Shacharit and Mincha he should not begin to pray because of the Kedusha which precedes the Kaddish. And it is only in Ma'ariv that it is conceivable when he comes to the synagogue and the congregation is standing in the Amidah — he should not start praying with them if he will not finish before "Amen, Yehei Shmei Rabba." But in the primary ruling, it also applies to Shacharit and Mincha, when he arrives during the chazzan's repetition after "Modim" — he should not pray the Amidah if he will not finish before the Kaddish after Tachanun. However, it is possible that we are not concerned with this Kaddish, since there is another full Kaddish after "Uva LeTzion." But in Ma'ariv, even though there is another Mourner's Kaddish after "Aleinu," it is not as essential as the Kaddish after the prayer. According to this, also in Mincha, he should not pray if he will not finish before the full Kaddish after the prayer.

And I have seen someone who wrote that for Kaddish one must wait because it has no fixed time, and only the Kaddishim from "Aleinu" and onwards are not included in this (Magen Avraham, section 3). According to this, many new laws arise for us: one should not stand to pray at the time of saying "Uva L'Tzion" even though he heard the half-Kaddish after Tachanun. Similarly, on Rosh Chodesh when Hallel is recited, one should not stand to pray unless he finishes before the Kaddish after Hallel, even though he will hear more Kaddishim. And so on and so forth. However, it seems that the custom is not like this. On the contrary, it appears to my humble opinion that if there is only one Kaddish from the prayer that he will hear more – it is sufficient. According to reasoning, since it has no fixed time – one is enough. And "Barchu" is also like Kedusha, and if he has already heard "Barchu" or Kedusha, or knows he will hear it later – he does not need to wait (there). According to our words, Kaddish is also the same. And it is clear that during the Torah reading one should not stand to pray, as he needs to hear the Torah reading. And there are several "Barchus" and "Amens", and the Kaddish after the Torah reading. And it seems clear that even before the reading he should not stand to pray unless he finishes before the reading. And even if he is in Pesukei D'Zimra or the blessings of Shema – he should wait and hear the Torah reading, and respond "Barchu" and "Amen, yehei shmei rabbah", but not the "Amens".

One who comes to the synagogue for Mincha after the Kedusha, and if he prays he will not say "Modim" and "Amen, Yehei Shmei Rabbah" – he should wait until after the complete Kaddish. However, if the time will pass, or he will not be able to pray Ma'ariv with the congregation, there is an opinion that the communal prayer is more important and he should pray immediately (there, subparagraph 2). And there is an opinion that disagrees, and holds that Kaddish is more important than communal prayer (Eliyah Rabbah, subparagraph 7). And this is the main opinion, for regarding Kedusha it is clarified that it is more important than communal prayer, and all the more so "Amen, Yehei Shmei Rabbah," which is greater than Kedusha as I have written. And even though he will hear Kaddish in Ma'ariv, nevertheless in Mincha he will not hear it. And even according to what we have explained that one Kaddish is sufficient, nevertheless, for each prayer, one Kaddish is necessary. And it is obvious that "Amen, Yehei Shmei Rabbah" is much preferable to "Modim." Therefore, if when he prays immediately he will not say "Modim" but will finish by Kaddish, and if he waits until after Kaddish the prayer time will pass – then he should not pray Ma'ariv with the congregation and should pray immediately (there). And also when he comes close to Kedusha – he should wait until after Kedusha and then pray immediately. And wait until after "Amen" of the "El Hakadosh" as will be explained (and Kaddish is preferable to Kedusha).

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote that the "Amen" after "HaEl HaKadosh" and "Shomea Tefillah" has the same status as Kaddish and Kedusha. These are his words. This is derived from the Jerusalem Talmud. However, Rabbi Yosef Karo (the Beit Yosef) did not concern himself with this because it is not mentioned in our Talmud. Additionally, neither the Rambam nor the Tur brought it up, and even the Tosafot and the Rosh mentioned this in a different context, see there. There is no proof that they ruled accordingly, and they only wrote that one should be careful with these "Amens," see there. 

Regarding the "Amen" after "HaEl HaKadosh," there is no practical difference in the law, and thus, when waiting for Kedusha, one should wait a few more moments until after the blessing. Likewise, regarding the "Amen" after "Shomea Tefillah," it seems to me that there is no practical difference, since it is adjacent to "Modim." Even though from his language it appears to be of the same status as Kaddish and Kedusha, which are more important than "Modim," nevertheless, it seems to me that this is not necessarily what he meant. It is only because the author (the Shulchan Aruch) was discussing Kaddish and Kedusha that he wrote this, especially since many completely disagree with this (as implied by the Levush).

In truth, every "Amen" is a mitzvah to respond.
