If the time is not passing (i.e., there is no risk of missing the proper time for prayer), it is good to wait until after the repetition by the Shaliach Tzibbur and to respond "Amen" to each blessing (see Taz in the name of the Rema MiPano). One who arrives when the congregation is answering "Amen, Yehei Shmei Rabbah" should respond with them, even if he was not there from the beginning, and similarly with Kedusha (ibid). Some say that he should start from "Yehei Shmei Rabbah" and not say "Amen, Yehei..." And when interrupting to say "Amen, Yehei Shmei Rabbah," he should not start from "Amen" because "Amen" refers to the previous statement (Magen Avraham, subsection 2). 

I am puzzled: even though "Amen" refers to the previous statement, as I wrote in Siman 56, nevertheless, it also applies to the future, as we find with the kings and in Jeremiah: "Amen. Thus says the Lord." If so, why should one not start with "Amen"? This is indeed the common custom.

In "Modim" one may initially pray if he arrives only at "Modim" or one of the blessings where one bows, since bowing with the congregation no longer appears as if he is a denier. It has already been explained in Siman 66 that between redemption and prayer it is forbidden to interrupt even for Kaddish or Kedusha, and therefore he should wait at "Shira Chadasha" as I wrote there. However, if out of habit he said up to "Ga'al Yisrael" and is therefore required to begin the prayer, what should he do when the Shaliach Tzibur reaches Kedusha? Should he remain silent? And similarly for Kaddish, as I wrote in Siman 104. And when the Shaliach Tzibur reaches "Modim" and he is in the middle of a blessing, he should bow with them. But if he is at the end or beginning of a blessing, he should not bow, as one does not bow at the beginning or end of a blessing except where the sages instituted it, which is in Avot and "Modim". And even though he is bowing only to avoid appearing as a denier, and indeed there are those who disagree with this (see Beit Yosef), the intention is that this can easily be done by starting the blessing and stopping in the middle, as this can be done in a moment (so it seems to me).

Maimonides wrote at the end of chapter ten: "One who enters a synagogue and finds the congregation praying silently, if he can begin and finish before the chazzan (prayer leader) reaches Kedusha, he should pray. If not, he should wait until the chazzan begins to pray aloud, and then pray silently word for word with the chazzan until the chazzan reaches Kedusha. He should answer Kedusha with the congregation and then continue the rest of the prayer on his own." This is his wording. And he says with the chazzan "Nakdish" or "Nakdishach", "U'le'umatam Baruch Yomru", "Uvdivrei Kodshecha Katuv Leymor", and "L'dor Vador Nagid Godlecha..." (Magen Avraham, subsection 7). Regarding praying on one's own after Kedusha – this applies when he can finish before the chazzan reaches "Shomea Tefillah" (ibid). If not, he should pray with the chazzan word for word until the end of the prayer, as this is also like answering "Amen" because he finishes the blessing with the chazzan. When the chazzan reaches "Modim", he should bow with him, and similarly at the end of the blessing. If he wishes, he can aim to finish the blessing at the same time the chazzan reaches "Modim". If he prays in tandem with the chazzan until the end, there is uncertainty if he should say with the chazzan "Barechenu Bivracha Hamshuleshet". Even though on a fast day the poskim (decisors of Jewish law) wrote that one should not say the "Aneinu" blessing with the chazzan between "Goel" and "Rofeh" but rather in "Shomea Tefillah" as an individual (according to the Mahari"l and the Mateh Moshe), this is because it is a blessing with God's name and was not established for individuals. But "Barechenu" is merely a request. In my humble opinion, one may say it with the chazzan.

And know that this ruling of the Rambam was also written by the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch in Section 2, but they wrote it in different language. See there. And our Rabbi, the Rema, wrote on this, and this is his language: "But ideally, one should not begin until after he has said Kedusha and 'the Holy God'." However, if he needs to start because the time is passing, or to connect redemption to prayer, this is the law. Up to here is his language. And these words are puzzling, for the Rambam wrote to do so ideally, and so did the SeMaG. And there are those who strained to interpret the language of the Tur to mean this (Prisha), but it is not so. And how could he not mention the words of the Rambam? Moreover, why should he not do so, since he says the Kedusha with the chazzan (and I found that the Eliyah Rabbah questioned this)? And it is clear to me that some error has occurred here. For in the Shulchan Aruch printed with the Eliyah Rabbah, this gloss is written in Section 1, and since it does not belong there, it was written that it belongs to Section 2 (and so did the Be'er Hetev write). And it seems clear to me that it refers to Section 3, on what the author wrote that when standing in prayer and the congregation says "Keter," one should be silent and not respond with them. On this, it was written that ideally, one should not begin until after Kedusha. (And this fits well with the words of the Magen Avraham in Subsection 9, who wrote that one should be silent and listen, see there. And it is surprising: does he not say with the chazzan? But regarding Section 3, it fits well. And see Pri Megadim, and his words are puzzling and strained. Be precise and you will find clarity.)

An individual who is standing in prayer, and when he reaches the place of Kedusha (the sanctification), the congregation is reciting the Kedusha of "Uva Letzion" or of "Yotzer Or" — he should not recite it with them, for the Kedushot are not the same. And Rabbi Yosef Karo wrote that it appears that the same law applies if he is standing in Shacharit (the morning prayer), and the congregation is reciting the Kedusha of "Keter" during Mussaf (the additional prayer) — he should not recite Kedusha with them, but rather should remain silent and have intent for what they are saying, as hearing is like responding. However, he should not begin this initially, as I wrote in the previous section. Nevertheless, Rabbeinu the Rema wrote that the individual can answer with them, as both are the Kedusha of the Amidah and their sanctity is equal. And this appears to me to be the primary ruling. This is the end of his words. And this is the common custom.

The Sages taught in a Mishnah (Berakhot 28b): Rabban Gamliel says: Every day a person should pray the Shemoneh Esrei (Eighteen Blessings). Rabbi Yehoshua says: A prayer in the style of Shemoneh Esrei. Rabbi Akiva says: If his prayer is fluent in his mouth, he should pray the Shemoneh Esrei; if not, a prayer in the style of Shemoneh Esrei. The halacha follows Rabbi Akiva (Rambam and Ra'avad in their commentary on the Mishnah). The Gemara explains: What is "a prayer in the style of Shemoneh Esrei"? This is the "Havineinu" prayer, in which one says the first three blessings and the last three blessings, and the middle blessings are included in one blessing in the following formula: "Grant us understanding, Hashem our God, to know Your ways, and circumcise our hearts to fear You, and forgive us so that we may be redeemed, and distance us from our pains, and make our land fertile, and gather our scattered from the four corners, and those who err in judgment shall be judged, and against the wicked raise Your hand, and may the righteous rejoice in the rebuilding of Your city and in the repair of Your sanctuary, and in the flourishing of the horn of David Your servant, and in the setting up of a light for the son of Yishai, Your anointed. Before we call, You will answer. Blessed are You, Hashem, Who hears prayer." See there. For in this, all the middle blessings are included, as explained by Rashi and Tosafot Yeshanim; see there.

In the Gemara there, it states: Abaye cursed anyone who prays "Havinenu." The SeMaG and the Hagahot Maimoniot (Chapter Two) wrote that this applies to someone who regularly does so without any pressing need. Thus are their words. And the Rif wrote: The Rabbis said: This only applies in a time of pressing need, but if it is not a time of pressing need, one should not pray "Havinenu." Thus are his words. And this is the language of the Rambam at the beginning of Chapter Two: In every daily prayer, a person should pray these nineteen blessings in order. In what case does this apply? When one’s mind is focused and one’s tongue can quickly articulate. But if one is preoccupied and pressured, or if one’s tongue is unable to pray quickly, one should pray the first three blessings, one blessing that encompasses all the middle blessings, and the last three blessings, and thereby fulfill one’s obligation. And this is the blessing they instituted...: "Havinenu..." Thus are his words. According to his words, what Rabbi Akiva said: If it is fluent... and if not, one should pray something similar to the Eighteen, this is interpreted either as not being fluent due to the inability of the tongue or due to preoccupation and pressure.

The Tur wrote: "And these words apply in a time of pressing need, such as when he is on the road or similar situations. And when he comes to his house, he does not need to pray again. But when it is not a time of pressing need, one should not say it." Thus are his words. And he did not mention that his speech was shortened from praying, even though the main explanation of the Mishnah is so, it appears to me because nowadays, when the text is available in all prayer books, it is not relevant to say that his speech was shortened from praying. It was only in the time of the Talmud when they would pray by heart that it was relevant to say that it was not fluent in his mouth, but not in this time when they pray from prayer books. And also, Rabbeinu the Beit Yosef did not mention this; see there. Rather, he wrote it in different language, and these are his words in section 1: "In a time of pressing need, such as when he is on the road or standing in a place where he is preoccupied, and he fears that he will be interrupted or that he will not be able to pray a long prayer with concentration – he prays... and he needs to say it standing... thus are his words." And what he wrote "and he fears that he will be interrupted" refers to "on the road," meaning that travelers will interrupt him. And what he wrote "or that he will not be able to pray with concentration" refers to "standing in a place where he is preoccupied."

And this which is written that one needs to say it while standing, meaning: even though it has been explained in Siman 94 that one who is walking is permitted to pray while walking, that is when one wants to pray the Amidah properly, which is lengthy, and if one stands, they will be confused. Therefore, they permitted him to pray while walking. But if he wants to pray "Havineinu," which is short, he is obligated to pray specifically while standing. And know that our Sages of blessed memory said there that one does not pray "Havineinu" on the conclusion of Shabbat and holidays because one needs to say Havdalah in "You graciously grant knowledge." Similarly, not during the rainy season because one needs to say "dew and rain." And even though these can also be included in "Havineinu" as is obvious, nonetheless, we are concerned that he might get confused (Gemara). Meaning: since it is an occasional prayer, and if changes are also made in it from time to time, he will become confused. And it is stated in the Gemara there that confusion only applies to "dew and rain" because it is in the middle of "Havineinu." But Havdalah can be included without causing confusion because it is at the beginning. And the Gemara remains with a question: why not include it? See there. And the Rashba wrote in the name of the Gaon that wherever the Talmud does not state a refutation, the law is not nullified, and this is the law. (And for the answer to this, see Beit Yosef, and Bach, and Magen Avraham, section 6. And in my humble opinion, there is no difficulty at all: for certainly according to Shmuel who says this, he believes that even in this case, one would become confused. However, the Talmud says to Rav Bibi who mentioned the rainy season, why did he not also mention the conclusion of Shabbat? Because he believes that with Havdalah, there is no confusion. But Shmuel does not hold this way. And you should know that there is a disagreement regarding the concept of confusion: for in the Jerusalem Talmud there, it indeed says concerning the rainy season that one can include it, see there. And if so, it is not held that there is confusion even with "dew and rain." And it is no wonder if Shmuel and Rav Bibi also disagree regarding Havdalah, and the law is according to Shmuel. And in the Jerusalem Talmud there, it says that in the blessing "Havineinu," when he concludes the last three blessings, he should say: "Blessed is the Lord who hears the voice of my supplications." See there.)

Know that there is an opinion which states that when time is running out, one should pray "Havineinu" (Magen Avraham, subsection 1, in the name of Kenesset HaGedolah). From this, it appears that he holds that if one began praying before the end of the time for prayer and it extended past the time, it is not considered as having prayed within the proper time. For certainly, his intention is that the time has not yet passed, for if it were not so, what difference would it make? Therefore, he holds that one should pray "Havineinu" and finish within the proper time, but if he were to complete all eighteen blessings, he would finish after the time. However, in my humble opinion, it seems from Tosafot in Berachot (7a, in the commentary beginning "Sha'almaley") that we go by the beginning, and if one began within the time for prayer, it is considered "prayer in its time" even if he finishes after the time. See there.

If someone prayed the "Havineinu" prayer not in a time of pressing need, some say he has fulfilled his obligation (Atzei), and some say he has not fulfilled his obligation (Eliyah Rabbah). It appears to me that the primary opinion is the first one, for it has already been explained that Abaye cursed one who prayed "Havineinu" — this is when it was not in a time of pressing need. And if you would think that he did not fulfill his obligation, a curse would not be applicable here; rather, it would need to state that he did not fulfill his obligation. Therefore, it is certain that he has fulfilled his obligation, but he did not act properly, and therefore he was cursed. However, in our times, we have never heard of anyone praying "Havineinu." The reason is simple: in their days, when they had much intention in prayer, they instituted "Havineinu" for times when they could not concentrate. But nowadays, we do not concentrate so well regardless, as I have written many times. Therefore, why would we need "Havineinu"? (It would be appropriate, however, to accustom soldiers who are pressed for time in their duties to pray "Havineinu.")

The law according to the Talmud (16a) states that laborers working for an employer, if they are only provided with food and not monetary wages, are to recite the full Shemoneh Esrei (Eighteen Blessings). However, if they are paid wages, they should recite the abbreviated “Havineinu” prayer. Even if they are not paid wages, they should not lead the prayer service nor perform the Priestly Blessing if they are Kohanim in places where the Priestly Blessing is performed daily. This implies that they must return to their work immediately after Kedusha, as otherwise, what difference would it make whether they lead the service or perform the Priestly Blessing, since in any case, they would delay until after the prayer? There is a question as to whether providing food for the worker's wife and children is considered equivalent to paying wages or not. Similarly, if the employer provides wages but not food, and the wages are only enough for sustenance, whether this is considered as paying wages or not. All this applies to daily wages, but if the worker is hired on a contract basis, it makes no difference to the employer, and the worker should pray the complete prayer like all of Israel. Our sages have written that nowadays, it is not customary to be strict about this, and in any case, one prays the complete prayer, as it is assumed that workers hire themselves with this understanding. There is a question whether nowadays, if the employer stipulates with the worker that he should only pray “Havineinu,” if this stipulation is effective or not. It would seem that it is effective, but one could argue that it is not within the employer’s power to nullify the worker’s prayer against the custom. However, whether a worker may go to the synagogue to pray nowadays depends on the local custom (Magen Avraham, subsection 7) if it was not explicitly stipulated otherwise.

Section 110, Subsection 8: The Rabbis taught (29b): One who is walking in a place of wild animals or bandits prays a short prayer: “The needs of Your people are many, and their understanding is limited. May it be Your will, O Lord our God, to give each and every one sufficient for their sustenance, and to every body enough for its needs. Blessed are You, O Lord, who hears prayer.” This prayer does not require the first three or the last three blessings and is not comparable to “Havineinu,” which fulfills the obligation of prayer. However, with this short prayer, one does not fulfill the obligation of prayer, and when he reaches a settled area and his mind is calmed from fear, he must return and pray the full Shemoneh Esrei. If he did not pray, it is as if he completely forgot to pray, as I wrote in Section 108 that this short prayer does not exempt one from the obligation of prayer. Therefore, it is permitted to pray it while walking, and only if he wishes to stand, he may stand. If you ask: If so, why pray it at all, why not wait until he reaches a settled place to pray the full prayer? It seems to me that the Sages were concerned that he might not reach a settled place during the time of prayer, and therefore, they said he should at least pray this short prayer. Furthermore, it seems to me that even if he reaches a settled place after four hours, he should pray the full prayer until noon. However, if he arrives after noon, he is exempt with this prayer and does not need to pray the afternoon prayer twice. Note that the Rif’s version after “enough for its needs” includes “and do what is good in Your eyes,” see there. This is also the version in the Rosh, Rambam, and Tur, see there. (See Magen Avraham, subsection 8, who wrote that if one is walking, he must return and pray, as I wrote in Section 94. Until here is his wording. I am puzzled because the Magen Avraham himself in subsection 11 disagrees with this, see there.)

Anyone who goes on a journey recites the Traveler's Prayer (Berachot 29b). And this is its text: "May it be Your will, Lord our God, that You lead us in peace, guide us in peace, support us in peace, and rescue us from the hand of every enemy and ambush on the way, and send blessing upon the work of our hands. And grant us grace, kindness, and mercy in Your eyes and in the eyes of all who see us. Blessed are You, Lord, who hears prayer." In the Rif, the version is: "and support us in peace, and return us to our home in peace," see there. In the Tur, this version does not appear, but at its conclusion, he writes: "for You hear the prayer of Your people Israel with mercy." And at its beginning, he writes: "Our God and God of our ancestors," see there. It is surprising that in the Rambam, no law regarding the Traveler's Prayer is found. Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, has already pointed this out in his great book, see there. Even though at the end of the tenth chapter of Berachot he wrote the prayer for entering and leaving a city, which is explained at the beginning of the chapter "One Who Sees," and wrote there: "Just as You have taken me out in peace, so too lead us in peace and guide us..." see there, similar to the text of the Traveler's Prayer. It could be said that he intended to include them in one prayer, and also that his intention was to conclude with "who hears prayer" even though he did not explain this (see Beit Yosef, Siman 230). In any case, there are several laws in the Talmud regarding this as will be explained, so why did he not explain them? This requires further investigation.

One must recite it in the plural form: "that You lead us" and not "that You lead me," and so for all of them. Even if one is traveling alone, there are many who travel, and it is better to include oneself with the many, for a prayer is more readily heard in the plural. There is an opinion that "and grant me favor" should be said in the singular form (Magen Avraham, subsection 10). However, there are those who disagree with this (the GRaI"B). 

It is a mitzvah to engage in Torah study while on the way, but one should not delve into halacha, lest he becomes distracted (Taanit 10a). But if he is sitting in a wagon, he can delve into halacha. One should not eat more than two portions on the way, because of the potential for digestive issues (ibid.). A person should always enter a city when it is good and leave when it is good, not at night (beginning of Pesachim). However, if leaving his city and he is not traveling alone, it is permitted to leave even at night (Tosafot there, and see Magen Avraham, subsection 10).

One may say the Traveler's Prayer (Tefilat HaDerech) even while walking. However, if possible, he should stand while reciting it and not walk, and it is preferable to say it standing rather than sitting. Nevertheless, if he is riding an animal, he is not required to dismount and may say it while riding. However, if possible, he should stop the animal, as riding is considered like walking. Similarly, if he is sitting in a carriage, he is not required to get out, and he may say it while sitting in the carriage. If it is easy to stop the horses, it is proper to do so. Those traveling by train should say it standing, as it is easy to stand, and the same applies when traveling on large ships. It is obvious that one must say the Traveler's Prayer when traveling by sea, rivers, or railroads. If he wishes to add additional supplications and requests, he may do so, but the Traveler's Prayer as found in the Talmud must be recited for any type of travel.

One needs to say it only once a day; however, on any day that one is traveling, one is obligated to recite it on the first journey of the day. Moreover, even if one intended to stay overnight, and then decided to continue traveling or return home, one must recite it again. Since one originally intended to stay overnight, the prayer recited in the morning is considered concluded. Therefore, if one changes one's mind, one must say it anew, and conclude with "Blessed" using the Divine name. However, if one stops to rest at some place during the day with the intention of continuing the journey later that day, one does not need to say it again. If one wishes to recite it without concluding with "Blessed" on every journey of the day, one is permitted to do so, because without the conclusion it holds no formal status. But once a day, one is obligated to say it with the concluding blessing. There are those who mistakenly do not say it with the concluding blessing every day, based on what is printed in some prayer books, but this is a significant error and was printed mistakenly.

One should recite it (the traveler’s prayer) after they have started on their journey, and not say it within the city limits (Magen Avraham, section 14). There are those who write that it should not be said within the city’s boundary, which is strange. Similarly, there are those who write that as soon as one prepares to leave, even if they have not yet departed, they can say the traveler’s prayer (Taz). This is also not clear. (The proof brought from the first chapter of Horayot, referring to page 4, see there – is irrelevant. How is this related, since over there it follows one’s preoccupation? On the contrary, from Eruvin 52b, there is explicit proof that as long as one has not left their house, it is not considered “starting the journey.” However, if one takes even a few steps away from their house, it is considered “starting the journey.” See there, where it says to leave it until one descends a step. Rashi explains that this is considered “starting the journey.” Therefore, when one leaves their house and immediately recites the traveler’s prayer, they fulfill the obligation.)

The Tur wrote: The reason it does not begin with "Blessed" was explained by Rabbi Yitzchak, because it is merely a prayer, where one prays to the Holy One, blessed be He, to lead us in peace. It is not like the blessings over enjoyment, nor like the blessings instituted for specific events, but rather a request for mercy. And because it contains an extended text, it concludes with "Blessed". And Rabbi Meir of Rothenburg, when he would go on a journey in the morning, would say it after the morning blessings in order to juxtapose it to the blessing of "He bestows kindnesses...", so that it would be a blessing adjacent to another blessing. See there. And consequently, he would also recite the blessings on the way. And even when one travels in the middle of the day, he can juxtapose it to another blessing, such as eating or drinking something and then juxtaposing it to the after-blessing. Or he can urinate and juxtapose it to the blessing "Who formed". And a wise person has his eyes in his head.

One should not recite the Traveler's Prayer unless they are traveling a distance of a parasang (approximately four mil), as anything less than a parasang is not considered a "journey." However, if the route is dangerous, then one can recite it even for a shorter distance. If one did not recite it immediately upon leaving the city, they may still recite it as long as they are on the way, provided that the distance to the place where they intend to rest is not less than a parasang. Beyond that, they should recite it without a blessing. Ideally, it is best to recite it within the first parasang. A parasang is four mil, and in the measurement of our country, Russia, a parasang is four versts. (When one sets out on a journey, it is good to receive permission from a Torah scholar in the city, and the scholar should say to him: "Go in peace," not "Go to peace." Additionally, one should not travel without provisions, tefillin, a prayer book, and a book for study.)

It is stated in the Gemara (Berachot 28b): Upon entering the Beit Midrash (house of study), one says: "May it be Your will, Lord my God, that no mishap occur through me, and I do not stumble in a matter of Halacha and cause my colleagues to rejoice over me. And let me not say regarding something impure that it is pure, nor regarding something pure that it is impure. And let not my colleagues stumble in a matter of Halacha, and I will rejoice over them." So far his words. This means that they will rejoice when they correct me from an error, and likewise, I will rejoice in them. And upon leaving, one says: "I thank You, Lord my God, that You have set my portion with those who dwell in the Beit Midrash, and You have not set my portion with those who dwell in street corners. I rise early, and they rise early; I rise early for words of Torah, and they rise early for idle words. I toil, and they toil; I toil and receive reward, and they toil and do not receive reward. I run, and they run; I run to the life of the World to Come, and they run to the pit of destruction." See there. And nowadays, this is not practiced, and it seems because currently those who study in the Beit Midrash do not issue Halachic rulings, and the rabbi who issues rulings sits at home. The Ari z"l would say it every morning, and he would say: "For the Lord gives wisdom; from His mouth come knowledge and understanding. Open my eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of Your Torah."

However, even for someone who sits alone, and especially when he is a decisor of Jewish law, it has been written that it is proper for him to say: "May it be Your will, Lord my God and God of my forefathers, that You illuminate my eyes with the light of Your Torah. And save me from any stumbling and error, both in matters of prohibition and permission, and in matters of monetary law, both in instruction and in study. 'Uncover my eyes and I will behold wonders from Your Torah.' And regarding what I have already erred – set me straight to the truth. Do not let a word of truth leave my mouth at all. 'For the Lord gives wisdom; from His mouth come knowledge and understanding'" (Taz, subsection 8). And the prayer "Modeh Ani" should be said every evening by someone who studies Torah all day (Magen Avraham, subsection 16).

One must be very careful to connect the blessing of redemption ("Ga'al Yisrael") to the Amidah prayer without any interruption. Our Sages, of blessed memory, said (Berachot 9b): "Anyone who connects redemption to prayer will not be harmed throughout the entire day." And in the Jerusalem Talmud (First Chapter, end of Halacha 5): "Immediately after redemption, prayer," as it is stated: "May the words of my mouth... and my redeemer" – this refers to redemption, and it is followed by: "May the Lord answer you on the day of distress," which refers to prayer. Anyone who connects redemption to prayer, the Satan does not accuse him on that day. And anyone who does not connect redemption to prayer, to what is he comparable? To a friend of the king who comes and knocks on the king's door. The king comes out to see what he wants, and finds that he has gone away – so the king also goes away. See there.

The Tur wrote: However, saying "Amen" after "Who redeemed Israel" is not considered an interruption. And so ruled our master, the Rema. But our master, the Beit Yosef, ruled not to answer "Amen" after "Who redeemed Israel." And this is according to the Zohar, and so we practice, as I wrote in Siman 66, that even for Kaddish, Kedusha, and "Barchu" one should not answer between redemption and prayer. One should wait in the new song, as explained there. The Tur wrote that some have the custom to say verses before, such as: "O You who hear prayer, unto You all flesh will come," "For I will proclaim the name of the Lord; ascribe greatness to our God" - and one should not say them, as they are considered an interruption. But "O Lord, open my lips, and my mouth will declare Your praise" is not considered an interruption, because the Sages instituted it in the prayer - it is considered like an extended redemption (Gemara). However, in the Mussaf and Mincha prayers, one can say "O Lord, open my lips" before starting if one wishes, but not afterwards.

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote that some say that the need to juxtapose redemption (geulah) to prayer (tefilah) is specifically on weekdays or on Yom Tov, but on Shabbat it is not necessary. However, it is good to be stringent unless there is a need for it. This is his language. The reasoning for this opinion is that since we derive this from "May the Lord answer you on the day of trouble," and Shabbat is not a day of trouble. And Yom Tov is like a weekday because we are judged on it, as it is taught in the first chapter of Rosh Hashanah: "On Passover, we are judged for grain; on Shavuot, for the fruit of the tree..." However, many great authorities have agreed that the verse "May the Lord answer you" is merely a support for this, but the juxtaposition of redemption to prayer is a fundamental aspect of the prayer itself. Therefore, it applies also on Shabbat, and this is the custom. Only in the evening service (Maariv) is it less stringent than in the morning service (Shacharit), and this will be explained in Siman 236, with the help of Heaven.

The prayer leader, when he needs to repeat the prayer out loud, should first say "Lord, open my lips..." And at the end, he should say quietly "May the words of my mouth..." And even though we do not find a prohibition for the prayer leader to interrupt between the silent prayer and the out-loud prayer, nonetheless, it is proper not to interrupt. And no other verse should be said except "Lord, open my lips..." (see Magen Avraham, subsection 4). And if, before he has recited the Shema, he finds the congregation praying, he should not pray with them, but rather pray in the proper order so that he can connect redemption to prayer, which is preferable to the prayer of the congregation. This applies in the morning. But in the evening it is not so, as will be explained in Siman 236 with the help of Heaven.

Even though in the middle blessings, each person can add any request when needed, in the first three and last three blessings, it is forbidden to add. The first three are like a servant who recounts praise before his master, and since he is arranging the praises of the Blessed One, how can he interrupt with a personal request? Similarly, the last three, where he gives thanks to his master, how can he interrupt with requests? However, this applies to the needs of an individual. But for the needs of the community, it is permitted. Therefore, we say "Ya'aleh V'yavo" in the Avodah blessing, and during the Ten Days of Repentance, we say "Zochreinu L'chaim," "Mi Kamocha," "U'chtov," and "B'sefer...". And on Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, we extend with "V'chein Tein Pachdecha...". For the community is very beloved before the Holy One, blessed be He, and they are given permission to interrupt, unlike an individual. Our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote that one should not say piyutim (liturgical poems) or kerovot (additional prayers). This is not comparable to what the Men of the Great Assembly instituted in all those we mentioned, as their strength was considerable. But our master, the Rema, wrote that there are those who permit it, since it is for the needs of the many. And thus is the practice in all places to say them. Thus far his words. And so is the simple custom and it should not be changed. And we have already written in Siman 68 that one of the great ones abolished the piyutim in his place, and he did not complete the year (Bach there).

It is stated in Megillah (17b): One hundred and twenty elders, including several prophets, instituted the eighteen blessings in order. And it is stated in the Aggadah: What is meant by "in order"? This refers to the order of the world. The eighteen blessings of the prayer were always arranged one after the other, and when the Men of the Great Assembly came, they consolidated and instituted them in their sequence. When Abraham was saved from the fiery furnace, the ministering angels began, saying "Shield of Abraham." When Isaac was bound, they said "Who revives the dead." When Jacob arrived and encountered the gates of mercy and sanctified the name of the Holy One, Blessed be He, they said "The Holy God." When Gabriel taught Joseph the seventy languages, they said "Who grants knowledge." When Reuben repented for the incident with Bilhah, they said "Who desires repentance." When Judah confessed in the incident with Tamar and said "Bring her out, and let her be burned," and he said "She is more righteous than I," and his sin was forgiven, they said "Gracious One who abundantly forgives." When the Holy One, Blessed be He, said to Israel in Egypt, "I will redeem you," they said "Redeemer of Israel." When Raphael healed Abraham, they said "Healer of the sick of His people Israel." When Isaac sowed and found a hundredfold, they said "Who blesses the years." When Jacob came to Egypt and the tribes gathered together with Joseph, they said "Who gathers the dispersed of His people Israel."

When the Holy One, blessed be He, said to Moses, "And these are the ordinances," they said, "A king who loves righteousness and justice." When the Egyptians were drowned in the Red Sea, they said, "He who breaks enemies and subdues the wicked." When the Holy One, blessed be He, said to Jacob and Joseph, "He shall place his hand upon your eyes," and afterwards it was fulfilled, and Jacob trusted in His word, they said, "Support and trust for the righteous." When Solomon built the Temple, they said, "Builder of Jerusalem." When Israel crossed the Red Sea and sang a song, they said, "He who makes the horn of salvation sprout." When Israel sighed and cried out, and the Lord heard their groaning, they said, "Hearer of prayer." And when the Divine Presence descended into the Tabernacle, they said, "He who returns His Presence to Zion." When Solomon brought the Ark into the Temple and was answered and gave thanks, they said, "Your name is good and it is fitting to give thanks to You." And when Israel entered the land and it was fulfilled for them, "I will give peace in the land," they said, "He who blesses His people Israel with peace." (The Beit Yosef brought this from Shibolei HaLeket and Orchot Chaim, see there.)

The Tur wrote in Siman 113 in the name of his brother, Rabbeinu Yechiel, that the pious ones of Ashkenaz would count all the words in each blessing of the Eighteen Blessings: in the first blessing, forty-two words; in the second, fifty-one words (this includes "Mashiv HaRuach U'Morid HaGeshem"); in the third, fourteen; in the fourth, seventeen; in the fifth, fifteen; and in the sixth and seventh, he did not count the number of words. However, in the book Pri Etz Chaim by the Arizal (page 60a), he also counted the words and wrote the same numbers as the Tur, see there. And he wrote that in the sixth blessing there are twenty words, and in the seventh, seventeen, see there. (And in the first blessing he wrote forty-eight, and this includes the verse "Hashem, open my lips.") And in the eighth, the Tur and Pri Etz Chaim wrote twenty-seven words, in the ninth, thirty words, and in the tenth, ten. In the eleventh, the Tur did not count, and in Pri Etz Chaim, it is written as twenty-four words. In the twelfth, which is the blessing "V'lamalshinim," they wrote twenty-nine words; in the thirteenth, forty-two words; in the fourteenth, twenty-four; and in the fifteenth, twenty. In the sixteenth, which is "Sh'ma Kolenu," the Tur did not count, and in Pri Etz Chaim, it is written as thirty-five words. And in the seventeenth, eighteenth, and nineteenth, the Tur also did not count, and in Pri Etz Chaim, it is written that in the seventeenth, there are thirty-four words; in the eighteenth, eighty-six; and in the nineteenth, it is not clarified even in Pri Etz Chaim, see there. Behold, the Tur wrote all this as hints and simple intentions, and in Pri Etz Chaim, he wrote great and awesome secrets about this, see there.

And behold, although none among us knows to what extent, and would that we could at least understand the simple meaning of the words. Nevertheless, every Jewish person must understand the great value of the Amidah prayer, for Shimon the Righteous was from the remnants of the Great Assembly, as it is stated at the beginning of Pirkei Avot, and his great stature is well-known in the Talmud, as discussed in Yoma (39b) and at the beginning of Tamid. And how much more so the men of the Great Assembly themselves, and all the more so the prophets among them. And if they labored with their holy spirit to arrange the prayer, how many profound intentions must be embedded within it! Every single word stands at the pinnacle of the world. Therefore, fortunate is the person who prays with careful attention to these holy matters.

The first blessing is "Avot" (Patriarchs). And from where do we know that we mention the Patriarchs? As it is stated: "Ascribe to the Lord, O sons of the mighty" (Megillah 17b) – refer to the mighty ones of the earth (Rashi). And from where do we know that we say "Gevurot" (Mightiness)? As it is stated: "Ascribe to the Lord glory and strength." And from where do we know that we say "Kedushot" (Holiness)? As it is stated: "Ascribe to the Lord the glory due His name; worship the Lord in the beauty of holiness."

We begin with "God of Abraham," as Reish Lakish said: What is the meaning of the verse: "And I will make you a great nation"? This refers to saying "God of Abraham." "And I will bless you"? This refers to saying "God of Isaac." "And I will make your name great"? This refers to saying "God of Jacob." Could it be that we should conclude with all of them? The Talmud teaches: "And you shall be a blessing" – we conclude with you, saying "Shield of Abraham," and not with all of them (Pesachim 117b).

And the reason we say "God of" each one individually is because each of the Patriarchs was worthy on his own for the name of God to be associated with him, just like the entire people of Israel say "God of Israel." (And the reason we don't say "and God of Israel" but rather "and God of Jacob," I have heard is because the numerical value of "the Patriarchs" is thirteen, and similarly, the Matriarchs – Sarah, Rebecca, Rachel, and Leah – also have the numerical value of thirteen, and together they total twenty-six, corresponding to the name of Hashem. This is what the scripture means when it says: "If it had not been the Lord who was on our side, let Israel now say." Reflect on this and you will find it straightforward.)

And there are forty-two words in it (Tur). And with the verse "O Lord, open my lips," there are forty-eight (Pri Etz Chaim).

This blessing begins with "Blessed" because it is the first one. And even though it follows "Who redeemed Israel," it is still considered the first within the context of the prayer. It ends with "Blessed" because it is lengthy and includes various praises of the Blessed One. The other blessings conclude with "Blessed" but do not begin with "Blessed" because they are considered subsequent to each other. Although it is established that any blessing without mention of the sovereignty of God is not a valid blessing (Berachot 40b), and we might ask why it does not begin with "King of the Universe," the phrase "God of Abraham" is considered equivalent to mentioning sovereignty because our forefather Abraham declared the sovereignty of the Holy One, Blessed be He, over the entire world by making His kingship known (Tosafot there). Additionally, the phrase "the great, mighty, and awesome God" is also considered equivalent to mentioning sovereignty, as we see in Rosh Hashanah (32b) that "Hear O Israel" is considered an expression of sovereignty (Tur).

When one says "Blessed are You" – one should bow. For it is taught (at the end of the fifth chapter of Berachot): these are the blessings in which a person bows at the beginning and end: in the blessings of "Avot" and "Hoda'ah." When one says "Blessed are You" – one should bow, and when one says "Lord" – one should straighten up, as it is written: "The Lord straightens the bent" (Psalms 146:8). If one wishes to bow at the end of each and every blessing – they are taught not to bow, so as not to undermine the enactment of the Sages, lest each person says: I will bow wherever I wish (Tur). Only the High Priest would bow at the beginning of each blessing. And a king, once he bows – he does not straighten up again, as it is said: "And it was when Solomon finished praying…, he arose from before the Lord from kneeling on his knees" (1 Kings 8:54). For the greater a person is, the more they need to demonstrate submission before the Holy One, blessed be He. Therefore, ordinary people who bow more than what the Sages enacted show themselves as if they are great individuals and need more submission, and it appears as arrogance (Tosafot there).

The Tur and the Shulchan Aruch wrote that specifically at the beginning and end [of the Amidah prayer], one should be taught not to bow, but in the middle [of the blessings], one may bow. Meaning: one should not be rebuked for doing so. And even though if one comes to ask whether or not to bow, the answer is that one should not bow; however, if one bows on their own in the middle, one is not rebuked, because bowing in the middle of the blessing is not relevant at all. Bowing is only at the beginning or the end. This is also the custom with a human king. Therefore, someone who bows in the middle does not violate the ordinance of our sages, nor is there a concern of arrogance. (This also resolves the question of the Taz, Section 2, and also what the Magen Avraham questioned in Section 1. Examine and you will find it easy.) Therefore, those people who are accustomed to bowing during the Amidah prayer on Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur should be careful to straighten up at the end of each blessing. And even in a place where one is obligated to bow, one should first straighten up slightly and then bow, so that it appears that the bowing is due to the obligation set by our sages. And at [the mention of] "Hashem," one should straighten up, and then if one wishes, they may bow again. (The Ba’er Hetev wrote in Section 1 to have intention in the first bow at the letter Yud of the Name of Hashem and at the Aleph of the Name Adonai, in the second bow at the second letters, in the third bow at the third letters, and in the fourth bow at the final letters of these Names. Refer there. There is no need to elaborate on such matters. Those who are initiated into the secrets of Hashem know many hidden intentions.)

Our Sages of blessed memory said (Berachot 34b): One who bows during the Modim (thanksgiving) of Birkat Hamazon when saying "We thank You..." and during the Hallel when saying "Give thanks to the Lord for He is good" – this is considered reprehensible, for one should only bow in the places established by the Sages. There is a question about this: If so, how do we bow when we say "And we bow," and on Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, we fall on our faces? And also during the service of Yom Kippur? However, the explanation of the matter is as follows: Certainly, in places where there is no established practice by our Sages of blessed memory – there is no concern about this, as I have written regarding bowing in the middle of blessings in the previous section. Therefore, there are those who bow also when saying "Barechu" and in the Kaddish.

The matter is as follows: In truth, the term "blessing" or "thanksgiving" does not imply bowing at all, but rather it denotes giving thanks and praise. When the Sages instituted four bowings in the Amidah prayer, they knew precisely why they did so. Therefore, one who bows during the thanksgiving blessing of Birkat Hamazon or during the thanksgiving of Hallel is acting inappropriately, meaning it is foolishness. Similarly, when saying in the "Nishmat" prayer, "For You alone we give thanks," or in "Vayevarech David," "And now, our God, we give thanks to You," it is foolishness. Also, in "Nishmat," when saying "And every stature shall bow before You," it is merely recounting words. However, one who bows in any place of praise or supplication, or for some reason that appears to him appropriate to bow in that place, or due to custom such as bowing in Kaddish or in "Barchu," or if his heart is inflamed in prayer, it is praiseworthy and is not considered as adding to the decrees of the Sages, for our Sages of blessed memory did not institute any decree in this matter (according to the Gra"z). This is what was said about Rabbi Akiva, that when he prayed by himself, he would increase in bowings and prostrations. And when saying "And we bow," it is proper to bow. Similarly, during the Yom Kippur service, in memory of what we used to do in the Holy Temple, it is good and proper to do so (there). However, all these bowings should be done slightly, except on Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur when we fall on our faces in memory of our Holy Temple.

The person praying must bow until all the vertebrae in his spine protrude. This means that the joints between his vertebrae should be prominent (Tur). He should not bend in the middle of his back with his head remaining upright, but rather he should also bend his head like a reed. Nevertheless, he should not bow so much that his mouth is opposite the belt of his pants, because bowing too much appears arrogant. This applies to a healthy person. However, someone who is slightly ill or elderly, for whom it is difficult to bow until the joints of his vertebrae protrude, it is sufficient for him to incline his head, since it is clear that he wishes to bow but finds it difficult. When bowing, he should bow quickly in one motion. When straightening up, he should do so slowly, first raising his head and then his body, so it does not appear burdensome. It has already been explained that when bowing, he bows at "Baruch." According to the Zohar, when he says "Baruch," he should bow with his knees, and when he says "Atah," he should bend (Magen Avraham, subsection 4), and he straightens up at the name [of God]. If during prayer, at the time he needs to bow, an idol appears before him, he should not bow at all, so it does not appear as if he is bowing to it, even though his heart is directed towards Heaven. He should pray without bowing (see Magen Avraham, subsection 5, who questions this from Yom Kippur when they would bow upon hearing the name, see there. I am puzzled: there, they bowed out of fear of the explicit name, what relevance does this have? But indeed, what is written "God straightens the bent" is not an absolute requirement, as the Magen Avraham writes in section 127, subsection 2. There is proof from the king and the high priest, and it is merely a hint).

It is forbidden to add to the descriptions of the Almighty more than "the great, mighty, and awesome God," because when one says more than what the Rabbis established, it appears as if he has concluded all His praises. And who can declare all His praises? Even these three descriptions, if not for the fact that Moses our teacher said them in the Torah, and the Men of the Great Assembly established them in the prayer, we would not say them. Therefore, one should not add to the words of the Sages. And this applies specifically to the Amidah prayer. But in supplications or personal requests that one makes outside of the fixed prayer, one may say as he wishes, because he says them out of his need in his request and supplication, and not to mention the praises of the Almighty. This is not the case in the fixed prayer, which is arranged to praise the Almighty, for the requests begin with "You graciously grant knowledge." Nonetheless, even there one should not increase praises since he is standing in prayer. According to Maimonides, it is forbidden in any case because, in his opinion, praising the Almighty should only be done in the way of negation, as he wrote in his Guide for the Perplexed. According to the Kabbalists, this is not so, and the main ruling is according to the first opinion. Nevertheless, it is good for one who wishes to say praises to say them in verses, for this is permitted even according to Maimonides. It is forbidden to say in supplications "on the good Your name will be remembered," for a person is obligated to bless for the bad just as he blesses for the good. It is also forbidden to say, "Just as Your mercy reached the bird's nest, as You said 'you shall surely send away the mother bird'—so too may Your mercy reach us." For the commandments of the Holy One, blessed be He, are decrees and not merely out of mercy, and we are commanded to fulfill the decree of the King.

What we say, "And He remembers the kindnesses of the patriarchs, and brings a redeemer..." – the Tur explains that the meaning is: even if the merit of the patriarchs has ceased, He will bring the redemption for the sake of His blessed name, see there. Additionally, it seems to me that what we say, "for the sake of His name, with love" is based on what is mentioned in the Midrash Ruth: one verse states, "For your sake, for your sake I will do," and another verse states, "For My sake, for My sake I will do" – here, when Israel performs His will, it will be for their sake, and here, when they do not perform His will, it will be for the sake of His blessed name and not for our sake. And this is what it means when it says that even if the redemption will be for the sake of His name and not for our sake, nevertheless, it will be with love and affection.

The second blessing is "You are mighty," and its conclusion is "Who revives the dead," as the resurrection of the dead is one of the greatest acts of might in this world. And they included in it the mention of the might of rains, and we say: "You revive the dead; You are great to save; You cause the wind to blow and the rain to fall," for rains also descend mightily (beginning of Taanit), and both were not given to an emissary (there). That is to say, both are beyond nature, and both are eternal life. And thus our sages of blessed memory said (there, 7a): Since it is equivalent to the resurrection of the dead, they therefore established it in the blessing of the resurrection of the dead. And the fact that "wind" is placed next to "rain" is not because saying "He causes the wind to blow" is essential, but because, typically, the winds bring the clouds, and from them the rain descends. Therefore, they were placed next to each other.

There is a question regarding this: Why do we say "rain" (גשם) in the mention (of God's might) and "rain" (מטר) in the request (for rain)? It appears to me that "rain" (גשם) is called so when it descends from the heavens while still above, as it is written: "If the clouds are full of rain (גשם)." And in the flood it is written: "And the rain (גשם) was restrained from the heavens." On the other hand, "rain" (מטר) is always near the earth, as it is written: "The rain (מטר) of your land," "And rain (מטר) did not fall upon the earth." And in Job it is written: "He gives rain (מטר) on the face of the earth." Therefore, it is written: "And rain (גשם) upon rain (מטר), and rain (גשם) of His mighty rains (מטרות)," for initially it is "rain" (גשם) and afterward it is "rain" (מטר). Although there are exceptions in the Scriptures, this is their main interpretation. Therefore, in the mention of might, we say "rain" (גשם), since the might is primarily above, and in the request where we ask "and give dew and rain (מטר) upon the face of the earth" – it was established to say "rain" (מטר). It seems that if one said "rain" (מטר) in the mention and "rain" (גשם) in the request, he has fulfilled his obligation and does not need to repeat it, although he changes from the language of the Sages.

Mentioning (rain) is not the same as requesting (rain). For requesting, each country requests according to the time of its rainy season, as will be explained in Siman 117. But mentioning (rain) is done by the entire world on the same day. For requesting, where one asks the Holy One, blessed be He, "Give dew and rain," it follows that each person asks when they need it. But mentioning is only to recall the mighty deeds of the Holy One, blessed be He – everyone mentions it at the time when His mighty deeds are recognized, which is when the rainy season begins in the Land of Israel, and then we all mention it. This is on the last day of the Sukkot festival, which is Shemini Atzeret, because then it is the rainy season in the Land of Israel. And even though requesting (rain) in the Land of Israel starts on the seventh of Cheshvan as I wrote there – this is so that the pilgrims can reach their homes (there, 10:2). And this blessing contains fifty-one words (Tur and Pri Etz Chaim).

In the Musaf Amidah, we begin to mention [the phrase "He causes the wind to blow and the rain to fall"], and we mention it throughout the winter until the Musaf of the first day of Passover. And why do we not begin mentioning it in the Maariv Amidah? Because not everyone is in the synagogue, and this one will mention it and that one will not mention it, and there will be divisions. And so we say in the Jerusalem Talmud there: And also in the Shacharit [Amidah], it is impossible to mention it because we only begin if there is an announcement before the prayer, as will be explained, and in Shacharit it is impossible to interrupt with an announcement between redemption (Geulah) and prayer (Tefillah) (Magen Avraham, subsection 1). And for this reason, we also interrupt in Musaf as in the beginning, so that it will be equal and publicized among the congregation. For until Musaf, everyone is in the synagogue (see Taz, subsection 3).

It is forbidden to mention rain until everyone has heard an announcement for this, or until the prayer leader, when he stands in silent prayer, says "He who causes the wind to blow" out loud. However, according to this, it would also be possible to do so in the Shacharit (morning) prayer. Yet, it is not proper etiquette to do so, and not everyone is in the synagogue at that time. Therefore, it is better that the sexton announces after the half-Kaddish "He who causes the wind to blow and the rain to fall." This is the common practice, and it should not be changed. Hence, an individual should not begin the Musaf (additional) prayer before the congregation. However, even an individual praying at home, even if he did not hear the announcement, should say "He who causes the wind to blow." He should aim to pray at the same time the congregation is praying, as it is not possible to do otherwise. (See Taz, subparagraph 4, and Magen Avraham, subparagraph 2, and you will understand why I was compelled to this. Be precise and you will find it easy.) Even if he is sick or coerced, he is not allowed to pray before the congregation. But if he knows that it has been announced, even if he did not hear it, he mentions it. For this reason, one who comes to the synagogue while the congregation is praying Musaf prays with them and mentions it even if he did not hear it.

The sages said (Taanit 3:1) that dew and winds were not required by the sages to be mentioned, but if one wants to mention them, one may mention them. Therefore, in Sephardic tradition, "He makes the dew fall" is said during the summer, while in Ashkenazi tradition, it is not said. The reason "He causes the wind to blow" is mentioned because it relates to rain, as I have written that wind is connected to rain. If it was not said, it does not invalidate the prayer. When asking for rain, "and give dew and rain for a blessing" is said, because we are asking for blessed dew as well, for there is dew that is not a blessing (Talmud). However, if one only said "and give rain" without mentioning dew, it does not invalidate the prayer. Therefore, if one said "He causes the wind to blow" during the summer without "He makes the rain fall," or during the rainy season only said "He makes the rain fall," one is not required to repeat the prayer. Similarly, regarding dew according to the Sephardic custom, if it was mentioned during the rainy season, or not mentioned when asking, or not mentioned during the summer, one is not required to repeat the prayer. Ashkenazim do not mention dew at all in the mention, neither in the summer nor in the rainy season, only in the request. In Sephardic tradition, if one did not mention dew during the summer, even if they have not yet completed the blessing, they do not need to go back to mention it because there is no obligation at all (Magen Avraham, subsection 4). The same rule applies to winds during the rainy season; they share the same law.

Our teacher, the Rema, wrote in paragraph 3: "There are those who say that the prayer leader (Shaliach Tzibbur) should stop mentioning [‘Mashiv HaRuach U'Morid HaGeshem’] in the Musaf prayer of the first day of Pesach, but the congregation continues to mention it and does not stop until Mincha, since they have already heard from the prayer leader who stopped mentioning it in the Musaf prayer. And this is the practice." Thus are his words. The explanation of this is: During the Amidah, the sexton announces "Mashiv HaRuach U'Morid HaGeshem." But during the break it is impossible to announce, so they do not say it, as it might appear as if they are rejecting the rain (Levush and Magen Avraham, subparagraph 5). Additionally, how can it be announced not to say "Mashiv HaRuach"? Concerning winds, there is no strictness, as I have written (Taz, subparagraph 9). Without an announcement, it has already been clarified that it is impossible to announce to say "Morid HaTal" because in Ashkenaz, they do not say it as has been clarified. Therefore, it is necessary to say it quietly. And in Sephardic practice, it would seem that the sexton announces "Morid HaTal," though I do not know if this is their custom. From the words of the Tur in the name of the Ra'avad, it is clear that they announce, as he wrote: "It is forbidden to mention until the Shaliach Tzibbur announces 'Mashiv HaRuach U'Morid HaGeshem' or 'Morid HaTal.'" Thus are his words.

If one said "He makes the wind blow and the rain fall" during the summer, we make him go back, because there are times in the summer when rain is harmful to the world, such as during the harvest season. Therefore, throughout the summer we make him go back (Taz, sub-section 10). Additionally, so as not to create divisions, where some mention it and others do not. Where does he go back to? To the beginning of the blessing "You are mighty." This is if he has not finished "Who revives the dead." But if he has finished, he goes back to the beginning of the prayer, as the first three blessings are considered as one. It seems to me that he needs to say the verse "O Lord, open my lips" again, because the Sages instituted saying it before the prayer, and his previous recitation was interrupted by the blessings and thus they are nullified, therefore he needs to say it anew. Even in countries that need rain during the summer, we make him go back if he mentioned rain or both rain and dew, as there is a practical difference only in the petition, not in the mention, as I have written. (And in Shaarei Teshuva it is written not to say "O Lord, open my lips" again. This requires further study.)

In the rainy season, if one did not mention rain, they must repeat [the prayer]. This applies when one did not mention dew, but if one mentioned dew, they do not need to repeat [the prayer]. Accordingly, the Sephardic custom to mention dew during the summer months is appropriate, so in the rainy season, even if one does not mention rain, they will still mention dew as per their habit. Even in regions that do not need rain during the rainy season, one still must repeat [the prayer], because in mentioning [rain], there is no difference between one region and another, only in requesting [rain], as I have written. And even though in a request, one does not fulfill their obligation by mentioning dew instead of rain – this is because in such a situation, both dew and rain are needed, which is not the case in mere mentioning, which was instituted alongside the resurrection of the dead because rain is life for the world. Dew is also life for the world and is relevant to the resurrection of the dead, as the dead will be revived through dew. Therefore, mentioning dew suffices (see Taz, Orach Chaim 117:3). Additionally, for a request, one must ask for something that can sometimes be withheld, and dew is never withheld, so it is not appropriate to request it. Therefore, one does not fulfill their obligation solely by mentioning dew. However, in mentioning, which is merely praise to the Holy One, Blessed be He, there is praise in mentioning dew just as there is in mentioning rain, and thus one fulfills their obligation by mentioning dew (Magen Avraham 117:7).

And this that we said, that when one does not mention rain, he is returned [to the beginning] – this is specifically when he finished the entire blessing and began the next blessing. Then he returns to the beginning of the prayer. But if he remembers before he finished the blessing, he should say it where he remembered. And although it is attached to "You revive the dead and are great to save," and now he will say it after "Who releases the bound" and similar, nevertheless it is ultimately within the blessing of the resurrection of the dead, whose main part is in the closing. And even if he finished the blessing of "Who revives the dead," if he has not yet begun "You are holy," he should say "Who makes the wind blow and the rain fall. You are holy..." This ruling was written by the Rosh and the Mordechai at the beginning of Taanit, and the Tur here in the name of Avi HaEzri. And there are those who disagree and hold that once he has finished the blessing, he returns to the beginning. However, our master the Beit Yosef decided according to the first opinion, and he did not bring the dissenting opinion in the Shulchan Aruch at all (see Beit Yosef). And the same law applies to "dew and rain" in the request; if he has not begun "Sound the great shofar," he should say there "and give dew and rain" (ibid.). And even though now they remain without a blessing, one can say that it refers to "Blessed are You, Hashem, who revives the dead, who makes the wind blow..." as if he concluded with this as well (Levush). And it does not apply here to say one does not conclude with two [blessings], for it is all one matter (ibid.). According to this, this law applies only if immediately when he said "Who revives the dead," he said "Who makes the wind blow," and similarly with "dew and rain" (Eliyah Rabbah and Taz, subsection 12). But it does not seem so (Taz). And it seems to me that it certainly does seem so, for he does not interrupt between blessing and blessing, and consequently if he remembers at the end of the blessing, it is immediate. (And one should not ask: why did we not differentiate in section 8 between finishing and not finishing? For there it is different, as he mentioned what he should not have mentioned, and it is necessary to return to the beginning and not mention, which is not the case when he did not mention what he should have mentioned – he should mention it in another place in the blessing.)

A fundamental principle is that the first three blessings (of the Amidah) are considered as one unit, and in any place where one makes an error in them, one must return to the beginning, whether one is praying individually or as a community. This specifically refers to matters that are essential, such as mentioning rain during the summer season, or failing to mention it during the rainy season, or during the Ten Days of Repentance if one did not say "the Holy King," or in other concluding blessings such as not saying "Shield of Abraham" or "Who revives the dead." However, any error in the middle of the blessings, where one added or omitted a small part, does not invalidate the prayer. There are many variations in the text of the prayers (as noted in Magen Avraham, section 9), and these do not constitute a deviation from the form established by the Sages. Nevertheless, if one recited any of the blessings in a completely shortened form, like the blessings for fruit or commandments, it is certainly considered a deviation, and one must repeat it (as noted there). There is a question regarding the blessing "the Holy God" if one concluded with "the Holy King" during the rest of the year, whether this constitutes a change, or perhaps "the King" is preferable and one has fulfilled their obligation. From the language of Rashi in Berachot (12b), who wrote that the reason for saying "the Holy King" during the Ten Days of Repentance is because during these days He shows His kingship by judging the world, it seems that this is not relevant throughout the rest of the year. If so, it would be akin to speaking falsehoods, and one must repeat the prayer. (See also Siman 118, further investigation is required.)

Our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 7: "In any case where we say 'he returns to the blessing where he made an error' – this applies only if he made an error unintentionally. But if he erred intentionally and deliberately – he returns to the beginning." Thus is his wording. And similarly, the Tur wrote in the name of Avi HaEzri, see there. Meaning: for example, if he said "He makes the wind blow and the rain fall" in the summer and did not complete the blessing, we say he returns to the start of the blessing – this is if it was unintentional and not intentional. And similarly, regarding the middle blessings, the rule is that if he erred, he returns to that blessing, or for the last three blessings, he returns to "Retzei" – this is all if it was unintentional. But if it was intentional, it is as if he did not pray at all, and he returns to the beginning of the prayer. There are those who question that our master, the Beit Yosef, contradicts himself, for he wrote in section 104 that even if he spoke intentionally, his ruling is the same as if it were done under duress, and we explained this there in section 12 (Bach). However, there is no contradiction at all: for only in the case where he spoke intentionally did he rule thus, where he prayed correctly but interrupted with speech, which is not the case here where he did not say something as ordained by the Sages intentionally – his entire prayer is an abomination, and he needs to pray a completely different prayer (and so is written in the Chiddushei HaHagot on the Tur).

If one is unsure in the summer months whether he said "He makes the wind blow and the rain fall" and must repeat the prayer, or he did not say it and prayed correctly, or if he is unsure in the winter months whether he did not say "He makes the wind blow and the rain fall" and must repeat the prayer, or if he did say it and prayed correctly. This is the case in Ashkenaz. But in Sefarad, there is no difference in the winter months, because even if he did not say "He makes the wind blow and the rain fall" – he said "He makes the dew fall" and fulfilled his obligation with that, as I wrote in section 9. And for thirty days, he is presumed not to have prayed correctly, because he is accustomed to say according to the previous season. After thirty days, he is presumed to have said it correctly, because he is already accustomed to it. And so ruled the Jerusalem Talmud in the first chapter of Taanit.

Our rabbi writes in section 9: If on the first day of Passover, one says "You are mighty" until "He makes the dew descend" ninety times, corresponding to thirty days where it is said three times each day, and from then on, if one does not remember if they mentioned rain – they have a presumption that they did not mention rain, and they do not need to repeat it. Thus far his words. And this is according to the Sephardic custom. According to the Ashkenazic custom, our Rabbi the Rema wrote: Similarly, for us, if one says up to "Who sustains life" without "Who makes the wind blow and the rain fall" during the rainy season. And similarly, if one said on Shemini Atzeret ninety times from "You are mighty" until "Who makes the rain fall", if afterwards one is unsure whether they mentioned it or not – there is a presumption that they mentioned it. Thus far his words. And although in thirty days there are more than ninety prayers because of the additional prayers of Shabbat and Rosh Chodesh, nevertheless the intention of the Jerusalem Talmud, which said thirty days, is for regular days that only have three prayers. This law is from Maharam of Rothenburg, brought by the Rosh and the Tur. They questioned it: for it is not comparable to make it fluent in his mouth by training himself for thirty days to saying it ninety times in one go. And there are more objections (see Beit Yosef, Bach, Taz, and Magen Avraham). It seems to me that he found a reason and relied on it because indeed a person who prays properly certainly says it correctly. But many times he forgets afterwards whether he said it correctly or not, and according to the law, he would need to repeat it. Indeed, this is very difficult, as it is more likely that he said it correctly. Therefore, he established this so that he would have a way to exempt himself according to the law as it is. And if he is a prayer leader – he can exempt himself in fifteen days since he also prayed out loud. But in the evening prayer, there is no repetition, and there are only seventy-five prayers, so he needs another five days, of course. ("And He maintains His faith to those who sleep in the dust." And the word "yeshanei" does not have a shva, and it is like: "For Your salvation I hope, O Lord.") And in the blessing "You are holy" there are fourteen words (Tur and Pri Etz Chaim).

The fourth blessing is "You graciously give knowledge." And why do we say it after the "Sanctification"? It is written in Isaiah: "And they shall sanctify the Holy One of Jacob," and immediately following it says: "And those who err in spirit shall come to understanding" (Megillah 17b). And it contains seventeen words (Tur and Pri Etz Chaim), corresponding to the number of words in the verse "And you shall speak unto all that are wise-hearted" (ibid.). And since the distinction of man over beast is understanding and intellect, therefore they established it as the first of the middle blessings. And if there is no understanding, there is no prayer (ibid.). And we recite the Havdalah in it on the conclusion of Shabbat and Festivals, as it is a matter of wisdom to distinguish between one thing and another (ibid.). That is to say: the distinction in spiritual matters, such as between holy and profane, is great wisdom. And the main petition is to ask the Blessed Name to grant him knowledge to shun evil and choose good (Eliyah Rabbah). And see what I wrote in Siman 294.

The fifth blessing is "Return us." And why do we say it after "Understanding"? Because understanding leads to repentance, as it is written: "Make the heart of this people fat, ... lest they see with their eyes, ... and understand with their heart and return and be healed" (Megillah there). And it has fifteen words corresponding to the fifteen words in the verse: "Let the wicked forsake his way" (Tur and Pri Etz Chaim). And great is repentance that reaches up to the Throne of Glory, and from the earth to the firmament is five hundred years, and likewise all the air between each firmament. And there are found seven firmaments and six airs between them, and the air from the earth to the first firmament, and the air from the seventh firmament to the Throne of Glory - there are fifteen (there). And the blessing begins with a "hey" and ends with a "hey," corresponding to the Ten Days of Repentance (there).

The sixth blessing is "Forgive us." It pertains to repentance, as it is written: "And let him return to the Lord, and He will have mercy upon him, and to our God, for He will abundantly pardon" (Megillah there). The reason we say "Our Father" in these two blessings is because a father is obligated to teach his son Torah. Therefore, we say: "Return us, our Father, to Your Torah." And in "Forgive us," we invoke mercy, asking that He have mercy on us as a father has mercy on his son, and that He abundantly pardon our sins (Tur). It contains twenty words (Pri Etz Chaim).

The seventh blessing "See our affliction." This is the wording in the Tur, and the number of words in this blessing is not counted. However, in the book Pri Etz Chaim, it is counted as I wrote in Siman 113, and it states that it is seventeen words. According to this, one should say "See our affliction" and not "See, please," and this is also the opinion of the Maharshal in his responsa (Siman 64). There are those who wrote to specifically say "See, please" (Magen Avraham), but I do not know who can decide contrary to the opinion of the Ari z"l, and the Maharshal supports him. And why did they establish redemption in the seventh? Because we are destined to be redeemed in the seventh – they established it in the seventh (Megillah there).

The eighth blessing is "Heal us." And why did they choose to say the blessing for healing in the eighth position? Because circumcision is on the eighth day and requires healing, therefore they established it in the eighth position (Megillah 17b). And there are twenty-seven words in it corresponding to the twenty-seven verses in the section on circumcision, and corresponding to the twenty-seven words in the verse "He said, 'If you listen carefully...for I am the Lord who heals you'" (Tur). And there are twenty-seven letters in the verse "For they are life to those who find them, and healing to all their flesh" (ibid).

The Ri"F, of blessed memory, at the end of the fourth chapter of Megillah, brought a Tosefta which states that one should not deviate from the language of the scripture. Based on this, they questioned: How do we say "Heal us, O Lord, and we shall be healed" in the plural form? For in Jeremiah it is written in the singular: "Heal me, O Lord, and I shall be healed." They answered that this applies to one who reads the verse or translates it, but not to those who say it as part of a prayer. And the congregation does not intend to recite the verse verbatim – they may alter it as necessary (Tur in the name of the Ramah). Furthermore, this is specifically regarding one who recites the entire psalm; however, when reciting selected verses within prayers, even if one intended this specific verse, since he is not reciting the entire psalm, he may alter it (there in the name of Rabbeinu Yonah). And this was agreed upon by the Rosh, of blessed memory. Therefore, regarding the verses in the Havdalah prayer, according to the first explanation, it is forbidden to alter them, but according to the second explanation, it is permitted (Taz). And similarly, in other matters of this nature. And one should say "Healer of the sick of His people Israel," with the 'lamed' of 'cholei' in a tzeirei (see Taz).

The ninth blessing is the blessing for the years [the blessing for sustenance]. It was established as the ninth blessing corresponding to those who artificially raise prices, as David said in the ninth verse: "Break the arm of the wicked," referring to those who artificially raise prices (Megillah 17a). Even though in our text it appears in Psalm 10, our sages of blessed memory received the tradition that "Happy is the man" and "Why do the nations rage" are one section (Berakhot 10b). And there are thirty words in it corresponding to the twenty-three words in the verse "The Lord will open for you..." and the seven words in the verse "You open Your hand" (Tur). 

Some say "satisfy us with Your goodness," and so wrote the Rosh in a responsum. Others say "satisfy us with its goodness," referring to the land. Some in the city say "with its goodness" and while traveling "with Your goodness," and to this, the Kabbalists agreed (as written by the Shlah in his Siddur).

In the Land of Israel, we begin to say "and give dew and rain" from the night of the seventh of Marcheshvan, because it is a land of mountains and valleys, and therefore it needs rain immediately after the festival [of Sukkot]. And the reason we do not ask for rain immediately after the festival is for the sake of the pilgrims who will return to their homes (Mishnah Ta'anit 1:3). Even though according to this reasoning, in our times, they should ask for rain immediately after the festival, nevertheless, the enactment has not changed.
