There is another reason given in the Gemara (Ta'anit 4b): because of the fruits that are left in the fields until the seventh of Marcheshvan, and we do not request rain then so that the fruits do not rot (see Ran on the first chapter of Ta'anit and Beit Yosef). The Rif did not bring this reason. His reasoning seems to me to be that so they do not say that if there are no fruits in the field, they should start immediately, which is not the case, as the Sages did not differentiate in their enactment. (And the reason he brought the matter of the pilgrims is because this reason is in the Mishnah there, and he brought the Mishnah in its form as is his way. But the reason is not because of this, but because the enactment has not changed.)

In Babylonia, which is a low-lying land and does not require as much rain, they begin asking for rain in the evening prayer on the sixtieth day after the autumnal equinox. The day of the equinox is included in the count of the sixty days, even if the equinox occurs in the middle of the day or later, as long as it is a bit before nightfall. For example, if the equinox is on Sunday, the request for rain begins in the evening prayer on Tuesday night, which corresponds to Wednesday. There are thus two full days between the equinox and the request for rain, Monday and Tuesday. (Therefore, the Pri Hadash is lenient regarding the first evening prayer if one forgets to say "dew and rain," because there are not yet sixty full days, and consequently also in the morning prayer if the equinox was later. The Pri Megadim does not agree with this, see there. The sexton announces "dew and rain" after the half-Kaddish so that everyone knows. If he did not announce it, it does not invalidate the prayer.)

And we, the people outside of the Land of Israel, follow the customs of the people of Babylon in all matters of law, even though at first glance this may not seem related to legal matters. The Rambam already wrote in his commentary on the Mishnah in Ta'anit that this matter depends on the countries, based on when they need rain. Therefore, in most European countries, where they sow after Pesach, we should technically say "dew and rain" in the summer, and in the winter, we do not need rain at all. The Rosh has already discussed this at length in his responsa. This is not comparable to individuals who need rain, as they say it in the "Shomea Tefillah" blessing, as will be explained, because we are not individuals but large communities. Nevertheless, the Rosh himself wrote that his words were not accepted at all; see there. It is as if a heavenly voice decreed to act like the people of Babylon. This is also clear from the words of the Rambam in his compilation in the second chapter, where he did not write as he did in the commentary on the Mishnah; see there. This is also the conclusion of our Rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, and this is the law. Anyone who questions this is deserving of punishment. Until when do we ask for rain? Until the evening of the first day of Pesach, and from then on, we cease asking (see Magen Avraham, subparagraph 2).

If one asked for rain during the summer months, he is made to repeat [the Amidah], whether he mentioned "dew" or did not mention it (Beit Yosef). And what is the ruling regarding his repetition? If he lifted his feet [to take three steps back], he must return to the beginning of the prayer. If he did not lift his feet, he returns to the blessing of "Bless Our Year." Even if he remembered before finishing the blessing, he still returns to the beginning of the blessing. This is not similar to the case of not mentioning [dew], where he can say it at the place where he stands, as I wrote in Siman 114 regarding the mention of rain, see there at the end of section 10.

Similarly, if one did not ask for rain during the rainy season, even though he mentioned "dew," he is made to repeat [the Amidah]. This is not similar to the mention [of rain], where one fulfills his obligation with "dew" as I wrote there, because regarding mentioning the might of the Holy One, Blessed be He, it suffices with dew since they [the dead] will live through dew, as I wrote there. However, regarding the request [for rain], without "rain" Heaven forbid, all crops are ruined – it does not suffice without rain. But if one asked for "rain" and did not ask for "dew," it does not prevent [fulfillment], and he is not made to repeat [the Amidah].

And what should one do if he forgot to say "mashiv haruach u'morid hageshem" (He who makes the wind blow and the rain descend)? If he remembers immediately within the blessing, or immediately after the blessing before he begins "Teka b'shofar" (Sound the great shofar), he should say there "Veten tal u'matar al p'nei ha'adama" (Give dew and rain upon the face of the earth), as I wrote regarding the mention (of rain) in Siman 114. If he remembers after he has started "Teka b'shofar," he should say it in "Shomea Tefillah" (Who hears prayer). In this case, it is better than the mention, since the mention does not belong in a prayer of request. However, the request can be said there, "Veten tal u'matar al p'nei ha'adama, ki Ata shomea..." (Give dew and rain upon the face of the earth, for You hear...), since any requests can be asked there, as will be explained in Siman 119. And even if it is a fast day when he needs to say "Aneinu" (Answer us) there, he should precede it with "Veten tal u'matar," because "matar" (rain) is essential and "Aneinu" is not essential if it was not said. But if he does not remember until after "Shomea Tefillah," if he has not yet started "Retze" (Be favorable), he should say "Veten tal u'matar al p'nei ha'adama" there, as after the blessing of the years. If he started "Retze," he goes back to "Barech Aleinu" (Bless us). When are these words said? When he has not lifted his feet. But if he has lifted his feet, he returns to the beginning of the prayer. And "lifting his feet" is not literal, but when he has completed the entire prayer, meaning "Hamevarech et amo Yisrael bashalom" (Who blesses His people Israel with peace), even if he has not yet lifted his feet, it is as if he has lifted them and he returns to the beginning. However, when he says supplications after the prayer, like "Elokai netzor" (My God, guard my tongue) and the like, if he has not yet finished the supplications, it is called "not lifted his feet." If he has finished them, it is as if he lifted his feet. And if he is accustomed to saying "Yihyu l’ratzon" (May the words of my mouth) after the supplications, it is not called "lifted his feet" until he says "Yihyu l’ratzon" that is after the supplications. (Magen Avraham in Siman 622, subsection 2, see there. And be precise and you will find it light.) (See Chayei Adam, General Rule 24, subsection 15, who wrote that "lifting his feet" literally is required. This needs investigation.)

Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote in Section 2: Individuals who need rain during the summer should not request it in the Blessing of the Years, but rather in "Shomea Tefillah" (the blessing of hearing prayers). Even a large city like Nineveh, or an entire country like all of Spain or all of Ashkenaz, are considered like individuals in "Shomea Tefillah." However, if an entire country needs rain during the summer and an individual mistakenly asked for rain in the Blessing of the Years, if he wishes, he can repeat the prayer as a voluntary prayer without requesting rain in the Blessing of the Years. But he is not obligated to repeat it at all. These are his words. Accordingly, it would seem that the reverse is also true: in our country during the winter, when we do not need rain, if one did not mention "dew and rain," he also does not need to repeat the prayer, just as in the summer when he did request it, as I wrote, for it is the same reasoning. And also, to pray as a voluntary prayer, we distance ourselves from this due to our lack of proper intent, as Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote in Section 107, see there.

But I have not seen any of the great authorities who said this. And all those who abbreviate the laws wrote simply that during the rainy season, if one did not say "dew and rain" – they must repeat [the prayer]. And they wrote this regarding our country, and in all our regions we do not need rain in the winter at all. And perhaps they reasoned to differentiate: that specifically if one said "dew and rain" when we need it, they do not need to repeat, but not when it is not said at a time when we do not need it, since according to the law one must say it – one is obligated to repeat. In my humble opinion, there is no distinction in this matter. And I have never ruled this way, nor have I ruled the opposite. And so I have accepted from my youth, that in the generation before us, there was one of the great authorities of the generation who did not want to rule this way. And know that the great authorities wrote that in any place where one needs to repeat, if one can hear the prayer from the public emissary from beginning to end – they have fulfilled their obligation. And one should be careful then not to interrupt with any conversation, and also not to answer "Blessed is He and blessed is His name," but only answer "Amen" alone. And this requires further study. (See Magen Avraham, subsection 4, who wrote that during the harvest season if one said "dew and rain" in the summer – they certainly need to repeat.)

And know that there are among the great authorities who warned that even during a period of drought in our region during the summer months, as we have written to request rain in the blessing of "Shomea Tefillah," in any case, one should not say "Ve'ten Tal u'Matar" (Give dew and rain), but rather increase in supplications with verses and psalms about rain. And it is written that two great authorities were punished for this (Bach, and brought by the Magen Avraham, small section 3). But there are those who disagree with this (Taz, small section 2), and this is the common custom among us. And it has already been printed in the prayer books, a prayer for a drought period in "Shomea Tefillah," which includes "Ve'ten Tal u'Matar," and there is no need to doubt this. However, one should be careful not to say this prayer except during a significant drought when it is seen that the crops are damaged, and not during a minor drought. And it is also written that even on Shabbat, they mention the thirteen attributes of mercy and recite verses about rain (Magen Avraham there). This is not the custom in our country.

The tenth blessing is "Sound the great shofar." For the redemption will be through the sounding of the shofar, as it is written: "And it shall come to pass on that day, that a great shofar will be sounded..." And why was this blessing established after the blessing of the years? Because it is written in Ezekiel (36) concerning the redemption: "But you, O mountains of Israel, you shall shoot forth your branches and yield your fruit to My people Israel, for they are soon to come. Behold, I am for you..." And it contains twenty words (Tur and Pri Etz Chaim) corresponding to the verse: "And on your joyous days... and you shall blow the trumpets..." which also contains twenty words (Tur, end of Siman 117).

The eleventh blessing is the blessing of "Restore," for once the exiles have been gathered, judgment is made upon the wicked, as it is written: "And I will purge away your dross as with lye, and remove all your alloy, and I will restore your judges as at the first" (Megillah there). And it contains twenty-four words corresponding to the twelve words in the verse "And I will restore," and corresponding to the twelve words in the verse "And I will betroth you to Me forever" (Pri Etz Chaim, page 60b).

The conclusion of this blessing is "King who loves righteousness and justice," and during the Ten Days of Repentance, "the King of justice." It is stated at the end of the first chapter of Berakhot that this is essential, and if one did not say it, he must be returned. If he has lifted his feet, he must return to the beginning of the prayer. If not, he returns to "Hashiva." Nevertheless, our teacher the Rema wrote, and this is his language: However, if one said "King who loves righteousness and justice," he does not need to return. They only said to return in a place where the whole year one says "God who loves righteousness and justice," and see further in Siman 582. Until here are his words. There are those who disagree with this, saying that even according to this version, throughout the year righteousness is primary, and during the Ten Days of Repentance justice is primary, and mentioning righteousness is inappropriate (Taz, section 2). But many agree with this (Magen Avraham, Bach, Shelah, and Magen Tzedek). However, in any case, it seems that even if the primary version is to say "God who loves righteousness and justice," we still say "King who loves righteousness and justice." If so, we can resolve the doubt we had in Siman 114, section 11: If one said "the Holy King" throughout the year, does he need to return? It seems that he does not need to return, contrary to what I wrote there. Or perhaps it can be distinguished, and it requires further study. (And in Shaarei Teshuva, he brought different opinions on this matter.)

And the twelfth blessing is "against informers." It was established after the blessing of justice, for once justice is enacted, the informers are eliminated. For after "And I will restore your judges as at first" it is written "and the sinners shall be broken together" (Megillah ibid.), which includes the wicked among them (ibid.). For afterwards it is written: "And those who forsake the Lord shall perish," and these are the wicked who act willfully against the Holy One, blessed be He, and they are the informers, heretics, and the willful sinners. This blessing contains twenty-nine words, corresponding to the Written Torah, the Oral Torah, and twenty-seven letters, for with the final forms (מנצפ"ך) there are twenty-seven letters (Tur and Pri Etz Chaim). And because in this blessing the texts are not consistent in the siddurim due to errors by the proofreaders, I will write the correct text. And it is as follows: "And for the informers let there be no hope, and may all the heretics and all the wicked perish instantly, and may all Your enemies be swiftly cut off. And may the willful sinners be swiftly uprooted, broken, cast down, and subdued in our days. Blessed are You, O Lord, who breaks enemies and humbles the wicked." And thus I found it in an old book.

The thirteenth blessing "On the righteous." After the uprooting of the slanderers, the horn of the righteous will be exalted, as it is written: "And all the horns of the wicked I will cut off, but the horns of the righteous shall be exalted" (Megillah there). And this blessing contains forty-two words (Tur and Pri Etz Chaim). According to this, there is no need to say "May Your mercies be stirred" but rather "May Your mercies stir." Similarly, one should not say "the remnant of their scribes" but "the remnant of the scribes." And so it is in accurate prayer books. According to this, there are forty-two words; with these two additional words, there would be forty-four. (And these forty-two words correspond to the Name of forty-two with which the world was created, as explained by Tosafot at the beginning of the second chapter of Chagigah. And for the sake of the righteous, the world was created, as written in Pri Etz Chaim there. In the Tur, there are hints from verses; see there.)

The fourteenth blessing, "And to Jerusalem, Your city." Where does the exaltation of the righteous from the previous blessing rise? In Jerusalem, as it is said: "Pray for the peace of Jerusalem, those who love you will be serene." Meaning: the righteous, who are His beloved, will live in peace (Megillah, there). And it contains twenty-four words corresponding to the twenty-four letters in the verse "The Lord builds Jerusalem..." And according to this, one should not say "And the throne of David, Your servant, prepare quickly within it," because then there would be twenty-five words. Rather, "And the throne of David, quickly... (This count is in Tur and Pri Etz Chaim there). The fifteenth blessing is "The offspring of David." They established it after "Who builds Jerusalem," because once Jerusalem is built, David comes, as it is said: "Afterward, the children of Israel will return and seek the Lord their God, and David their king" (Megillah, there). And it contains twenty words like in the verse "For the Lord has comforted Zion" (there).

The sixteenth blessing is "Hear our voice." It is placed next to "The offspring of David," because when David comes, prayer arrives, as it is said: "I will bring them to My holy mountain and make them joyful in My house of prayer" (Megillah, there). This blessing contains thirty-five words, and your mnemonic is: "Is this how you repay Hashem?" These are the same number of words as in the psalm "A Psalm of David" from "Hear, O Lord, righteousness" to "I have resolved that my mouth will not sin" (Pri Etz Chaim, there). The other blessings will be explained in Siman 120 with the help of Heaven.

If one wishes to add any request, he may do so in any of the middle blessings, each one according to its appropriate theme. How so? If he has a sick person in his house or family, he may ask for mercy for them in the blessing of "Heal us." If he needs sustenance, he requests it in the blessing of the years. Similarly, for all other needs: if he wants to ask God to strengthen his heart towards Torah, he should ask in "You graciously bestow knowledge." If he seeks help in repentance, he should ask in "Bring us back." If he wishes for forgiveness of sins, he should ask in "Forgive us." And so on. However, in the blessing of "Hear our voice" he can request anything he desires, because it is general and not specific, and it encompasses all requests. One should not begin his request at the start of the blessing, but rather begin with the blessing itself, as the main focus is the text established by the Sages. Before reciting the conclusion of the blessing, one should make his request and ensure that his request concludes in a manner similar to the closing of the blessing. When asking for mercy for a sick person, if he is praying in the presence of the sick person, he does not need to mention the person's name but should say: "Please send healing to this sick person," as Moses our teacher said: "Please, God, heal her now" (Berakhot 34a). However, if he is not in the presence of the sick person, he needs to mention the person's name, along with the name of their father or mother, to specify in his prayer for whom he is asking for mercy. For prayer must be clear. (See Rashi on Taanit 14b, beginning with "And in 'Hear our voice'," where he writes that all requests should be made only in "Hear our voice." This is quite surprising and requires further investigation.)

And know that it is a simple matter that our sages of blessed memory did not permit adding to the Shemoneh Esrei except in a case when necessary. But to add a fixed and permanent prayer to the Shemoneh Esrei is excessive audacity and insolence toward the Men of the Great Assembly. On this, every Torah scholar and everyone who has the fear of Hashem within him will agree. Therefore, it is appropriate to cry out against the printers who added in the Siddurim a fixed prayer in the "Shma Koleinu" section: "Please Hashem, I have sinned... You are the one who sustains and provides...". And many of the common people say this always as part of the Shemoneh Esrei, and my heart is in pain over this practice. And I heard that one of the great sages of the previous generation already protested against this. But due to our many sins, the world has been handed over to the foolish, and the printers do as they please, and we are unable to protest. And that which they brought from the Zohar that it is good to always ask for one's sustenance even if he is wealthy, or to confess his sins (Magen Avraham, small section 1) – this is indeed correct, but not to make it a fixed text within the prayers of the Men of the Great Assembly. If one wishes, he can say them after the prayer, after "Yihyu L'ratzon", and who will protest against him? And it has already been said in the Gemara that after the prayer one can say even the order of Yom Kippur.

Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote that according to Rabbeinu Yonah, when one adds a request similar to the blessing, if he adds it for all of Israel, he should say it in the plural form and not in the singular form. He should only add it at the end of the blessing and not in the middle. However, if he asks for his own needs, such as if he has a sick person in his house or he needs sustenance, he may ask even in the middle of the blessing, and he should ask in the singular form and not in the plural form. In the blessing of "Shomea Tefillah" and at the end of the prayer, whether before "Yihyu L'ratzon" or after it, he can ask either in the singular or plural form, whether for his own needs or for the needs of the community. This is the end of his words.

There are those who say that according to Rabbeinu Yonah, even in "Shomea Tefillah" it is forbidden to speak in the plural form (Magen Avraham in the name of Bach). In any case, the community is permitted even in the middle of a blessing (there in the name of Beit Yosef), and therefore in old synagogues, it is customary that in the middle of "Selach Lanu" they say all the supplications on the day they say supplications.

Know that Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote these laws in the name of Rabbeinu Yonah and did not write them as a general rule, because in his major work he wrote that Rambam and the Rosh do not hold these principles. According to them, in any case, it is permitted, and the law follows them, but it is good to be concerned about the words of Rabbeinu Yonah, see there. Therefore, he wrote them in his name, to inform that one can act contrary to his words according to the basic law.

It is further written in Section 2: There is an opinion that if one adds to the blessing for the sake of an individual, he should not prolong it. Thus is his wording. But after the prayer, one is permitted to prolong it (Magen Avraham). And if it is for the sake of a great person, the congregation can prolong it even in the middle of the blessing. When the Maharil was ill, the congregation recited Selichot, for since they needed his Torah, it was considered as if it were for the many (ibid.). And it seems that they said the Selichot in the blessing of "Forgive us," as was their custom in reciting Selichot.

The middle blessings are not like the first three, for all of them are considered as one unit, and if one errs in one of them, he returns to the beginning. The middle blessings are not considered as one. Nevertheless, they must be in order, meaning: one should not precede a later blessing to an earlier one. Therefore, if one erred in one of them in a way that requires him to return, or if he did not say a particular blessing at all and skipped it, and he remembered after he had already recited other blessings – he returns to the blessing in which he erred or which he skipped, and recites from there onward in order. Even those he already recited – he repeats them. However, he does not need to return to the beginning of "You graciously bestow knowledge." This applies when it was done unintentionally or by mistake. But if he intentionally skipped a particular blessing, or did not recite it in accordance with the ordinance of the Sages – it is as if he did not pray at all, and he returns to the beginning of the prayer, as I wrote in Siman 114 (Magen Avraham, subsection 5).

If the prayer leader forgot to say "Aneinu" between "Goel" and "Rofeh" and started "Refa'einu," if he has not yet finished the blessing, he should return to "Aneinu" and then pray in order. However, if he has finished the blessing, and if he returns to "Aneinu" he would need to say the "Refa'einu" blessing again because he must pray in order as has been explained, and in truth, "Aneinu" is not essential and it is not possible to add another blessing to the congregation, it would be a blessing in vain and he should not say it at all now. Instead, he should say it in "Shomea Tefillah" like an individual, and he can conclude with "Blessed are You, Hashem, who answers in times of trouble and hears prayer." However, saying it only in "Shomea Tefillah" is sufficient, for it includes everything, as is obvious (Magen Avraham, section 7). Similarly, if there were not ten people fasting in the synagogue and he did not say "Aneinu," and after "Refa'einu" they arrived – he should do the same (there). And if he forgot to say it even in "Shomea Tefillah," he should say it as a separate blessing after "Sim Shalom," for in that case, the order does not matter when saying it completely after the prayer (there). Nevertheless, if he said it before "Re'eh Ve'anyenu," it seems he must return and say it after "Re'eh Ve'anyenu" as the sages instituted (there), because he is still within the prayer. There is, however, one who disagrees and holds that he does not need to return and say it after "Re'eh Ve'anyenu," and also when he says it after "Sim Shalom" he should not conclude with the name but only "Blessed is the one who hears prayer" (some later authorities have written this). According to Rashi, he should say "Aneinu" as a blessing in the middle of the blessings, and this will be explained in more detail in section 566 with the help of Heaven.

The last three blessings have the same status as the first three. They are considered as one unit, and if one makes a mistake in any of them, he must return to the beginning of them, to "Retzei." These are the seventeenth, eighteenth, and nineteenth blessings. Although it is called "Shemoneh Esrei" (the Eighteen Blessings), the blessing against heretics was added later in Yavneh, and Shmuel HaKatan composed it. The seventeenth blessing is "Retzei," and it contains thirty-four words, corresponding to the verses from "I will enter Your house with burnt offerings" to "which He has done for my soul" (Pri Etz Chaim, page 61a). 

Our sages, of blessed memory, have already said in Berachot (34a) that the last three blessings are like a servant who has received a reward from his master and is taking leave. Therefore, before leaving, he offers thanks to his master and requests that he establish peace among us, which is the essence of the blessing. Before this, he asks that his prayer and sacrifices be accepted, which is "the offerings of Israel," as it is written regarding the sacrifices in Leviticus: "an offering made by fire, a pleasing aroma to the Lord," and similarly in the section of the Tamid. Even though there are no sacrifices now, the prayer takes the place of the sacrifices (Tur). According to this, the interpretation is as follows: "the offerings of Israel and their prayers, which are in place of the offerings, accept with favor," and "the offerings of Israel" refers to what is below (Beit Yosef). 

There is a simple explanation that it refers to what is above: "Restore the service to Your sanctuary and the offerings of Israel," and there is no difficulty at all. In the Midrash, it is said that Michael, the great prince, offers the souls of the righteous on the heavenly altar, and for this, they established "the offerings of Israel" (Tur and Tosafot at the end of Menachot). Michael is the high priest above, just as Aaron was in this manner below. This is hinted at in the eighth day of the consecration, when Aaron was appointed in this manner, and Michael was also appointed above in this manner, as it is written there: "for today the Lord will appear to you." The word "will appear" contains the letters of "Aaron," and "to you" contains the letters of "Michael" (so I have seen). The matter of offering souls is that the souls achieve such delight in their attachment to the supernal light, and it is a delight without measure or limit, and this is the term "offering," meaning drawing close. These matters are ancient. 

This is why the blessing of "Retzei" is placed next to "Shomea Tefillah," for when prayer is present, service is present, as it is written: "I will bring them to My holy mountain and make them joyful in My house of prayer; their burnt offerings and their sacrifices will be accepted on My altar, for My house will be called a house of prayer..." (Megillah 18a). Therefore, we say "Modim" afterward, for when service is present, thanksgiving is present, as it is written: "He who offers thanksgiving honors Me" (ibid.). The priestly blessing follows "Modim," as it is written: "Aaron lifted his hands toward the people and blessed them; and he came down after making the sin offering..." – thus, the priestly blessing follows the service. Service and thanksgiving are one matter, for thanksgiving is also considered service (ibid.). Consequently, since the priestly blessing concludes with peace, we say "Sim Shalom." This is the summary of the last three blessings (and another reason will be explained).

Our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote: "We say 'Retzei' in all prayers, contrary to those who have the custom not to say it at Mincha." Thus far his words. The explanation of his words: The Tur wrote in the name of the Geonim that they would only say 'Retzei' at the time of the Priestly Blessing, for then the priests ascend to the platform, as I wrote in Siman 128. But at Mincha, when there is no Priestly Blessing, they would begin with 'Ve'ishei Yisrael'. The Tur was already puzzled by this; see there. Therefore, he wrote that we say 'Retzei' in all prayers.

We have already written about the reason for the juxtaposition of the "Modim" blessing to the "Retzeh" blessing. And there are eighty-six words in the "Modim" blessing, and similarly in the psalm "For the conductor, on the death of the son" until "declare among the nations His deeds" there are eighty-six words (Pri Etz Chaim there). For it is written there: "I will thank the Lord with all my heart, I will recount all Your wonders," and similarly this blessing is one of thanksgiving, and we say "and for Your wonders and goodness..." And this number in gematria is "Elohim," to signify that all thanksgiving is only to God alone. And even at a time when we do not feel wonders, nevertheless there are always wonders, as it is written: "Give thanks to the Lord for He is good, for His kindness endures forever." For one who experiences a miracle does not recognize his own miracle, as expounded in the Midrash (Yalkut Shimoni Isaiah remez 417) on the verse "Who alone does great wonders." And this is "for His kindness endures forever." Therefore, we say in the "Modim" blessing: "for Your miracles that are with us every day, and for Your wonders and goodness at all times..."

One bows during "Modim" at the beginning of the blessing and at the end of the blessing, when saying "Blessed are You, Hashem, Your name is good...". If one happens to have saliva in his mouth, he should not bow until the saliva exits his mouth (Magen Avraham), because if he spits while bowing, it appears as if, Heaven forbid, he is spitting on this. Anyone who says "Modim Modim" (repeats "Modim" twice) is silenced, because it appears, Heaven forbid, as if there are two authorities. Therefore, one should say "Modim" only once. In general, one should avoid saying any word twice; now, if before a mortal king, one would not do this, how much more so before the King of Kings, the Holy One, Blessed be He?

Our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote: An individual should not recite the Priestly Blessing. This is his language. And our master, the Rema, wrote on this: This is the main ruling, and it seems to me that this is the practice we should follow. However, the common custom is not like this, but even an individual recites it whenever it is appropriate for the Priestly Blessing, and it does not appear otherwise. This is his language. And in our days, we have never heard of an individual reciting the Priestly Blessing. However, from this, we can at least learn that one who prays with the prayer leader word by word should recite it together with the prayer leader. And in a house of mourning, the Priestly Blessing is not recited. This is the common custom and should not be changed, although there are those who question this.

The Tur wrote: The nineteenth blessing is "Sim Shalom." It was instituted after the Priestly Blessing, as it is written: "And they shall place My name upon the children of Israel, and I will bless them." And the blessing of the Holy One, Blessed be He, is "peace," as it is written: "The Lord will give strength to His people; the Lord will bless His people with peace." Thus far his words. And it is taught at the end of the tractate Derech Eretz in the chapter "Great is Peace" that the prayer concludes with "peace." Neither the Tur nor the Pri Etz Chaim counted the number of words in this blessing. There are fifty-three words in it, and those who say "life, grace, kindness, and mercy" have fifty-four words. (And it appears to me that this corresponds to the verse: "And the spirit clothed Amasai..." until "and peace," look there. And there are fifty-three letters in it. However, this verse is in Divrei HaYamim I 12:19, and every "David" in Divrei HaYamim is spelled with a full Yud, making fifty-four letters. And both versions are correct. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

Rabbeinu the Beit Yosef wrote: If one wishes to interrupt and respond to Kaddish or Kedusha between the Amidah and "Yehiu L'ratzon" – he should not interrupt, since "Yehiu L'ratzon" is part of the prayer. However, between "Yehiu L'ratzon" and other supplications – it is permissible. Thus far his words. There is no novelty in this, for are supplications a requirement of the prayer? Rather, it informs us: for instance, we who always recite a specific supplication, namely "Elokai Netzor," and there was room to say that we have accepted it upon ourselves as an obligation similar to the eighteen blessings of the Amidah, and thus should not interrupt it – it informs us that it is permissible to interrupt to respond to Kaddish… And it seems that even "Amen" is permissible to answer, for although it is compared to the blessings of the Shema as will be explained, in any case, it is not exactly so. (See Taz, subsection 1, and his words need examination, for according to what I wrote, it is explained well with good reason. And I do not know his reasoning. Delve and you will find it easy.) (And what compelled me to this interpretation will be explained in subsection 3).

And afterwards he wrote: However, one who is accustomed to saying supplications after his prayer, if the prayer leader begins to arrange his prayer and reaches Kaddish or Kedusha, he should shorten and conclude. And if he did not shorten, he may interrupt in the manner one interrupts in the blessing of the Shema, even in the middle. Thus far his words. The explanation of his words is as follows: Certainly, it is a mitzvah and obligation to say "May the words of my mouth be acceptable" immediately after "Who blesses His people Israel with peace," for our sages of blessed memory instituted to say beforehand "O Lord, open my lips..." and afterwards "May the words of my mouth be acceptable." And just as it is forbidden to interrupt between "O Lord, open my lips" and the first blessing, so too it is forbidden to interrupt between the last blessing and "May the words of my mouth be acceptable." And indeed, this is how one should conduct oneself, and so all Torah scholars practice. And one who wishes to say "May the words of my mouth be acceptable" again after the supplications may do so, and there are those who practice this way. (And so wrote the Magen Avraham, subsection 1, in the name of K.A. and L.A.).

This is what is written later in section 2, and this is its wording: It is not proper to say supplications before "May the words of my mouth be acceptable." Rather, after finishing the Amidah, one should immediately say "May the words of my mouth be acceptable." If one wishes to repeat it again after the supplications, he may do so. This is the end of its wording. However, the matter of supplications depends: one who does not make a fixed practice to always say them, or sometimes says this supplication and sometimes another, as in the Gemara there are many supplications that each person would say after the prayer, if he practices this way, the interruption is entirely permitted. However, one who regularly says one supplication always and makes it obligatory upon himself, like we have adopted the prayer "My God, guard my tongue" always, and it is obligatory upon us; therefore, although it is not exactly like the Amidah, it still has the status of "middle of the prayer." This is what our master the Beit Yosef says: and if one is accustomed to say a single supplication regularly and makes it obligatory upon himself, even if he said "May the words of my mouth be acceptable" beforehand, it is still not considered an interruption. Therefore, it is better to shorten and say "Who makes peace." However, if he did not shorten, he may interrupt like in the blessings of the Shema, and it is not exactly like the Amidah. And we have already written that even a simple "Amen" may be answered. Interruption for anything else is forbidden, as he has not yet taken his steps back. However, in any case, the intention of our master the Beit Yosef is even if he said "May the words of my mouth be acceptable" before the supplications. (See Magen Avraham, section 2, who writes: If there is no time to step back, one should immediately say "May the words of my mouth be acceptable" and answer. This is the end of his wording. I am puzzled that he copied this from the words of the Rema in Darkei Moshe, and the Rema does not hold like this as will be explained. And the Beit Yosef does hold that it is necessary to say "May the words of my mouth be acceptable" before the supplications. This requires further study. Examine and you will find it easy.)

However, our teacher, the Rema, on the matter of not interrupting for Kaddish or Kedusha between the Amidah and "Yihyu L'ratzon," wrote the following, and this is his language: Specifically in a place where they are accustomed to say "Yihyu L'ratzon" immediately after the prayer. But in a place where they are accustomed to say supplications before "Yihyu L'ratzon" — one also interrupts for Kaddish and Kedusha. And in these places, it is customary to interrupt in "Elokai Netzor" before "Yihyu L'ratzon," and therefore one also interrupts for Kaddish, Kedusha, and "Barchu." Thus far his language. And behold, several of the great ones have protested loudly against him, arguing how it is possible not to say "Yihyu L'ratzon" immediately after the Amidah? (Taz, Bach, Levush, and this also appears to be the opinion of the Magen Avraham in subsection 1 and the Elya Rabbah.)

And certainly, you are correct that this is the preferred method, and whoever wishes may also say it after the supplications. However, our master, the Rema, who loved the Jewish people, recognized that this was the custom in his time and did not want to make it seem as if they were violating the Talmudic law. Even in our times, I have heard that the majority of Jews do not say "May the words of my mouth" until after "My God, guard my tongue." Therefore, it is necessary to clarify this matter. 

One who examines the Tur will clearly see that he also holds this view, that "May the words of my mouth" should not be said until after the supplications, as he wrote: "And after he concludes the eighteen blessings, before 'My God, guard my tongue' – he may respond to Kaddish...," thus far his words. There are those who wrote that his intention is after concluding the eighteen blessings and after saying "May the words of my mouth" (Bach). Besides the difficulty, as the Tur's method is to explain and not to obscure, it is also problematic: if so, what is he teaching us? Although Rabbi Yosef Karo resolved this because he prefaced by saying one should not interrupt before "May the words of my mouth," the Tur did not mention this at all. Similarly, later in this section, the Tur wrote: "After 'Do it for Your name's sake' – 'May the words of my mouth.'" See there. And if you think that he also said this previously, why is it needed afterward? And although we wrote that one may say it, nevertheless, there is no obligation. What need do we have to bring from the Tur? It is explicitly stated in the Gemara (Berachot 17a) that Mar the son of Ravina, when he finished his prayer, would say: "My God, guard my tongue from evil..., and disrupt their plans. May the words of my mouth..." See there. It is clear that "May the words of my mouth" is after "My God, guard my tongue." Perhaps this is why we chose the prayer "My God, guard my tongue" from all the prayers in the Gemara, because it explicitly states that "May the words of my mouth" comes afterward.

The matter is as follows: Upon careful examination, we see that the Tur wrote in the name of Rav Amram Gaon, and this is his wording: "From this point onward, after the eighteen blessings, it is forbidden to speak in praise of God, as it is written: 'Who can utter...'. However, if one wishes to say after his prayer 'Our King...', 'My God, before I was created...', 'My God, guard my tongue...' up to 'my Rock and my Redeemer', he may do so." This is his wording. 

We must understand: if it is after "May the words of my mouth...", one may say whatever he wishes. And if it is because he has not yet taken three steps back – it is explicitly stated in the Gemara that after the prayer, one can even recite the order of the Day of Atonement. Moreover, what is the meaning of what he wrote "up to 'my Rock and my Redeemer'"? 

Rather, it is certainly this point that is the main novelty: even though he has not yet said the "May the words of my mouth", he may still say supplications. They derived this from the Gemara there, which stated that one master said this after his prayer, and another master said that, see there. 

And what is the novelty, since anyone can arrange supplications for himself? Rather, it informs us that one master said this after his prayer before "May the words of my mouth", and another master said that before "May the words of my mouth". Therefore, it is forbidden to extend it too much, because the "May the words of my mouth" would become very distant from the eighteen blessings. However, a short prayer is permitted. Therefore, the author of the Gemara says that one master said this short prayer, and another master said that short prayer. Therefore, it is also permitted to say Kaddish and Kedusha.

And the reason for this matter is that "May the words of my mouth be acceptable" is not similar to "O Lord, open my lips." For there, at the beginning of the prayer when he says "and my mouth will declare Your praise" – it is indeed obligatory to say the praises that our sages of blessed memory instituted. But at the end of the prayer, where he is merely asking that his prayer be accepted favorably – what harm is there if he requests something additional? After all, even in the middle of the prayer, in the middle blessings, he can ask for what he needs, and all the more so at the end of the prayer? And it is clear that this is the opinion of the Tur and the Geonim. And they wrote that after "My God, guard my tongue from evil" one should say "Do for the sake of Your name, do for the sake of Your right hand, do for the sake of Your holiness, do for the sake of Your Torah." For it is said in the Aggadah: Whoever habitually says these words merits and receives the Divine Presence. And we customarily add the verse "So that Your beloved ones may be delivered, save with Your right hand and answer me." And additionally, it is customary to say a verse that begins with the letter of his name and ends with the letter of his name. In any case, one should not extend the supplications too much.

When one finishes their entire prayer, they should bow and take three steps back while still bowed, akin to a servant taking leave of their master by bowing and walking backward. One should not take more than three steps, as it would appear arrogant (Beit Yosef). Why three steps? The Geonim explained that when a person stands in prayer, they stand in a place of holiness with the Divine Presence above their head, and when they conclude their prayer, they step backward to leave to a mundane place. It is found in the Midrash that at the time of the giving of the Torah, Israel distanced themselves three miles from Mount Sinai; and Moses our teacher entered through three partitions before the Holy One, blessed be He: darkness, cloud, and thick darkness. When he exited, he exited through these three partitions. Similarly, the priest, upon completing the service on the altar, would descend the ramp, which also involved three steps (there). The steps should be heel to toe. It is mentioned in the Midrash Shocher Tov that one should lift their left foot first (there).

After taking three steps back, while still bowing before straightening up, when saying "He who makes peace in His heights," one should turn his face to his left, which is the right of the Divine Presence, for the one praying envisions the Divine Presence opposite him, and thus his left side is the right side of the Divine Presence. When saying "He will make peace upon us," he turns his face to his right. When saying "and upon all Israel," he bows forward like a servant taking leave of his master. It is customary to say "May it be Your will… that the Temple be rebuilt…", because the prayer substitutes the sacrifice, and thus we ask that the Temple be rebuilt so that we may offer the sacrifices in actuality. There is another reason: our Sages of blessed memory said (Sanhedrin 96b) that Nebuchadnezzar was rewarded for some steps he took, with the destruction of the Temple. Therefore, we ask the opposite: that in reward for our steps, we merit its rebuilding. We conclude with "and give us our portion in Your Torah," as the Mishna in Avot concludes. This is straightforward, because then we will also merit the light of the Torah much more than now, through the light of the Temple from the Divine Presence. Some also conclude with the verse "and there we will serve You…".

In a place where one has finished the three steps back, he should stand there and not immediately return to his original place. If he does so, it would have been better had he not prayed at all. The Gemara says about this that it is like a dog returning to its vomit (Yoma 53b), for he has taken leave of his Master, and now it appears that he is retracting from his prayer and request for forgiveness, and wants to sin again (Beit Yosef). Therefore, he should not return to his place until the prayer leader reaches the Kedusha, because then everyone will see that he is returning to his place for the sake of Kedusha. If the space is too tight to stand there, he can return to his place when the prayer leader starts the repetition of the Amidah. This is the opinion of the Rif. Similarly, when piyutim (liturgical poems) are recited, he may return to his place at the beginning of the piyut, as in this way it is clear to all why he is returning to his place: either for the recitation of the piyut or to hear the repetition of the prayer leader from his place. As long as the prayer leader has not started, he should not turn his face to another direction but should stand with his face to the east, for if he turns his face, it will cause those who are still praying to lose their concentration as they will look at him (Taz, subsection 5). But when the prayer leader has started, he may turn his face, and he should stand until the Kedusha. There are those who wrote that while standing there, he must align his feet as in prayer (Magen Avraham, subsection 5, in the name of Radach). These are astonishing words: what relevance does aligning feet have there? (I examined Radach, house 23, and it refers to Kedusha, see there.) This is not necessary at all, and it is not customary to do so, as there is no reason for it. (Also, what Magen Avraham brings from Binyamin Ze'ev is not there at all, as Eliyah Rabbah wrote.)

Some have the custom to be particular that when stepping back after completing the prayer, no one should pass between them and the place where they prayed. The reason for this is that some say that six steps are required because a "step" is only considered such when both feet are moved. This was also the custom of the sages of France, and they have support from the verse at the beginning of Ezekiel regarding the creatures of the chariot: "And their feet were straight feet," "their feet" implying two, and "foot" implying one, making three. And later it is written: "And the sole of their feet was like the sole of a calf’s foot," again making three. Therefore, they count the three steps that one takes back to their place during the Kedusha in addition to the initial three steps. According to this, there should be no interruption between them (see Beit Yosef). However, there are those who, upon seeing someone about to interrupt, quickly return to their place. This is a mistake, for not returning to one's place is a matter of Talmudic law, while avoiding an interruption is merely a matter of enhancement. Therefore, one should not do this, and if an interruption occurs, it occurs. 

Additionally, there are those who, upon completing their prayer and stepping back, quickly return to their place if the prayer leader begins the Kedusha. This also does not seem correct to me, even though it is clear that they return because of the Kedusha. Nevertheless, one should not nullify a matter of Talmudic law for this reason. It is better to recite the Kedusha where they stepped back rather than return immediately, and at the very least, they should wait the time it takes to walk four cubits. Furthermore, one can stand until the prayer leader reaches "Kadosh" (Holy), which is where the main Kedusha begins.

It is questionable whether one fulfills the requirement with steps taken to the side. This is because sometimes the space behind him is constrained, and perhaps stepping to the side is also considered as taking leave from before the king? There is no proof from the statement "to the rear," for certainly that is generally the case, but when it is impossible, stepping to the side is also acceptable. It seems to me that there is proof for this from what is said in Yoma (53a): "And so too, the priests in their service... did not turn their faces and go, but rather they turned their faces to the side and went." And so too, a student taking leave from his teacher... turns his face to the side and goes. See there. And thus I practice in places where there is great constraint behind me.

Rabbi Moses Isserles (Rema) wrote in paragraph 2: The prayer leader should stand the distance of four cubits before returning to his place and praying out loud. Similarly, an individual praying should stand in the place where his steps ended for this duration before returning to his place. And an individual praying in a congregation, who finished his prayer before the prayer leader – it is forbidden to turn his face to the congregation until the prayer leader has finished his prayer. Thus far his words. When the prayer leader finishes – it is permitted to turn his face even before the prayer leader begins to pray out loud. There are those who are stringent that an individual praying should not return until the duration in which, if he were in a congregation, the prayer leader would say Kedusha. For only for the prayer leader did they permit the four cubits because of the exertion of the congregation, and only between one prayer and another did they permit this duration in section 105 (Bach and Magen Avraham, subsection 8). Regarding the reason for the prohibition of turning the face, we have already written a reason. Additionally, there is another reason: so that he will not be suspected of having skipped parts of the prayer (Levush).

And we have already written that when stepping back, one should lift the left foot first. There are those who wish to say the reason for this is to show that it is difficult for him to part from the prayer. According to this, a left-handed person should lift his left foot, which is considered the right foot for others (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 10). But we have already written the reason is because this is the right side of the Divine Presence (there, subparagraph 6), and according to this, a left-handed person should also do the same. The steps should be heel-to-toe. One should not take larger steps than this, as it appears as if he is fleeing. There are three steps: first the left one, then the right foot to the heel of the left, and then the left foot to the heel of the right. Some do it this way: they lift the left foot, then place the right foot next to the left, lift the left again and place the right next to it, and so on for the third step. In this way, it becomes six steps (see Maadanei Yom Tov in Lechem Chamudos at the end of the fifth chapter, letter 67. And in Magen Avraham, subparagraph 10, he brings this in a "pressed" language, see there).

It has also been clarified that adding more than three steps is considered arrogance, as it seems that one is showing more honor to the Shechinah (Divine Presence) than other people do (Taz). Furthermore, the prayer leader (Shaliach Tzibur) must also take three steps when praying silently. However, when he repeats the prayer out loud, he does not need to take the three steps again, relying instead on the Kaddish recited after "Uva L'Tzion" to take the steps during "Oseh Shalom." Even though there is an interruption, it is still considered part of the prayer (Magen Avraham, subsection 11). Nevertheless, if he is accustomed to taking the steps, he should not be reprimanded (ibid). Similarly, if he did not pray silently but only out loud, he should take three steps immediately after the loud prayer. When repeating the prayer, the prayer leader should say the verse "Hashem, open my lips" at the beginning. However, he does not say "May the words of my mouth..." at the end of the prayer, relying instead on the "Tiskabel" said after the prayer. Some are accustomed to saying "May the words of my mouth..." as well (ibid, in the name of the Shelah), and this is our custom. (The reasoning of the Taz in subsection 9 is strained.)

From the enactment of the Men of the Great Assembly, after the congregation has completed their prayer, the prayer leader repeats the entire prayer aloud. And it was taught at the end of Tractate Rosh Hashanah: Just as the prayer leader is obligated [to pray], so too is every individual obligated [to pray]. Rabban Gamliel says: The prayer leader fulfills the obligation on behalf of the public. But the halacha follows the Sages. And in the Gemara there, Rabban Gamliel asked the Sages: If so, why does the prayer leader go before the ark [to lead the prayer]? They said to him: To fulfill the obligation on behalf of one who is not proficient in prayer, but one who is proficient does not fulfill his obligation with the prayer of the prayer leader. This is what the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch wrote: After the congregation has completed their prayer, the prayer leader should repeat the prayer, so that if there is someone who does not know how to pray, they can direct their attention to what he says and fulfill their obligation through it. And the one who fulfills his obligation with the prayer of the prayer leader must direct his attention to everything the prayer leader says from beginning to end. He should not interrupt or speak. And he takes three steps backward as one who prays individually. Up to here is their language.

Know that the commentators explained that the one who is "not proficient" is someone who is not proficient in praying, but nevertheless understands what the prayer leader is saying. For if this were not the case, it would not be relevant to say that he should have intent (Beit Yosef and Taz, Section 1, and Magen Avraham, Section 2). However, it is not clear, for what should one do if he does not understand as well? It seems that their intention is as I wrote later in Siman 193 regarding the Grace After Meals: that one who understands fulfills his obligation by listening, and one who does not understand should recite word by word with the prayer leader. Then he fulfills his obligation even though he does not know the meaning of the words, just like one who prays by himself without understanding the holy language and fulfills his obligation. For it is only when praying in another language that one needs to understand the language, as I wrote in Siman 62. And behold, in Siman 193, it is explained that Rashi disagrees with this and holds that women fulfill their obligation by listening even in the case of Kiddush, which is a Torah obligation, even if they do not understand. And the commentators there wrote that the custom follows Rashi, see there (Beit Yosef and Magen Avraham there, Section 2). And if so, it is obvious that one fulfills his obligation in prayer. And it is possible to say that in this matter, prayer is more stringent, for in Kiddush and Grace After Meals and all blessings, one fulfills his obligation by the blessing of his friend when he does not know, as it is stated in the Gemara: "A scribe blesses, and a boor fulfills his obligation." But in prayer, it is not so, for one fulfills his obligation only in the prayer of the prayer leader, as Tur wrote later in Siman 594 in the name of R' Yitzchak Gaon. Because prayer was instituted to be recited quietly, and so sent Rav Sherira Gaon that one who prays is not permitted to raise his voice to fulfill the obligation of one who is not proficient until he descends before the ark. Until here is his language. However, there are those who disagree: the Ran at the end of Rosh Hashanah, and Mordechai and Hagahot Ashri (see Beit Yosef). And even according to the opinion of the Gaon and R' Yitzchak Gaon, it still appears that the prayer leader fulfills the obligation for everyone by their listening. And surely they are no worse than the people in the fields, for whom the prayer leader fulfills their obligation even without their listening, as explained there, and all the more so these.

And know that the Tur wrote another reason for the repetition of the prayer leader: because of Kedusha (the sanctification prayer), see there. And it seems that he could also have said it is because of the Priestly Blessing, which cannot be done without the last three blessings. We must understand: if so, when Rabban Gamliel asked the sages why the prayer leader descends before the Ark, what was he informing us? Isn't it necessary due to Kedusha and the Priestly Blessing? And also, why did the sages need to respond to him, "to fulfill the obligation of one who is not proficient"? 

In my humble opinion, he was teaching us something significant with this. For they asked from the Rambam, of blessed memory: in a synagogue where everyone is proficient, why is the repetition of the prayer leader needed? And he answered them that since the sages instituted it, it is a fixed ordinance, and there is no difference whether there are proficient individuals or not (brought in the Beit Yosef). 

Nevertheless, it must be understood: why did they institute praying in vain when it is not needed? However, the matter is that part of the repetition of the prayer leader is necessary, even without the reason of those who are not proficient, namely the first three blessings for Kedusha and the last three for the Priestly Blessing (see Bach). But because of those who are not proficient, they had to institute that the prayer leader repeats the entire prayer. And since they instituted it, their ordinance remains even when everyone is proficient. Because the first three and last three blessings are obligatory in any case, therefore they instituted completing all the middle blessings so as not to divide the ordinance. And the Rambam spoke well.

And do not ask: why should the prayer leader (Shaliach Tzibbur) pray twice? Let him not pray silently at all. And if the reason is that the primary prayer is the silent one, since he can fulfill the obligation for others out loud, because it is not possible in another manner – let him fulfill it for himself as well. Why should he pray in vain? But this too is understandable. For on Rosh Hashanah, the sages asked Rabban Gamliel: according to you, why does the congregation pray? And he answered them: so that the prayer leader can arrange his prayer. Meaning: even though it is said there that arranging the prayer is only necessary for certain sections, as I wrote in Siman 100 – that is for praying by oneself. But for praying before the congregation, where there is the fear of the congregation – the prayer leader is compelled to arrange the prayer silently first, so that his prayer will be fluent when he prays before the congregation. And now the logical inference is clear: if Rabban Gamliel permitted the entire congregation to pray for this reason, even though they do not need it – all the more so did the sages permit the prayer leader alone for this reason. (And this resolves all the meticulous points of the Magen Avraham in subparagraph 3. Be precise and you will find it simple.)

A prayer leader who enters the synagogue and finds that the congregation has already prayed the silent Amidah, and he needs to lead the prayer service immediately – he goes before the ark and prays aloud for the congregation. He does not need to repeat the silent Amidah, because since he fulfills the obligation for others, all the more so for himself. And although the primary form of prayer is silent for one who can pray, nevertheless, since he is compelled to pray aloud, he automatically fulfills the obligation of prayer.

And our Rabbi, the Rema, wrote in Section 2: "Similarly, if it is a time of distress and he fears that the time for prayer will pass, he may pray immediately aloud, and the congregation prays with him word for word silently until after 'HaKel HaKadosh' (the Holy God). It is good that there should be one person who answers 'Amen' after the blessing of the prayer leader." This is his language. And some have interpreted that what he wrote, "that the time for prayer will pass," means that they will not be able to complete all eighteen blessings within the time for prayer (Magen Avraham, Subsection 4). And certainly, their intention is regarding the prayer leader, that he will not finish, for if it were about the congregation, what would be their remedy now? Accordingly, it seems that he holds that the completion also needs to be within the time, unlike what I wrote above in Siman 110, Section 5, see there. But indeed, it seems more likely that his intention is that the prayer leader will not be able to start within the time, but as for the completion, there is no concern, as I wrote there.

And this is what he wrote: "And it is good that one person answers 'Amen'" – it is obvious that this is not a strict requirement, since even the prayer leader (shaliach tzibur) only prays once, and there is no blessing in vain here. Rather, he is simply saying it is good, so that the prayer should not be without "Amen." According to this, our custom is better, where the prayer leader prays out loud until after "Ha'El HaKadosh" (the Holy God) and everyone answers three Amens, and then the congregation prays silently (this is also written in Ma'adanei Yom Tov). And earlier in Siman 109, section 2, our teacher the Beit Yosef wrote regarding an individual who should pray with the prayer leader for the entire prayer, see there. And perhaps it is difficult to do so in a congregation, but in truth, if they wish – they can do so. And later in Siman 232, our teacher the Rema leaves it ambiguous, writing that the congregation should pray with the prayer leader, see there; it could imply both ways. (And with this, it resolves what the commentators struggled with. And the words of the Magen Avraham in section 5 are not understood at all. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

And we have already written that even if the entire congregation is proficient in prayer, nevertheless, the prayer leader should recite the repetition of the Amidah aloud. The prayer leader begins when the majority of the congregation has finished their prayer. However, if the majority of the congregation rushes, it is proper to wait for one who prays word by word, neither too long nor too short. Therefore, in most places, they wait for the rabbi, who presumably will not extend his prayer excessively due to the inconvenience to the congregation. If there are individuals who prolong their prayer, the congregation should not wait for them, even if they are prominent members of the community. Also, if the rabbi extends his prayer significantly, he should instruct that they not wait for him.

Similarly, at the beginning of the prayer, when the time has arrived and there is a minyan present, they should not wait for the others who have not yet arrived, even if they are among the prominent members. The general principle is that the inconvenience to the congregation is very significant. Therefore, if the rabbi is unwell and needs to leave in the middle of the prayer or during the Torah reading, the congregation should not wait for him. Likewise, if he has not arrived at the synagogue on time for the prayer due to some reason, they should not wait for him. (What the Magen Avraham wrote in subsection 7 in the name of the Sefer Chassidim – it is difficult to act this way, and we have never heard of such a practice. Why should one feel ashamed before mockers, and is this not a shame? And it has already been explained in Siman 1 that one should not be embarrassed by those who mock.)

When the prayer leader repeats the Amidah, the entire congregation should be silent and concentrate on what the prayer leader is saying and respond "Amen." If there are not nine people focusing on his blessings, it is close to his blessings being in vain, for public prayer requires ten, with one of them being the prayer leader. Therefore, each person should act as if there are not nine without him and should focus on the prayer leader's blessings. Someone who cannot hear because his ears are blocked does not count towards the nine, although he is included in the minyan, because listeners are specifically needed (Taz, subparagraph 2). One should not study or recite Psalms during the repetition of the prayer leader, even if he responds "Amen" at the end of each blessing. Anyone who does so should be rebuked (see Magen Avraham, subparagraph 8). Some say that the entire congregation should stand during the prayer leader's repetition, and this is the proper practice, unless one is not in good health, in which case he is permitted to sit. This is the practice of all who fear Heaven.

The Tur wrote in the name of the Rosh that his father instituted that for every blessing a person hears, they should say "Blessed be He and blessed be His name." For even when mentioning a righteous person of flesh and blood, one needs to bless them, all the more so the Righteous One of the world, may He be blessed and exalted. And this is what Moses said: "For I will proclaim the name of the Lord; ascribe greatness to our God," see there. And it is clear that this applies to general blessings, where the responder does not need to fulfill their obligation with it. But when one needs to fulfill their obligation with it, such as the blessings of Kiddush and Havdalah, the shofar blowing, and the reading of the Megillah, it is forbidden to respond, as it constitutes an interruption. For this reason, many of the great authorities are not pleased with this practice, because the masses do not know this and think it is obligatory to respond "Blessed be He and blessed be His name" to every blessing. And they do not fulfill their obligation with these blessings because they respond even during these. And fundamentally, I do not understand the rationale, for what relevance does it have that one needs to bless? Is not the one making the blessing already blessing, by saying "Blessed are You, Lord"? Furthermore, if so, throughout the entire prayer when mentioning the name of the Lord, should we say "Blessed be He and blessed be His name"? This requires further investigation.

And they should respond "Amen" after every blessing. This is an obligation upon everyone who hears the blessing to respond "Amen," whether those who have fulfilled their prayer obligation or those who have not. And one who does not respond "Amen" is committing a great transgression. "Amen" has three intentions: the first is "may it be so," as in "Amen, so says the Lord." The second is an expression of "faith," which applies to all the blessings of the prayer. For example, "He who revives the dead"—one should intend that they believe in the resurrection of the dead. In "Shield of Abraham," one should intend it as "truth," meaning: it is true that You shield Abraham. Similarly, in "the Holy God," and in all blessings of enjoyment and commandments. Likewise, at the beginning of the intermediate blessings. In the blessing "Redeemer of Israel," one should intend: it is true that You are the Redeemer of Israel, and I believe in this with complete faith. And similarly in other blessings. The "Amen" of the morning blessings and the Psalms of Praise, and the blessings of the Shema reading—all are expressions of "truth." In the Kaddish prayers, one should have the first interpretation in mind, such as: may it be His will that His name be magnified and sanctified. And similarly, "may His great name be blessed." The essence of faith depends on "Amen." Therefore, one should teach their young children to be careful to respond "Amen." And as soon as a child responds "Amen," they have a share in the World to Come. And anyone who responds "Amen" with all their strength—the gates of the Garden of Eden are opened for them (Shabbat 119b). Its numerical value proves it, as it matches the combined numerical values of the names Havayah and Adnut. (And there are those who focus on the combination. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

And one should not engage in idle talk while the prayer leader is repeating the Amidah. If one does speak – their sin is too great to bear and they should be rebuked. Even words of Torah are forbidden to speak, for there is a time for Torah and a time for prayer. However, the rabbi who sits on the seat of instruction, if asked a question during the prayer leader's repetition – it is permitted and obligatory for him to answer, and he should not wait until after the prayer, as the timing of the question might be urgent. However, due to our many sins, it has become widespread to speak during the prayer leader's repetition, and it is impossible to protest. There are even those who are scholars who desecrate the name of Heaven by speaking, and fortunate is the one who is careful about this. This causes a desecration of God's name in front of the nations, as is well known.

One should not answer "Amen" hastily, meaning as if the aleph is vocalized with a sheva (a hurried pronunciation). Similarly, one should not hasten and answer it before the one reciting the blessing has finished. One should also not answer a "cut-off" Amen, meaning omitting the pronunciation of the nun so that it is not distinctly heard. Additionally, one should not pause in the middle of the word, nor should one prolong it excessively. Our Sages of blessed memory also said in Berachot (47a) that one should not "throw" a blessing from one's mouth, meaning one should not answer absentmindedly. One should not answer with a short Amen but rather a slightly extended one, so that one can say "El Melech Ne'eman" (God, Faithful King), which forms the acronym of "Amen." For most Amens, their intention is related to faith, as I have written. One should not prolong it excessively, for the word's pronunciation is not heard properly when it is overly extended. If some of those answering prolong it excessively, the prayer leader does not need to wait for them to finish before starting another blessing, except for Amens in blessings where many fulfill their obligation, such as the reading of the Megillah and the sounding of the shofar. Similarly, for Birkat Kohanim (the Priestly Blessing), Kiddush, and Havdalah, one should wait before starting another blessing until everyone has answered (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 15). Immediately when the prayer leader finishes the blessing, one should answer "Amen." In the Kaddish, when the prayer leader extends the melody in "V'imru Amen," one should not wait but answer immediately (ibid., subparagraph 14).

Our sages of blessed memory said in Berachot there, that one should not respond with an "orphaned amen." Rashi and Tosafot explained that this means when one does not hear the blessing from the mouth of the prayer leader, and also does not know which blessing he concluded – it is forbidden to respond "amen," since he does not know on which blessing he is answering, akin to an orphan who has no father. However, when one knows which blessing is being said, even though he did not hear it from the prayer leader – he may respond. And this is what we say in Sukkah (51b) that in the synagogue of Alexandria in Egypt, they would wave cloths when the prayer leader concluded the blessing and everyone would respond "amen," even those who did not hear it, because due to the size of the synagogue, the voice of the prayer leader did not reach those standing far away. Nevertheless, they knew which blessing the prayer leader was reciting.

However, in the matter of the Sukkah, the Tosafot cite Rav Nissim Gaon, who explains the difference as follows: The prohibition against an "orphaned" Amen applies to a blessing where the listener is obligated to fulfill their obligation through it. The case in Alexandria refers to a situation where each individual prayed by themselves and did not need to fulfill their obligations through the blessings of the prayer leader or the Torah reading. In such cases, they could respond even if they did not hear the blessing from the prayer leader. This is also explicitly explained in the Jerusalem Talmud at the end of the chapter "These Are the Things," where it says: What is an "orphaned" Amen? It is when someone is obligated in a blessing but does not know to what they are responding, see there. In practice, it is possible that the two explanations do not contradict each other: for a blessing where one needs to fulfill their obligation, they must hear it from the one reciting it. For a blessing where they are not obligated, they do not need to hear it, but they must know which blessing the prayer leader is reciting. This is the law, and this is also the ruling of our teacher, the Rema, in section 8, see there.

Based on this, if while a person is praying the prayer leader finishes a blessing, and before the congregation finishes saying "Amen" the person finishes his own prayer, and he knows which blessing the prayer leader said even though he didn’t hear it – he can respond with "Amen," since "Amen" is considered part of the blessing. Therefore, the congregation’s saying of "Amen" is regarded as if the prayer leader finished his blessing just now. The same law applies to Kaddish, Kedusha, and "Barchu"; even if he only hears the congregation's response and not the prayer leader’s words, he can respond with them. This is because these responses are not considered obligatory in a way that requires hearing them specifically from the prayer leader. They are not deemed obligatory except for things that can be said individually, and these matters are only for the congregation (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 18). This is also the ruling of our Rabbi, the Rema, in paragraph 11. One should not question this based on what our Rabbi, the Rema, wrote later in Siman 139, that if the congregation did not hear "Barchu" from the one blessing, even if they heard the prayer leader respond "Blessed...", they should not respond "Blessed" but rather "Amen." That is different because there the entire congregation didn’t hear. Furthermore, there it is an individual blessing. But regarding the "Barchu" in prayer said by the prayer leader, where most of the congregation hears, even one who did not hear "Barchu" from the prayer leader but from the congregation responding "Blessed is the Lord..." can also respond with them "Blessed is the Lord who is blessed forever and ever." (This is difficult according to the Magen Avraham in Siman 57, subparagraph 1, who ruled similarly regarding the "Barchu" in prayer; see there. It is clearly explained here that it is not so. I am puzzled why later authorities did not note this. Be precise and you will find clarity.)

Rabbeinu the Beit Yosef wrote in paragraph 10: If someone forgot to say "Ya'aleh Veyavo" on Rosh Chodesh or Chol HaMoed, or any instance where one must repeat [the Amidah] because of it – he should focus his intention and listen to the Shaliach Tzibbur (prayer leader) recite all eighteen blessings from beginning to end, as if he were praying by himself. He should not interrupt or engage in conversation, and he should take three steps back [at the end]. Since he has already prayed but forgot to mention [the required addition], even though he is proficient, the Shaliach Tzibbur fulfills his obligation. Thus are his words.

And it is obvious that he should not respond "Blessed is He and Blessed is His Name." However, even answering "Amen" I am uncertain about, because since it is as if he is also praying, how can he respond? Nevertheless, it seems he should answer "Amen," since the Shaliach Tzibbur fulfills the obligation of one who is not proficient, and in any case, he responds "Amen." This is not considered an interruption since there are blessings where one responds "Amen" after one’s own blessings, as explained in the Gemara. And we only practice this in Birkat Hamazon in the blessing of "Boneh Yerushalayim." However, in any event, it is not considered an interruption. But "Modim D'Rabbanan" he certainly should not say. And when the Shaliach Tzibbur says "Modim" quietly and he does not hear, he should say it himself up to the words he does not hear from the Shaliach Tzibbur. And if he is not sure that he will hear from beginning to end, it is better that he repeats the prayer himself.

And know that there are those who say that if he missed an entire blessing, listening to the Shaliach Tzibbur does not help (see Taz, paragraph 5). But Rabbeinu the Beit Yosef has already determined in his great book that there is no difference in this matter. Nevertheless, it appears to me that if he forgot "Ya'aleh Veyavo" and began "Modim," he should return to "Retzeh," say "Ya'aleh Veyavo," and complete his prayer, and should not rely on the Shaliach Tzibbur in such a case. And I have seen someone who does not say this, and it does not seem correct to me.

There are three sanctifications in the order of prayer: the sanctification of "Yotzer," where we recount how the angels sanctify His blessed name; and the sanctification of "Uva Letzion," which was instituted for the purpose of study, as it is mentioned at the end of Sotah and will be explained in Siman 132.
