The principal sanctification is in the Amidah prayer, in the blessing of "You are Holy," where we ourselves sanctify His blessed name. Therefore, we are obligated to stand during this sanctification, with feet together as in the Amidah itself, which is not the case for the other two sanctifications. Ideally, we should say "Holy, Holy..." immediately after the chazzan finishes "Who revives the dead," but there is no sanctification without an invitation. Therefore, the chazzan first invites us to say "Holy" by preceding with "We will sanctify and revere You" or "We will sanctify Your name." This serves as a preparation and invitation to say "Holy," similar to how before "Amen, yehei shemei rabba," which is the main part of Kaddish, the chazzan first says "May His name be magnified and sanctified," which is also a preparation and invitation.

Our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote: The congregation does not recite "Nekadesh" with the prayer leader but remains silent and concentrates on what the prayer leader says until reaching the Kedusha. Then the congregation responds with "Kadosh." Thus is his wording. This is because, as we have explained, the prayer leader prepares and invites them to recite "Kadosh." Just as the congregation does not say "Yitgadal v'yitkadash" but starts from "Yehei Shmei Rabbah," similarly with Kedusha: the congregation should start from "Kadosh" and not say "Nekadesh." There are still some places where this custom is maintained. However, in all our regions, the congregation also says "Nekadesh" or "Nekadesh." There is no strictness about this, and we all prepare ourselves for the Kedusha. According to this, we should also say "L'umatam Baruch Yomru" and "U'v'divrei Kodshecha...," but we do not practice this (see Beit Yosef and Taz). One could say that we only prepare ourselves before the Kedusha, but within the Kedusha itself, we do not wish to interrupt the preparation of the Kedusha, and it is sufficient for the prayer leader alone. (And one should not question the starting from "Kadosh" which is in the middle of the verse, as we have already explained at the end of Siman 51 that in Kedusha there is no concern, see there.)

And one should lift their eyes to the heavens when saying the Kedusha, but their eyes should be closed. This matter is brought by the Tur in the name of the Sefer Heichalot, that the Holy One, blessed be He, commanded us to lift our eyes to the heavens when saying the Kedusha. And thus said the Holy One, blessed be He: "I have no pleasure in the world like that moment when their eyes are lifted to My eyes, and My eyes to their eyes. And at that moment, I hold the throne of My glory in the likeness of Jacob, and I embrace and kiss it, and I recall their merit and hasten their redemption." See there. And so, they sway their bodies and lift the heels of their feet off the ground. And so it is stated in Midrash Tanchuma (Parashat "Tzav" 8) on the verse "and with two they flew" – from here they established to fly on their feet when saying "Kadosh, Kadosh, Kadosh." And similarly, at "Baruch kevod Hashem mimkomo" and "Yimloch" they should fly on their feet (Magen Avraham in the name of Shelah). And it seems to me that all three "Kadosh" should be said in one lifting. (And it appears this is what the Magen Avraham wrote: not like those who jump and skip, see there in subsection 2. And perhaps he means a complete jump off the ground.)

The congregation should not respond "Kadosh" until the prayer leader finishes saying "And one called to another and said." Nevertheless, if one responded while the leader was still saying "And one called," they have fulfilled their obligation. There are those who say they have not fulfilled it (see Sha'arei Teshuvah, subsection 2), but the primary opinion follows the first view. It is clear that the additions on Shabbat, "Then, with a voice..." and "From Your place...", as well as those in the Musaf service, are not essential parts of the Kedushah, and in a situation where interruptions are forbidden, one should not say them. One should say "as stated in the songs of Your might" with the "ha" of "ha'amur" pronounced with a kamatz (Magen Avraham). The prayer leader should ensure to finish "Opposite them, they say 'Blessed'" and "And in Your holy words it is written, saying" before the congregation responds "Blessed" and "He shall reign" (ibid.). Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote that if someone has already recited the Kedushah and then comes to the synagogue during the Kedushah, they should repeat it with the congregation, see there. Even many times, contrary to those who say Kedushah should only be said once (see Beit Yosef). It has already been explained that one should position their feet together when reciting Kedushah with the prayer leader. The Ari, of blessed memory, was very strict about this. It is forbidden to speak during the Kedushah, just as during the Amidah. One should intend, during Kedushah, to sanctify God's Name, so that holiness from above will rest upon them. One should also intend to fulfill the positive commandment of "I will be sanctified among the children of Israel." The Ari, of blessed memory, was very strict about this. Note that among Sephardim, the prayer leader also says "You are holy." Among Ashkenazim, it is customary for him to say "From generation to generation we will declare..." It seems to me that an individual who is reciting Kedushah as is customary among us should say "You are holy," for "From generation to generation" was only established for the prayer leader in a communal setting.

If a prayer leader (shaliach tzibur) makes a mistake in one of the blessings by skipping it inadvertently or out of haste, and when reminded, he knows how to return to his place, he is not removed from leading even that prayer, even if he made mistakes in two, three, or more blessings. However, if he skipped the blessing of "Velamalshinim" (the blessing against informers), he is immediately removed from leading that prayer, as we are concerned that perhaps heresy has entered him. Therefore, even though this is merely a suspicion and we do not permanently disqualify him from serving as a prayer leader, for this prayer, he should not continue. He should descend from the podium, and another should take his place unless he himself remembers and recites it. Additionally, if he began the blessing and stumbled or made an error, he is reminded to correct it, as this indicates it was not due to heresy. But without this indication, he is removed from leading that prayer since there is no loss to him in doing so. Although he may feel embarrassed, he should have been more careful. All of this applies if the mistake was inadvertent or due to error. However, if he intentionally skips any blessing, even a minor one, he is disqualified from ever serving as a prayer leader until he repents completely, as there is no greater act of irreverence than this. Similarly, if in the "Velamalshinim" blessing he mistakenly recites the end of the blessing without its beginning, he is also reminded to correct it. (Magen Avraham, small section 1. From his words, it appears that in some versions there is "Velakofrim," see there.)

And know that in the Jerusalem Talmud, in the chapter "One does not stand," it says that there are two other blessings that are similar in law to "And for the slanderers": The blessing "He revives the dead" because we are concerned that perhaps he denies the resurrection of the dead, and "Builder of Jerusalem" because perhaps he does not believe in the coming of the Messiah. And in our Talmud, this is not mentioned. The Tur brought this Jerusalem Talmud, and our teacher, the Beit Yosef, in his great book, wondered why he brought it, since it is against our Talmud? And in my humble opinion, it seems clear that if we were to be concerned – it is obvious that there are also concerns with these. The distinctions that the commentators wrote are strained, as is evident to the one who examines them. And it is clear to the Tur that our Talmud does not disagree with this. And what is stated in the Gemara (29a) only about this blessing, is because in truth this is not an independent statement in the Gemara there but rather an incident that happened with Shmuel HaKatan who forgot it. And on this the Talmud questions why they did not remove him, see there. And those blessings are not discussed there, but certainly, in practice, there is no difference. However, regarding the resurrection of the dead, it works out well in any case, for "He revives the dead with abundant mercy" is not at the beginning of the blessing, and if so, in any case: if he began with "You are mighty" – then also in "And for the slanderers" we do not remove him, as has been explained. And if he did not begin with "You are mighty" – then it does not relate to the resurrection of the dead. And perhaps the Jerusalem Talmud does not hold the distinction between beginning it or not beginning it. And the language of the Jerusalem Talmud clearly implies that it is concerned specifically with the end of the blessing, see there. And if so, it follows that it does not agree with our Talmud. And perhaps the opinion of the Tur is that our Talmud refers to the beginning of the blessing, and in this, this blessing differs from those two. And the Jerusalem Talmud refers to the end of the blessing, and in this, they are all the same, and our Talmud would also agree to this. And this all needs to be considered.

Indeed, I am mainly surprised by the fundamental points: the matter of the Jerusalem Talmud is not at all relevant to the words of our Talmud. And thus it is stated there (Halacha 3): For all, we do not return him, except for one who did not say "He Who revives the dead," "He Who humbles the arrogant," and "He Who builds Jerusalem"... see there. And it does not at all speak about his removal but rather about the matter that if he already said it further along – we do not return him due to the burden on the congregation, except for these three blessings. And what relevance does this have to our Talmud? And the Tur wrote about the Jerusalem Talmud using the term "remove," which is puzzling, and perhaps that was the version he had. However, in any case, from this Jerusalem Talmud it is clear that if one skipped one of the blessings, and at the time the congregation did not notice, and he prayed further along – we do not return him because of the burden on the congregation, and all the more so if he finished his prayer. And we do not hold this way, as will be explained in section 5. (And I found that even the Rashba brought this version that we have. And see Beit Yosef and Bach who wrote that even in this we do not hold like the Jerusalem Talmud, as will be explained with the help of Heaven.)

The prayer leader who made an error in one of the blessings and is unable to return to his place even when reminded due to his agitation, and another person must take his place – the new person should immediately take his place without any hesitation, as I have written in Siman 53. From where does he start? If the error occurred in the first three blessings or the last three blessings – he returns to the beginning, as it has already been explained that the first three are considered as one unit, and likewise the last ones. He starts from "Retzeh". However, if the error occurred in the middle blessings – he returns to the beginning of the blessing where the error occurred, and from there he continues in order, even if the one who made the error had already recited some blessings beyond that.

This is the language of the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, Section 3: Any situation where an individual must repeat the prayer, the prayer leader must also repeat the prayer if he makes the same mistake while praying aloud, except for the morning prayer of Rosh Chodesh. If the prayer leader forgets and does not mention "Ya'aleh Ve'Yavo" until he completes his prayer, he is not required to repeat it due to the burden on the community, since the Musaf prayer, in which Rosh Chodesh is mentioned, is still ahead. However, if he remembers before completing his prayer, he returns to "Retzeh," and this does not impose a burden on the community. Thus far their words. And our teacher, the Rema, wrote that some say if one errs in the morning prayer of Shabbat and Yom Tov, its rule is like Rosh Chodesh, and this is the custom. Thus far his words. And the reason here too is because the Musaf prayer mentions Shabbat. In truth, the Tur wrote that there is no reason to differentiate between Rosh Chodesh, Shabbat, and Yom Tov. And our teacher, the Beit Yosef, in his great book, wrote the reason: because on Shabbat and Yom Tov there is no work disruption, they were not concerned about the burden on the community. See there. It is difficult: on the contrary, we find that they were more lenient in prayer on Shabbat and Yom Tov than on Rosh Chodesh, for due to the burden they did not institute eighteen blessings on Shabbat and Yom Tov, as I wrote in Siman 268 (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 4)? Furthermore, what connection is there between the burden on the community and work disruption? Perhaps the reason is that just as on weekdays they repeat it and do not rely on saying this prayer during Mincha due to the long interval between Shacharit and Mincha, as the poskim wrote (see Beit Yosef), so too on Shabbat and Yom Tov, the readings are long, there are many who go up, and there is also the Maftir, Haftarah, vows, and donations as customary, creating a long interruption like between Shacharit and Mincha. However, in any case, these laws do not align with the interpretation of the Jerusalem Talmud we brought in Section 3. (And all of this is based on the Beraita at the end of the fourth chapter (Berachot 30b): if one errs and does not mention... and it was taught regarding the congregation according to the interpretation of the Ba'al Halachot Gedolot that Rashi brought, and this is the interpretation of the Rif. They do not have the version "in Musaf we do not repeat," see Beit Yosef. But according to Rashi's interpretation that it refers to an individual, since he can hear it from the prayer leader, one can uphold the method of the Jerusalem Talmud, see there. However, in practice, we hold like the Tur and Shulchan Aruch. This is also the opinion of the Rambam, Rif, and Rosh.)

The Rambam writes in the tenth chapter, law 2: But if the prayer leader (Shaliach Tzibur) made a mistake when praying silently, I say that he does not go back and pray again because of the burden on the congregation, but relies on the prayer that he will pray aloud. And this is on the condition that he did not make a mistake in the first three blessings, for if he made a mistake in them, he always goes back, just like an individual goes back. Thus are his words. This is the version we have before us, and similarly, Rabbeinu the Beit Yosef wrote in section 4. And it is not understood: what difference is there between the first three blessings and the entire prayer in this matter (Lechem Mishneh)? And the Levush wrote that this is when he remembered before he finished his prayer; see there. And this too is not understood, for according to this, if he remembered before the end of the prayer, he goes back to the beginning even if he prays all eighteen blessings again, and there is no greater burden on the congregation than this. And this does not make sense at all. (And see Magen Avraham section 5, and it requires further study.) And in my humble opinion, it seems the opposite, that this is what it means: if he made a mistake in the first three blessings and remembered there that he made a mistake, he goes back to the beginning, for there is not so much burden since he is still at the beginning of the prayer. But if he remembers afterward, he does not go back. However, the Tur brought the words of the Rambam in a corrected version, and this is his wording: The Rambam wrote... And if he made a mistake in that which he prays aloud, he always goes back like an individual. Thus are his words; see there. And he did not mention any difference between the first three blessings and the entire prayer. And that which he wrote "always goes back," this is only regarding the Shacharit of Rosh Chodesh, as the Rambam himself wrote there and as I wrote above. And it seems in my humble opinion in practice: if he made a mistake in the first three blessings and remembered afterward, one should rely on the version of the Tur, and on our interpretation according to our version, and he does not go back.

And know that there is an opinion that, just as it is clarified regarding the morning prayer of Rosh Chodesh, when the prayer leader does not say "Ya'aleh V'Yavo," he can rely on the Musaf prayer, so too an individual can rely on the Musaf prayer, for the after-the-fact status of an individual is not worse than the ideal status for the public (Magen Avraham, subsection 3, in the name of RMA). And this is even when praying alone, for if praying with the congregation, even without the reason of Musaf, one can hear it from the prayer leader, as I have written in Siman 124, and one can rely on this after the fact (there). And also, regarding what is clarified that if a prayer leader made a mistake and another took his place, starting from the beginning of the blessing — there are those who say that on Shabbat and Yom Tov in the Musaf prayer, where the wording is long, and he made a mistake in "Umipnei Chata'einu" — he does not need to return to "Atah Vechartanu." For the main part of the blessing is the additional sacrifices and its conclusion, and he can start from the middle of "Umipnei Chata'einu" and in the middle of "Tikanta Shabbat."

When the prayer leader (Shaliach Tzibbur) reaches "Modim" (the thanksgiving blessing) – the congregation bows with him. For it is taught in the Jerusalem Talmud in the first chapter of Berakhot (Halacha 5): everyone bows with the prayer leader in thanksgiving. And the Rambam wrote in the ninth chapter, law 4, and this is his wording: "When the prayer leader reaches 'Modim' and bows – all the people bow slightly, but they should not bow excessively." See there. Because he holds that there are only four complete bowings: at the beginning and end of the Avot blessing, and at the beginning and end of the Modim blessing. And our sages of blessed memory were strict about not bowing in places where the sages did not say to do so, as I wrote in Siman 123, and in our Talmud in Sotah (40a). For there it is mentioned about this "Modim," but it is not mentioned there that one needs to bow, only in the Jerusalem Talmud. The reason being: since the prayer leader says aloud "we give thanks to You" – it follows that the congregation also needs to show submission. Therefore, the Rambam wrote to bow slightly. And in the Jerusalem Talmud it also says: as long as one does not bow excessively. And the Rambam explains that this applies only to "Modim."

The Tur objected to [the ruling], and his objection is not understood. See there (and see Taz, subsection 1, who also expressed astonishment). Our teacher, the Beit Yosef in the Shulchan Aruch, omitted the ruling about "bending slightly" and only wrote "and should not bend excessively." It seems to me that he follows his reasoning in his larger work, where his intention is that one should bow as in all the other bowings, and for all the bowings, he said not to bend excessively. See there. This is very puzzling: if so, why did he write it here and not in the fifth chapter, law 12, where he explained the laws of bowing? Furthermore, how can this be said, for he explicitly wrote there that bending slightly is only valid after the fact (bediavad). See there, and here he wrote it as an initial requirement (lechatchila)? (And also, the Bach wrote that this applies only to "Modim." And the words of the Taz, subsection 1, are also puzzling. See there.)

The term "Modim" is referred to as "Modim deRabbanan." It appears that the formulation of this prayer is attributed to several Amoraim, as explained in Sotah there and in the Jerusalem Talmud there, where there are several different versions. It also concludes with the phrase "Blessed are You, Lord, for the thanksgivings," as mentioned there. However, our custom follows the Talmud Bavli without concluding with the Name, and the version is well-known in the prayer books. Some say that one should bow again at the end, and our master the Beit Yosef wrote that it is good to be concerned with this opinion. Our master the Rema wrote that some say one should recite the entire prayer with one bow, and this is the custom. This is the end of his words. Among us, not everyone practices this way. Rav Sherira Gaon wrote: Some bow again when they conclude, and some conclude while standing upright. The sages did not object to either practice (Beit Yosef). In the Jerusalem Talmud it says: Rabbi Zeira would stand close to the prayer leader so he could bow with him at the beginning and the end. It appears that the interpretation is that he would say "Modim" with some length so he would finish at the same time as the prayer leader and bow with him at the end. Therefore, it is permissible to follow either practice.

In Spain and all the lands of Ishmael, the Kohanim raise their hands in blessing every day during Shacharit. Therefore, our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote: If there are no Kohanim present, the prayer leader says: "Our God and God of our forefathers, bless us with the threefold blessing..." until "and I will bless them." The congregation does not respond "Amen" but rather "So may it be." Thus are his words. And with us, it is so every day, as we do not raise hands except on Yom Tov, as I have written in Siman 128. We only recite up to "peace," and we do not say the verse "and they shall place My name." The first "bet" in "b'bracha" is pronounced with a patach. The response "so may it be" is only at the end. Our custom is to say after each blessing between the verses: "by the merit of Abraham, by the merit of Isaac, by the merit of Jacob." When saying "may He bless you," he should turn his head to his right, "and guard you" to his left, "may He shine..." to his right, "and be gracious to you" to his left, "may He lift..." to his right, "and give you" to his left. When finishing "peace," to his right. This is our custom. There are those who wrote: "may He bless you," to the right, "may He shine," towards the sanctuary, meaning straight ahead, "His face to you and be gracious to you," to the left (Magen Avraham). But we conclude to the right, to strengthen the right over the left. This is not said at Mincha, when it is not a proper time for raising hands. Rabbi Rema wrote that the custom is to say "Sim Shalom" in Shacharit, and whenever "Our God..." is said (as in Mincha on a fast day). But otherwise (Mincha and Ma'ariv), "Shalom Rav." Some begin to say "Sim Shalom" in Mincha on Shabbat because it is written there "for with the light of Your face, You gave us, Hashem our God, a living Torah," which is the Torah read at Mincha on Shabbat. Thus are his words. In the siddur of the Ari z"l, it always says "Sim Shalom," and this is the custom of the Sephardim. (The reason for the Ashkenazim: "with the light of Your face" is not said in Mincha and Ma'ariv, which are times of judgment. Therefore, on Shabbat, Yom Tov, and Rosh Chodesh, it would be correct to say "Sim Shalom" also in Mincha and Ma'ariv, as well as on the eve of Shabbat and Yom Tov in Mincha, which are times of favor. Note and you will find it easy.) (It implies that in the house of mourning, "Our God" is said, as it is not mentioned. This requires further investigation.)

There is a positive commandment upon the Kohanim to bless Israel, as it is stated: "Thus shall you bless the children of Israel." This obligation is constant even in our time. The Rambam at the beginning of the laws of prayer included this in the count of commandments, see there. And in the time of the Temple, they would bless after the offering of the incense and after the offering of the limbs of the daily offering, as the Rambam wrote in the sixth chapter of Tamid, and as it is taught in the beginning of the seventh chapter of Tamid. (See Tosafot Berakhot 11b s.v. "Birkat Kohanim", which needs investigation. It seems to me there is a printing error. Be precise and you'll find it easy.) This matter is explained in the Torah on the eighth day of the inauguration, as it is written: "Aaron lifted up his hands toward the people and blessed them, and he came down from the sin offering..." That is to say, with this the service was completed. Hence, after the completion of all the sacrificial procedures is the time for the priestly blessing. This is explicitly stated in Torat Kohanim there, and Rashi also wrote this in Sotah (38b s.v. "and he came down").

And this applies both in the Temple and in the provinces, and similarly in our times at the conclusion of the prayer, which corresponds to the offering. The prayer concludes with "Shome'a Tefillah" where the requests end, and therefore we say "Retzeh B'amcha Yisrael Uv'tefilatam." Therefore, the obligation is to move their feet to the place of the platform at "Retzeh" as will be explained. And they established it to bless before "Sim Shalom" because the priestly blessing ends with "peace." And also there is the conclusion of the prayer, so they placed it there. And they need to remain on the platform until after the blessing "Who blesses His people Israel with peace," so that the entire prayer is completed perfectly. And afterward, they descend just as Aaron descended at the conclusion of the service (thus it appears to my humble opinion with these reasons).

From where do we know that the Holy One, blessed be He, desires the Priestly Blessing? As it is said, "And they shall put My name upon the children of Israel, and I will bless them" (Sotah there). For the scripture ties this matter to them, that this blessing would be the placing of His name upon His people, and it is not for the sake of Israel, but for the sake of the Omnipresent (Rashi). And regarding the explanation of "and I will bless them," the Tannaim disagreed in Chullin (49a): Rabbi Yishmael says: We have learned that the blessing for Israel comes from the mouths of the priests, but for the priests themselves, we have not learned. When it says "and I will bless them," it means: the priests bless Israel, and the Holy One, blessed be He, blesses the priests. Rabbi Akiva says: We have learned that the blessing for Israel comes from the mouths of the priests, but not from [the mouth of] the Mighty One. When it says "and I will bless them," it means: the priests bless Israel, and the Holy One, blessed be He, agrees with them. And the blessing for the priests, Rabbi Akiva derives from "and I will bless those who bless you." And this is what Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said in Sotah there: Any priest who blesses is blessed, and one who does not bless is not blessed, as it is said: "and I will bless those who bless you," see there. And this is according to Rabbi Akiva. And a priest who omits one word does not fulfill the commandment, and his blessing is in vain, as it is written, "Thus shall you bless" – as an imperative.

Any kohen who does not ascend to the platform (to bless the people), if he does not have any of the disqualifying factors that will be explained later, transgresses three positive commandments: "Thus you shall bless," "Say to them," and "They shall place My name" (from Numbers 6:23-27). And it is not exclusively him, as Rambam writes at the end of the Laws of Prayer, and this is his language: Even though he nullified one positive commandment, it is considered as if he transgressed three positive commandments. See there. And similarly, Rabbeinu the Beit Yosef wrote in section two. See there. And know that there is someone who wrote that even for an Israelite, there is a positive commandment to be blessed (Shaarei Teshuva in the name of Chareidim). And it is not exclusively him, for where do we find such a positive commandment? Rather, it means that there is an obligation upon him to be blessed by the kohanim, and if he does not care about this, it is as if he spurns the blessings of the Holy One, blessed be He, and he is deserving of punishment.

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote in Even HaEzer, Siman 3, that someone who comes and says, "I am a Kohen" is believed to perform the priestly blessing (Birkat Kohanim). See there. They raised an objection against him: Even the lenient authorities on this matter were only lenient regarding calling him first to the Torah, which was instituted merely for the sake of peace. But concerning the priestly blessing, there is a positive commandment that a non-Kohen is prohibited from performing the blessing, as stated in Ketubot 24a, "Thus you shall bless" – you (Kohanim) and not a stranger. The prohibition derived from a positive commandment is indeed a significant issue, and he is certainly not believed about himself (Magen Avraham, beginning of the Siman). However, we have already explained in Even HaEzer, Siman 3, Seif 5, that his words are correct, for according to Torah law, every person is believed about his own status even in matters involving a presumption of prohibition, as I have written in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 127. He should also be believed regarding Terumah of Torah law, but because Terumah affects lineage, and in matters of Kohanic lineage many precautions were taken, therefore, even regarding Rabbinic Terumah, he is not believed. This was during the time of the Talmud when Terumah was still Rabbinic – they were concerned about lineage. This is not the case now, and there is no concern in this regard. We have further elaborated on this with Divine assistance.

It is stated in Shabbat (118b): Rabbi Yossi said, "In all my days, I have never transgressed the words of my colleagues. I know within myself that I am not a Kohen, but if my colleagues told me 'Go up to the platform,' I would go up." The Tosafot wrote that Rabbi Yossi did not know what prohibition there is for a non-Kohen to go up to the platform, unless it is due to a blessing in vain, as the Torah commanded the Kohanim to bless Israel. This is their language. And many are puzzled because there is a positive commandment prohibition, as explained. And the simple understanding is this: Certainly, Rabbi Yossi did not bless, for why would he make a blessing in vain just to fulfill the will of his colleagues? And if so, merely ascending without reciting (the blessing), what prohibition is there in this? Is it forbidden to stand among the Kohanim? (Maharsha. And see Magen Avraham, subsection 1, who also explains this in the words of the Gemara. And I do not understand, for if so, why did he not also explain the Tosafot this way? And the words of the Taz, subsection 2, who wrote that there is no obligation for a non-Kohen, but there is also no prohibition in this matter, and so wrote the Magen Avraham there. And it is very puzzling: for if so, what is the question in Ketubot there whether one can raise from the priestly blessing to lineage, since there is no proof of priesthood from this? And besides this, it explicitly does not imply so. And the correct interpretation is like the words of the Maharsha. And what the Magen Avraham wrote to resolve the issue in Ketubot is forced.)

And our teacher, the Rema, explained to distinguish between when there are other Kohanim and when he is alone. And many wondered about him: What difference does this make? And it seems to me that his words are clear, and this is their explanation: He did not want to explain that Rabbi Yossi did not say anything at all. Rather, certainly he said "May He bless you" with the Kohanim, but certainly did not bless. If so, the distinction is simple: When he is alone and stands and blesses Israel – certainly there is a prohibition of a positive commandment even without a blessing, for blessings are not essential. But when there are other Kohanim and they are the ones blessing, then what difference does it make to us if he recites the verses? And what does he accomplish by this? Behold, he does not intend to bless Israel but rather says the verses with them, and what of it? But when he is alone and stands on the platform, and the people gather around him and receive his blessings – he certainly transgresses a positive commandment. (See Bach. Analyze and you will find it easy.)

There is no Priestly Blessing with fewer than ten people. The priests are included in the count, because they too are part of the blessing (Taz). One should not question: Why is this similar to matters of sanctity, since it is merely a blessing like all other blessings? This is not so, because since it is written "And I shall bless them" – it requires the Divine Presence, and the Divine Presence does not dwell with fewer than ten. Therefore, it is similar to matters of sanctity, which require ten for this reason. It has already been explained that any priest who does not ascend to the platform transgresses a positive commandment if he is not hindered by something that prevents him from blessing. There is a distinction in this: if the hindrance fully prevents him, he is forbidden to bless. If the hindrance only exempts him from blessing, but if he wishes, he may bless as will be detailed in this section – it exempts him from the act, but there is no prohibition involved (Taz, small section 3). Nevertheless, it is proper for him to leave the synagogue (there).

There are times when even if a Kohen does not have any of the disqualifications which exempt him, he still does not transgress the positive commandment. For example, if he was not in the synagogue when the prayer leader called "Kohanim," or if he did not move forward during "R'tzei," and they did not tell him to ascend or to wash his hands. Similarly, if he ascended once on that day, he does not transgress even if they told him to ascend again.

All the details of these laws will be explained later. The Tur wrote in the name of the Ra'avad that even if he is the only Kohen, he does not transgress, as it is written: "Say to them." The Tur disagrees, stating that it refers to Aaron and his sons, and "say" implies to each one individually. Many have questioned the Tur because it is explicitly explained in the Gemara there that for one Kohen, the prayer leader does not call "Kohanim" because "say" implies two. They gave a forced answer (see Beit Yosef, Bach, and Taz).

In my humble opinion, it seems there is no difficulty at all: while it is true that "say" implies two, the Torah does not prohibit an individual from blessing. On the contrary, it is a duty for him to bless, but the prayer leader does not call "Kohanim." This is what the Tur means: "say to them" – to each one individually. That is, the duty of the blessing is on each one individually. Therefore, if they told him to ascend and he did not, he transgresses the positive commandment.

In truth, we can say that the Ra'avad also agrees with this. Rather, the Ra'avad means that an individual does not transgress because it is written "say to them," meaning we derive from it that the prayer leader does not call "Kohanim" for one. Since the prayer leader did not call "Kohanim," he does not transgress, as I wrote. He does not discuss if the congregation told him to ascend. The Tur necessarily discusses such a case (so it appears in my humble opinion).

Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in Section 4: When the Kohanim do not want to ascend to the platform, they are not required to remain outside the synagogue except at the time when the chazzan calls "Kohanim." However, so that people do not say they are disqualified, they have the custom not to enter the synagogue until the priestly blessing is completed. Thus are his words. The explanation of the matter is: they do not want to ascend because they do not have the strength; otherwise, why would they neglect a mitzvah intentionally? And we find in the Jerusalem Talmud at the end of the chapter "Ein Omdin": Rabbi Yehuda, when he was weak, would lean his head and stand behind the pillar. Rabbi Elazar would go outside. This means: Rabbi Yehuda would tie his head as a sign that he was weak, so he would not be suspected. And he would stand in the synagogue behind the pillar. And certainly, at the time of the chazzan's call "Kohanim," he would not be in the synagogue at all, for otherwise, he would transgress a positive commandment. Rather, he would be present at the time of the blessing. And Rabbi Elazar did not rely even on this and would go outside the synagogue until after the priestly blessing. According to this, our teacher, the Beit Yosef, ruled like Rabbi Elazar. And it appears that even if one makes a sign like Rabbi Yehuda, it is acceptable. And the Mordechai wrote that they should leave before the chazzan begins "R'tzei," so that they would not be suspected when they do not ascend at "R'tzei." And this is correct. And it seems to me that if one makes a sign, it is permitted, and only at the call of "Kohanim" must he go out. And it is clear that if it is forbidden for him to ascend to the platform, even if the prohibition is rabbinic, he can be in the synagogue at the chazzan's call "Kohanim." He does not transgress a positive commandment because he is not refraining by his own decision, but the sages have prevented him. They have the authority to do so, contrary to the opinion of those who disagree (Magen Avraham, Section 4, see there).

From the decree of Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai, the priests should not ascend to the platform with their sandals, but rather they should remove them. The reason: their sandals were tied with straps, and there was a concern that a strap might break, leading the priest to sit down to tie it, causing a delay and preventing him from blessing alongside his fellow priests. People might then say that he is the son of a divorced woman or the son of a chalutzah, which would disqualify him from the platform (Sotah 40a). The intention is not that they should stand barefoot, as this is considered disgraceful, but rather they should stand in their stockings. And even though our shoes do not have straps and this concern does not exist, nevertheless, the decree remains in force, as it is akin to something prohibited by a formal enactment, which remains prohibited forever until greater sages come and annul it. And it is obvious that we are as donkeys compared to Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai.

And behold, it is certain that a sandal or shoe that is not made of leather is permitted, for regarding Tisha B'Av and Yom Kippur they are not called "shoes." However, if they also have straps, it seems that it is forbidden, as one should follow the reasoning. But if they do not have straps, it is obvious that it is permitted. Although regarding a shoe it is forbidden because the Sages did not distinguish, in this case, they did not decree. And behold, in the glosses of the Maimonides at the end of the Laws of Prayer, it is written that in boots it is permitted, as I have written. And it is obvious that they mean leather, for if not, even in shoes it would be permitted. According to this, one must wonder about our teacher, Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) in Paragraph 5, who wrote regarding the permissibility of boots that some are stringent if they are made of leather, and in some places, the custom is to be lenient. Thus his language. And how can one say this? For if not made of leather, even shoes are permitted. One must say that he means boots that have straps, for in such a case, shoes are forbidden as I have written. And in boots, it is permitted, for they did not decree on these straps that are on the leg (see Beit Yosef). Therefore, in leather, which resembles shoes, it is forbidden even with such straps. (And it is clear that this is the intention of the Magen Avraham in Subsection 5. See there.) And there is one who wrote that if they are made of fabric and covered with leather, it is permitted in any case (there). In my humble opinion, it seems that this is only when they do not have straps, for then even such a shoe is permitted. But with straps, it is forbidden as I have written, for one should follow the reasoning. (And what the Rambam wrote "barefoot" is not precise.)

It is stated in Sotah (39a): Any Kohen who did not wash his hands should not raise his hands [to bless], as it is written: "Lift up your hands in holiness and bless the Lord." And Rashi explains that this refers to one who did not wash his hands before the Priestly Blessing. It is clarified that this is not due to the impurity of the hands, and if his hands are pure from the morning washing, he does not need to wash them again. Rather, it is a scriptural decree. And so write the Tosafot, see there. It is obvious that one must recite the blessing "on the washing of the hands," as the Tur also writes. And this is the language of the Rambam in the fifteenth chapter of Prayer: "What is the impurity of the hands? A Kohen who did not wash his hands should not raise his hands. Rather, he washes his hands up to the wrist in the manner of sanctification for service, and then he blesses…" until here is his language. And it seems that if it is due to a concern for impurity, and his hands are clean, he does not need to [wash]. For in the Temple service, it is ruled in the fifth chapter of entering the Temple that one sanctifies once in the morning and serves with that sanctification all day and all night (Beit Yosef). Therefore, out of doubt, he does not need to bless "on the washing of the hands," and so is the custom.

And this is the wording of our teacher the Beit Yosef in section 6: Even though the Kohanim have washed their hands in the morning, they must wash their hands again up to the wrist, which is the connection between the hand and the arm… And if the Kohen washed his hands in the morning and recited the blessing "Al Netilat Yadayim" (for the washing of the hands), he does not recite the blessing again when washing his hands for the Priestly Blessing. This is the end of his words. The reason is because of the uncertainty of the law, as I have written. However, it is certain that if before the Priestly Blessing he needed to relieve himself and washed his hands, he certainly recites the blessing "Al Netilat Yadayim," because the morning blessing of "Al Netilat Yadayim" is now nullified. However, this is not the custom (Magen Avraham, section 9), and there is no reason for this. And there is someone who wrote that the Tur is unique in this, requiring the blessing "Al Netilat Yadayim" (Elya Rabbah, section 13). This does not seem correct at all, for since it is stated in the Gemara that one is obligated to wash hands, it follows that a blessing is required. And it seems to me another reason for this: because it is customary for the Kohanim to prepare themselves for the platform, and when they need to relieve themselves, they go beforehand and wash their hands on their own, not intending to go up to the platform, as for the platform, the Levites pour water on their hands. Therefore, since his hands do not require washing, he does not need to recite a blessing now due to the uncertainty, as I have written. And if it is because he did not recite the blessing "Al Netilat Yadayim" earlier – indeed, the blessings are not an impediment. And in Sepharad, where they bless every day, there are varying customs, and they are not known to us. And it is written that in Egypt, in the morning they do not wash, but at Musaf they wash (Beit Yosef and Magen Avraham). (And what the Magen Avraham deduced in section 9, why the Beit Yosef wrote "and recited Al Netilat Yadayim": it is obvious, wrote the Elya Rabbah in section 12, his intention is that if he did not have water in the morning and rubbed his hands with a stone and recited the blessing "Al Nekiyut Yadayim" (for the cleanliness of the hands), then he does not need to recite afterwards "Al Netilat Yadayim." And then when he goes up to the platform, he recites "Al Netilat Yadayim.")

The common custom is that the Levites pour water on the hands of the priests, according to the Zohar in the section "Naso," because the Levites are also called "holy." Additionally, it can be said this is in remembrance of our Holy Temple, where the Levites served in guarding the Temple under the authority of the priests, and therefore, they also serve the priests now. If there is no Levite in the synagogue, then the firstborn sons pour, specifically those who are the firstborn to their mother, for they are also holy. A learned Levite should not pour for an ignorant priest. Some have warned strongly against this, so as not to disgrace the Torah. However, nowadays it is not possible to adhere to this strictly, as it may lead to disputes, and everything is for the sake of Heaven.

Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 6 that the Levite must also wash his hands beforehand. His reasoning appears to be as we say elsewhere: "Let the pure come and purify the pure." But our teacher, the Rema, wrote that the custom is not for the Levites to wash their hands first but to rely on their morning washing. Thus far his words. And so is the common practice. It is clear that water fit for the washing of hands is required, following all the laws of handwashing for eating, and it must be done with a vessel. It is not permissible to add fragrances to the water, as we require water that has not changed from its original state, as I wrote in Siman 160 (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 8).

The priests should wash their hands before the "R'tzeh" prayer, because once the prayer leader begins "R'tzeh," all the priests must leave their places to ascend to the platform. Even if they do not reach the platform until the prayer leader finishes "R'tzeh," it is acceptable. However, if they did not leave their places during "R'tzeh," they should not ascend, even if they were prevented by something like being in the middle of praying. Nonetheless, if they did ascend, they do not come down (Siman 10). Moving one's feet from one's house to the synagogue is not considered as leaving unless the house is adjacent to the synagogue (ibid). It appears to me that if, after the fact, they left their places during "R'tzeh" to wash their hands, this is also considered leaving, as they are moving themselves from their place to ascend to the platform by washing their hands.

When the kohanim lift their feet to ascend to the platform, they say: "May it be Your will, Hashem our God, that this blessing which You commanded us to bless Your people Israel be a complete blessing, and let there be no stumbling block or sin in it from now and forever." They prolong this prayer until the congregation finishes saying "Amen" to the thanksgiving blessing. And the language of the Gemara there is: What does he say when he lifts his feet? "May it be Your will..." Rashi and Tosafot explained that this is said upon reaching the platform. The Rambam, the Tur, and the Shulchan Aruch wrote the language we have stated, that they begin to say the "May it be Your will" while they are walking. Our custom is to say this after "Modim." The reason seems to be: because we only perform the priestly blessing on Yom Tov, and we say the prayer "Veha'arev." On Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, there is also the prayer "Avinu Malkeinu, remember Your mercy..." If they were to start immediately upon standing on the platform, they would finish long before the thanksgiving blessing, and so they start afterward. Additionally, "Modim" would be an interruption (see Magen Avraham, subsection 12). In their times, they would say "Modim" while walking (ibid). The reason for this blessing seems to me to be: since it is a decree of the King that Israel should be blessed through the kohanim, if the kohanim have bad deeds, they are not fit for the blessing to be imparted through them. Therefore, they pray that the blessing should be complete without any stumbling block or sin, like the concept: "and let not sin and iniquity impede our prayer."

When they ascend the platform – they stand with their faces towards the sanctuary and their backs towards the people, with their fingers bent into their palms, unlike during the blessing itself. This is until the prayer leader concludes the blessing "Your name is good…" and the congregation responds "Amen," and the prayer leader calls out loudly "Kohanim" – then they turn their faces towards the people and their backs towards the sanctuary. For so the Holy One, blessed be He, commanded: "Thus you shall bless" – face to face, as a person speaks to his friend (Sotah 38a). And how beloved are Israel before the Holy One, blessed be He, that He permitted the Kohanim to stand with their backs towards the sanctuary for the sake of blessing Israel. The prayer leader should not say at all "Our God and God of our fathers, bless us…" as it has no relevance to the Priestly Blessing. Even those who have the custom to say it should ensure to say it quietly. When he reaches "Kohanim" he should say "Kohanim" out loud, and "with Your holy people as it is said" quietly. This is the custom in these countries. There are some prayer leaders who err by saying "Our God…" out loud, and they should be warned about this. It is also explicitly proven in Sotah (39b) that it says there: the one calling is not permitted to call "Kohanim" until the "Amen" is completed by the congregation – this shows that the calling of Kohanim is directly adjacent to the blessing. The prayer leader only calls "Kohanim" to two or more, as it is written: "Say to them". But if there is only one Kohen – he ascends by himself, turns his face, and blesses, for even an individual is commanded by the Torah to bless as I wrote in paragraph 9. However, since the prayer leader does not call him, he does not transgress a positive commandment if he does not ascend unless others tell him "ascend". Some say that for an individual it is only a rabbinic obligation (Tosafot Menachot 44a). But the opinion of the Tur is not so, as I wrote there. (And even the Tosafot did not write this conclusively, and on the contrary, they wrote that at the very least it is a rabbinic obligation. See Magen Avraham section 16. Consider this and you will find it clear.)

In most places, it is known that the Holy Ark is in the east, and the priests turn their faces to the west. If the Holy Ark is in the south or the north, there is an opinion that they should turn their faces towards the prayer leader and not to the west (Magen Avraham, Section 15). And there are places that are not particular about this (ibid.). In truth, I do not understand: the Torah warned about the faces of the majority of the congregation, and therefore it is simple that they should turn their faces to where the majority of the congregation stands. Know that the primary standing place of the priests is by the Holy Ark. This is the place of the platform, similar to the Temple where they stood in a designated place on the platform, which means a designated place like a "bench," as the Ra'avad wrote at the end of the second chapter of Middot. And from this language in the Mishnah in Kelim, Chapter Seven: since it has a receptacle. And the Targum explained on "Lift up your hands in holiness" – "Raise your hands, priests, on the holy platform." Therefore, they need to stand there. If there are many priests, they should stand at the sides of the platform by the eastern wall, and this is the common custom in all countries. Therefore, the priest should not stand in his usual place, for he needs to move from his place as I wrote in Section 16. Many priests do not know this law, and therefore it is necessary to inform them so that they do not do this.

In the Gemara, it is not explicitly clarified whether the blessing that the Kohanim recite, "Who sanctified us with the sanctity of Aaron, and commanded us to bless His people Israel with love," is to be recited with their faces towards the sanctuary or towards the congregation. The Rambam, at the end of the fourteenth chapter, explicitly wrote that they recite the blessing with their faces towards the sanctuary, and after the blessing, they turn their faces towards the congregation; see there. However, the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch in section 11 wrote that initially they turn their faces towards the people, and then they recite the blessing. And this is the custom among us. There are those who start the blessing with their faces towards the sanctuary, and in the middle of the blessing, they turn their faces towards the people (Pri Chadash). This is certainly puzzling. The prevalent custom follows the words of the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch.

And that which we say "with love," it is explained according to the Zohar that any Kohen who does not love the people, or the people do not love him, should not raise his hands (Magen Avraham, subsection 18). According to this, the Kohen should accept upon himself at the time of the act to love the congregation, and likewise the congregation should love the Kohanim. Each of the Kohanim recites this blessing, not that one blesses and all answer "Amen." And even though in all other blessings it is better that one blesses and fulfills the obligation of the many, because "in the multitude of people is the King's glory" as it is stated in Berachot (53a) – here it is not possible so that there should not be confusion. (And this is the intention of the Magen Avraham in subsection 17.)

The priests raise their hands opposite their shoulders and lift their right hand slightly higher than the left. They extend their hands and separate their fingers. The reason for lifting the right hand higher is because it is written: "Aaron lifted up his hands." And it is written "his hand"? To teach that one is higher than the other, and it is the right hand to strengthen the right, which is kindness, over the left, which is strength. They intend to create with their two hands five spaces, which are: between two fingers and two fingers, between a finger and a thumb, and between a thumb and a thumb; between the two fingers on two hands are two spaces, and similarly between a finger and a thumb, and one between a thumb and a thumb, as it is written: "peering from the lattice" – from five spaces. They spread their palms so that the inside of their palms faces the ground and the back of their hands faces the sky. And even though the right hand is lifted slightly, care must be taken to place the right finger on the left so that they do not separate from each other, so that there will not be more than five spaces (Magen Avraham, small section 19). Some inscribe the name of God with their fingers (there), and some inscribe Shaddai (Beit Yosef). This requires great precision, and not everyone is skilled in this, and therefore it is avoided. We only do what is explained in the Tur and Shulchan Aruch.

The priests begin to say "May He bless you" without being prompted by the prayer leader, as there is no concern for error in the first word. Afterwards, the prayer leader prompts them word by word, and they repeat after him each word until they complete the verse "May He bless you," and the congregation responds "Amen." Similarly, for "May He make His face shine upon you," the prayer leader prompts them, and the congregation responds "Amen" after "and be gracious to you." The same procedure is followed for "May He lift up His countenance upon you" until "peace," and the congregation responds "Amen." 

Afterwards, the prayer leader begins "Grant peace." At this point, the priests turn their faces back towards the ark and say: "Master of the Universe, we have done what You decreed upon us. Now You do what You promised us: 'Look down from Your holy dwelling from heaven and bless Your people Israel'." They should extend this prayer until the prayer leader finishes "Grant peace," so that the congregation responds "Amen" to both. If they cannot extend it for that long, they should say "Mighty in the heights," as I wrote later in section 130. On Rosh Chodesh and Yom Kippur, when the prayer "This day strengthen us..." is prolonged, they should not start saying "Master" until the end, so they finish together with the congregation.

Regarding what we wrote that they say "May He bless you" on their own, our master the Rema wrote in section 13 that there are those who say that the prayer leader should also prompt them for "May He bless you" initially, and this is the custom in all these countries. Thus far his words. This is because there are additional hidden reasons for why the prayer leader prompts them.

One only recites the blessing in the Holy Tongue (Hebrew) and not in any other language. This is essential, for even if it was done after the fact (bediavad), one has not fulfilled the obligation, as it is written: "Thus shall you bless," meaning in the Holy Tongue. And it must be done while standing, as it is written: "to serve Him and to bless in His name" – just as the service is performed while standing, as it is written "to stand to serve," so too the blessing must be recited while standing. And it must be done with the raising of hands specifically, as it is written: "Aaron lifted up his hands toward the people and blessed them." And it must be with a loud voice, as it is written: "Say to them" – like a person speaking to his fellow. This means it should be in a medium voice: not too loud and not too soft. The priests are not allowed to turn their faces until the prayer leader begins "Sim Shalom." They are not allowed to bend their fingers until they have turned their faces back and are standing there. They are not allowed to move from their place until the prayer leader completes "Sim Shalom," and the reason is written in section 2. Some say they need to wait until the congregation finishes responding "Amen" after "Who blesses…," and this is the custom. It is customary to say to the priests "Yasher Koach" (may your strength be firm), and they respond "Baruch Tihyeh" (may you be blessed).

When they turn their faces towards the people, they should turn via the right side. This means that when standing facing east, they should turn their faces via the south. And afterwards, when they turn their faces back towards the sanctuary and are standing facing west, they should turn via the north. For we have a principle that every turn you make should be via the right side. And when they descend from the platform, they should descend backwards, like a student taking leave of his teacher, so that their faces are towards the Ark of the Covenant as they descend. When they put on their shoes, they should do so with a cloth on their hands. And if they put them on with their hands, they should wash their hands, for they still have some prayer left to do.

How was the Priestly Blessing conducted in the Temple? After the priests completed the service of the morning Tamid offering, as I wrote in Section 1, they would ascend to the platform. The location of the platform was between the Court of Israelites and the Court of Priests. There was a step there, one cubit high, that extended the entire length of the courtyard, and upon it was placed a dais one and a half cubits high. They ascended to it by three steps, each half a cubit high. This was the place of the platform, where the priests stood in their priestly garments and blessed the Priestly Blessing. It seems to me that it is also valid without the priestly garments, as this is not part of the sacrificial service. And the proof is: for standing requires a textual basis, as I wrote in Section 24, and perhaps this same teaching implies that priestly garments are required, since the Torah connects it to service. This requires further examination. Note that the Rambam wrote in Chapter Six of the Laws of the Daily Offering that the location of the platform was on the steps of the Hall, see there. And perhaps he explains what we have learned in Middot, Chapter Two (Mishnah 6): Rabbi Eliezer ben Jacob said: There was a step one cubit high, and the platform was placed upon it, and it had three steps... This was the platform of the Levites. However, the Rash and the Ra'av interpret that the priests blessed from there, see there.

And after they ascend the platform, they raise their hands above their heads, except for the High Priest who does not raise his hands above the frontlet because of the Name inscribed on it. They spread their fingers, and another person prompts them word by word as is done outside the Temple. The difference is that outside the Temple, "Amen" is answered after each verse as I have written, but in the Temple, "Amen" is not answered. And thus it is taught in Sotah (37b): the Priestly Blessing in the Temple is one blessing, but outside the Temple, it is three blessings. Therefore, the three verses are recited without interruption. When they conclude with "peace," all the people respond: "Blessed be the Lord, the God of Israel, from everlasting to everlasting." This is explicitly stated in Nehemiah (9:5): "Stand up and bless the Lord your God from everlasting to everlasting." And so they would respond to each blessing (Sotah 40b) and not with "Amen."

(The reason "Amen" is not answered in the Temple: the Maharsha writes there that "Amen" is a combination of the two Names, the Tetragrammaton and Adonai. Therefore, it is relevant outside the Temple where the Name is not pronounced as written, but not in the Temple. See there. And the rule is that if so, after the death of Shimon the Righteous, they would answer "Amen." In my humble opinion, it seems that "Amen" strengthens the blessing, as the blessing flows through the House of God, "and this is the gate of heaven." But those standing and blessing there, the flow has already descended from the source. Scrutinize and you will find it easy to understand.)

The Kohanim in the Temple would pronounce the Name as it is written with Yud-Kay-Vav-Kay. And the Rambam wrote that this is the explicit Name mentioned everywhere. And in public, they would pronounce it with its substitute, Aleph-Daled. From the time of the death of Shimon the Righteous, the Kohanim ceased to bless with the Name as written, even in the Temple, due to the corruption of the generations, so that an unworthy person would not learn it. The earlier sages would only teach this Name to their worthy students and children once every seven years, as the concealment of the Name is a form of greatness for His exalted and awesome Name. So wrote the Rambam there, and this is explained in Kiddushin (71a), see there.

The prayer leader does not call "Kohanim" until the "Amen" is finished from the mouths of the entire congregation, who respond after the blessing of "Modim." And even though it is explained in Siman 124 that it is not necessary to wait for those who extend their "Amen," nevertheless, the Priestly Blessing is different because everyone is obligated to listen (Taz, Siman 12). The Kohanim are not permitted to begin the blessing "Who has sanctified us with the sanctity of Aaron" until the word "Kohanim" has been completely spoken by the prayer leader. After the Kohanim have recited this blessing, they are not allowed to start "Yevarechecha" (or the prayer leader when prompting) until the "Amen" has been finished by the entire congregation responding after the blessing "Who has sanctified us...". Similarly, they are not allowed to begin any word until the prompter has finished his recitation. The prayer leader should not begin the word following this one until all the Kohanim have finished the previous word. The congregation does not respond until the blessing has been completed by the Kohanim, and the prayer leader should not begin another verse until everyone has become silent. The Kohanim should not say "Veyishmerecha" until the congregation has finished "Ribono shel Olam," and similarly "Vichuneka" and "Shalom."

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote in section 18 that the Kohanim should not begin "Ribbon" after the Priestly Blessing until the "Amen" from the congregation is completed. Thus are his words. And this is surprising: For it was previously explained that they should not say it until the prayer leader begins "Sim Shalom" (Beit Yosef), and then they turn their faces and say "Ribbon" as I wrote in section 23, which is later than the "Amen" that the congregation responds. And there is one who says that the prompter does not actually need to wait for the entire congregation, and therefore the prayer leader can begin "Sim Shalom" before everyone responds "Amen" (Magen Avraham, subsection 28). But this does not seem correct (Elya Rabba, subsection 37). And in my humble opinion, it appears that indeed the Kohanim can say "Ribbon" before the prayer leader says "Sim Shalom", for what is the connection between the two? The delay is only because of the "Amen". And that which was written previously "until he begins Sim Shalom" is merely a sign, for presumably the prayer leader does not begin "Sim Shalom" until the "Amen" is completed, and he is proficient in this. Therefore, it teaches us here that the delay is only because of the congregation's "Amen" that they respond to "Shalom".

Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote in section 19: The prayer leader is not permitted to answer "Amen" after the blessing of the priests. Thus are his words. And this is a Mishnah in Berachot (34a): The one who leads the prayers should not answer "Amen" after the priests because of confusion. Rashi explained: So that his mind will not be confused and he will not make a mistake, as he will not be able to focus on beginning the next blessing. Similarly, Rambam wrote in chapter 14. From this, Tosafot deduced that "Amen" is not considered an interruption, since it did not state the reason as being due to an interruption, see there. Because these Amens are for the need of the prayer, and according to this, if he is confident that he will not be confused – he is permitted to answer "Amen" as per the ruling that will be explained. And this is explicitly stated in Midrash Rabbah, Parashat "Ki Tavo". But if so, why did the poskim (decisors) not explain this? Therefore, there are those who say that one does not derive halacha from a Midrash. And specifically in the law below, where the blessing of the priests would not be nullified completely, we rely on the fact that he will not be confused, and not because of his answering "Amen" (Bach and Tosafot Yom Tov there). According to this, there are those who say that after the first blessing of the priests, meaning after the blessing "Who has sanctified us with the sanctity of Aaron" – he can answer, because if he has not yet begun, there is no confusion (Taz at the end of 114). And there are those who say that we hold like the Midrash, that if he is confident – he can answer all the Amens in the priestly blessing (Magen Avraham, section 29, and Pri Chadash). And this is not the custom. And perhaps because we do not have anyone who is confident in this matter, as it is indeed difficult to dismiss the words of the Midrash. And what relevance is there to "one does not derive..." in this case, since there is no contradiction in the Gemara regarding this? And each Kohen blesses and does not fulfill the obligation with the blessing of another, for each Kohen is obligated to bless by himself in the priestly blessing.

If the prayer leader (Shaliach Tzibbur) is a Kohen and there are other Kohanim present, he should not perform the Priestly Blessing (Birkat Kohanim). They should not tell him to ascend (to the platform) or to perform the blessing before the "Retzei" blessing; if they did tell him, he would be obligated to ascend so as not to transgress a positive commandment. However, after "Retzei," we do not concern ourselves with this, as has been explained. Therefore, even though he himself calls out "Kohanim," he is not transgressing, because nothing was said to him before "Retzei." 

There are those who write that some have the custom that even when there are other Kohanim, since he is a Kohen, another person, an Israelite who has heard the entire repetition of the prayer leader, stands next to him and prompts the Kohanim and also says the "Sim Shalom" blessing and concludes the blessing, while the prayer leader recites the Kaddish (Bach). But the prayer leader does not go to wash his hands (Magen Avraham, section 31). In some places, he does go to wash his hands (ibid.). 

It seems to me that according to these customs, there is no reason to distinguish between whether he is assured of returning to his prayers or not, since the other person completes the entire prayer. However, all these customs are perplexing, and it is explicitly implied from all the halachic authorities that when there are other Kohanim, not only does he not wash his hands, but he also does not say the blessing with the Kohanim. Rather, he prompts them, and no one else should prompt them (as the Magen Avraham also writes there). And this is the main ruling in practice.

However, if there is no other Kohen present except for him, and in order not to completely nullify the priestly blessing, if there is another Israelite who has heard the entire repetition of the prayer leader, the prayer leader should move slightly from his place before "Retzeh" and return to his place. He should then recite up to "Hatov Shimcha," and the Israelite should prompt him, and he should ascend to the platform (duchan). The Israelite should prompt him up to "HaMevarech..." and then descend from his place and recite the full Kaddish. However, he does not need to wash his hands, since he is in the midst of prayer and his hands are clean – he can rely on the morning hand washing. If there is no other who has heard the entire repetition of the prayer leader, it is taught in Berachot that if he is not confident that he will not become confused, he should not perform the priestly blessing, and the priestly blessing should be nullified. However, if he is confident that he can return to his prayer without confusion, since there is no other Kohen present, he should perform the priestly blessing so that it is not completely nullified. And how should he do this? He should move his feet slightly during the Avodah and return to his place, recite "Retzeh" up to "Hatov Shimcha," ascend to the platform, and another should prompt him. After "Shalom," he should descend from the platform and complete "Sim Shalom." (This seems correct to me. See Magen Avraham, subsection 33, who writes in the name of the Bach that even if there is another who has heard, and the other says "Sim Shalom" as well, nonetheless, we require that he be confident to return to his prayer. This is not entirely understood, and Magen Avraham also critiques this. See there. Also, see Taz, subsection 15, but the primary ruling is as I have written. Study and you will find it easy.)

Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote in section 22: "It is preferable that the one who calls out ('makrei') to the Kohanim be an Israelite. And when the chazzan (cantor) is a Kohen, an Israelite should stand next to him and call out 'Kohanim' and prompt them, while the chazzan remains silent." These are his words, and this comes from the Rambam in Chapter 14. He provided a reason based on the verse "Say to them," implying that an Israelite should prompt the Kohanim. According to this, as explained, if there are other Kohanim present, the chazzan should not raise his hands in blessing, but still, he should not prompt; rather, he should stand silently. This is not like I wrote in section 32, where he himself calls out 'Kohanim'—see there—because this he should not do. However, it is preferable that the one who prompts be an Israelite, meaning that the chazzan should be an Israelite (Magen Avraham section 34), so that we do not need someone else to prompt instead of the chazzan. But the Levush wrote that this is not mandatory, and the chazzan who is a Kohen can also be the prompter—see there. The reasoning behind "Say to them" is merely a support to indicate it should be specifically from an Israelite. Indeed, in Sotah (38a), there is an opinion that says the opposite: that the prompter should be a Kohen. They derive "Say to them" as meaning from among themselves—see there. And although we do not rule this way, the derivation of "Say to them" is just that they should be prompted, but who does the prompting is not critical. And I believe this is also the practice. (See Taz section 17, who wrote that the plain meaning of the verse is that the prompter should be an Israelite. His words are perplexing: if so, how could Rav Chisda argue there and say the opposite, that the prompter should be a Kohen? See there.)

The priests are not permitted to chant multiple tunes during the Priestly Blessing, whether two or three tunes, because it could lead to confusion. They should only chant one tune from beginning to end. This is what Rabbi Yosef Karo wrote in section 21. From this, it somewhat implies that at the very least, they should chant one tune. Seemingly, why shouldn't they remain completely silent? Perhaps because from this, they might be stirred and inspired to bless with proper intention, in the manner of "and it was that whenever the musician played, the spirit of God came upon him." And the custom of Israel is Torah.

When the Kohanim bless the people, they should not look around or divert their attention, but their eyes should be directed downward, as is customary when standing in prayer. The congregation should focus on the blessings and face the Kohanim but should not look at them. The reason is not because anyone who looks at the Kohanim during the blessing will have their eyes dimmed, as stated in Chagigah (16a), for that only applied in the time of the Temple, as explained there. Rather, the reason is so they do not divert their attention. Additionally, it serves as a remembrance of the Temple (Magen Avraham, Section 35, and Taz, Section 19). The Kohanim themselves should also not look at their hands for the reasons mentioned. Therefore, it has become customary to drape the tallit extensively over their faces, with their hands outside the tallit. In some places, the custom is that their hands are inside the tallit so that they cannot look at them and others cannot look at their hands either, as the tallit covers the hands. This is the common custom among us.

"Thus you shall bless" — face to face, as it is written: "Say to them" — like a person speaking to a friend (Sotah 38a). Therefore, the sages said that people who are behind the Kohanim are not included in the blessing, as they are not face to face. It does not necessarily mean they must stand directly in front of their faces, but even from the sides, as long as they are face to face, meaning: the Kohanim face west and the Israelites face east. Only the sides in front of them and not the sides behind them, meaning if they form a line, they will be behind the Kohanim. Therefore, the custom is that all the people move from the eastern wall onward, because the Aron Kodesh (Holy Ark) protrudes greatly, and the Kohanim stand before the Aron. Therefore, those in the east will be on the sides behind the Kohanim. Some have written that if one stands in his designated place, he does not need to move, as he is considered compelled (Bach). But this is only when the people are numerous and crowded. When there is available space, why should he not move to fulfill the law (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 36)? Those standing in the courtyard can remain there as long as they face the Kohanim. The partition does not create a separation, as even an iron partition does not separate between Israel and their Father in Heaven (Eruvin 92b, Tosafot s.v. "Ta'aseh"). Moreover, even people in the fields are included in the blessing because they are compelled, being occupied with their work and unable to come — they are included in the blessing. But one who is not compelled is obligated to come and hear the blessing. (See Taz, subparagraph 20, who tries to reconcile the words of the Bach with a very forced reasoning. See there.)

It is stated in Sotah (38b): A synagogue where all the attendees are kohanim, if there are more than ten – those exceeding ten will bless, and ten will respond "Amen." And even though with Israelites we do not insist that specifically ten respond "Amen," this is because the mitzvah is for the kohanim to bless Israel, and it suffices with one since the mitzvah is fulfilled properly. However, when the listeners are also kohanim, there must be at least ten listeners, for the Shechinah dwells among ten and not fewer. And if there are only ten kohanim – all will bless. And to whom do they bless? To their brethren in the fields. And who responds "Amen"? It is stated in the Jerusalem Talmud, Berachot chapter five, that women and children respond "Amen" after them. And why do we not say that they bless the women and children, for they are also included in the blessing as we say in Sotah there? It seems to me because the husbands of the women and the fathers of the children presumably hear the blessings somewhere and are blessed, and therefore all the members of their household are blessed. For is the blessing only upon the man alone? And if he does not see blessing in his wife and offspring, there is no greater curse than this, as it is written: "Your wife will be like a fruitful vine, your children like olive shoots. Thus shall the man be blessed who fears the Lord." Therefore, they said only to the people in the fields. (See Taz, subsection 22, Magen Avraham, subsection 37. And according to our explanation, it fits simply and straightforwardly.)

When the priests bless, the people should not recite verses. Rather, they should remain silent, listen, and respond "Amen." After all, is there a servant who is being blessed and does not listen? This is the ruling in the Talmud there. As for our practice of saying "Master of the Universe" regarding the nullification of a bad dream, it is because there is danger involved, so it was permitted (Taz, Section 24). Moreover, we actually say this while the priests are singing. One can also say verses at that time, as Rabbi Moses Isserles (Rema) wrote in Section 26: "And now that the priests prolong their melodies, it has become customary to also say verses, as I wrote above in Section 57 regarding 'Bless.' However, it is better not to say them." This is his wording. One can say them when the cantor is reciting the word (Magen Avraham, Section 39). However, this is only when he prolongs the word slightly with a melody; otherwise, there is no time (Taz, Section 25). We do not have the custom to say them at all. It is better to remain silent and focus on receiving the abundance of blessings, since the law has been decided not to say them, why should we do otherwise?

A Kohen should not add to the blessings and should not say: Since the Holy One, Blessed be He, gives me permission to bless, I will add from my own, such as "May the Lord, the God of your fathers, add to you," and similar. It is forbidden for him to do so. If he does so, he transgresses the prohibition of "You shall not add," as it is written: "Thus you shall bless" – and no more. All the more so, it is forbidden to subtract, and if he subtracts, he transgresses the prohibition of "You shall not subtract." Nevertheless, a Kohen who has raised his hands (to bless) and afterwards went to another synagogue and found a congregation that had not yet reached the priestly blessing – he may raise his hands again.
