He does not transgress the prohibition of "You shall not add," because "You shall not add" only applies to adding to the essence of the commandment, but not to performing the commandment multiple times. Just as with taking the lulav, one can take the lulav many times in a day, and in any case, if he did not bless, he does not transgress a positive commandment since he already blessed once. It is advisable for him to leave the synagogue so that no suspicion falls upon him. And in all cases that have been explained and will be explained where one should not ascend to the platform – they should leave the synagogue (Taz, small section 26).

A Kohen who is in the middle of prayer, if there are other Kohanim present, should not interrupt his prayer. However, if there are no other Kohanim except him, he should interrupt his prayer and go up to the platform (to bless the congregation). Even though it is generally forbidden to interrupt prayer for other matters, the priestly blessing is different because it is a positive commandment. Since the commandment cannot be fulfilled without him, he is obligated to interrupt. If he is told to go up to the platform, even if there are other Kohanim present, he must interrupt so as not to neglect the positive commandment.

Similarly, a Kohen who has not yet prayed and finds the congregation praying and standing at the priestly blessing, should go up to the platform and bless the congregation first, and then pray afterward, because the prayer does not prevent him from performing the blessing. If he sees that the time for prayer will pass, he should go outside the synagogue and pray. If he is told to go up to the platform, he is obligated to do so to avoid neglecting the positive commandment (Magen Avraham, section 41), since the priestly blessing is a Torah obligation and prayer is rabbinic. Similarly, if there is no other Kohen besides him, he is obligated to go up even if the time for prayer will pass. If he sees that the time for the recitation of Shema will pass, he should recite the first verse and then go up to the platform, even if there are other Kohanim present (this seems correct to me).

There are situations in which the Sages decreed that a Kohen should not ascend the platform (to bless the people), such as if he has a blemish on his face or hands which are very noticeable. For example, if his hands are spotted, covered with small blemishes, crooked, or bent sideways, or if he cannot separate his fingers. Similarly, if he has a facial blemish that makes his face appear different from other people, the Sages said that he should not ascend the platform because the people would look at him and not listen to the blessings. It is better that he leave the synagogue than cause the people to miss out on the mitzvah. Even if they tell him to ascend, he should not do so. He does not transgress a positive commandment by not ascending, because he is following the Sages' decree. The Sages have the authority to establish such decrees.

Similarly, one who has blemishes on his legs in a place where people walk barefoot without leggings, or one whose saliva drips onto his beard, or whose eyes constantly tear, or who is blind even in one eye, should not perform the priestly blessing. However, if they are familiar in their city and people recognize them, they may ascend the platform, for since they are accustomed to them, people will not stare at their blemishes as it is not new to them. Even if he is blind in both eyes, he can ascend the platform and is like any other Kohen. Anyone who has resided in the city for thirty days is considered "familiar in his city." This is specifically in his own city, but if he goes temporarily to another city, even if he stays there for thirty days, he is not considered "familiar," as he is a visitor and people will look at him. He is only considered "familiar" when he comes to permanently reside there, in which case after thirty days he is considered "familiar." This does not mean he must live there forever, but rather a fixed residence for a period, such as coming to be a teacher, a scribe, a servant, or a craftsman for a year or even half a year, he is considered "familiar in his city" after staying for thirty days (and the Bach permits even for a temporary stay).

All of this applies in places where the hands and faces of the kohanim are exposed during the priestly blessing, as there is a concern that people might look at them. However, if it is the custom of the place for the kohanim to drape the tallit over their faces, then there is no concern about looking at blemishes on their faces. And if the custom is also for their hands to be under the tallit, as is our custom, then there is no concern about blemishes on their hands either. But in a place where this is not the custom, even if they want to start doing so now, it does not help, as this itself will cause people to look because of the change they are making (Magen Avraham, subsection 45). However, the fact that the congregation covers their faces with their tallitot does not help, because many young men do not have a tallit. Additionally, the listeners sometimes uncover their faces, which is not the case with the kohanim. Therefore, this does not help. (See Taz, subsection 28, who raises this issue. According to what I have written, there is no difficulty at all.)

And there is a question regarding this matter: It is explicitly implied that the Sages decreed this only because of the issue of gazing, and by law, a blemished priest is allowed to ascend to the platform. And why should he not be disqualified by law, just as he is disqualified from the service in the Temple? For indeed, the blessing is likened to the service, as I have written (Section 16, Subsection 27). The answer to this is: Because in the priestly blessing it is written: "Speak to Aaron and to his sons" – which includes even blemished priests, as Rashi explained in the portion of "Emor," see there. Furthermore, this is not a question at all, for regarding a blemished priest it is written in the portion of "Emor": "Whoever has a blemish, he shall not come near to offer..." – thus the Torah explicitly explains that it is forbidden only for the sacrificial service. And aside from all this, this matter is explained explicitly in the Gemara in Taanit (27a): If a blemished priest serves, is he not allowed to bless?... Behold, it is likened to a Nazirite. And the Tosafot wrote that from here it is clear that a blemished priest is permitted to perform the priestly blessing, see there and in the Tosafot at the end of Menachot. (And it is astonishing that the Tosafot there brought from Taanit: “I likened it to standing, not to anything else,” see there. And this is not found at all in Taanit. And they have already noted this in the glosses, see there.)

And so too, if his hands were stained with woad or madder, which are types of dyes that cannot be removed by washing, he should not lift his hands (to bless the congregation), because the people will look at them. But if his hands are blackened from soot of the ovens, he can wash them. And if the majority of the city works in this trade, he may lift his hands, because people will not look at them as they are accustomed to it. Similarly, if it is customary in his city, it is allowed (Beit Yosef). And so too in places where the hands are covered under the tallit, as I have written. And one who does not know how to pronounce the letters correctly, for example, he pronounces alephs like ayins, and ayins like alephs, and chets like heys, and so forth, in a place where everyone speaks properly, he should not lift his hands, because he does not say the blessings properly. This was in their times and in their country. But among us, everyone pronounces an aleph like an ayin, and an ayin like an aleph. And even a Kohen who cannot pronounce a right shin, like saying "sibbolet" instead of "shibbolet" – there is no concern among us because there are many like him, and this is not considered a significant change in the letters (see Taz, subsection 30).

It is taught in the Megillah (24b) that a minor does not raise his hands [to bless the people]. And in Sukkah at the end of the third chapter, it is said that a minor who knows how to raise his hands is given a portion of terumah, implying that a minor does raise his hands. And at the end of the first chapter of Chullin (24b), it is said that even an adult, if his beard has not yet filled out, does not raise his hands. See there. The Tosafot and the Rosh wrote there that there are also distinctions: a minor who has not brought two pubic hairs does not raise his hands at all when he is alone, but with other priests, he does raise his hands. This is the case in Sukkah and Megillah. And when he has brought two pubic hairs, he can raise his hands even when he is alone. However, this is only occasionally, but to raise his hands regularly, it is only if his beard has filled out. This is the case in Chullin, where it refers to a permanent prayer leader. And thus ruled Rabbeinu Bet Yosef in Section 34. He wrote that "filled out beard" is called when his years have reached this stage, even though it has not yet fully filled out. See there.

The words of the Rambam here require examination, as he wrote in Chapter 15, Law 4: How is it with two? A young priest should not lift his hands until his beard is full. And it explicitly implies that before this he does not lift his hands at all, as he counts it among all the disqualifications. And it is true that the Tur also wrote this, and these are his words: A minor or even an adult whose beard has not filled out does not lift his hands. However, the Tur concludes: And this applies when he is alone. But with others, once he knows how to lift his hands, he lifts them with them. Until here are his words. According to this, he will explain the matter in Chullin when he is alone, and similarly in Megillah and Sukkah with others. And one should not ask about the matter in Megillah: Why specifically a minor, even an adult whose beard has not filled out? For it is indeed so. However, in Megillah, it does not deal with the law of lifting hands but with the laws of a minor, and it also includes the matter of lifting hands. But regarding the Rambam, it is difficult. There are those who wrote that the Rambam also agrees with this distinction (Beit Yosef). And this is certainly surprising, for if so, why did he not mention it? There are those who wrote that the Rambam interpreted the matter in Sukkah that only if he knows how to spread his hands, they share with him the terumah, but to lift his hands he is not allowed (Lechem Mishneh). And this is more forced. However, they toiled in vain over his words, for the Rambam had a different version in Sukkah, as explained from his words at the end of Chapter 12 of Terumot, where he counts among the ten who are not given terumah: a minor who does not know how to guard his conduct, see there. And so it is in the Tosefta, Chapter One of Chagigah, see there. And it does not refer at all to the lifting of hands, but that he does not know how to guard his conduct in a sensible manner. (See Kesef Mishneh there who explained "to guard his conduct" as referring to the lifting of hands. And it is a puzzling matter.)

And one should not be surprised, whether according to the opinion of the Rambam, who holds that if his beard has not yet filled out, he does not lift his hands at all, or according to the opinion of the Tur that he does not go up alone, or according to Tosafot and the Rosh who say that he cannot consistently ascend to the platform alone, and if there is no other priest, the priestly blessing is nullified. Where did our sages of blessed memory derive this? After all, an adult is obligated in all the commandments? It seems to me that we derive this because it is written: "Speak to Aaron and to his sons, saying: This is how you shall bless..." and Aaron and his sons had filled-out beards. Therefore, according to Torah law, he is completely exempt as per the Rambam's view. According to the Tur, when there are others with him, it is an obligation on the others. According to the Tosafot and the Rosh, we do not compare it to Aaron and his sons, except if it was consistently like Aaron and his sons. (This seems to be my humble opinion. And see the Taz, section 31, who wrote that the Tur did not bring the distinction of occasional cases because in Ashkenaz they only perform the priestly blessing on holidays, and it was always occasional, see there. His words are puzzling: should the Tur not write for the sake of the Sephardim? Moreover, the main point is not so, as the Rosh fled to Spain with all his sons, as is known. The primary explanation is as I wrote, that the Tur does not make this distinction. The issue in Megillah is not specifically about a minor, but because it discusses matters of a minor, as the Lechem Mishneh wrote, see there. Additionally, the Tur did not mention this custom at all. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

According to this, I say regarding what our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, wrote at the end of this section: A Kohen, even if he is unmarried, may lift his hands (to bless). But some say he should not lift his hands, for one who is without a wife is without joy, and one who blesses must be joyful. So far their words. They brought this in the name of the Zohar, Parashat "Naso" in the Raaya Meheimna (page 145b), and this is the language of the Zohar: Because the Shechinah does not dwell in one who is not married... And therefore it is written: "Speak to Aaron and his sons...". So far its words. At first glance, these words are puzzling: From where do we derive this? Additionally, it has been objected: Only the High Priest on Yom Kippur was forbidden to perform his service without a wife (Magen Avraham, subsection 64). According to our explanation, it works well. This is what the Zohar alludes to by writing "And therefore it is written: Speak to Aaron and his sons...", meaning: We require the likeness of Aaron and his sons, who had wives and also joy – we learn from there, as it is written: "And all the people saw and rejoiced." And with this, we can also provide a proper reason why we only lift our hands on a festival, because it is a time of joy, as it is written: "Thus shall you bless" – and we require the likeness of Aaron and his sons on that day, when they lifted their hands on the eighth day of the inauguration, which was a time of complete joy.

And know that regarding what our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote: A minor who has not brought forth two pubic hairs does not raise his hands (to bless the congregation). One of the commentators on the Shulchan Aruch (Magen Avraham, subsection 48) wrote, and this is his language: It implies that even if he is thirteen years old, it is forbidden. Therefore, one must be meticulous about this matter so as not to come to a blessing in vain. Thus far his language. And it is implied from this language that we do not rely on age as we do in all Torah laws, where we do not say there is a presumption that he has brought signs (of maturity). And this is surprising: What blessing in vain is there? Behold, even a minor raises his hands with the other priests, and the minor recites all the blessings. Moreover, according to the Tosafot, there is only a rabbinic prohibition regarding a blessing in vain (Magen Avraham in Siman 215), and in rabbinic matters we do rely on the presumption that he has brought signs. Therefore, the primary ruling is that when he reaches thirteen years and one day, we presume him to be an adult regarding raising his hands in the general case (Eliyah Rabbah, subsection 58), unless we know clearly that he has not brought signs. (See Machatzit HaShekel who struggled to interpret the Magen Avraham in this way, but it does not seem so. And also the Pri Megadim did not understand his intention this way, see there. And the primary ruling is like the Eliyah Rabbah wrote. Be precise and you will find it straightforward.)

The Rambam writes in Chapter Fifteen, Law 6: A Kohen who does not have any of these things that prevent him from performing the Priestly Blessing—despite not being wise or meticulous in commandments, or if people gossip about him, or if his business dealings are not conducted justly—he still performs the Priestly Blessing. We do not prevent him, because this is a positive commandment upon every Kohen who is fit for the Priestly Blessing. And we do not say to a wicked person: "Increase your wickedness and refrain from the commandments." And do not wonder and say: "What benefit is there in the blessing of this common person?" For the acceptance of the blessing does not depend on the Kohanim but on the Holy One, Blessed be He, as it is said: "And they shall place My name upon the children of Israel, and I will bless them" — the Kohanim perform the commandment they were commanded, and the Holy One, Blessed be He, in His mercy, blesses Israel as He wishes. Thus far his words. 

And this follows Rabbi Akiva in Chullin (49a), that "And I will bless them" refers to Israel whom the Holy One, Blessed be He, blesses. See there. And more than this is found in the Jerusalem Talmud, Chapter Five of Gittin (Halacha 9), and these are his words: You might say, "This person commits adultery and sheds blood, and he is blessing us?" The Holy One, Blessed be He, said: "Who is blessing you, is it not I who bless you?" as it is said: "And they shall place My name...". See there.

However, the Rambam earlier wrote: A Kohen who has killed a person, even though he has repented, should not lift his hands [to bless], as it is stated: "Your hands are full of blood." And when you spread out your hands, I will hide My eyes from you." And a Kohen who has worshiped idols, whether intentionally, unintentionally, or under duress, even though he has repented, may never lift his hands, as it is stated: "The priests of the high places shall not go up..." And blessing is like service, as it is stated: "To serve Him and to bless in His name." Similarly, a Kohen who converted to idol worship, even though he has returned, may never lift his hands. Other sins do not prevent [him from lifting his hands]. Thus far his words. The case of killing a person is in Berakhot (32b). The case of idols is at the end of Menachot. The case of killing a person contradicts the Yerushalmi, and he ruled according to our Talmud. And there are those who say that the Yerushalmi is only dealing with suspicion of bloodshed (Beit Yosef). However, Rashi ruled that if he repented, he may ascend to the platform (Tur). And our Rabbi, the Rema, wrote in section 35 that we should be lenient with penitents and not lock the door in their faces. And so is the custom. Thus far his words. Similarly, our Rabbi, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 37 regarding one who converted, that there are those who say that if he repented, he may lift his hands, and this is the main ruling. See there. He also wrote that if it was under duress, according to everyone, he is permitted to lift his hands. Thus far his words. And it is surprising: Even though he did not rule like the Rambam, how could he write "according to everyone it is permitted"? For the Rambam prohibited it (and in the Beit Yosef he struggled with this).

A person who circumcised a baby and the baby died – he may still lift his hands (to bless the congregation), as he intended to perform a mitzvah. Additionally, perhaps the baby would have died regardless. Furthermore, perhaps the baby was a stillborn. Additionally, perhaps the wind disturbed him. We find this reasoning in Gittin (9a) regarding exile, when someone killed inadvertently and the victim did not die immediately, see there. Similarly, this applies here in the case of circumcision. And even if the person killed inadvertently and the victim did not die immediately (Magen Avraham, subsection 52). And even if people gossip about him, accusing him of being a murderer, since the matter is not clarified – he is permitted to lift his hands. However, if he knows for certain that he did indeed spill blood – he should not lift his hands. However, if he has repented, there is room to be lenient, so as not to close the door on him, as I have written.

And an uncircumcised person whose brothers died because of circumcision – some say he is disqualified from lifting his hands just as he is from performing sacrificial service (Bach). And some say he is qualified (Magen Avraham, subsection 54), as it is not analogous in all respects. And perhaps even an intentional uncircumcised person is qualified (there), as other transgressions do not disqualify. However, in practice, it is difficult to be lenient, as it seems to be a complete analogy to sacrificial service. And this is the opinion of the great later authorities (Taz, subsection 35; Elyah Rabbah, subsection 69; and Knesset HaGedolah).

The Rambam wrote in Chapter 15, Law 4: One who drinks a quarter-log of wine at once should not raise his hands [to bless the congregation] until the wine has worn off, because the blessing is compared to the Temple service. If he drank a quarter-log of wine in two sittings, or if he added a little water to it, it is permitted. But if he drank more than a quarter-log, even if it was diluted, and even if he drank it in several sittings, he should not raise his hands until the wine has worn off. And how much is a quarter-log? Two fingerbreadths by two fingerbreadths in height, and half a fingerbreadth plus a fifth of a fingerbreadth in volume. This is the finger with which the entire Torah is anointed, which is the thumb, also called "thumb of the hand." So far his words. And even if he drank wine from the winepress, which is still not good wine, he is disqualified just as in Temple service (Magen Avraham, end of subparagraph 55). Some say that this comparison of blessing to service is merely a supportive reference (Beit Yosef). And some say it is a complete comparison (Taz, subparagraph 35). The practical difference arises concerning other beverages, as will be explained.

And know that other beverages besides wine—for work (in the Temple) it is prohibited by a negative commandment, but there is no death penalty as there is with wine. According to this, regarding the priestly blessing when one is intoxicated with other beverages, such as strong wine, mead, and beer, some say it is prohibited just as with work (in the Temple) (Taz there), since it is a complete analogy. However, in Ta'anit (27a) it is explicitly stated that it is merely a rabbinic support, see there. Therefore, in truth, Rabbeinu Yerucham (brought in Beit Yosef) wrote that an intoxicated person, specifically when he has reached the level of Lot's intoxication, should not raise his hands (for the priestly blessing). This is his wording. And his intention is regarding other beverages (Perisha). And the explanation of his words: In Ta'anit there, we learn the prohibition of wine for the priestly blessing from a Nazir, see there. A Nazir is completely permitted to consume other beverages, and for work (in the Temple) as well, there is no death penalty for other beverages. Therefore, for the priestly blessing, it is completely permitted; only when he reaches the level of Lot's intoxication, at which point he is exempt from all commandments, should he not raise his hands (and this is the intention of the Magen Avraham in section 55). However, Rabbeinu the Beit Yosef in his great book wrote: Even though he also holds that it is merely a rabbinic support, nevertheless, his opinion is that even without reaching Lot's level of intoxication, it is prohibited to ascend the platform. And it is not less than prayer, as explained in Siman 99, that even without reaching Lot's level of intoxication, it is prohibited to pray. And this seems to be the primary ruling of the law. (And the Magen Avraham there disagreed with the Beit Yosef. His words are not clear to me, see there. Examine and you will find clarity.)

It has already been explained that other transgressions do not prevent one from performing the Priestly Blessing (Nesi'at Kapayim). There is an opinion that this only applies if he has repented (Magen Avraham, subsection 56, in the name of Ra'anch). However, these words are astonishing, for it is explicitly stated in the words of the Rambam and the Jerusalem Talmud that we have cited, that even if he is currently wicked, he may still ascend to perform the Priestly Blessing. There should be no doubt about this, as there is no uncertainty in this matter.

It is clear that a חלל (a disqualified descendant of a priest) should not raise his hands (to bless the congregation), as he has lost the sanctity of priesthood. However, a valid Kohen who marries women prohibited to priests does not disqualify himself from the priesthood, as his offspring are disqualified, but not he himself. Nonetheless, it is taught in Bechorot (45b): one who marries women in violation (of priestly prohibitions) is disqualified until he takes a vow of abstinence. And there, it is referring to the service in the Temple, and regarding the raising of hands it is not clarified what the law is. Neither Rambam nor Tur mention this at all. However, Rabbeinu Beit Yosef writes in section 40: a Kohen who marries a divorced woman should not raise his hands. He is not accorded honor, even to be called first to the Torah. And even if he divorces her or she dies, he is disqualified until he takes a vow of abstinence regarding many women who are forbidden to him. This is his language. And he explained the reason in his major work: since the Sages penalized him concerning Temple service, it is obvious that he is disqualified rabbinically from all priestly matters until he takes a vow of abstinence with the consent of many. Similarly, the Rashba wrote in a responsum, see there. And certainly this is correct. It appears to me that in this matter, it is stricter in our times than in the times of the Temple because in the times of the Temple perhaps it was sufficient to penalize him by not allowing him to serve in the Temple. But in our times, if we do not penalize him regarding the raising of hands and being called first to the Torah, how will we penalize him? And indeed, we see from the Mishnah in Bechorot that the Sages imposed such a penalty on him.

In Bechorot, it is taught that a priest who becomes impure through contact with the dead is disqualified from performing the Temple service until he accepts upon himself not to become impure again through contact with the dead. In this case, our Sages of blessed memory did not require him to take a vow of abstention, but only in matters of forbidden relationships where the impulse is strong did they require a vow of abstention, and not in transgressions where the impulse is not strong. And since this is due to a penalty, therefore, in this case, too, Rabbeinu the Beit Yosef wrote in section 41: If he becomes impure through contact with a corpse that is not one of the seven relatives for whom a priest is commanded to become impure, he is disqualified from the platform and from all functions of the priesthood until he repents and accepts not to become impure again through contact with the dead. So far his words. And I am astonished: From his language, it seems that if he became impure only once, he is disqualified, whereas from the language of the Mishnah we cited, it seems specifically when he is accustomed to making himself impure and not when he made himself impure once, for it states "one who becomes impure through contact with the dead" and not "one who becomes impure through contact with a dead body." And this is also clearly implied by the language of the Rambam in the sixth chapter of Biyat Mikdash. Similarly, regarding women, it is written: A priest who marries women in transgression implies that he is accustomed to doing so. But if he did it once, he divorces her and that suffices. This requires significant study, for in my humble opinion, the main legal ruling is as I have written.

And regarding what was written that one should vow with the intent of the public, so too wrote the Rambam in the sixth chapter of Hilchot Bi'at Mikdash, see there. And certainly, according to the Talmudic discussion in Bechorot there and in Gittin (36a), this is only necessary if one does not need to specify the vow, because then we are concerned that he might go to a sage and have the vow annulled. Therefore, it must be with the intent of the public, as that cannot be annulled. But for us, who hold according to Yoreh De'ah, Siman 228, that one must specify the vow—it does not need to be with the intent of the public. And many things have been said about this (see Magen Avraham, Siman 58, and Beit Shmuel in Even HaEzer, Siman 96, and Eliyah Rabbah). And it seems simple to me that certainly, in any way we can be stringent upon him—we are stringent. And in the Gemara, it is the opposite, as it questions the Mishnah that one makes him vow, and why not be concerned that he might have it annulled by a sage. And it answers that he must specify... and it questions: this is fine... and it answers that we make him vow with the intent of the public. Meaning: then according to all opinions, it is effective. But it is not explained: that for the one who says the vow must be specified—it does not need to be with the intent of the public, and why not make the strongest reinforcement possible?

Rabbi Rema wrote in section 41 that some say that if someone has a daughter who has converted to another religion, or who has committed adultery, one is no longer obligated to sanctify her, "for she has desecrated her father." Thus far his language. And they wrote that the primary obligation is due to adultery, as he should have guarded her so that she would not be secluded with a man. As it is said in Ketubot (45a): "See the product of what you have raised." Therefore, they stone her at the door of her father's house; see there. And they wrote that if she converted, it is certain that she committed adultery, for with other transgressions, what can the father do (Magen Avraham section 62 and Eliyah Rabbah)? And they also wrote that this is only in regard to honoring him to open first in the Torah reading or at a meal. But he can still perform the priestly blessing (there and Taz section 36). According to this, I do not know why it was written in this section. In truth, in his book "Darkei Moshe," he wrote this law in section 135 regarding the Torah reading, and similarly, the source of the law in Mordechai Sanhedrin chapter 7 is explicitly about the Torah reading. It seems to me that in the Shulchan Aruch it was mistakenly copied into this section, and its place is in section 135. And we have already written that a desecrated priest does not perform the priestly blessing. Even a rabbinically desecrated priest, such as if his father married a woman who was released from levirate marriage, which is a rabbinic prohibition. The detailed laws of a desecrated priest are explained in Even HaEzer section 7; see there.

An onen (a mourner before the burial) is forbidden to lift his hands (to perform the priestly blessing) because he is prohibited from performing service, and the lifting of hands is considered a service (Magen Avraham, subsection 64). Additionally, he is exempt from all commandments in the Torah. However, a mourner during the days of mourning, meaning within the seven days, we do not find that he is exempt from this commandment. Therefore, it is good for him to leave the synagogue before the priestly blessing. Nevertheless, if they called him, he is obligated to go up, or if he was in the synagogue at the time the chazzan (prayer leader) said "Kohanim" (calling the priests). Also on Shabbat, he should leave the synagogue. Some say that on Shabbat he should go up to the platform and fulfill the positive commandment (Pri Chadash). It seems that if there is no other kohen there but him, he definitely needs to go up. (See Magen Avraham, subsection 65, and it requires further investigation. Also, the wording is somewhat unclear, see there.)

However, our teacher, the Rema, wrote in section 43 that some say that during the entire period of mourning, even up to twelve months for one's father and mother, one does not perform the Priestly Blessing. And this is the custom in these regions. This is his language. And for other relatives, until thirty days. Certainly, this custom is puzzling. For this is included in the general custom observed in his land, not to ascend to the platform all year, as will be explained. And there is no proper reason for this other than what we explained in section 49 based on the words of the Zohar, see there. And our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 44: A Kohen, even if he is single, performs the Priestly Blessing. And our teacher, the Rema, wrote that some say he does not perform the Priestly Blessing, for one who is without a wife is without joy. And the one who blesses should be in joy. And the custom is that he performs the Priestly Blessing even if he is not married. Nevertheless, one who does not want to perform the Priestly Blessing is not protested against, as long as he is not in the synagogue at the time they call "Kohanim" or tell them to wash their hands. This is his language. For if they call them to ascend, or if they are present at the time of the saying "Kohanim," they transgress a positive commandment if they do not ascend. This too is among the puzzling matters, and we explained it there in section 49. However, among us, the custom is that the young Kohanim ascend to the platform, especially since among us it is a cherished mitzvah only on holidays. And this is very proper.

Rabbeinu the Rema wrote: It is customary in all these lands that they do not raise their hands (for the priestly blessing) except on Yom Tov, because then they are immersed in the joy of Yom Tov, and a good heart will bless. This is not the case on other days, even on the Sabbaths of the year when they are preoccupied with thoughts about their livelihood and the cessation of their work. Even on Yom Tov, they do not raise their hands except during the Musaf prayer, when they leave the synagogue and rejoice in the joy of Yom Tov. And in all Shacharit and Musaf prayers in which they do not raise their hands, the prayer leader says "Our God and the God of our fathers" as mentioned above in Siman 127. And on Yom Kippur, they do raise their hands like on Yom Tov (even though there is no joy of eating and drinking). In some places, they raise their hands during the Ne'ilah prayer, and in some places even during Shacharit. This is because of the inherent sanctity of this holy day.

Certainly, here is the translation:

And indeed, there is certainly no valid reason for our custom to nullify the positive commandment of the Priestly Blessing throughout the entire year. It has been written that it is a poor custom. But what can we do, as if a divine voice has decreed that we not lift our hands in blessing the entire year? And I have received that two great leaders of the generation before us, each in his place, wanted to institute the lifting of hands every day. And when they designated a specific day for this, the matter became confused and did not succeed. And they said that it appears that from Heaven it was decreed so. And according to the law, it can be said based on what I wrote in section 49 according to the Zohar, that we need joy similar to Aaron and his sons on the eighth day of the inauguration. And for this, it is said: "Thus shall you bless." However, the custom from earlier times that on a Yom Tov that falls on Shabbat they would not lift their hands – this has already been nullified in our days, as there is no reason or sense in this custom, as the commentators on the Shulchan Aruch have elaborated (Taz, subparagraph 37, and Magen Avraham, subparagraph 70). And a man who has had a seminal emission is permitted to lift his hands in blessing (Beit Yosef). And one who is stringent to immerse will have a blessing come upon him. However, in the Land of Israel and in Egypt and throughout Asia, the kohanim lift their hands in blessing every day.

These are the places where the priests turn towards: the South and the North. Meaning: they turn their faces there, so that the blessing spreads to all directions (Eliyah Rabbah). And these are: "Yevarechecha" (May He bless you), "Veyishmerecha" (and keep you), "Eilecha" (toward you), "Vichuneka" (and be gracious to you), "Eilecha" (toward you), "Lecha" (toward you), "Shalom" (peace). And our master the Rema wrote in section 45: "It is customary to extend the melody of these words, because each of them is the end of a blessing in itself." Thus are his words, meaning: in the Priestly Blessing, there are six blessings, as Rashi explained in the Chumash. And these are: "Yevarechecha" is one blessing. "Veyishmerecha" is the second. "Eilecha," which is the end of the blessing of "Ya'er," is the third. "Vichuneka" is the fourth. "Eilecha" of "Yisa," which is the end of the blessing of "Yisa," is the fifth. And "Lecha Shalom" is the sixth. Therefore, "Yevarechecha" is also considered the end of a blessing, since it is a blessing in itself. And "Eilecha" of "Vichuneka" is the end of the blessing of "Ya'er," and "Eilecha" of "Yisa" is the end of the blessing of "Yisa," and "Lecha Shalom" is one blessing (this resolves the question of the Magen Avraham in section 72). And they say "Ribbono Shel Olam" (Master of the Universe) as I wrote in section 130. And when do they say this? When the priests extend the melodies at the end of the verses: "Veyishmerecha," "Vichuneka," "Shalom." But not during the recitation of the words, but when the prayer leader finishes "Veyishmerecha," they sing, and the congregation says "Ribbono Shel Olam." And when they finish, the priests say "Veyishmerecha." Similarly with "Vichuneka" and "Shalom." The one prompting, meaning the prayer leader, should not say "Ribbono Shel Olam," because it is forbidden for him to interrupt. Rather, he stands silent. (See Magen Avraham section 73, from which it appears that the priests sing within the word itself at its end. This is not our custom.) (And even if someone else prompts, they should not say "Ribbono Shel Olam.")

Rabbeinu the Rema wrote at the end of this section: It is forbidden to use a Kohen (priest) even in this time, as it is akin to misusing consecrated property unless he forgives it. Until here is his language. At first glance, this is not understood: for if it is akin to misusing consecrated property, what benefit is there in forgiveness? Therefore, we need to explain this law, which early and later authorities have grappled with. The source of the law is from the Jerusalem Talmud, Chapter Eight of Berachot (Halacha 5), and this is what it says there: Rabba bar bar Chana and Rav Huna were sitting and eating, and Rabbi Zeira was standing and serving them. He handed them a cup and oil with one hand. And Beit Hillel says there that one should take the oil in his right hand and the cup in his left hand. Rabba bar bar Chana said to Rabbi Zeira: Is your other hand amputated that you brought them with one hand? And Rabba bar bar Chana's father became angry with him and said: Is it not enough that you are sitting and he is standing and serving? Moreover, Rabbi Zeira is a Kohen, and Shmuel said: One who uses a Kohen is guilty of misuse. But you also disgrace him? Therefore, I decree that you shall stand and Rabbi Zeira shall sit, and you shall serve him. And from where do we know that one who uses a Kohen commits misuse? Rabbi Elazar said in the name of Shmuel, as it is written in Ezra (8:28) when he handed over silver, gold, and vessels to the priests for the Temple, Ezra said: "You are holy to the Lord, and the vessels are holy." Just as one who uses the vessels is guilty of misuse, so too one who uses the Kohanim is guilty of misuse. Until here is the language of the Jerusalem Talmud. And it is necessary to scrutinize: if so, why did Rabba bar bar Chana's father remain silent until he disgraced him, and did not protest when Rabbi Zeira served them?

And in the Hagahot Maimoniot, Chapter Three of Avadim, regarding the law that a Kohen's servant cannot be pierced (as an eved ivri), but it is permitted to sell him as a Hebrew servant, it is written that from this it implies that serving a Kohen is permitted. This is difficult from the Yerushalmi that says one who uses the priesthood commits sacrilege. He remains with this difficulty; see there. And it is surprising: What is his difficulty? From this very Yerushalmi itself it is proven that it is permitted, for Rabbi Zeira served before them. And the Sefer Mitzvot Gadol in the positive commandment 3 regarding the law of a Hebrew servant explained this, and this is the language of the Sefer Mitzvot Gadol: From here it can be proven that even though it says in the Yerushalmi Berachot that one who uses the priesthood commits sacrilege, nevertheless, for a wage it is permitted to make him serve. This is his language. And it is not understood: Does a Hebrew servant take a wage? Behold, he is sold for his theft. And in the Mordechai Gittin in the glosses, he brought (see Taz section 39) an incident of a Kohen who poured water on the hands of Rabbeinu Tam. And a student asked: Have we not learned in the Yerushalmi that one who uses the priesthood commits sacrilege? And Rabbeinu Tam answered: There is no sanctity nowadays, for we hold that if their garments are upon them, they have sanctity. And if not, they do not. And the student asked: If so, should we not perform any forms of sanctity? And Rabbeinu Tam was silent. And Rabbeinu Peter answered that even though there is sanctity, he can waive it, as we say: A Kohen's servant is not pierced because he becomes blemished. And if not for this reason, he could be made to serve. This is his language. And Rabbeinu Tam's answer is not understood at all. And how did he say there is no sanctity nowadays? Behold, the incident in the Yerushalmi occurred in this time, in the time of the Amoraim.

Indeed, the clarification of the matter is as follows: The Torah sanctified the priests for the service of the Temple, and called them "holy" as it is written: "They shall be holy to their God ... for they offer the offerings of the Lord, the food of their God; therefore they shall be holy." And the Holy One, blessed be He, also commanded us to sanctify them, as it is written: "And you shall sanctify him, for he offers the bread of your God; he shall be holy to you." This is a commandment that we should sanctify them.

We need to clarify: it is understandable that the Holy One, blessed be He, sanctified them to serve in the Temple and commanded that they should not marry divorced women and prostitutes — this is appropriate. But how can we sanctify them? The explanation is that we should honor them as something holy. Therefore, the Sages said in Gittin (59b): "And you shall sanctify him" applies to all matters of sanctity: to be the first to open [with the Torah reading], to be the first to bless, and to take a good portion first. This means that he should be honored by you.

Accordingly, it is clear that in what the Holy One, blessed be He, sanctified them, they have no power to change, and it is not dependent on their will, for it is a royal decree. But in what we are commanded to sanctify them, meaning to honor them — they have the ability to forgo it, for even a teacher who forgoes his honor, his honor is forgone. Therefore, in all matters they can forgo, except for the Torah reading to bless first, which the Sages instituted that he cannot forgo for the sake of peace. This will be explained in section 135.

Know that the term "Me'ilah" (trespass) does not specifically refer to the obligation of a Me'ilah sacrifice. Every transgression is called "Me'ilah," as it is written: "And they acted treacherously against the Lord, the God of their fathers." Onkelos translates "Me'ilah" as an expression of falsehood, see there. Similarly, it is written: "To trespass against the Lord in the matter of Peor." Explicitly, we learned in Me'ilah (18a): Me'ilah is nothing but a change. And it says (Numbers 5:12): "If any man's wife goes astray, and acts unfaithfully toward him." And it says: "And they acted treacherously...," see there. Anyone who acts against the Torah is called a "Mo'el" (one who commits Me'ilah). With this understanding, everything becomes clear, as we will explain with the help of Heaven.

Rabbi Zeira, when he served Rabba bar Bar Hannah and Rabbi Chiya of his own goodwill, there was nothing for Rabba bar Bar Hannah's father to complain about. However, when Rabba bar Bar Hannah reprimanded him for not serving properly and insulted his honor, it was as if he was forced to serve him. Therefore, his father became angry and said to him: "Is it not enough that you sit while he stands and serves you?" Meaning, that he shows you honor. Additionally, he is a priest and has waived his priestly honor. Yet you also insult him, making it as if you are forcing him to serve you. And one who makes use of a priest is considered to have violated sacred trust. Meaning, one who uses a priest without his consent commits a transgression, altering the sanctity of Heaven, as the Torah commanded "and you shall sanctify him," and you are degrading him. And Shmuel said: Since Ezra said "You are holy and the vessels are holy" – just as one who uses the vessels without permission commits a sacrilege, so too one who uses the priests without permission commits a sacrilege, meaning he transgresses.

Accordingly, the Hagahot Maimoniot rightly questions, for indeed we sell a Hebrew slave due to his theft, and this sale is against his will, obviously. And someone who uses priestly privileges without consent is guilty of misappropriation. However, the Sefer Mitzvot Gadol (SeMaG) answered that it is permitted to use him if it is for his wages. In other words, if he rented himself out willingly, it is permitted, for he forgoes his honor. Therefore, the Torah's will should not be less important than his own will, as the Torah 'rents' him out to repay his theft. He is compelled to accept the will of the Torah, so he will say "I am willing." And they force him until he says "I am willing," as is known from the laws of divorce and sacrifices.

And Rabbeinu Tam is of the opinion that the primary sanctity is during the time when they wear the priestly garments. And explicitly, we say in Zevachim (17b): "And you shall gird them with a sash... and it shall be for them a perpetual priesthood," when their garments are upon them – their priesthood is upon them, when their garments are not upon them – their priesthood is not upon them. However, according to this, why did they say "you shall sanctify him"? To allow him to open first..., and this is when their garments are not upon them. Therefore, Rabbeinu Tam is of the opinion that when their garments are upon them – their sanctity is not under their control, and they cannot waive it. But when their garments are not upon them – their sanctity is under their control, and they can waive it. And this is what Rabbeinu Tam hinted at in his response. The student did not understand until Rabbeinu Peter explained it to him. And Rabbeinu Tam's intention was that since when their garments are not upon them they can waive, especially since it is an honor to serve a great person like Rabbeinu Tam, and it is understood that Rabbeinu Tam would not want to say this himself; therefore he hinted that only when their garments are upon them does the waiver not help, but now it does. And the student did not understand until Rabbeinu Peter explained it to him.

Accordingly, the law is clear: a kohen (priest) may, of his own will, serve and officiate as he wishes. This is contrary to the opinion that if the kohen does not receive any benefit, it is prohibited, and his consent does not help (Turei Zahav, end of subsection 39). This opinion has already been challenged (Eliyah Rabbah, subsection 90, and Ba'er Heitev, subsection 83). Similarly, I do not agree with the view that with an ignorant kohen it is permissible to use him (Mishneh LaMelech there), for did the Torah differentiate between an ignorant person and a scholar? It is clear later in section 135 that the common practice is that even an ignorant kohen precedes a great scholar of Israel to be called up to the Torah; see there. Some have also written leniently, claiming that nowadays there are no priestly lineages. Heaven forbid to say this, and to cast aspersions on the sanctity of the kohanim. This has already been vehemently protested (Eliyah Rabbah, end of section 56). The essence of the law is this: without the kohen's consent, it is forbidden to use him; with his consent, it is permitted. It seems to me that even for a kohen to use another kohen, it is forbidden. Or it is possible that "you shall sanctify him" applies only to Israelites, and all that our sages considered under "you shall sanctify him" such as being called first... does not apply from kohen to kohen. This requires further examination in practice. There is also a question whether it is permissible to use a kohen with a blemish, since he is unfit for service, and we do not say about him "for he offers the food of your God." This also seems to be the main point.

The Priestly Blessing (Nesi'at Kapayim) is only performed during the Shacharit and Musaf prayers, and during Ne'ilah on a day when the Ne'ilah prayer is recited, such as Yom Kippur. Additionally, on a public fast day during the times when the Ne'ilah prayer was customarily recited, as in the time of the Mishnah. However, it is not performed during Mincha because by that time the people would have already eaten, and the priests might have drunk wine, and a priest who is intoxicated is prohibited from performing the Priestly Blessing. Even on a fast day, the Priestly Blessing is not performed during Mincha, as a decree was made to prevent confusion with the regular Mincha prayer of any day.

In what case are these words said? In fasts during which we pray the Mincha and Ne'ilah services. However, a fast that does not have Ne'ilah, such as Tisha B'Av, the seventeenth of Tammuz, and the tenth of Tevet, as well as any public fast day among us, since the Mincha prayer is recited close to sunset, it appears as if it is Ne'ilah and is not confused with the daily Mincha service. Therefore, there is the priestly blessing (Nesi'at Kapayim) during Mincha. And if a Kohen transgressed and went up to the platform (Duchan) to bless during the Mincha of Yom Kippur, since it is known that there is no drunkenness there, he may perform the priestly blessing. He is not removed from the platform due to suspicion, so that people should not say he was disqualified and therefore removed. So wrote Rambam at the beginning of chapter fourteen of Hilchot Tefillah, see there. Similarly, it is written by the Tur and Shulchan Aruch. And in the name of Behag, the Tur wrote that on Yom Kippur, the priestly blessing is given during Mincha, because there is an abundance of supplications and it is also close to sunset. And the Tur wrote that in Ashkenaz, this is not the custom, see there. And among us, in any case, aside from Mussaf, there is no priestly blessing. (From this it appears that they used to pray Mincha every day several hours before nightfall, because they wanted to eat after Mincha. So wrote the Magen Avraham in subsection 2 in the name of the Ran. And only on fast days would they pray close to sunset.)

And Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote: Therefore, we say during the Mincha (afternoon) prayer on Yom Kippur, "Our God… bless us…" even though it is not appropriate for the priestly blessing (Nesiat Kapayim), nevertheless, since if the Kohen ascends he does not descend – it is considered somewhat appropriate. And this is the custom in these countries, even though there are those who disagree. Thus far are his words. And all the more so on any fast day when we say "Our God," for indeed it is appropriate for the priestly blessing. And our custom when we say "Our God" is to say "Sim Shalom" and not "Shalom Rav." Nevertheless, for those who fast until noon and then pray Mincha Gedola (early afternoon prayer) – the custom is not to say "Our God" and they say "Shalom Rav." And even though, according to the reasoning that if he ascends he does not descend, this should apply then as well since they have neither eaten nor drunk, nevertheless, this is not the custom (see Magen Avraham, small section 1).

Our Sages of blessed memory said in Berachot (55b): One who sees a dream but does not know what he saw should stand before the Kohanim when they ascend to the platform and say the following: "Master of the Universe! I am Yours, and my dreams are Yours. I dreamed a dream and I do not know what it is. (May it be Your will, Hashem my God and God of my fathers, that all my dreams be for my benefit.) (This is not in the Gemara.) Whether I dreamed about myself…" until "for good." And we conclude, "and protect me" (corresponding to "and safeguard you") "and be gracious to me" (corresponding to "and be gracious to you") "and accept me" (corresponding to "peace"). From this it is understood that this is only effective when one does not know the dream, but if he knows it, he specifically needs the interpretation of the dream (as the Maharshal wrote). He should try to conclude his prayer simultaneously with the Kohanim, so that when the congregation responds "Amen," it will also apply to his prayer. For "Amen" is very effective in having one's prayer accepted, as our Sages of blessed memory said: Greater is the one who answers "Amen" than...

In the Gemara it states: "And if not, say the following: 'Mighty in the heights… May it be Your will to bestow upon us and upon all Your people, the house of Israel… peace.'" It seems to me to explain "And if not," meaning: if one did not manage to say "Master of the Universe" before the priests turned their faces back, he should say "Mighty in the heights" (and it seems to me that this is what the Ma'adanei Yom Tov intended, see there). However, the commentators of the Shulchan Aruch explained: "And if not," meaning: when they have finished "Master of the Universe" and the priests have not yet finished, he should also say this (Taz and Magen Avraham). According to this, the phrase "And if not" is not precise. There are those who explain "And if not," meaning: if he does not have the strength to say the lengthy "Master of the Universe," he should say "Mighty in the heights" (Eliyah Rabbah in the name of Agudah).

And know that our custom, after the priests turn their faces back, is to say "Adir Bamarom." This does not align with our version in the Gemara, but the custom is based on the version of Rif and Rosh who read it this way: "And when the priests turn their faces back, they should say...," see there. Additionally, our custom is that everyone says "Ribbono Shel Olam" (Master of the Universe), even those who did not have a dream, because we only ascend the platform on Yom Tov. If not now, they will never say it. Perhaps it is believed that this prayer is effective even without a dream that night. Rabbi Rema wrote that in places where they do not ascend the platform, all this should be said when the cantor says "Sim Shalom," and he should conclude together with the cantor so that the congregation can respond "Amen." This is his language. If he sees that he will not be able to finish with the cantor, he should start when the cantor says "Yevarechecha" (May He bless you) (Magen Avraham). But this should not be said every day (Taz).

And after the prayer leader concludes the repetition of the Amidah – they fall on their faces and supplicate. The matter of falling on the face is to arrange the prayer in three orders: initially a prayer while seated, which refers to up to the Amidah, then a prayer while standing, and then the falling on the face, as Moses our teacher did, as it is written: "I sat on the mountain"; and it is written: "And I stood on the mountain... and I fell before the Lord" (Tur). Therefore, we say afterward "we do not know what to do," meaning: we have prayed in every possible manner, and beyond this, we do not know what to do, and our eyes are upon You (this is implied in the Tur, see there).

The Tur wrote in the name of Rav Natronai Gaon: "Nefilat Apayim (the Tachanun prayer) is a voluntary practice and not an obligation," see there. Therefore, it is easily omitted for various reasons as will be explained. And it seems to me that now that all of Israel has adopted this practice, it has taken on the status of an obligation, whether in a small measure or a large measure. We also find in the Gemara that although it is voluntary, its significance is very great. From Heaven, they hasten to respond to Nefilat Apayim, as we say at the end of the chapter "HaZahav" regarding the case of the oven of Achnai, that Rabbi Eliezer had a grievance against Rabban Gamliel the Nasi, and Rabbi Eliezer's wife was the sister of Rabban Gamliel. She did not allow him to fall on his face every day. Once, she was not attentive, and he fell on his face, and immediately Rabban Gamliel was punished, see there. It is explicitly stated that it is not an obligation, for if it were an obligation, he would not have heeded her. It is also explicitly stated that its power is great, for his prayer was accepted immediately.

And our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote: One should not speak between the prayer (Amidah) and Tachanun (Nefillat Apayim). Thus are his words. And they were precise in this, for in Siman 51 it is explicitly stated that it is only forbidden to speak until after the Amidah, see there. And they explained that it is specifically forbidden to interrupt and engage in another matter, but casual conversation is not an issue (Magen Avraham, subsection 1). And how strained is this explanation. However, his intention is as follows: the prohibition is not meant in the sense of an actual prohibition, for how can there be a prohibition since it is only optional? However, our teacher the Beit Yosef follows his own reasoning in his great book, where he wrote in the name of the Rashba that it would not have been possible for Rabbi Eliezer's wife to prevent him from performing Nefillat Apayim except by engaging him in conversation, and then his Nefillat Apayim would not be effective in achieving its purpose (see Beit Yosef, and Taz subsection 1. And not like the interpretation of the Rivash brought by the Magen Avraham there, who said he would forget to perform Nefillat Apayim, see there). And this is what our teacher the Beit Yosef means when he says: "One should not speak...", meaning: if one speaks, the benefit of the prayer through Nefillat Apayim will not be achieved.

The main aspect of "Nefilat Apayim" (falling on the face) is the spreading out of hands and feet with the face flat on the ground, similar to what we do on Yom Kippur. And this is the language of the Rambam at the end of the fifth chapter of Tefillah: "How is bowing done? ... One sits on the ground, falls on his face to the ground, and pleads with all the supplications he desires. 'Kneeling' mentioned everywhere refers to on the knees, 'Kiddah' on the face, 'Hishtachavayah' is the spreading out of hands and feet until one is lying flat on the ground. And when one does 'Nefilat Panim' after prayer, some do 'Kiddah' and some do 'Hishtachavayah.' It is forbidden to do 'Hishtachavayah' on stones except in the Temple. And a distinguished person is not allowed to fall on his face unless he knows he is as righteous as Joshua. Instead, he tilts his face slightly and does not press it to the ground... until here are his words. The reason he is not allowed to fall on his face unless he is as righteous as Joshua is explained by Rashi (Megillah 22a) to avoid disgrace if he is not answered immediately. This is also clarified by the Rif and the Rambam. It also appears from the Jerusalem Talmud in the second chapter of Ta'anit, which says that it is specifically in public that one should not do so, but in private, it is allowed; see there. According to this reasoning, it is clear that in private there is no such concern, as not everyone knows. This is the reason mentioned in the Gemara, that Abaye and Rava, when they fell on their faces, they tilted to the side slightly as is customary among us, and did not fall to the ground. Thus, we certainly are not worthy to fall with our faces to the ground. And this is the common practice.

Therefore, the Rambam in the ninth chapter of the order of prayer wrote in this law that after completing the entire prayer, one should sit and fall on one's face, tilting slightly, he and the entire congregation, and beseech while falling, then sit and raise his head, he and the rest of the people, and plead a little in a loud voice while sitting. Thus far his words. Meaning: that after the supplication, they say something, like we say "Guardian of Israel" or "And we do not know." And it is clear from his words that the supplication is only while sitting. And even the prayer leader, as he wrote: "And he falls and sits." However, this is not our custom, for the prayer leader tilts on his side while standing at the podium. And so wrote our teacher, the Beit Yosef, in section 2: "Falling on the face is done while sitting and not while standing." Thus far his words. And he explained in his great book that according to the Kabbalah, it is essential. Therefore, even if he finished his prayer now and is standing where he ended his steps – he should not fall there while standing but should sit there. And if it is not possible to sit there – he waits the time it takes to walk four cubits, and returns to his place and sits (Magen Avraham, section 5). But the Rivash and the Maharil wrote that it is not a strict matter, and he can fall while standing (there). And we, although we follow the first opinion, nevertheless, many times it happens that it is impossible to sit, such as when his fellow is standing in prayer within his four cubits, and it is forbidden to sit according to the Talmudic law as explained in section 105. And Heaven forbid to transgress the Talmudic law because of this, and then we fall while standing. (And the Rosh and the Tur wrote that the reason Abaye and Rava prayed while leaning was not because an important person is not allowed…, but because although according to Torah law, there is no prohibition to fall on a stone floor except with outstretched hands and feet, nevertheless, by Rabbinic decree, it is also forbidden to fall on a stone floor in a regular manner, see there. According to this, it is also forbidden in one's home. And we must say according to their opinion that the Jerusalem Talmud which permitted it – was not on a stone floor.)

On which side should one fall [during Tachanun]? The Tur writes in the name of a Gaon that an important person should fall on the left side. The reason given is that this is how they would lay down the Tamid offering when they slaughtered it, on its left side (Beit Yosef in the name of the Kol Bo). Another reason: because leaning to the left is called "leaning," which is the leaning of free people. And on the side where one appears as a free person, one must submit before the Divine Presence (ibid., in the name of Rav Hai). A sign for this is: "His left hand is under my head" (ibid.). Another reason: when one prays, the Shechinah (Divine Presence) is on his right, as it is written: "The Lord is your shade upon your right hand"; and it is written: "I have set the Lord always before me." Therefore, when one leans to the left, his face is towards the Shechinah. If he leans to the right, it will be the opposite, and it is not proper to do so (ibid., in the name of the Ra'avad).

The Tur wrote that in Ashkenaz they have the custom to lean to the right side, and this is stated in the Midrash on the verse "and His right arm embraces me." So far his words. And so wrote the Rokeach: We lean to the right because the Shechinah is opposite the person, and when he leans to his right and the Shechinah is opposite him, "His left arm is under my head, and His right arm embraces me." So far his words (Beit Yosef). And so wrote the Rivash in a responsum in the name of Rashi in the name of his teachers, that it is proper to lean to the right side, as it is written: "...and His right arm embraces me." And so it is in Bereshit Rabbah (there). And Rabbeinu the Rema wrote in Section 1 that the primary practice is to lean to the right side in the morning when he has tefillin on his left arm because of the honor of the tefillin, and in the evening or when he does not have tefillin on his left arm, he should lean to the left side. So far his words. And there are those who wrote that even in the morning with tefillin he should fall on the left but turn his head to the right, and in the afternoon he should lean to the left. And our custom is according to Rabbeinu the Rema, and so agreed the later authorities (Taz and Magen Avraham, Section 3). And when he falls, he should not fall on the flesh of his hand but on a garment, for the hand is not considered a covering as I wrote in Siman 91 (there, Section 2). And the prayer leader should lean his head towards the lectern (there, Section 3) and not to the sides. And likewise, one who sits opposite the Ark should lean towards it (there), for it is better this way as it appears as bowing towards the Holy Ark. And he does not need to fall specifically in the place where he prayed, for it is permitted to pray in one place and fall in supplication in another place.

In the Tur, it is written to say at the time of Tachanun (falling on the face): "Master of all worlds and Lord of lords, the great, mighty, and awe-inspiring God, have mercy on us, for we are Your servants and the work of human hands… What are we, what is our life… What can we say before You, Lord our God, for we have sinned and transgressed. We have no priest to perform our obligations, nor a High Priest… nor an altar… Therefore, may it be Your will that our prayer be accepted and considered before You as bulls and sheep as if we had offered them on the altar, and may You find favor with us." Until here is his wording. There is also another prayer there from the Jerusalem Talmud, see there. But our custom is to say the Psalm "Merciful and gracious, I have sinned…" up to "they shall be ashamed momentarily." And some say first the verse "And David said to Gad, I am in great distress…" but we are not accustomed to say it. The Sephardic custom is to say the Psalm "To David, to You, Lord, I lift my soul," and so it is in the Zohar. And one should intend to surrender their soul. And it is warned that if one does not intend with full concentration but with a distant heart, it will cause them to leave this world before their time, see there. Therefore, they refrained from saying it in Ashkenaz (Magen Avraham at the end of subsection 5).

After raising his head after the "falling on the face" (Tachanun), he should plead a little, each place according to its custom. Our custom is to say "Guardian of Israel..." until "and save us." Afterwards, we say "We do not know what to do." It has been written that it is proper to say "We do not know" while sitting, and "what to do" while standing and in a loud voice (Magen Avraham, subsection 4, in the name of the Shelah). The reason seems to me to be based on what I wrote in subsection 1 that we prayed in every possible manner: sitting, standing, and falling. Therefore, now we hint at this: Have we not fallen, sat, and stood? What more can we do? Now our eyes are only on You, remember Your mercies. Afterward, the prayer leader says the Half Kaddish. Then we say "Ashrei", "Lamnatzeach Ya'ancha", "Uva L'Tzion", as will be explained in Siman 132. Our teacher, the Rema, wrote at the end of subsection 1 that even on days when Tachanun is not said, "Lamnatzeach" is said, except on Rosh Chodesh, Chanukah, Purim, Erev Pesach, Erev Yom Kippur, and Tisha B'Av. Thus are his words. And likewise, "El Erech Apayim" on Mondays and Thursdays, as will be explained in Siman 134. But the Sephardic custom is that "Lamnatzeach" is equivalent to Tachanun, and on days when Tachanun is not said, "Lamnatzeach" is also not said.

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote in Section 2: Some say that the practice of "Nefilat Apayim" (falling on the face) is only performed in a place where there is an Ark with a Torah scroll inside it, but otherwise, one says the supplication without covering the face. And this is the custom. And the courtyard of the synagogue that is open to the synagogue, or when the congregation is praying, then even an individual in his home says the supplication with "Nefilat Apayim." These are his words. This law is from the Rokeach, who provided a sign for it from Joshua in the battle of Ai: "And he fell on his face before the Ark of the Lord." (See Taz, Section 5, who questioned from the episode of the concubine in Gibeah, where it is written: "And they wept before the Lord"; see there. And I am puzzled because there it is written "Ark," and it needs further study.) And Rabbi Yosef Karo, in his great book, wrote that if it is a tradition, we will accept it, and if it is a matter of law, there is an answer. These are his words. And it appears to me that his intention is: for the primary source of "falling" we learned from Moshe Rabbeinu where it is written "And I fell," and there was no Ark. And if because at Mount Sinai it is the primary dwelling of the holiness, in any place where a person prays, the place is holy; and when he prays, the Divine Presence is opposite him, and he is like one standing before the king, as has been explained several times. Furthermore, the Rosh in Megillah ruled that an individual in his home is permitted to fall on his face to the ground, and in his home, it is assumed there is no Torah scroll (Taz there). Nevertheless, the common custom is like the Rokeach and like the ruling of Rema. And in the courtyard of the synagogue that is open to the synagogue, when the door is open, they fall in the courtyard, but not when the door is locked. And in the women's section, they fall (Magen Avraham, Section 7). And similarly, the small rooms surrounding synagogues and study halls have the same status as the synagogue and study hall concerning this matter. And regarding the statement that even an individual in his home, when the congregation is praying, falls on his face – some interpret that this is specifically at the time when the congregation says the supplication (there, Section 8). And some interpret that only during the congregation's prayer time can one fall (Taz, Section 7). And certainly, when praying with a quorum in his home at the time of the congregation's prayer, they fall there even without a Torah scroll (there). And this seems to be the primary intention of Rabbi Rema, although the custom is not like this.

There is no falling on the face at night. Therefore, in the evening prayer, there is no falling on the face, as it is accepted by the sages that falling on the face is an allusion to the attribute of the night, and one does not fall on their face, and it is close to cutting down saplings (Beit Yosef). However, during the days of Selichot in the pre-dawn hours, it is permitted to fall on the face because it is close to the day (ibid.). And after midnight is a time of mercy, but at the beginning of the night, the judgments are strong (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 9). Nevertheless, if the supplication extends from Mincha until twilight, there is no concern as long as it is not definitely night (Taz, subparagraph 8).

Maimonides wrote at the end of the fifth chapter: It is a widespread custom among all Jews not to fall on their faces (for Tachanun) on Shabbat, Yom Tov (festivals), Rosh Hashanah, Rosh Chodesh (the beginning of the new month), Chanukah, and Purim. Nor during the Mincha (afternoon) prayer on the eve of Shabbat and festivals, nor during the Ma'ariv (evening) prayer every day. There are individuals who do fall on their faces during Ma'ariv. On Yom Kippur, they fall on their faces during every prayer because it is a day of supplication, petition, and fasting. This is his language. We do not know or have not heard of this custom to say Tachanun on Yom Kippur or for individuals to fall on their faces during Ma'ariv.

Our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, wrote in section 6: It is customary not to fall on their faces on the 15th of Av, the 15th of Shevat, Rosh Chodesh, and the Mincha prayer before it, and not during Chanukah. Some say also during the Mincha prayer before it, and this is the practice. On Purim, they do not fall on their faces, nor on Lag Ba'omer. Similarly, on the eve of Yom Kippur and the eve of Rosh Hashanah, even during Shacharit (morning) prayer. It is a widespread custom not to fall on their faces during the entire month of Nissan, nor on the 9th of Av, nor between Yom Kippur and Sukkot, nor from the beginning of Rosh Chodesh Sivan until after Shavuot. This is their language. There are places where they do not fall on their faces for seven days after Shavuot because the festival's offerings can be compensated for all seven days (Magen Avraham, section 18). They did not consider Pesach Sheni (the second Passover), which is perplexing, and the Sephardic custom is not to fall on it. Some have the custom not to fall on their faces from after Sukkot until after Rosh Chodesh Mar-Cheshvan, because most of the month was without falling on faces. This is not a primary custom. 

Know that on Lag Ba'omer, one must be very careful. There was an incident with a great person who used to say "Nachem" in prayer every day, and he said it on Lag Ba'omer and was punished (Magen Avraham, section 13, in the name of the Kavanot). Know that from the words of our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, it is clear that during the Mincha before the 15th of Av, the 15th of Shevat, Lag Ba'omer, and Purim - one does fall on their faces, as they explicitly wrote only about Rosh Chodesh and Chanukah. Our custom is not so, as is known.

They also wrote in section 4: It is customary not to fall on one's face [for Tachanun] neither in the house of mourning, nor in the house of the groom, nor in the synagogue on the day of a circumcision when there is a groom. And specifically if the circumcision or the groom is in that synagogue. But if the circumcision is not in the synagogue, even though it is in another synagogue – Tachanun is recited. And on the day of the circumcision when Tachanun is not recited, it is specifically in the morning service when the baby is circumcised. But in the afternoon service, even if they pray near the circumcised baby, Tachanun is recited, which is not the case with a groom, for Tachanun is not recited all day when praying near the groom. And it is only called "groom" on the day he enters the chuppah. Thus far his words.

There are those who say that the reason for mourning is based on the verse: "I will turn your festivals into mourning" (Beit Yosef). But I do not understand: even though we derive from here that the seven days of mourning are similar to a festival, what does this have to do with this issue? On the contrary, it is the opposite of a festival! It seems that the reason is to not intensify the attribute of judgment in a house that is already under judgment (and so writes the Levush). Therefore, no supplications should be recited there, nor the Psalm "May the Lord answer you in the day of distress" (Magen Avraham, subsection 10), nor "And He, the Merciful One" on Mondays and Thursdays. None of these should be recited by the mourners or those praying there during the seven days of mourning. Those praying there, when they return home, should recite "And He, the Merciful One" (Taz, subsection 9). However, they should not recite the Tachanun (supplication) at home (ibid.), as it is only recited immediately after the prayer service. Hallel should not be recited in the house of mourning (Magen Avraham, ibid.). Some say that during Chanukah it should be recited there because it is an obligation, whereas on Rosh Chodesh it is only a custom (ibid. in the name of the Tanya). Others say that even during Chanukah it should not be recited (ibid. in the name of the Maharil). The correct practice is that mourners should not recite it at all, and those praying there should recite it when they return home (ibid.). This applies during Chanukah, and on Rosh Chodesh it is not necessary since it is only a custom. The verse "And as for Me, this is My covenant" in "Uva L'Tzion" should be recited in the house of mourning (ibid.); even though it is not recited on Tisha B'Av, this is because all of Israel is prohibited from studying then. Selichot can be recited in the house of mourning, but not confessions and supplications (Machatzit HaShekel, ibid.). This all applies when there is a mourner present. However, if people are praying in a place where someone has died but there is no mourner present, everything should be recited (ibid.). Similarly, when a mourner is sitting in the synagogue, none of this applies, as he is nullified by the synagogue and it is not appropriate to call it a "house of mourning," obviously. Only he himself should not recite. (And a house of mourning, even if the deceased passed away elsewhere, still seems to be considered a "house of mourning.")

In the house of the groom, one should not recite Tachanun, because it is not appropriate to invoke the attribute of judgment during his time of joy. And even when they return to their homes, they do not need to recite "Vehu Rachum" (Taz, Section 10). Similarly, during a circumcision, because they are exempt due to the joy. This is not comparable to the house of a mourner, where they are not exempt, but rather because it is not appropriate to invoke judgments there, as I have written. And what they have written, that even when the groom or the circumcision is in the synagogue, everyone is exempt, there is no need to ask why this is not the case with a mourner, as I have written. This is not comparable, because in the case of a mourner, the exemption is because of the deceased. And even though the deceased is in another place, nevertheless, the house of the mourner is exempt due to the matter of the deceased. How does this relate to the synagogue? This is not the case with the groom and the circumcision, where the exemption is due to themselves, and therefore, wherever they are, the joy is present and it spreads to everyone (so it appears to me).

And know that the primary joy of the groom is during the seven days of feasting. And this, that they wrote that one is not called a "groom" except on the day he enters the chuppah—this is not intended for the future but for the past. Meaning, one might think that he is called a "groom" from the time of his preparation for the chuppah, as we find in Ketubot (8a) that they used to say "that the joy is in His dwelling place" from the time of betrothal or from when the gates were set up..., see there. And I would say that this applies also regarding Tachanun, since it is only optional. Therefore, it teaches us that only on the day of the chuppah itself and not before. (And this answers the question of the Taz at the end of subparagraph 10. And also what he wrote that one should not come to the synagogue is rejected, see there.
