And be precise and you will find ease.) And it is explained from their words that on the day of the chuppah, even in the morning, one is exempt from Tachanun. And regarding a circumcision in the afternoon, Tachanun should be recited as I have written, but there are those who say it need not be recited (Magen Avraham subparagraph 11 and Bach in the name of Rashal). The correct practice is that if the meal is after Mincha, Tachanun should not be recited, and if the meal was before Mincha, then it is appropriate to recite it. And it seems to me that this is indeed the custom. Additionally, our custom is that even if the circumcision is not in the synagogue, if the father of the child, the mohel, or the sandak prays in the synagogue, Tachanun is not recited. (And we have heard that there is a custom not to recite Tachanun in the entire city when there is a circumcision in the city. This is brought in the Atzei Zayit, see there.)

And know that the seven days of the groom are not from moment to moment, hour to hour. Once the seven days of feasting have passed, even if the wedding was in the evening, we still say Tachanun on the morning of the eighth day. In any place where Tachanun is not said on weekdays, “Av Harachamim” and “Tzidkatcha Tzedek” are also not said on Shabbat. If there is a groom on a fast day, or a circumcision on a fast day, we recite Selichot, and we say Viddui and “Avinu Malkeinu”. Only Tachanun and also “Vehu Rachum” are not said. (And the words of the Rema in section 5 have no understanding, as the Magen Avraham wrote in subsection 13. And see there in subsection 14 regarding the custom of legumes. This custom is not known among us.).

Our masters, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, wrote at the end of this section: "A distinguished person is not permitted to fall on his face when praying on behalf of the community unless he is certain that he will be answered, like Joshua the son of Nun. Similarly, it is forbidden for anyone to fall on their face with outstretched hands and feet, even if there is no stone floor. However, if one leans slightly to the side, it is permitted if there is no stone floor. This is also the practice when falling on one's face on Yom Kippur, if they spread grass there to create a separation from the ground. And this is the custom." Thus far is their language.

And behold, regarding what they wrote about praying on behalf of the community, there is an opinion that interprets it as specifically in the presence of the community (Taz, small section 13), as I wrote in section 4. The language does not imply this. It seems to me that their intention is that only when praying on behalf of the community, even at home, we are concerned about slander if the prayer is not answered. Indeed, there are those who interpret the Jerusalem Talmud we mentioned there in this way (Raavad at the end of the fifth chapter in the first explanation, see there).

And regarding what they wrote that falling on one's face with outstretched hands and feet is forbidden even without a stone floor, meaning even a floor that is not made of stones – this is neither the view of the Rambam nor the Rosh, as we explained in section 4. It is a singular opinion brought by the Rivash, as Rabbi Yosef Karo wrote in his major work. And he was puzzled by this, see there. I am astonished that Rabbi Moshe Isserles was concerned about this.

And regarding what they wrote "if they spread grass there" – it should be said "or they spread" (Taz, small section 15). And the explanation is: without grass or another covering, one should lean, but with grass, there is no need to lean. (And similarly, the Magen Avraham wrote in small section 22. And from his words, it is clear that on Rosh Hashanah during "Aleinu" there is no need to fall on the ground with one's face, see there. And the custom is to act as on Yom Kippur.)

And after the Half-Kaddish, they should say "Ashrei," and "Lamnatzeach Ya'ancha," "Uva L'Tzion," and "V'Atah Kadosh...". The reason for "Ashrei" is because it is stated at the beginning of Berachot (4b): Anyone who recites "Tehillah L'David" three times every day is assured of a place in the World to Come. Therefore, it was instituted to recite it twice in Shacharit: once before the prayer and once after the prayer; and in Mincha once before the prayer. Just as in Shacharit there are two Kedushot, apart from the Kedusha of "Yotzer" which is merely a recounting of how the angels say Kedusha, hence there are two recitations of "Ashrei" in Shacharit. And in Mincha, there is one Kedusha, so they instituted "Ashrei" once. And in Maariv, there is no Kedusha, so it was not instituted at all. For even in "Ashrei," there is the sanctity of the Holy One, Blessed be He, as it is written: "I will exalt You... every day I will bless You, the Lord is great, generation to generation, the splendor of Your glorious majesty, and Your awesome deeds," to indicate that He, blessed be He, is exalted above all blessing and praise, which is the essence of "Kadosh Kadosh." That is to say: holy and separate from all the upper creations, and all the more so from the lower creations. And just as in Kedusha we say "the whole earth is full of His glory," meaning: even though He is holy and separate, nevertheless, the whole earth is filled with His glory, so too in "Ashrei," that despite His immense greatness, He is gracious and compassionate, good to all, and His mercies are upon all His works, and the eyes of all look to Him, and He gives them their food in its season, He opens... in the manner they said: in the place where you find His greatness, there you find His humility...

And another reason for "Ashrei" is that since we have prepared the nourishment of the soul through the recitation of Shema and prayer, and with the tallit and tefillin, and the unification of God's name and love for Him; therefore, we now request that He graciously provide us with the nourishment of the body, that He gives us our food in its proper time, and that He arranges for each person sufficient sustenance. And this is [the meaning of] "You open Your hand." The two verses that we add before "Tehillah L'David" and one after "Tehillah L'David," namely "Ashrei yoshvei veitecha," "Ashrei ha'am shekacha lo," and the verse "Va'anachnu nevarech...," are because in the verses of praise (Pesukei D'Zimra) we have added them for the reason explained at the beginning of Siman 51, see there. Therefore, we also add them here to make them consistent with one another.

And since we are asking for our livelihood, therefore we recite the Psalm "May the Lord answer you in times of trouble." And as it is stated at the end of Berakhot: Why is it written "May the name of the God of Jacob protect you" and not "the God of Abraham and Isaac"? From here we learn that one who bears the beam should enter into the thickness of the beam. Rashi explains: if he comes to move the beam from place to place. That is to say: Jacob, whose children were all his and who toiled to raise them, sought mercy for them. Thus far his words. For Jacob had the distress of raising children and toiled to provide for them. He faced many troubles from Esau and Laban, and the Holy One, blessed be He, delivered him from all of them. Similarly, He will deliver us from our troubles. And in the Midrash Shocher Tov, it is said about this verse: The Holy One, blessed be He, said: At the time when trouble comes upon Israel, and they seek Me... I answer them, and I am with them in trouble. Therefore, we conclude with "May the King answer us when we call." The initials of these three words are numerically equivalent to 112, the same as the numerical value of the names Havayah-Adonai-Ehyeh, which are the primary names of His blessedness from which our sustenance flows. Therefore, we first say "Some trust in chariots... but we call upon the name..." meaning: everyone else has livelihood through natural means, but we trust only in His blessed name. Because naturally, since the destruction of the Temple, we are like those hanging in the air. And it is further stated there in the Midrash that David said this Psalm after eighteen Psalms, and similarly, we say it after the eighteen blessings. (And in our books, it is Psalm 20, but our Sages said that "Ashrei Ha'ish" and "Lama Ragshu" are considered one.)

Afterward, we say "And a redeemer shall come to Zion" as the prophet Isaiah said (Isaiah 59:19): "For distress will come like a river, and a redeemer shall come to Zion." And we also, after "May He answer you on the day of distress," say "And a redeemer shall come to Zion." Afterward, we say the verse "And as for Me, this is My covenant…" which Isaiah also said after the verse "And a redeemer shall come to Zion." This means one should not fear that due to the multitude of troubles, the Torah will be forgotten by Israel. It is not so, for "[the words of Torah] shall not depart from your mouth…" And we have seen this with our own eyes, that after the destruction of the Temple when the Romans decreed harsh and severe decrees upon us, the Torah was actually strengthened during the times of the Tannaim and Amoraim…

And afterwards, they say "Ve'ata Kadosh" (And You are Holy). This is the "Kedusha D'Sidra" mentioned at the end of Sotah, that from the day the Temple was destroyed, there has not been a day without a curse, and each day’s curse is greater than the previous one, as it is said: "In the morning you will say, 'If only it were evening...'" And upon what does the world stand? Upon the "Kedusha D'Sidra" and "Amen, Yehei Shemei Rabbah..." And Rashi explained: The order of Kedusha that was instituted so that all of Israel would engage in Torah with a small matter, by saying its reading and its translation, is as if they are engaged in Torah study... And there is the sanctification of the name and Torah study, and it is beloved. And so too with "Yehei Shemei Rabbah..." until here is his language. It is not understood: How does this relate to the removal of the curse? However, it appears to me that the matter is as follows: As in the Midrash that we brought in section 3, it says: "May the Lord answer you on the day of distress," this is as the verse says: "He will call upon Me, and I will answer him; I will be with him in distress." The Holy One, blessed be He, said: At the time when distress comes upon Israel and they seek Me, My honor is joined with them. At that time I answer them, as it is said: "He will call upon Me, and I will answer him." When? "For I am with him in distress." It is compared to a pregnant woman who had a quarrel with her mother, and her mother went upstairs, and at the time of her childbirth, she was crying out from below, and her mother heard her voice from above, and she too cried out in response... Even though I am angry with her, I cannot bear her crying out, the distress of her daughter is the distress of her mother. Until here is his language. And since the primary help in saving from troubles is to join His, blessed be He, honor with our distress, and also in the Gemara, they said similarly: Whoever associates the Name of Heaven with his distress, his sustenance is doubled (Berachot 63a). And therefore, when the curse increased upon us, and we prayed to Him, blessed be He, we are associating His great name, blessed be He, with our distress. That is to say: distress, as it were, comes to Him, blessed be He, for indeed, the whole earth is filled with His glory, and now His glory is not recognized at all. And we are distressed over the lack of Torah study, which is all His joy, blessed be He. And therefore, we say "The Lord will reign forever and ever." That is to say: When will His reign be revealed? And we say "May His great name be magnified and sanctified," which is entirely built upon the exile of the Shechinah. And in this, the Holy One, blessed be He, as it were, cries out in response to us, removes the curse from us, and bestows upon us our sustenance.

And we precede with the verse, “And You are holy, enthroned upon the praises of Israel.” That is to say: Even though You are holy, nevertheless, You sit and await the praises of Israel. Therefore, all that we add in prayer, praises, and songs – it is pleasing to You, as it were. This serves as an introduction to our preparing ourselves to recite the Kedusha for the third time, for seemingly it is not proper etiquette to repeat and triple something three times. For this, we say that His blessed will is in this. And the reason we translate the Kedusha is so that everyone can understand, because they spoke the language of translation (Aramaic) in Babylon. There are also profound reasons for this. There are those who wrote that the translation should be said softly, and there are those who are not concerned about this (Pri Etz Chaim, 73a: My teacher was not concerned about this…).

Afterwards, we say “Hashem, God of Abraham… preserve this forever to form…,” because this verse was said by David at the end of his prayer in Chronicles (I 29:18). The meaning is as follows: Everything is in the same manner as before, that the increase of curses upon us is due to our sins, and for this, we ask to preserve the order of holiness we have established, to subdue our inclinations and prepare our hearts for His service, may He be blessed. And for the sins of the past: “And He, being merciful, forgives iniquity…, for You, Hashem, are good and forgiving…”. Afterwards, we say “Your righteousness is everlasting…,” which is like justifying the judgment upon us for the great curse from the time of the destruction. Then, we comfort ourselves and say: “Grant truth to Jacob…,” meaning: we are confident that You will grant the kindness promised to Abraham to us, and the truth promised to Jacob. In Jacob, truth is relevant because the promise was already made to Abraham, and He, may He be blessed, will fulfill His word. Then we say, “Blessed be Hashem day by day, He bears our burden,” meaning: we look forward to great goodness in the future, but even now, we are assured that You will provide for our sustenance every day. We say these three verses: “Hashem of Hosts is with us,” “Hashem of Hosts, blessed is the man who trusts in You,” “Hashem, save us,” because in the Jerusalem Talmud, the fifth chapter of Berachot, it is said that these verses should never be omitted. Then we give praise and thanks to Him, may He be blessed, for creating us for His glory and giving us the true Torah. Then we pray for this: “That we may keep Your statutes and merit…”. Then we say verses of trust to strengthen us in our sustenance, that we may trust in Hashem, and He will send us His help from holiness. We conclude with the verse “Hashem desires for the sake of His righteousness to magnify the Torah and make it glorious.” It seems to me that this has two intentions: the first is that because of our limited sustenance, we are preoccupied with livelihood and do not have the time to engage in Torah. But we must know that Hashem desires to magnify the Torah and make it glorious. Therefore, even though we immediately go to engage in sustenance, we must remember that this is His main desire to magnify the Torah and make it glorious. Hence, one should raise his children to study Torah and support those who study Torah. This is an obligation even for those preoccupied with their livelihood. The second intention is regarding what is written in Isaiah (42:22) after this verse: “But this is a people robbed and plundered… Who gave Jacob to be plundered… Is it not Hashem, against whom we have sinned…”. The interpretation is: we complain about our lowliness, to which the prophet responds that the purpose of creation is to magnify the Torah and make it glorious. This is our sin that we did not do so and acted oppositely. Therefore, “this is a people robbed and plundered…”. However, we did not establish to say these verses to avoid concluding the prayer with something negative. But the intention should be as I have written. The reason for “Aleinu” and the Song of the Day will be explained in Siman 133, as the Tur explains there as well, see there. And with this, the order of prayer is completed. (There are also lofty and elevated intentions in the sanctity of the order, which in essence, the intentions are not similar to the sanctity of the Shemoneh Esrei. We have explained according to their plain meaning, and those who come into the secret of Hashem will intend more. Be precise, and you will find ease.)

And our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, wrote: One translates the Kedusha of "Uva Letzion." And one must be very careful to say it with intention. Regarding if an individual says it – its law is like the law of the Kedusha in "Yotzer," and see above in Siman 59 (where it is ruled permissive). And in the Kedusha that is in translation – an individual says it and not two people. And one should not say it out loud. And it is forbidden to leave the synagogue before the Kedusha of Seder. Thus far their language. For anything that is in the language of translation – one should not say it publicly (Taz in the name of the Zohar). And there is a reason for this based on the esoteric, and your mnemonic is: twice the Scripture and once the translation. And when making announcements – they should be made before "Ashrei," and not between "Ashrei" and "Uva Letzion" (Magen Avraham). And what is written that an individual who comes to the synagogue at the time when the congregation is saying the Kedusha of Seder should say it with them, see there – our custom is not so, since we hold the law that an individual says it like the Kedusha in "Yotzer." And the Levush and the Magen Avraham wrote here the customs of Kaddish and their laws, and among us, everyone says it together. And who precedes the prayer leader, and what are the laws of Kaddish are explained with divine assistance in Yoreh Deah at the end of Siman 376, see there.) (It seems to me that it is good to say "Ashrei" and "Uva Letzion" while seated.)

After "Uva L'Tzion," the prayer leader says the "Tiskabel" Kaddish, as the prayer service has concluded. However, we have the custom to say afterward the great praise of "Aleinu L'Shabeach," which the ancients said was instituted by Joshua the son of Nun at the conquest of Jericho. And the Ari, of blessed memory, warned to say it after every prayer, aloud, standing, and with joy. And one bows at "Va'anachnu Korim." Also, our teacher the Rema in the previous section warned to say it with intention. One should pause slightly before "Va'anachnu Korim" (so it should not be understood to refer to the previous part, God forbid). And we say the Mourner's Kaddish after "Aleinu." And even if there is no orphan in the synagogue, someone who has no parents should say it. Even someone who has parents can say it if they do not object. Until here is his language. This Kaddish has its source to complete four Kaddishes in Shacharit. By saying "Aleinu," our faith is strengthened, and that there is no power besides Him, blessed be He, and the hope to perfect the world under the sovereignty of the Almighty (see Beit Yosef). Some say "and His glorious throne is in the heavens above." Some say "and His honored seat," and the Tur wrote that this is the version in the Sefer Heichalot, see there. In any case, we say "and His glorious throne" for reasons known to us.

And afterwards, they say the Song of the Day, in remembrance of the song of the Levites in the Temple. And during the Mincha (afternoon) service, it is not customary to say it, even though they also sang a song in the Temple during the afternoon Tamid offering. It is explicitly stated in the Mishnah at the end of Rosh Hashanah that once the Levites erred in their song, referring to the afternoon service; see there. Nevertheless, since it is merely a remembrance, it suffices to say it in the morning service. In Rosh Hashanah (31a), reasons are explained for each day's song, indicating why each song is pertinent to that particular day; see there. And in Tractate Sofrim (Chapter Eighteen), it brings this Mishnah regarding the song the Levites would sing in the Temple at the end of Tractate Tamid, and concludes that anyone who mentions a verse in its appropriate time is regarded as if they built a new altar and offered a sacrifice upon it. Thus ends his words. Therefore, one should be careful about this. And after the Song of the Day, there is no need for Kaddish, for we have already said four Kaddishes, and we should not add more Kaddishes, as I wrote in Siman 55; see there. However, orphans have the custom to say Kaddish after it, and therefore, when there is no orphan in the synagogue, this Kaddish is not necessary.

And know that on a day when there is a Musaf (additional) offering, the Levites would say the song of the morning after the daily morning offering, and for the Musaf there were other songs, as explained in Masechet Sofrim regarding Rosh Chodesh and Yom Tov. According to the law, on Shabbat, Yom Tov, and Rosh Chodesh, the song of the day should be said after the Shacharit prayer. This is indeed the custom of the Sephardim and it is proper. However, we do not follow this custom, as we say it after Musaf. Additionally, we do not have the custom to say the Musaf songs at all, which is astonishing. The Sephardim say on Rosh Chodesh "Barchi Nafshi," which is the song for the Musaf of Rosh Chodesh. On Yom Tov, they also do not say it, and I do not know why. It is also perplexing to me that for Shabbat Musaf, it is explained in Rosh Hashanah that they would say a song from the portion "Ha’azinu," but in Masechet Sofrim it is not mentioned. Additionally, those who say the Musaf songs on Yom Tov, and they have already been printed in the machzorim, why is it that on Shabbat there is no one who says them? This requires much investigation.

The custom in Sephardic communities is to say after "Uva Letzion" the psalm "A Prayer of David, Incline Your ear, O Lord," which is Psalm 86. Afterwards, they say "Hoshianu," the Song of the Day, and then they say "Ein Keloheinu," "Pitum Haketoret," the teaching of the school of Elijah: "Anyone who studies halachot...," Rabbi Elazar said in the name of Rabbi Chanina: "Torah scholars increase peace...". They then recite the Rabbi's Kaddish, because of their statement at the end of Sotah, which we brought in the previous section, where the Talmud says "Amen. Yehei Shmei Rabbah" of the Aggadah. After that, "Aleinu." Their custom is proper and good, and so it is written in Pri Etz Chaim.

However, our Rabbi the Rema wrote in Siman 132, and this is his language: Some wrote to say "Pitum Haketoret" from a written text and not by heart, because the recitation is in place of the actual offering, and we are concerned lest one omit one of its ingredients. And it is said that one is liable to death if one of its ingredients is missing. Therefore, the custom is not to say it on weekdays, as people are hurried to their work and we are concerned lest they skip. And when leaving the synagogue, one says "Hashem, guide me...," and bows and exits. This is the end of his words. And the Mahari”l performed three bows, and when he left the synagogue, he did not leave with his back to the ark but turned sideways (Magen Avraham). And when the bimah is in between, it does not matter, as another domain separates between the ark and the entrance.

(Therefore, in Ashkenaz, the custom is not to say "Ein Keloheinu" and "Pitum Haketoret" for the reason written by the Rema. However, anyone who says it is praiseworthy. And due to the concern of missing one of the ingredients, some have the custom to count on their fingers, so they won’t make a mistake, as is obvious. And a Torah scholar certainly should say them. And so wrote the Magen Avraham in small section 5, that the meticulous ones have the custom to say it every day, see there. And what he elaborated in small section 4 regarding the Song of Mincha – there is no need to elaborate on this as there is no doubt regarding it, and the proper way is as I wrote. Be precise and you will find light.)

Our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, wrote: On Shabbat and Yom Tov, "Barchu" is not recited after the final Kaddish, even in places where it is customary to say it on weekdays in case there were individuals who were not in the synagogue when "Barchu" was recited. Nevertheless, on Shabbat and Yom Tov, it should not be recited because everyone comes to the synagogue before "Barchu." Thus is his language. This custom is not known to us, and we do not say it, neither on weekdays nor on Shabbat and Yom Tov.

On Mondays and Thursdays, it is customary to add supplications because they are days of favor. For Moses, in regards to the second set of Tablets, when God was reconciled with him, ascended on Thursday and descended on Monday, as explained in the Midrashim (Tur). Additionally, these are days of judgment, as the earthly and heavenly courts sit in judgment then (Shabbat 129b). Mars, which signifies the attribute of judgment, is influential on these days, appearing twice daily (ibid). Therefore, we also read from the Torah on Mondays and Thursdays with three readers. This was instituted by Ezra (Bava Kama 82a) to protect the world from being destroyed by the attribute of judgment, for the Torah protects and saves.

Therefore, we say "VeHu Rachum" at length as printed in the siddurim. The ancients wrote that it was instituted by three elders through a miracle that happened to them, that the Holy One, Blessed be He, saved them from the fire that did not harm them when a certain governor burned them. Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote that it should be said aloud. If it is not said while standing, one transgresses the ordinance and is called a "breacher of the fence." So far his words. However, our teacher, the Rema, wrote that it is customary to say it while standing, but it is said quietly... so far his words. Because it was instituted corresponding to the Shemoneh Esrei prayer (Magen Avraham), and this is the custom. He further wrote that it is customary to fast on these days. That is, when certain fasts are decreed, they decree on Monday and Thursday, and likewise Monday, Thursday, and Monday after Passover and Sukkot. Some have the custom to say the confession "Ashamnu," and "El Erech Apayim Ata...," and the Thirteen Attributes. After "VeHu Rachum" they say Tachanun and "Hashem Elokei Yisrael Shuv...," "Habet...," "Zarim...," and "Shomer Yisrael...". "El Erech Apayim" is said after Kaddish. And it is said while standing because it includes "we have sinned" and is like a confession, which is specifically said while standing (there).

Our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote: "One shows the writing of the Torah scroll to the people standing to its right and left, and then turns it to face those in front and behind. For it is a commandment for all men and women to see the writing, bow, and say 'And this is the Torah…', 'The Torah of the Lord is perfect, restoring the soul.' Thus far is his wording. This is also stated in Tractate Soferim (Chapter Fourteen). This is what we call 'Hagbah,' and among us, we do the Hagbah after the reading. The Sephardim do it before the reading, as implied in Tractate Soferim there. It is astonishing that we say 'And this is the Torah… by the mouth of the Lord, by the hand of Moses,' and this is also printed in the prayer books. This is very difficult for several reasons: Firstly, this is not a verse found anywhere. 'And this is the Torah' is in 'Va'etchanan,' and 'by the mouth of the Lord, by the hand of Moses' is the end of a verse in 'Beha'alotcha' in the journeys. Additionally, in Tractate Soferim, it is not so, as I have written. When one lifts the Torah, one rolls the Torah scroll on three columns, shows it to the people, and the writing faces the one who lifts it. And whoever looks carefully at the letters as is proper will receive great light if he is worthy of it (see Magen Avraham section 3)."

When the Torah scroll is taken out, "Vayehi binsoa ha'aron," "Brich Shmei" from the Zohar Vayakhel, and "Gadlu" are recited by the prayer leader facing the ark. The Torah scroll is slightly lifted and bowed, and "Lecha Hashem HaGedulah," "Av Harachamim…" are said. On Shabbat and Yom Tov, "Shema Yisrael" and "Echad Eloheinu" are recited facing the congregation. The prayer leader then turns back to face the ark and says "Gadlu," "Al Hakol Yitgadah Veyitkadash…" The Torah should be held on the right side, and the person holding it walks towards the north with the Torah. The first person called to the Torah says "Baruch Sh'natan Torah…," "V'atem Hadveikim…" (see Magen Avraham, subsection 6). Refer to section 141, clause 10 for additional notes.

Maimonides wrote at the beginning of Chapter 12 of the Laws of Prayer: Moses our teacher established for Israel that they should read from the Torah publicly on Shabbat and on Monday and Thursday mornings, so that three days should not pass without hearing the Torah. And Ezra established that they should read it at the Mincha service on every Shabbat because of those who sit idly on the corners. He also established that three people should read on Monday and Thursday, and that they should not read less than ten verses. Thus far his words. Meaning: On Shabbat morning, Moses our teacher established what should be read, which is the entire weekly portion and seven readers. But for Monday and Thursday, he did not establish how many readers or how many verses, and one reader and one verse would have sufficed. Ezra, however, established the number. All of this is explained in Bava Kamma (82a). The explanation of "those who sit idly on the corners," Rashi explained as "those who sit in shops" who did not read on Monday and Thursday, see there. And he established an additional reading before them even though they read in the morning. And some explain: so that they would not go and get drunk at the corners, as that is the time of drunkenness. Therefore, he established a reading, so they would come to the synagogue. And this is why we say the verse "But as for me, may my prayer be to You, O Lord, at an acceptable time" at the Mincha service on Shabbat, because earlier it is written: "Those who sit at the gate talk about me, and I am the song of the drunkards." And David said: They sit and get drunk at the corners, but I come to the synagogue and pray before You; it is an acceptable time, for even Elijah was answered only at the Mincha prayer (Shita Mekubetzet there).

And so Moses our teacher instituted the reading of the Torah on festivals, Rosh Chodesh (the new month), and Chol HaMoed (the intermediate days of festivals), as it is taught in the fourth chapter of Megillah (31a): "On Passover they read...," as it is stated: "And Moses declared the appointed seasons of the Lord to the children of Israel" (Leviticus 23:44) - it is a commandment that they should read each one in its proper time. And so we learned in the Jerusalem Talmud there, and the Rif and the Rosh brought it there: Moses instituted for Israel that they should read the Torah on Sabbaths, festivals, Rosh Chodesh, and Chol HaMoed, as it is stated: "And Moses declared...". The Jerusalem Talmud added "Sabbaths" which is not in the Mishnah. The readings for the Ninth of Av and public fast days were instituted later on as well; and this too is by the decree of Moses our teacher, as he instituted to read everything in its proper time. 

The Haftarot are mentioned in the Mishnah in Megillah there, and it seems that the Men of the Great Assembly instituted this. Therefore, it is necessary to read some verses from the Torah as well, so that the Prophets are not read without the Torah. The reading of the Torah for the Maftir on festivals, Rosh Hashanah, and Yom Kippur is not mentioned in the Gemara. The Geonim instituted the reading during the Mussaf from "Pinchas." However, the reading of the Maftir on Rosh Chodesh that falls on Shabbat and the four special Parshiyot are mentioned in the Mishnah there, and it appears that this too is from the enactments of the Men of the Great Assembly. The Parasha of "Zachor" is of Torah origin, and some say that the Parasha of "Parah" is also of Torah origin. These will be explained in their place with the help of Heaven. (The Bach in Siman 284 wrote that the Haftarah was due to a decree that forbade reading from the Torah, see there.)

How many people are called to the Torah on Mondays, Thursdays, and during the Mincha service on Shabbat? Three — neither less nor more, due to the concern of work disruption. Although there is no concern of work disruption during the Mincha service on Shabbat, the sages did not want to burden the congregation excessively, as they were accustomed to delivering sermons all day (Rashi, Megillah 21a). Additionally, they had already read from the Torah in the morning. Therefore, there is no Haftarah read from the Prophets due to the reasons already explained. The number three corresponds to the Torah, Prophets, and Writings, as well as to the Kohanim, Levites, and Israelites (Gemara, same source). The number of verses read is no less than ten, corresponding to the Ten Commandments and the ten utterances by which the world was created (same source). There are additional reasons mentioned in the Gemara there. Two individuals read three verses each, and one reads four verses. The identity of the person who reads four verses will be clarified in Siman 137.

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote in Section 1: "And if there are two grooms in the synagogue, and they are Israelites, it is permitted to add a fourth person to read, for to them it is like a holiday on which it is permitted to add. And it appears that the same applies regarding two people with a brit (circumcision), for it is their holiday." Thus is his language. This was written by the Mordechai in the name of the Riva, and the Hagahot Maimoniyot in the name of the Ritzba. However, we have never heard of anyone who does this, and so have written the later authorities (Levush, Magen Avraham, and Taz). Moreover, even on a holiday we do not have the custom to add. In any case, it appears in my humble opinion that in a situation where there could be a dispute, we can rely on the words of these rabbis and read for both of them, and the fourth will read what the third read. However, according to custom, one goes up to the Torah and the other for the lifting, and similarly with other obligations. (The Taz in subsection 2 elaborated to question the Ritzba and the Rema: What comparison is there between an individual's festival and a communal festival? And also because of the cessation of labor, see there. And I am astonished that he says: In a place where it is necessary and incidental, and the community consents, there is room to say that this is not considered violating the decree of the sages, for they permitted us in such a manner. Reflect and you will find leniency.)

In the place where we stop on Shabbat morning, which is at the end of the Torah portion, we begin reading at Mincha from the portion of the upcoming Shabbat. We repeat it on Monday and read it a third time on Thursday. Why didn't they establish that on Monday we read the second section and on Thursday the third section? Because this section doesn't count toward the total, since on the next Shabbat we begin from the start of the portion. Therefore, why trouble people to read something new? It is sufficient to read the first section at Mincha, on Monday, and on Thursday. This is a dispute among the Tannaim at the end of Megillah (31b), and the halacha is decided in the Gemara this way. The reason appears to be as I have written. According to this, it seems to me that even though on Shabbat, if they made a mistake and read a different portion, they certainly go back and read the correct portion that is fixed, nevertheless, at Mincha and on Monday and Thursday, if they made a mistake and read a different portion, whether from this Torah portion or another, they do not need to go back and read again. Since it doesn't count for the public reading, as on the next Shabbat we will read it anew, and it was only established so that three days should not pass without Torah, and because of those who sit in the marketplaces – therefore, whatever they read, they have fulfilled their obligation. And even if they remember in the middle of the reading, it seems to me that whatever was read is considered read, and the remainder should be read as required for that day. If they skipped one verse, it will be explained in Siman 137.

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote in Section 2 that if the community missed reading the Torah portion one Shabbat, the following Shabbat they should read that portion along with the portion designated for that Shabbat. This is his language. The same applies if they left off in the middle – they read from where they left off along with the portion for that Shabbat. There are those who say that if on that Shabbat there were two portions combined, they should not read them the following Shabbat, because it is not customary to read three portions at once (Magen Avraham, Section 4). According to this, the same applies if the following Shabbat also has two portions; they likewise should not be read. These are puzzling matters: since it is an obligation to complete what was not read, what difference does it make whether it is two or three portions? Even if several Shabbats were missed, it seems obligatory to complete them all, and I have seen someone who ruled this way (Elya Rabba, Section 2, who also cited this from the glosses on customs). There are also those who say that if the missed portion was at the end of one book, it should not be read the following Shabbat along with the portion from the next book, because the fourth person called up to the Torah would have to read from both portions, and it is not possible to combine readings from two books (Magen Avraham there). This is puzzling: is it really essential that one person combine two portions? Furthermore, what prohibition is there in combining them? The main principle seems to be that in any case, it is obligatory to complete the reading the following Shabbat. It seems that it can only be completed the following Shabbat, but if they wish to complete it during the week, it is not possible, because the enactment of seven readers is only for Shabbat. Reading it on Monday or Thursday with three readers together with the regular portion would not fulfill the enactment of the Sages. However, it is certain that if they can read it at Shabbat Mincha, they should have seven readers and include the following portion as well (this seems correct to me).

And all this is regarding Shabbat. But on Mondays and Thursdays, when the Torah reading is canceled, or on Shabbat at Mincha, it seems that they do not need to make it up since they will read it on the upcoming Shabbat. There is an opinion that if the reading was canceled on Monday, they should read it on Tuesday so that three days do not pass without Torah (Elya Rabba in the name of the commentary on Magen Avraham). However, it does not seem appropriate at all to read from the Torah and recite blessings on a day that the Sages did not institute. There is another opinion for a different reason: this ordinance was established only for the Shabbat morning service so that the reading of the section is not entirely nullified (Elya Rabba ibid.). Similarly, on Rosh Chodesh, Yom Tov, and public fast days, when the reading is canceled, they do not need to read it on another day, and this is the ruling. Likewise, on Shabbat morning when they read the entire section but the maftir and haftorah were canceled for some reason, they do not need to make it up, as this ordinance was established only for this specific section and not for another. Additionally, it seems to me that when the section was not read and they complete it on the following Shabbat, then the maftir must recite both haftarot since the section for it was read.

And who are the three called up? A Kohen (priest) reads first, after him a Levi (Levite), and after him an Israelite. This is a Mishnah in Gittin (59a). In the Jerusalem Talmud, there is a disagreement: Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai says this is from the Torah, as it is written: "And he gave it to the priests, the sons of Levi," and then "to all the elders of Israel." Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi holds that this is rabbinic. In our Talmud, it is clearly implied that it is from the Torah, see there. And regarding what we learned in the Mishnah that this is for the sake of peace, the Gemara explains that this is what it means: Even though in all manners of honor that we are obligated to give to a Kohen, such as blessing first at a meal and taking a good portion first, as it is written "and you shall sanctify him," meaning we are obligated to honor him – he can waive it, as we explained at the end of Siman 128, see there. And I might say that he can also waive this, that he should not be called first to the Torah – it comes to teach us that the sages instituted this for the sake of peace, so that the matter should not come to dispute, and he does not have the ability to waive it.

And this is what our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 4: The simple custom is that even an unlearned Kohen (priest) is called to read before a great sage of Israel. This is provided that the Kohen knows how to read, for if he does not know how to read, how can he bless the Torah? However, if he can read along with the Shaliach Tzibur (prayer leader) word by word, that suffices, as will be explained later in section 139. So far his words. And now the practice is not to be particular about this at all, and in any case, the Kohen is called first (Magen Avraham, sub-section 5). And our master, the Beit Yosef's intention is that even if the Kohen waives his right, it does not help. And although in his major work, he clarified some opinions from the Geonim that with a waiver it is permitted, nevertheless he concludes there himself that this is not the custom, and even a waiver does not help. And this is the simple custom in all places (as the Taz wrote at the end of sub-section 3). And there are now places that are not Torah observant, and the affliction has spread among them that they do not pay attention to the Kohanim at all, and they call up an Israelite in place of a Kohen, even though there are several Kohanim present. And they do not even ask for their waiver, even though it does not help as I have written. They are deserving of great punishment. And I have seen this with my own eyes, and I protested against them until they accepted not to do so. And it was almost a wonder in their eyes.

And know that in the Gemara there it clarifies that only on Shabbat and Yom Tov, when many people are commonly found in the synagogue, did they enact that the Kohen cannot forgo his honor. But on Monday and Thursday, he can forgo. And this is also written by the Rosh and the Tur. However, Tosafot wrote there that nowadays, many people are found in the synagogue on Monday and Thursday just as on Shabbat and Yom Tov, and so wrote the Ra'avad. Therefore, it is forbidden, and this is the opinion of our Rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, who did not mention this at all. Nevertheless, I am puzzled: since the Rosh and the Tur hold this way, why did they not mention their opinion at all? And this requires further study. Additionally, it is brought in the Gemara that Rav read in the place of the Kohen and so did Rav Huna, even on Shabbat and Yom Tov, because they were heads of the exile and all of Israel was subservient to them. Therefore, this is not applicable nowadays. And even Rambam, who in his commentary on the Mishnah wrote that it is forbidden to precede an ignorant Kohen to a wise Israelite, because he holds that the precedence of a Kohen is only when they are equal in status, and a scholar precedes an ignorant Kohen, as they said, "A mamzer who is a scholar precedes an ignorant Kohen" – nonetheless, in his work, he did not write this. He wrote that the custom is to give precedence even to an ignorant Kohen over a greatly wise scholar. The reason for the custom is that he holds that the precedence of a scholar is for other matters, but regarding the aliyah to the Torah, which the sages enacted that a Kohen reads first, there is no distinction (Beit Yosef). And like Rambam in his commentary on the Mishnah, Ra'avad also wrote. And with all this, he wrote that the custom is not so, see there, even though he holds that also in the aliyah to the Torah, the scholar precedes. And we must say another reason, which is that in recent generations this could lead to disputes, as one might say, "I am greater than you." Therefore, the opinion now is for the sake of peace (Tosafot Yom Tov). According to this, there is no permission to precede an Israelite to a Kohen even if the Kohen forgoes, unless they wish to leave the synagogue before the Torah reading, in which case it is necessary to call an Israelite.

It is stated there in Gittin: We hold that if there is no Kohen present, the bundle is separated. There are three explanations for this: One explanation is that of Rashi, that the Levite (Levi) does not read at all. And so wrote the Rambam in Chapter Twelve. It appears to me the reasoning behind this matter is that seemingly, since the Torah prioritized the Kohen before the Levi, and the Levi before the Israelite, consequently, when there is no Kohen, the Levi should precede the Israelite. This comes to teach us that it is not so, that when did the Torah sanctify the Levi to precede the Israelite? When there is a Kohen. But when there is no Kohen, his lineage is insignificant. And this is what we learn from the verse "the priests, sons of Levi" – meaning, when are they "sons of Levi" to precede the Israelite? When there is a Kohen. Accordingly, we might say the opposite: that he should be allowed to be after the Israelite. And this comes to teach us that this too is not so, for in any case, he is more sanctified than the Israelite and it is not proper for the Israelite to precede him, and thus he does not go up at all. And if you might say he should go up first and then the Israelite, not because of the law of precedence? One could say that if he goes up first, people will say it is by Torah law that he precedes the Israelite, and the Torah was particular that his obligatory precedence is only when there is a Kohen. Therefore, the Levi remains deprived from both sides and does not go up at all. (See Taz, subsection 6, who held that there are two explanations, but indeed there are three.)

And the second explanation was also written by Rashi: "The bundle is separated, there is no order to the matter, and whoever wishes may go first." Meaning: The Torah sanctified the Levite only in the presence of a Kohen, but without a Kohen, he is like an Israelite. Therefore, there is no strictness and no precedence, and they can act as they wish, like an Israelite and an Israelite, whoever wishes may go first. And the third explanation was written by the Rosh: If the Israelite is greater than him – the Israelite goes first, and then the Levite. But if the Levite is greater, or even if they are equal – the Levite goes first, see there (and also the Tosafot have this intention, see there). And it appears that he holds that certainly even without the Kohen, he has more sanctity than the Israelite, as it is written: "At that time the tribe of Levi was set apart" – thus he is inherently sanctified. Therefore, when they are equal, he precedes the Israelite. And only in this regard is he not as elevated as when the Kohen is present, for the Kohen precedes even if the Israelite is greater than him unless he is the greatest of the generation, as was explained. Consequently, the Levite also precedes the Israelite even when the Israelite is greater than him. But when there is no Kohen, if the Israelite is only slightly greater in rank than him – he goes first.

Our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in Section 6 that if there is no Kohen in the synagogue, an Israelite should read in the place of the Kohen, and a Levite should not follow after him. This is his exact wording. This corresponds to the first interpretation. Our master, the Rema, wrote about this: "But the first one may ascend..." This is his exact wording. There is someone who says that according to the first interpretation, this is also the case (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 10). However, this is not so, as this applies only to the third interpretation. The reason it is not written in the form of "there are those who say" is because, according to the wording of the author, there is no necessity that it is not so, and this is his way everywhere. According to this, the practical law is that the first one may ascend, but after the Israelite, another should not ascend. And this is the simple custom. When they call him, they call "in place of the Kohen" so that there is no mistake that he is a Kohen. (Also, the Taz in subparagraph 6 rules this way and writes not like the Magen Avraham, that this is also according to the first interpretation. However, what the Taz holds that this is according to the second interpretation and partially disagrees with the Rema, I am puzzled by him: this is exactly the third interpretation, which is the interpretation of the Rosh and the Tur, and thus it applies only when they are equal. But when the Israelite is greater, the Israelite reads and after him a Levite. However, this is not the custom. And in this, we have taken the first opinion that the Levite does not ascend after the Israelite. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

If the Torah scroll is open, and the Kohen is reciting the Shema – he is not permitted to interrupt, and an Israelite reads in his place. They do not wait for him out of respect for the congregation (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 7). And that which was explained earlier in Siman 66 that the Kohen interrupts – this is when he was called, but initially, they should not call him. There is no concern for his honor, since he is engaged in the recitation of the Shema and its blessings. However, during the Pesukei Dezimra (verses of praise), it is permitted to call him initially (ibid., subparagraph 6). 

Our teacher, the Rama, wrote that the same applies on a fast day after Passover and Sukkot when "Vayechal" is read. If the Kohen is not fasting – an Israelite reads. And it is better for the Kohen to leave the synagogue. Thus far is his language. This means: according to the law, he does not need to leave, since he is not related to this reading at all. However, it is better for him to leave, because not everyone knows that he is not fasting, and it may lead to a blemish (in his honor). The same applies to all public fasts when the Kohen is not fasting. However, it is the usual manner that on all public fasts, it is presumed that he is fasting, but on the Monday, Thursday, and Monday fasts, not everyone fasts.

It appears to me that no honor should be given to one who is not fasting, such as lifting and rolling the Torah, taking it out and putting it back. And know that some say that on a public fast, since the Torah reading is an obligation of the day, even one who is not fasting can be called up. In my humble opinion, this is not the case, and it will be clarified with the help of Heaven in Siman 606.

If a Kohen enters the synagogue after the Yisrael has started reciting the blessing over the Torah, he does not interrupt. However, if the Yisrael has only ascended or even said "Barchu et Hashem hamevorach" – he should allow the Kohen to recite the blessing, because "Barchu" is not considered a beginning until he says "Baruch Atah Hashem." It appears to me that the Kohen does not need to say "Barchu" again, but starts with "Baruch..." And since the Yisrael has already ascended, he should remain there until the Kohen and Levi are called, and then he will be called, for otherwise it would be a disgrace for him. It appears to me that if the Yisrael is not particular about this, he may descend and another can be called up.

If there is no Levite in the synagogue, an Israelite is not called in place of the Levite, nor do they call another Kohen. Rather, the same Kohen ascends in place of the Levite, completes the final blessing, and then begins "Barechu" and reads what the Levite would have read, and recites the final blessing. There is no concern here of unnecessary blessings since these blessings were instituted due to the reading of the Torah, and all who ascend bless. Therefore, each time one ascends, they must bless. The reason for this is that if they call another Kohen, people might say that the first one was disqualified. Similarly, if they call an Israelite, people might say he is not a Kohen, since they called an Israelite after him, as not everyone knows there is no Levite present. Additionally, they do not call one Levite after another Levite, as there is also a concern for disqualification of the second, where people might say he is not a Levite. But with one Kohen after another Kohen, there is no concern of disqualification for the second, because either way: if he is disqualified as not being a Kohen, then he is also not a Levite. However, with one Levite after another Levite, it could be said about both that they are Israelites. (See Taz, subsection 8, and Magen Avraham, subsection 12. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

If there were a Kohen and a Levi in the synagogue, and they thought there was no Levi, and the Kohen was called for the second reading—if he has only said "Barchu" and then they saw the Levi, the Kohen should leave his place and the Levi should go up. But if the Kohen has already begun the blessing, he should not be interrupted. Even though it may be a slight to the Levi, nevertheless, the Kohen must complete the blessing so that it is not rendered in vain. Furthermore, it is more reasonable that people will understand the truth—that they did not know the Levi was present—because it is something unusual for one person to have two consecutive readings. Thus, people will inquire about it and discover that this was the case. (This seems to be the reasoning of the Rashba as brought by the Magen Avraham in subsection 11; see there. Examine this carefully and you will find it straightforward.)

Our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in paragraph 9: "Similarly, two Levites should not be called up one after the other, so that people do not say that one of them is flawed." Thus are his words. And in the Gemara there it is stated that it is due to the flaw of both. See there. And the explanation is as follows: It is indeed true that the Torah commands to precede a Kohen to a Levite, and a Levite to an Israelite. But why should a Levite not be called up after another Levite? For this, they said it is due to a flaw, so that people do not say that the second is not a Levite but an Israelite, since the people are accustomed to the order of Kohen, Levite, Israelite. Or they might say that the first one is flawed and they erred with him, and therefore they called the second one a true Levite. And what is stated in the Gemara due to the flaw of both – the intention is either the flaw of the first or the flaw of the second. And a city that is entirely Levites or entirely Kohanim will be explained in paragraph 26.

Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote in paragraph 10: The custom is to call a Kohen after a Kohen with an Israelite intervening between them. And the cantor says when calling the second one, "even though he is a Kohen." Similarly, the custom is to call a Levi after a Levi. These are his words. The explanation of the matter is: Even though it is not customary to call a Kohen after a Kohen or a Levi after a Levi, this applies when a Kohen, Levi, and Israel have not yet been called. But if they have already been called, there is no issue. As the Tur wrote in the name of Rav Amram, after a Kohen, Levi, and Israel have been called, one may call whomever they wish, and if a Kohen wishes to be called a second time, it is permissible. These are his words. However, even afterward, one should not call a Kohen after a Kohen unless an Israelite intervenes between them. This is explained by the Tur beforehand, and these are his words: There are places where the custom is to call many Kohanim with an Israelite intervening between them. There is no concern that people will say the first one is disqualified since an Israelite was called after him. Rav Amram also wrote this... These are his words. Hence, it is clear that the custom and Rav Amram are one matter, meaning that after a Kohen, Levi, and Israel have been called, it is permissible to call as many Kohanim as one wishes, provided an Israelite intervenes between them. The same rule applies to Levites.

It is clear that the intention of our master, the Beit Yosef, is as we have explained. There is no concern either for the first Kohen or for the last one. Regarding the first Kohen, people will not say he is disqualified since a Levite and an Israelite are called after him, as per the sages' ordinance. Regarding the last one, there is also no concern of disqualification unless the order established by the sages is not followed. But if it is followed, why should there be a concern (Taz, subsection 9)? This is why we require an Israelite to be called between them, so it does not contradict the Gemara which states that a Kohen should not be called after another Kohen (Beit Yosef). Furthermore, for this reason, our master the Beit Yosef says that the prayer leader should announce "even though he is a Kohen." Although this is not strictly necessary according to what we have written, it is done as an additional safeguard. The same rule applies to a Levite after a Levite. If there is no Levite at all, and the first Kohen reads twice and then an Israelite follows him, the second Kohen may also read after him, followed by an Israelite, then a Kohen, and so on indefinitely (Magen Avraham, subsection 14). The Levush explains that even the second time, the order should be Kohen, Levite, and Israelite, and so on; see there. One of the commentators on the Shulchan Aruch also explains this way (there). Similarly, if there is no Levite, the second Kohen reads twice, followed by an Israelite (there). These matters are puzzling. (Also, the Taz there, the Perisha, and the Eliyah Rabbah, subsection 12, have written similarly to what I have written. The conclusion of the Beit Yosef is also thus, although he initially brought this in the name of the Eshkol. The Eliyah Rabbah also writes there that the conclusion of the Beit Yosef is not so; see there. Examine and you will find clarity.)

And our Rabbi the Rema wrote regarding this that it is therefore permissible to call up [a Kohen] for Maftir in such a manner. And if one calls up [a Kohen] for Maftir without specifying, there is no concern of defect, for they do not mention his name. Thus are his words. And it is not understood: What is he trying to teach us? If it is permitted to interrupt with an Israelite among the seven readers, all the more so it should be permitted for Maftir. And perhaps it comes to a precise point and to be stringent, meaning: It is specifically permitted to interrupt with an Israelite, and when an Israelite is called for the third reading, and a Kohen for the fourth, and an Israelite for the fifth, and a Kohen for the sixth, and an Israelite for the seventh, then it is permitted to call a Kohen for Maftir. But if Israelites were called for the fifth and sixth readings, and a Kohen for the seventh, it is forbidden to call a Kohen for Maftir. And then he says that if one calls up a Kohen for Maftir without specifying, there is no concern of defect, meaning: regarding what the author wrote that the chazzan needs to say "even though he is a Kohen" to remove any defect, as I wrote in the previous section. To this he says that for Maftir it is not necessary when the Maftir stands without mentioning his name, as this was their custom, that without mentioning his name, there is no concern of defect.

Another opinion states: Some say that one should not call a Kohen or a Levi for the count of the seven [aliyot], but after the count is completed, one may call a Kohen or a Levi. This is the custom in these lands. However, in a situation of necessity or pressure, one can rely on the first opinion. Thus far his words. Meaning: to call a Kohen or Levi also within the seven readers with an interruption of an Israelite. However, at present, our custom is not to call a Kohen or Levi even after the seven readers, except for the last one and the Maftir, and one can call a Kohen for the last one and a Kohen for the Maftir. This is our simple practice. This is not like calling a Kohen after a Kohen, since they are interrupted by Kaddish. Likewise, on Simchat Torah, for the Bridegroom of the Torah and the Bridegroom of the Beginning, and the Maftir, it is customary to call all of them Kohanim or Leviim, because these are separate matters and each one is read from a different Torah scroll (Eliyah Rabbah). But on a fast day, one should not call a Kohen or Levi for Maftir, because he is part of the count of the readers (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 16). And even if there is no Israelite who knows how to read the Haftarah, one should prompt him (ibid.). Also, the simple custom when there are grooms or societies requiring many aliyot, is to call seven readers on part of the portion, and afterwards start with a Kohen, Levi, and five Israelites on another part of the portion, and similarly further until the entire portion is completed. The last one is called as a Kohen or Levi as I have written. Care should be taken not to have to read the same section twice, as the Kabbalists are very particular about this. However, this is not strictly observed. Some of the poskim permitted this practice, and praiseworthy is he who is cautious about it. Nevertheless, one should not protest against those who do so.

One of the commentators on the Shulchan Aruch (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 7) wrote: If the custom is to purchase with money the right to be called first at the beginning of the Torah with "Bereshit," and if a Jew buys it – the Kohen waives his honor and exits the synagogue. Once, a Kohen did not want to leave the synagogue, and it is permissible to compel him by the authorities to leave the synagogue so that the custom and the honor of the Torah are not nullified. Thus far his words. Afterwards, he wrote that there is an opinion that even if the Kohen does not leave, the Jew should still be called up. However, from the language of Maharik, it does not seem so. Thus far his words. 

Behold, this matter has caused a great stumbling block for the common people, as I have seen in my youth. Because of this, they disrespect the honor of the Kohanim and say that they need to be brought into the synagogue, and they disgrace the Kohanim by not calling them first. Woe to the ears that hear such things, and to the eyes that see such things! They rely on the law that has been elucidated.

In truth, they did not find their hands and feet. The source of this law is from the Maharik (root 9), where it was a fixed custom in all places that on Shabbat Bereishit, one of the congregation would volunteer money for the synagogue's lighting for the entire year in order to read first at the beginning of the Torah. The custom was that if there was a Kohen suitable for this, he would purchase it, and if not, he would leave the synagogue. This was a fixed custom from time immemorial. There was honor for the Torah in this, namely that for the aliyah of opening the Torah, they would donate a significant amount, sufficient for the synagogue's lighting for the entire year. Once, it happened that there was a stubborn Kohen who neither wanted to purchase nor to leave. They asked him to go to another synagogue, where he would be called first and not cause the loss of this great charity here, nor diminish the honor of the Torah. He also refused this. The Maharik ruled that they did well by forcing him through the authorities to leave the synagogue. He elaborated on this because since there it was a fixed custom with the consent of the Kohanim, and in this custom, there was honor for the Torah and significant income to suffice for the lighting for the whole year, and they also wanted to call him first in another synagogue, certainly such a Kohen is not among the upright Kohanim, and he does not have the authority to annul a fixed custom. He elaborated on this, see there. Therefore, one should not learn from this matter, which was a fixed custom once a year for the honor of the Torah and for the lighting oil, and the Kohen was stubborn. Therefore, they should be careful and guard the honor of the priesthood, and one should not learn from this incident. (And also what the Magen Avraham wrote in subsection 15, in places where it is customary for the town sage to read the Thirteen Attributes even if he is a Kohen, he can read third. Until here is his language – we have never heard of such a custom.)

There are those who say that if the chazzan calls a Kohen or Levite and they are not present, and it becomes necessary to call another Kohen, he should not call the other by name due to the potential disgrace to the first. Instead, the other should go up by himself. However, if the Kohen who was called is praying in the synagogue, they can call the other by name, as there is no disgrace to the first since everyone sees that he is standing and praying (there in subsection 17). And this is the custom. And our teacher, the Rema, wrote in subsection 11: "A chazzan who is a Kohen can call another Kohen to the Torah." This is his language. Meaning, there were some of the early authorities who prohibited doing so because of the potential disgrace to the chazzan, as people might say he is disqualified. And others disagreed, arguing that everyone knows that since he is the chazzan, it is impossible for him to go up every time, and he must necessarily call others (Levush). And it is obvious that in places where the mitzvot are sold, he has no permission to call anyone other than the purchaser (Taz subsection 10). Similarly, if the purchaser is a Kohen, he can honor another Kohen, as everyone knows that this is the usual practice of those who purchase to honor others (there). And there are those who wanted to say that if the vice-chazzan is a Kohen, he should not command to call another Kohen. But this is not correct, for it is well known that he also must necessarily call others (see Magen Avraham subsection 19).

Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote in Section 12: A city that is entirely composed of Kohanim, if there is one Yisrael among them – that Yisrael reads first for the sake of peace. Thus is his language. And it is also explained in the Jerusalem Talmud, Gittin, Chapter 5, regarding this Mishnah that a Kohen reads first. And they wondered about this: for in the Jerusalem Talmud it is explicitly stated that this is according to the one who holds that the entire law of a Kohen reading first is rabbinic, see there. And it has already been explained in Section 8 that our Talmud holds that it is a Torah obligation (see Beit Yosef and Magen Avraham, Subsection 20). And it appears to me that it is fine even if it is a Torah obligation, for it has already been explained there that according to the Torah, the Kohen can waive his right. But the Rabbis decreed that he cannot waive it, and therefore in such a case, they can waive it because this will promote peace, and this is Rabbeinu Beit Yosef's intention. And if indeed they do not wish this – the Kohen will go up first. (And see Beit Yosef, who wrote in the name of Maharik that Tosafot and Mordechai hold that it is rabbinic. And I do not know its source. And in Mordechai, it is explicitly stated that it is a Torah obligation, see there.)

And it is obvious that if there is also one Levite there, they should call a Kohen, then a Levite, and then an Israelite. After that, they should call the Kohanim one after the other (Taz, subsection 11, and this is also the opinion of the Magen Avraham at the end of subsection 20, contrary to the Levush). Since it is possible to first uphold the order as established by the Sages, why should we not uphold it? And it is also obvious that when calling the Kohanim one after the other, the more distinguished one should be called first. If there are two Levites and two Israelites, they should call twice in the order of Kohen, Levite, Israelite, and the last one should be a Kohen (ibid).

And this is the language of our master, the Beit Yosef, in section 12: "And whenever there are not enough Israelites to suffice, or if there are no Israelites at all - a Kohen calls up another Kohen. There is no issue of defect here, as everyone knows that there are only Kohanim present. The same applies to a city entirely composed of Levites." Thus far his words. 

What he wrote, that if there are not enough Israelites to suffice, a Kohen calls up another Kohen - his intention is not that the Israelites should not be called up at all, as there is no reason for this. Rather, what he means is: if there are Israelites who are insufficient to complete the required number of aliyot, then a Kohen will call up another Kohen. For instance, if there are three Israelites, a Kohen will be called up first, followed by a Levite if there is one. If there is no Levite, the Kohen will be called up again, and then the three Israelites will be called up, with the sixth and seventh being Kohanim. It is also possible to call up a Kohen for the fourth aliyah, an Israelite for the fifth, a Kohen for the sixth, and an Israelite for the seventh. 

It is preferable to call up an Israelite for the sixth aliyah and a Kohen for the seventh, as explained, since the last one can easily be a Kohen. What was written, "a Kohen after a Kohen" - should not be understood as necessarily only when there are no more than two Israelites. In summary, the principles have been explained: when there is no alternative, a Kohen calls up another Kohen, and a Levite calls up another Levite. When there is an alternative, an Israelite must separate them. Therefore, one should consider the situation at hand. (Further examination is needed regarding Magen Avraham at the end of subsection 20, who wrote: "Then all the Israelites are called up, followed by the Kohanim," see there. Why do we not separate with an Israelite between Kohanim? This is indeed the primary ruling. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

In Siman 282 it is explained that even though, according to the law, a minor can be counted among the seven called to the Torah, nevertheless, for us, since all those called up recite blessings, a minor is not called among the seven readers, except for Maftir. See there for more details. Consequently, the same rule applies for Mondays, Thursdays, and Shabbat during Mincha – a minor is not counted among the three readers. Similarly, on Rosh Chodesh and Yom Tov, a minor is not called up. Even on a public fast day for Maftir, a minor is not called up, because the Maftir is counted among the readers. The same applies on Yom Kippur during Mincha. Whether a blind person is permitted to be called to the Torah will be explained in Siman 139 with the help of Heaven.

Our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, wrote in Section 14: People who are imprisoned – a Torah scroll is not brought to them, even on Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur. This applies specifically at the time of reading. But if a Torah scroll is prepared for them a day or two beforehand – it is permitted. And if the person is important – it is permitted in any case. Thus far his words. 

Explanation: It is not respectful to the Torah to move it from one place to another unless it is for an important person. Therefore, if they are not important, the Torah should not be moved for them, even if they are compelled and unable to come to the synagogue, such as people who are imprisoned and the like. But for an important person – it is permitted even without compulsion. This is what was written that "if the person is important, it is permitted in any case," meaning: even if he is not compelled. This is clearly implied in the Jerusalem Talmud, Chapter Seven of Yoma, that for this reason a Torah scroll was brought to the High Priest, see there – even though he was not compelled.

Some interpret that two conditions are necessary: compulsion and an important person (Magen Avraham, subsection 23). According to this, we must say that when they wrote "in any case it is permitted," their intention was whether the Torah scroll is prepared beforehand or whether it is brought at the time of the reading. Although in the Jerusalem Talmud it mentions bringing the Torah scroll only due to importance, we can say that the High Priest is different because he is unique to all of Israel, and similarly the Exilarch as explained there. But an ordinary important person requires compulsion as well. However, in truth, some say that one of these conditions suffices: either compulsion, such as a sick person or one confined in prison, or importance (mentioned there in the name of Or Zarua, and similarly written in Darkei Moshe, section 10). The language of the Jerusalem Talmud implies this, as it says: "In every place, they go after the Torah, but here they bring the Torah to him? Only because they are great, the Torah is elevated with them." This is its language. Thus, it is explicitly discussing a situation where they can go to the Torah, for otherwise, "they go after the Torah" would not be applicable. Therefore, one who rules in this manner is not to be disregarded. And on the portion of "Zachor," it is permissible to bring the Torah scroll according to all opinions. It appears to me that the same applies to all four portions.

And they further said that this is only when the Torah is brought from the synagogue at the time of the reading, and afterward it is returned to the synagogue. But if it is brought beforehand and placed in an ark or a box, which has a designated place for a certain amount of time - there is no issue. And the custom is to be meticulous to read from it three times, for this is considered as established, and there is no disgrace in moving it from the synagogue. But if it is moved for less than three times, it is considered temporary, and there is disgrace even if it was brought beforehand. And from all that has been explained, it is clear that many of the common people do not act properly on Rosh Hashanah, Yom Kippur, and Simchat Torah, when before the reading they take a Torah scroll from the synagogue to read in another place, and after the reading, they return it to the synagogue. Their intention is to be called up to the Torah on these sacred days, but their reward is lost by committing a transgression on these sacred days and not considering the honor of the Torah. Therefore, it is proper to protest against them and decree that they should not do so. And those who heed will receive a good blessing.

In Gittin (60b), it is explained that after a Kohen and Levi, Israelites are called up, and the one who precedes in rank is given precedence in being called up to the Torah. Thus, our Sages of blessed memory said that after a Levi, Torah scholars appointed over the community are called up. Following them, Torah scholars who are fit to be appointed as leaders of the community are called up, meaning those who are asked about a halachic matter everywhere and can answer. After them, the sons of Torah scholars whose fathers are appointed over the community are called up, in honor of their fathers. Afterward, the heads of congregations and all the people are called up. It appears, from the fact that they did not also mention the sons of Torah scholars who are fit to be appointed, that this honor of the fathers is only specifically when they are already appointed. This is the practice on Shabbat, Yom Tov, Rosh Hashanah, and Yom Kippur.

It is explained from this that, in essence, there is no inherent superiority in one Torah aliyah (calling to the Torah) over another. Nowadays, the third and sixth aliyot are considered the more significant. Among Ashkenazim, the third aliyah is held in high regard, and the rabbi of the community is called up for the third aliyah if he is neither a Kohen nor a Levite. Among Sephardim, the sixth aliyah is considered more important, as per the Zohar. It is understood that we cannot act strictly according to the Talmudic law, as, due to our many sins, we lack communal leaders and scholars to consult in every situation. Certainly, when aliyot are sold, the purchaser ascends. However, if someone purchases all the aliyot and honors others with them, it should be done respectfully and without dishonoring the Torah. Wealthy individuals are also honored with aliyot because they contribute to the synagogue's income. It is a great mitzvah to nullify the common people's belief that a certain aliyah is of lesser importance. Anyone who can personally ascend for an aliyah deemed less important performs a great mitzvah, as, due to our many sins, many disputes arise from this, may God have mercy. Indeed, there is no greater foolishness than this, as it is all one Torah and one blessing. This is nothing but the work of the Satan, as it is stated in the Midrash that he only provokes Israel. (See Magen Avraham, who wrote that the community leaders take precedence over all if there is no distinguished scholar present. The most prominent member of the community ascends. In places where it is customary for the communal leader to ascend, he is not permitted to forgo it in favor of another. Refer there. All this does not apply to us, of course. Examine and you will find the truth.)

Who are the obligated ones, and who comes first? There are no specific laws regarding this from the Talmud or early authorities, only based on established customs. The Maharal of Prague instituted that the groom on the day of his wedding or on the Sabbath following the wedding takes precedence over all others, followed by a bar mitzvah boy, then the groomsmen, then the sandek (the one who holds the baby during a circumcision), then the mohel (the one who performs the circumcision), then the father of the baby, and then a yahrzeit (memorial anniversary of a death) (Eliyah Rabbah). The one marrying a virgin takes precedence over one marrying a widow, a widow over a chalutzah (a woman released from levirate marriage), and a chalutzah over a divorced woman (Kenesset HaGedolah). And we have different customs, which will be explained in section 282 (and also the Magen Avraham explains there).

It has already been explained at the beginning of Siman 135 that it is an enactment of Ezra not to read less than ten verses on Mondays, Thursdays, and Shabbat during Mincha, for three men, for reasons that were explained there. The verse "And the Lord spoke" also counts towards the total. And although it does not contain any specific matter, nevertheless, it is Torah, and if one letter is missing from it, the entire Torah is invalid. And although on Purim we read "And Amalek came," which contains only nine verses, that is different because the matter is concluded, and the Sages did not want to start from another matter beforehand. Additionally, there is a reason in the Jerusalem Talmud, because he performed a truncated action, meaning: Haman and Amalek wanted to truncate the strength of Israel, therefore their section is truncated.
