(The first reason is written by Tosafot in Megillah 21b, and the second reason is brought by the Beit Yosef and the Taz from the Jerusalem Talmud. The Taz elaborates on this in Siman Katan 1, see there. And I am puzzled: for I did not find this explanation in the Jerusalem Talmud. On the contrary, in the Jerusalem Talmud, Perek "HaKoreh" Halacha 2, it is explained like Tosafot, that it questions: But what about the section of Amalek? And it answers: It is different because it is the order of the day, see there. And this requires further investigation.)

And since there are ten verses for three people, it follows that one of them will read four verses. The sages said that it does not matter who reads the four verses, and they can arrange it as they wish. The reason is that each has a virtue: the first is honored by being first, the third by the principle of ascending in holiness, and the middle one because, in the Menorah, the middle lamp was considered more important. Therefore, the sages did not want to establish that specifically the first should read four verses, as they established that the Kohen reads first for the primary aliyah. One could say the reason they did not do this is that when someone else reads for them, they need to honor the first, but when they read the Torah themselves, as was the practice in the time of the Gemara, the sages did not see a need to establish this due to the aforementioned reasons. And even now that the reader reads, we cannot change it because each has a virtue, as I have written.

(And perhaps this is the reason why the Maharshal, as brought by the Magen Avraham in subsection 1, said that now that the chazan reads, the middle one should not read four verses so as not to embarrass the last or the first. This is his language. The Pri Megadim and the Machatzit Hashekel had difficulty understanding his intention, and their words are puzzling; see there. In my humble opinion, it is a printing error, and it should say: so as not to embarrass the first. Meaning: as in the actual reading, the first is more honored. The Bach questioned: From where do we know this? According to what I wrote, it is understood with good reason. The Prisha and the Eliyah Rabbah brought a different version in the Maharshal, which also does not make sense; see there. In my humble opinion, it seems as I wrote. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

And know that Rashi, of blessed memory, wrote in Megillah there, and this is his language: "And if they have a space in the portion, and each one reads four verses – all are praiseworthy." Until here is his language. And I do not understand this: is there not space in all the portions, as each portion is very long? Moreover, why indeed did the sages not establish it this way? Rather, surely it is because of the burden on the congregation, and if so, how can each one read four verses? And it seems to me that Rashi’s intention is to wonder about our custom, that in the portion "Bereshit" the Levi reads only three verses, and the Kohen reads four, and the Israelite reads five – this is acceptable, as there are open portions there and it is not possible otherwise. And to have one person read two portions is considered a burden on the congregation. But in "Noach," where the Kohen reads eight verses, and the Levi and Israelite each read three, why is it done this way? And similarly in "Lech Lecha," the Kohen reads three verses and the Levi reads six verses, and there is no open or closed portion there, why is it done this way? And similarly, there are many portions to scrutinize. And this is what Rashi says, that where there is space – it is good for each one to read four verses. But what can we do that this is not the custom? And we have further to question our custom in the portion "Vayelech," where we read only nine verses, and the Israelite ends with "and to all the elders of Israel," and there are not ten verses. And recently it has indeed been printed in the prayer books that the third should read until "to inherit it," but this is not the custom. And perhaps because the portion is small, and until "to inherit it" would be four portions and almost half the portion, and it is not proper to do so since on Shabbat it will be read again. Therefore, it is considered like the portion "And Amalek came" which is considered a concluded matter. And this requires investigation. (And conversely, there are some places with a strange custom in "Naso" where the Israelite continues beyond "son of Aaron the priest," and there are many verses there and this is unnecessary. And similarly in "Beha'alotcha," there are those who continue beyond "and the Levites shall be mine," and this is unnecessary, see there.)

If one skips a verse on Monday, Thursday, or Shabbat during Mincha, as well as on holidays, if he reads ten verses without the skipped verse – he does not need to go back, because this reading will occur again on Shabbat. If not – he must go back. It is possible that nine verses suffice, since there are three verses for each of the readers. However, in the eleventh chapter of Massechet Soferim, it is implied that specifically ten verses are required, as this was the ordinance (see Magen Avraham, subparagraph 4). On Yom Tov, fifteen verses are required, because there are five readers. But on Shabbat morning, in any case, one must go back and read, even if seven readers completed without this verse; even after returning the Torah and saying Kaddish, and even after praying Musaf, because this verse remained unread and without a blessing. Therefore, the Torah scroll is opened, and one recites a blessing before it, reads this verse along with two additional verses, and recites a blessing after it. This is also stated in Massechet Soferim there. It seems that the two additional verses added to this verse should follow this verse. However, if the skipped verse is before an open or closed paragraph, one must begin two verses before it.

And similarly, if one of those called to the Torah read only two verses and then recited the blessing after it – it is as if he did not read, and his blessings are in vain. He needs to read those two verses again along with one additional verse. On Shabbat, another person can come up and read, but on Monday, Thursday, and the Mincha service on Shabbat, he himself should come up again, so it does not appear as if there are more than three people called up. On Shabbat, even if seven people have already been called up, it is not effective, because those two verses are considered as if they were not read and not blessed. If they realize immediately after he has recited the final blessing and before another has read, he does not need to recite a blessing before it because the last blessing was in vain; he should read one more verse and then recite the blessing after it (Taz, Section 4). Only if they realize after another has been called up does he need to recite both blessings as I have written. (See Magen Avraham, Section 8, that on Shabbat and Yom Tov he should not read again but another should; see there. It does not seem so, and also the Eliyah Rabbah, Section 7, disagrees with him; see there. However, regarding Eliyah Rabbah's disagreement with the Taz, and his opinion that even if they realize immediately, a blessing before it is also needed; see there – in my humble opinion, the main ruling follows the Taz. Be precise and you will find ease.)

And if they only read nine verses, even though ideally ten are required, nevertheless, after the fact, since they read three verses for each, they do not need to go back and read again. This is no worse after the fact than the portion "And Amalek came," where ideally they read nine. It is not similar to skipping verses, which we wrote requires going back and reading again, as skipping is a deficiency. And our teacher the Beit Yosef wrote in section 4: "But if they read less than nine, they need to go back and read again." This is his language. And there is someone who explained the reason is because three verses were not reached for each one. According to this, if they read three verses, such as if one verse was read by two of the readers, they have fulfilled their obligation (Magen Avraham, small section 9). I am astonished: if so, what is relevant about less than nine verses? And it cannot be said that in such a case all need to go back and read again, from where can this be derived? Since according to this opinion the obstacle is only from less than three, if so, only the one who did not read three verses needs to go back and read again. Therefore, it seems to me, in my humble opinion, that reading less than nine verses is not considered "reading" at all, since it was not done according to the ordinance. Therefore, if they have not yet removed the Torah and have not said Kaddish, the third can complete up to three verses even though he has already recited the blessing after. And if they have already removed the Torah or said Kaddish, they all need to go back and read again. (And also the Eliyah Rabbah in small section 8 disagrees with him. And I am astonished at the Magen Avraham who did not see the words of the Levush who wrote this explicitly, see there. And what the Magen Avraham wrote from the Ma'amadot - we do not learn from a reading that is not constant, only in the time of the Temple. Be precise and you will find ease.)

Kol Bo writes: There was an incident with a cantor who was reading the "Parah" portion and stopped at "to the foreigner who sojourns among them." He rolled up the Torah scroll and sat down. The Rabbi was upset about it and said: You have not read the portion. It is as if we did not read it at all, for we have only mentioned it in a general way. They went back, opened the scroll, and started from the beginning of the portion. The reader recited the blessings before and after, by the Rabbi's ruling, and they completed the entire portion until "he shall be unclean until the evening." This is the end of his words, and it is briefly mentioned in the Shulchan Aruch, Section 5. 

It seems to me that this is specifically because he stopped at "to the foreigner who sojourns among them," as the main laws of the purification of the red heifer had not yet been clarified. For it is written further: "He who touches the dead body shall purify himself..." But if he had concluded at "living water into a vessel," even though he did not finish the entire portion, he does not need to go back and read. This is evident from his wording, as he wrote "we have only mentioned it in a general way," meaning that the main laws of the purification with the water of purification had not yet been clarified (see Magen Avraham, Subsection 11). 

It is obvious that one does not need to go back due to skipping a verse (ibid.). This applies similarly to portions like "Chodesh" or the festivals. Also, here, if only the final blessing was recited and they immediately remembered, there is no need for the initial blessing or to start from the beginning of the portion again; rather, they complete the reading and recite the final blessing (Taz, Subsection 5). There are those who disagree with this (see Eliyah Rabbah), but it is not conclusive.

An incident occurred on the first Shabbat of Chol Hamoed Sukkot, where the Maftir was supposed to read "On the second day [...] and on the third day," but he only read "On the second day," and had already rolled up the Torah scroll. One of the great authorities ruled that he should read "On the third day" without a blessing before or after (Responsa of Rabbi Meir of Lublin, Siman 85). Others disagree with this, arguing that we are knowledgeable about the intercalation of the months, and the primary reading is "On the third day" (Magen Avraham, subsection 6, and Eliyah Rabbah, subsection 10). Some agree with the first opinion (see Be'er Hetev, subsection 4). It seems that in cases of doubt regarding blessings, we should be lenient, even though the reasoning appears to support the dissenting opinion. Nevertheless, since this is not the Shabbat morning reading of the parashah, it is not of such great concern.

It is clear that each of those called to the Torah must read different verses from those read by the previous ones. Otherwise, why did our sages of blessed memory trouble themselves regarding the division of the Ma'amados on a fast day, where they read the section of "Bereshit"? How to divide a section that does not contain six verses? One should read it first and then the second. But certainly, it does not suffice. And although there is no prohibition in this, nevertheless, for the count of those called to the Torah, the one who repeats does not count (see there, small section 13). 

And as for the matter on Chol HaMoed Sukkot, when the sacrifices of the festival are repeated, it is because it cannot be otherwise, as there is not enough for all those called to the Torah to read, as is known. However, if one reads what the first one read and adds another three verses that the first did not read, he certainly counts towards the number. And even if he adds only two verses, he counts, for on Rosh Chodesh we do so with the Levite who starts with "And you shall say" that the Kohen read, and adds another two verses. But one verse does not suffice, as we require the majority of three. 

And this only in a pressing situation, but ideally, one should not start at all from what the first read, even if he adds many. And even what we wrote, that if it does not count towards the number of those called to the Torah there is no prohibition in reading what the first read, not everyone agrees with this. Some prohibit it entirely, and it will be clarified with the help of Heaven in Siman 282.

Our Sages of blessed memory said in the Megillah (22a) that one who reads from the Torah should not leave less than three verses in a section, meaning one should not conclude with less than three verses remaining adjacent to an open or closed section. The reason for this is because of those who leave the synagogue at that time, who will not hear how many verses the next reader reads, and they will say that the next reader read only two verses until the section. And even though it is not proper to leave during the reading of the Torah, nonetheless, they were concerned because between one person and another it is permitted to leave if necessary, such as for bodily needs and the like. And why would they say this? Because they would say: Why did the previous reader not read until the end of the section? Rather, it is certain that he left it for the next reader. And if you would think that the next reader would read from another section, the previous one should have read until the end of the section (this is implied from Taz, small section 1; see there). And what is noted in the Chumashim as "Shlishi" etc. – this is not a section.

Similarly, the reader should not conclude with less than three verses from the beginning of the portion, even though he read a lot from the previous portion. The reason: due to those who enter after the next reader has begun, and they will hear that he started two verses after the portion and will say that the previous reader only read these two verses. For if you think that he read from the previous portion, then certainly he read from it three verses, as we do not leave two verses close to the portion as I wrote in Section 1. And if so, why would he read another two verses from this portion? Rather, it is certain that he only read these two verses. But when he concludes at the portion, even though the portion after it is only two verses, there is still no concern that those leaving will say that the next reader will only read the two verses of this small portion, for who would force them to say so? After all, they do not see any change, since he concluded at the portion (Taz there). Moreover, necessarily in this case there is no concern, for in the portion of "Pekudei" there are many portions at its end that are only two verses, and there is even a portion of one verse, see there. And it is impossible otherwise, so there is no concern. And this is the simple custom. (And know that Tosafot and several of the Rishonim questioned our practice of beginning on a public fast from "Vayechal" which is two verses from a portion, and similarly "Vehikravtem" on Chol HaMoed Pesach. And it needs investigation, for in our books "Vayechal" is four verses from a portion, and "Vehikravtem" is three verses from a portion. It must be said that for them it was two verses from one verse, as they wrote in Kiddushin 30a, see there. And the Torah scroll does not have verse breaks, and this is only in printed Chumashim, and there is no fault in this.)

If one made a mistake and concluded two verses after a section or near a section, and has already recited the final blessing, he does not need to go back and read again (Eliyah Rabbah, subsection 1). Specifically, if he read only two verses, thereby transgressing the primary enactment of Ezra, he must go back and read again. But in this case, since it is only a concern of recitation, there is no need. Nevertheless, the next one called up should start from the beginning of the section, or from three verses before the end of the section (Magen Avraham, subsection 1, in the name of Agudah). There are those who say that even this is unnecessary (Eliyah Rabbah there, and Magen Avraham at the end of this subsection also wrote this; see there). And I do not know what the reasoning is, because it is possible to rectify this. And if it is because initially it is not proper to read what the first one read, in any case, there is no prohibition in this, and why shouldn't we do everything that can resolve the concern of our sages of blessed memory? (And his proof is not conclusive, see there. Analyze and you will find leniency).

The one called for Maftir should not begin two verses after a section, even though everyone knows that he is only repeating what has already been read (see there, subsection 2). Therefore, if a section has five verses at the end of a parsha, the Maftir should read all five verses, even if he only needs to read three. There are those who write that it is permissible to begin after two verses (see Eliyah Rabbah subsection 2), but this is not the main opinion. This is also the simple custom, and it should not be changed (as the Rokach wrote, see Magen Avraham there). He should always intend to begin with something good and end with something good, as it is written: "Do not stand by an evil thing." The good of idol worshippers is not good, and their evil is not evil. And when he reads the blessings, he should not intend specifically for any individual, and certainly not for the curses. If someone is blind, he should not be called to read the section "blind or broken." And someone suspected of illicit relations should not be called to read the section about illicit relations. This applies only to someone merely suspected; but if it is clear that he committed the illicit act, if he has not repented, it is fitting to call him so that he will be ashamed and repent (Eliyah Rabbah). One should not interrupt in the forty-two journeys mentioned in "These are the journeys" (there).

The Tur and the Shulchan Aruch wrote: The one who reads the [Torah] portion must first arrange it twice or three times by himself. Like the case of Rabbi Akiva, who was called to the Torah and did not want to go up because he had not arranged it beforehand. And he derived it from the verse: "Then he saw and recounted it; he prepared it and also searched it out." This is their language. And the story of Rabbi Akiva is in the Midrash on the portion "Ki Tisa", and this is the language of the Midrash there at the beginning of section 40: A person needs... when he seeks to say them in public, he should not say: Since I know it well, when I enter to expound, I will say it. Rabbi Acha said, you learn from God, when He sought to tell the Torah to Israel, He said it four times to Himself before He said it to Israel, as it is said: "Then He saw..." and afterward: "And He said to man...". Rabbi Yochanan ben Torta came before Rabbi Akiva. He said to him: Stand and read the Torah! He said to them: I have not reviewed the portion. And the Sages praised him, thus "Then he saw and recounted it." This is the language.

And based on this, there is a question on the Tur and Shulchan Aruch who wrote "two or three times," whereas from the Midrash it is clear that four times are required? It seems to me that this is because in the Midrash Bereishit (Parsha 24) it states: "Then He saw and recounted it" – the Rabbis and Rabbi Acha. The Rabbis say: Every word that came out of the mouth of the Holy One, blessed be He, to Moses, He would say it twice in His heart, and then He would say it to Moses. What is the reason? "Then He saw and recounted it" – one... And Rabbi Acha said: four... until here is his language. And the Midrash on "Ki Tisa" says Rabbi Acha, and the ruling was according to the Rabbis. And this was in the time of the Talmud when the person called up would read. And now that the prayer leader reads – he is obligated to repeat the portion twice beforehand, even if he is proficient. And if he read the section twice on the eve of Shabbat – he has fulfilled this. And there is one who wrote that it is a mitzvah for the one called up to also arrange (B'er Heitev in the name of Knesset HaGedolah). And there is no reason for this, as he says it silently after the prayer leader. And also the custom is not so.

Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote in Section 2: One who does not know how to read should be prevented from being called up to the Torah. However, if there is a need for this person who does not know how to read because he is a Kohen or a Levi, and there is no other available, if when the prayer leader reads to him word by word he knows how to say and read it from the text, he can be called up. If not, he should not be called up. Thus far are his words. And indeed, it is certain that "knows how to read" was only necessary in the times of the Talmud when the one called up would read for himself. But in our times, why is it necessary for him to be able to read by himself? However, it is certainly necessary that he be able to repeat after the prayer leader word by word, for otherwise his blessing would be in vain. According to Rabbeinu Beit Yosef, he needs to be able to read from the text. This follows his reasoning in Section 4, that a blind person does not read because it is forbidden to read not from the text. But according to Rabbeinu Rema, who brought in the name of Mahari”l that nowadays a blind person reads, it is not necessary for him to be able to read from the text. Even so, it is certainly necessary for him to be able to read after the prayer leader, as Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote later in Section 141:2, that the one called up must read quietly with the prayer leader; otherwise, his blessing would be in vain, for how can he bless on what another reads? However, the great authorities have already written that even a complete ignoramus who cannot read even after the prayer leader can still be called up to the Torah because listening is like responding, and he can bless (Taz there, Subsection 3, and Keneset HaGedolah). Even Rabbeinu Beit Yosef himself in his major work wrote based on the Zohar in "Vayakhel" that in this case, listening is like responding. See there. And this is the prevalent custom in most Jewish communities.

One should not go up to the Torah by oneself until they are told "come up." Therefore, the custom is that the prayer leader says "So-and-so, the son of So-and-so, shall stand." And for the one whom the prayer leader calls – he is obligated to go up immediately, and if he does not go up, he causes a shortening of his days. And thus it is said in Berachot (55a): three things shorten a person's days and years, and one of them is one who is given the Torah scroll to bless and does not bless, see there. And now this is considered giving the Torah scroll when they call him "stand up..." And even the gabbai who is the head of the congregation or the cantor – they should not go up by themselves until they are told to come up.

And our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 3 that the custom is that when the prayer leader (Shaliach Tzibbur) wants to, he blesses and reads without asking permission, because it is as if from the moment he was appointed as the prayer leader, he was authorized to do so. Thus are his words. And our teacher, the Rema, wrote about this that in these countries, this is not the custom, and the prayer leader only ascends when the assistant (Sgan) tells him to ascend. However, they do not call him by name like the other people who are called by their names, "So-and-so the son of So-and-so." Thus are his words. In the country of our teacher, the Beit Yosef, the prayer leader calls on his own accord to all those who are called, and consequently, it is as if they gave him permission to ascend by himself, for otherwise, who would call him? But in these countries, the prayer leader only calls those whom the assistant tells him to call, and therefore the assistant also calls him only by name—it is not appropriate to call him since he is standing next to the Torah scroll and it is not appropriate to say "stand up" since he is already standing there. Rather, he tells him that he will be one of those called up. (Thus it appears to me the reason from the Darchei Moshe, section 1, and the Gra, section 5.)

He also wrote that if someone's father is a transgressor of the entire Torah, they are called by the name of their paternal grandfather but not by the name of their father alone, so as not to shame him publicly. This is specifically when the person has never been called by their father's name. However, if the person is an adult and has become accustomed in that city to be called by their father's name, and later the father turned to wrongdoing, they continue to be called by their father's name as they were accustomed, so as not to shame them publicly. Similarly, if there is a concern for animosity or if the person is an 'asufi' (foundling) or a 'shetuki' (of uncertain paternity), they are called by the name of their maternal grandfather. If the name is not known, they are called by the name "Abraham" as a convert would be. So far his words.

Now, a 'shetuki' is someone whose mother is known but not the father. An 'asufi' is one whose mother is also not known, as stated at the beginning of the chapter "Ten Lineages". So how can the name of the maternal grandfather be known? Nevertheless, it is possible even for an 'asufi', as explained in Even HaEzer, Siman 4, Se'if 32, see there. (See Taz, Section 1, who hesitates to write "by the name of the maternal grandfather" because of a get (divorce document), see there. This requires further study, as if so, there should also be concern regarding the name of the paternal grandfather and the name "Abraham". This was also questioned by the Eliyah Rabbah in Section 4. However, there is no concern here as the rabbi investigates at the time of the get. See Machatzit HaShekel, Section 2, and Pri Megadim, Section 1, and in Beit Shmuel, Even HaEzer, Siman 129, Sections 19 and 39, and in Taz there, Section 15. Examine and you will find clarity.)

Our master, the Beit Yosef, ruled in Section 4 that a blind person does not read [the Torah], because it is forbidden to read even a single letter not from the written text. Thus is his language. And our master, the Rema, wrote that nowadays a blind person reads the Torah, just as we prompt the Torah reading for an unlearned person. Thus is his language. And he wrote this in the name of the Mahari"l, meaning: this is the custom even though his [the Mahari"l's] opinion is not so, as he wrote in his book Darkei Moshe, see there. And thus the leading later authorities have ruled. They wrote that it has already become the custom for a blind person to read in the presence of the great sages of the world, and they did not protest (Bach and Magen Avraham, Section 4, and Taz in Siman 141, Section 3, and Eliyah Rabbah, Section 5), because since nowadays the chazzan reads and not the one called up himself – there is no concern in this. However, in any case, the blind person needs to repeat the words after the chazzan (see Magen Avraham there). And do not wonder that this one blesses and cannot read, and how can another read for him? For we learned in the Tosefta of Megillah and the Jerusalem Talmud (Chapter Three): an incident occurred with Rabbi Meir who read while sitting, and gave it to another who then blessed over it. And it questions: does this one read and this one bless? Rabbi Yirmiyah said: from here we learn that one who hears is as if he reads (Taz there). But there is no proof from this at all, for there the one who blessed was fit to read, but a blind person is not fit. As we say elsewhere: all that is fit for mixing – mixing does not prevent it.

And I have a great perplexity regarding this matter about our teacher, the Beit Yosef, in his great book in Siman 141, where he wrote in the name of the Sefer HaEshkol, and this is his language: That which we learned in the chapter "The Reader of the Megillah": A blind person does not read from the Torah – it means to say that he does not read by heart. But another person stands in for him... End of his language. And indeed, this is not a Mishnah in any place, and on the contrary, it is stated there (Megillah 24a): An improperly dressed person recites the Shema, but he does not read from the Torah... A blind person recites the Shema... See there. And it does not mention at all about a blind person reading from the Torah. And on the contrary, it is to be inferred the opposite, since regarding an improperly dressed person it taught it, and regarding a blind person it did not teach it – we learn from this that it is permitted. However, it is possible that there was no need to mention this for a blind person since he cannot see, and certainly this was the version they had in the Mishnah. And so I found this version in the Rif. However, the simple custom is that a blind person goes up to the Torah. (And what we questioned: that he is not fit to read – it can be said according to what the Tosefot Yom Tov wrote in Yoma 70a that this matter of things that are written you are not permitted to say by heart is only for the most preferred way but not as an absolute requirement, see there. And if so, a blind person, where it is not possible in any other way – it is permitted initially. And with this it is reconciled, for we find Rav Yosef and Rav Sheshet who said the Haggadah as explained in Pesachim 116b, and there are many verses there. And we have already explained this matter above in Siman 49, see there.)

Each of those called to the Torah recites a blessing before and after the reading. This practice is not related to the general blessings on the Torah, as these blessings were instituted to honor the Torah. Even if one has already recited the blessings over the Torah and is immediately called up to the Torah, they still recite the blessings in the usual manner. One should not argue that since they have just recited the blessing "Who has chosen us" for themselves, how can they immediately repeat the same blessing without any interruption? There is no concern in this, as they are following the enactment of the sages. Additionally, in reality, there is an interruption with the verses or the Mishnah of "These are the things" that are recited after the blessings over the Torah. Even if there is no time, one can still say a short verse, such as "May He bless you," as they go. However, if one is called to the Torah before reciting the blessings over the Torah for themselves, they are already exempt from reciting the blessing "Who has chosen us," as it is no less than one who is exempted by reciting "With great love," as I have written in Siman 47. They should only recite the blessings "to engage in the words of Torah" and "make sweet." Even though this means that "Who has chosen us" precedes these blessings, and this is not the order in the Torah blessings, there is nonetheless no concern.

The first blessing on the Torah is "Who has chosen us...", which is the most exalted of blessings (Berachot 11b) because it includes gratitude to God, praise for Israel, and for the Torah (Rashi). The final blessing is "Who has given...", which refers to the Written Torah, and "eternal life He has implanted within us" refers to the Oral Torah, since the primary study of the Torah is the Oral Torah. The Holy One, blessed be He, only made a covenant with Israel for the sake of the Oral Torah (Gittin 60b). This blessing is appropriate to be said after the reading, for on what merit do we have eternal life? It is because of the study of Torah. Therefore, after the study, which is the reading, this blessing is appropriate. (And if one reversed it and said "Who has given" before the reading, and "Who has chosen" after the reading, he has fulfilled his obligation. Magen Avraham, Section 5.)

In the time of the Mishnah, not all those who were called up to the Torah would recite blessings. Rather, the first person called up would recite the blessing before the reading, and the last person called up would recite the blessing after the reading. All those called up would read without a blessing, and everyone fulfilled their obligation with the blessing of the first and last person, as it was all considered one matter. This is what we learned in the Mishnah at the beginning of the [fourth] (third) chapter of Megillah. The sages of the Gemara instituted that each person called up should recite the blessing before and after their reading, as a decree due to those who enter in the middle of the reading—they might say that there is no blessing before the Torah reading. And due to those who leave, they might say there is no blessing after it, because they saw several people called up without reciting a blessing (Megillah 21b). It seems to me that we only need this reason when the person called up reads themselves. But according to our custom, where the public reader (Shaliach Tzibbur) reads, it is necessary for each person called up to recite the blessings; otherwise, how would it be recognized that they are being called up to the Torah?

The one who is called up to the Torah opens the Torah, looks at the verse that needs to be read, and blesses while it is open. At the end of Tractate Megillah, the Tannaim disagree about this: Rabbi Meir holds that one looks, then rolls up the Torah scroll and blesses, and after the blessing opens it again and reads. The reason is that if one blesses while it is open, people might say that the blessings are written in the Torah. Rabbi Yehuda says: One opens and looks, and blesses while it is open, and we are not concerned that people might say the blessings are written in the Torah. The halacha is decided in the Gemara there according to Rabbi Yehuda, that one opens, looks, and blesses. This is also ruled by the Rambam in Chapter Twelve of Tefillah, and by the Tur and Shulchan Aruch in Section 4, and this is the custom. However, our Rabbis, the Tosafists, wrote there that ideally one should roll it up, see there. It seems they hold that even Rabbi Yehuda agrees that it is preferable to roll it up, but he holds it is not necessary (as the Bach wrote). Some have this custom. I do not know if it is correct to do so, as it does not appear so from any of the other poskim. They understand that according to Rabbi Yehuda, one must bless while it is open, for since one needs to read it, how can it be closed? Therefore, they all ruled that after the reading, one should roll it up and bless, because once the reading is finished, it should be closed until the next person comes up and opens it. (In Pri Etz Chaim, page 72b, he also wrote like the Tosafists. See Magen Avraham, Section 6, Taz, Section 4, Bach, and Eliyah Rabbah, Section 7. They all agreed with the ruling of the Tur and Shulchan Aruch. What the Taz wrote—that the Tosafists differentiate between their time and our time—see there, I do not know what compelled him to say this. Their reasoning is as I have written, and so wrote the Bach.)

And our Master the Rema wrote that at the time one recites the first blessing, one should turn their face to the side, so it does not appear as if they are blessing from the Torah itself. And it seems to me that one should turn their face to their left. Thus far his words. For the left side is the right side of the Holy One, blessed be He, as I wrote in Siman 123 (Magen Avraham, Subsection 8). And I do not understand what the connection is to there, for there it is in the context of prayer and it is as if one stands before the king, but in all places the right side is considered more important. And in my humble opinion it seems that the reason is because the reader stands to his left as is known, and therefore he faces him. And I have seen that it is customary that during the final blessing one turns their face to their right, and this is proper. But there are some of the great ones who objected to this entire ruling, and wrote that if so, why does Rabbi Meir say to close it so that people do not say blessings are written in the Torah, he should have said to turn the face (Taz there, and Bach and Eliyah Rabbah)? And in my humble opinion it seems that this is not a contradiction. And one could say that Rabbi Meir holds that this recognition is not sufficient, and Rabbi Yehuda holds that this is sufficient. And the fact that this was not mentioned is because one can make some other form of recognition. And there are some of the great ones who would look outside the Torah scroll, and not look at the writing (Eliyah Rabbah in the name of Keneset HaGedolah).

There are those who are accustomed to bow during the blessing over the Torah. And there are those who object to this, arguing that one should only bow in the instances ordained by the Sages (Ma'adanei Yom Tov at the end of the fifth chapter of Berachot). Some have written that the early sages did this out of respect for the Torah (Magen Avraham, small section 6, in the name of the Shach), and similarly wrote the Rokeach (section 319, and Rama section 256). Nevertheless, we do not practice this custom. Instead, one should shake the Torah when saying "and gave us His Torah," and similarly in the final blessing when saying "Who gave us the Torah of truth" (Magen Avraham, small section 12), to indicate that this is our Torah. It is understood that this is not a requirement but merely a custom, and where it is customary – it is practiced. The shaking involves slightly lifting it by the handles held in one's hands.

One must hold the pillars of the Torah scroll during the blessing and during its reading. This is based on what is stated in Joshua: "This book of the Torah shall not depart from your mouth," which implies holding it in one's hand. After the reading, one should kiss it. Our custom is to kiss it with a tallit or a cloth, before the blessing and after the reading, to show our affection for it. Some have the custom that before the blessing, they hold both pillars, and during the blessing, they remove their left hand to strengthen the right hand (as stated in the small section 13 in the name of intentions). Others have the custom that during the blessing, they hold the Torah scroll's sheets with both hands, through a cloth or the tallit, and after the blessing, they remove the left hand (as stated in the name of writings). If saliva happens to come, one should spit and then kiss, not the other way around (as stated there). Know that in the verse "This book shall not depart," it is written: "Be strong and courageous." From this, it has become customary to say to someone who finishes reading from the Torah, "Chazak, chazak, ve'nitchazek!" Some prefer that "chazak" be said three times, which numerically equals "Moshe," and this is appropriate.

Our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in paragraph 5: "It is customary to cover the writing with a cloth between each person called to the Torah." End of quote. This means that after the reading, instead of rolling up the Torah, it is customary to leave it open and cover the writing with the Torah's mantle until another person is called up. However, our custom is different, as our master the Ramah wrote that in these countries, the custom is to roll it up between each person called to the Torah. And this is the main practice. End of quote.

The one who ascends says "Barchu" and the blessings out loud. And one who says them quietly is mistaken, for they should only be said in the presence of ten. And if ten do not hear and do not respond "Amen," his blessing is in vain (Beit Yosef). The same applies to Kaddish and "Barchu" in prayer (Magen Avraham, subsection 10). Some of our rabbis ruled that if one blessed quietly, he must repeat and bless out loud so that the congregation can hear and respond "Blessed is the Lord who is to be blessed..." (Rif). Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, brought this opinion in subsection 6. It seems to me that even according to the opinion explained in Siman 124 that one can answer "Amen" even without hearing the blessing as long as he knows which blessing it is, nevertheless, "Barchu" must be heard from the mouth of the one who blesses. And after the people respond "Blessed is the Lord who is to be blessed..." the one who blesses repeats "Blessed is the Lord..." to include himself among those who bless, for earlier he said "Barchu" for others to bless. And our teacher, the Rema, wrote in subsection 6 that if the congregation did not hear the one who blesses when he said "Barchu," even though they heard the chazan respond "Blessed...," they should not respond with him but rather respond "Amen" to the words of the chazan. Thus far his words. And we have already explained in Siman 124, subsection 16, that for "Barchu" in prayer it is not so; and there, if most of the congregation heard "Barchu" from the one who blesses, then even an individual who did not hear, when he hears the congregation responding "Blessed...," he can respond with them "Blessed...". And see what I wrote in Siman 57.

It states in the Jerusalem Talmud, fifth chapter of Berakhot (Halacha 3): If one was reading from the Torah and became unable to continue, the one who stands in his place should start from where the first began. If he said "from the place where he stopped," the first ones would be blessed before but not afterward, and the latter ones would be blessed afterward but not before. And it is written: "The Torah of the Lord is perfect, restoring the soul" – it should be completely perfect. This is the language of the Jerusalem Talmud, and it was brought by the Rif at the end of the third chapter of Megillah and the Tur in this section. All the early authorities explained it as follows: This second person who goes up to read blesses before the reading, starts from where the first one began, reads until the end of the section, and blesses afterward. For if not, but rather he starts from where the first stopped without a blessing – then the verses read by the first one would not have a blessing afterward, and what the second reads would not have a blessing before them. And if you say: he should start from where the first stopped and bless before it? Still, the first verses would not have a blessing afterward. Therefore, he starts like the first and blesses before it, and consequently, when he blesses afterward – the blessing also applies to the previous verses since he read them. And even nowadays when the chazzan (public reader) reads, it is still all one, for he reads in place of the one going up, and it is as if the one going up read them (Tosafot R”Y in the fifth chapter of Berakhot). And even if he did not delay long enough to finish the section – he must do so (Magen Avraham, small section 2). And although in the time of the Mishnah all those called up relied on the blessing of the first and last – this was because they intended it so, which is not the case now where everyone blesses – no one intends to fulfill their obligation with another’s blessing. Therefore, every section needs a blessing at the beginning and end (ibid.).

However, Rambam in Chapter 12 of Hilchot Tefillah, Halacha 6, wrote: "If one read [from the Torah] and then became incapacitated, another should stand in his place and begin from the place where the first person who became incapacitated had started, and he should recite the blessing at the end." Thus far is his language. And it is clear from his words that the blessing before [the reading] relies on the earlier [person's blessing]. And the reason one needs to read the verses that the first person read is to show that it is one continuous reading, and if they were to start from where the first person left off, it would appear as two separate readings. Consequently, the earlier verses would not have a blessing following them, and the later verses would not have a blessing preceding them. And this is the intention of the Yerushalmi, meaning that therefore it is necessary to start from the earlier point, but not concerning the blessing (Beit Yosef).

Our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 2: One who stands to read from the Torah, and has recited the blessing before it, and read some verses, and then stopped and spoke words of Torah or mundane matters – this is not considered an interruption, and he does not need to recite the blessing again. Thus are his words. Meaning: Even though if one became silent and another person stood in his place, the second person would need to recite the blessing before reading, according to the opinion of most decisors, as has been explained – this is because the first person did not intend his blessing to cover what the second person would read, according to our custom where each person recites the blessing. But if he himself paused – he intended his blessing to cover what he would read even after the pause. And if it is because of the interruption itself – it is of no consequence, just like an interruption during a meal does not require one to recite the "Hamotzi" blessing again, because he intended his blessing to cover the entire meal. Similarly, with the blessings of the Shema, when one makes an interruption in the middle – he does not need to start from the beginning again, and here too it is the same.

However, it seems from the language of our teacher, the Beit Yosef, that it is specifically when one read a little after the blessing, whether one read three verses or fewer, in any case, there was no interruption between the blessing and the reading. But if one interrupted immediately after the blessing – one needs to recite a new blessing, as it is with all blessings. And even though regarding the morning blessing of the Torah it is explained in Siman 47 that it is not considered an interruption – that is because of the reason explained there, that the obligation remains upon them all day and it does not pertain to interruption. This is not the case with the blessing on the Torah which is only for reading this portion. And so wrote one of the great authorities (Eliyah Rabbah, Siman Katan 2). Moreover, there are also those who disagree, as I wrote there. Nevertheless, it seems to me that one only needs to repeat the blessing. But "Barkhu" does not need to be said again, since he has already fulfilled his obligation by saying "Barkhu" and the congregation responded "Blessed is the Lord…".

Our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in Section 3: One who ascends to read from the Torah, and they showed him the place where he needs to read, and he blessed over the Torah, and he began to read, or did not begin to read, and they reminded him that he needs to read a different portion, and he rolled the Torah scroll to the place he needs to read – some say that he does not need to bless again, and some say that he does. So far his language, and he is very brief in this. Those who require him to bless again have a simple reason: since his intent was not on this place at all, it is like one who blessed over this fruit and it fell from his hand and was lost, and he had to take another one which he did not intend to eat at all, he needs to bless another blessing as will be explained in Siman 206. And here too it is the same. And those who do not require him to bless again hold: since the entire Torah is before him – the blessing applies to the entire Torah. And this is strained (see Beit Yosef). And our master, the Beit Yosef’s opinion is like those who say the second opinion that he needs to bless again, as is explained in his great book. Therefore, he wrote both opinions using the language "some say," to indicate that the latter is the main opinion (Drisha, end of Siman 206).

And so the great Achronim concluded in law, that if they showed him in this column or even in another column on the same matter, he can read. Meaning, if they showed him several verses after the place he needs to read – he does not need to make a new blessing, since his intention during the blessing was to read here, and indeed he will read here but just start a little earlier (this is implied in Taz, subparagraph 4, and Magen Avraham, end of subparagraph 4). And this is also the case with fruits: if his intention was to eat several fruits, and he took one and blessed it and it was lost – he takes another without a blessing, as will be explained in Siman 206. However, if they showed him above his reading place where he has already read, or even below his reading place but very far from his reading place in a manner that it certainly did not occur to him to read up to there – he needs to make a new blessing. And see in paragraph 9.

And there are those who say that even if they showed him above the place of his reading, since they showed him within this portion, he does not need to recite a blessing, for he is permitted to read what the previous one read, as I have written in Siman 137, see there (Magen Avraham there). But these words are perplexing: what relevance does this have to that? It is obvious that his intention was not on this place at all. Therefore, the primary ruling is that in such a case, he needs to recite a blessing, and so agreed the great authorities (Eliyah Rabbah, subsection 5, and Drisha in Siman 206. And this is also implied in Taz, subsection 4, who wrote: specifically if it was possible to call him to this portion, see there). (And what Magen Avraham wrote at the end of subsection 5, see the end of Siman 624, that it is not so, see there).

There is also an opinion that all of this is specifically when they realized their mistake immediately after the blessing. But if they began to read some verses and afterward realized their mistake, they do not need to recite a blessing again, because the interruption does not invalidate it, as I have written. And if it is because their intention was not on this place, it is similar to one who ate fruit and recited a blessing on it, and then they brought him more of the same type; he does not need to recite a blessing again (Magen Avraham there). However, there is one who disagrees with this and holds that a blessing is required (Eliyah Rabbah there). And this seems to be the main opinion, for even with fruits, if it was clearly his intention not to eat more and he decided to eat more, he indeed needs to bless again. And here it is certainly a complete change of mind, for he did not intend at all for this place. We only exempt him from a blessing when they showed him below his place of reading, not far from his place of reading, as I wrote in section 6. And this is also the ruling. And it seems to me that when he returns and blesses, he only repeats the blessing itself but does not say "Barchu" again, as I wrote in section 4.

And know that I am puzzled by the very essence of this law, to which all the great authorities agreed, that when one has shown him a little below this place, he does not need to recite a blessing, as I have written. But the Jerusalem Talmud insists that it is necessary for all the verses to be blessed, as I have written in section 1. If so, here too: Even if his intention was also on this place, nevertheless, in any case, for those verses up to this place, he had no intention at all in his blessing. If so, those verses have not been blessed. This requires further investigation.

The one who reads from the Torah must specifically read it standing up. In the Megillah (21a), we learn this from the verse: "And you, stand here with Me" — as if, even the Holy One, blessed be He, was standing when He taught the Torah to Moses our Teacher. And in the Jerusalem Talmud, it says that just as it was given with awe and reverence, so too we must behave with awe and reverence, see there. At the giving of the Torah at Mount Sinai, all of Israel were standing, and Moses with them, as it is written: "I stood between the Lord and you" (see Beit Yosef). And in the Jerusalem Talmud, it is uncertain whether this is due to the honor of the Torah or the honor of the congregation. It says there that it would seem it is due to the honor of the congregation, because if it were not so, even one who reads alone would be obligated to stand. It resolves that even if it is due to the honor of the Torah, they only obligated standing in public, not when reading alone. For if you require him to stand, he might become lazy and not study at all, see there. There is an opinion that even after the fact, he has not fulfilled his obligation (Beit Yosef). However, others disagreed, holding that certainly after the fact, he has fulfilled his obligation (Magen Avraham, subsection 1, Pri Chadash, and Eliyah Rabbah). Proof of this is from the Jerusalem Talmud, for it is certain that if the reason is due to the honor of the congregation, he does not need to go back and read again. And if so, the same applies if the reason is due to the honor of the Torah, for otherwise, the Jerusalem Talmud would have made a distinction in this matter.

It is obvious that the one who is called to the Torah must stand, for the reader reads in his place. However, the entire congregation does not need to stand, and this is the ruling of the early authorities. Nevertheless, there are those who are meticulous to stand. And certainly, this is proper, for at the giving of the Torah at Mount Sinai, we all stood. Additionally, from the days of Moses until Rabban Gamliel the Elder, they studied Torah while standing (Megillah there). This is what is taught at the end of Sotah, that with the death of Rabban Gamliel the Elder, the honor of the Torah ceased. The Mordechai wrote that this was the practice of Maharam, and even today, the pious do so, and it is an honor for the Torah. However, between one person and another, there is no strictness at all (Bayit Chadash). This will also be further explained in Siman 146, Section 8. See there.

And also to lean on something — it is forbidden. For we say in Zevachim (19b) that standing by means of leaning is not considered standing. Therefore, both the one who is called up and the one who reads must actually stand. And if they cannot see the Torah due to poor eyesight, they may bend their heads towards the Torah scroll. However, they should not lean on anything, not on the wall, not on the table, and not on the lectern, unless they are corpulent, in which case they are permitted to lean somewhat. And how much is "somewhat"? As long as if the object they are leaning on were to be removed, they would not fall (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 2). And even though in Choshen Mishpat, at the beginning of section 17, it is clarified that standing by means of leaning is considered "standing" with regard to witnesses — there it is different because the standing there is not essential. But here, even though post facto it is not necessary to repeat (as I wrote), nonetheless, initially, it is essential out of respect for the Torah. And this also constitutes a slight irreverence in the reading of the Torah (Eliyah Rabbah, subparagraph 2, and with this, the difficulty of Magen Avraham, subparagraph 2, is resolved. See also Taz, subparagraph 1).

Two people should not read the Torah simultaneously, for two voices cannot be understood at the same time. Therefore, if the one reading is also the one who was called up, he alone should read, and the prayer leader standing next to him should remain completely silent. This was the practice in ancient times. However, in our practice, the one who is called up does not read; only the prayer leader reads. The Rosh and the Tur wrote that the reason for this custom is because not everyone is proficient in the cantillation notes, and the congregation does not fulfill their obligation with his reading. He might think he knows how to read, and if he is not called to read, it could lead to disputes. Therefore, the custom is uniformly that the prayer leader reads for everyone, so the prayer leader takes the place of the reader. Now, if the person called up does not read at all, his blessing would be in vain. Therefore, they wrote that the one called up should also read quietly along with the prayer leader. The rule that two voices cannot be understood applies when both are speaking audibly. But if the second person speaks quietly, there is no issue, and he should read quietly, not loud enough to hear himself. However, if he does hear himself, there is no concern, similar to the silent prayer (Amidah). Nonetheless, if he does hear himself, he should not be prevented from doing so, as I wrote in Siman 101.

However, in any case, from the words of the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch, it is clarified that the one who is called up [to the Torah] is required to read quietly after the reader. And if not, it is considered a blessing in vain. And our master, the Beit Yosef, in his great book, wrote that one can say that even if he did not read at all, it is considered as if he heard and responded ("Shomea Ke'oneh"). And this is explicitly proven from the Jerusalem Talmud, Megillah, Chapter Three, where it questions: "Is it that one reads and the other blesses?" And it answers that the listener is like the reader. And we have already brought this in Siman 139, Section 7; see there. In any case, it is certainly better for the one who is called up to read quietly. However, if he did not, for example, if he is an unlearned person who cannot do even this – one can rely on this Jerusalem Talmud. (The Taz in Section 3 brought this as proof for a blind person. And we wrote there that for a blind person, it is not a proof, and even in the Jerusalem Talmud, it can be said that the one who was called up read quietly. And when it says "Shomea Ke'oneh," it means as if he read before the congregation, where the congregation does not hear what the one who was called up reads. And from the language of the Rosh and the Tur, it is explicitly implied that if the one who is called up is completely silent – it is a blessing in vain. And so is our custom.)

There are places where the custom is that each person who is called to the Torah reads according to the rules of the Gemara. To avoid embarrassing someone who does not know the cantillation marks, they appoint a prompter beside the one called up. The prompter says each word first, and then the reader repeats it. This is the custom of the people of Romania (mentioned in the Beit Yosef). There is support for this from Rashi in Shabbat (12b, in the commentary beginning "Roshei") who wrote that he assists the seven readers with the vocalization and cantillation quietly. See there. This is not considered two voices, since that applies when both speak simultaneously. But here, when the prompter speaks, the reader is silent, and afterwards, when the reader speaks, the prompter is silent. This is done for every word (as mentioned in the Beit Yosef). From Rashi's language, it is clear that since the prompter speaks quietly, we have no concern. Therefore, care should be taken even now, as I have seen in simple places where not even one person knows how to read. One looks into a Chumash and prompts the reader who reads from the Torah. This is impossible to do in such a way that the prompter remains silent when the reader speaks, and to do this for every word is impractical and will not be followed. Therefore, at the very least, the one prompting from the Chumash should speak quietly to the reader from the Torah.

In the Jerusalem Talmud, Megillah, it states that just as the Torah was given through an intermediary, meaning through Moses our teacher, similarly, during the reading of the Torah, it must be through an intermediary. Therefore, in our practice where the chazzan (cantor) is the one reading – the chazzan is the intermediary. And in their times when the one called up (to the Torah) would read – they required that the chazzan stand beside him. If the chazzan himself wants to be called up and read – another must stand beside him. In our practice, we meticulously ensure that on both sides of the one called up there are individuals standing, that is, the reader on one side and the assistant on the other side, as it was at the time of the giving of the Torah: the Holy One, Blessed be He, Moses, and Israel. This is also written by the Levush, see there.

The congregation is not permitted to answer "Amen" until the blessing is completely finished by the reader. Similarly, the reader is not permitted to begin reading from the Torah until the "Amen" has been completely finished by the entire congregation. Even those who prolong their "Amen" must be waited for, as is the case with the Priestly Blessing that we explained in Siman 128, paragraph 29, which is not similar to what we wrote in Siman 124 where it is not necessary to wait for those who prolong their "Amen," because in the case of the Priestly Blessing everyone is obligated to listen. Refer there for further details. Here too, in the case of the Torah reading, everyone is obligated to listen.

By law, it is permissible for two brothers to be called to the Torah one after the other, or for a son to be called after his father or vice versa. However, the custom is to refrain from this due to the "evil eye." Even if one is the seventh Aliyah and the other is the Maftir, this concern still applies. This is specifically on Shabbat when the Maftir reads from the same Torah scroll that everyone else read from, but on Yom Tov, as well as Shabbat Rosh Chodesh, Chanukah, and the Four Parshiyot, where the Maftir reads from a different Torah scroll, there is no concern of the "evil eye." Certainly, there is no concern for the one doing Hagbah (lifting the Torah) or Gelilah (rolling the Torah). If someone is not particular about this concern, they may do as they wish. (On Chol Hamoed Pesach, when there are two Torah scrolls, there is also no concern.)

The one who ascends to the bimah to go up to the Torah should go from his place by the shortest route to him. And when he descends, he should go to the other side by the longer route to him, to demonstrate that parting from the Torah is difficult for him. Therefore, when the bimah is in the middle of the synagogue, those standing on the south side should go towards the south when ascending, and when they descend, they should descend via the north. And those standing on the north side should do the opposite, as is obvious. And those standing in the middle of the synagogue, for whom both routes are equal, should go to their right when ascending, meaning towards the north which is to their right, and when descending, they should go to their left, which is towards the south. For every turn you make should be to the right.

And similarly, as explained at the end of Siman 134, the Torah is brought to the bimah (reading platform) towards the north because this is the way to the right, and when returning it from the reading towards the south – this applies when both ways are equal, as is customary when the ark and the bimah are positioned exactly in the middle of the synagogue. However, when one path is long and one is short, when carrying it to be read – it is taken via the short path, and when returning it, via the long path, similar to the one called to the Torah (Magen Avraham, Subsection 7).

The one who ascends to the Torah should not descend from the platform after his reading as long as another has not yet ascended, so as not to leave the Torah scroll without someone standing by it. Some wait until after the next person says "Barechu…". And our prevalent custom is that he stands until after the next person has read, and then he descends between one person and the next, as he then has time to return to his place before the one after him recites the blessing.

The reader must be very careful with "Keri" and "Ketiv" to read according to the "Keri," as this is a law given to Moses at Sinai, that it is written one way and read another way, even when reading it by heart. For this is how we were commanded from Moses by Divine instruction. And our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 8 about an incident where someone read it as it is written, and the "Keri" in the name was not as the "Ketiv." This happened in the presence of the great sages of the generation, Rabbi Yitzchak Abohab, Rabbi Eliezer Valansi, and his son Rabbi Shlomo Valansi. They warned him to read according to the tradition we received from Sinai, but he refused. They cursed him, distanced him, and removed him from the platform. See there.

Maimonides wrote in Chapter Twelve, Halacha 6: If one reads and makes an error, even in the pronunciation of a single letter, he is made to go back and read it correctly. Thus is his language, and so ruled our teacher, the Beit Yosef. And in the Jerusalem Talmud, Megillah, beginning of Chapter Four, it says: Even though the translation is not essential, if one errs, he is made to go back. See there. And it is a fortiori: if in the translation the error is corrected, certainly in the Torah itself. And furthermore, there (Halacha 5): If one errs between one word and another, he is made to go back (like "keves" instead of "kesev"). Rabbi Yirmiyah said to Rabbi Zeira: And do they do this (to embarrass him in public)? He said to him: And you still doubt this? Even if he errs between "im" and "ve'im", he is made to go back. See there. It is explicitly clear like the opinion of Maimonides (see Beit Yosef).

And this is the language of the Tur: The author of the Manhig wrote: If the reader, or the cantor who recites for him, makes an error – it is better not to correct him publicly, so as not to embarrass him. For even if he made a mistake in it – he has fulfilled his obligation of reading. For it is stated in the Midrash that if one reads "Aharon" as "Haron" – he has fulfilled his obligation. And the Rambam, of blessed memory, wrote... until here is his language. And the words of the Manhig are perplexing from the Jerusalem Talmud that we brought. And the proof from the Midrash is even more perplexing, for this Midrash is in Shir HaShirim on the verse "He has brought me to the house of wine," and this is the language of the Midrash: Rabbi Acha said: An unlearned person who reads "love" as "hatred," the Holy One, blessed be He, said: "And his skipping is for me love." Rabbi Yissachar said: A child who reads... "Aharon" as "Haron"... – and his mispronunciation is for me love. Until here is his language, behold it is referring to a child and an unlearned person who read by themselves, and not in public reading. Moreover, what proof is there from there? In a name, they cannot say it properly, but why should the reader not say it properly, and what relevance does embarrassment have here? And if so, even in prayer when he errs, we should not correct him for the reason of embarrassment. (And the Bach wrote that we follow the Manhig and not the Rambam, see there. And it seems to me that we follow the Rambam, but according to what we will explain with the help of Heaven, it fits well.)

It seems to me, in my humble opinion, that both are true. Certainly, if the mistake is in the essence of the word, such as "keves" ("lamb") instead of "kesev," "im" ("if") instead of "ve-im" ("and if"), and similar cases, even though the meaning does not change – nevertheless, we make him go back. But if he made a mistake in the cantillation marks – we do not make him go back, and this is the intention of the leader. He brings proof from "Aharon" ("Aaron") versus "Haran," meaning: from what we say in the Midrash about those who read by themselves even with word changes, it is beloved before the Holy One, blessed be He; all the more so for one who reads the Torah and errs in the cantillation marks. And the Rambam's intention is about word changes. Proof of this is from the words of the Terumat HaDeshen (Siman 181), who wrote: I have seen several times before my teachers and other great ones that the readers erred in the precision of the cantillation marks, and also in patach and kamatz, segol and tzeirei. And although they rebuked them a bit, nevertheless they did not make them go back. Thus far his words. This is clearly as I have written.

And know that a change in vowel points is only significant when it does not alter the meaning, such as "שָמַים" with a kamatz or "שַמַים" with a patach, or "אָרֶץ" with a kamatz or "אֶרֶץ" with two segol vowels, and similar cases. However, in cases where the meaning changes, like "חָלב" with a kamatz and "חֵלב" with a tzeire, and similar instances—certainly, one must correct it. This is what our teacher, the Rema, wrote: specifically when the meaning changes because of it. But if he erred in the cantillation or the vowel points—one does not correct him, but reprimands him. Until here are his words. And it seems to me that this is the explanation: his intention is not regarding a change of the word, for with a change of the word, even where the meaning does not change, like "כבש" and "כשב"—one corrects him. His intention is regarding vowel points when the meaning changes, like "חָלב" and "חֵלב", that one corrects him. But where the meaning does not change, one does not correct him. (See Magen Avraham, Beit Yosef, and Bach. Study carefully and you will find it easy.) And know that in all this there is no difference whether the reader himself is reading, or whether the chazzan is reading, for he stands in the place of the reader. And so ruled our teacher, the Rema, unlike those who differentiate in this matter (see Beit Yosef).

All of this applies post facto. However, ideally, the reader is obligated to read with the proper cantillation marks and precise pronunciation according to the law: not to leave a moving vowel unpronounced, nor to pronounce a resting vowel, and to maintain the distinction between hard and soft letters. Thus wrote our teacher, the Beit Yosef, in his major work, and he wrote that all of this has significant mystical roots; see there. Nevertheless, he wrote in section 2 that in a settlement where there is a quorum, but no one knows how to read the Torah properly with the correct pronunciation and cantillation marks, they should still read the Torah with a blessing according to the law, and read the Haftarah from the Prophets. This is his exact wording, because it is impossible otherwise. And how should they proceed? One person looks at the Chumash and whispers into the ear of the reader from the Torah scroll, and the reader reads aloud from the Torah scroll after him, for when no other option is available, the rules differ.

One does not read the Torah with fewer than ten Jews, who are adults and free men, excluding slaves. Even if one is half a slave and half free, although we hold that we compel his master to free him, nonetheless, as long as he has not been freed, he does not count towards the ten (Eliyah Rabbah, subsection 1). If they began with ten and some of them left, they complete the reading for all those who are required, but no more, similar to the rules of prayer in Siman 55. However, they do not call up the Maftir, as this is a separate matter (ibid., subsection 2). Some say that the seventh reader is the Maftir and he should recite the blessings along with the Haftarah (Magen Avraham, subsection 1). In the Jerusalem Talmud, Megillah, Chapter 4 (Halacha 4), it explicitly supports the first opinion, stating: "One does not read the Torah with fewer than ten; if they began... they complete it. One does not read the Haftarah with fewer than ten; if they began... they complete it. And regarding all of them it is said: 'Those who forsake the Lord will perish.'" Thus concludes its language. Clearly, one does not read the Haftarah unless there are ten present at the beginning of the Maftir. However, it seems to me that if the Maftir read from the Torah with ten present, and then some individuals left, it is permissible for the Maftir to recite the blessings of the Haftarah, since his reading from the Torah certainly constitutes the beginning.

One may only read from a complete and kosher Sefer Torah. If each Chumash (individual book of the Torah) is written separately, even if it is written on a scroll and on parchment like a Sefer Torah, one may not read from it until all five Chumashim are sewn together, meaning the entire Sefer Torah in its completeness. Thus, it is stated in Gittin (60a): one does not read from separate Chumashim in public because of the honor of the congregation. Our Chumashim, even when they are all together, do not have the sanctity of a Sefer Torah, and one may not read from them. Not only those printed on paper, but even those written on parchment, since they were not written with the sanctity of a Sefer Torah, one may not read from them. All the laws of a Sefer Torah are explained in Yoreh De'ah from Siman 271 to Siman 276. Even in villages that do not have a kosher Sefer Torah, one does not recite a blessing over the Chumashim. They should read from it without a blessing, so that the practice of reading the Torah is not forgotten. The chazzan (prayer leader) reads the entire portion, and everyone listens, but Heaven forbid to bless over it (Magen Avraham, subsection 2). There are those who permit reading from a complete Chumash when it is written according to the law of a Sefer Torah, on parchment and as a scroll, and written for its sake, but this is not acceptable (Eliyah Rabbah permits it occasionally because this is only due to the honor of the congregation). In a place where there is a Sefer Torah, but there is no chazzan proficient in the cantillation by heart, some have the practice that the chazzan reads from the Chumash with vowels and cantillation marks, and the one called to the Torah reads after him from the kosher Sefer Torah. If those called up also cannot do this, as they cannot read with cantillation even when prompted, and according to our custom where those called up do not read but the reader reads, the chazzan stands by the Sefer Torah, and another person stands by the Chumash and prompts the chazzan, who then reads from the Sefer Torah. As I wrote at the end of the previous Siman, see there.

If a mistake is found in a Torah scroll in the middle of the reading, what should be done? Indeed, the Rashba and the Rosh, and the Tur in Yoreh De'ah, Section 279, ruled that one must read again from another Torah scroll, and what was read from the invalid scroll is considered as if it was not read at all. This also seems clear from the words of the Rambam in the Laws of Torah Scrolls. And this is the language of the Rosh in a responsum (Klal 3, Din 8): "Regarding a Torah scroll in which a mistake was found, since it is invalid, the reading that was read from it is considered as nothing. Therefore, the blessing recited is also not a blessing..." Up to here is his language. Similarly, the Rashba wrote in a responsum (Section 227), and this is his language: "Anything that necessitates reading again, the blessing must also be repeated, for the mitzvah is to read from a kosher Torah scroll. The blessing on the first reading was in vain..." Up to here is his language. However, concerning the reading that was done from the invalid Torah scroll, we rely on the words of the Rambam in a responsum (Section 19), who ruled that one may bless on an invalid Torah scroll, and that this was the custom of the great sages of the world. This is also written by the Kol Bo in the name of the sages of Narbonne (Beit Yosef there). We have adopted their words regarding the past reading, but not regarding what still needs to be read. So, how should they proceed? Opinions on this matter are numerous.

The opinion of our master, the Beit Yosef, in paragraph 4 is that if an error is found in the Torah scroll, another Torah scroll is brought out, and they begin reading from the place where the error was found, completing the readings for those who read from the erroneous scroll. This applies when the error is found after the final blessing of one of the readers, and in this, no one disagrees. However, if the error is found in the middle of the reading, whether three verses have already been read or not, one stops there without a final blessing and begins reading from a valid Torah scroll from the place where the reading was invalidated. No blessing is recited before this reading, relying on the blessing recited over the invalid scroll. Our master the Rema agrees with this when three verses have not yet been read. But if three verses have already been read and it is possible to stop there, such as when it is not within two verses of a paragraph, one stops there, recites the final blessing, and completes the count with the other Torah scroll that is brought out. Nonetheless, he does not write this in the language of disagreement with our master, the Beit Yosef, but rather as an explanation of his words, because it is not explicitly clarified in the words of the Beit Yosef that even when three verses have been read, no final blessing is recited. Therefore, he does not write it in the language of dispute, and this is his method in many places (and this resolves the question of the Taz, paragraph 1). We have already explained this in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 279.

However, many have completely rejected these views, questioning how it is possible not to recite a blessing on a valid Torah scroll beforehand and to rely on the blessing of the invalid one. Even from one valid scroll to another, a new blessing is required since he did not have the other Torah scroll in mind at the time of the blessing (Bach and Magen Avraham, subsection 4). Therefore, they ruled like the Mordechai, who states that one always recites the concluding blessing on the invalid scroll. This means that if he has already read three verses – he recites the blessing. If he has not yet read three verses – he reads from the invalid scroll until he completes three verses, recites the erroneous text orally, and then recites the concluding blessing before switching to the valid scroll to complete the reading. Similarly, even if he has already read three verses but cannot stop there because there are only two verses remaining until the end of the section, he continues reading from the invalid scroll until the end of the section and then recites the concluding blessing as I have written. This is the practice of all the great sages of the world. This is also our practice and the primary ruling in law, as we have already explained in Yoreh De’ah there. We have also explained there what the law is if an error is found in the Maftir reading.
