Refer there for the distinction between the Maftir reading on all Sabbaths, where he reads what was read earlier, and the Maftir reading on festivals and similar occasions, where a different section is read.

One does not take out another Torah scroll unless there is a clear error, even if there is no change in its meaning, like "כבש" instead of "כשב", or "רחבו" instead of "רחבה" which can be read as "רחבה" with a "cholam" and would be like "רחבו", or "מגרשיהם" instead of "מגרשיהן" and similarly in all such cases - another Torah scroll is taken out since the error is clear. However, if the error is in the presence or absence of letters – another scroll is not taken out, because our Torah scrolls are not so precise that we can say that the other one will be more kosher. This is the ruling of Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema). And this is the explanation: even if in this case the error of the missing or extra letter is clear, nevertheless, who can say that the other scroll we take out does not have some error in terms of missing or extra letters? Therefore, even though this is a clear invalidation and it is necessary to correct it after Shabbat, nevertheless, since in this we are not certain about the other one – we are compelled to rely on the Geonim who permit reading from it, as stated by Maimonides (Rambam) in a responsum that we have brought. (And so wrote the Magen Avraham in subsection 7. And what the Tzemach Tzedek wrote regarding "מגרשיהם" instead of "מגרשיהן" that there is no need to take out another one – this was already contested by the Chacham Tzvi in Siman 54.)

Furthermore, the great authorities have written that if a defect is found in the middle of the reading, and there is no other Torah scroll available, they can complete the reading of the seven aliyot with this Torah scroll and rely on the lenient opinions of the Geonim, as I have written (Taz, sub-section 2 and Magen Avraham, sub-section 8 in the name of Maharil of Lublin, see there). And more than this, our Rabbi the Rema wrote: In an extenuating circumstance where the congregation has only the invalid Torah scroll and there is no one there who can fix it, some say that one should read from it in public and make the blessings over it, while others disqualify it. If one section is complete without error, one can be lenient and read from that section even though there are errors in other sections. Thus far are his words. In practice, we follow the opinion of those who disqualify it. Regarding one section, we may be lenient in extenuating circumstances, as the Ran wrote in Gittin (61a) that since the reason is due to the honor of the congregation, one can be lenient in extenuating circumstances. He also wrote this as a ruling but not for practical implementation, see there. Therefore, in extenuating circumstances, one may be lenient occasionally but not regularly. (This is how it seems to me, and this also appears to be the opinion of the Magen Avraham in sub-section 9.)

Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote in Section 5: Synagogues that do not have anyone who knows how to read except for one person – he should recite the blessing and read a few verses and recite the blessing afterwards, and then repeat the blessing at the beginning and read a few verses and recite the blessing afterwards. He should do this several times, according to the number of people called up on that day. So far his words. It appears that this law does not apply in our times, since those who are called up do not read by themselves but rather the public reader reads. In such a situation, everyone can be called up to the Torah, and the one who knows how to read will be the one who reads. And this is the practice.

It is taught in the Megillah (24a): We may skip in the Prophets, but we may not skip in the Torah. This means that we may skip in the Prophets from one place to another, such that one reads certain verses from one prophet and other verses from another prophet. But in the Torah, it is forbidden to skip, since the listener's mind is not settled when the reader skips from place to place. When is it that we may not skip in the Torah? In cases of two different topics, like from the section about afflictions to the section about discharges (Rashi). But if it is one topic, like the High Priest on Yom Kippur who would read "After the death" and "But on the tenth" from the section "Emor," since it is one topic, there is no confusion for the listener, and skipping is permitted. And in the Prophets, skipping from one topic to another is allowed. Why were they not concerned about confusing the listeners in the Prophets? Because in the Prophets, there are no laws, they were not concerned about this, unlike in the Torah, where there are laws, they were concerned that confusion might lead to error.

This that we have said, that in the Prophets one may skip even from one prophet to another, applies when it is regarding one topic. However, for two different topics, one may not skip from one prophet to another. Within the same prophet, one may skip even from one topic to another. In the Torah, even within one book, one may not skip from one topic to another. 

It appears that the reason for the distinction between the same prophet and a different prophet is because each prophet has his own style of language, as no two prophets prophesy in the same style. Therefore, when skipping from one prophet to another on two different topics, since both the topic and the language change, the confusion is great, and they will not listen at all. However, when the change is in only one aspect, either in the topic but not the language (as in the same prophet) or in the language but not the topic (as in different prophets on the same topic), the confusion is not so great.

And all of the Twelve Minor Prophets are considered like one prophet, and one may skip within them even from one prophet to another and on different topics. The reason is that they are small in quantity, and it has become customary to learn them together, and there is not as much confusion from the change in language as with one prophet.

Even in a place where skipping is permitted, one should not skip backwards, meaning from the end to the beginning, but rather from the beginning to the end. And it is not specifically the beginning and end, but the main point is that going backwards is forbidden, for it is not respectful. There are those who permit skipping backwards within the same prophet, but one should not skip backwards from one prophet to another, even within the Twelve Minor Prophets (this is the opinion of the Beis Yosef, as written by the Magen Avraham, section 4). Any skipping that is permitted in the prophets is only allowed if the reader does not delay much in his skipping to the extent that the congregation stands in silence, such as in their times when one person would stand by the reader and translate each verse into the vernacular – the reader should not delay in his skipping more than the translator's recitation. And for us, since we do not have a translator, as it is of no benefit to us because we are not familiar with the language of translation, the pause must be very brief, meaning when written in booklets one can make a mark and search quickly (section 3).

And know that even though the High Priest on Yom Kippur was permitted to read "On the tenth" from the Book of Numbers by heart, as explained in the seventh chapter of Yoma, nevertheless, for us, it is forbidden to do so, because it is forbidden to read even one word not from the written text. And in such a case where they permitted it, the Gemara explains that it was because it was not possible in any other way, see there (see Magen Avraham, small section 2). I am astonished at the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch for writing this law that we do not skip in the Torah: this law is not applicable at all nowadays, for all the readings are arranged for us, and where would we skip? And if it is because of the readings of the holidays which are in different places, and also other readings which are on different topics, like Shabbat Rosh Chodesh, Shabbat Chanukah, and the Four Parshiyot – these are two different people, and skipping is only with one person. Otherwise, how could our sages of blessed memory establish such? And if it is because it is one topic, there are readings that are not on the same topic as the Torah reading, like Shabbat Rosh Chodesh and Chanukah and the Four Parshiyot. And we must say that because with regard to the Prophets we also have skips, as there are Haftarot composed of several places, like on Shabbat Shuva where we read from Hosea, Joel, and Micah, and similarly, there are several Haftarot in such a manner. Therefore, they also wrote the law for the Torah scroll, even though it is not relevant nowadays.

Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote in Section 2: It is customary on a Shabbat when there is a groom to recite after the Haftarah of the week two or three verses from the Haftarah "Sos Asis." And when Rosh Chodesh falls on Shabbat and Sunday, after reading the Haftarah for Shabbat Rosh Chodesh, they recite the first and last verse of the Haftarah "Vayomer Lo Yehonatan Machar Chodesh." One should not object to this practice. This is his language. And even though they are skipping from one prophet to another in two different matters, nevertheless, one should not object. They wrote the reason: because now they do not delay much as it is written in pamphlets (Beit Yosef and Taz, Section 3). And I am puzzled: for from one prophet to another in such a manner is also forbidden. Furthermore, this is in reverse order, as the Haftarah for Shabbat Rosh Chodesh is from the end of Isaiah, and "Machar Chodesh" is from Samuel. And the Levush wrote the reason: that for a groom with "Sos Asis," it is like a mere song, and we do not object to it. And the matter of Shabbat Rosh Chodesh he did not mention at all, see there. And this is for the reason we wrote. And perhaps because they only say two verses – we do not worry about it. And indeed, this is not our custom. Also, the Haftarah for a groom "Sos Asis" is not practiced in all our communities. The Sephardim used to have this custom. And some of them also had the custom to call the groom to the Torah for the portion "Ve'Avraham Zaken," and in our regions, this is not known at all.

Our sages of blessed memory stated in Yoma (69a) that one should not roll the Torah scroll in public because of the honor of the congregation. This means that it is not respectful to the congregation to wait until the Torah scroll is rolled to the place where it needs to be read that day. This responsibility falls on the sexton or the reader to roll it before the prayer and prepare it at the place where it needs to be read that day. Many are not careful with this rule and it is necessary to warn them because they do not know that there is a prohibition involved.

Rabbeinu the Beit Yosef wrote in section 3 that if they have only one Torah scroll and need to read two portions, they roll it, and the honor of the congregation is deferred. This is his language. And so is the common custom on festivals, or on Shabbat when it is also Rosh Chodesh, or Hanukkah, and the four parshiyot, when they need two Torah scrolls but only have one—they roll it, since it is not possible otherwise. And even though in the Temple the High Priest would read by heart for this reason, as it is stated in Yoma there—this was because all of Israel was present and it was burdensome, and who would bear it? But each congregation individually—we testify that they waive their honor and the inconvenience, and they are content to wait until the Torah is rolled to the place of the reading, and that the Maftir reads from the Torah and not by heart (Magen Avraham section 7).

Rabbeinu the Beit Yosef wrote in section 4: One does not call a single person to read from two Torah scrolls, due to the disparagement of the first (lest people say the first scroll was invalid, hence he read from another one). However, three individuals reading from three Torah scrolls, such as on Rosh Chodesh Tevet that falls on Shabbat – there is no issue of disparagement. Thus far his words, and this is in Yoma there. From this we learn that one person can be called to the Torah twice. This is not a blessing in vain, since the blessing is for the honor of the Torah – therefore, each time he is called, he blesses, just like a Kohen who reads twice when there is no Levi, as I wrote in Siman 135. Only with two Torah scrolls, one person should not be called even for two different matters, so that people do not say the first scroll was defective. But with one Torah scroll, he can be called twice. Similarly, he can be called for the first and third readings, since he interrupted with the second – there is no disparagement. And when it says "three individuals" – it is speaking in the usual manner (Magen Avraham, subsection 3). Some have reservations about this (Eliyah Rabbah, subsection 4). In general, one should not allow a person to be called twice unless in a pressing situation (there). It is written that Mahari”l was called to the Levi and also for Maftir, and perhaps he was compelled to do so for some reason.

In the days of the Talmudic Sages, it was customary to translate every verse of the Torah, because they spoke Aramaic, and they translated so that the people would understand the meaning of the Torah. The reader is not permitted to read to the translator more than one verse at a time. Rather, he reads a verse and then translates it, and afterwards he reads another verse and translates it, and so on forever. And it appears that the reason is so that they would not get confused and understand well. The translator is not permitted to translate until the reader has finished the verse, and the reader is not permitted to read another verse until the translation is finished by the translator. The reader is not permitted to assist the translator, so that people will not say that the translation is written in the Torah. The reader is not permitted to raise his voice more than the translator, nor the translator more than the reader, as it is written: "Moses would speak, and God would answer him with a voice" - with the voice of Moses (Berakhot 45a, and see the Rif's explanation and Tosafot there). (And this concern does not apply in the blessings that people will say "they are written in the Torah" in Siman 139, because regarding the translation, there is more concern since it is the explanation of the Torah. Magen Avraham, subsection 2.)

A minor can be translated by an adult, but it is not honorable for an adult to be translated by a minor, as is indicated in Yoma (2b). Additionally, it is implied there that if it happened that the adult was the translator for the minor, he should finish, and another should not replace the minor in the middle of the translation, for we elevate in matters of sanctity and do not lower. Look there for further details. And now, the custom is not to translate because there is no benefit, since we do not know the Aramaic language. And if you would say, let us translate into our vernacular? One could say that translation is unique because it was established by divine inspiration (Tur). From this, one can derive a moral lesson against the modernists who say that in "Shnayim Mikra Ve'echad Targum" it is not necessarily referring to the Targum. This will be further explained in Siman 285 with the help of Heaven. And do not wonder: how can we nullify the translator that was established earlier? Because even in their days, there were not translators in all places, as explained in Megillah (23b). Look there for further details. The Tur brings the Jerusalem Talmud, from where we see that the sages would go out for a fast and read without translating. This indicates that the translation is not essential. This is the language of the Jerusalem Talmud at the beginning of the fourth chapter of Megillah. It further states there: although the translation is not essential, if a mistake was made, they would correct it. Look there for further details.

It is stated in Berakhot (8b): What is the meaning of the verse "And those who forsake the Lord will perish"? This refers to one who leaves the Torah scroll open and goes out. This means not only during the reading is it forbidden, but even between verses when the translator is translating according to the custom of their days—it is also forbidden, since the Torah scroll is open and it will soon be read. However, between one person and another, when the Torah scroll is not open but is rolled up or covered with a cloth as I have written in Siman 139—it is then permissible to go out if there is a great need (Magen Avraham, subsection 1) and a complete compulsion (Elyah Rabbah in the name of Agudah and Sefer HaYirah). It is explained that in the middle of the reading, even in such a case, it is forbidden. And although for a forced situation the Merciful One exempts, nevertheless, as much as one can force oneself, one is obligated to force oneself and not go out. There is a doubt whether one who needs to relieve himself, who would transgress "do not make yourself disgusting," has the same law as in the middle of Pesukei Dezimra or Shema and its blessings, and should go out, or has the same law as during the Amidah prayer and should finish his prayer? In my humble opinion, it seems that it has the same law as the Amidah prayer, as the honor of the Torah is as great as the honor of the Divine Presence, as they said: If only they had abandoned Me but kept My Torah. And one must wait until the one who is called up finishes, if only he is able to hold himself back.

It is stated in Sotah (39a): Once the Torah scroll has been opened, it is forbidden to speak, even about matters of Halacha, as it says in Nehemiah (8:5) when Ezra opened the Torah scroll to read before the people of Israel, it is written: "And when he opened it, all the people stood up." And "standing" means silence, as it says in Job (32:16): "And they stood, but did not answer anymore." And further, it is written there in Nehemiah: "And the Levites explained the Torah to the people, and the people stood in their place," meaning: they were silent. It is forbidden even to issue a Halachic ruling on any question. This is also the ruling of the Rif in the first chapter of Berachot (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 4). However, there are those who wrote that a temporary ruling is permitted (Darkei Moshe in the name of the Riva). It seems to me that the Rabbi should consider the nature of the question: if it is urgent, he should respond; if not, he should signal to the questioner to wait. This is also our practice, for sometimes a question arises due to an error found in a Torah scroll in a certain congregation, which necessitates an immediate response, or a question about matters of health—certainly, one must answer immediately. But for general questions, the questioner can wait until "between one person and another."

And know that what the Gemara says, "Once the Torah scroll is opened, it is forbidden to speak," refers to the time from when they begin to read. This is also written by the Rambam in Chapter Twelve. Some wish to say that from the moment it is opened, even before the reading begins, it is forbidden (see the Magen Avraham, subsection 3). But this is not the case, as Rashi explicitly explained there: once he begins to read, see there. And so ruled the great authorities (Ma'amar Mordechai and Eliyah Rabbah, subsection 3). And know that our master the Beit Yosef wrote that it is forbidden to converse even between one person and another. Some permit conversing between one person and another, especially nowadays when the "Mi Sheberach" prayer is extended (Bach and Magen Avraham). And indeed, the intention of our master the Beit Yosef is due to the concern that one might be drawn into extended conversation (Eliyah Rabbah), hence a brief matter is permitted. In all this, there is no difference whether or not one has already read "twice the Scripture and once the translation" (Beit Yosef).

And know that in Berachot there it is said: Rav Sheshet would turn his face away and study. He said: "We are engaged in our own matters, and they (the congregation) are engaged in theirs." And our Rabbis questioned this from Sotah, where it is stated that it is forbidden to be involved in anything else during the Torah reading, even in matters of Halacha. And the Ba'al Halachot Gedolot (BaHaG) answered in the laws concerning communal needs, and this is his language: "These words apply when there are ten people paying attention to the Torah reading. But if there are not ten people paying attention – no." Up to here is his language. And in the case of Rav Sheshet, there were ten besides him. And the Rif in the fourth chapter of Megillah brought this and wrote a different answer: "Rav Sheshet is different because Torah is his profession," see there. And our Rabbis, the Tosafists, answered that it is forbidden to study aloud, so as not to confuse the listeners. And Rav Sheshet studied quietly, see there. And the Rambam in the twelfth chapter of the laws of Prayer, Halacha 9, wrote that one whose Torah is his profession – it is permissible to study during the Torah reading, see there. And this is like the Rif. And the Tur brought all the answers.

And the students of Rabbeinu Yonah wrote in Berachot there that Rav Sheshet was different, as he was blind and exempt from reading the Torah, for matters written in the Torah are forbidden to be recited by heart. But for everyone else – it is forbidden. And in the name of their teacher, they wrote that one who prepares himself before the reading to study, and turns his face to show that he is removing himself from the Torah reading and wishes to study – it is permitted, see there. And our Rabbeinu Beit Yosef in paragraph 2 brought all the opinions in the name of "some say." And in my humble opinion, it seems that all our rabbis do not disagree, for certainly if there are not ten who remain to hear the Torah reading – in any case, it is forbidden. And also in a loud voice – in any case, it is forbidden, only in a whisper. And one whose Torah study is his profession, and prepares himself for this before the reading – it is permitted. And certainly among us in any case, it is forbidden, so that the common people do not learn from this to be lenient in the Torah reading, unless one has already heard the Torah reading and sits aside to study, for all see that he has already heard the Torah reading.

And besides this, none of these explanations clarify the phrase "anan b'didan, v'inhun b'didehu" for us. In my youth, I heard that one of the great scholars explained that Rav Sheshet would turn his face and study while the translator was translating the verse. He said "anan b'didan" — because we do not need the translation, "v'inhun b'didehu" — because those who do not know the meaning need the translator. But during the reading itself — it is forbidden. And in our time, we have neither seen nor heard that even the greatest Torah scholars study during the Torah reading unless they have already heard it, as I have written.

And our master the Beit Yosef wrote that reading "twice the scripture and once the translation" during the time of the Torah reading is permitted, because he is engaged in the same matter. Some are stringent and do not allow assisting the reader from a Chumash. Some wrote that it is proper to read quietly along with the public reader, as this allows for better concentration (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 5). Additionally, our master the Beit Yosef wrote that all this does not apply to the portion of "Zachor" and the portion of the Red Heifer, which are biblically mandated to be read with a quorum of ten, and one must intend to hear them from the reader. It is proper that in all portions, one who is meticulous in their actions should intend their mind and hear them from the reader. It is forbidden to converse while the Maftir is reading from the Prophets until he finishes, just as with the Torah scroll. Thus far his words.

Our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, wrote in subsection 4: One does not need to stand while the Torah is being read. However, there are those who are stringent and stand, as did the Maharam. Thus is his language, and we have already written about this in Siman 141, subsection 2, see there. And one does not need to stand before the Torah scroll except when it is being carried. But when it is placed on the Bimah, even those standing there do not need to stand (Magen Avraham, subsection 6). And between one person and another, it is obvious that it is permitted to sit (ibid). However, when the reader says "Barechu" and the congregation responds "Baruch...", they must stand, for in every matter of sanctity, they must stand on their feet (Taz, end of subsection 1).

It is forbidden to hold a Torah scroll bare without a cloth. Thus our sages of blessed memory have said in Shabbat (14a): One who holds a Torah scroll bare forfeits the mitzvah he was engaged in. If he studied from it or rolled it, he will not receive reward for the study or the rolling, see there. For this reason, it is said regarding the eighteen decrees in Shabbat (14a), that hands which touched a Torah scroll render the terumah impure. They decreed this so that people would be careful not to touch the Torah with their bare hands. However, later they decreed that all hands would render the terumah impure, and this is from the eighteen decrees. Consequently, hands that touched a scroll are included in this general decree, as they are not less significant than ordinary hands. And so the Rambam wrote in his commentary on the Mishnah in Yadayim (Chapter 3, Mishnah 3) that when the decree regarding ordinary hands was renewed, they abandoned the original matter, see there.

It is simple and logically understood that there is a distinction between the first decree and the second decree: the second decree, which renders hands that have not been washed as impure with respect to terumah (consecrated food), is because hands are active and might have touched an unclean place. According to this, if they touched terumah immediately after washing hands, the terumah remains pure. However, regarding the first decree, which is intended to prevent touching a Torah scroll, it does not matter whether it is before or after washing hands, as it is forbidden to touch a Torah scroll without a barrier in either case. This is also written by our Rabbis, the Tosafists, in Shabbat (refer to the relevant discussion). Nevertheless, from the language of Maimonides that we have cited, it appears that they abandoned the first issue. It implies that after the second decree regarding unwashed hands, even hands that touched a Torah scroll are not considered impure unless they touched without washing hands, otherwise, they would not have abandoned the first issue.

It appears to me that this is the reasoning of the Mordechai, which our teacher, the Beit Yosef, brought in his great book. He wrote that if one has washed his hands and has not diverted his attention, he is permitted to hold the Torah scroll while naked (this is also brought by the Magen Avraham). Indeed, our teacher, the Rema, in his book Darkei Moshe, disagrees with this; see there (ibid). At first glance, the words of the Mordechai seem perplexing: What reason is there for this? However, according to the words of the Rambam, it makes sense: This was established after the second decree because of the principle of "we do not differentiate." Our teacher, the Rema, follows the approach of the Tosafists. Indeed, from the words of the Rambam in his work, the tenth chapter of the Laws of Torah Scrolls, law 6, it also seems this way, as he wrote: It is forbidden to hold a Torah scroll while naked; see there. He did not distinguish between before washing and after washing, and this is the main ruling. Therefore, our teacher, the Beit Yosef, did not bring this matter in the Shulchan Aruch.

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote: Some say that the same applies to other holy writings—that it is forbidden to hold them when naked without a cloth. However, this is not the common practice. It is good to be stringent if one has not washed his hands. But with a Torah scroll, even in such a case, it is forbidden. Thus far his words. And this requires explanation: Now, the opinion of those who say this is found in the Tosafot on Shabbat there, and this is their wording: "One who holds a Torah scroll when naked"—it somewhat implies that this does not specifically refer to a Torah scroll, for it is taught in the third chapter of the tractate Yadayim that "all holy writings render the hands impure." Thus far their words. And their intention is not that because they render the hands impure it is forbidden to hold them when naked, for tefillin and straps are also taught there to render the hands impure, and it is permitted to hold them, as the Tosafot wrote in Chagigah (24b), see there. Rather, this is their explanation: They follow their reasoning that a Torah scroll has a prohibition even close to washing hands as in the original decree. And if so, that which is taught "all holy writings render the hands impure" applies even close to washing hands. And since a Torah scroll is included with all holy writings, it is inferred that all are equal in this regard. And if you would think that all holy writings are permitted to be held naked, and their impurity is only from the second decree, of the eighteen things decreed that hands and books should render the hands impure for reasons explained there, then close to washing hands, they would not render impure. And it is simple that "other books" refers to the Prophets and the Writings, written on parchment like a Torah scroll, and not to printed books.

And this is the opinion of the "yesh omrim" (there are those who say). And our master the Rema (Rabbi Moshe Isserles) says: But the custom is not so. Meaning, even prophets and writings written on parchment – one may hold them with hands, as is our custom. And the reason for the custom is according to the Mordechai we mentioned and according to the explanation of the Mishnah by the Rambam, that the original decree was abandoned. If so, that which it is taught: All sacred writings defile the hands – this refers to hands that are not certainly clean, and because of the decree of the eighteen matters that invalidate the terumah. And nowadays there is no terumah, so this decree does not apply. And only with a Torah scroll does the prohibition remain, because of the prohibition of holding it bare, even though the original decree was abandoned – this is regarding the stringency close to washing, since it is uncommon to touch immediately after washing, as the Tosafot wrote there, see there. But the essence of the prohibition of not holding a Torah scroll bare remains as it stands, and who can annul this? Therefore, our master the Rema says that it is good to be stringent if one did not wash his hands, and with a Torah scroll even in such a case it is forbidden. Meaning, even if he washed his hands. And he follows his view that with a Torah scroll it is forbidden even close to washing, as I wrote in paragraph 3. But nevertheless, also with other books without washing hands – it is good to be stringent according to the Tosafot's view. (So it seems according to my humble opinion. And the Magen Avraham in section 1 labored on this, and wrote that the words of the Tosafot contradict each other. And the intention of the Rema is about the printed ones, and that which he wrote "and it is good to be stringent" is an additional matter, see there. And according to our words everything fits well. Be precise and you will find ease.)

And know that holding the pillars of the Torah scroll with one's hands without a cloth, the great authorities have disagreed on this matter: Some permit it on the grounds that they are only items used for sacred purposes (Taz, subsection 1; Pri Chadash; and Noda B'Yehuda). And some forbid it (Bach and Magen Avraham). Their main reasoning is that since it is taught in the tractate Yadayim that they render the hands impure, therefore it is forbidden to touch them barehanded. 

And I am astonished, as there is no connection between the two: If so, it should also be forbidden to touch tefillin and their straps. The primary view is in accordance with those who permit, and so is the custom. There is no doubt about this matter at all. (Magen Avraham follows his reasoning in subsection 1, that Tosafot in Shabbat holds that this is dependent on each other. According to them, it is indeed forbidden to touch tefillin and mezuzot, and they disagree with Tosafot in Chagigah there. And we have already explained their words in subsection 4. And what Magen Avraham wrote that the main reason for the impurity of the hands is so that they should not hold it barehanded, look there – I am astonished: Certainly, the original decree was so, and only regarding the Torah scroll itself and its parchments. But afterwards, they decreed on all books, and on tefillin and mezuzot, and on anything attached to the books, the impurity of hands in the eighteen decrees, because they were storing terumah next to sacred writings and not because of holding barehanded, as explained in Shabbat there. And what connection is there between the two? Pay attention and you will find it easy.)

In the decree of the eighteen matters, they decreed regarding all holy scriptures, and on tefillin and mezuzot, and the straps and cases of books when they are attached to the book, like the sheets with which they bind the books and are called "tables" – all these render terumah impure if they touch it. And as explained in the words of the Rambam in the ninth chapter of the Laws of Impurity. The reason for the decree was that they used to place terumah food next to all the items we mentioned, because they said, "This is holy and this is holy – let them be placed next to each other." And mice would come to eat the food, and they would damage the books and all the items we mentioned. Therefore, in order to distance them from each other, they decreed that all these, when they touch terumah, the terumah becomes impure, and hands that touch any of these will render the terumah impure. And it is understood that now we do not have terumah, and this decree does not apply, because they did not decree regarding non-sacred items, and it is permissible to touch all these items with hands, except for a Torah scroll. However, it is obvious that when one knows that their hands are dirty – it is forbidden to touch any holy item, even printed ones, because permission was only granted for hands that are generally clean, but not when they are certainly not clean. And all of Israel is careful about this. And when it is necessary to handle a book when one’s hands are not clean – one should handle them with a cloth.

It is stated at the end of Megillah: Ten people who read from the Torah—the greatest among them rolls the Torah scroll. And the one who rolls it receives a reward equivalent to all of them. Some say: Specifically, the greatest among the readers. And others say: The greatest in the synagogue, even if he is not among the readers (Ran there). The Tur brings both opinions in the name of the Itur, see there. And our master, the Beit Yosef, in section 1, holds the first explanation, and this is his language: The greatest among those who read from the Torah rolls it. And it is customary to purchase this mitzvah for a high price to show love for the mitzvah. Thus far his language. And it is not understood: Why is the reward for the one who rolls so great? Why should it be increased, what has he done? Indeed, one of the early authorities wrote that this does not refer to the rolling after the reading, but to the rolling before the reading, when the Torah scroll is placed at the place of the reading, and if so, he is the one who prepares the readings to be read from them. Therefore, his reward is great (Shiltei Giborim in the name of Riaz, and brought by the Bach, see there). But the Tur, Shulchan Aruch, and all the poskim did not hold this. If so, why is his reward so great? And it is possible because he does not leave the Torah scroll open after the reading, and this is an honor for the Torah scroll.

However, from the words of the Rambam in Chapter 12 of Prayer, Law 18, I have learned a different explanation for this. This is the language of the Rambam: "And whoever is great in wisdom precedes in reading. And the last one who rolls the Torah scroll receives a reward equivalent to all. Therefore, he ascends and completes even if he is the greatest in the congregation." Until here are his words. According to this, the last one is the one who rolls. And this is what the Gemara says: "The great one rolls and receives a reward equivalent to all." This is its explanation: The great one can ascend last and roll, even though it is a disgrace to be the last of the readers. And he receives a reward equivalent to all because he merits two commandments: the commandment of reading and the commandment of rolling. And I am astonished at the Tur and Shulchan Aruch for not bringing his words at all. And know that I am astonished at our custom, which honors a distinguished person with lifting the Torah, and the roller is a simple person. For from the Gemara it is clear that the main reward is for rolling. Therefore, indeed, in our country in the study houses of the Chassidim, they lift the Torah, return and place it on the bima, and roll it themselves, then return, take it, and sit on a bench, and a simple person wraps the mantle and dresses the coat. It is clear that they do this for this reason. And the custom of the Ashkenazim is puzzling. It can be said that the lifting, which shows the Torah scroll to the people, and everyone stands up out of respect for the Torah – this is greater than the rolling. But in the time of the Talmud, there was no lifting after the reading, only before the reading, and this is still the custom of the Sephardim today. And we have already written this in Siman 134, see there. Therefore, for them, the rolling is the main thing, but not for us.

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (the Rema) wrote: There are those who say that if the mantle is linen on one side and silk on the other side, the silk should be turned towards the book and rolled up. This is not the custom. These are his words. The reason for the custom is simple: the main honor of the Torah is before the eyes of the observers, and therefore, on the contrary, the silk should be on the outer side, which increases the honor of the Torah. Therefore, indeed, there are those who say that the cloth used to wrap the Torah scroll should have the silk side towards the Torah scroll because it is not visible to us as the mantle is worn over it. The mantle should have the silk side outward (Magen Avraham, subsection 4, quoting the Agudah). This is the correct practice. And it is even better if both sides of the cloth are equal (Eliyah Rabbah, subsection 3). However, in this case, one must always be careful that the side which was next to the Torah scroll remains next to the Torah scroll and not be turned over since the boards of the Tabernacle had marks so that the side that stood above would not be turned below (there, quoting the Agudah). One should not roll a Torah scroll in a torn cloth unless there is no other option. Even in such a case, it should be repaired, and regarding this, it is said: "Offer it now unto your governor..."

Additionally, it is written that one should not make a cover for a Torah scroll from old materials that were previously used for a mundane purpose. This is the wording: "And the basis for this was brought from Mahari”l in a responsum (Siman 114), from what we say in Menachot (22a): 'On the wood... which is on the altar': just as the altar was not used for mundane purposes - so too the wood... And it is taught in the Tosefta, second chapter of Megillah: utensils that were initially made for mundane purposes - should not be made for sacred purposes." This is the wording. And it seems from this that even if they were just made initially and not yet used - it is forbidden, even though it is merely designation. And perhaps the stringency of the Temple is different (Magen Avraham, small paragraph 5). However, this is certainly true that if they made a change, such as sewing it differently or the like - it is certainly permitted (ibid.). And there is proof from the laver that was made from the mirrors of the women who assembled (ibid.), and also: 'bracelet, nose-ring, ring, and body ornament' that were donated for the repair of the Temple (Eliyah Rabbah, small paragraph 4) because they made a change. And even though with the wood of the altar a change does not help - we do not learn from the altar (ibid.). Furthermore: the offerings themselves come from animals that were used for mundane purposes, but they undergo a change through their slaughter. And some wrote that there is no absolute prohibition in this matter, but when asked, they say: do not make it from something that was used for mundane purposes. And if they bring it - we have no issue with it. And even without change (ibid. and this is implied from Mahari”l), for we do not learn from the Temple. And some wrote that even if you want to be stringent - it is only with items used for sacred purposes, but not for items used in service of sacred items. And in Siman 154 it will be explained what is considered an item used in service of sacred items (Taz in Yoreh De'ah Siman 282).

Anyone who wishes may purchase the right to hand over the mantles to the one who rolls the Torah, and the one rolling it cannot object. For although he has acquired the right to roll the Torah, he has not acquired the right to take the mantles. The same applies in similar cases. Likewise, in places where it is customary to purchase the rights to take the Torah out and put it back, the chazzan (cantor) cannot object, for this does not pertain to the chazzanim (cantors) (Rema, section 2). Among us, the sexton assigns this honor each time: to one person the honor of taking the Torah out, to another the honor of putting it back, to another the honor of lifting (hagbah), and to another the honor of rolling (gelilah). No person should take an honor for himself, for this does not show respect for the Torah.

The one who rolls the Torah scroll should position it against the seam. That is to say, the seam should be between the two staves, meaning the edge of the sheets and not the middle of a sheet. The reason is that if, perhaps, due to the pulling of the staves it tears, it will tear at the seam, which is easy to repair, and it will not tear in the middle of the sheet, which is difficult to repair. When rolling, he should wrap the mantle around the Torah scroll several times. But he should not roll the Torah scroll around the mantle, for this is disrespectful. In some places, every Torah scroll stands in its own case. Therefore, at the time of rolling, it should be taken out of the case, and it should not be rolled while still in the case, because in such a manner it is easy for it to tear. And the one who rolls the Torah scroll while it is in the case is making a mistake.

It is stated in the Gemara at the end of Megillah: "He who rolls a Torah scroll should roll it from the outside and not from the inside. And when he tightens it, he should tighten it from the inside and not from the outside." And Rashi explained: "He who rolls a Torah scroll from one section to another, and he is alone with the Torah scroll resting on his knees, should roll it from the outside, meaning the column that is farther from him he should roll. And he should roll from the outside towards the inside, because if he grabs the inner column and rolls towards the outside, the outer part will expand and fall to the ground. And when he tightens it, when he finishes rolling and comes to tighten it, he should grab the inner part and tighten it over the outer part, so that the writing is not covered by his arms. For it is a mitzvah to show the writing to the people..." Until here is his language.

However, the Tur explains: When the scroll stands before him, he should turn the writing towards himself and begin to roll from the outside. After finishing the rolling, he should tighten the end of the cloth from the inside, so that when he comes to read from it, he will find the tight end inside and will not need to turn the scroll towards the tightened side. This is his language. And this is the explanation of the Tosafot and the Rosh. Similarly, Rabbeinu the Rema wrote and added that it seems this applies when one person does all the rolling. But now that the custom is for one person to lift and another to roll, the writing should face the one who lifts. And this is the custom, as he is primarily the one who rolls and holds the Torah scroll. This is his language. Know also that lifting and rolling are commandments to be seen, for in the multitude of people is the King's glory. And one should not leave the synagogue before the lifting and rolling, unless he is going to another commandment (Eliyah Rabbah, subsection 5, and this also seems to be implied in the seventh chapter of Yoma, see there).

The one who recites the Haftarah does not begin the blessings until the Torah scroll has been rolled, so that the one rolling the scroll is not preoccupied and can hear the blessings and the Haftarah. However, on Mondays and Thursdays when "Yehi Ratzon" is recited after the reading, there is no need to wait for the one rolling the scroll, as this is merely a custom and there is a concern of work interruption (Magen Avraham, Section 10). Nevertheless, on a public fast day at Mincha, the one reciting the Haftarah should not begin until the rolling is finished. (See Magen Avraham at the end of Section 11, who writes that raising the Torah is preferable to rolling it, and rolling it is preferable to handing over the coverings. Refer to what I wrote in Section 9. Study carefully and you will find clarity.)

Our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, wrote in paragraph 8: On a day when there are two Torah scrolls, do not open the second one nor remove the cover until the first one has been rolled up. The first one is not removed until the second one has already been placed on the table, so that they do not divert their attention from the commandments. Both scrolls are brought out together, and the second one is held until after they have read from the first one. This is the end of his words, and this is the simple custom. And even though it is stated in the Jerusalem Talmud, Yoma, Chapter Seven, that Rabbi Yossi would instruct the synagogue attendant... when there are two, one should be removed and the other brought, see there. This has already been questioned by all, and no correct answer has been provided. (See Darkei Moshe, Magen Avraham, and Korban HaEdah there in the Jerusalem Talmud, and Pnei Moshe in the Jerusalem Talmud Sotah, Chapter Seven, Halacha 7.) In my humble opinion, it is clear that the interpretation in the Jerusalem Talmud is not as stated, for there it discusses the High Priest who would read "on the tenth" by heart. And we have established earlier in Siman 144 that among us, when it is necessary to read from two Torah scrolls and the congregation only has one Torah scroll, it is rolled in public, which is not comparable to the High Priest. See there. 

And this is the language of the Jerusalem Talmud there: Rabbi Yossi instructed the synagogue attendant in Babylonia, when there is one Torah scroll, it should be rolled next to the curtain. When there are two, one should be removed, and the other brought. This is the end of his words. And this is its meaning: He instructed him the law that was explained, that when it is necessary to read from two places in the Torah, if there is only one Torah scroll, it should be rolled next to the curtain in public. Unlike the High Priest who read by heart, as I wrote in Siman 144. But when you have two Torah scrolls, do not read from one and roll it in public. Rather, after the first reading, move it aside, and immediately take the second from the one holding it and read from it. According to our custom, this does not involve taking them from the Ark, but as I wrote. And it is customary to say Kaddish on the two Torah scrolls, both of which are placed on the table. When there are three Torah scrolls, all are placed at the time of Kaddish (Magen Avraham, paragraph 12). It is customary for the boys to kiss the Torah scroll when it is being carried, to accustom them to the love of the Torah. (See Magen Avraham, paragraph 11, who is meticulous about bringing two Torah scrolls together from "one does not perform commandments in bundles." It seems to me that this does not apply here, for it is one matter, as we say in Pesachim 102b: Havdalah and Kiddush is one matter. It is not comparable to two infants for circumcision, for they would also read from one if there were not two Torah scrolls. For this reason, it is not comparable to all those cases in Sotah, for here the reading is not increased. And the reason we do not read from one as in Pesachim there, for one matter is said over one cup, is because we do not roll the Torah scroll in public. Investigate and you will find it easy.)

We learn in Sotah (39b): The prayer leader is not permitted to undress the ark in public while they are in the synagogue. Rashi explains that they were accustomed to bring the Torah scroll from another house where it was kept to the synagogue and spread fine garments around the ark (the platform) and place it on the ark. And when they leave there and take the Torah scroll to place it in the house where it is kept - he should not undress the ark in front of the public, as it is a burden on the congregation to stay there with the Torah scroll. Instead, he should take the Torah scroll and the people should go out after him. Afterwards, he returns and undresses the ark. Thus are his words.

In Siman 132, it is explained that a person should not leave the synagogue until after "Ashrei"-"Uva Letzion". According to our custom, we place the Torah back in the ark before "Ashrei"-"Uva Letzion". However, the Sephardic custom is to return the Torah to the ark on Torah reading days after the complete Kaddish following "Ashrei"-"Uva Letzion". Therefore, it is forbidden for a person to leave the synagogue until after the Torah scroll has been returned to the ark. This is as stated in Sotah (39b): the congregation is not permitted to leave until the Torah scroll is taken and placed in its place. This is also the language of the poskim (legal decisors). Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote: However, if only individuals leave and not the entire congregation, it is permissible. This is his wording. Meaning: One by one, provided that most do not leave (Magen Avraham, small paragraph 2). I am very perplexed by this: although there is someone who says this (see Beit Yosef in the name of the Rosh), nevertheless, Rashi explicitly explained otherwise. This is Rashi's wording there: and a person should not leave through the entrance before the Torah scroll. This is his wording. And from the Gemara itself, in the entire discussion, it is clearly proven that every individual is included in "congregation", as it is said there: the congregation is not permitted to answer "Amen" until the blessing from the priests is concluded; the congregation is not permitted to answer "Amen" until the blessing from the reader is concluded, see there. And this applies to every individual, and here it is also the same. Therefore, it seems to me in my humble opinion that this prohibition applies to every individual. (And also, Tosafot R"Y only said this because they were not careful about this, see Beit Yosef. None of the Rishonim said this. And our proof is compelling.)

And this applies in places where the Torah scroll is stored in the holy ark within the synagogue itself, like in our own places. However, in ancient times, there were places where they would store the Torah scroll in a different house, as I wrote in the previous section. In that case, the law is as follows: If the synagogue has only one entrance, they must wait until the Torah scroll exits, and then follow it to the place where it is stored. A hint to this is found in the verse: "After the Lord your God shall you walk" (Talmud, there). If the synagogue has two entrances, they may leave through one entrance before the Torah scroll exits through the other entrance, provided that they subsequently follow the Torah scroll and accompany it to the place where it is stored.

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote: In places where the Torah scroll is placed in the ark in the synagogue, it is a mitzvah for anyone passing before it to accompany it until in front of the ark where it is placed. Similarly, the one who rolls the Torah scroll should go after the Torah scroll until in front of the ark where it is placed, and remain there until the Torah scroll is placed in its location. This is also the custom for the one who lifts the Torah scroll, as he is essentially the one who rolls it, as I wrote in Siman 147. Some have written that children come to kiss the Torah to educate and encourage them in mitzvot, and this is indeed the custom. Thus far is his language. Some have written that even when taking the Torah out of the ark, one should accompany it until the bimah (Magen Avraham, section 3). But some, on the contrary, refrain from this because it appears as arrogance, as if showing oneself worthy of accompanying the Torah. However, when returning from the bimah after the Torah scroll, it is necessary to go after it and it does not appear as arrogance. Therefore, it seems that each person can do as they wish, as long as their intention is for the sake of Heaven.

Residents of a city can compel each other to build a synagogue and to purchase Torah, Prophets, and Writings. In modern times, they can compel each other to purchase Mishnah, Talmud, the four sections of Shulchan Aruch, and other necessary books. This has already been explained in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 163; see there. It appears to me that even if they have a place to pray in a minyan by renting a house for prayer, if their situation indicates that they are capable of building a synagogue, they can compel each other to do so. However, if they already have one synagogue, they cannot compel each other to build another synagogue even if the first one is cramped, as each person can say, "For me, this synagogue is sufficient." If the synagogue requires essential repairs, such as leaking rain or damaged walls and the like, they can compel each other to contribute money for repairs. But for mere beautification, it seems to me that they cannot compel each other. If one person claims it is essential and another claims it is not, it depends on the judgment of the Beit Din (this is how it appears to me in these laws).

I have seen it written that regarding the collection for the construction of a synagogue, the collection should be according to wealth and not according to the number of people. And when renting a place for prayer, the collection should be according to the number of people (Kenesset HaGedolah and Atzei HaLevanon). There is also an opinion that half should be according to wealth and half according to the number of people (Eliyah Rabbah, subsection 1). According to the custom in our country where places are sold, this does not apply at all. They set a price for each place, and whoever wants a particular place pays accordingly, and another place has a different price. The pricing of the places is determined by the Beit Din (Jewish court) if they cannot reach an agreement among themselves. Similarly, for repairs to the synagogue, payment is according to the places. This is the common custom among us, that the eastern places pay more, and each person pays according to the value of their place. In all matters of disputes in the synagogue, such as whether to sell the aliyot (honors) or not, or renting a cantor, or other arrangements and expenses of the synagogue, if they cannot come to an agreement, they rely on the Beit Din, and they will rule according to the law. In Choshen Mishpat, section 163, we have further explained these matters, see there. And earlier in section 55, it was explained that when there is not always a quorum in the synagogue, they compel each other with fines to always have ten. And in a place with few Jews, they do not compel to hire to complete a quorum except on the High Holy Days, see there.

It is stated in Shabbat (11a): Any city whose rooftops are higher than the synagogue will eventually be destroyed, as it is said: "To raise the house of our God and to establish its ruins." And in the Tosefta, third chapter of Megillah, it is taught: One should only build a synagogue at the height of the city, as it is said: "She calls at the head of the noisy streets." Meaning, to build it in a place where the land is high, and then even if the building itself is not very high, since it stands on a high place, it will naturally be elevated above all the houses of the city. The Tur and Shulchan Aruch write that this applies only to houses that are used. But towers and turrets that are made only for beauty and not for use - it is permitted. And so it is stated in the Gemara there.

And from this it is clear that the reason is not merely out of respect, meaning that the synagogue should be higher than all the buildings in the city. For if so, why are tall buildings and towers permitted? Rather, the reason is so that one using the roof of their house should not stand higher than the roof of the synagogue. Therefore, they said: Any city whose roofs are higher…, because in their times the roofs were level and they used the roofs. Thus, in truth, regarding our roofs, the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch wrote that a sloped roof, which is not suitable for use, should be measured up to the place that is suitable for use. That is, if there is an upper story under the roof, it should not be higher than the synagogue. So far their language. Accordingly, it is clear that one should not use the upper story of the synagogue, as will be explained in Siman 151. (The Taz's gloss, Section 1, requires further study.)

And it appears to my humble opinion that the Rambam has a different understanding in this matter. This is his language at the beginning of chapter eleven of Tefillah: "When building a synagogue, it is only built at the height of the city. And it is elevated until it is higher than all the courtyards of the city." Until here is his language. He changed from the term "roofs" to "courtyards," and also omitted the permissibility of towers and fortresses mentioned in the Gemara. The language of the Gemara is as follows: "And these words apply to houses. But regarding towers and fortresses, we do not concern ourselves." And Rashi explained "towers and fortresses" as fortresses and towers. And so wrote the Rosh, and from this he permitted our roofs, and this is the way of the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch. But it seems to me that the Rambam interprets it according to the explanation of the Aruch (entry "Averuri"), that "Averuri" is the city wall, and in Persian language it is "Kashkush." And if so, it is not part of the city buildings but the encompassing wall around the city. Therefore, he omitted it because it is not relevant to us, obviously. But any type of building is forbidden, and the reason is out of respect alone: that it should be higher than all the buildings in the city. Therefore, he wrote "courtyards of the city" and not "roofs," as the reason concerns usage. And according to this, even our roofs would be forbidden. And I am astonished at the poskim who did not notice this.

And one who raises his house higher than the synagogue, some say that we compel him to lower it. However, from Rashi’s commentary, it seems that this requirement is only initially, but after the fact, we do not compel him to lower it (Beit Yosef and Bach). And Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote in paragraph 3 that if he made one corner of the building higher than the synagogue, this suffices. These are his words: meaning, even if the height is not over the entire synagogue, but only on one side, it is permitted. And specifically, this refers to an actual building, such as a roof or an upper story. But merely inserting a column does not help at all (Magen Avraham, subsection 3).

And it seems to me that for this reason, most of our synagogues are made significantly higher in the middle, and not over the entire synagogue. And know that this law does not apply to study halls. And thus, the custom is to make the synagogue very high, but not the study hall. And although we hold that the sanctity of the study hall is greater than the sanctity of the synagogue (as Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi in Megillah 27a), nonetheless, in this matter, the synagogue, which is a place of prayer for the entire city, is more stringent, as the impression is more noticeable in the synagogue than in the study hall. And the verse states: "And I will gather them in My house of prayer."

(What the Rema wrote in paragraph 2, that in a pressing situation or if they do not allow building the synagogue according to its law, it is permitted to pray in a house even though people live in an upper story above it, provided they conduct themselves with cleanliness in the upper story. These are his words. This will be further explained in section 151, paragraph 17. And see Magen Avraham, subsection 2, and Eliyah Rabbah, that now that there are other taller buildings, they are not particular about this. This requires further study.)

In Choshen Mishpat, Siman 154, it is explained that one who builds opposite his neighbor's window must distance himself four cubits so as not to block the light, see there. And four cubits suffices. But one who builds opposite the window of a synagogue or a study hall – distancing himself four cubits is not sufficient because it needs a lot of light, and he must distance himself enough so that the light remains as it was before. For it is no worse than a portico that requires a lot of light (Bava Batra 7a). And this is specifically when the public has established a right to the windows (Magen Avraham, subsection 4). An individual can open his windows facing the courtyard of the synagogue, since it is a place of entry for the public – it is considered like an open alley where there is no damage of sight, as I wrote in Choshen Mishpat there. But the public does not have the right to open windows into an individual's courtyard. And if the courtyard of the synagogue is not a place visible to the public, and it is sometimes used for private purposes – they can also protest against the individual who comes to open his windows there (there in the name of the Responsa of the Rema). And they need to be careful when it is permissible to open windows, that it does not establish a right for him in this, and they should protest against him building in front of his windows when needed. And he indeed does not have an established right, only that currently they cannot protest, but when they need to build there they can darken his windows (ibid.). And this should be written in a notebook as a reminder.

It is taught in the Tosefta, Chapter Three of Megillah: One does not open the entrance of synagogues except to the east, as we find regarding the Sanctuary, whose entrance was to the east... And the reason is that they used to pray facing west. Therefore, the entrance was to the east so that upon entering, they would bow toward the Ark, which was in the west. Consequently, for us who pray facing east, because we stand to the west of the Land of Israel as I have written in Siman 94, the entrance should be in the west. This is what the early authorities wrote, and this is the simple custom, and it should not be changed. This is what our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in Section 5: One does not open the entrance of a synagogue except toward the side one prays... so that they bow from the entrance toward the Ark... until here is his language. (And see Beit Yosef who wrote in the name of Hagahot Maimoniot: and similarly north and south, see there. It seems to me the intention is also that those who pray facing south should open to the north, and similarly vice versa. And from the Levush and Perisha it implies that it is not indispensable, see there. And further study is needed.)

Maimonides wrote in Chapter 11 of the Laws of Prayer, Law 3: "One sets up the bimah in the middle of the synagogue so that the one who reads from the Torah or the one who speaks words of admonition to the people can be heard by everyone." And our teacher, the Rema, ruled similarly in Section 5. Recently, there have been those who have come to change the customs of Israel by placing the bimah to the side. Their punishment is great, for they change an ancient custom without reason or understanding, a custom that even logic supports. They seem to desire to change it out of spite. According to the Zohar, the bimah should not have more than six steps. The prayer leader prays facing the ark, and no one should sit between the bimah and the ark with their back towards the ark. The arrangement of seating in the synagogue, as written by the Tur based on the Tosefta, is that the elders sit facing the people, and the rest of the people sit in rows facing the ark and the elders. See there. And it is good in the eyes of the Lord not to change the custom of the forefathers, and about this it is said: "Ask your father, and he will tell you."

Synagogues and study halls possess great sanctity because people pray and study Torah in them. They are akin to the sanctity of the Temple, as our Sages expounded in Megillah (29a): "And I have been to them as a minor sanctuary"—these are synagogues and study halls. And regarding what is written: "O Lord, You have been a dwelling place for us"—these are synagogues and study halls. See there. Even in their state of ruin, they retain sanctity, as it is written: "And I will bring desolation to your sanctuaries"—their sanctity remains even when they are desolate (Mishnah there 28a). Therefore, synagogues and study halls should not be treated with frivolity, such as laughter, mockery, and idle talk. The AriZal was very careful not to speak in the synagogue except words of prayer. He did not even speak words of moral instruction, lest it lead to mundane conversation (Magen Avraham, small section 3).

One may not eat or drink in them, even a casual meal or drink. One may not adorn oneself in them, nor stroll in them, nor enter them to escape the heat or rain. However, Torah scholars and their students are permitted to eat in them in pressing circumstances. Some say that in a study hall, it is permitted even without pressing circumstances, because they sit there most of the day to study, and it would result in a loss of Torah study if they had to leave to eat. But to enter to escape the rain or the heat and cold is prohibited even for a Torah scholar, unless it is necessary to study there, or in a synagogue to pray (Shulchan Aruch, Orach Chaim 151:1). It is stated in the Jerusalem Talmud that a Torah scholar is permitted to lodge in a study hall (Jerusalem Talmud, Yoma 1:4). And it also appears from Pesachim (101a) that guests are allowed to eat in a synagogue. However, the Tosafot there wrote that this refers to the rooms adjacent to the synagogue, see there (Tosafot, Pesachim 101a). (See Taz, Orach Chaim 151:1, and his words are perplexing. Also, Ramban only wrote that it is permitted due to a condition, see there).

And one should not calculate accounts on them (Shabbat and Yom Tov) unless they are for a mitzvah, such as the accounting of a charity fund or the redemption of captives and similar matters. One should not deliver eulogies on them unless it is for a great person or if the eulogy is related to a great person of the city, where all the townspeople gather to eulogize, such as if a member of the household of the great person has died, and in his honor, everyone comes for the eulogy. (See Rashi on Megillah 28b, who explains "a public eulogy" refers to a Torah scholar who has died… If so, what does the Talmud mean: What is the case of a public eulogy? Perhaps, since it does not specify that a Torah scholar has died, it implies even for a member of his household, due to his honor. See there. Examine it closely and you will find clarity.)

And what should a person do when he needs to enter a synagogue or study hall, for instance, to call someone from there or something similar? He should enter and read a bit of scripture or some halacha, and then call the person, so that it does not appear as if he entered for his own purpose. And if he does not know how to read or study, he should ask one of the children, "Recite to me the verse you are reading." Alternatively, he should wait a bit, as sitting is also a mitzvah, as it is said: "Fortunate are those who dwell in Your house." Then he can call the person he needs. The measure of sitting is the time it takes to walk through two doorways, as I wrote in Siman 90. It is not necessarily sitting; standing also suffices (Bach). "Sitting" means lingering, as it is written: "Like the days you dwelled." However, he should intend it for the purpose of the mitzvah of sitting in the synagogue or study hall. It seems that in such a case, it is also permitted to enter because of the sun, cold, or rain. Even though it appears that he entered for that reason, since he learns a verse or halacha, it does not seem so apparent that he entered because of the rain or the sun or the cold.

There is room to wonder about the current leniency regarding speaking in the synagogue and study hall after prayer about various mundane matters, which has become like a permissible act. It seems to me that they hold according to the opinion of the Ramban, which will be explained, that the synagogues in Babylonia were built with a condition that even in their inhabited state, it is permissible to speak there out of necessity. And we consider this to be a necessity, each person according to his own situation. However, certainly smoking bitter leaves there, as is the custom, and creating smoke there, is certainly a complete prohibition, and there is no greater frivolity than this. It is only permitted for those who sit and study there all day or half the day, for whom it is like eating. Therefore, it is permitted for them in the study hall but not in the synagogue. For other people, it is a complete prohibition, and for this, a condition does not help. Therefore, it is appropriate to rebuke those who do so.

And one should not sleep in the synagogue, even a temporary sleep. However, in the study hall, it is permitted for someone who studies there. For the needs of the synagogue, it is permitted to eat and sleep within it, but not to bring a bed there (Magen Avraham, subsection 4). For this reason, people sleep in the synagogue on the night of Yom Kippur to guard the candles, so that no mishap occurs. Additionally, those who sleep there recite many Psalms and songs of praise. Similarly, for the purpose of a mitzvah, it is permitted, as in ancient times when they would enter the synagogue for the intercalation of the year and would not go to their homes at all—they could eat and sleep there. However, they would only consume bread and legumes. Likewise, when completing a tractate, and all the more so for multiple tractates, it is permissible to eat a little in the study hall, as this is a mitzvah meal. To establish a large meal there seems unfit and should only be done under great necessity. This applies specifically to a mitzvah meal related to Torah study, and not to other mitzvahs like a circumcision feast, the redemption of the firstborn, or a wedding—it is forbidden, as these have no connection to the study hall.

Some say that the sanctity we attribute to study halls only applies to public ones, similar to a synagogue. However, if an individual designates a room in his house for study and for his personal use, it does not possess the sanctity of a study hall. There is no doubt about this, for its initial construction was for a regular house. Even now, when he designates this room for his study, he did not intend to consecrate it with the sanctity of a study hall. There is no need for an explicit condition about this, as this is the default assumption.

And one must not use them as a shortcut. This means that if there are two entrances, it is forbidden to enter through one entrance and exit through the other in order to shorten the way, for it is forbidden to enter the synagogue or the study hall without a purpose. How can one enter and exit merely to shorten the way? Therefore, if one did not initially enter to shorten their way, but rather needed to enter for a mitzvah, they may exit through the other entrance, even though this shortens their way. All the more so, if one entered to pray, it is permitted to exit through the other entrance. There is also a mitzvah in this, as it is written: "He who comes in by way of the north gate shall go out by way of the south gate" (Tur). Similarly, if before the synagogue was built, the path went through there, it is permitted afterward as well. It appears to me that this applies only to the synagogue itself, but to pass through the courtyard of the synagogue to shorten the way is permitted, and daily practice supports this. Similarly, passing through the vestibule of the synagogue to shorten the way is permitted.

It is permitted to enter a synagogue with one's staff, bag, and large pockets. Even though it was forbidden to enter the Temple with these items, the Temple is different due to its greater sanctity, similar to the prohibition of wearing shoes in the Temple, which is permitted in synagogues (Berachot 62b). Likewise, spitting was forbidden in the Temple but is allowed in synagogues because one should not prohibit in synagogues what is customary in one’s home (ibid.). In some Muslim countries, people go to the synagogue without shoes. This is not a proper custom and was learned from Muslims; it should be abolished. When spitting, one should rub it with one’s feet, since it is disgusting and should not be visible in holy places. On Shabbat, one should place their shoe over it until it is crushed (Eliyah Rabbah, Section 12). If there is sand or straw, or if the spit is not visible, one may spit there. Spitting is allowed even after the prayer (Bach), as this is customary in one's home. Certainly, during the prayer, if not spitting would cause distraction. The Ari (Isaac Luria) was particular about not spitting (Magen Avraham, Section 9), as his holy body could endure this, which is not the case for us.

Rabbeinu the Beit Yosef wrote in Section 6: "Some forbid entering it with a long knife or with an uncovered head." This is his language. It is not understood: what is the connection between these two? Furthermore, it is prohibited to have an uncovered head in any case. It seems that one should say: with a long knife and with an uncovered [knife], meaning when the blade of the knife is uncovered and not in its sheath, for when it is in its sheath it is permitted (Eliyah Rabbah, Section 10). Therefore, specifically a long knife, for a short one can be hidden under one's clothes or in one's pocket (see Taz who worked on this). The reason for the prohibition is because iron shortens a person's life, while Torah and prayer lengthen a person's life – it is not appropriate for that which shortens life to appear in this sacred place. It is forbidden to slaughter in a synagogue or study hall. Additionally, one should not enter with mud on his feet. It is appropriate to clean them before entering, and also the shoes should be clean. It is proper that there should be no dirt on him or his clothes. It is also customary to honor them by sweeping the floor, sprinkling water to prevent dust, and cleaning the walls. It is customary to light candles in their honor. (What the Magen Avraham wrote in Section 10 in the name of Sefer Chassidim, that Rabbi Yitzchak would clean before the Ark with his beard, see there – it is a surprising thing to demean his beard. Many are not pleased with this.)

Even after they have been destroyed, they still retain their sanctity. Just as they are treated with respect when they are in use, so too are they treated with respect when they are in ruins, whether in the Land of Israel or outside of it. However, sweeping and sprinkling water for dust control do not apply when they are in ruins. And thus it is taught in the Mishnah in Megillah (28a): A synagogue that has been destroyed – one does not eulogize within it, and one does not stretch ropes within it, and one does not spread out fruits on its roof, and one does not make it a shortcut, as it is stated: "And I will make your sanctuaries desolate" – their sanctity remains even when they are desolate. If grass has grown in it, one should not pluck it because of grief, so that the people will see it and their spirits will be stirred, and they will endeavor to rebuild it. Accordingly, if they do not need to rebuild it, for example if they have built another one elsewhere and do not intend to rebuild the old one, they do not need to pluck the grass. Rather, they should erect a fence around the place to prevent disgraceful activities from taking place there. Additionally, they may sell it according to the details that will be explained in section 153 (paragraph 16, subsection 3). It is stated in the Jerusalem Talmud, chapter 4 of Megillah (halacha 3), that Rabbi Yossi cursed the women who would spread out their clothes to dry in the air of the study hall. It appears that this refers to the Mishnah, and even in their ruins, it is forbidden. Certainly, washing clothes there is undoubtedly forbidden.

Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 11: If, at the time of building the synagogue, they stipulated that they could use it, it is permitted to use it in its state of ruin. However, in its inhabitable state, the stipulation does not help. And even in its state of ruin, for a disgraceful use, such as planting or communal accounting, the stipulation does not help. What are we talking about? Synagogues outside the Land of Israel. But for synagogues in the Land of Israel, the stipulation does not help. Thus ends his wording. 

And the stipulation is specifically when they explicitly made it. But in a general sense, we do not say "they were made on condition" for synagogues outside the Land of Israel. And specifically in Babylonia, their custom was that all their building was on such a condition generally, but not in other countries outside the Land of Israel (Magen Avraham, subsection 12). Also, regarding a ruin, the stipulation helps when they do not intend to rebuild it. But if they intend to rebuild it, the stipulation does not help (ibid., subsection 13). And there are those who disagree with this (Eliyah Rabbah, subsection 18). 

There are also those who question the distinction between Babylonia and other countries (ibid., subsection 17).
