And if one stipulated to pray in it until a certain time, and afterwards they will not pray in it at all, it is permitted to use it for any use he wishes from then on, even if it is still intact, because it was consecrated explicitly for a certain time (ibid., in the name of the Bach, in section 153).

And behold, this is the opinion of Tosafot, the Rosh, the Tur, and the Shulchan Aruch, that what we say there, that they are made on condition, even if they explicitly stipulated about the time of its construction – it is effective only after its destruction, as I have written. But the opinion of the Ramban and the Ran is that even during its construction, a condition is effective for something essential, such as that the poor may eat and sleep there, and likewise for all immediate needs of the poor. And this is what is stated in Pesachim (101a) that the sanctity of the synagogue benefits those who eat in the synagogue. But Tosafot and the Rosh explained there that this refers to the rooms adjacent to the synagogue, as I have written in section 5.

And know that this law is not found in the Rambam at all. It seems to me that he interpreted it differently: for indeed, what relevance does a condition have against the laws of their sanctity? For as long as they are in their state of sanctity, it is necessary for their sanctity to remain upon them, just like someone who consecrates something to the Temple treasury and stipulates that he can use it? Indeed, he has certainly committed a trespass. And certainly, it does not help whether they are in their state of construction or destruction, for who can remove the sanctity that is against the law? Rather, he interprets it as a condition that it should be possible to sell them to a layman, as will be explained in Siman 153. And this he explained in the eleventh chapter there. And this is permissible since they make a condition to completely remove their sanctity, which is like consecrating for a limited time. But as long as they are used for sacred purposes, all the laws of sanctity necessarily apply to them forever. (See Magen Avraham, subsection 14, who questioned why in the case of construction a condition does not help from Siman 154, for even for the Ark a condition helps? And he answered with difficulty, see there. And in my humble opinion, it seems according to the reasoning we have written: that there initially he does not consecrate it for the Torah scroll, and it is like a Torah scroll placed in a non-sacred ark, for it is not obligatory to make an ark. But a synagogue is obligatory, and necessarily since they pray there, it becomes a synagogue, and its sanctity is upon it, and a condition does not help in its construction. Investigate and you will find it easy.) (And see what I wrote in Siman 153, section 4.)

Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote in section 12: One should be careful not to use the upper floors above the synagogue for a permanent disgraceful use, such as lying there. As for other uses, it is questionable whether it is permissible to use them. Thus are his words. The question is whether the roofs and upper floors are sanctified with the sanctity of the synagogue. For in the Temple, it is said in Pesachim (85b) that in the entire courtyard, the roofs and upper floors were not sanctified, but in the Sanctuary, they were sanctified. See there (Beit Yosef). And it seems clear from there that, by law, the sanctity of a house does not extend to the roofs and upper floors, and in the Sanctuary, it is explicitly stated in the scripture that the upper floors were sanctified. See there. If so, what is the doubt in this matter? It appears that the doubt is not from the fundamental law. Rather, perhaps it is appropriate to make a memorial in the "small sanctuary" (synagogue), similar to the sanctity of the Sanctuary (and this also seems to be implied from the language of the Maharik, brought by the Beit Yosef, see there).

However, I am puzzled to the contrary: even though there is no sanctity on the roofs, nevertheless, it is explained in Siman 150 that the prohibition against having all the roofs higher than the synagogue is because they used to utilize the roofs. Therefore, they ruled that in our case, where we do not use the roofs, the prohibition is only up to the point that is suitable for use, as I wrote there in section 4. If so, it is forbidden to use any place in the city that is higher than the synagogue. If so, it is obvious that it is forbidden to use the roof of the synagogue itself. If so, what doubt is there about this? And even though according to the Rambam's opinion, which we explained there in section 5, the reason is not because of usage, but his opinion was not brought at all. See there, and it requires great investigation. (And with difficulty, one could say that only when the whole city uses the higher place consistently is it a disgrace, but not when the synagogue itself occasionally uses it. Nevertheless, it does not seem so. Examine carefully and you will find the truth.)

And our master, the Rema, wrote: "All of this applies specifically to a permanent synagogue that was initially built for that purpose. But a house that was designated as a synagogue after it was built – it is permitted to lie above it." Thus are his words. Since it was not initially built as a synagogue, a condition is effective even during its usage (Magen Avraham, subsection 17). Nevertheless, one who guards his soul should distance himself from this (ibid.). And there is one who says that all the more so, if at the time the synagogue was built, a dwelling house was built above it, it is permitted, for the upper part was not sanctified at all. Only a significant disgraceful use like defilement and the like is forbidden (Taz, subsection 4). And I am very astonished by this, for it seems to me that in such a case it is certainly forbidden, for it is forbidden to have a fixed usage in a place that is higher than the synagogue, as I have written and as explained in Siman 150. (And the words of the Taz are very perplexing. He wrote that he himself was punished for this, see there. Therefore, it is obvious that it is forbidden, and it is not similar to the law of the Rema where it was never sanctified with the sanctity of a synagogue and does not require the condition we mentioned; it is just a house in which they pray. But whenever there is a synagogue below, it is certainly forbidden to live above the synagogue. Be precise and you will find truth.)

One may not demolish a synagogue in order to build another one in its place or elsewhere. This is not only if the demolition is not for the purpose of building another, such as when one is constructing a new synagogue elsewhere from new wood and stones, where it is obvious that the old one should not be demolished until the new one is built. Even if it is necessary to demolish the old one first in order to build another in its place, or if one is building elsewhere but needs to demolish the current one to take its wood and stones to build the other – in any case, it is forbidden (Beit Yosef), as we are concerned that some mishap might occur preventing the construction of the new one. Therefore, one should build the new one first and then demolish the old one. Even if they do not want to demolish the entire structure but only one wall to expand it, the same rule applies: they should first build the new wall and then demolish the old one. This is permitted even in large cities. Although it is entirely forbidden to sell a synagogue in large cities, as I wrote in Siman 153, this is because perhaps not everyone is agreeable. However, for building a new one, it is certainly agreeable to everyone (Magen Avraham, subsection 2).

Some say that even if there are two synagogues in the city or more, it is forbidden to demolish one of them until another is built in its place (Shulchan Aruch, small section 1). And some say that in such a case, it is permitted. The reason is that we do not worry that an unforeseen event will occur which will prevent it from being built forever, as this is an unlikely concern. Rather, the concern is that an unforeseen event might occur which would delay the construction for a long time, and in the meantime, they would not have a place to pray. Therefore, when there is another synagogue in the city where they can pray, there is no issue (Taz, small section 1, Bach, and Eliyah Rabbah, small section 1). And since the majority of the authorities hold this way, one can be lenient in such a case. (The Rashba, Ran, and Nimukei Yosef explicitly permit in such a case, only the Beit Yosef wrote that according to Tosafot and the Tur, it is not so. They elaborated to explain that even according to Tosafot and the Tur, it is so.)

We state in the Gemara (beginning of Bava Batra) that this prohibition only applies when there is no defect in the old structure. But if we see a defect in it—under all circumstances, it is permitted. That is to say, only when the old structure is still strong and there is no concern of damage, then it is forbidden to demolish it until the new one is built. However, if its foundations have crumbled, or its walls are leaning to fall, or there is danger in the roof or beams—they demolish it immediately. They just begin building the new one by day and night if possible, and hurry its construction so that it does not extend for a long time. And in the Gemara there, it mentions an incident of this nature, where one of the sages brought his bed there to hasten its construction. (And see Magen Avraham, subparagraph 4, that the intention is near the synagogue, see there. And it is not necessary, as Eliyah Rabbah wrote in subparagraph 4 that for the need of the synagogue—even within the synagogue it is permitted. And also what he wrote in subparagraph 5 against the Bach follows his reasoning in subparagraph 1. And it is not so, as I wrote in subparagraph 2. And also the intention of the Bach is not as he wrote, but when the person is standing in the middle of the building. And Machatzit HaShekel has already pointed this out, see there.)

Our teacher, the Rema, wrote that it is forbidden to take stones from an old synagogue to build a new one. That is his language. Meaning: What has been clarified that it is forbidden to demolish the old synagogue – this applies even when the stones are needed for the construction of the new synagogue, and we have already explained this in paragraph 1. Furthermore, it informs us that even if the construction of the new synagogue has already begun and is in the middle of construction – it is forbidden. (Eliyah Rabbah and Magen Avraham, subsection 5. However, what the Bach wrote permitting in such a case – that is when they have another synagogue, as I wrote in paragraph 2. And the Magen Avraham took it with a different intention, but it is not so as I have written. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

He further wrote that it is forbidden to demolish anything from the synagogue unless it is done with the intention to rebuild. Thus are his words. The explanation of his words: It is found in the Sifrei on the portion "Re'eh": From where do we know that one who removes a stone from the Temple, from the courtyard, or from the altar is transgressing a negative commandment? It is derived from the verse: "You shall not do so to the Lord your God." And since the synagogue is considered a "small sanctuary," it is forbidden to demolish or dismantle anything attached to it. However, if his intention is to dismantle in order to rebuild, and through this dismantling he is improving – it is permitted, for this is not considered dismantling. Some prohibit making even a small hole in the wall to insert a piece of wood or metal for a shelf (Taz, Orach Chaim 151:3). And some permit it (Eliyah Rabbah 151:7), as long as it is not done destructively – it is permitted, as Maimonides wrote in the first chapter of the Laws of the Temple, even concerning the Temple itself, and certainly regarding a synagogue. And this is the main ruling and the common custom. Both the synagogue and the study hall have the same law in all aspects of this section. (And from Makkot 22a it is evident that even something detached is forbidden.)

The sanctity of a Beit Midrash (study hall) is greater than the sanctity of a synagogue, for in a Beit Midrash they study Torah and in a synagogue they pray, and Torah is greater than prayer. Therefore, it is permitted to convert a synagogue into a Beit Midrash, but it is forbidden to convert a Beit Midrash into a synagogue, for we elevate in sanctity and do not downgrade. And this allowance to convert a synagogue into a Beit Midrash applies specifically to a communal Beit Midrash. However, for the private study of an individual, it is forbidden, for it does not have the same sanctity as that of the public. There are those who are uncertain about this (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 1), but there is no doubt that it is certainly forbidden (Eliyah Rabbah, subparagraph 1). I have proof of this from the Megillah (3b), which states that the Torah study of an individual is lighter in weight compared to service (sacrifices), see there. All the more so compared to prayer, which is in place of service. Additionally, it appears to me that although it will be explained later regarding selling that it is forbidden to sell the synagogues of large cities, nevertheless converting a synagogue into a Beit Midrash is permitted even in large cities. The reasoning for selling is that perhaps the public will not agree, but elevating to a higher sanctity, everyone agrees. And although in the case of selling, the proceeds are used for a higher sanctity, as will be explained, nevertheless the synagogue building itself is desecrated, unlike here where the building itself is elevated in its sanctity.

In this section, it will be explained that the residents of a city are permitted to sell a synagogue or other sacred objects to a layperson to use as a dwelling, provided that the money obtained is used to create something with a higher level of sanctity than the original. There is a disagreement regarding whether the money can be used for something with equal sanctity, as will be explained. It will also be clarified that it is permissible to give these items as a gift, because it is assumed that the recipient of the gift has provided some benefit in return; otherwise, they would not have given it as a gift. A significant question arises from this overall issue: since the synagogue is sacred, how does its sanctity become nullified? The Talmud in Nedarim (29a) straightforwardly asks: "Where did its sanctity go?" It cannot be said that this is similar to the sanctity of items dedicated to the Temple treasury, where redemption is effective—the money becomes sanctified, and the consecrated object becomes ordinary. If that were the case, how could it be permissible to give it as a gift? Is consecrated property redeemed for prior benefit?

The earlier authorities of blessed memory were aroused by this inquiry. And the Ramban of blessed memory answered that a synagogue and anything similar to it do not have intrinsic sanctity. Rather, they are treated as articles used for a mitzvah, like a sukkah, shofar, lulav, and tzitzit, which are respected as sacred objects as long as their mitzvah is in effect, but after their mitzvah is completed, their sanctity is removed. Therefore, when people cease to pray in a synagogue, its sanctity is nullified. It is only the Sages who established guidelines and distinctions, whether it was sold by the townspeople alone without the seven trustees of the town, or if it was sold by the seven trustees of the town, as will be explained. And the Ran of blessed memory answered that all these sanctities are rabbinic. The Rabbis imposed sanctity upon it and they specified the details in this matter, and in some instances, they saw fit to prohibit, and in others, they saw fit to permit, according to the laws that will be explained (Ran, chapter "Bnei Ha'ir").

From the words of the Rambam, it appears to me there is another explanation. We have already written in Siman 151, Section 14 that the Rambam omitted the case of the synagogues of Babylonia being built conditionally. And we explained there that "conditionally" means that if they wish, they have the ability to sell them, see there. According to this, it could be that the sanctity is from the Torah, as the plain meaning of the language of the Gemara there (Megillah 26a) suggests, which calls the synagogue a sacred place like the Temple. And as they expounded: "And I have been to them as a small sanctuary" — these are synagogues and study halls. And this is explicitly implied in the Yerushalmi there, which says: it is one thing if it was built as a synagogue, but if it was built as a courtyard and then sanctified, what is the status? See there — it clearly calls it "sanctified". And it is difficult to say that the intention is a mitzvah or rabbinic. And this that it says the synagogues of Babylonia were built conditionally… this is its interpretation: because there is a difference between village synagogues and city synagogues as will be explained, and therefore it says that in Babylonia even in cities, they were built conditionally, because they are built with the consent of the leader of the city. And as Rav Ashi said (Megillah 26a): this synagogue of Mata Mechasya… since it was built with my consent… if I wish, I can sell it. And also here that it says the law of the synagogues of Babylonia… (Megillah 28b), in his days it was so throughout Babylonia. And this law was written by the Rambam there in Chapter Eleven of the Laws of Prayer, Law 19, see there. And he did not mention Babylonia or Mata Mechasya, because in those places it was only so in their days. But the main reason for the Rambam is that every synagogue is presumably built with this condition, that it is possible to sell and give them, and it is like temporary sanctity. And the Rabbis differentiated in this with specific laws, as will be explained with the help of Heaven. And all this because it is as if they stipulated so. And there is proof of this from the language of the Rambam there when he differentiates between villages and cities, as will be explained in Section 16.

We learned in the Mishnah at the beginning of the fourth chapter of Megillah: The residents of a city who sold a synagogue may use the proceeds to purchase an ark, which is the cabinet where the Torah scroll is kept. This is the Holy Ark, whose sanctity is greater than that of the synagogue because the Torah scroll is placed there. The same applies to the table on the platform: if the Torah scroll is placed directly on it without an intervening cloth, its sanctity is like that of the Holy Ark. However, if the Torah scroll is not placed directly on it without an intervening cloth, its sanctity is only like that of the synagogue. Similarly, the platform itself has sanctity only equivalent to that of the synagogue, as will be explained in Siman 154.

If they sold an ark, they can buy with its proceeds a Torah mantle, which is holier because the Torah scroll is dressed or wrapped in it, and the cover and the mantle share the same level of sanctity. If they sold a mantle, they should buy with its proceeds books, specifically Torah scrolls written on parchment like a Torah scroll. Similarly, they can buy Prophets and Writings written on parchment, as these are holier than the mantles, even though the mantles serve the Torah scroll, and the Torah scroll is holier. Nevertheless, the intrinsic sanctity is weightier than an object serving a holy item, even if the latter's sanctity is greater. If they sold books or Prophets and Writings, they should buy with their proceeds a Torah scroll. But the reverse is not allowed. That is, if a Torah scroll was sold, it is forbidden to buy books, Prophets, or Writings with the proceeds. If they sold books, Prophets, or Writings, it is forbidden to buy a mantle. If they sold a mantle, it is forbidden to buy an ark. If they sold an ark, it is forbidden to buy a synagogue. The Prophets are greater than the Writings. Some say they are equal, as I wrote in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 282. The sanctity of Torah scrolls is greater than that of the Prophets and Writings, as I wrote there. All this applies to those written on parchment as a proper Torah scroll. But printed ones have lesser sanctity, and their sanctity is equal, as we explained in Siman 22. Nevertheless, it seems to me that their sanctity is still greater than that of the mantles, as they contain the essence of sanctity and many Divine names. Therefore, it is forbidden to sell them and use the money to buy items serving sanctity, but the reverse is allowed. A Torah scroll found with an error has the sanctity only of Torah scrolls. Even though it can be corrected, as long as it is not corrected, it does not have the sanctity of a Torah scroll (Magen Avraham, Siman 3). Know that even if they bought something of greater sanctity than what was sold, and there remained some money from the sale, it is still forbidden to use the remaining money to buy something of lesser sanctity, because the sanctity of the sold item applies to all the money (Talmud there).

Rabbeinu, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 4: If it is permissible to buy with the money of one sacred item another sacred item similar to it—there are those who prohibit and those who permit. These are his words. And behold, concerning a Torah scroll, there is certainly no difference of opinion, for initially, it is clear that it is forbidden to sell it in order to buy another, as I wrote in Yoreh De'ah, section 270. And in the Gemara there, it was a question that was not resolved and thus is forbidden. And after the fact, it is clear that it is permitted to buy another Torah scroll. For what else would be bought, since there is no sanctity higher than the sanctity of a Torah scroll? And the disagreement is only regarding other items. And some say that all items have the same ruling as a Torah scroll. And there is no argument here, for initially, it is forbidden and after the fact, it is permitted (Ba”ch and Derisha). And there is no proof: for although it is certainly forbidden to sell initially, in any case, after the fact, it is not similar to a Torah scroll, for there is no other sanctity higher than it. But concerning other items, one can buy a higher sanctity, and on this, there is a disagreement. And so, the precise wording of Rabbeinu, the Beit Yosef, indicates that he is referring to after the fact, but initially, all agree that it is forbidden. (And the objections of the Derisha and the Ba”ch are in vain. And also the question of the Taz in Yoreh De'ah there is puzzling, for there it is initially and here it is dealing with after the fact. And so wrote the Eliyah Rabbah in section 7. Also, what the Magen Avraham wrote in section 4, that after the fact it is permitted—I do not know from where he derived this. And there is a disagreement about this, and the words of the Beit Yosef are clear. Be precise and you will find ease.)

However, from the wording of Maimonides (Rambam) in Chapter 11, it is evident that it is even initially permissible to sell a synagogue in order to purchase another synagogue. He wrote: "The residents of a village who wanted to sell their synagogue, or to build another synagogue with its proceeds...," see there. It is clear that he permits selling a synagogue initially in order to purchase a sacred item of similar sanctity, and this applies to all items. Only with a Torah scroll is there an initial prohibition, because there is a slight disgrace in making a trade with a Torah scroll. But for all other items, it is initially permissible to sell in order to purchase another of similar sanctity. And so it is our custom to sell books and purchase others, and many have agreed that this is indeed the opinion of Maimonides (Rambam). (Tosefot Yom Tov there, and Eliyah Rabbah there. And so wrote the Magen Avraham there. The distinction made between a Torah scroll, because its sanctity cannot be diminished, is stricter, see there – this has no reason, and on the contrary, for this reason, it is more preferable, as is evident. The main reason is as I have written, and the world seems to have adopted Maimonides' opinion as primary. Examine and you will find clarity.)

Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote in Section 5: If money was collected to build a synagogue or a study hall, or to purchase an ark, a cover, or a Torah scroll, and they want to change its use from what it was collected for – it can only be changed from a lesser sanctity to a greater one. However, if they used the money for the intended purpose and there is a surplus, they may change the surplus to whatever they want. This is his language. In this matter, money is treated more leniently than the sacred object itself, for with sacred objects it is forbidden to change even the surplus, but with collected money, it is permitted to change the surplus. This permission of the surplus is explicitly stated in Megillah 27a, and the Rambam and the Tur also wrote this in his language, see there. And one of the early sages already wondered why it is forbidden to change the money, for we hold that designation is not significant? Even if they built a synagogue, as long as they have not prayed in it – it is permitted to change its use, as will be explained. All the more so with money, where there isn't even a designation. (And it is like weaving for a fabric; Beit Yosef in the name of Ramach.)

There is an opinion that explains that indeed, it is not because the money acquires sanctity, but rather due to a vow. And also in a law that will be explained later, that it is permissible to change it, but it is necessary to build another synagogue to fulfill the vow, and here too they are permitted to change these funds as long as they substitute with other money (Taz, subsection 2). However, this cannot be said, for if so, why is it permitted to change them to a higher level of sanctity when they vowed for a lower one? There is an opinion that says that for a higher level of sanctity, they certainly agree (Pri Megadim). But this is not so, for since they vowed for this specific mitzvah, it is forbidden to change it to another, even a greater one. And this matter is explicitly stated in the Mishnah in Menachot (107b), that in the same type, if one vowed to bring a small one and brought a large one, it is a dispute whether he has fulfilled his obligation, but with a different type, he has not fulfilled his obligation even with a greater one. And this is also clarified by Maimonides in Chapter 16 of the Laws of Sacrificial Procedures, see there.

There are those who explain: since the people of the city donated for this mitzvah, it is forbidden to change its use without their consent. Only the public has the authority to change it because it was given with their intention (Magen Avraham, Subsection 5), which means the seven leaders of the city in the presence of the townspeople (Machatzit Hashekel). According to this, we must say that when changing to a higher level of sanctity, it is not considered a change.

There are those who explain that collecting money constitutes an act and not just preparation (Shach, Yoreh De'ah, Siman 259), since the money was given to the treasurer, it is considered an act. And even though building a synagogue is certainly an act, and nonetheless it is permissible to change its use, this is because their intention is that as long as they do not pray in it, the sanctity does not apply, which is not the case with money (Eliyah Rabbah, Subsection 8, and this resolves the question of the Magen Avraham there. Also, what is questioned from Sanhedrin 48b is not difficult at all, since there it deals with surplus, see there. And this is also the answer of the Beit Yosef and the Bach, who wrote that since it came into the hands of the treasurer, it is forbidden to change its use. The Taz there was astonished by this, see there. And it is not difficult at all, since their intention is that by this it is considered an act. This reasoning was written by the Tosafot in Sanhedrin 48a, beginning with "surplus," see there. And here it is even better. Investigate and you will find it easy.)

Our master, the Beit Yosef, further wrote: If, when the funds were collected, they stipulated to do as they pleased with the surplus money, even if they bought and sold, and then bought sanctity with part of the money – it is permissible to use the surplus. But if they did not stipulate when collecting, but only when selling, it is forbidden to use the surplus. Thus are his words.

The explanation of his words: If they purchased with all the money and then sold, and then bought again with part of the money, even if they stipulated at the time of the sale – it does not help, because the sanctity applies to all the money from the first purchase. Only if they stipulated at the time of collection – it helps even in such a case. (The Gra and the Eliyah Rabbah questioned this, for if so, what is Abaye's question to Rava in Megillah there: The reason is that they stipulated, but if they did not stipulate – they cannot? Let us say it refers to such a case, see there. And I do not understand: for the Baraita stands on the Mishnah of "and likewise with their surplus," and the Mishnah does not refer to such a case, see there. Reflect on it and you will find it easy.)

And know that regarding what has been explained about leftover money, that they can use the surplus for whatever they want, some say that it is even permitted for discretionary matters (Magen Avraham, subsection 6), and only for communal needs (Eliyah Rabbah, subsection 9). And there are those who write that it is only permitted for lesser sanctity, and not for discretionary matters (Taz, there). The main ruling follows the first opinion, for otherwise, what is meant by the phrase "for whatever they want"? (And the question posed by the Taz is answered by the Eliyah Rabbah; see there. This is also necessitated by the language of the Talmud; see there. Study it and you will find it straightforward.)

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote: If they bought wood and stones with these funds that were collected, the sanctity of the money transfers to the wood and stones, and it is forbidden to change them except for a higher level of sanctity. And if they brought wood and stones for the purpose of building the synagogue, if they came into the hands of the treasurer, it is forbidden to change them except for a higher level of sanctity. And before they came into the hands of the treasurer, it is permitted to change them, but in any case, they cannot retract. Thus far his words. 

The explanation of his words: Even though one who donates wood and stones, before they come into the hands of the treasurer, it is permitted to change them as explained in Yoreh De'ah, siman 259, in any case, if they were acquired through the collection of money that came into the treasurer's hands as I wrote, and the wood and stones were bought with this money, they have the status of the money even before they came into the treasurer's hands. And afterwards he says that if they brought wood and stones as a donation for the building of the synagogue, if they came into the hands of the treasurer, it is forbidden to change them except for a higher level of sanctity, and only seven distinguished members of the city are allowed to change as will be explained. And before they came into the hands of the treasurer, it is permitted to change them, meaning to borrow them and replace them with others (Magen Avraham, section 8). And this is what he wrote "but in any case, they cannot retract," meaning due to his donation which is like a vow. (See Taz, section 3, who follows his reasoning. And according to what I wrote, it fits well.)

And since it has been explained that one may sell these items for the sake of a higher level of sanctity, all the more so may they be sold in order to study Torah and to provide for students (Levush). Even a Torah scroll, for what benefit will there be in them and in the Torah scroll if they do not study it? The merit of the one who studies is greater than the merit of the Torah itself (ibid.), and the entire world was created only for the sake of Torah study. Similarly, one may sell a Torah scroll to marry off orphans with its proceeds, and this has already been mentioned at the beginning of Even Ha'ezer. There are those who say that this applies specifically to male orphans and not female orphans, because women are not commanded in the mitzvah of procreation (Chelkat Mechokek there, and see there in Beit Shmuel). However, this is not so, for on the contrary, we find in Ketubot (67a) that a female orphan precedes a male orphan in marriage. And so the Levush writes here, for regarding "to settle the world" everyone is commanded. The disgrace of a female orphan is greater than the disgrace of a male orphan, and this is the established ruling. (And so wrote the Magen Avraham and the Eliyah Rabbah in subparagraph 12. And so wrote in a responsum R’ Meir Alshakar.)

It is stated in Megillah (26a) that the sale of a synagogue applies specifically to that of villages. But a synagogue of cities, since people come to it from all over, it cannot be sold, because it belongs to the public, and everyone is its owner, and the townspeople do not have ownership over it (Rashi). According to the Ramban and the Ran, which we mentioned in section 3, that a synagogue does not have sanctity except as a means of performing a mitzvah or rabbinic sanctity, it is not understood why the Sages differentiated between those of villages and those of cities. One must force an interpretation. According to what we explained in section 4, following the Rambam's opinion that the sanctity is from the Torah, and the reason it is permitted to sell is that initially, the townspeople build it on this condition; and even though they did not explicitly state it, it is as if they did, for the townspeople always consider the possibility they might need to sell it. According to this, the distinction between villages and cities makes good sense: in cities, it does not depend solely on them, and what benefit is their condition? The masses of the world certainly do not have this condition in mind, as what concern do they have for the needs of the city? This is also precisely the language of the Rambam in this law in Chapter 11, Law 16, and this is his language: What are we discussing? ...of villages, which were made only with their intention alone... But those of cities, since they were made not solely with their intention... they belong to all of Israel. They can never be sold. Thus are his words. Meaning, that the condition of the townspeople is of no benefit, for they are not the sole owners? And all of Israel cannot be assumed to have intended this condition.

And know that there is no distinction regarding which funds were used to build it. For in villages, even if it was built from donations from the world, it is permitted to sell it, since the donations were given with their [the villagers'] intent. But in cities, even if it was built from the city's funds, they cannot sell it, because since it was built in a city with the intent that people from all over the world would come to pray there, it belongs to all of Israel. However, even in a city, if individuals built a synagogue for themselves, they can sell it like in a village (Taz, section 6). This is explicitly stated in the Gemara there (Megillah 26a), regarding the synagogue of the Tarseans in Jerusalem which they sold, see there. Since it was designated only for craftsmen or a minority of the public, it belongs solely to them. Specifically, the synagogue of the entire city in a city cannot be sold, but in a village, even in such a case, it can be sold.

It has already been clarified that the money from a sold synagogue retains its sanctity and can only be used for a higher level of sanctity, and it is forbidden to lower its sanctity. However, this is specifically when the townspeople sell it without the consent of the seven community leaders, or the community leaders sell it without the presence of the townspeople. But if the seven community leaders sell it in the presence of the townspeople, they are permitted to use the money for any purpose, even for non-sacred matters, as the money completely loses its sanctity. According to the Ramban and the Ran, the reason must be that the sages established it this way. According to the Rambam, it appears the reason is that initially, the townspeople had this intention, that if the sale would be conducted by the seven community leaders in the presence of the entire town, the money would completely lose its sanctity, and it is as if it was consecrated conditionally. And what we have written, that it must be in the presence of the entire town, is not to be taken literally; rather, it should be with the agreement of the entire town. Therefore, if the seven community leaders sell it publicly, it is considered "in the presence of the townspeople" even if they did not say anything, as long as they did not object. Therefore, if some of the townspeople objected, the money would not lose its sanctity. Similarly, if the townspeople agreed at the time of the sale that whatever a specific individual does with the money is permissible, then whatever he does is valid, and he can use it for non-sacred matters, and it is as if the seven community leaders sold it in the presence of the townspeople.

And also regarding city synagogues, which we said it is forbidden to sell even if it was built with their own funds, our teacher the Beit Yosef wrote in Section 7: But for city synagogues... it may only be sold if it was originally stipulated to follow the opinion of an individual, in which case the individual may do with it as he wishes with the consent of the community. The same applies to all sacred objects mentioned here, for they all follow the synagogue. Thus far his words. This means: at the time of construction, it was stipulated to follow the opinion of an individual, then he may do with it as he wishes. And there is no novelty in this, for it is obvious that an initial condition is effective, so what is it teaching us? And why does it need to say that it was stipulated to follow the opinion of an individual, for an explicit condition without this is also effective? Furthermore: if it was explicitly stipulated to follow the opinion of an individual, why is the community's consent needed? However, the matter is thus: there was no explicit condition, but rather the entire construction was dependent on the opinion of an individual, that he would build it according to his opinion and he would be involved in the construction expenses. In this case, it is as if he was given permission to do with it later as he wishes, even to sell it and use the money for non-sacred purposes (and this is also implied in Taz, subsection 7). Therefore, the community's consent is needed, for the final ruling is like the initial ruling, just as initially there was the community's consent over him, so too whatever he does with it later requires the community's consent.

And there are those who say that this applies specifically when they built it with their own funds, as it is then considered a condition. But if they built it with the money of others who are not from that city, what benefit is there in their opinion alone, since perhaps the others do not agree with this (Magen Avraham, subsection 12)? And this is a correct reasoning, but if so, why was this not clarified? Also, the language of our teacher, the Beit Yosef, who wrote "even if they built it with their own funds, it is not sold unless it was conditioned on the opinion of an individual...", implies that all the more so, if it was built with the funds of others, it is not sold, and this refers to the case where it was conditioned on the opinion of an individual. Therefore, it appears to me, in my humble opinion, that even if it was built with the funds of others, if at the time of collecting the donations they stated that the entire building depends on a certain individual – everyone gave with that understanding. But if they did not say this – it is prohibited to sell it even if only a small portion of the funds came from others, according to the law of a community (and perhaps even the Magen Avraham would agree to this).

And so it is with all sacred items that have been explained; they all have the same laws, that there is a distinction between villages and cities. In villages, when the seven good men of the city sell [sacred items] with the agreement of the town, it is permissible to use the money [for other purposes]. This applies to all synagogue utensils, benches, and curtains (Magen Avraham, subsection 15). Curtains that are spread over the ark are considered like the ark itself (ibid.). However, not all sacred items have the same status regarding their use. A synagogue itself can be sold even for secular use. Similarly, all items used for a mitzvah, when sold, may be used for secular purposes, as will be explained. However, items used for sacred purposes, like the ark and the curtain and similar items, retain their sanctity even when sold, and they may only be sold to someone who will use them for sacred purposes, similar to a Torah scroll. This will be explained in section 154 (ibid., subsection 14).

It is a clear matter that the permission to sell a synagogue in villages applies when they have another synagogue to pray in. Otherwise, it is forbidden to demolish it in order to build another until the other is built first, as I have written in Siman 152. Unless they wish to sell it to buy another synagogue with the proceeds, and in a situation where there is no concern of negligence, then it is permitted. But in cities, it is forbidden in all cases (there, subsection 17). There are those who want to say that the permission to sell in villages when they have another synagogue means that they have now built another one. But if they have not now built it, even if they have two synagogues, it is forbidden to sell one, for even to demolish one is forbidden, as I have written in Siman 152, and all the more so to sell (there, subsection 16). These matters are puzzling, and the entire sugya in Megillah and in all the Rishonim does not imply this. The prohibition to demolish is certainly correct, but when the sale is necessary, they permitted it. However, if they only wish to demolish and build another, they were concerned that they might not build. What is the connection between these matters? (And conversely, what is written in subsection 17, that to purchase a more sacred item is permitted even if they do not have another synagogue, is also puzzling. The Eliyah Rabbah already disagreed with this in subsection 18, see there. This is also implied in Yoreh De'ah, beginning of Siman 252. Also, what the Magen Avraham wrote in subsection 33 requires examination. What the Shach and Taz wrote there is specifically in the context of redeeming captives, as the Shach wrote there, or for the needs of the synagogue as the Taz wrote there. But to sell a synagogue for a more sacred purpose when they do not have another synagogue, we certainly have not heard of. Investigate and you will find it easy.)

And certainly, in the case of cities, even if another one is built – it is forbidden to sell the first one, because it does not depend solely on them. However, regarding the law of demolition as explained in Siman 152 – there is no difference between villages and cities, since they intend to build another in its place. If so, why should the distant ones care? Nevertheless, the wood, stones, and land retain their sanctity, and it is forbidden to use them or sell them, because perhaps there is someone at the end of the world who does not agree to their sanctity being nullified (Magen Avraham, subsection 16). And there are those who permit it (there in the name of Masat Binyamin). And it is proper to be stringent. (Eliyah Rabbah, subsection 18, ruled like Masat Binyamin to permit, and disagreed with Magen Avraham, see there.)

There are those who have written that a "city" (כרך) is defined only as a city where merchants regularly gather for commerce, or where people regularly gather for some other reason, like provincial cities and the like. However, if many people merely pass through there without a permanent residence in the city, it is not called a "city" (כרך), because what significance do the passersby have to the synagogue of this city? And anything that is clear to us that it was not built with the intention for everyone is considered in this regard a "village" (כפר), and it can be sold (Magen Avraham, Section 17, in the name of Masat Binyamin). And this also seems logical. Therefore, in our times, there are few synagogues that are judged as a "city" (כרך) in this regard. And an individual who built a synagogue and handed it over to the public – its status is like all the synagogues in the city, and the individual has no say in its sale. But if he reserved any power for himself – it cannot be sold except with the consent of both parties, meaning: the consent of the public and his own consent or that of his heirs after his death. And if before his death he gave all his power to the public – they do not need the consent of his heirs. And see Section 39.

Any sacred object that is sold and permitted to be altered can be sold without public announcements, even in the case of land, which typically requires an announcement. There is no issue of overcharging (ona'ah) even with movable items, where such concerns usually exist (Taz, subparagraph 8). The reasoning is that the main purpose of announcements is to prevent overcharging, and even gifts are permitted (there). Additionally, announcements are only relevant when collecting for others, not when we are selling something that belongs to us (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 18, in the name of the Ran, see there). The reason there is no issue of overcharging with movable items is that it is akin to a homeowner selling his own belongings, where overcharging does not apply, as explained in Choshen Mishpat, section 227. However, if it is forbidden to alter the item, and therefore it cannot be given as a gift, an announcement is required, because without an announcement, it is considered a devaluation of the sale (there, subparagraph 20). Consequently, there is overcharging with movable items as with all movable items, whereas with land, there is no overcharging, as overcharging does not apply to land. Some say that with movable items, there is overcharging even if it is permitted to alter the item unless it was known from the outset that its value was more or less. But if it is forbidden to alter the item, there is overcharging even with land, as its status is like that of an agent, where any sale is void even with land, as explained in Choshen Mishpat there (there, and Eliyah Rabbah, subparagraph 19).

It is well-known that with all items of holiness and commandments, we hold that "preparation is not significant" until it is verbally designated and an action is taken. Therefore, if a synagogue is built, as long as prayer has not been conducted in it, it does not have the sanctity of a synagogue. Even if it was built merely as a house, if it was subsequently dedicated as a synagogue, it has the status of a synagogue, but it does not become sanctified until prayers are held in it. However, if prayers were conducted in it even by individuals or by guests temporarily, since it was used for prayer and designated for it, it becomes sanctified. If it was dedicated temporarily, it depends on what was stipulated, as a condition is effective in all matters. Regarding the funds, if it was built from donations intended for the synagogue, it is prohibited to change their use, as explained (Magen Avraham, section 21). However, if an individual donated and built a synagogue from his own funds and on his own land or on the land of others, although it does not become sanctified until prayers are conducted in it, he cannot retract his donation because it is considered a vow, as will be explained in section 36 (there).

The villagers, when they sell a synagogue as will be explained, can sell it as a permanent sale. The buyer can do with it whatever he wishes, except for four things which he is prohibited from doing: a bathhouse, a tannery, a ritual bath, and a bathroom. However, if it was sold by the seven good men of the town in the presence of the townspeople, the buyer can even do these four things, for in such a case, the sanctity is completely removed, both from the synagogue and from the money, and the seller can do whatever he wishes with the money. The same applies to all holy items that have been clarified, except for a Torah scroll and books, which necessarily remain in their sanctity (Levush). However, with the money, the seller can do whatever he wishes (there), since it was sold by the seven good men of the town in the presence...

Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote in section 10: There are those who say that an individual with his own Torah scroll – even a Torah scroll – is permitted to sell it and use the money for whatever he desires, as long as he did not consecrate it for public reading. And there are those who prohibit this unless it is to learn Torah or to marry a woman. Thus are his words. The first opinion is that of the Rosh and the Tur, and they hold that what our sages of blessed memory said, "One may not sell a Torah scroll except to learn Torah or to marry a woman," and similarly, the entire discussion in Megillah – all of this applies to a communal Torah scroll or an individual who entrusted it to the community. But any individual with his own Torah scroll, even if he made it with the greatest sanctity like a Torah scroll, initially his intention was that when he needs, he will sell it and use the money. Similarly, if he built a synagogue or study hall only for himself – he can always sell it or change it, because from the outset, he made it with this intention. And it is not similar to what I wrote at the end of section 26 that in any case it is a vow – this is when they have not yet prayed in it at all or studied in it at all. But here, since they have already prayed and studied and fulfilled the vow – he can rightfully do with it as he pleases as long as he did not entrust it to the public. The "there are those who prohibit" is the opinion of the Rambam in [Rambam, Laws of Tefillin, Mezuzah and Torah Scrolls, Chapter 10 of Torah Scrolls], who wrote: One may not sell a Torah scroll… – and he did not differentiate between an individual and the public. And I am astonished by this: for the Rosh and the Tur also wrote this in the laws of Torah scrolls in Yoreh De'ah, section 274, see there. And despite this, they differentiated here between an individual and the public, so what is the proof that the Rambam disagrees with this? And in my humble opinion, it seems to say that in "Torah scroll" it refers to the one Torah scroll that every person is obligated to have as explained there, and therefore even an individual is prohibited from selling it. Whereas here it refers to another Torah scroll, where the prohibition is due to its sanctity – in this, we differentiate between an individual who made it for himself and one who entrusted it to the public, and there is no disagreement at all. This requires further investigation. However, in practice, it seems that Rabbeinu Beit Yosef also holds like the first opinion, and one of the greats also wrote this. (Eliyah Rabbah, section 22, and similarly the Rema wrote in Darkei Moshe that the custom is like those who permit, see there.)

There is someone who raised a difficulty regarding this law from what is written in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 248, about someone who said, "My property to so-and-so," whether a Torah scroll is included in "my property" since it is forbidden to sell it. This is from the Gemara in Bava Batra (150a). It refers to an individual, because if he had consecrated it to the public, he would not be able to sell it. They forcefully explain that it refers to giving it to the public to read from, but not handing it over completely, because in such a case, he also would not be permitted to sell it. And they are astonished at the custom of the world, which is to sell it even in such a case (Magen Avraham, Siman 22). According to what I have written, it is not difficult at all: there, it refers to a single Torah scroll that he is obligated to write, and therefore it is forbidden to sell it. The world that has the custom to permit this does so because they hold like the opinion of the Rosh in Yoreh De'ah, that nowadays the mitzvah is with books and not with a Torah scroll, see there. And in Yoreh De'ah, I further explained this, see there. However, it is certain that the seller will not see a sign of blessing in the money, as I wrote in Yoreh De'ah there. (And know that according to what I wrote there in Yoreh De'ah, the prohibition of selling is only because of the disgrace to the Torah scroll being sold like other objects, and therefore, even if one has several Torah scrolls, one should not sell them, as I wrote there – this has no relevance at all to the laws in this Siman. And therefore, there is no proof from the Rambam at all. Examine this well and you will find it easy to understand.)

Just as it is permissible to sell a synagogue in villages, so too it is permitted to give it as a gift. The recipient of the gift may do with it as he wishes, just as in a sale. The reason is that if they did not derive benefit from it in matters concerning the synagogue, they would not have given it as a gift. Therefore, the gift is considered like a sale, and this requires the presence of seven community leaders in the presence of the townspeople. In cities, it is forbidden (Magen Avraham, subsection 26), and the reason is explained in sections 3 and 4. Giving it as a gift to a distant city, where they certainly did not derive any benefit from it, is definitely forbidden (ibid., subsection 27). Likewise, wood and bricks from an old synagogue that was demolished with permission, as explained in Siman 152, may also be sold or given as a gift, just like the synagogue itself.

Just as it is permitted to sell or give a synagogue as a gift, it is likewise permissible to exchange the synagogue or its wood and stones for another, so that the other takes on the sanctity of the synagogue, and similarly, the wood and stones. The original synagogue and its wood and stones then become desecrated. What difference does it make if it is sold or exchanged? And even though all these things are permitted, lending, renting, or pawning them for mundane purposes is not permitted. The reason is that they only permitted it when another item would take on their sanctity, such as the money from the sale or the exchanged item. However, in the case of lending, renting, or pawning, no other item takes on their sanctity, because they themselves remain in sanctity after the lending, renting, or pawning period is over. Therefore, they would become desecrated without any replacement, and this is forbidden. The reason why gifting is permitted is due to the previous favor, which is considered like an exchange, and it is forbidden even with the consent of the seven good men of the city and in the presence of the city residents. Although in such cases, the money also becomes desecrated as I wrote in paragraph 18, at the time of the sale they take on sanctity. But afterward, the seven good men of the city, in the presence of the city, have the power to desecrate them, which is not the case here (see small section 28). And even if we say that the rental money also takes on sanctity, it is still forbidden because they themselves remain in sanctity – it is impossible for another to take on their place. (In this way, we understand the language of the Tur and Shulchan Aruch in paragraph 11, which states that they still remain in sanctity, as there is nothing else to replace… until here is their language. They are like two contradictory statements, but according to our explanation, it is well understood. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

And know that everything explained regarding the permissibility of selling (a synagogue) does not apply in towns; this is all when selling it to remove its sanctity, for since its sanctity is being removed, something else must be designated for the sanctity to rest upon, with the agreement of all. Therefore, in towns, it is prohibited, as explained. However, one may sell a synagogue to others, provided it retains its sanctity as a synagogue. There is no need at all for something else to bear its sanctity (Magen Avraham, section 27, contrary to the Bach). This is permissible even in towns, but according to the Tosafot (beginning of the fourth chapter, s.v. "I would hire"), it is forbidden to sell from many to an individual, see there. One must say the reason is that it diminishes its honor. However, most authorities disagree with this and hold that even from many to an individual is permitted, as long as its sanctity is not removed. This is the opinion of our master, the Rema, at the end of section 11, who wrote: "Specifically in a manner that diminishes their sanctity. But it is permitted to lend even a Torah scroll to read from, even from many to an individual." Thus far his words. All the more so with a synagogue and study hall and other holy objects, one can lend, rent, pawn them, and also sell them, provided they remain in their sanctity with the purchaser. Even in towns, if an individual donates a holy object, if he gives it to the public, it belongs to the public. If not, or if the custom is that the public uses it temporarily, and when he wishes, he takes it and sells it, the custom is followed. This matter is explained in Yoreh De'ah, section 259. See also later, section 154.

One of the great authorities (Magen Avraham there in the name of Masat Binyamin) wrote: If a new synagogue is built, and the old one is demolished by the decision of the seven representatives of the city in a formal assembly... – the sanctity of the old one is removed and transferred to the new one. They are then permitted to do whatever they wish with the old one, as it is no worse than a gift. However, without this, not even the seven representatives of the city in a formal assembly have the authority to treat it as a secular building, since there is no other entity for its sanctity to be transferred to. This is also implied in the Tosefta... thus far his words. And it has been elucidated in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 259, that the seven representatives of the city have the authority to change the use of a synagogue's candelabrum for secular purposes. Nonetheless, a synagogue itself, which is primarily made for sacred use, cannot have its sanctity nullified without transferring it to something else (Magen Avraham). However, in the responsa of the Rosh (Klal 5), it is written that the seven representatives of the city have the authority to convert a synagogue into a residential house, similar to the candelabrum. This requires further investigation: how can its sanctity be nullified without anything in exchange? We must say that the Rosh's intention is when they build another synagogue in its place, thereby transferring the sanctity to the new one. However, this explanation is very puzzling: it is explicitly stated in the responsa of the Rosh that they built upper rooms for the study hall, and afterward decided that they should study in the synagogue there, and they rented out the upper rooms as residences, see there. The Rosh responded that the seven representatives of the city... can change it for secular use, and there is no exchange required for the sanctity to be transferred to something else. Additionally, this is very puzzling: the Rosh brought the ruling that the seven representatives of the city can sell even for secular use, and it is explicitly stated in the Gemara there that renting is forbidden, as written by the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch. And the Rosh himself mentioned this in Megillah there and wrote the reason: since there is nothing for the sanctity to be transferred to. Therefore, in my humble opinion, we do not derive from this responsa, and it requires significant examination. (And the main ruling is that it is forbidden. Also, what the Magen Avraham wrote in the name of the Nimukei Yosef, we do not hold by the Nimukei Yosef as the Mechatzit HaShekel wrote. And I am astonished at the Mechatzit HaShekel, the Pri Megadim, and the Eliyah Rabbah for not commenting on this.)

Our Rabbi, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 12: "One who has a condition with the community that only he and his descendants can build the synagogue cannot sell his right to another." Thus is his wording. And it is written that this is specifically when he was honored with this. But if he purchased this right, he acquired all rights like any other acquisition (Taz, subsection 11, and Eliyah Rabbah, subsection 24). However, it does not seem so from the source of the law in the Mordechai, in the chapter "HaChovel," where the case was that they inherited this right and the heirs sought to sell this right, and it was ruled that they do not have the ability to do so, see there. And if you would think that they honored their father with this, what kind of inheritance is it? The truth is that even when he purchased this right, we testify that it was granted to him on the condition that he would not sell to another without their permission, for perhaps he would sell to someone unworthy. (And the Taz himself wrote: "In any case, it is clear that he should only sell to someone as worthy as he is, for it was granted to him with this understanding." Thus is his wording. If so, why was it necessary to say that they honored him with this? And the intention of the Beit Yosef is also that he cannot sell without their consent.)

The Rambam wrote in Chapter Eight of the Laws of Gifts to the Poor, Law 11: If money was collected for the construction of a synagogue and a mitzvah (commandment) opportunity presented itself, the money can be used for the mitzvah. However, if stones and beams were purchased, they should not be sold for a mitzvah except for the redemption of captives. Even if the stones were brought and dragged, and the beams were trimmed and prepared for the synagogue construction, everything can be sold only for the redemption of captives. But if they built and completed the synagogue, it should not be sold, and funds for the redemption should be collected from the community. This is the Rambam's language, and our master the Beit Yosef copied it in this section, law 13. This law has already been explained in Yoreh De'ah, section 252, see there. In truth, its place is in the laws of charity, as it is not related to the sanctity of the synagogue in this section, as it was explained above that if money was collected for the synagogue construction, it is forbidden to change its purpose. However, the reason here is that the redemption of captives is greater than all commandments, and therefore, according to the decision of the seven good men of the city in the presence of the city inhabitants, it is permissible to change its purpose to the redemption of captives. This is also stated in Yoreh De'ah there. This is explained in the Talmud at the beginning of Bava Batra. In the Talmud, it is only explained that the money should be given for the redemption of captives. The Rambam, who wrote that it is permissible to use the money for another mitzvah, must have had that version in the Talmud. Also, it must be said that his intent was to borrow this money for that mitzvah and then others would repay it for the synagogue construction, as I wrote in section 10. However, our master the Beit Yosef in his major book in Yoreh De'ah there wrote that even for another mitzvah, it is permissible to change its purpose with the agreement of the seven good men of the city… It must be said that this is through the seven good men of the city, and above it refers to without the seven good men of the city, as I wrote in section 11. What they wrote, that if the synagogue was built and completed it should not be sold, is not because it is forbidden but because it is not customary to sell a person's residence. Therefore, even before it has been prayed in, it should not be sold. (Magen Avraham section 31 and section 33. And what he wrote in section 32 that in the Rambam the version is "they built and completed", see there – our version in the Rambam is like in the Shulchan Aruch. However, the ruling is certainly so, that even if the building is not yet completed, it should not be sold, for it is not less than a person's residence as explained in the Talmud. And be precise and you will find it light.) (And according to the Magen Avraham, there is no need for the Taz's difficulty at the end of section 13.)

Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote in Section 14: Reuven said, "I am donating this land to build a synagogue on it," but the idolaters did not allow them to build the synagogue, and the community wants to build a study hall (Beit Midrash) on it, and Reuven says, "I did not vow with this intention" – Reuven cannot retract. If Reuven did not live there – they could change its use, but if he is from that city – they are not permitted to change it if he stands and protests. Unless there is a city official (Chaver Ir), because everything that comes is done with his intention. This is his (Rabbeinu Beit Yosef's) language. The explanation of his words: If Reuven wants to completely retract from his dedication of the land for a synagogue because "I did not vow with this intention" – he cannot, since he did not say at the time of dedicating the land "on condition that they allow building it immediately." And although he said it was to build a synagogue on it, it could be that over time they will allow it. But regarding changing it to a study hall, if Reuven does not live there – he donated based on the intention of the city's people, and it is obvious that they are permitted to change it to a higher sanctity. But if he is one of the city's people – we testify that his intention was that even without his consent it should not be changed. Therefore, when he stands and protests – they should not change it even to a higher sanctity. However, when there is a city official, we testify that at the time of dedication – he dedicated it based on the intention of the city official completely. And now he wants to retract, and he cannot.

And our master, the Rema, wrote that the seven good men of the city have the same status as a member of the city council. Thus are his words. And I am astonished: for it is understandable that a member of the city council, everyone gives according to his sole decision. But the seven good men of the city need the consent of the townspeople as explained, and behold he is one of the townspeople and protests? (The Eliyah Rabbah also raised a similar difficulty, see there. And he ruled not like the Rema in subsection 28.) On the contrary, there are those who raised the difficulty (Magen Avraham, subsection 36) that in Yoreh De'ah, section 259, it is explained that charity donated for the synagogue can be changed for the study hall, even if the owners object, see there. And here they ruled that the owners object. (And what Magen Avraham wrote that in Yoreh De'ah it refers to owners who are not from the city, see there and the difficulty is evident. Also, the words of the Levush here are puzzling, see there. And in Eliyah Rabbah subsection 27, he also expressed astonishment at him.)

And it appears clear to me that the words of our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, are correct. And the matter is as follows: It has already been explained that to elevate to a more stringent sanctity, seven community leaders (tovei ha'ir) are not needed, but for a lesser sanctity or for secular matters, seven community leaders are required. And any person who dedicates something perpetual, like money or land, certainly does not nullify his intention against the entire community or against any individual. But against the community council or the seven community leaders and the agreement of the entire community, he certainly nullifies his intention, unless he specified at the time of the dedication that he does not nullify his intention against them. According to this, everything fits well: Initially, it was written that without his knowledge, it is forbidden to change even to a more stringent sanctity. But when there is a community council or seven community leaders with the agreement of the entire community, certainly his initial intent was that his intention would be nullified against the seven community leaders with the agreement of the entire community, and he is like one of the other community members who does not agree with the seven community leaders. And "the entire community" is not to be taken literally; the intention is the majority of the community. And even if he now says that this was his intention, he is not believed. And in Yoreh De'ah it refers to the seven community leaders, and it was not expanded upon there because the main laws are here. And in Yoreh De'ah, section 7, we wrote another method regarding this, such as when the one who donated is not from this synagogue. (And with this, we can uphold the words of the Magen Avraham that we brought. However, it appears more as I wrote, that it refers to the seven community leaders. Analyze this and you will find it clear.)

It is obvious that in cities, the seven trustees of the city do not have authority, for how could they benefit another city? The reason for the prohibition in cities is because the entire world has a share in it, as explained. Therefore, how could the seven trustees of this city help? Additionally, the seven trustees of the city require the consent of the city's inhabitants, and here there is no consent from all the cities. Nevertheless, the great authorities have written that nowadays the seven trustees of the city can sell even in cities just as they can in villages (Magen Avraham, subsection 37, in the name of the Maharshal, and Beit Yosef in the name of the Mordechai). This is when they built it with their own funds (there). Similarly, one of the great authorities acted to sell the land of a synagogue when they saw it was impossible to build there because of oppressors. They sold it with the seven trustees of the city, even though it was in a city and built by others, because certainly all of Israel would agree to this (there in the name of Maharal of Lublin regarding the synagogue of the Lukov community). This matter should be understood according to the time and circumstance, and it is impossible to explain everything in writing. Additionally, above in section 24, we explained that the law of "city" as mentioned in the Gemara is rare in our times, see there.

In Yoreh De'ah, section 224, it is explained: Since a partner can forbid his portion to his fellow, therefore, in a synagogue where everyone is a partner, one can forbid his portion to another. This is according to the strict law. However, the enactment of the early sages was that a person cannot forbid his portion of the synagogue or the books. If he does forbid, it is of no consequence, for the declaration of the court is considered ownerless property. They enacted this to prevent disputes: today one might get angry at another and forbid his portion to him, and tomorrow the other will do the same, leading to endless conflict. Regarding a charity box, if one forbids what is inside it to another, his prohibition is of no legal consequence, for once given to the charity box, it no longer belongs to him. Similarly, one cannot forbid tithe money, for it is not considered his, as explained in Nedarim (83b); see there in detail (Magen Avraham, subsection 38).

In Yoreh De'ah, Siman 221, it is explained that if one lends his house to another, he cannot prohibit its use for the entire duration of the loan. However, the borrower can prohibit its use, as for the entire duration of the loan, it is considered as belonging to the borrower; see there. Therefore, if someone lends his house to a synagogue, if he lends it for a specified period, he cannot, during that period, prohibit its use by the congregation or any individual. But if he does not set a specific period and just lends it indefinitely, or if the specified period has passed, he can prohibit its use by the entire congregation. However, he cannot prohibit its use by some individuals or a portion of them, because since he consents to the majority using it, it is not considered his in a way that he can prohibit its use by individuals. However, if he initially stipulated that he can object whenever he wishes or did not explicitly lend it to them but merely allowed them to enter his house, he has the right to object as he wishes. Conversely, if he lent his house to the synagogue and it was used for a long time, and later the congregation wants to move to another place, they are not permitted to do so. As it is stated in Gittin (61a): "We establish an Eruv in an old house for the sake of peace," so that people do not say that the members of his household are suspected and therefore they moved away. Even if there is some reason for wanting to move from there, it is not proper to do so (Magen Avraham, Siman 40). Unless they build a permanent synagogue, in which case everyone sees the reason. And similarly in all such cases. (And regarding what the Magen Avraham wrote that he can say "I do not wish to go far," see there—I do not understand. What difference does it make to them? Why should this compel them? Rather, the main reason is because of suspicion, as I have written.)

Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in paragraph 18: "There is an opinion that the holy vessels made of silver, which are customarily brought to the synagogue during festivals, cannot be taken out for secular use or sold by their owners. The community can claim them so that they remain in the possession of holiness after the death of the dedicant." This is his wording. Nowadays, the common practice is that they remain in the possession of the owners, and if so, even without an explicit condition, it is as if they had stipulated this (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 43). The words of our teacher, the Beit Yosef, are perplexing, for later in paragraph 20, he wrote the opposite. This is his wording: "There is an opinion that a Torah scroll that was established as belonging to Reuven's ancestors cannot be claimed by the community." This is his wording. Now, the matter is a fortiori: If a Torah scroll, which has a great level of sanctity and is always in the synagogue, yet if it was established as belonging to his ancestors, the community cannot claim it—how much more so with silver vessels that are always in his house and only brought to the synagogue during festivals, that the community cannot claim them. (And the Elyah Rabbah, subparagraph 32, addressed this and resolved it with difficulty; see there.)

And behold, these two laws are from the Maharik (Siman 70 and Siman 161). I have examined there, and there is no contradiction, as in the case of silver vessels, it refers to when the congregation argued that their ancestors completely donated them to the synagogue, and in the case of a Torah scroll, it refers to the opposite: it was established that it belonged to his ancestors, who never handed it over to the synagogue. And it is written that the assumption held by the congregation is not valid, because it was given to read from and not to become their property. And witnesses do not help because they all have a vested interest, see there. And this is also the intention of the Shulchan Aruch. Therefore, what the later authorities (Taz, section 15, and see Taz) brought, that the Maharshal in his responsa (Siman 16) disagrees regarding the Torah scroll, ruling that not only are the heirs not believed, but even he himself would not be believed to say "I did not hand it over to the congregation," see there - there is no disagreement here. For certainly, in a general case, he must clarify that he did not completely hand it over to the congregation, and the Maharik is referring to when it is known that he did not completely hand it over. And this is also how it should be ruled: if it is known that he did not hand it over to the congregation, the congregation does not have an assumption. And when it is not known, he must bring proof, and if he does not bring proof, he loses.

It is further written in Section 19: There is an opinion that if, after a person's death, a written document is found stating that they dedicated utensils (to the Temple), and there are no witnesses and it was not handed over to the community — nevertheless, it is considered dedicated. Thus are his words. And even though in Choshen Mishpat, Section 255, it is explained that with regard to dedications, we also say that a person might say something just to make themselves seem pious, nevertheless, writing is different. This is explicitly implied from the Mishnah in Ma'aser Sheni, at the end of Chapter 4, see there. And although in Choshen Mishpat, Section 81, Paragraph 17, it is explained that in writing for oneself, we also say that a person might say something just to make themselves seem pious, see there — this applies to ordinary matters and not to dedications, as is proven from the Mishnah there. (And this answers the question of the Magen Avraham in Subsection 44.)

Our Master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in paragraph 21: "One should not purchase cloaks that were used by a common person for sacred use." So is his language. And this specifically applies without any change, but with a change, such as sewing it in a different manner than it was originally, or similar modifications – it is permitted. And we have already explained this above in Siman 147, paragraph 11, see there. And our Master, the Rema, wrote: "It is forbidden to make an item of mitzvah, such as a synagogue or a Torah scroll, from the earnings of a prostitute or the price of a dog." And this specifically refers to the earnings themselves, but if they gave her money as payment – it is permitted to purchase an item of mitzvah with it. And 'prostitute' only refers to a forbidden relationship, but those unmarried women who dedicate something – it is permitted to accept from them. So is his language. And 'forbidden relationship' also refers to those who are liable to a negative commandment, and a maidservant and a non-Jewish woman. And there is one who says that a non-Jewish woman the first time is not called a 'prostitute' (see Magen Avraham, paragraph 48). And according to this, in the opinion of the Rambam at the beginning of the Laws of Marriage, that any unmarried woman who isolates herself for promiscuity violates a negative commandment – what our Master, the Rema, wrote is not correct, but he follows the opinion of those who disagree with the Rambam. And we have explained this in Even HaEzer, Siman 26, see there. And know that a change is permitted in payment when the item given to her has been altered. Similarly, if one had relations with her and then gave her payment – this is not considered payment. And it is only forbidden if he gave her and then had relations with her.
