And if she gave him – it is permitted. And there are many more laws regarding this and the price of a dog, which have been explained in the Rambam, Chapter Four of the Laws of the Altar (and see Magen Avraham, paragraph 46, who elaborates on this).

It has already been explained in section 41 that one should not change the house in which they prayed to another house. The same applies to anything that a person has established in a mitzvah even once—if they have established it in a manner of permanence, it should not be taken from them. Similarly, if someone has attained an honor, it should not be taken from them. There is an opinion that if someone has fulfilled a mitzvah for several years and then dies, if their son takes their place, he also merits this mitzvah (Sha'arei Teshuvah, subsection 27, in the name of Knesset HaGedolah). This is compared to an appointment where the son takes precedence. However, this is a perplexing matter, as this is merely an honor. It also seems that the custom is not like this.

And a person who is accustomed to a particular mitzvah, such as rolling the Torah or any other mitzvah, and an unforeseen circumstance or poverty occurred such that the community gave the mitzvah to someone else, and afterward he became wealthy and wants the mitzvah returned to him, our master the Beit Yosef ruled in section 22 that if at the time the mitzvah was given to another he was able to give what he used to give each year but did not desire it, and he agreed along with the rest of the community to give it to another – he lost his right. However, if at the time it was given to the second person, the first was unable to give what he used to give, and now that he is able, he wants to reclaim his mitzvah and give what he used to give initially – he returns to his mitzvah. This is the end of his words, and the mitzvah is not changed even from an ignoramus to a scholar. From his words, we learn that if the first person was away for several years and the community gave it to another – when the first person returns, he reclaims it, because he was compelled. However, if there is evidence that he despaired of it – he lost his presumption (Magen Avraham, section 49).

In the time of the Talmud, it was customary during a fast to gather in the street of the city and pray there. Nonetheless, our sages of blessed memory stated at the beginning of the fourth chapter of Megillah that there is no sanctity in this practice at all, because it is not a fixed arrangement but rather a temporary one. Based on this, the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch wrote that the same law applies to houses and courtyards where people gather to pray occasionally – they hold no sanctity, see there. Based on this, Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote in section 2 that if one rents a house and prays in it – it does not have the status of a synagogue. Thus far his words. He carefully chose to say "it does not have the status of a synagogue," and did not write "it has no sanctity" as before, because here it is not due to the temporary nature since they rent it for a year or more. Rather, the reason is that they do not have the power to make it a permanent synagogue, as the Levush wrote, and these are his words: since the property is not owned by them, and today or tomorrow the landlord may take it back…, see there. Therefore, he wrote "it does not have the status of a synagogue," meaning: the sanctity and laws of a synagogue do not apply to it. However, it is sacred for its time, and one should not do anything disgraceful there. (This seems to be my humble opinion. And the Pri Megadim stated that the reason is because it is temporary and had difficulty with the words of the Levush, see there. But this is not so. And this is also the intention of the R.Y. Chaviv in Beit Yosef and Taz, small section 1. Be precise and you will find clarity.) (Also, what the Taz and R.Y. Chaviv wrote about behaving with cleanliness in the upper rooms above the place of prayer, according to what the Rema wrote at the end of section 151 – this applies only in a permanent synagogue. And the Taz wrote there that the prayer does not ascend above when the upper place is not clean, see there. This is a measure of piety, and it is proper to be careful about it.)

We learn in Megillah (26b): The Rabbis taught: Items used for a mitzvah may be discarded after their mitzvah has been fulfilled. Items used for holiness must be stored away. These are items used for a mitzvah: sukkah, lulav, shofar, tzitzit. This has already been explained above in Siman 21, see there. And these are items used for holiness: the bags (or boxes) of books, tefillin, and mezuzahs, the cover of a Torah scroll, and the case and straps of tefillin. The fact that the straps are referred to as "items used for holiness" and not as "holiness" itself indicates that the knots of the hand and head tefillin, which have the letters yud and dalet, are not complete letters and are not a law given to Moses at Sinai (Tosafot there). There is a difficulty with Rashi, who holds that they are a law given to Moses at Sinai, see there. One must say according to Rashi that this refers to the entire strap except where the knot is. Additionally, even if it refers to the whole strap, one cannot do more than store them away. After all, even a Torah scroll that has become invalidated has no remedy other than being stored away.

The curtain that is hung before the Ark – it has sanctity and must be stored away properly. This is stated in the Talmud there, and in the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, section 3. And in section 6, Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote that the curtain we hang before the Ark does not have the sanctity of the Ark, only the sanctity of the synagogue. These are his words. And this is not a contradiction, for it is certainly so, as it is merely an accessory of an accessory. That is to say: the Ark serves the Torah scroll, and the curtain serves the Ark. However, in the Talmud, they explained that in their times, they used to spread the curtain on the table and place the Torah scroll on it, and therefore, it was an accessory of sanctity, which is not the case in our times. And it is perplexing that the Tur and Shulchan Aruch did not explain this. But in any case, their intention is also so, as it is explained in the Talmud. (And so wrote the Taz, section 3, and the Magen Avraham, section 7.)

Books that have been eaten by worms, or the coverings of the books that have been eaten and are close to decay, require burial (Shabbat 91a). In the language of the Mishnah, this is called "decayed books," see there. And a chair on which a Torah scroll is placed, if sometimes the Torah scroll is placed on the chair without a covering, the chair has the status of an item used for holiness. If not, it is considered an item used for an item used for holiness, and it only has the sanctity of a synagogue. Therefore, the bimah only has the sanctity of a synagogue, as does the table on which the Torah scroll is placed, since among us it is not placed without a covering, the table only has the sanctity of a synagogue. The covering itself has the status of an item used for holiness. Similarly, the parochet (curtain), the kaporet (cover), the poles, and the bars on which the parochet hangs only have the sanctity of a synagogue. Likewise, the steps that lead up to the ark, and the entire structure there, as well as the reading stand.

A fundamental principle must be understood regarding what is called "objects of holiness" and what is called "secondary objects" which only have the sanctity of a synagogue. An item in which something of inherent holiness is placed, such as the Holy Ark, or the cloth that is wrapped around the Torah scroll, and the mantle that is placed on the Torah scroll, or if the Torah scroll is placed on it without any separation. Or if something is placed on the Torah scroll, even if it's only placed for the sake of honor, like in ancient times when they used to place thin and beautiful boards on the books, and they would place a silk or other kind of cover on the boards; this is only for the sake of honor, but still, in the end, the cover is placed on the holiness – it is considered an "object of holiness" and it is forbidden. But the cover on the cover of the boards, which is made only to protect the cover – it is considered a "secondary object." And similarly, all such cases. Likewise, silver and gold apples made for the Torah scroll for decoration, and placed on the Torah scroll – these are considered "objects of holiness," as I wrote in Yoreh De'ah, section 282. However, the wood or bone that is made like a pointer, to show the reader the place of the reading of the day's obligation – they do not even have the holiness of a synagogue, as they are neither for decoration nor for clothing, only for marking. Therefore, the poles from which the curtain is hung should not be used to make this pointer, as they should not be downgraded from their sanctity, and the "pointer" is considered a downgrade in comparison. It appears that this is the case if the pointer is not hung on the Torah scroll. But in our practice, where it is hung on the Torah scroll for decoration, it can be said that it is called an "object of holiness" and has greater sanctity than the poles.

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) writes in Section 1: There are those who say that something is not called a "Holy Ark" unless it is in the form of a box made solely for the honor of the Torah. However, an ark built into the wall, which is made for protection, is not considered a "sacred object." And certainly, if the books deteriorate in it, it is permissible to remove them from there. This is his language. That is to say: it will only have the sanctity of a synagogue, because since it was not suitable from the outset, the sanctity does not apply to it, as it is not a sacred object but rather damages the sanctity (Magen Avraham, Section 3) and is considered like a consecration made in error. The same applies to an ark built into a wooden wall, which is like an ordinary room (ibid., Section 2). It seems that even if one attaches wooden boards with nails inside a hollow wall made in the form of a Holy Ark, it is nullified in regard to the wall and has only the sanctity of a synagogue. But if they build a box-like structure outside and insert the box into the hollow wall, the box has the status of a Holy Ark and is considered a sacred object.

The courtyards of the synagogue do not have the sanctity of the synagogue, even if prayers are occasionally held there. However, if prayers are regularly held there, they do acquire the sanctity of the synagogue. Similarly, a women's section in the synagogue has the sanctity of the synagogue since women pray there. It is obvious that a courtyard surrounding the synagogue, or a garden surrounding the synagogue, or an orchard or benches surrounding the synagogue do not have any sanctity, even if they are open to the synagogue. Nevertheless, one should not use them for disrespectful purposes. Similarly, it is forbidden to wash Torah scroll covers in urine, out of respect.

All sacred items that have become worn out and damaged should not be burned, as it is written: "You shall not do so to the Lord your God" (Magen Avraham, Small Paragraph 9). All the more so, it is forbidden to burn sacred writings. And so wrote the Rambam in the Book of Commandments (Negative Commandment 65), that one who destroys sacred writings transgresses a prohibition. Therefore, for a Torah scroll that has become worn out, our sages said that it should be placed in an earthenware vessel and buried in the grave of a Torah scholar; even if he only studies Mishnah and not Gemara, he is considered a Torah scholar for this purpose. The reason for the earthenware vessel is that it lasts for many years. Similarly, worn-out tefillin and mezuzot, and Torah scroll coverings can be made into shrouds for a deceased mitzvah-obligated person, and this is their proper burial. A "mitzvah-obligated person" refers to a poor person who has no shrouds. It also seems that an ark and table that have become worn out can be made into an ark for a Torah scholar, since the sanctity of the coverings is like the sanctity of the ark, and there is no difference between them (this is my opinion). In my humble opinion, it also seems that the directive to bury a worn-out Torah scroll in the ground in an earthenware vessel near the grave of a Torah scholar is not an obligation. Certainly, if one has a secure place to store it in his home, in a box or the like, or in the synagogue, it is preferable to burying it in the ground. However, if there is no appropriate place to store it respectfully, it is permitted to bury it in the ground as I have written. Some have written that this is a specific obligation (see Pri Megadim). It is difficult to say so. (And where it is written in the Shulchan Aruch regarding coverings "they can..."—this also applies to the Torah scroll that follows. And in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 282, where the law of the Torah scroll is mentioned first, this wording is not used, see there.)

It has already been explained that one should not downgrade from a higher level of sanctity to a lower level of sanctity. Even within the same level of sanctity, if one is constant and the other is not constant, it is considered a "downgrade." Therefore, our sages of blessed memory said that one should not make a chair for a Torah scroll from an ark, because the Torah stands in the ark constantly, whereas on the chair it is only during the reading. And if the Torah is not placed on the chair except with a cloth – it is still forbidden, for its sanctity is lesser, as I wrote in Section 4. However, it is permissible to make a small ark from a large ark. Similarly, it is permissible to make a small chair from a large chair, as they are of the same sanctity and serve the same purpose. It is forbidden to make a footstool from a chair, which is a small chair that stands under the large chair, and does not have the same sanctity as the large chair, and it seems to be for supporting the legs. It is also permissible to make a small curtain from a large curtain, or to make from it a cover for the Torah scroll, which is an elevation in sanctity. But to make from it a cover for a Chumash is forbidden, as it would be a downgrade in sanctity. This refers to the curtain from the time of the Gemara, as I wrote in Section 3. But for our curtains, it is permitted, because ours are only secondary usage, as I wrote there. It seems that a secondary usage from a high sanctity may be made for a lower sanctity. A Torah scroll cover should not be used to wrap Haftarot or other books of Prophets and Writings. A cloth spread on the reading table should not be spread on the lectern (Magen Avraham Section 12). Cloths spread on the Torah scroll may be hung on the walls of the synagogue. Likewise, silver utensils placed on the Torah scroll may be placed on the synagogue's stands (Eliyah Rabbah Section 10). It is permitted to make from a parochet a cloth for the table on which the Torah scroll is placed (ibid. Section 11). For our parochot, it is even permitted to make them into a cloth for the lectern (ibid.). But it is forbidden to make from it a wedding canopy (ibid.).

Our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, wrote in Section 8: The ark and everything made for the Torah scroll – it is effective to make a condition to use them for other purposes, even mundane ones. And it has become customary to benefit in various ways from sacred items, such as book coverings, synagogue tables, and Torah scroll covers. They wrote the reason: because since this is the custom and it is impossible to be cautious – the heart of the court makes a condition from the outset, so that people do not come to transgression. And even though they did not explicitly make a condition – it is as if they did. Thus their words. And even though regarding the synagogue itself, a condition does not help except in its destruction according to most authorities, as I wrote in Siman 153 – there it is different, because since they pray there and always recite sacred matters – it becomes sanctified against their will. This is not the case with items of sanctity, when we do not designate them at all initially solely for sacred purposes – the sanctity of sacred items never descends upon them (it seems to me).

However, to say that if they did not stipulate, it is as if they stipulated, is certainly a forced interpretation. This is also explained in the source of this law in Terumat HaDeshen (Siman 273), where he struggled to justify the custom of the world (see Beit Yosef). Indeed, there are things for which we must necessarily say so, for we see that people place invalid Torah scrolls in the Holy Ark and put parchment scrolls there, which is technically forbidden. We must therefore say that it is as if they stipulated. Similarly, in places where they make canopies from the Torah curtain, which is completely forbidden as I have written, we must necessarily say that it is as if they stipulated. We also see on Simchat Torah that boys carry flags as is customary, and they tie the flags with Torah scroll covers, and we must necessarily say that it is as if they stipulated. However, the better way is that when they do these things, they should explicitly say that they are doing it on the condition that it is permissible to use them (Magen Avraham, subsection 15). Therefore, it is understandable why on Hoshana Rabbah, they take all the Torah scrolls to the platform and place a candle in the Holy Ark. This is completely forbidden, and they have already protested against this (Taz, subsection 7). Similarly, putting other books in the Holy Ark (there and Magen Avraham, subsection 14). We must necessarily say that it is as if they stipulated. (And what the Taz wrote there, that an ark made for a temporary period has no sanctity, is straightforward. And what the Magen Avraham wrote there about placing one book on top of another, is explained in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 282. And what the Magen Avraham protested against bookbinders, who make pages from sacred writings - we have already protested about this. Some are careful, and some are not careful and need to be rebuked. And even though the Eliyah Rabbah, subsection 10, sought to justify it – he admitted himself that it is a forced interpretation, see there. It is not just forced, but a complete prohibition.)

And we can bring proof to the ruling of our rabbis from the Jerusalem Talmud (Megillah, Chapter Three, Halacha 1), where it says: Rabbi Yirmiyah went to Gwalna and saw them placing items inside the Holy Ark. He went and asked Rabbi Ami. He said to him: I say that they must have stipulated this from the beginning. Thus far is his wording. And certainly, it was not known that they had stipulated this, for if it had been known, Rabbi Yirmiyah would not have been astonished by it. Rather, Rabbi Ami told him that since they had this practice, it must be assumed that their original intention was such. And even though they did not explicitly stipulate it, it is as if they had stipulated it. It is further stated there: All the utensils of the synagogue are like the synagogue itself, such as benches and candelabras... see there. And behold, our eyes see that benches and tables of the synagogue and candelabras are borrowed for joyous occasions, and this is certainly a complete prohibition. Rather, we must certainly say that it is as if they had stipulated from the beginning, since this is the custom.

And behold, our master the Beit Yosef wrote in Section 10: Those who have the custom to place the crowns of the Torah scroll on the head of the one who completes the reading of the Torah – we do not object to them. But those who place them on the heads of ordinary grooms – we do object to them. Thus are his words. And it is obvious that if they explicitly stipulated, it is permitted. However, he says that placing it on the head of the one who completes the reading of the Torah is presumably agreed upon because it is for the honor of the Torah. But placing it on the heads of ordinary grooms, which are for mundane purposes, is presumably not agreed upon (Magen Avraham, Section 16). However, from the Jerusalem Talmud that we brought, it is proven that if such is the custom, we say that even for mundane purposes they agreed upon, for there they placed a mundane object in the Holy Ark. And it is also clear from the simple custom that they borrow synagogue items for joyous occasions, as I have written.

Furthermore, it is written in Section 9: Those who donate a Torah scroll and place the coverings in the synagogue — it is permissible to use them for any scroll, as they were dedicated with this intention. However, those who place them in their home and then consecrate them, since they were made with the intention for that specific scroll and used for that specific scroll — it is forbidden to place them on another Torah scroll. Some permit this, and this is the current practice because it is assumed that the court's intention is to allow this practice. Thus are his words. And so is the prevailing custom, that the covering and cloak are sometimes used for one scroll and sometimes for another; for the donor also intends this way and does not mind if they are placed on another Torah scroll, and initially dedicated them with this condition.

In Yoreh De'ah, Siman 139, it is explained that candles belonging to idolaters, if extinguished by a non-Jewish servant, are nullified from their prohibition and permitted for ordinary use. However, for the purpose of a mitzvah, they are still considered repulsive and are forbidden. Therefore, if their servant sells or gives them to a Jew, it is forbidden to light them in a synagogue. Similarly, if a complete transgressor, who is an idol worshiper or publicly desecrates the Sabbath, donates wax or candles to the synagogue, it is forbidden to light them, as it is akin to a sacrifice that is not accepted from him (Magen Avraham, Section 18). Nevertheless, some say that a house that was used for idol worship may afterward be used for prayer, as it is considered attached. And even though the house was originally detached and later attached, making it considered detached concerning idolatry, since the house itself was not worshiped, it is permissible to be lenient with such an attached structure (ibid., Section 17). It is certainly permissible if it was originally a synagogue and then idol worship was introduced; it does not become forbidden even while the idol is there, as it has come into the synagogue’s domain (ibid.). Similarly, if a mouse is found in the synagogue’s oil, if it is repulsive, it is forbidden to light it in the synagogue due to "Would you present it to your governor?" Even when permitted for ordinary use, such as when there is sixty times the volume against the mouse, some say that if there is sixty times and it is permitted for ordinary use, it is also permitted to light it in the synagogue (Taz, Section 10). This is also explained in the Torat HaBayit by the Rashba (see Magen Avraham, Section 19), that since there is sixty times, it is not considered repulsive. (Anything related to idol worship is forbidden for use in the synagogue and for any mitzvah.)

From the law, it is forbidden to read by the light of the synagogue candle except for sacred matters and not for mundane matters. Certainly, it is forbidden to light a common candle from the synagogue candle. Some say this applies while the candles are lit for their mitzvah purpose. However, when they need to be extinguished, it is permitted. Rabbi Rema wrote in section 14, and this is his language: "However, it is not customary to be strict about this, and they light from them a candle for a significant need. It is also possible that the court's intention is to stipulate this." Similarly, in all matters where it is customary to be lenient, it might be for this reason. This is the end of his language. It has been written that the custom of lighting a candle on Saturday night to go home is considered a mitzvah matter (Taz, section 11). Some have written to differentiate between someone who vowed a candle for the synagogue, which is forbidden to light from it a Havdalah candle, and when the treasurer buys candles, in which case we say the court's intention is to stipulate and it is permitted (Magen Avraham, end of section 20). The candles standing before the menorah are certainly forbidden (there), and all the more so the candles before the pillar. And know that nowadays, this is not observed at all. People read letters by the candles before the menorah and the pillar, and they light from it for making tobacco and all common needs, even without significant need. It must be said that since this is the custom, everyone who donates candles does so with the understanding that they will be used for common purposes. No one takes care to observe this in our times, and fortunate is the one who is careful about this. The Havdalah candle has no sanctity (there).

Our master the Beit Yosef wrote in section 15: Residents of a city who bought a Torah scroll and stipulated that if one of them leaves the city, the remaining residents will pay him his share, and the value of the scrolls increased; if one of them leaves, they only give him back what he originally paid. Thus are his words. And even though in any other partnership, if there was such a condition, they would need to pay him according to the current value, in this case, we say that presumably the intention was not to evaluate it at that time, but they stipulated a known amount according to what he had initially paid. For this reason, if the value had decreased, they would still need to pay him the original higher amount. However, there is another reason: the matter is uncertain regarding their intention, and since the scroll remains with them for certain, and he needs to extract money from them, they can say: "Bring proof that our intention was to pay according to the current value." According to this, even if the value had decreased, they only need to pay him according to the current value, because they can say the opposite: "Bring proof that our intention was to pay you according to the original value." And the burden of proof is on the one who wants to extract money from his fellow (Levush based on Maimonides' Responsa, Mishpatim, section 12). According to this, if the condition was that he would pay them the money and take the Torah scroll, he is considered the one in possession. And even if he later agreed to take the money and leave the Torah scroll with them, they are not considered in possession for this reason, since he has the right to remove them (Magen Avraham, subsection 23).

There are those who wrote that if one finds an item in the courtyard of a synagogue, he acquires it. We do not say that the courtyard acquires it for the consecrated property, because a courtyard acquires by virtue of being an extension of one's hand, and consecrated property has no hand (as cited there in the name of the Agudah). This requires further study, for we hold in Choshen Mishpat that consecrated properties of our times, whether for the poor, a synagogue, or a Torah scroll, are not considered consecrated in the full sense but rather as ordinary property—see there. However, Rav Hai Gaon’s opinion in the Book of Transactions concerning “speaking for the higher authorities is like handing over to a common person” is that our consecrations are treated like those of the Temple maintenance fund. We have brought his words in Choshen Mishpat at the end of Siman 66, see there. Nevertheless, the finder acquires it regardless, as it is a place frequented by the public, and the finder there acquires it as if it were his own, as I wrote in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 260, see there. (And it requires examination why the reason that consecrated property has no hand is necessary. This requires study.) The Rashba ruled in a responsum that someone who donates an item to the synagogue or another mitzvah can write his name on it. However, it is better that every mitzvah be performed by many rather than by one individual alone. An individual who obstructs and does not want others to have a part in the mitzvah will be punished (Sefer Chassidim). There are those who ruled that when selling mitzvot, if one person gives a little and another gives a lot, and the second person retracts, the first person is obligated to accept it according to the value he gave (Tzemach Tzedek). This is not the custom (Magen Avraham there). And even though it was so with consecrated property, as it is taught in the seventh chapter of Erchin, we do not learn charity from consecrated property (Pri Megadim).

We learn at the end of Berachot: Anyone who leaves the synagogue and enters the study hall to engage in Torah study merits and receives the presence of the Divine, as it is said: "They go from strength to strength, every one of them appears before God in Zion." Therefore, after the prayer, one should establish a fixed time to study Torah. One should not neglect this time even if he thinks he can earn a lot, and he should trust in God that He will give him his reward and he will not lose out because of the Torah. Whatever has been decreed for him to earn, he will earn. A person's initial judgment is only on matters of Torah (Sanhedrin 7a). And when a person is brought to judgment, they ask him: Did you conduct business with integrity? Did you set fixed times for Torah study (Shabbat 31a)? Even one who does not know how to study should go to the study hall, and the reward for the effort is in his hand. Alternatively, he should establish a place and study a little of what he knows, and reflect on his deeds to see and examine if there is any element of transgression, and he should refrain from it. Through the Torah, the fear of Heaven will enter his heart. The Torah is the tree of life. Without the Torah, there is nothing good in the world; everything else is vanity and striving after wind.

And even if he must go out for a very urgent matter, he should learn one verse or one halacha. And before he goes to the Beit Midrash, he can eat breakfast bread if he is accustomed to it, and it is good that he should get accustomed to it. Our Sages of blessed memory said that breakfast bread brings much health to the body. And they said (Bava Metzia 107b) that there are eighty-three diseases dependent on the gallbladder, and all of them are nullified by breakfast bread. And thirteen things are said about breakfast bread: it saves from the sun, and from the cold..., and sixty runners run and do not reach a man who eats breakfast bread. And the Rabbis said: Rise early and eat in the summer because of the heat, and in the winter because of the cold. And it is written: "And you shall serve the Lord your God" - this refers to the recitation of Shema and prayer, "and He will bless your bread and your water" - this refers to bread with salt and a jug of water. From then on: "And I will remove illness from your midst." (And regarding what they said that breakfast bread is only from grain that is distant from habitation..., the Magen Avraham wrote well that someone heard and erred, for it refers to "pota" in Shabbat 66b. He erred in saying it about "pita," see there. Thus it is explicitly in Shabbat there.)

Afterwards, he should go to his work. For any Torah that is not accompanied by work will ultimately become null and lead to sin, because poverty causes a person to lose his reason and his awareness of his Creator. And one who has a craft, this is a good thing. And so our sages of blessed memory said in Kiddushin (29a) that a person is obligated to teach his son a craft, and anyone who does not teach him a craft - it is as if he teaches him to be a robber. And many err in this, saying that a craft is something disgraceful, for many Tannaim and Amoraim were craftsmen. And it is stated in Midrash Rabbah Bereshit (Parashah 74): Work is more beloved than the merit of the fathers, for the merit of the fathers saved wealth, and work saved lives, as it is said: "Had not the God of my father, the God of Abraham... you would have sent me away empty-handed. God saw my affliction and the labor of my hands and rebuked you last night." Meaning: Laban did not kill Jacob when he met him. And it is a great virtue for one who earns his livelihood from the work of his hands, as it is said: "When you eat the labor of your hands, you shall be happy, and it shall be well with you." You shall be happy in this world, and it shall be well with you in the world to come, which is entirely good.

Nevertheless, one should not make his work primary and his Torah study secondary. Rather, he should make his Torah study fixed and his work temporary, and both will be sustained in his hands. It seems to me that this applies to a Torah scholar whose main occupation is Torah study, as explained in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 246. But for an ordinary householder, this doesn't apply. For an ordinary householder, there is no obligation other than to establish fixed times for Torah study, and it is those times that they will be questioned about on the Day of Judgment: "Did you establish fixed times for Torah study?" For a Torah scholar whose main occupation is Torah study, it is not relevant to ask "Did you establish fixed times?" since he is obligated to study continually, day and night, except for what is necessary for his livelihood, as I have explained in Yoreh De'ah there.

"Conducting business with integrity" – the intent is not merely to avoid theft, robbery, or using false measures and weights; for these actions are not included in this category, as anyone who does so is a complete evildoer. It is forbidden to steal, rob, or defraud, whether from a Jew or a non-Jew. According to the Torah, one transgresses the prohibition of theft and robbery of a non-Jew just as one does with a Jew, as Rambam writes in the first chapter of Hilchot Geneivah, and as stated in the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, Choshen Mishpat, Siman 348. Rather, the intent is that one's "yes" should be just, and one's "no" should be just. When one says that a certain merchandise costs a certain amount and that it is good, one should not lie even slightly. One's business dealings should be conducted peacefully and one's speech should be gentle, without shouting, insulting, or anger. Ultimately, this leads to one's business being reputable, one's livelihood being readily available, and everyone trusting in them. And one who trusts in God will be surrounded by kindness.

Within the scope of business dealings with faith, one should not take an oath, neither a light oath nor a severe oath, until he becomes known to all as reliable by his word alone. He must be very careful not to mention the name of Heaven in vain, for wherever the mention of the name is common without cause – death is common. He should be careful not to swear even truthfully. And Yannai the king had a thousand cities, and they were all destroyed because of the sin of truthful oaths, as they were very accustomed to it (Midrash Eicha). He should be careful not to enter a partnership with an Arab, lest he be obligated to take an oath and swear by his oath, thereby transgressing "it shall not be heard upon your mouth." There are those who are lenient in this time because they do not swear by the stars; for their intention is to the Creator of heaven and earth, but they associate the name of Heaven with something else. And we do not find that this falls under "do not place a stumbling block before the blind," for they are not commanded regarding association in terms of an oath. And to engage in business dealings with them without partnership – according to everyone, it is permitted outside of their festival days. These laws are explained in Yoreh De'ah, sections 147 and 148, see there.

People's temperaments and traits differ from one another. Some are quick-tempered, and some are soft-hearted. Some are arrogant, and some are humble. Some are cruel, and some are compassionate. Some are stingy, and some are generous. The proper path is to hold to the middle way, for the extremes are not good. Only in the case of arrogance is it appropriate to distance oneself to the utmost extreme, for it is very loathsome. And this is what we have learned in Pirkei Avot: "Be exceedingly humble." And a person should not say: "What can I do since this is my nature?" For a person is obligated by their intellect to overcome their nature, and this is the entire duty of a Jewish person. The sages said: "A person should always incite the good inclination against the evil inclination." And it is written: "And you shall walk in His ways" – just as He is merciful, so you should be merciful; just as He is gracious, so you should be gracious. One should train their nature according to the way of the Torah and the commandments. Increase in silence, and speak only words of Torah and words of commandments, and in matters of business and necessary things.

There is a positive commandment to cleave to sages and their disciples in order to learn from their deeds. Concerning this, it is said: "And to Him you shall cleave," for whoever cleaves to sages is as if they cleave to the Divine Presence. Therefore, a person must endeavor to marry the daughter of a sage, marry his daughter to a sage, eat and drink with a sage, and engage in business with a sage (Ketubot 111b). Thus, it is said in Avot: "Let your house be a meeting place for sages, sit in the dust of their feet, and drink their words thirstily."

It is a mitzvah to love each Jew as oneself, as it is said: "Love your neighbor as yourself." Therefore, one must speak well of him and care for his property, just as one desires respect for oneself and cares for one's own property. And one who attains honor through the degradation of his fellow has no share in the World to Come (Maimonides, Laws of Character Traits, Chapter Six). However, the intention is not to love him as one's own soul and to share one's possessions with him, for this is not written at all in this context. For this verse is written in the context of the prohibitions against "You shall not go about as a talebearer," "You shall not hate," "You shall not take vengeance nor bear a grudge"—from this, we learn that the commandment is not to harm him, and in matters that do not cause monetary loss (this seems to me). And a wicked person who does not accept reproof—it is a mitzvah to hate him. About him, David said: "Do I not hate those who hate you, O Lord" (Maimonides' Glosses there). (And the Ari wrote to accept before prayer the positive commandment of "Love your neighbor as yourself.")

Loving the convert (in ancient times) who has come and entered under the wings of the Divine Presence involves two positive commandments: one because he is included in "friends," and one because he is a convert, as it is stated: "And you shall love the convert." And anyone who hates even one Jew transgresses a negative commandment, as it is stated: "You shall not hate your brother in your heart." There is no flogging for this prohibition since it does not involve an action. And when a man sins against another man, he should not harbor hatred and remain silent; rather, he should say to him: "Why did you do such and such to me?" This is what is meant by (the verse): "You shall surely rebuke your fellow." And if the offender repents and asks for forgiveness, one must forgive him. One should not be cruel, as it is stated: "And Abraham prayed to God..." Even though Abimelech wronged him without cause, Abraham nonetheless forgave him and even prayed for him. Therefore, we, as his descendants, must adhere to the traits of our forefather.

One who sees his fellow sinning, or going on a bad path, it is a mitzvah to return him to the right path, and to inform him that he is sinning, as it is said: "You shall surely rebuke your fellow." One must rebuke him privately, and speak to him gently and with a soft language. If he accepts it from him, it is good; and if not, he should rebuke him a second and third time. And thus, he is always obligated to rebuke him until he scolds him (Sefer Mitzvot Gadol and Rabbi Yosef in Arakhin 17b). And Rambam in the sixth chapter of De'ot ruled until striking (like Rav there). And anyone who can protest but does not protest is held accountable for those he could have protested against. And even if he is doubtful whether they will accept his words, he must rebuke them. But if he knows for certain that they will not accept his words, he is exempt from rebuking them, and it is better that he remains silent. And this is the language of the Sefer Mitzvot Gadol, positive commandment 11: And if it is clear to the rebuker that they will not accept from him, and the transgressors are inadvertent, it is better for him to remain silent, as we say (Beitzah 30a)... "Leave Israel alone, it is better that they be inadvertent..." But if the transgressors are intentional, and it is clear to him that they will not accept, although he is exempt from punishment... nevertheless, from the positive commandment of "You shall surely rebuke," he is not exempt... And I say that even with intentional sinners, one should remain silent, as it is said in Yevamot (65b): Just as it is a mitzvah for a person to say something that will be heeded, so it is a mitzvah not to say something that will not be heeded, as it is said: "Do not rebuke a scoffer lest he hate you." Thus far is the language of the Sefer Mitzvot Gadol, and the first opinion is that of Rabbeinu Eliezer of Metz in Sefer Yereim. All the more so now, due to our many sins, heresy has increased and rebuke is not applicable at all. And it is not appropriate to argue with a Jewish heretic who has become even more heretical, as our sages said in Sanhedrin (38b).

One who rebukes his fellow should not speak to him harshly to the point of embarrassing him, as it is said: "and do not bear sin because of him." Thus the Sages said: Can you rebuke him and his face changes [from shame]? The verse teaches: "and do not bear sin because of him" – from here we learn that it is forbidden to shame a fellow Jew, and all the more so in public. And although one does not receive lashes for this prohibition, it is a grave sin. The Sages said (Sanhedrin 107a): One who whitens the face of his fellow in public has no share in the World to Come. Therefore, one must be careful not to embarrass a person in public, whether they are great or small, and not to call them by a name they are ashamed of, even if they are accustomed to it (Bava Metzia 58b). For this sin, people descend to Gehenna and do not ascend (ibid).

In what context were these words said? In matters between a person and his fellow. But in matters concerning Heaven, if he does not repent in private, he is shamed publicly, and he is exposed and insulted to his face, and he is degraded and cursed until he returns to the proper path, as all the prophets did in Israel.

And someone whose friend sinned against him, and he did not want to rebuke him or speak to him at all because the sinner was extremely ignorant or his mind was confused, and he forgave him in his heart and did not bear a grudge against him nor rebuke him – this is considered an act of piety. The Torah only insists against bearing a grudge. So wrote the Rambam there.

A person is obligated to be cautious with orphans and widows because their spirits are low and their souls are depressed. Even if they are wealthy, even if they are the widow or orphan of a rich man, we are warned about them, as it is written: "You shall not afflict any widow or orphan." One should speak to them gently and treat them with respect. One should not cause them physical pain through labor or distress their hearts with harsh words, and one should be more concerned about their property than one's own. Anyone who causes them pain or angers them, or distresses their hearts, or oppresses them, or causes them to lose their property, transgresses a negative commandment. How much more so does this apply to someone who strikes or curses them. Although this prohibition does not carry the punishment of lashes, its punishment is explicitly mentioned in the Torah: "My wrath will be kindled, and I will kill you with the sword." It is a covenant with them that whenever they cry out, they will be answered, as it is said: "I will surely hear their cry." 

To what does this apply? When one torments them for one's own purposes. However, if one afflicts them in order to teach them Torah or a trade, or to guide them on the right path, it is permitted. Nevertheless, one should still manage them in this context with gentleness and compassion. This applies equally to an orphan from the father and an orphan from the mother. Until when are they called "orphans" in this regard? Until they no longer need an adult to rely on and care for them, but can manage all their needs by themselves like adults (Rambam, ibid.).

The Rambam wrote in Chapter Seven of De'ot: A talebearer about his friend transgresses a negative commandment, as it says: "You shall not go about as a talebearer among your people." And even though one does not receive lashes for this transgression, it is a great sin and causes the death of many souls in Israel. Therefore, it is juxtaposed to "You shall not stand by the blood of your neighbor" – go forth and learn what happened to Doeg the Edomite. What is a talebearer? One who carries words and goes from this one to that one, saying "So-and-so said such-and-such, and I heard such-and-such about so-and-so." Even though he speaks the truth, he destroys the world. And there is a sin even greater than this, which is included in this prohibition, and that is "lashon hara" (evil speech), which is speaking derogatorily about one's fellow even though he speaks the truth. But one who speaks falsehood is called "one who spreads a bad name about his fellow." But a "ba'al lashon hara" (master of evil speech) is one who sits and says, "So-and-so did such-and-such, and such-and-such were his ancestors, and I heard such-and-such about him," and says things of disgrace – about this it is said: "May the Lord cut off all flattering lips." Thus far are his words. And according to the Rambam, lashon hara is more severe than talebearing, and according to the Ra'avad in his critiques, the opposite is true; see there. And in the Jerusalem Talmud, it is said that it is permitted to speak lashon hara about those who cause disputes, and it is derived from the incident of Zadok and Bathsheba in the rebellion of Adonijah (Sefer Mitzvot Gadol). All the more so about those who are irreverent towards the Torah.

Our sages of blessed memory said that lashon hara (evil speech) is equivalent to three major transgressions: idolatry, forbidden sexual relations, and bloodshed (Arakhin 16b). It is as if one denies the fundamental principles of faith (ibid.). Lashon hara kills three people: the one who speaks it, the one who accepts it, and the one about whom it is spoken; and the one who accepts it is worse than the one who speaks it. However, if one sees clear evidence, it is appropriate to be cautious about it (Hagahot Maimoniyot, letter 4, and this is also implied in the Gemara). 

There are things that are considered "dust of lashon hara," not full-fledged lashon hara. How so? For example, when one says, "Who will tell so-and-so to remain as he is now," or when one says, "Be silent about so-and-so; I do not want to disclose what happened and what was," and similar things. Anyone who speaks the praises of his fellow in the presence of his enemies is engaging in "dust of lashon hara," because this causes them to speak ill of him. Similarly, one who speaks lashon hara in a joking and frivolous manner, without the intention of actual lashon hara, about this Solomon said: "Like a madman who casts firebrands... and says, 'I am only joking...'" – in the end, it is still lashon hara, and its sin is very great. 

Also, one who speaks lashon hara deceitfully, as if speaking innocently as though he does not know, but the Lord examines hearts, and before Him, the impurity of his thoughts is significant. (According to Rashbam, one should not praise his fellow even not in the presence of his enemies, and this is considered excessive.)

There is no difference between Lashon Hara (slanderous speech), whether it was said in the presence of the person or not, if these words were heard from one person to another and caused harm to someone's body or property, or even just caused them distress or fear without any damage – this is considered Lashon Hara. And if these words were said in the presence of three people – the matter is already known and public. If one of the three recounts the matter again, it is not considered Lashon Hara, provided they do not intend to spread the rumor further. All these individuals are considered speakers of Lashon Hara, and it is forbidden to live in their neighborhood, and certainly to sit with them and listen to their words. The decree against our ancestors in the desert was sealed solely because of Lashon Hara. So wrote the Rambam there. And what he wrote, that when it is said in the presence of three it is no longer Lashon Hara – this is in general. But if the speaker in the presence of the three said, "Do not recount these words I have said," and one of them tells the matter – it is considered Lashon Hara (Hagahot Maimoniot). And in the first chapter of Yoma (4a), it is said: From where do we derive that if one tells something to another, it is under the prohibition of "do not say" until he tells him "go and say"? It is derived from the verse: "From the Tent of Meeting to say." Meaning: "Go and tell them."

It is written: "You shall not take vengeance nor bear a grudge against the children of your people." We learn that one who takes vengeance against his fellow transgresses a negative commandment, and similarly one who bears a grudge. And although there is no flogging for this transgression because it involves no action, it is nevertheless a very bad trait. Rather, it is fitting for a person to rise above their emotions regarding all worldly matters, for all worldly matters are considered vanity and emptiness by those who understand, and they are not worth taking vengeance over. 

How is vengeance defined? If one's fellow said to him, "Lend me your axe," and he did not lend it, and the next day the one who refused needed to borrow from his fellow and his fellow said, "I will not lend to you just as you did not lend to me" — this is vengeance, and it transgresses a negative commandment. Rather, one should lend with a complete heart and not mention the matter at all. And concerning this, David said: "If I have repaid those who did good to me with evil..."

And what is bearing a grudge? If one lends to his fellow but says, "I am not like you who did not want to lend to me; I am lending to you" — this too transgresses the negative commandment, for he is bearing the grudge, and this can lead to vengeance. Rather, one should erase the matter from their heart completely. The Torah guides us towards correct, beautiful, and clear traits, and not to follow the counsel of the evil inclination that confuses the world. Rather, one should follow the way of the Torah, about which it is said: "And all its paths are peace."

There are many good and bad traits, and it is impossible to list them all. One who wants to follow the path of the Torah should turn to the good traits and not the bad ones, and should forgo his own inclinations. Whoever overcomes his own traits will have all his transgressions forgiven. Those who are insulted but do not insult in return are the ones about whom it is said, "and His lovers are like the sun going forth in its might." When a person asks for advice, one should give him proper advice and not lead him astray from the straight path in the matter for which he is seeking counsel. Regarding this, it is said, "and before a blind person…" And it is stated in the Midrash: If a person does not have a commandment that is fixed for generations, what benefit does he have?

It is forbidden to eat and drink in a gluttonous and drunken manner, as it is said: "This our son is a glutton and a drunkard." The Rambam counts this as a full negative commandment in the enumeration of the mitzvot, number 195. Instead, one should eat with proper conduct, and not eat in the market or while standing. This will be further explained in Siman 170, with the help of Heaven.

The fourth hour from the time one rises from bed is the mealtime for everyone. However, if he is a Torah scholar and engaged in his studies, so as not to interrupt his learning, he may wait until the sixth hour and eat at the beginning or the end of it, as I have written in Choshen Mishpat, Section 5, Paragraph 11. See there. But he should not delay more than this, as it is like throwing a stone into a flask if he does not taste anything in the morning. (See Magen Avraham that one should relieve oneself before the meal. If he cannot – he should walk four times ten cubits, or ten times four cubits. And not to prepare a dish from one day to the next, see there. And people are not careful with this. And to prepare something to clean the hands when touching milk, see there.)

The sages instituted washing the hands with water when one wishes to eat bread. As it is taught in Chagigah (17b): one washes hands for non-sacred food (chullin), for tithe (ma'aser), and for terumah. And the Gemara explains: "For chullin" – for eating, "and for terumah" – even for touching, because ordinary hands are considered second-degree impurity, and a second-degree impurity causes a third-degree impurity in terumah. They decreed washing the hands for eating chullin because of the concern for terumah (Chullin 106a), for if people are not accustomed to washing their hands for chullin, they might also neglect washing hands for terumah. They did not impose the stringency for touching chullin, as it is sufficient if we accustom ourselves to washing for eating chullin. And even though we do not have terumah in this time, nevertheless, the Temple will soon be rebuilt, and we will have terumah, and we will know to be careful with it (Levush).

The truth is that they did not decree this solely for this reason. Rather, we derive this from the verse "and you shall sanctify yourselves" – this refers to the first waters (Berachot, end of chapter eight). The concept of sanctity is as it is stated in Sotah (4b): Anyone who eats bread without wiping their hands – it is as if they eat impure bread, as it is said: "And the Lord said: Thus shall the children of Israel eat their bread impure..." For without wiping the hands, the hands are considered repulsive, and something repulsive is akin to impurity, as it is written: "Thus..." – meaning that something repulsive is called impurity (Rashi). And this is the concept of sanctity, the opposite of impurity, for this is the will of the Holy One, Blessed be He, that we conduct ourselves with cleanliness, sanctity, and purity, for cleanliness leads to purity, and purity leads to separation and sanctity. And even though they said this regarding wiping the hands, in any case it is obvious that for the main act of washing, it certainly would be like impure bread, because hands are busy. Additionally, there is a support for washing hands from the Torah, from the verse "and his hands he did not wash with water," as it is stated in Chullin there. (And with this, it is understood what is written there: the washing of hands is because of the concern for Terumah, and also because it is a mitzvah to heed the words of the Sages. And Tosafot explained it as a matter of cleanliness, see there – and it is not understood at all. But according to what I have written, it fits well, for the words of the Sages are derived from "and you shall sanctify yourselves," and we can say that this is also the intention of Tosafot. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

One must be very careful with the washing of hands, and anyone who is negligent with the washing of hands will come to poverty (Shabbat 62b) and be uprooted from the world (Sotah 4b). In the fifth chapter of Tractate Eduyot, it is taught that there was someone who was negligent with the washing of hands, and they cursed him, and he died from the curse. Anyone who transgresses the words of the Sages is liable to death. The obligation of washing hands was only imposed for bread upon which the blessing "Hamotzi" is recited, even if there is no known impurity. One recites the blessing: "Who has sanctified us... concerning the washing of hands," because since the Sages instituted this, it is appropriate to say "and commanded us" based on the verse "You shall not deviate" (Deuteronomy 17:11). It is also appropriate to say "Who has sanctified us," since this is based on the verse "and you shall sanctify yourselves" (Leviticus 11:44). However, for bread that does not require the blessing "Hamotzi," such as rolls or pastry (pat haba'ah b'kisnin), which are blessed with "Mezonot," hand washing is not required. If one establishes a meal on them and recites "Hamotzi," then hand washing with a blessing is required. There are those who are uncertain about this, but there is no doubt. The Rashba wrote this in "Torat HaBayit," and this is also clarified in the language of the Rambam at the beginning of the sixth chapter of Hilchot Berachot, where he wrote: "Anyone who eats bread upon which 'Hamotzi' is recited requires the washing of hands." This is also agreed upon by the commentators on the Shulchan Aruch (Taz and Magen Avraham, subsection 2), and this is how it should be instructed: to wash hands with a blessing. Why was this not instituted for these breads? Because the institution was only for a fixed meal, which involves "Hamotzi" and Birkat Hamazon, where sanctity is evident. But not for food blessed with "Mezonot," which is eaten casually and has a short after-blessing, where sanctity is not as evident. Therefore, for less than an olive's volume (kazayit), hand washing is not required, because it does not involve Birkat Hamazon. There are those who say that even for less than an egg's volume (kebeitza), hand washing is not required, because all food impurity is considered with an egg's volume. Therefore, one should wash hands without a blessing. However, most of our sages do not hold this view, because since Birkat Hamazon and "Hamotzi" are required, the Sages did not make a distinction, and one should wash hands with a blessing (this is implied in Magen Avraham, subsection 3). But some say this applies only to Terumah (Gra, subsection 6). When in doubt about blessings, one should be lenient. There are those who say that even for less than an olive's volume, one should wash without a blessing (Eliyah Rabbah, subsection 4), because one needs to bless "Hamotzi." However, it seems that this is not the practice in the world, and for less than an olive's volume, hand washing is not required. (As Magen Avraham wrote in subsection 4, that the entirety of subsection 3 in Shulchan Aruch is from a mistaken manuscript, and there is no disagreement on this matter.)

We learn in Pesachim (115a): Anything that is dipped in liquid requires washing of hands. Some have explained the reason: Just as they decreed concerning bread because of the concern for terumah, where a secondary level of impurity can create a tertiary level in terumah, and with liquids we hold that anything that disqualifies terumah can render liquids as a primary level of impurity even in non-sacred food; if so, when one does not wash his hands, the hands will render the liquids a primary level of impurity, and the liquids will render the food impure, as a primary level makes a secondary level in non-sacred food (Tosafot of Rabbi Yitzchak in Berachot, Chapter 8). According to this, a blessing should be required as with bread. However, Tosafot wrote in Pesachim there that this washing is not due to sanctity and cleanliness like with bread, but so that the liquids do not become impure and become forbidden to drink, thereby disqualifying the person... Therefore, it seems that one should not recite a blessing on this washing, since there is no commandment here to heed the words of the Sages... Thus are their words. Meaning: In truth, regarding impurity and purity, it does not apply to us, for are we careful about impurity? The primary obligation of washing hands is from "and you shall sanctify yourselves," which applies only to bread in a fixed meal as I have written. The rationale of concern for terumah is an additional reason, and since in this case the obligation of "and you shall sanctify yourselves" does not apply, a blessing is not appropriate. Many of the early authorities hold this view. According to this opinion, there is no obligation at all in our times to wash hands for dipping in liquid, and this was only in ancient times when they ate in a state of purity. The Tur explicitly wrote this later in Siman 473 in the name of Rabbi Meir of Rothenburg. For this reason, we are lenient nowadays in this matter. (The Levush wrote according to this opinion that it is only for cleanliness. His words are puzzling, for Tosafot explicitly wrote that it is not for cleanliness, as the Tur wrote in Siman 473 that nowadays this rule does not exist, see there. The words of Rabbeinu Yerucham in the Beit Yosef misled the Levush, as he wrote: "There are those who explain that it is only for cleanliness," see there. It is a printing error, and it should say: "that it is not for cleanliness." It is known that the books of Rabbeinu Yerucham are full of errors, and in the glosses of the Levush the matters are correct, see there. Also in Taz, Section 6, there is this error of Rabbeinu Yerucham.)

When one is required to wash for dipping in a liquid — even if his hands do not touch the part of the food that is wet; for we are concerned that they might touch, even if only the tip of the vegetable or the tip of the fruit is dipped. For any type of dipping in a liquid, one should wash without a blessing, due to the differing opinions that have been explained. There are some of the great authorities who have extensively explained that the main opinion follows the first view, which is the opinion of the Geonim and the Rambam, and one should make a blessing (see Gra, subsection 12). However, this is not the customary practice, for even those who are careful with dipping in a liquid, we have never heard them make the blessing "on the washing of the hands." And in cases of doubt with blessings, we are lenient, especially in a matter that most people are not careful about at all.

"Liquids" are only seven liquids and no more, and they are: wine, honey, oil, milk, dew, blood, and water. And your mnemonic is: י"ד שח"ט ד"ם (yod-shin-chet-tav dalet-mem). But other types of moisture, such as fat, sweat, and fruit juices, are not included in "liquids," for only these seven liquids can render something susceptible to impurity and can themselves become impure, as it is taught in the Mishnah in Tractate Machshirin, Chapter Six (Mishnah 4). And these liquids, as long as they are moist enough to make something else moist, are called "moist." But less than this amount, they are considered dry and do not require washing. And know that honey refers only to the honey of bees as we have, but date honey is considered fruit juice and not a liquid. Similarly, hornet and wasp honey are not considered liquids. And "blood" that we mentioned is not relevant here at all, since it is forbidden to eat blood. And the blood of fish and locusts is not considered a liquid, but since in Machshirin it is considered one, the poskim (decisors) also considered it here, following the language of the Mishnah there. And it is obvious that vinegar is included in wine, and if it is made from water, it is included in water. Similarly, our beer is included in water, as is distilled wine. Even strong spirits called "spirit" are included in water. I have heard from someone who wants to say that sweat generally is included, but it is not so, for a lot of water enters them. And similarly, with all the beverages found in cellars, their immersion in a liquid is relevant.

The one who drinks beverages does not need to wash his hands, since drinking is done by means of a vessel. And even if he dips his finger into the beverage and sucks it, he does not need to wash his hands (Magen Avraham, subsection 5, in the name of Radbaz), because they did not decree on something that people do not normally do. And for this reason, even if one dips food into a liquid in a manner that people do not normally do, he does not need to wash his hands, because his intention is nullified by that of everyone else (there). However, for something that people normally dip into a liquid, even if he dips it using a fork or spoon, he must wash his hands, because the Sages did not differentiate (Be'er Heitev, subsection 12, in the name of Knesset HaGedolah). Nevertheless, it is certain that for something that is normally eaten with a spoon, like soup, or with a fork, like fish and meat, he does not need to wash his hands, as this is considered like drinking. And those who soak fruits in water to clean them from dirt or other impurities, and eat them while the water is still moist on them, must wash their hands (Shaarei Teshuvah, subsection 4). But if they dry them, even if there is still some moisture on them, they do not need to wash their hands. (And what the Taz wrote in subsection 10 regarding honey requires further investigation.)

The liquid inside eggs is considered like fruit juice. Similarly, the fat of animals and birds, and congealed water, according to the Tosefta in Taharot, are not considered a liquid (as brought by the Rash in the third chapter of Taharot, Mishnah 2). If they liquefy again, they become a liquid (there). Snow is not considered a liquid; if one intended it to be used as a liquid, it becomes a liquid (Niddah 17a). It seems that this is the case when it has not melted, but once it melts, it becomes regular water. The Rambam writes in the first chapter of Hilchot Tum'at Ochlin, Law 19: Congealed oil is neither food nor a liquid. If one considers it as a solid or a liquid when congealed, his intention is disregarded. Congealed milk is neither food nor a liquid. If one considers it as a liquid, his intention is disregarded. See there. The same applies to wine and honey; when they liquefy, they revert to being liquids. Milk in the stomach or udder is not a liquid (there). From this, we learn that butter is not a liquid unless it has melted. Eating something with butter does not require hand washing, even if he spread it with his hands. There is no difference in the congealed state, whether it congealed through cooking or cold. However, if it only thickened slightly and is still pourable and moist enough to make other things moist, it is considered a liquid, and hand washing is required (Magen Avraham, Section 7).

Various types of confections that are fried in honey, such as Aingimatz, Teiglach, and Piyoreskes, and similar items, there are those who say that they are not considered a liquid. As it is taught in the Tosefta of Taharot: Honey that drips from the comb is subject to impurity as a liquid. If one intends it for food, it is subject to impurity as food. Therefore, honey confections, since they are intended for eating, are not called "liquid" (Magen Avraham). And there are those who say this is a mistake, that this applies to honey that drips by itself and one intends it at the time of dripping. But honey that is extracted from the comb, it is taught there that it is subject to impurity as a liquid. And it does not help to intend it for food, as intention does not override action. And even though they are fried and this is an action that overrides intention – this applies to utensils, but with food, until it becomes unfit for a dog to eat (Taz, subsection 7). In my humble opinion, even though it is true according to the latter opinion, nevertheless, the main ruling is according to the first opinion, for certainly due to the essence of honey it is considered a liquid. But it is stated in Shabbat (144b) that a liquid that comes to food is considered food. And in Yoma (80b): Any food preparation is considered food, see there. And here indeed it comes to food, to prepare the food, and it does not require washing. And there is no distinction to say: because there it did not previously have the status of "liquid" before it came to the food, and therefore when it came to the food it became food. But here it already had the status of "liquid" before. For this is not so, for here too we say: now, when we obligate washing because of the liquids – it has already mixed with the food and prepared the food. And the obligation is only if now one puts a food item into a liquid. (And what the Magen Avraham wrote at the end of subsection 7, that if they solidify and then melt again, they are not considered liquids, see there – this is the opinion of Tosafot. But Rambam did not rule this way as I wrote.)

And there is a matter of doubt regarding types of preserves where the concern is for the liquid, such as when fruits are squeezed, and the liquid is cooked with syrup which is called "sugar." They are all fruit juices, and it is customary to mix a little water during the cooking process. Similarly, even when the fruits are cooked whole, like our types of compotes which contain a lot of liquid, the main component is the syrup, with only a little water mixed in. Also, all types of preserves we now make with syrup and not with honey, and they are fruit juices with a little water mixed in, do they require washing of hands? It appears they do not require washing, because the majority are fruit juices compared to the water – the water is nullified in relation to the fruit juices. And this is explicitly stated in Bekhorot (22a) in the discussion of one who buys fish brine, see there. And regarding what we learned in Makhshirin (Chapter 6, Mishnah 3) that pure brine into which any amount of water fell becomes impure, they explained in Bekhorot there (23b) that it was already half and half, see there. And the words of Maimonides in Chapter Sixteen of the Laws of Impurity of Foods, Law 4, where he explained the Mishnah literally – they have already questioned him on this, see there. However, the ruling is as I have written, and there is no need to wash hands for our preserves unless they were cooked in honey. And this is the main ruling.

Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote in section 5: Roasted meat, there is an opinion that even if the liquid from the meat is still on it, it is treated like fruit. And a dish of grains that are dry – it is treated like fruit. His words mean that it refers to roasted meat that is roasted on a spit over a fire, and therefore the liquid that comes out from the meat itself is treated like fruit juice. And even though it was certainly washed with water, nevertheless it is assumed that it dried from the water immediately before being cooked. And a dish of grains that are dry – it is obvious that it does not require hand washing. And some say that even if there is moisture on the meat or grains, they do not require hand washing, because the decree was only on something that is dipped in a liquid, not on food that has liquid on it (Yam Shel Shlomo, chapter 8 of Chullin, section 18), since once it is cooked, it is called "food" (Magen Avraham, subsection 10, in the name of Maharit). And some disagree, for the Rashba wrote (in Torat HaBayit) that fruits, meat, and fish that have moisture on them, or are dipped in liquid, require hand washing (Taz, subsection 9). This is not evidence, for this is when it is not cooked, but when it is cooked, it is called "food". And so it appears in Rashi, Berachot (52a, s.v. "ein keli"), who wrote: liquids of a cooked dish that moisten the hands – are not considered liquids but rather food. And what Magen Avraham wrote in subsection 10 that this is about its own liquid, see there – I do not know from where we say this. But from the Mishnah at the beginning of the third chapter of Taharot, it is clear that it is considered liquid, see there. But according to what Yam Shel Shlomo wrote, although it receives impurity, nevertheless they did not decree about this. Understand and you will find ease.

One who washes his hands for fruit – this is considered arrogance, as it shows that he is stricter than the Sages. The Sages only decreed washing hands for bread because the tithing of fruit is rabbinic. And even if it were from the Torah, as it appears from the words of Rambam in the first chapter of Terumot, nevertheless, they are eaten casually, and the decree was only for regular meals as I have written. This specifically applies when one washes them as an obligation. But if he washes them merely for cleanliness, and particularly if he knows his hands are not clean – it is acceptable. Similarly, one who drinks does not need to wash even one hand, because he always drinks using a vessel and there was no decree in this case. And even if he washes his hands in river water – this is incidental, and they did not decree in such a case (see Magen Avraham, subsection 11). Likewise, when cooking dough types in water – they do not require washing, because they are eaten with a spoon (Taz, subsection 9). And it seems to me that even if he eats them with his hands, since it is an uncommon matter – the Rabbis did not decree on it. And when frying dough in butter that is eaten with hands, if there is wet butter on them which is enough to make another surface wet – washing is required. If not – washing is not required. And if they were fried in fat in any manner, washing hands is not required, as these are fruit juices (Taz there). Similarly, meat from soup is not typically eaten except with a fork, and washing is not required. Likewise, potatoes in a dish, when eaten with melted butter, require washing hands.

He washed his hands for something that is dipped in a liquid, and afterwards he decided to eat bread; or he washed his hands not for eating at all, such as if they were dirty, and after washing and drying them he decided to eat bread – this depends on the opinions that will be explained in Siman 159 whether intention is required for washing hands for eating bread or not. For if intention is required – he certainly needs to wash again with a blessing. And if intention is not required – he does not need to wash again at all, unless he had a distraction from the previous washing. The opinion of our Rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch later, tends towards not requiring intention, and therefore here he should wash without a blessing. It turns out that his eating now is without a blessing, for initially he certainly did not bless, and also now he will not bless. And it cannot be said that he should now bless for the previous washing, for we hold that even after drying, one blesses "Al Netilat Yadayim" – it is impossible to say this, for this applies to a washing intended for bread. But here, in the first washing, he did not intend for washing hands for bread (Magen Avraham, Small Paragraph 13), and therefore he does not bless at all. And blessings do not impede. And if he touched unclean places on his body in the middle of his meal – he should wash his hands again and bless "Al Netilat Yadayim." All the more so if he went to the restroom in the middle of the meal, he needs to wash again and bless "Al Netilat Yadayim."

At the end of the first chapter of Eruvin (17a), it is taught that in a military camp they are exempt from washing hands because it is a place of danger, and even if there is water within four mil, they do not need to go. The same applies to travelers in the desert or someone who is on the road in a dangerous place and has no water – they are exempt from washing hands. Similarly, someone who is in prison and has no water can eat without washing hands. And even though we find that Rabbi Akiva, when he was in prison, did not want to eat without washing hands (Eruvin 21b) – he was stringent upon himself, but by law, he was exempt. It seems that he does not need to wrap his hands in a cloth and eat, because since the Rabbis exempted him, he is completely exempt. However, there is an opinion that he needs to wrap his hands in a cloth (Eliyah Rabbah, Section 20, quoting Ma'adanei Yom Tov). But it does not seem so from the language of the Mishnah, because since it taught that they are exempt – it should have said they permitted it with a cloth, as in the Gemara, it is permitted with a cloth for those who eat Terumah (Chullin 107b). And it is stated in the Jerusalem Talmud there that just as they permitted it during their journey to the camp – so too on their return, see there.

It has already been explained that one must be very careful with the washing of hands, for neglecting it can lead to removal from the world and result in poverty. A sign for this is that the initial letters of "Al Netilat Yadayim" (on the washing of hands) spell "ani" (poor), meaning that it saves one from poverty (Levush). And even though the measure is a Revi'it (a quarter of a log), one should wash abundantly. As Rabbi Chanina said: "I used to use handfuls of water, and they gave me handfuls of goodness" (Shabbat 62b). This means that he poured a lot of water on his hands, and they gave him much wealth from the heavens. And those people who belittle and doubt the words of our sages, of blessed memory, will ultimately face destruction and have no share in the world to come. About them, the prophet cries out: "Woe to those who call evil good and good evil," for in the washing of hands there is great cleanliness. Nevertheless, due to the evil inclination of their corrupt nature, they despise this delicate mitzvah and eat with dirty hands. Woe to them and to their souls.

When one washes his hands, he should take the vessel in his right hand and transfer it to his left hand, and then he should wash his right hand first, because in all places, honor is given to the right side. There is also another reason for this (see Magen Avraham at the beginning of this section). And according to what we uphold, that for all commandments one recites the blessing before performing them, one should ideally recite the blessing "Al Netilat Yadayim" before washing the hands. Nevertheless, the custom is not like this, and we recite the blessing after the washing. And this is the primary ruling in practice, because in most cases, a person’s hands are not clean and it is impossible to recite the blessing at all. Therefore, even when occasionally the hands are clean, we do not differentiate. Moreover, even when one recites the blessing after washing, it is still considered before performing the act, because one blesses before rubbing the hands together, which is the way of people and is considered as before the completion of the commandment. Especially if one washes the first time with less than a revi’it (a specific measure of water), the hands are not purified until after the second pouring of water, as will be explained. And one blesses before the second pouring, which is considered before performing the act. And even if one completely blesses after the washing, since one blesses before drying the hands, it is considered before performing the act.
