For drying the hands is also essential, as they said at the beginning of Sotah, that anyone who eats without drying the hands is as if he eats impure bread.

Therefore, one must be careful to dry the hands well, and the main aspect of this law is due to the impurity of the water, as will be explained. When one washes the first time with a lot of water, the water is not impure, and similarly when one immerses them in a river. However, in any case, we have never seen anyone eat with wet hands, and it is unseemly. Therefore, drying the hands is also considered part of the mitzvah, and when one blesses before drying, it is considered "over la'asiyatan" (before performing the mitzvah). This is the common custom and should not be changed (and this resolves the precise wording of the Taz in subparagraph 12). If one forgot to bless before drying, one should bless afterward, just as with immersion where one blesses after immersing, as explained in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 200. There is an opinion that after drying one should not bless (Taz, subparagraph 12), like with "Hamotzi" where one does not bless after finishing the meal, as I wrote in Siman 167. But this is not comparable, because there it was appropriate to bless before "Hamotzi", and it was seen and then dismissed, so it does not return to be seen. This is not the case here, where in most washings it was not appropriate to bless beforehand, and it is considered a rejection from the outset, and we hold in the entire Shas that this is not considered a rejection. And so the great Acharonim agree that one should bless afterward (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 16, and Eliyah Rabba, subparagraph 23), and this is the main ruling. However, after the blessing of "Hamotzi" one does not bless "Al Netilat Yadayim" (there), because it is considered as if its time has already passed since one has begun another matter. (And one should not dry their hands with a robe or garment, as this causes forgetfulness. And the Birkei Yosef writes that if immediately after Birkat Hamazon they brought before him something that is dipped in a liquid, he does not need to wash his hands.)

One who immerses his hands may, according to the law, eat without drying them, as the hands have not become impure. And seemingly, even when one pours a quarter-log over his hands at once, the water has not become impure. Nevertheless, it is written that this is not the case, for drying is a rabbinic enactment, and they established it in every situation, except for immersion (Rashal, Bach, Taz, and Magen Avraham, subsection 18). Even for one who immerses, there is an element of repulsiveness if he finds it distasteful and he needs to dry them (there). However, our master the Beit Yosef in section 13 ruled that if one pours a quarter-log at once over both hands, or a quarter-log over each hand, it is considered as if he has immersed, see there. And the great later authorities did not rule this way, as I have written. How to bless upon immersion will be explained at the end of section 159.

One may only wash their hands using a complete vessel. We derive this from the laws of the red heifer, which require a vessel, as it is written: "living water shall be put into a vessel." Similarly, for the sanctification of the hands and feet, a vessel is also required, like the laver and similar items. Additionally, since a person's table is like an altar (end of Chagigah), and just as before the service of the altar one needed to sanctify their hands from the laver, so too before eating, one should sanctify their hands using a vessel. It is taught in the Mishnah (Yadayim 1:2): one may wash their hands with any kind of vessels, even with vessels made of dung, stone, or earth. Even though these are not considered vessels for the purposes of contracting impurity, they are still considered vessels, and what difference does it make if they can contract impurity or not?

And know that regarding a hole in a vessel, whether it invalidates it, and what size hole invalidates it – there is confusion among the decisors. Therefore, it is necessary to elucidate the law from its source. We learn in Chullin (107a): Rava said: A vessel that has a hole the size of "koness mashkeh" (that allows liquid to enter) – one may not use it for washing hands. And if we say the reason is because it loses its status as a "vessel" in terms of impurity, since with such a hole the vessel becomes pure, as it appears from the words of the Rambam in Chapter Six of Hilchot Berachot, Law 11, where he wrote: And vessels that were broken to the extent that they become pure from impurity – one may not use them for washing hands, because they are broken vessels. This is his language, and he did not mention "koness mashkeh" at all; and also in the law of the pipe, mentioned in the Gemara there with "koness mashkeh", which will be explained in section 29, and the Rambam wrote it there in Law 14 – he also omitted "koness mashkeh", see there. It seems clearly that he holds that the reason of Rava is because with this hole it becomes pure from impurity, as it is like a broken vessel. If so, this rule applies only to earthenware vessels specifically used for liquids, as Rava himself said in Shabbat (95b): There are five measures for earthenware vessels: if it has a hole the size of "koness mashkeh" – it is pure for sanctifying with the waters of purification, but it is still a vessel for the preparation of seeds…, see there. And the mention of "koness mashkeh" is because it is the first level of nullification of a vessel, as Rashi explained in Niddah (49a). He says there also that the measure for an earthenware vessel is "koness mashkeh", and Rashi explained that this is the smallest measure that nullifies it from being a vessel. This is his language. (And even though a "gistra" is like "motzi mashkeh" (that allows liquid to exit), this is initially a broken vessel, see there.)

According to this, this law applies specifically to earthenware vessels designated for liquids. However, if it is designated for food, the size of the hole that invalidates it is as large as an olive, as explained there. Similarly, if it is a wooden vessel, its measure is as large as a pomegranate, as stated in the Mishnah, Chapter 17 of Keilim. If it is a metal vessel, there are different measurements, as explained there in Chapter 14 and in the Rambam, Chapter 11 of Keilim. Rava relied on the measurements specified in the Mishnayot of Keilim, which are known to all, and he began with the first measurement as in Niddah. Even though he did not specifically mention earthenware vessels here, it is implied, as it is known that the measure of "koness mashkeh" (a hole that allows liquid to enter) applies only to earthenware vessels. This is what the Rambam wrote: if a vessel is broken in a manner that purifies it, it is invalid for washing hands. It seems to me that this is also the opinion of the Sefer Mitzvot Katan (Semak), which the Tur cited. His words are: The Semak wrote that if it is designated for olives, it retains the status of a "vessel" and it is permitted to use it for washing hands if it holds a revi'it (a specific measure), until it is perforated to the size of an olive. This is his language, which aligns exactly with the Rambam's view. The Tur objected to this with the following language: It is possible to differentiate that specifically regarding impurity, designation for olives is effective, but regarding washing hands, whose measure is "koness mashkeh," once it is perforated to this measure, it is no longer considered a vessel. This is his language. For the Tur, it was obvious that Rava's measure of "koness mashkeh" applied to all vessels, and therefore it is not related to impurity. But according to the Rambam's opinion, this depends on each other, and perforce, one must say as we explained with the help of Heaven.

However, the Sefer Mitzvot Gadol (SeMaG) in the laws of washing hands wrote: Rava said: A vessel that has a hole large enough for liquid to enter - one cannot use it for washing hands, as it no longer has the status of a "vessel". Even if the hole is above the level of a revi'it (a quarter-log). My teacher wrote that Rabbi Yitzchak used to practice this even with vessels made of metal, even though this measure was only mentioned with regard to earthenware vessels. This is his language. Similarly, the Tosafot wrote in Niddah: And even though throughout the entire discussion, the measure of a hole large enough for liquid to enter was mentioned only with regard to earthenware vessels... and not with wooden vessels, nevertheless, what Rava said in Chullin: A vessel that has a hole large enough for liquid to enter - one should be stringent with all vessels..., since he did not specify "earthenware vessel" but rather "vessel" in general. This is their language, and the intention is not merely a stringency but a fundamental aspect of the law. Their reasoning seems clear to me: for all vessels, when designated for water, the status of "vessel" is nullified if it has a hole large enough for liquid to enter. And indeed, even for earthenware vessels, the law is the same - when designated for olives, a hole large enough for an olive to pass through is required. Therefore, the reason wooden vessels require a hole large enough for a pomegranate to pass through is because they are generally used for that purpose. But when designated for water, a hole large enough for liquid to enter is sufficient. The proof for this is: we also learned there that for metal vessels, when designated for wine or oil, their purity is determined by having a hole through which wine or oil can drip, see there. Furthermore, according to the opinion of the Rambam and the Sefer Mitzvot Katan (SeMaK), how should we judge vessels made of earth... which do not become impure, as they cannot be broken for their purification from impurity, since they never become impure. Rather, it is certain that any vessel used for washing hands loses its status as a "vessel" if it has a hole large enough for liquid to enter. According to the Rambam and the SeMaK, we must also say this for these vessels, as they have no other measure. See section 11.

However, according to these two opinions, there is certainly no difference whether one takes the water from the vessel through its upper opening or through a hole, even if a quarter-log remains below the hole. Since the reasoning is that it is considered a broken vessel, in any case, it is prohibited to use it for hand washing. There is clear proof for this from the Sefer Mitzvot Gadol (SeMaG), who wrote the following: "If the vessel is punctured on its side less than the size that allows liquid to gather, and it holds a quarter-log below the hole, and the water comes through the hole to his hands, it is pure. However, if one takes from the water that passes outside the hole and falls through the edge of the vessel, it is invalid... for from the hole and onward, it does not have the status of a 'vessel.'" But below the hole, it has the status of a 'vessel,' since it was not punctured to the extent that allows liquid to gather. Until here is his language. It is explicitly stated that if the hole is as large as the size that allows liquid to gather, the entire vessel is invalid. And if it is less than that size, what is above the hole does not have the status of a 'vessel,' and what is below does have the status of a 'vessel,' and one must take water through the hole. According to the Rambam, it is obvious that this is the case, as he explicitly wrote that when a vessel is broken to the extent that it purifies, one cannot use it for hand washing, because they are considered broken vessels. Until here is his language. And it is obvious that with a broken vessel, it is invalid to use it for hand washing from any part of it. However, regarding a puncture less than the size that allows liquid to gather, the severity of the SeMaG is not found in the other halachic authorities.

However, the Rosh and the Tur have a different approach to this. For the Rosh in Chullin there writes: A vessel that was perforated and holds a quarter-log below the perforation—it is permissible to draw water through the perforation but not through its mouth, because above the perforation it is not considered a "vessel." Thus are his words. And this is the wording of the Tur: If it was perforated enough to admit liquid… it is nullified from the status of a "vessel." And one cannot draw water from it for washing hands, even if it holds a quarter-log from the perforation and below. And these words apply when one draws through its mouth above, for what is above the perforation is not considered a vessel, and consequently, the water does not come from the vessel. But if one draws water through the perforation—it is permissible, since it holds a quarter-log from the perforation and below. And it is written in the Smak… and it is possible to distinguish… Thus are his words. Their opinion is that it does not depend on the laws of impurity and purity, for indeed one can draw water even with vessels that do not accept impurity. Rather, this is the ruling according to Rava: Any vessel that was perforated enough to admit liquid is not considered a vessel regarding washing hands, because the water flows out in abundance through the perforation when it admits liquid, which is much more than when it just lets out liquid. Therefore, if one draws water through the perforation—it is acceptable, since there is a quarter-log from the perforation and below, disregarding the upper part. And it is implicitly proven from their words that if it was perforated less than enough to admit liquid—it is permissible to draw water even through its mouth, because it is still considered a "vessel," since the water does not flow out in abundance. (And therefore the Tur criticizes the Smak, since in his opinion it does not depend on impurity and purity.)

However, it is obvious that a vessel which has been purified from its impurity through breaking – even the Rosh and the Tur agree that it is invalid for washing hands. Therefore, one should not use the sides of vessels, as will be explained. And on the contrary, they are stringent that even with a vessel that has not yet been purified from its impurity and is considered a complete vessel regarding impurity, nevertheless, regarding washing hands, it is not called a "vessel" if it has a hole that can admit liquid. And it is forbidden to wash from it through its mouth, but washing through the hole is permitted. And in this they are lenient against the Rambam, the SeMaG, and the SeMaK, for according to them, with an earthenware vessel designated for liquids, the entire vessel is invalidated by a hole that can admit liquid, and it is forbidden to wash even through the hole. But according to the Rosh and the Tur, it is permitted.

And the opinion of the Rashba in Torat HaBayit (Bayit 6, Shaar 3) is not clearly understood at first glance, as he wrote: "A vessel that has broken, even though it can hold a quarter-log below the break, it is written in Sefer HaTerumah that it is forbidden to take from it; because anything above the break does not have the status of a 'vessel,' and it is considered a fragment of a vessel. Nevertheless, if water flows through the break, it seems permissible because it is like a spout. And it seems that even if it is broken, as long as it has not become pure due to its breakage, it is still considered a vessel, and we do not divide the vessel into two. As long as it can hold a quarter-log and its break is not so significant as to purify it from its impurity – it is permitted to use it for washing hands." Thus far is his wording.

And behold, his words are obscure. In my humble opinion, the explanation is as follows: Initially, he brings the words of the Sefer HaTerumah, which aligns with the opinion of the Rosh that anything below the break retains the status of a "vessel" if it contains a quarter-log and can pour through the break. What is above the break is considered a broken vessel. When he writes that it is like a spout, he does not mean literally like a spout, as a spout is made that way from the beginning. But here, it is a break. Rather, the explanation is that it is no worse than pouring through the hole of a spout, with the upper part removed from here. He does not mention the size of the hole, as he is referring to Rava's statement that the hole must be capable of admitting liquids; he did not feel the need to specify this explicitly because he holds that this is not relevant to the laws of impurity and purity according to the Rosh – it follows that the hole is as one that admits liquids, where water flows out in a stream, and this is not considered a vessel for the purpose of washing hands. This is the opinion of the Sefer HaTerumah.

And afterwards, the Rashba wrote: "And it seems..." - meaning to say: that he disagrees with the Sefer HaTerumah on two points: one leniently, in that Sefer HaTerumah holds that any break invalidates the vessel for hand washing, he says it is not so: that as long as it was not purified due to its breakage – it is still considered a vessel. Meaning: it is completely valid, according to the opinions of the Rambam and the Smak. And then he says that one does not divide the vessel into two, meaning: in this he disagrees stringently, and this is that according to the Sefer HaTerumah, the lower part, if it contains a revi'it (a quarter-log) and one can wash from the break – it is always valid. And he (the Rashba) holds that one does not divide it into two, meaning that if the break is sufficient to purify it from its impurity – the entire vessel is invalidated, according to the opinion of the Smag that we mentioned. (This is how it appears to my humble opinion in his intention.)

According to what we have clarified, the Rambam, the Smak, and the Rashba hold the same view that a vessel is not rendered invalid by a hole unless it has been purified from its impurity through such a hole. The measure of "able to absorb liquids" applies only to an earthenware vessel specifically designated for liquids. However, if it is not designated for liquids but for foods, and similarly, wooden vessels, metal vessels, bone vessels, and glass vessels designated for foods, the hole does not render it invalid unless it is the size of an olive. Likewise, dung vessels designated for liquids are governed by the measure of "able to absorb liquids"; and when designated for foods, they are governed by the measure of an olive. Even though they do not accept impurity, nevertheless, regarding the matter of ritual hand washing, they should not be treated differently from other vessels. Conversely, we are stringent that when there is a hole that purifies, the entire vessel is invalid, even the part below the hole.

The opinion of the Rosh, the Tur, and Sefer HaTerumah is exactly the opposite: it does not depend on impurity and purity, but in any vessel, a hole that "admits liquid" invalidates it. Contrary to this, there are those who are lenient regarding the lower part of the vessel such that when it contains a quarter-log and one can draw from the hole, it is always valid even if the vessel has been purified from its impurity. The SeMaG adopts the stringencies of both views, that in any vessel a hole that admits liquid invalidates it, and this is also the opinion of Tosafot in Niddah there. Furthermore, the SeMaG is stringent according to the view of the Rambam that a hole that admits liquid also invalidates the lower part of the vessel. He is even more stringent than the Rambam, for according to the Rambam, SeMaK, and Rashba, this applies only to earthenware vessels specifically designated for liquids, but according to the SeMaG, this law applies to all vessels, and only with a hole that allows liquid to exit is the lower part permitted. However, according to all our Rabbis, a hole that is less than "admits liquid" is entirely valid even for the upper part. Know that the Tur at the end of the matter also brought the words of the Rambam, see there. It appears that his opinion is that in this, he agrees with the Rambam, that if the vessel has been purified from its impurity with such a hole, it is totally invalid. Our Rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, wrote entirely according to the words of the Rosh and the Tur and did not bring at all the words of the Rambam or the other authorities, which requires investigation. (Their reasoning is that the Beit Yosef in his great book got very entangled with the words of the Rambam, SeMaK, and SeMaG, see there. Also, the TaZ in subsection 1 elaborated a lot, and his words are not understandable, as wondered by the Pri Megadim. The Levushai Srad tried to resolve it with great difficulty. The Magen Avraham in subsection 3 brought the words of the Rashba and thought that the Rashba interprets the words of Sefer HaTerumah, see there. According to what I wrote, this is not so, but for practical law, he almost agreed as I wrote. He also wrote that a vessel that has been purified from its impurity is invalid even for drawing through the hole, see there. And certainly, it is so, since the Tur also holds this way; even though from the Rosh and Sefer HaTerumah it doesn't appear so, nonetheless, for practical law, this is the main opinion. Be precise and you will find ease.)

And know that in the Mishnah Parah, Chapter 5, Mishnah 7, regarding the sanctification of the water of purification, it is taught: If it was punctured from below and plugged with a rag, the water inside is invalid... from the side and plugged with a rag, the water inside is valid... see there. And so ruled the Rambam in the sixth chapter of the laws of the Red Heifer, law 7, and this is his language: If it was punctured from the side and plugged, it is valid to fill it and sanctify and sprinkle from it. Thus far his language. And now, the reasoning is clear: If in the sanctification of the water of purification, which is a Torah law as it is explicitly written "living water in a vessel," it is valid in such a manner, all the more so in the case of washing hands, which is rabbinic. And I am astonished that none of the decisors mentioned this. And one of the great ones wrote on this Mishnah, and this is his language: We learn from this that it is permitted to wash hands with a vessel punctured from the side... and it cannot be said that here it is when the water is below the hole, but what is above is not considered a vessel, for if so... (the Gra in Eliyah Rabbah). And so wrote one of the commentators on the Shulchan Aruch (Magen Avraham, subsection 6), and this is his language: And if the vessel was whole, and it was punctured and something else was inserted, it is effective... since it was sealed, it is properly considered a vessel. Thus far his language. However, he did not differentiate between below and from the side. And it appears that his intention is on a proper sealing with wood or iron that would last. However, the Rosh in his commentary there explicitly wrote the opposite, and this is his language: But from the side, they sanctify with the water below the hole, even if it was not plugged with a rag... thus far his language. And so it seems from the Rash, see there. But the Rambam ruled as I wrote. (And the Taz at the end of subsection 1 brought this Mishnah and wrote that washing hands is more stringent, see there and his words are puzzling. And I am astonished why he did not bring the words of the Rosh? And for the ruling, one may rely on those who are lenient, as the Terumat HaDeshen wrote in Siman 161 that in washing hands we follow the lenient opinion, see there. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

How large is the hole that qualifies as "absorbing liquid"? If you place it on water, the water will enter through the hole. This is larger than a hole through which water exits, as water can exit even through a very small hole, and such a hole is not considered invalid according to most authorities. Even if the hole is at the bottom of the vessel, it is permitted, except according to the Sefer Mitzvot Gadol (SeMaG) who prohibits it, as I have written. There is also another sign for "absorbing liquid," which is if water drips from it drop by drop, it is known that it absorbs liquid (Niddah 49b). 

Some say that if it is cracked from top to bottom, even if the hole only allows liquid to exit and does not absorb liquid, it is invalid for washing hands, because it has become purified from its impurity (Beit Yosef). If it has indeed been purified from its impurity in this manner, it is certainly invalid for washing hands, but this law is not clearly stated anywhere (Taz, Section 1). On the contrary, in the eleventh chapter of Keilim, Mishnah 11, it is proven that a crack and a hole have the same law, look there. Every crack mentioned in the Mishnah represents a significant separation, as explained in the ninth chapter of Keilim, Mishnah 7, where it is taught: if it is cracked from the oven to the side, its measure is the width of a weaver's comb. Similarly, at the beginning of the eleventh chapter of Oholot, in a house that is cracked, the minimal measure is the width of a plumb line, look there. And at the end of Shabbat, a crack is measured by a handbreadth, look there. Therefore, this law does not apply.

Therefore, any type of vessel that has a hole, if it does not have the size of "a liquid entering" – it is permissible to use it for washing hands. Similarly, if there is a chip at the top or a crack even over its entire surface, if the water cannot enter through the chip or the crack – it is permissible to use it. Likewise, if the hole or the chip or the crack is very large, to the extent that one could wash one's hands through the hole or the chip or the crack, and there still remains below it a quarter-log (a biblical measurement of liquid) – it is permissible to use it for washing hands according to the Rosh, the Tur, the Sefer HaTerumah, and our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch. Similarly, if one closed the hole or the chip or the crack with any material – it is permissible to use it even through its mouth according to the Rambam and many of the great authorities as I wrote in section 13. According to the Rosh, this is not so, as I wrote. And we have already written that in the matter of washing hands, one should rely on the lenient opinions.

It is taught in the first chapter of tractate Yadayim (Mishnah 2): One does not pour water for washing hands from the sides of vessels, or from the bottom of a broken vessel, or from the stopper of a barrel. The Rash, the Rosh, and the Ra'avad explain that "the sides of vessels" and "the bottom of a broken vessel" refer to fragments of vessels. And "the stopper of a barrel" is invalid because it is not made for use inside but rather as a cover for the barrel, see there. According to this, even if they can hold a quarter-log and are standing without support, they are invalid for washing hands (Magen Avraham, subsection 3). The reason is that they are not called "vessels." They are also invalid for the sanctification of the waters of purification, as it is taught in the fifth chapter of Parah (there). And it is taught in the Tosefta there: the bottoms of bone vessels, glass vessels, and wooden vessels - one does not wash hands with them. If one has repaired and smoothed them and made them into vessels, one may wash hands with them. Until here is his language. And this is its explanation: "the bottoms of vessels" refers to fragments of vessels. However, if one has repaired and smoothed them, which is like the Mishnah in the thirtieth chapter of Keilim that teaches: the bottoms of a bowl... that were prepared for use - they are pure. If one has cut or smoothed them with a file - they are impure. This means: merely designating them for use does not help, and they do not contract impurity because they are considered fragments of vessels. Only if one has cut and repaired them through action and made them smooth, or has smoothed them with an iron tool, do they become vessels. Here too, regarding washing hands: if one has not performed an action on it, one may not wash with it; if one has performed an action on it, it is permitted to wash with it. (And in the Tosefta it says: fragments of earthenware vessels that hold a quarter-log - it is permitted to wash hands with them. And this is puzzling.)

And our teacher, the Beit Yosef, in his great book, followed a different path in this matter. He holds that the invalidity of the walls, bottoms, and covers is due to their inability to stand without support. Based on this, he wrote in paragraph 3: A vessel that holds a revi'it (a specific measure of liquid) when supported, but if not supported, the water will spill and it will not hold a revi'it – it is not considered a "vessel." Therefore, the cover of a barrel, which is sharp and does not hold a revi'it without being supported – one may not use it for ritual washing. But if it is widened at the bottom so that it holds a revi'it when it stands without support – one may use it for ritual washing. Thus far his words. And indeed, the law is correct. However, what he wrote that the invalidity of the cover is because it does not hold a revi'it without being supported – this is not so, for even if it stands without support, it is invalid until a correction is made as I have written. A mere designation does not help. (Magen Avraham, small paragraph 4. And the Beit Yosef follows the method of the Tur.)

There are those who say that one should not wash hands from the container called a "giskan" through the protruding spout, because it was not made for receiving (water) (Sheloh). And they were astonished by this: for the basin, the priests would sanctify their hands and feet from the basin through the spouts of the basin (Magen Avraham, subsection 4). And they resolved that in the basin, the spouts were made like tubes that receive water, but when it is made like a pipe that is open at the top and is like a half-circle – no (ibid.). Alternatively, in the basin, the protrusions were not higher than the body of the vessel but protruded evenly from the sides. But when it protrudes upwards – no (Eliyah Rabbah, subsection 6). And behold, these matters are obscure and require explanation.

And it appears to me that the explanation of the matter is as follows: The intention is not that at the time of receiving the water, the water must enter through there, for through all the spouts of the vessels, water is not introduced, and yet the priests washed their hands from the spouts of the laver. Rather, the explanation is that it is necessary for the water to be held there, excluding those vessels called "kanan"—some part of the vessel protrudes above the body of the vessel, and in that protrusion, the water is not held as can be clearly seen. And therefore, they said that in the laver it was not so, or even if the spouts were above, in any case, each of the spouts was surrounded all around, and consequently, the water is held there. Or the protrusions were not above the laver but level with the laver, and consequently, the water is held there. This is the explanation of the matter.

According to this, with our utensils, when there is no protrusion rising above the utensil, it is permissible to wash one's hands through the protrusion. However, when it protrudes above, it is not permitted to wash one's hands through the protrusion. But if it is not through the protrusion, it is permitted. For metal vessels designed to heat hot water, called a samovar, which have a spout at the bottom from which the hot water is poured through a tap known as a kran, as well as a large vessel called an ant pass into which a lot of water is poured, and at the bottom, there are spouts, and when one wants to take water from them, they lift the spouts upward, and the water flows out through there. When they remove their hands, the spouts return downward and seal the water outlets, it is permissible to wash through there. However, one should ensure that with each pouring, the spout is lifted and lowered so that the water comes by human force, as will be explained. Similarly, with the spout of the samovar, one should do the same. And through the spout of the tsaník standing on the samovar, one can wash through its spout, as well as through the tap in the barrel. But with each pouring, one should remove the tap and replace it so that the water comes by human force, as I have written. From this, we can understand for all types of utensils.

It has already been explained that for all vessels one can use them for washing hands. However, this specifically applies to those which are typically used for drawing water, to exclude sacks, baskets, and felt items, which are hats or shoes made of felt called "pilsetz." Even if one prepared the sack to stand without support and coated it with pitch so that it can hold liquids, one should not use them for washing hands because they are not made to hold liquids. Similarly, felt items, even though they are hard and the water does not drip from them, still they are not made to hold water. And our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in Section 4 that in a pressing situation, they are permitted because travelers are accustomed to drinking from them. This is his language. But some disagree, stating that even in a pressing situation, it does not help (Yam Shel Shlomo). And one who relies on our teacher, the Beit Yosef, has not lost (Eliyah Rabbah, subsection 5). This applies only to felt hats, which are sometimes used to drink water, but not to sacks and baskets. Leather vessels are like all other vessels, and one can use them for washing hands, for many use leather flasks for liquids, as it is written, "And she opened the skin of milk and gave him a drink." However, for washing hands, we require a vessel that can stand without support, and the flasks are like mere bags. But when they want to fill them with liquid, they blow them up, and this is not suitable for washing hands. Therefore, a leather wineskin or flask that has been prepared and made with a base so that it can stand without support can be used for washing hands.

And that which has been clarified that the vessel from which one pours water for washing hands must stand without support, this applies to regular vessels. However, there are types of vessels that are initially made in such a way that they cannot stand without support, and their primary use is with support – one may use them for washing hands, since their primary use is indeed this way, and they are considered properly a "vessel." Therefore, our hand-washing basin, where the handles are underneath it, and it does not stand on the ground or on a bench, but is affixed with nails to the wall and hangs in the air – one may use it for washing hands, since this is its primary use.

And similarly, regarding our requirement that there be no hole in the vessel, if it is a vessel that was originally made with holes, as Rambam wrote in Chapter Eighteen (Halacha 6) of [the Laws of] Vessels, and this is his wording: "A 'titros,' even though it is perforated and coins fall out, becomes impure, because the water gathers in its sides, and it is made to receive [liquids]." This is the end of his wording, and it is a Mishnah in [the tractate of] Kelim. Therefore, a vessel that is full of holes at its bottom, and its mouth is narrow at the top, and when a person places his finger on it, the water does not exit, but when he removes it, the water exits — it is permitted to use it for washing hands, even though it does not hold anything; since it is made to receive in this manner, and this is its primary use — it is called a "vessel." All the more so, a vessel that has a faucet below, like our modern faucets, even if it has large holes that the faucets stop, since it was originally made to receive in this manner — one may use them for washing hands. Similarly, a whole vessel that became perforated and one plugged it with something to permanently seal it — this is effective, because since it was sealed, it is called a "vessel" (Magen Avraham, Subsection 6). And see in Siman 162, Subsection 22.

There are those who wrote about pewter vessels called "giskan," which are used during meals for washing hands, and these vessels have a large hole at the top near their mouth, made for decoration. Nonetheless, one should not be lenient and wash through the mouth of the vessel, but rather through the hole. This is not similar to a vessel full of small holes, which we explained is permissible to use for washing hands, because there the holes are small, unlike this large hole. Even though it is made for decoration, it is still a large hole and invalidates what is above it (Taz, subsection 6). Moreover, there are those who disagree even with the small holes. Nonetheless, we rely on the lenient view for these, but not for a large hole. Therefore, it seems to me that in our "leika," which draw liquids from a barrel with large holes on both sides – it is prohibited to wash hands from them, since the hole on the other side is also large, and it is not similar to a "titrus" as explained. This is also the practical ruling.

Since one needs to wash from a vessel specifically, it is understood that Reuven is forbidden to scoop water with his hands and pour it over Shimon's hands, for the water on Shimon's hands did not come from a vessel. Moreover, even if Shimon himself were to wash one hand from the vessel, then scoop water with this hand and pour it over his other hand, this washing would not be valid for his other hand, even though the water in his first hand came from a vessel. He would need to wash the second hand again. However, some of our great rabbis permitted in such a case, arguing that since the water in his one hand came from a vessel, he may pour the water from his hand over the other hand. The custom is to be lenient according to this opinion. Nevertheless, the primary view is the first opinion, and therefore, one should be stringent initially. However, even according to the lenient opinion, one must be careful that the water in his one hand is not impure, meaning he should pour a quarter-log (revi'it) at once, covering the entire hand, both palm and back. Then, when he pours on the second hand, he fulfills the requirement according to the lenient opinion. Otherwise, the water would become impure and render the second hand impure. These laws cannot be fully explained here as this is not the appropriate section. They will be explained in Siman 162 with Heaven's help. Refer there to section 23.

As long as a vessel is needed, the water must also come through the force of "giving," meaning: through the force of a person giving it. It is not sufficient if one immerses his hands in a vessel, as it says regarding the laver: "Aaron and his sons shall wash from it" — and not inside it (Zevachim 21a). Even though immersion of hands in forty seahs of water is valid, as will be explained, this applies to a mikvah in the ground suitable for bodily immersion, all the more so for washing hands. But in a vessel, immersion is not valid; only pouring from the vessel by human force is valid. Without human force, such as if a barrel tips over for some reason and the water pours out, and one places his hands under the stream — this does nothing, because the water did not come by human force. However, any person is acceptable. And so it is taught at the end of the first chapter of Yadayim: anyone is fit to pour water on the hands, even a deaf-mute, a mentally incompetent person, and a minor. The same applies to a woman and a Samaritan. Whether specifically a human being is required, or also other animals like a monkey that acts like a human — there is a dispute, as the Sages permit and Rabbi Yosi disqualifies. The decisors are divided: some rule like the Sages and some like Rabbi Yosi. The words of those who permit seem more reasonable. Even though a monkey is disqualified for slaughter, slaughter is a Torah-level requirement. Nonetheless, it is preferable to be stringent initially, and there are those who are stringent with a Samaritan and a menstruating woman. But for practical law, it is not so, because we are all impure anyway, and being careful about this is only a pious practice. Similarly, some are stringent with a deaf-mute, mentally incompetent person, and a minor under six years old, but the main ruling is as I have written (see Taz, sub-section 15, and Magen Avraham, sub-section 22). In section 32, it will be explained that some permit immersion of hands in a vessel.

And since it is required that the water comes through human effort, therefore, a person who draws water from the river or from a well that is a spring, and pours the water into the conduit in front of him, and from the conduit the water flows to irrigate fields – it is not permissible to put his hands into the conduit before the arrival of the water, and for the water to pour over his hands upon arrival, because the human effort of the one who poured has already ceased, and it turns out that this water is not coming through human effort. This applies specifically when he places his hands in the conduit far from the place where the water was poured into the conduit. However, if he places his hands close to the place where the water was poured, even though he does not place them directly under the pouring, the washing is valid, because as long as they are close to the place of pouring, they are still coming through his effort.

And this is when the water comes upon his hands. But if he immerses his hands into the pipe, in any case, it does not count as a valid washing, because the water is drawn and the vessel is attached to the ground. And with something attached to the ground, a vessel does not help, and even if it is not attached, there are those who invalidate it as will be explained. And this applies when the drawer pours into the pipe itself. But if he pours them outside the pipe, and they flow into the pipe and he immerses in it – his hands are pure, because even regarding a mikvah, we hold in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 201, that drawn water that is led (into the mikvah) is valid. And even for those that invalidate it for a mikvah, nonetheless for the washing of hands which is rabbinic, everyone agrees it is valid.

Even if one draws water and pours it into the pipe itself, if the bucket with which he draws is perforated at the back with a hole that allows liquid to enter, and while he pours through its mouth into the pipe, it flows from the back into the river or spring – one may wash their hands with it and they are pure. This is considered as if he immersed them in the river, for this connection joins the vessel to the river, and the water in the pipe is regarded as connected to the river water. And even though such a connection is not considered a connection for immersion, unless the hole is as large as a wineskin stopper as explained in Yoreh De'ah, section 201, nonetheless, regarding washing the hands, one may be lenient. There are those who disagree and hold that even for washing the hands, such a connection is not considered valid. Certainly, it is preferable to be stringent initially, but if one does not have a vessel – one may be lenient in washing the hands according to the opinions that permit it.

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote in Section 7: One should not wash their hands from stones that are fixed into a wall, even if they have a receptacle and a tap. However, if they were originally vessels and then were attached to the wall, one may wash from them. End of his words. The explanation of the matter is that something attached (to the ground) does not have the status of a "vessel"; only if it was detached and then attached, such as if it was initially a vessel, it is permissible to be lenient regarding hand washing, since it is considered detached. There are those who are lenient in all cases (Taz, Section 8). The main opinion follows Rabbi Moshe Isserles, since if it did not have the status of a "vessel" at all when detached, then it is considered fully attached, and it is not effective for washing with a tap nor for immersion in it, even if it contains forty seah, because it is prohibited for immersion (Pri Megadim). It is possible that for immersion, one may be lenient if it contains forty seah regarding hand washing (ibid.).

The water that is drawn through hollow reeds from a distance, such as aqueducts, to take from the reeds themselves is certainly forbidden, as it does not come through human effort, being far from the source of the water that a person manipulates. However, it is permitted to immerse one's hands in a stone basin that stands before the reeds, as it is considered as if it is connected to the river or spring at the time the reeds are flowing with water, and it is regarded as a connection for the purpose of washing hands as I have written. But when the flow from the reeds stops, it is forbidden to immerse hands in it, as it is no longer connected to the river or spring water (see Taz and Eliyah Rabbah). And to take from the flumepin (fountain) is certainly forbidden, as they are not vessels (Be'er Heitev, subparagraph 8).

If one places his hands into a vessel of water and shakes his hands in it, if the vessel is connected to the ground, the washing is certainly not valid, because in a connected vessel, it is definitely not considered "washing" (netilah) but rather "immersion" (tevillah); and immersion is not valid with drawn water, even if there are forty se'ah. However, if the vessel is detached, not connected to the ground, some say that the washing is valid, because only for a sink do we expound "from it" and not "in it," as I wrote in Section 26. But in the case of rabbinic hand washing, this is considered a type of washing. And some say that it is not valid, as I wrote there. The main ruling in terms of prohibition is that the majority of decisors hold this view. Nevertheless, in a pressing situation, one can rely on the lenient opinion in rabbinic hand washing. If subsequently, water with a vessel becomes available, he should wash his hands and not recite a blessing if it was after the blessing of "Hamotzi" (Eliyah Rabbah, Section 12). And beforehand, he should not bless either. There is one who says that he should bless beforehand on the immersion (Magen Avraham, Section 15), but this does not seem correct; rather, he should bless afterward if it is still before the blessing of "Hamotzi." This seems to be the main opinion. There is one who says that even those who permit this only do so if there are forty se'ah in the vessel (Bach in the name of Hagahot Ashiri). This is not so, because if that were the case, why would we need a verse to prohibit in a sink, where there are not forty se'ah, and it is certainly forbidden? (Taz, Section 10, see there. This is not a precise argument, for one could say that the verse comes to exclude even when there are forty se'ah in the sink. Nevertheless, the opinion of most decisors is that the lenient opinion, which is that of the Bahag, permits in all cases. The Yam Shel Shlomo rules that even in a pressing situation, one should not rely on the lenient opinion, see there and in Taz, Section 11.)

A barrel that contains water, and he does not have a vessel, nor is there another person to lift the barrel to pour on his hands, if it is small – he should place it on his knees and take water from it for washing his hands. This means he should shake it with his knees for each and every stream (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 16). This is considered "human force," for what difference does it make whether he pours with his hands or tilts with his knees? And if it is large and resting on the ground, and the water streams out without his manipulation, but rather it rolled by itself and he placed his hand under the stream – this does not count as proper washing. And if there was a faucet in the hole, and he removed it and received the water on his hands – this is considered proper "human force," provided that for each and every stream he removes and replaces the faucet, and then removes it again, for only the first stream is considered "human force." There is an opinion that all the pouring is called "human force" (Yam Shel Shlomo), but this is not the main opinion (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 20). Nevertheless, if he tilted a barrel full of water, and went and sat down, and the barrel continues to pour water all day because of his tilting, and he washed his hands from it – this counts as proper washing, for this is considered "human force." This is not comparable to removing the faucet, which needs to be removed for each stream, because in that case he did not act upon the water itself, but rather upon the faucet. But in tilting the barrel, he acted upon the water itself – thus all the streams are considered "human force." This is also not comparable to what we explained in paragraph 27 regarding a pipe, which is not considered "human force," because there it is far from the place where his force acts, unlike here. Therefore, when he has a large barrel and no vessel, if it is full of water – he should tilt it on its side and place his hands under the hole, and the water will come upon them, and this will fulfill the requirement of washing the hands.

In the tractate Chagigah (18b), it is explained that one does not need intention for washing hands for non-sacred (chullin) matters, only for terumah (priestly gifts); this is also explained in Chullin (31b). Nevertheless, the Rashba in Torat HaBayit was stringent about this, based on what is taught in the Tosefta: "If the one who washes intends and the one who pours does not intend, or if the one who pours intends and the one who washes does not intend, his hands are pure." It is explicitly implied that one of them needs to have intention: either the one washing or the one pouring over his hands. We must say that in Chagigah and Chullin, the discussion is about touching and not about eating. However, all the poskim (halachic decisors) did not write this way, and they did not concern themselves with the Tosefta because the Gemara states otherwise, or because this is referring to terumah. Nevertheless, our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, were concerned with the Rashba's opinion initially, and this is their language: "Initially, the one washing should intend for the washing that prepares for eating. The intention of the one pouring is also effective even initially, even if the one washing did not intend at all." This is their language, and it is based on the Tosefta we brought. There are those who were concerned with the Rashba's opinion even post facto (Magen Avraham, subsection 25), and this requires investigation. (And one should not ask: if intention is not needed, why did we rule in Siman 158 that if one washed his hands for dipping in liquid, he needs another washing for a meal? This is not difficult at all, for when one intends for something else, it is worse than if he had no specific intention. Examine and you will find it easy.)

He immersed his hands in spring water, even if it does not contain forty se'ah, the immersion is valid. For a spring purifies with any amount, even for the body, and all the more so for the washing of hands, provided that all his hands are covered by the water at once. If he immersed them in mikveh water, which is rainwater, some say that it requires forty se'ah like the immersion of the body, and some say that its law is like that of a spring. Their reasoning: since from the Torah one can immerse vessels in a mikveh when there is a revi'it of water, but the Rabbis nullified this and required forty se'ah for vessels as explained in Yoreh De'ah, Section 201, therefore we rely on the lenient opinion for the washing of hands, which is a rabbinic requirement. This is the main ruling, and only ideally should one be stringent. Therefore, one who is traveling and does not have a vessel can immerse his hands in a puddle of rainwater or in a small cavity of rainwater, provided that both hands are covered by the water. However, the water must be stationary, meaning it must remain in one place and not be flowing, for a mikveh is invalid if the water is flowing. Rabbi Yosef Karo wrote in Section 15: rainwater that is flowing, meaning that it is moving and not collected, if it contains forty se'ah, there is a doubt whether one can immerse his hands in it. This is his language. Because flowing water is invalid even for the immersion of vessels.

Maimonides wrote in Chapter Six of Blessings, Law 5: Anyone who requires hand washing and immerses his hands in a mikvah does not need anything else. But if he immerses them in water that does not have the quantity of a mikvah, or in drawn water that is on the ground, he has done nothing, because drawn water does not purify the hands except through washing. So far his words. Now, regarding the quantity of a mikvah, it was explained in the previous section that there is a disagreement, and its law is like that of a spring. Also, regarding disqualification with drawn water that is on the ground, the Raavad disagreed with him and ruled that in forty se'ah of drawn water on the ground, since those who had seminal emissions immerse in it, as we learned in Mikvaot, Chapter Eight, it is also valid for hand washing by immersion. And drawn water that was conducted entirely – even according to Maimonides, one may immerse hands in it.

It is written in this language: Regarding snow, some forbid and some permit. And R. Avigdor did not want to use snow, even in pressing circumstances. Until here are his words. The intention is to throw snow on one hand, and then on the other, and to rub them until they melt like water. But to immerse one's hands in a pile of snow that has forty seahs – it is obvious that it is permitted, for even for the immersion of the entire body many permit, as I wrote in Yoreh De'ah there. All the more so for washing hands (Taz, subsection 20). And see what I wrote in Siman 160, subsection 16.

One should not take water from a river with one hand and pour it over the other hand, because in this case, it is neither a valid washing nor immersion. "Washing" requires a vessel, and here there is no vessel. However, if one immerses one hand and washes the other hand using a vessel, it is permitted, and the hands are pure. One who immerses their hands does not need to immerse them twice, as this is only necessary for washing when pouring less than a quarter-log, as will be explained in Siman 162, but not when pouring a quarter-log, and certainly not for immersion. Additionally, there is no need for drying the hands or raising them, as these requirements apply only when the water is impure, as I have written there.

One who immerses his hands does not recite the blessing "al tevillat yadayim" (on the immersion of the hands) but rather "al netilat yadayim" (on the washing of the hands), for the primary enactment was washing; however, included in the greater number is the lesser, and certainly this is true for immersion. Therefore, the blessing is as the primary enactment. And there are those who say that he recites "al tevillat yadayim," and this is the principal opinion. For how can he say "netilah" (washing) when he is not washing? And there is one who decided that if he immersed in waters that are valid for netilat yadayim (hand washing) – he blesses "al netilat yadayim." And if they are invalid for washing as will be explained in the next section – he blesses "al tevillat yadayim" (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 38). And one who acts according to this – has acted correctly, and one who acts according to that – has acted correctly. However, if one hand is washed and the other is immersed – he certainly blesses "al netilat yadayim" (ibid., subparagraph 30).

Maimonides wrote in Chapter 6 of the Laws of Blessings, Law 7: "Four things invalidate the water: change in appearance, exposure, usage for work, and spoilage that prevents an animal from drinking them. How so: water whose appearance changed, whether in vessels or on the ground, whether due to something falling into them or due to their location – these are invalid. Similarly, if they were exposed and the exposure prohibits drinking – they are invalid for washing hands." End of quote. 

Now, regarding exposure, the Tur wrote that nowadays we do not worry about exposure – they are valid even for washing hands. End of quote. Indeed, we have no knowledge at all of the matter of exposure since snakes are not common among us, as stated in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 116. And regarding what he wrote, 'whether on the ground,' certainly he means drawn water on the ground, and he follows his own opinion, as we explained at the end of the previous Siman, that drawn water on the ground, even if it contains forty se'ah, one should not wash hands in it. For in a place where it is permissible to wash hands, a change in appearance does not invalidate, as a change in appearance does not invalidate a complete mikveh, as explained in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 241 (Ba"ch), except that he follows his own opinion, and we have already explained there that others disagree with him.

However, regarding what was written: "with a change in color, whether due to something that fell into them or due to their location," even though in the Mishnah Yadayim, Chapter 1, it only states: "If ink, gallnut juice, or vitriol fell into them and their appearance changed - they are invalid," nonetheless, the Rambam holds that a change due to their location is like a change caused by something that fell into them, since the reason is not due to the essence of the water. And if the change is due to the water itself, such as if they stood for many days and turned green, the Rambam did not invalidate them, for even regarding the water of the red heifer it is taught at the end of Chapter 8 of Parah: "Water that changed, and the change is due to themselves - is valid," and all the more so for washing of the hands, which is rabbinic.

And according to this, the words of the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch in Section 1 are very puzzling, where they wrote: "Water that has changed its appearance, whether due to itself, or due to something else that fell into it, or due to its location, is invalid." Their words end here. And from where do we derive to invalidate water that changed due to itself? The commentators (the Taz, the Magen Avraham, and the Bach) have already questioned this and ruled that it is valid. In my humble opinion, the main ruling follows the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch, as it is known that water standing in a vessel for many days until its appearance changes to a greenish color, if one examines it closely, they will find many flies and worms in it, and through this, its appearance changed. It turns out that all the changes are due to something else, but in the language of people, they call it 'changed due to itself.' And proof of this is from the Mishnah in Parah there that we brought, that if it changed due to itself, it is valid. And at the beginning of Chapter 9 of Parah, it is taught in a vessel of purification water: "If creeping things and insects fell into it and they burst or its appearance changed, it is invalid." This implies that it is common for water to change due to insects, and if so, why is it not taught at the end of Chapter 8? Rather, certainly, there it is referring to a spring, and it is not common for it to change due to insects, as is known by observation, but in a vessel, it is common for water to change due to them. And another proof from Chullin (107a): Rav Sheshet asked Ameimar: Are you particular about appearance? He replied: Yes. And it is difficult, what kind of question is this, it is an explicit Mishnah in the first chapter of Yadayim as written. And Tosafot and the Rosh explained that in the Mishnah it can be said that it is referring to Terumah. And it is not understood at all, as all the laws there are for ordinary (non-consecrated) items. And according to the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch, it is straightforward, as in the Mishnah it is referring to something else: due to ink or gum, etc., as written, and he asked him about appearance due to itself, and he replied that we are stringent, and the reason is as written. Therefore, it appears to me that the Halacha and practical ruling follow the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch, that even if it is due to itself, it is invalid, as in truth, it is not due to itself, as written.

How is performing labor defined? It was taught there: "If one performed labor with them or soaked bread in them—they are invalid. If he washed dishes with them or wiped measuring vessels with them—they are invalid. If he washed new or already cleaned dishes with them—they are valid." See there. We also learned there: "Water in which a baker dips loaves—invalid, but if he washes his hands in them—they are valid." See there. The explanation is as follows: Performing labor with them refers to what is necessary for the labor, such as cooling drinks (Rosh there) or soaking bread, or washing dishes that need washing, or wiping measuring vessels where liquids have stuck, or dipping loaves, which are all necessary for the task at hand—this constitutes labor and is considered like wastewater and is invalid for handwashing. However, if one washed already cleaned or new dishes, which do not require labor at all—they are valid, as this is not considered labor. And a baker who washed his hands in them, even though it is needed, nevertheless, the water he needed was taken from the vessel, and the remainder did not perform labor (Rambam). See Section 8.

And bread that was soaked in them is invalid, even if one did not intend for this, but rather the bread fell there and got soaked (Taz 1), if the soaking of the bread is necessary, and all the more so if one intended to soak in this vessel and it fell into this vessel, it is invalid. However, if the bread fell and he immediately took it from the water, it is valid (Magen Avraham 4). And a baker who washes his hands in the water, of which we said is valid, this is when he scooped some water with his hands to spread on the surface of the baked goods, or he immersed his hands and spread the surface of the baked goods, for now the necessary water was taken, and the rest of the water in the vessel did not perform any labor. But if he washed his hands in the water in the vessel, it is invalid, for he performed labor with all of it (Taz 3). And some of the early authorities permit even in such a case (Beit Yosef in the name of Sefer HaTerumot), and the reason is that they hold this is not called labor at all, but this is not the opinion of the Rambam, the Tur, and the Shulchan Aruch (Taz there). Similarly, if he washed vegetables in them, they are invalid if washing them is necessary, but if they were clean, they are valid (Magen Avraham 5), as they are like clean vessels. However, if he soaked the vegetables in them so they would not wilt, it is certainly called labor and they are invalid (there). The same law applies if he placed vessels in them during the summer that cracked and would shrink in the water, the water is invalid (there). But if he placed live fish in them so they would not die, it is not called labor (there), for the water does not act upon them at all but rather saves them from death, and even if they died there, the water is valid (Elya Rabbah 6).

And know that our Rabbi the Rema wrote at the end of section 2, and this is his language: "And the same applies to water in which the baker washes his hands from the dough that sticks to them," end quote. According to the arrangement of matters, this refers to purification, see there. But this is not according to the method of the Rambam, but according to the method of some of the early authorities that we wrote in the previous section. And indeed, there are those who disagreed with our Rabbi the Rema on this (Taz section 4 and Yam Shel Shlomo and Eliyah Rabbah). Furthermore, he should have written 'and there are those who say,' since he explicitly disagrees with our Rabbi the Beit Yosef, who wrote the reason that the remnants did not perform any work, see there. Consequently, if he washes his hands in them, then all of them have performed work and require purification. And it seems to me more that there is a printing error, and this gloss should be a bit earlier, on what our Rabbi the Beit Yosef wrote: "And if the baker dipped the rolls in them - they are invalid," end quote. On this, he says: "And the same applies to water in which the baker washes his hands, etc.," meaning they are invalid, and this is the established ruling (and even though the Taz's question from the water before the blacksmith is not so much of a question, see there, nevertheless the truth is that this is not according to the previous method).

It is stated in Gittin (53b) that there are utensils in which they make marks for the weight of the meat. They put water and meat into them, and when the water rises to this mark, the weight is such, and when it rises to that mark, the weight is such - this is called making use of them for work, see there. And there is one who wrote that if one put something into the water for a good fragrance, it is called making use of them for work and they are invalid (Magen Avraham, section 5 in the name of the Shlah). This is a surprising matter to invalidate for this reason, for the reason that making use of them for work invalidates is because it is like pouring, and here he intended to improve them by doing so, and he improved them. Additionally, there are proofs to permit them (see Magen Avraham there). Therefore, in practice, they are certainly valid (there), and see the end of section 17.

And know that as explained, cooling liquids within water is considered as performing work with them and invalidates them. It is surprising regarding the common custom of placing bottles of beer or types of water in a vessel of water so they do not warm, and despite this, they take from them for washing hands. It seems to me that they hold like what one of the great authorities said, that cooling does not invalidate them unless they placed hot items to cool in the water, but if they placed cold items so they would not warm - it is not considered as performing work with them and they are valid (Eliyah Rabbah section 6 in the name of Atzei Tzvi and Damascus Eliezer). And know that there is someone who wrote that if one checks a vessel with water to see if it is whole or broken, the water is invalid (Shu”t in the name of Birkei Yosef), but in my humble opinion, this is not so because this is not considered performing work, for the vessel is made for water and one checks if it is suitable or not suitable, and this is not a side work.

Water that is in front of a blacksmith, even if its appearance has not changed, is invalid because it is known that work has been done with it, meaning that hot iron was quenched in it. Water that is in front of a barber, which he uses when cutting others' hair, if its appearance has changed, is invalid; if not, it is valid. This is from the Tosefta in Yadayim, and all the early authorities brought it without explaining what the barber does with the water. According to the context, it seems that he only takes a small amount of water in his hands from the vessel, and therefore the rest remains valid since no work has been done with it. This is similar to a baker who washes his hands, as discussed at the end of paragraph 4.

Water from which chickens have drunk or from which a dog has licked—there are those who are concerned to disqualify it based on the Mishnah in Parah: that any bird which drinks from it disqualifies the water, except for a dove, because all birds raise their heads when they drink, causing drops to fall back into the water (Parah 9:3). Similarly, it is taught there that if an animal or beast drinks from it, it is disqualified for the same reason. However, this opinion is not acceptable, as the disqualification in that context is not because of work being done with the water, since this is not considered a form of work, but because it is no longer "living water" in a vessel (Tosafot Chullin 9b). And even if it were considered work, these few drops would be nullified within the water in the vessel (Taz, note 5). Furthermore, should we learn from all the stringencies concerning the water of purification to the laws of washing hands? The main ruling is that the water is valid regardless of who drank from it—whether an animal, beast, or bird. However, in the case of a dog or pig drinking, it is appropriate to be stringent, as the water becomes repulsive and is considered like waste water (Magen Avraham, note 7). This is brought from the Tosefta (ibid.), though I did not find this in the Tosefta.

The Rambam wrote in Chapter 11 of the laws of Mikvaot, Law 9: "A vessel that had within it a quarter-log of water that is valid for the washing of hands, and a small amount of water that is invalid for the washing of hands was added to it—these waters are valid (because the invalid water is nullified by the majority). If one took from the vessel the amount that was added and only a quarter-log remains as it was—this is invalid, because the invalid water completes the measure of the quarter-log." End quote. He wrote this based on the Gemara in Zevachim (22a), see there, and Rashi explained there (s.v. 'to exclude') that this is only in the case of exactly a quarter-log, as such a small measure is not considered significant to nullify, see there. This interpretation is necessary, for otherwise it would be puzzling, as even in prohibitions we say that once they are nullified, they are nullified, and all the more so in the washing of hands, which is lighter since it is Rabbinic. Therefore, he explained that this applies only to exactly a quarter-log, but if there was more than a quarter-log and a small amount of invalid water fell into it, it is nullified even if one later took out the amount that was added. One can also say that this is the Rambam's intention. However, even in the case of exactly a quarter-log, the Tosafot found this stringency puzzling and wrote (s.v. 'for a quarter-log') that it was not said regarding the washing of hands but rather regarding the immersion of vessels, see there. It seems that this is the opinion of all the poskim who did not mention this law at all, and even according to Rashi and the Rambam, it is an uncommon situation to have exactly a quarter-log. Nevertheless, the halacha is that invalid waters that were mixed with valid waters less than half—are nullified and permissible for the washing of hands, and it is clear that this is only when their appearance has not changed (see Beit Yosef in Bedek HaBayit and Magen Avraham sec. 7, and examine it well).

Work only invalidates [the water] if it involves drawn water, whether it is in a vessel or on the ground in less than forty se'ah, but not in the waters of a mikveh or a spring while they are still connected. There is an opinion that only concerning work is there a distinction between a mikveh and a spring compared to vessels, but regarding a change in appearance or if they were invalidated by animal drinking, they are also invalid (Taz, subsection 6). These are puzzling matters, for since they are valid for body immersion, all the more so for hand washing. And in Yoreh De'ah, section 201, it is explained that these matters do not invalidate a complete mikveh, see there (also the Pri Megadim struggles with his words, see there).

Water heated by fire – one may use it for washing hands. And even though it is not suitable for washing after meals, as will be explained in Siman 181, this is because after eating, the hands are full of grease and the hot water would cause it to spread, as explained there. However, for the initial washing of hands, it is permitted, even if the water is so hot that the hand recoils from it. There are those who prohibit using water that is that hot, and the Talmud (Chullin 107b) presents two opinions on this matter. This all pertains to water heated by fire, but with regard to the hot springs of Tiberias, meaning hot water that comes from the mountains, one may not use them for washing hands because they are bitter and not fit for a dog to drink. However, if one finds natural spring water that is fit for a dog to drink, one may use it for washing hands. Therefore, seawater may not be used for washing hands, as it is not fit for a dog to drink. Nevertheless, there is an opinion that if seawater is boiled, it becomes fit for a dog to drink and may then be used for washing hands (Magen Avraham, Siman 12, citing Radbaz). However, Rabbeinu Yonah in the eighth chapter of Berakhot writes that the water must be suitable for a person to drink in a pressing situation, while Rambam in the sixth chapter writes "fit for animal consumption." In the case of washing hands, one who relies on the lenient opinion has not lost out.

Therefore, one can immerse their hands in the hot springs of Tiberias when they contain forty se'ah, as they are not invalid for immersing the body, and certainly they are fit for hand immersion. However, one should not take water from them with a vessel, because they are not suitable for drinking. And Rashi in Chullin (106a) explained the reason, that when the Rabbis instituted the regulation, it was not regarding hot water, and these are worse than heated water because they never had a moment of being fit [for use], end quote. According to this, even if they are fresh water, it is forbidden to use them for hand-washing, contrary to what was stated in the previous section. However, the Rambam, the Rashba, and all the poskim wrote that the reason is because they are not fit for drinking. And what we wrote that forty se'ah are required for hand immersion, this is when the spring is not in its place, for in its place there is no need for forty se'ah, as a spring purifies no matter the amount. The requirement of forty se'ah is if the water is drawn through a channel in the ground outside of its place, and the channel is in the ground and separates from the flowing spring, then forty se'ah are required. And although in Siman 159, section 35, we brought that some say even in a mikveh forty se'ah are not required, nevertheless, the hot springs of Tiberias are worse, and all agree that forty se'ah are specifically required (see Taz and see Magen Avraham, subsection 10). And even if this channel is connected to the flowing spring as hot water connected to other water, nevertheless, Rashi and the Rashba hold that one cannot immerse their hands in them if there are not forty se'ah, because we decree that one might take them with a vessel. And Rabbeinu Yonah disagrees and holds that forty se'ah are not required, since it is a spring. However, when there are forty se'ah in the channel, even Rashi and the Rashba agree that immersion is permissible (Beit Yosef).

Therefore, salty water or putrid water or bitter water that a dog cannot drink from is invalid for washing hands, even though it is valid for a mikvah for immersion. And murky water due to mud mixed in it, if a dog can drink from it, is valid both for washing hands and for a mikvah. If a dog cannot drink from it, it is invalid for both, even for a mikvah, as this is worse than bitter water which is still considered water. However, water mixed with mud is not considered water, and see Yoreh De'ah, Siman 201, where several laws regarding this matter are clarified.

One may wash their hands with anything that originates from water, such as red worms if they are crushed until they become like water, as well as fish oil if it is crushed, and snow, hail, frost, and ice, which are frozen water that we call ice. Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 12 that if they are crushed until they become water, one may wash with them and immerse in them if they have the required measure. It implies that without crushing them, one may not wash their hands with them. Earlier, in section 159, paragraph 37, we wrote that it is certainly permissible to immerse one's hands in a heap of snow of forty seahs. It can be said that our teacher, the Beit Yosef, also holds this view, and the requirement to crush is for washing the hands or immersing when there is not forty seahs. In Yoreh De'ah, section 241, he wrote that in a pressing situation, one may permit immersing one's hands in forty seahs of snow. Therefore, it can be said that here he speaks not in a pressing situation, and one should be lenient in practice as he wrote there (similarly, the Magen Avraham wrote in subparagraph 16).

Some say that washing hands (for ritual purposes) can only be done with water and not with other liquids or fruit juices, because they made hand washing similar to immersion, which can only be done with water. As it says, "and his hands he did not wash with water." This is the opinion of the Ra'avad, and also the Rosh holds this view in the seventh chapter of Berachot (section 31), bringing proof that even water whose appearance has changed is invalid for hand washing; how much more so other liquids. Rashi, however, holds there (50b) that one may wash hands with fruit juices and other liquids. One can differentiate between these and water whose appearance has changed, as the water has changed from what it was, but they (fruit juices and other liquids) have not changed (see Tosafot there). The Rashba's opinion is that although from the perspective of hand washing they are valid, one should not wash hands with wine, whether water has been added to it or not, so as not to disrespect something as important as wine, which has improved from the original fruit to the extent that it warrants its own blessing. Therefore, it should not be done initially. It also seems that with all liquids there is an issue of "bal tashchit" (not wasting), except in a pressing situation when there is no water, one may wash with fruit juices. If he does not have fruit juices or wine, he is necessarily permitted to wash his hands with them. Certainly, in a pressing situation, it is allowed to wash hands with beer or honey-water (called mead), as they are boiled and primarily water. One should not say that since the appearance of the water has changed, it is invalid, because it can be said that since it has changed for the better, we do not concern ourselves with it (Magen Avraham 19 and its question requires investigation, as there are certainly three distinctions; pay attention carefully). Some say that only with white wine is it permitted to wash, but not with red wine, and most opinions lean towards permitting it (and what the Taz wrote in 10 has already been challenged by the Elya Rabba 24).

And it also appears from the words of the Rambam in Chapter 7 of Berakhot, Law 9, that among the laws he wrote there regarding the prohibition of disrespecting food, he wrote: "One does not wash their hands with wine, whether it is undiluted or mixed, and likewise, one should not waste other foods and drinks in a way that shows disrespect and contempt." End quote. And this is certainly true that washing hands with beverages is considered disrespectful, for they were created by the Holy One, blessed be He, to be drunk and not to be poured out. However, from the essence of the law of hand washing, it is permitted. Therefore, if there is no water, it is permitted, as it is done not out of disrespect but out of necessity.
