Any doubt concerning the hands is considered pure, following the principle that doubts in rabbinic matters are treated leniently. Therefore, if there is doubt regarding water — whether it was used for work or not, or if one washed their hands and there is doubt whether there was the required amount, which is a quarter-log, or if the water is impure or pure, or doubt whether one washed their hands or not — we rule leniently. Nevertheless, some say that although the basic law is certainly so, if one has water available, they should be told: 'Arise and wash your hands without a blessing,' so as not to come to poverty (Levush). This applies when there is doubt whether the initial washing was proper. But when the initial washing was proper and the doubt arises later — whether the hands became impure, or if one is unsure whether they were distracted, or if they touched something unclean, or similar cases — one does not need to wash again, not even as a stringency, because we maintain the original status. (See Magen Avraham section 13, who questions the Yam Shel Shlomo, as distraction disqualifies. His question is puzzling, as the doubt here is whether there was distraction, for if there was definitely distraction, it is obvious one needs to wash as stated in section 164. Investigate further).

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote in section 11: "If someone did not wash their hands and touched the water, that water is not invalidated for washing and is not considered impure water. However, it is forbidden to wash one's hands with water that someone else has already used for washing." End quote. The explanation of his words is as follows: Even though it will be explained in Siman 162 that if someone washes one hand and it touches the other hand, it becomes impure, and therefore it would seem all the more so if it touched the water before washing. This is not the case, since only at the time of washing, when purifying the hands, is impurity relevant, according to the details that will be explained there. However, before washing, the Rabbis did not decree, and as long as the water is in the vessel, it is not invalidated. The proof for this is that it has been explained in section 4 that when a baker rinses his hands in water, it is permissible to wash hands with that water, and this is a clear Mishnah as stated there. And the baker did not wash his hands for eating, yet the water is still valid. Therefore, even if someone comes out of the bathroom and immerses their hands in a vessel of water, and then takes some water in their palms and pours it outside, the remaining water in the vessel is not rendered impure (Yam Shel Shlomo), since this is before the washing. However, if they did not take water in their palms but immersed their hands in the vessel and left the water there, all the water becomes impure (Taz, section 9). And even though it is not for washing, nevertheless, the water becomes impure during the washing from the bathroom impurity, and it is considered like washing (see Eliyah Rabbah, section 20, who is uncertain about this but did not decide to be lenient). And this is what Rabbi Moshe Isserles concludes: "However, etc.," meaning do not say that just as there is no impurity before washing, so too after washing. This is not the case, because the washing water has already become impure, and how can it be rendered valid again? And even if one washed with a lot of water, nevertheless, the impurity remains on it and it is forbidden to wash with it again (and that which he wrote, "that someone else washed," is the usual way of speaking, and the same applies to one's own washing, and this is obvious).

It is taught at the beginning of the tractate Yadayim: "A quarter of a log of water can be given for the washing of hands for one person or even for two; from half a log for three or four; from a log for five, ten, or even a hundred," which means it is an exaggeration, and the intention is as long as there is enough water to pour over each person (Tur). The explanation is: The Sages instituted that precisely a quarter of a log of water should be used for washing the hands, and less than a quarter of a log is not sufficient, and this is even for one person. However, a quarter of a log also suffices for two people if the first person only poured half, as the Sages estimated that half a quarter of a log is enough for the hands, and therefore the second person washes with the remaining half of the quarter of a log, because this water comes from the remnants of purity (Chullin 107a). Now, according to this measure, a quarter and a half log would suffice for three people, but since the number of people is greater, we are concerned that they might not be careful to wash up to the wrist properly, and therefore they said half a log. However, after the fact, if there is a quarter and a half log and the first person washed with half a quarter log, then certainly the remaining quarter will suffice for two people, but if the first person washed with more than half a quarter log, the remaining amount will only suffice for one person (Ra'avad there).

However, there is a dispute regarding this matter. Some say that all must wash simultaneously, while others say even one after the other. And this is the language of our master, the Beit Yosef, in paragraph 13: "There must be a quarter-log of water, and this applies to one person. But for two who come to wash together - the latter does not need [a separate quarter-log] even one after the other, as long as the flow is not interrupted. How so? There was a quarter-log of water in the vessel, one person extends his hands and another pours on his hands, and the second comes and extends his hands below him close to the first person's hands, and the flow descends on the hands of the first and onto the hands of the second below him - the hands of both are pure, even though the measure of the quarter-log diminishes when it reaches the hands of the second - his hands are pure, because they come from the remnants of purity."

"And some permit even when they wash one after the other, since at the time the first began to wash there was a quarter-log, therefore it also counts for the second because it comes from the remnants of purity. And in this manner, they wash from half a log for three or four, and from a log for several people, as long as the water is sufficient to pour on each one's hands three times. And it is also permissible for four or five to place their hands next to each other or one above the other and wash together, provided they relax their hands in such a manner that the water reaches each one." End of quote. And all this is when from the beginning both intended to wash together, but if initially one intended to wash for himself and afterward the second decided and extended his hands below him - his hands remain impure as they were, and he needs to dry them and wash them again (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 20).

Know that Maimonides' words on this matter are puzzling, as he wrote in Chapter 6, Law 10: "One may wash four or five [people's hands] side by side or one on top of the other with a single pouring, provided that they loosen their hands so that the water can reach them, and there must be a quarter-log for each one." This is perplexing because he requires a quarter-log for each individual, contrary to the Mishnah. However, Maimonides follows his own approach as explained in his commentary on the Mishnah and his introduction there, that the initial waters are not less than a quarter-log for each person, and this Mishnah refers to the second waters, which were more lenient. And this stringency is only for terumah, but for non-sacred purposes (chullin), second waters are not required at all. Therefore, he completely omitted this rule in the Laws of Blessings and wrote this rule in the Laws of Mikva'ot, Chapter 11, in relation to terumah. The Tur and Shulchan Aruch did not bring his opinion at all because he is singular in this interpretation, and there is no need to be stringent in the washing of hands due to this stringency. Nevertheless, the simple custom is according to his words, and two people do not wash from one quarter-log.

A quarter-log must be contained in one place and in one vessel because if one takes from an eighth of a log and then takes from another eighth of a log, his hands are impure as they were, and he is obligated to dry them and then wash them again with a quarter-log. For if he does not dry them, the second washing will not help because the water will be defiled by the hands, as it is stated in Siman 162. A quarter-log, as mentioned, is required whether one washes both hands or only one hand, whether for the hands of a small person or for the hands of a large person, for the Rabbis did not differentiate. If two people wash, one washing one hand and the other washing one hand, and then the second person washes his other hand, it is considered as if three people washed because the second hand is now regarded as another person since he did not initially wash but one hand. Therefore, if there was initially half a log in the vessel, their hands are pure, but if not, the second person's hand is not pure for the reason we mentioned, that one cannot wash with less than half a log for three people lest they not be exact, as stated in section 21, and there is no difference between one hand and two hands.

One must be careful about any obstruction during the ritual washing of the hands (netilat yadayim). The Gemara (Chullin 106a) states that anything that constitutes an obstruction during immersion for purification (tevilah) of the body also constitutes an obstruction during the washing of hands for non-sacred purposes. The reason is that anything the Rabbis instituted, they did so in a manner similar to Torah law. The Tosefta in Mikvaot (Chapter 6) teaches that for non-sacred purposes, obstructions do not apply; this refers to situations where non-sacred items were handled while maintaining the purity standards of terumah (as explained by Tosafot there).

All the laws of obstruction are detailed in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 198. However, one must be particularly careful in the washing of hands regarding something very common: that there should be nothing under the fingernails. For example, if there is excrement under the nail not adjacent to the flesh, such as when the nail is long and extends beyond the flesh of the finger, it is considered an obstruction. However, if the excrement is adjacent to the flesh, it is not considered an obstruction because this is common and people are not particular about it. But if there is dough under the nail, even if it is adjacent to the flesh, it is considered an obstruction because it is not common and people are particular about it. According to this, if it is known that a person is not particular about it, it is not considered an obstruction.

The Levush wrote that the reason is that excrement against the flesh is not tightly bound and water can enter there, but dough is very tightly bound and water does not enter there. However, his words are perplexing. In Yoreh De'ah, he himself wrote as I said, that the reason is due to concern, as stated there in Section 18. This is also clarified from the words of the Tur, who wrote: "For excrement not against the flesh, if one is not particular, it does not constitute a barrier." The truth is that the Rashba in Torat HaBayit wrote two reasons for this: because it is not well adhered and because one is not particular. However, the main reason is due to concern, and when they wrote about the reason of tightness, they wrote it concerning river mud, as stated there. Similarly, a bandage on the flesh constitutes a barrier if it can be removed (Taz, subparagraph 2), and so too does river mud and potter's clay constitute a barrier. This is when it covers the majority, but if it covers a minority and one is not particular, it does not constitute a barrier. If it covers the majority of the hand, even if one is not particular, it constitutes a barrier (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 3). One should not ask, as it was explained in Section 162, that if something is found on the hand, it is impure, because it can be said that this is regarding something that is not nullified in relation to the hand. But here, it is nullified in relation to the hand (there, subparagraph 4). Also, if one poured a quarter-log of water on the hand, impurity does not apply at all, as will be explained there (there).

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote that for this reason, it is not customary to clean the mud under the nails for the purpose of washing [the hands], because it is considered a minor obstruction that one is not particular about. Since there is no concern about this for washing, but if one were particular, it would be an obstruction, and one would need to clean it, and this is the primary ruling. It is possible that they have adopted leniency regarding obstructions for washing because some say that obstruction does not apply to washing at all, but the main opinion follows the first reasoning. In other words, people are not accustomed to clean the mud under the nails that are against the flesh because they are not particular about it. However, if one is particular, even though others are not, one must clean it. But for the mud not against the flesh, certainly, there is a way to be particular, and it must be cleaned, even if he is not particular, as written in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 198 (there, subparagraph 5). And on Shabbat, it is forbidden to clean due to the prohibition of smoothing, as explained in Siman 302, therefore, one should wash them with water (there). And then it says: "And it is possible that they have adopted leniency regarding obstruction for washing," meaning that earlier it was said the reason for leniency is because they are not particular, and now it says that perhaps they have adopted leniency even in what they are particular about, due to the opinion that obstruction does not apply to washing at all. And the intention is not literal, for certainly there is obstruction, but its explanation is as follows: the Rashba in Chullin there wrote in the name of the Tosafot that saying that excrement and mud under the nail obstruct is a mistake, for it does not obstruct except for the mud of potters or builders that sticks well like dough. But ordinary mud or excrement that is not compact and stinky, and a person removes it all the time, does not obstruct at all (this is brought by the Beit Yosef in Yoreh De'ah there), and perhaps people rely on this opinion. But the main opinion follows the first reasoning, which is the view of most poskim. And now most of the common people do not clean because they are not particular at all.

A nail that is partially detached - it needs to be cut, and it is considered a barrier, as stated in Yoreh De'ah there, and there are detailed laws about this explained there. The general principle is: anything that one is particular about - is a barrier, and anything that one is not particular about - is not a barrier. If it is typical for one person to be particular and another person not to be particular, for the one who is particular it is a barrier, and for the one who is not particular it is not a barrier. Similarly, if someone’s occupation involves working with dye and his hands are stained with dye - the dye is not a barrier on his hands even though there is a substance of the dye on his hands. But if he is not a dyer and his hands are stained with dye and there is a substance of the dye - it is certainly a barrier. Similarly, dry ink is a barrier, but wet ink is not a barrier, and for someone who writes regularly, even dry ink is not a barrier (Magen Avraham, section 8). Similarly, if he is a butcher and sells fat - blood and fat on his hands are not a barrier. This issue is discussed in Zevachim (98b), and we are lenient regarding hand washing (there). However, for someone who is not accustomed to this, it is a barrier even though he is not particular (according to the Gra), because most people who are not butchers are particular.

The mud of pits and the mud of potters, which adhere strongly and prevent water from coming underneath them, as well as other types of mud that adhere strongly, constitute a barrier even against the flesh, because most people are particular about it. Even if the individual is not particular, it constitutes a barrier, unless it is a very small amount that people do not care about. Women who customarily dye their hands for beauty and the like, that dye does not constitute a barrier, and all this applies to a minority of the hand. But on the majority of the hand, in any case, it constitutes a barrier if it has substance. As for the pus that comes out of a wound and dries and turns into a scab, if he is not particular about removing it or it causes pain to remove it, it is considered as if he is not particular and it does not constitute a barrier. Although we are stringent regarding immersion as stated in Yoreh De'ah, nevertheless, concerning the washing of hands, the law is lenient.

A ring that is tightly fastened on the finger is considered a barrier (chatzitzah), but if it is loose, it is not a barrier, because the water can reach underneath it. This specifically applies when one pours a quarter-log (revi'it) of water at once; otherwise, the ring becomes impure from the water, as will be explained in Siman 162. Ideally, one should remove the ring even if it is loose, since we are not experts in determining what is considered loose, and in a matter where there is no trouble, why enter into doubt? If it was tight and pressed against the finger, it is a barrier even after the fact (bedi'eved). 

To what does this refer? When it is customary to remove it occasionally, such as if it has a gemstone and one is particular to remove it when washing, or a woman who, even if there is no gemstone, is accustomed to remove it when kneading dough so that it does not become dirty. Therefore, for a woman, in any case, it is a barrier if it is tight. For a man, if there is no gemstone, he is not accustomed to be particular about removing it. If it is known that he is particular to remove it occasionally, it is also a barrier for a man. However, it is said that the ring is at the end of the third segment of the finger, and some say that only the first two segments require washing, as will be explained. Consequently, it would not be considered a barrier. But in truth, we do not hold by this opinion, and this needs further examination.

How far must one wash their hands? According to Rashi, the obligation of washing only extends to the two joints of the fingers, which means up to the middle of the fingers and no further (Chullin 106b). Since this is due to the concern of impurity in relation to Terumah (tithes), it suffices if one washes the parts of the fingers that touch the food (ibid.). The Rokeach (Siman 328) also wrote similarly, stating: "Rings on women's fingers are not considered a barrier because they are above the middle joint of the finger. It is stated in Chullin: 'up to here for Chullin,' meaning the middle joint of the finger. If it were necessary to wash the entire hand, it would constitute a barrier." This is his exact wording. Rabbeinu Tam in Tosafot there explained that it means up to the first joint (ibid.), while the Raavad and the Rosh wrote that the washing extends to all three joints of the fingers, which means up to where the fingers connect to the palm of the hand. 

Even according to Rashi and Rabbeinu Tam, it is possible to say that the conclusion of the discussion there, which states "up to here for both Chullin and Terumah as a stringency," refers to all three joints, as explained there. Therefore, according to the conclusion, it appears they agree with the Raavad and the Rosh. This is the opinion of most Halachic authorities. The Talmidei Rabbeinu Yonah in the eighth chapter of Berachot also wrote that Rashi's opinion is up to the end of the fingers (ibid.), although this is not evident from the Rokeach as mentioned.

It also appears from the words of the Rambam in Chapter 6, where he wrote, "Washing hands up to the wrist," without specifying which wrist, presumably he means the final wrist, and so it was explained in the Hagahot Maimoniot. However, in the name of the Rif, the Rosh wrote that one should be stringent and wash up to the end of the palm where it connects to the arm, and he wrote that this is an excessive stringency. The Tur also wrote this, but in truth, in the Rif's text before us, there is no proof of this. However, the version of the early authorities in the Rif is "for non-sacred purposes up to the knuckle," which means up to the end of the finger joints, "and for terumah up to the wrist," which means the connection of the hand and the arm. Therefore, in the end, when he says to be stringent for non-sacred purposes as for terumah, it naturally means up to the connection of the hand and the arm (Terumat HaDeshen). This is also written in the name of the Laws of Eretz Yisrael. And in the Zohar on Ekev (p. 272b), it is explicitly stated like the Raavad that it is up to the end of the fingers, as it says there washing hands up to the joints of the 14 phalanges, and in each finger there are three joints and in the thumb two joints, which totals 14, and this is the main law. The world customarily washes the entire hand according to the Rif's opinion, and one should initially stipulate that it should not be obligatory to do so always, as perhaps he will not have so much water available (and measuring half a revi'it for the hand also supports the Raavad, as for the entire hand, how would half a revi'it suffice).

It is stated in Sotah (4b): "For the first water, one must raise their hands upwards, and a sign for this is: 'and he shall lift them and carry them up.' The reason is so that the water that is outside the wrist does not come back and render the hands impure. As it is taught in the Mishnah Yadayim (Chapter 2): 'The hands are susceptible to impurity and can be purified up to the wrist. How so? If one poured the first water up to the wrist and the second water outside the wrist and it flowed back to the hand – it is pure. If one poured the first water and the second water outside the wrist and it flowed back to the hand – it is impure.' And the Tur wrote that the interpretation is as follows: The law of washing is that a person pours twice from a vessel on their hand – the first water is impure and the second water purifies the first water, and their impurity and purification are specifically up to the wrist. Therefore, when one pours the first and second water outside the wrist – the second water does not purify the first water that went outside the wrist, and if one lowers their hands and the first water that is outside the wrist returns and flows on their hands – they are impure. Therefore, one must raise their fingers upwards."

The general principle is that hands do not render liquids impure except until the wrist. However, liquids that touched beyond the wrist remain pure. Similarly, the second waters do not purify the first waters except while they are within the wrist, but if they fall beyond the wrist, they do not purify them. This is what we have learned: if one washed both hands beyond the wrist and then they returned to the hand, they are impure. The meaning is that they were washed within the wrist and then extended beyond the wrist. Therefore, the first impure waters were not purified by the second waters, as they do not purify beyond the wrist and the waters remained in their state of impurity. If, afterwards, one lowers them and the waters go from beyond the wrist to within the wrist, they will render each other impure. Therefore, one should raise them and not lower them.

And one should not ask, if so, why should he raise his hands? He should lower them from the beginning to the end, as now the water will not go beyond the wrist, as is obvious. It can be said that this is certainly so, and this is what our Rabbi, the Rema, wrote in Section 1, and this is his language: "And the same applies if he lowers them from the beginning of the washing to the end, that it is acceptable, only he should be careful not to first raise the tips of his fingers and then lower them, because then the water will go beyond the wrist and return and make the hands impure." End quote. And he precisely said "the tips of his fingers," and similarly, earlier regarding what the author wrote: "the one who washes needs to raise his hands," he wrote that it refers to the tips of his fingers there. And his reasoning: since we hold according to most opinions that the washing of hands is only up to the end of the cutting of the fingers, as it is written in the previous section, then up to the wrist is called up to the end of the fingers, and the first waters, if they go down to the palm and return to the fingers, it is called that they went from outside the wrist to inside the wrist and the waters became impure. According to this, what we learned in the Mishnah: "up to the wrist" means up to the cutting of the fingers, and beyond the wrist from there onwards, which is on the palm of the hand.

But I found that our early sages did not say so, and they held that "until the joint" means until the connection of the hand and the arm, for even though the ordinance of washing only extends to the cutting off of the fingers, nevertheless, regarding the impurity and purity of the water, it extends until the connection of the hand and the arm. And this is the language of the Raavad in Sefer Tamim De'im (Siman 66): "And it appears to me that the decree of impurity of hands was only decreed until the upper joint, the place where the arm and hand connect, and until here was the sanctification of hands in the Temple... the first waters that require washing up to the joint, meaning: up to the palm of the hand where the fingers end." End of quote. And the explanation of the matter: even though the palm of the hand is not included in the washing of hands for ordinary purposes, nevertheless, since in the sanctification of hands in the Temple it is included in the washing, therefore regarding impurity and purity of the water, they are included within the joint. And similarly, the Ra'ah wrote in Bedek Habayit in the laws of washing hands according to the Rashba in Torat Habayit (Shaar 2) and this is his language: "And the entire hand is included in this decree of impurity until the connection of the arm bone, and nevertheless, they only decreed washing until the joint, etc." End of quote, and this is according to the words of the Raavad, and I think that also the Rosh and the Tur followed this approach.

However, the Rashba, of blessed memory, has a different approach to this matter, as he explained in a responsum (Part 3, Siman 260), that the statement in Sotah is not to be taken as halacha, and therefore he did not write about it at all in his book Torat HaBayit regarding the laws of washing hands. The reason it says in Sotah that one needs to raise their hands upwards is because he holds that washing the hands only extends to the fingertips, and therefore the water that returns from the palm to the fingers will render the water impure. But if washing extends to the connection of the hand with the arm, this rule does not apply at all, because the water that descends on the arm does not have any impure status, and even if it returns to the hand, it will not render it impure. Most of the poskim do not hold this view, because since the water comes from the hand to the arm, when it returns, it renders the water impure. Refer to what I wrote in paragraph 10 according to the Rambam's opinion.

Now, the Rashba holds, regarding the washing of hands, like the Rif, that one needs to wash up to the connection of the hand and the arm, as he wrote in Torat HaBayit there. And I am astonished at our master, the Beit Yosef, who also wrote like the Rashba. This is his language in section 1: "The one who washes needs to raise his hands upwards so that the water does not go outside the wrist and then return and render the hands impure. And this is when he does not wash the entire hand up to the place where the hand connects with the arm. But if he washes up to there, he does not need to raise his hands," end quote. And this is surprising, because since he holds that the matter from Sotah is according to the halacha, where do we get the distinction in this matter? In truth, our master the Rama wrote that there are those who disagree, see there. And indeed, we have not seen earlier authorities who disagreed on this, but our master the Beit Yosef holds that one may be lenient in the washing of hands. (The Magen Avraham, at the beginning of the section, at the end of his words, was astonished at the Rama who was lenient in lowering the hands from beginning to end, saying this is not according to the opinion of the Rashba, see there. And I am astonished at his astonishment, for certainly it is so, that the Rama does not hold like the Rashba, and the Rashba is unique in his position as we have written. And also, the Yam Shel Shlomo in section 36 holds that even in lowering, one should be stringent, see there, but we should not make stringencies in the washing of hands, and the main ruling follows the Rama.)

If one pours a quarter-log of water over both hands or over one hand at once, there is no need for secondary water at all, for the quarter-log completely purifies, as we have learned in the Tosefta of Yadayim (Chapter 1). Consequently, since there are no impure waters at all, there is no need to raise one's hands. Similarly, one who immerses his hands in a mikveh does not need to raise his hands, for there are no impure waters at all. Although there are those who disagree with this (see Beit Yosef), nevertheless, our master Beit Yosef ruled this way in practice since it is explicitly stated in the Tosefta, and this is the law. However, despite all this, it is proper to raise the hands in any case, since in the Gemara they based it on a verse as I have written. There are those who recite the verse "Lift up your hands in holiness" while raising their hands, but we do not follow this custom to avoid interrupting between the washing and the blessing. Nevertheless, whoever raises his hands will be blessed, as the Kabbalistic sages have warned, and why should we not do so in something that involves neither effort nor loss? This is also our custom (and this is also the view of the Rambam, as I have written in section 10).

And our master the Rema wrote that there are those who say that if one pours over their hands three times, there is no need to be careful about all this, and this is the custom to be lenient, end of quote. The reason is that with three times, certainly the first waters have already been removed completely (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 2). And one should not question that the first waters would render the second waters impure, and the second waters would render the third waters impure (ibid.), for indeed there is a significant question here: how can we say that the second waters purify the first waters, for logically, if the first waters are impure, why would they not render the second waters impure? However, the Ra'avad in the book "Tamim De'im" explained this matter, and this is his language: "The primary impurity of the hands is not actual impurity but rather the impurity of dirt due to contact with sweat and excrement, or having killed a creature, and they decreed upon that dirt as if they had touched impurity, and they made them second-degree impurity to disqualify terumah through their contact, and that one should not eat with them except by rinsing, etc., and this is what is meant by 'the second waters purify the first waters', meaning they wash away the cloudy waters from the dirt on the hands, etc." end of quote. And according to this, all these matters are a rabbinic enactment, and with a single revit (quarter-log) at once, the hands are completely cleansed, and likewise, with three times, the first waters are removed as mentioned.

And with this, it is understood why the Sages instituted washing the hands twice with a revi'it (a quarter of a log of water). Why not wash them once? Because with two washings, the dirt is removed from the hands better than with a revi'it at once. Nevertheless, if one washed with a revi'it at once, we do not require him to use a second water, but ideally, they instituted washing twice.

Behold, we have already written in Siman 160, Section 23, that the Rambam's opinion is that one must use a quarter of a log of water at once, and there is no need at all for a second washing in non-sacred contexts, only for terumah, as mentioned there. According to this, there is no need to raise the hands. However, the Rambam does not hold this view, for he wrote in Chapter 6 of Berachot, Halacha 16: "For the first washing, one must raise their hands upwards so that the water does not go beyond the wrist and return to contaminate the hands." We must say that he was not concerned with the Tosefta we mentioned because the Gemara disputes it, and he does not agree with the Rashba that the Gemara is not according to the halacha as we wrote in Section 5. He holds that the water of the washing, when it goes beyond the place of washing, becomes impure. Most of the poskim do not hold this view, and his opinion is not mentioned at all in the Tur and Shulchan Aruch.

And behold, all the halachic authorities mentioned only the first and second waters for washing hands before a meal and no more. However, the Mordechai in the chapter "These Things" wrote that the morning washing requires three times, the washing before a meal twice, and the final waters once, and your mnemonic is "and to remove water from a cistern." But the Tur wrote in the name of the SeMaG a new thing, that three times are required, and this is his language: "What is mentioned regarding the first and second waters is specifically for water that comes to purify, but besides these, one needs to pour again to remove dirt and anything that forms a barrier, and these were not mentioned in the Mishnah. Therefore, one needs to pour three times: once to remove the dirt and twice to purify them." End of quote. Consequently, when one's hands are clean without dirt and barriers, twice is sufficient (Beit Yosef), and so our master the Beit Yosef ruled in the Shulchan Aruch, section 2, and this is his language: "One who washes his hands pours a bit of the quarter-log to remove the dirt and anything that forms a barrier, and then pours a second time, and even this water is impure, and then pours a third time to purify the water on the hands. And if there is no dirt or barrier on the hands, he pours a quarter-log over both hands at once, and no second water is needed." End of quote. And our master the Rema wrote on this: "And the same applies if he had much water (much more than a quarter-log), he first washes a little to remove the dirt and then pours a quarter-log at once, and no second water is needed." End of quote. (And in the Shulchan Aruch it is written "third," and it is all one and the same, examine it well).

I am astonished at our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, who were concerned about a singular opinion regarding the washing of hands, since all the poskim (decisors) have clearly written to pour once and then pour a second time. And for the decisors of halacha, it is not appropriate to say that they did not mention the previous water to remove the dirt. Moreover, there are those who explicitly wrote that the first pouring is to remove the dirt. Even the Tur, who brought the words of the Sefer Mitzvot Gadol (SeMaG), it seems to me that he did not bring them as halacha, since the Rosh explicitly says to pour twice. Rather, he brought it in his way of mentioning all opinions, but establishing it as halacha is astonishing. Furthermore, it is a stringency that leads to a leniency, for according to the SeMaG, when one washes with a revi'it (a specific measure of water), there will not be half a revi'it for each washing, only a third of a revi'it. And perhaps it will not wash every part of the hand that requires washing. Also, this is not the custom, and it requires further study. In any case, since they ruled this way, one should be careful about it. However, if one pours a revi'it at once, no further washing is needed at all.

The Rashba wrote in Torat HaBayit (there): "If one pours a large single pouring on his hand, and it is sufficient for two pourings, this is considered as two pourings, and there is no need for two separate pourings. But if he pours a large single pouring on both hands, it is not pure unless it contains a quarter-log (revi'it), and without this amount, it does not help, even if it comes from the remnants of purity," end quote. And there are those who require even with a quarter-log a second pouring (Magen Avraham in subsection 3 in the name of the Raavad), and we have already explained that according to the Rambam, for non-sacred (chullin) one does not need a second pouring at all, only for terumah.

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote in section 2: "One who washes his hands needs to rub them together," end quote. The Tur wrote: "Even if one pours a quarter-log on each hand," see there. Therefore, even if one immerses in a river, rubbing is necessary, for a quarter-log is equivalent to immersion (Taz, subsection 4). And it is explicitly stated in the Tosefta: "One who washes his hands needs to rub them," see there. However, the reason for this rubbing is not explained to us. Indeed, I have seen someone who wondered why this rubbing is necessary: if it is for purification, the hands are already purified; furthermore, if they are not yet purified, how will rubbing purify them, and what will the rubbing accomplish? And if it is to clean from dirt and grime, that has already been removed (Drisha). Indeed, some of our Rabbis have explained that this rubbing is for drying (Rash in Chapter 2 of Yadayim, Mishnah 2). And there are those who wrote that rubbing is permitted (Bach), meaning because when one washes one hand, it is forbidden to rub it with the other, as will be explained, it is stated here that when one washes both hands, rubbing is permitted. However, Maimonides wrote explicitly in his commentary on the Mishnah that rubbing is required, and this is also evident from the language of the Rosh, the Tur, and the Raavad. But Maimonides wrote the law of rubbing in his work in Chapter 11 of Mikvaot regarding Terumah, and in Chapter 6 of Berachot, he only mentioned drying. It seems that the reason for rubbing is that they were concerned that perhaps some stubborn grime remained that the water did not remove, so by rubbing, this would be removed. Maimonides held that this concern applies only to Terumah, while the Raavad, the Rosh, and the Tur held that this concern also applies to ordinary food, and thus the custom is to rub. However, certainly, if one did not rub, it does not invalidate the washing. And some say that the rubbing is after the first pouring (Magen Avraham, subsection 8), but this is not the custom.

If one washed part of his hand and then returned and washed the remaining part of his hand, his hand remains impure as it was, for there is no partial washing. However, if there is still moisture on the part of the hand that was washed first, sufficient to wet another surface, then it is considered pure, for moisture that can wet another surface is considered connected in the context of washing hands, and it is as if he washed his hand all at once. This is valid only after the fact, but initially, it is forbidden to do so (Magen Avraham, section 5). Some are concerned even after the fact (Bach and Taz, section 5), but Maimonides in Chapter 11 of Mikvaot ruled this way, see there, and it is obvious that one can rely on him after the fact. Even according to the stringent opinions, in any case, with a vessel that has a narrow mouth, it is permitted to wash, and even though it does not pour over the entire hand at once, since there is no interruption, it is not considered washing half the hand and then the other half, for this only applies when there is an interruption between them and not when it flows without interruption (Taz there). Some are stringent even in this regard (see Magen Avraham, section 5), but this is surprising (Taz), and there is no basis for this stringency.

And the prohibition against washing the hands partially applies to the first waters (i.e., the initial washing), but for the second waters (i.e., the rinsing), one may wash part of the hands and dry them, and then wash the other half. The reason for this distinction is simple: the first waters are impure as they become defiled by the hands, and it was instituted that the second waters would purify them, but this only works if the first waters were poured all at once. However, if they were washed partially, then the second waters do not purify; rather, they become defiled by the first waters. Even if one used a quarter-log (revi'it) all at once, or even if one used a quarter-log on half the hand and another quarter-log on the other half, it still does not fulfill the requirement if done partially (as explained in Gittin 15b). But for the second waters, which come to purify, it does not matter, as the second waters are not obligatory if a quarter-log was used all at once, as previously explained. The Ra'avad, in his commentary on Chapter 11 of Mikva'ot, disagrees, holding that even the second waters do not purify if done partially. His reasoning appears to be that just as bodily purification cannot be done partially, so too with hand washing. Note that "partially" refers to half the fingers. However, if one poured on all the fingers and then on the palm, it is not considered partial, as most authorities do not require washing the palm at all, as stated at the end of Siman 161. (And Maimonides, who established this rule in the laws of Mikva'ot and not in the laws of blessings, perhaps meant it only for terumah, and this requires further investigation. All the authorities wrote this regarding our hand washing.)

When pouring water on one hand, one must be careful not to touch the other hand before washing it, because if he touches it, the washing is not valid even if he later pours water on both hands. This is because the water poured on the first hand becomes impure, and when he touches the other hand, it renders it impure as well. Similarly, the water on the first hand becomes impure from the second hand, and the second water only purifies the water that became impure from the hand itself, not the water that came from the other hand. If it happens that he touched the second hand, he should dry them and wash them again according to the law. Similarly, if another person touched his hands after the washing but before drying, and the other person has not yet washed his hands, the other person renders the hands of the first person impure. He must dry them and wash them again. However, if the other person has washed his hands, there is no concern in his touch since both are pure. See section 22, where drying is not necessary.

Therefore, the best way for one who washes his hands is for another person to pour water on his hands and not to do it himself. If one does it himself, there is a concern that when he raises his hand, the water will flow beyond the wrist, and then, necessarily lowering it to pour on the other hand, the water will return from beyond the wrist to within the wrist and render it impure. Likewise, there is a concern that he might hold the handle of the vessel with a wet hand, and the handle will become impure from his wet hand. If he then touches the handle again, his hand will become impure from the handle. For this reason, the washing is only effective if he dries his hands first, as stated, for water from another place does not purify the second time. If he must wash by himself, he should hold the edge of the vessel and pour on both hands simultaneously, holding the edge of the vessel with his fingertips.

These concerns do not apply when one uses a revi'it (a specific halachic measurement, approximately 3.3 ounces), for with a revi'it there are no impure waters, and there is no concern if the water returns from beyond the wrist to within the wrist. Additionally, there is no concern about the vessel's rim touching the water, for the vessel does not become impure. The same applies if one has already poured twice on the first hand; these concerns do not exist, as the initial waters have already been purified. Therefore, we are not particular about having someone else pour for us or about holding the vessel by the fingertips, as we pour a revi'it on each hand. Similarly, our practice is to pour twice on the first hand and then on the second hand, and we do not have these concerns as described.

However, when one hand touches the other before the second hand has been washed, there is no difference between a quarter of a log and less than a quarter of a log, nor between one washing and two washings. Even if one pours a quarter of a log on each hand twice, if the wet hand touches the dry hand before washing, the water on the hand becomes impure. Certainly, if another person touches it before washing the other hand, although the water is not impure and will not render anything impure by touch, the second hand is still considered impure before washing. This is why we require washing of the hands. When the second hand touches the water, which is susceptible to impurity, it becomes impure from the second hand. The same applies when someone else is about to wash. But if they are not about to wash, we are not concerned with it (and this is the intention of the Magen Avraham in section 9, see there and examine it thoroughly).

Therefore, one should pour a *revi'it* (a quarter-log) on each hand or twice, and after washing both hands, one should rub them together, but not before. It has already been explained that one who washes with a *revi'it* and pours the entire *revi'it* does not need a second washing. (And in the Shulchan Aruch at the end of section 4 it is written: "Therefore, one must be careful when pouring the third water, which is the second in addition to the first, not to touch one hand to the other until this has also been poured on the second hand, etc." His intention is as previously stated, that three times are required as mentioned in section 11, consequently the third pouring is considered the second, and before the third pouring, one hand should not touch the other.)

Some say that even though it was explained that a hand that was washed, if it touches the other hand, becomes impure, and seemingly it would require drying just like touching any other impurity, because the other water does not purify side impurity that came onto the water, in this case, drying is not necessary. Rather, one pours more water on the hand and it becomes purified (Yam Shel Shlomo and Magen Avraham). The reason is that since the hands were already completely pure, even though they became impure from the other hand, the other water helps. Consequently, the same rule applies if someone else touched his hands: drying is not necessary; rather, he pours water on the hands again and they become purified. And even though we do not find this leniency among the earlier authorities, nevertheless in the matter of washing hands, one can rely on this leniency. (And what the Magen Avraham wrote about a vessel that was punctured at its bottom, which is like our anthaphas [type of vessel], has already been explained in Siman 159, Section 23, and it is clear that touching the hands then does not matter, as this is the way of washing, and pay attention to this.)

From what we have written, it will become clear to you that which is taught in the second chapter of Yadayim, that a hand becomes impure by rubbing against its fellow. This is when one has washed one hand and then touches the other hand before it has been washed. However, if one wishes to wash both hands at once initially, one may do so, as both hands are considered as one hand and do not render each other impure. Even four or five people who place their hands next to each other or one on top of the other with a slight separation so that the water can enter under each and every hand—these are considered as one hand and do not render each other impure. Similarly, after each hand has been washed individually twice or with a quarter-log of water (revi'it) at once, they are permitted to touch each other. Likewise, after everyone has washed their hands, they are permitted to touch each other even before drying. Whether it is permissible to take water in one’s fists and pour it on the other hand is explained in Siman 159, section 25. See there.

Touching hand to hand is permitted only after pouring a quarter-log of water at once or after the second waters, when one pours over both hands simultaneously or one after the other. However, if one poured the first waters over one hand and similarly over the second hand and then decided to join hands before pouring the second waters, and then poured the second waters over both hands at once – this accomplishes nothing and his hands remain impure as they were, and even the water on the hands becomes impure. For the first waters on each hand are impure, and each hand contaminates the other as well as the water on the other hand. The second waters do not purify the first waters because they were contaminated by the other hand; rather, the second waters also become impure from them, and one needs to dry his hands and wash them again. Certainly, one needs to be careful when two times water is poured on one hand and once on the other, that they do not touch each other, and all this applies when a quarter-log was not poured at once. This is what our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in paragraph 7: "If one rubbed his hands together, he should be careful not to touch outside the area where the water fell, because they contaminate each other.” His intention is when one washed only up to the end of the fingers, then he should be careful not to touch a wet hand on the palm so it does not become impure from it. Although according to most authorities, it is not considered washing, nevertheless regarding impurity it is considered a hand. But when one washed up to the connection of the hand and the arm – touching outside the area of the water is not relevant, for from there and onward it is not an area of impurity as stated in paragraph 4 (and so is written in the Eliyah Rabbah, section 16).

It is taught in the Mishnah in Masechet Yadayim, Chapter 2: "If one washed one hand and rubbed it with the other – it is impure; but if he rubbed it on his head or on the wall – it is pure." This means that even though the second hand, before it is washed, contaminates the washed hand while it is still wet, as stated in Section 23, nevertheless, other parts of the body do not contaminate. Therefore, if he touched his wet hand to his head – it is pure. Similarly, another object does not contaminate the wet hand, so if he touched the wall – it is pure. The main point is that impurity is only on the hands before washing. It is taught in the Tosefta there that if, after drying, he touched the water on his hand to his head or to the wall – it is impure, because that water is impure and it returns and contaminates the hand that touched it. This applies when he did not wash with the second water or with a quarter-log of water, for if he washed with the second water or with a quarter-log and touched his head or the wall – then there is no impure water there. But if he touched from the first washing and not with a quarter-log, and he then washed with the second water, then if he touched the water on his head or on the wall which are from the first waters – his hands are impure even if he touched them after drying, and certainly before drying.

And know that just as we have written, so it appeared to my humble opinion to explain the words of the Tosefta that we brought, that according to this, the laws are aligned as explained throughout this section. However, there are those who interpret that even if one touched his head or a wall after the second waters, nevertheless, since he did not wash with a quarter-log (r'vi'it) at once, even the second waters are impure when they fall on another place (Taz, subparagraph 7), and this is also explicitly implied in the words of Rabbeinu Shimshon in his commentary on the Mishnah there, who brought the Tosefta and explained it thus. And also Rabbeinu Beit Yosef in paragraph 8 followed this path, and this is what he concludes with these words: "Even though as long as he did not rub, they purify with rubbing, now that he touched again, it is worse," end of quote. This is from Rabbeinu Shimshon there, and this is its explanation: that even though as long as he did not rub his head or the wall, they purify with rubbing after the second waters when he rubs his hands together, nevertheless, when he touched again these waters that fell on another place, it is worse, and the matter is strained. And some explained it the opposite, that it refers to when he did not pour the second waters at all, and therefore the waters are impure. However, the rubbing stands in place of the second waters, as through rubbing the first waters alone suffice (Levush and Magen Avraham, subparagraph 16). And this is certainly puzzling and it is impossible to say this at all, and this is contrary to the fundamental laws of washing hands (and already the Taz there rejected these words and lamented that the Levush wrote this, also the words of the Magen Avraham in subparagraph 14 who explained that it refers to touching his head with his hat on, and his intention was that if not so, another washing would be required due to touching the head, and his words are puzzling, as only when one scratches his head is washing hands required, not merely touching, and so wrote the Eliyah Rabbah in subparagraph 17, and also the Pri Megadim was puzzled by this, and it is explicitly stated earlier in section 4, see there).

There is one who wrote: "If one wiped with a cloth in the manner of those who wipe, even if he returned and touched it, it remains pure" (Ma'adanei Yom Tov in Divrei Chamudos, letter 85). This means that even in a case where the water on the head and wall is impure, nevertheless, on the cloth, it is pure, since it is the manner of wiping (as it is written there). And there is one who disagrees with this (Magen Avraham, section 16). And there is one who wrote that if the water is absorbed into the cloth, there is no concern of touching after wiping (Taz, end of section 7). Now, this applies when he wiped after the first waters, but after the second waters, and certainly when he poured a quarter-log at once, there is no impurity in the water on the cloth, even if the water is not absorbed. Therefore, we do not guard ourselves from touching the cloth. (The Ma'adanei Yom Tov and the Magen Avraham refer to the first waters according to their previous opinion, as mentioned there, and the Taz, although according to his opinion he refers to the second waters, nevertheless it is obvious that a cloth used in its customary manner is not like the head and wall, and regarding a quarter-log, all agree. And examine this well.)

When pouring the first waters on one's hands, one must be careful that there is no pebble, splinter, or any other item left on the hand. This is because the second waters only purify the water on the hand and not anything else, as explained. If so, the water on the pebble would render the water on the hand impure, and the purification would not be effective until one dries the hand and washes it again. However, if one pours a full revi'it at once, there is no need to be concerned about this, as there are no impure waters. 

There is an opinion that snow and hail that are not crushed are considered like a pebble (Magen Avraham section 17), and the same applies to things that originate from water (ibid). This is an extra stringency, and our teacher the Beit Yosef ruled in his great book that anything originating from water does not create a separation, like Rabbi Shimon ben Gamliel, who holds this in the Mishnah in Yadayim, chapter 2, Mishnah 2. This is also implied clearly in Zevachim (22a) that the halacha follows Rabbi Shimon ben Gamliel. In the winter, it is common for a little ice to remain on the hands.

Even though one must wash the entire hand and if one washes it in parts, the washing is not valid as explained, nevertheless, if someone has a wound or pain in a finger or several fingers, and it is difficult for them to wash there - they should wash the rest of the hand and it is considered pure. In such a case, the Rabbis did not institute that it should invalidate the washing. And if one has a bandage on the wound, they should be careful that the water does not reach the bandage, because if the water reaches there, it will never purify, as stated regarding a pebble or splinter. And if one pours a quarter-log (revi'it) at once, there is no issue, since the water does not become impure. Therefore, we are not careful to avoid pouring on the bandage, because we pour a quarter-log at once. And know that even though the final waters (mayim acharonim) are not poured on the ground, as stated in Siman 181, this is because an evil spirit rests upon them, as stated there, but the initial waters (mayim rishonim) can be poured either into a vessel or on the ground, see the next Siman, section 2.

It is stated in Chullin (107b): They permitted using a cloth for those who eat terumah, but they did not permit using a cloth for those who eat taharot. Rashi explained that for those who eat terumah, they permitted wrapping their hands in a cloth and eating bread without washing their hands, because those who eat terumah are careful and will ensure that their hands do not touch the bread. But for those who eat taharot, meaning those who eat non-sacred foods in a state of purity, they did not permit this. The Rambam also holds this view, as he ruled in Chapter 8 of the Laws of Ritual Impurity. He believes that it was only for those who observe taharot that they did not permit this, but for regular non-sacred foods, it is permitted. Therefore, the Rambam ruled in Chapter 6 of the Laws of Blessings that one may wrap their hands in a cloth and eat bread.

But all the early authorities disagree with him, and they hold that in the case of non-sacred foods, this was not permitted at all, unless one is on the way and cannot obtain water within four mil ahead or one mil behind. In such a case, it was permitted, but not otherwise. This is the ruling of the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch, and this is how we rule. One who is at home must go four mil, and those who guard gardens and orchards need only go one mil, as implied in the Jerusalem Talmud. If there is doubt whether water can be found within four mil or within one mil, one can rely on the Rambam and eat using a cloth (Magen Avraham). Similarly, one who is traveling with a group and fears being left alone can also rely on the Rambam. Likewise, someone who has a wound on their hand and finds it difficult to wash completely, even around the wound, can wrap their hands in a cloth and eat. If one hand is healthy, they should wash that hand and wrap the other in a cloth, and not recite the blessing for washing hands. Similarly, if one has water that is not fit for washing hands and has no other water, they should wash without a blessing (Be'er Heitev in the name of Knesset Hagedolah), and it is forbidden to eat using a spoon or fork, and likewise with something that is dipped in a liquid.

It is further stated there in Chullin that one who feeds others, even though he touches the bread, does not need to wash his hands. Conversely, one who eats, even if the feeder places the bread into his mouth, still needs to wash his hands and recite a blessing, and similarly, one who eats with a fork. It is forbidden to feed someone who has not washed his hands because of "Do not place a stumbling block before the blind," and even if the bread is his, one should not help him bring it closer to himself (see Magen Avraham). Certainly, it is forbidden to give him bread. However, if there is doubt whether he will wash his hands, it is permissible to give it to him, and say to him: 'Go and wash your hands' (Eliyah Rabbah), and if he does not listen, it is not a sin for the giver for what more can he do, and the wicked one will bear his own iniquity.

It is stated in Chullin (106b): A person may wash his hands in the morning and stipulate that this washing will suffice for the entire day, allowing him to eat without further hand washing, provided he takes care not to dirty or contaminate them (Rashi). This rule applies specifically when he explicitly stipulates that this washing will suffice for all his meals throughout the day. If he does not make this stipulation, it is ineffective even if he keeps his hands clean. The reason seems to be that even if intention is required for hand washing, as most authorities hold that intention is not necessary (as stated in Siman 159, Section 34), without this stipulation, it is as if he is eating without washing his hands. For the Sages instituted hand washing for eating even when one knows his hands are clean, as stated at the beginning of Siman 158. Therefore, how can he eat without washing just because his hands are clean? However, when he makes a stipulation, the washing is valid for the meal, meaning that in the morning his intention was for the meal. Although generally hand washing must be close to the meal, in this case, the Sages were lenient. Nonetheless, the stipulation still constitutes a valid hand washing for the meal, but without intention, it is ineffective. There is a question whether the stipulation must be made verbally or if thinking it in his heart is also sufficient. I found that some are uncertain about this (Bach at the end of Siman 158), while others say that thinking it is enough (Elya Rabbah). However, I have seen that it is stated in the name of Shibolei HaLeket and Tanya that he must say: "With this washing, I will be permitted to eat all day" (there). This seems to me to be the main opinion, for otherwise, there is no clear indication that he washed his hands for the meal. Note that from the language of the Gemara which states "the entire day," the stipulation is only effective until nighttime. Although one might say that it means until bedtime, what difference does it make between day and night? Nevertheless, since this is a significant leniency, it suffices for the entire day and no more.

When making the condition, one should be careful not to divert their attention from it and not to soil it, such as by wearing gloves and the like. There is someone who asked that if one does not divert their attention, why is a condition needed? From this, they proved that intention is needed for washing hands (Magen Avraham, section 2). However, this is not a proof at all, for even if intention is not needed, at the very least it must be recognizable that this is a washing of the hands for eating, as stated in section 1. If one diverts their attention and a long time passes from the washing, then it is not recognizable at all. The proof for this is that our master, the Beit Yosef, ruled in section 159, paragraph 13, that intention is not indispensable, and it is only preferable to have intention. Nevertheless, he ruled here that one should not divert their attention. Also, Rambam and the Tur wrote that one should not divert their attention, and they did not explain anywhere that intention is needed. On the contrary, from Rambam’s words in the laws of primary sources of impurity and in the laws of Mikvaot, chapter 9, it is clear that for non-sacred purposes, intention is not required.

In the Gemara, there are two versions: one version states that even not in a time of necessity, one can stipulate, and in another version, it states that only in a time of necessity. And the Tur brings a dispute regarding this, see there, and our master the Beit Yosef ruled that even not in a time of necessity. However, several great Acharonim ruled that it is only effective in a time of necessity, such as when one is traveling on the road and it is not easy for him to obtain water, and similar situations (Yam Shel Shlomo, Magen Avraham, and Eliyah Rabbah), and many of the Rishonim ruled similarly (see Eliyah Rabbah). Moreover, one of the great ones wrote that nowadays, the world custom is not to stipulate at all (there in the name of Knesset Hagedolah), and indeed, we have not heard in our times of anyone doing so. Nevertheless, in a time of necessity, such as when one is traveling with non-Jews and it is difficult for him to find water, he can do so.

Even when one made a condition, if later, at the time of the meal, water becomes available, he should not rely on the condition and should wash his hands without reciting a blessing. The Tur wrote that the condition is effective only in the morning. There is someone who wants to say that this is because, in the morning, we recite the blessing "Al Netilat Yadayim," and this has some connection to the meal (Beit Yosef). However, our master the Rema does not agree, as he wrote: "The condition is effective only for washing that is not for the purpose of eating, similar to the washing in the morning. But if one washes for the purpose of eating, the condition is not effective for that washing." 

The explanation of his words: Seemingly, how can a condition be effective, for it is said in Berachot (52b): "Immediately after washing hands, [one should proceed to] the meal." However, this applies to washing for eating, where the washing must be immediately followed by the meal. But if one washes not for the purpose of eating, but for another reason, such as after leaving the bathroom, for dipping in a liquid, or if his hands were not clean, there is no need for the meal to follow immediately after washing. This is similar to the morning washing, meaning the washing is not for the purpose of eating. And even though there is no blessing, since at the time of washing a blessing is not relevant because he does not intend to eat immediately, and before eating he does not wash his hands, nevertheless, it does not matter because in such a case no blessing is needed (Taz). 

And certainly, if one washes his hands for eating and makes a condition that it should be effective for all meals of the day, it is effective (Magen Avraham, section 6). And it is even possible that no condition is needed if he keeps his hands clean (ibid.), not like the one who wants to say that from one meal to another the condition is not effective. However, it certainly seems that washing is necessary for some purpose, but if there is no need at all for washing now and he washes only for eating later, it is not effective.

One who is sitting at a meal and touches their leg or thigh or other covered parts of the body, or unclean places that have sweat or scratches the head or similar actions, or remembers that they touched these places after washing, and similarly if they diverted their attention from keeping their hands clean, and certainly if they went to relieve themselves in the middle of the meal, they must wash their hands again and recite the blessing 'Al Netilat Yadayim'. Some have written that one should only recite the blessing if they walked a significant distance (see there in Shach, section 8, in the name of the Maharshal), however, if one went to relieve themselves, everyone agrees that they must recite the blessing (see Magen Avraham, section 7, who wrote that if one touched a slice of bread while it was in their mouth, it is forbidden to swallow until they wash their hands. In my humble opinion, this is an excessive stringency, and I bring proof to this from Tractate Terumot, Chapter 8, Mishnah 2, according to Rabbi Eliezer, and in this certainly Rabbi Yehoshua agrees; see there and scrutinize).

One who has relieved themselves, whether for minor or major needs, and wants to eat, inquired of Rashi whether it is necessary to wash twice. Rashi responded that he had asked Rabbeinu Yaakov ben Yakar, who said that one must wash twice: the first time with the blessing "Asher Yatzar" and the second time with the blessing "Al Netilat Yadayim." However, Rashi himself holds that one washing suffices for both purposes. Rabbeinu Yaakov's reasoning is because of the blessings: if one were to first bless "Al Netilat Yadayim" and then "Asher Yatzar," there would be an interruption between the washing and the blessing over the bread ("Hamotzi"). Conversely, if one were to first bless "Asher Yatzar" and then "Al Netilat Yadayim," there would be an interruption between the washing and the blessing "Al Netilat Yadayim." Rashi holds that it is not considered an interruption, since both blessings are necessary and thus do not constitute an interruption, similar to the sequence of "Yayin, Kidush, Ner, Havdalah, and Zman" (Yaknehaz) where there is an interruption between the blessing over the wine and the drinking, and it is not considered an interruption. Similarly, with these blessings, one may recite them in any order. Additionally, Rashi is not pleased with two washings, because after the hands are already clean, how can one wash and bless "Al Netilat Yadayim" again? This is close to a blessing in vain. Some have written that the first washing should not be done in the manner of a ritual washing, or one should touch a dirty place in between (Magen Avraham 2). The Tur and Shulchan Aruch wrote that if one does not wish to wash more than once, after pouring water once over their hands and rubbing them, they should bless "Asher Yatzar," and then at the time of drying their hands, bless "Al Netilat Yadayim."

And behold, with regard to the two washings [of hands], there are many complications and clarifications, as the commentators have extensively discussed for the corrections that have been clarified, and not everyone is proficient in this. The most correct way is according to Rashi, of blessed memory, and it is more correct to precede the blessing of "Al Netilat Yadayim" to "Asher Yatzar," and "Asher Yatzar" is not considered an interruption between the washing of hands and "Hamotzi," as it is not worse than "Gvil L'Tori" which is not an interruption. And indeed, it is certain that if one needs to relieve themselves in the middle of the meal, they should first bless "Al Netilat Yadayim" and then "Asher Yatzar," as there is no "Hamotzi" there. And indeed, regarding the blessing of "Asher Yatzar" itself, there is an opinion that one should first bless "Al Netilat Yadayim" as the Tur writes in Siman 7. If so, what concern is there if one does this? And so we practice. Especially since this is a very common matter, as some have warned to check oneself before eating (Shl"a, Seder HaYom, and Eliyah Rabba). Therefore, one who does so will go on their way securely, especially since Rashi ruled so. However, if one needed to bless an after-blessing such as "Borei Nefashot" or a blessing of the type of three and then went to relieve themselves, when they wash their hands they should first bless "Asher Yatzar" and then the after-blessing, as "Asher Yatzar" is considered more frequent in comparison, and it also does not have a set measure (Magen Avraham, Siman 3). All the more so if one went to relieve themselves before Birkat HaMazon, they should first bless "Asher Yatzar" and then bless Birkat HaMazon.

If many are reclining at the meal, the greatest among them washes his hands first. For it is taught: “The first waters start with the greatest” (Berachot 46a), and it questions: “Should the greatest sit and guard his hands until everyone has washed?” and it answers: “Immediately they bring the dish before him and he eats.” According to this, it seems that if the greatest must wait to say 'Hamotzi' until everyone has washed, like on Shabbat when the two loaves are only before the head of the household, he must wait until everyone has washed so they fulfill their obligation with the two loaves, it is not proper etiquette for the greatest to wait for everyone. Therefore, indeed, the Rosh would wash his hands last, as the Tur wrote in Siman 166 and our teacher the Beit Yosef in this Siman (and what was written about not interrupting, etc., doesn't apply here and take note). There is someone who disagrees with the Rosh and holds that even now they start with the greatest, and so it appears from the Rambam in Chapter 7 of Berachot where he wrote this law (Maharshal), because the simple understanding of the Talmud says so even after the explanation we wrote, meaning that in any case the greatest should wash first even if he must sit and wait (Bach), and so the custom now is that the greatest washes his hands first.

It also states there: "What is the order of reclining? When there are two couches (as their seating was on the couch), the elder reclines at the head and the second one below him. When there are three: the elder reclines at the head, the second one above him, and the third one below him." And we learn in Bava Batra (57b): "What is the table of a Torah scholar like? Two-thirds covered and one-third uncovered," upon which there are bowls and cups. And this is its explanation: Two-thirds of the table towards those eating is covered with a cloth to wipe their mouths and to place the bread and food, and the outer third is uncovered to place bowls and cups on it. And it explains there on which side the ring of the table should be, but our tables do not have rings and there is no need to explain this. And further we say there: "What is the bed of a Torah scholar like? One that has nothing underneath it except sandals in the summer and shoes in the winter, whereas the bed of an unlearned person resembles a storage room," as he leaves everything under the bed. One should not do this, for food and drink under the bed have an evil spirit resting on them (Pesachim 112a), and this is explained in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 116.

After thoroughly drying one's hands, one should immediately recite the blessing of 'Hamotzi' without any significant interruption, even in silence, and certainly not by speaking. Even speaking words of Torah is prohibited, for it is stated in Berachot (42a), "Immediately after washing hands – the blessing," and it is further stated there (51b), "Immediately after washing hands – the meal." However, some of our rabbis have said that one does not need to be careful about not pausing for a long time in silence between washing hands and 'Hamotzi', provided that one does not lose focus. For the statement 'immediately after washing hands – the blessing' refers specifically to the washing of hands after the meal, and 'immediately after washing hands – the meal' means that one should not interrupt with other actions or speech, which can cause distraction, but pausing in silence is permitted. The Tur wrote that this is also the opinion of the Rif and Rambam, and the opinion of Rabbeinu Beit Yosef leans towards this view, as he wrote: "Some say that it is not necessary to be careful about pausing between washing and 'Hamotzi', and some say one should be careful, and it is good to be careful," end quote. This shows that he only wrote it is good to be careful, but his main opinion is that it is not necessary to be careful. However, speaking is certainly prohibited, unless it is for the sake of the meal, such as bringing salt, as will be explained (16), and certainly performing an action, such as pouring a cup of hot water, is prohibited (Magen Avraham). Some distinguish between the prohibition of interruption on weekdays and Shabbat, as on weekdays one should not interrupt because one might lose focus and not eat at all, thus even pausing in silence is not proper. But on Shabbat, it is permitted because one is compelled to eat, so even if one wants to wash hands and then make Kiddush, it is also permitted (ibid.), and in the Yerushalmi (Chapter Elu Devarim, Halacha 2), it implies like the first opinion.

And our Master the Rema wrote that if one delays the time it takes to walk 22 cubits, it is considered an interruption. This is derived from the Tosafot in Sotah 39a, who learned this from "immediately after the laying of hands comes the slaughter," as mentioned in Zevachim 33a, where it was not possible for the leper’s guilt-offering because the leper was not permitted to stand there and would stand at a distance of 22 cubits. From this, it is proved that such a measure is not called "immediately." It is also possible that even less than this is not called "immediately," but this measure certainly is not "immediately," as also implied in Zevachim there (see Magen Avraham, section 3, where his difficulty is resolved, as written by the Bechor Shor). And certainly, this is like "immediately after redemption comes prayer." The truth is that it all depends on the matter at hand, and in a situation of necessity, it is not considered an interruption. For example, if the place of washing hands is far from the eating area, even more than 22 cubits, it is not considered an interruption because it is necessary for the matter. An interruption is only when one delays without needing to delay, and this is the intention of our Master the Rema. And you should know that this is true, for in the previous section it was explained that the eldest washes his hands first and waits to say the blessing of 'Hamotzi' for all those reclining, and he delays a lot, but certainly, anything necessary for the matter is not considered an interruption at all. And I have seen those who are particular that the place of washing hands be near the table for this reason, but this is not essential at all. The essential point is as I have written, and the washing place can be far from the eating place, and this is the main ruling. Some have written that it is permissible to recite the Psalm "The Lord is my shepherd" between washing hands and the blessing of 'Hamotzi,' but Heaven forbid to do so (see Magen Avraham who got entangled in section 2 concerning washing hands last, and I am astonished what difference it makes between the elder and the younger, for is the younger allowed to interrupt? But according to what I have written, there is no interruption at all in what is necessary, and understand this well).

It is stated in Sanhedrin (102b) that one must recite the blessing "Hamotzi" on bread from a place where it is well baked. Rashi explains: from a place where the surface of the bread in the oven is crusty, that is, from the top or around it, etc., but not from its middle. Another interpretation: from where it first bakes, from the place that bakes first, and this is the same. Another interpretation: from where it finishes baking, from the place where the bread is very baked, etc., and the first opinion seems correct, end quote. The Rambam in Chapter 7 of the Laws of Blessings wrote: "One should break from the place that is well baked," end quote, and this is like the last interpretation. The Tur also wrote similarly and added: "From the best part of the bread, from the place that is well baked," end quote, and so wrote Rabbeinu Beit Yosef like the Rambam.
