According to all interpretations, in our bread, it is from the top, where it is nice and well baked and bakes quickly, and if one breaks from a piece, one should do so likewise, and not from the soft part in the middle. And Rabbeinu the Rema wrote: "One should break from the side of the bread in our bread, and cut a bit from the upper and lower side," end quote, because there are those who hold that it starts baking from the bottom first. Some add that this is opposite the side that cracks, but this is not so with all breads. In our bread, we fulfill all opinions, but one should not break from the soft part unless one has no teeth. In our round bread, which is called bagel or thin bread called kokosh, all places are equal (see Taz and Magen Avraham, section 2, as I have written).

In the Mishnah of Berakhot (20b), it is taught regarding one who experienced a seminal emission that he recites the blessing after the meal, because Birkat Hamazon (Grace After Meals) is of Torah origin, as it is written: "And you shall eat and be satisfied, and you shall bless" (Deuteronomy 8:10). However, he does not recite the blessing of 'Hamotzi' before the meal because it is of rabbinic origin, like all the blessings instituted by the Rabbis. And even though regarding bread there is an a fortiori argument (kal vachomer), that if he blesses when he is satisfied, all the more so should he bless when he is hungry (Berakhot 35a), and an a fortiori argument can be used for derivation, nonetheless, it is not a conclusive a fortiori argument (Tosafot there), because one could argue, on the contrary, that when he is satisfied it is like a blessing of thanks, which is not the case before eating. And the Sages said there that it is forbidden to benefit from this world without a blessing, and whoever benefits without a blessing is as if he benefited from sacred things, as it is written: "The earth and its fullness are the Lord's" (Psalms 24:1), but once he blesses, he is permitted to benefit, as it is written: "The heavens are the heavens of the Lord, but the earth He has given to the children of men" (Psalms 115:16). And the Sages instituted a blessing for each type of benefit: for fruits of the earth, 'Who creates the fruit of the ground'; for fruits of the tree, 'Who creates the fruit of the tree'; except for wine, due to its importance in gladdening the heart, as it is said: "And wine gladdens the heart of man" (Psalms 104:15), they instituted a special blessing: "Who creates the fruit of the vine." Similarly, for bread, they also instituted a special blessing due to its importance in sustaining the heart, as it is written: "And bread sustains the heart of man" (Psalms 104:15), they instituted the blessing 'Hamotzi'.

It is a preferred mitzvah to bless over the bread when it is whole, and not to cut it first and then bless over it if a whole one is brought before him. And even if he cuts a piece - he should bless when the piece is whole, and he should not cut it until after the blessing, and the entire blessing needs to be completed while it is whole or the piece is whole. And if there are others at the table who respond 'Amen' after him, he should not cut until the response of 'Amen' from most of the responders is finished. This is specifically when they are fulfilling their obligation with his blessing, for then the response of 'Amen' is part of the blessing. But if they are not fulfilling their obligation with his blessing, he does not need to wait for their response of 'Amen'. Now, whether he should not start cutting at all or should start cutting during the blessing is a matter of debate, as will be explained with the help of Heaven.

The language of the Gemara in Berachot (39b): "The halacha is that one blesses and then breaks [the bread]." And the language of the Rambam in Chapter 7: "One completes the blessing and then breaks [the bread]." But Tosafot and the Rosh wrote that the intention is not to separate the piece from the bread until after the blessing, see there. And this is the language of the Tur: "One should cut the piece of bread for breaking and leave it attached to the bread, and start to bless, and after finishing the blessing, separate it, so that the blessing concludes while the bread is still whole." End of quote. And their reasoning: If one starts to cut after the blessing, there will be a significant interruption between the blessing of 'Hamotzi' and the eating (Tur).

And what amount should remain attached? Our master, the Beit Yosef, explained as follows: "One must cut a little so that if one holds the slice, the rest of the loaf will rise with it. If not, it is considered a slice. One should leave it attached to the loaf and begin the blessing, and after finishing the blessing, separate it so that the blessing concludes while the bread is still whole." End of quote. However, on Shabbat, one should not begin cutting at all until after the blessing, so that one blesses over two whole loaves. Even though when attached in this manner it is still called a whole loaf, we are concerned that one might cut more than this amount before the blessing is finished, or might completely cut it before the blessing is finished, thereby not blessing over two whole loaves. This is the simple custom and should not be changed. It seems to me that with thin bread that is immediately cut, even on weekdays, one should finish the blessing first, and at the conclusion of the blessing, immediately cut or break it, because with thin bread, partial attachment is not relevant as is known. (Nevertheless, on Shabbat, if one did as on weekdays, it does not cause harm.)

One should not cut a very small piece for "Hamotzi" because it appears stingy, nor a piece larger than an egg because it appears gluttonous, and this is not the proper way. This applies on weekdays. However, on Shabbat, it is a mitzvah to cut a large piece that will suffice for the entire meal, and it does not appear gluttonous since one does not do this every day (as per the Gemara there according to Rashi's explanation). Similarly, on weekdays, when one eats with their household members or guests who fulfill their obligation with his blessing, and the host gives them from his piece, it is a mitzvah to cut a large piece so that it will suffice to give from the piece to each of the participants, and not from the remaining bread. The measure of this piece for one person: some say it should be the size of an olive and one should consume it all at once (Magen Avraham 7), and some say it does not need to be the size of an olive (ibid.), since even any amount is fit for a blessing and half an olive's worth is sufficient, and so is the custom (the Gra). With our bread, the simple custom is to cut a large part from the whole loaf and from it to cut the required amount for "Hamotzi," because given the large size of our loaves it is almost impossible otherwise, but with smaller loaves, one should do as explained.

All blessings over enjoyment must be in the past tense, for this thing has already been created. And the reason we bless using the term 'Borei' (Creator), such as 'Borei Minei Mezonot' (Creator of various kinds of sustenance), 'Borei Pri Ha'etz' (Creator of the fruit of the tree), 'Borei Pri Ha'adamah' (Creator of the fruit of the ground), is because 'Borei' is also in the past tense, as it is written: "Borei Hashamayim" (Creator of the heavens), "La'oseh Orim Gedolim" (To the Maker of the great lights) (Psalms 136:7). We are obligated to use the language of the scripture in every way possible. It appears to me that the scripture chose this term because it also includes the present tense, as the Holy One, blessed be He, renews the act of creation every day continuously, and similarly, He creates at all times and at every moment, as His supervision does not cease for even a moment. Therefore, we use a term that includes everything, for what we eat is in the past tense and also in the present tense, meaning that even now, at this very moment, He is creating. Therefore, in the blessing of 'Shehakol' (that everything) one should say 'Nihyeh' with a Segol vowel under the Yod, which is a participle tense like 'Borei' (Magen Avraham, Siman 204:14, and also written in Ma'atz and Machatzit Hashekel). Some wish to say 'Nihyah' with a Kamatz vowel under the Yod (see Magen Avraham 8), which is strictly past tense, but this is not the main opinion. The main opinion is to say it with a Segol under the Yod.

And regarding the blessing of 'Hamotzi,' there is a consideration. In the Gemara (Berachot 38a), it is said that 'Motzi' certainly implies the past, as Balaam said: "El Motziam miMitzrayim" ("God who brought them out of Egypt"), and they had already left. Regarding 'Hamotzi,' there is a dispute: some hold that 'Hamotzi' also implies the past, as it is written: "Hamotzi lecha mayim mitzur haChalamish" ("Who brings forth water for you from the rock"); while others hold that it implies the future, as it is written in Parashat Va'era: "Hamotzi etchem mitachat sivlot Mitzrayim" ("Who will bring you out from under the burdens of Egypt"), which is a promise to bring us out. Nevertheless, the Gemara concludes: "And the halacha is 'Hamotzi,'" implying there that the reason is to show that the term 'Hamotzi' also refers to the past. 

In truth, this is not clear, as in all cases, one should choose the clearest language. However, we find a similar situation in the first chapter of Pesachim regarding the blessing 'Al Biur Chametz.' In the Jerusalem Talmud, it is said that this is to avoid the merging of letters, meaning the world ends with a 'mem,' and if one says 'Motzi,' the two 'mems' will merge. Although 'lechem min' also places two 'mems' together, this is because the verse states: "Lehotzi lechem min haaretz" ("To bring forth bread from the earth"), and it is impossible to change the language of the scripture, which is not the case with 'Hamotzi' (Tosafot there), and the explanation is not satisfactory, as is clear.

I have seen someone write that if we scrutinize the phrase 'Hamotzi lechem min haaretz,' it is as if bread actually comes out of the earth. The intention is to hint at the future when ready-made loaves will come forth, and thus the term 'Hamotzi' is preferable as it includes the future as well (see Taz, section 4). In my opinion, it appears as I stated earlier, that intentionally the phrase was chosen to denote the present, which includes both past and future. For the phrase "Hamotzi lecha mayim mitzur" refers to both past and present, as at the time Moses said this, water was coming out from the rock. Therefore, to show that the Holy One, Blessed be He, never removes His providence from the world, even for a moment, and continually brings forth bread to the world, and even during baking, the providence of the Holy One, Blessed be He, ensures the bread bakes. 

However, because it is continuous, it is called 'nature,' and nature itself is divine providence. But because it is continuous, we are not amazed by it, but to those who reflect, these are constant miracles. This is the meaning of "Shiviti Hashem lenegdi tamid" ("I have set the Lord always before me"), meaning that in everything I see, it is only the Lord alone, and there is none else. One should pause between 'lechem' and 'min' to avoid merging the letters. 

If many are gathered and want to fulfill their obligation with the blessing of the one breaking the bread, they should intend to hear the blessing and respond 'Amen,' and the one blessing should intend to the 'Amen' they say. However, among us, everyone recites 'Hamotzi' for themselves, and still, there is an obligation to respond 'Amen' to one's friend's blessing. Even before one's own blessing, one can respond 'Amen,' and it is not considered an interruption. But after the blessing, one should not respond 'Amen,' even if hearing another also recite 'Hamotzi,' so as not to appear as if responding 'Amen' to one's own blessing, as stated in Siman 51, see there in section 4, as ruled by our teacher, the Beit Yosef.

In the Jerusalem Talmud at the end of the first chapter of Challa it says: "A person performs ten commandments before eating a piece of bread: Do not plow with an ox and a donkey together, do not sow mixed seeds, do not muzzle an ox while it is threshing, gleanings, forgotten sheaves, and the corner of the field, terumah, first tithe, second tithe, and challah (this requires examination, as there are also bikkurim). When Rabbi Yitzchak came to sit, he would stretch out his ten fingers" (see there). Therefore, our master the Beit Yosef wrote in section 4: "One should place both hands on the bread during the blessing, as there are ten fingers corresponding to the ten commandments related to bread. Thus, there are ten words in the blessing of 'Hamotzi,' ten words in the verse 'He causes grass to grow for the cattle,' ten words in the verse 'The eyes of all look to You with hope,' ten words in the verse 'A land of wheat and barley,' and ten words in the verse 'And He will give you'" (end of quote). And if one has a cast, it must be removed. When saying the name of God, one should lift the bread, and on Shabbat, one should lift both (Magen Avraham subsection 10). One must be careful not to recite the 'Hamotzi' blessing before holding the bread, as every blessing must be immediately before the action, as written regarding the lulav in section 651 (see there). The reason we say 'bringing forth bread from the earth' and not 'from the ground,' as in the blessing 'who creates the fruit of the ground,' is because in the verse in 'Bless the Lord, O my soul,' it is written: 'to bring forth bread from the earth,' and there are additional reasons for this (the Eliyah Rabbah wrote in subsection 5 in the name of the Shlah that one should have more intention in the blessing over the table than in other blessings, because eating and drinking can lead a person to coarseness of nature, and one must contemplate to draw his heart towards the desires of the Holy One, Blessed be He, and not towards the desires of food and drink, end of quote). The Magen Avraham wrote in subsection 2 that the Mahari"l would cut around the bread like a ring, leaving the middle attached, and would break from the bottom to the top, and with a thin cake, he would place eight fingers on top and two thumbs below, recite the blessing, and break (end of quote). I do not understand why he did this only with a thin cake, and perhaps it is not specific.

It is stated in the Gemara (Berachot 40a): "One who breaks bread may not break it until they bring salt or a condiment before each and every one." Rava visited the house of the Exilarch; they brought out bread for him, and he ate immediately, without waiting for them to bring salt or a condiment. They asked him why he did so, and he replied: "This bread does not require waiting." Rashi explained: this is an expression of delay, as in "his chariot tarried" (Judges 5:28), meaning this is clean bread and does not need a condiment. Based on this, the Tur and Shulchan Aruch wrote in section 5: "One should not break bread until salt or a condiment is brought before him to season the piece he breaks. If the bread is clean or seasoned with spices or salt like ours, or if one intends to eat dry bread, it is not necessary to wait." The Tur did not mention "if one intends to eat dry bread," and the Rambam in chapter 7 mentioned only this, as we will explain, and there is a significant difference between them.

And this is the language of the Rambam: "The one who breaks (the bread) is not permitted to break until they bring salt or a condiment before each and every one, unless they intend to eat dry bread." End of quote. And our master the Beit Yosef wrote everything. And in my humble opinion, it is not possible to say this, for one who is meticulous in the language of the Tur, who wrote: "salt or a condiment to dip the piece of the breaking (bread) in," it seems clear that it does not refer to the condiment for the entire meal, but rather to something for the piece of 'Hamotzi' (the blessing over bread) because of its honor. For if it is coarse bread, it needs to be dipped in salt or a condiment, and if it is fine or spiced bread or salted, it has a good taste even without salt or a condiment. This is according to the explanation of Rashi and Tosafot there. But the Rambam did not mention: 'to dip the piece of the breaking (bread) in,' but rather 'until they bring salt or a condiment,' meaning what one wants to eat in the meal. If one eats only bread with salt, it is enough to bring salt. And if one wants to eat some condiment, they need to bring the condiment before them. And the reason is that since the blessing of 'Hamotzi' exempts also the condiment of the entire meal, they need to be before him at the time of 'Hamotzi,' and not because it is necessary to dip the piece of 'Hamotzi' in them. Therefore, the Rambam did not mention a distinction between coarse bread and fine bread, for it does not depend on this. Rather, he mentioned that if they intend to eat only dry bread, they do not need to wait. And he explains in the Gemara what Rava said: 'This one does not need to wait,' meaning it applies to himself, that he does not need to wait because he intends to eat only dry bread. And if so, our master the Beit Yosef, who followed the method of the Tur, should not have mentioned this intent to eat dry bread, since this is because of the honor of the piece of 'Hamotzi.' And I have not seen anyone who has raised this issue, and it requires further investigation. And according to what we have explained in the intention of the Rambam, the first dish should be on the table at the time of the blessing of 'Hamotzi.'

And our teacher the Rema wrote: "Nevertheless, it is a mitzvah to bring salt to every table before breaking bread, because the table is akin to the altar, and eating is like a sacrifice, as it is said: 'On all your sacrifices you shall offer salt.' And it protects from misfortune." The Midrash states that when the Israelites sit and wait for one another, Satan accuses them, but the covenant of salt protects them (Magen Avraham). The Kabbalists instructed to dip the piece of bread in salt, and this is the practice of all God-fearing people. It is forbidden to kill a louse on the table on which one eats, and similarly, not to do anything repulsive on it, since it is likened to the altar, as it is written: 'This is the table that is before the Lord.' (See Magen Avraham, who wrote that it is good to speak words of Torah rather than sit idly, but better than both is not to interrupt at all. This is the main halacha.)

After reciting the blessing of "Hamotzi," one should eat immediately and not engage in any conversation between the blessing and the eating. Similarly, as long as one is chewing, one should not speak until swallowing the piece of "Hamotzi." If one spoke between the blessing and the eating, one must recite the blessing again. However, if one spoke while chewing, there is no need to recite the blessing again. Even if one spoke about something related to "Hamotzi," such as "bring salt" or "bring a condiment," or even if it is not related to "Hamotzi" but pertains to the meal, such as saying "give so-and-so to eat" or even "give food to the animal"—which is also considered a need of the meal since it is forbidden to eat before feeding one's animal, as it is written: "I will provide grass in your fields for your cattle," and afterward it says, "and you will eat and be satisfied" (Talmud, Berakhot 40a)—in such cases, these words and similar ones are not considered an interruption after the fact, but it is ideally prohibited to say even these things. It is written that a person should drink before their animal, as we find with Rebecca, who said: "Drink, and I will also water your camels" (Magen Avraham, section 18, quoting Sefer Chasidim).

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote regarding the aforementioned law, and this is his language: "The matter of one who speaks idle words needing to repeat the blessing, this applies specifically if he spoke before the one who breaks the bread ate. However, after he has eaten, the conversation is not considered an interruption, even though the others who are reclining have not yet eaten. For they have all fulfilled their obligation with the eating of the one who broke the bread, since it is not necessary for everyone to eat from the piece of the one who broke the bread; they only do so to show their affection for the mitzvah." End of quote. The source of this law is from the Rokeach (Beit Yosef). He compared this to the cup of Kiddush, where ideally it is proper for all those reclining to taste from it, but after the fact, everyone fulfills their obligation with the drinking of the one who recited the blessing. Similarly here, ideally it is proper for everyone to eat from the piece of the one who broke the bread, but after the fact, everyone fulfills their obligation with the tasting of the one who broke the bread. And since he tasted, it is as if everyone tasted. Therefore, their conversation is not considered an interruption between the blessing and the 'Hamotzi,' but as if it occurred after the 'Hamotzi.'

Many great authorities disagree on this matter, and they hold that this is not a valid comparison at all. There, it is a blessing on a mitzvah, and after the fact, if the one who recites the blessing drinks, everyone fulfills their obligation, and they themselves do not drink from it. But here, everyone needs to eat, and it is a blessing of enjoyment. Is it possible that the listener would be better off than if he had recited the blessing himself and then interrupted, in which case he would need to recite the blessing again? Just because he listens, he should not need to recite the blessing again (Magen Avraham 19). And since he interrupted with conversation before deriving benefit, the blessing is nullified, and he derives benefit without a blessing (Taz 8). Furthermore, the primary aspect is their response of "Amen," which is considered as if they themselves had recited the blessing. Therefore, one should not interrupt between his "Amen" and his eating (ibid.). Additionally, in truth, only with Kiddush and similar blessings do listeners fulfill their obligation through the drinking of the one who recites the blessing alone. But with the blessings of the meal, they do not fulfill their obligation through his tasting, and each person at the table must taste for themselves (Eliyah Rabbah 13). And also, our master the Beit Yosef in his major work disagrees with this ruling, see there.

In my humble opinion, I do not see any objection to all of this. As the Rokeach and Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) have stated: the tasting that the one who breaks bread tastes is as if everyone has tasted, for it is certain that for both Kiddush and Havdalah, each individual is obligated to sanctify and perform Havdalah and to drink the cup, but we say that everyone fulfills their obligation through the blessing and tasting of the one who sanctifies. Similarly, we say that everyone fulfills their obligation through his blessing and tasting as if everyone had blessed and tasted. Additional proof can be found in what will be explained in Siman 271, that if the one who sanctifies does not taste and another tastes, he has fulfilled his obligation. Now, the argument is even stronger: if the tasting of another is like his tasting, certainly his tasting is like the tasting of another. Even according to the Geonim who disagree regarding Kiddush, they agree with other matters there. And if the concern is that they will eat by themselves afterward and their washing is for eating, nonetheless, what difference does it make? Is the obligation to drink, which the Torah mandates, less than the desire to eat? In any case, in the end, we must say that his tasting is as if all the participants have tasted. (And the proof that the Magen Avraham brought from Tosafot Pesachim 101 regarding Rabbi Yitzchak is puzzling to me, for what comparison is there between a change of place and speaking? And even though Rabbi Yitzchak holds that a change of place when one has drunk does not require a new blessing, nonetheless, without drinking, it is certainly not comparable. From the Rosh and Mordechai, it is clear that there is no proof for one who investigates there. And what the Taz wrote regarding tefillin is completely puzzling, as is clear to one who examines his words there thoroughly.)

Our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in Section 7: "Reuven was washing his hands for eating, and Yaakov was reciting the blessing of 'Hamotzi' with the intention to fulfill the obligation for the listeners. Afterward, Reuven dried his hands and recited the blessing 'Al Netilat Yadayim' – this is not considered an interruption, and he fulfills his obligation with Yaakov's blessing and does not need to recite 'Hamotzi' again." End of quote. The reason is that this is not worse than other needs of the meal that are not considered an interruption, as explained. It appears to me that even if he himself forgot and recited the blessing of 'Hamotzi' before the blessing of 'Al Netilat Yadayim' – it is also not considered an interruption for the same reason. And it is obvious that the one reciting the blessing must intend to fulfill the obligation for others, and the listeners must intend to fulfill their obligation and answer 'Amen'.

If one forgot and ate without reciting the blessing of "Hamotzi": if he has not yet finished his meal, it is obvious that he should recite the blessing for what he eats afterwards. If he has finished his meal, he should not recite the blessing. However, it is proper that he should recite the blessing and eat an olive-sized portion while it is still before Birkat Hamazon, for according to the Raavad, one must recite the blessing even afterwards, though we do not follow this opinion. Therefore, it is proper to do so (Magen Avraham, section 21). And if one is in doubt whether he recited the blessing of "Hamotzi" or not, it is like any other doubt concerning rabbinic blessings, and he should not recite the blessing. And what the Tur states in the name of the Rambam that he should recite the blessing is not so according to the version of the Rambam that we have (Beit Yosef).

If one recited the blessing "Shehakol" over bread, he has fulfilled his obligation, because it is a general blessing. However, if one recited "Borei Minei Mezonot" or "Ha'adama," he has not fulfilled his obligation. There are those who say that one has fulfilled his obligation with the blessing "Borei Minei Mezonot" (Shu”t Siman 13 in the name of Birkei Yosef and Even HaOzer), and the reason seems to be because bread is certainly a type of sustenance. But in my humble opinion, it seems that one has not fulfilled his obligation, because it is not a clarified blessing and it is not the blessing instituted by the sages for bread, therefore one has not fulfilled his obligation. It is not comparable to "Shehakol," which includes everything. And if you argue that bread is sustenance, since we bless in the Grace After Meals: "for the land and for the sustenance," everything is called sustenance (Eruvin 30a), and yet if one recited "Borei Minei Mezonot" over fruit of the tree or fruit of the ground, he has not fulfilled his obligation. The same applies to bread, and this requires further study.

If one recited the blessing over bread: 'Blessed is the Merciful One, Ruler of the Universe, Master of this bread,' or even if he did not conclude with 'bread' – he has fulfilled his obligation, for blessings can be recited in any language. Even the Grace after Meals can be recited in any language, as it is taught in the chapter "These are Recited," and all the more so for blessings before eating, which are only rabbinic in origin. This is explicitly stated in Berachot (40b). 

It is not specifically that he recited the blessing in Aramaic; the same rule applies if he recited it in any language, provided it translates to: 'Blessed are You, Lord our God, King of the Universe, etc.' – he has fulfilled his obligation. And although 'Master of this bread' is not the same wording as 'Who brings forth bread from the earth,' we are not concerned about this, as the essential meaning is present in this blessing. 

This is what they said in the Gemara there, that even if it is not said in the sacred language as the Sages instituted, he has fulfilled his obligation, see there. The intention is regarding the conclusion of 'Who brings forth bread from the earth,' but concerning 'Lord our God, King of the Universe,' it is certainly required and indispensable, as we say there. However, if he said: 'How beautiful is this bread, blessed is the Omnipresent who created it' – he has not fulfilled his obligation (there), and although in the Jerusalem Talmud it is explained that even in such a case he has fulfilled his obligation, see there, in our Gemara it is not so. This is included in the rule: 'Anyone who changes from the formula that the Sages instituted in blessings – has not fulfilled his obligation' (this seems to be my humble opinion and it is puzzling that the Tur and Shulchan Aruch did not mention this law).

The Sages taught in the Mishnah (Berachot 42a): "If they were sitting – each one blesses for himself; if they reclined – one blesses for all of them." This means that if they ate without any formal arrangement, but were simply sitting and each one began to eat without agreeing to eat together, they do not join together, and each one blesses for himself. But if they reclined, one blesses for all of them (Tosafot Rid). Specifically for them, who ate while reclining, they needed to recline. However, our sitting is considered a fixed arrangement for us, similar to their reclining, because they were accustomed to each one reclining on his own bed at his table, but now we all eat at one table. And when we eat together, it is our fixed arrangement (Tosafot). And Rav Hai Gaon explained 'reclined' in the sense of surrounding, when they all sat around, which indicates a fixed sitting arrangement, as translated: "And they sat to eat bread" – "and they surrounded to eat bread" (Tosafot Rid).

And it is said in the Gemara there, and so it is in the Rif, that if they say: "Let's go and eat bread in such-and-such a place," even though they did not recline, even if each one eats from his own loaf, it is considered as if they are established together, and one blesses for all of them. As it is taught: "Ten people who were walking on the road, even though they all eat from one loaf, each one blesses for himself. If they went up and sat down, even though each one eats from his own loaf, one blesses for all of them." And we establish: such as when they say: "Let's go and eat bread in such-and-such a place," so concludes the Rif.

And so wrote the Tur, and he wrote that if they are two or many, one blesses for all of them. His words: This means that even though for Birkat Hamazon (Grace After Meals) they do not combine unless there are three for a zimun (invitation to bless), for Hamotzi (blessing over bread), even two can have one bless (Beit Yosef). And the reason is: for Birkat Hamazon, where they are about to separate from each other, we require specifically three. But for Hamotzi, where they are coming together, even two suffice (Bach and Magen Avraham, section 23). The Tur further wrote: that the head of the household with his household members is considered a fixed group even without reclining, and nowadays, when we are not accustomed to reclining, our sitting is considered a fixed group even for members of a group, as their reclining is similar. And so wrote our Rabbi, the Rema, in section 11, that the head of the household with his household members is considered as if they reclined, even if they sit without reclining (Magen Avraham, section 24), and this is from the Jerusalem Talmud there. And I am puzzled by our Rabbi the Rema, why he wrote this law, since nowadays it suffices even for guests to sit, and the head of the household with his household members also requires sitting. If so, there is no difference now between guests and the head of the household with his household members. Also, it is difficult regarding the Tur, and to say that they wrote this according to the Talmudic law is not their way, and it requires further investigation.

And know that there is an opinion that with reclining, it is not necessary for everyone to recline; if only some of them are reclining, one can recite the blessing for all, even if others are not reclining (there, sub-paragraph 25, in the name of Sh"G). According to this, it would seem that for us, since sitting is considered like reclining, even if some are sitting and some are standing. However, it cannot be said this way, for standing is certainly considered a temporary manner, and we require that all should be sitting, and even the head of the household with his household members need to all be sitting, and one standing does not fulfill his obligation with the blessing of the head of the household. Also, this primary ruling that we do not require all to recline is not mentioned by the poskim, but even if we say so regarding reclining, it is not said regarding sitting (and even though in the context of Havdalah the Tosafot wrote on page 43 in the commentary "since" that even standing they fulfill their obligation because they establish themselves to fulfill it there, nevertheless, in the context of a meal it does not apply, for certainly, throughout the meal they sit, as it is not customary to eat the entire meal standing, and this is the primary ruling in law).

And this is the language of our master, the Beit Yosef, in section 11: "If there were two or many people, one recites the blessing for all of them, and this is specifically when they recline... But if they were sitting without reclining... And if they said, 'We will eat here or in a certain place'... it is considered fixed even without reclining. And nowadays... our sitting at one table or without a table with one cloth is considered fixed... And for us, even if they set a place for their eating or the homeowner with his household members - it is not effective unless they are sitting at one table or with one cloth" end quote. And it appears to me that what he wrote: "or with one cloth," meaning even without a table, this is according to the custom of their country where they would sit on the ground and not always eat at a table, but in our country, anything without a table is not considered fixed at all.

Additionally, it is written in section 12: "If they were riding and said, 'Let us eat,' even though each one eats from his own loaf, without dismounting from their animals – they combine, provided they stopped in one place. But if they were eating while walking – they do not combine. And if they were eating in a field, scattered and dispersed, even though they all eat at the same time and from the same loaf, since they did not establish a place and are eating scattered – they do not combine." End of quote. The explanation of his words: although it was explained above that merely saying [to join together] does not help except to prevent separation, nonetheless they need to sit at a table when they are indoors. However, in a field, saying [to join together] helps even while riding if they stopped. But if they eat while walking – saying [to join together] does not help, and similarly, if they eat while scattered even if they sit on the ground – saying [to join together] does not help. And when sitting in a wagon, there is someone who is uncertain if saying [to join together] helps (Magen Avraham section 27), and it appears that it does not help if they eat while the horse is moving, unless they stop the horse, in which case saying [to join together] helps. And on a boat, saying [to join together] helps (ibid.), and also in train cars, saying [to join together] certainly helps, as this is just like an actual house, provided they sit next to each other and not scattered or dispersed. And it has already been explained that there is no difference in all this whether each one eats from his own loaf or they eat from the same loaf.

Additionally, it is written in section 13: "In a case where they did not establish a place (for eating), where we say that each one blesses for himself, if the one who blesses had the intention to include them and they intended to be included, they are included." In other words, after the fact, they are included in the blessing of one of them even without establishing a place, if they prepared themselves to be included in his blessing and the one blessing prepared himself to include them. And even though it is obvious that even when establishing a place, they need to intend to be included and he needs to intend to include them, when establishing a place, it is typically so, but without establishing a place, they need to prepare for this, which means by verbally stating: 'We intend to be included in his blessing,' and he says: 'I intend to include them,' for this itself acts as establishing a place. There are those who reject this from the law, because the Rosh explicitly wrote that if they did not recline, even though hearing is like responding and even if they said 'Amen' - they are not included, and he similarly wrote this in the name of Rashi (Magen Avraham, section 28). I say that this is not a contradiction, as it certainly is so and it is explicit in the Talmudic discussion, and even though hearing is like responding in everything, it states in the Jerusalem Talmud that this is except for the Grace after Meals, and similarly for 'Hamotzi' (there). The reason is that since one benefits individually, he must bless individually unless there was an establishment of a place, but our master the Beit Yosef is referring to explicit preparation, which itself acts as establishing a place (this is how it appears to me in my humble opinion). And know that all these laws apply to bread, but concerning wine and the blessing over grains and other items, whether one can fulfill his obligation with his friend's blessing and the law regarding establishing a place will be explained, with God's help, in Siman 174 and Siman 213.

And know that among us, there is no custom at all for everyone to fulfill their obligation with the head of the household's blessing of "Hamotzi," and all the more so for guests who are eating together in a fixed manner; rather, each member of the household or guest recites the blessing for themselves. And in the Gemara (Berachot 53a), it is explicitly explained that it is a greater mitzvah for one person to recite the blessing for everyone, because "In the multitude of people is the King's glory," as it says there. And similarly, one of the great early authorities wrote that it is better when one person recites the blessing for everyone (Kesef Mishneh, Laws of Blessings, Chapter 1, in the name of the Ra'avad). We must say that the reason among us is because it is not customary to wait to recite the blessing of "Hamotzi" until everyone has washed their hands and is seated around the table. Rather, each one washes their hands and recites "Hamotzi" while others have not yet washed, and even those who have washed are not yet seated at the table. Therefore, it is entirely impossible for one person to fulfill another's obligation with the blessing of "Hamotzi." According to this, if there is a place where the head of the household waits to recite "Hamotzi" until everyone has washed and is seated at the table, it is certainly better for the head of the household to recite "Hamotzi" and for them to answer "Amen," and he should intend to fulfill their obligation, and they should intend to fulfill their obligation with his blessing. (And it is possible that they hold according to the words of the Rambam in a responsum brought there by the Kesef Mishneh, even though it has no resolution there; see and understand.)

We hold that the head of the household recites the blessing of 'Hamotzi' in order that he may break [the bread] generously. And even if there is someone greater than him at the table, nonetheless, he recites the blessing. There is an opinion that if there is a distinguished guest, he can honor the guest [to recite the blessing] (Magen Avraham 32, in the name of the Levush), but this does not seem to be the case in the Gemara there, which brings an incident where Rabbi Avahu honored Rabbi Zeira to break [the bread], and he did not want to because the head of the household recites the blessing. And if you would think that he could honor [someone else], Rabbi Zeira should not have gone against the words of the head of the household, for 'whatever the head of the household tells you, you should do', but because it is against the law, therefore he did not want to (and the words of the Magen Avraham are perplexing, and the Machatzit Hashekel struggles with this, see there). And if it is not in the house of the head of the household but in an inn and they are all guests, the greatest among them recites the blessing. And if there is a Kohen there who is equal in stature to all the diners or even slightly less, it is a mitzvah to give him precedence, but if he is an ignoramus, the Torah scholar takes precedence over him, and it is forbidden for the scholar to give him precedence. However, if he is only slightly less, it is a mitzvah to give him precedence and he will have long life because of it, but there is no obligation to give him precedence. And the one who recites the blessing should first say: 'With the permission of my masters and teachers', but among us, there is no such custom because everyone recites the blessing for himself, as it is written (see Magen Avraham 33, and Eliyah Rabbah 22 disagrees with him, see there and delve deeply).

And the one who recites the blessing is not permitted to break the bread until the majority of those responding have finished saying 'Amen', and there is no need to wait for those who prolong it excessively. The participants are not permitted to taste [the bread] until the one who recites the blessing has tasted it, but it is permitted to give each person their portion from the piece of 'hamotzi' before he eats. This is not considered an interruption between the blessing and the eating, as this is also part of the eating since he is blessing on behalf of everyone. However, in the Jerusalem Talmud, it is stated that Rav would take a taste of the 'hamotzi' with his left hand and distribute it with his right hand (Magen Avraham, section 34). Nonetheless, in any case, the participants are forbidden to taste before the one who recites the blessing tastes. All of this applies if they need the one who recites the blessing to give them from his loaf, but if each person has his own loaf before him and does not need the one who recites the blessing to give them from his loaf, they are permitted to break the bread before the one who recites the blessing tastes. However, on Shabbat, they are not permitted to taste before, even if each person has his own loaf before him, unless each has two loaves before him, for otherwise, they fulfill the obligation of the two loaves with the one who recites the blessing, and they are compelled to wait for him until he tastes.

The one who breaks bread gives a piece before each person and should be careful not to give it by throwing, as it is forbidden to throw bread. He should also be careful not to give the piece of bread directly from his hand to the hands of those seated, rather he places it before them, and they take it from the table. There is no prohibition in this, but it is considered a bad sign to give directly from hand to hand, and your sign for this is: "Zion spreads forth her hands." However, to a mourner, one does place it from hand to hand, as it is stated in the Midrash Eicha and also written by the Rambam in Chapter 7, Law 5. On Shabbat, even to a mourner, one does not give it to his hand, because there is no mourning on Shabbat. The one who breaks the bread extends his hand first to the bowl to eat, and if he wants to honor someone greater than himself, he is permitted. There is no question that if there is someone greater, why does he break the bread, as it can be said that he is the master of the house, and as it is written, only the master of the house breaks the bread. Our teacher, the Rema, wrote in Paragraph 20 that one should eat the piece of 'hamotzi' in its entirety before eating other bread so that it is eaten with appetite due to the affection for the mitzvah. One should not feed the piece of 'hamotzi' to a non-Jew or an animal, and some want to say to leave a bit of the piece of 'hamotzi' until the end, but we follow the words of our teacher, the Rema (in Tosafot 47, it is explicitly proven that the groom needs to break the bread).

And one who does not eat cannot recite the blessing of 'Hamotzi' for someone else, and this is true for all blessings over enjoyment. For only in the blessings of commandments can one person bless on behalf of another because all of Israel are responsible for one another. When one does not fulfill, it is as if he himself did not fulfill. But this is not the case for blessings over enjoyment, which are not recited unless one benefits. However, for minors who cannot bless for themselves, one may bless even if he himself does not eat, to educate them in the commandments. And even on Shabbat, when there is an obligation to eat bread, one should not bless for his fellow if he himself is not eating. Only the blessing of 'Borei Peri Hagafen' for Kiddush, both at night and during the day, and 'Al Achilat Matzah' with the blessing of 'Hamotzi' on the first night of Passover, which are complete obligations like all commandments, can one bless on behalf of his fellow.

There is a priority in the quality of bread to bless 'Hamotzi' when both types are before him and he wishes to eat from both. This means that wheat bread takes precedence over barley bread, whole bread takes precedence over sliced bread, clean (refined) bread takes precedence over unclean (less refined) bread, large bread takes precedence over small bread, whether in slices or whole loaves. However, a small whole loaf takes precedence over a large slice, even if the whole loaf is not as refined as the slice. This means if the slice is made from fine flour and the whole loaf is made from simple flour, and even though the slice has two advantages over the whole loaf, the whole loaf still takes precedence when they are of the same type (see Magen Avraham, subparagraph 1). And for two slices, one large and one refined, the refined one takes precedence, as refinement is superior to size. Similarly, with two whole loaves, one large and one refined, the refined one takes precedence (there, subparagraph 7). Rabbi Yosef Karo wrote in section 4: "And if both are refined and one is whiter than the other, he blesses on the whiter one" (end quote). If the other one is larger, it is questionable (there, subparagraph 8), and he can do as he wishes. It seems to me that with our bread, this rule does not apply at all, since in our case, the whiter it is, the more refined it is.

And this is all with one type, but if one is wheat and one is barley—the wheat takes precedence even if it is a piece and small and not clean, and the barley is whole and large and clean. Because it is written: "A land of wheat and barley," and the verse mentions wheat before barley, it takes precedence in all matters. And it is stated in the Gemara (Berachot 39b) that a God-fearing person fulfills both, for if he has before him a whole [loaf] of barley and a piece of wheat—he places the piece within the whole and breaks from both together and blesses. And so ruled the Rambam, the Tur, and the Shulchan Aruch. And even though the Gemara itself states that the primary law is that the piece of wheat takes precedence, only that for extra piety a God-fearing person does so, nevertheless, since it is possible to act as a God-fearing person, it follows that one must do so since there is no loss in this. And this is specifically with barley bread because it is mentioned in the Torah, but with our rye bread that we call "karein," even though it is a type of barley, nevertheless, since it is not explicitly mentioned in the Torah—there is no need for even a God-fearing person to do so (see there, section 2). Therefore, we do not do so, and besides this, with our bread, it is impossible to place the piece within the whole.

Some have written that if there are two people, one should bless over the whole loaf of barley bread and the other over the piece of wheat bread (Rashal, Bach, Shlah, and Mat'e Moshe). It seems to me that the explanation is as follows: Certainly, if one person fulfills his obligation with the blessing of the other, it is not possible to say this, but rather, for example, in our case where each person blesses for himself and both sit equally at the table. Consequently, one takes the piece of wheat bread as is proper, and then the other can take the whole loaf of barley bread and bless. There is no need to wait until the first finishes the blessing and cutting; at that moment it is as if there is no other bread before him, and he blesses over the whole loaf. The reason for this is that since we see that the Talmud took care to fulfill the obligation for both, we do the same out of respect for the whole loaf. This applies when there is a piece and a whole loaf of two different types, but when both are whole loaves or both are pieces, or both are of the same type, it should not be done this way. Rather, both should bless over what the law dictates. For example, if both are whole loaves or pieces and one is wheat, they should both bless over the wheat. If both are wheat or barley, each should bless over one of them. If one is wheat and one is barley, they should both bless over the wheat, and one should wait until the other blesses and then he blesses (see Magen Avraham 2, who questioned this, but according to what I have written, it is understandable, and examine it well).

Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in paragraph 4: "Bread made from barley and bread made from spelt - one blesses on the barley bread because it is one of the seven species, even though spelt is better," end quote. Similarly, the Tur wrote, and it is from the Jerusalem Talmud, Chapter 6 of Berachot. The intention is that even though spelt is a type of wheat, nevertheless, since barley is explicitly mentioned in the Torah, it has an advantage over spelt even though it is a type of wheat, just as wheat has an advantage over barley because it is mentioned first in the Torah. Therefore, this is specifically regarding barley bread itself. But for barley-like species, such as our rye bread, surely spelt comes first because it is a type of wheat. And we do not know at all about spelt (and this is also the intention of the Magen Avraham in subsection 6, and the Taz in subsection 4 struggled with this, and the matter is simple as I wrote).

It has already been explained that all this applies when one wants to eat from both of them. But if one only wants to eat from one of them, he should recite the blessing over that one, and he does not need to be concerned about the other, even if it is more significant or preferred by him. Conversely, when one wants to eat from both, he should recite the blessing as explained, even if the second bread is more preferred by him. This is what our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in his great book. There is an opinion that according to the Rambam, which will be explained in Siman 211 regarding fruits, that one follows what is preferred, the same applies here (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 6). In my humble opinion, it seems that this is not the case. Specifically with fruits, where there is no set meal, one follows the Rambam's ruling to go after what is preferred. But not when it comes to a set meal when one's intention is to eat from both. And there is proof from the Rambam himself, who wrote this law in chapter 7 without mentioning the preference, and in chapter 8 regarding fruits, he did mention it. Rather, it is certainly as I have written (and I have seen in the Ba'er Heitev, subparagraph 3, that the Yad Aharon also challenged this opinion).

Bread of non-Jews and bread of Jews, and that of non-Jews is better, and that is when it is clean and the bread of Jews is not clean. If he is not careful about the bread of non-Jews, he may bless over whichever he prefers, for each bread has an advantage: this one because it is clean, and this one because it is of a Jew. If he is careful about the bread of non-Jews, he blesses over the bread of a Jew. Nevertheless, he should remove the clean bread of non-Jews from the table until after the blessing of 'Hamotzi', for although he is careful, since there is no prohibition by law and many people eat it, it is good to remove it from the table. Some say that since he is careful, he does not need to remove it, and if he is not careful, he should remove it and bless over the bread of a Jew (Bach and Taz section 5, and see Magen Avraham section 9). And it truly seems so, that if he is careful and does not intend to eat it, why should he remove it? Even without this, since he does not intend to eat it, we do not worry about it, as explained in the previous section.

There are those who provide a general rule in this matter: one should follow the superior qualities of the bread. If the bread belongs to a Jew, it has one advantage. Therefore, if the bread of a gentile has two advantages, such as being clean and whole, while the bread of a Jew is sliced and not clean – one should bless on the bread of the gentile when not being particular. Conversely, if the bread of a gentile is whole but not clean, and the bread of a Jew is clean but sliced – one should bless on the bread of the Jew since it has two advantages (see Taz in the name of Rashal). And certainly, if each has an advantage, one may bless on whichever they prefer. If there are two people at the table, one can bless on one and the other on the second. If it is one person, he should place one within the other. All this applies when one is not being particular, but if one is particular, nothing extra is needed.

And if the homeowner and his household are reclining at the table, and he (the homeowner) is the one who breaks the bread, and he is careful not to eat bread baked by non-Jews and he has no intention of eating from it at all, but his household members are not careful and they will eat from the bread of non-Jews, nevertheless, since the homeowner who breaks the bread is careful, he should bless over the bread that is not from non-Jews. This is what our Rabbi, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 5, that if the homeowner is careful about bread baked by non-Jews and a Jew who is not careful about this dines with him at the table, since it is the homeowner's obligation, he should break from the best of the non-Jewish bread. And since it is permitted to break [bread], it is permitted for the entire meal, end quote. In truth, there are those who disagree with this (Bach), stating that there is no valid reason to be lenient in this matter (see Magen Avraham 12 who struggled with this). Therefore, it seems to me that this leniency applies only to a guest, where there is a mitzvah of hospitality, and it is appropriate for the homeowner to honor him and make the 'Hamotzi' over the bread that the guest eats, and consequently, it is permitted for the entire meal. But with his household members, this does not apply, obviously. And even though it does not seem so from the commentators, nevertheless, this seems to me the main point, since this law is a novelty, let us not add to it.

And our master, the Rema, wrote about this law, and this is his language: "Specifically when that bread is dear to him, but if it is not dear to him and there is no prohibition of non-Jewish bread, he does not need to prioritize it." End of quote. His words require explanation, for is it really dependent on what is dear to him? It only depends on whether he wishes to eat that bread or not, as stated, and what is he teaching us? It seems that even for our master, the Rema, this law was difficult, so he explained that the matter is as follows: Even though he is careful about their bread, since there is no absolute prohibition in this, and for the honor of the guest, this clean bread is dear to him, meaning he wishes to eat from it, therefore it is permitted. But if it is not dear to him, meaning that even now he has no desire to eat from it at all, he does not need to prioritize it even without this consideration. This also seems evident from the source of the law in Terumat HaDeshen (Siman 32, and this is also the intention of the Magen Avraham Sk12). All this applies if the homeowner is careful. But if the homeowner is not careful and does not intend to eat the entire meal except from their bread because it is clean, and his household members or guests are careful and only eat the unclean bread of Israel, and these two types of bread are placed on the table, it is obvious that he should break bread over their clean bread, since he is the one breaking bread and does not intend to eat from any other bread. In this case, everyone agrees that there is no need to remove it from the table, since he does not wish to eat from any other bread (there Sk10).

Two loaves that were joined together during baking, and a part of one was cut while the other remained whole, it is advisable to separate the piece from the whole one so that it appears whole rather than leaving it attached, even though it might appear larger. And one should not break off a piece from the place where it was attached to the other loaf, because there it appears as a slice. Instead, one should break from the whole part. However, with an actual slice, there is no need to be careful to break from the whole part, since it is already a slice; rather, one breaks from the side (see the Gra and the Magen Avraham, section 5).

Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote in paragraph 2: "If a person has two halves of bread and does not have a whole loaf, he should join them together with a stick or something else so that the connection is not visible, and it will have the status of a whole loaf, and he can even join them on Shabbat." But if the connection is visible, it does not help. And on Shabbat, one must be careful not to take a stick that is muktzeh, but to prepare it before Shabbat (Magen Avraham, subsection 4). It is not customary to join them at all during the week (ibid). This rule is from the Rokeach, but in Tosafot Zevachim (105b, s.v. 'Chibur') it implies that it does not help (B'er Heitev in the name of the Pnei Moshe), but it is possible that they wrote this regarding an etrog, and there is no proof for other things, and we have not seen this custom even on Shabbat.

Even though for Birkat Hamazon (the Grace After Meals) one needs an olive's bulk (kezayit), nevertheless, regarding the blessing of 'Hamotzi' (the blessing over bread) - even less than an olive's bulk suffices. However, for the blessing after eating, one does not recite anything for less than an olive's bulk. And this rule is not just concerning bread but applies to any type of food and its respective blessing: the initial blessing is recited even for any amount, but the concluding blessing is only recited for an olive's bulk. It appears to me that if one ate half an olive's bulk and did not intend to eat more, and then decided to eat another half an olive's bulk, he must recite the initial blessing again, and he must also recite the concluding blessing if he ate both within the time span it takes to eat half a loaf (b’kdei achilat pras). There are those who are uncertain about this (B’er Heitev, section 21 in the name of the Leket Yosher), but it seems to me as I have written (and proof of this can be derived from what will be explained regarding pastries, when one starts eating without intending to make it a meal and then decides to make it a meal, that he must recite Birkat Hamazon; similarly here, the concluding blessing is not dependent on the initial intent).

The measure of an olive (kezayit) is half an egg, and we have already written in Yoreh De'ah, section 324, that three great sages of the world have said to now double all the measures, because they found in the two measures of challah written by our rabbis—that is, one measure in eggs and one measure in fingers—that these measures contradict each other. Therefore, they said that the eggs of our time have decreased to half the size of the eggs that existed in the time of the sages of the Talmud. Hence, now the measure of an olive is like an egg and a quarter, as three eggs displace water (Noda BiYehuda, the Gaon of Vilna, and the Alter Rebbe), and thus all pious individuals are meticulous with the cup for Kiddush and Havdalah. According to this, an olive is like an egg. Yet one of the great sages of the generation disagreed with them (Chatam Sofer, Orach Chaim, section 127), and we have also explained there that eggs are generally the same size, but the eggs themselves are not uniform and differ from country to country. This matter was explained by the Tashbetz (Part 3, section 33), and this is his wording: "Because fingers are the same in all places, etc., and it is more accurate than the measure of eggs, which are not the same in all places, etc." End of quote. The Tashbetz also wrote this in his book Yavin Shemuah, and this is his wording: "I am astonished by those who measure with our eggs, because not all places have the same eggs; some are large like in the lands of Edom, and some are small like in the lands of Ishmael." End of quote. We also learned in Keilim (chapter 17, mishnah 6): "The egg they spoke of is neither large nor small but medium-sized." End of quote. And we have also seen this with our own eyes: in the chickens from Prussia or Galicia, when they came to our country, the egg was much larger than our chicken eggs. Now they have intermingled, and the difference is not so noticeable. Additionally, we brought evidence from sensory perception that it is impossible to say at all that an olive is like our egg, for the sages said that the gullet holds an egg of a chicken, and according to them, it would be like two of our eggs, which sensory perception contradicts. Therefore, certainly, even now, half a medium egg is the measure of an olive, and this is the main ruling.

It is stated in the Gemara (Berachot 42a) that for "pas haba'ah b'kisnin" one blesses "Borei Minei Mezonot" and not "Hamotzi". What is "pas haba'ah b'kisnin" will be explained later. However, this is when one eats it as a casual snack, but when one establishes a meal on it, one blesses "Hamotzi" and says Birkat Hamazon, and it requires washing hands. If initially one intended to eat a small amount and blessed "Borei Minei Mezonot" and then ate a lot, one must say Birkat Hamazon. This is if one did not initially decide to eat a lot but ended up eating a lot, thus "Hamotzi" and washing hands are not relevant here. Even if in the middle of eating one decided to eat a lot, nevertheless, if the time from the decision until the end of the eating is not enough to establish a meal, one does not need to wash hands and bless "Hamotzi". But if at the beginning of the eating one decided to eat a lot, one must wash hands and bless "Hamotzi" (and this is the intention of the Magen Avraham, Orach Chaim 168:14).

The determination of a fixed meal is not dependent on what an individual considers a fixed meal for themselves, but rather on the amount that others would consider a fixed meal. This is called a fixed meal, and one is obligated to wash their hands, recite 'Hamotzi,' and Birkat Hamazon (Grace after Meals). As it says in the Gemara there: "Anything that others consider a fixed meal requires a blessing," see there. If one eats an amount that others do not consider a fixed meal, even if the individual is satisfied from it and considers it a fixed meal, they still only recite the blessing 'Borei Minei Mezonot' and 'Al HaMichya,' which is a condensed version of the three blessings, because the individual's opinion is nullified in the face of everyone else. The reason is that such an amount is not considered bread that requires the blessings 'Hamotzi' and Birkat Hamazon. If it were only a matter of being satisfied, it would be similar to being satisfied from foods whose blessing is 'Shehakol,' 'Ha'adama,' or 'Ha'etz.' The reason for all this is that, according to Torah law, the obligation is only for the amount that satisfies, as it is written: "And you shall eat and be satisfied and bless," and according to some halachic authorities, even one blessing for Birkat Hamazon suffices according to Torah law. However, the Sages instituted four blessings and for the consumption of an olive-sized portion (kazayit). They only instituted this for complete bread, and for such bread, they only instituted it for the amount that everyone considers a fixed meal (as explained by the Alter Rebbe in Shulchan Aruch and his Siddur, both reasons are necessary, and study this carefully).

Some say that four eggs is the measure for establishing a meal, meaning that when one eats this amount of "pat haba b'kisnin" (a type of bread), it is considered establishing a meal (Eliyah Rabbah, section 17, citing Or Chadash). There are those who disagree and say that this is the minimal measure for a poor person’s meal, which was estimated for an eruv, but a proper meal is about half an omer. After all, the manna descended for each person every day as an omer per person for two meals. And regarding this, our sages said in Eruvin (83b): "One who eats this amount is healthy and blessed" (Gra). According to this, the measure for establishing a meal is half the measure of challah, which is one and a half litra. Indeed, we see with our own eyes that the measure of four eggs does not suffice for satiety at all; it is considered a casual eating (as the Chayei Adam also wrote in section 54 of Nishmat Adam, citing the Gra, who was not pleased with the measure of four eggs, and it is clear that his reasoning is as stated).

There are those who say that if one eats this with meat or other cooked dishes, and in this manner, it constitutes a fixed meal, even though when eaten alone it does not constitute a fixed meal - it is considered a fixed meal, and one must wash their hands and recite the blessing of 'Hamotzi' and Birkat Hamazon (Magen Avraham, section 13, and Eliyah Rabbah, section 17). And if one is satisfied from it even without a condiment, whereas others are not satisfied with this amount unless with a condiment - the same law applies (ibid.). Some add that even if one eats it with a condiment and is satisfied, and others are also satisfied in such a manner, nevertheless, it requires the measure of four eggs (the Gra, section 8). I am perplexed by all these statements, for even regarding an Eruv where many are lenient concerning the two meals for the Eruv of boundaries, Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda hold in the Mishnah in Eruvin (40b) that we estimate with a small amount of bread eaten with a condiment, and nevertheless, we do not rule like them but like the Tannaim who disagree with them, and hold that we estimate with bread alone. All the more so that we do not adopt a stringent approach in this matter, for if we did, these would be things without measure, as many wealthy people eat many good cooked dishes and eat only a little bread, and what is the measure of four eggs for this? And if it is because one is satisfied, it is like someone who is satisfied with fruits, and what relevance does this have to 'Hamotzi' and Birkat Hamazon? Therefore, it seems to me in my humble opinion that we should estimate with bread alone, and this is not found in the early authorities. (And the Magen Avraham brought proof from Tosafot and Sefer Mitzvot Katan who wrote about rolls that people establish a meal on them like on Purim, and he inferred from this that on Purim they do not eat only bread. I am astonished, for is this what they meant? They only said that on Purim it is customary to establish a meal on rolls because during the rest of the year it is not customary to establish a meal on them, and what relevance does this have here? And also what the Gra wrote that up to six eggs, if one is not satisfied, one should recite 'Borei Minei Mezonot', and if one is satisfied, one should wash hands and recite 'Hamotzi' and Birkat Hamazon, and from six and above up to half an issaron, if one is not satisfied, one should recite on other bread - I do not know these measures. Do we not follow the majority of people? And since he himself wrote that half an issaron is the measure of a meal for everyone, what more do we need? And I think there are mixed-up matters in the new prints that were copied from his Siddur, and the matters are not aligned with what he wrote in his Shulchan Aruch. Pay close attention.)

Know that many great scholars have cried out vehemently about the practice that has spread in our generation throughout the country, that at times of joyous occasions, tables are set with various kinds of fish and meats, and people eat with pat haba'ah bekisnin (pastries) without washing their hands (netilat yadayim), without the blessing of "Hamotzi," and without Birkat Hamazon (Grace after Meals), but rather they make the blessing over "Mezonot" and afterwards "Al HaMichya." They eat a lot of pastries and oil-baked challah, which is called "boimel challah." There is no doubt that they need to wash their hands, recite "Hamotzi," and Birkat Hamazon. Even if they are careful not to eat a lot of bread, according to the opinion of the great authorities mentioned previously, if they are satisfied from the side dishes, they must wash their hands and so forth, even if they eat a little bread. Certainly, they eat the volume of four eggs. Only a few of the God-fearing are careful when sitting at such a table not to eat a lot, or they wash their hands and recite "Hamotzi" over plain bread. But the majority of the common people do not guard themselves in this matter. Therefore, it is certainly forbidden to act in this manner, but it is known that we do not have the power to protest.

(And to teach a bit of merit, it seems to me in my humble opinion, a leniency from the words of the Rif in this matter, who wrote in these words: "The conclusion: where one eats it as a snack, one blesses 'Borei Minei Mezonot,' etc., and where one eats it as a fixed meal, one blesses 'Hamotzi' and the three blessings." From his words, it appears that it does not depend on the quantity that establishes the meal but on the manner of eating, whether it is prepared as a casual eating or as a regular meal. It is known that in a complete meal, they remove their outer garments and sit around the table, but in these eatings, they snatch and eat as they are without preparation. Some eat standing and walking, as is known, and they think that this does not constitute establishing a meal. And as was said in the Gemara: "Anything that others establish, etc." this also needs to be interpreted in the manner we have written. Every God-fearing person should distance himself from this, and may He, the Merciful One, atone for sin.)

And what is called "pat haba'a bekisnin," there are many opinions on this matter: Rashi of blessed memory explained that after a meal they were accustomed to bring roasted grains, and these are called "kisnin," and they would bring with them bread kneaded with spices, similar to our "oblyash," etc., in which they put many spices and nuts and almonds, etc. This implies that the bread was kneaded with water and flour, but they mixed in many spices and nuts and almonds, and this type is unknown to us at all. Similarly, the Tur wrote that it is bread made like pockets filled with sugar, almonds, and nuts, and various spices, etc., and this is the explanation of Rabbeinu Chananel as written by Rabbeinu Yonah there, and so wrote the Aruch, and also the Rashba wrote something similar: that they fill it with honey, almonds, and various spices. And in the name of Rav Hai Gaon, they wrote that "pat haba'a bekisnin" are cakes, which is bread whether seasoned or unseasoned, made like dry cakes that are chewed in the banquet hall and eaten in small amounts, and this too is unknown to us. However, for our rabbis, the essence of the bread is made with water like ordinary bread, for if it were kneaded with liquids, they would have clarified it.

And this is the first opinion that our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 7, and this is his wording: "Pas HaBa'ah B'Kisnin: Some explain it as bread made like pockets that are filled with honey or sugar and nuts and almonds and spices, etc.” End quote. And the intention in eating them is for the filling and not for the bread itself, but because it is a type of grain, it is not nullified to the filling, and therefore one blesses 'Borei Minei Mezonot' (Magen Avraham 16). If one eats only the filling, one blesses according to the blessing of the filling (ibid.). There is no difference whether the filling is fruits or meat and fish (Taz 6). And there is someone who wrote that from this type are those made on Purim, where the bread is filled with sesame seeds (ibid.). In my humble opinion, it is not similar, because on Purim, the main aspect is the bread like all types of bread, except that they also put sesame seeds in them, and it is considered complete bread, and one blesses 'Hamotzi' on it, and this is the common custom. And our rabbis who explained the filling meant that the main aspect is the filling and the bread is almost nullified to the filling, except because grain is not nullified as mentioned. But on Purim, the main aspect is the bread, and according to Rashi, there is no filling but it is kneaded together, and nevertheless, because of the abundance of spices, the bread is not considered significant at all and it is like a filling according to their explanation.

However, the explanation of Rav Hai Gaon is not included in this, for he wrote: "Whether it is seasoned or unseasoned," and Rabbeinu Beit Yosef cited it as the third opinion, and this is his language: "And there are those who explain that it is bread, whether seasoned, etc., which they make like dry cakes and nibble on them, and they are called 'biscuit'." End quote. And this is not understood at all, for since it has no seasoning, it is indeed regular bread, for just because it is dry does not mean it is not bread. And they wrote that they are nicely arranged like fine rolls, and this refers to the "kichelach" made for meals to stimulate appetite (Taz, subparagraph 8). And I do not know how to interpret this, and our "kichelach" are kneaded with eggs and not with water, and what resemblance does this have. And if this was also the intention of the Gaon, he should have explained that this is the main point, and explicitly wrote that it is kneaded with water (Gra). And it must be said that since it is very hard, it is not considered bread, and this requires further study.

However, the Rambam in Chapter 3 wrote: "Similarly, dough kneaded with honey or oil or milk, or if he mixed in various spices and baked it, which is called 'pas ha'ba'ah b'kisnin,' even though it is bread - one blesses 'Borei Minei Mezonot' over it. And if he establishes his meal on it - he blesses 'Hamotzi.'" End quote. And here, the Rambam also mentioned 'that he mixed in various spices' as explained by Rashi, and it seems to me that his intention was that only this is called 'pas ha'ba'ah b'kisnin' and not when it is kneaded with honey, etc., because that is obvious since it is not kneaded with water, and this is the second explanation brought by our teacher the Beit Yosef there. And he added to say that only if the taste of the fruit juice or spices is noticeable in the dough, end quote, meaning that certainly if the main ingredient is water and the fruit juice or spices are minimal, even if their taste is recognized, nonetheless, since they are not noticeable in the dough - one blesses 'Hamotzi,' but they must be the main ingredient to be noticeable in the dough, meaning that it should be visibly noticeable that there are fruit juices or spices, and therefore he did not say noticeable by taste.

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote regarding this: "And there are those who say that this is considered full bread, unless it contains a lot of spices or honey like sweet foods called 'lekach,' where the honey and spices are almost the main ingredient, and this is the custom." End quote. And I do not understand, for it seems that the opinion of our teacher, the Beit Yosef, is also as we have explained, that it cannot be said that the intention of our teacher, the Rema, is that there should be no water at all, for if so, he would not have said that the honey and spices are the main ingredient, since there is no water at all. Rather, certainly there is also water, but the water is not the main ingredient (and so the Taz wrote in section 7, see there). And it appears that he (the Rema) holds that the opinion of our teacher, the Beit Yosef, is that it is sufficient if the taste is recognizable (Taz there), but indeed it seems as I have written. However, in practice, all the opinions that have been explained regarding 'pat haba'ah b'kisnin' (bread-like items) are true according to the law, as our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote that the law is according to all of them, that all these things are given the laws we mentioned regarding 'pat haba'ah b'kisnin,' end quote. And they wrote the reason that it is a Rabbinic doubt, and we rule leniently. And there are those who questioned that if one does not recite the appropriate blessing, they transgress the commandment of "Do not take [God's name in vain]" (Bach). And this is not so, for certainly the blessing of 'Mezonot' exempts even regular bread according to the Torah, for it satisfies (as the Taz wrote in section 6), and also the blessing of 'Al HaMichya' exempts according to the Torah for many poskim, for according to the Torah, only one blessing is needed. However, in my humble opinion, it seems that it is not necessary to say it is due to 'Rabbinic doubt,' but that this is the fundamental law, only that the poskim disagree on the interpretation of 'pat haba'ah b'kisnin,' but in practice, they do not disagree with each other, and behold, the Rambam included almost all of them as I have written (and what the Magen Avraham wrote in section 18 is a stringency without any reason at all, and the primary opinion is like the Taz).

Accordingly, all of our cakes, whether they are kneaded with eggs and called Eier Cakes, or kneaded with milk or butter and called Butter Cakes, and also the round ones called Eier Bagels, when they contain a lot of eggs or a lot of milk or a lot of butter, even if they also contain water - they do not require the blessing of 'Hamotzi' (the blessing for bread). And we do not follow the majority and minority in this regard, for it is known that even if the quantity of these ingredients is less than the water, their quality is significant because of the nature of fatty substances which have a greater spread.
