The main point: if it is evident to the eye that this is not ordinary bread, and everyone sees that it is egg bread or butter bread or milk bread or oil bread, like those baked from dough kneaded with plain oil called Patschani Maslana (and the majority and minority mentioned in this context refer to this, and consider it carefully).

According to the explanation of Rav Hai Gaon, "pat haba’ah b’kisnin" (a type of baked good) is dough kneaded only with water and without spices, but its preparation is not like ordinary bread, as it is very dry. For this reason alone, it does not receive the blessing of 'Hamotzi.' The reason, as the Levush writes in section 6, is as follows: The sages did not establish 'Hamotzi' and the three blessings even for an olive-sized piece except for bread upon which most people typically establish their meal. This means dough kneaded only with water, where the flour and water are the main components, and it is baked in the usual manner without any changes or additions, as it is considered significant by everyone and warrants its own blessing due to its importance. However, anything that has undergone a change, which most people do not typically make or establish a meal upon, is not required to have the blessing of 'Hamotzi' and the three blessings unless one ate a quantity upon which people establish their meal. (This explanation resolves several nuances regarding this matter, so study it well).

And know that in my youth, when I was in the province of Raissin, it spread there among the bakers to cook barley grits in water, strain the water, and knead dough with this water to bake loaves from them. They would bless upon them 'Mezonot' and 'Al HaMichya,' and they said that this was instructed by one of the great rabbis of the previous generation. His reasoning appears straightforward based on what we say in Berachot (39a): that the water of cooked vegetables is like the vegetables themselves concerning the blessing, and consequently, it has the status of fruit water. And even though the Rosh wrote that the primary cooking is for the sake of the vegetables, and here the primary cooking of the barley is for the sake of the water, nevertheless, the Rosh wrote that even if one cooks vegetables for the sake of their water, since everyone in the world cooks them for eating, the blessing of the water does not change because of this. (This is mentioned in Magen Avraham, Siman 206, Sif Katan 6), and here the barley is cooked by everyone for eating. It is not similar to fruits cooked in water, as explained in Siman 202, where one blesses 'Shehakol,' because there the reason is that it is not customary to cook them, as explained there. But grits are only for cooking, not for any other purpose. Nevertheless, there is no clear proof from this that all such things have the status of fruit water. Therefore, I am accustomed to tell them that it is difficult to rely on this alone, and it is necessary to add a bit of oil or milk or butter so that at least the taster will taste the flavor of oil or the flavor of milk and butter.

I have also seen in some places that they knead with whey, which is called "seravotka," and they recite the blessings of 'mezonot' and 'al hamichya' over it, considering it to be like fruit juice. It appears that there is evidence for this from what is stated in the Mishnah (Makhshirin, Chapter 6, Mishnah 5): "Whey is like milk," and it is explained that this refers to the liquid separated from the cheese when the milk is coagulated. And even though in Chullin (114a), Reish Lakish said: this applies only to rendering seeds susceptible to impurity, but concerning cooking meat with milk, it is not like milk—it is nevertheless clear that even there, the interpretation is not that it is not like milk at all, but rather like water. If it were only like water, what relevance would it have to rendering seeds susceptible to impurity, whether it is like milk or not? For if it were merely like water, it would obviously render them susceptible, since the primary source of susceptibility is water, as it is written: "When water is put on the seed" (Leviticus 11:38). Rather, it must certainly be that it is not like milk but like fruit juice or mere liquid. However, in any case, regarding the blessing of 'hamotzi,' it is not like water. (And even aside from this, why should we compare it to cooking meat with milk? Let us compare it to rendering seeds susceptible to impurity, which is a rabbinic matter. And even though regarding vows, it is not like milk, as stated in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 217, this is because in vows we follow common language. And the proof is that if it is called by the name of milk, it is forbidden, as stated by the Rema there, and examine this well.)

It is stated in the Gemara (Berachot 42a): "For rolls: If one establishes a meal on them, one recites 'HaMotzi'; if not, one recites 'Borei Minei Mezonot'." And Rashi explained: "Rolls - oblias in foreign language," but we do not know what this is. The Tosafot challenged this, saying that oblias is regular bread, and they explained that it is nilish, as also written by the Rosh, but this too is unknown to us. However, from the words of Rabbeinu Beit Yosef in section 8, it is explained that it is kneaded with water. According to Rashi, its dough is thick, and according to Tosafot, its dough is soft. This is the language of Rabbeinu Beit Yosef: "Rolls: Those with thick dough, called oblias, are considered regular bread, and one recites 'HaMotzi' and Birkat HaMazon over them. Those with soft and very thin dough, called niblas, one recites 'Borei Minei Mezonot' and Al HaMichya. If one establishes a meal on them, one recites 'HaMotzi' and Birkat HaMazon." End quote.

And behold, even regarding pat haba’ah b’kisnin, Rashi explained: bread kneaded with spices, which is like our obliaush, as mentioned in section 19, and why did the Tosafot not question this there. However, the truth is that obliaush is not named because of the spices but because of the manner in which it is prepared and rolled, that is, it is rolled until it becomes very thin, and spiced bread is also made in this manner. This is what Rashi wrote: "like our obliaush," meaning that its preparation is like our obliaush, and Rashi held that since its preparation is different, it is not considered regular bread, and this is similar to the explanation of Rav Hai Gaon regarding pat haba’ah b’kisnin that we explained there. And perhaps the obliaush is also hard, which is precisely the explanation of the Gaon, but the Tosafot and the Rosh did not agree with this. And I saw someone who wrote that the words of Rabbeinu the Beit Yosef in section 8 contradict his words in section 7, where he wrote regarding pat haba’ah b’kisnin that it is spiced bread like Rashi's explanation, which is obliaush, and how did he write in section 8 that it is regular bread (Even HaOzer). But it is not so, for obliaush does not contain spices but as mentioned, and there is no contradiction here. And although in section 7 he also brought the words of the Gaon, according to our interpretation, these are rolls according to Rashi's explanation as mentioned, but Rabbeinu the Beit Yosef did not hold this and held that rolls are not very hard and are not similar to the kisnin of the Gaon, as the Gaon's kisnin are not for eating but for dessert (Magen Avraham section 19). And there are those who wrote that obliaush is baked without rolling, just mixing the dough with water to make a thick dough (Taz section 9). This is a great wonder, for it is explicitly implied that rolls are an important food, and its name proves: "rolls," meaning thin bread, as the Aruch explained that it is like pat haba’ah b’kisnin, and so it is clarified from the Rif there, and if so, how can we say that it is without rolling. Rather, on the contrary, it is rolled a lot until it becomes thin.

And some (the Nili"sh) have explained that this is what they call "nalasinki," where they mix flour with water in a pot like porridge, and pour it onto wide vegetable leaves and bake them in the oven with the leaves (there in the Beit Yosef and Magen Avraham, Seif Katan 20). However, this is not understandable, because if so, it is not considered bread at all. Indeed, the Rashba rejected the Tosafot’s explanation for this reason, and it appears that he agrees with Rashi there. In my humble opinion, it seems that in the manner we have explained, where its preparation is very thin, it is possible that even Tosafot and the Rosh would agree with Rashi. Nevertheless, in any case, we do not know the nature of such breads, and there is no need to elaborate further on this.

Additionally, our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote that if one eats these rolls during a meal not because of the meal (not eating for satiation but for pleasure), they require a blessing before eating but not after (as Birkat Hamazon covers it). However, those thin wafers on which jam is spread are secondary to the jam, and the blessing on the jam covers them. This is because the intention is not to eat the wafers at all, but rather to use the wafers so their hands do not get dirty from the jam (Magen Avraham, section 23). Therefore, even if one eats them together, they recite a blessing over the jam, and it covers the wafers, as per the rule that the primary food exempts the secondary food. But when one eats the wafers alone, one recites 'Borei Minei Mezonot' (Taz, section 11).

According to this, the same rule applies to all "pat haba'ah b'kisnin" (bread-like pastries), that when eating them during a meal, a blessing is needed beforehand. However, this is not an absolute rule, for it is taught: "If one has blessed on the bread, it exempts the appetizers," and the Tosafot explained this as referring to sweet pastries and fruits, and Rashi also explained appetizers as referring to pastries and rolls. However, the correct explanation is that when one eats them as a meal or cooked dish intending to be satisfied, the blessing on the bread exempts them. But if the intention is merely for dessert or enjoyment, the bread's blessing does not exempt them. The majority of the later great authorities (Shaloh, Magen Avraham, and Eliyah Rabbah) agreed with this. There is someone who disagrees (Taz), but the law follows the majority, and reason also supports this.

According to this, when we eat during a meal thick cookies or cakes or any kinds of pastries filled with fruits or spices, they certainly come to satiate and to continue the desire for food, and no blessing is needed at all. But when one eats thin cakes or tarts and sugar cakes and honey bread and small sweet breads and thin crackers like wafers - a blessing is required before them, for all these are not typically eaten for satiation but purely for enjoyment and as a dessert. And even someone who intends to eat them for satiation, his intention is nullified by the general practice of people, and this is how it should be instructed (and kreplach and blintzes and donuts are considered part of the meal).

It is stated in the Gemara (37b): "This porridge, even though it does not contain pieces the size of an olive, one recites 'Hamotzi' over it, provided it has the appearance of bread." And before this, it is taught: that when bread is cooked while the pieces are intact, initially one recites 'Hamotzi' over it, and afterwards the three blessings. And if the pieces are not intact, initially one recites 'Borei Minei Mezonot' and afterwards a blessing of 'Me'ein Shalosh'. And the Jerusalem Talmud explains that 'intact pieces' means that they are the size of an olive, and 'not intact' means that they are not the size of an olive. It is further stated there that bread, even if it is crumbled until it returns to flour, one recites 'Hamotzi' over it. Refer there, and Rabbeinu Yonah divided these matters into three categories, which were agreed upon by the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch in section 10, as will be explained.

And this is the case when the pieces are cooked in boiling water in a primary vessel, whether they stick together or not. If each piece is at least the size of an olive (k'zayit), this is called intact pieces, and one must recite the blessing "Hamotzi" and the Grace After Meals (Birkat Hamazon). There is no difference if they retain the appearance of bread or not, and this is according to the Baraita and the Jerusalem Talmud. If the pieces were not cooked but were instead stuck together by means of soup, honey, milk, or other liquids, this is called "chavitza," which is of a lesser status. Even if the pieces are less than the size of an olive, one must recite the blessing "Hamotzi" and the Grace After Meals if they retain the appearance of bread. However, if they are less than the size of an olive and do not retain the appearance of bread, one recites the blessing "Mezonot" and the abridged Grace After Meals (Bracha Me'ein Shalosh). If they were cooked and are less than the size of an olive, even if they retain the appearance of bread, one recites the blessing "Borei Minei Mezonot" and the abridged Grace After Meals, and this is the statement of the Gemara regarding chavitza. All the more so when they are of the size of an olive, even if cooked, there is no difference. If they are neither cooked nor stuck together but are finely crumbled, like when matzah is ground and sifted through a sieve, which is called "matzah meal," even though it is less than the size of an olive and does not retain the appearance of bread, one recites the blessing "Hamotzi" and the Grace After Meals when eating them dry.

There is someone who wrote in this manner: It is stated in the Gemara that if one crumbles bread until it returns to the state of flour, and then kneads it together again and bakes it, one must recite the blessing of 'Hamotzi' even if it no longer has the appearance of bread, because this is considered crumbs that have the size of an olive, and an olive-sized piece does not require the appearance of bread. And it is implied there that even if it is fried in oil at the beginning, similar to the meal offerings, and if so, those who make 'charamzelach' from crumbled bread or from bread soaked in water must recite 'Hamotzi', since originally it was bread and does not lose the status of bread until none of the pieces are the size of an olive (Magen Avraham 168:28).

And all his words are puzzling, for what he wrote: "If later they stick together, it is considered crumbs that have the size of an olive," is not correct as the Levush wrote, that if before cooking there was not the size of an olive in the crumbs, even if they stick together through cooking, it is not considered that they have the size of an olive, see there. And the Gemara which says that if he crumbled and then kneaded them together he blesses 'Hamotzi,' means he baked them again, as Rashi explained, see there. But if he cooked or fried them, like our knaidelach that we make on Passover and cook them, or the chremslach that are fried in honey and fat – their sticking together does not matter, and since before they did not have the size of an olive in the crumbs, and when they stuck together through cooking like knaidelach or through frying like chremslach, they already lost their form of bread, and their sticking together now is not considered sticking, and one blesses 'Borei Minei Mezonot.' And certainly, if eggs and fat are mixed in them before cooking or frying, there is no reason to bless 'Hamotzi' on them, as the great later authorities (Eliyah Rabbah and Even HaEzer as mentioned by Machatzit HaShekel) have written. Similarly, 'taigachatz' that is made on Passover from broken matzah into small pieces, none of which is the size of an olive, and mixed with eggs and fat, and then fried, and it is obvious that they have lost their form of bread – it is clear that one blesses 'Mezonot' on them, and this is the custom of the world and there is no concern about this at all (and even the Magen Avraham himself at the end of his words wrote this in the name of Kenesset HaGedolah, and wrote it requires further investigation, see there, but there is no investigation at all and it is clear in law without any doubt at all).

And know that in the case of those foods that have lost their status of requiring the blessing 'Hamotzi' and Birkat Hamazon (Grace After Meals) due to being cooked, combined, or fried, such that they no longer have the appearance of bread at all, even if one eats an amount that would normally establish a meal, one does not need to recite 'Hamotzi' and Birkat Hamazon, but rather 'Borei Minei Mezonot' and the shorter blessing Me’ein Shalosh. And what has been clarified, that if one establishes a meal they must recite 'Hamotzi' and Birkat Hamazon, this applies to baked items that have the appearance of bread, such as kichlach and puter kochen and similar items, for which the exemption applies because 'Hamotzi' and Birkat Hamazon were only instituted for bread in the context of a meal. However, for those that were once bread and lost their status through crumbling, cooking, combining, or frying, they no longer have the status of bread at all, and 'Hamotzi' and Birkat Hamazon do not apply to them. All the more so with our fried dough items like kreplach, blintzes, and pancakes, which do not require 'Hamotzi' and Birkat Hamazon even if one eats a lot of them, since they do not have the status of bread at all (Magen Avraham there).

There are those who say that crumbs less than the size of an olive that are placed in water and the water becomes whitened because of the crumbs, such as if they soaked for many hours, lose their status as bread, and one only recites 'Borei Minei Mezonot' and the blessing of 'Al Hamichya'. And even if they were soaked in cold water and were not in the water for a full day, which is said to be like cooked, since they lost the form of bread and the crumbs were less than an olive in size, and all the more so if they were soaked in hot water, as their form of bread is lost in a short time. And know that there are those who wrote that the same law applies to pieces of bread that are dried on coals in beer and called "Panyitz" (as mentioned in Shulchan Aruch, Orach Chayim 168:29 in the name of the Shlah), but I do not know the explanation for this, as our "Panyitz" which are dried in a hot oven and called "Sukhariyot" are considered complete bread. And one should not question what we established in Siman 460 that one fulfills the obligation with soaked matzah, even though one does not recite 'Hamotzi' on it, as it can be said that the pieces have the size of an olive (as mentioned in Shulchan Aruch, Orach Chayim 168:30), and furthermore, in truth, one does not soak the matzah until it loses its form.

And there is one who says that bread soaked in red wine and soaked until the bread becomes red loses its status of bread, as it has lost its form, and it is like "pat haba'ah b'kisnin" whose blessing is 'Mezonot' and 'Al HaMichya' if one did not eat a fixed meal from it. However, this is only if it has crumbled or in pieces that do not contain an olive's bulk, for if they do contain an olive's bulk, even by cooking it does not lose its status of bread, and certainly not by soaking. And regarding the blessing on the wine - it is not needed, as one blesses 'Borei Minei Mezonot' on the soaked bread and exempts the wine absorbed in it, as it is taught in the Tosefta (chapter 4): "Rice and wine," meaning that the wine is absorbed in the rice - one blesses on the rice and exempts the wine, as per the rule of the primary item exempting the secondary (there). And therefore, if his intention is only to suck the wine within it - he blesses 'Borei Pri HaGafen' on the wine (there), and if his intention is on both, as both are considered primary to him - he blesses on both (there), and the detailed laws will be explained in Siman 177 on this matter, and the same law applies to all kinds of drinks absorbed in foods. And if one crumbles a bit of thin bread in a drink to give taste to the drink and not for the sake of the bread - there is no need to bless at all on the bread (there).

And know that regarding cooked bread, there is a great wonder in the words of the Rambam in chapter 3, law 8, where he wrote: "Bread that has been broken into pieces and cooked in a pot or kneaded into a soup, if the pieces are the size of an olive or it is recognizable that they are bread and their form has not changed - one blesses 'Hamotzi' initially. If they are not the size of an olive or their form has changed in cooking - one blesses 'Borei Minei Mezonot' initially." His words contradict themselves from the beginning to the end. In the beginning, he is stringent that if the pieces are the size of an olive, the change in form does not matter, and if they are less than the size of an olive, the change in form is necessary, as all the decisors hold. But in the end, he says the opposite, that if the pieces are not the size of an olive, even if their form has not changed, and if they are the size of an olive, the change in form matters. All the sages of the generations have struggled to explain his words (see Kesef Mishneh, Lechem Mishneh, Bach, and Taz section 12). The correct interpretation is as stated by the great sages of Spain, that there is a mistake in the 'or' in the latter part, and it should say: 'And if they are not the size of an olive and their form has changed, etc.' According to this, his words are like those of all the decisors (Kesef Mishneh in the name of R. Yitzhak Alfasi). However, he differs in that he does not distinguish between cooking and soaking in soup. Some say that the beginning refers to soaking in soup and the end to cooking (Kesef Mishneh), and according to this, he is lenient in cooking that even if the pieces are the size of an olive, if their form has changed, one blesses 'Borei Minei Mezonot,' unlike all the decisors as explained. Others distinguish between the phrase 'their form has not changed,' which indicates that it is clearly recognizable and has not changed at all, in which case even less than the size of an olive one blesses 'Hamotzi,' and if it is the size of an olive, even though it has changed a bit and is not clearly recognizable, one blesses 'Hamotzi,' and the phrase 'their form has changed,' meaning their form has completely changed, in which case even if it is the size of an olive, one blesses 'Borei Minei Mezonot,' and this applies to cooking and not to soaking in soup as is clear (there in the name of R. Yosef Shushan, R. Yitzhak Alfasi, and Abarbanel). According to this, it is possible that all the decisors would agree with him in this detail when it is really like a cooked dish, and this requires further study (and also the Lechem Mishneh agreed with this, see there). Some wrote that what was written at the beginning 'if they are the size of an olive' means after cooking, and before it was less than the size of an olive but became the size of an olive through cooking (Taz there), and in any case, regarding the ruling, whatever the intention of the Rambam, the law follows Rabbeinu Yonah, the Tur, and the Shulchan Aruch (there).

Our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 13: "Even a thick dough mixture, if it is cooked or fried - one does not recite 'HaMotzi' over it, even if it has the appearance of bread and even if it is obligated in challah, because the blessing of 'HaMotzi' follows only the time of baking. However, there are those who disagree and say that if the dough was originally thick, even if it was later softened with water and made into doughnuts and then cooked in water or fried in oil - one still recites 'HaMotzi' over them. The custom is to be lenient. A God-fearing person should fulfill both opinions and not eat it unless he first recites the blessing over another bread." This will be explained further on.

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote on this: All this refers only when, after baking, it retains the appearance of bread. But if it does not retain the appearance of bread, such as lakshen that are called "vermicelli" - according to everyone, one does not recite the blessing 'Hamotzi' nor the three blessings, as it is not called bread. But pastries and kreplach are considered to have the appearance of bread, and one should not eat them unless one first recites a blessing on other bread. And all this refers only to dough that does not contain oil and honey and the like, but is fried in them. But if they are kneaded with them, their law has already been clarified regarding 'pat haba'a b'kisnin' (cake-like bread). And their words need further explanation.

And the explanation of the matter is thus: Until now, we have clarified the law of pat haba'ah b'kisnin, where its kneading is not like regular bread, and we have clarified the law of chavitza, which is regular bread even after baking, but then it was cooked or stuck together with soup. Now, we clarify the law of bread whose kneading is like regular bread, meaning it is made with water alone like regular bread, and its dough is thick like regular dough, but it was not baked like regular bread. Rather, it was cooked or fried and retains the appearance of bread. This seems contradictory, as cooking removes the appearance of bread as explained earlier. The intention is not actual cooking, but rather baking it in a pan with a little water (Magen Avraham, section 31), which is similar to cooking but retains its form. Similarly, frying it in a little oil or butter also falls into this category, making it subject to challah as stated in Yoreh Deah, section 329. However, for 'HaMotzi,' it is exempt because the obligation of challah applies at the time of kneading, while the obligation of 'HaMotzi' applies after baking, and its baking is not like regular bread. Some disagree and say that 'HaMotzi' follows the same law as challah in this regard, but the custom is according to the first opinion.

And all this our Rabbi, the Rema, came to explain so that one would not err in the expression 'cooked in water or fried in oil', which would be considered actual cooking and actual frying. If so, it does not have the form of bread, and according to everyone, one is exempt. For even according to Rabbeinu Tam, who is stringent and holds that 'Hamotzi' depends on the obligation of challah, as brought in Tosafot and the Rosh and all the poskim, this is all when it has the form of bread. And according to Rabbeinu Tam, indeed even for pastry made with pockets filled with liquids, one is also obligated to say 'Hamotzi' if it has the form of bread. However, in this case, our Rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, did not worry to bring his opinion, considering it a lone opinion, since its kneading is not like ordinary bread (and this resolves the difficulty raised by the Eivan HaEzer, see there). And only here, where its kneading is like ordinary bread, they were concerned to bring his opinion, and even in this case, they wrote that the custom is to be lenient. Only a God-fearing person who is concerned should first bless on another piece of bread.

And our teacher, the Rema, added that if it does not have the form of bread, everyone agrees that one does not say 'Hamotzi' and the three blessings. What he wrote, that pastida and krepelach are considered as having the form of bread, is not like our pastidot and krepelach. His intent was that meat or cheese is placed between layers of dough and baked in the oven, which is actual bread. This is similar to our Hamantaschen on Purim, where sesame seeds are filled in the bread, and it is complete bread. So too, the pastida and krepelach he wrote about are actual bread, with something placed inside them. This is not similar to the "pas haba'ah b'kisnin" mentioned in section 7, according to the first opinion, where they are filled with many spices, almonds, and nuts. There, the dough is filled to such an extent that the main intent is the filling, as stated in section 20. But here, the main element is the bread, and it is filled in the manner of pastida and krepelach, which are filled with meat and cheese or similar items. However, the main element is the bread. He then wrote that all this only applies to dough that does not contain oil, honey, etc., meaning the kneading is like any other bread. Otherwise, it would be considered "pas haba'ah b'kisnin" according to the Rambam, which is the second opinion in section 7. (This is the explanation of their words. The Even HaOzer wrote that section 13 contradicts section 7; however, there is no contradiction. Also, what the Bach wrote, that if one intended to bake it and then decided to cook it, one should say 'Hamotzi,' was already refuted by the Magen Avraham in subsection 32. There is no need for what the Taz wrote in subsection 16 and 19. The Rema used the phrase "baking" to indicate that the terms "cooking" and "frying" used by the Beit Yosef are not exact, as we explained. As the Magen Avraham wrote in subsections 31 and 36, see there. However, regarding the Magen Avraham's doubt in subsection 38 if one needs to say 'Hamotzi' with a fixed meal when the dough was kneaded with oil and honey and then fried slightly as mentioned, in my humble opinion, since it is not actual frying but slight frying, one should say 'Hamotzi' with a fixed meal).

In their days, there was scalded bread, meaning that they scalded the dough in boiling water and then baked it in the oven. It is considered complete bread, and one recites "Hamotzi" and Birkat Hamazon. In our times, bagels are dipped in boiling water, and it is complete bread. Similarly, when flour is scalded in boiling water and then baked in the oven after kneading, it is also considered complete bread. Even dough with a soft mixture, when baked in the oven, is considered complete bread, and one recites "Hamotzi" and Birkat Hamazon. Even if it is baked in a pan, as long as it is baked without any liquid at all, even if the pan is greased with a little liquid, it is not considered a liquid since this is done to prevent the bread from burning, and one recites "Hamotzi" and Birkat Hamazon. However, if some liquid is added to the pan for the purpose of frying, the previous law applies, that even with a thick mixture, one does not need to recite "Hamotzi." There we brought the opinion that equates it to challah, but with a soft mixture in such a case where it is fried with a little liquid, it is not considered bread according to all opinions (this is the explanation of Shulchan Aruch, section 14, and see Magen Avraham 39 who wrote in the name of Riva that even if it was fried in oil and then baked, one recites "Hamotzi," and he does not mean complete frying for in such a case it would be like pastries, but he means a slight frying, and since the kneading and baking are like regular bread, the slight frying in the middle does not prevent it).

The Tur wrote: "Troknin, which is when one makes a hole in a stove, puts flour and water in it, mixes them, and bakes them in the hole, is obligated in challah, and one blesses 'Hamotzi' over it, and a person fulfills their obligation on Passover with it. Since it is in a hole and combines together, it becomes like complete bread. But Trita, which has a soft mixture, and is where one takes flour and water, mixes them, and pours it on the stove where it spreads and bakes, does not have the status of bread, and one blesses 'Borei Minei Mezonot' over it." End quote. And if one established a meal on it, the Tur ruled that one must bless 'Hamotzi,' while Rabbeinu Beit Yosef ruled that even if one established a meal on it, one blesses 'Borei Minei Mezonot,' as he holds that it is not considered bread at all. And regarding Troknin, he ruled that only if one established a meal does one bless 'Hamotzi,' but if one did not establish a meal, one blesses 'Mezonot.' Refer there. The Talmudic discussion (37b) is explained according to Rabbeinu Beit Yosef, while the Jerusalem Talmud implies like the Tur, and Rabbeinu Yerucham explicitly states like Rabbeinu Beit Yosef. However, some say that with Trita, if one established a meal, the law follows the Tur, and the difference between Trita and Troknin is only regarding challah. In Rabbeinu Yerucham, there is a printing error (Magen Avraham section 48). There is no need to elaborate on this because we do not have these types of foods at all.

They further wrote: "Bread of the spit, which is dough baked on a spit and smeared with oil or egg wash, and similarly bread made for kutach that is not baked in an oven but in the sun - the blessing over it is 'Borei Minei Mezonot' (Who creates various kinds of sustenance)." And the Tur wrote: "If it is made like a fine bread, meaning arranged and attractive like a cake, it is obligated in challah and the blessing over it is 'Hamotzi' (Who brings forth bread from the earth)." And it is not known why our master, the Beit Yosef, omitted this, as it is explicitly stated in the Gemara there, and this is regarding the bread made for kutach, as mentioned there. However, this does not apply to the bread of the spit, as is evident. And behold, these types do not exist among us, and there is no need to elaborate on this.

Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 17: "A pastry baked in an oven with meat, fish, or cheese - one recites 'Hamotzi' and the Grace After Meals" [end of quote]. Our teacher, the Rema, wrote: "This is specifically if it is baked in the oven without liquid, but if it is baked in a pan with liquid - one does not recite a blessing over it and it should only be eaten within a meal, as explained" [end of quote].

This pastry is considered full bread, but it is filled with meat or cheese, similar to what we do on Purim when we fill bread with sesame seeds. This ruling has already been explained in section 46. The reason for not eating it outside of a meal when baked in a pan with liquid is because the liquid might nullify its status as bread, certainly if there is a small amount of liquid. But if there is a lot of liquid, it definitely nullifies its status as bread, as explained in section 44 there.

Know that there is someone who wrote in the name of Tanya that this pastry is blessed with 'Hamotzi' only when setting a meal, but without that, one recites 'Mezonot', and this remains questionable (Magen Avraham section 144). However, there is no question at all according to what we explained in section 46 about the difference between this and pastries filled with fruits and spices, where the spice is primary and here the bread is primary, as explained there. Therefore, it is clear that Tanya refers to cases where it is filled with a lot of meat until the meat is primary or fried slightly, but the pastry as explained is undoubtedly full bread according to the ruling of our masters, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch.

I have seen someone who differentiates between this and pastries filled with fruits and spices, arguing that fruit fillings nullify the status of bread more than meat fillings (Magen Avraham section 137). In my humble opinion, it seems clear that both are the same, and it depends only on the quantity. If the filling is not in large quantity, the bread is primary, and if the filling is large, the filling is primary. This seems to me to be the correct ruling (and it is surprising that the Magen Avraham himself in section 144 wrote in this language that the five species are primary, etc., and it is possible that all fillings with fruits also have the same ruling, as explained there. Consider this carefully).

And know that there is someone who wrote that dough kneaded with egg water without fat and baked — it is considered regular bread, because eggs are also nourishment and do not nullify its status as bread. And this is also implied in Beitzah (16b) in Tosafot s.v. "Kimcha," end quote (there, section 144). However, his words are puzzling, as what relevance does nourishment have, for anything not kneaded with water is considered "pat haba'ah b'kisnin" (a type of bread-like pastry). And it is common practice in all Jewish communities to eat cakes kneaded with eggs with the blessing of "Borei Minei Mezonot," unless one establishes a meal on them. And what he brought from Tosafot, they explicitly wrote that if one establishes a meal, etc., see there. Also, in Chullin (64a) in Tosafot s.v. "Simanim," they wrote regarding dough kneaded with eggs that one blesses "HaMotzi," see there, their intention is also when establishing a meal. And in Shibolei HaLeket, it is explicitly written that when kneaded with eggs, it is like kneaded with honey (Magen Avraham there). (And similarly, the Even HaOzer wrote at the end of this section: "Bread that is kneaded with wine... or with eggs or with other fruit juices — its blessing is 'Borei Minei Mezonot,' see there. And so ruled the Gaon Noda B'Yehuda in Dagul Mervavah at the end of this section, and this is his language: "Also, if kneaded with eggs, one blesses 'Borei Minei Mezonot,' see there. And this is the primary ruling in law).

Any food that causes a person distress when they are not given a taste upon smelling it—namely, a food that has a good smell or strong aroma and the one who sees it before him desires it and feels distressed and could become ill (Rashi, Ketubot 61a)—therefore, it is an obligation for the host, when the servant serving him brings such food and he eats it, to immediately give the servant a small portion of the food to taste. And thus it is stated in the Gemara there: The general rule is: anything that has a smell or a strong aroma, and Rashi explained: the smell or strong aroma harms the one who sees others eating it and is not eating himself. It implies that the primary desire occurs when the other begins to eat and not before. It is a pious practice to give him a portion from each type of food immediately, but according to the law, it is only necessary to give him from one type, as this quenches his desire. Also, according to the law, it is only necessary to give it to him after eating, but it is a pious practice to give it to him before eating (Gemara there). It seems to me that nowadays, this practice is not observed because the servants taste the food themselves in the kitchens, and furthermore, these matters apply only to the wealthy, and among the wealthy, the servants eat as they wish. However, a condition does not help in this matter because the reason is due to distress (Magen Avraham 1), but in other matters, a condition helps.

However, one should not give food to a servant when the cup is in the hand of the host or in the hand of the servant. As it is taught in Chullin (107b): One should not give a piece to a servant, whether the cup is in the servant's hand—because perhaps while he is preoccupied with the piece, he will spill the cup—or whether the cup is in the hand of the host—because perhaps the host will look to see what was given to the servant and will spill the cup. This is explained by the Tur. Rashi, of blessed memory, explained that this applies to one of the guests. And this is only for the servant; but the other participants in the meal may give to each other even when the cup is in the hand of the host, because he does not mind regarding them. There is no difference whether he is dining with his household members or with guests; they may give to each other, because since he invited them, he does not mind regarding them. But to give to someone who is not part of the meal—his status is like that of a servant. And now we do not concern ourselves with this, because among them, drinking wine was a fixed practice at every meal, which is not the case among us. Therefore, even if we happen to drink a little, we do not worry about it.

It is further stated in the Gemara there that one should not give a piece (of bread) to the attendant unless he knows that he has washed his hands. And it is implied from Rashi there that this concern applies only to the attendant, because he is preoccupied with serving at the table and might forget to wash his hands, but we do not have this concern with others—why should we assume such a thing about a Jewish person? However, Rabbeinu Yonah wrote that this law applies to everyone. From this, he also deduced that one should not give food to someone unless he knows that the person will recite a blessing, as Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote in paragraph 2. There are those who wrote that only in regard to washing hands should we be concerned, because he must wash his hands before taking the piece (of bread) into his hand, but for the blessing of Hamotzi, he must give it to him before reciting the blessing. And after he has given it to him, if he does not recite a blessing, what can he do about it (Bach)? Rabbeinu Yonah also wrote that one may be lenient if giving to a poor person as charity, as brought by Rabbeinu Rema, and this is the explanation: Charity is a mitzvah, and one must give it to him, and he cannot withhold the giving due to the doubt that perhaps the recipient will not bless, for a doubt does not override a certainty. This applies only to the blessing of Hamotzi, but regarding washing hands, he must wash beforehand. Similarly, if giving to someone as a gift and not as charity, he should not give until he knows that the recipient will bless. And if he knows for certain that the recipient will not bless, it is forbidden, even in the case of a poor person (Magen Avraham, Subsection 6), and this is the proper ruling.

Our Master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in Section 3: "The attendant recites the blessing 'Borei Pri HaGafen' over each and every cup given to him, as he is considered to be as if he decided to drink more wine, but he does not recite a final blessing until the end. He does not need to bless each piece of bread if there is an important person at the meal who knows that he will be given all the bread he needs (not specifically bread, as this applies to all foods; see Taz). However, if there is no important person at the meal, he needs to bless each piece of bread as he does with the wine." If the attendant had in mind at the time of the first cup he blessed to include all subsequent cups, he does not need to bless each cup individually, and the same applies to the pieces of bread (as noted there, subsection 7). There are those who disagree, arguing that his intention does not help as he does not know if more will be given to him (Taz, end of section 179), and the matter requires further investigation (Eliyah Rabbah). This will be explained at the end of section 179, with God's help. Our Master, the Rema, wrote: "When two people eat together, the attendant eats with them without needing permission so that they can form a zimun (quorum for Grace After Meals)," and this will be explained in the next section.

One should not speak in the middle of eating. Our Sages stated in Taanit (5a): "Do not converse during a meal, lest the windpipe precede the esophagus and cause danger," because when one speaks, the cover over the windpipe opens, allowing food to enter and posing a risk (Rashi). It seems that between one food and another it is permitted, but some say that even between one food and another it is prohibited as long as one intends to continue eating, because since it is a matter of danger, they were cautious in every situation (Perisha). Even words of Torah should not be spoken (Magen Avraham 1), and this is also implied in Taanit there. One should not question this based on the Mishnah in Avot (Chapter 3): "Any table that does not have words of Torah spoken over it is as if they ate from offerings to the dead," because many agree that Birkat Hamazon alone does not suffice. If so, how is this accomplished? One can say that it is achieved after eating, or before washing hands when preparing for the meal, or after the blessing of 'Hamotzi' before one starts eating, just the 'Hamotzi' itself. In our practice, we fulfill this by reciting 'Al Naharot Bavel' before Birkat Hamazon, and on Shabbat, Yom Tov, and Rosh Chodesh, we recite 'Shir Hama'alot B'Shuv.' However, one who can manage to study actual words of Torah, it is all the better.

It is difficult to understand why nowadays people are not careful about this law and speak during the meal. Some say that this concern was specifically for their [ancestors'] time when they would eat while reclining, as then the esophagus was above and the windpipe below, and food could enter the windpipe when it opens, as mentioned. But for us, who sit upright and the windpipe is not below, there is no concern (Pri Megadim). However, this distinction is not mentioned anywhere (there), and furthermore, if so, why didn't he respond during the fast that he should sit upright and answer? Additionally, even if the windpipe is level with the esophagus, it still seems that food could fall there. 

Perhaps they hold that the statement "one should not converse during the meal" refers to extensive matters, like discussing Torah matters during the fast there, as questions in Torah can lead to lengthy discussions. But to respond with a few words, we do not concern ourselves, as perhaps this does not open the windpipe. Therefore, indeed, we do not speak in the middle of eating, only between dishes, and we do not worry about the opinion in the first clause that one should not speak even between dishes, as this does not seem correct. In the middle of the meal, we speak little by little. 

Another possible explanation is that since many are accustomed to it, "The Lord protects the simple" (Shabbat, end of chapter 18), and this seems to be the main explanation. The previous answer has a contradiction from the Jerusalem Talmud, chapter 6 of Berachot, which says not to interrupt eating even to say "Gesundheit" to someone who sneezes, as mentioned by the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch. From this, it is clear that one should not speak even a single word in the middle of eating.

The Talmud in Yoma (30a) states: The Rabbis taught: If a person leaves during a meal to urinate, meaning he leaves in the middle of the meal to urinate, he must wash one hand upon returning—the hand that wiped the droplets that fell on his legs (Rashi)—and he must recite the blessing 'Al Netilat Yadayim' (Magen Avraham, section 2). When washing, he should not wash outside, but rather in a way that everyone will notice that he washed, so that he will not be suspected of not washing. Perhaps someone saw him wiping the droplets and might suspect him (Magen Avraham, section 3). Therefore, if he did not actually wipe the droplets and did not touch private areas, he does not need to wash at all. However, if he defecated, he must wash in any case. 

What we said about not washing outside due to suspicion applies if he does not intend to eat more but only to drink, and with drinking, one also eats a little, leading to suspicion that he is not strict about washing his hands. But if he needs to eat more, he can even wash outside, as everyone knows that in such a case, anyone meticulous would certainly wash their hands. 

In the Gemara there, it states: "Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak said: Even when I drink, people know that I am delicate (fastidious)," meaning I am meticulous (see there). The Tur and Shulchan Aruch omit this, as we do not compare ourselves to them, and similarly, the Rambam omits this in Chapter 7 (see there).

If during the meal, one leaves the table and talks to his friend at length, meaning he spends a lot of time talking away from the table—he must wash both hands upon returning. Since he spent an hour or two, he diverted his attention from his meal and did not take care to keep his hands clean, as they are busy (Rashi). It appears that he does not need to recite a blessing nor the 'Hamotzi' blessing, as stated in Siman 178 (Magen Avraham, section 4). Whenever one spends a long time, he must wash in a noticeable manner, as he will certainly be suspected (Magen Avraham, section 5).

Note that the requirement to wash for drinking applies only during a meal, due to the concern that he might also eat. But for drinking outside of a meal, washing is not required, meaning the rules of handwashing do not apply. If his hands are not clean, he washes them however he can without a blessing.

It is stated in Berakhot (47b): "Two people wait for each other at the table, but three do not wait for each other; the one who breaks bread extends his hand first, etc." At first glance, it appears that the explanation is as follows: that one should not start eating from the table before the other, and the one who breaks the bread extends his hand first, and immediately after, the second person extends his hand. However, if the second person is not yet ready, the first person should also not start. However, our teacher, the Beit Yosef, in his major work, explained this in a different manner, which is that if, in the middle of the meal, one person stops eating from the table in order to drink or for some other reason, his companion should also stop eating from the table until he finishes drinking or the other matter. But if there are three, the two do not stop because of the one. And it seems that this applies when they are eating from one dish; therefore, out of respect, this should be done. However, when each one is eating from his own dish, this law does not apply. Nevertheless, the explanation we initially provided is certainly correct according to the law.

It is stated in Eruvin (53b): "One does not leave a portion in the pot, but one does leave a portion in the bowl." Rashi explains: "When the servant pours from the pot into the bowl, it is not customary to leave anything in the pot for himself. However, each person leaves a portion in the bowl and returns it to the servant, and this is the servant's food." These are his words, and similarly wrote the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch in section 3. And even though it is necessary to give to the servant also at the beginning of the meal, as written in the previous section, at that time, he gives him a small amount. Furthermore, not all foods follow this rule, as stated there. But here, they leave him a substantial amount, and this applies to all types of food. And even if he is not serving at the meal but only cooks the food, and even if his sustenance is not dependent on it, one must leave something for him (Magen Avraham, sub-section 8).

And know that in the Tractate Derech Eretz (Chapter 6) it is taught: "One leaves a portion (pe'ah) from a dish made in a pan, but one does not leave a portion from a dish made in a pot," because leaving from a dish made in a pan appears gluttonous if one does not leave some, but not so with a dish made in a pot. And the Tosafot in Eruvin there brought the opposite: leaving from a dish made in a pot but not from a dish made in a pan, because leaving from a dish made in a pot appears gluttonous and not from a dish made in a pan, see there. And there it appears that it is not for the sake of leaving some for the servant, but rather this is a measure of proper conduct. And now the custom is that the guest leaves a little, but the host in his house does not leave, and perhaps the intention of the Baraita is also such, and so it seems in the Gemara and in Derech Eretz that they brought this regarding one who comes to an inn, see there. And perhaps for this reason the custom has spread that the guest leaves some when he does not pay for his meal.

Rambam wrote in Chapter 7: "One should not look at the face of someone who is eating nor at their portion, so as not to embarrass them." This is his conclusion. I have not found this in any other place, but logically it is certainly correct. This applies to a guest who is eating for free, for when people look at him or at his portion, it seems to him that they are scrutinizing what he eats. It is taught in Derech Eretz Zuta (Chapter 4): "Scholars are pleasant in a group, but the unlearned are not pleasant in a group," meaning that scholars conduct themselves with proper manners and speak with dignity, unlike the unlearned, who are coarse and lack proper manners. And there in Chapter 5, it is taught: "A scholar should not eat standing up nor lick his fingers... A person should always be aware of who he is sitting with, standing with, reclining with, and speaking with... Scholars are recognized by their pockets, their cups, their anger, and their attire, and some say even by their speech."

We learned in Tractate Derech Eretz, Chapter 6: "When one enters a house, one should do everything the homeowner decrees." And in Pesachim, at the end of Chapter 7, we say: "Whatever the homeowner tells you to do, do, except 'leave,'" meaning if he tells him to leave the lodging, he does not need to leave, as it is said in Arakhin (16b) that one does not change lodging. And a person should not be strict during his meal, meaning he should not get angry or upset, because it is difficult for the household members and the guests to eat then, as they worry that he might be upset about their eating (see Taz).

It is stated at the end of the seventh chapter of Pesachim: "One who drinks his cup in one gulp is a glutton; in two gulps, it is proper conduct; in three gulps, it is haughty." Therefore, one should be careful not to drink the cup in one gulp. However, if the cup is small, he may drink it in one gulp (there). There is no fixed measure for this; rather, it depends on the drink and the person (see Magen Avraham, section 13). Similarly, for a very large cup or a very strong drink like potent liquor, one may drink it even in four or five sips. And it is stated in Bechorot (44b): "One does not drink water in front of many people," and so it is in Tractate Derech Eretz Zuta, chapter 6: "If one comes to drink in public, he should turn his face to the other side and drink" (see there). And it is not proper for a woman to drink an alcoholic beverage, except a little if she is accustomed to it (Ketubot 65a and see Magen Avraham, section 7).

It is taught there at the end of Chapter 6: "One should not drink two cups and then recite the Grace After Meals, because it appears gluttonous." The language of the Tur is as follows: "One should not bring two cups to his meal and then recite the Grace After Meals, because it appears gluttonous." The language of our teacher, the Beit Yosef, in Section 11 is like the language of the baraita, except that he adds 'at once'. And the matter is not understood; if the intention is that one should not drink two cups consecutively, what does this have to do with the Grace After Meals? And all that is said about this is not sufficient, and it requires further investigation. And know that it is a measure of proper conduct to refuse a little when asked to eat or drink, but one should not refuse a great person and should do so immediately.

It is stated in Beitzah (25b): A person should not eat garlic or onions from their head, but rather from their leaves. If he eats from the head, he is considered greedy. A person should not eat in a greedy manner, meaning he should not eat a large slice of bread the size of an egg. Even if he does not eat it all at once but holds a large slice in his hand and bites from it, he is considered gluttonous, except on Shabbat with the blessing of 'Hamotzi'. Additionally, he should not bite a slice and place it on the table while it is bitten, as it is considered disgusting. Thus we have learned in Tractate Derech Eretz Zuta (Chapter 6): A person should not recline in the presence of someone greater than himself, meaning if he eats with a great person, he should not recline. When he comes to break bread, he should break it in the place of the roast, meaning the hard part. If he comes to eat radish and onion, he should eat from the leaves. He should not take the loaf and tear it with his teeth and then put it back on the table.

It is obvious that one should not do something at the table that others find repulsive, such as spitting forcefully either from the mouth or the nose, nor should one pick their teeth, which involves opening the mouth in a way others cannot bear to see. Similarly, throat clearing, known as "gargling," is recognized as something people find disgusting. Additionally, any repulsive behavior is forbidden in front of another person even when not eating, as it is stated in Chagigah (5b): "For God will bring every deed into judgment, including everything hidden" (Ecclesiastes 12:14), this refers to spitting in front of another person and being repulsive to them. And in Eruvin (99a), it is stated: "Spitting or clearing one’s throat in front of one’s teacher is punishable by death."

We learned in Chapter 7 of Tractate Derech Eretz: "When two people are sitting at one table, the greater of them extends his hand first, and afterward the lesser one; if the lesser one extends his hand first, he is considered greedy." This applies even if each one is eating from his own bowl or from types of fruits that are before each of them (Bach and Magen Avraham, section 17). And in Chapter 8, we learned: One who enters a house should not say to them, 'Give me [something] to eat,' until they say to him, 'Eat.' But if they place food before him, he does not need them to tell him to eat. The proof is from Eliezer who said, "I will not eat until [I have told my errand]," and they had not yet told him to eat. But since it is written, "and food was set before him to eat," he did not need a further invitation (Magen Avraham, section 18). It seems that this applies to someone eating for free, but in the case of a guest paying for lodging, he may say, 'Give me [something] to eat,' and this is the common practice. We also learned there: "When they pour him a cup, he waits and drinks, etc." (see Taz, section 6, and it appears that the blessing of 'Hamotzi' is different).

We also learned there: "A person should not say to his friend: 'Come and eat what you fed me,' as this is a form of interest." Meaning, it is as though he is repaying a debt, which appears as if he had lent him, and he might feed him more, raising concerns of interest. However, it is permissible to say: 'Come and eat with me and I will eat with you another time,' and it is permissible to eat with him afterward even at a larger meal, since the intention is not repayment but rather from the way of friendship.

At the end of Horayot, it is taught that there are foods that are detrimental to memory. It lists the heart of an animal, the heart of a wild animal, the heart of a bird, and olives. It is written that one who eats olives with intention enhances memory (Magen Avraham, section 19). It is written that the Ari z"l would eat wild herbs that are not sown by human hands, to fulfill the verse: "And you shall eat the herb of the field," which was said to Adam after the sin (see Pesachim 118).

We also learned in Tractate Derech Eretz (Chapter 9): A person should not place a piece of bread on top of the bowl, but one may wipe the bowl with a piece of bread. The reason for not placing it on the bowl is that it might fall from the bread into the bowl and become repulsive. However, at the end of the meal, one may wipe the bowl with the piece of bread. A person should not collect crumbs and place them on the table because it is distasteful to others. One should not bite a piece of bread and then offer it to someone else or put it into the bowl, as people's sensibilities differ, meaning some may find it repulsive. One should not drink from a cup and then give it to someone else because of the danger to life, meaning there are some people who cannot drink from what others have left, and out of embarrassment, they might drink and come to harm. However, when someone takes it for themselves and drinks, there is no issue. In the will of Rabbi Eliezer the Great, he strongly warns against drinking from others' cups because some people have illnesses, and their breath enters the cup, posing a danger to the drinker (Taz, section 8). One should not drink from a cup and place it on the table, as someone might find it repulsive. Instead, one should hold it in their hand until the servant comes and takes it. Nowadays, we are not careful about this because at most tables, it is not possible to wait for the servant, and it is not our custom, nor have we seen anyone who is particular about this.

We also learned there: One who enters a meal should not take his portion and give it to the servant, lest something go wrong with the meal. Rather, he should take it and place it before him, and then he may give it to him. And this is its explanation: Behold, a guest may give from his portion to the servant, but perhaps the host will not have enough to give to all the guests because something might go wrong with the meal. Therefore, he should not hasten to give until all the portions are distributed, and afterwards, he may give if he wishes (Levush and Taz, Subsection 9, and the reasoning of the Magen Avraham, Subsection 22, is strained; see there). And guests who enter the host's home are not permitted to take from their portions and give to the host's son or servant unless they have received permission from the host. This does not contradict the previous rule, for the servant who serves at the meal does not need to receive permission from the host (Perisha). And it is said in Sanhedrin (23b): "The refined people of Jerusalem would not recline at a meal unless they knew who would be reclining with them," because it is disgraceful for a Torah scholar to sit at a meal with an ignoramus.

It was taught at the beginning of Chapter 7 of Berachot: A servant who is serving two people can eat with them even if they did not give him permission, since it is certainly agreeable to them so that he can join in the zimun (invitation to recite Grace After Meals). If he is serving three people, he may not eat with them unless they give him permission. It seems to me that only a servant can join two people without their permission, since they would need to give him food in any case as explained, but for someone to come from the marketplace and eat without their knowledge is certainly forbidden, as who says they would be agreeable to give their food to a stranger for the sake of the mitzvah of zimun? And when they are eating something that does not warrant a zimun, the servant also should not eat without permission (Taz, sub-paragraph 10), and this is obvious.

After you have drunk from the cup and there is wine left in the cup for your friend to drink, if it is wine, you should wipe the place where your mouth touched the cup because of repulsiveness. Do not pour out some of the wine because of the prohibition of “wanton destruction” (Bal Tashchit), unless your friend does not want to drink in any other way. But after drinking water, you should pour some out from that spot, and this is the custom to pour a little. After all your eating, eat salt, and after all your drinking, drink water. This applies when there was no salt in the bread or the foods that you ate, and you did not drink any beverage that contains water. But otherwise, there is no need for concern. And so, it is customary not to be meticulous about eating salt and drinking water for this reason.

The Sages prohibited using food items in a way that disrespects them, because it appears as if one is contemptuous of the blessings of the Holy One, blessed be He. However, other uses that do not disrespect the food are permitted, even with bread, which is the primary food, as long as it does not render the food repulsive. But if it does render the food repulsive, it is prohibited, as it disrespects the bread and all types of food. Therefore, one should not place raw meat on it, as it makes it repulsive, nor should one pass a full cup over it, lest it spills on the bread and makes it repulsive. Similarly, one should not place a bowl filled with soup or porridge or anything that makes it repulsive on it, lest it falls on the bread and makes it repulsive. However, if it does not contain anything that makes it repulsive, it is permitted to use it, as this is not disrespectful, since a person may use bread for all his needs, and certainly for other foods.

Similarly, when something is done for human needs, even if it results in loss, since it is not done in a disrespectful manner, it is permissible. For example, sprinkling wine in the house or anointing the body with oil. Likewise, we say in Shabbat (108a): A person may soak bread in wine and place it on the eye for medicinal purposes, even though the bread will certainly become repulsive. Nevertheless, since it is done for healing and not for destruction, it is permissible. Similarly, it is permitted to make wine mixtures and wash with wine, and to use wine for washing hands when there is no water, as stated in Siman 160. However, when there is water available, it is forbidden to wash hands with wine, whether undiluted or diluted, even for washing not related to eating. But to remove dirt, it is permissible to use either wine or oil. And so it is taught in Berakhot (53b): Oil prevents the blessing, and they supported it with a verse, see there. Rashi explained: "Oil that they were accustomed to bring at the end of the meal to anoint the hands to remove their dirt" (end quote). Therefore, one may use wine for the final washing of hands, as stated in Siman 181, because it removes the dirt (see Taz and Magen Avraham). And this is the language of the Rambam in chapter 7: "One does not destroy food in a disrespectful and contemptuous manner," see there. But as long as it is not done disrespectfully and is for one's needs - it is permissible.

And one should not throw bread, even though it does not become soiled, because the act of throwing itself is a form of disrespect. Just as one should not throw bread, so too should one not throw other foods. However, there is a distinction in this regard: the prohibition regarding other foods applies only when they become soiled and repulsive through throwing, but if they do not become soiled, such as nuts, almonds, pomegranates, and quinces which have hard shells and the food does not become repulsive – it is permitted. And it is not comparable to bread, upon which a person’s life depends and therefore it requires a certain degree of respect, but not other foods. And even though there are those who hold that there is no distinction, this opinion is not considered (see Beit Yosef and Levush).

And that which we said that it is forbidden to support a bowl of soup with bread lest it spill on the bread and make it repulsive, this is when one is not eating this bread at the time. But to eat the bread with the soup - it is permitted to use the bread for the soup, meaning that one eats the porridge with the bread, and the bread serves in place of a spoon, as one takes the porridge with the bread and eats them together. And according to the law, even if one does not eat them together but afterward - it is also permitted, for this is not a manner of disrespect but a manner of eating. Nevertheless, the meticulous ones eat each time they put a bit of the bread into their mouth, and the rest they eat afterward. And they should not leave it, for it becomes repulsive to others, and so it is proper to do, for if not, one is using the bread as if it were just wood, and it is not proper to do so (see Magen Avraham, section 3).

A person should not sit on a basket full of figs and dried figs if the basket is soft, because he will press them with his body and render them unfit, and certainly it is forbidden to sit on bread. However, one may sit on a circle of pressed figs or on a basket full of legumes, as these are not rendered unfit by doing so. Whether it is permissible to sit on a box containing books is explained in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 282, see there. 

Pouring wine through pipes before a bride and groom was a custom in ancient times, and this does not constitute disrespect for the wine since it is done as a good omen, meaning that their tranquility will continue, and it is done for the joy of the bride and groom, provided that it does not go to waste but is collected in a vessel at the end of the pipe. Throwing roasted grains and nuts before them in the summer, when they do not become spoiled, is allowed, but not in the rainy season when they do become spoiled. Even though they are in their shells, nevertheless, because of the mud and mire, they become completely spoiled.

It is always forbidden to throw cakes, as bread is distinct from other foods in regard to throwing, as stated in paragraph 3. Those who throw wheat before bride and groom must ensure to throw it only in a clean place and also to sweep it up from there so that it is not trampled underfoot. If one sees food lying on the ground, one should not pass by and leave it but should pick it up, unless there is a concern of witchcraft (see Magen Avraham, Subsection 1). It is stated in Taanit (20b) that human food should not be fed to animals, see there (in Shabbat 50a it states that it is forbidden to crush olives even if one's intention is to sweeten the fruit because doing so renders them unfit; the Rif explained that it refers to wanting to use the olives for washing hands and it is possible to clean with soap, see there and in Magen Avraham there).

If one forgot and put food into his mouth without a blessing: If it is something that would become disgusting if he spits it out, he should move it to one side of his mouth and bless. If it is something that would not become disgusting, he should spit it out and bless. And why is it not sufficient to move it to one side of his mouth and bless? Because it says, "My mouth will be filled with Your praise." However, after the fact, if he moved it to one side and blessed, his blessing is valid. If he did not remember until after he had eaten and it had gone down into his stomach, he does not bless, as it is stated in Siman 167, since once it is rejected, it is rejected. He should only recite the after-blessing if there is an olive-sized portion (of food), and this applies to food.

But if one forgets and places liquids into their mouth without a blessing, even though they have not yet swallowed them, they should swallow them and not recite the initial blessing on them. Since they have entered the mouth, they cease to be considered liquids, as they are no longer fit for anyone and are like food after it has been swallowed. Since they have been set aside, they remain set aside, and one should only recite the after-blessing if there is the requisite amount. This is also implied by the language of the Rambam in Chapter 8, where he writes: "Swallow them and bless on them at the end," meaning the after-blessing. However, our teacher, the Rema, wrote that some say one should bless on them, and this seems to be the main opinion. And this is the opinion of the Rosh, who wrote that it is not comparable to food after swallowing, because here, since it is still in the mouth, it is similar to before the act. Some also interpret the Rambam's words to mean that one should bless on them the initial blessing at the end, but this does not seem to be the case. The more correct opinion, as stated by the Raavad, is that if one has no other liquids and is compelled to this, then they should swallow without a blessing. However, if they have other liquids or are not compelled to this, it is better to spit it out and not swallow without a blessing. And this is also agreed upon by the later authorities, for according to our teacher, the Rema, there is a difficulty in how to conduct the after-blessing, as we do not find two blessings adjacent to each other in the blessings of enjoyment without an interruption of something in between. Nevertheless, according to him, for the seven species, one should recite the after-blessing, as it is a Torah obligation (see Magen Avraham, Section 3).

Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote: "Washing hands between courses is optional, and this applies between one dish and another. But between a meat dish and a dairy dish—it is mandatory." End of quote. He was very brief, and this is not understandable. The matter is as follows: At the end of the eighth chapter of Berachot, the Rabbis based the practice of washing hands before and after a meal on verses, but there is no mention at all of washing hands between courses. However, in Chullin (105b), it is said: "Washing hands between courses is optional. Rav Nachman said: this was only taught between one dish and another, but between a meat dish and cheese—it is mandatory." Rashbam explained that between one dish and another refers to when both dishes are either meat or both are dairy, meaning that washing is for cleanliness alone. But between a meat dish and cheese that follows—it is mandatory, so that the cheese in one's hands does not stick to the meat dish. And Rabbeinu Tam explained that between one dish and another also includes between a meat dish and a dairy dish, and the sages did not worry about this. But between a meat dish and actual cheese, it is mandatory. The Tur also explained it this way.

And one should not ask, when there is an obligation to wash one's hands, why a blessing was not instituted for this, as it can be said that this is like a preparation for food, similar to deveining and salting (Tosafot there at the end of s.v. 'water'), and it is not appropriate to recite a blessing for this. And behold, according to this, it is not related at all to the laws of the meal but rather to the laws of meat and milk, as explained in Yoreh De'ah, section 89. And indeed, Rambam did not mention this in the laws of blessings, but rather in chapter 9 of Forbidden Foods, and he also did not mention the term 'washing' but rather 'rinsing,' as mentioned there. According to this, the words of our teacher, the Beit Yosef, can be interpreted according to both explanations. He also wrote that between meat and fish it is obligatory to wash because it is harmful to leprosy, and danger is more severe than prohibition. There is a slight proof for this from Pesachim (76b), and Rambam did not mention this, and it was written that nowadays the nature of people has changed (Magen Avraham), and also Tosafot at the end of the first chapter of Moed Katan wrote similarly. And we do not eat fish after meat, only meat after fish, and we have heard that there are places where they eat meat and then fish.

Our Master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in Section 3: "All the practices that apply to the last waters (mayim acharonim) also apply to the middle waters (mayim emtza'im), whether to be lenient or stringent, except for the diversion of attention (hesach hada'at), which invalidates the middle waters because one still intends to eat and their hands require guarding, and except for drying the hands, as the middle waters require drying like the first waters (mayim rishonim)." End quote. And our Master, the Rema, added that some say the middle waters specifically require water, unlike the last waters, as mentioned later in Siman 181, because other liquids do not clean the grease and food, though there are those who disagree with this (Magen Avraham in the name of the Rashal), and drying is necessary because of repulsiveness (there). I do not understand what relevance the diversion of attention has to the middle waters, which are an interruption between milk and meat, and if it is because of the diversion of attention regarding the first waters, then what does this have to do with the middle waters? This requires further study.

Even though all beverages drunk during the meal do not require a blessing, as will be explained, nonetheless, wine requires a blessing. Even wine drunk during the meal, which is to facilitate the digestion of the food in the intestines and is like items that come because of the meal, which the blessing of 'Hamotzi' exempts, still requires the blessing of 'Borei Pri Hagafen'. The reason, as stated by the Sages in Berachot (42a), is that wine is unique in that it warrants its own blessing, as it is used in several contexts where blessings are recited over it even though its consumption is not necessary (Rashi), such as for Kiddush, Havdalah, and the blessings of betrothal and marriage. 

One should not question why, in this case, Birkat Hamazon (Grace After Meals) does not exempt the after-blessing for wine, because it is different. Birkat Hamazon exempts even items that are not part of the meal, unlike the initial blessing (Rashba). The reason, it seems to me, is because Birkat Hamazon is a Torah obligation. Furthermore, the primary importance is given to the initial blessing, and the after-blessing naturally follows due to the obligation of drinking (this seems to be the intent of the Ramban in the chapter "Arvei Pesachim," and the Gra (Rabbi Elijah of Vilna) addresses this in his commentary. What Tosafot says there, 103a, in the commentary "Rebbi Eliezer" seems puzzling to me, as we do not follow Rebbi Eliezer's opinion but rather Mar Zutra's, and the previous explanation is clearer – examine this well).

There is additional importance to wine, for just as bread exempts all kinds of food during a meal, so too does wine exempt all kinds of drinks (as stated in the Talmud), even from the initial blessing and even not during the meal. During the meal, it is not necessary for wine to exempt them because bread exempts them, just as bread has the quality of satiating, so too does wine have the quality of bringing joy, as it is written: "And wine gladdens the heart of man, and bread sustains the heart of man." It appears to me that this is specifically when one sits to drink in a fixed manner like with bread, and there is also a fixed manner with wine, as mentioned in Siman 213. Some say that this is only when other drinks are in front of him, but otherwise, it does not exempt (Taz, subsection 2, in the name of Mordechai). Some say that even if they are not in front of him, but he has them in mind, it exempts (the Gra) when he sits in a fixed manner to drink the wine (as stated in the Talmud). I have seen someone write that even if he does not set himself to drink wine but drinks a little wine for a mitzvah purpose, such as Kiddush or Havdalah, and then drinks many other drinks afterward, they are exempted by the blessing over the wine if he had them in mind (the Gra). In my humble opinion, it seems that without a fixed manner, it does not exempt, for the Talmud compares it to bread, and with bread, there is a fixed manner. However, Kiddush and Havdalah are considered fixed manners, for Kiddush is certainly a fixed manner, as Kiddush must be in the place of the meal. Even Havdalah is also considered a fixed manner, as Tosafot wrote in Berachot (43, starting from 'since'), and this appears to me to be the primary ruling (and I found this also in Mordechai, chapter "How to Bless", and it is explicitly stated in Or Zarua HaGadol, Siman 155).

Know that I did not find in the Rambam or the Tur this ruling that a blessing on wine exempts all other beverages, and I do not know why, as it is explicitly stated in the Gemara in Berachot (41b) and in Chullin (111b). Only our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote this ruling in section 2, and also the Rosh ruled this way in chapter 6 (section 26), and so did the Terumat HaDeshen rule there. It appears to me that according to the Talmudic discussion, the law is not so, and this is what it states there: "It was stated: if they brought figs and grapes during the meal: Rav Huna said: one blesses before them... and it contradicts Rabbi Chiya, for Rabbi Chiya said: bread exempts... and wine exempts" etc. And we hold like Rav Huna, and consequently, the law is not like Rabbi Chiya.
