However, the Rosh and the Terumat HaDeshen wrote there that although the law is not like Rabbi Chiya regarding bread, it is like him regarding wine. And the Rambam and the Tur do not think so. And indeed, I do not understand the opinion of the Rosh and the Terumat HaDeshen, for just as bread does not exempt figs and grapes because they are not related to the meal, so too, it is clear that other beverages are not related to wine, and why should they be exempt to us who do not hold like Rabbi Chiya regarding bread. We must say that the Rosh and the Terumat HaDeshen believe that there is a closer connection between other beverages and wine than there is between figs and grapes and bread. Also, from the words of the Rif, it seems he does not hold this way, as he wrote: "and it contradicts Rabbi Chiya etc.," and if you would think that regarding wine he ruled like him, he would have explained, but certainly, he rejected it from the law. And we are compelled to say so, for otherwise, why did he write at all "and it contradicts Rabbi Chiya," for if it was regarding figs and grapes, he had already brought the words of Rav Huna, but certainly, he wrote it because of wine, meaning that also in this we do not hold like Rabbi Chiya. According to this, it would be a doubtful law, but consequently, we are lenient in rabbinic doubts. The Bahag ruled it as law there in chapter 6, and so did the Or Zarua the Great (section 155), but our rabbis, the Tosafists, wrote there that also regarding wine, the law is not like Rabbi Chiya (and it is questionable if those who hear the blessing "Borei Pri HaGafen" and fulfill their obligation with his blessing, whether they also exempt all other beverages from a blessing if they did not drink from the cup of blessing, and see Tosafot Pesachim 100a s.v. "and Rabbi Yosef").

If one is sitting at a meal and has only one cup of wine, he should not drink it during the meal. Instead, he should leave it until after the meal, recite the blessing over the cup, and then drink it. Even if the cup came to him earlier (Taz, paragraph 3). Nevertheless, there is an opinion that if one is thirsty for the wine, and we do not have the custom of using a cup for the Grace After Meals, and he holds like the one who says that the Grace After Meals does not require a cup, and our master the Rama ruled later at the end of Siman 197 that according to the Torah, if one is thirsty to drink, he is not obligated to wait until the Grace After Meals, therefore it is better to drink before the Grace After Meals (Magen Avraham, paragraph 2).

Our Sages said that wine before the meal exempts the wine during the meal and the wine after the meal, meaning after they have withdrawn their hands from the bread to drink wine and eat fruits before Birkat HaMazon (Grace After Meals). But for us, there is no concept of "after the meal" because we are not accustomed to this practice and we do not withdraw our hands from the bread until Birkat HaMazon, as will be explained in Siman 177. Therefore, for us, everything is considered "during the meal." Wine during the meal does not exempt wine after the meal, and the reason is: the wine before and after the meal is for drinking, while the wine during the meal is merely to rinse the food in the intestines. Drinking is considered more significant than rinsing, and therefore what comes for drinking exempts what comes for rinsing, but not the reverse, for what is less significant does not exempt what is more significant. And for us, as mentioned, there is no "after the meal." It has been clarified that one must make a blessing on the wine during the meal, that is when one did not drink beforehand.

(6) The Tur and Shulchan Aruch write in section 4, "If one established to drink before the meal, there is no need to bless on the wine during the meal, etc." This is not specifically about establishing to drink, as the same applies even without establishing. Their intent with "establishing" was that he intended to drink during the meal, excluding if he had no intention to drink at all during the meal but later decided to drink. In such a case, the wine before the meal does not exempt the wine during the meal since he had no intention to drink at all (Taz, subsection 4). However, establishing is not required. Only if he drank before the meal does it exempt the wine he will drink during the meal and after the meal, provided he intended to drink.

And similarly, the wine used for Kiddush and Havdalah exempts the wine consumed during the meal. Not only Kiddush, which is related to the meal, but even Havdalah, which is not related to the meal — nevertheless, if at the time of Havdalah it was his intention to eat immediately and drink wine during the meal, then the wine of Havdalah exempts it. This is no less than wine before the meal on weekdays, which exempts it, and what is the deficiency of Havdalah? However, some say that Havdalah is deficient. For on weekdays, when one drinks voluntarily before the meal, it is called wine before the meal. But Havdalah, where one is compelled to drink for the sake of the mitzvah, has no connection to the meal at all. It is not comparable to Kiddush, which is only in the context of a meal. According to this opinion, the wine of Havdalah only exempts if he washed his hands for eating before Havdalah, and this is not considered an interruption between washing the hands and the blessing of 'Hamotzi,' since his intention is to eat. And it is not specifically that he washed his hands, for even if he did not wash his hands but established himself for a meal (Magen Avraham 296:6). Therefore, one who performs Havdalah before washing and before establishing the meal, which means arranging the table for eating, should intend not to exempt the wine during the meal. However, if he did not intend this, he should not recite a blessing, as we are lenient in cases of doubt regarding blessings of rabbinic origin.

If one did not drink wine before the meal, they should recite a blessing over the first cup of wine they drink during the meal. This blessing covers all the wine they will drink throughout the meal, similar to how the blessing over bread covers all the food eaten during the meal. This is not similar to the first night of Passover, where a blessing of 'Borei Pri HaGafen' is recited over each cup of wine, as there the drinking is not part of a meal.

However, this applies only when one intends to drink more wine beyond the first cup. If one initially did not plan to drink more but later decides to have another cup, a new blessing is required, and this rule applies universally. This is true for all foods, whether fruits or bread. For example, if someone purchased a loaf of bread to eat, finished it, and then decided to buy another loaf, they must recite 'Hamotzi' again. 

However, this does not apply to a homeowner eating bread in their own home, as there is no set limit to bread, and their intention encompasses all they will eat (Taz, subsection 6). But with wine, which is for enjoyment, even a homeowner at home who initially only wanted to drink one cup but then changes their mind and drinks another cup, must recite a new blessing. If there was no specific intention regarding further drinking, it depends on the situation: if the person usually drinks several cups during a meal, no new blessing is needed; if they do not usually drink multiple cups, a new blessing is required.

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote in paragraph 5: "Similarly, one who comes to a meal and they offer him many cups, he must bless on each and every one, as it is considered a change of mind," end quote. This means that initially, Reuven offered him a cup, and he blessed and drank. Afterwards, Shimon offered him another cup, and he must bless again. However, if they give him multiple cups at once before he blesses on the first one, it is obvious that one blessing covers all of them. Similarly, if he knows that they will give him more cups, he blesses on the first one and it exempts all of them, and everything follows the logic we have explained, as is clear.

Additionally, he wrote: "Similarly, if someone recites a blessing over the cup for the wedding blessings and does not know to whom the cup will be passed, each person must recite the blessing, as it is considered as if he changed his mind." End of quote. And similarly, our teacher the Beit Yosef wrote at the end of section 190, see there. This requires clarification, for it is certain that with the cup of Kiddush, Havdalah, and the cup of Birkat Hamazon, everyone tastes from the cup without a blessing, as they fulfill their obligation with the blessing of the one reciting the blessing. Even when each person has their own cup before them, they fulfill their obligation with the blessing of the one reciting, as is evident in Pesachim (106a), see there.

However, the matter is as follows: It is certain that with a blessing where each of the assembled must fulfill their obligation, such as the cup of Kiddush, Havdalah, and the cup of Birkat Hamazon, all the assembled intend to fulfill their obligation, and the one reciting the blessing intends to fulfill it for them. But with the wedding blessings, that is, the Sheva Brachot or 'Asher Bara,' there is no obligation on the assembled. Only if the assembled are few and everyone knows that the cup will reach them, they intend to fulfill their obligation, and the one reciting the blessing intends to fulfill it for them. But when the assembled are many and know that the cup will not reach everyone, naturally, there is no intention from either the one reciting the blessing or the listeners. Therefore, each person must recite the blessing.

And among us, the custom is that the one reciting the blessing gives to those close to him, and they do not recite the blessings, as this is their initial intent. See what is written at the end of section 190.

And even though in the first blessing bread does not exempt wine as we said, nevertheless concerning the final blessing, Birkat Hamazon exempts it, and the reason we explained in section 1. And even the wine before the meal does not require a final blessing, for Birkat Hamazon exempts it, because it is also considered part of the meal since it comes to open the intestines and arouse appetite for food (Magen Avraham section 9 and see there section 8, and it is difficult because during the meal this reason is not needed), and even if he did not drink during the meal. And also wine that comes after the meal is also exempted by Birkat Hamazon, because wine also satiates and is like bread (there). According to this, the previous reason is not needed at all, however in truth we do not rely on this reason alone obviously, but since he drank it before Birkat Hamazon, this reason is added, and it has already been explained that for us there is no rule of after the meal. And even though Birkat Hamazon exempts wine before the meal, nevertheless concerning Havdalah, if it exempts it from a final blessing when he ate immediately, there is a dispute, and it will be explained in section 299, because Havdalah is different as it is not related to the meal at all. But on weekdays when one takes wine or another drink before the meal, his intention is to open the intestines as we said (see Magen Avraham section 10).

All that has been explained pertains to wine, but water or other beverages consumed during the meal do not require a blessing before them, as this is all considered part of the meal. For there is no eating without drinking, and everyone knows that it is customary to drink water or other beverages during the meal. The blessing of 'Hamotzi' exempts them even if one did not bless over them before the meal. Wine also does not need a blessing during the meal, except because of its importance it requires a blessing as stated in section 1, but this is not the case with other beverages, and they are all considered part of the meal. I have seen someone write that spirits (liquor) do not come to stimulate appetite and require a blessing (there, section 11), but I do not understand the meaning of this, and this contradicts sensory experience. In our time, everyone knows that spirits are only to stimulate appetite and strengthen the heart for eating, and therefore do not require a blessing, and this is the custom of the entire world. It is simple and should not be changed.

Even though most of our rabbis have agreed, and the Rashba wrote in Berakhot (41b) that Rashi and Rabbeinu Tam and all the great rabbis of France used to drink during the meal without a blessing, nevertheless, there are those who say to bless on water during the meal. This is because with wine, since it is significant, our sages said that without its importance one would not need to bless it, but water has no connection to the meal and requires a blessing, and similarly for all types of beverages. Some are even stricter and say to bless on them each time one drinks water, as it is assumed that one changes their mind each time. This does not apply to other beverages, for only with water, since it has no taste, does one change their mind, but beer and mead do not involve such a change of mind (Magen Avraham, section 13).

One who wants to fulfill these opinions and remove any doubt should sit before washing hands in the place of their meal and bless on water or liquor "Shehakol" with the intention to drink during the meal. Therefore, some are meticulous to take a little liquor before washing their hands. This is only for extra piety, but the main ruling is that one does not need to bless on water or other beverages "Shehakol". Moreover, even if one was thirsty before eating and drinks during the meal, which seemingly is not related to the meal since they were already thirsty, nevertheless, one does not need to bless. The reason is that if they did not drink before the meal, it was because they were afraid it would harm them, and during the meal, it will not harm them, so it is considered part of the meal, and this is the simple custom (see Taz, section 10, who also wrote that one should bless on liquor, and Atarot Zekenim wrote in the name of the Gaon Rabbi Feivish that if the liquor is on the table, then one does not need to bless as Be'er Heitev, section 8, wrote. They held that liquor is not related to the meal at all. However, times have changed, and in our days, we do not know another way, and for us, liquor is only for the time of eating to enhance the appetite for food, and one does not need to bless, and this is the simple custom).

Some are uncertain whether one who drank a revi'it (a specific measure) before the meal needs to recite a concluding blessing (bracha acharona). If we say that he does, then according to what has been explained, to satisfy all opinions, he should drink less than a revi'it before the meal. For if he drinks a revi'it, he would have to recite a concluding blessing, and how would that cover what he drinks during the meal? However, from what has been clarified, that Birkat Hamazon (the Grace After Meals) covers wine drunk before the meal, it implies that one does not need to recite a concluding blessing because it serves to open the intestines, as mentioned in section 11. This applies to all beverages (Taz, subparagraph 9). There is an opinion that only wine serves to open the intestines and not other beverages, thus requiring a concluding blessing (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 14). But it is known to us that other beverages also serve to open the intestines, especially spirits (liquor), which significantly increase the appetite, as is known. However, spirits, being strong, are difficult to drink a revi'it before the meal. But the main ruling is that even for a revi'it, one does not need to recite a concluding blessing (see Taz, end of section 177). This is not comparable to Havdalah in section 299, where Havdalah has no connection to the meal, as explained in section 7. Similarly, coffee weakens the appetite and is related to the meal and is exempt from a blessing, but tea is not related to the meal and requires a blessing (and also the Gra in section 176 wrote that spirits are like wine, see there).

Even though when many are gathered together, they can all fulfill their obligation with the blessing of the one who blesses, nevertheless, for the wine blessing during the meal, when they need to bless over it, such as when they did not drink before the meal, each one blesses for himself and does not rely on the blessing of the one who blesses and answers "Amen," because each one is involved in eating, and there is a danger in speaking lest the windpipe precede the esophagus, as stated in Siman 170. Furthermore, because of the eating, they do not hear the blessing. Therefore, our master the Rema wrote in Section 8: that some say if the one who blesses says before the blessing, "S'vri Maranan" (meaning, pay attention to hear the blessing), indicating that they intend to fulfill their obligation with his blessing, and they do not eat and hear the blessing and have intent to fulfill their obligation and answer "Amen," in such a case, one blesses for all of them. And so is the custom that whenever they bless over wine, they say "S'vri" and not "Birshut" (with permission), for "Birshut" is just requesting permission out of respect and so that they hear the blessing. And thus, they say this for all beverages when they fulfill their obligation with the blessing of the one who blesses, except for wine, where they say "S'vri," due to the wine during the meal as explained. (And what the Magen Avraham wrote in subsection 16, we have already explained there. See and understand.)

In the time of the Talmud, they would bring incense after the meal to create a pleasant aroma, and it is taught in the Mishnah: "And he says a blessing over the incense," meaning, he blesses. Rashi explains: the one who blessed over the wine also blesses over the incense, because once he has begun the concluding blessings, he completes them. Similarly, the Tur writes that the one who blesses over the wine after the meal blesses over the incense. The Geonim explained that this refers to the one who blessed 'Hamotzi'. This all applies when the incense is brought before the Grace After Meals, but when it is brought after the Grace After Meals, the one who blessed the Grace After Meals blesses (Magen Avraham 17 in the name of the Maor). And some say that the eldest blesses, because even though he gave permission to another to bless the Grace After Meals, it returns to him afterward (there in the name of the Raavad). And although we do not have incense at all and are not familiar with it, nevertheless, there is a practical difference for other matters to learn from this law (and in this section, the laws of drinks during the meal are explained, whether they require a blessing or not, and in section 177, the laws of foods and which require a blessing will be explained).

It is stated in Berakhot (59b): "A change of wine does not require a blessing […]. But one says, 'Blessed is He Who is good and does good.'" Rashi explained: If one drank wine during the meal and they brought him another wine better than the first, he does not need to bless "Borei Pri HaGafen" again. Thus far his words. And it is clear from his words that the blessing "Hatov VeHameitiv" is only for better wine. Similarly, Rambam wrote in Chapter Four, Law 9, and this is his language: If they were reclining to drink wine, and another type of wine came to them, such as they were drinking red wine and brought black, or old and brought new, they do not need to bless the wine blessing again. But they do bless: "Blessed are You, Hashem, our God, King of the universe, Who is good and does good." Thus far his words. And certainly, Rambam agrees with Rashi that a different wine which is better is not worse than another type. And Rashi would agree with Rambam, obviously. And it is also explained in the Jerusalem Talmud at the end of Chapter Six of Berakhot: Old wine, new wine requires a blessing. A change of wine does not require a blessing… Rabbi, for every barrel he opened, he would bless on it. And what would he say? "Blessed is He Who is good and does good…." Thus far his words. And the barrels differed from each other, either better than the previous one as Rashi explained, or a different type as Rambam explained. And the point of this blessing: although for all types of food and drink, one blessing applies to all varieties of that type – even the superior ones to the previous ones, such as one who blesses on one type of food and they brought before him two types, and he blessed on the inferior one, it exempts the superior one, or this one is white and that one is black – in any case, it exempts. Only for wine, they instituted this because of its importance, that for this, they established a specific blessing. And although bread is also important, in any case, wine gladdens the heart of man, and we only sing songs over wine. Additionally: in Yavneh, they instituted "Hatov VeHameitiv" for Birkat Hamazon because of the casualties of Beitar (Berakhot 48b), and it is stated in Gittin (57a) that they harvested their vineyards for seven years with the blood of the slain. Therefore, they also established this blessing for a change of wine (beginning of Chapter Nine, Section 15). And the explanation of "Hatov VeHameitiv" for a change of wine is not like "Hatov VeHameitiv" in Birkat Hamazon: "Hatov" (the good) – that they did not spoil, "VeHameitiv" (Who does good) – that they were given to burial. What relevance does that have here? Rather, its explanation is like "Hatov VeHameitiv" when a man's wife gives birth to a son, and similar cases as will be explained in Section 223, where its meaning is that the Holy One, Blessed be He, is good and does good for His creations. And in Birkat Hamazon, they instituted it like this because of the casualties of Beitar, meaning: that even at a time of strong judgment like with the casualties of Beitar, nevertheless, He, Blessed be He, is good and does good in the matter of calamities as well, and that is what it means that they did not spoil and were given to burial. But here, its meaning is simple as I have written.

Now, according to Rashi and Rambam, this blessing is only for wine that is better than the previous one or a different type. Similarly, Behag wrote in the laws of Kiddush, and this is his language: "From bad wine to good wine, one says 'Blessed is He who is good and bestows good.'" See there. And likewise, the Rashbam wrote in Pesachim (101a), and this is his language: "Change of wine, when they brought him from another barrel, and it has a different taste or is inferior or superior – one does not need to bless again on the wine. But 'He who is good and bestows good' one blesses if it is superior to the first..." This is his language (see Or Zarua HaGadol, Siman 157). However, Tosafot and the Rosh wrote in the name of Rabbeinu Tam that even on inferior wine one must bless 'He who is good and bestows good,' because the blessing is on the abundance of wines. And it is explained in the Jerusalem Talmud that we brought that Rabbi disagrees with the previous statement that said specifically old and new, rather on every barrel that he opened he would bless, whether better than the previous or inferior to the previous, as long as it is not much inferior. And Tosafot themselves wrote that only when there is doubt whether it is better than the first or not – one must bless. And so is the case with Rabbi in the Jerusalem Talmud. But when it is certainly inferior – one does not bless. And so it appears to be the opinion of the Rosh, see there. And I do not understand what relevance there is to a doubt in something that can be clarified by tasting. This requires further investigation. And the Rashba in Berachot there agreed with the interpretation of Rabbeinu Tam, because the blessing is only on the abundance of wine, see there. And the Tur brought both opinions. And see in section 4.

Our masters, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, only wrote according to the opinion of the Tosafot. And this is their language in section 2: "We bless 'HaTov VeHaMeitiv' (He who is good and bestows good) for any change of wine as a rule, even if one does not know that the second wine is superior to the first, as long as he does not know that it is inferior. And there is no difference whether both are new, or one is new and the other is old. And even if one drank from it within thirty days." End quote. 

This means: Since there are those who say that within thirty days of drinking, the wine is not cherished, and one should not bless it at all; it informs us that this is not so, as there is wine that is cherished by a person even if it is drunk frequently. And it is obvious that it refers to when it is better than the first, since we do not follow the opinion of Rabbeinu Tam, who says that even on definitely inferior wine we bless, but rather we follow the opinion of the Tosafot and the Rosh, who say specifically when it is not known. And here, since he drank from it within thirty days, he knows which wine it is. Therefore, one needs to say as I have written. And regarding new and old, one also needs to say that initially he drank the new and afterwards the old (and this is also written in the Taz); or for instance, that this new one is better than the previous old one, such as it being of a better type than the previous one. (And the Levush wrote the reason: because the primary blessing is only on the increase, see there. And his words are puzzling: for this is only according to the opinion of Rabbeinu Tam, and they ruled like the Tosafot. Examine and you will find straightforward.)

I am astonished at our Rabbis for completely omitting the opinion of the four pillars of the world: Rashi, Rambam, Behag, and Rashbam. While it is understandable that they omitted the opinion of Rabbeinu Tam and the Rashba because of the principle of leniency in cases of doubt regarding blessings, they should have ruled that one only recites a blessing on something superior, in accordance with the opinion of the four great authorities. At the very least, they should have mentioned their opinion. Especially since the reasoning of our Rabbis, the Tosafists and the Rosh, is not clear, as I wrote in section 2, since it is possible to taste [the item]. And one must say that the reasoning of our Rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, is as follows: just as in Scriptural law we say a double doubt (safek sefeika) leads to leniency, so too in Rabbinic law we say a double doubt leads to stringency. And here, when it is not known if it is better than the first, there is a double doubt: maybe it is better than the first, and if you say it is not better, maybe the law follows Rabbeinu Tam and the Rashba, who say one blesses even on something inferior. And maybe the reasoning of the Tosafists and the Rosh is also similar: that they did not require tasting beforehand, because since Rabbeinu Tam's opinion is that one blesses even on something inferior, we are not obligated to taste; for even if it is inferior, we can rely on the great opinion of Rabbeinu Tam, because the plain reading of the Yerushalmi in the case of Rabbi implies this, as it does not say that Rabbi required tasting.

Our Teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in Section 1: If they bring them another wine, one does not recite "Borei Pri Hagafen" but recites over it "Hatov VeHameitiv." And it is not specifically when they bring them a new wine, but the same applies if they had two wines from the start—they recite "Hatov VeHameitiv" over the second wine. Thus are his words. And in Section 3, he wrote: If they brought him a bad wine and a good wine together—he should immediately recite "Borei Pri Hagafen" over the good one and exempt the bad one. And he should not recite "Borei Pri Hagafen" over the bad one first in order to later recite "Hatov VeHameitiv," for one should always bless over the primary and preferred item first. Thus are his words. Meaning: Even when they can be covered by one blessing—it is necessary to prioritize the primary and preferred item to bless over it, as will be explained in Siman 211. All the more so here, for if he blesses over the good wine, he will not need another blessing. But if he blesses over the bad wine, he will need another blessing, as one should not cause an unnecessary blessing. And what is written in Section 1, that if they initially brought two wines, they bless "Hatov VeHameitiv" over the second wine, one could say that his intention is not that both wines were before him at the time of the blessing, but that they brought the second wine after the blessing.

And this is the intention of our teacher, the Rema, who wrote regarding this: "Specifically, when they were not in front of him together when he blessed 'Borei Pri Hagafen'. But if they were together – he does not need to bless except 'Borei Pri Hagafen' as will be explained in section 3." This is his language, and his intention is as I have written. However, we do not need this, as it can be explained that they were together at the time of the blessing, but they were of two kinds, like black and red, or the like, and both are good; and he is compelled to bless on one 'Borei Pri Hagafen', and on the other 'Hatov Vehametiv' (and this fits the language written by the Taz in subsection 4). There are those who wish to say that initially, he should bless on the inferior one so that he may afterward bless 'Hatov Vehametiv' on the better one (there). They compare this to what will be explained in Siman 211, that if two items are brought, one with the blessing 'Shehakol' and one with 'Borei Pri Ha'etz', he should not bless 'Shehakol' first to exempt the fruit blessing. However, this is not a valid comparison: there the fixed blessing is 'Ha'etz', whereas here the blessing for both is 'Borei Pri Hagafen'. Therefore, the primary ruling is as I have written. Nevertheless, if it is unknown which is better and which is inferior – he should certainly bless on one 'Borei Pri Hagafen' and on the other 'Hatov Vehametiv' according to the ruling of Tosafot and the Rosh as I have written. (And so wrote the Taz there, and this is certainly correct.)

And regarding what was explained that when one brings another wine, he blesses "HaTov VeHaMetiv," our teacher the Rema wrote: Even though he no longer has any of the first wine. This is his exact wording. Meaning: not only when there is still some of the first wine, but even if all the first wine has already been consumed. For there are those who say that in truth, one does not bless "HaTov VeHaMetiv," since the second wine was not brought due to a change in wine but because the first one was finished (Magen Avraham, Small Paragraph 1, in the name of Ra'avad and Radbaz). This teaches us that it is not so. And indeed, this is certainly when their intention from the beginning was on the second wine, for otherwise, he would need to bless "Borei Pri HaGafen" on the second wine like with all other fruits, as will be explained in Siman 211. But certainly, as I have written. (And according to this, it could be said that they do not disagree, but it does not seem so from the Magen Avraham there. And the Magen Avraham was concerned with the opinion of those who disagree, see there. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

The Mahari"l wrote: There are those who say that one does not bless "HaTov VeHaMetiv" on the night of Pesach, so as not to increase the number of cups. Thus his language. And surely his intention is not regarding the four cups, for one must bless "Borei Pri HaGafen" on each one, and there is no "HaTov VeHaMetiv" blessing here. Furthermore, what is this statement about not increasing the cups? Rather, his intention is regarding the wine during the meal, where one is permitted to drink as much as he wants without needing a blessing. And for this, he says not to bless "HaTov VeHaMetiv," for when there is a blessing, it appears as if he is adding to the cups (Mishnah Berurah). And there are those who say that one should be careful to bring from the same wine he drank previously. And if he brings a different type, he is compelled to bless "HaTov VeHaMetiv," since it is a Talmudic law (Magen Avraham. And it requires examination what he wrote that in Birkat HaMazon one does not need to bless "HaTov VeHaMetiv," for they said in Birkat HaMazon, see there. And it is fine anyway, for one must bless "Borei Pri HaGafen," and how can he bless two blessings? Ponder this and it will become clear.)

Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote in section 4 that one should not recite the blessing of "HaTov VeHaMeitiv" unless another person is with him, as the meaning is: "He is good to him and bestows goodness upon his friend." The same applies if his wife and children are with him. But if he is alone – no [he does not recite it]. Until here are his words. For this is the law in every "HaTov VeHaMeitiv" blessing, as I wrote in Siman 223. And even though in Birkat Hamazon one blesses also alone, this is not related to "HaTov VeHaMeitiv" of Birkat Hamazon, as I wrote in section 1. And if the homeowner drinks with a guest – the homeowner blesses and not the guest, because the wine is his. But two guests, and the homeowner is not with them – they bless (see Taz). And there are those who say that a guest with the homeowner – even the homeowner does not bless, because we require that the other has a share in this (Magen Avraham section 4). And his wife and children, since they are at his table – it is considered as if they also have a share in it and they bless (there). And similarly, if the homeowner places a wine jug on the table for the guests to drink – it is considered as if he gave them the wine, and it is deemed theirs, and they bless (there).

If they were gathered to drink, one person blesses for everyone, as "in the multitude of people is the glory of the King." However, if they were sitting in a meal, each person blesses "HaTov VeHaMeitiv" for himself, and one does not bless for everyone, because we are concerned that since they are engaged in eating, someone might swallow improperly and come to danger when they respond "Amen." Additionally, when eating, one does not pay attention to the blessing of his friend, unlike with drinking without eating. And even according to the opinion in Siman 213 that there is no fixed setting for drinking, and for the blessing "Borei Pri HaGafen" one does not exempt his friend, nevertheless, for "HaTov VeHaMeitiv" one person can exempt his friend (Eliyah Rabbah, subsection 8), because this is not the primary blessing for the wine.

Our master the Beit Yosef wrote in Section 6: Wine from two barrels, if it is from the same type, if within forty days of its harvest it was placed in two vessels – it is considered as two types, and one recites "Hatov Vehametiv" over it. But if it was divided after forty days – one does not recite this blessing, since it is all of the same type. Thus are his words. And it appears that within forty days there could be a different taste from one to the other, but not after forty days. And we are not knowledgeable in this, as in our country wine is not common. And know that the opinion of the Raavad, of blessed memory, is that even over two types of bread one recites "Hatov Vehametiv" (see Beit Yosef). But all our Rabbis disagreed with him on this. And only over wine do we recite it for the reason we wrote in Section 1.

The sages taught in the Mishnah (Berakhot 42a): If one recited a blessing over the appetizers before the meal, he has exempted the appetizers after the meal. If one recited a blessing over the bread, he has exempted the appetizers. If one recited a blessing over the appetizers, he has not exempted the bread. Beit Shammai says: not even the cooked dish is exempted. According to the first tanna, the cooked dish is exempted, and the law follows the first tanna. In the Gemara, there remains a doubt whether this statement about the cooked dish applies to bread or to appetizers. A doubt of rabbinic origin is resolved leniently. Therefore, in practice, when one recites a blessing over the appetizers, the cooked dish is exempted. This is what our master, the Rema, wrote: If one recited a blessing over the appetizers, he exempts the cooked dish, which is porridge and similar items. Similarly, if he recited a blessing over the cooked dish, he exempts the appetizers. Thus is his wording. This is also the ruling of Rabbi Ovadiah of Bartenura in his commentary on the Mishnah. The Tur did not mention anything about this. It appears to me that his reasoning is based on the Jerusalem Talmud, which explicitly states the opposite: But if he first recited a blessing over the appetizers, everyone agrees that he does not exempt the bread nor the cooked dish, see there. This is the opinion of Maimonides in the fourth chapter, law 6. The commentators challenged him based on the Talmud’s discussion (see Kesef Mishneh and Lechem Mishneh). Some wished to amend his words, see there. It is clear that he ruled according to the Jerusalem Talmud because the Babylonian Talmud leaves this matter in doubt, whereas the Jerusalem Talmud is unequivocal, thus he ruled according to the Jerusalem Talmud. This is also his approach in several places. Therefore, the Tur also omitted mention of this. Tosafot Ri wrote similarly, and this is their wording: If one recited a blessing over the appetizers, he does not exempt the cooked dish... thus is their wording. Our master, the Rema, wrote in his work Darkei Moshe that this was written according to Beit Shammai, see there. This is a great wonder: did they not write this as the halacha? Some wished to delete the word "not" (D"T). It is clear that their approach is based on the Jerusalem Talmud, and apparently our master, the Rema, did not see this Jerusalem Talmud. This seems to be the primary ruling.

And what is "parperet" and "ma'aseh kederah"? The Rambam wrote in his commentary on the Mishnah that it refers to condiments and all kinds of delicacies... and "ma'aseh kederah" refers to dishes such as porridge and groats... thus far his words. Tosafot, the Rosh, and Tosafot R' Yitzchak explained in the name of Rabbeinu Chananel: such as dry bread in a bowl that does not have the form of bread, upon which we bless "Borei Minei Mezonot". This means: that it is mixed with honey or other sweet things (Tosafot R' Yitzchak). Also, very thin wafers (there). And the term "parperet" includes many things that are not the main part of a person's meal, but rather come for enjoyment and to stimulate the appetite; as Rashi wrote there that this is parperet: things that benefit the heart, both before and after eating, see there.

The Tur wrote all the laws, and this is his language: If one recited a blessing over the appetizer before the meal, it exempts the appetizer after the meal. Explanation: after finishing the meal but before the Grace After Meals... If one recited a blessing over the bread, it exempts the appetizer during the meal... If one recited a blessing over the appetizer, it does not exempt the bread. This is his language, and he omitted "cooked dishes" for the reason we explained. However, our teacher the Beit Yosef wrote only: If one recited a blessing over the bread, it exempts the appetizer, meaning fine crumbs of bread that were mixed with soup or honey. If one recited a blessing over the appetizer, it does not exempt the bread. This is his language, and he omitted the rule that the appetizer before the meal exempts the appetizer after the meal. Perhaps his reason is that since among us there is no "after the meal," as we do not withdraw our hands from the bread, as Tosafot and all the early authorities wrote, and so did our teacher the Beit Yosef write in Siman 177. Therefore, it only applies to the appetizer during the meal. And for this, we do not need the appetizer before the meal, as the bread exempts it. But regarding the Rambam, it is difficult, as he also omitted this law, and it is not his way to omit a Talmudic law, especially a Mishnah law. Besides this, his words need explanation, as will be clarified in the next section with the help of Heaven.

And this is the language of the Rambam: If one recited a blessing over bread, it exempts the parperet (side dish) that is eaten with the bread, from types of cooked dishes, fruits, and similar items. But if one recited a blessing over the parperet, it does not exempt the bread. If one recited a blessing over a cooked dish, it exempts the cooked food. If one recited a blessing over the cooked food, it does not exempt the cooked dish. Until here is his language. 

And it is difficult: why does the cooked food not exempt the cooked dish, and vice versa it does exempt? And it must be said that because a cooked dish is considered a complete meal, but the cooked food is merely a parperet. And so it appears from the words of Tosafot R”I, who wrote that a cooked dish exempts a parperet and not vice versa, see there. And their reasoning is that according to our Talmud it is doubtful for both, and only in the Jerusalem Talmud it is explicit that a parperet does not exempt a cooked dish as I wrote, but vice versa it remains according to the doubt in the Gemara and doubt in Rabbinic law is lenient. 

But why did he change the language from "parperet" to "cooked food"? And also why did he omit that parperet before the meal exempts the parperet after the meal? This requires further investigation.

And know that from what we have learned, that the appetizer before the meal exempts the one after the meal, and before the meal means before washing hands and "Hamotzi" as the commentators have written; and it necessarily must be so: for if it were after "Hamotzi," there would be no need for a blessing on the appetizer, since the bread exempts it. From this, it is clearly proven that when one eats an appetizer before the meal, there is no need for a concluding blessing, because this also relates to the meal, and the Grace after Meals exempts it. For if it were not so, and one would recite a concluding blessing, how could it exempt that which comes after the meal, since one already recited the concluding blessing?

And so it is explicitly stated in the Jerusalem Talmud, Chapter Six (end of Halacha 4), and this is its wording: Rabbi Zeira said: From what we see of the Rabbis, they go up to Rosh Chodesh and eat grapes, and do not recite a blessing afterwards, if they intend to eat bread. Until here is its wording. This "not" is not literal but in the language of the Jerusalem Talmud, meaning: Therefore, they do not recite a final blessing because they intend to eat bread, and the Grace After Meals covers them. And I have also seen one of the great scholars who wrote similarly, and this is his wording: And similarly, one who eats before the meal appetizers, such as sweets or fruits, to open the appetite and stimulate the heart for eating... does not need to bless after them before the meal; they are covered by the Grace After Meals just like wine before the meal. But if he eats them purely for enjoyment, and not to stimulate the heart for the meal – he must bless after them; they are not covered by the Grace After Meals just like the wine of Havdalah. (The Gra in this section. And he also wrote that distilled wine (brandy) has the same rule as wine and does not require a final blessing, as I wrote in Siman 174, section 14, see there.)

However, I found in the Rashba's commentary on Berakhot (41b) the following text: "There is still a fourth category that has not been explained, which is items that come before the meal when one intends to eat bread afterward. This is because one might say that they are like items that come after the meal, which require a blessing before and after them; or we might say that they are like items that come during the meal but are not part of the meal, which also stimulate appetite and increase food intake, and therefore do not require a blessing afterward. The first reasoning is primary, that anything before the meal is not considered part of the meal at all. It seems to me that this is a dispute in the Jerusalem Talmud, as we read there: Rabbi Zeira said: From when we see... (as we brought in the previous section). It appears that according to Rabbi Zeira, as long as one intends to eat bread, even if he ate grapes before starting the meal, it is as if he ate them within... and does not need to bless afterward. But further down it says in the Jerusalem Talmud: Rabbi Ba inquired about one who ate fine flour when he intends to eat bread; what is the ruling regarding blessing on the flour at the end? The rabbis of Caesarea resolved: He needs to bless at the end. And this seems to be the main ruling." Thus far is the Rashba's text. He concluded the opposite, that one must recite a blessing afterward. And I am very puzzled: How can this be reconciled with the Mishnah that states appetizers before the meal?

I am also puzzled by the contradictions in the Yerushalmi: If the Rashba’s interpretation were correct, the Yerushalmi should have stated that there is a disagreement. In my opinion, there is no dispute here: This teaching of Rabbi Ba appears later on the Mishnah concerning appetizers, and this is the language of the Yerushalmi: "But if he blessed on the appetizer first, everyone agrees that he has not exempted the bread nor the cooked dish." Rabbi Abba inquires about one who ate fine flour with the intention to eat bread afterward… It is difficult: What is his question, as this is an appetizer? And if it does not exempt the bread, it clearly does not require an after-blessing as I have written. It appears to me that this is its explanation: Certainly, one who prepared to eat an appetizer before the meal does not need an after-blessing, and this is our Mishnah that states if one blessed on the appetizer before the meal. But Rabbi Abba inquires: What about one who ate fine flour without intending to eat it before the meal as an appetizer to stimulate the appetite but rather intended only to eat the fine flour, and while eating, decided to eat bread. In this case, it concludes that it does not exempt him from an after-blessing, as it has no relation to the meal since he did not eat it as an appetizer before the meal. There is no contradiction here at all. Furthermore, in the Yerushalmi there earlier (in Halacha 4) on the Mishnah of "If there were many kinds before him," Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi and Rabbi Abba disagree if one intended to eat bread, whether an after-blessing is needed on the fruits. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi holds that it is not needed, and Rabbi Abba holds that it is needed. And now, not only if we follow Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, but even according to Rabbi Abba, it seems to me that this applies specifically to regular fruits that do not come to stimulate the appetite for the meal. But for those that do stimulate the appetite, they do not require an after-blessing. This also appears to be the intention of the Rashba. And although his language does not imply this, it is better to interpret his intention this way rather than say something contradicting the Mishnah. Certainly, on Shabbat, when after Kiddush they give out sweet things and other items, and they intend to wash their hands and eat bread shortly thereafter, they definitely do not need an after-blessing, as the Kiddush is in the place of the meal, and it is all part of the meal. (And although in Magen Avraham, section 249, subsection 6, it does not imply this, it can be said that they did not eat the meal immediately. The Chayei Adam, section 41, subsection 4, struggles with this, see there. But there is no need. And the Chayei Adam also ruled not to make an after-blessing on Shabbat, but his reasoning does not seem correct to me. In my humble opinion, the main ruling is as I have written according to the opinion of the Gra and the Rashba, as I have explained. Examine and you will find it clear.)

Bread exempts all types of foods that come during the meal, which are part of the meal. This refers to things that are typically eaten as part of a meal, to accompany the bread, such as meat and fish, eggs, vegetables, butter, cheese, milk, porridge, and all types of cooked dishes meant for eating and satiation, as well as all types of salty foods. Even if one eats them without bread, they do not require a blessing before them, because the blessing of "Hamotzi" covers them; nor after them, because the blessing of Birkat Hamazon covers them. For those foods that a person eats with the bread itself, we do not need the reason, because the blessing of "Hamotzi" covers them, as they are exempt due to the principle of primary and secondary. Rather, the reason for the blessing of "Hamotzi" for those eaten without bread is implied from Tosafot on Berachot 41b, "Halacha," see there. And note carefully and you will find it easy. Thus, there are two exemptions: one, that bread exempts, meaning the foods eaten with bread, and the exemption is because of the principle of primary and secondary. The second, that the blessing of "Hamotzi" exempts, meaning all that comes for eating and satiation, which includes most of our cooked dishes that are the main part of the meal.

And based on this, I have seen someone who is uncertain: if he does not intend to eat a lot of bread in this meal and eats only a little bread, are the foods exempt from a blessing because he does not intend to eat a lot of bread (Magen Avraham, subsection 1)? There is no doubt about this: if the exemption were solely due to the bread, it would indeed be questionable. But the exemption is also due to the "Hamotzi" blessing. Since he recited "Hamotzi," all the foods that come because of the meal are exempt, even if he ate only an olive's worth of bread, because less than an olive's worth does not allow him to recite the Grace After Meals. And after all, we also need the Grace After Meals for the foods to exempt them from the final blessing, as I have written. And there are many wealthy people whose meal consists of a little bread, and will we differentiate between them and everyone else? (And the end of Magen Avraham's words in subsection 1 are unclear. Machatzit Hashekel struggles with his intention, see there and in Yad Ephraim. And the main ruling is as I have written. So too wrote Even Ozer, see Shaarei Teshuva. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

If one eats during the meal items that are not considered part of the meal, meaning they are not typically used to accompany bread, and they are not usually part of a meal for satiation purposes, such as figs and grapes and all types of fruits, as well as types of pastries that are not meant for satiation like thin crackers, sponge cakes, and tarts, and all that was explained in Siman 168, Section 33, where we elaborated in detail, see there – if one eats them without bread, they require a blessing beforehand; for the blessing of "Hamotzi" does not exempt them, as they are not part of the main meal. However, they do not require a blessing after eating, as everything eaten during the meal is covered by Birkat Hamazon (the Grace after Meals); for Birkat Hamazon is more comprehensive than the blessing of "Hamotzi" in this regard because it is from the Torah, as I wrote at the beginning of Siman 174. But when one eats bread with the fruits, no blessing is needed due to the principle of primary and secondary foods, as the fruits are secondary to the bread. Similarly, when one eats thin crackers or sponge cakes or tarts with bread, the same applies, as the bread is primary over everything. However, it is not customary to eat sweets with bread. Nevertheless, if one eats them, no blessing is needed, as in this regard we do not follow the majority of people, for each person eats according to what seems fit to them (this seems correct in my humble opinion).

However, one who eats something after the meal, meaning what the Gemara refers to as things that come after the meal, before Birkat Hamazon; for in the time of the Talmudic sages, their custom at the end of the meal was to withdraw their hands from the bread and remove it, and then set themselves to eat fruits and drink. Therefore, at that time, anything brought before them, whether items that are part of the meal like fish and meat, or items that are not part of the meal – requires a blessing, both before and after. For even Birkat Hamazon only exempts what comes during the meal, not what comes after the meal (except for pat habaa b'kisnin, which is like bread), which is considered like eating without a meal. According to Rashi's view, this is only for items that are typically eaten after the meal. But items that are typically eaten during the meal, even if eaten after the meal – do not require a blessing. This also seems to be implied by the language of the Rambam at the end of the fourth chapter, where he wrote: "And items that come after the meal, whether part of the meal or not part of the meal – require a blessing, both before and after." Until here is his language. However, according to this, it is not clear why he wrote "whether part of the meal...". Therefore, it seems more likely that he holds like the view of Tosafot, the Rosh, and all the early authorities. This is why he wrote "whether part of the meal," meaning: whether items that are part of the meal (as the Kesef Mishneh and Lechem Mishneh also wrote). And if one began during the meal – he does not need to bless after them.

Our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote at the end of section 2 about this ruling, and this is his language: "This last ruling is not common among us, since we do not remove our hands from the bread until after the Grace After Meals." Thus far is his language. Similarly, this was written by the Tosafot, the Rosh, and all the early authorities. And it is found that among us, it is always called "during the meal." There are those who wrote that in large meals, even now the custom is the same as in the time of the Talmud (Levush). There are those who disagree with this (Bach and Magen Avraham, subsection 7), and they wrote that in the time of the Talmud they were accustomed to remove the tables, as they had small tables; and now that the table is large and it is not removed, everything is called "during the meal." And in cases of doubt regarding blessings, we are lenient. And it seems to me that now in large meals, as well as among the very wealthy, fruits are eaten after the Grace After Meals. (The Magen Avraham, subsection 6, brought a Tosefta: "Salted food that comes first before the meal, and bread that comes with the salted food after the meal, requires a blessing... and I do not know why he brought it, for these are the words of an individual, and the first Tanna disagrees with this? And thus it is taught there: 'Salted food and a slice of bread - one blesses on the salted food and exempts the bread.' Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel says: 'Salted food that comes first...' Moreover, this is regarding the primary and secondary status, not regarding the bread exempting, and it belongs to Siman 212. And even there, we do not hold like Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel but like the first Tanna. Investigate and you will find it lenient.")

It has already been explained that someone who eats fruits with bread does not need to recite a blessing over the fruits because they are secondary to the bread. There are times, however, when even if one eats them without bread in the middle of a meal, they do not require a blessing. How so? For example, if someone has established their meal as usual, and in the middle of the meal fruits are brought to him to accompany the bread, and he eats a little of them with bread, intending to eat more of them with bread. Then, even if he eats them without bread in the meantime, they do not require a blessing because they were brought to accompany the bread, and he intends to eat more of them with bread. Even if he later changes his mind and decides not to eat them with bread, nonetheless, since at the time he ate them without bread, he intended to eat more with bread, it is not an issue. However, what he eats after changing his mind requires a blessing.

And this applies when they brought them in the middle of the meal to accompany the bread. But if they brought them not to accompany the bread but to eat them for enjoyment, like the way fruits are eaten, and he ate them with bread not with the intention to accompany the bread but because he wanted to for some reason, such as it being pleasing to him to eat them with bread and the like, and his intention is to eat them further with bread for this reason, it is obvious that those he eats with bread are exempt from a blessing. But if in between he eats them without bread – he needs to recite a blessing even though he eats them at the beginning and end with bread. And even if he brought the fruits to accompany the bread, but began to eat them without bread – he needs to recite a blessing. For it is specifically when he began to eat them with bread, and his intention is to eat more with bread – then the intermediate ones are exempt, but not at the beginning. And know that there are those who disagree even in such a case, not to exempt the intermediate ones from a blessing (Sefer Mitzvot Gadol and Hagahot Maimoniyot, see Beit Yosef). And even though the main ruling is according to those who exempt, and our teacher the Beit Yosef ruled in section 1, and it is also clear from the language of the Tur, see there – nevertheless, all the great authorities wrote that it is good to act when fruits are brought to him in the middle of the meal, even if his intention is to accompany the bread with them, still he should eat a little of them without bread and recite a blessing on them, to fulfill all opinions. And every God-fearing person should act accordingly. But the main ruling is as I have written. (And so wrote the Magen Avraham in subsection 3, and the Taz at the end of subsection 3, see there. They lean towards this ruling because of concerns, see there.)

All that has been explained applies when one did not initially set his meal upon the fruits but rather brought them in the middle of the meal to accompany the bread. However, if one initially sets his meal solely upon the fruits, like the poor in countries where fruits are cheap and cooked dishes are expensive, and he sits to eat bread with fruits – in this case, the fruits are considered as things that come because of the meal itself, and even if he eats them first without bread, they do not require a blessing; just like when one eats meat without bread, it does not require a blessing neither before nor after. Yet, in this matter, there are those who disagree and hold that even in such a case one needs to eat them first with bread, and afterwards he can eat them without bread. But the initial eating must be specifically with bread. The reason is that since it is not customary to accompany bread with them but he chose them, therefore, he must begin eating them with bread. This is not similar to other cooked dishes (Sefer Mitzvot Katan and Maimonides' Glosses). Therefore, it is good to initially eat them with bread, and then, even if he eats them afterwards without bread, they are exempt from a blessing; even if he does not return to eat them later with bread, since the main establishment of his meal was upon them. Some have written that dates, in any case, are exempt from a blessing because they satiate like bread (Magen Avraham, Section 3). This requires further investigation for the law. It is proper to first eat some other fruit and bless "Ha'etz," and thus cover the dates in any case.

And know that in any situation where the fruits are exempted by the blessing over bread, even if the fruits were not on the table – they are exempted, since it was his intention to bring them. And in any situation where they are not exempted by the blessing over bread, even if they are placed on the table – they are not exempted. And our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in paragraph 5: If after he blessed over the bread, they sent him from another house, which he does not rely on to feed him, and it was not his intention to receive the gift, even if it is something that is usually eaten with bread – he needs to bless over them, as is the law for something reconsidered. Thus far his words. And it is clear. And our teacher, the Rema, wrote about this, and these are his words: And I have not seen people being careful about this. And perhaps the reason is that the general intention of a person is for everything that is brought to him during the meal. Thus far his words. And this is not a sufficient reason, obviously, unless in a place where it is customary for neighbors to send to each other, or relatives send to each other. But otherwise, if someone sends his friend some cooked dish in the middle of the meal – he needs to bless over it with its proper blessing; unless he eats it with bread, for then it becomes subsidiary to the bread and he does not need to bless. And it is obvious that if they sent him fruits he needs to bless in any case, even if it is customary to send to him, unless he eats everything sent to him with bread (see Magen Avraham, small paragraph 10).

And know that according to all the laws explained in this section, for us, all foods made from flour that are fried in butter or fat, such as kreplach, blintzes, taigech, pampushkes, and the like, even if they are filled with fruits – they are all considered part of the meal because the flour is primary and the fruits are secondary. And even though they are considered a delicacy for the wealthy, nevertheless, ultimately they satiate the body and do not require a separate blessing. Similarly, when potatoes are cooked with meat or fat, and fruits like plums (which are called ploymen) are added, and this is called tsimmes, which is commonly eaten by us on Friday night – the ploymen are secondary. And they do not require a blessing even if one eats a little bit of them without the potatoes. Unless one does not want to eat the potatoes at all, but only the ploymen by themselves, then one would need to recite the blessing "Borei Pri Ha'etz". And see in paragraph 11.

But when fruits are cooked alone, such as apples, pears, plums, raisins, and quinces, and these are served at the end of the meal, one is required to recite a blessing over them, for this is considered "not because of the meal"; they are only for enjoyment and do not satisfy the body. And know that it is customary to say that when fruits are cooked with meat or fat, they are considered "things that come because of the meal" and are exempt from a blessing (see Magen Avraham, subsection 3). There is no valid reason for this unless they are eaten with bread, and it is good to do so. All kinds of sweets such as cake or tarts require a blessing even if they contain fat. However, on pastries, no blessing is required, as they are considered part of the meal, as is known, for they are indeed dough and satisfy the body.

It appears to me that even though someone who eats fruits before the meal, which are not related to the meal but were simply desired to be eaten, and then sits down for the meal, must recite a blessing after eating the fruits (as the Magen Avraham writes in subsection 3). Nevertheless, if he wishes to eat more of the fruits but intends to eat them during the meal, he does not need to recite an after-blessing nor a before-blessing when he eats them during the meal, as they are covered by the previous blessing. Consequently, the after-blessing will be covered by the Grace After Meals, as explained during the meal in subsection 3.

Maimonides wrote in the fourth chapter: If one was eating in this house, and he interrupted his meal and went to another house (or room), or if he was eating and his friend called him to speak with him, and he went out to the entrance of his house and returned, since he changed his place – he needs to bless retroactively on what he ate. Then he blesses again with the initial blessing of "Hamotzi" and afterward he completes his meal. Thus is his language. And it is obvious that he needs to wash his hands again, and this has already been clarified in Siman 170, see there. And it appears to me that he should wash without a blessing, since his hands are clean. 

According to Maimonides' words, one who went out in the middle of a meal to stroll in the courtyard has finished his meal and needs to bless the Birkat Hamazon on what he ate previously, and afterward "Hamotzi." The Raavad has already disputed this, and this is his language: He exaggerated in this, for every "to the entrance of his house" is not considered an interruption. And all the more so if he sees his place, it is not an interruption at all. Thus is his language. (And it is obvious that according to the Tosafot, the Rosh, and the Rashbam, whose opinions will be clarified – this law does not apply at all, as its source is a Tosefta in section 2. And that Tosefta is taught together with a Baraita of the members of the group in Pesachim 101b. According to these Rabbis, this Baraita is rejected from the law; only the Rif and Maimonides hold it as law, as they ruled according to Rav Sheshet there. But these Rabbis ruled according to R' Chiya there. Examine and you will find it light.)

And also in the Tosefta (Chapter Four) it is explicitly stated not like the Rambam, for it was taught: A homeowner who was reclining and eating, and his friend called him to speak with him – he does not need to bless retroactively… If he went far – he needs to bless retroactively. And when he returns – he needs to bless initially. Thus phrased. And “went far” implies that he went with him to a distance. And it seems that the Rambam interprets “went far” as when he left the doorway of his house (see Kesef Mishneh). And this is a wondrous thing. And it seems to me that the Rambam interprets “went far” in terms of time, meaning: he delayed for a certain amount of time, like half an hour or something similar. And also, the Rambam's intention is indeed included in his language, as he wrote: his friend called him… and he went out… – which indicates a delay of time. And I wonder at our teacher, the Beit Yosef, who copied his words into the law in Section A, besides what others have already wondered at him (Bach) for ruling like the Rif and the Rambam against the Rashbam and Tosafot and the Rosh and most of our Rabbis, who ruled differently as will be explained. And in rabbinical matters, we go leniently. Furthermore, there is a wonder even according to this approach: for also from the Rif it is evident that what constitutes an interruption of a meal is walking to some place, like going out to greet a bridegroom or something similar as the Ra’avad wrote. And this is also proven in the Gemara there. And it is also evident from the Tosefta itself, as I have written. And how can he rule in rabbinical blessings such a stringency? This requires investigation.

The Rambam also wrote: Friends who were sitting to eat and went out to greet a groom or a bride, if they left behind an elder or a sick person (as is customary, since they cannot go out) – they return to their place and finish their meal, and they do not need to recite the blessing again. But if they did not leave anyone there when they went out – they need to recite a blessing for what they have already eaten. And when they return, they need to recite a blessing at the beginning. Thus are his words. It is clear that in the previous ruling, his intention was also when they did not leave anyone there, and he relied on what he would explain later. This is why he wrote earlier that upon their return, they need to recite a blessing for what they have already eaten, and here he wrote that when they go out, they need to recite a blessing for what they have already eaten, and certainly, they should have done so earlier as well. However, because in that case, they went out based on their friend's call and did not know that they would go far, they did not bless earlier. But in the latter case, they went out on their own and knew they would go far, therefore they need to bless before their departure. And certainly, in the former case as well, if they knew they would go far, they would need to bless earlier (and so wrote the Ran in Pesachim there, see there).

The Rambam also wrote: Similarly, if they were gathered for drinking or to eat fruits, anyone who changes their place has interrupted their eating. Therefore, they must bless retroactively for what they have eaten, and then bless again initially for what they need to eat. If one changes their place from one corner to another within one house, they do not need to bless again. This is his language. And what he wrote "similarly" is puzzling, as it is a fortiori. For even those who dispute the previous law in the Gemara when they were sitting in a meal agree regarding drinking and fruits, which are items that do not require a blessing after them in their original place, as will be explained with Heaven's help. And it is possible to say that his intention is: that in this case, it does not help even when people remain in their place. Therefore, he said "similarly," meaning: similarly, in drinking and fruits, in any situation, one needs to bless. And this detail will be further elucidated with Heaven's help. (And the Magen Avraham, small section 3, wrote the opposite. And similarly, here it helps, see there.)

However, our Rabbis, the Ba’alei Tosafot, Rashbam, and Rosh, disagree with all these matters. They ruled according to the opinion in Pesachim that there is a distinction between a meal, which is considered fixed and requires a blessing after it in its place, and other eating and drinking, which do not require a blessing after them in their place. It will be clarified before us what are the things that require a blessing in their place, and what are those that do not require a blessing in their place: For things that require a blessing in their place, one does not need to bless at all for what one eats in another place, because everything follows the meal since it has a fixed nature. And it is not necessary if it was initially intended that in the middle of the meal he would go to another place to finish his meal there, or eat there and then return to his original place, he does not need to bless at all. It is all one matter, and there is no difference whether he finishes his meal in another place and blesses the Birkat Hamazon there or returns to his original place to finish it; as long as he did not divert his mind from eating – there is no other blessing here. Even if he did not intend to eat in another place, but in the middle of the meal it happened that he was called to another place, and he did not divert his mind from eating – he can go to the other place, finish the meal, and bless there, or return to his original place and bless. It appears to me that when he returns to his original place – he needs to eat a little there before Birkat Hamazon. Furthermore, it seems to me that he does not need to wash his hands again, since he did not divert his mind from eating. However, it is certain that if he diverted his mind from keeping his hands clean, he needs to wash his hands with a blessing, as I wrote in Siman 170, Se’if 3.

And even regarding items that do not require an after-blessing, they disagree with the first opinion, arguing that a final blessing is needed for what was previously eaten and an initial blessing for what will be eaten. Our Rabbis believe that only an initial blessing is needed and not a final blessing, for the blessing that is recited afterward will automatically cover what was eaten previously. To what is this similar? To someone who intended to stop eating but then decided to eat more, we require him to recite an initial blessing again as will be explained in Siman 179, but not a final blessing for what was previously eaten. The first opinion holds that this is worse than diverting one's attention. Diverting one's attention happens in one place, but not in two different places; one should not move from the first place without reciting a final blessing, because moving to a different place is considered entirely like another meal.

And regarding what was explained according to the first opinion, that if some of the participants in the meal remain, one does not need to recite a blessing, our teacher, the Rema, wrote that this is also the case according to this opinion for things that do not require a blessing after them in their place. Meaning, if many people were sitting to eat fruits or drink, and one of them went to another place and returned, when he returns he does not need to recite a blessing because the original matter has not been concluded, since he left some of the group there. However, there are those who disagree with this and hold that it is only according to the first opinion, for things that require a blessing in their place, which is a matter of permanence, that this distinction applies. But for things that do not require a blessing in their place, there is no permanence, and there is no difference whether he left some of them or did not leave some of them, and in any case he is required to bless (Bach and Taz, subsection 6). However, there are some of the great authorities who agreed with the words of our teacher, the Rema (Magen Avraham, subsection 3, and Eliyah Rabbah, subsection 4). And similarly, it appears from the Talmudic discussion there, and in cases of doubt regarding blessings, we are lenient. And especially, it appears to be the words of our teacher, the Rema, that since he left some – there is no interruption of attention, and he does not need to bless. However, this is certainly when he returns to his original place, but if he remains there – it is obvious that he needs to bless before and after.

And behold, the world has adopted the approach of our sages according to the second opinion. They customarily begin eating at home for the wedding feast and then go to the wedding feast and finish the meal and recite the blessing there (Taz, subsection 9). We also see this behavior on Purim and festivals, where they do likewise. And even though this is only acceptable after the fact, but ideally, it is certainly not correct to do so, as our teacher, the Rema, wrote, and these are his words: "And this is the custom in these regions. Nevertheless, ideally, one should not leave his place without a blessing, for we are concerned that he might forget to return and eat." However, for a pressing mitzvah need, such as when the time for prayer has arrived, it is permitted. These are his words. It is also explained in the language of the baraita in Pesachim there: "A group that was reclining, and they uprooted their feet to go out to greet the groom...," see there, implying because it is a pressing mitzvah. Nevertheless, it seems that the world also considers this a pressing mitzvah according to the time, such as the joy of a mitzvah like a wedding or Purim feast and the like, where it is necessary to eat both at home and at a friend's house. But without a mitzvah, it is not correct to do so ideally unless a necessity arises where it is imperative, such as being called by a great person or some official where he had to go, and similar cases. (See Magen Avraham, subsection 8, who wrote that if one is invited to eat elsewhere, and he had this intention at the time of the blessing "Hamotzi," it is completely permitted, for in such a case there is no concern of forgetting, see there. And see Eliyah Rabbah, subsection 5, who has some reservations about this.)

And what is called "things that require a blessing in their place"? Some say specifically bread (Rashba and Hagahot Maimoniyot). And some say all types of grain, meaning also those things over which one recites "mezonot" (Tur in the name of R"i). And some say that all seven species require a blessing after them in their place (Rashbam and Rosh). And it is clear that regarding the requirement to bless in their place, one should be stringent according to the last opinion. And regarding the law that was explained, one should be stringent according to the first opinion. And this also appears from the language of the Rambam that we brought, as he wrote the term "meal," and meal applies only to bread. (And even though the end of his language does not imply this, as he wrote drinking or fruits, nevertheless this seems to be his intention. Examine it and you will find it easy.)

What is considered a "change of location"? In one room, even if it is very large, it is all considered one place. If one eats in this corner, he can eat in another corner, or go to another corner to speak there, as it is considered one place. Similarly, even from one room to another, if one can see part of the first room from the second room where he ate, it is not considered a change of location. Even from a house to a courtyard, it is not considered a change of location in such a case, as I have written in Siman 273 regarding Kiddush in the place of a meal. And it is explained there that even from a house to a sukkah is not considered a change of location. And there are some details explained there. It seems to me that in our houses, all the rooms that are open to the dining room are considered one place, as it is inevitable that one can see part of the dining room from the other rooms. Therefore, it seems to me that one who eats fruits in this room or drinks something hot can finish eating or drinking in the other room that is open to it, and it is not considered a change of location.

It is further explained there that if his intention was to eat in another place, it is not considered a change of place. And Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote that this is specifically in one house, meaning from room to room within one house, even if he cannot see from one to the other – his intention suffices. But to another completely different house – his intention does not suffice. And from a house to a loft or vice versa – it also suffices since both are within one house. The Levush explains here and in Siman 273 that his intention suffices even for another house. This requires examination (and the Eliyah Rabbah also questions this), for this law is from Tosafot and the Rosh based on the Shulchan Aruch, and so wrote the Tur later in Siman 273. However, it is certain that all that is under one roof is considered one house, for this matter, so that his intention suffices even if they are separate houses, such as when a gatehouse interrupts between them, which is called a "foyer." Therefore, one who wishes to drink hot beverages in several rooms should have the intention at the time of the blessing not to drink in only one place, but rather to drink a little here and a little there, and then he may drink based on this blessing in all parts of the house under this roof. The same applies to eating fruits. This is very necessary in our times when we linger over drinking hot beverages and move from room to room. Therefore, it is proper that he have this intention from the beginning.

It states in the Jerusalem Talmud at the end of the sixth chapter of Berakhot: If one ate on the eastern side of a fig tree and then went to eat on its western side, he must recite a blessing. This is also the ruling of the Rambam there.
