And even though moving from one corner to another within a house does not constitute a change of place, this is because the walls surround and make the entire room as one place, which is not the case with a fig tree standing in the open air. The Ra'avad wrote: This is specifically when he did not originally intend for this, see there. And it is obvious that if he originally intended for this, it is no less than moving from one room to another. Now, the Tur did not bring this ruling. It seems his opinion is that the law is not in accordance with this Jerusalem Talmud, as it is no worse than moving from one corner to another. But our master the Beit Yosef did bring this at the end of paragraph 2. I am puzzled why he did not bring the words of the Ra'avad, for it cannot be said that he disagrees with him, as he himself wrote in paragraph 3 that one's intention helps even from one tree to another, as will be explained. It seems he did not bother to bring it, because this is a simple matter. And know that this is specifically when the fig tree is large and thick enough that when standing on its eastern side, one cannot see its western side. But with an ordinary tree, this law does not apply at all. And even though in one room, even if there is an obstruction such that one cannot see from place to place, such as a stove standing in the middle of the room, it is still considered one place for this matter, such that if one eats on one side, he can finish on the other side even though it is not visible from there, this is all within a house that has walls, as I wrote (Magen Avraham, small section 5). Furthermore, it seems to me that this law only applies to a fig tree, because not all its fruits ripen at once, as we say at the beginning of the chapter "Klal Gadol," see there. Therefore, when he picked from its eastern side, it did not occur to him that the western side had also ripened, unlike other fruits. (And if not for the words of the Beit Yosef, I would interpret that it does not refer to one fig but to many, such that if he ate from the figs on the eastern side and then went to eat from the figs on the western side, he must recite a blessing. The Beit Yosef added "this fig," but it is not so in the Jerusalem Talmud and the Rambam, and it refers to the species. Examine and find it easy.)

Our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in paragraph 3: There is an opinion that if one is in a garden and wants to eat from the fruits of each tree, since he has already blessed over one tree, he does not need to bless over the others. This applies if at the time of the blessing he intended to eat from the others. But from garden to garden, one needs to bless even if they are adjacent, and even if when he first blessed he intended for all. Thus far is his language. For from tree to tree is like from room to room, and from garden to garden is like from house to house; since each garden is enclosed by partitions, the entire garden is considered a single unit. And even if the garden is very large such that one cannot see from one side to the other, nevertheless, one's intention at the time of the blessing is effective just like from room to room. (Refer to Eliyah Rabbah that from tree to tree, if one sees the other, no intention is needed. However, the Taz at the end of subparagraph 9 did not write this, and this is also implied by the language of the Shulchan Aruch. And similarly, it is implied by the Magen Avraham in subparagraph 9, see there carefully. Be precise and you will find clarity.)

He further wrote in Section 4: If one ate bread in one place and then ate again in another place, he only recites the Grace after Meals in the second place, just as travelers who eat along their way sit and recite the Grace after Meals at the place where they finish eating. This is his language. The explanation is: He follows his own reasoning, ruling like the Rambam, that even for things that require a blessing after them in their place, it is still forbidden to go to another place without reciting the Grace after Meals. And if he left, he should return to his original place and bless. Therefore, he says that if he transgressed this and went and ate in another place and does not wish to eat more, he must recite the Grace after Meals there, and it will also cover the first place. It is clear that he has no other way to do so, even if he wanted to eat more in the first place, since ultimately he ate in two places. According to the Rambam, he must bless specifically in the place where he ate. Thus, he must bless in one place to fulfill the obligation for the other place. He explains this so that one does not wonder how one can fulfill the Grace after Meals for the second place by blessing here. He explains and compares it to travelers, whose way of eating is such, and they can do so initially. Therefore, here, after the fact, he fulfills the obligation in any case. All this is a novelty for this opinion. But according to the opinion of our Rabbi, the Rema, all this law is unnecessary, as it has already been clarified that according to this opinion, one can initially eat in two places for a mitzvah. Therefore, this law is not novel at all.

Prayer in the middle of a meal does not constitute an interruption that would require another blessing. Therefore, if one forgot to pray and remembered in the middle of a meal, one can pray without reciting Grace After Meals and without the blessing of "Hamotzi" afterward. Not only if there is still time after the meal to pray, then it is not necessary to interrupt. But even if there is no time to finish the meal and pray, thus making it necessary to interrupt, it still does not constitute an interruption since one did not leave their place (Tosafot Pesachim 102a). However, washing hands is required, as it constitutes a distraction of the mind (Magen Avraham, subsection 13). Some say that washing hands is not necessary (Eliyah Rabbah, subsection 11); similarly, it is written in Yam Shel Shlomo, chapter six of Chullin (Siman 10), that prayer does not constitute a distraction of the mind. This applies to praying in one's place. But going to the synagogue to pray, according to Rabbeinu Beit Yosef, is prohibited, and according to Rabbeinu Rema, it is permitted as per the opinions explained. Note that this specifically applies to items that require a blessing after them in their place. However, for items that do not require a blessing after them in their place, prayer certainly constitutes an interruption. (And Taz, subsection 9 and 10, extensively argued against the Shulchan Aruch. Eliyah Rabbah (subsection 10) has already written that his arguments are insufficient for refutation, see there. Even the Even Ozer extensively argued on certain details. We follow the ruling of Rabbeinu Rema, which is agreed upon by Magen Avraham and Eliyah Rabbah.)

A person who falls asleep during their meal with a brief nap—it does not constitute an interruption. This is not comparable to a distraction of the mind that requires a new blessing beforehand, as this does not divert his attention. He does not even need to wash his hands again if he is certain that he did not touch covered areas. Similarly, if he pauses for other permissible matters, such as needing to relieve himself or similar instances; however, in this case, he does need to wash his hands with a blessing, since his hands have been soiled. See also Siman 170, Paragraph 3.

The Tur writes: "If one has finished his meal and has washed his hands for 'Mayim Acharonim' (the final washing)... it is forbidden to eat or drink until he first recites the blessing. Since he has washed his hands in preparation to bless, he has removed his mind from eating and drinking, and the original blessing does not cover anything he wishes to eat or drink afterward... And if he said 'Give us and let us bless,' it is considered a removal of thought just like the washing of hands... thus far his words. However, the Grace After Meals (Birkat Hamazon) for what he already ate does not require this. All our Rabbis agreed that the removal of thought only necessitates a blessing beforehand, but the Grace After Meals can still be recited afterward. And is it forbidden to interrupt between eating and the Grace After Meals with any other matter, as long as he has not moved from his place? Only between the final washing and the Grace After Meals is it forbidden to interrupt. And it is certain that the final washing he performed becomes nullified, and he should wash his hands again before the Grace After Meals."

Our master the Beit Yosef in his great book was astonished at the Tur, who equated "He lifted his hands" with "Give us and we will bless." But it is not so: for "He lifted his hands," since immediately after washing one recites the blessing, it is as if he began the Grace after Meals, and he is forbidden to eat or drink until he blesses the Grace after Meals. And with "Give us and we will bless," there is no need for the Grace after Meals, only the initial blessing on what he eats. Based on this, he wrote in the Shulchan Aruch, and this is his language: "He finished his meal and washed his hands with the final waters – he cannot eat or drink until he blesses the Grace after Meals. And if he said, 'Give us and we will bless,' it is considered a distraction, and it is forbidden for him... unless he blesses on it first." Until here is his language. However, all the commentators on the Shulchan Aruch disagreed with him and clarified with clear evidence that there is no difference in this matter. And the main ruling is according to the Tur (Taz section 1, Magen Avraham section 2, Eliyah Rabbah section 1, and so wrote the Ba"Ch and the Derisha). And it is explicitly stated in the Ba"Ha"G, and this is his language: "And if he wants to drink water or taste something after he washed his hands – he blesses and drinks, and then blesses the Grace after Meals." Until here is his language. And from his language, it somewhat implies that there is also no need for the final waters afterward. But all the commentators did not write this. And aside from what our master the Beit Yosef wrote that "He lifted his hands" is stricter than "Give us and we will bless," the Rashba in his innovations (42b) wrote the opposite: for "Give us and we will bless," he spoke with his mouth that he is removing himself from his meal, which is not the case with "He lifted his hands," see there. Therefore, the main ruling is according to the Tur. (And some wrote that in any case, one should not do so initially, and the Eliyah Rabbah objected to this there. And it is also clearly proven from the language of the Ba"Ha"G; and so wrote the Levush, see there.)

Some of our Rabbis differentiate between eating and drinking. That is to say, with eating, even if a person has removed themselves from eating, and even if the table has been cleared, and even if they said "bring us [the food] and we will bless" – this is not considered a removal, and one can eat without a blessing beforehand, but if they have washed their hands, they need to bless. However, with drinking, if a person has removed themselves from drinking – it is considered a removal and a blessing is required. And when sitting at a meal, drinking is also permitted (Taz, small section 2). And this is the opinion of Rabbeinu Yonah in the sixth chapter of Berachot, and the Ran in "Arvei Pesachim." It appears that this is also the opinion of the Ra'avad in the fourth chapter, law 7, who wrote: They did not say this regarding eating but only regarding drinking. But regarding eating, it is not considered an interruption except for the final waters… so far his words. (In this way, the two sugyot of Berachot 42b and Pesachim 103b align well. Tosafot and the Rosh wrote a different answer, see there. And the Eliyah Rabbah ruled according to the first opinion, see there. And in my humble opinion, it seems that this remains at any rate a doubtful law, as they did not mention that the Ra'avad also stands by this opinion. And it seems that in cases of doubt regarding blessings, we are lenient. Delve and you will find ease.)

And the Rambam in the fourth chapter has a different approach to this matter, and the Tur and Shulchan Aruch did not bring his opinion at all. And this is the language of the Rambam: If one decided in his heart to stop eating or drinking, and afterward reconsidered and wanted to eat or drink, even if he did not change his location – he must recite a new blessing. But if he did not decide in his heart and still intended to eat and drink, even if he paused the entire day – he does not need to recite a new blessing. Until here is his language. And they were astonished at him: for the Talmud in Berachot there explicitly concludes that deciding is not considered a cessation except for the final washing of hands. However, the truth is that the Rambam was interpreting this concerning Birkat Hamazon (the blessing after meals) and not the initial blessing (Lechem Mishneh). And the law regarding the final washing of hands he wrote at the end of the sixth chapter, that after this it is forbidden even to drink water until he blesses, see there. And "Give us and we will bless" is for him like the final washing of hands, as he wrote after the previous law, and this is his language: If they were drinking and said "Come and let us bless Birkat Hamazon…" – it is forbidden for them to drink until they bless… until here is his language. And he wrote in the language of the Talmud in Pesachim there that this was the practice, as it is his way not to change the language of the Gemara, but there is no difference between eating and drinking. And his main intention is that "Give us and we will bless" is like washing his hands. And behold, regarding the law, we hold like the Tur as I wrote, that this is the approach of most of our rabbis. Nevertheless, it is appropriate to be concerned about the opinion of the Rambam. Additionally, we learn from his words a leniency, that if he did not divert his mind from eating and drinking, even if he paused for many hours in his place – it is not an issue. And this is simple, that if during all this time he diverted his mind from guarding his hands, he needs to wash his hands in any case. And it is possible that he does not need to bless, since he does not know that he touched covered places.

The Tur and Shulchan Aruch wrote that saying "Give us and let us bless" is only relevant for the owner of the house, as it constitutes a distraction of the mind and requires a blessing beforehand, as I have written. However, for someone who relies on another's table, such as a guest, if he says "Give us and let us bless," it is meaningless and does not constitute a distraction of the mind until the owner of the house says it. It seems that also his sons and sons-in-law who rely on his table when they eat together – their saying it does not constitute a distraction of the mind. But when they eat without him, it appears that their status is like that of the owner of the house. Similarly, a guest in an inn who pays for his meal – his status is like that of the owner of the house, since he is eating his own (meal). And by the saying of the owner of the house, all those who are seated are prohibited if they agree with his words (Magen Avraham, Small Paragraph 4). But if they do not agree with his words, no blessing is required. And this is obvious. And all this is regarding "Give us and let us bless." But when he washes his hands – there is no difference between the owner of the house and another. And there is one who says that even in "Give us and let us bless," if the guest decided in his mind that he would not eat any more even when the owner of the house eats, and then changed his mind to eat – he needs to bless (there, Small Paragraph 3). However, this does not seem to be the opinion of the Poskim. (Nevertheless, also the Eliyah Rabbah, Small Paragraph 7, agrees with the Magen Avraham. And it requires further study.) And know that also taking the cup for a blessing is like washing hands. And this is the language of our teacher the Beit Yosef in Paragraph 3: If he did not say "Give us and let us bless" and also did not wash his hands, once he took the cup to bless – it is a distraction of the mind. Until here is his language. (And the Magen Avraham wrote in Small Paragraph 5 that it is like washing hands.)

It appears to me that saying "Bring us [the cup] and let us bless" is not considered a distraction when the host mistakenly thought there was nothing more to eat, and he was informed that there is still more to eat and the meal is not yet finished – this is considered an error in distraction. If he had known, he would not have said "Bring us [the cup] and let us bless"; because for this reason, the guest's statement means nothing since he relies on the host's table and does not know if the meal has ended. Therefore, the same applies to the host. Similarly, if a guest in an inn who pays money says "Bring us [the cup] and let us bless," and he is informed that there is still more to eat – this is also considered an error in distraction. It is only when the host has firmly decided in his mind not to eat any more, even though there is still more to eat, that it is considered a distraction and not an error. The same applies to the guest. (This is my humble opinion, for follow the reasoning. Delve deeply and you will find it easy.)

Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in Section 4: If someone enters his friend's house and there are many groups eating there, and each one offers him a cup, there is an opinion that says he should recite the blessing of "Borei Pri Hagafen" on each cup, because each time he changes his mind [about drinking]. This is the end of his words. Meaning: when he enters for a different purpose. But if he enters to sit with them and drink, certainly he only needs to bless on the first cup (Taz, Subsection 3). And it is not specifically when they give him a cup, for the same law applies if they give him various kinds of food. Rather, it is customary to mention a cup, as it is the way of those sitting together to offer a cup for drinking. And there is an opinion that even if he has not yet finished drinking the first cup and they offer him a second cup, he needs to bless again (Magen Avraham, Subsection 6). Indeed, there is a dispute about this, and it will be explained in Siman 206 with the help of Heaven. (And there is a printing error in the Magen Avraham. It should say: "It is not similar…" as the Pri Megadim wrote. The Gra in his notes wanted to correct it to "does not need to bless," see there. But it is not conclusive. The Pri Megadim and the Machtzit HaShekel also held this. The final ruling will be explained there. Pay attention and you will find it light.)

Furthermore, it is written in Section 5: Guests in the house of a host, who come to eat various fruits and are served one after the other, only need to recite a blessing over the first one. This is the language used. This is because they rely on the host, and their intention is for everything the host will give them. This is not similar to the case of a servant in Siman 169 who needs to bless each time, because the servant does not usually eat while the diners are eating, and therefore his intention is only for what is in front of him. But guests know that the host will give them more (Beit Yosef). The proof for this is that even in the case of a servant, it is explained there that if there is an important person at the meal, he does not need to bless on each piece, since he knows he will be given more, see there. All the more so for guests. There are those who disagree with this. They hold that only when it is certain for the guest that the host will give him more, he does not need to bless. But if it is doubtful, he needs to bless (Taz, Subsection 4). This is not so, the guest does not need to be certain. And this is also clarified from the language of the Talmud in Berachot (42a), see there. The main ruling follows the Beit Yosef. (Also, the Eliyah Rabbah in Subsection 8 criticizes this, and the Be'er Hetev quotes the Yad Aharon. Also, the Pri Megadim is not pleased with this, see there. The primary reliance on the forced language of Tosafot in their commentary on the word "leaning" (the second one) has been corrected properly. It is just like the Beit Yosef, see there, and nothing more. Be precise and you will find ease.)

If one has eaten any food but has not eaten salt, or has drunk any beverage but has not drunk water, he should be concerned during the day because of bad breath, and at night he should be concerned about two things: bad breath and "askara" (a disease that chokes the throat) (Berachot 40a). One who eats salt should not eat it with his thumb afterward, as this is detrimental to fathering children; nor with his little finger, as this causes poverty; nor with his index finger, as this causes severe boils (Eliyah Rabbah); rather, he should eat it with his middle finger or ring finger. This is a mystical matter according to the tradition of the ancients. There is no need for a blessing over this, since it is solely for medicinal purposes. We do not adhere to this practice because our bread always contains salt, and our dishes always contain water. This has already been clarified at the end of Siman 170, see there.

Furthermore, the Gemara there states: one who rinses his meal down with water will not come to intestinal illness. One who regularly eats lentils once every thirty days prevents "askara" from entering his house. However, eating them daily is not advisable, as it causes bad breath. One who eats mustard regularly once every thirty days prevents illnesses from entering his house. However, eating it daily is not advisable, as it is harmful to the heart. One who regularly eats small fish will not come to intestinal illness. Moreover, small fish increase fertility, multiply, and strengthen a person’s entire body. One who regularly smells "ketzach" (a spice) will not come to heart pain. However, one should not eat it, as it is harmful to the body; rather, it should be attached to the bread during baking, and then peeled off so that only the aroma remains.

Rashi explains "ketzach" as "nigella," which is not known to us. In the Aruch, I have seen that it is what we call "cumin," and some people put it in bread. It is also stated in Gittin (70a): Three things weaken a person’s body: eating while standing, drinking while standing... and five things bring one closer to death than to life, and these are: eating and standing immediately afterward, drinking and standing, letting blood and standing, sleeping and standing, engaging in marital relations and standing. Rather, one should wait a little and then get up, see there. Similarly, it is stated in Shabbat at the end of Chapter 18, see there.

One should not remove the tablecloth and bread until after the Grace After Meals (Birkat Hamazon). And that which is implied in Berachot (42a) that they would remove the tables before the Grace After Meals, this is because each person ate at a small table by himself, and they would remove the tables from before those reclining and not from before the one leading the blessing. But for us, where we all eat at one table, it should not be removed until after the Grace After Meals (Tosafot and Rosh there). And it appears that for this reason there are places where it is customary to leave the bread and the tablecloth in front of the one leading the blessing, as the Tur writes, see there, in order to do as it was done in their times.

And the reason for this is: because a blessing does not rest upon an empty thing, as we find with Elisha and the Shunammite woman, to whom he said: "Do you have anything in the house?" And in Sanhedrin (92a): anyone who does not leave bread on his table will never see a sign of blessing. And so it is in the Zohar Yitro (87b), and this is his wording: it is forbidden for a person to bless on an empty table, for the blessing from above does not rest on an empty place... And so it is in the Zohar Terumah (4, 157b), see there. And our master the Beit Yosef wrote: but one should not bring a whole loaf and place it on the table. And if he did so, it appears like those who prepare a table for Gad, as the prophet Isaiah said (65:11). And it is specifically forbidden to bring, but if a whole loaf was already placed on the table beforehand, it does not need to be removed (Taz and Magen Avraham). Therefore, on Shabbat when the second challah of lechem mishneh is placed, it should not be taken from the table. But pieces of bread must be present, and if there are no pieces of bread left on the table, they should be brought from elsewhere. And in Job (20:21) it is written: "There was nothing left for him to devour; therefore, his prosperity will not endure." From this, our sages derived that one should leave bread on the table, as it is understood from this verse that the leftover refers to pieces of bread, as that is the meaning of "remnant."

And there are several reasons for leaving over bread: so that it will be ready for a poor person when he comes (Rashi). Additionally, to give thanks to the Blessed Hashem for His kindness and goodness, that we have eaten and have leftovers, as it is written: "Eat and have leftovers." Furthermore, so that it will be evident to all that we bless the Blessed Hashem for preparing food for all His creatures. Additionally, so that His blessing will rest upon this table and this house, as we say in "Harachaman"— "May the Merciful One send us abundant blessing in this house and upon this table that we have eaten upon." And for all abundance of blessing, there needs to be something upon which the blessing can rest, as I have written. (Two of these reasons are found in the Levush.)

During the days of the Talmudic sages, when they would remove the small tables in front of the diners before washing for mayim acharonim (the final washing of the hands), and they would wash the mayim acharonim in the place of the tables—they needed to sweep the floor of the house where the tables had been before washing, so that crumbs of bread would not remain and become soiled by the washing water. And even though it is permitted to destroy crumbs that are less than the size of an olive, there is still a concern that the attendant might be an unlearned person, and it is permitted to use an unlearned attendant. When he removes the bread from the table, he might leave crumbs that are the size of an olive, and then they might fall when the table is removed from there and become soiled by the washing water. Therefore, they would sweep first.

However, for us, since we do not remove the table and we wash our hands in a place where there is no concern of crumbs—when we wash our hands on the table with a vessel, we ensure that the water does not fall on the tablecloth, and consequently, it does not reach the food. This is not like them, who would wash with a vessel on the ground, and it was not customary to be meticulous to prevent the water from falling on the ground. Therefore, we do not need to sweep the house first.

And know that although it has been clarified that it is permitted to destroy crumbs that are less than the size of an olive, this applies to throwing them in water or fire. But it is forbidden to throw them in a place where people tread, because stepping on bread crumbs causes poverty, as stated in Chullin (105b). (See the Beit Yosef, who is stringent even now to sweep because they wash before the table; see there. According to what I have written, there is no concern in this, and this is not the custom. Only the tablecloth is sometimes cleaned a bit. Look into it and you will find it easy.)

The early authorities wrote that it was customary to cover the knife during the Grace After Meals (Birkat Hamazon). However, on Shabbat and Yom Tov, it was not customary to cover it. The reason is that the table is likened to the altar, and it is written about the altar: "You shall not wield iron over them." For iron shortens a person's life, whereas the altar prolongs a person's life, and it is not proper for the shortener to be wielded over the prolonger. Additionally, the table also causes the prolongation of life through hosting guests and atones for sin, and iron is the strength of Esau. Therefore, on Shabbat and Yom Tov, there is no evil inclination and no harm. And the custom of Israel is Torah. Another reason given is because of an incident that happened with a certain righteous person who, when he said "and rebuild Jerusalem…", was very distressed over the destruction of the Temple, took the knife, and killed himself (see Beit Yosef). Therefore, they decreed to cover the knife. However, they did not decree this on Shabbat and Yom Tov, because the incident occurred on a weekday, and they only decreed similar to the incident that happened, as we say in Shabbat (60b) regarding the nailed sandal, see there. Additionally, on Shabbat and Yom Tov it is forbidden to be distressed, and such a mishap cannot occur. And know that nowadays people are not accustomed to be careful about this, and they do not cover the knives during the Grace After Meals.

Maimonides wrote at the end of Chapter Six: Immediately after washing one's hands for the final time, one should recite the Grace after Meals, and one should not interrupt with anything else; even drinking water after washing one's hands for the final time is forbidden until one recites the Grace after Meals. This is his language. The Tur and the Shulchan Aruch in Siman 179 wrote similarly. And Rashi also wrote in Berachot (42a) that immediately after washing hands for the final time, one should recite the blessing and should not eat anything until one blesses the food. This is his language. From all this, it seems that only eating and drinking are forbidden as interruptions. But speaking is not considered an interruption (Kesef Mishneh and Magen Avraham at the beginning of Siman 179). And even according to the opinion at the beginning of Siman 166 that speaking is forbidden between washing hands and the blessing of "Hamotzi," in the case of the final washing, it is permitted. The reason seems to be that an interruption by speaking is only relevant where there is a blessing, and the blessing needs to be adjacent to the action. But in the case of the final washing, there is no blessing. And in the case of the initial washing, the sages established not to interrupt between the blessing of "Al Netilat Yadayim" and the blessing of "Hamotzi." But in the case of the final washing, what relevance does an interruption by speaking have? And while eating and drinking are forbidden because the blessing of "Hamotzi" would be nullified after washing, why should speaking be forbidden? (And Magen Avraham at the beginning of Siman 179 disagreed with Beit Yosef, see there. According to what I have written, the words of Beit Yosef are correct. And the reason one should not converse over the cup of blessing in Siman 183 is out of respect for the cup, not because of an interruption.)

The Sages based the practice of "Mayim Acharonim" (ritual washing after a meal) on a verse at the end of the chapter "Elu Devarim": "And you shall sanctify yourselves"—this refers to "Mayim Rishonim" (ritual washing before a meal); "and you shall be holy"—this refers to "Mayim Acharonim", see there. They were stricter with "Mayim Acharonim" than with "Mayim Rishonim": for in the camp, they exempted from "Mayim Rishonim" but not from "Mayim Acharonim", as it is found at the end of the first chapter of Eruvin, see there. And we say in Chullin (105a): "Mayim Rishonim" is a mitzvah; "Mayim Acharonim" is an obligation; because there is salt from Sodom that blinds the eyes, and there is danger if one does not wash his hands. Therefore, because it is a matter of danger, they did not institute a blessing (Rambam).

Based on this, our Rabbis, the authors of the Tosafot, as cited by the Tur, wrote that nowadays we do not practice washing the hands after a meal (mayim acharonim) because Sodomite salt is not prevalent among us. However, the Rosh and Tosafot Ri at the end of the eighth chapter have already questioned this: how can one say such a thing? If so, what relevance does sanctity have here, as we expound from "And you shall be holy"? Rather, certainly the reason of danger is an additional reason to the sanctity of the commandment, and the sanctity is to remove the filth from the hands which are soiled from eating, and soiled hands are unfit for blessing. In the name of the Gaon, they wrote that the one who blesses, who needs to mention the Name, his washing is a commandment due to sanctity. For the participants, it is only due to danger, see there. (Also, the Gra in section 12 objected to the Tosafot and wrote that what they said about mayim acharonim being obligatory means in addition to the commandment, as I have written. And he ruled so in practice, see there.)

However, if so, why do we not bless as we do for the first washing of hands? The opinion of the Ra'avad in the sixth chapter is indeed that a blessing is required. He wrote this in the name of the Shemuot HaGeonim, stating that one must bless upon washing hands. There, he differentiates between when one eats something that has dirt, such as meat and fish and all moist items, which then requires a blessing, and when one eats dry items that do not have dirt, which do not require a blessing. But all our rabbis wrote simply that the last washing of hands does not require a blessing.

And it appears to me in my humble opinion that just as the blessing of "Hamotzi" covers all the foods in the meal, so too the blessing of "Al Netilat Yadayim" covers all the washings in the meal. However, according to the Tosafot, there is no blessing here at all. And it is explained in the Rambam there, who wrote: "And for the last washing of hands, one does not bless, as it is only due to danger." Thus, it is clear that he agrees with the Tosafot. And according to them, we must say that what our sages based on a verse is only a mere hint, since there is nothing that is not hinted at in the Torah. And proof of this: as it is derived there "for holy" – this refers to oil that they would anoint the hands with after the last washing (Rashi). And this certainly is not an obligation, and this enactment did not spread; but as mentioned.

And this is the language of the Tur: "And the Tosafot wrote…, and since we do not practice as the verse says 'for I am holy' – this refers to fragrant oil, we also do not practice the washing." And it is not considered for us as dirty hands, since we are not accustomed to wash, and we are not strict about it. However, if there is a person who is particular and accustomed to wash his hands after the meal – for him, it is considered dirty hands, and he must wash before the blessing after the meal. But he should not bless on it at all. Thus far is his language. And in this language, also wrote Rabbeinu Beit Yosef in section 10, see there. And such a person who is particular, even if he wants to bless on the wine and his hands are dirty – he must clean them first (Magen Avraham small section 9).

And now, regarding the law of mayim acharonim (ritual washing of the hands after a meal), it is not only according to the opinion of many of our rabbis that essentially the obligation still applies even in our times, as we have explained. But even according to the opinion of the Tosafot that there is no obligation in our times, it is undoubtedly written in order to justify the custom in their days. However, even the Tosafot agree that it is necessary even in our times, for who can say that Sodomite salt is not present even now? And it seems to me that sea salt contains a concern of Sodomite salt. And what they wrote that now there is no Sodomite salt, it is because in their country they ate salt that is quarried from mountains; and even now it is so there. But in our country, many eat sea salt, and there is a concern of Sodomite salt. And also in the Zohar "Pinchas" (page 246a) it warned about this, and all the kabbalists warned about this (Magen Avraham, small section 10). And in a response from Heaven to one of the early sages, it is explained that anyone who is lenient with mayim acharonim - his sustenance will be lessened from Heaven. Therefore, one should be very careful about this, and this is the practice of all God-fearing individuals. Every head of the household should warn his household members to be careful about this.

If he does not have water for the first or last washing – the first washing takes precedence, since there are those who are lenient regarding the last washing, as has been explained. Nevertheless, on Shabbat during the second meal, if he washes his hands for the last washing, he will not have water for the first washing for the third meal – he should forgo the third meal and wash his hands now for the last washing, since he is already obligated in it (Magen Avraham in the name of Beit Yosef). And if he has a cup for the blessing – he should mix the cup, and then wash his hands with the last waters (ibid.).

One does not wash mayim acharonim (the final waters) on the ground, because an evil spirit rests on them, but rather in a vessel. Nevertheless, one should not immerse his hands in the vessel, but rather pour from the vessel onto the hands as with the first waters. Only for middle waters, between dairy and meat or between fish and meat, is it permissible to immerse the hands in the vessel for those who practice this, but not for the first and final waters. If one does not have a vessel, he should pour on the floor, as the evil spirit only rests on the ground and not on the floor. If there is no floor in his house, he may wash on thin wood or similar materials, so there is some separation between the water and the ground. If this too is not available, he may wash on the ground in a place where people do not usually walk. He may also wash under the table, which is not a place of walking (Magen Avraham). One should not wash with hot water that would burn the hand, because it causes the hands to swell and does not remove the dirt. The preferred practice is to wash with cold water (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 3, in the name of Rashal). It is only necessary to wash up to the second joint of the fingers, as that is where the dirt from the food reaches. One should lower the tips of his fingers downward so that the dirt will run off. Mayim acharonim can be washed with any kind of liquid, including water that is unfit for the first waters, such as water that has been used for work and is not clean (ibid., subparagraph 7). One does not recite a blessing over mayim acharonim, as has been explained. There is no need for drying. Rambam wrote that drying is necessary. It is written that only the one who blesses needs to dry, as he dries and then blesses. But the others at the table do not need to dry (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 6, in the name of Yam Shel Shlomo).

Kolbo writes in the name of the Ra'avad: These are the differences between the first waters (for washing before a meal) and the last waters (for washing after a meal): The first waters require a revi'it (a specific measure of water), while the last waters only need enough to wash the hands. The first waters must be poured from a vessel, while the last waters can be from any source. Human force is not needed, and interposition does not invalidate them. All types of water are valid for the last waters, even if they were used for work or are very murky. Even if an animal would not drink from them, or even the hot waters of Tiberias which are bitter. The first waters should not be done in halves, but the last waters can be done in halves. If one rubbed his hands against his body or a wall after using the first waters, he needs to wash again, but not so with the last waters. This is the end of his words. All these matters are the halacha (Eliyah Rabbah, section 3). And know that I have seen people who are particular that there should not be a revi'it in the last waters, but specifically less than a revi'it. I have not found this anywhere. Many of the great ones of the generation do not follow this practice and use a revi'it or more than a revi'it (and I have heard some reasoning for this, but it was not acceptable to me).

The one who leads the blessing washes his hands first for the final waters, because since he is honored with leading the blessing, he is also honored with washing his hands. When does this apply? When there are up to five people including the one leading the blessing, as the sages estimated that during the time it takes for the other four to wash their hands, he can contemplate in his heart the four blessings of the Grace After Meals so that he will not make a mistake in them. Therefore, when there are more than five people, it is not proper etiquette for him to wash his hands, and he should wait until everyone else has washed. Moreover, it is ideally not proper to interrupt so much, as the blessing should follow immediately after washing. And even though we explained in section 1 that speaking is not considered an interruption, and certainly not silence, it is still not proper to do so ideally. Therefore, the others should begin to wash their hands. They should not honor one another to wash first, as there is no honoring with soiled hands. Rather, they should wash in order as they are seated around the table until it reaches five people, then the one leading the blessing should wash, and afterwards the four, for the reason explained. It is customary to say "By the rivers of Babylon" before the final washing. And on Shabbat, Yom Tov, and Rosh Chodesh, they say "A Song of Ascents, when the Lord returned..."

Maimonides, at the end of the seventh chapter of Berakhot, ruled that Birkat Hamazon (Grace after Meals) does not require a cup [of wine]; the same is the opinion of the Rif in the chapter "Arvei Pesachim," see there. Similarly, the Rashba ruled in Berakhot (52a), and so did the Sefer Mitzvot Gadol (SeMaG). However, the Rosh and the Tur ruled that a cup is needed even for an individual, and so did the Tosafot in Pesachim (105a), see there. Similarly, the Rashbam ruled, and so did Rabbeinu Yonah at the end of the seventh chapter of Berakhot. Some of our rabbis ruled that only with a zimun (quorum) a cup is required (Hagahot Maimoniot there in the name of the Ri and Rabbeinu Elchanan, see there). Similarly, it is in the Zohar Pinchas (page 246), and this is its wording: "Because of this, fewer than three do not need a cup; for three, a cup is needed." See there (and so wrote the Beit Yosef in the name of Midrash HaNe'elam on Ruth). They wrote that those who are concerned about this: when they bless individually, they place the cup on the table and do not take it in their hands (Beit Yosef). And there are those who hesitate about this: is it then, according to the Zohar, forbidden to take a cup individually? The Zohar said it is not needed, so why should one not take the cup in his hand (BaCH)? Indeed, in our country, we do not practice using a cup at all, because wine and other beverages are expensive for us, and all our drinking is water, as is known. And it seems we have adopted the opinion that no cup is required. Nevertheless, some are meticulous on Sabbaths and festivals, when there is a zimun, to bless over a cup if it is possible to obtain one.

Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, in the first section brought all the opinions and wrote that according to the one who says a cup is necessary – one must seek it out. And if he does not have a cup to bless over – he should not eat if he is anticipating and it is possible that he will get one, even if he has to miss one mealtime. According to this, if two people are eating together – each one must take a cup for the Grace after Meals. This is his language. The Tur also wrote this and brought proof from Havdalah, see there. But this is not a comparison: before Havdalah it is forbidden to eat, but before the cup, it is permitted to eat? And if later he does not have a cup, what should he do (Magen Avraham, small section 1)? However, we find in Pesachim (102b) on Motzei Shabbat, if he does not have a cup for the Grace after Meals – he eats without Havdalah and then makes Havdalah over the cup for the Grace after Meals, see there. Thus, the cup is so significant that they permitted him to eat before Havdalah, and all the more so that without it, he should not eat if it is possible that he will get a cup later and now he does not have one, that he must wait (Elya Rabba). (And what the Magen Avraham questioned from Pesachim 105a – I do not know what his question is, for there it does not discuss the Grace after Meals at all. And perhaps he holds that a cup is not required, or that he has a cup for the Grace after Meals. And from Eruvin 40b, on the contrary, it implies that he will not have a cup at all, and waiting does not apply, see there. Examine and you will find it easy.)

It is clear that even according to the opinion that it does not require a cup [of wine], it is still a beautification of the mitzvah to bless over a cup. And in the Talmud, it implies that they would all bless over a cup because wine was inexpensive for them. Therefore, in regions where wine is available and inexpensive, it is certainly appropriate for every God-fearing person to bless over a cup, especially when there is a zimmun. And in our country, it is not possible because we do not have wine, and even the wine we make from raisins is expensive, and even beer is expensive, and we cannot afford to have a cup of blessing for every meal. However, the wealthy who drink beer at every meal—it is certainly fitting for them to bless over a cup. And may the listener be blessed from Heaven.

And our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, wrote in Section 2: The cup for the Grace after Meals should only be of wine and not of other beverages, even if one fixed their meal on them. However, if wine is not available in that place, and beer or other beverages are considered the common drink of the region, one may bless on them, except for water. The custom in these regions to bless on beer should not be protested, for there are those who say that a cup is not required at all. Additionally, the main common drink in these regions is beer, and people establish their meals on it. Although wine is available in the city, it is not considered "available" for this purpose because it is expensive and it is not possible to buy wine for every meal to bless on it. However, it is preferable to bless on wine. Some are particular when blessing alone with wine not to hold the cup in their hand, but to place it on the table before them. This practice is proper according to the mystical tradition. Thus far is his wording.

It appears to me that what they wrote, that the cup for Birkat Hamazon (Grace after Meals) must be only with wine, is not comparable to the reasoning for Kiddush, which must be only with wine, as I wrote in Siman 271. For in the case of Kiddush, there is a verse, "Remember the Sabbath day to sanctify it" (Exodus 20:8) — remember it over wine (Pesachim 106a). The term "remembering" is associated with wine: "We will remember your love more than wine" (Song of Songs 1:4, Tosafot ad loc.). And even according to those who say this is merely an asmachta (a rabbinic support), as will be explained there, nonetheless, it is an asmachta. But in Birkat Hamazon, the Talmud does not mention "wine" but rather "requires a cup." The reason, however, is that for them, most of their drinking was wine (Shabbat 78a), and in Pesachim (107a), there is a curse for one who makes Kiddush over beer, "May his beer become vinegar." And even now, in the Land of Israel and in Babylonia, most of their drinking is wine, which is considered the local beverage. However, this is not the case with us; even beer is beyond our reach, and only the wealthy drink beer regularly. It seems to us that distilled wine is considered the local beverage, but even this is not feasible for two reasons: one, because it is expensive, and secondly, because it is not suitable for drinking after a meal, as is known. Some of us are lenient to bless over a cup of tea, which we call "kvas" in our language, but we have not seen anyone who does this. However, on mead, which we call "mead," it is certainly appropriate to bless. As for licorice, one should not bless (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 2). Similarly, one should not bless over lemonade or seltzer, for they are merely water. Regarding what they wrote, that an individual should not hold the cup in his hand, we have already written that there are those who question this. And even according to those who do, it applies only to wine, not to other beverages (Ba'er Heitev and Magen Avraham, subparagraph 6).

Every cup used for a blessing, such as the cup for Birkat Hamazon (Grace After Meals) and for Kiddush and Havdalah, if one tastes a bit from the cup, even though there still remains a revi'it (a specific measure) or more, it is invalid. Thus, our sages of blessed memory said (Berachot 52a): "If he tasted it, he disqualified it," because it is like the leftovers of a cup (Rambam in the twenty-ninth chapter of Shabbat). It is like a blemish in an animal, and regarding this it is said: "Offer it now to your governor" (Levush). 

There is a question whether this applies specifically to those who hold that Birkat Hamazon requires a cup, or if it is possible that even if a cup is not needed, nevertheless, if one blesses over a cup, it must not be blemished, just like the ten things said about the cup of blessing which Rambam wrote at the end of the seventh chapter. Here are his words: "Even though Birkat Hamazon does not require wine, if he blessed over wine, it must be rinsed..." see there. However, from this itself, it is a proof: since he did not write that it must not be blemished. 

In Kiddush, in the twenty-ninth chapter of Shabbat, he wrote that it must not be blemished—this implies that because he holds that Birkat Hamazon does not need a cup, therefore, we are not concerned about being blemished. It is surprising that the Rif did not mention the law of blemished at all, not in the eighth chapter of Berachot regarding the cup of blessing, nor in "Erev Pesachim" regarding Kiddush and Havdalah. This requires further investigation.

A cup is considered blemished only if someone drank directly from it. However, if someone poured from the cup into their hand and then drank from their hand, it is not considered blemished. This is because just as there are people who are fastidious and find it difficult to drink from a cup that someone else drank from directly with their mouth, similarly it is considered a blemish regarding the cup of blessing. If one did not drink directly from the cup, fastidiousness does not apply, and thus it is not considered a blemish. According to this, it would seem that it is only when one placed their mouth on the cup in the manner of drinking. But if one opened their mouth and poured from the cup into their mouth without their mouth touching the cup, it would not be considered blemished. However, I have seen one of the great authorities (the GR”A) who did not write this way. 

It is not only drinking from a cup that causes it to be blemished; even if one drank from a pitcher, it is considered blemished, and even from a small barrel. But if one drank from a large wooden barrel, there is no need to be concerned. Some people are strict even about this, so it is best to be cautious from the outset (Magen Avraham, subsection 8). There are those who are so stringent about blemish that even if one needs to dilute wine with water, if the water is blemished, it is forbidden to dilute the wine with it. The reason is that anything blemished is not fit for matters of sanctity. 

And do not wonder why we need a reason of blemish when the cup is lacking, for even if the cup holds more than a revi'it, it is still not full, and one of the conditions of the cup is that it should be full, as will be explained. One could say that one can pour it into a smaller cup (Magen Avraham, subsection 7), or if one drank a tiny amount, it is still considered full (Taz, subsection 3). However, there is a remedy for this, as will be explained later.

How is a damaged cup (kos pagum) repaired? By adding a little wine to it. The blemish is due to having drunk from it, and when one adds to it, it is thereby repaired, similar to the blemish of the altar which is sealed and thereby repaired. Similarly, if the wine from the damaged cup is returned to the flask, it is nullified by the majority and becomes fit. It appears to me that even if the wine in the cup is more than the wine in the flask, it is also nullified, because the main concern of nullification is the small amount of wine that the mouth touched; the wine below is not blemished, as for this reason, adding a little wine is sufficient as I have written. In truth, it is not necessary to return the entire cup to the flask. However, some are hesitant and say that this repair is only effective after the fact (b'diavad) (Magen Avraham, subsection 9), but ideally (l'chatchila) one should add a little wine, then pour it into the flask, and afterward fill the blessing cup from the flask. The reason for this is: we need to repair the blemish in the cup, just as the blemish originated from the cup. And so we customarily do, and this is proper. It is not only by adding a little wine that it is repaired; the same applies to adding water or other beverages that do not spoil the wine. However, water is preferable because wine is typically diluted with water (see Magen Avraham, subsection 11). Therefore, even if one has more wine, one can repair it with water if the wine will not be spoiled by the excessive water. Just ensure that the water is not blemished, as I have written.

And our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in paragraph 4: If the participants' cups are blemished, one must pour from the cup of blessing into them. Some say that it is not necessary. Thus is his wording, meaning their custom was that each participant would have a cup, and the one who blesses would fulfill their obligation, and each would drink from his own cup. Consequently, it is necessary that the participants' cups not be blemished. Therefore, it is necessary to pour a little from his cup into theirs. It is obvious that he should pour before he drinks (Taz, small paragraph 4), because otherwise, even his cup would become blemished for them. And the "some say it is not necessary" hold that we are not particular about a blemished cup, except for the cup of the one who blesses. And know that the opinion of the Rashbam in Pesachim there, from the fact that the Talmud uses the term "particular" regarding a blemished cup, implies that there is no absolute requirement after the fact; and if he has nothing with which to fix it, he can bless even when it is blemished. And one cannot say that he can fix it with a little water as explained, because it could be that it would spoil if water were added (Taz, small paragraph 7). And there are those who disagree with the Rashbam. Nevertheless, the Rashbam is reliable to rely upon in pressing circumstances (Tur and Shulchan Aruch, paragraph 7). According to what we have explained, it is clear that the Rif's opinion is the same, and in the Grace After Meals, the opinion of the Rambam is also the same as I wrote in paragraph 6.

It is stated at the end of the seventh chapter of Berachot: Ten things were said regarding the cup of blessing: rinsing and washing, undiluted and full, adorning and wrapping, taking it with both hands and then holding it in the right hand, raising it a handbreadth from the ground, and looking at it. Some say even sending it as a gift to the members of one's household. Rabbi Yochanan said: We have only four of these: rinsing, washing, undiluted, and full. And it was taught: rinsing inside and washing outside. This means not only must the inside of the cup be clean, but even the outside. And it was taught in the Tosefta that if one wipes it well, it is acceptable. This means that rinsing and washing with water are not strictly necessary; the main thing is that it be clean. Therefore, if one wipes it well, that is sufficient. And if it is clean otherwise, nothing more is needed (Beit Yosef). One should be careful that there are no remnants of cups in it, meaning what remains from bread dipped in the cup. And in the Zohar Pinchas (page 245a), it implies that rinsing and washing with water are absolutely necessary in every case. See there. (See Beit Yosef, who wrote in the name of Mordechai and the R"Y that this is the custom of the world. He wrote that if it is clean, it is not necessary. See there. I am puzzled that he did not bring the words of the Zohar which require this. Examine and you will find clarity.)

"‘Undiluted’ does not mean without mixing, for this is impossible with their wines, which were strong and could not be drunk without mixing. Rather, this is its interpretation: they would pour undiluted wine from the barrel into the cup, and when they reached the blessing 'on the land and on the sustenance' – they would add water to mix it. And why at the blessing of the land? To make known the praise of the land, that its wines are strong and require mixing with water. And even though we bless outside of the Land, nonetheless, since he does not mix it until the blessing of the land – it proves that his intention is to praise the land. And with our wines which do not require mixing – there is no need to mix it at all. (And in the Beit Yosef, it is written that in some places they always had the custom to mix, as there is a matter according to Kabbalah. Look there, for water is kindness, and it comes to sweeten the wine which is red.)"

And the water should be added at the beginning of the blessing of the land, when one begins to say "We thank You…" (Beit Yosef). And Rabbeinu Tam explained that "alive" means "mixed and not mixed," meaning: that even at the beginning, a little water should be mixed, but in the blessing of the land, a little more water is added. This explanation aligns with the Talmudic discussion; see there. This is also clarified from the language of the Rambam at the end of the seventh chapter, where he wrote: And when he reaches the blessing of the land – he adds a little water to it, see there. Indeed, it seems necessary to interpret it this way for another reason: if not, how could one begin to bless over a cup that is not full? But if we say a little water – it is satisfactory, as initially, it is also considered full, but a few drops of water are added. The first opinion is that of the Rif, and indeed there are those who say that the Rif's intention is also so (Bach). And Rashi of blessed memory explained that "alive" means that he mixes it in the cup itself; and not that he mixes it in another vessel and pours it into the blessing cup, as the wine must come to the cup pure as it is, and in it, he mixes it with water. Further, he explained "alive" to mean that it is taken from the barrel close to the blessing, see there. And for us, who do not have barrels, each person should pour from the pitcher close to the blessing. And if he sends to the wine seller, who has a wine barrel – he should send it close to the blessing. There are others who interpret "alive" as referring to the cup, meaning: that the cup should be whole and not broken, as in vessels we say "their breaking is their death." Therefore, when it is whole, it is called "alive." And even if the break is at the bottom of the vessel, meaning at the base of the vessel – it is still not proper except in pressing circumstances. And "full" is to be taken literally, that the cup should be full. And anyone who blesses over a full cup – is granted an inheritance without boundaries, as it is said: "And the blessing of the Lord is full, the sea and the south he shall inherit." And he inherits two worlds: this world and the world to come (Talmud there). And "alive" should ideally satisfy all opinions (Tur) if possible. However, with our wines, this is almost impossible, because if a little water is added, it will be completely spoiled.

"Adornment": Rav Yehuda would adorn himself with students, seating them around him at the time of the blessing. Rav Chisda would adorn himself with cups, meaning: with cups surrounding the cup of blessing. And "Wrapping": Rav Pappa would wrap himself and sit, Rav Ashi would spread a cloth over his head. It is written that every God-fearing person should not bless with the thin head covering on his head, but should place the hat on his head (Magen Avraham, subsection 5). And this is the custom. However, in the Zohar it is explicitly stated so that one should not bless with an uncovered head, see there. And there are those who also practice wrapping with an upper garment (there), but we have neither seen nor heard of this custom.

And he receives it with both hands to show the preciousness of the mitzvah, that he accepts it with all his strength. And when he begins to bless, he takes it in his right hand, so that it does not appear as a burden to him. The right hand is primary, and he should not assist with the left; even holding his right hand with his left hand is not proper, unless he cannot manage otherwise. If the one blessing is left-handed, he holds it in his right hand, which is the left hand of others. It is forbidden to hold the cup with gloves, as this is a disgrace to the cup, as if he does not want to hold it with his own hand. Therefore, if he is wearing gloves, he must remove them during the blessing over the cup. Some have written that it is proper for the cup to be held on the palm with the fingers surrounding the cup upright, and not to place it on the fingers. Others require specifically on the fingers. Our master, the Rema, rules that it is only forbidden for the left hand to touch the cup, but one may place it under the right hand to assist the right. He lifts it a handbreadth from the ground if he is sitting on the ground. If he is sitting at a table, he lifts it a handbreadth from the table, as it is written: "I will lift the cup of salvation..." so that it would be visible to all those seated and they will gaze upon it. He should focus his eyes on it to avoid distraction. The Rema writes that therefore one should not use for the cup of blessing a vessel with a narrow mouth, called a "galok glas," to bless over, since one cannot look at the wine. Some have contested this, saying the intention is to look at the cup, not the wine. There is also another reason: because it is a mitzvah to drink the cup of blessing in one gulp, and with a narrow vessel, this is not possible. This too has been contested, as the main point is that it should not enter the intestines little by little but rather into the throat, and one can pour it into the throat little by little without swallowing until most of it is poured. And in the Zohar, it is explicitly indicated that the gazing is at the wine in the cup. He sends it to his wife for her to drink from it, even if she is not eating with him at the table.

And behold, Rabbi Yochanan said: "We have only four." And so it is explained by the Rambam at the end of the fourth chapter, see there. But the Tur wrote in the name of the Geonim that all ten things are needed, since we find that Rav Pappa and Rav Ashi, who are later authorities, performed the wrapping, and we do not follow Rabbi Yochanan in this. And we do all of them except the wrapping (Tur). And know that even according to the opinion that Birkat Hamazon does not require a cup, nevertheless, when one blesses over a cup, one should practice these things, as the Rambam rules there, see there.

The one who recites the blessing immediately upon receiving the cup of blessing – it is forbidden for him to speak, so that he does not divert his attention from the cup. It is also proper for those seated to refrain from speaking at that time, but according to the law, they are not prohibited from speaking except from when the one reciting the blessing begins to bless. And it is not only during the time that he is blessing, when they are obligated to incline their ears and listen, for if they did not hear or engaged in idle chatter, they do not fulfill their obligation; but even between blessings when the one reciting is silent – they should not speak. If they spoke during that time, they do not need to repeat the blessing. Even the one reciting, if he spoke between blessings, does not need to repeat the blessing. But if he interrupted with speech in the middle of the blessing, he must start the blessing over. If he paused in silence, even if he waited long enough to complete the entire blessing, he does not need to start over. Refer to what I wrote in section 65. 

Know that all this is according to their custom, where everyone remains silent and fulfills their obligation through the blessing of the one reciting. However, we each recite our own blessing, only finishing the blessing before the one reciting so that we can respond "Amen," because we cannot rely on hearing, as I wrote in section 59. Our master, the Beit Yosef, also wrote in subsection 7: It is proper for each person seated to quietly recite each blessing along with the one reciting, even the conclusions, and to finish before the one reciting so that they can respond "Amen." These are his words. There are those who practice that until "He who sustains all" they fulfill their obligation through the blessing of the one reciting, as this is the main part of the Zimun blessing. This is the main practice (Magen Avraham, subsection 12). Nonetheless, we do not follow this practice. It is written that the cup of blessing should only be given to one with a good eye (Talmud Sota, chapter 7), who hates unjust gain and is charitable with his wealth (Rashi), as it is stated: "He who has a good eye will be blessed" – do not read "will be blessed" but "will bless" (Talmud). If there is no such person, the greatest among them should bless.

The Grace After Meals must be recited while seated: whether one ate while walking around the house, or ate while seated, or ate while reclining – one must only recite it while seated, in order to concentrate properly. And one should not recite it while reclining, as that is a manner of arrogance; rather, one should sit with reverence. This applies not only to the one reciting the blessing, but also to all those present: they should not sit in a light-hearted manner but with reverence. And if, after the fact, they recited it while walking – they have fulfilled their obligation, but it was not done in the optimal manner. However, if one was walking on the road and eating – one may recite it while walking initially, and does not need to sit down because his mind is not settled, and it would be bothersome. And it is forbidden to recite the Grace After Meals while engaged in one's work, and this will be explained in section 191. Some say that even the blessing "Me'ein Shalosh" should be said while seated, even though the blessing is rabbinic. There is support from the Torah for sitting during the Grace After Meals, as it is written: "And you shall eat and be satisfied, and bless" – "sit and bless" (Tosafot at the end of the chapter "These are the Things"). Regarding interrupting in the middle of the chapter or between chapters, some say its law is like that of prayer, and it is forbidden to interrupt at all except in the case of danger, and it is stricter than the Shema. The reason why it should be stricter than the Shema is not understood. It is clear that "Hatov Vehameitiv" is not included in this, as it is rabbinic. (And the Gra provides a somewhat reason, but it is not sufficient, see there. And it seems that even to hint with one's eyes is forbidden during the Grace After Meals, since we compare it to prayer.)

Grace after meals (Birkat Hamazon) must be recited immediately after finishing the meal, specifically in the place where the meal was eaten. It has already been explained in Siman 178 that some say all seven species (of produce for which the Land of Israel is praised) require a blessing in their place specifically. Others say only the five species of grain require a blessing in their place; even those whose blessing is "Borei Minei Mezonot" (Who creates varieties of nourishment) require a blessing in their place. But those whose blessing is "Ha'etz" (Who creates the fruit of the tree), even if they are among the seven species, do not require a blessing in their place. Refer to that section. What constitutes "a change of place"? Moving from one room to another. However, within one room, even if it is very large, one can eat in one corner and bless in another corner. Additionally, moving from one room to another, if part of the original room is still visible, is considered as one place. If one ate with the intention to bless in another room, it is permissible, as I have written there.

If someone ate and left without reciting the blessing at the place where he ate, the Rambam (Maimonides) rules in the fourth chapter that if it was intentional, he must return to his place and recite the blessing. If it was unintentional, he may recite the blessing at the place where he remembers. Even if it was intentional, if he did not return to his place and recited the blessing where he remembered, he has fulfilled his obligation. However, the Tur rules that even if it was unintentional, he must return to his place and recite the blessing. If he did not do so and recited the blessing where he remembered, he has fulfilled his obligation. But if it was intentional, even if he recited the blessing where he remembered, he has not fulfilled his obligation and must return to his place and recite the blessing again. (The Tur rules according to Beit Shammai at the beginning of the eighth chapter, while the Rambam rules according to Beit Hillel. See Tosafot 52b, s.v. "Bekulei.")

However, many have wondered about the Tur: From where do we derive that if one intentionally recited the blessing not in its proper place, he must recite the blessing again? This is not explained anywhere. Granted, he committed a transgression, but nevertheless, since according to Torah law he certainly fulfilled his obligation just as in the case of unintentional transgression, for according to Torah law there is no distinction between intentional and unintentional transgression, it is clear. If so, one must say that the Rabbis decreed to differentiate between intentional and unintentional transgression, that in the case of intentional transgression, even after the fact, he did not fulfill his obligation. This is not found in the Talmud at all, and none of the early authorities wrote this. Therefore, even though some commentators have struggled to uphold the Tur's words based on Talmudic discussions, these interpretations are not at all necessary. And according to the law, one should not recite the blessing again (Taz, end of section 1 and Eliyah Rabbah). Anyone who is stringent in this regard is only among those who cause wonder and brings about blessings in vain (Eliyah Rabbah). There is no difference between intentional and unintentional transgression; in both cases, he should return to his place and recite the blessing, and if he did not do so but recited the blessing in his place, he has fulfilled his obligation. It has already been explained in Siman 178 that matters requiring a blessing in their place have the same status as bread, and therefore, even in these cases, one is obligated to return to his place and recite the blessing, even unintentionally. It is possible to rely on the opinion of the Rambam that in the case of unintentional transgression, one should recite the blessing in the place where he remembered, and this appears to me to be the primary ruling. (This is a case of a double doubt: perhaps we follow the Rambam, and if you say we follow the Tur, perhaps only bread requires a blessing in its place. Although from the Magen Avraham, section 6, it does not seem so, see there, nevertheless, it appears so. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

And our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 2: "Regarding what matters are we speaking? When he has no other bread. But if he has other bread – he may eat a little in the second place and bless, as long as he is not hungry from the first meal." End of his words. This means: Even if he ate less than an olive's volume there, nevertheless, since he finished eating there – he can bless there, as I wrote in Siman 178. However, this is according to the opinion of the Rosh. But according to the Rambam, it is explained there that he must make a blessing beforehand on what he will eat, and a blessing afterward on what he has eaten, see there. And also our master, the Beit Yosef’s intention is the same, for earlier he said, "And if by mistake, according to the Rambam, he should bless where he remembered, and according to the Ri and the Rosh, he should also return to his place and bless" – to this he says: "Regarding what matters are we speaking...". Meaning: According to the Rambam, he can bless there, and according to the Ri and the Rosh, he should eat in the second place. And that which he wrote: "as long as he is not hungry from the first meal" is simple, for if much time has passed since his meal – the Grace After Meals would no longer be relevant. (And the words of the Magen Avraham in subsection 3 are not understood at all, as written by the Pri Megadim and the Machtzit HaShekel, see there. And the main difficulty is not difficult at all, for it is obvious that the Beit Yosef earlier is referring to the opinion of the Rosh. And know that if until he returns to his place the food will be digested – according to all opinions he should bless where he remembers. Consider this well and you will find it easy.)

If one ate and does not know whether he recited the Grace after Meals or not, he must recite it out of doubt because it is a biblical commandment, and in cases of doubt regarding a biblical commandment, we are stringent. This is specifically when he ate to the point of satisfaction, as it is written: "And you shall eat and be satisfied and bless." However, if he did not eat to the point of satisfaction, his obligation is rabbinic, and in cases of doubt regarding a rabbinic commandment, we are lenient. When he repeats the blessing out of doubt, he also includes the blessing "HaTov VeHaMeitiv" even though it is rabbinic; because once he becomes obligated, he is obligated in the entire blessing, as it was established that each time one recites the Grace after Meals, one also recites "HaTov VeHaMeitiv." Nevertheless, he cannot fulfill the obligation for someone else who ate and definitely did not bless, because a case of doubt cannot exempt a case of certainty. Even though someone who ate a rabbinic measure can exempt someone who ate a biblical measure, this is because it is considered certain in any case. But not when one blesses due to doubt (see Sha'arei Teshuvah in the name of Pri Chadash, and this is the main ruling). And see what I wrote in Section 9.

Furthermore, it seems that this applies specifically when he definitely ate and there is a doubt whether he blessed, so he is obligated to bless. But if there is a doubt whether he ate or not, or he ate and there is a doubt whether he ate bread or not, he does not bless. And the reason: because it seems that it is not appropriate to say here that we should be stringent and he is obligated to bless, for there is a leniency in that if he already blessed, his blessings now would be in vain. Rather, the matter is as follows: when he definitely ate, and the obligation to bless is definitely upon him, therefore in a doubtful situation of Torah law, you cannot exempt him from the obligation that is definitely upon him. However, if there is doubt regarding the fundamental obligation, you cannot impose upon him to bless, for perhaps he is not obligated to bless at all, and his blessings would be in vain. (See Ba'er Hetev, small section 6. What appears to my humble opinion I have written. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

Until when can one recite the blessing? Until the food in his stomach has been digested. And what is the measure of digestion? As long as he is not hungry due to that meal (Gemara Berakhot 53b). From the moment he begins to feel hungry, even though the food has not been completely digested, since it has started to be digested, he can no longer recite the blessing. The same applies to drinking or eating fruits: if he is not thirsty or hungry for those fruits, even if he has an appetite for other fruits, he should recite the blessing if he is not sure whether the food has been digested. Indeed, it is difficult to measure this, because digestion refers only to the beginning of digestion, as complete digestion takes a long time, not less than six hours, but the beginning of digestion (Magen Avraham, subsection 9). And if so, who can measure this? All the more so with eating fruits and drinking. Additionally, this measure only applies when one has eaten to satisfaction, but if one has eaten a little, on the contrary, his appetite increases more, and still, he is obligated to recite the blessing. And what should the measure be in this case? (See Taz, subsection 2 and Magen Avraham, subsection 9).

In the Gemara there, it states that the duration of digestion is the time it takes to walk four mil. According to Rashi's interpretation, for a large meal, it is four mil, and according to Tosafot, for a small meal, it is four mil. However, this is according to the opinion there that the measure of digestion is as long as one is thirsty due to his eating. But according to what we hold, that it is as long as one is not hungry, as I have written, there is no proof, as they hold this way regardless, and there is no proof that they disagree on this. Therefore, indeed there is someone who says that for a small meal, it is four mil, as concluded by our Rabbis, the Tosafot, and for a large meal, it is as long as one is not hungry due to his eating (Taz there). The measure of four mil is one hour and twelve parts of an hour. However, we still do not know how much is considered a large meal and how much a small meal. Nevertheless, in any case, it is certain that up to four mil, one must recite the grace after meals, and therefore there is no other way when one delays longer than this measure than to eat an olive-sized portion now and recite the grace after meals (Magen Avraham there). And one should do this, and similarly for the after-blessing of other foods. However, in this case, if one diverted his attention, he must also recite the initial blessing. And it appears to me, in general, when a person is in doubt whether he delayed the duration of digestion or not, for bread he must recite the grace after meals, and for other foods, he should not recite a blessing due to doubt (this seems to me in my humble opinion).

The measure of eating to recite the Grace After Meals is an average olive's size, and this is by rabbinic decree. Biblically, however, it is specifically to the point of satiation (Magen Avraham, subsection 18). The Levush wrote that an egg's size is from the Torah, see there. And there are some from the early authorities who hold this view (R"Y, Ra'ah, and Rivav like Eliyah Rabbah wrote in subsection 9).
