But most of our rabbis do not hold this view, and it will be further explained in section 197 with the help of Heaven. (And know that in the case of doubt if one blessed, that one is obligated to bless the Grace After Meals as I wrote, this also applies to women. And see Shaarei Teshuva, subsection 7. Delve and you will find ease.)

Birkat Hamazon (Grace After Meals) can be recited in any language, as it is stated: "And you shall bless the Lord your God" – in any language that you bless (Sotah 33a). It appears to me that this is specifically when one does not understand Hebrew. This is implied in the Jerusalem Talmud there, which states that Birkat Hamazon can be recited in any language so that one knows to whom they are blessing, and similarly in prayer, so that one knows how to request their needs. It is explained that this is why they permitted it in any language, but if one understands Hebrew, they certainly know to whom they are blessing. Thus, it is only when one does not know Hebrew. Furthermore, the Jerusalem Talmud says regarding the Megillah that if one knows how to read it in Hebrew and in another language, they fulfill their obligation only in Hebrew. If so, the same applies to Birkat Hamazon and prayer as well. When the Gemara says "in any language that you bless," it does not mean any language you want; rather, it means if you do not understand Hebrew, you should bless in any language you understand for blessing. (However, from Rashi's language there, where he wrote: "The text did not establish a specific language," it does not seem so, and this needs to be reconciled. Delve and you will find clarity.)

Behold, in the generation before us, there arose a congregation of evildoers outside our country who prayed and recited the Grace After Meals in a foreign language, basing themselves on the Mishnah in Sotah that states, "These are recited in any language." The great sages of that generation annulled their words. And I say that this evil congregation did not understand the sages of the Talmud at all. For in the Mishnah, many things are enumerated that can be said in any language, and the Gemara provides reasons for each one why it can be in any language; and many things that specifically must be in the Holy Tongue, and the Gemara explains for each one why it must be specifically in the Holy Tongue, see there. And it is not understood: if logically we would not say that it must specifically be in the Holy Tongue, why do we need a verse for those that can be in any language? And if logically we would say that it must specifically be in the Holy Tongue, why do we need a verse for those that must specifically be in the Holy Tongue?

However, the main points are as follows: Certainly, since the Torah was given in the Holy Tongue, and it is the sacred language through which the world was created, it is surely a commandment and obligation that anything related to Torah and mitzvah must be in the Holy Tongue specifically, for one who knows the Holy Tongue. Even for one who does not know the Holy Tongue, we would not permit him to say it in another language. Therefore, a scriptural verse is needed to permit someone who does not know the Holy Tongue, as per the words of the Jerusalem Talmud that we brought. Consequently, these matters do not require the Holy Tongue to be indispensable, and even if one knows the Holy Tongue but prayed or made a blessing in another language, he has fulfilled his obligation according to the Torah, although he has committed a transgression. It is unreasonable to say that someone who does not know the Holy Tongue can initially say it in another language, while someone who knows it, even post facto, has not fulfilled his obligation (and this is the intention of Rashi there, which we brought in section 1). Accordingly, a scriptural verse is needed to permit, initially, someone who does not know the Holy Tongue. For those matters that require the Holy Tongue indispensably, a scriptural verse is needed to state that even post facto, they have not fulfilled their obligation. Based on this, it is obvious that it is absolutely forbidden for us to pray and bless in another language. It has already been clarified in Siman 101 that when using another language, it must be translated exactly from the Holy Tongue to the other language, word for word, with precision. See there.

If it is necessary to understand the language? Later in Siman 690, it will be explained regarding the Megillah that in a foreign language, one must understand, and if not, one has not fulfilled the obligation. But in Hebrew, even if one does not understand, one has fulfilled the obligation, both the reader and the listener, see there. And Rashi of blessed memory learned from this that the same applies to all commandments; as Mordechai wrote in his name in the eighth chapter of Berachot, see there. According to this, one who prays or blesses in Hebrew has fulfilled the obligation even though they do not understand, and so too the listener. This is also explicitly implied in Berachot (45b), where it is taught: Two who ate together—it is a mitzvah to separate (each one should bless for himself). When does this apply? When both are literate. But if one is literate and the other is illiterate—the literate one blesses and the illiterate one fulfills the obligation, even though the illiterate one does not understand Hebrew at all.

However, our rabbis, the authors of the Tosafot, wrote there, and this is their language: "Concerning women, it requires investigation whether they fulfill their obligation with the blessing of the zimun of men, since they do not understand. And some bring proof that they fulfill their obligation, from what is said later: 'A scribe recites the blessing, and an unlearned person fulfills his obligation...' However, it can be rebutted, for an unlearned person understands the Holy Tongue and knows somewhat what is being said, though he does not know how to bless. But women who do not understand at all, one can say that they do not fulfill their obligation. And that which is said in Megillah (17a): 'A foreigner who heard it in Hebrew fulfills his obligation' — the reason is solely the publicizing of the miracle, as it is said there... So far their language, and so wrote the Rosh and the Mordechai there. And so wrote the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch in Siman 193, see there. 

But I do not understand the opinion of our rabbis: from where do we know that the unlearned person understands the Holy Tongue? For there are many unlearned people who do not understand at all, and did the Baraita distinguish between one unlearned person and another? And indeed, in the Sefer Mitzvot Gadol (Mitzvah 27) this rebuttal is not found, except regarding that of the Megillah that publicizing the miracle is different, see there. And also this rebuttal I do not understand, for in Megillah it says: 'Do we know the meaning of "the couriers riding the royal steeds"? Rather, the mitzvah of reading and publicizing the miracle.' Thus, besides publicizing the miracle, it also says the reason 'the mitzvah of reading' — thus one fulfills his obligation with this reading even though he does not understand. (And from the language of the Rosh and the Mordechai it implies that in their version, it was only for the reason of publicizing the miracle, see there. And also in Maimonides, Chapter Five, Halacha 15, it clearly implies not so, and so in the Behag and the Rif. And so the Sefer Mitzvot Gadol there wrote in the name of the Ri according to the opinion of Rashi, see there.)

However, even according to these rabbis, this applies only to the listener. But someone who recites a blessing for themselves or prays, even if they do not understand anything, has nevertheless fulfilled their obligation. Similarly, the Levush writes in Siman 193, Section 1, and this is his language: "And this is the difference between the one who recites the blessing and the listener: the one who recites the blessing fulfills their obligation with their own blessing even if they do not understand, since this is the format of the blessing. The listener, however, does not fulfill their obligation unless they understand what the one reciting the blessing says." This is the end of his language. And so wrote several great authorities (Magen Avraham at the beginning of Siman 62, and Ateret Tzvi and Pri Megadim at the beginning of Siman 193). They also wrote that the common custom follows Rashi, that women fulfill their obligation by listening even if they do not understand anything (Bach in Siman 193, and Magen Avraham there, Subsection 2, and see there in Taz). Similarly, our teacher the Rema wrote in his book Darkei Moshe there, and it is also made clear from his words in Siman 199, Section 7, as I wrote there. And indeed, this is also the opinion of the Bahag, the Rif, and the Rambam, as I have written.

And know that one of the great sages made a distinction: Even if someone recites the blessing themselves, if they do not understand the words of the blessings that came out of their mouth, they have not fulfilled their obligation, even if it is in the Holy Tongue (Rabbi Zalman in this section). He wrote the reason: since they do not understand the words, I do not consider it as "and you shall bless the Lord your God" even though they know to whom they are blessing, see there. This is very puzzling: since they know to whom they are blessing, it is indeed considered "and you shall bless the Lord your God," meaning that they are giving praise and thanks to the Blessed God. And indeed, lack of intention does not invalidate even the recitation of Shema except for the verse "Shema Yisrael" as I wrote in Siman 60, and in prayer only during the Avot as I wrote in Siman 101. Furthermore, if we say so, it turns out that thousands of Jews have not fulfilled their obligation in Birkat Hamazon, and it is unthinkable to say so. Moreover, according to the opinions of Rashi, the Ba'al Halachot Gedolot, the Rif, and the Rambam, even one who hears (the blessing) has fulfilled their obligation even if they do not understand, so how can we create such a far-reaching dispute according to those who disagree that even the one who recites has not fulfilled their obligation? Therefore, the main ruling is as I have written. Additionally, the world holds primarily according to the opinion of Rashi as I have written, as this appears to be the straightforward understanding of the Talmud's language. And also, our Rabbis who disagree do not state it as a definitive matter, as is clear from their words to one who examines them. All this is in a situation of after the fact. But certainly, ideally, and the main mitzvah is to understand what one is saying and hearing with attention. And likewise, when one fulfills their obligation by hearing from another, the listener must intend to fulfill their obligation, and the one reciting must intend to fulfill it for them, and this is essential even after the fact.

Maimonides wrote in the first chapter of Blessings, Law 5: The formulation of all the blessings was established by Ezra and his court. It is not proper to change them, nor to add to any of them, nor to subtract from them. Anyone who changes from the format established by the sages in the blessings is mistaken. Any blessing that does not include the mention of God's name and sovereignty is not a blessing, unless it is adjacent to another blessing. All blessings can be recited in any language, provided that the essence of what the sages established is maintained. If one changes the format, as long as the mention of God's name, sovereignty, and the essence of the blessing are included, even in a secular language, one fulfills the obligation. Thus far his words. The explanation of his words "anyone who changes from the format established by the sages is mistaken" means that he still fulfills the obligation, as he concludes that as long as the mention of God's name, sovereignty, and the essence of the blessing are included, one fulfills the obligation. The first law applies when one blesses in Hebrew, and the second law applies when one blesses in a secular language. (He ruled according to Rabbi Meir in Berachot 40b and not according to Rabbi Yossi there, and according to the opinion of all the halachic authorities. Thus wrote the editor in the glosses of Maimonides, letter B. The Kesef Mishneh and the glosses of Maimonides assumed he ruled according to Rabbi Yossi, and what he wrote "is mistaken" means he does not fulfill the obligation. They raised a difficulty that in the Jerusalem Talmud it rules explicitly according to Rabbi Meir, and the Kesef Mishneh struggled with this interpretation, see there. This is unnecessary, and his intention is as I wrote and according to the opinion of all the halachic authorities. Examine and you will find it easy.)

He further wrote: All blessings require that one should make them audible to their own ears. If one did not make them audible to their ears, they have fulfilled the obligation, whether they articulated it with their lips or blessed in their heart. Thus is his wording. And he ruled thus based on what is taught (Berakhot 15a): A person should not recite the Grace After Meals in their heart. But if they did, they have fulfilled the obligation. See there. And it must be said: even though we hold that contemplation is not equivalent to speech regarding the Shema, as I wrote above in Siman 62, Section 6, and we proved there that this is also the opinion of Maimonides, see there. However, regarding blessings, he holds that it is equivalent to speech, because regarding the Shema it is written "and you shall speak of them," as I wrote there.

However, Rashi of blessed memory wrote that the statement in the Baraita, "And if he blessed, he has fulfilled [his obligation]"—this means that he did not make it audible to his own ears. For this is how he explained "in his heart," that he did not make it audible to his own ears; see there. His intention is: It is impossible to interpret "in his heart" literally, for we hold that contemplation is not equivalent to speech. And this is also the opinion of all our early sages, and so it is ruled in the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch in section 2. This is its wording: "And if he did not make it audible to his own ears, he has fulfilled [his obligation], provided he articulated it with his lips." This is the end of its wording. But with contemplation alone, he has not fulfilled [his obligation] (Magen Avraham, subsection 1). And if due to illness or another unavoidable circumstance he recited it in his heart, he has fulfilled [his obligation] (there); for this is also the case with the recitation of the Shema, as I have written in section 62. And so should one do in a place that is not completely clean, as our teacher the Rema wrote there; see there. And it seems to me that in the case of the final blessing, when one is in doubt whether he has blessed or not, he does not need to bless again, except for the Grace after Meals, which he should contemplate in his heart, for in any case he has fulfilled [his obligation] according to the Rambam.

Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in paragraph 3: There are those who say that a homeowner, along with his children and wife, must recite the blessing out loud so that they fulfill their obligation through his blessing. Thus are his words. This applies when they are unable to recite the blessing themselves, as it is stated in the Gemara: "A scribe recites the blessing and an unlearned person fulfills his obligation." He wrote "There are those who say," because the Tosafot and the Rosh wrote that perhaps this only applies to an unlearned person who understands what is being said, and not to women who do not understand at all, as I wrote in paragraph 5. Therefore, he wrote "There are those who say." This is proof that even our teacher, the Beit Yosef, does not hold like the Tosafot and the Rosh, as I wrote there. (And the Magen Avraham in subparagraph 2 wrote: It requires investigation why he wrote "There are those who say," see there. His words are perplexing, as I wrote, for in Siman 193 he himself wrote like the Tosafot and the Rosh, see there. Therefore, he wrote "There are those who say." Delve deeply and you will find it easy.)

The Tur brings a passage from the Jerusalem Talmud (Terumot, Chapter One): What is the law regarding a drunk person making a blessing? A certain pious individual asked Elijah. He said to him: "And you shall eat and be satisfied, and you shall bless" – even if he is in a dazed state. This means: asleep and not in a clear state of mind. Until here is his wording. The Tur and the Sefer Mitzvot Gadol (positive commandment 27) explain "in a dazed state" like "an inanimate stone," meaning: drunk and unable to speak properly, see there. And elsewhere, it is explained that sometimes due to an excess of eating and drinking, sleep overcomes him, and he is not clear-minded, and nevertheless the Torah says "and you shall bless" (so the Prisha brought in his name). And it is explained there in the Jerusalem Talmud that even if he cannot speak before the king, see there. But in prayer, it is not so, as I wrote in Siman 99. And it is similarly explained in Eruvin (64a): Even when slightly intoxicated, if he can still speak before the king, he should not initially pray, but if he did, his prayer is a prayer. But if he is drunk and cannot speak before the king, even after the fact, his prayer is not considered a prayer, as I wrote there. But for Birkat Hamazon and all blessings, even in such a state, he blesses initially. And this is the language of the Jerusalem Talmud there (Halacha 4): One who is slightly intoxicated should not pray. If he prayed, his prayer is supplication. One who is drunk should not pray, and if he prayed, his prayer is blasphemous. What is considered slightly intoxicated? Anyone who drank a quarter-log. Drunk is one who drank more. There they say: Anyone who cannot speak before the king... What is the law regarding a drunk person making a blessing? "And you shall eat and be satisfied, and you shall bless" – even if he is in a dazed state. See there. Thus, it is explicitly stated that even if he cannot speak before the king, he blesses Birkat Hamazon. And the same applies to all blessings.

However, our Rabbis, the authors of the Tosafot in Eruvin there, did not write so, and this is their language: "Drunk... – and it requires investigation whether blessings should be equated to prayer regarding excrement and drunkenness. And necessarily, they are not similar in all matters, for a person who is slightly intoxicated should not pray until he becomes sober... And it is obvious that someone slightly intoxicated recites Birkat Hamazon and all the blessings, as it says in the Jerusalem Talmud in Berakhot: 'And you shall eat, be satisfied, and bless' – even if he is somewhat muddled. Until here is their language."

Thus, they only adopted the words of the Jerusalem Talmud concerning someone slightly intoxicated and not someone drunk, and necessarily they had a different version of the Jerusalem Talmud. And they wrote that the Jerusalem Talmud is in Berakhot, but in our version, it is only found in Terumot. The Rosh also wrote similarly, see there. However, in Berakhot (31b), they themselves brought the Jerusalem Talmud from Terumot, that a drunk person can recite Birkat Hamazon, see there. And similarly, the Rosh wrote so, see there. And their words contradict each other. The main ruling is as I wrote in Berakhot, as ruled by the Sefer Mitzvot Gadol and the Tur (from the eve of the holiday) and the Mordechai.

Based on this, what our master the Beit Yosef wrote in section 4: even if one has become so intoxicated that he cannot speak properly – he can still recite the Grace After Meals. This is his precise wording. It is clear that his intention is even when one cannot speak before a king. However, from what he wrote afterward in section 5, and this is his wording: if one blessed, and there was excrement in front of him or he was intoxicated – the Tosafot and the Rosh were uncertain whether he needs to recite the blessing again. But regarding urine, it is clear that he does not need to recite the blessing again. This is his precise wording. And this is according to their statements in Eruvin, which contradicts what he wrote previously. Indeed, the Levush omitted "intoxicated," see there. However, it seems that our master the Beit Yosef’s opinion aims to reconcile their statements and to differentiate in the case of intoxication between one who cannot speak properly and one who cannot speak at all. But the main ruling is that in any case, one can recite the Grace After Meals, except when he has reached the level of Lot's intoxication. Also, the commentators on the Shulchan Aruch (Taz and Magen Avraham) agreed with this ruling, and this is also clarified from the words of our master the Rema at the beginning of Siman 99, see there. It is also explicitly stated in the Zohar, Terumah (page 153b); and there it explains the reason for the difference between prayer and the Grace After Meals, see there.

Women are obligated in Birkat HaMazon (the Grace After Meals), as it is a positive commandment not bound by time, for whenever one eats, one is obligated to bless. Nevertheless, there is a doubt in the Gemara (Berachot 20b) whether their obligation is from the Torah or only rabbinic, and from the Torah they are exempt, because it is written: "And you shall bless... for the good land..." – and women did not take a portion in the land (Rashi). And even though the priests and Levites also did not take a portion in the land, nevertheless, they had the cities of refuge. Additionally, since they took tithes and offerings from the produce of the land, it is as if "they have a portion in the land", which is not the case for women. Furthermore, since in the blessing of the land one is obligated to say "for Your covenant which You have sealed in our flesh, and for Your Torah which You have taught us", and women are neither in the covenant nor in the Torah (Tosafot). And one cannot say: even if they are exempt from the blessing of the land, why would they be exempt from the blessing of "He Who sustains"? For initially, Moses instituted the blessing of "He Who sustains" when the manna fell for them, and Joshua instituted the blessing of the land when they entered the land, and David and Solomon instituted "Who builds Jerusalem" (Berachot 48b). And when Moses instituted it – surely he also instituted it for women, for the manna fell for them as well. If so, how were they exempted afterward? And similarly, why are they exempt from "Who builds Jerusalem"? One can say that since we derive from the verse "And you shall bless" – this is the blessing of "He Who sustains...," "for the land" – this is the blessing of the land, "the good" – this is "Who builds Jerusalem" (there). Therefore, anyone obligated in the blessing of the land is obligated in all of them, and anyone not obligated in the blessing of the land is exempt from all of them. Additionally, because women’s sustenance is the responsibility of their husbands, as the man is obligated to provide for his wife. Therefore, one could say that even the main blessing of "He Who sustains" does not pertain to them. Similarly, the main aspect of the building of Jerusalem pertains to men, and women are secondary to men (so it seems in my humble opinion).

And it is stated in the Gemara there that there is a practical difference whether the obligation is from the Torah or from the rabbis: if it is from the Torah, women can fulfill the obligation for men, but if it is rabbinic, they cannot, for rabbinic law cannot fulfill a Torah obligation. And even though we hold that someone who ate an olive's bulk of grain can fulfill the obligation for someone who ate to satiety, even though from the Torah the obligation is only for eating to satiety, as it is written: "And you shall eat and be satisfied"—this is not comparable. Firstly, according to the Ra'avad in the fifth chapter of Berachot, even from the Torah there is an obligation for an olive's bulk, see there. And even according to the Rambam and Tosafot that an olive's bulk is only rabbinic, nonetheless, since the main obligation is from the Torah, in truth from the Torah he could fulfill the obligation for others even if he did not eat at all, just like any blessing over commandments, since all Jews are responsible for one another; and it is not similar to blessings over enjoyment, where one cannot fulfill the obligation for others if he did not benefit, because blessings over enjoyment are not obligatory. But the Grace after Meals following eating is obligatory and is like blessings over commandments, except that rabbinically it is said that as long as one has not eaten an olive's bulk of grain, he cannot fulfill the obligation for others. And this is explicitly stated in the Gemara. (Berachot 48a; and Shimon ben Shetach held it should be completely compared to commandments, see there. Analyze and you will find it easy.) Therefore, if one only ate an olive's bulk, he can fulfill the obligation for others, which is not the case for women if they are not obligated at all (Rashba there 48a). And that which we say in the Jerusalem Talmud, the third chapter of Berachot, that Grace after Meals is not comparable to all commandments, because it is written: "And you shall eat and be satisfied and bless"—he who ate should bless—this is rabbinic (there). And the Tur brought the opinion of Rabbi Yitzchak that in truth, even one who did not eat can fulfill the obligation for others, see there. And this is the opinion of Tosafot in Berachot there (end of the commentary beginning with "until"), and they wrote that what we say in the Gemara that one must eat an olive's bulk of grain—this is regarding the invitation to say "we have eaten of His," but without the invitation, he can fulfill the obligation for others. And the Tur disagrees with this, see there. And this is how we rule, as this seems to be the opinion of most authorities. (And the opinion of the Rambam in the fifth chapter is that in truth, one who only ate an olive's bulk cannot fulfill the obligation for one who ate to satiety. And the Rashba wrote this in the name of the Ba'al Halachot, see there. And this is the opinion of the Bahag, see there.)

The opinion of the Raavad and the Rashba is that the question has been resolved, and women are obligated in Birkat Hamazon (Grace After Meals) by Torah law and can also fulfill the obligation for men. Nevertheless, regarding the matter of a zimun (invitation to bless), they do not join together because of impropriety, as will be explained in Siman 199. However, the opinion of Tosafot and the Rosh is that the question has not been resolved and it remains a halachic doubt, and this is also the opinion of the Rambam in the fifth chapter, see there. And so ruled Rabbeinu the Beit Yosef in section 1. Therefore, they can only fulfill the obligation for those whose obligation is rabbinic, such as women and minors. A slave has the same status as a woman. A tumtum (person of indeterminate sex) and an androgynous (person with both male and female characteristics) are of uncertain status as either male or female, therefore a woman cannot fulfill the obligation for them, and they cannot fulfill the obligation for a man; nor can they fulfill the obligation for each other, since one may be male and the other female. There are some poskim (halachic authorities) who are certain that the conclusion of the Talmudic discussion is that women are only obligated by rabbinic decree, and this is the opinion of Rabbeinu Yonah (see Beit Yosef). This is also the opinion of the Zohar on Terumah (168b), see there. (See Magen Avraham, subsection 1.)

When a minor reaches the age of education, the father is obligated to train him in the recitation of the Grace After Meals (Birkat Hamazon) by rabbinic decree. A woman, however, cannot fulfill the obligation on behalf of a man, according to those who hold that her obligation is of doubtful or definite biblical origin. The minor's obligation in education applies even if he only ate an olive's bulk (kezayit), for whatever the Sages instituted, they did so in a manner similar to biblical law (Eliyah Rabbah). The same applies to women. A minor cannot fulfill the obligation for an adult unless the adult only ate an olive's bulk, in which case his obligation is rabbinic, and similarly, a woman cannot fulfill the obligation for a man unless he only ate an olive's bulk. This is what we learned in Sukkah (38a): "A son blesses for his father, a woman for her husband, and a servant for his master"; because they ate to satiety and their obligation is rabbinic, they can fulfill the obligation for those who ate only an olive's bulk, whose obligation is also rabbinic. If they also ate only an olive's bulk, they cannot fulfill the obligation, for two rabbinic obligations cannot discharge one rabbinic obligation (Tosafot at the end of the second chapter of Megillah 19b, s.v. "And Rabbi Yehuda"). Some dispute this (Magen Avraham, subsection 3). From the language of the Rambam in Chapter 5, Law 16, it also seems more in line with this opinion that there is no distinction, see there. According to the Raavad, who holds that an olive's bulk is a biblical obligation, in any case, they cannot fulfill the obligation for adults. The fact that a son blesses for his father and a woman for her husband does not mean they fulfill their obligations, but rather that the father or husband responds to what they say and then blesses on his own. The need for their recitation is due to his lack of familiarity. Therefore, it is indeed taught there: "A curse be upon a man whose wife and children bless for him," see there. (And daughters are not obligated in the educational aspect of Grace After Meals.)

The three blessings of Birkat Hamazon are from the Torah, as it is taught (Berachot 48b): From where do we derive that Birkat Hamazon is from the Torah? As it is stated: "And you shall eat and be satisfied." "And bless" – this refers to the blessing of "He who sustains." "The Lord your God" – this refers to the blessing of the invitation. "For the land" – this refers to the blessing of the land. "The good" – this refers to the blessing of "Who builds Jerusalem." And so it says: "The good mountain…" The blessing of "He who is good and does good" was instituted in Yavneh. And that which we said earlier there, that Moses instituted the blessing of "He who sustains," Joshua the blessing of the land, and David and Solomon "Who builds Jerusalem" – the intention is not that they instituted the essence of the matter, for this is from the Torah, but rather that they arranged the texts of the blessings (Rashba).

The first blessing opens with "Blessed" and concludes with "Blessed," as it is a long blessing that includes several matters; it has praise that the Blessed Name sustains the entire world, and a prayer that "we should never lack sustenance forever." Besides that He, Blessed be He, provides the necessary sustenance without which one cannot live, He also "provides for all and is benevolent to all" even in luxuries; and also prepares sustenance for every creature so that they find their sustenance in their place, as David said: "He gives bread to all flesh, for His kindness endures forever," and they established it in the first blessing. Some add "for His kindness endures forever with us," but this should not be said because His kindness is with all living creatures (Tur). Similarly, some add at the beginning of the blessing to say "Blessed is He who satisfies the hungry, Blessed is He who gives drink to the thirsty, Blessed are You... who sustains the world..." – but this should not be said, as it is not part of the blessing's text. Whoever adds, subtracts, and changes from the formula established by the Sages (Tur). Also, what is printed in some siddurim before the blessing, "Blessed is He and Blessed is His Name" – this is an error. Whoever changes from the formula established by the Sages is simply mistaken, even though he fulfills his obligation, as I wrote in Siman 185, Section 8, see there.

In the Sephardic version, there is, before the conclusion: "As it is said: You open Your hand...". The Kol Bo wrote that this is not correct, for how can we bring a verse that David said to support the words of Moses our Teacher? And this is not definitive (Beit Yosef), for we find this several times. The main intent of the Kol Bo is that this is like "a supporting reason" (Drisha), meaning: this is only for the purpose of faith that the Blessed Name sustains the entire world, and since Moses our Teacher established to say "Who sustains the entire world with His goodness...", why do we need proof from David who said "You open Your hand..."? And in my humble opinion, another intention in this addition seems to be that the Blessed Name ingrained in the nature of every living being to be joyful and content with its sustenance, and to reject other food. This is the meaning of "and prepares food for all His creatures which He created," meaning: He has prepared this nature in the living being specifically for its sustenance. And he brings proof for this from what David said: "You open... and satisfy the desire of every living being," meaning: every living being is filled with desire from its sustenance. He brings proof from this verse that this was the intention of Moses our Teacher. (And one should not question this version from the Jerusalem Talmud, first chapter of Berachot, end of Halacha 5, that one does not say a blessing with a verse, see there. For there the intention is after the blessing; and even according to the interpretation of the Chareidim there in the name of R. Eliezer that it refers to before – it is also not applicable here, as it speaks in praise of the Omnipresent. And proof: for even before the Blessing of the Land it concludes with the verse "and you shall eat and be satisfied". And be precise and you will find it light.)

"In favor, kindness, and mercy," and some versions say "in favor, in kindness, and in mercy." It is all the same, as we also find in the Torah that the conjunctive vav (and) is only added at the end, like "with livestock, with silver, and with gold." Our version reads: "and with mercy He gives food to all flesh." Some do not include "He," but rather "and with mercy gives food" (Eliyahu Rabbah). It appears to me that our version is more accurate; the meaning of "favor, kindness, mercy" seems to be that there are three levels among people: there are very wealthy individuals, which corresponds to "in favor," as in "Noah found favor." This means an excess of blessing. Then there are middle-class householders who easily obtain all they need without luxuries. This is "in kindness," where God, blessed be He, bestows His kindness so that one can easily acquire all necessities. Finally, there are the poor whose bread comes with difficulty; this is "in mercy," for mercy is invoked only where the attribute of judgment prevails. After this, we say: "He gives food to all flesh," meaning He gives food to all. However, to one He gives in this measure, and to another in that measure. "For His kindness is everlasting," meaning even for the poor, it is for their benefit, to increase their reward in the World to Come or to atone for their sins or another reason, as stated in Pesachim (118a), see there. Additionally, "gives food to all flesh" includes all creatures besides humans, so it is appropriate to say "He," meaning the One who sustains humans sustains all creations.

"And in His great goodness He has never lacked for us," the ḥet is with a kamatz and the samekh with a pataḥ. "And may He never lack for us," the yod is with a segol and the ḥet with a sheva nach. And some say "He has not lacked for us" with the ḥet in ḥirik, "and may He not lack for us" with the yod in sheva and the ḥet in pataḥ. And the primary version is like the first version (Shlah). "For His great name's sake, for He is a God who sustains and nourishes…"; and some read "for He sustains and nourishes" (see Eliyah Rabbah), "sustains" with food and "nourishes" with other needs. "Sustains and nourishes all, and benefits all" with a cholam, "and prepares food for all…" with a kamatz, for it is adjacent to "His creatures," unlike the previous ones which are separate as is obvious. And some read "and in His great goodness He is always with us…", which is not satisfactory: for indeed "His great goodness" is for the entire world and not only with us. It is more comfortable without "with us," meaning: and in His great goodness which is over the entire world, He has never lacked for us, for we too are included in the whole world. "His creatures" the bet is with a small ḥirik and the resh is nach. And some say the bet is with a sheva and the resh with a ḥirik.

The Tur wrote: If one did not recite the Blessing of "HaZan" but instead said, "Blessed is the Merciful One, the King, Master of this bread" — he has fulfilled his obligation. Thus is his language. And it must be said that his intention was when he said "King of the world," for later in Siman 214, it is established that any blessing that does not include "King of the world" is not a blessing, see there. However, the Tur did not mention this there, and it is possible that he holds that this is not indispensable. Indeed, in the words of our master the Beit Yosef in Section 1, one certainly needs to say so. But the Rashba, of blessed memory, disagrees with this, for although the Blessing of the Meal can be said in any language, in any case, we still require it to follow the form established by the Sages, meaning with an opening and closing of "Blessed." Therefore, if one said, "Blessed is the Merciful One, Master, King of the world, who gives this bread, and by His great goodness always provides for us and will not let us lack, blessed is the Merciful One who sustains all" — he has fulfilled his obligation, and not in any other manner. And this too is considered altering the form established by the Sages. And the opinion of the Tur is puzzling, for it is strained to say that he holds that ex post facto the closing is not indispensable. (And it seems to me that the Tur holds that indeed the Blessing of "HaZan" is a short form. And in the Jerusalem Talmud, Chapter One, Halacha 5, it indeed raises a question about "HaZan" and leaves it unresolved, see there. And it seems that because Moses initially ordained only the Blessing of "HaZan," he therefore ordained it with a closing, and similarly, it resolves there concerning Havdalah, see there. Therefore, even afterwards, it was not nullified, and therefore post facto, one fulfills the obligation without a closing. Examine and you will find this easy.)

The second blessing is the Blessing of the Land, and it does not begin with "Blessed" because it is adjacent to the blessing of "Who sustains." The Tur writes that Rabbi Meir of Rothenburg would say: "We acknowledge You, Lord our God" and not "We acknowledge You," because the latter implies "We acknowledge You and someone else." However, the custom is not like this. Additionally, it is written in the verse, "We will acknowledge You forever; for generations, we will recount Your praise" (Psalms 79:13). This is his language. Nevertheless, we also find phrases like "All Your works will thank You, Lord," "I will thank You for answering me," "You are my God, and I will thank You," and many such phrases in the Psalms. The verse "We will acknowledge You forever" is found only once, and this is the reasoning of Rabbi Meir. In any case, the custom follows the Tur, and there is no strictness in this matter.

In the formula of Birkat Hamazon according to the Rambam: "We thank You... for the inheritance of a desirable, good, and spacious land that You gave to our forefathers, for the covenant and the Torah, and for bringing us out...". The Rosh disagrees with this, for we say "for Your covenant which You sealed in our flesh, and for Your Torah which You taught us," and it is sufficient to mention it once. And so is the custom according to the Rosh. And if one does not mention "covenant" or "Torah" in this blessing, he must repeat it. Rabbi Rema writes that women and slaves should not say "covenant and Torah," for women are not part of the covenant and slaves are not part of the Torah. This is his language. And women are also not in the Torah, but the custom is that women do not skip "covenant and Torah," and the commentators have labored to find a reason for this (see Magen Avraham, subsection 3). Indeed, they are not required to say it, but there is no issue if they do, as the explanation of "covenant and Torah" is written that when Abraham was circumcised, a covenant was made with him, and when the Torah was given, the land was given to them, as it is written: "And He gave them the lands of nations, that they might observe His statutes and keep His laws" (Beit Yosef). Consequently, from that time, women also drew closer to God. Accordingly, when they say "for the inheritance of a desirable land to our forefathers...", they are explaining the reason that this is from the time of the covenant and Torah. And when they say "for Your covenant... and for Your Torah," it refers to all of Israel. (And I found a support for this in the Prisha, see there.)

This blessing includes thanks at the beginning and the end, as we also say at the end, "And for all... we thank You...". If one did not say the thanks at the beginning or the end, one must repeat it (Magen Avraham, subsection 2). Some say "we thank You", but it is better to say "we" as "we" can also imply mourning, as it is written: "and we mourned Pethahiah", "and we the fishermen" (Eliyah Rabbah). We say "that You sustain and provide for us continuously, every day, at every time, and every hour". An "et" is a quarter of a day, six hours (ibid). There are four changing times each day: from morning to midday, from midday to night, and similarly at night (ibid). To me, it seems that "et" is like the term "onah" in the Talmud, which is twelve hours (end of Avodah Zarah [75a]). Additionally, "et" refers to cold and heat, summer and winter (Magen Avraham, ibid). One needs to say "she'atah" with the "shin" having a kamatz gadol, to broaden the aleph (Eliyah Rabbah). On Chanukah and Purim, we say "for the miracles" before "and for all". If one did not say it, one does not need to repeat it. Nevertheless, one can say it within "Harachaman", saying: "The Merciful One will perform miracles and wonders for us, as You did for our ancestors...", and see later in section 682. One should say "in the mouth of all living" and not "in the mouth of all life".

The third blessing is about the rebuilding of Jerusalem, and it was established by David and Solomon: David instituted "for Your people Israel and for Jerusalem..." and Solomon instituted "and for the great and holy house upon which Your name is called." The Tur wrote that this does not mean that they did not bless these until David and Solomon came, for all of them are derived from Scripture. Rather, they fixed the wording according to the additional goodness that came to Israel. Certainly, before the conquest and building of the land, they did not say as after the conquest and building; just as we do not say the wording coined by David and Solomon, for we ask for the restoration... and the rebuilding of the house, while they would ask for the continuation of the peace of the land, the kingdom, and the house. So far his words. The explanation of his words: Before the conquest, they would say "Have mercy on Your people Israel." But Jerusalem, Zion, and the Kingdom of the House of David were not yet in the world, and necessarily they also did not say "and rebuild Jerusalem... builder of Jerusalem," but rather concluded with "Savior of Israel." Similarly, in the blessing of the land, they did not conclude "for the land and for the sustenance" but "He who bequeaths lands and for the sustenance"; and after they conquered the Land of Israel, they concluded "for the land and for the sustenance." After David acquired Jerusalem, he added "and for Jerusalem...". After Solomon built the Temple, he added "and for the great house...". And in the conclusion, they did not say "and rebuild Jerusalem... builder of Jerusalem," but they said "may Your kingdom continue," and concluded with "Savior of Israel." After the destruction, our version was established. (So it seems in my humble opinion. And with this, it is understood why it is said in Berachot 49a: Anyone who concludes "He who bequeaths lands... and Savior of Israel" is an ignoramus, see there. Meaning: Do not say that since they concluded so before, it is still effective now. Pay attention and you will find it easy to understand.)

"Have mercy, O Lord our God" – the letter 'chet' (ח) is pronounced with a tzeire (צירי). Some say "Have mercy, please" and "please" (נא) is a term of request and also means "now," as Rashi explains on the verse "Behold now, I know that you are a beautiful woman...", see there. And one concludes with "Builder of Jerusalem." The Mordechai wrote in the name of the RaM to say "Builder of Jerusalem in His mercy," and so is the custom. For we find the building of Jerusalem mentioned with mercy, as it is written in Jeremiah: "I will have mercy on his dwellings," and in Zechariah: "How long will You not have mercy on Jerusalem," "I have returned to Jerusalem with mercy, My house shall be built in it." Additionally, since we begin with "Have mercy," we also conclude with mercy. According to this, it is understandable why in prayer we do not say this. And even though in the name we say "and to Jerusalem, Your city, return in mercy," it is possible that here the opening word is "Have mercy." Indeed, there are those who dispute this and say only "Builder of Jerusalem." But the majority of the world says "Builder of Jerusalem in His mercy."

And respond "Amen" after "Boneh Yerushalayim." Even though one does not respond "Amen" after one's own blessing, here, since it is the conclusion of the biblical blessings, one responds, as "HaTov VeHaMeitiv" is not from the Torah. According to the Talmud, at the conclusion of all kinds of blessings, one must respond "Amen" to one's own blessings to indicate that they are finished (Tosafot Yeshanim at the beginning of the seventh chapter). However, the people did not adopt this practice (Tosafot 45b, s.v. "Ha BeBoneh"), except in Birkat HaMazon at "Boneh Yerushalayim" at the conclusion of the Torah blessings. Therefore, this "Amen" should be said quietly, so that people do not realize that the blessing of "HaTov VeHaMeitiv" is not from the Torah and come to disrespect it. This is the law according to the Talmud (45b). However, people are not careful about this and respond loudly. It is written that nowadays there is no concern for disrespect (Beit Yosef and Magen Avraham, subsection 1). Nevertheless, it is certainly more correct to be meticulous and follow the Talmudic law, and to say it quietly.

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote in section 2, and this is his language: "It appears that it is specifically when one blesses alone and others do not answer 'Amen' after other blessings. But when there is a zimun, they answer 'Amen' as they do after other blessings. And even though the one who blesses also answers, in any case, it is not so noticeable since others also answer with him. And so is the custom in these lands, to say it aloud even the one who blesses himself when there is a zimun. And perhaps it is for this reason." This is the end of his language. And besides the fact that his reasoning is strained, in any case, according to his words, when one blesses without a zimun, he should say it quietly, and indeed the custom is not so. And it seems more reasonable to say: since in the Gemara we find that one sage responded aloud and another responded quietly, the world understands that there is no strictness in this, and each one can do as he wishes. And even though according to the reasons mentioned there, there should be a distinction between times, as Tosafot and the Rosh wrote, see there— the world understands that it is not so, and in practice, there is no strictness in this (see Taz, small section 1). And so it appears from the Rambam, who did not mention this law at all. And the Rif also did not bring this at all, because there is no strictness (Taz there).

It is stated in the Gemara (Berachot 48a) that anyone who does not mention "the kingdom of the House of David" in the blessing of "Boneh Yerushalayim" (Builder of Jerusalem) has not fulfilled his obligation. This is why we say, "Have mercy… and upon the kingdom of the House of David, Your anointed." If one did not say this, they must repeat the blessing. We do not say that since prior to the kingdom of the House of David it was not said, as I wrote in section 1, therefore now it is also not essential; it is not so, as I wrote there. One should not mention the kingdom of Heaven at all in this blessing, so as not to equate it with the kingdom of flesh and blood. Therefore, one must be careful not to say, "and upon Your kingdom and the kingdom of the House of David, Your anointed," and anyone who does so should be rebuked. Hence, we say there "Our God, our Father, our Shepherd, our Sustainer…" and one should not say "our King" for the reason explained. In sum: in this blessing, since one is obligated to mention "the kingdom of the House of David," they must be careful not to mention the kingdom of Heaven here at all. (And Maimonides wrote (Chapter 2) the reason: to indicate that we have no complete consolation except with the return of the kingdom of the House of David, see there. And see at the end of section 7).

They say "re'inu zonenu"; "re'inu" with a sheva under the resh, "zonenu" with a shuruk under the zayin. This is a language of prayer, as if to say: "May it be Your will to shepherd us and sustain us." And even on Shabbat one can say this. And although there are no supplications on Shabbat, nevertheless, this is the format of the blessings. This is also explicitly stated in the Jerusalem Talmud. And they say: "For only from Your full, open, holy, and expansive hand, so that we will not be ashamed or humiliated forever and ever." And some also say "and not stumble." And there are siddurim where instead of "the holy" it is written "the abundant," meaning: a language of abundance, as if to say, giving with a full hand and abundance. And it concludes with "the builder of Jerusalem" or "the builder of Jerusalem in His mercy," as has been explained. And some say "the builder of Jerusalem in His mercy" (Magen Avraham, Siman 3). And one of the great rabbis would conclude: "Blessed is the Lord, the God of David, and the builder of Jerusalem" (ibid). And some conclude: "The comforter of Zion with the building of Jerusalem." And there are those who do not begin this blessing with "Have mercy" but with "Console us" on Shabbat and festivals. Their reasoning is that "Have mercy" is a language of supplication, and one does not say supplications on Shabbat and festivals. But it is not so, for "Console us" is also a language of supplication, and they are the same; and this is the format of the blessings, and it is permitted to say them on Shabbat and festivals. This is also the custom (Tosafot, Berachot 58b, s.v. "starts," see there). And the Rambam in the second chapter also wrote that on both Shabbat and weekdays one can begin with either "Have mercy" or "Console us," see there.

On Shabbat, one says before "U'vneh" (in Birkat Hamazon): "Retzei Ve'hachalitzenu...U'v'ratzoncha Haniach Lanu..." The word "Haniach" should be pronounced with a kamatz under the hey and a chirik under the nun, and not "hanach lanu" with patachs, because the latter is not a prayer but a narrative, indicating that the Holy One, Blessed be He, has given us rest on Shabbat, that there should be no distress, sorrow, or sighing on Shabbat. This means that mourning is not observed on Shabbat, and no worries should be mentioned on Shabbat, as it is written: "And you shall call the Shabbat a delight." And when we say "V'harenu Hashem Elokeinu b'nechamot Tzion..." it is not a prayer or request but rather words of comfort, similar to what we say in the Shabbat prayer: "May our eyes behold..."

On a festival and Rosh Chodesh, one says: "Ya'aleh V'yavo." When these days fall on Shabbat, "Retzei" is recited first followed by "Ya'aleh V'yavo," because Shabbat, in relation to the festival and Rosh Chodesh, is more frequent and more sanctified. It seems to me that if one said "Ya'aleh V'yavo" first and then "Retzei," he does not need to repeat it, because the order of frequency and sanctity does not invalidate it post facto, as proven in Zevachim (91a). One does not mention Shabbat in "Ya'aleh V'yavo." Even according to the opinion mentioned later in Siman 487, that in the morning prayer on a festival, Shabbat is mentioned in "Ya'aleh V'yavo," see there – this is because the Shabbat matter has not yet concluded, as one will subsequently say "V'hasi'enu" and conclude with Shabbat. This is not the case with Birkat Hamazon, where Shabbat is already concluded with "Retzei Ve'hachalitzenu." Similarly, on a Rosh Chodesh that falls on Shabbat, Shabbat is not mentioned in "Ya'aleh V'yavo" during the morning prayer, because Shabbat has already been concluded, as explained in Siman 425, see there. Likewise, the festival and Rosh Chodesh are not mentioned in "Retzei Ve'hachalitzenu."

(One should not conclude "Ya'aleh V'yavo" with "for You are a gracious and compassionate King" but rather "for You are gracious..." for the reason explained in section 5, that one should not mention the Kingdom of Heaven together with the kingdom of flesh and blood. The Rema writes in section 3 that this is proper, but it is not the custom. Thus far are his words. It is written that since this is distant from the mention of the House of David, it is not a concern. The Levush does not bring this, see there. In our times, many follow the Rema. See Taz and Magen Avraham section 2.)

In the Gemara (48b), there is a dispute regarding whether one who mentioned "Retzeh VeHachalitzenu" on Shabbat in another blessing besides the blessing of "Boneh Yerushalayim" has fulfilled his obligation or not. The Tanna Kamma and the Sages disagree: the Tanna Kamma holds that he has fulfilled his obligation, while the Sages hold that he has not. See there. The Rif, Rambam, and Rosh did not mention this at all, nor did the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, and I do not know why. Regarding the law, it seems that the halacha follows the Sages, that he has not fulfilled his obligation (Magen Avraham, subsection 5). There is proof for this from what will be explained: if one forgot the special Shabbat mention and started "HaTov VeHaMeitiv," he must return to the beginning. If it were to be thought that mentioning it in "Boneh Yerushalayim" is not indispensable after the fact, then he could mention it there, as mentioning it separately is no worse than mentioning it in another blessing. Therefore, it is certain that even after the fact, it is indispensable, as the Sages say. Perhaps because of this, our Rabbis omitted it, since they explained the law of "if he forgot..." they did not need to mention this as well.

Regarding the main laws of Birkat Hamazon (Grace After Meals), if one recited a later blessing before an earlier one, for instance, if one recited the blessing for the Land before the blessing "Who sustains," or "Who builds Jerusalem" before the blessing for the Land, it is uncertain whether he has fulfilled his obligation or not. It appears to me that he has fulfilled his obligation. The proof: at the beginning of the second chapter of Megillah, it is taught: if one reads out of order, he has not fulfilled his obligation. And it is taught in a Baraita: the same applies to Hallel, the reading of Shema, and prayer. See there. And from the fact that Birkat Hamazon is not mentioned – we infer that the order does not prevent one from fulfilling the obligation in Birkat Hamazon. Moreover, in Berachot (48b), we derive the order of Birkat Hamazon from the verse "and you shall bless" – this refers to the blessing for sustenance, "the Lord your God" – this refers to the blessing of invitation (Zimun), and indeed Zimun precedes the blessing for sustenance? Thus, it is certain that the order does not prevent one from fulfilling the obligation, and therefore, although Zimun certainly precedes, they placed "Who sustains" before Zimun to indicate that the order does not prevent the obligation (this is how it seems in my humble opinion).

If one made a mistake and did not mention the Shabbat until he finished "Boneh Yerushalayim" and has not yet begun the blessing of "Hatov V'Hametiv," he should say: "Blessed are You, Hashem, our God, King of the universe, who has given Shabbats for rest to His people Israel with love, as a sign and a covenant. Blessed are You, Hashem, who sanctifies the Shabbat." This is the ruling of the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, Section 6. This also appears to be the implication of the Rambam's words at the end of the second chapter, where he writes: If one forgot and did not mention the sanctity of the day on Shabbat or a festival, if he remembers before beginning the fourth blessing on Shabbat, he says: "Blessed is Hashem who has given rest… Blessed…" up to here is his wording. And even though he did not mention "our God, King of the universe," nevertheless his intention is such since he mentioned Hashem (as also written by the Lechem Mishneh).

And behold, in the Gemara (49a) it is stated: If one made a mistake and did not mention Shabbat, he says: "Blessed is He Who gave Shabbats…". See there. It is possible to say that the intention is without mentioning God's name and sovereignty, and so wrote the Tur in the name of the Raavad because it is not a fixed blessing, similar to the case of the zimmun, even though it is from the Torah, it does not include God's name and sovereignty; because it is not fixed, for when there are not three who ate - there is no need for zimmun. But Rambam, the Tur, and the Shulchan Aruch hold that without mentioning God's name and sovereignty, it is nothing. And one should not ask: In the main part of "Retzei VeHachalitzenu" there is no mention of God's name and sovereignty, so how in the case of forgetfulness would there be God's name and sovereignty in its place? It is not so, for in "Retzei VeHachalitzenu" there is God's name and sovereignty since it is included in "Boneh Yerushalayim", which is adjacent to the Blessing of the Land, and the Blessing of the Land is adjacent to "HaZan" and in "HaZan" there is God's name and sovereignty, and it is as if in "Boneh Yerushalayim" there is God's name and sovereignty; and it also concludes with "Blessed". Therefore, in the case of forgetfulness, where a blessing is required in its place - it also needs God's name and sovereignty, and it also concludes with "Blessed", even though it is short, since it comes in place of a long blessing (this seems to me). And one who does not know this version – returns to the beginning (Taz, section 4).

And so too on Yom Tov: If one made a mistake and did not mention "Ya'aleh V'Yavo," he says: "Blessed are You..., Who has given festive days to His people Israel for joy and for gladness, this day of [specific festival]. Blessed are You, Hashem, Who sanctifies Israel and the seasons." And if Yom Tov falls on Shabbat, he says: "Blessed are You... Who has given Shabbats for rest to His people Israel with love, as a sign and as a covenant, and festive days for joy and for gladness, this day of [specific festival]. Blessed are You, Hashem, Who sanctifies the Shabbat, Israel, and the seasons."

And all this applies if he remembers before beginning the blessing of "Hatov VehaMeitiv." But after he has begun "Hatov VehaMeitiv," this blessing does not help, and he must return to the beginning of Birkat Hamazon, which is the blessing of "HaZan." It is not sufficient to return to the blessing of "Boneh Yerushalayim," because all three blessings are considered as one, just like in the prayer where the first three blessings are considered as one. And so ruled the Rambam there. Therefore, despite the fact that in the "Ya'aleh Veyavo" of the prayer on Rosh Chodesh, if one is accustomed to say supplications after his prayer, he returns to "Retzeh" and not to the beginning of the prayer, as I wrote in Siman 422, and if so, here too the blessing of "Hatov VehaMeitiv" is not inferior, even though he began it with supplications, and we are also accustomed to say "Harachaman," which is like supplications, and he should have returned only to the beginning of the blessing of "Boneh Yerushalayim." And indeed, this is the opinion of the Raavad there, see there. Nevertheless, we do not hold this way, because all three blessings are considered as one, like the first three and last three blessings of the prayer which are considered as one regarding interruptions, as I wrote in Siman 104, see there. And here too, it is the same.

Nevertheless, we have a significant question in this matter: since the Talmud there compares it to prayer, then just as in "Ya'aleh V'Yavo" of the prayer, if one remembers before "Modim" they say "Ya'aleh V'Yavo" before "Modim," as I wrote in Siman 622; and if so, here too on a festival: if one remembers before "HaTov V'HaMeitiv," why did they establish a separate blessing? Let them say "Ya'aleh V'Yavo" there, just like in prayer. Similarly, on Shabbat, let them say "R’tzei V’Hachlitzeinu" there. And it seems to me the reason for this is: it is certainly not a proper rectification to say "Ya'aleh V'Yavo" or "R’tzei V’Hachlitzeinu" there, for they were established within the blessing and have the status of "with God's name and sovereignty," as I wrote, and after the blessing, it is not with God's name and sovereignty. Therefore, they established a blessing with God's name and sovereignty as per the essence of the law. But in prayer, they could not do this, for if they did, there would be four blessings in the last three, and they only established three blessings. Therefore, they sufficed with saying "Ya'aleh V'Yavo" immediately after the blessing, and it is as if it was said within the blessing since another one has not yet begun. But in the Grace After Meals, it does not appear as an addition, for the biblical blessings have already been completed and it is a different matter. Additionally, one can say that since the Grace After Meals is from the Torah, and it is written: "And you shall bless the Lord your God" – they were concerned to establish the matter as it was instituted and did not worry about the concern of a blessing in vain; for everything is included in "And you shall bless the Lord your God," as this too is a blessing. This is not the case with the prayer, which is rabbinic; they did not want to add another blessing and were concerned about a blessing in vain, and thus established that it be said after the blessing.

And this applies to Shabbat and Yom Tov, where there is an obligation to eat bread, and their mention is obligatory. But on Rosh Chodesh and Chol HaMoed, even though it is forbidden to fast on them, nevertheless, there is no obligation to eat bread specifically, and their mention is not mandatory. Therefore, if one forgot to say "Ya'aleh Veyavo" in Birkat Hamazon and did not remember until after starting "HaTov VeHaMeitiv," one does not go back at all. This is not comparable to prayer, where one must go back, because prayer is an obligation, whereas mentioning it in Birkat Hamazon is not a complete obligation; since one could exempt oneself from it by not eating bread. Therefore, even though Birkat Hamazon itself is obligatory, its mention is not. See what I have written in Siman 429, Section 3.

And this is when he has already begun "HaTov VeHaMeitiv." But if he has not yet begun, it is said in the Gemara there: If he made a mistake and did not mention Rosh Chodesh, he says, "Blessed is He who has given new months to His people Israel for remembrance..." And I do not know if he concludes with a blessing or not, see there. The Rif and the Rambam ruled that he does not conclude with a blessing, since it remains in doubt in the Gemara, and so ruled Rabbeinu the Beit Yosef in section 7. And it seems clear from the fact that the conclusion is in doubt in the Gemara, we infer that the opening is certainly with a blessing and sovereignty. For if not, what relevance is there to doubt in the conclusion, for if there is no opening, there is no conclusion? And so wrote the Levush that he opens "Blessed are You, Lord, our God, King of the universe, who has given new months..."

And what is not mentioned in the Gemara about a blessing and sovereignty in the opening is because even on Shabbat and Yom Tov it is not mentioned. But from the Rambam, who mentioned it on Shabbat and Yom Tov and did not mention it on Rosh Chodesh, as well as the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch who mentioned it on Shabbat and Yom Tov but not on Rosh Chodesh, it seems that there is no need for a blessing and sovereignty even in the opening. However, in our version of the Rambam, it is also not found even on Yom Tov, see there. And necessarily, he relied on Shabbat; if so, one can say the same for Rosh Chodesh. But from the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch, there is proof; and perhaps they also did not bother to mention it on Rosh Chodesh, relying on the previous context.

However, the main point is perplexing: how can we establish a blessing with a name and sovereignty on something that is not mandatory? And I am astonished at the commentators on the Shulchan Aruch who did not address this (and the Eliyah Rabbah raised this issue, see there). And there are some of the greats who followed the Levush (the Gra and the Chayei Adam). In my humble opinion, it is proper to rely on the Raavad, who held that even on Shabbat and Yom Tov one should not bless with a name, as I wrote in section 11, and rely on him at least on Rosh Chodesh, especially since from the language of the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch it explicitly implies this. (And some of the poskim hold that Rosh Chodesh is like Shabbat and Yom Tov, as explained in Beit Yosef. But this is not our established ruling, and in cases of doubt regarding blessings, we are lenient.)

On Chanukah and Purim, if one forgets "Al HaNisim" (the section of prayer for miracles), he is not required to repeat the prayer, as is the case in the Amidah prayer. Nevertheless, it is appropriate to say in the "Harachaman" section: "May He perform miracles and wonders for us, as He did for our forefathers in those days...". Similarly, on Rosh Chodesh (the new month) and Chol HaMoed (intermediate days of festivals), our master the Rema wrote that it is possible to say it within the other "Harachaman" sections, just like with "Al HaNisim". Perhaps a distinction can be made because "Ya'aleh V'Yavo" (another prayer section) includes mention of divine names, and it should not be said in vain. This seems correct to me, and this is the custom. End of his words. And it requires investigation, for we say supplications throughout the day and they include mention of divine names, so why should this be different from other supplications (Magen Avraham, subsection 11)? It is possible that when it is said as an obligation, it is different because it is not said as a supplication. Know that on Rosh Chodesh there is no difference between night and day, even though regarding prayer there is a difference because we do not sanctify the new month at night; in prayer, it is not mentioned at night to avoid interrupting the prayer, but in the Grace After Meals, the blessings of the Torah have already been completed, and therefore, if one has not started "Hatov V'Hameitiv" (the fourth blessing), he says "Blessed" as explained (the Gra).

If Rosh Chodesh falls on Shabbat, and one forgets to mention Rosh Chodesh but does mention Shabbat, the Mordechai's opinion is that one does not need to repeat the prayer if they have begun "Hatov Vehametiv". Even though today one is required to eat bread, nevertheless, due to Rosh Chodesh they are not obligated to repeat the prayer, since the obligation is because of Shabbat, and they have mentioned Shabbat. However, the Rashba ruled that one must repeat, because since on this day one is required to eat bread, the obligation also applies to Rosh Chodesh on this day; as we say in the Ne'ilah prayer on Yom Kippur that falls on Shabbat, one is required to mention Shabbat even though on Shabbat there is no Ne'ilah, nevertheless, since on this day one is obligated in the Ne'ilah prayer, the obligation of Shabbat also applies. Here too, the same principle applies. The Tur also brings both opinions, see there, as he tends towards the obligation to repeat. But our teacher, the Beit Yosef, in section 7 ruled like the Mordechai that one does not repeat, and follows his reasoning in Siman 623 regarding Ne'ilah when one forgets Shabbat. There too, there is a disagreement whether one repeats or not, and he ruled there that one does not repeat, see there. And the halacha is that in cases of doubt regarding blessings, we are lenient.

And this is when one forgot only [the mention] of Rosh Chodesh. But if one forgot also [the mention] of Shabbat, if one remembers before beginning "HaTov VeHaMeitiv," one includes both and says: "Who has given Sabbaths for rest, and New Moons for remembrance," and concludes "Who sanctifies the Shabbat and Israel and the New Moons." And our teacher the Beit Yosef in section 7 wrote that there are those who say that in such a case one concludes with the blessing of Shabbat and does not conclude with the blessing of Rosh Chodesh, see there. And his reasoning is because on Rosh Chodesh it is without a conclusion as I have written. And it is very puzzling: for on Rosh Chodesh it was a doubt in the Gemara as I have written. But here where one mentions the Name for Shabbat, if so, why not conclude also for Rosh Chodesh? Therefore, there is no basis for this opinion (Magen Avraham section 14), and one concludes also for Rosh Chodesh. And it is obvious that if one began "HaTov VeHaMeitiv" one needs to return to the beginning, mentioning both Shabbat and Rosh Chodesh.

And know that since the reason has been clarified that on Shabbat and Yom Tov one needs to repeat [the blessing] because there is an obligation to eat bread on Shabbat and Yom Tov, it follows that if one eats an additional meal, such as eating a fourth meal on Shabbat, and on Yom Tov the obligation is one meal during the day and one at night, as is customary, if one eats a third meal, there is no need to repeat [the blessing] because there is no obligation for this meal. Furthermore, our teacher the Beit Yosef wrote in section 8 that the third meal on Shabbat is like Rosh Chodesh. This is his language. And his reasoning: since there are those who say that one fulfills the obligation with various kinds of delicacies, as I wrote in Siman 291, therefore there is no obligation to eat bread, even though everyone agrees that ideally there is an obligation to eat bread, as I wrote there. And indeed, there are those who disagree regarding the third meal on Shabbat and ruled that one must repeat [the blessing] like for other meals; this is the opinion of the Rambam who ruled in the 30th chapter of Shabbat that one is obligated to eat bread in the third meal; and consequently, what he ruled that on Shabbat one must repeat from the beginning – this applies also to the third meal. For so wrote the Tur at the end of this Siman, that according to the one who obligates eating bread – one must repeat. And many of our Rabbis hold this view. And therefore, although our teacher the Beit Yosef ruled simply that one does not need to repeat due to doubt, obviously, but anyone who accepted upon himself the obligation to eat three meals – certainly must repeat, because he holds that it is a legal obligation to eat. (And there is proof for this from Baal HaMaor who was brought by the Rosh at the beginning of the chapter "Tefillat HaShachar". And even according to the Rosh who rejected this, it is not comparable to this case as I wrote. And also from the Gra in section 20 it seems to me so, and this is how one should rule in my humble opinion. And pay attention and you will find it easy.)

And behold, even on Yom Tov there is a dispute whether one is obligated to eat bread. The Tosafot in Sukkah (26a) hold that there is no obligation to eat bread on Yom Tov except on the first night of Pesach and Sukkot. Indeed, they wrote that if one made a mistake and did not mention Yom Tov in the Grace After Meals, he does not need to repeat it. And that which we say that on Shabbat and Yom Tov it is not sufficient without eating — this applies to the night... thus is their language. The Rosh in the seventh chapter of Berachot (Siman 26) brings a dispute regarding this, and it seems that his opinion leans towards the obligation to eat bread on every Yom Tov. This also appears to be the opinion of the Tur and Shulchan Aruch in this siman, who wrote simply that Yom Tov is like Shabbat. And it is explicitly explained that this refers to every Yom Tov. This also seems to be the opinion of the Rif and Rambam, and this is how we rule. Even on Rosh Hashanah it seems that one needs to repeat; although there are those who hold that it is permissible to fast on Rosh Hashanah — we do not hold this way (see Magen Avraham, small section 7). And know that in all these cases where we said one does not need to go back to the beginning — this is when he started "HaTov VeHaMetiv". But if he has not yet started, he should say "Blessed...," as it is no less than Rosh Chodesh (there, small section 16).

Our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 9: "Three who ate on Shabbat or Yom Tov, and forgot to mention the special addition for the occasion, and they need to go back to the beginning of Birkat Hamazon – each one should bless by himself; because they have already fulfilled the obligation of Zimun." These are his words. This means: even though it is as if they did not say any of the blessings, since they need to go back and bless, nevertheless, they have already fulfilled the obligation of Zimun. The proof: they only go back to the blessing of 'Ha-Zan' and not to the Zimun blessing. The reason: the Zimun blessing is considered a separate blessing, as it is only recited when eating with a Zimun.

Additionally, it is written in section 10: If one was eating and Shabbat ended – they mention Shabbat in the Grace After Meals (Birkat Hamazon), because we follow the beginning of the meal. The same applies to Rosh Chodesh, Purim, and Chanukah. Thus far his words. The commentators on the Shulchan Aruch have elaborated on this. The main ruling is according to our teacher, the Beit Yosef, that we only follow the beginning of the meal. Therefore, if Rosh Chodesh falls on Motzei Shabbat, one does not mention Rosh Chodesh. However, if one prayed Maariv before Birkat Hamazon, it is impossible to mention Shabbat: because since one has already considered it a weekday in prayer, how can one mention Shabbat? That would be a contradiction. The same applies to Rosh Chodesh, Chanukah, and Purim. Similarly, if one recited Havdalah, or said "Hamavdil bein kodesh lechol", one does not mention Shabbat. Conversely, if one was eating during the day and continued eating into the night, and at night it was Rosh Chodesh, and before Birkat Hamazon one prayed Maariv, one is compelled to mention "Ya'aleh V'yavo" in Birkat Hamazon, because one has already considered it Rosh Chodesh in prayer. This is not because we follow the end of the meal, but because one is compelled to make this mention obligatory. The same applies in similar cases. There is no difference whether one ate bread at night or not, the main point is the beginning of the meal. (The Taz and the Eliyah Rabbah's opinion is also to follow the end of the meal, but this is not the opinion of the Bach and the Magen Avraham. The Magen Avraham's opinion is that if one ate bread at night, one must mention the night, see there. It is explicitly proven that this is not so. All their difficulty arises because of the Baraita in Pesachim 102a where they were reclining and the day sanctified itself upon them, Rabbi Yossi holds the first one says Birkat Hamazon and the second one says the sanctification of the day. And it is taught in the Tosefta that one mentions Shabbat in Birkat Hamazon, as the Rosh wrote in his responsa, section 22. In my humble opinion, there is no difficulty at all, because there, since by the letter of the law one needs to say the sanctification of the day on that cup, as the Gemara in Pesachim questions Rabbi Yossi: "Let him say both over one cup", and answers that we do not make bundles [of mitzvot], see there. However, the obligation is upon him in any case to sanctify immediately, and it is as if the Kiddush is ready and standing, so how can one not mention Shabbat? But in all other meals, we only follow the beginning. This is the main ruling.)

The fourth blessing, "HaTov VeHaMeitiv" (Who is good and bestows good), is not from the Torah. Rather, the Sages instituted it after the war of Beitar. After the conquest of Beitar and the multitude of casualties, it is said in the Jerusalem Talmud, Taanit, Chapter 4, Halacha 5, and in the Midrash Eicha on the verse "The Lord has swallowed up…", that Hadrian had a large vineyard measuring eighteen by eighteen mil. It was surrounded by the slain of Beitar, stacked full height, and they were not given burial until another king arose and allowed them to be buried. It is stated that when Beitar was destroyed, the horn of Israel was cut off, and it will not return until the coming of the Messiah. Therefore, this blessing was established next to "Boneh Yerushalayim" (Who rebuilds Jerusalem) as if to say: May it be Your will that the horn of Israel be restored with the coming of the son of David, which is the rebuilding of Jerusalem (Rosh). It seems to me that the reason they did not establish it in the prayer next to the blessing "Boneh Yerushalayim" is because there it is in the middle of the prayer; unlike in the Grace After Meals where it is after the conclusion of the blessings. Additionally, in Gittin (57a), it is said that "He has cut down in fierce anger all the horn of Israel" refers to the slain of Beitar. This is as I have written, that then the horn of Israel was cut off. And in the prayer, we say after "Boneh Yerushalayim": "And may our horn be exalted with Your salvation," which is not the case in the Grace After Meals.

Furthermore, the essence of this blessing is more appropriately connected to the Grace After Meals (Birkat Hamazon). For so the Sages said there: At the time when the slain of Beitar were given burial, they instituted in Yavneh the blessing of "HaTov VeHaMeitiv" ("He who is good and bestows good"). "HaTov" ("the good") because they did not decompose, and "HaMeitiv" ("and bestows good") because they were given burial. This teaches us that even at the time of the Holy One, blessed be He’s anger towards us, He performs miracles and wonders for us. For there are no greater miracles than those of the slain of Beitar, who lay for many years on the ground and did not decompose, and afterward were given burial.
