This is a sign that the Holy One, blessed be He, will never abandon us, even when we sin before Him, as it is written: "The Lord has chastened me sorely, but He has not given me over to death." And, because the principal affliction is poverty, as Job said: "With all this, I have chosen my poverty"; and as our Sages said (Bava Batra 116a): Poverty is harder to bear than fifty lashes. Therefore, so that we should not worry that, Heaven forbid, we will be lacking bread, they instituted the blessing of "HaTov VeHaMeitiv," and as it is instituted in this blessing: "He who has done good, He who will do good […] and may we never lack all good." Therefore, this is appropriate only for the Grace After Meals (so it seems to me).

This blessing begins with "Baruch" (Blessed), as it is not adjacent to its companion because it was established independently for a different matter, as I have written. And it does not conclude with "Baruch" because it is considered a short blessing: initially, it was only established to say "Blessed is the One Who is good and does good," and later, three kindnesses and three goodnesses were added to it, as will be explained (Tur). Furthermore, they did not want to make it superior to the blessings of the Torah that precede it (Rashba), meaning: the blessing of the land and "Builder of Jerusalem" have a conclusion without an opening, and therefore here, where there is an opening, there is no conclusion. Additionally, in truth, all the matters in this blessing are all one matter, and it is one format with different words describing the Almighty's goodness to us, and its status is like a short blessing where the intention is a single matter (Tosafot R"Y).

And our sages of blessed memory said (Berachot 49a) that three mentions of kingship are required, meaning: one for itself like all the blessings, where we say "King of the universe." And one for "Builder of Jerusalem," as we wrote in the previous section that it was impossible to mention kingship there due to the kingship of the House of David, so they added another mention of kingship here for it; and this is what we say: "God our Father, our King, our Creator." And since they established this for "Builder of Jerusalem," they also established it for the blessing of the land, and this is what we say: "The good King who does good to all." But for the blessing of sustenance, it is not necessary, as it already contains "King of the universe," since it begins with "Blessed."

And our Rabbis have written, based on the Midrash, that since we say three [mentions of] kingship in it, we also say three [mentions of] goodness, which are: "He has done good, He does good, He will do good for us"; and three [mentions of] recompense: "He has recompensed us, He recompenses us, He will recompense us...". And Rambam did not mention any of this, only the three kingships, see there in the second chapter, and also in his version of the Grace after Meals it is not mentioned. According to his version, it is indeed a short blessing, see there. The matter of the three goodnesses and recompenses pertains to the past, present, and future, and our version is well-known in the prayer books. And there are those who recite: "In every goodness for us He has done good for us, He does good for us, He will do good for us." And there are those who recite: "He has done good, does good, will do good." And the primary version is according to our text. And we say "that every day He has done good...". And some object to the version "that every day," rather they should say "in every day" (Magen Avraham, section 1). This wording is not convenient at all (Taz, section 2). The explanation is: that every day it is so, as we first say "the good King who does good to all," meaning that every day "He has done good...".

The mourner adds in this blessing: "The Almighty, our Father, our King... the Holy One of Jacob, the living King who is good and bestows good, the True God, the True Judge, the Righteous Judge, who takes souls in justice, and who rules in His world to do as He wishes, for all His ways are just; and we are His servants and His people, and we are obligated to thank Him and bless Him for everything. He who repairs breaches, may He repair this breach from upon us for life, peace, and all good." And the rest of those present also say this blessing, and they add, "from upon us and from upon this mourner for life and peace..." And it is explained in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 379, see there. It is also explained there whether this is said on Shabbat, see there.

The end of the blessing is "may we never lack," and there one should answer "Amen." The "HaRachaman" that we say is not part of the blessing; rather, it is an additional supplication, similar to the prayers said after the Amidah. And this is the language of the Tur: My brother Rabbi Yechiel z"l wrote: It is customary to extend the blessing of "HaTov VeHaMetiv" with "HaRachaman" in various ways, and I do not know where this practice of increasing requests between Birkat HaMazon and the blessing over the wine (when blessing over the cup) comes from. It is possible that they adopted this practice from what was said: the guest blesses. This is the end of his language. And it seems to me that there is no interruption here. We find a greater example in the blessing of the circumcision, where prayers are said for the child…, and this interrupts between the blessing and the drinking. This is the end of the Tur's language. At any rate, it is important to correct the misconception among the masses who think that "HaRachaman" is part of Birkat HaMazon, and they answer "Amen" after "HaRachaman" and not after "may we never lack"; this is a significant error, and they need to be informed. The guest blesses the host (Moed Katan 41), and the wording of the blessing will be clarified in Siman 241. It concludes with "and say Amen." On weekdays, one says "Magdil," and on Shabbat, Yom Tov, and Rosh Chodesh, one says "Migdol," as it is written in Samuel. There is a reason for this. (And know that all the letters are present in Birkat HaMazon except for the letter 'Peh,' because one who blesses Birkat HaMazon with intention is not affected by anger, rage, or wrath, and his sustenance is provided for him with honor all his days. So it is written in Ateret Zekenim in Siman 185 in the name of Sefer HaChinuch and Sefer HaGan, see there.)

After completing the Grace After Meals, one should bless "Borei Pri HaGafen" if blessing over a cup. There is an opinion that one should say "Savri Maranan" (see Taz), but this is not the custom. This seems correct, for everyone is prepared to listen at the conclusion of the Grace After Meals which everyone has recited. One should not question: Why is it that for Kiddush and Havdalah, the blessing over "Borei Pri HaGafen" precedes the other blessings, while in the Grace After Meals it follows? It is not the same, for Kiddush and Havdalah are the beginning of the matter, and the cup's blessing precedes the other blessings, and it is not an interruption as it pertains to the matter. But the Grace After Meals is the conclusion of the meal and the removal from the meal, and the cup is a matter in itself; if one were to bless before the Grace After Meals, the Grace After Meals would be an interruption. (See Magen Avraham. And what he wrote about the cup at weddings – because of "Lo Plug" (we do not differentiate), the Beit Shmuel in Even HaEzer, Siman 62, wrote a different reason: that if they were to bless "Borei Pri HaGafen" before the seven blessings, it would appear that the blessing is only for the Grace After Meals, see there.)

After the blessing of "Borei Pri HaGafen," the one reciting the blessing should taste [the wine]. It is a mitzvah to take a substantial sip, due to the love of the mitzvah. There is no obligation for the others present to taste from the cup, since the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch ruled in Section 4 that if the one reciting the blessing does not want to taste, one of those present should taste, as noted there; and all the more so, the tasting of the one reciting the blessing suffices. However, if others come to taste, they should not taste before the one reciting the blessing, whether they drink from his cup or pour from his cup into their own cups. But if each has their own cup of wine, they may taste before the one reciting the blessing. If each has their own cup of wine but they are blemished, the one reciting the blessing must pour a little from his cup into theirs. Some say this is not necessary, as a blemished cup is only invalid for the one reciting the blessing. This has already been clarified in Siman 181, see there. 

One should not question the first opinion: How can there be invalidity in blemished cups, given that there is no necessity for those present to drink, as I have written? This is not difficult at all: Certainly, if they do not drink at all, there is no issue. But if they drink, they must drink from unblemished cups, since the designation of "the cup of Birkat Hamazon" applies to them. 

If the one reciting the blessing interrupts between the blessing and the drinking, he must return and bless again, as will be explained in Siman 271, see there. It is obvious that if he drank the required amount, as will be explained, he must recite a concluding blessing. However, if he intends to drink more, he should bless after he finishes drinking. If he has recited the concluding blessing and wants to drink more, he must recite the initial blessing again. 

There is one opinion that if he originally intended to drink more, he does not need another blessing if he intended to drink immediately (Magen Avraham, Section 3). This is a surprising view, since he has already recited the concluding blessing (and the Eliyah Rabbah did not agree with his words, see there).

The Tur and the Shulchan Aruch wrote in section 3: The measure of drinking to be obligated in an after-blessing is uncertain whether an olive's volume (k'zayit) suffices or if a quarter-log (r'vi'it) is required. Therefore, one should be careful to drink either less than an olive's volume or a quarter-log to avoid the doubt. However, here it is impossible to drink less than an olive's volume, because anything that requires a cup – one must drink from it a cheekful, which is the majority of a quarter-log. Therefore, he should drink a full quarter-log. Thus far his words. 

Explanation of the matter: Behold, the Rambam in the third chapter ruled that for an after-blessing on wine or other beverages, a quarter-log is required, and the measure of drinking a cup of blessing he did not clarify. But since he explained in the twenty-ninth chapter of Shabbat that for Kiddush a cheekful is needed, and this is also stated in Pesachim (107a), it follows that every cup of blessing is the same. And in this, no one has ever disagreed. And "cheekful" is less than a quarter-log, for this is a cheekful: anything that, when moved to one side, appears as a cheekful, like in the matter of Yom Kippur. And if so, consequently, according to this, when one drinks a cheekful – he does not need an after-blessing.

However, our rabbis, the Tosafists in Yoma (79a) and Sukkah (26b), and the Rosh in the chapter "Three Who Ate" (siman 24), were uncertain about the obligation of the after-blessing: perhaps it suffices with an olive's bulk (kezayit) like eating. And this is less than a cheekful (melo lugmav), as a cheekful is the majority of a revi'it, and a kezayit is much less than that; for a kezayit is half an egg, and a revi'it is an egg and a half. Therefore, a cheekful is close to an egg. And although a solid kezayit is equivalent to a liquid revi'it, as stated at the beginning of the eighth chapter of Shabbat, see there, nevertheless we are in doubt whether a liquid kezayit suffices. This is why the Tur and Shulchan Aruch wrote that for all drinks, a person should either drink less than a kezayit or a revi'it, to avoid a doubt regarding the blessing. According to this, for a cup of blessing where one must drink a cheekful, one should drink a full revi'it. (The Taz in subsection 3 wanted to innovate that even for the majority of a revi'it one blesses an after-blessing, see there. The Eliyah Rabbah in subsection 5 already disputed this. His proof from siman 480 is not a proof, as that is when one drank the entire revi'it. The Rashba in his responsa, siman 625, wrote that one should drink the entire revi'it for the cup of Grace after Meals, and this is because of the after-blessing. What he said that "and the blessing" refers to the cup of Grace after Meals is not found anywhere; and how can he rule against the clear position of the Rambam? The Tosafists themselves wrote that it is a doubt, and in cases of doubt regarding blessings, we are lenient. The Beit Yosef himself in siman 210 wrote that the opinion of the Rambam is primary, see there. And also what the Taz wanted to innovate that for burnt wine (brandy), a revi'it is not needed because it is strong – the Magen Avraham in this siman, subsection 4, already disputed this, see there. The sages did not differ in measurements, and one who drinks less than a revi'it does not need an after-blessing. Our custom for every cup of blessing is to drink the majority of a revi'it, which is like a cheekful as I wrote, because we hold the opinion of the Rambam as primary. And wine is expensive for us, but a person with a very large mouth, whose cheekful is more than the majority of a revi'it – must drink a revi'it, as the Magen Avraham wrote in subsection 5, see there. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote in Section 4: If the one reciting the blessing does not want to taste, one of the participants should taste the required amount. The drinking of two people does not combine. Nevertheless, it is an optimal mitzvah for everyone to taste. So far his words. And later in Siman 271 regarding Kiddush, the Tur and Shulchan Aruch bring the opinion of the Geonim that specifically the one making Kiddush must drink. The Tur writes there that regarding the cup of Birkat Hamazon, the Geonim agree, see there. Therefore, he did not bring their opinion here, because here they agree that it is sufficient for another to drink. On the other hand, I am puzzled by Rabbeinu Beit Yosef, who brought an opinion that it is not necessary for one person to drink a full mouthful, and it is enough if each person drinks a little, see there. This is the opinion of the Ritva in the name of the Tosafot, see there. And since he brought this opinion regarding Kiddush, all the more so he should have brought this opinion here, for Kiddush is more stringent than Birkat Hamazon, as is evident from the Geonim. This requires further examination. (Additionally, in his major work, he brought the opinion of the Ra’aviah that a full mouthful is not required at all for the cup of blessing. He derives this from the Talmud in Pesachim there, which says: if the one making Kiddush tasted a full..., and the term "tasting" implies a small amount. In my humble opinion, a more compelling proof can be found in Berachot 52a, which says: the one reciting the blessing must taste..., if he tasted, it is disqualified, see there where it is clearly explained that it is merely tasting. However, since most poskim do not hold this way, we are compelled to bow our heads. Nevertheless, regarding combining [the amounts], this requires further examination. I saw in the Shulchan Aruch of the Gra that he compared this to the libation on the altar, see there. I do not understand: what is the connection between this and that? Moreover, if so, it should require the entire amount like on the altar. And for us, where wine is expensive, as are all beverages, in my humble opinion, we should at least rely on the opinion of "some say" in Siman 271 regarding combining. Examine this and you will find it easy.)

He further wrote: When dining at a large meal and it is uncertain to whom the cup of blessing for Birkat Hamazon will reach, each person who is unsure if it will reach them must recite "Borei Pri Hagafen." Thus is his wording. However, if the one reciting the blessing had the intention for all the diners, and they also intended that if the cup reaches them, they would fulfill their obligation with his blessing, they do not need to recite the blessing (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 7). And this is the common custom. And earlier, in Siman 174, paragraph 10, we explained that this only applies at a wedding feast; see there. For Kiddush, Havdalah, and Birkat Hamazon where everyone needs to fulfill their obligation, it is obvious that they do not recite the blessing individually.

The one who blesses over the cup must hold the cup in his hand during the Grace After Meals. Our custom is to hold it until "HaRachaman," and afterward place it on the table. When finishing "HaRachaman," one takes it in his hand and blesses. Some require holding it in the hand until drinking (Sha'arei Teshuva in the name of Chacham Tzvi). However, if one did not hold the cup in his hand at all – it does not invalidate the blessing after the fact (the Gra in section 2). But at the end of the chapter "Three Who Ate," it somewhat implies that this is mandatory, basing it on the verse "I will lift the cup of salvation," and one raises it a handbreadth. See there. This requires further examination for practical ruling.

The workers who perform labor for an employer, due to the potential loss of the employer's work, the Sages were lenient with them to shorten the Grace After Meals, as it is taught in Berachot (16a). Just as they were lenient with them in prayer to recite the "Havineinu" prayer, as I have written in Siman 110, so too they were lenient with them in the Grace After Meals. How is this done? The first blessing is recited in its complete form since it is the primary obligation, and therefore, it is not shortened. But in the second blessing, they begin with the blessing of the land and incorporate the blessing of "Builder of Jerusalem" within it. This is how it is said: We thank You, Lord our God, for the heritage of our forefathers, a good and spacious land, and for Jerusalem, Your city, that will be rebuilt speedily in our days, and for Your covenant that You have sealed in our flesh, and for Your Torah that You have taught us. We thank You. Blessed are You, Lord, for the land and for the nourishment. The blessings of the land and the blessing of Jerusalem are similar (Rashi). That is to say, even though they are from the Torah, nonetheless, from the Torah there is no necessity for each to be a separate blessing, but they established it that way (Magen Avraham). All the more so since there are those who hold that the number of blessings is not from the Torah (Beit Yosef and Bach). Therefore, for workers, due to the potential loss of work – they established it according to the Torah principle (see Tosafot there).

And this is when the homeowner is not reclining with them, for he might be particular about the interruption of work. But when he is reclining with them, they may recite the blessing properly with him, since he knows and forgives. And from whichever perspective: if he is particular, he will tell them to shorten it. However, Jews are not suspected of being particular about such a small amount of time, and if he is particular, he is particular. But not in his presence, they should not be lenient with others' work. And even if he is not reclining with them, this only applies when they are receiving payment in addition to their sustenance. But if they are working only for their sustenance, or they are receiving money just to sustain themselves, they do not shorten it and recite the blessing properly, for in such a case the sages were not concerned about his particularity.

And it is clear that the blessing of "HaTov VeHaMeitiv" is not recited, because it is rabbinic. And one does not wait for the zimmun (Sma, Siman 337). And there are those who question this (Magen Avraham). It appears that if the zimmun is in front of them, they should recite it with the zimmun. For it seems that it is from the Torah, and it only takes a few moments. However, waiting is forbidden. And regarding the blessing of "Hamotzi," according to our version in the Gemara and also in the Rambam in the second chapter, it is not recited. The reason: because it is rabbinic. But in the Rif and the Rosh, the version is: and they recite it before them. Similarly, the Tur wrote, and this appears to be the main opinion (Maadanei Yom Tov). For although it is rabbinic, nevertheless, one says it in a brief moment, and there is no nullification of work. Likewise, all blessings before eating and drinking are obligatory. And also the final blessings are obligatory, for they are brief and do not cause nullification of work.

The halachic authorities have written that all this was in their days. However, nowadays, we always bless all four blessings in their proper order, as it is not the way of people now to be particular about this. Presumably, workers are hired with the understanding that they will bless all four blessings in their proper order. And even if one later claims to be particular, we do not heed him. And this is also the case now with prayer, as I wrote in Siman 110. Furthermore, it appears to me that even if one hires them on the condition that they shorten their prayer and the Grace After Meals, we do not heed him. Since everyone does not conduct themselves in this manner, and it is as if they have accepted this as an obligation, an individual does not have the ability to exempt himself from the community and nullify the commandment.

In the Jerusalem Talmud, it questions: why should one not always recite the blessings in their proper order, and instead recite the two blessings "Builder of Jerusalem" and "He Who is Good and Bestows Goodness" while they are engaged in their work? They answered that this implies it is forbidden to engage in work while reciting a blessing. This applies to all blessings and all commandments, that it is forbidden to engage in any other matter while reciting the blessing or performing the commandment. Concerning this it is said: "And if you walk with Me with casualness"—meaning that you perform My commandments in a haphazard and coincidental manner, without intention. It is even forbidden to think about words of Torah while reciting a blessing, for every blessing requires intention (Taz).

The Sages taught in the Mishnah (Berachot 45a): Three who ate together are obligated to perform a zimun. This means that they must bless together and add another blessing, which is the Birkat HaZimun. We derive this from the verse "And you shall bless the Lord your God" – this refers to the Birkat HaZimun (Berachot 48b). And it is written: "Magnify the Lord with me, and let us exalt His name together." This means when there are three, one says to the other two, "Magnify the Lord with me" (Gemara). Similarly, Moshe Rabbeinu said: "For I will proclaim the name of the Lord; ascribe greatness to our God" (Deuteronomy 32:3). This also means that one says to the other two: "Ascribe greatness."

They did not institute the use of the Divine Name and kingship in the Birkat HaZimun because it is not a fixed blessing since one or two are exempt from it. They only commanded to mention the Divine Name with a quorum of ten, when they say "Let us bless our God," as will be explained. It is written: "In congregations bless God" (Psalms 68:27), meaning when there is a congregation or assembly, they mention "our God," as "assembly" is not less than ten (Levush). Even though any blessing without the mention of the Divine Name and kingship is not considered a blessing, as I wrote in Siman 214, the Birkat HaZimun is different because it is a preparation and invitation to several blessings. Therefore, it is called the Birkat HaZimun, and it is as if it also contains the Divine Name and kingship. This is why we say in the Birkat HaZimun "Let us bless Him of whose bounty we have eaten," meaning: let us bless with the Divine Name and kingship. Even though the main intention is for them to respond "Blessed be He of whose bounty we have eaten," nevertheless, this is also included. (This seems to be my humble opinion.)

In Pesachim (103a), it implies that before the blessing of the Zimun, they would say "Hav lan v'nivrich" (Give us [the opportunity] and let us bless), see there. Perhaps from this comes our custom of saying beforehand "Rabosai mir vilin bentchin" (Gentlemen, we want to bless), and they respond "Yehi Shem Hashem mevorach me'atah v'ad olam" (May the name of the Lord be blessed from now until forever). Similarly, in the Zohar on Devarim, it is stated that there must be an invitation for this, to indicate that they are preparing themselves. And in the Zohar before us, it is in the portion of Balak (page 186b), see there. And the matter appears to me as follows: Behold, whenever people intend to carry out something significant, they make preparation and invitation beforehand. In the generation of the dispersion, when they sought to rebel against God, it is written: "Come, let us build us a city." And Pharaoh, when he wanted to destroy Israel, said: "Come, let us deal wisely with them." And "come" (hava) is a term of invitation. Similarly in matters of holiness, as the scripture says: "Ascribe to the Lord glory and strength." And Moses our teacher, when he was commanded to appoint judges and officers, said: "Provide (havu) for yourselves men." Therefore, every commandment requires preparation. Now, in all practical commandments, there is a blessing beforehand, which serves as the preparation. But in the Grace after Meals, where the commandment is the blessing itself, preparation is needed before the blessing; hence, we say "Hav lan v'nivrich," using the term "hava," which means preparation. (And this is the language of the Zohar: see David, who required preparation, and said "I will bless...". And if you say why is there no preparation for other blessings? Because the act of blessing itself is the preparation... likewise for the blessing of Zimun... "Hav lan v'nivrich...". Thus far its language, see there. And be precise and you will find it easy.)

How is the Grace after Meals (Birkat Hamazon) recited with a zimun (invitation)? The one leading says, "Let us bless [the One] from whose food we have eaten," and those seated answer, "Blessed [is the One] from whose food we have eaten and by whose goodness we live." The leader then repeats this, and they respond "Amen," as this marks the conclusion of the blessing. There are those who question this practice, but it is not the primary halachic opinion (see Magen Avraham and Eliyah Rabbah). 

Why doesn't the leader say "Bless" (as is done in prayer and Torah reading)? Because "Bless" is not said with fewer than ten people, as is derived from the verses "Magnify" and "For there" as I have written. Therefore, the leader must include himself and say "Let us bless." According to this, if there are four people seated, he could say "Bless," and certainly if there are ten. However, to standardize all Birkat Hamazon recitations, it was established to always say "Let us bless." Additionally, this avoids excluding himself from the group.

In prayer and Torah reading, "Bless" is not said in this manner because when he says "the blessed One," he does not exclude himself. Furthermore, in those contexts, even if one has already fulfilled his obligation, he can still say "Bless" to fulfill the obligation for others and does not need to include himself again. But in Birkat Hamazon, one only recites if he has personally eaten and is obligated in the blessing, thus he cannot exclude himself from the group (Magen Avraham, section 2). In retrospect, if there are four or more people and he said "Bless," he fulfills his obligation (ibid., section 1). This is also written in the Tur.

And why does he not first say "And in His goodness we live"? Because initially it is only a command to all those gathered to bless God for feeding us this meal, and it is also a preparation and invitation, and there is no need to mention more. And they, when they respond, say "And in His goodness we live," meaning: not only in this meal did we eat from His, but we always live from His goodness, blessed be He. Therefore, the one who blesses is obligated to repeat and say "Blessed...", because he has not yet said "And in His goodness we live." There were those who had the custom that the one who blesses, when he said "Let us bless the One from Whose food we have eaten," would also finish with "And in His goodness we live," but their words were rejected (see Bach and Taz). And now this custom is not practiced anywhere. If there are ten, he should bless with the Name, meaning he should say "Let us bless our God," and they also respond "Blessed is our God," and he repeats and says "Blessed is our God...". He should not say "Let us bless to our God" with a "lamed" (to), because in the blessing it is not written with a "lamed," as it is written: "Bless God, peoples, in the congregations bless God" (Tosefta Berakhot).

And immediately we begin with the blessing of "Who sustains." There are those who say beforehand "Blessed is He and blessed is His name"; but this is incorrect, as we do not find this in the Gemara or in the poskim. Even though this language appears in the Tur, it has been written that this is a printing error, as it has no relevance at all and it constitutes an interruption between the blessing of the zimun and the blessing of "Who sustains." However, it is also found in the Rokeach (in Siman 284) and likewise in the Abudraham. Some have written that this is when blessing in a group of ten, because since the name of God is mentioned, they give Him a blessing, as it is written: "For I will proclaim the name of the Lord; ascribe greatness to our God" (Beit Yosef). But it is more correct not to say it; and this is the common custom in our country, and this also seems to be the opinion of most of the poskim. There is no difference between ten, a hundred, a thousand, or more, as we do not say more than "Let us bless our God" (the halacha follows Rabbi Akiva in the Mishnah 49b). 

And why is the name "Elokim" used in the zimun and the name "Hashem" used in Torah and prayer? Because providing sustenance to the creatures is a matter of justice that He, blessed be He, provides sustenance to all creatures, and therefore we mention the name "Elokim," which signifies the attribute of justice. But the Torah is a Torah of kindness, and therefore we mention the name "Hashem" (Eliyahu Rabbah, small section 6). Additionally, sustenance was prepared at the time of the creation of the world, and all the acts of creation are done in the name "Elokim," as it was established from the time of creation; whereas the Torah and prayer are above this world and emanate from the hidden treasures above. Therefore, we mention the name "Hashem" blessed be He. 

And why is the name mentioned in a group of ten and not less? Because wherever ten gather, the Divine Presence rests. And furthermore, because of the verse "in assemblies" as I wrote in section 1.

Anyone who deviates from the formula established by the sages and from the set text is simply making a mistake. For example, one who says, "Let us bless the food we have eaten," which implies that one is blessing the food itself. Therefore, when there are ten present and the name of God is mentioned, one can say this, as it is understood that the blessing is directed to God for the food we have eaten. Similarly, one should not say, "Let us bless the one from whom we have eaten," as this implies blessing the host. Even with ten present, one should not say this, because although it does not imply the host, it could still be misconstrued, Heaven forbid, as implying that we have eaten from a deity, as if there are two powers, Heaven forbid (according to the Bach and Magen Avraham). One also should not say "from His goodness" instead of "in His goodness," as this implies only a part and diminishes the kindness of the Holy One, blessed be He. Only in requests and petitions can one use such language, like "satisfy us from Your goodness," because it is not proper etiquette to ask for too much, but not in His praises (as per the Talmud). Additionally, one should not say "in the place of our life" instead of "life," and one who says this is considered ignorant, as they have excluded themselves from the community (according to Rashi).

If there were ten, and the one leading the blessing and those responding erred and did not mention "our God" – they cannot go back and bless using the name, for they have already fulfilled the obligation of the invitation (zimon), and it is considered an error that cannot be corrected. However, if they have not yet responded after him, since the obligation of the invitation has not yet been fulfilled – the one leading the blessing should go back and say it using the name, and then they should respond after him.

It has already been explained in Siman 167 that blessings over enjoyment (Birkat Hanehenin) are not similar to blessings over commandments (Birkat Hamitzvot). For blessings over commandments, one can exempt his fellow with his blessing even if he himself is not obligated, because all of Israel are responsible for one another. However, with blessings over enjoyment, one who does not benefit cannot exempt one who does benefit; and even one who benefits cannot exempt another who benefits unless they are joined together in something that establishes them as one, such as bread or similar items where their establishment joins them to be as one entity and one blessing for everyone. And this is only for the first blessing, where their intention is to join and establish themselves together to eat. But for the after-blessing, since they are about to separate from each other, they do not join together in this to exempt everyone with one person's blessing. Therefore, in other after-blessings, one does not exempt his fellow; rather, each one should bless for themselves.

And similarly with the Grace After Meals (Birkat Hamazon): if two people ate together, they need to separate, and each one should bless for himself. But if three ate together, since they are obligated in the Zimun (invitation to bless) and say together "Let us bless" – the Zimun makes them as if they are connected together. And the one who leads can recite the entire Birkat Hamazon, and the listeners should have intent to fulfill their obligation through their listening and answer "Amen," even if they are proficient in reciting the blessing themselves. This clearly appears from the Talmud and the Poskim (decisors of Jewish law), that since the Zimun connects them – their status is like a prayer in a congregation, where the prayer leader fulfills their obligation. And even though in prayer the leader does not fulfill the obligation for one who is proficient, as I wrote at the beginning of Siman 124 – this is a special law in prayer because it is a supplication for mercy, and each one needs to ask for mercy. But in other matters, it is preferable that one person blesses and all listen because of "In the multitude of the people is the King's glory," like in Kiddush and Havdalah and similar cases. And why should Birkat Hamazon be any less, since the Zimun connects them? And the reason we do not practice this way is because among us it is not customary to fulfill blessings by listening, except for Kiddush and Havdalah, and blessings over commandments like Shofar and Megillah. But according to the essential law, it seems clear that this is the case. And so it is explicitly explained from the words of Rabbeinu Beit Yosef earlier in Siman 183, where he wrote: it is proper that each one should say quietly along with the one who blesses… see there, for the reason that perhaps they will not hear well. But according to the law, it is not necessary for each one to bless for himself. (And so wrote the Bach there, and so it appears from the words of the Magen Avraham in Subsection 2.)

And this, where two people each say the blessing for themselves, is when both are able to recite the blessing. But if one can recite the blessing and the other is an ignoramus – the one who can recite says the blessing and the ignoramus fulfills his obligation. The ignoramus must intend for each word that the one reciting says. The Tur and the Shulchan Aruch wrote in Section 1 that this applies when he does not know how to recite the blessing. However, if he understands Hebrew […], see there. But if he does not understand at all, he does not fulfill his obligation by hearing it. The Tur concludes that therefore women do not fulfill their obligation with the men's blessing, since they do not understand at all. And what is their remedy? They should say word by word after the one reciting, for when they say it themselves, they fulfill their obligation even if they do not understand at all (Levush). This is the difference between Hebrew and a foreign language, for in a foreign language one must understand what is being said, as I wrote in Section 185; not like "there are those who say" that even in Hebrew one must understand, as I wrote there in Section 7, see there.

And know that the opinion of Rashi, of blessed memory, is that even one who hears in the Holy Tongue fulfills his obligation even if he does not understand; and also the Tosafot and the Rosh did not explicitly disagree with him but were uncertain. And we have already wondered above in Siman 185 about the basis of this opinion, and also the great later authorities wrote that the custom follows Rashi (Rema in Darkei Moshe, and Bach, Taz, and Magen Avraham in subsection 2). And women who are unable to recite the blessings listen to the men and fulfill their obligation even if they do not understand at all. And even for the biblical mitzvah of Kiddush, women and unlearned men fulfill their obligation by listening (there). And it is obvious that the one who listens must intend to fulfill his obligation, and the one who recites the blessing must intend to fulfill it for them.

And know that in the Mordechai at the beginning of the seventh chapter, it is written, and this is his language: Rabbi Eliezer of Worms wrote in the name of Rav Hai Gaon that three who ate from the seven species are obligated to recite the zimun. Until here is his language. According to this, we would find ourselves often in situations when eating in groups with cakes and fruits of the seven species, and they do not recite the zimun at all. There are those who wrote that it is good not to establish a meal on the seven species (Bach and Magen Avraham there), and this is almost impossible in cases of honors, celebrations, guests, and the like. However, in truth, there is no need to worry about this, and no other halachic authority has brought this opinion at all. And our rabbis, the Ba'alei HaTosafot (Bava Batra 37a, in the discussion beginning with "Nathan") explicitly wrote the opposite. Similarly, the Rambam, the Tur, and all the halachic authorities explicitly wrote that three who ate bread are obligated to recite the zimun; and in Chullin (106a) it is said that one does not recite the zimun over fruits, and this applies to all kinds of fruits, even from the seven species, since it does not say "except for the seven species." The reason it does not say "one recites the zimun only over bread" is because the discussion there is about an incident involving fruits, and several laws are derived from this incident, hence it uses this language. And the Rif brought this in the eighth chapter of Berachot (and similarly wrote Tosafot Rid), therefore there is no need to worry about this at all. And it appears that there was an error in the Mordechai, and it should say: "one is not obligated to recite the zimun" (and so it is written in Sha'arei Teshuvah in the name of Pri Chadash and Baruch Yosef, see there).

Three people who ate together are not permitted to separate, as they are obligated in Zimun. Even if two people ate together, it is a mitzvah to seek out a third person to join them for Zimun. This is the ruling of the Rosh, the Tur, and the Shulchan Aruch, section 1. However, we do not see anyone being careful to fulfill this mitzvah. Furthermore, it is perplexing that our master, the Beit Yosef, in his major work at the beginning of section 197, wrote in the name of the Rashba that if two people ate together and a third person comes, there is an obligation to invite him to join. Look there. So why are people not careful about this?

It seems to me to justify the practice: Their proof is from the beginning of the chapter "Three Who Ate": The servant who was serving two people is allowed to eat with them, even though they did not give him permission, in order to join in Zimun. In truth, the Rif and the Rambam did not bring this at all (and the Baal Ein Mishpat referenced it, but it is not so). Even the Rosh himself in the chapter "Arvei Pesachim" (section 32) wrote that there is no obligation to seek out a third person except on the first night of Passover. Look there (Ma'adanei Yom Tov). And the case of the servant is not proof, for they are obligated to give the servant a taste of each type of food, as I wrote in section 170. 

Another proof they bring is from Chullin (105a), where Rava bar Bar Chana said: I was standing before Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi, and they brought a basket of fruit before them, and they ate and did not give me any. This implies that one does not recite Zimun over fruit. For if they did, they would have given me some to join in Zimun. Besides the fact that one should not derive law from the holy ones, it also appears clearly that they were not at home, and the fruit was not theirs; in such a case, they would have certainly invited him as well. This is not the case with a homeowner eating at home with one other person; how can we impose upon him that when another person comes, he should invite him to eat as well? Usually, the meal would not be sufficient. Therefore, people are not careful about this. (This is what seems to my humble opinion to justify the practice of the general Jewish community.)

And just as three who ate together are forbidden to separate, so too four or five are forbidden to separate. For even though if two out of five separate, three will still remain for a Zimun, nonetheless, those two will not fulfill the mitzvah of Zimun which they were obligated in. But six can be divided into groups of three, for then there will be a Zimun for both groups. Similarly, seven, eight, or nine can be divided until they reach ten. For ten are obligated to bless with the Divine Name, and if they separate, they will not bless with the Divine Name. It is a mitzvah to strive for a group of ten to bless with the Divine Name. Ten cannot be divided until they are twenty. It is understood that with twenty, there is no obligation to divide, but if they wish to divide, they can. Similarly, with six, there is no obligation to divide.

The Tur and the Shulchan Aruch write in section 1: However, if many are gathered together and they cannot hear the blessing of the zimun from the one leading, and they are not permitted to divide into groups of ten each because they would need to recite the blessing out loud and the householder would hear and become upset with them—they can divide into groups of three each and recite quietly so that the householder does not hear. This is better for them than not fulfilling the obligation of the blessing of the zimun, since they cannot hear it from the one leading. Thus far is their language. This applies specifically when they cannot hear the blessing of the zimun from the one leading. But if they can hear the blessing of the zimun, even if they cannot hear the entire Grace After Meals from the one leading—it does not matter, since they can recite it themselves, and they are not permitted to divide into groups of three (Taz, subsection 5). And there is an opinion that says that even if they cannot hear the end of the blessings and respond "Amen," it is better to divide into groups of three each (Magen Avraham, subsection 4). The language of the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch agrees with the first opinion. (And the Eliyah Rabbah agreed with the Magen Avraham, and this requires further study.)

From what has been explained, it seems to me that in large meals, which last many hours, and there are individuals for whom it is difficult to remain seated and they wish to leave the meal, and it is not possible for them to gather ten from among those present to bless, they can bless with three. This is all the more so from the previous ruling, where due to the homeowner’s insistence they were exempted from this, certainly here, where it is entirely impossible to bless with ten, they are compelled to bless with fewer than ten. (And this ruling is sourced from Berachot 51a, from the incident with Rabban Gamliel. And it seems to me from Rashi there, in the commentary beginning "mevarchinan," that specifically when they wish to stay until after the meal is over, the Talmud needed to search for reasons, but when they wish to leave earlier, all this is unnecessary, see there. Delve deeply and you will find it simple.) (And the Taz wrote similarly in Siman 200, see there.)

All the more so, if they need to go to perform a mitzvah in the middle of the meal, they can divide into groups of three (Magen Avraham, subsection 7). There is room to question whether if another person needs to leave the meal to perform a mitzvah and cannot find even three people to bless with a zimun, if he is allowed to bless by himself due to the principle of "one engaged in a mitzvah is exempt from another mitzvah." It seems to me that this is forbidden, for he has already become obligated in the blessing of zimun; this does not exempt him from the mitzvah but rather makes him as one transgressing a commandment. It is not similar to what is permitted with fewer than ten, for there the mitzvah of zimun is still fulfilled, only it could have been performed in a more optimal manner. This is not the case when it would not be fulfilled at all.

Some of the poskim (halakhic authorities) have said that it is specifically when all three sat down to eat together from the beginning that they are not permitted to separate. But if initially, two sat down to eat and in the middle of the meal the third one came and ate with them, they are allowed to separate because the obligation of zimun (invitation to bless) did not take effect at the beginning of the meal (Tur in the name of R”Y). However, the Rosh rejected these words, stating that since he sat down to eat with them, the obligation of zimun takes effect on all of them, and it is forbidden for them to separate. This is the ruling we follow; and likewise, our teacher, the Beit Yosef, ruled in section 2 and did not mention the first opinion at all, see there. Even if they joined together only at the end of the meal, they are obligated to perform zimun, and it is forbidden for them to bless without zimun. There is no difference whether two ate first and the third came, or one ate first and then two came. This is straightforward.

And our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote: Nevertheless, if one eats with them without a fixed setting, they are permitted to separate, unless he is a servant. So are his words. That is to say, if the third person, when he comes, does not sit with them at the table but eats standing or walking, the obligation of Zimun (invitation to say the Grace After Meals) does not apply to them; because three who eat with a fixed setting are obligated in Zimun, but not without a fixed setting. And only the servant, this is his way of a fixed setting. The novelty is that even though the two are eating with a fixed setting, we do not say that the third is secondary and it is as if all of them are eating with a fixed setting, as it is not so. And our teacher, the Rama, wrote: Nevertheless, even in a place where they are permitted to separate, it is better to have Zimun, because "in the multitude of people is the King's glory." So are his words. That is to say, the third should sit with them for the Grace After Meals at the table and they should perform Zimun. And we do not say that there is no obligation of Zimun at all and it is forbidden for them to perform Zimun, as it is not so. And it seems clear to me that this is specifically in a case where the law permits them to separate, as in the case explained here - it is better to perform Zimun. But in a place where we say they do not combine for Zimun, such as when all ate dispersed and separated and similar cases, in such a manner it is certainly impossible for them to perform Zimun at all.

The Mishnah teaches: "Three people who ate together are obligated to form a zimun." Certainly, this applies when they ate at one table, or at small tables as was common in their times, but close to each other. However, when they ate separately, such as in our case where each person eats at their own table, even if they are all in one room—they do not combine for a zimun, as this is not considered "together." This will be explained in Siman 195, where it is discussed that two groups can combine—this is when each group has three people. (The Magen Avraham writes similarly in subparagraph 8; see there. However, what I wrote in the intent of the Rema in the previous paragraph, that his intent is that they should all eat a little together with the intent of establishing a meal, see there—in my humble opinion it does not seem so from his language. For in that case, it is not necessary, since two sit together with intent and the third also stands with them—they can form a zimun, similar to a servant. But there is no obligation for them to form a zimun, for if according to the Magen Avraham without this it is not relevant to zimun at all, how can the servant combine? And this is also implied by the Elyah Rabbah in subparagraph 6, and by the Taz in subparagraph 7; see there. Delve deeply and you will find it simple.) (And in Siman 195, paragraph 4, another answer will be explained regarding the case of two groups; see there.)

If they were riding and said "Let us eat," even though each one eats from his own loaf and they did not dismount from the animals, they join together, since they stood in one place. But if they were walking and eating, they do not join together. Similarly, if they were eating in a field scattered and separated, even though they all eat at the same time and from the same loaf, since they did not establish to eat in one place, they do not join together. And those traveling in a wagon, if they stopped the horses and three ate in the wagon, they join together. But if they ate while the horses were walking, it seems to me that they do not join together. However, those traveling in a ship, it seems to me that they do join together even while it is moving, because a ship is considered a fixed place (so it appears in my humble opinion).

Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote in Section 4: Three people who sat down to eat and recited the blessing of "Hamotzi," even if each one is eating from his own loaf, and even if they haven't yet eaten an olive's worth of bread – they are not permitted to separate. So far his words. And there are those who say that the obligation applies specifically when they are eating from one loaf, even if they haven't yet eaten an olive's worth. But when each one is eating from his own loaf – the obligation only applies if they have eaten an olive's worth of bread (Bach and Magen Avraham, subsection 10). There is also an opinion that if they began to eat together, then even if one wants to finish his meal before the others – it is forbidden, because they are all obligated in Zimun. But if one started eating before and then the second and third started, then if one wants to finish his meal earlier, he can finish and bless by himself (Taz, subsection 6). And so wrote the Tosafot at the beginning of the chapter "Three Who Ate," see there. And they wrote this based on their interpretation of the Jerusalem Talmud, see there. But the Rashba and the Rosh interpreted it differently, and according to them, this distinction does not exist, as is clear. Therefore, Rabbeinu Beit Yosef did not bring this matter (Eliyah Rabbah, subsection 6). Therefore, one should not be lenient in this. And see what I wrote in Siman 200, Section 2.

Three people who came from three groups of three people each, who ate but have not yet recited the Grace After Meals, and these three joined together – certainly the obligation of Zimun (invitation to bless) applies to them. They are required to now bless with Zimun, even if they did not eat together now but each one by themselves, for if they had not eaten here at all, it would be impossible for them to bless here at all; as I wrote in Siman 178 that one must bless only in the place where one ate. According to Maimonides, in such a case, it is also forbidden. Rather, it refers here that they all ate in one room, but these ate in this corner, these in another corner, and these in a third corner, for regarding the Grace After Meals, the place of eating is considered as one place. This is when there was no Grace After Meals in the initial places at all by these three separated individuals, for since they did not perform Zimun in their place, they became obligated in Zimun. But if they performed Zimun in their place, for example, if one waited for the other two who recited the Grace After Meals with Zimun, and he paused his eating until the blessing of "He Who sustains" or until the blessing for the land according to the opinions that will be explained in Siman 200, and afterwards he ate more – they will no longer join together for Zimun, even if they ate together afterwards and finished their meal; for the obligation of Zimun has already left them, and each one blesses by himself. And even if one did this for his group – he no longer joins for Zimun. Only two remain, and with two there is no Zimun. (See Taz, subsection 8, and Magen Avraham, subsection 13, and we have already included their words. Be precise and you will find ease.)

There are times when even if those who separated did not join in a zimun (invitation to bless) at all in their previous groups, the obligation of zimun leaves them, and they are no longer able to join in a zimun even if they eat together later. For example, if there are three groups of four people each, and one person from each group leaves and joins another group, and the remaining three in each group recited the zimun – the obligation of zimun has completely left those who separated, since their group already performed the zimun. Similarly, if each group had only three people, and one person from each group separated and joined together, but three others came to each of the remaining pairs in each group and ate with them, and each group then performed the zimun separately – the obligation of zimun also leaves those who separated, because their groups already performed the zimun, even though they did not do it with them. The reason for this matter is that zimun is only obligatory for three who are obligated, and how can the one who separated from the group now perform zimun, since their group already performed it? Now he is left as an individual.

And all this is in a situation where they have already separated after the fact. But initially, three who ate together – it is forbidden for one to separate from the two and join with two others who are obligated in a zimmun, for he will nullify the obligation of zimmun that was incumbent upon the two who remain. However, from a group of four who ate, one is permitted to separate from them and join with two others who are obligated in a zimmun, for there will still remain three for the zimmun.

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote in Section 3: The custom is not to recite the Zimun (invitation to bless) in the house of a non-Jew. It seems to me that the reason is that they cannot establish themselves in his house due to fear of him, and it is as if they ate without establishing a fixed meal. Additionally, there is a concern for danger if they change the wording of the blessing and do not say, "May the Merciful One bless the master of this house." Therefore, from the outset, they did not establish themselves to bless together, but each one would bless alone. Therefore, the custom should not be changed; even if these reasons were not sufficient, since the custom has already been established, it is as if they did not establish themselves together. This is the end of his words. However, many great authorities have disagreed with this, and they hold that one can recite the Zimun there, and "this master of the house" refers to the host of the meal. Many great authorities have acted accordingly in practice, especially now that inns have special rooms for guests where they recite the Zimun. And so we practice, unless they are eating there casually and not in an established manner, in which case they do not recite the Zimun there. (The Levush, the Bach, the Mateh Moshe in the name of the Maharshal, and the Magen Avraham in Section 9 in the name of the Mahari”l – all ruled that one should recite the Zimun there.)

Three people who ate together and forgot to recite the zimun, and each one recited the blessing individually— the zimun is nullified for them. They can no longer recite the zimun, as there is no retroactive zimun. Meaning: the zimun must precede the other blessings and not follow them, and what is distorted cannot be corrected. Similarly, if two of them recited the blessing. But if only one of them recited the blessing—the remaining two can still perform the zimun with him; since he is also obligated in zimun, and the majority of the group has not yet recited the blessing, it is considered that the zimun is in order and not retroactive, as we follow the majority. He has not fulfilled the mitzvah of zimun, as there is no retroactive zimun. And you might say: How can he say "Blessed is He of whose we have eaten," since he has already blessed over his eating? This is not the case, since he did not bless according to the proper order—it is no worse than having eaten a leaf of a vegetable. Therefore, even according to those who hold that a leaf of a vegetable does not combine, this is better since he did not bless according to the proper order. (This seems to me the reason for the matter. And what the Tur wrote that it is no worse than a leaf of a vegetable, is not a reason for the zimun as the Magen Avraham wrote in subsection 1, but regarding the phrase "of whose we have eaten." And so it is explicitly in the Tur. According to this, the rationale of the law is properly understood. The Gaon of Vilna worked on this, and according to what I have written, the reason is understood. Consider and you will find ease.) (And it has already been explained in the previous section that when one performed the zimun with others—he nullified the mitzvah of zimun for the other two. It is forbidden to do so, see there.) (The Rif omitted this law, and his reason is not known.)

Three who ate together, and one of them went out to the marketplace before the Grace After Meals – they call him and inform him that they want to recite the zimun so that he comes and intends to join them, and he answers with them the Blessing of Invitation (zimun). They fulfill their obligation, and even if he does not sit with them at the table but stands at the entrance – they fulfill their obligation, and he also fulfills his obligation. This applies to three. However, with ten, since they need to mention the Divine Name – it is not proper etiquette that he does not sit at the table, and he is required to sit with them until the end of the Blessing of Invitation. This will be explained in section 200.

It is well known that in the Grace After Meals, either everyone recites the blessing together with the leader according to our custom, or the leader recites the blessing and everyone listens and responds "Amen," as I wrote at the beginning of the previous section. And when two of them are unlearned, it is necessary that only the leader recites all the blessings, and they listen and respond "Amen." But if all of them are unlearned, they have no one to recite for them. And our sages of blessed memory said (Berakhot 46a according to the Rif) that if three people ate together and none of them knows to recite all the blessings; rather, one of them knows the first blessing, another knows the second blessing, and another knows the third blessing—they are obligated in the invitation to bless (zimmun), and each one recites the blessing he knows, and the other two respond "Amen." The same applies to the second and third blessings. And even though none of them knows the blessing of "HaTov VeHaMeitiv," it does not prevent them from fulfilling their obligation, since this blessing is of rabbinic origin. But they should not split a blessing in half, meaning if one knows half of the blessing and the other knows the other half—they should not perform the zimmun, because a blessing cannot be split, and it is not divided into two parts. And it is obvious that they need to know also the blessing of the zimmun. Similarly, if two people ate together, as we established at the beginning of the previous section that the one who knows should recite and the other fulfills his obligation, if one knows one or two blessings and the other knows the third—they should proceed accordingly: the first person recites the first and second blessings, and the second person the third, and similarly in all other cases. And all the decisors ruled this law.

There is a question regarding this matter: From this it implies that if none of them knows even one of the three blessings, the invitation (zimun) is nullified. This seems unreasonable, and why shouldn't they invite based on the blessing they do know? The answer is as follows: They are certainly obligated to recite the blessing they know, but the mitzvah of zimun is only applicable when there are three blessings. Since we derive the blessings of zimun and the three blessings from the verse "And you shall eat and be satisfied and bless" (Berachot 48b), therefore, when there are three blessings, there is zimun; and when there are not three blessings, there is no zimun. From this it is proven that all three blessings are of Torah origin. If not, why would they prevent zimun? For "HaTov VeHaMeitiv," which is rabbinic in origin, does not prevent zimun. (And so wrote the Magen Avraham in subsection 3. And see there what he wrote in the name of the Ramban, that the blessings do not prevent one another, and he objected to it from this source. But according to what I have written, this is not an objection, for this is only said regarding the blessing of zimun. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

The Sages taught in the Mishnah (50a): Two groups that were eating in one house, if some of them can see each other, they can combine for a Zimun. If not, these make a Zimun by themselves, and those make a Zimun by themselves. And it is stated in the Jerusalem Talmud: This is needed for two houses. Meaning: Concerning one house, it is not applicable to say "if some of them can see each other," because in one house, they can all see each other. Rather, certainly, there is no difference between one house and two houses. And the Mishnah that mentioned "one house" informs us that even in one house, they can make a Zimun separately if each group has ten, or if even together they would not be ten. For the Mishnah that states "they can combine for a Zimun" – it is certainly not necessary for them to combine, and if they wish, each group can make a Zimun by itself (and so wrote the Bach). This informs us that even in one house, they can divide, as I wrote in Siman 193. And it is obvious that they all need to be able to hear from the person leading the blessing (there).

And it is taught there that even the attendant joins them, meaning: even if they do not see each other, the attendant joins them if he serves both groups, even if they are in two different houses. However, if a public domain separates between the two houses, they are not joined in any manner, even if they see each other, and even if one attendant serves both. And it is not specifically a public domain, but even a private path that separates them—they do not join (Taz, subsection 2). But in the case of a wedding feast, the public domain does not separate, since it is all considered one wedding feast (there, subsection 3). And it is explained further in Even HaEzer, Siman 62, that even if they do not see each other and there is not one attendant serving them, they are still joined, see there. And so wrote the Tur in the name of the Rosh, see there.

In Siman 193, Se'if 12, we explained that those eating at two separate tables do not combine together. And the reason that two groups can combine is when there is a zimun in each and every group, see there. However, even this is not necessary because the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch wrote here that this is the case when they initially entered with the intention to combine together. And this is based on the Jerusalem Talmud. Therefore, we properly combine them even when they are sitting at two tables. And it is possible that in such a case, it is necessary for them to combine, contrary to what I wrote in Se'if 1. However, it is not possible to say this, because even in one group they can separate if they wish, when there is a zimun for each one or ten, as I wrote there.

Based on this, we derive a new ruling: That which was explained there, that at two tables they do not combine for a zimun (invitation to say grace after meals), if they initially entered with that intention, they do combine. And even if there are not three at each table, they are obligated in zimun. And that which we wrote there, that when there is a zimun in each group they combine, is not definitive, and the custom is to combine. And this requires careful consideration in practice. (See Beit Yosef who raised a difficulty: The Rosh holds that even joining at the end is effective, as I wrote in Siman 193. But this is not a difficulty at all: Here, even at the end, there is no joining. And so wrote the Bach and the Magen Avraham in subsection 2. And see Taz in subsection 1 who elaborated at length, but this is not necessary at all. And the Beit Yosef in his major work wrote because of this difficulty: that it is not required that they entered with the intention to combine except in two houses and not in one house, see there. Based on this, we would need to say as I wrote there, that when there is a zimun at each table, they combine. This is the intention of the Magen Avraham at the end of subsection 2, see there. But from the language of the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, it is understood clearly that it also applies to one house, as the commentators wrote. Therefore, there is no need for what I wrote there. Be precise and you will find it simple.)

If some ate part of the meal inside the house, and some ate part of the meal outside the house, if the one reciting the blessing sits on the threshold of the house and can see both groups, he combines them, as it is considered as if each part sees the other. And our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, wrote in Section 3: "In any situation where two groups are combined, both groups must hear the words of the one reciting the blessing of the Zimmun clearly. For the rest of the Grace After Meals, each person should recite it by themselves. However, if they want the one leading the Zimmun to fulfill the obligation for everyone, they must hear the entire Grace After Meals, as without this they have not fulfilled their obligation at all." This is the end of their words. And if someone cannot hear, they respond "Amen" (Magen Avraham, subsection 5). And several authorities wrote that in any situation, they should hear the entire Grace After Meals from the one reciting the blessing (ibid., subsection 4). And in Siman 193, Section 8, we explained this, see there.

It is taught at the beginning of the chapter "Three who ate": If one ate untithed produce, first tithe from which its terumah was not separated, or second tithe and consecrated items that were not redeemed – one does not include him in a zimmun. And Rambam wrote at the end of the first chapter: Anyone who eats something forbidden, whether intentionally or unintentionally – does not recite a blessing over it, neither before nor after. How so? If one ate untithed produce of their decrees... he does not bless; and needless to say, if he ate carcasses and treif, or drank libation wine and the like. But if he ate demai... – he does bless before and after, and similarly all similar cases. So far his words. The explanation of his words: Indeed, even someone who eats a rabbinically prohibited item should not bless. But something with a lighter prohibition like demai – he does bless. And since he wrote "and similarly all similar cases", it clearly implies that there are other light rabbinic prohibitions upon which one blesses. And it appears to me that this includes foods cooked by non-Jews and milk milked by a non-Jew, where they were lenient to allow the kashering of earthenware vessels, as I wrote in Yoreh De'ah, section 113, see there. (And in the Ba'er Hetev, it is written about their non-Jewish wine, see there. But this does not seem correct to me. Consider it and you will find it light.)

However, the Ra'avad disagreed with him and wrote that for all prohibitions, one is obligated to recite a blessing both before and after since he derives benefit. It is only regarding the matter of a zimun (invitation to bless) that he does not join, because there is no fixed status for something prohibited, and it is like eating fruits, which do not have a fixed status for zimun. According to the Rambam, we must say that the rule mentioned in the Mishnah about zimun is to emphasize that not only is it forbidden for him to bless by himself, but even to join in a zimun where another person blesses and he is just joining is also forbidden (Bach). The Rosh agreed with the Ra'avad, as the Tur wrote. Look there.

However, our master the Beit Yosef in his great book brought an explicit Tosefta like the Rambam (Demai, Chapter Two), and this is the language of the Tosefta: "A Jew should not give a limb from a living animal to a Noahide, nor a cup of wine to a Nazirite... and we do not bless over them, nor do we include them in a zimun, nor do we answer 'Amen' after them." Thus far its language. Likewise, in the Jerusalem Talmud, Chapter One of Challah: "Stolen matzah is forbidden to bless over, and 'one who blesses over it blasphemes...'. Rabbi Yose says: A transgression is not a mitzvah. Rabbi Ila said: These are the commandments; if you perform them according to their commandment - they are commandments. If not - they are not commandments." Thus far its language. It is explicitly like the Rambam, and it is also explained from the Mishnah in Demai: "We bless over demai and include it in a zimun," which clearly implies that specifically demai we bless over and not other prohibitions, even rabbinic ones. And so ruled Rabbenu Yonah and the Rashba like the Rambam. And it is also evident from Rashi's language in the Mishnah of "three who ate," see there. And so ruled our master the Beit Yosef in section one. And it appears to me that if one ate bread with forbidden meat, even the Rambam agrees that one should bless over the bread before and after. For with bread there is no prohibition, so why should one not bless over it?

There is an opinion that if one ate something forbidden unintentionally, they should recite a blessing over it (Taz, subsection 1). This means that if one becomes aware after eating that it was forbidden, they should recite Birkat Hamazon or another blessing. This opinion brings proof from what Rabbi Yosef Karo ruled in subsection 2, that if one ate something forbidden in a life-threatening situation, they should recite a blessing over it. The argument is, what difference is there between a life-threatening situation and unintentional consumption?

However, this argument is questionable: in the case of unintentional consumption, although the person is not liable, ultimately they have consumed something forbidden, and this does not fall under the category of a blessing. But in a life-threatening situation, what they are eating is permitted by the Torah, and it is considered as if it were fully permitted. So how can these two cases be compared?

(Regarding what was written from the response of the Rashba, Part 1, Siman 994, concerning a sick person on Yom Kippur: the Rashba did not elaborate on the reasons since he ruled that one should recite a blessing. Moreover, the Rashba’s words there are puzzling because he agreed with the Raavad, while in his commentaries at the beginning of the chapter "Three who ate" he explicitly ruled according to the Rambam. See there. Therefore, this response is not as it should be. Analyze it well and you will find it easy.)

Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in his great book: If one stole wheat, ground it, and baked it, even though he acquired it through a change – he does not bless, neither at the beginning nor at the end. And like the case in Bava Kamma (94a), where one who blesses in such a situation is actually blaspheming. And so is the ruling regarding the lulav, as explained later in Siman 649; look there. Because regarding a blessing, a change does not help, as one does not mention God's name over something whose essence involves a transgression (Tosafot Sukkah 30a). However, there is an opinion that since Birkat Hamazon (Grace After Meals) is a Torah obligation, it is different, because according to the law it is considered his. Furthermore, regarding the lulav, there is uncertainty about this; look there. Therefore, in the case of Birkat Hamazon, which is a Torah obligation, we are stringent. (Magen Avraham. And this has support from the words of the Maggid Mishneh in Chapter Six of the Laws of Chametz and Matzah, Law 7; look there.)

In Arakhin (31a), it is stated that priests (kohanim) and Israelites (Yisraelim) can combine for a zimun (invitation to bless after a meal), even though the Israelite cannot eat terumah (priestly food). However, since the kohen can eat regular food (chullin), it is considered a joint meal and they can combine for a zimun. Based on this, our sages deduced that in any similar case, such as when three people are eating and one is eating bread of the Samaritans and the other two avoid it, nevertheless, since the one eating can eat from their food, they combine for a zimun. But if neither can eat the other's food, such as one who is a kohen eating terumah or challah and the other is an Israelite eating Samaritan bread and the kohen avoids it; since the Israelite cannot eat the kohen's food and the kohen avoids the bread the Israelite is eating—they do not combine for a zimun.

And similarly, if there are three people and two of them are forbidden to benefit from each other – they do not combine for a zimmun (invitation to bless after a meal), because one is prohibited from the other’s benefit. And even though they can annul their vows through a sage, nevertheless, at this moment, they have not annulled them. And our teacher, the Rema, wrote that this is specifically when each one eats from his own loaf. But if they eat from the loaf of the host – they do combine, because they are eating from one loaf. Thus far his words. And at first glance, there seems to be no novelty in this, and what is he teaching us? However, in truth, there is a great novelty here, as it is explained in Yoreh De'ah, section 221, that they are forbidden to eat from one bowl at the host’s place, because perhaps one will eat less than the other, and it will turn out that he benefits him, unless there always remains food in the bowl, see there. And thus, he is teaching us that with bread, we do not worry about this, as it is assumed that the host provides plenty of bread. (See Taz, subsection 3. According to his words, it should have been explained that there is plenty. And according to what I have written, it fits well, as it is generally the case. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

Translation:
From the aforementioned law, the poskim (Jewish legal decisors) have deduced that if one person is eating meat and another is eating dairy, they can still join together (for a zimun). Even though the one who ate meat cannot eat dairy for six hours, by which time the food will have been digested, nevertheless, since the one who ate dairy can eat meat immediately after rinsing and rinsing (his mouth), they can join together, as explained regarding terumah (tithe) and chullin (non-sacred food). However, if the one who ate dairy does not eat meat at that time, such as before the Ninth of Av, they do not join together. Similarly, if he ate hard cheese, which requires a long wait, they also do not join together.

However, there is a difficulty: What does meat and dairy matter when they are eating bread? If not, zimun (invitation to bless) is not applicable, and they can eat bread together. In truth, this is not a difficulty at all, for the essence of zimun is eating together, and two people who are eating, one meat and one dairy, must eat separately. It is forbidden to place them at the same table, or they need to make a distinction like using two tablecloths or something similar, as I wrote in Yoreh De'ah, section 88. Therefore, how can they join for zimun? If you say that even if one eats dairy and the other meat, they cannot join together, it is not so, for the dairy eater can immediately join the meat eater. Even if he does not join, since he is able to join, it is considered as joining. This is not the case when both cannot eat from the other.

Note that it is customary for the dairy eater to lead the blessing and not the meat eater, because the dairy eater can eat the other’s food (Magen Avraham, subsection 1). In my opinion, this is not so strict, since the Gemara in Arakhin did not specify that the kohen (priest) must lead the blessing. However, it can be said that it did not need to specify since in any case the kohen blesses due to "and you shall sanctify him," as I wrote in section 241. Nonetheless, it is not reasonable, for if the meat eater cannot bless, how can he join for zimun? Therefore, it is certain that they said this initially, but if for the sake of honor they want to honor the meat eater, there is no strictness. This seems to be the custom. (What the Taz wrote in subsection 2, the Eliyah Rabbah refuted in subsection 3, see there.)

Our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 4: One does not include in a zimun someone who ate less than an olive's bulk. Thus is his wording, and it is an obvious matter. However, it teaches us that even according to the opinion that will be clarified in the next section that someone who ate vegetables can also join a zimun, and I might have said that bread less than an olive's bulk is not worse than vegetables – it teaches us that it is not so. (See Taz section 4. According to our words, it is straightforward and simple. Examine and you will find it easy.)
