If two people ate together and a third person came, and the two had already finished their meal but had not yet recited the Grace After Meals nor washed their hands for the final washing, and had not yet said, "Let us bless," the Tur writes that he joins them. And so is the language of the Rosh (Chapter Seven, Siman 18), and this is his wording: Therefore, if two people ate and a third came and ate before the two said, "Let us bless," he joins them. This is the end of his wording. And it is explained from their language that he joins without any condition. (For they explain in Berakhot 47a: If they would bring me a delicacy..., would we not eat? Meaning, it is inevitable that every person, even if he is full, would find some food agreeable, and he would eat if they brought it to him.)

However, the Rambam in Chapter 5, Law 9 wrote: "Two people who were eating and completed their meal, and a third person came and ate, if they are able to eat with him anything at all, even from other foods, he joins with them." Thus are his words. He states a condition: "if they are able to eat with him." This is further clarified in the Sefer Mitzvot Gadol, which writes: "We assess their mindset: if they have not eaten so much that, if delicacies and a favored item were brought to them, they would still be able to eat – he joins." Thus are his words. It is explicitly stated that if not, he does not join. This is even more explicitly stated in the Ba'al Halachot Gedolot, and these are his words: "And in a case where two were eating bread and completed their meal, and another person came and wanted to invite them, we see if they bring something favored by them more than what they ate... and they do not eat – he does not join with them. But if they eat – he joins with them." Thus are his words. (They interpret: "if they would bring...", meaning: it is necessary to see if they would eat if it were brought to them or not. And from the Ba'al Halachot Gedolot it is clear that it requires specifically from the foods they have eaten, unlike the opinion of the Rambam. Examine this and you will find it easy.)

According to this, our teacher the Beit Yosef wrote in section 1: "Two people who ate together and finished, and a third one came, wherever if he brought them something they could eat from - he joins them. And they are obligated to give him to eat so that he may join them. And this is provided that he came before they said 'Let us bless.' But if they said 'Let us bless' and then the third one came, he does not join them." Thus far his words. And behold, he wrote explicitly like the Rambam and not like the Tur. And this is the established law that the halacha follows the majority, and the third one does not always join except under the explained condition. And I am astonished that the commentators did not note that the early authorities disagreed on this. (And the Levush wrote from his own reasoning that it depends on a condition. And the Perisha critiqued him that it does not depend on a condition, and in any case, he joins. See there. And they did not see that the early authorities disagree on this.)

And that which our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote that we are obligated to give him food so that he can join us, we have already explained this in Siman 193, Section 6, see there. And regarding what he wrote that when they said "Give us and we will bless" he does not join, our master the Rema wrote that washing hands for the final waters is akin to "Give us and we will bless." Until here is his wording. And certainly washing hands for the final waters is more significant than "Give us and we will bless," for in "Give us" there are those who disagree and hold that he joins (Magen Avraham, Section 2, in the name of the Ran, and see Siman 179). And also, "Give us and we will bless" only applies to the host and not to a guest, whereas for the final waters there is no distinction as I wrote in Siman 179. However, his intention is this: that in "Give us and we will bless" it is explained there that if he wants to bless for what he will eat – it is allowed. Not so with the final waters, as I wrote there. Therefore, he says that here, for the purpose of joining for a zimun, his ruling is like "Give us and we will bless," meaning: that they can bless and eat and join in the zimun with the third person (Magen Avraham, Section 3). And there are those who wrote that it is a mitzvah to wash his hands, bless "Hamotzi," and eat a little (there in the name of the Bach). These matters are puzzling and are close to gluttonous eating (Eliyah Rabbah). And we have never heard anyone who would consider doing so.

The Gemara (48a) states regarding ten people who bless using the Divine Name: nine who ate grain and one who ate vegetables can combine to bless with the Divine Name. The same applies if he drank a cup of wine (Tosafot), as drinking is considered like eating and he can say "who ate from His [bounty]" (there). And it is not specifically wine, as the same applies to other beverages, except for water which has no significance at all and cannot combine. Even if he only dipped with them in brine, he can combine. This is specifically when he ate an olive's worth of the vegetable or other food, or drank a quarter-log of wine or other beverages or brine. And it is specifically if he did not recite the final blessing, as after the final blessing he cannot combine. The Gemara also states that it is not specifically one who combines, as the same applies to three who combine. And so they said there that if seven ate grain and three ate vegetables, they can combine. But if four ate, they cannot combine even though the majority ate grain, because we need a majority that is significantly noticeable. It is obvious that the one who blesses must be one of those who ate bread. There are those who want to say that even water can combine, because drinking is included in eating (Magen Avraham, subsection 6). The main opinion appears to be like Rabbeinu Beit Yosef, who ruled in subsection 2 that it does not combine. The reason is that we need something that has at least some significance. According to this, it is possible that properly prepared water like seltzer, lemonade, or types of kvass can combine. This also seems to be the main practical ruling.

The one joining must recite the concluding blessing on what they ate or drank. For Birkat Hamazon does not exempt either the "Borei Nefashot" blessing or the "Me'ein Shalosh" blessing. Birkat Hamazon only exempts what is during the meal. And even those who are eating together, on items that come after the meal, need a blessing before and after, as I wrote in Siman 177. All the more so those who did not eat at all during the meal, and their joining is only for the Zimun. Therefore, if they joined even through eating mezonot, they need a separate blessing. They should wait until the one leading the Zimun finishes the blessing, as will be explained in Siman 200, and then they should recite the concluding blessing. There are those who wish to say that wine and dates are exempted by Birkat Hamazon, because they satiate like bread (see Beit Yosef and Magen Avraham, sub-paragraph 7). This requires further study. Therefore, it is good for them to intend not to fulfill their obligation with the blessing of the one leading the Zimun.

The Rif and Rambam wrote that only for ten people can even someone who ate vegetables join; but for three, only someone who ate bread specifically can join, for in this regard three are more stringent than ten. For with ten, since the main aspect of the zimun has those who ate bread, adding "Elokeinu" in the recitation is because they ate something, and the Shechinah (Divine Presence) rests and they can say "Elokeinu." However, for the main zimun, it requires those who ate bread specifically, as it states: "Three who ate," meaning at a meal. And there is no meal except with bread. And even though in the Jerusalem Talmud it is taught: two who ate grain and one who ate vegetables join, it is clearly understood there that this is the opinion of an individual, and the Sages disagree, see there. And behold, in the Rambam it is written explicitly: "an olive-sized portion of bread." But in the Rif it is written "an olive-sized portion of grain," and therefore some say that it does not specifically mean bread, for even a blessing on mezonot (grain-based foods) suffices, as it is grain (Kol Bo). But the opinion of the Rosh and the Ri is that even vegetables suffice, for if they can join for ten, all the more so for three. And behold, our Master the Beit Yosef in his larger work ruled like the Rambam, but in the Shulchan Aruch, Section 3, he brought all three opinions. And since his inclination is towards the ruling of the Rambam, he wrote, and this is his language: Therefore, if two ate and a third came, if they can compel him to eat an olive-sized portion of bread, it is preferable. And if he does not want to, they should not give him to drink or any other food. And if it happened that they gave him to drink or another food, they should zimun with him, even though he does not want to eat bread. Thus far his words. And he retracted from what he wrote in his larger work, because Maharam of Rothenburg did so in practice (there). And the great later authorities wrote that even initially they do so, because the main ruling is like the words of the Rosh (Magen Avraham, Small Section 9, and Bach and Knesset HaGedolah).

It is well known that the Rambam in the fifth chapter, and Tosafot and the Rosh and most of the authorities hold that the obligation of Birkat Hamazon (Grace after Meals) from the Torah is only if one ate to the point of satiety, and the obligation for an olive-sized portion is only Rabbinic. Except for the Raavad there, who holds that an olive-sized portion is a Torah obligation. And there are those who hold that an egg-sized portion is a Torah obligation, as I wrote in Siman 184, see there. Therefore, a group that ate, some of whom ate to the point of satiety, and some only ate an olive-sized or egg-sized portion – ideally, the blessing should be recited by those who ate to the point of satiety, and not by those who ate an olive-sized or egg-sized portion, for it is better that one who is obligated by Torah law blesses for those who are obligated only by Rabbinic law, and not the reverse. However, after the fact, or if among those who ate to the point of satiety there is no one who knows how to bless – one who ate an olive-sized portion may bless, and everyone fulfills their obligation. The reason is: since the obligation of Birkat Hamazon is to bless, it is like the blessing over mitzvot, where one can discharge the obligation for another even if he did not perform the mitzvah at all, due to the principle of "all of Israel are responsible for one another." And it is not comparable to blessings of enjoyment, where one cannot discharge the obligation for another unless he also enjoyed. However, with Birkat Hamazon, one cannot discharge the obligation without any eating at all, for how can he say "that we have eaten from His," when he did not eat? Therefore, he must eat an olive-sized portion. But once he ate an olive-sized portion – it is sufficient, and he can discharge the obligation for others (Tosafot 48).

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) writes in section 4: "And some say that one is not obligated to recite a blessing from the Torah if one has not drunk and is thirsty to drink. It is good to be cautious initially that if some have drunk and some have not drunk, the one who drank should recite the blessing." This is his wording. And this is its explanation: There is an opinion that is concerned with the words of Rabbi Meir who expounded that "you shall be satisfied" includes drinking. According to him, the obligation from the Torah is for the measure of an olive. But if one wants to drink and does not drink, the obligation is only rabbinic. Therefore, to be cautious of this opinion initially, it is proper that the one who drank should recite the blessing; because if someone who did not drink recites the blessing, perhaps he wants to drink and his obligation is only rabbinic. And if some have eaten to satisfaction without drinking, and some have eaten an olive's worth and have drunk, it is better that the one who ate to satisfaction should recite the blessing, because most authorities hold that satisfaction is an obligation from the Torah and not drinking (Magen Avraham, section 12). And all of this is initially, as in the previous law. But after the fact, it does not invalidate at all, as in the previous law. (And the Taz in section 4 understood that the Mordechai's intention is also after the fact and was astonished by this; see there. But this is not his intention; see there.)

Three people ate together and began to recite the blessing, and someone who did not eat entered; if he enters when the one reciting the blessing says "Let us bless Him of whose food we have eaten" – he responds after them "Blessed and praised is His name always and forever." This is because when he hears the one reciting the blessing calling on everyone to give a blessing to God, all those who hear are obligated to bless, for otherwise, Heaven forbid, it would appear as if he does not want to... And because he cannot say "of whose food we have eaten," since he did not eat – he says "Blessed and praised..."

But if he enters when the diners are responding "Blessed is He of Whose food we have eaten," he should respond after them with "Amen." He does not need to say "Blessed," since he did not hear when they said "Let us bless." It appears to me that the response of "Amen" comes after the one who leads the blessing repeats, "Blessed is He of Whose food we have eaten," since certainly every "Amen" response is at the end of the matter, and how could one not respond at the end? If we were to say that he should respond both to them and to the one leading the blessing, it would be strange to answer two "Amens" to one matter almost simultaneously. Therefore, it appears to me as I have written. Additionally, it seems to me that even if one enters while the leader is saying "Let us bless," and responds "Blessed and praised," in any case, he should still respond "Amen" after "Blessed is He of Whose food we have eaten," since one is obligated to respond "Amen" to every blessing that one hears. The distinction made in the Gemara and the poskim (decisors of Jewish law) between entering at "Let us bless" and entering at "Blessed" is explained as follows: if one enters at "Let us bless," he needs to say "Blessed" as well, but if he enters at "Blessed," he should only respond "Amen." It is obvious that if ten are blessing, he should say "Blessed is our God and blessed be His name forever and ever." If he drank water, or even more so other beverages, and has not yet recited the final blessing, he can respond "Blessed is He of Whose food we have eaten," since drinking is included in eating, as I have written. It is clear that there is no difference between entering when they began to bless or sitting there during the meal without eating or drinking. Similarly, if he enters when the leader repeats "Blessed is He of Whose food we have eaten," he should also respond "Amen." There are those who disagree with this, but their opinion is not primary. (See Taz, whose words are not clear. Also, the Eliyah Rabbah disputes him; see there. The Gra"z ruled not to respond "Amen" when responding "Blessed," which requires further investigation. Also, in Siman 192, we ruled similarly; see there.)

The attendant who ate an olive-sized portion - one can include him in a zimun, even though his eating is not done in a formal setting, sitting at the table, but rather while he is walking or standing. Nevertheless, he is included, because since it is his usual way, his walking and standing are considered his formal setting. But for another person, this is not the case, as I have written in Siman 193. And the Cuthean, who is from the Samaritans, nowadays they are considered complete idol worshipers in all respects. And an ignoramus, according to the strict law, one cannot include him in a zimun, because his company is not appropriate. However, we hold that one can include an ignoramus in a zimun, relying on those Tannaim who hold: Who is an ignoramus? Anyone who does not recite the Shema in the morning and evening, or does not wear tefillin. And we do not have such ignoramuses among us. And even though we hold in the Gemara there that even if one learns Scripture and Mishnah but did not serve Torah scholars, he is still considered an ignoramus, nevertheless, it is impossible to uphold this now, for if so, they would go and build an altar for themselves. And in a similar manner our sages said in Chagigah, and we rely on this. Nevertheless, someone who does not recite the Shema or does not wear tefillin, one does not include him in a zimun, for he is a wicked person. And certainly a heretic and an apostate – one does not include them in a zimun, and similarly, a convert (in ancient times) who was circumcised but did not immerse – one does not include him in a zimun. And certainly, one does not include an idol worshiper, even if he blesses God. But if he was circumcised and immersed – one includes him in a zimun. And one should not ask: How can he say "for the inheritance of the desirable land you gave to our ancestors"? For this is not a question: the land was given to Abraham, and Abraham is called "the father of many nations"; meaning, anyone who enters under the wings of the Divine Presence is considered a child of our father Abraham. And an onen, during the time he is in mourning, is not included in a zimun, because he is exempt from all commandments. And even according to those who hold that he can perform commandments, nevertheless, he has no connection to zimun. Furthermore, we do not hold this way, as I have written in Yoreh De'ah Siman 341. And on Shabbat, when mourning does not apply to him – he is included in a zimun. And the mourner is always included in a zimun, and with him, the blessing of "He who is good and does good" is added as I have written in Siman 189.

It is stated in the Gemara (Berachot 45b): Women may form a zimun (invitation to bless) amongst themselves, and slaves may form a zimun amongst themselves. Women, slaves, and minors, if they wish to form a zimun together—they do not form a zimun due to concerns of promiscuity. According to Rashi there, it is not obligatory for women to form a zimun. However, if they wish to do so, they may. The Tosafot agree with this. But the Rosh wrote that women are obligated to form a zimun, as it is explicitly implied at the beginning of Arakhin that says: "Everyone is obligated in zimun… to include women," see there. Similarly, the students of Rabbeinu Yonah wrote this. However, even according to Rashi and Tosafot it is understandable, for certainly, women are obligated when they ate with three men—they are also obligated to listen to and respond to the zimun blessing. But for themselves, there is no obligation. And they are not included with men for a zimun, as the mingling of men and women is considered promiscuous. And even a husband and wife and his daughter do not join together for a zimun, but only when there is a zimun without them, they are obligated (Sefer Mitzvot Gadol). The custom of the world follows Rashi and Tosafot, and we have never heard of women forming a zimun by themselves. Also, from Maimonides in the fifth chapter there is evidence for the opinion of Rashi and Tosafot: for Maimonides’ words are concise like the language of the Talmud, but he wrote that they do not form a zimun with the Name, see there. And if you would think that they are obligated, why would they not form a zimun with ten using the Name? Rather, certainly, there is no obligation on them, and therefore the Name is not mentioned where there is no obligation. And so ruled our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch. They wrote that women fulfill their obligation with our zimun even though they do not understand, and we explained this in section 193, paragraph 4. (And see Magen Avraham, small paragraph 5. Look carefully and you will find it easy.) And in the Tur, he brought an opinion of someone who ruled that a woman can be included in a zimun. But we do not rule this way, and we have never heard or seen anyone who ruled this way. (And the Taz, who extended himself in small paragraph 2, did so not for the law but to explain the words of R. Yitzchak HaKohen in the Tur.)

The Tur and the Shulchan Aruch wrote: "An androgynous person can lead a zimun (invitation to bless after eating) for their own kind, but cannot lead for men or women. A tumtum cannot lead a zimun at all." Until here is their language. Because an androgynous person is a unique entity, and everyone agrees on this. However, a tumtum can be either male or female, and therefore their kind cannot fulfill the obligation. And someone who distanced themselves due to sin, or who transgressed a regulation as explained in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 334 – they are not included in a zimun.

In the case of a minor, there is much disagreement among the early authorities. Our master, the Beit Yosef, ruled that a minor who has reached the age of discernment, approximately nine or ten years old (according to the Magen Avraham), and knows to whom blessings are directed - can be included in a zimun and counted either among three or ten. This is his language. However, our master the Rema wrote that there are those who say that he cannot be included at all until he is thirteen years old, for then he is presumed to be an adult who has produced two pubic hairs. And this is the custom, and it should not be changed. As for a deaf person and a fool, if they have intention and understanding - they can be included in a zimun, even though the deaf person cannot hear the blessing. This is his language. And even though, in Torah law, we do not assume a thirteen-year-old minor to have produced two pubic hairs without examination, nevertheless, for inclusion in a zimun there is no concern. However, for him to fulfill the obligation for others, an examination is specifically required (there). But if everyone blesses on their own, and he only says the blessing of zimun - there is no concern (there). And so is the common practice, that one who becomes Bar Mitzvah and has a celebratory meal - he blesses. And what was written about the deaf and the fool - it does not refer to a completely deaf and foolish person; for such individuals have no understanding at all and are worse than a minor. Rather, it refers to a deaf person who cannot hear but can speak, and a slightly foolish person. Therefore, if they have intention and understanding - they can be included. And a mute person who can hear but cannot speak, it seems to me that he cannot be included because he cannot respond and bless (see Magen Avraham, subsection 8, and so writes the Eliyah Rabbah).

Our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote: When three people have eaten together, one must stop against his will for the two and respond with them to the blessing of Zimun. And even if he does not want to stop, they can still include him in the Zimun whether he responds or not, as long as he is standing there. However, two are not obligated to stop for one. Therefore, the obligation of Zimun does not apply until they agree to stop for one and bless. If they do not want to stop, and he initiated the Zimun upon them, it is of no effect. If they do not want to stop, he is also not permitted to bless and go out to the marketplace until the two finish and he can perform the Zimun with them; for he is already obligated in Zimun, and how can he bless without Zimun? Thus are his words.

In his great book, he ruled that if it is necessary for an individual to leave, he may recite the blessing and leave. This is because the Rashba wrote in the name of Rav Hai Gaon that an individual does not need to wait for the other two and can recite the blessing alone. The obligation of Zimun (invitation to bless) only applies at the conclusion of their meal, and as long as the other two have not finished their meal, the obligation of Zimun does not apply to them, and the individual can bless for himself. What was explained in Siman 193 that the individual is not permitted to separate, is when all have finished their meal and wish to separate. But as long as they have not finished the meal, he is permitted to bless for himself. This is also the ruling of the great Acharonim (later authorities) (Bach, Magen Avraham, subsection 2, and Eliyah Rabbah, subsection 3 in the name of Raavan, see there). And it is certain that without necessity, one should not do so. However, if it is necessary for his business or some other need, he may do so (Eliyah Rabbah there). There is an opinion that distinguishes: if they began eating together, he is not allowed to bless alone. And if they did not begin eating together, he is permitted (Taz, subsection 1). And we have already written there in subsection 14 that this opinion is not agreed upon, see there.

To what point must an individual interrupt their eating for the blessing of the zimun? There is a dispute in the Gemara (Berachot 46a): One opinion is that it is until the blessing of the zimun, meaning that once the leader says "Blessed is He from whose food we have eaten and through whose goodness we live," the individual can return to eating, for this is the main part of the zimun blessing that the individual does not say. Another opinion is that it is until they finish the blessing "Who nourishes all." The reason is that the blessing of the zimun does not include the mention of God's name and kingship, and therefore without the blessing of "Who nourishes all," it does not appear as a complete blessing (Tosafot there). The poskim (halachic authorities) also disagree on this matter. Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, ruled that it is until the blessing of the zimun, while our teacher, the Rema, ruled that it is until "Who nourishes all." This is also the prevailing custom, and it should not be changed. This is also the ruling of the Baal Halachot Gedolot (BHG).

If someone stopped eating and resumed, he may continue eating without a new blessing, as he intended to eat more. However, if he did not intend to eat more and then changes his mind, he must recite a new blessing (Magen Avraham, subsection 5). When he finishes eating and recites the blessing, he should start from the blessing of "HaZan." Even if he paused until the completion of the blessing "HaZan," he must recite it again, for although he was exempted by hearing it for what he ate before the blessing, he is not exempted for what he ate afterward. Even if he did not eat afterward, he must still recite the blessing, as he did not intend to be exempted by hearing it. If he indeed intended not to eat more and to be exempted by hearing it, he starts afterward from "Nodeh Lecha."

If one person interrupted for two others, and afterwards two other people came and ate with him, he joins them for a zimun (invitation to bless). We do not say that he has already fulfilled his obligation of zimun with the previous pair, because now that two others have joined him, he is obligated again (Bach and Magen Avraham, Siman 3). It seems to me that this is specifically if he ate after he interrupted for the two others. But if he did not eat, he does not join again. All the more so in a group of five or six or more, who interrupted for three or more of them, they should not bless with a zimun afterwards, even if they ate afterwards, because the obligation of zimun has already left them once they all interrupted for the blessers. However, if it was a group of nine, and one interrupted for two blessers, he may join two others afterwards, and then two others after that; since only he interrupted and they remained in their obligation, he joins them. If there was a group of five people, and one interrupted for two, he cannot join the remaining two, since there is no longer an obligation of zimun among them (Magen Avraham, Siman 3). However, if they all ate afterwards, they are obligated to make a zimun on what they ate afterwards (as implied by the Gra). This is not similar to what we wrote that even if they ate afterwards, they do not make a zimun, for that applies when all interrupted for the blessers. But when only one interrupted, and the others have not yet fulfilled their obligation of zimun, therefore, even though only two remain, nevertheless, if they all ate afterwards, he joins them in their obligation. This is how it appears in my humble opinion in these laws. (The Eivan HaOzer disagrees with the Magen Avraham. According to what I have written, there is no disagreement. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

And the Tur wrote that if they are ten, and three interrupt for seven – they only need to interrupt until they have said "Blessed is our God." And if the three return and eat – they can recite the zimun together. Thus far is his language. Meaning: even if one of those interrupting for two needs to wait until "He Who nourishes all" [is said], this is because without him there is no zimun. But three interrupting for seven, since there is still a zimun without them, their interruption is only for the mention of God's name. Therefore, they only need to interrupt until they have said "our God." Thus, when they return and eat, they can recite the zimun together. And it is not called "the zimun has flown away from them" as in the previous law, since they did not interrupt on account of the zimun but on account of the mention of God's name. And they can join with another seven for the mention of God's name, for in this, "the zimun has flown away from them" does not apply, since the Divine Presence rests on every group of ten (Magen Avraham, end of subsection 3).

We hold that the most distinguished person at the meal recites the Zimun and the Birkat Hamazon (Grace After Meals) (Berachot 46b), as the participants are obligated to honor him; even if the distinguished person arrives at the end of the meal. If the distinguished person wishes to grant permission to someone less distinguished than himself, he may do so, as this is not considered a lack of honor since he himself is giving the permission (Bach). This is also not included in what was stated (Berachot 55b) that one who is given the honor to bless and does not do so shortens his days, since the participants did not give him the honor to bless. And even though according to the law he should bless, it is because of his honor; and since he waived his honor, his honor is waived, and he is no longer obligated to bless. On the contrary, the one who was honored by the distinguished person is obligated to bless. And it seems to me that if the participants honored the distinguished person, he is not permitted to honor another. However, if the distinguished person has to clear his throat, which is called "huston," he may pass the honor to another because there would be an interruption due to the repulsive spitting, and the participants would find it objectionable (Magen Avraham).

It appears to me that all of this applies when there is no host with guests, but rather a gathering where each person eats their own food or at a communal mitzvah meal. However, when there is a host and everyone is eating from his food, he takes precedence over everyone else since it is his meal. Nonetheless, he has the authority to honor whomever he wishes. It seems that it is incumbent upon him to honor the most distinguished guest. Thus, our sages have said (Baba Metzia 46a): "The host breaks bread and the guest recites grace," so that the guest may bless the host, even if the host is greater than him; this is for the benefit of the host so that he may be blessed. This is not an obligation on the host but rather good advice and proper conduct; if the host relinquishes this blessing and prefers to recite the grace after meals himself, he is permitted to do so. He can also honor whomever he wishes, even if that person is not the most distinguished guest. (This is the intention of the Rema at the end of section 1 and resolves the question of the Magen Avraham in subsection 2; see there. Examine closely and you will find it easy.) It is obvious that someone who pays for his meal, like at an inn, is not considered a guest but a host. (There, and regarding what is written, "if two eat..." his words are not clear to me.)

What is the blessing that the guest recites for the host? "May it be Your will that this host should not be shamed in this world, nor humiliated in the World to Come; and may he be very successful in all his possessions, and may his possessions and our possessions be successful and close to the city; and may Satan not have power over his handiwork nor over our handiwork, and may no sinful thought or transgression or iniquity come before him or us from now and forever." This is the version in the Talmud (Berachot 46a). It is clear that nowadays, when everyone recites the Grace After Meals, every guest is obligated to recite this blessing even if the host did not honor him with the invitation to recite the zimun. (And perhaps now we do not say at all that the guest blesses, because we follow the reason. Pay attention and you will find it easy.)

It is a simple matter that a Kohen (priest) takes precedence over everyone, as it is a commandment to honor him, which is included in "and you shall sanctify him." However, a Jewish scholar (Talmid Chacham) takes precedence over an ignorant High Priest (Kohen Gadol Am Ha'aretz). The scholar is not required to honor him according to the laws and customs of priesthood, but the scholar may give him permission to bless as a form of respect. And a Kohen who is a scholar should be given precedence. All of this applies when there is no homeowner present. Also, the Kohen can honor someone else, which is not comparable to being called up to the Torah, as I wrote in Siman 135; see there. A Levi (Levite) does not have precedence. And one who is given the opportunity to bless and does not do so shortens his days. This only applies when there is a cup of blessing (Magen Avraham, subsection 5). It is a commandment to ensure he is given a cup of blessing to bless if he is worthy of it.

A general rule appears to me regarding blessings: Any blessing that the Sages established for a specific type [of food] – one does not fulfill his obligation with a different blessing, even though that type of food has a connection to the blessing. And only in a place where the Sages explicitly said that one fulfills his obligation, such as if one blessed "Borei Pri Ha'adama" (Creator of the fruit of the ground) on the fruit of a tree, or "Shehakol" (by whose word everything came to be) on any item, as it is taught (Berachot 40b): "If he blessed on the fruits of the tree 'Borei Pri Ha’adama', he has fulfilled his obligation; and for all [foods], if he said 'Shehakol', he has fulfilled his obligation." But regarding what is taught at the beginning of the chapter "Keitzad Mevarchin": "On the fruits of the tree one says 'Borei Pri Ha’etz' except for wine, for on wine one says 'Borei Pri Hagafen'; and on the fruits of the ground one says 'Borei Pri Ha’adama' except for bread, for on bread one says 'Hamotzi' etc.," if one blessed "Borei Pri Ha’etz" on wine or "Borei Pri Ha’adama" on bread, he has not fulfilled his obligation. A clear proof of this is that if it were not so, why did the Mishnah not teach that if one blessed 'Ha’etz' on wine or 'Ha’adama' on bread, he has fulfilled his obligation, just as it taught that if one blessed 'Ha’adama' on the fruit of the tree, he has fulfilled his obligation, or that for all [foods], if he said 'Shehakol', he has fulfilled his obligation. Rather, it is certain that in these cases, he does not fulfill his obligation because the Sages completely removed [these blessings] from their previous context, and so I have seen written in the name of our Rabbis, the Ra’ah and Ritva, and other great [authorities] (Birkei Yosef, Siman 207, Shiyurei Beracha). And there are those who wrote that one fulfills his obligation with bread if he blessed 'Ha’adama' (Chaye Adam, Klal 58, Nishmat Adam), and there are those who are uncertain (Kesef Mishneh, Chapter 4, Halacha 6). And so wrote one of the commentators on the Shulchan Aruch in Siman 208: that if one blessed 'Borei Pri Ha’etz' on wine, he has not fulfilled his obligation (Magen Avraham, Sk22). And it also appears to me that if one blessed 'Borei Minei Desha’im' (Creator of the various kinds of herbs) on vegetables, he has not fulfilled his obligation (since we hold according to the Rabbis in the Mishnah there, and see what I wrote in Siman 208). Anyone who deviates from the formula established by the Sages has not fulfilled his obligation and must bless again properly.

Our Sages said (Bava Kama 30a): "He who wishes to be pious should observe the matters of blessings." The explanation seems to be as follows: A pious person goes beyond the letter of the law. Now, regarding blessings, it is established that 'in cases of doubt concerning blessings, one should be lenient.' The pious person removes himself from this leniency. For example, if he is in doubt whether he recited the "Borei Nefashot" blessing or not – and one need not recite it in cases of doubt – the pious person will eat or drink something more and then recite the "Borei Nefashot" blessing. Similarly, if there is something for which it is doubtful whether to say the blessing "Ha'etz" or "Ha'adama," the general rule is to recite "Ha'adama." The pious person will eat two different things, one requiring "Ha'etz" and the other "Ha'adama," to ensure he properly fulfills the blessing requirement. Likewise, if there is doubt whether a final blessing is needed, such as not knowing if he consumed an olive's volume within the specified time – and one need not recite it in cases of doubt – the pious person will eat enough to ensure it is within the specified time and will then recite the blessing. The same applies to drinking hot beverages and similar cases. In all types of doubts, the pious person seeks to remove himself from uncertainty. Certainly, a pious person will not rely on what is stated in the Mishnah: "For all [types of food], if one said 'Shehakol' he has fulfilled his obligation," and one who absolves himself in every case with the "Shehakol" blessing is considered ignorant (Eliyah Rabbah, section 1, in the name of the AriZal).

And it appears to me, in my humble opinion, that there is a legal remedy to absolve oneself from any doubt regarding the after-blessing. For example, if one is in doubt whether they recited the after-blessing or not, or if they need to recite the after-blessing or not, there is a way to remove oneself from the realm of doubt. This is because it is established for us that if one says, "Blessed is the Merciful One, Master of the Universe, for this bread" — they have fulfilled the obligation of the blessing of HaMotzi, as I wrote in Siman 167. Therefore, one can say: "Blessed is the Merciful One, Master of the Universe, Creator of numerous souls, etc." If one is obligated in this blessing, they have fulfilled it with this; and if they are not required to bless, they have not taken the name of Heaven in vain, as there is no mention of God’s name at all, and one can say "Merciful One" a hundred times. This applies similarly to other blessings, and one should intend in their heart that if a blessing is required, this is for the sake of a blessing; and if not, it is merely a statement. This is my practice many times when drinking hot beverages (and I have seen someone write that this too is considered a blessing in vain, but it does not seem so to me at all).

Another important principle regarding blessings: One is required to recite a blessing before eating or drinking any amount, as long as the intention is to eat or drink it. However, if the intention is only to taste the dish to see if it is good or not, no blessing is required. There are differing opinions on this, which will be explained in section 210. When one takes something for medicinal purposes: if it does not taste good, no blessing is necessary; if it tastes good, a blessing is required, since in any case the palate derives pleasure from it, as will be explained in section 204. If others force someone to eat or drink and he does not want to, Rabbi Rema rules that even if he derives pleasure from it, no blessing is necessary. However, there are differing opinions on this, which will be explained there with the help of Heaven.

And this is regarding the first blessing, but for the final blessing: for eating, one needs an olive's worth, and less than this does not require a final blessing. And this is the measure of half an egg, and some say a third of an egg, and we hold primarily that it is half an egg. Consequently, the pious person will eat either less than a third or about half an egg. In drinking, the opinion of the Rambam in chapter 3 is that a quarter of a log is needed, and the Tosafot and the Rosh are uncertain about this, as perhaps an olive's worth is sufficient. And this has already been written by the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch in siman 209, and our master, the Beit Yosef in siman 210, holds primarily like the Rambam, as it appears there, and it is reasonable that a doubt does not override a certainty, and thus we are accustomed to rule by a quarter of a log, and the pious person should see himself to remove the doubt. And we have already written in siman 209, section 4, that an olive's worth is much less than a quarter of a log, as mentioned there.

The measure of eating an olive's bulk is only when one eats the olive's bulk within the time it takes to eat half a loaf of bread. However, if one eats it in more time than this measure, one does not need to say the final blessing. And how much is the time to eat half a loaf of bread? According to Maimonides, it is the time it takes to eat three eggs, and according to Rashi, it is the time it takes to eat four eggs, as written in section 612 [of the Shulchan Aruch]. And with regard to a complete entity, there is doubt, perhaps one does not need an olive's bulk, as written in section 210, and it will be clarified there with the help of Heaven, and the pious person should be careful about all of this. 

Regarding the measure of drinking a quarter-log, Maimonides ruled on the matter of prohibitions in Chapter 14 of Forbidden Foods, Law 9, and this is his language: "Similarly, one who drinks a quarter-log… little by little… or drank blood little by little: if the time from beginning to end was sufficient to drink a quarter-log, they combine; if not, they do not combine," end quote. And he ruled similarly regarding Yom Kippur in Chapter 2 of Resting on the Tenth [Day], and similarly regarding terumah in Chapter 10 of Terumot, see there. And in the Tosefta of Yoma, Chapter 4, it is explicitly stated thus, and this is the language of the Tosefta: "He drank and drank again: if there was from the beginning of the first drinking to the end of the last drinking the time sufficient to drink a quarter-log, they combine; if not, they do not combine," end quote. 

And one should not be astonished about what is relevant in drinking a quarter-log to the time it takes to drink a quarter-log, for this is the explanation: it is not usual to drink a quarter-log in one go, for that is gluttony, as we say: "One who drinks his cup in one go is a glutton, in two goes is the way of the world," and it is customary to pause a little and drink leisurely, which requires some time. Therefore, according to Maimonides, even for the final blessing, it is the same: if one waited more than the time it takes to drink a quarter-log, one does not need to say the final blessing. Refer to what I wrote in Yoreh De'ah, section 85.

According to this, when drinking hot beverages like tea or coffee, where one takes some time to drink a revi'it (a specific measure), there is no need for an after-blessing. However, a pious person should try to drink a revi'it without delay in order to say the after-blessing, due to the opinion of the Ra'avad which will be explained. One should not argue that since it is customary to drink hot beverages little by little, they are not comparable to other drinks, for we have already explained in Section 290, Paragraph 4, that there is no distinction between different types of drinking, to counter the opinion of those who believe that for strong spirits one should say an after-blessing even on less than a revi'it. The sages did not differentiate between different types of drinking, as agreed upon by the great later authorities.

Indeed, the Tur and Shulchan Aruch later in Siman 612 regarding Yom Kippur brought that the Ra'avad holds that the combining of drinking [amounts] is also considered like the eating of a "pras" (half a loaf) as eating. And many agreed with his words, as it is explicitly stated in Keritot (12b) regarding impurity, that the invalidation of the body by combining drinking is like combining eating, see there. And the Rambam himself ruled so in Chapter 8 of the Laws of the Fathers of Impurities, see there. And one must say that he holds that we do not learn from impurity, and we do not derive prohibitions from impurity, or one might say that since bodily impurity is rabbinic, they did not want to differentiate between eating and drinking. And behold, in any case, there is a dispute regarding the measure of combining a quarter-log of drinking. And there is a great difference between them, for the eating of a "pras" is certainly like three or four minutes, and the drinking of a quarter-log certainly does not reach half or a third of this measure. Therefore, the pious person should be cautious about this as mentioned in the previous section or accustom himself to bless "Blessed is the Merciful," as mentioned in Section 3.

Here is the translation of the passage:

"Behold, regarding prohibitions, the Rambam writes in Chapter 14 of Ma'achalot Asurot that an olive-sized portion is exclusive of what is between the teeth, but what is between the gums counts. If an olive-sized portion of forbidden fat or carrion... was left in the sun and reduced in size - one who eats it is exempt. If it was then left in the rain and swelled - one is liable for karet or lashes. If it was less than an olive-sized portion initially and swelled to an olive-size - it is forbidden but one does not receive lashes for it," end quote. And it seems clear that the same applies to the after-blessing; we go according to the current state of the food. If it currently has an olive-sized portion, one recites an after-blessing. If it does not currently have an olive-sized portion, even if it initially had an olive-sized portion, one does not recite an after-blessing. If it did not have an olive-sized portion initially and then swelled to an olive-size, one does not recite an after-blessing. And it is clear that in spongy food that has many holes, the holes do not combine to form an olive-sized portion (as the Shulchan Aruch writes in Siman 210 in the name of the Pri Chadash). It further seems to me, as taught in the beginning of Chapter 3 of Taharot: "The broth and the grits and the milk: when they are liquid to the touch - they are considered primary, if they congealed - they are considered secondary." Meaning, since they congealed, they are considered as food - similarly, regarding the after-blessing, if the water congealed and one ate them in their congealed state, one must recite an after-blessing on an olive-sized portion, and similarly for other liquids. In this matter, there is no distinction between impurity and other matters. And it further seems to me that one who eats snow or hail or frost and ice and enjoys it, such as if he is thirsty and the like - must recite an after-blessing on an olive-sized portion. And even though for a mikvah they complete forty se'ah as water, as stated in Chapter 7 of Mikvaot, nevertheless, in terms of eating it now, it is considered eating and not drinking, and this is a fortiori from the broth of the Mishnah in Taharot that we mentioned (and see Niddah 17a, and this requires further study)."

All foods combine to make up an olive's bulk (kezayit), and all beverages combine to make up a quarter-log (revi'it) (Magen Avraham 210:1). Even if one ate half an olive's bulk of something that requires the blessing "Al HaMichya" and half an olive's bulk of something that requires the blessing "Borei Nefashot" — they combine for the blessing "Borei Nefashot." Similarly, for beverages, if one drank half a quarter-log of wine and half a quarter-log of other beverages — they combine for the blessing "Borei Nefashot." However, eating and drinking do not combine (ibid), as their measures and benefits are not the same. 

All preparations for food that come to enhance the food itself are considered food, like sauce on vegetables or liquid absorbed in food, and they combine to make up an olive's bulk (ibid). However, when the liquid stands alone, it does not combine. Hence, foods fried in honey like tayglach, peretzkas, or ayin gimachts, or foods fried in butter like kreplach, blintzes, pampushkas, taygach, or foods fried in the fat of the butter or the fat on the food — they combine to make up an olive's bulk, for liquid that comes for food is considered food (Shabbat 144b).

It seems to me that foods stuffed with meat, eggs, or cheese — the meat, eggs, and cheese do not combine to make up an olive's bulk for the blessing "Al HaMichya," since they stand on their own, and if there is not an olive's bulk of flour, one blesses "Borei Nefashot" if these fillings make up an olive's bulk. Similarly, when butter is spread on bread or crackers — the butter does not combine, since it is a solid and stands on its own. However, when oil or fat is spread, it combines, as it is absorbed into them and is like the sauce on vegetables (so it seems according to my humble opinion in these matters).

One does not recite a blessing over food or drink until the food or drink is in front of them, as stated in Siman 206, and it must also be ready to be eaten or drunk. For example, if one is eating nuts or almonds: one should not recite the blessing until the first nut or almond is cracked, because if one blesses before cracking it, the act of cracking constitutes an interruption. This is not similar to the cutting of bread, where one completes the cutting after the blessing of "Hamotzi," as stated in Siman 167, because in the case of bread, the food is visible before us, and the completion of cutting is immediate, which is not the case with nuts where the food is covered and the cracking is not immediate. Therefore, one should crack it before the blessing. Similarly, if one is eating an apple and does not intend to eat it until it is peeled, one should bless after peeling it so that the peeling does not constitute an interruption. This applies to all similar cases. Likewise, in the case of drinking, if the beverage is in a jug and it is poured into a cup and drunk from the cup, one should not bless until it is poured into the cup. Similarly, if the food or drink is very cold or very hot, making it impossible to eat or drink until some time has passed, one should not bless until it is fit to eat or drink. This applies to all similar cases. (See Eliyah Rabbah, Siman 1, who brings someone who says to bless before cracking the nut or peeling so that one blesses over the whole item, but this is not reasonable at all. See there that his conclusion is also not so, and examine it well.)

For all fruits of the tree, whether from the seven species or from other species: their initial blessing is 'Who creates the fruit of the tree'. And although their growth is from the ground like the fruit of the earth, and therefore, in truth, if one blessed 'Who creates the fruit of the ground' on them, he has fulfilled his obligation, nevertheless, initially, they established a more specific blessing for them due to their importance, for the more important something is, the more specific its blessing should be, to give praise to the Holy One, blessed be He, who created such an important thing. And the wording of the blessing is 'Who creates the fruit of the tree' and not 'the Creator', for every blessing must refer to the past. And although 'the Creator' is also a past tense, like 'Who brings forth bread from the earth', nevertheless 'creates' is more specific language, and in 'Who brings forth' the reason is to avoid mixing the letters, as stated in Siman 167. And even according to the other reason we wrote there, to show precision in language, 'Who brings forth' suffices, and therefore all the blessings are without the definite article, like 'Who creates the fruit of the tree', 'Who creates the fruit of the ground', 'Who creates various kinds of sustenance' (Machtzit Hashekel subparagraph 1). And we have already explained there in paragraph 7 that this is present tense language, indicating His providence at all times and every moment, see there.

And for wine, due to its importance, they established its own blessing: "Borei Pri Hagafen" ("Who creates the fruit of the vine"), whether it is undiluted or cooked. Even though cooked wine is inferior to undiluted wine and does not have the status of yayin nesech (wine used for idolatrous purposes), and according to Rashi, one does not sanctify on it nor bless "Borei Pri Hagafen" over it, as the Tur writes later in Siman 272, most of our Rabbis disagree on this as the Tur writes there. Similarly, our Rabbis, the Tosafists, write in Bava Batra (97a) and the Rosh there, and so the Tur and Shulchan Aruch conclude in Siman 1. Likewise, diluted wine is also blessed with "Borei Pri Hagafen." This refers specifically to their wines which were strong, but our wines, when mixed with a little water, lose their wine taste and the blessing is "Shehakol" (the general blessing). However, not all wines are the same in this regard. And if one blessed "Borei Pri Ha'etz" (the blessing for fruit of the tree) on wine, he has not fulfilled his obligation, as stated in Siman 1. Furthermore, if one made konditon from wine, meaning adding honey and pepper to it, its blessing is still "Borei Pri Hagafen," and this is not widely known to us.

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote in section 1: If wine was mixed with beer, we follow the majority: if the majority is wine, one blesses 'Borei Pri HaGafen', and if the majority is beer, one blesses 'Shehakol'. And we do not follow the taste, because since both are obligated in a blessing, it follows that we go after the majority, which is primary (Taz, subsection 1). Additionally, it appears to me that certainly if there is no wine taste present, one does not bless 'Borei Pri HaGafen' on it even if the majority is wine. Here, we are discussing fig beer (Magen Avraham, subsection 3) that has sweetness similar to wine. But our beer or other beverages that nullify the taste of the wine - the majority wine does not help at all. And when the wine is less than the fig beer, even if it has a wine taste - we follow the majority and bless 'Shehakol'.

And know that for wine made from raisins, we bless over it 'Borei Pri HaGafen' (Who creates the fruit of the vine), and we use it for Kiddush and Havdalah as mentioned in Siman 272. Indeed, even regarding libations in the Temple, it is valid after the fact, as it is stated in Bava Batra (96a). And in all our regions, wine is not available at all, except what is made from raisins, as is known. However, I have always been troubled by this, for behold, the Rif there, and the Rambam in Chapter 29 of Shabbat, and the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch in Siman 272, explicitly wrote that we require that even from the raisins themselves without water, a little wine should come out, but otherwise it is not considered wine, as mentioned there. And behold, our raisins from which we make wine have no moisture of wine at all, and only by soaking them in water for a long time does the water have the taste of wine. How then do we bless over it 'Borei Pri HaGafen' and use it for Kiddush and Havdalah and bless 'Borei Pri HaGafen'? And if we come to change and say to bless 'Shehakol' (Who creates everything) they will not heed us, for this is our custom from our forefathers and no one protests, and we ourselves do so, and how have we found our hands and feet in this matter?

And it is necessary to justify the custom of Israel, for it is known the dispute among the early authorities regarding the principle of "taste as substance." Rashi and the Rambam hold that it is of rabbinic origin, as the Rambam writes in Chapter 15 of Forbidden Foods, that even if the substance of the prohibition is dissolved within the permitted substance, if one does not consume an olive's bulk of the prohibition itself within the time it takes to eat a piece of bread, he is not liable for lashes, and certainly this applies when it is only the taste. But Rabbeinu Tam and the Raavad rule that "taste as substance" is prohibited by Torah law, as the Tur writes in Yoreh De'ah, Section 98, see there. According to this, we can say that the Rif and the Rambam, who required that some wine must come out from the raisins themselves, followed their opinion that "taste as substance" is of rabbinic origin, and we rely on Rabbeinu Tam and the Raavad that "taste as substance" is of Torah origin. If so, it follows that when the water absorbs the taste of the wine hidden in the grapes, and there is no greater example of "taste as substance" than this, therefore, we bless over it "Borei Pri HaGafen." However, it is certain that with our raisin wine, if even a little water or other beverage is mixed in, it completely spoils the taste, and we bless over it "Shehakol." And the laws that have been explained, like conditon and mixtures of wine with beer, do not apply to our raisin wine, and in Section 204, Clause 16, a good reason for this will be explained, see there.

Every fruit of the tree, as soon as the fruit has grown a bit and one wants to eat it, one recites the blessing "Borei Pri Ha'etz" (Who creates the fruit of the tree) even though it has not fully ripened, as long as it is fit to be eaten, even with difficulty, since it is intended to be eaten and he is eating it. However, if it is not fit to be eaten at all, even with difficulty, such as if it is very bitter or very astringent, which is called "zoyar," one does not bless on it at all, and it is considered like a regular tree. And if it is made fit by fire, one blesses "Shehakol" (Who creates everything), for it is still not considered a fruit of the tree. Therefore, all types of apples, all types of pears, and all types of cherries, even though they have not fully ripened yet, since they can be eaten with difficulty, one blesses on them "Borei Pri Ha'etz."

And with grapes, it is not so, for as long as they are still immature and have not reached the size of a white bean, one blesses over them 'Borei Pri Ha'adama' (Who creates the fruit of the ground). The reason for this is because the primary purpose of grapes is to make wine from them. Therefore, as long as they have not reached this size, they are not suitable for making wine, and their blessing is not 'Ha'etz' (the fruit of the tree) but 'Ha'adama' like other fruits of the ground, as the name 'grapes' is not applicable to them. The size of a white bean is not known to us, and therefore one always blesses 'Borei Pri Ha'adama' on them until it is visibly apparent that they are fully ripe. This is not against the law, for if one blessed 'Ha'adama' on 'Ha'etz', he has fulfilled his obligation after the fact. Therefore, as long as there is doubt, one blesses 'Ha'adama'.

And there are those who say that one does not bless 'Ha'etz' on carobs until they appear in clusters like carob chains, and similarly with olives until the blossom grows around them, for before this they do not have the status of fruit at all and one blesses 'Ha'adama' on them. And our Rabbi, the Rema, wrote that this is the primary opinion, but there are those who disagree with this (see Magen Avraham, section 5). And we have no knowledge in this matter because they do not grow in our country.

Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote in Section 3: "The seeds of fruits: if they are sweet, one recites 'Borei Peri Ha'etz' (Who creates the fruit of the tree) over them, but if they are bitter, one does not recite a blessing over them at all. If they are improved by fire, one recites 'Shehakol' (Who creates everything) over them." This is because he considers seeds as the fruit itself, as they are subject to the laws of Orlah, as it is taught in the first chapter of Orlah: "The shells of nuts and the seeds are subject to Orlah." From this, Tosafot and the Rosh in Berachot (37b) deduced that their blessing is 'Ha'etz'. However, the Rashba disagrees, maintaining that seeds are certainly not considered part of the fruit, and one does not recite 'Ha'etz' over them but 'Ha'adamah' (Who creates the fruit of the ground). Regarding Orlah, there is a derivation that includes what is secondary to the fruit from 'its fruit', but this does not apply to blessings. Many great authorities were concerned with his opinion and ruled to recite 'Ha'adamah' over seeds, while some are careful to recite only 'Shehakol' (see Ba'er Hetev and Shulchan Aruch HaRav 6 and Magen Avraham 7). It is best to recite 'Ha'adamah', as this way we fulfill the opinion of Tosafot and the Rosh, since one fulfills the obligation with 'Ha'adamah' even on the fruit of the tree in a post-factum situation. (The Magen Avraham 7 questioned why it was ruled to recite 'Shehakol' if improved by fire, what is the difference from almonds, see there, and I am puzzled as he himself ruled this way in section 5, see there and examine well.) In section 23, the difference between various types of seeds will be explained, see there.

All liquids that come from any fruits, such as when one squeezes them and extracts juices - they are considered mere sweat and their blessing is 'Shehakol' (the general blessing for food and drink), because people do not plant fruit with the intention of extracting juice, except for olives and grapes, whose primary planting intention is for oil and wine. For these, their blessing is 'Ha'etz' (the blessing for tree fruits), and for wine, a special blessing 'Hagafen' is established due to its importance. However, for oil, the blessing is 'Ha'etz' like for the olives themselves. 

Nevertheless, it is a rare situation to bless on olive oil, because if one drinks oil as it is, it would harm them and one would not bless on it at all. If one eats it with bread, the bread is considered the main item and the oil secondary, so one blesses on the main item and it includes the secondary. The only case you would find is when one drinks oil for medicinal purposes and eats a little bread with it so the oil does not harm them, then one blesses on the oil because the main intention is on the oil (as stated there, section 8). Similarly, when one mixes the oil with other liquids so the oil does not harm them, and their intention is only for the oil - they bless 'Ha'etz' (as stated there). 

And even though their intention is for medicinal purposes, since they derive benefit from it - they are obligated in a blessing. And only because it is the nature of oil to harm the palate when drunk alone, they take something else as well, but their main intention is for the oil. The Rambam in chapter 8 ruled that if one drinks oil, they bless 'Shehakol', and this is questionable, and the Tur already criticized him.

And similarly, it is stated in the Gemara (Berachot 36a): for example, someone who has a sore throat and drinks oil as a remedy mixed with beet juice, which is called “anigron,” then not only does it not harm him, but on the contrary, it benefits the throat. In this case, the oil is considered primary, and he recites the blessing "Borei Peri Ha'etz" (Who creates the fruit of the tree) on it, even if the oil is less than the beet juice (there, 9), because his main intention is for the oil, so he blesses "Ha'etz." Therefore, if he does not have a sore throat and his intention is not for healing but for eating, then the anigron is considered primary, even if it is less than the oil, and its blessing is "Shehakol" (Who creates everything), because the anigron is primary and the oil is secondary, and he blesses on the primary and exempts the secondary (from all this, it is evident that there is benefit in drinking oil, and among us, this is not known. Perhaps their oil was better than ours, and this requires further investigation).

There are two types of almonds: sweet and bitter. The sweet ones are like all other fruits. The bitter ones, when they are mature, are not fit for consumption due to their bitterness and do not fall under the category of [fruits that require a blessing]. They are used as a spice, but in and of themselves, they are not fit for consumption at all. However, when they are small, the peel around them is sweet, and they are eaten because of the peel. Many people plant them for this purpose, to eat them when they are small, and therefore, one recites the blessing "Borei P'ri Ha'etz" over them. When the mature ones are prepared through fire or another method, one also recites "Borei P'ri Ha'etz" over them. This is not similar to the seeds mentioned in section 19, where one recites "Shehakol" in such a case, because there, the seed is not the primary part of the fruit. Therefore, when they are only fit for consumption through fire, they are not considered fruit. But here, the almond is the primary part of the fruit, and its consumption is through fire, and they are planted for this purpose, to sweeten them through fire. This is their primary method of consumption, and it is proper to recite "Borei P'ri Ha'etz" (according to Levush, and this is the intention of the Magen Avraham in section 13). What is this similar to? To vegetables that are only eaten after being cooked, and we recite "Borei P'ri Ha'adama" over them, as stated in Siman 204. The same applies here.

In the time of our Rabbis, there was a type of tree called a caper bush, which has four edible parts: the first is the main fruit called 'aviot', the second is a large peel that grows around the fruit similar to thin walnut shells and is called 'kapritsin', the third are the leaves which are also edible, and the fourth are the shoots that grow among the leaves. The planting is primarily for the main fruit, and therefore on the 'aviot' one blesses 'Borei Pri Ha'etz' (Who creates the fruit of the tree), and on the 'kapritsin', leaves, and shoots one blesses 'Borei Pri Ha'adama' (Who creates the fruit of the ground). The general rule for the fruits of trees is: for whatever the main intention of the planting is, one blesses 'Ha'etz', and for whatever the intention of the planting is not, one blesses 'Ha'adama'. Seeds, for which one blesses 'Ha'etz', are because the intention is for the seeds themselves, as there are fruits where the main taste is in the seeds. When there is doubt whether the planting is for this intention, one blesses 'Ha'adama'. According to this, it seems clear to me that what has been explained, that one blesses 'Ha'etz' on seeds, only applies to fruits that are full of seeds, like raisins, figs, pomegranates, and similar, where when eating them, one eats them with their seeds. But the seeds of apples, pears, and similar fruits, which are eaten without their seeds, one does not bless 'Ha'etz' on the seed but rather 'Ha'adama' or 'Shehakol', and this appears to me to be the main ruling (and according to the Rambam in chapter 11 of Terumot, there is a distinction in types of seeds, see there).

The Rambam wrote in Chapter 8, Law 4: "Dates that one has mashed by hand and removed their pits, making them like a dough—one blesses over them first 'Borei Pri Ha'etz' and afterward 'Me'ein Shalosh.'" This means that one should not think that the blessings 'Borei Pri Ha'etz' and 'Me'ein Shalosh' apply only when eating the fruit as it is, with its form recognizable, but that when one mashes it into a kind of dough, it loses its status. This is not so. And this is the language of the Gemara (38a): "And the halacha is that if one makes dates into a mash, one blesses over them 'Borei Pri Ha'etz'. What is the reason? Because they remain in their original form." And it is obvious that this is the same law for all fruits. Therefore, our povidla, where the fruits are mashed and cooked until they dry and are cut into pieces, one blesses over them 'Borei Pri Ha'etz'. And so wrote Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) in his commentary on the words of Rabbi Yosef Karo in paragraph 7, who quoted the Rambam's language: "And accordingly, for the lutarin called povidla, one blesses over them 'Borei Pri Ha'etz'."

However, afterward, it is written that there are those who say to recite "shehakol" over them. And it is good to be stringent initially and recite "shehakol," but if one recited "borei pri ha'etz," he has fulfilled his obligation, as this seems to be the main ruling. And it has been clarified that the opinions of our masters, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, are to recite "ha'etz," except that our teacher, the Rema, was stringent initially according to the opinion of those who say otherwise. And this is the opinion of the Terumat HaDeshen in Siman 29, who ruled to recite "shehakol." And in my humble opinion, the matter of the Terumat HaDeshen is entirely different, so I am compelled to explain them. But first, we will explain the words of the Tur, which seem very perplexing at first glance, and afterward, we will explain the words of the Terumat HaDeshen, with God's help.

And this is the language of the Tur: "Dates that have been slightly crushed but not completely mashed - one says the blessing 'Borei Peri Ha'etz' (Creator of the fruit of the tree), but for the honey that flows from them, one says 'Shehakol' (that everything was created by His word). And the Ba'al Ha'Itur wrote that this is specifically if water was mixed with it, but if it is in its original form, one says 'Borei Peri Ha'etz'. And Rabbi Yitzchak did not differentiate. And Rambam wrote: Date honey - one says 'Shehakol', but dates that were mashed by hand and made into a dough - one blesses 'Borei Peri Ha'etz' initially and at the end... And it is possible that Rabbi Yitzchak also agrees with this matter, since they are in their original form - they are considered the main fruit according to everyone." End of quote. 

And he contradicts himself, for earlier he wrote specifically that if they are not completely mashed one says 'Borei Peri Ha'etz', and it is explicitly implied that if they are completely mashed, one does not bless 'Borei Peri Ha'etz', as this is implied from Rashi's explanation on the matter of Terima, where he wrote that Terima is something that is slightly crushed but not mashed. End of quote. 

And it is seemingly explained that if they are mashed, their blessing is not 'Borei Peri Ha'etz'. If so, how could the Tur write afterward that according to everyone they agree with Rambam, since Rambam's case is with completely mashed dates as they are like dough. And the commentators on the Tur (Beit Yosef and Bach) wrote that indeed he retracts his earlier opinion and rejects Rashi's explanation in favor of Rambam. There, and the forced interpretation is evident.

But in truth, it seems to me as the author of the Drisha wrote, that there is no contradiction here at all. And this is what he wrote: "they are not completely crushed" – this means that they are not crushed to the extent that they become like a liquid or honey, for in such a case, Rambam would certainly agree since the food status has been nullified. And Rambam is referring to when the appearance of food is still upon it, but it has become like a dough and its appearance has been mixed up, but nevertheless it is still food, like our "povidla," and in this case, even Rashi agrees that we bless on it "the tree" (and in practice, the Taz also rules this way in section 4, although he struggles with Rashi's wording – see there. According to the Drisha, there is no difficulty, and it is a completely different matter as he wrote). And the term "crushing" means that it becomes like a liquid, as in "we do not crush the snow."

And according to this, I say that the words of the Terumat HaDeshen also pertain to a different matter, and this is his language: "Question: Regarding 'twirga' that is made from dates, which they call 'weinakslin,' they cook them until they are completely dissolved and mix them with spices and honey, should one bless 'Shehakol' or 'Ha'etz' over them? Answer:… indeed, when we carefully examine Rashi's explanation on that matter of 'trima'… it implies that if they are very crushed, we bless 'Shehakol' over them… because they are completely dissolved, etc." End of quote. And our master, the Beit Yosef, in his great book, Siman 204, was astonished at him, questioning why he did not mention the words of the Rambam at all, as he rejected his words. But in truth, this matter is not related at all to the words of the Rambam, who was referring to something that is completely dissolved until it becomes like a liquid, as explained in his language, and this we also have, where they crush the fruits and squeeze them and fry them in honey or syrup, and certainly the blessing on this is 'Shehakol,' and they call this 'sirof.'

Behold, I also found in the Mahari"k (Shoresh 43) and this is his language: "Regarding grapes that are cooked until they become thick and are called 'konfit,' and you were uncertain whether to bless 'Shehakol' or 'Ha'etz' since they have changed for the better... it seems to me that one should bless 'Shehakol'... but this konfit which does not have the appearance of grapes nor the taste of grapes at all... and has not changed for the better but for the worse, etc." End quote. And earlier he wrote that konfit does not come in its usual manner of eating at all, and it was not planted with this intention, etc. End quote. He did not bring the words of the Rambam nor this of terima, but certainly he is referring to when it becomes like a thick beverage. And even in this, he wrote because it changed for the worse and does not have the taste of grapes at all and was not planted with this intention. But our povidla, which is food as before, except that its appearance has become confused and it has also improved as known, and it tastes of the fruit - there is no doubt that one blesses on it 'Borei Pri Ha'etz,' and so I practice and so it should be ruled in practice. (And also the words of the Magen Avraham in Siman 218 support this, differentiating between completely dissolved by cooking and not completely dissolved, but his language is brief, and his intention is not to differentiate between cooked and uncooked. See there well. And see in the Levush who differentiates between crushing and crushing, and already they have contested him. See Eliyah Rabbah Siman 211 who struggled to reconcile it, but according to our words, there is no need for all this. Pay attention well.)

The halachic authorities are divided on what blessing to recite over orange peels: Some say to recite "borei pri ha'etz" (Magen Avraham, section 17), since regarding orlah (the prohibition of eating fruit from a tree during its first three years), we hold that the peel and the seed are subject to orlah (36b), and if so, just as we have ruled that over seeds we recite "borei pri ha'etz," so too over peels. Others say to recite "borei pri ha'adamah" (Taz in section 204, sub-section 15). Their reasoning is that although it is subject to orlah, this is because it protects the fruit, and we derive from the phrase "its fruit" that it includes what is secondary to the fruit, but not for the purpose of the blessing, for one does not plant with the intention of using the peels, and it is like the caper bush's capers, leaves, and shoots mentioned in section 23. Others say to recite "shehakol" (Eliyah Rabbah in section 203, sub-section 2). I do not come to decide the matter, but I have heard clearly that most of our oranges that come from Italy are not the peels of lemons or apples as is commonly said, but they are the primary part of the plant and are like the fruits themselves, as they grow with such peels, and they harvest the fruits and cut them into oranges. If so, surely we bless "borei pri ha'etz" over them. From the day I heard this, I have been blessing "borei pri ha'etz" over them, especially since the first opinion holds this way even if they are peels of fruit (and also the Panim Meirot in section 65 ruled like the Magen Avraham as the Be'er Heitev wrote in sub-section 13, perhaps for the reason we mentioned, and I do not have his book to examine it, and so ruled the Chayei Adam in section 52 to bless "borei pri ha'etz," see there).

We have already written that liquids extracted from all kinds of fruits through squeezing are blessed with "Shehakol" (the blessing for "everything"), as they are considered mere sweat, except for olives and grapes. Therefore, even honey that drips from dates is blessed with "Shehakol." The opinion of the Bahag (Ba'al Halachot Gedolot) is to bless "Ha'etz" (the blessing for "the tree"), as mentioned in Section 26, and perhaps his reasoning is because in the Torah it is written "honey" and it is written "a land flowing with milk and honey," indicating that this is the essence of the fruit. However, all the poskim (halachic decisors) disagree with him, as the honey mentioned in the Torah refers to dates, and they are like all fruits whose blessing is "Shehakol." Similarly, the end-of-season grapes that never ripen fully, and it is impossible to make wine from them and they are made into vinegar, therefore they are not considered grapes, and the blessing on them is "Shehakol." This is not comparable to immature grapes (boser) on which the blessing is "Ha'adamah" (the blessing for "the ground"), because immature grapes are destined to grow, and even now it is possible to make wine from them, therefore they only drop from the level of "Ha'etz" to "Ha'adamah." But these (end-of-season grapes) are treated like the vinegar that comes from them. Similarly, dates called "novlot," which have ripened, burned by the heat, dried out, and it is impossible to make honey from them at all, are not considered dates, and the blessing on them is "Shehakol," as they have significantly deteriorated.

It is stated in the Gemara (39b): "The water of beets is like beets, and the water of turnips is like turnips, and the water of all cooked vegetables is like all cooked vegetables," and similarly the water of dill, which is a vegetable that is put in the pot to sweeten it but not to be eaten (Rashi). From this, it is clear that when vegetables or fruits are cooked in water, one blesses over the broth as one would over the vegetables and fruits themselves. This is not comparable to fruit juices, which are considered mere exudate and their blessing is 'Shehakol,' as stated in the previous section, because there the taste is not like the taste of the fruits. However, the water of cooked vegetables has the same taste as the cooked vegetables themselves, and therefore one blesses over the broth with the same blessing as the fruit itself (Rosh, Chapter 6, Siman 18).
