Similarly, if one cooks a tree fruit and the taste enters the cooking water, one blesses 'Ha'etz' on the water. Accordingly, if one cooks plums or raisins, one blesses 'Ha'etz' on the water as well, and if one cooks carrots or beets, one blesses 'Ha'adama' on the water.

And this is the language of the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch in Siman Reish Heh, Paragraph 2: "For the water in which vegetables were cooked, one recites the same blessing that is recited over the vegetables themselves, even though they only contain the flavor of the vegetable. And these words apply when they were cooked without meat, but if they were cooked with meat, one recites 'Shehakol' over it." End quote. Because there is another flavor besides the flavor of the vegetables, the taste of the vegetable is not primary. Consequently, the same rule applies if vegetables were cooked in vinegar or kvass or beer: one does not recite 'Ha'adamah' over the broth but 'Shehakol,' because there is another flavor besides the vegetables (Taz there, Section 5). According to this, the same rule applies when milk or sour cream is added to cooked beets or other vegetables, as is customary; one also does not recite 'Ha'adamah' over the broth but 'Shehakol.' The general rule is: one does not recite 'Ha'adamah' over vegetable broth unless the vegetables were cooked with water and nothing else was added, so that it only contains the flavor of the vegetables. Whenever the broth has a flavor besides the vegetables, one recites 'Shehakol' over the broth.

All of this applies to vegetables, but regarding fruits, our master the Beit Yosef wrote in this chapter, section 10: "Fruits that were soaked or cooked in water, even though the taste of the fruit enters the water, one only blesses 'Shehakol' on that water." And the Rosh wrote that it is possible that where the taste of the fruit enters the water, one should bless 'Borei P'ri Ha'etz.'" End of quote. The first opinion is that of the Rashba, who differentiates between vegetables and fruits, as he wrote that specifically vegetables that are usually boiled and are not eaten without boiling, like cabbage and beets, the primary way they are eaten is through cooking, and therefore their water is like them. But fruits, whose primary way of eating is when they are raw, and therefore when they are cooked, the broth does not have the status of the fruits. And when there are fruits that are usually only cooked, like dried plums, one blesses 'Ha'etz' on the broth according to the Rashba (Taz, section 8), and similarly with dried apples and pears that are only eaten through cooking, one blesses 'Ha'etz.' (Bach) The same applies to dried apricots, and similarly, dried raisins whose majority of consumption is through cooking.

However, there are those who disagree with this, and they hold that according to the Rashba, one does not recite the blessing of "Ha'etz" on any fruit soup. The reason of the Rashba is that we require items that are primarily planted for cooking purposes, such as vegetables like karvit (cauliflower) and borikas (possibly referring to a type of vegetable). But all types of fruits are primarily planted to be eaten raw, and it does not help that they are dried until they are not fit to be eaten without cooking (Levush and Magen Avraham 222). According to this, even on soup made from plums or any soup made from dried fruits, one would recite "Shehakol". And thus, in practice, due to the principle of doubt in blessings, we are lenient and recite "Shehakol", as after the fact, even according to the Rosh, one fulfills their obligation with this blessing.

And according to the Rambam, there is a different approach to all of this in Chapter 8, Halacha 4, and I am amazed that our rabbis did not mention his words at all. And this is the language of the Rambam: "Vegetables that are usually boiled: if one boiled them, he blesses on their boiling water 'Who creates the fruit of the ground,' provided that he boiled them to drink their water, since the water of boiled vegetables is like the vegetables in a place where it is customary to drink them." End quote. Thus, according to his view, this does not apply to all types of boiled vegetables of ours, like carrots and beets which are cooked to be eaten with the soup, and according to the Rambam, it is only specifically when they are cooked just for their water. And certainly, this does not apply to fruits. And in this matter, his opinion clearly seems to be like that of the Rashba, that this law applies only to vegetables, and even with vegetables, only when the cooking is solely for their water. 

And we also have a practice where they cook whole beets for the broth, and this is called 'rasil,' meaning that the beets are discarded or given to animals. According to this, in practice, we do not bless on any boiled vegetable the specific blessing of the fruit, but only 'Shehakol,' unless one cooks a vegetable for the water, and there is no meat or milk in it, for then according to all opinions, one blesses 'Ha'adama.' And it seems to me that even if one flavors the 'rasil' with one or two eggs as is customary, nevertheless its blessing is 'Ha'adama,' since the eggs are not at all recognizable in the soup as is known, unless one poured many eggs into it. But meat or milk or clotted milk called 'smetana' give a significant flavor to the 'rasil' and one blesses 'Shehakol,' and thus it seems to me to be the practical law.

It appears to me that there is proof for the words of the Rambam that the essence of this matter is that it is made for drinking. For behold, at the beginning of "How to Bless," the Talmud says regarding oil that one drinks it through "Anigron," as Rava said: "Anigron is the water of beets, Ansigron is the water of all cooked vegetables" (see there). Thus, the Talmud calls it drinking. And here, it also says: "Water of beets, water of all cooked vegetables." And it also seems evident from the words of Rabbeinu Yonah, who asked: Since the water of cooked vegetables is like the cooked vegetables themselves, why don't we bless 'the ground' on barley beer as we do on the barley itself? And he answered: Because the way of eating them is with bread (see there). And if you think that when they are cooked it is to eat with the vegetables, this is not similar to beer, but certainly, they are similar to beer, which is cooked initially only for the sake of the drink. And it also becomes clear to me from the words of the Mordechai (see there). (See Magen Avraham, Siman 206, Subsection 6, and there it will be further elucidated with Divine help, see there, and see Nishmat Adam, General 52, what he wrote regarding the intention of the Rambam, and there is no taste in them, see there and examine well).

And regarding the broth of pickled vegetables such as the brine of cabbage and of cucumbers, it appears that their law is like cooking, for the taste is like the vegetables themselves and most of their planting is with the intention that they be pickled, and they eat the vegetable with the broth when they are pickled. Therefore, according to the Rosh and Rashba, when one drinks them, he blesses 'Ha'adama'. But according to what we have explained, according to the Rambam, the blessing is 'Shehakol', because they are not pickled solely for their liquid. Nevertheless, it appears to me that for cabbage, since no water is added but the cabbage itself releases broth, according to the Rambam, one blesses 'Ha'adama' because it has the taste of the cabbage itself, and it is not similar to fruit juices as mentioned in section 32. But the brine of turnips: when one drinks it raw, he blesses 'Shehakol' according to all opinions, because it is not customary to drink it raw but only cooked. And there are those who wrote that the brine of cucumbers is meant to be poured out (Chayei Adam there), but this is not so, and many poor people eat it with bread, and it is also served on the table of the wealthy as is known. And the kvass of beets or from apples - certainly its blessing is 'Shehakol', for it does not have the taste of the fruit and it is merely water, and this is the simple custom (and this is also what the Chayei Adam wrote) (and see Taz at the end of section 10 and his words are puzzling and investigate thoroughly).

Our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 11: "One who drinks the water of soaked raisins or figs or their cooking water - blesses 'Shehakol' [the general blessing for food and drink] and fulfills his obligation according to the Rosh as well. However, regarding the blessing after drinking, there is a doubt whether one should recite 'Borei Nefashot' [a general after-blessing] or 'Me'ein Shalosh' [an abridged version of the three blessings said after eating certain foods]." His words end here.

That is to say, since according to the Rosh, fruit water is like vegetable water, and according to the Rashba, it is not so, as explained. Now, concerning the initial blessing, when one blesses 'Shehakol' according to the Rashba, he also fulfills his obligation according to the Rosh, because for all blessings, if one says 'Shehakol,' he fulfills his obligation. But for the blessing afterward, what should he do? Since they are from the seven species, according to the Rosh, one needs to recite 'Me'ein Shalosh' as for the fruit itself. And if he blesses 'Borei Nefashot' according to the Rashba, he does not fulfill his obligation according to the Rosh. Therefore, 'in cases of doubt regarding blessings, one should rule leniently' and not bless either 'Me'ein Shalosh,' which would be a blessing in vain according to the Rashba, nor 'Borei Nefashot,' which would be a blessing in vain according to the Rosh. Therefore, our master, the Beit Yosef, endeavored to find a solution as will be explained.

It seems to me that if there is no solution, one should bless 'Borei Nefashot,' for we have already explained that the Rambam also holds like the Rashba on this matter. So too, it seems from Rabbeinu Yonah and the Mordechai, and they are many, as I wrote in section 37 (this seems correct in my humble opinion).

And he further wrote: "Therefore, a God-fearing person should only drink within a meal, or eat a fruit of the seven species and also drink water, so that he will need to bless one after-blessing of 'Al HaMichya' and 'Borei Nefashot.' And if he soaked the raisins and separated them from the water - it becomes wine and he blesses 'Borei Pri HaGafen' and one after-blessing of 'Al HaMichya.' This is provided that the raisins have moisture, so that if they were pressed, their juice would come out. But if, when pressed, no moisture or juice comes out - then not." End of quote. And what he wrote previously, that the blessing over the water in which raisins were soaked is 'Shehakol,' is because as long as the raisins are mixed with the water, they do not have the status of wine, but when he soaks and separates them from the water, they have the status of wine, as stated in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 123. There are those who wrote that after three days, even when the raisins are in the wine, they have the status of wine (Taz, Siman 10), and there are those who say that this is also the intention of the Beit Yosef, that when he wrote: "if he soaked and separated them from the raisins," it does not mean that he separated the raisins from the wine, but that the raisins are still mixed with the water, but he drew only the water with a vessel, and previously it referred to taking the water with the raisins in a vessel (Magen Avraham, Siman 27). And what he wrote that it is specifically when they have moisture, we explained in Siman 16, see there. And what he wrote that one should bless 'Al HaMichya' and 'Borei Nefashot,' there are those who say that one should first bless 'Borei Nefashot,' because if he blesses 'Al HaMichya' first, it might exempt 'Borei Nefashot.' But this is not so, because water is certainly not exempted by the blessing of 'Al HaMichya,' and one can precede whichever blessing he prefers (see Magen Avraham, Siman 26).

And know that in the dispute between the Rosh and the Rashba regarding fruit juices, there is still uncertainty that cannot be resolved according to all opinions. For example, if one drinks fig water and also eats figs, what should be done regarding the after-blessing? According to the Rosh, one recites the "Me'ein Shalosh" (a shortened version of the three blessings) on both. However, according to the Rashba, one recites the "Me'ein Shalosh" on the figs and "Borei Nefashot" on the fig water. Therefore, one should also drink regular water or eat something whose after-blessing is "Borei Nefashot" and recite both blessings (Magen Avraham, section 24).

For any fruit that is good both raw and cooked, such as apples and pears, one recites the blessing "Borei Pri Ha'etz" (Who creates the fruit of the tree) whether eating them raw, cooked, or when they are pickled in honey, vinegar, or another liquid. For fruits that are only good raw and lose their taste when cooked, one recites "Ha'etz" (the tree) on the raw fruit and "Ha'adama" (the ground) on the cooked fruit. For pickled fruits: if they are good when pickled, one recites "Ha'etz"; if not, "Ha'adama." Conversely, if the customary way is to eat them cooked and not raw, one recites "Shehakol" (everything) when they are raw and "Ha'etz" when they are cooked or pickled. 

The reason we do not recite "Ha'adama" when they are raw, as we do for unripe fruits, is that since they were planted with the intention to be eaten only after cooking, they are not considered fruits until cooked. This distinction is necessary according to the Tur and Shulchan Aruch in paragraph 12, where "Shehakol" is recited, as well as according to the Tosafot 38b s.v. "Mashkachat" and the Levush.

Our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, wrote in section 13: "A fully matured nut fried in honey, known as Nianadu or Noyat - one blesses 'Borei P'ri Ha'etz' over it. A soft nut that is cooked in honey and is called Nuss Mushkada - one blesses 'Shehakol' over it. Similarly, those nuts that are cooked in honey while they are still green - one blesses 'Shehakol' over them." This is their exact wording.

Now, we are not familiar with this at all, but from the context, it appears that a fully matured nut is suitable for eating even before cooking, and after cooking it is not as good on its own without honey, but in honey it is much better than when it is raw. Therefore, its blessing remains 'Ha'etz' as before cooking. Even though the primary improvement in its cooking is due to the honey, and indeed for this reason the Tur brings an opinion that one should bless 'Shehakol' over it after cooking, the Tur rejects this and his reasoning is clear: since it is good for eating even while raw, its status does not diminish because of the honey, even though the honey improves it. In any case, the nut remains primary and it is the nut that the eater intends, not the honey.

However, the soft nut is not suitable for eating at all while raw, and it can only be eaten through cooking in honey. Therefore, the honey is primary and one blesses 'Shehakol'. Nevertheless, if it were a complete fruit that people plant with the intention of eating it this way, like orange peels, one would bless 'Ha'etz' over it. But it is not a complete fruit and people do not plant it with this intention, therefore its blessing is 'Shehakol'. This is also the reason for the nuts that are cooked in honey while they are still green, which are blessed with 'Shehakol'. There is someone who wrote that this is the same as the soft nut. (The Magen Avraham wrote in section 31 that what is printed as 'similarly those nuts' is a mistake, and it should say 'and they are those, etc.' see there).

The Tosafot and the Rosh (36b, s.v. 'Bartiva') wrote that on sugar, one blesses "Borei Peri Ha'etz" because "the honey of the forest" refers to sugar. Rabbeinu Yonah wrote there that on sukkar (sugar), one blesses "Borei Peri Ha'adama," and he brought this from the Ba'al Halachot Gedolot (BHG). And the Rambam in Chapter 8, Law 5 wrote: "The sweet canes that are squeezed and their liquid is cooked until it solidifies and resembles salt: all the Geonim say that one blesses 'Borei Peri Ha'adama' over them, and some said 'Borei Peri Ha'etz,' and they also said that one who sucks on those canes blesses 'Borei Peri Ha'adama.' But I say this is not fruit, and one does not bless over it except 'Shehakol,' for the honey of these canes, which has changed through intense heat, should not be different than date honey, which has not changed through heat, and one blesses 'Shehakol' over it." End quote. The Tur objected to this, arguing that there is no comparison to date honey, where the primary fruit is the dates, and the honey is like any other liquid that comes from fruits. But for sugar, the primary intent of planting is for the honey, and this is its main fruit, so one blesses "Borei Peri Ha'etz." However, the Rambam's intention seems to be that he considers these canes not to be classified as fruit at all, similar to the Geonim who say to bless 'Ha'adama' because they do not consider it a tree but merely a type of planting. The Rambam holds that it is not fruit at all but merely canes with sweetness. The Tosafot brought proof from the verse "forests with honey" which calls it a forest and thus a tree. The Rambam interprets 'forests' not as referring to 'honey,' but rather the meaning is: forests with honey within the forest. And when he wrote: "the honey of these canes... should not be greater than date honey," his meaning is: certainly, something that produces honey is not called fruit, for date honey is not called fruit even though the Torah called dates 'honey,' nonetheless it is clear to the Rabbis that the intention is on the dates and not the honey, and they removed the verse from its literal meaning, because it is unreasonable to say that honey is fruit. All the more so for these canes, which cannot be called fruit because of their honey, which becomes honey through cooking. Consequently, for the law, we are concerned for the Rambam's opinion and bless 'Shehakol,' which satisfies all views, and so ruled Rabbeinu Beit Yosef in section 15. (This seems to me the Rambam's intention, and on the words of the Kesef Mishneh, the Taz in sk13 and the Gra objected. And what the Magen Avraham wrote in sk32 that it is similar to fruit juices, it is even more difficult, why are they similar to fruit juices, for this is their main fruit. According to our explanation, it is clear, and ponder this well.)

Things that are not normally eaten by themselves but are used as spices in food mixtures, such as dried pepper and ginger, which are called "ingver," and the clove of "gropel," which is called "nagelach," and galangal and cinnamon, and similar items – one does not bless on them at all, because they are not considered food for people, and one who eats them is disregarding the norm of all people, and it is like blessing on mere wood. However, on nutmeg – one blesses "Borei P'ri Ha'etz" ("Who creates the fruit of the tree"), and although it is also used as a spice in foods, nonetheless, it is also eaten dry on its own (Magen Avraham, section 334). And if someone has diarrhea and adds nutmeg to beer to stop it, if he is not thirsty and the primary intention is the nutmeg – he blesses on it "Ha'etz" as with oil in section 20, see there. But if he is thirsty, he blesses "Shehakol" on the beer, because it is primary (there). And on cinnamon, which is "zimring," when eaten dry – one blesses "Ha'adamah" ("Who creates the fruit of the ground"), and although its primary use is as a spice, it nonetheless has a good taste even when eaten by itself, and it is not like ginger. And on pepper and ginger when they are fresh – "Borei P'ri Ha'adamah," because then they are good for eating. And although they are trees, nonetheless, most are planted with the intention that they will dry, and the intention is not to eat them fresh; therefore, their blessing is "Ha'adamah," and their status is like unripe fruit (see Magen Avraham, section 335). The general rule is: any fruits known to be primarily fruits – one blesses on them "Borei P'ri Ha'etz," and those that are not primarily fruits – one blesses "Borei P'ri Ha'adamah," and if one is unsure whether it is primarily a fruit or not – one also blesses "Ha'adamah." And if one does not know at all what it is – one blesses "Shehakol," and one who has not learned should go to a wise person and learn from him the laws of blessings (Talmud Brachot 35a).

On fruits of the earth, one blesses "Who creates the fruit of the ground." And why do we not bless "Who creates the fruit of the land"? Because the term "land" does not refer to the clods of soil, but rather to the name of a country, like "the Land of Israel" or "the Land of Egypt." "Ground" is the term that refers to the actual soil, as it is written: "And the Lord God formed man from the dust of the ground." This is also explained in the section of the first fruits: "And it shall be when you come into the land... and you take from the first of all the fruit of the ground... and now, behold, I have brought the first of the fruit of the ground." 

And why is "fruit of the tree" not written there? Because all seven species are obligated in the first fruits, and among them are wheat and barley. However, vine and fig, etc., are also included in the "fruit of the ground," for this reason, if one blessed "Who creates the fruit of the ground" on a fruit of the tree, he has fulfilled his obligation, and we learn this explicitly from this verse. And this is why in the blessing "Me'en Shalosh" (the condensed version of the three blessings after meals), we conclude with "for the land" and not "for the ground," because that term indeed refers to the Land of Israel. Therefore, in the Land of Israel, we conclude "for the land and its fruits," as it is stated in Siman 208. 

Therefore, it seems to me that if one mistakenly blessed "Who creates the fruit of the land" on a fruit of the ground, he has not fulfilled his obligation and must return and bless "Who creates the fruit of the ground."

There are certain items where it is unclear whether their blessing is "Borei Pri Ha'etz" (Who creates the fruit of the tree) or "Borei Pri Ha'adamah" (Who creates the fruit of the ground). This is because for fully developed trees, whether large or small, their blessing is certainly "Ha'etz", and for types of seeds that are planted every year, their blessing is certainly "Ha'adamah". However, there are small fruits that grow in fields and forests called yagidas, which come in black, red, sweet, and sour varieties. These are not planted but rather grow on their own among the grasses like very small branches, and they are harvested every summer. There is a dispute regarding these. It is clear that if it is difficult to determine according to the depth of the law or if there is doubt, one should recite "Ha'adamah", as this blessing covers even if the proper blessing is "Ha'etz". However, we will clarify according to the halachic determination with the help of Heaven.

And this is the language of the Gemara (40a): "How do we bless 'Creator of the fruit of the tree'? If when you pick the fruit, the branch remains and produces more fruit (Rashi explains). But if when you pick the fruit, the branch does not remain and does not produce more fruit, we do not bless 'Creator of the fruit of the tree' but rather 'Creator of the fruit of the ground'. According to this, even though the main part of the tree remains until the next year, if the branch perishes, we bless 'the fruit of the ground'. And this is the opinion of the Geonim that the Tur brings, and this is his language: 'Any tree that dries up in the winter and its branches and leaves completely perish and then it grows again from its roots - we bless on it 'Creator of the fruit of the ground'' end quote. And this also seems to be the opinion of Behag in chapter six of Berachot.

And this is also the intention of our Rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, in Section 2, where they wrote: "For mulberries that grow on a bush, one recites 'Borei Pri Ha'adama,' because it is not called a tree unless it produces leaves from its wood, but if it produces leaves from its roots, it is not called a tree. And since these completely lose their wood in the winter and then blossom again from their roots, one recites 'Borei Pri Ha'adama' over them." End quote. And "from its wood" means from its branches. According to this, all types of our blackberries, the blessing over them is 'Ha'adama,' even the black ones called 'Schwarzbeeren,' which grow on a small low tree and whose root survives from year to year. Nevertheless, since its branches perish in the winter, one recites 'Ha'adama' over them. I am puzzled by those who wrote that one recites 'Ha'etz' over blackberries (Magen Avraham 1), for this is only according to the opinion of the Rosh in the Tur, who holds that only when the tree survives from year to year does one recite 'Ha'etz.' But we hold like the interpretation of Rashi and the words of the Geonim. Further, I am even more puzzled by the poskim who did not notice that the Rif and Rambam omitted all of this. It seems to me, in my humble opinion, that they interpreted that in the Gemara, this is explained according to Rabbi Yehuda, but according to the Rabbis, a full tree is required. A proof of this is from the Jerusalem Talmud at the end of Chapter 5 of Kilayim, where it concludes that although an item of Kilayim is considered a tree, for the purpose of blessing, it is 'Ha'adama.' (Tosafot there brought this.) This implies that one does not recite 'Borei Pri Ha'etz' unless it is a full tree. Therefore, the Rif and Rambam did not need to bring this down.

Based on this, all types of our strawberries, whether black or red, sweet or sour - we bless over them "Borei Pri Ha'adama" (Who creates the fruit of the ground). There is a type found in winter called "kalinas" which are not suitable for eating at all and people only suck the juice from them - we bless "Shehakol" (everything by His word). And our master the Beit Yosef wrote in section 3 that on the "maazinush" we bless "Borei Pri Ha'etz" (Who creates the fruit of the tree), and we do not know what this is, and similarly on "bromber" and "arper" (Magen Avraham), and we also do not know what these are. But on "vineberries", "smorodines", "agrisin", and "malinas" - we bless "Ha'etz", as they are complete trees and persist well throughout the winter. And I saw someone write that on "malinas" we bless "Ha'adama", which is astonishing, and we indeed bless "Ha'etz" on them. And "rabbinas" are not suitable for eating at all and are put into drinks, and it seems to me that nevertheless, if someone eats them and tastes them - they should bless "Shehakol".

For fruits produced by non-fruit-bearing trees, one recites the blessing 'Shehakol' (that everything was created by His word). This is the ruling of our master, the Beit Yosef, in section 4, and the reason is that these fruits are very poor in quality. However, if they are indeed good for eating, one recites the blessing 'Borei Pri Ha'etz' (who creates the fruit of the tree) (Taz and Magen Avraham, section 2). Therefore, small nuts that are picked from forest trees and are good for eating, their blessing is 'Borei Pri Ha'etz' (ibid.). And he further wrote: Regarding the fruits of the asa tree, even though they are cooked and become like regular fruits, one only recites 'Shehakol' because they are not considered significant at all and are like the fruits of non-fruit-bearing trees, and we have no knowledge of this matter at all. (See Shulchan Aruch HaRav, who wrote in the name of the Arizal to bless 'Ha'etz' on them, and I say that his intention is also when they are fit for good eating, as per the words of the Taz and Magen Avraham. Note this well.)

For ginger, which they call "ingber" that is candied while it is moist - the blessing is "Borei Pri Ha'adamah" (Who creates the fruit of the ground). And even though most ginger is sold in its dried form, nevertheless it is also planted to be eaten in its moist state. It seems that the same rule applies if one candies it when it is dry, since by doing so it becomes fit for eating - the ginger is primary and not the honey, because the intention is for the ginger, and one blesses "Borei Pri Ha'adamah" over it. Similarly, when one roasts ginger and eats it for medicinal purposes - one blesses "Borei Pri Ha'adamah" over it, since it is made fit for eating in this manner (Magen Avraham, Section 4). 

For citrons (etrogim) which they call "cimarin" it is possible that the blessing is "Shehakol" (Who creates everything) since it is made only for flavoring and not for eating (ibid.). For peppercorns when they are candied - the blessing is "Borei Pri Ha'adamah" (ibid.). However, according to our knowledge in the present time, it is clear that they are made only for flavoring, and in our time, we have never heard of candied peppercorns. Maybe in places where they grow, they have a good taste and they do so, but we are not aware of this. 

For ground spices mixed with sugar - the spices are primary and one blesses on them according to the blessing for the spices, whether they are from the fruit of the tree or from the fruit of the ground or "Shehakol".

Radish (tznon) - one blesses "Borei Pri Ha'adama" (Who creates the fruit of the ground) on it. And even though it eventually hardens and is not suitable for eating, nevertheless, its primary planting is to eat it before it hardens. Therefore, on radishes (reita"ch) - one blesses "Borei Pri Ha'adama," and similarly on onions and garlic, because many are eaten raw in our times. On turnips (ribi"n) - one blesses "Ha'adama." As for Brussels sprouts, most are eaten cooked and their primary planting is for this purpose, if one eats them raw - one blesses "Shehakol" (by Whose word all things come into being). It seems to me that the same applies to horseradish (ma'ari"n), but turnips (ribi"n) are mostly eaten raw and are planted with this intention. Horseradish (tamcha), which is called chrain, is not suitable for eating at all, only eaten with meat and fish, and then the horseradish is secondary to them. If one eats horseradish by itself and derives pleasure from it, it seems to me that one should only bless "Shehakol." However, on salad (salata) - one blesses "Ha'adama," because it is good for eating. When frying radish (reita"ch) in honey, called ein gimachtz - one blesses "Ha'adama," even when mixed with nuts, the radish is primary. If the nuts are the majority - one blesses "Ha'etz" (Who creates the fruit of the tree). Similarly, in any case where one fries two types, one from the fruit of the tree and one from the fruit of the ground, follow the majority. When frying sesame in honey, called manalak - one blesses "Ha'adama."

For items that do not grow from the ground, such as the meat of domestic and wild animals, birds, fish, eggs, milk, cheese – one recites the blessing 'Shehakol Nihiyah Bidvaro', which is a general blessing for all things in the world. And even though all living creatures are sustained by the ground, nonetheless their growth is not from the ground (see Eruvin 27b). And we need to understand why the language was changed in the blessing 'Shehakol', and it should have said: 'Who creates everything by His word', just as we say: 'Who creates various kinds of sustenance', 'Who creates the fruit of the tree', 'the fruit of the ground'. Similarly, we should have also said here the language 'Who creates everything by His word'. And it seems that the term 'creation' (Beriah) only applies to something that renews every year, like grain and fruits, for the term 'creation' is about renewal, as in 'In the beginning, God created'. But anything that is continuous, like living creatures and water, the term 'creation' does not apply to them, but rather the term 'existence' (Havayah), meaning 'He spoke and it came to be', and this is why we say 'Shehakol Nihiyah Bidvaro'. And 'Nihiyah' has a segol under the yud, indicating the present tense, and not a kamatz, which would indicate the past tense. For all blessings, we use the intermediate tense that includes both the past and the future, because His providence is constant without a moment's interruption, as stated in Siman 167:7.

And similarly, bread that has become moldy and slightly spoiled, such that it is not as good for eating as before, and similarly a dish whose appearance has changed and is not as good as before, and wine that has curdled and become slightly spoiled to the extent that its smell is like wine but its taste is like vinegar - one blesses over them "Shehakol" (the blessing for foods that do not have a specific blessing), because it is impossible to bless on them their original blessing with the wording "Borei" (Creator), since they have deteriorated from their original creation. And it is obvious that we are discussing a case where it is still possible to eat them with difficulty, because if they are not fit for consumption at all, they are not subject to a blessing, and it is like eating wood and stones.

And similarly, fruits that were damaged from the beginning of their creation, which the Talmud refers to as 'novlot', and these are those that fell from the tree before they ripened (Bach, Magen Avraham, Taz), or dates that ripened and then were scorched by the heat and dried up - their blessing is 'Shehakol'. And it seems to me that falling from the tree only applies to those fruits whose nature is such that they never ripen and their way is to fall before ripening, but those whose nature is to ripen on the tree but fell before ripening - their blessing is 'Borei Pri Ha'etz', for with all fruits except grapes, we bless 'Ha'etz' even while they are still unripe, as it is written in Siman 202, Se'if 17 (and this is also explicitly stated by the Taz, Sk 3).

And so too for the gubai, which are kosher locusts, and for salt and saltwater—one recites "Shehakol." Similarly, for meat broth—one recites "Shehakol," in a case where there is only broth alone. However, if there is any food in it, its blessing follows the blessing of the food when eaten together, as the food is primary and the broth is secondary, unless the food is very minimal and only there to give flavor to the broth like soup, in which case the broth is primary and one recites "Shehakol." The details of this law will be explained with the help of Heaven in Siman 208.

And regarding truffles and mushrooms which are called "she'amalach," when they are eaten on their own after being cooked – their blessing is 'Shehakol.' And even though they also draw sustenance from the ground, nevertheless their growth is from the air, and it is not possible to bless over them 'Borei Pri Ha'adamah.' Truffles are those that are created under the ground and derive their substance from the earth, and mushrooms are a different type that sometimes grow on trees (Pri'sha). And it appears to my humble opinion that if, after the fact, one blessed 'Ha'adamah' on them – he has fulfilled his obligation, since they draw sustenance from the ground. And it is obvious that if they are added to a dish, they are secondary to the dish, and no blessing is recited over them separately.

Our Sages said (Bava Batra 36b) regarding a "korah" (the top of a palm tree when it is soft; see Arukh, entry 'kor'): Rashi explained: "The soft part of the palm tree (dates) when its branches grow every year. The part that grows in this year is soft, and in the second year, it hardens and becomes like wood." End of quote. It is suitable for eating when it is soft, and its blessing is 'Shehakol,' because people do not plant with the intention of eating the 'korah' (Talmud). One might question why we do not bless it as 'Ha'adamah' like we do for 'kaprissin' (caperberries) as mentioned in Siman 202. The difference is that with caperberries, it is known that they will be eaten, albeit they are not the main fruit, and therefore, it only drops one level from 'Ha'etz' to 'Ha'adamah.' But with 'korah,' the planter does not intend for them to be eaten at all, as it is planted to harden and become wood. Therefore, it is not considered a fruit at all, and its blessing remains 'Shehakol' (this appears to me).

Therefore, even those vine shoots that are eaten when they are soft - their blessing is also "Shehakol," because they are not planted with the intention of being eaten at all (Tosafot). Similarly, almonds when they are soft and their outer shell is eaten, and they are not planted with the intention of being eaten at all but rather to eat the kernels when they mature - their blessing is also "Shehakol" (ibid.). This is not similar to unripe grapes (boser), because unripe grapes are eaten as fruit, whereas here the shell is eaten and people do not plant with the intention of eating the shell (Rashba). Therefore, one who eats the pods of legumes while they are still soft and green - also recites "Shehakol," since the main purpose of planting them is so that the pods and legumes will dry out, at which point the pods are not fit for human consumption. However, some say that this applies to legumes in the fields, but for those in the garden where a small amount of legumes are planted to be eaten while still soft - one also recites "Ha'adama" over the pods like on the legumes, because they are planted with this intention (Taz, subparagraph 4). Others say that when the pods are eaten by themselves - the blessing is only "Shehakol" (see Shulchan Aruch, subparagraph 5), and this seems correct, for even if we say that they are planted to be eaten, nevertheless they are like caperberries on a caper bush, since the main intention is for the legumes and not the pods. Therefore, the blessing should be "Shehakol," which satisfies all opinions. However, if one eats them together with the legumes - the blessing is "Ha'adama," which also covers them, as they are secondary to the legumes.

And for "chaziz," which is grain fodder that has not reached a third of its growth, we recite 'Shehakol,' because its growth is not complete (Eruvin 28b). And even though for fruit from the tree we recite 'Ha'etz' even for unripe fruit in all fruits, as stated in Siman 202, Section 17, it is possible to say that anything that has not grown a third is not even considered like unripe fruit from the tree. This also seems to be the implication from the language of the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, Section 1, where they refer to it as 'fodder,' indicating that it is not considered grain at all. And in Bava Batra (36a), it is explained that 'fodder' is animal feed. According to this, if it has passed the stage of being fodder, even if it is not fully ripened, we recite 'Ha'adamah.' Therefore, I am puzzled by those who wrote that for any fruit of the ground that is not fully ripened, we recite 'Shehakol' (Magen Avraham, Sk 7). In my humble opinion, it is clear that this is not the case, and it is similar to unripe fruit from the tree for which we recite 'Ha'etz.' Similarly, for fruit of the ground, we recite 'Ha'adamah,' and there is no reason to differentiate between fruit of the tree and fruit of the ground (see Pri Megadim) as there is no source to support this differentiation (and the words of the Machatzit HaShekel are puzzling; see there and examine carefully). I am also puzzled by the Tur and Shulchan Aruch as to why they did not write that garden chaziz should be blessed with 'Borei Pri Ha'adamah,' as it is explicitly mentioned in the Gemara, and so the Tosafot write there (and this is also proof for our position; see there and examine carefully).

They also stated in Berachot (36a) that for eating raw gourd, one recites "Shehakol" (the blessing for "everything comes into being by His word"). This refers to a type of squash that is not typically eaten raw but rather cooked, similar to our zucchini. Therefore, if one eats it raw, the blessing is "Shehakol." For consuming barley or wheat flour, one also recites "Shehakol" if it provides any enjoyment. Even though when eating whole grains of wheat or barley, one recites "Ha'adama" (the blessing for "the fruit of the ground"), as mentioned in Siman 208, in the case of flour where it has completely changed, the blessing is "Shehakol." This is not comparable to olive oil, where it is considered an enhancement, but here the enhancement is in bread. Therefore, it is no longer considered grain and has not become bread (as discussed in the Gemara). Nowadays, we are not familiar with any common way to eat flour, but in their time, they had a type of consumption for it. (Also, it is not similar to fruit preserves for which the blessing is "Ha'etz" (the blessing for "the fruit of the tree"), as mentioned in Siman 202, where the entire fruit is intact, only crushed, and this is its way of being eaten, which is not the case for flour.)

And similarly, for date beer and barley beer, one recites "Shehakol" (the blessing "By Whose word all things came to be"), even though the main components are the dates and barley. Nevertheless, since it becomes a beverage, its primary identity is considered to be on account of the water. This is not comparable to cooked vegetable water, for which one recites "Borei Pri Ha'adama" (the blessing "Who creates the fruit of the ground"), because in that case, the flavor of the vegetables enters the water. However, beer has a different taste derived from the dates and barley (see Taz section 7 and Magen Avraham section 9). Similarly, barley water that is cooked for a sick person, since the main intention is for the water, one recites "Shehakol." This is not limited to a sick person, for the same applies to a healthy person if he cooks a barley dish and his intention is not for the barley at all but only for the water, and he only adds a little barley to give it flavor, he also recites "Shehakol." However, this is uncommon because in a dish, one usually intends for the barley and recites "Borei Minei Mezonot" (the blessing "Who creates various kinds of sustenance"), as will be explained in section 208. But for a sick person, the intention is only for the water. And the same applies if for a sick person the intention is for the barley, one recites "Borei Minei Mezonot."

The Tur writes in the name of the Raavad: Herbs that are not planted intentionally - one blesses "Shehakol" on them, because since they are not planted intentionally, they are not considered important produce. This is the explanation: Certainly, fruits are considered important even if they are not intentionally planted, like all our types of berries or nuts, where one blesses "Ha'adama" or "Ha'etz". However, for herbs, since they have no importance at all and are also not intentionally planted, they are not considered produce, and the blessing on them is not "Ha'adama" but "Shehakol". Therefore, on shatzavim, one blesses "Shehakol", and this is the custom (as the Taz writes in subparagraph 8). There are those who wrote that the Arizal would bless "Ha'etz" on those that come from a tree and "Ha'adama" on those that come from the ground (Magen Avraham subparagraph 10), and perhaps he did this only for those that were important. The horseradish, which is also called chrain, also grows on its own, and see what I wrote at the end of Siman 203. Know that on batzvina, which are the leaves of the burdock, one also blesses "Shehakol", since they are not planted for their sake.

They also wrote: that for Shabeta, Shablilata, Kamona, and Kusbarta – the blessing is 'Shehakol' (that everything was created by His word), and thus said the Baal Halachot. And his reasoning is that all of these are made for flavoring and not for eating. And Shabeta is what they call anise, Shablilata is fennel, Kamona is as it sounds, and Kusbarta is coriander, as stated by the Tur. And kamon is cumin, and Shablilata and Kusbarta are not known to us. This which was explained at the end of Siman 202, that on spices one does not bless at all, is because they are not fit for eating at all, but these are fit for eating and have good taste, only they were not made for that purpose. Therefore, they require a blessing, but their blessing is 'Shehakol'.

And our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote: If vinegar is mixed with water and is fit for drinking, one blesses "Shehakol" over it. However, over pure vinegar, no blessing is recited because it is harmful. And this applies to their vinegar, which was very strong and not suitable for drinking without mixing with water. Even now, there exists such vinegar brought from afar that cannot be drunk at all. But our vinegar is fit for drinking even without mixing with water, and we bless "Shehakol" over it. This is the common custom. Any wine that smells like vinegar but tastes like wine is considered wine, and we bless "Borei Pri HaGafen" over it. Conversely, if it tastes like vinegar but smells like wine, it is considered vinegar, and its blessing is "Shehakol." The general rule is: anything that people refrain from drinking because of its sourness, we do not bless "Borei Pri HaGafen" over it but rather "Shehakol." It appears to me that our raisin wine does not need these distinctions, and as soon as it is slightly spoiled, we do not bless "HaGafen" over it but "Shehakol."

Wine dregs that are fit for drinking - one blesses over them "Borei Pri HaGafen." This applies when not too much water has been added to them (see Magen Avraham, section 15, and see Rashbam, Bava Batra 96b, entry "Shamrei" and examine well). However, if much water has been added: if three measures of water were added and one finds four measures, where one measure is from the wine itself - this is considered diluted wine, as the dilution is one part wine to three parts water according to their wines, and one blesses over it "Borei Pri HaGafen." But if less than this amount is found - it is merely a weak mixture, even if it has the taste of wine, and one only blesses "Shehakol." This applies to their wines which were strong, but our wines, which are not so strong, even if three were added and four were found - one does not bless over it "Borei Pri HaGafen." Our master the Beit Yosef wrote in section 5 that the measurement is according to the amount of water that is diluted in that place, end of quote, and our master the Rema wrote: provided that there is not one part wine to six parts water, for then it is certainly nullified, end of quote. And know that our wines are not fit for dilution at all, and with a little water they become spoiled, and their blessing is "Shehakol."

However, the main point of our teacher the Rema is very puzzling, for even with their wines, which were very strong, one does not recite 'Borei Peri HaGafen' when there are more than three parts water, and all the more so with our wines. How could he have written up to six parts? Indeed, the Levush omitted this, see there. And I saw written in the name of the Mahari"l, and this is his wording: "And if the wine is more than one part in six, we go according to the taste, if it is wine that is fit to drink with such a great dilution, and people drink it in place of wine with this dilution, we do not say that his opinion is nullified by everyone else's" (end of quote, Magen Avraham, section 16). At first glance, it is not understood what 'fit to drink' means; is water not fit to drink? Rather, it is certain that his intention is wine that is fit to drink as wine, as he concludes. But this is even more puzzling, for what does 'for its name' have to do with this, and what does it help that he drinks it as wine since it is not wine?

Therefore, it appears to me that in truth, the Mahari"l and our teacher, the Rema, introduced a new ruling in this matter. If we scrutinize, we find that throughout the Talmud, a judge (dayan) requires that there be at least one-fourth water, even with the strongest wines, and with less than this, it is considered water. If so, why do we maintain in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 134, that up to six parts constitutes yayin nesekh (forbidden wine)? After all, it is merely water. And perhaps you might say that the principle of taste being principal (ta'am k'ikar) is from the Torah, then we should prohibit it up to sixty parts. However, the clarification of the matter is as follows: The nature of wine, what is called wine, is not a halacha given to Moses at Sinai, but rather according to the custom of the land. If the people of the country consider this to be wine, then it is wine, since it has the taste of wine in any case. And in the time of the Talmud, they considered that anything less than one-fourth was not called wine. But in some places, up to six parts is considered wine, and therefore they were stringent regarding yayin nesekh to the utmost limit. And this is what the Mahari"l wrote: "People drink it in place of wine," meaning that many consider even up to this measure to be wine, and it isn't an individual opinion that we can disregard. But beyond this measure, no place considers it wine, and therefore even if an individual considers it wine, his opinion is nullified compared to everyone else. And these are the words of our teacher, the Rema, as is clear.

(According to this, we have a great justification for our raisin wine, which is not proper wine, and we have already wondered about this in Siman 202:15. However, according to what we have written, it is satisfactorily explained with good reason, that since the entire country considers this to be wine, it is indeed wine, and we can make Kiddush on it and bless 'Borei Pri Hagafen' over it.)

And our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, wrote in section 6: "Temed (a type of drink) made from grape seeds upon which water is poured has the same status as wine dregs. This applies when they have been pressed with a press, but if they were merely trodden with the feet, even if one poured three measures of water and found only three or less - one blesses over it 'Borei Peri HaGafen' because it is considered wine and the water is absorbed into the grape skins, and what comes out contains more wine. And grape skins upon which figs were placed to strengthen the power of the wine, even though the majority are skins - nevertheless, all the power of the figs is in the liquid, and one does not bless 'Borei Peri HaGafen' over it." And even if this is not clear, in any case, one cannot bless 'Borei Peri HaGafen' due to the doubt, but with 'Shehakol' one certainly fulfills the obligation. However, for the after-blessing, if there is a doubt, one does not fulfill it with 'Borei Nefashot', and therefore it is good to also drink certain wine and bless 'Al HaGefen', and also eat figs and bless them with 'Me'ein Shalosh', because perhaps the fig water is the main part and perhaps their water is like them (Magen Avraham 17). But from 'Borei Nefashot' one is certainly exempt, because even if these are considered as water, in any case, since he also drank wine, it exempts all kinds of drinks.

One who drinks water to quench his thirst - recites the blessing 'Shehakol' before drinking and 'Borei Nefashot' afterwards. However, if he does not wish to drink but drinks for another reason, such as if he has something stuck in his throat and drinks water to remove it, or to taste some bitter or salty medicine or the like - he does not need to recite a blessing either before or after drinking, because water has no taste if one is not thirsty, and the palate does not derive any pleasure from it. But for other beverages in such situations - a blessing is required both before and after drinking, because all foods and drinks that a person consumes for medicinal purposes, as long as the palate derives pleasure from them - a blessing is required both before and after, since there is a good taste to them. Therefore, if they do not have a good taste - no blessing is needed, similar to water. The text of the blessing 'Borei Nefashot' will be explained in Siman 207 with the help of Heaven.

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote in section 8: "If one is coerced to eat or drink, even though the palate benefits from it, one does not recite a blessing over it since it was forced upon him." End quote. And our teacher, the Beit Yosef, ruled in section 9: "If one eats a forbidden food or drink due to danger, one recites a blessing before and after." End quote. The commentators on the Shulchan Aruch were puzzled by our teacher, the Rema, for if one eats forbidden food due to danger, he is also considered coerced, and yet he recites a blessing over it. Therefore, if one is coerced, he should also be obligated to recite a blessing. What difference does it make if he was coerced by another person or by Heaven? They refuted his words (Taz, subsection 12 and Magen Avraham, subsection 20). 

We already wrote in section 196 that the words of our teacher, the Rema, are correct, for in that case, the Torah commanded him to eat, and it is considered as entirely permissible. Therefore, even according to the Rambam, who holds that one does not recite a blessing when eating forbidden food, in a case of danger, there is no prohibition. This is not the case when one is coerced to eat, for there is neither an obligation nor a permission, and he does not wish to eat. Thus, he does not derive enjoyment from it, for if he did enjoy it, he would eat willingly. Therefore, it is not considered enjoyment, and he does not need to recite a blessing, and this is the primary ruling in law. It is not comparable to being coerced to eat matzah, where one fulfills a mitzvah (and this seems to be the opinion of the Eliyah Rabbah, subsection 13, and it is not similar to one who inadvertently engages with forbidden fats and illicit relations, where he enjoys willingly, which is not the case with enjoyment under coercion, as it is not considered enjoyment).

Bee honey is like other honey, and one only recites the blessing "Shehakol" over it. That is to say, we do not say that since it is always being renewed, one should bless "Borei Hakol Bidevaro" (for otherwise, what distinction would there be in this case), as explained in Section 1. Instead, one blesses "Shehakol." And our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in Section 11: "Quinces or fragrant gourd or roses and other types of fruits and herbs that are preserved in honey—the fruits and herbs are primary and the honey is secondary, even if they are very finely ground. Therefore, one blesses 'Ha'etz' on quinces and fragrant gourd and 'Ha'adama' on herbs and roses," end quote. And this is the custom with all our kinds of confections. Specifically, this is when the fruit is recognizable, but if they are very crushed until they become like a thick drink, one blesses "Shehakol." Therefore, with our confections, when they are completely mashed and strained through a strainer and called syrup, one blesses "Shehakol." Similarly, when fruits are placed in water and sugar or honey, like vischnik (cherry liqueur) or malinovik (raspberry liqueur) and the like, one blesses "Shehakol" over the drink.

And know that "veradim" (roses) refers to "rosin" and their blessing is "Borei Pri Ha'adama" (Who creates the fruit of the ground). And even though they grow on a tree, nevertheless, they are not the main fruit, and they contain seeds that are the main fruit (Magen Avraham 23). And the "veradim" that are the leaves are like capers in the caper bush, and therefore their blessing is "Borei Pri Ha'adama." These roses cannot be eaten raw or cooked, only fried with honey. Despite this, the honey is not the primary component; the primary component is the rose, and the honey merely prepares it for eating. They are like vegetables that are not eaten raw but only cooked, and their blessing is "Borei Pri Ha'adama" (Magen Avraham and Beit Yosef). Even if the vegetables require some preparation by cooking, their blessing remains "Borei Pri Ha'adama" because that is the way they are eaten. Similarly, with roses, this is the case, and the same applies to anything similar.

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote: Any concoction that healthy people do not normally consume, but only for medicinal purposes, one blesses over it "Shehakol" (the blessing for things that do not have a specific blessing). This means that even though we hold that if one eats or drinks something for medicinal purposes, if the palate derives pleasure from it, a blessing is required, this is certainly so. However, in this case, there are no specific blessings. Even if it is something whose blessing would normally be "Ha'etz" (the blessing for fruit from trees), in this case one only blesses "Shehakol." The reason is that since it is mainly food for the sick, the ill person does not concern themselves with the specifics, as their intention is not for eating but for healing. It is only because the palate derives pleasure that the blessing is "Shehakol," which is a general blessing. But if it is something that healthy people also consume, even if one eats it for medicinal purposes, one cannot change the format of the blessing from that of healthy people. And although there are those who disagree with this, nonetheless, the ruling is to be lenient in cases of doubt regarding blessings, and with "Shehakol" one has certainly fulfilled their obligation. There are those who explain that it refers to things that are not good for eating, and therefore their blessing is "Shehakol," but if they are good for eating, their blessing is "Ha'etz" or "Ha’adamah" (the blessing for things that grow from the ground). And I am puzzled by this, for if so, it should have been explained and not left ambiguous. Furthermore, if so, there would be no blessing at all. (And "Machatzit HaShekel" struggled to explain that they are neither good nor bad for eating, see there, but this is just conjecture and forced, and the main point is as I wrote, and pay careful attention).

And know that regarding what is taught (44a) that the primary exempts the secondary, the Rambam divided this in Chapter 3 into two parts: mixed secondary and unmixed secondary. That is to say, if one eats two things where one is primary and the other is secondary, such as a salted fish and an onion, the salted fish is primary and the onion is secondary, and one blesses on the salted fish and exempts the onion. This is called unmixed secondary, and this will be explained in Siman 212. Mixed secondary refers to when one cooks a dish and mixes into it another item; we determine which is the primary and which is the secondary. And this is the language of the Rambam there: "What is mixed secondary? For example, if one cooks turnips or cabbage and mixes into it flour from one of the five species to bind it, he does not bless 'Borei Minei Mezonot' on it, because the turnip is primary and the flour is secondary. For anything that is mixed to bind, or to give scent, or to color the dish - this is secondary. But if it is mixed to give flavor to the mixture - it is primary. Therefore, types of honey that are cooked and wheat milk is added to bind and make sweets - one does not bless 'Borei Minei Mezonot' on it, because the honey is primary." End quote.

And seemingly, his words are not understood at all, as if there is no mixed dish that contains elements that are neither for fragrance, nor for dye, nor for taste, but rather several things are cooked together, and one must see which is the primary and which is the secondary. However, his intention is indeed as follows: there certainly are such cases, and this is the main law of primary and secondary, which will be explained in Siman 212. However, the Rambam states something different: that previously, he was referring to the laws of the five species [of grain], where in any food that contains one of the five species, even if they are minimal compared to the rest of the food, one still recites the blessing "Mezonot" over it, because the five species are primary compared to other foods. This will be explained in Siman 208, as it is stated in the Gemara (Berachot 36b): "Anything that contains one of the five species, one recites 'Borei Minei Mezonot' over it," meaning that with other kinds of mixtures, one follows the majority, but when there is one of the five species, even if it is minimal, the other foods are secondary to it, and one recites 'Borei Minei Mezonot'. This is what the Rambam wrote earlier, and these are his words: "Flour of one of the five species that was cooked in a pot, whether by itself or mixed with other things... Likewise, any cooked dish in which one of the five species was mixed, whether it be flour or bread - one recites 'Borei Minei Mezonot' over it." This is the end of his words.

According to this, the five species are always considered primary, and other foods are secondary. However, this is only when they come to be eaten. But when they come merely to bind, they become secondary. And this is his language: "When is this said? When this species is significant to him and not secondary. But if one of the five species is mixed as a secondary ingredient, one only blesses on the primary... This is a rule regarding blessings... How is the secondary ingredient mixed? For example, a turnip or cabbage that was cooked and mixed with flour from one of the five species to bind it, one does not bless 'Borei Minei Mezonot'...". This is the explanation: How is the secondary ingredient mixed with the five species? But this does not apply at all to other things. Therefore, he says afterward: "But if it was mixed to provide flavor in the mixture, it is primary." Meaning, if his intention with the five species is for the purpose of taste, it is primary even if it is a small amount. And this is what he says afterward: "Therefore, types of honey... and wheat flour is added to bind... one does not bless 'Borei Minei Mezonot' because the honey is primary," and this does not refer to the previous case of providing flavor, because it is the opposite of this, but rather to an earlier previous case. Meaning: since we said that when they come to bind, they are not primary, therefore not only against other types of foods, but even regarding honey, they become secondary. And this clarifies the words of the Rambam (and this is the intention of the Magen Avraham, section 25).

According to this, our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, who brought these words of the Rambam in this section, paragraph 12, it is not relevant here at all (and this is the critique of the Magen Avraham there). Nonetheless, their words are correct, and they also understood the Rambam's intent, but because there are practical differences in the laws of this section, as will be explained, they brought his words briefly according to the matter relevant here. And this is the language of our Rabbi, the Beit Yosef: “Anything that is the main part... And anything that is mixed to bind or for fragrance or to color - this is secondary. But if it is mixed to give flavor... Therefore, varieties of honey, etc.” End quote. He did not bring all the words of the Rambam except for the matter previously explained, that varieties of fruits and herbs cooked in honey, the honey is secondary, and for this he brought the words of the Rambam that if for the five species the Rambam wrote that when they come to bind, for fragrance, or for appearance, they are not primary and the honey becomes primary, all the more so for herbs when they come in such a manner, like there are herbs that improve appearance and give a good fragrance as is known, if his intention is for this - the honey is primary and we bless 'Shehakol'.

And our teacher, the Rema, added to this matter and this is his language: "It seems that the rule that if one mixes to give flavor to a mixture, which is the primary reason, applies specifically when there is substance from the item giving the flavor that is significant. But spices that are added to a mixture, even though they are intended to give flavor, do not require a blessing on them, because they are nullified in their minority even though they impart flavor. Therefore, the custom is to only bless on the mixture and not on the spices within it." End quote. And the explanation of his words is as follows: Because our teacher, the Beit Yosef, learned from the Rambam's ruling regarding the five species as mentioned, and according to this, one might mistakenly equate it entirely with the five species, that if there is even a small amount, if the intention is to give flavor, one blesses 'Borei Minei Mezonot.' But in truth, for other items, it is not so; it is specifically the five species, which are very important, that this rule applies to. But for other types of food, even if the intention is to give flavor, we still require a significant substance at the very least. And a majority is not required because since it is intended for flavor, it has importance even without a majority. However, we do require a significant substance. Therefore, for spices that are added for flavor, since they are very minor, they do not have the importance to warrant a blessing (the Magen Avraham wrote there that a majority is required and brought proof from rice, see there, but this is not comparable because certainly any food that gives flavor requires a majority, and here we are discussing a significant flavor like spices and similar, and investigate thoroughly).

Nowadays, there are many in [the region of] Kandinerska who preserve fruits with a lot of sugar, and the sugar covers all the fruits. Nevertheless, their blessing is 'Borei Pri Ha'etz' (Who creates the fruit of the tree), as they are the main part (as also written in Ba'er Heitev, section 19). Our master the Beit Yosef wrote in section 13: "Anything whose blessing is doubtful – one should bless 'Shehakol' (by whose word all things came to be)." Thus he wrote. And there is no novelty in this, as it is impossible to do otherwise, and this has been explained in several places. It seems to me, in my humble opinion, that his intention is: in this case, we do not follow the majority opinion as we do in other laws, but rather, unless one is certain about blessing 'Ha'etz' or 'Ha'adama' (the blessing for produce of the ground). But if one is not certain and there are differing opinions, even if the opinion of 'Shehakol' is the minority against the opinions of 'Ha'etz' or 'Ha'adama', one should bless 'Shehakol' (thus it seems in my humble opinion).

The Sages taught in the Mishnah (Berachot 35a): "For vegetables, one says, 'Who creates the fruit of the ground.' Rabbi Yehuda says: 'Who creates types of grasses.'" The Gemara rules that the law does not follow Rabbi Yehuda. And even though the reasoning of Rabbi Yehuda is explained in the Gemara, because [it is written: "Blessed is Hashem day by day"], meaning that for each and every day, give it a blessing appropriate to it: on Shabbat, a blessing for Shabbat, on a festival, a blessing for the festival, and similarly for each type, give it a blessing appropriate to it. In a similar manner, Rabbi Yehuda and the Sages dispute in Sukkah (46a): If many mitzvot are before him, the Sages hold that he should say: 'Who has sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us concerning the mitzvot,' and Rabbi Yehuda holds that he should bless each mitzvah individually: for tzitzit individually and for tefillin individually. And Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning is also from this verse, that for each and every mitzvah, give it a blessing appropriate to it. And there, the law follows Rabbi Yehuda, as the Rambam wrote in chapter 11 of Berachot (and one of the great ones of the previous generation raised a great uproar with this question).

However, in truth, it is not similar at all, because here, even when we bless "ha'adamah," it also includes each type with its own appropriate blessing. That means the fruit of the tree by itself, the fruit of the ground by itself, and other things by themselves. Furthermore, what difference is there between seeds and grasses regarding "ha'adamah"? By any logic, if we bless on grasses "Who creates various kinds of grasses," we should bless on seeds "Who creates various kinds of seeds." And indeed, in the Tosefta of Berachot (Chapter 4), we learned thus: "On the seeds, one says: 'Who creates various kinds of seeds,' on the grasses, one says: 'Who creates various kinds of grasses,' and on the vegetables: 'Who creates the fruit of the ground.'" But in the Mishnah, which excludes only grasses from "ha'adamah," we rightly rule that the law does not follow Rabbi Yehuda, and this is our established practice, and heaven forbid to doubt this. (Furthermore, there is no fixed name for this, and in the Jerusalem Talmud at the end of Chapter 5 of Kilayim, it is taught: "Rye, wheat, rushes, and all other things that grow in dust are a type of grasses," thus rye and wheat, which are types of barley, are also included in grasses) (and there is clear proof from the Ba'al Halachot Gedolot at the beginning of the chapter "How to Bless" who brought this derivation).

The general rule for vegetables is as follows: any type of vegetable that is typically eaten either raw, cooked, or pickled - one recites the blessing 'Ha'adama' (who creates the fruit of the ground) whether it is eaten raw, cooked, or pickled. The same rule applies to all types of fruits and legumes: if they are good both raw and cooked - their blessing after cooking is the same as before cooking. Dried raw legumes, like certain types of beans, are not suitable for eating, and their blessing is 'Shehakol' (who creates everything) [Magen Avraham, section 1]. Any type of vegetable that is eaten raw but not cooked, like cucumbers when they are raw – the blessing is 'Borei Pri Ha'adama' (who creates the fruit of the ground), and when they are cooked: 'Shehakol' (who creates everything), but pickled - the blessing is 'Borei Pri Ha'adama' because their main purpose is for pickling, as is known. If they are typically eaten cooked and not raw, like carrots: when they are raw - the blessing is 'Shehakol', and when cooked – 'Ha'adama'. Pickled carrots receive the blessing 'Ha'adama' because most of them are used for pickling and they are very good when pickled. However, other vegetables are not suitable without cooking, even when pickled, and from this, you can deduce the blessing for all types of vegetables that are not found among us.

And this is the wording of our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, in section 1: "But [for] pumpkins, beets, cabbage, and similar items that are better cooked than raw: when they are raw – one blesses 'Shehakol,' and when they are cooked – 'Borei Peri Ha'adamah.' And garlic (knab'l) and leeks: when they are raw – 'Borei Peri Ha'adamah,' and after they are cooked – 'Shehakol,' because they are considered downgraded, even if they are cooked with meat and improved, the improvement is not due to themselves but due to the meat within them." This is the end of their words. And even though with a nut fried in honey, where the improvement is also due to the honey, nevertheless, we bless 'Ha'etz,' as we said in Siman 202, this is because the nut is the main element and the honey comes to improve the nut. However, garlic and leeks are not the main elements in the dish, and the meat is the main element (there in subsection 5). And indeed, when vegetables are fried in fat and meat, and the vegetables are the main part of the dish, we bless 'Borei Peri Ha'adamah' (there). And there is one who says that for garlic and leeks – even when they are raw, one blesses 'Shehakol' (Bach) because they are not so suitable for eating, but for onions, one certainly blesses 'Ha'adamah,' as they are good for eating. And for pickled cabbage, one blesses 'Ha'adamah' (Magen Avraham in subsection 2), and likewise when it is salted, as it is good when salted (there), and we are not familiar with these varieties.

There is no difference regarding vegetables between cutting them into large pieces or cutting them into small pieces, and even if they are very finely crushed, as long as they still have the form of food, their blessing does not change, as it is written in Siman 202 concerning fruits, and the same law applies to legumes. However, vegetables from which juice has been extracted – their blessing is 'Shehakol' because their form has deteriorated. This is the ruling of the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch, paragraph 3. The Tur brought in the name of his brother, Rabbeinu Yechiel, that one should bless 'Ha'adamah,' and he refuted this, as seen there, and he brought proof from the juice that comes from fruits, where the blessing is 'Shehakol.' In truth, one could say that it is not comparable, as in fruits, the taste of the juice changes from the taste of the fruit, but in vegetables, it does not change. In any case, since the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch have ruled thus, one should not deviate from their words, as with 'Shehakol,' one certainly fulfills the obligation (see Taz, subparagraph 6).

Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 2: "For water in which vegetables were cooked, one recites the same blessing as on the vegetables themselves, even though it only has the flavor of the vegetable. This applies when they were cooked without meat, but if they were cooked with meat, one recites 'Shehakol'." And we have already elaborated on this in Siman 202 from section 32 to section 42, where we brought three opinions on this matter. According to the ruling, one should not recite 'Ha'adama' on any soup unless it was cooked specifically for the sake of the liquid, which is the opinion of the Rambam, of blessed memory, and when it was cooked without meat as explained here. According to our foods, we only have cooking in a primary manner. (See the Magen Avraham section 6, who elaborates on this and brings different opinions, and it is difficult to ascertain his intention. However, the ruling is as stated based on the words of the Rambam, and the Rema in Darkei Moshe also relies on the Rambam as brought by the Magen Avraham there. And what the Taz wrote in section 5, that when vegetables are cooked with borscht or vinegar, one does not bless the liquid as one does on the vegetables, and certainly so, for it is like meat, and we have already written this there).

It is also written in section 5: "Raw turnip - one blesses 'Shehakol' over it, and if it is cooked or pickled in vinegar or mustard - 'Borei Peri Ha'adama'." And even if it is cooked with meat, one blesses 'Ha'adama' because the main component is the turnip. It is not similar to garlic and leeks mentioned in section 4, and it is like a nut in Siman 202. Know that it was written by the Ribi"n and Ma'ari"n that when eating it raw, one blesses 'Shehakol' (Taz, Sk 1), but according to what is known to us regarding the Ribi"n, one should bless 'Ha'adama', as it is primarily eaten raw and is very good for eating (as also indicated in Magen Avraham, Sk 9). For sesame seeds, one blesses 'Borei Peri Ha'adama' even if they are ground, because they are typically enjoyed in that form (Shulchan Aruch, Sk 7 in the name of Even HaEzer). There is an opinion that if they are ground, one blesses 'Shehakol' (Magen Avraham there), but the main opinion seems to be the first one. Similarly, for radishes, even if they are crushed, one blesses 'Ha'adama' because they are primarily eaten that way, and some mistakenly bless 'Shehakol', which is an error (Shulchan Aruch there). Even when cooked in water, called Krupnik or Zupah, if there are many radishes, one also blesses 'Borei Peri Ha'adama', but if the water is the majority and the radishes are few, one blesses 'Shehakol'. However, for barley groats from the five species like barley, oats, rye, groats - their blessing is always 'Borei Minei Mezonot', as will be explained in Siman 208 with the help of Heaven.

If he blessed on fruit of the tree "Who creates the fruit of the ground" – he has fulfilled his obligation, because the essence of a tree is the ground. But Rambam in Chapter 8 ruled that he has not fulfilled his obligation, and his reasoning seems to be according to the Talmudic discussion which links this to first fruits (Bikkurim 40a), and regarding first fruits, we hold: that if the tree was cut down – he does not recite [the blessing], because he cannot say "from the ground which You, O Lord, have given me" (Deuteronomy 26:10), indicating that the essence of the tree is not the ground. Nevertheless, the Tosafot, the Rosh, and all the poskim ruled that he has fulfilled his obligation, like the anonymous Mishnah in Berakhot (40a), and even though the Talmud linked the two, it is not meant to be taken literally, and the Yerushalmi there rejected that it is dependent on first fruits, therefore Rambam's opinion was not brought at all in the Tur and Shulchan Aruch. And in our version of Rambam it also is explained that he has fulfilled his obligation, but all the Rishonim cited in his name that he has not fulfilled his obligation (see Beit Yosef and Kesef Mishneh), and perhaps he retracted and corrected that he has fulfilled his obligation, but in any case, this is the law. And for fruit of the ground, if he blessed "the tree" – he has not fulfilled his obligation, because "tree" is included in "ground" but "ground" is not included in "tree". Therefore, in any case of doubt or dispute whether to bless "the tree" or "the ground" – he should bless "the ground" and thereby fulfill his obligation in any case.

However, initially, it is forbidden to bless "Borei Pri HaAdama" on something whose blessing is certainly "Borei Pri HaEtz." Even if he has before him two items that he wants to eat, one with the blessing "HaEtz" and one "HaAdama," such as a radish and an olive, he should not bless "HaAdama" on the radish with the intention to exempt the olive. Instead, he should first bless "HaEtz" on the olive and afterward bless "HaAdama" on the radish, because the blessing "HaEtz" precedes the blessing "HaAdama." And even if he first blessed "HaAdama" on the radish, if he did not explicitly intend to exempt the olive, he should afterward bless "HaEtz" on the olive. This does not increase blessings unnecessarily, since this is not the primary blessing. However, after the fact, if he blessed "HaAdama" on the radish and intended to exempt the olive, he has fulfilled his obligation and it is forbidden for him to subsequently bless "HaEtz" on the olive, as this would be a blessing in vain. It has already been explained that for all items, if one said "Shehakol," he has fulfilled his obligation, even for bread and wine, and certainly for other items. Similarly, when there is a fruit of the tree for which the blessing is "HaAdama," such as unripe grapes or capers from the caper bush, as per the laws explained in Siman 202, if he blessed "HaEtz" on them, he has fulfilled his obligation, as they are ultimately fruits of the tree (Magen Avraham 1), and the same applies to fruits of the ground regarding "Shehakol" in a similar manner.

It appears to me that even though we hold that if one recited the blessing "ha'adamah" (the blessing for vegetables) on a fruit that requires the blessing "ha'etz" (the blessing for tree fruits), he has fulfilled his obligation, this applies to the fruits that are in front of him and not to fruits that are not in front of him. This means that if someone is eating apples and recited the blessing "ha'etz" and then more apples are brought before him, he has fulfilled his obligation with the first blessing, as will be explained. This is when he recited "ha'etz."
