However, if he recited "ha'adamah" and did not specifically intend to exempt the apples that would be brought later, he must recite "ha'etz" on the apples brought later. For initially, one should not recite "ha'adamah" on fruits that require "ha'etz," but if he did so, he has fulfilled his obligation only for what is before him and not for what will be brought later. Certainly, if he recited the blessing on a radish intending to exempt olives, and then other olives are brought, he must recite "ha'etz" on them. (And the Taz in section 2 wants to say that even in such a case, he exempts, and he questions the Shulchan Aruch. And his words are puzzling, as the Sha'agat Aryeh in section 27 already questioned him, and the Maharil and Rashba have no proof at all. And it also seems to my humble opinion that in all blessings where one fulfills his obligation post facto, like "shehakol," this applies only to what is before him and not to what will be brought later. Pay attention to this matter.)

It is forbidden to pause between the blessing and the eating for longer than the time it takes to say a greeting, which is the time it takes for a student to greet a teacher: 'Peace be upon you, my teacher and master.' If one pauses in silence for longer than this duration, some say that one should repeat the blessing (Beit Yosef), and some say one should not repeat the blessing (there, Siman 140), and this is the primary ruling (Magen Avraham, subsection 4). However, if one speaks in between, it is obvious that one needs to repeat the blessing (there). One should not pause between the blessing and eating, neither out of respect nor out of fear. This is not comparable to the blessings of the Shema, where we do not bless to recite the Shema and therefore the interruption is not a nullification of the recitation of the Shema, which is not the case with blessings of enjoyment (there). Additionally, in just a moment, one can taste a bit of the food or drink so that the blessing will not be in vain, and therefore a person must be very careful about this.

One must recite every blessing in a manner that he can hear it with his own ears, and not like those who recite in a whisper to the extent that they themselves cannot hear and they rush through the blessing. Rather, he should recite it quietly, word by word, so that he can hear it with his own ears. However, after the fact, if he did not hear it with his own ears, he has fulfilled his obligation, as it is no more stringent than the recitation of the Shema, as long as he articulates it with his lips. But if he only thought the blessing in his heart, he has not fulfilled his obligation according to the majority of authorities, except for the Rambam in Chapter 1 of Berachot, and that is a singular opinion. Therefore, it seems to me that if someone ate a little based on thinking the blessing, he should recite the blessing and then eat the rest, and the same applies to drinking, as it is a clear ruling among the authorities that contemplation is not considered like speech. And blessings can be recited in any language, and we have already explained this in Siman 185 that it is not possible for us to do so. See there.

It is forbidden to recite a blessing while naked until one's nakedness is covered. What are we discussing? A man whose nakedness is exposed, but a woman who is sitting with her lower parts pressed to the ground and reciting a blessing, in such a case her nakedness is considered covered. This is explained in detail in Siman 74, see there. Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in paragraph 3: Even if he is not naked, if his heart sees the nakedness or his head is uncovered, it is forbidden to recite a blessing. And the law regarding the heart seeing the nakedness is explained in Siman 74, where it is also clarified what interruptions or coverings are sufficient, see there. In paragraph 5, we explained that if, after the fact, one recited a blessing while his heart saw the nakedness, he does not need to repeat the blessing, see there. All the more so, if he recited the blessing with an uncovered head, he does not need to repeat it. It is also explained there that seeing the nakedness with the eye is forbidden by Torah law, see there.

Any item over which one recites a blessing to eat, drink, or smell must be held in the right hand while blessing. However, this is not strictly required after the fact, as even if he held it in his left hand or did not hold it at all but it was placed before him on the table, his blessing is still valid. Ideally, one should not insert a knife into the item being eaten at the time of the blessing, as there is no blessing with a sword, but after the fact, this is not a hindrance. However, the item to be eaten, drunk, or smelled must be in front of him, even after the fact, and one does not bless over food or drink until it is brought before him. If he blessed and then it was brought before him, he must bless again. This is the ruling of the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, Section 5. It seems to me that this only applies if the food or drink was not present at all and there was a significant delay until it was brought before him. But if he saw the food through a window and it was immediately brought to him, or if he blessed in one room and the food was in another room and he immediately went to the other room or a third room and ate it, his blessing is valid, and he does not need to bless again. This can be proven from Yoreh De'ah, Section 19. All this applies after the fact, but ideally, the item should be directly in front of him, and he should hold it in his right hand as stated.

The Tur wrote: "One who recited a blessing over fruits that were before him and afterward more of the same type was brought to him - he does not need to recite a new blessing, even though they were not before him when he first blessed." This implies specifically the same type, but for a different type, a new blessing is required (Bach). However, our teacher the Beit Yosef in his great work wrote that there is no difference between this type and another type, since the blessing is the same. Based on this, he wrote in section 5: "One who recited a blessing over fruits that were before him and afterward more of the same type or a different type whose blessing is the same as the first - does not need to recite a new blessing." This is certainly the case if he explicitly intended at the time of the blessing for all that would be brought to him, it is obvious that he does not need to recite a new blessing even for a different type, since his intention was for this. Conversely, if he explicitly intended only for those placed before him, it is obvious that a new blessing is required even if more of the same type is brought to him. In these two cases, no one would disagree. Whether there are still some of the fruits that were present at the time of the blessing in front of him, or whether he has already eaten them, it makes no difference, as is understood.

However, the disagreement is in a case of uncertainty, meaning when one did not intend to eat more, and also did not intend not to eat more. According to this, it is possible to say that there is no disagreement at all, and our master the Beit Yosef's intention is when it was explicitly his intention to eat more, or he was in another's house and relied on the host's table, as stated in his larger work in Siman 179. In Yoreh De'ah Siman 19, section 13, we wrote that his intention could also be that there were still some of the first fruits before him; therefore, there is no need to bless over the others even if it was not his intention, since he also did not intend the opposite, or he explicitly intended at the time of blessing that they would bring him more. Now, regarding the second explanation, certainly no one disagrees, but regarding the first explanation, there are those who disagree when it comes to a different type. And from the words of our master the Rema, who wrote regarding the words of our master the Beit Yosef in this manner: "It is good to be cautious initially to have in mind all that they will bring him," end quote, it is clear that he interprets the words of our master the Beit Yosef in a case of uncertainty.

Regarding the matter of the law, one of the great latter authorities has ruled that if the fruits upon which the blessing was recited have already been eaten, even if they bring more of the same type, a new blessing is required unless it was explicitly intended at the time of the blessing to bring and eat more fruits (Magen Avraham end of section 7). This is because the consumption of fruits is considered casual, and a person’s intention is only on what is before him. However, if it was explicitly intended to bring other fruits or fruits whose blessing is the same as the first ones, it is obvious that no new blessing is required. Even if his intention was for other items, if they bring something entirely different, such as eating fish and intending to bring more fish, but they brought beer, even though both share the same blessing of "Shehakol," if his intention was not explicitly for beer, a new blessing is required (as indicated in Magen Avraham there). This does not apply when one is dining at a friend's house, as one relies on the host's table, and in this case, no new blessing is required for anything brought, as stated in Siman 179. This ruling applies similarly in all such matters (and the opinion of Taz section 7 also appears to be the same, and logically this is the case).

And as long as these fruits have not yet been consumed, but some of them still remain and other fruits are brought, and it is unclear whether his intention was to eat more or not to eat more, then regarding the same type, certainly no blessing is needed. However, when a different type is brought, there is a dispute as we have mentioned, and consequently, it is understood that in cases of doubt regarding blessings, we rule leniently. This is specifically when a different type is brought, but both are fruit of the tree. However, for the blessing of 'Shehakol' on two completely different types, like fish and beer and similar items, it is obvious that a blessing should be recited unless he had explicitly intended otherwise.

If one has before him many types of fruits, all of which have the blessing "borei pri ha'etz" or all "borei pri ha'adama," and he wishes to eat all of them, he should recite one blessing for all of them. It is forbidden for him to bless one type with the intention of not covering the other types with this blessing, and then bless the second and third separately to increase the number of blessings. This practice is considered as making blessings in vain, and regarding such practices, the prophet said: "To what purpose is the multitude of your sacrifices unto Me? says the Lord." Even on Shabbat and festivals, when one's intention is to complete one hundred blessings, it is forbidden to do so. However, he may act in this way: he can bring one type before him, bless it, and intend not to cover the other types with this blessing. Then he can bring the second type and bless it, intending not to cover another type, and so on. Even in this case, there are those who have reservations, arguing that since he intends to eat all of them, why not bring them all and make one blessing? However, regarding this matter, to complete one hundred blessings, one may rely on those who permit it, but not when all the types are before him (Eliyah Rabbah, section 8, in the name of Rabbi Moshe Galanti).

The Rambam wrote in Chapter 4, Law 10: "If someone took food, blessed over it, and then it fell from his hand and was burned or swept away by a river - he should take another piece of the same kind and bless over it again. … A person stands by a stream, blesses, and drinks, even though the water that was before him at the time of the blessing is not the water he drank, because that was his initial intention." This is from the Jerusalem Talmud (Chapter 6, Law 1). It is clear that the other piece he takes was not initially intended to be eaten, because if it were, why would it say, 'even though it is of the same kind'? It should teach us an even greater novelty: even if his intention was to eat it. Therefore, it is certain that in such a case, he does not need to bless again. And all the more so from the case of the stream, where even though the water he drinks was not before him at the time of the blessing, because his intention was on that water, he fulfills his obligation. All the more so with another fruit that was before him and his intention was to eat it after the one he held in his hand, that he does not need to bless again.

However, the language of the Tur and Shulchan Aruch in Section 6 is different, as they wrote: "If one took a fruit to eat it and made a blessing on it, but it fell from his hand and was lost or became unfit - he must make another blessing, even though he had more of the same type of fruit before him when he blessed the first one." From this language, the commentators understood that their intention was even if he had in mind to eat them (Taz Sk 8 and Drisha), and from this they questioned our master the Rema who wrote: "Only if he did not have in mind to eat it," and they wrote that this is the opinion of Rabbeinu Tam and Rabbeinu Yonah. But the opinion of the Rambam, the Rosh, the Tur, and the Beit Yosef is that even if he had in mind to eat them, he must bless again. In my humble opinion, their words are perplexing, and the words of our master the Rema are correct. Besides, there is no reason to require another blessing in such a case. Why did they say: 'even though he had more of the same type before him'? They should have said: 'even though he intended to eat them.' Rather, it is certain that in such a case, they agree that no blessing is needed. And they wrote a greater novelty than the Rambam, that even if he had more of the same type before him, since he did not intend to eat them, he needs to bless again, and this is the main ruling (as also written by the Levush).

And there are those who say further: that even if it was a neutral intention, where he did not explicitly intend either to eat or not to eat, if the fruits are placed before him - he does not need to recite a blessing (Magen Avraham section 8 in the name of the Mabit). However, some disagree, stating that in a neutral case, one must recite a blessing (Magen Avraham ibid.), and this seems to be the inclination of the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch, as understood. Nonetheless, if it is the habit of this person not to be satisfied with one fruit and to eat two or more - it is as if he intended to eat more, and he does not need to recite a blessing.

It is stated in the Jerusalem Talmud there: When one needs to recite a different blessing and it turns out that the first one was in vain, he should say: "Blessed be the Name of His glorious kingdom forever and ever," as this is a remedy for a blessing recited in vain. So wrote the Rambam, the Tur, and the Shulchan Aruch. They also wrote that if one has only said: "Blessed are You, Lord," he should conclude with: "Teach me Your statutes," as this is a verse, and it is considered as if he is reading from the Torah. And if one blessed over water and then discovered that he needs to pour it out because of a dead body or because of the season, in any case, he should drink a little so that his blessing will not be in vain, and "one who observes a commandment will know no evil" (Magen Avraham there). And if one made a mistake in the blessing and recited a different blessing, it will be clarified in Siman 209 with Heaven's help. (The reason for the remedy of saying "Blessed be the Name of His glorious kingdom forever and ever" for a blessing recited in vain is not explained, and perhaps it is because one has uttered God's name in vain, therefore he needs to accept upon himself the yoke of the kingdom of Heaven).

The difference in blessings between 'ha'etz' (fruit of the tree) and 'ha'adamah' (fruit of the ground) and between the blessing 'shehakol' (everything) is only in the initial blessing. However, for the blessing after eating, they are all the same except for the seven species, which have a unique blessing, and that is the 'borei nefashot' (Creator of souls). And everything that the Rabbis instituted, they instituted in a manner similar to the Torah. Since, according to the Torah, the main blessing is the Grace After Meals following consumption, as it is written: "And you shall eat and be satisfied and bless." Therefore, it was impossible to leave other things without a blessing after consumption. And not only for items that provide some nourishment and important items like meat, fish, and eggs, but even for vegetables and water, which are not important and do not provide nourishment, one is still obligated to say a blessing after consuming an olive-sized portion (k'zayit) and drinking a quarter-log (r'vi'it), provided the k'zayit is eaten within the time it takes to eat a half-loaf of bread (k'dei achilat pras) and the r'vi'it is drunk within the time it takes to drink a r'vi'it (k'dei shtiyat r'vi'it). (See the end of chapter 'Ketzad Mevarchin' (Berachot 44b), Tosafot s.v. 'Avidna', and this is also written by all the poskim, pay close attention.)

What is the proper text? "Blessed are You, Lord our God, King of the Universe, Who creates numerous living beings with their deficiencies," and some have the version "with their deficiencies" (HaGri"B). The reason is that "living beings" (נפשות) is a feminine term, as we say "numerous living beings" (נפשות רבות) and not "numerous" (רבים). If so, it should end with a final nun (ן) and not with a mem (ם), as it is written concerning the daughters of Zelophehad: "And Moses brought their case" (משפטן). Throughout the Torah, "soul" (נפש) is in the feminine form: "And if a soul sins and hears..." (נפש כי תחטא ושמעה), "If a soul commits a trespass and sins..." (נפש כי תמעל מעל וחטאה). However, in the Tur, the version is "with their deficiencies," and so it is printed in the siddurim (prayer books), and this seems to be the main version. For in the Torah as well: "And if a soul sins and hears... and he is a witness... he will bear his iniquity" (ונשא עונו), which is in masculine form. Similarly, in "If a soul commits a trespass... and brings" (והביא), it is in masculine form because it refers to a person, and people are generally referred to in masculine form, though the soul part of a person is in feminine form. So here too, "with their deficiencies" refers to people.

"For everything that He created to give life, etc."—this is the version in the Tur. There are those who have the version: "that You created" in the second person (Magen Avraham and Eliyah Rabbah in the name of the writings). Even though the beginning of the blessing is "Creator" in the third person, one can still say afterward in the second person, as this is the way of blessings. For we say: "Blessed are You" in the second person, and then we say: "Creator" in the third person, since the Holy One, blessed be He, is revealed more than all that is revealed and hidden more than all that is hidden. We intentionally say it this way, as we say: "You are He" as mentioned in Siman 5. There are those who have the version: "And for everything that He created, etc." (Mayim Chaim), but the principal version is without the conjunction "and," as found in the prayer books (Eliyah Rabbah). "To give life with them to every living soul, Blessed is the Life of all worlds"—'Life' with a tzeirei (a vowel mark). In the Tur, it concludes: "Blessed are You, Hashem, the Life of all worlds," which is based on the Jerusalem Talmud. However, our master the Beit Yosef wrote that this blessing is without the Divine Name, as it is not found in the Talmud and it is a short blessing. This is our custom, and it should not be changed.

The Tur writes its explanation: "Who creates numerous living beings and their deficiencies"—everything they lack, such as bread and water which are essential (Beit Yosef), "for all that You have created, etc."—that is, and for the other things that were created in the world which the living beings would not have lacked if they had not been created, which are only for enjoyment, "to give life to the soul of every living being"—meaning that the Holy One, blessed be He, is good and bestows goodness and even provides things that are not essential for the sustenance of the soul (and perhaps for this reason, the Jerusalem Talmud holds that one should conclude with the Name, because they are two different matters and it becomes a long blessing).

The blessing of "Me'ein Shalosh" (a condensed version of the three blessings) as it appears in the Gemara (44a) and in the Tur is as follows: "Blessed are You, Lord our God, King of the universe, for the sustenance and for the nourishment, for the produce of the field, and for the desirable, good, and spacious land which You desired and gave as an inheritance to our forefathers, to eat of its fruit and to be satisfied with its goodness. Have mercy, Lord our God, on Israel Your people, on Jerusalem Your city, on Zion the dwelling place of Your glory, on Your altar, and on Your sanctuary. Rebuild Jerusalem, the holy city, speedily in our days; bring us up into it and make us rejoice in its rebuilding (this phrase is not in the Tur), for You, Lord, are good and do good to all (this phrase is not in the Tur). Blessed are You, Lord, for the land and for the sustenance."

In the Tur, an additional phrase "and for the nourishment" is included, but the halachic authorities did not agree with this, and thus Rambam and SeMaG (Sefer Mitzvot Gadol) wrote (as cited in Beit Yosef), and so too is our custom and it should not be changed. In the prayer books, an additional phrase has been added before the conclusion of the blessing: "and we thank You for the land and for the sustenance," and our custom is to recite it so that the ending of the blessing should be similar to the conclusion. 

This blessing is for the five species of grain included in wheat and barley, and for the five types of fruits: vine (grapes), fig, pomegranate, olive, and date (which is also referred to as honey), but it begins with: "for the tree and for the fruit of the tree," and for wine: "for the vine and for the fruit of the vine," with the conclusion: "for the land and for the fruits." This will be further explained with Divine assistance in Section 6.

And it is called "the abridged three blessings" because it includes all three blessings of the Grace after Meals. How so? "On the sustenance" corresponds to the blessing of "He who sustains," and similarly for fruits and wine, "on the tree and on the vine." "And on the desirable land" corresponds to the blessing of the land, "Have mercy" corresponds to the blessing of building Jerusalem, "For You, O Lord, are good and do good" corresponds to the blessing of "He who is good and does good" that the Rabbis instituted. Indeed, the Rambam wrote in chapter 8 that there are some who have the custom not to say it because it is only necessary to say an abridged form of three blessings, not four. However, the Tur wrote that this is the case in all versions, and it is called "the abridged three" based on the three Torah blessings in the Grace after Meals, and this is the common custom in all Jewish communities.

If the blessing of "Me'ein Shalosh" (abridged grace after meals) is from the Torah like the full grace after meals, or if it is rabbinic like other blessings, is unresolved. From the words of the Rambam in chapter 8, where he first explains all the blessings including "Me'ein Shalosh", and then writes in law 12: "All these blessings, if one is uncertain about them... he does not go back and bless neither at the beginning nor at the end because they are from the words of the Scribes," it is clearly explained that it is not from the Torah. For regarding the grace after meals, he ruled in chapter 2 that one goes back and blesses because it is from the Torah (as he also wrote there in the Kesef Mishneh). 

And there are those who say it is from the Torah (Magen Avraham, Siman 172, Sk. 3), and this is the opinion of the Tur at the end of Siman 209 where he writes regarding the words of the Rambam that we brought, and this is his language: "It appears that only the initial blessing is rabbinic... but the final blessing of 'Me'ein Shalosh' for the seven species is from the Torah, as he supports it with a verse, one returns." 

And the language 'supports it with a verse' is not understood, as it implies it is merely a supportive proof (Beit Yosef). And also, the Sefer Mitzvot Gadol (SeMaG) wrote that it is rabbinic, because if it were from the Torah, we would bless three blessings. And indeed, Rabban Gamliel holds so in the Mishnah (Berachot 44a), where he understands that "and you shall bless" applies to all seven species, but the Sages disagree with him and hold that "and you shall bless" only applies to bread, as it is written there: "A land where you will not eat bread in poverty," and this verse is written after the verse about the seven species, interrupting to tell you that "and you shall bless" only applies to bread. And throughout the Talmud, we only find that the grace after meals is from the Torah. 

And the Rashba in his novellae (beginning of chapter 6) explicitly wrote that it is from the Torah, and so did the Rosh (there, Siman 16) who wrote that it is from the Torah. And since it is a dispute among the authorities, it is considered a doubtful law, and it will be explained at the end of Siman 209. (And to our Rabbis who say it is from the Torah, we must say that what we say there "the land interrupts the matter" is regarding the three blessings and not one blessing. And the Drishah wrote on the Tur that we do not learn this from this verse but from another verse or from a tradition given to Moses at Sinai, and the difficulty is clear, and there is no need to elaborate on this).

And one should not question that if this blessing (the after-blessing for the five species of grains and the seven species of fruit) is of Rabbinic origin, why is it different from other fruits whose after-blessing is "Borei Nefashot" (Who creates numerous living beings), for the reason is simple: For the fruits of the five species with which the Land of Israel is praised, they instituted an important blessing similar to the three blessings (of Birkat Hamazon), while for other fruits "Borei Nefashot" suffices. And even though for the initial blessing there is no difference between them, because it is impossible to differentiate since they are all fruit of the tree. And proof: For the five species of grain, when they are cooked, their initial blessing is different from other foods, for their blessing is "Borei Minei Mezonot" (Who creates various kinds of sustenance) due to their importance, and this cannot be instituted for the five species of fruit, for they are not considered sustenance. But for the after-blessing, it is possible to institute an important blessing for all the seven species due to the importance of the Land of Israel.

The Tur wrote in the name of the Ra'avad that one should not say "and for the produce of the field" regarding fruits and wine, as this expression only applies to types of grain, as it is written: "And he ate the produce of the field." However, in the versions of the Gemara, the Rif, and the Rambam, it is also written as such, and this is the common custom. In truth, Rashi explained that "and he ate the produce of the field" refers to the fruits of the Land of Israel, which are light and ripen quickly, etc., thus it applies to all fruits. Furthermore, the root 'nov' means growth and development, as it is written: "They shall still bring forth fruit in old age," "A man will flourish," "And the face of the world be filled with produce." Likewise, grammarians explain that it refers to the growth and development of fruit, as elucidated in Meir Nativ.

When concluding: "for the fruits of the land, etc.": outside of the Land of Israel, one should say "for the land and for the fruits," and in the Land of Israel, one should say "for the land and for its fruits." Similarly, if one is eating fruits of the Land of Israel outside of Israel, one should also conclude "and for its fruits," and conversely, when eating fruits from outside of Israel in the Land of Israel, one should say "and for the fruits." And our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 11 regarding the condensed blessing that one should not conclude "for the vine and for the fruit of the vine," but rather "for the land and for the fruit of the vine" or "for the land and for the fruits," as he concludes, for he holds that concerning the conclusion, wine is treated like all other fruits. However, there are those who disagree and hold that one must mention the vine even in the conclusion; therefore, one should say "for the land and for the fruit of the vine," as in this manner all opinions agree (Taz, subparagraph 14), and this is the common custom. And after the fact, if one concluded "for the vine and for the fruit of the vine," one has also fulfilled their obligation (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 17). This applies to the final conclusion, but before the final conclusion, everyone agrees that one must say "and we thank You for the land and for the fruit of the vine." And for fruits, one should say "for the land and for the fruits" even in the Land of Israel, as it is sufficient in the final conclusion to say "its fruits" (so it appears to me).

One mentions in this blessing Shabbat, Yom Tov, and Rosh Chodesh, for since it is a long blessing, one must mention the occasion as in the Grace After Meals. This means that before "and we thank You," one says on Shabbat: "and grant us rest on this Shabbat day," and on Yom Tov one says: "and remember us for good on this [specific] festival day," and some say: "and gladden us for good on this [specific day]," and on Rosh Chodesh one says: "and remember us for good on this Rosh Chodesh day," and on Rosh Hashanah: "on this Day of Remembrance." In all these cases, if one did not mention it, he has fulfilled his obligation and is not required to repeat it. However, regarding Chanukah and Purim, one does not mention them at all, since even in the Grace After Meals and prayer, it is not essential after the fact.

If one ate mezonot (grain-based foods), drank wine, and ate fruits of the five species, he should not make a separate blessing for each one but rather include them all in one blessing, and say: "for the sustenance and for the nourishment, for the vine and for the fruit of the vine, for the tree and for the fruit of the tree," prioritizing sustenance over vine, and vine over fruits. At the end, he should also say: "and we thank You for the land and for the sustenance and for the vine and for the fruit of the vine and for the fruits. Blessed are You, Hashem, for the land and for the sustenance and for the fruit of the vine and for the fruits." This is not considered as signing off on two things, which is generally not done, because the land produces everything. Some say that in such a case, it is sufficient to say: "for the sustenance and for the fruits," and there is no need to mention the vine (Magen Avraham 20, citing Mordechai and Agudah).

The five species of grain, which are: wheat, barley, oats, rye, and spelt – when one makes bread from them, one blesses 'HaMotzi', and when one makes them with fruit juice or eggs, one blesses 'Mezonot' and afterwards 'Al HaMichya', if one does not eat enough to establish a meal, as explained in Siman 168 regarding 'Pat HaBa'ah B'Kisnin' (bread-like products). But if one eats raw grain, one of the five species, or roasts them over fire, or even cooks them in a pot with water, but the grains remain whole as they come from the threshing floor without removing their husk (Magen Avraham, siman 5) – one only blesses 'Borei Pri HaAdamah' and afterwards 'Borei Nefashot', as it is taught (Berakhot 36a): "One who chews wheat – blesses 'Borei Pri HaAdamah', if he grinds, bakes, and cooks it – blesses 'Borei Minei Mezonot'." The reason is that eating them in this manner does not make them considered as bread or food, and the verse 'And you shall eat and be satisfied and bless' does not apply in this case, and they are considered like any other produce of the ground that has not been elevated to the status of bread or grain products. However, our Rabbis, the Tosafists, were uncertain regarding the final blessing, as it is not explicitly stated in the Gemara, and perhaps they require the 'Me'ein Shalosh' blessing (the abridged form of Grace after Meals). Therefore, they wrote that it is proper not to eat them except within a meal, and the Grace after Meals will cover them, or one should eat with them grain products and something that requires 'Borei Nefashot'. If it happens that one eats them alone – one should bless 'Borei Nefashot' (Magen Avraham, siman 7), as this is the opinion of most authorities, and in our country, we do not know at all of such eating.

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote in section 4: That which one blesses "Borei Pri Ha'adama" (Who creates the fruit of the ground) over them refers to eating wheat and similar grains that are fit to be eaten as is. However, if one eats whole barley grains, even if they are roasted in fire, they are not fit to be eaten except under pressing circumstances, and one should only recite "Shehakol" (By whose word all things came to be) before eating them. And it appears in our lands that even wheat is not fit to be eaten except under pressing circumstances, and we have never heard of anyone eating it even under pressing circumstances. Also, concerning "Kali and Carmel" (parched grain) mentioned in the Torah, we have not heard of this with our wheat, and the matter requires investigation for the law. When one eats dry flour or flour roasted in fire, even wheat flour, according to the Gemara, one only blesses "Shehakol" before eating and "Borei Nefashot" (Who creates many souls) afterward, whether it is finely ground or only somewhat ground and still has the taste of wheat. The reason is that the blessing "Ha'adama" is lost because the form of the fruit is no longer upon them, and they have not reached the status of bread or food, therefore their blessing is "Shehakol," and this too is unknown to us.

But one who makes dough and cooks or fries it - he blesses 'Borei Minei Mezonot' (Who creates various kinds of sustenance) and afterwards 'Al HaMichya' (the blessing after eating grain products), even if he ate a lot as a fixed meal. There are details regarding frying which are explained in Siman 168, where certain types of frying, if eaten as a fixed meal, require the blessing 'HaMotzi' (Who brings forth bread). And flour from one of the five species of grain, when it is boiled and mixed with water or other liquids: if it is thick enough to be suitable for eating and chewing, meaning it is thick with substance, even if it doesn’t need to be chewed with the teeth because it is soft - one blesses 'Borei Minei Mezonot' and afterwards 'Al HaMichya'. But if it is thin to the extent that it is suitable for drinking - this is not considered eating, like beer, and one blesses 'Shehakol' (Who creates everything) and afterwards 'Borei Nefashot' (the blessing after drinking) as with all kinds of drinks. And Rabbi Yosef Caro wrote in paragraph 3: When flour is added to almonds made for a sick person, if this is done to satiate the heart - the blessing is 'Borei Minei Mezonot', and it is good to be stringent and consume it within the meal after the blessing 'HaMotzi' and be exempt in any case, end quote. And it is obvious that we are referring to it being thick with substance, because if not, in any case, one blesses 'Shehakol' as mentioned. And what he wrote: 'to consume it' is not literal, and his intention is to eat it. And sugar candies made from sugar with flour added - they are only for binding and their blessing is 'Shehakol'. But cakes (lekach), even though they contain a lot of honey and spices, still, their main purpose is for eating and their blessing is 'Borei Minei Mezonot' (and see Taz paragraph 4, whose words require examination, but it is not the custom as mentioned).

Rambam wrote in Chapter 3, Law 4: "Flour from one of the five species that was cooked in a pot, whether by itself or mixed with other things such as fritters and the like, and similarly, grain that was split or crushed and cooked in a pot such as groats and parched grain and the like, all of this is called 'pot dish', and similarly any cooked dish in which one of the five species was mixed, whether flour or bread initially - one blesses over it 'Borei Minei Mezonot' (Who creates various kinds of sustenance)." These are the concluding words of the Rambam, and something similar was written by the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch, Section 2.

And the explanation of the matter is: This refers to thick flour that has substantial edibility, and therefore even if it was mixed with other ingredients that are the majority compared to the flour, nevertheless the flour is primary. And thus it is stated in the Gemara (36b): "Anything that contains one of the five species [of grain] - we recite upon it 'Borei Minei Mezonot'," meaning even if they are a minority compared to the other ingredients in the pot. And this is the wording of the Tur: "A cooked dish that contains one of the five species [of grain], even if it was mixed with other ingredients until they became the majority - one recites upon them 'Borei Minei Mezonot' and afterwards the one blessing that encapsulates three [Birkat Hamazon]. But if they were only added to the dish to thicken it or bind it - they are nullified in the dish." End quote.

And the Rambam did not mention a blessing at the end of the meal similar to the 'three blessings' because this is not a general rule. Even though for foods made from the five species of grain one always recites a blessing when there is even a small amount of flour from the five species, nevertheless, the final blessing of "Al Hamichya" is only recited when there is an olive's worth of flour within the time it takes to eat a pras (a specific quantity of food). This is what the Tur is referring to. Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, explained this in section 9, where he wrote: "If one mixed millet flour and other types of legumes with the flour of the five species of grain and cooked it in a pot, one recites 'Borei Minei Mezonot' and 'Al Hamichya'. If one made it into bread, one recites 'Hamotzi' and the Grace After Meals. But this is only if there is enough of the flour from the five species to eat an olive's worth of grain within the time it takes to eat a pras. However, if it does not contain this amount from the five species, one does not recite the Grace After Meals, but rather initially recites 'Hamotzi' because it has the taste of grain even though it does not contain an olive's worth within the time it takes to eat a pras, and at the end, 'Al Hamichya'. If it was cooked in a pot, one initially recites 'Borei Minei Mezonot' and afterwards 'Borei Nefashot'." End of quote. This that he wrote regarding bread, if it does not contain an olive's worth within the time it takes to eat a pras, one recites 'Al Hamichya' at the end, and it would seem that one should recite 'Borei Nefashot' like when it was cooked in a pot. Some have questioned this (Magen Avraham, section 15). However, his reasoning is that when there is not an olive's worth within the time it takes to eat a pras, we descend one level and no more. Therefore, for bread, where an olive's worth within the time it takes to eat a pras requires the Grace After Meals, when there is not an olive's worth within the time it takes to eat a pras, we descend to 'Al Hamichya'. And for a cooked dish, where an olive's worth within the time it takes to eat a pras requires 'Al Hamichya', when there is not an olive's worth within the time it takes to eat a pras, one recites 'Borei Nefashot' (Eliyah Rabbah, section 13, and in the Drisha another explanation is given though it is strained, see there. The Magen Avraham wrote regarding rice, see there, and it will be explained later in section 23, pay attention).

And this is what the Rambam wrote: "And similarly, grain that has been split or crushed and cooked in a pot, such as porridge, etc.," end quote. The explanation of the matter is as follows: It has already been explained in section 9 that when whole grains of grain are cooked without their husks being removed, one blesses "ha'adama" over them. Therefore, he says: "grain that has been split or crushed," meaning that whole grains were not cooked but rather the grains were split, like our groats made from barley or oats where one grain of barley or oats is made into several pieces, and consequently their husks are removed and they become small pieces. And afterwards he says: "or crushed," meaning that even though the grains were not split but rather crushed so much that their husks were removed, and much of the food itself was also removed, as they used to crush the groats or pearl barley, which is barley ground in mills but not ground into fine pieces like groats, rather each barley grain is crushed by the stone until its husk is removed and much of the barley itself is also removed, as is known. Therefore, their blessing is "mezonot," and afterwards "al hamichya." And their status is like that of flour, as explained, that even if they are the minority in the dish, their blessing is "mezonot." And if there is an olive's bulk in the measure of the time it takes to eat a pras, one blesses afterwards "al hamichya." And if there is not an olive's bulk in the measure of the time it takes to eat a pras, one blesses initially "borei minei mezonot" and afterwards "borei nefashot," just as with flour of the five species, as explained.

And the language of our teacher, the Beit Yosef, in this matter requires clarification, as he wrote in paragraph 2: "The five species of grain that were boiled or crushed and made into a dish, such as porridge, thick soup, grits, and pudding, even if he mixed a lot of honey or other ingredients with them more than the grains themselves - one blesses 'Borei Minei Mezonot' over them and afterwards 'Al Hamichya'. But if he only added the grain to the dish to bind it and thicken it - it is nullified in the dish." These are his words. And behold, all this has already been explained, but what he wrote at the beginning of his words: "The five species of grain that were boiled" is difficult, as it implies that even if they were boiled whole, and it has already been explained that if they are whole, their blessing is 'Borei Pri Ha'adama' (Magen Avraham, Section 2). And they wrote that his intention is that they were boiled so much that they were mashed and stuck together (there), meaning that in such a case, even if they were cooked whole - one blesses 'Borei Minei Mezonot'.

Based on this, I have heard that there are those who mistakenly say that when cooking our groats, if they do not stick to each other—and that means they have to shrink a lot until they stick to each other—one should bless "Ha'adama" (the blessing for things that grow from the ground). This is a complete mistake. Firstly, this is only when cooking whole grains and not when they are split, like our groats, as explained by the Rambam. Also, it does not apply when they are crushed, like our split groats. Besides this, it is clear that there is a small printing error in the words of Rabbeinu Beit Yosef. Instead of "ששלקן" (when boiled), it should say "שחלקן" (when split), as he is copying the language of the Rambam in his holy way, and why would he change his words for no reason? How could he not copy what the Rambam wrote? Certainly, they erred by confusing the "ח" of "שחלקן" with the second "ש" of "ששלקן." However, the law they innovated that even when they are cooked whole and have been mashed and stuck to each other is also correct, because in such a case, their peel is definitely removed, and it is like they are split or crushed (and I found that Rabbi Zalman Margolies wrote similarly in Yad Ephraim that it is an error, and so it is written in the name of Eshel Avraham).

Based on this, when we cook items such as lakshen (noodles), farfel, kreplach (dumplings), barley groats, oats, or pearl barley grits, even if we mix in types of legumes like chickpeas or potatoes which are called kartoffel and they are much more in quantity than the groats or lakshen, etc., nevertheless, we recite the blessing 'Borei Minei Mezonot' (Who creates various kinds of sustenance) on the dish. However, with regard to the blessing afterward, 'Al Hamichya', one needs to assess if he will eat an olive's size of the groats or lakshen, etc., within the time frame of 'Kedei Achilat Pras' (the time it takes to eat half a loaf of bread) from the entire dish, which is approximately the equivalent of three or four eggs - then he blesses 'Al Hamichya'. If not, he blesses 'Borei Nefashot' (Who creates all living things). And there is no difference whether the groats are stuck together or not, or whether they are mashed or not mashed. And even if they are stuck together and mashed, if they were cooked whole, their blessing is 'Borei Minei Mezonot'. 

And know that rice or buckwheat are not included in the five species of grain and their blessing is always 'Ha'adama' (Who creates the fruit of the ground), and this is known to most people. All this applies when the groats or lakshen, etc., were added for the purpose of eating, but if they were added merely as a binder to the other foods, they are nullified in relation to the other foods.

It is obvious that if they cooked groats for a sick person, or even for a healthy person where the main intention is for the groats and they add a little flour just to bind it or to give sweetness to the groats or for medicinal purposes—the blessing is 'Shehakol.' And even if, when one takes a spoonful of the groats, some flour is mixed in, it is secondary. If one separates the flour alone and eats it—they bless 'Borei Pri Ha'adamah' (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 7), and certainly for green peas. And one does not bless 'Ha'adamah' on a dish of green peas unless there are many peas in the dish, and the intention of the dish is for the peas and not for the broth. Certainly, in the case of green beans, one blesses 'Ha'adamah' and not, as some mistakenly say, 'Shehakol.' And similarly, in all kinds of legumes or potatoes, it depends on the intention in this dish, whether for the broth or for the food (see Taz, subparagraph 11, who wrote that for potato soup one blesses Shehakol, and if it is peas, these are perplexing matters).

And know that we have types of very small groats called "manna groats." Some of them are made from wheat and their blessing is 'Mezonot,' and some are made from groats and their blessing is 'Borei Peri Ha'adama.' It is necessary to distinguish between them because they look similar to the eye; therefore, one must inquire as to what they are. Our teacher, the Rema, wrote in Section 8: "One who makes a dish from other types of legumes, if they remain whole and good, cooked as if they were raw, one blesses 'Borei Peri Ha'adama.' If they have completely disintegrated or are not good when cooked as they are when raw, one blesses 'Shehakol'." And this is what is written: 'completely disintegrated' means when they are disintegrated in a perforated vessel (Magen Avraham, section 13), as they are not typically eaten this way (Beit Yosef), similar to what we have when legumes are strained and only a thick broth remains, and this is called "Gezayta Arba'os," or when the legumes are ground and made into food from the flour, which is also just like a thick broth. However, when they are mashed with a spoon, as this is their usual way of eating and their substance remains, one blesses 'Borei Peri Ha'adama' (Magen Avraham there). The same applies to potatoes when they are mashed with a spoon and called "Kasa Bulba," or fried mashed potatoes in butter or fat - their blessing is 'Borei Peri Ha'adama,' as Maimonides wrote in Chapter 8 regarding fruits that are mashed and made like dough that their blessing is 'Borei Peri Ha'etz,' as written in Siman 202:24, and similarly in all types of cooked dishes. And know that in some places there is a type of dish called 'manna,' which is collected in the summer mornings from the dew and dried, and they look like groats, and their blessing is 'Shehakol' because it is not a type of seed. There is also another type of dish made in factories called 'Saga' which are round, and I do not know their nature or from what they are made.

Rice is "rayz" and millet is "hirz," and even though there have been doubts about this, it has now been clarified that this is indeed the case, and there is no doubt about it. Both are types of seeds, and their blessing should be "Ha'adama" like all other seeds. However, our Rabbis of blessed memory ruled that on rice, one blesses initially "Borei Minei Mezonot" and afterward "Borei Nefashot" (Berachot 37b), because it is satisfying and satiates the heart, they said this regarding the initial blessing (Rosh there). Similarly, if one bakes bread from rice, one blesses "Borei Minei Mezonot" and afterward "Borei Nefashot," and the opinion of the Rosh is that the same rule applies to millet, as it is also satisfying and satiates. However, this is not the opinion of the Rif and the Rambam, and millet is like all other seeds, and this is the practice of the world.

Therefore, one who chews raw rice recites the blessing "Borei Pri Ha'adama" (Who creates the fruit of the ground), as it is no different from chewing raw wheat, and afterward recites "Borei Nefashot" (Who creates numerous living beings). However, if one cooks it or grinds it and makes it into bread, the blessing is "Borei Minei Mezonot" (Who creates various kinds of sustenance) and afterward "Borei Nefashot." And our Rabbi, the Rema, wrote about this in paragraph 7: "If it is cooked until it becomes soft," end quote, meaning that if it is not completely softened, since one eats them whole, they are no better than whole wheat, for which cooking does not change the blessing to "Mezonot," but rather the blessing remains "Ha'adama" as stated in paragraph 9, and so it is here as well. However, it is not exactly the same, because the usual way to eat rice is different from wheat. And so wrote the Kol Bo in the name of R"Y, and this also appears to be the opinion of our Rabbi the Beit Yosef in his major work, that rice always retains the blessing of "Borei Minei Mezonot." It seems to me that the intention of our Rabbi the Rema is not that it is completely mashed until each grain is no longer distinct, but rather that it is well-cooked so that each grain swells as is usual with good cooking. And it seems to me that this is the common custom, that any rice that is well-cooked is blessed with "Borei Minei Mezonot," and this is the main ruling in law (Eliyahu Rabbah in subparagraph 9 disagreed with the Rema, and also the Magen Avraham in subparagraph 10 shares this view, and also the Gra in subparagraph 21, and the Taz in subparagraph 8 had difficulty with this. In my humble opinion, the intention of the Rema is also not that it is completely mashed, and pay close attention).

And regarding rice that has been cooked, our teacher the Beit Yosef wrote in section 7: "This is only if it is not mixed with something else but is rice alone. If it is mixed with another dish and the other dish is the majority, one blesses over it according to the blessing of that dish." These are his words. That is to say, even though its blessing is 'Mezonot' like all five species of grain, nevertheless its law is not the same as theirs. For them, even when they are a minority in the dish, one blesses 'Borei Minei Mezonot' as stated in section 13. However, rice, when it is a minority, is nullified in relation to the other dishes in the pot. There is also another deficiency with rice compared to other dishes. In section 14, it is clarified that although the five species of grain, even when they are a minority, one blesses 'Borei Minei Mezonot,' nevertheless, regarding the 'Al HaMichya' blessing, one needs to eat an olive's bulk (kezayit) within the time it takes to eat a portion (kedei achilat pras). And in the Jerusalem Talmud, the first chapter of Challah says that rice is dragged after, meaning that the nature of rice when mixed with wheat becomes like the wheat itself. And thus it is taught in the first chapter of Challah: "One who makes dough from wheat and rice, if it has the taste of grain, it is obligated in Challah, and a person fulfills their obligation with it on Passover." The Ramban and the Maggid Mishneh ruled that even if the wheat does not have an olive's bulk within the time it takes to eat a portion, because the wheat drags the rice along, and if so, the same applies to the 'Al HaMichya' blessing. However, the Raavad and the Rashba disagree with this, and it will be explained with Heaven's help in Siman 593. Therefore, one should not act upon this (see Magen Avraham, section 15, who also states that the Rambam and the Rosh agree with the Ramban and the Maggid Mishneh; what the Magen Avraham questioned regarding why one blesses 'Al HaMichya,' we have already resolved in section 14 in the name of the Eliyah Rabbah, and pay close attention).

Even though bread stands in a superior position compared to all other cooked foods, due to its importance we bless "Hamotzi" over it, and even with rice it does not diminish in its significance, nevertheless with millet and other types of legumes it diminishes in significance. If one makes bread from them, one only blesses "Shehakol" over it, because it is not customary for people to make bread from them at all, and it is not classified as a fruit, so it is impossible to bless "Ha'adamah" over them. Therefore, the blessing is "Shehakol" and afterward "Borei Nefashot."

Our Sages said (Berachot 41a): “Items that come after the meal but are not because of the meal require a blessing both before and after.” And seemingly, why is a blessing required afterward, for is Birkat Hamazon (Grace After Meals) inferior to an abbreviated blessing or to 'Borei Nefashot'? From this, our rabbis deduced that indeed, Birkat Hamazon does not exempt even the smaller blessings, and Birkat Hamazon does not cover the 'Al HaMichya' blessing (Tosafot Rid). The reason appears from Rashi's explanation, who wrote: “For Birkat Hamazon does not cover them because they are not sustenance (mezonot)” - meaning that Birkat Hamazon only exempts matters of sustenance, which is the bread by which a person lives. And this is what our master the Beit Yosef wrote in paragraph 17: “The blessing of three does not exempt the 'Me’ein Shalosh' (abbreviated three blessings), for if one ate porridge, Birkat Hamazon does not exempt it (if one erred and recited Birkat Hamazon). But with wine, the blessing of three exempts it, for if one recited Birkat Hamazon over wine instead of 'Al HaGefen' – he has fulfilled his obligation. And the same applies if one recited Birkat Hamazon over dates instead of 'Al HaEtz' – he has fulfilled his obligation. And even if he only said the 'Hazan' blessing over wine or dates – he has fulfilled his obligation. If he remembers before concluding the 'Hazan' blessing, he should start 'And for the inheritance of the desirable, good, and spacious land for our fathers,' and conclude with the blessing of 'Me’ein Shalosh'” – end quote.

And the reason that wine and dates exempt [from further blessing] is because they too are nourishing. Nevertheless, this matter is perplexing, for we testify that porridge is more nourishing than wine and dates, and indeed, there are those who question this for that reason (Ba'al HaGoleh). There are those who say the reason is because porridge has another elevation over bread (Magen Avraham 25), but in any case, it is not understood what the connection is. In truth, from the words of the Rosh in the discussion of things that come as part of the meal in the name of Ba'al HaGoleh, it implies that Birkat Hamazon exempts porridge. And similarly, the Rashba wrote there regarding pat haba’ah b’kisnin, and these are his words: "However, after it, it does not require a blessing, for Birkat Hamazon exempts it, for it too is nourishment, and it is logical that Birkat Hamazon exempts it, etc.” Therefore, even though Rabbeinu Yonah ruled that Birkat Hamazon does not exempt them, and Rabbeinu Beit Yosef rules similarly, nevertheless, since from the words of the Rosh and the Rashba it implies that they disagree, it remains a doubtful matter of law, and if one blessed Birkat Hamazon on porridge or on pat haba’ah b’kisnin, it is impossible to instruct to bless 'Al HaMichya,' and it requires further investigation (and the opinion of the Eliyah Rabbah 25 seems to agree, see there).

Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote further in section 13: "If one ate fruits of the seven species and also ate apples, it is not necessary to recite the 'Borei Nefashot' blessing on the apples, as they are included in the 'Al Ha'etz' blessing, since they are also fruit of a tree. But if one ate apples and drank wine, one must recite 'Borei Nefashot' on the apples. All the more so, if one ate meat or fruit of the ground and drank wine or ate from the seven species, one must recite a blessing on each one separately. Similarly, if one ate meat and fish and also ate from the five species (of grain), the 'Al HaMichya' blessing does not exempt the meat and the fish." End of quote. The general principle is that the 'Al HaMichya' blessing does not exempt the 'Borei Nefashot' blessing.

Now, the Tur wrote that his opinion was that the 'Al HaMichya' blessing should exempt soup because it is also nourishing, but the Rosh did not agree with his words. The reason given is that soup does not satisfy in the same way and has no connection to it (Beit Yosef). Furthermore, in the 'Al HaMichya' blessing, nourishment is not mentioned, and soup is not a sustainer (Taz, section 16). I am very puzzled by this, as we say in Eruvin (30a) that all things are called nourishment except for water and salt, so the 'Birkat HaMazon' (Grace After Meals) should exempt all kinds of food. And if it is because the blessing was not established for this purpose, why does it exempt wine and dates? Furthermore, it is not clear what the difference is between sustenance and nourishment.

Therefore, it seems to me that the main reason of the Rosh is that since this blessing was not established for that type of food, one does not fulfill the obligation with it. Wine and dates are different because we find in the Gemara that they are similar to bread. Concerning wine, the Talmud (35b) states: "Bread satisfies and wine satisfies and gladdens." It asks: If so, should we recite the three blessings on it? And it answers: No, because one does not establish a meal on it. Concerning dates, it says there (12a) that if one ate dates and began the blessing with bread and concluded with dates, one fulfills the obligation. Even if one concluded with bread, one fulfills the obligation, because dates are nourishing. Therefore, what we find in the Gemara is established, but for other things, each must be blessed with the specific blessing the Rabbis established and not another blessing.

He also wrote: "If one drank wine and recited the blessing 'Borei Pri HaGafen' (Creator of the fruit of the vine) and then ate grapes, he must recite the blessing 'Borei Pri HaEtz' (Creator of the fruit of the tree) for the grapes. Similarly, in the after-blessing, he must mention 'al ha'etz ve'al pri ha'etz' (on the tree and the fruit of the tree). However, if he mistakenly recited 'Borei Pri HaGafen' for the grapes or 'al ha'gafen' (on the vine) after them, he has fulfilled his obligation. If he drank wine and water, he does not need to recite 'Borei Nefashot' (Creator of many souls) for the water, as the blessing over the wine covers it, just as the initial blessing over wine covers all kinds of beverages." End quote. 

This applies only when the beverages were in front of him at the time he recited the blessing over the wine (Magen Avraham, section 24). This is in the case of drinking wine in an incidental manner, but if one drinks in a fixed manner, even if the beverages were not in front of him, he does not need to recite a separate blessing (ibid.). The reason that one fulfills his obligation for grapes with the blessing 'Borei Pri HaGafen' is that the primary purpose of grapes is for wine, similar to the case where one recited 'HaAdama' (Creator of the produce of the ground) for a tree fruit and fulfilled his obligation, so too in this case (Beit Yosef). Therefore, if he drank wine with the intention to exempt the grapes, he indeed fulfilled his obligation (ibid. and Magen Avraham section 23). If he mistakenly recited 'Borei Pri HaEtz' for the wine, he has not fulfilled his obligation and must recite 'Borei Pri HaGafen' again (ibid., section 22). Although there are those who disagree, the primary ruling follows what we have written in the previous section (as also written by Yad Efraim).

Our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, wrote in paragraph 18: "One should not include any additional blessings in the 'Me'ein Shalosh' (the shortened form of the three blessings) out of doubt, even though he is not adding the name and sovereignty. For example, if one drank a beverage and is uncertain whether its blessing is 'Al HaGefen' or 'Borei Nefashot', he should not eat something whose blessing is 'Borei Nefashot' and something whose blessing is 'Al HaEtz Ve'al Pri HaEtz' and also include 'Al HaGefen Ve'al Pri HaGefen' out of doubt," end quote, because it constitutes an interruption in the blessing if it is not necessary. There are those who say that this is only initially, but after the fact, one can do so since there is no other remedy (Taz 19 and Eliyah Rabbah 17). And it is obvious that someone who ate a fruit of the tree and is uncertain whether its blessing is 'Al HaEtz' or 'Borei Nefashot' should eat something whose blessing is definitely 'Al HaEtz' and thereby exempt both. There is an opinion that in doubt, one can say 'Borei Nefashot' (Levush), but this is not clear, for it is more concerning to say a blessing in vain than not to say a blessing at all (Magen Avraham 26 and Eliyah Rabbah), and if there is no way to resolve the doubt, he should not bless at all.

According to Rashi's opinion in the first chapter of Berachot (12a): If one took a cup of water or beer, whose blessing is 'Shehakol,' but he thought it was wine and its blessing is 'Borei Pri Hagafen,' and he began the blessing: 'Blessed are You, Hashem, our God, King of the universe' intending to say 'Borei Pri Hagafen,' but at 'King of the universe' he remembered and correctly said 'Shehakol Nihiyah Bidvaro' - it is a doubtful matter whether he fulfilled his obligation because he said the correct blessing, or did not fulfill it because at the mention of the Name and Kingship he intended to say the incorrect blessing. But in the opposite case: If he took a cup of wine and thought it was water or beer and began to say: 'Blessed…' intending to say 'Shehakol,' and upon reaching 'King of the universe' he remembered and said 'Borei Pri Hagafen' - he certainly fulfilled his obligation, for even if he had finished with 'Shehakol,' he would have fulfilled his obligation, since for all of them if one said 'Shehakol,' he has fulfilled his obligation. However, in the first case, it is a doubtful matter, and it will be explained further how the law is practically.

Many have wondered what doubt there could be in this case, for he said the blessing properly: 'Blessed… that everything, etc.', and why should it matter to us that he intended to say 'Borei Pri HaGafen.' Not only if mitzvot do not require intention, but even if intention is required, this means the intention to fulfill the mitzvah, but what he intended to say does not matter to us, since he said the blessing properly with his mouth (Rosh in the name of the Raavad and Ramban in Milchamot, and according to what was stated, the question of the Maadanei Yom Tov section 3 is resolved, see there and examine well).

Indeed, there is no difficulty at all, for certainly in a commandment that involves an action, intention is not essential according to the opinion that 'commandments do not require intention.' However, for a commandment that involves only speech, intention is certainly required according to all opinions, since the main aspect of the saying is in the heart. If one did not intend properly in his heart, then he has accomplished nothing (Tosafot). And in this case, where the main intention at the time of the primary blessing was for a different intention, it is worse than having no intention at all (Rosh). And this is true for all commandments, even if we say that commandments do not require intention, but if one intends the opposite - he has not fulfilled his obligation (Tosafot in the name of Rashbam).

And the Rambam's method in Chapter 8, Law 11, is even more perplexing. According to him, even if one recited a blessing improperly, for example, if one blessed on beer with "Borei Pri HaGafen" (the blessing for wine), if at the moment one said "Baruch Ata Hashem" etc., one intended to say "Shehakol" (the appropriate blessing for beer) but stumbled with the tongue and said "Borei Pri HaGafen" instead, one has fulfilled the obligation. And these are the words of the Rambam: "If one took a cup of beer in hand and began the blessing intending to say 'Shehakol' but erred and said 'Borei Pri HaGafen,' one is not required to repeat it. Similarly, if one had fruits of the earth before them and began the blessing intending to say 'Borei Pri HaAdamah' (the blessing for fruits of the earth) but erred and said 'Borei Pri HaEtz' (the blessing for tree fruits), one is not required to repeat it. Likewise, if one had a grain dish before them and started to say 'Borei Minei Mezonot' (the blessing for grain dishes) but erred and said 'Hamotzi' (the blessing for bread), one has fulfilled the obligation, because at the moment of mentioning the name and sovereignty which are the essence of the blessing, one intended only the appropriate blessing for that type. Since there was no error in the essence of the blessing, even though there was an error at the end, one has fulfilled the obligation and is not required to repeat it." End quote.

And his words are exceedingly puzzling. How can he say that there was no fundamental error in the blessing, when the entire blessing is in error since he concluded with a different blessing? For the essence of the blessing is the conclusion. If a person were to only say: "Blessed are You, O Lord our God, King of the universe" and nothing more, would that be considered a blessing? Surely, this is merely taking the name of Heaven in vain, as the earlier authorities have already criticized. 

In my humble opinion, it seems that the Rambam's intention is as follows, consistent with his view in the first chapter of the Laws of Blessings, that one fulfills their obligation with intention in the heart alone. According to this, he rightly says: “When he mentioned the Name and Kingship, which are the essence of the blessing, he intended only the appropriate blessing, etc.” This means that since at the time of mentioning the Name and Kingship he intended in his heart to say it properly, it is as if he completed the blessing in his heart and has fulfilled his obligation. Therefore, what does it matter to us that he concluded verbally inappropriately, since he already fulfilled his obligation with the intention of his heart?

(And as for the blessings of the Shema, where we follow only the closing as stated by himself in the first chapter of the Laws of the Shema, it is because they are very lengthy and it is not plausible that he intended the entire appropriate text in his heart, obviously. This is not the case with blessings over enjoyment, which are short. The Kesef Mishneh and the Lechem Mishneh have already elaborated there, as have many of the commentators and in his response to the sages of Lunel who found it perplexing. In my humble opinion, as I have written, this is the most correct way to reconcile his words. Pay close attention.)

The approach of the Rif is clearer, and this is what the Talmud questions: When one takes a cup of water or beer in hand and says, "Blessed… who creates the fruit of the vine," and immediately realizes and also says "shehakol," thus saying, "Blessed are You, Lord our God, King of the universe, who creates the fruit of the vine shehakol nihyeh bidvaro," do we say that he has fulfilled his obligation since he concluded with "shehakol," or since he said this after "who creates the fruit of the vine," it is like it is after the blessing? But conversely, when one takes wine and says, "Blessed… shehakol who creates the fruit of the vine" - surely he has fulfilled his obligation, for with "shehakol" alone one fulfills the obligation for all items. And the Rif ruled that in cases of doubt regarding blessings, we are lenient and do not require him to repeat it, and the Ramban and the Rosh agreed with his interpretation and version. But the Rashba is puzzled by this, questioning what benefit there is in saying it after the conclusion of the entire blessing. It appears that since the conclusion was in error, we do not consider it a conclusion but merely an interruption, and although it is forbidden to interrupt in the middle of a blessing with other speech, nevertheless, after the fact, we do not say that the interruption invalidates the blessing since he corrected himself within the time it takes to speak and said it properly. Furthermore, this is not considered an interruption like other interruptions, for he is saying that the Holy One, blessed be He, created this and that (Ramban in Milchamot).

Here is the translation of the passage:

"And behold, the Rambam according to his approach and the Rif according to his approach ruled leniently according to the principle of 'in cases of doubt regarding blessings, one should be lenient,' and presumably Rashi also follows this approach. However, the Tosafot wrote there that Rabbeinu Yitzchak would rule stringently, that one needs to bless again, see there, and this is not understood at all, since this is a clear law that in cases of doubt regarding blessings, one should be lenient. However, from their words, it later became clear what their intention was. They wrote: 'And Rabbeinu Tam would say, if he knew clearly that he erred in his speech... that within the time it takes to say "Shalom Alecha Rebbe" he can correct himself. And similarly, on Yom Tov if he erred between "Who sanctifies Israel and the times" and said "Who sanctifies the Sabbath" and corrected himself within the time it takes to say "Shalom Alecha Rebbe" — he has fulfilled his obligation, since he knows it is Yom Tov.' End quote. And this is according to the explanation of the Rif, evidently. It turns out that they differentiate between if he knew it was water but mistakenly said 'the creator of the fruit of the vine,' in such a case, in cases of doubt regarding blessings, one should be lenient. But if he did not know at all that it was water and thought it was wine as appears from Rashi's explanation, in such a case, we do not say 'in cases of doubt regarding blessings, one should be lenient,' because in the essence of the blessing he did not know at all that it was water but thought it was wine, and there is no blessing here at all (and also the Prisha wrote this distinction from his own reasoning, and we derived this carefully from the words of the Tosafot themselves)."

And this is the language of the Tur: "If one had in his hand a cup of water and thought it was wine, and he began and said: 'Blessed are You, Hashem, our God, King of the Universe,' intending to say 'Who creates the fruit of the vine,' and then realized it was water and finished with 'by Whose word everything comes into being' — he has fulfilled his obligation. All the more so if he had a cup of wine and thought it was water, and began intending to say 'by Whose word everything comes into being,' and then realized it was wine and finished with 'Who creates the fruit of the vine' — he has fulfilled his obligation, as even if he finished with 'by Whose word everything comes into being' he has fulfilled his obligation. Similarly, if he erred and said over wine: 'by Whose word everything comes into being, Who creates the fruit of the vine,' or said over water: 'Who creates the fruit of the vine, by Whose word everything comes into being' — he has fulfilled his obligation. The same law applies to fruits of the tree and fruits of the ground, where he was supposed to bless on one of them and began with the intention for the other and then realized and finished correctly, or said both — he has fulfilled his obligation." So are the words of the Tur. And this is the explanation of Rashi and the explanation of the Rif, who ruled leniently, and the explanation of the Rambam was not brought at all. According to our understanding, this makes sense, since the main reason of the Rambam is that blessings can be fulfilled through contemplation, and all the poskim disagree with this, as we have written in Siman 185 that only if one did not hear it with his ear he has fulfilled his obligation, but not through contemplation. Therefore, according to the explanation of the Rambam, it is certain that one must return and bless the blessing of 'by Whose word everything comes into being.'

Our master, the Beit Yosef, in section 1 first brought the explanation according to the Rambam and afterwards according to Rashi, and ruled in both that one fulfills their obligation. In section 2, he brought the explanation of the Rif according to the language of the Tur. Some say that according to the explanation of the Rif, which deals with a case where one said both blessings: "Borei Pri HaGafen" and "Shehakol, etc.," and they ruled that one fulfills their obligation, this is only when one knew it was water but stumbled with their tongue and said "Borei Pri HaGafen," and therefore it is effective when they subsequently said "Shehakol" within the time of "toch kedei dibur" (within a short interval). And some say that even after "kedei dibur" it is effective (Magen Avraham, subsection 4, in the name of R. Yehuda HaLevi). However, our master the Beit Yosef was meticulous to say specifically within "toch kedei dibur," and so wrote the Ramban, and this is also implied by the language of the Tur, and this seems to be the primary ruling, that after "kedei dibur" there is no connection to the blessing. And certainly, according to the explanations of Rashi and the Rambam, who do not deal with a case where both were said, there is no difference between "toch kedei dibur" and after "kedei dibur," and not according to the Rif (and so wrote the Gra, subsection 6).

However, in any case, the opinion of the great authorities is that according to the interpretation of the Rif, if one did not know at all that it was water - he has not fulfilled his obligation even after the fact and must go back and recite the blessing "Shehakol" (Magen Avraham subsection 3 and Prisha). This is also the opinion of the Tosafot, as mentioned in Section 7. But the Levush wrote that even if he did not know it was water, see there. However, later in Siman 487 it seems to support the first opinion. There are those who want to differentiate between the blessing of prayer there and the blessing of enjoyment here (Eliyah Rabbah), but this is a forced explanation. And even though there is a principle of leniency in cases of doubt concerning blessings, in this case, it is not a doubt, because since neither his intention nor his speech was proper - it is not considered a blessing at all.

And our master the Rema wrote: "If others were also drinking and had wine before them, and his intention was also on the wine, thinking that there was wine in his cup, and he blessed 'Borei Pri HaGafen' (Who creates the fruit of the vine), and it was later found that his cup had water or beer, when he subsequently drinks wine, he does not need to recite the blessing again. He fulfills the obligation with the blessing he made on his cup, even though it was in error, because his intention was also to drink other wine and to fulfill the obligation for others who were drinking there. Therefore, his blessing is valid." End of quote. 

The explanation of his words seems to me: If no others were drinking, and he alone was drinking this cup, and his intention at the time of the blessing was also to drink other cups that contained wine, and he thought that this cup also contained wine, and he blessed 'Borei Pri HaGafen' (Who creates the fruit of the vine), and it was found that it contained water, this is exactly the law explained in Siman 206 regarding blessing on fruit and it being lost. If his intention was to eat more of that type, he does not need to bless again. However, this applies only if he did not taste the water in the cup. But if he tasted it, it constitutes an interruption between the blessing and the wine, and he must bless again. 

But if others were also drinking and he was the one making the blessing and fulfilling the obligation for all of them, and they all drank based on his blessing, and there was no interruption between the blessing and their drinking, then even though he interrupted with drinking water, it does not matter (and this resolves what the Taz in subsection 2 and the Magen Avraham in subsection 5 questioned; see there and understand well). (And what the Magen Avraham wrote regarding the blessing 'Pokeach Ivrim' (Who gives sight to the blind) or Havdalah does not need to be explained, as it can be learned from the previous law).

Rabbi Yosef Caro wrote in section 3: "For all blessings, if one is uncertain whether he recited the blessing or not, he does not recite the blessing either initially or subsequently, except for Birkat Hamazon because it is of Torah origin." The Tur wrote that also the blessing "Me'ein Shalosh" is of Torah origin for the Seven Species. Therefore, it is proper for every God-fearing person to eat another olive-sized portion of that species so that he can recite the blessing with certainty (Taz, section 3). This law remains a doubtful case, as there is a disagreement among the authorities, as mentioned in Siman 208, section 3.

It has already been explained that the first blessing has no fixed measure, for even if one ate or drank any amount, one is required to recite a blessing. The measurement of an olive's bulk (kezayit) and a quarter-log (revi'it) is only relevant to the final blessing, not the initial one, as it is forbidden to derive benefit from this world without a blessing. Each person's blessing is according to the amount they consumed, even if it is less than a kezayit, contrary to the opinion that for less than a kezayit one should only recite "shehakol" (see Beit Yosef). This is not the case; rather, the blessing for less than a kezayit is the same as for a kezayit, and the same applies to beverages.

As we have explained at the beginning of Siman 202, all foods combine to make up a kezayit, and all beverages combine to make up a revi'it, and one should consume the kezayit within the time it takes to eat a half-loaf of bread.
