There is a disagreement regarding the time it takes to eat a half-loaf and the combination of beverages, and beverages that are on foods are considered like foods.

Regarding the primary law concerning beverages, that one needs a revi'it for the final blessing, this is the opinion of the Rambam in Chapter 3, both for wine and other beverages. Our Rabbis, the Tosafists, were uncertain if wine requires a revi'it or if a kezayit suffices for the final blessing, and therefore one should be careful to drink either less than a kezayit or a revi'it. The general consensus follows the Rambam, and this appears to be the opinion of the authors of the Shulchan Aruch. Some hold the measure to be a "mouthful" (see Siman 190).

Furthermore, we have explained there that there is no difference between one beverage and another, contrary to the opinion that for strong liquor, a final blessing is required even for less than a revi'it (see Taz, subsection 1), which is not the case. For all types of beverages, a revi'it is required. The measure of a revi'it is as much as displaces an egg and a half from a vessel full of water (Eliyah Rabbah, and Magen Avraham, subsection 2, requires wine, which is not necessary), and this is measured with medium-sized eggs.

There are those who wish to double the measures nowadays because eggs have become smaller, but we have already explained that this is not so, and the measurements have not changed and will not change, as there are always large and small eggs. We have brought this from the words of the Tashbetz and other poskim as we wrote in Siman 168. Some say that a revi'it holds as much as fills two shells of a hen's egg (Shelah), which is the measure of displacing an egg and a half from the water. We customarily measure a revi'it as one percent of a hin, and this measure is called a "quarter" or "zwertka." 

If an olive's bulk (kezayit) shrinks and becomes less than a kezayit, a final blessing is not required, and conversely, if it increases, a final blessing is required. Holes in food do not combine to make up a kezayit. All this we have explained in Siman 202.

There is someone who wrote in this language: "It seems to me that if one ate less than the minimum required amount (a kezayit) and went outside and then returned to his place, he must recite a new blessing at the beginning, even for bread, because he does not need to recite a concluding blessing, and his status is like other foods. Therefore, it is questionable if he returned and ate less than the minimum required amount whether these portions combine, as it could be considered an interruption of intention. It seems to me that they do combine." End of quote (Magen Avraham, end of section 1). In my humble opinion, it seems that since it was explained at the beginning of section 158 that for less than the size of an olive (kezayit) of bread, one does not need to wash hands, therefore it depends on this: If he washed his hands, certainly the portions combine and he also does not need to recite a new blessing, because certainly his intention was to eat a kezayit or more than a kezayit, as some say that until an egg-size (kebeitza) one does not need to wash hands, as explained there. And if he did not wash his hands, he needs to recite a new blessing and the portions do not combine, because if you say that they combine, then if he eats many times, each time less than a kezayit, it turns out that he ate without washing hands (so it seems in my humble opinion).

In the Jerusalem Talmud (Chapter 6, Halacha 1) it is stated: Rabbi Yochanan ate an olive and blessed it both at the beginning and the end, even though when the pit is removed, which is inedible, there is not a kezayit (olive's bulk) remaining, because something that is a complete entity does not require a kezayit. And it says there: even if one ate a single grape, it requires an after-blessing even though it does not have a kezayit. According to this, if one eats a single pulse or lentil or one bean, an after-blessing is required. But our Rabbis, the Tosafists (Bava Metzia 39b s.v. 'Batzar') were uncertain about this, because this incident is also mentioned in the Talmud there, and it questions Rabbi Yochanan similarly to the Jerusalem Talmud, and answers that Rabbi Yochanan ate a large olive, that even though the pit is removed there remains still a medium-sized kezayit, and the measure of a kezayit is medium-sized. And since the Talmud does not answer from the reason of a complete entity, we learn from this that our Talmud does not hold like the Jerusalem Talmud in the law of a complete entity, and the law follows our Talmud. However, it is possible to say that the incident in our Talmud is not the incident in the Jerusalem Talmud, and in our Talmud it refers to eating a salted olive, and it is possible that the pit was already removed from it and it is not in its complete form, and therefore it needed to answer that he ate a large olive. In any case, the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch ruled that the law of a complete entity is a doubtful law, therefore every person should distance themselves from eating a complete entity less than a kezayit and eat many of them, because otherwise one will come to a doubtful blessing. And the Rambam did not mention this at all, from which we understand that he holds that the law is not like the Jerusalem Talmud.

And some say in this manner: if it is something that is not normally eaten with the pit, such as an olive or plums with hard pits and the like, where the pit is a hard shell – it is not considered a "whole entity" (beriah), since it will never be a complete entity, because if you remove the pit as is customary, it is not whole. But something that is customarily eaten whole with the pit, like grapes, figs, pomegranates, and our small fruits like gooseberries or little grapes and all kinds of berries – it is indeed considered a "whole entity" (beriah) (Terumat HaDeshen). And this is the practice of our master, the Rema, who wrote that it is not called a "whole entity" unless it is eaten as is, but if the pit is taken from it, it is not called a "whole entity." And if one eats what is inside the pit, where there is food inside the hard shell, some say that it is considered a "whole entity" (Magen Avraham, Siman 4). And it is obvious that if even a small part is missing or if one did not eat it all, even if he left a small part – it is not considered a "whole entity." However, if a small part naturally falls off due to cooking, it is still considered a "whole entity." It also appears that an external shell does not invalidate, and if one eats a broken nut, since he ate all the food inside, it is considered a "whole entity." If the edible shell is not eaten, it is an invalidation and it is not considered a "whole entity"; therefore, with nuts, if one peels the soft shell covering the food, it is not considered a "whole entity," and similarly with legumes. And know that there are those who eat tiny seeds, and they are very small and are peeled and eaten, and it is unlikely that one would eat an olive's worth in the time it takes to eat half a loaf, as is known. And it is proper for one who fears Heaven to be cautious and avoid any doubt, and to eat at the time of action something that definitely contains an olive's worth or to drink a quarter-log, so that he can make an after-blessing without doubt.

The Tur wrote: "One who eats from the seven species less than an olive's bulk, and therefore cannot recite the 'me'ein shalosh' blessing, Rabbi Yitzchak wrote that he should recite 'borei nefashot.' And my master and father, the Rosh, of blessed memory, wrote that this does not seem correct, as it is logical that for something that is worthy of the 'me'ein shalosh' blessing, due to the lack of the required amount, it should not be subject to a different blessing. This also appears to be the view of the Rambam, of blessed memory, who wrote: 'One who eats less than an olive's bulk, whether from bread or other foods, and one who drinks less than a quarter-log, whether from wine or other beverages, recites the appropriate blessing before it but does not recite any blessing afterward.' He does not differentiate between a whole entity and other items, nor between the seven species and other species." This is the end of the quote, and he also does not differentiate in the quarter-log measure between wine and other items. (Were it not for the words of our Rabbis regarding the whole entity in the Jerusalem Talmud, I would say that the Jerusalem Talmud follows Rabbi Shimon, who holds in Makkot 17 that one grain of wheat is considered a whole entity, and our Talmud follows the Sages who believe that only a living soul is considered a whole entity, and we follow the Sages in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 100, and this is the reason why the Rif and the Rambam omitted it).

It is stated in the Gemara (14a): "One who tastes [food] does not need to make a blessing, and one who is fasting can taste and it is not an issue. Up to how much? Up to the measure of a revi'it." And the Tur wrote: "It appears that even if he tastes and swallows [the food], and so wrote the Rambam, of blessed memory (in Chapter 1): 'Generally, one who tastes does not need to make a blessing up to a revi'it.' But Rav Hai Gaon explained that it is specifically when he tastes and spits out [the food], but if he swallows - even any amount requires a blessing. However, when he spits out - he does not need to bless even if it is a large amount," end quote. And this is not understood, for the Gemara explicitly states up to a revi'it, and according to Rav Hai Gaon, it is specifically when he spits out. So how can he say that even more than a revi'it does not need a blessing? It must be said that he holds this only regarding fasting, but regarding a blessing, since he spits it out, how can he bless? And what difference does it make whether it is less than a revi'it or more than a revi'it, after all, his stomach did not benefit from it (Beit Yosef).

And the Rambam implies that he interprets "spitting out" only in the context of fasting and not for blessings. For in the context of blessings, he wrote in Chapter 1: "One who tastes does not need a blessing," and in Chapter 1 of the laws of fasting, he wrote that it is permissible to taste up to a quarter-log and then spit it out, as he believes that for a blessing, one does not need to even if he swallows, since his intention is not for enjoyment at all. And in the context of blessings, he also mentioned up to a quarter-log because beyond a quarter-log it is no longer considered just tasting. And this is what our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in Section 3: "One who tastes... does not need to bless up to a quarter-log even if he swallows it. And some say that if he swallows, he needs a blessing and is exempt only if he spits it out, and then even for a large amount, he does not need a blessing, and in doubtful blessings, we are lenient." This is the end of his words, and the first opinion is the view of the Rambam. And regarding eating, when one tastes, he also needs to chew and spit out. And there are those who wrote that if he swallows, he certainly needs a blessing even for a minimal amount (Magen Avraham section 10), and I am astonished because this is against the opinion of the Rambam. (And also what he wrote in section 6 to differentiate between tasting and tasting needs further examination, and the story of Yonatan that he brought is a contradiction to his words. Also, what he wrote in section 7 that even from many pots it is permissible, needs further examination if it is also permissible to swallow in such a manner. And what he wrote regarding the blessing on tobacco smoke will be explained with the help of Heaven in section 216, and pay close attention).

Maimonides wrote in Chapter 8, Law 13: "If one has many types of foods before him, if their blessings are the same, he recites a blessing on one of them and that exempts the others. If their blessings are different, he recites a blessing on each one according to its proper blessing, and he may choose to bless whichever one he prefers first. If he does not have a preference, if one of them is one of the seven species, he blesses on it first. The one mentioned first in the verse is prioritized for the blessing. The seven species mentioned in this verse are: 'A land of wheat and barley, vines and fig trees and pomegranates, a land of olive oil and honey.' This honey is date honey, and dates take precedence over grapes, for dates are second to 'land' and grapes are third to 'land.'" End of quote.

Explanation of his words: Initially, he wrote that when their blessings are the same, one blesses over one of them and exempts the rest. This means that it is forbidden to bless on this one and intend not to exempt the second one and to make a separate blessing on the second one, and similarly for all of them, as this is close to a blessing in vain, since it is one blessing and his intention is to eat all of them - it is forbidden to increase blessings without need, as stated in Siman 206, Se'if 12. However, if their blessings are not the same, one blesses on each one with the appropriate blessing. This means the opposite, for it is known that when one blesses "Ha'adamah" on a fruit of the tree, he fulfills his obligation, and with "Shehakol" he fulfills his obligation for all things. Therefore, if before him are items whose blessing is "Ha'etz," items whose blessing is "Ha'adamah," and items whose blessing is "Shehakol," and he wants to minimize the blessings, meaning that he will bless "Ha'adamah" and intend to exempt also the fruit of the tree, or bless "Shehakol" to exempt all of them - this too is forbidden initially. Certainly, if he did so, he does not bless another blessing, but initially it is forbidden to do so. Rather, he should bless on each one with its appropriate blessing: on the fruit of the tree he blesses "Ha'etz," on the fruit of the ground "Ha'adamah," and on other items "Shehakol." This does not yet deal with the law of precedence at all (see there).

And now we are dealing with the law of precedence, and it is stated that whichever of them (foods) one wishes to prioritize, one may prioritize. This means that one should prioritize the food that one currently desires more, that is, the food that is currently more cherished to eat than the other. This applies both to blessings that are the same, where one blesses over the more cherished food to exempt the rest, and to blessings that are not the same, one prioritizes the blessing appropriate for it (as noted). There is no difference even if one of them is from the seven species and the other is not, as long as the non-seven species food is more cherished at that moment, one blesses over the cherished one to exempt all or to prioritize its blessing over the others. It was not mentioned that there is any preference for the blessing "Borei P'ri Ha'etz" (fruit of the tree) over "Borei P'ri Ha'adama" (fruit of the ground) or "Borei P'ri Ha'adama" over "Shehakol" (everything), as we only follow what is currently cherished. However, if in terms of preference they are all equal, then the seven species are superior to other foods, and whatever is mentioned earlier in the verse takes precedence for the blessing. (This follows the opinion of the Rif who ruled according to the sages of the Mishnah 40: that one blesses over whichever one wishes, meaning the one currently cherished, and not according to Rabbi Yehuda who says the seven species take precedence over the cherished one. According to their view, we must also say in the case of the incident with the students of Bar Kappara (39.) that "Ha'adama" is preferable to "Shehakol", this is all according to Rabbi Yehuda and not according to the sages, and therefore it was not mentioned by the Rif or Rambam. However, in a case where there is no cherished food - certainly this is the case and there is no need to explain further as it is simple).

However, all our Rabbis disagree with him and hold that one of the seven species is preferable over what is more cherished. Similarly, the blessing "Ha'adama" precedes "Shehakol," even if what requires the blessing "Shehakol" is more cherished, and likewise the blessing "Ha'etz" precedes "Ha'adama." However, the opinion of the Rosh is that regarding "Ha'etz" versus "Ha'adama," there is no significance, and more will be explained on this matter (and the halacha follows Rabbi Yehuda and not the Sages, as the Talmudic discussion supports his view). 

However, this is when the blessings are identical, but when their blessings are not the same, some say there is no order of precedence at all, and even if one is from the seven species and is also more cherished by him, nevertheless, he can bless the second one first. Since he needs to bless each one individually, there is no connection between them at all (Rosh). 

And one should not be surprised by what we said—that there is no order of precedence at all when their blessings are not the same, and we said that "Ha'etz" precedes "Ha'adama" and "Ha'adama" precedes "Shehakol," even though their blessings are not the same. The matter is thus: when their blessings are not the same, there is no superiority of the seven species and no advantage of what is cherished, and also there is no significance of the blessing "Ha'etz" over the blessing "Ha'adama." However, the advantage of "Ha'etz" and "Ha'adama" over "Shehakol" remains even when their blessings are not the same (I learned this from the Rosh, as mentioned there, and also the Tosafot there needed to explain it this way, as mentioned there, and examine it closely).

And there are some of our rabbis who hold that even when their blessings are not the same, only the precedence of the seven species is not removed, but after that, we follow the precedence of what is cherished (Sefer Mitzvot Katan, brought in the Tur, and similarly written in the name of Rabbenu Shmaiah in the name of the Gaon, see Beit Yosef and Bach). And regarding the explanation of what is cherished, they also disagree with the Rambam, for according to the Rambam, it means what is currently preferred by him, and they interpret it as what is generally always dear to him, even if at this moment he prefers another food. And behold, this is the essence of the opinions on this matter.

And know that what we have said according to the previous opinion, that when their blessings are not the same, there is no precedence for the seven species, nor is there a precedence for what is preferred. According to the opinion in the previous section that there is no precedence for the seven species, this applies when one is from the seven species and the other is not, such as a radish whose blessing is 'borei pri ha'adama' and an olive whose blessing is 'borei pri ha'etz,' where one can precede the radish to the olive because they have no connection to each other in any way. But when both are from the seven species and their blessings are not the same, such as chewing wheat whose blessing is 'borei pri ha'adama' and an olive whose blessing is 'borei pri ha'etz,' the wheat precedes because it is mentioned earlier in the verse (and this is the intention of the Magen Avraham in section 2). And some say that what we have said, that when their blessings are not the same, there is no precedence for what is preferred and one can precede whichever one he wants, means that we do not follow what is always preferred to him, but what is preferred to him at this moment (Bach and Taz section 1 and Perisha). Therefore, if one of them is from the seven species, it precedes, even if he currently prefers the other (there), because we hold that the seven species are more important than what is preferred, and it does not appear this way from the Rosh (Magen Avraham there).

Our master, the Beit Yosef, after bringing the opinions of the decisors and the opinion of the Rambam, wrote in section 3: "If they brought before him something whose blessing is 'Borei Pri Ha'etz' (Who creates the fruit of the tree) and something whose blessing is 'Shehakol' (by whose word all things came to be) - 'Borei Pri Ha'etz' precedes because it is significant, as it does not cover anything else, and similarly 'Borei Pri Ha'adamah' (Who creates the fruit of the ground) and 'Shehakol' - 'Borei Pri Ha'adamah' precedes. And if they brought before him 'Borei Pri Ha'etz' and 'Borei Pri Ha'adamah', he may precede whichever he prefers, and some say that 'Borei Pri Ha'etz' precedes" - end quote. The first opinion is that of the Rosh who holds that 'Ha'etz' is not considered more important than 'Ha'adamah'. It seems to me that the Rosh did not say that there is no significance between them except when he currently desires the fruit of the ground more, but if he does not prefer one over the other - 'Borei Pri Ha'etz' precedes. And this is also implied by the language of the Rosh who wrote: that the blessing 'Borei Pri Ha'etz' is not considered so much more significant than the blessing 'Ha'adamah', etc., and it is clearly implied that there is some significance.

Here is the translation:

And behold, the fact that "Ha'etz" (the blessing for fruits of the tree) and "Ha'adamah" (the blessing for fruits of the ground) precede "Shehakol" (the general blessing) applies even if "Shehakol" is more beloved to him (as mentioned there in subsection 3) and even if it could be one of the seven species, because "Shehakol" compared to "Ha'etz" and "Ha'adamah" is considered nothing. And regarding the opinion that "Ha'etz" precedes "Ha'adamah," it has already been clarified in subsection 4 that there are those who say there is no precedence at all when their blessings are not the same. According to the opinion in subsection 5, we follow what is more beloved, and this is also the opinion of the Rambam. If so, how can we find a case where "Ha'etz" precedes "Ha'adamah"? If both are from the seven species, like chewing wheat and eating grapes, isn't wheat first as stated in subsection 6? However, this is the opinion of the Bahag that "Borei Pri Ha'etz" always precedes "Borei Pri Ha'adamah," even against the virtue of the seven species and against the virtue of what is beloved. Nonetheless, in practice, we follow what is beloved, for according to the Rambam, what is beloved always takes precedence, and according to the Smak in this law, what is beloved also takes precedence, and according to Rashi and the Rosh, one blesses on whichever one he prefers, and this is also the opinion of the Gaon. Therefore, the Bahag stands alone in this regard (as mentioned there in subsection 4).

And there are those who wrote in this language: "Regarding the halacha, there is no concern here, as in all the ways there is someone to rely upon: If the blessings are the same and there is one of the seven species, one can take the species of the seven and bless on it and exempt the one that is not of the seven species, and this is the opinion of most of the poskim. And one can take the one that is not of the seven species if it is more cherished to him and exempt the species of the seven, and this is the opinion of the Rambam. And if there is no one among them from the seven species - certainly the more cherished is preferable if the blessings are the same, and when their blessings are not the same it has already been explained that however he does, he has upon whom to rely. And regarding the explanation of cherished: if he takes what is cherished to him now, he fulfills according to the Rambam, and if he takes what is always cherished to him, he fulfills according to the other poskim" (Taz Sk. 1).

And it is stated in the Gemara (Berakhot 41b) that anything mentioned earlier in the verse "A land of wheat and barley" is given precedence in the blessing. In the middle of the verse, it is written "A land of olive oil and honey," and the word 'land' interrupts between them to teach us that what is closer to the second 'land' takes precedence over what is later to the first 'land'. Therefore, honey, which are dates, precedes grapes, since grapes are third to the first 'land' and honey is second to the second 'land'. This rule can apply to all authorities, even according to the Rambam who follows what is more beloved. This means that if they are all equally beloved to him, then according to all opinions, he should give precedence to what is earlier in the verse. This is what our teacher the Beit Yosef wrote in Section 5, that wheat and barley take precedence specifically when they are made into a dish or bread, but chewing wheat, for which the blessing is 'Who creates the fruit of the ground,' does not take precedence over the blessing 'Who creates the fruit of the tree'. His precise wording was 'does not take precedence,' but he did not write that 'Who creates the fruit of the tree' takes precedence, because he already wrote in Section 1 that when the blessings are not the same, there is no preference at all. According to the Rambam and the Sefer Mitzvot Katan, one follows what is more beloved. Only according to the Ba'al Halachot Gedolot does one need to give precedence to 'the tree,' as we have explained (and the words of the Taz in Subsection 5 require examination; see there and investigate).

Based on what has been explained that dates precede grapes, our teacher Rabbi Moses Isserles (Rema) writes in paragraph 4: This is specifically when one eats grapes as they are. But if one makes wine from them, which has its own designated blessing of 'Borei Pri HaGafen' (Who creates the fruit of the vine), it is considered significant and one should bless on it first. However, a dish made from the five species of grain is more significant than the blessing for wine, because its blessing is 'Mezonot' (Who creates various kinds of sustenance) and it precedes wine in the verse (Tur). It will also be explained later in the order of precedence that after 'Hamotzi' (Who brings forth bread from the earth), the blessing of 'Mezonot' takes precedence over all other blessings. According to the Rambam, it seems that in all matters one follows what is preferred, but most decisors do not hold this view, especially concerning the blessings for 'HaGafen' and 'Mezonot'. Our teacher Rabbi Moses Isserles also wrote: Anything mentioned close to the first instance of 'land' in the verse precedes what is mentioned close to the second instance of 'land', assuming they are equal in their proximity to 'land'. This means that wheat precedes olives, and barley precedes dates. This rule only applies according to the Rambam who does not consider precedence in blessings, such as when all are equally preferred. But according to other decisors, this scenario does not arise. If one makes a dish from them, the 'Mezonot' blessing takes precedence. If one chews them and their blessing is 'Ha’adama' (Who creates the fruit of the ground), when the blessings are not equal, there is no precedence as explained. According to the Ba'al Halachot Gedolot (BaHaG), on the contrary, 'Ha'etz' (Who creates the fruit of the tree) precedes, as he wrote. But according to the Rambam, it is consistent (and resolves the question of the Magen Avraham in section 8, see there and examine carefully).

Furthermore, it is written in paragraph 5: "The blessing of 'Hamotzi' precedes the blessing of 'Borei Minei Mezonot,' and certainly other blessings, even if the other item is more important or preferred by him." This ruling seems applicable only when one eats bread less than the size of an olive, for which there is no need to wash hands, as stated in Siman 159. In such a case, 'Hamotzi' takes precedence. However, if one washes hands and eats a fixed meal, this does not apply, for after washing hands, one is required to immediately recite the blessing of 'Hamotzi.' If it is before washing hands, it is common practice on Shabbat and festivals to eat various sweets before washing hands. In such a case, the rule of precedence does not apply since they are two separate matters, and there is an explicit Mishnah: "If one blessed on the appetizer, he has not exempted the bread" (Berakhot 41b.), indicating that one eats the appetizer before the bread, which means before washing hands. (All the words of the Magen Avraham in section 9 are not clear to me at all, and it is a common practice even on weekdays to taste from the dishes and bless on them before washing hands, so what relevance is there to a blessing that is not required when he intends to eat before washing hands, and this is indeed the simple custom of the world).

It has already been explained that the blessing of "Borei Minei Mezonot" (Who creates various kinds of sustenance) takes precedence over other blessings, except for "Hamotzi" (Who brings forth bread from the earth). And not only for types of cooked dishes made from wheat and barley which are explicitly mentioned, but even if there is before him a cooked dish made from spelt flour, oats, and rye, which is called K.A.R.N., which are not explicitly mentioned but are included under wheat and barley — in any case, their blessing takes precedence over grape, fig, and pomegranate which are explicitly mentioned, and even over wine which is considered very important. This is for several reasons: First, since they are included under wheat and barley, they are considered like them themselves. Additionally, since they are important, as they can be made into bread for which one recites "Hamotzi" and Birkat Hamazon (Grace after Meals), they take precedence even when not made into bread. And even barley and its types, which are second to "land," precede the olive which is first in the second mention of "land," because their blessing is "Mezonot" and takes precedence over the blessing of "Borei Peri Ha'etz" (Who creates the fruit of the tree). (Regarding what the Magen Avraham wrote in section 13 that the olive precedes, there is a need for further examination, and all the five species precede it. See Machatzit HaShekel and analyze well.)

In any situation where we have said that one item takes precedence over another, this applies when one wishes to eat both items. Therefore, one should prioritize the seven species, or the preferred item, or the more important item. However, if one does not wish to eat both items, one only recites a blessing over the item they wish to eat, even if the other item is also in front of them, as mentioned in Siman 168 regarding the blessing of 'Hamotzi'. In cases where one must prioritize due to the significance of the seven species, even if one item is a half-fruit and the other is a whole fruit (Magen Avraham section 1), and likewise in prioritizing among the seven species themselves, such as wheat bread taking precedence over barley bread, even if the wheat bread is sliced, as stated in Siman 168. However, in cases where preference is due to the factor of preference (chaviv), it seems that a whole item is preferable (there), when both are equal in the significance of the seven species or when neither is from the seven species. And there is proof from there when both are wheat or both are barley, and one is clean and one is whole, that the whole item is preferable, see there.

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote that all of this necessity to precede [the blessing] is specifically an initial preference. However, if one transgressed and blessed on the second [item], if the blessings are identical, he fulfills his obligation and does not need to go back and bless on the one he should have preceded, provided that he also had intention for it in his blessing. Even if both of them were before him, there is a requirement to explicitly intend to exempt it, as it is not proper to exempt the less important with the important one implicitly, unless he explicitly intends for it. But the important one can exempt the less important one even implicitly (Magen Avraham, section 11). And if the second one is not before him, even the important one does not exempt the less important one implicitly (ibid.), unless he explicitly intended for it. These matters are explained in Siman 206, see there.

According to my humble opinion, what our Rabbi, the Rema, wrote—that something of lesser importance does not exempt something of greater importance by default, even when both are before him—applies to a Torah scholar who knows the law and nonetheless blessed on the less important item. It can be said that by default, it is as if he explicitly did not intend to exempt the more important item. However, in the case of someone who does not know the law at all and unintentionally blessed on one of the items, certainly, by default, it is as if he intended to exempt the other item, for this is known to everyone. And even regarding a Torah scholar, perhaps he holds like the Rambam that the beloved item takes precedence, and for him, this item was beloved. Therefore, this ruling of our Rabbi, the Rema, requires further investigation, and it cannot be ruled this way in practice.

Order of precedence: 'Hamotzi', 'Borei Minei Mezonot' on wheat, 'Borei Minei Mezonot' on barley, olives, dates, grapes, figs, and pomegranates. Some say that olives come before 'Borei Minei Mezonot' on barley (Magen Avraham, section 13, though it is puzzling that he omitted dates), but in my humble opinion this is not so (and so wrote the Eliyah Rabbah). 'Ha'etz' and 'Ha'adamah' come before 'Shehakol', and 'Ha'etz' comes before 'Ha'adamah'. However, if 'Ha'adamah' is more beloved, one should bless 'Ha'adamah' first and intend not to exempt 'Ha'etz'. Among the seven species, any of them has precedence over those not of the seven species, and whichever comes first in the verse has precedence in the blessing. The one closest to the word 'land' [in the verse] has a higher status than the third of the 'land' series. 'Ha'adamah' of the seven species, such as chewing wheat, with 'Ha'etz' not of the seven species: according to the Ba'al Halachot Gedolot, 'Ha'etz' takes precedence, but other poskim (decisors) disagree, and according to the Rambam, what is beloved takes precedence over everything else. According to the Rambam, what is considered beloved is what is currently beloved to him, while according to the Rosh, it is what is always beloved to him. Eating and drinking precede fragrance (there), and it seems to me that eating precedes drinking. Those who drink schnapps with cake, according to all opinions, should bless 'Mezonot' on the cake first, even if the schnapps is more beloved to him, even according to the Rambam, because it is unreasonable that drinking and 'Shehakol' should precede eating and 'Mezonot'. And so should the practical halacha be taught (and 'Borei Pri Hagafen' precedes other blessings except 'Hamotzi' and 'Borei Minei Mezonot').

The Sages taught in the Mishnah (44a): "This is the rule: any food that is the main part and has with it a secondary part - one blesses on the main part and exempts the secondary part." And there are two types of secondary parts: one is mixed and the other is not mixed. How is a mixed secondary part defined? For instance, when two items are cooked together and eaten together, such as when legumes are cooked with groats or groats with potatoes called kartoffels or bulbs. Now, if there is an item in this mixture whose blessing is 'Mezonot', like certain types of groats (oats, barley groats) - even if they are in the minority, their blessing is 'Mezonot', because anything that contains one of the five species of grain, even in small amounts, becomes the primary part due to its importance, and one blesses 'Borei Minei Mezonot' on the whole dish, unless it was not added for eating but merely as a binder, or if the flour was mixed with water until it became soft and is considered a drink and not food, in which case the blessing is 'Shehakol'. But with other types of mixtures, one follows the majority, as stated in Siman 208, where it is explained that rice, even though its blessing is 'Mezonot', does not have the importance of the five species to be considered the primary part if it is a minority, and it is treated like other foods where one follows the majority.

And one should not question, based on this, our practice of cooking dishes with meat and blessing the dish with its specific blessing and the meat with "Shehakol," that one of them should be the primary and the other secondary. This is not a question, because in the context of a mixed secondary item, the primary and secondary concept only applies when they are eaten together, such as when cooking barley with legumes or with potatoes, and taking both together with one spoon. In that case, even if only one type is taken with the spoon, it is still secondary. But if the meat is eaten separately, either before or after the dish, it is not considered primary and secondary. The same law applies if one picks out the potatoes from the dish and eats them separately; one should bless "Borei Pri Ha'adama" if the dish’s blessing is "Mezonot" or "Shehakol," and similarly, if the meat is cut into small pieces and eaten together with the dish, they become nullified and secondary to the dish, and the same applies to all such cases. It is obvious that all this refers to eating the dish and meat outside of a meal, because if they are eaten within a meal, they are all secondary to the bread, and the blessing of "Hamotzi" exempts them, as is the law with items eaten within a meal where the bread exempts them, as stated in Siman 177. Similarly, dough filled with fruits or with eggs or with cheese, like our fried foods—the dough is primary, and there is no need to bless on the filling, even if one eats a little of the filling by itself. However, if one takes the filling and eats it without eating the primary part at all, it is obvious that one blesses on the secondary item the appropriate blessing, because at that moment it is not secondary but primary, and this is the rule in all cases of mixed primary and secondary items.

A secondary item not mixed in, how is it defined? For example, if one eats a salted fish and takes an onion to mitigate the saltiness, and eats the salted fish and then the onion – there is no need for a blessing on the onion. But if he eats the onion first, even though his intention is to mitigate the saltiness of the fish he will eat afterward – nevertheless, he must recite the blessing 'Ha'adama' on the onion. The general rule regarding a primary and secondary item that are not mixed: if one eats the secondary item first – it is not considered secondary and requires its own blessing. Additionally, when eating the primary item, one must have in mind the secondary item. However, if one did not have the secondary item in mind at all, but after eating the primary item felt weak and took the secondary item – he must recite a blessing on the secondary item. And it appears to me that in such a case, even if the secondary item shares the same blessing as the primary item, for example, if one drank liquor and felt weak and took cheese to strengthen the heart, and both have the blessing 'Shehakol', nevertheless, since at the time of drinking he did not have the intention to eat the cheese – he must recite 'Shehakol' on the cheese separately, and similarly for all such cases.

And this is the language of our teacher, the Rema, in Section 1: "The rule that one recites a blessing on the primary food and it exempts the secondary food applies when one eats them together or eats the primary food first. But if one eats the secondary food first, for example, if one wants to drink and wants to eat first so as not to drink on an empty stomach, or if one eats fruit pits to sweeten the drink (that follows) – one recites a blessing on the food first even though it is secondary to the drink. And one only recites the blessing 'Shehakol' on it, since it is secondary to something else." And we learn from his words that even though a blessing is required for the secondary food when eaten first, nevertheless, its blessing is only 'Shehakol' if the primary food's blessing is 'Shehakol' (Magen Avraham, Subsection 4), meaning one blesses the secondary food, and consequently, no blessing is required on the primary food. There are those who wish to say that even if the primary food's blessing is not 'Shehakol,' still one only blesses 'Shehakol' on the secondary food even though it has a different blessing, because since it is secondary, the main blessing is removed from it, and afterward, one blesses the primary food with the appropriate blessing (Terumat HaDeshen). However, this is not clear (Magen Avraham there). And know that some have written that if the secondary food is always more desirable to him – he blesses the secondary food in all cases (Taz, end of Subsection 7 and Eliya Rabba). This is two opposites in one subject, for if it is desirable to him, it is not secondary, and if it is secondary, it is not desirable to him (and the law is true, but in such a case, the name 'secondary' is nullified from it, and in Section 6 this will be further explained).

There are times when even bread, which is more important than anything else, is secondary. And this is the language of our teacher, the Beit Yosef, in Section 1: "Even bread, which is more important than anything else, if it is secondary, such as eating salted fish and eating bread with it so that it does not harm the throat - one blesses the fish and exempts the bread since it is secondary." End of quote. This means that he does not desire the eating of bread at all, and since the primary eating is not for the bread - he does not bless it (Magen Avraham, Subsection 2, in the name of Turei Zahav). According to this, when one desires to drink brandy and prepares some bread or a small cake to revive the heart and the primary intention is not their consumption, one blesses the brandy with 'Shehakol' and exempts them. And know that it is certain that any secondary [food] is only a small amount to revive the heart or to prevent harm to the throat, and then no blessing is needed for the secondary, neither a preliminary blessing nor a concluding blessing. But when one eats a lot - it cannot be called secondary. Therefore, all God-fearing individuals refrain from taking even a small amount of bread or a small cake as secondary after drinking a little brandy as is customary, because who can measure this?

And our master, the Rema, wrote: "And some say that if the secondary item is precious to him, he blesses on it and then blesses on the primary item." And we already wondered in section 4 that if it is precious to him, it is not secondary. We must say that this is according to the explanation of the Rosh that we brought in Siman 211, that 'precious' refers to what is always precious to him. According to this, it can be said that now it is not precious to him, and therefore it is secondary. However, since it is always precious to him, it requires its own blessing, and the primary item does not exempt it if its blessing is not the same as the primary item (and so wrote the Gra in section 9. What he wrote further about this and several things he wrote in this Siman were not clarified to me; refer there and examine closely).

It is simple that when one soaks bread in whisky or cake or lekach (honey cake) and tart, even though his intention is for the whisky absorbed in it - nevertheless, they are primary and the whisky is secondary, and he blesses 'Hamotzi' and requires washing of the hands, or he blesses 'Mezonot' and exempts the whisky absorbed in it, and similarly when soaking in wine or other beverages. There is someone who distinguishes between before eating, where then he blesses on the bread, and after eating (Magen Avraham, end of section 3), but in my humble opinion, there is no distinction in this matter, for if it is during the meal, no blessing is needed, and if it is after Birkat Hamazon, for us 'Shehakol' is considered within the meal as stated in Siman 177, and certainly also then the bread is primary and it requires further investigation, and we have never seen anyone do this after Birkat Hamazon and it is proper to avoid this. If one desires a drink after Birkat Hamazon, he should drink the beverage alone and bless over it.

Rabbeinu the Beit Yosef wrote in section 2: “A confection that is placed on thin wafers, those wafers are secondary to the confection, as it is known that one does not intend to eat bread.” This is because they are only used to support the confection so that the hands do not get soiled with honey. Nonetheless, if one eats the confection by itself and then eats the wafers, one must bless 'Mezonot' on them because they become primary (Taz, subparagraph 8). However, in our times this is uncommon, and the confection sticks to the wafers to give flavor to the wafers (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 5), and therefore the wafers are primary and the confection is secondary, and one blesses only 'Borei Minei Mezonot'. The same law applies to lekach (honey cake). And know that there is a type of confection in certain places called ingberlach, which is fried cinnamon with nuts and almonds, and it depends on which is primary. If they mix in farfel and their intention is only for binding, one blesses 'Ha'adamah', but if not, one blesses 'Mezonot'.

It has already been explained that the blessing of enjoyment (Birkat Hanehenin) is not like the blessing over commandments (Birkat Hamitzvot), where one person can fulfill the obligation on behalf of another even if he has already fulfilled his own obligation, due to the principle that all of Israel are responsible for one another. However, with the blessing of enjoyment, this is not the case. If the person is not currently deriving benefit, he cannot recite the blessing on behalf of others, for in this case, the principle of mutual responsibility does not apply, as it is not a mandatory obligation on the person. Therefore, the person reciting the blessing cannot fulfill the obligation for others unless he eats and drinks with them. In that case, they can fulfill their obligation by listening to his blessing if he intends to fulfill their obligation and they intend to be fulfilled by his blessing, even if they did not respond 'Amen,' since listening is like responding, provided they do not interrupt with speech while he is reciting the blessing. Similarly, if they did not hear the blessing from the beginning to the end, even if they responded 'Amen,' they do not fulfill their obligation and must recite the blessing themselves. Likewise, if he does not eat and drink with them and recites the blessing on their behalf, his blessing is in vain, and they are obligated to recite the blessing themselves (Magen Avraham, subsection 7), unless they recited with him together and responded after him to what he said.

In Siman 167, Se'if 21, it is explained that during a meal, regarding the blessing of 'Hamotzi,' the participants do not fulfill their obligation with the blessing of the one who recites it unless they are reclining. For us, sitting around the table is like reclining for them, as we are not accustomed to reclining. The Tur and the Shulchan Aruch write in Se'if 1: "For all fruits and other items except for bread and wine, if the eaters are two or more, one can exempt the other even without reclining. However, sitting is still required, and specifically bread and wine, which are significant, require reclining. For us, sitting is like reclining for them. According to this, for us who do not recline, there is no difference between bread and wine and other items. When sitting, even for bread and wine, one person can recite the blessing for everyone, and without sitting, even for other items, each person must recite the blessing for themselves." End quote.

Explanation of the matter: In the Gemara (43a), the rule regarding other items is not mentioned at all. It is only mentioned there regarding bread that reclining is necessary. Concerning wine, there is a dispute in the Gemara there whether reclining is needed or sitting is sufficient, or if even reclining does not help because it does not have a fixed status. The poskim (decisors of Jewish law) ruled according to the version that wine is like bread because wine is important and most banquets are with wine. Regarding other matters, they concluded logically that reclining is certainly not applicable because they do not have such a fixed status. Without sitting, one cannot fulfill the obligation for others, as it is even taught regarding bread: "If they were sitting, each one blesses for himself." For us, if there is no fixed sitting, each one blesses for himself, and all the more so for other foods where fixed sitting is necessary. The sitting needs to be fixed, and if they intend to leave their place immediately, it is not considered sitting at all, and each one blesses for himself (see Magen Avraham, Section 1).

And all of this applies only to the first blessing when they are sitting together to eat or drink and it constitutes a fixed setting, then one can recite the blessing for the others. However, for the final blessing when they are about to part ways, they need to divide, and one cannot recite the blessing for another, and each one must recite it for himself. This is not similar to the zimun of the Birkat Hamazon, for through the zimun they are all united together, but with fruits, zimun does not apply, as there is no zimun for fruits and they are considered as separate individuals. It appears to me that even when eating pastries whose blessing is 'Mezonot', since they are eaten without a fixed meal and without the quantity of a fixed meal - their law is like that of fruits, and it is not similar to wine which is drunk in large quantities. And when they eat the quantity of a fixed meal, then it requires washing of hands, 'Hamotzi', and Birkat Hamazon, and it is considered like actual bread.

And since the Gemara does not mention a law regarding other items, therefore some of our Rabbis hold that, on the contrary, since they do not have importance, they are not subject to either reclining or sitting and are always considered separate, and it is impossible for one to exempt others in any manner. And this is the opinion of our teacher, the Rema, who wrote: "And some say that for all items other than bread and wine, reclining does not help, and the same applies to sitting for us, and therefore the custom now is that for fruits, each one blesses for himself." And the great ones wrote that nowadays, even for wine, there is no fixed setting, and each one blesses for himself, except if the wine and fruits come at the end of the meal or during the meal, then one blesses for all, because since reclining or sitting for us works for bread, it also works for these items.

And behold, in practice, the common custom is that one person does not discharge another’s obligation in any matter, and each person recites the blessing for themselves. For even in the cases of 'Hamotzi' (the blessing over bread) and Birkat Hamazon (the Grace After Meals), it is rare in our times for one person to discharge another's obligation, and certainly in other matters. Nevertheless, if it happens with fruits or other items that one person recited the blessing, and the others heard and intended to fulfill their obligation with his blessing, and he intended to discharge their obligation: if they were sitting - they have fulfilled their obligation after the fact, both for the initial blessing and the concluding blessing. But if they were not sitting, but rather standing or walking - they have not fulfilled their obligation even after the fact, not even for the initial blessing (Magen Avraham 4 and in Siman 167, and see Machatzit Hashekel).

And know that we have already explained several times that even in a case where one person can fulfill the obligation on behalf of another, and in the Gemara (53a) it is explicitly indicated that this is preferable in such a situation because "In the multitude of the people is the King's glory," nevertheless we do not practice this way because it is unlikely that each person will attentively hear the blessing from the other. Only for Kiddush and Havdalah does one person fulfill the obligation for everyone, even while standing, because they prepare themselves for this, and it is considered as a fixed arrangement (Tosafot 43a, end of s.v. "since"), and this will be explained in Siman 298. Similarly, regarding incense, the Gemara states that one person blesses for everyone, and it seems that sitting is not required, and the reason is because the fragrance reaches everyone equally at the same time, and it is not something that enters the body that would require a fixed arrangement. In conclusion: aside from Kiddush and Havdalah, we are not accustomed at all for one person to fulfill another's obligation with his blessing; rather, each person blesses for themselves (see Shulchan Aruch, Siman 1 and Siman 2, and there is no practical difference for us, and consider this well).

In every blessing, there must be the mention of the Name and Sovereignty and the phrase "King of the Universe": "Blessed are You, Lord our God, King of the Universe." Any blessing that does not contain the Name and Sovereignty is not a valid blessing. If one omits the Name or Sovereignty, he must repeat the blessing, and even if he only omits the word "the Universe," he must repeat the blessing, for "King" alone is not considered Sovereignty (Tosafot 40b, s.v. "Amar"). However, if one omits the word "our God," it seems that he does not need to repeat it. This applies to blessings that have both an opening and a closing formula; the closing does not include "King of the Universe," because since it was mentioned in the opening, it need not be mentioned in the closing. When one says in the closing, "Blessed are You, Lord," it refers back to the opening (this seems to me to be the intention of the Tosafot there).

And this that in the blessing of the Patriarchs in the prayer there is no 'King of the Universe,' since when we say 'God of Abraham,' it is equivalent to kingship, for our father Abraham proclaimed the Holy One, blessed be He, as King over the entire world. Similarly, in the blessing of 'Shield of the Patriarchs,' since we say: 'the holy King unparalleled' or 'the holy God unparalleled,' it is equivalent to 'King of the Universe' (Tosafot there). And similarly in 'My God, the soul' according to the opinion that it is not adjacent to the blessing of 'Who formed,' and does not contain kingship, since it mentions that the Holy One, blessed be He, creates souls and breathes them into bodies and then takes them from them and then returns them to them, there is no greater kingship than this (Beit Yosef). And a blessing adjacent to its companion does not require 'King of the Universe,' since the opening of the first applies to all of them.

And some say that what our Sages said: 'Any blessing that does not include [mention of] kingship is not a blessing,' applies to blessings over enjoyment, blessings over commandments, and blessings of seeing, which are acknowledgements to the Holy One, blessed be He. In these, it is appropriate to mention Him as 'King of the Universe.' But in prayer, whose primary purpose is to request one's needs, although one must first arrange the praise of the Omnipresent, our Sages did not say this; therefore, in prayer, there is no [mention of] 'King of the Universe' (Beit Yosef in the name of Rabbeinu Yaakov Pollak, and similarly written by the Beit Yosef in the name of the Rokeach). The reason seems to me that in all the blessings we considered, all of humanity benefits from His creation, and therefore, it is necessary to mention 'King of the Universe.' But in prayer, which is unique to us, where we say 'Our God and the God of our fathers, etc.,' what relevance is there to 'King of the Universe'? And in the blessings over commandments, we say 'King of the Universe' because we say 'Who sanctified us with His commandments,' meaning from all the nations, it is necessary to say 'King of the Universe,' obviously.

The Rambam wrote in Chapter 11 of Hilchot Berachot, Halacha 5: "One who performs a mitzvah and did not recite a blessing, if it is a mitzvah whose performance is still ongoing - he may recite the blessing afterward. For example, if he wrapped himself in a tallit or donned tefillin or sat in a sukkah and did not recite the blessing - he may recite it afterward, for he is still engaged in the mitzvah. But if it is something where the mitzvah has already been completed - he does not recite the blessing afterward, such as if he slaughtered an animal and did not recite the blessing, or if he covered the blood and did not recite the blessing, etc." These are his exact words. However, there are those who disagree with him, maintaining that even in such cases, if one did not recite the blessing, he may recite it afterward, except for blessings over enjoyment, which are not recited afterward, nor for blessings over mitzvot. This is explained in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 19, see there.

If one hears a fellow Jew reciting any blessing, even if they only hear the end of the blessing, they are obligated to respond "Amen," even if they themselves are not obligated in that particular blessing. There is an account of a prominent individual who was studying with his teacher, and a child ate fruit and recited a blessing aloud. This prominent individual did not respond "Amen," and his teacher severely rebuked him, as explained in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 334. He observed a period of rebuke and then appeased his teacher, who forgave him on the condition that he would teach everyone how serious the punishment is for someone who hears a blessing and does not respond "Amen." He even recounted a terrifying story related to this matter (Levush, introduction). Additionally, when one hears a "Mi Shebeirach" (a special prayer for someone's well-being) being recited, it is proper to respond "Amen," thus fulfilling the commandment of "Love your neighbor as yourself." This is also the reason why we respond "Amen" after the phrase "HaRachaman" (May the Merciful One) (Magen Avraham, Sk 3).

However, if the one reciting the blessing is a Samaritan who worships Mount Gerizim, or a heretic, or a child who does not understand at all what he is saying, or an adult who deviates from the proper formula of the blessings, one does not respond 'Amen' after him. Similarly, one does not respond 'Amen' after a child when he is learning the blessings in front of his teacher, for it is permitted to teach children the blessings in their proper form even though they are reciting them in vain during the learning. But an adult during his learning should not pronounce the name explicitly; rather he should say 'Hashem', and similarly 'Elokenu'. Also, those who give public sermons and mention a verse that includes names of God should not pronounce the name explicitly but should say 'Hashem'. Even though there are those who permit it, it is proper to refrain from this, and this is our custom. However, if a child recites a blessing to fulfill his own obligation and understands what he is saying and has reached the age of education, one responds 'Amen' after him. Similarly, after a child who recites the Haftarah in the synagogue, one responds 'Amen' after him. It appears to me that for a young girl who has not reached the age of education, one does not respond 'Amen' after her until she is twelve years and one day old.

Rabbeinu the Rema wrote in Section 2: "One responds [Amen] after a non-Jew if he heard the entire blessing from his mouth." These are his words. And it is true that a similar notion is found in the Jerusalem Talmud, but there are those who disagree, and this is also evident from the words of the Rambam in Chapter 1 and from his commentary on the Mishnah in Chapter 8, see there. The Jerusalem Talmud is at the end of Chapter 8 of Berachot. And it seems to me, in my humble opinion, that his intention is not regarding a standard fixed blessing, but rather when he said a blessing to the God of Israel or something similar, see there.

One should only answer "Amen" after another person's blessing, not after one's own blessing. If someone answers "Amen" after their own blessing, it is considered improper (Gemara 45b). In my humble opinion, the reason is that a blessing channels divine influence, and answering "Amen" strengthens and affirms that this is indeed so. It is not appropriate for a person to affirm that their own blessing is effective in channeling divine influence, and therefore it is considered improper. Others can affirm this, but not oneself.

Only after completing a series of two or three blessings can one answer "Amen" at the end, as we do in the Grace After Meals after the blessing "Boneh Yerushalayim," which concludes the Torah-mandated blessings; "Hatov Vehametiv" is not from the Torah. However, this practice is not followed for other types of blessings.

Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote that it is customary to answer "Amen" after "Yehallelucha" and "Yishtabach." Rabbeinu Rema wrote regarding this: "Some say that one should only answer 'Amen' after the blessing 'Boneh Yerushalayim' in the Grace After Meals, and this is the widespread custom in these regions and should not be changed. In places where it is customary to answer 'Amen' after 'Yehallelucha' and 'Yishtabach,' one should also answer 'Amen' after the blessing 'Shomer Amo Yisrael La'ad.'" Consequently, on Shabbat and Yom Tov, one should answer "Amen" after "Haporeis Sukkat Shalom," but in our practice, we only answer "Amen" in the Grace After Meals after "Boneh Yerushalayim." Perhaps this is to distinguish between Torah-mandated and Rabbinic blessings. Therefore, it is not customary to answer "Amen" for other blessings, as it is not an obligation but a permission; at the conclusion, it is permissible but not obligatory to answer "Amen" after one's own blessing.

Anyone who recites a blessing that is not necessary is considered as one who takes the name of Heaven in vain, and it is as if he has taken a false oath. It is forbidden to answer "Amen" after such a blessing. Even though this is not a direct Torah prohibition like taking a false oath or mentioning God's name in vain, as those involve mentioning the name without a blessing, in the case of a blessing the prohibition is rabbinic (Tosafot at the end of Rosh HaShanah and Rosh in Kiddushin, Chapter 1). And what is said in Berachot (33a) that one who recites a blessing that is not necessary transgresses the commandment of "You shall not take [the name of the Lord your God in vain]" is merely an asmakhta (a rabbinic support for a biblical idea). Nonetheless, it is a very serious prohibition. There is one who wishes to say that Rambam in Hilchot Berachot, Chapter 1, Halacha 15, holds that it is a Torah prohibition (Magen Avraham, Subsection 6), but this is not definitive (Eliyah Rabbah, Subsection 5). There are those who wrote that when one mentions God's name in vain, he should remove his shoes, sit on the ground, humble himself, and ask three people to release him from the vow (there in the name of Ramban). And one who curses using God's name, such as saying "May the Lord afflict you" and similar expressions, his punishment is very severe (there). One should not increase blessings unnecessarily, as we have explained in Siman 206, Section 12 (and all the laws that Magen Avraham wrote here in Subsection 6, we have explained there).

It is taught in Berachot (43b): From where do we know that we bless on fragrance? As it is stated: “Let every soul praise God” (Psalms 150:6). What is something that the soul benefits from and the body does not benefit from? You must say this is fragrance. This means to say that one should not think that a blessing is only necessary for something that enters the body, like eating and drinking where the enjoyment is felt, and in this case, it is appropriate to say that it is forbidden to benefit from this world without a blessing, and not for mere fragrance which does not enter the body at all. Therefore, the verse teaches that there is also an obligation to bless on good fragrance. It is called the enjoyment of the soul because, compared to eating and drinking, it is a spiritual pleasure attributed to the soul and not the body. Therefore, it is as if it is written about the Holy One, blessed be He: “A pleasing aroma to the Lord” (Leviticus 1:9), hence fragrance is called such because it is a spiritual matter.

Therefore, just as it is forbidden for a Jew to benefit from food and drink before reciting a blessing, it is likewise forbidden to benefit from a pleasant aroma before reciting a blessing. One should bless before enjoying the aroma, just as one blesses before eating and drinking. Even though it is not exactly the same, since with eating and drinking if one blesses afterward it would not be considered "prior to enjoyment," which is not the case with an aroma where one can continue to enjoy the smell. Nevertheless, the primary blessing should be recited before enjoying the aroma, similar to eating and drinking (Bach). It is obvious that this is not comparable to eating and drinking in the case where one did not bless beforehand. If one ate and drank without a blessing, it is forbidden to bless afterward, whereas with an aroma, this does not apply; one can bless and then continue to enjoy the aroma. There is only an initial blessing for an aroma and no final blessing, as the enjoyment is minimal. This means that every final blessing requires a measure of an olive's bulk or a quarter-log, and this does not apply to an aroma (this seems to be the intention of Rashi in Niddah 52a, and the Taz in subsection 1 explains it is because it is similar to being assimilated in one's intestines, but I do not understand why this is necessary).

And because it is a minor pleasure, therefore eating and drinking take precedence over it if both come at the same time, as the Tur wrote at the end of Siman 212: "If they brought before him wine and good oil to smell, he holds the wine in his right hand and blesses over it first, and afterward takes the oil in his right hand and blesses over it," end quote. And so it is in the Gemara (43b), and for this reason, we do not recite the 'Shehecheyanu' blessing on a fragrance, and also because it lasts from year to year (Magen Avraham section 1). And there are many types of pleasures upon which we do not recite a blessing, such as bathing in hot water, anointing, pleasant music, or the light of a candle when sitting alone in the dark on Motza'ei Shabbat, and the like, because any pleasure that does not enter the body does not require a blessing. Nevertheless, fragrance is different, for its spirituality enters into the body and all the limbs are affected by it, but it is a spiritual pleasure and therefore it is called a pleasure of the soul and is not similar to all the aforementioned.

There are those who wonder why we do not recite a blessing when inhaling tobacco smoke through the mouth or nostrils, even though it has pleasant scents. This is not a wonder at all, for it is well-known that the primary purpose of this is not for its pleasant scent. On the contrary, it is strong and bitter to the extent that many people, especially women, cannot tolerate this smell at all. Its initial use was for stomach ailments, to dispel thoughts, and to pass the time. Therefore, even if some mix a pleasant scent into it, their intention is not for the pleasant scent but to dispel the strong and bitter smell of the tobacco. It is akin to the spices of the bathroom, over which one does not recite a blessing, as will be explained in Siman 217.

Just as there are several types of blessings for foods, so that one blesses each type with a specific blessing, so too with fragrances one must bless according to the source of the fragrance. How so? If the source of the fragrance is a tree or tree product, one blesses "Who creates fragrant trees," meaning that the Holy One, blessed be He, created trees that give a good smell. If it is an herb, one blesses "Who creates fragrant herbs." If it is a fruit that is eaten and gives a good smell, like an etrog or a good apple, one blesses "Who gives a good smell to fruits." If it is neither a tree, herb, nor fruit, like musk which comes from an animal, one blesses "Who creates various kinds of spices," which is a general blessing like "Shehakol" in eating and drinking. Therefore, just as if one says "Shehakol" for all foods one fulfills the obligation, so too if one says "Who creates various kinds of spices" for all fragrances, one fulfills the obligation. And just as with food, if there is doubt about the proper blessing one says "Shehakol," so too with fragrance one says "Who creates various kinds of spices" which is a general blessing. However, if one blessed "Who creates fragrant herbs" on a tree product or vice versa, one does not fulfill the obligation and must bless again, as well as with the fragrance of fruits. Therefore, on Motza'ei Shabbat we always bless "Who creates various kinds of spices" and do not scrutinize the source of the spices, because we are not so knowledgeable, and with this blessing, we fulfill the obligation for all types of spices as mentioned.

This is what we said: if someone smells a fruit that has a good fragrance, they recite a blessing. This applies when they took it specifically to smell it or if their intention is both to eat it and to smell it. However, if they took it only to eat and not to smell, even though it naturally gives off a good fragrance, they do not recite a blessing, since it was not taken for its fragrance. Therefore, one must have the intention to smell it. But for items specifically made for fragrance, even if their intention is not to smell but merely to move it to another place, since it gives off a good fragrance, they recite a blessing (this is explicitly stated in Magen Avraham 5 and in the Shulchan Aruch there). Nevertheless, in practice, this needs further examination, because if one does not intend to smell it, why should they recite a blessing? And if it is because it is inevitable that they will smell it involuntarily, it seems that this reasoning does not apply to blessings (but from Pesachim 25b it is explicitly implied that if one inevitably smells it, it is considered as if they intended, according to Rava, see there). Therefore, it seems to me that if it is possible for them not to hold or move it, they should recite a blessing. If it is not possible, such as if they need to move it to another place, then it is considered unintentional and they do not need to recite a blessing. And take note.

When one takes a fruit to eat and to smell, there is an opinion that the blessing for eating precedes the blessing for smelling (Aruch HaShulchan), as the blessing for eating takes precedence. However, there is another opinion that since the smell comes to him immediately, the blessing for smelling should be recited first (Eliyah Rabbah, subsection 6), and this seems to be the main ruling. As for the etrog used for the mitzvah on Sukkot, some say it is forbidden to smell it because it has been designated for its mitzvah for all the days of the festival, while others say it is permissible to smell it since it has only been designated from eating and not from smelling. Therefore, it is proper not to smell it, but if one does smell it, one should not recite a blessing, as in cases of doubt regarding blessings, we are lenient (Magen Avraham, subsection 22). And know that what we have said that for a fruit that has a good smell, one blesses 'Who gives a pleasant scent to fruits,' even if the fruit is not fit for eating except through a mixture, it is still called an edible fruit, and this blessing is recited (ibid., subsection 4).

Regarding nutmeg, which is primarily a fruit, and cinnamon, which is called "zimring" and "cloves," which is "nagelach," even though it is not primarily a fruit, nevertheless, since its main purpose is for eating, therefore it is considered a fruit for its fragrance. Similarly, all types of spices that are primarily for eating, even if they require preparation, one blesses "Who gives a pleasant fragrance to fruits." But for the rose, which is called "roza," and cinnamon, which is Indian wood, and rose water, which is called "rosenwasser," and frankincense and "metzitich," which is a type of resin that drips from a tree, and similar items—one blesses "Who creates the spices of trees." And even though they can be eaten when prepared, their primary purpose is not for eating but for fragrance. Therefore, one blesses "Who creates the spices of trees" since they are a type of tree and not a type of herb. Similarly, anything whose stalk is hard is considered a tree and not an herb.

Regarding balsam oil, which is very precious and grows only in the Land of Israel, a special blessing was instituted for it: "Creator of pleasant oil." For olive oil that has been crushed or ground until its fragrance is noticeable, one blesses "Creator of the trees of spices," because the olive is a tree. But other oils that do not grow on trees, if their fragrance is noticeable by their nature, their blessing is "Creator of various spices" and not "trees of spices," since they do not come from a tree. If spices were added to the oil, such that because of this their fragrance is noticeable, like the anointing oil used in the Temple, if the oil was scented with tree spices, one blesses "Creator of the trees of spices," and if with herb spices, one blesses "Creator of the herbs of spices." This follows the primary source of the scent when the scent remains in the oil. If it contained both wood and herb spices, one blesses "Creator of various spices." If the spices were filtered out, some say that one blesses "Creator of pleasant oil" like for balsam, because the oil became pleasant due to this. Others say that one does not bless it at all, because this pleasantness does not come from the oil itself but was absorbed from something else, and this is like a scent that has no source, and no blessing is recited on it. This is similar to the incense of utensils, as explained in Siman 217, where a blessing is not recited for a similar reason. Since there is doubt, it is proper to avoid smelling it, and if one does smell it, they do not bless, as we rule leniently in cases of doubt regarding blessings. There is an opinion that one blesses "Creator of various spices" (Bach), arguing it is not similar to scented utensils which did not absorb the scent from the essence of the spice, and here there is merely a doubt about the blessing, and "Creator of various spices" covers everything (ibid.). There are arguments for both sides (see Magen Avraham, Siman 213:13, and Taz 217:2 who wrote not to bless, ibid.).

Our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in Section 7: "Simlak and Chilfei Dima - one blesses 'Borei Atzei Besamim' (Who creates fragrant trees). Simlak, some interpret it as rosemary, some interpret it as jasmine, and some interpret it as a herb that has three rows of leaves one above the other, with each row having three leaves. Chilfei Dima is spikenard which is called ishfak, and this is Spikenard (Taz). "Sigli, which is violets - 'Borei Isvei Besamim' (Who creates fragrant herbs), Nargis, which is a lily, and some say it is a lily of the valley: if it grows in a garden - 'Borei Atzei Besamim' (Who creates fragrant trees), and if it grows in a field - one blesses 'Borei Isvei Besamim' (Who creates fragrant herbs)” end quote. We do not know these species at all, and 'Isvei' should be pronounced with a chirik under the ayin, a shva under the shin, and a tzeirei under the bet (Taz, section 12). The reason for the distinction between what grows in a garden and what grows in a field is that in a garden it is watered and maintained even when the wood dries out, therefore its blessing is 'Atzei Besamim'. However, in the field, it is not watered, nor is it cared for, and it only remains while it is an herb, therefore its blessing is 'Isvei Besamim'.

If one has before him trees of spices, herbs of spices, and species of spices, he blesses each one with the appropriate blessing, just as with types of food, where one should not initially include them all under the blessing of 'Shehakol'. Similarly, one should not include them all under the blessing of 'Minei Besamim'. He first blesses 'Atzei Besamim', then 'Isvei Besamim', and then 'Minei Besamim'. From the Tur, it appears that when all the spices are before him, he blesses 'Borei Minei Besamim' and it covers everything. The reason seems to be that it is not like food, as the scent comes from all of them together, and one must bless for everything at once. Our teacher, the Rema, wrote in Section 10, and this is his language: "And if he blessed 'Minei Besamim' on all of them, he has fulfilled his obligation." End of quote. It is not understood what he is informing us of, as this has already been explained in Section 1, but his intention is that it is permissible to do so initially.

If they bring before him myrtle and oil to smell: if their blessings are the same, he blesses on the myrtle and exempts the oil, for myrtle is more important than oil. This is according to the versions of the Rif and Rambam. According to the versions of Rashi and Tosafot, he blesses on the oil and exempts the myrtle. If their blessings are not the same, he blesses on the myrtle first and holds it in his right hand, for on what he blesses he must hold in his right hand. The blessing for myrtle is 'borei atzei besamim' and it is more important, just as 'borei peri ha'etz' precedes 'shehakol' (which resolves the difficulty raised by the Magen Avraham, section 19).

In the time of the Talmud, they would bring incense at the end of the meal and place coals on it so that the fragrance would rise before those reclining [at the meal]. And when does one recite a blessing over the incense? From when its smoke begins to rise before the fragrance reaches him, in order that the blessing precedes its enjoyment. But one should not bless before the smoke rises, for it must be adjacent to its performance, as stated in Siman 25 regarding tefillin. And the incense also follows the same rule as other spices: if it is from wood, one blesses "Who creates species of trees with pleasant scents" (Borei Atzei Besamim), and even though the fragrance comes after it is burned, its essence is from wood. If it is from herbs, one blesses "Who creates species of herbs with pleasant scents" (Borei Isvei Besamim), and if it is from other types, "Who creates various kinds of spices" (Borei Minei Besamim). And among us, there is an incense that is taken from the apothecary, small black round pieces, and they are placed in the morning on the windows, and they are lit and give off a good fragrance. If the intention is for the fragrance, one blesses "Who creates various kinds of spices" (Borei Minei Besamim), and if the intention is to remove bad odors, no blessing is needed as will be explained in Siman 217.

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote at the end of this section: "Some say that one who smells warm bread should recite the blessing 'Who has given a pleasant fragrance to bread,' and some say that one should not bless over it, therefore one should not smell it," end quote. I do not understand what pleasant fragrance there is in bread, and perhaps it refers to bread made with butter and spices. We have never heard of blessing over this, and many good fragrances arise from various cooked dishes when they are hot, and we do not bless over them, for the intention is not for the fragrance.
