It seems that one who smells fruit peels that have a pleasant fragrance, such as apples and the like, if his intention is to smell, he should bless 'Who has given a pleasant fragrance to fruits.'

One who enters a perfumer's shop that contains many types of fragrances, and he intended to benefit from the smell (Taz, Seif Katan 1) - he blesses "Borei Minei Besamim" which includes everything as was mentioned in the previous section. If he stays there all day, he only blesses once. If he enters and exits repeatedly - he blesses each time he intends to smell. This is specifically when he did not intend to return, but if he intended to return, he does not bless, and this is specifically when he intended to return immediately (Magen Avraham, Seif Katan 2). 

Even though for things that do not require a blessing after them in their place, it was explained in Siman 178 that with a change of place one needs to bless, and all the more so with scent where there is no final blessing at all, if so, even upon returning immediately he should need to bless. This is not so, for in the case of food, he eats something different from what he ate before, which is already consumed, but here he is smelling the same fragrances he smelled before, and therefore, upon returning immediately, he does not need to bless (there, Seif Katan 3).

However, if indeed he smells different fragrances, it is possible that he needs to bless (there), but it can be said that since with fragrances no action is lacking, for as soon as he enters he smells, therefore it is not similar to eating, and even with different fragrances, he does not need to bless when he enters immediately (there). And it is obvious that if he enters another perfumer's shop, he needs to bless again.

(Note that this which we wrote that one needs to intend to smell, and this is from the Taz, the Bach did not write so, rather since it is customary to smell as will be explained, therefore even if he did not intend to smell, he is obligated to bless, and Eliyah Rabbah agrees with him, see there. In my humble opinion, the primary view is like the Taz, that this was not possible and he did not intend, as explained in Pesachim 25b that it is permitted, see there, and certainly for a blessing. And here it is considered not possible, for he is forced to enter there for some matter, as we wrote in the previous Siman, Seif 6, see there, and this aligns with the custom of the world, and examine thoroughly).

And know that in the Gemara (53a), there is a question about the ruling that one should bless on a perfume shop, asking how one can bless on such a shop when it is not made for smelling. The Gemara answers that it is indeed made for smelling, as the intention of the perfumer is that the scent will spread and people will smell it so that they come to buy from him. According to this, perfumes that are stored in a room and not in a shop made for selling do not require a blessing, and so ruled the great authorities (Magen Avraham, Siman 216:1). The Gemara likens this to the perfumes in a bathroom, on which no blessing is made because they are meant to remove a bad smell. 

However, this seems not to be a valid comparison, because when something is made to remove a bad smell, it is not made for a good smell. But a perfume made for sale, which also has a good smell, why should it be worse than the smell of fruits made for eating, and in any case, if one smells them, one must bless, just like the smell of good foods—if one intends to smell them, one blesses. Why should a perfume shop be worse than these things? On the contrary, a perfume shop’s main purpose is for perfumes. (According to the explanation of the Bach in the previous section, it works out well, as here it concerns one who did not intend to smell, and in that case, it is similar to perfumes in a bathroom. Likewise, with fruits, if one did not intend to smell, he does not bless. And when it answers that the perfumer’s intention is that people will smell it, one must bless even if he did not intend to smell, and it is better than fruits. This is also explicitly stated in the language of the Rosh there. According to this, even in a room where many perfumes are placed, if one intends to smell, he must bless, as it is like fruits. But according to the Taz, this matter requires great study and consideration.)

In my humble opinion, it appears that if one enters a situation where it was necessary at that moment, one does not recite a blessing unless one intended to smell. Without such intention, it would be considered unintentional and not directed. However, if one did not need to be there at all but entered to stay there for a short while, then even if one did not intend to smell, one must recite a blessing. And if it is placed in a room, intention is always required.

One does not recite a blessing on a fragrance unless it was made for the purpose of smelling. That is to say, even though one recites a blessing on any pleasant fragrance even if its primary purpose was not for smelling, such as the pleasant scent of fruits, and all the more so if its primary purpose is for smelling, nonetheless, if this fragrance was made for another purpose, like to neutralize a bad odor, or to remove filth from the hands, or if the scent is intended specifically to go elsewhere with the intention of the fragrance being for a prohibited purpose - one does not recite a blessing on such fragrances. For a blessing requires a pleasant scent that is neither for a bad purpose nor for a prohibited purpose, and that there is no intention for the fragrance to go elsewhere.

Therefore, one does not recite a blessing over the spices of the dead that are placed above the bier, for they are intended only to remove the stench of the dead. But for those placed below the bier, one does recite a blessing, for they are intended to honor the living by providing a pleasant scent. Similarly, one does not recite a blessing over the spices that a delicate person carries with them to the privy, as they are intended only to remove the stench of the privy, nor over the oil used to wash hands after eating, as it is intended merely to remove the filth from the hands. Therefore, one does not recite a blessing over soap, even if it has a pleasant fragrance, for the primary purpose of soap is to remove the filth from the body and head (see Rashi and Tosafot 53a, s.v. 'ain' and Magen Avraham 5).

Similarly, incense used to perfume utensils does not warrant a blessing, since the scent is intended solely to impart fragrance to the garments, and it is akin to a scent meant to remove foul odors, given that the scent has another purpose. Likewise, one who smells utensils that have been perfumed with incense does not recite a blessing, because there is no primary source of fragrance, only a scent without substance. This is what Rambam wrote in Chapter 9, Law 8. Therefore, those who smell a vessel that contained spices or where spices were crushed and the vessel absorbed the scent do not recite a blessing (Taz, subparagraph 2), because it is a scent without substance.

Forbidden fragrances, how so? A woman who carries spices to emit a pleasant scent and draw others closer to her, even if she is unmarried - it is forbidden to bless such spices, as they assist in a sinful matter, and these are fragrances of immorality. Therefore, when a box of spices is hanging from her neck, in her hand, or in her mouth - it is forbidden to smell them and to bless them, lest this lead to kissing or physical closeness (see Magen Avraham 6 and Eliyahu Rabbah 7 who disputes this). Similarly, spices used for idolatry should not be blessed, as it is forbidden to smell them. Therefore, at a gathering of idolaters, one should not bless their spices, as their gatherings are generally for idolatry. Hence, if one was walking outside the city and smelled a pleasant scent: if the majority of the city are idolaters - one does not bless, if the majority are Jews - one blesses. If a fragrance that requires a blessing is mixed with one that does not, follow the majority, and there is no need to elaborate on these laws as we are not accustomed to these scents at all.

Even though our existence and our continual standing are always miraculous, as we say in the prayer of Modim: "And for Your miracles that are with us every day, and for Your wonders and Your favors at all times, etc.," nevertheless, all of these are hidden miracles intertwined with nature. However, one who sees places where open miracles were performed for our ancestors, such as the Exodus from Egypt and similar events, we are obligated to bless with the name and sovereignty: "Blessed are You, Hashem, our God, King of the Universe, who performed miracles for our ancestors in this place." Thus, our Sages taught in the Mishnah at the beginning of the ninth chapter of Berachot: the miracles done for our ancestors are relevant to us in every generation, just as we bless on the days when miracles were performed for our ancestors, like Chanukah and Purim, "who performed miracles for our ancestors in those days at this time," so too we bless for the places where miracles were performed for our ancestors. And these blessings are with the name and sovereignty as explained in the Jerusalem Talmud, and in the Gemara we derive it from what Jethro said: "Blessed be the Lord, who has delivered you out of the hand of Egypt" (and the Tur cited in the name of the Raavad that these blessings are not with the name and sovereignty, but all our rabbis disagree with him, see there).

And these are the places: such as the crossing of the sea, the place where Israel crossed the sea; the crossing of the Jordan, the place where Israel crossed the Jordan; the crossings of the Arnon streams, which are the valleys where the Amorites hid themselves to kill Israel, but the Ark of the Covenant that went before them leveled the land, and the mountains joined together and killed them all, and their blood flowed out. Israel saw this great miracle and sang a song, as it is written: "And the slopes of the valleys... then Israel sang, etc." And the hailstones that fell from the heavens on the Canaanites, as it is written in Joshua: "And it came to pass, as they fled from before Israel on the descent of Beth-horon, that the Lord cast down great stones from heaven upon them." And the stone that Og sought to throw on Israel, and the stone upon which Moses sat during the battle with Amalek, and the wall of Jericho that fell beneath it, meaning the place of the wall. For all of these, one blesses with the name and sovereignty: "Blessed is He who performed miracles for our forefathers in this place." Similarly, all the blessings of sight that will be explained are with the name and sovereignty.

And behold, regarding the miracles explained, there are some where the miracle itself is visibly apparent as it was, such as the hailstones and the stones of Moses and of Og. But regarding the splitting of the sea and the Jordan River, behold now the sea and the Jordan are full, except that in those places the sea and the Jordan split. And if so, the same should apply to the surroundings of Jerusalem when seeing the place where the army of Sennacherib fell, they should also be required to bless. However, our rabbis did not write so. And indeed, they wrote this in relation to the hailstones (Tosafot 54: s.v. ‘stones’), and certainly, it is not comparable to this, but in relation to the sea and the Jordan, why is it not comparable? And from the words of the Mordechai there, it implies that the places where Israel crossed the sea and the Jordan are more well-known than the place where the army of Sennacherib fell. And I do not know how to align these matters, and they themselves wrote that the place is known around Jerusalem, and this requires further investigation (also the words of the Magen Avraham 1:1 require further investigation).

For a miracle that was not performed for all of Israel or the majority of Israel, but only for a portion of Israel, even if it was performed for several tribes, since they are not the majority of Israel - we do not recite a blessing over it. And even though, with regard to the ruling of the court, we hold that one tribe is called a "community," as the Rambam writes in Chapter 12 (Halacha 1) of "Shgagot" (Laws of Errors), nevertheless, not for all matters is this the case. For instance, with regard to the Pesach offering brought in impurity, they are not considered the majority. However, in the matter of rulings, it is different, for it is written "community," and one tribe is called a community but not a public (Magen Avraham, section 3). Furthermore, regarding rulings, since each tribe had its own Sanhedrin, the tribe is considered a public in terms of an erroneous ruling, but not in other matters.

These blessings are like many of the blessings of sight, which are obligatory every thirty days. This is excluding the two days of sighting. And if one sees them again within this time frame, there is no need to bless, as each thirty-day period is considered as something new. Therefore, it is called a 'month' (chodesh), which is derived from the term 'new' (chadash), because the moon renews itself in it, and Israel is compared to the moon. And even though it is not exactly thirty days, this is the general practice, as we do not count hours for a month. Therefore, also in the redemption of the firstborn, mourning, and in certain calculations, the count is based on thirty days. Similarly, in the blessings of sight, after thirty days it is obligatory to bless as one did the first time.

One who sees a place where a miracle occurred for an individual or for many individuals does not recite a blessing. However, the individual for whom the miracle happened recites a blessing with the name and sovereignty of God: "Blessed... Who performed a miracle for me in this place." And even if the miracle is not evident from the place (Magen Avraham section 1), for he does not bless the place but the miracle itself. Similarly, all descendants, sons and daughters, recite: "Blessed... Who performed a miracle for my father or for our father in this place," even if the descendants were born before the miracle (Magen Avraham section 6). If one also needs to recite the blessing of "HaGomel," this will be explained at the end of section 219; see there.

And know that what we have written that his descendants are obligated to bless, so wrote our teacher, the Beit Yosef, in this language in section 4, see there. However, this requires explanation, for behold in the Gemara it is not found at all about his descendants at the beginning of the chapter "HaRo'eh", see there. Rather, the Rif wrote there that he and his son and his grandson are obligated to bless, and likewise the Rambam wrote in chapter 10, law 9, that he and his son and his grandson are obligated to bless. And similarly, the Tur wrote in the name of Rav Hai Gaon, see there. And our teacher, the Beit Yosef, in his great book ruled likewise, see there. According to this, our teacher, the Beit Yosef, should not have written in the Shulchan Aruch "his descendants". However, the Tur brought those who say that it is not specifically his grandson, but rather the same applies to all his descendants, meaning until the end of all generations, see there. And this is his intention in the Shulchan Aruch. But it requires examination, for behold, in cases of doubt regarding blessings, we are lenient, and furthermore, if so, regarding the miracle of a particular tribe, all of Israel would be exempt from the blessing, and they should have explained that the members of that tribe are obligated. Therefore, in practice, it seems to me in my humble opinion that only his son and grandson are obligated to bless with the name and sovereignty, and not other generations. And the reason seems to me to be because it is stated in the Midrash that up to the fourth generation a father's mercy extends to his son. And even though it implies that the fourth generation is also included, in any case, for this matter, since the reason is due to honoring his father, for this reason also the earlier descendants are obligated in the blessing, and honoring at most is only for his grandson, as our teacher the Rema wrote in Yoreh De'ah, section 240, see there (so it seems in my humble opinion).

And one to whom many miracles occurred, when he reaches one of the places where a miracle was performed for him, he must also mention the other places, and he can include all of them in one blessing. That is to say, he should say: "Who performed a miracle for me in this place, and in such-and-such a place, and in such-and-such a place." He does not need to mention the details of the miracle, only the places where the miracles occurred for him (Taz, subparagraph 1), and he should mention the miracle of the current place first (Gemara).

One must recite a blessing for the miracle of his teacher just as he does for the miracle of his father, and this is due to the honor of his teacher. It is clear that this applies only to the teacher himself and not to his descendants. He should say: "Blessed are You... who performed a miracle for my teacher in this place," and this applies specifically to a distinguished teacher. Some say that if a person sees someone who experienced a miracle, he should bless him just as he blesses the place where the miracle occurred. This means that if one is obligated to bless the place, such as for his son or his student, he also blesses the person, as the person is no less significant than the place. An example is Jethro, who saw Moses and Israel and blessed (Levush).

For a miracle that happened to a specific person, such as Yoav ben Tzeruya and his companions, or for a miracle where the name of Heaven was sanctified through a person, such as Daniel and his companions, one who sees the lion's den into which Daniel was thrown, or the fiery furnace into which Chananiah, Mishael, and Azariah were cast, blesses: "Blessed is He who performed a miracle for the righteous in this place." There are those who question this blessing for a specific person through whom the name of Heaven was sanctified (Magen Avraham, section 9), and there are those who uphold it (see Eliyah Rabbah and Machtzit Hashekel). Nowadays, it is certainly difficult to find such cases.

The one who sees Lot's wife blesses two blessings: for her, he says, "Blessed are You, Lord our God, King of the universe, the True Judge," and for Lot, he says, "Blessed are You, Lord our God, King of the universe, who remembers the righteous," referring to our father Abraham, in whose merit Lot was saved (Rashi), as it is in the Gemara. And it appears that the blessing for Lot is only incidental, for since one blesses for his wife, it naturally follows to mention Lot as well. But without this, there would be no place for this blessing, and so it seems in the Levush as well.

Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote in section 9: "Some say that one does not recite a blessing for a miracle unless it is a miracle that goes beyond the natural order. But a miracle that follows the natural order and its consequences, such as thieves coming at night and one being endangered and saved, and similar cases - one is not obligated to recite a blessing. And there are those who disagree, and it is good to bless without mentioning God's name and kingship." And they wrote about this that no one disagrees with this; how could it be considered a miracle if it follows the natural order (Magen Avraham section 12)? And although one could explain his words, practically there is no difference, and one only recites a blessing for a miracle that goes beyond the natural order. For a natural event, one recites the blessing of 'HaGomel', as will be explained in the next section.

Our sages stated (Berachot 54b): "Four people must give thanks: those who travel by sea, those who journey through the wilderness, one who was ill and recovered, and one who was imprisoned and released." All of these are explained in Psalms (107): "Give thanks to the Lord... Let the redeemed of the Lord say so, whom He has redeemed... They wandered in the wilderness... and they cried to the Lord... and He led them... to a settled city. Let them give thanks to the Lord for His steadfast love... Those who sat in darkness and the shadow of death... and they cried to the Lord... He brought them out of darkness and the shadow of death... Let them give thanks to the Lord for His steadfast love... They drew near to the gates of death and they cried to the Lord... Let them give thanks to the Lord for His steadfast love... Those who go down to the sea in ships... and they cried to the Lord... Let them give thanks to the Lord for His steadfast love... Let them exalt Him in the congregation of the people and praise Him in the assembly of the elders."

The explanation of the matter is as stated at the beginning of the previous section, that all our vitality and existence are based on miracles and not on nature, as we say: "For Your miracles that are with us every day, etc." And anyone who contemplates the life of our people, the children of Israel, throughout our prolonged exiles and the great dispersion, will see with open eyes that God dwells among us always, as He promised us in His holy Torah: "And yet for all that, etc." And this is what our Sages, of blessed memory, said: "They were exiled to Babylon and the Divine Presence went with them, etc." Meaning that everyone sees that the existence of the children of Israel is not natural at all. Even in generations that do not act well, nevertheless His Presence does not depart from us, as it is written: "Who dwells with them in the midst of their impurity." Rather, He chastises us, and about this it is said: "The Lord has chastened me sorely but He has not given me over to death." This is the general state of our situation, both collectively and individually.

However, miracles are divided into two extremes with an intermediate path. One extreme is when miracles are completely revealed and entirely break the bounds of nature, such as the miracles of Egypt and similar events. For such miracles, one must recite a blessing: 'Who performed miracles for our forefathers' or 'Who performed a miracle for me.' These are the laws explained in the previous section. The other extreme consists of miracles that are entirely intertwined with nature, such as all our sustenance and existence. For these, a specific blessing is not applicable, and one fulfills their duty through the regular prayers that include expressions of thanks: "We give thanks to You... and for Your miracles, etc."

There is also a third type, which is intermediate between miraculous and natural events. This means that the matter proceeds according to nature but deviates slightly from the natural order towards the realm of miracles. For example: one who travels by sea. This is natural, but when strong winds and storms arise, it is very difficult by natural means for the ship to be saved. Nevertheless, it does not entirely depart from the natural order, as is evident. All the more so, those who travel in deserts are in great danger. Similarly, one who is imprisoned or a sick person whose illness has become severe. Therefore, it is impossible to bless with the language of a miracle, but rather one gives private thanks to the Blessed Holy One for this matter and justifies the judgment upon himself with the blessing, acknowledging that the suffering he endured was due to his sins, and his rescue is a gracious act from the Blessed Holy One even for those who are guilty.

And your mnemonic is: "And all the living will thank You, Selah," with "living" being an acronym for "sick," "suffering," "sea," and "desert." And he blesses: "Blessed are You, Lord our God, King of the universe, who bestows good things upon the guilty, who has bestowed every good thing upon me." And those who hear respond 'Amen' and say: "He who has bestowed every good thing upon you, may He bestow upon you every good thing, Selah." And this is like a consolation and blessing for the soul that has endured suffering. And he does not bless until he has completely emerged from the distress: those who go down to the sea until they come to dry land, those who travel in the desert until they reach habitation, and one who was sick and recovered until he goes out to the market, and one who has come out of prison until he is completely free from his judgment and not released on bail. And there is no difference whether he was imprisoned for monetary reasons or because of capital matters.

Since it is written: "And let them exalt Him in the congregation of the people, and praise Him in the assembly of the elders," therefore our Sages said that one must bless in the presence of ten, as they are called a congregation, and two of them should be scholars who are referred to as elders in the language of Scripture, and the minimum of elders is two. And Maimonides wrote in Chapter 10 that the blessing should be recited standing, and it seems to me that his reasoning is because since one blesses in the presence of ten, and among ten the Divine Presence rests, it is not respectful to sit. For this reason, it seems that the custom is to recite this blessing after being called to the Torah, for then there are certainly among the ten some who are scholars and it is recited standing. All this, however, is not essential, for if there are not two scholars among them, one still fulfills the obligation (Mordechai). The Tur wrote that even without ten one fulfills the obligation, while others say one does not fulfill it, and it is good to bless again later in the presence of ten without the mention of the Name and Kingdom. It is proper to be careful not to delay this blessing more than three days after one is able to bless, and if the listeners did not respond "Who has bestowed good upon you, etc.," it does not invalidate (Magen Avraham, subsection 2). A minor should not recite this blessing, and women customarily do not recite it, although there is no reason for this other than the custom of reciting it during the Torah reading, leading to the assumption that women are not obligated in this blessing. Therefore, it is proper for them to bless. Perhaps because it is written: "in the congregation of the people," and women are not called a congregation, and it is not respectful for them to bless in the presence of men, they have refrained from this (see Magen Avraham).

If someone recited the "HaGomel" blessing for himself and intended to also fulfill the obligation for his friend who is also required to recite this blessing, and his friend heard the blessing from him and intended to fulfill his obligation through it, he has fulfilled his obligation even without responding "Amen," since the one reciting the blessing is also obligated in this blessing, as stated in Siman 213. And we have already written not to delay this blessing more than three days; however, if he delayed, he can still make it up as long as he wishes. It seems to me that if a long time passed until the matter was forgotten, he should no longer recite the blessing and the opportunity for the blessing is lost (some say up to five days).

Our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, wrote in section 4: "If another person blessed and said: 'Blessed are You, Lord our God, King of the universe, who has bestowed upon you all good,' and [the one who was blessed] answered 'Amen' – he has fulfilled his obligation. Similarly, if he said: 'Blessed is the Merciful One, the Master of the world, who has given you to us,' and [the one who was blessed] answered 'Amen' – he has fulfilled his obligation. This is not considered a blessing in vain for the one who blessed, even though he himself was not obligated in this blessing, because he is only blessing as a way of praise and thanksgiving for the goodness of his friend in which he rejoices." 

This means that a blessing of thanksgiving is like a blessing of enjoyment, where one person does not bless on behalf of his friend if he himself is not obligated. According to this, it could be said that it is a blessing in vain and does not fulfill the obligation of the one who is required to bless. Therefore, it states that this is not the case, and if this person is very happy about the salvation of his friend, he can bless the blessing of thanksgiving for his friend's good fortune, and it is not a blessing in vain. Therefore, when he answered 'Amen,' he fulfilled his obligation, but without answering 'Amen,' he did not fulfill it. This is not similar to the previous law where the obligation was fulfilled even without 'Amen,' since there the one blessing was obligated in it, which is not the case here where he blesses on behalf of another, necessitating the 'Amen' response.

From this, they learned that if a woman is obligated to recite the blessing of 'HaGomel,' her husband can recite it on her behalf. Therefore, when she gives birth and is saved from danger, her husband can recite: 'Who has bestowed all goodness upon you,' and she will respond 'Amen,' for there is no greater love and concern for her welfare than from him, as his wife is like his own self (Bach and Magen Avraham, section 4). This is contrary to those who question this (see Beit Yosef and Taz, section 3). However, this is not the common practice. It is clear that if someone recites it for another person who is not as close and beloved as himself, such as a father for a son, a son for a father, or a brother and the like, but does so to appear as if he loves him – this is considered a blessing in vain, and it does not fulfill the obligation (Taz, there).

Our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 7: "In Ashkenaz and France, they do not recite the blessing when traveling from city to city, as they only required it for those traveling in deserts where wild animals and bandits are common. But in Spain, they customarily recite the blessing, because all the roads are presumed to be dangerous. However, for less than a parasang, they do not bless, and if it is a place known to be particularly dangerous, even for less than a parasang, they do bless." End of quote. And in our times, the blessing of 'HaGomel' is not relevant at all, even for long journeys, unless it is by sea or through deserts. But on land and in settled areas, the blessing of 'HaGomel' does not apply in our times, and in our days we have never heard of anyone reciting the blessing of 'HaGomel' upon returning from a regular journey. Only the prayer of the traveler, as mentioned in Siman 110, is obligatory to say in every place, as stated there.

It is further written in section 8: “For any illness one must recite the blessing, even if it is not a life-threatening illness or a wound of the body cavity, but any illness where the person has been bedridden and then recovered, because it is as if he was taken to the gallows to be judged. And there is no difference whether the illness is chronic and recurs from time to time or whether it is not chronic” (end of quote). That is to say, even though in the case of a chronic illness one has been cured from it several times, nevertheless, since he has been bedridden and recovered - he must recite the blessing, because a miracle does not happen at every moment (Magen Avraham, subsection 7). And our teacher, the Rema, wrote about this: “And some say that one only blesses for an illness that is life-threatening, such as a wound of the body cavity, and this is the custom in Ashkenaz” (end of quote). And likewise, the sick person who has been bedridden for more than three days must recite the blessing (Taz, subsection 8). And some have written that the main opinion follows our teacher, the Beit Yosef (Bach and Eliyah Rabbah, subsection 13, and see Magen Avraham, subsection 8), and the custom follows our teacher, the Rema.

Additionally, it is written in section 9: "These four [situations] are not specific, as the same applies to someone to whom a miracle happened, such as if a wall fell upon him or he was saved from being trampled or gored by an ox, or if a lion stood over him to devour him, or if thieves or nighttime robbers came upon him and he was saved from them. All similar cases require the blessing of 'HaGomel'. Some say that the 'HaGomel' blessing is only recited for these four situations specifically, and it is better to bless without mentioning the name and kingdom [of God]." This is the end of the quote. In truth, without mentioning the name and kingdom, it is not a blessing at all. The latter authorities wrote that one should bless for any dangerous situation when saved from it, and this is the common custom and should not be changed (Levush and Taz section 7 and Magen Avraham section 10). And even now, this is the custom.

Regarding the blessing of the miracles mentioned in the previous section: whether one also needs to recite the blessing of 'HaGomel,' there are differing opinions, as explained in the great work of our teacher, the Beit Yosef. There, he cites in the name of the Rivash that one must also recite the blessing of 'HaGomel,' and it appears that his opinion leans towards this. See there (and this is also the opinion of the Magen Avraham in section 218, sub-section 12. See there).

Regarding dreams, there is much discussion, and some of our Rabbis of blessed memory advised not to recount a bad dream nor interpret it, and then it has no substance. Thus, they said in the chapter "Haroeh" (Berachot 55b): "A dream not interpreted is like a letter not read." Rashi explained: A dream not interpreted is like a letter not read, neither good nor bad; all dreams follow the interpretation, end quote. They learned this from what is written: "And it was as he interpreted to us, so it was" (Genesis 41:13).

And there it was said: "Rava raised a contradiction: It is written, 'In a dream I will speak to him' (Numbers 12:6), and it is written, 'And dreams speak falsehood' (Zechariah 10:2). There is no contradiction: Here, it is through an angel; here, it is through a demon." Meaning, a person who is pure and whose thoughts are in Torah and fear, and who sleeps without a full stomach, the dream of such a person certainly has substance, as they show him from Heaven through the angels guarding the complete person, as it is written: "For He will command His angels concerning you, etc." (Psalms 91:11).

But for ordinary people immersed in the vanities of the world, they are complete demons who rob a person of true success, and the demons are created to harm and rob true success – their dreams speak falsehood and have no substance. All the more so those who eat a lot before sleeping, whose rising vapors confuse the imaginative faculty, and there is no truth in them at all. Similarly, if one dreams of ideas he thought about during the day, it is obvious that the imaginative faculty shows him something similar to his thoughts, and such dreams have no substance.

And Shmuel, when he saw a good dream, would say: "Do dreams speak falsehood? Is it not written: 'In a dream I will speak to him'?" And when he saw a bad dream, he would say: "Dreams speak falsehood" (Berachot 55b). And it was said there that generally, a good person is shown good, but upon waking, he forgets it.

He who rises early and a verse happens to enter his mouth - this is a small prophecy (there). And three types of dreams are fulfilled: a morning dream, a dream that someone else dreams about him, and a dream whose interpretation is revealed within the dream. Some also say a dream that is repeated, as it is said: "And because the dream was repeated... it is certain, etc." And one who sees in a dream a river, a bird, or a pot should anticipate peace (56:), and all kinds of beverages are good for a dream except for wine: some drink it (in a dream) and it is good for them, and some drink it and it is bad for them; but for a Torah scholar, it is always good. And one who sees King David in a dream, or the Book of Psalms, or the Song of Songs should anticipate piety, and one who sees the Book of Kings should anticipate greatness, and one who sees Solomon or Ezekiel or the Book of Proverbs should anticipate wisdom, and likewise the Book of Ecclesiastes. And one who sees the Scroll of Esther will have a miracle happen to him, and one who sees Isaiah should anticipate consolation, and one who sees Jeremiah or Ahab or Job or the Book of Lamentations should worry about calamity (there 57:), and should increase in prayer and good deeds, and charity saves from death, and all the more so from other calamities.

The one who sees a river in a dream should rise early and say: "Behold, I extend peace to her like a river" (Isaiah 66:12). The one who sees a bird in a dream should rise early and say: "As birds flying, so will the Lord of hosts protect" (Isaiah 31:5). The one who sees a pot in a dream should rise early and say: "The Lord will judge peace for us" (Isaiah 26:12). The one who sees grapes in a dream should rise early and say: "I found Israel like grapes in the wilderness" (Hosea 9:10). The one who sees a mountain in a dream should rise early and say: "How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of the messenger of good news" (Isaiah 52:7). The one who sees a shofar in a dream should rise early and say: "And it shall come to pass on that day, that a great shofar shall be blown" (Isaiah 27:13). The one who sees a dog in a dream should rise early and say: "But against any of the children of Israel, a dog shall not sharpen its tongue" (Exodus 11:7). The one who sees a lion in a dream should rise early and say: "The lion has roared, who will not fear?" (Amos 3:8). The one who sees someone shaving in a dream should rise early and say: "And he shaved and changed his garments" (Genesis 41:14). The one who sees a well in a dream should rise early and say: "A well of living waters" (Song of Songs 4:15). The one who sees a reed in a dream should rise early and say: "A bruised reed he will not break" (Isaiah 42:3). The one who sees an ox in a dream should rise early and say: "His firstborn bull, majesty is his" (Deuteronomy 33:17). 

All these because a sign is a matter, and all dreams follow the mouth, and therefore one should interpret them for good. And if one goes to sleep with joy from a mitzvah, one is shown a good dream (Shabbat 30b).

Our Sages said in Berachot there: If one sees a dream and it distresses him, he should have it interpreted before three friends and say before them: 'I saw a good dream.' The idea is that it is better for a person to train himself not to pay attention to dreams, as most of them have no substance, as it is written in Ecclesiastes (5): "For a dream comes with much concern," and Rashi explains: For it is the way of a dream to come with many thoughts that one contemplates and muses over during the day. And it is said (there): "For with many dreams come vanities and many words, but fear God." He equates dreams with vanities. The main thing is to fear God, and then he will not fear the dream. However, if it distresses him, causing him anguish and worry, the remedy for this is that three friends interpret it for good. Perhaps because of this, the custom in many places is that someone who has a bad dream comes before the rabbi of the city to ask him to interpret the dream for him, and the rabbi provides a positive interpretation, for in monetary matters, an expert individual can serve as three laymen, and presumably, the rabbi is a friend to the entire city, fulfilling the directive of our Sages to have it interpreted before three friends, and the rabbi says that it will be for good.

And the explanation of 'I had a good dream', that is to say, the dream I saw should be for the good, as we say during the Priestly Blessing: "And just as You have turned... so too should You turn all my dreams for good." And it is customary to say it three times, as is the manner with all incantations, and the three respond to him: "You had a good dream, it is good and it will be good. May the Merciful One make it good. Seven times they shall decree upon it from Heaven that it be good. It is good, and it will be good." This is the text of the incantation. And it is not necessary to say it seven times, but three times; however, the Tur wrote that it is customary to say it seven times, see there. And they should say three verses of transformations: "You have turned my mourning into dancing, etc.," "Then the virgin will rejoice... and I will turn their mourning into joy, etc.," and "But the Lord your God did not want to listen to Balaam... and the Lord your God turned the curse into a blessing for you." And three verses of redemption: "He redeemed my soul in peace, etc.," "And the redeemed of the Lord shall return, etc.," and "And the people said to Saul... and the people redeemed Jonathan, etc." And three verses of peace: "Creator of the fruit of the lips, peace, etc.," "And the spirit clothed Amasai... peace to you, etc.," "And you shall say, 'All is well,' and peace to you and your house, and all that you have is peace." And afterwards, they say to him: "Go, eat your bread with joy, etc." Some reverse it to say: 'Go with joy, eat your bread' because of the acronym 'אבל' (mourning), but some are not pleased with reversing the language of the verse, and the final letters form the word 'כלה' (bride) (as per the tradition of Rabbi Yitzchak Tzemach), and the text has already been printed in the prayer books, and the dream will be improved after the Shacharit prayer or before the prayer. And it has already been explained in Siman 130 that there is a remedy for a dream to say: "Master of the Universe, I am Yours, etc." during the Priestly Blessing or during the chazan's recitation of 'Sim Shalom,' see there. And the general rule is: a person should not habituate themselves to these things, and one who is good before God will escape from it, and when a dream is improved for him, he should remember the dream in his thoughts at the time of the improvement (Magen Avraham, section 1).

There are those who wrote in this manner: "And if two people are interpreting dreams at the same time, the third person must also interpret for him even though he did not dream that time" (ibid.), and this has no understanding, and many have already labored over this. And there are those who explained that it refers to the interpreters, that when there are two who want to interpret for the dreamer, it is a commandment for the third to involve himself in this even though he did not dream that night (Machatit HaShekel, and it is understood that this has no relevance, and Pri Megadim wrote that he does not know its meaning, see there). And there are those who explained that if two people are interpreting, the third should also respond to them: 'Your dream' in the singular form and not in the plural, and it refers to each one individually. Therefore, it says that three are needed and it is not said that two are sufficient and one of the interpreters should respond to one of them, and then the second should respond with the two to the former, because we require that all the interpreters be not among the dreamers, even though he did not dream that time (Magen HaElef at its end), and this certainly has no reason or sense as understood.

And it seems to me that the explanation is as follows: It is certain that the improvement of a dream (i.e., interpreting a dream positively) should only occur on the day after the night in which the dream was had, and not after a few days have passed since the dream, just as a fast due to a dream should only take place on that same day. According to this, if someone comes who did not dream on the previous night to request an improvement of a dream, they are not obligated to attend to him. Even though it might help, since it is not explicitly stated, there is no need to attend to him. This applies when there is no improvement of a dream happening at all, or even if there is an improvement of a dream happening but only one person is having their dream improved and they answer him in singular form: "Your dream is good," it will not help the other person. If we say that indeed they should answer them: "Your dreams are good" in plural form, and since this does not require much effort, we might say that perhaps it does not help the other person, and therefore it would not help the one who dreamt on that night either, since it was said in one speech. Therefore, if there are two people who need their dreams improved, in this case, the interpreters of dreams must say to them: "Your dreams are good" in plural form. Consequently, the third person who did not dream on that occasion can also have his dream improved with them, and in any case, if it helps him, good; if not, the focus is not on him, since even without him they need to improve in plural form, and the phrase "Your dreams are good" will apply to the two.

Our Sages said in Shabbat (11a): A fast is effective to annul a bad dream like fire to flax, and specifically on that day, even on Shabbat, as will be explained in Siman 288. And there it will be explained that they say one fasts on Shabbat for three types of dreams: seeing a Torah scroll being burned, seeing tefillin being burned, or seeing Yom Kippur during the Ne'ilah prayer, or seeing the beams of one's house or one's teeth falling out. It is proper not to fast on Shabbat (Magen Avraham there, Subsection 7), and even on weekdays, one should not become accustomed to it, because this was only said regarding a pure person and not on a full stomach, and otherwise, it has no substance. And in Midrash Kohelet, it is written that they interpreted for a woman who saw in a dream the beams of her house falling, that she would give birth to a male child, and so it was for her, as it is there. This is analogous to a child falling from her body. And we are accustomed to interpret dreams positively, and thus it is our duty, and thus it is good for us, for all dreams follow the mouth, as it is said.

In the Mishnah of "The One Who Sees," we learned: "For rains and good news, one says: 'Blessed is the One who is good and does good.'" It is not clarified when this blessing for rain is to be recited, for if one were to bless every time it rains, it would have no end and no rationale. The words of the Tur are also not explicit. The language of our master, the Beit Yosef, in Section 1 is as follows: "If they were in distress due to a lack of rain and rain fell, they bless for it, etc.," and similarly wrote the Levush. I am puzzled that in the laws of fasting for rain, this blessing is not mentioned at all, only the recitation of Hallel as elucidated in Taanit and Rambam and later in Siman 575. It must be said that there it refers to a prolonged drought, whereas here it applies even for a minor delay, and further investigation is needed.

However, from the words of the Rambam in Chapter 10, Halacha 5, I have learned a different intention in this matter. And this is the language of the Rambam: "When many rains fall, if one has a field, etc." end quote. According to this, the explanation is as follows: If the rainfall is average as in all years, there is no need for a blessing. But when the rains are abundant, and in the Land of Israel, abundant rains do not damage the crops as they do in our countries, and in the Land of Israel, the more it rains, the more blessing there is. Therefore, a blessing is required. According to this, it is clear why we do not recite this blessing, and our teacher, the Rema, wrote, and this is his language: "The reason we do not practice the blessing on rain in this time is because these countries are accustomed to regular rains and they are not withheld so much," end quote. This is a major difficulty, as there are many years when we experience a withholding of rain. According to our explanation, it makes sense, for since the blessing is for abundant rains, and in our case, abundant rains are a great curse, and there is more expense with abundant rains than with a withholding of rains, this blessing does not apply to us.

And from when do we bless for the rain, meaning, what is considered an abundance? When the water increases on the ground and bubbles rise from the rain on the surface of the water, and the bubbles move towards each other. And what blessing does one recite? If he has a field, he blesses 'Shehecheyanu'. If it belongs to him and others, he blesses 'Hatov Vehametiv', as will be explained in the next section. For any goodness that is solely for oneself, the blessing is 'Shehecheyanu', and for any goodness that benefits both oneself and others, the blessing is 'Hatov Vehametiv', meaning good for oneself and beneficent to others. And even though when the field is solely his, there are still other fields, why does he not bless 'Hatov Vehametiv'? The reason is that we require that the very same goodness that reaches him also reaches others in a shared manner.

If he has no field at all, a special blessing is not relevant to him. However, he must still give thanks to Hashem, blessed be He, since this matter concerns everyone. And he should say: "We thank You, Hashem our God, for every single drop that You have brought down for us." He should then say from the text of Nishmat: "And if our mouths were as full of song as the sea..." until "they would acknowledge and bless Your Name, our King." And he concludes: "Blessed are You, Hashem, the source of many thanks and praises." This is how it is in the Rambam. In the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, "and praises" is not mentioned, only "the source of many thanks and the thanks," see there. And be aware that the Rosh ruled that even if one has a field only for himself, he still blesses "He who is good and does good" because of other fields, as mentioned. However, our teacher the Beit Yosef did not bring his opinion at all.

And our master the Rema wrote in section 2: "And there are those who say that one who hears that rain has fallen blesses 'He Who is Good and Does Good'." That is to say, when he has a field by himself, according to the Rambam, he blesses 'Shehecheyanu', this is in seeing, because here he sees only his own benefit. But in hearing, he also blesses according to the Rambam 'He Who is Good and Does Good', because in hearing there are many partners in the benefit (so it seems to me, and it resolves the question of the Magen Avraham in section 2, examine it well). And in Egypt, one who sees the Nile increase blesses 'Shehecheyanu' (there in the name of the Radbaz) because this is like a new fruit.

It is taught at the beginning of "HaRoeh": "For good tidings, one says, 'Blessed is He who is good and does good.'" The Gemara (59b) explains that when the good news is for him alone, he blesses "Shehecheyanu" (Who has kept us alive), but if it is for him and others, he says "HaTov VeHaMeitiv" (Who is good and does good) — good for him and beneficial for others. This is specifically when he hears the news from a trustworthy person (Magen Avraham 1:1, and what is said regarding a wealthy woman requires further investigation and careful consideration). It is not clear what is considered good news, but it seems that it must be significant good news that brings much joy, whether it is financial joy or another kind of joy. In financial matters, it depends on his wealth or poverty, for what is a great matter for a poor person is a small matter for a rich person, and it all depends on the context. These blessings are recited with the full Name and Kingship (i.e., using God's name and the phrase "King of the Universe").

And for bad news, one blesses "Blessed are You, Lord our God, King of the universe, the True Judge." In this, there is no difference whether the misfortune is solely for him or also affects others, as this is the justification of the judgment of Heaven, as it is written: "The Rock, His work is perfect, etc." There is no distinction between bodily harm and financial loss, and similarly, each person according to their situation, as was written regarding good news.

The Sages taught in the Mishnah in Berakhot (54a): "A person is obligated to bless for the bad just as he blesses for the good." This means to bless for the bad with complete understanding and a willing soul, just as one blesses joyfully for the good. For the bad is beneficial and joyous for the servants of God, since they accept with love what God has decreed upon them. One should think that everything is an atonement for their sins, and thus, by accepting this bad, they are serving God, and the service of God is a joy for them. This is what is written: "And you shall love the Lord your God... with all your might," with every measure that He measures for you, whether it is a good measure or the opposite, you should thank Him very much. This is what David said: "I will sing of kindness and justice," meaning, whether He deals with me with kindness or with justice, I will always sing. And Job said: "The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away; blessed be the name of the Lord." A person should always be accustomed to say: 'All that the Merciful One does is for good' (Gemara 60b), and the wise person will understand in his mind and intellect that the matters of this world are vanity and emptiness, a fleeting moment like a passing shadow and like a dream that flies away.

One recites the blessing "HaTov VeHaMetiv" (Who is good and does good) on good fortune, even if one fears that misfortune may follow from it. For example, if someone finds a valuable item and fears that robbers might hear about it and take everything he owns, since now it is a good thing and it is not certain that misfortune will follow, one recites the blessing "HaTov VeHaMetiv." Similarly, one recites the blessing "Baruch Dayan HaEmet" (Blessed is the True Judge) on misfortune, even if good may come from it. For example, if one's field is flooded, even though after the flood it will be beneficial because it irrigated the field, at present it is a misfortune due to the significant damage caused. Therefore, even if the good will certainly come, the damage that occurred remains damage. It is obvious that if there is no damage at all, one does not recite "Dayan HaEmet," and also one does not recite "HaTov VeHaMetiv" for the irrigation of the field, as this does not constitute sufficient joy to warrant the blessing "HaTov VeHaMetiv." Note that for several misfortunes that come or are heard about at the same time, one recites one blessing for all of them. Similarly, regarding good fortune, if several good things happen at once or one hears several good pieces of news at once, one recites the blessing "HaTov VeHaMetiv" once for all the good fortunes.

If his wife gave birth to a male child, he recites the blessing "HaTov VeHaMeitiv" (Who is good and does good), as this is a benefit for him and also for his wife, as she too prefers a male child (Gemara 59b). There is no difference whether he was present at the birth or in another city and the news reached him – he recites the blessing, and she too is obligated to recite "HaTov VeHaMeitiv." However, with the birth of a female child, this blessing is not recited, as the joy is not as great as with a male child. It does not matter whether he has fulfilled the commandment to be fruitful and multiply or not, nor does it matter whether they are genuinely happy about the birth of the male child or not. There is an opinion that one should bow towards the east and recite the blessing (Magen Avraham, section 2), but I do not know the reason for this.

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote: "If his wife dies in childbirth, he recites the blessing 'Shehecheyanu,' because there is no benefit for others. Similarly, if the father dies before the birth, the woman recites 'Shehecheyanu.' Some have written that the custom is to be lenient with this blessing, viewing it as optional rather than obligatory, and from this, it has spread that many are lenient with these blessings." End of quote. 

And this is not sufficient, for we do not find in the Talmud that this blessing is optional except for the blessing of 'Shehecheyanu' on a new fruit (Eruvin 40b), but regarding the blessing of 'Hatov Vehametiv' (He Who is Good and Bestows Good) when a man’s wife gives birth to a son, this is an explicit Baraita (Berachot 59b), and they already raised a similar objection (Magen Avraham section 3). 

In my humble opinion, the reason for this leniency in this blessing seems correct, for I have not found this law in the Rif or Rambam in chapter 10 at all, and I am astonished that the decisors did not notice this. And since the Rif and Rambam dismissed this from Halacha, it is clear that we should not enter into the doubt of a blessing. 

And the reason of our sages seems to me as follows: the language of the Baraita is: "They said to him that his wife gave birth to a son, he blesses...if his father died, etc." It is difficult why it says 'they said to him' when his wife gave birth to a son, but not when his father died. Surely, it is because in general, one does not bless, and the Baraita refers to a person who is anxious and eager for the birth of a son, as in Nazir (12b): "I will become a Nazirite when I have a son," and the people who heard from him came and told him his wife gave birth to a son, meaning they brought him good news that the Holy One, blessed be He, fulfilled his desire. 

(And this also explains the question there: "In any case where there is no benefit for others, one does not bless 'Hatov Vehametiv,' but it teaches: if she gave birth to a son, etc." and answers: "there, etc., his wife, etc." and it is not understood what it means. According to what I explained, it is clear: in general, one does not bless, only here he eagerly desired this, but from her we did not hear, and hence he thought the benefit was only for him alone. And it answers that this is not so, for generally, if he desires, she also desires a son. And understand this well).

If one's father dies, one recites the blessing "Blessed is the True Judge" because for all deceased for whom one mourns, this blessing is obligatory, and certainly for one's father. Even for a Torah scholar or a respectable person, one initially should recite "Blessed is the True Judge" when they die, for it is no less than hearing bad news, except that the custom is not to recite it with the Divine Name and Kingship. See Yoreh Deah, section 340 (and see Bach and Magen Avraham, subparagraph 4). However, for one's father, it is obvious that one recites it with the Divine Name and Kingship, and this is not surprising at all. The novelty is that if one's father left him a significant amount of money as an inheritance, after reciting "Blessed is the True Judge," one recites "Shehecheyanu" over the inherited money. We do not say, "How can one recite 'Shehecheyanu' at the time of his father's death?" because this is a separate matter. However, when does one recite "Shehecheyanu"? When he is the sole heir. But if there is another heir, he recites "HaTov VeHaMeitiv" (Who is good and does good), good for him and good for the others, because the rule is that one does not recite "HaTov VeHaMeitiv" unless the benefit also extends to others. And we do not say that even when he is the sole heir, the benefit extends to his wife and children, for they are dependent on him. It is not similar to when his wife gives birth to a son, where she also has an actual share in the child, but money is entirely his. And this is not limited to the inheritance of one's father; the same applies to any inheritance.

It is taught: "If one builds a new house or acquires new utensils, one recites: 'Blessed are You, Lord our God, King of the universe, Who has kept us alive, sustained us, and brought us to this time,'" and the reason is because it brings him joy. And it seems to me that even though regarding exemptions from military service, as it is written: "Who is the man who has built a new house, etc.," and it is taught in the eighth chapter of Sotah: "Whether one builds a house of straw, a house for cattle, or a storage house" — see there, all of these are included in the term 'house'. Nevertheless, the 'Shehecheyanu' blessing is only recited on a proper house, as this brings much joy, unlike a house of straw, etc. However, it is taught there: "Whether one builds, buys, inherits, or receives as a gift," the same applies here, for regarding joy, all these scenarios are equal. There is a question whether in the cases of military exemptions, where three things are considered: building a house, planting a vineyard, and marrying a wife, how the law applies to 'Shehecheyanu'. Since the blessing for seeing a vineyard or a wife is not mentioned, it is understood that one does not recite a blessing for these. For a vineyard, one could say that it does not bring the same joy as a house, but for a wife, it is surprising why 'Shehecheyanu' should not be recited, as it is a great joy, and we recite: 'Who has joy in His dwelling'. It could be suggested that at the time of betrothal, the joy is not complete, and it is not possible to recite 'Shehecheyanu' then, and at the time of marriage when the joy is complete, it is not possible to recite it because the matter was already concluded at the betrothal. Therefore, even among us, where betrothal and marriage are as one, it is not customary to recite it because they did not recite it, so we also do not recite it. Similarly, for a vineyard, 'Shehecheyanu' was not instituted because at the time of planting there is no joy yet, as the fruits are forbidden for three years due to 'Orlah', and afterward it is not appropriate to recite it because the matter is already concluded. Therefore, only a house, which is used immediately upon completion, is mentioned.

In the case of a new house and new utensils, even if he already had similar items, he must recite the blessing "Shehecheyanu," because they are new to him. Moreover, even if he once bought similar items and bought similar ones again, even though this is not the first time he is purchasing them, he still recites "Shehecheyanu." This is according to the Talmudic discourse, and so ruled the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch. However, the Rambam in Chapter 10 only mentioned having similar items, and did not mention buying and then buying again (see there for further details). And it is mentioned in the Jerusalem Talmud there: that even if they are not new, since they are new to him, he recites "Shehecheyanu," because these were never his before. They only said "new" to exclude if they were his and he sold them and then bought them back, in which case he does not recite the blessing, since they were previously his and thus it is not such a joy. (The Magen Avraham in Section 5 wrote that people are not careful about this, see there, and it seems to me that nowadays people are careful about this, but only because it needs to be an important item as will be explained. Therefore, if it is not clear that such an item is important to him, some refrain from reciting the blessing).

One should recite the blessing at the time of acquisition, even though they have not yet used the item, because the blessing is made due to the joy in the heart that one feels from the purchase. However, this is only when the matter is completed properly, but if the house is not yet completely finished, or the vessel requires repair, or the garment needs mending, one should not recite the blessing until all the repairs are completed. For a garment, when one puts it on to go out, one should recite: "Who clothes the naked," and the blessing of 'Shehecheyanu' precedes this (see Magen Avraham, section 6, although his words are difficult to understand, see there).

Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 5: "If one buys utensils that he and his household use, he recites the blessing 'HaTov VeHaMeitiv' (Who is good and does good). If they were given to him as a gift, he recites 'HaTov VeHaMeitiv,' as it is good for him and the giver." This is his exact wording. If one buys utensils for himself alone and also for his household separately, he recites 'Shehecheyanu' for his own and 'HaTov VeHaMeitiv' for those of his household (Bach and Magen Avraham, section 7), for he also uses those of his household. (See Taz, section 4. According to what I wrote, the Magen Avraham is not as he stated but rather as I wrote, and the Magen Avraham questioned the benefit to the giver from Even HaEzer, at the end of section 37. Were it not for the words of the Rosh, I would have said that this law comes from the Jerusalem Talmud, and the intention is that when one buys with his own money, even though his household also uses them, the primary ownership is his. But the giver of a gift intends for the whole household to use it, and therefore the blessing is 'HaTov VeHaMeitiv.' Understand this well.) (See also Ba’er Hetev, section 15 and Shach, section 13. According to what I wrote, it fits well. Understand this well.)

This is the wording of the Tur: "The Tosafot wrote that one should only recite a blessing on important matters, similar to building a new house. But on something that is not so significant, such as a robe, shoes, or slippers, one does not recite a blessing. And my master, my father, the Rosh, of blessed memory, wrote: It appears to me that everything depends on the person: there is a poor person who rejoices in his robe more than a rich person with valuable items." End of quote. And our master, the Beit Yosef, ruled in paragraph 6 according to the opinion of the Rosh. And there are those who say that the Tosafot also agree with this, and they were not referring to a poor person (Maginei Avraham, subsection 10, in the name of Radbaz). But our master, the Rema, wrote: "And there are those who say that even a poor person does not recite a blessing on a robe, shoes, and the like, and so is the custom." End of quote. The explanation of his words: The opinion of the Tosafot is indeed that even for important items like clothes and valuable utensils, it depends on one's wealth and poverty. For a poor person, even a simple garment is significant, and he recites "Shehecheyanu" on it, whereas a rich person only recites the blessing on an expensive garment like silk or fine wool, and the like. In this, everyone agrees, including the Rosh and the Tur. However, the Tosafot add that on a robe, shoes, or slippers, even a poor person does not recite a blessing, even though they are significant to him. This is for a different reason: because for the blessing of "Shehecheyanu", we require something that comes infrequently, similar to "from time to time", where "Shehecheyanu" is relevant. This applies to garments that are not commonly worn as new. But robes, shoes, and slippers are frequently renewed, and it is not appropriate to recite "Shehecheyanu" on them. And so is our custom. Regarding books: there are those who say one should not recite a blessing, because commandments were not given for our enjoyment (Maginei Avraham, subsection 5), and there are those who disagree (there and Shulchan Aruch). And someone who completed a composition, there are those who say to recite "Shehecheyanu", but our custom is not so (see Shulchan Aruch, subsection 2). And on the construction of a synagogue, one does not recite a blessing since it belongs to the public, unlike those who instructed that the prayer leader should recite "Hatov Vehametiv" (there, subsection 1). And someone who was privileged by God to write a Torah scroll, there are those who say that upon its completion, he should recite "Shehecheyanu" on the fulfillment of the mitzvah, and this is correct, though I do not know if everyone practices this.

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote: "The custom is to say to someone who wears a new garment: 'May you wear it out and renew it.' There are those who wrote that this should not be said regarding shoes or garments made from animal hides, because if so, it would necessitate killing another animal first, so that another garment could be made from it. And it is written: 'His mercies are on all His works.' Behold, the reasoning is very weak and it does not seem appropriate, but nevertheless, many are careful not to say it." End of quote.

One who sees a Mercurius (a type of idol) or other forms of idolatry says: "Blessed are You, Lord our God, King of the universe, who has given forbearance to those who transgress His will." This means that you should not think that because it continues to exist for a long time, He does not care about it, as it were, but rather this is from the attribute of forbearance, that the Holy One, blessed be He, is patient and slow to anger. If one sees it within 30 days, he does not repeat the blessing, for all blessings of sighting are from thirty days to thirty days. And our teacher, the Rema, wrote that nowadays this blessing is not recited. There is no need to elaborate on this.

One who sees a place from which idolatry has been uprooted, if it is in the Land of Israel, says: "Blessed are You, Lord our God, King of the universe, who has uprooted idolatry from our land," and if it is outside the Land of Israel, he says: "who has uprooted it from this place." And in both cases, he says: "Just as You have uprooted it from this place, so may You uproot it from all places, and return the hearts of its worshippers to serve You." And if it has been uprooted from one place and moved to another place, he blesses upon the place from which it was uprooted: "Blessed... who has uprooted, etc.," and upon the place to which it was moved, he blesses: "Blessed... who is long-suffering, etc."

It is recorded in the Tractate Avodah Zarah (18b): "The Sages taught: One who goes to stadiums... this is considered a gathering of scorners, and similarly one who goes to theaters and circuses, about this it is said: 'Happy is the man that has not walked, etc.'” See there. And if it happens in your city, be careful not to see it, for then you will merit to witness the delight of Leviathan and the ox. And if you hear the sound of singers and players of flutes and all musical instruments, sigh and say: "Master of the Universe, Your people whom You brought out of Egypt have sinned doubly and have been punished doubly. Their palaces You have destroyed, their joys You have ceased, their happiness You have marred, their delight You have turned. Will You, O Lord, be angry with us forever? May it be Your will that You rebuild Jerusalem, Your holy city, speedily in our days, Amen." (Bach in the name of the Eshkol, see there).

One who sees wicked Babylon says: "Blessed are You, Lord our God, King of the Universe, who has destroyed wicked Babylon." If he sees the house of Nebuchadnezzar, he says: "Blessed... who has destroyed the house of Nebuchadnezzar the wicked," and even if he sees it from afar, for from close up it is impossible, as snakes and scorpions surround it, as Isaiah the prophet cursed. If one sees the lion’s den or the fiery furnace in Babylon, he blesses: "Blessed is He who performed miracles for the righteous in this place," and this has already been explained in Siman 218. There is a place in Babylon where any animal that passes over this place cannot go further unless they put some of the soil from that place on it, and it is a sign of a curse for it as it is written: "I will sweep it with the broom of destruction." When one reaches this place, he says: "Blessed is He who speaks and does, blessed is He who decrees and fulfills." And I do not know if this is with the name and kingship or not, and it seems that it is not with the name and kingship, for if it were with the name and kingship, it would not be appropriate to say 'blessed' twice (and know that all that we wrote in this section is not brought by the Rambam at all in Chapter 10, and I do not know why, and in the Gemara there is indeed no twofold 'blessed', and the Levush wrote with the name and kingship).

One who sees six hundred thousand Jews together recites the blessing: "Blessed are You, Lord our God, King of the Universe, Knower of secrets," for their minds are not alike, nor are their faces alike. Just as they are different in their opinions, which is the inner form, up to six hundred thousand, so they are different in their outer form. This encompasses all opinions, and it is the ultimate extent beyond which there is no further form. Therefore, the Torah was given to six hundred thousand to include all opinions and wisdoms, with nothing to be added to them (Maharsha on Berachot 58). The Holy One, blessed be He, is the Knower of secrets, meaning that although they are wise and their speech and thoughts are not the same, and each one's wisdom is different, nevertheless He knows what is in the heart of each one (Levush). And one who sees a multitude of idolaters says: "Your mother shall be greatly ashamed; she who bore you shall be humiliated. Behold, the least of the nations shall be a wilderness, a dry land and a desert" (Jeremiah 50:12).

One who sees a wise man among the sages of Israel who is great in Torah should recite the blessing: "Blessed are You, Lord our God, King of the universe, who has given of His wisdom to those who fear Him, for the portion of the Lord is His people, Jacob the lot of His inheritance." And one who sees a wise man among the non-Jews who is great in other wisdoms should recite: "Blessed… who has given of His wisdom to flesh and blood." The measure of greatness in Torah or other wisdoms is not clarified, and therefore this blessing is now avoided. One who sees a king from among the kings of Israel during the time of the Temple would say: "Blessed… who has given of His glory to those who fear Him," and one who sees a king from among the nations of the world should recite: "Blessed… who has given of His glory to flesh and blood." Even a blind person who cannot see blesses, and even if one sees through a window or from a distance, they bless. It is a mitzvah to strive to see a king, but if one has already seen him once, they should not interrupt their learning to see him again, unless he comes with more honor and splendor than the first time. The Rambam wrote at the end of the third chapter of "Mourning" that a Kohen is permitted to become impure by rabbinic impurity to see a king. All blessings for seeing are already explained to be from thirty days to thirty days, but when seeing a different king, one blesses even within thirty days.

Our Rabbis taught (Berachot 58b): "One who sees the homes of Israel in their inhabited state says: 'Blessed... who establishes the boundary of the widow.' In their desolation, he says: 'Blessed... the true Judge.' For the homes of idolaters in their inhabited state, he says: 'The house of the proud will the Lord uproot' (Proverbs 15:25). In their desolation, he says: 'O Lord, God of vengeance; O God of vengeance, shine forth' (Psalms 94:1)." Rashi explained: "The homes of Israel in their inhabited state, such as during the settlement of the Second Temple and in the land of Israel" (Magen Avraham, section 8), and according to this, this blessing does not apply now. And the Rif wrote: "One who sees the synagogues of Israel in their inhabited state," see there. There are those who wrote that it refers to the homes of great wealthy individuals who give much charity and conduct themselves with the fear of God (Beit Yosef). In any case, we do not practice this blessing due to the differing interpretations, and in cases of doubt regarding blessings, we are lenient.

One who sees Jewish graves recites the blessing: "Blessed... who formed you in justice, and sustained you in justice, and provided for you in justice, and gathered you in justice (and in the Rambam and Tur the version is: 'and caused you to die in justice,' and this is the custom), and who will in the future restore you in justice, and knows the number of all of you in justice, and He will in the future revive you and sustain you. Blessed are You, O Lord, who revives the dead." In the Jerusalem Talmud, it adds before the conclusion: 'He will uncover the dust from your eyes,' see there. One who sees the graves of idolaters says: "Your mother is ashamed, etc.," as stated in section 5. All blessings on seeing [graves], if one sees them within thirty days, one does not bless, as stated. However, if one sees the cemetery after [thirty days], one blesses even within thirty days. Similarly, if graves have been added to the cemetery, one also blesses again. If there is doubt whether graves have been added, one does not bless, and should bless when near the graves within four cubits. For a single grave, one does not bless. A Kohen, who cannot come near the graves, it seems he can bless from a distance as long as he sees them. Similarly, one who is traveling or riding in a wagon, since he sees the graves, it appears he blesses.

Know that in Eruvin (40b) it is explicitly explained that the blessing of 'Shehecheyanu' on holidays that come from time to time is obligatory, while the blessing of 'Shehecheyanu' on new fruits is optional, as stated there. Therefore, it seems to my humble opinion that all types of the 'Shehecheyanu' blessing that come at fixed times, such as on Chanukah and Purim, are obligatory, and other 'Shehecheyanu' blessings are optional. Consequently, many are lenient regarding this. However, regarding new fruits, it has been accepted as obligatory, and everyone is careful about it. It is found in the Jerusalem Talmud (Kiddushin, Chapter 4) that there was someone who would save small coins from his expenses to buy every new fruit and taste it, and it says there that he will be held accountable for not having eaten.

One who sees his friend, who is dear to him and he is very happy to see him: if it has been thirty days since he last saw him, he recites the blessing of "Shehecheyanu" with the [Divine] Name and Kingship. If he has not seen him for twelve months, he recites the blessing of "Mechayei HaMeitim" (Who revives the dead), and in that case, he does not recite "Shehecheyanu." This applies when there has been no correspondence from him, but if he has received a letter from him, he does not recite "Mechayei HaMeitim." However, regarding "Shehecheyanu," there is no difference; even if he received a letter within the thirty days, he still recites "Shehecheyanu." The reason is that the blessing of "Shehecheyanu" is due to the joy of seeing him face to face, but the blessing of "Mechayei HaMeitim" is because it is now known that he is alive. Therefore, since he already knew he was alive through letters or heard from others that he is alive, the blessing of "Mechayei HaMeitim" is not applicable. The measure of twelve months seems to be because a deceased person is not forgotten from the heart until twelve months (this seems to me, and see Be'er Heitev and Shach Taz section 1). And if one has never seen him before, even though he knew of him, such as if he sent him letters and he was pleased to see him, nevertheless, he does not recite a blessing upon seeing him.

There is no distinction in this ruling between males and females. Only if one is very joyful upon seeing them does one recite the blessing of 'Shehecheyanu.' However, in the case of females, this applies only to one's wife, mother, daughter, sister, and similar relations. Nowadays, people are very lenient with this blessing. Nevertheless, someone who knows that he derives pleasure from seeing the person and is very joyful, especially a son for his father or a father for his son, or a brother for his brother, and the like, must recite the blessing.
