Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote in section 2: "There are those who say that when one's son becomes a Bar Mitzvah, meaning when he is thirteen years and one day old, the father should bless: 'Blessed are You, Lord our God, King of the universe, who has exempted me from the punishment of this one,' and it is good to bless without using God's name and kingship." The essence of this blessing is because until now, the father was punished when the son sinned due to not educating him properly, and the son also suffered due to the father's sin. But when he becomes a Bar Mitzvah, the father is no longer punished for the son's sins nor the son for the father's (Magen Avraham 5) as it is written: "Each person shall die for their own sin." And what is written: "He visits the iniquity of the fathers upon the children," refers to when they continue their fathers' deeds (Sanhedrin 27). And the reason for blessing without God's name and kingship is because we do not find this blessing in the Gemara, but it is found in the Midrash at the beginning of Toldot. There are several blessings we recite even though they are not found in the Gemara, like the blessings 'Who gives strength to the weary' and 'Who sanctifies His name in public.' Many have the custom to recite this blessing with God's name and kingship when the Bar Mitzvah boy is called up to the Torah, if the day he becomes a Bar Mitzvah is a Torah reading day or the following day (ibid. 4). It is a mitzvah to make a feast on the day he becomes a Bar Mitzvah, and it is considered a seudat mitzvah (ibid.). If the boy delivers a discourse, even if the feast is not on the same day, it is still considered a seudat mitzvah (ibid. in the name of the Yam Shel Shlomo).

It is a mitzvah to taste every new fruit, as it is mentioned in the Jerusalem Talmud that we brought in Section 1. The reason is simple: in order to give praise and thanks to the Blessed Holy One, Who renews the fruits from year to year for the enjoyment of human beings. And we bless on every new fruit that renews from year to year the blessing of "Shehecheyanu." The common practice is to first recite the blessing for the fruit and then "Shehecheyanu," and I have also seen that the great authorities wrote this way due to the principle of frequent and infrequent (the frequent takes precedence) and other reasons (Gr"iP and in the name of the Leqet Yosher). However, in my humble opinion, it seems appropriate to precede the blessing of "Shehecheyanu," and the principle of frequent does not apply here, as this principle only applies when the obligation of both blessings comes at once. But here, the blessing of "Shehecheyanu" applies first, as the primary blessing of "Shehecheyanu" is for seeing the fruit, not for eating it, although we customarily bless it at the time of eating. However, the blessing for the fruit is only at the time of eating. Furthermore, in all blessings over enjoyment, there should be no interruption between the blessing and the eating, and therefore, it is appropriate to precede the blessing of "Shehecheyanu," and this is how I practice.

The primary blessing of 'Shehecheyanu' is on seeing [a new fruit], as the Rambam writes at the beginning of Chapter 10: "One who sees a fruit that is renewed from year to year, upon first seeing it - blesses 'Shehecheyanu,'" end quote. Similarly, Rashi of blessed memory wrote in Eruvin (40: s.v. 'on a new gourd'), and this is his wording: "When I see a new gourd from year to year, I say the 'Shehecheyanu' blessing," end quote. The Tur and the Shulchan Aruch, in Section 3, wrote: "One who sees a new fruit that is renewed from year to year - blesses 'Shehecheyanu,' even if he sees it in his friend's hand or on the tree. However, the custom is not to bless until the time of eating, but one who blesses at the time of seeing does not lose out. One should not bless until the fruit's growth is complete, and if he did not bless at the first sighting, he can bless at the second sighting," end quote.

The reason for the custom can be explained by the fact that we are not experts in determining when the fruit has fully developed. Some opine that one should bless when the fruit reaches the size of a white bean (Magen Avraham, section 8, in the name of Radbaz), while others say that if one blessed before the fruit was fully developed, they must bless again when it is fully developed (ibid, in the name of Rashba). Based on this, it would be unclear at the time of seeing whether the fruit is fully developed, and therefore, our custom is to bless at the time of eating, as it is then clearly determined. Another possible reason is that the essence of the blessing of "Shehecheyanu" is due to the joy of the occasion. In earlier generations, people were wholehearted and rejoiced at seeing new fruit, giving thanks to God for His goodness and kindness to the world, and therefore, they could bless upon seeing. However, we do not experience the same joy and gratitude except at the time of physical enjoyment during eating, and thus we cannot bless upon seeing. 

This is why it is written: "If one blessed upon seeing, they have not lost out," meaning it is not considered a blessing in vain for us. It is also written that if one did not bless at the first sighting, they may bless at the second sighting. Accordingly, for us, if one did not bless at the first eating, they may bless at the second eating. However, many disagree with this and hold that if one did not bless "Shehecheyanu" the first time, they should not bless again, and this is the practice to follow, especially since the blessing of "Shehecheyanu" is discretionary (ibid, section 9, in the name of Rabbi Meir, Sefer Mitzvot Katan, and Radbaz).

They wrote in Section 4: "If one recited the 'Shehecheyanu' blessing on sherezash, when he eats gindash, he must recite the 'Shehecheyanu' blessing again, as they are considered two types of fruits, similar to two types of cherries such as weinkeshol and kirsen and the like." And even if they differ only in taste and not in name, such as white figs and black figs, they are considered two types (Levush and Magen Avraham). There are those who wrote that even if they have the same taste but differ in appearance, such as red and black, they are considered two types (there in sub-section 10 in the name of Ma'aseh Tuvya). And in the name of Maharil, it is written that even two types of pears or two types of apples or nuts, one must recite the 'Shehecheyanu' blessing on each type (there). According to this, the number of 'Shehecheyanu' blessings would increase for us, as there are many types within each species, and among the small fruits like kirsen and weinperlach, there are different colors such as red, black, white, and green, and they also differ in taste. Thus, we would need to recite the 'Shehecheyanu' blessing on each one, but this is not the custom.

In truth, there is one who disagrees with this and holds that the individual varieties within each species are not considered different species regarding the blessing of 'Shehecheyanu.' The reasoning of those who are stringent is because it is taught in the fourth chapter of Terumot that black figs do not elevate the status of white figs. Since, concerning the nullification of prohibitions, they are considered two species, the same applies to the 'Shehecheyanu' blessing (see Beit Yosef). However, in reality, there is also a dispute in the Talmud about this. Additionally, according to Rabbi Akiva, whose ruling is followed, it depends on whether one knows what fell, whether it was black or white. If one knows what fell, they do not nullify each other, but if one does not know, they do nullify each other. This would imply the opposite, that they are considered one species. The reason they do not nullify each other when known is because they were not included in the doubt of the prohibition, and how could they nullify the prohibition? Even within the same species, those that were not included in the prohibition do not contribute to nullification (see Gra, section 3, and Knesset HaGedolah who also questions this). Therefore, our custom is to recite the 'Shehecheyanu' blessing on the combined species and not on the individual varieties within each species (and there is proof for this from the law that will be explained in section 10, and ponder this well).

Our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 5: "If one recited the 'Shehecheyanu' blessing (who has kept us alive) on grapes, when he drinks new wine, he does not need to recite the blessing again," because it is considered the same joy even though they have different names, as it is all one happiness (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 11). And the Mahari”l would refrain from eating grapes until drinking the freshly pressed wine (there), and according to this, when one drinks new wine and has not yet eaten grapes, he must recite 'Shehecheyanu'. This applies specifically when it is freshly pressed wine, but when it is ordinary wine, there is no need to recite 'Shehecheyanu', because with wine there is no distinction between new and old (there), and wherever there is no distinction between new and old, the 'Shehecheyanu' blessing does not apply. And we are not proficient in distinguishing between freshly pressed wine and ordinary wine, because we do not have wine.

A fruit that does not renew from year to year, even if many days pass without eating it - one does not recite the 'Shehecheyanu' blessing. Therefore, one does not recite 'Shehecheyanu' on new birds or new fish (see there, section 12). And for a fragrance that renews from year to year, some say to bless 'Shehecheyanu' and some disagree (see there), as mentioned in Siman 216, and this is the primary ruling. And for a fruit that renews twice a year, one needs to recite 'Shehecheyanu' each time because it renews from time to time; a year is not specifically required. But for anything that does not have a fixed time for its growth - one does not recite a blessing on it. And our teacher the Rema wrote in section 6 that therefore one does not recite 'Shehecheyanu' on new vegetables, because they stand in the ground all year, end quote. And in our region, we do not know of such a vegetable at all. And some have written that it refers to vegetables that are buried in the ground all year (see there). And this too we do not know, and the language does not imply this. Perhaps there are countries where the vegetable stands all year.

There is one who wrote that one should not recite the blessing of 'Shehecheyanu' on any type of vegetable (cited there in the name of the Shelah). However, we do not follow this practice. For important vegetables such as cucumbers (ugerkes), cabbages (kavennes), and similar vegetables, we do recite 'Shehecheyanu', as they do not last from season to season. Even though they can be preserved when pickled, all fruits can be preserved when pickled, and that is a completely different reason. But for simple vegetables like lettuce (salata), onions (tsviyin), squash (tsavina), and similar vegetables, we do not recite 'Shehecheyanu'. Similarly, for types of turnips like brisca, radishes (merin), horseradish (retach), and sesame seeds, we do not recite 'Shehecheyanu', as they last from year to year. Also, for potatoes (kartofel), we do not recite [the blessing] for this reason, and likewise for carrots (karoit) and beets (burikas), since there is no noticeable difference between the new and the old. However, for strawberries (riben), we do recite 'Shehecheyanu', because they do not last from year to year and they have sweetness. For types of legumes, we do not recite 'Shehecheyanu', such as beans (arbes), lentils (linsin), and similar legumes, because they last from year to year. Similarly, for all types of bread, we do not recite [the blessing], since there is no noticeable difference between the new and the old, and similarly for wheat (terkesa veyitz), we do not recite, and this is what we call 'kikes', which also last for a long time. However, for fruit of the trees and all types of berries (yagidess), we do recite 'Shehecheyanu', except for gooseberries (brosnitses) and cranberries (zorolines), because they are not significant and also last from year to year. Rabbi Yosef Karo wrote in section 7 that one does not recite 'Shehecheyanu' on unripe fruit ('boser') until the grape clusters ripen, and similarly for all other fruits, only when they have finished growing. And this is obvious, and it has already been clarified at the end of section 6 (what the Magen Avraham wrote there that one recites the blessing on 'rifot', I do not know what that is).

Just as one recites a blessing over a new fruit, so too one recites a blessing over an unusual creature, for it is also something new. However, the "Shehecheyanu" blessing does not apply here, obviously, and one recites with the full formula: "Blessed are You... who changes the creatures." Therefore, one who sees a very black person, a very red person, a very white person, a very tall and thin person, or a person with a very large and unusual belly to the extent that it appears, due to its thickness, as if his stature is diminished, a very short person, a person full of warts, a person whose hair clumps together, an elephant, or a monkey - recites the blessing "who changes the creatures." Similarly, one who sees a crippled person, a person missing limbs, a blind person, a person afflicted with boils, or a person with vitiligo (i.e., covered in small white spots) - if they were born this way, one recites "who changes the creatures." If they became this way later, such that they became crippled, lost limbs, blind, afflicted with boils, or developed vitiligo, one recites "Blessed is the True Judge" as one would for any misfortune, heaven forbid. Some say that this blessing of "Blessed is the True Judge" is only recited by someone who is greatly distressed by it, but not by someone who is not distressed. The blessing "who changes the creatures" is only recited the first time and not every 30 days, because the first time the change appears very significant and is a wonder, but not so the second time. Some say that one recites the blessing every 30 days, like all blessings of sight, if they have not seen another like it within 30 days, and it is clear that for another person one blesses even within 30 days.

And one who sees beautiful trees that are uncommon, or exceptionally beautiful creatures, whether male or female (Eliyah Rabbah), whether Jewish or non-Jewish, and even when one sees a beautiful creature from among the animals and birds, he blesses with the name and sovereignty: "Blessed is He who has such in His world," and this is a blessing of praise and thanks to the Creator. And one only blesses upon them the first time and not more, neither on them nor on others, because beyond the first time there is no astonishment, unless they are more beautiful than the first ones (and although one should not stare at a woman, etc., this refers to extensive staring, but mere sighting is involuntary, and there is no issue with that. See Eliyah Rabbah).

The one who goes out during the days of Nisan and sees trees blossoming says: "Blessed are You, Lord our God, King of the universe, who has not left anything lacking in His world, and created in it good creatures and good trees for human beings to enjoy." This means he gives praise and thanks to the Holy One, blessed be He, who created even things not necessary for human life, such as fruit trees, for the benefit of man. Therefore, this blessing is not recited on seeds and vegetables, as those are necessary, unlike fruits. And one blesses at the time of blossoming, as it is then evident that they will produce fruits. In our region, this is not in Nisan but rather in Iyar or the beginning of Sivan, and that is when we bless. This blessing is only recited once a year even if one sees other trees, as this blessing is a general thanksgiving for His kindness and goodness, blessed be He. And for one who is careful with this blessing, it is said: "See, the smell of my son is like the smell of a field which the Lord has blessed" (Eliyah Rabbah).

The Tur and Shulchan Aruch wrote that if one delays reciting the blessing until after the fruit has fully ripened, he should no longer recite it. However, the Mordechai wrote that he should still recite it. And some say that they do not actually disagree, as the Mordechai is referring to a situation where he did not see the fruit at all until after they had fully ripened, while the Tur and Shulchan Aruch refer to a case where he saw them before they ripened and did not bless, in which case he should not bless afterward (Bach). There is also someone who rejected this explanation, arguing that it is certainly not dependent on the first sighting (Prisha). It is also possible to say that the Tur and Shulchan Aruch are referring to a situation where he did not see them until after they had completely ripened, at which point the "Shehecheyanu" blessing would apply, while the Mordechai refers to a time before they had fully ripened (and this interpretation is supported by the Eliyah Rabbah, see there and also see Prisha), and this is the practice that should be followed. However, this blessing is generally neglected among the masses (and see Bedek HaBayit who wrote in the name of R”Y that it is not customary to recite this blessing, but all Torah scholars and God-fearing individuals are careful to observe this blessing).

It was taught at the beginning of the chapter "Haro'eh" (Berachot 54a): "On comets (zikin), earthquakes (ze'ot), lightning (brakim), thunder (ra'amim), and strong winds (ruhot), one recites a blessing with the phrase 'Blessed... whose power and might fill the world.'"

Comets (zikin) are like a star shooting across the sky from place to place, and its light trails like a rod, or alternatively, a star that appears to have a long tail (Ra'avad). Earthquakes (ze'ot) are the shaking of the earth. 

Lightning (brakim) is well-known and is called "blitz." There are two types: one that comes with thunder and the other that appears on summer nights when it is hot and many flashes of lightning are seen at night. Thunder (ra'amim) is also well-known; it is the sound heard in the sky from clouds pouring water onto each other, as it is written: "At the sound of His giving, a tumult of waters in the heavens" (Jeremiah 10:13). 

Strong winds (ruhot) are uncommon winds that blow with great force and only occur occasionally. 

Here, five phenomena are listed because the earth contains the four basic elements: fire, wind, water, and earth, and the heavens are the fifth element. Comets (zikin) are a star from the heavens, earthquakes (ze'ot) come from the earth, lightning (brakim) are fire, thunder (ra'amim) are the sounds of water, and strong winds (ruhot) are the element of wind (the explanation of the Gra on the Mishnah).

For all these things, one blesses: "Whose strength and power fill the world," because they are visible and audible over a great distance. One can also recite the blessing "Who makes the works of creation" for all these things, as they and their occurrences are from the creation of the six days of Genesis. This is stated in the Gemara and is ruled by the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch. Accordingly, at the time of thunder which is preceded by lightning, one may recite one blessing for both (Magen Avraham), whichever blessing one prefers. The common custom is to bless "Who makes the works of creation" for lightning and "Whose strength and power fill the world" for thunder. However, in my humble opinion, the second blessing is a blessing in vain (the Taz also protested against this, see there, and the Eliyah Rabbah tried to justify it but did not succeed, see there. This is only according to the Raavad brought by the Beit Yosef, who wrote to bless both, as is implied from Rashi. But why should one involve oneself in a blessing that most authorities consider to be in vain? Therefore, they should be warned not to do so, and examine this carefully).

When one has blessed over thunder and lightning, one should not bless again for additional thunder and lightning as long as the rain continues and the clouds are gathered. However, if the clouds have dispersed, the rain has stopped, and the sun has shined, and then there is lightning and thunder again, one blesses over them once more. This continues indefinitely, as it is considered a different occurrence. It is stated in the Jerusalem Talmud: if one is sitting in the bathroom and hears thunder or sees lightning, if he can exit and bless within the time it takes to say a greeting, he should leave and bless. If not, he should not exit. This is almost impossible unless he has not yet relieved himself, has not touched a soiled area, and has water in front of him (see Magen Avraham). In my humble opinion, the Jerusalem Talmud does not mean he entered to relieve himself but rather entered for some other purpose. In such a situation, he could exit within the time it takes to say a greeting, although the phrase "was sitting in the bathroom" does not seem to fit this interpretation very well.

At the beginning of the chapter "Haroeh" (Berachot 54a), it is taught: "On mountains, hills, seas, rivers, and deserts, one says: 'Blessed is He who makes the works of creation.'" Rabbi Yehuda says: "One who sees the Great Sea says: 'Blessed is He who made the Great Sea.'" It is clear that for mountains and hills, we require them to be notable in their height, such as the Alps, the Pyrenees, Mount Kazbek, Mount Ararat, and similar. Rivers, too, must be large and well-known worldwide, and not small rivers that do not have a global reputation.

The words of the Rambam and the Tur are concise, like the language of the Mishnah, but the language of our teacher, the Beit Yosef, is as follows: "One does not bless over all rivers, but rather over the four rivers mentioned in the scripture, like the Tigris and Euphrates, and that is if one sees them in their natural course, not altered by humans. One does not bless over all mountains and hills, but specifically over mountains and hills that are distinct and demonstrate the might of the Creator." This is the end of his words. Now, what he wrote: 'only on the four rivers in the Torah' is a puzzling matter, and it has already been questioned (see Magen Avraham). And in the Mordechai it is written: "like the four rivers," meaning rivers that have a name similar to the four rivers in the Torah. Furthermore, his language is not understood; what does he mean by saying: 'like the Tigris and Euphrates,' as if we do not know the rivers in the Torah. Therefore, it seems to me, in my humble opinion, that it should be stated: 'but rather similar to the four rivers mentioned in the scripture.' And this is why he says: 'like the Tigris and Euphrates' because they are well-known, unlike the Gihon and Pishon which are not known to us. According to this, certainly on large rivers like the Volga, Danube, Rhine, and the like - one must bless. (And this ruling follows Rabbi Yehuda, as the Rambam wrote. The Tur was puzzled by this, see there, but it is not difficult at all, as he holds that Rabbi Yehuda is not disputing, see Beit Yosef and Bach).

And what is the "Great Sea"? Our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote that it is the sea that people cross to reach the Land of Israel and Egypt. This is the sea in the middle of the inhabited world, whose one end is near Jaffa, which is the border of the Land of Israel, and whose other end is at the edge of the land of Spain. Some have written that it is the Ocean that surrounds the entire world (Magen Avraham in the name of the Levush). Seemingly, this is the main interpretation, for although the Torah calls the sea adjacent to the Land of Israel the "Great Sea," this is because, of the seas surrounding the Land of Israel, it is the largest. However, in the language of the Mishnah regarding the blessing, it makes sense to call it the "Great Sea," as it is insignificant compared to the Ocean. Furthermore, in Mikvaot (Chapter 5, Mishnah 4), Rabbi Yehuda also says: "The Great Sea is like a mikveh," and there it is explained that it refers to the Ocean.

In my humble opinion, it seems that the primary understanding aligns with the view of Rabbeinu, the Beit Yosef. When we delve into the account of Creation, where the Holy One, blessed be He, said: "Let the waters be gathered into one place, and let the dry land appear," the waters referred to are the ocean waters that surround the earth. It is then written: "God called the dry land Earth, and the gathering of the waters He called Seas." It appears to me that this means: 'the gathering of the waters' within the dry land—these are all the seas within the earth's sphere—He called Seas. Thus, according to this, the ocean is called 'waters,' which is the fundamental element of water, and 'seas' are those within the terrestrial sphere. Within this terrestrial sphere, the sea near the Land of Israel is the largest of all the seas within the sphere, as is known from maps of the land, and this interpretation also applies to mikvaot (ritual baths). (Rabbi Meir says: 'All seas are like a mikveh,' meaning all the seas within the sphere. Rabbi Yehuda says: 'The Great Sea is like a mikveh,' meaning the sea near the Land of Israel, into which many seas and rivers flow, as is known. However, the commentators did not explain it this way. Therefore, in practice, it seems appropriate to recite the blessing 'Who performs the act of Creation' on all of them, even on the sea near the Land of Israel and also on the ocean, due to the varying interpretations. Examine this closely.)

One who sees a rainbow says: "Blessed are You, Lord our God, King of the Universe, who remembers the covenant, is faithful to His covenant, and keeps His promise." This refers to the covenant that the Holy One, Blessed be He, made with Noah that He would not bring a flood upon the world, as it is written: "And the rainbow shall be seen in the cloud, and I will remember My covenant." He, Blessed be He, is faithful to His covenant not to bring a flood upon the world. Since there is nothing new under the sun, the rainbow was not created now but was already created from the six days of creation. It is one of the ten things that were created on the eve of the Sabbath at twilight, as it is taught in Avot. Therefore, we conclude: "and keeps His promise," meaning that the essence of the rainbow was already created by His command during the six days of creation (as explained by the Maharsha, Nedarim 59b), but now He shows it to us.

Our Sages said (there) that it is forbidden to gaze extensively at a rainbow, and only a mere glance is permitted, not an excessive gaze. And about this, they said: "Anyone who does not show regard for the honor of their Creator - it would have been better for them not to have come into the world" (beginning of Chapter 2 of Chagigah), as it is written: "Like the appearance of a rainbow, so was the likeness of the glory of Hashem." And it is forbidden to fall on one's face when seeing the rainbow, because it appears as if one is bowing to the rainbow (Berachot 59a), and one who gazes at the rainbow, their eyes become dim (there).

One who sees the sun during the spring equinox at the beginning of the great cycle, which is every 28 years, and at that time the equinox is at the beginning of the night of the fourth day, as it was during the six days of Creation when the luminaries were placed at the beginning of the night of the fourth day. Therefore, when one sees the sun on the first year of the great cycle on Wednesday morning, one blesses with [God's] name and sovereignty: "Blessed... who performs the acts of creation," and this will, God willing, be in the year 5657 (1897) coming upon us for good. The blessing is recited until three hours into the day. However, if the sky is covered with clouds, one can bless until midday and no later. If it remains cloudy until midday, the blessing is no longer recited.

And similarly, when the moon returns to the beginning of the constellation Aries at the start of the month and is not inclined either to the north or to the south, and similarly when each of the five stars—Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Venus, and Mercury—return to the beginning of the constellation Aries and are not inclined either to the north or to the south, and similarly at any time when the constellation Aries appears rising slightly in the east, for each of these one recites the blessing: "Who performs the act of creation," because these seven stars—Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, the Sun, Venus, Mercury, and the Moon—are the primary stars that influence the earth according to His command, blessed be He. Therefore, when one sees them in their position as they were at the beginning of creation during the six days of creation, one blesses over them 'Who performs the act of creation.' And Aries is the first of the constellations, and when they stand at its beginning, it is as at the beginning of their creation. However, we do not recite this blessing on the moon and the stars because we are not proficient in this matter, and there are other explanations for this. The main explanation, as written, is that this is the interpretation of Rashi and Rambam (and the Tur also brought the explanation of the Aruch when the sky was covered with clouds for three days, see there).

It is logically understood that the matter of prayer is only for the future and not for the past. For what benefit is there in praying for the past? Regarding the past, only the language of thanksgiving is appropriate, to give thanks to the Blessed One for the good He has done. And for the future, the opposite is true: thanksgiving is only appropriate for what has already occurred, and prayer is relevant for the future, where one requests from the Blessed One to do such and such.

Therefore, one who enters a city and hears the sound of crying in the city from some calamity that has occurred there, and says: 'May it be Your will that this is not in my house' - this is a vain prayer, for this is a prayer about the past and what has happened has already happened. But one can say: 'I am confident that this is not in my house' if he is a completely righteous person, like the incident with Hillel the Elder who said so, and concerning him it is said: "He will not fear bad news; his heart is steadfast, trusting in the Lord" (Berachot 60a). And the matter can be explained in two ways: One, in its straightforward sense, that he is confident that this is not in his house; and the second, because he has accustomed his household to accept everything with joy, both the good and the opposite, and if so, even if, God forbid, some calamity has occurred, they will not cry out loudly but will accept it with love and silence.

And similarly, one whose wife is pregnant and wishes for a male child, until 40 days he may pray and say: 'May it be Your will that my wife give birth to a male,' because until 40 days it is considered mere water. But after 40 days, when the form of the fetus has already been formed, if he then prays: 'May it be Your will that my wife give birth to a male,' this would be a vain prayer, for what has been, has been, and it will not change. And even though we find that Dinah was transformed from a male to a female, this occurred within 40 days, and even if it was after 40 days, we do not mention miraculous events (there), and all matters concerning our holy ancestors were entirely miraculous.

When entering a city, one should say: "May it be Your will, Hashem, our God and the God of our forefathers, that You bring me into this city in peace." This is a prayer for the future. And when one enters the city in peace, one should say: "I give thanks before You, Hashem, my God, for bringing me into this city in peace." This is a prayer of gratitude for the past. Similarly, upon leaving, when one wishes to depart, one should say: "May it be Your will... that You take me out of this city in peace." And when one leaves, one should say: "I give thanks... for taking me out of this city in peace. Just as You have taken me out in peace, so too may You guide me in peace," etc. This is the traveler’s prayer as explained in Siman 110, see there. And Rambam wrote in his commentary on the Mishnah that this is neither a prayer nor a blessing but merely a general request. Therefore, nowadays we are not accustomed to this, because Rashi explained that in a city, accusations are prevalent, see there. In our times, this does not apply. Nevertheless, one who is careful with the words of our Sages would do well to say it, especially since there is no blessing involved that we might worry about saying in vain.

One who enters to measure his granary says: "May it be Your will, O Lord my God, that You send blessing upon this pile," which is a prayer for the future. Once he begins to measure, he says: "Blessed is He who sends blessing upon this pile," because he is assured that there will be a blessing. If he measured and then blessed, it is a vain prayer, for blessing is not found except in something hidden from the eye, so that it should not appear plainly contrary to nature, for most miracles are hidden. 

One who enters a bathhouse, and in their bathhouses where it was heated from below and they were always in danger, says: "May it be Your will, O Lord my God, that You bring me in peace and bring me out in peace, and save me from this fire and the like in the future." And when he comes out in peace, he says: "I thank You, O Lord my God, that You have saved me from this fire." Nowadays, this is not customary because the furnace stands to the side and there is no danger (Beit Yosef and Taz and Magen Avraham), and so it is explicitly in the Jerusalem Talmud, Chapter 10 of Berakhot. 

One who enters to let blood says: "May it be Your will... that this act shall be for me as a healing, for You are a free healer," and after letting blood he says: "Blessed is the Healer of the sick." There are those who say this with mentioning God's name and sovereignty (Taz, section 3), and it is also found in the Rambam with the name as well (and so wrote the Beit Yosef in the name of the Sefer Mitzvot Gadol). It is appropriate that for any medicine one takes, he should say: "May it be Your will, O Lord my God, that this shall be for me as a healing," and so the meticulous practice. A person should always be accustomed to say: "Whatever the Merciful One does, He does for the good." 

In summary, a person should always pray for the future and request mercy from the Blessed One, and give thanks for the past, and praise and glorify according to his ability, and whoever increases in giving thanks to God, it is praiseworthy, as the scripture says: "It is good to give thanks to the Lord, and to sing praises to Your name, O Most High."

It is stated in Sukkah (26b): "It is forbidden for a person to sleep during the day for more than a horse's sleep. And how long is a horse's sleep? Sixty breaths... Abaye would sleep while traveling from Pumbedita to Bei Kuva, and Rav Yosef would recite about him: 'How long will you lie down, O sluggard?'" See there. However, the Rambam does not mention this at all, and his reasoning is simple—since Abaye slept a lot, as Rav Yosef recited about him 'How long, etc.', and Rashi explained that this is six Persian miles, see there. And even though we do not know Rashi's source for this, in any case, we understand that the law is not so, as it is clear that he slept more than sixty breaths. It is clear that this is why the Rambam omitted this. 

Certainly, in such matters, it all depends on the person. Furthermore, from Tractate Avot, Chapter 3, there is evidence for this, as it is taught there: "Morning sleep and afternoon wine... remove a person from the world," meaning that morning sleep causes one to miss the time for reciting Shema, but afternoon sleep is not mentioned. Additionally, we have seen that great individuals would sleep during the day for an hour or two, as needed due to their weakness and their regimen.

However, the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch ruled accordingly, and in any case, the words of the Tur can be reconciled. This is the language of the Tur: "After he finishes his meal, he should return to learning, and if he cannot learn without an afternoon nap, he may sleep provided he does not extend it too much. It is taught in Sukkah... Abaye would sleep sixty breaths... Rav Yosef commented on this, etc." End quote. According to this, it is not ruled that it is forbidden to sleep more than sixty breaths, but rather that one should not extend it too much. That is to say, sleeping many hours as at night is certainly forbidden, for if so, when would his Torah be accomplished? Afterwards, he brought the matter from Sukkah to inform us that there are those who were stringent up to sixty breaths and those who were lenient in this, but in any case, one should not sleep a lot.

However, the words of our teacher, the Beit Yosef, are perplexing, as he wrote: "If one cannot study without an afternoon nap, he should sleep, provided that he does not extend it, as it is forbidden to sleep during the day more than the sleep of a horse, which is sixty breaths." End of quote. It is difficult to understand the source of this prohibition, as the Rambam does not mention this at all, and the Tur also does not write a prohibition on this. The Tur was precise in his words, as I have written, so how could he [the Beit Yosef] write the language of prohibition regarding something that is clearly demonstrated from the Talmud, where Abaye did not act in this manner? It must be said that our teacher, the Beit Yosef, believes that there is no disagreement here, and even Abaye agrees with this, but he holds that everything depends on the individual. Abaye could not suffice with sixty breaths, while the Beit Yosef wrote this for someone whose health is robust and can suffice with sixty breaths. Nonetheless, he should not have left the matter ambiguous, and it is difficult to grasp. After the prescribed duration of his nap, he does not need to recite the blessing of 'Elokai Neshamah,' as this is only for the morning. Some say that before sleeping during the day, one should recite 'Vihi Noam' due to harmful spirits (Magen Avraham), but we do not follow this practice.

And even in this little sleep that one gets, his intention should not be for the pleasure of his body but rather to strengthen his body for the service of the Almighty, such as to study Torah or engage in mitzvot. Similarly, one who needs to support his wife and children through work or commerce and needs to rest during the day in order to toil for his livelihood, is also permitted. Likewise, in all worldly pleasures, the primary intent should not be for the pleasure of the body, as this is the behavior of an animal, and all matters of this world are fleeting, futile, and empty. Rather, everything should be for the sake of Heaven. On this it is said: "In all your ways acknowledge Him" (Proverbs 3:6). And our sages of blessed memory said in Avot (2:12): "And let all your deeds be for the sake of Heaven." Even discretionary matters such as eating, drinking, walking, sitting, standing, marital relations, conversation, and all your bodily needs should all be for the service of your Creator or for something that leads to His service (Tur in the name of Rabbeinu Yonah).

Eating and drinking, how should it be done: It goes without saying that forbidden items are prohibited, but even when eating and drinking permissible items and one was hungry and thirsty, if one does so solely for bodily pleasure, it is not praiseworthy, unless one intends to be healthy for the service of one's Creator. And sitting, standing, and walking, how should it be done: It goes without saying that one should not sit in the company of scoffers, nor stand in the path of sinners, nor walk in the counsel of the wicked, but even to sit in the company of the upright, to stand in the place of the righteous, and to walk in the counsel of the innocent, if one does so for personal pleasure to fulfill one's own desire and craving, it is not praiseworthy, unless it is done for the sake of Heaven.

Lying down—how should one do it? It goes without saying that when one is able to engage in Torah and mitzvot and instead he indulges in sleep to pamper himself, it is not appropriate to do so. Even when one is tired and needs to sleep to rest from his weariness, if he does so for bodily pleasure, it is not praiseworthy. However, if he intends to fulfill the needs of his body so he can serve his Creator, and he gives sleep to his eyes and rest to his body for the sake of health, so that his mind is not confounded in Torah due to weariness, this is commendable.

Regarding marital relations—how should one conduct them? It goes without saying that one should not commit a sin, but even during the times prescribed by the Torah, if he engages in relations for his bodily pleasure or to fulfill his desire, it is disgraceful. Even if he intends to have children who will serve him and take his place, it is not praiseworthy. However, if he intends to have children to serve his Creator, or if he intends to fulfill the commandment prescribed by the Torah like a person who pays his debt, this is commendable.

Conversation, how so? It goes without saying that speaking gossip and foul language is forbidden. However, even relating words of wisdom requires that one’s intention be for the service of the Creator or for something that leads to His service. In summary: A person must direct their eyes and heart towards their ways and weigh all their actions on the scales of their intellect. When they see something that will lead to the service of the exalted Creator, they should do it, and if not, they should refrain from doing it. Someone who possesses these qualities serves their Creator all their days, even during times of sitting, standing, walking, conducting business, eating, drinking, and all their needs. Regarding them, it is said: "Happy are those whose way is blameless, who walk in the law of the Lord."

Our rabbis, the Ba'alei Tosafot in Pesachim (107a), posed a question: Why is this prayer called 'Mincha'? If it is because of the meal offering (minchat ha-tamid) and the accompanying libations, these offerings were also part of the morning (Shacharit) sacrifice. They answered: As it is stated in Berakhot (6b), Elijah was only answered during the Mincha prayer, and perhaps he was answered at the time of the Mincha offering. Therefore, it is called 'Mincha prayer' because that was an auspicious time. However, it is still not clear why it was specifically at the time of the evening Mincha offering that he was answered and why it was an auspicious time, for the same applies to Shacharit. 

It seems to me that the matter is as follows: It is known that at the time of the Mincha offering, they would pour the wine libation and the Levites would sing with musical instruments. This was true for both the morning Tamid offering and the afternoon Tamid offering. There is no greater auspicious time than this. However, the afternoon is more auspicious because Mincha comes at the end of all the day's services, as mentioned in Yoma (34b), making the afternoon Mincha the last service of the day. It is cherished and accepted like the Ne'ilah prayer on Yom Kippur. Therefore, it is an auspicious time. 

David also said: "Let my prayer be set forth as incense before You, the lifting up of my hands as the evening Mincha offering" (Psalms 141:2). This shows that the evening Mincha is more cherished. (And in the Jerusalem Talmud, chapter 4, halacha 1, it is derived that Mincha is compared to incense, see there. The Magen Avraham cites the Jerusalem Talmud that it was established at the time of the incense offering, although he references chapter 3, which is not correct, see there, and this can be reconciled. The Abudraham explained that it is called 'Mincha' because it means rest, as when the sun sets in the west it is as if it is going to rest. However, according to this, it should be called 'Menuach,' and 'Mincha' means a gift. Perhaps according to the Rambam, who holds that prayer is a Torah obligation and only once a day, as mentioned in Siman 89, then Shacharit is the payment of a debt and Mincha is a gift. This requires further study.)

It is stated in Berakhot (6b): "A person should always be careful with the Mincha prayer, for Elijah was only answered at the time of the Mincha prayer, as it is said: 'And it came to pass at the time of the offering of the evening sacrifice, that Elijah the prophet came near.'" The reason is that the time for the morning prayer is well known; in the morning, upon rising from his bed, he should pray immediately before becoming involved in his affairs. Similarly, the time for the evening prayer is well known; at night, when he comes home and is free from his affairs, he prays. However, Mincha is in the middle of the day, while he is still engaged in his affairs. He needs to be mindful of it, set aside all his affairs, and pray it. If he does so, his reward is very great.

Therefore, the Sages prevented everyone from engaging in fixed tasks close to the time of Mincha, as it is taught: "A person should not sit before the barber close to Mincha time until he has prayed" (Tur). The Rambam wrote similarly in chapter 6 of Tefillah, that what they forbade was getting a haircut and other activities that will be explained, close to Mincha and not in the morning, because they only decreed close to Mincha, which is common and most people are involved in it, whereas in the morning, it is uncommon, so they did not decree about it. There is a Mincha Gedolah and a Mincha Ketana, which will be explained in the next section, where it will also be clarified which is the primary one.

The afternoon prayer (Mincha) is like the morning prayer (Shacharit), where the congregation and the prayer leader (Shaliach Tzibur) pray silently, and then the prayer leader repeats the prayer aloud. The congregation responds with 'Amen' and Kedusha, and this is the primary ordinance as stated in Siman 124. However, our master the Beit Yosef wrote: if the time is pressing, they should pray silently, and afterward the prayer leader should say 'Magen' and 'Mechaye,' respond with Kedusha, and conclude with 'HaEl HaKadosh,' if there is not enough time in the day to complete the eighteen blessings. And why do they not all pray equally, the congregation silently and the prayer leader aloud? Because the mitzvah of prayer is to pray silently, and the prayer leader does not fulfill the obligation if he only prays aloud (Beit Yosef). And although above in Siman 124 it is ruled that a prayer leader who enters the synagogue and finds that the congregation has already prayed should immediately begin praying aloud and fulfills the obligation this way, this is because it is not possible otherwise due to the inconvenience to the congregation. But whenever it is possible to pray silently, it is preferable (this is the intention of the Magen Avraham in subparagraph 1).

However, our master the Rema indeed wrote this, and this is his language: "And there are those who say that the prayer leader prays with the congregation out loud, and this is the custom." End of quote. It seems that his intention is as follows: The congregation prays silently, and the prayer leader prays out loud. When they reach 'Mechayei Hameitim' (the blessing of the resurrection of the dead), they say the Kedusha. The prayer leader says 'Nakdish' or 'Nakdishach,' and the congregation does not say this because they are in the midst of the prayer. Rather, they respond 'Kadosh,' 'Baruch,' and 'Yimloch.' 

But if so, why should the prayer leader pray out loud after 'HaEl HaKadosh'? After all, the congregation cannot respond 'Amen' because they are in the midst of the prayer. We must say that his intention is indeed as follows: The prayer leader prays out loud until after the Kedusha, and afterwards, even the prayer leader prays silently. This is also implied from his words earlier in Siman 124, see there. His words here are somewhat unclear, as he writes there in section 7, see there.

However, on a public fast day, it is impossible to do this, for the prayer leader must say 'Aneinu' as a separate blessing between 'Goel' and 'Rofeh,' and the congregation says it without a blessing in 'Shomea Tefillah.' Consequently, he must also now pray the entire Shemoneh Esrei out loud and say 'Aneinu' between 'Goel' and 'Rofeh,' while the congregation prays silently and says it in 'Shomea Tefillah,' because there is no other way. Even though, according to this, they will not be praying in unison with the prayer leader (and this is the intention of the Magen Avraham in section 2).

Even though according to the approach of our teacher, the Rema, there would be no recitation of 'Amen' at all in this prayer, and this is the reasoning of our teacher, the Beit Yosef, who, according to his method, the congregation would respond with three Amens, nevertheless, we are not concerned with this. For the obligation of 'Amen' is only when the prayer leader repeats the prayer aloud after having first prayed silently, and then without 'Amen' it would be a blessing in vain, as is written in Siman 124. But according to the approach of our teacher, the Rema, the prayer leader prays only once, and there is no obligation to respond with 'Amen' as is evident. All this is according to the words of our Rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch.

However, our custom is different, and it is the superior way: If time is pressing, the prayer leader (Shaliach Tzibbur) stands and recites the Half Kaddish after 'Ashrei', and then recites the first three blessings aloud while the congregation remains silent and responds with the three 'Amens' and the Kedusha. After the prayer leader completes 'Ha-El HaKadosh', the congregation stands and prays silently, and the prayer leader also prays silently from 'Ata Chonen'. In this manner, we benefit because, in any case, the congregation responds 'Amen' and the prayer leader recites most of the prayer silently. We have already written about this in Siman 124 (and this was also written by the Ma'avit). However, the Ari (Rabbi Isaac Luria) was very strict and instructed that the congregation should pray as usual with the prayer leader silently, and afterwards, the prayer leader should pray aloud as in all prayers, even if it is after sunset. This is our constant practice.

Indeed, this applies in the synagogue and the study hall where there are many people and it is assured that there will be ten to answer "Amen." But when praying at home and there is a limited quorum, or even slightly more, and some people converse during the repetition of the prayer leader and do not pay attention to answer "Amen," then it is better to perform the Kedusha as mentioned, for if the prayer leader repeats the prayer there, certainly not everyone will answer "Amen," and all the blessings will be in vain, and it will be a mitzvah that comes through a transgression. Therefore, it is better to do as mentioned, and this is the common custom and should not be changed, except in a place where it is ensured that everyone will answer "Amen," for then, certainly, it is better for the prayer leader’s repetition to be done properly and as originally instituted.

The Sages taught in a Mishnah in the first chapter of Shabbat (9:2): "A person should not sit before a barber close to the time of Mincha until he has prayed, nor should a person enter a bathhouse, nor a tannery, nor to eat, nor to judge. And if they have started, they do not need to stop." The Gemara establishes that this 'close to the time of Mincha' refers to Mincha Gedolah, which is half an hour after midday, and 'close to it' means half an hour before, which is from midday. The Talmud questions why it is forbidden since there is still much time left. It answers that it is not referring to a regular haircut, a regular bathhouse, a regular tannery, a regular meal, or the conclusion of a case. Rather, it refers to a haircut like that of the High Priest, where each hair is meticulously cut next to the base of the other hair, which takes many hours. A bathhouse not just to sweat briefly, but to stay for a long time to rinse, bathe, sweat, and wash thoroughly. A tannery not just for a brief inspection but a large tannery at the beginning of the process, inspecting all the leather preparations. Eating refers to a large meal like a wedding feast or a circumcision meal, which takes many hours. And judging refers to the beginning of a case, and who knows how many hours it will last. Therefore, we are concerned that the time for Mincha might pass and they will not pray at all. Hence, they forbade starting these activities.

And afterwards, there is an establishment in the Gemara, that it always refers to a simple haircut, a bath only to sweat, a tannery only to inspect, and a simple meal of any homeowner in his home, and for judgment when the judgment is concluded. Nevertheless, the Sages prohibited these even close to the time of Mincha Gedola due to a decree: concerning a haircut, lest the scissors break in the middle of the haircut and he needs to obtain another pair of scissors; concerning a bath, we worry lest he faint due to the heat; concerning a tannery, lest he sees a loss in the hides and he is preoccupied with this all day; concerning a meal, even a small meal, lest he end up being drawn into eating meat and drinking wine and it will last several hours; and concerning judgment, even when the judgment is concluded, we decree lest the judges find a reason to overturn what they initially intended to rule and start anew, which will take many hours.

And if you ask why the Talmud expends effort on this, let us establish our Mishnah as referring to near the time of the Mincha Ketanah (the smaller afternoon prayer). The answer to this is because the Talmud first states that if it were near the time of the Mincha Ketanah, then why does it teach: "And if they began, they do not interrupt"? For didn't Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi say that once the time for the Mincha Ketanah prayer arrives, it is forbidden for a person to taste anything before praying Mincha? All the more so, they must interrupt, for it is obvious that tasting is less severe than interrupting, and even so, it is forbidden, and certainly, they must interrupt. And even though in Berachot (28b) the Talmud rejects Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi’s opinion and rules that it is permitted to taste, nevertheless, it holds that while in terms of tasting we do not follow his view, in terms of interrupting, certainly, one must interrupt (see Tosafot s.v. 'in haircut' at the end, there).

The Rif and the Rambam in Chapter 6 of Tefillah ruled completely stringently, in accordance with the second answer, that even a small meal is forbidden close to mincha gedolah (the larger mincha time), and all activities such as haircutting, tannery work, bathing, and concluding a judgment are forbidden. Similarly, our teacher the Beit Yosef ruled in Section 2 according to his usual practice of ruling like the Rif and the Rambam when their words align. According to this opinion, we would be unable to function in our generation and in previous generations, as most of our eating is after midday. It is clear that all of Israel did not accept upon themselves the stringency of this opinion, and it is almost impossible to uphold it. It will be explained further that even according to this opinion, there is some leniency.

However, our Rabbis, the Tosafists, Rabbeinu Tam, and the R”i, as well as the Rosh, ruled according to the first explanation, that it is specifically a large meal, or the haircut of the High Priest, etc., a bathhouse or large tannery, or the beginning of a court case that are forbidden close to Mincha Gedolah. But a small meal, such as any individual with his household, even on Shabbat and Yom Tov, is permitted close to Mincha Gedolah. Similarly, all other activities are permitted in such a manner. However, close to Mincha Ketana, which is from the beginning of the fourth hour, meaning Mincha Ketana is nine and a half hours, which is half an hour into the fourth hour after midday—it is forbidden to start any meal. And even in this, we have not fulfilled our obligation, as many eat in the summer even after this time. 

There is another opinion by the Baal HaMaor, agreed upon by the Rashba and several other Rishonim, that even a large meal and similar activities are permitted close to Mincha Gedolah. The reason is that since the Talmud did not specify Mincha Ketana due to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, and since we do not rule according to him, it is dismissed, and we establish it close to Mincha Ketana. But close to Mincha Gedolah, everything is permitted. However, close to Mincha Ketana, even a small meal is forbidden.

There is yet another opinion, brought by the Rosh and the Tur in the name of the R”i, that a small meal is permitted lechatchilah (from the outset) close to Mincha Ketana, and similarly for all other activities in such a manner. The reasoning behind this opinion is that they hold that our Mishnah discusses a large meal and close to Mincha Gedolah, as per the Tosafist view we have written, but does not discuss a small meal at all. And since we do not rule according to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, it is permitted to start a small meal even close to Mincha Ketana (Drisha).

The commentators (Bach and Magen Avraham, section 15) wrote that even according to this opinion, it is only permissible to begin a meal close to the Mincha time, but once the time for Mincha Ketana has arrived, it is forbidden to start. According to this, even following this view, we do not fulfill our obligation, for it is known that in the summer, many important people eat after the fourth and fifth hour, and no one protests. All these opinions were brought briefly by our master, the Rema. However, there is another opinion in the Mordechai that the prohibition only applies to a large meal and close to Mincha Ketana, but a large meal before close to Mincha Ketana and a small meal even after the time of Mincha Ketana is permitted from the outset, as cited in the name of the Mordechai (Magen Avraham there). I did not find this in the Mordechai; on the contrary, he wrote the opposite. Here is the language of the Mordechai: "But a small meal is not forbidden to begin until Mincha Ketana arrives, which is at the end of nine and a half hours." Hence, clearly, once the time for Mincha Ketana has arrived, it is forbidden to begin. If so, how do we act, and this requires scrutiny. Similarly, there are many things we do in the summer after the time of Mincha Ketana, such as bathing, haircuts, and beginning a court case, and it is common practice in all courts to begin cases even well after the time of Mincha Ketana.

And our master, the Rema, wrote regarding the words of our master the Beit Yosef, who ruled according to the Rif and the Rambam that even a small meal is forbidden and even close to Mincha Gedola (the earlier Mincha time), he wrote as follows: "And there are those who disagree and hold that a small meal is permitted, and it is only forbidden in the case of a wedding feast or a circumcision feast. And some say that even a large meal close to Mincha Gedola is permitted, and some say that a small meal is permitted even close to Mincha Ketana (the later Mincha time). And the custom is to be lenient according to two opinions, that is, a large meal close to Mincha Gedola, and a small meal close to Mincha Ketana. And it is possible that the reason is because nowadays they call people to the synagogue, we do not worry that one might become negligent and not pray. Nonetheless, for a large meal, one should be stringent even close to Mincha Gedola, etc." End of quote. 

And it needs to be understood, that if the reason for leniency is the calling to the synagogue, then why did he only permit it close to Mincha Ketana, for even after Mincha Ketana this leniency should apply. It must be said that indeed this is his true intention, but because in the aforementioned opinions only those who are lenient close to Mincha Ketana were mentioned, but once the time of Mincha Ketana has arrived, there is no opinion that is lenient as mentioned. And on this he wrote that the custom follows the lenient opinions, and he provided the reason for the leniency because they call to the synagogue. But in truth, according to this leniency, it is also permitted afterward, as is customary in the world.

However, in truth, this leniency does not apply nowadays in most places, as we do not read from the Torah in the synagogue at Mincha time. It appears, in my humble opinion, that people rely on the Jerusalem Talmud, which comments on this Mishnah: "We learned near Mincha, Rabbi Chiya taught: near darkness… Rabbi Chananya said: Our Mishnah refers to the common people, what Rabbi Chiya taught refers to scholars. The sages of Caesarea say: Our Mishnah follows Rabbi Yehuda (who says the time for Mincha extends until the middle of the afternoon), what Rabbi Chiya taught follows the Rabbis (who say the time for Mincha extends until evening)." According to this explanation, our custom is not difficult at all, because we follow the Rabbis who say that the time for Mincha extends until evening, and therefore, it is permitted to eat until near darkness, as well as to engage in all activities such as bathing, shaving, leatherwork, and judgment.

Furthermore, our Talmud does not contradict this, as it can be said that the Talmud's discussion follows Rabbi Yehuda's opinion. Why should we create a dispute between the Babylonian Talmud and the Jerusalem Talmud? Also, according to the previous explanation that our Mishnah refers to the common people and Rabbi Chiya's teaching refers to scholars, meaning Torah scholars, it also fits well, as it is known that we do not consider ourselves to be common people, as explained in many places. (Only according to this, I do not understand the relevance to common people sitting in judgment, unless it refers to the litigants or the courts in Syria, as mentioned at the beginning of the chapter "This one selects," see there.) Moreover, the first explanation in the Jerusalem Talmud, which refers to "near Mincha" and means "near darkness," and the rule that a tailor should not go out near darkness also refers to near Mincha. This is certainly not according to the method of our Talmud, and examine this carefully.

Some have proposed another leniency regarding our practice of eating after the time of Mincha Ketana. As explained earlier in Siman 89 concerning studying before the morning prayer, if one prays individually, it is forbidden to study, lest one become engrossed and miss the time for prayer. However, one who regularly prays in the synagogue is permitted [to study beforehand]. The same applies here: the prohibition on all matters applies to one who prays Mincha individually. But one who prays with a minyan, since the minyan gathers at a fixed time, will not forget to pray (see Magen Avraham, subsection 8, in the name of the Mahari Weil). This is certainly a strong rationale. Therefore, one who does not pray Mincha with the community is certainly obligated to pray Mincha before eating when the time is close to Mincha Ketana, and even more so after this time. But one who prays with the community can rely on the leniencies we have written.

There is a doubt regarding the law of sleeping during the time of Mincha Ketana (the later afternoon prayer). Seemingly, since it is stated in the beginning of Berachot (4b): "A person should not come from the field in the evening and say... I will sleep a bit," and this is referring to the half hour before the time of prayer as written in Siman 235, and all the more so when the actual time of Mincha arrives. Alternatively, one could say that there, at night, which is a time for sleep, we are concerned that he might continue sleeping all night long as people typically do, but during the day it is not customary to sleep for long, and it is also possible to wake him from his sleep. And although in such a case it is stated in Sukkah (26a): "Your guarantor requires a guarantor," this is regarding tefillin, where even a short time is considered significant due to the concern of passing gas, but regarding Mincha, where there is still much time, it could be said that it is permitted, except close to the end of the time for Mincha. And the common custom is also to permit this, and certainly it is proper for one who wants to sleep after the time of Mincha Ketana to pray Mincha beforehand.

And our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 3: "The prohibition against eating a small meal pertains when one establishes it as a meal, but to taste, meaning the eating of fruits, is permissible. The same applies to eating bread up to the size of an egg in the manner that a person eats without establishing a meal - it is permissible." These are his words. And behold, he wrote this according to the view of the Rif and the Rosh, and the same applies to all opinions even for Mincha Ketana, as we do not hold like Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi that even tasting is forbidden once the time for the Mincha prayer arrives, and until one prays, tasting is permitted. And behold, he permitted bread up to the size of an egg, implying even bread that requires washing hands, the blessing of Hamotzi, and the Grace after Meals. This is astonishing, for who can ensure that one will not eat more? And if his intention was bread that does not require washing hands and Hamotzi but rather the blessing of Mezonot, he should not have used the term 'bread'. Indeed, the Tur only wrote about fruits. We must say that our teacher, the Beit Yosef, holds that a small meal is only considered as such with preparation, but without preparation, it is considered casual eating and is permissible even with washing hands, Hamotzi, and Grace after Meals. More than the size of an egg is considered a fixed meal (Magen Avraham, section 17), and similarly, drinking more than the size of an egg is forbidden, lest one become intoxicated (ibid.), specifically with intoxicating beverages like wine and strong drink, but not beer and the like. Similarly, fruits are permissible even in large quantities, and similarly pastries, which are blessed with 'Mezonot', are permissible even more than the size of an egg, for all these are considered casual eating.

The Mishna teaches: "If they have started, they do not interrupt." Our sages agreed that even if they started in a prohibited manner, such as according to the Rif and Rambam, if they started shortly after Mincha Gedolah, or according to Tosafot and the Rosh, shortly after Mincha Ketana, nevertheless, they do not interrupt but rather complete the meal, haircut, bath, tannery work, or legal case. This is specifically when there will still be time to pray afterwards. However, if there will not be time remaining, even if they started in a permitted manner, they must interrupt. And even if there is still much of the day left, if one knows that their meal will extend until night, they must interrupt (Siman 231:11).

However, the Rosh and the Tur wrote that if one starts a meal close to Mincha Ketana, they must interrupt, for the rule of "if they started, they do not interrupt" applies only to a large meal close to Mincha Gedola, but for a small meal close to Mincha Ketana, one must interrupt. However, from the language of the Tosafot in Berakhot (28b, s.v. 'since') it is explained that there is no need to interrupt (Ba"ch), and this is also the opinion of several poskim (see Taz, section 3). It is clear that in a place where there is a concern of drunkenness, one certainly needs to interrupt. Therefore, for large meals where it is common to become drunk, one must interrupt and pray Mincha (there, section 2). This is what our teacher the Rema wrote at the end of section 2: "However, for a large meal, it is proper to be stringent even close to Mincha Gedola, and even if one started earlier, when it reaches Mincha Ketana and the time is passing, one must rise and pray" (end of quote). Certainly, his intention is not that the time for Mincha should pass entirely, because if so, the term 'to be stringent' would not apply since it is a fundamental law. Rather, his intention is that this could occur due to excessive drinking, as is common in large meals. Therefore, even if there is still much of the day left, one must interrupt (Magen Avraham, section 16, and Taz, section 4). Therefore, when there is a wedding on Shabbat and they do not eat until after midday, they should pray Mincha first and then eat, since a wedding is certainly a large meal and it is forbidden to start it close to Mincha Gedola. Even those who permit it in other cases agree that after midday, when it reaches the time of Mincha Gedola, it is certainly forbidden to eat until one prays. This also applies to a meal for a Brit Milah and similar occasions (there).

And since if they have begun, they do not interrupt, it is necessary to know what constitutes a beginning. And so the sages said there: "From when is the beginning of a haircut? From when the barber places the cloth on his knees. And the beginning of the bathhouse? From when he removes his upper garment. And the beginning of the tannery? From when he ties the garment between his shoulders in the manner of tanners. And the beginning of judgment: If they were previously engaged in a case, the beginning is from when the litigants begin to argue. And if they were not engaged in a case, the beginning is from when the judges wrap themselves. For us, since we do not have wrapping, it is from when they sit with the intent to judge. And the beginning of eating is from when he washes his hands. And one who customarily loosens his belt during eating, it is from when he loosens his belt, even before washing (Magen Avraham section 12), as it is explained in Shabbat there, see there. And even though this is not an exertion at all, nevertheless, they do not interrupt. And know that in the Jerusalem Talmud it is said regarding this 'and if they began, they do not interrupt,' that if one interrupts, he is called a fool. For anyone who is exempt from something and does it, is called a fool. This is not similar to other stringencies, because since it is explicitly taught: 'they do not interrupt,' he has no right to be stringent. Nevertheless, it appears to me that this is only if he began permissibly, but if he began prohibitedly, he is allowed to interrupt since he began in a prohibited manner. And see what I wrote in Choshen Mishpat, section 5."

Regarding the end time for the Mincha prayer, it is stated at the beginning of Chapter 4: "The Mincha prayer [may be recited] until evening; Rabbi Yehuda says: until the middle of the Mincha period," which is an hour and a quarter before nightfall. The time for Mincha Ketana is at nine and a half hours, which is two and a half hours before nightfall, and half of it is one and a quarter hours. According to the Rabbis who say Mincha [can be recited] until evening, the time for Maariv begins in the evening and not before. According to Rabbi Yehuda, the time for Maariv begins from the middle of the Mincha period, which is an hour and a quarter before nightfall. It is clear that when the time for the Mincha prayer ends, the time for the Maariv prayer begins. This is agreed upon by our Rabbis, the Tosafot, the Rosh, the Rashba, and all the halachic authorities.

And the halacha is decided in the Gemara (Berachot 27a) that there is no fixed law in this matter, and one can do as they wish: either like the Rabbis or like Rabbi Yehuda. Our Rabbis agreed that the interpretation is as follows: it does not mean that one should sometimes act like the Rabbis and sometimes like Rabbi Yehuda, but rather that he has the discretion to always follow either the Rabbis or Rabbi Yehuda. If he wishes to follow the Rabbis, he should always pray Mincha until the evening and not pray Maariv before nightfall; and if he wishes to follow Rabbi Yehuda and prays Maariv after Plag Hamincha, he should be careful not to pray Mincha after Plag Hamincha.

And behold, in ancient times they followed the opinion of Rabbi Yehuda and prayed the evening prayer before nightfall, as all of this is explained in the Tosafot, Rosh, Rashba, and the students of Rabbeinu Yona at the beginning of Berachot. Nowadays, in most countries, they pray the Mincha prayer until evening, and consequently, they do not pray the evening prayer before nightfall. However, if one did pray the evening prayer with the intention of fulfilling it from the time of Plag HaMincha and onward, he has fulfilled his obligation and we do not require him to pray again (Talmidei Rabbeinu Yona). Similarly, on Shabbat, one may ideally pray the evening prayer of Shabbat from Plag HaMincha and onward due to the addition of Shabbat, for once he has accepted Shabbat, it is considered as if it is actually night (Pnei Yehoshua at the beginning of Berachot, in the discussion of 'therefore' and in Chapter 4, page 27, in the discussion of 'and now', see there for details).

However, it is necessary to examine the words of the Rambam in chapter 3, law 4, where he wrote: "You have learned that the time for the 'Mincha Gedolah' (the greater afternoon prayer) is from six and a half hours until nine and a half hours, and the time for the 'Mincha Ketana' (the lesser afternoon prayer) is from nine and a half hours until there remains one and a quarter hours of the day, and one may pray it until the sun sets." These are his words. Rabbeinu Beit Yosef explained in his work Kesef Mishneh that this means: if one wishes, he may pray until one and a quarter hours before the night as per Rabbi Yehuda, and if he wishes, he may pray until sunset as per the Rabbis. But it is impossible to say this, for if so, a crucial element is missing from the text, and moreover, he later wrote: "The time for the evening prayer begins at the start of the night, etc.," and according to this explanation, when following Rabbi Yehuda, its time would be one and a quarter hours before the night.

It appears to me that according to the Rambam, he had a different approach to this matter, and the Mincha prayer is not dependent on the Ma'ariv prayer, meaning that when the time for Mincha ends, the time for Ma'ariv begins. In truth, there are puzzling statements in the Gemara about this, as it says there (Berachot 27a): "Now that it was not stated as a definitive ruling neither like this one nor like that one, one who acts like this one has acted correctly, and one who acts like that one has acted correctly." And this is puzzling, for since it was not stated as a definitive ruling neither like this one nor like that one, we revert to the general rule: "An individual and the many, the law follows the many," as is the case throughout the Torah, and there is nothing comparable to this in the entire Talmud. Furthermore, earlier (Berachot 26b) it brings a Baraita about this dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis, and this is what it says there: "And why did they say the Mincha prayer is until the evening? Because the afternoon Tamid offering was brought and continued until the evening. Rabbi Yehuda says: until the midpoint of the Mincha period, because the afternoon Tamid offering was brought and continued until the midpoint of the Mincha period." This is astonishing, for could they have argued about when the offering was made in the Temple? Moreover, the term "because" implies a clear matter, and these are two contradictory things.

However, according to my humble opinion, this is the matter: The Mincha prayer corresponds to the afternoon Tamid (daily offering). Since every day it was sacrificed at nine and a half hours, as stated in the beginning of the chapter "Tamid is slaughtered," and as the Rambam wrote there before, it is well known that its offering did not extend until the night, as they needed to offer the incense, the meal offering, the wine libation, and the song. At most, its offering did not extend more than half of this time, which is an hour and a quarter. Therefore, Rabbi Yehuda rightfully says: "For it is sacrificed until the middle of the Mincha," meaning this was its usual time of offering. The Rabbis rightfully say: "For it is sacrificed until the evening," meaning if it happens that it was not offered at nine and a half hours, it is still permissible to offer it until the evening. Accordingly, the Talmud rightfully says: "Now that it has not been stated as law, etc.," meaning that in this case, it is not appropriate to say "the law follows the majority," for certainly the Rabbis also agree with Rabbi Yehuda that the main time is until the middle of the Mincha, since this was the practice every day. However, they disagree because Rabbi Yehuda holds that one should not pray after the middle of the Mincha, as most days the offering was not delayed past this time. But the Rabbis hold that ideally, it is better to pray until the middle of the Mincha, but if one did not pray, he can still pray until the evening (and this is explicitly found in Rambam, Chapter 3, Halacha 7, and there is no need for the strained interpretation of the Kesef Mishneh there, and consider this carefully).

According to this, it turns out that in reality, we follow the ruling of the Rabbis, but it is not possible to state this explicitly. For if we did, it would imply that one may initially delay until the evening, and this is not so. Therefore, it is said: "One who acts in accordance with the opinion of this authority has acted [correctly], etc.," meaning that one should rule in accordance with both views: initially, one should strive to pray until "Plag HaMincha" (1.25 proportional hours before sunset), but if this was not done, one may pray until the evening. This is exactly the view of the Rambam who wrote: "The time for the 'Mincha Ketana' prayer is from nine and a half hours until there remains an hour and a quarter," meaning that one should ideally strive to pray then. Afterward, he says: "And one may pray until sunset," meaning that if one did not pray earlier, one may pray afterward, according to the Rabbis. Thus, according to this, the matter does not concern the evening prayer at all. And we who pray close to sunset are also not following this view, which is the more clarified opinion. However, what can we do, as it is difficult to gather a quorum before "Plag HaMincha"? And whoever can do so, or prays individually, it is a mitzvah and an obligation to pray before "Plag HaMincha."

In addition to this, we must cry out against the custom in our country to delay the Mincha prayer until actual sunset. For in the Gemara (Berakhot 29b), it is stated explicitly that in the West (i.e., Eretz Yisrael), they curse one who prays Mincha with the setting of the sun. And that which is stated in the Jerusalem Talmud at the beginning of the fourth chapter that Rabbi Yochanan would pray with the setting of the sun, refers to the Shacharit (morning) prayer, as it concludes there: "So that the fear of Heaven shall be upon him all day" (and there is a significant difficulty in the Hagahot Maimoniyot there; see there and scrutinize). However, a defense for this practice is that our preoccupation with our livelihood is very great, may God have mercy, and therefore we delay.
