Nevertheless, one who fears the word of God should strive to pray earlier, especially according to the Rambam's view that we have explained, that the primary time for Mincha ideally is before Plag HaMincha, as we have written.

Another puzzling matter exists in this issue: The Rambam wrote that the end time [for the afternoon prayer] is until sunset. Why then did our master, the Beit Yosef, write in section 1 that the main time is from nine and a half hours until nightfall? But nightfall is when the stars come out, which is much later than sunset. And indeed, the words of the Rambam are explicit in Zevachim (56a) that the blood of the daily offering becomes invalid at sunset. Since the prayer corresponds to the daily offering, it follows that one should not pray after sunset.

Furthermore, the Tur also wrote "until nightfall," but the language of the Gemara and the poskim is "until evening." The term "evening" includes everything, as is understood. Perhaps the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch hold that since twilight is a doubtful period, whether it is day or night, they were lenient regarding a rabbinic prayer. And as for the matter discussed in Zevachim, one could say that the time for prayer corresponds to the burning of the offering, which could occur afterward. Or they interpret the end of sunset to mean the time when the stars come out (see Tosafot Menachot 20a, s.v. "invalid"). Nevertheless, it is still puzzling that they did not cite the words of the Rambam. Therefore, one should certainly be concerned with his opinion and take care not to pray Mincha after sunset.

And this is the language of our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch: "And we conclude that one should act according to one of the opinions consistently... This means he should always follow one of them. If he follows the Rabbis and prays Mincha until nightfall, he cannot then pray Ma'ariv from Plag [HaMincha]. And if he follows Rabbi Yehuda and prays Ma'ariv from Plag [HaMincha], he must be careful not to pray Mincha at that time. And now that the custom is to pray Mincha until nightfall, one should not pray Ma'ariv before sunset. However, if he prayed Ma'ariv from Plag [HaMincha] after the fact, he has fulfilled his obligation, and in a pressing situation, he may pray Ma'ariv from Plag [HaMincha] and onwards. For us, who have the custom to pray Ma'ariv from Plag [HaMincha], one should not pray Mincha afterward. If, after the fact or in a pressing situation, he prays Mincha until nightfall, which means the appearance of the stars, he has fulfilled his obligation." End of quote. And these matters have already been clarified. However, it appears that if on one day he prays both Mincha and Ma'ariv in Plag [HaMincha], he has not fulfilled his obligation, as this would be contradictory on the same day. However, some follow this practice because it is difficult to gather the congregation again (Magen Avraham, section 7), and it will be explained in siman 235. It is possible to say the reason is that the Ma'ariv prayer corresponds to the burning of the limbs and fats, which are valid both by day and by night, and this will be explained with Heaven's help.

There is a "great Mincha" and a "small Mincha," as explained by the Rambam there, and this is his wording: "Since the daily offering was sacrificed every day at nine and a half hours, they established its time at nine and a half, and it is called the small Mincha. And since on the eve of Passover that fell on the eve of Shabbat they would slaughter the daily offering at six and a half hours, they said that one who prays after six and a half hours fulfills his obligation. And once this time arrives, the obligatory time has arrived, and this is called the great Mincha." End of quote. And it is clear from his words that the main time is the small Mincha because most of the year the daily offering was sacrificed at this time, and if one prayed the great Mincha, he has fulfilled his obligation. When he says that once this time arrives the obligatory time has arrived, he does not mean that it is obligatory to pray, but rather that it is forbidden to engage in eating, haircuts, bathing, leatherwork, and judgment until one has prayed, as this is his opinion as written in the previous section.

According to this, one may even initially pray Mincha Gedola (the early afternoon prayer) when necessary, such as when wanting to eat or similar needs. This isn't like the usual distinction between l'chatchila (ideally) and b'diavad (after the fact) where l'chatchila is prohibited. Here, it is not so. Rather, it means that if one has no specific reason to prefer Mincha Gedola, it is better to pray Mincha Ketana (the later afternoon prayer). But if there is any slight reason, one may initially pray Mincha Gedola. Therefore, our custom during the days of Selichot, when some fast until midday, is to pray Mincha Gedola. Additionally, from the words of the Rosh and the Tur, it seems that the primary preference is for Mincha Gedola (Beit Yosef). I have seen in the writings of one of the early authorities who specifically advised praying Mincha Gedola (Rabbi Shimon Farhon in the root "Menach" or "Palel" wrote: Therefore, poverty is prevalent in the land of Edom because they do not pray Mincha Gedola. And especially among us, where they pray close to sunset and are not careful to pray before "Plag HaMincha" (one and a quarter hours before sunset), which is when the continual offering was always sacrificed, as written. Rather, they follow the time when it is permissible to sacrifice the offering. If so, it is obvious that one can pray Mincha Gedola, as understood. And delve into this).

And behold, the time for the "Mincha Gedola" (the early afternoon prayer) begins six and a half hours [after sunrise]. And even though the time truly begins immediately after six hours, for at that time the "bein ha'arbayim" (afternoon period) begins and the sun starts to incline to the west, as it is clearly explained in the Mishnah which states: "The morning prayer can be recited until midday... the afternoon prayer can be recited until evening," and we are compelled to interpret this as from midday until evening. Otherwise, it should have stated "the afternoon prayer from six and a half hours until evening." However, this is indeed the case, and at the beginning of the third chapter of Yoma, the Gemara explains this matter, that because it is difficult to determine the exact middle of the day, they extended it by half an hour. Therefore, even the "Tamid" (daily offering) was not sacrificed before six and a half hours, even in pressing circumstances. 

And proof for this is that they said in Pesachim (94a): "Half of the sixth hour and half of the seventh hour, the sun stands at the height of every person." And seemingly, it is not understood, for at half of the sixth hour the sun is still in the east, and at half of the seventh hour it is in the west. Rather, because at that time, it moves so slowly that there is almost no noticeable difference between half of the sixth hour and half of the seventh hour except for someone who is very precise about this, and to the naked eye, there is almost no difference. Therefore, it says there that at half of the sixth hour and half of the seventh hour, the sun stands at the height of every person, meaning to the naked eye. Therefore, in the Gemara and the Poskim, the time for the "Mincha" prayer is from half of the seventh hour.

And there are those who say that if one prayed before half of the seventh hour, he has not fulfilled his obligation (Magen Avraham sect. 1), and it is difficult to say this, because since this is only due to a concern for error and the prayer is Rabbinic, why should he not fulfill his obligation. And one of the great ones wrote simply that he has fulfilled his obligation (Pri Chadash in this section), and he brought several proofs for this, see there. And from the Mishnah about the morning prayer, there is a clear proof as I have written.

And our master, the Rema, wrote: These hours are calculated according to the context of the day, and even if the day is long, we measure it as twelve hours, and these are called "seasonal hours." And similarly, wherever the Sages calculated in hours, we measure with these hours. End of quote. Meaning, since the day is always twelve hours, if so, in the winter when the day is short and you divide it into twelve hours, necessarily the hours are short, and conversely, in the summer when the day is long, the hours are long. Therefore, for the time of Mincha Ketana, which is nine and a half hours, it will be in the winter before the accustomed three and a half hours, and in the summer it will be after the accustomed three and a half hours. The accustomed hours are only during the months of Nissan and Tishrei when the days and nights are almost equal. And know that midday is always equal in both summer and winter; when the clock strikes twelve, it is midday, and similarly at night. For the hours that are added or shortened are divided half before midday and half after midday, and therefore, midday is always the same. The calculation of the twelve hours begins from sunrise until sunset (Levush and Magen Avraham, section 3).

Our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, wrote in section 2: "If one has water, he must wash his hands before praying, even though he does not know of any dirt on them, and he does not make a blessing. Even if he interrupts his learning, he washes his hands before praying, and if he does not have water available, he does not need to wash." End quote. And it has already been explained in Siman 192 that for every prayer one needs to wash hands, and if there is no water, one should clean with earth, pebbles, or other materials. The measure of not having water available has been explained there: if in front of him up to four mil and behind him one mil, see there, and here they did not explain anything. It is possible that for Mincha they were lenient in all respects when there is no water available before him, and this is also implied by their language when they wrote: "And if he does not have water available, etc.", and in the Tur he brought a dispute on this, see there. Similarly, if he stood up from eating, he needs to wash his hands, but one who washes his hands for prayer, even though he learned before the prayer, does not need to wash his hands afterward. Similarly, one who comes to the synagogue to pray and washes his hands, even though he stayed a long time in the synagogue, since he did not leave the synagogue, he does not need to wash again (Eliyah Rabbah, and see Magen Avraham section 8).

Since the Mincha prayer has nothing preceding it, it is not proper etiquette to come and pray immediately, as our Sages have said: "A person should always organize the praise of the Omnipresent and then pray." Therefore, they instituted the recitation of 'Ashrei' before the prayer. However, one who comes to the synagogue and the congregation is already praying should begin praying immediately in order to pray with the congregation. After 'Ashrei', the prayer leader recites the half-Kaddish, and even though there is no Kaddish without a preceding recitation, here there is something preceding it, which is the recitation of 'Ashrei'. Therefore, one must ensure that 'Ashrei' is recited with a quorum of ten, since for the recitation of Kaddish, ten are required to have said something, as explained in Siman 55. After the prayer, they recite Tachanun, the full Kaddish, Aleinu, and the Mourner's Kaddish.

There are those who have the custom to recite the passage of the Tamid and the Ketoret before "Ashrei," and it is a beautiful and proper custom, as they offered the afternoon Tamid and Ketoret just as in the morning. Why should we not fulfill "the offering of our lips" (Hosea 14:3)? Therefore, those who are meticulous have the custom to recite them every day before Mincha. Specifically, this should be done before the prayer, but after the prayer, one should not recite the passage of the Tamid and the Ketoret, nor should they recite "Ashrei" after the prayer, and they warned about this very much. And know that if a situation arises where one delays until close to sunset, they should stand in prayer immediately and not recite "Ashrei" nor the passage of the Tamid and the Ketoret, for we do not push off the main for the secondary. It is necessary to warn simple people about this, for to them, everything is the same. See section 7.

And Rambam wrote in Chapter 3, Law 3: "Many people have the custom to pray the large and small [Mincha], and some of the Geonim have ruled that it is not proper to pray a voluntary prayer except the large one, and this is indeed the correct ruling, because it corresponds to something that does not occur every day. And if one prayed the large one as an obligatory prayer, he should only pray the small one as a voluntary prayer." End quote. And one should not be surprised how a voluntary prayer can precede an obligatory one, for even in the case of a compensatory prayer which is obligatory, it should not be prayed before the obligatory one, as written in Siman 108, all the more so a voluntary prayer should not precede an obligatory one. It can be said that here, since the main obligation is during the time of Mincha Ketana, it is considered as if the time for the obligatory prayer has not yet arrived.

However, the Tur brings from his father, the Rosh, who responded that one should distance oneself from a voluntary prayer, because we require that a person recognizes in himself that he is diligent and capable of concentrating properly from beginning to end without any distraction. But if he is not in this category, we say about him: "Why do I need your numerous sacrifices? says the Lord," and so ruled our master the Beit Yosef in this section and in section 107. And indeed, we have never heard of this in our times, and it would be fortunate if we could maintain the obligatory prayer. Therefore, in our times, it is forbidden to pray a voluntary prayer, and this is how it should be instructed.

However, the Rosh responded, and this is his language: "But Rav Alfas ruled that a person can pray a voluntary prayer, and since you follow his practice, it is reasonable that once six and a half hours have arrived, which is the time for Mincha, the first is obligatory and the second is voluntary." End of quote. This is contrary to the words of the Rambam who ruled that the first prayer should be voluntary. And our master, the Beit Yosef, in his great book at the beginning of Siman 233, inferred from this that the Rosh holds that the initial time for Mincha is from six and a half hours, see there. In my humble opinion, there is no proof from this, only that the Rosh holds that since it is, in any case, now a time for prayer, one should not advance a voluntary prayer before an obligatory one, as stated in section 3. Also, what he inferred from the Tur who wrote there: "And its time is from six and a half hours, etc.," that he holds the primary time is Mincha Gedola, is also not a proof, for the Tur wrote the basic law. However, from the fact that the Tur did not write like the Rambam that initially one should pray Mincha Ketana, we understand that he holds they are equal. And we have already explained in the previous Siman that there are some of the early authorities who make Mincha Gedola primary.

If one forgot to pray the Mincha (afternoon) prayer, he should pray the Ma'ariv (evening) prayer twice. The first is for the obligation and the second is as compensation. If he reversed the order, he has not fulfilled his obligation, as stated in Siman 108. One should say 'Ashrei' before the second prayer. The detailed laws of compensation are explained in Siman 108, see there.

And we have already written that one should say "Ashrei," and someone who recites the passage of the Tamid offering and the incense should say "Ashrei" afterward. There are those who wish to say that the passage of the Tamid should be recited after "Ashrei" (Taz, subsection 2, and Magen Avraham), but this is not the custom, and in my humble opinion, the primary practice is as follows. Their reasoning is that "Ashrei" is considered a prayer, and in the Temple, they would pray the afternoon prayer before offering the Tamid. However, in truth, "Ashrei" is not a prayer but rather a praise of the Blessed One. Nevertheless, I assert that for this reason, many do not recite the passage of the Tamid during the afternoon prayer, because in the Temple the prayer preceded the offering, and therefore they did not want to recite it before the Shemoneh Esrei prayer. And we have already written that ten people are required to say "Ashrei" so that they can recite Kaddish (Magen Avraham, subsection 1, and see Taz who writes otherwise, but the main opinion follows Magen Avraham. What Magen Avraham wrote in the name of Maharil is perplexing, and Eliyah Rabbah has already challenged this, and this is the custom, that even if the prayer extends into the night, they still say Kaddish).

It is known that in ancient times, they would pray the evening service while it was still very much daylight. Now, according to the Rambam, its time is from the onset of night. According to Rabbeinu Tam, Rabbeinu Yitzchak, all the Tosafists, the Rosh, and other early authorities, its time is from "Pelag HaMincha" (an hour and a quarter before sunset) for those who follow Rabbi Yehuda, who does not pray the afternoon service after Pelag HaMincha. However, those who pray Mincha until nightfall should not advance the evening service before nightfall. All this we explained in Siman 233. Many great ones have exerted themselves to determine from where this custom of advancing the evening service while still daytime came, and all the early authorities justified it by saying it was due to the public hardship of gathering at night, though it is understood that this is not a sufficient justification, and it is necessary to find merit for Israel. I say that this matter is clarified in the Mishnah, the Gemara, and the Jerusalem Talmud, and from the basic law, this is indeed so, as we will explain with the help of Heaven.

It was taught at the beginning of the fourth chapter: "The morning prayer [may be recited] until noon, the afternoon prayer until the evening, and the evening prayer has no fixed time." And the Gemara asks (Berakhot 27a): "What is meant by 'has no fixed time'? If it means that one may pray throughout the entire night, then let it state: 'The evening prayer [may be recited] all night.' Rather, what does 'has no fixed time' mean? It follows the opinion that the evening prayer is optional." This is difficult to understand, for if so, why not simply say 'the evening prayer is optional'? Furthermore, if that were the case, why did it not specify the time as it specified the times for the morning and afternoon prayers? And even if it is optional, one would still need to know the time frame for this optional prayer. Additionally, how can it be said that 'has no fixed time' does not mean that its time is all night, when it is explicitly taught there (Berakhot 26a): "And why did they say the evening prayer has no fixed time? Because the limbs and fats that were not consumed during the day may be offered all night." This clearly indicates that 'has no fixed time' refers to the entire night.

However, the truth is that the explanation is as follows: Certainly, the expression "it has no fixed time" means that it has no set time, that is to say, since it corresponds to the burning of the limbs, and it is known that the burning began during the day after the burning of the fats, but it was also valid all night. Therefore, the prayer also begins during the day and continues all night. However, the Gemara states that since it is not explicitly taught this way, we learn from it that the evening prayer is optional. But the main explanation is as stated. According to this, even according to the Rabbis, who hold that the Mincha prayer is until evening, one is still permitted to pray the evening prayer from the time of the burning of the limbs, which is approximately from the time of "Plag HaMincha" and onward. This is all the more so on Shabbat, where the main prayer should be during the day, since the limbs of the daily offering of the evening of Shabbat eve are forbidden to be offered at night on Shabbat, as we say in Shabbat (24b): "Nor a weekday burnt offering on Shabbat.”

And even according to the opinion that the prayers were instituted by the Patriarchs, it is also proven [that the evening prayer starts before nightfall], as it is stated there that Jacob instituted the evening prayer. And Tosafot asked, in Chullin (91b) it is explicit that Jacob prayed while it was still day. And they answered that according to Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that the time for the Mincha prayer extends until the midpoint of the afternoon, it works out well, because the time for the evening prayer begins from the midpoint of the afternoon. And yet, it is still difficult according to the Rabbis. However, according to our explanation, it works out well, for even according to the Rabbis, the time for the evening prayer begins while it is still day. (And with this, the words of the Rambam in Chapter 3, Law 7 are understood, and even though he attributes it to the fact that it is optional, nevertheless, the main reason is as I have written, and examine this well).

And thus it is evident in the Jerusalem Talmud (beginning of chapter 4) where it says: "Rabbi instructed Abdan to announce to the congregation: Whoever prays should pray from the evening until the day rises, and so Rabbi Chiya would announce" (see there). At first glance, this appears to be only according to Rabbi Yehuda, and if so, how can our Talmud state that the law was not established neither according to the Rabbis nor according to Rabbi Yehuda, when in practice both Rabbi and Rabbi Chiya ruled according to Rabbi Yehuda? Rather, it is certain that the evening prayer is not related to the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis, and even according to the Rabbis it is permissible to pray while it is still day. (And this requires further study according to what we say: "Since Rav would pray the Shabbat prayer on the eve of Shabbat, we conclude that he holds like Rabbi Yehuda." And the Talmud rejects this: "On the contrary, since Rav Huna and the Rabbis would not pray until it was evening, we conclude that the law is like the Rabbis" (see there). According to our explanation, even according to the Rabbis, this is the case for the evening prayer. And we must say that indeed it could be refuted in this manner, and it could also be refuted by the reason of the addition to Shabbat, as it is mentioned in the Jerusalem Talmud there that regarding Shabbat it is obvious (see there). Rather, it rejects this because from this there is no proof at all. We are compelled to say this, for otherwise what does "on the contrary" mean, let us say indeed that there is a dispute in this matter. Rather, certainly this is its explanation: from the evening prayers there is no proof at all, just as we cannot infer from Rav Huna that the law is according to the Rabbis, for according to Rabbi Yehuda, one may not pray at night; similarly, we should not infer from Rav that the law is according to Rabbi Yehuda, since even according to the Rabbis one can do so. According to this, on the contrary, it would be a proof for our words. And the Talmud rejects: from the evening prayer there is no proof for the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis, and examine this thoroughly).

And behold, all of this concerns the matter of prayer. However, regarding the recitation of the Shema in the evening, all our early and later sages ruled that its time is at night when three medium stars appear, as stated in the plain Mishnah at the beginning of Berachot, where it is taught: "From when do we recite the Shema in the evenings? From the time the priests enter to eat their Terumah," and it is taught in the Baraita that this is the time of the appearance of the stars. Therefore, although the time of prayer is earlier, nevertheless, since the time of the recitation of the Shema is at night and it is necessary to juxtapose redemption (the blessing following the Shema) to prayer, one must pray at night. And already all our sages at the beginning of Berachot have investigated this regarding their custom to recite the Shema and pray before nightfall.

The viewpoint of Rabbeinu Tam is that just as for prayer, from "plag hamincha" (one and a quarter hours before nightfall) is considered the time for prayer according to Rabbi Yehuda, so too it is considered the time for the recitation of Shema. The Rosh challenged this, questioning what relevance prayer has to the recitation of Shema, as for the recitation of Shema we require "when you lie down," which is the time of lying down, as explained there. It is possible to say that indeed, this is considered the time of lying down, for just as it is considered night for prayer, so too for the recitation of Shema (Bach). And even though the Mordechai wrote that the Ra'avyah agreed with this, nevertheless, this opinion was not accepted by most of our rabbis, as explained in the Tur there. In truth, regarding the recitation of Shema, which is a Torah obligation, it is impossible to be lenient as with prayer, which is rabbinic. In the Jerusalem Talmud, it is stated that even if one recited the Shema during twilight, one must recite it again at night. The reason is simple: twilight is a doubtful time, and the recitation of Shema is a Torah obligation, and a doubtful Torah obligation requires stringency (as also written by the Sha'agat Aryeh, Siman 3).

Therefore, it is written in the name of Rav Hai Gaon that if the congregation advances the time to recite the Shema and to pray while it is still day, one should pray with them, for prayer with the congregation is a very significant matter. One should also recite the Shema with its blessings and pray with them, and then at night, he should recite the Shema again, all three sections without the blessings. And if one is concerned about reciting the blessings of the Shema during the day, we do not worry about it, for the Rashba has already written in the name of the Geonim that the blessings of the Shema are not intrinsically connected to the Shema and are considered a separate matter; they were merely juxtaposed to the Shema. Therefore, when one later recites the Shema without the blessings, it is acceptable. And if one is concerned about saying in the blessings "Who rolls light before darkness" and "Who removes the day and brings the night" and similarly "Lay us down" and it is still day, we do not worry about it, for since one can pray the evening prayer, one can also say these blessings. Only the Shema itself needs to be recited again at night, and this is the proper and praiseworthy way. This is also our practice when welcoming Shabbat, that we pray while it is still day, after the time of the afternoon prayer, and when we come home, we wait until night and recite all three sections of the Shema, then we sanctify the wine and eat. This is our obligation and it is fitting for us.

And this is also the opinion of our Rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, in section 1, where they wrote: "The time for reciting the Shema at night is from when three small stars become visible. If it is a cloudy day, one should wait until the doubt is removed from his heart. If he recited it earlier, he should repeat it without the blessings. If the congregation recites the Shema early, before nightfall, he should recite the Shema and its blessings with them and pray with them. When the proper time arrives, he should recite the Shema again without the blessings. However, he should not pray again at night, even if the congregation prays much earlier than nightfall, unless he is accustomed to other forms of piety and devotion, in which case it does not appear as arrogance for him to pray again." This is the end of the quote. Even if they prayed two or three hours before nightfall, as was their custom, as explained in Terumat HaDeshen (Siman 1). However, in our times, we have not heard of this custom, and only on Shabbat do we pray a little earlier before sunset. In such a case, it is certainly forbidden to pray again, for after Plag HaMincha it is considered a complete prayer by law, as we have explained, even according to the Rabbis. But one should not rely on the Shema recited before going to bed (Magen Avraham, section 3). And know that even though the evening prayer is technically optional, the Rif has already written that we have accepted it upon ourselves as an obligation. Therefore, the decisors did not mention this at all, and there is no difference between it and the morning and afternoon prayers. (See Taz, section 2, who extended at length his disapproval of the Shulchan Aruch's approach, but I do not understand why, as their approach is correct. And what the Shulchan Aruch wrote about "small stars" is not precise, but rather to exclude large stars. See Magen Avraham and Taz, section 1. And what Magen Avraham wrote in section 3, that someone who is accustomed to praying at night and mistakenly began the blessings of the Shema with the congregation before nightfall, should complete the blessings with the congregation and at night recite the Shema without the blessings and pray, and not connect redemption to prayer, is certainly correct. But why should one act this way, as Rav Hai Gaon has already warned to pray with the congregation before nightfall, and so wrote the Shulchan Aruch. How can one act against their words? Consider this well).

Rashi of blessed memory explained at the beginning of Berachot that those who pray and recite the Shema while it is still daytime do not intend to fulfill their obligation with this recitation of the Shema, but rather they fulfill it with the first paragraph that they recite on their bed, as he explained there. Therefore, those who follow Rashi's opinion need to recite the Shema on their bed with the intention to fulfill their obligation of the Shema. One should not ask, how can they eat before the recitation of the Shema, since it will be explained later that it is forbidden. It can be said that since they have already prayed and recited, even though they have not yet fulfilled their obligation, they did not consider it a concern. And even though they only recite the first paragraph, it can be said that from a Torah perspective, this suffices. Certainly, it is better to recite all three paragraphs or at least also the paragraph of "Vehaya Im Shamoa". As for the fact that they recite without the blessings, we have already written that the recitation of the Shema is not dependent on the blessings, and the great authorities have already elaborated on this. However, the most straightforward way is as we mentioned earlier.

Just as it is forbidden to eat close to Mincha, as mentioned in Siman 232, so too, half an hour before Ma'ariv it is forbidden to eat until one has recited the Shema and prayed. And in fact, this is more stringent than Mincha, because with Mincha, even if one started eating inappropriately, one does not have to stop, as mentioned there, but with Ma'ariv, one must stop. There is a similar reason in the Gemara (Shabbat 10a), because in the evening, drunkenness is more common. Additionally, since in the evening there is time all night, one is not afraid that the time will pass, and meanwhile, the entire night might pass, which is not the case with Mincha, as mentioned there. The primary reason is because the recitation of the Shema is a Biblical obligation, whereas prayer is Rabbinic.

And this is the language of our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, Section 2: "It is forbidden to begin eating half an hour before the time for reciting the Evening Shema. If one began eating after its time has arrived, he must interrupt and recite the Shema without its blessings, finish his meal, and afterward recite it with its blessings and pray. However, he is not required to interrupt for prayer, since he started eating. But if he has not begun eating, even if he washed his hands, he must interrupt. If there is not enough time to pray, he must interrupt even for prayer." End of quote. The explanation of their words: If one began permissibly, that is, before the half-hour close to the evening, he does not need to interrupt even for the Shema because there is still sufficient time to pray. But if indeed there is not enough time left, that is, if he is eating before dawn, he must interrupt even for prayer, even if he began permissibly, as stated in Section 232. But if he began eating forbiddenly, he interrupts for the Shema but not for prayer, as in Section 232 regarding Mincha. There is only this difference: there, beginning is considered even if he washed his hands, as stated there, but here it is not considered a beginning, because drunkenness is common at night and the entire night is its time, as stated in the previous section. Since beginning to eat is not considered a significant start for prayer, only for Shema, which is from the Torah. But regarding washing hands, which is a minor beginning, they were stringent even for prayer in the evening for the explained reasons. And it seems to me that this is when he has not yet recited the blessing 'Al Netilat Yadayim', but if he has recited it, he must eat so that there will not be an interruption between washing and the blessing of 'Hamotzi'. There are those whose words imply that even in such a case, he must interrupt (see Magen Avraham, Subsection 6), and this seems strange to me (as written by the Taz). There are those who wrote that even if he blessed 'Hamotzi', he must interrupt, as this is not considered a complete beginning (Eliyah Rabbah in the name of the Pesakim of Tosafot), but I have not found any of the early authorities who say this. And know that when we say there is enough time to pray, we mean until the light of day, but anything that continues after midnight, we do not consider, even though it is ideal to pray before midnight as will be explained. Nonetheless, regarding interruption, we need the actual end time." (So it seems in my humble opinion).

There are those who say that the half-hour is not precise, but rather a little before the time, as the Tur wrote that once its time has arrived, it is forbidden, etc. (Taz at the end of section 3). Similarly, Tosafot wrote (Berachot 4a, s.v. "ukorei"): "From here it implies that from the time the evening Shema's time arrives, one should not eat a meal until he recites the Shema and prays the evening service." This is also implied by the language of the Rambam in Chapter 6 and by the language of the Rosh (Siman 9) there. Only the Rashba and the Tur's Rishonim inferred from the language of the Gemara that even a little before the time is forbidden there. Therefore, it is enough to be stringent a little before and not exactly half an hour. And our masters, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, who wrote half an hour, likened this to the proximity to Mincha in Siman 232, which is half an hour before, see there. Therefore, one who wishes to be lenient and begins eating half an hour before has upon whom to rely.

The commentators of the Shulchan Aruch wrote that only a fixed meal like a formal meal is forbidden, but tasting a small amount is permitted (Magen Avraham section 4, Taz section 3, and Eliyah Rabbah section 6). This is also evident from the wording of the Tosafot that we brought, which states: "One should not have a formal meal, etc.," and similarly, the Tur wrote: "When the time for reciting the Shema arrives, it is forbidden to establish a formal meal until one prays," end quote. It is clearly explained that only a formal meal is forbidden. And even though the language of the Baraita (4:) is: "A person should not come from the field in the evening and say, 'I will eat a little, drink a little, and sleep a little, and afterward I will recite the Shema and pray,' but rather, etc.," and the term 'a little' implies a small amount, and furthermore, we are forced to say that the intention is not that only all three together — eating, drinking, and sleeping — are forbidden, but rather it means 'either or,' (as the Taz wrote there), if so, the interpretation is: eat a little or drink a little, and drinking is not considered a fixed activity, yet it is still forbidden. Therefore, eating a small amount is also forbidden.

However, in truth, this is not precise, for it is based on the words of people. That is to say, because one wishes first to eat and sleep a little, and then to recite the Shema and pray, he says to himself that there is no concern that he might not pray at all. To this, it says: "Behold, I will eat and drink a little, and sleep a little," and it does not state "either or," for he says all of them together. He says that there is no concern that he might sleep the entire night, for he will eat a little, drink a little, sleep a little, and then rise immediately. But the sages were concerned that he might eat and drink a lot and then sleep a lot. And the mention of drinking is because, with most meals, one also drinks. This is also evident from the language of the Rambam in Chapter 6, Halacha 7, where he wrote: "Even though the evening prayer is optional, a person should not come from his work and say: I will eat a little and sleep a little, etc., but rather he should pray the evening prayer and then eat and drink or sleep." This proves that he omitted drinking first completely. And then he also wrote: "He eats and drinks or sleeps," because drinking follows eating. He carefully said: "I will eat a little and sleep a little," meaning that by eating a little, he will not sleep a lot. This is also evident from the Baraita itself, which concludes: "And he recites the Shema and prays, and eats his bread and blesses." This implies that it refers to a fixed meal, as this is the term 'bread.' And this is the main ruling. (There is someone who wished to be stringent even regarding a taste, but this is not the main opinion.) Even if the time for the evening prayer has arrived, and even afterward, it is permitted to have a taste, meaning not in a fixed meal. This is the custom of the world, and there is no need to doubt this at all, for this is the main ruling.

And know that the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch only mention the prohibition of eating, but the Rashba wrote that all these activities are prohibited close to Mincha time, which include haircutting, bathing, leatherworking, and judgment, and this is also evident from the language of the Levush. However, from the language of the Rambam, the Tur, and the Shulchan Aruch, it is clear that only eating is prohibited because it leads to sleep, but other activities do not lead to sleep, and the night is long, so there is no concern that the night will pass without praying. This was also written by one of the greats (Eliyah Rabbah, section 6). Furthermore, if all these activities were also prohibited at night, why does it state in Shabbat (9b) only close to Mincha, and it should have said close to Mincha and Arvit. Therefore, it is certain that at night only eating is prohibited, and that is why it does not mention Arvit in the Mishnah. This is also evident from the language of the Rambam there, for after he wrote that one eats after the Arvit prayer, he wrote: "And it is permitted to get a haircut and enter the bathhouse close to Shacharit, for they only decreed close to Mincha, etc." See there. And why did they associate it with Arvit? Rather, this is the explanation: in these laws, Arvit is equivalent to Shacharit, for in eating both are prohibited, in Shacharit because it is forbidden to eat before the Shacharit prayer, and in Arvit the sages decreed as mentioned. But all these other activities are permitted in both, because they only decreed this close to Mincha, and the reason is explained because most people engage in these activities during the day. (And there is a need to examine what the Magen Avraham, section 9, wrote: "And it is forbidden to do all the activities mentioned in section 232," and he cited the Beit Yosef and the Rashba there, and the Beit Yosef brought it for a different matter there, and since he did not bring it in the Shulchan Aruch, it is understood that he did not hold this, as the Eliyah Rabbah wrote).

The Tur wrote: "Regarding the end time, it is taught: The Sages say until midnight, and Rabban Gamliel says until dawn, and the law follows Rabban Gamliel, as Shmuel said: the law follows Rabban Gamliel (8:), and even ideally one can wait to recite until dawn." End of quote. And so wrote the Rosh there, that only eating and drinking are forbidden once the time arrives, and similarly the Rashba wrote in his commentary that it is permissible ideally to study and perform work before the recitation of the Shema and the evening prayer until an hour before dawn, except for eating and all those labors that are forbidden close to Mincha, but other than these, all labors are permitted ideally until before dawn. And we have already written that all the poskim (legal decisors) disagree with him regarding what he forbids in all those that are forbidden close to Mincha, and only eating is forbidden as we wrote in the previous section.

However, this is not the opinion of the Rambam and the Sefer Mitzvot Gadol (SmaG), as the Rambam wrote in the first chapter of the laws of Kriyat Shema: "Its mitzvah is from the time of the emergence of the stars until midnight. But if one delayed and recited it before dawn, he has fulfilled his obligation, because the sages only said until midnight to distance a person from negligence." End quote. And this is the language of the SmaG: "From when do we read... from the emergence of the stars until midnight according to the words of the sages. But if one delayed and recited it before dawn, he has fulfilled his obligation, for the law follows Rabban Gamliel who holds this. The sages only said until midnight to distance a person from transgression." End quote. (For the reason of their disagreement, see Beit Yosef and Bach). I am puzzled by our master, the Beit Yosef, who wrote in paragraph 3: "Initially, one should read the Kriyat Shema immediately after the emergence of the stars, and its time is until midnight. But if one delayed and recited it before dawn, he has fulfilled his obligation." End quote. Behold, in ruling like the Rambam and the SmaG and not mentioning at all the opinion of the Rashba, the Rosh, and the Tur, this seems primary to him according to his great understanding. But in what he wrote that initially, one should read the Kriyat Shema immediately after the emergence of the stars, where do we get to rule against the Rashba, the Rosh, and the Tur, for in the Rambam and SmaG this is not explained. And even though the students of Rabbeinu Yonah wrote this at the beginning of Berachot and brought proof from the prohibition of eating even a little before its time, nevertheless, it is a singular opinion against the Rashba, the Rosh, and the Tur, and also his proof is not so simple. Therefore, the words of our master, the Beit Yosef, require investigation (and this explains why many are not meticulous about this).

One who recites the evening Shema after dawn has broken has not fulfilled his obligation, unless he was in a situation beyond his control, such as being sick or drunk. This is specifically if he began drinking before the time for reciting the Shema arrived, but if he started afterwards, he is considered negligent and cannot recite it (Taz, subparagraph 4). There are those who are uncertain about this (Eliyah Rabbah). Certainly, if he began drinking after the time for reciting the Shema arrived, but did not intend to become drunk and it happened unintentionally, he is also considered to be in a situation beyond his control (Magen Avraham, Siman 99, subparagraph 3). 

One who recites the Shema after dawn should not say the blessing ‘Hashkiveinu,’ as it is not a time for lying down then. However, ‘HaMa’ariv Aravim,’ ‘Ahavat Olam,’ and ‘Emet VeEmunah’ up until ‘Ga’al Yisrael’ should be recited, and certainly the Amidah prayer should be recited.

The sages taught in the Mishnah (11a): "In the morning, one recites two blessings before [the Shema] and one after it; and in the evening, two before it and two after it." This is because in the evening, the blessing of 'Hashkiveinu' is added, which has no relevance in the morning. Altogether, these are seven blessings. And it is stated in the Jerusalem Talmud there, in reference to the verse "Seven times a day do I praise You" (Psalms 119:164), that the verse is not clear on where these seven praises are each day; rather, it refers to these blessings of the Shema. And this is its explanation: "Seven times a day do I praise You for Your righteous judgments," as the recitation of the Shema is the righteous judgment, containing the yoke of the Kingdom of Heaven and the yoke of the commandments. And although we have already written in the name of the Geonim that these blessings were not instituted specifically for the Shema, nevertheless, the sages connected them to the Shema before and after it, and this was the primary enactment. Furthermore, it is stated there: that whoever fulfills "Seven times a day do I praise You" is as if they fulfill "You shall meditate on it day and night" (Joshua 1:8). And it appears to me that the reason is because it is written earlier: "I love Your Torah" and later it also states "Great peace have those who love Your Torah" (Psalms 119:165). This is also evidence that it refers to the blessings of the Shema, which include the love of the Torah in 'Ahavah Rabbah' of the morning and 'Ahavat Olam' of the evening.

The first blessing is 'Who at His word brings on the evenings,' and it opens and closes with "Blessed," for it is a long blessing. And it says in it: 'He rolls away light before darkness and darkness before light,' and behold, 'light before darkness' pertains to the night, but 'darkness before light' pertains to the day. And our Sages said (Berakhot 11a): in order to mention the attribute of day at night just as we include the attribute of night during the day, as we say: 'Who forms light and creates darkness' to show that one God created and fashioned them. And why the expression 'rolls away'? Because on the globe there is no moment without day and no moment without night, since the earth is round as known, and this is the meaning of 'rolls away,' as if the sun rolls around the globe, and in one place light dispels darkness and in another place darkness dispels light, and thus it is a continuous matter without interruption. Therefore, we first say: 'and arranges the stars in their watches in the firmament according to His will.' And one must pause between 'according to His will' and 'creates day and night' (Magen Avraham), because 'according to His will' refers to the former, meaning the Holy One, blessed be He, arranged the position of the stars in the firmament, each star in its watch, so that day and night will always come upon the globe, and light is rolled away before darkness and darkness before light as we have explained, and all this is because so arose in His blessed will. Therefore, we conclude: 'the Lord of Hosts is His name,' meaning that He, blessed be He, established His hosts in this manner, and all is from Him, blessed be He, and the stars are in His hand, blessed be He, like a hatchet in the hand of the hewer, having no power of their own, as it is written: "and the host of heaven worships You."

The Ashkenazim add before the conclusion: 'El chai v'kayam tamid yimloch aleinu l'olam va'ed' (The living and eternal God will always reign over us forever), and this is not similar to the conclusion. The Rosh justified the custom, saying that this too is similar to the conclusion, for when it is fulfilled in us: "The Lord will reign forever," then in the evening there will be light. And since in the evening prayer we say: 'Emet v'emunah' (Truth and faith), and it is said about this: 'And Your faith at nights,' referring to the exile which is compared to night, and we believe that He will redeem us as explained in Emet v'emunah: 'The God who exacts vengeance... and Who gives recompense...', therefore we say that we hope and anticipate that the living and eternal God will soon reveal His kingdom over us and bring light to us, contrary to the Babylonians (see Bach). And there is also the attribute of day and the attribute of night, light and darkness, and we pray that He will bring light to us.

The second blessing is 'Ahavat Olam'. Even in places where they say 'Ahava Rabba' in the morning, nevertheless in the evening they say 'Ahavat Olam', as established by the Geonim (Tosafot 11a and Rosh there). And we say: 'And Your love do not remove, etc.', and some say 'will not be removed', but the first version is primary. This blessing does not begin with 'Baruch', as it is considered a blessing adjacent to its companion, and so too the blessings after the Shema, as in the morning, where the recitation of the Shema is not considered an interruption (Tur). And in 'Emet V'Emunah' we conclude 'Who redeemed Israel' and not 'Who redeems Israel' as in the prayer, for here it refers to the past (ibid). And we have already explained in Siman 66 that those who conclude the evening prayer with: 'King, Rock of Israel and its Redeemer', the sages do not approve of them. And even though some justify the custom, nonetheless, why should we enter into a problematic breach. And now, in most places, they have instituted to conclude 'Who redeemed Israel' in the evening service of Yom Tov.

The second blessing after the recitation of the Shema is "Hashkiveinu," and it concludes with "Who guards His people Israel forever," because the night requires protection from harmful forces. And even though we hold by Rabbi Yochanan, who said that the evening prayer also requires the juxtaposition of redemption (the blessing "Ga'al Yisrael") to the prayer (Amidah), as Rabbi Yochanan said (Berachot 4b): "Who is destined for the world to come? He who juxtaposes the redemption of the evening prayer to the evening prayer." If so, how can we interrupt between "Ga'al Yisrael" and the prayer with the blessing "Hashkiveinu"? However, since the Sages instituted the recitation of this blessing, it is considered as an extended form of redemption (Berachot 4b), similar to how they instituted the recitation of the verse "O Lord, open my lips" (Psalms 51:17) before the prayer. Additionally, "Hashkiveinu" is related to redemption because when God passed over to smite the Egyptians, the Israelites were terrified and prayed to the Holy One, blessed be He, that the destroyer should not enter their homes to smite them. Corresponding to that prayer, they instituted the recitation of "Hashkiveinu," so it is also related to redemption. Before the conclusion, we say: "Guard our going out..." so that the content near the conclusion resembles the conclusion. The Sephardim end with: "For You are God who guards and saves us," which is better, because "Guard" is a prayer, but "Who guards His people Israel" is a promise. Similarly, "For You are God who guards us" is also a promise.

Regarding the eighteen verses "Blessed is the Lord forever, Amen and Amen," etc., and the blessing "May our eyes see" that we add, I have seen different reasons given by our Rabbis of blessed memory. The Tosafot (4b) wrote: "And we, who say 'May our eyes see' and other verses after 'Lay us down,' it seems, since the Rabbis instituted them, it is considered like an extended redemption, for they instituted to say this so that in the meantime, one's fellow may also pray and not leave the synagogue until everyone has finished their prayer. And also, in those verses, there are eighteen mentions [of God's name], corresponding to the eighteen blessings of the Amidah, and while they instituted to say those verses, they also instituted to say the conclusion of 'May our eyes see.'" End of quote.

And the Rosh wrote another reason, and this is his language: "This custom was practiced by the masses because in earlier days their synagogues were in the fields, and they were afraid to stay there until after the evening prayer. So, they established the recitation of these verses, which contain eighteen mentions [of God's name], corresponding to... and they later established the blessing 'Yir'u Eineinu' and Kaddish. And even now that we pray the evening prayer in the synagogue, the original custom has not been nullified." End of quote. And the Tur Yoreh Deah wrote in the name of Rabbi Yitzchak, and this is their language: "At first, when the evening prayer was optional, they would say these verses... and conclude with them and say Kaddish and leave. And afterwards, even though it was established as obligatory, the practice remained as it was originally, and it is not considered an interruption between redemption and prayer, because from the beginning they instituted it with this in mind, so it is not called an interruption." End of quote.

It appears to me that they all intended the same thing, which is that if the evening prayer (Maariv) were not optional, or if there were no fear of lingering in the synagogue in the fields, they would not have come to this [practice]. But since it is optional, and there was the fear factor, they began to be lenient with the prayer, finding it difficult to not pray at all. Therefore, they recited these eighteen verses and "Veyare'u Einenu," and some would pray the Amidah. This is what Tosafot wrote: “Meanwhile, his fellow would also pray, etc.,” meaning that by the time these people finished reciting the verses, the others would have completed their prayer. The Rosh wrote that the primary reason for the enactment was due to fear, and the Tur wrote it was because it was optional, and both reasons are needed. However, in any case, once this enactment spread, it became a fixed practice, akin to a prolonged redemption. These verses contain many themes of redemption, as does "Veyare'u Einenu" and the blessing "The King in His Glory," etc., all relating to redemption. Likewise, the Kaddish primarily concerns future redemption, when His name will be magnified and sanctified, especially according to those who say, "May His salvation sprout and His Messiah come near," which is the essence of redemption. Therefore, even the Sephardim, who do not recite these verses, still say Kaddish, because Kaddish is the essence of redemption. Thus, even though initially the Kaddish was enacted for reciting these verses, as the Rosh and Tur wrote, and it is evident that in the morning service there is no Kaddish after "Ga'al Yisrael," if so, the Sephardim who do not have the custom of reciting these verses should not say Kaddish either. Nevertheless, due to the sanctity of the Kaddish and because it is the essence of redemption, the Kaddish remained even among the Sephardim. (It is surprising that the Rambam, in Chapter 1 of the Laws of Reading the Shema and at the end of Chapter 7 of the Laws of Prayer, mentioned only the two blessings after the Shema, and in the order of prayer mentioned all the verses and "Veyare'u Einenu" there, without mentioning the origin of this enactment, and did not mention the Kaddish at all there.)

Therefore, on Shabbat and festivals, it is not customary to recite these verses, because we do not pray the eighteen blessings, and also the fear was not as great, for Shabbat itself protects Israel. Furthermore, since the prayer time is earlier while it is still day, there was no fear for everyone to remain there. And although the blessing of the Patriarchs was instituted for protection against harmful entities, as mentioned in Siman 268, nevertheless, in this case, they were not concerned, and they also considered the burden on the congregation. However, the Kaddish remains as on weekdays due to the reason we explained, that Kaddish is the essence of redemption. The verses recited on Shabbat: "V'shamru," on festivals: "Vayedaber Moshe," on Rosh Hashanah: "Tiku," and on Yom Kippur: "Ki vayom hazeh," we do not know when they were instituted, and this will be explained with Heaven's help in Siman 266.

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote: "I have seen meticulous individuals who customarily stand when reciting the eighteen verses of 'Blessed is the Lord forever, Amen and Amen,' and it is a fine custom because they were instituted in place of the Amidah prayer. Therefore, it is proper to stand for them as one does in prayer." However, many disagree and hold that it is better to sit, so that it should not be said that one fulfills the obligation of the Amidah prayer with this (Eliyah Rabbah, section 6). This was also the practice of the Maharshal, and the Maharil also wrote to sit until the half-Kaddish. (Similarly, the Magen Avraham, section 2, wrote in the name of the Mateh Moshe, and the Megaleh Amukot wrote that this is based on Kabbalah. The Magen Avraham also wrote that when praying with the congregation, one first prays the Amidah and then recites the Shema and its blessings as will be explained, and in that case, one can recite these verses standing.)

The halacha has been determined that one must also connect redemption to prayer in the evening service, according to Rabbi Yochanan (Berachot 4b), as ruled by the Rif and the Rambam at the end of chapter 7, and also by the Rosh, the Tur, and the Shulchan Aruch. Here are the words of the Rambam: "In the evening prayer, one recites the Shema and blesses before and after it, and connects redemption to prayer and prays, etc." end quote. One should not ask, if so, how did he write in chapter 3, law 7: "One is allowed to pray the evening prayer of Shabbat on Friday before sunset, and similarly to pray the evening prayer of the end of Shabbat on Shabbat, because the evening prayer is optional and one need not be precise about its time, provided that the Shema is recited at its proper time after the appearance of the stars" end quote. If so, one would not connect redemption to prayer. Indeed, the Raavad objected for this reason and wrote that this should only be done in a pressing situation. It can be explained that the Rambam holds that only when the time for the Shema has arrived, there is an obligation to connect redemption to prayer, but not when the time has not yet arrived. This is also written by one of the greats (Shagat Aryeh, Siman 3). Earlier in Siman 111, it was explained whether one must connect redemption to prayer also on Shabbat and Yom Tov, and the main opinion is like that of Rabbeinu Beit Yosef in his great book, that there is no difference, and also on Shabbat and Yom Tov there is an obligation to connect redemption to prayer (and so ruled the Shagat Aryeh, Siman 16).

And since there is also an obligation in the evening prayer to connect the blessing of redemption to the prayer (the Amidah), one must be careful not to speak between the blessing of "Guardian of Israel forever" and the Amidah. Similarly, those who recite the eighteen verses "And let our eyes see" must be careful not to interrupt between the end of the blessing "The King in His glory" and the Amidah. However, the announcement of the prayer leader of "Ya'aleh Veyavo" on Rosh Chodesh, or "Tal Umatar" (prayer for rain), or "Al Hanissim" (prayer for miracles) is not considered an interruption, since it is necessary for the prayer. As for other rules, such as interrupting between sections and in the middle of a section, their laws are the same as in the morning prayer. It seems to me that regarding these eighteen verses, between one verse and another is like between sections, but from "And let our eyes see" until the end of the blessing is considered like the middle of a section.

And our Rabbi the Beit Yosef wrote in section 3: "If one finds a congregation that has recited the Shema and wishes to stand in prayer, he should pray with them and then recite the Shema with its blessings afterward," end quote. For prayer in a congregation is preferable to the juxtaposition of redemption and prayer, even if the congregation is praying while it is still daytime (Magen Avraham, subsection 3). And if he can recite the Shema and its blessings without saying "Blessed is the Lord forever and ever, amen and amen" and "May our eyes behold," he should do so, since these verses are merely a custom (ibid.). And he does not need to recite them afterward, for they were only instituted after the blessings of the Shema and not on their own. 

And if he comes to the synagogue at the time they begin "Barechu" and he has not yet prayed Mincha, he should pray Mincha, and afterward, when the congregation reaches the Amidah, he should pray the evening prayer with them, and then recite the Shema with its blessings. But he should not pray Mincha together with the congregation when the congregation is praying the evening Amidah, for this is not considered prayer in a congregation, as for him it is still day, while for the congregation it is considered night (ibid. and Turei Zahav, subsection 4).

It is further written in paragraph 4: "After 'Who guards His people Israel' one says 'Amen' after one's own blessing, and does not respond Amen after the blessing of the King in His glory," end quote. And he follows his reasoning in Siman 216 that here one responds 'Amen' after one's own blessing just like in the Grace After Meals at 'Who rebuilds Jerusalem,' and therefore he says to respond after 'Who guards' etc. and not after 'May our eyes see,' just like in the Grace After Meals one does not respond after 'Who is good and does good.' But it has already been clarified there that we do not have the custom at all to respond 'Amen' after one's own blessing, except in the Grace After Meals at 'Who rebuilds Jerusalem.' And know that in the blessing of the King in His glory one must say 'May He always reign over us,' that the word 'always' should be connected to the following phrase and not the preceding one. However, there are those who say the opposite, that it connects to the preceding phrase (Pri Shoshana).

The custom is to recite the verse "But He, being merciful, forgives iniquity" before 'Barchu', because in the morning and afternoon there are the daily offerings that atone, but not so in the evening. Therefore, we request "But He, being merciful, forgives iniquity" (Tur). There are additional reasons in the Tur and Kolbo (see Beit Yosef). There is also a reason based on Kabbalah: there are three appointed angels in Gehinnom—Mashchit, Af, and Chemah—who judge the wicked at night since their deeds were done in darkness. Hence, we mention "and does not destroy completely, and frequently withdraws His anger, and does not arouse all His wrath." Therefore, we do not say this on Shabbat, because on Shabbat the wicked have rest in Gehinnom (Eliyah Rabbah in the name of Asarah Ma'amarot). "And does not arouse all His wrath" means He does not arouse any of His wrath, similar to "and the poor has nothing" (Eliyah Rabbah in the name of Rabbeinu David Abudraham). But Rashi of blessed memory explained that He does not arouse all of His wrath, but He does arouse part of it, and so it is in the Yalkut, see there.

There are those who have the custom to also recite "A Song of Ascents, behold, bless the Lord, etc." before 'Barchu' or before 'V'hu Rachum' or afterwards. The reason is that in the Talmud it says: "If one is accustomed to reading, he reads... and afterwards he recites the Shema and prays," and they have adopted this Psalm because it is written in it: "who stand in the house of the Lord at night." Some add the verse: "By day the Lord commands His loving-kindness, and at night His song is with me," which is relevant to the matter, and they also add the verse: "But the salvation of the righteous is from the Lord; He is their stronghold in time of trouble," because night is likened to troubles, therefore we beseech the Blessed One to be our stronghold in times of trouble. And they recite the three verses: "The Lord of hosts, etc.," because in the Jerusalem Talmud, in the chapter Ein Omdin, it says that these verses should never depart from your mouth, see there, and all our trust is in these verses that the Blessed One is with us and our stronghold, and He will answer us on the day we call. And they recite the Half Kaddish, but only when there are ten who have recited these verses, and after the Kaddish, the prayer leader says 'Barchu,' etc.

There is no repetition of the Amidah (the standing prayer) in the evening prayer because it is considered optional. This is also written by the Rambam in Chapter 9, Halacha 9, and this is his wording: "One does not repeat the evening prayer aloud because the evening prayer is not obligatory. Therefore, one should not recite blessings in vain, as there is no person who is obligated in them to fulfill his obligation." End of quote. And even according to the Geonim who said that since one has prayed once, it becomes obligatory, nonetheless, from any perspective, if he is proficient, the prayer leader does not fulfill his obligation, and if he is not proficient, he has never prayed (Beit Yosef in the name of the Rashba). And even according to several of the Rishonim who wrote that we have already accepted it upon ourselves as obligatory, nonetheless, regarding the repetition of the prayer leader, we have not accepted it. However, in truth, there are hidden reasons for why there is no repetition of the prayer leader at night. And we do not recite the Kedusha (sanctification) at night, and only the prayer leader says the full Kaddish, and we say Aleinu and the Mourner’s Kaddish, and then we depart to our homes in peace (and there is no falling on the face (Tachanun) in the evening prayer, and see the Tur, and with us, it is not so as the Tur himself wrote, and delve deeply).

Maimonides wrote at the end of Chapter 3 of the Laws of Torah Study: "Even though it is a mitzvah to study by day and by night, a person learns most of his wisdom at night. Therefore, anyone who wishes to merit the crown of Torah should be careful with all his nights and not waste even one of them on sleep, eating, drinking, talking, or similar activities, but rather engage in Torah study and words of wisdom. And the sages said, the song of Torah is only at night, as it is stated, 'Arise, sing out at night.' And anyone who engages in Torah study at night, a thread of kindness is extended to him during the day, as it is stated: 'By day, the Lord commands His kindness, and at night, His song is with me' (Psalms 42:9), and this song refers to Torah. Any house in which words of Torah are not heard at night, fire consumes it (Sanhedrin 99a), and this is expounded in the Gemara from the verse, see there."

Therefore, one must be more careful in studying at night than during the day, and one who neglects it is severely punished. They said in Eruvin (65a): "The moon was created only for study," and they also said there: "The night was created only for sleep," and Tosafot wrote that this refers to the nights of the summer solstice. There are those who explain that the Talmudic phrase in the first statement, "The moon was created only for study," means that at the beginning of creation, the night was entirely dark, and from the time of the creation of the luminaries, it has light through the moon. For most of the month, the moon does not shine all night, so when it is completely dark at night, it is a time to sleep, and when the moon shines, it is a time for study (Maharsha). 

The great scholars wrote that from the period when we read the Book of Ruth, where it is written: "Lie down until morning," until the Ninth of Av, where it is written in Lamentations: "Arise, cry out in the night"—one should lie down, meaning that the nights are short and there is no need to study at night. From "Arise"—that is, the Ninth of Av—until "Lie down"—that is, Shavuot—one should rise, meaning one should get up and study at night (Magen Avraham and Bach). They wrote that the measure of sleep is eight hours, as it says: "I slept, then I was at rest," and "then" numerically equals eight. Some wrote four hours, as "I slept, then I was at rest" numerically equals "forty" hours. The truth is that it all depends on one's weakness or strength and the number of one's days, and everything should be for the sake of Heaven.

Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote: "If a person has a fixed practice to study a certain amount each day, and he was preoccupied during the day and did not complete it, he should complete it at night immediately." This is because one who says, 'I will study this chapter' has made a great vow to the God of Israel (Nedarim 8a), and one who consistently practices a good deed with the intention of always doing so, it is considered a vow, as is written in Yoreh De'ah, Section 214. Therefore, it is good that anything a person wishes to practice regularly, he should say: 'without making a vow' (Magen Avraham). And regarding what is written: 'he should complete it at night immediately,' the intention is not immediately upon the onset of night, for how would we know to say that? For its source is from Eruvin there: "Rav Acha bar Yaakov would borrow and repay," rather the intention is that he should complete it that night and not leave it for the next day, and so it appears in the Tur there.

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi stated: Even though a person recites the Shema in the synagogue, it is a mitzvah to recite it on their bed, as it says, "Speak in your hearts on your beds." This means to say what is written "upon your heart" on your beds, as it says "when you lie down" (Rashi). If the person is a Torah scholar, they do not need to do this, as their regular study of Mishnah suffices (there). However, even a Torah scholar needs to say one verse of supplication, such as, "Into Your hand I entrust my spirit, etc." This means that while a Torah scholar does not need to recite the Shema, which is akin to studying Torah, since they are accustomed to Torah study, they still need to say a verse that is like a prayer. Anyone who recites the Shema on their bed is as if they are holding a double-edged sword in their hand, as it says, "Let the saints exult in glory, let them sing for joy on their beds," meaning it wards off harmful entities, as it says there: "Anyone who recites the Shema on their bed, harmful entities keep away from them." The idea is that these entities distance themselves so that they do not cause the person to have evil thoughts during their sleep and thereby emit seed wastefully.

It is stated there in the chapter "Haroeh" (Berachot 60b): "One who goes to sleep on his bed recites 'Shema Yisrael' until 'Vehaya im shamoa', and says: 'Blessed is He who casts the bonds of sleep', etc." From this, it is implied that one first recites 'Shema' and then the blessing of 'Hamapil'. However, Maimonides in the beginning of Chapter 7 of Hilchot Tefillah wrote the opposite, and this is his language: "When a person goes to bed to sleep at night, he blesses: Blessed... Who casts the bonds of sleep, etc., and then recites the first paragraph [of Shema]" and then sleeps, the end of his words. The Tur and the Shulchan Aruch wrote like the language of the Gemara, and they wrote that this is the primary way (Magen Avraham, section 2, and Shnei Luchot HaBrit), and the Levush wrote like Maimonides. It is astonishing that Maimonides changed the language of the Gemara, and indeed also in the Rif the version is like in the Gemara, see there. And it seems to me that Maimonides intentionally changed from the language of the Gemara, for a reason that will be explained in section 5.

The Tur and Shulchan Aruch wrote that one should recite: "He who dwells in the covert of the Most High..." This is called the "Song of Afflictions," which protects against harmful forces (Shevuot 15b). One should also recite: "O Lord, how many are my foes..." until "Salvation belongs to the Lord." Additionally, one should say: "Blessed is the Lord by day, blessed is the Lord by night, blessed is the Lord when we lie down, blessed is the Lord when we rise up," and "The Lord said to Satan, 'The Lord rebuke you, Satan...'" and "The Lord is your keeper..." and "From now and forever, into Your hand I entrust my spirit..." and "May the Lord bless you and keep you...and grant you peace." One should also recite "Lay us down..." until near the conclusion.

It is explained in Shevuot there that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi would recite these verses and then sleep, meaning he would fall asleep while reciting these verses. The Talmud queries: Is it not forbidden to use words of Torah for healing? It answers: protection is different. That is to say, if one is ill and seeks to be healed by them, it is forbidden because one should not use Torah for bodily healing, as Maimonides writes in Chapter 11 of Laws of Idolatry, Law 12: “For they are among those who deny the Torah, making words of Torah a physical remedy, while they are only for the healing of souls. But a healthy person who recites verses and a Psalm from Tehillim so that their merit will protect him and save him from troubles and harm—this is permitted.” This is clarified in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 179. The primary purpose of reciting the Shema before bedtime is solely to protect against harmful forces. The Talmud did not question this because the Shema is always recited as an obligation; if it also serves as protection, there is no wonder. However, these verses, which are not an obligatory recitation, were thought to be forbidden, and the Talmud clarifies that this too is permitted (Tosafot, beginning of Berachot). The Rif also brings this in the first chapter there.

One must be puzzled by Maimonides (Rambam) in Chapter 7 of the Laws of Blessings regarding the recitation of the Shema before bed, as he did not mention this at all. It seems to me, in my humble opinion, that Maimonides dismissed the matter from the Talmud Bavli based on the Talmud Yerushalmi in the first chapter of Berachot (Halacha 1), which states: "Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani, when he would go down to the marketplace, would stay with Rabbi Yaakov Grosso, and Rabbi Zeira would hide among the baskets to hear how he would recite the Shema. He would recite and repeat the Shema until he fell asleep. And what is the reason? Rabbi Acha and Rabbi Tachlifa, in the name of Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani, said: 'In your hearts, on your beds, and be still, Selah.' 'Be still' refers to sleep, and this verse is part of the recitation of the Shema as written." And the Yerushalmi says: "The words of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi disagree, for Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi would recite additional Psalms after it." This is the end of the quote, and this is what Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi mentioned in Shavuot about reciting all these verses. Since many of the Amoraim disagree with Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, Maimonides ruled according to them, and according to them, one only needs to recite the Shema and repeat it until falling asleep, as Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani did. This is not against the Talmud Bavli in Shavuot, as the Bavli states that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi did so, but did not rule the Halacha according to him, since in the Yerushalmi many disagree with him, and the Halacha follows the majority.

The reasoning of all these Amoraim is that although it is permissible for protection, it is not considered a commandment, and it suffices with the recitation of Shema, which is often said as an obligation, as we wrote at the end of Section 3. According to this, it also makes sense why the Rambam placed the blessing of 'HaMapil' before Shema, because according to his opinion, one should fall asleep after reciting Shema and not after the verses. Therefore, it is necessary to say Shema after 'HaMapil' so that one reads and re-reads until sleep comes, as Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani did in the Jerusalem Talmud. And even though in the tractate Berakhot the Talmud places Shema before 'HaMapil', the Rambam did not consider this, because in the first chapter it is proven that it is not a hindrance, since Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi innovated in the first chapter that one must recite Shema upon his bed, as stated in Section 1, and according to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, it precedes 'HaMapil', and thus the Talmud arranged it so. But from there itself it is proven that it is not so, for Abaye says there that even a Torah scholar must say one verse of mercy, which is after 'HaMapil', thus proving that 'HaMapil' is not the last. The Rambam wrote in Chapter 7, Law 2, and these are his words: "And he recites the first paragraph of the Shema and sleeps, and even if his wife sleeps with him, he recites the first verse or verses of mercy and then sleeps. And if sleep overtakes him, he recites even the first verse or verses of mercy and then sleeps." End of quote. And it seems that the Rambam holds that even the paragraph of Shema is not a hindrance; therefore, if his wife is with him or sleep overtakes him, it suffices with the first verse of Shema or other verses of mercy, and his source is from what we say in the first chapter that a Torah scholar only needs to say verses of mercy, which implies that 'Shema' is not a hindrance. (And see Magen Avraham, subsection 2, who wrote similarly, but regarding what he wrote that 'Shema' is not for protection, we have already brought from Tosafot Yeshanim that it is for protection, but it is not similar to the verses as explained there. And regarding his question on the Rema who wrote that if one recited Shema and could not sleep, he should recite it several times, etc., this is not according to the Beit Yosef's way. The Magen Avraham assumed that the Rema's intention was on the paragraph of Shema. To me, it seems that it includes reciting Shema as we also recite it, and his intention is both on Shema and on the verses, and the main thing is to fall asleep with words of Torah, and contemplate this well).

Some have written, based on the Midrash, to recite all three sections of the Shema, which contain 248 words, as a safeguard for the 248 limbs (Magen Avraham 1). However, since the Gemara explicitly mentions only the first section, it is not necessary to recite more, and this is the simple custom. Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote that one should recite the Shema near their bed, and one should not eat, drink, or speak after reciting the Shema near their bed, but should sleep immediately, as it is stated: "Say in your hearts upon your beds and be still, Selah." See above in section 63 whether it is permissible to recite it while lying down. If one recited the Shema and cannot fall asleep immediately, they should repeat it several times until they fall asleep, so that their recitation is close to their sleep, and no blessing is recited on the Shema near the bed. This is certainly not to say that after the blessing of 'Hamapil' there should be no interruption until sleep, as is the case with other blessings where interruption is prohibited between washing hands and 'Hamotzi' and similar cases, for after all, verses are recited afterwards, and according to the Rambam, the Shema section. Even though these are for protection, if it were prohibited to interrupt, what benefit would there be that they are for protection? Therefore, it is certain that here the interruption is not forbidden as with other blessings.
