The reason is that sleep is not in a person's control, and this reasoning is written in Sukkah chapter 4 by the Rosh and the Mordechai, which is why no blessing is recited over sleeping in the Sukkah. This blessing is obligatory concerning a person's sleep, and hence it is said that one should try to bring sleep closer with all their ability (see Magen Avraham 3). When one needs to fulfill marital duties, they should recite the Shema afterward, wash their hands, and recite it if they are clean from seminal emission. Regarding the question of whether it is permissible to recite while lying down, this is if one intends to fulfill the obligation of reciting the Shema with this recitation, as per Rashi’s opinion mentioned in section 235. However, if one has already fulfilled the obligation, it is better to recite it lying down (there), and this is the simple custom. When it says "repeat it several times," it means either the Shema, verses, or other words of Torah, and if one contemplates Torah, no more is needed (there). The reason no blessing is recited on the Shema near the bed is simply that the obligation is only in the blessing of 'Hamapil', and it is not appropriate to have a blessing on a blessing. It appears that women are also obligated in the blessing of 'Hamapil', and most of our women are careful about this (see Magen Avraham 2).

If one sleeps naked, he should not remove his shirt while sitting, which would expose his nakedness, but rather he should lie down in his bed and cover himself with a sheet, and then slowly remove the shirt over his head, with the sheet covering him as he removes it. (See Magen Avraham, subsection 7, who is not pleased with the practice of saying the deathbed confession every night, because one should never open his mouth to the Satan. He also mentioned not to sleep alone in a house; some interpret this as not to sleep in a house that stands alone.)

Maimonides wrote at the end of Chapter 4 of De'ot: "Semen is the strength of the body, its life, and the light of the eyes. Whenever it is excessively emitted, the body deteriorates, its strength diminishes, life is lost. This is what Solomon said in his wisdom: 'Do not give your strength to women.' Anyone who is excessively engaged in intercourse, old age jumps upon him, his strength wanes, his eyes become dim, a foul odor emanates from his mouth and armpits, the hair of his head, eyebrows, and eyelashes fall out, the hair of his beard, armpits, and legs increases, his teeth fall out, and many other pains come upon him. The wise physicians said: One out of a thousand dies from other illnesses, and the thousandth from excessive intercourse. Therefore, a person must be cautious in this matter if he wishes to be well. He should only engage in intercourse when he finds his body healthy and very strong, when he becomes aroused without intending to, and distracts himself with something else while the arousal persists, feeling heaviness from his loins downward as if the cords of his testicles are being pulled, and his flesh is warm—this is a sign that he needs to engage in intercourse, and it is therapeutic for him to do so. Additionally, one should not engage in intercourse when sated or hungry, but only after the food in his intestines has digested. He should check his bowels before and after intercourse. One should not engage in intercourse standing, sitting, in a bathhouse, on the day he enters the bathhouse, on the day of bloodletting, or on the day of travel, neither before nor after." End quote. And what is stated in Yevamot (62b) that a woman yearns for her husband when he is about to travel and that he must visit her—this applies when he travels by carriage, not by foot. Regarding our statement 'not on the day of departure or return from a journey,' it refers to when he travels by foot and becomes fatigued, or possibly he should visit her the night before (see Levush and Taz).

A person should consider that this desire was not created by the Holy One, blessed be He, for the sake of desire itself, but for the sake of the continuation of the species. Evidence for this is that when the seed is emitted, the desire ceases until, after a period of time, more seed gathers and the desire intensifies again. According to intellect and nature, a person should view this matter with disdain, as our Sages of blessed memory expounded in Shabbat (152a): "'For He commanded and it was created' – this refers to woman; 'He established it and it stood firm' – this refers to children. It was taught: A woman is a pouch full of excrement, and her mouth is full of blood, yet everyone runs after her." If not for the decree of the King, it would not be proper to desire her, but 'for He commanded and it was created,' for the sake of the continuation of the species, for He did not create it to be desolate but formed it to be inhabited. Therefore, every wise and God-fearing person should contemplate this, walk securely in his way, and not stumble in this world, nor be shamed in this world. It is well known that in this matter lies the source of the sanctity of Israel.

And even when he is with his wife, he must be modest in this matter, as it is written: "And walk modestly with your God" (Micah 6:8), meaning that even when you are only with your God and no one else sees, you should still walk modestly (Levush), and be ashamed before the Lord your God, for before Him, darkness is as light (there). And one should not be overly familiar with his wife, but only according to the times stated in the Torah. For example, those who are idle and have their sustenance readily available and do not pay taxes—their time is every day. Workers who work in another city and sleep at home every night—once a week; and if they work in their own city—twice a week, and in Even HaEzer, Siman 76, there is a dispute regarding this, see there. Carters—once a week, camel drivers who travel far—once every 30 days, and sailors who go to sea—once every six months. The Rambam explains that these "idle" people are healthy and pampered individuals. The times for Torah scholars are from Sabbath to Sabbath, as they are occupied with Torah all week, and about them it is said: "Who gives its fruit in its season" (Psalms 1:3). It is forbidden to sleep in a room where a man and his wife sleep, and even if she is in a state of impurity (niddah), another person should not sleep there (Eruvin 63b), because she takes pleasure when she is in one room with her husband, talking and asking him whatever she wants, but when another person is there, she is embarrassed. Regarding them, the prophet said: "You drive the women of My people from their pleasant homes" (Micah 2:9).

And every man is required to attend to his wife on the night of her immersion and when he is about to embark on a journey, if he is not going for a mitzvah-related purpose. Similarly, if his wife is nursing and he notices that she is enticing him with words and adorning herself before him to attract his attention, he is obligated to attend to her even if it is not her designated time. Moreover, when he is with her, he should not intend solely for his own pleasure but rather as someone who is fulfilling a debt, and the debt is what the Torah obligates him—that he should not diminish her designated times, and to fulfill the commandment of his Creator so that he will have children who engage in Torah and uphold the commandments in Israel.

And similarly, if one intends to benefit the fetus, for in the last six months of pregnancy, marital relations are beneficial to the fetus, as through this the fetus will be born more developed and vigorous, it is permissible. However, in the first three months, marital relations are harmful to the fetus and difficult for the woman, and in the middle three months, it is difficult for the woman and beneficial to the fetus, and in the last three months, it is beneficial for both. And similarly, if one's intention is to protect oneself from sinning because he sees his inclination gaining strength and desires that act, there is also a reward for this. However, it would be better for him to overcome his inclination and subdue it, for a person has a small organ; if he starves it, it is satisfied, and if he satisfies it, it is hungry. But one who does not need it but arouses his desire to fulfill his lust, and this is not during the time of his wife's conjugal duty, this is the way of the evil inclination, and from what is permissible, it will lead him to what is forbidden. And regarding this, it is said in the Talmud Niddah (13b): "One who purposely causes arousal should be cursed."

One must fulfill the obligation of conjugal relations even during pregnancy and nursing. If someone maintains ritual immersion for his ritual purity, and during the winter it is difficult for him to immerse, can he exempt himself from the obligation of conjugal relations? They asked the Arizal, and he replied that if she is not pregnant or nursing, he is certainly obligated. But if she is pregnant or nursing, he still needs her forgiveness, and if not, he is obligated to fulfill the conjugal duty even if he cannot immerse (as noted at the beginning of this chapter in the Magen Avraham), since according to the Talmudic law, the obligation of immersion was nullified. 

A Torah scholar has the same obligation on Shabbat, as well as on Yom Tov and Rosh Chodesh. As an act of piety, one should not have marital relations on the first night of Pesach, the first night of Shavuot, and the night of Shemini Atzeret, except on the night of immersion (as mentioned there in the writings), and similarly on Rosh Hashanah. All this is not from the law, for according to the law, the prohibition applies only on Tisha B'Av and Yom Kippur. Therefore, someone who finds it difficult is permitted on Rosh Hashanah, Pesach, Shavuot, and Shemini Atzeret. 

One should not drink from this cup and set his eyes on another cup, meaning he should not think of another woman during the act, even if both are his wives, such as in countries where it is permissible to take two wives, for this is somewhat similar to the exchange of sacrifices, which will be explained.

Our Sages said in Nedarim (20b): It is written, "And I will purge from among you the rebels and those who transgress against Me"—these are the children of nine types: the children of a woman who was raped, even if it was not actual rape but she was not willing. Therefore, he should appease her and only then have relations. And so our Sages said in Eruvin (100b): "It is forbidden for a man to force his wife in the matter of a mitzvah, as it is said, 'And he who is hasty with his feet sins,' and anyone who forces will have children who are not proper, as it is written (there), 'Also, without knowledge, the soul is not good.'" We should learn proper conduct from the rooster, who appeases and then has relations. And so they said there that we should learn modesty from the cat, which does not defecate before people and covers its excrement, and theft from the ant, as it is written, "She prepares her food in the summer," and does not steal from others, and chastity from the dove, which mates only with its partner, and proper conduct from the rooster.

And the second [category] is the children of a hated wife, when he does not love her at the time of cohabitation. But if he loves her at the time of the act, even though she was hated, it is permitted (Tur). And the third [category] is the children of distance, meaning that he or she are distant from the court, as stated in Yoreh Deah, Siman 334. And the fourth [category] is the children of exchange, such as when he thinks at the time of the act that she is someone else, meaning he intended for a different body than she is, even if both are his wives. But if he intended for this body but was mistaken about her name, such as thinking her name was Rachel when her name is actually Leah, there is no issue (see Magen Avraham, section 9).

The fifth [case] is the children of a rebellious wife, who says: 'I do not want you,' and nevertheless he has relations with her. And even though she is agreeable at the time of the act, since she says 'I do not want him' and is intending to get divorced - it is forbidden to have relations with her until she fully consents and retracts her previous statements. The sixth [case] is children conceived in drunkenness, whether he is drunk or she is drunk. The seventh [case] is children of a heart-divorced [couple], when he has decided in his mind to divorce her for any reason, even though he loves her. Therefore, when he has resolved in his heart to divorce her, he should not come upon her. The eighth [case] is children of confusion, meaning for instance when he is with her but his mind is on another woman, as we wrote at the end of paragraph 6. The ninth [case] is children of an insolent woman, who demands him openly, and she is like a harlot. But if she does not demand him directly, rather she pleases him and adorns herself before him so that he may set his mind on her, she will have proper children. And so our Sages said in Eruvin (100b), look there.

It is forbidden to gaze at that place, and anyone who gazes there has no sense of shame and transgresses 'and walk discreetly,' and removes the shame from his face, for anyone who feels shame does not sin, as it is stated: "And so that His fear shall be upon your faces"—this refers to shame, and it is written (there) "so that you do not sin," for "upon your faces" implies shame (Ran on Nedarim there), and anyone who fears feels shame (Rosh there). Furthermore, it incites the evil inclination within oneself, and certainly, anyone who kisses there transgresses all of these, and also transgresses "do not make yourselves abominable." During the act, he should be on top and she below, but the reverse is considered a brazen manner, and if they both engage equally, it is considered a perverse manner.

It is forbidden to engage in marital relations in the presence of any person who is awake, even if there is a partition of ten [handbreadths] separating them. In the presence of an infant who cannot speak, it is permitted, but once the child can speak, it is forbidden even if he does not understand the matter, as he might recount what he saw, which is improper. In a room that contains a Torah scroll or scrolls of the Five Books of Moses made in the form of a Torah scroll, it is forbidden to engage in marital relations unless there is a partition of ten [handbreadths] in front of them. Covering the Torah with one vessel inside another does not help, as the honor of the Torah is stringent, and a curtain is not considered a partition since it is not fixed and moves around. Therefore, if it does not move and stands as if it is fixed, it is considered a partition. Even with a partition, it is only permitted if there is no other room available, but if another room is available, it is forbidden until the Torah scroll is moved to the other room.

If there are tefillin or printed books in the room — whether they are scriptures, Mishnah, Talmud, or legal codes — it is forbidden to engage in marital relations until they are placed in a double covering, where the second covering is not designated for them, as mentioned earlier in section 40. However, if both coverings are designated for them, even a hundred coverings are considered as one. If a garment is spread over a box of books, it is considered a double covering. If the box is large and holds forty se'ah, which is an area measuring one cubit by one cubit with a height of three cubits, no additional covering is needed as it is considered a separate domain (Magen Avraham, section 19). It is also written that a mezuzah requires a double covering, but we have explained in Yoreh De'ah, section 286, that a mezuzah does not need a double covering. Since the mezuzah is required to be there, a single covering suffices. When it is fixed on the doorpost of the room and covered with paper, glass, or another material, it is sufficient, and daily practice confirms this.

It is preferable not to engage in marital relations at the beginning of the night or at its end, so that one does not hear the sound of people and become distracted by others, but rather in the middle of the night. However, if it is not possible in the middle of the night, there is no strictness about this. One should engage in marital relations with awe and reverence, as it was said about Rabbi Eliezer (Nedarim ibid.) that he would uncover a handbreadth and cover a handbreadth and it seemed as if a demon had forced him, meaning the awe and reverence made it seem as if a demon had forced him. Some explain "uncover a handbreadth, etc." to mean that he would not excessively clean the member during the act to minimize his pleasure, making it seem as if he were doing it under duress. Others explain "uncover a handbreadth of the woman," meaning that now he uncovers it for the purpose of the act and now he covers it, as he would not prolong the act, and it seemed to him as if a demon had frightened him and he abandoned the act, thus he would greatly shorten the marital relations.

The Ra'avad of blessed memory raised a difficulty: Didn't we say that as a reward for delaying on the belly, one is granted male children? And he answered: This is all for the sake of Heaven, for God searches all hearts, and one who is confident in himself that he can perform this act without any other thoughts entering his mind and delays himself so that she derives pleasure from him and thus she emits seed first, and he intends to perform a commandment, the Holy One, Blessed be He, rewards him with male children. And one who is not confident in himself and hastens the act in order to be saved from sin, so that he does not think of another, he also performs a commandment, and the Holy One, Blessed be He, rewards him as well with male children, and this is what we have learned: "All your actions should be for the sake of Heaven." And some explain that she reveals a handbreadth over the apron she was wearing, that even at the moment of the act she needed to wear it, and she reveals only a handbreadth of herself and then covers immediately in order to minimize his pleasure. And even though it is explained in Even HaEzer, Siman 76, that it is not possible to force her to engage in intercourse while wearing her clothes, see there, but the apron is not considered a garment, and furthermore, when both agree, it is permitted in all manners, and this is a measure of modesty (Magen Avraham, section 22). All the explanations are true, and a person of spiritual refinement should be careful with them when he has the ability.

One should not converse with her about matters unrelated to conjugal relations, neither during the act nor beforehand, so that his mind does not turn to another woman. However, discussing matters related to conjugal relations is permitted in order to increase his desire (Tur), and see Even HaEzer, Siman 25. Nevertheless, such conversation should be measured and weighed, and regarding this, it is said in Chagigah: "He tells a person what they have spoken" – even trivial conversation between a man and his wife is recounted to a person at the time of judgment. And if he is angry with her, it is forbidden to engage in conjugal relations until he appeases her, and he may converse with her before the act in order to placate her.

It is forbidden to engage in marital relations by the light of a candle, even if one darkens it with a garment, for this is not the way of modesty. However, if one makes a partition ten handbreadths high in front of the candle, even though the light is visible through the partition, since there is an interruption with the sheet, it is permitted, for this is not considered direct light. Similarly, if the light is visible above the partition, such as when the partition does not reach the ceiling, it is also permitted. Nevertheless, one must still darken it with a garment so as not to gaze at the nakedness. The Kabbalists wrote that one should not see any light at all, even when she is pregnant, as this causes epilepsy in the offspring (Magen Avraham, section 24). One who sleeps in a canopy bed, which is called "paliah rabah" in Yiddish, if the curtains are thick, even if they do not darken completely, it is permitted (ibid.). If the moonlight shines directly on them through the window, it is forbidden to engage in marital relations, but if it illuminates the house and not directly on them, this is not so much of a concern (ibid.). Similarly, it is forbidden to engage in marital relations during the day unless it is a dark house, and a Torah scholar may darken it with a garment, and it is permitted, for the Torah scholar will be careful not to look at the nakedness. The Talmud explains the reason is lest he see something repulsive and she become repulsive to him (Niddah 17a). The Rambam wrote that this is only resorted to due to great need, and whether it is permitted to make a partition with a sheet on Shabbat for this purpose will be explained in Siman 315.

The sages said in Ta'anit (18a) that it is forbidden to engage in marital relations during years of famine, because the entire world is in distress. They learned this from the verse that states, "And to Joseph were born two sons before the year of famine came" (Genesis 41:50). And it is said there in the Jerusalem Talmud that the same applies to other troubles that are like a famine. However, if one is childless and has not yet fulfilled the mitzvah of procreation, it is permitted.

It is stated in Ketubot at the end of chapter 4 that it is forbidden to engage in marital relations in a guest house if there is no private room for him and his wife. But if they have a private, closed room, it is permitted, provided that he does not sleep in the host’s bed linen, as it might become unclean and disgrace him, and it is also improper, as the host did not provide it for this purpose (see Yoma 18a).

(And regarding the difficulty raised by the Magen Avraham in section 127, that without a separate room it would also be forbidden in one's own home, this is not difficult at all, as we were careful to write "closed," as without this there is a concern that someone else might enter, but in one's own home there is no such concern. And see Eliyah Rabbah section 121, who explained that in one's own home, if there is another person sleeping in the room, it is permitted, but in a guest house, even in such a case, it is forbidden. There are many distinctions to be made; scrutinize well).

The sages said in Pesachim (112b) that one who engages in marital relations on a bed where a child is sleeping will cause the child to fall ill with epilepsy. This is specifically if the child is not yet one year old, but if the child is one year or older, it is not an issue. Even if the child is not yet one year old, this applies only if the child is sleeping at the foot of the bed, but if the child is sleeping at the head of the bed, it is not an issue. Even if the child is at the foot of the bed, this is only if the person does not place their hand on the child during the act, but if they place their hand on the child, it is not an issue. Although we do not understand this, our holy rabbis received this tradition based on true wisdom. In the Zohar Vayikra, it is stated that a woman should not nurse the child after marital relations until the time it takes to walk two miles, and not less than the time it takes to walk one mile, which is eighteen minutes. One who comes out of the bathroom should not engage in marital relations for one hour, and after marital relations, one should wash their hands. It is proper to think about righteous individuals during marital relations, as this will benefit the child if conception occurs from that union. The bed on which one sleeps with their wife should have its head and foot positioned such that one side faces north and the other south, and there are various interpretations for this (see the responsa of Rabbi Yosef Shalom Elyashiv, siman 1).

It is stated in Niddah (17a): "There are four things the Holy One, Blessed be He, hates: one who enters his house suddenly, and needless to say someone else's house; one who grasps his membrum and urinates; one who urinates naked in front of his bed; and one who engages in marital relations in the presence of any living creature." Urinating naked in front of his bed is not specifically about being naked, but it is the usual manner of the matter, for when he is naked, he is lazy to go outside (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 1). And urinating means on the ground.

And so it is said in Shabbat (62b): One who urinates while naked in front of his bed will come to poverty, as the demon of poverty is named "Naval," and it dwells in any place that is unclean and not kept tidy. This specifically applies when he faces the bed, but if he faces outward, it is not a concern, as the stream flows outward. And this is specifically when he urinates on the ground, but if he urinates into a vessel, it is not a concern. A Torah scholar should cover it with a vessel or urinate into a vessel so that it will be permitted for him to contemplate words of Torah, as it is impossible for a Torah scholar to be without contemplation of Torah. (And it is written that one who cuts his nails in order will also come to poverty, and this is written in the name of Abudraham and the sages of France and Provence, as brought in Ateres Zekeinim).

The Tur writes: "There are pious individuals and men of deed who are stringent upon themselves and immerse before praying. This is an excessive stringency, for even according to the Rif, who wrote that some require immersion for prayer, it is not specifically immersion but rather washing with nine kabin (a measure of water)." And I have written above that neither immersion nor washing is necessary, and this has already been explained in Siman 88, and one who is stringent will be blessed. The Tur further writes: Before dawn breaks, one should hasten to rise with alacrity for the service of the Creator, may He be exalted, and not let the morning wake him, but rather he should wake the morning. This has been explained in Siman 1.

The holy Sabbath is the great sign between the Holy One, blessed be He, and His people Israel, as it is written: "For it is a sign between Me and you throughout your generations, that you may know that I am the Lord who sanctifies you." This means that although the Sabbath is a remembrance of the act of creation, "For in six days the Lord made the heavens and the earth, and on the seventh day He rested and was refreshed," and therefore "God blessed the seventh day and sanctified it, because on it He rested," as it is written in the account of creation. If so, it pertains to all creatures of the world, unlike the festivals, which are a remembrance of the Exodus from Egypt, to which other nations have no connection, as they did not come out of Egypt. But in the act of creation, all were created. Nevertheless, the Holy One, blessed be He, gave the sanctity of the Sabbath only to Israel. This is "to know that I am the Lord who sanctifies you," meaning that you are holy to Me, as it is written: "You shall be holy," and therefore I gave you the sanctity of the Sabbath. The Sabbath and Israel are the purpose of creation. (This is why we say: "And You did not give it" etc. "to the nations of the lands, nor did You make it the inheritance" etc., meaning that although it might seem that it pertains to everyone. This is what they said in the first chapter of Shabbat: "I have a good gift in My treasury, and its name is the Sabbath; go and tell them to Israel" etc., meaning that although it is possible to give it to all creatures, and understand this well.)

The sanctity of Shabbat is above all other sanctities, and its blessing is above all other blessings. Therefore, it was sanctified and blessed from the beginning of creation, as it is written: "And God blessed the seventh day and sanctified it." It is the source of blessing for all the weekdays. Therefore, the Israelites were commanded about the Shabbat in seven sections of the Torah: in 'Beshalach', 'Yitro', 'Mishpatim', 'Ki Tisa', 'Vayakhel', 'Emor', and 'Va'etchanan', to teach that all seven days of the week depend on Shabbat. Therefore, we mention Shabbat every day, saying in the Song of the Day: "First day of Shabbat," "Second day of Shabbat," and so on.

Shabbat is the essence of belief in the Holy One, blessed be He, who created His world in six days and rested on the seventh day. Anyone who does not observe Shabbat has no faith. Therefore, our sages of blessed memory equated in all of the Talmud the desecration of Shabbat to the worship of stars. Anyone who desecrates Shabbat is as if he denies the entire Torah. Thus, as soon as the Israelites left Egypt, they were commanded about Shabbat in the Parashat "Beshalach," even before the giving of the Torah, because the exodus from Egypt is a testimony to His providence, blessed be He, in His world, to reward those who do good and the opposite for those who do evil, like the Egyptians and their ilk. It is a testimony to His ability, blessed be He, to change nature, as with the plagues of Egypt, the splitting of the Red Sea, the descent of the manna, the quail, and the well. If they do not acknowledge that the Holy One, blessed be He, created His world, they deny all these things. Therefore, He gave them Shabbat immediately upon their exodus from Egypt. Thus said our sages of blessed memory, that Shabbat and laws were given at Marah, the first encampment after the splitting of the Red Sea, as explained in the Torah. And indeed, we see on the first Shabbat that some people desecrated Shabbat and went out to gather the manna, and the Holy One, blessed be He, said: "How long will you refuse to keep My commandments and My instructions?" This explicitly states that Shabbat encompasses the entire Torah and commandments. (Therefore, at the end of Ki Tisa, it is written: "You shall observe the Festival of Unleavened Bread," and afterward: "Six days shall you work, but on the seventh day you shall rest," and throughout the Torah, Shabbat precedes the festivals, as it is constant and sanctified. This is to teach that for the Festival of Unleavened Bread, it is essential to observe Shabbat, and without Shabbat, there is no Passover and no Torah).

The prophets, when they reproved Israel about violating the Torah, specifically reproved them about the desecration of the Sabbaths themselves. He said: "Blessed is the man who does this... who keeps the Sabbath from desecrating it and keeps his hand from doing any evil" (Isaiah 56:2), meaning that the merit of keeping the Sabbath will cause him not to do any evil. And furthermore, it says: "Everyone who keeps the Sabbath from desecrating it and holds fast to My covenant," meaning the covenant of the Torah. It is therefore explicitly stated that one who desecrates the Sabbath thereby violates the covenant of the Torah.

Jeremiah said: "Thus said the Lord, guard yourselves and do not carry a burden on the Sabbath day, nor bring a burden out of your houses on the Sabbath day, and do no work, and sanctify the Sabbath day" etc., "It shall be, if you listen to Me" etc., "then kings and princes who sit on David's throne shall enter through the gates of this city" etc., "But if you do not listen to Me to sanctify the Sabbath day and not to bear a burden" etc., "then I will kindle a fire in its gates, and it will consume the palaces of Jerusalem and it will not be quenched." Therefore, our Sages said about the Sabbath, that in a place where Sabbath desecration is common, fire is common. And Ezekiel said: "They rebelled against Me" etc., "They desecrated My Sabbaths, and I resolved to pour out My wrath" etc., "because they did not perform My judgments and they despised My statutes, and they desecrated My Sabbaths" etc. Therefore, an Israelite man should focus his heart on observing the holy Sabbath and accept it well before sunset, not close to sunset, because based on this, many among the masses and women and the ignorant light candles after sunset. And behold, concerning the prohibition of chametz on the eve of Passover after midday, which is only a negative commandment, the Sages made a safeguard of about two hours; and our Sages explained in Pesachim the reason, because chametz is common to all. All the more so, with the desecration of the Sabbath, which is a capital offense, and is entrusted to all the people of Israel, young and old, men and women, that lighting candles should be distanced far, far before sunset. Certainly, the city rabbi and the pious are obligated to light much earlier, so that the masses, although they won't light as early, will still not come to desecrate the Sabbath. This is unlike if they themselves light close to sunset, where the masses will light after sunset, as we have heard and seen in many places. Previous generations would accept the Sabbath much earlier, as explained in Terumat HaDeshen (Siman 1), that after prayer and after eating they would go for a walk, and by then it was sunset, see there. (And the Shla in his Siddur before the acceptance of the Sabbath explains that one who says "A Psalm, a Song for the Sabbath day" after sunset brings great danger, see there where he elaborates on this with his great sanctity and wisdom).

The reward for observing Shabbat is very great, as explained by the prophets and our sages. They said: Whoever delights in Shabbat is granted an inheritance without bounds, is saved from subjugation [by kingdoms], and is given the desires of their heart (Shabbat 118a). The delight of Shabbat is a commandment from the prophets, as it is written: "And you shall call the Shabbat a delight" (Isaiah 58:13). And everyone agrees that on Shabbat we need [to do things] for your own enjoyment (Pesachim 68b), as it is written: "And you shall call the Shabbat a delight." We will further explain this with the help of Heaven in section 42.

The laws of Shabbat are numerous and profound. Our rabbis, the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch, despite their extensive length, only wrote about what is forbidden and permitted. However, they did not write about the principles of the primary categories of work and their derivatives, the Torah obligations and Rabbinic decrees, and the general principles of the roots of Shabbat labors. The Rambam, of blessed memory, explained everything. For the sake of the completeness of this holy work, we wish to also elucidate a bit on this, including the differences between the view of the Rambam and several of our rabbis like Rashi and Tosafot, and other early authorities, as we will explain with G-d's help.

And this is the language of the Rambam at the beginning of chapter 1 of Shabbat: Cessation from labor on the seventh [day] is a positive commandment, as it is stated (Exodus 20:9): "But on the seventh day you shall rest." And anyone who does work on it has nullified a positive commandment and transgressed a negative commandment, as it is stated: "You shall not do any work." And what is he liable for doing work? If he did it willfully with intent, he is liable for karet (excision). And if there were witnesses and warning, he is stoned. And if he did it unintentionally, he is liable for a sin offering. And anytime it is said on Shabbat "exempt," it means exempt from Torah law, but it is forbidden by rabbinic law. And so the Sages said at the beginning of Shabbat: All exemptions of Shabbat mean exempt but forbidden, except for those three, etc., unless it is stated "permitted" or "not liable at all." And for "exempt but forbidden," if one transgressed and did it, he is given lashes of rebellion (makkat mardut).

At the beginning of Parashat Vayakhel (Exodus 35:1) it is written: "And Moses assembled" etc., "These are the things that the Lord has commanded to do: Six days work shall be done, but on the seventh day it shall be holy for you" etc. The explanation is that he commanded them regarding the work of the Tabernacle, and that on Shabbat it is forbidden to do the work of the Tabernacle, as explained in the Mekhilta. From this, the tradition came to our Sages to derive great principles and fundamentals concerning the work prohibited on Shabbat; since the matter of Shabbat is juxtaposed with the work of the Tabernacle, we learn all the labors of Shabbat from the labors that were in the Tabernacle. Thus, the Sages taught (Shabbat 49b): One is only liable for a labor that was similar to one performed in the Tabernacle. They planted, and you shall not plant; and planting was in the Tabernacle for planting herbs (Rashi). They harvested, and you shall not harvest, etc. From this, we learned the 39 primary labors on Shabbat, as will be explained, because these labors were significant in the Tabernacle (beginning of Bava Kama). And although there are several primary labors that are similar to each other, like winnowing, selecting, and sifting, all of which are to separate the food from the refuse, but the separation is not in the same manner: winnowing is done with wind, selecting by hand, and sifting with a sieve. Nevertheless, since they were all significant labors in the Tabernacle, we call them primary labors; and other labors that are similar to the primary ones, we call them derivatives (there and Shabbat 73b).

And if you ask: What practical difference is there between a primary category (av) and a subsidiary category (toldah)? For indeed, one is liable to stoning and excision, and a sin-offering if done inadvertently, for both. However, there is a significant practical difference: if a person performs two labors, if one is a primary category and the other is its subsidiary, he is liable for only one sin-offering. But if they are two primary categories, or if it is a subsidiary from another primary category, he is liable for two sin-offerings. And so wrote the Rambam in Chapter 7 (Halachah 7), see there. According to our Rabbis, the Tosafists (Shabbat 73b s.v. 'mishum zoreah'), there is a reason that there is a distinction regarding the warning, that one must warn about the subsidiary specifically due to the primary category. If so, there is a significant practical difference between a primary category and a subsidiary. And so it seems in Shabbat. However, the Tosafists themselves were uncertain about this, and it can be said that even if warned due to the subsidiary, one is also liable. But it is clear that if warned about the subsidiary due to another subsidiary, even if it is from the same primary category, it is not a valid warning, unless warned about the specific subsidiary he desires to perform, or its primary category. According to this, it is necessary to know what is called a primary category and what is called a subsidiary.

What are the primary categories of labor? This is what the Sages have taught in the Mishnah of "Klal Gadol": The primary categories of labor are forty minus one. Sowing, plowing, reaping, gathering sheaves, threshing, winnowing, selecting, grinding, sifting, kneading, and baking; shearing wool, bleaching it, combing it, dyeing it, spinning it, stretching the threads, making two loops, weaving two threads, separating two threads, tying, untying, sewing two stitches, tearing in order to sew two stitches; trapping a deer, slaughtering it, skinning it, salting it, tanning its hide, scraping it, cutting it; writing two letters, erasing in order to write two letters; building, demolishing, extinguishing, kindling, striking with a hammer, transferring from one domain to another—these are the primary categories of labor, etc. And it is stated in the Gemara (Shabbat 75b): Salting and tanning are considered one and are not counted as two separate primary categories. There is also another primary category, which is marking lines (for cutting), see there. This is not a deficiency in the Mishnah, for indeed the interpretation of "tanning" includes this, as it is stated in the Jerusalem Talmud and this is its language: What tanning was done in the Tabernacle? They would mark lines on the hides to even out the sides, see there (and in our Talmud, where it says "remove" etc., it can also be explained this way, and examine it well).

The Tur and Shulchan Aruch did not mention the labors in detail, and it is impossible for us to deviate from the structure of the Tur and Shulchan Aruch. Therefore, we have decided to append these labors in detail, each labor to the section that has some relevance to it. There, with the help of Heaven, we will explain the primary categories and their derivatives. We will note the sections that mention sowing, plowing, and reaping in section 336. Gathering, shearing, combing, spinning, warping, making two heddles, weaving, unraveling, writing, and erasing in section 340. Winnowing, selecting, and sifting in section 319. Kneading, grinding, skinning, tanning, smoothing, cutting, and ruling in section 321. Baking and slaughtering in section 318. Threshing, laundering, and dyeing in section 320. Tying and untying, sewing and tearing in section 317. Trapping in section 316. Building, demolishing, and striking with a hammer in section 313. Extinguishing and kindling in section 334. Transferring from one domain to another in section 301.

And behold, each primary category (av) has many derivative categories (toladot). In the Jerusalem Talmud, it is stated that Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish studied the primary categories of work for a long time and found that each primary category of work has thirty-nine derivative categories. The Rambam wrote in Chapter 7 (Halacha 5): A derivative category is a type of work that is similar to one of these primary categories. How so? One who cuts vegetables into very small pieces to cook them is liable because this is a derivative of grinding, as grinding involves taking one entity and dividing it into many parts. Anyone who performs an action similar to this is performing a derivative of grinding. This is the language of the Rambam. The details of this law will be explained in Siman 319, as this only applies to vegetables that are not eaten raw. The Rambam also wrote that each type of work has derivative categories in this manner. From the nature of the work, one can understand which primary category it belongs to, as this is clear to those who understand. One must know the definitions of the primary categories, and with Divine assistance, we will mention the definitions when we come to each of the types of work.

According to what has been explained, a person could be liable for thirty-nine sin offerings on Shabbat if he transgresses all the forbidden labors inadvertently, and no more, because all the labors in the world are included in these thirty-nine labors. Regarding a primary category and its derivative, it has already been explained that one is only liable once. And from where do we learn that one is liable for each primary category of labor separately? This is what our Sages said (Shabbat 70a), as it is written: "Do not kindle a fire," and kindling was included in all the labors. Why was it singled out? To teach about the division of labors, that just as one is liable for kindling separately, since it was singled out, so too for each and every labor. This is one of the thirteen principles, that anything that was included in the general category and was singled out, it was not singled out to teach about itself, but to teach about the entire category. And so wrote the Rambam in Chapter 7 (Halacha 2) of Shgagot, see there. (And it must be said that we do not hold by this opinion of Isi at the beginning of the tractate, who said that there is one labor out of the thirty-nine for which one is not liable for a sin offering, see there. And the reason is that since Rabbi Yochanan said (Shabbat 69a) regarding the Mishnah of primary labors, that if one performed all of them in one lapse of awareness, he is liable for each and every one, we do not concern ourselves with Isi, and certainly Rabbi Yochanan knew that the Sages disagreed with Isi, and understand this well).

Rambam wrote at the beginning of Chapter 2 of Shgagot: "A person is not liable for a sin offering for his inadvertent act until he is inadvertent from beginning to end. But if he was inadvertent at the beginning and intentional at the end, or intentional at the beginning and inadvertent at the end, he is exempt. How so? For example, if he carried an object from one domain to another on Shabbat. If he lifted it intentionally and put it down inadvertently, or lifted it inadvertently and put it down intentionally, he is exempt, until he lifts it inadvertently and puts it down inadvertently. And the same applies to all similar cases," end quote. And if his beginning and end were inadvertent, even if in the middle he was intentional – he is liable for a sin offering. And this is clearly implied in Shabbat (102a in the context of Rav Ashi, see there). And know, that this is not limited to carrying where it was in his power not to complete the act, but even if he threw, where after it left his hand he could not retrieve it, nevertheless, if he remembered before it came to rest – he is exempt from a sin offering. And this is explicitly stated in Shabbat there. And I am astonished at the Rambam, why didn't he illustrate this law with throwing, especially since the language of the Mishnah there is like this, and it requires investigation. And it seems to my humble opinion that the Rambam intentionally changed from the language of the Mishnah, because the Jerusalem Talmud indeed obligates in the case of throwing, on the grounds that it is not in his power to retrieve it (and this is the language of the Jerusalem Talmud, Shabbat, Chapter 11, Halacha 6: "This is the explanation of the Mishnah, and he was intentional. And it is difficult, if he shot an arrow to kill a person, and they warned him, and he retracted, would it be anything, etc.?" see there. And the commentators explained it in a strange way, see there. And the truth is that in the Jerusalem Mishnah the version in the Mishnah is: the one who throws and remembers before it leaves his hand, see there. And this is what it says, this is the explanation of the Mishnah and he was intentional, meaning, that this is the version, that he was intentional until it left his hand, and therefore when he threw, it was intentional and he is exempt from a sin offering; for if not, but according to the version of the Babylonian Talmud, it is difficult, why should he be exempt? And indeed he cannot retrieve it! And therefore the Rambam, to distance himself from controversy, wrote the language of carrying, and understand this well). (And in the laws of Shgagot we wrote another explanation, see there).

Furthermore, he wrote: "If one transgressed a sin and knows it is a prohibition but does not know that it incurs karet (excision), this is considered inadvertent, and he brings a sin-offering. However, if he knows that it incurs karet but is unaware whether it mandates a sacrifice or not, this is considered intentional, as ignorance regarding the sacrifice does not constitute inadvertence for sins that incur karet." This is his language. But for a transgression that does not incur karet but rather lashes, if one intentionally violates a prohibition, it is not considered inadvertent, and he is flogged. Now, on Shabbat, there is one matter that is a prohibition without karet, which is driving an animal (to perform labor). Nevertheless, even if he did so intentionally, he is exempt from lashes because this prohibition is derived from the verse "You shall not do any work" etc., "nor your animal" etc., and within this prohibition is also included the death penalty if one performs work himself. And any prohibition that is given as a warning for the death penalty administered by the court does not incur lashes. This is explained in several places in the Talmud, due to the reason that this prohibition was given for the death penalty and not for lashes. And so Rambam ruled at the beginning of the first chapter of Shabbat, see there. All the more so, if done inadvertently, he is exempt from a sacrifice, as a sacrifice is only brought when there is karet for intentional violation, and not for a prohibition punishable by lashes (see Tosafot Shabbat 154a, s.v. 'b'lavo').

And know that regarding the inadvertent transgression of Shabbat, there are two scenarios. For example, if one reaped on Shabbat, knowing that it is Shabbat, but thought that reaping is permitted on Shabbat; or if one knew that reaping is forbidden on Shabbat, but did not know that it was Shabbat. It turns out that the liability for the death penalty is only when one knew that it was Shabbat and knew that reaping is forbidden on Shabbat, which carries a death penalty. 

Now, it seems that it makes no difference whether one intentionally violated Shabbat and inadvertently performed a forbidden labor, or intentionally performed a forbidden labor and inadvertently violated Shabbat. But in truth, it is not so, for if one knew that it was Shabbat and performed many labors because he did not know they were forbidden, he is liable for each and every labor, if they are distinct primary categories. However, if he knew that the labors are forbidden but did not know that it was Shabbat, he is liable for only one sin-offering. 

The reason is simple: the liability for a sin-offering is due to inadvertence. When he inadvertently transgressed Shabbat, it is considered one inadvertence; but when he inadvertently performed forbidden labors, there are many inadvertences, as he was unaware of this labor and that labor, etc. This is what the Sages taught in the Mishnah in "Klal Gadol," and so ruled the Rambam in chapter 7 of "Shgagot." Similarly, if he inadvertently transgressed Shabbat and also inadvertently performed forbidden labors, he is liable for only one sin-offering. The reason is that the inadvertent transgression of Shabbat is primary (Tosafot Shabbat 72b s.v. "Amar"). And although in other transgressions there are also similar cases of dual inadvertence, nevertheless, they have one ruling.

Even though it has been explained that one who performs a primary labor along with its derivatives is only liable for one sin-offering, nevertheless, this is true for the same Sabbath. However, if one performed the primary labor on this Sabbath, and performed the derivative or even the primary labor itself on the next Sabbath, he is liable for two sin-offerings. This is not only the case if he performed both with the intentional violation of the Sabbath and unintentional violation of the labors, for since the mistake is about the labor, they are two separate mistakes, as each Sabbath is considered a separate entity. Just like one who has relations with two menstruating women during one lapse of awareness is liable for two offerings, because each body is considered a separate entity, so too each Sabbath is a separate entity. 

Rather, even if he performed them with an unintentional violation of the Sabbath and intentional violation of the labors, where it is one mistake over all the Sabbaths, meaning he did not know that it was the Sabbath, he is still liable for each Sabbath. The reason is that it is impossible that he would not become aware during the week that it had been the Sabbath, and therefore each Sabbath is a separate mistake, as they are considered two lapses of awareness. This is what our sages said in Kritot 16b, that the days between Sabbaths are considered knowledge to divide the liability, see there. And so ruled the Rambam there, see there.

Even though there are differences between the inadvertent performance of a prohibited labor (melacha) and the inadvertent observance of Shabbat, as explained, nevertheless, if one performed the same labor twice on one Shabbat—where the first time he knew it was Shabbat but erred in the labor, and afterward he forgot it was Shabbat but knew that this labor was forbidden, and he repeated the labor due to his forgetfulness of Shabbat—in any case, if he becomes aware of both actions, he brings one sin-offering. Even though the second lapse is somewhat different from the first, it is ultimately considered one lapse (Rashi, Shabbat 71a, s.v. "ketzira," see there). Similarly, even though it has been explained that in any case, for every Shabbat one is obligated to bring a separate sin-offering, nevertheless, a child who was captured by non-Jews and did not know about Shabbat at all, or someone who completely forgot that there is such a thing as Shabbat, and performed many labors on many Shabbatot, is only obligated to bring one sin-offering, because in all of these instances, it is considered one continuous inadvertence, as he did not know about Shabbat at all. Thus, the Sages taught in the Mishnah in the chapter "General Rules," and likewise, Maimonides ruled there, see there in Chapter 2 (and he ruled in accordance with Rav and Shmuel in Shabbat 68b, and not according to Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish; see there in Kesef Mishneh. Seemingly, according to the general rules of the Talmud, he should have ruled according to Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish, which requires further investigation).

And from the juxtaposition of the work of Shabbat with the work of the Mishkan, the tradition came to the Sages to also learn that we require specifically intentional work for the labors of Shabbat, just like in the Mishkan. And this depends on great principles and foundations. That is, one must intend for the work that he is doing; but if he does not intend it at all, for example, if he intended to throw two cubits, which is permitted, and he threw four cubits, he is exempt (Bava Kamma 26b). Similarly, if a stone was placed in his lap, and it fell from his lap and caused a bruise to an animal, he is exempt (ibid.), since he did not intend this work at all, even though for several things he is liable even without intention, such as for damages and other matters (ibid.). For in the Mishkan, every work they did—they intended to do it, as it is written in "Vayakhel" (Exodus 35:32-33): "And to devise plans" etc. "to do all works of craftsmanship."

And for this reason, it is well-known throughout the entire tractate of Shabbat that an act done without intention is a point of dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon. According to Rabbi Shimon, it is permitted from the outset, and according to Rabbi Yehuda, although it is forbidden from the outset, it is only prohibited by rabbinic decree. In other prohibitions, Rabbi Yehuda holds that it is forbidden by Torah law (Tosafot Shabbat 41b s.v. 'Meicham'). Even Rabbi Shimon, who holds that in other prohibitions it is permitted by Torah law, as proven in Pesachim and Shabbat, agrees that in certain matters, even if done without intention, one is liable, such as in cases of damages and those liable for exile (Bava Kama 26b). And from the words of Rambam in chapter 10 of Kilayim, law 18, it appears that he ruled that even in cases of Kilayim (forbidden mixtures), one is liable even if it was done without intention (see there in Kesef Mishneh and examine carefully).

Similarly, it is included in the category of "skilled work" (melechet machshevet), which we require specifically to be a craftsperson's work, as it was in the Tabernacle, which involved the work of artisans and designers. However, anything that is not craftsmanship is not considered work on Shabbat (Beitzah 13b, Rashi s.v. "rather"). Therefore, one who stacks a pile of grain on Shabbat, if there is no other work involved, is not liable from the Torah (ibid.), but it is prohibited rabbinically due to mundane activities (uvdin dechol) and muktzeh. For this reason, even regarding tying a knot, which is one of the primary categories of work, one is only liable for tying a craftsman's knot, as Rambam wrote in Chapter 10 (Halacha 1) of Shabbat, and it will be explained in Siman 317, and all this is because we require "skilled work."

Therefore, those who cause damage are exempt, unless they cause damage with the intention to repair. But one who causes damage alone, such as demolishing a building without the intention to rebuild it, is exempt according to Torah law, because this is not considered "thoughtful work," as all the labors in the Tabernacle were for the purpose of repairing and not for damaging. Similarly, work that is not needed for its own sake, for those who exempt it, as will be explained, is also due to the reason of "thoughtful work" (Chagigah 10b), as our rabbis, the Tosafists, wrote in Shabbat (94a, s.v. 'R. Shimon'), and this is also necessary according to Rashi, see there and take note. And those who obligate, do so because they consider this to be "thoughtful work." For this reason, one who is engaged in permitted labor and accidentally performs forbidden labor, such as intending to cut a detached item and cutting an attached one instead, is also exempt due to the reason of "thoughtful work." Even if one intended to perform forbidden labor but did so on a different item, such as intending to cut one attached item and cutting another, is also exempt for this reason (Tosafot, Shabbat 72b, s.v. 'intended to cut', see there). However, there are those who disagree on this, as will be explained. Similarly, if one intended to perform one labor and then another labor, but ended up performing them in reverse, is also exempt for this reason, since it was not done as he thought, as Rambam wrote in Chapter 1, Law 11, see there. Further clarification will be provided with Heaven's help in paragraph 27.

And know that I found one matter where the requirement of "skilled work" (melechet machshevet) is a stringency. This means that one who winnows grain using the wind is liable. This is one of the primary categories of labor (avot melachot). And even though the primary work is done by the wind, and in matters of damages (nezikin) one would be exempt, nevertheless, on Shabbat, one is liable. This is because it is considered "skilled work" (melechet machshevet), for this is the way winnowing is done, and his intention was fulfilled, as it is beneficial to him that the wind assists him (Bava Kama 60a).

Maimonides wrote in Chapter 1, Law 8: "Anyone who intends to perform a task and ends up performing a different task that he did not intend to do is exempt from liability because his intention was not fulfilled, etc. All the more so if he intended a minor prohibition and a major prohibition occurred, etc. If he intended to do something permissible but ended up doing something else, such as intending to cut something detached and instead cutting something attached, he is not liable at all, and so too in similar cases," up to here is his language. This case of intending to cut something detached and instead cutting something attached is in the Gemara (Shabbat 72b). According to Rashi's explanation, it means he intended to cut this gourd which was detached but instead cut another gourd which was attached. Our rabbis, the Tosafists, questioned this, arguing that even if he intended to cut this attached item and instead cut another attached item, he would also be exempt, as explained in Keritot, that if he intended to pick this fig but picked another fig, he is exempt because his intention was not fulfilled, and this is not considered deliberate work. So why specify intending to cut something detached, where there was no intention for any prohibition at all? Even if he intended for a prohibition, he would still be exempt! Rather, it is certain that intending to cut something detached and instead cutting something attached means he cut the gourd he wanted but thought it was detached and found it was attached. He is exempt due to "misdeal," as he was engaged in permissible activity and ended up with a prohibition, see there thoroughly.

However, from the words of the Rambam, it seems explicitly like Rashi, and so agreed the commentators, as it is explained from his words later on, that if one intended to detach this attached item and ended up detaching a different attached item, if there is no difference between this and that – indeed he is liable, for this is considered purposeful work. And the Raavad objected to him from the matter of Keritot. But the Rambam dismissed the matter of Keritot because of the sugya in Shabbat (Lechem Mishneh). And furthermore, it seems to my humble opinion, that also the sugya in Keritot according to the conclusion holds this way (for certainly at first the Gemara thought like Tosafot and the Raavad, and explains the case of intending to pick figs and picking grapes, that it implies figs and figs – liable, because he forgot what he picked from his mind. But Rava who said there afterward: "precedence makes a difference," holds that figs and figs – liable if there is no difference between them, and precedence is worse, because he did not do as he thought. And therefore also in intending to throw four and throwing eight – exempt also, because it did not happen as he thought, that there is a change in this. But fig and fig when there is no difference between them – this is not a change, and this is the approach of Rashi and the Rambam, and take note).

He further wrote: "If one intended to pick black figs but picked white ones, or if one intended to pick figs and then grapes, but the matter was reversed and he picked grapes first and then figs, he is exempt. Even though he picked everything he thought of, since he did not pick in the order he intended, he is exempt, because it was done without intention, and the Torah only forbids deliberate work. If there were two candles before him, either lit or extinguished, and he intended to extinguish this one but extinguished the other, or to light this one but lit the other, he is liable, because he performed the work he intended to do. What is this similar to? To one who intended to pick this fig but picked another fig, etc. However, if he intended to light the first one and then extinguish the second one after it, but the matter was reversed and he extinguished the first one and then lit the second one after it, he is exempt. If he extinguished this one and lit this one in one breath, he is liable, because even though he did not precede, he also did not delay, and similarly in all such cases. And anyone who performs work inadvertently without intending to do so is exempt," until here is his language. (And he intended what they said in Shabbat 72b: If one intended to lift the detached and cut the attached, he is exempt. And the Ra'avad, Ramban, and Maggid Mishneh argued with him about what he wrote regarding one who intended to pick this fig but picked another that he is liable, and in Keritot it establishes it specifically when he forgot what he was picking, see there. But according to what I wrote, it is good, for Rava does not hold thus. And this is also the opinion of Rashi. And to precede is worse, for the change is noticeable and it is not considered deliberate work; and whenever the change is not noticeable, it is called deliberate work, and everything is good and study it well). (And this is what Rashi wrote in Keritot there 20a at the end of "to precede": "But in general inadvertence, where he only intended for one and did not do it, but did another, all agree he is exempt," until here is his language - this is with black and white figs, for Rabbi Yehuda holds that this is one name, as he wrote earlier in "with two names," see there. And further, for Rabbi Shimon Shazuri and Rabbi Shimon indeed hold as the Rambam ruled, see there, and who says that the law is not like them against Rabbi Yehuda, for they are many? And as is proven from the simple reading of the sugya in Shabbat there. And a proof that we do not need exactly as he thought when there is no change is from one breath that he is liable as it says there, even though he did not precede, he also did not delay, see there. And it is difficult, for in any case, it is not according to his thought to precede! Rather, certainly, since the change is not noticeable, it is not called a change and it is considered deliberate work, and study it well).

It has already been clarified that the matter of "a deed done without intention" and "a labor not needed for its own sake" is a dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon throughout the entire Talmud. Rabbi Yehuda holds that a deed done without intention is forbidden by rabbinic law, and a labor not needed for its own sake incurs a sin-offering because it is considered a complete labor. Rabbi Shimon, on the other hand, holds that a deed done without intention is permitted from the outset, and a labor not needed for its own sake is exempt by Torah law because it is not considered purposeful labor as it was in the Mishkan (Tabernacle). In the Mishkan, when they performed labor, they needed the labor itself and its purpose, but it is forbidden by rabbinic law. (And Rabbi Yehuda considers it purposeful labor. One could explain his reasoning, that certainly in the Mishkan there was extinguishing to prevent the excessive fire from ruining the herbs, and this is a labor not needed for its own sake. Rabbi Shimon, however, holds that in the Mishkan they were surely careful not to let the fire grow too much, as Tosafot wrote in Shabbat 94b s.v. "Rabbi Shimon," see there, and there was no extinguishing except to make charcoal, which is needed for its own sake, as Tosafot wrote in Shabbat 31b s.v. "and dismantles," see there).

Regarding the law, in matters where there is no intention, the Talmud explicitly rules according to Rabbi Shimon, who says: "And now that we hold like Rabbi Shimon, it is permitted even ab initio" (Shabbat 95a). However, regarding a labor that is not needed for its own sake, the halacha is not explicitly decided. Our rabbis, the Tosafists, the Raavad, the Ramban, and the Rashba, all ruled according to Rabbi Shimon even in the case of a labor that is not needed for its own sake. Firstly, because Rava at the beginning of the chapter "Notel" holds like Rabbi Shimon, and secondly, because at the end of Shabbat it is said that throughout Shabbat the halacha follows Rabbi Shimon. But the Rambam in chapter 1, law 7, ruled according to Rabbi Yehuda, and also the opinion of the Rif seems to be the same (Magid Mishneh). Their reasoning is that according to the principles of the Talmud, between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon, the halacha follows Rabbi Yehuda. And even though Rava holds like Rabbi Shimon, nevertheless, there are Amoraim who hold like Rabbi Yehuda. Additionally, in the Mishnah (Shabbat 93b), our holy teacher established in the Mishnah that if one carries a corpse on a bed, he is liable, like Rabbi Yehuda, and stated it in the plural form. And what is said that throughout Shabbat the halacha follows Rabbi Shimon, there it only refers to issues of muktzeh, see there. (However, according to the Jerusalem Talmud, Shabbat chapter 2, halacha 5, where Rabbi Yossi also holds like Rabbi Shimon - certainly the halacha follows Rabbi Yossi over Rabbi Yehuda. And in our Talmud (Shabbat 31b), there is a dispute regarding whom Rabbi Yossi holds like, see there. And in the Jerusalem Talmud, Shabbat chapter 9, halacha 6, it is explicitly understood that we rule like Rabbi Shimon, see there and examine it well.)

And what is a "labor not needed for its own sake"? For example, when one performs a prohibited labor but does not need it for its prohibited purpose, rather for a different purpose. For instance, when one digs a hole, the prohibition is the digging, but he does not need the hole at all, rather he needs the dirt. "Needed for its own sake" is when one needs the hole, to store something in it or to use it. Similarly, extinguishing a candle, the labor is the extinguishing. If he needs the extinguishing itself, that is to make a coal, it is called "needed for its own sake." But if he does not need the coal, rather he wants to save the oil or the wick or the vessel, it is called "not needed for its own sake." Likewise, if one carries a thorn four cubits in the public domain, the labor is the carrying, and he does not need this, rather he removes it from its place so that many will not be harmed by it, or extinguishes a coal so that many will not be harmed by it - this is "not needed for its own sake." Similarly, if one traps a snake so that it will not bite him, the labor is the trapping, and he does not need the trapping at all, and so too in all similar cases. And in the Tabernacle, when they performed the labor, they needed it for the purpose of the labor. (And Rashi also holds this way. And what he wrote in the Mishnah about "the dead in a bed," and this is his language: "for labor that is only needed to remove it from oneself, and not for its own sake" (Shabbat 93b s.v. 'and R. Shimon') look there, this is only an explanation, meaning: that for the purpose of the labor he does not need, and it was not his intent. And the Tosafot (94a s.v. 'R. Shimon') who were precise about him, were only precise about his language, but the intention is clear, and scrutinize it well).

And know that it is well-known throughout the Talmud that even though an unintentional act (דבר שאין מתכוין) — even according to Rabbi Yehuda, it is only a rabbinic prohibition, and according to Rabbi Shimon, it is permitted ab initio, and so is the law as we have written. Nevertheless, this is in a case where the action may or may not result in a prohibited labor. But in a case where the action necessarily results in a prohibited labor, even Rabbi Shimon agrees that one is liable according to Torah law. Thus, it is stated in several places in the Talmud: Rabbi Shimon agrees in the case of "inevitable occurrence" (פסיק רישא ולא ימות). And this is the language of the Rambam in Chapter 1, Law 5: "Things that are permitted to do on Shabbat, and during their performance it is possible that a prohibited labor might be done or might not be done, if one did not intend that labor — it is permitted. How so? A person may drag a bed, chair, or bench on Shabbat, provided he does not intend to dig a furrow in the ground while dragging them. Therefore, if the ground is dug — he is not concerned with it, since he did not intend [to dig]. But if he did an action, and as a result a labor that will definitely occur due to that action, even though he did not intend it — he is liable, because it is known that it is impossible for that labor not to occur. How so? If one needs a bird's head to play with for a child, and he cuts off its head on Shabbat, even though his ultimate goal is not merely to kill the bird — he is liable, because it is known that it is impossible to cut off the head of a living being and it remains alive; rather, death comes as a result of it. And so it is with all similar cases," thus far his words.

There is a significant question here: How can Rabbi Shimon be held liable for a "p'sik reisha"? Since he does not intend for it, it is obvious that he does not need its outcome, and if so, it is at any rate a melacha she'eina tzericha legufah (a labor not needed for its own sake)! However, from the words of our Rabbis, the Ba'alei HaTosafot, in Shabbat (41b, s.v. 'Michaem'), Yoma (34b), and Keritot (2a), it seems that the explanation is as follows: Any "p'sik reisha" where we can testify that he benefits from it, he is liable even if he does not intend for it, and against his will it is as if he intends for it. And in any case where we can testify that he does not benefit from it, meaning it does not matter to him, it is considered a melacha she'eina tzericha legufah. According to the view of the Aruch (in Tosafot 103a), any "p'sik reisha" that he does not benefit from is permitted even initially, see there. But Rashi, of blessed memory, wrote explicitly (75a, s.v. 'Tfei') that Rabbi Shimon concedes in a case where it does not matter to him whether it happens or not, unless he specifically wants the opposite, that this labor should not be done, see there.

And behold, we have found that the son of the Rambam was asked about this, and he responded in the name of the Rambam in this language: "The difference between a labor that is not needed for its own sake and 'psik reisha' is: Regarding 'psik reisha' - he does not intend the labor at all, but it is an inevitable act, such as someone who closes the door of his house and there was a deer there; he did not intend to trap the deer, but the labor is done inevitably. However, a labor that is not needed for its own sake - he intends the labor itself, but he does not intend its purpose (Kesef Mishneh Chapter 1, Halacha 7). The great scholars of the world have struggled with his intention, and I have not seen words on this that settle well in the heart.

In my humble opinion, it seems that the matter is as follows: For example, in the matter of commandments, there are authorities who hold that intention is necessary, and there are authorities who hold that even if one does not intend, he fulfills the obligation, as it is considered as if he intended. Nevertheless, if one explicitly intends not to fulfill the obligation, all agree that he does not fulfill it. The same applies to the labors prohibited on Shabbat. Certainly, when performing a prohibited labor, one must intend to do it; intention is not a hindrance, for if it were, one could perform all the labors and claim that he did not intend to do so. Rather, even if one performs without any intention of labor at all, since he is performing the labor in the usual manner, what difference does his lack of intention make? It is necessarily considered as if he intended. This is the concept of "psik reisha". However, if one indeed intends to perform the labor but does so for a different purpose, it is like a commandment where one intends not to fulfill the obligation. Here, too, it cannot be said that it is as if he intended, for he certainly intends, but he intends for a different purpose and not for the prohibited aspect of the labor itself.

Therefore, in the case of trapping a deer, he does not intend anything, and similarly with the bird's head for a child's play, he does not intend anything. This is not the case with digging a pit where he only needs the dirt, for he certainly intends to dig, but for a different purpose, namely for the dirt. But in the case of trapping a deer, he does not intend to trap at all, and similarly with the bird's head for a child's play, he does not intend to kill at all, and it is even worse, for the labor is performed against his will, and it is considered as if he intended. 

(And there is an opinion that in the case of "psik reisha", if it is inevitable that the prohibited outcome will occur as a result of the "psik reisha", it is forbidden, but if it is not inevitable, then it is permitted even in "psik reisha". This is written by the Shiltey Gibborim in Chapter 3 of the section on weaving, see there, and see also the Ran and Rashba).

In all the labors of Shabbat, there are specific measures, and each will be clarified in its place. And half a measure—this is forbidden by Torah law, as with all Torah prohibitions, except that one does not incur lashes for half a measure. Certainly, one is not executed nor brings a sacrifice for half a measure, but nevertheless, its prohibition is from the Torah (Rashi 73b, s.v. "And"). However, in the prohibition of transferring (objects on Shabbat), there is a difference: For transferring from a private domain to a public domain, which involves both uprooting and placing down, if one performs uprooting without placing down or placing down without uprooting—there is no Torah prohibition, but there is a Rabbinic prohibition, and this is explicitly stated in the first Mishnah of Shabbat and in the Gemara there. And for carrying four cubits in a public domain, it is evident throughout Shabbat that less than four cubits—it is permitted to carry even by Rabbinic law. One must understand why in the prohibition of transferring there is no Torah prohibition of half a measure. One can say that since the reason for half a measure is because it is fit to combine, as written at the beginning of the last chapter of Yoma (73b), and in transferring this does not apply, since when one transfers from a private domain to a public domain, the uprooting is fit to combine when placing, but placing is not fit to combine, as is evident. And since there is no Torah prohibition of half a measure in placing, it follows that there is no Torah prohibition of half a measure in transferring. Nevertheless, the Rabbis forbade it, because through uprooting one can come to be liable for a sin-offering, and thus the Talmud at the beginning of our tractate refers to it as such; see there. And if one carries two cubits in a public domain and stops, it is not fit to combine further, as placing one's body is like placing an object, and therefore even by Rabbinic law, half a measure is not forbidden. (And in the Tosefta Beitzah, chapter 4, halacha 2, it implies clearly that half a measure on Shabbat is forbidden only by Rabbinic law; see there, and it requires great examination. And it must be said that it is not precise, and according to what we will write at the beginning of section 343).

Rambam writes in Chapter 1, Law 16: "Any labor that an individual can do alone, and two people do it together, whether one does part of it and the other does part of it, or whether both do it together from beginning to end - they are exempt. But if neither of them can do it alone until they join forces, both are liable, and [the measure of liability] is the same for both. If one has the strength to carry this beam alone, and the other cannot carry it alone, and they both carry it together: the first one who can do it alone is liable, and the second one is merely assisting, and one who assists is not liable at all, and similarly in all such cases." Thus far is his wording.

The Aruch Hashulchan further writes: "All those who cause damage are exempt. How so? If someone injures an animal or a person with the intent to destroy, or if someone tears clothes, burns them, or breaks utensils with the intent to destroy, he is exempt." This is his language. However, it is rabbinically forbidden, as all exemptions on Shabbat are exempt but forbidden, as has been explained. He carefully states "with the intent to destroy," because we find that injuring (chovel) is liable, as it is stated in the beginning of chapter "Eight Sheratzim" (Shabbat 107a), and as the Rambam writes in Chapter 8 (Halacha 9), see there. But there it is not with the intent to destroy, such as if his intention was to capture them in that manner. Likewise, tearing that is not with the intent to destroy, such as tearing for a deceased or tearing in anger and through the tearing his anger is settled, the Rambam rules in Chapter 10 (Halacha 10) that he is liable, see there, as he follows his opinion, ruling like Rabbi Yehuda in a labor that is not needed for its own sake. But according to most authorities, who rule like Rabbi Shimon, he is exempt even in such a case, and this is explicit in the Gemara (Shabbat 105b), see there.

He also wrote: "If one digs a pit and only needs the dirt, this is considered destructive and he is exempt, even though he performed labor, since his intention was to cause damage — he is exempt," thus far his words. And this is also necessary according to his approach, because according to the majority of the decisors he is exempt regardless, as it is a labor that is not needed for its own sake.
