And know, that in the Gemara (Shabbat 73b) it is proven that it is only in a house that it is considered destructive and not in a field. However, this is certainly not specific, but rather it is the usual manner of the matter, and therefore, since it is written "and his intention was to cause damage," it follows that in a place where his intention is not to cause damage, he is liable according to his approach (see Magid Mishneh and Kesef Mishneh).

He further wrote: "Anyone who destroys something with the intention to repair is liable. How so? If one demolishes in order to build in its place, or erases in order to write in the place that was erased, or digs a pit in order to lay foundations within it, or anything similar - they are liable, and the measure is the same as that of repairing." This is the end of his words. Now, in the Gemara (Shabbat 31b), it is explicitly implied that this is only according to Rabbi Yehuda, who holds one liable for a labor that is not needed for its own sake. But according to Rabbi Shimon, even if one demolishes in order to build in its place, they are not liable, unless by demolishing they improve the second building more than if there had never been a building there at all, such as when one burns wood and extinguishes it to make charcoal, see there. And according to the Rambam, this is correct, as he rules according to Rabbi Yehuda. Nevertheless, even according to Rabbi Shimon, it is necessary to say this, because demolishing in order to build is one of the primary labors, and in this case it is impossible to say that it repairs more by demolishing than if there had never been a building there at all. And it must be said that in such a case - even according to Rabbi Shimon, one is liable. And even though this is like a labor that is not needed for its own sake, obviously, still, in the Mishkan, there was certainly demolishing in order to build, and therefore one is liable (Tosafot there, s.v. 'and demolishes'). And here we have explained a little of the many general and primary laws of Shabbat with the help of Heaven, and give to a wise person and they will become wiser still.

Since the Torah blessed and sanctified the Sabbath day, it is therefore obligatory for every Jew to honor this holy day and to delight in it, as the prophet said (Isaiah 58:13): "And you shall call the Sabbath a delight, the holy of the Lord, honorable." And this is the language of Maimonides in Maimonides' Laws of the Sabbath, chapter 30 (halacha 1): "Four things were said about the Sabbath, two from the Torah, and two from the words of the Scribes, and they are explained by the prophets. From the Torah: 'Remember' and 'Keep'; and those explained by the prophets: honor and delight, etc. What is honor? This is what the Sages said (Shabbat 25b), that it is a commandment for a person to wash his face, hands, and feet in hot water on the eve of the Sabbath, because of the honor of the Sabbath, and to wrap himself in a fringed garment, and to sit with solemnity, anticipating the Sabbath, like someone who goes out to greet the king. The early Sages used to gather their students on the eve of the Sabbath, wrap themselves, and say: 'Come, let us go out to greet the Sabbath Queen.' Until here is his language. And now we gather in synagogues and study houses, and say five psalms, from 'Come, let us sing joyfully to the Lord' (Psalms 95:1) until after 'The Lord reigns; let the peoples tremble' (Psalms 99:1), because these psalms are about the future, when one will say to another: 'Come, let us sing joyfully to the Lord' (Radak), and then 'The Lord reigns,' meaning the fulfillment of the scripture that says (Zechariah 14:9): 'On that day the Lord will be one and His name one.' And because the Sabbath is a hint to that time, a day that is entirely Sabbath, we will then sing to the Lord a new song; for all the songs are in the feminine language, and the song of the future is in the masculine language, as stated in the Midrashim. Therefore, we say these psalms. And we also say the psalm of the seven voices (Psalms 29), because it also hints at the seventh millennium, a day that is entirely Sabbath, and then 'The Lord sat enthroned at the Flood; the Lord sits enthroned, King forever,' and then 'He will bless His people with peace'; and the Sabbath is a semblance of the World to Come, and therefore we say it. And these are six psalms, corresponding to the six days of the week, all of which draw their influence from the Sabbath, for it is the source of blessing. And afterwards, we say the song 'Lecha Dodi' to greet the bride, and at its conclusion, we turn our faces to the west and say: 'Enter in peace, crown of her husband, enter, O bride, enter, O bride,' and we say this standing. And this is like the early Sages, who would say: 'Come, let us go out to greet the Sabbath Queen.' And afterwards, we say 'A psalm, a song for the Sabbath day' (Psalms 92:1), and this is the main acceptance of the Sabbath (and the holy Shelah wrote in his prayer book, to be careful to say 'A psalm, a song for the Sabbath day' before sunset, for if not, the harmful spirits created on the eve of the Sabbath at twilight are aroused from their place to cause harm, see there and examine well).

Out of respect for Shabbat, one should wear clean clothing, and weekday clothes should not be like Shabbat clothes. If one does not have a change of clothes, they should let down their garment (Shabbat 113a), meaning they should let their garments hang down to appear longer, as this is the custom of wealthy individuals who sit in their homes and do not need to lift their garments from the ground for work, and it is an honor for Shabbat (Rashi). It is a decree from Ezra that people should wash their clothes on Thursday in honor of Shabbat (Bava Kamma 82a), and they should not wait until Erev Shabbat, so that Erev Shabbat will be free for the preparation of Shabbat (Shitah Mekubetzet). Nowadays, all Jews change their shirt for Shabbat, and also change other clothes, including the hat, to signify the honor of Shabbat. They also go to the bathhouse in honor of Shabbat. Many also immerse in a mikvah to purify themselves for the sanctity of Shabbat. For all that is done in honor of the Shabbat Queen, the reward is very great.

The Rambam wrote (ibid., Halacha 7): "What is considered delight? This that the Sages said that one must prepare a particularly rich dish and a fragrant drink for Shabbat, all according to a person's means. And whoever increases their expenditure for Shabbat and prepares good and plentiful foods is praiseworthy. But if one cannot afford it, even if they only make a simple dish or something similar in honor of Shabbat, this is considered Shabbat delight. One is not obligated to trouble themselves or to borrow from others in order to increase their Shabbat meals. The early Sages said (Shabbat 118a): 'Make your Shabbat like a weekday and do not become dependent on others.'" Thus far is his wording.

And behold, what is written, that the Sages said to prepare a dish that is especially rich, is not found. In the Gemara (Shabbat 118a) it states: How does one delight in it? With a dish of beets, large fish, and heads of garlic, see there. However, the Rambam holds that this is certainly not specific, and if one does not like fish, what should he do? Rather, the main point is a dish that he enjoys and it should be especially rich, as is the way of the wealthy. The Gemara mentioned according to what was in their days, that these dishes were beloved to them. And there are also those now who are particular about having fish in every Shabbat meal, and there is a hidden reason for this. And one should not have less than two cooked dishes (Magen Avraham, sub-paragraph 1).

And this is what is written that one does not need to ask from others, even though at the beginning of the second chapter of Beitzah it is stated that all of a person's provisions are fixed for him from Rosh Hashanah, except for the expenses of Shabbat and Yom Tov, for if one adds [to their expenses] — they add to him, and it is said there that the Holy One, blessed be He, says: "Borrow on My account and I will repay." However, this all applies to someone who has some kind of business, and therefore, even if he currently does not have [money], he can borrow and hope in God that he will profit and repay. But someone who has no business at all, it was said about him: "Make your Shabbat like a weekday and do not become dependent on others." And what Rambam wrote, that one does not need to ask from others, either he meant to request a gift, or if he meant it in the sense of asking [for a loan], he was speaking in such a context. And on this it was said in Shabbat there: even a little bit for the honor of Shabbat — this is considered delight, see there. And our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 1: "Even someone who depends on others, if he has a little of his own — he needs to make an effort to honor Shabbat. And they only said 'make your Shabbat like a weekday' etc., for someone who is in extremely difficult circumstances. Therefore, one should cut back on other days in order to honor Shabbat," until here is his language. And he holds that someone who depends entirely on others, that is, his livelihood comes from the communal fund of the city or from charity — this one does not need anything. But if he also earns a little himself — about this they said: even a little bit, and he cuts back on other days and saves for Shabbat. (See Taz and Magen Avraham. And what Magen Avraham wrote regarding the third meal, the main point is that even the poor need to eat, as Rambam wrote in his commentary on the Mishnah. And regarding what was said that they borrow with interest for the needs of the Shabbat meal, this is according to permission, like from a Cuthean, or with an investment document. And the commentator in the Jerusalem Talmud, Moed Katan chapter 2, end of halacha 3, wrote about rabbinic interest, see there, and it is a great leniency, and the clarified opinion is as I wrote, and so wrote the Pri Megadim. And the novelty is that it is proper to do so for the sake of the mitzvah) (And see Pesachim 112b, and it needs examination, and pay close attention).

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote: "It is customary to knead the amount required for challah at home, to make from it loaves to break bread on them on Shabbat and Yom Tov, and this is in honor of Shabbat and Yom Tov and should not be changed," thus far his words. Additionally, to fulfill the mitzvah of challah which is incumbent upon the woman, as this is one of her commandments, because she lost the challah of the world, which was Adam the first man, whom she caused to sin, as stated in the Midrash (Rashi Shabbat 32a "I am"). And it is one of the three sins which cause women to die, as it is taught in Shabbat. All the more so those who eat non-Jewish bread throughout the week - should eat kosher bread on Shabbat (see Magen Avraham subparagraph 4). He also wrote: "There are those who wrote that in some places it is customary to eat a dish called pashtida on Friday night, as a remembrance of the manna which was covered above and below. But I have not seen a reason to be concerned about this," thus far his words. And the pashtida is similar to our kreplach, which is covered with dough above and below, and in between is meat. And it is stated in the Gemara at the beginning of the second chapter of Beitzah, that Shammai would eat all his days in honor of Shabbat. If he found a nice animal, he would say: this is for Shabbat. If he found another nicer one, he would set aside the second and eat the first, see there. And it is good if one sets aside good food for Shabbat, as this way one always remembers the day of Shabbat and honors it. (See Magen Avraham who wrote that if the price of fish becomes expensive, it is proper to enact that fish should not be purchased, see there).

Know that besides the thirty-nine primary categories of labor, there are many other rabbinic prohibitions on Shabbat which are derived from verses, as it is stated in the Mekhilta on the verse "and in all things that I have said to you, take heed" (Exodus 23:13): "Why is this stated? Because it says, 'You shall not do any work'; this refers only to things that are classified as work. How do we know about things that are rabbinic prohibitions? Therefore, it says, 'and in all things that I have said to you, take heed.'" This is the language of the Mekhilta. And in the portion of Ki Tisa, the Mekhilta states: "However, you shall observe My Sabbaths" (Exodus 31:13), why is this stated? Because it says, 'You shall not do any work'; this refers only to things that are classified as work. How do we know about rabbinic prohibitions? Therefore, it says, 'observe My Sabbaths,' to include things that are rabbinic prohibitions." This is the language of the Mekhilta.

And it appears to me that both are necessary, for there are two types of rabbinic prohibitions on Shabbat: one, which is forbidden for a person to do himself; and the second, just as it is forbidden for him to do it himself, so too it is forbidden for him to instruct a non-Jew to do it. (And indeed, the Sefer Mitzvot Gadol in the laws of Yom Tov brings the Mekhilta from the portion of Bo on the verse "no work shall be done on them," which means you shall not do it, nor your friend, nor a non-Jew – see there. This is brought by the Taz at the end of this section and by the Beit Yosef in section 244. However, the version of the Gra is the opposite and reads: "but it shall be done" etc. – see there. And regarding the version of the Sefer Mitzvot Gadol, I am perplexed, for later there Rabbi Yonatan says: it is not necessary etc., and isn’t it an a fortiori argument: if for the stringent Shabbat one is not warned about the work of a non-Jew, how much more so for the lenient Yom Tov etc. This is the end of his language. From here it is clearly explained according to the version of the Gra).

And so wrote the Rambam at the beginning of Chapter 21, and these are his words: "It is stated in the Torah 'you shall rest': even from things that are not work, one is obligated to rest from them. And there are many things that the Sages prohibited because of 'resting,'" thus far his words. And behold, we find that the prophets mentioned these rests. Isaiah said (Isaiah 58:13) "If you restrain your foot on the Sabbath from pursuing your affairs on My holy day, and you call the Sabbath a delight and the Lord’s holy day honored; and you honor it by not engaging in your own ways, seeking your own needs or speaking of mundane matters"; and Nehemiah son of Hacaliah (Nehemiah 13:16) cried out about the Tyrians bringing fish and selling them on the Sabbath to Israelites, and it is written: "And I quarreled with the nobles of Judah and said to them, 'What is this evil thing that you are doing, profaning the Sabbath day?'" Behold, buying something on the Sabbath is considered a desecration of the Sabbath.

And so wrote the Ritva in the name of the Ramban, that it is a received tradition among us that the prohibitions of Shabbos rest (shvut) are not like other rabbinic prohibitions, but rather they are like Torah prohibitions. And the proof for this is, if it were not so, but rather we say that from the Torah only actual labor is forbidden, but business dealings are permitted, then would this be called a day of rest and cessation, where everyone would engage in their trade, sit in their shops, and buy and sell? This is indeed an astonishing notion! Rather, the main point is that for actual labor, the Torah mandated stoning, but for the shvut prohibitions, it did not mandate stoning. However, their prohibition is a complete prohibition, like a Torah prohibition.

Behold, regarding resting on Shabbat, there is a concept of "telling a non-Jew to do work" - which is a rabbinic prohibition. This means that any work that we are forbidden to do ourselves, we are also forbidden to tell a non-Jew to do for us, whether we tell him on Shabbat, or before Shabbat to do it on Shabbat, or on Shabbat to do it after Shabbat, as Maimonides writes at the beginning of Chapter 6. He writes that even if one does not need the work on Shabbat, it is prohibited so that Shabbat should not become light in their eyes and they might come to do it themselves. See there.

But Rashi, of blessed memory, in the first chapter of Avodah Zarah (15a, s.v. "since") writes as follows: "And the reason it is forbidden for a Jew to tell a non-Jew 'do this for me' is because of 'finding your own pleasure and speaking words' - speaking is forbidden." Thus far is his wording. And at the end of the first chapter there, he explains another reason, because it appears as if he is his agent. See there.

Both reasons are necessary: for the reason of "speaking words" - the prohibition is only when he tells him on Shabbat itself, but if he tells him before Shabbat, this does not apply, and in such a case the prohibition is because of agency. And although a non-Jew cannot be an agent, nevertheless, as a stringency, there is agency (Bava Metzia 71b).

The Rambam writes in Chapter 6, Law 8: "A Jew who tells a non-Jew to do this work for him on Shabbat, even though he has transgressed and we flog him with lashes of rebellion, it is permitted for him to benefit from that work after Shabbat, after waiting the amount of time it would take to perform that work. And they only forbade the waiting period in all cases because of this reason: if you say it is permitted immediately, then perhaps he will tell him to do it, and he will find the matter ready immediately. And since they forbade it until the time it would take to perform the work has passed, he does not gain anything," thus far his language. And even if the non-Jew did it by himself for the Jew, and the Jew did not ask him at all to do it, nevertheless it is forbidden on that day, and in the evening, one must wait the amount of time it would take to perform the work, as will be explained in Siman 325 with several detailed laws about this. (And the wage for Shabbat is completely forbidden, as will be explained in Section 16).

And if a Jew is obligated to protest when he sees a non-Jew doing work for him, and the non-Jew is doing it in a concealed place—since if it were in public, it is obvious that he is obligated to protest even in a place where it is technically permitted by the basic law, as will be explained in this section. But even when he is doing it in a concealed place, such as in his own home or the like, it is stated in the Jerusalem Talmud (Chapter 1, Halacha 9), and this is its language: "If he gave his garment to a non-Jewish launderer, and he came and found him working on it on Shabbat—it is forbidden. Rabbi Yudan said: He should tell him not to work. This applies when it is for a benefit. But if it is for wages—he is preoccupied with his own work." Thus far is its language.

It is explained from this Jerusalem Talmud that whenever the non-Jew is doing it only for the benefit of the Jew, the Jew is obligated to protest. But when the non-Jew is doing it for his own wages, the Jew is not obligated to protest, and so it is written in the Mordechai's glosses in the first chapter of Shabbat. The details of these laws will be explained with the help of Heaven in Siman 252; see there. (And what is stated on page 121a that one does not need to protest when the non-Jew comes to extinguish a fire—this is because he knows he will be compensated well and is doing it for his own sake. Furthermore, they were lenient in the case of a fire, as will be explained in Siman 334).

Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote in Section 1: "A person should not rent out his bathhouse to a non-Jew, because it is associated with the name of the Jew, and [the non-Jew] does work in it on Shabbat. Generally, a bathhouse is not used for sharecropping, and people will say that all the profit belongs to the Jew, and he hired the non-Jew for a certain amount per day, making it seem as if the non-Jew is working on behalf of the Jew. However, it is permitted with a field, as it is common practice to lease a field for sharecropping. Even though it is known that it belongs to a Jew, people assume that it was leased for sharecropping and that [the non-Jew] is working for himself. An oven has the same law as a bathhouse, and a mill has the same law as a field," end of his words. And Rabbeinu Rema added, saying that even though the non-Jew took it only for a third or a quarter, and the Jew benefits from the work done on Shabbat, it is still permitted because the non-Jew is working for his own sake, end of his words.

And to explain the matter, the fundamental principle is that if a non-Jew rents something from a Jew for a year or two and pays the Jew a fixed amount each year, and the whole business operation is his, it is permissible for him to work on Shabbat, because he is working for himself. For the Jew, it makes no difference whether he works on Shabbat or not. Moreover, even if the non-Jew takes it from the Jew on a sharecropping basis—half, a third, or a quarter, as is the way fields are taken on a sharecropping arrangement—even though the Jew's portion increases from what is done on Shabbat, it is still permissible, because he is working for himself and not for the Jew. The fact that the Jew's portion increases as a result does not matter, since this is an incidental benefit, and it is merely an indirect cause, where the non-Jew causes the Jew to profit. And even regarding a full-fledged labor on Shabbat, it was said (Shabbat 120b): "You shall not do any manner of work"—it is the act of doing that is forbidden, but indirect cause is permitted, see there, and certainly in this case. Thus, there is no prohibition if the non-Jew rents from the Jew the bathhouse, the field, the oven, or the mill, and takes the profits for himself, while paying the Jew a fixed amount, or taking a share—half, a third, or a quarter.

But if all the profit belongs to the Jew, and he pays the non-Jew for his labor a certain amount per day or per week or per year, it is prohibited by law. And even though in this case too the non-Jew is working for himself to receive his wages and is acting on his own behalf, nevertheless, the primary business is being conducted for the Jew, since the non-Jew himself does not receive any profit, only a fixed wage. Therefore, the non-Jew is considered the agent of the Jew to conduct the business for him, and he is paid for his agency. And since the agent of a person is like the person himself, it is as if the Jew himself is doing the work on Shabbat. However, when the non-Jew has a share in the actual profit of the business, he is not considered the agent of the Jew but is primarily doing the business for himself, and the Jew benefits incidentally. (And what is written in the Shulchan Aruch: "And he hired the non-Jew for such and such per day" applies equally to a year).

Nevertheless, our Sages said (at the end of the first chapter of Avodah Zarah) that it is forbidden to lease a bathhouse even under a sharecropping agreement, but a field is permitted. The reason is that it is customary to lease a field under such agreements, so there is no suspicion. However, it is not customary to lease a bathhouse under a sharecropping agreement because its income is entirely concealed. The income from a bathhouse comes from those who enter to bathe and pay a certain amount, and the income is minimal, and who knows how many will bathe? Therefore, it is customary for the income to go to the owners, who then hire someone to sit and collect the fees, leasing it by the year, month, or day. Hence, even though it is now leased under a sharecropping agreement, people will still suspect that all the profit belongs to the owner. But for a field, they will not suspect him. The poskim (decisors of Jewish law) said that a mill has the same status as a field because it is customary to lease a mill under a sharecropping agreement. An oven, where one who bakes in it pays a certain amount, has the same status as a bathhouse because it is not customary to lease it under a sharecropping agreement. (And because the prohibitions of Shabbat are very severe, akin to Torah prohibitions as we have written, our Sages decreed even on the suspicion of violating it. It is necessary to make such a fence, otherwise breaches will lead to more breaches, as these matters are public.)

One of our Rabbis wrote (Ran, end of the first chapter there): From this we learn that since the non-Jew has a share in the produce of the field, even though the Jew benefits, it is permitted because the non-Jew works for his own benefit, and the Jew's benefit comes incidentally. This is not similar to a partnership between a Jew and a non-Jew, as will be discussed later in Siman 245, which is prohibited, because there the work of the field is also the responsibility of the Jew. But here, the entire responsibility lies on the non-Jew and not on the Jew at all. All the more so, it is permitted to rent one's field to a non-Jew for a fixed amount, because in such a case, when the non-Jew works, he does so for his own benefit, and the Jew does not benefit at all, etc. 

Regarding contracting, such as when a non-Jew takes upon himself to do all the work of the Jew's field for a specified amount: whether it is permitted for the Jew to allow him to work on Shabbats and holidays: there is an opinion that permits it, because since we say that sharecropping is permitted, contracting should also be permitted, as the Jew does not benefit from the work done on Shabbat at all (for if it is not done on Shabbat, it will be done on a weekday). But there is another opinion that contracting in this manner is prohibited, as it is not similar to sharecropping. In sharecropping, since the sharecropper receives a portion of the produce, people do not say that he is a hired worker. But in this case, where the owners take all the produce, it appears to people as if he is a hired worker, etc. And so wrote the Rambam, of blessed memory, in Chapter 6, etc., until here is his language. Those who prohibit compare this to contracting for building a house, which is prohibited according to most authorities, as will be explained in Siman 244. Those who permit it hold that it is not similar to a house, where the usual practice is to build with hired workers, which is not the case with fields (and the Shulchan Aruch there simply prohibits it).

And even according to those who permit it, this is only in a field, because it makes no difference to the Jew what is done on Shabbat, since he must do all the work of his field, and if it is not done on Shabbat, it will be done on a weekday, and the Jew derives no benefit from this. But in a bathhouse, a mill, or an oven, everyone agrees that it is forbidden by contractual work, for in these cases all the benefit accrues to the Jew from what is done on Shabbat. The work is not like in a field, but whenever people come to bathe, grind, or bake, the non-Jew must attend to it, and the non-Jew's wage is the same whether it is much or little. Therefore, what is done on Shabbat is primarily beneficial to the Jew. And so agreed the great later authorities (Magen Avraham and Taz, section 2), and even in a field they agreed to the prohibition. Therefore, one must be careful in any business handed over to a non-Jew, that the non-Jew should have a share in the actual profit of the business, such as when he sells, he should receive a certain amount from each measure or from each loaf, and similarly in all such cases.

Our master the Beit Yosef wrote in paragraph 2: "Even a bathhouse or an oven, if one rented them year after year and it became known that he does not hire workers but rather rents them out, and similarly if it is the custom of most people in that place to rent them out or to give them as sharecropping - it is permitted to rent them out or to give them as sharecropping," until here are his words. And one of these reasons is sufficient, as explained by the words of the Tur who wrote in the name of the Gaon, that if one rented them out year after year - it is permitted, and according to this, he wrote in the name of the Rosh that when this is the custom, it is permitted. Similarly, the Rambam wrote in Chapter 6, Law 15, that anything identified with a Jewish owner, and it is not the custom of most people in that place to rent it out or to give it as sharecropping - it is forbidden to rent it out to a non-Jew, because they will work on Shabbat and it will be referred to by the name of its owner, until here are his words. Thus, it is explicit that if the custom of the place is to rent it out or to give it as sharecropping – it is permitted. (And one should not ask: how did he act in the first years before it became known? For one can say that at that time it was indeed not used on Shabbat and holidays).

And our master, the Rema, wrote: Even in a prohibited place, if the bathhouse or oven is not owned by a Jew, but rather rented from a non-Jew and then re-rented to another non-Jew – it is permitted, for the name of the Jew is not called upon it. Thus are his words. In truth, this reasoning applies not only to renting from a non-Jew, but also to purchasing from a non-Jew. However, in the case of purchasing, the permission is only if the matter has not yet aged and become established. But if the matter has aged – the name of the Jew is indeed called upon it. Similarly, if the Jew enters this house immediately, it is forbidden, because immediately the name of the Jew is called upon it. But with renting – in all cases it is permitted, for everyone knows that it belongs to the non-Jew and the Jew has rented it. (See Magen Avraham, subparagraph 3, and according to what I wrote, it is clear, and see Eliyah Rabbah, subparagraph 7). And likewise with purchasing, even immediately, if he purchased publicly, such as in courts, etc. – it is immediately forbidden, as opposed to renting (Tosefet Shabbat, subparagraph 3).

He also wrote: "Similarly, if there is a bathhouse in a residence, and only those in the household bathe in it, and they know that the renter is not Jewish, it is permitted," thus far his words. This means that the prohibition of renting a bathhouse to a non-Jew applies only when the bathhouse is in his courtyard, and others besides the household members bathe in it. In such a case, those who see the bathhouse being heated on Shabbat will assume that a Jew instructed the heating. Or even if only household members bathe in it, if the bathhouse is situated on the street, it is also forbidden, as everyone sees it being heated on Shabbat, leading to suspicion. But if it is in his courtyard, not everyone sees it. And regarding the concern that someone entering the courtyard might see it, that is inconsequential, as it is not widely known that there is a bathhouse there, given that only household members bathe there. Similarly, if the bathhouse is in someone else's domain, neither in his courtyard nor on the street, then even if others bathe there, it is permitted, as it is not widely known that the bathhouse belongs to a specific person; only the neighbors know, and they know it was rented to a non-Jew. This is the opinion of our teacher, the Rema. Some are stringent, permitting only when it is in someone else's domain and only household members bathe there; otherwise, it is forbidden. However, many great authorities agreed that one should not be stringent in a rabbinic prohibition (Eliyah Rabbah section 8 and Tosefet Shabbat section 4), and it is explicitly stated in the Mordechai in the chapter "Kol Kitvei" that when the bathhouse is in someone else's domain, it is permitted. (What the Taz wrote, that regarding appearances, even in the innermost rooms it is forbidden, applies to a biblical prohibition. And what he wrote in the name of Sefer Mitzvot Gadol that this is a biblical prohibition, we have already explained that it is very stringent. But who does not know that this is a rabbinic issue? And what he wrote about being concerned for guests is not relevant to something within one's home. And what the Magen Avraham wrote in section 4, that people will see smoke coming out, we have already explained that this is inconsequential, as they will attribute it to something else. The Gra (Gaon of Vilna) leans towards the Magen Avraham’s view, see there. The main ruling follows the Rema, and study this well.)

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (the Rema) wrote: If one transgressed and rented it out in a place where it is forbidden, some say the rent is permitted, and some say it is forbidden, and the main opinion is that it is forbidden. Thus far his words. The great authorities agree that in a place where it is forbidden by law to rent it out, the rent is forbidden. But in a place where it is permitted by law, and the prohibition is only due to appearance, the rent is permitted (Beit Chadash, Magen Avraham subparagraph 5, Eliyah Rabbah, the Gaon Rabbi Zalman, and Tosefet Shabbat). This will be further clarified with Heaven's help in Siman 245; see there.

Even in a place where it is permitted to rent out a bathhouse, a mill, an oven, or similar items to a non-Jew, such as when they are rented out year after year, or this is the local custom, as has been explained - nevertheless, one should not rent them to him on the eve of Shabbat, for reasons which will be explained in Siman 246. Similarly, one should not rent to him by the day or by the month at a rate of such-and-such per day, because if so, he would be receiving payment specifically for Shabbat. One must not earn money on Shabbat in a way that it is noticeable that he is being paid specifically for Shabbat, due to the prohibition of buying and selling. Instead, he should rent it to him at a rate of such-and-such per week, or such-and-such per month, or such-and-such per year, so that the payment for Shabbat is included within the payment for the other days, and it does not appear as payment specifically for Shabbat. Payment for Shabbat is forbidden even after the fact (Perisha).

In the previous section, it was explained regarding the business dealings of a Jew that are set up for profit, such as fields, baths, ovens, and mills – how it is permissible to rent them to a non-Jew. And this permission is only in the case of sharecropping, or if the non-Jew rents them completely and pays the Jew a fixed amount annually. However, if the non-Jew rents on a contract basis, meaning the earnings go to the owners and the owners pay him a fixed amount annually – there is a disagreement, and many prohibit it, and this is the main ruling, as explained there in paragraph 11. Even those who permit it only allow it in the case of a field, as explained there in paragraph 12, see there.

In this section, we will clarify matters that are not related to business profits but are simply human needs, such as clothes, shoes, building houses, and similar items. If a non-Jew performs these tasks for a Jew—who hired him to sew his garment or make his shoes, whether using the Jew’s materials or his own—the law is as follows: If he was hired by the day, meaning he is paid for each day he works a certain amount, it is prohibited in all matters, even if he does the work in his own home. However, when the work is done on a contractual basis, meaning that a set amount is given for sewing the garment, making the shoes, or building the house, in such cases involving movable items—like clothes and shoes—it is permitted. This is different from the previous section, where the Jew profits from the work done on Shabbat as it is a business matter. Here, the Jew does not profit at all; what difference does it make to the Jew whether the work is done on Shabbat or a weekday? The task must be completed regardless. Even if the Jew prefers the work to be finished on Shabbat so he can wear it immediately after Shabbat, as long as he does not explicitly instruct the non-Jew to work on Shabbat, the non-Jew is doing it for his own benefit, to complete his work and receive his payment. What concern is it to us if this results in a benefit for the Jew? An incidental benefit is permitted even in profit-making, as explained in the previous section, paragraph 8 (see there, and also as written by the Gaon Rabbi Zalman). This is specifically when the work is done in the non-Jew’s home; however, if it is done in the Jew’s home, it is prohibited. It is also forbidden to tell the non-Jew to work on Shabbat, and the contract must be made before Shabbat. More on this will be explained in section 252. But for a day laborer, it is completely prohibited because the labor is not his own, and his intention is not to complete the task but to work for the Jew on that day. Thus, his entire intention is to work for the Jew, and this is forbidden.

And all this applies to work with detached materials, which the non-Jew does in his own home, and the matter is not well-known, and not everyone recognizes that this work belongs to a specific Jew. And even if some know about it - we do not concern ourselves with it, since it is done discreetly within his home (Magen Avraham subsection 2). But regarding work with attached materials, such as building a house for him - both Rambam in Chapter 6 and the majority of our sages agree that it is forbidden even on a contract basis. This is not similar to a field, where we permitted sharecropping and the like in the previous section, because a field is generally maintained under a sharecropping arrangement, unlike buildings, which are mostly worked on by day laborers, and thus there is suspicion. And even though one of our great sages thought to permit building on a contract basis - he did not do so in practice, and the majority of our sages agreed on the prohibition, and so is the law.

The primary distinction is not between detached and attached items, but rather between private and public activities. Since, as a rule, detached items are handled privately, and attached items necessarily involve public activity, we distinguish between the two. In reality, detached items handled publicly, such as the construction of a ship known to belong to a Jew, are treated like attached items and are prohibited. However, with attached items, everything is prohibited. The construction of a ship is prohibited when done in a well-known place where many people see it. But if not done in a well-known place, it is permitted, as will be explained in Siman 252. Even attached items in places where they are not seen, such as beyond the Shabbat boundary, are permitted, as will be explained, and all the more so with detached items.

And this is the language of our teacher, the Beit Yosef, in Section 1: "A person may make an agreement with a non-Jew regarding work and set a price, and the non-Jew does the work for himself. Even though the non-Jew works on Shabbat, it is permitted. In what case are these matters stated? When it is done privately, so that not everyone recognizes that this work being done on Shabbat is for a Jew. But if it was known and publicized, it is forbidden, because when one sees the non-Jew working, he does not know that an agreement was made, and he will say that so-and-so hired the non-Jew to do work for him on Shabbat. Therefore, if one makes an agreement with a non-Jew to build his courtyard or his wall or to harvest his field, if the work is in the city or within the boundaries, it is forbidden to let them do the work on Shabbat, due to onlookers who do not know that an agreement was made," thus far his words, and this is from the words of Maimonides in Chapter 6. And he was stringent regarding the harvesting of a field, even though it is permitted to sharecrop a field in the previous section - this is when he truly takes a portion of the produce. But here, when they will see that the Jew takes all the produce and see that he is not a sharecropper, they will suspect him of being a day laborer (Magen Avraham, Subsection 5). And Maimonides, according to his view, forbids contracting even in a field, as explained there in Section 11. And it appears to me that even according to those who permit it there - this is in contracting the entire work of the field, plowing, sowing, and harvesting. But harvesting alone - it is customary to do by day laborers, and it is like building a house.

Rabbi Moses Isserles (Rema) wrote that even if one lives among non-Jews, one must be concerned about guests who come there or his household members suspecting him. This is his language. And even though in the case of the bathhouse in the previous section we did not worry about the suspicion of household members, this is because they know the truth, that the non-Jew was hired by him. But in the case of building, they think the homeowner hired them for days and not by contract (see sub-section 7). Additionally, in the case of work connected to the ground, they were very stringent on Shabbat, and therefore we are concerned even for guests, even though they are not very common, as it is understood. And the Jerusalem Talmud in the third chapter of Shevi'it says that the concern of appearance is only for the townspeople and not for others. Nevertheless, on Shabbat they were stringent (see sub-section 6). Therefore, in the case of building, it is forbidden in any manner, even if one lives alone in the city and there are no other Jews there. And even if it is not yet known that the house belongs to him, nevertheless, there is concern for the neighbors who know it is his (see sub-section 4 there). And perhaps in the case of one who is alone in his city, there is room to be lenient in such a situation.

If the construction is outside the city's boundary, and there is no other city within the boundary of the place where the work is being done – it is permitted, as there is no suspicion involved. Even if there is just one Jew living within the boundary of the work area – it is prohibited, as they were stringent within the boundary even if it is far from the city, and it is not common for many people to go there. Regarding vows, the boundary is not considered part of the city, as explained in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 217. Nevertheless, concerning Shabbat, they were stringent because of the concern that an individual might go there and see. Similarly, if a single Jew lives within the boundary of the work area – it is prohibited for this reason. However, outside the boundary, even by one step – it is permitted, and even though those standing within the boundary can see – they were not stringent about this, as the Sages did not differentiate in this matter. Later, in Siman 537, it will be explained regarding a non-Jew who brings manure into a Jew’s field and does so on his own without receiving payment for it – there is no need to protest against him, as it is not considered a complete form of labor. But in the case of complete labor – even in such a situation, one is obligated to protest against him.

And know that there are those who sought to find a leniency in the construction of synagogues and study halls in times of pressing need, allowing them to be built on Shabbat by non-Jews, reasoning that for communal needs there is no suspicion. But Heaven forbid to say so! For do the public themselves hire the workers?! It is the appointed official who hires them! Moreover, this reasoning is only said in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 141, regarding protruding images that are openly visible to the public, because there is a concern of idolatry. But in a matter where the prohibition is not known to all and is not public – perhaps we do not say this reasoning. Furthermore, there is no greater desecration of the Name than this in the eyes of the nations, that we should allow construction on the holy Shabbat. (See Magen Avraham, Subsection 8, regarding the cleaning of garbage from the streets, see there. And certainly, if Jews hire workers to clean the streets on Shabbat – it is certainly forbidden. However, if the city official hires them, even at the expense of the Jews – it is permitted, because the work is done by order of the city official and his name is associated with it).

It is stated in the Jerusalem Talmud, the first chapter of Shabbat: "It was taught: Non-Jewish craftsmen who perform work for Jews inside the house of a Jew – it is forbidden, but inside their own houses – it is permitted. Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar said: In what case are we speaking? When it is on a contract basis, but on a daily wage basis – it is forbidden. In what case are we speaking? Concerning detached items, but with attached items – it is forbidden. However, in a different city, in any case, it is permitted. What does 'in any case' mean? Whether detached or attached, provided it is on a contract basis. And the halacha follows Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar," thus far the language of the Jerusalem Talmud. 

From this, we learn that within the house of a Jew, in any case, it is forbidden. Similarly, with daily wage workers, it is forbidden in any case, as we have already explained. Furthermore, we learn that with attached work – even the labor of detached items is forbidden, for it is prohibited even within their own houses when connected to attached items. How does this apply? Certainly, for example, when fixing beams or doors and windows, and the non-Jew fixes them to install them in the house of the Jew. This is what the Tur and Shulchan Aruch wrote in section 2, that to shape the stones and fix the beams – even in the house of the non-Jew, it is forbidden, since it is for the purpose of something attached. And if they did so – they should not be embedded in the building, thus far their language. 

The reason for this stringent ruling is that otherwise, people might be lenient in this matter and allow building the structure itself, as people do not distinguish between this and that. This applies specifically when the beams and stones are designated only for this building. However, if the contractor fixes beams and stones or similar items and still has the option to use them in another building, even if he places them in this building – it is permitted, for it is not explicitly designated for the Jew (Sha'arei Teshuvah subsection 6 in the name of the Dagul MeRevavah). 

And regarding the ruling that even after the fact it is forbidden, the commentators on the Tur and Shulchan Aruch (Bach, Taz, and Magen Avraham subsection 10) agreed that in the case of a contract, one may rely after the fact on the opinion of Rabbeinu Tam, and it is not forbidden after the fact. It seems to me that if they were informed by halachic authorities that it is forbidden to do so and did not heed their words – then even after the fact it is forbidden.

And this is what the Jerusalem Talmud says, that in another city, even with something attached (to the ground) it is permitted. There are those who explain that this refers to preparing beams and stones, and bringing them to this city (Korban HaEidah). It seems that this is the opinion of Rabbeinu the Rema, who wrote on this law: "Some say that if it is not known to be owned by a Jew, it is permitted," end quote. And this applies when it is done in another city or similar situations. But to build something actually attached (to the ground) is forbidden, even if it is not known to be owned by a specific person, when the building is in the city, such as in another city. Therefore, he only wrote this law in section b, regarding the preparation of beams, and not in section a, regarding the construction itself. However, there are those who explain that the intention of the Jerusalem Talmud also applies to the construction itself in another city, that it is permitted since it is not known to be owned by that Jew (Pnei Moshe), and I do not know why the early authorities omitted this. And perhaps they reasoned, since they wrote regarding something attached (to the ground) the reason is due to publicity, consequently, when building in another city where it is not known, it is permitted. And for the practical ruling, further investigation is needed.

And it has already been explained that even with detached items, when the publicity is great, such as with a ship, it is also prohibited. But if the publicity is not as great as with a ship, if the Jewish owner's name has already become associated with it, it is forbidden. However, if the Jewish owner's name has not yet become fully associated with it, for example, if a Jew hired a non-Jew on a contractual basis to make new vessels for him and they were made publicly, and even if it became known that they were made for a particular Jew, nevertheless, they have not yet been explicitly called by his name to be known as his vessels since they have not yet come into his possession at all (according to the ruling of the Alter Rebbe, section 5), it is not similar to the publicity of a ship. In any case, although this is the essential law, it is praiseworthy for a pious person to be stringent in this matter, and one who is stringent will be blessed. And if the work is not done publicly but within the home or similar situations, there is no stringency at all, and it is permissible from the outset even for a pious person.

And our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, wrote in Section 3: If a non-Jew built a house for a Jew on Shabbat in a prohibited manner - it is proper to be stringent and not enter it. However, if the Jew stipulated with him not to do work for him on Shabbat, and he did it against the Jew's will to hasten his work - there is no need for concern, until here is his wording. And we have already explained in Section 9 that the major later authorities agreed that when the work was done on a contractual basis, the building is not forbidden post facto.

This is simple: A day laborer who performed work—such work is prohibited even after the fact. There is an opinion that with a day laborer, it is not effective even if he stipulated with him not to perform the work and the non-Jew did it on his own for the benefit of the Jew. For whenever it is done for the benefit of the Jew, even if the non-Jew did it on his own and the Jew objected—it is prohibited even after the fact (Magen Avraham, section 12). This is an excessive stringency, for since he objected, what more could he have done? And if the reason is that he should have appeased him with money so that he would not do it—we do not find that one is obligated to spend his money for this. Therefore, it seems that it should not be prohibited after the fact if he objected. (And so wrote the Eliyah Rabbah, section 9).

Maimonides writes in Chapter 6, Law 12: "A person may make an agreement with a non-Jew regarding work and set a price... Similarly, if one hires a non-Jew for many days, it is permitted, even though he works on Shabbat. How so? For example, if one hires a non-Jew for a year or two to write for him or to weave for him, he may write and weave on Shabbat as if he set a price with him to write a book or weave a garment, which he can do at any time he wishes, as long as he does not reckon with him day by day." This is the end of his wording. This means that just as it is permitted to make an agreement with him regarding specific work when done as a contract, where he sets a price for such-and-such work, similarly, even if he does not hire him for specific work but rather for a specific type of work, meaning he hires him for a year to do this specific work whenever needed, it is also permitted because he is doing it as a contract, receiving a set amount for the work of that year, since he can do it whenever he wishes. It is specifically when he hires him for specific work, such as writing or weaving, that it is certain he will have many free times when he is idle, and thus the Jew does not benefit from him writing or weaving on Shabbat, for if he does not do it on Shabbat, he will do it on a weekday. But if he hires him for all the work he needs, it is forbidden for him to do it on Shabbat, for then it is certain the Jew will benefit, as when he works on Shabbat, he will have time left on weekdays for other work. The Raavad disagrees with him and holds that even for specific work, it is also forbidden for this reason: if he works on Shabbat and then needs to do the same work tomorrow, and he does it, the Jew benefits from what was done on Shabbat (see Magen Avraham 315:15). The Tur and the Shulchan Aruch agree with Maimonides, and his reasoning seems correct, as it is unlikely he will constantly need one type of work. Therefore, Rabbeinu the Beit Yosef only brings the Raavad's opinion as a "yesh omrim" (some say), see there. And the reason for the statement "as long as he does not reckon with him day by day" is simple: so it does not appear as if he is paying him Shabbat wages. And it is obvious that if he hires him to always weave or always write, it is forbidden for him to do so on Shabbat.

Based on this, if a Jew has a workshop and employs non-Jewish workers who are hired for a year to perform a specific task, such as weaving, spinning, or quarrying, it is forbidden for him to allow them to work on Shabbat. Even though they are hired for a specific task, since the work in the workshop is done all day, it results in benefit to the Jew from work done on Shabbat. This is akin to hiring them for all tasks, and even Maimonides agrees that it is forbidden, as we have written. The only solution is selling, as will be explained in section 24.

Similarly, non-Jewish maidservants in a Jewish home are forbidden to perform any work on Shabbat for the Jew, even if they do not do it in the Jew's home, because this is considered as if they are hired for all tasks, as is obvious. However, for their own needs, they are permitted to work even in the Jew’s home. There are some who forbid this within the Jew's home due to suspicion that people might say the work is for the Jew (Taz, Section 1), but this is not the main view. Explicitly, it is written in the Mordechai’s glosses at the end of the first chapter of Shabbat that it is permitted; see there, and why should they suspect it is for the Jew? Everyone knows she also needs to work for herself (as Eliyah Rabba wrote in Section 11). And what Taz wrote from Mordechai’s glosses that it is forbidden is referring to work for the Jew, otherwise it would contradict itself. This is the main ruling in law, and consider it well.

Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote in section 6: "A Jew who buys a customs duty and hires a non-Jew to collect the customs on Shabbat - it is permitted if it is on a contract basis, meaning that he tells him: When you collect one hundred dinars, I will give you such and such an amount." This is his wording, for he [the non-Jew] is acting on his own behalf, as the more he collects, the more he profits, and work performed on detachable items is permitted on a contract basis. And even though he designates the work for Shabbat, and in such a case it is forbidden even if he specifies a set amount, as it is written in Siman 252, and furthermore, there is no greater public display than this, and in all cases it is forbidden, as explained in section 4 regarding a ship - nevertheless, in this case, where the loss would be very great, it is permitted (Beit Yosef in the name of Maharam). And the proof for this is from what is taught in the Mishnah (Shabbat 153a): If night fell upon him on the way, he gives his purse to a non-Jew. And the Gemara explains, because a person does not restrain himself concerning his money, and if you do not permit it, he will come to carry it four cubits in the public domain (there). And even though it is not entirely analogous, for here the money is not yet his, it is not so, because he pays customs duty also for Shabbat, and it is a loss from his pocket. And you might say: He should not have taken the customs duty at all? It is not so, because at the time of taking the business he takes it permissibly, and when Shabbat arrives - he faces a great loss (Beit Yosef). Furthermore, if so - all businesses would be closed to us, and it is impossible to endure this. And there is no difference whether the non-Jew needs to perform only a rabbinic prohibition, like collecting the customs only, which is merely a rabbinic prohibition, or if he needs to perform a Torah prohibition, such as needing to write the customs, so agreed the poskim. And indeed, there is almost no business in the world that does not require writing for the business, as is known.

There is a question regarding this matter: since we have said that due to significant loss we are not concerned, neither about designating the work on Shabbat nor about publicity, then why do we not permit using an oven and bathhouse in the previous section when there is significant loss? There, it is only a concern of suspicion, and it is obvious that we should permit it. And it is understandable regarding something attached (to the ground) and a ship in this section, we can say that the reason we do not permit it in any situation is because there the publicity is very great, as everyone sees the workers performing complete labors all day, which is not comparable to collecting a tax, obviously. But an oven and bathhouse that are used in the house, their publicity is no greater than that of collecting a tax, so why do we not permit it in cases of significant loss?

The answer to this is that it is not comparable at all. The oven and bathhouse are his, and it is not considered a loss if he cannot profit on Shabbat, for it is forbidden for a Jew to engage in business on Shabbat. However, the tax is not his; he rents the tax collection and pays for each and every day, so it turns out he is losing from his own pocket directly. This is similar to someone who was delayed, as explained (and all the more so for someone building a house or making a ship, which is forbidden to do on Shabbat, and the Magen Avraham and Taz have delved into this issue; see there).

Furthermore, the fundamental matter is not comparable: something that is inherently his, like a bathhouse or an oven, to something that is not inherently his, like a tax, which he also leases from the authority or the government. For something that is not inherently his, he sells it completely to the non-Jew for the Sabbath, meaning he sells all rights he has in this business. Therefore, it truly does not belong to the Jew at all. To what is this similar? To someone who knows merchandise will arrive for him on the Sabbath, and he sells the merchandise to a non-Jew on the eve of the Sabbath. However, with something that is inherently his - it remains his even on the Sabbath. And although it is not comparable to merchandise, because merchandise exists in the world and can be sold, whereas a tax is like something that does not yet exist and cannot be sold. This is not the case, for if so, how did the Jew lease it? In any case, it does not belong to the Jew on the Sabbath, because all the rights the Jew has in this business are transferred to the non-Jew. (This is the intention of the Magen Avraham at the end of section 18, and it resolves the difficulty raised by the Tvu'ot Shor in section 17. See there and examine it well.)

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) writes: "Similarly, one can lease the tax collection to a non-Jew for all the Sabbaths, and the non-Jew will take the Sabbath profits for himself. We are not concerned that people will say it is being done for the sake of the Jew, for in a case of significant loss, such as this, they did not worry," end quote. This is not understood, for what did he add to the words of Rabbi Yosef Karo (Beit Yosef)? On the contrary, it is a fortiori: Rabbi Yosef Karo permitted even by means of a fixed payment, meaning if you collect one hundred dinars, I will give you such and such, where the Jew gains from what is collected. All the more so if the non-Jew takes all the Sabbath profits for himself. At the very least, he should have said: "All the more so, one can lease the tax collection for all the Sabbaths." However, his words are correct. If we consider something that a Jew holds from others as his own property, the permit of Rabbi Yosef Karo is much more lenient than that of Rabbi Moshe Isserles. In a fixed payment, it is permitted in any matter that is completely his own, like a field or a mill, as stated in the previous section, because the non-Jew acts with his own intention, as explained there. This is not the case if he leases it for a fixed amount, as permitted by Rabbi Moshe Isserles, because the non-Jew must pay the tax collector the total amount for all the Sabbaths of the year, obviously. Therefore, if we consider it as his own, it is certainly forbidden. However, if we consider something that is not inherently his as not his own, because he sells all his rights in this business, as we explained in the previous section, the permission of Rabbi Moshe Isserles is more lenient. Regarding the permission of Rabbi Yosef Karo, who leases it with a fixed payment, it is not so applicable to say that he sells all his rights, as he takes a part of the profit, and the business remains his own. This is not the case when he leases it for all the Sabbaths of the year, and he will give the tax collector the amount for the Sabbaths, and he will take all the profits for himself. Hence, the Jew has no involvement in the business on the Sabbaths of the year. Since the matter is balanced, he wrote 'similarly' (this seems clear to me, and thus everything that the Magen Avraham questioned in section 18 is resolved, see there and examine closely).

Additionally, he wrote that an Israelite who is appointed over the king's coinage is judged like one who is appointed over customs, even though there is noise made on Shabbat from the striking of the coinage. This is his language: meaning that he can give money to a non-Jew on the eve of Shabbat on a contractual basis, so that if he makes such and such from the money, he will give him such and such, as permitted by our teacher, the Beit Yosef, or he can lease him all the profit of all the Sabbaths of the year, as permitted by our teacher, the Rema. This is even more lenient than customs because it makes noise and the publicity is great, and everyone knows that this Israelite rented it from the king, and it is called by his name. Nevertheless, because there is a great loss involved, they did not worry about the appearance of the matter. Therefore, in a case where there is not a great loss, such as another person who gave him money to make utensils, it is not permitted even on a contractual basis, unless the non-Jew does this work in his own home and in private, as explained in Siman 243. Also, he is allowed to give money to a non-Jewish craftsman to make utensils in the non-Jew's home, and even though there is noise, in any case, it is not publicized that this belongs to the Israelite, and he is doing it on a contractual basis (Magen Avraham, subsection 19).

Additionally, it is written to be cautious that a Jew should not sit next to a non-Jew on Shabbat when he is engaged in his work with currency or collecting customs duties. So far his words. And there are those who say that even if he rented it out for all Shabbats and has no involvement in the matter, it is still forbidden to sit there, lest people say he is doing it for his own benefit (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 20). And there are those who say that the prohibition applies only if he sits there to understand the work being done, as that is akin to examining the business. But if he sits and does not examine the work, rather to ensure that there is no theft, it is permitted (Taz, subparagraph 7). In a pressing situation, one can rely on this, as all prohibitions of appearance were permitted in cases of great loss as explained, and the concern of theft constitutes a great loss. And know, it is a simple matter that a Jew himself is forbidden to collect any customs duties, even food items that are not muktzeh and were not brought from beyond the Shabbat boundary, for any collection done as customs duties is considered business transactions on Shabbat, and the verse says (Isaiah 58:13) "refrain from your own needs" (Magen Avraham there).

A Jew who has leased the salt cooking from the government—it is permissible to hire workers on a task-based arrangement, that if they produce a certain amount of salt, he will pay them a certain amount (Rashal in his responsa, siman 100). It is permitted for them to work on Shabbat even with the Jew's utensils, for we are not commanded to rest our utensils. Also, the wood can belong to the Jew, for the utensils and wood are not considered to be called by the Jew's name (ibid.), and it is not similar to an oven, which is called by the Jew's name (ibid.). However, he should prepare the utensils and the wood before Shabbat, for on Shabbat itself it is certainly forbidden for the worker to take the utensils or the wood from the Jew's house. 

Nevertheless, some say that it is not similar to a tax, which we permitted to lease for Shabbat alone, for there it is a great loss (Tosafot Shabbat and Chayei Adam, and this also appears so from the Gra"z). But some say it is exactly like a tax, and all the permissions regarding the tax apply here as well (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 17, and Pri Megadim there). And this seems to be the main opinion, according to the reasons explained in paragraph 18, that something not inherently his—he can lease it for Shabbatot and we are not concerned about the appearance, due to the great loss, and I do not know how to differentiate between this and that. (And the words of the Gra"z in paragraph 21 are not clear to me, who told them that in the case of the tax it is a great loss, and in the case of the salt it is a minor loss? This is only a wonder. Therefore, it seems to my humble opinion in accordance with the Pri Megadim who holds this way in the Magen Avraham, and therefore he connected it to the law of the tax, and also the Rashal would agree to this, except that there it was sufficient with the permission of the task-based arrangement, so why permit more? And examine this well.).

From what has been explained, we learn for all types of businesses in the world that Jews receive from the government or from lords, if it is possible for such a business that the workers can perform it on a contract basis, such as in the business of digging earth where one is paid a certain amount per excavation or per unit of measure, and similarly, one can hire workers on a contract basis in such a manner, and similarly in other such cases, the permission is straightforward that the workers can also perform on a contract basis. And for businesses that cannot be done on a contract basis, if there is a significant loss, one can lease out the business for the Sabbath days entirely, as allowed by our master, the Rema, in section 19.

However, in businesses that cannot operate without day laborers, such as the production of whiskey and beer, as well as those who maintain postal services for the government and keep horses, there is no remedy for this, as we are commanded to rest our animals on Shabbat. And all the more so for those people who have factories for merchandise, where it is necessary to employ day laborers—there is no remedy other than selling the entire business to a non-Jew with a legally valid transaction according to halacha. Even though it is done publicly and everyone knows it belongs to a Jew, it is still permitted, as it has already been clarified that in cases of significant loss, we do not concern ourselves with the appearance of impropriety, as long as it is not done in the house where the Jew lives. And this is the common custom now in all countries, to make sales contracts for all leased businesses from lands, where it is obviously not possible to employ contractors, and it is necessary to sell the horses and animals used for labor. The manner of the sale cannot be explained here, as there are many laws concerning it, and they are explained in Choshen Mishpat. Each person needs to make the sale contract with the community rabbi, and the rabbi will inform him how to do it. In particular, it is necessary to inform them that the sale of horses and animals only applies to the horses and animals currently in their possession, but what they acquire afterward is not included, and a new sale is needed, and many common people do not know this.

In the previous sections, it was explained that on a contractual basis, it is permissible for a Jew to allow a non-Jew to work on Shabbat, because in a contractual arrangement, the non-Jew works for his own benefit, except in the case of work connected to land, as explained there. This is specifically when the business belongs solely to the Jew. However, if a Jew and a non-Jew are partners in a business, it is prohibited in such a manner. And do not wonder why it is worse because the non-Jew has a share in the business itself, and how can one say so? The reasoning is as follows: when the business belongs solely to the Jew, and he hires the non-Jew on a contractual basis, the non-Jew is not considered his agent but works for his own benefit, as explained there. The fact that the Jew profits from this is incidental, as explained there. But when two partners have a business, it is incumbent upon both to work. If the non-Jew works alone on Shabbat, he will certainly expect that on weekdays the Jew will work alone one day in return for the Shabbat that he worked, which is essentially like saying: 'You work for me on Shabbat, and I will work for you on Sunday,' making the non-Jew essentially the Jew's agent. There are detailed laws regarding this, which will be explained with Divine assistance. There is no difference whether the business is inherently theirs or if they rented it from someone else to operate it as partners, for in the end, they are partners. See Section 7.

And this is what the Sages taught at the end of the chapter "Before Their Festivals" (Avodah Zarah 22b): A Jew and a non-Jew who received a field in partnership, the Jew should not say to the non-Jew: "Take your portion on Shabbat and I will take mine on a weekday," because he makes him his agent for half of the day that is incumbent upon him (Rashi). However, if they stipulated from the beginning - it is permitted. That is to say, if before taking on the business, they stipulated that the business of Shabbat would be yours and that of Sunday would be mine - it is permitted, because the Jew did not take on the business of Shabbat at all, and the non-Jew is not his agent (there). And if they come to an accounting - it is prohibited. And Rashi explained it as follows: when they did not stipulate from the beginning but took it on without specification and operated without specification, and the non-Jew worked on Shabbat and the Jew on weekdays, and they came to an accounting after some time to say: "How many Shabbat days did you take, and I will take corresponding weekdays" - it is prohibited, because he is taking the wages of Shabbat. In other words, later it does not help if he wants the Shabbat days to belong solely to the non-Jew and for one of the weekdays to belong solely to him, because since they already partnered without specification - they are compelled to be partners on all days, and he becomes his agent for Shabbat.

There are some of our Rabbis who explained that the phrase "And if they came to an agreement" refers to an initial agreement, and this is its explanation: that even if they initially agreed, nevertheless, if when they came to an accounting they divided the overall profit equally, it is forbidden. This is because if the non-Jew did not take the profit from the Sabbaths, whether it was large or small, and correspondingly the Jew did not take the profit from the weekdays, whether it was large or small, it turns out that their initial condition was merely a deceit (Ran in the name of Raavad). And it is possible that Rashi does not disagree with this, for it is certain that if they initially agreed, it is necessary that each one takes the profit of his day, whether it is much or little. And Rashi, who explained that the phrase refers to when they agreed, did so because without an agreement, even in such a situation where one takes the Sabbath profit and the other takes the weekday profit, it is also forbidden. And in this matter, the second opinion also agrees. And behold, the words of the Rambam in Chapter 6, Law 17, are also like Rashi, as will be explained. And according to what we have written, there is no disagreement at all. And I saw someone who wrote that according to the Rambam, it is permitted if they agreed to divide equally, since he did not explain the phrase "if they came to an agreement" as referring to an agreement (Beit Yosef in the name of Mahari Abohab), and according to this, Rashi would also hold this way. However, according to our words, one should not create a dispute among the poskim (decisors of Jewish law), and everyone agrees that even if they agreed, it is forbidden to divide equally. And this explanation that it refers to without an agreement is because without an agreement, even in such a situation, it is also forbidden, as we have written. (And also the Bach rejected the words of Mahari Abohab. But the Taz in subparagraph 2 agreed with Mahari Abohab, see there). And further clarification will be provided with the help of Heaven in section 5, where there is room for leniency, see there.

And this is the language of the Rambam there: "One who partners with a non-Jew in work or in merchandise or in a shop, if they stipulated from the beginning that the profits of Shabbat would belong solely to the non-Jew, whether it is small or large, and a profit of another day corresponding to Shabbat would belong solely to the Jew - it is permitted. But if they did not stipulate from the beginning, when they come to divide the profits - the non-Jew takes all the profits of the Sabbaths alone, and the rest they divide (and the Jew does not benefit from Shabbat at all) and he does not add anything corresponding to the day of Shabbat, unless he stipulated from the beginning. Similarly, if they accepted a field in partnership, the law is the same. And if they did not stipulate and came to divide the profits, and the Shabbat profit was not known, it appears to me that the non-Jew takes alone a seventh of the profit, and the rest they divide," thus far his language, and so wrote our Rabbi the Beit Yosef in section 1. And it is simple, that what he wrote a seventh of the profit - this is in a matter where the profit is equal every day. But in a shop and the like, where there is a market day once a week, which provides more sustenance than all the week - it is not necessary to calculate in this manner, but rather to calculate a sixth of the profit from six days that are not market days.

And behold, even though we wrote that it is possible to say that Rashi and the Rambam agree with the opinion in section 3, that even if they stipulated [a division] it is forbidden when they calculate and divide equally. However, our rabbis, the Tosafists, wrote there that when they stipulated, it is obvious that it is permitted, see there. According to this, it can be said that Rashi and the Rambam also hold this view. According to this, it makes sense what our master, the Beit Yosef, was lenient about in section 2, where he wrote, and this is his language: "Where they stipulated at the beginning, if afterwards at the time of division the non-Jew agreed to divide equally, it is permitted," until here is his language, and we say that he is giving it as a gift. (And it makes sense the ruling of the Beit Yosef even without the words of the Maharai, because since Rashi and the Rambam are not decisive, but it is the Raavad who forbids, and since the Tosafists are lenient and the prohibition is Rabbinic - we follow to be lenient. Moreover, the Rosh certainly holds this way, as will be explained, and thus two against one, and pay attention).

It is stated there in the Gemara: They inquired, what is the law of a "stam"? And the question was not resolved, see there. And Rashi explained: "Stam" – that they accepted it simply and acted simply, a non-Jew on Shabbat, and a Jew on a weekday, and the Jew never said "take you on Shabbat and I on a weekday" – what is the law of dividing simply and equally, without the Jew mentioning Shabbat? Until here is his language. The explanation of the matter: Perhaps the prohibition is only when he says to him: "Take you on Shabbat and I on a weekday," for this is as if he says explicitly – be my agent on Shabbat and I will be your agent on a weekday. But simply – everyone knows that it is forbidden for a Jew to conduct business on Shabbat even through an agent, and consequently, the non-Jew acts for himself on Shabbat and the Jew acts for himself on a weekday. And although they do not calculate that one will take the profit of Shabbat and the other the profit of a weekday – it is not the way of partners to be meticulous about this and they waive it for each other.

And behold, the Rosh ruled leniently on this issue. He wrote the reason that since it is a rabbinic doubt, we follow the lenient opinion. See there. And this is what our master, the Rema, wrote in section 1, that there are those who permit the profit after the fact, even if they did not stipulate, and divided it simply. And it seems to me that in a case of significant loss, one can rely on them; thus far his words. But without significant loss, it is forbidden. The reason is that the Rif omitted this issue, and also from the words of the Rambam it appears clearly to be forbidden, for the Rambam speaks in general terms, and this is the opinion of our master, the Beit Yosef. And even though one might say that they did not write this except as an initial ruling, but not after the fact – this cannot be said, for if so, they should have clarified that it is permitted after the fact. Moreover, since the Rambam was strict that the non-Jew should receive a seventh part of the profit when the profit from the Sabbaths is not known, it is clear that he was very stringent on this matter. (And the reasons of the Rif and the Rambam, see the Ran there. And see the Magen Avraham section 3 who brought in the name of Rabbeinu Yerucham another explanation on the general rule, that the non-Jew took the profit of the Sabbath for himself, and then the Jew took the profit of a weekday, see there. And it is necessary to explain this, for otherwise, it has no explanation, and for the practical law, it is all the same. And from the Rosh, it is proven that he holds like the Tosafot in the case of a stipulation, and not like the Raavad, that since he is lenient in general terms, all the more so in the case of a stipulation, and understand this well).

There is no difference in this law whether they partnered in something that through its execution on Shabbat increases the portion of the Jew even in the essence of the business, like a field or a vineyard and similar things, where through the work done on Shabbat the actual field and vineyard are enhanced, or whether it is not enhanced through the work done on Shabbat, like an oven or a store and similar things, where the work of each day stands on its own, for in the end it is as if he is his agent, as has been explained. Therefore, even though the Gemara only mentioned a field, in any case, it is all the same. And in the Tosefta of Demai at the end of Chapter 6, it is mentioned that they have a bathhouse in partnership, see there.
