And a bathhouse - the business is not enhanced by the work done on Shabbat, obviously (Tosafot there in the name of Rabbeinu Tam and the Ri). Therefore, Rabbeinu the Beit Yosef intentionally wrote in Section 1: a Jew and a non-Jew who have a field or an oven or a bathhouse, etc. (And the fact that the Talmud mentioned only a field, it seems to me because indeed in a field there is a greater novelty, for the profit is not immediate on Shabbat, but there could be some profit over time. This is not the case with an oven, bathhouse, and store, where the profit is immediate on Shabbat and it is obviously forbidden. With this, the words of the Rambam are understood, who wrote: "One who partners in a work or in merchandise or in a store, etc.", and afterwards wrote: "And likewise if they received a field in partnership, etc.", until here are his words. And it is not understood, for a field that the Talmud mentioned is at the end. But because in the previous cases the prohibition is more evident for the reason I have written, and examine this well).

Some of our rabbis have written that the prohibition in partnership is only when the Jew works alone on a weekday corresponding to the day the non-Jew worked alone on Shabbat, for then he is like his agent, as explained. However, if they work together throughout the entire week, and the non-Jew does not demand that the Jew work alone on a weekday, and the non-Jew independently gives the Jew half of the Shabbat profits, it is permissible to take it, for the non-Jew acts on his own behalf. Even though this results in profit for the Jew, it is not a concern, similar to the sharecropper situation mentioned in Siman 243. Additionally, it is not considered solely in the name of the Jew, as everyone knows that the non-Jew is a partner in this, and the prohibition only applies when the Jew works alone against him for one day (Ran there). Nevertheless, he should not take Shabbat wages except as part of the overall payment for the rest of the days, but not separately, as it appears like Shabbat wages (there). And so ruled our Rabbi, the Rema, in Siman 1. Even though from the language of the Rambam it is not clear that the main prohibition depends on this, the general interpretation is as explained, since he wrote in the condition that the Shabbat wages are for the non-Jew and the weekday wages for the Jew, see there – it implies that it depends on this. Furthermore, it is logical that this is the case, as the non-Jew would certainly not forgo this, as is the way of partners, but if it happened so, it is permissible (see Beit Yosef and Bach).

And this prohibition applies only when they themselves are engaged in the activity in their own physical bodies, such as a shop, mill, field, and similar. But if they themselves are not engaged at all, such as an oven where anyone who wants to bake and cook fires it up, bakes, and cooks, and pays for the use of the oven, and similarly with a mill if they do the same - they are allowed to share the profit equally, provided the Shabbat payment is included in an encompassing manner. The reasoning is that in this case, it cannot be said that he is his agent, since he does nothing (Magen Avraham, section 1). And if it is because people will say that the Jew profits on Shabbat from his oven business - everyone knows that the non-Jew has a share in the oven, and he will not allow it not to be fired up on Shabbat, and if so, it is on his own account that he allows baking there, and the profit comes to the Jew incidentally, like with a sharecropper, as we wrote in the previous section.

And it appears to me that even in businesses that they run themselves, like a store or similar, if they themselves are not involved at all, but rather hire workers to operate them - it is also permitted for the Jew to receive payment for Shabbat as part of a broader payment, even if the workers are hired on a daily basis. For what concern is there? For the non-Jewish partner is not considered his agent, since he is not acting on his behalf. And if the concern is because the worker is hired on a daily basis, indeed if he had the power to prevent them from working on Shabbat, he would certainly be obligated to do so. However, the non-Jewish partner will not allow him to do so, and if so – the workers are employed for their own benefit, and the profit for the Jew comes naturally, and he may take payment for Shabbat as part of a broader payment in accordance with the previous rules (this is how it appears in my humble opinion).

And similarly, if the oven or other business belongs solely to the Jew, and he partners with a non-Jew so that the non-Jew always heats the oven and bakes for anyone who wants to bake, and in return takes half the profit – he may divide the earnings of Shabbat by inclusion. This is not considered as if the non-Jew is acting as his agent, since the Jew has no involvement at all, and the non-Jew is doing it for himself. This is like a contract work, where he is doing it for his own profit, and the Jew's profit comes incidentally (Magen Avraham section 3 and the Alter Rebbe’s Shulchan Aruch section 9). However, he should not say to him: you take Shabbat and I will take another day – because in such a case it is forbidden, as it would be like giving wages for Shabbat. This is not the same as the oven, where they are partners in the actual oven, and half of it entirely belongs to the non-Jew. But when the oven belongs solely to the Jew – in such a case it is like wages for Shabbat. Instead, they should divide all the earnings of the entire week by half (Tosafot there in the name of Rabbeinu Elchanan, see there), or by a third or a quarter, as they agreed between them. However, all this applies in a place where it is permitted to rent out one’s oven to a non-Jew, based on the details explained in Siman 243, section 13, such as when it is well-known that he does not hire daily workers, but rather as contract work, or if that is the custom of that place, as it says there. But otherwise, since the oven belongs entirely to him – it is prohibited to rent it out to a non-Jew due to suspicion, as explained there.

There is another leniency when they are partners in the actual oven, where the Jew rents out his portion to the non-Jew on a contractual basis, as Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote in paragraph 3, and this is his wording: "And if he wishes to rent his portion to the non-Jew for Shabbat or on a contractual basis – it is permitted, as explained in section 244 regarding taxes and currency, which is permitted. All the more so here – it is permitted with a non-Jewish partner," end quote. And here, on a contractual basis, meaning that he gives him for his portion such and such – it is certainly permitted, as it is no worse than if the entire oven were his, that is, the contract should cover all days of the week, and the Shabbat wages are included. However, what he permitted regarding his portion on Shabbat alone is perplexing, as it was clearly explained there that we only permit this with taxes and currency, due to significant loss, and also because the business itself is not his, as explained there. Therefore, some have rejected his words in this detail (Taz, subparagraph 3). And it must be said that Rabbi Moshe Isserles's intention is thus: since the non-Jew is a partner in the actual oven and will not allow it to remain unoperational on Shabbat, and thus the Jew cannot prevent him – what difference does it make if he receives half the wages or agrees on a specific amount, and this is better than half the wages, obviously. And his intention is not to specifically mention Shabbat, but to say to him: 'Give me for my portion such and such per day' (and this is also implied by the Magen Avraham at the end of subparagraph 8 and by the Alter Rebbe in paragraph 14). And it is obvious that this must be said before Shabbat, and even after they have become partners (and therefore, he wrote this in paragraph 3, and pay attention). And before they become partners, he can also mention Shabbat in this manner, meaning that he says to him: I will partner with you in this manner, that the Shabbat days will be entirely yours, and for this, you will give me such and such (this is also implied by the Magen Avraham there. According to this, Rabbi Moshe Isserles's words can be interpreted in two ways. This is not Shabbat wages, but merely a condition that in this manner, he partners with him, committing to give him such and such money, and Shabbat is entirely yours, and pay attention).

It has already been explained that if they stipulated from the outset, it is permissible to tell the non-Jew: "You take your share on Shabbat, and I will take a corresponding day during the weekdays." But if they did not stipulate from the beginning and simply acquired in partnership, it is forbidden. However, there is a solution for this. If one wishes to say so, they should void the previous partnership. This means that if they acquired in partnership, they should ask the seller to return the money and tear up the bill of sale. Then, they should make the stipulation between themselves and purchase from the seller with a new transaction. Or, if they formed a partnership in a shop or another business, they should void the partnership and release each other from the conditions between them. If they created a partnership document, they should tear it up, then make the stipulation and form the partnership anew. If they partnered in a shop and both left money or goods, they should void this, take back the money or goods, make the stipulation, and then form the partnership. We do not say that this is merely a subterfuge, because certainly, it is within their power to void the partnership! And even if they do so for some reason, who can protest against them? The same applies afterward in the second partnership. And even if we call it a subterfuge, it is still permissible in Rabbinic law, even if it is recognizable, as is evident in Shabbat regarding the ferry in 139: see there. And as written later in Siman 339 in Tur. And even though we only permitted this for a Torah scholar, that pertains to something public and very recognizable, not in this matter, which is a business transaction done in private, and they have the ability to act as they wish, as I have written. (And this also seems to be Rashi’s implication there in the commentary on "subterfuge," where he concludes: "to pass there before everyone," see there, and it clearly implies that the first subterfuge regarding the ferry is not applicable in private matters, see there and pay attention).

Maimonides wrote in Chapter 6 (Law 18): "If one gives money to a non-Jew to invest, even though the non-Jew conducts business with it on Shabbat, they share the profit equally. This is the ruling of all the Geonim," thus far his words. Similarly, it is permissible to give him merchandise under these conditions, as the Jew is not commanding him to do business on Shabbat, and he acts on his own accord because he has a share in the profit, or he is allotted a wage such that from any amount he redeems, he will be given a certain amount, in which case he works for himself to earn more. However, if he is a day laborer – it is forbidden, as he works for the Jew. Therefore, the permission is only if he is allotted a wage or has a share, and it has already been clarified that the Shabbat wage must be absorbed (in a larger payment). It is not prohibited due to the appearance of impropriety, that people might say he is the Jew's agent, because not everyone knows that this money and merchandise belong to the Jew (Rabbi Maggid). According to this, if the business is in a fixed place, such as a store or another specific location, and everyone knows that it is the Jew's business – it is forbidden in any case (see Shulchan Aruch Harav sub-section 2), and this is a simple matter.

And all this applies when the non-Jew is working alone. But if each one works on his day, and for the Sabbath day that the non-Jew works, the Jew must work one weekday in its place – then he is considered the Jew's agent on the Sabbath. However, if the non-Jew does not require that the Jew work one weekday in place of the Sabbath day – it is permitted, and this is clarified from the previous laws. But when he is obligated to exchange one day for it – there is no solution for benefiting from the Sabbath profits. However, if it is a significant loss – one can rely on the opinion of the Rosh in paragraph 7, who permits them to work in a general manner and divide the profits generally, see there.

A Jewish person who took an oven as collateral for a loan from a non-Jew, and the non-Jew asked him that the oven should remain under his control, and whatever profit the oven generates he will give him as a return for his money - it is permitted for him to receive rental income from it even without it being included in a larger sum, because the oven itself belongs to the non-Jew and the Jewish person has no ownership in it, only a general lien. Additionally, he is not telling him to work on Shabbat; rather, the non-Jew is working on his own accord for his own benefit, to repay the debt he owes for the money. Therefore, there is no prohibition at all. And it is not specifically an oven; the same applies to any other similar item - it is permitted.

Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote in section 6: "If non-Jews baked in the oven of a Jew on Shabbat against his will (and they did not listen to the Jew, who did not want to allow them), and they gave him bread as payment for the oven - it is forbidden to benefit from it," thus his wording. Similarly, if they gave him money, it is forbidden to benefit from it (Eliyah Rabbah, sub-section 7). The reason for the prohibition is that it constitutes Shabbat wages. The Levush wrote that the reason is because it was baked for him; see there. According to this, if they gave money, it would be permitted, but it does not appear so (ibid). Similarly, there is one who says that it is only initially forbidden to accept from them, but after the fact, it is permitted (Shelah on the Mordechai), but this does not seem to be the implication from the wording of Rabbeinu Beit Yosef. However, it is certain that if they baked also during the weekdays, it is permitted to accept the Shabbat wages as well by means of inclusion (Bach, end of Siman 243). In such a case, it is permissible even without coercion, but it is impossible to imagine this, for it is forbidden for him to allow them to bake in his oven on Shabbat. There is one who says that even if he committed a prohibition, the wages should not be forbidden after the fact by means of inclusion, since it is merely due to the appearance (Mishnah Berurah, sub-section 23). This does not seem correct, for we say this only in a case of great loss, but in this case - on the contrary, it is fitting to penalize him, and this is the main ruling.

Maimonides wrote in Chapter 6, Law 16: "It is permissible to lend or rent utensils to a non-Jew, even though he performs work with them on Shabbat, because we are not commanded to have our utensils rest. However, it is forbidden regarding one's animal and servant, because we are commanded to have our animals and servants rest." End quote. And from the fact that Maimonides did not write that it is forbidden to lend or rent utensils on the eve of Shabbat, it implies that he holds that it is also permissible on the eve of Shabbat, even though it is taught: "A person should not rent his utensils to a non-Jew on the eve of Shabbat, but on Wednesday and Thursday it is permitted," he holds that the law is not according to this teaching, and this is also the opinion of the Rif, who omitted this Baraita. (And he holds that it follows the opinion of Beit Shammai, who maintains the requirement for utensils to rest, as explained there. And the Tosafot raised an objection, that if so, even on Wednesday and Thursday as well. It seems to me that since lending and renting constitute a partial transaction, but not entirely, as will be explained, therefore on Wednesday and Thursday we do not worry, as perhaps no Torah-level prohibition will be done with them on Shabbat, and on the eve of Shabbat they were concerned. And carefully consider this.)

But our Rabbis, the Tosafists and most of the poskim (decisors of Jewish law), hold that this baraita (teaching) is legally binding, and the reason is not because of the resting of utensils, but because when one rents it out on Friday, it appears as if he is receiving payment for Shabbat. Even though the payment for Shabbat is included with the other days, for if not, in any case, it is forbidden to take payment specifically for Shabbat, nonetheless, since he rents it out on Friday and the first day of the rental begins on Shabbat, it appears as if he is being paid for Shabbat and it is forbidden. And if he rents it and calculates each day individually, it is forbidden even on Wednesday and Thursday, for this is essentially payment for Shabbat. According to this interpretation, it is forbidden to rent out any kind of utensils on Friday, even those that do not involve labor.

There is another opinion from Rabbeinu Yonah, who interprets this Baraita not regarding all utensils, but specifically those utensils used for labor, such as an axe, a plow, and similar items. And it is not due to the prohibition of "resting of utensils" (Shevitat Kelim), but rather because when one rents out such a utensil on the eve of Shabbat, and the non-Jewish renter begins to use it on Shabbat, it appears as if he is the agent of the Jew, doing work on Shabbat on his behalf. However, utensils that are not used for labor may be rented out even on the eve of Shabbat, as this does not appear as hiring for Shabbat, since the rental is for a week or month, and thus the Shabbat is included (in the overall rental period). The proof for this is that if we said that renting out on the eve of Shabbat appears as hiring for Shabbat, then it would not matter whether the renter is a non-Jew; even renting to a Jew should be forbidden for this reason (Rosh, there). And if you ask, since they did not worry about this, why did they worry that people might think he is his agent? We could say that the reason is that it is not customary to rent out for a daily rate, but rather for a week or a month, and in such cases, the Shabbat is included in the overall rental period and there is no suspicion. But in this case, certainly, there is suspicion that he is his agent doing work on his behalf. (And behold, the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch did not bring the opinion of the Tosafot at all, and this requires examination, for most of the poskim agree with the Tosafot. And the Beit Yosef wrote that Rashi agrees with Rabbeinu Yonah, and perhaps since according to the Rif and the Rambam it is permissible in all cases, and Rashi does not agree with the Tosafot, therefore they did not concern themselves to bring this opinion. Consider this well.)

And this is with renting, but to lend him a utensil – it is allowed even on the eve of Shabbat. And it is not only according to the opinion of Tosafot that with lending it is not considered as if one is paying for Shabbat, since he is not taking anything, but even according to the opinion of Rabbeinu Yonah who discusses a utensil used for work, and the prohibition is because it appears as if the non-Jew is his agent to do work – nevertheless, with lending they did not worry about this, because the concern is only when the Jew takes money and benefits from the non-Jew’s use of it on Shabbat – it is reasonable to worry that people might say [he is his agent]. But with lending – they did not worry. And the proof for this is from what will be explained in Siman 252, that it is permitted to give hides to a tanner and utensils to a launderer on the eve of Shabbat. And why did they not worry that people will say he is his agent, but because there the Jew does not benefit from what the non-Jew does on Shabbat, and it is not the same with renting. (See Beit Yosef).

Our master, the Rema, ruled in accordance with Rabbeinu Yonah, and his reasoning seems to me to be because it is a balanced view between the Rif and Rambam, who permitted renting any utensils on the eve of Shabbat, and the view of the Tosafot, SeMaG, and other poskim who forbade it for all utensils, as explained. And Rabbeinu Yonah permitted it for utensils that do not perform work and forbade it for utensils that do perform work, and the halacha is according to the one who mediates. He also wrote that it is permitted to lend him on the eve of Shabbat even though the condition is that the non-Jew will return and lend it back to him, and we do not say in such cases that it is like renting, end quote. That is to say, even though this is akin to renting, for what difference does it make if he pays him with money or with the use of utensils, nevertheless, since it is not in the manner of actual renting - they were not concerned about this (Beit Yosef) in a matter that is only a concern of suspicion.

However, on Shabbat itself, it is forbidden to lend any utensil to a non-Jew. Moreover, even on the eve of Shabbat, if it is close to nightfall in such a way that the non-Jew does not have enough time to take it out of the Jew's house before nightfall, it is also forbidden. The Rambam wrote the reason for this is that when the non-Jew leaves the Jew's house on Shabbat, it will appear as if he borrowed it or pawned it or made a deal with him or bought it from him on Shabbat. According to this reasoning, it is forbidden even in a city that has an eruv, and carrying is permitted. But our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 2 that the reason is because the observer might think that the Jew commanded him to take it out, and this reasoning is written in Sefer HaTerumot, that they might suspect the Jew of commanding the non-Jew to carry his object into the public domain, and commanding a non-Jew is a rabbinic prohibition (shvut). Therefore, in a place that is not a public domain but only a karmelit, which is only a rabbinic prohibition, it is a double rabbinic prohibition (shvut d’shvut) and we do not decree a decree for a double rabbinic prohibition. (Taz, subparagraph 3) Alternatively, it is possible that even for a double rabbinic prohibition, we do decree (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 6). However, in a place with an eruv, there is no concern at all. It is a matter of concern that our master, the Beit Yosef, omitted the words of the Rambam, for according to the Rambam, it is forbidden in all cases. (There) It seems that since the Sefer Mitzvot Gadol and Sefer HaTerumot omitted his reasoning and did not worry about it, therefore he also omitted it. (Ateret Zekeinim, subparagraph 8) In any case, one should be concerned about his words and only be lenient in a time of need, and likewise, if it is clear that it is a loan, it is also permitted even according to the Rambam, because in such cases there is no concern, as is obvious.

And if indeed he sold it to him on the eve of Shabbat or gave it to him as collateral or to do work with it or lent it to him for a long period more than thirty days, which is considered as a sale as mentioned above in Siman 14 — according to everyone, it needs to leave the entrance of his house during the day, even in a place where there is an eruv, because there is a concern that it will be known to the observer that the Jew sold it to him or gave it as collateral or for work or lent it to him as mentioned, since this is the truth, and they will suspect him of having done so on Shabbat. This is not the case with a simple loan; when the truth becomes known, there is no suspicion at all, even if it seems to him that he lent it on Shabbat, for it is permitted to lend on Shabbat. And know that all these matters are when the items belong to the Jew. But items of a non-Jew that were deposited with a Jew and he came to take them on Shabbat — he can take them even if he takes them out to the public domain, as mentioned in Siman 325 (the Alter Rebbe).

And this is all regarding utensils, as we are not commanded to rest utensils. However, it is forbidden to lend one's animal to a non-Jew even in the middle of the week if it is used for work, such as an ox that is used for plowing or a horse that pulls a wagon and the like, because the non-Jew will use it for work on Shabbat, and the Torah states: "So that your ox and your donkey may rest." Similarly, one should not lend his slave or maidservant who are owned by him, as it is stated: "So that your male and female servants may rest as you do." However, the owner can warn them not to work on Shabbat, but an animal does not have the capacity for understanding. And even if the borrower promises not to use it for work on Shabbat, he is not trusted. It appears to me that if the borrower leaves a collateral with the Jew and stipulates that if it becomes known that he used it for work on Shabbat, the Jew will take the collateral entirely, it is permitted, since the borrower will be afraid to use it on Shabbat, lest the Jew finds out and he loses his collateral. Refer to Siman 305.

It is also forbidden to rent one's animal to a non-Jew for them to perform work with it on Shabbat. Even though in the context of acquisitions and the laws of overcharging, rental is considered like a sale, and rental for a specified period is considered a sale (Bava Metzia 56b), this applies only to those specific contexts. However, the animal does not become like the renter's own; the essence of the animal remains with the owner. The Sages explicitly stated in the chapter "Before Their Festivals" (Avodah Zarah 15a) that rental does not confer ownership. There are those who wish to argue that for stringency, it should be considered a form of acquisition, and according to this, a Jew who rented an animal from a non-Jew would be prohibited from allowing it to perform work on Shabbat (see Magen Avraham 308:8 and Bach in Choshen Mishpat, end of Siman 312). However, it is explicitly proven there that even for stringency, it is not considered an acquisition (and the Shach already objected to the Bach in Choshen Mishpat 313:1 regarding this matter, bringing proof from a Jew who rented a cow from a Kohen, that he feeds it with terumah produce. Even though Tosafot wrote there that its sustenance is the responsibility of the Kohen, as the Magen Avraham brought, they wrote this for a different reason, because otherwise, how could he feed it terumah? In truth, the Rosh at the end of Terumot wrote not like Tosafot, and the sustenance is the responsibility of the Jew, yet still he feeds it terumah. Hence, from the Rosh it is explicitly proven that even for stringency, it is not considered a sale).

And it does not help if he makes a condition with him that he will not do work with it on Shabbat, nor that he will not accept rental payment for Shabbat, because he is not believed, unless he fears losing by this, as stated regarding a loan. However, he can lend or lease it on the condition that it will be returned to the Jew before Shabbat, and in this case, there is no issue of credibility, for he will certainly lose by this, as he will be sued in court for not fulfilling his condition. Nevertheless, if it happened that he lent or leased it on this condition and did not return it, our master the Beit Yosef (Rabbi Yosef Karo) ruled in Section 3 that he should declare it ownerless between himself before Shabbat, or say: 'My animal is acquired by him,' in order to avoid a Torah prohibition. And our master the Rema (Rabbi Moses Isserles) wrote about this, that if he wants, he can declare it ownerless before three people, as is the law with other ownerless property, and even so, no one else can acquire it, for certainly his intention is only to remove the Shabbat prohibition from himself, and his words require explanation.

The explanation is as follows: one who wishes to declare something ownerless (hefker) - according to Torah law, it becomes ownerless even if he declares it so privately, but by rabbinic decree, three people are required. This is the language of the Gemara at the end of the fourth chapter of Nedarim (45a): "By Torah law, even with one person it is considered ownerless, but why did they say three are required? So that one can acquire it and the other two can testify." Similarly, this is found in the Rambam, Chapter 2 (Halacha 16) of Nedarim. Many hold that the Rambam believes that at least one person is required by Torah law, but Tosafot and the Rosh there wrote that the same applies even privately. According to this, there is no necessity from the Rambam that one is essential. We have already written this in the name of one of the greats in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 273, Section 7. According to this, Tosafot and the Rosh wrote there that in a case like this, where the non-Jew did not return the animal to him, he can declare it ownerless privately, as per Rabbeinu Beit Yosef. It seems to me that the reason they did not require three people in this case is that there is a concern that someone else might acquire the animal.

However, the Tosafot in Shabbat (18a, s.v. 'd'Mafkara') wrote that one must declare it ownerless specifically in the presence of three people, and this is explicitly stated in the Tosafot Yeshanim there, see there. And it seems to me that their reasoning is as follows: Firstly, since by rabbinic law, three are required; and furthermore, if he declares it ownerless by himself, there is still suspicion for the observer, who will say that a Jew's animal is performing work on Shabbat. And this is what our teacher the Beit Yosef precisely meant when he said 'to avoid a Torah prohibition', meaning, however, the prohibition of 'marit ayin' (appearance of wrongdoing) still exists, but due to this, we do not impose upon him that he lose his animal if another person acquires it. Therefore, our teacher the Rama comes and says that he can declare it ownerless in the presence of three, so that it will be a complete ownerlessness by rabbinic law, and the prohibition of 'marit ayin' will not exist, because through the three, it will become known that he declared it ownerless. Nevertheless, he will not incur damage, because another cannot acquire it, as we are witnesses that he only declared it ownerless so that he would not transgress the prohibition of resting his animal. And one should not ask what kind of ownerlessness this is, as there is a solution to declare it ownerless only for Shabbat, for temporary ownerlessness is valid, as stated in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 273, Se'if 8, where it is learned from the Jerusalem Talmud, chapter 6 of Peah, that ownerlessness is derived from the Sabbatical year, as we explained there. And on Shabbat, no one is permitted to acquire it, since it is still under the domain of the non-Jew, and after Shabbat, it returns to him, as our teacher the Beit Yosef wrote in his great book. (See Taz, note 5) And our teacher the Rama says that even if he did not explicitly state this, we say that his intention was so. (See Magen Avraham, note 11, from which it is implied that even when declared ownerless so that no one acquires it, it is effective, even though it is not a complete ownerlessness, as the Maharshal wrote. And see Pri Megadim, Taz, note 5, and these are puzzling matters, and therefore, in my humble opinion, the main point is as I have written, and scrutinize it well).

Nevertheless, ideally, it is forbidden to rent or lend [an item] to a non-Jew, relying on the condition that he will make it ownerless in front of three people on the eve of Shabbat. There are those who permit doing this from the outset (Magen Avraham, section 9, citing Bach), but one should only rely on this in cases of great necessity, such as being compelled by government orders to lend or rent it, or similar situations. Otherwise, it is strictly forbidden to permit this from the outset. Additionally, in the case of a sale, it is not permitted to sell it solely for the day of Shabbat; rather, it must be sold completely (Magen Avraham, ibid.).

And this is what our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote: "Or he should say, 'My animal is owned by a non-Jew.'" There are those who say that he must specifically say to him in his presence, "My animal is owned by you." (see there, subsection 10) And transferring ownership through another person does not help, because transferring ownership is considered an agency, and he does not have the status of an agent as stated in Choshen Mishpat, section 182. (Magen HaShulchan there) And one should not ask what benefit there is in a mere statement, as a mere statement is not a transaction. This can be explained that since the animal is in the possession of the non-Jew, automatically when he says to him, "My animal is owned by you," his possession acquires it for him, and this is considered an acquisition by possession. This is not like what one of the great authorities questioned, and we have explained this in Choshen Mishpat, section 194, subsection 12, see there. According to this, it is possible to say that the words of our master, the Beit Yosef, are correct, that it suffices to say this not in the presence of the non-Jew. The reason is that although in every transaction the buyer's intent is also needed, here it is different since he is a complete thief, as he agreed to return it on Shabbat and he does not return it. Therefore, his intent is to steal it, and automatically when he says, "My animal is owned by him," it is no less than abandonment, and there is here both abandonment and transfer of possession, and automatically his possession acquires it for him. (This seems to be my humble opinion, and see Orach HaShulchan, subsection 11, who also agrees with the Beit Yosef for another reason, see there, and the acquisition is considered as a gift.)

Some say that we are only commanded to have our animals rest on Shabbat and not on Yom Tov, as it is written, "so that your ox and your donkey may have rest" (Exodus 23:12), and similarly, "you shall not do any work, neither you, nor your beast" (Exodus 20:10) — these are written regarding Shabbat and not Yom Tov. On Yom Tov it is written, "no work shall be done on them" (Exodus 12:16) — which applies only to humans. It seems to me that according to this opinion, the rest of a slave or maidservant is also not required on Yom Tov, as these are written regarding Shabbat and not Yom Tov. Others say that Yom Tov is like Shabbat, and it is explicitly taught: "There is no difference between Yom Tov and Shabbat except for the preparation of food." And in the Jerusalem Talmud, Tractate Beitzah, Chapter 5 (Halacha 2), they said that one should not ride an animal due to the requirement for the animal's rest. (Rashal in Yam Shel Shlomo there, and see Magen Avraham, Section 12, who agrees with Rashal, but Taz in Section 495, Subsection 3, agrees with Rema. Also, see Beit Yosef later in Section 495 in his major work, who also agrees with Rashal).

Regarding the halacha: Some have ruled it forbidden (the Gra and the Gra"z), and some have ruled it permissible (Tosafot Yom Tov at the end of chapter 2 of Beitzah and the Pri Chadash later in Siman 495). Note that even according to those who hold that there is a prohibition of "Shvitat Behemah" (resting of animals) on Yom Tov, this only applies to performing labor that is forbidden on Yom Tov, like plowing and similar activities. But to place a burden on [an animal] on Yom Tov is certainly not a Torah prohibition, for on Shabbat the prohibition is in a public domain and not in a courtyard, as stated in Siman 305, and on Yom Tov there is no difference, for on Yom Tov there is no prohibition of carrying. And if you say that on Yom Tov it is forbidden even in a courtyard, then Yom Tov would be stricter than Shabbat. Additionally, it is explicitly stated in Shabbat (153b) that it is impossible to prohibit more with animals than with humans, and on the contrary, animals are more lenient there. And the prohibition of "mechamer" (leading a laden animal), which we derive from "you shall not do any work, you, your animal" (there), does not apply on Yom Tov except according to the Rashba, who holds that the prohibition of "mechamer" applies even in a courtyard. But the Ran in the chapter 'Lifnei Eideihen' refuted his words, and wrote that "mechamer" only applies in a public domain, and so wrote the Rivash in his responsa (Siman 24), and consequently, this does not apply on Yom Tov either. And so wrote explicitly the Ramban in Shoresh 14 of the count of mitzvot, that "mechamer" does not apply on Yom Tov. (This is discussed in the context of "mechamer" and he wrote that it does not apply on Yom Tov and the Sabbatical year, and according to this, the words of the Talmud in Beitzah 37b, which says the reason for not riding an animal is a decree lest one cut a branch, and did not say because of "Shvitat Behemto," because on Yom Tov this rest does not apply. However, also the Rambam regarding Shabbat in the first chapter wrote the reason of the Talmud, and we must say it is because the living carries itself. And the Yerushalmi in Beitzah there that says because of "Shvitat Behemto," see Magen Avraham subparagraph 12 that wrote it means lest one go beyond the boundary, and also because it is a distress to it as will be explained in the next paragraph, and scrutinize this well).

Seemingly, since a person is commanded to ensure the rest of his animal on Shabbat, meaning that it should not perform prohibited labor, we should not allow it to stand on grass and eat, as it would be uprooting it from the ground. However, in the Mekhilta of Mishpatim (Parasha 20), it is taught: "So that your ox and donkey may rest"—the verse added another form of rest, allowing the animal to uproot from the ground and eat. Or should it be confined within the house? You would say that this is not rest but distress. (The Tosafot on Shabbat 122, s.v. 'ma'amid' brings this in a different language).

It appears to me that this is merely an asmachta (a supportive scriptural reference), for if not, we would say the same about a servant and maidservant, as it is written there: "and the son of your maidservant may be refreshed." And it is certain that they are prohibited from performing all labors just like their masters themselves. (And there is no distinction between the term "rest" and the term "refreshed.") 

However, the matter is as follows: Surely, regarding an animal, which has no understanding at all, the prohibition of labor does not apply to it. The prohibition is on the owner when he makes the animal perform labor. But without the owner, meaning in a matter where the labor does not involve the owner himself, the prohibition does not apply to the animal. Therefore, they said in Shabbat there: "A person may place his animal on grass." But regarding the servant and maidservant, who have understanding, the prohibition applies to them, and the owners are commanded to supervise them so that they do not perform any labor. Moreover, it is written in the latter commandments: "So that your servant and maidservant may rest like you." (According to this, one could say that this is a complete derivation, and regarding a servant and maidservant, the scripture included them. And examine this closely).

There are those who say that if a non-Jew rides on the animal of a Jew, there is no need to be concerned, because a living being carries itself. However, one should be concerned about the saddle that is under the rider. But to ride outside the boundary is forbidden. (Atoret Zekenim) This is not clear at all, for in any case, the animal suffers, and according to the Mechilta that we brought, it is a complete prohibition. (And this was brought in the name of the Levush in section 305, but it is not found in the Levush.) It is not comparable to what is permitted to sell a horse for this reason, as Maimonides wrote in chapter 20, because there the concern is merely about proximity to idol worshippers, as it is stated in 'Lifnei Ideihen,' and they did not worry about such cases. However, to allow a non-Jew to ride - it is certainly forbidden. And know that even though the rest of one's animal is only with one's own animal, nevertheless, leading one's animal - the prohibition is the same whether it is with one's own animal or with another's animal, even of a non-Jew, because since the animal goes due to his voice, there is no difference, for this prohibition is one that he himself performs. (Ran in the chapter 'Lifnei Ideihen').

Our master, Rabbi Yosef Karo, wrote in section 4: "A Jew who rents oxen to a non-Jew to plow with them, and he plows with them, there are those who permit it if the non-Jew accepts responsibility for death, theft, robbery, inflation, and depreciation. And there are those who say that since the Jew cannot sell them if he wishes, the oxen are still considered the Jew's property." End quote. The primary opinion is the first one, as Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) also rules in section 5, see there. Additionally, this is also the law regarding interest, as explained in Yoreh De'ah at the beginning of section 177, see there. However, if the non-Jew does not accept responsibility for inflation and depreciation, it is forbidden. Nevertheless, I am puzzled because even if the intrinsic prohibition is permitted, there is still the issue of "marit ayin" (appearance of wrongdoing). Perhaps they relied on what is written in section 244, that in cases of significant loss, we do not worry about this, see there. However, I do not know if this is considered a significant loss. Therefore, it should be said either that it is publicized that the non-Jew accepted all the responsibility, or that it is not yet known that these oxen belong to the Jew, or that he is working with them outside the boundary, in which case, even in construction, it is permitted, as written there.

It seems clear to me that when a Jew and a non-Jew are partners in an animal, if the non-Jew performs work with it on Shabbat, the Jew transgresses the commandment of resting his animal. If he can protest, he is obligated to protest. If he cannot protest, he should not partner with him except in permissible ways, as will be explained. Similarly, it is written in the responsa of the Riva”sh, a Tosafist (brought in Hagahot Maimoniyot, the first chapter, and in Beit Yosef at the end of Siman 245), and this is his language: "Regarding your question about a Jew and a non-Jew who are partners in fields and oxen, for the fields there is no prohibition... but concerning the oxen, it is forbidden, because a person is commanded regarding the resting of his animal, and there is no solution except to sell, etc." End quote. And so the words of our Rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, tend towards this in every section 5, as will be explained. (And the Magen Avraham in section 13 brought in the name of the Rivash that there is no concern of the resting of his animal, since the non-Jew has a share in it. This causes a stumbling block for those who study it, for in the Rivash, Siman 151, it is explicitly written that the non-Jew will not obey and will act against his will, and indeed he wrote at the end: "Regarding the resting of his animal - there is none, since he acts against his will because of his share, but he initially made a prohibition by partnering with him, etc." End quote. And the Magen Avraham abbreviated as usual, and examine it well).

If a Jew wants to partner with a non-Jew in an animal that performs work, he should proceed as instructed in the previous section regarding partnerships in a field, oven, or bathhouse. This means that at the time of purchase, they should make a condition that the non-Jew will take all the profits from the animal on Shabbat, and the Jew will take a corresponding day during the weekdays. When accounting, the non-Jew will take the profits of Shabbat and the Jew the profits of the weekday. In cases where this would result in a loss, they can divide the profits equally, as mentioned there. Therefore, even if both share equal responsibility throughout the week, it is permitted, since in the end, they stipulated that the animal's work on Shabbat belongs entirely to the non-Jew. However, if this condition was not made initially, and they later agree that the non-Jew will take Shabbat and the Jew the weekdays, it is as if the Jew appointed the non-Jew as his agent on Shabbat, as stated in section 245. Instead, the non-Jew should take the earnings of all Shabbatot, and the earnings of the weekdays should be divided, as mentioned there. Still, this causes a prohibition, as half of the Jew's animal worked on Shabbat. Even though he cannot prevent the non-Jew from working on Shabbat, he should not have partnered in this manner, as stated in the previous section. (The Magen Avraham there wrote in such cases that they should divide the profits generally, according to the Rama, and in cases of great loss, as he himself explained, and examine carefully.)

Nevertheless, a remedy can be found even if no prior stipulation was made, aside from the solution mentioned in Siman 245 to dissolve the partnership and stipulate beforehand. This involves lending the animal to the non-Jew as a complete loan, granting him the right to use it without the permission of the Jew, and recording the debt against the non-Jew, with the non-Jew also assuming responsibility for the oxen. Some permit this even if the non-Jew does not have the right to use it without the Jew's permission, by recording the debt against the non-Jew as a loan, and the non-Jew making the animal a pledge (apotiki) to the Jew. This means that if he does not repay the debt, the Jew will collect from the animal, and only from the animal, not from anything else. Alternatively, the Jew can hold the animal as collateral, with the non-Jew taking it and working with it, and the non-Jew stating that if he does not repay the debt, the Jew will collect from the animal. However, care must be taken that the non-Jew does not say that if he does not repay, the animal will belong to the Jew from now, because if he does not repay, it would turn out that the animal belonged to the Jew, as stated in Siman 441.

Another leniency was written by our master, the Beit Yosef, in section 5, and this is his language: "And some permit it by having the Jew warn the non-Jew not to perform work with it on Shabbat. If he transgresses and does work, the responsibility will be upon him, even for unavoidable circumstances, and this should be written in their courts. For now, if he comes to do work with it on Shabbat, it is not considered the animal of the Jew, since the non-Jew has acquired it to be responsible for any unavoidable circumstances." End quote. And what he wrote, "that it should be written in their courts," is not exact, and the main intention is that this should be publicized to avoid suspicion. One should not question what benefit there is in accepting responsibility, for even according to the first opinion in section 4, one must accept upon himself both the increase and decrease in value, as mentioned in section 19. And it must be said that this applies when the entire animal belongs to the Jew, but when they are partners, it is sufficient to accept responsibility alone, provided he warns him not to perform work on Shabbat. Some interpret this to mean that he also acquires it concerning the increase and decrease in value (Rabbi Akiva Eiger), but if so, the main point is missing from the text, for only unavoidable circumstances are mentioned, and this is explicitly indicated in his large book at the end of section 245. (And so wrote the Eliyah Rabbah in subsection 13). The reason is that since the borrower, due to his liability for unavoidable circumstances, is like the owner, it still is not considered an acquisition. This applies when the borrower takes it willingly, but if unwillingly, he is like a thief and it is entirely considered his. Therefore, when he stipulates not to do work, and if he does, it is in his possession for unavoidable circumstances. Since he transgressed, he is like a thief, and it is entirely considered his. (So it seems in my humble opinion).

And Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote that all these leniencies are halachically valid, and one can choose any of them that he wishes, even if the entire animal belongs to a Jew—it is considered as if it were in partnership with a non-Jew, provided that it is publicized that it was done in a permissible manner. And he holds that even if it entirely belongs to a Jew, since he changed the usual manner and thus became liable for accidents, it is considered as his own for the reasons we have explained. All these leniencies apply when the non-Jew is performing his own work. However, for a Jew to perform his work, these leniencies do not apply at all, for it is forbidden for a Jew to allow a non-Jew to perform his work unless he sells the entire business in a complete and publicized sale, as we have written at the end of Siman 244. (See Taz, section 15, who wrote regarding what is stated in the Shulchan Aruch that one should warn not to do work on it on Shabbat, and if one transgresses, the responsibility is upon him—that it must be said "from now" so that it should not be considered a mere pretext. See there.)

Rambam writes in Chapter 6, Law 2: "One who gives a letter to a non-Jew to deliver to another city, if he agreed upon a payment for the delivery - it is permitted, even if he gave it to him on Friday at twilight, provided that he leaves from the entrance of his house before Shabbat. But if he did not agree upon a payment, if there is a regular person in the city who collects letters and sends them to each city with his messengers - it is permitted to give the letter to the non-Jew, provided that there is enough time in the day for him to reach the house adjacent to the wall before Shabbat, because perhaps the one who collects the letters and sends them - his house is adjacent to the wall. But if there is no regular person for this task, and the non-Jew to whom the letter is given is the one who delivers it to another city - it is always forbidden to send the letter through him, unless he agreed upon a payment" (end quote). (Regarding what he wrote: "because perhaps... adjacent to the wall," see Magen Avraham, subsection 3 and Bayit Chadash, who disagree with Beit Yosef).

In all tasks delegated to a non-Jew, it is required to establish a fixed payment, as stated in Siman 244 and Siman 252. However, regarding a letter, there is a leniency even without a fixed payment if there is an established person in the country who collects letters. Therefore, the Gemara and the Poskim explained this law separately. (See Magen Avraham 1) Additionally, according to the Rambam, who holds that without a fixed payment, it is forbidden to send it by his hand even not on the eve of Shabbat, as he wrote, it is always forbidden to send a letter by his hand, even though it might arrive before Shabbat based on estimation. In other tasks, it is permitted even without a fixed payment if it can be completed before Shabbat. And even if it is done later on Shabbat, it is not of concern, as stated in Siman 252. But regarding a letter, it is not so, for if it is not done during the week and is done on Shabbat, and everyone sees that the non-Jew has the Jew's letter in his hand, they will say that it was given to him to carry on Shabbat (see there in the name of Sefer HaTerumot). According to this, if the letter does not belong to a Jew, it is permitted (see there).

And one should not ask, if so, according to this concern, what benefit is there in stipulating payment? For they will still say that it was given to him on Shabbat. It can be said that once the payment is stipulated, since he is acting on his own behalf, he will not tell anyone, nor show them the letter. This is not the case without stipulation, for then he acts on behalf of the Jew, and if he does not want to carry it on a weekday and carries it on Shabbat, he will tell everyone that he is carrying it on behalf of the Jew and show them the letter, and they will say that it was given to him on Shabbat.

For this reason, some say there is also a distinction between letters and other matters. For other matters, it is not necessary to stipulate the payment in such and such a manner, but only that it should not be a daily wage. The allowance is if it is done on a contractual basis, where he says, "Do this work for me and I will pay you for the work." It is not necessary to stipulate how much he will pay him, as the non-Jew relies on him to pay appropriately. But for a letter, a specific amount must be stipulated for delivering the letter to a certain city. This is also for the reason mentioned, that if the payment is not fully stipulated, he still acts somewhat on behalf of the Jew and will tell everyone he encounters that he is carrying a letter for the Jew, and they will see the writing and suspect that it was given to him on Shabbat. (Mordechai, Chapter 1, and in the explanation of the Shlah in the B"G, see there). And there are those who disagree with this, as will be explained in section 8.

And furthermore, I say that the law regarding a letter contains an even greater novelty than any other labor. It is indeed perplexing, for although from the perspective of the labor performed by the non-Jew there is no prohibition—since when he is paid a fixed amount, he works on his own accord—nevertheless, the letter of the Jew is being carried beyond the Shabbat boundary. And indeed, a person's belongings are restricted to the boundary of their owner, as it is taught in Beitzah (37b): "An animal and vessels follow the feet of their owner." So how is it permissible to hand a letter to a non-Jew on Friday close to nightfall when he is paid a fixed amount, as he will carry it beyond the boundary? Even though he is not explicitly instructed to carry it on Shabbat, it is still known that he will do so. How then is it permissible for a Jew to allow his belongings to be carried beyond the boundary? And even though regarding a letter it could be said that once it leaves his hand, he no longer needs it and it is not considered his belongings, nevertheless, this surely also applies when he sends money or objects to his home, which is permitted with a fixed amount, and this is practiced daily all over the world by sending objects and money to their homes via the post office. How then can we reconcile this with the fact that our belongings are carried beyond the boundary?

It appears to me, in my humble opinion, that the reason for this matter is that since the letter was given to the non-Jew on Friday before twilight, which is close to the time of acquiring the Shabbat rest, the letter was taken out of its place of rest and does not acquire the rest of its owner. For even someone who fell asleep on the road and it became dark for him, the Sages in Eruvin (45a) hold that he does not acquire rest because he did not intend to acquire rest. And although we hold like Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri who disagrees and holds that he does acquire rest, as stated later in Siman 401, this is because since he was awake and acquired rest, even if he fell asleep he also acquires rest, as explained there in the Gemara. But if not for this reason, he would not acquire rest. Therefore, all the more so, if he intentionally gave it to the non-Jew during the day, it is not considered among his belongings that acquire his rest. This is not comparable to what is stated in Siman 405, that one who gives his animal to a shepherd may not take it out beyond the Shabbat boundary, because there it is still in his domain and he does not intend to take it out of his rest. This is not the case with a letter or other items, where if he gives them to a non-Jew to take to another city and he gave them during the day, he intentionally took them out of his rest. However, in any case, there is a significant novelty in sending a letter, which is not found in all other labors, and therefore the Talmud and the poskim (decisors) explained this law separately.

It is a clear matter that even if one hired a non-Jew with a fixed salary, it is forbidden to tell him to go on Shabbat, for this is essentially like sending an agent on Shabbat. And even if one does not explicitly say so, but rather sends him on Friday to a distant place and tells him: "See that you are there on Sunday or Monday or Tuesday," and it is known that it is impossible to be there unless he travels on Shabbat – this is also considered as if he told him "go on Shabbat." (Magen Avraham, Section 2) Rather, one should give him general instructions to go there, and he can go whenever he wishes. And even though it would be beneficial for the Jew if the non-Jew hurries to go on Shabbat, nevertheless, the non-Jew is acting on his own accord, and the benefit comes by itself, similar to profit in other such cases which is permitted, as stated in Siman 244. Therefore, one must be very careful not to explicitly say to go on Shabbat, and likewise any language that implies he should go specifically on Shabbat.

And regarding the Rambam's prohibition without specifying a payment amount always – several authorities disagree with him. And this is the language of the Rosh (Chapter One, end of Siman 36): "One may not send letters in the hand of a non-Jew on Friday, but on Wednesday and Thursday it is permitted, because it is only on Friday that it appears as if he is telling him to hurry on his mission, and telling a non-Jew [to perform work] is a rabbinic prohibition, even if he told him before Shabbat to do it on Shabbat. But if it is well before Shabbat, it does not appear as if he is saying to him: 'Do my work on Shabbat,' and similarly, hides to be tanned and utensils to be laundered are permitted on Wednesday and Thursday even without specifying a payment amount." End of quote. 

And the reason is that although he did not specify a payment amount, nevertheless, he is not compelling him to go on Shabbat, and when he goes, he does it on his own accord. And our teacher the Rema wrote in Section 1 that one can rely on this opinion if necessary, end of quote, and even if it is known that he would not be able to arrive there before Shabbat (Magen Avraham Subsection 4), for indeed he can go on Sunday and who can prevent him. And even according to the Rambam, if he sends him on Monday or Tuesday and it is known that the place is not far and he can arrive there comfortably before Shabbat, it is permitted. (See Magen Avraham there and examine closely).

And also regarding what we wrote in Section 3 that in a letter there are those who say that a complete agreement is necessary, see there, the Rashba, of blessed memory, disagrees with this, and our teacher the Beit Yosef in Section 2 ruled like him, and this is his wording: "If he stipulated with him that he would give him his wages, even though he did not specify how much he would give him - it is considered as if he set a price, because the non-Jew relies on it (that he will be paid appropriately), and he is working for himself. But if it was unstated, even though he intends to give him wages - it is forbidden, because he does not rely on it, and he is working for the Jew himself." End of quote. Meaning, it is not only when he does not expect any payment that it is forbidden, but even if he expects payment - it is forbidden since it was not promised to him. (See there, Subsection 5) And it is not similar to what will be explained that if he carries it for him for free - it is permitted, because this is different, as he agreed to do it for free due to some favor the Jew did for him, and it is considered as if a price was set. But here he does not want to do it for free but for wages, and since it was not promised to him - he is doing it with the Jew in mind. Moreover, even regarding this, there are those who disagree, as will be explained.

Even according to the opinion of the Rambam, that without a fixed payment it is forbidden even on the fourth and fifth day (i.e., Thursday and Friday) — this is only when no fixed payment was made at all. But if a fixed payment was made for each and every day, meaning that his wage for each day he goes and returns is a set amount per day, and he explicitly tells him that he does not care on which day he goes — it is permitted on the fourth and fifth day, but it is forbidden on the eve of Shabbat. For when he goes out on Shabbat, it appears as though he made such an arrangement with him, and what he said, that he does not care, applies to the other days, but the day immediately following his dispatch appears as though he is his emissary. This is not similar to a completely fixed payment, which is permitted even on the eve of Shabbat, because when he sets a fixed amount for his work, it is clear that he is acting on his own behalf, and it is not at all noticeable that his going on Shabbat is for the sake of the Jew. But with daily wages, and if the first day is Shabbat, it appears as though he is his emissary.

If a non-Jew delivers a letter for free, even if it was given to him on Friday, it is permitted, since he is doing it on his own accord. Certainly, he is doing it out of gratitude to the Jew for a favor the Jew did for him, and it is as if he has been paid. Even if the Jew initiated by saying to him, "Take this letter there," and he agreed, since without the favor, the Jew would not have asked him, and the non-Jew would not have agreed, it is considered as if he has been paid. However, some disagree and hold that whenever it is done for free, it is forbidden if the Jew initiated the conversation, as it is likely that the non-Jew is doing it with the Jew in mind. But in a case where the non-Jew initiates with the Jew to deliver it for free, it is certainly because of the favor he received from the Jew, and it is permitted, as he is doing it for his own benefit, akin to being paid, as previously mentioned.

Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote in Section 5: "If the non-Jew goes on their own to a certain place, and the Jew gives them a letter - it is permitted in all cases," end quote. This is because the non-Jew is not going for the sake of the Jew but for their own sake. There is a question on this, for in any case, the non-Jew is performing labor on behalf of the Jew by carrying the letter from one domain to another and transporting it four cubits within a public domain or a karmelit. (Magen Avraham, Subsection 8) Meaning, it would be understandable if the non-Jew were receiving payment, as they would be acting for their own benefit, but in this case, even though the journey is not for the sake of the Jew, the carrying of the letter is for the sake of the Jew. I am puzzled by this, for if so, it should be more problematic, as how is it permissible to allow the non-Jew to carry the Jew's belongings beyond the Shabbat boundary? This is similar to actively handing over the letter for them to go beyond the boundary. Rather, it is certainly as stated in Section 5, that since the letter was handed over before Shabbat, it is removed from the Jew's domain for Shabbat. According to this, it is like ownerless property that does not acquire a Shabbat boundary, and thus it is entirely removed from the Jew's domain, and it is not considered the property of a Jew at all. (And the Magen Avraham explained that the intention is in all cases, even if there is no established postal service in the town, and anyone can see that the language does not support this at all. The Taz, Subsection 9, explained because certainly, the non-Jew would be paid something, and they are acting for their own interest, and this is only prophetic words, and the intention is even for free as the Magen Avraham initially stated, and it is clear as stated. Nevertheless, practically, it is advisable to be stringent as the Gra"z wrote in his commentary, because from the responsa of Maharam of Rothenburg, Siman 202, it appears that even if the non-Jew is going anyway, it is forbidden. But the Gra agreed with the Shulchan Aruch. Also, in Maharam, it can be said that his intention is that sometimes they do it for free because they have a way there, but the baraita can be said not to refer to such cases. Nevertheless, practically, it is better to determine a small payment for the non-Jew, and take heed).

If he has a non-Jewish employee hired for a year or two, it is forbidden to send him with a letter on Friday, as it is stated in Siman 244:14, that such an employee is not allowed to be left to work on Shabbat. Consequently, it is forbidden on Friday, as it is considered as if he was not contracted for a specific task. However, on Wednesday and Thursday, it is permitted even according to the Rambam, who forbids it without a specific task even on Wednesday and Thursday, because there is reason to say that even such an employee can be allowed to work on Shabbat (see Beit Yosef there). And although we do not hold this way, and we ruled there to prohibit in such cases, nevertheless, their opinion can be combined with those who hold in this Siman that on Wednesday and Thursday it is permitted even without a specific task (the Gra). But if he is not hired for all tasks, but only for carrying a letter, it is certainly permitted even on Friday, as this is exactly like a specific task, as mentioned there in Siman 244.

And this is all on the eve of Shabbat. But on Shabbat, it is forbidden in any manner to deliver, even a letter prepared the day before, to the postman. Even if he positioned the non-Jew before Shabbat to place it on the post on Shabbat and agreed on his payment, it is completely forbidden. For it has already been clarified that instructing a non-Jew to do work is a rabbinic prohibition, even if he told him on the eve of Shabbat to do it on Shabbat. And I have seen someone who permits it in the case of a great loss through a non-Jew who places it on the post, as it is considered a double rabbinic prohibition in the place of a mitzvah, and a loss is treated as a mitzvah. (Mishnah Berurah endnote 118) This is not so, as there is another prohibition here, for the letter has established its resting place with him (the Jew), and how can he place it on the post to be taken beyond the Shabbat boundary, unless the post goes out on the evening following Shabbat, or if the letter or items he wishes to send, or money, is given to the non-Jew before Shabbat and he acquires it as a gift, thereby making it the non-Jew’s from the eve of Shabbat and similar cases. Even in this, it is only permitted in a case of great necessity.

And this distinction that the Rambam makes between whether there is a person established in the city who gathers the letters and sends them to the places to which they were sent—this is according to his explanation in the Gemara (19a), which says that when there is a fixed postal service in the town, it is permissible to send letters on Friday even without a set fee, and when there is no fixed service, it is forbidden. Rashi explained: "Postal service" refers to the city official to whom the letters are sent. If he is always in the city, it is permissible as long as the letter can reach a house near the wall before Shabbat. But if he is not regularly in the city, we are concerned that he might not be found in the city, and one might need to go after him on Shabbat. The Rambam explained it according to his interpretation, which we have written in paragraph 1. It is clear from Rashi’s interpretation that without a set fee, it is forbidden to send letters on Friday to anyone, even if it can reach there before Shabbat, because he might not be found at his home. And even according to the Rambam's interpretation, it is proven that without a fixed service, it is forbidden even on the fourth or fifth days, even if it can arrive, because he might not find him there. Only when it can comfortably reach its destination before Shabbat is it permitted according to the Rambam, as we wrote in paragraph 7 (as the Magen Avraham wrote in subparagraph 4). Now, in government-established post offices in every city and town, it is obvious that it is permissible to deposit letters, items, and money on Friday before dark, as all the permissions are present in them. But on Shabbat itself, it is forbidden in any manner, as we have written, and this is the common custom in all countries, and there is no need to elaborate on this. Telegraphs are forbidden on Shabbat, since one needs to command writing.

In the Gemara (Shabbat 19a), it is stated: "The Rabbis taught: One may not set sail on a ship less than three days before Shabbat. In what context was this stated? For a voluntary matter, but for a mitzvah (commandment-related matter), it is permitted. And one should stipulate with the captain that he intends to observe Shabbat, but if he does not observe it, these are the words of Rabbi. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says: It is not necessary. And from Tyre to Sidon, even on the eve of Shabbat, it is permitted." Our Rabbis have disputed the reason for this prohibition: The Tosafot explained that it is due to the exertion involved, and even within the Shabbat boundary, it is forbidden (see there). This means that just as one may not float on the water because of the decree lest one make a floating vessel, as we wrote in Siman 339, so too it is forbidden on a ship. Hence, it is obvious that it is forbidden to cross on a ferry. This is not considered a decree upon a decree, for it is all one decree—to not cross water by floating, whether with one's body or by means of a vessel. And since it is forbidden on Shabbat, it is naturally also forbidden before Shabbat if one will be there on Shabbat. However, before three days, it is permitted, as there will be a noticeable difference, and he will not make a floating vessel. This is how our master the Beit Yosef wrote in his great book. The measure of three days is because three days before Shabbat pertain to the coming Shabbat (end of chapter 7 of Gittin). Additionally, it seems to me that the reason is that after sitting there for three days, it becomes like his home. According to this explanation, there is no difference between seas and rivers, or between places that are ten tefachim deep or not, and between within the boundary and outside the boundary as we wrote. And for a mitzvah, they did not decree.

And Rabbeinu Chananel explained the reason as being due to the prohibition of boundaries. That is to say, certainly in a large ship that goes only in deep waters more than ten handbreadths deep - it is permitted in every manner, because there are no boundaries above ten handbreadths in water, as stated in Siman 404. But here it refers to a small ship, and we are concerned that perhaps the depth of the water is not ten handbreadths, and it will go beyond the boundary. And what they permitted before three days is because then, if it goes beyond the boundary, it is considered compelled. But three days before Shabbat, which are connected to Shabbat, it is as if he is intentionally planning to violate Shabbat. And even for the sake of a mitzvah, the Rabbis did not decree regarding water, as there is no Biblical prohibition of boundaries in water. (Bach)

The Rif and the Rambam in Chapter 30 wrote that the reason [one may not sail on a ship within three days before Shabbat] is because of the delight of Shabbat. Most sea travelers, during the first three days, suffer from seasickness, and their minds are not settled. Some vomit, and some lie down unable to stand on their feet, and therefore it is forbidden. However, for the sake of a mitzvah, they did not worry about the disruption of Shabbat delight, for one who is engaged in a mitzvah is exempt from [another] mitzvah. According to this, the prohibition applies only to seas and not to rivers, even the largest of them, for it is not the nature of rivers to disturb a person's mind (Tur). Only the sea disturbs the mind because of the abundance of salt in it. And the reason the Talmud did not mention this is because the language "one does not set sail in a ship" applies only to seas, which involve distant voyages, and not to rivers. Similarly, in the Mishnah in Eruvin, beginning of Chapter 4: "and their ship set sail in the sea," and on "the depths froze in the heart of the sea," the Jerusalem Talmud translates: "the great sea split." And the Rambam in Chapter 24, law 6, wrote: "One may set sail on the great sea on the eve of Shabbat for the sake of a mitzvah, etc." - to emphasize that even on the great sea, one may set sail for the sake of a mitzvah. But this, that one may not set sail for a non-mitzvah purpose, applies to all seas. Therefore, indeed, in Chapter 30, law 13 regarding the prohibition, he wrote: "One may not set sail in a ship less than three days before Shabbat," and he did not mention 'the great sea.' (And with what we have explained, several precise points are clarified; see Beit Yosef and examine it well).

The opinion of Ba'al HaMaor is that the prohibition is because the sea is presumed to be dangerous due to the inherent risks for those who travel by sea, as it is written: "Those who go down to the sea in ships... they mount up to the heaven, they go down again to the depths... and they cry unto the Lord, etc." and it is likely to lead to the desecration of the Sabbath. Therefore, three days before the Sabbath, which is called "before the Sabbath," it appears as if one is making a condition to desecrate the Sabbath. The same applies to venturing into deserts and any dangerous places, where it is likely that one will be forced to desecrate the Sabbath because nothing stands before the preservation of life; thus, it is forbidden to venture out three days before the Sabbath. For this reason as well, the prohibition applies only to the seas and not to rivers.

The Ramban wrote another reason, which is that the ship is going only for the sake of the Jew, and the one steering the ship is compelled to perform Torah-prohibited labor on Shabbat such as tying and untying and similar activities. Therefore, when the Jew hires it, it is clearly seen as if he is his agent in desecrating the Shabbat. However, three days before Shabbat, he does it on his own accord. Therefore, in a ship that is not going specifically for the Jew, like our ships, it is permitted for a Jew to board whenever he wants. (Ran, first chapter of Shabbat) According to this, our custom and the custom worldwide, to sail on a ship even on Friday and even on Shabbat through acquiring a resting place, as will be explained, is correct. According to the Rif, Tosafot, and the Maor, we do not find a clear basis for this. However, according to Rav Hai Gaon, our custom is also correct, as the majority of ships do not even sail on rivers unless the depth is ten tefachim. (Or perhaps people rely on the Rashbam in Tosafot Eruvin 43, who rejected this Baraita from the law, but the earlier authorities did not accept his words at all, see Beit Yosef. However, the Baal HaMaor, which the Tur brought, seems to agree with him as the Gaon Avuhav, cited by the Beit Yosef, wrote, but the Beit Yosef rejected his words, see there and examine it well.)

And in order to teach merit on behalf of the entirety of Israel, it appears to my humble opinion that there is proof from within the text of the Baraita itself for the opinion of the Ramban, of blessed memory, from what it is taught: "And he makes an agreement with him on the condition to rest, but he does not rest." This means that he is obligated to make this condition with the owner of the ship, and if afterwards he travels on Shabbat, there is no need to protest against him. This applies to a matter of a mitzvah when he sets sail on the eve of Shabbat or within three days. (Taz, Siman 1) And the reason we do not require this for all work done on a contract basis is because in this situation, the Jew himself is present on the ship. (ibid.) However, in any case, if one were to think that this refers to a large ship carrying cargo and most of the passengers are not Jews, it would be ridiculous for the Jew to make a condition with the ship owner to stop on Shabbat; they would laugh at him and say 'go away'. If we say that he reveals to him that even if he does not comply he should not be concerned, this is even more perplexing, and there is a desecration of God's name, as is evident. But according to the Ramban's words that the ship travels for the sake of the Jew, this is fitting. Regarding the core dispute between Rabbi and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel on whether one needs to make this condition, the Rambam and the Shulchan Aruch ruled according to Rabbi that one needs to make the condition, and the Tur ruled according to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.

However, according to the opinions of the Rif, the Tosafot, and the Me'or, our teacher the Rema taught in section 4 a merit for all of Israel, and this is according to the opinion of Rabbeinu Tam—that for a discretionary matter, it is only considered as such if one goes for a stroll. But if one goes for business or to visit a friend, it is considered a matter of a mitzvah. And this is the language of our teacher the Rema: "There are those who say that any place a person goes for business or to visit a friend—it is all considered a matter of a mitzvah, and it is only considered a discretionary matter when one goes for a stroll. Therefore, in some places, they have the custom to be lenient regarding the departure of ships and the traveling of caravans within three days, because they consider everything as a matter of a mitzvah, and one should not protest against them, for they have upon whom to rely." And even if someone has sustenance and goes for business to increase his wealth—it is considered a matter of a mitzvah (Magen Avraham, section 19), and all the more so to collect debts that are likely to be lost, and all the more so to go for a minyan of ten. However, regarding the ferry called a 'parom' and a small boat that goes in shallow waters, the great authorities have disagreed—some prohibit and some permit, and in Ashkenaz they have the custom to be lenient. (See Shulchan Aruch, section 1, in the name of Chavos Yair, Shev Yaakov, Avodas HaGershuni, Nesivos Chaim, and the responsa of Rabbi Ziskind Rothenberg) Nonetheless, outside the domain—it is obvious that it is forbidden.

Three days before, meaning on Sunday, Monday, and Tuesday, it is permitted even in a ship that is pulled by animals, meaning that the animals pull it along the riverbank by ropes. This is not comparable to traveling in a wagon, which is prohibited due to the concern that one might cut a branch, because since the animals are far from the ship, they did not decree a prohibition in this case. It is obvious that the animals belong to a non-Jew, and it is permitted even in a place that is not ten [handbreadths] deep, as stated in section 2 according to the opinion of Rabbi Hananel, that before three days it is permitted. Consequently, if afterward a danger occurs, it is permitted to desecrate the Sabbath due to the principle of saving a life (pikuach nefesh). Therefore, even if one himself needs to perform labor and steer the ship, it is permitted, since he entered with permission.

It has already been explained in a Baraita (Shabbat 19a) that in a nearby location, such as from Tyre to Sidon, it is permissible to set sail even on Friday morning, since it is only a one-day journey, because it is possible to arrive there with a good wind before Shabbat.
