Therefore, even if there is no good wind at the moment, one can rely on the possibility that there will be a good wind (Magen Avraham sec. 5 and Beit Yosef). And if afterward there is no good wind and he does not arrive before Shabbat, it does not matter, since he set out permissibly. However, if it is just an hour or two away, it is forbidden, because even with a good wind, he would not arrive. All this depends on the distance of the location, so that the calculation is based on a good wind allowing one to arrive before Shabbat. In a place where the custom is not to set sail at all on Friday, one should not set sail even for a short distance, and the children cannot change what their fathers accepted upon themselves not to set sail, even if the time is pressing, for their fathers have already accepted this custom upon themselves. (Pesachim 50b).

Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, followed the approach of the Rif and the Rambam, as is his custom, that the reason [for the prohibition] is due to the disruption of Shabbat enjoyment, and specifically during the day. But in rivers - it is permitted, as stated in section 3. However, he wrote in section 2 that this is only when it is not known to us that the depth is not ten tefachim. But in a place where it is known to us that from the bottom of the ship to the bottom of the river is less than ten tefachim - it is forbidden to go beyond the Shabbat boundary due to the prohibition of boundaries. Nonetheless, within the boundary - it is permitted, and we do not decree that one might go beyond the boundary. And although according to their opinion this was not mentioned in the Gemara, the Rambam clarified in his responses that when it travels below ten tefachim - there is a prohibition of boundaries, as will be explained in Siman 404. And this requirement of our teacher, the Beit Yosef, that there must be from the bottom of the ship to the bottom of the river ten tefachim - some disagree, saying that as long as the river's depth is ten tefachim, even if the ship is somewhat submerged in the water and there is not ten tefachim from its bottom to the river’s bottom - it is not a problem, especially for one sitting above. Nevertheless, the main ruling follows our teacher, the Beit Yosef (Magen Avraham Section 7 and Eliyah Rabbah Section 7). And know that from the precision of his language, it is clear that we do not need to be concerned that there might not be ten tefachim, but rather we assume there are ten tefachim, and therefore the prohibition only applies if it is clearly known that there are not ten tefachim.

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote in Section 2: "Similarly, it is forbidden to board a ship within three days before Shabbat if the Jew will need to perform work on Shabbat, even if they are flowing rivers, and they are more than ten [handbreadths deep]" (end quote). That is to say, even though we adhere primarily to the reason of the Rif and not to other reasons that have been explained, and if so, in rivers it would be permitted – this is only when it is not known that it will lead to desecrating Shabbat. However, in a situation where it is likely to lead to desecrating Shabbat, it is forbidden to set out within three days, but before then it is permitted. And it is not that we know for certain that there will necessarily be a desecration of Shabbat, for if that were the case – it would be forbidden even on Sunday. Rather, it is likely, similar to those who travel in deserts. Therefore, anyone who embarks permissibly, if afterwards it becomes necessary to desecrate Shabbat due to danger to life – what can he do (thus it appears in my humble opinion). Similarly, Rabbi Yosef Ibn Lev wrote in his responsa that when it is known for certain that it will be necessary to desecrate Shabbat – it is forbidden even on Sunday. And similarly, what our master the Beit Yosef wrote in Section 4: "Those who go out with a caravan in the desert and everyone knows that they will need to desecrate Shabbat, etc." (end quote), the intention is not that it is known for certain, but that it is likely to come to this. (See Magen Avraham Section 14 who brought this from Rabbi Yosef Ibn Lev and from the Radbaz that certain desecration of Shabbat is forbidden, and it is obvious that this is the case).

Our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, wrote in Section 3: "In a situation where it is permissible to set sail on the eve of Shabbat, if one boards a ship on the eve of Shabbat and establishes residence on it, even though the ship continues to sail on Shabbat - it is permitted, as long as he does not disembark from the ship from the time he established residence. And there are those who say that even if he disembarks from the ship - it is permitted, for since he established residence on it on the eve of Shabbat - it is permitted to board it again on Shabbat and set sail. And there are those who say that they make Kiddush on the ship and then return to their home and sleep there, and the next day they return to the ship and set sail. And thus is the custom in some places, and one should not protest." These are their words, and clarification is needed.

And the explanation of the matter is as follows: The Ba'al Halachot Gedolot (BHG) wrote: "If one established residence (acquired Shvitah) on the eve of Shabbat, one is permitted to enter it even on Shabbat." This means, despite the fact that the Gemara only permitted it on the eve of Shabbat in a place where it is allowed, such as for a mitzvah or in rivers according to the Rif, or above ten handbreadths according to R. Chananel, and not on Shabbat itself. The reason is that this appears as if one is initially going out of the Shabbat boundary on Shabbat. Even though there are no boundaries above ten handbreadths in water, nonetheless, since one established residence on land and on Shabbat went far away, it appears as going out of the boundary. Therefore, if one acquired residence during twilight in a boat, it is like one's home. Hence, some permit even going out afterward and entering the city, and the next day to return to the boat, because since at the time of establishing residence one was in the boat, one did not establish residence in the city. Some even perform Kiddush in the boat to publicize that residence was established there, but it is not mandatory. Only the Rashba hesitates about this and holds that from the time one acquires residence, one should not leave the boat. The reason is that since the boat is above ten handbreadths, it is not a place for establishing residence, because there is doubt whether there are boundaries above ten handbreadths, and in water, certainly, there are no boundaries above ten handbreadths. This will be explained in Siman 404. Therefore, how could one establish residence there? Hence, if one goes out afterward to the city, one establishes residence in the city, since one has not yet established residence. Rather, one must establish residence there and not leave it. But the custom follows those who disagree with him, that even if one leaves, since one goes above ten handbreadths, it is also considered the place of residence, as it was at the time of establishing residence. Another implication is that when they arrive at the port the next day, it will be permitted to go out. This will be explained with God's help in Siman 404, see there. This applies if one did not leave the boat. But if one left, it is forbidden. However, within the boat, one can always walk, and this will be explained with God's help in Siman 405.

Those who travel in a caravan in the desert, and it is likely that they may come to desecrate the Sabbath, whether by a Torah prohibition or a rabbinic prohibition, and the desecration is due to danger, such as if the caravan travels on the Sabbath more than the Sabbath boundary and he fears to remain alone because of bandits or wild animals, or even if he is concerned about the theft of his animal, property, or clothing, that if he walks on foot or naked he will be in danger, in all these cases when such things happen, it is permitted to desecrate the Sabbath for this, because this is actually a matter of saving a life, yet it is not certain. Therefore, its law is like that of a ship: from Wednesday onward it is forbidden, but before then it is permitted, and if later he encounters danger, it is permitted for him to desecrate the Sabbath. 

And for the sake of a mitzvah, such as going up to the Land of Israel to settle there, even if he intends to return, it is also a mitzvah to spend some time in the Land of Israel. And if a caravan is available to him, even on the eve of the Sabbath, he can travel with them, and the Israelites speak and agree with the leader of the group to stop on the Sabbath, and for the caravan, it is not a loss, because they must rest one day from the toil of the journey. And if afterward they do not comply and travel on the Sabbath, it is necessary to go with them because of the danger. And when they enter the city on the Sabbath, they are permitted to walk throughout the city. For although one who goes out beyond the boundary has only four cubits, this applies to one who goes out voluntarily, but for the sake of a mitzvah, he has two thousand cubits in every direction, as is stated in Siman 407. And even if they left him outside the city and he wants to enter, since he went out for the sake of a mitzvah, he has two thousand cubits in every direction. The same applies even for a non-mitzvah matter when he went out with permission, that is, on Sunday, Monday, and Tuesday, the law is also the same, as stated there. And likewise, if he was mistaken and thought it was permitted to go out on Wednesday and Thursday, it is also permitted, for one who says it is permitted is considered mistaken. (Magen Avraham, Siman 418).

In the time when Israel dwelled on their land, it was taught: (Shabbat 19a) "One does not besiege cities of idol worshippers less than three days before Shabbat, but if they started, they do not stop. And so said Shammai: 'Until it is conquered' - even on Shabbat." The reason is also due to the enjoyment of Shabbat, as during the first three days the warriors are anxious until they settle down. The Tur wrote in Siman 249 that for the sake of a mitzvah, it is permitted (see there), and this is similar to the law of a ship.

It is stated in the Talmud (Sukkah 44b) that a person should not travel on Friday more than three parasangs, in order that he may arrive while it is still day, so that it will be possible to prepare for him the necessities for Shabbat, whether he is going to his own home or to the home of others. For if he arrives just before nightfall and nothing has been prepared for him in his house, he will become upset, and there will be nothing for him or them to eat in honor of Shabbat. Similarly, if he goes to the home of others, either he will have nothing to eat, or if they give him their portion, they will be left without. There is also another concern, that certainly they will want to prepare for him, whether in his own home or in the home of others, and they will delay and end up cooking as it gets dark. It is obvious that if he has notified his household or others in advance, either by letter or by sending a messenger, that he will be arriving for Shabbat, it is permissible to travel more, since they will prepare for him. Similarly, if he is traveling to a regular inn where it is known that they prepare for guests who arrive before dark, it is also permissible, as they are accustomed to expecting guests.

However, all this applies when he is in a settled area after traveling three parasangs. But if he is not in a settled and secure area – he is compelled to continue traveling. And this is specifically if he is in a settled area, where he is able to prepare for Shabbat. But when even there it is not possible to prepare for Shabbat – it is better for him to go to his home or to someone else's home, for in this place he also does not have what he needs for Shabbat. And if it is because they will prepare for him at his home upon his arrival and thereby desecrate Shabbat – he will not permit them, since he also has nothing here, and it is better for him to be at his home or at the home of an acquaintance. And similarly, if he prepares the needs of Shabbat here and takes them with him to his home or to someone else's home – this is also permitted, for we follow the reasoning.

The great authorities have written that all this applies to someone traveling on foot. However, if one is sitting in a carriage or riding on a horse or donkey, he may travel more than three parasangs (approximately 12 miles) (Bach and Magen Avraham; see also Taz), because in these modes of travel, the journey is faster than on foot. Therefore, it is not customary now to be stringent about this. Nevertheless, one should be careful to arrive while it is still broad daylight, so as not to come to desecrate Shabbat. All the more so, when traveling by train, one must calculate the timing very carefully, for even when the train stops and one arrives at his destination, he may still need to travel by carriage to reach his home. Therefore, if it appears that the train will arrive close to sunset, one should be careful to stop at the previous station. Usually, Satan accuses on Friday afternoon, so one should be very careful about this, and his reward will be doubled from Heaven. He will be among those who sanctify the holy Shabbat, and not among those who desecrate it, God forbid.

The Rambam wrote in Chapter 30, Law 4: "It is forbidden to establish a meal or feast on the eve of Shabbat out of respect for Shabbat, but it is permitted to eat and drink until it becomes dark. Nevertheless, out of respect for Shabbat, one should refrain from establishing a meal from the time of Mincha and onwards, so that one enters Shabbat with an appetite to eat." The Maggid Mishneh explained that the intention is that a meal or feast that is not customary on weekdays is forbidden the entire day, even from the morning. This is what is stated in Gittin (38b): There was a family in Jerusalem that established a meal on the eve of Shabbat and was uprooted. However, eating and drinking without establishing a meal is permitted until nightfall. Even establishing a meal that is customary on weekdays is also permitted according to the law, as we hold at the beginning of Erev Pesachim (Pesachim 99b). However, out of respect for Shabbat, one should refrain from establishing a meal even one that is customary on weekdays from Mincha and onwards, which is from the ninth hour and onwards, which is three quarters of the day. There are those who explain his words that initially he is referring to a meal and a feast, meaning drinking, as it is forbidden all day lest one become intoxicated and neglect the Shabbat meal. In the latter part, he is referring to establishing a meal without drinking. (Taz, Sk 1) There is no difference between the explanations, as even according to the first explanation, it is a meal that is not customary on weekdays, which is a feast with an abundance of food and drink. (And I do not understand the lengthiness of the Taz and what he innovated over the explanation of the Maggid Mishneh, see there).

And this is the wording of the Tur: "One should not set a meal on Friday afternoon out of respect for Shabbat, but it is permitted to eat until it gets dark. In any case, it is forbidden to set a meal so that one enters Shabbat hungry." This means, according to him, that what we hold regarding the eve of Passover, that one may eat and continue until it gets dark, applies without setting a meal. But setting a meal is forbidden the entire day. Certainly, he does not mean to prohibit any meal, even a small one, the whole day, for that is not reasonable at all. Rather, his intention is to prohibit a large meal that one is not accustomed to. And our master, the Beit Yosef, explained his words in his great book, even though the plain meaning of his words implies that he prohibits any type of meal, but it is necessary to explain it this way. (It can also be explained that he prohibits any set meal, only permitting casual eating, and this is evidenced by what he writes afterwards that pious individuals fast the whole day. However, it is difficult to say so, and also on the eve of Passover, it does not seem to imply so there.)

The primary enhancement of the mitzvah and the honor of Shabbat is that one should eat the Shabbat meal with an appetite, that he should be almost hungry. And we find in the Jerusalem Talmud, Tractate Ta'anit, Chapter 2 (Halacha 12): "Rabbi Avun would fast the entire eve of Shabbat," as he was delicate and only ate once a day, and if he would taste food on the eve of Shabbat, he would not eat at night with an appetite, therefore he fasted. And it is proper for every God-fearing person that during the winter days, when the days are short, not to eat any meal on the eve of Shabbat, only slight tastings, and also during the summer days to eat a small meal in the morning. According to the Ra'avad, it is forbidden to establish a meal after midday. (According to the version of the Maggid Mishneh there) In summary, "the wise person has his eyes in his head," and the honor of Shabbat is very, very great.

A mitzvah meal whose time is set for Erev Shabbat, such as Purim that falls on Erev Shabbat, or a Brit Milah even not at its proper time, since it can be done today—one transgresses a positive commandment if he does not perform the circumcision today. Similarly, a Pidyon HaBen whose time is today—if it is postponed from its time, it can be delayed to Sunday. Also, a Yom Tov that falls on Erev Shabbat, even the second day of Yom Tov—it is permitted to establish even a large meal. And if the concern is that one will not eat at night with appetite—the one engaged in a mitzvah is exempt from the mitzvah. The same applies to a Bar Mitzvah meal whose time is today. Nevertheless, they should see that the meal begins before noon, or at the very least before the tenth hour. However, if they did not begin earlier, they can still start even after the tenth hour, since it is a mitzvah in its proper time. Some refrain even from a mitzvah meal if there are enough participants for the meal without them. The Shelah, of blessed memory, wrote about his teacher who was a Sandak and did not want to attend the meal since there was a quorum without him. (Magen Avraham, section 6) Also, those seated at the meal should not fill their stomachs and should leave room for the honor of Shabbat. (See Taz, section 2) The meal of consolation can be eaten on Erev Shabbat, as this too is a mitzvah. (ibid.) And Chol HaMoed and Rosh Chodesh—I believe they are like weekdays regarding Shabbat. And know that on Hoshana Rabbah, where it is customary to have a large meal like on Yom Tov, if it falls on Erev Shabbat—I do not see a permit for this. Even on regular weekdays, I do not know the source of this custom, for at night it is Yom Tov, and Yom Tov is like Shabbat in this matter. All the laws we wrote regarding the Erev Shabbat meal also apply to Erev Yom Tov. However, the world considers Hoshana Rabbah as a Yom Tov, and this requires further investigation. (And later in Siman 664, Hoshana Rabbah is mentioned only for the multiplicity of prayers and not for a Yom Tov meal, see there).

Our teacher, Rabbi Yosef Karo, wrote in paragraph 2: “It is forbidden to establish a meal or a banquet on Friday that one does not usually have during the weekdays, even if it is an engagement meal, etc.,” and this also applies to a wedding meal. (Bach) And there are those who say that this applies when the engagement or wedding did not take place today. But if it occurred today, it is certainly considered a mitzvah meal, as stated in Siman 444 (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 3). However, the language of our teacher, Rabbi Yosef Karo, does not seem to indicate this. It appears to me, in my humble opinion, that this is why he did not write about weddings, for certainly a wedding meal is a mitzvah tied to its time, since it is necessary to recite the Sheva Brachot. Therefore, if one marries on Friday morning, one should have the meal. But an engagement meal, although it is also a mitzvah meal, is not obligatory on that day, as it is not the completion of the mitzvah and there is no blessing specific to the meal, and it can be postponed to Sunday. However, if it cannot be postponed to Sunday, such as if the groom or bride is traveling to another place, they can have the meal today, and this is the context referred to in Siman 444. (And this is also written by the Elya Rabbah, subparagraph 4).

The Tur and the Shulchan Aruch wrote in Section 3: "The way of pious people is to fast every Friday." These words only apply to a delicate person, who if he eats during the day, he will not eat at night. But otherwise, one should not fast on Friday, so that he does not enter Shabbat in a state of affliction (Magen Avraham, Subsection 7). It is better to taste something while it is still daytime, and this depends on one’s constitution and the length of the day, as mentioned in Section 6. Additionally, what they wrote about fasting only applies to a person who can eat well and with appetite after the fast. But there are those who become weakened by fasting and are unable to eat at all – these individuals are forbidden to fast (Taz, Subsection 3), and everything depends on the person.

It is established for us at the end of the third chapter of Eruvin: "The law is - one fasts and completes [the fast]." This means not only an obligatory fast such as the Tenth of Tevet that falls on a Friday, but even a voluntary fast, such as one who accepted upon himself to fast on a Friday - he must fast until the appearance of the stars, unless he specified at the time of accepting the fast that he would only fast until the congregation completes their prayers, according to their custom of praying the Friday evening prayer while it is still daytime, as stated in Siman 242. It is proper to do and specify this. (See Taz, subsection 2, and his words require study and scrutiny.) There are those who say that even if he did not explicitly specify this but accepted it generally - he is permitted to eat after the congregation completes their prayers, as this is considered completion, fasting until after the acceptance of Shabbat. However, on a weekday - it is not considered completion until the appearance of the stars, and therefore in an individual's fast, he does not complete it until after the prayer. Nevertheless, it is good to specify this at the time of accepting the fast, since the first opinion does not hold this way. But in a public fast - this does not apply, and one fasts until the appearance of the stars, and this is the custom. Likewise, in a fast due to a dream - one must fast until the appearance of the stars, as this is considered an obligatory fast.

In all the fasts that one has accustomed oneself to observe, such as on the eve of Rosh Chodesh and the Ten Days of Repentance, as well as what will be discussed later in Siman 679 or a Yahrzeit fast, if one completed the fast the first time until the appearance of the stars, one must always do so. Even if the first time occurred on a weekday and was completed, one must complete it afterward even when it falls on the eve of Shabbat. There is an opinion that this is not dependent on weekdays, but only on the eve of Shabbat. If the Yahrzeit once fell on the eve of Shabbat and one completed the fast, then one must always complete it. However, if the fast was completed on a weekday, it does not obligate one on the eve of Shabbat, and one who is lenient not to complete it on the eve of Shabbat has not lost out (Taz, subparagraph 3). This is specifically if one intended the first time to always observe it this way. But if one did not intend it as a vow, it is not obligatory at all even if it falls on a weekday. We have already explained this in Yoreh De'ah, end of Siman 282, and see there in Siman 214.

It is written in the Or Zarua HaGadol, Hilchot Erev Shabbat (Siman 21): "Rabbeinu Eliezer of Metz explained: It is a mitzvah for a Jew to eat the Shabbat meal with appetite... and the main Shabbat meal is dependent on bread... Since it is so... it is forbidden to eat 'gremazal' before the meal on Shabbat, because one will not eat the main Shabbat meal with appetite, and whoever does so is not fulfilling the obligation." End of quote. 

Afterward, it brings the words of the Rashbam in Arvei Pesachim, that we hold like Rabbi Yossi that one does not need to interrupt, but spreads a cloth and sanctifies. The Or Zarua wrote that from his words it sounds that one does not need to enter Shabbat with an appetite, and according to this, it is permissible to eat 'gremazal' before eating the bread. And it is also written that on Erev Shabbat, after sanctifying over the wine, they would bring 'gremazal' before Rabbeinu Kalonymus and before the elders, and they would bless over them 'Borei Minei Mezonot' and afterward the blessing 'Me'ein Shalosh' to increase and complete one hundred blessings, and afterward, they would eat bread and the needs of the meal. End of quote from Or Zarua. (And all of this was brought in the Darkei Moshe, and the Magen Avraham in Siman 6 thought that the Darkei Moshe challenged the Or Zarua and questioned him there because, in his days, the Or Zarua had not yet been printed).

It is certainly the case that even according to the Rashbam, in any event, there is definitely a mitzvah to eat the Shabbat meal with appetite, and it is better that after Kiddush, one should eat bread and Shabbat dishes. Among us, at night, everyone does this, and in the morning, many have the custom of eating sweets and then eating the meal. Regarding the blessing after eating: if one washes their hands immediately, there is no need for the blessing after eating, but if some time has passed, a blessing after eating is required. And the incident with Rabbeinu Kalonymus certainly happened this way, that they did not eat immediately. We have explained this matter with its reasoning above in Siman 176, section 5, see there.

And know, that which is written: "Rabbeinu Kalonymos intended to complete one hundred blessings," its meaning is - he did so for this purpose. However, it is obvious that there were foods that were not typically eaten during the meal but before the meal, such as the sweets we eat, and so too were the "grimizli" that they ate. But if there were items that are usually eaten during the meal and one ate them before the meal in order to increase the blessings - this is not proper, for it is forbidden to needlessly increase the blessings, as we wrote above in Siman 215. (The Alter Rebbe in section 11, but what he wrote that it is forbidden to precede them to the blessing of "hamotzi," as written in Siman 211, see there - the Magen Avraham in section 25 wrote this according to the custom to wash before Kiddush, see there, and perhaps his intention is also there, and examine carefully).

A person should always rise early on Friday morning to toil and prepare for the needs of Shabbat, as Moses our teacher warned at the descent of the manna: "and prepare that which they bring," and the bringing was in the morning as it is written: "and they gathered it every morning." He commanded to prepare immediately upon bringing it, thus the preparation was in the morning. And so our Sages said (117a): "A person should always rise early to prepare for Shabbat, as it is said: 'and prepare that which they bring' - immediately." And in the book Shibolei HaLeket, he brought a Midrash: Rabbi Chisda said, from where do we know that anyone who prepares for Shabbat, it is a mitzvah to rise early and prepare from the morning as it is said (there): "and it shall be on the sixth day, etc.", and the Sages expounded that "and it shall be" means immediately, as it is said: "and it came to pass when the Philistine arose" in the matter of Goliath and David, and it is written there: "and the Philistine approached early, etc." Rabbi Zeira said, even though a person prepares from the morning - it is a mitzvah to add and prepare again before the evening, as it is said (Exodus 16:5): "and it shall be double," meaning that they should prepare again.

It is a mitzvah to wait until Friday to buy food, even though it is more effort, because this makes the honor of Shabbat more recognizable. However, what cannot be found on Friday must necessarily be prepared beforehand. And if they sell in the morning, it is a mitzvah to go even before prayer, provided that it does not pass the time for the recitation of the Shema. One should not engage in Torah study before preparing the needs of Shabbat. (A.R.) And for everything one buys, one should say: "For the honor of Shabbat." (ibid.)

Maimonides wrote in Chapter 30, Law 6: "Even though a person is very distinguished and it is not his custom to take things from the market or to engage in household tasks, he is obligated to perform tasks necessary for Shabbat with his own body, for this is his honor. The early sages, some would chop wood to cook with, others would cook or salt meat, or make wicks or light candles. Some would go out and buy things needed for Shabbat, food and drink, even though it was not their custom. And whoever increases in this matter is praiseworthy." (Shabbat 119). And one should not say 'for it degrades my honor' – for this is his honor, that he honors the Shabbat. And he wrote this in the language of obligation, though the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch did not mention it as an obligatory language. And even he did not intend it as an absolute obligation, for many great individuals do not do it themselves. Furthermore, in the Talmud there, it is considered praiseworthy for those who did it themselves – implying that many did not do it themselves, but it is an enhancement of the mitzvah. And among us, our wives prepare and make things themselves in honor of Shabbat, and a man's wife is like his own self. (See the later pamphlet by the Gra and examine it closely and thoroughly).

We have already written in Siman 242, Section 40, that it is a mitzvah to prepare throughout the week for the needs of Shabbat, see there. And it is written that one should sharpen the knife for the honor of Shabbat, and there is a hint to this in the verse "and they shall prepare that which they bring," where the word "that" (את) hints at knives and pruning tools. It is also proper to clean the walls from spider webs, which are called "puzina." It is proper to taste from all the Shabbat dishes on Erev Shabbat, "those who taste it merit life," and all of this is for the honor of Shabbat, like one who prepares himself to receive a great person, tasting the dishes and cleaning the house, and sharpening the knife to prepare oneself for eating. One should increase in meat, wine, and delicacies according to his ability, and whoever adds, they add to him from Heaven, provided that he intends only for the honor of the holy Shabbat.

It is stated at the beginning of the chapter "Makom Shenahagu" (Pesachim 50:): that one who performs work on Friday from Mincha and onwards will not see a sign of blessing from that work. Nonetheless, he is not punished, but he is warned not to do it. Some explain that it refers to "Mincha Gedolah," which is half an hour after midday, and some explain that it refers to "Mincha Ketana," which is from nine hours and onwards, and this is the main opinion in halacha. (Taz and Magen Avraham, and the Taz and Bach endeavored to explain the Talmud's question there of "why specifically in the afternoon," etc., but they did not see the words of the Ran there, who explained it very well; see there.)

Specifically, labor is prohibited, but commercial transactions are permitted, as well as sitting in a shop. Additionally, labor is only prohibited when done in a consistent manner, but if done temporarily and not as a regular occupation, it is allowed. Therefore, it is permitted to write greeting letters and similar items. Also, repairing one’s clothes and utensils on the eve of Shabbat, for the sake of Shabbat, is permitted all day. The same applies to repairing a friend’s clothes for Shabbat, provided no payment is received. However, if one is poor and wishes to use the payment for the honor of Shabbat, it is also permitted (Taz, sub-section 2). The same rule applies to someone who writes books for himself as part of his study. Certainly, writing Torah insights is permitted all day, but writing for a friend for payment is prohibited like all other labors.

They may get a haircut all day, even if a Jew is cutting the hair, even if it is done by a professional, and even if it is for payment, since it is for the honor of Shabbat and it is evident to all that it is for the honor of Shabbat. This is not similar to repairing clothes, as explained (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 5). All the more so, cutting nails is permitted all day. The Ari Zal was careful not to shave after Mincha on Erev Shabbat, and certainly not on a weekday, because he had not yet prayed Mincha, following the opinion of the Rif and the Rambam in Siman 232, see there (see Magen Avraham there and Eliyah Rabbah). Some are stringent regarding the prohibition of work on Erev Shabbat after the time of Mincha, to not shave after midday (see Biur HaGra), but the common practice is not to be stringent. Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote: a person should reduce their study somewhat to prepare for the needs of Shabbat. Therefore, if his wife prepares for him, he does not need to reduce his study (see Magen Avraham, subparagraph 6, it requires further examination). In regard to the cancellation of Torah study, one must be very careful, especially nowadays when craftsmen do not cease their work, all the more so for Torah study. "If not for My covenant..." (Jeremiah 33:25).

And it is surprising that in our times, craftsmen do not cease their work until close to sunset, and we have never heard of anyone protesting against them. Perhaps this is due to the pressure of making a livelihood. Furthermore, it can be said that in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 331, it is explained that a worker does his work for the employer until close to sunset, so that he can roast a small fish for him, as mentioned there, and this is based on the Yerushalmi. If so, the rule of ceasing work applies only to the employer and not to the workers. Nowadays, most craftsmen have workers, and they are the ones working. Additionally, it can be said that they are not starting new work but finishing some work, which is less stringent. Moreover, it can be said that the reason for ceasing work is because one needs to prepare for Shabbat, and nowadays women prepare everything. This seems to be, in my humble opinion, a way to justify their actions, but the God-fearing individual will follow the enactments of the Sages, and it will be well for him.

It is written: "Six days you shall labor and do all your work, but the seventh day is a Sabbath to the Lord your God, on it you shall not do any work." This means that for six days you shall perform your work with your hands, but on the seventh day you shall not work with your hands. However, if the work was done by his hands before the Sabbath and the work is completed on its own during the Sabbath, it is permitted (Jerusalem Talmud, Chapter 1, Halacha 5). For example, one places bread in the oven before the Sabbath or meat in a pot to cook, and the baking and cooking are completed in three hours, which means the completion occurs on the Sabbath, it is nevertheless permitted, since it is done on its own and he is not doing anything. (This is the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel in the first chapter concerning many laws: according to Beit Shammai, it needs to be cooked before the Sabbath, and Beit Hillel permits it, and the law follows Beit Hillel).

And there is a question in this matter, since we only follow the beginning of the action, why then regarding the obligation of stoning do we follow the completion? For example, one who places dough in an oven on Shabbat or places a pot with food in the oven on Shabbat, if he were to remove them immediately from the oven, he would not have done anything. But if he leaves them until they are baked or cooked, he is liable, even though he only performed the beginning and not the completion. Rather, you attribute the completion to him as if he completed it with his own hands. If so, even when he began with his hands before Shabbat and it completed itself on Shabbat, we consider it as though he also performed the completion. (In Menachot 56b, if one placed leaven on dough and went and sat down, and it became leavened on its own, he is liable for it as an action on Shabbat - see there)

However, the matter is as follows: it is certain that the final outcome is judged based on the beginning, and when the beginning was on Shabbat, the final outcome is judged based on the beginning, as if he also performed the final outcome with his hands. And when the beginning was on Erev Shabbat, the final outcome is also judged based on the beginning, meaning as if the final outcome was also on Erev Shabbat. For the Torah states that the beginning of the act with one’s hands is considered as if he completed the entire work at that time. We see further regarding the work of Shabbat, that even if the final outcome occurs after several days, one is liable for stoning and a sin offering, like one who plants on Shabbat and the seed takes root three days later, and he is liable because it is considered as if he completed the work on Shabbat. Conversely, one who plants on Thursday, even though the seed takes root on Shabbat, it is nothing, as it is considered as if the seed took root on Thursday, for the Torah does not hold one liable for work that completes itself on Shabbat.

Nevertheless, one should not infer from this regarding someone who placed dough and a cooked dish into the oven on Shabbat right before dark, as the baking and cooking occurred at night on a weekday. Why should he not be liable just like someone who sows on Shabbat? In truth, there is no comparison, for in the case of sowing, the entire act of sowing is completed in the usual manner of people who sow, whereas baking and cooking are not considered complete unless they are baked and cooked to the point of being fit for consumption. Thus, he has done nothing on Shabbat. And if you say that if so, then even on the eve of Shabbat in such a manner, he has still done nothing, and the main work will be on Shabbat. This is not difficult at all. On the contrary, if he has done nothing, why should he be liable for what happens by itself on Shabbat? After all, he has done nothing with his hands, and the Torah only forbade actions performed with one's hands on Shabbat, and also that the completion of the work in the usual manner of people should be on Shabbat. Nevertheless, the matter is not clear to me, for perhaps with baking and cooking right before dark on Shabbat, he is liable, just as in such cases on the eve of Shabbat it is permitted, similarly on Shabbat he is liable by Torah law, and further investigation is needed for the ruling. (See Nimukei Yosef in the second chapter of Bava Kama, regarding "his fire is like his arrows").

Therefore, it is permitted to start a task on Friday close to dusk, even though it cannot be completed before Shabbat and it completes itself on Shabbat, such as soaking ink and dyes in water and they soak all of Shabbat, or placing bundles of flax in the oven so that they whiten, and whitening is one of the primary categories of forbidden labors. Similarly, flax that has been taken out from soaking and placed in fire to dry, which involves the prohibition of cooking. (Mordechai, Chapter 1) And why do we not decree in this case that one might stoke the coals, as we decree in all matters on the fire, as will be explained in Siman 253? The Gemara (18b) explains that since the wind would spoil the flax, one would not open the oven to stoke the coals. Similarly, it is permissible to place wool into the dyeing pot on Friday close to dusk, and the wool gets dyed throughout Shabbat. However, there is a concern that one might stoke the coals on Shabbat to hasten the cooking, and therefore, it is only permitted when the pot is not on the fire, having been removed from the fire. (Gemara ibid.) Even if it is not on the fire, it still requires that the pot be covered, and the cover must be sealed with clay all around, because otherwise, we are concerned that one might stir it with a spoon, and stirring a boiling pot, even if not on the fire, incurs liability for cooking, as this hastens the cooking, as stated in Siman 318. Even though it will be explained there that this applies to a dish not fully cooked, but for a fully cooked dish there is no issue of cooking with stirring, this applies to a dish, but for dyeing, even when fully cooked, the color continues to be absorbed, and this constitutes dyeing, which is one of the primary categories of forbidden labors. However, when it is sealed with clay, there is no concern that one will remove the seal with the cover and stir, because this would take a lot of time, and one would remember that it is Shabbat. But when it is not sealed, and one can remove the cover and stir quickly, there is a concern that one might forget that it is Shabbat. Similarly, it is permissible to spread traps for animals, birds, and fish on Friday close to dusk, and they are trapped throughout Shabbat. Even though the trap performs an action by capturing the animals, we have already explained at the beginning of Siman 246 that we are not commanded to rest our utensils. (See Beit Yosef there that the Rokeach is of the opinion that even Beit Hillel holds that resting utensils is required when they perform an action, but all the poskim do not hold this way, as explained there.)

And similarly, it is permitted to open a water source to a garden, and the water flows and continues throughout the Sabbath, watering the seeds. And similarly, it is permitted to place a thick poultice on the eye, which is a medicinal remedy, and it heals throughout the Sabbath, even in a manner that is forbidden to do on the Sabbath itself, and this refers to a situation where there is no danger, as mentioned in Siman 328. And similarly, one may place incense under garments, and they become perfumed and remain so all day long, following the custom of placing frankincense and various spices on the fire to smoke the clothes so that their fragrance spreads. (Gemara there) And similarly, one may place sulfur under utensils on the fire; these utensils are silver vessels that are decorated with flowers and designs, and they are smoked with sulfur, causing them to darken and become distinct. (Rashi there) And even if the incense and sulfur are placed in a vessel - we are not commanded to have our utensils rest, as mentioned.

And it is also permitted to place barley into a vat of beer to soak, and they will soak all of Shabbat and become beer, and similarly with other types of alcoholic beverages. Likewise, one may load the beams of the olive press on olives to make oil from them, or on grapes in the winepress to make wine from them, and the oil and wine will flow out throughout Shabbat. It is permitted to load them just before nightfall, but the oil and wine that comes out of them are forbidden to drink on Shabbat. For if we permit them, we fear that one might come to squeeze them by hand, reasoning that just as they were whole before nightfall and were pressed on Shabbat, what difference does it make whether they are squeezed by hand or by a beam? Squeezing by hand incurs the penalty of stoning and a sin offering.

Therefore, if one loaded the beams while it was still day in such a way that the olives and grapes were already crushed before nightfall, then even if one were to squeeze them by hand, there would be no Torah prohibition. It is permitted to drink the liquids that come out of them on Shabbat. Although there is a rabbinic prohibition even if they were crushed, nonetheless, they did not decree to forbid the liquids that come out of them, as this would be a decree upon a decree. (Magen Avraham, section 118)

According to the Tur, it is only permitted to drink the liquids on Shabbat if they were initially crushed on the eve of Shabbat and then the beams were loaded on them. This will be explained, with God's help, in section 321 (see Taz, section 6). And it will also be explained there whether it is permitted to complete the pressing by hand on Shabbat if they were crushed before Shabbat. Similarly, crushed grapes and grains that were crushed before Shabbat, the liquids that come out of them on Shabbat are permitted. But if they were not crushed before Shabbat, the liquids that come out on Shabbat are forbidden even if they come out by themselves. For in their case, there is also a Torah prohibition on Shabbat: for grapes, because of squeezing, and for grains, because of threshing. This will be explained there, with God's help.

But for other fruits and garlic, which are not designated for liquid extraction, the liquid that comes out of them on Shabbat is permitted in any case. (Magen Avraham, section 119) And there are those who disagree, as mentioned there.

It is also permissible to place wheat and barley into a water mill just before nightfall, and it will grind all of Shabbat, for we are not commanded to rest our utensils. The same law applies to a windmill. However, an animal-powered mill is forbidden because we are commanded to let our animals rest. Similarly, a mill operated by a person is forbidden if done by a servant or maidservant, as we are commanded to let them rest, and similarly, it is forbidden by a hired day laborer. However, it is permissible if done under a contract, as stated in Siman 244. There is a significant point regarding mills compared to other activities we have considered: mills produce a sound, which can be seen as a desecration of Shabbat. In the Gemara, there is a dispute about this, and most authorities rule permissively. In truth, some forbid mills for this reason, saying people might claim that someone’s mill is grinding on Shabbat. This applies in all cases where there is concern about noise, and this is the established custom. However, in cases of financial loss, one may be lenient, as this is the primary ruling. It is also permissible to lease it to a non-Jew. (See there, Siman 22). One should not question those who forbid noise on Shabbat by asking how we can set up weight clocks, known as "zeiger," on Friday, which make noise on Shabbat. It can be said that everyone knows they were set up the day before, as it is customary to set them up beforehand. See further in Siman 338.

And if the millstones belong to a non-Jew, it is obvious that if the Jew gives him the wheat before Shabbat, even if he gives it to him on Shabbat, it is permitted, for he is doing it for his own sake, as long as the Jew does not stand beside him, for it would appear as if he is his agent. However, in a case of a mitzvah, such as grinding wheat for Passover, it is permissible to sit at a distance, as long as he does not get involved in the work but only supervises the kashrut, as stated at the end of Siman 244, when he watches to ensure that nothing is stolen, as the Taz writes there in sub-section 7, and we have already explained this there (see Magen Avraham sub-section 20, who wants to say that by giving wheat to a water mill there is no Torah prohibition, but all the great authorities—the Eliyah Rabbah, the Pri Megadim, and the Taz—have already protested against him, saying his reasoning is flawed, as the Maharsha and all the great authorities have written, and it is unthinkable to entertain such an idea, especially in light of what is written at the beginning of this Siman).

It is also permissible to sell an item to a non-Jew near the onset of Shabbat and to load the item onto his shoulder or his donkey, provided that he leaves the entrance of the house while it is still daytime. That he carries the item in a public domain or outside the boundary - we do not concern ourselves with, for it is his. However, if he does not leave the house before Shabbat but rather on Shabbat itself, it is forbidden for two reasons: firstly, the primary acquisition is considered when he leaves the house; secondly, an observer might think that he sold it to him on Shabbat. Therefore, even in a city where it is permitted to carry within it, it is forbidden for this reason. Some permit it if a place in the house was designated for him at the time of the sale, allowing him to leave even on Shabbat. This only addresses the reason of acquisition, but regarding the suspicion that it was sold on Shabbat, this does not help. This reason was written by the Rambam in Chapter 6, and we brought his words earlier in Siman 246. Therefore, one should be stringent in all cases and only be lenient in great necessity or in pressing circumstances, or if the buyer is strong-armed (insistent), then it is permissible even without designating a place, as in such cases the Rabbis did not decree (Taz Sk 3 and see Magen Avraham Sk 5), and it is proper to avoid this. The law regarding lending him a utensil and renting to him is explained in Siman 246, see there.

And similarly, it is permitted to give one's clothes to a non-Jewish launderer, and hides to a craftsman who processes them, on Friday close to nightfall, provided he leaves his home while it is still day. The payment should be determined as a contract, where he receives a certain amount for each garment or hide, and he should not instruct him to perform the work on Shabbat, and also the non-Jew should perform the work in his own home. And if the payment for the laundering is known, it is also considered as if it were contracted. And nowadays, giving items to a launderer is generally considered as if it were contracted, as it is a known matter, especially if he is the regular launderer, for it is not necessary to contract with him each time. (Magen Avraham, Section 6) Therefore, the simple custom is to give items to a laundress on Friday close to nightfall without specifically contracting payment now, because the payment is known. (ibid) And similarly, it seems to me that with hides for processing, if he regularly does work for him and they have already established the payment for each hide, he can give it to him without specifying the payment each time.

And it has already been explained in Siman 247 that in any transaction, it is not necessary for one to state how much he will pay him. If he stipulates that he will pay him, it is sufficient because he relies on him to pay him appropriately, and he acts with this understanding. Similarly, even if he does not give him anything, but the non-Jew does it for the benefit he received from him, it is also considered as if he stipulated, because ultimately he acts with his own understanding for the benefit he received from the Jew. However, if he does not do it for free and expects payment and did not speak with him, even though he intends to give him, it is forbidden, because then he acts with the understanding of the Jew, as it is written there.

If he did not set a fixed price, it is forbidden to give it to him on Friday unless there is enough time to complete it during the day. Otherwise, according to the Rambam, it is forbidden even on Sunday if there is not enough time to finish it before Shabbat. However, Rabbi Rema rules earlier in Siman 247 according to those who disagree with the Rambam, and he holds that on Wednesday and Thursday it is permitted even without a set price, even if it cannot be completed before Shabbat, because he is not telling him to do it on Shabbat, and only on Friday does it appear as if he is telling him to do it on Shabbat. And even though in a letter he did not permit in such cases unless it was necessary, that is because in that case when he goes every day, it appears as if he told him to go on Shabbat. But here, where he is doing it in his house, and for the Jew it makes no difference when he does it, it is permitted in all cases. (There, Section 8)

If a Jew went on Shabbat to the launderer or tanner and sees that he is doing his work on Shabbat, if he set a fixed price with him as explained - he does not need to say anything to him. However, if he did not set a fixed price and gave it to him on the fourth or fifth day as per the opinion of our master, the Rema, in the previous section, which is also the opinion of most authorities - he is obligated to tell him not to work on Shabbat. This is also the case if the work is done for free as a favor. If the non-Jew listens - all the better, but if not - he is still exempt. The reason for this is that when a fixed price is set, it is obvious that the non-Jew is working for his own benefit, and what concern is it to the Jew? This is similar to seeing a non-Jew doing his own work on Shabbat; should one intervene? In the same way, this applies here. However, if there was no fixed price or if the work was done as a favor, which is not exactly like setting a fixed price, although we permit it because we are not obligated to know when he will do the work, when we see him doing it on Shabbat, it is certainly possible that he is doing it with the Jew in mind. Therefore, he is obligated to protest, to show that he does not desire the work to be done on Shabbat. If the non-Jew does not listen - then it is obvious that he is working for his own benefit. (And doing work as a favor is similar in this regard to not setting a fixed price, that even if given to him in the middle of the week - one must protest when seeing him work on Shabbat.)

And this is what we said, that with a contracted worker, one does not need to protest when he sees him working on Shabbat—this applies to private work. But when the work is done publicly, one is obligated to protest even with a contracted worker because of those who see, so they do not say that the work of a Jew is being done on Shabbat. And if you ask, didn't we prohibit public work even with detached items in Siman 244? Indeed, this is certainly true, but here the Jew did not tell him to do it on Shabbat, and therefore, when he sees him doing it, he must protest. Therefore, initially, it is permitted to give it to him, as we do not need to worry that he will do it on Shabbat. However, there is also a distinction here, for something that is not yet known to be the Jew's property—one must protest, and if he does not comply, he does not comply. But for something well-known to be the Jew's property, one is obligated by law to protest and to make every possible effort to prevent it from being done on Shabbat, as with attached work in Siman 244. (This I learned from the words of the Magen Avraham, section 10, see there).

If a non-Jew performs work for a Jew on Shabbat and brings it to him on Shabbat, if the work was not pre-arranged (not fixed), it is certainly forbidden for the Jew to wear or use it on Shabbat. Since it was not pre-arranged, it can be assumed that the non-Jew did the work with the Jew in mind, resulting in the Jew benefiting from Shabbat labor. However, if the work was pre-arranged, it is permitted to wear and use it, as it is certain that the non-Jew did it for himself. There is no issue of muktzeh (set aside) or nolad (something new), as the item existed beforehand and was merely completed, and anything finished by human hands is not considered muktzeh, as will be explained in the laws of muktzeh and nolad. However, some prohibit wearing or using it if it is known that it was completed on Shabbat, as one still benefits from Shabbat labor, and it is necessary to wait until evening for the time it would take to make it. On Yom Tov, if it was made on the first day, it is permitted on the second day, as will be explained in Siman 515. The primary opinion follows the first view, and therefore, if it is not urgent, it is proper to be stringent like the others say, but if it is urgent, it is permitted. Certainly, if it is not known for sure that it was completed on Shabbat, it is permitted in any case, and similarly, if the main part of the item was completed beforehand and it was only finished and polished on Shabbat, it is also permitted in any case. (Magen Avraham, Seif Katan 13)

Know that all this applies when the non-Jew brings it to the Jew’s house. But to send someone to take it from the craftsman's house is forbidden in any case, as one may not take items from a craftsman's house even on Chol HaMoed, as stated in Siman 534, and all the more so on Shabbat and Yom Tov. Even through a non-Jew, it is forbidden to bring it. (ibid., Seif Katan 14)

Rabbeinu the Rema writes at the end of Seif 4 that all this applies to items made for the Jew (meaning the Jew gave him the material). But if a non-Jew makes shoes (from his own materials) for sale, it is permitted for a Jew who knows him to go and buy from him on Shabbat and wear them, provided he does not fix the price. This is in a city where the majority are non-Jews, but where the majority are Jews, it is forbidden, as he is making it for them, and it is like lighting a candle for a Jew’s need, which is forbidden for a Jew to use its light, as stated in Siman 276. However, some entirely disagree with Rabbeinu the Rema and hold that going to his house to take it on Shabbat is forbidden in any case unless he brought it to the Jew’s house. (ibid., Seif Katan 15) And this seems to be the main ruling.

A person should not go out into the public domain with an object in his hand close to nightfall, as a decree lest he forget and carry it on Shabbat. And even though if he forgets about the object and carries it, there is no Torah prohibition, for this is not considered a deliberate act. From the Torah, one is only liable for a sin offering if he forgot that it was Shabbat or was unaware of the prohibition, but if he forgot about the object, he is not liable for a sin offering, as stated in Siman 342. And since in such cases there is no obligation to bring a sin offering, there is no need to decree to prevent this, as we do not make one decree to prevent another decree (as per Rava, Shabbat 11a). Nevertheless, we are concerned that he might forget about the object until it becomes night and not put it away, and at night he will remember the object and forget that it is Shabbat (Tosafot there).

However, it is permitted to go out on the eve of Shabbat with a needle stuck in his garment, because in such cases, even if he forgets, he will not be liable for a sin offering, as this is not the usual manner of carrying, as stated in Siman 301. And even a tailor, for whom it is usual to go out in this manner, and there is a dispute in the Gemara whether an artisan in his usual manner is liable or not, the Rambam ruled in Chapter 19 that he is exempt (even though he ruled like Rabbi Meir against Rabbi Yehuda, see Magid Mishneh, because the Sugya follows Rabbi Meir) and so did the Tur rule in Siman 301. And since there is no Torah prohibition, we do not decree to prevent this, as stated.

According to this, for us, who hold that nowadays there is no public domain (as defined by Torah law), this law does not apply for this reason. But with tefillin on his head, it is permitted even in a complete public domain to walk close to nightfall, even though there is a liability for a sin offering with tefillin on his head, because the main way of walking with tefillin is in this manner (Bach, not like Beit Yosef there). And even though for another reason one is exempt with tefillin, even when going out with them on Shabbat, because they are considered a garment (Shabbat 61a), nevertheless, on Shabbat it is forbidden to go out with them, because when he needs to relieve himself, he will remove them from his head and may come to carry them four cubits in the public domain (Rashi there).

Nevertheless, close to nightfall, it is permitted, and we are not concerned that he will forget about them, since distraction of mind is forbidden with tefillin. And even though it was explained in Siman 28 that distraction of mind is only frivolity (see there), nevertheless, since frivolity is forbidden, he will remember them and remove them from his head before nightfall. (But otherwise it would be forbidden, and in this case, it is not considered a decree to prevent a decree, because this is certainly the usual manner of people, see Taz, subparagraph 8).

It is stated in the Gemara (12a): "A person is obligated to check his clothes on the eve of Shabbat at twilight, lest he forget and go out [with something prohibited]." Similarly, this is the language of the Rambam at the end of Chapter 19. And I am astonished at the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch, Section 7, who wrote "it is a mitzvah to check," etc., and changed it from an obligation to a mitzvah. Even for us who do not have a public domain [in the halachic sense]—nevertheless, perhaps there is something muktzeh [prohibited to move on Shabbat] in them. And this is the language of the Rokeach: "A person needs to check his pocket or his belt lest there be a pocket or a knife hanging from it, or in the belt of his pants, and a woman in her pocket or in the sleeves of her dress or in the kerchief on her head," end of quote. And the Gemara concludes that this is a 'great halacha for Shabbat,' meaning a great safeguard for Shabbat.

It has already been explained at the beginning of the previous section that it is permissible to begin work on Friday even if the work will be completed on Shabbat. Therefore, a person can place a pot with food on the fire on Friday close to nightfall, or meat in the oven or on coals, and they will continue to cook on Shabbat. However, there are certain matters in this regard that the Sages prohibited, due to a decree lest one stoke the coals on Shabbat in order to hasten the cooking. This is because stoking is done in an instant, and in his desire to eat, it is likely that in that moment he will forget that it is Shabbat and will stoke the coals, thereby coming to a Torah prohibition. For by stoking the coals, the cooking will be hastened, and he will be cooking on Shabbat. Therefore, the Sages made certain safeguards for this, as will be explained with the help of Heaven.

Due to the fact that there is a disagreement among the authorities on this matter, and also because their method of cooking was different from ours, it is necessary to first explain their method of cooking: In their time, the oven was not open from the side like ours, nor was it as large as our oven. They had three types of ovens: a kirah, a kupach, and an oven. None of these were usually attached to the ground, and their openings were at the top. They would light a fire at the bottom, and the flame would rise. They would place the pot on the mouth of the kirah, kupach, or oven, which means on their walls, and the entire pot was opposite the cavity. The kirah was made to hold two pots and was long and short, being equal at the top and bottom. The kupach was also equal at the top and bottom, but it was smaller than the kirah, meaning it was made for one pot. Consequently, since it was not long, it retained heat more than the kirah. The oven was also made for one pot and was wide at the bottom and narrow at the top, consequently retaining more heat than the kupach. Additionally, they would stoke the oven more than the kirah. (Rashi, Bava Batra 20a, s.v. 'And in a kirah.' It is puzzling regarding the Tur, Choshen Mishpat beginning of siman 155, who wrote in the name of the Rashbam that the kirah was open from the side. Also, the Nimukei Yosef there brings this from the Jerusalem Talmud, which says the kirah was made like a dovecote. This is surprising, as the explanation is that it was equal at the top and bottom like a dovecote, and not like an oven which is narrow at the top.)

And their fuel was either straw and stubble gathered from the field, from which the fire is very weak and contains only a few coals, or olive pulp, which is the residue of olives or sesame. The fire from olive pulp was very strong and contained many coals, and similarly with sesame pulp, although it is not as strong as olive pulp but stronger than straw and stubble. And similarly with wood, the fire is very strong and contains many coals. Additionally, they would use animal dung as fuel, and it is stated in the Jerusalem Talmud at the beginning of Tractate Kira: that the dung of small animals is like olive pulp and wood, and that of large animals is like straw and stubble. It is surprising that Maimonides in Chapter 3 wrote the opposite, as we will bring his words, and it must be said that this was his version in the Jerusalem Talmud.

Their custom on Friday evening was to leave the cooked dishes in their pots, meaning to place them on the stove, the hearth, or the oven so that they would remain warm until they ate the Shabbat evening meal. They did the same for the second meal on Shabbat morning. This is called "shehiyah," meaning that they left the pot on the stove, etc. Some would also, after taking the pot off the stove on Shabbat and removing a bit of the dish, return it back to its place on the stove. This is called "chazarah," meaning that they took it and then returned it. This is much more stringent than "shehiyah," as it is done on Shabbat itself, whereas "shehiyah" is done on Friday evening. Some, after taking the pot off the stove, would insulate it with cloths or other materials, wrapping it above, below, and around the sides. This is called "hatmanah," and these laws will be explained in Siman 257. However, in this Siman, only the laws of "shehiyah" and "chazarah" are discussed.

And this is the language of the Rambam in Chapter 3, Law 4: "A dish that has not been fully cooked or hot water that has not been fully heated, or a dish that has been fully cooked and as long as it continues to cook it benefits - one may not leave it on the fire on Shabbat even though it was placed there before Shabbat, as a decree lest one stoke the coals to complete its cooking or to enhance it. Therefore, if one raked the coals or covered the stove's fire with ashes or with fine flax, or dampened the coals so that they are like covered with ashes, or if he kindled with straw or stubble or with animal dung so that there are no burning coals - it is permitted to leave it there, for he has diverted his attention from this dish, and we do not decree lest he stoke the fire." End quote. Meaning, that he has diverted his attention from this dish regarding stoking, since he performed an action to reduce the fire - we no longer fear the concern that he might stoke. (This is the intention of the Kesef Mishneh and it answers the question of the Ra’avad there.) And it is not necessary to extinguish until there is no fire visible at all; merely any reduction suffices, (Ran, Beit Yosef, and Magen Avraham paragraph 3) since he has revealed his intention that he does not need the coals - it suffices. (ibid.) Therefore, it is said in the Gemara (37b) that even if he reduced and re-ignited - it is permitted to leave it, and even with the coals of broom, which are strong in their heat as it is written: "the coals of broom" - nevertheless it is permitted, since he has shown that he does not need to stoke. And the Rambam omitted this law, and likewise the Rif, Tur, and Shulchan Aruch did not mention this, and it is questionable, for no one disagrees with this. And know, that some say that "grufa" does not mean to remove the coals from the oven - rather to push them to one side of the oven (Ran and Maor) as we do, but the Rambam, Tur, and Shulchan Aruch do not hold this way.

And the Rambam wrote: "What are we talking about? With a stove that has minimal heat. But an oven, even if the fire has been swept out or covered with ashes, or if it was fueled with straw or stubble, one cannot leave food inside it, on top of it, or near it if the dish is not fully cooked or if it is fully cooked but improves with continued cooking. Since its heat is very intense, he does not divert his attention from it, and we are concerned that he might stoke this small fire, even if it is made of straw and stubble or covered. And why did they prohibit leaving food in an oven even though it has been swept out? Because the one who sweeps out the fire only removes most of it, and it is impossible to sweep out all the fire so that not even a single spark remains. Since its heat is intense, we are concerned that he might stoke it to ignite the remaining sparks in the oven." End quote. And even though covering the coals indicates that he does not intend to stoke, it can be said that this is only for a stove with minimal heat, and when it is covered, it is close to being completely extinguished, which is a clear indication of his intentions. This is not the case with an oven where the heat is very intense; this is not a clear indication at all. It can be said that the covering was to temper the fire from its intense heat so that it does not burn the dish, and when he later sees that the fire has completely subsided, he might stoke it to increase it a bit. And indeed, there are some of the great authorities who hold this view, that the prohibition with an oven applies only when it is swept and not when it is covered, because covering indicates his intention as mentioned. And similarly, when it is fueled with straw and stubble where the fire is weak, there is also no difference between an oven and a stove. (This is found in the name of the Ra'avad.) But most of the authorities follow the Rambam's opinion.

And he further wrote: "The kupach (a type of stove) generates more heat than a kira (a regular stove) and less heat than a tanur (an oven). Therefore, if it was fueled with pomace or wood, it is like a tanur, and one cannot leave a dish in it, on it, or adjacent to it if the dish is not fully cooked or if it improves by remaining on the heat, even if it was raked out or covered with ashes. But if it was fueled with straw or stubble, it is like a kira that was fueled with straw or stubble, and one can leave a dish on it, and it is permitted to place a dish adjacent to the kira on the eve of Shabbat, even if it is not raked and covered." These are his words. This means that even if it was fueled with pomace and wood, they were not stringent regarding placing a dish adjacent to a kira. "Placing adjacent" means placing the pot on the side of the kira so that it heats by its walls, like in our ovens. And there are those who say that it is also permitted to place adjacent to a kupach if it is raked and covered, and the Talmud, which prohibits, refers to when it is not raked and covered. (This is how it appears in the name of the Ramach.) And the opinion of the Rambam is that if fueled with pomace and wood, the kupach has the exact status as a tanur. From the words of the Rambam, it is understood that "leaving" refers both to placing the pot on top or inside, like in our ovens. And know that the prohibition in all these matters only applies when the inside of the oven, kupach, or kira is hot enough that the hand would recoil from it. But if they have cooled down to the point where the hand does not recoil from them, even if there are still coals, it is permitted to place something on or in them in any manner. And this is not only on the eve of Shabbat but even on Shabbat itself, since they are not suitable for cooking. (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 9)

And everything that was explained regarding the prohibition of leaving food [on the stove]—this applies when the dish is fit to be eaten at night, meaning it has already been cooked substantially before Shabbat, but requires further cooking or benefits from being left on the heat. Even though his intention is for the next day, we still worry that he might decide to eat it at night. However, if there is proof that it is not fit to be eaten at night, such as placing a raw dish shortly before evening, such that it would not be adequately cooked by the time of the evening meal, and he will necessarily leave it until the next day—in such cases, it is entirely permissible to leave it [on the heat] even in an oven. And even though it might be cooked within three or four hours of the night, we do not worry that he will delay the Shabbat evening meal for such a long time because it is customary for Jews to eat the Shabbat meal at the beginning of the night, as this is part of the honor of Shabbat.

This is the language of the Rambam there: "A raw dish that has not been cooked at all, or one that has been fully cooked and then shrinks and deteriorates - it is permitted to leave it on the fire, whether on a stove or an oven. And similarly (even) any dish that has been partially cooked, or fully cooked and then shrinks and improves, if one throws a raw piece into it close to twilight - the entire dish is considered as raw and it is permitted to leave it on the fire, even though it has not been raked or covered, because he has already diverted his attention from it and will not come to stir the coals." These are his words. This means that until the next day there is plenty of time for it to cook, so why would he stir the coals? And this applies specifically to raw meat that requires a long time to cook, but raw vegetables and the like that cook quickly - it is forbidden. (Taz section 2 and Magen Avraham section 4)

And know that the things we permitted for leaving on the stove, such as a stove or a range that was fueled with straw and stubble, or a dish that was fully cooked and only deteriorates when left longer, or a raw dish or a piece of raw meat that was placed into it, which we permitted even in an oven — this is only permitted for leaving on the stove on Friday close to sunset. But for returning, meaning that it was removed on Shabbat and they want to return it to the stove, range, or oven — it is forbidden, because when one returns it on Shabbat, it appears as if he is cooking from the outset. And there are those who forbid returning it even before nightfall, as long as it cannot be cooked before Shabbat begins (Tosafot beginning of “Kirah” s.v. ‘uBeit Hillel’), but the opinion of the Rambam does not appear to be this way.

This is the language of the Rambam there: "Anything that is permitted to be left on the fire, when it is taken off on Shabbat, it is forbidden to return it to its place. And one should never return it (even if it shrinks and deteriorates or an uncooked dish) except on a stove that has been swept (because in this case it does not appear like cooking) or on a stove or oven that has been heated with straw and stubble (also for the reason explained), provided that the pot was not placed on the ground. But once it has been placed on the ground, it should not be returned (because in this case it always appears like cooking), even on a swept or covered stove, and it should not be returned to an oven or stove that has been heated (so it should be said) with peat or wood (and in an oven even with straw and stubble), even though it has been swept or covered (even if it shrinks and deteriorates or an uncooked dish) because its heat is very intense. And anything that cannot be returned to - cannot be leaned on during Shabbat," end quote. And regarding leaning on a stove, some disagree and permit, as stated in section 7. And all this is the opinion of the Rambam who follows the opinion of his teacher the Rif, and this was agreed upon by the Ramban, of blessed memory. (For the question at the beginning of the chapter on whether our Mishnah deals with leaving or returning - the Rif proved that the conclusion is stringent, that it was taught about leaving, see there, and so the Baal HaMaor wrote there).

But according to the opinions of Rashi, Tosafot, the Rosh, and the Rashba, and similarly, Rav Hai Gaon and Rabbeinu Chananel believe that all the prohibitions that were explained apply only to returning (food to the heat source) and not to leaving it (there from before Shabbat). And with leaving it, it is only prohibited if it began to cook and has not yet reached the stage of Ma'achal Ben Drosai, which is one-third cooked according to Rashi and half cooked according to the Rambam. However, once it has reached this stage, even if it improves by simmering, it is permitted, for we hold like Chananya (Shabbat 20a) that anything that has reached the stage of Ma'achal Ben Drosai is permitted to leave on the stove, even if it is not swept or covered. According to the Rambam, this only applies to roasted foods, as will be explained in Siman 254, and not to cooked foods in a pot. According to these Rabbis' opinions, the laws are more lenient, as we will explain with God's help.

And according to this view, the law is as follows: As long as it has begun to cook but has not yet reached the stage of Ma'achal Ben Drusai (which was a bandit who ate food partially cooked) – it is forbidden to leave it on top of a stove that is not swept and covered with ashes, or on an oven even if it is swept and covered, and even if it was fueled with straw and stubble. And a stove fueled with straw and stubble – it appears that it is permitted, and a double stove with straw and stubble – is like a stove, and if fueled with pressed waste and wood – it is like an oven. (This seems to be the case in my humble opinion, that according to this view, before it has reached the stage of Ma'achal Ben Drusai – it is like the Rambam, from where do we say otherwise, and Hananiah only argues regarding Ma'achal Ben Drusai. And it is possible that according to this view, a stove and an oven are equal in terms of leaving [food on them], and in any case, the main point is as I wrote, and so it seems in the Ran, see there. And regarding an oven – it is also forbidden to place [food] near it, and regarding a stove – it is always permitted to place [food] near it, and regarding a double stove, there is a dispute as I wrote in section 7.)

And anything that has reached the stage of "Ma'achal Ben Drusai" (the food of Ben Drusai, i.e., partially cooked), even if it continues to cook and improve, it is permissible to leave it on top of a stove, oven, or kupach (a type of stove) (Tosafot 38b, s.v. 'Tanur' and Maggid Mishneh there). And even if it was fueled with pomace and wood (there in Maggid Mishneh), because once it has cooked to the stage of Ma'achal Ben Drusai, it will continue to cook on its own, and we do not worry about stoking, since for the sake of drying out [the food], one will not come to stoke the coals. And all the more so if it is raw, and if it is fully cooked and continues to cook and worsen. 

The difference between a stove and an oven is with regard to returning a pot. For a stove that was fueled with straw or stubble, it is permissible to return a pot onto it even if it is not swept out or covered with ashes. But if it was fueled with pomace and wood, it must be swept out or covered. An oven, however, is forbidden even if it is swept out or covered, and even if it was fueled with straw and stubble. 

And a kupach, when fueled with straw and stubble, is treated like a stove, and when fueled with pomace and wood, it is treated like an oven. And with an oven, even placing close by is forbidden in all cases when returning a pot, whereas with a stove, it is permissible in all cases, and with a kupach, there is a dispute as I wrote in section 7.
