Sometimes, an action is considered "placing" ( סמיכה) even when it is done on a stove, such as in the case of two stoves built together with only a wall separating them. This wall is made of earthenware, and one stove is raked out and covered ( גרופה וקטומה) while the other is not. It is permissible to place [a pot] on the raked out and covered stove even though it was fueled by pressed grape skins and wood, and the same applies to the second stove. Even though the first stove adds heat due to the heat rising from the second stove, it is still considered only "placing" and is permissible (Gemara, 37). The Rambam and the Tur did not mention this, and it requires further investigation.

The Tur wrote: "An oven that has been swept and covered, and the pot was removed from it—even on Shabbat, it is permissible to return it as long as it is still boiling. And specifically on top of it, such as on its edge or on a cover over its cavity, and while it is still in his hand and his intention is to return it. But into the cavity of the oven, or if he placed the pot on the ground, or even if it is still in his hand but his intention was not to return it—it is forbidden. And even if he did not place it on the ground but hung it on a stick or placed it on a bed, or transferred it from one pot to another—it is forbidden." End of quote. And in this, he was very stringent against the Rambam, as the Rambam did not differentiate between on top of the oven and inside the oven (see Beit Yosef and requires further examination). The Gemara there explicitly supports the Tur, stating: "They only taught [this ruling] regarding on top of it, but into it—it is forbidden," and concludes that this ruling is said regarding returning. And the Rambam did not mention this matter, and his reasoning seems clear to me: the one who says this believes that our Mishnah is discussing returning, and therefore, the Rambam, who ruled that it is discussing leaving it, nullified this statement. According to the Rambam, returning is only permitted in an oven or stove that was heated with straw and stubble and has been swept and covered, as mentioned in section 11, and in such cases, there is no relevance to differentiate between inside it and on top of it, obviously. But the Tur, who ruled that it is discussing returning, rightly ruled according to this statement. And in this, he was also stringent against the Rambam, as the Rambam only forbade it when placed on the ground, and did not require that his intention be to return it, and the Tur was stringent in this regard. And in the Gemara, there are two versions regarding this, which is also for the reason we explained, that according to the Rambam, where returning is entirely forbidden except in an oven or stove heated with straw and stubble and swept and covered—it is not relevant to be so stringent, unlike the Tur. (And this is clear with the help of Heaven)

And know that "inside it" is only considered when the bottom of the pot is standing on the bottom of the stove. But when it is not touching the bottom of the stove, even if most of the pot is inside the stove and is held by the width of the stove from above - this is considered "on top of it" and is permitted. (Magen Avraham 22) And our ovens, which have the same law as a stove as will be explained, and in them there is no "on top of it," as they are always placed inside - there is no difference in this, and "inside it" is like "on top of it." (This is the intention of the Shiltei Giborim brought by the Magen Avraham there)

And what has been explained that it is permitted to return [a pot] even on Shabbat - this is when the dish is fully cooked and has not yet cooled down. But if it is not fully cooked or it has cooled down - it is obvious that it is forbidden to return it when the hand feels the heat there, because this is exactly like cooking. And with a fully cooked dish that has not cooled down - it is permitted to return it even to a different stove, and even if the heat is greater than the first one, since there is no concern of cooking. And if it is not fully cooked or it has cooled down - it is forbidden to return it even to the same stove when the hand feels the heat there. And what we permitted even to a different stove - this is because it is from one placing to another placing, and it is all the same. But when the pot was in insulation and one wants to place it on the stove - it is forbidden, and all the more so to take it from the stove and insulate it, as will be explained in Siman 257, see there.

Rabbeinu the Rema wrote in section 2: "And some say that all of this prohibition only applies when it was taken from the stove while it was still day and not returned until after dark. But if it was taken from there after dark, it is permitted to return it, even if it was placed on the ground. And thus, the custom is to be lenient with our ovens, which have the status of a stove, and rely on the words of those who are lenient. However, it is good to be stringent. Yet if it has cooled down, it is prohibited according to everyone. And some say that if one took food out of the oven on Shabbat, it is forbidden to place it in pillows and blankets." End quote. 

The explanation of his words is that some say the entire prohibition of returning, which the sages forbade, only applies when it was taken on the eve of Shabbat and returned after dark. In such a case, even if it was fully cooked and boiling, it is forbidden, as this is considered leaving it initially on Shabbat. But when it was taken on Shabbat and returned on Shabbat, this is not the returning that the sages forbade, since cooking is not relevant here, and there is no concern of stoking, as it is boiling and fully cooked, and it is considered as if it was left. Even if it was placed on the ground, the initial leaving has not been nullified. And on this, people rely when they take pots from our ovens, which are fired with wood and not raked and covered, and take a little food and return the pots to the oven. However, it is truly good to be stringent, as this is only a singular opinion (Ran of blessed memory). And when it has cooled down, it is obvious that it is forbidden. And what he wrote, "that it is forbidden to place it in pillows and blankets," is a simple matter, as even if they do not add warmth, it is forbidden on Shabbat, as stated in section 257, but because some used to do so thinking that the prohibition of insulating on Shabbat only applies to the initial insulation, but once it stood on the stove it is permitted, just as it is permitted to transfer from one stove to another, it informs us that it is forbidden. (Thus it appears to me in his intention).

The Tur writes: "If it is not swept and covered with ashes, it is prohibited to return [a pot to the stove]. This is not only on Shabbat, but even during the day, after all the cooking of the pot is completed, and it is left on the stove until evening to keep it warm. If it is removed from the stove, it is forbidden to return it even while it is still boiling, if it is so late in the day that there would not be enough time to bring it to a boil if it were cold. This is because we decree [against returning it] lest one come to return it on Shabbat. For if we permit returning it during the day, one may come to return it if it was taken off on Shabbat. However, as long as it is not fully cooked, or even if it is fully cooked and there is enough time in the day to bring it to a boil if it were cold, it is permitted to return it. And in an oven, even if it is swept and covered with ashes, it is prohibited to return it. And a double stove (kupach), if it is heated with straw and stubble, it is treated like a stove (kira); if it is heated with peat and wood, it is treated like an oven." End of quote.

And behold, regarding what is written: "If you permit it before Shabbat, one might also return it when it was taken on Shabbat" – this does not align with the opinion brought by our Rabbi, the Rema, who states that if it was taken on Shabbat, it is permitted to return it. However, we have already written in section 19 that this is a singular opinion, and the Tur does not hold this way. But even according to this opinion, there is a decree lest one take it on the eve of Shabbat and return it on Shabbat. (According to this, it fits well that the Rema also brought this and ponder it.) Similarly, what was written: "When there is time during the day to heat it, it is also permitted" – this fits well, because in such cases it is not considered returning but rather delaying, for if not, we would forbid returning anything on the eve of Shabbat. However, what is written: "Even when it is not yet cooked, it is permitted to return it" – this is not understood. The commentators wrote that the reason is that in such cases we do not decree that one might do it on Shabbat, because certainly, they will not cook on Shabbat. (Magen Avraham section 26, and see Taz section 15) This is certainly puzzling, for we do decree lest one forgets that it is Shabbat and stokes the coals. Indeed, there are authorities who disagree with this (see Magen Avraham there and Bach), and our Rabbi the Rema did not bring this. His reasoning seems to be that if it is not yet cooked, it does not apply to call it returning but rather delaying, and the proof is that returning is permitted even on Shabbat as explained, and on Shabbat, it is obvious that one does not return in such cases. In summary, the term "returning" only applies to something that is completely cooked.

And our teacher, the Rema, brought this as well, and this is his language: "There are those who say that any time it is close to nightfall, or close to 'Barechu,' which is the acceptance of Shabbat for us, if it is so close that if the pot cools down it will be impossible to reheat it before Shabbat starts, its status is like it is on Shabbat itself. And there are those who are lenient about this, and the custom is to be lenient, but it is good to be stringent where there is not much need. And this is specifically on the stove itself, but to place it near – even near the fire in a place where the hand recoils is permitted, even close to nightfall. And in an oven, there is no difference between returning it to the oven and placing it near it. And specifically in a place where the hand recoils, but if the hand does not recoil there – it is permitted even on Shabbat, as will be explained later in Siman 318." End of quote. 

And regarding placing it near, it is permitted even if it has completely cooled down (Magen Avraham, section 29), for if not, even on Shabbat it would be permitted to place it near, as will be explained later in Siman 318. (ibid.) And know, that which is written: that close to 'Barechu' is like close to nightfall – there are those who disagree with this, that one should not be stringent in something that is only a decree lest one stoke close to 'Barechu,' for even if one were to stoke close to 'Barechu' – there is no Torah prohibition here, and therefore one should be lenient about this. (ibid. section 26) And this is according to their custom, where they would pray the Shabbat evening prayer while it was still considerably daylight.

Our master, the Beit Yosef, writes at the end of section 1: "All this is regarding leaving (food to heat), where the pot is sitting on an iron chair or on stones and does not touch the coals. But insulating on coals - according to everyone, it is forbidden." These are his words. Meaning, when the pot touches the coals, as in our ovens, this is not considered leaving, but insulating, and it is forbidden in all circumstances. According to this, there is no permission for us to place pots on Friday close to darkness unless it is raked and covered, and many are not careful about this. Therefore, according to this opinion, there is no permission for our ovens at all, but our master the Rema disagrees with this, as will be explained.

And our master, the Rema, wrote on this: "There are those who say that even if the pot is standing directly on the fire, as long as it is uncovered on top, it is not considered 'hatmana' (insulating) and is permitted. And this is the custom, but they are careful to slightly detach it from the fire before Shabbat so that a Jew can remove it from there. If it was not detached from the fire and was found on the fire on Shabbat, it should be removed by a non-Jew. If there is no non-Jew available, a Jew is permitted to remove it, but he should be careful to take it off gently and not to stir the coals. And even if he stirs them slightly, it is considered an unintentional act and is permitted." Thus he concluded. According to his words, in our case, it is not considered 'hatmana,' because only when the walls of the oven are closely surrounding the pot, it is called 'hatmana.' This is like insulating with materials such as cotton and the like, which encircle the pot and cover it also on top, and this does not apply to placing pots in our ovens. This is only considered 'shehiya' (leaving it). However, regarding what he wrote that the Jew himself should remove it from the fire, this is a significant leniency and should only be done in pressing circumstances. Nonetheless, if the coals are placed around the pot, it is obvious that it is forbidden for a Jew to move it himself, as he will move the coals, ignite the upper ones, and extinguish the lower ones, which is close to a Torah prohibition. And even through a non-Jew, it is difficult to be lenient. However, through a non-Jew, there is room to be lenient, as we do not tell him to stir the coals but only to take the pot. If he extinguishes or ignites, he does this on his own accord." (Magen Avraham, Siman 318)

And behold, regarding our ovens, our master the Rema ruled in Section 1 that their status is like that of a stove, because they are much larger and their opening is on the side, allowing the air to escape. There are those who dispute this (Tiferet Shmuel in the name of the Maharshal, see there), but we follow the ruling of our master the Rema. This is also written by the Kol Bo and other early authorities, and common sense supports this. How can we compare them to the ovens of the time of the Gemara, which held only one pot and were narrow at the top? When placing a pot on the top of such an oven, which was sealed on all sides, the strength of the fire would affect the entire pot all around. What comparison can there be to our ovens? It is sufficient to treat them as stoves. Similarly, our modern stoves (plite'os) are certainly like stoves, since the pots stand on top and they are made for several pots, being uniform both above and below. This is precisely like a stove and not like an oven. Our small portable stoves (kakhlakh), where a space is made in the walls of the oven with a small iron door—this is exactly like the support mentioned, and similarly, placing on the oven is also like support. The same applies to placing in front of the oven, which we call a Kaminak, which is in front of the oven opening, and some call it a Yamka—this is also like support.

Our custom is that on Friday afternoon before evening, those dishes that need to be eaten at night are taken from the oven and placed in front of the oven or on the oven or on the coals. It is obvious that placing them near the oven is permitted on a stove even if it is not raked and covered, according to all opinions, as explained. For the dishes for the next day, called "cholent," they are placed in the oven, and the fire is raked to one side of the oven. Some also place ashes on the coals. The pots are placed in the oven where there are no coals at all, and it is customary to seal the mouth of the oven with clay or ashes or with rags that have been soaked in water. This is called sealing the oven, where the oven door is tightly sealed with the oven itself such that the next day it requires force to open it. Refer to what is written in Siman 254, paragraph 4.

According to our custom, it is permitted even according to the view of the Rambam, as it is stated in the Gemara (18b) that when the mouth of the oven is sealed, we do not fear the stirring of coals, as will be clarified in Siman 254. The reason is that the concern for stirring coals is only when one can stir them immediately and might forget that it is Shabbat. However, something that takes time — by the time he stirs the coals, he will remember that it is Shabbat.

Even if the mouth of the oven is not sealed, if one placed a pot with raw food close to nightfall, it has already been clarified that it is permitted according to all opinions, even in an oven. If one placed it about an hour before nightfall, so that by nightfall it has not yet reached the stage of Ma’achal Ben Derusai (the food of Ben Derusai), it is prohibited according to all opinions in a stove that is not swept and covered. If one placed ashes on the coals, this is considered covered, and it is permitted according to all opinions. If one did not place ashes, it is not considered swept according to most authorities, except for those who say in paragraph 5 that it is considered swept.

If one placed it two or three hours before nightfall, so that by nightfall it has reached the stage of Ma’achal Ben Derusai, according to Rashi and Tosafot, it is permitted, as they permit leaving it in a stove that is not swept and covered. According to the Rif and Rambam, it is prohibited unless it is considered swept and covered. Therefore, if ashes were placed, it is permitted according to their opinion as well. If ashes were not placed, it is not permitted according to their opinion, except for those who say in paragraph 5.

Jews are holy and follow all stringencies, sweeping the coals to one side, placing ashes, and sealing the oven. The laws of returning a pot to the stove have also been explained. According to Rashi and Tosafot, returning is permitted in a swept and covered stove. According to the Rif and Rambam, it is prohibited unless the food is fully cooked, shrinks and becomes worse, and the stove is swept and covered. Among us, we use wood and not straw and stubble, and the prohibition of returning a pot only applies where the hand recoils from the heat.

Maimonides writes in Chapter 3, Law 9: "Any cooked dish that is forbidden to leave [on the fire]—if one transgressed and left it, it is forbidden to eat it until after Shabbat, and one must wait the amount of time it takes to cook it after Shabbat. If one forgot [and left it]: If it is a dish that was not fully cooked, it is forbidden until after Shabbat; but if it is a dish that was fully cooked and improves by continued cooking (that is, even if it improves by continued cooking), it is permitted to eat it immediately on Shabbat." This is the end of his words. The Tur equates intentionally leaving it with forgetting it, see there. Our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, ruled like Maimonides in section 1, see there. When it is forbidden, it is forbidden for everyone, even for others (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 11), and there is one who permits it for others, but this is not the main opinion (ibid.). If a non-Jew returned it to the oven on Shabbat for the Jew, it is treated as if he forgot and left it; if it was not fully cooked, it is forbidden, but if it was fully cooked, it is permitted. If the Jew returned it on Shabbat in a place where it is forbidden, even unintentionally, it is treated as if he transgressed and left it; even if it was fully cooked, it is forbidden if it improves by continued cooking, because the act of returning on Shabbat is treated stringently even if done unintentionally. However, if it was fully cooked and deteriorates by continued cooking, it is certainly permitted in any case, for the delay or return ruined it. There is one who says that if it was returned unintentionally, it is permitted for others immediately (ibid., subparagraph 14).

One who rises early in the morning and sees that his dish is burning and fears it will burn further, and he wishes to place it on another pot to distance it from the heat of the stove - he may remove it and place an empty pot on the stove, and set this pot on the empty pot, provided it is an old pot. For if it is a new pot, there is a concern of libun (heating to white-hot), as mentioned later in Siman 502. And even though there our master the Beit Yosef ruled leniently, that is when there is food in it, but if it is empty, there is a concern of libun. (There, Skale) And he should also be careful not to place the removed pot on the ground while it is still boiling, for if not, it is forbidden to return it on Shabbat. However, it has already been explained in Section 19 that the world is accustomed to be lenient even if it was placed on the ground, for they hold that if it was taken and returned on Shabbat, this is not considered the prohibited form of returning.

Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 4: "One should protest against those who have the custom of placing a kettle of hot water [to insulate] before the onset of Shabbat, and then placing it into the pot on Shabbat when the dish is shrinking." End quote. And our teacher wrote to examine section 318, and his intention is that we do not hold this way. For the reason of our teacher, the Beit Yosef, is because sometimes one is scalding hot and the other is not, and they cook each other, and this follows the opinion that in such cases, there is cooking after cooking. But, according to what will be explained later in section 318, as long as it has not completely cooled down, there is no issue of cooking, and it is done daily to put legumes or kasha into the bowl, making it a secondary vessel, and pouring soup from a primary vessel onto it. Similarly, if one first puts the soup and then adds the legumes or kasha, which is a solid and very hot, and we are not concerned with this - if so, we also do not agree with the ruling of our teacher, the Beit Yosef. (See Magen Avraham, subsection 32, and what he wrote about not stirring with a spoon - he himself wrote in subsection 44 that the custom is to permit it, and it will be explained there with God's help).

It is permitted to place on top of a hot pot on Shabbat, even if it is near the fire, a fully cooked dry dish from before Shabbat, such as bread similar to tiegachatz (a type of bread) and our kugel and similar items, in order to warm them, since this is not considered cooking even if they have completely cooled down. On this matter, everyone agrees in Siman 318 that a dry item which was fully cooked before Shabbat is no longer subject to the prohibition of cooking. Therefore, dry meat and dry kassah (a type of food) are permitted in these cases. However, if there is a lot of congealed fat, it is forbidden, because when the fat melts it is considered creating a new entity, as will be explained there, with God's help.

And this that we said to place it on top of a hot pot, we permitted only in such cases. But to place it on top of a stove or inside the stove is forbidden, because even though it does not involve cooking, nevertheless, leaving it there initially on Shabbat is forbidden even if it is boiling and diminishing and harmful. (The Gra) Therefore, to place it inside our oven when the oven is very hot and the hand recoils from it is completely forbidden. Similarly, it is forbidden to place any food on the hot plates when they are very hot. This practice of sometimes putting fish or meat or kugel into the oven in the evening during the winter is only when there is not much heat in the oven, but only a small amount of heat like our ovens, where the great heat dissipates after midday. But on the warming stove, it is permitted to place, as placing is permitted on a stove as explained, and similarly on the oven or in front of the oven. Therefore, we only permitted placing on a hot pot, because in this case it does not appear as cooking or leaving it there initially, since the pot interrupts. Therefore, if there are clothes on the pot that insulate the pot, it is forbidden to place the food under the clothes, because this is considered insulating and is forbidden on Shabbat. (And the prohibition to place inside the oven or on the stove is even if it is swept and covered with ashes, because even though we permitted returning, we did not permit leaving it there initially on Shabbat. Pay close attention.)

There are those who permit placing food into an oven that was baked in before the onset of Shabbat, and no dishes were insulated in it for Shabbat. Since it was only used for baking before Shabbat, there is certainly very little residual heat, and there is no concern for cooking. This applies when placing the food in the oven on Shabbat morning, as by then, such an oven does not have much heat. However, at night, it is clear that it retains a lot of warmth and is therefore forbidden. Nevertheless, this permission is only valid if the food has not completely cooled down, for if it has completely cooled, it is considered as initial placement (hesei'ah), and perhaps the surface is still too hot to touch. There are those who are stringent even if it has not completely cooled, as long as the surface is still too hot to touch, as this too is considered initial placement on Shabbat. It is obvious that if the surface is not too hot to touch, it is permitted in all cases. We have explained many times that if the surface is not too hot to touch, there is no prohibition to place food there, even if it is moist to take off the chill, and certainly with dry food.

And know that anything forbidden for us to do ourselves is also forbidden to tell a non-Jew to do, for instructing a non-Jew is a rabbinic prohibition. Even for a rabbinic prohibition, it is forbidden to instruct a non-Jew. However, in the case of a rabbinic prohibition that is a "double rabbinic prohibition," in the context of a mitzvah, the Rabbis did not decree against it. And if the dish is needed for the honor of Shabbat, it may be permitted. It seems that there are those who act in this way and they have what to rely on. Therefore, one must know what is a Torah prohibition and what is a rabbinic prohibition. It is clear that anything involving the concern of cooking is a Torah prohibition, whereas anything involving concern of leaving, returning, or insulating (food) is a rabbinic prohibition.

This is the language of our Rabbi, the Rema, in section 5: "And all things that are forbidden to do, it is also forbidden to tell a non-Jew to do them. Therefore, it is forbidden to tell a non-Jew to heat up a pot if it has cooled down, and if he does so, it is forbidden to eat it even if it is cold. However, if it has not cooled down so much, and is still suitable to eat, if the non-Jews heat it, it is permitted to eat. Therefore, it is customary that the non-Jews take the pots out of the ovens in which they are insulated and place them near or on the winter oven, and then the servant kindles that oven, and through this, the pots reheat. But through a Jew, it is forbidden in such cases. However, if the pots are still hot, it is permitted to place them near the winter oven, as it has been explained that our ovens have the status of a stove, and placing near a stove that is not swept and covered is like placing on a stove that is swept and covered regarding placing on it. And it has already been explained that it is customary to be lenient with returning on Shabbat, even if it was placed on the ground, and the same applies to placing near an oven that is not swept and covered, since the pot is still hot and fully cooked, and this is the simple custom to permit. See further in section 318." End of quote.

The explanation of his words is that it is forbidden to tell a non-Jew to heat the pot if it has cooled, as this is a prohibition akin to a Torah prohibition. Therefore, if one did so, it is forbidden to eat even cold (food), even though one does not benefit from his (the non-Jew’s) work; nevertheless, they penalized him to wait until after Shabbat for the amount of time it would take to do the work, because the non-Jew performed the work due to his command. Therefore, if the non-Jew did it without his command, it is permitted to eat it cold. However, if it has not cooled so much and the non-Jew heated it, even by his command, although he transgressed, still, he is not penalized to forbid the food from being eaten. And know, all this applies even to a dry item that does not have a concern of cooking; nevertheless, there is a prohibition of leaving it (on the fire), as explained. And in the Agudah, it is written: "There was an incident where the maid insulated hot water after dark, and they forbade the dish that was cold and permitted the meat that was fit to be eaten cold" (Magen Avraham 319). And know, that when a Jew sees a non-Jew doing so, he must rebuke him, and this suffices. And even though he may not comply, nevertheless, it is his duty to protest, since he is doing it for the Jew. But when he does it for himself, it is obvious that there is no need to protest, and then the Jew may also eat, as per the ruling that any work a non-Jew does on Shabbat for himself, a Jew may benefit from it, as stated in Siman 325.

And it says further: "Therefore, it is customary that the non-Jews remove the pots from the ovens and place them next to the winter stove, etc." Meaning, since it has been clarified that it is forbidden to tell a non-Jew to heat the food, therefore the custom is that the non-Jew removes the pot from the oven and places it on the stove of the winter house before the stove is ignited, as at that point, he is not yet doing anything. Afterwards, he ignites the stove of the winter house, and consequently, the food gets heated. There is no prohibition in this, for his intention is to ignite the winter house stove, which is permitted, as everyone is considered ill when it comes to cold, and the food gets heated incidentally. And even though there is an element of subterfuge in this, it is the non-Jew who is doing the subterfuge, so what of it? Therefore, even if the food was cold and got significantly heated, it is permitted to eat, whether it is dry food or liquid food. (And perhaps it is permissible to tell the non-Jew to do so, meaning to ignite the winter house stove, even though this will heat the food. However, to tell him to place the food before the ignition - it is obvious that this is forbidden.)

All of this applies when the non-Jew does it, but if a Jew does so, placing the cooled pots on the winter stove, and then the non-Jew heats the stove causing them to warm up, it is completely forbidden and is close to a Torah prohibition, similar to one who places the fire and another who places the water, where both are liable. However, this is when the pots are cold. But if the pots are still warm, it is permitted for the Jew himself to place them on the winter stove, because it has already been explained that our stoves have the same status as a stove, and placing on the stove is considered leaning. Leaning on a stove that is not swept and covered is like the law of leaving or returning on a swept and covered stove. This has already been explained, that we permit returning on Shabbat even if it was placed on the ground, as stated in paragraph 23, and thus the same rule applies to leaning on a stove that is not swept and covered, that it is permitted as long as the pot is still warm and fully cooked. This is also the widespread custom to permit, and see further in chapter 318 where the primary laws of cooking are explained. (This is the intent of the Rema.)

And know that all this permission applies to our ovens, where placing [a pot] on the oven constitutes leaning. But with ranges, which are called English cooking ranges, where the main cooking is done by placing the pots on them, it is forbidden in all cases. And not only if the Jew himself places the pot on it, relying on the non-Jew to light it afterward, which is considered full-fledged cooking and incurs a sin-offering, but even if done by a non-Jew, it is also forbidden. This is because it constitutes leaving and returning [a pot] on a stove that is not swept and covered, and this is considered initially leaving [a pot] on the stove on Shabbat, which is forbidden according to all opinions, whether the dish is hot or cold. Moreover, in this case, the intention of the non-Jew is certainly to cook, as this is their usual method of cooking. Therefore, it is absolutely forbidden to do so. And placing a samovar before Shabbat and drinking from it at night is forbidden unless there are no burning coals in it, as we have learned in the Mishnah (40a): "A swept mulier, one can drink from... but not if it is not swept." (And our samovar is like a mulier and not like an antique in the Mishnah obviously, all according to Rashi's interpretation there and not according to Tosafot's interpretation there).

In the previous section, paragraph 8, it was explained that the delay which the Sages prohibited close to evening, out of concern that one might stoke the coals, applies only to a dish that is fit for the evening, meaning it has already begun cooking. However, a raw dish, which will not be cooked by the evening and is intended for the next day, is permitted to leave on the stove, because by the next day there is plenty of time, and one will not come to stoke the coals. This, however, is for a dish that is cooking in a pot, and even for a roast in a pot, which is called "pot roast," meaning it is roasted without water. Still, since it is in a pot, it requires a lot of time to cook. But if one roasts meat by the fire, not in a pot, but places it near the fire or on the coals where it cooks quickly, it is prohibited even if it is raw, until there is enough time for it to roast before nightfall. This is what the Sages taught in the Mishnah: "One does not roast meat, onions, or eggs unless there is enough time for them to roast before nightfall." However, we do not require complete roasting, but rather as much as the food of Ben Drusai, which is a third or half cooked. We hold like Chananya who said: "Anything that is like the food of Ben Drusai is permitted to leave on the stove, even if it is not raked or covered." And even though the Rambam's opinion is not like Chananya, as mentioned in the previous section, this is regarding delay, but for roasting, he ruled like Chananya. And although in the Rambam, Chapter 3, Law 16, he wrote: "so that they roast before nightfall and are fit for eating," it must mean up to the stage of the food of Ben Drusai, as explained by the Maggid Mishneh, and this is supported by the Gemara. For Rav on the topic of the stove rules that something which improves by being left is prohibited, which is not like Chananya, and there Rav said: "so that they roast like the food of Ben Drusai," which is the intention of the Rambam, as brought by the Kesef Mishneh. Also see Tosafot 37a, s.v. "If you say," who wrote that Rav is not like Chananya from the topic of eggs, and this needs clarification, as Rav on the Mishnah of meat, onions, and eggs says like the food of Ben Drusai. We must say that eggs on the coals do not improve by being left, which is the opinion of the Rambam who prohibits something that improves by being left, but permits it for eggs. This must be true, for in the Gemara 38a: "Dried eggs left on the stove improve by being left," which does not apply to those roasted on coals. Therefore, the words of Tosafot need clarification, and examine this well.

And this is the language of the Tur: "Even though raw meat is permitted to be left [before Shabbat] - this applies to a pot that does not cook quickly, and he has diverted his attention from it until the next day, and we do not worry that he might stoke [the coals]. But for roasting that is by the fire - even raw meat is forbidden to be left close to dusk, because it roasts quickly and it is possible for it to be roasted to be fit [to eat] while it is still night, and he does not divert his attention from it and he will come to stoke [the coals]. But if it is in an oven sealed with clay - it is permitted even with goat meat, since the wind is not strong on it and we do not worry that he will open and stoke, because it is sealed with clay. (As Rashi explained, page 18b, 'and sealed,' that for all this he does not trouble himself and remember, see there.) And a kid [goat] that the wind is strong on it - even if it is not sealed, it is permitted, as we do not worry that he will open and stoke, because the wind is strong on it, and such as when it is cut into pieces, then the wind is strong on it. But if it is whole, or a goat even if it is cut into pieces, and the wind is not strong on them, if the oven is not sealed with clay - it is forbidden." End of quote.

According to the opinion of the Tur, any sealing of the oven mouth makes everything permissible, even dishes in pots, because the reason is that one will remember to remove the seal. This is the reason why it is customary among us to seal the oven mouth close to the evening, as mentioned in the previous section, paragraph 27. This leniency follows the opinion of the Tur, which is not the case according to the Rambam, as will be explained. However, regarding goat meat, the Tur is stringent, as according to his opinion, the permission for goat meat is because the wind is harsh on it. According to this, the permission is only when it is roasted inside the oven and the oven is covered. But if the oven is not covered or it is roasted on coals before the oven, there is no permission, and this is not the opinion of the Rambam, as we will explain, with God's help.

And this is the wording of the Rambam in Chapter 3, Law 13: "An oven into which meat was placed before Shabbat and it remained there on Shabbat, if it is the meat of a kid or something similar - it is permitted, because if one were to stoke the coals the meat would become singed, as it only requires the heat of the fire. But if it is the meat of a goat or ox - it is forbidden, lest one stoke the coals to cook it. And if the mouth of the oven was sealed with clay - it is permitted, because if one were to open the oven and stoke, the wind would enter, harden the meat, spoil it, and cool down the oven, thus ruining the meat. Similarly, anything that the wind spoils, we do not decree that one might uncover it and stoke... And if one placed a whole kid into the oven - it is like the meat of a goat or ox, and it is forbidden to leave it lest one stoke, unless the oven was sealed, etc." End of quote. It is clear that he did not write the reason for sealing due to remembering before uncovering, but because the wind would spoil the meat. Based on this, for dishes in a pot - sealing the oven does not help, unless we say that they too would be spoiled by the wind. And regarding the meat of a kid, he wrote the reason: that the meat would become singed, so even if the oven is uncovered or when it is roasted near the oven - it is permitted.

And this is the intention of our teacher, the Rema, who, after the words of our teacher the Beit Yosef, which align with the words of the Rambam, wrote the following: "There are those who are stringent and hold that if the oven is plastered with clay, everything is permitted, and on an exposed fire, everything is forbidden. And in an oven whose opening is covered but not plastered with clay, it is necessary to differentiate between a kid and a bird (which has the same status as a kid), and other meat as previously explained, and this is the custom following this opinion." End quote. This is the opinion of the Tur. And when he wrote that there are those who are stringent, he refers to the matter when they are on an exposed fire, that according to the Rambam, it is permitted due to the fact that it will be singed, but according to the Tur, it is forbidden. However, regarding the plastering of the oven, on the contrary, the Tur is lenient. And this is what he wrote: "And this is the custom," meaning to plaster the opening of the oven, as he wrote in the previous section, paragraph 27. And there is no difference in roasting whether it is completely raw or partially cooked, for where it is permitted, it is completely permitted, and where it is forbidden, it is completely forbidden, even if it has reached the stage of Ma'achal Ben Drusai (partially cooked). (Magen Avraham, note 4) And know that it is considered whole as long as the body is intact, even if it does not have its head and legs. And a kid is in its infancy, and it is called a goat when it grows up. A bird is similar to a kid, (and in the Gemara 'kid and lamb' are mentioned, that is, a ram, and the poskim hold that a goat is treated like a ram because of its size, or they interpret 'lamb' as a male goat, see Aruch under the entry 'lamb') and see in paragraph 8.

And the Rambam wrote there in Law 16: "One does not roast meat, onions, or eggs over a fire unless they have been roasted before Shabbat and are fit for eating (like the food of Ben Drusai). If they remain on the fire during Shabbat until they are well-roasted, it is permitted because it shrinks and becomes worse, for if one would stoke the fire, it would scorch them, as they are directly on the fire." And it seems that here he is not referring to kid meat, for kid meat is permitted in any case, as mentioned earlier in Section 4. And what he wrote there, that for other meats it is forbidden if the oven is not sealed with clay, applies when it has not reached the stage of Ben Drusai's food before Shabbat. But if it has reached the stage of Ben Drusai's food, it is permitted, as explained here.

However, from the words of our teacher, the Beit Yosef, in section 2, it does not seem so, as he wrote: "One may not roast an onion, egg, or meat on coals unless it will roast from both sides before Shabbat, like the food of Ben Drosai, which is half-cooked. Even if it is goat meat, since it was placed on coals, one does not worry except that it will roast quickly, even though it might burn. Therefore, we are concerned that one might stoke the coals. But once it is roasted like the food of Ben Drosai, we are not concerned that one will come to stoke the coals, even if it is ox meat, since it is already fit for eating, why would one stoke the coals and risk spoiling it?" Thus his words end. According to him, in the previous law, it is referring to roasting in an oven not on coals. Therefore, goat meat is permitted for the reason explained, as it only needs light heating. But when placed on coals, or very close to them, which is like being on them, since the heat is very strong and necessarily one is not concerned about burning, for if one were concerned, one would not do so - therefore, it is forbidden even with goat meat. Conversely, in the previous law, it is forbidden even if it has reached the stage of Ben Drosai's food, because since it is not on the coals and the heat is weak, one worries that it will not cook, and might come to stoke the coals. But here, on the coals, one will not be irrational to stoke after it has reached the stage of Ben Drosai's food, even with ox meat, for stoking would spoil it. And know, that it is not literally on the coals, but near the coals, for otherwise, how would one remove the meat from the coals, as one might come to extinguish, or wait until the coals are extinguished (Magen Avraham, section 7).

However, we are compelled to say that the Tur does not hold this way, for in the previous law he also wrote "roasted next to the fire," as he wrote in section 2. In this law, he only wrote the language of the Mishnah: "One does not roast meat, onions, or eggs unless they can be roasted before Shabbat as the food of Ben Drusai," and he did not explain it in the language of the Rambam. From this, we understand that it is all one law, and consequently, in the previous law, the prohibition is also only if it has not reached the stage of being as the food of Ben Drusai. According to this, there is a question on our master the Rema, as we mentioned in section 5, that he did not mention this leniency. (And this is the intention of the Taz in section 31.) It seems that because these matters are not explicitly clear neither in the Rambam nor in the Tur, although it is certainly the case, nonetheless, since it is not explicitly clear, he did not want to bring it. And perhaps even in practice, he agreed with our master the Beit Yosef, and one who relies on the Tur in a time of need does not lose out.

If one transgressed or forgot and roasted [food] on Shabbat in a prohibited manner, it is forbidden. This is the ruling of our master, the Beit Yosef, in paragraph 3, and he does not differentiate between intentional transgression and accidental forgetfulness. Even though regarding leaving food on the stove in the previous section, he differentiated in paragraph 1, stating that in the case of forgetfulness, we are not stringent if the food was fully cooked, even if it improves by cooking longer, as we explained there in paragraph 27. Here, he follows the opinion of the Rambam concerning roasting in an oven not heated directly by the fire and not sealed with clay—it is forbidden in any case, as he wrote. The reason seems to be that, on the contrary, here even if one transgressed, his intention is not to prohibit it once it has reached the stage of Ma'achal Ben Drusai (the food of Ben Drusai, a certain level of cooking), especially if it is fully cooked. This applies to the rule of roasting meat, onions, and eggs, where the prohibition is only until it reaches the stage of Ma'achal Ben Drusai, as explained. There is an opinion that when placing [food] in the oven, in any case, it is not forbidden if one transgressed or forgot, since there are authorities who completely permit it when the oven is covered, even if it is not sealed with clay. (Magen Avraham, section 11, and his intention is for the authorities who rule like Rav Ashi, who permits it when the oven is covered but not sealed, as mentioned in Tosafot and Rosh).

Fruits that are eaten raw - it is permitted to place them around the pot near the coals, even though they cannot be roasted before nightfall, because since they are fit to be eaten raw - it is considered as if they have reached the stage of Ma'achal Ben Drusai (partially cooked). This is not similar to onions, which we prohibited, because they are not as good raw as fruits are. In truth, anything that is not good to eat raw as it is when cooked, like wild apples and similar items - is prohibited unless they reach the stage of Ma'achal Ben Drusai before nightfall. However, even though we permitted this with fruits, one must still be careful that if they were covered and then uncovered after nightfall - not to replace the cover after nightfall, and not to add any cover after nightfall, because this hastens their cooking - and it is as if one is cooking on Shabbat, and one must be very careful about this, as the common people do not recognize this as cooking. And it is obvious that on Shabbat it is forbidden to place them on a winter stove that a non-Jew will later heat because of the cold, (as mentioned in the previous section, paragraph 38). However, through a non-Jew - it is permitted in such cases, as mentioned there in paragraph 37.

Our sages taught in the Mishnah (19:): "One may not place bread in the oven as it gets dark, nor a cake on coals, except to the extent that its surface will crust over before the onset of Shabbat." And once its surface crusts over, meaning that the bread forms a crust and skin due to the fire, it is sufficient. Even though for cooked food, according to the opinions of Rashi and Tosafot, it must reach the stage of Ma'achal Ben Drosai (a third to a half cooked), and according to the Rambam, even that is not sufficient, as we wrote at the beginning of the previous section, nevertheless, bread is not comparable to cooked food, and it suffices if its surface crusts over. The reason is found in the Jerusalem Talmud, which explains that women are more diligent with bread than with cooked food, meaning they are careful with bread so it does not burn, and therefore we do not worry about stoking the coals. This is what the Rambam wrote there: "One may not place bread... except to the extent that its surface will crust over... and if they remain afterward... if one were to stoke the coals, it would spoil them" - end quote. (And the commentators of the Jerusalem Talmud explained this with a strange interpretation, as mentioned there.)

However, the main issue is puzzling, as it is clear from the Mishnah that in order for its surface to crust, it is permissible to initially put bread into the oven, and the baking will be completed at night. It is not understood what to do with it upon removing it from the oven, as removing bread from the oven is prohibited on Shabbat, as will be explained. Unless we say that one should leave it in the oven until the end of Shabbat, which is difficult, as it would certainly burn, obviously. And perhaps since the Sages said (117b) that removing bread from the oven is a skill and not a labor, and they permitted it occasionally, as will be explained, therefore if it appears that the bread will be ruined if it remains until the end of Shabbat, one can tell a non-Jew to remove it from the oven, as this is not a complete rabbinic prohibition. Moreover, a double rabbinic prohibition in a situation of loss is permitted.

The Tur writes regarding the crusting of the surface: "So that its surface, which is stuck to the oven, or the surface facing the fire, becomes crusted." The Rambam's language is also similar to this, see there. And our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote regarding bread: "the surface that is stuck to the oven," and regarding a cake: "its surface facing the fire," see there, because he holds that it suffices if one of them is crusted. Therefore, with a cake, where the surface facing the fire cooks faster, he wrote "the surface facing the fire," and with bread, it could be that the part stuck to the oven cooks faster. But the main point is that it suffices if one of them is crusted, and as long as you can break it and the threads do not stretch, it is called crusted. This is also true regarding matzah as mentioned later in Siman 461. 

It seems to me that crusting of the surface occurs much earlier, but when the threads do not stretch, it has definitely reached the stage of crusting. (We must say so, because when the threads do not stretch, it is somewhat edible, as is evident from matzah. If so, also regarding a cooked dish, it is permissible when it is as cooked as the food of Ben Drusai, according to Rashi and Tosafot. If so, what is the Jerusalem Talmud's distinction between bread and a cooked dish? Rather, it is certainly as I have written, and examine this well.)

And Rabbi Moshe Isserles (the Rema) wrote: "Regarding a pastida or a paladin — it is necessary that its surface be crusted both on the top and bottom, and that what is inside be cooked to the extent of Ma'achal Ben Drusai" (partially cooked). There are those who understand this as differing with Rabbi Yosef Karo (the Beit Yosef), and if so, he should have said 'there are those who say' (Magen Avraham, section 16). However, this is not the case, as with thin bread or a wafer, crusting on one side suffices, but not with these which are thick (Gra). According to this, with our bread which is thick, even Rabbi Yosef Karo agrees that both sides need crusting. Additionally, there is no comparison between paladin and pastida and bread, since they are filled in the middle; thus, the upper and lower doughs are two separate doughs, and it is like two wafers, and of necessity, both the top and bottom must be crusted (Dagul Mervavah). Also, what is inside needs to be cooked to the extent of Ma'achal Ben Drusai, and it cannot be said that it is nullified regarding the dough, as this is not applicable to the prohibitions of Shabbat. And anyone who knows that it has not yet reached the extent of Ma'achal Ben Drusai must be concerned lest he stoke the coals (so it seems to me).

It is simple that with bread, cake, and similar items, even if they are placed raw in the oven close to evening, it is forbidden [to leave them there], because it is not like a pot dish that requires a long time to cook, but rather it is like roasting. And if they were placed close to dusk and their surfaces did not form a crust before the onset of Shabbat: if done intentionally, it is forbidden until after Shabbat for the amount of time it would take to prepare them, even if one has nothing to eat. And if done unintentionally: if one has nothing to eat, we do not penalize an unintentional act due to an intentional one, for "man lives by bread," and it is not comparable to other dishes. Therefore, it is permitted for him to remove from the oven enough for three meals for himself and his household, and he can also tell others who have nothing to eat: "Come and remove for yourselves enough for three meals." And when he removes it, he should not use the peel [a baker's shovel] as he does on weekdays, but rather his hand or a knife or something similar, so that he does not act in the same manner as on weekdays. And if it is impossible to remove it with a change, he may use the peel, for this is not considered work. And if it was placed in the oven so that its surface could form a crust before Shabbat, and no prohibition was committed: if the bread is needed for Shabbat, he may remove it in the usual manner, and if it is not needed for Shabbat, it is forbidden even with a change, because removing bread from the oven is a rabbinic prohibition. In all of this, there is no difference between our bread and ovens and theirs, contrary to the opinion of those who wish to permit more than three meals with our ovens. (See Magen Avraham, subsection 17.) And we have already written that if done by a non-Jew, it may be permitted if there is a loss, as stated in section 12. See also section 17.

And it is clear that with a stove that has been swept out or covered with ashes, it is permissible to place bread close to nightfall, as it is no different from a cooked dish. (Orach Chaim 253:16) Therefore, with our ovens which are considered like stoves, if they have been swept out or covered with ashes, it is permissible to place bread close to evening. However, removing the bread is forbidden unless it is done as explained, either for the sake of Shabbat or by a non-Jew. Cakes or types of dough that are baked in a pot are also treated like bread, provided they are not filled with meat, eggs, or fruit, (ibid.) because then they are considered as cooking in a pot. Pastries and flans that we mentioned as being like bread are so only when they are not in a pot. It seems to me that in a frying pan, it is not considered like a pot, and likewise, all that has been explained applies only to an oven that is not sealed with clay. But if it is sealed, it is permissible in all respects, as it is no different from a cooked dish. Similarly, if one is not baking for the sake of Shabbat but for after Shabbat, since there is time to bake it, it is also permissible, as in such cases we do not worry that one might stoke the coals, for why would one stoke them? This is like leaving it for tomorrow, which we permitted in the previous section. The reason we do not permit it here for the sake of tomorrow is because we fear one might eat it at night. However, with a cooked dish, this concern does not exist, as it is not fit for night because it requires much cooking, which is not the case with bread. One might argue that the same should apply even when one needs it for after Shabbat, but we do not decree thus, because it is forbidden to remove it on Shabbat. But when one's intention is for tomorrow, it is clear that the intent is to remove it either with a change or by a non-Jew. Therefore, there are those who say that with our ovens, where the prohibition of removing is not so strict, it is forbidden even when one's intention is for after Shabbat, due to the concern that one might remove it at night and come to stoke the coals (ibid. 253:20). In my humble opinion, this does not seem correct, for is our removal a complete permission? And do not ask how it is permissible for after Shabbat, as covering (Hatmanah) is forbidden for after Shabbat, as stated in Siman 257. One can say that the prohibition of covering itself is a novelty, and let us not add to it. (Taz)

Know that what we wrote at the end of Section 15, that there is no difference between our ovens and theirs—this applies when it was placed in the oven in a prohibited manner. But if it was placed permissibly, such as by lining the inside of the oven during the day, there is a difference, as our master the Beit Yosef wrote in Section 7, and this is his language: "In our ovens, which do not require raking out, it is permitted to remove more than three meals' worth with a knife or any other instrument that can be inserted (and certainly with one's hands). However, one should not remove it with a baker's peel, because it appears like weekday labor." This refers to when it was placed permissibly (as the Magen Avraham writes in Subsection 23), and it is comparable to a cake on coals, which is not prohibited like raking bread. This is also specifically when one intends to eat on Shabbat, for then it is permitted even for more than three meals. But to rake out the oven for a weekday need—moving items on Shabbat for a weekday need is forbidden, as the Maimonides' Glosses state, that it is forbidden to bring wine on Shabbat for use after Shabbat, and see Section 323. It has already been clarified that only for bread did they permit three meals' worth, and not for cooked dishes. However, if one has nothing to eat except for the cooked dishes, it is obvious that it is permitted, for it is forbidden to fast on Shabbat. And know that regarding the three meals that are permitted, if one took one loaf that has the measure of three meals, there are opinions that say it is forbidden to take more, even though one will not have two loaves for each meal, and will not have a whole loaf at each meal—nevertheless, it is forbidden, for this is not such a strict obligation, and there are those who are uncertain about this. It has already been explained that if the bread will spoil by the end of Shabbat and cause a loss, it is permitted to remove all the bread from our ovens and theirs through a non-Jew, and there are those who permit in our ovens even by oneself in a case of loss. This is correct, but ideally, it is certainly better to do it through a non-Jew.

If one placed bread into the oven on Shabbat, whether he did so unintentionally, not knowing that it was Shabbat, and immediately remembered, or whether he did so intentionally—it is permitted for him to remove it immediately before the bread begins to form a crust, in order to avoid the prohibition of stoning and a sin offering. And even though one would not be liable for a sin offering, because all those who are liable for a sin offering are only liable if both the beginning and the end of the act were done inadvertently, and here he remembered—nevertheless, in any case, he would still be performing a primary labor unintentionally. And even though removing bread from the oven is a rabbinic prohibition, and especially in their days when removal was considered somewhat of a labor, since the bread was stuck to the walls—nevertheless, it is better for him to transgress a light rabbinic prohibition than to transgress a primary labor. And even in the case of intentionality, although if we prohibit him from removing it and he wants to remove it, he would not be liable for stoning since we do not permit him (Tosafot 4a s.v. 'before') because if not, it is clear that he would not listen to us (there) in any case, the Sages permitted him initially so that he would not perform a primary labor, even though he did so intentionally. (See Magen Avraham section 21 who scrutinized the language "even intentionally," and according to what was explained, it is clear and pay attention).

And it is obvious that if one can remove [the bread] by making a change, he is obligated to do so. (ibid.) And specifically, it should be done by himself or by a non-Jew, and this is certainly better than doing it himself if possible, because by the time a non-Jew is found, he should not start to become closer [to transgressing]. However, another Jew is forbidden from removing it, because since removing the bread [from the oven] is a rabbinic prohibition, we do not say to a person "commit a minor sin so that your friend does not commit a major prohibition," since the prohibition was not caused by him, and also his friend was negligent by placing [the bread in the oven]. (ibid.) For even if it was done unintentionally, it is considered close to negligence, and the main point depends on the reason of negligence. (ibid.)

It was taught (Shabbat 18b): A woman should not fill a pot with beans or lupines and place it into the oven on the eve of Shabbat as it gets dark, and if she did, they are forbidden to be eaten after Shabbat until the time it would take to prepare them has passed. Similarly, a baker should not fill a barrel with water and place it into the oven on the eve of Shabbat as it gets dark, and if he did, it is forbidden to be used after Shabbat until the time it would take to prepare it has passed. The reason is that he might stoke the coals. Rashi explained (s.v. 'this pot') that they require a long time to cook, and the entire night and day are not enough for them. Regarding the barrel of water, the reason is that they are accustomed to heat it on a low fire and are concerned that it might cool down, leading him to stoke the coals (Tosafot there).

However, the Rambam wrote there the opposite: that these and anything similar, even though they have not been cooked at all, are considered like a dish that has not been fully cooked, because they do not require much cooking and one's intention is to eat them immediately. Therefore, it is forbidden to leave them in the oven, and if one transgressed and left them, they are forbidden until after Shabbat, and one must wait the amount of time it would take to cook them. And the same applies to a stove and a small oven when they are not cleared of coals or ashes and it is possible to stoke them, and in a small oven, even if it was cleared, it does not help when it was heated with peat and wood, as mentioned in the previous section, and straw and stubble do not require clearing as mentioned, and only in a stove when it was heated with peat and wood does clearing help. And water, even though it is fit to drink raw, nevertheless it is not comparable to fruits, since raw water is not as good as cooked, or if it needs washing, it specifically requires hot water. Therefore, all types of water need to be left from before daybreak. And there is a difficulty with the Rambam’s explanation from what we say in Shabbat (74b): "Lupines are different, as they are boiled seven times," as it is explained that they are hard to cook. And regarding cooking tea, it will be explained in section 318, and also to place the samovar near darkness seems forbidden, as there is a concern one might stoke the coals, and furthermore, when one removes the teapot on Shabbat and returns it to the samovar, it constitutes complete cooking.

As explained, the sages were concerned about food placed close to darkness, fearing that one might stoke the coals. Similarly, they decreed regarding wood piles set close to darkness that one should not benefit from them unless they were lit during the day in such a way that they no longer need assistance to continue burning on their own. Therefore, one should not make a wood pile close to darkness unless the fire has sufficiently taken hold in a way that the flame rises by itself without the need for additional wood. If it is a single piece of wood, the fire must have gripped most of its thickness on the inside and most of its circumference on the outside. If it has not been lit to this extent, it is forbidden to use it on Shabbat to sit by it or to use its light, lest one stoke it to make it burn well and thereby move the wood to enhance the flame. Even if it is fully lit afterward, it remains forbidden, just as we forbid food even after it has finished cooking. The same rule applies here. However, if it was lit to the required extent before nightfall, one may use it for any purpose, whether to warm oneself by it on Shabbat or to use its light, whether it is on the ground or on a lamp, even if it is made from materials that are not used for Shabbat wicks, as explained in Siman 264, where we decree lest one tilt it, since it is merely a lamp. But with a bonfire that has a large flame, there is no concern of tilting it. See Siman 275.

There are those who say that in any case, when one sits by a bonfire, one should not sit close to the burning ends of the logs (called "halavaska"), because there is a concern that he might touch them and turn them over so that they burn better, as people tend to do. (Taz, Orach Chaim 274:6) However, there are those who disagree, saying that specifically regarding study, which requires deep concentration, they decreed this concern, as during the distraction of study, one might forget and do it. But when not engaged in study, but merely sitting to warm oneself, we do not find this decree. (Taz) And that which they prohibited when the flame has not yet risen by itself is due to the concern that it might be completely extinguished. But once this concern is removed, there is no longer a worry, and this seems to be the main opinion.

The Tur wrote that with coals, even if the fire has not gripped them except slightly, it is permitted because they continue to burn on their own. These are his words. This is not mentioned in the Rambam, and in the Mishnah at the end of the first chapter, there is a dispute about this. The sages did not mention this, and only Rabbi Yehuda says this about coals, even slightly. They questioned the Tur, asking how he could rule according to an individual against the majority. Some have written that he believes Rabbi Yehuda is explaining, but it is far-fetched to say this, as this is only said when he states 'In what case are these words said' or 'When.' (See Beit Yosef) But the truth is that this is proven in the Jerusalem Talmud, that the law follows Rabbi Yehuda there.

A bonfire made of pitch and sulfur (it seems to me that this refers to wood coated with pitch and sulfur, and examine this thoroughly) and of straw and stubble, even if the fire has only slightly caught on them - it is permitted, for they continue to burn. Similarly, a bonfire made of thin reeds and date pits, when they are scattered. But if the reeds are bundled and the pits are in a basket - they do not catch fire as easily, and the flame needs to rise on its own, as with other wood. This is according to the version of the Rif and the Rambam in the Gemara (end of the first chapter); however, according to the version of the Rosh and the Tur, it is the opposite, that when they are scattered - the flame needs to rise on its own, and when they are gathered - even if the fire has only slightly caught on them. And the Tur wrote in Siman 502: "A bonfire made of thin wood - it is permitted to remove from it, as long as the fire has not caught on them" see there, and the same applies on Shabbat in these types of cases if the wood is not set aside (muktzeh). (And similarly, someone who arranges wood and lights it from afar with a long rope until it reaches the wood, as long as it has not reached the wood - it is permitted to take from them on Yom Tov or Shabbat, when the wood is not set aside).

When Israel was in their place, they would blow six blasts on the eve of Shabbat after midday. Not specifically a "tekiah" (a long blast), for "tekiah" encompasses everything, and thus they would blow: tekiah, teruah, tekiah; tekiah, teruah, tekiah. (Rashi 35a: s.v. 'six') These blasts were signals for preparing for Shabbat as will be explained. According to Maimonides at the end of Chapter 5, they would also blow one blast at the end of Shabbat after the appearance of the stars, to announce that work was permitted. However, Nachmanides and Rashba disagreed, stating that the blast is only for the entrance of Shabbat and not its exit.

How is the order of the shofar blasts: The Rambam wrote there that they would blow the shofar from a high place to be heard throughout the city and beyond the city. The first blast was after the large Minchah (afternoon prayer), and with the first blast, the people in the fields would stop plowing, digging, and doing any field work. Those nearby were not allowed to enter the city until those far away had heard and all entered together, to avoid suspicion. The second blast would be at the time of the small Minchah, which is two and a half hours before nightfall (according to Magen Avraham), at which point the shops would be closed (Talmud 35b), and the craftsmen in the city would cease their work. After some time, they would blow the third blast, at which point pots were removed from the stove if they were prepared for the night's meal, and pots prepared for the next day were insulated, and the candles were lit. Then they would wait a little to roast a small fish, and they would blow three blasts—Tekiah, Teruah, and Tekiah—and they would accept Shabbat. The one blowing the shofar would place the shofar where he blew it and not take it home, as they had already accepted Shabbat (Talmud 35b). I do not know why the Rambam omitted this. When a festival would fall on the eve of Shabbat, they would still blow the shofar, as the sanctity of Shabbat is stricter. It seems to me that the first two blasts were not done then, as on a festival, one does not do work or engage in commerce. On the conclusion of Shabbat, they would not blow the shofar even if a festival fell on Sunday, as the blast is only for the entrance of a more stringent holiness.

Rabbeinu the Rema wrote that it is customary in holy communities that an hour before Shabbat, the shaliach tzibbur announces to prepare themselves for Shabbat, and this serves in place of the sounding of the shofar in earlier times. And this is a proper practice. And now, even this is not possible, but we send a designated person to chase people out of the market and the shops, because there is a great stumbling block in this, as most often, in the late afternoon, the deeds of the Satan cause people to come and buy, and this requires much strengthening. And it is clear that the holy Shabbat rewards those who are careful with it. One should advance the prayers of Kabbalat Shabbat and Maariv while it is still day, and one should not wait for a distinguished person who has not yet arrived at the synagogue, and this is a great merit. (Magen Avraham) And in our many sins, now they delay the prayers very much, and they think it is a mitzvah to pray Maariv at its proper time. Woe to this mitzvah, for it is tested and proven that because of this, many people in the city come to desecrate Shabbat, and we have elaborated on this in Siman 242. Fortunate is the person who strives to pray Maariv while it is still day, for there is no end to his reward, and Shabbat will advocate on his behalf.

The matter of insulation is that after they have left the pots on the stove or oven, they take the pot from there and insulate it with materials that add heat to strengthen its warmth, or with materials that do not add heat but rather maintain its warmth. And why do they do this? Because usually the insulation is needed for the next day (Tosafot 47b, s.v. 'With what do we insulate'), because they are concerned that if it remains on the stove all night, it will cool down since it is exposed and not covered. Therefore, they take it from there and insulate it to retain its heat. And usually, they would insulate during twilight, as it is taught (34a): "When it is uncertain whether it is dark or not... they insulate the hot food."

The Sages forbade insulating on Shabbat itself, even with something that does not add heat. They only permitted it during twilight, as mentioned. However, with something that adds heat, they forbade insulating even before Shabbat. The reason for the prohibition with something that does not add heat on Shabbat, even though it does nothing other than maintain the existing heat, is because we are concerned that he might come to boil it. That is to say, when he wants to insulate it and finds that his pot has cooled, he might first boil it, and thereby he would be cooking on Shabbat (Rashi). But during twilight, we do not decree this, because typically pots are still hot at twilight (Gemara). It seems to me that the intention is not that he would boil it and cook it completely, for we have already explained in Siman 253 and 254 that the concern is only with stoking the coals, which is done in a moment. But something that requires time, we do not decree, just as we do not decree with an oven sealed with clay that he might remove the seal and stoke the coals (as per Rashi’s explanation). Rather, here too, the intention is that he might stoke the fire all around until it boils, for he has removed it from the stove. (And this resolves Ramban’s difficulty in his Milhamot on this version, for he is not suspected of this. See there and examine well.)

And I have a great question about this, as it is explained in Siman 253 that raw meat is permitted to be left even in an oven, because it is for the following day, and we do not worry that one might stoke the coals, as it will cook on its own by the next day. If so, why did they decree against insulation (hatmana) for the following day? However, the explanation seems to be as follows: If someone does not insulate for the following day but leaves it on the stove or in the oven, it is because he knows that it was properly heated and the fire is strong, and it will not cool off by morning even if it stands uncovered. Therefore, there is no need for stoking. But someone who removes it from the stove and insulates it does so because he knows that the fire is not strong, and if he leaves it on the stove until the next day, it will cool off. Therefore, he wants to insulate it. According to this, it is reasonable to be concerned that when he comes to insulate it, he will see that it has cooled off a bit and will reheat it, meaning he will stoke the few remaining coals that are still hot, and he will stoke the coals on Shabbat, which constitutes cooking. Therefore, they prohibited it and did not differentiate in their decree between insulating at night for the following day or insulating on the next day, as the rabbis did not make distinctions in their decrees, and they prohibited insulating on Shabbat itself in any substance, even in something that does not add heat.

And regarding something that increases heat, it is forbidden to insulate even from before Shabbat, due to the reason that we decree that one might insulate in embers that contain a coal, meaning ashes mixed with coals (Rashi), as this also increases heat, and in this case, we certainly have to be concerned that one might stoke the coals. This is not considered a decree upon another decree, as it is all one single decree (Rambam in his commentary on the Mishnah). And even though it is for the next day, nevertheless, we are concerned that one might worry that it will cool off by the next day. This is not similar to leaving food on a stove for the next day, where the heat is much greater as we explained, unlike insulating with embers, where despite everything, it does not have the same warmth as a stove that is stoked with many woods. And here, the main concern is that there are few embers and ashes, and we are concerned that it will cool off and one might stoke them. (And the Rif and Rambam have a version in the case of something that does not increase heat - "lest one insulate in embers," and in the case of something that increases heat - "lest it boil," and according to Rambam, in the case of something that increases heat, it is forbidden from before Shabbat but permitted during twilight, as he wrote in Chapter 4, and everyone was puzzled by this. From the Rif, it is not necessarily so, as the Ra'avad wrote, since the question is why it is permitted during twilight in the case of something that does not increase heat. According to the law, there is no practical difference between the versions, and most decisors agreed with Rashi’s version, so we explained it accordingly. In the Yerushalmi, there is another reason for something that increases heat, because one might take it on Shabbat and return it, and when taking it, it cools down, and upon returning, it heats up, which is like cooking on Shabbat, so pay attention and understand.)

And know that regarding insulating, there is no difference between whether the food has been cooked to the level of Ma'achal Ben Drusai or not, whether it has been fully cooked or not, and even if it has been fully cooked and is deteriorating - it is forbidden. The reason is that it is not similar to leaving on the fire, where stirring is due to cooking. Therefore, we do not worry about deterioration when it is fully cooked or has reached the level of Ma'achal Ben Drusai, according to the opinions explained in Siman 253. However, with insulating, stirring is due to the food cooling down, so this applies in all cases, obviously. Additionally, with insulating, even a little stirring is effective, since the insulation retains the heat even with minimal stirring. But leaving it (on the fire) for the next day - minimal stirring is not effective (Rosh), and thus one would not stir. This is the opinion of most of our Rabbis, and this is also clear from the words of the Rambam, who in Chapter 4 of the laws of insulating does not mention specific distinctions as he does in the laws of leaving (on the fire) in Chapter 3.

Nevertheless, some of our teachers have said that the laws of insulation are like the laws of leaving food on the stove, where the prohibition only applies to food that is partially cooked and has not reached the stage of Ma'achal Ben Drusai (the level of cooking suitable for the consumption of a thief). But if the food is either raw or cooked to the level of Ma'achal Ben Drusai, it is permissible to insulate it just as it is permissible to leave it on the stove. (Rashbam in Tosafot at the beginning of "Bameh Tomnin") And it seems that this is also the opinion of Rashi, who wrote at the beginning of "Kirah" that the prohibition of leaving food on the stove is also due to additional heat, as mentioned there. If so, it is one matter. All the opinions explained in Siman 253 regarding leaving food on the stove apply equally to insulation. Furthermore, insulation was only prohibited for what is needed for the evening, but not for what is needed for the next day. According to this opinion, even though the standard practice of insulation is for the next day, if it is suitable for eating at night, it is forbidden, as stated in Siman 253. This is the law for leaving food on the stove, or it is possible that according to this opinion, there are types of insulation that are also for the night. However, all our teachers completely rejected this opinion. It is also not understood how insulation can apply to something that is not fully cooked, as it is not a place of cooking.
