Although in the case of something that adds heat, one could say that the heat aids in cooking, still, in the case of something that does not add heat, it is clear that cooking does not apply. The Talmud did not differentiate between something that adds heat and something that does not, except that one is prohibited even before Shabbat, and the other is prohibited only on Shabbat. In any case, they are the same in one respect, and this opinion is questionable. (And it is necessary to say that it is considered that they are not the same in one respect.)

And this is what our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, wrote in paragraph 7, and this is their language: "In any case where we prohibit insulating, even with a pot that is fully cooked, we prohibit, even if it shrinks and is detrimental, and this is the main ruling. And there are those who are lenient and say that anything which is completely raw or fully cooked - is permitted to insulate as with leaving it on [the stove], as we wrote above in Siman 253. And in a place where they have the custom to be lenient according to this reasoning, one should not protest against them, but one should not act this way in other places." End of quote. Because certainly the main ruling is that in all cases insulation is prohibited, and the opinion that permits it is a singular opinion. However, in a place where they have the custom to be lenient - we do not protest against them in rabbinic matters and mere decrees, but the main ruling is according to the majority of the authorities.

And I am puzzled by our teacher, the Rema, who wrote in Section 1: "There are those who say that all this is only prohibited when done for the sake of the night, but when one insulates for the sake of the next day, it is permitted to insulate during the day with something that increases heat, and after the fact, one can rely on this, provided that it is not done regularly." This is only according to the opinion of the Rashbam, who equates the law of insulation with that of leaving something (on the stove), as all our teachers—the Tosafists, the Rosh, the Rashba, and the Ran at the beginning of Chapter 4—explicitly wrote that insulation is for the sake of the next day, and this is the primary prohibition, and in this they rejected the words of the Rashbam. Furthermore, the sources cited for this law from the Mordechai at the beginning of "Kirah" and from the Shibolei HaLeket (in Beit Yosef, end of Section 253) do not provide any conclusive proof upon examination, and even if we were to say so, it would be according to the Rashbam. (And so wrote the Shelah in "Bigdei Yesha") Similarly, in Shibolei HaLeket, it is explained that this is according to Rashi, which is the opinion of his grandson, the Rashbam, as mentioned in Section 6. If so, why did our teacher, the Rema, divide this into two laws? He should have written this in Section 7. Additionally, why did he change the wording? There he said that in a place where they are accustomed to be lenient, one should not protest, but one should not act this way in other places. However, in Section 1, he said: "After the fact, one can rely on this, provided that it is not done regularly." And it is known that all his words are very precise. (And also the Magen Avraham, sub-paragraph 8, wrote that this is the opinion in Section 7)

It seems clear to me that his intention is as follows: Certainly, the ruling in Section 7 follows the approach of the Rashbam (Rabbi Shmuel ben Meir), and the same applies in Section 1, but there is no necessity that the Rashbam himself holds the ruling of Section 1. The proof for this is that the Tosafot and all the early authorities who cited the Rashbam's approach - only mentioned it regarding the matter in Section 7, i.e., that if it is fully cooked or cooked to the extent of Ma'achal Ben Drusai (partially cooked), there is no prohibition of insulating. However, the ruling in Section 1, which permits it for the next day, they did not mention, and even in the Mordechai it is not conclusive as stated. In truth, it is certainly surprising to say this, as the main issue of insulating is for the next day. Therefore, our teacher, the Rama, did not bring this in Section 7, but only here in Section 1, which does not deal with the specific laws of insulating, but rather discusses the prohibition of the dish if one insulated it before Shabbat. For this, he stated that some insulate for the next day and hold that the Rashbam also permitted this, as written in the Shibolei HaLeket. Therefore, he said: In retrospect, one can rely on this, meaning that the dish should not be prohibited, provided that one does not make a habit of doing so. Meaning, that another time, it is forbidden for him to do so even according to the Rashbam's approach, because it is likely that the Rashbam did not permit this. But in Section 7, he says that in a place where they are accustomed to rely on his approach, one should not protest against them, meaning that they can always rely on his approach and act accordingly.

What is called "hatmana" (insulation)? When the pot is covered on top and from the sides with the insulating material. But if the insulating material does not touch the pot, this is not considered hatmana. Therefore, placing pots in our ovens and sealing the oven's opening is not called hatmana, since the pots are not directly adjacent to the oven walls. There are those who wrote that one should be careful not to place the pot next to the wall, as this would be considered like hatmana (Taz, section 6). However, even in this case, there is no concern, since only a small part of the pot is close to the wall, and most of the pot is exposed. Hatmana is when the entire pot is covered with the insulating material, and we have already written this in Siman 253. Similarly, when the covering is not for the purpose of insulation, but to protect it from mice or from getting dirty with dust, it is permitted. Therefore, although a fully cooked dish is forbidden to insulate on Shabbat, even with a material that does not add heat, and even if it only deteriorates and is not improved by further cooking, nevertheless, placing utensils on it to protect it from mice or dirt or dust is permitted, as this is not considered like insulating to keep it warm, but rather as protecting it, like putting a cover on the pot to protect it.

Even though it is permitted to leave a pot on a stove, as stated in Siman 253, and even if there are coals in it, according to the methods and approaches explained there, nevertheless, one must be careful not to cover the pot with clothes, even during the day, as it is considered something that adds heat. Although the clothes themselves do not add heat, nevertheless, due to the fire underneath them, they do add heat and it is forbidden. And although in the Gemara (49a) it is questioned whether we require something that adds heat by itself specifically, and the opinion of the Rif there is explained that the conclusion is indeed so, nevertheless, the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch, who wrote their words without qualification, it is clearly explained that they hold there is no distinction. The reason is because the Rambam in Chapter 4, Law 1, explains that due to another factor, it is considered even more as adding heat, see there, and it is possible that the Rif also explains thus. (See Bach and Drisha) Additionally, heating due to fire certainly adds a lot of heat, and it is forbidden.

However, if the clothes are not touching the pot, even though there is a fire underneath, since it is not done in the manner of insulation, it is permitted. Therefore, if one places a pot on a stove or a small oven that contains coals, and the bottom of the pot does not touch the coals, this is considered as leaving [the pot to stay warm] and is permitted, according to the methods explained in Siman 253. And according to our teacher the Rema there, even if the pot touches the coals, it is permitted, since it is not entirely covered, as we explained there in paragraph 24, see there. Similarly, if one places a wide utensil on the pot that does not touch the sides of the pot, and places clothes on that wide utensil, it is permitted, because since the clothes are on the utensil and the utensil does not touch all the sides of the pot, this is not considered insulation.

It is also permitted to place a pot in our ovens by putting a piece of raw meat inside, even according to the opinion of the Rif and the Rambam in Siman 253, provided that the pot does not touch the coals. According to Rashi and Tosafot there, it is permitted even without a piece of raw meat, and according to Rabbeinu the Rema, it is permitted even if it touches the coals, as he wrote. And even though one covers the mouth of the oven with clothes, since the clothes do not touch the pot, it is not an issue, as he wrote, because this is not considered insulation. The insulation that is done in these countries, where they insulate in the oven and smear the mouth of the oven with clay, is permitted according to all opinions. The smearing is only for things that cook quickly, but for raw meat, there is no need for smearing, as he wrote in Siman 253. And in places where the custom is not to smear with clay or any other substance, it is forbidden to put there dough products or legumes or kas'a or potatoes, unless they cook to the extent of Ma'achal Ben Drusai before Shabbat, or cover the coals with ash (Magen Avraham, Siman Kaf-Tet), and we have already explained this in Siman 253. It is a mitzvah to insulate hot food for Shabbat in order to eat hot food on Shabbat, as this is part of honoring and enjoying Shabbat. Anyone who forbids eating hot food on Shabbat is considered a heretic, which is the way of the Sadducees, and they should be checked. However, someone who, according to their health, should not eat hot food, may eat cold food, and everything depends on their nature. Most Jews are meticulous to eat hot soup made from beef or chicken, and they eat cholent and kugel, and the custom of Israel is Torah. (But anyone who is not in good health should not eat, and should do as the doctors instruct and not be stringent in this matter, and anyone who is stringent in this matter does not meet the approval of the Sages).

Besides this, our ovens do not have the law of "hatmanah" (insulation), because the pots were already in the oven before the insulation. Additionally, since the oven is attached to the ground, it is considered like the ground, and "hatmanah" only applies to something detached from the ground. Furthermore, the Rosh wrote there, and this is his language: "There are places where, after cooking the pots, they remove the fire and rake out the coals, and place the pot there for the next day, and cover it with cold ashes... But in a place where the pot was cooked all day, the initial placement of the pot there was not for the purpose of insulation, and it is also not appropriate to insulate within the ground. Hence, there is no concern." End quote. He permitted this for these reasons even when the pot is covered with ashes, which is really "hatmanah," and certainly in our case, where we do not cover the pot with ashes. However, one must be careful, as I have heard that there are places where they take the pot from the oven and cover it with pillows and cushions - this should not be done on Shabbat. But from before Shabbat, it is allowed, for this is like the case of materials that do not increase heat, as will be explained, and it is permitted from before the day.

And behold, we have explained the matter of insulation, and therefore one must be careful not to insulate on Shabbat even with something that does not add heat. However, during twilight (bein hashmashot) it is permitted to insulate, because typically pots during twilight are boiling, and there is no concern that one might come to boil it. And it will be explained in Siman 309 that it is prohibited to insulate for the sake of after Shabbat, but with bread it is permitted, as stated in Siman 254:16. And with something that adds heat, it is forbidden even before Shabbat. And if one insulated with something that adds heat, the dish is forbidden even post facto. And even if one insulated unintentionally, it is forbidden, because they were very stringent regarding insulation (Magen Avraham, Siman 4). The reason seems to be that it does not appear to people as a prohibition, since there is no fire and coals present. And when do we prohibit it? Specifically, with something cold that was heated or something that improves with time, but if it remains warm, it is not prohibited post facto. Similarly, one who insulates on Shabbat with something that does not add heat, it is not prohibited post facto for this reason, since it just remains warm, as it does not add heat (ibid., Siman 6). And some say that if one forgot and unintentionally insulated with something that adds heat, it is permitted in any case, since it was unintentional, particularly with a dish that was fully cooked. But if it finished cooking on Shabbat, it is obvious that it is forbidden (ibid., Siman 7, and see Taz, Siman 2, who wished to say that there is no dispute here, since when the primary insulation is with something that adds heat, all agree it is forbidden, and the opinion that permits refers to when the primary insulation was with something that does not add heat, and the first opinion agrees with this, see there).

These are the things that add heat: the refuse of sesame seeds and even more so of olives. However, there is a distinction between them. If one insulated with something that does not add heat and placed the container on sesame refuse, which is their waste product, it is permitted, for they do not have enough heat to raise the temperature of the insulated container. But on olive refuse, it is prohibited, for they emit heat. (Talmud 48b) The Rif and the Rosh brought this, but the Rambam, the Tur, and the Shulchan Aruch did not mention this, and it requires further study. Similarly, with other items that add heat, as will be explained, it is permitted to place the container that was insulated on them, for they only prohibited olive refuse that has significant heat. Likewise, in Choshen Mishpat, section 155, regarding maintaining distance from the wall with something that damages the wall, they only prohibited olive refuse as explained there. (However, according to this, manure, salt, lime, and moist sand should be considered like olives since they are equal to olives in terms of maintaining distance as explained there, and perhaps indeed this is the case. And from sand, there is also proof, for insulation is stricter than maintaining distance from the wall, since with insulation even dry sand is prohibited as will be explained, and not so with maintaining distance as stated there. It is puzzling that the poskim did not discuss this at all and requires careful study.) (And it is implied in the Jerusalem Talmud that refuse after twelve months does not add heat.)

And so manure, salt, lime, and sand, whether moist or dry, and straw, grape skins, and soft materials, which includes anything soft like cotton and similar substances, and herbs when these four are moist, as they then increase heat. And in the Gemara there, they had a question whether it is specifically when they are moist by themselves or even when they are moist due to something else, and the Rosh ruled leniently there, and the Rif wrote that the conclusion is that it was taught when they are moist by themselves, and it seems also that his intention is like the Rosh. But the Rambam in Chapter 4 explains that on the contrary, when they are moist due to something else, they heat more, as he wrote: "Moist, even by themselves" there. And the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch wrote indeterminately. And it seems that this is their reasoning, because according to the Rosh, moist due to something else is less severe, and according to the Rambam, moist by themselves is less severe, and consequently, both are forbidden. Therefore, they wrote simply: 'Not with moist soft materials', and consequently, everything is included. (And in the Gemara 49a, they asked: when are soft materials moist by themselves, and they answered from the wool that is sheared from between the legs of the animal, which is full of sweat and is moist by itself there).

These are the things that do not add heat: clothing, fruits, pigeon wings, and other feathers. According to this, cushions and pillows do not add heat, and similarly, flax tow, which is the waste of flax. It appears that flax itself is the same, as it is not inferior to clothing. The reason they mentioned 'tow' is because it is common to insulate with tow, as it is worthless, being the fine particles that fall from the flax. Similarly, wood shavings, which are the fine particles that fall from the wood when it is planed, called "flek" or "polovina." All these, when they are damp, add heat; therefore, when they are not damp, they do not add heat.

And our master, the Rema, wrote in paragraph 3: "There are those who say it is permitted to insulate with rocks even though they increase the heat, because for something uncommon the Rabbis did not decree." This means that even though it is explained in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 155, that one must distance rocks from the wall, and they are hard stones, due to the fact that they contain much heat and damage the wall, and if so, it is obvious that they increase the heat, nevertheless, since insulation with them is uncommon, because they are likely to break the pot and spoil the food - therefore the Rabbis did not decree concerning this. And hot ashes without coals do not increase the heat. (Rashal in his responsa)

Even though it is forbidden to insulate on Shabbat, even with something that does not add heat, nevertheless, if one insulated with it while it was still day and it became uncovered after nightfall, it is permitted to re-cover it. And one can even initially uncover and re-cover it if there is a need. (Tosafot 51a, s.v. "kasehu", and see Taz, sect. 4, and Beit Yosef) However, if it became uncovered while it was still day, it is forbidden to re-cover it after nightfall, as this is considered as initially insulating. (Magen Avraham, sect. 12) But from Tosafot (ibid.) it is clear that only if he uncovered it during the day is it forbidden to re-cover it after nightfall; but if it became uncovered by itself, it is permitted. See there. However, our teacher the Beit Yosef, in his major work, ruled from the Jerusalem Talmud that even if it became uncovered by itself, it is forbidden; see there. And indeed, in the Jerusalem Talmud it remains in doubt; see there. And also the Rosh wrote like Tosafot; see there. And know that it seems there is no difference whether he uncovered it with the intention to re-cover it or without the intention to re-cover it, as the decisors did not distinguish in this matter. (And in this manner, it would be possible to reconcile the disagreement, that even in the case where it became uncovered by itself, we could distinguish between if he saw and did not care to cover it and later decided to cover it, and if immediately when he saw he wanted to cover it. Consider this carefully.)

Just as it is appropriate to cover it when it becomes uncovered on Shabbat, so too it is permitted to add to the cover on Shabbat with materials that do not add heat. Similarly, if one wishes to remove the entire cover and replace it with another cover in its place, it is permitted, whether the first is hotter than the second or the second is hotter than the first. Since it was already covered, this is not considered new insulation and is permitted. Furthermore, even if there was a light cover on the pot, such as a sheet, one can remove it and cover it with a thick garment. All this applies when the pot is fully cooked, even if further cooking would improve it, since there is no cooking involved. However, if it is not fully cooked, it is forbidden even to add to the cover, because this addition might cause some cooking. Additionally, one might place it as it is covered on a stove with coals. It should be done in a permissible manner as explained in section 12, where the clothes do not touch the pot, or by using a wide vessel as mentioned there. (This is also written by the Magen Avraham in section 13, but the language does not imply this. Therefore, it seems that their intention is as we explained in the first reason, and furthermore, in the insulation mentioned here, there is no permission, and consider this well.)

Insulating with something that does not add heat - they only prohibited it with something hot that was heated in a primary vessel. But it is permitted to insulate something cold, insulating it so that it does not get too cold or so that its coolness diminishes. Even an important person is allowed to do this, as we find in the Gemara (51a) that Rav Nachman did so (see there). Furthermore, even if one transferred the cooked food on Shabbat from the pot in which it was cooked to another pot, it is permitted to insulate it with something that does not add heat, since it has been removed from the primary vessel. There is no concern that it will come to a boil, because by transferring it to another pot, he is cooling it down, so how could it come to a boil? (See the Gemara there.) Even though placing it on a stove is worse when transferring from one pot to another, as we wrote in Siman 253, that is when placing it on a stove with coals, because there his intention is necessarily to heat it up, which is not the case with insulating with something that does not add heat. (See Magen Avraham, subparagraph 14.) It is possible that even in the primary vessel itself, if it has cooled somewhat, meaning if it was removed from the stove and left for some time on the ground or on the table, one is permitted afterwards to insulate it with something that does not add heat for this reason, since his intention is to cool it somewhat. (See there.) However, all of this is with something that does not add heat, but with something that adds heat - it is prohibited even to insulate something completely cold, and even from before Shabbat it is also prohibited, as this is like insulating in embers, where the Sages made no distinction. (But in a weekday cold setting, it is permitted as proven in the beginning of the second chapter of Bava Batra, and see Turei Zahav there.)

The Rambam wrote at the end of Chapter 4: "One may place a kettle (of copper) on top of another kettle on Shabbat, and a pot (of earthenware) on top of another pot, and a pot on top of a kettle and a kettle on top of a pot, and seal their mouths with dough. Not so that they will be heated, but so that they will retain their heat. For it was only prohibited to insulate on Shabbat, but placing a hot vessel on top of another hot vessel so that they will retain their heat is permitted. However, one may not place a vessel containing a cold item on top of a hot vessel on Shabbat, for it generates heat in it on Shabbat. If it was placed from before the onset of Shabbat, it is permitted, and it is not considered insulating with an item that adds heat." End quote. (And this is also the text in the Gemara at the end of the chapter "With What May One Insulate," and not as the text before us which states that placing a kettle on a pot is prohibited, and Rashi there also wrote like the Rambam according to the Tosefta, see there.)

Explanation of the matter: When one places a hot utensil on top of another hot utensil, this does not involve the prohibition of cooking, since both are hot and equal in their heat. However, if they are not equal, it will be explained in Siman 318. Additionally, there is no issue of insulation here, since the upper utensil is exposed, and this is not considered insulation. This is also not similar to leaving it on the stove, where there are coals and the heat is very intense, which is not the case with a hot water urn on another hot water urn. Only placing a cold utensil is prohibited because it generates heat, but from before Shabbat it is permitted since this is not considered insulation, as we have explained. It is obvious that what was stated about sealing their openings with dough refers to when the dough was kneaded before Shabbat, and the sealing is permitted because it is only for a short time. It is also clear that when a pot is on the fire, it is forbidden to place another pot or hot water urn on it, as this is considered actual leaving (shehiya). There is another reason why this is not considered insulation, because the heat gradually diminishes. Even though coals and embers also gradually cool, their heat is very strong and is not comparable to the heat of hot water. However, this consideration is only needed according to the opinion that considers placing the bottom of the pot on coals as insulation, but it has already been explained that according to our accepted view, as long as the entire pot is not covered, it is not considered insulation. See further in Siman 318, Section 36.

There are those who criticize people who, during the winter, take a vessel containing a cold beverage and place it within another vessel filled with hot water to take the chill off, saying that this constitutes complete insulation. We have not heard of anyone doing this, except that we have heard of women who take the vessel containing kugel and place it entirely within a large pot of cholent, and this is complete insulation in something that adds heat, since the pot is within an oven full of coals, and it is prohibited even from before Shabbat. This is unless we follow the reasoning of the Rosh that we mentioned in the previous section, paragraph 14, which permits this because the pot was initially in the oven and this is considered connected, as explained there. However, it is certainly better not to do this. (Or because the oven is sealed, and also with insulation, it is permitted just like with leaving it [on the fire]).

One must also be cautious regarding drinking hot beverages on Shabbat morning. We place in the oven an earthenware or copper vessel with water, which is called a "lyak," as well as a "tsanik" with tea, and we place them in the oven. In the morning, we take them out of the oven and drink. We must be careful not to cover either the "lyak" or the "tsanik" with a cloth or any other object, for this constitutes complete insulation from the outset on Shabbat with something that does not add heat, and it is forbidden as explained.

It is well known that anything not suitable for permissible use on Shabbat, or even if it is suitable but not designated for such use, is considered muktzeh and is forbidden to move. Therefore, if one insulated with garments or cushions and pillows, or with materials like cotton wool and soft, sheared wool of animals, and did not designate them for permanent insulation—for if he designated them, they would be deemed suitable and designated for insulation and permitted to move. But if he did not designate them and only insulated with them once, then they are not considered designated for that purpose, and they remain muktzeh as before and are forbidden to move because the insulation was incidental. Therefore, there is an opinion that if he insulated twice, it is considered as though he designated them for insulation and they would be permitted to move. (Bach)

According to the Rif and the Rambam in Chapter 26, Law 12, even if one insulated with wool shearings that are not so significant, they are forbidden to move if they were not designated for that purpose. Only if one insulated with hides, whether of a homeowner or a craftsman, they are permitted to move, because he is not particular about them. But according to most authorities, wool shearings are like hides, and if one insulated with them once, they are permitted to move. This is also the general ruling of the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch, Section 1. However, this applies to ordinary shearings that are not intended for trade. But if they were placed in storage for trade and he is particular about them, they are forbidden to move without designation, or if he insulated with them twice.

It is obvious that when insulating with manure, lime, sand, or straw, one must designate these materials for this purpose; otherwise, they will certainly be discarded, as they hold no significance and are therefore considered muktzeh (set aside and not to be moved on Shabbat). Therefore, these materials must be designated for insulation permanently. Similarly, when placing stones or bricks around a pot, they must be designated for this purpose permanently, as otherwise, they are insignificant to him and will be discarded. Thus, it is forbidden to move them unless they are stored and designated for insulation. However, stones placed on top of a stove are permitted to be moved, as they are designated for use. (Magen Avraham, section 7) In our practice of sealing the oven opening, some support the oven cover with wood intended for burning, which is forbidden to move unless designated for this purpose. (ibid.) Women are not careful about this due to their lack of knowledge of the laws of muktzeh, and they should be warned about it. Similarly, when sealing the oven opening with worn-out rags, they need to be designated for this purpose; if not designated, they are forbidden to be moved. When opening the oven, one should let them fall and not touch them. (Refer to the Bach, who wrote that for stones, repetitive insulation does not suffice, which requires further examination.)

How should one act when he insulated [a pot] with something that is forbidden to move, if part of the cover is exposed without the fleece or other insulating material? He should shake the cover and they will fall off, meaning he should take the pot cover from the area free of fleece, and the cover has the status of a utensil. Even though the fleece is on the cover, and when he moves the cover, he is effectively moving the fleece, this is considered indirect movement, as he is not moving them directly. And we hold that indirect movement for the sake of something permitted is allowed, as will be explained in Siman 311. The reason we do not say that the cover becomes a base for the fleece, as is the rule for a base for something forbidden, is because this would apply if the cover served the wool, but here, on the contrary, the wool serves the pot to keep it warm. Therefore, it is not appropriate to say that the cover becomes a base for the fleece. If the entire cover is covered by the fleece, the only solution is to take a fork or knife or another object and lift the cover with the fleece together. (Magen Avraham, subsection 5, and see Taz, subsection 2, who questions from the barrel in Siman 311, that when one needs the place, it is permitted to move the barrel, so why not permit it here. His words are puzzling, and indeed, they only permitted it when one needs the place, and the Peri Megadim already questioned him there. Examine this carefully.)

One who buries a pot in a basket filled with wool fleeces that are forbidden to be moved, such as those designated for sale and he is particular about them, and he removes the pot, such as when its top was not covered with fleeces, and afterwards wants to return it into the basket, as long as the indentation has not been spoiled, it is permitted to return it, since he is not touching the fleeces. But if the indentation has been spoiled, and it is necessary to move them around with the pot, it is forbidden to return it. And although moving indirectly is permitted as we have said, this applies to general movement, but not when it is necessary to move them a lot, for then it is considered as if he is moving them directly with his hands. (Tosafot 50a: s.v. 'hakol' see there) Nevertheless, we do not prohibit taking the pot out lest the indentation be spoiled, because in any case, if it does not get spoiled, he will return it, and if it gets spoiled, he will not return it.

And this is regarding an item that cannot be handled on Shabbat, but if it was insulated with something that can be handled, it is self-understood that there is no concern in returning it even if the insulation pit was damaged, since it is permitted to repair it with one's own hands, because it was insulated with something that can be handled. This is according to the opinion of Rashi and Tosafot. (There)

However, the Rambam in his commentary on the Mishnah wrote a different reason for the prohibition of returning it when the insulation pit was damaged. It is not because of the principle of muktzeh, but rather because when the insulation pit is damaged and it is repaired, it appears as if one is initially insulating on Shabbat. Therefore, there is no difference between an item that can be handled and an item that cannot be handled, as it is prohibited in both cases. (See in the Jerusalem Talmud at the end of the chapter "With What May One Insulate" and examine closely)

If one insulated a pot with something that cannot be handled on Shabbat and covered it with something that can be handled, he may uncover it and grasp the pot to remove it, for certainly the top of the pot is free from something that cannot be handled. Similarly, if he covered the pot with something that cannot be handled and insulated it with something that can be handled, he clears around it and grasps the pot to remove it, for the pot does not become a base for the cover, as mentioned, and this is considered indirect handling, as mentioned. Even if he insulated and covered it with something that cannot be handled, if part of the pot is exposed, he may take and return it. If not, he may only move it if he uses a fork or knife to lift the cover, as mentioned in section 4.

Our ovens, which are sealed at their openings with a board and coated with clay - it is permissible to dismantle this seal on Shabbat morning to open the oven, and there is no prohibition of demolishing a structure, since this would only apply if it were sealed for a long duration. However, here it is only sealed to be opened in the morning. One can remove the cooked dishes and then reseal it if possible as before, but usually, the clay has already dried and it is not possible to reseal it as before, except by using just the board to seal it. However, if there are still burning coals in the oven, and by opening the oven, they become kindled by the air as usual - it is forbidden for a Jew to seal the oven opening, because through sealing, the coals will be extinguished, and even if they are not completely extinguished, their burning will be reduced, which constitutes extinguishing. This cannot be considered as "an unintended action" because it will inevitably happen, making it a "psik reisha" (an inevitable consequence). Therefore, if it is possible to do it through a non-Jew, one should instruct the non-Jew to seal the oven opening - this is preferable, and it does not constitute "commanding a non-Jew to perform a Shabbat prohibition", since we are not commanding him to extinguish the coals, but to open the oven, and the extinguishing happens incidentally. If it is not possible through a non-Jew, one should be careful not to cover the entire oven opening but leave part of it open or position the cover diagonally, so that one side remains open.

There is an opinion that forbids even opening the oven when there are glowing coals inside, because by opening it, the wind will ignite the coals (Magen Avraham 11 in the name of Terumat Hadeshen). This is also considered a "pesik reisha" (an inevitable consequence). However, the custom is not like this, as our women open the oven even when there are glowing coals inside. This is also evident from the words of our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, who wrote in paragraph 7 that if there are glowing coals, it is permitted to close it by a non-Jew but not by a Jew. Why did they not also forbid opening it? Certainly, there is no concern in opening it. This is not similar to what is written in Siman 307, where one opens the door of the house and the wind enters from the courtyard. Additionally, there the main concern is due to an unusual wind, and we make a decree for a usual wind because of an unusual wind (Taz there, paragraph 4). But when one opens the oven into the house and not into the courtyard, there is no concern of igniting or extinguishing. Even though we see that after opening the oven for some time the coals appear glowing, which were previously covered, nevertheless at the time of the action he does nothing, and even afterward it is not a complete ignition, it is only indirect causation (grama), and it is explicitly stated in Shabbat (120b) that grama is permitted. (I am puzzled by what the Magen Avraham wrote regarding this law from Terumat Hadeshen, because there in Siman 59 it does not discuss at all opening the mouth of the oven but rather opening the window opposite the candle. It seems that the intention of the Magen Avraham is that he considers opening the oven similar to opening the door, but this is not a proper comparison, and examine this well.)

I have also seen someone write that there are those who prohibit sealing an oven with glowing coals because of the concern of stoking the fire, as the wind exits through a small hole, and it is similar to a bellows and kindles the oven more than if it were completely open. According to this, when sealing the oven, one would need to leave a large opening. But in truth, these things are puzzling, and many disagree with this. The prohibition of sealing is due to extinguishing, not due to stoking. It is obvious that when the fire is burning inside, it is forbidden to seal it completely, as it will certainly be extinguished. However, if a place is left open, it is permitted, and certainly, there needs to be an open place for some duration, because if not, it is meaningless.

However, regarding the matter that has been clarified—that there is no prohibition of demolition concerning an oven—our teacher, the Rema, wrote that there are those who are stringent and do not permit the demolition of an oven sealed with clay by a Jew if it is possible to have it done by a non-Jew. Similarly, if it is possible to have it done by a minor Jew, an adult Jew should not do it. And if it is not possible, an adult may do it with some modification, and this is the common custom, end of his words. But among us, the custom is not so. And thus wrote one of the great scholars (Elya Rabba 316:15), that Maharshal, the teacher of the Mahari"l, permitted doing so from the outset.

He further wrote: "The permission to seal the oven applies during the day, when all the pots have already fully cooked. But at night, close to the time of insulation, there is a concern that perhaps the pots have not yet fully cooked - it is forbidden to seal the oven, as it causes cooking, as explained in Siman 257, and even through a non-Jew it is forbidden, as explained above at the end of Siman 253." Therefore, one must be very careful about this, unless it is known that the dishes are already fully cooked, in which case it is permitted through a non-Jew. But otherwise, if it was done by a Jew, the food is forbidden even after the fact, until after Shabbat, in order to allow the time it would take to do the action. However, if it was done by a non-Jew, even though it was done in violation, nevertheless, the food is permitted after the fact, since it would have cooked even without this action. (Magen Avraham, Subsection 12)

There is a doubt whether, if it is necessary to open the oven for a sick person or someone in danger, and it is permitted by a Jew, or if there is no danger and it was opened by a non-Jew, if it is allowed to subsequently instruct the non-Jew to close it, similar to things that were permitted at the end due to their beginning (Beitzah 11b), or if it was not permitted. And it seems that it is allowed by a non-Jew. Furthermore, since if the oven is not closed, there will be nothing to eat on Shabbat morning, it is permitted to instruct a non-Jew in such cases, and it is much better than what Rabbi Rema permitted later in Siman 276, to instruct to light a candle for the Shabbat meal, see there, because here it was necessary to open for the sick person, which is not the case there, where it could have been prepared before Shabbat, and therefore it is permitted by a non-Jew.

In their time, some would insulate with stones, that is, they would arrange the stones like a structure, setting the stones around the pot one on top of the other. Therefore, on a Yom Tov that falls on the eve of Shabbat, there are those who prohibit insulating with stones, because it appears like building on Yom Tov. And there are those who permit it, as it does not appear like building, and for the honor of Shabbat, they did not decree against it. Therefore, when it is possible to insulate in another manner, one should not insulate with stones (Magen Avraham, Subsection 10). And now, we do not know at all about this type of insulation.

And now that all the laws of Shehiyah (leaving food on a heat source before Shabbat) and Hatmanah (insulating food) have been explained, and it has already been clarified that our ovens do not have the status of Hatmanah at all, but rather of Shehiyah, and their status is like a Kirah (a type of stove) and not like an oven from the times of the Gemara. If the oven is plastered with clay, it is permitted according to all opinions. However, if it is not plastered, it depends on the opinions explained in Siman 253, section 27. But if ashes were placed on the coals and the coals were swept to one side of the oven, it is also permitted according to all opinions. We adhere to the view of Rashi and Tosafot, that Shehiyah is permitted with a Kirah that is not swept and covered, as long as the food reached the stage of Ma'achal Ben Drusai (partially cooked) before nightfall. Placing food on top of the oven or in front of the oven, which is called a "yamakka" or "kaminack," and similarly with "kakhlakhs" - this is considered mere support and is permitted, as mentioned there. However, we must be careful not to open the oven on the eve of Shabbat until the food for the next day is fully cooked, as this would be a Torah prohibition if the oven is then resealed. Additionally, care should be taken not to wrap any pot or vessels (like the "laya'kas" from which hot beverages are drunk and the "tsanikas") in any material on Shabbat, as this constitutes Hatmanah. Everyone should ensure that members of their household do not do this. They should also be warned against supporting the oven's closure with wood or stones, unless these were designated for this purpose permanently. Since this practice is very common and women are often unaware of this prohibition, it is necessary to warn them, as mentioned in section 3.

It is written: "And You have removed my soul far off from peace; I forgot prosperity" (Lamentations 3:17). The Sages expound (Shabbat 25b): "'And You have removed my soul far off from peace' - this refers to the lighting of the Shabbat lamp; 'I forgot prosperity' - this refers to the bathhouse or washing one's hands and feet with hot water on the eve of Shabbat." Therefore, most Jews have the custom to go to the bathhouse on the eve of Shabbat, due to the honor of Shabbat. And some have the custom to also immerse in the mikvah because of the sanctity of Shabbat, and fortunate is their lot, for through this, they draw upon themselves an abundance of sanctity from the Holy Shabbat. They also wear a white shirt in honor of Shabbat.

And this is what the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch wrote: "It is a mitzvah for every person to wash their entire body in hot water on the eve of Shabbat, and if that is not possible, they should wash their face, hands, and feet" (see there). In the Gemara, "face" is not mentioned, because it is something obvious, as we have already learned there (50b): "A person washes their face, hands, and feet every day in honor of their Creator" (see there). And similarly, it is stated there regarding Rabbi Yehuda, that every Friday evening they would bring him a basin full of hot water, and he would wash his face, hands, and feet (see there). And the fact that the face is not included in 'the good practice' is not because the face does not need to be washed, but because the face is not part of 'the good practice.' Meaning, washing hands and feet in hot water in the evening was considered a remedy, as it is said there (108b): "A drop of cold water in the morning and washing hands and feet in hot water in the evening is better than all the balms in the world" (see there), and the verse does not refer to the eve of Shabbat, hence it does not mention the face. And indeed, it is certain that bathing the entire body is a greater mitzvah than washing just the face, hands, and feet, and the fact that Rabbi Yehuda did not do so, I have seen some who labored over this (A.R. Sk. 1). But it seems to me that the reason is simple, because Rabbi Yehuda had a headache, as stated in Nedarim (49b), and someone who has a headache cannot enter a bathhouse because of the heat, and therefore he did not wash his head either.

It is stated in the Talmud (Shabbat 61a): When one washes, he should wash his right side first and afterwards his left side. When he anoints, he should anoint his right side first and afterwards his left side. And if one wishes to anoint his entire body, he should anoint his head first because it is the king over all the limbs, as stated there. Accordingly, if one washes his entire body, he should wash his head first for the same reason. The reason this is not mentioned regarding washing is because most washing in the time of the Talmud was done in a bathhouse, as it is stated in Nedarim (41b): "And he washes with him in the bathhouse." Therefore, it is necessary that his feet enter the water first; hence, it only mentions washing the hands, starting with the right and then the left. Consequently, one who washes outside of a bathhouse should first wash his head along with his face, then his heart, which is considered superior to all limbs after the head, then his right hand and then his left hand, and afterwards his feet, starting with the right and then the left. This procedure should also be followed when anointing with soap, which is called "zeif."

It is stated in Nedarim (40a): "Messiness of the head leads to blindness, messiness of the clothes leads to a state of neglect, and messiness of the body leads to boils and sores." This means that when one does not regularly comb their hair, it will lead to eye problems; when one does not regularly wash their clothes, it will lead to filth and a state of neglect and confusion; and when one does not regularly wash their body, it will lead to boils. And it is stated in Pesachim (111b): One who combs their hair when it is dry will become blind, and one who puts on shoes while their feet are still wet will also become blind, as is stated there. Therefore, it is customary for all Jews to wash their bodies on Friday afternoon, to comb their hair after washing, and to put on clean, white garments. By doing this, one avoids all three of these harmful outcomes, and it is considered a delight for Shabbat.

It is proper to cut the nails on the eve of Shabbat, and to shave the head when necessary, one should shave or get a haircut on the eve of Shabbat. However, one should not shave after the time of Mincha if it has arrived and he has not yet prayed, as we mentioned earlier in Siman 232. Also, it is forbidden to go to the bathhouse, as we wrote there. However, people are lenient about this because our bathhouses are not like theirs, which had a lot of steam and danger since they were heated from underneath, which is not the case with our bathhouses. Earlier in Siman 232, our master the Rema wrote a leniency regarding eating, see there, and we wrote in section 15 a leniency based on the Jerusalem Talmud, see there. Consequently, the same applies to the bathhouse, even if we do not differentiate between our bathhouses and theirs.

Some have written, based on the will of Rabbi Yehuda HaChasid, not to shave or cut nails on Rosh Chodesh, even if it falls on a Friday (Magen Avraham), due to danger (Ba'er Heitev). And some have written not to cut the nails of hands and feet on the same day (ibid.). And some have written not to shave or cut nails on Thursday, because they start to grow on Shabbat (Magen Avraham). This is contrary to an explicit Mishnah in Taanit (Chapter 2, Mishnah 7), where the members of the priestly watch would shave on Thursday. Also, what prohibition is there if they start to grow on Shabbat? Rather, out of respect for Shabbat, it is better to get a haircut on Friday. However, if one knows that he will not have time on Friday, he can simply shave and cut nails on Thursday.

They also wrote that when cutting nails, one should not cut them in order; he should start with the ring finger on the left hand and the index finger on the right hand. The mnemonic for this is "D-B-A-G-A" on the left hand and "D-A-G-H-A" on the right hand. The Arizal did not care about this and mocked it (Magen Avraham). Nonetheless, it is worthwhile to be cautious initially (ibid.). All these matters have no basis in law; whoever is particular about them, it is as if he is particular, and whoever is not particular, it is as if he is not particular. One should cut the nails of the right hand first and then the left, although the Kolbo brings the opposite, to cut the left hand first (Eliyah Rabbah, subparagraph 6), and I do not know the reason.

One should be careful not to throw the nails on the ground, lest a pregnant woman pass over them and miscarry (Moed Katan 18a). Therefore, in a place where no woman is present, like a study hall, there is no concern (ibid.). Similarly, if the nails have been moved from their original place where they were thrown, there is no concern (ibid.). Also, if one cuts something with a knife after throwing the nails, the concern is removed (Niddah 17a). They also said there that regarding nails: a pious person burns them, a righteous person buries them, and a wicked person throws them away. All the words of the Sages are very trustworthy, and they are mystical matters beyond the understanding of the intellect.

It is obvious that all these matters—bathing, cutting nails, and shaving—are better done after midday, as it is more apparent that it is for the honor of Shabbat. Nevertheless, if one did them before midday, it is also good, as anything done on Friday is considered for the honor of Shabbat, as explicitly stated in Nazir (5a). Some delay going to the bathhouse and mikvah and claim that this is based on kabbalah, but they are mistaken, and they should be rebuked. On the contrary, if it is only after midday, it is a mitzvah to hurry (and there is no contradiction from the Rema at the end of Siman 262).

We learned in the Mishnah (34a): "A person must say three things in their home on Friday evening as it gets dark: Have you tithed? Have you made an eruv? Light the candle." This does not pertain to a question form, for he sees that the candle is not lit. And in our case, one must say 'Have you separated challah?' Our women are diligent and do not wait for their husbands' promptings. One must speak gently and calmly (Gemara), and also warn them to cease from work. When an eruv for courtyards is needed, he should do it himself and not rely on others.

It is taught in the Mekhilta (Yitro, Chapter 7): "Remember and observe - remember beforehand and observe afterward. From here, they said: one must extend the sanctity into the mundane. It is comparable to a wolf that attacks from before and from behind." This is the end of the quotation. And this is its explanation: the way of the wolf is that it does not kill the animal in the middle of its body, but either from the front at its neck or from behind. And just as the wolf kills the whole body by attacking from the front or from behind, so too, if one does not extend the sanctity into the mundane from before and from behind, it is as if one desecrates the entire Sabbath. Therefore, the Torah warned about this. And similarly, it is stated in the Midrash Rabbah (Bereishit, Chapter 10): "A human being, who does not know his times or moments, extends the mundane into the sanctity." See there. And in Yoma (81b), regarding the extension of Yom Kippur, we say: From where do we derive that Sabbath and festivals also require extending the mundane into the sanctity? It says, 'You shall rest on your Sabbaths.' From this, you learn that wherever it says 'rest,' meaning cessation, one must extend the sanctity into the mundane. (And that which we say in Moed Katan 4a, 'We derive the word 'rest' from the six days of creation, just as there it is forbidden and beforehand is permitted, etc.,' Tosafot writes there that this is a minor detail. See there. And according to the words of the Midrash, it is not difficult at all, for it is necessary to add, and there it refers to the thirty-day addition of the Sabbatical year. And similarly, the Yerushalmi at the beginning of Shevi'it, 'Just as the Sabbath of creation, you are allowed to do work until sunset, etc.,' also has this explanation. See there. But Tosafot in Rosh Hashanah 9a, s.v. 'and Rabbi Akiva,' did not interpret it this way. See there and understand well.)

And this is what our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 2: "There are those who say that one must add from the mundane to the holy." See there. And he wrote in the language of "there are those who say," because the Rambam and the Tur only mentioned this in regard to the addition of Yom Kippur in terms of affliction alone, as they wrote in the laws of Yom Kippur, and this depends on the discussion in Yoma there. However, most of our Rabbis: the Ba'al Halachot Gedolot, the Rif, the Rosh, the SeMaG, the SeMaK, the Yereim, the Ran, and the Maggid Mishneh, ruled that the addition of Shabbat and Yom Tov is from the Torah. Nevertheless, in practice, it seems to me that there is no practical difference, for it is obvious that one must cease from work a little before sunset, as it is impossible for a human being to ascertain the exact moment, as the Midrash we brought states. And after sunset begins "bein hashmashot," which is a doubtful period concerning capital punishment, and one who performs work during "bein hashmashot" on the eve of Shabbat and at the end of Shabbat at the same time - in any case is liable to bring a sin offering (Shabbat 35b). And so the Rambam ruled in chapter 5, see there. If so, since one ceases from work before sunset - there is also an addition here, for there is no measure for the addition.

However, regarding the exact time of bein hashmashot (the twilight period between sunset and nightfall), there is a disagreement among the poskim (Jewish legal scholars). As explained in the Gemara (Shabbat 34b), the time of bein hashmashot extends for the duration it takes to walk three-quarters of a mil after sunset, and afterwards it is considered night. According to the calculation that the time to walk a mil is eighteen parts of an hour, three-quarters of a mil is thirteen and a half parts. The Gemara (Shabbat 35a) also states: "One star – it is still day; two stars – it is bein hashmashot; three stars – it is night. These are not large stars visible during the day or small stars visible only at night, but medium-sized stars." And this is the language of the Rambam in Chapter 5, Halacha 4: "From the time the sun sets until three medium-sized stars are visible, that is the time called bein hashmashot everywhere, and it is uncertain whether it is considered day or night, and we rule stringently… And these stars are not large ones, etc." End quote.

His words are not understandable, for in the Gemara it is said that one star is still day, and we must conclude that this is not referring to stars visible during the day, for it later explains: "and not the large stars visible during the day." Therefore, we must conclude that it refers to medium-sized stars, which are visible after sunset while it is still day, and how can he rule that from sunset it is twilight? And indeed, many have questioned him on this. (Ralbach in his commentary on the laws of sanctifying the month, chapter 2, see there.) Furthermore, why did he omit the measure of three-quarters of a mil? One cannot say that there is a disagreement, for the Rif brought both sayings, see there, from which we understand that there is no disagreement. Perhaps the Rambam intentionally wrote so, because this matter is taught to many, including women and the unlearned, and who can precisely measure the three-quarters of a mil, or distinguish between large, small, and medium stars? Therefore, he chose a definitive matter, that is, the sunset, which everyone recognizes. So immediately with the sunset, it is twilight, and work is forbidden, and three stars indicate definitely night. The practical difference is for someone who wishes to recite the Shema at night, or to make Kiddush, or similar matters. And even though not everyone is skilled in recognizing stars, there is no stumbling block in this. However, on the conclusion of Shabbat, one must know the medium stars to avoid mistaking them for large ones. And it is written in the Jerusalem Talmud, first chapter of Berakhot: the three stars must be close together, not scattered. And this is the language of the Jerusalem Talmud: "Provided that three stars appear that seem like one cluster," see there. Therefore, at the conclusion of Shabbat, one must be careful with this sign. (This version was brought by the Ran, see there.)

And behold, according to the opinion of the Rambam, twilight begins immediately after sunset. This is also the opinion of the Rif and the Geonim. However, our Rabbis, the Tosafists, wrote in the name of Rabbeinu Tam a different approach to this matter, and this was also agreed upon by the Ramban, the Rashba, and the Rosh in Taanit (Chapter 1, Siman 12) and by the Ran at the end of the second chapter of Shabbat, because these Rabbis found it difficult to understand how it could be said that from sunset until nightfall is only three-quarters of a mil, when in Pesachim (94a) it is stated that from sunset until nightfall is four mil. Therefore, Rabbeinu Tam explained that there are two sunsets: the first is the beginning of sunset, and from it, there are four mil until nightfall. And on Shabbat, we speak of the second sunset, which is when the sun is already set in the sky, but it has not yet passed behind the horizon, the sign for which is that the sky's face reddens opposite its location. Therefore, from the beginning of sunset until three and a quarter mil, it is still considered day, which adds to the observance of Shabbat, and from then twilight begins, and three-quarters of a mil later, it is night.

There is an approach among the early authorities (the Ra'avan and Rabbi Eliezer of Mitz in the Yereim) who, due to this difficulty, stated that the measure of three-quarters of a mil for twilight is before sunset, while the sun is still on the earth. According to this opinion, even before sunset, it is uncertain whether it is night. According to their view, one must refrain from work and light the candles a considerable time before sunset. However, this approach was not accepted. (And the Bach wrote that one should be concerned about it). Indeed, in previous generations, people would accept Shabbat almost two hours before nightfall (Bach), and fortunate are they. We have already discussed this in Siman 242, Section 5, and in Siman 256, Section 3. (And so wrote the Magen Avraham in subparagraph 9).

Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, in Section 2, only brought the view of Rabbeinu Tam and held it as the main opinion. And this is his wording: "Some say that one must add from the weekday to the holy day, and this additional time is from the beginning of sunset, when the sun is no longer visible on the earth, until the time of twilight. And this period, which is three and a quarter mil, if he wishes to make it entirely additional time, he may do so; if he wishes to make part of it additional, he may do so, provided that he adds some certain time from the weekday to the holy day. And the duration of twilight is three-quarters of a mil, which is the walking distance of one thousand and five hundred cubits before nightfall." End of quote. This is the opinion of Rabbeinu Tam.

(And perhaps he [the Beit Yosef] holds that since the words of the Rif and Rambam are the language of the Talmud, then everything that is explained in the Gemara will be explained in their words. However, this is a great difficulty, and so wrote the Radbaz in his commentary on the Laws of Sanctification of the Month, Chapter 2, that the Rambam does not hold like Rabbeinu Tam, but immediately after sunset it is twilight, and so wrote the Maggid Mishneh in Chapter 5.)

Many of the great authorities of the world rejected the approach of Rabbeinu Tam entirely (the Gra and the Baal HaTanya in his Siddur, among other greats) and determined that immediately after sunset is Bein HaShmashot (twilight), and after three-quarters of a mil it is night. The reference in Pesachim is not to the appearance of stars throughout the Talmud as three stars, but rather when the entire sky is filled with stars. This is implied in the Jerusalem Talmud which states: just as it says for the evening, once three stars are visible, even though the sun is in the middle of the sky, it is night, and one should say the same for the morning. Meaning, why do we consider it day from dawn onwards? It is clear that it is called night when the sun is in the middle of the sky, meaning it has not yet passed the entire thickness of the sky, and thus all of Israel practice. On Motzei Shabbat, the practice follows the words of Rabbeinu Tam. (In our book "Or L'Yesharim" siman 181, we explain Rabbeinu Tam's approach with the help of Heaven). Know that all the measurements that Chazal estimated are based on the situation in Eretz Yisrael and Babylonia, and during the times of the equinoxes of Nissan and Tishrei, when days and nights are equal. Consequently, in our northern countries during the winter, it becomes night immediately after sunset. Therefore, in winter, one must caution the people to start much earlier while the sun is still on the land, and now the calendars print the time of sunset for all days of the year, and one must light candles at least no later than half an hour before the time printed on the calendar. Anyone who is careful and diligent in hastening the holy Shabbat is granted blessings from Heaven.

And one who is not proficient in these measurements should light while the sun is at the top of the trees. If it is a cloudy day, light when the roosters sit on the beam during the day. If it is in the field where there are no roosters, light when the crows sit during the day. There is also a herb called 'Adani' in the language of the Gemara (35a), which is a type of rose whose leaves incline towards the sun. In the morning, they incline to the east; at noon, they stand upright; and in the evening, they bend greatly to the west (Rashi there). And in our large cities where it is not customary to raise roosters, and it is a cloudy day, certainly he or his neighbor has a clock, which is very common these days, and calendars are also in everyone's possession. They should ensure that the clock is not delayed, and half an hour before the time on the calendar, they should light the candles, not later.

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote in Section 2: "If one wishes to accept the Sabbath early, from the time of 'Pelag Hamincha' and onwards, he is permitted to do so." And it was explained that he adds to the opinion of Rabbi Yosef Karo (Beit Yosef) three parts of an hour, which is three minutes in an hour. According to Rabbi Yosef Karo, four mil (a measure of time) are seventy-two minutes, and 'Pelag Hamincha' is one and a quarter hours before nightfall, which is seventy-five minutes. (Magen Avraham, section 10) These things are perplexing, as three minutes are added, and besides this, what does it add to the words of Rabbi Yosef Karo who wrote this same law in Section 267, Paragraph 2? However, the true intention of Rabbi Moshe Isserles is that many calculate the time of 'Pelag Hamincha' as one and a quarter hours before sunset, and indeed this is the clarified method as the Levush wrote in Section 267, and the Vilna Gaon in Section 459. All calculations of the day are not from dawn until the appearance of the stars, but from sunrise until sunset. If so, there is an addition to the words of Rabbi Yosef Karo by one and a quarter hours, and this is the main ruling in law. (And even according to the Magen Avraham, who calculates from dawn until the appearance of the stars, it also fits well, as Rabbi Yosef Karo follows the opinion of Rabbi Tam. But according to Maimonides, who holds that three-quarters of a mil after sunset is 'Pelag Hamincha,' it is one and a half mil before sunset. If so, there is also a significant addition, and this should be carefully considered.)

The sages taught in a Mishnah: (34:): If there is doubt whether it is dark or not, that is, during twilight - one does not tithe definite produce, meaning produce that is definitely untithed, because one is rectifying on Shabbat. And even though it is generally a rabbinic prohibition - he holds that they decreed on rabbinic prohibitions during twilight (Rashi). And even according to the opinion that we hold 'that anything that is a rabbinic prohibition - they did not decree on it during twilight', as stated in Siman 307 - this is for a mitzvah or if there is a significant need. Therefore, if one truly has nothing to eat on Shabbat - it is permitted to separate during twilight as stated there. But otherwise - it is forbidden even to tithe rabbinically obligated produce. And similarly, it is forbidden to separate challah during twilight, and in this case, it is not permitted even if there is a need to eat, because we hold that challah outside the Land of Israel - one eats and continues and then separates, and in the Land of Israel it is permitted. And similarly, if Shabbat falls on the eve of Passover and one forgot to separate - one separates during twilight, for it is impossible to leave a part until after Shabbat due to chametz.

And similarly, one may not immerse vessels, whether to elevate them from impurity to purity, which is not practiced nowadays, or for the immersion of new vessels, as all of these are considered as fixing (something). However, if one does not have vessels with which to eat on Shabbat, it is permitted to immerse them during twilight, for they did not decree (against it) in a case of great need during twilight, as it is stated. There is an opinion that does not permit this, because one can give them as a gift to a non-Jew, who does not need immersion. (Taz, Section 1). And I am astonished by this, for is giving a gift on Shabbat permitted when it is not for the sake of a mitzvah? Surely it is forbidden (Magen Avraham, Section 306, Subsection 15), so what is the difference between this and that? Furthermore, as explained in Section 323, this ordinance applies to Shabbat itself, but during twilight, it is better to immerse them oneself and recite a blessing. There is also an opinion that says that metal vessels, which require immersion by Torah law, may not be immersed during twilight (Shulchan Aruch, Section 56). The decisors did not make such a distinction, and there is no reason for this if one needs the vessel to use on Shabbat.

And it is all the more so forbidden to light candles during twilight—it is prohibited in every case, as it is potentially punishable by stoning. However, if one does not have a candle, it is permissible to instruct a non-Jew to light a candle for him during twilight for the reasons explained. Similarly, it is permissible to instruct [the non-Jew] to perform any labor that is for the sake of a mitzvah or if one is preoccupied and hurried about it, for in any case of significant need or substantial loss, the rabbinic prohibition of instructing a non-Jew is permitted. Likewise, to light a Yahrzeit candle, it is permissible to instruct a non-Jew to light it during twilight, since people consider this to be a mitzvah. However, for entirely mundane purposes, it is prohibited even if one is distressed about it, unless there is a substantial loss involved. (Magen Avraham, section 6, in the name of the Rashal)

But it is permitted during twilight to tithe demai, because this is not a complete correction, as most of the common people do tithe, and for several matters, demai was permitted without separation. And one may establish an eruv for courtyards during twilight, as there is no prohibition in this and it is a matter of a mitzvah, but not an eruv for boundaries, as this is like acquiring a domain and is forbidden. Nevertheless, if one made an eruv, the eruv is valid, as we will say later in Siman 415. And one may insulate hot food during twilight with something that does not add heat, and this is in a post facto situation. But ideally, one should instruct their household to insulate before twilight, as we mentioned in the previous Siman. And know that everything forbidden during twilight is also forbidden in a case of doubt regarding twilight. (There in subsection 1) This is not considered a double doubt for several reasons: Firstly, a doubt due to lack of knowledge is not included among doubts, and furthermore, it is all one doubt – whether it is day or night, and there are additional reasons. And everything that is forbidden on Friday twilight is also forbidden on Saturday night twilight. (And some say that this is the ‘doubt as to whether it is dark’ mentioned in the Mishnah – a doubt as to darkness on Friday evening, a doubt as to not darkness on Saturday night, and consider this well.)

Our teacher, the Rema, wrote in Section 1: "Similarly, one who accepts Shabbat an hour or two before nightfall can instruct [someone else] to light the candle and do other necessary things." And although accepting Shabbat before "Plag HaMincha" (the time for the afternoon prayer) is not effective, as mentioned later, nevertheless, two hours before nightfall is calculated from "Plag HaMincha," according to the opinion we brought that "Plag HaMincha" is an hour and a quarter before sunset and an hour after sunset, which totals two complete hours. And as mentioned there, in previous generations, they would accept Shabbat about two hours before nightfall. 

The reason he can instruct to light the candle, as mentioned at the end of Section 263, is that since, if he wished, he would not yet accept Shabbat. The general rule is that whenever there is a permissible way, it is allowed to instruct, as mentioned in Section 307. If most of the city has accepted Shabbat, the individual becomes secondary to them, even if he has not yet accepted Shabbat. However, it is still permitted to instruct a non-Jew because there are places where Shabbat has not yet been accepted. It suffices that we do not perform the action ourselves, and in such cases, the Sages did not decree against instructing a non-Jew. Therefore, approximately half an hour before sunset, when Shabbat is certainly accepted everywhere, it is prohibited to instruct a non-Jew. However, for the sake of a mitzvah, it is permitted. And in Section 263, it will be explained that if one comes to a city and the residents have accepted Shabbat, he too is prohibited from performing work on the eve of Shabbat. (All this I learned from the words of the Magen Avraham in Subsection 7, see there.)

Our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 4: "After the response of 'Barechu,' even though it is still daytime, one should not make an Eruv or insulate (food), because they have accepted Shabbat upon themselves. For us, the recitation of 'Mizmor Shir L'Yom HaShabbat' is equivalent to their response of 'Barechu.'" According to this, for us who say 'Lecha Dodi,' this is considered Kabbalat Shabbat. And even though later in section 293, subsection 2, our master the Beit Yosef brings two opinions on whether it is permitted to make an Eruv during twilight when one has accepted the addition of Shabbat, why did he rule here simply to prohibit it? It can be said that there he is referring to an individual who accepted the addition of Shabbat, but here he is referring to the community, and therefore it is more stringent, even during twilight. There are those who explain that there he is referring to accepting the addition of Shabbat, while here it is the acceptance of the actual sanctity of Shabbat. (Dagul Mervavah) I do not understand this reasoning, because necessarily, before nightfall, it is considered an addition. Therefore, it seems to me that the primary explanation is as I have written. However, regarding instructing a non-Jew for the sake of a mitzvah, it is permitted just as during twilight. (Magen Avraham, subsection 7, and see what I wrote in subsection 13, and for us, it is considered acceptance, and scrutinize this).

Rashi, of blessed memory, wrote in Shabbat (34b, s.v. "Lemai") that one who performs labor during twilight (bein hashmashot) is liable for a provisional guilt offering (asham talui). And at the beginning of the chapter "Suffers Doubt" it is taught: "If it is Shabbat and a weekday, and one performs labor on one of them but does not know on which, he brings a provisional guilt offering," and it can be said that twilight is similar to this case. The Tosafot wrote there that on Saturday night during twilight one is liable for a provisional guilt offering, even according to the opinion that requires a specific piece from two pieces where the prohibition is established, because here the prohibition is established for the entire day of Shabbat. However, on Friday evening during twilight, it is not called an established prohibition.

It is stated in Shabbat (119b): "Two ministering angels accompany a person on the eve of Shabbat from the synagogue to his home, one good and one bad. When he arrives home and finds the lamp lit, the table set, and the bed made (as they used to sit on the beds) - the good angel says: May it be God's will that it be like this for another Shabbat, and the bad angel answers 'Amen' against his will. But if not - the bad angel says: May it be God's will that it be like this for another Shabbat, and the good angel answers 'Amen' against his will." Therefore, one must be very careful to arrange the table, and the lamps should be lit, and the beds should be made and prepared for sitting, and among us, the chairs are prepared for sitting. Nevertheless, the beds in the rooms should also be made with respect, as if an important guest is coming. The house should be swept during the day, and also the preparation of the tables, beds, and chairs - everything should be ready during the day, and the dishes, spoons, and knives should be clean and polished in honor of the Holy Shabbat. All aspects of the house should be prepared, and spider webs should be cleared from the walls and ceilings in honor of Shabbat. Everything should be done during the day so that upon returning from the synagogue, everything is found to be beautiful and orderly.

All the tables in the house should be covered with cloths, and the cloths should remain on the tables all night and all day until the end of Shabbat. It is considered a great dishonor to Shabbat when the table is uncovered. The Maharshal would place two cloths on the table where he ate, in addition to the cloth spread over the bread, so that when the cloth on which they ate was removed to shake off the crumbs, the table would not be exposed. (Magen Avraham, subsection 1) This practice has spread throughout all the communities of Israel, that cloths should be on the tables all Shabbat day and all Yom Tov day. (And the Ari HaKadosh was particular to eat specifically on a table with four legs, resembling the table in the Temple, and to bless over two bundles of myrtle. On Friday night, he would place on the table until the next day the cup used for Birkat Hamazon with a little wine in it, and also crumbs on the table, but not whole bread, as it is written in Yoreh De'ah, section 179. Regarding what the Magen Avraham wrote about throwing something outside the table, see there; we are not aware of this. And the house is to be swept with something permissible, as it is written in section 337, see there.)

And one should strive to have nice clothes for Shabbat, as it is written: "and honor it" [Isaiah 58:13], and we expound (Shabbat 113a) that your Shabbat clothing should not be the same as your weekday clothing. And regarding what we say (Shabbat 119a): "And [call] the Holy of the Lord honorable - this refers to Yom Kippur, when there is neither eating nor drinking; the Torah says to honor it with clean clothes" - this refers to expensive and beautiful clothes, like we are accustomed to wearing a white garment on Yom Kippur. But to change clothes - also on Shabbat one must change from weekday clothes, though they do not need to be expensive clothes. And if it is not possible for him to change his clothes, it is said there that he should let them hang low, and this refers to the clothes of their times, and for us, this doesn't apply. And it is good to change all clothes in honor of Shabbat, even the undergarment (Magen Avraham), and to wear Shabbat clothes until after Havdalah (ibid.).

And women also customarily wash their faces and hands and wear Sabbath clothes before lighting the candles. However, they should be cautious because perhaps the sun will set, and they will light the candles, and afterward, they will wash and wear Sabbath clothes, especially in the winter days. And if they do not comply, the husband should light the candles because women are less discerning and do not distinguish between the enhancement of a mitzvah and a complete prohibition. And know that what our master the Rema wrote in paragraph 3: "That one should wear Sabbath clothes immediately after washing, and this is the honor of the Sabbath, and therefore one should not wash for the Sabbath except close to the evening so that one can immediately wear Sabbath clothes [end quote]" – this applies to washing one's face and hands at home. But going to the bathhouse – God forbid to go close to the evening, as it says in Siman 260 at the end of paragraph 6, because this can lead to the desecration of the Sabbath, God forbid, and many are mistaken in this as it says there, and they should be admonished and prevented from doing so. (And this is also written in the Mishnah Berurah)

He should wear Shabbat clothes and rejoice in the coming of Shabbat as if going out to greet a king, or going out to greet a bride and groom. As it is stated in the Gemara: "Rabbi Chanina would wrap himself and stand on the eve of Shabbat. He said: 'Come, let us go out to greet Shabbat the Queen!' Rabbi Yannai would put on his garments on the eve of Shabbat and say: 'Come, O bride! Come, O bride!'" And now we recite psalms and "Lecha Dodi" in honor of her, and in the last stanza, we stand and turn our faces towards the entrance and say: "Enter in peace… Come, O bride! Come, O bride!" Some would go out to the field to welcome Shabbat, and some to the courtyard of the synagogue, but we are not accustomed to this.
