The Tur wrote: One should increase in meat, wine, and delicacies according to his ability, and whoever increases in honoring it, whether in his person, his clothing, or in eating and drinking – this is praiseworthy. (And it is explicitly implied in Gittin 52 that Satan strives to cause discord in the home when Shabbat is being brought in, therefore one must be very careful about this) (See Shabbat 113 and 119, and Rambam Chapter 30, and this requires further examination).

Maimonides writes at the beginning of Chapter 5: "Lighting the Shabbat candle is not optional, where if one wants he lights and if he does not want he does not light, nor is it a commandment, where one must pursue it... rather, it is an obligation. Both men and women are required to have a lit candle in their homes on Shabbat. Even if one does not have what to eat, he must beg at the doors and take oil to light the candle, for this is part of the delight of Shabbat. And one must bless before lighting: 'Blessed are You, Lord our God, King of the Universe, who has sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us to light the Shabbat candle,' just as one blesses over all things that are obligatory by rabbinic decree." These are his words. And even though we do not bless over all aspects of the delight of Shabbat, the lighting of the candle was an independent enactment, as we say (25b): "Lighting the Shabbat candle is an obligation," and Rashi explains the reason, that it is an honor of Shabbat, as a meal is not considered significant except in a place with light similar to daytime. These are his words. And according to Rashi, this is not part of the delight of Shabbat, but rather it is part of the honor of Shabbat.

And the Rambam himself in Chapter 30 considers the lighting of the candle as an honor for Shabbat, as he wrote there: "There should be a lit candle, a set table, and a made bed, for all these are for the honor of Shabbat." Thus, it is necessary to say that both aspects are present: in the place where one eats, it is for the honor of Shabbat, and in other rooms, it is for the delight of Shabbat, so that one does not stumble while walking there. And this is what they said there: "And you have cast off my soul from peace – this is the lighting of the Shabbat candle," for when there is a candle, there is peace, and people do not stumble and fall. Therefore, since it encompasses both honor and delight, the Sages were stringent about it and made it a distinct mitzvah, to the extent that a blessing is recited over it specifically. Moreover, since according to the view of Baal Halachot Gedolot, which will be explained, this act constitutes the acceptance of Shabbat for the woman who lights the candle – it is certainly appropriate to recite a blessing over it. (And in Hagahot Maimoniot, section 1, and in the Mordechai, they brought this blessing from the Jerusalem Talmud, Chapter 4 of Beitzah and Chapter "HaRo'eh", that one blesses: "Who has sanctified us… to light a candle in honor of Shabbat," but I have not found this in the Jerusalem Talmud. Refer to Tosafot on Shabbat 25b, where it is stated that in the place of eating it is called delight. And his words are perplexing, and they are against the words of Rashi and the Rambam in Chapter 30 that we have brought, and also from the language of the Rambam here, where he wrote: "Even if he has nothing to eat," it is evident that this is not so. Examine this carefully.)

And one should not infer from Rashi's words that if one does not eat in this room, one should not recite a blessing on this lighting, for Rashi himself wrote there on the exposition of "and You have disdained my soul's peace" — this refers to lighting a lamp on Shabbat. And Rashi explained that in a place where there is no lamp, there is no peace, for one stumbles and walks in darkness, end quote. And this is considered enjoyment. Thus, even Rashi did not attribute the reason solely to eating, and this is as I wrote that both reasons are required. Furthermore, there is evidence from Rabbeinu Meshulam, who raised the question of how we can bless over the lighting of a Shabbat lamp, when we say in Menachot (42b) that any commandment whose performance is not the completion of the commandment, we do not recite a blessing over it. Here, the completion of the commandment is at the time of eating. And Rabbi Yitzchak of the Tosafists answered him that here too it is the completion of the commandment, for one sees by it to serve the house and to place utensils on the table (as brought in the Korban Netanel on the Rosh, chapter 2, note 33). Hence, the commandment is also for the use of the house.

Therefore, it seems to my humble opinion that a woman who recites the blessing, if she can do so in the place where they are eating, it is certainly better. However, if another woman is reciting the blessing in the place where they are eating, she can also recite the blessing in a room where they are not eating. Similarly, a guest in an inn who has a private room can recite the blessing there even if he eats in another place. And this is what our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in paragraph 9: "Those who light in the corner of the house and eat in the courtyard, if the candles are not long enough to burn until nightfall, it is a blessing in vain" - end quote. It implies that the concern is when they eat in the courtyard. But if they eat in the house, we do not have this issue, and at first glance, it is not understood what the difference is between the two cases. According to what we have explained, it makes sense, because when they eat in the house, even though it is not yet completely night, it is still in honor of Shabbat to have light during the meal. But when they eat in the courtyard and the candle is only for the sake of pleasure and household peace so that they do not stumble, this applies only at night and not before nightfall, even if the daylight has diminished. Therefore, if that place was indeed somewhat dark, in a manner that the candle would be useful even before nightfall, he has fulfilled his obligation. (See Magen Avraham, section 17, and there in section 16, and this is as mentioned, and examine it well).

The Shabbat candle is like the Chanukah candle, in that it is a mitzvah and an obligation for each person to light it, meaning that every family is obligated to light the candle. Therefore, a man in his home, when his wife lights and blesses, even if he has a separate room—he does not need to light with a blessing, for his wife blesses on his behalf, and her blessing includes all the candles in all the rooms. However, he needs to light so that he does not stumble in his walk. And if he is on the road in an inn: if he has a separate room—he needs to light and bless, for the blessing in his home does not exempt the candle in a completely different place. And if he does not have a separate room—he does not need to light or bless, for the mitzvah of Shabbat candle lighting is fulfilled in his home by his wife. And if he does not have a wife and he is in an inn, like young men who go to study away from their home, or if his wife has died—they need to light a Shabbat candle in their room and bless over it, even if they have parents in another place who light, since he is an adult, he is like the head of a household on his own, and the mitzvah of the Shabbat candle applies to him. This is not similar to when he is in his father and mother’s house, where he is included in the family. And if such a man does not have a separate room—he needs to participate with coins with the head of the household where he stays, and thus fulfill his obligation, and I am puzzled that this is not the custom. And over the synagogue candles, one should not bless, for they are made only for the honor of the synagogue, not to provide light. (Magen Avraham, section 16)

Our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 8: "Two or three householders eating in one place: some say that each one should bless on his own candelabrum, and some hesitate on this matter. It is proper to be cautious in matters of blessings, and only one should bless." The Rema wrote: "But we do not practice this way." The explanation seems to me that if they come to light at the same time, all agree that all can light and bless, like all commandments incumbent on every Jew, and like the Chanukah light. However, if one blessed earlier and then another comes to light, the second opinion holds that perhaps this constitutes a blessing in vain, for here the obligation did not fall on the second person, since the primary commandment is for the light, and here there is already light. And although the commandment is incumbent upon him—in any case, he cannot fulfill this commandment here. The first opinion holds that he also fulfills this commandment, because with the increase of lights, the light is increased, and the more light there is, it adds to the commandment of peace in the home and greater joy. And we hold according to this opinion, and our master, the Beit Yosef, was concerned for the second opinion. However, even according to the first opinion, two should not bless on one candelabrum that has many branches. (There, in the name of the Shelah) The reason is that in one candelabrum, only a little light is added, unlike when each one lights on his own candelabrum. (And what the Magen Avraham wrote there concerning women on the night of immersion who light in the synagogue—this is not our custom, and our custom is that they bathe in the morning and prepare for immersion, and in the evening after lighting the candles, they go to the mikveh.)

This mitzvah is especially incumbent upon women, as it is taught (Shabbat 31b): "For three transgressions... for not being careful with niddah, challah, and lighting the candle." The reason, as written by the Rambam there, is because they are usually at home and engaged in household affairs. In the Midrash, it says that because Adam HaRishon was the light of the world, as it is written: "The soul of man is the candle of the Lord," and she caused him to stumble with the tree of knowledge and extinguished the light of the world, therefore her mitzvah is the Shabbat candle to atone for the light she extinguished. Even if the husband wants to light, she can object, and even if she is a niddah, she can still recite the blessing as we mentioned above in Siman 88, except for a woman who has given birth during the first Shabbat, as she is presumably not clean - the husband should recite the blessing. Jewish daughters customarily recite the blessing each on her own even when they are with their mother, even if the husband does not recite and relies on his wife's blessing, as mentioned in section 5, because the obligation is only on the family as stated there. Nevertheless, the daughters, because they are commanded more as explained - each one recites the blessing, and it is good for each one to bless in a separate room. However, in any case - two should not bless on one candelabrum as stated.

If one cannot afford to buy a candle for Shabbat and wine for Kiddush, the Shabbat candle takes precedence, because it is for the sake of peace in the home, and Kiddush can be made over bread. Similarly, if one cannot afford to buy a candle for Shabbat and a candle for Chanukah, the Shabbat candle comes first for the sake of peace in the home, for there is no peace in the home without a candle. One cannot fulfill both with a single candle for both Shabbat and Chanukah, because the Shabbat candle is meant to be used for its light, while the Chanukah candle is forbidden to be used for its light, as will be explained later in section 673. If one has only one candle for Shabbat, that suffices, and the remainder can be used to buy wine for Kiddush or a Chanukah candle. However, bread takes precedence over a candle, for eating takes precedence over everything. Nevertheless, if one has bread, the Shabbat candle takes precedence over other foods. (Magen Avraham, comment 4) And this is what Maimonides wrote: "Even if one does not have food to eat, he should beg at the doors and buy oil to light the candle," as stated in section 1. The intention is not that this takes precedence over bread. Rather, the explanation is: even if one does not have food to eat and is compelled to buy bread with the small amount of money he has, nevertheless, he should ask, etc. (there, and with this, the proof we brought at the end of section 2 is resolved).

There are those who say that a blind person should recite the blessing to light the Shabbat candles, and it is an a fortiori argument from the Chanukah candles, for which a blind person is obligated, as stated at the end of Siman 675. However, this is not comparable at all, because regarding the Chanukah candles, the lighting is the mitzvah, and using the light is forbidden, so both the sighted and the blind are equal. This is not the case with Shabbat, where the primary purpose is to use the light for eating and other activities, and for a blind person, this is of no benefit at all, so how can they recite a blessing? This is also not comparable to what is stated in Siman 69, that a blind person recites the blessing 'Yotzer HaMe'orot' (Who creates the lights), because that blessing is for the light of the world, for otherwise people could not walk in the streets and marketplaces due to pits and thorns, as stated in Megillah 24b. Therefore, even for a blind person, there is a benefit, as others can see them and help them avoid stumbling. But in a house, there are not so many obstacles, and every blind person is familiar with their own home. Therefore, it seems to me, in my humble opinion, that a blind person should not recite the blessing, and there is proof from the Havdalah in Siman 298.

In regard to the Hanukkah candle, it is established for us later in Siman 675 that the lighting constitutes the mitzvah. If it was already lit and standing not for the sake of the mitzvah of Hanukkah, one must extinguish it and relight it for the sake of Hanukkah. Additionally, it must be lit in the place where it is required to stand, and not lit in one place and then brought to its proper location. This applies on Shabbat as well (Tosafot 25b, end of s.v. "Chovah"). Therefore, the Sages said one should not light much earlier before Shabbat, in such a way that it is not evident at all that it is being done in honor of Shabbat. However, one should also not delay lighting until a short time before sunset, for then, God forbid, one might come to the doubt of violating the prohibition of stoning. When do we say not to rush to light much earlier? When one does not wish at that moment to accept the additional sanctity of Shabbat. But if one wishes to accept the additional sanctity of Shabbat, one may light even while it is still significantly daytime, for since one immediately accepts Shabbat, it is not considered early. In any case, one should ensure that it is after the time of "Pelag HaMincha" and before sunset, which is one and a quarter hours when the days and nights are equal. The main thing is to be cautious not to delay, God forbid, and enter the doubt of twilight. Fortunate are those who light early.

It is stated in the Gemara (23b): "Rav Huna said: One who is accustomed to lighting the Shabbat candle will have children who are Torah scholars, as it is written: 'For the commandment is a lamp and the Torah is light.' Through the commandment lamp of Shabbat and Chanukah, the light of Torah comes." (Rashi s.v. 'children') Therefore, one should be careful to make a beautiful candle, and some are particular to make two wicks: one corresponding to 'Remember' and one to 'Keep.' Some even make the candles intertwined, because 'Remember' and 'Keep' were said in one utterance. But our custom is not like this. We light each candle separately, and one can light three or four candles or more, as is the custom. Some light seven candles and some ten. (Shelah) It is written that if a woman forgets once to light the Shabbat candle, she should add an additional candle permanently to what she was accustomed to lighting until now. If she forgets twice, she should add two candles. This is so that she will penalize herself and be more careful in the future. Therefore, if she was forced and could not light, she is exempt. (And what the Rema wrote that if she forgets, she lights three, his intention is when she initially lit two, as he is referring to the words of the Mechaber to make two wicks.)

Just as on Shabbat we are commanded to light candles, so too on Yom Tov, for it is obvious that Yom Tov is a time of joy, and there is no joy without light. Therefore, one must recite the blessing: "Blessed are You, Hashem, our God, King of the Universe, who has sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us to light the Yom Tov candle." The Mordechai, the Agudah, and the Hagahot Maimoniot brought this from the Jerusalem Talmud, but I did not find this in the Jerusalem Talmud before us. Our women also recite the "Shehecheyanu" blessing when lighting the candles on Yom Tov, and one should not protest against them, for most of the time on the eve of Yom Tov, they light in the evening itself, and the "Shehecheyanu" applies to Yom Tov. Some are uncertain about this, but let the daughters of Israel continue their practice. On Yom Kippur, some bless and some do not bless; our custom is to bless, and this will be explained in Siman 620.

It is well known that all blessings must be recited prior to performing the associated mitzvah (commandment). Accordingly, one should recite the blessing before lighting the candles. Nevertheless, the custom is to recite the blessing after lighting. The reason for this is that lighting the candles is considered an acceptance of the additional sanctity of Shabbat, and the primary acceptance happens with the blessing, as will be explained. Therefore, if one were to recite the blessing and accept Shabbat, how could she then be permitted to light? Even though it is possible to recite the blessing and intend not to accept Shabbat, women are generally not accustomed to this and their understanding is limited in this regard. Additionally, there is an opinion that such a condition is not effective, as will be explained. Therefore, they light all the candles and then recite the blessing. To ensure that this is considered "prior to the performance," they cover their eyes with their hands after lighting, so they do not benefit from the light, recite the blessing, and then uncover their eyes. This is considered as "prior to the performance." 

However, on a Yom Tov (festival), when lighting is permitted, one should recite the blessing beforehand to ensure that it is truly "prior to the performance." (Derisha) There is an opinion that disagrees with this due to the principle of "we do not differentiate" (not making distinctions). (Magen Avraham, section 12) Many disagree with this opinion, arguing that Shabbat and Yom Tov are two different matters, and this is the primary ruling. (Nevertheless, when a man recites the blessing on Erev Shabbat, he should do so before lighting and intend not to accept Shabbat. It is also written that a woman should pray at the time of lighting that the Holy One, Blessed be He, grants her children who are enlightened in Torah. What the Magen Avraham writes in section 11 regarding a wedding canopy - he himself later disagreed with this, and the best practice when the wedding canopy is delayed is to light the candles first and then proceed with the wedding canopy, and we once did so.)

The Ba'al Halachot Gedolot (BaHaG) wrote that the acceptance of Shabbat is dependent on the lighting of the candle, for once the Shabbat candle is lit, Shabbat has commenced. His reasoning is that we have observed that the custom of the sages was that the last task on Friday afternoon was the lighting of the candle, and certainly, the enactment was that no further work should be done after this. This is because the lighting is a mitzvah task for the sake of Shabbat and is obligatory. Therefore, it is considered as the beginning of rest and its acceptance. One who lights the candle has already resolved in their mind not to do any further work after lighting, and there is no greater acceptance of Shabbat than this. (Ran, Chapter 2) When lighting many candles, the intention is until all the candles are finished being lit. Based on this, Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote in paragraph 10 that for this reason, some women have the custom that after lighting the candles with a blessing, they throw down the wick they used to light and do not extinguish it. It appears that these women bless before lighting, for if they were blessing afterward, they could still extinguish the match before the blessing. It is certain that before the blessing, the acceptance of Shabbat has not yet occurred. Accordingly, our women who bless after lighting, as mentioned in the previous paragraph, can indeed extinguish the match and then bless, and it seems to me that this is the custom and there is no concern about it.

And he further wrote: There are those who say that if she makes a condition before lighting [the candles] that she does not accept Shabbat until the chazzan (precentor) says "Barechu," it is effective. And there are those who say it is not effective for her. And there are those who disagree with the Ba'al Halachot Gedolot (BaHaG) and say that the acceptance of Shabbat is not dependent on the lighting of the candle but on the evening prayer, for once the chazzan says "Barechu," everyone ceases from their work. For us, once they begin "A Psalm, a Song for the Sabbath day," it is like "Barechu" for them. And for us, "Lecha Dodi" is the acceptance of Shabbat, as is written at the end of Siman 261. And Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote about this: The custom is that the woman who lights accepts Shabbat with the lighting, unless she made a condition beforehand, and even a condition in her heart is sufficient. But the other members of the household are permitted to do work until "Barechu." And the primary lighting is dependent on the candle on the table and not on the other candles in the house. And one must place the candles where they are lit, and not light them in one place and then move them to another place. Their words need further explanation.

And it appears to me that this is its explanation: According to the BeHaG (Ba'al Halachot Gedolot), the lighting of the candles constitutes the acceptance of Shabbat for all members of the household, for the reason explained in section 14. Just as the recitation of "A Psalm, a Song for the Sabbath Day" serves as an acceptance for everyone when the majority of the city recites it, as will be explained, similarly, the Sages established that in every household where candles are lit, this constitutes the acceptance of Shabbat for all its members. However, a stipulation is effective, and why should it not be effective, since she explicitly intends not to accept Shabbat with this lighting. Nevertheless, some say that a stipulation is not effective. The reason is because there is a blessing involved, and the blessing necessarily brings them into the sanctity of Shabbat, since it mentions "to light the Shabbat candle," and if not, it would be a blessing in vain (see Beit Yosef in the name of the Kol Bo). Another reason appears to me: since according to the BeHaG, it was the enactment of the Sages that the candle lighting be the last act, so that this would serve as the acceptance of Shabbat, an individual cannot exempt themselves from this through a stipulation. And all this is according to the opinion of the BeHaG.

Indeed, the Tur, citing the Tosafot and Ramban, disagrees with the Ba'al Halachot Gedolot (BHG) on this fundamental issue. They hold that the lighting of the Shabbat candle was never connected to the acceptance of Shabbat. We also find that after the lighting of the candle, people would still insulate hot food and remove tefillin. (See Shabbat 35b for Rabbeinu Nissim's explanation, and there he quotes the Ramban who states that even the roasting of fish took place afterward, and see there in Tosafot.) According to this opinion, the lighting of the candle was just one of the many preparations for Shabbat. Therefore, even those who believe in the Talmud that it was the last act of labor do not see it as a sign of accepting Shabbat. And as for the blessing, what of it? The blessing is on the ordinance established to light the Shabbat candle, and it has no connection to the acceptance of Shabbat.

The custom that our teacher, the Rema, wrote about is a kind of compromise between the opinions. Certainly, for all the members of the household, lighting the candle is not related to accepting Shabbat. However, for the one who lights, since she blesses and mentions Shabbat, it is assumed that she has accepted the addition of Shabbat, unless she explicitly stipulates otherwise, and even a mental stipulation is sufficient. The primary candles are those on the table, for although there is an obligation to light all the candles, even in rooms where one does not eat, as we have mentioned, nevertheless, the main ones are those candles on the table where the Shabbat meal is eaten, for they honor the Shabbat, as we have mentioned. And what he wrote about not lighting in one place and placing them in another place – we have already explained this in section 10, that it is like the Chanukah candle which needs to be lit in its place. And what is called its 'place' – the place where one intends the candle to stand during the night. It seems that in one room, from one place to another, this is not considered changing its place. However, the place where one eats is the main place, and one should specifically bless in the name of those candles that will stand during the meal. (See Magen Avraham section 23, and I have written what seems to me in my humble opinion, and delve into it) And there is no question of how to move the candles after lighting, for one can say that another person will move them, or she herself can move them by making a stipulation beforehand. (See Magen Avraham section 22)

Even though a condition works for lighting according to most authorities, and even according to Bahag, who holds that lighting constitutes acceptance of Shabbat as explained – nevertheless, a condition does not work for prayer. For example, if an individual prays the Shabbat prayer while it is still daytime, even though the congregation has not yet prayed – in any case, Shabbat is accepted upon him, and from that moment he is forbidden to perform labor, even if he says he does not want to accept Shabbat. For since he has prayed the evening service of Shabbat and blessed 'Who sanctifies the Shabbat', he has unwillingly accepted Shabbat, and it is as if one would say at night: 'I do not want to accept Shabbat'. It seems to me that in such cases, even if it was before Plag HaMincha – he has unwillingly accepted Shabbat. And even though it is explained in Siman 261 and also in Siman 267 that one should not add [to Shabbat] before Plag HaMincha, see there, and certainly, initially, one should not do so, but if one did so, who can protest against him, for do we have a measure for the addition [to Shabbat] that we can say that before this time it does not work? And I have seen that someone wrote that this is specifically from Plag HaMincha, (see Mishna Berura) and these are astonishing words. But with the recitation of 'Mizmor Shir LeYom HaShabbat' or 'Lecha Dodi' – it is generally considered acceptance of Shabbat. But if he explicitly says that he does not want to accept Shabbat – it works, for there is no prayer or blessing in vain. And similarly, if he said this before Plag HaMincha – it is possible that it is not an acceptance. (According to the Magen Avraham in Siman 161:10 in the name of the Rivash) But in prayer – it is obvious that it is an acceptance. And we also find that the early authorities would pray the evening service up to three hours before night, and they accepted Shabbat upon themselves. (See Terumat HaDeshen Siman 1 and Shevut Yaakov part 2 Siman 20)

If the majority of the congregation in the synagogue have accepted Shabbat upon themselves, meaning they have recited 'Lecha Dodi', and it is after the time of Plag Hamincha - then even the minority who were not in the synagogue are drawn after them and are forbidden to perform work, for the rule is that the minority follows the majority. However, another synagogue is not drawn after this synagogue, and even if the one that has already accepted Shabbat is the larger one in the city - nevertheless, each synagogue is considered a separate community for this matter. Therefore, one who comes to the synagogue while the congregation is accepting Shabbat and reciting 'Lecha Dodi', and he has not yet prayed Mincha - he should not pray Mincha in that synagogue, since the sanctity of Shabbat has already taken effect there. Rather, he should go outside the synagogue to the courtyard or an adjacent room and pray Mincha there, and afterwards, he can enter the synagogue and accept Shabbat. And one should not question how he can pray a weekday prayer, since the sanctity of Shabbat has already taken effect upon him as well, because it can be said that the prohibition of work applies to him stringently, but not leniently to exempt him from the weekday prayer. Therefore, this applies specifically when he has not accepted Shabbat with them, but if he did not pay attention and has not yet prayed Mincha and accepted Shabbat with them – then he himself has accepted Shabbat, and it is forbidden for him to pray a weekday prayer. Instead, he should pray the Shabbat evening prayer twice, as is the rule for one who forgot to pray, as stated in Siman 108.

And this is when [one arrives] during the congregation's recitation of "Lecha Dodi." But if he arrives earlier, even during the recitation of the psalms that precede "Lecha Dodi," which it is customary to say, he may pray Mincha even though he knows his prayer will extend beyond the acceptance of Shabbat, since he began permissibly. There is one who says specifically that he thought he would finish before the acceptance of Shabbat, but if he knows he will not finish, he should not begin. (Taz, section 2) This does not seem correct, for this is not one of the prohibitions that would prevent him from starting to pray, but merely a matter of preference. (This is also implied in Magen Avraham, section 29, and is written by the Eliyah Rabbah, section 37) And this is the primary ruling in practice. However, in such cases, if he wishes, he may leave and pray in another place, but he is not obligated to do so.

According to what has been explained, that the individual follows the majority of his synagogue, it is questionable if, in the case where the synagogue has already accepted Shabbat and he is still at home and prohibited from performing work, whether his household members are also prohibited from performing work. If they have not yet lit candles in his home, they are still forbidden to light, because they follow the head of the household. Alternatively, it might be that only he is prohibited from performing work, but his household members are permitted. This cannot be compared to what was explained in Section 18, where a woman who has lit candles has accepted Shabbat, and all her household members are permitted to perform work, since a woman is not considered the principal figure for her household to follow her. But it is possible that the household members follow the man. The law is uncertain, because perhaps this is considered a "secondary following," where he follows his synagogue and they follow him, and we do not say "secondary following," similar to what is mentioned in Shabbat regarding liability for a sin offering (70a). However, it is certain that if the majority of the city has already accepted Shabbat, then everyone, both men and women, are prohibited from performing work. If they have not lit candles, they should have a non-Jew light them.

Even a guest who comes to the city on Friday evening, when the people of the city have already accepted Shabbat upon themselves by reciting 'Lecha Dodi' – he is immediately forbidden from doing work, even though there is still much daylight left. If he has money or other items that are muktzeh (set aside and not to be moved on Shabbat) – he should not carry them but should go into a room and let them fall by moving them indirectly. This applies if it is after the time of 'plag hamincha' (an hour and a quarter before sunset), and despite this, he is still permitted to pray the weekday Mincha (afternoon prayer), as stated in section 20. There is an incident recorded in the Shibolei Haleket regarding Rabbi Avraham and his brother Rabbi Yaakov who arrived in a city after the congregation had left the synagogue. They were not greeted, nor were they allowed to enter the synagogue the next day. On Sunday, they decreed upon them fifty consecutive days of fasting, and to complete these three days with fasts and lashes. Additionally, they decreed upon them to donate from their money as a redemption for their souls to the charity fund, etc., as it says there. (Beis Yosef)

If the community mistakenly accepted Shabbat, such as when it was a cloudy day, and they thought it was close to night, and they lit candles and prayed the evening prayer of Shabbat, and afterward the clouds dispersed and the sun shone and it was still daytime: if when they prayed it was after the time of "Pelag HaMincha" (one and a quarter hours before sunset) - they do not need to pray the evening prayer again, because we do not burden the community. (Berachot 27b) But if an individual made this mistake - he must pray the evening prayer again. Regarding the performance of labor - whether it is the community or an individual, it is permitted, since the acceptance was made in error. Some say that an acceptance made in error by the community is still considered an acceptance, because since we do not burden them to pray again - consequently their prayer is valid and they are prohibited from performing labor. Therefore, those who lit candles are prohibited from performing labor, but the minority is not drawn after them, and those who did not light or pray are permitted. (This seems to me to be the explanation of the first opinion mentioned in paragraph 14, as explained by the Magen Avraham in section 26. The words of the Taz in section 1 are not clear, and study them carefully.)

In regard to the mistake that has been clarified, our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote at the end of section 14 that some say that the candle lit for the sake of Shabbat is forbidden to touch and add oil to, and even if it is extinguished, it is forbidden to move it. This is not understood at all, for why should it be forbidden to touch, add oil, or move it if one has not yet accepted Shabbat? He himself was puzzled by this in his larger work. There is an opinion that holds that an acceptance made in error is considered an acceptance, as previously stated, and therefore this candle is set aside for its mitzvah. The prohibition against touching it is a decree lest one come to use it. But there is no reason for this, for from where do we derive such a decree, and why not add oil to it?

In my humble opinion, it seems that this is not related to the prohibition of muktzeh, but rather that even though we maintain that a mistaken consecration is not a consecration, nonetheless, because we do not trouble the public, we say that their acceptance is an acceptance, and consequently, this candle is set aside for its mitzvah. Therefore, it is forbidden to use it for a secular purpose until the conclusion of Shabbat. His intention is that it is forbidden to touch it and add oil for a secular purpose, and even if it is extinguished, it is forbidden to move it for a secular purpose until the conclusion of Shabbat.

Similarly, one who lit candles for Shabbat and stipulated that they are not yet accepting Shabbat, nonetheless, the candles are set aside for their mitzvah and are forbidden to be used for a secular purpose, whether by the person who lit them or by others.

Our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, wrote in Section 17: "There are those who say that if one accepts the Sabbath upon themselves before nightfall, they are permitted to tell another Jew to perform work for them, and they are allowed to benefit from that work on the Sabbath, and certainly after the Sabbath. And someone who delays praying on the night after the Sabbath or extends their meal into the night is permitted to tell another Jew who has already prayed and made Havdalah to perform work for them, to light candles and to cook for them, and it is permitted to benefit and eat from their work." And there are two reasons for this: one is that since it was within their own power to be permitted in this matter, such as on the eve of the Sabbath, if they wanted, they could have not yet accepted the Sabbath, and on the night after the Sabbath, if they wanted, they could have made Havdalah themselves. And as long as it is permitted for them, they can tell their friend, and there is no prohibition of "speaking about work." As it is said in the Talmud (150b): "A person is allowed to tell their friend, 'I am going to such and such a place tomorrow,' if there are huts there, they may go." And as we will explain later in Section 307. Another reason is that we do not find a prohibition of speaking about work except in matters that are forbidden to all Jews. But in matters where it is permitted for the other, such as in these cases, why should they not be able to tell their friend to do something that is permitted to them? (Taz, Subsection 3) And according to the first reason, the night after the Sabbath is less stringent than the eve of the Sabbath, because on the eve of the Sabbath, although they could have not yet accepted the Sabbath, at this moment, they do not have permission. But on the night after the Sabbath, it is within their power at any moment to say 'Havdalah' and be permitted to do work, as it is stated in Section 299. (Magen Avraham, Subsection 31) There are those who want to dispute this ruling, but their words were rejected. (See Taz, Drisha, and Bach who rejected the words of the Levush who disagreed in this matter) And it is clear that if one says 'Havdalah' in the middle of the meal, they are permitted to perform work, but it is questionable whether they will be able to say 'Retzeh' in the Grace After Meals. (Magen Avraham, Subsection 33)

And know that even though it is explained that on Friday afternoon the minority follows the majority when the majority has accepted Shabbat upon themselves, nevertheless on Motzei Shabbat (Saturday night) it is not so. Even if the whole city continues Shabbat late into the night, an individual is still able to pray, perform the Havdalah, and do work. The reason seems to me to be similar to Friday afternoon before the time of Plag HaMincha, where the minority does not follow the majority, as we have said, and the same law applies on Motzei Shabbat when the time of weekday has already arrived, there is no reason for their extension.

There are those who wish to say that according to the first reason mentioned in section 26, where one does not have to accept Shabbat, if someone is in a synagogue where they have already accepted Shabbat, and he also accepted it with them, he is prohibited from asking someone else from the synagogue to perform work for him. This is because, in such cases, the reason of "if he wants, he would not accept" does not apply, as the individual follows the community. (Magen Avraham) However, this does not seem reasonable at all, because as long as there is the possibility of not accepting it, it is permitted. Similarly, if he wishes, he could go to another synagogue. 

There are also those who wish to say that accepting Shabbat early is considered a vow, and one can annul it. (Levush in his gloss) This is a surprising statement, because since we hold according to most authorities that the addition to Shabbat is from the Torah, and there is no defined limit to this addition, then one who makes a large addition is indeed following the Torah law. I have not seen this mentioned in any halachic authority, and therefore, one should not rely on this in practice. 

It is clear that one should not wait for a prominent person in the synagogue if he has not yet arrived, nor for any other reason in the world. (In Magen Avraham's commentary, a mistake fell where it says "close to the synagogue," it should say "close to twilight." And where it says afterward "it is better, etc.," it means there were places where they waited and said it is better, etc. He wrote that this is only in a place where there is permission, meaning when praying in a minyan. But in a synagogue, we do not say it is better that they be inadvertent sinners, etc., and one should protest so they do not wait for someone who has not prepared his food, even if it is not close to twilight, and understand this well.)

During the time of the sages of the Talmud, they did not light candles as we do today with tallow and wax candles. Instead, they would light with oils, making wicks and placing them into the oils, similar to how we light with our kerosene today. The sages said that there are wicks that should not be used for lighting because the flame flickers with them, meaning its light is not steady and fixed in one place; rather, it flares up and dies down (Rashi 21a), or the oil does not enter the wick but surrounds it from the outside (ibid), causing the flame to jump. Similarly, there are oils that should not be used because they do not draw well into the wick, which could lead someone to adjust the lamp on Shabbat (ibid). With wicks that cause the flame to flicker, we are concerned that one might fix the wick on Shabbat (Bach).

And thus the sages taught in the Mishnah (20:): "With what may one light and with what may one not light?" One may not light with "lechesh" – which is a type of cedar that has something like cotton between the wood and the bark, nor with "chusen" – which is uncombed flax that has refuse in it, nor with "kalach" – which is the refuse of silk, nor with the wick of "eidan" – which is a type of willow that has something like cotton between the bark and the wood, nor with the wick of the desert – which is a type of long grass and the fluff inside it is suitable for lighting, nor with the green substance on the surface of the water – which is the green stuff that grows around a ship when it stays in one place on the water. And these are all invalid wicks, and similarly, one should not make wicks from wool or hair. It appears that from all types of wool, whether from sheep, camels, or goats – one may not light. According to Rashi, one may also not light with hemp, which is called "kanapolia," or with cotton, which is called "baoul." Rabbeinu Tam disagreed with him, saying that these wicks are very good, and the practice is according to Rabbeinu Tam. And thus far are the invalid wicks.

From this point onward, certain oils are invalid: neither pitch nor wax, meaning to melt wax and place a wick in it like in oil - this is forbidden, but our wax candles are good for lighting. (Tosafot there) And not castor oil, and there are three interpretations in the Gemara about this, see there. The Rambam in his commentary on the Mishnah wrote: "Vegetable seeds that are oily, and the oil is very thick." The Tur wrote: "Oil made from cotton seeds," and both interpretations are in the Gemara there. There is another interpretation in the Gemara that there is a type of bird called 'kik,' and they put its fat in the lamp, and it burns, see there. This was not mentioned because it is not common at all. (Drisha) And not with 'burnt oil,' which is oil of terumah that became impure and is prohibited for consumption and is only meant for burning. There are two explanations in the Gemara (23b): One is that it refers to every Erev Shabbat, and the prohibition is even though the oil is good and draws after the wick, nevertheless, since there is a commandment to burn it, we are concerned that one might tilt the lamp so it burns faster. The second explanation is that it refers to Erev Shabbat that falls on Yom Tov, and the prohibition is because one does not burn sacred things on Yom Tov. According to the Rambam, it is clear that he understood this, because he did not mention this at all regarding Shabbat, and in Yom Tov, chapter 3, he mentioned this regarding impure challah, see there, and by extension, the same applies to terumah, for they are the same.

One should not use the fat of a tail or suet for lighting, as one does with oil, but our candles made of suet are very good. One should not use pitch, which is a byproduct of tar and initially drips thickly and does not follow the wick, and later drips clearly. Even though it follows the wick, since it has a bad smell, we are concerned that one might leave it and go out. It is an obligation to eat on Shabbat in a place with a candle. (Gemara 25b)

And regarding our practice of lighting with our petroleum, which is called gas, even though it does not have a good smell, it is not considered a bad smell either. Furthermore, when it is enclosed in a candlestick with a glass cover, like our lamps, it does not smell at all, and it is also lit in the homes of the nobility. 

The primary concern of 'lest one leaves it and goes out' is not applicable since many people are accustomed to eating in the courtyard. We can say that the candles are commanded for delight and not for distress, and if one enjoys eating in the courtyard more because of the air or because of the flies in the house, it is certainly permissible to eat in the courtyard. (Bach in the name of the Hagahot Maimoni) However, in any case, there should be no distress from the candles themselves.

One should not light with balsam, which is the resin that drips from trees called "kaf", because it has a very pleasant smell, and we are concerned that one might use it. (Gemara ibid.) And it is taught in the Tosefta: "One who adds oil to a lamp is liable for kindling, and one who uses it is liable for extinguishing." (Rashi)

The Gemara provides another reason for balsam, because it is flammable and can stick to the walls of the house and set the house on fire, and we are concerned that one might become anxious about his property and come to extinguish it. (Tosafot ibid.)

From here, we can learn not to seal the oven with wood for this reason, as it often leads to the desecration of Shabbat. (Magen Avraham, section 9) In our case, we seal the oven because it is large, and the coals are trimmed and far from the cover, so there is no concern.

Our sages said there that the nature of these bad oils is that if you add even a small amount of good oil to them, they will be drawn after the wick. Nevertheless, even in such cases, the sages prohibited it, because if you permit it by mixing in good oil, one might come to light it without mixing, leading to tilting. This is not considered a decree upon a decree, because it is almost certain that one will come to tilt, and moreover, it is all considered one decree, for when they decreed not to light with them, they decreed it for all situations, whether they are used alone or in mixtures. (Taz, subparagraph 4) The main reason is like the first explanation, as our rabbis, the Tosafists, wrote. (23a, s.v. 'decree' and this is his language: when it is not mixed, one will certainly tilt because it does not draw, etc. see there)

One may kindle with fish oil, but not with fish innards that have melted, even though they draw after the wick. However, we decree melted innards because of unmelted ones, and unmelted ones do not draw after the wick. Similarly, cooked and melted fat, even though it also draws after the wick, the Sages prohibited, as we decree because of fat that is not melted, which does not draw. However, if one mixed a bit of good oil with melted fish innards or melted fat, one may kindle with them, and we do not decree because of cases where no oil was added, or where the innards or fat are not melted. This is a decree upon a decree, and we do not issue such decrees. (Talmud, there) But in the previous ruling, it was not a decree upon a decree, for the reasons we explained in the prior section. Moreover, here there are three decrees, and we do not issue so many decrees. (And the Ran required that the melted fat be from the beginning of its extraction from the animal, as noted there, but this is not implied by all the poskim, and this is the intent of the Magen Avraham in section 11, see there.)

The same law applies to invalid wicks: if one wraps something that can be lit around something that cannot be lit, even though the flame does not flicker now, one may not light it, because we decree that one might come to light something that cannot be lit by itself, similar to the decree regarding oils. However, this is only if the intention was for both to be lit. But if the intention was not for both to be lit, but rather that because it was thin, he added something to thicken it, it is permitted even though both are burning, because in this case, there is no concern that he will come to light it by itself, as his intention was not at all to light it. And from Rashi there it appears that if he intended to thicken it, he does not wrap them together, for he does not do this for the thickness but so that the valid wick does not sink in the oil; he places the invalid wick below and supports the valid one on it. And there are those who want to say that according to Rashi, it is forbidden in all cases where both are lit (see Beit Yosef and Taz, subparagraph 2). In my humble opinion, it seems that Rashi would also agree with the Rif who permits it, but he interprets the Gemara with a different intention. (And the wording of the Beit Yosef in section 2, which writes: "And if he intended to harden it… so that it would not sink below," there it begins with the language of the Rif and ends with the language of Rashi. See Tur and Beit Yosef and examine closely.)

Due to the reason explained, it is permitted to wrap something that can be ignited around a reed or straw, in order to place the wick in a lantern, since one does not intend to ignite them. Similarly, it is permitted to place a grain of salt or a split bean on the mouth of the lamp on Friday afternoon so that it will burn well on Shabbat, as this is a remedy to ensure it burns well, and there is no concern about it. Other wicks aside from those we mentioned are permitted to be used, and it appears that cotton wool is the best among them, as its light is clear and it follows the wick well. Similarly, all oils aside from those we mentioned are permitted for lighting, but olive oil is the choicest mitzvah. Other oils are preferable to wax, and wax is preferable to tallow. (Magen Avraham, Section 12) However, in our place, refined tallow is better than wax candles, as we can see clearly. It has already been explained that the prohibition of wax and tallow applies when lighting as oil, but if one wraps wax or tallow around the wick like our candles, it is permitted to light with them, as well as with pitch. If one wraps invalid oil and an invalid wick together, it is forbidden to light with them. (ibid, Section 13) And oil, although it follows the wick very well, the sediment of oil does not follow and is forbidden for lighting on Shabbat. (ibid, Section 7)

All those disqualified for lighting, whether disqualified wicks or disqualified oils, are forbidden both in the candles on the table for eating and in other candles in the house, because all of them are made for light and to benefit from their illumination for various uses. If one lights with forbidden items, it is prohibited to use their light even for activities that do not require scrutiny, because we are concerned about tilting [the lamp]. (Shulchan Aruch 1:1) And even if there is another person with him, it is still forbidden. (Magen Avraham 1:3) This is not similar to what is written in Siman 275 regarding the prohibition of learning by the light of a candle due to the concern that one might tilt it, where it is permitted for two people, because there the concern is that due to the need for scrutiny, one might forget it is Shabbat because of the concentration, and when there are two people, the other will remind him. But here, since the concern is that the lamp does not burn well and one might forget and tilt it, we are concerned even if there are two people, as they might forget due to the lack of light. This is not similar to scrutiny, where it is unlikely that two people would be deeply engrossed in concentration and forget that it is Shabbat.

However, our teacher the Rema wrote in paragraph 1 that some say that if there is one permissible candle, it is allowed to use the light of the others. Similarly, something that can be done without a candle is allowed to be done even near the other candles, and for the sake of Shabbat, it is permissible after the fact. And there are those who explain that the meaning is if there is one permissible candle, it is allowed to use it near the forbidden ones, even if they are in a different room, because since there is one permissible candle, one will remember and not tilt [the forbidden ones] even in other places. And something that can be done without a candle, such as drawing wine from the cellar and the like, is always allowed even without a permissible candle, and it is permissible to be lenient for the sake of Shabbat. And when the forbidden one is next to the permissible one, it is allowed in any case to use them, even if there is not such a great need for Shabbat. (Magen Avraham)

The Levush omits this entirely, and in truth, these are significant leniencies, and there are questions on this from the Talmudic discussion, and most of the poskim (halachic decisors) do not seem to hold this way. Furthermore, it is not logical at all that when there is a valid candle one would also remember the invalid ones, and also what is written 'even by other candles' is completely redundant, for we are dealing with other candles. Therefore, it appears to me that the correct explanation is that when there is a valid candle present in a room where there are invalid candles, it is permitted to use their light, as one will not come to tilt (the candle) because he has good light from the valid one, but in another room, it is forbidden. Afterwards, it says that something that can be done without a candle is permitted to do even when there is no valid candle at all, and so it appears to me in my humble opinion that this is how one should instruct, and not to be overly lenient. (And this is also implied by the words of the Eliyah Rabbah, section 3)

The one who lights the candle needs to light most of the wick that extends from the candle, because otherwise it is likely to be extinguished. Similarly, for a wax or tallow candle, most of the wick at the top of the candle needs to be lit. However, it is not necessary to singe the wick, since we do not follow the opinion that requires singeing, as it will burn well even without it. Nonetheless, the Ba'al HaMaor rules that one should not light with rags, which are worn linen garments, nor with a wick that has not been singed. It must be said that although we rule that singeing is not required, this refers to complete singeing, meaning lighting it well and extinguishing it so that it becomes nearly ash, which then makes it easier to relight. But some singeing is necessary, because without it, it will not burn well. Therefore, one should not light with rags, as they cannot be singed due to their fragility. (Refer to Beit Yosef, and you will understand what compelled me to explain this, and study it well.) Women have the custom to light the wick and then extinguish it, so that it becomes singed and the fire catches well. One should not light on the table with an old clay lamp (Magen Avraham section 216) because it is repugnant. However, if it is coated like porcelain or made of glass, it is not repugnant and it is permissible to light with it.

A festival that falls on the eve of Shabbat - one should not light with a piece of cloth that is exactly three by three fingerbreadths, for anything that measures three fingerbreadths by three fingerbreadths is considered a utensil regarding ritual impurity. And since one has lit it a little, it becomes a broken utensil, and one should not light with broken utensils on a festival, as stated in Siman 501. However, if one prepared it as a wick before the festival, it has already lost its status as a utensil and it is permitted to light with it. (Gemara 28b)

Our teacher, the Beit Yosef (Rabbi Yosef Karo), wrote in section 1: "One may not place a perforated vessel filled with oil above a lamp so that it drips into it, due to a decree lest one take from it and be liable for extinguishing. However, if one attaches it with lime or clay, it is permitted, since it becomes a single vessel, and one refrains from it due to the prohibition of Shabbat." This is derived from a Mishnah in Shabbat (29b): "A person should not pierce an eggshell, fill it with oil, and place it above the lamp so that it drips, even if it is made of earthenware" - because it is repulsive. Nevertheless, we are concerned lest one take from it, because it is in a separate vessel and not within the lamp, it does not appear to people as a prohibited act. The Beit Yosef did not mention 'even if it is made of earthenware,' because since he wrote generally 'vessel,' it includes everything. Only in the Mishnah, where it mentioned the eggshell, one might have said that earthenware is permitted, it comes to teach us that this too is forbidden. They also said there in the Gemara that we do not require a professional connection; rather, even if the homeowner connected it, which is a weak connection, it is still permitted, because once they are a single vessel, one refrains from it.

And there is much to wonder about our teacher, the Beit Yosef, who wrote: "When in doubt, one is liable for extinguishing." What relevance does this have to extinguishing? After all, the oil is in a separate vessel. Indeed, the Rambam in Chapter 5, Halacha 12, and the Tur did not mention that one is liable for extinguishing; rather, it is merely a prohibition. Since it was designated for the lamp, it is forbidden to benefit from it, but there is no liability for extinguishing. And the Tosafot in Beitzah (22a) already wrote that one who benefits from the lamp is liable for extinguishing because he diminishes the light, which is not applicable when the oil is in a separate vessel. However, Rashi in the Mishnah also wrote that one is liable for extinguishing, which requires further investigation. (Additionally, Rashi's language there requires investigation, as he wrote: "And since it was designated for the lamp, one is liable for extinguishing," thus beginning with muktzeh and concluding with extinguishing. And I found that the Pnei Yehoshua addressed this, writing that the Rambam's reasoning is muktzeh.)

And in the Jerusalem Talmud, it gives a completely different reason – because of kindling. This means that even though it is permitted to light a candle on the eve of Shabbat so that it burns all Shabbat, this is only when everything is together. But here, where the oil is separate and drops drop into the candle, there is no connection between this drop and the other, and it turns out that the drop that falls on Shabbat is like one made by hand, or because we decree that perhaps one will pour from the tube into the candle on Shabbat and will be liable for kindling. And according to the Rambam and the Tur, it seems that the prohibition is because of muktzeh, but it is puzzling because of extinguishing. (And the Lechem Mishneh there questions the Rambam why he did not write because of extinguishing, and his question is puzzling.)

And I found someone who wrote that here it could be complete extinguishing, for there is no concern that one might take a little from the tube, but rather that one might take the entire tube while the drops are still descending, and then it would be completely extinguished. (Yam Shel Shlomo, Beitza, Chapter 2, Siman 28). However, the Rosh in Chapter 2 of Beitza (Siman 17) brought a proof from this Mishnah against the Tosafot, that the reason for liability for taking is because it reduces the flame, for here the flame is not reduced, and yet one is still liable for extinguishing. Rather, the reason is because it causes extinguishing, for when one takes from it, it causes it to extinguish faster, and in such causation of extinguishing, everyone agrees that it is considered extinguishing. (And the Panim Yafot there wrote that Rashi's intention was not complete extinguishing, but something akin to extinguishing, and he did not mention the words of the Rosh that we brought, and the Gra in his Shulchan Aruch, Siman 1, seems to align with the words of the Yam Shel Shlomo. Investigate this well.) (And this is only a labor not needed for its own sake, as is clear, and see Magen Avraham, Siman 1).

We also learned there: A person should not fill a bowl with oil and place it beside the lamp and put the end of the wick into it so that it will draw, due to a decree lest one come to use it. Here, the prohibition can indeed be because of extinguishing, since the end of the wick is within the oil. But from the Rambam it is clear that this is only due to muktzeh (set aside), as he equates this law with the previous one. We must say that since the oil is in a vessel by itself, it is not considered extinguishing if one uses it. This is also evident from the Tur, who equates the two laws. One should not ask that since the end of the wick is in the oil, how can one use it, because it can be said that since the oil is in a vessel by itself, it does not appear prohibited to people. The Gemara implies that, on the contrary, this is more lenient to people than the previous case, because there is the separation of the vessel. And it is stated in the Jerusalem Talmud that the same applies to lighting a wick in two vessels, with the end of the wick in one vessel and its other end in another vessel, and lighting both – it is also forbidden to do so due to the concern that one might come to use it. The reason is that as long as the wick and oil are only in one vessel, it does not seem stringent to people, and they might mistakenly think that there is no prohibition to use the oil.

It is written in the gloss of the Rosh: (there) that if there are several pieces of fat in a burning candle and one piece is taken - one is not liable for extinguishing. And it seems that even according to the opinion of the Rosh that we brought, that with a tube one is liable due to causing extinguishing - here he would agree, because there, all the oil is connected to each other and they are all like one piece, which is not the case with pieces of fat, each piece is separate and has no connection with the others, and causing extinguishing does not apply here. And even though on Shabbat it is forbidden anyway because of muktzeh, nevertheless, there is a practical difference regarding Yom Tov, that it is permitted to move the fat for lighting and extinguishing is forbidden, and therefore on Yom Tov it is permitted to take one piece from the vessel.

One may not place a vessel under a candle on Shabbat to catch the dripping oil, because this would nullify the vessel's preparedness, meaning that prior to this, the vessel was fit for carrying, and now on Shabbat, he makes it muktzeh (set-aside) and prohibits carrying it. Rashi explained in Shabbat (154b) that this is akin to dismantling, meaning that since he cannot move it from its place, it is like dismantling the construction of the vessel. And Tosafot (43a) wrote that it is like building, meaning since he cannot move it from its place, it is like a permanent building on the ground. However, if placed before Shabbat, it is permitted, but the dripping oil is forbidden to use on Shabbat, because the oil was set aside for its mitzvah for the entire Shabbat, and the vessel is also forbidden to carry because it becomes a base for the oil. However, if no oil fell into it, it is permitted to carry, and it is not prohibited because of the thought that oil would fall into it and it would become a base for a prohibited item, because mere thought is nothing. (Magen Avraham 3) And although he set aside the vessel with his intention, he did not set it aside except for the oil, and it is like an explicit condition that he does not set it aside unless oil falls into it.

Some place a vessel under a wax or tallow candle on Shabbat, so that if the candle falls, it will not fall on the table or the ground and cause a fire, but will instead fall into the vessel. This does not constitute "nullifying a vessel from its preparedness," because one can shake the candle out of the vessel by moving it indirectly. However, the oil cannot be shaken out to fall on the ground, as this would waste the oil. But the candle is not wasted in this manner, and therefore the vessel does not become a base for a prohibited item, even according to the opinion in Siman 309 that if one intentionally places it, it becomes a base for a prohibited item, even if it was not intended for the entire Shabbat—this applies when it was on it during twilight, as we say: "Since it was set aside during twilight, it is set aside for the entire day." But outside of twilight, everyone agrees that it is not called a base. (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 2) Furthermore, this is not at all related to the concept of intentionally placing, which is only relevant when one specifically wants the muktzeh (prohibited item) to be within the vessel, but here, on the contrary, one does not want the candle to fall into the vessel at all. It is only that if it falls, one places the vessel so that it will not fall on the table or the ground, and this is not considered intentional placing. (Drisha) However, dripping oil necessarily drips and falls into the vessel. (See Tosefot Yom Tov at the end of Kira, who wrote that according to Rashi, it seems that even during the day one should not initially place a vessel under the oil, as we are concerned that one might move the vessel afterward as well, and this is against the Tur and Shulchan Aruch who permitted it initially, and it is a new decree. Also, Tosafot wrote on page 42: "And if they placed it," that it is permissible even initially, and according to Rashi, there is no proof, as it refers to the language of the Mishnah. Investigate this thoroughly.)

And even with an oil lamp, where there is a prohibition to place a vessel due to the issue of nullifying a vessel from its preparedness, as explained, but causing a vessel to be nullified from its preparedness is permitted. For example, if one placed a vessel under the table before Shabbat, and after the meal moved the table from its place, causing the hanging lamp above to be positioned over the vessel and the oil to drip into the vessel, thereby causing on Shabbat the vessel to be nullified from its preparedness by moving the table - in any case, it is permitted. And even if causing such extinguishing is prohibited, as explained, nonetheless causing the nullification of a vessel from its preparedness is permitted (Magen Avraham, Siman 262), because the prohibition is only rabbinic. And sometimes it is also permitted to place a vessel under the oil on Shabbat, such as when there is something permissible and of some significance in the vessel, and it is not possible to shake it out of the vessel. Thus, even if the oil drips into it - it is permitted to move the vessel, as it is considered a base for something forbidden and something permitted, as will be explained at the end of Siman 310, that there is no issue of muktzeh and it is permitted to move it, and it does not nullify the vessel from its preparedness. (ibid.) But when it is possible to shake the permissible item out of the vessel - it is prohibited, as explained there.

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote in paragraph 3: It is forbidden to touch a lit candle when it is hanging, even though one is not moving it and there is no issue of muktzeh (an object that cannot be moved on Shabbat) by merely touching it—nevertheless, it is forbidden, lest it sway a bit from one's touch and one might tilt it. His words clarify that the principle that muktzeh is permitted by mere touch, as stated in section 310, means that even if it sways from the touch, it is not a concern. This is evident from his statement 'lest it sway and tilt'—it clearly implies that the concern is only about tilting the oil, which is akin to kindling, but the swaying itself is not a concern. However, it is impossible to say this since he himself wrote in section 308, paragraph 3, that swaying is forbidden. Therefore, it appears to me that his intention here is the same, and when he concludes with 'and tilt,' it is because without this concern, we wouldn't worry about the swaying. It is not comparable to an egg in section 513, as an egg is round and will certainly sway. However, due to the concern that one might tilt (which is a Torah prohibition), we are cautious even with a hanging candle. Therefore, when it is not lit, we are not concerned, but if it will certainly sway, it is forbidden like the egg. Also, Rabbi Yosef Karo (Beit Yosef) in section 310, paragraph 6, who wrote 'provided he does not touch it'—his intention is through moving it, which is swaying, as Rema explained his words at the beginning of section 513 regarding the statement of the Shulchan Aruch 'an egg… it is forbidden to touch it,' Rema wrote that it means moving it. Similarly, we should interpret it here. Some have written that Rabbi Yosef Karo holds that it is forbidden even by mere touch for a prohibited purpose, and they also questioned Rema for contradicting himself. In my humble opinion, there is no contradiction or disagreement here. (See Magen Avraham, section 4; section 310, comment 3; section 513, comment 2; and Taz here and there, and what seems correct in my humble opinion I have written; examine it well.) (And what is written in section 5 is simple).

But one may place a utensil under a candle to catch sparks, and this does not constitute nullifying a utensil from its preparedness, because the sparks have no substance and they quickly extinguish and are considered as if they never were. Therefore, it is permitted to move the utensil as before. This applies specifically to sparks, but to place it under to catch coals that fall from the candle is forbidden, because they have substance and it would be impossible to move the utensil. And even though one can shake them off, it is still forbidden, because shaking them off happens after they have extinguished and this requires some time, and during this time the utensil is nullified from its preparedness. Therefore, it is not comparable to a wax candle that we permitted for this reason in section 8, because there one can shake it off immediately. But with burning coals, when one shakes them off, they will certainly extinguish somewhat. (Magen Avraham section 6, as written by the Tosafot in Menachot end of 'while they are still' - see there)

It is not permitted to place a vessel with water under a lamp so that sparks will fall into it, even on the eve of Shabbat. And it is not just on Shabbat that this is forbidden. Even though causing extinguishing is permitted on Shabbat to prevent loss, as stated in Siman 334, where it is permitted to place vessels with water in front of a fire so that the vessels will break and the water will extinguish the fire, and similarly, if a garment has caught fire, it is permitted to pour water on it from the side, and if it extinguishes the fire, it is extinguished, because this is considered indirect extinguishing. But here, it is not called indirect extinguishing but rather proximate extinguishing, since there is no barrier between the fire and the water except for air, and the water is directly under the sparks. However, in the case of a fire, there is a barrier. Additionally, there is a concern that one might lift the vessel at the moment the sparks fall (as per Tosafot at the end of the tractate Kira). Therefore, it is prohibited even on the eve of Shabbat. This is not comparable to other labors that are permitted on the eve of Shabbat, because here we decree it due to Shabbat itself, since placing a vessel under the sparks does not appear to people as a significant prohibition, and therefore, it was necessary to be stringent in this case.

Nevertheless, it is permissible to place water under the oil in a lamp that is lit. One places the water on Friday afternoon and then places the oil, doing so in order to raise the oil. Since the intention is not to extinguish the flame but to elevate the oil, there is no concern that one might do this on Shabbat, as raising the oil is not relevant on Shabbat, given that one does not light flames on Shabbat. Our master, the Rema, wrote in paragraph 4: "Some say that even if one intends to extinguish, it is permitted, since the water is under the oil and not visible—it is considered only indirect extinguishing, and this is the custom." In other words, in this case, the decree about Shabbat does not apply, even if it were conceivable to do this on Shabbat. This is truly an indirect extinguishing, as in Siman 334, since there is a separation between the water and the flame. Therefore, there is no reason to decree a prohibition on Friday because of Shabbat, as there is no Torah prohibition here on Shabbat itself. Moreover, it is impossible to do this on Shabbat, as was mentioned. And even though the previous rule also does not involve a Torah prohibition, as the extinguishing is a labor not needed for its own sake, it is still considered a labor. Additionally, according to the Rambam, one is liable for a labor not needed for its own sake, as mentioned in Siman 312. But here, there is no labor at all, only an indirect labor. (His words are clear, and the Tosafot there wrote the reason because the intention is not to extinguish—they spoke the truth. However, even if one intends to extinguish, there is no prohibition on Friday. The difficulty posed by the Magen Avraham in section 10 from the Sefer Mitzvot Gadol and the Sefer Mitzvot Katan is not a problem at all, as the Tosafot also wrote this because it is indeed the truth. Moreover, placing water on Friday within a candle that holds a tallow or wax candle is not prohibited, as one would not do this on Shabbat. Only in another vessel do we decree, lest one does it on Shabbat, as people do not perceive a prohibition in this. And the conclusion of the Magen Avraham seems to agree with this, as he wrote in section 10, and this was the custom in his time. Initially, he wondered about this, and then he wrote the leniency we have explained. As for what the Magen Avraham wrote that the Rema omitted this—it is not an omission, as it is implicitly understood. Moreover, if he had wanted to prohibit it, he would have clarified it, since the custom was to do so, as the Eliyahu Rabbah wrote. Therefore, it is certain that there is no prohibition regarding this on Friday. Be diligent in understanding this.)

The sages taught in the Mishnah (153b): "If nightfall overtakes someone on the way, he gives his purse to a non-Jew." Even though he is appointing him as an agent to carry the money, they were compelled to permit this due to the reasoning stated in the Gemara: 'The sages understood that a person will not restrain himself regarding his money, and if you do not permit him, he will come to carry it four cubits in the public domain.' Rashi explained: He gives the purse before nightfall. However, Rambam in Chapter 6, Law 22 wrote that it is also permitted after nightfall, and similarly wrote the Rosh, the Tur, and the Shulchan Aruch, stating that it is obvious that even though after nightfall there is also the prohibition of muktzeh, they permitted it so that he would not come to violate a Torah prohibition. And Rashi's intention is also the same, that certainly one should strive to give it before nightfall to avoid the prohibition of muktzeh. But if he did not give it before nightfall, Rashi also agrees that he can give it after nightfall. And from the precise language of the Rambam, it also seems so, as he wrote: "He gives his purse... and even if he gives it to him after nightfall, it is permitted." And this is its explanation: He gives it before nightfall, and even if he gives it after nightfall, it is permitted.

And this is the language of the Rambam and the Shulchan Aruch: "If one was on the road and the day became holy (Shabbat) and he had money with him, he gives his purse to a non-Jew to carry it for him, and after Shabbat, he takes it back from him, even though he did not pay him for this. And even if he gave it to him after dark, it is permitted, because a person is anxious about his property… And if you do not permit him to do this, which is only forbidden by rabbinic decree, he will come to carry it himself and violate a Torah prohibition." End of quote. And this that it is written: "And after Shabbat, he takes it back from him" – this is when he is far from his home, outside the Shabbat boundary. But if he was within the boundary and he comes to his home, the non-Jew can also bring the purse to his home and place it there. Only if he is compelled to rest on the road, Rambam warns that it is forbidden for him to take it from the non-Jew all of Shabbat, for it is considered muktzeh (set-aside).

Nevertheless, regarding what was written, "even though he did not pay him for this," there is room to consider: if he were to pay him, there would be a permissibility in the matter, as he is engaged in his own matter, as stated in Siman 243. If so, why did the Sages not decree that he should pay him something, so that it would not be directly as the emissary of the Jew? It seems to me that indeed this is so: if he hands over the purse before Shabbat, he needs to assure him some payment. However, the Rambam is referring to a situation after nightfall, where there is a prohibition to hire on Shabbat. In this case, we gain nothing from this, and what difference is there between the prohibition of sending an emissary and the prohibition of hiring on Shabbat? Hence, he concludes: "And even though he paid him after nightfall, it is permitted," meaning that when did we permit without payment? When he paid him after nightfall.

There is an opinion that says since the main reason is to prevent one from coming to a Torah prohibition of carrying four cubits in a public domain, or transferring from a public domain to a private domain, therefore, nowadays when we do not have a public domain, we should not permit a rabbinic prohibition. Since even if he were to carry it himself, it would only be a rabbinic prohibition (Magen Avraham, section 3), as the Tur writes later in section 334, that they did not permit moving muktzeh due to loss for this reason. However, in truth, it is not comparable, as there the rabbinic prohibitions are the same in any case, as explained there.
