But here, regardless, if there is no public domain, and when he carries it himself it is a rabbinic prohibition, then giving it to a non-Jew is a rabbinic prohibition upon a rabbinic prohibition, which is much lighter than a single rabbinic prohibition. In several matters, they permitted a rabbinic prohibition upon a rabbinic prohibition in the case of a mitzvah or loss, even without concern that it might lead to a greater prohibition. (And the Magen Avraham himself in section 3 brings the opinion of the Bach to permit it, as explained there, and see Machatzit HaShekel and examine it thoroughly).

This allowance to give the purse to a non-Jew applies even if one has a donkey or horse upon which the purse could be placed—nevertheless, it is preferable to give it to the non-Jew, because with your animal, you are commanded that it rest. Therefore, specifically if the animal is his own, but if the animal belongs to the non-Jew, who he hired along with the animal—it is preferable to place it on the animal. And even if he rented the animal and is leading it himself—he should still do so, for it has already been explained in Siman 246 that renting does not acquire. However, there are those who say that stringently, it does acquire, and if so, one is commanded that it rest, but it has already been explained there that the primary ruling is that renting does not acquire at all. Nevertheless, one should be careful not to walk behind it while it carries the load, as this would be considered driving [the animal], and there is no difference in driving whether it is his animal or a non-Jew's animal, as explained there, and this will be further clarified with G-d’s help.

And if there is no non-Jew with him - he may place it on the animal. But how should he do so without violating the prohibition of leading a laden animal? For it is understandable that the resting of his animal, when it is not his, does not violate anything, but regarding leading a laden animal, there is no distinction, as we have mentioned. So, what should he do?

The Tur wrote: "He should place it on the donkey while it is walking and be careful to remove it every time it stops, and when it resumes walking, he should place it back on it." This is also in the Gemara there. The Gemara explains this matter, for the essence of the prohibition of carrying on Shabbat is only through lifting and placing down, and that he himself does this. But if his friend places the load on him while he is walking - even if he stops, he is exempt by Torah law because his friend did the lifting and he did the placing down, and when two people do it together, they are exempt.

Therefore, even when the Torah prohibits the labor of carrying with his animal, the obligation is only when the animal does both the lifting and the placing down. But when he places it on the animal, even if it stands still - it has performed the placing down without the lifting, and it is impossible to obligate his animal more than himself. Therefore, even though with two people in such a case they are exempt by Torah law but prohibited by rabbinic law - nevertheless, with his animal, it is permitted from the outset in such cases.

(As stated in the Gemara there) The straightforward understanding of the Gemara and the language of the Tur clearly indicate that he places it on the animal after it has lifted all its body. According to this, we must say that our master, the Beit Yosef, who wrote in section 2: "He places it after it has lifted a hand and a foot" - does not mean one hand and one foot, but rather it is a general statement, and his intention is that it has completely lifted both hands and both feet, as the Levush also wrote. (And the Radvaz and also the Eliyah Rabbah, section 6, wrote not as on the eve of the festival, see there. And Rashi, who wrote the expression "foot," also meant this, as it is written: "Those who send forth the foot of the ox and the donkey.")

And this regulation applies only when there is no Gentile with him or when he does not trust him. But otherwise, one should not do so, even though it is entirely permissible, because he might not be careful, and the animal may perform the lifting and placing. (Ran and Magen Avraham, Section 6) And it becomes clear from the words of the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch that when one makes this correction with the animal to place it on while it is walking, that is sufficient, as the Rashba also wrote. However, the Rambam in Chapter 20, Law 6 added a condition in this matter.

And this is the wording of the Rambam: "He places his purse on it while it is walking, and when he wants it to stop, he removes it from it, so that it does not stand with the purse on it, and so that there is neither lifting nor placing there. And it is forbidden for him to guide it even with his voice as long as the purse is on it, so as not to be leading on Shabbat." End of quote. He added two things: First, before stopping, he must remove the purse from it, and besides this, it is forbidden for him to guide it even with his voice, even when it is neither lifting nor placing. The Rashba disagrees with him and holds that since there is no lifting and placing here, there is no prohibition of leading even when guiding. And our teacher, the Beit Yosef, did not mention at all the requirement to remove the purse before stopping, and regarding the prohibition of guiding with the voice, he wrote in the name of some who say, because his opinion on the basic law follows the Rashba. And indeed, the words of the Rambam are puzzling, as from where did he derive this?

And behold, regarding the requirement to remove [the burden] from it before it stands, it appears to me that this is proven from the Talmudic discussion, where it says that when it is walking, one places it on it, and when it is standing, one removes it from it. And it questions: if so, even [with] his friend as well, etc. And it is difficult: if you think that it is really standing, then how does it question ‘if so, even [with] his friend as well,’ for in the first Mishnah of Shabbat it states: ‘if a poor person extends... and the homeowner takes from it – both are exempt,’ and the Gemara there explains that they are exempt but it is forbidden, because lifting without placing or placing without lifting is forbidden by Rabbinic decree. And if it is really standing and has done the placing, how is it permitted for his friend initially? Rather, it must be that the intent is before it stands. And if you ask, how does one know that it wants to stand, one can say that any animal that carries a load does not suddenly stand, but rather prepares itself to stand, walking not as quickly as before until it stands. Therefore, when he sees that it intends to stand, he should remove the bag from it.

And regarding the matter of "mechamer" (having an animal carry a load on Shabbat), he also had a different view. If we examine closely, we find that there are two prohibitions concerning animals on Shabbat: the rest of one's animal, derived from "so that your ox and your donkey may have rest" (Exodus 23:12), which applies when the animal is carrying a load even without its owner, and the entire chapter "With What May an Animal Go Out" (Bava Metzia) is based on this. The second prohibition is "mechamer," meaning that one drives their animal, derived from "you shall not do any work, you, nor your animal" (Exodus 20:10). And what is the work performed by both? This is "mechamer," where the animal is carrying a load and the person is driving it (Rashi there). 

It is not clear why both prohibitions are needed. For the rest of one's animal, "mechamer" is necessary because the rest of one's animal applies only to one's own animal, but "mechamer" applies even to the animal of a non-Jew, as the Ran writes there. But why is the rest of one's animal necessary? Isn't "mechamer" alone sufficient? 

Rather, certainly the rest of one's animal applies only to lifting and placing (the load), as stated, but "mechamer" applies only when one is driving it while the load is on it, even if it is not performing lifting and placing—one is liable because of "mechamer." This is also clarified in the beginning of chapter 20 there. Therefore, it was necessary to say that it is forbidden to drive it, etc. According to the Rashba and the Tur, we must say that the Torah prohibited both when the animal alone is carrying a load if it is his, and when he is driving it even if it is not his. If the Torah had written only "mechamer," I would say that the Torah prohibited only when both are involved. 

(It is also possible to say that according to the Rambam, "mechamer" applies only to one's own animal, and if so, "mechamer" would be completely redundant, but certainly, "mechamer" does not require lifting and placing).

And for us, who travel by carriage: if the driver is not Jewish and he is not far from the city, and he sees that the sun is close to setting—he should get off the carriage and place his money and belongings in the carriage and walk by foot, and the driver will drive to his home, and he will walk on foot, provided that he enters the city's boundary before it gets dark, so as not to walk outside the boundary after dark. And if the horse or the driver is Jewish, and how can the horse go with the saddle and tied to the carriage after dark, this transgresses the commandment of resting one's animal on Shabbat—he is certainly obligated to plan beforehand and rest in some place before sunset. However, if he did not do so, and staying on the road is impossible—it seems that he should declare the horse ownerless, place his money and belongings on the carriage, and let it go by itself while he walks on foot until he enters the city, and he should ask a non-Jew to take the money and belongings from the carriage and bring them into the house, and also to untie the horse from its restraint. Perhaps he can do this himself, as this is not considered labor. And those who travel by train, when they come close to nightfall and need to enter the city near the station they disembarked at—they should ask or hire a non-Jew to carry their belongings and money into the city to their home or inn, and they should walk on foot. They should not carry anything in their hands or pockets, and if they carry a watch—they should also hand it over to the non-Jew in a place where carrying is prohibited. The general principle is that a wise person has foresight and should be careful not to come to such a situation.

And Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote in paragraph 2: "He should not ride on a donkey but should walk on foot. However, if he needs to go beyond the Shabbat boundary because he is afraid of bandits or other dangers, even if it is within the boundary, he may sit on the donkey and ride." End of quote. The explanation of the matter is as follows: If someone is on the road and Shabbat begins, and he is compelled to go beyond the boundary because he has no place to rest, and he has with him a donkey or a horse, some say it is better for him to ride than to walk on foot beyond the boundary. This is because when he rides and his feet are above ten handbreadths, the boundary does not apply above ten handbreadths, which is not the case when walking on foot. And if the concern is about the rest of his animal, it is said that a living being carries itself. And if the concern is about the saddle, the saddle is considered nullified in relation to the rider. But if he walks on foot, he will violate two prohibitions: he will walk beyond the boundary and violate the rest of his animal because it is carrying the saddle. (See Beit Yosef and Magen Avraham, subsection 7)

But our master the Rema disagrees with this and holds that, on the contrary, one should walk on foot and not ride. For riding also involves a rabbinic prohibition, as it involves using animals, and what would be gained by this? Even if he goes beyond twelve mil, which according to the Rambam is a Torah prohibition, nevertheless, there is also a prohibition of boundaries in riding, as riding is considered like walking. Just like traveling in a wagon that is ten tefachim high off the ground, where there is still a prohibition of boundaries, as it is considered like walking on the ground, as stated in Siman 404, the same applies to riding. Rather, he should walk on foot, and if there is a saddle on the animal, he should remove it, for we do not permit violating the rest of his animal due to the loss of the saddle (see Magen Avraham there). Additionally, it is not conclusively stated that there are no boundary limitations above ten tefachim, as mentioned there. However, all this applies when there is no danger in his walking, but he cannot remain there for the entire Shabbat. But if there is danger in his walking, such as being attacked by bandits or other dangers, and he needs to hasten his journey, it is clear that he should ride the animal to hasten his journey even within the boundary, for there is no prohibition at all with his feet, as nothing stands before the preservation of life. (This appears to be my humble opinion in its explanation.)

We have already explained in section 11 how one should act when traveling in a wagon, and now we will add to this: Know that if the wagon itself, without the wheels, is ten handbreadths high and four handbreadths wide, it is considered a private domain, and it is forbidden to transfer items from it to the public domain. Therefore, if one is sitting in the wagon and it becomes dark, he should not descend from the wagon with his money and belongings that are in his clothes, but rather he should remove his belongings into the wagon while still sitting in it, and then descend from the wagon. However, if the wagon itself is not ten handbreadths high, the wheels are not included, because it would be considered a partition that goats can breach if there are three handbreadths from the wheels to the ground, and the wagon is considered a neutral area even if it is four handbreadths wide, since there is no 'carmelit' in vessels, and he may descend from the wagon with his belongings. And even if it is considered like a post, which is a 'carmelit'—nonetheless, according to us who do not have a true public domain but only a 'carmelit,' it is permissible to transfer from one 'carmelit' to another (Magen Avraham, sec. 7). And if the wagon and the horse belong to him or another Jew, there is no solution except through relinquishing ownership, as stated there. (And the Magen Avraham wrote that there is no issue of the rest of his animal here and this needs further investigation, and furthermore, the saddle and bridle are on it, and it is obvious that there is an issue of the rest of his animal; ponder this well.)

If he has with him a donkey, a deaf-mute, an imbecile, and a minor, he should place it on the donkey and not give it to any of these individuals. The reason is that they are considered a type of person, and one may come to confuse them with a competent adult. (Rashi there) And if he only has a deaf-mute and an imbecile with him, he should give it to the imbecile because he has no intelligence at all, whereas the deaf-mute has limited intelligence. (Yevamot 113) If he has an imbecile and a minor, he should give it to the imbecile, because the minor will eventually gain intelligence when he grows up. If he has a deaf-mute and a minor, he can give it to whomever he prefers, since they are equal: the deaf-mute has limited intelligence and will never achieve complete understanding, whereas the minor has no intelligence at all but will eventually gain full understanding.

And even though it is forbidden to feed them forbidden food directly, so how is it permitted to give them [loads] to carry on Shabbat? But in truth, the Geonim said that we must treat them as we explained regarding a donkey: to place [the load] on them while they are walking, and when they stop, to take [the load] off them, and afterward, when they start walking again, to place it back on them. However, our teacher, the Rema, wrote in paragraph 6 that this is specifically when one gives it to them after nightfall. But if one gives it to them while it is still day, it is permitted in any manner. And the reason is that at the time he gives it to them, it is still day, and afterward, when they go at night with the load, they are doing it on their own, and a minor who eats non-kosher food is not required to be prevented by the court, as stated in Siman 343. But there are those who disagree and hold that even if one gives it to them during the day, one must act similarly, for in any case, he is giving it to them directly. This is the opinion of the Rashba, while the first opinion is that of the Rambam. (See Magen Avraham section 8, Taz, and Machatzit HaShekel)

If he is alone, with no other person or any animal, and he is by himself, what should he do? The sages have provided another leniency, but they did not want to reveal it because it is close to leading easily to a prohibition. It involves carrying it by himself less than four cubits at a time. Before completing four cubits, he should stop to rest in between. He should do so with every less than four cubits, for if he does not, even if he stops, the distances combine together. There are those who require specifically to sit, but this is not essential. (See Magen Avraham, subsection 9.) It seems that the same applies in our times when there is no public domain (reshut harabim) – one must also do so, pausing before completing each four cubits. (And this is also indicated in Taz, subsection 4.) It is obvious that to transfer from a public domain to a private domain, stopping to rest does not help, for in this case, the four cubits are not needed. (There) And just as in a public domain, this leniency is only when he is alone, without a person or animal with him, so too in our times when there is no public domain, the leniency applies, as long as there is no animal or types of people together with him.

The Sages said (there): All these permissions are specifically for his money or belongings that were already with him, and they had to permit it because a person does not restrain himself concerning his money, as stated at the beginning of the section. But if he found a lost item, they did not permit it at all; rather, he should leave it and go, because in this case, he can restrain himself and not breach a boundary, as his inclination does not overpower him so much, since it has not yet come into his possession. Therefore, if the lost item has already come into his possession, it is considered his money, and all the permissions that were explained apply. And know that, seemingly, since the reason is that a person does not restrain himself concerning his money, this only applies to a lot of money or many belongings, and not to a small amount of money or few belongings. However, we do not find this distinction in the Talmud or the legal decisors, and since they permitted it, they permitted it even for a small amount of money, because the Rabbis did not differentiate in their decree.

And know that the Rambam wrote in Chapter 6 and Chapter 20: that which is forbidden regarding a found object - this only applies to other leniencies, but the leniency of carrying less than four cubits - is permitted even for a found object, see there. And all the sages of the generations have already been astonished by this, for on the contrary, this leniency is more stringent than all of them, and indeed it was not permitted when there is another leniency. How can we say that for a found object itself, the opposite is true? And the sages of Lunel asked him, and he replied that it seemed to him logically, because this leniency is not a well-known matter and is done discreetly, when no one is with him, and even an animal is not with him and he is alone, therefore, it is permitted even for a found object. (Kesef Mishneh) And it is understood that his words are not sufficient, and it is astonishing that the Raavad did not challenge him on this. And the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch did not bring his opinion at all, because it is a surprising matter. However, the later greats found an explicit Gemara according to his words (Avodah Zarah 70a): "Rabbi Yitzchak said: One who finds a purse on Shabbat - carries it less than four cubits at a time," see there. (And from this, he derived this ruling, but it was not mentioned when they asked him) (And it cannot be explained as one who takes a purse out of his house, for if so, what benefit is there in carrying less than four cubits, since bringing it into the house is forbidden. And if we explain it as taking it out of his house - presumably the arrangement is to bring it into his house, which is impossible. But if we explain it as finding, meaning a found object - it is not explained as bringing it into his house, but rather to a guarded place, and scrutinize this).

Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 8: "Some say that this specifically applies to someone who was overtaken by nightfall on the way, thinking that there was still time in the day. But if he left his house close to nightfall and forgot and carried into the public domain, none of these methods were permitted for him," end quote. This is considered close to intentional. However, if he left much earlier than close to nightfall, it is permitted, for this is not close to intentional. 

There is someone who challenges this from the Gemara we brought: "One who finds a purse on Shabbat should carry it less than four cubits at a time," which implies that even if he finds it on Shabbat, it is permitted, and all the more so if it is close to nightfall. He struggled to differentiate that there it refers to someone who forgot, and here we are speaking of someone intentional. (Magen Avraham, section 10). But in truth, the term ‘finds’ is a language of finding, not a language of carrying out, and in all the books, the version is ‘finds,’ which means finding, and not ‘brings out’ with a yud, which implies carrying out, and from this, the Rambam derived his ruling as mentioned. (What the Taz wrote in section 4 about the word 'its place' is in section 331).

We learned in the Mishnah about someone to whom nightfall came (Shabbat 153a): if he reached the outer courtyard, he may take the vessels that may be carried on Shabbat, and those that may not be carried on Shabbat—he unties the ropes, and the sacks fall by themselves. They did not permit him to move muktzeh (items prohibited to be moved on Shabbat) when he reached a guarded place. It seems obvious that here we are dealing with someone who is traveling on the road and has not yet reached his city. For if he had reached his city, the concept of the outer courtyard does not apply; he should continue to his house and do so there. Alternatively, it is possible that even if he reached his city, they only permitted him to go as far as the first courtyard of the city, which is a guarded place. This also seems to be implied by the fact that the poskim (decisors of Jewish law) did not distinguish in this regard, and it also seems somewhat implied by the language of the Rambam in Chapter 21, Law 10.

Know that I have seen someone who raised a difficulty regarding this law, that when [the animal] stands a little before the entrance, it brings [items] from a public domain into a private domain. And he answered that concerning one's animal, the Sages were not so stringent (Magen Avraham, subsection 11). There are those who explained that it is done in an indirect manner, and there are other far-fetched explanations (see Pri Megadim, Maharsha, and Tosefot Yom Tov there). Were it not for their words, it would seem to me that indeed the intention is not to bring it into the courtyard, but rather the matter is as follows: as long as he is on the road, the Sages were compelled to permit him to avoid standing on the road, for he could come to harm from robbers or wild animals. But when he reaches the city, where there is no fear of these things, he should stand by the courtyard and place his pouch and items there, and guard them until the end of Shabbat or appoint a guard, but the intention is not to bring them into the courtyard. And it is not similar to the law that will be explained regarding when his bundle is on his shoulder, where he runs beneath it until he reaches his house and throws it in an indirect manner as will be explained—this applies when he is walking in his city and the burden is on his shoulder, they permitted him in such cases, but not for one who was delayed on the road. And according to several authorities, this was only permitted for a bundle and not for a pouch, as will be explained, and here we are dealing with a pouch. Furthermore, a person himself can do this, not his animal, and therefore in my humble opinion it seems as I have written. (And in the commentary on the Mishnah by the Rambam, there are things that are not understood, where he wrote: 'until he reaches the entrance of his house, and he will take it off from him while he is walking, and throw it into his house in an indirect manner'—see there. And it is difficult, as it was taught regarding the outer courtyard, not his house, and also the Ra'avad wrote that reaching the outer courtyard does not refer to one who was delayed—see there. And perhaps he holds that in his city it was permitted to his house, as we wrote in the first opinion in the previous section, and this requires further study and consideration).

It is simple that they did not permit untying the ropes and allowing the sacks to fall except when they are placed on the animal, for then, due to the suffering of living creatures, it is necessary to do so. And even if it were carrying a load of more than fifteen se'ah, which is forbidden to unload on Shabbat, as stated in Siman 333, they permitted it due to the suffering of living creatures. But when the load is placed on a wagon, as is customary among us, it is obvious that it is forbidden to untie the ropes and remove the load, even if it is not muktzeh, but rather it should remain so until the end of Shabbat. (Magen Avraham, section 12)

This which has been explained, that when the load is on the animal, he unties the ropes and the sacks fall off – this is with merchandise that will not break when it falls to the ground. But merchandise that does break, such as glassware and earthenware vessels – he should unload them by hand, since they are not muktzeh (set aside), and it is permitted to move them on Shabbat, as they are fit for use on Shabbat. But if they are glass items that are muktzeh and it is forbidden to move them, such as cups used by bloodletters, or window glass or lamp glass and similar items, what should he do? He should place many pillows and cushions on the ground so that they fall on them and do not break. This applies specifically to small loads, which he can remove from under them gently and they do not become a base for a forbidden object, since he did not place them there during twilight, and furthermore, he placed them with the intention of removing them. (See there, section 14) But if they are large and heavy, and it is impossible to remove the cushion from under them – it is forbidden to place them underneath because it would be nullifying a vessel’s preparedness. And there is no remedy for this except to unload them gently from the animal in a way that they do not break, and he should not leave them on the animal, due to the suffering of animals. And it is obvious that if he can unload the merchandise through a non-Jew – he should do so, as it is a rabbinic prohibition overridden in a place of animal suffering, and it is certainly permitted. But from a wagon – it is forbidden, unless he fears theft, in which case it is permitted through a non-Jew. And even though he can guard it himself until the end of Shabbat – nevertheless, this is also a form of suffering for him, and it is permitted as a double rabbinic prohibition. (And the Ran wrote that even temporarily, it is forbidden to nullify a vessel’s preparedness except in a place of great loss, and in the Gemara there it says that window glass breaking is a minor loss, and the poskim omitted this. And it seems to me that the truth is as such, that in their time when the windows were small – it was not a great loss, but not now, and we see clearly that when a glass window box breaks, it is almost a total loss, see Magen Avraham there)

If one is overtaken by night on the road with his tefillin on his head, or if he is sitting in a field's study hall and night falls upon him, he should place his hand over them until he reaches his house, for tefillin worn in the manner of clothing does not constitute a Torah prohibition. Although it is initially forbidden, in order that they should not remain in disgrace, left in the field, they permitted him to bring them in while they are on his head and arm. However, they required him to cover them by placing his hand over them because of observers. (Rashi, Beitza 15.)

The Sages said at the beginning of "Mi Shehichshich": If a bundle of load was placed on his shoulder, he should run with it to his house, so that he remembers that he is forbidden to stand, so that he does not perform an uprooting and placing on Shabbat, since the uprooting of his body is like the uprooting of an object. However, now his uprooting was before the onset of Shabbat. Therefore, he should not walk slowly, because if there is no noticeable sign, he will come to stand and rest, and will be liable for a sin-offering. But standing to adjust his load, he is exempt, as the Rambam wrote in chapter 13. However, when he runs, there is a noticeable sign, and he will not stand. And when he reaches his house, and there will be an entry from the public domain to the private domain, even though he did not perform an uprooting after nightfall, but near his house it is unavoidable that he will delay a bit. Therefore, his remedy is to throw the load in an unusual manner, that is, from his shoulder backwards. And some say that this leniency was only granted for a bundle of load, because in this case, running is noticeable since it is not usual to run with a heavy load. But for his purse, in such cases where he carries it, they did not permit it, because in this case, his running is not noticeable. And some say the same applies to his purse, and if he wishes, he can carry it less than four cubits at a time. (See Magen Avraham section 18, and according to what is written in section 22, this does not pertain to the law of one who was overtaken by night on the way, and scrutinize this well.)

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote in section 12: "One who forgot his purse on him on Shabbat: if he is in his house, he can go with it to a room, untie his belt, let it fall there, and hide it. But if he is in the marketplace, he is not allowed to bring it to his house; he should only untie his belt in the marketplace and let it fall, and tell a non-Jew to guard it. And if he brought it [to his house], there is no concern." End of quote. And the reason he permitted when he is in his house to go to a room and let it fall there, and did not require him to let it fall here and not carry the muktzeh to the room, is because since the muktzeh is already in his hand, he can place it wherever he wishes, as will be explained in section 308, see there. And they questioned him, asking how he could write simply that it is forbidden in the marketplace, when it has already been explained that there is a disagreement whether they permitted also a purse like a bundle or not, and according to the one who permits, he could do like with a bundle. (Taz section 6) And in matters of Rabbinic prohibition, we follow the lenient opinion. (ibid.) And it seems to me that our teacher, the Rema, holds that even those who permit with his purse only permit it if he was walking on the eve of Shabbat and the day sanctified while he was walking, but not if he went out on Shabbat. (And see Magen Avraham section 20 which implies a distinction if he fears to leave it in the marketplace, see there.) And our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 13: "If one found a wallet on Shabbat, he is not allowed to pick it up even though he fears someone else might precede him." End of quote. And it is also forbidden to tell a non-Jew to pick it up. (Magen Avraham section 21) And we have already brought in section 19 the opinion of the Rambam, that less than four cubits, even with a found object, is permitted, see there.

One must know how to conduct oneself now in a place where it is forbidden to carry, when one finds money or objects in his pocket. Nowadays, it is not relevant to untie the belt, and it is necessary to take the items from the pocket by hand due to our clothing. How can one carry the muktzeh (objects prohibited to move on Shabbat) with his hands? It is obvious that if there is a non-Jew present, one should tell him to put his hand into the pocket and take out the money, and consequently, he will bring them to his house. If there is no non-Jew present: if one is in a public domain, he is obligated to remove his garment in the market and shake them out of his pocket. If one is in a karmelit (a semi-public domain), like in most of our towns where there are not sixty myriad (600,000 people) and it is not considered a public domain, human dignity is of great importance, and he should go to his house and there remove his garment and shake them out. It seems that it is also permitted through a child; it is good to tell the child to take them out of the pocket and bring them to his house, even in a public domain when it is not possible to leave them here, because a person does not control his impulse regarding his money. Also, in a karmelit, it is better through a child than to do it himself. (This is what it seems to me in my humble opinion.) If the pocket is sewn into the garment with the money, it will be explained in Siman 310.

They enter the synagogue and pray the Mincha (afternoon) prayer as on weekdays, except that they do not fall on their faces because of the honor of Shabbat. And even those who pray half an hour after midday also do not fall on their faces (Pri Megadim). And not only on Shabbat, but on all days when supplications are not recited, they do not fall on their faces in the preceding Mincha prayer. And know that for us, where we do not add to Shabbat as early as in ancient days, we should be careful to light the candles in the synagogue before Mincha. For if we delay until after Mincha, it will lead to the desecration of Shabbat. And so is the simple custom, and it should not be changed even when we pray earlier. There are those who recite before the Mincha of Erev Shabbat the Psalm "Four must give thanks," and "Petach Eliyahu" from the Tikkunim, and the poem "Yedid Nefesh," and the section of the daily offering, and the incense – all before Mincha, which requires a lot of time. They must be very, very careful to come to the synagogue a long time before sunset, because if not, they will delay the Mincha prayer time until evening, and all God-fearing people should be careful about this.

After Mincha, we say five psalms: "Come, let us sing joyously to Hashem," "Sing to Hashem a new song," "Hashem reigns, let the earth rejoice," "A psalm, sing to Hashem a new song," and "Hashem reigns, let the nations tremble," because these psalms refer to the future, to the days of the Messiah, which is a time that is entirely Shabbat. Therefore, we say them as we welcome Shabbat. Then we say "A psalm of David: Ascribe to Hashem, sons of the mighty," because it contains seven voices, corresponding to the seven blessings of the Shabbat prayer (Berachot 29a). These are six psalms corresponding to the six weekdays. Afterward, we say "Ana B'Koach," which is a Name of 42 letters, a Name associated with the act of Creation (Tosafot, beginning of the second chapter of Chagigah, see there). And because Shabbat is a remembrance of the act of Creation, we say it before accepting Shabbat. Then we say "Lecha Dodi... Let us greet the Shabbat bride," and conclude with "Come, bride, come, bride!" as it says in Shabbat (119a): Rabbi Chanina would wrap himself and stand at the eve of Shabbat. He said, "Come, let us go out to greet the Shabbat queen." Rabbi Yannai would put on his garments and say, "Come, bride, come, bride!" After that, we say "A psalm, a song for the Shabbat day," which alludes to the day that is entirely Shabbat, as we learned at the end of Tamid, see there. With this, we have accepted upon ourselves the holy Shabbat. Then we say "With what do we light?" Some have the custom to recite a passage from the Zohar, "Kegavna" until "Benehiro De'anpin" (Zohar Teruma 135a).

And afterwards, they pray the Maariv (evening) prayer. The Tur and the Shulchan Aruch wrote that one should pray the Maariv prayer earlier than on regular weekdays. Similarly, the Rambam wrote in the third chapter of Hilchot Tefillah (Halacha 7): "From the time of Plag HaMincha, one can light (candles) and accept Shabbat with the Maariv prayer," which is an hour and a quarter before sunset. And even though on weekdays one prays Mincha at that time, nevertheless on the eve of Shabbat one can pray Maariv at that time. This is not contradictory, because due to the addition of Shabbat, one can do so. There is also a significant reason to pray the Shabbat Maariv earlier, as the Maariv prayer was instituted corresponding to the limbs and fats that were offered at night from the daily afternoon offering. Now, it is forbidden to offer them at night, as it is written: "The burnt offering of the Shabbat on its Shabbat" – and not the weekday burnt offering on Shabbat (Shabbat 114a). Therefore, it is necessary that they offered the limbs and fats before nightfall, and hence the prayer that corresponds to them is during the day (Magen Avraham, small section 1). However, the Mincha prayer on the eve of Shabbat must necessarily be prayed before Plag HaMincha because it is impossible to do two contradictory things in one day. Some say that in a congregation, even in such a case, it is permitted (Derech HaChaim).

However, in any case, we see that our early sages instructed us to pray the evening prayer before nightfall. This is a significant safeguard for the Sabbath for the masses, women, and the unlearned, whose only concern is the time of prayer in the synagogue. If they delay praying in the synagogue, many in each city will light the candles after sunset. As our eyes see and our ears hear, to our heart's sorrow, in many large and small towns, they delay lighting the candles and come to desecrate the Sabbath. May the Merciful One save us from this great punishment. It is a sacred duty of the rabbi and the devout in the city to pray before nightfall to prevent the desecration of the holy Sabbath. Some strive to pray the evening prayer at its proper time on the Sabbath and will ultimately be held accountable, for it is known that this delay causes the desecration of the Sabbath in the city. One who hastens the entrance of the Sabbath – the merit of the holy Sabbath will protect him. We have already elaborated on this in several places, for it is known to us that the early prayer establishes the Sabbath and its holiness in its proper place.

And just as one can pray before nightfall, one can also recite Kiddush before nightfall, as the Rambam wrote in Chapter 29, Law 11, and this is his wording: A person may recite Kiddush over a cup [of wine] on Friday afternoon, even though Shabbat has not yet started. So far his wording. And the Maggid Mishneh wrote: Even though he sanctified [the day] in the afternoon, he is permitted to eat in the evening with that Kiddush… So far his wording. And there is room for doubt regarding his intention: If his intention is that eating must specifically be at night, and therefore he says that the Kiddush is valid for him, and if it is required that Kiddush be in the place of a meal, he can eat a kezayit (olive's volume) of grain products after Kiddush. Or his intention might be that if he eats at night, he fulfills the obligation with this Kiddush, but he can always eat in the afternoon, and thereby fulfill the obligation of the Shabbat meal. And so it is explained in the words of our teacher, the Beit Yosef, who wrote: In the time of mincha, one can light and accept Shabbat with the evening prayer and eat immediately. So far his wording. And so it is written in the book Terumat HaDeshen (Siman 1) that they would finish the Shabbat meal in the afternoon. And even in the days of the Gemara it seems to have been so, for at the beginning of Berachot it is said: "From the time people enter to eat their bread on Friday evenings," and the Tosafot wrote there at the beginning of Berachot that it was in the afternoon, see there. Therefore, this is the main ruling in law. And there are those who wrote in the name of Sefer Chassidim that one must eat a kezayit at night (see Magen Avraham there), and it is a mere stringency of piety (and so it is proven in Magen Avraham). And the reasoning: that any time after the time of mincha, when one accepts the addition of Shabbat, it is considered completely as night (there). And it is not necessary to say according to most of the poskim that the addition of Shabbat is from the Torah, but even according to the Rambam who does not hold of the addition as we wrote in Siman 261, nevertheless, since he accepts the addition, it is considered completely as night, regarding that he fulfills the obligation of Kiddush made in the afternoon for his obligation at night, since he will immediately come to obligation. Therefore, he can continue it even earlier with the added sanctity, for the Torah has given him permission for this. (And this is the intention of the Mordechai in the second chapter of Megillah, brought by the Magen Avraham. And what he questioned from Siman 186 regarding a minor not fulfilling the obligation for an adult, even though he would come to obligation when he grows up, see there – as we explained, it is not similar at all. Be precise and you will find ease.)

Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, in his great work, posed a question: How did they eat while it was still day, when it is forbidden to eat before reciting the Shema? He answered that since they recited it from the time of Pelag HaMincha, even for those who hold that one must recite it again after nightfall, it is nevertheless permissible to eat beforehand. (The Magen Avraham challenges this in Siman Katan 2 of the Rosh, and it is not understood at all. The Tosafot Shabbat wrote that his intention was regarding before Pelag HaMincha; see there. If so, what did he challenge the Beit Yosef on? Also, the Pri Megadim seems to interpret like the Tosafot Shabbat; see there. The Machtzit HaShekel seems to interpret based on what the Rosh wrote at the beginning of Berachot, that prayer is not related to the recitation of the Shema; see there. But this is not relevant to Erev Shabbat, as due to the addition of Shabbat, it is considered like night. However, I am accustomed to recite the Shema before Kiddush, as our eating is always at night, since we do not advance it so much, and it is certainly proper to do so. Delve and you will find clarity.)

In the blessing of "Hashkiveinu," one should not conclude with "He who guards His people Israel forever," because Shabbat itself is a form of protection. Therefore, we recite the verses of "V'shamru" because when we observe Shabbat, then Shabbat protects us. It is also a type of redemption, as it is said that if Israel would observe two Shabbats properly, they would be immediately redeemed (Tur). Instead, we conclude with "He who spreads the shelter of peace... and upon Jerusalem," as the Divine Presence shelters us. Consequently, one must first say "Spread over us the shelter of Your peace," so that the conclusion will be similar to the beginning of the conclusion. In the Tur, it is noted that even in "Spread over us," one should mention Jerusalem, since it is mentioned in the conclusion, and it should be said: "Spread over us and upon Jerusalem the shelter of Your peace." However, this is not the custom, and the reason is that Israel and Jerusalem are considered one (Eliyahu Rabbah, Section 6). There is proof for this from Berachot (49a), see there.

According to this, we should not say "For God who guards us... and guards our going out..." on Shabbat, and this is the custom of the Sephardim. However, we have the custom to say it, and the reason is that Shabbat guards those who observe it properly, and we do not consider ourselves to be in that category (Taz, Section 1). Additionally, in the Zohar Vayakhel (Page 204b), there is a distinction between the community and the individual, and an individual needs protection even on Shabbat. Therefore, "He who guards His people Israel," which refers to the entire Jewish people, should not be said on Shabbat, but the preceding phrase, which refers to each individual, should be said (Magen Avraham, Section 3). If one concluded with "He who guards His people Israel," he has fulfilled his obligation and is not required to repeat it (Eliyahu Rabbah, Section 7, citing the Kol Bo). It seems to me that the reason is that is Shabbat our guardian? Rather, it is the One who commanded us about Shabbat who guards us, and if so, "He who guards His people Israel" is also fitting, as He guards us in the merit of Shabbat. However, on Shabbat, one must differentiate from the weekdays with the phrase "He who spreads a shelter of peace." But after the fact, one has fulfilled his obligation. It also seems to me that if one concluded with "and guard our going out," and when he said "Blessed are You, Lord" he remembered, he should still finish with "He who spreads a shelter of peace" and not "He who guards His people Israel." Even though this is not immediately related to the conclusion, one can say that it is also somewhat related, for through the spreading of peace, we are guarded, and indeed, this is a superior form of protection.

The cantor says the Half Kaddish, and we stand to pray the seven blessings: the first three are like on weekdays, since they are praises of the Holy One, Blessed be He, and Shabbat is similar to weekdays in this regard. However, the middle blessings are requests, which should not be said on Shabbat. In the Siddur of Rav Amram Gaon, there is also an addition in the first blessing on Shabbat, for when it reaches "and brings a redeemer to their children's children," it adds: "Be pleased and grant Shabbat as a heritage to their descendants for rest, for the sake of His name, with love," and does not say "and brings a redeemer to their children's children." It seems to me that the reason is that this is not a request but a praise, meaning that the redemption will come through the merit of Shabbat, and as our Sages said (Shabbat 118b): "If Israel were to observe two Shabbatot according to their laws, they would be immediately redeemed." Therefore, when saying "Be pleased and grant, etc.," it is as if saying "and brings a redeemer, etc.," but this is not our custom. (See Beit Yosef, who struggled with the reasoning of the Gaon, and according to what I have said, it fits well with good reasoning.)

Afterwards, one recites one blessing in the middle, and its main part is: "Our God... be pleased with our rest" until "Who sanctifies the Sabbath," and this is the main part and it is the same in all prayers of the Sabbath. However, the Men of the Great Assembly added themes to each prayer, that is, at night, which is the time of the Sabbath's entrance, they mention the sanctity of the Sabbath and the creation of the world, and they say: "You sanctified... the culmination of the creation of heaven and earth," because the culmination of the days is the Sabbaths. And the term "culmination" has two meanings: one is the completion, in which the work of creation was finished, and the other is the purpose, as explained. And they say "Vayechulu" as it is stated in Shabbat (119b): "Whoever prays on the eve of the Sabbath and says 'Vayechulu' - it is as if they become a partner with the Holy One, blessed be He, in the creation of the world," and so it is written in your Torah: "And they were finished..." meaning that it was stated about the culmination of the creation of the heavens and the earth, and about "and He blessed it above all days and sanctified it above all times" it is written: "And God blessed the seventh day and sanctified it." (Tur) And the Sephardim also say "They shall rejoice in Your kingdom" in the evening prayer as in the morning and additional prayers, but the Ashkenazim do not say it in the evening, and I do not know the reason for this. However, it seems to me that if one did not say "You sanctified" but only "Our God... be pleased" until "Who sanctifies the Sabbath" - they have fulfilled their obligation and do not need to repeat. But if one did not say "Blessed are You, Lord, Who sanctifies the Sabbath" - they have not fulfilled their obligation and need to repeat, as this is the main part. And it seems to me that even if one only said: "Blessed are You, Lord, Who sanctifies the Sabbath" alone, and did not say also: "Our God... be pleased" - they have also fulfilled their obligation, and the same applies in the morning and afternoon prayers, only in the additional prayer it is necessary to mention the verses of the additional offerings. Then one says the last three blessings as on all weekdays, and it is customary to also say "My God, guard my tongue" on the Sabbath, and even though it is not customary to make requests on the Sabbath, nevertheless, since everyone says this on weekdays - it is considered as part of the arrangement of the prayer, only one should be careful to say "May the words of my mouth" before "My God, guard my tongue."

If one made a mistake and began with "Ata Chonen" (the weekday blessing) - he should complete that blessing, because it would have been appropriate to pray the full eighteen blessings even on Shabbat, since it is a fixed prayer, and this is not considered a special request on Shabbat. The order of the prayers is such that they would also add the Shabbat-specific blessings. However, the Sages did not want to burden us, and since he began the blessing, he must complete it. (Berachot 21a) There is no difference between the blessing of "Ata Chonen" and any other blessing, contrary to those who differentiate. (See Beit Yosef) Even if he said several weekday blessings and began another one after them - he should complete it and then say "Ata Kidashta," and this applies to all Shabbat prayers. Some say that in the Musaf prayer, he should stop even in the middle of a blessing, because there is no Musaf on weekdays, and it is not relevant to say that it would have been appropriate to pray it like a weekday. The first opinion holds that since it is called a prayer - it would have been appropriate to pray the eighteen blessings even in it. This is the opinion of the Tur, but the Rambam's opinion is like that of the "some say" view, and our master the Beit Yosef in his major work ruled like the Rambam. I am puzzled why in Shulchan Aruch, section 2, it is written in the name of "some say," and it is obvious that in practice one should be concerned about a blessing in vain, and he should stop during Musaf. (Bach and Ateret Zekeinim)

Our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 2: "If one thought it was a weekday and began with the intention of the weekday, and immediately when he said the word 'Ata' he remembered before he said 'Chonen' - it is considered as having begun the weekday Amidah, and he completes that blessing. But if he knew it was Shabbat, and unintentionally began with the word 'Ata,' even if it is during the Shacharit prayer which does not begin with 'Ata' - he does not complete the blessing of 'Ata Chonen,' because we consider it as if he erred in the Shabbat prayer between one and another, for he can say 'Ata Kidashta' or 'Ata Echad.'” This means that this does not invalidate it in retrospect.

Here is the translation of the passage:

And behold, this ruling that if one begins with the intention for a weekday, he must complete it, follows his earlier view in Siman 209, where he ruled according to the Rambam's opinion that the primary factor in prayer depends on the intention in the heart. And even if he verbalized it correctly, nevertheless, since he intended in his heart the opposite, the blessing is null. And although he also brought the opinion of Rashi there, that if one intended at the beginning of the blessing for a different blessing, if he completed it correctly, he has fulfilled his obligation - this is because it is a question in the Gemara whether we follow the intention at the beginning of the blessing or at its end. But in any case, even according to Rashi, the main factor is the intention in the heart. And he did not bring at all the opinion of the Ra'avad and other poskim, who hold that intention is not significant. Therefore, he ruled here that since when saying "You" he intended for a weekday, he must complete it, and his intention applies to all the prayers of Shabbat, as the Levush wrote. (See A.R. 5 and T.S. 4) There are those who explained that his intention was only for Shacharit, which does not start with "You", but for Ma'ariv and Mincha, even our teacher the Beit Yosef agrees. (M.A. 3) But this is not so, for we are dealing with Ma'ariv, and furthermore, according to his view, it fits well as he wrote. However, in practice, it is certain that intention does not prevent fulfillment, and also in Siman 209 we hold so, not like the words of our teacher the Beit Yosef there. And also, regarding the main issue, it is not comparable to there, for there he said: "Blessed are You, Lord our God, King of the universe" with a different intention that is the essence and core of the blessing, but with the word "You" alone, what difference does it make. And it seems that the main reasoning of our teacher the Beit Yosef is because it is proper to pray the eighteen blessings on Shabbat, but the Sages did not want to burden us as they wrote, and therefore, even with the word "You" alone, it is not stringent if he completes the blessing. Nevertheless, in practice, we do not hold so. (See M.H. who apologized for the M.A. that his intent was according to the Ra'avad's view, and it is very perplexing, for the Beit Yosef did not bring the Ra'avad's view at all in Siman 209)

And based on what has been explained, when one knows it is Shabbat and unintentionally starts with "You," even in Shacharit, he does not finish the weekday blessing because he can say "You sanctified" or "You are One." This implies that if not for this reason, he would need to finish the weekday blessing. Therefore, if he said "You grant intelligence," he would need to finish the blessing of intelligence. However, reason does not support this, for since he knows it is Shabbat, but due to lack of intention and the flow of language he said "You grant intelligence," why should he need to conclude? Therefore, it seems to me that even if he started several words, in such a case, he interrupts and says the Shabbat version. The reason written is not precise, but since it discusses the word "You," it is convenient to provide this reason and to inform us that even in Shacharit, when he said "You sanctified" or "You are One," it is acceptable. Consequently, it follows that the same applies in Maariv if he said "Moses rejoices" or "You are One," and similarly in Mincha if he said "Moses rejoices" or "You sanctified," as all of Shabbat is one. (Thus it appears in my humble opinion, and see Be'ur Halacha which remains in doubt)

And if one forgot and did not pray the Friday night Maariv, and prays the Shacharit twice – it is obvious that initially, he should pray 'Yismach Moshe' in both, as it is not appropriate during the day to initially say 'Atah Kidashta', which is only said at the entrance of Shabbat. (Shu”t in the name of Shlah) Similarly, if he did not pray Shacharit and prays Mincha twice – he should say 'Atah Echad' in both. However, after the fact – there is no hindrance in how he said it. And it seems to me that in Shacharit when he prays twice: the first is for the obligation and the second for the compensation of Maariv, and he must precede the obligation before the compensation, and if not, he does not fulfill his obligation, as stated in Siman 108. According to this, if he said 'Atah Kidashta' in the first and 'Yismach Moshe' in the second, even though there is no hindrance in the matter as explained – nonetheless, he has not fulfilled his obligation, because he revealed his intention to precede the compensation before the obligation. And he needs to pray another prayer afterwards for the compensation, and however he says it, he fulfills his obligation, but initially, he should say 'Yismach Moshe' as stated. This law can be derived from the law of Havdalah as explained there.

It is obvious that although it has been clarified that if someone thinks it is a weekday and begins the blessing of 'Ata Chonen' or another blessing, they need to complete it, if they did not complete it and interrupted in the middle and returned to the Shabbat prayer and completed the Shabbat prayer, we do not concern ourselves with this, and there is no need to return to 'Ata Chonen' or another blessing to complete it. (Shu”T in the name of Machzik Beracha) There are those who want to say that if one continued with the weekday blessings until 'Mevarech HaShanim' during the winter and did not say 'Tal u'Matar' and completed the blessing, then remembered and returned to the Shabbat prayer and completed the prayer, they would need to go back and say 'Tal u'Matar'. This ruling is astonishing, and there is no doubt that since they returned to the Shabbat prayer, even though they have not completed the prayer yet, there is no need to return to the weekday blessings in any case. (ibid.)

Our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, wrote in section 4: "One who prayed a weekday prayer on Shabbat and did not mention Shabbat has not fulfilled his obligation. But if he mentioned Shabbat within the eighteen blessings, even though he did not establish a blessing specifically for Shabbat, he has fulfilled his obligation. And in the Musaf prayer, even if he only said: 'And we shall perform our obligations with the daily offerings and the Musaf offering,' he has fulfilled his obligation." End quote. 

This ruling, that mentioning Shabbat even without establishing a specific blessing for Shabbat fulfills the obligation, is not mentioned in the Gemara or the early poskim (decisors of Jewish law), and our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote this ruling in his great book from his own reasoning. According to this, Shabbat is not as stringent as Rosh Chodesh, where a mere mention suffices. This is perplexing, because since the Rabbis instituted a special blessing for Shabbat and Yom Tov, even if the specific text is not essential, why wouldn't the main aspect of the blessing be essential? And why is this different from 'the holy King' during the Ten Days of Repentance, or 'He who makes the wind blow' and 'the dew and rain' in the winter, which are essential? And if the reasoning is that ideally one should pray all eighteen blessings as written, nevertheless, in the end, they did institute a blessing for Shabbat.

Moreover, it is taught in Eruvin (40b): "When Shabbat coincides with Rosh Chodesh or Chol HaMoed: for Ma'ariv, Shacharit, and Mincha, one prays the regular seven blessings and mentions the special occasion in the blessing of Avodah. If he did not mention it, he must repeat the prayer. For Musaf, he begins with Shabbat, ends with Shabbat, and mentions the sanctity of the day in the middle." If it were to be thought that even on Shabbat it suffices to mention it incidentally, it should have taught us that if one did not pray the Shabbat prayer, he fulfills his obligation by mentioning it incidentally. Similarly, the Rambam in Chapter 10 of Hilchot Tefillah, Halacha 7, wrote: "One who erred and prayed the weekday Amidah on Shabbat has not fulfilled his obligation." He should have said: "If he mentioned Shabbat incidentally, he has fulfilled his obligation," as this would be a significant novelty. Furthermore, in Berachot (21a), it says: "Those who erred and mentioned weekday in their Shabbat prayer, they complete the blessing," as stated in Section 4. It should have taught us a greater novelty, that even if he prayed the entire weekday Amidah, he fulfills his obligation if he only mentioned Shabbat. Additionally, it is a clear ruling that everything follows the conclusion, (Berachot 12a), and this law requires further study. (Also, the Magen Avraham in Siman 267 questioned from Siman 487, that if one concluded on Yom Tov with 'Who sanctifies Shabbat', he has not fulfilled his obligation, even though he mentioned Yom Tov in the middle, and he answered that this is worse. In Siman 487, he wrote that it refers to someone who did not mention Yom Tov in the middle, and this was already questioned by the Eliyah Rabbah in Section 7 and Taz in Section 6. The truth is, he labored to resolve it in this way and that way. In any case, the commentators did not disagree with the Beit Yosef in practice.)

If one is unsure whether one mentioned Shabbat in their prayer or not: According to the words of our teacher, the Rema, later in Siman 282 - one does not need to repeat, but there are those who disagree and hold that one must repeat (Bach and Magen Avraham there) because it is certain that the weekday habit prevailed. There are those who say that if before the prayer one had the intention of Shabbat - one does not need to repeat, because it is assumed that one mentioned Shabbat. But if one did not have the intention of Shabbat - one must repeat, because it is certain that the weekday habit prevailed (Taz there) and this is the primary ruling in practice.

If one made a mistake and prayed the weekday prayer on Shabbat and did not mention Shabbat: if he has not yet moved his feet, meaning he has not finished his prayer, or even if he finished his prayer until "He who blesses His people, etc." and has not yet said "May the words of my mouth," or even if he said "May the words of my mouth" but has not yet said the supplications he is accustomed to say after the prayer, such as "My God, guard my tongue," or he is accustomed to other supplications - all of this is considered as if he has not moved his feet, and he does not return to the beginning of the prayer, but only to the Shabbat section. But if he completed all these things - it is considered as if he moved his feet, even though he did not physically move them, and he must return to the beginning of the prayer. And a prayer leader (Shaliach Tzibur) who made a mistake in the silent prayer - he may rely on the repetition of the prayer leader when there is a repetition, like in the morning prayer, and does not need to pray again silently, as mentioned above in Siman 126, see there.

If one makes a mistake in the Shabbat prayers and switches one for another, he does not need to repeat it, because they are all considered one; the main part is the blessing "Retzeh Bimnuchateinu" as we mentioned. However, if he remembers in the middle, he should stop and begin the appropriate prayer for that time, as there is no interruption in the middle since they are not blessings but merely praises. (Magen Avraham section 7)

There are those who say that if one switches the Musaf prayer with another, or another with Musaf, he must repeat it, since the Musaf prayer does not relate to the other prayers. In "Tikanta Shabbat," we speak only about the matters of Musaf which have no connection to the other prayers, and in the other prayers, Musaf is not mentioned at all. Therefore, it is worse than praying a weekday prayer and mentioning Shabbat, which is valid according to our master Beit Yosef because there is no falsehood there. But here, in all the prayers, when mentioning Musaf, it is as if one is speaking falsehoods, and conversely, in Musaf, if another prayer is mentioned, the Musaf offering is not mentioned at all, and the person has not fulfilled their obligation even if they mentioned Shabbat.

The first opinion holds that since, in any case, one prayed the Shabbat prayer, even though Musaf was not mentioned, he has fulfilled his obligation. This is a surprising matter. (See Magen Avraham section 9 and Eliyah Rabbah section 11 who disagree with Beit Yosef and hold that one must repeat, and so it appears in Tosafot at the end of Rosh Hashanah. Also, this is the ruling of the Gra in section 11, who completely omits the first opinion, and Taz section 9 tried to refute it, but his words have no substantial basis. It seems the main opinion is like the "yesh omrim" and study this well.)

(Yom Tov has the same ruling as Shabbat in prayer, and the second day of Yom Tov is also the same.)

There are places where in the blessing "Retzei Bimnuchateinu" during Maariv (the evening prayer) they say "V'yanuchu Va," and in Shacharit (the morning prayer) they say "V'yanuchu Vo," and in Mincha (the afternoon prayer) they say "V'yanuchu Vam" (Magen Avraham, subsection 3). It appears to me that the reason is as follows: The Torah sometimes refers to Shabbat in the feminine form, as in "Zachor ki kadosh hi lachem, mechaleleha mot yumat" (Exodus 31:14) - here it is feminine. And it is written in Vayakhel: (Exodus 35:2) "U'vayom hashevi'i... kol ha'oseh vo melacha," and similarly it is written: (Exodus 20:8) "Zachor et yom haShabbat lekadsho," and also "Shomer Shabbat mechalelo" (Isaiah 56:2) - here it is masculine. Therefore, at night, when the Torah uses the feminine term "laila" - they say "va," and "yom" (day) is always masculine in the Torah - therefore they say "vo." And in Mincha, which is close to the evening and includes both aspects, they say "vam." (And according to the measures, this also makes sense, and delve into it). They say: "Yisrael mekadshei shmecha" so that it will be similar to the ending of the blessing, and some have written "ohavei shmecha" which is puzzling, and also this is not the custom. (See Magen Avraham there).

And after the prayer, they say "Vayechulu," and even though each individual already said it in their prayer, nevertheless, everyone repeats it together aloud and standing. For although we all already testified quietly, and in pressing circumstances, one fulfills their obligation with this testimony, still, the best form of testimony is for everyone to testify together and aloud, as it is written, "And he heard the voice of the oath, and he is a witness, etc." Additionally, for the sake of a holiday that falls on Shabbat, where "Vayechulu" is not said in the prayer, and also to include those who do not know how to say it. Therefore, an individual praying without a minyan should not repeat "Vayechulu," and if they want to say it, they should not intend it as testimony, but rather as a recitation from the Torah. (Taz, section 5)

Afterward, the prayer leader (shaliach tzibbur) recites the blessing of "Me'ein Sheva," which is: "Blessed... Shield of the Fathers... accept our rest" until "Sanctifier of the Shabbat." Even though there is no repetition of the Amidah in the evening service, this blessing was instituted because their synagogues were in the fields, and some people would come late to the synagogue for the evening prayer. This blessing was established so that while the prayer leader recited it, individuals would complete their prayers and not remain alone in the field, which could be dangerous. Therefore, this enactment remains even today, although our synagogues are in the city. 

This blessing reflects the seven blessings of the Shabbat Amidah in a condensed form, as follows: "Shield of the Fathers by His word" corresponds to "Shield of Abraham," "Reviver of the dead by His command" corresponds to "You revive the dead," "The Holy God without comparison" corresponds to "You are holy," "Who grants rest to His people on His holy Shabbat" corresponds to "accept our rest," "Before Him we will serve with awe" corresponds to "accept," etc., "The service of Israel, Your people" and "We give thanks to His name" correspond to "We thank You," "Master of peace" corresponds to "Grant peace" (as explained by the Ateret Rosh citing Avudraham).

Therefore, on a Yom Tov that falls on Shabbat, the mention of Yom Tov is not included in this blessing because the enactment was solely due to the danger, and thus they did not establish to mention Yom Tov in it, and it is recited as on all other Shabbatot. Even when Yom Tov falls on Friday night, when everyone is available and not late to the synagogue, the enactment remains, and the prayer leader still recites this blessing, as the Sages did not differentiate.

And the entire congregation is obligated to listen to this blessing from the mouth of the prayer leader (Shaliach Tzibbur), and not to talk at all, and also during the recitation of 'Vayechulu' it is forbidden to talk. However, an individual should not say it, as it was only instituted for the prayer leader in the context of the repetition of the Amidah. The custom is for the congregation to say 'Magen Avot' until 'Zecher Lemaaseh Bereishit', as there is no concern of a blessing in vain. Nonetheless, there are places where the congregation does not say it at all, and this is proper. Similarly, an individual praying alone should certainly not say this blessing, but if he wishes to say from 'Magen Avot' until 'Zecher Lemaaseh Bereishit', he is not prevented. This blessing was instituted even for a congregation only in a synagogue or a fixed study hall with a regular minyan, but when praying in a temporary place, such as in a bridegroom's house or a mourner's house or for another reason, it is not said at all. Some say 'Magen Avot' until 'Zecher Lemaaseh Bereishit', and they are not prevented, but it has no taste or aroma. In summary, it was only instituted in a fixed minyan where there is a Torah scroll. (Shnei Luchot HaBrit) Therefore, when a minyan is established for a certain period, and there is a Torah scroll there, they say it, but if not, they do not say it, and if one says it, it is considered a blessing in vain. Similarly, there are places that say after the full Kaddish 'Mizmor LeDavid Hashem Ro'i' and half Kaddish and 'Barchu', and this too is only in a fixed minyan like the blessing of 'Magen Avot', and there are those who err in this and they need to be warned about it. (See Magen Avraham, Siman 14, who wrote regarding the blessing of Me'ein Sheva in a non-fixed minyan that they are not prevented when they say it, but the great ones disagreed with him as written in Pri Megadim there, that there is a concern of a blessing in vain, see there)

If one prayed the weekday prayer and did not mention Shabbat, or did not pray at all, our teacher the Beit Yosef rules in section 13 that if one hears the abridged blessing of the Shabbat prayer from the prayer leader from beginning to end, he has fulfilled his obligation, and it is preferable to recite it along with the prayer leader. (There, section 15) The reason we are lenient in this case is because the evening prayer is optional. (There) And the Tur raised a difficulty with this ruling, see there, and indeed it has been clarified many times that for us it is considered obligatory. Nevertheless, all the great authorities agreed to this ruling. However, it is certain that if one did not hear it from the prayer leader, he should not recite it alone, as it was only instituted for the prayer leader in a communal setting. However, if he did recite it, it counts for him. (There, and there is an opinion that on Shabbat the evening prayer is not optional, but this does not seem to be the opinion of our Rabbis, and if it is because of Kiddush, he can sanctify over the cup. And according to this ruling, if Shabbat coincides with a festival and one prayed the festival prayer and did not mention Shabbat, he can rely on hearing the abridged blessing from the prayer leader.)

In the time of the Talmud, they would make Kiddush in the synagogue. And even though there is no Kiddush except in the place of a meal, in their times there were adjacent rooms in the synagogue, and guests were commonly found there, and for them it was a place of a meal. (Pesachim 100a) Therefore, in a place where there are no guests adjacent to the synagogue, the Kiddush is not effective at all. Hence, the Tur protested against our custom of making Kiddush in all synagogues, considering it a blessing in vain, since we do not have guests with us. And so wrote our rabbis, the Ba'alei Tosafot in Pesachim (100a s.v. "Yedei"): "And where there are no guests adjacent to the synagogue, one should not make Kiddush, for it is a blessing in vain, as we hold according to Shmuel that there is no Kiddush except in the place of a meal." End quote. And so wrote the Rosh there.

However, some of our rabbis have written that it is a fixed ordinance and cannot be annulled even when there are no guests, like the 'Me'ein Sheva' blessing, whose ordinance was because of harmful spirits, which nowadays is not relevant as mentioned in the previous section; nevertheless, it has not been annulled, and this is also the case here (Ran, there). Similarly, we find in the Rambam, who responded to someone who asked him: If in a place where everyone is proficient in prayer, is the repetition of the Shaliach Tzibbur (congregational leader) necessary? He responded with the following language: "Since the Sages decreed to appoint the Shaliach Tzibbur... just as they decreed the Kiddush in the synagogue because of guests, and all synagogues are obligated even though there are no guests, etc." (Teshuvot HaRambam, end of Teshuvot Harashba, Siman 31). 

I have seen someone write that there was never a fixed ordinance about this, but rather it became customary by itself, and it is not comparable to the ordinance of the repetition of the Shaliach Tzibbur and the 'Me'ein Sheva' blessing (Bach). In my humble opinion, it seems clear from the language of the Talmud there: 'And why does Shmuel need to sanctify in the synagogue,' it implies that it was a fixed ordinance, for if not, it should have questioned why we allow them to sanctify in the synagogue, as it questions similarly in Rosh Hashanah (15b). 

Similarly, the Rashba wrote in his responsa (Siman 37 and 323), and this is his language: "Initially, they decreed to sanctify in the synagogue, and the essence of the decree was because of guests, and they decreed to sanctify whether there are guests or not, similar to the 'Me'ein Sheva' blessing, etc." He further wrote there that this is an old dispute among the great ones of the world, for Rav Hai Gaon and Rabbi Yosef Ibn Giyyat are among those who prohibit when there are no guests, and Rav Natronai is among those who permit, along with a group of prophets, and the ruling has already spread according to them. 

Similarly, the Maggid Mishneh wrote in chapter 29, law 8, on what the Rambam wrote: And why do we sanctify in the synagogue because of the guests, etc., and he wrote: "Nevertheless, now... even though there are no guests eating, since it was decreed - the decree has not moved from its place."

The Rosh, in the name of Rabbeinu Yonah, wrote that Kiddush in the place of a meal is only a rabbinic requirement, but according to Torah law, one has fulfilled the obligation even not in the place of a meal. And since there are people who do not know how to make Kiddush, it is better that they hear it in the synagogue and thus fulfill their Torah obligation at the very least. This, however, is not agreeable to most of the authorities who hold that Kiddush over wine is only a rabbinic requirement, and according to Torah law, one fulfills the obligation through prayer, as stated in Siman 271. If so, even for those who do not know how to pray, there is no benefit, for according to Torah law they have already fulfilled the obligation through prayer, and according to rabbinic law, there is no benefit unless we say that the benefit is for those who also did not pray, which is not common nowadays. Or it is possible that Rabbeinu Yonah holds that Kiddush over wine is a Torah obligation, and this will be explained in Siman 271 with God's help.

Our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote: "It is customary to recite Kiddush in the synagogue, but the one reciting it should not taste the wine of the Kiddush, rather he should give it to a child to taste, because Kiddush is only valid in the place of a meal. Initially, it was instituted only for the sake of guests... and now... the enactment has not been nullified... but it is better to establish the custom not to recite Kiddush in the synagogue, and this is the custom in the Land of Israel." End quote. In Ashkenaz, it is customary to recite Kiddush, and this is also the custom in our country in all synagogues and study halls. However, those who pray in the Sephardic rite do not customarily recite Kiddush. Our master, the Rema, wrote that it is customary to stand while reciting Kiddush in the synagogue. End quote. This means that although at home Kiddush is recited while seated, as it is written in Siman 271 that the custom is to recite Kiddush while seated, nevertheless, in the synagogue, Kiddush is recited while standing, and the reason is out of respect for the congregation. This applies to the prayer leader who recites the Kiddush, and not to the entire congregation, as the Levush also wrote. Some interpret that the entire congregation needs to stand (Elya Rabba), and they wrote that it is a segulah (remedy) for knee pain, but we have never seen this custom practiced. Also, what the Tur wrote in the name of the Gaon, that it is a segulah to put the wine into the eyes, see there. We have also not seen this custom with Kiddush, only with Havdalah. (And in Berachot 43b, it equates Kiddush with Havdalah in this regard).

And this that he wrote: 'that they taste it for the minor' - this is not like feeding a minor prohibited food by hand, for there are those who opine later in Siman 343 that even a rabbinic prohibition is forbidden to give by hand. For in this case, there is no prohibition at all for the minor, for we do not prohibit feeding the minor without Kiddush, as in this case, we are not obligated to educate him so that he does not become weak-hearted, similar to fasts where we do not educate them at all (see Magen Avraham). And there are those who wrote that it is given to a minor who has not yet reached the age of education (Bach), and so the custom now is to give many minors little by little, and these are minors who have not reached the age of education. But in the name of the Rashba, it is written to give specifically to minors who have reached the age of education for the reason we have written. And if there is no minor in the synagogue, an adult should drink the entire cup, and rely on the opinion in Siman 273 in the name of the Geonim, that in such cases it is considered 'in the place of a meal,' and he can eat elsewhere, as mentioned there. Or the one making Kiddush should drink the entire cup and intend to fulfill his obligation with this Kiddush, and at home make Kiddush for his household. And the custom is to purchase this mitzvah of wine for Kiddush and Havdalah with money (Magen Avraham), and they consider this a great mitzvah.
