And in the 'Mi Sheberach' on Shabbat after the reading of the Torah, they established a blessing for one who gives wine for Kiddush and Havdalah, as written in the siddurim.

The custom is to recite the chapter "Bameh Madlikin" because it contains the laws of kindling lights, and perhaps someone did not follow the law and lit with oils and wicks that are forbidden to use; he will then go and correct it. Additionally, because it contains the Mishnah: "A person must say three things in his house on the eve of Shabbat as it gets dark: 'Have you tithed?', 'Have you made an eruv?', 'Light the candle,' and through this saying, he will remember to do so.

According to this, we should say it before the evening prayer, because after the evening prayer we cannot correct it, as we have already accepted Shabbat with the recitation of "Barchu." There are places where this is said after the evening prayer, and this is not correct. There is an opinion that since in our times we do not use forbidden wicks and oils, we do not need to be concerned about this. (Bach) However, it seems to me there is another reason: In ancient times, when they would pray the evening prayer while it was still day, and their acceptance of Shabbat was with "Barchu," it made sense as a correction for someone who violated this. But now, when we do not pray so early, and for us, the acceptance of Shabbat is with "Mizmor Shir Leyom HaShabbat" and "Lecha Dodi," even if we say it before "Barchu," we have already accepted Shabbat and it is impossible to correct it. Additionally, in most places, it is after sunset, and therefore, they do not practice this stringency. We have already written in Siman 267 that there are those among us who do not say "Bameh Madlikin" at all, but rather a passage from the Zohar, "K'Gavna" etc., as explained there, and all this is for the reason we have explained.

Some do not recite it on a Yom Tov (festival) that falls on the eve of Shabbat or during Chol HaMoed (the intermediate days of a festival). Also, on a Yom Tov that falls on Shabbat, they do not recite the psalms and "Lecha Dodi," but only "A Psalm, a Song for the Shabbat day." For if we say then "Let us welcome the Sabbath," it would be disrespectful to the Yom Tov, implying that we do not welcome the Yom Tov. However, the Sephardim begin from "A Psalm of David," and everything follows the custom. There are those who wrote that one does not say "Bameh Madlikin" on Shabbat Chanukah, but this is not the custom. (See Bach, Taz, and Magen Avraham)

We learned in a Baraita in Pesachim (106a): "Remember the Sabbath day to sanctify it (Exodus 20:8) - remember it over wine at its entrance." For "remembrance" is written in connection with wine - "its remembrance is like the wine of Lebanon" (Hosea 14:8), "we will remember your love more than wine" (Song of Songs 1:4) (Tosafot). It seems that the Kiddush over the wine is an Asmachta (a rabbinic support for a biblical text) (ibid). Additionally, it can be said that the Kiddush over wine is a Torah commandment, but the requirement that the one who blesses must taste it is rabbinic (ibid). Our sages, the Tosafists, were uncertain whether Kiddush over wine is a Torah commandment or rabbinic. And the Rambam at the beginning of chapter 29 wrote: "It is a positive commandment from the Torah to sanctify the Sabbath day with words, as it says: (Exodus 20:8) 'Remember the Sabbath day to sanctify it,' meaning remember it with words of sanctification. And one must remember it both at its entrance and at its exit: at its entrance with the Kiddush of the day, and at its exit with Havdalah... And from the words of the scribes (rabbinic) to sanctify over wine and to differentiate over wine, etc." Thus, he explicitly wrote that from the Torah, one fulfills the obligation with words alone. According to this, from the Torah we fulfill our obligation in prayer, in the blessing of 'Retzeh Vahachalitzenu' where we bless 'Who sanctifies the Sabbath,' and the Kiddush over the cup is rabbinic. In the Mechilta it is stated: 'Remember the Sabbath day, etc. - sanctify it with a blessing,' and thus it is concluded by the great authorities that this is rabbinic (Magen Avraham 271:1 and Sha'ar HaTziyun 50). Similarly, the SeMaG (Sefer Mitzvot Gadol) wrote in the positive commandments (29) that from the Torah it is with words alone.

But from the words of Rashi in Berachot (20b), who wrote: "Kiddush of the day is a positive commandment that is time-bound, 'Remember the day of Shabbat to sanctify it' - remember it over wine," it is clearly implied that it is from the Torah. Similarly, the commentator at the beginning of Nazir (4a) wrote that Kiddush over wine is an obligation from Mount Sinai. And likewise, the Ran in Pesachim there wrote that Kiddush of the day over a cup is rabbinic, but the Kiddush of the night is from the Torah, as it is a complete derivation. And this is also evident from his words in the second chapter of Shabbat, where the Talmud says (Shabbat 23b) that the Chanukah candle takes precedence over the Kiddush of the day because of publicizing the miracle. The Ran questioned how we can set aside the Torah obligation of Kiddush of the day in favor of the rabbinic Chanukah candle, and he answered that one can make Kiddush over bread. And if you think that from the Torah one fulfills the obligation merely by reciting words in prayer, his question would not even begin. (See there in Anshei Shem, and it is not so; examine it well.) According to his words, it is not specifically wine, as bread would also suffice, but for some matter one must make Kiddush from the Torah. And in the name of the Ra'avan, they brought that it is specifically wine that is from the Torah, as it is a complete derivation 'remember it over wine,' and so wrote the Or Zaru'a HaGadol. (Siman 25)

And in my humble opinion, it seems that there is proof for this view from what we say in Pesachim (117b): "Rabbi Acha bar Yaakov said: One must mention the Exodus from Egypt in the Kiddush of the day, as it is written here: 'Remember the day,' and it is written there: 'So that you remember the day you left the land of Egypt'." Now, if you think that by Torah law one fulfills the obligation with prayer, then it should have been enacted to mention the Exodus in the prayer, for that is the essence of Kiddush by Torah law. And even if we say that mentioning the Exodus is merely a rabbinic support, still, how could we abandon the essence of Kiddush by Torah law? Rather, it is certain that even by Torah law, one does not fulfill the obligation with mere words. This is also clarified by the Jerusalem Talmud in Berachot, at the beginning of the chapter "These are the things," where Rabbi Zeira says that we learn from both opinions: we make Havdalah without wine, but we do not make Kiddush without wine. This does not specifically require wine, but the same applies to other beverages. And in the rabbinic enactment, it is explicitly stated in the Jerusalem Talmud in the chapter "One does not stand" that Havdalah is also made over a cup, and Rabbi Zeira himself says there that they enacted both in prayer and over a cup. Rather, it is certain that by Torah law, Kiddush also requires some substance, hence they were stringent about using wine specifically. But for Havdalah, prayer alone suffices by Torah law, and therefore they were not stringent about requiring specifically wine.

And this is the language of the Ba'al Halachot Gedolot (Section 12): "We are obligated to sanctify the Sabbath day and the holy days in prayer and over a cup of wine, as it is written: 'Remember the Sabbath day to keep it holy'—remember it with wine upon its entry. From here, the Sages derived the obligation of sanctification (Kiddush) of the day from the Torah. This only teaches about the Sabbath; from where do we learn about Passover? It is stated: 'That you may remember the day you came out of the land of Egypt' (Deuteronomy 16:3). From where do we learn about the Festival of Weeks? It is stated: 'And you shall remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt' (Deuteronomy 15:15). From where do we learn about the Festival of Booths? It is stated: 'And you shall remember...', etc. And although we mention it in Kiddush, it must also be mentioned in prayer and in the blessing after meals. What is the reason? 'Remember' and 'you shall remember that you were a slave...', etc.—these are two verses, and we learn the festivals from the Sabbath: Just as the Sabbath is sanctified in prayer and over a cup, so too are the festivals sanctified in prayer and over a cup." End of quote. And he does not count Rosh Hashanah, because it does not need a separate derivation, as it is explicitly called a 'remembrance of the sounding of the shofar' (Leviticus 23:24), and since the derivation is from the term 'remembrance', it is obvious that Rosh Hashanah is similar to the Sabbath in this regard. And from his wording, it implies that it is of Rabbinic origin, as he says: 'From here the Sages derived, etc.', and furthermore, he equates the Sabbath with a festival, and the sanctification of a festival is certainly of Rabbinic origin, as stated by the Maggid Mishneh in Section 18. (Magen Avraham, Section 1) And the sanctification of the day is also of Rabbinic origin, only for the honor of the day. Therefore, they did not institute [specific] words for it, because the primary Kiddush is at night upon the entry of the Sabbath, as stated by the Ra'avad in Chapter 29, see there.

Women are obligated in the sanctification of the day (Kiddush) according to Torah law, and even though it is a positive time-bound commandment, because the commandment 'Remember' is juxtaposed to 'Observe', and since these women are included in 'observing' (which is a prohibition), and women are obligated in prohibitions - they are also included in 'remembering' (which is Kiddush). (Berachot 20b) And our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 2: they can fulfill the obligation for men, since they are obligated by Torah law just like men. Even according to those who hold that Kiddush over the cup is Rabbinic, since according to Torah law one fulfills the obligation through prayer - nonetheless, men and women are equal in this regard, and whatever the Rabbis instituted resembles the Torah law. And also, for women, since according to Torah law they fulfill the obligation through prayer, and over the cup they are obligated by Rabbinic law, they stand on the same level and can fulfill the obligation for men. Some wish to say that women cannot fulfill the obligation for men, as in the case of the Megillah later in section 689. (Rashal and Bach) This is not the main opinion, since there, because it is in public, it is considered disrespectful, as Tosafot wrote in Sukkah 38a, which is not the case with Kiddush. This is also written by the commentators on the Shulchan Aruch. (Taz and Magen Avraham paragraph 2)

It appears at first glance that when one person fulfills the obligation for another, it is when either both have prayed or neither has prayed, as their obligations are equal. But if one has prayed and the other has not, the one who prayed does not fulfill the obligation for the one who has not prayed, according to the poskim (decisors) who hold that the obligation of prayer is from the Torah. In that case, the one who has already prayed has an obligation only from the Rabbis, and the one who has not prayed has an obligation from the Torah, and a Rabbinic (obligation) cannot fulfill a Torah (obligation). However, according to this, we would not find our way in all families, where the head of the household recites Kiddush and fulfills the obligation for his wife, daughters, and daughters-in-law, even though they have not prayed. But the truth is that this applies only to blessings of enjoyment and blessings of sustenance, but not to blessings of the commandments, where one person can fulfill the obligation for another even if he has already fulfilled his own obligation, because "all Israel are guarantors for one another," as it is stated at the end of the third chapter of Rosh Hashanah. Therefore, a man and a woman can fulfill the obligation for each other in all aspects. There are those who want to say that a woman is not included in this guarantorship, and this is a surprising assertion. The Rosh, who wrote this reasoning at the beginning of the third chapter of Berachot, only meant it in a commandment that is not relevant to a woman, but in what she is obligated, she is completely equal to a man. (And so wrote the Gra in his glosses to the Shulchan Aruch and in his responsa).

It is obvious that a minor cannot fulfill the obligation for an adult or a woman, as they themselves are not obligated. Even when a boy is thirteen years and one day old, if we do not know for certain that he has grown two pubic hairs, he cannot fulfill the obligation for a woman who has not prayed, because her obligation is from the Torah, and in matters of Torah law, we do not rely on the presumption that he has grown signs of maturity, as stated in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 35 regarding testimony (Magen Avraham, Siman 682). However, if she has prayed, her obligation is only rabbinic, and in rabbinic matters, we do rely on this presumption. Although there are those who hold that Kiddush over a cup of wine is a Torah obligation, as we have written, in this case, we can rely on those who hold that from the Torah, prayer alone suffices, because even in the primary matter of not relying on this presumption in Torah law, there is some room for doubt. (See Tosafot, Bava Batra 154, s.v. 'And moreover', and Noda Biyhuda, Even HaEzer, Siman 61, and in our work Or LeYesharim, Siman 8, Ot 3).

And know that according to the opinion mentioned earlier in Siman 193, even in the Holy Tongue (Hebrew), one cannot fulfill the obligation on behalf of others unless they understand the language. However, when they do not understand, they do not fulfill their obligation unless they repeat word for word after the person reciting, for in such cases, even if they do not understand, they fulfill their obligation. Therefore, our women, most of whom do not know the Holy Tongue, do not fulfill their obligation in Kiddush unless they repeat word for word after the one reciting Kiddush, and this is not the custom. However, in truth, we explained there in Section 4 that the main opinion follows Rashi, that in the Holy Tongue, even one who does not understand fulfills their obligation by merely listening, and the custom serves as proof for our words. See there.

It is stated in Pesachim (105b) that the honor of the day takes precedence over the honor of the night. If one does not have enough wine or delicacies for both meals, the honor of the day takes precedence because the mitzvah of delight (oneg) is greater during the day than at night. I have seen that the Maharshal (Yam Shel Shlomo, Gittin, Chapter 4, Siman 51) criticizes the custom of eating fish on Friday nights and not in the morning. Since the honor of the day takes precedence, one should save the fish for the second meal. This was his practice.

In my humble opinion, I seek to justify the custom. Rashi and Rashbam specifically interpreted "much wine and delicacies" to mean fruits, as it is written "fruit of delights." This is because certain foods cannot be as good during the day as they are at night, such as hot fish, soup, and hot meat, which would spoil if left for the next day. This is similar to the concept of "decay of form" in sacrificial offerings. It is obvious that we should not leave good food for the day if it cannot be preserved. 

For example, wheat bread is better at night than during the day, as is well-known. However, the Torah did not command us to refrain from eating at night because we won't have the same quality the next day. Therefore, they interpreted it concerning wine and fruits, which do not spoil overnight, and in this case, the honor of the day takes precedence.

Therefore, since hot fish is more preferred by people than cold fish, and it cannot be the same during the day, we eat it at night, as well as hot soup. Conversely, we prepare foods that require long cooking, like kugel, for the day, and the holy community acts correctly.

This also clarifies the Zohar in Yitro (157a) cited by the Magen Avraham (Siman 271, Seif 4): "One should set the table on Friday night with bread and delicacies; Rabbi Yitzchak says, even during the day of Shabbat." This seems difficult—why “even,” if the honor of the day takes precedence? According to the above, it means that one should set the table on Friday night with bread and delicacies, even though the bread and delicacies are better at night because they are hot. One might think that since it cannot be as good during the day, one should not set the table at all but merely eat something small. Therefore, it teaches us that we should prepare as well as we can.

And that which the honor of the day takes precedence—this is regarding other items necessary for the meal. But if one has only one cup of wine, the sanctification (kiddush) of the night takes precedence over that of the day, for the main sanctification is at night, as we have said. Therefore, if one cannot afford both wine for kiddush and provisions for the meal in honor of the night and the day, and for the day’s kiddush, it is better to buy wine for the night’s kiddush than to prepare meal provisions or to buy wine for the day’s kiddush. However, bread takes precedence over everything, so that one should not be hungry and can fulfill the obligation of the three meals. It seems that the day’s kiddush also takes precedence over other foods of the day, except for bread. There is one who says that perhaps the honor of the day is preferable to the day’s kiddush, for the kiddush is due to the honor. (See Magen Avraham, section 263). But the main ruling is as we have stated, and this is also made clear in the Jerusalem Talmud brought by Tosafot in Pesachim (113a), which says: ‘What is the honor of the day?—the blessing over the fruit of the vine.’ (And so wrote Eliyah Rabbah, and Magen Avraham was also uncertain about this matter.)

Our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in Section 1: "When one comes home, one should hasten to eat immediately," his words end. This means to make Kiddush in order to remember Shabbat upon its entrance (Magen Avraham, Subsection 1), and consequently, one should eat immediately, due to the requirement of Kiddush in the place of the meal, even before it gets dark (Taz, Subsection 1). And one can eat by means of this Kiddush (ibid.), and we have already explained this in Section 267, see there. And it is obvious that if one is not yet able to eat, one can wait a few hours into the night (Responsa of Maharam Alshich). I have seen someone write that one should make Kiddush specifically before nightfall, because at the beginning of Shabbat night, the constellation is Mars, and at the end of Friday, the constellation is Jupiter - therefore one should make Kiddush under Jupiter (Magen Avraham, ibid.). In my humble opinion, this is astonishing, for heaven forbid to say that we are under the influence of the constellations. On the contrary, I have seen among the ancients that the ancient nations would sit in darkness and weep on Shabbat because the constellations of Shabbat indicate evil. And the Holy One, blessed be He, commanded us the opposite, to light many lights and to delight ourselves, to show that we are above the constellations. And the Lord took us to bring us out from under the system of the heavens, and how can we say such a thing? It is difficult to understand, and one who trusts in the Lord, kindness will surround him (Magen Avraham ibid. brings the Jerusalem Talmud at the beginning of Berachot that the custom was to eat an hour or two into the night, see there. However, see the commentary of the Chareidim that "two" means two parts of an hour, and the reason is that synagogues were in fields far from the city, and by the time they arrived, time would pass naturally. On the contrary, from the explanation there regarding those who lived in villages, it implies that it is a mitzvah to eat earlier, and consider this well).

Once the time for Kiddush has arrived, meaning after nightfall, even if one has not yet accepted Shabbat, it is forbidden to eat or drink anything, even water, or even to taste anything at all, until one makes Kiddush, out of respect for Shabbat. For Shabbat has established itself upon arrival of its time, even if one has not yet accepted Shabbat, and the obligation of Kiddush takes effect, and it is forbidden to taste anything until one makes Kiddush. However, rinsing one's mouth is not a concern since one does not intend to taste. (Magen Avraham, Section 5) And if one has accepted Shabbat while it is still day, it is forbidden to eat, drink, or taste anything until one makes Kiddush, since one has accepted Shabbat. One can make Kiddush, eat, and then pray Ma'ariv (the evening prayer) afterward, provided it is more than half an hour before the time for reciting the Shema of Ma'ariv. If not, it is forbidden to eat due to the obligation of Shema, as stated in Siman 232. And know that even if one has only one cup of wine and wishes to save it for Birkat Hamazon (Grace After Meals), Kiddush takes precedence, even according to those who hold that Birkat Hamazon requires a cup. This is despite the fact that for Havdalah it is not so, as stated in Siman 296. (ibid.) And even if one can make Kiddush over bread, one should not do so but should make Kiddush over wine and recite Birkat Hamazon without a cup.

Not only is it forbidden to begin eating and drinking when the time for Kiddush arrives—this also applies to Havdalah—but even if they were gathered to eat while it was still daytime, in such cases with Havdalah, if they began eating during Shabbat while it was still day, they do not need to stop, even if the meal continues for several hours into the night. However, with Kiddush, this is not the case. Out of respect for Shabbat, one must interrupt their meal and make Kiddush. However, it is not necessary to completely stop by clearing the table and reciting the Grace after Meals. Rather, one spreads a cloth and makes Kiddush. This means that just as on every Shabbat, they bring the two loaves (lechem mishneh) before Kiddush, place them on the table, cover them with a cloth, and make Kiddush, as will be explained. This is also done now, and this is the decided halacha. (Pesachim 100.)

And since he is in the middle of the meal, how should he proceed with the blessing of "Borei Pri HaGafen" for Kiddush and the blessing of "Hamotzi"? The opinion of the Meor and the Sefer Mitzvot Gadol (SMaG) is that he performs Kiddush without the blessing of "Borei Pri HaGafen," and he eats without the blessing of "Hamotzi," since he is in the middle of the meal. But the Rif wrote: He spreads a cloth and performs Kiddush, and then he recites the blessing of "Hamotzi," finishes his meal, and recites Birkat Hamazon. From his words, it’s clear that the blessing of "Borei Pri HaGafen" is not necessary, but "Hamotzi" is necessary, and so wrote the Ba'al Halachot Gedolot (Bahag). The reason: The blessing of "Hamotzi" serves as an interruption for Kiddush, because once the day is sanctified, eating is forbidden (Rosh), and since eating is forbidden and he is obligated to make Kiddush, these two things require him to recite the blessing of "Hamotzi." However, the blessing of "Borei Pri HaGafen," which is before Kiddush, even though drinking is forbidden, still, since he has not yet interrupted with Kiddush, there is no need to bless. This matter is explicitly stated in the Jerusalem Talmud, Berachot (Chapter 1, Halacha 5), that there is no need for "Borei Pri HaGafen," see there. And consequently, it is understood that if he performs Kiddush on bread, there is no need for "Hamotzi," since it is like the blessing of "Borei Pri HaGafen." The Tur brought an opinion that also the blessing of "Borei Pri HaGafen" is necessary before Kiddush, and the reason is that since drinking is forbidden, the obligation of the blessing automatically applies, as it is like a complete interruption, but we do not find anyone who explicitly holds this view. (See Beit Yosef and Taz, section 5, and it is not compelling.) And even if someone were to hold this view, we do not concern ourselves with it, since it is against the Jerusalem Talmud, and also because we see that it is not considered a complete interruption, since we do not obligate him to recite Birkat Hamazon, only regarding "Hamotzi," it is considered an interruption due to Kiddush and the prohibition together, as mentioned, and it is like one who decides to eat more after finishing his meal, who needs to bless "Hamotzi" again, and similarly here. Nevertheless, the opinion of the Rambam in Chapter 29, Law 12, is like the Meor and the SMaG, see there. And for the practical law, our Rabbi the Beit Yosef ruled in paragraph 4 like the Rif, because the Rosh ruled so, and regarding the Rambam’s words, he was uncertain in his large book, see there, and he wrote the opinion of the Meor and the SMaG in the name of some who say so, see there. (And from the words of the Maggid Mishneh there, it is clear that he deduced a fortiori from "Borei Pri HaGafen" to "Hamotzi" that it is not necessary, see there and examine well.) (And the Magen Avraham wrote in section 8 that also for the wine within the meal, there is no need to bless, for there is no interruption between the Kiddush cup and drinking wine within the meal, see there. And it is obvious that this refers to when he drank wine during the meal while it was still day, for if not, it is obvious that he must bless on the wine, but when he performs Kiddush on bread, he should not bless.)

All that has been explained pertains to one who is in the middle of his meal when Shabbat enters. But if he has finished his meal, the Rambam writes there, and these are his words: "If he was eating and finished his meal with the entrance of Shabbat, he should first recite the Grace After Meals (Birkat Hamazon) and then sanctify (make Kiddush) over a second cup (of wine). He should not recite the blessing and sanctify over one cup, because we do not perform two mitzvot with one cup, as the mitzvah of Kiddush and the mitzvah of Grace After Meals are two separate Torah obligations." End quote. And the language of the Talmud (Pesachim 102b) is: 'Because we do not bundle mitzvot together,' and from the language of the Rambam it implies that this rule only applies to two mitzvot that are Torah obligations. According to this, in his view, since one fulfills the obligation of Kiddush from the Torah with words alone, if Kiddush was made with words, both (Kiddush and Birkat Hamazon) can be done over one cup. All the more so with the blessings of betrothal (Eirusin) and marriage (Nisuin), since both are rabbinic blessings, they can be done over one cup. However, our Rabbis, the Tosafists and the Rosh, wrote differently there. And it is possible that the Rambam did not specifically mean 'Torah obligations,' but since this is the truth here, that both are Torah obligations, he wrote so, and the same would apply to two rabbinic mitzvot, as the reason is that it should not appear burdensome. (Rashbam there, and Rashi and Tosafot in Sotah 8a, though in Sotah only Torah obligations are considered there, and see Berakhot 49b, this requires further study and precision.)

One should not ask, "Isn't it required to make Kiddush in the place where the meal is eaten?" for it can be said that the meal that was previously eaten, when Kiddush is made immediately, is considered as being in the place of the meal. (Ran there) And the Tur and Shulchan Aruch write in section 6: "One must mention Shabbat in the Grace After Meals, even if one blesses before making Kiddush for Shabbat, and even if they did not eat at night at all." And even though it was clarified in section 188 that we follow the beginning of the meal, it can be said that Shabbat is different, because since it is established by itself, it is necessary to mention Shabbat. Additionally, since Kiddush is made immediately, Shabbat obligations automatically take effect. (See Magen Avraham section 14, who writes that this is due to doubt, and Taz section 8 who compares it to one who did not pray on Friday evening, who then prays twice for Shabbat on Shabbat, and I do not understand the comparison. In my humble opinion, it seems as I have written, but it is also written in the Rosh in this manner, and it must be said as we have explained, due to the fact that Shabbat has taken effect upon him. Based on this, all is one, and analyze this well.)

Indeed, our Rabbi the Rema (Rabbi Moses Isserles) wrote that there are those who say that one does not mention the Sabbath [in the blessing after the meal], as we follow the beginning of the meal, and this is the main opinion. And in the Tosefta of Berachot, we learned that one does mention the Sabbath, and this is when they also ate at night, but not when they finished while it was still daytime. Therefore, if indeed they also ate after nightfall, it is obvious that one must mention [the Sabbath]. (Magen Avraham, section 15) And know that there is a disagreement about whether one should taste from the cup of the blessing after the meal before sanctifying [the Sabbath]. Some say that one should not drink from it until after the Kiddush, and some say that one blesses on it and drinks, (ibid, section 16) and consequently, one should not bless on the cup of Kiddush [in this case].

And all this follows the opinion of the Rambam, who holds that one recites Birkat HaMazon and then Kiddush of the day. Even according to this view, some hold that one is required to eat a little before the Kiddush, so that the Kiddush will be in the place of a meal, and not rely on the meal that preceded the Kiddush. However, the opinion of the Rosh is completely different: even at the end of one's meal, one does not recite Birkat HaMazon first, rather one covers the bread with a cloth, recites Kiddush, then recites HaMotzi and eats a little, and afterwards recites Birkat HaMazon. And so it should be done if such a situation occurs, to avoid the dispute. And know that even according to the Rambam, this is only when one has already washed one's hands for Mayim Acharonim, but as long as one has not washed one's hands, even if one said 'Let's bless,' one should cover the bread and recite Kiddush. Those who disagree hold that even if one has washed Mayim Acharonim, one should cover the bread and recite Kiddush. However, in such cases, it is obvious that one should recite the blessing 'Borei Pri HaGafen' on the Kiddush, and also wash one's hands and recite 'Al Netilat Yadayim' and 'HaMotzi,' for after Mayim Acharonim the previous meal has already been concluded.

The Rambam wrote in the fourth chapter of Berakhot, Halakha 8: "If they were drinking and said, 'Come and let us recite the Grace after Meals' or 'Come and let us sanctify the day with Kiddush' - they are prohibited from drinking until they recite the Grace or the Kiddush. If they wish to return and drink before reciting the Grace or the Kiddush, although they are not permitted to do so, they must first recite the blessing 'Borei Peri HaGafen' (Creator of the fruit of the vine) and then they may drink. However, if they said, 'Come and let us recite Havdalah' - they do not need to recite the blessing again." So are the words of the Rambam.

Our master, the Beit Yosef (Rabbi Yosef Karo), copied this law regarding Kiddush only in Section 5, and from the words of the Rambam it is clear that even with 'Come and let us recite the Grace after Meals' it is forbidden to drink. However, our master the Beit Yosef ruled differently above in Siman 179, where he held that 'Come and let us recite Grace' does not prohibit drinking, but rather one must recite a blessing. We have already explained his opinion in Section 4 there. (See Taz, subparagraph 6).

It is clear from his words that for Kiddush, one must say 'Come and let us sanctify,' but without this, it is permitted - this applies during the day. However, once it is dark, even if they did not say 'Come and let us sanctify,' drinking is prohibited because Shabbat establishes itself. (And this answers the objection of the Raavad there). Even if there is a doubt whether it is dark, they must stop drinking (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 10). The law regarding Havdalah will be explained in Siman 299, with G-d's help.

In this law, when they said 'Come and let us sanctify' and they need to recite Kiddush, they do not need to recite 'Borei Peri HaGafen' on the Kiddush cup. Nevertheless, one should be careful not to come to such a situation because there are different opinions on this matter, and indeed, we have never heard of anyone doing so.

If someone forgot to recite Kiddush until after the blessing of "Hamotzi" and remembers before eating, he should recite Kiddush over the bread and then eat. He should not recite Kiddush over wine, as this would render the "Hamotzi" blessing void, since it would be interrupted by the Kiddush. It is obvious that if he already ate the "Hamotzi," he should pause his meal and recite Kiddush over wine. If he only has bread, he should take an uncut whole loaf and recite Kiddush without the "Hamotzi" blessing.

Similarly, if he has not yet eaten the "Hamotzi" but has already cut the loaves, he should take another whole loaf and combine it with the second whole loaf if he cut one, or two other whole loaves if he cut both, and then recite Kiddush. It seems to me that with two other loaves, he should also recite the "Hamotzi" blessing, since these loaves were not originally before him when he first recited "Hamotzi," and they were not in his intention.

(See Magen Avraham, Siman 271:11, whose intention is as I stated.)

However, regarding Havdalah, if it happened that he recited the "Hamotzi" and forgot to say Havdalah and remembers before eating, he must eat the piece of "Hamotzi," as Havdalah cannot be recited over bread, and his blessing would be in vain. Therefore, it is better to eat a little before Havdalah than to cause a blessing in vain, and afterward, he should pause and recite Havdalah.

There is an opinion that even for Havdalah, he should not eat and should first recite Havdalah and then recite "Hamotzi" again and eat, even though the first blessing will be in vain, because it is forbidden to eat before Havdalah. (See Magen Avraham, Siman 271:12, in the name of Ritzba.) However, Rabbi Rema in Siman 271:5 ruled as I stated earlier.

Even though it is forbidden to taste [food] before Kiddush, nevertheless, if one tasted or even ate, they should recite Kiddush immediately upon remembering, even at night. For it is established (Pesachim 107a): "If one tasted, they still recite Kiddush; if one tasted, they still recite Havdalah." And it appears to me that even if one did so intentionally, they still recite Kiddush or Havdalah afterward. And if someone did not recite Kiddush at night, whether unintentionally or intentionally, they should recite Kiddush the next day and say the nighttime Kiddush, except for "Vayechulu," which they do not say, because "Vayechulu" is only said at the entrance of Shabbat, since at the beginning of the night God completed His work. And perhaps you will ask: if so, how do we say "Vayechulu" when we recite Kiddush several hours into the night? This is not a question, for the entire night is considered one period. And it appears that when one recites Kiddush the next day, they fulfill the obligation of the daytime Kiddush as well, and there is no need to recite a separate Kiddush for the day, and one Kiddush suffices for both night and day.

There should be a cloth on the table under the bread, and another cloth spread over the bread, and this is the custom in all Jewish communities. This should be arranged before the onset of Shabbat. In the time of the Talmud when they ate at small tables, and each person had a table before them, they would arrange the table in another place, and after Kiddush they would bring the table before the person, and there was no need to cover the bread. But now that the table is large and always stands in the place of eating, and the challot are on it, it is necessary for the challot to be on the table at the time of Kiddush, so that the meal begins with the Kiddush, which is the honor of Shabbat. Therefore, it is necessary to place a cloth over the challot so that the bread's shame is not seen, as Kiddush is not made over it. According to this, after Kiddush one may remove the cloth. But the Tur wrote another reason: this is a remembrance of the manna, which was covered above and below. According to this, the cloth should remain until after the blessing of "Hamotzi," and this is the custom. Some bring the challot after Kiddush, but this only suffices for the reason that the bread's shame should not be seen, and it is not proper to do so. Moreover, even when making Kiddush over the bread, it should be done this way.

One sanctifies over a cup full of wine that is not blemished, and it requires everything that a cup for Grace After Meals requires: the cup should be whole, it requires rinsing on the outside and washing on the inside, it should be full, and the wine should not be blemished, as it is written in Siman 183. This requirement applies for both the morning Kiddush and Havdalah. The general rule is: everything that is required for the cup of Grace After Meals is also required for these, as well as for the Kiddush of Yom Tov. The one sanctifying holds the cup with both hands, then holds it with his right hand alone, lifts it a handbreadth from the table, and looks at the cup as it is written there, and says 'Vayechulu'. Even though it was said in the synagogue, one must repeat it over the cup to fulfill the obligation of 'Vayechulu', to testify about God’s creation of the world, for his children and household members who have not yet said it, such as those who were not in the synagogue. After that, he blesses 'Borei Pri Hagafen' and the Kiddush.

If it is necessary to perform Kiddush standing or sitting—it is not explicitly clarified in the Talmud or the poskim (decisors of Jewish law), and it appears that there is no strict requirement. From the end of the laws of Sukkah in the Rambam, it is explicitly clarified that they performed it sitting, as it is written there that on the first night of Sukkot, one must perform Kiddush standing so as not to sit before the blessing of "to sit in the Sukkah," and the Ra'avad objected to him, saying that even then they perform it sitting. It is explicitly clarified that they performed it sitting. And it is also clarified from Tosafot in Berachot (43a) that anything involving eating or drinking where one must fulfill others' obligation with his blessing must be done sitting, and they also wrote regarding Havdalah that it is better to perform it sitting, implying that they performed it sitting. The kabbalists wrote to perform it standing, and this was the custom of the Ari (Arizal), as he would hold the cup against his chest and perform Kiddush standing, saying that blessings for the bride must be performed standing, and the Sabbath is called a bride, as we say: "Come, bride, come, bride." According to the law, there is no strict requirement, and Tosafot already wrote there that even when performed standing, if everyone prepares themselves to listen, they fulfill their obligation with his blessing also standing. Only "Vayechulu" according to everyone should be done standing, as this is testimony. However, even in this, there are those who do not stand except for "the sixth day and the heavens and the earth were finished," as the initial letters form the name of God, blessed be He, and they stand in His honor.

And this is the language of our Rabbi, the Beit Yosef, in paragraph 10: "And he says 'Vayechulu' while standing, and afterwards, he says 'Borei Peri HaGafen,' and then the Kiddush." End of quote. And from the plain language, it implies that after 'Vayechulu' one needs to sit. And our Rabbi, the Rema, wrote on this, and this is his language: "He can stand during the Kiddush, but it is better to sit (because of the words of the Tosafot that we have brought). And it is customary to sit even when saying 'Vayechulu,' except when beginning, they stand a bit to honor the name of God, because they start with 'the sixth day' (meaning even though the verse starts with 'Vayechulu') and 'the heavens were finished,' and the name of God is hinted at in the initials. And when beginning, one should focus their eyes on the candles, and during Kiddush on the cup of blessing, and so it seems to me." End of quote. And focus one's eyes on the candle and the cup, and focusing on the cup is by law, as with all cups of blessing, and on the candle it is a hidden matter, for the healing of the eyes (see Magen Avraham, section 23). And if one forgot to say 'Vayechulu' before Kiddush - they say it during the meal over the cup (ibid., section 21). And behold, the words 'the sixth day' are the end of the verse 'And God saw all that He had made, and behold, it was very good. And there was evening, and there was morning, the sixth day' (Genesis 1:31). Therefore, some have the custom to say this entire verse quietly, and to begin from 'the sixth day' out loud. And the reason: so that the beginning is not in the middle of the verse, and this is proper.

The number of words in Kiddush is found in the Kabbalistic texts, which state that there should be 70 words: 35 in "Vayechulu" and 35 in the blessing, and with "Yom HaShishi" it totals 72, corresponding to the Name of 72, which is a combination of the Name of the Blessed Hashem. The blessing "Borei Peri HaGafen" is not included in the count, as it is a blessing over the wine, and this is also stated in the Zohar Vayakhel (page 247b). According to this, it is not necessary to say "Ki Hu Yom" nor "Ki Vanu Vacharta Ve'otanu Kidashta Mikol Ha'amim." However, we have the custom of saying them, and Heaven forbid to change any version. (Magen Avraham section 22) In Rashi (Ketubot 7b) and in Tosafot (Pesachim 104a), "Ki Hu Yom" is mentioned in Kiddush, see there. (And see Machatzit Hashekel section 22, and in my humble opinion, it also seems that according to our version, the beginning and end of the blessing are not counted in the number of words, like the blessing "Borei Peri HaGafen," which is missing 11, and here 10 are added, and they are 71 corresponding to the Sanhedrin of Moshe above them, and so it is in the Sanhedrin above, and you should examine closely.)

In that we say in the Kiddush "a remembrance of the Exodus from Egypt," and it is explicitly stated so in Pesachim (117b), the Tur was troubled by this, for the Sabbath is a remembrance of the act of Creation. He explained that it refers to "holy convocations," first of the holy convocations which are a remembrance of the Exodus from Egypt. In the name of the Rambam, it is written that the Sabbath itself is a remembrance of the Exodus from Egypt, because through the Exodus from Egypt it became clear that the Blessed One is an eternal God, who renews, desires, and is capable, and this is the essence of the Sabbath. However, the Ibn Ezra wrote according to its plain meaning, that the Sabbath itself is a remembrance of the act of Creation, and the rest of the servant on the Sabbath is a remembrance of the Exodus from Egypt, and this matter is explicitly stated in the last utterances: "So that your servant and your maidservant may rest as you do, and you shall remember that you were a servant in the land of Egypt" etc. (Deuteronomy 5:13-14).

There are those who have written that this is the reason we do not say in the Shabbat prayer: "You have chosen us from all the nations," because the commandment for Shabbat was given at Marah, and He had not yet completely chosen us until after the giving of the Torah (Taz, section 13, in the name of Orchot Chaim). Therefore, there are those who object to the wording "for You have chosen us, etc." I am puzzled by this reasoning, for if so, we should also not say "You have chosen us" on Passover, since the commandment for Passover was given in Egypt before Marah. Moreover, we were chosen from the time of the Exodus, as it is written: "I will take you to Me as a people, etc." (Exodus 6:7). Furthermore, as we have already explained at the beginning of section 242, it is more fitting to say that He chose us regarding Shabbat, because Shabbat pertains to all creations, as it is a remembrance of the act of creation, whereas the festivals have no such relevance. However, the truth is that it is fitting to say "You have chosen us" every day, and a clear proof for this is that we say every day in the blessing of the Torah: "Who has chosen us from all the nations, etc." The reason is that on Shabbat, there are other preambles in the prayer specific to Shabbat alone, such as "You sanctified," and similarly, all the Shabbat prayers as is known. But on a festival, we have no other preamble except "You have chosen us," which is a matter that includes every day, every time, and every moment. In Kiddush, we say "because You have chosen us," and this is a reason for what was previously said: for what we said "and His holy Shabbat in love and favor He gave us, a remembrance of the act of creation." It is difficult to understand, for this pertains to all creations, so we say "because You have chosen us"—to give Shabbat only to us, as explained in section 242. And on a festival, in Kiddush, we also say "because You have chosen us" for what was previously said: "and sanctified us with His commandments"—why? Because "You have chosen us," but in truth, this applies more to Shabbat than to any of the festivals, as mentioned there. (This seems clear to me with the help of Heaven.)

Rabbeinu the Beit Yosef wrote in section 11: "If one has only one cup, he should recite Kiddush over it at night and not taste from it, so as not to render it 'pagum' (blemished for further ritual use). Instead, he should pour from it into another cup and taste the wine of Kiddush from the second cup. The next day, he should recite Kiddush with what remains in the first cup. If there was only a precise 'revi'it' (a specific volume) and some was consumed at night, he should dilute it the next day to make up a full 'revi'it'. This is specifically when he has another cup for Havdalah, for if not, it is better to save it for Havdalah, which cannot be done with bread, rather than use it for Kiddush and not have wine for Havdalah. If he has two precise cups after dilution, he should recite Kiddush at night with one and Havdalah with the other, and not recite Kiddush during the day, as Kiddush of the night is preferable." End of quote. 

Some disagree with what was written, that one should taste from the second cup, asserting that the tasting must be from a 'revi'it'. Rather, it should be the opposite, that he should taste from the first cup and then add to it from the second cup (Magen Avraham, section 24). Additionally, some disagree with the statement that Havdalah is preferable to Kiddush, maintaining that Kiddush is preferable (ibid., section 25). It seems that this refers to Kiddush of the night, but for the day, Havdalah is preferable. It is clear that if he has beer for Havdalah, then even the daytime Kiddush is preferable over Havdalah (ibid.), as Havdalah can be done with beer, but not Kiddush, as one’s soul is repulsed by beer in the morning (ibid.). This is also explicitly stated in the Jerusalem Talmud at the beginning of the chapter 'These Things': that Havdalah can be done without wine, only with beer, but Kiddush cannot be done without wine. And even though it seems to refer to the night Kiddush, it is still a significant proof. However, it is certain that if one has only beer, Kiddush can be made on it if it is a common beverage in that place.

From the words of our teacher, Rabbi Yosef Karo (the Beit Yosef), who wrote: "And the next day one sanctifies with what remains in the first cup," we learn that even though one does not have a full cup, one may still sanctify on it if there is at least a revi'it (a specific measure). The requirement for a full cup is when it is possible, but when it is not possible, one sanctifies even if it is not full. We also learn from what he wrote: "that he should taste the cup of Kiddush from the second cup," that even though we require a full mouthful or the majority of a revi'it, in pressing times, such as when there will not remain a revi'it for the Kiddush of the next day or for Havdalah, one fulfills the obligation with just a taste. There is an opinion that interprets this as referring to having a full mouthful more than a revi'it and drinking it, but this does not seem reasonable at all, for if so, what kind of language is 'tasting'? 'Tasting' means simply tasting, like 'tasted - blemished'. And what we say in the Gemara: "the one who blesses needs to taste" also depends: if possible, he should drink a full mouthful, and if not possible, just tasting is sufficient. Additionally, in the Gemara (Pesachim 105b) it says: "from this we learn that the one who blesses needs to taste, and from this we learn that if he tasted, he blemished," indicating that just as blemishing occurs with any amount, so too the requirement to taste is the same, as it is one expression, and this is evident in Berachot. 

Although from the words of the Tosafot there in Pesachim it seems to align with the opinion that interprets it that way, from the words of Rashi and Rashbam there, it clearly does not appear so, and this is explicitly stated in the Mordechai there. For indeed, where did Tosafot get the idea to say that the teaching "he has only one cup" refers to having more than one full mouthful in addition to one cup? And the Mordechai explicitly wrote: "because it is impossible to measure exactly, there will necessarily be a bit more," but not a full mouthful, for where did he get this interpretation and this precision? However, the Mordechai wrote there that the rejection of Rav Ashi is for this reason, that one needs to drink a full mouthful, and here it is not so. Therefore, it is not an inference, as the reason is because tasting blemishes. However, according to Tosafot there, Rav Ashi's rejection is that there is no proof, and for the law, he does not disagree. Therefore, the matter requires further study. In pressing times, one can rely on the language of the Beit Yosef, as it seems from Rashi and Rashbam, and one can fulfill the obligation in pressing times with less than this. Note well. (Dilution does not apply to our wines).

Maimonides wrote in Chapter 29, Law 9: "If one desired bread more than wine, or if he did not have wine - he washes his hands first, recites the blessing 'Hamotzi', and sanctifies (Kiddush), and then he breaks and eats... And if one intended to sanctify over wine on Friday night, but forgot and washed his hands before sanctifying - he should sanctify over the bread, and does not sanctify over the wine after washing his hands for the meal." End of quote. And they wrote the reason, that since he washed his hands, he revealed his intent that bread is more precious to him, for otherwise he would not have washed his hands first. (Ran and Kesef Mishneh) And I do not understand the reason, for indeed he forgot and washed his hands, and if he had remembered, he would not have washed. If so, why should he not sanctify over the wine, unless we say it is due to the interruption of Kiddush between the washing of the hands and the eating, and this is as explained by Rashbam in the Talmud (Pesachim 106b). Or we could say the reason is that it appears as though he is washing his hands for fruit, which is considered arrogant (Rashbam there).

And our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in paragraph 12: "After one sanctifies over the cup, he washes his hands and recites the blessing 'Al Netilat Yadayim.' If he washed his hands before Kiddush, this reveals that bread is more important to him, and he should not sanctify over the wine but over the bread." These are his exact words. And according to this language, the reason is clear, for he did not write 'and he forgot,' and this is also the language of the Rif. It can be said that indeed his intention was to sanctify over the bread, because at that moment, bread was more important to him than wine. If so, the law is that one should sanctify over what is more important to him. However, the Rambam, who wrote that he intended to sanctify over the wine but forgot and washed his hands, certainly cannot explain this reason, but as mentioned. Nevertheless, according to this view, one should not wash his hands before he sanctifies over the wine, and if he did, he should not sanctify over the wine then. This aligns with our custom where we sanctify over the wine and then wash our hands, and when we sanctify over the bread, we wash our hands first. In these situations, it is not considered an interruption, since it is forbidden to eat until one sanctifies. Similarly, 'Vayechulu' is not considered an interruption between washing hands and 'Hamotzi,' since this is the order of Kiddush, and it is not worse than 'bringing salt for the bread' which is not considered an interruption, as mentioned earlier in Siman 167. All the more so, Kiddush, which completely prevents eating by a complete law. And although Rabbeinu Tam's opinion is not to sanctify over the bread, as mentioned in Tosafot and Rosh there, the Rambam and most of our rabbis disagree with him, and this is the simple custom in all Jewish communities.

However, our master the Rema (Rabbi Moses Isserles) wrote: "And some say that ideally one should wash his hands before Kiddush and recite the Kiddush over wine, and this is the prevalent custom in these regions, and it should not be changed except on the night of Passover," end quote, because the Haggadah constitutes a significant interruption. But Kiddush itself is not considered an interruption, even when recited over wine. This is based on the opinion of Rabbeinu Tam, who maintains that one does not recite Kiddush over bread, which necessitates a different interpretation of the Talmud there—that even when reciting Kiddush over wine, one washes hands first, due to the principle that Kiddush is only recited in the place of a meal, as explained in Tosafot and the Rosh there. This was the practice in his time, but in our time and for many generations before us, this custom was not known. In truth, the Tur (Rabbi Jacob ben Asher) also questioned this practice, and all the great Halachic authorities did not agree with it (see Beit Yosef, Bach, and Taz, who did not agree with this). Indeed, why should we abandon the opinion of the majority of the Halachic authorities? And our master the Rema, because this was the custom in his time and because they adhered to the opinion of Rabbeinu Tam as primary, wrote thus. But the later generations have ruled according to the majority of Halachic authorities (see Magen Avraham).

Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote: "One must drink from the cup of Kiddush a 'melo lugmav' (a cheekful), meaning enough to fill one side of the mouth and appear full, which is most of a 'revi'it' (a specific measure). If the one making Kiddush did not taste it but someone else at the table tasted a 'melo lugmav', they have fulfilled the obligation. The drinking of two people does not combine to make up a 'melo lugmav', but it is nevertheless preferable for everyone to taste. Some say that if, collectively, they drank a 'melo lugmav', they have fulfilled the obligation, as the drinking of all combines to the required measure. The Geonim hold that if the one making Kiddush did not taste, he has not fulfilled the obligation, and it is proper to be concerned about their opinion. This is specifically in regard to Kiddush, but for other matters requiring a cup, the Geonim agree that the tasting by another suffices." These words need clarification.

It appears that the matter is like this: Behold, it is explicitly proven in Eruvin (40b) that the cup of blessing is not invalidated if the one who recites the blessing does not drink it, but someone else does. For it says there in regard to Yom Kippur, according to the opinion that one should recite Shehecheyanu over a cup, that "What should he do? If he blesses over it and drinks, then once he says the Shehecheyanu, he has accepted Yom Kippur, and it is forbidden to give it to a child, etc." And Rashi explains that the statement "the one who blesses must taste" is not literal, as it can also be another person who tastes, because the reason is that it is disrespectful for the cup of blessing not to be enjoyed by someone immediately, making the blessing unnecessary, etc. But the Geonim said that Kiddush is different, as it is stated in Pesachim (107a) that "one who recites Kiddush and tastes a cheekful has fulfilled his obligation, and if not, has not fulfilled it," implying that the one who recites Kiddush himself must drink and enjoy a cheekful. And indeed, it is not understood, for regarding the cup of blessing, it is also stated, "the one who blesses must taste" (Berachot 52b), and yet another can drink, so the same should apply here. And the Rashbam there explains thus: "one who recites Kiddush and tastes a cheekful... and if none of those reclining tasted, but one of them did taste, they have all fulfilled their obligation, even though not all tasted," and this is the opinion of most poskim (decisors). (See Beit Yosef, who wrote the reason we mentioned, and Taz section 18 wrote the reason because Kiddush is a Torah obligation, and it is not understood, for a blessing in vain is also considered a Torah prohibition, and what is the connection?)

The reason for the first opinion that the amount of a cheekful of wine does not combine from the drinking of two people is because less than a cheekful does not provide complete enjoyment, and we require that one of them derives complete enjoyment. However, the Ritva wrote in Eruvin (79b) in the name of the Tosafot that the drinking of several people combines to make up a cheekful. The reason is simple, for certainly there is enjoyment even from a small amount of wine, and therefore, one blesses even on a minimal amount, because it is forbidden to derive benefit without a blessing. And it appears to me, in my humble opinion, that there is a clear proof that the drinking combines to make up a cheekful, for even in what is explicitly written in the Torah regarding the mitzvah of eating - nevertheless, the consumption of many individuals combines when many partake in this mitzvah. This is exemplified by the showbread, as it is written in Parshat Emor: "And they shall eat it in a holy place," and each eating is with an olive-sized portion as is known. Nevertheless, the sages said at the beginning of the fourth chapter of Yoma: each priest received a double portion, which is less than an olive-sized portion according to Rashi's explanation there. Therefore, we are compelled to say that the eating of all combines. Furthermore, there is proof from there that not all those present are obligated to taste from the cup, for it is stated that modest priests would withdraw their hands and not eat at all. This is difficult, for the Torah commanded to eat, but certainly since the Torah commanded the entire group of priests, it does not mean that each one individually is obligated to eat, but rather that it should be consumed among all of them, and they fulfill their obligation through the eating of others. And if so, all the more so regarding Kiddush, for according to most authorities it is on the cup by rabbinic decree, and even if it were by Torah law, there is no explicit commandment regarding its drinking as there is with the showbread's eating.

If one recited Kiddush and before he tasted [the wine] he interrupted with speech, he must recite the blessing 'Borei Peri Hagafen' again, but he does not need to recite Kiddush again. However, if he spoke about matters related to the Kiddush, or even matters related to the meal, it is not considered an interruption because Kiddush is a necessary part of the meal, like "preparing the ox" in Siman 167 or "bringing salt and spices" mentioned there. (Magen Avraham, Sif-Katan 31)

Our master the Beit Yosef wrote in Section 15: Similarly, if the cup spilled before he tasted from it, he should bring another cup and recite the blessing 'Borei Peri Hagafen' on it, and he does not need to recite Kiddush again. This is his exact wording. He explained in his major work as follows: "What we said, 'if he did not taste, he did not fulfill [the obligation],' means to say that he did not fulfill the mitzvah in its proper manner. There is support for this from what the Tur wrote in the name of Behag, and similarly, it is written in Orchos Chaim."

The Tur brings in the name of Behag: "One who makes Kiddush and before he tastes speaks - he must recite 'Borei Peri Hagafen' again, but does not need to recite Kiddush again." If it were thought that without drinking it is not considered Kiddush at all, then the Kiddush would be nullified before drinking due to the interruption of speech in between, just as the blessing 'Borei Peri Hagafen' is nullified. Rather, certainly the Kiddush is valid even without drinking after the fact, and this is why one needs to bless 'Borei Peri Hagafen' and drink it, because certainly, as much as possible, we try to correct the situation so that he drinks wine. Similarly here, he wrote for this reason that one should bring another cup and bless 'Borei Peri Hagafen' on it, but this is not related to Kiddush. This is a great proof for what we wrote in Section 30, that in a pressing situation, one fulfills the obligation of Kiddush even without drinking a full mouthful, and certainly from this law when he did not drink at all. Also here, since it is written, "if it spilled before he tasted," it clearly implies that if he tasted a little and then it spilled, nothing further is required.

I have seen someone write that without tasting a mouthful (of wine) - one has not fulfilled the obligation at all, even after the fact. And our teacher, the Beit Yosef, retracted in the Shulchan Aruch from what he wrote in his larger work, and therefore he wrote here that one should bring another cup and drink, and this cup is exactly like the cup of Kiddush, and with it, one fulfills the obligation of Kiddush. (Magen Avraham 32) But these words are puzzling, for in his larger work his intention is the same, as he brought proof from the Bahag, and the Bahag explicitly wrote that one needs to bless 'Borei Pri Hagafen' and drink, and the same is true here for the reason we explained. But what is the relevance of another cup to Kiddush? This matter has already been rejected (Eliyahu Rabbah and Taz), but certainly, this is the opinion of our teacher, the Beit Yosef - that without tasting, the mitzvah is not performed properly, but one has still fulfilled the obligation of Kiddush. (And what Magen Avraham questioned, that later he brings in the name of the Or Zarua the opposite - this is according to the Geonim, see there, but we do not hold like that. And what Magen Avraham compared another cup to the cups of the diners - this is just a wonder, for the cups of the diners were present at the time of Kiddush, and this has already been refuted. And what the Machatzit HaShekel wrote that they are defective cups, see there - this has no substance, for if someone makes Kiddush on a defective cup, does he need to redo the Kiddush?)

If one thought that there was wine in the cup and made Kiddush on it, but it was actually water, he must repeat Kiddush. (This is stated in the name of the Terumat HaDeshen and the Taz 19) This is not similar to a case where the wine spilled, because in that case, at least the Kiddush was initially made on a cup of wine. However, here, there was no wine at all, only water, and one does not make Kiddush on water. It seems to me that this applies specifically to water. But if it was whiskey or beer, even though one would need to say the blessing "shehakol" again, nevertheless, regarding Kiddush, one has fulfilled his obligation, since one can make Kiddush on them if they are considered a local beverage, as it is stated in Siman 272. Furthermore, even with water, if there was other wine on the table that he intended to drink during the meal, no new blessing is needed, as stated in Siman 206. Nevertheless, Kiddush must be repeated, since Kiddush was made on water and it is invalid. (Magen Avraham there and as written by the Machatzit HaShekel) There is an opinion that in such cases, even Kiddush does not need to be repeated, (Taz there) and although logically the first opinion seems correct, in practice, one should not make another Kiddush if there was wine on the table. (This also appears from the Eliyah Rabbah there) It is clear that someone who has only a small amount of wine should be careful not to drink more than a mouthful, so that he will have wine left for Kiddush during the day or for Havdalah. (Magen Avraham 30)

There are those who say that if one recited Kiddush in the morning over beer and the cup spilled, there is no need to bring another cup, because there are those who say that one fulfills the obligation with bread, as stated in Siman 272 (section 132). This means that if one blessed over wine and has another wine available, they must bring another wine, as against wine, one cannot rely on the opinion that bread suffices. But against beer, one can rely on that opinion. The same applies at night; however, at night, one does not recite Kiddush over beer. Furthermore, at night, it is not relevant to say to bring another and rely on the Kiddush over it, because at night there is the blessing of Kiddush, and if one brings another cup and blesses 'Shehakol', this is not the blessing of Kiddush. And to perform the entire Kiddush again, we have already ruled that it is not necessary if it spills, as stated in section 37. However, for the daytime Kiddush, which only has the blessing of the beverage, it is relevant to say that one fulfills the obligation of Kiddush. (See the glosses of R' Akiva Eiger, and it must be said that this is his intention.) Nevertheless, if one wishes to bring another cup of beer, they may do so, and they should not bless over it, as the first blessing already exempted it, which also exempts the beverage during the meal, and consequently, it is exempt from a blessing. (Magen Avraham, not like Taz) Even with wine, if one brings another cup, there is no need to bless 'Borei Pri Hagafen', unless they did not intend to drink more wine, as explained. There are those who disagree, and hold that since the beer spilled, one is obligated to bring another cup (there) and not rely on the Kiddush over bread, as most authorities prohibit Kiddush in the morning over bread. And know that beer is not specific, as the same applies to whiskey and mead, which are called 'mead'.

The participants are not permitted to taste from the cup of Kiddush before the one reciting the Kiddush. In what case does this apply? When they need the cup of the one reciting Kiddush, such as when they do not have their own cups, or they have cups that are defective or completely empty, requiring them to pour from the cup of the one reciting Kiddush. However, if they have intact cups of their own, they can drink beforehand. When two people are making Kiddush, and each one is saying the blessing for himself: one should bless and the other should answer Amen, and afterwards, the second should bless without answering Amen between the blessing and drinking, as that would be an interruption. It is better that one blesses with the intention to include the second person, and the second person should intend to fulfill his obligation, answer Amen, and drink. Why should they need two blessings?

When each of those seated has a complete cup in front of them, the one who blesses does not need to pour a little from his cup into theirs. But when their cups are blemished, he needs to pour from his cup into theirs. And if some of the cups are blemished and some are not, he pours into the blemished ones and not into the unblemished ones. And if they have no cups at all in front of them, they drink a little from his cup. All of this is ideally, but after the fact, it does not prevent the fulfillment of the obligation. And when the one who blesses pours into their cups, he pours before he drinks himself. If he has already drunk, they drink from the remnants of his cup.

It is stated in Bava Batra (97a): "We do not recite the sanctification of the day (Kiddush) except over wine that is fit for libation on the altar." And it is explained in the Gemara there: that things which are acceptable after the fact (bedieved) for libations, even though they should not ideally (lechatkhila) be brought, are nevertheless valid for Kiddush even ideally (lechatkhila). And these are: wine from the press, which has not yet been properly clarified - should not be brought for libations, but if brought, it is valid; and for Kiddush, it is valid even ideally, 'for Rava said: A person may squeeze a cluster of grapes and recite Kiddush on it.' (Bava Batra 97b) Similarly, wine from the press may be used for Kiddush, but it is preferable (to use) old wine. (Magen Avraham section 3) Similarly, one does not bring for libations from the top of the barrel, because it contains some particles, nor from the bottom of the barrel, because of the sediment, but rather from the middle; and if brought, it is valid. For Kiddush, it is permitted even ideally to use wine from the top or bottom of the barrel, but if there is a white film on it, one should not use it for Kiddush. (ibid section 4) Some prohibit in any case if there are particles in it, and it must be strained to remove the particles ideally, and for libations, even with straining, it is prohibited ideally. (This is necessary and study it well)

Black or very white wine, or wine that is very sweet and weak, or from a cellar, meaning that among them are found barrels that emit a vinegar smell but taste like wine, or wine made from raisins—all of these are initially forbidden for libations but are permitted post facto, and for Kiddush—even initially permissible. However, it is a mitzvah to choose good wine for Kiddush. The Ramban, of blessed memory, disqualifies white wine for Kiddush even post facto, and the 'white' mentioned in the Gemara there is not truly white, but rather tends towards whiteness, and therefore it is called 'green' in the Gemara there, referring to the sheen of whiteness. However, one can make Havdalah over it, as Havdalah does not require as good a quality as Kiddush. The custom of the world is not like the Ramban, but rather they make Kiddush on white wine. (Beit Yosef)

And wine that is invalid for libations even after the fact - for Kiddush, some say it is valid and some say it is invalid. How so? Wine that is pungent, whose smell is like vinegar but its taste is like wine - it is invalid for libations. And what has been explained that wine from the cellar is valid - this is because in the cellar most of it also has the smell of wine, but if it is known that its smell is like vinegar - it is invalid for libations. However, for Kiddush - it is valid, as we hold: 'If its smell is like vinegar and its taste is like wine - one recites the blessing of "Borei Pri Hagafen" over it', and it is valid for Kiddush. But the opposite, if its smell is like wine and its taste is like vinegar, meaning any wine that people refrain from drinking because of its sourness - even after the fact, it is invalid for Kiddush and for Havdalah, and one does not recite "Borei Pri Hagafen" over it. (Taz, subsection 3) And see above in section 204. And this is not included in the principle that one sanctifies only with wine that is fit for the altar, as wine whose smell is like vinegar and taste is like wine is invalid for the altar not because it is not wine, but because it is written with regard to sacrifices 'a pleasing aroma', and we require that its smell be like its taste. But for Kiddush, which is for taste alone - we do not care about its smell.

And similarly, diluted wine, even though it is invalid for libations, is valid for Kiddush even initially. Its invalidity for libations is because it is written "strong drink"—something that intoxicates. And we derive from the Sifrei: "And you shall pour a quarter of a hin as a libation—undiluted you pour and not diluted." But for Kiddush, it is obvious that diluted wine is preferable to undiluted, as undiluted wine is not so suitable for drinking. Nevertheless, even on undiluted wine, even though it is very strong and can take three parts water, one may make Kiddush on it. However, it is better to dilute it so that it is more suitable for drinking, provided it is diluted properly and not excessively with water. All this was regarding their wines, but our wines are better without dilution, as they are not so strong. Those that are suitable for dilution may indeed be diluted. And it is obvious that our raisin wine is not suitable for dilution at all, and if diluted, one would recite the blessing "Shehakol" and not make Kiddush on it, because even with a little dilution, it becomes like water, as is well known.

Wine with a bad odor is invalid for libations and also invalid for Kiddush, even if its taste and smell are like wine. What is considered a bad odor? It is when it smells bad (Rashi there), because its invalidity is due to its repulsiveness. Concerning this, the prophet said: "Offer it now to your governor; will he be pleased with you?" Therefore, it is invalid for all mitzvah purposes, including Kiddush, Havdalah, and the cup for Birkat Hamazon. Similarly, wine that has been left uncovered is invalid for libations, as there is concern that a snake may have drunk from it, making it repulsive and dangerous. Consequently, it is also invalid for Kiddush, even nowadays when we are not particular about uncovered wine. In truth, our wines are kept in covered bottles, and if they remain uncovered for a short time, it is not a concern (Magen Avraham, Sk 1), and even the governors and officials are not particular about this (there). However, if it remained uncovered all night or even for many hours, one should not use it for Kiddush, Havdalah, or the cup for Birkat Hamazon, although we bless "Borei Pri HaGafen" on it in our countries where snakes are not common and people are not cautious about uncovered wine. But for a mitzvah purpose, it falls under "Offer it now to your governor." For uncovered wine, filtering it through a strainer is not effective (Talmud there) for the reason explained, and it is important to warn about this, as not everyone is aware of this ruling.

Since it is explained in section 1 that the wine remaining at the bottom of the barrel, even though it contains sediment, is valid for Kiddush, therefore, wine sediment or grape seeds upon which water has been poured: if it is fit to recite the blessing "Borei Pri Hagafen" on it, as explained in Siman 204, one may use it for Kiddush. If not, one may not use it for Kiddush. And regarding the ruling that one may use raisin wine for Kiddush, the Tur writes as follows: "One may use raisin wine for Kiddush, whether they have shriveled naturally or whether they shriveled due to the sun or due to heat, such as by placing them in hot water to hasten their shriveling or by hanging them in smoke. This is provided that some moisture is extracted when they are pressed. But if they contain no moisture and nothing comes out of them except by soaking them in water - then not." End quote. This is also written by Rabbeinu the Rema in section 6, and indeed, this matter is also written by the Rif and the Rambam in chapter 29, see there.

And according to this, it is astonishing beyond measure how we sanctify (make Kiddush) on our raisins, for it is well known that the small raisins from which we make wine throughout our countries do not have any moist wine content, and how can we justify this? And we have already wondered about this above in Siman 204, Se'if 15, and we wrote there to teach favorably: that according to the Rif and the Rambam who hold that 'Ta'am Ke'ikar (the taste is like the substance) is not a Torah law' - it is sufficient if the wine itself from the raisins has a little wine content. But we hold like Rabbeinu Tam and the Ra'avad that 'Ta'am Ke'ikar is a Torah law,' therefore if soaking the raisins in water imparts a wine taste - it is considered as having the essence of wine, and it is regarded as wine. And in Siman 204, Se'if 16 we wrote another leniency: that wine depends on what the world considers wine, and what can we do since wine is not readily available among us, and also the laws of Temed (fermented drink) are explained there.

The Rambam wrote in chapter 29, law 14: "One may only recite Kiddush over wine that is fit for libation on the altar. Therefore, if honey or leaven has been mixed with it, even a mustard seed's worth in a large barrel, one may not recite Kiddush over it. This is how we teach throughout the West. However, there is someone who permits reciting Kiddush over it and says that 'wine fit for libation on the altar' was mentioned only to exclude wine that has a bad smell, is uncovered, or cooked, none of which may be used for Kiddush." End of quote. The explanation of the matter is as follows: It has already been clarified that not everything unfit for the altar is unfit for Kiddush, and the general rule applies only to what is blemished for the altar, such as having a bad smell or being uncovered, due to "offer it now to your governor" (Malachi 1:8), but not to other matters. The Rambam holds that the mixture of leaven or honey is also considered blemished because the wine remains as it was, and if so, why is it unfit for the altar? It is because it is considered blemished, akin to being uncovered. The dissenting opinion argues that this is not due to a blemish but because the Torah prohibited leaven and honey on the altar, as it is written: "For any leaven and any honey you shall not burn" (Leviticus 2:11), but this is not related to Kiddush and is akin to diluted wine, which is unfit for libations but fit for Kiddush. Most authorities agree with the one who permits it, and the opinion of the Rambam is not mentioned at all in the Shulchan Aruch. The Rashba brought proof from the Jerusalem Talmud in the chapter on the Four Cups, which states that one fulfills the obligation with spiced wine, which is wine mixed with honey and spices. This is also the opinion of the Ramban and the Ritva in chapter six of Bava Batra, and the Rivash wrote similarly, as did Rabbeinu Yerucham, who added that even if it contains so much honey and pepper that it changes, one may still recite Kiddush over it. (Beit Yosef)

And behold, the Rambam wrote that even cooked wine is invalid for Kiddush, and also in the name of Rashi it is written that one blesses over it 'Shehakol', and so wrote one of the Geonim (Tur). But Rabbeinu Tam, the Ri, the Itur, and the Rosh wrote that cooked wine is valid for Kiddush, and certainly one blesses over it 'Borei Pri Hagafen' (Tur).
