And their reasoning is clear: the Torah invalidated cooked wine for libations not because of its inferiority, for we have learned in a complete Mishnah at the beginning of Chapter 11 of Terumot that cooked wine is considered better there (see there), but because it changed from its original state, and it is written "sacrifice and libations"—just as the sacrifice did not change, so too the libations should not change (Bechorot 17). And this has no relevance to Kiddush. The first opinion holds that its taste changed for the worse, and the Mishnah in Terumot means that it improves in terms of lasting much longer than uncooked wine, but always loses the status of wine. And our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in paragraph 4: "One may sanctify over cooked wine and wine with honey, and some say one should not sanctify over them." Thus he concluded. And he took as primary the opinion of those who permit, and therefore wrote the opinion of those who prohibit as 'some say'. And so wrote our teacher, the Rama: that the custom is to sanctify over them even if one has other wine, only that it is not as good as the cooked wine or the wine with honey. And this is why the mixture of leaven was not mentioned—because it is not customary to mix leaven with wine, but if a little leaven fell into a lot of wine in a way that did not change the taste at all—it is also valid, according to those who disagree with the Rambam.

The Rambam writes there in Law 17: "A region where most of its wine is beer, even though it is invalid for Kiddush, it is permitted to make Havdalah on it, since it is the common drink of that region." This means that most of the drinking of the people in that region is beer. However, for Kiddush, it is forbidden in all cases, as Kiddush was only instituted over wine and not over any other drink. Consequently, if he does not have wine, he makes Kiddush over bread. Similarly, if he desires bread more than wine, he makes Kiddush over it, as explained earlier there, which we brought in the previous section 31. And from the fact that it was not explained that this applies specifically to the night Kiddush, we can infer that he holds there is no difference between the night Kiddush and the day Kiddush, for if it were otherwise, he would have explained it. And even though for the day Kiddush, when he makes Kiddush over bread, there is no distinguishing mark for Kiddush, since there is only the blessing of 'Hamotzi,' nevertheless, what of it? The distinguishing mark is the two loaves and his intention for the sake of Kiddush.

Here is the translation of the passage:

And behold, the Rif also wrote in the chapter "Arvei Pesachim" that one should only sanctify on wine, except if bread is preferred, one sanctifies on the bread. This is the opinion of the early Geonim: Rav Amram, Rav Tzemach, and Rav Nissim. Similarly, this is the opinion of the Raavya and the Maharam of Rothenburg. (Hagahot Maimoniyot there) However, the Rosh in the chapter "Arvei Pesachim" (Siman 17) wrote that one may sanctify on beer if it is a local beverage, and this is also the opinion of Rabbi Yehudah, the author of the Tosafot, and the Raavan, and the majority of the Geonim agreed with this. And indeed, from the Gemara (Pesachim 107a) it is clearly implied that there is no difference between Kiddush and Havdalah, as it says there that Rav and Shmuel hold: just as one does not sanctify on beer, so too one does not make Havdalah on beer. If so, just as we do not hold this way for Havdalah, so too for Kiddush. Furthermore, it is stated there that Rav sanctified on beer, which contradicts what the Talmud previously brought in the name of Rav. It is necessary to say that initially, it refers to a place where beer is not a local beverage, and where Rav sanctified on beer, it was a local beverage, and this serves as proof for those who permit it. In any case, there is no proof for those who prohibit it. However, in the Jerusalem Talmud, Berachot, beginning of chapter 8, it is explicitly stated like those who prohibit, as it says there: "One makes Havdalah without wine only on beer, but one does not sanctify without wine" there. And those who permit did not take this into account, since in the Gemara it is the opposite, and furthermore, the Rosh wrote there that one could say this is in a place where beer is not a local beverage there. (And those who prohibit are not satisfied with this, for if so, Havdalah should also be so, and the plain meaning of the Jerusalem Talmud does not imply this there)

Our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, concluded in paragraph 9 according to the Rosh, and this is their language: "In a place where wine is not readily available: there are those who say that one may recite Kiddush over beer and other beverages except for water, and there are those who say that one should not. According to the Rosh: at night one should not recite Kiddush over beer but rather over bread (and place his hands upon it), and in the morning it is better to recite Kiddush over beer, blessing 'shehakol' before the blessing 'hamotzi', for if one blesses over the bread first - there is no difference. These are logical words, and the common practice is in accordance with the Rosh. And if there is wine in the city - one should not recite Kiddush over bread," end quote, because the opinion of Rabbeinu Tam is that one should not recite Kiddush over bread. Nevertheless, one should not initially recite Kiddush over beer at night, because this is against the opinion of the Rif and the Rambam. But during the day - it is necessary to act against their opinion, for otherwise there is no distinction and change as mentioned. And it turns out that in practice they concluded not like the Rambam and not like Rabbeinu Tam, but where we can fulfill their opinions - we are obligated to do so, and if it is not possible - we abide by the law. (And we strive more to fulfill the opinion of the Rambam than to fulfill the opinion of Rabbeinu Tam, because the opinion of Rabbeinu Tam is a singular opinion, and pay attention to this).

However, what they wrote: that when there is wine in the city, one should not make Kiddush on bread, for certainly wine is the preferred mitzvah both at night and during the day. Nevertheless, even the great scholars of the generation customarily blessed on beer in the morning. (See Bach and Magen Avraham who noted that the Maharshal and Rashak did so, and they had wine available, as mentioned.) The commentators have labored to provide reasons for this: Some wrote that they wished to exempt the beverages during the meal, (Bach) and some wrote because wine was expensive, (Taz, section 6) and some wrote that in our country beer is considered the common beverage, (Magen Avraham, section 9) or perhaps the beer was beloved to them. For this reason, even today in our time many make Kiddush in the morning on whiskey, because for most people whiskey is preferable before eating, and for us it is the common beverage. Some wrote not to make Kiddush on whiskey unless in countries where most of the common people's drinking every day is whiskey, (ibid, section 6) and that one should be able to drink a cheekful at once. (Eliyahu Rabbah) And in our place, it is indeed so, where people do not drink such strong beverages, and it is the common beverage.

However, all the reasons are not satisfactory, because ultimately wine is certainly better than other beverages. So why didn't they make Kiddush over wine during the day, since they had wine in their homes or cities? In my humble opinion, there seems to be a clear reason: The Tur writes that what is considered other beverages that can be used as "local wine" is when there is no wine growing within a day's journey from the city. The Mordechai writes that it is when the vineyards have been damaged.

Now, all our early sages, as well as the ancient Geonim, were in Babylonia, Spain, France, and Germany, where there is a lot of wine, as grapes grow abundantly in all these regions. But in our northern regions, it is known that we do not have any wine at all, and the wine imported from other regions is prohibitively expensive, and many God-fearing people do not want to drink it due to concerns about its kosher status. We only have raisin wine, and that wine is barely sufficient to bless over it "Borei Pri Hagafen," as we have discussed earlier in sections 202, 204, and 272.

Therefore, the great scholars in our regions distanced themselves from this wine, and it was enough for them to make Kiddush at night. Indeed, the raisin wine is a heavy burden for us, but when there is no choice, we are forced to make Kiddush over it. Some have written that it is necessary to ensure that the raisins are at least one-sixth of the water. (Taz)

Moreover, we have seen that the great scholars made Havdalah over milk or sweet tea, even though these certainly do not qualify as "local wine," but due to the pressing circumstances, such as when one has no wine or beer, or is cautious about new wine. Kiddush is made at night over bread and in the morning over whiskey, but for Havdalah, when it is difficult to drink whiskey, it is necessary to use some other beverage. Milk is considered a beverage and sweet tea is also widely consumed. Truly, when we scrutinize, there is no "local wine" at all here except for whiskey, as most householders in our regions do not drink wine or beer with every meal during the week, so it cannot be called "local wine."

Therefore, in such great hardship, it suffices to use whatever beverage is available. However, it is certain that wine is better than all other beverages, whether for Kiddush, Havdalah, or the cup of blessing.

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) writes in Section 9: One who does not drink wine due to a vow may still recite Kiddush over it, and others who are dining with him can drink it. If there are no others with him, he should recite Kiddush over bread instead of wine, or hear Kiddush from others. There are those who disagree with this if others know how to recite Kiddush, questioning why they themselves don’t perform the Kiddush. However, it appears that Rema's intention refers to the Kiddush for the night, such as when the others do not know how to recite Kiddush themselves. 

Know that it has been clarified that if one prefers bread, he may recite Kiddush over bread at night, and this is explicitly stated in the Gemara (Pesachim 106b). This is not an obligation but an option; if he wishes to recite Kiddush over wine, he may do so, and this is clear. Among us, there are those who prefer spirits (strong alcoholic beverages) and recite Kiddush over them even at night. The sages do not approve of this; at night, one should use either wine or bread. If one prefers spirits, he should drink them after the Hamotzi blessing. However, in the morning, one may recite Kiddush over spirits. 

As for those who claim that spirits do not qualify as a drink because a Midrash states that oil surpasses all drinks and spirits do not – this is incorrect. Only very strong spirits are not surpassed by oil, and we drink spirits that are not so strong. Moreover, we do not derive halachic rulings from Midrashim, and our eyes see that spirits are considered a common beverage.

The blessing over wine for Kiddush exempts the wine that is drunk during the meal and after the meal before Birkat Hamazon (Grace After Meals), and it also exempts all kinds of beverages. There is no need for a blessing after drinking the wine because Birkat Hamazon covers it, whether one recites it over a cup or not. Additionally, in the morning, if one eats pastries after Kiddush and immediately washes hands and eats the meal, there is no need for a concluding blessing on the pastries either, as stated in Siman 176.

There is someone who wrote in this language: "If it is on the eve of Shabbat in a place where there is wine, and he knows that on Shabbat he will not have wine, he should sanctify (make Kiddush) during the day on the wine and drink, and afterward it is forbidden to do work." (Magen Avraham, beginning of this section) And indeed, this is found in the Ba'al Halachot Gedolot in the laws of Kiddush, and this is his language: "And where it is certain to him that by twilight he will not find wine for Kiddush, and he happens upon wine in the afternoon... - he sanctifies (makes Kiddush) during the day and says 'Vayechulu,' and in the evening when he comes home - he sanctifies on bread to fulfill the obligation for his children and household." End of quote, and certainly the intention is after the 'Plag HaMincha' (the half-hour period before sunset). (And this is clearly stated in the Magen Avraham there, and thus wrote the Machatzit HaShekel and the Pri Megadim, and there he wrote that Kiddush precedes communal prayer, meaning Kiddush on wine if he cannot obtain both, and in any case, it remains questionable. And in my humble opinion, it does not appear so, and he should sanctify on the bread, and communal prayer should not be like one who prefers bread. Pay close attention.)

We hold that there is no sanctification (Kiddush) except in the place of a meal, meaning one should sanctify (recite Kiddush) in the place where one eats and not in another place, as it is written: "And call the Sabbath a delight," where you call the proclamation of the Sabbath, where you sanctify it - there should be the delight of the meal (Rif and Rashbam). And even the daytime Kiddush, although it does not mention the Sabbath specifically, is nevertheless in honor of the Sabbath. Moreover, it is logical because Kiddush has been established over wine, as it is taught: "Remember it over wine" - presumably over the wine that is at the time of the meal, as it is significant (Rashbam there). Consequently, the same applies to other beverages, for it is not the way of a respectable person to drink without eating (Chullin 4). It is clear that just as one needs to eat in the place of Kiddush, so too one should not delay the meal for a long time after Kiddush, so that there is no significant interruption in between. If one interrupts for a long time, the meal will not be recognized as being for the sake of Kiddush. However, a short delay is not an issue. Similarly, one should not take a long walk to the market after Kiddush, but a short walk to the courtyard is not an issue. See what will be explained in Section 4.

There are three distinctions regarding Kiddush in the place of the meal: In one room, from corner to corner, it is considered the place of the meal. Not only if one made Kiddush in this corner with the intention to eat in the other corner, but even if during the Kiddush one intended to eat in the corner where the Kiddush was made and afterward decided to eat in the other corner, it is acceptable. (See Magen Avraham, section 1, whose words are puzzling as written by the Gra, and examine it thoroughly.) Even if it is a large hall, there is no issue, for this is not considered a change of place, as written in Siman 178. This is also the ruling of the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, and although the Mordechai in Pesachim holds that even from corner to corner one must have the intention during Kiddush to eat in the other corner, we do not hold this way. The same applies from the house to the sukkah when there is no other room in between—it is considered like from corner to corner because the sukkah is a temporary dwelling and is nullified to the house, so it is considered like from corner to corner. The partition between the house and the sukkah is not considered a partition to interrupt because it is only for the mitzvah of sukkah. Some say further, that as long as one can see the place from where the Kiddush was made to the place where the meal is eaten, even from room to room if they can see each other, and even from the house to the courtyard if they can see each other, and even if one can see part of the place or only through a window and not through a doorway, it is considered like from corner to corner. One can rely on these opinions in practice, and it is also written this way above in Siman 178.

The second division: [This concerns] one building from room to room where they cannot see each other, or from a house to an upper floor or from an upper floor to a house. If, at the time of the Kiddush, he intended to eat in the second place - it is permitted, but if he did not intend - it is forbidden, and this is as stated above in Siman 178, see there. And it appears to me that whenever they are in one building, even though there is a courtyard separating them, it is still called from room to room. The third division: [This concerns] two buildings from house to house - it does not help even if he intended at the time of the Kiddush to eat in the second house, and he is obligated to eat an olive's worth of food at the very least in the place of the Kiddush, and if not - he must make Kiddush in the place of the meal again. Similarly, from room to room or from a house to an upper floor, if he did not have the intention at the time of the Kiddush to eat in the other room but only in that room, and then he changed his mind to eat in the second room - he needs to make Kiddush again, and the same applies when he did not explicitly intend to eat in the second room. (And what is written in Shulchan Aruch in section 2: 'If he made Kiddush with the intention to eat there, etc.' - it is not specifically, for the same rule applies in general, and if he made Kiddush and did not eat anything - he has not fulfilled the obligation of Kiddush at all).

And our teacher the Rema wrote in Section 3, that one must eat in the place of the Kiddush immediately, or it was his intention to eat there right away, but otherwise, even in the place of the Kiddush – he does not fulfill his obligation. And if it was his intention not to eat there immediately, but he changed his mind and ate – he has fulfilled his obligation, end quote. This means that we follow both scenarios leniently: if it was his intention to eat immediately, even though due to some reason a lot of time passed – he has fulfilled his obligation. And similarly, if it was his intention not to eat immediately or to eat in another place, and he changed his mind and ate immediately and in the place where he made Kiddush – he has also fulfilled his obligation, unless it was not his intention to eat immediately and he did not eat immediately – then he has not fulfilled his obligation. 

And it seems to me that "immediately" does not literally mean without any delay at all, but rather that one should not delay for a long time. And the term 'immediately' is not literal, as explained in Gittin (27b) that there is some short amount of time allowed, as mentioned there, and as I wrote in Section 1. And a clear proof for this is that it is explained that when one makes Kiddush in the house with the intention to eat in the upper floor – it is considered the place of the meal, and this requires a short amount of time to go up to the upper floor. Therefore, certainly the intention is not literally immediately, and the Torah was not given to the ministering angels, and usually after Kiddush people change their clothes, but the intention is not to delay for a long time. (And what the Magen Avraham wrote in subsection 5 in the name of the Mahari”l, that there is no difference between a short time and a long time, it also means a very long time and a short time, meaning not that long. And also what the Magen Avraham wrote: if one leaves his place in the meantime – he needs to make Kiddush again, it also means a long departure to the marketplace, but not going out to the courtyard or the street adjacent to the house. And I have seen someone who did not explain it this way, and it does not seem right to me, and from the words of the Shiyurei Knesset HaGedolah there is proof to my words, see there and examine well).

A person can recite Kiddush for others, whether for men, women, adults, or children, even if he is not eating with them there. Even though the Kiddush does not fulfill his own obligation in that location, nevertheless, for them it is considered the place of the meal, and they fulfill their obligation with his Kiddush. For we hold that for all commandments, a person can fulfill the obligation on behalf of others, even if he has already fulfilled his own obligation or has not yet fulfilled it. This is unlike blessings over enjoyment, where one cannot fulfill the obligation for others unless he also benefits with them, for a mitzvah is different. Since the obligation of the mitzvah rests upon the listeners to fulfill, all Israel are responsible for one another, and one person can fulfill the obligation for his fellow even when the fulfiller does not currently need it himself. Therefore, not only can he make Kiddush for them, but he can even recite the blessing of 'Borei Pri HaGafen' of the Kiddush for them. And even though without Kiddush he would not be able to recite the blessing over wine for others unless he also benefited with them, nevertheless, since it is part of Kiddush, it is considered a mitzvah blessing itself, and he can fulfill it for them even though he does not benefit. The same applies to the Kiddush of the daytime in the morning, he can do so even though it only involves a blessing, nevertheless it is called Kiddush and is considered a mitzvah blessing. The same applies when the Kiddush is over bread, he can make Kiddush for them and recite the 'Hamotzi' blessing for them, and they drink the wine or eat the bread. But for other meals of Shabbat, he cannot recite 'Hamotzi' for them if he is not eating with them, for even though it is a mitzvah, its primary function is a blessing over enjoyment. (Taz, subsection 3)

And it is obvious that this applies when they are unable to make Kiddush themselves. But when they can make Kiddush themselves, he should not make Kiddush for them if he has not fulfilled his own obligation with this Kiddush. However, if he also needs to fulfill his obligation with this Kiddush, it is preferable for him to make Kiddush and fulfill the obligation for everyone, rather than each person making Kiddush individually, even though each one can make Kiddush for themselves. This is due to the principle of "In the multitude of the people is the King's glory" (Berachot 53a), as mentioned in Siman 298. This is also the custom in many places. In some places, each person makes Kiddush for themselves, but this is not appropriate. It is proper to prevent this practice and to teach them that it is a greater mitzvah for one person to make Kiddush for everyone. He should have the intention to fulfill their obligation, and they should have the intention to fulfill their obligation through him. This is as long as they listen to the Kiddush from beginning to end and respond "Amen." They should not say "Blessed is He and Blessed is His Name," as this constitutes an interruption and they do not fulfill their obligation with the blessing.

If someone sanctifies [the Shabbat] in his house, and his neighbor in another house hears the Kiddush and intends to fulfill his obligation through it, and the one reciting the Kiddush intends to include him, the neighbor fulfills his obligation of Kiddush. Even though the one reciting the Kiddush is not in the place where he will eat, nonetheless, for his neighbor, it is considered the place of the meal, and the hearing is as if the Kiddush was made there. However, if the neighbor hears the Kiddush in the house of the one making the Kiddush, he cannot go to his own house to eat there if they are two entirely separate houses, because he did not hear it in the place of the meal, unless it is two rooms in one house, in which case his intention makes it valid as explained, but not in two entirely separate houses. It is not similar to when he hears it in his own house, where he fulfills his obligation, because hearing is like speaking, and he heard it in the place of the meal and established himself in that place to hear the Kiddush. This is not the case when he hears it in the house of the one making the Kiddush, where it does not help. (This seems correct to me, and the words of the Shulchan Aruch HaRav in paragraph 1 are not clear to me, and perhaps his intention is also like this, see there).

And know that the Geonim introduced a significant innovation regarding the requirement of Kiddush in the place of a meal, and they said that if one drinks a full quarter-log cup of Kiddush wine, it is considered as the place of the meal. And if you ask, in that case, how is it possible to have Kiddush not in the place of a meal, the answer is if one drank only a cheekful or drank a little here and a little there. And this is the language of the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, Section 5: "The Geonim wrote: The matter that Kiddush must be in the place of a meal, even if one ate a small amount (such as foods made from the five species of grain) or drank a cup of wine that requires a blessing, he fulfills the obligation of Kiddush in the place of a meal and may complete his meal elsewhere. This applies specifically to eating bread or drinking wine, but if one ate fruits, it does not suffice." End quote. And it is obvious that one needs an olive-sized portion of bread, and the bread is from the types of grain foods, and this is the simple custom among us for the morning Kiddush of Shabbat. And it is better to immediately eat the Shabbat meal in its entirety, for this is the essence of Kiddush in the place of a meal.

Based on this, our master the Rema wrote the following: "According to this, it would be permissible for the mohel and the sandak to drink from the circumcision cup on Shabbat morning if they drink the appropriate measure, but the custom is to give it to a child." End of quote. Similarly, our master the Beit Yosef wrote in his major work. From their words, it is evident that the intention of the Geonim is to drink the entire Kiddush cup, which is a revi'it (a quarter of a log). The Levush wrote that the intention of the Geonim is to drink a revi'it apart from the Kiddush cup, and the commentators on the Shulchan Aruch agreed with him (Taz section 4, Bach, and similarly in Magen Avraham section 12 and Eliyah Rabbah section 8). One of the great scholars elaborated to refute their words (Aha'u'Z) and concluded that with the Kiddush cup, if one drank a revi'it, he has fulfilled his obligation, for any drink that requires an after-blessing is considered significant drinking, and in this we apply the verse "and call the Shabbat a delight." Indeed, it is not understood what the difference is between one cup and two cups, for if one fulfilled his obligation with Kiddush wine at the meal, he fulfills it with one. If not, what will the second help? This is like saying there is no difference between one olive-sized piece of bread and two olive-sized pieces, and so it is here as well. And one who relies on the Geonim as understood by our Rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, has not lost out. (And the Alter Rebbe ruled like the later authorities, and in my humble opinion, it appears as I have written).

Some say that one should only recite Kiddush by the light of a candle, and the reason is that since lighting a candle on Shabbat is obligatory due to the honor of Shabbat, and the essence of Shabbat is the Kiddush, it follows that Kiddush should be recited by the light of the candle. Others say that Kiddush is not dependent on the candle, and if one benefits more in the courtyard due to the air or because of the flies, one may recite Kiddush in the courtyard and eat there, even though one does not see the candle, since the candles were commanded for enjoyment and not for discomfort. This seems more reasonable, but one should ensure that there are large candles or a lot of oil so that they burn into the night, for if they go out before nightfall, the blessing over the candle would be in vain, as mentioned earlier in Siman 263, that the candles are for the enjoyment of Shabbat, not only for eating but for light, so that one does not stumble in the dark and can use the space comfortably, which is when the light continues into the night, obviously. This is only if it is very distressing to eat where the candles are, but otherwise, it is proper and a mitzvah to eat where the candles are. (Refer to the Magen Avraham, Siman Kaf Yud Daled, that for the Kiddush in the synagogue, which is only customary, one does not fulfill the obligation unless one intends to fulfill it. And this requires examination, for is the custom contrary to the law? The custom is to fulfill the Kiddush according to the law for the reasons explained, and usually, the Shaliach Tzibbur intends to fulfill it, and therefore, if someone eats in the Beit Midrash or nearby, why should they not rely on the Kiddush of the Shaliach Tzibbur? And it seems to me that this is indeed the custom).

We learn in the Talmud (Shabbat 117b): "Rabbi Abba said: On Shabbat, a person is obligated to break bread over two loaves, as it is written: 'double portion of bread.' This refers to the manna, as it is written: 'And it was on the sixth day they gathered a double portion of bread, two omers for each one,' and the phrase 'double portion of bread' is superfluous, as it could have simply written 'they gathered two omers for each one.' This redundancy implies an additional matter, and its interpretation is that the bread for Shabbat meals should be double. Similarly, it is written in the Mekhilta: 'double portion of bread' – Rabbi Yehoshua says it means a doubled bread.' From this, it appears that this is a Torah law and not just a rabbinic support, since indeed the phrase 'double portion of bread' is entirely superfluous as mentioned."

And it is stated there: "Rav Ashi said: I saw Rav Kahana take two [loaves] and cut one. He said, 'It is written "they shall gather" (Exodus 16:22), which implies taking, but it does not say "they shall cut."' (Rashi) Rav Zeira would cut an entire large slice for the whole meal, and this was sufficient for that meal, and it seemed as though he cherished the Shabbat meal by strengthening himself to eat a lot. (ibid.) And the Rashba's version is "for the entire meal," meaning that he cut both loaves. And Rav Hai Gaon wrote as follows: "If a person blesses on Shabbat over two [loaves] and cuts one like Rav Kahana, it is acceptable, and if he cuts both like Rav Zeira, it is also acceptable." These are his words. However, the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch did not bring this at all; they only brought the words of Rav Kahana that one takes two and cuts one, and it is a mitzvah to cut a large slice that will suffice for the entire meal, as per Rashi's explanation. This is also the opinion of the Rambam in Chapter 7 of [the Laws of] Blessings and Chapter 30 of [the Laws of] Shabbat, and he also explains it according to Rashi. It appears that they did not want to create a dispute between Rav Kahana and Rav Zeira, and furthermore, Rav Kahana derives it from the verse that only the gathering is mentioned in pairs, not the cutting as mentioned. Additionally, in the Kolbo, the Mekhilta is brought in this language: 'On the eve of Shabbat, the manna descended for them in two omers, and from an omer they made two loaves, one of them on Friday morning and the other on Friday night, the third on Shabbat morning, and the fourth for the third meal.' These are his words. (Brought in the Eliah Rabbah, section 1) And although I did not find this in the Mekhilta before us, nevertheless, it was written before them, and thus it is a clear proof like Rav Kahana, and this is the custom of the majority of the world. (And so wrote the Gra”z)

And the Maharshal would practice in the evening to break one [loaf] and during the day two loaves, because the honor of the day precedes the honor of the night. (Bach and Magen Avraham) And now there are many meticulous individuals in the regions of Lithuania, Russia, and Zamut, who have been practicing for several generations according to the Gra to break two [loaves] at every meal. And I do not understand this, for even though the interpretation of Rav Zeira is as the Gaon and the Rashba, nevertheless, Rav Ashi and Rav Kahana do not hold this way, and they are later authorities against Rav Zeira. And if we say that even Rav Ashi and Rav Kahana do not disagree with Rav Zeira, but rather they hold that even with one [loaf] one fulfills [the mitzvah], and Rav Zeira holds specifically with two - from where do we derive this, for it seems that they explicitly said to take two and break one, from the precision of ‘they gathered’ as explained by Rashi as I wrote. Furthermore, if the preferred mitzvah is according to Rav Zeira - why did Rav Kahana not perform the preferred mitzvah? Additionally, the Mekhilta states that our ancestors did so in the desert as I wrote, and therefore I remain puzzled by this. (And the Kabbalists practice with twelve loaves like the showbread, and so it is in Pri Etz Chaim, Sha'ar HaShabbat, chapter 17, and it is written there to kiss the hands of one's mother, and the Magen Avraham brings this at the beginning of this section)

Women are also obligated to break bread over two loaves, as (cited in Mordechai), all matters of Shabbat are equal for women and men. Therefore, meticulous individuals practice that the head of the household, after washing his hands, does not break the bread until all the participants have washed their hands and are seated at the table. Then he breaks bread over the two loaves, and everyone fulfills their obligation through this. Even in places where each participant has their own two loaves, it is still not customary to place two loaves in front of the women. Therefore, the head of the household needs to wait for them. Thus, the proper practice, as mentioned, is that the two loaves should be placed only in front of the head of the household, and he should wait until all the participants, men and women, are seated at the table. This is the most commendable way to perform the mitzvah.

And also on Yom Tov, one needs to have two loaves of bread (lechem mishneh) just as on Shabbat, as it is stated in the Mekhilta in the section on the manna: "Shabbat there will be none – this includes Yom Tov when the manna did not descend." (See Rashi and Tosafot at the beginning of Beitzah). The loaves must be whole and not missing, for it is not respectful if they are incomplete. Therefore, if mice gnawed at them, they are not suitable for lechem mishneh. And earlier, at the beginning of Siman 168, it was explained that if one does not have a whole loaf and has two halves of a loaf, one can connect them with a toothpick in such a way that they appear from the outside as completely whole, and one must be careful not to use something muktzeh (an object that is restricted to move on Shabbat) to connect them. And even though for something that needs to be whole according to Torah law, such as an etrog, certainly this kind of connection would not suffice, because human joining is not considered a connection, as stated at the end of Chapter 2 of Ohalot. Nevertheless, regarding lechem mishneh, since "whole" is not explicitly mentioned in the Torah, and even a piece is still called bread, this connection is effective. However, if it is truly missing, even a little, it is not considered whole. There is someone who wants to say that if the missing part is the size of the portion for challah, it does not matter, as with an eruv in Siman 366. But this is not a valid comparison, as there the reason is due to animosity, but it is not considered whole. However, if one does not have any whole loaves at all, one should take two pieces, for at the very least, it is lechem mishneh, even though it is not respectful. (See Sha'arei Teshuvah and Taz).

He holds two loaves in his hand and does not cut them at all before the blessing, as we require them to be whole at the time of the blessing. Instead, he marks them with his knife and blesses over both of them. On Friday night, he breaks the lower one, and on the night and day of Yom Tov and Shabbat day, he breaks the upper one. The reason is based on kabbalistic principles. Some object to breaking the lower one, arguing that we do not pass over commandments, and they wrote to always break the upper one. (Bach) Some wrote that therefore one should first place the lower loaf on top of the upper one, and at the time of the blessing, place it underneath the upper one. (Magen Avraham) Some wrote that the lower one should be closer to him. (Taz) This is also the custom. However, some say that the principle of not passing over commandments only applies when one wants to perform both, not when performing only one. (Taz) This is as Tosafot wrote in Yoma (33a).

It has already been explained that it is a mitzvah to break a large piece of bread on Shabbat, sufficient for the entire meal. However, those who customarily break on two loaves together do not need to follow this practice, as their interpretation of the Talmud is different, as explained. The guests are not permitted to taste from the piece used for "Hamotzi" until the one breaking the bread has tasted it. However, if each person has their own two loaves, they may taste even if the one breaking the bread has not yet tasted, since they are not relying on his bread. 

Every Jew, whether man or woman, is obligated to eat three meals on Shabbat: one at night and two during the day. Moses our teacher hinted to this in his holy Torah: "And Moses said, 'Eat it today, for today is a Sabbath to the Lord; today you will not find it in the field,'" where the word "today" is mentioned three times. 

The night meal and the morning meal certainly require bread, and there are differing opinions regarding the third meal. However, the primary opinion is that bread is required there as well, as will be explained in Siman 291. If, due to some reason, one did not eat at night, they should eat three meals during the day. Ideally, however, the obligation is to eat at night, contrary to the opinion of some who believe there is no obligation at night at all. 

Each Shabbat meal should consist of more than the volume of an egg in bread, so that it is not considered a casual meal. However, if one can only eat the volume of an olive, they fulfill their obligation. This is what is meant by the statement in Shabbat (119b): "A person should always set their table on Friday night, even if they only need an olive's volume." This is under pressing circumstances, but ideally, one should eat more than the volume of an egg. (See Magen Avraham Siman 291, Sifkat 1, and what is written here in Sifkat 2 about not being particular about eating on Friday night - this was due to extenuating circumstances, as explained in Pesachim.)

It is forbidden to use the light of an oil lamp for activities that require a great deal of scrutiny, such as inspecting one's clothes for lice, checking tzitzit, distinguishing between similar utensils, and the like, as well as reading a book by the light of the lamp. This prohibition is due to the concern that, in the course of such scrutiny, one might forget that it is Shabbat and tilt the lamp to bring the oil closer to the wick for better lighting, thereby kindling a flame on Shabbat. (Rashi 11a, s.v. 'and not') Even if one is not reading the book aloud but merely looking at it and studying it in thought, it is still forbidden, as one is still engrossed in scrutiny and may come to tilt the lamp. See further in Section 15.

There is no doubt that the concern of potentially adjusting the lamp applies only in situations where there is a fear that the light will diminish from its original state when lit, and one might adjust it to restore the light to its former state. This is similar to their method of lighting, where they would put oil in a vessel and place a wick inside it, with the wick positioned at the edge of the vessel. Consequently, as the oil decreases, the light diminishes, and one might adjust the wick to bring the oil closer to it, to improve the light so that it burns properly. This is how Rashi explained it, and also the Ran and the Ra'av, and similarly, the Rambam in his commentary on the Mishnah mentioned 'to improve the light'. 

However, in a situation where the light remains constant from beginning to end, like in our case where we light gas lights in lamps, where the light is at the top center of the vessel, the wick is wide and fixed in the middle of the candlestick with a glass cover above it, and its light remains consistent from beginning to end until the fuel runs out, then adjusting it would not help. This means pulling the wick out slightly more using the mechanism on the side because it would inevitably extinguish. As long as the fuel is not exhausted, its light remains as consistent as when it was first lit. 

It is possible to say that in this scenario, the concern of adjusting does not apply. This reasoning can serve as a justification for many Jews who study by our lamps. We have already wondered about the source of the custom to permit this, and according to what we have explained, it makes sense. (I have also seen in the book Mishnah Berurah that he wrote in the name of the Masgeret HaShulchan that he heard from several great rabbis that they permit this based on their reasoning, and he did not bring the words of Rashi, the Rambam, the Ran, and the Ra'av, which clearly indicate this, and one should examine this carefully.)

It is stated in the Gemara (12b): "And one should not read by the light of a lamp. Rabbah said: even if it is two stories high, even if it is two plowshares high, even if there are ten houses one on top of the other." And Rashi explained: "Even though there is no concern of tilting the lamp, the Rabbis did not differentiate" (i.e., the prohibition still applies). Afterwards, it says that only an individual is prohibited from reading, but two people are permitted, because if one comes to tilt the lamp, his companion will remind him. Similarly, an important person who is not accustomed to tilt the lamp even on a weekday due to his importance, is permitted to study by the light of the lamp on Shabbat, as there is no concern that he will tilt it, since he does not do so even on a weekday. And it is also said there that with a nafta (a type of oil) lamp, it is permitted because one would not come to tilt it, as it has a bad smell and one would not come to tilt it. This is according to Rashi's interpretation. (This is not the case according to the Rambam's interpretation, which will be explained in section 16).

And there is a question about this, because we said that even if it is as high as two stories, there is no concern for bending [towards the light] – the Rabbis did not differentiate and prohibited in any case. If so, why did they permit it for two people, for an important person, and for something that smells bad? Let us say that the Rabbis did not differentiate. Some have explained that distinctions concerning the lamp itself are not made by the Rabbis, but distinctions concerning the person are not decreed; therefore, they did not decree two people because of one person, or an important person because of an unimportant person (Taz, Section 1). However, this explanation does not settle the issue of why they did not decree concerning naphtha because of oil, according to Rashi's explanation of the Talmud passage there. But indeed, one of our early authorities (Ran in Chapter 23) already addressed this and wrote that Raba's statement refers to when they equalized their measures within one kind, but to be stringent with another kind because of that kind – even Raba agrees that we are not stringent. For we say that if it is an important person, it is permitted, and we do not decree because of an unimportant person. And regarding oil, they also differentiated between oil and naphtha and did not decree one because of the other. And this is a clear explanation. (And in the Jerusalem Talmud, this is compared one to another).

And this is the opinion of our master, the Beit Yosef, in Section 1, who wrote: "One must not separate or read by the light of the candle... even if it is ten stories high and one cannot reach it, because the sages did not make distinctions in this matter. And for this reason, it is forbidden even if it is in a lantern or fixed in a hole in the wall," end quote. And there is someone who wrote that if it is locked with a key, it is permitted, and thus did the Maharam and the Rosh and their students, and there are those who prohibit it. (Magen Avraham, Subsection 2) And the opinion of the permitter is astonishing, for since the sages did not make distinctions, then in all cases it is forbidden, and what difference does it make whether one cannot tilt it because of its height or because it is locked. And there is no doubt in the matter, that according to what has been explained, it is forbidden in all cases. (And there are those who made distinctions, but it is not clear)

And if you ask, if so, how did the great ones permit locking a door, it seems to my humble opinion that it is clear that they did not interpret as Rashi did, that the reason for the prohibition with something very high is because the Sages did not differentiate, but rather because even with something high, there is concern that one might come to tilt it. This matter is explicitly stated in the Rambam, Chapter 5, Law 14, where he wrote: "One does not examine [for lice]... and even if there are ten houses one above the other and the lamp is in the upper one - he should not read nor examine by its light in the lower one, lest he forgets and tilts it," end quote. It is clearly explained that the reason is not because 'the Sages did not differentiate,' but because there is a concern of tilting even at a height. And this is the reason the great ones permitted locking a door, because in such cases it is impossible to tilt, and I am astonished at the commentators who did not notice the words of the Rambam that we brought. (See Beit Yosef, who labored over the words of the Rambam and interpreted it differently, because of his words in Chapter 22 regarding a mirror fixed in the wall, which he forbids. And I am astonished, for it is explicitly stated in Rashi 149, in the commentary 'of metal' - that it itself shaves, see there. But Rabbi Meir holds that before he shaves, he will remember, and the Sages do not have this reasoning, and it is exactly like here. And this has no relevance to a place where it is impossible to tilt, like when it is locked, and if you worry that he might bring the key - there is certainly no concern in this, for in such cases it is obvious that he will remember, since this is the reason he locked it. But with a lantern or a hole where it is possible to tilt - he will not remember, and if indeed it is impossible to tilt - it is permitted, and this is a major principle in this matter, and pay careful attention.)

And our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote: Similarly, with a wax candle - it is forbidden. The reason is not because of 'lo plug' (a general prohibition not to make distinctions), since it has already been clarified that we do not make decrees on one type because of another type, but rather the matter is as follows: There is a dispute whether inclining (adjusting) a wax candle is similar to oil, or not. There are those who permit it, and our teacher, the Beit Yosef, in his great book, ruled for prohibition, and this is his wording: "It seems obvious to me to forbid it, because one can trim and cut the wick's head," end quote, for by doing this the light increases and it constitutes kindling. This is how it appears in my humble opinion. And so we say in Beitza (32b): "One trims the wick on Yom Tov, what is trimming - to remove the darkness," meaning to remove the darkness so it will shine more, and it is kindling. And that which we explain later in Siman 514 that this is extinguishing - it is certainly also true, since the wick that is trimmed is extinguished, and regarding Yom Tov, there is no prohibition of kindling, only of extinguishing, therefore we refer there to extinguishing. But on Shabbat, where kindling is forbidden - it is obvious that this includes kindling.

Therefore, I am very astonished at those who disagree with our master, the Beit Yosef, and the commentators on the Shulchan Aruch (the Taz, subsection 2; the Magen Avraham, subsection 3; and the Eliyah Rabbah) who wrote that the reason is that since the prohibition is due to extinguishing, there is no Torah prohibition because it is a form of labor that is not needed for its own sake. Extinguishing from the Torah is only for making charcoal, as we explained in Siman 242, and for rabbinic prohibitions, we do not decree. And it is very puzzling, for surely there is also kindling here, unless we say that it is their opinion that the light is not increased at all, but rather the wick darkens it, and when it is removed, the original light shines more brightly, but not that the light is increased. (See Taz in Siman 278) And it is obvious that a tallow candle is like a wax candle, and on the contrary, with a tallow candle there is even more allowance, as it is repulsive, and when one trims its light with one's hands, a bit of the foul smell of the rancid tallow remains on the fingers. And people customarily permit studying before a tallow candle, and all the more so a tallow candle that has hardened, called "stearin licht," which has no wick that turns to ash and does not need to be trimmed at all—it is obvious that it is permitted from the outset to study and perform work before them, and so we practice. (In the large Or Zarua that was printed, Siman 32, he elaborates to prove that the law does not follow Rabba, even if it is two stories high, and the law follows Abaye and Rav Acha later in Siman 149, who dispute Rabba, and this is a new matter.)

It has already been explained that only one person is prohibited from reading by the light of a lamp, but two people are permitted, because if one of them comes to tilt the lamp, the other will remind him, as it is unlikely that both will forget at the same moment that it is Shabbat. And this is specifically when they are engaged in the same topic, even if they are using two different books, because when they are engaged in the same topic, they see what the other is doing. But if they are engaged in two different topics, even if they are using the same book, it is prohibited, because one does not pay attention to the actions of the other. And some say that with two different books, even on the same topic, it is prohibited for this reason, that with two different books, one does not pay attention to the other. Therefore, it is forbidden to recite liturgical poems on a Yom Tov that falls on Shabbat on Friday night when everyone is using their own machzor, even in a synagogue with a large congregation, because one does not pay attention to the other. And so the custom is not to recite the evening liturgical poems on the night of a Yom Tov that falls on Shabbat. But the prayer itself is permitted from the siddur, even for an individual in his home, because it is familiar to everyone and one will not come to tilt the lamp.

And specifically, reading from a book is permitted with two people, but other types of examination, such as inspecting one's clothes or examining the differences between utensils, are also prohibited with two people because each one is engaged in their own task. Even with one garment, if they are working on it, one person is engaged with one corner of the garment and the other person with another. However, if one person is engaged in the task and another is sitting idly beside him to supervise, it is obvious that in all tasks it is permitted, and certainly when reading from a book. Therefore, when reading from a book, if there is another person with him, even if he is not reading, and he says to him, "Pay attention to me so that I do not deviate," it is permitted, and the same applies if he says this to his wife. But with a minor, it seems to me that one cannot rely on him, even if the minor says he will watch him, because he does not have sufficient understanding to prevent him before he deviates, and certainly a non-Jew does not help.

And it has already been explained that an important person who does not customarily lean on weekdays is permitted in all cases. This is as stated in the Gemara there, and in the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, section 4, but the Rambam omits this, and I do not know why. However, it is also difficult regarding the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, for it is explained in the Gemara that one who conducts himself regarding words of Torah as a commoner, like Rabbi Yishmael ben Elisha, is forbidden there. So why did they omit this? Perhaps they reasoned that this is not common in our generations. It seems that this is the reason of the Rambam, for since a mishap occurred to Rabbi Yishmael ben Elisha, as explained in the Gemara, because he conducted himself regarding words of Torah as a commoner—certainly this could also happen in our generations. And perhaps the Rambam holds that all Torah scholars fall under this category, and an important person means a wealthy person who is not a Torah scholar. Since it is impossible to make a definitive rule in this matter, he omitted it, and it is forbidden for all. And some say that it is specifically when it is clear that he does not customarily lean on weekdays, but in an unspecified case, we do not say this (Taz, section 5). According to this, it also makes sense why the Rambam omitted it, because it is impossible to know this clearly.

It is further stated in the Gemara there: that by a bonfire, even ten people are prohibited from reading, because since they are sitting far from each other, they will not notice one another. And even if they are sitting close to each other, still, one will not notice the other because the ends of the logs are near them, and one will not notice when the person sitting next to him comes to stoke and adjust the log. And it is specifically reading from a book that is forbidden opposite the bonfire, because wanting to look well at the book will lead one to stoke the fire. But if one is sitting by the bonfire to warm up, it is permitted even if he is sitting close to the ends of the logs, because why would he stoke since he does not need to look closely. There are those who are stringent and say that even in these cases, one should not sit close to the logs, for the reason that he might come to stoke (Taz, subparagraph 6), and it seems to me that this is an excessive stringency. (And also the Eliyah Rabbah, subparagraph 9, objected to this, as did the Taz, subparagraph 10.) And it seems clear that just as it is permitted to study by a candle when another person is sitting next to him supervising, as stated in paragraph 10, the same applies to a bonfire, that since another person is sitting alone to supervise him, it is not comparable to two people reading. There are those who are stringent in these cases with a bonfire (Taz there), but in my humble opinion, it seems as I have stated.

The Rambam (Maimonides) also omitted the law regarding the bonfire, and I do not know his reasoning. Perhaps he interpreted the Gemara there differently, where it questions the opinion that two people are permitted: 'But it has been taught: Neither one nor two,' and Rabbi Elazar explains: Here it is in one matter, here it is in two matters, as we have explained. Afterwards, it states regarding the bonfire that even ten people are prohibited, and then it says that a distinguished person is permitted with a candle. It is difficult, why did he interrupt with the law of the bonfire between the laws of the candle? He should have stated the law of the bonfire after the law regarding the distinguished person. Therefore, the Rambam explains that the law of the bonfire is a response to the Baraita that prohibits two people. That is to say, the Baraita is dealing with a bonfire and disagrees with the previous explanation that distinguishes between one matter and two matters, and we hold by the first explanation, thus he omitted it from the law. (It is possible that his version read: Rav Huna said regarding the bonfire etc., see there and examine well.)

Children in school can read by the light of a candle because the fear of their teacher is upon them, and they will not come to tilt [the candle]. The Rambam and the Tur wrote: "Before their teacher," and it seems that this is correct, for then the fear of their teacher is upon them. The Rashba holds that even not in the presence of their teacher, they are fearful, and the language of our teacher, the Beit Yosef, in paragraph 6 is like the Rashba. (Taz and Magen Avraham, section 7)

It is permissible to read the chapter "With What May One Light" by the light of a candle, since it mentions the prohibition of Shabbat, and how could one forget to tilt [the candle]. Specifically because one is studying the laws of lighting, but when studying other laws of Shabbat - it is forbidden. Similarly, Shabbat hymns, if one is not familiar with them - it is forbidden to read them from a book by the light of a candle, because even though they mention Shabbat - nonetheless, one could forget for a moment, which is not the case when studying the laws of lighting.

Similarly, on the night of Yom Kippur, it is customary to say the prayers from the prayer book by the light of the candle, because the awe of Yom Kippur is upon them, and they will not forget that it is Yom Kippur and come to tilt [the candle]. Specifically during prayer, for then the awe is great, but it is forbidden to study from a book on the night of Yom Kippur as on Shabbat, for after the prayer - the awe is not as great, as is tangibly felt, and one might forget that it is Yom Kippur and come to tilt [the candle].

Similarly, on the night of Passover that falls on Shabbat - it is permissible to read the Haggadah by the light of a candle from a book, because every Jew, even the common folk, are familiar with the main points, and they will not come to tilt [the candle], and it is like prayer, which is permissible for this reason.

The teacher who instructs children can look by the light of a candle to see from where the children should read, and he can arrange the beginnings of the sections orally from the book, and then recite the rest of the section from memory, since the children themselves read from the book. When he sees the beginning of the section, he places the book in their hands (Rambam). This is not specifically about the beginnings of sections, as the general rule is: as long as one knows the section by heart and occasionally needs to look in the book, it is permitted. Since he does not constantly look in the book, he has awareness and will not come to tilt the candle. In other words, since he does not need to examine the book extensively, he will not forget that it is Shabbat and come to tilt the candle. The same applies to anything a person is familiar with, such as studying Mishnah and Gemara. If he is well-versed in the subject he is studying but occasionally needs to look in the book, it is permitted for this reason. The part that he needs to see in the book can also be articulated verbally (Beit Yosef), and see paragraph 1.

Utensils that are similar to each other and require careful examination to distinguish between them - it is forbidden to inspect them by the light of a candle. And even to differentiate between his clothes and his wife's clothes, if they are similar - it is forbidden to check them by candlelight, even though he is accustomed to them, and certainly with other items. The Rambam wrote: "Therefore, a servant who is not regular should not check cups and plates by candlelight because he is not familiar with them, whether it is an olive oil lamp or a lamp of naphtha which has a strong light. But a regular servant is permitted to check cups and plates by candlelight, as he does not need much examination. And if it is an olive oil lamp - one should not instruct him to check even though it is permitted, as a decree lest he might take some of it for his own use." These are his exact words, and he wrote this according to his version in the Gemara there.

However, according to Rashi's version and interpretation, a regular attendant is more stringent than a non-regular attendant because the regular attendant must be very meticulous due to the fear of the owners. But with regards to a lamp fueled by kerosene, everything is permitted because it smells bad and there is no concern he will tilt it. And with an oil lamp, the regular attendant is forbidden and the non-regular attendant is permitted if he does it on his own, but we do not instruct him to permit it. Rashi interprets "non-regular" as one who is not regularly in the service of this homeowner, but rather serves occasionally, and therefore is not very meticulous. Rambam interprets "non-regular" as one who has not been in the service of this homeowner for a long time, meaning he is not yet established and is not familiar with the utensils, and therefore needs to be more meticulous. Tosafot, Rif, and Rosh interpret a non-regular attendant like Rashi, but they are stricter, reasoning that since he is not yet established, he is more meticulous to find favor in the eyes of the owners, so they will hire him regularly. Even according to them, with a kerosene lamp, it is permitted in any case, firstly because its light is great, and secondly because it smells bad and he will not take from it. With an oil lamp, the non-regular attendant is forbidden, and the regular attendant, if he comes to check it, we do not prevent him; but if he comes to ask, we do not instruct him to permit it initially. According to Rambam, we are concerned that the attendant might take from the oil, but we are not concerned about this with other uses of people because he comes close to the lamp (Beit Yosef). Also, there is no need to ask about permitting a regular attendant because there is no need for much scrutiny, just as there is no less scrutiny than distinguishing between his clothes and his wife's clothes, and the reason they were lenient is for cleanliness (Ran). The Jerusalem Talmud states: "But he looks at what is in the cup and what is in the bowl and does not worry," and the reason is either due to cleanliness, as there is danger if it is not clean, or because it is for a short time, and there is no concern he will tilt it. For the reason of cleanliness, it is permitted to select vegetables from waste as stated in the Jerusalem Talmud (Magen Avraham, section 10), and this is during the meal when he selects and eats, otherwise, there is a prohibition of selecting. Our master, the Rema, wrote that it is customary to cover the young children so that they are not naked in front of the candles due to the disrespect to the mitzvah, as the Rokeach wrote, and there is danger in this. (See Pesachim 112)

In Siman 325, it is explained that if a non-Jew performs work on Shabbat for his own benefit, it is permitted for a Jew to benefit from it, provided there is no concern that the non-Jew might increase his work for the Jew's sake on Erev Shabbat. However, if the work was done specifically for the Jew, then no Jew is allowed to benefit from it on Shabbat. This is not comparable to something brought from outside the Shabbat boundary (techum), which is permitted for another Jew, since techum is a rabbinic prohibition, and additionally, the boundary is not an absolute prohibition, as what is outside the boundary for one may be inside the boundary for another (Ran, Chapter 16). There is a practical difference between the explanations: according to the first explanation, if a rabbinic prohibition work was done for the Jew, it is forbidden for the one for whom it was done, but permitted for others, similar to the case of techum. According to the second explanation, even a rabbinic prohibition is forbidden for everyone. And there in [Siman 125] (325), it appears according to the first explanation.

Now, earlier in Siman 244, it was also clarified that work done by a non-Jew for the sake of a Jew is forbidden for the Jew to benefit from. It was explained there that this applies when the work is done for the Jew's benefit. However, if it is done for the non-Jew's own benefit, such as when he is paid for his work and the work is contracted rather than paid by the day, it is permitted because he is doing it for his own sake and not for the Jew's benefit, as mentioned there. But here, there is no distinction; even if he does it for his own benefit, such as being paid on a contract basis where he is paid a set amount whenever the Jew needs the work done, and now he is doing it for his own sake, it is still forbidden. The difference is that there we are discussing the Jew benefiting from it on a weekday. Therefore, if the non-Jew does it on his own initiative, it does not appear as if he is the Jew's agent. But here we are talking about the Jew benefiting from it on Shabbat itself. Therefore, even if the non-Jew entirely did it on his own, since he did it for the Jew, it is forbidden for the Jew to benefit from this work on Shabbat itself.

Therefore, if a non-Jew lights a candle for a Jew, it is prohibited for anyone to benefit from it, even for someone for whom it was not specifically lit. There is no difference whether he was paid or not, whether he did it as a contractor or as an employee, because since the Jew benefits from the actual work done on Shabbat, it is prohibited in any case. However, if he lit it for his own need, it is permitted for any Jew to use its light. The same law applies if he lit it at the request of a Jew for a sick person who is not in danger, as we hold that it is permitted to instruct a non-Jew for such a purpose, or for the needs of children, who are considered like a sick person not in danger. In such cases, it is permitted for any Jew to use it, because anything lit with permission is allowed.

Seemingly, since it is forbidden for a Jew to derive benefit from a candle lit by a non-Jew on his behalf, it follows that if it was dark in the house and the non-Jew lit it for the Jew, the Jew would be compelled to benefit from its light, and we would obligate the Jew to leave the house. However, this is not the ruling of our master, the Rema, at the end of section 1, and this is his language: "However, if the non-Jew did it in the Jew's house of his own accord, the Jew does not need to leave, even though he benefits from the light or the fire." And the reason for this matter is: this benefit is considered as a benefit that comes to a person against his will, for he did not intend for it, and this too is called: it is impossible to avoid this benefit, and how can we tell him to leave his house. And in a situation where it is impossible and he did not intend for it – it is certainly permitted, as it is stated in Pesachim (25b), and only to look at a book or other things is forbidden by this light. And it appears to me that drinking hot water is also permitted, for even in the dark it is possible to drink, only with light, it is more comfortable, and this too is considered as a benefit that comes against his will. However, it is clear that he is obligated to protest to him from now on and to tell him that if he does it again, he will drive him out of his house, (Magen Avraham, section 4), for if not, he will always do so, knowing that it pleases the Jew.

It appears that if a non-Jew lights [a candle] for himself and for a Jew, it is permissible for the Jew to use its light, unless the primary purpose was for the Jew and the non-Jew’s need was secondary. This is what our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in Section 3: "If a person tells his servant or maid to go with him and they lit the candle, even though they also need it, it is not considered for their need, since the primary purpose of the walk is for the Jew," end quote. It is clearly implied that this is because the primary purpose of the walk is for the Jew. But otherwise, even if his intention is also for the Jew, since he also intended it for himself, it is permissible. See Section 8.

The Tur wrote: Specifically when one lights a candle for his own use, it is permitted for a Jew to benefit from its light. However, if he lights a fire for his own use or for a sick person who is not in danger, it is forbidden to warm oneself by it, lest he add more fuel on his behalf. That is to say, if he made a bonfire to warm himself against the cold, and it is customary that for two people more wood is needed than for one, since a small fire will not suffice for two to warm themselves by it – we are concerned that he might add more wood on his behalf. And even though it is explained later in Siman 325 that we are only concerned about adding more fuel when he knows him, nevertheless with a bonfire it is customary that when another person comes to warm himself by it, a little more wood is added even if he does not know him, because when he sits beside him, it is as if he knows him for this matter (see Beit Yosef). There are those who disagree with this (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 3).

However, our master the Beit Yosef brought two opinions on this matter and leans towards permitting it. This is his language: "And the same applies to making a bonfire for one's own need or for the need of a sick person, and there are those who prohibit a bonfire because we decree that he might add more wood for his benefit." End quote. He first brought the opinion of the one who permits, and explained this in his major work: that the Sefer Mitzvot Gadol, Sefer HaTeruma, Mordechai in the first chapter, and the Hagahot Maimoniot wrote that it is permitted for a Jew to warm himself by a fire that a non-Jew made for his own need or for the need of a sick person. And there are those who say that they do not disagree at all; those who permit are referring to when the bonfire was burning from before Shabbat, made permissibly for the Jew, and afterward on Shabbat, the non-Jew added wood - then it is permitted. And those who prohibit refer to when the non-Jew made it on Shabbat for himself - then it is prohibited, (according to the Bach) but this does not seem to be the case. All this is regarding a bonfire, but in the case of heating a stove in a winter house - it is certainly permitted according to all opinions, because there is no concern of adding more wood for his benefit, and it is like a candle, as a candle for one is a candle for a hundred (according to the Magen Avraham section 3).

And know, that in what we have written that when a candle is lit for both him and for the Jew, it is permitted, there is someone who says that for both of them—it is forbidden. (See there, Subsection 6) And his proof is from later in Section 515, where if something was brought from outside the boundary or fruits were picked for both him and the Jew—it is forbidden. See there. And this is a wondrous thing, what is the connection between this and that? For there, when he does it for both of them, he increases more than if he did it for himself alone. But here, a candle for one is a candle for a hundred, and why should it be forbidden since he also did it for himself, and there is no relevance to increase in this case. (And see Eliyah Rabbah, Subsection 7, who also refuted this, except that he was confronted with the words of Maimonides in the commentary on the Mishnah at the end of the chapter “Kol Kitvei”, where it implies that it is forbidden. But in truth, Maimonides’ intention there is when the principal act was done for the Jew, as explained by the Ra’av in his words there. And similarly, the Rashba wrote at the end of the chapter “Kol Kitvei” according to the Jerusalem Talmud there. And there are variant readings in the Jerusalem Talmud; see Beit Yosef at the end of this section, and the Rashba’s ruling is to permit).

A Jew and a non-Jew who recline together, and a candle is lit: if the majority are non-Jews, it is permitted to use its light, but if the majority are Jews, it is forbidden to use its light, for it is presumed that it was lit for the majority. And even if it is half and half, it is forbidden, for it is not clear that it was lit not for the Jews. However, if there is some proof that it was lit for himself, such as if we see that immediately upon lighting it, he uses its light, then even if the majority are Jews, it is permitted, for we see that it was lit for himself. And even if we say that his intention was for both, it is also permitted, as stated in section 5. However, if the non-Jew is in the Jew’s house and knows that it is forbidden for the Jew, and he pretends to light the candle and use it a little so that the Jew can use it, it is certainly forbidden, for his main intention is for the Jew. (Piskei Tosafot, Chapter "Kol Kitvei") And I remember in my youth, on winter Shabbat nights, when the nights were long, they would call a non-Jew and ask him: Do you want a glass of brandy? He would say that he does, and they would reply: We want to give it to you, but what can we do since it is impossible to find it in the dark? And he would light a candle, drink the brandy, and leave, and they would use its light. And it seems that this is a complete permission with a non-Jew who is not regular, and there is no concern that he is pretending. And even though the Jew is pretending in this, nevertheless, what does it matter to us, in the end, the lighting is for him alone. This is not the case if the non-Jew is pretending – then the lighting is for the Jew, and it is forbidden. And this is the main point: if according to our understanding he is not pretending to do a favor for the Jew, but is doing it for himself, then even if he is a household member, it is permitted. And if not, even if he is not a household member, it is forbidden, but generally, a household member can be pretending, and therefore it needs to be understood accordingly.

Our Rabbi, the Beit Yosef, wrote in Section 4: "If there is a candle in a Jewish home and a non-Jew comes and lights another candle, it is permitted to use its light while the first candle is still burning. However, after the first one goes out, it is forbidden to use the light of the second one. Similarly, if the non-Jew added oil to an already lit candle, it is permitted to use the light until the originally present oil is consumed, but afterward, it is forbidden." These are the exact words, and they are from the Tur. And our Rabbi, the Beit Yosef, wrote in his larger work: Even those who permit a bonfire prohibit this case because the initial lighting of the second candle is for the sake of the Jew. Thus, he ruled here generally in prohibition. However, some say the opposite, that even those who prohibit a bonfire permit this case because, with a bonfire, there is concern that the non-Jew might add more wood for the Jew, thereby lighting for the Jew. This is not the case here because at the moment the non-Jew lit the other candle, even if it was done for the Jew, there was no benefit to the Jew since the first candle was still burning, making it as if nothing happened. Therefore, the prohibition cannot apply afterward, since the primary prohibition is related to the time the act is done. (See Bach and Taz Section 3) However, if the non-Jew’s intention was to provide light for the Jew after the first candle goes out, there is reason to prohibit (there), and thus, we assume so by default. (there) Nevertheless, according to those who permit a bonfire, it is certainly permitted here (Taz there).

And behold, regarding the matter of a bonfire, we find in the Hagahot Maimoniot (Chapter 6, note 6) the following language: "I remember when I was with my teacher (which is Maharam of Rothenburg) in the tower of Weissburg, we made a bonfire on Friday evening to warm ourselves by it on Shabbat. And when we sat until the bonfire was almost extinguished, servants came and made it large again. And they explicitly said that they did this for our enjoyment, and we sat by it and rejoiced in the matter." End quote. And since Maharam, the teacher of the Rosh, acted leniently regarding a bonfire, therefore, even though there is a distinction between a candle, as explained elsewhere, nevertheless, one who is lenient even after the initial extinguishing has not lost out. (ibid.) And one should not say that the permissibility was because the cold was great, and it is permitted to tell a non-Jew to heat the oven as will be explained, for if so, this is not a novelty, and from his words, it is clear that the permissibility is because the bonfire was arranged before the Sabbath. And behold, in these laws, there are distinctions in logic, but since this is not a Torah prohibition, one should not rebuke those who rely on the lenient opinions.

In the northern countries where the cold is severe during the winter days, it is obvious that everyone is considered ill due to such intense cold, and one may tell a non-Jew to perform work. All the more so if the non-Jew is heating the oven—it is permissible to benefit from this, and one who is stringent about this is simply being perplexing. Rabbeinu Yerucham wrote that Rabbeinu Yaakov of Orléans would instruct a non-Jew to light the fire and fix it on Shabbat, because everyone is considered ill due to the cold. However, if the cold is not severe in that place, or if on that particular day the cold is not severe, it is certainly forbidden to tell a non-Jew to heat the oven, and even if the non-Jew did it on their own accord, one must protest. But if there are small children in the house, it is permitted to tell a non-Jew to heat the oven, because small children are considered ill due to the cold even when it is not so severe, and in that case, adults may also benefit from the heat since it was lit permissibly for the sake of the children. (See Magen Avraham, section 15, who wrote that the world is lenient even when the cold is not severe and for the sake of adults, as they believe it is permissible to violate a rabbinic prohibition in the case of distress, as written in Siman 328. But we hold that only a double rabbinic prohibition is allowed in the case of distress, as written in Siman 307, and therefore one should be careful not to instruct on Shabbat to heat—see there. It is difficult to determine when the cold is considered severe and when it is not, and in our countries during the months of Tevet and Shevat, the cold is very severe, and it is impossible to make a clear-cut rule, as not all people are the same in this regard).

Rabbi Moshe Isserles writes in Section 2: "There are those who say that it is permissible to tell a non-Jew to light a candle for the Shabbat meal, because they hold that it is permissible to instruct a non-Jew to perform even a complete labor in the context of a mitzvah. Based on this, many have the custom to be lenient in this matter, to instruct a non-Jew to light candles for the meal, particularly for a wedding or circumcision meal, and nobody protests against them. However, one should be stringent when there is no great need, as the majority of legal authorities disagree with this opinion. See further in Siman 307, Section 5." 

Explanation: It is stated in Eruvin (67b) that it is permissible to tell a non-Jew to bring hot water for the needs of a circumcision through a courtyard that is not enclosed. From this, the Rambam deduced in Chapter 6 that any instruction to a non-Jew is permissible for a rabbinic prohibition in the context of a mitzvah or slight illness.
