Our teachers, the Tosafot, in Bava Kamma (80b) wrote that they did not permit instructing a non-Jew to perform any rabbinic prohibition for all mitzvot, but only for the needs of circumcision. This is the opinion of the Tur in Siman 338. However, the Ran at the end of Chapter 19 brings that the Baal HaItur wrote that even for a Torah prohibition, it is permissible to instruct a non-Jew to perform it in the context of a mitzvah, interpreting the ruling in Eruvin to permit instructing a non-Jew to bring hot water through a public domain, and equating all mitzvot with circumcision. (See Beit Yosef in Siman 307). The Tosafot and the Tur differentiate circumcision from other mitzvot because circumcision itself overrides Shabbat.

And now the matter is puzzling, to rely on the opinion of an individual where all the other authorities disagree with him. It should suffice for us to rely on the opinion of the Rambam to compare all commandments to circumcision regarding rabbinic prohibitions. It is evident that our master, the Rema, himself was not comfortable with this, but he came to somewhat justify those who act in this manner. In truth, they wrote, "It is better that they be inadvertent sinners rather than intentional sinners," and therefore we do not protest against them. (Bach and Magen Avraham section 9) But if it is possible to protest - it is obvious that we are obligated to protest, and in our times we have not heard of anyone being lenient in this. (And so wrote the Shlah, that Heaven forbid to be lenient in this, and so wrote the Eliyah Rabbah, and now it is possible to protest because they will listen to us.)

And know that what has been explained, that a non-Jew who lights a candle for himself - it is permitted for a Jew to use its light, this is even when the non-Jew needs to light for himself for the sake of the Jew’s business. For example, the maidservants in a Jewish household who need to clean the Jew's utensils after a meal, and they lit a candle for this - it is permitted for a Jew to use its light, because since the work of the Jew is incumbent upon them - it is considered that they are lighting for themselves what they need to do. And a proof for this is from the words of our master the Beit Yosef in section 3, where he wrote: "If a person tells his servant... to go with him and they lit the candle... - this is not for the sake of the non-Jew, because the main purpose of walking is for the Jew," end quote. And it is explicitly understood that they are engaged in the Jew’s work, and even so, the prohibition is only because the Jew called them to go, and the main purpose of the walk is for him. But if they went by themselves - it is certainly permissible, and so too in all similar cases.

And our master, the Rema, wrote regarding this: It is permitted to tell a non-Jew to go with him to take an already lit candle, since he is only carrying the candle and not doing anything else. This means that even though in the case of a Torah prohibition, such as lighting a fire, it is forbidden if the primary purpose of the action was for the Jew, as our master the Beit Yosef wrote, since this is not considered as if he is doing it for himself—however, in the case of a rabbinic prohibition of muktzeh, it is permitted, and it is considered as if he is doing it for himself. But if the non-Jew has no personal need at all, it is forbidden to tell him to carry the candle, for the sages did not permit instructing a non-Jew in a rabbinic prohibition except for the sake of a mitzvah or for some illness, as has been explained. But without this, it is forbidden. Nevertheless, it is still not understandable, for even with all this, when the non-Jew does it, it is considered as if he is doing it for himself. But in any event, why is it permitted to tell him to do it? One must say that since he is doing it for his own benefit, it is permitted, as will be explained at the end of Section 307, that it is permitted to tell him to do work for himself. (As our teacher explained in the Magen Avraham, subparagraph 11, that the permission is because he needs it, and see there subparagraph 10 that one should not forbid it on account of the oil moving, since he does not intend for this, and see there in the name of the Radbaz that this permission is only for Torah scholars, lest they become habituated to it.)

According to what has been explained, it is forbidden to tell a non-Jew to move a candle for us from place to place, yet the common practice is to permit this. The truth is that the Hagahot Maimoniot in the name of Rabbeinu Tam permits telling a non-Jew to bring a lit candle, as the prohibition is only due to muktzeh, and indirect handling (tiltul min hatzad) is allowed with muktzeh for oneself. Since there is a leniency for a Jew using indirect handling, it is therefore permissible to tell a non-Jew to move it directly. (See subparagraph 11) And in Siman 325, Subparagraph 10, our teacher, the Rema, brings this opinion regarding telling a non-Jew to bring beer or other drinks through a karmelit for this reason, since it is possible to go there and drink. He writes there that this is only allowed for the needs of Shabbat and in pressing circumstances, but otherwise, one should be stringent. Why did he not mention this here? (See Taz there subsection 10 who raises this question) It seems to me that it is different here, as going outside is more noticeable. Additionally, here there is another reason for leniency, as the reason for telling him to move the candle is because one wants to take something or use that place, and this can be done with difficulty even without the candle, which is not the case there. (See Magen Avraham who mentions this reasoning in the name of the Hagahot Maimoniot)

It is further written in section 4: that it is permissible to protest against a non-Jew who comes to light a candle or add oil. That is to say, we should not mistakenly think that just as it is forbidden for us to command him to perform labor, so too it is forbidden for us to prevent him from performing labor - it teaches us that this is not the case. On the contrary, if the candle belongs to a Jew, one is obligated to protest against him. Only in the case of a fire did they permit it because of potential loss, as stated in section 334. And some say that if one protested and he still lit the candle, it is permissible to use its light (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 13, in the name of Bach), for it is as if he lit it for himself, since he was protested against (Bach). However, there should be no deceit in this matter (Magen Avraham, ibid), meaning if the non-Jew understands that the protest is merely superficial and that the Jew actually desires him to light it - in such cases, it is clear that it was done for the Jew, and it is forbidden to use it. Nevertheless, even without deceit, the permission is puzzling, for in the end, he lit it for the Jew, so why should it be permissible to use it? (And so wrote Eliyah Rabbah, subparagraph 16). It seems that one is not obligated to leave his house, as Rabbi Moses Isserles wrote at the end of section 1, and we explained in section 4, but one should not actually use its light. (It seems to me that this is what Magen Avraham hinted at in subparagraph 13 when he wrote to refer to the end of section 1; see there and examine it carefully).

It is stated in the Gemara (120b): "It was taught: A candle that is behind the door - one opens and closes it normally, and if it goes out, it goes out." And we conclude that this is not the case, and it is forbidden because it is a 'psik reisha' (an inevitable consequence). According to Rashi's explanation, this is when the candle is placed directly opposite the door, such as if the door is in the west and the candle is fixed in the eastern wall of the house directly opposite the door in the west, and the room is small, so to someone standing outside, the candle is behind the door. When one opens the door, the wind enters, and there is a concern that the wind might extinguish it, since it is close to the door because of the smallness of the room. (Bach, and this resolves Tosafot's difficulty). The prohibition only applies to opening the door, not to closing the door. (ibid.) According to this, regarding the prohibition of opening, there is no difference whether one opens it normally all at once or whether one opens it little by little, since the prohibition is due to the wind from outside which enters when the door is opened. (This is what the Magen Avraham wrote in subparagraph 1, that what is written 'normally' is a mistake, because according to Rashi's explanation, there is no difference).

And even though a normal wind does not extinguish the candle, nevertheless they decreed because of an uncommon wind, as will be explained in the introduction regarding the bonfire. According to this, there is no difference between opening all at once and opening gradually as mentioned. Our teacher, the Rema, who wrote that the prohibition is to open in the usual manner, it is written that this is a printing error (Magen Avraham there). But in truth, also in the Rosh there it is specifically written "in the usual manner," and the Rivash in his responsa (Siman 394) explained this: And this is the language of Rashi of blessed memory who explained that it is a certain outcome that the wind extinguishes, not referring to the wind entering through the opening… but rather referring to the wind that is generated by the movement of the door and its opening, for this is like fanning with a fan in front of the candle, etc., end quote. According to this, the prohibition is only when one opens in the usual manner all at once, for then wind is generated, and not when one opens gradually. (And the Korban Netanel there explained so from his own understanding and so wrote the Eliyah Rabbah, and the Magen Avraham did not see the Rivash).

According to this explanation: with this interpretation, the prohibition of opening the door applies only when it is done in the usual manner, but if done gently, it is permitted. This applies in the case of a regular wind, but with an unusual wind, it is certainly forbidden due to the wind from outside. One should not ask why we do not decree against a regular wind because of an unusual wind, as we do concerning a bonfire, which will be explained. It can be said that it is not similar, because with a bonfire, where the fire spreads over a large area, it is inevitable that some part will catch fire. But with a candle that gives a small light and is somewhat distant from the door, it is not certain that it will be extinguished. Therefore, it is sufficient to prohibit it in the case of an unusual wind, but not to decree against a regular wind because of an unusual wind (this is my opinion). See Paragraph 7.

And Rabbeinu Chananel explained: that the candle is placed on the wall behind the door, and when one opens the door, it knocks against the wall, and there is concern that it might extinguish. According to his explanation, the prohibition is only in opening [the door]. And Rabbeinu Yitzchak explained that the candle is fixed on the door itself behind it, and therefore it is forbidden to open and close it, for in both cases it brings the oil closer to the wick and it is considered kindling, or it distances it and it is considered extinguishing. It appears that this is the explanation to which the Rambam in Chapter 5, Law 17, alluded, where he wrote: "A candle behind the door – it is forbidden to open and close the door as usual because it extinguishes it, but one should be careful when opening and closing," end quote. Meaning, one should take care to open or close gently. And that which he wrote 'because it extinguishes it' – is because he holds that through the movement, the oil distances from the wick. And the Maggid Mishneh wrote that the Rambam explains like Rabbeinu Chananel, which is surprising, for if so, why is it forbidden to close [the door]? According to this explanation, the prohibition is only with an oil candle and not with wax or tallow, unlike the previous two explanations, obviously. But in practice, all the explanations are true, and they only disagreed in the interpretation of the words of the Gemara, but in practice, they did not disagree.

And know that in the Jerusalem Talmud, Tractate Kira (Halacha 7), it states: "A candle that is placed behind the door – one may open and close [the door] on Shabbat, provided that one does not intend to extinguish or ignite [the candle]. Rav and Shmuel explained this as referring to one who forgets, and they curse anyone who does so intentionally: 'May the Lord cut off the man who does this...’ (Malachi 2:12)." This is its explanation: One may open and close [the door] gently, provided that one does not intend to extinguish or ignite [the candle], meaning that one should not intend to distance the oil or bring it closer. Consequently, when one opens and closes the door in the usual manner – it is a "psik reisha" (inevitable consequence) according to our Talmud. And Rav and Shmuel said that this also applies to one who forgets, as it is necessary to permit opening and closing gently. However, one who initially places a candle behind the door and lights it on Shabbat – they curse him, because it is close to leading to a Torah prohibition. And according to this, we learn from the Jerusalem Talmud that if one has a fixed candle behind the door – one should not light it initially for Shabbat. (And it is necessary to interpret it this way, as Rav and Shmuel say so, and in our Talmud (Shabbat 120b), 'Rav cursed it,' and we are compelled to understand it as referring to opening and closing gently. And what the Ketzot HaChoshen explained, that in the case of one who places [the candle], it becomes a base for something prohibited – this contradicts the words of Tosafot there, and it is clear as I have written. And the Taz in Siman 2 wrote that according to this explanation, opening and closing gently does not help, and this is against the words of the Rambam that we brought. And it is clear that gently is permitted, as the Bach also wrote there, and also what is written in the Shulchan Aruch according to the explanation of Rabbeinu Chananel, that even closing is forbidden – the Bach and the Magen Avraham in Siman 4 already objected to this, and the Taz in Siman 1 tried to explain it with far-fetched arguments, and examine it well.)

Candles that are on the table on Friday night and there is a window opposite them - it is forbidden to open the window on Shabbat, lest the wind extinguish them. And even in a usual wind, it is forbidden, as it is like a candle behind the door according to Rashi's interpretation, and so rules our teacher, the Rema, in section 1. However, to close it is permitted, and even though we see with our senses that when the window is open, the candles burn more strongly due to the wind, and when it is closed, they do not burn as strongly - nonetheless, this is not considered extinguishing, as the amount of fire is the same, but the wind causes it to burn more strongly, and this is neither igniting nor extinguishing. The prohibition of opening is so that they do not get extinguished entirely because of the wind. It is obvious that this applies when the table is not far from the window, but if it is far, we do not concern ourselves with it.

And we have seen that the common people are not careful about this, and in the summer during the heat, they open the windows at night during the meal to get fresh air, and they should be warned about this. (And it is possible to judge them favorably since the main prohibition is due to the decree concerning an uncommon wind, and in the summer, uncommon winds are not frequent. This is unlike a bonfire which will be explained, which is in the winter to warm oneself by it, as then winds and storms are common, as is known. And take note and examine further.) And see in section 7.

It is forbidden to open a door opposite a bonfire that is somewhat close to the door, because the wind could fan the flames if the wind is very strong. Therefore, even if there is only a common wind, we decree against it due to the possibility of an uncommon wind. And even though an uncommon wind is rare, which is why it is called an 'uncommon wind'—nonetheless, they decreed this. Perhaps the bonfire is made in the rainy season to warm oneself against it, and during that time, winds and storms are common, as mentioned. However, it is permitted to close the door when it was open opposite the bonfire, and this does not constitute extinguishing. Even for those who prohibit blocking an oven in Chapter 259, here it is permitted, because in the house there is a lot of air, and it is not comparable to an oven. (Magen Avraham, Section 6) Know that what we have written follows Rashi's opinion that the primary prohibition is due to an uncommon wind, as mentioned in Sections 2 and 3 and also in Section 6 regarding opening a window opposite a candle, and so the Bach explicitly writes according to Rashi, and this is his language: "Our teacher explains in Rashi's commentary that it is not an inevitable result except with an uncommon wind, but we decree...like with a bonfire." End quote. I have seen it written that with a candle, it is forbidden by the letter of the law even with a common wind. (Magen Avraham, Chapter 514, Section 10) I am puzzled as to where this is derived from, and I have not seen any of the decisors who hold this view. However, he also writes that when there is no wind at all, Rabbi Moshe Isserles permits it there, and he disagrees. According to this, one can also justify those who are not careful about opening a window opposite candles, as mentioned in Section 6. (The Magen Avraham compares the law of this chapter to that of there, and in my humble opinion, it is not comparable at all, because there Rabbi Moshe Isserles says to place the candle where the wind prevails, and it refers to a festival day, where the intention is to move the candle outside—and in this case, even a common wind will certainly extinguish it. But here on Shabbat, where the candles stand indoors on the table—a common wind will not extinguish them. Examine this well.)

If one placed a candle on a table, or on a bench, or on a chest while it was still daytime, and it was not his intention to leave it there, but he forgot to remove it before nightfall, and he needs the place where the candle is to use on Shabbat, he may shake the table, bench, or chest, and the candle will fall to the ground, and he can move them to any place he wishes. For in the case of forgetting, the object does not become a base for something forbidden. Provided that he does not intend to extinguish the candle by shaking it, and if it does extinguish, it is an unintentional act, as this is not a certainty (psik reisha), for it is possible that the candle will fall and not extinguish. And this applies to a wax or tallow candle, or even an oil candle if there is no more oil in the candle and only the wick is burning, for if there is oil, it is forbidden to shake it, as the oil will necessarily move, causing either extinguishing or kindling, which is a certainty, and all the more so if the oil spills, it is extinguishing. Nevertheless, through a non-Jew, it is permitted, as any certainty (psik reisha) is permitted through them, as written in Siman 253. And even with a wax or tallow candle, it is better to do it through a non-Jew if one can easily obtain one and tell him. And if he needs the entire place of the table, bench, or chest, he can move it with the candle on it, as this is indirect moving for a permitted purpose, and it is allowed as will be explained in Siman 311.

And all of this applies when one forgot to remove the candle before nightfall. But if he intentionally left the candle there to be present at the onset of Shabbat, then the table or the bench and the chest have become a base for the forbidden item, and they are considered muktzeh like the candle itself, and it is forbidden to shake them. Shaking does not help, because even after the candle is removed, they remain forbidden to move, and only touching is permitted, as is the law with all muktzeh items that are allowed to be touched but not moved, even in the case of a wax candle. Only through a non-Jew is it permitted to move it, as all muktzeh is permitted through a non-Jew, as mentioned in Siman 276. Similarly, shaking it is permitted through a non-Jew, even with an oil lamp, even though it is a "psik reisha" as mentioned. But touching is permitted by oneself, as mentioned. The same law applies to touching the candelabras in the synagogue even while the candles are burning in them, but one must be careful not to shake the candelabra. Therefore, with a hanging candelabra, which is called a "hanging light," it is forbidden to touch it, because it will certainly be shaken. Refer to what is mentioned in Siman 308 and Siman 309, paragraph 11.

And know that what we have written, that if one placed [a candle] so that it would be there at the entrance of Shabbat, it becomes a base for a prohibited item, will be explained later in Siman 309. There are those who say that a base for a prohibited item only applies if it was his intention that it should remain there all of Shabbat. But if his intention was to remove it on Shabbat morning through a non-Jew, or by moving it indirectly, like shaking it off, or the like - its status is like one who forgot, and it does not become a base for a prohibited item. In a case of loss, one can rely on this opinion, to shake it off the table or the board or the chest if it is a wax candle and there is no oil, such as if it fell on the table and he fears it will burn the tablecloth or the table - he should shake the candle off it, and it will fall to the ground. And if there was bread or dishes on the table at the entrance of Shabbat - the table does not become a base at all, even if his intention was that the candle should remain there all of Shabbat, because it also becomes a base for the bread or the dishes, and it is a base for both a prohibited item and a permitted item, and it is permitted as explained there. (The Gra in paragraph 6 wrote that also the tablecloth does not become a base for the candle, following his reasoning in Siman 309 paragraph 9. But this is not how the Taz ruled in Sk. 1, and it will be explained there, and there are several other laws regarding this matter, which will be explained there. And a candle attached to a stand is not a base for the candle.)

It is permitted to place a Shabbat candle on a tree before Shabbat, and it can remain there for the entire Shabbat. However, on Yom Tov, it is forbidden. The reason is simple: on Yom Tov, when the candle is allowed to be moved and lit, we are concerned that someone might climb the tree on Yom Tov to take it, thereby using something attached to the ground, which is forbidden, as stated in Siman 336. But on Shabbat, since the candle is forbidden to be moved, this concern does not exist. And even though it is permitted through a non-Jew, it does not matter if the non-Jew uses something attached to the ground, since for the Jew, the candle is forbidden to be moved even after it is extinguished, as it is considered muktzeh.

It is permitted to invert an earthenware bowl over a burning candle to prevent the fire from catching onto a beam or for any other purpose. (See Taz, subparagraph 8, and there is no difficulty at all, for this is the language of the Gemara, 43a, and it follows the usual manner of expression.) It is obvious that a little air must be left between the bowl and the candle, for if not, the candle will be extinguished, and this would constitute extinguishing. There is no novelty in this ruling, for why should it be prohibited? After all, there is no nullification of a vessel's preparedness when it is inverted over it, and it can be removed. Rather, because in the Gemara there is someone who holds that a vessel may only be moved for the sake of something that may be moved, and not for the sake of something that may not be moved, and according to him, it is prohibited to move a permissible vessel in order to invert it over the candle. Therefore, it comes to teach us that we do not hold this view, as the Talmud concludes there.

The sages taught in a Mishnah (29:): One who extinguishes a lamp because he fears gentiles, like the Persians who did not allow light during their festival except in their house of worship (Rashi), or because of bandits, so that they should not see him and come upon him (ibid.), or because of an evil spirit, melancholia that comes upon him, and when he does not see the light, he is more comfortable (ibid.), or there is a type of illness where when he sees the light, he flees and distances himself from human nature (Rambam in his commentary on the Mishnah), or there are people who imagine illusions during their sleep if the lamp is burning, in a way that they come to an evil spirit and lose their minds (Prisha), or if he extinguishes it for the sake of a sick person so that he may sleep - he is exempt. And all exemptions on Shabbat - exempt but forbidden. The Gemara establishes that it is obvious that in a place of danger, it is permitted from the outset, and the Mishnah deals with a situation where there is no danger, and what is exempt by Torah law is because it is a labor that is not needed for its own sake. This is according to the Tur and most of the poskim, for we hold like Rabbi Shimon, that a labor that is not needed for its own sake is exempt. But according to the Rambam, who rules like Rabbi Yehuda, that a labor that is not needed for its own sake is liable, here too, one would be liable. And we have already written about their dispute in Siman 242. The Rambam would interpret the Mishnah according to the first establishment in the Gemara, that it deals with a place of danger, and indeed, it is permitted from the outset. And the reason the Mishnah uses the term 'exempt' is because of the latter part of the Mishnah.

The Tur, who rules according to Rabbi Shimon, indeed writes in this language: "One who extinguishes a candle because he is afraid... where there is no danger - he is exempt but it is forbidden, and if there is danger - it is permitted from the outset. And if he extinguished it because he is concerned about the candle, or the oil, or the wick - he is exempt, but if he extinguished it in order to singe the wick - he is liable." This is because it is necessary for the act of extinguishing itself, so that the wick will be easy to catch the flame, and therefore it is necessary to extinguish it and then relight it, and it is like extinguishing to make charcoal, which is called "necessary for itself." And our teacher, the Beit Yosef, only wrote: "It is permitted to extinguish the candle so that a dangerously ill person may sleep," and wrote nothing more, as he did not want to enter into this dispute, because in any case, there is a rabbinic prohibition even according to Rabbi Shimon. And in all the laws of Shabbat, our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, only differentiated between what is forbidden and what is permitted, as it is stated in Siman 242. (And see the Taz who wrote that it is permitted to study by a wax candle, because there is no Biblical prohibition if one trims the candle, as it is a labor not needed for its own sake, and we have already explained this in Siman 274, Section 7, that it can be said there is also a prohibition of kindling. And what the Magen Avraham wrote in the words of the Kesef Mishneh, Chapter 1, about the difference between a labor not needed for its own sake and "inevitably resulting," we have already explained in Siman 242. And what they questioned about the Tur who ruled in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 424, that one who wounds his fellow is exempt from payment because of "Kam Lei B'deraba Minei," and this is a labor not needed for its own sake, it is clear that the Tur holds that just as one is liable for destructive acts in wounding and kindling, so too he is liable for a labor not needed for its own sake, contrary to the words of the Tosafot. This will be explained further elsewhere, with the help of Heaven.)

Know that in this section, as well as later in the laws of muktzeh, the laws regarding a candle, whether it is permissible to move it or forbidden, have been explained. This is because it serves as a base for the light and due to the principle of "migo de'itkatzai bein hashmashot" (since it was set aside at twilight), as will be explained. Therefore, if it was not lit on Shabbat, it is permissible to move it. Similarly, some say it is permissible through a condition, as will be explained. This all pertains to their candles, which were vessels like all other vessels, and they would put oil in them and light them. If not for the lighting, it would be a permitted vessel. However, with our candles which we call "Leuchter" or our candlesticks which we call "Lampin"—they themselves are muktzeh because they are not suitable for any use other than lighting. They are considered a vessel whose primary function is forbidden (muktzeh machmat issur) and are not suitable for any permitted use at all. They are completely muktzeh even if they were not lit at all. And because there are those who err in this, we have written this: our candles and candlesticks are always forbidden to be moved on Shabbat.

A candle that was lit on that Shabbat, even if it went out, is forbidden to be moved. Since it was set aside during twilight (bein hashmashot) and served as a base for something forbidden, it remains set aside for the entire day. This is a fundamental principle in muktzeh, because twilight, which is the beginning of Shabbat and its primary time, if the prohibition of muktzeh applies then, we say: 'Since it was set aside during twilight, it is set aside for the entire day.' This is similar to the concept of acquiring a resting place (keniyat shevita), where the primary time is during twilight. 

Even according to the opinion in Siman 309 that we do not say it becomes a base for something forbidden unless it was intended to remain there all Shabbat, and not if it was intended to be removed the next day, as stated in Siman 277, section 10 - they agree regarding 'since it was set aside during twilight, it is set aside for the entire day,' even if it was expected to go out in the middle of Shabbat. The reason seems to be that if the base is only because the muktzeh was placed on it, like placing a candle on a table or a stone on the mouth of a barrel, and similarly in all such cases where one can remove the muktzeh whenever they want by shaking or moving it from the side - in this case, some say it needs to be left for the entire Shabbat. But in a base like this one, where once the candle is lit, it cannot be removed from the fire - in this, according to all opinions, it depends only on twilight, even if it was expected to go out in the middle of Shabbat. (So it seems in my humble opinion, and see Taz in section 2, and it seems to me similarly from all the poskim, and scrutinize well).

However, a candle that was lit in the middle of Shabbat, for example, if a non-Jew lit it, or it was lit for a woman in childbirth or for a dangerously ill person—it is permitted to move the candle after it has extinguished, according to what we hold in Siman 310, that there is no muktzeh (prohibition of moving objects) for half of Shabbat. That is to say, we only say "since it was set aside at twilight, etc." but not in the middle of Shabbat, we do not say "since it was set aside for part of Shabbat, it is set aside for the whole of Shabbat." Therefore, when it has extinguished, it is permitted to move it. This is also proven in the Gemara (45a), that if there is fear that one will be punished—it is permitted to move the candle after it has extinguished. (And what Rashi wrote there "danger"—is not precise, and the Magen Avraham Se'if Katan 1 took it literally, which is surprising, and see in Machatzit HaShekel. And in Turei Zahav it is written in the name of Birkei Yosef that someone who suffers from his eyes and the candlelight harms him—even so, it is forbidden to move it, see there, and this is also very surprising. However, if it can be done by a non-Jew or a child—it is certainly better, and if not, it seems to my humble opinion that it is permitted to do it oneself, for an eye ailment is close to danger).

And similarly, the leftover oil from a candle that was lit on that Shabbat—it is forbidden to move it or to make use of it on that Shabbat, even after it has extinguished. Since during twilight (bein hashmashot) it was forbidden to make use of the oil due to the prohibition of extinguishing, we say, "Since it was set aside (muktzeh) during twilight, it remains set aside for the entire day." Additionally, there is the reason that it was set aside for its mitzvah. However, due to this reason alone, it would not be forbidden to move it on Yom Tov, since it is permissible to light (on Yom Tov). But for the first reason, it is also forbidden on Yom Tov since extinguishing is prohibited on Yom Tov, as will be explained in Siman 514. Regarding Shabbat, there is no difference in this matter. (See Magen Avraham, sk 2) There it will be explained concerning a wax or tallow candle—that it might be permitted even according to the first reason. See there.

This candle that we have said is forbidden to move—it is forbidden even for its use or its place. And it is not similar to any [other] muktzeh whose primary use is forbidden, which is permitted for its use or its place, as stated in Siman 308, because there even during twilight it was allowed to move it for its use or its place, for anything whose primary use is forbidden was never prohibited for its use or place, as written there. But the candle at the time it is lit, since it becomes a base for the flame—it is obvious that it is forbidden even for its use or its place, and therefore it is forbidden for the entire Shabbat in such cases. (Beit Yosef) There are those who permit it, but our teacher the Beit Yosef wrote in paragraph 2 that their words are not accepted, as explained. And there are those who wrote that the reason for those who permit it is because they hold like the second opinion in Siman 309, that a base is only such when it is intended to be there all Shabbat, and with the candle it was not intended for the entire Shabbat, and therefore it is permitted after it is extinguished for its use or its place. (Taz, subsection 2) And I am astonished by this, for if so, the muktzeh would be entirely nullified after it is extinguished, and why only for its use or its place? Surely, in this case, all agree that it does not need to be for the entire Shabbat, for the reason we wrote in paragraph 2. (And behold, the one who permits is the Mordechai at the end of Chira, and he also permits muktzeh due to a financial loss for its use or its place there, because he holds that anything that is a utensil is permitted for its use or its place, and he also permits with a candle. And it appears that even during the lighting, according to his view, it is permitted, but we do not hold accordingly. And also the Shelah in his explanation there brought that the Maharshal disputed him there, and if so, his reasoning is clear, and therefore the Beit Yosef rejected his ruling from halacha, examine it carefully.)

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) writes in Section 2: "There are those who say that if someone is delicate and the candle is repulsive to him, he is permitted to remove it, as for him it is like a chamber pot, and one who is stringent does not lose out." End quote. This is not understood, as surely one who is stringent does lose out. It has been suggested that this is a printing error, and it should say: 'One who is stringent should be stringent, and one who is lenient does not lose out' (Bach, Taz, and Magen Avraham Section 3). There are those who wrote that one who is stringent does not lose out on the mitzvah of Shabbat delight (Elya Rabba Section 7).

But the main issue is puzzling. If so, for any item that is repulsive, we should say it is like a chamber pot. In the Talmud, there is a dispute regarding items that are repulsive, but no one ever disputed the status of a chamber pot. And if you say that the dispute is when the repulsive item is not in one's seating area, in the Mishnah it states that a new candle can be moved but not an old one because it is considered repulsive (according to Rashi's explanation). The candle is on the table, and nowhere do the Talmud and the poskim (decisors) mention that repulsiveness is like a chamber pot. 

Moreover, we cannot say that a delicate person is different, for if so, you have given the law over to each individual, and today one would say he is delicate regarding this repulsive item, and tomorrow regarding another, and many repulsive items would be nullified. Additionally, why wasn’t this mentioned anywhere? This is the intention of the Taz in Section 3, and the Taz's criticism in Turei Zahav is unwarranted.

Certainly, for anything repulsive, it does not apply to call it a 'chamber pot' except where the sages specifically mentioned, for otherwise there is no boundary to the matter, as I have stated. Furthermore, the chamber pot that the sages permitted, they did not differentiate between a delicate person and one who is not. And in the Talmud (47b), Abaye wanted to say that ash in a pan is like a chamber pot, and Rava challenged him, saying a chamber pot is repulsive and this (ash) is not repulsive. And the candle is no better than ash. From there, it is clear that a chamber pot is something repulsive to all people, like excrement and similar items. (See Bach, who is certain that for everyone, even one who is not delicate, it is permitted, as it is surely like a chamber pot, and this needs further investigation).

And also in the primary source of the law in the Mordechai at the beginning of Beitza, it appears as we have stated. This is his language there: "If so, a candle that was lit on Shabbat is forbidden to move. There are those who permit it, comparing it to a chamber pot, but this is not correct, as every fool will claim that they are delicate, and it is only permitted for someone who is truly delicate by nature, and one who is stringent does not lose out." End of quote. This is not understood, as still every fool will claim they are delicate. It seems to me that indeed this is its explanation, refuting the words of those who permit it on the grounds that everyone will say so, and indeed it is only permitted for someone who is delicate by their nature. And who can decide this in a matter of prohibition? Therefore, one should be stringent for everyone, and one who is stringent, even if they are delicate, does not lose out compared to other people for whom it is forbidden by law (this is how it appears in my humble opinion).

Ramban and Rashba, of blessed memory, ruled that making a condition is effective for a candle that was lit on Shabbat, since it is meant to be extinguished. One should make the condition during the day that he does not withdraw from it, so that when it extinguishes, it will be permissible to move it (Maimonides, Chapter 25, Halacha 10). There are those who questioned this leniency, arguing that necessarily, during twilight, one withdraws from it while it is lit, and therefore, 'since it was set aside during twilight, it is set aside for the entire day' (Rivash, Siman 93). This is not analogous to what is stated in Beitza (30b) regarding the decoration of a Sukkah, where if one says, 'I do not withdraw from them throughout twilight,' they are not considered set aside, for there, even during twilight, one does not withdraw from them. This is not the case here, where necessarily one withdraws from it during twilight. Nevertheless, one can say, since the candle itself is not inherently set aside but rather because it is a base for the flame, therefore the condition on the candle when it extinguishes is effective (Beit Yosef in the name of Tashbatz), since it is its nature to be extinguished. (See Magen Avraham, note 6, who criticizes Tashbatz, and indeed also Tashbatz's intention is such, and we need two conditions: that it is not inherently set aside but a base for what is set aside, and also that necessarily the set-aside status will be removed from it. Therefore, we do not say this for any base, and not for what is inherently set aside, unless one does not withdraw even during twilight as with the decoration of a Sukkah. Therefore, the condition does not work with a flimsy Sukkah in Siman 518, and the opinion of Magen Avraham is beyond me and requires further study and scrutiny.)

And the halachic ruling is as follows: Our master, the Beit Yosef, ruled in Section 4 permissively, and this is his language: "If one made a condition regarding this candle that he will move it after it goes out - it is permitted to move it after it goes out." And he explained his words in his major work, that since this is a Rabbinic prohibition, and the Ramban and the Rashba ruled leniently - we listen to them, and even the Rivash did not have the heart to reject their words there. Nevertheless, our master the Rema wrote: "There are those who say that a condition does not help, and this is the practice in these countries." For it seems to him that since during twilight one must separate from it - a condition does not help. And even according to those who hold in Siman 518 that a condition helps in a rickety sukkah regarding the wood of the sukkah - it is also not comparable, for there the sukkah was made beforehand, and now during twilight he sits and waits for it to fall. This is not the case with a candle, where its primary designation is during twilight, and how would the condition help, for during twilight he actively sets aside the candle to be a base for the flame for the sake of Shabbat, as Tosafot wrote. (M. D. end of 'Shebener,' and see Magen Avraham Section 7).

And it is also written that it is customary to move it by a non-Jew, and there is no prohibition of instructing a non-Jew, since this is the custom—it is as if it was stipulated from the beginning and is permitted. And the reason for needing this rationale, when it is already ruled in Siman 276 that moving by a non-Jew is permitted, is because there the non-Jew also needs it (as explained by the Magen Avraham in Sk 11) and as we explained there in Section 16. And even according to what we wrote there in Section 17 in the name of Rabbeinu Tam, that even for the need of a Jew himself it is permitted, it is because the Jew could do it himself by means of indirect handling, as we wrote there, and this is when the Jew needs it for his own body, then indirect handling is permitted. But here the permission is even when it is not needed for his body, but rather he moves it to store it in a concealed place so it will not be stolen, and in such cases, it is forbidden even by indirect handling, as we wrote in Siman 311, see there, and consequently, it is also forbidden to instruct a non-Jew. Therefore, we needed the rationale that it is as if it was stipulated from the beginning, and this stipulation is effective even for those who prohibit it. (See Magen Avraham Sk 9 who wrote this on the words of the Rema, and the Rema only permitted it because the non-Jew also needs it as he himself wrote there in Sk 11, but according to the words of Rabbeinu Tam, it fits well, and examine it carefully).

In Siman 311, it will be explained that a base for something prohibited and something permitted is allowed to be moved. Based on this, some mistakenly place bread on a candle on Shabbat and move it, but this is a complete error. The base for the prohibited and the permitted must be established during the day. And even though we say regarding a corpse: 'Place a loaf or a child on it and move it,' as mentioned in Siman 311, the Sages actually said (142b) that placing a loaf or a child was only permitted for a corpse when it is lying in the sun, due to the dignity of the deceased so it does not decompose. This does not apply to other muktzeh (items that are set aside and not to be moved on Shabbat). For other muktzeh items, since during twilight it became a base for prohibition only, it does not lose its prohibited status. What benefit would it be to add something permitted on Shabbat? The primary status of the base is determined during twilight.

Therefore, if one placed bread on the candle before Shabbat, there is room to permit it. However, even in this case, there is reason to doubt, because we require in any event that the permitted item should have at least as much importance as the prohibited item. Otherwise, it is nullified to the prohibited item, and this is evident in the Gemara (47a). Regarding the oil and flame that illuminate on Friday night, the bread has no significance compared to them, for it is needed for them now. Hence, the primary basis is for the prohibited item, and therefore, one should not rely on this leniency. Nevertheless, one could argue that the bread is effective because it acts as if there were a condition in the matter, since it is as if one stated that he does not divert his attention from it during twilight, which is permitted according to our master the Beit Yosef in paragraph 9. Even according to our master the Rema there who forbids conditionality, in any event, one can combine this with the basis (and this is the intention of the Magen Avraham in subparagraph 5). Indeed, this reasoning, that the primary basis is for the oil and flame because they are needed now, is not so clear, because if the bread has importance, it does not matter that the oil and flame are needed now. In the Gemara there, it implies that it depends only on the inherent importance, not on the timing. (And what the Magen Avraham wrote there, bringing proof from Rashi 47a, s.v. "for the prohibited item," that Rabbi Shimon concedes that the vessel is secondary to the flame, I do not understand, for certainly it is so, because there is no permitted item there, as the oil is also secondary to the flame as Tosafot wrote there s.v. "place", and this has no relevance to bread).

A candle that was lit on Shabbat for a woman in labor or for a sick person, and the woman gave birth or the sick person recovered — it is permitted to handle it after it is extinguished, for this is not considered an act of nullifying the prohibition by hand, since it was lit permissibly. Moreover, there is no concept of muktzeh (an object that cannot be moved on Shabbat) for part of Shabbat, as mentioned in section 3. Therefore, even if one lit the candle on Shabbat unintentionally, it is permitted to handle it after it is extinguished. The same applies if it was lit deliberately, because the reasoning is as stated, except that it is not possible for a Jew to do so deliberately. However, if one lit it for a woman in labor or a sick person before twilight, it is considered muktzeh for the entire Shabbat. Although muktzeh does not apply to them because it is permissible to light for them even on Shabbat, nevertheless, since the candles were lit during twilight, they are set aside for the entire day. For at this time, when there is a candle, it is prohibited to light for them (so it seems to me).

A candle that was not lit on that Shabbat - it is permitted to move it, and even if it is made of earthenware and is repugnant - it is permitted to move it for its own use or its place, as with a utensil whose primary function is prohibited, as stated in Siman 308. And even if it is made of petroleum and has a foul smell - it is permitted, for we hold that an object set aside due to repugnance is permitted, as stated there. And we have already written at the beginning of the Siman, that all this does not apply to our candles, see there. And a candelabrum, whether large or small, if it is composed of segments that are joined together - it is not to be moved, because we are concerned that it might fall apart and one would reassemble it, thus creating a utensil on Shabbat. And this does not relate to the principle of "there is no building with utensils," because when making a new utensil - everyone agrees that there is building, as stated in Siman 314, see there. And even if it is not made of segments, but has grooves around it and resembles a segmented one - it is forbidden to move it, because of a decree due to those who see and might say it is a segmented one and they will come to permit a segmented one, which is close to leading to the desecration of Shabbat, hence the Rabbis did not differentiate. And utensils that do not usually fall apart when they fall - it is permitted to move them. And similarly, even if they are segmented, if it is common for them to be loose - they are permitted to be moved, and even if they fall - it is permitted to reassemble their segments, as stated in Siman 313, see there.

The Tur writes that one recites the Shema on Friday night just as on other nights, as mentioned there. Meaning, one should not say that since we do not recite "He who guards His people Israel forever" on Shabbat, because Shabbat guards us, as stated in Siman 267, therefore, we should also not recite the verses of the Shema which serve as protection from harmful forces on Shabbat. The Tur informs us that we do need to recite it. (Bach) The reason being, we are not proficient in observing Shabbat properly, and furthermore, there is a difference between an individual and a community, as mentioned there.

It is stated in Ketubot (62b): "Whose fruit yields in its season - this refers to a Torah scholar who has marital relations from one Shabbat eve to the next Shabbat eve," which is a night of delight and rest and bodily pleasure (Rashi). The marital obligation of a Torah scholar is from one Shabbat to the next (ibid.), and it is mentioned there that one of the sages was punished for not adhering to this. And the language of the Rambam in Chapter 30 is: "Marital relations are one of the delights of Shabbat, therefore the marital obligation of healthy Torah scholars is to engage in marital relations from Shabbat eve to Shabbat eve" (see there). This excludes someone who is weak in health, who is not obligated in this. It is also clarified above in Siman 240 that the marital obligation of a Torah scholar is from Shabbat to Shabbat because the whole week he is engaged in Torah study (see there), and regarding them it is said: "Thus says the Lord to the eunuchs who keep My Sabbaths," and there is a hint to this in the Torah in the initial letters of the words of the verses: "And the children of Israel shall keep the Sabbath" (Rosh at the end of Perek Merubeh). It is a mitzvah to eat garlic on Shabbat eve or on Shabbat night, as it increases seed. (ibid. in the Gemara) However, we do not practice this, perhaps because it is found in Sefer Chassidim (Siman 490) that garlic diminishes desire, only roasted garlic increases seed (see there), and we are not proficient in roasting it. Additionally, it is written that all salty foods diminish seed, and cooked legumes and lentils when not salted increase seed. And in the first chapter of Yoma (18a), it is said that milk, cheese, egg, wine, fatty meat, and garlic increase seed, and it lists other things there that we are not proficient in (see there).

It is established that it is permissible to consummate a marriage with a virgin initially on Shabbat. (Ketubot 7.) There is no prohibition in this due to the suffering she experiences in the first intercourse, nor is there a prohibition due to wounding by causing blood to be released, since the blood of virginity is not absorbed in the walls of the womb, but rather it is gathered there, like it is stored within a vessel, and it is merely like opening a vessel from which the blood comes out. Additionally, there is no prohibition because of creating an opening, for one reason, this is a type of labor that is not needed for its own sake, and furthermore, it is a form of damage, as a virgin is considered more valuable than a non-virgin. All of this matter is explained in Ketubot there. There are those who are stringent about this, but there is no sense or reason in this, and one who is stringent about this is considered among the perplexing. (Taz) Nowadays, everyone practices leniency in this matter according to the main law. (The Magen Avraham posed a difficulty, asking how those who ate in a state of ritual purity and terumah could do so, since someone who has immersed and waits for sunset is prohibited from these, see there. I do not understand, and what did the priests who ate terumah or those who served in the Temple do? In truth, they did not have intercourse on Shabbat, as the obligation is only on those who are able. Some evidence can be drawn from what is stated in Niddah 38: that the early pious ones would have intercourse from Wednesday onward, see there. It is difficult, as the scheduled time for Torah scholars is on Shabbat, and what is their virtue? Rather, there were several obstacles on Shabbat due to some reason, as mentioned, and study it well.)

We learn in Megillah (23b): On Shabbat they hasten to come to the synagogue, as everything has already been prepared on the eve of Shabbat, and it is good to hasten their arrival to recite the Shema like the early pious ones (Rashi). And they hasten to leave for the sake of the enjoyment of Shabbat (ibid.). And in Tractate Sofrim (Chapter 18, Halacha 4) it says: On Shabbat they hasten to come in order to recite the Shema like the early pious ones, and they delay their departure in order to hear the explanation of the Torah portion, meaning the section of the weekly reading. According to this, it is surprising about our teacher, the Rema, who wrote in this section: "The custom is that on Shabbat they come to the synagogue later than on weekdays, because regarding the daily offering on weekdays it is written: 'in the morning,' and regarding Shabbat it is said: 'on the day of Shabbat,' which implies later" (end of quote). This is contrary to the Talmud and Tractate Sofrim. Perhaps he holds that what was said 'they hasten to come' is not in comparison to weekdays, as the Talmud does not mention weekdays, but in comparison to a festival, where it says 'they come later' because of the need to prepare for the festival meal. In contrast, it says that on Shabbat 'they hasten to come,' meaning more than on a festival, but compared to weekdays, they come later. And the reason he wrote based on what is written 'on the day of Shabbat' is merely a hint, since this is written regarding the additional offerings, but because it is written 'in addition to the regular burnt offering,' it implies they are adjacent to each other. The main reason is because on Shabbat people sleep more than on weekdays, and this is also the source of the law in Mordechai (Chapter "Kol Kitvei") there, because sleep on Shabbat is a pleasure (see Bach and Magen Avraham, and according to what I have explained, everything fits well. It is puzzling about the Rif, the Rambam, the Rosh, and the Tur, who omitted this from Megillah).

They enter the synagogue and arrange the morning blessings, the Binding of Isaac, the section on the sacrifices, and the Mishnah "Which is the Place" just as on weekdays. However, for the sacrifices, they say "and on the Sabbath day," because they do not read the additional sacrifice of the Sabbath from the Torah, unlike on Yom Tov, when they read the section on the additional sacrifices from the Torah. And as for Rosh Chodesh, when they say "and on your new moons," even though they read from the Torah – it is because not everyone comes to the synagogue on weekdays and does not hear the Torah reading. But on the Sabbath and Yom Tov – everyone comes to the synagogue. And the reason we say "and on the Sabbath day" before Shacharit, which is the additional sacrifice – is in order to mention all the sacrifices together: the daily offering, the incense, and the additional sacrifices.

And I have a question: regarding all the sacrifices, they instituted to say in reference to "And we will pay with the offering of our lips," so why did they not institute the mention of the section of the "bazichin" on Shabbat, which refers to the showbread and the "bazichin" and their burning at the end of Parshat Emor. It appears to me the reason is because it is stated in Yoma (33a) by Abaye who arranged the order of the "ma'aracha" (the arrangement of the wood on the altar), that the additional offerings precede the "bazichin," because it is written twice "on the day" in reference to the "bazichin" — after the eve of Shabbat. And it is stated at the beginning of "Tamid Nishchat" that according to the opinion that holds this, the additional offerings were brought at the sixth hour and the "bazichin" at the seventh hour on the eve of Shabbat, and according to this, the "bazichin" would not be burned before noon. Therefore, it is impossible to say them in the morning, as this would be like someone who says the sacrifices before the light of day. According to this, what I have seen in some prayer books that printed the section of "bazichin" before the Kiddush of the day on Shabbat morning — is not correct, and this is only appropriate when reciting Kiddush after midday, and it is forbidden to fast on Shabbat until midday, as written in Siman 288.

Additional psalms are included in the Pesukei D'Zimra: "The heavens declare," "By David, when he feigned madness," "A prayer of Moses," "He who dwells in the secret place," "Praise the name of the Lord," "The Great Hallel," "Rejoice, O righteous," "A psalm, a song for the Sabbath day," and "The Lord reigns, He is clothed with majesty." The Sephardim add another psalm, "Sing to the Lord a new song," and "A song of ascents," and "The grandeur and the faithfulness," without concern for the ruling of Maharil not to say "The grandeur and the faithfulness" in congregation except on Yom Kippur (Magen Avraham, siman 665, sk 5). The Ashkenazim recite these psalms after "Baruch She'amar," because even on weekdays they say "Hodu" after "Baruch She'amar." The Sephardim, who say "Hodu" before "Baruch She'amar" on weekdays, also say the psalms beforehand, except for "A psalm, a song for the Sabbath day," which they say immediately after "Baruch She'amar," just as they say "A psalm of thanksgiving" on weekdays after "Baruch She'amar." On Shabbat, "A psalm of thanksgiving" is not recited, because the thanksgiving offering is not brought on Shabbat. The Tur objects to this, arguing that it is not said for the sake of the offering, but for gratitude (Beit Yosef). Nevertheless, this is the established custom, and it should not be changed.

And after the Song of the Sea, we add 'Nishmat' because it mentions the miracles of the Exodus from Egypt, and therefore we say this on Shabbat and Yom Tov. Similarly, we say 'Shochein Ad' and 'Uv'mak'helot.' One should extend and beautify the hymns, and one should not protest against those who extend them, even though the protester intends to prevent the neglect of Torah study. However, this is not like the lengthy singing of the cantors, which the sages do not approve of. (Magen Avraham section 4) We say 'Hakol Yoducha' and 'El Adon,' with the first two verses consisting of five words, and the rest four words, and at the end, six words, and this should not be changed. (Zohar Terumah) The Sephardi version reads 'Seraphim, Chayot, and Ofanei HaKodesh,' and this is also found in the Tikkunei Zohar. This seems correct, for the Ofanim are lower than the Chayot, as explained in the vision of Ezekiel's Chariot. Nevertheless, the Ashkenazi version reads: 'Seraphim, Ofanim, and Chayot HaKodesh,' as it appears in the Zohar Terumah (page 132), and we also say in Yotzer: 'And the Ofanim and Chayot HaKodesh.' It seems to me the reason is because the Ofanim do not have their own elevation; all their life force comes from the Chayot, as it is written in Ezekiel: "For the spirit of the living creatures is in the wheels, and when the living creatures went, the wheels went beside them, etc." Therefore, the Ofanim are mentioned first, not because they are higher in rank, but on the contrary, like we say the Ofanim depend on the Chayot HaKodesh, not that they have power on their own.

And they say 'To the God Who rested', and our teacher, the Rema, wrote that for any matter, if it was not said, one is not made to go back, except if 'To the God Who rested' was not said, one is made to go back, see there. The reason can be explained that in all other praises, Shabbat is not explicitly mentioned; rather, because Shabbat is a day of rest and sanctity, additional praises were included. However, 'To the God Who rested', the primary sanctity of Shabbat is mentioned there, therefore one is made to go back. And they were astonished at him, asking whether this is mentioned in the Talmud, and furthermore, the Tur wrote that in certain places they do not say it, see there, so how can we say that if it was not said, one is made to go back. (Magen Avraham) However, our teacher, the Rema, did not mean that one should go back to the beginning of the blessing, but rather he means to say it at the place where one stands. (ibid) And for the other songs, since one has passed the place where it is said and did not say it, one does not say it at all.

And we pray the first three blessings, which are only praise, and the middle blessing. The main part is the blessing of 'Be favorable with our rest... Who sanctifies the Shabbat,' but we precede it with 'Moses rejoiced,' just as in the evening service we precede it with 'You sanctified.' The intention of 'Moses rejoiced in the gift of his portion' is because he chose the day of Shabbat for rest while they were still in Egypt, as it is stated in the Midrashim. And when they were commanded about the Shabbat, Moses rejoiced in the gift of his portion, that the Holy One, blessed be He, chose the portion that he (Moses) had chosen. And it contains fifty-five words, corresponding to the fifty-five words from 'However, you shall keep My Sabbaths' until 'And He gave to Moses.' (Tur)

If one did not mention Shabbat [in the prayers], one must repeat: If one has already taken three steps back, one returns to the beginning of the prayer. If one has not taken three steps back, one returns to the mention of Shabbat (there). The prayer leader repeats the prayer, and in the Kedusha, they add "Then with a voice" and "From Your place, our King, appear and reign, etc." and says the Priestly Blessing and a complete Kaddish, and they say "There is none like You, etc." The Sephardim say "You have been shown, etc." because this was said regarding the acceptance of the Torah, which was given on Shabbat (there). The Sephardim say the Song of the Day after Shacharit, and this is correct, for the Song of Musaf was different, "the ziv lach," as it is stated in Rosh Hashanah (31a), and how can we say it after Musaf. It is surprising that in the Tractate Soferim, chapters 18 and 19, it lists the songs of the additional offerings, but it does not mention Shabbat. Also, those who have the custom on Rosh Chodesh to say "Bless the Lord, O my soul" after Musaf, which is the song of the additional offering of Rosh Chodesh, and similarly on every festival, they say the song related to the Musaf of that day as printed in the machzorim, why is the song of the Shabbat Musaf not mentioned at all, and this needs investigation. Know that in our custom, in Shacharit, we do not say "They will rejoice in Your kingship," but begin with "With the sanctifiers of the Seventh," and in Musaf we begin with "They will rejoice." The Sephardim begin with "They will rejoice" even in Shacharit, but they do not conclude with "a memorial to the work of Creation" in Shacharit, and the reason is unknown. One should not bow during "Nishmat" when saying "To You alone we give thanks," because one should not bow in prayer except in the places the Sages specified, no more. The reason we bow in "Aleinu" at "and we bend the knee" is because it is after the prayer, and we say that we are bending the knee, and similarly, we bow before the Torah scroll during the lifting, but not during the prayer. (The commentators have toiled in explaining "He saw and set the form of the moon," and it seems simple that it refers to the diminishing of its light, as explained in the Midrash, and in the future it will be filled. This is "and set," meaning He fixed it for the future and now diminished it; see Tur).

After Shacharit, the Torah scroll is taken out of the ark, and everyone stands in its honor. They are not permitted to sit until it reaches the reading table and is placed upon it. They recite 'Vayehi Binsoa HaAron' and 'Berich Shemei' from the Zohar (Parashat Vayakhel 206a) until 'Letav Ulchaim Ulshalom Amen.' One person is honored with taking out the Torah scroll and hands it to the chazzan (cantor), but the chazzan himself should not take it out of the ark, as it is considered more honorable this way, as explained in the Mishnah at the beginning of the seventh chapter of Yoma. 

The chazzan takes the Torah scroll, facing the congregation, and recites aloud: 'Shema Yisrael...' and the congregation responds after him. Then he says: 'Echad Hu Elokeinu, Gadol Adoneinu Kadosh Shmo' (Our God is One, Great is our Lord, Holy is His Name), and on Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, they say: 'Kadosh V’norah' (Holy and Awesome). However, in Tractate Sofrim, Chapter 14 (Halacha 10), it is stated that 'Kadosh V’norah' should always be said to include three praises: Gadol (Great), Kadosh (Holy), and Norah (Awesome), corresponding to the three Patriarchs and the three sanctifications, and the congregation responds after him, 'Echad Hu Elokeinu...'

Afterwards, the chazzan turns his face towards the ark, bows slightly, and recites 'Gadlu L’Hashem Iti...' (Magnify the Lord with me), and the congregation responds 'Lecha Hashem Hagedulah...' (To You, Lord, is the greatness), 'Al Hakol Yitgadal V’yitkadash...' (Above all, may He be exalted and sanctified), and the chazzan walks with the Torah scroll to the right, until the reading table, and places the Torah scroll on the table. Some have the custom to walk behind the Torah scroll, as mentioned in Tractate Sofrim there (the end of Halacha 14), which states: "This is what the noble-minded people of Jerusalem would do: When they took out the Torah and returned it, they would walk behind it in its honor," and there is an allusion to this in the verse 'After the Lord your God you shall walk' (see Sotah 39a).

Some refrain from walking behind the Torah scroll, as it might appear haughty, as if one is worthy to walk behind the Torah scroll. Know that in Tractate Sofrim there are different verses, the maftir (the one who reads the Haftarah) is the one who recites the verses, and the lifting of the Torah (Hagbah) is done before the Torah reading. We cannot change from our custom, and there is no strict requirement in this matter.

It has already been explained at the beginning of section 135 that Moses our teacher instituted for Israel to read each Torah portion on its respective Sabbath, and it is forbidden to exchange one portion for another. There are fifty-four portions in the Torah, although in the Zohar it is consistently mentioned as fifty-three. It appears to me that the intention is regarding the Sabbaths on which the portions are read, excluding "Vezot Haberacha," which does not have a Sabbath but is designated for the last festival day of Sukkot; in the Land of Israel - on Shemini Atzeret, and outside the Land - on Simchat Torah. But all fifty-three portions are specifically designated for the Sabbaths of the year. And since in a regular year there are not fifty-three Sabbaths, and aside from the festival days that fall on a Sabbath, when the portion is not read, and in a leap year there are more than fifty-three Sabbaths - therefore, there are portions that are combined and read together on one Sabbath. It has already been explained there that if for some reason the portion was not read on a particular Sabbath, it is read on the following Sabbath along with the portion designated for that Sabbath, and even if there are then two portions, both the portion of the past Sabbath and that of the current Sabbath are read together.

The Zohar (Vayakhel, page 206b) writes: "It is forbidden for one who reads the Torah to interrupt a section, or even a single word, except at the place where Moses divided the sections for the holy people." End quote. This does not refer to each of the readers, that they should only stop at a section, meaning an open or closed section, because if so, where would we find seven readers? For there are portions that do not contain any open or closed sections at all, like 'Vayetze', 'Miketz', and some that contain only one section, like 'Balak', 'Ha'azinu', and many portions that do not have seven sections. Rather, the intention is regarding the completion of the readers, that they should finish exactly at the end of the portion, neither earlier nor later by even a single word, and certainly not more, as he concludes later and writes: "And one should not interrupt the words of the portion of this Shabbat for the portion of another Shabbat... because when they complete the divisions of the entire year and are crowned before the Holy One, blessed be He, they say, 'I am from such-and-such Shabbat from such-and-such congregation... and it is forbidden for us to mix these with those... even by a hair's breadth and even by a single word." End quote. This strictness applies only to Shabbat morning and not to Mincha, nor to Monday and Thursday, since those readings are not part of the general count. And the proof is, that on Shabbat morning, we read those same portions again, just like the readings for Rosh Chodesh and festivals. (See Magen Avraham. And what they said in Berachot 12b, 'Any section that Moses did not divide, we do not divide,' refers to establishing it regularly, like the verses of Balak that they sought to establish in the Shema reading, as mentioned there. But for the Mincha of Shabbat and on Monday and Thursday, since we complete it on Shabbat, we do not concern ourselves with this, except that it is forbidden to stop in the middle of a verse, as stated in Taanit 22b. And what they said in Megillah 29b, that in the West (Eretz Yisrael) they divided it into three years, the truth is, they did not concern themselves with this, and therefore their custom did not spread, and all Israel completes it in one year. And the fact that in the Temple they divided the portion of Ha'azinu – there it was not for the study of Torah for all Israel, but the Levites would sing it in song, as stated in Rosh Hashanah 31a. See there and pay attention.)

And we take out the Torah scroll and read from it seven aliyot, no fewer. But we may add to the number of aliyot if necessary, as it is taught at the beginning of the third chapter of Megillah. From the Levush, it appears that it is a virtue to add, as he wrote that we elevate in matters of holiness. However, this does not seem to be the opinion of all the poskim (decisors of Jewish law), but rather that permission is given to add. According to Rashi’s explanation there, the reason is because it does not cause a loss of work. According to the Ran, it is because its sanctity is great. According to Rashi’s opinion, it is also permissible to add to the number of aliyot on Yom Tov, since it does not cause a loss of work. This is also the opinion of the Rambam in the 12th chapter of Tefillah. However, according to the Ran, it is only permitted to add on Shabbat and not on Yom Tov. This is the custom in these countries, except on Simchat Torah when many are added. The maftir (the one who reads the Haftarah) is not counted among the aliyot, even on Yom Tov when a different section is read for him, and certainly on Shabbat when he repeats what the seventh has read.

In the time of the Mishnah, not everyone would recite the blessings; rather, the Kohen would recite the first blessing, and the last person would recite the final blessing. As it is stated there: "The one who begins recites the blessing before, and the one who concludes recites the blessing after." In the time of the Gemara, it became the practice for each person who was called up to recite a blessing before and after. It is mentioned there (21b) that the reason is due to a decree concerning those entering and those leaving. See there. And now, it is clearly necessary to do so, because in the time of the Talmud, each person called up would read [from the Torah]. But now, since the reader reads, if the one who is called up does not recite the blessing, how will it be evident that he has been called up to the Torah?

Therefore, some say that even though according to the Mishnah it is permissible to add to the number of those called up to the Torah on Shabbat, this applied to their time when each person did not recite a blessing. But when each person recites a blessing, and if additional people are called up the number of blessings will increase, it is likely that there will be blessings in vain, since these blessings were not instituted (Magen Avraham, section 1, in the name of the Tashbatz). And although these are certainly valid points, nevertheless, this opinion has not been accepted. And most of the decisors did not agree with this (ibid.), for even in the time of the Gemara each of those called up would recite a blessing, as I have written, and yet all the early authorities wrote that additional people may be called up. And this is the prevalent custom. Some have instituted that no more than three additional people should be called up, meaning up to ten in total, excluding the Maftir (Eliyah Rabbah). However, even now there are those who do not add more than seven people called up, and this is very proper. And this is how one should conduct oneself except for occasions like a wedding or a circumcision and the like (Magen Avraham, ibid.).

Even according to the opinion that on Yom Tov it is not permissible to add [additional aliyot], when it falls on Shabbat it is permissible to add, and likewise on Yom Kippur that falls on Shabbat. There are those who are particular not to add on Yom Kippur even when it falls on Shabbat, because the headings of the sections are aligned with matters of atonement, and it is better not to change them (there, subsection 2). However, what can we do if they do not listen to us, saying they are compelled to add because of the complaints of the householders who want to be called up to the Torah? Since there is no prohibition in the matter, it is not worthwhile to create a conflict and protest against them.

Rabbeinu the Beit Yosef wrote in section 2: It is permitted to call up many people [for aliyot], even though one reads what another has already read and repeats the blessing – it does not matter. Thus far his words. And Rabbeinu the Rema wrote about this: And some prohibit it. And so is the custom in these regions, except on Simchat Torah because they are accustomed to increase the readers, and they follow the first opinion. Thus far his words. And even at a wedding or when there are many obligatory readings – they did not customarily call up someone to read what another has already read (Magen Avraham, subsection 4). And some are lenient at a wedding (ibid.). But it is better to avoid this, because the proofs of those who prohibit are clear from the Taanit (27b) that they did not permit skipping backwards, and the one who permits only did so when there was no other choice. And in the Mordechai at the end of Megillah, it is brought that Rabbeinu Ephraim left the synagogue in great anger because of this, see there. (And it is proper to distance from this. And it is obvious that even according to those who permit, this does not apply to the count of the seven readers when one reads what another has already read. And from the Gemara, it seems that the main importance is the third reader, but from the Zohar, Parashat Shelach, page 164b, it is explained that the sixth is preferable. And so it is in Pri Etz Chaim, Shaar HaShabbat, end of chapter 19, that it is the foundation. See there, and examine and you will find easily.)

Everyone may be counted towards the seven [who are called to the Torah], even a woman, even a minor who knows to whom the blessings are recited, i.e., who has some understanding that the blessing is directed to the Blessed One. However, the Sages said that a woman should not read in public because of the dignity of the congregation. Even according to strict law, they are only counted towards the seven, but it should not be that all of them are women or minors. Yet, a minor cannot be the one who reads until he has grown two pubic hairs (Magen Avraham, subsection 5). A minor is only counted towards the seven, but not towards the three on Monday and Thursday or Shabbat at Mincha (ibid.). It is not clear what the difference is between these cases. However, based on what will be explained, that not all aliyot can be given to a minor, it becomes clear. It is further written that even a minor who is a Kohen, if there is no adult Kohen present, may be called up. But if there is no Levi, to call the minor Kohen twice is certainly not correct (ibid.). There are those who question calling a minor Kohen, arguing that the verse "and you shall sanctify him, for he offers the bread of your God" does not apply to him since he is disqualified from offering sacrifices (ibid.). This is not a valid proof, for he will eventually be eligible to offer sacrifices, and he also eats from the most holy offerings. Moreover, a Kohen with a blemish can be called up first, even though he is disqualified from offering sacrifices.

Know that from the words of Pri Etz Chaim it is explained that when the Sages said, "everyone can be counted among the seven (called to the Torah)," this applies only to the seventh aliyah. The reason given is that it is of lesser importance than all the others, see there. And in the Rivash (Siman 321), it is written in the name of Rabbeinu Tam that a minor can be counted among the seven, but only for Maftir when there are two Torah scrolls, as only one person reads from the second Torah - a minor should not be called up. See there. I saw someone write in his name that a minor is only called up for Maftir among the seven (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 6). This is perplexing to me, as this is the wording of the Rivash there: "And for this reason, the Manhig wrote in the name of Rabbeinu Tam that on a day when there are two Torah scrolls, and the Maftir reads what is obligatory for the day, a minor should not read Maftir." And although we hold that a minor can be counted among the seven, nevertheless, it implies that for what is obligatory for the day, where only one reads, it must be an adult. But for the count of seven, a minor can be included if the others are adults. This is his language, clearly supporting our position. And in the Rokeach (Siman 53), it is written: "And a minor reading the Haftarah in the Prophets should not read less than twenty-one verses," implying that a minor only reads for Maftir (as the Magen Avraham also wrote in his name). But this is not so, as later (Siman 56) it is written: "A minor does not count among the three, but for the seven, he counts." This is his language.
