We must say that what was written earlier is because it is customary to call a minor for Maftir. And so is our custom now that a minor is only called for Maftir. But from the fundamental law, we have not seen any of the poskim who prevent a minor from being counted among the seven, except for the Arizal, who only permitted it for the seventh, as I have written. However, for the count of three, many poskim hold that a minor cannot be called, as I have written. And certainly, this applies also on Rosh Chodesh, Yom Tov, and Yom Kippur; only on Shabbat, where there are seven, a minor can be called. And according to the Arizal, only for the seventh. And when Maftir is from the second Torah scroll, a minor is not called, as I have written in the name of the Rivash. And in the Jerusalem Talmud, Megillah (Chapter 4, Halacha 3), it is stated that a servant can be counted among the seven, see there. And Rabbeinu Ramah wrote that his status is like that of a woman, meaning that ideally, he should not be called up due to the dignity of the congregation. But if his mother is an Israelite, he may be called up initially because he is considered a full Israelite, as he follows his mother. He also wrote that a mamzer is permitted to be called to the Torah. And it is forbidden to read with an uncovered head, meaning without a proper covering. Even a light covering, like in prayer where a hat or tallit on the head is required, as I wrote in Siman 91, paragraph 6, see there. He also wrote that there is no prohibition to call an esteemed and wealthy ignoramus before a Torah scholar. This is not a disgrace to the Torah scholar but an honor to the Torah as it is honored by great people. This is his language. And it is understood that this is when necessity brings to this. And earlier in Siman 137, the order of aliyot is explained, see there. (See Magen Avraham, subparagraph 8, and according to what I have written, it fits well. Be precise and you will find clarity.)

And know that it is found in Masechet Soferim (Chapter 18, Halacha 4): "That women are obligated to hear the reading of the Torah scroll like men… and it is proper to translate for the people, for women and children, every portion and prophet of Shabbat after the reading of the Torah." End quote. And it seems to me that it is not a complete obligation, but similar to children, for she is exempt from the study of Torah, and furthermore, there is no greater time-bound commandment than this. And regarding a woman being counted among the seven who are called to the Torah, the Tosafot have already written in Rosh Hashanah (33a, s.v. 'Ha'), that this is like they bless on all positive time-bound commandments, or it refers to the time of the Mishnah, when not all those called up would recite blessings, and moreover, these blessings are not because of the study of Torah. And one should not compare this to the commandment of Hakhel, where the Torah commanded: "Assemble the people, the men, the women, and the children," because this is a special commandment once every seven years, where the king himself would read from the book of Deuteronomy, which are words of admonition. But to say that they are obligated every Shabbat in the reading of the Torah - surely this is a surprising matter, and daily practice will prove it, and most of the time it is impossible for them to hear. Rather, Masechet Soferim speaks in the manner of ethical instruction, at a time when they would translate, that it is proper to translate before them and before the children to instill in their hearts the fear of G-d and His love, blessed be He. (See Magen Avraham, subsection 6, who is uncertain about this, and in my humble opinion it is clear as I have written, similar to children, and so wrote the Perisha there).

The common custom when two Torah portions are combined is for the fourth aliyah to read the end of the first portion and the beginning of the second, so that the seven aliyot (readers) are evenly distributed between the two portions. The Levush wrote that where additional readers beyond the seven are added, this practice is not beneficial, as the second portion will still have more readers than the first. Instead, if adding, for example, three readers to make a total of ten, five should read from the first portion and five from the second. However, the custom does not follow his view, as the main requirement is the seven readers. I find his opinion puzzling because it is necessary to say this; otherwise, there is always a maftir, and thus four read from the first portion and four from the second. And even if the maftir just repeats what the last reader read, in the case of 'Vayakhel-Pekudei' when they are combined, and one of the four special portions is included, the fourth reader combines them. But one could argue that since the maftir reads from another place, he is not counted. Nevertheless, the main point is that the seven readers are essential, and our custom is correct. (See Magen Avraham section 9, who wrote that there was a custom to sell the sixth aliyah separately, but we are not familiar with this custom).

The matter of the Maftir (the one who reads the Haftarah) is because there was a time when oppressors decreed that the Torah should not be read, and they instituted the reading of the Prophets with twenty-one verses, corresponding to the seven readers, each reading three verses. They also instituted blessings for this before the Haftarah and after it. Later, when the decree was annulled, they did not want to abolish the practice, and they decreed that the Maftir should first read from the Torah out of respect for the Torah, so the honor of the Prophets would not be equal to the honor of the Torah. Consequently, the Maftir blesses before and after, like all those called to the Torah. To make a distinction, they arranged that he reads what his predecessor read. There is a dispute whether the Maftir counts towards the number of the seven readers or not, but the main ruling is that he does count. Nevertheless, on Shabbat, Yom Tov, and Yom Kippur, where it is permitted to add readers according to the primary law, they decreed that the Maftir should not be counted among the readers, to satisfy those who hold that he does not count. Even according to those who hold that he does count, it is permissible to add readers. However, on Yom Kippur at Mincha, on Tisha B'Av, and on any public fast day at Mincha when it is forbidden to add readers, it is necessary to adhere to the primary law that the Maftir is among the readers, and the third reader is the Maftir. The Geonim instituted saying Kaddish before the Maftir to indicate that he is not among the readers. Therefore, at Mincha on a public fast day, when the Maftir is among the readers, Kaddish is not said before the Maftir.

But on a day when two Torah scrolls are taken out, the one who reads the haftarah does not repeat what the previous reader read; rather, he reads from the second scroll. Nevertheless, the Kaddish is recited beforehand, because the number of those called to the Torah has already been completed in the first scroll. Therefore, on a day when three Torah scrolls are taken out, such as Rosh Chodesh Tevet and Rosh Chodesh Adar that fall on Shabbat, where the seventh reader reads from the second scroll, in truth, Kaddish is not recited on the first scroll but on the second. The general rule is that Kaddish on Shabbat and Yom Tov is always recited before the haftarah.

There is a question regarding this, since we said that the one who reads the Haftarah portion from the Torah does so not for the essence of the reading itself, but out of respect for the Torah. Therefore, he does not read a new section but rather what was already read by the previous reader. If so, why on a festival does the one who reads the Haftarah read a new section? We should have established that first one of the regular readers should read the portion from the second scroll, and then the Haftarah reader should read it, as is done on Shabbat. And while it might be said that for a festival, the reading of the additional portions by the Haftarah reader is not mentioned in the Talmud and is an ordinance of the Geonim, and therefore they were not concerned about it, what can we say about the Haftarah reader on Shabbat Rosh Chodesh, Chanukah, and the four special portions which are mandated by the Talmud, why do we not do as we do on every Shabbat?

The answer to this is that certainly it would be possible to do so, but the sages did not wish to burden the congregation by having them listen to the same portion twice. Only on regular Shabbatot was it necessary to do so to complete the weekly Torah portion, for if not, it would not be possible to recite the Kaddish in the middle of the portion, and the Kaddish is necessary to indicate that the number of readers has been completed. But on these special Shabbatot, since the number of readers has been completed and it is possible to recite the Kaddish, they did not want to burden the congregation by having one of the readers read the Haftarah portion first and then have the Haftarah reader read it again, as it would place an undue burden on the congregation. (And so wrote the Gra in section 14). And if there are places with different customs in this matter, they should follow their custom, but our custom is primary and consistent with the halacha.

And our master, the Rema, wrote in section 4: That a minor can read in the Musaf portions or in the four additional portions added in Adar, and this is the practice even though some disagree, end quote. And some say that a minor should not be called up for the portion of Zachor, for it is a Torah obligation, and everyone is obligated in it, so how can a minor fulfill their obligation? And those who permit it argue that the minor is not the one reading the portion, but rather the adult who reads it fulfills their obligation. And there are those who do not allow a minor to be called up for Maftir on the first day of Shavuot, when the Haftarah is from the Chariot, nor on the seventh day of Passover when the Song of David is read, nor on Shabbat Shuva which calls the people to repentance. And in our country, it is not customary to allow a minor to be called up for Maftir in all the four additional portions, and this is proper and should not be changed. And know that the minor who is permitted must be one who knows and understands the matter well, for if not, he should not be allowed to be called up to the Torah.

If there is no one available to recite the haftarah except for those who have already been called up to the Torah, and if the chazzan has already recited Kaddish after the Torah reading, one of the individuals who was previously called up should go up again and recite the blessings before and after the haftarah, even if it is the seventh person who was called up, since Kaddish has already been recited. However, if Kaddish has not yet been recited, the person who was called up seventh should recite the haftarah, and their Torah reading is considered as if they are the one reading the haftarah. For why should the fact that they were the seventh person be a disadvantage, since in any case, the Torah reading takes place before the reading of the Prophets. Therefore, Kaddish should not be recited until after the haftarah and its blessings, because if Kaddish is recited before, it would create a separation between the Torah reading and the haftarah, and then the haftarah would no longer be connected to the Torah reading, leaving the haftarah without a preceding Torah reading. Instead, Kaddish should be recited after the blessings of the haftarah. This is not considered an interruption, since the haftarah is itself connected to the Torah reading, as instituted by the Sages (Magen Avraham, section 16). However, it is preferable to find someone who has not yet been called up to the Torah. And do not be troubled by our statement that if Kaddish is recited, one of those who were called up should recite the Torah blessings again, even though they have already blessed once. This is not a problem, because the blessings are due to the honor of the Torah, and each time someone goes up, it is an honor to the Torah. If someone was called up to the Torah in one synagogue and then goes up again in another synagogue, they are required to recite the blessings again. Moreover, a Kohen who goes up in place of a Levi blesses twice, as stated in Siman 135, and blesses one after the other immediately and in the same place.

If the shaliach tzibbur (prayer leader) made a mistake and concluded the Torah reading with the sixth aliyah and recited Kaddish, it is not necessary to call another person for the seventh aliyah. Instead, the portion read for the sixth aliyah should be read again together with the maftir, and the maftir counts towards the seven aliyot. This is the primary ruling as stated in section 13. If the Torah portion was read but one verse or even one word was omitted, it must be read again, including that verse along with two additional verses, with a blessing before and after. Even if the maftir was already read and the Musaf prayer was recited, and even if it is already the time for Mincha, it must still be read again as stated. This is also mentioned in the end of chapter 11 of Tractate Soferim. However, if this occurs during Mincha on Shabbat or on Monday and Thursday, it is not necessary to read it again since the portion will be read on the upcoming Shabbat. The details of these obligations will be clarified in the next siman (section), with God's help.

The reason we do not take out a second Torah scroll on Shabbat to read the maftir, to read "On the Sabbath day" like on a holiday, is because it contains only two verses. And to start earlier is not relevant, unlike Rosh Chodesh where there are four readers. Furthermore, the main purpose of reading the sacrifices is to atone for our sins, as stated in Ta'anit (27b), and in the additional offering of Shabbat, there is no sin offering for atonement (Tur). And although burnt offerings also atone for positive commandments that were not fulfilled, their primary purpose is as a gift, and only secondarily do they atone (Zevachim 7b, and see there in Tosafot). Additionally, on holidays, since they already interrupt the sequence of the weekly Torah portions, the Geonim instituted that we read also from the section of the additional offerings, but not on Shabbat (Ran, chapter 4 of Megillah). Furthermore, if so, there would be a single haftarah for the entire year, as the haftarah needs to be related to the reading of the maftir. (The Tur writes that therefore we say in the additional prayer: "You established the Shabbat, You desired its offerings," because it does not include a sin offering, see there. This means that a sin offering is not for appeasement, and it is better not to sin. Therefore, on Rosh Chodesh we say: "And the goat offerings will be for appeasement," because in the future there will be no sin, and then even the goat sin offerings will be for appeasement.)

Regarding the obligations - there are no fixed laws but customs. In the enactments of Maharal of Prague, it is stated that the precedence is as follows: first is the groom on his wedding day or on the Shabbat after the wedding, followed by the Bar Mitzvah boy, then the groomsmen, then the mohel, then the sandek, then the father of the newborn, and lastly, the one observing a yahrzeit (Eliyahu Zuta in Levush).

There are those who write that a groom on the day of his wedding takes precedence over all obligations, and on the Shabbat before the wedding, if he is a bachelor, he is equal to a bar mitzvah boy, and they should draw lots between the two of them. After them comes the father of a newborn when she goes to the synagogue after giving birth. Following him is the groom after the wedding, if he is a bachelor or she is a virgin, and the wedding was on a Wednesday or later. After that come those involved in a circumcision: the sandak (who holds the baby during the circumcision) precedes the father of the boy, and the father of the boy precedes the mohel (the one who performs the circumcision). A man whose wife gave birth to a daughter precedes the father of the boy before the circumcision day, if the circumcision is not on Shabbat itself, and similarly a yahrzeit (anniversary of a death) precedes him. The yahrzeit is last of all the obligations, except for the father of the boy on the day before the circumcision (Magen Avraham), and according to this, all the more so that he precedes the mohel. (Even though it is not explicitly explained in Magen Avraham to differentiate between if the circumcision is on Shabbat itself or afterwards, it seems to me that this is the case.) There are other customs, and each river flows according to its path (Magen Avraham).

The reason it is called "Maftir" and "Haftarah" is because during the time of persecution, they would exempt themselves from reading the Torah with it, as stated in Siman 282 (Levush). Additionally, since during the Torah reading it is forbidden to speak, and afterwards it is permitted to speak, it comes from the expression "they shall conclude with a speech" (ibid). It seems more likely that it is an expression of beginning, as found in the Midrash: "he made a conclusion," similar to "one does not conclude after the Passover with Afikoman" at the end of Pesachim, meaning he begins with the words of a prophet. They established this term in Aramaic to explain to the masses, and therefore during the time of the Talmud they would translate the Haftarah. The reason they instituted all the Haftarahs from the Prophets and not from the Writings is explained in the Mishnah at the beginning of "Kol Kitvei" that we do not read from the Writings on Shabbat because it would disrupt the study in the Beit Midrash (study hall), as mentioned there. (The Levush elaborates on this reason there.) The Maftir recites seven blessings: two on the Torah, one before the Haftarah, and four after it, corresponding to the seven readers. Even though there is a break at "Emet V'Tzedek," one does not respond "Amen" because it is in the middle of a blessing. The break is because in their days, when the Maftir reached "Ne'eman Atah..." the congregation would say this, and then the Maftir would say it, as explained in Tractate Soferim Chapter 13 (Halacha 10), and this is its wording: "for all His words are true and righteous, and immediately the people stand and say: 'You are faithful...', and then the Maftir repeats and says: 'You are faithful'." (See Tosafot Pesachim 104b, s.v. "Chutz") It is obvious that when there is no Torah reading, there is no Maftir.

It is stated in Gittin (60a) that, according to the law, it is prohibited to read from the book of Haftarot. This means that they would write all the Haftarot on parchment in one scroll, and it is prohibited to read from it if it is not a complete book of the Prophets, similar to the Torah scroll which should not be read from if it is not complete. However, they permitted it due to "a time to act for the Lord, they have nullified Your Torah" (Psalms 119:126). In other words, because it is not possible for every community to write a complete book of the Prophets, they therefore permitted writing only the Haftarot. The Levush wrote: "I have always wondered why they do not write the Haftarot in the form of a book like the Megillah, because it seems to me that one does not fulfill the obligation of reading the Haftarot in public when reading from printed Chumashim, since they are not written according to the laws of a Torah scroll, and this requires further investigation." And it is clear that his intention is not to write the complete books of the Prophets, as the Gemara permitted this because it is not feasible, but rather his intention is why not write the Haftarot on parchment with ink and sinews like a Torah scroll as was done in the time of the Gemara, as this is feasible for every community, as it is a minor matter. And certainly, one does not fulfill the obligation with printed books, even if we say there is sanctity in print like in writing - still, there is no parchment and no ink but merely color. Additionally, not all the Haftarot are connected together, and we must do as the sages of the Talmud did, and in my humble opinion, his words are clear.

And those who came after him disagreed with him: There are those who explained that in a pressing situation, even orally it is permitted (A.Z. in the name of A.T.), and there are those who explained that not every congregation has the ability to write a complete book of Prophets, and if they write only the Haftarot, it is of no use, since it is not a complete book (there in the name of Ma'aseh Yom Tov). And I am astonished, for does the Levush require a complete book? He requires only the writing of the Haftarot alone according to the law on parchment and with ink, and is he more knowledgeable than the Sages of the Gemara? And I do not understand what he says that there is no benefit in this, for the Sages of the Talmud permitted reading from a Haftarah scroll. And the words of the Levush are clear in their reasoning, for why should we not do as the Gemara in Gittin commands us there.

There are those who explain that since the primary reason the Sages permitted it was due to "a time to act," because it was not feasible for every community to write a complete set of Prophets, therefore now that the art of printing has been revealed and books are inexpensive, it is forbidden to write the Haftarot, as printing is considered an elevated form of writing. And if the concern is that they are written on paper, the Sheiltot Givorim writes in the chapter "Kol Kitvei" that other books besides the Torah can be written in all kinds of colors, and if so, it follows that they can also be written on paper and do not require a scroll (Magen Avraham). He also writes that this is what Tosafot writes there. However, all these matters are questionable, for Tosafot explicitly concludes there that this is regarding saving them from a fire, and so it is in Sheiltot Givorim, but to read from them publicly is forbidden, as stated there. He also writes this himself later in Siman 334 (section 18), that even nowadays, one may not read from them if they are not written in ink, as stated there. (And so the Gra"z critiques him in his Kuntres Acharon, as stated there.) And regarding what he wrote that blessings are recited over printed versions of Song of Songs and Lamentations on paper, this requires verification, and furthermore, among us, we do not recite blessings over them at all.

Furthermore, it is written in the responsa of the Rashba (Siman 487) that it is specifically prohibited with a Torah scroll, but not with Haftarot. Refer there. I am puzzled because the Rashba did not mention this. Here is the language of the Rashba there: "One does not read in public except from a Torah scroll that is made properly... and to read the Haftarah in a place where they did not read from a Torah scroll - no, for it was only instituted after the reading of the Torah scroll," end quote. Therefore, he did not mention at all the permissibility of writing the Haftarot when they are not written properly according to the law of the Talmud, and this was not the question at all. The question was about the custom of reciting the blessings when reading from the Prophets even though they did not read from a Torah scroll, and some read from a Torah written on notebooks, and he responded that both are prohibited, and nothing more is found in all of the Rashba's responsa. He further brought from the Kol Bo in the name of the Rashba, and this is his language: "And regarding the Haftarah that you asked about - I say that they are not particular about it, and they bless on the reading without a scroll," end quote. In my humble opinion, this is its interpretation: even when there is not a complete book, as it is stated in Gittin. There, however, the Haftarot are written according to the law. Moreover, it is difficult for me, because even according to his words, now that books are readily available in print and cheaply, it is prohibited to read from a Haftarah. If so, we should read the Haftarah from a Tanach or a complete Prophet, and indeed we read from Haftarot that are in Chumashim. If so, it is obvious that it is prohibited according to his words, which state that even from a Haftarah scroll written on parchment - it is prohibited, because it is possible to have a complete printed book, and all the more so it is prohibited with printed Haftarot.

And there are those who refute his words for another reason, and here are his words: "The Haftarah was not instituted at all to be read from a valid book, but it is forbidden to read it by heart. And even though in their times it was forbidden to write individual sections, whether from the Torah, the Prophets, or the Writings unless it was a complete book, nevertheless, they permitted writing Haftarot because of 'a time to act for the Lord.' And even now, with the advent of printing and the availability of books at a low cost, it is still permitted to print or write only the Haftarot, because even if a complete book of the Prophets were printed on paper, it would not be permitted to read from it except because of 'a time to act for the Lord,' since it is not on parchment and not written in a scroll, etc." End of the quote. (The Gra"z in section 4).

And his words are not understood at all, for where does he get the idea that the Haftarah was not instituted to be read from a valid book in public? Furthermore, if that were the case, why did they say in the first chapter of Bava Batra (13b) that one must leave four lines between each prophet and three lines between each of the Twelve Minor Prophets, and that each prophet must be written separately? Since it was not instituted to be read from a valid book in public, all the more so for ordinary study, and why did they not say the same for the Writings? Rather, it is certain that this is because it must be read in public with the same validity as the Torah scroll, and the Sefer Haftarah mentioned in Gittin was written according to the law on parchment, with ink, and in scroll form, but it was not a complete book because it was not possible.

Besides this, it is impossible to say so, for we say in Gittin there that we do not read from Chumashim in public because of the respect of the congregation, and all the more so they would not institute reading the Haftarah from an invalid book because of the respect of the congregation. And certainly, even now with printing, it is not to be read except when written like a Torah scroll, but not complete books of the Prophets, only a book of Haftarot, which the sages permitted. And the Levush correctly said so. And in Lithuania, there are many places where they write complete books of the Prophets, and there are those who write only the Haftarot, and this is our obligation and this is proper for us, but they should be warned not to make two columns like a Torah scroll but one column, as we say there in Bava Batra (15a). And so wrote the Eliyah Rabbah.

One concludes with a reading from the Prophets related to the theme of the Torah portion, as printed in the Chumashim (Pentateuchs), and one does not read fewer than 21 verses, corresponding to the seven people called to the Torah, with each reading three verses. However, if the topic concludes earlier, such as "Add your burnt offerings to your sacrifices" and similar cases, it is acceptable. Truly, this is not an absolute requirement, as the Tur wrote that in places where there is a translator, ten verses suffice, as stated in the Tractate Soferim (Chapter 13). On Yom Tov, when five people are called, fifteen verses suffice. Accordingly, on Tisha B'Av and public fasts, nine verses suffice, although the topic there typically extends further. We have already written that the Maftir and Haftarah were instituted only for public readings after reading from the Torah, but otherwise, it is forbidden to recite them with blessings before and after. However, without the blessings, it is permissible. It is appropriate to read the Haftarah after reading the Torah portion twice and the translation once, and this is the custom.

If Rosh Chodesh falls on Shabbat, one does not mention Rosh Chodesh in the blessing of the Haftarah in "Al HaTorah Ve'al HaAvodah" because there is no prophet for Rosh Chodesh. Some say that even though it is not mentioned in the concluding blessing of "Mekadesh HaShabbat" for Rosh Chodesh, it is nevertheless mentioned within the blessing by saying "and on this Shabbat day and on this Rosh Chodesh day." This is the opinion of the Rambam in Chapter 12 of Tefillah, where he writes: "Similarly, if Rosh Chodesh falls on Shabbat, the one who reads the Haftarah mentions Rosh Chodesh in this blessing, just as it is mentioned in the prayer." This also appears to be the opinion of Rashi in Shabbat (24a) and the opinion of Rabbeinu Yonah in the Rosh there. Nevertheless, the custom is not so because our teachers, the Ba'alei HaTosafot, wrote there that it is not necessary to mention it at all, and it depends on the Talmudic discussion. (For the statement "and the law is not..." the Tosafot wrote that it does not apply to Rav Gidel, see there.)

We have already written that before the Haftarah, there is one blessing: 'Who has chosen good prophets'. Some want to say that it is two blessings, as in the middle, it states, 'Blessed are You, Hashem, Who has chosen the Torah, etc.' However, it is truly one blessing. Initially, we bless 'Who has chosen good prophets' and not false prophets. And because there are many matters in the prophets that appear as mere storytelling, it states 'and desired in their words spoken in truth', meaning that it is not mere storytelling but words of truth that the Holy One, Blessed be He, desired. And they wanted to give honor to the Torah, which is of higher status than the prophets, and to Moshe, the master of all prophets. It would appear as if mentioning them after the prophets would not be respectful. Therefore, it states 'Blessed are You, Hashem, Who has chosen the Torah and Moshe His servant, etc.' to juxtapose it to 'Blessed are You, Hashem', and afterwards 'and the prophets of truth and righteousness', as the prophets are of lower status than Moshe Rabbeinu, and the words of the prophets are of lower status than the Torah (so it appears in Chapter 12 of Prayer, law 15). And this is why it first states: 'Who has chosen' in the past tense, and then 'Who chooses' in the present tense - this is similar to the blessing of the Torah, where it first states 'Who has given', and then 'Who gives the Torah', to indicate that each and every day the Holy One, Blessed be He, gives His Torah and chooses it, as they have said: 'Each and every day, they should be in your eyes as if new'. Furthermore, new insights in Torah are revealed each and every day to those who engage and toil in it for its own sake, as our Sages said: 'What is this like, etc.'

And after the Haftarah, there are four blessings. As we have already written, "faithful" is in the middle of a blessing. There is a question regarding this: Why does it begin with "Blessed," since it is adjacent to the blessing before the Haftarah, and the Haftarah is not considered an interruption? Similar to "Yishtabach," which does not begin with "Blessed" because it is adjacent to "Baruch She'amar," even though the verses of praise interrupt in the middle, as we wrote in Siman 54. The answer is that they wanted to liken it to the blessing of the Torah, which begins with "Blessed" after the reading, as explained in Siman 139. This is because in the time of the Mishnah, not all who were called up recited a blessing, only the first and the last, and there was a significant interruption. Therefore, they enacted the same for the Prophets (Levush in his glosses). Additionally, it seems that because there were those who would translate the Prophets to make them understandable to the common people, and there was a significant interruption, they enacted to begin with "Blessed." The other three blessings do not begin with "Blessed," as is the rule for blessings that are adjacent to their companion. The first blessing after the Haftarah begins and ends with "Blessed" because it contains several matters and is considered a long blessing. (And perhaps they also judged the first one before it as long: "Who chose" and "was pleased with their words," and afterwards mentions the Torah and Moses. There is no need for what is written in section 9; examine it well.)

This is what we say: "And not one of Your words will return empty," and at first glance, the word "empty" seems superfluous and lacking understanding. It appears to me that its interpretation is as follows: It is a simple matter that all the words of the Torah and all the words of the prophets will be fulfilled, God willing, and anyone who doubts this has no share in the God of Israel. However, seemingly, in matters that have already passed, we have no benefit from their words, and Heaven forbid, it is like a mere story. But the truth is that the past still shines at all times and in every moment, like the Exodus from Egypt, where in every generation a person is obligated to see himself as if he himself came out of Egypt, and therefore at every moment it is the Exodus from Egypt. Similarly, all the words of the prophets that have already passed have not passed and will not pass; they always shine and have an effect at all times, and this is the virtue of our holy Torah. Therefore, we say, "And not one of Your words will return empty," meaning even those that are now in the past and have already occurred — they too will not return empty, and they are perfect Torah. In the blessing of "Rachem," we say, "And for the downtrodden soul, save quickly in our days," and the Sephardim say, "Save and rejoice," because they conclude with "He who makes Zion rejoice" — it should be similar to the conclusion close to the conclusion. The Ashkenazim were not concerned with this, because salvation and joy are one and the same. In the blessing of "Simchenu," we conclude with "Shield of David," as the Sages commanded in Pesachim (117b): "In prayer — 'Who causes the horn of salvation to sprout,' in the Haftorah — 'Shield of David,'" as mentioned there, as God promised David: "I will make for you a name like the names of the great ones" (I Chronicles 17:8), just as we conclude with "Shield of Abraham," so too do we conclude with "Shield of David." However, in prayer, it is impossible to conclude with "Shield of David," for we need to conclude with a language of mercy. Additionally, since we conclude with "Shield of Abraham," it is impossible to mention "Shield of David" (Rashbam in the name of Rashi there).

Every person must intend to listen to the blessings of those who read from the Torah and the blessings of the Maftir, and to answer "Amen" after them. This will count towards completing the count of one hundred blessings that are lacking on Shabbat, as mentioned earlier in Siman 46. Based on this, it is obligatory for those who are called up to bless in a loud voice, and if someone says it quietly, they should be reprimanded. A minor can recite the Maftir, and he should be taught to say it in a loud voice. If someone is called to be Maftir and does not know how to recite the Haftarah, another person can recite it, similar to the Torah reading where one person blesses and the reader reads. However, this should not be done initially. The reason is that with the Torah, which needs to be read with cantillation, if the person does not know the cantillation, the reader reads, and the one called up repeats quietly after him. But for the Haftarah, which is read from a printed Chumash, if the person is so ignorant that he cannot read from a Chumash, it is not proper to call him for Maftir. Therefore, in our region, where in many synagogues there are complete prophetic scrolls, the reader reads as with the Torah, and this is the common practice. (This seems to me to be the explanation of the Rema in paragraph 4, and there is no need for the words of the Magen Avraham in sub-paragraph 3. Also, what he brought from the Beit Yosef in Siman 282, the Beit Yosef there did not agree with that. See and be precise.)

Rabbeinu the Beit Yosef wrote in Section 5: If the one reading the Haftarah becomes mute in the middle of the reading, the one who comes to complete it should not start from where the first one stopped, but must go back and start from where the first one began, just as with the Torah reading. These are his words. This means, as he wrote above in Siman 140: "If the one reading the Torah becomes mute, the one who stands up to read should start from where the first one began and recite the blessings before and after. According to the Rambam, he does not need to recite the blessing before." These are his words. And even in a situation where the Shliach Tzibur (prayer leader) is reading, the same rule applies. Here too, the blessings before the Haftarah need to be recited, but according to the Rambam, it is not necessary. This is derived from the Jerusalem Talmud, Chapter 5 of Berachot (Halacha 3), and there we explained it with the help of Heaven. (This is not analogous to the Shliach Tzibur who becomes mute, as mentioned by the Taz in subparagraph 2, or the Shofar mentioned by the Magen Avraham in subparagraph 4, where all have already fulfilled their obligation. This is not the case with the Haftarah, where the one called up is obligated to recite the blessings before and after, as is the case with the Torah reading in Siman 140.)

The one who recites the Haftarah does not begin the blessing before the Haftarah until the one who rolls the Torah scroll has finished rolling it (Sotah 39b). The reason is so that the one who rolls the scroll can hear the blessings and the Haftarah. Additionally, there is a disrespect to the Torah scroll if it is not yet rolled and they are already engaging in the needs of the Haftarah (see Beit Yosef). When he blesses after the Haftarah, they should not remove the scroll of the prophets until after the blessings, so that it is evident what he is blessing on. Our master, the Beit Yosef, in his great book, did not agree with this (see there), and it can be said that for anything one blesses on, the item must be in front of him (see Taz, section 3). Two people should not recite the Haftarah simultaneously, as two voices cannot be heard. This applies only when the reader reads from the Prophets, or the one who recites the Haftarah reads from a Chumash and everyone listens. But in most places in the country, everyone recites the Haftarah from the Chumashim in their hands, and this is also the opinion of the Arizal (see Magen Avraham, subsection 5), and in these situations, this law does not apply (and this is the intention of the Magen Avraham there). And know that on Shabbat where two portions are read, the Haftarah is from the second portion, and also for 'Acharei' and 'Kedoshim' they recite the Haftarah 'Are you not like the children of the Ethiopians' from Kedoshim, and not like those who say to recite 'Will you judge' (see Levush and those who critique him).

After the Haftarah, it is customary to say "Yekum Purkan," "Mi Sheberach," and a blessing for the king. We also mention the souls of the deceased, because on Shabbat there is also rest for the dead, and we pledge charity on their behalf. This has support from the Sifrei: "Atone for Your people Israel"—these are the living, "whom You have redeemed"—these are the dead, teaching that the dead also require atonement. We recite "Av Harachamim," "Ashrei," and "Yehalelu," and the congregation says "Mizmor LeDavid Havu," etc., because it contains seven voices, from which we learn the seven blessings of Shabbat. On Shabbat when Tachanun is not said, if it were a weekday, and likewise on Shabbat when we bless the new month, we do not say "Av Harachamim" nor mention the souls. Nevertheless, if it is necessary to mention, we do so, for we also mention souls on Yom Tov. During the days of the Omer counting, we say "Av Harachamim" even when blessing the new month, and similarly when blessing Rosh Chodesh Av, because these days are days of decrees. If Rosh Chodesh Iyar or Rosh Chodesh Av falls on Shabbat, we do not say "Av Harachamim." Likewise, if there is a wedding or circumcision, we do not say "Av Harachamim," and every place follows its custom. (See Magen Avraham section 6 that if there is no Chumash in the synagogue and there is no Eruv, ten people go to a house that has a Chumash and read the Haftarah there, even though the Torah reading was in the synagogue, and they can read by heart if there is no other option. This is not the general custom with us. The other things he wrote are not our custom.)

It is stated in Berachot (8b): "A person should always complete his Torah portions with the congregation, [reading] twice from the Torah text and once from the translation; even [the verses] 'Atarot and Dibon.' For anyone who completes his Torah portions with the congregation, [reading] twice from the Torah text and once from the translation, his days and years are prolonged." This means that before the congregation reads the portion in the synagogue, he should read it at home, whether on the morning of that Shabbat itself or during the entire preceding week, but he should not do so before that week. There are people who have the custom to read a little bit each day of the week and complete it on Shabbat (Turei Zahav). Therefore, even though everyone hears the Torah reading every Shabbat in the congregation from the reader, nevertheless, each person is obligated to read the weekly portion for himself every week, twice from the Torah text and once from the translation. (And the Levush wrote a mnemonic: "And these are the names of the children of Israel"—the initial letters of "וה״שב"י" stand for "A person is obligated to read the portion twice from the Torah text and once from the translation," and this obligation applies to all "the children of Israel.")

The reason for this matter is not known to us, but certainly, at the time that Moses our Teacher instituted the reading of the Torah, he also instituted this ordinance, that each person should read the Torah portion twice in the original Hebrew and once in the Targum (Aramaic translation). The Levush wrote: in order that one should be proficient in the Torah, see there, but this is obviously insufficient. It appears that the obligation in the Torah includes hearing and learning, as we say in the blessing of Ahavah: "to hear, to learn." Now, the hearing is done on Shabbat from a kosher Torah scroll, written according to the law. Therefore, one should first study from a Chumash and then ascend in holiness to hear from the Torah scroll. 

It is stated in Sotah (37b): "General principles and specific details were said at Sinai, repeated in the Tent of Meeting, and taught a third time in the plains of Moab," see there. Therefore, one needs to study three times, even a verse that has no Targum, as will be explained, corresponding to these three. However, where there is a Targum, they chose the Targum for the third time, so that one understands what he is studying. The Targum is close to the Holy Tongue and was given at Sinai, as we say in Nedarim (37b): "And they read from the book of the Law of God, distinctly," (Nehemiah 8:8) "distinctly" – this refers to the Targum. It was given at Sinai as explained there, but it was forgotten and Onkelos reestablished it, as we say at the beginning of Megillah, see there. (And something similar I saw in Eliyahu Zuta in the name of Mateh Moshe. It was not explained properly, see there.) And some say: it corresponds to the two who read and the one who translates (Raavan).

And there is a doubt: Do we specifically require two readings of the Scripture first, and then the translation, or does one fulfill the obligation if one reads Scripture, translation, and then Scripture again? From the words of the Levush, it is clear that his opinion is the latter, as he wrote: "It seems to me that if a person reads one Scripture and one translation by himself, and then when the congregation reads the portion in the synagogue, he reads word for word with the cantor—this fulfills 'twice Scripture and once translation.'" See there, where it is explicitly stated that the translation can be in the middle. And even though it is written there that Rabbeinu Beit Yosef does not hold that this fulfills the obligation—that is because he believes that one does not fulfill the obligation from the cantor’s reading, see there, but not because the translation is in the middle. And the great authorities have already written that Rabbeinu Beit Yosef does not actually disagree on this point, but rather he is discussing that one does not fulfill the obligation by listening. But if one says it word for word with the cantor—he fulfills the obligation (Perisha and A.Z.). And there are those who say that even by listening, one fulfills the obligation (Magen Avraham, subsection 8). And there are also those who say that if one hears 'twice Scripture and once translation,' one also fulfills the obligation, provided one intends to listen (Sha'arei Teshuvah in the name of Radbaz). In my humble opinion, the requirement is specifically study and not listening, as I have written. And see paragraph 13.

There is an opinion that the reading of "twice the scripture and once the translation" is to be done in the following manner: read each section, whether it is an open or closed section, twice, and then the translation (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 1 in the name of the Rashal and the Shelah). And this seems logical, for the Holy One, blessed be He, said each section to Moses together, and between sections, there was a pause, as it is stated in Torat Kohanim at the beginning of Vayikra: What purpose did the pauses serve? To give Moses time to contemplate each section. And Rashi brings this in his commentary on the Chumash, see there. And perhaps for this reason, they commanded to read "twice the scripture and once the translation," as it is stated in the Midrash (Yalkut on Job 28): Every word that the Holy One, blessed be He, said to Moses, He would say twice in His heart, and then He would say it to Moses. What is the reason? "Then He saw and recounted it" (Job 28:27) – once, etc., see there. In any case, the Holy One, blessed be He, said each section to Moses individually. And at the beginning of Megillah (4a), they said: I will pass a section and review it, see there. And a "section" is called either open or closed. And what is indicated in the Chumashim as "third," "fourth," etc., is of no consequence. (And in Berakhot 8b, where they said: A person should always complete his sections with the congregation, which implies that each series is called a "section" – it is not so, for the explanation is: the sections of the series.)

However, according to this, there is a question when there is a paragraph in the middle of a verse, such as in Pinchas: "And it was after the plague," and in Vayishlach: "And the sons of Jacob were twelve," and in Devarim: "From Eilat and from Etzion Geber" – what should be done if one stops there and repeats the paragraph? After all, it is in the middle of a verse! Nevertheless, it seems that one should do so. And if the concern is "any verse that Moses did not divide, we do not divide" – here Moses did indeed divide it. Similarly, in the Ten Commandments with "You shall not murder," etc., where there is a paragraph. Look there.

Some have written to read each verse twice, and then the Targum (the Arizal, and the Ma'adanei Yom Tov there, in Divrei Chamudos section 41), and at the end of the portion, to read the verse again after the Targum in order to conclude with the Torah (Magen Avraham there). And there is proof for this from the language of the Gemara: "twice Mikra and once Targum," which is in masculine form, and "Parsha" is in feminine form, and "Pasuk" is in masculine form. However, it can be said that it refers to a person, that the person should say twice Mikra and once Targum. And it seems to me that this depends on the reasons: for the reason written in section 4 – it certainly refers to "Parsha," and also for the reason written in section 2. But for the reason of the "yesh omrim" at the end of section 2, it certainly refers to each verse (see there in Divrei Chamudos).

And there are those who read the entire portion, and then a second time, and then the translation. This also somewhat implies from Rashi's language in Berakhot there, and from the language of the Gemara which says: "Rav Beivi bar Abaye intended to complete all the portions of the entire year on the eve of Yom Kippur, etc.," and the intention is all the portions. Afterwards, it says: 'He intended to precede them,' and Rashi explained (beginning of "to precede them"): "to arrange all the portions in one Shabbat," see there, and so he called the portion a "parasha." And this is also explained from the words of the Or Zarua HaGadol (Siman 12), and this is his language: "He intended to complete all the portions of the entire year. Rashi reads the portions of the entire they are four portions read in Elul, and four portions read in Adar, etc."; until here is his language. So he called the portion a "parasha." Therefore, it seems to my humble opinion that there is no strictness, and one can do as he wishes, for all have a basis in Halacha. And it is also possible that he can sometimes do it this way and sometimes that way. And if it were thought that there was strictness to do it specifically this way or that way – our early sages would not have been silent about explaining it. And there are those who wrote that if he is proficient in the cantillations – he should read from the Torah scroll, and immerse after the reading, and cut his nails before the reading (Magen Avraham there). This is a measure of piety, and for those who read it all on Shabbat eve. And there are those who wrote that it is forbidden to interrupt with speech during the reading of twice the scripture and once the translation (Be'er Heitev section 1). It is puzzling to say this, for without a blessing, what relevance does interruption have? As Tosafot wrote in Berakhot (14a beginning of "days") regarding Hallel. And if it is because one should not interrupt Torah study with worldly matters – if so, this does not pertain to the reading of twice the scripture and once the translation, and presumably, he interrupts for necessary matters. Moreover, those who read a portion every day – indeed interrupt a lot, therefore this has no basis in law.

What is considered "with the congregation"? The Tur wrote: The entire week from Sunday onward is considered "with the congregation" because the Torah portion begins on Shabbat at Mincha. (And this is "with the congregation," meaning: when the congregation begins.) It is an optimal mitzvah to complete it before eating on Shabbat. (The Or Zarua writes there that we are concerned that due to the abundance of eating, one might not read it at all.) If one did not complete it before eating, they should complete it after eating and before Mincha. But from that point onward, since another portion has begun, the time for this portion has passed; thus far is his wording.

It is clear from his words that there is no special enhancement to complete [the reading] before the Torah reading, only before eating, as he refers to this as "a mitzvah of the most preferred kind." It is also clear from his words that after Mincha – its time has already passed, because the congregation has already begun another [prayer], and it is not considered "with the congregation." It is also clear from his words that if one completes it on Friday evening – this is not a mitzvah of the most preferred kind. And so wrote the Mordechai in the first chapter of Berachot, that specifically on Shabbat morning before eating, see there (and see Beit Yosef).

But there are those who wrote that the primary enhancement (hidur) is on Friday; some say before noon, and some say after noon. And thus was the custom of the Arizal to read from the Torah scroll on Friday after the prayer (see Be'er Heitev and Sha'arei Teshuvah, subsection 1). And there are those who say that it is an optimal mitzvah to read a little every day and to complete it on Friday, as is printed in the book Chok L'Yisrael. And there are also those who say: Whoever did not complete [the reading] on Shabbat should complete it by Wednesday, for this is still considered after Shabbat, as we say at the end of the seventh chapter of Gittin (77a). And there are others who say that one can complete it until the end of the year, until the completion of the Torah in Eretz Yisrael on Shemini Atzeret, and outside of Eretz Yisrael on Simchat Torah. And then he should read all the portions he did not read, reading them twice in Hebrew and once with the translation. And so it appears from the words of our Rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch and the later authorities, and so should one practice.

And it has already been explained in their saying of blessed memory that for everything, translation is required, even verses of names like "Reuven and Shimon" – a translation is necessary. This is not because of the translation itself, for even in the language of the translation, the names remain the same as in the original text, but rather because it must be done three times, as we have explained according to the reasons. And in the Gemara, it is said: even "Atarot and Divon." This has an even greater novelty, as Rabbeinu Bachya wrote, because the translation refers to names of idol worship, and one might think it is better not to mention them – it comes to teach us that this is not the case. (The commentators have labored on this matter, see Taz and Magen Avraham, and see Tur and Terumat HaDeshen. And according to what I have written, it is clear, be precise and you will find it easy.)

The Tur wrote: If one learns the portion with Rashi's commentary, it is considered like the Targum (Aramaic translation), for the intent of the Targum is only to understand the matter. But if one reads in other languages, it is not so. Thus far are his words. This is because other languages do not convey the intent as it was transmitted from Sinai. However, the Targum explains as it was given from Sinai, as I wrote at the end of section 2. Similarly, Rashi's commentary is based on the interpretations of our Sages of blessed memory, which is the clear truth as from Sinai. And our Master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 2: A God-fearing person should read the Targum and also Rashi's commentary, for the Targum was given from Sinai and Rashi's commentary helps to understand the portion well. The great authorities agreed that only the Targum of Onkelos is valid, and one does not fulfill their obligation with anything else, as the Targum is sacred and was given from Sinai. This is also in accordance with the wisdom of the Kabbalah, and so all Israel practices, and it is forbidden to change this. If one does not have the Targum at hand, they should read the scripture twice, and when they obtain the Targum, they should read it (Magen Avraham, section 4). And if one does not expect to obtain the Targum, in my humble opinion, they should read the scripture three times, for the reasons that have been explained.

One can read "Shnayim Mikra ve'Echad Targum" during the Torah reading; so wrote our teacher the Beit Yosef in section 5. Its explanation is that one can recite "Shnayim Mikra ve'Echad Targum" during the Torah reading, even if it is not in sync with the reader. The reason is explained in the Mordechai there, because he is engaged in this matter, see there. There are those who say that even by listening, one fulfills the obligation, but we have already written that this is not so (and so also wrote the Kenesset Hagedolah and the Ateret Shlomo). Teachers of children who read the portion throughout the week with the children several times fulfill their obligation of reading. If they read with them the Targum or Rashi's commentary, they also fulfill the obligation of Targum. See what I wrote in section 12. Similarly, anyone who learned the portion twice during the week does not need to repeat the portion on Shabbat. The Haftarot do not need to be read individually, but it is customary to read them after "Shnayim Mikra ve'Echad Targum". Likewise, what is read on Rosh Chodesh, festivals, and the High Holidays does not need to be read individually, as each one has already been read on its Shabbat. Our teacher the Rema wrote: On the Shabbat of a wedding, the Haftarah of Shabbat should be read, and not "Sos Asis"; thus far his words. In his days, the custom was to read "Sos Asis" for a groom, but in our days we do not know of this custom. (And all that the Magen Avraham wrote in sections 11 and 12 – we do not know of such customs. Also, what he wrote in the name of the Kenesset Hagedolah, that the one who reads "Shnayim Mikra ve'Echad Targum" should read the Haftarah of the weekly portion and not of the four special portions – needs investigation.)

Before the Musaf, one recites Kaddish, and this refers to what was recited beforehand: 'Ashrei' and additional items, for there is no Kaddish without preceding items. The Musaf prayer consists of the first three blessings and the last three blessings, the sanctity of the day, and the Musaf offerings in the middle. The main part is the verses of the offerings: "On the Sabbath day, two lambs, etc.," and the blessing "R'tzeh Bimnuchateinu." Additionally, they included "Tikanta Shabbat" just like in Shacharit they added "Yismach Moshe." Because the sanctity of Musaf is greater than that of Shacharit, they also mention the future redemption: "that You will bring us joyfully to our land, etc.," and this is the case in all Musaf prayers.

And they instituted 'Tikkun Shabbat' based on the reversed Aleph-Bet: תשר"ק, צפע"ס, נמל"ך, יטח"ז, והד"ג, ב"א. The hint to this is: תשר"ק - based on "I will whistle to them and gather them" (Zechariah 10:8), צפע"ס - "the mountains shall drip sweet wine" (Joel 4:18), צ"ף like ט"ף, meaning that the sweetness will be seen everywhere, נמל"ך - "God will be king" (Zechariah 14:9), יטח"ז - "they will shoulder together to serve Him," and ח"ז is a term for prophecy - "for eye to eye they shall see" (Isaiah 52:8), והד"ג ב"א - "Leviathan will come and companions will feast upon him" (Bayit Yosef). 

How good and beautiful is the Sephardic version: 'Then from Sinai they commanded two actions properly,' which includes the letters מנצפ"ך, and מנצפ"ך refers to the prophets, as from the word צופים, as stated at the beginning of Megillah. Therefore, they say 'from Sinai they commanded,' meaning that all are from Sinai. And 'Tikkun' has some versions written with a 'kuf,' meaning repair, and some with a 'kaf,' meaning 'I have made ready, etc.' 

The explanation of 'You desired its offerings' is explained by the Tur, that although there is labor involved - nevertheless, you permitted the offering of the daily and additional sacrifices on Shabbat, see there. Alternatively, the additional sacrifices of Shabbat are acceptable because they do not have the measure of a sin offering (see Bayit Yosef). 'You commanded its explanations with the arrangement of its libations' - this refers to the section 'Command the children of Israel,' where the Shabbat offering is detailed, 'You commanded its offerings' - those specified in it, 'with the arrangement of its libations' - they are the six rows of showbread, and its interpretation is six arrangements, and its libations are from the term 'libation vessels' (Bayit Yosef). 

It would be better to say 'explanations' with a left 'shin,' in the sense of 'he spread the tent over the tabernacle,' and similarly here, the spreading of the showbread on the table, with the arrangement of its libations - they are the bowls, which are the libation vessels. 'Those who delight in it shall inherit honor forever' - it is stated in the Pesikta: by virtue of three things, Israel delights before the Holy One, blessed be He, by virtue of Shabbat, etc., as it is written: 'then you shall delight in the Lord.' 'Those who taste it merit life' - those who honor it with various foods and delicacies. Some have the custom to taste a dish before Shabbat (there), like one who invites a king to his table, who must first taste to see if it is good to eat. 'And those who love its words have chosen greatness' - it appears to me that in Jeremiah (17:24-25) it is written: 'And it shall come to pass, if you diligently hearken, etc., to sanctify the Sabbath day, etc., then there shall enter through the gates of this city kings and princes, etc.' And in Shabbat (119a) it is said: the wealthy of other lands, why do they merit - because they honor the Sabbath, and Yosef who honored the Sabbath became very wealthy, and similarly, the butcher who reserved the best animal for Shabbat became very wealthy as explained there. 'Then from Sinai they commanded two actions properly' - meaning even though Shabbat was commanded at Marah before Sinai, nevertheless, the proper laws of Shabbat were commanded at Sinai, and similarly, the Ashkenaz version 'Then from Sinai, etc., and you commanded us to offer, etc.' - at Marah, offerings were not commanded. 

And some explained 'Then from Sinai' as meaning before Sinai (Bayit Yosef), but this is a great stretch and it is more correct as I have explained with God's help.

In the repetition of the Amidah, the Sephardim recite the Kedushah of "Keter," which is of the highest level. The Ashkenazim recite "Na'aritzcha," because they believe that the Kedushah of "Keter" is not appropriate outside of Israel. It should not be questioned about the Kedushah of "Keter" where it is said, "A crown they shall give You, the multitudes above and Your people Israel gathered below, all of them together shall thrice declare Your holiness." How can this be said, since it is stated in Chullin (91b) that the angels do not say their song until Israel first says theirs, and that song refers to the Kedushah, so how can we say "all of them together shall thrice declare Your holiness"? One can say that since Israel has already said the Kedushah during Shacharit, therefore in Mussaf, they can say it together with Israel. We say "Where is the place of His glory," and "Where" (איה) is an acronym for "Remember the Sabbath day" (פרי עץ חיים), because on Shabbat, the sovereignty of the Holy One, Blessed be He, is recognized by those who sanctify the Sabbath properly, and they stand on the same level as the angels who feel a great sanctity. Therefore, they ask "Where is the place of His glory," because this cannot be comprehended, as His holiness has no end. In the Kedushah of Mussaf, we say "Shema Yisrael" because once there was a decree forbidding the recitation of the Shema, and they would say "Shema Yisrael" in every Kedushah. When the decree was annulled, the sages of that generation decreed to retain it in Mussaf as a memorial, so that the miracle would be publicized for generations, because in Mussaf there is no recitation of Shema, but in Shacharit, the Shema has already been recited in its proper order. (Or Zarua HaGadol, Siman 50, in the name of Rav Sherira Gaon, head of the academy)

And we say "He is our God" and not "One is our God," because we do not say "One" twice in succession, as it would be like saying "Hear, hear" or "We give thanks, we give thanks," which we silence. Some prayer books have it written twice as "One" – but this is incorrect (see Magen Avraham). "He is our God" – meaning that we accept His divine sovereignty upon us, "He is our Father" – every father wishes to fulfill the desires of his children, but may not have the capability, whereas the king has the capability, and thus we say "He is our King." Therefore, we are confident that "He is our Savior," and assured that "He will let us hear in His mercy once again before the eyes of all living beings," meaning publicly, as it was during the Exodus from Egypt. In the Sephardic version, it is clarified further: "He will save us and redeem us again soon… Behold, I have redeemed, etc.," for on Shabbat we mention matters of redemption, as our sages said, "If they observe… they will be immediately redeemed" and the verse states: "For thus says the Lord to the eunuchs who keep My Sabbaths… and I will bring them to My holy mountain, etc." And some do not pause between "to be your God" and "I am the Lord your God" (Or Zarua there).

In Ashkenaz, during the Mussaf prayer, they say "Na'aritzcha V'Nakdishcha" ("We will revere You and hallow You"), as it is stated in the end of the 16th chapter of Massechet Sofrim, to precede "Na'aritzcha" before "Nakdishcha." The Sephardim, during the Shacharit prayer, say "Nakdishcha V'Na'aritzcha" ("We will hallow You and revere You"), as the prophet said: "They will hallow the Holy One of Jacob and revere the God of Israel" (Isaiah 29:23).

It is worth noting that during the Shacharit prayer, everything is in the masculine form: "V'lo natato" ("and You did not give"), "V'lo hinchalto" ("and You did not bequeath"), "V'gam b'menuchato lo yishkenu areilim" ("and also in His rest, the uncircumcised shall not dwell"). In the Mussaf prayer, the language is feminine: "Ratzita korbanoteha" ("You desired its offerings"), "Tzivita perusheha sidurei niskeha ma'angeha toameha divareha" ("You commanded its explanations, the ordering of its libations, those who delight in it, those who taste it, its words, etc.").

Although "Shabbat" can be both masculine and feminine, as stated in Siman 268, nevertheless, why did they choose this way for Shacharit and that way for Mussaf? We have already written there that during the day it is masculine, and in Mussaf itself they say: "U'vashvi'i ratzita bo chemdat yamim oto karata" ("And on the seventh day, You desired it, the most coveted of days, You called it"), "V'yanuchu bo" ("and they rested in it").

Perhaps because the primary acceptance of holiness from the additional soul's influence is during Mussaf, as is known, and all acceptance is in the feminine form, as is known. It is possible that for this reason "Tikanta" is in the Tashrak order and "El Adon" in the Shacharit is in alphabetical order. The Shelah in his Siddur and the Ramak were very perplexed by this, see there. According to what I have explained, it fits well, as all inversion is from strength, and this is its measure—pay attention.

After the Musaf repetition of the Chazan, a full Kaddish is recited, and we say 'Ein Kelokeinu', 'Pitom HaKetoret', and the Mishna 'The Song that the Levites would say in the Temple'. This was instituted for two reasons: the first, to mention the main sections of the song for each day on the holy Sabbath, to indicate that they all draw their sustenance from the Sabbath, for it is the source of blessing and the culmination of the days of the week. The second reason is that in this Mishna it is explained that the Sabbath alludes to the day that will be entirely Sabbath, and those who observe the Sabbath will merit this. We say the saying 'Anyone who learns Halachot', and 'Torah scholars increase peace in the world'. Some say the Rabbi's Kaddish here, but in our community, we do not interrupt with Kaddish here. We say 'Aleinu' and the Mourner's Kaddish, and then 'Anim Zemirot', which is a sacred and beautiful song to say on Sabbaths and holidays when holiness dwells. In some places, they also say 'Shir HaYichud', and then the song of the day and 'Adon Olam', each place according to its custom. It is proper to be careful not to increase the number of Kaddishes, as is written in Siman 55. (The Tur wrote: It is customary in Spain to say a chapter of Mishna, and see the Bach, Prisha, and Taz who discussed this, and perhaps the intention is the Mishna of 'The Song that the Levites would say', and he called the chapter 'one' because the word 'one' is written ten times within it, and it is the last Mishna of Tamid, see there.)

The Tur and Shulchan Aruch write in Section 1: The time for the Musaf prayer is immediately after the Shacharit prayer, which begins in the morning, corresponding to the Musaf sacrifice whose time is immediately in the morning. For in the Tractate Yoma, it requires a verse stating that the libations precede the Musaf offerings, and if not for the verse, the Musaf offerings would be valid to precede, even though it is written regarding the libations 'in the morning.' This implies that the time for the Musaf offering is immediately in the morning, and since its time is in the morning, it is good to perform it immediately after the Shacharit prayer (Tur). The explanation of this matter: Seemingly, since it is not written regarding Musaf 'in the morning' but rather 'on the Sabbath day,' (and in the Taz, Section 1, there is an error regarding this), and the expression 'on the day' as stated in Yoma (34a) means later, as 'on the day' implies when it is fully light and not in the morning (Rashi there), and if so, it would disqualify it in the morning. Therefore, it says that if so, why require a verse that libations precede, since regarding the libations it is written 'in the morning,' therefore it is certain that the time for Musaf is immediately in the morning. Based on this, our teacher the Rema wrote in Section 1, that if one prayed Musaf before Shacharit, he has fulfilled his obligation.

In my humble opinion, these matters are perplexing. Indeed, the Tosafot there raise this question, and this is their language: "It is puzzling, why did he not state the reason that something mentioned 'in the morning' should precede something mentioned 'during the day'? And in any case, the verse 'sacrifice and libations' is needed for another interpretation, that libations are only sanctified through the slaughter of the sacrifice, as it is stated in Menachot (79a). And it seems to me that it is necessary for the opinion that the incense precedes the additional offerings... since 'during the day' does not imply afterward, etc." End quote. 

Now, since we hold that the additional offerings precede the incense, like Rabbi Akiva at the beginning of the chapter "Tamid was slaughtered" and like Abaye in the order of the arrangement, and so the Rambam ruled in the sixth chapter of Tamidin, then indeed we do not need the verse 'sacrifice and libations' for this, but rather because 'in the morning' should precede 'during the day'. Therefore, it would not be correct if the additional offering was done before the morning offering.

Even if we say that the Tur does not agree with Tosafot, since the words of the Tur come from the Rosh at the beginning of the fourth chapter of Berakhot, it is still difficult regarding our teacher, the Rema, who ruled this way in practice and did not consider the words of Tosafot that we cited. It is also difficult regarding the Rosh and the Tur, for perhaps the true intention of the Gemara is: "Zevach u'Nesachim," meaning just as the sacrifice is in the morning, so too the libations are in the morning. And even though it is written regarding the libations themselves: "in the morning," "like the morning meal-offering and its libation," the Gemara did not bother to elaborate. And because it previously said that the meal-offering precedes the Chavitin due to "Olah and Minchah," therefore it concludes the end of the verse with "Zevach u'Nesachim." And if you say, why do we need this verse, this is not a question, for we need it for the meal-offerings mentioned in the previous section. I have seen someone who raised another question on the Rosh, perhaps we need two verses: one for the initial requirement and one to make it essential (as stated in Yom Tov there). Meaning, because in matters of sanctity, the Torah needs to repeat it to make it essential, as we say everywhere. But the truth is that this verse is not superfluous at all, as I have explained. And I have seen that our teacher, the Beit Yosef, in his great book wrote: that the Rashba wrote that it appears from Tosafot that if one offered the Musaf sacrifice before the Shacharit sacrifice, he has fulfilled his obligation. And I did not find this in the Rashba, neither in his novellae nor in his responsa, and from Tosafot, it does not seem so either. This is the language of Tosafot: "The time for Musaf is all day, even from the morning, for indeed sacrifices can be offered immediately after the Tamid offering, so too the Musaf prayer can be prayed immediately from the morning." And since they wrote that one can offer immediately after the Tamid, it follows that the prayer, which is in place of the sacrifice, is also specifically after Shacharit. And what they wrote "from the morning" is regarding the time, and so Tosafot R”Y explicitly wrote, and this is his language: "But the time for Musaf is all day, only that one should precede the Yotzer prayer first."

The intention of the Rosh and the Tur is the same, that from the perspective of time it is valid, but in any case, not before the morning prayer, as the Tur explicitly states that the time for the Musaf prayers is immediately after the morning prayer, etc. Therefore, our teacher the Beit Yosef, because he saw the weakness of the matter, did not bring this in the Shulchan Aruch, and the words of our teacher the Rema need further investigation. However, if we say that in the Temple, when they offered the Musaf before the Tamid, it was valid after the fact, then the same applies to prayer, and the words of our teacher the Rema are understandable. Seemingly, there is proof for this since we hold that "the frequent and the infrequent, the frequent comes first," and in any case, if they offered the infrequent first, it is valid after the fact, as is proven in Zevachim (91a), and so writes the Rambam in Chapter 9 of Temidin, see there. However, in my humble opinion, it seems that this applies to other matters and not to the Tamid, as we say in Pesachim (58b): From where do we derive that nothing should precede the morning Tamid? The verse states "the burnt-offering" - the first burnt-offering. And at the beginning of "Kol HaTadir" we expound from the verse "besides the morning burnt-offering." And Tosafot there questioned why two verses are needed and answered that one is for the sprinkling of the blood and one for the burning of the limbs, see there. And in the Tosefta of Pesachim, Chapter 4, we learned that all the sacrifices that were offered before the morning Tamid are invalid, see there. And our Rabbis, the Baalei Tosafot in Pesachim and Menachot there, wanted to infer that it is valid, but in any case, they wrote that it is rabbinically invalid, see there. If so, it seems to my humble opinion that also in prayer, if one prayed Musaf before the morning prayer, he has not fulfilled his obligation and needs to pray again after the morning prayer. This seems to be the law, but in practical terms, one should deliberate, as I have not found any of the great authorities who disagree with our teacher the Rema.

We learned in the Mishnah at the beginning of the chapter "Tefillat HaShachar": "The Musaf prayer [may be recited] all day." And it is stated in the Gemara: "Rabbi Yochanan said: He is considered negligent if he delays it." The reason seems to be that Rabbi Yehuda disagrees in a Beraita and says [one may pray Musaf] until the seventh hour. Therefore, even though the halacha is according to the Sages, since one can also fulfill Rabbi Yehuda's position, why not do so? The proof for this is from the words of the Rambam in Chapter 3 of Tefillah, Law 5, where he wrote: "The time for the Musaf prayer is after the morning prayer until the seventh hour of the day. If one prays it after the seventh hour, although he has been negligent, he has fulfilled his obligation, since its time is all day." Thus it is explicitly clear that ideally, we should be concerned with Rabbi Yehuda's words. This is what the Tur wrote: "Its time is all day, but the primary mitzvah is until the end of the seventh hour, and it is forbidden to delay it ab initio," as he wrote there, and so wrote Rabbeinu Beit Yosef. He further added: If one forgot and did not pray until its whole time has passed, there is no makeup prayer," as he wrote there. This is unlike other prayers which have a makeup prayer in the next adjacent prayer, as stated in Siman 108, where the reason for the difference is explained. (This also clarifies why the Rif brought the words of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi who said: "One who prays Musaf after the seventh hour, according to Rabbi Yehuda, about him the verse says 'I have gathered the mourners of the appointed time.' It is difficult to understand why he brought this, as the halacha is not according to Rabbi Yehuda. According to what we have said, it makes sense, for ideally, we need to be concerned with his words. The Kesef Mishneh there brought in the name of the RaMaCH who wondered why one is considered negligent, as he wrote there. According to what we have said, it makes sense, and consider it well.)

The Tur and the Shulchan Aruch wrote in Section 2: Every individual is obligated to pray the Musaf prayer, whether there is a congregation in the city or not. This means that even though there is an opinion in the Talmud (Berachot 30a) that when there is a congregation in the city, an individual does not pray Musaf, but rather only the chazzan (prayer leader) does — the law is not like this. Rather, it is like all other prayers. Consequently, the chazzan repeats the prayer afterwards, just as with other prayers. Rambam did not mention this, and his reasoning is that since it is not different from other prayers, there was no need to mention it. Additionally, the priestly blessing (Nesiat Kapayim) is included in it. And even though it is permissible to eat a little before Musaf, as will be explained, still, drunkenness is not common in it. Therefore, it is not like Mincha, which does not have the priestly blessing because drunkenness is common there. And for us, the priestly blessing is only done on festivals during Musaf, as we wrote earlier in Section 128.

Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote in Section 3: It is permissible to taste something before the Musaf prayer, meaning eating fruits or even a small amount of bread, even a tasting that is enough to sate the heart, but a meal is forbidden. And the Tur brought proof that a meal is forbidden from what we say in Ta'anit (26a) that during Musaf there is the priestly blessing, because in Musaf drunkenness is not common. And if you would think that a meal is permitted - then drunkenness would be common. But there are those who disagree with Rabbeinu Beit Yosef, and they hold that by law, even a meal is permitted, and the Tur did not mean it as a prohibition, but rather that there is no custom to eat a fixed meal before Musaf, as it is not the way of people to do so, and therefore drunkenness is not common (Bach and Magen Avraham 1). Therefore, someone who is weak-hearted, and finds it difficult to pray Musaf before eating a fixed meal - can eat a fixed meal and then pray afterward (ibid.), and there are those who uphold the words of Rabbeinu Beit Yosef (Taz 2).
