In my humble opinion, it seems there is a proof for permissibility, for the prohibition of eating before prayer is derived in Berakhot (10b) from "And Me you have cast behind your body" etc. - after this one has become haughty, he accepts upon himself the kingdom of Heaven, see there, and the kingdom of Heaven is only in the morning with the recitation of Shema, and between redemption and prayer, and the prayer. Furthermore, since one has already prayed Shacharit - it does not apply to say "And Me you have cast." However, this is not the custom, but someone who is weak can simply rely on the opinions that permit it.

And regarding what he wrote 'eating fruits,' they were puzzled by this, for we require Kiddush in the place of a meal. But it seems to me that he is not referring to this case, and it is obvious that one needs to eat an olive's bulk of food. Rather, what he means is that one is permitted to eat many fruits or even bread to satiate the heart, which means more than an egg's bulk. And there are those who explain that his intention is to rely on a cup of wine, as it is written in Siman 273, or that he should pray and then eat bread (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 1). In my humble opinion, it seems that this constitutes an interruption and is not called 'in the place of a meal' (as the Taz also wrote), and it is clear as I have explained. And without Kiddush, it is obvious that it is forbidden to eat, for the obligation of Kiddush has already taken effect.

If one did not pray Musaf until the time for Mincha arrived, which is half an hour after midday, the Gemara (Berachot 28a) rules that he should pray Mincha first and then Musaf, because Mincha is more frequent compared to Musaf, and when there is a frequent and an infrequent commandment, the frequent one takes precedence. The Rambam wrote at the end of Chapter 3 of Tefillah that there is an opinion that one should not do this in a congregation, so that people do not make a mistake. And our Rabbis, the Tosafists, wrote there that this is only when one needs to pray both now, such as if one wants to eat and is forbidden to eat until he prays Mincha, according to those who hold this view above in Siman 232. But if he does not need to pray Mincha now, he may pray Musaf first. However, when the time for Mincha Ketana arrives, the early authorities brought from the Jerusalem Talmud that one is necessarily obligated to pray Mincha first. Nevertheless, in any case, if one prayed Musaf first, he has fulfilled his obligation after the fact, even in a situation where he was required to pray Mincha first. And our Rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, brought all of this into law in Section 4, see there.

At first glance, it is not understood, since something that is more frequent takes precedence by law, how is it possible to differentiate between a congregation and an individual, and between whether one needs to pray Mincha now or does not need to. However, in truth, there is a basis for this in the fundamental law, as at first glance this entire law is not understood. How is it possible to prioritize Mincha over Musaf, given that prayers were established in place of the sacrifices? Based on this, one must say that if they delayed offering the Musaf sacrifice until after midday, they would offer the afternoon Tamid (daily offering) first. This is certainly not possible, as it is forbidden to offer any sacrifices after the afternoon Tamid, since "upon it complete all the sacrifices," as stated in Pesachim (59a) and Yoma (33a).

However, the reason is as stated in Zevachim (91a): since the time of the Mincha [afternoon offering] arrives, it is as if both [offerings] have already been slaughtered, see there. According to this, it is well understood, that in the Temple they did not offer the afternoon Tamid offering earlier because the Tamid offering had not yet been slaughtered. But concerning prayer, since it is as if it has already been slaughtered, it is obvious that the regular [prayer] takes precedence to offer, and therefore one prays Mincha first. This applies when one is now compelled to pray Mincha automatically, as it is as if both have been slaughtered. But if one does not need to pray Mincha now, it is not as if both have been slaughtered, and its law is like the offering in the Temple, where in any case the Musaf [additional] offering is offered first. Similarly, for a congregation, we judge them as in the Temple, and do not say it is as if both have been slaughtered. However, in the case of the small Mincha [Mincha Ketana], in any case it is as if both have been slaughtered, and therefore, after the fact, if one offered the Musaf first, he has fulfilled his obligation as in the Temple. (And therefore, among us, we have not heard of anyone praying Mincha before Musaf, even if Musaf is delayed until Mincha Ketana, because we eat even after Mincha Ketana, as stated in Siman 232, since we rely on the sexton's call to the synagogue, and see Magen Avraham subparagraph 3, and therefore among us it is not as if both have been slaughtered in any case. And the Magen Avraham wrote that if it is close to evening and there is no time to pray both, one should pray Musaf, as Mincha has a make-up time, see there. And what is written in Shulchan Aruch, paragraph 5, that on Shabbat and Yom Tov we do not say 'Barechu' after the final Kaddish - among us, even on weekdays, this custom does not exist, as stated in Siman 133, see there.)

It is stated in Shabbat (12a) that Beit Shammai prohibit comforting mourners and visiting the sick on Shabbat, because it is distressing (Rashi), and also so one does not come to cry out on Shabbat (Rif). But Beit Hillel permit it, because it is considered an act of loving-kindness, and moreover, it alleviates their distress. It is with difficulty that they permitted comforting mourners and visiting the sick on Shabbat for the reasons explained, but the Sages permitted it as stated. However, those who do not go during the weekdays and only go on Shabbat are not acting properly (Magen Avraham), except for one who is preoccupied during the weekdays and cannot go (Shulchan Aruch).

The Sages taught: One who enters to visit the sick should say, "It is Shabbat, we are prevented from crying out, and a speedy recovery is likely to come because of the merit of Shabbat," and he should expand their mind with comforting words (Rashi). This refers to a sick person who is not in immediate danger, because if the person is in immediate danger, it is permitted to cry out and plead on Shabbat, as stated in Siman 276. Rabbi Meir says that the visitor should say, "May it be Shabbat's ability to have mercy on you," if they honor it by not being distressed (Rif). Rabbi Yehuda says that the visitor should say, "May the Omnipresent have mercy on you and on the sick of Israel," as the merit of the public is great. Rabbi Yossi says that the visitor should say, "May the Omnipresent have mercy on you among the sick of Israel," because including the sick person with others is more effective. Shevna, a man of Jerusalem, would say "Peace" upon entering to visit the sick, and upon leaving, he would say, "It is Shabbat, we are prevented from crying out, a speedy recovery is likely to come, His mercies are abundant, and Shabbat is in peace." The Rambam in Chapter 24 wrote according to the language of the first Tanna, and the Tur and Shulchan Aruch wrote according to the language of Shevna, as he did not intend to argue but to add slightly, and our custom follows the Rambam. Similarly, when making a "Mi Sheberach" for the sick in the synagogue, one should not say as during the week, "May the Omnipresent send a complete recovery," but rather "It is Shabbat, we are prevented from crying out, etc." (Gra"A). However, in our communities, we bless "and may He send a complete recovery... It is Shabbat, we are prevented from crying out, etc.," and this is also printed in the prayer books. I do not know who permitted this, except in the case of a critically ill person who is in immediate danger, as mentioned.

The Talmud does not specify what language to use when comforting mourners, and it appears that one may use the weekday phrase: 'May the Omnipresent comfort you among the mourners of Zion and Jerusalem.' However, some say that one should use the phrase used for the sick: 'It is Shabbat, and we are not to mourn, and comfort is near to come, and His mercies are abundant, and rest in peace' (Rashal and Bach). See Yoreh De'ah, section 393. In our community, it is not customary to comfort mourners on Shabbat.

It is forbidden to fast on Shabbat, and for the sake of a fast—even for one hour—it is prohibited. Moreover, one must eat before midday, as it is stated in the Jerusalem Talmud at the end of the third chapter of Taanit, that it is forbidden to fast on Shabbat until the sixth hour, and even if one is engaged in Torah study or prayer, it is prohibited. Certainly, this refers to a general case, for if it is for the sake of a fast, even one hour is forbidden. 

The reason for the sixth hour seems to be because the last time for eating is in the sixth hour, which is the meal time for Torah scholars, as stated in Siman 157. From that time onward, it is like throwing a stone into a flask, as mentioned there. Therefore, one should not delay eating until after this time. And although it is explained there that for regular people their meal time is in the fourth hour, nevertheless, since from that time onward it is not like throwing a stone into a flask, we are not concerned. Furthermore, the primary concern is for Torah scholars, as we learn in the Jerusalem Talmud (brought by Beit Yosef): "Shabbatot and holidays were given only for eating and drinking, and Shabbatot and holidays were given only for engaging in Torah study." The Midrash Tanchuma explains that there is no disagreement, for Torah scholars who engage in Torah study all week, Shabbat was given more for eating and drinking, and for those who work all week, it was given more for engaging in Torah study.

And it is clear that if one sanctifies and eats an olive-sized portion before midday, one can also wait until after midday. It also seems to me that when one drinks something warm before prayer, it is also permitted to wait until after midday, since one has exited the category of fasting. And this is a common practice every day: they make Kiddush and taste something, and delay the second meal until after midday.

In truth, according to my humble opinion, the second meal should only be before midday, as the third meal must only be after midday, as will be explained in Siman 291. The reason seems to be that since we derive the three meals from the three mentions of ‘today’ in the verse: "And Moses said, Eat it today, for today is a Sabbath to the Lord; today you will not find it in the field" (Exodus 16:25), each meal must have its own specific time: one at night, one during the day before midday, and one after midday. But I am puzzled as to why none of the poskim (decisors of Jewish law) mentioned this, and many are not concerned with it. Perhaps the reason the third meal is not before midday is not due to the three mentions of 'today', but because each meal must have its own name: the night meal is the evening meal, the day meal is the morning meal, and the third meal is the afternoon meal, which is only after midday. However, according to this reasoning, the morning meal should not be after midday either. And if we were to say that one does not fulfill the obligation of the third meal unless one has prayed Mincha first, it would make sense, but this is not the case, as stated in Siman 291. Therefore, I say, even though the poskim did not mention this, it is still clear that the second meal should begin, in any case, before midday, and this is how I conduct myself.

Our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 2: "There are those who say that a person for whom eating is harmful, so that it is a delight for him not to eat - should not eat." And it is obvious that this is the case, for it was given for delight and not for distress. And he wrote in the language "there are those who say" not because there are those who disagree with this, but because it is his custom to write in this manner when he bases the ruling on a single authority. And afterwards, he wrote in section 3: A person who fasts every day, and eating on Shabbat is distressing for him due to the change in routine - there are those who say that they saw several pious individuals and men of deeds who fasted on Shabbat for this reason, and it was also said that our master, Rabbi Yehuda the Pious, acted in this way.

And seemingly, this is the law stated in Section 2, but in reality, it is not so. Initially, it says that someone for whom eating causes harm is exempt [from eating], and then it says that even someone for whom eating does not cause harm and perhaps even benefits, but because of a change in their constitution they also experience some discomfort as is evident, where the palate senses the sweetness of the food but the change in constitution causes some discomfort in their intestines - they too are exempt, for in any case, this is not called "Shabbat delight." And know that even in the case where it is written that someone for whom eating causes harm is exempt, even if at the moment they enjoy it but later it harms their health - they too are exempt, and this is simple [to understand]. Likewise, someone for whom a particular food is not pleasant to the palate - should not eat it on Shabbat, for this is not considered delight.

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote: "And similarly, one who has pleasure if he cries, to relieve the distress from his heart—it is permitted to cry on Shabbat." His intention is clear: even in cases of distress from worldly matters, whether from a death or a financial loss, it is certainly forbidden to be distressed on Shabbat. However, if he cannot alleviate the distress from his heart until he cries, since it is the way of people that through crying the distress is eased—it is permitted for him to cry, as this too is a form of pleasure, for through this the distress leaves his heart. It is stated in the Aggadah that the students of Rabbi Akiva found him crying on Shabbat, and he said, "I have pleasure." And there are those who explain that this was due to his intense attachment to the Holy One, blessed be He, like those who pray with intention, as we find with Rabbi Akiva in the Zohar Chadash, that when he recited Shir HaShirim, he wept, because he understood the depth of the matter. But to cry over distress—it is certainly forbidden, for if so, anyone in distress would cry, and this is puzzling about our teacher, the Rema (Taz, sec. 2).

In my opinion, the words of our master, the Rema, are very correct. Certainly, the matter of the story in the Aggadah is different from that of the Zohar Chadash. If it were like this story, the students would not have been astonished by his weeping, and he would not have needed to say that it was a pleasure for him, for it is obvious that these are tears of joy, an emotional response to the sacred secrets in the holy Torah. Rather, it is certain that he wept from some distress, and for this reason they asked him, and he replied that through this he experiences pleasure. As for the question that if so, anyone who is distressed and weeps—behold, our master, the Rema, explicitly says: "Specifically when through this the distress leaves his heart," otherwise, it is forbidden (as the Taz also wrote), and this is the law.

However, regarding a fast for a bad dream, our Sages said (Taanit 12b): "A fast is effective to nullify a bad dream like fire to straw," and specifically on that same day, even on Shabbat, in order to alleviate his physical distress (Rashi). But he must subsequently fast on Sunday, for having fasted on Shabbat. And even though the fast is a delight for him, nevertheless he has nullified the delight of Shabbat, and therefore he requires a fast for his fast (Tur). This is not comparable to the previous laws, where one nullified the delight of Shabbat because eating would harm him, or due to a change in his usual cycle, where he does not need to fast for his fast, because in those cases, the prevention is not due to his desire but due to his inability. But in the case of a dream, if he wishes to disregard the dream, he is permitted to do so, and most dreams are vanity, as Kohelet (Ecclesiastes) said: "For in the multitude of dreams and vanities, etc." However, because he desires to heed the dream, and who can say there is any substance to it, perhaps he nullified the delight of Shabbat unnecessarily, and therefore he requires a fast for his fast.

If a public fast falls on Sunday, one must fast another day, because since atonement is needed for having nullified the pleasure of Shabbat, it is not atonement when one is compelled to fast (Magen Avraham 3). Even if it is not a public fast, but rather a fast that one is accustomed to always observe, such as Erev Rosh Chodesh or the days of Selichot, it does not count (ibid.). However, if one is not accustomed to fasting, or does not always complete the fast and now completes it, it does count. Some say that even a complete fast counts for this (Taz 3), and a proof is from the fact that we hold that one fulfills the obligation of festive peace offerings on Yom Tov with vow and voluntary offerings, and so too this fast counts for both purposes. And since it is a doubtful matter of law and concerns rabbinic matters, one who finds fasting difficult can rely on the lenient opinion. In my humble opinion, the main view is like the "some say," for we find even in matters of atonement that this is the case. For example, a woman who brings her obligatory offering of a pair of birds, one for a sin offering and one for a burnt offering, it is said in Zevachim (5a) that if she had violated several positive commandments, she is atoned for with this burnt offering, as a burnt offering atones for the violation of positive commandments. Thus, it is explicitly clear that even though she was obligated to bring the burnt offering because of the obligation of a woman who gave birth, nevertheless it atones for other positive commandments. All the more so, this fast atones also for the fast observed on Shabbat, and this is a clear proof. (What Magen Avraham wrote about "atonement in vain" – perhaps he said it as a kind of rhetorical expression, and what relation does it have to this, for there it means atonement without the giving of money, as Rashi explained in Zevachim 37b).

The matter of "fasting for his fast" – it is not necessarily for the next day specifically. If it is difficult for him to fast two consecutive days, he should not fast on the first day and instead fast afterward. All the more so if the first day was Rosh Chodesh, Chanukah, Purim, or a festival, even the second day of a festival observed in the Diaspora – he should not fast until afterward. Similarly, on other days when one does not fast, he should postpone the fast until afterward.

There is, however, an opinion that on other days that are only a custom, one should fast, as it is implied in Sefer Chassidim that if one fasted a dream fast on a festival, he should fast the next day, which is Isru Chag. Consequently, for all days except Rosh Chodesh, Chanukah, and Purim, the same rule applies (Magen Avraham, Section 4). I do not understand this, for since there is no necessity to fast on that specific day, why should one nullify such a custom that all Jewish communities have adopted, prohibiting fasting on those days? This is also written in the Perisha, that one should not fast on those days. (And similarly, it is written in the Eliyah Rabbah and the Taz. In Sefer Chassidim, it seems to me there is a different intention, and it does not necessarily mean the next day, but rather it teaches that if one had a dream on the first or last day of a festival and fasted on both, it suffices to observe one fast day for his fast. Look there and examine it well.) (And in the Zohar, Vayakhel 247b, it implies specifically the next day. Look there.)

And this is what they said in Berachot (31b): "Anyone who fasts on Shabbat - they tear up his decree of seventy years." Our rabbis explained that this refers to a fast due to a troubling dream (Tosafot in the name of Rabbeinu Chananel). And when one fasts because of a troubling dream on Shabbat, Behag explained that he says "Aneinu" in "Elokai Netzor" and even establishes it as a separate blessing, since it is not within the eighteen blessings (there). But the Tur and Shulchan Aruch in section 6 wrote: "One who fasts on Shabbat - says 'Aneinu' without a concluding blessing after finishing his prayer, and includes it in 'Elokai Netzor'" - end of quote. And he should say after his prayer: "Master of the Universe, it is revealed and known before You that our desire etc." as on a weekday, and he can say "My God, before I was formed etc." And even though he concludes with: "May it be Your will that I do not sin anymore," and supplication is forbidden on Shabbat - this applies to requesting personal needs, but not in matters of sins to ask that he not sin (Magen Avraham, subsection 11).

Rabbeinu the Rema wrote in paragraph 4: "There are those who say that if someone sleeps a nap in the afternoon and has a bad dream, he should fast from midday until midnight and then make Havdalah, and on the first day (of the week) he should fast as if he had fasted the entire Shabbat," this is the end of his words. Even though he did not fast the entire day and ate before midday, and if he wanted, he could have refrained from eating until night, nevertheless, since he did not eat for the sake of the fast, he needs atonement (there, sub-paragraph 6). And from this, it is clear that even for a dream that he dreamt during the day, there is reason for concern, although people usually say that a daytime dream has no substance. 

Additionally, the Tur writes later in Siman 608 in the name of Rav Amram and Rabbeinu Kalonymus that one should not fast a "ta'anit chalom" (fast for a bad dream) on Shabbat in our times because we are not proficient in interpreting dreams as they were in the times of the Talmud. And here he mentioned it according to the law of the Talmud. Furthermore, he did not write an obligation regarding this, but rather for one whose soul is troubled and is concerned about the dream, and the fast would be a delight for him. However, there is no obligation here (as the Taz also wrote in sub-paragraph 3). 

It is better not to pay attention to dreams, especially a dream that one contemplated during the day—it is obvious that it has no substance. Similarly, if one filled his stomach with food and drink, then the vapors rising to the head show him visions and imaginations, and they have no substance.

And this is the language of our teacher, the Beit Yosef, in section five: "There are those who say that one should not fast a dream fast on Shabbat unless the dream was seen three times. And there are those who say that in our times one should not fast a dream fast on Shabbat because we are not skilled in the interpretation of dreams to know which are good and which are bad. And people say that it is found in ancient books that for three dreams one fasts on Shabbat, and they are: one who sees a Torah scroll that has been burned (the same applies to tefillin according to the Magen Avraham), the beams of his house or his teeth that have fallen out (and in the Midrash of Parshat Miketz it was interpreted for a woman that she would give birth to a boy, and so it was), and some say one who sees Yom Kippur even if not during the Ne'ilah prayer (and all the more so during Ne'ilah), and some say one who sees himself reading from the Torah, and some say one who sees himself marrying a woman. And regarding seeing one's teeth that have fallen out - it refers specifically to the teeth, but if his cheeks fall - it is a good dream, as it means that those who counseled evil against him have died. And it appears to me that the dreams mentioned in the chapter "The One Who Sees" that are bad - one also fasts for them on Shabbat" end of quote. And a person needs to be precise, as many things depend on the name in language, such as 'shunra' (cat) 'shinra' (demon) (Magen Avraham section 10). And one should not fast for dreams that involve financial loss, but only for something that desecrates Shabbat (there in the name of Sefer Chassidim).

And even regarding the three dreams that have been clarified for which one fasts – there are those who have written that one should not fast for them unless one's soul is distressed, and when one fasts, one will find comfort. I am accustomed to rule that one should fast for two days during the week (there in subparagraph 7 in the name of the Shlah). There are those who have written that if one's soul is distressed, one should fast for all dreams, and for these three, one should fast even if one's soul is not distressed (there in the name of the Bach). It seems reasonable to be lenient and not fast, as fasting on Shabbat is a Torah prohibition (there). There are those who have written in this language: 'If a person is not particularly concerned about a bad dream, or if fasting is harmful and causes more distress than the fear of the dream, it is forbidden to fast on Shabbat, and even on a weekday it is not a mitzvah' (there in the name of the Rivash). And it is clear that if one had thoughts during the day or slept with a full stomach – there is no substance to the dream as it is written. Nowadays, it is customary to go to the wise person in the city to interpret the dream, and he interprets it for good and blessing, and one should not become accustomed to dreams.

It is stated in the Gemara (119a): It is written regarding Shabbat, "And you shall honor it" (Isaiah 58:13). Rav said: To advance the time of eating compared to weekdays, and this is its honor (Rashi). And Shmuel said: To delay it compared to weekdays, and this is its honor, because he desires to eat (there). And they do not disagree, for this depends on one's nature: If advancing the meal is a delight for him, such as when the nighttime meal has been digested - he should advance it. And if delaying the meal is a delight for him, such as when it has not yet been digested - he should delay it.

And it says there further: The sons of Rav Pappa bar Abba said to Rav Pappa, "For us, who have meat and wine available every day, with what should we make a distinction?" He said to them, "If his custom is to eat earlier, he should eat later; if his custom is to eat later, he should eat earlier." Therefore, one who is wealthy and eats good food every day should make a change on Shabbat by eating a little earlier or a little later, and through this, there will be a recognition of the honor of Shabbat. It seems to me that the same applies if one eats on Shabbat in a more beautiful room than the one he eats in on weekdays—this too would be a recognition of the honor of Shabbat. Similarly, if one uses expensive utensils on Shabbat and does not use them on weekdays, and all similar matters. (And it is unclear why Rav Pappa did not command in this manner).

One does not fast on Shabbat for any distress at all, and if there is an incident that requires mercy and the time is pressing, one should pray and fall on their face privately (Magen Avraham 13). One does not cry out on Shabbat nor give a public alarm for any distress, except for distress due to lack of food, for which one cries out verbally on Shabbat but not with a shofar. Similarly, a city that is surrounded by enemies, or surrounded by water, or a ship that is being tossed in the sea, and even an individual who is pursued by enemies or robbers or has been seized by an evil spirit, which is a danger of the day - one may cry out and plead in prayers on Shabbat. However, one does not blow the shofar unless it is to gather people to help their brothers and save them, which is considered saving lives, and this will be explained further in Siman 276.

A person pursued by an evil spirit is considered to have a dangerous illness. There are those who want to kill themselves by drowning in the river or by strangling themselves. The same applies to any patient who is in mortal danger that day – people cry out, plead, and pray. Likewise, it is customary to say prayers and supplications for patients in mortal danger that day, to bless them in the synagogue, to change their name, and to recite Psalms on their behalf if the danger is very great on that day. But for an ordinary patient, this is not done; instead, they bless them with the "Mi Sheberach" prayer and say "Shabbat Hi Miliz'ok" (It is Shabbat, so we do not cry out), as mentioned in Siman 287. A woman experiencing difficulty in childbirth is included in the category of a patient in mortal danger on that day. One can bless the patient even if they are in another city, and we do not fear that perhaps they have died, as most patients live, unless they were left in a state of death throes. In that case, we do not bless them unless it is known that they are alive. (See Shach, Siman 3, who brought in the name of the Maharil something puzzling – that one does not bless a patient who is not in the city due to fear that they may have died. Undoubtedly, the Maharil was referring to a severely ill patient close to death).

And one's table should be set in the morning on Shabbat in honor of the second meal, and the beds should be made, and in our case, the chairs we sit on should be arranged as if awaiting an important guest, and a cloth should be spread over the bread just as it is done for the evening meal. And the Sages said in Pesachim (105b): the honor of the day takes precedence over the honor of the night. For example, if one does not have much wine or delicacies, he should reserve them for the daytime meal (Rashi) and not for the evening meal. Similarly, all good foods that can be prepared for the daytime meals take precedence over those for the evening meal. See what is written in Siman 271, Section 9. And one should not question that if the honor of the day takes precedence over the honor of the night, why is Kiddush at night a Torah obligation and during the day a Rabbinic one? This is not due to the meal, but because of the entrance of Shabbat. On the contrary, the Kiddush during the day is specifically because of the honor of the meal. If not for this, what place would there be for this Kiddush, as it has already been sanctified upon its entrance? Rather, it is certain that the Kiddush is in honor of the meal.

And the reason that the honor of the day precedes (the honor of the night), it seems to me, is because the main meals are during the day and not at night (see Tosafot at the end of Avodah Zarah, s.v. "bat yoma"). Additionally, at night, one has already eaten during the day on the eve of Shabbat, and it is impossible for the meal to be as beloved to him as it is during the day of Shabbat. Furthermore, in the Temple, the primary sanctity was evident during the day when they offered the additional sacrifice, and not at night when there was no work of Shabbat. Moreover, the main strength of the time is during the day, as it is stated in Shabbat (89b) in the argument of Isaac in the future: "Remove half of the nights, etc." See there. And in Eruvin (65a), "We are workers of the day." See there.

And also during the day, one must recite Kiddush over a cup of wine before the meal by rabbinic decree, and they supported this from the verse "Remember the Sabbath day to sanctify it" (Pesachim 106a). This is not because "day" implies day and not night, for "day" is from evening to evening, as it is written: "And there was evening and there was morning, one day." Rather, the term "day" here is somewhat superfluous, as it could have written: "Remember the Sabbath to sanctify it." The reason for this Kiddush is due to the honor of the day and the meal, as stated in Section 1. I found support for this in the Sheiltot of Yitro (Siman 54) brought by Rashbam in Pesachim, where it says: "A cup of wine is brought, and one blesses and drinks for the honor of the Sabbath, to distinguish between the measures of Sabbath and weekday." This shows that the main reason for Kiddush is purely out of respect. Therefore, it only contains the blessing "Borei Peri HaGafen," and in the Gemara it is called "Kiddusha Rabba" euphemistically, and also because this blessing is found in all Kiddushim (Rashi and Rashbam there). Some recite verses of "Remember the Sabbath day" before the Kiddush, and some start with "Therefore, the Lord blessed," even though it is in the middle of a verse, as their intention is not the verse but to preface with words. Others say "A Psalm of David, The Lord is my shepherd," and some say the section of the Bazichin. But from the Gemara there, it is proven clearly that they did not say anything, and only began with the blessing over the wine and drank. (As it says there: "Rav Elazar visited... since all blessings begin with 'Borei Peri HaGafen'... he bent down and drank." And regarding the Bazichin, we explained in Siman 283 that it is not proper to say it before midday, and I also saw in my youth that the great ones did not say anything before this Kiddush).

And after the Kiddush, he should wash his hands for the meal with two loaves of bread, just as in the evening, and then eat. There are those who have the custom to eat sweet things after the Kiddush, like cake and other foods. If he eats immediately, there is no need for an after-blessing, as we clarified earlier in Siman 176. But if he eats after some time has passed, it is obvious that an after-blessing is required. However, we have already written in Siman 249, Section 12, that the early authorities were not at all pleased with the practice of eating sweet things after the Kiddush. Instead, after the Kiddush, one should wash his hands and have the meal. And before Kiddush, it is forbidden to taste anything, even water, just as in the evening. However, before the prayer, it is permitted to drink hot beverages, since the obligation of Kiddush has not yet taken effect. Before Mussaf, though, it is forbidden until Kiddush is made, as stated in Siman 286.

This Kiddush is not recited over bread. Even though at night one can recite Kiddush over bread, because at night it is recognizable as Kiddush due to the blessing of Kiddush, during the day, when there is only the blessing of "Hamotzi" (over bread), Kiddush is not recognizable at all. Therefore, in a place where wine is not available, one should make Kiddush over whiskey or beer or other beverages. Even though at night we did not permit this according to all opinions, as some hold that one should specifically use bread when there is no wine, as mentioned in Siman 272, in the morning everyone agrees for the reason explained. Even if it is not the local beverage, what loss is there in this, since there is only the blessing for it, and at the very least, it will be recognizable as Kiddush. So wrote our teacher the Beit Yosef in his great book. (See Magen Avraham, subparagraph 3.) According to this, it seems to my humble opinion that if there is no beverage at all, one can recite Kiddush even over milk so that it will be recognizable. If there is no beverage at all, one should eat without Kiddush, meaning he should recite "Hamotzi" over bread and intend for it to be for Kiddush. This means that he should not eat anything before this because what can he do since he has nothing. If he does not even have bread, he should eat other things, for what else can he do? (See there, subparagraph 4).

It is a mitzvah to increase on Shabbat in fruits, delicacies, and pleasant fragrances for two reasons: first, because of the delight of Shabbat, and second, to complete the one hundred blessings which are lacking on Shabbat, as stated in section 46. And even though there is a remedy to hear the blessings from those who are called up to the Torah, as stated there, nevertheless, it is better to bless by oneself, which is achieved through an abundance of fruits. However, one must be careful not to make unnecessary blessings, which would be considered a blessing in vain, as stated in section 215. This means that if there are several types of fruits before him that all have the blessing of 'ha'etz' (the fruit of the tree), he should bless on one and intend to include all of them, and generally, this is the practice. If he wishes to bless on one and intend not to include the others, this would be a blessing in vain, as stated in section 206, paragraph 12. The only way to fulfill this is by ensuring that not all the fruits are brought before him at once but rather one by one, and he should intend to only bless the type that is in front of him. And even though there are those who prohibit this because it would be considered an unnecessary blessing, nevertheless, to complete the one hundred blessings, one may do so, as stated there. If one is accustomed to taking an afternoon nap, he should not cancel it, as it is a delight for him, and sleeping on Shabbat is a delight. It is forbidden to say: 'I will sleep in order to perform work in the evening,' and even to study in the evening, as this is preparing from Shabbat to a weekday. Rather, he should sleep in order to rest on Shabbat.

After the morning meal and after sleeping, people establish a study session to read from the Prophets and to expound upon words of Aggadah (non-legalistic exegetical texts). The Tur brought a Midrash that the Torah said before the Holy One, blessed be He: When the Israelites enter the land, this one will run to his vineyard and that one to his field, and what will become of me? He said to her: I have a partner for you, and its name is Shabbat, and they will be idle from their work and will be able to engage with you, as it is written. And in Tanchuma, Parasha Vayakhel: From the beginning of the Torah until here, there is no portion that begins with the word 'assembly' except this one, and why is that? The Holy One, blessed be He, said to Moses: Go down and make great assemblies for me on Shabbat, so that future generations will learn to enter synagogues and study halls to study Torah publicly. If you do this, I will consider it as if you have crowned Me in My world, etc., end quote. And it is even more incumbent upon householders, who are preoccupied with their livelihood on all the other days of the week, to engage in Torah study on Shabbat, as is written at the beginning of Siman 288, see there.

It is forbidden to establish a meal during the time designated for the study hall, as it is stated in Gittin (38b): "In these three matters, householders lose their property, and one of them is that they establish a meal on Shabbat during the time of the study hall." And so is the custom among us that the study and sermons continue until Mincha, and after Mincha, they go to eat the third meal. (And the Eliyah Rabbah writes that if the preacher continues for a long time until there is no time left for the third meal, one should go to fulfill the mitzvah of the third meal.)

And one should be very careful to fulfill the third meal, and our sages said (Shabbat 118a): Whoever fulfills the third meal is saved from three calamities: the birth pangs of the Messiah, the judgment of Gehinnom, and the war of Gog and Magog. And Rabbi Yossi said: May my portion be with those who fulfill the three meals on Shabbat. And the Levush wrote that they are from the Torah, as it is written three times 'today' regarding Shabbat. And if it is possible that they are not directly from the Torah, nevertheless, they are certainly from the ordinance of Moses our teacher, as he received it from Sinai. And they allude to the three patriarchs, to Torah, Prophets, and Writings, and at the time when the manna was given to them, it was given for three meals, as it is stated in the Mekhilta which the Tur brought here, and we brought it above in Siman 274. And great and awesome matters are dependent on these three meals, and they are explained in the Zohar in several places.

Therefore, one should be careful about this, and thus the Sages said: A person is obligated to eat three meals on Shabbat, and even if he is satisfied, it is sufficient for him to eat bread the size of an egg and a little more, as the size of an egg is considered a minimal meal. And even though in the Gemara (119b) it implies that an olive's size is sufficient, and for this reason, there are those who indeed disagree with this (Eliya Rabba in the name of Maavar Yabbok) — however, we have already written at the end of Siman 274 that this is in a case of necessity, and certainly, one fulfills the obligation with an olive's size, but ideally, more than an egg's size is required, as noted there. And if it is absolutely impossible for him to eat, he is not obligated to cause himself distress. A wise person has his eyes in his head and will not fill his stomach at the morning meal, in order to leave room for the third meal, and Heaven forbid to nullify this great mitzvah. And one who did not eat on Friday night should eat the three meals during the day, and similarly on a Festival: one who did not eat at night should eat two meals during the day, and also recite the Kiddush of the night (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 2).

And its time is when the time of Mincha arrives, which is from six and a half hours and onward. If one performed it earlier, they have not fulfilled the mitzvah of the third meal. The reason for this we explained in Siman 288, Section 2, refer there. And know that from the words of all our sages, it is clear that the third meal is not connected to the Mincha prayer, and even before one prays Mincha, they can eat the third meal. One of our great sages forbids eating after Mincha, as explained in Tosafot Pesachim (105, in the name of Rabbeinu Tam), because it is found in the Midrash that it is forbidden to drink water between Mincha and Maariv on Shabbat.

Behold, according to the view of the Rif and the Rambam in Siman 232, even a small meal is forbidden even close to the time of Mincha Gedolah (early Mincha) - it is obvious that one must pray Mincha beforehand, unless one began eating before midday and continued eating past midday, as will be explained. However, according to the dissenting opinions there, one may eat beforehand. The Kabbalistic sages wrote that one should eat only after Mincha, as every meal was ordained to follow the prayer associated with that meal. Thus, we find three opinions on this matter: the first is that one should eat only before Mincha, the second is that it does not matter and one may do as he wishes (this is the opinion of most of the poskim who did not discuss this matter, implying that it is not a stringent requirement), and the third is that one should eat only after Mincha. Our custom follows the third opinion; however, if there is a reason that one cannot eat after Mincha or it is difficult for him to eat after Mincha, he may eat before Mincha, and this is the prevalent custom. It is clear that women are also obligated in the third meal (Seudah Shlishit), as in all matters of Shabbat, women are obligated just like men. There are many who are unaware of this, and it is necessary to inform them and caution them to observe the mitzvah of Seudah Shlishit.

And this is the language of our master, the Rema: "There are those who say it is forbidden to drink water between Mincha and Maariv on Shabbat, for then the souls return to Gehinnom. Therefore, one should not eat the third meal between Mincha and Maariv, but rather eat it before Mincha. And there are those who say it is better to pray Mincha first, and this is the initial practice in all these countries. In any case, one should not drink water from the rivers, but in the house, it is permitted, and certainly other drinks are permitted. And there are those who say that it is only forbidden within twelve months of one's father and mother, and there are those who say that this prohibition on drinking water is only on the eve of Shabbat." End quote. The explanation of his words: The first opinion holds that one should eat before Mincha because of the prohibition of drinking water, as generally one drinks during the meal. The latter opinion holds that it is better after Mincha due to the prohibition of eating before Mincha (see Magen Avraham, section 5). As for the prohibition of drinking water, it is only from the rivers, and furthermore, other drinks are permitted and one should drink other drinks. Additionally, this is only during the twelve months of mourning, and besides this, some say the intent of the Midrash is for the eve of Shabbat. The first opinion did not concern itself with the prohibition of eating before Mincha, as it follows its reasoning in Siman 232 that with a small meal there is no concern, see there.

There are those who wrote that if one began the third meal (Seudah Shlishit) before midday and it extended until after midday, he has fulfilled his obligation, as he has eaten after midday. But if he knows that his meal will extend until after midday, it is forbidden (Magen Avraham, section 3). There is no reason for this, and on the contrary, it seems more logical that if he knew his meal would extend until after midday and his initial intention was for the third meal, why should he not fulfill his obligation? And if he did not know that his meal would extend until after midday and it happened incidentally, and he did not intend it to be the third meal, it seems that he has not fulfilled his obligation. And even if we say that in such cases he has fulfilled his obligation if he already performed the second meal, as we do not require specific intent for the third meal, nevertheless, if he knew it would extend and intended it as such, it is obvious that he has fulfilled his obligation. There is no reason to say that he has not fulfilled his obligation in such cases, and this is the primary ruling in law. (Also, the Taz was puzzled by this and wrote that there is certainly a printing error there, see there. The Pri Megadim and the Mahatzit HaShekel inclined his intention due to the prohibition of eating before Mincha, see there. These thoughts are perplexing, as the law has already been decided in Siman 232 not according to the Rif and the Rambam, and furthermore, what relevance does it have here? The Eliah Rabbah wants to say that even if it extended, he has not fulfilled his obligation, as we follow the beginning of the meal, and his opinion was not agreed upon. In this matter, the main ruling follows the Magen Avraham, and examine this well.)

Our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 3: If the morning meal extends until the time of Mincha (afternoon prayer), one should interrupt the meal and recite the Grace After Meals (Birkat Hamazon), then wash one's hands and recite the blessing of Hamotzi and continue the meal. And this is proper, for if one does not do so, since the morning meal extended until that time, one will not be able to eat later except with a sense of heaviness. This is because as long as one is eating, the stomach is open and can receive food, which is not the case afterward (Taz and Magen Avraham). However, it is good to take a short break by engaging in words of Torah or by taking a walk (ibid.).

It is clear to me that this [washing hands after Birkat Hamazon] is merely for enhancement, but after the fact, even if one did not pause at all but immediately after Birkat Hamazon washed his hands, he has also fulfilled his obligation. There are those who wrote that those who remain in their place have not fulfilled their obligation, as it is considered one meal. (Magen Avraham, section 6, in the name of Maharil) But in my humble opinion, this is not the case. Rather, according to the Tosafot in Shabbat (118a, s.v. 'in Mincha'), who prohibit splitting the morning meal into two, they were concerned about an unnecessary blessing. But we hold like the Rosh and his teacher Mahar"m of Rotenburg, who wrote that it is proper to do so, for since he does it for the purpose of the third meal, there is no issue of increasing blessings, and they themselves did so in practice. And in the Tashbetz, it is written that in the winter, when the days are short, Mahar"m would make the third meal immediately on the table after Birkat Hamazon (Beit Yosef), and the Tur wrote that this is what his father, the Rosh, would do as well, without mentioning any need to pause. However, in the Mordechai, it is written that it is good to pause, but not as an absolute requirement. This is also implied by all the Poskim, and this is the main ruling in practice.

And all this applies to someone who finds it difficult to eat after Mincha or has another reason. But someone who knows that he can eat after praying Mincha with the congregation should not ideally have the third meal before Mincha. However, if he did so, he has fulfilled his obligation. Even on Shabbat that falls on the eve of a festival, if he can eat before the tenth hour, he should not initially split the morning meal into two. (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 8) The general principle from this is that not all natural tendencies are the same, provided his intention is for the sake of Heaven, meaning that according to his nature, it is proper for him to eat in this or that manner as explained.

Maimonides wrote in Chapter 30, Law 9: "A person is obligated to eat three meals on Shabbat: one in the evening, one in the morning, and one in the afternoon. One must be careful with these three meals not to diminish them at all (it is permitted to add), and even a poor person who is supported by charity must eat three meals. If one is sick from excessive eating or continually fasts, they are exempt from the three meals. Each of the three meals should be established with wine, and one should break bread over two loaves, as is also done on a festival." End of quote.

It appears that he requires a cup for Kiddush even at the third meal, which is puzzling, as we do not find in the Talmud that Kiddush is made more than once during the day, as in the night. Therefore, it is written that his intention is not for Kiddush but that one should drink wine during the meal as is done at an important meal (so explained the Kesef Mishneh). However, the opinion of the Kabbalists is that even at the third meal, one needs a cup of wine for Kiddush, though we have never heard of anyone doing so. (And this is the language of the Shelah in his Siddur: "He takes the cup in his hand, and although he is not obligated... according to the sages of truth, one must also make Kiddush at the third meal, etc." see there. But in Pri Etz Chaim, Sha'ar HaShabbat, the end of Chapter 23, it is written, and this is his language: "It is not proper to make Kiddush on wine at this meal... in the middle of the meal one should drink wine, etc." End of quote. This is precisely as Maimonides explained according to the Kesef Mishneh, and so it is written in Mishnat Chassidim, page 99. Be that as it may, Maimonides of blessed memory aligned with the words of the Kabbalists, which is astonishing. It is not our custom to cover the bread at the third meal, and see Orach Chayim 299:14).

And this is what the Rambam wrote, that two loaves are required, and several of our rabbis have written similarly. However, the Tur and the Mordechai brought from the Mechilta that for the third meal, one loaf suffices, as this was the case when they ate the manna on Friday, and we brought this at the beginning of Siman 274, see there. Based on this, some are lenient regarding the third meal to break bread over one loaf, and it is not appropriate to do so unless it is impossible to obtain a second loaf, as this is the opinion of most of the authorities. Additionally, from the language of the Talmud (117b): "A person is obligated to break bread over two loaves on Shabbat" - it is explained that this applies to all the meals. Therefore, some say that if one eats more than three meals, they also need to have two loaves (see there in the name of a Gaon). And what is written "and likewise on Yom Tov" - refers to the two loaves and not to the third meal.

The Tur wrote: "Some say that one can fulfill the obligation of the third meal with 'minei targima,' a food made from the five species of grain... However, Rabbi Yehuda said that since we derive the obligation of the three meals from the three instances of 'today' written in connection with the manna, it must be done with bread." This is the end of his words. It seems clear that this is the conclusion of the Tur, that it must be specifically with bread (Beit Yosef), and it is necessarily so, for with the manna, they set aside one loaf for the third meal (there). And these are the words of our Rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, in section 5: "One must make it with bread. Some say that one can make it with one of the five species of grain (for which the blessing is 'mezonot'), and some say that one can make it with foods that are eaten with bread, such as meat and fish, but not with fruits. And some say that even with fruits one can make it. The primary opinion is the first one, that it must be made with bread, unless one is very full or in a place where it is impossible to eat bread, such as on the eve of Passover that falls on Shabbat." This is the end of their words. It is clear that the authors of the Shulchan Aruch also hold that the primary ruling is that it must be with bread, and since the Rif, Rambam, Rosh, Tur, and Shulchan Aruch all hold that it must specifically be with bread, it is forbidden to be lenient in this matter. It is a great transgression for those who are lenient and fulfill the obligation with 'minei targima.' One must strongly warn about this, and there is no permission except for the ill. Those who belittle the third meal and fulfill their obligation without bread will have to answer for it. (See Magen Avraham at the beginning of this section, and it is surprising, and what of it, let him set aside a little bread for the third meal there, and delve deeply into this matter.)

We recite 'Ashrei' and 'Uva Letzion', as we say them every day in the morning service, and on Shabbat, since the morning service is already lengthy, we have moved it to the afternoon service. We then say the Half Kaddish. After that, we recite the verse 'Va’ani Tefilati', based on the Midrash which explains the verse: 'Those who sit at the gate talk about me, and I am the music of the drunkards'. David said before the Holy One, blessed be He: Even though we drank, my prayer is to You, Hashem. Meaning, while other people drink and get drunk and engage in frivolity, when I drink, I engage afterward in Torah and prayer. Therefore, on Yom Tov when there is no Torah reading, we do not say it. Additionally, 'Et Ratzon' (a time of favor) is only on Shabbat during Mincha, referred to in the Zohar (Shemot 88b) as 'Ra’ava D’Ra’avin' (the will of wills), and this is only on Shabbat as known. Therefore, on Shabbat, even when praying alone or in a place without a Torah scroll, we still say it (see Magen Avraham 1), and so it is in Zohar Terumah.

The prayer leader says the Half Kaddish, and they take out the Torah Scroll and say "When the Ark would travel," "Blessed is His Name," "Exalt [the Lord] etc.," but they do not say "Shema Yisrael" as in the morning, and I do not know the reason for this. Perhaps it is because in Tractate Sofrim, Chapter 14, it is explained that the one who is called for the maftir is to say "Shema Yisrael," therefore when there is no maftir, they do not say it. They stand when the Torah Scroll is taken out, and it is customary to stand during the Kaddish, and consequently, they also stand during the saying of "And as for me, my prayer," as it is not appropriate to sit for just a few moments. There is someone who says that it is proper to stand during the saying of "And as for me, my prayer," but I do not see any reason for this, and the custom is due to the reason we have explained.

And they read from the Torah from the upcoming weekly portion ten verses for three people: Kohen, Levite, Israelite. This is an ordinance of Ezra for those who sit in the marketplaces, as mentioned in Siman 135. And no Kaddish is said after the reading, because thereafter nothing is recited. That which is recited, "A Psalm of David, the earth is the Lord's and all it contains," "And when it rested, he would say" - is not of the essence of the law. And if they were to say Kaddish after the reading, there would be no basis to say Kaddish before the leader begins the prayer. Therefore, they left the Kaddish of the Torah reading to be said before the prayer. And likewise in all Torah readings of Mincha, like on a public fast day, on Tisha B'Av, and on Yom Kippur, all for the reasons we have explained. And after the Torah scroll is returned to the ark, the prayer leader stands and says Kaddish, and the congregation prays, and the leader repeats the prayer aloud, and they say Kedushah. (And there are those who have the leader say Kaddish and the congregation prays before the Torah scroll is returned to the ark, but it is not proper to do so, for the one carrying the Torah scroll passes in front of those praying).

And also on a Yom Tov (a festival) that falls on Shabbat, we read from the weekly Torah portion and not from the topic of the festival, for there is no special Torah reading for Yom Tov, and only the prayer is that of Yom Tov. We pray "Atah Echad" (You are One), and the main part of the prayer is "Retzei Bimnuchateinu" (Accept our rest) "Who sanctifies the Shabbat," only we precede with "Atah Echad" as in all Shabbat prayers, where we precede first. Three things were instituted: "Atah Kidashta" (You sanctified), "Yismach Moshe" (Moses rejoiced), and "Atah Echad" corresponding to three Shabbats: "Atah Kidashta" corresponds to the Shabbat of Creation, "Yismach Moshe" corresponds to the Shabbat of the Giving of the Torah, and "Atah Echad" corresponds to the Shabbat of the future. (Tur) And we say "U'Mi K'amcha Yisrael" (And who is like Your people Israel), and it is stated in the Midrash: Three testify about each other, the Holy One, Blessed be He, Israel, and Shabbat. The Holy One, Blessed be He, and Israel testify about the Shabbat that it is a day of rest, Israel and Shabbat testify about the Holy One, Blessed be He, that He is One, the Holy One, Blessed be He, and Shabbat testify about Israel that they are unique (there).

And we say: 'Abraham will rejoice, Isaac will exult, Jacob and his children will rest in it,' as it is stated in the Midrash: "The father of a righteous one will greatly rejoice" (Proverbs 23:24) - this refers to Abraham when he was told 'This one will not inherit you' - he felt joy. And joy filled his heart as it is said: "And Abraham fell on his face and laughed." And since this verse refers to Abraham, and it says 'the father of a righteous one' - Isaac was righteous, and regarding the righteous it is written: 'Rejoice, O righteous' - and this is 'Isaac will exult.' 'Jacob and his children will rest in it,' as it is written about him: 'And he camped before the city,' and the Midrash says: this teaches that he established boundaries before the Sabbath - this tells us that Jacob and his children observed the Sabbath. But Abraham and Isaac's children did not all observe it, as neither Ishmael nor Esau observed the Sabbath. 'And grant us, with love and will, Your holy Sabbath,' and some say 'Your holy Sabbaths.' And also 'and they will rest in them,' because in the afternoon service it includes both the day and the night, as it is at the end of the day and close to the night.

After the repetition of the Amidah by the prayer leader, it is customary to recite three verses of "Your righteousness" (Tzidkatecha): "Your righteousness is an everlasting righteousness" (Tzidkatecha tzedek), "And Your righteousness, O God, reaches to the high heavens" (Utzidkatecha asher asita), "Your righteousness is like the mighty mountains" (Tzidkatecha k'harerei El). This is akin to justifying the judgment concerning the three righteous individuals of the world who passed away on Shabbat during the time of Mincha: Joseph, Moses, David. And although there is evidence that Moses our teacher died on Friday, as he wrote thirteen Torah scrolls on the day of his death as explained in the Midrashim, the truth is that he died on Friday and was lying in the wings of the Divine Presence until Shabbat during the time of Mincha, and then he was hidden away at the time of the Divine favor (Bach and Asarah Ma'amarot). The Sephardim say "Your righteousness is like the mighty mountains" first and "Your righteousness is an everlasting righteousness" at the end, and this is indeed the order of the psalms in Tehillim (Psalms). The Ashkenazim say "Your righteousness is an everlasting righteousness" first. It appears to me that this is because this verse corresponds to Moses our teacher, as the conclusion of the verse is "and Your Torah is the truth," and therefore, out of respect, they put it first.

And if it (Shabbat) falls on a day when, if it were a weekday, we would not recite Tachanun, such as Rosh Chodesh or the eve of Rosh Chodesh, or other days on which Tachanun is not recited – we do not recite Tzidkatcha and Tzidkatcha. And it is customary not to establish a study session between Mincha and Maariv, out of respect for Moshe Rabbeinu, peace be upon him, and for Yosef and David, for when a sage dies, his study hall is nullified. And there is no strictness except with a group, but not with one or two individuals studying Torah. And in the summer, we recite Pirkei Avot, and in the winter, we recite "Barchi Nafshi" and the Songs of Ascents, and some have the custom to recite Psalms in the evening, and "Ashrei Temimei Derech" and "Lamnatzeach Binginot," and each place according to its custom. (And the Perisha wrote that since we eat the third meal between Mincha and Maariv – we also establish a study session, and the Ma'avit wrote that the Maharal of Prague would give a sermon between Mincha and Maariv on Shabbat, as written by the Eliyah Rabbah, section 14, and also written in Or Zarua HaGadol, section 89, from the sages of the Rhineland.)

One delays the evening prayer on Saturday night, as Rabbi Yossi said: “May my portion be with those who bring in the Sabbath in Tiberias and those who end the Sabbath in Sepphoris” (Shabbat 119b), for Tiberias was in a valley and it appeared to be night earlier, whereas Sepphoris was situated on a mountain and it seemed to them that it was still day until the appearance of the stars, and they would delay much on Saturday night. The time for night is when three small stars are visible, and although by law it suffices with medium-sized stars, we are not proficient in identifying medium-sized stars. It is stated in the Jerusalem Talmud at the beginning of Berachot that the stars must not be scattered but rather appear together. If it is a cloudy day, one should wait until all doubt is removed from his mind. Therefore, for the evening prayer, one waits until after this to add from the mundane to the holy. Our custom is to wait from sunset an hour and twelve parts of an hour, each part being one-sixtieth of an hour. This way, we resolve all doubts, and then work is permitted. However, when the sky is full of stars, no other sign is needed.

Afterward, the prayer leader stands and begins "VeHu Rachum Yechaper Avon" and "Barechu," and he continues the words of "VeHu Rachum" and "Barechu" pleasantly and with a crying voice. This is stated in the Ba'al HaMaor at the end of the laws of Tzitzit: "A person should extend (the word 'Barechu' and the blessing 'Baruch Hashem HaMevorach' on the conclusion of Shabbat). This is necessary to be saved from the harm of that Shabbat," end quote, meaning to be saved from the harms of the coming week. And in the Or Zarua HaGadol (end of Siman 89), he writes as follows: "My teacher, Rabbi Eliezer of Worms, wrote: on Motza'ei Shabbat after saying 'VeHu Rachum'… 'Hashem Hoshia'… immediately the prayer leader says 'Barechu' with a prolonged utterance, because the souls return to Gehenna afterwards, and as long as he prolongs - they do not return. Additionally, due to the escorting of Shabbat, as one needs to escort the king - it is proper to prolong. Also, due to the delay in ending Shabbat, it is necessary to prolong… I also heard that Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Meshulam the Great, who was a prayer leader, would prolong 'Barechu' with all his strength, and similarly, it is found in the prayer order of Rabbi Amram Gaon: on Motza'ei Shabbat the prayer leader should prolong 'Barechu,' end quote. This is what our teacher, the Rama, wrote: "It is customary to say 'VeHu Rachum' and 'Barechu' with a prolonged pleasantness in order to add from the mundane to the holy," end quote. And although there are additional reasons, he did not feel the need to explain them all. The custom of Israel is Torah, and one should not change any custom established by the ancients.

Our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote: "One who is compelled, such as someone who needs to wait at the boundary for a mitzvah purpose, can pray the Maariv (evening) prayer for the conclusion of Shabbat from 'Plag HaMincha' (approximately one and a quarter hours before nightfall) onwards and recite the Havdalah (blessing separating Shabbat from the weekday) immediately. However, he should not bless over the candle, and he is prohibited from performing labor until the appearance of the stars." Thus far his words. And he should wait to recite the Shema until the appearance of the stars, even though he will not connect the redemption blessing directly to the Amidah prayer (according to the Magen Avraham). This means that he will pray the Amidah first, and then recite the Shema and its blessings afterward. This is specifically in a case where he does not have wine at the place where he waits at the boundary (there), or if he needs to pray while walking (there). However, in Siman 89, it is clarified that it is better to connect the redemption blessing directly to the Amidah and to pray while walking, see there. Nevertheless, in our times we have neither seen nor heard of anyone doing this, and it should not be done, as it is bewildering to many, especially in our times when we pray Mincha (afternoon prayer) until evening, and this is agreed upon by the great authorities (the Shach, Taz, and Magen Avraham).

Just as Kiddush is recited in prayer and over a cup [of wine], so too Havdalah must be recited in prayer, meaning that one adds in the blessing of "You graciously grant wisdom" the phrase "You have graciously granted us and distinguished, O Lord our God, between holy and profane, etc." and also over a cup [of wine]. Thus, the Men of the Great Assembly instituted that Havdalah must be recited both in prayer and over a cup, and one who does so will have blessings rest upon his head (Berachot 33a). They instituted Havdalah in the blessing "who grants wisdom" because it is wisdom to distinguish between holy and profane, and they established it in the blessing of wisdom (Tur, Orach Chayim 115), for through knowledge we recognize the significance of rest and know to distinguish between holy and profane (Rosh, Berachot 33a). If there is no knowledge, there is no distinction, for knowledge in the physical sense is animalistic knowledge, whereas true knowledge is spiritual, which is the knowledge of Torah and the observance of its commandments. This is why we say "You have graciously granted us the knowledge of Your Torah, and taught us to perform the statutes of Your will, and You have distinguished, O Lord our God, between holy and profane, etc." – thus, showing that one depends on the other.

Some say that since we say "Ata Chonantanu" (You have granted us knowledge), there is no need to say "Ata Chonen" (You graciously endow humans with knowledge), as it would be redundant. However, many prominent authorities require both, as they are two distinct matters: "Ata Chonen L'adam Da'at" (You graciously endow humans with knowledge) refers to the general intellect granted to all of humanity, such as basic understanding that distinguishes humans from animals. "Ata Chonantanu L'mada Toratecha" (You have granted us the knowledge of Your Torah) refers specifically to the wisdom of the Torah (Levush and Bach). 

Indeed, "Chaneinu Me'itcha De'ah Binah Vehaskel" (Grant us from You knowledge, understanding, and discernment) certainly refers to Torah wisdom. However, "Ata Chonen" may be said to refer to general human intellect. It is also possible that "Ata Chonen" refers to Torah wisdom, while "Ata Chonantanu" refers to the wisdom of distinguishing (between holy and mundane) (Taz, section 1). 

When we say "Ve'Chaneinu Me'itcha," it refers to the earlier statement. Some suggest saying "Ve'Chaneinu Me'itcha De'ah" twice: once before "Ata Chonantanu" and once afterward, but this opinion was rejected (see Bach and Taz). 

In the Jerusalem Talmud, Berakhot, chapter Ein Omdin (halacha 2), it is stated: the reason we say "Ata Chonantanu" at the beginning of the middle blessings is that just as one is forbidden to do work before making Havdalah (the separation between holy and mundane), similarly, one is forbidden to request their needs before making Havdalah. Therefore, we make Havdalah and then request our needs (the Gra elaborates on this, see there).

And I have a question about this, since the sages instituted for Havdalah, as they did for Kiddush, that it should be both in the prayer and over a cup as mentioned. This is explained in Berachot (33a): "For Kiddush, just as Kiddush even though it is sanctified in prayer, it is sanctified over a cup - so too Havdalah, etc." If so, why did they not institute a blessing for Havdalah in the prayer as they did for Kiddush in the prayer? It must be said that certainly two blessings for one matter are difficult to institute, as is evident. Therefore, they did not institute a blessing for Havdalah. And this that they instituted for Kiddush - it is not because of the obligation of Kiddush, but because of the obligation of prayer, as there is no other blessing in the Shabbat prayer. And it applies to all the prayers, even to prayers where there is no Kiddush like Mussaf and Mincha. But for Havdalah in the prayer, which has eighteen blessings - they did not want to add a blessing for Havdalah, and the Havdalah over the cup suffices.

I have another question: How can we recite in the "Ata Chonantanu" prayer the four distinctions: "between holy and profane, between light and darkness, between Israel and the nations, between the seventh day and the six days of labor"? For in Pesachim (103b), the Talmud questions this formulation based on the ruling: "One should not recite fewer than three distinctions, nor more than seven," and there is a specific requirement for these particular numbers as they signify certain matters (Tosafot there 104a, s.v. "Ve'omer"). The Talmud answers that "between the seventh day and the six days of labor" is not counted among the distinctions, but is included because we need a phrase similar to the conclusion near the conclusion itself. 

Now, this is difficult to understand. While it makes sense to require a phrase similar to the conclusion near the conclusion when reciting over a cup (of wine), where there is a formal conclusion, in the prayer where there is no formal conclusion, we should not say "between the seventh day and the six days of labor." While it is understandable in the Havdalah recited from Shabbat to Yom Tov that we say this formulation because there we do recite seven distinctions, as Tosafot mentioned there, it is difficult to justify this in the weekday prayer Havdalah. 

We must say that since this formulation is required over the cup, they did not want to change it in the prayer either, or perhaps the specific requirement is only for the cup. Nevertheless, this does not sit well with me, and it would have been better not to say it. This requires further investigation. (Later, I found this same opinion in Mordechai).

If one made a mistake and forgot to say "Ata Chonantanu" in the prayer, he does not need to go back, since he will perform Havdalah over the cup. And even though he did not follow the enactment of the Sages, he was mistaken, and he is forbidden to do work until he says "Hamavdil bein Kodesh lechol" (He who separates between holy and profane), as will be explained in Siman 299. And if he also made a mistake with the cup, for example, if he tasted before Havdalah, and even though we hold that if one tasted, he still performs Havdalah, there is still an error, and he needs to repeat the prayer. This is the ruling of the Rosh, the Rashba, Rabbeinu Yonah, the Tur, and the Shulchan Aruch. The source of this law is from what it says in Berachot: "If one made a mistake in both, he returns to the beginning," and our Rabbis explained that he made a mistake in the prayer and also with the cup, meaning he tasted before Havdalah, therefore he returns to the prayer and the cup.

And the Rambam in Chapter 10 of Hilchot Tefillah does not mention this law, and indeed it is not understood what rectification there would be for what he tasted if he returns and prays. And if it is because the Havdalah over the cup was not proper due to his tasting, and therefore he needs to recite Havdalah in the prayer—it would also not be proper in the prayer due to his tasting. And indeed the Tosafot Rid wrote there that it is a penalty because he tasted before Havdalah, as mentioned. And it is not understood, for what should be done if he tasted inadvertently? And if we say that this is only specifically when he tasted intentionally—our Rabbis should have explained this, and furthermore, if it is because of a penalty, let us penalize him for not having recited Havdalah in the prayer, and let him return to the beginning if he did not recite Havdalah in the prayer. Moreover, where do we find a penalty in the repetition of the prayer, for there are many blessings in vain. And although since the Sages instituted it, it is not considered in vain—why did they institute this to increase unnecessary blessings on a festival?

Therefore, it appears to my humble opinion that the Rambam, of blessed memory, would interpret the Talmud differently. "Erred in this and that" means: if one erred in any of the middle blessings, the rule is that he returns to the beginning of the blessing in which he erred as long as he has not completed his prayer, as stated in Siman 119. But here, if he erred and did not mention "Ata Chonantanu" as well, he returns to the beginning, meaning the beginning of the middle blessings. And even though for that alone he wouldn't have to return, nevertheless, because he needs to return for the other blessing, he also returns for this one as well. However, this interpretation was not brought. (And the Rashba wrote the reason that since he erred completely, he returns to the proper order, and your mnemonic is: if one comes to sift, he sifts the entire batch, as mentioned there. According to our interpretation, the analogy is better. However, the understanding of our sages is broader than ours.)

And since the reason one does not repeat the prayer if they made a mistake and did not recite Havdalah is because they can perform Havdalah over a cup [of wine], therefore, if one does not have a cup at night and believes they will also not have a cup the next day, they must repeat the prayer. And even though the time for Havdalah extends for three days, as stated in Siman 299, nevertheless, one cannot fast for three days (Perisha). That is to say, even if someone will have a cup the next day but wants to eat, it is obvious that they need to pray and recite Havdalah in the prayer, but it is customary that until the next day, one can resolve in their mind not to eat. And on Tisha B'Av, which falls on a Sunday, and one forgets "Atah Chonantanu" - they do not need to repeat the prayer, as they will perform Havdalah after the fast.

The Tur writes: "In a case where one has a cup [of wine], where there is no need to repeat the prayer, immediately upon concluding the blessing - one does not need to go back, even if one has not begun the following blessing. And Rabbeinu Eliezer writes: As long as one has not begun the following blessing, one goes back, and this applies to all matters for which there is no need to go back, such as 'Al Hanisim' etc." End quote. For Rabbeinu Eliezer holds that as long as one has not begun the following blessing, it is not considered a repetition, and it is as if one is still in the midst of the blessing. And our master the Beit Yosef in section 4 rules like the Tur that one does not need to go back, but before concluding the blessing, if one has not yet said the name [of God], even if one has said 'Blessed are You' - one goes back and says 'You have graciously given' (Bach). And one should not ask that if so, why do we rule in Siman 114 regarding 'He who causes the wind to blow' when one forgets, if one has not begun 'You are holy' - one says it there. For it is not similar, for certainly in a matter where there is an obligation to go back - it is not considered an interruption, but in a matter where there is no obligation - it is considered an interruption (Magen Avraham there, Subsection 8), and according to this, when one does not have a cup [of wine] - also here one says it even when one has concluded the blessing. And even more than this they wrote, that if one does not have a cup and remembers before the blessing of 'Hear our prayer' - one can say it in 'Hear our prayer' (Magen Avraham Subsection 3).

It seems to me that even though one does not need to repeat the prayer if he forgot "Ata Chonantanu," and also should not say it during "Shomea Tefillah" if he has a cup of wine, as it would be an interruption, still after "Yihyu Leratzon" he should say it. This is because after the prayer, it is not considered an interruption and is no worse than someone who is accustomed to saying supplications after the prayer. As for the concern that there is no blessing at all—what does it matter to us, since we hold that as long as one says "Hamavdil Bein Kodesh Lechol" he is permitted to do work even without a blessing, as will be explained in Siman 299. And the reason why the poskim did not mention this is because it is an obvious matter, and it is not a correction to the enactment of the sages who instituted Havdalah in the prayer, as this is not considered Havdalah in the prayer since it is after the prayer. And a proof for this is from "Aneinu" in Siman 605, where it is ruled that if one did not say it in "Shomea Tefillah," he should say it after the prayer, as mentioned there. The same applies here. And do not say that "Aneinu" has supplications, for here too we find: "Our Father, our King, bestow upon us the days… cleansed from all sin, etc."

The Tur also wrote: Rabbeinu Tam holds that even if one began the blessing that follows [the Amidah], one may go back if one wishes. Rabbeinu Tam also holds that in all matters where the Sages said one does not need to go back, nevertheless, if one wishes, one may go back as long as one has not completed their prayer. Rabbeinu Tam himself acted in this manner, as mentioned in Tosafot at the end of the chapter "Tefillat Hashachar."
