The Rosh disagrees, arguing that just as one does not go back after taking three steps back [at the end of the Amidah], similarly, one does not go back after completing the blessing. Our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 5: In instances where it was said that one does not go back, if one wishes to be stringent upon oneself and go back after completing their prayer, one may do so. But if one has not yet completed their prayer, one is not permitted to go back. His intention is to rule like the Rosh, that it is forbidden to go back after completing the blessing. He adds that, on the contrary, if one has completed their prayer, one may be stringent and go back, and this would be considered as praying a voluntary prayer. The main point is that this is the opposite of Rabbeinu Tam's opinion. According to Rabbeinu Tam, one may go back in the middle of the prayer but not after completing it, while according to the Rosh, one may not go back in the middle, but if one wishes, one may go back after completing it. However, it is obvious that even according to Rabbeinu Tam, if one has completed the prayer and wishes to pray a voluntary prayer, no one would prevent him from doing so (see the Tur and the Taz, section 3).

Some say that if one forgot to pray the Maariv (evening) prayer on Motza'ei Shabbat (Saturday night), when he prays the Shacharit (morning) prayer twice to make up for it, he should not say "Ata Chonantanu" (the Havdalah prayer) in the make-up prayer (Magen Avraham, section 1, in the name of Radbaz). However, there are those who disagree, arguing that since during Maariv there was an obligation to mention Havdalah, and initially, in the Gemara, Havdalah was instituted only in the prayer, and even now the main enactment is in the prayer, therefore, he needs to mention it (Magen Avraham). In my humble opinion, the primary view is like the first opinion, that certainly if he did not have a cup (of wine for Havdalah), he is obligated to mention it in order to fulfill the obligation of Havdalah in the prayer. But if he had a cup and already fulfilled the obligation of Havdalah, even though if he prays later he needs to mention it, nonetheless, when he prays the next morning, it is similar to one who did not pray Mincha (afternoon) on Erev Shabbat (Friday), who prays the Maariv (evening) prayer twice on Shabbat, as mentioned in Siman 108, and the same applies here. And during the day, there is no Havdalah, and the obligation of Havdalah has already been fulfilled.

Tur wrote in the name of Rav Amram Gaon: "The custom to recite 'Vayehi Noam' and the Kedusha D'Sidra with pleasantness and lengthiness at the departure of Shabbat is to delay the completion of the prayers of the Israelites, to prolong the time before the wicked return to Gehenna, for on Motzaei Shabbat the appointed angel over the spirits cries out: 'Return to Gehenna, for the Israelites have completed their prayers.'" He further wrote another reason for 'Vayehi Noam,' stating that it is a psalm of blessing in which Moshe blessed Israel upon the completion of the Mishkan, and the work of the Mishkan was completed on a Sunday, as it is taught in the Baraita of the Ten Crowns (Shabbat 87b). Therefore, we say it as a symbol of blessing for the six weekdays that come to us in peace. It is customary to repeat the verse 'Orech Yamim,' and the Tur wrote that by doing so, the Divine Name is completed. We do not know more than this (see Magen Avraham). According to its plain meaning, this verse is repeated in every place where it appears, such as in the Shabbat and Yom Tov morning psalms, where it is also repeated. Perhaps from 'Vayehi Noam' until after 'Orech Yamim,' there are sixteen verses, and we repeat it as a sign of the numerical value of 'Tov' (good). We begin with 'Ve'ata Kadosh' and not with 'Uva Letziyon Goel,' because there is no redemption at night. Nor do we recite the verse 'Vaani Zot Beriti,' because the main engagement in Torah is during the day, as it is stated in Eruvin (65a): 'We are daytime workers.' Furthermore, we want to juxtapose the verses of 'Yoshev B'Seter' to 'Ve'ata Kadosh,' meaning because this psalm explains how Hashem protects us: 'A thousand may fall at your side, etc.,' 'Orech Yamim, etc.' – to this, we sanctify His Name. Therefore, when 'Vayehi Noam' is not recited, 'Ve'ata Kadosh' is also not recited, which is when a Yom Tov falls in the middle of the week, as there are no six weekdays. Additionally, 'Vayehi Noam' was said by Moshe at the completion of the Mishkan, when the Divine Presence rested, and this is 'Ve'ata Kadosh Yoshev Tehilot Yisrael.' If Yom Tov falls on the Shabbat that follows, we do recite 'Vayehi Noam' and 'Ve'ata Kadosh,' since there are six weekdays. Some are hesitant about these customs, but the custom of Israel is Torah.

The cantor recites the Havdalah over a cup of wine to fulfill the obligation for those who do not have wine or who are not knowledgeable in the blessings. Each individual should intend to fulfill their obligation, but the cantor generally intends to fulfill the obligation for everyone. The cantor also intends to fulfill the obligation for women and those listening outside the synagogue. Those who are listening are required to respond 'Amen' to each blessing. Even though, typically, someone who fulfills the obligation for another must be seated to establish a fixed setting, and the congregation is standing, since they prepare themselves to listen, it is considered as if they have a fixed setting (Tosafot Berachot 43).

It is customary to recite verses of blessing: "Veyiten Lecha," "Hamalach Hagoel," and they are printed in the prayer books. These are said even when "Vayehi Noam" and "Ve'ata Kadosh" are not recited. However, on the eve of a weekday during Chol HaMoed, it is not appropriate to recite them at all, as these are not workdays, and it is disrespectful to Chol HaMoed.

It is customary to mention Elijah the Prophet on Saturday night, in hymns that are based on the mention of his name, and to pray that he will soon come to us with the Messiah, son of David. Since Elijah does not come on Friday evenings or the eve of holidays (Eruvin 43b), and there is also uncertainty if he would come on Shabbat due to the restrictions of traveling beyond the Shabbat boundary (ibid.), therefore, on Saturday night, we have the hope and pray for his arrival. Additionally, since Shabbat is a semblance of the World to Come, a time entirely of joy, and on Saturday night, sadness returns, we alleviate this with the hope of redemption, and place good signs in verses of blessing, peace, and redemption, and in the mention of Elijah the Prophet, who risked his life for the Torah and for the zeal of the Lord of Hosts. When we mention him, his merit protects us to walk in his ways and paths. Some say the prayer "Ribbono Shel Olam" which is printed in the prayer books, a small portion of which is found in the Jerusalem Talmud, chapter "Ein Omdin," and each place follows its own custom.

We learn in Tractate Shevuot (18b): "Anyone who recites Havdalah over wine at the conclusion of Shabbat will have male children, as it is written: 'To distinguish between the holy and the profane, and between the impure and the pure,' and at the end of the portion it is written: 'To distinguish between the impure and the pure,' and it is immediately followed by: 'A woman who conceives and gives birth to a male child.' And he will have children fit to issue rulings, as it is written: 'To distinguish between the holy... and to teach the children of Israel.' Now, although these interpretations are supportive references, nevertheless, if the primary commandment of Havdalah were not from the Torah, the sages would not have relied on scriptural verses to support it, to perform Havdalah over wine."

In truth, this is the opinion of the Rambam at the beginning of Chapter 29 of Shabbat, where he writes: "It is a positive commandment from the Torah to sanctify the Sabbath with words, as it is stated, 'Remember...' And one must remember it both at its entrance and at its exit: at its entrance with the sanctification of the day (Kiddush), and at its exit with Havdalah." These are his words. And from the Torah, it is sufficient with prayer, but the Rabbis instituted it over a cup of wine. The Rabbis based this on verses in the Talmud, Shevuot, where Havdalah is considered entirely similar to Kiddush. And this is what is stated in Berachot (33a), that the Men of the Great Assembly instituted blessings and prayers, sanctifications and separations; initially, they established it in prayer, etc. This refers to the formulations — how and what. And the proof is that Kiddush is said similarly, and Kiddush is clearly from the Torah. Rather, it is about the formulation of Kiddush that is being discussed, and similarly for Havdalah.

And so it is explicitly stated in the Sefer Mitzvot Gadol (Positive Commandments 29) and this is his language: "Remember the Sabbath day... and it is necessary to sanctify it at its entry and exit... one at its entry is 'Remember', and one at its exit is mentioned regarding 'Observe', as it says in the Midrash that this refers to the exit of the Sabbath." End of quote. And also in the Sefer HaChinuch, it is written thus. And so the commentator at the beginning of Nazir writes, who says: From wine and strong drink he shall abstain - to prohibit wine of a mitzvah. And he asks, what is it - Kiddush and Havdalah. And the commentator explains: That it is written 'Remember', I only have at its entry, from where do we derive at its exit, etc. And from the language of the Gemara itself, it is proven thus, as Havdalah is compared to Kiddush based on the scriptural derivation, thus it proves that the essence of Havdalah is from the Torah. And in the Pirkei DeRabbi Eliezer (Chapter 20), it says: That Adam the first man, when he knew that the holy day was separated, he said 'Blessed is He who separates between the holy and the mundane'. And it also says there that when one makes Havdalah over wine, the Holy One, blessed be He, acquires him as His treasured one, as it is said: "And I will separate you from the nations to be mine" (Leviticus 20:26), "And you shall be to Me a treasured possession" (Exodus 19:5), as it says there. And the intention is that it is derived like a verbal analogy 'to Me - to Me' (so it appears to me), nevertheless, from all this it clearly seems that it is from the Torah.

And the Maggid Mishneh there wrote that there are those who disagree, and he holds that Havdalah is only a Rabbinic obligation, see there, and according to them, all those verses are merely supportive references. The practical difference in law would be regarding women, for if it is a Torah obligation, women are also obligated, as they are equal in all matters of Shabbat. But if it is Rabbinic and it is not dependent on the observance of Shabbat but is a separate matter, and it is a time-bound commandment – women are not obligated in it (Beit Yosef at the end of this section in the name of Orchot Chaim). And there are those who say that even if it is Rabbinic – women are obligated, as it was decreed similarly to Kiddush (Maggid Mishneh there).

Based on this, our teacher the Beit Yosef wrote in Section 8: "Women are obligated in Havdalah just as they are obligated in Kiddush, though there are those who disagree." And our teacher the Rema wrote: "Therefore, they should not perform Havdalah for themselves, but rather hear Havdalah from men." There are those who dispute this, saying that even if they are exempt, they are permitted to recite the blessing, just as they recite blessings over several positive time-bound commandments like Sukkah and Lulav (Bach and Magen Avraham, Section 11). One of the authorities wrote that women are not permitted to perform Havdalah for themselves, meaning they are not obligated to do so, but if they wish, they are allowed (Bach there). Some reconcile the words of our teacher the Rema by saying that this applies specifically where men are obligated by Torah law, in which case women are permitted to bless. However, in the case of Havdalah, for those who hold that men are only rabbinically obligated, women should not bless (Taz, Section 7). This is puzzling to me, as the Lulav for the entire festival is only rabbinically obligated except for the first day, and women still bless. Some wish to differentiate, arguing that women can bless only on practical commandments, not on commandments that are purely verbal (see Magen Avraham there). This too is incorrect, for Havdalah involves the action of drinking the cup, and besides, what reasoning is there to differentiate in this way? Furthermore, most authorities hold that Havdalah is a Torah obligation and that women are obligated by Torah law and can even fulfill the obligation for men. Even if it is rabbinic, some authorities hold that both men and women are rabbinically obligated, and women can fulfill the obligation for men since both are rabbinically obligated. The opinion that women are not obligated at all is a minority view. While it is advisable to be cautious about women fulfilling the obligation for men, and it is better for them to hear it from men, it is clear that if there is no one to perform Havdalah for them, they should perform it themselves. I have seen some who question how women can perform Havdalah, given that women do not drink from the Havdalah cup. This surprises me, as this is not a rule, but merely a custom, and not all women adhere to it. It is clear that if women perform Havdalah, they must drink. I have seen it written that a man who has already performed Havdalah should not perform it for women, just as a man does not blow the shofar for women after he has fulfilled his obligation, as stated in Section 589 (Elya Rabbah, Section 18). However, it seems to me that this is not analogous, as with the shofar, there is clearly no obligation for women, but for Havdalah, most authorities agree that women are obligated. Even though we should be cautious for the minority opinion that they may be exempt, if they can perform it themselves, it is better, but if they cannot, it is permitted and a mitzvah for a man to perform Havdalah for them, as this is the view of most authorities. This is my humble opinion.

The order of Havdalah: wine, spices, candle, Havdalah, and your mnemonic is Y'B'N'H'. The reason for wine preceding all the other items is that it is frequent and it is the cause for separation (Berachot, beginning of Chapter 8). Spices precede the candle because the blessing over spices is also frequent compared to the blessing over the candle, which is only on the conclusion of Shabbat, while spices can be blessed several times a day. And the blessing of Havdalah obviously needs to be at the end, as it is the main component and conclusion of the matter, similar to Kiddush. The specific laws regarding spices will be explained in Siman 297, and the laws regarding the candle in Siman 298. One should be careful that the cup is not damaged, and also that the wine is not damaged. A damaged cup is when it is slightly broken or has a large crack, and damaged wine is when it has been tasted. These laws have been explained earlier in Siman 182 regarding Birkat Hamazon, see there.

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote in Section 2: "That it is better to recite Havdalah over a blemished cup of wine than over beer." And there are those who say that his intention is in a place where beer is not considered a significant beverage, but when it is a significant beverage, it is better to recite Havdalah over unblemished beer than over blemished wine (Magen Avraham, Subsection 5). And it is not permitted to recite Havdalah over a blemished beverage unless one has no other beverage at all (ibid.). However, this does not seem to be the case, as our teacher the Rema is referring to a place where beer is considered a significant beverage, as he discussed this earlier (see there). And the truth is that he holds that blemished wine is better than unblemished beer (Eliyahu Rabbah, Subsection 5), as it is also clarified above in Section 182 regarding Birkat Hamazon that one fulfills the obligation with blemished wine in retrospect (see there). Nevertheless, regarding the actual law, there is no decisive ruling on this matter, and the great authorities have agreed that unblemished beer is better than blemished wine (the Vilna Gaon and the Alter Rebbe).

In the synagogue, we begin with the blessing "Creator of the fruit of the vine," but each head of household in their home starts with verses for a good omen and success: "Behold, God is my salvation," "And you shall draw water with joy," "Salvation belongs to the Lord," "The Lord of Hosts is with us," and some add also "The Lord of Hosts, happy is the man," "Save us, O Lord," "The Jews had light," and they conclude with "So may it be for us" and say "I will lift the cup of salvation." And why are these not said in the synagogue? To teach the public that this is not part of the Havdalah, and furthermore, since they already said "And He shall give you" earlier, they have already recited many verses for a good omen.

And our master the Rema wrote that during Havdalah, one should look at the cup and the candle. This is from the Tur in Siman 299, where he wrote: "Those who respond Amen must look at the cup and the candle." There are those who explain that the one making Havdalah must also look at the cup and the candle (Derech HaChaim), but this is not implied from the language of the Tur, as is evident. However, one is compelled to say so, since it is one of the ten things said about the cup of blessing—to look at it (Berachot 51a), as we wrote above in Siman 183, and consequently, here where there is also a candle, one must also look at the candle. But the Tur states that even the listeners need to do so, and certainly the one making Havdalah himself. The reason for this is so that they do not lose their concentration. They did not require looking at the spices as well, because the spices are not essential for Havdalah, and many times Havdalah is made without spices.

It is also written: That it is customary to pour some wine from the cup onto the ground before completing the blessing of "Borei Pri Hagafen," so that the cup will not be considered blemished. The reason for the pouring is based on what is said in Eruvin (65a): Any household in which wine is not poured like water does not have a sign of blessing. This is done as a good sign at the beginning of the week. Additionally, wine is poured from the cup after Havdalah and used to extinguish the candle and to wash one's eyes because of the affection for the mitzvah. These are the words of the text. 

Now, regarding what is written that it is customary to pour so that the cup will not be blemished – this is not understandable at all. The Levush wrote that one should not pour at the beginning of the blessing in order not to bless over a blemished cup. This is also not understandable, as it is not considered blemished unless one has drunk from it. Moreover, the Levush wrote that one should pour when starting the blessing, and this is even more puzzling: if so, by the end of the blessing it would be blemished, if this is considered to be blemished (Taz, section 1). Furthermore, there is no greater disgrace than pouring onto the ground after the blessing (ibid.), and it is explicitly stated in Sefer Chassidim (section 111). 

Some have explained that a cup is only considered blemished if one has drunk from it, and this "blemish" refers to the notion of disgrace. That is, if one pours after the blessing, it is considered disgraceful as mentioned, and therefore one pours before the conclusion of the blessing (Magen Avraham, section 2). This too is puzzling: if there is disgrace at the end of the blessing, surely there is also disgrace before the conclusion of the blessing.

In truth, the commentators on the Shulchan Aruch have written not to follow his words, but rather, when filling the cup for Havdalah, to fill it to its brim in such a way that a little spills over onto the ground (Taz and Magen Avraham there), and this is the common practice. There are those who also object to this, suggesting to abolish the spilling entirely due to the waste of drink, but it is possible that a small amount is not an issue (there). And I say that this is indeed the intention of our master, the Rema, and moreover, he corrected it more because he is concerned about the waste of drink, and also did not want to entirely abolish the custom, therefore he advised to do it in this manner. And that which he wrote to pour from the cup, his intention is not to pour with the hands, and the proof is that he did not write to pour from the cup, as he wrote at the end: 'they pour from the cup after Havdalah.' Rather, the explanation is: not to pour a lot to the extent that when filling the cup it will spill onto the ground, as this involves waste as mentioned. Instead, fill it fully as required for the cup of blessing, but when starting the blessing and moving the hand slightly, a little will spill naturally. However, be careful not to spill a lot, which would cause a defect in the cup by not being full, but a little - it is still considered full, as it is impossible to be exact. And that which he wrote: 'so that the cup will not be defective' - the explanation is: that it should spill so that it will not be defective, meaning be careful not to spill a lot, and it is proper to do so. And that which he wrote: 'before finishing the blessing of Borei Pri Hagafen' - this is when starting from the blessing, and if starting from 'Hinei El Yeshuati' - it should spill then, and his main intention is, on the contrary, not to spill intentionally, but since it is really full, when taken in the hands and starting the Havdalah, and the hand moves a bit - it will spill naturally. And at the end, he wrote to pour from the cup after Havdalah, meaning after drinking, and they pour it directly onto the table or into a vessel and extinguish the candle with it, and wash the eyes for medicinal purposes and out of love for the mitzvah. (And in Mordechai at the beginning of Yoma, he brought the response of the Geonim that they put water into the Havdalah cup and drink, and what remains they wash their faces to show love for the mitzvah, and the remnants of the mitzvah prevent calamities, see there).

One does not perform Havdalah (the separation ceremony marking the end of Shabbat) over bread, for specifically Kiddush, which requires a meal, it is appropriate to recite it over bread and then eat the meal, as the meal is related to the Kiddush. However, regarding Havdalah, it is not related to bread, and it is necessary to perform Havdalah over a beverage. On a Yom Tov (festival) that falls on Motzaei Shabbat (Saturday night), which includes Kiddush to be recited over bread: some say that since there is Kiddush, one also performs Havdalah on it (the bread), and some say that it is better to perform both Kiddush and Havdalah over beer or another beverage. The primary view is according to the first opinion, that since one must eat, the Havdalah is also related to the bread, and it is not less significant than Kiddush.

And if he does not have wine, one sanctifies over beer or other beverages if they are considered "chamar medina" (a commonly consumed beverage in that place), excluding water. Even though most of their drinking is water, since it has no significance, one does not make Havdalah over it. It seems to me that even if the water is enhanced, such as our seltzer water or lemonade, or water with honey for taste or other types of fruit - in any case, it is still water, and one does not make Havdalah on it. And we have already written in Orach Chaim, Siman 272, Section 14, that when there is absolutely nothing else that one can drink, one can make Havdalah over milk or sweet tea, and this is not like plain water since it is cooked and not called water. 

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote that it is customary to make Havdalah after Pesach over beer and not wine, because it is cherished. And there are those who wrote that this is only in a place where beer is considered "chamar medina," but in Ashkenaz it is forbidden (Magen Avraham, Section 6), meaning since wine is available there. However, the language does not imply this, for if so, why mention specifically after Pesach because of its cherished status? Even otherwise, it would be permitted as explained. It seems that even in a place where there is wine, but they are also accustomed to beer, and beer is also considered "chamar medina," therefore, throughout the year one is obligated to make Havdalah over wine, and only after Pesach does one make Havdalah over beer because it is cherished (and this is also evident from the words of the Taz in Section 3, see there).

And if one does not have wine, beer, or any other beverage for Havdalah: some say that he is allowed to eat and rely on the Havdalah in the prayer, or he can say 'Hamavdil' without a cup and without a blessing, since the blessing is only recited over a cup, but without the blessing, similar to what will be explained at the end of Siman 299 (see Magen Avraham, subparagraph 7, and it is questionable if his intention is for the blessing and he compares it to the grace after meals, but this is not a comparison at all; see Pri Megadim and consider it well). Indeed, this opinion seems reasonable, for why should he fast if he does not have a cup, and if so, if the whole week he will not have a cup, should he not eat?! And although we find in Pesachim (107a) about Ameimar who did not eat - this was an act of piety and not the law. And some say that certainly, if he will not have [a cup] until the next night, we do not tell him to fast the whole day. However, if he expects that tomorrow he will have a cup, he is forbidden to eat today until tomorrow when he makes Havdalah. And although it is a mitzvah to eat on Motzei Shabbat, as stated in Siman 300, nevertheless without Havdalah the mitzvah is nullified. Therefore, for one who holds in section 12 that on a Yom Tov that falls on Motzei Shabbat, one does not make Havdalah on bread, and he has no beverage at all - he should not eat until tomorrow if he expects to have a cup tomorrow. And although it is a mitzvah to eat at night on Yom Tov, nevertheless since he did not make Havdalah, the mitzvah is nullified. (And this is the intention of the Magen Avraham, subparagraph 8). However, we have already ruled there that the main halacha is that one makes Havdalah on bread in such a case.

And similarly, for those who hold that Birkat Hamazon (Grace after Meals) requires a cup, and he has only one cup, and if he makes Havdalah (the ceremony marking the end of Shabbat) over it, he will not have a cup for Birkat Hamazon: if he expects that tomorrow he will have a cup, he should make Havdalah now and not eat until tomorrow. If he also does not expect to have one tomorrow, it is better that he eats before making Havdalah and says Birkat Hamazon over it, but does not drink the cup until he makes Havdalah and drinks it. However, for those who hold that Birkat Hamazon does not require a cup, he should make Havdalah over the cup and then eat, and say Birkat Hamazon without a cup. All this refers to a situation where he only has a precise quarter-log of wine already properly mixed, and if he adds a little water, it will spoil it. Otherwise, he could make Havdalah, drink a little, and then add a little water to complete the quarter-log and say Birkat Hamazon over it. And although ideally one should drink a mouthful, in a situation where it is not possible, even a small amount of drinking suffices, as stated in Siman 271, section 30. For us, this law does not apply at all, as we are not accustomed to using a cup for Birkat Hamazon at all.

If one cannot afford to buy wine for Kiddush and Havdalah, they should prioritize Havdalah, because Kiddush can be made over bread. Even though Kiddush during the day cannot be made over bread, Havdalah takes precedence since many authorities hold that it is a biblical obligation, as stated at the beginning of this section, and Kiddush during the day is universally regarded as rabbinic. Furthermore, Kiddush during the day can be fulfilled with bread in pressing circumstances, as stated in Siman 289, which is not the case with Havdalah. If one cannot afford to buy oil for the Chanukah lights and wine for Havdalah, the Chanukah lights take precedence even though they are rabbinic, due to the aspect of publicizing the miracle. We have already written in Siman 671 that bread for eating takes precedence over all other matters.

Our teacher, the Beit Yosef (Rabbi Yosef Karo), ruled that Havdalah should be recited while seated. The reason is that any matter that involves fulfilling an obligation on behalf of others must be done with a sense of permanence. Our teacher, the Rema (Rabbi Moshe Isserles), ruled that it should be recited while standing, and this is the custom in these regions. The reason is that escorting the king requires standing. And if the concern is for permanence, since everyone prepares themselves for it, it is considered permanent even while standing (Tosafot Berachot 43a). Nevertheless, some of the great authorities perform it while seated (and this is also implied by the Gra in section 6). 

The Beit Yosef wrote in section 6: One should hold the wine in the right hand and the myrtle in the left hand, bless over the wine, then take the myrtle in the right hand and the wine in the left hand, and bless over the myrtle, and then return the wine to the right hand. The reason is that one must hold the object over which they are blessing in the right hand, which is the primary hand. Know that holding in the left hand is not an obligation at all. Therefore, in our practice, we do not hold the spices during the wine blessing, and when blessing over the spices, we place the cup on the table and take the spices in our right hand. Rather, the main intention is to hold the wine in the right hand and the myrtle in the right hand during their blessings, and consequently, the second item will be in the left hand, but this is not mandatory.

Even if all the members of the household heard the Havdalah in the synagogue, if they intended not to fulfill their obligation or even if it was unstated and they did not intend to fulfill their obligation and their practice is always to perform Havdalah at home, they should perform Havdalah at home. This is not considered making unnecessary blessings, because on the contrary, it is good for every head of the household to perform Havdalah at home. There is an opinion that a Torah scholar should not rely on the Havdalah in the synagogue (Sema in Choshen Mishpat 291:27), and although there is no reason for this and it is disputed (Magen Avraham 10), nevertheless, it is certainly good for every head of the household to perform Havdalah at home. However, if their practice is always to rely on the Havdalah in the synagogue, they have fulfilled their obligation by default, unless they intended not to fulfill it. And we have already explained at the beginning of this section that many authorities hold that Havdalah is a Torah obligation, and women are obligated just like men.

The reason for [using] spices for Havdalah is because on Shabbat there is an additional soul, and at the conclusion of Shabbat it departs from the person, causing a weakening of the spirit, and the spices strengthen the soul, as any pleasant fragrance strengthens the soul. Moreover, on Shabbat, even Gehenna is at rest, and at the conclusion of Shabbat it begins to burn, and the fire of Gehenna emits a foul smell which weakens the soul, necessitating support and reinforcement. And although all these reasons are spiritual, nonetheless, every Jewish soul feels this, and a clear sign of this is that every Jewish person finds themselves changed at the conclusion of Shabbat, and even though they do not see it, their soul perceives it, and the two reasons depend on each other (Beit Yosef). Therefore, on the conclusion of a festival, one does not bless over the spices, because on a festival there is no additional soul. And on the conclusion of Shabbat that coincides with a festival, there are also no spices, because Gehenna rests on a festival as well.

And since the spices are not an essential part of the laws of Havdalah, therefore, if one has spices, he blesses over them, and if not, he does not need to seek them out. This is a fortiori reasoning from the light, whose blessing is primarily on the conclusion of Shabbat; nevertheless, one does not need to seek it out (Berachot 53a), and this will be explained in the next section. All the more so with spices, which are only to refresh the soul, one does not need to seek them out. However, those who are meticulous ensure they have spices for Havdalah, and so do all those who are God-fearing.

One only recites a blessing on spices that are intended for smelling, meaning spices in a shop or at home that are made for a pleasant fragrance. However, if the spices are placed to remove a bad odor or filth, such as spices placed near a toilet to remove the stench or spices placed above a corpse’s bed, and similar instances – one does not recite a blessing on them, as they are not intended for a pleasant fragrance but to remove the bad odor. So too, spices at a gathering of idol worshippers, as their primary purpose is for their worship – they are forbidden for benefit, and the details of this law are explained in Siman 217. If one recited a blessing on any of these – it is not valid, and his blessing is nearly in vain, even though he smelled a pleasant fragrance from them, because they are not for a pleasant fragrance but to remove the bad, and the good comes incidentally. Therefore, he must recite a blessing again on other spices if they are available in his house, and there is no concern of an unnecessary blessing, as he is always permitted to bless on other spices not specifically for the conclusion of Shabbat, and all the more so at the conclusion of Shabbat. Similarly, spices associated with licentiousness, such as those hanging on her neck or in her hand, even though they are made for smelling – one does not recite a blessing, lest it leads to a sinful habit as stated there. In this case, it seems that after the fact, one does not need to recite the blessing again since it is only due to a decree. Similarly, spices made to remove sweat – one does not recite a blessing, and likewise on incense used to perfume vessels or when smelling perfumed vessels – it would be a blessing in vain, and one must recite the blessing again, and see Siman 217 for the details of this ruling. One does not recite a blessing on a container used to crush spices even though it smells, as the fragrance is incidental and not intended for smelling (Taz there, Siman 262), and so too on any fragrance that has no source – one does not recite a blessing on them, as stated there.

In Siman 216, the laws of the blessing on fragrance are explained. Some of these blessings are "Who creates fragrant trees" or "Who creates fragrant herbs" or "Who gives a pleasant fragrance to fruits" or "Who creates pleasant oil," and the general blessing is "Who creates various kinds of spices" - which one fulfills their obligation with this blessing for all types of spices, similar to the blessing "shehakol" for matters of eating and drinking. Therefore, our custom is to bless "Who creates various kinds of spices" during the Havdalah ceremony on any type of fragrance that we smell, since not everyone is proficient in the laws of the blessing on spices, because we are not accustomed to using spices, and therefore we bless on everything "Who creates various kinds of spices."

There are those who debate whether one should recite the blessing for spices over pepper, but we have never heard of this, and one does not recite the blessing (see Magen Avraham and Taz, section 5). On ground ginger, which is called "ingever," one can recite the blessing (as noted in Ba’er Hetev in the name of the Ashel Avraham), and certainly one can recite the blessing over cinnamon. Some say that even over warm bread one can make Havdalah (see Beit Yosef and Magen Avraham), but we have not heard of anyone who does so. Sacks filled with spices that non-Jews place inside wine containers, as is customary in Eastern countries, although it is permissible to smell them because they are made so that the wine will absorb the fragrance and not the other way around, nevertheless, one does not make Havdalah over them because it is inappropriate for a mitzvah. Rabbi Yosef Karo wrote that the custom is to bless over myrtle whenever possible, since it is used for the mitzvah of the Four Species on Sukkot, it is fitting to use it for another mitzvah. Rabbi Moshe Isserles wrote that some say not to bless over dry myrtle because it has no scent, but to bless over other spices, and this is the custom in these countries. It is proper to also place myrtle with the spices, thus fulfilling all opinions. However, we do not follow this practice because our myrtles dry out and become useless, and they only have a faint scent, so we do not practice this.

In Siman 624, it will be explained that on Yom Kippur, one does not recite the blessing over spices at the conclusion of Yom Kippur, even if it falls on Shabbat, because due to the fast, there was no additional soul (neshama yetera). Nevertheless, one who fasts on Shabbat as a fast for a bad dream does recite the blessing over spices, since he ate at night and the additional soul did not depart from him. This is not the case on Yom Kippur. However, on Yom Kippur, there are also those who disagree, as mentioned there. Therefore, on the conclusion of Shabbat, it is obvious that one recites the blessing over spices even if he fasted.

Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in Section 5: "One who does not smell should not recite a blessing on the spices, unless he intends to fulfill the obligation for members of his household who are minors who have reached the age of education, or for someone who does not know how and is fulfilling his obligation." End quote. There are those who disagree with this (Taz and Magen Avraham), saying that the blessing on spices is not considered a mitzvah blessing, for which the rule 'even if he has fulfilled his obligation, he can still fulfill it for others' would apply, as the spices are not the main part of the Havdalah, but rather to restore one's spirit. And even though the sages instituted the blessing on spices in Havdalah, nevertheless, many recite Havdalah without spices at all. It is obvious that if one is performing Havdalah for others and does not want to smell at that moment, having already smelled, he should not recite the blessing on the spices, but rather the listeners should recite it. However, if he wishes to smell, he may recite the blessing, as one can smell the spices multiple times as desired. And know, that the listeners do not customarily fulfill their obligation with the blessing of the one reciting, but rather they recite the blessing on the spices themselves, and similarly for the blessing on the candle.

We recite the blessing over the flame on the conclusion of Shabbat because the firelight was created at that time (Pesachim 54a). On the conclusion of Shabbat, God granted Adam the first a form of divine inspiration, and he brought two stones and rubbed them against each other, producing fire (ibid.). In Pirkei DeRabbi Eliezer (Chapter 20), it is stated: At the twilight of Shabbat, Adam was sitting and pondering in his heart, saying, "Woe is me, perhaps the serpent that deceived me on the eve of Shabbat will come." A pillar of fire was sent to him to illuminate and protect him from all harm. Adam saw the pillar of fire and rejoiced in his heart, and said, "Now I know that the Omnipresent is with me," and he stretched out his hands towards the fire and blessed "Creator of the lights of fire." 

And it further states there: When Adam withdrew his hands from the fire, he said, "Now I know that the sacred day is distinct from the profane day, for one must not kindle fire on Shabbat." He then said, "Blessed is He who separates between the sacred and the profane." (The Levush wrote that the fire was created at the end of Shabbat, which is the first day when the light was created, as stated there, but this was already refuted by the Baal HaItur and the Eliyah Rabbah, as stated there.)

And one should not ask, if so, why don't we recite a blessing on other things that were created, for a candle is different since it was forbidden on Shabbat and it is as if it is being newly created now (Magen Avraham, section 1, in the name of the Rashba). That is to say, even though the main reason for the blessing on the candle at the conclusion of Shabbat is because it is the beginning of its creation, and only at the conclusion of Yom Kippur is the reason because it was forbidden all day, and therefore on Yom Kippur we specifically need a light that "rested," as stated in section 624, and on Shabbat we do not need a light that "rested," nonetheless, this reason also applies to Shabbat. And how is Shabbat any less than Yom Kippur, since on Shabbat it was also forbidden, and Shabbat is stricter than Yom Kippur, for Shabbat carries the penalty of stoning and Yom Kippur carries the penalty of excision. Rather, what we are saying is: on Shabbat we do not need a light that "rested" because of the reason that it is the beginning of its creation, but nonetheless, by necessity, this reason also applies, and therefore they instituted a blessing on this and not on other things that are newly created. Furthermore, it seems to me that this is not a question at all, for here we bless on its renewal because we benefit from its light, similar to the sun's light for which we bless every day "He who forms the lights," but for other things that are newly created, it is not relevant to bless. And on the contrary, the Tosafot in Pesachim (53b, s.v. "Ein") asked why we do not bless every time we benefit from the light, for it is forbidden to benefit from this world without a blessing. They answered that this applies to physical enjoyment and not merely the benefit to the eyes, and the reason we bless on the sun is because it is renewed every day, as explained there. Nonetheless, there is enjoyment in this, and it is not comparable to other created things. And although from everything that the Holy One, blessed be He, created in His world, there is benefit to man, it is not comparable to the enjoyment of light, which provides immediate benefit at the moment it is kindled.

It is stated in Berachot (53b): One does not seek out a flame in the same way one seeks out other mitzvot, and if one does not have a flame, one does not need to seek it out (Rashi). The reason is that [the blessing on the flame] is not intrinsically connected to Havdalah, for when Tisha B'Av falls on a Saturday night, one recites the blessing on the flame even without Havdalah. They simply arranged it [the blessing on the flame] at the time of Havdalah. And the primary obligation of its blessing is not so significant, for if it were due to enjoyment, we do not always recite a blessing for its enjoyment as we have said. The main reason is because fire was created at that time, and also because it was forbidden all day, and what obligation is there in this? It is not more obligatory than the blessing of Shehecheyanu, which we hold to be optional (Eruvin end of Chapter 3).

And know that the Rambam (Maimonides) in Chapter 29 and the Tur who wrote this law did not differentiate between Shabbat and Yom Kippur, and from the Rambam it is explicitly clear that it applies to both of them, see there. And the Tur, although he did not mention Yom Kippur in this section, also did not mention in Section 624 that on Yom Kippur one is obligated to seek out a light. And our master the Beit Yosef wrote in Section 1: “One blesses over the light… and there is no need to seek it out. And these words apply at the end of Shabbat, but at the end of Yom Kippur - some say one should seek it out,” end quote. And this is the opinion of the Raavad that the Rashba brought in Berachot there, and this is his language: “But for a light that rested on Yom Kippur - one could say that one should seek it out, for one blesses the Creator, blessed be He, who distinguished for us between this day and other days, since all day it was forbidden to use it and now it is permitted,” end quote. And I do not understand, for is it not the same on Shabbat, and because on Shabbat there is also the reason of the beginning of its creation, does it make it worse?! And one must say in his intention, that although on Shabbat there is also this reason, nonetheless the main institution on Shabbat was not for this reason, therefore we do not require on Shabbat a light that rested. Additionally, it is difficult, for the blessing over the distinction of the day is indeed recited in the Havdalah: 'who distinguishes between holy and profane' and everything is included, and it requires further study. And I am astonished that he did not bring that the Rambam and the Tur do not hold like the Raavad, and it requires further study. And one who does not have a cup for Havdalah, nevertheless when he sees a light - he blesses 'Borei Me'orei Ha'esh' (Creator of the lights of fire), and similarly he blesses over the spices, for they are not intrinsically connected to the Havdalah itself as written.

The blessing is 'Creator of the lights of the fire' and not 'the light of the fire'. The reason given by our Sages (there) is because there are several kinds of light in the fire: a red flame, a white flame, and a greenish flame (Rashi). We say 'Creator' (present tense) and not 'created' (past tense), as it says in Scripture: 'Who forms light and creates darkness' (there). If one said 'the light of the fire', he has not fulfilled his obligation (Beit Yosef). According to this, the same applies if one said 'created' instead of 'Creator', as he has changed the wording established by the Sages. However, as written above in section 167, if one only expressed the concept, he has fulfilled his obligation, as it is explained that if one said instead of the blessing over bread 'Blessed is the Merciful One', he has fulfilled his obligation (look there), and therefore, here too, if one said 'created', he has fulfilled his obligation (look there). But if he said 'the light' instead of 'the lights', he has not fulfilled his obligation, as this would imply speaking falsely, as it suggests that only one light was created, while in truth there are many lights, as mentioned (Acharonim). It is customary to perform Havdalah with a wax candle (Magen Avraham), and it seems the reason is that it needs to be a torch, which is made by intertwining several candles, something that cannot be done with oil or fat but can be done with wax, and this is evident to the senses. (In Pri Etz Chaim, Sha'ar Shabbat, chapter 24, there is a mystical reason for this, as 'wax' (דונג) in gematria equals 63, one of the permutations of the Divine Name, and wax represents the 370 lights illuminating the letters Vav and Heh, see there and delve into it).

It is stated in Pesachim (103b) that using a torch for Havdalah is the optimal way to perform the mitzvah. This means that while one fulfills the obligation even with a single candle, for the most preferred way of performing the mitzvah, a torch is required. The reason for this is so that there will be a large light, and also to clearly distinguish the three different wicks. Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 2 that there is an opinion that if one does not have a torch, they must light another candle specifically for Havdalah, aside from the candle designated to illuminate the house. However, we do not know the reason for this ruling. The Mordechai wrote the opposite, that if there is a candle in the house, one does not need to seek out a torch, and the custom follows our teacher the Beit Yosef. Additionally, the custom is that when there is no torch, one places candles next to each other, which is considered like a torch, and similarly, if there are two wicks in a candle close to each other, it is considered like a torch. One should not make a torch out of wood, as it is disgraceful, and sometimes they emit a tar-like smell which is repulsive. A wax torch is acceptable if the wicks are braided together, and this is the prevalent custom that should not be changed. (See Magen Avraham and Eliyah Rabbah)

One does not recite a blessing over the candle until benefiting from its light, meaning that one should be close enough to it to distinguish between the currency of this country and the currency of another country, which are similar in size but have different designs, requiring good recognition. The custom is to look at the palms of the hands and the nails. This is the wording of the Mordechai at the beginning of Yoma: "It is written in the responsa of the Geonim… and the reason we look at the nails is because one does not recite a blessing over the candle until benefiting from its light, until feeling the brightness of the Havdalah candle's light, and even though we recall the nails of the first man." And in Pirkei DeRabbi Eliezer (Chapter 20) it says: "He extends his hands to the fire's light and looks at his nails, which are whiter than the body, and says 'Blessed, etc.'"

And this is the language of the Tur: "One looks at their nails to see if they can benefit from it and to recognize the difference between one coin and another, just as one recognizes the difference between nail and flesh... And the early ones had the custom to look at the lines of the palms... because the lines on the palm of the hand are a sign for blessing. Additionally, we have the custom to look at the nails, and they say it is because they are fruitful and multiply forever." (And being fruitful and multiplying is a sign of blessing). And our Master the Rema wrote that one should look at the nails of the right hand and hold the cup in the left hand, and one should bend the fingers into the hand so that one sees the nails with the palms at the same time, and one should not look at the inner side of the fingers, end quote. And the thumb should be bent into the hand so that it is not seen outside, and the custom is to bend the fingers into the hand as mentioned, and then to stretch them out and look at them from behind (Magen Avraham section 5). And the customs of Israel are Torah, and they are based on the Zohar, and it appears that all these actions should be done only with the right hand and not with the left (and so it is written in Pri Etz Chaim there, and in Magen Avraham and in Shulchan Aruch HaRav).

And even though we do not require a light that rested, as we do on Yom Kippur, we still require a candle that was not used for a transgression, meaning it was not lit on Shabbat. It is not only if a Jew lit it, but even if a non-Jew lit it, which is permitted for him, still, since this light, if a Jew had lit it, would be a transgression, we do not recite a blessing over it, and even after the fact, one does not fulfill their obligation (Magen Avraham, subsection 6). However, a candle that was lit permissibly on Shabbat, such as for a dangerously ill person by a Jew, or for someone not in danger by a non-Jew, as well as for a woman in childbirth, when it was lit – we do recite a blessing over it, since there is no transgression here, and on the contrary, there is a mitzvah of saving a life. This is the difference from a candle lit by a non-Jew, where although there is no transgression, there is also no mitzvah. Any candle lit on Shabbat not for a mitzvah – we consider it a transgression, even though it is not actually a transgression, but rather concerning the candle itself, there is an element of transgression if a Jew had lit it. We do not recite a blessing over a candle lit for idol worship, even if it was lit from the previous day or was lit after Shabbat, because it is forbidden to derive benefit from it. Some say that if a non-Jew lit it for a sick person who is not in danger, it is considered as if it did not rest from a transgression, and only for a dangerously ill person is it permitted, whether lit by a Jew or a non-Jew; but for a sick person not in danger, if a non-Jew lit it – it is as if he lit it for himself (Elijah Rabba, subsection 10), and this is not definitive.

A non-Jew who lit a candle on Saturday night from a Jew's candle - one may recite a blessing over it, and this is obvious. Similarly, if a Jew lit a candle from a non-Jew's candle that was lit on Shabbat - one may recite a blessing over it, for although a transgression was committed with the first candle, nevertheless, now one blesses over the additional permissible light. However, in cases where a non-Jew lit from another non-Jew's candle - one does not bless over it, because we decree [against using it] due to the first candle, and since this is only a decree - it is permitted after the fact (Magen Avraham, sec. 11). And similarly, if a Jew lit a candle from an idolatrous candle - it is also permitted (ibid., sec. 8), and even though its flame is forbidden for benefit - this applies when it is attached to the coal and not when it is separated, for the flame has no substance. However, initially, it is forbidden to light from its flame, as it is prohibited to derive benefit from it. (See Magen Avraham, sec. 10, who wrote in the name of the "Me'orei Or" that a non-Jew who lit a candle for a sick person from his own bonfire - it is forbidden to bless over it, and similarly, if he kindled a fire on Saturday night from wood and stones - it is forbidden, and this is perplexing. However, even according to the Magen Avraham, it is permitted after the fact, and although the first ruling could be dismissed if a non-Jew lit from another non-Jew, in my humble opinion, if he lit it for a sick person it is different, but still, this can be said. But regarding the second ruling - I do not see any prohibition in it, and this seems to me from the words of the Tosafot, see there. And that which they said: 'If one was walking outside the city, if most of the inhabitants are non-Jews - it is forbidden,' this is because we are concerned they lit it before nightfall, but if it was lit at night - why should it be forbidden, and this requires further study. Pay careful attention to it.)

If one was walking outside of a city and saw a light that he could use, but he does not know whose light it is: if the majority of the city's inhabitants are not Jewish, one does not recite a blessing over it, because we suspect that it was kindled before nightfall, making it a lamp that was lit in violation (as explained earlier). However, if the majority are Jews, or even if it is half and half, one recites a blessing over it, because this is not a case where we require a majority specifically. Nevertheless, we do not apply the principle of "every established entity is considered as half and half" in the case of prohibitions to permit it even if the majority are not Jewish, because ultimately this light belongs to a non-Jew, and the principle of "established entity" does not help in this case. This law is not similar to other prohibitions. (See Magen Avraham 13 and what I have written there, which clarifies this.)

There is proof for this from the Jerusalem Talmud (Chapter 8 of Berachot), which states: "An alley that is entirely non-Jewish, and one Jew lives there, and a light comes out from it – one recites a blessing." The reason is that since he saw that the light came from there, it is certainly from the Jew, and we do not follow the majority in this case. Similarly, the reverse: an alley that is entirely Jewish, and one non-Jew lives there, and he saw that the light came from there – it is certainly from the non-Jew, and one does not recite a blessing over it. (The Eliyah Rabbah 17 writes that this contradicts our Talmud and enters into difficulties, as does the Taz, but in my humble opinion, the matters are clear, as this is not similar to other prohibitions, and see there.)

It is stated in Berachot (53b): If one was walking outside the city close to sunset on Shabbat, and saw someone walking with a candle in his hand: if the person walking is an adult, it is certain that he is not Jewish, and one does not recite a blessing on this light when it gets dark, for a Jew would not have kindled it during the day. But if the person walking is a child, one must investigate: if he is Jewish, one recites a blessing on it, and if he is not Jewish, one does not recite a blessing on it. All the decisors did not bring this ruling. (See Magen Avraham, subparagraph 13, who addressed this and offered a strained explanation. In my humble opinion, it seems they did well to omit it, for it is difficult to understand that even if the child is Jewish, how can one recite a blessing on it, since it was lit forbiddenly during the day. Rather, one must say it was a little before dark, and it is possible it was also night, except that it is not the way of Jews to light early. If so, who can determine such an exact measure? Therefore, the decisors omitted it.)

One recites a blessing over fire that comes from wood and stones, for Adam the first man blessed over this fire made from stones, as stated in Section 1. However, on the conclusion of Yom Kippur, one does not make a blessing over such fire, because at that time, the fire must have been kindled before Yom Kippur. Similarly, on the conclusion of Yom Kippur, one does not bless a candle lit by a Jew from a non-Jew, even though it is permitted on the conclusion of Shabbat as previously explained. Nevertheless, on Yom Kippur, the fire must specifically have been kindled before Yom Kippur, as will be explained in Siman 624.

Burning coals that are so hot that if one inserts a splinter among them it ignites—one recites a blessing on them when one can benefit from their light just like from a candle. But this only applies when they are meant to illuminate, for one does not recite a blessing on light that was kindled for another purpose, not to illuminate. Therefore, one does not recite a blessing on the light of a kiln at the beginning of the brick firing, since at that time it is intended for the bricks and not to illuminate. But after the bricks are fired, it is intended to illuminate, and one recites a blessing on it. The same applies in all similar cases, for since the blessing is for the light that illuminates for our needs, it must be such light.

Accordingly, one might question how we recite a blessing on the Havdalah candle, which is extinguished immediately after Havdalah, and it is not intended to illuminate but rather for the mitzvah of Havdalah. This is not the case, for on the contrary, since we make it for the mitzvah of Havdalah, our intention is necessarily for it to illuminate. Otherwise, we would not fulfill the obligation, and in truth, our intention is for it to illuminate at that moment, which is during Havdalah. Thus, during Havdalah, our intention is to illuminate, and this is its mitzvah.

The synagogue candle is not considered to be made for illumination, but rather for the honor of the synagogue, unless there is an important person there—in which case it is considered made for illumination, as it was lit to provide light for the important person. If there is no important person present, one does not recite a blessing over it. Some say the opposite: that if there is an important person present, one does not recite a blessing over it since it was made for his honor and not for illumination, and if there is no important person present, it is made for illumination and one recites a blessing over it. If there is an attendant in an adjacent room to the synagogue who eats there, and the room has a window to the synagogue, one recites a blessing over it since it provides light for the attendant, provided that the moon is not shining there, for when there is moonlight, he can eat by the light of the moon. It seems to me that nowadays one recites a blessing over synagogue candles, as it is known that their intention is to provide light for the people. Similarly, one does not recite a blessing over candles for the deceased or for grooms, since they are made for honor and not for illumination. This applies specifically to a case where, had they taken the deceased out during the day, they would have also lit a candle for his honor; in such a case, even at night, one does not recite a blessing. But if they would not have lit a candle for him during the day, one recites a blessing when he is taken out on the night after Shabbat with a candle. As for a groom, the candle is always for his honor, as is known, and in any case, one does not recite a blessing.

It is stated in the Gemara (there): They were sitting in the study hall and a flame was brought before them. Beit Shammai says each one blesses individually because of the disruption to the study hall, for if they all stop learning to hear the blessing from one person, they will be neglecting their Torah study. And Beit Hillel says one person blesses for everyone, because "in the multitude of people is the King's glory," for when they all respond "Amen" to the blessing of one, there is glory to the King. Therefore, they were not concerned with the disruption to the study hall. And it is understood that all the poskim (decisors of Jewish law) ruled according to Beit Hillel, for Beit Shammai in opposition to Beit Hillel is not considered. 

Based on this, it is perplexing regarding our custom, where there is no disruption to the study hall, and everyone listens to the Havdalah from the one who blesses, why for the blessing of "Borei Me'orei Ha'esh" ("Creator of the lights of the fire") the custom is that each one blesses individually, contrary to the words of Beit Hillel. And certainly, in our case, there is no issue of disrupting the study hall. And perhaps the custom was established according to the Tosefta in Berakhot, Chapter 5, where it is the opposite — Beit Shammai says one blesses for everyone, and Beit Hillel says each one blesses individually, as stated there. 

(And although according to the Tosefta, Beit Hillel only said this in the study hall, it is possible to say that they also always held this view, considering it similar to a blessing of enjoyment, where one does not fulfill the obligation for another, just as for the spices each one blesses. And even though for a blessing of enjoyment, when the one who blesses also benefits, he can fulfill the obligation for others, nevertheless, it is considered preferable this way. And the reason the Tosefta mentions "study hall" is because of Beit Shammai. In any case, it requires further investigation, since it is against the Gemara. And perhaps because our fire does not reach everyone at once, it would be considered an interruption.)

The Tur and the Shulchan Aruch wrote in Section 13 that a blind person does not recite the blessing 'Borei Me'orei Ha'esh' (Who creates the lights of fire) because he does not benefit from the light. This is not similar to the blessing 'Yotzer Ha'me'orot' (Who forms the luminaries) which the blind person recites, as stated in Siman 69, because it is not comparable at all, as we explained in Siman 263, Section 9. However, for the rest of the Havdalah, he must either recite the blessings or listen to them. The Rashba in his responsa (Siman 1379) wrote in the name of the Geonim that a blind person does not perform Havdalah at all but relies on the Havdalah in the prayer. This is not understood at all why he is exempt from the Havdalah over the cup. Perhaps the Geonim had a tradition that Havdalah over the cup was only instituted when there is also the blessing over the candle, and this requires further investigation. Therefore, there is reason to heed their words, and a blind person should not perform Havdalah himself but should listen to it from another.

It is stated in the Jerusalem Talmud (there): A candle within one's lap, or within a lantern, or within a glass lantern, one can see the flame but not use its light (if standing far away), or use its light but not see the flame (if standing from the side) – one does not recite a blessing over it until one can see the flame and use its light. And there was a question on the Rashba who wrote that a lantern is considered as seeing the flame, with a proof that seeing nakedness through a lantern prohibits reciting the Shema opposite it because of "and no nakedness shall be seen among you," as mentioned in Siman 75, but a lantern does not allow one to see the flame. And in my humble opinion, there is no difficulty at all, for a lantern is not a glass lantern, since a glass lantern is made of clear glass, and a lantern is a mirror, and this is explained at the end of Tractate Keilim. And a lantern is what they call a lamp. There are those where one can see the flame, such as those made of glass, and those where one cannot see the flame, such as those made of another material, and similarly with a mirror – sometimes one can see and sometimes not. And the Rashba is referring to a lantern where one cannot see the flame, while the Jerusalem Talmud is referring to one where one can see the flame, but a glass lantern always allows one to see. (And the Magen Avraham was forced to say that different matters were being stated, and see the Machatzit HaShekel there, but this is unnecessary, and examine it well). (The Arukh explained that a lantern is a lamp, see there).

It is forbidden to eat anything or drink wine or other beverages once it has become dark before making Havdalah. Even if one has recited Havdalah in the prayer, it is forbidden until one makes Havdalah over the cup, except for water, which has no significance at all and is permitted according to the law. The fact that we refrain from drinking even water is not actually a matter of law, but rather a custom explained in Siman 291 according to the Midrash, which states that this is the time when souls return to Gehinnom. But any food or drink is forbidden by the law of the Talmud, because the obligation of Havdalah applies to them. Even according to those who hold that Havdalah is of rabbinic origin, one is still obligated in Havdalah. The proof is that even according to those who say that Havdalah is of biblical origin, making Havdalah over the cup is certainly of rabbinic origin after one has recited it in the prayer, and still it is forbidden. Therefore, it is also forbidden according to those who hold that its primary obligation is rabbinic. Even in a case of doubt if it is dark, which is about half an hour before night, it is forbidden. One should not eat the third meal then, but before this time it is permitted. It is obvious that if one has not yet eaten the third meal, one must eat it even a little after sunset. (See Magen Avraham, Sec. 1, who writes that if one prayed Maariv while it was still daytime, it is forbidden to eat until one makes Havdalah. The Pri Megadim disagrees with this and writes that it is not comparable to Kiddush.)

Some people protest against large meals that begin close to nightfall on Shabbat, asserting that it is a definite prohibition (Bach and Magen Avraham). However, there are those who permit it, arguing that the prohibition only applies when it is definitively night (Taz, section 1). One of the great authorities cited the Piskei Tosafot, which stated that a pious person should be cautious about eating when it is uncertain if night has fallen, but one should not object to others who do so (Elya Rabbah, section 5). This also seems to be implied by the words of the Rambam in Chapter 29, Law 5, where he wrote: "Once the day has ended, it is forbidden to eat, drink, perform work, or taste anything until one has made Havdalah." Thus, it is only once the day has ended that it is forbidden. Additionally, since the comparison is made to work, which certainly does not apply before nightfall, it is clear. Therefore, in pressing circumstances, one may be lenient until it is definitively night. However, ideally, one should certainly be careful not to come to this situation and should begin eating at least during sunset. They will be blessed for this.

And this applies to starting a meal, but if one was already sitting at a meal before nightfall, and their meal extended for several hours into the darkness, they do not need to stop eating or drinking. This is not similar to the eve of Shabbat, where one must stop when it becomes dark, spread a cloth, and make Kiddush, as stated in Siman 271. On the contrary, just as on the eve of Shabbat one must stop for the honor of Shabbat, so too, for the honor of Shabbat, one does not need to stop once it has become dark. Not only that, but it is even forbidden to stop, as it appears like one is dismissing the king. It is stated in the Mechilta: "Guard it upon its departure" – like a person who does not want his friend to leave him. This is what they said in Pesachim (105b), that Shabbat establishes [the obligation] for Kiddush but not for Havdalah.

And this is the opinion of the Rambam there and the Rosh there, and so also wrote Rashi, Rashbam, and Tosafot (there 99:), and nevertheless, the Semag wrote that it appears from the Rif that this applies specifically in a case of doubt about darkness and not in definite darkness, and in definite darkness, one must stop and make Havdalah. This was also written by the Ba'al Ha'itur. And there are those who were concerned with their words, and it was written about the Maharshal of blessed memory that he stopped a wedding feast and went to the synagogue to pray and returned to the feast (Magen Avraham, subsection 2). And this is the opinion of the "yesh omrim" brought in the Shulchan Aruch, and this is its language: "And there are those who say that this matter applies in a case of doubt about darkness, but in definite darkness, even if he was sitting and eating, he spreads a cloth and makes Havdalah and then completes his meal." End of quote. But the main ruling according to the law is like the first opinion, which is the view of the majority of the poskim, and this is how the world practices, and so ruled our teacher the Rema.

And this is when they are sitting in a meal. But if he was sitting and drinking, or even if many were sitting and drinking and it became dark—they need to stop, for this is not considered a fixed meal, even if they are eating fruits and delicacies. It appears to me that even if they are eating foods made from grain, it is not considered a fixed meal, for if it were a fixed meal, they would need to wash their hands and recite the blessing of 'Hamotzi'. And since they did not do so, their eating is considered casual, and they need to stop.

If one began [a meal] in a prohibited manner, meaning if he sat down to eat after nightfall, it is obvious that he must interrupt for Havdalah, even if he has already recited the Shema. For if not, he must interrupt for the Shema even before nightfall if he began eating half an hour before nightfall, as stated in Siman 235. There is an opinion that this only applies to those who hold that Havdalah is a Torah obligation, but for those who hold that Havdalah is Rabbinic and one began eating, there is no need to interrupt, as with all matters that are Rabbinic (Magen Avraham 2). However, it does not seem correct to say so, for Havdalah is not like other matters, since it was specifically instituted at the beginning of the night, one is obligated to interrupt even if it is Rabbinic (the Alter Rebbe in the Kuntres Achron), and this is the primary ruling. However, if one began close to nightfall, since there are those who permit it as stated in section 2, he does not interrupt. But concerning the Shema, if he has not yet recited it, it seems that he must interrupt, therefore at the very least he should recite the Shema at his table.

Rabbeinu, the Beit Yosef, wrote in paragraph 2: "If they were drinking and said, 'Come, let us recite Havdalah,' if they want to continue drinking before reciting Havdalah, they do not need to recite a new blessing. However, there is an opinion that disagrees." This is his exact wording. It is not understood, for it has been clarified that one is required to stop drinking. However, in truth, this is not the issue here. The primary discussion here is about the blessing, and the first opinion follows the Rambam in Chapter 4 of Blessings. Even though regarding Kiddush, in similar cases when they said, 'Come, let us recite Kiddush,' it is considered an interruption, and they must recite a new blessing, as mentioned in Siman 271. Nevertheless, this is not the case with Havdalah. The reason is that just as Kiddush is stringent in terms of when the time arrives, one must cover the table and recite Kiddush, even if they are in the middle of a meal, whereas this is not the case with Havdalah. Similarly, regarding their saying: in Kiddush, it constitutes an interruption, and they must recite a new blessing if they wish to continue drinking, but not in Havdalah. The one who disagrees is the Raavad there, who holds that once they said, 'Come, let us recite Havdalah,' the obligation of Havdalah takes effect on them just like Kiddush, and they must recite a new blessing. This distinction applies specifically when there is no saying, because Shabbat establishes itself, not Havdalah. But when they said it, they willingly established the obligation of Havdalah at that moment. And if you ask, even without this, they are required to stop for Havdalah, it can be explained that this refers to when they said it before it became dark in a manner that they were still permitted to drink, and by saying it, it became prohibited, or they were in the middle of a meal, or they are indeed doing something wrong in this matter. (See Beit Yosef, Magen Avraham section 5, and Taz section 3)

When sitting at a meal and one wishes to interrupt to perform Havdalah in the middle of the meal before the evening prayer (Maariv) - one can perform Havdalah. If wine was already drunk beforehand, there is no need to recite the blessing "Borei Peri HaGafen" (Creator of the fruit of the vine) again on the Havdalah cup, as Havdalah is not considered an interruption, similar to how Kiddush is not considered an interruption in such cases, as written in Siman 271. However, there is an opinion that Havdalah is considered an interruption. The primary view is the first one, that the dissenting opinion holds it is necessary to interrupt as we wrote in Section 4, and therefore it automatically becomes an interruption. Even though for Kiddush it is necessary to interrupt according to all opinions, and nevertheless one does not recite "Borei Peri HaGafen" as written there, this is because Kiddush requires a meal, which is not the case with Havdalah. However, in practice, since we do not follow that opinion, as written in Section 4, therefore also here in practice we hold that it is not necessary to recite the blessing. This applies when they are sitting at the meal, but when they were only drinking and wished to make Havdalah, since we hold that they are obligated to interrupt, as written in Section 5, it follows that they need to recite the blessing "Borei Peri HaGafen" again on the Havdalah cup (this is according to the words of the Taz, Siman 4). There is an opinion that even when they were engaged in drinking - there is no need to bless, because Havdalah is not considered an interruption at all (Beit Hillel). There is another opinion that even if they were engaged in a meal - they need to bless, because Havdalah is worse as it has no connection to the meal at all (Magen Avraham, Siman 6). In my humble opinion, the primary view is the first one, and it is good to be cautious not to come to such a situation. In truth, we are not accustomed to this, rather we finish the meal, pray Maariv, and then perform Havdalah. However, if necessity compels one to perform Havdalah in the middle of the meal, one should not bless "Borei Peri HaGafen" on the Havdalah cup. (The Magen Avraham himself seems somewhat uncertain about this, and it is also clarified from the Eliyah Rabbah and the Turei Zahav that this is the main practical ruling).

When one was sitting at a meal, and we said that he does not need to interrupt, and he finished his meal—he can bless over the cup and drink from it. And even though after the Grace After Meals it is forbidden to drink—nevertheless, the cup of the Grace After Meals belongs to the meal, and it is permitted for him to drink it. However, this is when he always blesses over the cup—it becomes for him like part of the meal itself, but if he always blesses without the cup—then now too he should not drink from it (Magen Avraham, subsection 7). And this is when it is already night, but if it is still before night, even though it is after sunset and close to twilight—he is obligated to drink it in any case. However, if he does not have another cup for Havdalah—in any case, he should not drink it, rather he should bless over the cup and then make Havdalah over it, whether he makes Havdalah immediately or after the prayer. But if he has another cup for Havdalah—certainly he should drink it as explained, and make Havdalah over another cup (this is the explanation of what is stated in Shulchan Aruch, section 4, see there).

Our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in Section 7: "If one recites Havdalah over wine at his table, even if he performed Havdalah before washing his hands, it exempts the wine consumed during the meal from requiring a blessing. And some say it does not exempt unless he washed his hands before performing Havdalah," end quote. And our master, the Rema, wrote: "And if he first performed Havdalah, he must recite the 'Me'ein Shalosh' blessing afterward," end quote. 

Then, in Section 8, our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote: "When the wine consumed during the meal is exempt from requiring a blessing, there is also no need to recite a final blessing over the Havdalah cup. And if he has only one cup and expects more wine to be brought, and he performed Havdalah over that cup, and subsequently no more wine was brought and he recited the Birkat Hamazon without a cup, there is an opinion that he must recite a final blessing over the Havdalah cup," end quote. These matters require clarification.

And this is its explanation: It has already been clarified in Siman 174 that wine before the meal exempts the wine during the meal. Therefore, if one wants to eat immediately after Havdalah, the wine of Havdalah exempts the wine during the meal, and just because there is also a mitzvah involved, it does not degrade it. However, there are those who say that it certainly degrades it. On weekdays, when one drinks by choice, it is indeed called wine before the meal and exempts the wine during the meal. But Havdalah, which one is compelled to perform, has no connection to the meal at all and is not similar to Kiddush, which is only in the context of a meal. Therefore, it is their opinion that only if one has washed their hands before performing Havdalah does it exempt the wine during the meal, but if one has not washed their hands, it does not exempt it. And this is what our teacher, the Rema, says: Consequently, since it does not exempt it, one is obligated to recite the final blessing on the Havdalah cup, since it has no connection to the meal.
