But according to the first opinion, which exempts it, no final blessing is needed, and these are the words of our teacher, the Beit Yosef, in section 8.

And afterwards, he says: "And if he has only one cup, etc." and this is its interpretation: That even according to the first opinion which holds that the wine of Havdalah is like the wine before the meal, which exempts the wine within the meal and therefore does not require a final blessing as mentioned, there is still a distinction between it and the wine before the meal. For the wine before the meal, it is clarified in Siman 174 that it does not require a final blessing in any case, whether he drank wine during the meal or not, and whether he blessed over the cup or did not bless. But the wine of Havdalah is not exempt from a final blessing unless he had wine during the meal or blessed over the cup. Otherwise, he is obligated in a final blessing. It is also not similar to Kiddush, which is exempt in any case, as mentioned in Siman 271. The reasoning is that the wine before the meal, which comes for the purpose of opening the digestive organs, or the wine of Kiddush, where there is no Kiddush except in the place of the meal, the Grace After Meals exempts them in any case. However, the wine of Havdalah, which does not come to open the digestive organs, and also has no connection to the meal - how would the Grace After Meals exempt it from a final blessing? Rather, if he drinks wine during the meal, since it exempts it from the initial blessing, as explained, it also exempts the wine within the meal from a final blessing, and it is considered as one wine. Or even if he did not have wine during the meal but blessed over the cup, when he blesses the final blessing over the cup of the Grace After Meals, it automatically exempts it as well. But if neither of these applies, he is certainly obligated in a final blessing.

Therefore, if one knows that he will not have wine during the meal, nor will he have a cup for the Grace After Meals, it is obvious that he must recite the final blessing immediately. However, if he thought he would have wine during the meal or for the cup of blessing and did not recite the final blessing, and afterwards it turned out that he did not have it and did not drink during the meal and also recited the Grace After Meals without a cup, therefore, this is what our master the Beit Yosef wrote: Some say that he must now also recite the final blessing over the Havdalah cup. He wrote in the language "there are those who say" because there is a reasoning to say that since he initially thought he would have it and now it has changed, we might say that since he did not bless at the time until the Grace After Meals, the Grace After Meals exempts it in retrospect. The teaching comes to inform us that there are those who say that even in such cases, he needs to bless. (See Magen Avraham section 10 who raised a difficulty from the four cups, and I do not understand, for this is like Kiddush as the Taz wrote in section 7, and in Taz section 6 there are some printing errors, and scrutinize).

Our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in Section 9: "If one wishes to eat immediately after Havdalah, one must be careful not to bring bread to the table before Havdalah. If he did bring it, he should cover it with a cloth, since it is mentioned earlier in the verse, and it should be given precedence unless it is covered." This is difficult to understand. It makes sense with Kiddush, where one can sanctify over bread, so there is a notion of embarrassment. But with Havdalah, where one cannot perform Havdalah over bread, what embarrassment is there? We must say that this itself is the embarrassment, that it is not possible to perform Havdalah over bread, and wine now takes precedence over it (Taz, subsection 8 and Magen Avraham, subsection 12). There is proof of this from the morning meal, where we also do not sanctify over bread, yet the bread must still be covered with a cloth, as written at the beginning of Chapter 289. However, on Shabbat, there is another reason, as a remembrance of the manna, as written in Chapter 271. But we primarily hold the reason of embarrassment, and proof of this is that during the third meal, we do not cover the bread, as written in Chapter 291, end of Section 10.

It is established for us in Pesachim (107a): "If one has tasted [food], one can still recite Havdalah." In other words, even though it is forbidden to eat before Havdalah, nevertheless, if one forgot and ate, or even if one ate deliberately, Havdalah is not forfeited, but rather one recites Havdalah afterward. And furthermore, we say there: that one who did not recite Havdalah on Saturday night can continue to recite it until the end of Tuesday, for these three days are connected to the past Shabbat. But from then onward, one should not recite Havdalah, this is the version of Rashi, Rashbam, and Tosafot, and so wrote the Rambam in chapter 29 there. But the version of the Geonim that the Tur brings is: only on Sunday until nightfall can one recite Havdalah, and not afterward, and this is also the version of the Rif. However, in front of us in the Rif, the matter is puzzling, for first he wrote 'all day,' and at the end of his words he wrote 'until Tuesday,' see there.

It is obvious that on the next day or until Tuesday, one only recites the blessings "Borei Peri HaGafen" and "HaMavdil," but not the blessing over spices nor the blessing over the fire, as these are only relevant on the night following Shabbat. Additionally, it is written in the "Ba'al Halachot Gedolot" that the statement "someone who tasted food - separates" applies when one performs Havdalah on the night following Shabbat. But if one performs Havdalah the next day, it only applies if one has not tasted food; however, if one has tasted food, one does not perform Havdalah the next day, and certainly not until Tuesday according to our version. The Tur challenges this, asking what the difference is, and in my humble opinion, it seems that the Ba'al Halachot Gedolot holds that if one has nothing with which to perform Havdalah on the night following Shabbat, one is permitted to eat. And since we find in the Gemara that Amemar, when he did not have anything for Havdalah, fasted until the next day, why did he do so? It must be because if he had eaten, he would not have been able to perform Havdalah the next day. One could explain the reason that it is not understood why on Sunday, and even more so on Monday and Tuesday, one would say "HaMavdil Bein Kodesh Lechol," as the sanctity has already departed and it has long been a weekday. However, if one refrains from eating due to Havdalah, it is considered for him until now as a sort of sanctity in this matter, because the past sanctity prevented him from eating. But if he ate, what relevance does it have to say now "HaMavdil Bein Kodesh Lechol," as on the night following Shabbat, one says it about the time, but on Sunday, the time has already passed. Nevertheless, the main ruling is as our teacher the Rema ruled in paragraph 6 according to the first opinion, that one can perform Havdalah until Tuesday even if one tasted food, as this is the opinion of most authorities. Regarding whether one is allowed to eat before performing Havdalah the next day, this is explained in Siman 296, see there in paragraph 14.

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote: One who fasts for three days and three nights should hear Havdalah from others. If there is no one else with him, he may perform Havdalah during the day on Shabbat and drink, and then accept the fast upon himself afterward. This means that if he fasts for one or two days and has no one from whom to hear Havdalah, he can perform Havdalah after the fast on the third day. But when he fasts for three days, the time has passed, and he is compelled to perform Havdalah during the day. However, even if he only fasts for one day, if he begins the fast from the night of Motza'ei Shabbat and has someone from whom to hear Havdalah on Motza'ei Shabbat, it is better to hear it at its proper time than to perform it himself after the fast, and this is simple. (And so it is written in Eliyah Rabbah, section 11) One should not ask that since he performed Havdalah he has accepted the fast upon himself, as this applies to an obligatory fast and not to a fast that he has taken upon himself in this manner (Magen Avraham, section 9). This is specifically when he has taken upon himself to fast from the beginning of the night, but generally, the fast does not start from the evening, as we follow the common language of people, and in common language, a fast is only from morning until evening.

And one who fasts for two consecutive days from the conclusion of the holy Sabbath until Monday evening, if he did not hear Havdalah, he must recite Havdalah then as mentioned. If Rosh Hashanah occurs at that time, he should not recite Kiddush and Havdalah over the same cup, for we do not recite two sanctifications over one cup. This is not similar to when a festival falls on the conclusion of the Sabbath, for there it is considered one sanctification, as in Havdalah we say 'between holy and holy,' but not in the case of Havdalah for a weekday with Kiddush for a festival. Therefore, he should recite Kiddush over one cup and then Havdalah over another cup. If he does not have wine, he should recite Kiddush over bread, eat, and then recite Havdalah over beer. Even though it is forbidden to eat before Havdalah, in this case it is unavoidable, or he may also recite both Kiddush and Havdalah over beer. It is better to hear Kiddush from someone else and then recite Havdalah (there).

It is forbidden to perform work before Havdalah. Thus, our Sages said in Shabbat (150b): "A person is forbidden to attend to his affairs before he performs Havdalah." If one has recited Havdalah in the prayer, it is not necessary to perform Havdalah over a cup of wine in order to perform work, and he is permitted to work even before performing Havdalah over the cup. If one needs to perform work before the prayer, he should say: "He who distinguishes between holy and secular" without a blessing. This is the opinion of Rashi there, as it is merely a matter of recognition. The opinion of the Rosh is that one should say it with a blessing, that is, "Blessed are You, Hashem, who distinguishes between holy and secular." This is also explicitly stated in the Ba'al HaMaor, and the Rosh also opines that even if one has recited Havdalah in the prayer and wants to perform work, he must recite the blessing "Blessed are You, Hashem, who distinguishes between holy and secular." However, the custom of the world follows Rashi in both aspects: without mentioning the name of Hashem and if one has recited Havdalah in the prayer, nothing further is required. And our master the Beit Yosef in section 10 only brought Rashi's opinion, since this is the custom and it is a rabbinic matter, and also because mentioning the name of Hashem might be in vain. Therefore, one should not protest if the custom follows Rashi (Beit Yosef). On a festival that falls on the night after Shabbat, one says: "He who distinguishes between holy and holy" (Magen Avraham section 13), but regarding eating, there is no permission until one performs Havdalah over the cup (there).

And we should instruct the women who do not pray Maariv and do not say "Ata Chonantanu," and before the Havdalah over the cup they perform work, that they should say: "Hamavdil bein Kodesh lechol" (He who distinguishes between holy and secular). It appears that most of our women are not careful about this and light the fire at night before Havdalah. It can be said that they rely on what our teacher Rabbi Moses Isserles (the Rema) wrote in section 10, that some say all this applies to significant work, such as writing and weaving, but lighting a candle or carrying from one domain to another does not require this (saying "Hamavdil"). From this, the custom has spread to be lenient and light candles immediately when the congregation says "Barechu." However, the primary opinion is as the first opinion, end quote. But there is no reason to differentiate between light work and heavy work.

It appears to me that the reason for this opinion is because, ostensibly, there is no reason for this statement, and why is it necessary to say "He who separates between holy and secular," for it is already nighttime. Rather, the reason is that since the Torah required separation, as it is written: "to distinguish between the holy and the secular," and it is stated in "Remember" - "and you shall remember," from which we learn the requirement of separation, as it is written at the beginning of Siman 296, we see that the Torah required verbal separation and to say "He who separates between holy and secular." This is the reason of the Baal HaMaor and the Rosh, who required a blessing with God's name, as written in section 19, because this is a scriptural decree or an allusion. Indeed, according to them, there is no difference between one type of work and another. However, according to us, who follow Rashi, who does not require [mentioning God's] name, we must understand, for this is not a blessing at all. We must say that according to this opinion, the Torah's requirement of separation is not because without it work would be forbidden, but rather it is a commandment in itself, that the Torah commanded us to remember the sanctity of Shabbat at its entrance and exit. But the Sages said that since the Torah required separation, we too must make some noticeable sign even in work, not because of prohibition but to pay attention to remember some form of separation. Therefore, saying "Blessed" without God's name is sufficient, since it is merely for recognition as explained by Rashi, and thus paying attention and recognition only applies to work that is noticeable as labor, and not to something that is merely called work. This is to settle the custom. However, it is certainly more proper that every head of the household should teach in his home that when lighting the candle, they should first say "He who separates between holy and secular."

It is mentioned in the Jerusalem Talmud (Chapter "Makom Shenahagu," Halacha 1): "Those women who have the custom not to do work on the night following Shabbat – it is not a proper custom," meaning it is not a correct custom because there is no reason for it. "Until the order of the prayers is completed – it is a proper custom," meaning until they complete the prayer – it is a valid custom not to do work. And concerning this, our Talmud says: "One who does work on the night following Shabbat does not see a sign of blessing" (Tosafot there). There are those who wrote that women have the custom not to do any work the entire night following Shabbat (Magen Avraham, section 16), but we have not heard of this custom, which contradicts the Jerusalem Talmud. Our women only refrain from work until after the Havdalah, and afterward, they perform all types of work, and this is the main practice.

And know that in the Zohar Bereishit in the introduction (page 14b), it lists three things that someone who does them causes harm to themselves. It says there: "The third is one who lights a candle at the conclusion of Shabbat before the Jewish people reach the sanctity of the prayer service, for this causes the fire of Gehinnom to ignite within that fire before its proper time." And it says there that those who are punished in Gehinnom curse him who lights the candle before its time. (The Magen Avraham in section 17 mentions this Zohar, stating not to light the candle until after one has made Havdalah over the cup. However, this is not accurate, as the wording of the Zohar is as mentioned, but later he writes in the wording of the Magen Avraham. This is perplexing, as one needs to light the candle for Havdalah, and this issue has already been addressed in the margins of the Zohar in the path of truth. Refer there for the resolution. In my humble opinion, it appears that what is written later "until one makes Havdalah over the cup" means up to but not including, which means after the sanctity service, where one immediately performs the Havdalah by law. Study this well.)

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote that some say to draw water every Saturday night, because Miriam's well circles all the wells every Saturday night, and whoever encounters it and drinks from it will be healed of all his ailments. However, I have not seen this custom. Refer above to Siman 263 regarding one who adds from the weekday to the holy day, if it is permissible to tell someone else to do work for him after he has made Havdalah — the conclusion is that it is permissible, and he is allowed to benefit from that work. In Siman 295 it is explained that they say the verses "And He shall give you," and "Elijah the Prophet," and the "Ribon" of the Jerusalem Talmud.

It is stated in the Gemara (119b): "A person should always set his table on Motza'ei Shabbat (Saturday night), even if he only needs an olive-sized portion. Hot water on Motza'ei Shabbat is a remedy, and hot bread on Motza'ei Shabbat is a remedy. Rabbi Abbahu would prepare a third-born calf for Motza'ei Shabbat and would eat from its kidney. When his son Avimi grew up, he said to him, 'Why do you need to waste so much? Let's leave the kidney from Friday.' He left it, and a lion came and ate it." Thus concludes the Gemara.

The reason for this meal, the Rambam wrote in Chapter 30, is to honor the Sabbath upon its entrance and exit, meaning that it is like escorting the king with a dignified meal. Therefore, this meal is called "Melaveh Malkah" (escorting the queen). Hence, it is customary to recite poems and songs to accompany the Sabbath, just as one would escort a king at his entrance and exit (Beit Yosef). Therefore, it is proper to recite the songs after Havdalah (Taz). And the sages have written that there is one organ in a person called "neskui," and some say "luz," which does not benefit from any food except from the eating at the end of the Sabbath to accompany the Sabbath (Levush). From it, man was created. When one dies, this bone does not disintegrate; even if it is put in fire, it does not burn, in a mill, it is not ground, and with a hammer, it does not break. From it, the person will be revived in the time of resurrection, and its root and essence are from the bone of the heavens (Ateres Rosh in the name of Matta Melech).

Many are not careful with this meal, but one who fulfills it receives great reward. All God-fearing individuals strive to fulfill it and eat an olive-sized portion. It is proper for one who can eat meat to do so; if not, one should eat fish, which is also considered an important food, or good fruits if he has them. He should eat them with bread, and one who cannot eat bread at all should fulfill it with other foods and fruits. If one extends the third meal into the night and eats an olive-sized portion at night, he can also fulfill the Melaveh Malkah meal (A.R.). And it is explained in Tosafot Shabbat (118: D.H. Veha) that even a poor person traveling from place to place should be given a meal on Saturday night, see there.

The Maharil had a special tallit for Shabbat, and he would fold it every Saturday night in order to engage in a mitzvah immediately (Magen Avraham). It is also customary to fold the tallitot on Saturday night. It is customary to drink hot beverages on Saturday night as it is considered medicinal, as mentioned in paragraph 1. One should be careful not to make any signs on Saturday night for someone who seeks a loan or charity, saying, "It is Saturday night" as this is not a good sign and transgresses the prohibition of "do not practice divination" (Sanhedrin 66a), and it is considered one of the practices of the Amorites as stated in the Tosefta of Shabbat, chapter 8. Therefore, it is forbidden to say such things, and you should be wholehearted, etc.

Carrying from a private domain to a public domain is one of the primary categories of work and was present in the Mishkan (Tabernacle), for one is only liable for a type of work that was done in the Mishkan, as stated in siman 242. Besides its presence in the Mishkan, it is explicitly mentioned in the Torah, as it is written: "And Moses commanded, and they caused it to be proclaimed throughout the camp, saying: 'Let neither man nor woman make any more work for the offering of the sanctuary.' So the people were restrained from bringing" (Exodus 36:6). This implies that bringing is considered work (Rambam, Chapter 12). And there, it involved carrying from a private domain to a public domain, as Moses was sitting in the Levite camp, which was a public domain, because all of Israel would gather there, and he told the Israelites: Do not bring from your private domain to my public domain (beginning of the chapter "Hazorek" (Shabbat 96b)). And although for all other types of work we do not need to find explicit mention in the Torah, since they were in the Mishkan, they are included in "you shall not do any work." However, since carrying is considered a lesser form of work, for the object itself does not change, only its location changes, and all other types of work involve a change in the object itself, therefore, if the Torah had not explicitly revealed that it is considered work, we would not know that it is (Tosafot, beginning of Shabbat, s.v. "Pashat"). And in Jeremiah (17:22), it is also explained that it is considered work, as stated in siman 242, see there.

Our Sages said (there) that carrying out is considered a principal labor, and bringing in from a public domain to a private domain is considered a derivative. It is surprising regarding the Rambam who wrote there that both carrying out and bringing in are principal labors. Additionally, one who throws from a public domain to a private domain, or from a private domain to a public domain, is liable, as it is considered a derivative of carrying out (there). And one who transfers four cubits in a public domain or throws - this is a law given to Moses at Sinai that it is included in carrying out (there), and it is also considered a derivative. There is also one who hands over from a private domain to a private domain through a public domain when they are on the same level, which is also considered a derivative of carrying out, and it will be explained in section 346, with G-d's help. The liability for a public domain is only up to ten handbreadths from the ground, except for handing over, and it will be explained there.

And one who takes out, brings in, throws, or transfers is not liable until the object that he took out has the specified measure, as will be explained. Similarly, he is not liable until he himself performs both the uprooting and the placing down, and he takes the entire object into the public domain. Therefore, a basket that is full of items, even if it is full of mustard seeds, and he takes out most of it from one domain to another - he is exempt until he takes out the entire basket. The same applies to anything similar, because the outer vessel makes all that is inside it into one single entity, and it is considered as one object. This is what the Gemara says (91b): 'The binding of a vessel is considered a binding,' meaning the outer vessel binds all of them to be as one. Similarly, if he stops in the middle in an exempt area, he is exempt. This is what we learned in the Mishnah (there): "One who takes out food and places it on the threshold of a karmelit, and then takes it out again - he is exempt, because he did not perform the labor in one go."

And likewise, one is not liable until he carries out or throws in the usual manner. But if he does so in an unusual manner, meaning not in the usual way, he is exempt. How so? If one carries out whether with his right hand, his left hand, in his lap, that is, in some garment placed in his lap, or in pillows sewn into garments called "keshenah," or if he goes out with money or another item wrapped in his cloth, he is liable, because he carried out in the usual manner. Similarly, one who carries on his shoulder is liable, even though the shoulder is above ten handbreadths in the public domain, because this was the burden of the sons of Kehat, as it is written: "They shall carry on the shoulder" (Numbers 7:9), and all the labors we learn from the Tabernacle. And in the Jerusalem Talmud (Chapter 10), it is explained regarding the verse: "And the charge of Eleazar… the oil for the light, etc." (Numbers 4:16) - one oil in the right hand and one oil in the left hand, the incense in his lap, and the meal-offering on his shoulder (Rashi 92a).

However, if one carries in an unusual manner, meaning that he placed an object on the back of his hand, which is the side where the nails are, and carried it out, or with his foot or with his mouth an object that is not food, or with his elbow which is the 'alnavagan', where he bends his arm and places an object in it and carries it out, or in his ear - where he inserts the object into his ear or places it on his ear, or in his hair - where he ties the object in his hair and carries it out, or in a pocket sewn into his garment with the opening of the pocket facing down, yet the object does not fall because the opening of the pocket is narrow. And the Rambam wrote regarding a pocket: "sewn into his garment, with the opening of the pocket facing down between the garment and within the opening of his garment" end quote, or in his shoe or sandal or socks - he is exempt because he did not carry it out in the usual manner. All these are exempt from a Torah prohibition but are forbidden by Rabbinic decree, as all exemptions on Shabbat are exempt but forbidden. See section 99.

The Gemara states there: "One who carries a load on his head is exempt," and from Rashi there it is implied that this is specifically when he is not holding the load with his hands, but if he is holding it with his hands, he is liable. The Rambam there writes: "One who carries a load on his head, if it is a heavy load such as a full sack or a box and the like, which he places on his head and holds with his hand, he is liable, for this is the usual manner of carrying, and it is considered as if he carried it on his shoulder or in his hand. But if he took a light object, such as placing a garment or a book or a knife on his head and carried it out, and he is not holding it with his hand, he is exempt, for he did not carry it in the usual manner, as most people do not carry objects placed on their heads." And this is like the words of Rashi. His intention is not that for a light load, if he holds it with his hand he is liable, for then he would contradict the beginning where he requires specifically a heavy load, but rather he is speaking in the usual manner, that a light load is not held with the hands, and Rashi's intention must also be understood this way (and this is evident from the Maimonides Commentary, see there and understand well). However, I am puzzled, for if so, with regard to carrying on the shoulders, it should also be distinguished this way, as it is known that on the shoulders only heavy loads are carried. And it also seems from the Jerusalem Talmud, where Rabbi Yosi questions: "From now on, if one carried a dried fig on his shoulder, is he liable?" And it is in a questioning tone. And it is explicitly implied in the Mishnah there that carrying on the shoulder is similar to carrying in the hand and is liable in any case, and this requires further investigation. (And it must be said that the Jerusalem Talmud indeed questions this, as it is evident from the Mishnah that it is similar to carrying in the hand, and it is not the usual manner to carry a small load on the shoulder. And it answers that we learn from Eliezer, but even in its answer there seems to be a deficiency, as the text there is not as Rashi wrote in the Mishnah that we brought in section 4, and it does not consider at all what is on the shoulder, and similarly in the Midrash Bamidbar at the end of chapter 4, see there and understand well).

There are many laws regarding carrying out, in terms of the acts of lifting and placing and the domains, and all of them will be explained with God's help in Siman 347 because that is their place. Here, we need to explain the measurements for carrying out, which Rambam explained in Chapter 18, and what are the measurements for carrying out on Shabbat. And it's not only carrying out, as the same applies to bringing in, transferring, throwing, and handing over, but since carrying out is the primary labor, all of them are included under its name, but they all share the same law.

And this is the wording of the Rambam there: "One who transfers an item from a private domain to a public domain or from a public domain to a private domain is not liable until he transfers an amount that is useful for something. And these are the measures of transfer: one who transfers edible food - the measure is the volume of a dried fig, and they combine with each other, provided that the volume is the size of a dried fig from the food itself, excluding the peels, seeds, stems, bran, and coarse bran." End quote. Even those peels that are eaten with the fruit, such as lentil peels and the peels of all tree fruits - nevertheless, we require something significant. After all, people also eat bran and coarse bran when mixed with flour, and they combine for the measure of challah, as mentioned in Yoreh Deah, Siman 324. However, regarding Shabbat, they do not combine for this reason, and so it is (Gemara at the end of the chapter "Klal Gadol"). This is precisely the reason why we require the volume of a dried fig and not the volume of an olive as in all other Torah measures, because we require something significant, and a dried fig is larger than an olive. All the measures are a tradition from Moses at Sinai (and hinted at in the verse "a land of wheat and barley, etc.," and a fig is like a dried fig for the transfer on Shabbat as stated at the beginning of Eruvin, and it is larger than an olive as proven in "Hamatznia," 91a. We have not precisely determined the measure of a dried fig, see Tosafot Eruvin 80b, s.v. 'Agav').

He also wrote: "A quarter of a quarter (of a log), and if it is congealed - an olive's bulk," end quote. The reason is that it is taught: One who takes out wine - enough for mixing a cup of blessing, which is a quarter (of a log), and all wine carries with it three parts water, and therefore a quarter (of a quarter) is sufficient. And even though the three parts water are not present, in any case, since the main importance is the wine and the water is not considered with respect to the wine, and on Shabbat we only need something significant - therefore a quarter (of a quarter) is sufficient (Gemara Avodah Zarah). And I am amazed, how could Rambam state this plainly, for this applies only to the wine of their days, but our wines do not take in so much water. Therefore, in truth, the Tanna taught: 'for mixing,' meaning each wine according to its measure of mixing, and our wines which do not accept mixing at all - need a full quarter (of a log). And in the Gemara where Rav Nachman said: 'A cup of blessing - it needs to have in it a quarter (of a quarter of a log) etc.' - he was talking about the wines of his time, but how did Rambam rule plainly with a quarter (of a quarter of a log), it is difficult to understand. And that it congeals to an olive's bulk - because the quarter (of a log) when congealed will amount to an olive's bulk (Gemara there), and why is a full quarter (of a log) needed here - because Kiddush does not accept mixing (Rashi there).

Furthermore, it is written: "The milk of a kosher animal - the amount needed for a gulp, and the milk of a non-kosher animal - the amount needed to apply to one eye. Human milk and egg white - the amount needed to mix into a salve, oil - the amount needed to anoint a small toe of a day-old infant, dew - the amount needed to mix with eye salve. And eye salve - the amount needed to mix with water, and water - the amount needed to wash the surface of a mortar. Honey - the amount needed to apply to the head of a wound, blood and all other liquids and all pourable substances - a quarter-log." End quote. (Non-kosher milk is mentioned in the Jerusalem Talmud there). The measure 'the amount needed for a gulp' is not specified, and some say it is a mouthful, but it does not seem that way in Yoma (80a), although it is more than a dried fig's bulk (Tosafot there). And regarding what is written: 'water - the amount needed to wash the surface of a mortar,' ostensibly this contradicts the Mishnah which states: 'water - to mix with eye salve,' but the Jerusalem Talmud there explains that this refers to dew water, but plain water - the amount needed to wash the surface of a mortar. And the Jerusalem Talmud says 'to rinse,' and it is all the same. And although our Talmud does not indicate this, as it says there (78a) that drinking water is common, and this certainly refers to plain water, Rambam did not concern himself with this as it is explicitly stated in the Jerusalem Talmud, and our Talmud does not explain it as clearly. (And according to the Jerusalem Talmud, what Shmuel says there: 'Any mixture - is dissolved and diluted,' meaning the eye is healed except with water - this refers to dew water as mentioned there).

The one who takes out straw of grain – its measure is the full mouth of a cow, and even if he took it out for a camel, whose mouth is larger than that of a cow – he is liable. And straw of legumes, even if he took it out without specification – it needs to be the full mouth of a camel, which is larger than that of a cow, because the cow does not eat this straw except in a pressing situation. And if he took out straw of legumes the full mouth of a cow for a cow – there is a dispute in the Gemara there between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish: Rabbi Yochanan exempts, because eating in a pressing situation is not considered eating, and Reish Lakish obligates – because it is considered eating. And according to the general rules of the Talmud, the law follows Rabbi Yochanan against Reish Lakish, and the Rambam ruled there that one is liable, because his version read 'Rabbi Oshaya' and not 'Reish Lakish', and the law follows him against Rabbi Yochanan. However, this is not necessary, for even according to our version it works out well, as it says there earlier that Rabbi Yochanan retracted and agreed with Reish Lakish. And furthermore, since the reason depends on whether eating in a pressing situation is considered eating or not, and we have already established in Choshen Mishpat, siman 391, that it is considered eating, and this is explicitly stated at the beginning of the chapter 'How the Foot' there.

Bundles of straw, which are the hard stalks of grain, the measure is the amount that fills a lamb’s mouth. For herbs, the measure is the amount that fills a kid's mouth, which is a smaller measure than the mouth of a lamb. However, the straw bundles are not suitable for a kid. But herbs that are suitable for both – we follow the stricter measure (Rashi). Even if one takes out [the herbs] for a lamb, he is liable, just like the straw of grain that one takes out for a camel in the previous section. Garlic leaves and onion leaves, if they are fresh – the measure is the size of a dried fig, because they are suitable for human consumption. If they are dry – the measure is the amount that fills a kid’s mouth. All these do not combine with each other for the stricter measure, but they combine for the more lenient measure. How so: If one took out straw of grain and of legumes, if together they amount to the measure that fills a cow's mouth – he is exempt; but if they amount to the measure that fills a camel’s mouth – he is liable. The same applies to bundles of straw and herbs and all similar cases.

One who carries out wood [on Shabbat]—enough to cook a dried fig’s worth from a chicken’s egg, which is easier to cook than all other eggs, and also not to cook it alone, as this requires a lot of wood, but when it is beaten with oil or another liquid and placed in a frying pan, which hastens its cooking. And one who carries out a reed [on Shabbat]—enough to make a quill that reaches the tips of his fingers. There is a doubt in our time when reeds are not used for writing as to what its law is, and it seems that its law is like other wood, and even in their time, if it was thick and not suitable for writing or was broken—its measure is like that of wood.

We learned in the Mishnah (Chapter 9): "Spices - enough to season a light egg," and Rashi explained that it is the size of a dried fig from a light egg, which is a chicken egg, and certainly, this is the case, as can be inferred from the previous law. However, the Rambam wrote: "Enough to season an egg," and perhaps he also meant the same and relied on the previous statement. This is also explicitly stated in the Jerusalem Talmud (Chapter 8, Halacha 5), and this is its wording: "Every egg mentioned in vessels - is like a real egg; on Shabbat - it is like a dried fig from an egg." We also learned: that all types of spices combine with each other, and the Gemara explains - they taught this regarding sweet spices since they are suitable for sweetening the pot. This means that the term 'spices' includes everything, even salt, as the Jerusalem Talmud questions there, and this is its wording: "Is cumin and salt combined?" in astonishment, and it answers as well - they taught this regarding sweet spices, see there. It is surprising about the Rambam who wrote simply that spices combine with each other, and more so, his words in the Mishnah commentary where he wrote: like pepper and ginger, etc., and pepper is not a sweet spice (see Tosefot Yom Tov). It seems that the Rambam interprets 'sweet spices' - not literally, but those that sweeten the pot. Therefore, the combination of pepper and ginger and other things sweetens the pot. The Jerusalem Talmud only excluded salt, which merely prevents blandness, but all other types of spices combine, and this is how it is explained in the Gemara. (What was said: 'so too it is suitable for sweetening' - the interpretation is that all types of spices together are suitable for sweetening the pot to make it tasty).

One who carries out peppercorns, even the smallest amount, is liable because they are suitable for refreshing the mouth. This is not our pepper (according to Rashi), as our pepper is classified as a spice, and the measure for it is sufficient to season a dried fig or a light egg. The same measure applies to salt, in my opinion. Tar, which is the residue of pitch, even the smallest amount is liable because it is suitable for half-head pain. Any pleasant fragrance, even the smallest amount, and any foul odor, even the smallest amount, likewise any dye used for coloring purple is liable in any amount because it has a pleasant fragrance (according to Rashi), and foul odors are used for fumigating illnesses. Various aromatic spices, even the smallest amount, because any type of fragrance is liable in any amount. It seems to me that this applies to spices that are solely for fragrance, but spices used in food are classified as seasonings, and their measure was explained in the previous section. Hard metals, such as copper and iron, even the smallest amount, since they are suitable for making a small tool. (Gemara) A fresh rose petal, one, which is a type of rose, and the Gaon reads "a rose wick" made from dyed cotton resembling a rose, and they call it a rose (Arukh). Dust from the altar and stones from the altar and worn-out holy books and their wrappings, even the smallest amount, because they are stored for burial. A burning coal, even the smallest amount, and one who carries out a flame is exempt, as Rambam wrote. I am perplexed because in the Gemara (Beitzah 39a) it is clear that this only applies if he pushed the flame out by hand, but if he carried it out with a splinter or shard, he is liable, even though the splinter or shard has no measure. This should have been explained. However, if one carries out idolatrous accessories, even the smallest amount is exempt, even though Rabbi Yehuda says in the Mishnah (Shabbat 90a) that one is liable because there is a commandment to destroy them. In the Jerusalem Talmud, it is stated that Rabbi Shimon agrees, even though he holds that a labor not needed for itself is exempt, because Rabbi Shimon agrees in the case of items forbidden for benefit. And certainly, Rambam, who ruled that a labor not needed for itself is liable, still ruled not like Rabbi Yehuda, because in our Talmud at the end of the chapter "Kol HaKashar LeHatznia" it states to exclude asherah wood. Thus, it is evident that we do not follow Rabbi Yehuda in this case. Even if one is liable for a labor not needed for itself, this is repugnant and exempt. (This can reconcile the words of Tosafot in Shabbat 94a, s.v. "et ha-met," where they wrote that Rabbi Yehuda holds that a labor not needed for itself is liable from this Mishnah, and according to the Jerusalem Talmud, Rabbi Shimon agrees. However, our Talmud disagrees on this, so examine well.)

It seems to me that all measurements of 'any amount' must still have some substance, even if there is no fixed measure for it. The proof is from metals, which are considered in 'any amount' because it is possible to make a small needle from them, and even the smallest of small items requires some measure. Similarly, items meant for smelling are considered in 'any amount,' yet there must still be something to hold in one's hand, for otherwise, it would slip away. Therefore, it is certain that some substance is required. And regarding the expression 'any amount,' our Rabbis, the Tosafists, have already written in Shabbat (63b, s.v. 'weaving') that even 'any amount' has some small measure. (Although there is room to scrutinize their words from what they themselves wrote earlier in the s.v. 'from where do we know about weaving,' that initially he did not intend to add, etc., and if so, there is no proof. Examine there carefully. Nonetheless, they did write so, and pay close attention.)

One who takes out garden seeds that are not edible and are only for planting is liable even if it is less than a dried fig's bulk. However, it is unclear what the exact measure is, as "less" can include both slightly less and significantly less. Rambam in his commentary on the Mishnah wrote: "close to a dried fig's bulk," meaning slightly less, but it is also not clear how much less that is, and it might be that it needs to be more than half. One who takes out squash seeds – two seeds, and the same applies to gourd seeds and Egyptian bean seeds.

One who takes out bran – enough to place on the opening of a goldsmith's furnace, as in a place where there is no charcoal, gold is smelted with the fire of bran, according to Rashi. But according to this, it no longer applies nowadays. The bran with us is only for animal feed, and its measure is the amount to fill a kid's mouth. 

One who takes out coarse bran, which is the waste left in the sieve, if he takes it out for human consumption – its measure is a dried fig's bulk. If for animal consumption – its measure is the amount to fill a kid's mouth. If for dyeing – enough to dye a small garment.

Tender shoots of the carob tree, before they sweeten – a dried fig's bulk, because they are fit for human consumption. After they sweeten, they are only for animals, and their measure is the amount to fill a kid's mouth. 

But garlic, mustard, lupines, and all other pickled items, whether they have sweetened or not – their measure is a dried fig's bulk, and we are not proficient in these species.

We learn in the Gemara (90a): One who carries out date pits—Rashi explains, date pits—if for planting, it is two; if for eating, it is the amount that fills a pig's mouth, and how much is that? One. If for fuel, the amount needed to cook a light egg, which is the same as a dried fig. If for accounting, as a marker for each simple dinar (Rashi)—two. And the Rambam wrote: One who carries out date pits, if for eating—five; if for fuel—they are considered like wood; if for accounting—two; if for planting—two. His words end here, and presumably, this was his version in the Gemara. And in the Jerusalem Talmud (Chapter 7, Halacha 2): 'Median wheat—two, because they are cherished, they are treated like garden seeds that are not eaten,' and similarly at the end of Chapter 9, see there. The Rambam did not bring this, and perhaps because it is not brought in our Talmud, he presumably holds that their measure is like a dried fig, like all foods. However, it is difficult to reject the Jerusalem Talmud since there is no dispute about this, and it requires further investigation.

One who carries out hyssop for eating - the measure is like a dried fig; for an animal - the measure is the amount that fills a kid's mouth; for use as wood - the measure is the amount of wood needed for sprinkling, which is explained in Tractate Parah, Chapter 12, as the amount needed to dip the tops of the stalks and sprinkle. And the measure for it is explained there. 

One who carries out nutshells, pomegranate peels, woad, and madder, all of which are types of dyes, and also nutshells - the intention is the green shell while it is still on the tree - the measure is enough to dye a small cloth the size of a hairnet. The hairnet is something that girls place on their heads (according to Rashi and Rambam's explanations). 

Similarly, one who carries out urine aged forty days, Alexandrian natron, borit (alkali), kimonia, and ashleg, which are also types of grasses and earth used for cleaning like borit - the measure is enough to wash a small cloth the size of a hairnet, and the same applies to all other cleaning agents. 

If one carries out soaked dyes - the measure is enough to dye a sample for a weaver's shuttle, which is a very small amount. Specifically, with dyes as they are, the measure is enough to wash, etc., because a person does not bother to soak dyes for a small sample.

Ink - the amount needed to write two letters, whether the ink is taken out dry or with a reed pen, or whether it is taken out with an inkwell which is called "tinta" (ink). And the Rambam there wrote: "One who takes out ink on a reed pen - its measure is enough to write two letters, but if he took the ink out by itself or in an inkwell - it needs to be more than that, so that it can be used to write two letters with the reed pen. If there was enough ink in the inkwell for one letter and on the reed pen for one letter, or if there was enough ink by itself for one letter and on the reed pen or in the inkwell for one letter - this is a doubt whether they combine or not," and this is a question in the Gemara there. And it is clear that the same applies even if there are three letters, one in the ink, one on the reed pen, and one in the inkwell - it is also a doubt, but two letters in two reed pens or two inkwells - they combine and he is liable (Tosafot there). And if you ask: isn't he liable even without this on the reed pen or on the inkwell - it can be said that since there is ink in them, they are secondary to the ink, just like when someone takes out a living person on a bed - he is exempt for the bed as well, because the bed is secondary to him (Rashi there). And even with less than the required measure, the law is the same, as it is taught (Shabbat 93b): "One who takes out food less than the required measure in a vessel - he is exempt even for the vessel, because the vessel is secondary to it. And if he takes out two letters and writes them while walking - he is liable even though there is no resting, because writing them is their resting, and their resting is on the paper, and all the more so if he stood still to rest, he is liable even without writing, because his body standing still is considered like the object standing still. And if he takes out one letter and writes it, and then takes out another letter in one concealment and writes it - he is exempt, because the first letter is already lacking, and it is like taking out half a dried fig and placing it down and then taking out another half a dried fig, they do not combine, because he only took out half of the required measure each time. And this is when he lifted the first one beforehand as will be explained, or if he made the first one lacking a bit and burned it, and similarly, when he writes it on the paper, necessarily a bit of it becomes lacking when it dries a bit (see Rashi there).

The one who carries out kohl that is used to paint the eyes—enough to paint one eye, because men do not paint and only women do, and modest women who go wrapped and leave only one eye uncovered—paint only that one. Therefore, in villages where they do not need so much modesty and go with both eyes uncovered—one needs enough to paint both of them, and similarly in any place where it is customary to adorn only with both eyes. And this is when it is carried out for adornment, but if it is carried out for medicinal purposes—in any case, one is liable for enough for one eye. Pitch and sulfur—enough to make a small hole, a vessel in which they place raw silver, they seal its mouth with pitch or sulfur and pierce a thin hole in the seal to extract through it (Rashi 78b). Wax—enough to place on the mouth of a small hole of wine, but not of oil or honey, because wine flows through a smaller hole than oil or honey (there 80a). Glue—enough to place on the tip of the reed of a bird snare, for they place a small slat at the tip of the reed and put glue on it and the bird sits on it and sticks to it, and one needs to place enough there so that the bird sticks to it (there). Grease—enough to anoint under a small cake the size of a sela, and grease, Rashi explained—it is fat or oil (78b). And it is difficult, for with oil the measure was clarified in section 10 as enough to anoint a small limb, as mentioned there. And it is possible that both are the same measure, or it is possible that there are two types of oils, and what is suitable for one is not suitable for the other.

One who carries out earth – its measure is enough to make a seal for a letter, and it is written that this refers to a type of red earth. However, regular earth – certainly it does not have this measure, that is, dust whose measure will be explained – enough to cover the blood of a bird. Clay – enough to make the opening of a crucible for goldsmiths, manure or fine sand – enough to fertilize a leek, which is called "kaplutos," and coarse sand – enough to mix with a full trowel of lime. Potter's clay, which is crushed brick – enough to make the opening of a crucible for goldsmiths, and similarly, clay has this measure as stated, and it is measured enough to fertilize with this measure of clay. Lime – enough to apply to the smallest finger of girls, for they used to apply lime to their faces to remove hair and beautify themselves with it. Dust and ash – enough to cover the blood of a small bird, a pebble and a stone – enough to throw at an animal so it feels it, which is the weight of ten zuz. A shard – enough to hold a quarter-log.

The one who carries out a rope - enough to make a handle for a basket, and there is no difference between a regular rope and an Egyptian rope, and the handle is to hold it. Reed (translated on 'kaneh and sof' as 'kaneh and gemi') - enough to make a patch for a sieve or a sifter to hang them with. And it is questionable whether this applies even to a fresh reed that is fit for animal food (Shabbat 112a), or only to a dry reed, and for a fresh one, the measure is the mouthful of a kid. Palm leaves - enough to make a handle for an Egyptian wicker basket made of palm twigs. Fiber that grows around the palm like a garment - enough to place on the mouth of a small funnel to strain wine, soft material - enough to make a ball the size of a walnut (Tosefta, Chapter 10). Bone - enough to make a spoon, which is a spoon specifically for doctors, and its measure is known to them (Arukh). Glass - enough to scrape the head of a weaving shuttle, which is a weaver's tool with a sharp head (Rashi, Chapter 1), or enough to cut two threads at once.

One who removes two hairs from the tail of a horse or the tail of a cow is liable, as they are stored for trapping birds. If one removes one from the stiff bristles of a pig, he is liable, as it is suitable for a shoemaker to use at the top of the sewing. Palm twigs, which are the threads of the wood—two are for two heddles in the weavers' house. Palm fibers, which are the bark of the palm branches—one, as it is suitable for digging a gourd (Aruch). From cotton wool and from calach wool, camel wool, rabbit wool, and sea animals, and all other spun fibers—enough to spin a thread four handbreadths long (Tosefta there). One who removes from a garment or sackcloth or leather—as their measure for impurity is their measure for carrying out: the garment three by three [fingerbreadths], the sack four by four, the leather five by five, and it appears to me that here also they combine with the lighter measure and not the stricter measure, as in the case of animal food in section 12, and also in impurity it is so, as it is taught in Chapter 27 of Kelim there. It also appears to me that a mat six by six for carrying out is the same as for impurity there, but from the language of the Talmud (79a) which brings this Mishnah, and there it also has a mat, and it says about this: "And it was taught on this: the garment, the sack, and the leather—as their measure for impurity is their measure for carrying out, and a mat, hear from it"—hear from it that it is not so, and the reason for this I do not know, and also in the Rambam a mat is not found and it requires further investigation.

One who carries out leather that has not been processed at all and is still soft – its measure is enough to fashion a small weight that weighs a shekel. If it was salted but has not yet been processed with flour or gallnut – its measure is enough to make an amulet. If it was processed with flour but has not yet been processed with gallnut – its measure is enough to write a bill of divorce on it. Once its processing is complete – its measure is five by five [handbreadths]. According to Rashi, this is specifically when it was boiled in hot water and hardened to the point where one can sit on it, and it is made to cover beds and cushions. The reason for these measures is that the leather, when it is in this state, is suitable only for these purposes. Therefore, it could be that when its quality improves, its measure is greater than before it was improved, as explained in this law.

One who carries out processed parchment—[the minimum amount to be liable is] enough to write the Shema passage for tefillin, because tefillin are written on parchment, and the Shema is the smallest of all the passages. For duchsustus—[the minimum amount to be liable is] enough to write a mezuzah, because a mezuzah is written on duchsustus, as mentioned earlier in Siman 32 and in Yoreh De'ah Siman 288. For tefillin, duchsustus is invalid. What is duchsustus? This was explained there. 

One should not ask why for tefillin one is liable for a single passage, but for a mezuzah, the required amount is for the entire mezuzah, because a mezuzah is written on a single piece of skin, and with two pieces of skin, it is invalid as mentioned there. Tefillin of the head consists of four compartments, and thus one passage is sufficient for one compartment of the head tefillin. 

For paper—[the minimum amount to be liable is] enough to write two letters of a tax receipt, which the tax collectors give to those who pay the tax, and these letters are larger than our letters. One who carries a tax receipt is liable even though he has already shown it to the tax collector and has been exempted with it. Nevertheless, he always carries it with him to show that he is a person who pays taxes. 

For erased paper—[the minimum amount to be liable is] enough to wrap around the opening of a small flask of perfume, which is good-smelling spices. If there is enough of its whiteness to write two letters of a tax receipt, one is liable.

The one who carries a living person is exempt, because a living being carries itself. This is not due to the lightness of the load, for one is liable even for a lesser load than this. Rather, it is because in the Tabernacle they did not carry people, as this was not one of the labors of the Tabernacle (Tosafot, Shabbat 94b, "for the living"). The explanation is as follows: Even though we do not require that every detail exactly resemble the labor in the Tabernacle, as long as this labor was present in the Tabernacle, one is liable for this labor even if it was not exactly the same in the Tabernacle. Nevertheless, since carrying a living person is different from all other loads, as all other loads are fully carried by the one bearing them, but a person carries himself, it turns out that the one carrying him does not bear him completely. Indeed, if this had been in the Tabernacle, one would be liable, but since this was not in the Tabernacle, this labor was not present there. However, one who carries animals, beasts, and birds is liable, because they make themselves heavier (Talmud, Shabbat 94b), meaning they burden themselves downward and do not carry themselves, and this is similar to all loads. Additionally, one could say that this was in the Tabernacle, as they carried the red rams' skins that were needed for the work of the Tabernacle. Similarly, a child who cannot walk on their own, one is liable for carrying them, and so too for a sick person or someone who is bound, as all these do not carry themselves and are similar to all loads. And one could say that this was also in the Tabernacle, as the women who spun, if they had a child, would carry him, and similarly if one of the artisans became ill, it was necessary to carry him, and the bound and the sick are the same. (See Tosafot there; this is according to Rav Nachman and not according to the Rabbis, and examine this closely).

And know that there is a common mistake among the masses who carry children and infants in a place where it is forbidden to carry, and they are accustomed to say that one is exempt regarding a living being. They desecrate Shabbat because for an infant who cannot walk, one is liable according to Torah law, as we have written. Only allowing to toddle him is permitted, meaning that he stands on the ground if he can lift one foot and place one foot down. It is permissible to hold his hand and let him toddle. Even a big child who can walk and carries himself, although he is exempt according to Torah law, he is obligated rabbinically, as with all Shabbat exemptions that are exempt but forbidden, as we wrote in Siman 242. Therefore, it is necessary to inform the public so they do not stumble.

One who carries a living person on a bed is exempt, even for carrying the bed, because the bed is secondary to the person. Similarly, if the person is wearing clothes and has silver and gold rings on his fingers, he is exempt because they are secondary to him. However, if the clothes are not worn in the usual manner but are carried on his shoulder, he is liable. Similarly, if the rings are not on his fingers but in his hands, he is liable, since in these cases they are not considered secondary to him. Likewise, if one carries a living child who can walk and there is a purse hanging on his neck, placed there to amuse him or to quiet him from crying, one is liable for carrying the purse, since a money purse is not secondary to the child. But items that are normally hung on a child are considered secondary to him, and one is exempt.

(This ruling about the child is at the beginning of the chapter "Notel," and there it is according to Rabbi Nathan, who exempts in all cases involving living beings. Thus, according to the Rambam, who rules according to the Rabbis, he should not have brought this ruling. Therefore, I wrote "who can walk." However, regarding the main ruling where the Rambam does not follow Rav Nachman, I find it difficult, as Rava rules there according to Rav Nachman. How did the Rambam rule not according to Rava? Nonetheless, I do not find it so difficult regarding the Rambam, as it is also stated there that Rava holds like Rabbi Shimon in the case of a labor that is not needed for its own sake, and yet he rules like Rabbi Yehuda, as I wrote in the first chapter. But for all the authorities who disagree with him and rule like Rabbi Shimon because of this ruling of Rava, as the Maggid Mishneh wrote in the first chapter, then also in this case of "a living being carries itself," we also rule according to Rav Nachman because of this ruling of Rava. Investigate this thoroughly.)

We have learned in the Mishnah (90a): A living kosher locust — any amount [is significant], a dead one — [the amount of] a dried fig, because a living one is kept for a child to play with. Rabbi Yehuda says — even an impure one, any amount, because it is kept for a child to play with. And the Rabbis hold that an impure one should not be given to a child, lest it die and he eats it, and the law follows the Rabbis. According to this, it is puzzling why the Rambam wrote there simply: "One who carries out a living locust — any amount, and a dead one — [the amount of] a dried fig," without distinguishing between impure and pure. It seems to me, in my humble opinion, that certainly the law follows the Rabbis that it is forbidden to give a child an impure locust for the reason we explained, but if one gave it, indeed it is considered significant and one is liable for any amount, as it is not less than anything else that is not fit for keeping, and one kept it — the keeper is liable as will be explained, and therefore the Rambam stated it simply. And the prohibition to give it to a child — its place is not in Shabbat, and it is included in all prohibitions concerning a child explained at the end of Forbidden Foods. And know that in the Jerusalem Talmud it says that a dead impure locust is not [measured by] a dried fig but by the amount that fills a pig's mouth, as stated there, and the Rambam did not concern himself with this because it is not implied in our Talmud. And a bird of the vineyards, whether alive or dead — any amount, because it is kept for medicinal purposes, and likewise all similar things, and it is not clear to us what a bird of the vineyards is (see Aruch, entry 'Pele').

The corpse, the carcass, and the creeping animal – the measure of their impurity is also the measure for carrying them out: a corpse and a carcass – the size of an olive, and a creeping animal – the size of a lentil. If there was exactly an olive-sized amount and one removed half an olive-sized amount from it – one is liable, for one's actions have been effective in reducing the measure from causing impurity. However, if one removed half an olive-sized amount from an olive and a half – one is exempt, and similarly with all other impurities. And know that all this follows Rabbi Yehuda, who holds one liable for a labor that is not needed for its own sake, and therefore the Rambam ruled this way there, as he follows his approach in the first chapter that a labor not needed for its own sake is liable. But according to many of our Rabbis who ruled according to Rabbi Shimon – one is also exempt here, for Rabbi Shimon disputes this in the Mishnah (93b), since there is no need for the impurity itself, but rather to prevent it from causing impurity. And even if one takes out the corpse to bury it, which is a need for the corpse – one is exempt, for although the corpse needs this, the person does not need this (Gemara 94a).

All the measurements that have been explained apply only to someone who carries something out generally. Therefore, each person needs to follow the measurement that is relevant to their particular situation according to their own measurement. However, someone who carries something out for planting, for medicinal purposes, to show a sample, or similar purposes is liable even for the smallest amount, since for these purposes even the smallest amount is useful. 

And not only if he carried them out now for these purposes, but even if he set something aside for planting, for medicinal purposes, or for a sample and later forgot why he set it aside and carried it out generally, he is liable for the smallest amount, since he carried it out based on his original intention, and if he forgot, he will later remember. 

This only applies to the one who set it aside, but anyone else is only liable based on the measurements that have been explained, and we do not say that this person is liable based on another's intention. Similarly, even if this person carried it out for one of these purposes and thus became liable for the smallest amount, nonetheless, another person is only liable based on their own measurement. 

Even this very person, if he changed his mind and nullified his original intention for one of these purposes, even if he did not explicitly nullify it but threw the item into storage after carrying it out, even though its place is recognizable, his original intention is nullified, since he only performed a mental action and a thought nullifies a thought. Therefore, if he carries it out again, he is only liable based on the standard measurement.

The sages taught in the Mishnah at the end of the chapter "Klal Gadol": "And another general rule they said: Any item that is fit to be stored, and people store it, and someone carries it out on Shabbat - he is liable for a sin offering." And this is its explanation: Any item that is fit to be stored, which is made for human use, and people store it, if it is in a quantity that is suitable for storage - anyone is liable, even a wealthy person for whom this item is of no significance at all - nevertheless, he is liable. But any item that is not fit to be stored or is not stored in this quantity, but is cherished by someone and he stores it - that person is liable, but everyone else is exempt. And what is an item that is not fit to be stored even in a large quantity? The Gemara explains, for example, menstrual blood, even though someone might store it to feed a cat, or wood from an Asherah tree, even though there is a commandment to remove it from one's house - nevertheless, it is not called 'fit to be stored,' and only the one who stored it is liable. According to the Jerusalem Talmud, one is liable for wood from an Asherah tree, as mentioned above in paragraph 15, but this is not the case according to our Talmud, as mentioned there.

One who performs an action with half the required measure is exempt. Similarly, anyone who performs any of the forbidden labors with half the required measure is exempt. It is well known that all exemptions on Shabbat mean exempt but prohibited. This is not comparable to the case of carrying an object four cubits in the public domain with half the measure, which is permissible even initially, because in that case it is not fit to combine, as stated in Siman 342:35. However, half a measure is fit to combine. We have already explained there that half the measure of all the labors, except for carrying out, is forbidden by Torah law, just as with other prohibitions, and this is explicitly stated in Rashi (74a, s.v. "And if"). But in the Tosefta Beitza (Chapter 4, Halacha 2), it is explicitly stated that half the measure on Shabbat is only a rabbinic prohibition, see there, and this requires further investigation.

If someone carries out half a measure and places it down, and then carries out another half measure - he is liable. However, if he lifted the first half before placing down the second half, it is considered as if it was burned, and he is exempt. If someone carries out half a measure and places it down, and then carries out another half measure and passes it over the first within three handbreadths - he is liable even though he did not place it down, because anything within three handbreadths is considered as if it is joined (lavud), and for passing, placement is not necessary, because as long as it is in his hand - it is considered as if it is placed on something. Therefore, if one throws an object through the air within three handbreadths of the ground - he is liable only if it lands on something, otherwise, he is exempt. This is unlike carrying, as ruled by the Rambam there. In the Gemara, there is a dispute on this matter. Rava holds (80a) that within three handbreadths requires placement on something, but Rav Hilkiah disputes this (97a), and the Rambam rules here and in Chapter 13 like Rava, but Rabbeinu Chananel and the Ramban rule like Rav Hilkiah (commentary on Chapter 13, Halacha 17) (see Tosafot 80a s.v. 'Ha').

If one carries out half the required measure and then carries out another half measure, in one lapse of awareness, he is liable. If in two separate lapses of awareness, he is exempt. Even in one lapse of awareness, he is liable, even if the lapses of awareness were not equal, such as one being intentional violation of the Sabbath and unintentional regarding the labor, and the other the opposite (Rashi 71a, s.v. 'Ketzira'). We have already explained this in Siman 242, Section 19. And there it is regarding two full measures, that they are considered as one lapse of awareness, and it seems that the same applies to two half measures, that they combine. Moreover, in the case of a half measure, the awareness needs to be clearer than with a full measure, for Rabban Gamliel holds at the end of the chapter "HaBoneh" that awareness does not help at all for a half measure. And even though we do not rule according to him, in any case, it is certainly not worse than two full measures.

However, even in one period of forgetfulness, one is not liable unless he carries to one domain without an intervening domain between this half and that half. Therefore, even if the halves are not adjacent to each other, nevertheless, they are placed in one domain. But if there is an intervening private domain between them, or he brought them from a public domain to a private domain and there is an intervening public domain between them, he is exempt. However, if there is an intervening rabbinic domain like a karmelit between them, there is no issue, and he is liable (so explained the Rambam like Rabbah. Not like Abaye and Rava, as the law does not follow students in the presence of their master, so wrote the Maggid Mishneh, Halacha 24, see there).

One who carries out less than the required measure, and before placing it down it swells and becomes the required measure, or one who carries out the required measure and before placing it down it shrinks and becomes less than the required measure - is exempt, since the measure was lacking at the time of either the uprooting or the placing down. And even if there was the required measure in both the uprooting and the placing down, but it deteriorated in the middle, such as if one carried out the required measure and it shrank, and before placing it down it swelled again - this too is doubtful whether he is liable or not, for perhaps we require the measure to be maintained from beginning to end. This is not similar to inadvertence, where one is liable if he was inadvertent at the beginning and end even though he was deliberate in the middle, as stated in Siman 242, and this matter is explained in the Gemara (102a). Nevertheless, here there is doubt whether there is disqualification regarding Shabbat, meaning perhaps since it became less than the required measure, it is disqualified from its status, just as there is disqualification regarding commandments (Gemara 91a). See what I wrote in Yoreh De'ah Siman 85, Se'if 16, that in this law there is a distinction between Shabbat and other prohibitions.

One who carries out [an item] the size of a dried fig for eating and it shrivels before placing it down, and he then decides to use it for planting or for medicine, which does not require a specific measure - he is liable, because there is liability both at the initiation and at the placement, even though the intentions are not the same. Therefore, since it is not necessary for the intentions to be the same, it also applies leniently, for instance, if one carries out less than the required measure for planting and then, before placing it down, decides to use it for eating - he is exempt, because it lacks the required measure according to his intention at the time of placement. If it swells before placing it down and becomes the required measure - he is liable, because even if he had remained silent and not decided to use it for eating, he would still be liable based on his initial intention. (See the Gemara 91a, and in the Rambam, where it is written that it became the required measure before he decided to use it for eating, as otherwise there would be a period of time when he was not clearly liable, which would create a doubt as mentioned in the previous section - consider this carefully.)

In the Gemara (there), it remains uncertain regarding someone who threw an olive-sized piece of terumah into a house that is ritually impure, and there were foods there that were less than the size of an egg. This is the measure of impurity for foods, and this olive-sized piece combined to make up the size of an egg. Do we say that since it combines for the matter of impurity, it also combines for the matter of Shabbat, or perhaps for Shabbat we require the measure of a dried fig? And specifically if he threw it, because now the prohibition of Shabbat and impurity come together, for regarding Shabbat he is not liable for throwing until it comes to rest. But if he brought it in (carried it), he is certainly not liable, for regarding Shabbat the liability occurs immediately when he brings it in, since the placing of his body is like the placing of an object. But regarding impurity, the liability does not occur until it is with the foods (Tosafot there). And similarly, specifically an olive-sized piece of terumah, but less than an olive-sized piece, even though it completes the measure to the size of an egg, since there is no prohibition to eat it in impurity, it does not combine for the matter of Shabbat. And similarly, an olive-sized piece of non-sacred food does not help, because there is no prohibition in eating non-sacred food in impurity (there).

But the Rambam wrote there in Halacha 27: "If one threw an olive-sized portion of food into an impure house, and this olive-sized portion combined with other food that was there to form the volume of an egg, it is uncertain whether one is liable for the olive-sized portion because it completed the measure required for impurity, or if one is not liable." These are his words. And it appears that in his version, the word 'terumah' was not written in the Gemara, because since an olive-sized portion is significant everywhere and combines to form an egg-sized portion which is effective for impurity, there is a doubt as mentioned. But less than an olive-sized portion does not have significance, and we do not say that since it combines for impurity, it also combines for Shabbat. And it seems to me that this is only for food that has been prepared to receive impurity, but if it has not been prepared, it appears that it certainly does not combine for Shabbat (this is my humble opinion, and see there in the Maggid Mishneh).

If someone carries out food less than the minimum measure in a utensil, they are exempt even for the utensil, because the utensil is secondary to the food. And the Rambam explained there that this is because his intention is not to carry out the utensil but rather what is inside it. From this, it is clear that if his intention was to carry out the utensil, he would be liable. This law is a Mishnah in the tenth chapter (93b), and in the Jerusalem Talmud, it is explained that this applies only to foods that require a utensil, such as oily fruits, crushed foods, and the like. But when the food does not require a utensil, he is liable, as the Ra'avad wrote there. However, the Rambam did not bring this because it does not seem to imply this in our Talmud. Similarly, one who carries a living person on a bed is exempt even for the bed, because the bed is secondary to the person. Specifically, this is when the person is not bound and is an adult who can walk, but if it is a child who cannot walk or someone bound, one is liable for the person, as written in section 27. And one who carries a peddler's basket, even though it contains many kinds of items, and even if he carried them in his palm, he is only liable once, because they are all considered one act of carrying, and the same applies to all similar cases.

We were commanded by the prophets that just as the Torah prohibits carrying objects from a private domain to a public domain or from a public domain to a private domain, so too we were commanded that our manner of walking should be different on Shabbat than on a weekday. And the prophet said: "If you restrain your foot on Shabbat," and we expound from this (Shabbat 113a) and also from the verse "and honor it by not doing your own ways"—that your manner of walking on Shabbat should not be like your manner of walking on a weekday. On a weekday, it is customary for a person to run after their business and take large strides, even though it is burdensome for the eyes (there, Shabbat 113a). However, on Shabbat, it is forbidden to run and take large strides; rather, one should walk calmly, heel to toe, like a person at rest. 

What constitutes a large stride? More than an amah (a cubit). An amah is such that the foot itself is half an amah, and the space between one foot and the other is half an amah, so more than this is considered a large stride, unless it is impossible for him to walk in less than this measure due to the size of his foot and his manner of walking. But for a mitzvah, such as going to the synagogue or something similar, it is permitted and a mitzvah to run, because these are matters of heaven, as it is written (there): "finding your own pleasure"—your own affairs are forbidden, but matters of heaven are permitted. (The Magen Avraham, section 2, wrote in the name of the Agudah that a large stride is defined as lifting the second foot before placing down the first foot, see there. It is difficult to be cautious about this and we are not accustomed to this at all, and Rashi there explained that it is more than an amah in one stride, see there.)

This matter is part of the delight of Shabbat, as they say, "a day of rest," and those who are resting do not run or take large steps. Therefore, for someone who finds jumping and running to be a delight, such as young men playing and enjoying their jumping and running, it is permitted even initially, since this is their delight. Similarly, running to see something that one enjoys is permitted, even though there is some effort involved in running, but in any case, this is his delight because he hurries to see something he desires to see, since this is not due to mundane activities. (See Magen Avraham, section 4; there is a question because there it is to read.) It is stated in the Tosefta Shabbat (Chapter 17): "One does not run on Shabbat in order to exercise, but one may stroll in his usual manner even all day long."
