This means that for someone whose therapy involves running to exercise and sweat, it is forbidden on Shabbat for two reasons: one, because of therapy, and two, because during the act it is difficult for him to run and he suffers, but he does it for therapy. However, strolling in the usual manner is permitted even if it has a therapeutic benefit, since it is not evident that he is doing it for therapy, and he does not suffer but rather delights in the stroll. And this is what our teacher, the Rema, wrote in section 2 that it is permitted to stroll on Shabbat, meaning even though one intends it for therapy, just like all foods that a person eats for therapy, for otherwise, what is he teaching us? Why would strolling be forbidden? (And with this, the hesitation of the Magen Avraham in section 5 is resolved. See Taz, section 1, and Eliyah Rabbah, section 7, and according to what I have written, everything fits perfectly; examine it well.)

And even though it is forbidden to take large steps on Shabbat, and likewise to jump when there is no pleasure derived from it, nevertheless, when one is walking and comes upon a water channel and has three options before him: the first, to walk through the water; the second, to go around it; and the third, to jump over it. Now, the first option, to walk through the water, is entirely forbidden when walking for a non-mitzvah purpose, due to the decree lest he wring out his clothes that become soaked with water, and only for a mitzvah purpose was it permitted with a change, as will be explained. The second option, to go around it, also involves great effort, and therefore the third option, which is to leap and jump over it, is better. And even if it is so wide that he cannot place his first foot down before lifting the second, nevertheless it is better to leap than to go around, as it increases walking. However, if it is very wide, he is forced to go around it, and this is better than walking through the water because of the wringing out issue, as we said. And if there is no way to go around and he is compelled to walk through the water, it is entirely forbidden unless for a mitzvah purpose. From this, we learn that if there is no water in the channel, he should walk within it and climb out if he cannot jump over it, and jumping is better than descending into it, walking through, and climbing out, as this is as burdensome as going around, but this depends on the depth.

If one was going for the purpose of a mitzvah, such as to greet his teacher or someone greater than him in wisdom, and he needs to cross a body of water: if he can jump over it - he should jump, and this is preferable as with a non-obligatory matter. If he cannot jump - he should go around it, and if he cannot even go around - he is permitted to walk through the water, and this is the opinion of the authorities mentioned later in Siman 613. But the opinion of our teacher the Rema there is that since they permitted him to walk through the water - it is better than going around it, which would increase his walking. And how should he act when walking through the water - he should make a change, meaning he should not take his hand out from under the hem of his garment. This means that one who is walking through water usually lifts his clothes up high and puts his hand under them until his hand protrudes from the edge of his clothes to prevent them from falling, and on Shabbat he is not allowed to do so but should walk in his clothes as usual, and in this way it will be noticeable and he will not come to wring them. And it is forbidden to cross in sandals, because since he cannot tie and fasten them well - we are concerned that they might fall off and he will come to carry them in a place where carrying is prohibited, such as in the public domain or a karmelit. But shoes are permitted, as they are tied to his feet. This is according to the form of their shoes, and now it is necessary to understand according to the form of our shoes which can fall off the feet and which cannot. And it appears to me that none of our shoes can fall off, except for the higher shoes called galoshes which are likely to fall, and it is forbidden to walk in them in somewhat deep water.

In all these cases, they also permitted someone who was going to guard his fruits from being stolen, for this is permitted on Shabbat, as he is not doing anything but preventing thieves from entering, and guarding his property is also considered a sort of mitzvah. However, there is a distinction between guarding his fruits and performing a mitzvah. In the case of a mitzvah, they permitted also the return journey to walk along the waterway, just as they permitted the initial journey according to the details explained, for if we did not permit the return journey, he would not want to go there in the first place. But in the case of guarding his fruits, they only permitted the initial journey and not the return journey, and if he refrains, he refrains. Moreover, because of the potential loss of his property, he will not refrain from going, unlike with a mitzvah. (See Taz, subsection 3, who questions why this is not included in Beitzah among the things that were permitted at the end because of the beginning, and it is not a question at all, for there are several prohibitions there, but here there is no prohibition, only a mere concern.)

Since it has been explained that carrying out [an object] is a primary category of work (av melacha) and one is liable for stoning for it [if done intentionally], and for a sin offering if done unintentionally, it is therefore necessary to know what is considered carrying a burden, as it is written: "And do not carry a burden, etc." What is called a 'burden'? For what a person wears as clothing is not considered a 'burden,' for otherwise, would it be suggested that one should go naked on Shabbat? Similarly, their ornaments are not called a burden, since an ornament is not a burden. Therefore, anything a person wears in the manner of dressing, as well as ornaments which one adorns oneself with, is permitted. Only what one carries in one's hands or on one's shoulder is called a 'burden.'

And know that those who carry some burden and make it like a garment, for example, carrying a handkerchief to wipe the nose and making it like a neckerchief wrapped around the neck, if he does not have a neckerchief on his neck - it is permitted. But if he has a neckerchief wrapped around his neck - it is forbidden, for it is considered a burden. And if during the winter he wraps it around the outer garment on his neck because of the cold, so that the cold does not affect him - this is also permitted. But if he wraps it around his hand or around his leg - it is obviously a complete burden, and he is liable for stoning or a sin offering.

Some wrap it around their garment in the place of a belt to make it like a belt, and I do not see a permission in this: Firstly, because it is not customary to wear a belt in this way, and secondly, because it is not the manner of a belt, as it is a different type. And when a person wears this handkerchief in place of a belt, people will mock him. However, it is possible that if he unties the garment hooks in such a way that the garment remains open and it is not proper to walk like this - he may wrap the handkerchief to tie the two sides of the garment, and the hooks are not a burden, since they are secondary to the garment. In such cases, it might be permitted, although this too is a lenient ruling (this appears to be my humble opinion), and there is proof for this from Section 103, see there.

And know that due to the gravity of the prohibition of carrying and because it is something that people are accustomed to doing at all times and every moment, the sages were compelled to institute safeguards regarding this. That is to say, there are certain ornaments that they decreed should not be worn out of concern that one might remove them to show them off. This prohibition is especially relevant to women, as they are proud and love to show off in front of their friends. There are many specific laws related to this, which will be explained in Siman 303. There are also items that are prohibited because they are loose and there is a concern that they might fall off and one might come to carry them four cubits in the public domain. Some items are forbidden because walking in such a manner might cause people to laugh at the wearer, who might then remove and carry them four cubits in the public domain. Some things are prohibited due to the appearance of impropriety, and some are forbidden even though they are typically worn in battle, like armor, which will be explained, and although it is a garment, at times other than during battle it is considered a burden, and they decreed against this as will be explained.

Therefore, anyone who goes out with an item that is neither an ornament nor a garment, and carries it in the usual manner that one carries that item, is liable. For if it was carried in an unusual manner, like with the back of one's hand, one is exempt, as mentioned in Section 5. Similarly, any ornament that is loose and can easily fall off - it is forbidden to go out with it, and if one does go out with it, one is exempt from a sin offering. A woman should not go out with ornaments that are customarily removed and shown, and it will be clarified in Siman 303 whether this is forbidden only in the public domain or even in a courtyard or house.

Therefore, a person should not go out with a sword, even if it is girded on his belt, as one does on weekdays, nor with a bow or similar items, nor with a shield that protects his head and body from the enemy, nor with a club which is an iron stick, nor with a spear that one carries beside the body as warriors do. And if he goes out with them, he is liable to bring a sin offering. The reason is that these items are not inherently ornaments, but for warriors, they are like garments; however, for ordinary people, they are considered a burden (as explained by Rabbi Ovadiah in the Mishnah, Chapter 6, Mishnah 4, see there). Therefore, for a warrior, such as one who serves in the king's army, they are like garments. It seems clear to me that all these cases are talking about when these items are not carried in one's hands, for in such cases, even if they were ornaments, one would be liable for a sin offering. Rather, the discussion is about when they are attached to one's garments (as also indicated by the Magen Avraham, Section 27). I have seen someone write that carrying a spear in one's hand, if it were an ornament, would be permitted even in such cases, and therefore, it is permitted to carry a staff with a nice button in a karmelit (an area of semi-public domain, according to Tiferet Yisrael in his commentary on the Mishnah). Heaven forbid to say so, for it is a great mistake. If so, why do we decree for a woman that she might remove and show it, what difference does it make if it is an ornament? And even though it is not customary to carry such an ornament in the hands, nonetheless, it is not considered an ornament when carried in the hands. Therefore, in a public domain, one is liable for a sin offering, and in a karmelit, it is prohibited by rabbinic decree, and this is the primary ruling in law.

And similarly, a man should not go out wearing armor that he is dressed in, nor with a helmet which is an iron hat, nor with greaves which are iron boots, even though they are made like regular clothing, because they are not considered clothing except for warriors. Therefore, if he goes out with them, he is not liable for a sin-offering, because they are like clothing and are only prohibited rabbinically for the reason we have mentioned. And he should not go out with tefillin, and it is not necessary to say that it is forbidden to put them on during Shabbat and Yom Tov because these are not times for tefillin, but even if we say that these are times for tefillin and there is no prohibition, we still worry that he might need to go to the bathroom and remove them, and he might come to carry them four cubits in the public domain. And if he goes out with them, he is not liable for a sin-offering even if it is forbidden to put them on, because he carries them in the manner of wearing them during the week, and it is not considered carrying from the Torah (Gemara 61a). And similarly, one whose foot is small should not go out with a large shoe, lest it fall off his foot and he comes to carry it four cubits in the public domain, but he may go out with a large cloak, for he will not remove it and remain naked, and by itself, it will not fall off. But a garment seems to be forbidden, and it is not necessary to say if there is a concern that it will fall off by itself, but even if it will not fall off by itself, we worry that people might mock him and he will remove it and carry it (this is explicitly stated in Rashi 141a, s.v. "but" see there). And similarly, he should not go out with one shoe if he does not have a wound on his foot, lest people mock him and he comes to carry it. But if he has a wound on his foot, he may go out with the one that does not have the wound, and they will not mock him, for they see that he has a wound on the other foot and cannot wear a shoe. And some prohibit even in such cases, and in the Gemara (61a) there is a dispute about this, and it is proper to be stringent (Taz, section 4).

It appears to me that in all these cases where they decreed not to go out with certain items due to concerns that they might fall, be mocked, or one might need to use the restroom and similar concerns—they only decreed this in a public domain and not in a karmelit (an area that is not a public domain but has some of its laws). For us, since we do not have a public domain, we do not make this decree. A proof for this is from the argument between Abaye and Rava in the first chapter (11b) regarding the Mishnah that states: "A person should not stand in a private domain and drink in a public domain, etc."—this is a decree lest the vessel be brought to him. And what is the law in a karmelit? Abaye holds that they decreed a decree upon a decree regarding carrying (see Tosafot there, s.v. 'Amar'), and Rava holds that they did not decree, and it is permitted in a karmelit, as stated there, and as explained later in Siman 350. Thus, it is explicitly clear that in a place where they decreed due to the concern of carrying, they only decreed in a public domain. And even though they prohibited women’s ornaments also in a karmelit due to the concern that she might remove and show them off—that case is different, because they even prohibited them in a house and courtyard. The reason for this is explained by Rashi in the Mishnah at the beginning of the chapter "With What May a Woman Go Out", and this is his language: "And all those mentioned above are prohibited even in a courtyard, lest they become accustomed to wearing them in a public domain, and it is all one decree that they decreed not to adorn themselves with them on Shabbat at all"—end quote. But in other decrees, they only decreed in a public domain (this is how it appears to me in my humble opinion).

Rambam wrote in Chapter 19, Law 3: "A ring that has a seal on it is considered a man's ornament and not a woman's ornament. A ring that does not have a seal is considered a woman's ornament and not a man's ornament. Therefore, if a woman goes out wearing a ring with a seal and a man goes out wearing a ring without a seal, they are liable. And why are they liable? Since they carried them in an unusual manner, as it is not customary for a man to carry a ring that is not suitable for him on his finger, and similarly, it is not customary for a woman to carry a ring that is not suitable for her on her finger. However, sometimes a man will give his ring to his wife to store at home, and she will place it on her finger while she carries it. Similarly, a woman might give her ring to her husband to take to the craftsman for repair, and he will place it on his finger while carrying it until he reaches the craftsman's shop, thus they carried them in the manner that they are usually carried, and therefore they are liable." This is also the opinion of the Rif and most of the poskim, and it is found in the Gemara (62a). From this, we learn that carrying in this manner is considered carrying even though it is not always customary to carry it in this way, but occasionally it is, and it is considered the usual manner of carrying and one is liable. Similarly, regarding a garment, if it is customary to carry it occasionally in this manner, it is considered the usual manner of wearing and it is permitted to go out with it. (In the Yerushalmi, Chapter 6, end of Halacha 3, it says: If it was made for this and that purpose, meaning as an ornament and also to seal with, if one goes out to seal with it, they are liable, if one goes out as an ornament, they are exempt even if it has a seal, since the seal is secondary to the ornament)

It is further written: "A woman should not go out with a ring that does not have a seal, even though it is one of her ornaments, as a decree lest she take it out into the public domain to show her friends, as women always do. And if she goes out with it, she is exempt. But a man is permitted to go out with a ring that has a seal, because it is an ornament and it is not his way to show it. And all the people have the custom not to go out with a ring at all." End quote. And Rashi of blessed memory holds that it is also forbidden for a man, but Rabbi Tam's opinion is like that of Maimonides, and so it is proven in the Jerusalem Talmud that there is no concern for a man to remove and show it. And our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in paragraph 9: "But something that is an ornament for both a man and a woman is forbidden also for a man." End quote. And this is from the language of the Rosh and the Tur, and it is from the Jerusalem Talmud. And the reason is that since it is suitable for both, the Rabbis did not differentiate, and since a woman is forbidden, so too is a man. And now, since women also go out with ornaments and we are not concerned about removing and showing for reasons that will be explained in section 303, therefore a man is also permitted. And it is also written: A ring that has a fixed stone, or if letters are written on it, it is not called a seal, because it is not called a seal unless the letters or designs are engraved on it. End quote. And it is already explained in Yoreh De'ah, section 141, that protruding designs are forbidden even on weekdays. See there.

And know that in the time of the Gemara, it was not the way of a man to wear a ring on his finger without a seal. But now in our times, many wear such rings as ornaments, as is well-known. It is obvious that this matter depends on the customs of the place and time (Magen Avraham, section 15). Therefore, nowadays it is permitted to go out with a ring that does not have a seal. The Ran also writes this there, and this is his language: "There are those who say that now a man goes out even with a ring that does not have a seal, because even though it is said in the Gemara that the opposite is true for a man, that was according to their generation when men were not accustomed to rings without seals. But now that they are accustomed to it, it is considered an ornament for them and is permitted." And our teacher the Beit Yosef did not bring this, because in his great book he wrote that it does not appear so from the Rambam, who did not differentiate between times. And I do not understand, for it is known that the Rambam transcribes the language of the Talmud, and perhaps in the days of the Rambam and in his country it was like in the time of the Gemara. He also brought what the Rambam wrote, that people were accustomed not to go out with any ring at all. And I do not know what the relevance of custom is to the law; certainly, it is a measure of piety to do so. This is the language of the Maggid Mishneh there: "It is a custom of the pious in those lands, and if it were possible to return all places to that custom, it would be very good." Thus, it was not the custom in every place, as is clear from the words of the Ran. He also wrote there in the name of Rabbeinu Yerucham: that even though nowadays a ring without a seal is an ornament for a man, it should be forbidden because it is also an ornament for a woman. And anything that is an ornament for both a man and a woman is forbidden. However, now even women wear ornaments, as mentioned, so how can we forbid it for a man more than for a woman? Therefore, it seems to me clearly correct that it is certainly proper and correct not to wear rings on fingers on Shabbat. And even though the Rambam only wrote the main laws of the Gemara, he nevertheless wrote this custom because it serves as a safeguard for Shabbat. However, from the main law, there is no need to rebuke those who wear gold rings and precious stones on their fingers on Shabbat, since it is permitted according to the main law. And our teacher the Beit Yosef himself brought this later in Siman 303, section 18.

The Rambam also wrote (Chapter 19, Halacha 5): "A woman who goes out with a perforated needle is liable, but a man is exempt. And a man who goes out with an unperforated needle is liable, but a woman is exempt, because it is among her ornaments, and it is only prohibited because of a decree lest she show it to her friends." This is the way of the Rif there. The Rosh there already wondered how a man could be liable for an unperforated needle, since it is considered an unusual manner of carrying. That is, we are certainly referring to needles that are stuck in the garments, for if they are carried in their hands, it is always considered carrying, and thus it is an unusual manner of carrying. Similarly, one can question the woman, how she could be liable for a perforated needle in such cases. There are those who answered that with one needle it is common to carry it stuck in the garment, as it is not common to carry a single needle in the hand (Bach). These are puzzling matters, for the Rambam explicitly ruled there in Halacha 21 that even a tailor who goes out with a needle stuck in his garment is exempt because it is not the usual manner of carrying, and all the more so any person. Therefore, it appears clear to me that the Rif and the Rambam also agree with this, but here they were not dealing with this issue; rather, they came to teach that a man typically goes out with a perforated needle and a woman with an unperforated needle. And the exemption due to it being an unusual manner of carrying will be explained later. Here, the practical implication is in the primary law: for a woman, an unperforated needle is considered an ornament, but the reverse is considered a burden and is prohibited by rabbinic decree even if it is not the usual manner of carrying.

The Tur wrote: "One should not go out with a needle stuck in his garment, whether it is pierced or not, and if he goes out - he is exempt." The reason is because this is not the usual way of carrying, and it is rabbinically prohibited in both cases. The law regarding a needle for a woman is explained in Siman 303, see there. According to our explanation, the Rif and the Rambam also hold this view. There is another opinion that for a pierced needle, a man is liable, and this is what our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in paragraph 8: "One should not go out with a needle stuck in his garment, whether pierced or not, and if he goes out: with a pierced needle - he is liable, and with a non-pierced needle - he is exempt, and some say the opposite." There is no practical difference in this, for according to all opinions, a man is prohibited from going out with a needle stuck in his garment, whether pierced or not, and so is the law. However, it seems to me in my humble opinion that if the needle is used in place of hooks, which connect the two ends of the garment - it is permitted, just like for a woman when she fastens her ties with it, as written in Siman 303. Even though there are distinctions for a woman between different types of needles, this is because it is customary for a woman to adorn herself with one type and not the other. But for a man - adornment does not apply, and therefore if the needle serves instead of hooks - why should it be forbidden? (See Tosafot Shabbat 11b regarding the unusual way of carrying a needle stuck in one's garment. They wrote in the commentary beginning with 'And if': "And the teaching that if a woman goes out with a pierced needle she is liable - there it is entirely the usual way of carrying." This is their language. It is not understood why, and this is contrary to all the poskim we have brought. The Magen Avraham in Siman 303, subparagraph 7, brought this and explained that the Machatzit HaShekel interpreted it as follows: When it is stuck in the garment - it is the usual way of carrying, and Rabbi Meir only disagrees when it is stuck in a special place. I do not know what he means, for there it is taught: 'with a needle stuck in his garment,' see there. The Pri Megadim explains there that for a woman it is the usual way of carrying because she typically sews household items. This too is perplexing, for why should a woman be more liable than a tailor, who according to Rabbi Meir is exempt. It seems to me that their intention is when she goes out with it for tying, but does not use it for tying, yet all the poskim did not understand it this way, and examine this well.)

Our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, wrote in paragraph 11: "An item made for adornment and for use, such as elegant silver keys designed as an ornament, is prohibited [to carry in the public domain on Shabbat], for an observer might say that it is being carried for practical use. However, some permit it if it is made of silver. Nevertheless, it is forbidden to go out with a beril'in case, even if the case is made of silver, because the eyeglasses themselves are a burden. And if the key is made of copper or iron, even if it is attached and fixed to the belt, it is forbidden. Yet, some have written that the custom is to permit this." End of quote. Their words require explanation.

And this is its explanation: After it has been clarified that any type of ornament is permitted, and an item that is not an ornament but rather for use is considered a burden, according to this, we should permit an item that is both an ornament and made for use as well, such as attractive silver keys which are beautiful to adorn with. What difference does it make to us if they are also used? They brought a teaching from the Jerusalem Talmud that it is forbidden. The reason must be that one who sees it being used will say that its primary purpose is for its use, and there are those who permit it by interpreting the Jerusalem Talmud differently. Therefore, silver ones that are attractive are permitted, but iron and copper ones are not ornaments because they do not have beauty and are forbidden. Not only if they are by themselves, but even if attached and fixed to a belt, it is forbidden. We do not say that it is nullified in relation to the belt because it is a key and an important tool, it is not nullified to the belt, just like tzitzit are not nullified in relation to the garment due to their importance, as will be explained in this chapter. In any case, there are those who wrote that in this matter, the custom is to permit when it is attached and fixed to the end of the belt, where the body is girded, and the belt is fastened like a hook, and it has the image of a key. In such cases, it is nullified to the belt and included as part of the belt, even if made of iron or copper. But if it hangs in the middle of the belt and is a separate tool, it is forbidden. And even if it is at the end of the belt, it is only when the intention is to carry the item for the sake of the belt, but if the intention is to carry it for the sake of the key, it is forbidden. This matter is clarified in the Jerusalem Talmud which we brought at the end of paragraph 54.

And they further say that even according to the most lenient opinions on this matter, it is still forbidden to carry a monocle in a silver case with the case attached to a silver or gold chain and hanging around one's neck as an ornament. Even if one were to argue that the case is subordinate to the chain, or even if the case itself were made as an ornament together with the chain, nevertheless, the lenses inside it are not subordinate to the chain and the case, since their primary function is for a significant use, which is necessary for all those with poor vision. It is obvious that this is more important than tzitzit regarding a tallit. And regarding the lenses themselves, there is no allowance whatsoever, even if they are made of silver or gold, since everyone sees that they are a functional tool and not an ornament. And even if they are woven into the garment so that there is no concern they might fall, similar to what they do now and call it a "pince-nez," it is still a complete prohibition, and one is liable for a sin offering, for it is a completely functional tool and not at all considered a garment, but rather akin to a spoon, fork, or knife. 

And one cannot argue that it should be permitted because one needs them to read a book, similar to how it is permitted for a lame person to walk with a cane when they cannot walk without it, as will be explained. This is not analogous, because there the cane serves as a substitute for the leg, but here one can walk without them, and if it is because he cannot read a book without them, then he should not study. And if we do not say this, we would also permit him to carry a book to study from. And even if he cannot walk without the lenses, for instance, if the doctors commanded him to always wear them, nevertheless, it seems they are forbidden and he should stay at home. However, in such cases, it might be permitted if they are woven into his garment in such a way that they cannot fall off, for since he does not remove them from his body, they are considered as one of his garments. This is what seems to me, in my humble opinion, to be the law. But if he needs them only to read a book, it is forbidden to walk with them, and he is liable for a sin offering. Those who are lenient in this matter desecrate the Sabbath and will eventually be held accountable, and the fools have transgressed and been punished.

From these things that have been explained, it can be learned that a watch, which is called a "Zeiger," even if it is very beautiful and made of pure gold, it is forbidden to go out with it [on Shabbat], and there is an obligation of a sin-offering if carried in a public domain. One who is lenient in this matter will be held accountable. It is obvious that it is a useful tool to know the hours, and it is merely beautified as all useful tools are beautified. Proof of this is that if it breaks and does not work for a long time, one would store it away and not wear it until it is fixed. Even if one attaches a gold chain to it as an ornament, it is still clear that it is not nullified by the chain, more than tzitzit are nullified by the garment. Therefore, in a place where there is no eruv, it is forbidden to carry a watch on one's body on Shabbat, not due to stringency but by the essence of the law, and one who carries it is liable for a sin-offering. Someone who mistakenly considers it an ornament is mistaken in a clear ruling, as an ornament is only something that is not a tool for any use except as an ornament, like earrings, rings, and gold chains. However, anything whose primary purpose is for some use is a tool and not an ornament.

It is taught (Shabbat 11a): A tailor should not go out with his needle stuck in his garment, nor a carpenter with a chip of wood in his ear, nor a comb-maker with a thread in his ear, nor a weaver with a bit of yarn in his ear, nor a dyer with a sample around his neck, nor a money-changer with a coin in his ear. And if he goes out – he is exempt but it is forbidden, because this is not the usual way of carrying. Even if an artisan carries in his usual manner, he is exempt – these are the words of Rabbi Meir. Rabbi Yehuda says – an artisan carrying in his usual manner is liable, but all other people are exempt. Seemingly, according to the Talmudic principles, the law follows Rabbi Yehuda over Rabbi Meir. However, Rambam in Chapter 19, Halacha 21 ruled according to Rabbi Meir, because the Talmudic discussion proves this, as the Maggid Mishneh wrote there (and in Hagahot Maimoniot, it remains a question). Rashi explained: "An artisan who carries in his usual manner, meaning he occasionally goes out like this on weekdays, etc." (end quote). And then he wrote: "It seems to me that all those mentioned here are only cases where professionals put these items on themselves when going to the market so that people will recognize their trade and hire them for work" (end quote). It appears to me that there is no practical difference between these explanations in terms of the law, but Rashi explained the reason for this behavior – so that people will recognize their trade, etc.

And I have seen someone who wrote that it refers to a situation where it is inserted into his garment in a place where it is not normally completely taken out in that manner, but rather he did it to show that he is an expert. However, in a place where it is customary to insert it occasionally on weekdays - he is liable (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 19). And I am puzzled by this, for if so, Rashi should have explained, for according to his second explanation, this is not the same place as his first explanation, and it clearly implies that the places are the same. Additionally, the Talmud there raises several questions on this matter, and if you were to think that there is a difference between one place and another, it should have resolved that here it refers to this place and there to another place. From many of our Rabbis' words, it is clarified that there is no difference in this, and this is the main understanding. (Regarding what is written in Tosafot there, we have already explained their words in paragraph 58, see there. And I saw in the commentary of the Chacham Tzvi that the Chemed Moshe raises a difficulty on him, and I do not have his book to examine it. See also Pri Megadim on the Turei Zahav, subparagraph 10, who questions this matter, and in my humble opinion, the main understanding is as I have written, and delve into it).

A zav (a man with a discharge) should not go out with a pouch made to protect him from his discharge so that it should not soil him. Even though this is a labor that is not needed for its own sake, since he does not need the act of carrying itself but rather to avoid his clothes becoming dirty — according to the Rambam, we hold that a labor that is not needed for its own sake is still prohibited. Even according to most authorities who disagree with him, it is still prohibited by rabbinic law. Similarly, a menstruating woman who ties a garment in front of her to avoid it being soiled by her menstrual blood — it is prohibited for her to go out with it unless it is an apron made like a garment both in the front and the back. But if it is only in the back and she ties it with straps in the front, it is forbidden (Magen Avraham section 2). However, if she ties it to prevent pain or discomfort from the blood, she is permitted to go out with it. This is what we have learned in the Mishnah (64b): "A woman may go out... with a cloth prepared for her menstruation." But if it is not tied, it is prohibited, as it might fall and she would come to carry it.

And even though it is understood from this that anything a person wears to protect themselves from filth is considered a "melacha she'eina tzericha legufa" (a prohibited act on Shabbat that is not needed for its own sake), nevertheless, if it is something that is worn in the manner of clothing, even if it is worn only to protect from filth, it is permitted to go out with it on Shabbat. Therefore, it is permitted to wear a garment because of the rain, even an unsightly garment, as we say in Nedarim (55b): "One may go out with a thick sack, etc." And this is the language of our teacher, the Rema, in section 14: "Therefore it is permitted to wear a garment because of the rain or a hat on one's head, but it is forbidden for a woman to place a garment over her scarf because of the rain, for this is not the manner of wearing clothing." These are his words. This means that if only the head is covered, it is not considered wearing clothing, but if the body is also covered, it is considered wearing clothing (Taz, subparagraph 7 and Magen Avraham, subparagraph 23). However, if her intention is so that the rain does not cause her discomfort, it is permitted in any manner, even if it also protects from filth (ibid.). According to this, when it is raining and one covers their hat with a handkerchief, it is forbidden, because only the head is covered. However, if one also covers their face so that the rain does not cause discomfort, it is permitted, even though their intention is also to protect the hat from filth, as mentioned.

A person whose leg has been amputated – he cannot go out with his prosthetic leg, which is a form made in the shape of a leg with a hollow space to place his stump in it. He does not use it to walk, as he still needs a cane, but he uses it so that he appears to be lame rather than missing a leg. Since it is not necessary for walking, it is prohibited. According to Rashi, because it is considered a burden, and according to Tosafot, not because it is a burden, but because we fear it might fall off and he will come to carry it. Some explain this differently, where the stump is bent backwards and at the end of the stump, in place of the leg, he makes a prosthetic to appear as if he has a leg (Tosafot there according to Rabbi Porat's explanation). If this prosthetic reaches the ground and he steps on it – it is certainly permitted. But if it does not reach the ground, and he has another support that does reach the ground, and this prosthetic is only for appearance, since it does not reach the ground, we fear it might fall off and he will come to carry it (as explicitly stated in Tosafot there). According to the first explanation, even if it reaches the ground, it is prohibited. In Shulchan Aruch, section 15, only the first explanation is brought. However, it seems to me, in my humble opinion, that even according to the first explanation, if he steps on it properly, although he cannot walk without a cane, if it appears that if the prosthetic falls, the cane will not help – it is permitted to go out with it, and we do not fear it might fall and he will come to carry it, because if it falls, he cannot walk.

A person with an amputated leg who cannot walk at all on his thighs but sits on a chair, and when he moves from his place he supports himself on his hands and thighs and pushes himself forward, making supports out of leather or wood for the ends of his thighs or hanging legs, and when he leans on his hands and lifts himself up he also leans a bit on his legs - one may not go out with these on Shabbat, because since they are hanging and not placed on the ground, they might fall off. But with a chair and small stools in his hands, meaning he supports himself on them when he pushes himself forward - it is permitted to go out with them. And a person with amputated legs who walks on his thighs and knees and makes leather supports for his thighs - he may go out with them on Shabbat, because in this case there is no concern that they might fall off.

And our master the Rema wrote in section 16: "And it is also permitted to go out with a wooden shoe, where the foot enters it and there is no concern that it will fall off, and similarly with pattens that come off quickly and easily, and some are stringent and prohibit it." End quote. That is to say, with a wooden shoe it is permitted only if the foot enters it so that it adheres to the foot. But if it is much larger than the foot, it is forbidden, for we are concerned that it might fall off. However, pattens which are made of leather are permitted even if they are large, because they come off quickly, since they are made of leather or covered with tight leather and do not slip off, as one can walk in them. And it is not similar to a small child in a large shoe, which is forbidden to walk in, as stated in section 52, because there it does not fit the foot at all; but here it fits the foot, just with much space. And some indeed are stringent in such cases and compare it to a small child in a large shoe. And there is one who wrote that the main opinion follows the first view, because it is not customary to go barefoot in public, and if it falls off the foot, one will be compelled to put it back on (Taz at the end of subsection 27), and it is not similar to a small child in a large shoe, which is impossible to walk in at all. And one can rely on this in pressing circumstances, especially nowadays when no one goes barefoot. And everyone should be careful not to walk barefoot on Shabbat out of respect for Shabbat, even if he goes barefoot during the week, and also to remind himself that it is Shabbat, unless in a place where everyone goes barefoot. And besides shoes, one should also not go out on Shabbat in other clothes that he wears during the week, without something else to remind him that it is Shabbat, so that he does not come to desecrate it. And further, 'and honor it by not following your usual ways' – meaning that your Shabbat clothing should not be like your weekday clothing, as mentioned above in section 262, see there.

A lame person who cannot walk without a cane - it is permitted for him to walk with it even if it is not tied to him, as it is not considered a burden, since for him it is like his leg. And we are also not concerned that it might fall from his hand and he might carry it in his hand, since he cannot walk without it. However, if he is somewhat lame, or he is elderly and can walk without a cane, and at home he walks without a cane but takes it to walk more comfortably - it is forbidden even if he supports himself with it, because since he can walk without it - it is considered a burden. And certainly it is forbidden for a healthy person to walk with a fancy cane, as that would be considered carrying a load, and an ornament does not apply to something held in the hand. And a sick person who has recovered from his illness - his status is like that of a lame person if he cannot walk at all without a cane, meaning that even at home he walks with a cane. But otherwise - it is forbidden. However, an elderly or weak person, or someone who is somewhat lame, when he needs to walk on ice, or during icy times when it is impossible to walk without a cane lest he fall due to the slipperiness, since even for a healthy person walking is difficult as is known - it is permitted for him to walk with a cane (Taz 12).

And know that all those who we prohibited from walking with a cane—this is in a place where there is no eruv, but when there is an eruv—they are permitted, even though it may resemble weekday activities. A healthy person, it is obvious, is prohibited from walking with even a fine cane, as this is clearly a weekday activity. Nevertheless, all those for whom walking with a cane is better for them—they are permitted to walk with a cane. And what the Tur wrote: "One may not go out with a chair, meaning sitting in a chair carried by people, but if many need him—it is permitted," this is also in a place where there is an eruv (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 27).

And our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in paragraph 18 that a blind person is forbidden to go out with a cane, because if he is able to walk without a cane, it is considered a burden. However, in a place where there is an eruv, it is certainly permitted, and similarly, on the Sabbath, he is permitted to walk with a cane. It appears to me, in my humble opinion, that the prohibition applies only to a blind person in his familiar area, where he knows his way somewhat due to habit. But when he comes to another place, it is known that a blind person cannot walk at all without a cane to feel in front of him, and it is like a lame person, and without a cane, he would fall into a pit or stumble over something.

And one who is bound with chains on his legs, which are called "kletzlochs," as was done in ancient times - it is permissible for him to walk with them, for this is not considered a burden, as for him it is like a garment, and there is no concern that they will fall from his legs, for they are fastened well (Beit Yosef). And one may not go out with an "ankatmin," which is a type of donkey that jesters make, and it appears as if one is riding on it while it carries him and he walks with his legs. Similarly, one may not go out with "kesherim," which are high wooden clogs with a place for the foot to rest, used for walking in mud. Nor may one go out with "perami," which are masks that jesters wear on their faces to frighten children, for all these are considered burdens. Likewise, one may not go out with a chest on his head or a basket and mat, even if he carries them as a head covering, for they are considered a complete burden. However, one may go out with a sack, a curtain, and a thick cloak, even though these are thick and coarse garments that only simple people wear and are typically worn in the rainy season - nevertheless, they are considered garments. The term 'sack' refers to a garment made of sackcloth, and it is permitted to go out with them, as we have learned in the Tosefta in Chapter 10, and even in non-rainy times it is permitted to go out with them (Magen Avraham, Section 30).

One may go out with a cloth or sponge on a wound, and even though this is not a garment, since they provide healing, they are considered like an adornment for him. The same applies to a garlic or onion peel placed for healing, or a poultice, bandage, or plaster, as anything used for healing is considered like an adornment. If they fall off the wound, he should not replace them, as this would be considered like spreading an ointment. Certainly, one should not place them initially unless there is danger or they are placed by a non-Jew. The details of these laws are not discussed here and will be explained, with God's help, in section 328. One is permitted to tie the bandage with a thread or string to prevent it from falling off, and he may walk with it, tying and untying it. However, to wrap a thread or string around it for decoration and not for tying is forbidden, as they are not nullified to it and it is considered carrying. But those needed for tying are nullified to it (see Magen Avraham, subsection 31). Similarly, one may go out with types of herbs tied in knots and hung for healing, provided they were given by an expert or it is known that these herbs are beneficial. Otherwise, it is forbidden (this is my opinion).

And it is also permitted to go out with an expert amulet because it is like an ornament for him. But with a non-expert amulet, it is forbidden to go out even into a karmelit. And what is an expert amulet? According to Rashi, of blessed memory, if the maker of the amulet is established as an expert, his amulet is effective even for other matters for which he has not yet become accustomed. Similarly, if this amulet has been proven to heal, it is permitted to go out with it even if others have written it, because this incantation has been proven to heal. This also appears from the language of the Rambam who wrote in Chapter 12: "And what is an expert amulet? One that has healed three people, or one made by a person who has healed three people with other amulets. And if one goes out with a non-expert amulet, he is exempt because he took it out in the manner of a garment." And it is possible that what he wrote, "one that has healed three people" refers specifically to this writing, but it seems more likely that his intention is like that of Rashi, of blessed memory.

However, our rabbis, the Tosafists, have a different approach to this matter, and the Rosh, the Tur, and the Shulchan Aruch agreed with it. The concept of "the person is established but not the amulet" means, for example, that someone wrote one incantation on three different amulets, and all three amulets healed three different people, each healing one person. In this case, the person is established for this specific incantation he writes, as he has been proven effective with three incantations. However, for other incantations, he is not established, and the amulet itself is not considered established except through its writer. 

The practical difference is that if another person writes it, it is not established, and also, if this established person loses his effectiveness, for example, if he writes and it does not heal, he loses his established status for this one as well. The concept of "the amulet is established but not the person" applies when someone writes one incantation on an amulet and it heals three times. This amulet is considered established for anyone who carries it, even if it only healed one person three times - still, this amulet itself is considered established but not another amulet, even with the same incantation and even by the same writer.

The concept of "both the person and the amulet are established" applies when someone writes this incantation on three different amulets, and each amulet heals three times for three people or for one person - the person is established for this incantation in any amulet he writes, and these three amulets are established for any person.

But if [a person] wrote three amulets for one person and they healed three times, neither the individual [who wrote the amulets] nor the amulet is considered established, because we attribute it to the luck of the sick person, and only this sick person is permitted to go out with it, unless the individual [who wrote the amulets] lost his certification, as is written. (In Magen Avraham, section 339, there is a printing error, as is written in Machatzit HaShekel). And why don't we attribute it initially when each letter heals three times for one person to the sick person—because there were three letters, and we would need to attribute it to the luck of all three, and therefore we attribute it more to the individual [who wrote the amulets].

And know that when we say that both are established, this is when the two certifications come together, such as when he wrote a letter to Reuven and healed, and a letter to Shimon and healed, and additional letters to Shimon and healed twice, that no letters have yet been established for three times and he has not yet been established with three people. Afterwards, he healed with the third letter to Levi, and the two certifications came together. But if he gave three letters to three people and they were healed, and the person was certified, then the amulets are not certified anymore because we attribute it to the certification of the person. And if you wonder what difference it makes, the difference is if the person loses his certification, as it is written (there, Siman 338).

It is permitted to go out with an expert amulet, whether it is an amulet of writing or an amulet of roots, whether for a person who is in danger or for a person who is not in danger. And it is not only when the illness already exists and he hangs it for healing, but even if he has not yet been seized by the illness, but he is from a family that has this illness, and he hangs the amulet so that he will not be seized by the illness - it is permitted. However, with an amulet that contains verses, it is forbidden to go out with it unless it is covered with leather (as stated in the Gemara 61b), so that when he enters the bathroom it will not be exposed. And he may tie and untie the amulet in the public domain, and we do not worry that he might carry it four cubits in the public domain, because those who possess amulets are careful not to move from their place without the amulet. However, he should not tie it with a bracelet or a ring and go out with it into the public domain, because then there will be suspicion that people will say he is going out with it as an ornament, and this is forbidden, for it is not an ornament. And the physician is trusted to say about himself that he is an expert.

We learned in the Mishnah (Shabbat 67a): One may go out with a locust egg—a type of grasshopper—and it is for ear pain, and with a fox's tooth, which is a charm to induce sleep in the sick, and with a nail from a crucifixion, which is a remedy for wounds and tertian fever. And the version we have says, "These are the words of Rabbi Meir, but the Sages say even on a weekday it is forbidden because of the ways of the Amorites." According to this, it should be ruled as prohibited like the Sages. However, the Rambam, the Tur, and the Shulchan Aruch, Section 27, ruled it permissible, and this is based on the Jerusalem Talmud, which reads: "These are the words of Rabbi Yossi, and Rabbi Meir forbids," and the law follows Rabbi Yossi. Even according to our version, the law follows Rabbi Meir, because the Gemara there says: Abaye and Rava both said: Any matter that has medicinal value, meaning that experience has proven its efficacy, does not fall under the prohibition of the ways of the Amorites, and these have been proven effective. And this is what Rambam wrote: "And it is when doctors say it is beneficial," meaning that experience has proven to them its efficacy, and certainly when doctors prescribe natural remedies based on medical wisdom, it is permitted. But one who performs an action that has no natural medicinal value, and has also not been proven effective by experience, it is prohibited even on a weekday because of the ways of the Amorites. However, various incantations are permitted, provided they are not from idolatrous practices, and those that have been tested and found ineffective are prohibited. Some are concerned with any amulet that is not from an expert because of the ways of the Amorites, and the Rashba in his responsa (Siman 513) elaborated extensively on these matters but did not conclude with a clear ruling. And the clear matter in this is: Be wholehearted with the Lord your God, and only use expert doctors, prayer to God, and charity, as these certainly help.

One who has a wound on the sole of his foot and ties a coin on it to protect it from getting injured, and it is customary for this to be a hard metal object made of silver that has some moisture in it, and that it should have an image on it (Gemara and Rashi 65a). And so wrote the Rambam in his commentary on the Mishnah that this is one of the remedies (see there). There is an opinion that if it does not heal but only protects the foot from getting injured, it is forbidden (Magen Avraham, section 141). However, this does not seem to be the case in the Gemara there, and reason also does not support this view. The prominent authorities have also ruled leniently (Eliyah Rabbah, section 151; Taz, section 145, in the name of Maharshak, see there). And this is the main ruling in practice.

Children may go out with small bells, which are woven into their garments. However, if they are not woven in, it is forbidden, because we are concerned that they might fall off and the child will come to carry them. Similarly, if they are sewn in, it is considered as if they are woven. (See Magen Avraham, section 32, which requires further investigation, as the Tosafot write explicitly in Shabbat 66b, s.v. ‘bnei’ that if it is not woven, we are concerned that it might tear off, and what does he compare this to section 9? And what he brings from all the words of the Tosafot – they wrote this according to Rabbi Oshaya and not according to Rava, and this is also explicitly stated in the Bach, and also the Taz wrote so, and see Machatzit HaShekel, and there is no reason in his words. And behold, the Levush also wrote this because it might fall off and be carried, and it is questionable who compelled him to this, and the reason is simply because it might fall off and be carried, and consider this well.)

And our master, the Rema, wrote in section 23 that it is not effective if something is attached to the garment unless it is something that is ordinarily attached there. However, if one attaches something that is not ordinarily attached there - it is forbidden. And those green circles that the Persian government decreed every Jew must wear on their garment - it is permissible to go out with it even if it is not sewn to the garment but only slightly attached there. Similarly, it is permissible to go out with handkerchiefs used to wipe the nose, which are called "patsilyot," if they are attached to the garment. And the matter of going out with woven bells - it is specifically when they do not have a clapper and do not produce sound. These words need explanation.

And this is its explanation: Behold, the Mishnah permits going out with bells woven into a garment, and consequently, the same applies to those sewn into a garment, as there is also no concern with sewing that it might fall and be carried in one's hands. However, with tying – it is forbidden, as we worry that it might fall (and so writes the Taz in sub-section 14 in the name of the Sefer Mitzvot Gadol that specifically sewing is permitted). However, even with weaving and sewing, it was only permitted for something that is customary to do so, like bells in their time. But if someone wants to attach some ornament to a garment by weaving and sewing in a way that is not customary – it is forbidden because it does not become secondary to the garment and is considered a burden, and certainly, something that is not an ornament at all is forbidden. And if you ask, if so, how is it permitted to carry green circles – that is not a question, for on the contrary, this is even more lenient than an ornament of bells, and it does not require weaving and sewing but only a slight connection, because it is mandatory by the government to carry this on the garment, thus people are afraid to go out without it and ensure that it does not fall, and it is like the slave's collar (in the Gemara 58a). And even though there we worry that it might fall and he will place the garment on his shoulder – that is because its connection is weak, as will be explained in section 87, but here it is well connected, though not by weaving and sewing.

And afterwards, it is permitted even for something that is neither an ornament nor a decree but a necessity for the body, such as a handkerchief used to wipe the nose—it is permissible to attach it to clothing by weaving or sewing, and it is considered subordinate to the clothing. However, tying it is forbidden. And with a belt, even sewing does not help, because the belt is not significant enough for the handkerchief to be considered subordinate to it, and it is considered a burden (Magen Avraham, section 34, and concerning what he wrote about a capona and cloth, I do not know what they are). 

Know that there are those who permit tying the end of the belt to the end of the handkerchief with a non-permanent knot, making it like a long belt (Taz, section 14). This permission is not understandable: firstly, it requires sewing, and even if we say that a strong knot is like sewing (as explicitly stated in the Bayit Chadash), in any case, a non-permanent knot is certainly not like sewing, and there is concern that the knot will come undone, and it will fall and one may come to carry it. Besides this, everyone sees that they are two different things and it is not entirely a belt, therefore it should not be permitted (also the Eliyah Rabbah, section 43, and the Gra question this, as mentioned there, and the Turei Zahav wrote that clothing requires sewing and a belt is sufficient with tying, as mentioned there, and there is no reason for this).

And what the Rema wrote about not making a sound, the Magen Avraham questioned in section 35, as it is only forbidden with musical instruments, as mentioned there. It seems that the Rema's intention is the same, that they make a sound like musical instruments.

We learned in the Mishnah (Shabbat 60a): A man should not go out with a nailed sandal, which is made of wood with nails inserted above to strengthen the connection between the bottom and the top (Rashi). It is stated in the Gemara that this applies specifically when the nails are used for reinforcement, but if they are for adornment, it is permitted. The sign of adornment is when there are five or seven nails on each sandal. If one places a leather shoe inside and sews it, it becomes a shoe and not a sandal, and it is permitted. Similarly, if the nails are made in the shape of a horseshoe, like our pattens, it is permitted, as the decree only applied to simple nails. Additionally, if the entire sandal is covered with nails to prevent the ground from wearing it out, it is permitted. The reason for this decree was due to an incident where many Jews were killed on Shabbat out of fear caused by these sandals. Therefore, they decreed not to wear or handle them on Shabbat and Yom Tov. Nowadays, this ruling does not apply, as the Tur stated, because our nailed shoes are not included in this prohibition. The prohibition only applied to their specific form at that time, and ours are made of leather, not wood. Therefore, this is not brought in the Shulchan Aruch. The Rambam mentioned this briefly (the Tur wrote that some have the custom to prohibit, but we have not heard of this).

The Rambam wrote there, law 18: "A slave goes out with a clay seal around his neck, but not with a metal seal, lest it fall and he bring it" (end of quote). But a clay seal – if it falls, it will break, and why would he bring it. And it is explained in the Gemara (58a) that a seal on his garment – even a clay one is forbidden, because we are concerned that it might fall and break, and due to his fear of going without a seal – he will remove the garment and place it on his shoulders, see there. And it seems that it was attached to the garment easily, because if it were attached by sewing or weaving – why would we be concerned that it might fall. And the Tur and Shulchan Aruch did not bring this because now we do not have slaves, and the Rambam also shortened this as I wrote.

Maimonides wrote (there): "One who wraps himself in his tallit and folds it here and there in his hand or on his shoulder, if he intends to gather its corners so that they do not tear or become dirty, it is forbidden. However, if he gathers them to adorn himself as per the custom of the people of the place, it is permitted. One who goes out with a folded tallit placed on his shoulder is liable, but he may go out with a scarf on his shoulder even though it is not tied by a string to his finger. Any scarf that does not cover his head and most of his body, it is forbidden to go out with it. If it was a small scarf that is not wide, he ties its two ends below his shoulders, making it like a belt, and it is permitted to go out with it." End of quote. (The first law is from Rav Yehudah in the Gemara 147, which states: "If the intent is to gather, it is forbidden; to adorn, it is permitted." The second law is as the Gemara states: "If the tallit is placed on his shoulder, he is liable for a sin offering. There was an incident with Horkinus who went out with a scarf on his shoulder... and the Sages said even though it was not tied with a string, etc." The words of the Taz in section 2 are perplexing. The law regarding not covering his head and most of his body is also there on page 2, and also the small scarf is mentioned there.)

And the explanation of the matter is as follows, which is clear in my humble opinion: This is like our mitzvah garment (tallit) in which one wraps their whole body until their entire body, in front and behind, is covered by it. There are those who, out of concern for the edges of the tallit that hang over their hands and also reach in front, fold the two edges from here and there, and hold them in their hand or place them on their shoulder, and the tallit hangs down behind them to below, but it does not spread over their hands. And it appears from behind in the middle like a gutter, that because of the gathering of the sides, it becomes thick at its sides and in the middle like a gutter. This is the explanation of the "gutter" mentioned in the Gemara there. And it depends on his intention: if his intention is to protect the tallit, it is forbidden; but if it is to adorn himself, as even now the meticulous do not want the tallit to hang over their hands but rather over their shoulders, it is permitted. And also the Aruch in the entry "gutter" explained it this way, see there, and it is brought in Tosafot, see there. And in this, the Rambam wrote that it is only forbidden, but there is no liability of a sin offering, since after all, he is still wearing it as a garment. (And therefore, he preceded this law to the folded one, even though in the Gemara the folded one comes first, because he initially dealt with a rabbinic prohibition of a slave's seal, and included this with the seal, see there, and both are rabbinic, see there).

And afterwards, he wrote: "One who goes out with a folded tallit placed on his shoulder is liable." The explanation is as follows: a tallit is large enough to cover the whole body, and if one wishes to carry it only on his shoulder, there are those who completely remove it and then fold it from both sides as mentioned, and there are those who do not remove it but rather wear it on their shoulder while it is folded in half or quarters - in this case, one is liable for a sin offering, because in such forms it is not considered a garment at all. And this is regarding a tallit, but a scarf which is not so large, which scholars who were married used to wear on their heads, spreading over the shoulders as evidenced in Kiddushin (29b), and in Shabbat (147b) they said: 'a scarf - the secret of God is for those who fear Him', and similarly in Pesachim (111b): 'the master's scarf is like that of a scholar' - see there. Therefore, even if it is not worn on the head but only on the shoulders, it is permissible, because it is customary to wear a scarf this way since it is not large, and it has hard threads at its ends, which are held in the hands to prevent it from falling, and they are like small hooks, and even if the thread is not tied to his finger but he holds it in his hands. And then he said: And any scarf that does not cover his head and most of his body, that is, although the scarf is much smaller than a tallit, nevertheless it should not be so small that it does not cover his head and most of his body, and if it is indeed a short scarf that does not cover his head and most of his body, he should not wear it as a garment, but rather make it into a belt and tie its two ends with hooks below the shoulders around the body. And all these matters have no relevance to our garments, as is obvious.

However, our master, the Beit Yosef, in sections 29, 31, and 34, directed all matters towards a different intention. And this is his wording in section 29: "One who goes out with a folded tallit on his shoulders, meaning that after placing it on his head, he raises its edges onto his shoulders, is liable for a sin offering. But if it is not folded on his shoulders but rather hangs down broadly below his shoulders, it is permitted, because since he is wrapping himself in his tallit and covering his shoulders and body with it, even if it is somewhat shortened below, it is allowed. Based on this, it is permitted to wrap oneself in one's tallit under the cloak and bring it to the synagogue." And our master the Rema added: "Even though he places the right side on his left shoulder, as it is customary to wear it in this manner, it is only for adornment and is permitted." (This gloss is mistakenly printed in section 30, as the Taz wondered there, but the truth is it belongs to section 29, as is explained in the Beit Yosef there. There is no need for all the efforts on this matter. Pay close attention.)

And behold, this explanation about a folded tallit was written by Rashi, of blessed memory, see there, and similarly by the Tur. However, this is not the way of the Rambam. In any case, it is possible that regarding the law, the Rambam would not disagree with this ruling. According to this ruling, if one lifts the entire length of the tallit from its edges to the top and wraps it around his shoulders, this is not considered a garment at all, even if the edges are folded in front, and he is liable for a sin offering. But if he lets it hang down from his shoulders, even though much of it is wrapped around his shoulders in a manner that the tallit does not reach down, nevertheless, it is considered a garment because it covers most of the body from behind. This is the way we wear the tallit on Shabbat when walking to the synagogue, even if one places the right side on the left shoulder, which is the way we do during the wrapping as is known. However, according to what we have explained regarding the Rambam's intention in section 89 concerning the one law about folding it from here and there, the tallit needs to be lowered from the sides of the shoulders onto the hands as mentioned there, and this also seems to be from the explanation of the Aruch, and it also seems to me from the words of the Tur by the precision of his language, see there (for if not, what kind of adornment is there in this, and scrutinize well).

Indeed, the words of our master, the Beit Yosef, are perplexing, as they contradict his own words written later in Section 30: "It is permitted to go out into the public domain with a tallit around one's neck," end quote, which contradicts what he wrote earlier, that even over one's shoulders is forbidden, and all the more so just around the neck. The source of this law is from the responsa of the Rashba, who was asked from a certain place where they wear the tallit around their necks. He replied: All of Spain has the custom of going out in this manner as a sign of modesty, even in the courtyard, and it is considered a form of clothing for them. See there. The commentators have already labored over this (see Taz at the end of Section 19 and Levush). In my humble opinion, it is clear that here we are not dealing with a tallit like our tallitot, but with a small tallit similar to a scarf (as is explicitly stated in the Beit Yosef, see there). This is like what we call a shawl, which some call a scarf, which is wrapped around the neck, and it is for beauty and modesty. Our master, the Beit Yosef, in the Shulchan Aruch, did not bother to elaborate and explain, as is his way in the Shulchan Aruch.

Some have written: The scholars who hang the scarf over their shoulders as an ornament - it is forbidden to go out with it. In Constantinople, they are not careful about this, but those who are meticulous tuck the ends of the scarf into their belts, and now there is no concern that it might slip off. It seems that one must tie it to the belt (Magen Avraham 142:2 in the name of Kenesset HaGedola). This is also similar to the question of the Rashba, of blessed memory, regarding small scarves similar to our shawls. Those who forbid it do so because it is like a folded tallit on the shoulders, which is forbidden. In Constantinople, they permit it according to the opinion of the Rashba, as it is not similar to a tallit, as mentioned. However, there is a concern that it might fall and one might come to carry it, so they tuck the ends into the belt, and it is proper to be stringent and tie it to the belt. We wear scarves by inserting the right side into the left side of the garment and the left side into the right. In our case, there is no concern that they might fall because they are narrow in width and long in length and protrude significantly in the front. (Also, what Magen Avraham wrote in 143:3 in the name of Maharil that it is permissible to go out with our tallitot, see there, it must be said either that his intention is that it hangs below the shoulders or that it is a small tallit like our scarf, and his intention is also like the Rashba.)

In section 31, our master the Beit Yosef wrote: "One who goes out wrapped in his tallit and folds it here and there, etc.," as is the language of the Rambam that we brought in section 88. And afterward, he wrote: "This applies to their tallitot which were a single rectangular piece, but regarding our garments, when one is wearing them and extends his hands out from them—it is permissible to hold part of it in his hand to lift it so that its edges do not become soiled with mud, or so that it does not hinder him from walking," end quote. From this, it seems that he interpreted the Rambam's words "and folds it here and there" to mean folding it from the bottom up, not as we explained in section 89 that it is folded from the sides onto the shoulders. According to his interpretation, this would also be like the ruling of a folded tallit, except that there, it is raised completely to the shoulders, and here, only the edges are raised significantly. And I do not understand, in such cases, what relevance this has to aesthetic appearance, but for the ruling, it makes no difference to us. And behold, regarding our garments, he permitted it even without the intent of appearance, since they have sleeves and one inserts their hands in them—it is considered a complete garment. (And the Taz in subparagraph 21 disagrees on this matter, see there, and all his words need examination, and the words of the Beit Yosef are correct, and so wrote the Eliyah Rabbah in subparagraph 53. And it is possible that the Taz only prohibited when they are raised completely upwards, and in this, his words are certainly correct, and this is also the intent of the Beit Yosef as will be explained in the next section.)

This permission is only when they lift them from the ground, and in any case, it appears to all that it is considered a garment. But if they lift it up higher - it is certainly forbidden. And this is what the Maharil wrote (brought by the Magen Avraham 144:4): "Those women who let down and fold their garments under their arms to lift them so that their hems do not get soiled - it is forbidden… but they can lift them with their hands without any folding." End quote. And this is its explanation: If they lift them up high under their arms - the garment is no longer considered a garment; rather, they should lift them with their hands without folding, as naturally, they will not lift them up too high, as is understood (and so wrote the Magen Avraham there). And even in lifting from the ground, the Levush wrote that if they do not wear them on the wristbands to insert their hands into them - they should not lift them too much, near their shoulders, see there. In any case, it appears to me that lifting a little is not a concern. (In the Levush, the language is not precise, as it concludes differently than it started, but the intention is as I have written, see there).

In section 34, our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote: "A person may go out with a folded scarf on his shoulder even if there is no thread wrapped around his finger. However, if the scarf does not cover his head and most of his body, it is forbidden to go out with it, unless he ties the two ends of the scarf from his shoulders together." This is the end of his words. This is based on the language of the Rambam, except he added 'folded on his shoulder.' Indeed, this language is not found in the Gemara or the Rambam, but only the Tur wrote this. This is very puzzling, for if so, what is the difference between a scarf and a tallit? Many have already questioned this (Taz, subsection 24). Moreover, if you think it is so large, then how can it be said: 'if it does not cover his head and most of his body.' The Tur indeed did not write this language, but certainly, the scarf is small; some cover their head and most of their body, and some do not. (This is the "sachnita" mentioned in the Gemara there, and the Tur interpreted "sachnita" differently, as a large scarf that hangs between his shoulders and his head is wrapped in it, and we are concerned it might fall, therefore it needs to be tied. The Taz, subsection 24, elaborated extensively and it is difficult to understand his intention, but from the end of his words, it seems he agrees with what we wrote in section 89, that when carrying the tallit from the synagogue, it should be draped over the hands if praying in this manner. See there and understand.)

It is stated in the Gemara (147a): "One who goes out with coins wrapped in his cloth - is liable for a sin offering." This exact language is written by the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch, section 32, and the Rambam wrote it in chapter 12. In truth, at first glance, there is no novelty here, as this is a complete act of carrying. However, the main novelty is that we do not say this is an unusual manner of carrying and thus only prohibited by rabbinic decree, since the usual way for coins is to be in a pocket and not wrapped in a cloth. The teaching is that one is liable because this is the way of shopkeepers. This is what the Gemara says there: "And a shopkeeper who goes out [with coins wrapped in his cloth]... is liable for a sin offering, and not only a shopkeeper but any person, except that it is usual for a shopkeeper to go out with coins wrapped in his cloth."

And our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 33: "It is forbidden to go out on Shabbat with money or silver and gold sewn into one's garment." End quote. He did not use the term 'liable' as he did with bundles in one's sheet because this is certainly carrying in an unusual manner, and therefore it is only forbidden by rabbinic decree. Now, the Rambam wrote in Chapter 12, Law 13: "But one who carries with the back of his hand... or in a pocket sewn into his garment with the opening of the pocket downward... is exempt," and we brought this above in section 5. If so, it implies that only when the pocket's opening is downward is it considered carrying in an unusual manner, but if its opening is upward, one is liable. We must say that when the money is sewn without a pocket, it is considered carrying in an unusual manner in any case, but when it is placed in a pocket and the pocket is sewn into the garment, this is considered a typical manner of carrying unless its opening is downward. According to this, when one places the money in a pocket or another object and sews it into the garment, one is liable for a sin offering, and there is a practical difference in law, as we will explain with God's help.

Our master, the Rema, wrote on this: "There are those who permit [carrying money] in the case of a loss, such as if a caravan might rob him if he leaves it in the house and goes away from them. And so, the custom is to be lenient if one needs to go out. But if he can stay at home and not go out, he should not go out. And in a situation where it is not necessary and he can leave it at home, one should be stringent." End quote. The reason is that since it is an indirect form of carrying (Magen Avraham section 146), they permitted it in a case of loss. And according to what we have explained, the permission is only if the money itself is sewn [into the garment] without a pouch.
