But if it is placed in a pouch and then sewn, it is a biblical prohibition and one is liable to bring a sin offering. And because merchants now customarily rely on this leniency, as they do not want to entrust large sums to the innkeeper, and they sew the money into their garments, they should be careful not to sew it into a pouch or other wrapping. However, if they wrap it in paper and sew it, it seems this is like without a pouch, for a pouch is not made from paper. Nonetheless, the best practice is not to leave the inn all Shabbat, as our master the Rema wrote, and it is better to pray individually and not go to the synagogue than to follow this leniency. However, the merchants have adopted this as a complete leniency, so they should at least be careful not to place it in a pouch as mentioned.

There are those who say that just as we permit when they are sewn into his garment, so too, even if they are not sewn in and he holds the money between his garment and his flesh—it is permitted because of potential loss (Taz 23). And there are those who say that if they are not sewn in—it is completely forbidden (Magen Avraham there), and this seems to me to be the primary view, and this is close to a liability for a sin-offering, for they are certainly in a pocket. If not, how could he carry them? And regarding a pocket, we have already explained that even if they are sewn in, it constitutes a regular manner of carrying and he is liable for a sin-offering. And regarding the matter clarified that for coins wrapped in his garment he is liable for a sin-offering, our teacher the Rema wrote: that in the house it is permitted even if they are not wrapped, as long as they are perforated. But if he goes out into the public domain—he is liable for carrying, but in the house and a courtyard with an eruv—there is no carrying. And even though there is still the prohibition of muktzeh, to this I say that it is permissible, for he is not holding them in his hands but they are wrapped in his garment, and they are nullified regarding the garment in such a manner that it does not constitute carrying muktzeh with his hands. Moreover, if the coins are perforated such that they are suitable for hanging around the necks of boys and girls as an ornament—it is permitted to carry them even if they are not wrapped, just carrying them next to his garment or in a pocket of the garment. But to carry them directly with his hands—there is certainly no permission even if they are perforated (Magen Avraham 45, and what is written about carrying outside the eruv needs further study and should not be permitted, examine this thoroughly).

It has already been explained in section 73 that one may go out with thick garments such as sackcloth, a curtain, and a cloak. Rambam writes in Chapter 19, Law 17: "A cushion and a pillow, if they are soft and thin like garments, it is permitted to take them out placed on one's head on Shabbat in the manner of a garment. But if they are hard, they are considered a burden and are forbidden." Certainly, he is not referring to our cushions and pillows that contain feathers and where the feathers are the primary part, as it would not be appropriate to wear them. Rather, he refers to soft bedding, like thick sheets that are spread on beds. According to their custom, they would go out wrapped in them, as is still done today in the lands of the Ishmaelites. Therefore, if they are soft, they are like a garment, but if they are hard, they are like a burden. Consequently, with hard cloths, it is forbidden to wrap oneself in them and bring them through the public domain or a karmelit, but if they are not very hard, it is permitted. As for cloths, this refers to what is called "felt," and in our country, this is not considered a garment at all, even if they are soft. Only because of the rain do some women wrap themselves in sheets and similar items, and certainly, this is permitted in such cases. Hence, even without rain, if they go out with them, one should not rebuke them, as stated in section 73. However, men do not have the custom to carry them even in the rain, and it is forbidden for them to go out with them, as here it is certainly considered a burden. Nevertheless, regarding the law, it requires further investigation.

It is permissible to go out on Shabbat wearing two garments, one on top of the other, whether for one's own need or for the need of a friend, meaning that his intention is to bring it to his friend in a manner that is considered wearing it as a garment. The reason is that since it is customary to wear several garments because of the cold or for adornment, it is always considered a manner of wearing a garment. There is no difference whether they are two shirts or two overcoats, that is, outer garments, or other types of two clothes, and similarly, two belts one on top of the other even without a garment separating them. Some prohibit wearing two belts one on top of the other unless a garment separates them, as it is not similar to two garments, since with cold there is benefit from the second garment and it is customary to do so, but with two belts, what benefit does one have, and it is not customary to do so, and it becomes a burden. Only with a garment separating can one wear a belt over any garment. However, if it is customary with this garment to wear two belts, one above and one below, it is certainly permissible (Taz, subparagraph 25). Women who have garments with sewn-in ties to be worn with them, and afterwards they wear another belt of silk or silver, if it is their custom, it is certainly permitted. However, it is better that they do not wear the sewn-in ties so that the belt becomes necessary. Nevertheless, there is no prohibition with the sewn-in tie, and it is not considered a burden because it is secondary to the garment (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 149, and he writes that it is better not to wear it there, but there is no prohibition as mentioned, and we wrote such a suggestion in section 48 regarding a kerchief there). See section 106 and section 107.

It is certainly permitted to wear two coverings on the head, for this is how our ancestors walked with a small covering on the head and a larger covering like a hat over it. And this is what our teacher, the Rema, wrote in paragraph 36, that it is permitted to wear two hats one on top of the other, and his intention is also the same. For wearing two large hats together is certainly forbidden, as no one walks like that and it would be considered a burden, but his intention is as I wrote. And it seems to me that in a place where the government is strict about those who wear a small covering under the large one and punishes for this, it is forbidden to walk there in such a manner, for it is obvious that one should be concerned about being approached by a police officer, and out of fear, one might remove the covering from his head and hide it in his garment, as has happened several times in this matter. And one can wear two socks and two shoes one on top of the other, as it is now customary in the world to walk this way as is known.

Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in paragraph 37: "It is permissible to go out on Shabbat with gloves called guantesh, which in our language are called henchuch. There are those who are stringent and require that they be sewn to the sleeves of one's garments on the eve of Shabbat or that they be tied with a strong, secure knot, and it is proper to be concerned with their opinion." The reason for permitting is that it is considered a garment like all garments, as all garments are for the body, and these are garments for the hands. The reason for prohibiting is that it is known that one cannot properly feel the body with gloves, and we are concerned that one might want to feel and remove them and then carry them four cubits. Therefore, sewing or tying is required (Beit Yosef), for in such cases, it becomes as one with the garment. And there are those who say that tying does not nullify it to the garment, and it becomes a burden if one removes it (Taz, section 26). And for mittens, which in our language are called mofta, where both hands are warmed in them - it is certainly permissible, for even if one hand is removed, it remains on the other hand (ibid.). But for gloves (henchuch) - it is proper to be stringent, and this is the custom. However, if the cold is severe, it is permitted without question.

He also wrote in section 44: "One who comes to save his belongings from a fire—he may wear whatever he can wear and wrap himself with whatever he can wrap himself, and then he removes them, goes back, wears, and takes them out again," end quote, which is a clear Mishnah (120). And one should not ask, since even without a fire we permitted wearing two garments in section 103, as it can be said that in the case of a fire, they permitted even many layers one on top of the other. This is certainly forbidden without a fire because people do not normally do this even in cold weather, as is known, but in the case of a fire, they permitted even many layers.

A mosquito net, which is a type of garment spread out like a sheet and has many straps that are stretched out and the straps hang - it is permitted to wrap oneself in it and go out into the public domain, and the straps are not considered a burden because they are subordinate to the net. Therefore, a belt with straps hanging from it that are made to tie the shoes on one's feet - it is permitted to go out into the public domain with the belt, even though the straps are hanging and are not tied to the shoes, because they are subordinate to the belt. However, if the straps are made of silk, which are valuable - they are not subordinate, and it is forbidden if the shoes are not tied with them. The same applies to anything that is detached from a garment but one end is still attached, such as loops: if they are not important - they are subordinate, and it is permitted to go out with the garment, but if they are important - they are not subordinate. And here, a house garment that we call a "shtub chalate" which has long straps in the back that are sewn and wrapped around the garment like a belt - they are definitely subordinate to the garment, and it is permitted to go out with the garment even when it is not tied and the straps are hanging behind the garment, and the straps of the pants - they are subordinate to the pants. And those who wear suspenders on the shoulders that connect with clips on the pants in the loops of the suspenders, if the suspenders are not connected, meaning the loops of the suspenders are not inserted into the clips of the pants - it is forbidden to go out into the public domain or a karmelit, because they are considered a separate item and are a burden. And there is one who says that if there is one strap and the other is broken and he intends to fix it - it is forbidden to go out with it, because it is not subordinate to the garment, and these words are an error. (The Chayei Adam brought this from Tosafot 139:) (This is only in regard to tzitzit as explained in the Rambam and Ran, and pay attention).

Therefore, one who goes out on Shabbat with a tallit that does not have its tzitzit properly made is liable for a sin-offering, because those threads are important to him and he intends to complete and make them into tzitzit, and the significance of the mitzvah is considered importance. It seems to me that if his intention is to discard them, they are not considered significant and are nullified. And if it is properly made according to the halacha, even though we do not have techelet, it is permitted to go out with it on Shabbat, because its mitzvah now is with white alone, as stated earlier in Siman 13. Even on Shabbat night, when it is not the time for tzitzit, it is permitted since this is the way of wearing it. Nonetheless, it seems to me that it is prohibited to go out with a large tallit on Shabbat night, since it is not customary to wear it at night, except on the night of Yom Kippur when we do wear it, and it is permitted to go out with it then. However, if he does go out with it, he is not liable for a sin-offering, because it is a garment of a mitzvah (this is how it appears to me).

The Tur writes: "A hat, if it is not tightly secured on the head – it is forbidden to go out with it into the public domain, lest the wind blow it off and one come to carry it. But if it is tightly secured: according to Rashi, it is permitted even if it protrudes a tefach; according to Rabbeinu Tam, if it protrudes a tefach – it is forbidden due to the prohibition of making a tent even indoors, and if it does not protrude a tefach – it is permitted even in the public domain." End quote. And this is also the opinion of the Rambam, of blessed memory, at the end of chapter 22, and his words are: "A hat that is made for the head and has a surrounding brim that provides shade like a tent over the garment – it is permitted to wear it. But if it extends from the garment around the head or in front of the face like a tent, and it is tightly secured on the head and the brim that extends is very stiff like a roof – it is forbidden, because it makes a temporary tent." End quote. 

It follows that according to Rashi, our hats that we call "sliafa" or "hut" or "kapeloyis", if not tightly secured – it is forbidden lest it fall from the head and one come to carry it four cubits in the public domain, but when it is tightly secured on the head – we are not concerned. Similarly, if it is deep and the head enters into it, it is permitted. Also, if it is not customary to go in the street without this hat – it is permitted, because if it falls, one will immediately pick it up and place it back on the head (Magen Avraham, section 52), and all the more so if one does not wear a small covering on the head, that one would remain bareheaded, we are not concerned. And so, we are only concerned in the public domain and not in a karmelit, and therefore nowadays it is permitted according to Rashi, of blessed memory, and all the more so if it is tied with a strap under the chin.

However, regarding the issue of a tent, Rashi does not agree. One could say the reason is that there is no tent without partitions. Additionally, a tent is only considered as such if it resembles a building and not a garment, similar to how covering vessels is not considered a tent, as will be explained in Siman 315 with God's help. Another reason is that a tent made all at once is not considered a tent because the prohibition of a tent is due to building, and all building is done gradually (this reasoning was written by the Ran in the chapter "Tol'in" in the name of Rabbeinu Yonah, of blessed memory). See also what is written in Siman 315, section 12.

However, the opinion of Rabbeinu Tam and the Rambam, as well as the opinion of Rabbi Chananel, is that when it is a handbreadth wide, it is considered a tent when it is rigid, but certainly not when it is soft. Therefore, if one removes the tallit from over his head, even if more than a handbreadth is extended, it is not an issue, but when it is rigid, it is considered a tent. And even if we say that these rabbis also agree with the general rules of a tent that we explained in the previous paragraph, they still hold that this hat is considered a tent because it is made for shade initially to protect the eyes (see Taz, section 315, subparagraph 11). And if it goes in a slant like a beret, it is not considered a tent (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 51), and furthermore, according to this view, the prohibition of a tent is only when the intention is for shade, and in our case, that is not the intention, as is well known. It seems to me that those who are concerned about their eyes and place a wide piece in front of their eyes, which is called a berilik, even if it is a handbreadth wide and rigid and intended for shade, nevertheless there is no prohibition in this, because it goes in a slant, and also certainly, even according to those who prohibit because of a tent, it is not considered a complete tent, as is obvious, and therefore it is not prohibited for those with eye ailments.

And our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 40: "A hat that extends a tefach beyond one's head - it is forbidden to wear it on one's head even indoors because of [the prohibition of making] a tent." These are his words. He did not bother to explain that this applies only to a hard hat, and he was brief on this matter. Later, in section 41, he wrote: "To go out on Shabbat with a hat on one's head that is made to protect from the sun, there are those who prohibit it because the wind might lift it, etc." He adopted both opinions stringently, which is surprising. He initially wrote 'to wear it on one's head' and later 'to go out,' because according to the reason of a tent, if it is worn before Shabbat, it is permitted, and according to the reason of it falling, it is forbidden in all cases. The world is accustomed to permit this matter (see Bach, Eliyahu Rabbah, and Taz), as they hold like Rashi, and the SeMaG and Ran and other early authorities agreed with Rashi. Similarly, the Maharil wrote (Eliyahu Rabbah) that there is no prohibition of a tent, and the concern of it falling does not apply in our public domain, among other reasons that have been explained. Some refrain from placing the tallit on their heads out of concern for making a tent, as the tallit on both sides acts as walls, and what is on the head acts as a roof and forms a tent. However, this concern is baseless. In the Gemara (138b), this was said in a questioning manner, and it is soft and bends, and this is the way of wrapping, and now no one is concerned about this, and on the contrary, it is the main practice of prayer.

The parasol which they call "sherm" or "regensahn," and it is made to protect from the sun and from the rain, and it provides shade over a person's head, and it has many hooks and loops, and when it opens it becomes like a structure on Shabbat - it is forbidden to carry it on one's head even in a courtyard, for this is a complete tent and is made as a tent to protect the head and body. All the more so is it forbidden to open and close it, for this resembles building, and it contains a semblance of a Torah prohibition, and the great authorities of the world have already forbidden it. And anyone who wants to permit it with sophistry testifies about himself that he lacks fear of Heaven, and indeed it is a complete prohibition to carry it according to the law and not just as a stringency. And see what is written in Siman 315, section 12.

The Sages taught in the Mishnah at the beginning of the tenth chapter of Eruvin (95a): "One who finds tefillin - brings them in pair by pair." This means that if he finds them in a place where they are protected from dogs and wild animals so that they will not be soiled, he is not permitted to wear them on Shabbat even if they are not protected from thieves, because thieves will not disdain the tefillin. This is explicitly stated at the end of the first chapter of Beitzah (15a). However, if they are not protected from dogs, the Sages permitted him to wear them as on a weekday. And even though Shabbat is not a time for tefillin, nevertheless, it is not considered carrying, since it is in the manner of wearing them on a weekday. According to the fundamental law as explained in the Gemara there, since Shabbat is not a time for tefillin, he can wear two pairs at once, as there is enough space on the head to place two tefillin, and similarly on the hand. On a weekday, this would be forbidden due to "Bal Tosif" (adding to the commandments), but on Shabbat, "Bal Tosif" does not apply since he does not intend to fulfill the mitzvah of tefillin. However, even though this is the law, it is not possible to rule this way consistently, as this only applies when the tefillin are very small, so there is space for both, which is not the case when they are somewhat larger. If he places them not in their proper place, it becomes a burden (Magen Avraham, section 154). It can also be said that he is not permitted more than what he could carry on a weekday (there in the name of Maharsha).

There are additional detailed laws regarding this matter: if it is a time of danger, as in their days when there were decrees not to wear tefillin, he should cover them and go. And even without danger, if they do not have straps and it is possible that they are not tefillin but amulets, which in their days were made in the form of tefillin, he is also not permitted to carry them, but out of doubt he should cover them and go. Similarly, even if they have straps, which is a sign that they are certainly tefillin, nevertheless, if the straps do not yet have knots, he is unable to wear them, because making a tefillin knot on Shabbat constitutes a permanent knot, and he would be liable for a sin-offering. He should act as will be explained. However, if he can make a tefillin knot using a bow, he should do so (as explicitly stated in Eruvin 97a). Also, if there are many tefillin such that if he were to bring them pair by pair, he would not finish until nightfall, he should wait with them until nightfall and then bring them. If he fears waiting due to robbers, he should carry them less than four cubits at a time, or pass them from one person to another until they reach the outer courtyard. If there are few, he should bring them pair by pair as mentioned and wear them in the manner of wearing until he brings them all in. (The details of this were not clarified in the Tur and Shulchan Aruch because this is now an uncommon matter.)

There are those who say that a woman is prohibited from wearing tefillin if she finds them on the way on Shabbat. Even though an item that is considered clothing for one person is also considered clothing for another, even if it is not customary for the latter to wear it, women are different because they are like a distinct group (Magen Avraham 301:54). Consequently, a woman who goes out to the marketplace with a garment that has tzitzit is liable for a sin-offering for the tzitzit, as the tzitzit are not nullified to the garment, as we wrote in paragraph 108. Nevertheless, an item that is considered complete clothing for a man can also be worn by a woman (ibid.), but with tefillin and tzitzit, which women are not permitted to wear even if they wish, their status is not like that of men, unlike other garments. However, it is certain that if there is a concern she will be mocked for wearing such a garment, it is forbidden for her to wear it, because she might be mocked and then remove it and carry it in her hand. (And regarding what we learned 'whether a man etc.' it is explained in the Gemara, see there.)

If one finds a Torah scroll in a field, he should sit and guard it, wait until nightfall, and then take it with him. If there is danger, he should leave it and go. If it is raining and the scroll could become damaged, it is permitted for him to wrap himself in it with the parchments like a garment, then put a garment over it and enter with it. This is a Tosefta in the eighth chapter of Eruvin, and it has been ruled by the poskim (decisors). It is obvious that if one is afraid to sit until nightfall, he may carry it less than four cubits at a time or give it to another person, etc., as with tefillin. (See the Shulchan Aruch, chapter 178, that giving it to another person is preferable to carrying it less than four cubits at a time. But it seems to me that this is with regard to monetary matters, but with sacred items less than four cubits at a time is preferable, since passing it from one person to another is disrespectful. And know that this does not only apply to a Torah scroll and tefillin, but also to mezuzot and all books, even printed ones, should not be treated disrespectfully and are subject to the same laws as written.)

We learned in the Mishnah (146): If someone's garments fell into water on the way, meaning his clothes fell into water on Shabbat, he may walk with them and does not need to worry that people will suspect him of washing them (Ra'avad). Furthermore, there is no concern that he will come to wring them out, because the sages did not trouble him to remove his clothes due to this concern, as human dignity is important (Tosefot Yom Tov). Additionally, according to the law, we hold that there is no concern that he will wring them out, as will be explained. However, he should not spread them out to dry because of the appearance of wrongdoing, so that people will not suspect him of washing them on Shabbat. Even in a private room where there are no observers, it is forbidden, because anything the sages prohibited due to the appearance of wrongdoing is forbidden even in a private room, in matters where there is a concern of a Torah prohibition (Tosafot Ketubot 60, s.v. 'Mema'achan', and see Ran, first chapter of Beitzah). The prohibition is only against spreading them out on Shabbat, but if he spread out washed clothes before Shabbat, he is not required to remove them on Shabbat, because the main suspicion is only when he spreads them out on Shabbat. In that case, there is reason to suspect that he washed them today. If he had washed them yesterday, he would have spread them out yesterday. People will not say that they fell into water because they are unaware of this (Levush).

And our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 47: "A person should not spread out his clothes on Shabbat, even due to sweat," end quote. And this is from the Tosefta at the end of chapter 17, see there. And know that there is an opinion that says that this applies specifically when the clothes were soaked in water, but if a small amount of water fell on them, it is permitted to spread them out, because with a small amount of water there is no concern that people will say he washed them (Magen Avraham 155 in the name of the Yereim), and it is not similar to sweat which spreads throughout the entire garment and people will say he washed it. But with a small amount of water that fell on part of the garment, they will not suspect him, as they see that part of it is dry (and this resolves the difficulty raised by the Magen Avraham there).

Clothes that are soaked in water - it is forbidden to dry them near a fire, because of laundering and cooking, and therefore even a minimal soaking is prohibited. However, in a place where the hand does not recoil from the heat - there is no concern of cooking, and consequently, there is also no concern of laundering. If this were not the case, drying in the sun should also be prohibited. And with minimal soaking, we have explained that it is permitted, for if it were a significant soaking, it would be prohibited regardless due to the appearance (of wrongdoing), and we would not need the reasons of laundering and cooking. However, even with significant soaking, there is a practical difference in this law, which is when one heats them while wearing them, for in such cases there is no concern of appearance, but it is still prohibited for these reasons (Erev Yom Tov).

A person may dry themselves with a towel, which is a cloth used for drying after washing, and bring it with them, and we are not concerned that they might come to wring it out. And why are we not concerned? Because everyone who washes themselves dries off, and if you prohibit drying off, they will be unable to wash, and this is something impossible (Ran in Chapter "HaKoneis"). And even in our times, when we do not usually bathe on Shabbat, it is still permitted, since no decree was made concerning this (Magen Avraham, subsection 158). However, one should not hand the towel to the bath attendants, as they are suspected of wringing it out. 

Our Rabbi, the Rema, in section 46 regarding items soaked in water which are prohibited to dry near a fire, wrote the following: "It is forbidden to move them lest one come to wring them out, and this applies if one is particular about the water in them" (end quote). According to this, one could say that even with a towel, although we allowed him to bring it in his hand where there is an eruv and we are not concerned about wringing for the reason explained, nevertheless, after bringing it to his house, it is forbidden to move it further, since the reason we explained no longer applies, obviously. However, this does not seem to be the case, and the reason appears to be that since we permitted him to bring it, it is impossible to forbid it later for moving. Furthermore, with items soaked in water, one is certainly particular about the water, which is not the case with a towel, where one is certainly not particular, as it is customary to dry off with a towel (and so it appears in the Gra, see there). 

He also wrote: that it is forbidden to walk on Shabbat in a place where one might slip and fall into water, lest one's clothes get soaked and one come to wring them out (end quote). And his intention is if one goes there to stroll and the like, but if it is his usual path, what can he do? And the main ruling regarding someone whose clothes got soaked refers to such situations (it seems to me). See above, section 45.

It is permitted to wash one's hands in a river on Shabbat, provided that one does not move them with the water on them outside the river for four cubits, and also does not push the water in the river more than four cubits, as the water is considered a karmelit (an intermediate domain). The prohibition of moving water outside the river for four cubits applies when the area outside the river is also a karmelit, as then it is not prohibited to carry from the river to the area outside it within four cubits, since transferring from one karmelit to another is allowed. However, if the area outside the river is a public domain or a private domain, then even within four cubits it is prohibited, and one must dry their hands while they are still in the river (as also noted in the Mishnah Berurah). The laws regarding bathing in a river will be explained in section 326.

People who have scabs with wounds on their heads make hairpieces for themselves from combed flax or from carded wool and are permitted to go out with them on Shabbat, as for them it is like a garment or an ornament and not a burden. However, they need to prepare them before Shabbat so that they are not muktzeh, as stated in Siman 308. Therefore, we require that they either perform an action on them, such as dyeing or wrapping them for this purpose before Shabbat, or that they go out with them for at least one hour before Shabbat. Similarly, it is permitted to go out with a turban that hangs around the neck for someone who has a wound on their head or arm, as that was their custom in this matter. It is also permitted to go out with rags wrapped around the hand or finger when there is a wound, as for them it is considered a garment. Some require that they go out with it for one hour before Shabbat (Taz, Siman 29), while others do not require this (Magen Avraham, Siman 62), and this seems to be the main opinion. In any case, we certainly require preparation, for otherwise it would be muktzeh, but according to this opinion, no specific action is needed for the preparation. (The Be'er Heitev, Siman 135, cites the Derisha who prohibits going out with iron-nailed shoes like horse riders, meaning those with spikes. But without spikes, just with iron plates, it is permitted, see there.)

It is stated in the Gemara (147a): "One who shakes out a garment on Shabbat is liable for a sin-offering. This was only said regarding new garments, but for old garments, there is no concern. And it was only said regarding black garments, but for white or red garments, there is no concern, and this is only if he is particular about them." According to this, the prohibition applies only to new black garments and if one is particular about them. Rashi explained: 'Shaking off the dust — this constitutes laundering,' but Tosafot, in the name of Rabbi Chananel, wrote that it does not seem so, as shaking off dust does not constitute laundering but rather shaking off dew that is on it, which is related to washing and laundering.

According to the explanation of Rav Hai Gaon, which was agreed upon by the Rosh, the Ran, the Mordechai, and the Rashba, and this is also clarified by the Raavad in his glosses on chapter 10, as well as the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch (the words of the Raavad are brought in the Maggid Mishneh there). The Rambam, in his commentary on Halacha 18, explains it completely differently, and these are his words: "If one shakes a new black garment in order to beautify it and remove the white wool that clings to it, as craftsmen do, he is liable for a sin-offering. But if he does not care, it is permitted." End quote. Hence, according to his explanation, this only applies at the completion of the work, to remove the white wool that sticks to it during the work, and the liability is for striking the final blow, which is the liability for any completion of work. And according to his explanation, it makes sense that the concern is only with a black garment, because white on black is very noticeable. However, according to the explanation of Rashi and Rav Hai Gaon, it is not so clear why there would be no concern with white and red garments. Also, according to their explanation, it is not clear how long a garment is considered new; they wrote that it means it has not been used much and is still in its new state (Beit Yosef and Magen Avraham), and even this is without a clear boundary.

And behold, regarding the law, we certainly need to be concerned with all interpretations. However, the main ruling follows the interpretation of Rabbi Hananel (R"Ch) that the shaking off is from the dew, as this is the ruling of the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch, and this is the opinion of most of the decisors. And in the Gemara there it is explained that one who is not particular about shaking it off—it is permitted for him even initially to shake it off. The explanation of the Gemara's words is this: For red, white, or old black garments, it is presumed that one is not particular about shaking off the dew, but if we know that one is particular about shaking it off, it is certainly forbidden just like with new black garments. When it is known that he is not particular, it is permitted—the same applies in reverse.

Therefore, it is clear that this applies only to dew. However, rain that falls on a garment, and certainly a garment that falls into water – for all kinds of garments, one is particular to shake them if they are not very worn. And this is what our teacher, the Rema, wrote in paragraph 1: "All the more so, it is forbidden to shake a garment that fell into water or upon which rain fell, and specifically a new garment that one is particular about." This means that in such cases, one is particular about all garments when the garment is new, and it is not called an old garment. He further wrote: "Some say it is forbidden to shake a garment from the dust upon it if one is particular about it, and it is good to be cautious about this." This is the opinion of Rashi that we have mentioned.

As is known to us, people are particular about shaking off rain from all expensive garments, whether they be of silk or fine wool, and this applies not only to new garments but until they are completely worn out. Certainly, this applies even more so to garments that have good fur, such as sable, beaver, marten, fox, and other types of animal fur, as well as those who wear hats made of good fur. It is obvious that they are very particular about not allowing rain to fall on them, and anyone who shakes them off on Shabbat is certainly liable. Therefore, it is very important to warn the people about this, as this is the primary law and not merely a stringency.

It is stated in the Gemara (75b): "Someone who removes knots from a garment is liable for the prohibition of 'striking with a hammer.'" Rashi explains: 'The ends of threads hanging from the fabric at the place of knots, when a thread breaks and it is tied, and similarly, small sticks and thin splinters that were woven into it unintentionally and are removed from it after the weaving is completed - this is considered finishing the work, and one is liable for 'striking with a hammer.''" This is the language of the Tur: "One who removes splinters and knots that remain in the garment from the weaving, if he is particular not to wear it until they are removed - he is liable to bring a sin-offering," which is like the explanation of Rashi. He added: 'if he is particular,' for if he is not particular - there is certainly no prohibition, and so it is in the Gemara there.

And the Rambam there wrote: "One who removes burs from clothing, such as woolen burs, is liable for the prohibition of 'striking with a hammer.' This applies if he is particular about them, but if he removes them in the course of regular activity, he is exempt," end quote. Similarly, it is written in the Shulchan Aruch, section 2. He was precise in his wording not to say: "but if he is not particular," as this would imply that we need to know that he is particular, which is not the case, because even in a general situation we assume he is particular. Rather, what he means is: "if he is particular about them," meaning that his act of removing them is for the purpose of beautifying the clothing. However, if he removes them in the course of regular activity, meaning he is not concerned at all about wearing the garment until he removes them, but rather, he removes them now not for beautification but as a simple act without any specific intention, in such cases it is permitted. This is because it is assumed that generally people are indeed particular about this, as it is common for people to be particular about it. (And the explanation of the Gemara there: "and if he is particular about them" follows this reasoning, and this is the intention of the Magen Avraham, section 5, and the Taz, section 2. However, what the Taz wrote that this is like the Tur - according to what I have written, it is not so, and this should be carefully examined.)

And I have heard another explanation, which is that it is known that tailors first insert long threads into the garment with a few stitches in order to connect the upper and lower parts until they complete the sewing of the garment. At the completion of the garment, they remove all the threads from the garment, and these are called "stirigewanias." Therefore, the Gemara calls it 'akofi,' because these threads surround the entire garment, and this is the final task of the garment, and therefore one is liable for it due to the prohibition of "striking the final blow." According to the law, all interpretations are true, and there is no dispute in this matter, for all of them are considered the completion of the garment; rather, one interprets it this way and another interprets it that way. (And perhaps this is the intention of the Magen Avraham in section 5 in the name of the Shiltei Giborim, who wrote: 'the removal of the threads that tailors make,' see there.)

And Rabbeinu the Rema wrote in Section 1: "But it is permitted to remove feathers from a garment on Shabbat," end quote. And there is someone who was concerned about a prohibition (Magen Avraham, section 4, in the name of Zikhronot), but there is no disagreement here. Certainly, according to Rashi's interpretation, who explained that shaking a garment to remove dust incurs liability, it is also forbidden if one is particular about it, as is obvious. However, according to most authorities, who hold that one is liable only for removing mud but not dust, all the more so is there no concern regarding feathers. And Rabbeinu the Rema is saying as follows: Even though he previously brought up the concern for Rashi's interpretation, nevertheless, feathers are permitted. The reason is that most people are not particular about this, as we see many people go out with feathers on their hats. However, for someone who is particular, it is certainly forbidden, and this should be the ruling (this seems to me). And it is written that if flax seeds or cooked food fall on one's garment, it is permitted to peel them off (there), as this does not fall under the prohibition of laundering. And there are those who wish to be stringent with a new and black garment (Mishnah Berurah), but this is not reasonable, as laundering does not apply to this at all. And if one's garments get entangled in thorns, one may separate them discreetly and slowly to avoid tearing them, and if they do tear, one is not liable, as this is an unintended consequence (there). But to remove them forcefully, they will certainly tear, and this is a case of "inevitable consequence" (and what is written there in the name of Zikhronot, regarding blisters, that even if one is not particular it is forbidden, I am puzzled, for in the Gemara, it is the opposite).

Maimonides wrote in Chapter 22, Law 22: "It is forbidden to fix the sleeves of garments and to fold them in a meticulous manner as is done during the weekdays when laundering them. Similarly, one should not fold clothes on Shabbat in the same way they are folded during the week after laundering. However, if one does not have another garment to change into, it is permitted to fold it, spread it out, and cover oneself with it in order to adorn oneself on Shabbat, provided it is a new white garment, as it becomes creased and dirty immediately. When folding, only one person should do the folding, but folding with two people is forbidden." End of quote. It is explained that all these matters are due to the principle of fixing utensils, and this folding is not simple folding but rather professional craftsmanship, as mentioned with regard to the sleeves being creased, meaning folded with creases. However, with simple folding, there is no issue in any manner. The first law is found in Beitzah (23a), and the second is a Mishnah in Shabbat (113a). Additionally, we learned there: "One may arrange the beds from Friday night for Shabbat, but not from Shabbat to the conclusion of Shabbat." This law is also written by Maimonides in Chapter 23, Law 7, and there he also explains the reason as it appears as if one is fixing. The Ra'avad wrote that the prohibition is because it causes exertion for the weekday.

There is a practical halachic difference between the reasons. According to the Rambam, who does not consider the reason of effort (tircha), it is permitted to fold a garment with a simple fold that does not involve making it into a utensil, even for a weekday. According to the Raavad, it is prohibited due to the effort from Shabbat to a weekday. It appears to me that according to the Raavad, even folding clothes is prohibited for the sake of a weekday, even if it does not involve the reason of making it into a utensil, as this is the opinion of our Rabbis, the Tosafists, who wrote: "From here we learn that it is forbidden to fold the synagogue's tallitot because they are needed for tomorrow," end quote. And with a tallit, it seems that making it into a utensil through folding does not apply, but the prohibition is due to the effort. (However, to throw a garment without any folding at all is not the way of people, and the intention is also to a precise fold, but an imprecise fold, according to his view, is permitted, and this is the intention of the Mordechai in the next section.)

And in the Mordechai there, it is written as follows: "The Ra'avyah wrote, we learn from this that for tallitot (prayer shawls) which are white and not needed for the rest of the day after leaving the synagogue, it is forbidden to fold them, whether they are new or old, and even if done by one person. However, this applies to folding them in their original manner, but if not in their original manner, it is permitted even with two people." And our master, the Beit Yosef, brought this in section 3, and wrote that this is logical. And certainly, according to Tosafot and the Ra'avad, who hold that the reason is due to unnecessary effort, there is also a distinction between folding in its original manner and not in its original manner, and the Mordechai also holds this, hence the distinction. And the Tur explains the reason as being due to repair, writing that new and white items do not require as much repair. And from Rashi, it is also explained thus. And in our times, there are many who fold their tallitot on Shabbat, and it can be said that they hold that our manner of folding does not constitute repair, and they do not hold the reason of unnecessary effort, as per the views of Rashi, the Rambam, the Tur, and the Shulchan Aruch. And this is also written in the Kolbo, and these are his words: "And now that it has become customary to fold all garments, it is possible that our folding is not similar to their folding, as they were very particular about smoothing out creases, and we do not do so." (The Tur and the Shulchan Aruch wrote the law concerning the sleeve in the laws of Yom Tov in Siman 519, and the law concerning making the beds they did not bring at all, and this requires further study.)

And regarding the matter that one should not arrange the beds from Shabbat to the conclusion of Shabbat, it appears that this is when the beds are in the bedroom, where no one goes all day. But in our case, where it is one of the rooms of the house, and if they are not arranged it would be disgraceful — it is permitted to arrange them for the sake of the house’s appearance, and especially in honor of Shabbat (Magen Avraham, section 6), and this is the common custom everywhere. Additionally, one could say the reason is because we hold that the only concern is fixing something, and with our type of bed arrangements, it is not considered as fixing, as the Kol Bo wrote in the previous section, and indeed, people also customarily fold the good tablecloths after the meal, and we have not heard anyone objecting to this, and we are forced to say it is like the reason of the Kol Bo. And this is what the Mishnah meant: that one may arrange the beds from the eve of Shabbat for Shabbat, and the intention is to sleep in them better if they are arranged before the day (there). However, as known, the arrangement not for sleeping is more beautiful than the arrangement for sleeping, and therefore during the day, they are arranged with decoration in honor of Shabbat, not in the manner of sleeping, and after the meal, they are arranged for sleeping. See what I wrote above in section 262.

A homeowner's press, which is a tool used to press clothes after washing, consists of two wooden boards with clothes between them and something that tightens them. One may loosen the tightening to take clothes out for the sake of Shabbat. However, in the case of a professional's press, it is forbidden because it is tightly secured and loosening it is akin to dismantling. According to the Rambam, the reason is due to muktzeh (an item set aside and not used on Shabbat). To press clothes on Shabbat is certainly forbidden even with a homeowner's press (Mishnah 141). Regarding a professional's press, it is taught there that one should not touch it at all, either due to muktzeh according to the Rambam, as it is considered muktzeh because of monetary loss and one is particular about it, or because we are concerned that one might come to loosen it (see Magen Avraham, section 7).

After washing, a garment becomes stiff, and rubbing it with hands to soften it is permitted on Shabbat, since this is not considered laundering. His intention is only to soften it, and once it softens a bit, he stops rubbing it, and this is not like laundering. However, for a scarf, it is forbidden because his intention is to polish it, which is like laundering. Hats and other linen items have the same rule as a scarf. In our region, there are no scarves, and polishing hats is not known to us. It seems that this applies only to linen garments that become stiff after washing, and through rubbing, they soften, and their laundering brightens them through rubbing (as Rashi explains). In our region, there are no linen garments except for shirts and pants, and we have not seen them become stiff after our washing. It has been said in Ketubot (10b): "Our ironing is like their laundering," and Rashi explains: 'Their water was suitable for laundering... and with our laundering, the garment is not whitened until it is ironed.' (And the custom of the world is to rub them with hands, as the Magen Avraham wrote in section 8, and according to what I have said, this is understandable).

Mud on one's garment, and one wishes to remove it - he should rub it from the inside of the garment, because it does not appear as laundering, and it is not considered actual laundering since no water is being used (Rashi 141a). However, one should not rub it from the outside, as it appears like laundering. One may scrape the mud off with their fingernail or with a knife, as this does not constitute a prohibited labor. Some say this is only permitted when the mud is wet, but if it is dry, it is forbidden to scrape it off as this would be considered grinding. Although this is a labor that is not needed for its own sake, it is prohibited by rabbinic decree, and according to the Rambam, it is forbidden by Torah law. There is no difference regarding which type of garment it is, whether linen, wool, or silk (ibid. section 16). This is specifically when there is a substance of mud, such that when it is scraped, crumbs fall off, which resembles grinding. But if there is only the appearance of mud, it is permitted, as this is not considered grinding (Taz section 6). Similarly, this applies to all types of dirt on the garment, for in truth, the concern of grinding is only a stringency, as it is not a type of grinding, and there is no need for it, and one does not derive any benefit from it (ibid.).

However, a shoe – it is forbidden to scrape it whether with a knife or with a fingernail, whether it is new or old, because it peels the leather and this is considered smoothing. Mud on one's feet or shoes – one may wipe it on a wall or a beam but not on the ground, lest one come to level the ground. This means that one might forget and intend to level the ground, and if not for this, it would be considered an unintentional act and not a certain result (Magen Avraham section 10). And using iron on a shoe – it is forbidden, because it is considered smoothing if the iron is sharp at its tip. Therefore, in our place, where in front of the synagogue there is a sharp iron piece that is used on weekdays to clean shoes, one must be careful not to do so on Shabbat (Taz section 3). However, if the iron is thick at its tip – it is permitted, but in any case, it is proper to be stringent even in such instances (see Magen Avraham section 17). There are those who prohibit wiping on a stone wall because it appears like adding to the building, and there are those who permit it whether on a wall or on the ground, because on a wall it is not the usual way of building and on the ground it is considered an unintentional act. Similarly, it is permitted to remove mud or excrement with a small shard that is suitable for moving and is not muktzeh, such as something suitable for covering a vessel or the like.

If there is some dirt on the garment, like spit or excrement or similar, one may wipe it with a cloth but not with water. And it is not only forbidden to wash the spot with water, but even to pour a little water on the dirty spot is prohibited, because that constitutes laundering, and laundering is a primary category of forbidden labor because of whitening. Any soaking in water is forbidden for a garment, and even when wiping with a cloth, one should do so lightly and not with pressure lest one wring it. Whether it is permissible with other liquids will be explained in Siman 319, with God's help. But for a soiled shoe, it is permitted to pour water on it to rinse it, but to actually launder it, meaning to scrub one side against the other, is prohibited. The reason is that with hard leather, laundering is not applicable at all, and even with soft leather where laundering is applicable, it is only with complete laundering. But we do not say for leather what we say for a garment, that soaking it or putting water on it constitutes laundering (Rashi 142a), and it is also explicitly stated in Zevachim (94b) there. (And there are those who prohibit laundering leather in any manner, and this opinion requires further investigation.)

And Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote in paragraph 9: For a garment that does not have dirt on it, it is permissible to put a small amount of water on it, but not a large amount lest one come to wring it out, and some forbid it in any case. 

The explanation is as follows: Our Rabbis, the Tosafists, at the end of the fourteenth chapter, raised a difficulty regarding what we say in Yoma (77b): 'One who goes to greet his teacher on Yom Kippur goes into water up to his neck,' and in Beitza (18a), that a menstruating woman who does not have clothes can immerse in her clothes on Shabbat, even though soaking is considered laundering. 

They answered that we only say this when there is dirt on it, and because the dirt is removed by this, it is indeed considered laundering. But when there is no dirt on it at all, laundering is not applicable, since it does not need laundering. This is the opinion of the first view. Nevertheless, a large amount of water is forbidden, as a decree lest one come to wring it out. 

And the reason they did not decree in the case of a mitzvah is that the Rabbis did not make a decree in the case of a mitzvah. They further answered that we only say 'soaking is laundering' when one washes in a manner of cleanliness, but when it is in a manner of dirt, such as in the case where one goes into water and dirties his clothes, laundering is not applicable at all, since on the contrary, he makes himself dirtier with this. 

According to this answer, we do not say the first distinction between whether there is dirt on it or not, and in all cases it is forbidden. This is the opinion of those who forbid in all cases. 

And the poskim (halachic authorities) seem to have considered the second answer as the main one. (See Magen Avraham 319:19 that when one is not particular about his water, it is permitted, as mentioned in Siman 301:66, and I am puzzled because there it is talking about moving it when it falls into water, and not about putting water on it, and this needs further investigation).

Our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 10: "One who washes his hands - it is good to rub them vigorously and remove the water as much as possible before wiping them with a towel." And our master, the Rema, wrote about this: "There are those who wrote that one need not be concerned about this, for we do not say that soaking a garment is considered laundering in such cases, as this is merely a way of soiling it, and this is the common practice. Therefore, it is permitted to dry one's hands on a garment into which a child has urinated in order to nullify the urine, as this is merely a way of soiling. However, it is forbidden to pour actual water on the urine in order to nullify it." This is certainly a clear law that any manner of soiling does not constitute laundering, and our master, the Beit Yosef, also holds this view. Therefore, he did not write that one is obligated to rub them, but rather that it is good to rub them, because according to the first explanation of the Tosafot that we brought in the previous section, this reasoning is not needed as we have written. Hence, our master, the Rema, came to say that no one is concerned about this at all, because the second explanation is taken as primary by the decisors, as we have written.

There are those who have written that even though it is usually permissible to dirty (a cloth), nevertheless, to move it afterward is prohibited, as a precaution lest one come to wring it out (this is the intent of the Magen Avraham, section 22) when one is particular about its moisture. In my humble opinion, we only say this when there is a lot of water, and not concerning drying hands as previously explained. And to put actual water on it - it has been clarified that this is forbidden, and the proof is from the towel in the previous section, clause 121, see there. And drying hands only helps for urine and not for excrement (see section 24 there). 

It is advisable not to take a baby in one's lap to avoid the possibility that the baby might urinate on him, necessitating the search for a permissible way to clean it, and instead, take the baby on a pillow so that if the baby urinates, it will urinate on the pillow (see section 23 there). And a woman washing a baby in water should be careful to wash the baby with her hands and not with a cloth that she puts in the water (see there), because this involves complete wringing. 

And it has been clarified that it is forbidden to put actual water on urine – even to wash one's hands over it is forbidden (see section 26 there), and only drying one's hands on it is permitted. One should not question what benefit this provides, since in section 77 it has been clarified that even to reduce the quantity of urine, one needs a quarter-log of water to nullify it. This applies when the urine is in its original state, but here, when the baby has urinated, it is only moist enough to make something else wet, and therefore drying it is sufficient (see section 25 there).

If one’s hand becomes soiled with mud or excrement, one may clean it with the tail of a horse or a cow, or with a rough cloth made for holding thorns, like a sack or mat. However, one should not use a cloth that is typically used for drying hands, so as not to act in the same manner as on a regular weekday, which may lead one to wash the cloth. It seems to me that people are not careful about this, and it is possible that nowadays there is no concern about laundering, since even on weekdays it is not customary to wash it immediately when it gets dirty, but rather to wait until a significant amount of laundry has accumulated and then wash everything together or send it to the laundress. (This law is from the Tosefta in Chapter 17, Law 5, and there it does not conclude 'lest he come to launder' as it is here. Only Maimonides in Chapter 22, Law 19 concludes this way, and so it is written in the Shulchan Aruch, Section 11. According to the Tosefta, one can say it is only due to it being a weekday activity. It seems Maimonides found it difficult to understand what weekday activity applies here, and therefore he wrote the reason of laundering.)

Our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 12: "It is forbidden to wipe a cup that had water or wine in it with a cloth, because it might lead to squeezing"—end quote. And the entire world is not careful about this, as the Radbaz wrote in his responsa (Siman 213). The truth is that this prohibition is not understood at all, for does wiping a cup lead to squeezing? And is this worse than wiping hands, and if wiping hands is considered a manner of dirtiness—here too it is in a manner of dirtiness. And even if we say that his intention is regarding a narrow cup where squeezing is inevitable—it is also not understood, for is there enough moisture on the sides to lead to squeezing? Especially with wine, where many opinions hold that squeezing does not apply, as written in Siman 319, and even more so with a cloth designated for that purpose, it is certainly permitted (Magen Avraham sk27, see there), and the essence of this law requires further investigation.

Additionally, it is written in paragraph 13: "One should not look on Shabbat in a metal mirror that is sharp like a scalpel, as we are concerned that one might remove dangling hairs with it, even if it is fixed to the wall. However, it is permissible to look in a mirror that does not have this concern, even if it is not fixed." These are his words. And in Yoreh De'ah, Chapter 156, it is clarified when it is permissible to look in a mirror and when it is forbidden even on weekdays due to the prohibition of "a man shall not wear [a woman's garment] and so forth." The case of the sharp metal mirror like a scalpel is not common in our region, and we do not know what it is.

It has already been explained in Siman 301, Section 49 that due to the severity of the prohibition of carrying and due to the frequency of this activity, the Sages were compelled to establish safeguards in matters related to carrying. Specifically, they decreed that women should not wear certain types of jewelry on Shabbat. In the beginning of the tractate "Bameh Ishah" in the Jerusalem Talmud, it is stated: "Because women are boastful and they will remove it (to show it) to their friend - and they will forget and walk with it four cubits in a public domain." There are several reasons for this: some say that because a woman needs to immerse in the mikveh, she might remove the item before entering the mikveh and carry it four cubits in a public domain. Many prohibited it out of concern that she might wish to boast and show her jewelry to her friends, as mentioned in the Jerusalem Talmud. Others prohibited it because it might be loose and fall off, leading her to carry it four cubits in a public domain. Some prohibited it due to concerns of "mar'it ayin" (appearance of wrongdoing), and others because in this manner of walking, she may be mocked and remove the item, subsequently carrying it four cubits in a public domain. All these laws will be explained in this Siman.

A woman should not go out with woolen threads on her head, nor with linen threads on her head, nor with straps on her head. This refers to those that are wrapped around her head, for we are concerned that she might encounter an immersion on Shabbat and go with them to the immersion house. At the time of immersion, she needs to loosen them so that they are not tight and do not form a barrier during immersion. Therefore, we are concerned that while she is walking, she will remember she needs to loosen them, and she will remove them entirely from her head to hasten her immersion and carry them four cubits in the public domain. Similarly, upon her return, she will remove them from her head at the time of immersion, and after the immersion, she will hasten to go and forget it is Shabbat. Due to her haste, she will not put them back on her head but carry them in her hand and walk, carrying them four cubits in the public domain. And why do we not decree similarly regarding garments? Because it is not customary for a woman to walk in the street without all her clothes and large personal items, which is not the case with small items like these. Even on weekdays, she is not particular at times to carry them in her hand while walking. They decreed this for all women, even for virgins and elderly women who are not relevant to immersion, for the Sages did not distinguish (in their decrees).

And if the threads and straps are braided within her hair, she is permitted to go out with them because in such cases it is forbidden to untie the braid on Shabbat. Braiding hair is considered a form of work, as is untying the braid. Therefore, she must untie them before Shabbat and remove them from there. Similarly, when she wishes to braid them after immersion, it is obvious that it cannot be done on Shabbat; hence, she will not come to any transgression. However, there are those who prohibit even in such cases, and this is the opinion of Rashi at the beginning of "With What May a Woman Go Out" (Shabbat 57b). The reason is that we are concerned that she might loosen the braids enough for water to enter them, and she would be permitted to immerse with them. Then we return to the original concern that she might remove them completely afterward and carry them in the public domain. Nonetheless, we hold in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 198, that loosening does not help, as explained there. (See Taz, subparagraph 1, and his words need examination, as written in the glosses of the Alter Rebbe.)

If the threads are made like a net, as chains, and there is enough space in them and they cannot be tightened strongly on her hair, and water can pass through them and they do not create a barrier – it is permitted for her to go out with them on Shabbat even if they are not braided into her hair, because she will not need to remove them at the time of immersion. However, this is with respect to the issue of a barrier. But if there is a concern that she might want to remove them for another reason, such as if they are dirty with mud and she does not want to bring them into the mikveh water so that the mud does not dissolve in the water and dirty her body upon emerging, or conversely, because they are precious and she does not want to bring them into the water, such as if they are gold-plated or similar – it is forbidden to go out with them, because she might remove them before immersion and come to carry them four cubits in the public domain, as we have said. (See Magen Avraham sections 4 and 5, and according to what we have said, this is also the intention of the Shulchan Aruch, as Rashi explains there regarding "teichi chalilta", and so wrote the Gra).

And this applies to the strings at its head, but with the strings wrapped around her neck—a woman is permitted to go out with them, for there is no concern regarding immersion, as they are not tightly bound around her neck to prevent water from reaching them, as a woman does not strangle herself and they are loose, and the water reaches them and she does not need to remove them. However, if they are golden strings or similar, which she is concerned about immersing in water—it is forbidden, as we said regarding the head strings, and likewise if they are dirty with mud. And specifically with the strings around her neck, it is permitted for the reason explained, but with a "katla" around her neck, which is a garment hung around her neck against her heart, and it has a place where a wide strap is inserted and the strap is tied around her neck—it is forbidden for her to go out with it, because this strap is wide, and even if she tightens it around her neck, she will not strangle herself, and a woman wants to tighten it to make herself appear attractive as if she has more flesh, and this is a barrier to immersion, and the concern remains as with the head strings. Additionally, there is another prohibition due to a different concern, which is that if it is valuable and decorated as is common with "katla"—we are concerned that she may remove it to show it to her friends, admire its beauty and goodness, forget about the Sabbath, and carry it four cubits in the public domain.

And for this reason, she should not go out with a "totefet," which is similar to a headband and extends from ear to ear, nor with "sarvitin," which is also like a headband but only reaches the cheeks. She wraps it on her head and lets it hang on her cheeks on both sides, because we are concerned that she might remove it and show it off. This is specifically when they are not sewn into the "shavecha" on her head, which is like a veil. But if they are sewn into the "shavecha," she is permitted to go out with them, as she will not remove them from her head, since she will not take off the "shavecha" from her head and remain bareheaded. And some say this applies to a married woman who is forbidden to uncover her head, but maidens who are accustomed to uncover their heads are forbidden even if they are sewn, because we are concerned that she might remove them and show them off. And although regarding immersion we said that the Sages did not differentiate, this is a stringency and not a leniency, and in any case, we do not prohibit married women here because of maidens, for the main decree is for married women who are numerous and significant, and we do not decree because of the few maidens. The first opinion holds that even for a leniency the Sages did not differentiate. And know that all these ornaments that have been explained and will be explained are according to their time, and now we do not have all these ornaments.

She should not go out with a "kavul," which is a woolen cap, meaning woolen threads woven to a width of two fingers like the tzitz (frontlet), and she places it around her face as an ornament. There is a concern that she might remove it to show it to her friends. Similarly, she should not go out with an "istama," which is a cloth that has colored threads hanging from it, and they hang it in front of a bride to drive away flies from her face, as she is embarrassed to shoo them away herself and is distressed by them, so they make this for her. This is not considered an ornament at all but rather a burden, and because of this, she should not go out with it even though she needs it. This is the explanation of the Rif and the Rambam for the "istama" mentioned in the Gemara there. Rashi, of blessed memory, explained that it is a small headband that binds the hairs that come out from her braids and prevents the hair from coming out. The Aruch explained that it is a piece of gilded fabric with precious stones and pearls set in it, and according to this, the prohibition is because she might remove it and show it off, as with all ornaments.

She should not go out with a "City of Gold," and Rashi explains that it is a circular ornament depicting a city, with a clasp in the middle that attaches it to the garment. Rabbeinu Tam explains that it is a type of crown for the head. In the Talmud (Shabbat 59a), it mentions "Jerusalem of Gold," and thus it applies to any city. There is no difference in the ruling, as all ornaments that might be removed and shown off are prohibited. (And in the Aruch, under the entry 'Jerusalem,' it explains that it is a crown with the depiction of Jerusalem on it).

A kalila, which is an ornament placed on the forehead extending from ear to ear and tied with hanging straps, is permitted to go out with, whether it is made of pieces of gold threaded together or those pieces are fixed on a cloth. The reason is that ordinary women do not generally wear this ornament, and only distinguished women wear it, and a distinguished woman will not remove it and show it. Nevertheless, ornaments that all women wear, even a distinguished woman is prohibited [to go out with], because the Sages did not differentiate, as mentioned regarding the concern of immersion for maidens and elderly women in Section 2, see there.

A cloak, which means a wide piece of clothing, and the Aruch explains it as a leather girdle. If it has short straps hanging from it to tie and secure it around, it is permitted. If it does not have straps, it is forbidden. One should not go out with a "katla," which is a garment with slits like pants, and is important and adorned with gold, as we have already explained in section 5. One should not go out with nose rings, due to the concern that she might remove it and show it, but one may go out with ear rings in their time, because then women would cover their ears with their veils, and it would be troublesome for her to remove them because of the ties. Therefore, in places where it is customary to expose the ears, it is forbidden to go out with ear rings if they can be easily removed, due to the concern that she might remove and show them.

It has already been explained in Siman 301, Se'if 57 that a needle with an eye is not a woman's ornament, and if she goes out with it, she is liable to bring a sin offering. However, a needle without an eye is considered an ornament for a woman, as she inserts it into her bindings. For the needle without an eye is made with one end round and thick like an ornament, but the one with an eye is only for sewing. Therefore, the needle without an eye is like all other ornaments that have the concern of being taken off and shown. Now, the Rambam in Chapter 19 did not mention this distinction but simply wrote: "a needle without an eye is an ornament, and there is a concern of taking it off and showing it" (see there). However, the Tur wrote: "A woman should not go out with a needle that she parts her hair with, even if it is made to adorn herself with, but with a needle that she uses to hold her bindings, she can go out with it. And she should not go out with a needle with an eye, and if she goes out with it, she is liable. But with a needle without an eye, she should not go out, and if she goes out, she is exempt" (end of quote).

Explanation of the matter: In the Mishnah it is taught, "nor with a needle that is not perforated, and if she went out [with it] — she is not liable for a sin offering," for the prohibition is due to smoothing and combing. The Gemara (60a) explains that with a needle that is not perforated, which she uses to gather her hair and stick the needle into her head-covering, it is permitted to go out, for there is no concern of smoothing and combing, since when she pulls it out, her hair will be revealed. However, the Mishnah is referring to a needle that divides the hair here and there, which is an adornment and not a burden according to Rashi's explanation. And the Gemara asks: For what purpose is it suited on Shabbat, and it answers: It has a gold plate on its head, etc. And Rashi explained: For what purpose is it suited, after all, it does not divide the hair on Shabbat. It follows that according to this, it is indeed an adornment, only that on Shabbat it does not divide the hair. Tosafot, the Rosh, and the Rashba questioned him, why is it forbidden to divide the hair on Shabbat, and moreover, does this make it an adornment, after all, it is only a utensil and is considered a burden. Therefore, they explained that the truth is so, and this is its question 'for what purpose is it suited,' meaning to say, after all, it is a burden, and it answers: It has a gold plate, etc. Hence, according to these rabbis, a plain needle that is not perforated is a burden, unless it is made with a gold plate. It is clear that Rambam agrees with Rashi, for he did not bring any of this but wrote simply: that if it is not perforated, it is an adornment — thus it is explained according to Rashi. Also, I do not understand the words of our Rabbis, for we learned in the Mishnah (62b): "A woman should not go out with a perforated needle, and if she went out — she is liable for a sin offering," why specify perforated, even if it is not perforated, in such cases it is a burden. Similarly, the early authorities, Sefer Mitzvot Gadol, Sefer HaTerumah, Mordechai, and Rabbeinu Yerucham all wrote simply that a needle that is not perforated is an adornment, only that it is forbidden lest she pulls it out and shows it. And I am astonished that the commentators on the Tur and Shulchan Aruch did not discuss this, and inevitably, we must say that these Rabbis also agree that a needle that is not perforated is an adornment when she sticks it in her veil and shawl for decoration, only that they disagree with Rashi that the needle which parts the hair is not an adornment at all, and therefore, if the needle is designated for this — it is a burden.

And these are the words of the Tur who wrote: "And she should not go out with a needle that parts her hair, even if it is made to adorn her." This means that a needle used to part the hair is not considered an ornament, as per the words of the Tosafot. But with a needle that secures her ties, she may go out. And she should not go out with a perforated needle, and if she does, she is liable for a sin-offering, as it is not made at all to be stuck in her veil or the like. But with a non-perforated needle, she should not go out, and if she does, she is exempt if it is stuck in her veil or the like, because it is considered an ornament.

Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in Section 9: "A woman should not go out with a needle that has an eye, and if she goes out with it, she is liable. But if the needle does not have an eye, if it holds her knots, she is permitted to go out with it. If it does not hold her knots, it is forbidden." This means that if it holds her knots, she will not remove it, so as not to reveal her hair. If it does not hold her knots but is tucked into her scarf or something similar, it is forbidden, lest she remove it and show it. But if it serves no purpose at all, she is certainly liable for a sin-offering. The way to carry it is if it is stuck where her knots are, for that is where she customarily carries it. If it serves no purpose at all, meaning it does not hold her knots and serves no function, she is liable for a sin-offering. But if she tucks it into her garment, she is exempt because that is not the way she usually carries it, as is written in Siman 301 at the end of Section 58. And there are those who wrote that with a needle that has an eye, even if it holds her knots, she is liable for a sin-offering (Beit Yosef and Magen Avraham, Subsection 7, and Taz, Subsection 7 at the end), and some say she is exempt because that is not the usual way of carrying it (Bach and Eliyah Rabba, Subsection 12). In my humble opinion, this is completely perplexing, because if it serves as a function for her garments in any case, how can she be liable even if that is the usual way of carrying it? This is not considered carrying but a use for her garment, like we wrote in Siman 301 there regarding a man, that if the needle serves as a substitute for hooks, why should it be forbidden there? And I found similarly in the Shiltei Giborim, Chapter 6, which states: "The Rosh wrote that a woman may go out with a needle that holds her knots and also with a needle that gathers her hair, etc., and he does not differentiate whether the needle has an eye or not." However, regarding the actual matter of the appearance of our needles which are not pierced, there is no concern for removing and showing, for what beauty is there in this? We must say that for them, it had the appearance of an ornament, similar to what we have, large and beautiful, which women tuck into their scarves. (And all the words of the Taz are not clear to me, also the words of the Magen Avraham, Subsection 7, are questionable as I wrote, and his words in Subsection 8 where he objects to the Bach are certainly correct. However, what he wrote that if it is made as an ornament, even if it holds her knots, it is forbidden lest she remove it and show it, this is questionable, for in the Gemara it clearly does not imply this. In Beit Yosef, in the name of Sefer Mitzvot Gadol, it is not written about holding knots there, and this needs further investigation. However, in practical law now, there is no difference, for we are not concerned about removing and showing, and our women go out with ornaments as will be explained in this Siman. Only regarding a needle with an eye, which is forbidden even if it holds her knots, this needs further investigation, and it seems that the custom is to permit as written in Shiltei Giborim, and examine this carefully).

She should not go out with a ring that has a seal on it, and if she goes out with it, she is liable. And if it does not have a seal, she should not go out with it, and if she does, she is exempt. The reasoning for this matter is explained in Siman 301, Se'if 55, see there. She should not go out with a "kulyar," which is a type of ornament used to fasten the key of her cloak, and it must be said that if she removes it, the cloak will not open and her flesh will be exposed.
