If this were not the case, we would not be concerned about her removing it and showing it off, similar to a needle used to fasten her clothes. However, some explain that it is a type of shawl, and the Aruch explains that it is like a crown. She should not go out with a "koveles," which is a pouch that contains a pleasant-smelling fragrance, and a woman who has a bad odor wears it (Rashi 62b), and it is considered an ornament, and we decree that she might remove it and show it off (Gemara there).

If one is missing a tooth and places another in its place, if it is made of gold - she should not go out with it, because since it differs in appearance from other teeth, people might mock her, and she might remove it and carry it in her hand for four cubits in the public domain. But if it is made of silver - it is permitted, because since it is white, it resembles other teeth, and people will not mock her. All the more so, a tooth made of human material is permitted. Nowadays, doctors make teeth from bone, and their appearance is exactly like natural teeth.

A woman should not go out wearing a torn shoe, lest people mock her and she removes it and ends up carrying it. Nor should she go out wearing a new shoe, lest it does not fit her properly, unless she has tried walking in it beforehand to ensure it fits her. However, a man is allowed, as he is not as particular about this. Similarly, for all matters where there is a concern of mockery, a man generally need not worry in most cases. For other types of clothing, there is no concern even for a woman, as she will not remove her clothing while walking, except for a single shoe, where even a man should be cautious about being mocked, as mentioned in Siman 301, Section 52.

A woman can go out with hair ribbons designed to be worn on her head, called in our language "peruk," whether they are made from her own hair, another woman's hair, or even animal hair, as long as an elderly woman does not wear a young woman’s hairpiece and a young woman does not wear an elderly woman’s hairpiece, because both could lead to mockery. They may remove them and end up carrying them four cubits in the public domain (Tosafot 64b, s.v. 'u'vel'vad'). Rashi explained that this is also because they have their own hair, and white on black or black on white is repulsive, and they may come to remove and carry it.

She may go out with a knot made for the healing of "kituaf" [a type of wound] from the evil eye so it will not take effect, and with wool tied and fastened in her ear, and with wool in her sandal tied to the sandal, and with a sandal and a shoe that are closed on all sides—even if they are not tied, it is permitted, for they will not fall off since they are closed. And with wool that she prepared for her menstruation so that blood will not fall on her and cause her distress. However, if her intention is that the blood should not fall on her clothes and she carries it so her clothes will not get soiled, it is prohibited, for all protection from dirt is considered a burden, as stated in Siman 301:65 unless it is a proper garment, as stated there in section 66. However, when the intention is that it should not fall on her body, it is considered for her own need and is permitted even if it is not tied. And we are not concerned about it falling and bringing it, for since it is disgusting, she will not come to bring it, and even if it has a handle, because it is very disgusting. Similarly, she is permitted to go out with pepper in her mouth and with a grain of salt and with any perfume she places in her mouth, provided she does not place them initially on Shabbat, as a decree due to the grinding of medicines like all remedies. Alternatively, because she appears to be scheming to bring them out on Shabbat (Tosafot 64b, s.v. 'provided'). However, according to this reasoning, the wool we mentioned is also prohibited to place initially on Shabbat (ibid.). And if it falls from her mouth, she should not return it, whether it fell on the ground or on a utensil (Magen Avraham, section 11), and this is according to the second reason. But according to the first reason, only when it falls on the ground, as it would be considered a new placement.

And similarly, it is permitted to go out with leg bands that are tied with a string around the legs, even though the string is not tied to them, and we do not worry that they might slip down, because she certainly ties them well. And when we said even though it is not tied, we meant it is not permanently tied to the legs. And we do not worry that she will take them off and show them, for it is not an ornament, and even if it were an ornament, she would not reveal her leg (there, section 12). And she may go out with a bracelet that is placed on the arm or leg, provided that it clings to the flesh and does not slip off the arm or leg, and we do not worry that she will take it off and show it, because she would not reveal her arm or leg. And there is an opinion that forbids it on the arm, because we worry that she might take it off and show it, because the arm is sometimes revealed, unlike the leg which is always covered.

A great principle applies here: In everything that the Sages permitted her to go out with, as explained, she can untie it in the public domain, and we are not concerned that she will carry it four cubits. Since the Sages said that this item must be on her, it follows that if she unties it in the public domain, she will retie it. And anything that the Sages forbade her to go out with in the public domain is also forbidden to go out with in a courtyard that is not enclosed. This is stated in the Gemara (Shabbat 64b): "Rav said: Anything that the Sages forbade to go out with in the public domain is also forbidden to go out with in a courtyard, except for a ribbon and a wig, so that she should not be unseemly to her husband. Rabbi Anani bar Sason in the name of Rabbi Yishmael said: Everything is like a ribbon." All ornaments are permitted in the courtyard, and the Rif and the Rambam ruled according to Rav. The reason they also decreed regarding the courtyard is not a decree upon another decree, since the Rabbis knew that if she goes out in the courtyard, she will also go out in the public domain (Ran, see there). The Rambam wrote that the courtyard is one that is not enclosed, which is like a karmelit, but in an enclosed courtyard it is permitted, and all the more so in the house. The Ramban and the Rashba wrote that it is forbidden in an enclosed courtyard, and likewise in the house, as the Sages decreed that she should not adorn herself with them at all, because if she adorns herself, she will certainly go out into the public domain. But Rabbeinu Tam ruled like Rabbi Anani, that everything is like a ribbon and it is permitted with all ornaments to go out in a courtyard that is not enclosed, according to the first opinion. And know that according to those who prohibit adorning even in their house, there are those who prohibit carrying a key even in an enclosed courtyard except in one's hand and not in one's belt, lest one forgets and takes it out into the public domain. Anything a person goes out with as a garment, there is concern that they will go out with it into the public domain, unlike when the item is in their hand. Thus, in the house, it is also forbidden in the belt for this reason.

Behold, the early authorities have already raised the question as to why our women go out with all their jewelry into the public domain and no one protests against them. Indeed, some have written that it is forbidden, but since they will not listen to us, it is better that they transgress unknowingly rather than knowingly, but it is unthinkable to say such a thing. Therefore, our rabbis have begun to seek justification for them. Some have written that we follow the principal view of Rabbeinu Tam, of blessed memory, mentioned in the previous section, that all jewelry is like a tied ornament, and they are permitted to go out with all their jewelry into an unenclosed courtyard. And in our case, there is no true public domain, and our streets are considered a karmelit. Even though it is evident in the Gemara (102a) regarding a fire that a karmelit is stricter than an unenclosed courtyard, for one can save items from a fire to an unenclosed courtyard but not to a karmelit, that was in their time when they had a true public domain. In comparison to a true public domain, a karmelit is more similar than an unenclosed courtyard, but nowadays that we do not have a true public domain, they are equivalent (Tosafot 64b, s.v. 'Rabbi Anani').

And still, it is not sufficient, for this is based on the opinion that at present we do not have a public domain (reshut harabim) because we require six hundred thousand [people], but many great authorities do not hold this way, as I have written in Siman 345. Furthermore, nowadays there are large cities in the world that have six hundred thousand [people]. Therefore, some offer a different reason: because nowadays jewelry is common and women go out with them even on weekdays, there is no concern that they will remove and display them as in those days when it was not customary to go out with them except on Shabbat, and it was not common. Some have written that our women do not show their jewelry and rings. We can explain this matter as follows: In section 9, it was clarified that a collila (a type of jewelry) is permitted because whoever wears a collila is an important woman, and an important woman will not remove and display it, and all our women are considered important. Additionally, in my humble opinion, another reason is that it is known that in their days, women stayed in their homes and did not frequently go out to the street. When they occasionally went out, they were wrapped in their garments and did not have women's synagogues. Hence, they saw each other only occasionally and rarely entered each other's homes, so there was a significant concern that if they met each other on Shabbat while walking in the street, they might remove and display [their jewelry]. But now, women often go out frequently in the streets and markets, visit each other's homes, and see each other in women's synagogues. Consequently, they can show their jewelry to each other in their homes and synagogues. Certainly, it is not customary to remove jewelry in the street to show it to their friends, and we see with our own eyes that even on weekdays and holidays they do not do so. Why should we be concerned on Shabbat? This is a correct and clear leniency.

And it is obvious that this permission is only in regard to the concern of "removing and showing," and this applies to most ornaments. However, in a situation where there is a concern that they will mock her – even now it is forbidden. But this is not common among us, as is well known. Similarly, this permission does not apply in cases where it is considered carrying, such as a ring with a seal for a woman, and a ring without a seal for a man, and similarly a pierced needle for a woman, for these were not forbidden due to "removing and showing" but because they are considered carrying and one would be liable for a sin-offering. Nevertheless, there is also a rationale for permission in this case, for we have already written in Siman 301, section 56, that nowadays it is customary for men to wear rings without seals on their fingers, and if so, it is known that women also customarily wear rings with engraved seals on their fingers. Moreover, as is known, this is not done for the seal but for the ornament, as the engraving is something that pleases the eye, and the place of the seal itself is a beautiful ornament, and they are permitted to go out with them. Similarly, with needles, it is known that nowadays they secure their scarves and shawls with needles, whether pierced or unpierced, and they are considered accessories of the garments and are permitted. Nevertheless, they should be warned not to overdo it with needles, but only to use what is necessary to secure their scarves and no more, and in this way, they will listen to us since they have no benefit from more.

One must caution women not to carry a needle that is not perforated, whose point and tip have been removed. And it's not only when it was removed on Shabbat, but even if it was removed before Shabbat, if it was not designated for use, for instance to place it in their scarves or similar uses - it is considered muktzeh (set aside and not to be touched). The details of this law will be explained in Siman 308. There is an opinion that prohibits using a needle when either its point or tip is removed, but this is not the main opinion (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 16). And a perforated needle - even if it is whole - is forbidden, as has been explained.

Young girls who have their ears pierced to put in earrings when they grow older, and to ensure that the holes do not close up, they place small sticks in them—are permitted to go out with them. And even though it is not considered an ornament, it is still not considered a burden, since it is customary for them to go out this way. All the more so if they place threads in their ears, which is certainly not considered a burden. This applies as long as the sticks are not colored, but if they are colored, it is prohibited because it appears as an adornment. And even though we do not make this decree regarding ears, as was mentioned in paragraph 10, this applies to a married woman. But a virgin is not concerned about revealing her ears, especially in places where it is customary to go out with uncovered ears, as mentioned there (see Magen Avraham, subsection 16). The language of the Mishnah (65a) is: "Young girls go out with threads, and even with sticks in their ears." And it seems that this is not specifically referring to young girls, for the same applies even to adult women, as the Rambam wrote in Chapter 19, Halacha 12: "Women go out with sticks in their ears," see there. And perhaps he intentionally altered the language of the Mishnah to indicate that this does not apply exclusively to young girls.

We also learned in the Mishnah there: "Arab women go out veiled." This refers to Jewish women in Arab lands, and the custom of Arab women is to cover their heads and faces except for their eyes, and in Arabic, this is called veiled, which is the veils mentioned regarding women's ornaments in Isaiah (Rashi). And in the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, section 21, it is written that she covers her whole head except for the face. And the Rambam there wrote: "With the veils that are on their necks or on their garments," and he explained in his commentary on the Mishnah that they are like bells or jingles, and in the Aruch, it is explained like Rashi. And we learned: "Median women fastened," that is, Jewish women in Media go out fastened, meaning they wrap in a tallit and hang the strap on one edge against their neck, and on the other edge, they wrap a stone or a nut and tie the strap in a wrap, so the tallit does not fall off (there). And "fastened" means like hooks, which we translate as 'porphea,' and any garment connected to another is called 'fastened' (there). The Mishnah concludes that it is not specifically Arab and Median women, as this applies to everyone, but the Sages spoke of the common practice.

And she may fasten [the cloak] with a nut or a stone that was designated for this purpose before Shabbat and go out with it, for a stone can be designated without any action. But with a coin – it is forbidden to fasten on Shabbat, as it is not typically used for any other purpose during the week, and designation is not effective for it. It requires an action before Shabbat or to have been used for an hour during the daytime. Therefore, if she fastened it before Shabbat, it is permissible to go out with it on Shabbat, and all the more so if she used it for an hour during the daytime. (The Tur and Shulchan Aruch did not write this, because it is impossible to go out without fastening, and consequently, no going out is needed. Pay close attention.)

In the Gemara there: 'They asked: Can a woman employ a ruse and spread a mat over a nut to remove it for her small child on Shabbat?' and there in the Gemara it remains unresolved. It seems to me that although we find ruses even in Torah law, such as employing a ruse with the firstborn and similar cases, this is different because the ruse is evident. And since it remains unresolved, the Rambam, the Tur, and the Shulchan Aruch in section 23 ruled: if it is to a public domain, it is forbidden, but if to a karmelit (a semi-public domain), it is permitted, as the rule in all cases of doubt in Torah law is to be stringent, and in rabbinic law to be lenient. (And therefore the Talmud there compares it only to the ruse in the case of a fire, because there too it is evident, as explained in Berakhot 139: see there).

The Gemara states (66b): The Rabbis taught: One may go out with an "Eben Takumah" on Shabbat, which is a stone that pregnant women carry so that they do not miscarry, and in our language, it is called "Sterine Shus." According to Rabbi Meir, one may even go out with the weight of the "Eben Takumah" if something else was weighed against it, and if its weight is the same as the weight of the stone, it also has this protective quality. This applies not only if she has miscarried, but even if she might miscarry, and not only if she is already pregnant, but even if she might become pregnant and miscarry. It appears to me that this refers to a family with a history of miscarriages, and it is considered like an amulet, as explained in Siman 301, section 79. Otherwise, how could we permit this? "And it was intentional and coincidental," meaning the weight of the "Eben Takumah" should not be something they take and make equal to its weight, but rather that it naturally has the same weight. Abaye raises a question: What about the weight of the weight? Meaning, if it happens that they weighed the "Eben Takumah" and found another object with the same weight, does it work? Even though it naturally has the same weight as the "Eben Takumah," perhaps the protective quality is only effective if it was weighed directly against the stone itself. This remains a doubt, and therefore, it is forbidden. However, it might be permitted in a karmelit, similar to the previous section. (The poskim ruled according to Rabbi Meir, because Abaye's question follows his opinion, as for the first Tanna, even the weight is forbidden, and certainly the weight of the weight.)

It is forbidden for a woman to apply rouge to her face on Shabbat, which is a type of dye, due to the prohibition of dyeing. Since it is customary for her to do so, it is considered dyeing. This is not the case for a man, as will be explained at the end of Siman 320. This prohibition is of Rabbinic origin (Mishna 94:). For this reason, it is forbidden to apply kohl to the eyes on Shabbat, and for this reason, it is forbidden to apply dough to the face, because when it is removed, the flesh reddens, which is similar to a type of dyeing. Know that this is what is stated in the Gemara there: that applying kohl is forbidden due to dyeing. The Rambam in Chapter 23, Law 12 wrote that the prohibition is due to writing, as is mentioned there. This was his version in the Gemara, and so it is in the Aruch.

A woman is forbidden to braid her hair on Shabbat, as this involves a rabbinic prohibition related to building (Shabbat 95a). Even though braiding threads in a detached item incurs liability for weaving, braiding hair is not considered weaving since it is not meant to last and is intended to be undone (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 2). However, any form of building, even temporary, is prohibited. Consequently, since a woman is forbidden to braid her hair, she is also forbidden to undo the braid on Shabbat, akin to the general prohibition of building and dismantling on Shabbat. Even though dismantling requires the intention to rebuild to incur a Torah-level liability for stoning and a sin-offering, rabbinically it is forbidden in all forms. However, it is permitted to part her hair to either side, as it does not necessarily lead to hair being pulled out, and if it does, it is considered unintentional. Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) writes in section 26 that some prohibit parting the hair, specifically making a "shaitel" (wig), and the custom is to forbid doing so with a tool. But with just fingers, the custom is to be lenient. This means that Rashi's view (Shabbat 60a, "and on Shabbat") is that parting the hair on Shabbat is forbidden. The Tosafot and other early authorities questioned what prohibition exists in this. As we have written in section 12, Rashi's view is explained as referring to making a "shaitel," which involves parting the hair so much that it appears bald in the middle, and moving the hair to both sides strongly with a tool, as was customary for maidens in our times. This must be done with a tool, so there is a concern for pulling out hair, which is a certain outcome. But with just fingers, even Rashi agrees it is permitted (this seems to me).

It is forbidden to comb with a comb on Shabbat, even those made from pig bristles, as it is impossible that some hairs will not be uprooted, and this constitutes shearing, which is a primary category of labor. However, it is permitted to wash and scrub with one's hands. Some have written that those made from pig bristles are not considered a certain outcome (פסיק רישא), and there is proof for this from Nazir (42b), where the Talmud states that according to Rabbi Shimon, a nazirite is forbidden to comb his hair because he intends to remove the loose hairs that have not yet completely detached, as it is explained there. This clearly indicates that it is not a certain outcome. It seems to me that this refers to combs made from the thin bristles of a pig, as the thick ones certainly pull out hairs, and all the more so with any type of comb, it is a biblical prohibition (see Magen Avraham, section 322, who cites Mahari Beirav; his intention is as I have written, and examine this carefully).

Know that the laws of slaves are not applicable in our times, because according to the law of the land in all countries, a person cannot purchase a slave, and no person can be a slave to another. Therefore, it is only possible to have day laborers, yearly laborers, or contract workers. They are like the general populace of nations who have no connection to the laws of slavery mentioned in the Torah: "You shall not do any work, you... and your slave, etc." There is only the prohibition of instructing a non-Jew to perform labor on Shabbat, and these laws are explained from Siman 243 to Siman 248, and will be further elucidated in Siman 306 and 307. This Siman deals with the matter of slaves whose very bodies are owned by a Jew, as it was in ancient times.

It is written: "You shall not do any work, you, your son, your daughter, your male servant, your female servant, etc." Thus, a servant of a Jew is forbidden to do work by Torah law just like the Jew himself. This refers to a Canaanite servant, for an Israelite servant is a full Jew. According to the Raavad at the end of the first chapter, the prohibition from the Torah is on the servant and not on the master, since the servant has understanding. However, Maimonides ruled that the master is commanded by the Torah not to allow the servant to do work on Shabbat, and he derives this from the verse in Mishpatim: "So that your ox and your donkey may rest, and the son of your maidservant, and the stranger," just as the obligation for the ox and donkey rests on the owners, so too for the maidservant's son. There are those who question him, arguing that this verse does not refer to a full servant, as will be explained (Maggid Mishneh). But I say that Maimonides' main intention is that just as the "so that they may rest" in this verse refers to the owners, so too the verse "so that your male servant and your female servant may rest as you do" in the portion of Va'etchanan also refers to the owners. Many agree with Maimonides.

There are three types of slaves: the primary slave mentioned in the Ten Commandments "you, your son, your daughter, your male servant, and your female servant" - this is a slave sold to an Israelite who has undergone circumcision and immersion for the sake of servitude, and has accepted upon himself the yoke of the commandments. He is obligated in the commandments like a woman, and he is prohibited from labor on Shabbat by Torah law just like an Israelite, as stated in the Ten Commandments. The second type is a slave sold to an Israelite who has not undergone circumcision or immersion, but has accepted upon himself the seven Noahide commandments. His status is like that of a resident alien (ger toshav). It is stated in Keritot (9a) and in the Mekhilta that the verse "and the son of your maidservant and the resident alien may be refreshed" refers to this resident alien and resident slave who has accepted the seven commandments but has not undergone circumcision or immersion. It is explained there that he is permitted to do labor on Shabbat for his own needs, but it is forbidden by Torah law for him to do work for an Israelite, whether for his master or for another Israelite. The Tur wrote that it is forbidden for him to do his master's work - this is stated as a general rule, but it likewise applies that he is forbidden to do any Israelite's work, and the same applies to a resident alien, as the Rambam writes there. (See Yoreh De'ah at the beginning of section 267 for the conditions under which it is permitted to acquire such a slave.)

And the third case: A slave who has neither been circumcised nor immersed [in a mikvah], nor has he accepted upon himself the seven commandments [of the Noahides], and Maimonides (Rambam) did not mention this at all. On this matter, there is a dispute among the decisors: for Maimonides and Nachmanides (Ramban) hold that such a slave is not included in the commandment "that your manservant may rest," but is like any other hired worker. However, Rashba, Semag, and Sefer HaTerumot hold that he is included in the commandment "that your manservant may rest." This also appears from the words of the Tur, who wrote: "But if he has not been circumcised nor immersed, even if he accepted upon himself the seven commandments, he is like a resident alien, etc." Thus, he wrote "even if he accepted," and all the more so if he did not accept, implying that both cases have the same ruling.

However, Rashba wrote that the second and third types of slaves, whom the Torah forbids from performing work for a Jew, is only when there is a directive, when his master or another person told him to do work for him, and regarding this it is said "that your manservant may rest, etc." But if he is acting on his own initiative, his master is not obligated to stop him, and it is like a minor who eats non-kosher food, where the court is not commanded to stop him. Only regarding his master, if it is evident that he is acting on his master’s behalf, meaning he knows this is his master’s desire, must he be prevented. As for another person, even if he is acting on his own initiative, we do not concern ourselves with it, as long as he is not told to do it and the Jew does not benefit from that work on Shabbat. This is by rabbinic decree as stated in Siman 276, and it is clear to all opinions that a hired non-Jewish worker is not commanded to rest by his master.

And our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in Section 2: "Where it is permitted for the servant to perform work for himself, if the master tells him to do work for himself and sustain himself on Shabbat day, since he stipulated with him beforehand, he may do so for his own sustenance, provided it is done discreetly so that there should be no suspicion from onlookers." End quote. 

I do not understand why a stipulation is necessary for this and why we should be concerned about onlookers. However, it could be said that the onlooker might think he is doing it for the Jew. But why is a stipulation needed, since it is permitted for him to do work for himself? And even if his master sustains him, what difference does it make to us and what prohibition is there in this matter? Perhaps without a stipulation, it is assumed he is doing it with his master's intention, and this is forbidden with his master, as mentioned in the previous section.

Here is the translation of the given passage from the Aruch Hashulchan:

"According to what has been explained, our established law is that for the needs of a sick person who is not in danger, one may tell a non-Jew to do [work], and similarly, if someone dies on the first day of Yom Tov, our established law is that non-Jews should handle it. This is prohibited for a slave, whether he has been circumcised and immersed or whether he has not been circumcised and immersed but has accepted upon himself the seven mitzvot, and according to the Rashba, even if he has not accepted upon himself the seven mitzvot, since according to Torah law they are forbidden to do work for a Jew. Therefore, with regard to the work of a Jew, these [slaves] are treated like Jews and are not permitted to do [work] except in a situation of danger, like a Jew himself. However, according to the Rambam and the Ramban, one who has not accepted upon himself the seven mitzvot is permitted, and he may perform the needs of a sick person who is not in danger and [handle] a dead person on the first day of Yom Tov. And know that regarding Yom Tov, there is a dispute about the primary prohibition for a slave, as the Bahag holds that a slave is prohibited from working on Yom Tov just as on Shabbat, but the Ramban disagrees and holds that a slave is only warned [not to work] on Shabbat and not on Yom Tov. This dispute is brought by our master, the Beit Yosef, in his great book later in Siman 526. (This is the first "some say" in paragraph 1, and it pertains to Yom Tov. The Magen Avraham, section 5, believes that this is the opinion of the Rambam mentioned later, and he questioned the redundancy, but the Taz, section 5, wrote as I have stated, and examine carefully.)"

The Tur wrote: A servant may not go out with a metal seal, whether it is on his garment or on his neck, because since it is valuable and the master is particular about it, we are concerned that it may break and the servant will come to carry it. But if it is made of clay, which the master is not particular about, on his neck - it is permitted, because if it breaks, the servant will leave it, and there is also no concern that he will take it off his neck and carry it in his hands, because he fears his master, who might think he wants to remove his servitude from him. But on his garment - it is forbidden, because it might break, and the servant fears his master who would be upset that he is walking with his garment without the seal, so he will remove his garment and fold it over his shoulder, in which case he would have some excuse for why he did so (see Beit Yosef). This applies to a seal made by his master, but if the servant made the seal himself - in all cases it is forbidden, even if it is made of clay and even on his neck, because we are concerned that he will take it off his neck and carry it in his hands, since, not being made by his master, he is not afraid. (See Taz section 3 and Magen Avraham sections 11 and 12, and in our times this does not apply at all as stated in section 1)

In the case of an animal, there are two Torah prohibitions and one Rabbinic prohibition. The Torah prohibitions are: the resting of one’s animal, meaning that it should not carry any burden on Shabbat nor walk with a wagon, as it is written: "So that your ox and your donkey may rest." It is not specifically ox and donkey, but rather the same applies to all kinds of animals, beasts, and birds that belong to a Jew—it is forbidden for the owner to place any burden on them. Even if someone else places a burden on the animal, the owner is obligated to remove it. The obligation applies specifically to the initial lifting and placing down [of the burden], similar to a person. This commandment pertains only to one's own animal and not to the animal of a non-Jew. 

The second prohibition is "mechamer," which means that the animal is carrying a burden and the owner is leading it. This is derived from "You shall not do any work, neither you nor your animal" (Exodus 20:10). Which labor involves both the person and the animal? This is "mechamer" (Rashi 153:). This is prohibited even with the animal of a non-Jew, and we have already explained this in Siman 246, Section 10, where we also explained why both prohibitions are necessary.

The Rabbinic prohibition is that one should not use their animal at all on Shabbat, meaning leaning on it or similar actions. The law of "mechamer" is explained there, and the law regarding using an animal will be explained in this Siman and in Siman 339. The main laws of this Siman pertain to the resting of one’s animal that it should not carry any burden. Women are equal to men in the resting of an animal, as in all the laws of Shabbat, and this is explicitly stated in the Mishnah at the end of the chapter "With What May an Animal Go Out," regarding the cow of Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah.

And the essence of this matter needs clarification, for there are cases where the animal is compelled to carry certain items, such as for its protection, since without them it would not be guarded at all. Consequently, this is not considered a burden, just as clothing is not considered a burden for a person. There are also cases where the animal needs something for warmth, like a donkey that is naturally cold and needs a saddlecloth to warm it. Obviously, this is akin to clothing for a person. Similarly, if items are placed on animals for some beneficial purpose, such as on sheep to keep their wool clean, to preserve their milk, or to prevent males from mounting them, and similar matters—these are considered like clothing for a person. Even though this is not intrinsically necessary for the animal but for the person, it is still called a need for the animal itself, similar to something that protects it. Although the animal does not feel this need because it lacks understanding, if it did have understanding, it would desire it. Therefore, it is considered its garment. In contrast, a burden is considered labor and is akin to work, and concerning this, the Torah said: "You shall not do [any work]... so that your ox and your donkey may rest." But in all the cases we mentioned, it is for the animal's benefit since it derives good from it. This is the general principle.

And thus the Sages said: Anything that is for protection is permitted, but if it does not protect with this, it is considered a burden, for it provides no benefit in terms of protection. And any extra protection is also considered a burden, since it can be protected with less than this. Specifically, it must be recognizable that it is extra protection, but if it is not so recognizable, even though it might be possible to protect with a little less than this, nevertheless, it is impossible to be so precise and meticulous, for this is the way of the world (Beit Yosef in the name of the Ri"v, the Smak, and the Terumah). Similarly, anything that is for adornment, like hanging ornaments on horses, is prohibited, for this is not like clothing, as there are no ornaments for animals. And some say that adornments that are common on weekdays are permitted, for this is like clothing, and only adornments that are not common on weekdays but that some people occasionally do (Ran, Chapter 5). However, the Tosafot believe that any kind is prohibited, and this is the main ruling in practice. And it seems to me that even according to those who permit, it is only for adornment that is common not during work, but adornment during work, like the wealthy who decorate their horses while they ride them or travel in a carriage, it is obvious that this is prohibited, for this is an adornment of burden. And these are the specifics of this section, and the entire chapter "With What Animal" in Chapter 5 of Shabbat is based on this, see there.

Therefore, a she-camel, which requires more guarding than a male camel, goes out with a nose ring. This means that they take an iron muzzle, which is an iron ring, and pierce its nose when it is young, and insert the ring into its nose, and it is guarded by this (see Drisha). And a Libyan donkey, a donkey that comes from the region of Libya, as it is written: "Put and the Libyans were your helpers." Rashi explains that this is Egypt (another version:), and it seems to me that this is a part of Egypt, as it is written there Cush, Mizraim, Put, and the Libyans, etc., and if so, it is not Egypt itself but a part of the country. It is stronger and requires an iron bit that is placed between its jaws (Pri Toar), and a bit is a bridle that fits on its head and jaws, and in the language of the Mishnah, it is called a promby. A camel goes out with a halter, which is a rope bridle (Aruch), and a mule, donkey, and horse go out with a halter or a bridle, but not with both, as it is written in the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, Section A. There is a question, for with a bridle, there is only permission for a Libyan donkey (Taz, Subsection 2), and some have removed 'donkey' from the texts (Bach and Magen Avraham, Subsection 2). However, in truth, there is no need for this, for we explicitly find in Bava Metzia (9a): 'This one acquired a donkey and a bit,' see there, indicating that this is the usual way for a donkey. However, in truth, the Aruch explains (entry 'peg'): leather straps of a bridle placed on its jaws and forehead, where a bridle includes whether it is made of leather straps or iron. And for a Libyan donkey, the Talmud precisely says 'iron bit', and an ordinary donkey has a bit, not of iron. It is permitted to wrap the halter rope around its neck and it goes out with it, as this is its way during the week, and this is not considered excessive guarding. It is permitted to carry the halter and place it on it, and it is not considered muktzeh, since it is needed for this. However, one must not lean on it, as it is forbidden to use animals as stated. Any item that is an animal's garment is not considered muktzeh, and it is permitted to dress it just as it is permitted to feed and water it.

If one ties a rope in the mouth of a horse, it does not guard it well, as it slips out of its mouth. This is not comparable to a halter that is tied on its head and does not slip out. Since it does not guard it well, it is considered a burden. Conversely, a regular donkey is prohibited from going out with a "perumbia," which is an iron bridle, as it is considered excessive guarding. However, a donkey that is difficult to manage, which is wild and requires more guarding, is permitted to go out with it. Similarly, any animal that is difficult to manage, even though all other animals of its kind do not need strong guarding, since this one requires it, it is permitted to go out with it.

And all animals that have ornamental collars, such as hunting dogs and small animals that have a kind of bracelet around their necks with a fixed ring in which a strap is inserted and used to pull them, it is permissible for them to go out with the collar around their necks and be pulled with it. This refers to a situation where there is guarding with the collars, so if they try to run away, they can be caught with the halter's wrapping. The wrapping needs to be loose enough to allow a hand to be inserted (as explained in Tosafot 52a, "or"), but if it is solely for decoration, it is prohibited. Rashi, of blessed memory, explained there that even if it is solely for decoration, since this is their usual practice on weekdays, it is permitted. We have already explained this in section 3 (and see Bach). However, a dog that is not a hunting dog is prohibited from going out with a ring on its neck.

There is uncertainty regarding a place where this is done as a sign that the dog has an owner. If the dog does not have a ring on its neck, it is a sign that it does not have an owner and people will kill it. The question is whether it is permissible for it to go out with it or not. It seems that it is prohibited, and the proof is from what will be explained that chickens are not allowed to go out with strings that are made as a sign so they will not be exchanged. Therefore, anything made as a sign is considered a burden.

Rams go out with louvavin, which is leather tied beneath their genitals to prevent them from mounting the ewes, so they won't become emaciated. Ewes go out with khuzot, which is the opposite; it is tied above their genitals to allow the rams to mount them, so they will become pregnant and give birth. They go out with kavunot, which is a cloth tied around them to keep the wool clean. Goats go out with tzerurot, which is a tying of their udders. Specifically, if the tying is to shrink their udders so they won't give milk and will become fat, then it is tied tightly. But if the tying is to keep their milk from falling to the ground, it is forbidden, because in this case, it is not tied tightly, as they fear tightening it would cause the udders to shrink, and the intention is that they should give milk. Therefore, we are concerned it might fall off and be carried. One should not ask how it is possible for two opposites to be considered for their benefit; it is certainly so. There are goats that are naturally fat and benefit from milking, and those that are thin benefit from not milking. Moreover, since they are human property, whatever the person wishes for their benefit is considered for them like a garment. This is specifically when it concerns the body of the animal itself, but if it is made as a sign, it is considered a burden, as we have said.

The donkey by its nature is cold and requires warming, as people say: 'A donkey - even in the middle of summer, it feels cold.' Therefore, it always carries a saddlecloth, which is like a small saddle. It may go out with a saddlecloth tied to its body, because if it is not tied, there is concern that it will fall and one might come to carry it. Tying it on Shabbat is prohibited, because during the tying one needs to lean on the animal's body, which is considered using animals. Therefore, it must be tied on it before Shabbat. However, all other animals are prohibited [to go out with a saddlecloth], as they do not need warming and it is considered a burden. Also, placing a saddle on a donkey is prohibited even if it is tied from before Shabbat, because it does not warm the donkey but is merely for carrying. On Shabbat, it is permitted to place a saddlecloth on the donkey for it to walk in a courtyard, as it does not need to be tied, and just placing it does not require leaning on its body. Similarly, in a city with an eruv, it is permitted to go out [with a saddlecloth], and all things that were explained as prohibited due to being considered a burden are only in a place without an eruv. In a place with an eruv, everything is permitted, as it is not more stringent than a person, as mentioned in Siman 266. However, placing a saddlecloth on a horse is entirely prohibited, even in a courtyard, because it does not need it, and it appears as if one intends to load it with a burden. Removing a saddlecloth on Shabbat is prohibited whether from a donkey or a horse, because since they do not suffer if it is not removed, it is considered unnecessary exertion. A saddle is prohibited both to remove and to place, whether on a donkey or a horse, due to unnecessary exertion.

And when the cold is intense and the horse suffers from the frost, its law is the same as that of a donkey (Taz, note 6). Similarly, in the summer when flies bite it, it is permissible to place something on it to prevent the fly bites (ibid.). And the saddle on a donkey that has come from the road and is exhausted and needs to be removed to cool it down—one should not remove it by hand. Although the donkey experiences some discomfort from the heat of the saddle, it will cool down on its own when it rests. When one wants the saddle to fall off, one loosens the strap underneath it, as there is no need to rely on it, and leads it back and forth in the courtyard until it falls off on its own.

One may not hang a basket on a donkey's neck to place its food inside so that it eats from there, because since it can eat without this, it is considered unnecessary exertion, and further, it might come to lean on it. However, for calves and foals, which are young donkeys with small necks and have difficulty eating from the ground, it is permitted to hang a small vessel with food on them so they can eat from it. There is no concern of leaning for them because it is easy to hang things on them. And this is in a courtyard, but they should not go out with it into the public domain, as it is considered a burden. According to this, in our case, hanging a bag with oats on a horse's neck so it can eat is not proper, since it can eat from the trough or other vessels.

A horse may not go out with a fox's tail hanging between its eyes to ward off the evil eye, nor with a red ribbon that is used to adorn the horse, nor may goats go out with a pouch on their udders, which is tied on to prevent their udders from getting scratched by thorns. I do not understand this, for it is a great necessity for them. Indeed, in the Rambam, Chapter 20, this law is not found, and also in the Gemara (53b), this is not mentioned as a prohibition. Rather, it is told as a story about the goats of the house of Antochia, whose udders were large, and they made pouches for them so that their udders would not get scratched—see there. From the Rambam there, it is actually a proof to the contrary, for he wrote in Law 12 that male goats may go out with a leather strap tied on their hearts so that wolves do not fall upon them, and this is in the Gemara there. If so, what is the difference between this and that? The Tur and the Shulchan Aruch in paragraph 11, which brought this law, did not bring this law of the Rambam. It seems to me that the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch hold that for an animal, in order to protect it from damage, it is considered a burden, just like for a person when protecting from filth, it is considered a burden if it is not a complete garment, as stated in Siman 301, paragraph 65—see there. Therefore, they ruled this as forbidden. They did not rule according to the opinion in the Gemara there that permits the leather strap, but ruled like the other Amoraim, and they believe there is a disagreement, while the Rambam holds there is no disagreement, as the Maggid Mishneh wrote there. It is surprising to me that the commentators did not address this at all.

And furthermore, they wrote that a cow should not go out with a muzzle in its mouth, which is used to prevent it from grazing in other fields, nor any animal with sandals on its feet, to prevent it from being injured. I did not find this ruling about a cow not going out with a muzzle in its mouth in the Rambam. Regarding the reason for the sandal, one could say that perhaps it might fall off and one might come to carry it, for otherwise, why would it be forbidden? However, an animal may go out with a bandage on a wound and with splints on a fracture, which are boards tied around the broken bone, and with a placenta that has partially emerged and is hanging from it. One may also seal a bell around its neck and let it walk in the courtyard, but it should not go out with it into the public domain, even if it is sealed, whether it is on its neck or on its clothing. The reason is that it appears as if one is taking it to the market to sell it, and if it is not tied to it, it is also considered a burden (see Magen Avraham section 6). If the bell is not sealed, it is also forbidden in the courtyard because it makes a sound, and if it resembles the sound of a musical instrument, even slightly, it is certainly forbidden. Even otherwise, since it makes noise, it appears as if one is taking it to the market to sell (ibid. section 5). An animal should not go out with a seal, whether it is on its neck or on its clothing, because the seal is a sign, and this is forbidden for an animal, as will be explained regarding the threads on a chicken, as mentioned in section 5. Additionally, there is a concern that it might break off and one might come to carry it.

A camel may not go out with a saddlecloth, which is a type of small cushion placed under its tail, even if it is tied to its tail, unless it is tied both to its tail and to its hump or to its genitals. Because if it is tied to both, it will not fall off (Rashi 54a). But if it is tied only to its tail, we are concerned that it will fall off and one might come to carry it. And no animal may go out with its legs bound or hobbled, and "bound" means tying one of its forelegs with one of its hind legs, and "hobbled" means tying one of its legs upwards so it will only walk on three legs. The prohibition is because the reason for doing so is to prevent the animal from running away, and this is an excessive precaution, as such a level of guarding is not necessary.

And one should not tie camels one after another while holding the halter of the first, causing all of them to be led by him, because it appears as if he is leading them to sell (Gemara 54a). But if he holds several halters of camels in his hand, it is permitted. However, there is an opinion that prohibits even this, because in such a case too, it appears as if he is leading them to sell, and it is only permitted to lead one animal alone while pulling it with a rope. And even when leading one animal and pulling it with a rope, one must be careful that the head of the rope does not extend a handbreadth below his hand, because in such a case it will appear as if he is carrying the rope by itself, and that it is not attached to the animal. Also, he should not leave too much of the rope between his hand and the animal in a way that it drags and reaches a handbreadth near the ground, because if it reaches there, it also appears as if the rope is by itself and not tied to the animal. If the rope is long, he should wrap it around its neck and leave it loose between the rope and the neck, as stated in section 5.

A donkey may not go out with a saddlecloth that is not tied to it from before Shabbat, and the reason is explained in Section 7. Nor with a bell, even though it is plugged, as stated in Section 11. Nor with a ladder around its neck, which are boards tied around its neck so that it does not scratch its wound. This is not similar to a bandage on a wound, which is permitted because it is considered significant, and we are concerned that the tie may come undone, fall, and one may come to carry it (Rashi 54b). Nor with a strap on its leg, which is like a thick ring made of straw, tied to the animal's legs so that its steps are short and it does not strike its legs against each other. This is done to protect it from injuring its legs, or when its hooves are cracked, they tie it with a strap so that it heals and returns to its original state. The reason for prohibition is either because of concern that it may fall and one may come to carry it, or because it is unnecessary and is considered a burden. 

Chickens may not go out with strings tied to their legs as a sign, as this is considered a burden, as stated. Nor with a strap tied to their legs to prevent them from breaking vessels, as it is not necessary for the chickens themselves and is considered a burden. However, if it is to prevent them from running away, it is permitted, as this is considered necessary. 

Rams may not go out with a wagon under their tails, made to prevent their tails from dragging on the ground. The Jerusalem Talmud explains the reason for the prohibition is that the wagon digs into the ground. Goats may not go out with a known stick placed in their noses to make them sneeze and expel the worms in their heads, lest the stick fall from its nose and one may come to carry it. 

A calf may not go out with a small yoke placed on its neck, as it is considered a burden, nor with a muzzle placed on its nose to prevent it from sucking, as this cannot be considered necessary for it and is therefore a burden. A cow may not go out with a skin placed on its udders to prevent leeches from sucking, because it is not tied securely, and we are concerned that it may fall and one may come to carry it. Nor with a strap between its horns, whether for protection, as it does not need such protection and is considered excessive guarding, or for decoration, as an animal does not wear jewelry. 

Similarly, a cow or ox may not go out with a rope around its neck for this reason, as it does not need guarding, and it is considered excessive guarding unless its nature is bad, and it requires this guarding. Calves, however, are permitted, as they are easily rebellious and need guarding. Even if the rope is wrapped around their necks, it is permitted if there is space between the rope and the neck, enough to insert a hand. 

An animal may go out with an amulet that is expert for animals, but it may not go out with an amulet that is expert for humans, as an amulet expert for humans is not expert for animals, as humans have fortune (Gemara).

It is a general principle that anything the Sages prohibited regarding an animal because of carrying is permitted in a courtyard and even in a karmelit (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 6). However, there are those who prohibit it in a karmelit (Taz, subparagraph 27), and this is also implied in the Sefer Mitzvot Gadol (SmaG) which writes that a bell is prohibited in a karmelit (there). But this is not a proof, for it can be said that the reason for the bell is because it appears as if one is leading the animal to sell it, and this is certainly prohibited even in a karmelit. Indeed, the SmaG explicitly writes this reason there. And although he also writes "and furthermore because of carrying" there, this applies to a public domain. On the contrary, regarding other matters, the SmaG explicitly writes that it applies to a public domain there. Therefore, the primary opinion seems to be the first opinion. However, in a case where the reason is that it might fall off and one might come to carry it, it can be said that it is also prohibited in a karmelit (Magen Avraham there). And in a matter where the reason is because it appears as if one is leading it to sell, it is obvious that it is prohibited even in an alley that has an eruv, and indeed, even on Yom Tov this is prohibited, where there is no prohibition of carrying as stated in Siman 522 (there).

One may not ride on an animal or hang onto it, and even using it from the side is prohibited, for it is forbidden to make use of animals on Shabbat and Yom Tov, and this is one of the rabbinic prohibitions. Know that the prohibition against riding is a Mishna in Beitza (37b), and the Gemara explains the reason is lest one cut a branch, and Rashi explains this means to strike it, while the Rif and the Rambam in Chapter 21 explain it means to drive it. Why didn’t they say it’s because of using animals? Because the primary prohibition of using animals is also for this reason, lest one cut a branch (Tosafot Eruvin 43a, end of s.v. 'halacha'). In the Jerusalem Talmud, it says the reason is because of resting one’s animal, and Rabbeinu Beit Yosef explains in his major work that even though a living creature carries itself and there is no resting of one’s animal, nevertheless since it suffers from this, it is forbidden, for in this case there is no rest for it. According to this, it can be said that the Jerusalem Talmud and the Babylonian Talmud are of one reason, according to Rashi’s explanation that it is lest one cut a branch to strike it. In other words, there are two prohibitions: the prohibition of cutting a branch, and the prohibition of causing distress from the blows. In my humble opinion, it seems that the intention of the Jerusalem Talmud aligns with the explanation of the Rif and the Rambam, lest one cut a branch to drive it, and in this case, he will certainly transgress the prohibition of resting one’s animal when driving it with any load. The Jerusalem Talmud that says it’s because of resting one’s animal means that it can lead to a violation of resting one’s animal (see what I wrote above in Siman 246, Section 16).

It has already been explained in the previous section that even using the side (of an animal) is forbidden, but secondary sides are permitted. For example, if another object is placed on the side and one uses it, it is permitted, as they did not decree on secondary sides. A horse that pulls a wagon is considered as the wagon being the sides, since the whole act of the wagon is one, and the animal pulls it with the wagon, and the person sitting in the wagon is effectively using the sides of the animal. Moreover, if one uses the animal through another object, i.e., through the wagon, and the person sitting in the wagon is as if he is sitting on the sides of the animal itself. What difference does it make if the animal pulls the person through riding or through the wagon? On the contrary, through the wagon it is more severe, as the animal pulls both the person and the wagon, and in this case, the principle of "a living being carries itself" does not apply. Therefore, one who travels in a wagon is liable from the Torah, and even if the horse and the wagon belong to a non-Jew and he is driving it while the Jew sits in the wagon, it is considered as if he is riding and using an animal. This is what our master, the Rema, wrote in section 18: "It is forbidden to sit in a wagon that a non-Jew is driving on Shabbat, because one is using the animal, and also one might cut a branch," end quote. This means there is a prohibition of using the animal itself, and it is considered as sides, and perhaps even more than sides for the reason we explained. Additionally, since the main reason for the prohibition was that one might cut a branch, there is also this concern for someone sitting in the wagon, who, wanting the animal to run faster, might cut a branch or take another object and hit it, thereby committing several prohibitions as we mentioned. Outside the Shabbat boundary, the prohibition of boundaries is also added. In summary: one who sits in a wagon commits many prohibitions, and even pushing the wagon while the horse is in it is forbidden (see Magen Avraham sub-section 10, and according to what we have explained, everything is clarified as forbidden, and examine this well).

The Rambam writes in Chapter 21, Law 9: "One may not ride on an animal on Shabbat… and one may not mount it while it is still day in order to sit on it on Shabbat. If one climbed a tree on Shabbat inadvertently, one is permitted to descend; if done intentionally, one is forbidden to descend (since he would be using it by descending). However, with an animal, even if it was done intentionally, one may descend due to the suffering of living creatures. Similarly, one may unload a burden from an animal on Shabbat due to the suffering of living creatures. How so? If one's animal was laden with a bundle of grain, one should place his head under it and shift it to the side, and it will fall off by itself. If one was returning from a journey on Shabbat and his animal was laden, when he reaches the outer courtyard, he may remove the utensils that may be handled on Shabbat, etc." This has already been explained in Siman 266, see there. And even if the burden is muktzeh (set aside), it is permitted due to the suffering of living creatures (see Magen Avraham, Subsection 9).

An animal that has fallen into a water channel — if the water is deep enough that it cannot be sustained in its place, for if it could be sustained in its place, we would provide it with food there and it would remain until the conclusion of Shabbat when it could be pulled out — but on Shabbat, it is forbidden to pull it out even though there is a concern for the suffering of animals, as one cannot compare one rabbinic decree to another. (See there, subsection 11). However, it is clear that it is permitted to tell a non-Jew to pull it out because of the suffering of animals (see there). However, if there is no non-Jew present and it also cannot be sustained in its place and might die, the sages permitted even bringing cushions and pillows, lifting one of its legs and placing the leg on them, and then doing the same with the second, third, and fourth legs in order to lift it. If it climbs out, it climbs out. Even though this temporarily nullifies the use of a utensil, and perhaps it will not climb out and the nullification will last all of Shabbat, nevertheless, they permitted it because of the suffering of animals, but not to lift it directly with one's hands. Further laws concerning animals are clarified in Section 266 and will also be clarified in Section 324 and Section 332, and laws concerning cooling an animal will be clarified in Section 523 regarding Yom Tov, and the same applies to Shabbat. (See Orach Chaim 318:18 and it requires further study).

It is permissible to tell a non-Jew to milk his animal on Shabbat, because although milking is a prohibited activity due to extraction and telling a non-Jew to perform work is rabbinically forbidden, nonetheless, due to the suffering of animals when their udders are full of milk and they are not milked, which causes them great pain, it is therefore permitted to instruct a non-Jew to milk them. It is obvious that the milk is prohibited all of Shabbat due to being muktzeh and nolad. Some say that since the entire permission is due to the suffering of animals, one must purchase the milk for a minimal amount from the non-Jew, so it does not appear that the milking is for the benefit of a Jew. It is known that nowadays they give something in exchange for the milking, so even according to this opinion, we are compliant. Some say that for maids who are hired for a year, this is not necessary at all (Bach and Taz, section 12), because they certainly work with their own intentions, as it is their duty to do so. Some say, on the contrary, that maids are worse, as they certainly act with the intention of the owner, as stated in Siman 254 (Magen Avraham, section 13), and also that in a Jew’s house there is no permission to perform work at all as stated in Siman 252 (there). Nevertheless, the world customarily allows this (there), and it appears to me that the law is with them, as this is not similar to all other labors, for everyone knows that the Jew does not use the milk on Shabbat and derives no benefit from it since it would have been milked after Shabbat, and the milking is solely due to the suffering of animals, which is evident even to non-Jews. If there is no maid in his house, it is good to appoint a permanent non-Jew to come and milk on Shabbat, so he does not need to instruct her every Shabbat, and this is our custom. How to give food to animals on Shabbat will be explained in Siman 324. (Regarding what the Magen Avraham states in section 12 that it is permissible to tell a non-Jew to force-feed geese, we customarily prohibit force-feeding as stated in Yoreh De'ah Siman 33, and the laws of milking will be explained in Siman 320 there.)

Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote in Section 21: Cheeses that maidservants make on their own from the milk of a Jew are permitted, since he did not instruct them to do so. This means that if he knows they are making it, he is obligated to protest, but this refers to a case where they made it on their own. The source of this ruling is from the glosses of the Maimonides, Chapter 8, Letter 7, and he holds that if a Jew instructs a non-Jew to perform work for him on Shabbat, the Jew is prohibited from benefiting from that work forever as a penalty, according to the opinion of Rabbeinu Yerucham, which he brought in his major work in Section 307. This teaches us that the cheese is permitted since they made it on their own. And indeed, according to what Rabbeinu Beit Yosef ruled later in Section 307, Paragraph 20, even if the Jew instructed him to do the work on Shabbat, it is only prohibited for the time it takes to perform that work, but this law is still relevant. Nevertheless, his intention is as stated (and it resolves the difficulty raised by the Magen Avraham in Subsection 14).

If someone has a non-Jewish servant, and the servant waters the person's animal and leads it to drink while riding on it, there is no need to protest, because a living being carries itself and there is no Torah prohibition involved. Although it is rabbinically prohibited, this rabbinic decree does not extend to animals in such a way that the Jew would be required to prevent it. The Jew is not doing anything, neither in speech nor in action, except knowing that the non-Jew is performing a rabbinic prohibition with his animal. We do not find that one must prevent this. However, if the non-Jew places the Jew's clothes or other burdens on the animal, the Jew must prevent it, as there is a Torah prohibition involved. But there is no concern with a saddle, as it is considered part of the animal (Perisha). If something was left on the animal from before Shabbat, the owner is obligated to prevent it from walking in the public domain on Shabbat (Magen Avraham 16 and Eliyah Rabbah 23). However, if it is walking outside the Shabbat boundary, there is no need to prevent it (Eliyah Rabbah). 

It is permitted to hand over a horse, mule, or donkey to a non-Jewish shepherd, even though the shepherd might use them on Shabbat, as it does not matter because the shepherd does so without the Jew's knowledge and does not expect payment. If the Jew sees the shepherd using the animal on Shabbat, he should protest, and consequently, the shepherd will not use them. Why would the shepherd perform an act from which he gains no benefit? Therefore, when the Jew sees the shepherd using it, it is an isolated incident and will not be done regularly, so there is no issue. This is not the case with renting or lending to a non-Jew, for even if there is an agreement not to use it on Shabbat, it is ineffective, as it is certain the non-Jew will use it, as stated in Siman 246. But the shepherd has no benefit from using it.

Certainly, there is no concern that the shepherd will take the animals outside the Shabbat boundary, as this boundary is a rabbinic issue. Even beyond twelve mil according to several authorities is a rabbinic matter, and even if it were a Torah issue, we do not worry that the animals will go that far. However, it is forbidden to tell the shepherd to take them outside the boundary. If someone sends oxen to a distant place through non-Jews on a fixed payment basis, they should be sent before Shabbat, as it is forbidden on Shabbat, as stated in Siman 252 (this appears to me, and see Magen Avraham 18).

It is written: "If you refrain from trampling the Sabbath, from pursuing your affairs on My holy day, and you call the Sabbath a delight... and honor it by not doing your own ways, nor seeking your own affairs, nor speaking of them." This indicates that it is forbidden on the Sabbath to engage in business or commerce, even if it does not involve a primary category of prohibited work. This is referred to as "your affairs," meaning mundane matters. We are warned against both doing and speaking about them. The laws pertaining to speech will be explained in Siman 307. The Sages expounded (150b): speech is forbidden, but thought is permitted, meaning one is allowed to think about his business matters in his heart. Nevertheless, for the sake of Sabbath delight, it is a mitzvah not to think about them at all, and one should consider it as if all his work is done. The Sages permitted thinking about business only when it does not cause anxiety and worry, such as when his affairs are going well, successfully, and without mental distraction. But if thinking about them causes him worry and anxiety, it is forbidden, for there is no greater disruption to Sabbath delight than this. It is stated in the Mekhilta: "Six days you shall labor and do all your work" — one should consider all his work as done when the holy Sabbath arrives, for no one can complete all his work in one week. Rather, a person should see every Sabbath as if all his work is done, and there is no greater delight than this (Tur). Similarly, we say in the prayer: "A rest of peace, tranquility, calm, and security, a complete rest that You desire," and in the Grace after Meals we say: "Let there be no distress or sorrow on our day of rest" (Beit Yosef in the name of Rabbi Yosef). The reward for this is very great, and even in this world, his livelihood is rewarded, as we learned in the Baraita there: A story is told of a pious man whose fence was breached in his field, and he decided to repair it, but he remembered that it was the Sabbath and refrained from repairing it (even during the week, and he fined himself for thinking about it on the Sabbath). A miracle occurred, and a caper bush grew in it, and from it came his livelihood and the livelihood of his household (Shabbat 150b).

And what is this that is written, "from pursuing your own business" (Isaiah 58:13)? Is it not already written, "to do your own business"? What is the meaning of the term "from pursuing"? Rather, this is its explanation: Even to set up your activities is forbidden, meaning that doing something now which is entirely permissible, involving neither labor nor any rabbinic prohibition but is entirely permissible, yet by doing this you set up for yourself work that is forbidden to do on Shabbat, either because of labor or because of rabbinic decree—this too is forbidden. And even though this is only a thought (and thoughts are generally permitted), our sages explained in Eruvin (39a) that if it is something where the intent is not noticeable that it is for something forbidden on Shabbat, it is indeed permitted. But if it is something where the intent is noticeable, it is considered like speech and is forbidden.

How so? For example, if one is walking in his field to see what it needs in terms of hoeing and weeding, or if he is walking in his factory to observe what it needs, everyone understands that he is thinking in his heart about business matters. Similarly, in their times when the bathhouses were immediately after the city gate, and he stands at the city gate until dark, everyone sees that his intention is to go to the bathhouse when it gets dark. And thus we have learned in the Mishnah (150a): "One may not wait by the boundary to hire workers," meaning that he stands at the end of the boundary until dark, and everyone sees that since he stands at the end of the boundary, it is assumed that his intention is for something forbidden on Shabbat, and he waits by the boundary so that immediately when it gets dark, he will go outside the boundary and hire workers or engage in another matter that is forbidden on Shabbat. But within the boundary, it is permissible, as no one notices this, and it is considered as mere contemplation. (Tosafot there, s.v. "And one may not," and the words of the Magen Avraham in Siman 307:13 who wrote that waiting by the boundary is forbidden even if it is not noticeable, and rejects the words of the Mishneh Torah and the Shulchan Aruch based on the words of Tosafot there, is very puzzling, for Tosafot's intention is the same, and thus the Eliyah Rabbah objected to him in Siman 2. Furthermore, according to him, why is it permissible to wait to bring his animal, since even if it is not noticeable, it is forbidden? But according to what I explained, it is clear, and examine it well.)

However, one may wait at the boundary to bring his animal, because this could also be done permissibly. If there were huts within seventy and a fraction cubits of each other, it would be considered within the boundary. Similarly, it is permitted to wait at the boundary to bring detached fruits that are not set aside (mukzeh), since there is an aspect of permissibility if there were partitions from there to his house. But attached fruits or mukzeh fruits are forbidden, as there is no way to permit them (Gemara there). It is also forbidden to wait at the boundary to bring a small animal that cannot walk on its own and must be carried on one's shoulder, as there is no permissible way to do so on Shabbat; animals are considered mukzeh and are prohibited from being carried. However, it is permitted to wait to guard the small animal and the attached fruits, since guarding is allowed on Shabbat as well, and thus, one is waiting for something permissible. If one initially went for guarding and then decided to bring it, it is also permitted (the Gra"Z). Within the boundary, everything is permitted, since people do not notice it, as stated in the previous section. And what our Rabbi, the Rema, wrote in section 1 that it is also forbidden to walk to find a horse, boat, or cart to go out with, is talking about when it is evident that one is walking for that purpose (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 3), or if his intention is for the boundary (and it is apparent that it refers to this matter, see there).

However, it needs to be understood that since we have said that at the end of the boundary it is forbidden even though they do not know what he is waiting for until nightfall, but at the end of the boundary, they will say that presumably, it is for something forbidden as stated in Section 3. If so, what benefit is there if he waits until nightfall for something permitted, for they will still suspect him of waiting for something forbidden? However, the matter is clear that when he waits until nightfall for something permitted, they will see afterward that they suspected him for nothing. Furthermore, fundamentally, it is impossible to prohibit in such cases, for what is the reason we prohibit when they suspect him, and what difference does it make to us? Rather, since speaking is forbidden and thinking is permitted, if so, when they suspect him, he moves from the realm of thought to the realm of speech because it is evident what he is doing, as stated in Section 2. But when he waits until nightfall for something permitted, what do we care if they suspect him, for with him, there is neither speech nor thought involved (so it seems in my humble opinion).

If his animal is standing outside the techum (Sabbath boundary), he can call it, and it will come to him. Even though by calling it, it goes beyond its own techum, for example, if its techum was different from that of its owner, such as if he had given it to a shepherd before Shabbat as explained in Siman 397, it is still permissible to call it. This is because a person is not commanded regarding the techum of his animal. However, it is forbidden to bring it by hand if it is outside its own techum (Gemara 53b). And even if it is standing outside his own techum, he can call it, and we are not concerned that he will follow his animal and go beyond the techum. Since this is a rabbinic prohibition, we do not worry about it, similar to the case in Siman 350 where one is standing in a private or public domain and drinking in a karmelit, where we are not concerned that he will bring the vessel to himself. The same applies here.

Our Sages expounded from the verse "from pursuing your own affairs and speaking words" that your own affairs are forbidden, but matters related to Heaven are permitted. This means that one may attend to matters of Heaven, such as waiting at the boundary [of the Shabbat limit] and similar actions, as will be explained. There is a question about this: if so, we should also expound "doing your own affairs" and not the affairs of Heaven, and it should be permitted to perform a rabbinic prohibition (shvut) in matters of Heaven. However, the explanation is as follows: Certainly, when the Torah prohibited labor on Shabbat, it prohibited even for matters of Heaven unless it is a case of saving a life, as it is written: "You shall not do any labor," without differentiating between ordinary labor and labor for Heaven. Therefore, regarding sacrifices, the Torah needed to explicitly permit the burning of the limbs of the daily offering of the afternoon on the eve of Shabbat when the fire has already taken hold, based on the verse "You shall not kindle a fire in any of your dwellings on the Sabbath day," implying you shall not kindle a fire on Shabbat, but you may kindle for the limbs and fats of the eve of Shabbat, as stated at the end of the first chapter of Shabbat. Consequently, when rabbinic prohibitions were universally forbidden, they were also forbidden for the sake of a mitzvah, except in the Temple where rabbinic prohibitions do not apply, and even then, not all rabbinic prohibitions (see Tosafot Eruvin 102b, s.v. "vehayelyon"). Therefore, the verse "doing your own affairs" includes even matters of Heaven. However, here, where it is written "from pursuing your own affairs and speaking words," just as "speaking words" does not refer to words of Heaven, for on the contrary, it is a mitzvah to speak words of Heaven on Shabbat, so too "from pursuing your own affairs" does not refer to matters of Heaven.

Therefore, it is permissible to wait at the boundary to attend to the needs of a bride or the needs of the deceased or other essential matters of a mitzvah, such as bringing the bride her necessities or the deceased a coffin and shrouds, and the like. One can also tell another to wait until nightfall to bring it for him, because since it is permissible for him to do it himself, all the more so he can tell his friend to do it. He can also tell him to go to a specific place tomorrow to buy it, and if he doesn't find it in the first place, to go to another place, and if he doesn't find it for a certain price, to buy it for a higher price. As long as he does not specify an exact amount, meaning he should not say not to exceed a certain amount of money, because that is considered actual buying and selling, which is not permitted for the sake of heavenly matters. However, general preparations are permitted, and as long as he does not specify a fixed price, it is considered general preparation. Rabbi Rema writes in Section 3: If it is not possible otherwise, even specifying an amount is permitted in any case, because it is for the sake of a mitzvah, but some forbid it in any case, and this is the main ruling. The one who permits it holds that since this is not actual buying and selling, it falls under general preparation, meaning to acquire for the sake of the purchase. Those who forbid it hold that specifying a price is considered personal business, which is forbidden as mentioned. All the more so it is forbidden to say to the seller: "I took from you for eight dinars, give me more for two dinars, and I will owe you ten," because that is certainly forbidden as it is considered actual buying and selling. (It seems to me that in this everyone agrees it is forbidden, even though from the wording of Rema it does not appear so; examine it carefully.)

It is well known that it is forbidden to take payment for Shabbat even for something that is permitted to do on Shabbat, such as payment for guarding, unless it is included with the payment for other days, such as taking payment for a week or a month, where the payment for Shabbat is included within the payment for the other days.
