And even for guarding something that is a mitzvah, this is also the case, and we do not say in this context that "matters of Heaven are permitted." This is what is taught (Bava Metzia 58a): One who hires a worker to guard a cow, to guard a child, to guard seeds — meaning the treasurer of the Temple who hired a worker to guard the red heifer or the children being prepared for this or the seeds for the omer — does not give him payment for Shabbat; therefore, the responsibility for Shabbat is not upon him. If he was hired for Shabbat, for a month, for a year, or for a week (Shemitta) — he is given payment for Shabbat because it is included, therefore the responsibility for Shabbat is upon him. We have thus learned that even for a mitzvah it is forbidden, for this is not included in "your affairs" but rather in "your work," as it is not preparation for a matter but a complete prohibition, even though it was not explicitly spoken about. (This is the reason for the Tur who wrote: "It is forbidden to take payment for Shabbat," and the Bach wondered why he changed the language from the Gemara there, but to me it is clear that here regarding Shabbat this is the main law, but I am puzzled by the language of the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch in paragraph 4 who wrote this law in general terms of hiring and did not write the main novelty that even for a mitzvah it is forbidden, which is the main point relevant to this section. They wrote in the language of the Rambam at the end of chapter 6, but the Rambam does not deal there with the laws of matters of Heaven, see there and examine carefully).

When one hires a worker for a month or a week and the worker demands part of his wages, he is not allowed to say: 'Give me the wages for Shabbat', but rather he should say: 'Give me the weekly wage or the monthly wage,' or 'Give me part of the weekly or monthly wage,' and he can also say: 'Give me the wage for ten days.' It seems to me that he can also say: 'Give me the wage for seven days,' even though it appears as if he is mentioning Shabbat, it is permitted since it is included in a general payment, and this is like a week. However, even if he hired him for a month but stipulated that he would pay him for each day as it is due for the day, it is considered a daily wage, because if he dismisses him in the middle of the week, he would only pay him for the days worked and not for the entire week. Therefore, it is considered a daily wage and constitutes Shabbat wages (Magen Avraham, section 7). Therefore, if they agreed that he would pay him for the entire week if he dismisses him in the middle of the week, it is permitted. Hence, those who lend with interest based on a heter iska should ensure that when they pay, they calculate by the week and not by the day, so that it does not constitute Shabbat wages. This applies to all similar matters. However, for a deduction, it is permissible even to calculate daily, but for profit, it is forbidden to calculate daily (Magen Avraham, ibid., and so it is in Ketubot regarding the matter of a rebellious wife on page 64a, the difference between an addition and a deduction, see there).

And since it has been clarified that even for the sake of a mitzvah, it is forbidden to receive wages for work done on Shabbat, it is therefore prohibited to hire cantors to pray on Shabbat and to pay them a specified amount for this. However, it is permissible if they are hired for a week, a month, or a year. And even though the main intention is for Shabbat, as is known, the hiring is for the week according to the custom of cantors who receive wages on a weekly basis. Indeed, it is common practice among us that cantors who are traveling pray on Shabbat and receive payment for this according to the agreement with the gabbai (synagogue sexton), and according to this, it is a complete prohibition. Additionally, even when they are paid for a week, there is an opinion that they must pray every day (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 9), but this is not our custom. However, it can be argued that since they are obligated to go to a circumcision or a wedding, it is permitted. Yet, as is known, the primary hiring is for the prayers of Shabbat, Yom Tov, Rosh Hashanah, and Yom Kippur. Therefore, it constitutes wages for Shabbat and requires further examination.

And this is the language of our master, the Beit Yosef, in section 5: "It is forbidden to hire cantors to pray on Shabbat, and there are those who permit it," end quote. And here, the Tur later in Siman 585 ruled it as forbidden and brought proof from the case of one who hires a laborer that we mentioned in section 9. And our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote there in section 5: "One who takes payment... does not see a sign of blessing," see there. And despite the fact that here it seems he holds like the first opinion, since he writes the second opinion in the name of "there are those who permit," as is his usual manner, nevertheless, it seems that because he saw that this is the custom of the world, he did not rule it strictly forbidden there. And the one who permits brought proof from Pesachim (50a) regarding the four coins that do not show a sign of blessing, one of which is the wages of interpreters who stand before the sage on Shabbat and announce to the public, see there, where it is said the reason is that it appears like Shabbat wages. This implies that there is no prohibition, but rather that one does not see a sign of blessing. And there are those who say the difference is because in the case of hiring a laborer, the mitzvah is not dependent on Shabbat, but for interpreters and cantors, it is only dependent on Shabbat (Taz there, subsection 7). And this is not understood, because on the contrary, since it is specific to Shabbat, it would be a greater prohibition. The two opinions are in the Mordechai on Ketubot at the end of chapter 5, and the one who permits says there the reason is that it is for a mitzvah (and so wrote the Magen Avraham in subsection 8). And this is not understood, for is hiring a laborer for guarding the red heifer not a mitzvah? And it seems that they mean to say that because this mitzvah must necessarily be done on Shabbat, like the interpreters and cantors, and there is no one willing to do it for free, therefore it is necessary to pay them, and they indeed do not do well, and therefore they do not see a sign of blessing. However, they are also not committing a prohibition, because for them it is like compensation for loss of work, as they do not take payment for Shabbat itself but for the effort throughout the week. And it turns out that those who give are not in violation, because they are compelled to do so according to the law, and those who receive do not take Shabbat wages but compensation for loss of work on weekdays. And although among us there is no necessity for cantors who sing, as a simple person can lead the prayers, nevertheless, since the masses consider it a mitzvah and an honor for Shabbat and festivals, and also a pleasure, it thereby becomes a mitzvah. And even for the cantors who are passing through, they consider this a Shabbat pleasure, and the money is given as a donation. Therefore, there is no prohibition in this matter (so it seems in my humble opinion to justify, and the words of the Beit Yosef there require further investigation).

One is permitted to discuss matters related to mitzvot on Shabbat, such as calculations for charity or what is needed for a mitzvah meal, as well as to allocate charity. Although one may not consecrate or make valuations on Shabbat, this is because speaking to consecrate something to a sacred purpose is like physically transferring it to a secular domain, thereby moving it from one domain to another. However, our charitable donations, whether to the poor or to the synagogue, are considered secular, as stated in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 95, and therefore, there is no issue of transferring from one domain to another on Shabbat. It is merely verbalizing a mitzvah commitment, akin to making a vow, and it is permitted to make a mitzvah vow on Shabbat. Perhaps even if one were to hand over an item to a charity treasurer on Shabbat, it would also be permitted, as it is certain that the donation was pledged before Shabbat. However, it is better not to hand it over to the treasurer on Shabbat (see Taz, Subsection 2, and Magen Avraham, Subsection 11).

And similarly, it is permitted to manage communal affairs on Shabbat, for there is no greater heavenly concern than this, even when the matters are of a secular nature, such as matters of livelihood, property boundaries, and the like, for all communal needs are a great mitzvah. And even though no rabbinic prohibition or rabbinic prohibition of instructing a non-Jew was permitted for communal needs, nevertheless, mere speech, which is prohibited for one's own matters because of "speaking a word" (Isaiah 58:13), is considered a heavenly concern and it is permitted to speak about them and to organize matters through mere speech (Magen Avraham 12). Similarly, it is permitted to arrange a match between a young man and a maiden on Shabbat through mere speech, because this is a mitzvah matter, and certainly to speak with a teacher to teach a child a book, or with a craftsman to teach him a craft, for this is also a mitzvah, for if he has no craft, he will engage in theft. And specifically to speak if the teacher or craftsman wants to earn, but it is forbidden to finalize with him through a formal act of acquisition, and also to mention the price amount - it is forbidden, for only speech itself was permitted in this matter.

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote in section 6: "There are those who say that in places where it is customary for the one called to the Torah to make a 'Mi Sheberach' (blessing) and pledge charity or to the cantor – it is forbidden to pledge on Shabbat how much to give. However, the custom is to be lenient, as it is permissible to pledge charity." This means that it is not considered a transaction where one pays a certain amount for the aliyah (being called to the Torah), but rather it is simply charity. It is customary for those called to the Torah to pledge charity, and it is permissible to pledge charity. Even if they give it to the cantor and he is wealthy, it is still considered charity, since they give it in exchange for the mitzvah of prayer (Magen Avraham, section 15).

In a place where they sell the mitzvot, and there are those who hesitate about this, since it is really like buying and selling, where one person offers a certain amount and another increases it, nevertheless, this is not exactly like buying and selling, for is there any intrinsic value here? Rather, it is as if one says: If I merit this aliyah, I will give such and such to charity, and the other says: I will add to the charity if I merit this aliyah. Therefore, some of the early pious ones would pay the synagogue whatever they intended to give for the aliyah, even if the other person increased and ended up with the aliyah, because they considered it as a vow to charity. However, in terms of the law, this is not the case, as it is a conditional vow (see Magen Avraham there), and the custom of Israel is Torah and should not be questioned at all. And it is obvious that selling synagogue seats is forbidden on Shabbat and Yom Tov, as this is truly like buying and selling, since one sits in the place. But other mitzvot like the aliyah to the Torah, lifting and rolling the Torah, opening the ark, and wine for Kiddush and Havdalah are permitted, as this is merely charity, as explained.

The Rambam wrote in Chapter 23, Law 12: "It is also forbidden to buy, sell, rent, or lease due to a decree lest one come to write," end quote. I do not understand why this is needed, for the prohibition is clear due to 'finding your own pleasure and speaking your own words on My holy day,' since even speaking about it is forbidden (113:), and so wrote the Tosafot there, and it is explained at the beginning of Siman 307. However, also in Rashi (Beitzah 37a), this language is found: "Buying and selling is forbidden from the verse, as it is written: 'finding your own pleasure and speaking your own words,' or alternatively, buying and selling may lead to writing sales contracts. And if you say it is a decree on a decree - it is all one decree," end quote. And perhaps our Rabbis spoke of an additional reason beyond 'finding your own pleasure.' Similarly, a gift is like a sale, as it transfers ownership from one domain to another and is forbidden on Shabbat, but for the sake of a mitzvah and for Shabbat needs - a gift is permitted (Magen Avraham, Section 15 and Beit Yosef, Siman 667). And even though buying and selling, even for the sake of a mitzvah, is certainly forbidden, indeed, a gift is not comparable to buying and selling, for with a gift, 'finding your own pleasure' does not apply as much, as it is not for profit but rather out of love. And even though we find in the Gemara regarding a gift that if not for receiving benefit from him, he would not give him a gift, and thus a gift is like a sale (Megillah 26b), nevertheless, it is not for profit, and its law is like consecration, which is forbidden to consecrate on Shabbat. But what is needed for the day is permitted, as written in Siman 339, and it is explicitly stated in the Gemara at the beginning of the chapter "Shoel": "A person may consecrate his Pesach offering on Shabbat and his festival offering on Yom Tov," and the concern of writing does not apply to a gift, as writing in a ledger is specifically related to business matters. Some wonder about giving gifts to the groom on Shabbat (there), but in truth, there is no prohibition in this, as it is considered a matter of a mitzvah, for it is a mitzvah to bring joy to the groom and bride. And it is also needed for the day, as the custom is to make a feast on the first Shabbat after the wedding, and it is a time of joy for the groom and bride, and certainly, it is permitted to bring them joy with gifts. Similarly, the custom is to give the bride gifts at that time, and there is no trace of prohibition in this, and the custom of Israel is Torah (this appears to be my humble opinion).

And the Rambam wrote there: "Whether one sells by word or by delivery, it is prohibited, whether with scales or without scales. And just as it is forbidden to weigh, so too it is forbidden to count and measure, whether with a vessel, by hand, or with a rope." End quote. And we say at the end of Shabbat that it is permissible to measure on Shabbat for a mitzvah, such as measuring a hole to see if it has an opening of a handbreadth to impart impurity, as mentioned there. And it is permissible to measure a mikveh to see if it has forty se'ah. Even measuring for a charm, which women have the custom to measure the girdle of a sick person for healing and recite incantations over it, is permitted, as it is considered a measurement for a mitzvah.

In Choshen Mishpat, Siman 73, it is explained that if someone owes money to another and swears to repay it on a specific day in a specific month, and that day falls on Shabbat, if he does not repay before Shabbat, he must give a pledge on Shabbat and have it appraised, because without appraisal it is not considered repayment (Sema there), or transfer ownership of the object itself (Bach there). We explained there in Section 10 that this applies when the creditor demands repayment on Shabbat. Even though it is forbidden to make such a demand on Shabbat, once he has made the demand, the oath takes effect. However, if no demand is made, he does not transgress, as mentioned there. There are those who forbid appraisal and measurement (Magen Avraham, section 16), but in my humble opinion, this is not so, for measurement for the sake of a mitzvah is permitted, as we have said, and the same applies to appraisal for the sake of a mitzvah. In this case, it is a great mitzvah to fulfill his oath. If he is obligated to give money specifically, there is no solution, for moving muktzeh (items forbidden to move on Shabbat) is not permitted for this purpose. Instead, he should transfer ownership of the room where the money is located, and the money will be acquired through the principle of chatzer (yard), as mentioned there. Some say he should instruct a non-Jew to give the money (Magen Avraham there), but how will the lender receive it unless the non-Jew places it in the lender's house? It is obvious that if it is possible to appraise and measure through a non-Jew, it is better than doing so through a Jew; and if so, it is forbidden for a Jew to do it. If he has a pledge from a non-Jew and the non-Jew comes to exchange it on Shabbat, it is permitted, provided the non-Jew removes the first pledge through wearing it as clothing; if not, it is forbidden. This will be explained in Siman 325, with God's help.

Matters concerning a bride and matters concerning a deceased person - it is permitted to discuss them on Shabbat, as it is considered a mitzvah-related conversation. However, this is specifically regarding matters directly related to their needs. It is forbidden to tell a non-Jew to travel outside the Shabbat boundary to invite the bride's relatives to the celebration or the deceased's relatives to the eulogy, as this only pertains to their honor and is not permitted for this purpose.

However, if the sick person requests to send for his relatives and he is in a life-threatening situation, it is obligatory to send a non-Jew to fetch them, even if it means hiring a non-Jew on Shabbat to do so. This is because we are concerned that the sick person might lose his mental stability if his request is not fulfilled. Various regulations have been instituted for the benefit of the sick person, as explained in Choshen Mishpat, section 200. 

Nevertheless, for a Jew to personally commit a rabbinic prohibition (Shvut) has not been permitted, as this is not considered direct healing but rather a general concern. Therefore, in the matter of “finding your pleasure and speaking words” (Isaiah 58:13), we are concerned about this, but not about an outright prohibition.

It appears to me that if the doctor says there is danger if the sick person's words are not fulfilled, he is considered as any other person in a life-threatening situation, which will be explained in section 328, with God's help.

Maimonides wrote in Chapter 6, Law 11: "One who purchases a house in the Land of Israel from a non-Jew is permitted to tell a non-Jew to write a deed for him on Shabbat, for instructing a non-Jew to perform work on Shabbat is prohibited by rabbinic decree, but due to the importance of settling the Land of Israel, the Sages did not apply this prohibition in this case. Similarly, one who purchases a house from them in Syria, for Syria is considered like the Land of Israel in this regard." This is explicitly stated in Gittin (8b). The prominent early authorities explained that this does not mean to purchase on Shabbat, as that is certainly forbidden, but rather that if one purchased it on the eve of Shabbat and it is necessary to instruct a non-Jew to write the deed, it is permitted (Magen Avraham 19, in the name of the Rosh and the Rivash). The Tur omitted this, perhaps because he held that in the present time, when the Land is in ruins, this does not apply.

And know that it is clear to me, in my humble opinion, that a significant printing error occurred in the Shulchan Aruch, section 11, where it is written: "It is permitted to purchase a house in the Land of Israel from a non-Jew on Shabbat, and to sign and submit in the courts." This is incorrect. It should say: "It is permitted for the purchaser of a house in the Land of Israel from a non-Jew to instruct a non-Jew to sign, and to submit in the courts," as this is explicitly stated in the Gemara and Rambam there. There is no difference regarding the type of script used, as writing deliberately in any script and language incurs the penalty of stoning, and unintentionally incurs the penalty of a sin-offering, as Rambam writes in Chapter 11, Law 10, and this is his language: "One who writes in any script and any language - is liable," and all the early authorities wrote this. It is necessary to say this because even writing two letters makes one liable, as written in section 300. (In a gloss, it is written in this section that writing in their script is only prohibited rabbinically. This must be removed from the books, as many skeptics rely on this, unfortunately, and it has no basis in law, God forbid to say so, as the Magen Avraham writes later in section 340, sub-section 10, and the Mishnah Berurah elaborates on this, and the Levush did not write this, nor did the Gra, and it was printed as required. And what the Levush wrote, that it is only rabbinically prohibited, he referred to instructing a non-Jew, as the Avodas Zarah writes there, and as the Eliyahu Rabbah writes in sub-section 24.)

It is permitted to announce a lost item on Shabbat, even if it is something muktzeh (an object that cannot be moved on Shabbat), because the commandment of returning a lost item is a positive mitzvah and is considered a divine matter. If it is necessary to announce the loss also on Shabbat – it is therefore permitted as well (see Magen Avraham, subparagraph 11). It is permitted to resolve communal prohibitions on Shabbat, even if it is not for the sake of Shabbat, because Shabbat is a day of gathering for many and it is not possible to do this on a weekday – it is therefore considered a communal matter that is permitted to discuss. However, announcing a prohibition on Shabbat is only allowed for the needs of Shabbat, such as the annulment of vows that are only for the sake of Shabbat, as stated in Siman 341. Nonetheless, matters concerning the improvement of the city are permitted on Shabbat (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 24). In summary: any matter understood to concern the improvement of the city or the public, such as the practice of announcing at fairs about those who do not pay their debts (as stated in Beit Yosef, Siman 347), because even though this is an individual matter, it still pertains to the commercial dealings of the public – it is considered a public need and is permitted to announce on Shabbat, and this is the custom before the great sages of the world.

But to announce on Shabbat about land being sold, that anyone who has a claim to it should come and state their claim, and if not, they will lose their right - this is forbidden, as it constitutes rendering a legal judgment on Shabbat. Instead, it is permissible to make a general announcement that anyone who has a claim should come and state it, even though it is implicitly understood that if they do not come and state their claim, their right will be void. Nevertheless, the matter is not explicitly stated, and it does not constitute a legal judgment. And even though this is for the need of an individual, it is still considered a communal need, that is, for all sellers and buyers of land and houses (see Magen Avraham, section 26, and the Gra, section 25).

And Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote in section 13: "And it is also forbidden to announce the sale of wine on Shabbat, as it is considered a business transaction," end quote, and we do not know of this custom. It seems that they used to announce who has wine to sell so that it could be purchased for Kiddush and Havdalah. However, to announce the price of the transaction seems certainly forbidden, and so wrote the great authorities. Some wrote that they would announce even the price of the transaction, but it does not seem appropriate to do so (see Magen Avraham, section 28, and Taz, section 4).

If one is informed that there are those who wish to kill his daughter or to cause her to abandon her faith, it is a mitzvah to set out on a journey even on Shabbat to strive for her rescue, even beyond the three-parsah limit, and even to travel by horse-drawn carriage or to ride. If he refuses, he is compelled to do so, since this is a matter of saving a life, for which Shabbat is desecrated. This applies not only to her father but to anyone. The law explained in Siman 328, that if a person is being coerced to commit a transgression, Shabbat is not desecrated to save him, applies to a one-time transgression, as saving him from this transgression would result in the desecration of Shabbat. However, in a situation that affects all the days of her life, it is better to desecrate one Shabbat than for her to desecrate many Shabbatot throughout her life, as we say regarding saving a life, as will be explained there (see Taz, sk 5, and Magen Avraham, sk 29). If she herself is negligent in this matter, it requires further examination (see Beit Yosef), and one should act according to the understanding of the situation.

It is written: "and speak a word" – that your speech on Shabbat should not be like your speech on weekdays (113:). And Rashi explained: such as commerce and calculations. And Tosafot questioned this, for it is already derived from "finding your own pleasure" as mentioned there. And I do not understand, for "finding your own pleasure" refers to actions, performing permissive acts that bring one closer to doing something forbidden on Shabbat after its conclusion, as stated at the beginning of the previous section, like walking to the boundary to hire workers. And here it refers to speech about business matters, and what relevance does one have to the other? This is also explained in the words of the Rambam at the beginning of chapter 24, as mentioned there. And Tosafot explained that even general matters that do not pertain to business should not be discussed extensively on Shabbat as on weekdays. They brought this from the Midrash Vayikra, section 34: Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai had a grandmother, and he told her not to speak much on Shabbat. In the Jerusalem Talmud (end of chapter 15): "Rabbi Avahu said: Shabbat is for the Lord, just as the Holy One, blessed be He, ceased from speech, so you too should cease from speech... Rabbi Hanina said, due to pressing needs, it was permitted to inquire about another's welfare on Shabbat" as mentioned there.

The Tur and Shulchan Aruch have adopted both opinions, as they wrote: "And 'speaking of speech' - that your speech on Shabbat should not be like your speech on weekdays. Therefore, it is forbidden to say 'I will do such and such tomorrow' or 'I will buy such and such merchandise tomorrow' (like Rashi), and even engaging in idle talk excessively is forbidden" (like Tosafot). And it seems that the main ruling they adopted is like Rashi, and what is said in the Midrash and Yerushalmi is a matter of piety, which is appropriate for everyone to do in honor of Shabbat. And proof of this is from the words of our Rabbi the Rema, who wrote: "And people who find enjoyment in telling stories and news - it is permissible to tell them on Shabbat as on weekdays. But for one who does not enjoy it - it is forbidden to say them in order to delight his friend" end quote. And it needs to be understood, if it is a prohibition of 'speaking of speech', how is it permitted for the sake of enjoyment, and if so, we should also permit talking about business matters, and similarly permit 'seeking your own interests' in something that brings pleasure. Rather, it is certain that the main aspect of 'speaking of speech' is as Rashi interprets, and Tosafot's interpretation is a matter of piety, and since there is enjoyment in it, we do not impose such stringency (so it seems in my humble opinion. See Magen Avraham, section 1, who wrote regarding the matter of saying 'I will do such and such tomorrow', that it is forbidden even for a mitzvah matter. And it is puzzling, for heavenly matters are permitted, and the Eliyah Rabbah already questioned him. And what he wrote from the Sefer Chasidim is a different matter, that one says 'I will sleep on Shabbat to be able to perform a mitzvah tomorrow', and this is certainly forbidden, for it is done for the sake of tomorrow. And see Taz and Magen Giborim who labored to explain, but it is not the main point, and examine it well).

It is stated in the Gemara (116b, 149a) that it is forbidden to read secular documents. And Tosafot explains that this refers to documents of debts and similar business matters, but ordinary letters are not prohibited. And Rashi initially explained this as referring to letters, but later corrected himself to specify that it applies only to documents of buying and selling, and the reason is obvious because of "pursuing your own affairs and speaking words" (Isaiah 58:13). 

It is surprising regarding the Rambam in Chapter 23, Law 19, where he wrote: "It is forbidden to read secular documents on Shabbat, so that it should not be like a weekday activity and lest one come to erase," end quote. And similarly wrote the SeMaG. It is very puzzling why they needed this reason (and the Bach remained in doubt about this, see there). 

It seems to me that they intentionally wrote this. For certainly, reading aloud is due to "speaking words," but reading silently and contemplating without speaking, indeed, contemplation is permitted. And they inform us that in this case – even contemplation is forbidden, for the reason that one might erase if they see an error in the account. This is clarified from the words of the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch in Section 13, where they wrote: "Secular documents, meaning documents of debts and accounts, and any greetings of peace – it is forbidden to read them, and even to contemplate them without reading is forbidden," end quote. 

And it is difficult, for contemplation is permitted, except for the reason of the Rambam. Therefore, it is forbidden to contemplate any business or accounting document on Shabbat.

And this is what they wrote that even greeting another is forbidden, and this is the first explanation of Rashi, because this is the opinion of the Rashba, the Rosh, and the Ran there (Beit Yosef). And the Ramban agreed with Rashi, Tosafot, and Rambam, that it is permissible to read letters of greeting, and they wrote that this is the custom. And even the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch, who prohibited, wrote in section 14, and this is their language: "To read a letter sent to him, if he does not know what is written in it - it is permitted, but he should not read it aloud but should look into it. And if it was brought for him from outside the domain - it is good to be cautious not to touch it," end quote.

And the explanation is as follows: If one does not know what is written in it, it is permissible to read it, as there might be some matter of saving a life involved. However, one should not read it aloud but rather examine it silently, because to understand what is written, contemplation is sufficient, and even if it is a business letter, it does not violate the prohibition of "engaging in [weekday] activities," since contemplation is permissible. This is not the case if one reads it aloud, for if the letter is about business, it constitutes a transgression. 

One should not touch it because some hold that a letter that comes from beyond the [Sabbath] boundary is considered muktzeh (set aside and prohibited to move). Even though food brought from beyond the boundary for a Jew is allowed to be moved, as explained later in Siman 515, this is because it is allowed for another Jew, and thus it cannot be considered muktzeh for this Jew since others are permitted to eat it. But a letter is indeed considered muktzeh for all Jews (see Beit Yosef). However, if we are concerned about muktzeh, how is it permissible to read it? Therefore, some hold that the prohibition of touching it is for a different reason: we are concerned that the Jew might take the letter from the non-Jew's hand, causing the non-Jew to perform the act of lifting and the Jew to perform the act of placing, which is rabbinically prohibited. However, this concern only applies when bringing from a public domain to a private domain, not from a karmelit (a semi-public domain), and since we no longer have a public domain, there is no issue here. Additionally, once the non-Jew is standing in the Jew’s house, the act of placing is already completed, as the standing of his body is considered like the standing of an object. But one might still be concerned that the Jew might take it before the non-Jew stands still. 

In truth, many permit this, and the Levush wrote that he did not see people practicing this stringency (see there), especially in our times when mail is delivered by the postal service. This is not considered something that comes from beyond the boundary specifically for the Jew, as the postal service does not travel for the sake of this particular letter. However, some have the custom not to accept it directly from the postal carrier. If the letter is sealed, it is forbidden to tell the non-Jew to open it; rather, one should say, "I cannot read it," and the non-Jew will open it of his own accord. One should only read it once silently, not aloud, and afterward, one should not move it again and should put it away (see Taz 12 and Magen Avraham 20).

Due to the prohibition of reading "ordinary documents," the sages prohibited if one invited guests and prepared various delicacies for them, and wrote down in writing how many guests were invited and how many delicacies were prepared for them, it is forbidden to read it on Shabbat. And it is not only the writing that is forbidden, due to the concern that one might erase one of the guests' names or one of the delicacies, but even if it is written on a high wall, where there is no concern of erasure, and even without the concern that we have established in Siman 340 regarding the fear that one might tilt (the lamp to see better), as there is no difference whether one can tilt or not, such as if it is high up, where the sages did not differentiate as written there. Nevertheless, here it is forbidden due to the decree that one might read "ordinary documents," which are documents of debts and accounts, where it is forbidden even to examine them without reading, as mentioned. However, if it is engraved into the wall with sunken letters, it is permitted, as there is no concern of erasure, and a wall is not confused with a document, and we do not decree this due to that. But if the letters are protruding, it is forbidden, as we decree that one might erase, meaning that one might cut the protruding letters, even if they are high up, as the sages did not differentiate, as mentioned in Siman 340. But on a board or notebook, even if the letters are engraved, it is forbidden to read it, as it might be confused with a document. (The Tur and Shulchan Aruch in section 12 wrote regarding writing in a high place, the reason being due to the decree of "ordinary documents," it is difficult because according to what they ruled in Siman 340 according to Rabbah that even if it is two stories high, there is no need for this reason, and it requires further investigation.

And behold, with us, the attendants who call the invited guests to a wedding or a circumcision, and prepare a written list on the eve of Shabbat, and on Shabbat they read from the list whom to call, many wonder how they do this, as it seems against the established law. One can say the reasoning is that it is specifically the homeowner himself who is prohibited from reading from the list, lest he might come to think of erasing or adding and writing. But the attendant, since he does not have the authority to subtract or add, there is no concern that he might erase or write. And to be concerned that the homeowner might demand the list from him to examine it - we are not concerned, as we do not find such a decree. Additionally, there is no concern that he might read business documents, for in matters of a mitzvah, they did not decree, and this is for the sake of heaven and for the needs of the community. How could we decree concerning this because of business documents? (See Bach and Magen Avraham, Section 16).

A wall or curtain that has images of various animals or portraits of people depicting events, such as the battle of David and Goliath, and they write, "This is the image of so-and-so" and "This is the portrait of so-and-so" - it is prohibited to read it on Shabbat, as a decree lest one come to read ordinary documents, and even to examine it is forbidden just like ordinary documents, as stated in Section 3. However, on weekdays, it is permitted, and there is no concern that one may be drawn to it, as will be explained in the next section, because it is a minor matter and there is no concern of being drawn to it (Magen Avraham, Section 21). This applies to the writing under the portrait, but the portrait itself, the Gemara says (149a), is forbidden to look at even on weekdays, as it says: "Do not turn to idols, etc." See there. However, Tosafot writes there: "It seems that this is specifically for something made for idol worship, but for something made for decoration, it is permitted to look at it, and so is the custom." Elsewhere, it is explained from their words that even for decoration it is forbidden (Avodah Zarah 50b), but even according to this, only looking intently is forbidden, meaning to deeply focus and contemplate it. But a casual glance - we do not prohibit (Magen Avraham, Section 23).

Our teacher, Rabbi Yosef Karo, wrote in section 16: "Poetic and allegorical works of mundane conversation and erotic matters, such as the book of Immanuel and books of wars, are forbidden to read on Shabbat. Even on weekdays, it is forbidden because of 'a company of scorners,' and one transgresses 'Do not turn to idols'—do not turn to your own thoughts (see Rashi there). Erotic matters also provoke the evil inclination, and those who write, copy, and certainly those who print them cause many to sin." This is also the case for those who go to theaters and circuses, which are forms of entertainment and tricks (see there, section 22). It seems to me that newspapers are not included in this, and it is permissible to read them on weekdays, for they inform about current events, which many people need to know, both for business-related matters and other issues. However, matters that have already passed and are no longer relevant—why should we care to know them? Similarly, all foolish matters that involve mockery and frivolity, and certainly erotic matters, are a great sin. Unfortunately, due to our many sins, these have now spread in printed form, and it is beyond our ability to protest against them.

And our teacher, the Rema (Rabbi Moshe Isserles), wrote about this, and this is his language: "It seems that the prohibition against mundane conversations and war stories (on Shabbat) specifically applies if they are written in a foreign language, but if they are written in the Holy Tongue (Hebrew), it is permitted, and so is the custom to be lenient in this matter," end quote. And they questioned him: Is there sanctity in the language? After all, one can speak mundane matters in the Holy Tongue in the bathhouse (see Taz, Yoreh Deah 13, and Magen Avraham 24). In my humble opinion, it seems that the interpretation is as follows: Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote three things: parables and allegories, words of affection, and war stories. Now, words of affection are certainly a severe prohibition due to inciting the evil inclination. But the other two, for those who take pleasure in them, why are they forbidden? It has already been explained that those people for whom telling tales and new stories is a delight, it is permitted for them to tell them on Shabbat, as written in section 2. And if so, for those who enjoy mundane conversations and war stories, why are they forbidden? However, the truth is that telling and listening are permitted for those who take pleasure in them, but reading them is prohibited due to the decree concerning business documents. Therefore, our teacher, the Rema, says that the prohibition applies only if written in a foreign language, because then there is a decree concerning business documents. But when written in the Holy Tongue, there is no reason for a decree, as business documents are not written in the Holy Tongue. Therefore, for those who take pleasure in them, it is permitted to read them, and there is no decree concerning business documents, and it is not because of the sanctity of the language. (The Acharonim write that this does not include the book of Josippon and the Chronicles of Rabbi Joseph the Cohen and similar works, for one can learn much fear of Heaven and ethical teachings from them, and they are permitted even in a foreign language and on Shabbat).

They further wrote in section 17: "It is forbidden to study on Shabbat and Yom Tov except for words of Torah. Even books of wisdom are forbidden. There are those who permit it, and according to their reasoning, it is permitted to look at an astrolabe on Shabbat. This is a tool for stargazers, and it is permitted to turn it over and move it, as will be explained later in section 308." In other words, for those who prohibit studying this, it is inherently muktzeh (set aside and not to be used) since it has no use on Shabbat, but for those who permit it, it is allowed to move it, as it is not muktzeh. The one who prohibits it is the Rambam in his commentary on the Mishnah (Chapter 23), where he writes: "It is forbidden to study on Shabbat and Yom Tov except in the books of prophecies and their explanations, even if the book deals with wisdom." Since Shabbat is holy, we should only engage in matters of holiness. This is also implied in the Jerusalem Talmud (Chapter 15, Law 3) which states: "Shabbat and Yom Tov were given only for eating and drinking, and for engaging in words of Torah. One verse says: 'It is a Shabbat for the Lord,' and another verse says: 'A solemn assembly for the Lord your God,' so how should it be? Give a portion to Torah study and a portion to eating and drinking," implying clearly that it is not for other matters. Those who permit it are the Ramban and the Rashba (Beit Yosef), and their proof is that the decree was only on mundane documents. If you would think that even wisdom is forbidden to study, why specifically mention mundane documents? However, there is truly no disagreement, and both opinions are correct. Indeed, from the strict letter of the law, it cannot be prohibited; however, from a perspective of piety, every person should adopt this practice to honor this holy day, and it is a proper commandment that aside from words of Torah, nothing else should be spoken on Shabbat. (And regarding asking demons for healing, anything permitted on weekdays is permitted on Shabbat, as mentioned in Yoreh De'ah section 179, and see what is written there, and see Magen Avraham subsection 26. Also, all kinds of healing incantations are permitted on Shabbat, but it is forbidden to speak words of distress on Shabbat).

It is forbidden to hire workers on Shabbat, as it is written: "from pursuing your own affairs" (Isaiah 58:13). Even if one does not finalize the transaction, but merely discusses with them whether they will hire themselves out, or something similar, it is prohibited because of "speaking words" (Isaiah 58:13). It is even forbidden to tell a non-Jew to hire workers for him, even without a transaction, because of "speaking words," even though the Jew does not need the work until after Shabbat. For anything that is prohibited to do oneself, it is also prohibited to tell a non-Jew to do, as telling a non-Jew to perform a forbidden act is rabbinically prohibited (Shvut), and also because the speech itself is prohibited due to "speaking words" (and see Shabbat 150a for further discussion). Therefore, something that is only a strictness that one does not do oneself—it is permissible to tell a non-Jew to do it (Magen Avraham 306:2). Even to instruct him before Shabbat to do it on Shabbat is prohibited for the first reason, that whatever is forbidden to do oneself, it is forbidden to tell a non-Jew even before Shabbat to do it on Shabbat (and this resolves the aforementioned difficulty; study this well). But for the reason of "speaking words," there is no issue here, as one is not saying this on Shabbat itself. Similarly, if one does not tell him on the eve of Shabbat to do it on Shabbat but just to do it in general, it is also permitted, since he does not specify to do it on Shabbat, and this will be further explained. Similarly, it is permitted to say to him after Shabbat: "Why did you not do this on the past Shabbat?" even though from this the non-Jew will understand that he wants it done on the coming Shabbat, nevertheless, since he does not explicitly say so, it is permitted. And this is in a situation where it is permitted for the non-Jew to do this thing according to the details explained in Siman 252, and there are those who disagree, as will be explained.

And behold, the Tur disagrees with this, and this is his wording: "And in the Book of Commandments, it is permitted to tell him after Shabbat why he did not do so on Shabbat... and it seems somewhat to be forbidden." End quote. And similarly, our master the Rema at the end of this section wrote that anything that is forbidden to tell a non-Jew to do on Shabbat is forbidden to hint to him to do, but it is permitted to hint to him to do work after Shabbat. End quote. And it is possible to say that it is only forbidden to hint to him on Shabbat, but it is permitted to hint to him on weekdays (and therefore he did not correct in section 2 the words of the Beit Yosef, who did not consider the words of the Tur as written in the Beit Yosef and the Bach, see there).

And so it appears to be the main ruling that hinting to someone during the weekdays about something they did not do on the past Shabbat, so that they will know for the future, is permitted even with a clear hint, such as telling him: "Why did you not do such and such last Shabbat?" But on Shabbat itself, it is forbidden. And it appears to me in my humble opinion that this is with a clear hint, meaning: "Why did you not do such and such?" But with a general hint, like in the opening of a letter where he says: "Why did you not open the letter?" it is certainly forbidden. However, if he says: "I cannot read the letter because it is closed," why should it be forbidden, for he is not stating an act of labor? And as we find with the early authorities who said: "Wipe your nose," and by this, it was understood that they needed to remove the coal from the candle, or if he says: "I am very cold," and by this, the oven would be stoked—it seems that this is permitted, for there is no "and speaking of words" [on Shabbat], and what the non-Jew understands does not concern us. And there are those who say that according to Rabbeinu the Rema, all kinds of hints on Shabbat are forbidden (Magen Avraham 307:31), but in my humble opinion, the main ruling is as I have written. (And I have a support from the Maharit who would say on Shabbat: "The candle is not shining," and the maidservant would understand and trim the wick, as the Kenesset HaGedolah brought in the Be'er HaTeiv 307:24).

It is forbidden to give money to a non-Jew on the eve of Shabbat and tell him: "Buy for me tomorrow," but it is permissible to say to him: "Buy for yourself, and if I need it, I will purchase it from you after Shabbat." Even though the non-Jew understands that he is being told this because it is forbidden to tell him directly, it does not matter since he is not being told to buy on his behalf, and this is only a hint. Similarly, it is permissible even to tell him to buy, but one should not say: "Buy for me on Shabbat" or "tomorrow," rather request to buy in general, as he can buy after Shabbat, and if he buys on Shabbat, he does so on his own accord. However, if Shabbat is the market day, it is also forbidden in such cases, as it is akin to telling him: "Buy on Shabbat." Similarly, it is forbidden to give an item on the eve of Shabbat to sell, as this is like telling him: "Sell on Shabbat." But when the market day is not on Shabbat, it is permissible to give him clothes or other items to sell, provided he does not tell him to sell on Shabbat. All this applies to the eve of Shabbat, but during the rest of the week, it is permissible to give him items to sell or money to buy on his behalf, even if the market day is on Shabbat, because since it is several days before Shabbat, he can sell or buy before Shabbat, and if he waits until Shabbat, he does so on his own accord. (This clarifies the words of the Magen Avraham and Turei Zahav, see there).

And our teacher the Rema wrote in Subsection 4: "If someone hires a non-Jew to transport his merchandise, and the non-Jew comes and takes it from the Jew's house on Shabbat, it is forbidden, and it is appropriate to punish the one who does this." End quote. This means that the essence of the matter is permissible, for example, if he made a fixed arrangement with the non-Jew and not a daily hire. Nevertheless, the non-Jew should not take it from the Jew's house on Shabbat itself, but rather a bit before nightfall, as explained in Siman 252. Even if he designated a place for his merchandise, it is forbidden, for it has been explained there that on Shabbat itself there is no allowance. Therefore, it is appropriate to fine him according to his wealth, whether with money or other means, as deemed fit by the authorities. However, if it was done accidentally, there is no need to punish him, and he is believed to say it was accidental. Similarly, if he arranged for it to be taken before Shabbat, and the non-Jew was negligent and took it on Shabbat, and he could not prevent it, he is not at fault, for what could he have done? And if it was taken before Shabbat, there is no prohibition in transporting it on Shabbat, for the non-Jew is working for himself (Magen Avraham, Subsection 6), and the details of these laws are explained there. 

And the Taz wrote in Subsection 3: Even what is permitted with the sun, such as giving clothes to a launderer and similar cases, one should not say to him, "See that I need them on Saturday night," for this is like telling him to do it on Shabbat. Similarly, if one gave him money to buy something on Friday close to evening, and said to him, "I am traveling on Saturday night," it is forbidden, for this is like telling him to buy it on Shabbat. Also, in cases where it is permitted if he did not designate it to be bought on Shabbat, and it is not a market day on Shabbat, and he did not say, "I am traveling on Saturday night," it is still permitted in such cases. Nevertheless, if he bought it on Shabbat, the Jew should not benefit from it on that Shabbat, as it is like a non-Jew who performed labor for the Jew, which is forbidden to use on Shabbat. And I do not understand the comparison, for there the labor was done for him, but here it is merely buying and selling for him, and in essence no labor was done, and it requires further study and examination.

It is well known that all rabbinic prohibitions (shvut) are forbidden even in the context of a mitzvah, even in cases of financial loss, and even in cases of discomfort or minor illness. The same applies to the shvut of instructing a non-Jew to perform a Torah prohibition, meaning to tell him to perform a Torah-mandated labor (melacha de'oraita). This is only permitted in the case of a serious illness, even if there is no danger to life, as we hold: 'For a sick person who is not in danger, one tells a non-Jew to do [the prohibited labor],' as will be explained in Siman 328.

However, a shvut of a shvut, such as telling a non-Jew to do something that is rabbinically prohibited for a Jew, like buying or selling on their behalf, is forbidden for discretionary matters, as has been explained. But for a mitzvah, or in cases of minor illness or significant discomfort, or where there is a considerable financial loss, it is permitted. For a shvut of a shvut in the context of a mitzvah, the Rabbis did not issue a decree (Eruvin 68), and all these situations are considered as in the context of a mitzvah.

And this is the opinion of the Rambam in Chapter 6, Law 9, and this is his language: "A matter that is not a labor and is only prohibited to do on Shabbat because of a rabbinic prohibition – it is permissible for a Jew to tell a non-Jew to do it on Shabbat, provided there is some illness involved, or it is needed for a significant purpose, or for the sake of a mitzvah. How so? A Jew may tell a non-Jew on Shabbat to climb a tree or swim across water to bring him a shofar or a knife for circumcision or to bring him hot water from one courtyard to another where there is no eruv, to wash a child who is suffering, and similarly in all such cases." End quote. According to this opinion, even in a city without an eruv, if it is not a public domain as we assume that a city without sixty myriads is not a public domain, it is permissible to tell a non-Jew to bring his tallit to the synagogue or a siddur or a Chumash, and similarly food that he needs for Shabbat or a drink that he forgot to take before Shabbat or that would spoil if taken yesterday, since the enjoyment of Shabbat is considered a mitzvah, and similarly to send portions to a guest, which is also considered like a mitzvah, and similarly in cases of significant loss or great distress or minor illness, and this is the custom of the world. And although our Rabbis, the Tosafot, disagree with this and hold that only for the mitzvah of circumcision was the rabbinic prohibition permitted and not for other mitzvot, and certainly as explained, and the reason is because circumcision itself overrides Shabbat (Tosafot Gittin 8b). And the Tur brought both opinions and did not decide there, in any case, the world follows the Rambam. And it is also clear from the words of our teacher, the Beit Yosef, in paragraph 5, who ruled according to the Rambam and brought the opinion of the Tosafot as 'there are those who forbid,' and later in Siman 586, he did not bring the opinion of the forbidders at all, and earlier in Siman 276, he brought the opinion of the Itur to be lenient in matters of public need even for a complete rabbinic prohibition. And there are those who permit even in a public domain to bring through a non-Jew, because if there were partitions, the Jew himself could bring (Beit Yosef and Taz 4 in the name of the Ra'avyah). And there are rabbinic prohibitions that the sages permitted, such as buying a house in the Land of Israel, and there are those that were forbidden even through a non-Jew, such as extinguishing, which is a labor not needed for its own sake, and the rabbinic decrees are not compared to each other. However, in places where it is not explicitly stated, we follow the opinion of the Rambam, which is the middle path, and so it is proper to instruct (see Magen Avraham 7 and Taz there).

The Sages said (Shabbat 150a): Calculations that have no practical purpose are permitted to be made on Shabbat. In other words, in matters that have no consequence or benefit, such as state calculations and the like, and even personal calculations that are no longer relevant, for in such cases the prohibition of "finding your own pleasure and speaking words" does not apply, since he has no concern in them, and it is like other idle matters that are spoken on Shabbat, which also does not honor the Shabbat and any person of spirit should not do so, as mentioned in section 2. However, there is no prohibition of "finding your own pleasure and speaking words" in this. But if he still needs to pay the workers, or if he is uncertain whether the account with them has been settled or not - this is forbidden by law, for this is considered "your own affairs" and is strictly forbidden, and so with all similar cases.

Even though it is forbidden to say to one's friend, "I want to hire you for some matter," for it is even forbidden to say this to a non-Jew as has been explained, and all the more so to one's Jewish friend, since this is the main prohibition of "seeking your own needs and speaking words," nevertheless, it is permissible to say to one's friend, "Will you be available to stand with me in the evening?" And even though both of them know what he means, it is only considered a thought and is permitted (Rashi 150, s.v. "Will you be available"). But one should not say, "Be ready with me in the evening," because this is like a command, as if saying, "I need you for my business." However, when he says "Will you be available," he leaves it ambiguous, as if saying, "I will see if you will stand with me in the evening," and this is nothing. Therefore, when speaking in a foreign language, one must be careful how to phrase it. But the explanation of the matter is as we have said, and it is also permissible to say this to a non-Jew.

Since speech is forbidden and thought is permitted, any action that is forbidden on Shabbat cannot be verbally directed to be done tomorrow. However, if the action to be done tomorrow has a permissible aspect, such that if this permissible aspect existed, it could even be done on Shabbat, one may say, "I will do this tomorrow," even if the permissible aspect is not present. For example, one may say, "I am going to such-and-such a city tomorrow," because there is a permissible aspect if the buildings are close to each other within seventy cubits, as it would then be within the Shabbat boundary. The reason is that it is considered merely a thought, since the speech itself does not constitute a prohibition, as the same expression can be used in a permissible context. It is just that they know in their heart that the permissible aspect is not currently present, but this is considered a thought. Similarly, anything that has a permissible aspect to be done today can be mentioned to one's friend to be done tomorrow, provided that the mention of payment is not included. It is simple that one can say to go tomorrow, but not to travel by carriage, ride a horse, or travel by train, as these do not have a permissible aspect on Shabbat. Therefore, using the common expression of "traveling" in a foreign language is forbidden, but to sail on a ship tomorrow is allowed, as there is a permissible aspect even on Shabbat.

And know that there are some of our Rabbis who said that what we need for permission is when one says: "To such and such a city I am going tomorrow, come with me," because if not, it is obvious, what is he saying (Magen Avraham, Siman 11 in the name of Ramban and Rashba)? Meaning, there is no benefit in this statement, and it is not considered "seeking your own pleasure" and is like other trivial matters. According to this, one can also say: "I will ride tomorrow, I will work tomorrow" (there) since there is no benefit in this. And this is also explained by the Rambam at the beginning of Chapter 24 where he writes: "'Seeking your own pleasure and speaking words,' therefore it is forbidden for a person to deal with his affairs on Shabbat or even speak about them, such as discussing with his partner what he will buy tomorrow, etc." End quote. And even though he later wrote: "And likewise, a person can say to his friend: 'To such and such a city I am going tomorrow,' if there are inns, etc." there, and he did not write: "that he should say to him, come with me," it is because the language of the Talmud is like this, and the intention is to say to him, come with me.

However, there are those who disagree on this matter, and this is the opinion of our master, the Rema, in section 8, who wrote: "And likewise, one should not say, 'I will do such and such tomorrow.'" End quote. And also our master, the Beit Yosef, who wrote there: "One may say to his friend, 'I am going to such and such a city tomorrow,' and it is also permissible to say to him, 'Come with me to such and such a city tomorrow,' because today one could travel there by means of temporary huts." End quote. This clearly implies that the reason also applies to the first part, that he does not say, 'Come with me.' And it is also explained by the words of our rabbis, the Tosafot, there, who questioned this and said: "It is surprising, why is it specific to him? Even to his friend, he can also say, 'Come with me to such and such a city tomorrow, etc.'" There. And if you would think that this is also the intention of the Gemara, what is their question? Rather, it is certainly because they hold that even without 'Come with me' it would be forbidden, if not for the reason of the temporary huts. And it is also explained from the Tur, who wrote in this language there. And the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch did not bring any disagreement on this matter. And from his great book, it is clearly proven that there is no disagreement here. And I say that in truth, there is no disagreement here, as we will explain with God's help.

For in this matter, everyone agrees that if it is not for some benefit, it does not fall under "pursuing your affairs and speaking words." And if someone goes and says to himself, "I will do big business, I will buy houses," etc., is this "pursuing your affairs"? These are just idle words and trivial matters. Therefore, the Sages of blessed memory carefully stated: It is permitted to tell one's friend, "I am going to such-and-such a city tomorrow." And why did they say "to one's friend"? Because when one says it to oneself, it is considered idle words. But when one says it to a friend, there is certainly some substance to it, and the friend needs to know this. In such cases, it is indeed "pursuing your affairs." This is the intention of all the decisors. The Ramban and the Rashba explained that when he says to him, "Come with me," it is as if he is saying to him, "Come with me." The main issue depends on the intention: if his intention is merely idle chatter, it is considered trivial matters. But if he tells his friend so that the friend will know, it is forbidden unless there is a permissible reason on Shabbat itself. (This is the intention of the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch who wrote the language we brought, and this is its explanation: that he tells his friend, "I am going so that you know," and likewise if he explicitly said, "Come with me," and examine this well.) (And the Magen Avraham in section 11 considers this a dispute, but in my humble opinion, it is as I have written.)

However, regarding something that has no permissible way to be done today, even if it only involves a rabbinic prohibition, such as if someone has fruit outside the Shabbat boundary that is muktzeh (set aside and not to be used on Shabbat), since it is impossible to bring them today, it is forbidden to tell a friend to bring them tomorrow. Even if the fruits are within the boundary, it is still forbidden because they are muktzeh (as explained in section 112 and Taz section 8). Similarly, it is forbidden to wait at the boundary at the end of Shabbat to quickly go and bring them at night. However, within the boundary, it is permitted, and the reason for this we explained in the previous section, paragraph 3. But one can wait at the boundary to quickly go there to guard them, because even today guarding them is permissible if they were within the boundary. If he only intended to wait to guard them, he can also bring them afterward, and the reason we explained there. Likewise, it is forbidden to say, "I will do such and such tomorrow," if it is forbidden to do on Shabbat, if he intends any benefit from saying it as explained in the previous section. It is permitted to wait within the boundary to pick fruits and vegetables from his garden or ruin if it is not obviously apparent, because if it is apparent, it is forbidden even within the boundary, as explained in the previous section. This is the reason why it is forbidden at the end of the boundary, because the end of the boundary is apparent to all, as explained there. It is permitted to tell a friend, "Guard my fruits within your boundary and I will guard your fruits within my boundary," and everything is for the reason explained that it is permissible if they were within the boundary. (See Magen Avraham section 13 for what he questions from Eruvin and Tosafot there, and he writes that the end of the boundary is forbidden even without the reason that it is apparent there, and we already responded to his words in section 3 there. Look into it carefully.)

The Sages taught in a Mishnah at the beginning of Chapter 23: "A person may borrow jugs of wine and jugs of oil from his friend, provided he does not say 'lend me.' And if the friend does not trust him, he may leave his cloak with him and settle the account after Shabbat." The Gemara explains the difference between the language of borrowing (שאלה) and lending (הלואה). Lending tends to be written down, whereas borrowing does not tend to be written down. Rashi explained that this is because a loan is typically for a long period, as we hold that an unspecified loan is for thirty days, so one might write in his ledger: "I lent such and such" so as not to forget. But borrowing is returned immediately and does not tend to be written down. The Tosafot explained that the term "loan" implies something that is not returned in its original form and tends to be written down, while borrowing implies something that is returned in its original form and does not tend to be written down. And even though jugs of wine and oil are not returned in their original form, nevertheless, since the term "borrow" is used, he will remember and not come to write it down.

In a foreign language, where there is no distinction between the language of lending and the language of borrowing, one must say: "Give it to me as a sign," and can also finish with "and I will return it and give it back to you" (Taz 9), because if not, it would be considered as a gift and he would not agree to it. Therefore, he reveals to him that he will return it and give it back to him, and he only says this for recognition. Nowadays, we are not careful about this because it is customary among us to only record money loans in a ledger, and not loans of utensils, food, or drink. Also, among us, it is customary to demand immediate repayment of a loan (Magen Avraham 14). And that which the Mishnah permits leaving a collateral – this is specifically for something needed for Shabbat, but for something not needed for Shabbat, they did not permit giving a collateral, as this also resembles a type of acquisition. And when one gives a collateral, he should not say: "Here is the collateral," as this is a weekday-like activity. Rather, he should place the collateral with him without saying anything. Just as one should not borrow on Shabbat something that is not needed for Shabbat, similarly, one should not repay on Shabbat something that is not needed for Shabbat, as this also somewhat resembles buying and selling. However, for the sake of Shabbat, it is permitted, as it is evident that it is for the honor of Shabbat. And similarly, to repay something that is needed for Shabbat, such as if he borrowed wine or oil during the week, he can repay him with other wine or oil on Shabbat, if the lender needs it (this appears to me). (And some have written that repayment is prohibited due to the concern that one might erase, and I am puzzled by this, as the Rema in section 11 prohibits any repayment even in the language of borrowing. And that which is written: "Just as one should not borrow, etc." is not precise, as it is evident from the words of the Rivash brought by the Magen Avraham in 15 regarding the redemption of the firstborn, where writing is not relevant, as explained there, and examine it well.)

It has already been clarified that no rabbinic prohibition (shvut) is permitted on Shabbat due to financial loss. Therefore, merchandise that is being damaged on Shabbat due to rain or some other factor, or if a water channel is flooding and causing financial loss, or if a barrel of wine has cracked and will be lost – it is forbidden to tell a non-Jew, 'Go and save my property.' However, in such cases, it is permitted to call a non-Jew and show him, even though it is certain that he will save it. Similarly, one can say, 'Whoever saves will not lose,' and consequently, they will come to save in order to gain, just as it is permitted to say in the case of a fire, 'Whoever extinguishes it will not lose.' And although there are those who say that this permission to speak applies only in the case of a fire and not in other types of loss – nevertheless, one who is lenient has not lost out (Levush and Magen Avraham, Section 327).

And know that this prohibition for a Jew to tell a non-Jew, "Go and save [it]," applies when the non-Jew would be compelled to save it by performing a Torah-level labor. However, if there is no Torah-level labor involved, but only a rabbinic prohibition (Shvut), it is permissible to explicitly say to him, "Go and save [it], and I will pay you," for it has already been explained in section 17 that for a double rabbinic prohibition in a case of loss, the Rabbis did not decree, and all the more so when the loss is significant. The prohibition is only regarding telling a non-Jew to perform a primary category of labor (Av Melacha) or its derivative. Therefore, one must know or ask a teacher what constitutes a Torah-level prohibition and what constitutes a rabbinic prohibition. In a matter where there is no Shvut at all, but only some exertion, one can save it himself. This will be explained in siman 335 and siman 338, with God's help. The main principle is that in saving from loss on Shabbat, a person should not act on their own but should ask a wise scholar, the local authority, who will guide them according to the law of our holy Torah.

Maimonides wrote in Chapter 6, Law 8: "A Jew who told a non-Jew to do this work for him on Shabbat, even though he transgressed and is given rabbinic lashes - it is permitted for him to benefit from that work on the evening after he waits for the amount of time it would take to do it. And they did not prohibit waiting the amount of time it would take except for this reason: if you say it is permitted immediately, he might tell the non-Jew to do it for him, and the matter will be ready immediately. And since they prohibited until he waits the amount of time it would take - he will not tell him to do it, since he does not gain anything because it is delayed until the evening for the time it would take to do this thing that was done on Shabbat." End quote. And even though if he did the work himself on Shabbat, it is ruled there in Law 23: that if he did it intentionally - it is forbidden for him forever, see there, this is because he committed a Torah prohibition. According to this, it seems that if he himself committed a rabbinic prohibition - it is permitted for him to benefit on the evening after Shabbat for the time it would take, just as with telling a non-Jew in a Torah prohibition. And if he told a non-Jew to do a rabbinic prohibition for him - it is possible that he does not need to wait the time it would take. And similarly, if he told him inadvertently to do a Torah prohibition - also the same. And there are some poskim who hold that if he did it intentionally in a Torah prohibition, it is forbidden for him forever, just like in his own work (Beit Yosef in the name of the Ri"v), but our teacher the Beit Yosef in section 20 ruled straightforwardly like Maimonides, see there. And this is in a matter that is not public, for a matter done publicly - it is forbidden forever, as stated in Siman 325, (Magen Avraham subparagraph 28) and also clarified in Siman 244.

Another ruling is written there in Halacha 21: "A non-Jew who enters the house of a Jew and brings in his belongings - it is permissible, and even if he tells him, 'Place them in this corner' - it is still permissible." This is the end of his words. This is not understandable; what novelty is there in this? For there is no prohibition here since the belongings are those of the non-Jew and he is depositing them with him, so why should he not tell him, 'Place them in this corner'? Also, the source of this ruling is unknown to me (and see the commentary of the Maggid Mishneh, who seems also to be puzzled by this).

It appears to me, in my humble opinion, that what he means to say is this: Even if the belongings will eventually belong to the Jew, such as if they had already agreed that the Jew wants these belongings and now the non-Jew brings them, and they do not yet belong to the Jew but will be acquired from him after Shabbat - it is still permissible. This is exactly like the ruling written by our teacher, the Rema, at the end of this section, and these are his words: "Non-Jews who bring grain on Shabbat to a Jew who owes them money, and the Jew gives them the key to his storehouse, and the non-Jew places it there and they measure and count - there are those who permit it because the non-Jew is engaged in his own work and it does not belong to the Jew until after the measurement, and he will settle accounts with him afterward." This is the end of his words, and this is exactly like the ruling of the Rambam as we have explained his words.

However, if they bring the merchandise of the Jew - it is obvious that it is forbidden to accept it from them on Shabbat. If they do not want to wait until the end of Shabbat and if they take it elsewhere it will cause a loss to the Jew, it seems to me in my humble opinion that he may say to them, 'Do whatever you want, I cannot accept it on Shabbat,' and automatically they will unload the merchandise in his courtyard, and he will not speak with them until after Shabbat. For although it is forbidden in the house and courtyard of a Jew, as written in Siman 252, nevertheless, what can he do when they come on their own (see Magen Avraham, subparagraph 32).

Furthermore, our master, the Rema, wrote there: "Non-Jews who make cheese on Shabbat and the Jew sees it, he may buy it from them, for in any case the non-Jew does it for his own sake, and although the Jew stands by the herd for a month or two and the non-Jew does it with the intent to sell it to the Jew, it is permitted." These are his words. This means that the non-Jew makes cheese from his animals and he desires that the Jews buy it from him. He hires a Jew to stand by during the milking and cheese-making, and since the cheeses are not yet the Jew's, there is no prohibition regarding their production on Shabbat. Even though eventually they will come into the Jew's possession, they are not currently owned by the Jew. The Jew can stand by during their production for the sake of kashrut, and even if the Jew receives them as a debt payment, it is permitted, because they are currently owned by the non-Jew (see Magen Avraham, section 33, and what the Rema wrote earlier about it being forbidden to hint, etc., we explained his intention in section 14).

And our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 21: "It is forbidden to say to a non-Jew on Shabbat, 'Take this meat and cook it for your own needs,' even if their sustenance is not your responsibility. However, it is permissible to tell him to perform work for himself." This means that the principle we uphold: 'Instructing a non-Jew [to perform work on Shabbat] is rabbinically prohibited,' applies to our types of labor. But for his own needs, it is permissible to tell him, 'Cook for yourself and bake for yourself,' as it is of no consequence. Nonetheless, if one gives him the meat, it is forbidden, because the Jew's meat would be cooked on Shabbat, and similarly with all such matters. And know that it is stated several times in the Gemara that anything which is rabbinically prohibited is not decreed between sunset and nightfall for the sake of a mitzvah. Therefore, it is permissible to tell a non-Jew at twilight, 'Light the candle for me,' or other similar work. Similarly, one can perform rabbinically prohibited acts at twilight for the sake of a mitzvah, and therefore one can declare a tithe at twilight. However, to separate the tithe, it is taught: 'One does not tithe definite [produce].' Some say that if one was preoccupied all day, it is permissible, but this requires further study (see Magen Avraham section 31 and Eliyah Rabbah section 48). This will be further explained in section 342, and if it is also not decreed at the end of Shabbat during twilight, it will also be explained there, with God’s help.

In explaining the reasons for muktzeh, the Rambam wrote at the end of Chapter 24, and this is his language: "The sages prohibited moving certain objects on Shabbat in the same manner as one does during the weekdays. And why did they touch upon this prohibition? They said: If the prophets warned and commanded that one's walking on Shabbat should not be like one's walking during the weekdays, and one's conversation on Shabbat should not be like one's conversation during the weekdays, as it is stated, 'and speak a word,' all the more so that moving objects on Shabbat should not be like moving objects during the weekdays, so that it will not appear like a regular day to him, and he might come to lift and arrange utensils from one corner to another or from one house to another, or he might come to store away stones and similar items, since he is idle and sitting in his house and will seek something to occupy himself with, and it will turn out that he did not rest, thus nullifying the reason stated in the Torah: 'so that you may rest.' Furthermore, when he inspects and moves utensils whose primary purpose is forbidden labor, he might engage with them a bit and come to perform labor. Additionally, some people are not engaged in labor all their days, such as the leisure-seekers and those who sit at street corners, who rest from labor all their days. If it were permissible to walk, speak, and move objects as on other days, it would turn out that they did not have a noticeable rest. Therefore, resting from these activities is a rest that is equal for everyone. Because of these reasons, they touched upon the prohibition of moving objects, and prohibited a person from moving on Shabbat except for utensils that he needs." (End of quotation).

The Ra'avad challenged him, for it is explicitly explained in the Gemara (124b) that the prohibition of moving muktzeh was instituted because of the prohibition of carrying out, as moving is a prerequisite for carrying out, since it is impossible to carry out without moving. And if people are lenient with moving, they will be lenient with carrying out (as explained there in Rashi). Additionally, it is taught there (123b): "Initially, they said only three types of utensils may be moved on Shabbat... they permitted more and permitted more until they said: all utensils may be moved on Shabbat except for a large saw and the peg of a plow." Furthermore, it is stated there: "In the days of Nehemiah son of Hacaliah, this Mishnah was repeated, because initially... they were lenient with Shabbat as it is written: 'In those days I saw in Judah some treading winepresses, etc.'" See there. How then could Rambam devise his own reasons?

And it seems to me that the words of the Rambam are correct and necessary, for if you think that the original decree of muktzeh (items set aside) began in the days of Nehemiah, how could they permit and then re-permit it? For a later court cannot annul the words of an earlier court unless they are greater in wisdom and number than the earlier ones, and it is not reasonable that the later ones were greater than the earlier ones.
