And it is also not reasonable that in the days of Nehemiah themselves they permitted and then re-permitted it. Additionally, in the days of Nehemiah there were the prophets Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi, and when they prohibited, who would dare afterward to permit what they had prohibited? And Ezra was with them. Also, who forced them to permit what they had prohibited? Rather, it is certainly another matter, and thus is the presentation of the matter:

For we have already explained at the beginning of Siman 243 that the prohibitions of Shabbat rest (Shvut) are not similar to other rabbinic prohibitions, and they are like Torah prohibitions. This matter was clarified for us by the Rambam at the beginning of Chapter 21, where he wrote: "It is stated in the Torah 'you shall rest'—even from things that are not work, one is obligated to rest from them, and there are many things that the Sages prohibited because of Shvut." The Maggid Mishneh explained that the Torah entrusted these matters to the Sages, as it says there. And in the Mekhilta, the Torat Kohanim, and the Sifrei, it is stated several times: 'a Shabbaton of rest.' Earlier, we explained this in the name of the Ramban, of blessed memory, that it is impossible for it to be otherwise, because if not, there would be no Shabbat. And the prophets warned about the Shvutim and called it a desecration of Shabbat, as mentioned there. And at the time of the giving of the Torah, Moses our teacher commanded us all the Shabbat prohibitions by the word of God, and the Torah included it in the term 'you shall rest,' for without the Shvutim there is no rest at all. And all the words of the Rambam in these chapters follow from his introductory words at the beginning of Chapter 21. However, this is what the Holy One, blessed be He, commanded us—that these Shvutim are not counted among the forbidden labors, and one is not liable for stoning or a sin-offering for them, but the Holy One, blessed be He, obligated us to observe all the Shvutim as they are with us today.

According to this, the prohibitions of muktzeh (items that are set aside and not to be used on Shabbat) were in place since the Torah was given. Their status then was like after they permitted and then prohibited again, as explained in the Gemara: they permitted items whose primary use is prohibited for the sake of their use or their place, but not from sun to shade. Items whose primary use is permitted, even from sun to shade, as we have it today, as will be explained with G-d's help in these sections. However, in the days of Nehemiah son of Hacaliah, when they were lax in observing Shabbat since their time in Babylon, he, along with Ezra, Haggai, Zechariah, Malachi, and the Men of the Great Assembly, enacted additional stringencies for their generation. They only permitted three types of vessels. These decrees were not established for future generations, as our Rabbis, the Tosafists, explicitly wrote in Bava Kamma (94b, s.v. 'in the days of'), that these decrees were only for that generation. Therefore, later on, when they saw that they were careful with Shabbat again, they permitted and permitted again until it remained as the previous laws and as the halacha is with us. This is what Rambam explained regarding the reasons for the earlier muktzeh prohibitions. He explained with his great understanding that without muktzeh, there is no rest and cessation from work on Shabbat, and this is all included in the rest mentioned in the Torah, as written at the beginning of Chapter 21. It is obvious that even for carrying, it is a significant boundary as explained in the Gemara.

It is well known that throughout the entire tractate of Shabbat, Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon disagree regarding muktzeh and nolad. Rabbi Yehuda prohibits, and Rabbi Shimon permits, and the halacha is decided according to Rabbi Shimon. According to the Rif, Rambam, and the majority of poskim, we also hold like Rabbi Shimon regarding nolad. Therefore, Rambam did not mention the prohibition of nolad at all on Shabbat. Similarly, the Tur wrote in Siman 395: "On Yom Tov, they were more stringent than on Shabbat regarding muktzeh… However, Rabbeinu Tam differentiated, stating that the halacha follows Rabbi Shimon only regarding muktzeh, but concerning nolad, the halacha follows Rabbi Yehuda." End quote. All of our sages do not hold this view, and therefore you will see that the Tur and Shulchan Aruch in these simanim, from this siman until Siman 313, which discuss the matters of muktzeh, do not mention nolad at all. Furthermore, you will see that in Siman 320, which discusses the laws of squeezing fruits, the prohibition is due to the decree that one might come to squeeze (on Shabbat), and nolad is not mentioned. Similarly, at the beginning of Siman 322, it is written: "An egg that was laid on Shabbat is prohibited due to the decree of Shabbat following Yom Tov and due to preparation," as it is written there, but it was not prohibited due to nolad. This is because we hold according to Rabbi Shimon, as it is said at the end of Shabbat: In all of Shabbat, the halacha follows Rabbi Shimon. However, in the case of complete nolad, meaning something entirely new that did not exist in the world at all, Rabbi Shimon agrees that it is prohibited (Tosafot Eruvin 46a, s.v. "kol"). An egg is considered to have existed in the world, as it was inside the chicken and now has come out, and similarly, liquids that were absorbed in fruits (this seems to be my humble opinion).

And if you ask, since we hold by Rabbi Shimon that there is no concept of muktzeh, what is the nature of these muktzeh laws that are prohibited? The answer is: Indeed, even Rabbi Shimon agrees to many forms of muktzeh. For example, the muktzeh related to living animals, as it is stated (45b) that even Rabbi Shimon agrees that during their lifetime they are prohibited from being moved. Similarly, the muktzeh of figs and raisins that were set aside to dry and were intentionally put away – he agrees (ibid). Also, Rabbi Shimon agrees to the muktzeh of items that would incur significant financial loss if used (157a). Additionally, an object whose primary use is forbidden, even to move it from sunlight to shade without any necessity – Rabbi Shimon agrees that it is prohibited (Tosafot 36a, s.v. 'Ha Rabbi Shimon'). Similarly, something that emits a bad odor – even Rabbi Shimon agrees that it is prohibited to move (Rashi 46a, s.v. 'But' see there). And any item that has no designation as a usable object at all, like rocks and dirt and the like – Rabbi Shimon agrees (as discussed in the Gemara, which questions: 'But from now on, all rocks'). In summary: anything that is entirely unfit for Shabbat use, such as living animals, money, candles, and all types of metals that are not tools, as well as items that one would be meticulous not to use except for their specifically intended prohibited use, like a slaughter knife or large saw and the like, which is called muktzeh due to significant financial loss, and muktzeh due to intentional setting aside – Rabbi Shimon agrees to all of these.

Rather, what is this muktzeh over which Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon disagreed, and the law follows Rabbi Shimon? It refers to an object that is currently usable but has muktzeh status either in practice or by name, such as muktzeh due to being repulsive, like an earthenware lamp that was lit during the weekday and is repulsive, or muktzeh due to being stored away, or an item whose primary use is prohibited but can be used for a permitted purpose. And the law is decided according to Rabbi Shimon, that an item whose primary use is prohibited is allowed for a permitted use or for its place. And what is forbidden from sun to shade is because the person has no need for it, and it is like stones and dirt. However, there is a permission if one wants to save it from sun damage—he should use it for some purpose, as will be explained before us with God's help (and the Magen Avraham Section 8 brought this in the name of the Jerusalem Talmud, see there). Similarly, regarding something prepared for a person whether it was prepared for dogs, like a healthy animal or bird that died on Shabbat, Rabbi Yehuda holds that something prepared for a person is not considered prepared for dogs, as his intention was removed from the dogs, and Rabbi Shimon holds that it is permitted, and the law follows Rabbi Shimon. And there are two types of muktzeh which Rabbi Shimon agrees to: muktzeh due to a mitzvah, and a base for a prohibited item, such as a lamp when it is lit, because the vessel is secondary to the flame while it is in it (Rashi 47a, s.v. 'for a thing'). And this is what they said in the Gemara (45a): "There is no muktzeh for Rabbi Shimon except for the oil in the lamp while it is lit, since it was set aside for its mitzvah and set aside for its prohibition." Meaning that it has two types of muktzeh: muktzeh due to a mitzvah, since a Shabbat lamp is a mitzvah, and muktzeh due to its prohibition, meaning that it became a base for the flame which is completely muktzeh. And from this we learn all types of bases for prohibited items, as will be explained with God's help.

Indeed, there is one matter in which Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon disagree, and the law follows Rabbi Yehuda. The Ba'al Halachot Gedolot (BaHaG) explains the reason is because Rabbi Meir also holds like Rabbi Yehuda, and thus Rabbi Shimon is considered an individual opinion against the majority. This is regarding muktzeh at twilight, such as a candle that was lit at twilight and then extinguished. Rabbi Yehuda holds: "Since it was set aside at twilight, it is set aside for the entire day," while Rabbi Shimon holds that once the muktzeh is removed, it is permitted. In this, the law follows Rabbi Yehuda. And this is the language of the BaHaG in the third chapter of the laws of Shabbat: "And where chicks were on it all twilight, it is prohibited to move it all day, since it was set aside at twilight, it is set aside for the entire day... And the law does not follow Rabbi Shimon in a candle that was lit on that Shabbat, since Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda agreed with each other in this matter, and therefore he (Rabbi Shimon) is considered an individual opinion against the majority." End quote. And similarly, it is written in chapter 24 that in all matters the law follows Rabbi Shimon except for this. This is the general rule of muktzeh, and the details will be explained in the appropriate section with the help of Heaven.

Any type of vessel or any type of utensil, such as chairs, tables, beds, and boxes that are used to store items, or beams designated for sitting, even if they are very large and heavy, since they have the status of a vessel - they are permitted to be moved on Shabbat. And it is stated in Eruvin (102b): "That plank which was in the house of Rabbi Pedat," and "plank" refers to a beam (Rashi), which required ten people to lift it and place it on the threshold, and it was permitted because it had the status of a vessel, as it was suitable to sit on (there). And that large bench which was in the house of Mar Shmuel, which held half a kor - Mar Shmuel permitted it to be placed on the threshold. He said: it has the status of a vessel. (And the case in Shabbat 35b regarding the large sieve, Tosafot and the Rosh rejected it from the halacha there, because of the case in Eruvin. And even though in Eruvin there they differentiated the matter, and according to their opinion there, anything not usually moved on weekdays is prohibited, according to this our large cabinets and canopied beds and wardrobes would be prohibited to move. But this is not the halacha, for the Rif and the Rosh brought the case in Eruvin in the chapter "All the Utensils," and similarly, the Rambam in Chapter 25, Halacha 6 brought this, and the case in Shabbat there was not brought, and the Rosh rejected it from the halacha as mentioned, and so did the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, Section 2, therefore, the main opinion is according to Tosafot in Shabbat there.)

All utensils may be moved on Shabbat, except for those that are set aside due to financial loss. This refers to items that one is particularly careful with and refrains from using for anything other than their specific purpose, such as a slaughtering knife, a circumcision knife, a barber’s razor for shaving head hair, or a scribe’s knife used for sharpening quills. Similarly, any household owner with a small knife used for sharpening quills or similar items—these are prohibited from being moved because they are not suitable for permitted tasks due to their value. This is what is called "set aside due to financial loss," and even Rabbi Shimon agrees with this, as stated. Even for personal use or to move it out of the way, meaning for a permitted use or to use its place, it is forbidden to move it because one entirely sets it aside from their mind, as if rejecting it by hand. Moreover, even if it is sheathed together with other knives, it is forbidden to move it. We do not say that since it is sheathed together with other knives, one is not particular about it. However, the sheath does not become a base for it (a support for a forbidden item), which would make it forbidden to move, since it is also a base for other knives, making it a base for both a forbidden and a permitted item, and thus it is allowed. The same applies to a perfume hammer that one is careful not to dirty—it is considered set aside due to financial loss since one sets it aside from their mind for use. But if one is not particular, it is permitted. The same is true for items designated for trade that one is particular about, and if one is not particular, it is permitted. Presumably, if its value is high, one is particular, and if its value is not high, it is permitted unless it was placed in storage (as stated in the Magen Avraham, section 3). It is obvious that all types of merchandise in a shop are prohibited from being moved, not only merchandise that is not suitable for wearing or use, but even if it is suitable for use—presumably one is particular about them, and they are considered set aside due to financial loss and are forbidden. However, food and drinks in a shop are permitted to be taken and eaten, as there is no concept of being set aside due to storage with food and drinks, as will be explained in Siman 333, with God's help.

The Rambam writes at the beginning of Chapter 25: "There are utensils whose primary function is for permitted use, such as a cup for drinking, a bowl for eating, and a knife for cutting meat or bread, and a small hatchet for cracking nuts and similar items. There are also utensils whose primary function is for prohibited use, such as a mortar and millstones and similar items, which are prohibited to use for grinding and crushing on Shabbat. Any utensil whose primary function is for permitted use, whether it is made of wood, earthenware, stone, or metal - it is permitted to move it on Shabbat, whether for its own sake (which is from sun to shade as mentioned in the Gemara), for the sake of its place, or for the sake of its function. Any utensil whose primary function is for prohibited use, whether it is made of wood, earthenware, stone, or metal - it is permitted to move it on Shabbat for the sake of its function or for the sake of its place, but for its own sake it is prohibited."

How so? He may move a wooden bowl to eat from it, to sit in its place, or to prevent it from being stolen, and this is for its own sake. Similarly, if he moves it from the sun so that it does not dry out and break, or from the rain so that it does not swell and become ruined - this is moving it for its own sake and is permitted because its function is permitted. Likewise, he may move a millstone or mortar to crack nuts on it or to climb onto it, and this is for his own need, or to sit in its place. But he may not move it to prevent it from breaking or being stolen, and similarly in all such cases. And anything that is not a utensil, such as stones, coins, reeds, beams, and the like - it is forbidden to move them.

It is stated in the Jerusalem Talmud, in the fourth chapter (Halacha 2) and in Beitzah (beginning of chapter 5), that nets were spread out in the sun and were getting ruined because of the heat, and their use is normally prohibited because it is forbidden to move them from the sun to the shade. They asked Rav what to do, and he told them to now consider using them as a pillow, which would make it for a permitted purpose and thus allowed. And we learn from this that any object whose primary use is prohibited and one wishes to move it so it won't be stolen or to move it from the sun to the shade, if he can find a permissible use for it on Shabbat, he should think to use it that way and do so (Magen Avraham, section 8). And even though this might be deemed a trick, it is still permitted to prevent a loss. (And the Knesset HaGedolah explained there that he had thought about this from before Shabbat and therefore it becomes an object for permitted use, but this is not the case as the Magen Avraham wrote, and the Pri Megadim explained it well there.)

And behold, regarding handling an object for a permitted purpose, it has been clarified that it is allowed even from the sun to the shade and to prevent theft. Our teacher, Rabbi Yosef Karo, wrote in paragraph four that if there is no need at all, it is forbidden to handle it. Only holy writings and food are permitted to be handled even without any need at all, see there. This is not understood, for if he is handling it, surely he has some intention in doing so. It must be said that it is a case where he is merely engaging in an activity without any intention in handling it. However, if he derives pleasure from handling it, even though in the case of handling an object used for a forbidden purpose, we do not consider this a bodily need, nevertheless, in the case of handling an object for a permitted purpose, it is certainly allowed. (And regarding this primary law, there are those who disagree, as the Maggid Mishneh wrote there. And what he wrote that it appears so from the Rambam, in my humble opinion, there is no proof, as he adopts the language of the Talmud as is his custom, and the Ran is uncertain about this in the chapter "Kol HaKelim." And what the Maggid Mishneh wrote, why did Rava need to say "from the sun to the shade"? Let him say "with no need at all." I do not understand, for are we dealing with fools? Even on weekdays, when a person handles something, it is with some intention. And also the Rashba in the topic of the oven in the discussion that a vessel is only taken for something that is permitted to be taken, is uncertain about this, see there. However, who would come to be lenient in a matter that Rabbi Yosef Karo ruled, and there is no one who disagrees with him? And examine this well.)

Regarding a deceased person, it will be clarified in Siman 311 that although it is forbidden to move the deceased, as there is no greater example of muktzeh (an object that is set aside and may not be moved on Shabbat) than this, nevertheless, they permitted moving him when there is a need, by placing a loaf of bread or a child upon him. And it is stated in the Gemara (142b) that this permission was granted only for the deceased. However, there are those who permit moving any object whose primary use is prohibited, even from the sun to the shade or to prevent it from breaking, by placing a loaf of bread or a child upon it. And that which was said, that the permission was only for the deceased, refers to muktzeh similar to the deceased, such as pebbles, stones, and dirt. But an object, even if its primary use is prohibited, is permitted. There are those who disagree with this, and it will be further clarified in Siman 311, with G-d's help.

Tefillin, even though they are not to be worn on Shabbat, are nevertheless not considered muktzeh (set aside and prohibited from being moved) and it is permissible to handle them for any need, even from sunlight to shade, as they are not considered a utensil whose primary function is prohibited on Shabbat. This is because there is no prohibition against wearing them when one does not have the intention of fulfilling the mitzvah. Therefore, it is clarified in Siman 301 that one who goes out wearing tefillin on Shabbat is not liable, because it is considered a customary garment. They are not like sacred texts, which are permissible to handle even without any need, as stated in paragraph 15. Tefillin are not like this, but as long as there is some need, it is permissible. 

Some say that since it is clarified in Siman 31 based on the Zohar that it is forbidden to wear them on Shabbat and Yom Tov, they are considered like a tool whose primary function is prohibited, and therefore they are only allowed to be handled for their function or place (Taz, Sk 3 and Magen Avraham, Sk 11). According to this, they are only permitted to be moved for their place, as their function does not apply to tefillin, obviously. Nevertheless, one who relies on the first opinion does not lose out, because otherwise, we would say that they are muktzeh due to their value, as one is certainly particular about them. But certainly, since they are similar to sacred texts, they do not have the status of muktzeh at all (Taz, Sk 21).

The Megillat Esther is also not muktzeh, even though it is not read on Shabbat when Purim falls, because it is still considered sacred texts. There is one who prohibits (Pri Chadash), but it seems more permissible (Eliyahu Rabbah), and this will be further explained in Siman 688, with God's help.

A lulav and etrog on Shabbat are considered muktzeh because one is particular about them, as stated in Siman 658. A shofar is not something one is particular about, and its status is like a tool whose primary function is prohibited, and it is permissible for its function or place. Blank paper, if it is not set aside for writing and one is not particular about it, is permissible to handle, as it is suitable for covering a vessel or for wiping. If it is set aside for writing, one is particular about it, and it is considered muktzeh due to its value (Magen Avraham, Sk 10), and it is prohibited to handle. Certainly, papers with accounts written on them are prohibited to handle because one is particular about them. But past accounts or letters that are not needed are suitable for covering vessels or other matters and are not muktzeh unless they are thrown into the trash, in which case they need to be designated before Shabbat, as will be explained. Tzitzit that are not in a garment are muktzeh.

And know that there are rules regarding muktzeh. Specifically, a utensil whose primary function is for prohibited or permitted use is considered as if its primary function is for permitted use (ibid., sec. 9). Similarly, when we permit an object whose primary function is for prohibited use for the needs of its body or place, one is not obligated to put it down immediately when moving it from its place. Rather, since he is already holding it in his hand, he is allowed to carry it to any location where he wishes to place it. Even if he forgets that it is muktzeh and picks it up, he is permitted to carry it and place it wherever he wishes. The general rule is that once muktzeh is in his hand, he is allowed to place it wherever he wishes and is not obligated to drop it immediately, because the prohibition is in picking it up with his hands. Similarly, it is permitted to move muktzeh by blowing on it, or by pushing it with one's feet to another place, or with the back of one's hand, since this is considered moving in an unusual manner and is not classified as carrying (ibid., sec. 7). All muktzeh is permitted to touch without moving it, as only carrying is forbidden. Therefore, if touching it would cause it to sway, such as a candle hanging in the air, it is forbidden to touch it, but if it does not make it sway, it is permitted. Therefore, it is permitted to touch the candelabras in the synagogue that stand on the table or are attached to the wall even when the candles are burning in them. Similarly, it is permitted to touch a hot oven with a fire burning inside it. It is also permitted to take a permitted object that is on top of muktzeh, even if it causes the muktzeh to sway slightly, as indirect carrying for the sake of a permitted object is allowed, as will be explained in Siman 309 with God's help. All these laws are established. (However, regarding what we wrote that when holding muktzeh in his hand he is allowed to carry it wherever he wishes, some authorities say this applies only to utensils whose primary function is for prohibited use, but for complete muktzeh he is obligated to remove it immediately from his hand. There are also those who say this rule only applies when he picked it up in a permitted manner, but not when he forgot and picked up the muktzeh in his hand.)

All vessels that were broken on Shabbat - it is permitted to move their fragments, provided they are suitable for some use, even if not for their original purpose. For example, fragments of a kneading trough to cover the mouth of a barrel, and fragments of glass to cover the mouth of a flask. However, if they are not suitable for any use, they are prohibited to be moved. 

Know that regarding this law, Rabbi Yehuda and the Sages dispute in the Mishnah (Shabbat 124b): Rabbi Yehuda prohibits until they can be used for a purpose similar to their original function, and the Sages permit, and the law follows the Sages. The Gemara explains that they disagree on this reasoning: Rabbi Yehuda holds it is a case of "nolad" (something newly created), since on the eve of Shabbat it was not suitable for this use, whereas the Sages hold it is considered "prepared" (mukhan), meaning it is not "nolad" since it is suitable for some use. "Nolad" is only relevant on Yom Tov regarding kindling with broken vessels, as it is obvious that they were not intended for kindling from the eve of Shabbat—this is considered "nolad." But this is not called "nolad."

It turns out that even according to the opinion of R"T that we brought in section 6—it is also permitted. And I have seen someone explain that the Sages hold it is "nolad," but they do not hold the prohibition of "nolad," and according to this, for R"T it is prohibited in such cases until it is suitable for its original function (Magen Avraham 345:15). However, this is not so, as the Sages hold it is not "nolad" (and this is also explicit from Taz 345:5 and Ateres Zekeinim 345:15 and Aruch HaShulchan 345:26), only if a non-Jew made a vessel on Shabbat—this indeed is certainly called "nolad," and it depends on the dispute. But we have already written in section 6 that most poskim permit "nolad" on Shabbat, and the law follows the majority.

It is obvious that if the shards are in a place where people walk and they can cause harm, such as broken glassware or similar items, or if they broke on the table and can cause harm to the hands – one may remove them, for in a place of potential public harm, the Sages did not decree [against moving them] (Gemara 42b). However, it is better to gather them with a broom, called a "bazim," or with bird feathers made for sweeping, and this is permitted even if there is no known danger, such as shards of earthenware or similar items, for this is indirect handling for a need, which is permitted. And if one steps on the shards and they break further as a result – there is no prohibition, as this is considered an unintentional act, and there is no prohibition in breaking them in such a manner unless one intentionally breaks them with their hands (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 16).

And know that according to what has been explained, there is no difference between a vessel that broke on Shabbat and one that broke on the eve of Shabbat, for even if it broke on the eve of Shabbat, it must still be fit for some use, otherwise, it would be like pebbles and dirt and would be considered muktzeh. On the contrary, in one respect it is more lenient when it breaks on Shabbat than when it breaks on the eve of Shabbat, for if it broke on the eve of Shabbat and one threw the fragments into the garbage, they would be considered muktzeh even if they are fit for some use, since one has actively rejected them and nullified their status as a vessel. However, if they broke on Shabbat, throwing them into the garbage on Shabbat does not help, for once the status of a vessel has applied to them at twilight, one cannot nullify their status as a vessel on Shabbat (Darkei Moshe section 4 and Bach). Also, there is no difference whether the entire vessel broke or only a fragment broke from it, for even in such cases, even if it broke on Shabbat, if it is fit for some use, it is permitted. And there are those who want to say that if a fragment broke from it on Shabbat, it specifically needs to be fit for its original purpose, but there is no difference in this matter (Bach, and this is also the intention of the Magen Avraham section 17 and Taz section 6).

According to this, a piece of a clay vessel that broke or a piece of a glass vessel, even though the entire vessel, meaning the main vessel, remains intact, if this piece is fit for some use, such as to cover a vessel or the like, whether it broke on the eve of Shabbat or on Shabbat itself – it is not considered muktzeh and is permitted to be moved. This is true even in a place where there are no other vessels available to cover with, as we do not require that it be used immediately for its intended purpose. Rather, since it is fit for use – it is permitted. However, if it broke on the eve of Shabbat and was thrown away into the trash before Shabbat began, then it is forbidden to move it, as we have written. Even if the one who threw it away was wealthy and it was not important to him, nevertheless, it is also forbidden for a poor person for whom it would be important, because what is muktzeh to a wealthy person remains muktzeh for a poor person when the owners have set it aside. Unless the poor person took it before Shabbat and designated it for covering, then it is permitted both for him and for the wealthy person since it is no longer his, and the poor person, the new owner, has designated it for use, as will be explained in Section 75.

And this is beneficial if it is fit to cover a utensil - this refers to a shard that comes from a utensil, for since it had the status of a utensil before Shabbat, it does not lose its status on Shabbat unless it is completely unfit for any use. But something that does not have any connection to being a utensil, such as pebbles and stones, or utensils that broke before Shabbat and were thrown away before Shabbat into the garbage, and a poor person did not pick them up before Shabbat, then on Shabbat they are also like pebbles and stones. Even if they are fit to cover utensils, it is forbidden to move them on Shabbat unless they were designated for this purpose before Shabbat. And this is a fundamental principle in the laws of muktzeh: any item that did not have the status of a utensil before Shabbat is considered completely muktzeh and is forbidden to move even for its own use or for the use of its place. A wick is considered a utensil, but remnants of a wick are considered like pebbles. If the wick is fit for some use, it is permitted to move it for its own use or for the use of its place. But a candle made of tallow or wax that is not fit for any permitted use at all is forbidden to move even for the use of its place, since it has no use at all, and therefore it is like pebbles and stones. This is contrary to those who mistakenly say that a whole candle is permitted to move (Magen Avraham 318:18). Similarly, our candles that are used to light oil lamps or wax lamps, even if they were not lit on that Shabbat or were never lit at all, are considered completely muktzeh like pebbles and stones because they are not fit for any permitted use. This is not similar to those in the time of the Gemara, who used to light oil in complete utensils, and it is important to remember this and not make a mistake in this matter. We have already mentioned this above in Siman 279, Section 1. Similarly, wood is considered completely muktzeh (Taz 307:7).

Doors are considered utensils, as they are used to open and close. However, the doors of a house, although they are utensils, since they are attached to the ground, there is no greater muktzeh (a category of prohibited items on Shabbat) than this. When they become detached, whether during the week or on Shabbat, they are prohibited from being moved because they were not prepared to be moved (Rambam, Hilchot Shabbat 10:6). It is clear that if they became detached during the week and were designated for a detached use, such as to eat on or to sleep on or similar, it is permitted. But if they became detached on Shabbat, the designation does not help, because since they were set aside at twilight, they are set aside for the entire day. Certainly, to detach them on Shabbat from the hinges called "krokoas" involves the prohibition of demolition. Therefore, even if it is customary every day to detach them at night to sleep on them, on Shabbat it is prohibited because of the prohibition of demolishing a structure. If one wants to sleep on them on Shabbat, they must be detached before Shabbat and designated for sleeping use. Certainly, it is prohibited to lock them on Shabbat because of the prohibition of building. Similarly, it is prohibited to remove and replace windows, as they are also attached (Magen Avraham 308:22).

However, the doors of utensils, such as chests, boxes, and cabinets, can be removed from them, but it is forbidden to reattach them, due to a decree lest one might fasten them firmly with knives and pegs, which would be considered completing a task and would incur liability for the prohibition of striking the final blow (as per Rashi at the beginning of the chapter "All Utensils"). However, there is no issue of building here, as there is no building or dismantling regarding utensils (and it is questionable about the Magen Avraham, section 21, who wrote not according to Rashi; see there). Therefore, all utensils that may be handled on Shabbat, their doors that were detached from them during the week are permitted to be moved, and similarly, if they were detached on Shabbat, because they always retain the status of a utensil and are always suitable for their function, as even when detached, they can cover the utensils.

However, the door of a chicken coop, even though it is not a complete structure, nevertheless, since it is attached to the ground, it is prohibited both to remove and to replace it. And when they become detached, they are prohibited from being moved like the doors of a house, because since they are attached to the ground, they involve building and dismantling, and therefore, they are considered muktzeh (set aside). Similarly, the doors of porches, cattle stalls, and the doors of pits, even though they are made loosely and the doors hang loosely, nevertheless, since the buildings are attached to the ground, they have the same laws as the doors of a house.

And this applies to doors that are hung with iron or ropes, and they are like the building itself. But mere coverings, like the coverings of pits and cisterns, even though they are related to the building, nevertheless, since they are merely coverings, if there is a sign that this is a covering, such as if they have a handle - then it is permitted to move them. Without this, there is a concern because of building since it serves it. And coverings of utensils that are attached with clay to the ground - do not require a handle, since they are not actual buildings. Nevertheless, it is forbidden to move them until they are prepared and made suitable for this purpose before Shabbat, or if they were used for this purpose before Shabbat, because even though they have some connection to the ground, and we do not require a handle, some sign is still needed. And if the barrel is completely buried in the ground, its covering needs a handle, for this is like pits and cisterns. And even coverings of utensils that are not connected to the ground at all, there are those who say they require some preparation, for they do not have the status of a utensil like a broken shard from a utensil. But from the words of the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, section 10, it does not appear this way (see Magen Avraham, subparagraph 23, who writes this as a final law, and in my humble opinion as written). And know, that it seems that in a place where preparation is effective - thought is also effective, as will be explained regarding branches, and this is also the opinion of one of the great authorities (Taz, subparagraph 36, and this resolves the difficulty of the Eliyah Rabbah, subparagraph 25).

A hand needle, which is a small needle used for sewing clothes, is permitted to be moved in order to remove a thorn, as it is considered a tool whose primary function is prohibited, but it is permitted for a permissible use. The same applies if it is needed for its place. This is specifically when it is whole, but if its point or eye is removed, it is prohibited. Even though if the eye is removed it can still be used to remove a thorn, the Gemara (123a) gives two reasons for this: one, because it loses its status as a tool concerning impurity and thus also concerning Shabbat, and the main reason is that when its point or eye is removed, a person discards it among the broken pieces, effectively nullifying its status as a tool. Therefore, it is not similar to a broken tool that is permitted to be moved if it is still useful. A new needle that has not yet been pierced is permitted to be moved because sometimes a person may decide to use it as it is to remove a thorn (Gemara there). Note that in Keilim, Chapter 13, it is taught: A needle from which the eye or the point is removed - it is pure. If it is prepared for stretching clothes, it is impure. Accordingly, for Shabbat, if the eye is removed, it is still a tool, but if the point is removed, it is not suitable for removing a thorn. (See Magen Avraham, paragraph 24, and see Tur and Shulchan Aruch, paragraph 11, where they wrote, "a whole needle, etc." It seems to me that this is a printing error, and it should say "a hand needle," as it is in the Gemara and Rambam there, because there is a large needle used for sacks, which is not suitable for removing a thorn and is prohibited to be moved. Pay attention to this.)

In the time of the Talmud, they used to sit on mats, and therefore, remnants of mats that have worn out, even though they are no longer suitable to sit on – still, it is permitted to move them, because their status as a utensil has not been nullified, since they can still be used to cover some dirt, even if they do not measure three by three [handbreadths], and they are like a utensil whose primary use is permitted and it is allowed even to move them from the sun to the shade. But if they were thrown into the garbage before Shabbat – it is forbidden to move them, just like with any broken utensils that were discarded into the garbage. 

And it seems to me that nowadays, in our countries, where it is known that mats are not used for sitting or lying down and most are for merchandise, even the mats themselves – are considered muktzeh as items whose primary use is forbidden, and they are only permitted for use for their function or their place. And remnants of mats in our time, we see that they are generally considered as if they were discarded into the garbage, and therefore, in my humble opinion, they are entirely forbidden like pebbles and stones, unless they were designated before Shabbat for some permitted use. And if they were designated for a prohibited use – their status is like a utensil whose primary use is forbidden, which is permitted for its function or its place but not from the sun to the shade (this seems to me clearly in the laws of mats and their remnants).

Rags, which are remnants of worn-out garments: if none of the pieces is three fingerbreadths by three fingerbreadths, which is the minimum size for impurity, it is forbidden to move them because they are not suitable even for poor people and have lost the status of a utensil. If they are three by three: if they belong to a poor person, they are permitted to be moved by him and all poor people, because they keep them to patch their garments, and they are like remnants of utensils that are suitable for some use, and are permitted for their own use and their place. But for wealthy people, it is forbidden to move them unless each piece is three handbreadths by three handbreadths, as then they are significant even for the wealthy. Consequently, if they belong to the wealthy and are smaller, they are considered muktzeh even for the poor, since the householder has designated them as such, and if they were thrown into the garbage, they are forbidden to be moved in any case. But a whole garment or a complete utensil that was thrown into the garbage is permitted to be moved, because his intention is nullified by everyone else. Note that the neighbor follows the householder in these matters (according to the Gra). Some say that all garments, even if not three by three, are permitted to be moved because they are suitable to cover something repulsive, and these measurements apply to worn-out ritual garments that are forbidden for disgraceful use. The primary opinion follows the first view, as this is the plain meaning of the language of the Talmud and the codifiers, that suitability for such a disgraceful use does not qualify it as a utensil. If one designated it during the day for some permitted use, it is allowed in any case, and this is obvious.

The mold of the shoe, which is called a "kapul," is an object whose primary function is for a prohibited activity, but it is permitted to move it for its own use or for the space it occupies. Therefore, a shoe, whether new or old, that has the mold placed inside it and is tightly fitted, it is permitted to remove it, whether one removes the mold from the shoe or removes the shoe from the mold, since this is considered using the space it occupies. This means that one needs the interior space of the shoe in which the mold is situated. It is also permitted for its own use, such as to cover a utensil or something similar, as per the law of an object whose primary function is for a prohibited activity. Therefore, to move it for its own sake, such as if rain is falling on it or it is placed in the sun, it is forbidden to move it, unless one intends to use it for some permitted use, as stated in section 14 based on the Jerusalem Talmud. This is also the law for any object whose primary function is for a prohibited activity.

And our sandals, even those that have straps and the straps have broken—are permitted to be carried, because they are fit to be worn even without the straps, and they retain the status of a utensil in every regard. And it seems to me that our shoes and sandals, even if they are torn at the top or bottom or from the sides, as long as they can be worn in any manner—they are permitted to be carried. However, if most of the shoe is torn in such a way that a person would be ashamed to go out in it—it has the status of broken utensils that are not fit for any use at all, and their status is like stones and pebbles that are completely set aside (muktzeh), and are forbidden even for their place or their use (as it seems to me). And regarding them, the rule of "three by three" does not apply, as this only applies to garments that are soft, as well as socks and trousers and all kinds of clothing. But shoes and sandals that are hard, and are also not suitable to cover the mouth of a vessel because of their repulsiveness—are forbidden to be carried. (And what the Magen Avraham questions in section 21 about the nailed sandal that it says there to cover the mouth of the vessel, this is not a question, because there even a new one where there is no repulsiveness is forbidden, and what it says that it is fit for another use, they are hard.)

However, the sandals that existed in the times of the sages of the Talmud have a different law, because they had a different design. Without straps, it was impossible to wear them. They had two straps sewn on two sides: one on the outside and one between the legs, which were wrapped over each other, and people would walk in them this way. If both straps broke, they would lose their status as a utensil and be considered broken vessels that are not fit for anything. Even if one of them broke, if the one between the legs broke, it is permitted (to carry them) because it can be repaired and worn. But if the one on the outside broke, it is forbidden to carry it, because if it is repaired it will be noticeable to everyone, and it is disgraceful and people will mock him. Therefore, it loses its status as a utensil.

However, how is it possible to fix it on Shabbat? Thus, the Sages said: If it (a sandal strap) broke while he is walking in a karmelit, he is permitted to take a fresh reed suitable for animal fodder, which is allowed to be handled, and wrap it around the sandal and tie it so that it does not fall off his foot. But to tie or wrap it with a string or cord is forbidden, as we are concerned that he may leave it there permanently, resulting in a permanent knot. However, he will untie the reed after Shabbat, as it is not customary to walk in such a manner. Even with a fresh reed, they only allowed it in a karmelit, since it is impossible to store the sandal there for fear it might be stolen, and it is forbidden to carry it from a karmelit to a courtyard. But if it broke in a courtyard or a place where carrying is permitted and he can store it, using a reed is also forbidden; rather, he should store it. It seems to me that if he has no other sandal or shoe, it is permitted to tie it with a reed. Only in a public domain is this not possible, even if the reed is within four cubits, as we are concerned he might carry it beyond his four cubits. But in a karmelit, which is rabbinically prohibited, we are not concerned (as it seems to me). Tying with a bow is permitted even with a string or cord.

A garment that was washed and hung to dry using a rod, where the rod was inserted into the garment and it was hung on it before Shabbat, and the rod was not designated for this purpose and even now has not been designated for this, thus it remains in its original status of muktzeh. For if it had been designated for this purpose, it would have acquired the status of a utensil. But now that it has not been designated, how does one remove the garment from the rod? One should slide the garment off the rod, for in such cases, the rod is not being carried. However, it is forbidden to remove the rod from the garment. This is not similar to the shoe form mentioned in section 31, where the shoe form has the status of a utensil, even though its primary use is prohibited, and it is allowed to be moved for the sake of its place. This is not the case with the rod, which is completely muktzeh and is not a utensil, and it is forbidden to move it even for the sake of its place. Therefore, if a utensil, even one whose primary use is prohibited, was inserted into it, one may remove the utensil from it, similar to the shoe form.

A stove from which one of its legs has come off, meaning its supports that are fashioned like legs - it is forbidden to move it for its own use or for the use of its place. And even though a utensil whose primary function is prohibited can be moved for its own use or for the use of its place, and in this case, where one of its legs has come off, it has not lost its status as a utensil, nevertheless, for another reason it is forbidden, as a decree lest one may reattach it firmly (Talmud, Shabbat 138b), meaning lest one may return the leg and attach it strongly, which would incur the liability of building. And even though there is no building with utensils, nevertheless, a complete construction is forbidden, as we have written in Siman 313, and furthermore, from a rabbinic perspective, it is still forbidden. This is not considered a decree upon a decree, for in a matter that is likely to happen, we do issue a decree, and moreover, there is the issue of striking the final blow, which completes the work.

Therefore, a long bench from which one leg has been removed on Shabbat, or even before Shabbat, and certainly if two legs have been removed—it is forbidden to move it and place it on another bench and sit on it, unless one has sat on it in this way once before Shabbat without replacing the leg. In such a case, there is no concern that one might decide to reattach the leg on Shabbat. But if one did not sit on it beforehand, it does not help. And even though for the matter of muktzeh (set-aside) even thought alone helps, as will be explained regarding palm branches, here, since there is a decree lest one decide to reattach it, as long as one did not sit on it, we are concerned. Reattaching the leg on Shabbat is forbidden, even loosely, as a decree lest one attach it firmly, unless it is always loose, in which case it is permitted to reattach it as stated in Siman 313. 

All this applies when the leg has been removed. But if one or two legs have been broken, meaning a small part of the leg remains in the hole, making it impossible to reattach the leg as is obvious—it is permitted to take the bench and place it on another bench and sit on it, even if one did not sit on it before Shabbat. In this case, there is no concern of reattachment, since the end of the leg is still in the hole (Taz, Sk 14). And even on Shabbat, one may do so, as it has not lost its status as a utensil and is permitted to be moved. Similarly, if the leg has been lost for several days and one must make a new leg—even if it was removed, there is room to permit it (ibid.), as in such cases there is no concern of firm attachment.

It is stated in the Gemara (124b): Bricks that were left over from construction are permitted to be moved, because the remaining ones are used for sitting on and become like utensils, as it is not customary to set aside the leftovers for building. However, if one gathered them and arranged them one on top of the other, it reveals his intention to designate them for construction, and they are forbidden to move, as they do not have the status of utensils. It seems to me that this was in their times, when it was customary to sit on them, but now they are considered completely muktzeh (set aside) in any case, as it is not our custom at all to sit on them, and even the leftovers are usually designated for building or for making ovens, which are like construction. Similarly, it seems to me the opposite applies to what the Tur and Shulchan Aruch wrote in paragraph 19, and this is their language: "An attic ladder that is large and made for plastering the roof is forbidden to be moved. But a dovecote ladder is permitted to be tilted from place to place, but one should not carry it from dovecote to dovecote, so that it does not resemble weekday activities and lead to trapping." And behold, we do not have dovecote ladders at all, and even an attic ladder that is forbidden to be moved, although it is certainly a utensil like all utensils, and even if we say it is called a utensil designated for a prohibited use, nevertheless it is permitted for its own use or its place. We must say that since it is made for plastering the roof, it is considered like the construction itself and like the doors of the house (Magen Avraham, section 338). According to this, our ladders, which are not made for plastering the roof, are considered utensils and are permitted to be moved for their own use or their place, and it seems to me that this is also the custom.

A thorn lying in the public domain, and there is a concern that many might be injured by it - it is permissible to move it less than four cubits at a time until it is removed to the sides of the public domain. And through a non-Jew, it is permitted to bring it even into a courtyard. And even though there is also the prohibition of muktzeh - nevertheless, in a place where many might be harmed, the Sages did not enact their decree. And if the thorn is in a karmelit, like in our streets which do not have the status of a public domain - it can be moved in the usual manner even for many cubits in one go, because in a place where many might be harmed, the Sages did not enact their rabbinic prohibition. And one should not learn from the case of the thorn to other matters (see Magen Avraham, subparagraph 37).

Regarding an item that is muktzeh and one wishes to use it on Shabbat for a permissible purpose, such as stones or wood for sitting, there is a dispute in the Gemara (50a) as to what preparation is needed: One opinion says that actual physical action is required, such as bundling tree branches called "charioth" for sitting, which one must tie together before Shabbat. Another opinion says that even intention is sufficient, meaning that one should think before Shabbat that they will sit on them the next day. A third opinion says that this is not necessary at all if one sits on them before Shabbat, even without any action or intention.

The Rif and Rambam in Chapter 25, Halacha 21, rule that sitting on them alone is enough. Similarly, Rabbi Shimon the Elder in the Tosafot there rules this way, and certainly having intention is effective. Only Ramban holds that sitting is better than intention, and intention alone is not effective (see Beit Yosef). Rabbi Tam in the Tosafot there requires specifically an action, but this is not the opinion of most poskim. Rav Hai Gaon also believes that sitting on them a bit before Shabbat is sufficient. This is also the opinion of the Rosh and Ran as they write in the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, Section 2: Palm branches, meaning branches cut for burning, are muktzeh and it is forbidden to move them. If one sits on them a bit before Shabbat, it is permitted to sit on them on Shabbat, and certainly if one thought about them before Shabbat to sit on them even on a weekday, or if one tied them to sit on them. (This is the language of the Tur, and the Beit Yosef placed tying before intention, and his wording is: "And certainly if he tied or thought," see there. There is no practical difference, but the language of the Tur is more precise, and examine this well).

However, in the words of the Rambam there, there is room for examination regarding this, and this is his wording: "A row of stones that one thought about the day before: if he arranged them, it is permitted to sit on them the next day, and if not, it is forbidden. Palm branches that were gathered for wood, and he changed his mind about them on the eve of Shabbat for sitting - it is permitted to move them, and similarly, if he sat on them the day before - it is permitted to move them." End of quote. And since regarding the palm branches he ruled like all the poskim (decisors of Jewish law) that it is enough to have thought or even sat on them the day before, if so, why did he rule regarding the row of stones that it requires both thought and action? The Magid Mishneh answered that for the palm branches, since there are some that are designated for sitting and some that are designated for wood, they are not prohibited except because of his initial intention to use them for wood, and therefore it is sufficient to change his mind to sitting, which removes his initial thought. But for the row of stones, none are designated for sitting, and therefore an action is needed. Based on this, our Rabbi the Beit Yosef wrote in section 21: "But a row of stones, even though he thought about them the day before - it is forbidden to sit on them unless he arranged them, meaning he set them in order." End of quote. According to this, for our wood, an action is needed (Magen Avraham, section 40).

However, these matters are very perplexing. Besides the fact that this goes against the opinion of the Rif and many other poskim (decisors of Jewish law), how can one say this? If so, why would it require further thought for the action? Moreover, did not the case with the branches rule that even sitting alone is sufficient, so why was this not mentioned at all with the stones? In truth, according to my humble opinion, the Rambam did not intend this at all. Even with the stones, it is sufficient to sit on them somewhat before Shabbat, but it is understood that they must be suitable for sitting. If they are not suitable, what benefit is there in sitting or even in thought, as is obvious? And a pile of stones, if they are arranged very high, are not suitable for sitting. One must arrange them in a way that makes them suitable for sitting. This is what the Rambam means: in a case where something is not suitable for its intended use, an action is necessary. But if it is suitable, like the branches, thought and even sitting before Shabbat suffices. According to this, what our master the Rema wrote: “And there are those who say that the law of stones is like the law of branches, and this is the main ruling,” this is also the opinion of the Rif and the Mordechai. In my humble opinion, there is no disagreement at all. If they are fit for sitting, even the Rambam agrees. If they are not fit, it is necessary to make them fit, and this itself is the action required, and nothing more is needed. In my opinion, this is an explicit Mishnah in the chapter “All Vessels” (Shabbat 125b): “A stone in a gourd: if it can be filled and does not fall out, it may be filled, and if not, it may not be filled.” Rashi explains: a hollow gourd that is filled with water, and since it is light, it floats, and they put a stone in it to weigh it down. And it is difficult for those who hold that thought is sufficient, for here he certainly intended to fill it, so why is it not filled if it is not tied? Rather, it must be because if it falls out, it is not suitable for drawing water, and thought does not suffice. It is necessary to take some action to make it suitable for drawing water.

And one should not ask why it is taught (142:): "A stone on the mouth of a barrel - one tilts it on its side and it falls," and it is said in the Gemara: "They only taught this in the case of forgetting, but if it was intentionally placed, it becomes a base for something prohibited." And the Rif and the Rambam ruled this way, and so did the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch in Siman 309, for since they ruled that it is sufficient to sit on it during the day, if so, it should also be sufficient to place the stone during the day. However, the Ran already raised this difficulty and answered: This specifically works with branches, because it is customary to sit on them, but a stone, since it is not customary to place it on the mouth of a barrel to seal it, placing it during the day does not help, and this is according to the reasoning of the Maggid Mishneh that we brought.

However, the Rashba, of blessed memory, explained it in a different manner (as brought by the Ran in chapter four), that the Rashba did not agree with this reasoning, and for him, everything is equal to our reasoning. They asked him: If one designates a stone to crack nuts, is it permissible to move it, and he responded that it is permissible, but it is required that he designates it permanently for this use. But if he designates it only for this Shabbat, it does not help, and an action is required. And this is the reason for the stone placed on the barrel, that by placing it, it becomes a base for something prohibited because he did not designate it permanently. Thus, the Rashba did not agree with the distinction made by the Ran and the Meiri that it requires something that is intended for this or customarily used in this manner. The Ran, of blessed memory, there also rejected his words and held that even designation for one Shabbat is effective, but there it is because it is not customarily used in this manner, as he wrote. (And with this, it is well explained on page 125b in the dispute between Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Assi, and what the Gemara says: 'And they follow their reasoning,' and the Tosafot there are puzzled by this, as he wrote. However, according to the words of the Rashba and the Ran, a stone placed on the barrel is different, and therefore Rabbi Ami is stringent, and the law is according to him, and pay attention.)

In my humble opinion, the view of the Rambam represents a third opinion, as I have mentioned. He does not distinguish between different cases as the Rashba does, and we also do not find in his words that he requires designation forever. According to him, it depends on whether the item is fit for use as it is; if so, then mere intent suffices, and even sitting on it alone is sufficient. The reason why placing a stone on top of a barrel is not enough is because it is understandable that to seal a barrel with a stone requires some adjustment, and without this, it does not settle properly. Therefore, he holds that placing it makes it a base for a prohibited item, as we explained regarding a layer of stones. (And this is why the Talmud compares the case of a stone on top of a barrel to that of a layer of stones. However, Rabbi Assi holds that a stone is less severe than a layer of stones because a layer of stones, without some adjustment, is not fit at all, whereas a stone on top of a barrel can be placed as it is. Rabbi Ami holds that they are similar. Therefore, they ruled according to Rabbi Ami in this case, because Rav also holds this way in the chapter "Notel," see there. And even though there is no proof from Rav, as he follows his own reasoning in the chapter "Bameh Tomnin" (Shabbat 50a) that even with palm branches, an action is required, nonetheless, in the case of a stone on top of a barrel, Rabbi Assi is considered a minority opinion compared to them, and pay close attention.)

And this is the wording of our teacher, the Beit Yosef, in section 22: "It is forbidden to cover the mouth of a barrel with a stone or a piece of wood, or to close a door with them, or to strike with them on a faucet, even though one had thought about it before Shabbat — it is forbidden, unless one designated them for this purpose permanently. But if one designated them only for this Shabbat — it is not allowed. And this applies to something that is not usually designated for such a purpose, like those mentioned above. But for any item that is commonly used for this purpose, like cracking nuts, designating it for one Shabbat suffices. There are those who say there is no difference, and there are those who say that one needs to make some sort of modification to it before Shabbat." End of quote. And the first opinion is that of the Ran, the second is the opinion of the Rashba that for all items, one needs permanent designation, and the third is the opinion of the Mordechai, that for a stone, some action is required (see Beit Yosef). According to what is written in the opinion of the Rambam, it depends: if the item is merely fit for use, some use before Shabbat is permitted, and certainly if one thought about it before Shabbat. And it seems that since muktzeh (set aside) is rabbinic, one may rely on the lenient opinion. And it appears that our teacher, the Beit Yosef, took the opinion of the Ran, which is the primary opinion, and above in section 357 regarding insulation, it implies that permanent designation is not needed, and for insulation, modification with stones is not relevant (Magen Avraham section 144). And it is also simple that to sit on a heavy stone that does not move from its place when one sits on it — no action is needed, for muktzeh is only forbidden in moving it, not touching it. Therefore, it is permissible to sit on a stone or large beam even though they are muktzeh (see there section 141). And similarly, to sit on grass is permitted, since it is attached to the ground, and moving it while sitting on it is not considered moving, as it is attached to the ground and there is no moving here. And even if, perhaps, by sitting on it, some of them may be uprooted — it is considered an unintended act and not a certain result, and proof of this is from what will be explained in section 336 that it is permitted to walk on them, see there.

It is permitted to cut a branch from a palm tree before Shabbat and designate it for a permissible use on Shabbat, such as to wave over the table to chase away flies or to remove crumbs from the table, or to threaten a child or to play with it, and then it is permitted to handle it on Shabbat. It seems to me that if one designates it at the time of cutting, then, according to all opinions, it does not require permanent designation, since there is an action involved. Similarly, when one takes a branch from a broom called "bazim." However, if at the time of the action he did not have any specific intention, it later requires permanent designation according to the opinion that requires permanent designation, as explained in the previous section. When one designates it for these purposes, it is considered a complete utensil. But on Shabbat, it is forbidden to detach it through a non-Jew (Taz, Subsection 17), and even if the non-Jew detached it by himself, it is forbidden to handle it, for it is considered muktzeh, and on Shabbat, designation does not help. Even if the non-Jew detached it before Shabbat, if the Jew did not know about it until Shabbat, it remains muktzeh. There is a doubt whether the designation by the non-Jew is effective, and similarly, for any muktzeh item, whether the non-Jew's designation is effective. It seems that it is not effective, because for the Jew, it was muktzeh during twilight due to his lack of knowledge about it, and it remains muktzeh for the entire day.

Combed flax and carded wool that are placed on a wound—if one intended during the day to put them on the wound, or if they were placed on the wound for an hour during the day, or if they were dyed with oil which indicates that they are meant for the wound, or if they were wrapped in a bandage to be placed on the wound on Shabbat—since there is intention, action, or use from the day before, they are not considered muktzeh. And there is also no issue of healing, as it is similar to a garment that prevents his clothes from scratching the wound. Some say that mere intention is not sufficient. However, it is a complex issue because, according to everyone, mere intention is enough to permit carrying them. (See Magen Avraham 346:146 who raises this difficulty, and see Taz 369:169 who reconciles the words of the Beit Yosef. However, it makes no practical difference to the law, as the primary opinion follows the first view, as is evident from the Beit Yosef in section 24, where he cites an opinion that supports this.)

Dry hides, whether they belong to a craftsman or to a homeowner, are permitted to be moved, as they are fit for sitting. But moist hides are not fit for sitting and are prohibited from being moved. Some say that the hides of large animals, whether moist or dry, are permitted to be moved, but those of small animals are prohibited since they are not so fit for sitting, unless one designated them before Shabbat for sitting. It seems to me that this applies in the times of the Talmud, when people would sit on the ground and were accustomed to sitting on hides spread out on the ground. However, nowadays, all types of hides are considered muktzeh, as we are not accustomed at all to sit on hides, unless they were specifically designated before Shabbat for spreading or lying on. Their law is like that of utensils whose primary use is prohibited, which may be moved for the need of their use or their place, but not to protect them from the sun, as they certainly have the status of a utensil.

Planks belonging to a homeowner are permitted to be moved, since he is not particular about using them. However, those belonging to a craftsman are forbidden to be moved, as he is particular about them and they are only permitted if he intended before Shabbat to use them for placing bread for guests or for another use. Planks belonging to merchants and shopkeepers are also like those of a craftsman, because since they place merchandise on them, they are certainly particular about them. Nevertheless, it seems that their status is like that of a vessel whose primary use is forbidden, which is permitted for use if needed for their function or place. (In our times, homeowner's planks are not common, but craftsmen's planks are still found among us.)

Bones that are fit for dogs, even if they became separated from the meat on Shabbat, may be moved by hand from the table, for they are not muktzeh since they are fit for dogs. And even though before Shabbat they were prepared for human use and not for dogs, we hold according to Rabbi Shimon, who maintains: "That which is prepared for humans is considered prepared for dogs." And as for the concern of nolad (something that came into being on Shabbat), we hold that nolad is permitted on Shabbat, as stated in section 6. Indeed, according to those who hold that nolad is forbidden, it would be prohibited to move them, but we hold that nolad is permitted, following the opinion of the majority of the poskim (decisors of Jewish law).

Similarly, peels that are fit for animal consumption, even if they were peeled on Shabbat, and crumbs that do not contain the size of an olive, which are generally designated for animal consumption, may be moved from the table. However, hard bones that are not fit for dogs and peels that are not fit for animal consumption, such as nut shells, almond shells, and eggshells, among others, may not be moved. Instead, one should shake the entire table and move them to the side or outside.

The table does not become a base for a prohibited item, for this is only said if the muktzeh was on it during twilight (bein hashmashot) and not in the middle of Shabbat, as there is no concept of muktzeh for part of Shabbat. Additionally, there was no intention to leave them there all day, and furthermore, the table also held permitted items, such as bread. Additionally, this is not considered intentional placement, as one does not care where they fall, and their status is like that of forgotten items, which do not make the base a base for a prohibited item (see Magen Avraham, subparagraph 50).

If one wishes, he can throw them behind him with his tongue, meaning that while eating, he throws the peels with his tongue, and it is better to throw them behind than in front of him, so as not to litter the place in front of him. See section 55.

Nevertheless, this is not like a "graf shel re'i" (a chamber pot) which is permitted to be moved by hand, as it is not so repulsive. One should not ask, if so, how is it permitted to shake the table, since that would be moving it indirectly for the sake of something forbidden, which is prohibited as stated in Siman 311. It can be said that this is preferable to moving it indirectly. Additionally, since it is somewhat repulsive, although it is not exactly like a "graf shel re'i" which is explicitly permitted to be moved, in any case, moving it in this manner is certainly allowed. If there is bread on the table, it is permitted to lift the entire table and move it with the peels, because they are nullified due to the bread. Therefore, even though it will be explained in Siman 309 that a base for both something forbidden and something permitted is not allowed to be moved directly when it can be shaken off, nevertheless here it is permitted because they are nullified to the bread. However, if there is no bread, it is not permitted to place bread next to them and move them directly, as with a corpse. Some say that even here it is permitted, but the main opinion follows the first view (see Magen Avraham, Subsection 151). If one needs the space of the table, even if there is no bread on it but rather bones and peels that are not suitable for dogs or animals, it is permitted to lift the table and move them, because since the table did not become a base for them for reasons explained, he is moving a permitted item, and the forbidden item is moved incidentally. Only in a situation where shaking it off is sufficient, it is not permitted to move it directly, except when it is not possible in another manner.

Bundles of straw and bundles of soft wood that are suitable for animal fodder: if they were designated for animal feed, it is permissible to move them even if they are very large. However, if they were not designated, they are considered muktzeh, because typically they are intended for fuel. Therefore, in our region, where straw is not used for fuel but rather for animal feed or bedding, it is permissible to move it. There are places where straw is used to cover roofs, and in those places, it is forbidden to move it, like stones and pebbles, as they do not have the status of a utensil at all, and everything depends on the local custom. Dry hay, which is called "hay," is intended for animal feed and is permissible to move.

Any item that is suitable for consumption by a type of wild animal or bird that is commonly found—may be moved, even if it is not suitable for the majority of wild animals and birds, such as the squill plant, which is only suitable for deer, or mustard, which is only suitable for doves—may be moved in a place where deer and doves are commonly found, meaning in a place where it is customary for ordinary people to raise them and they are commonly found. It is not sufficient if they are only found with nobles. An item that is only suitable for a wild animal or bird that is not commonly found in that city—if one owns such a type of animal or bird—it is permissible to move the food that is suitable for them, and if not—it is forbidden.

Therefore, it is forbidden to move bones in a place where there are no dogs, such as if one is resting in a field or an inn where there is no dog, whether the bones were separated from the meat on the eve of Shabbat or on Shabbat. This applies to soft bones, but hard ones are forbidden in any place, and they are considered completely set aside (muktzeh) like stones and pebbles.

Date pits, in places where they are customarily fed to animals, may be moved. Nevertheless, a distinguished person should be stringent upon himself not to move them except in an unusual manner, such as placing a piece of bread or some other item that is permitted to move next to them and moving them together. This is because in many places they are not fed to animals at all, thus one should be stringent with them even in places where they are fed to animals. And all peels and seeds that are not fit for animals - one should eat the food and discard them behind him with his tongue. He should not discard them with his hands, nor should he discard them with his tongue in front of him, relying on the idea that when many accumulate in front of him, it will be considered like a chamber pot and it will be permitted to remove them by hand. For it is forbidden to create a chamber pot initially, and not everything can be considered like a chamber pot.

And the Rambam wrote in Chapter 26, Law 17: One may not move shards of glass even though they are food for ostriches, nor bundles of twigs even though they are food for elephants, nor colocasia even though they are food for ravens, because these and similar items are not commonly found among most people. Therefore, one who has them is permitted to move what is appropriate for him as stated, such as if he raises them for work or for beauty. However, it is forbidden to raise them for the purpose of killing them and selling the meat, as it is forbidden to trade in items that are forbidden to eat, as stated in Yoreh De'ah, Section 117.

He also wrote there: "We may handle putrid meat, meaning it is rotten, because it is food for animals. And we may handle raw meat, whether unsalted or salted, because it is fit for human consumption, and similarly, salted fish. But unsalted fish is forbidden to be handled." End quote. And in our place, where animals are not commonly found, it is forbidden to handle putrid meat, but the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch, section 31, wrote: because it is fit for dogs, and dogs are found everywhere, it is permitted to handle it. The Rambam uses the language of the Gemara (128b), see there. Concerning the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, one could say that in the time of the Gemara, animals were commonly found, thus it says: because it is food for animals. And in the time of the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, they were not commonly found, thus they wrote it is fit for dogs (see Kesef Mishneh there). However, this does not seem to be the language of the Gemara, see there. In fact, the Tosafot there explained that "putrid" does not mean rotten but rather unsalted meat, and this is also the explanation of Rashi on the Rif, see there for further study (and see Drisha).

And also what he wrote about raw meat being considered tasteless because it is suitable for human consumption, as our master the Beit Yosef wrote, there is a wonder about this. For in the Gemara there, it is stated that this applies only to wild goose and not to other meats. Therefore, the Tur truly wrote that tasteless refers to something suitable for dogs. 

And even though it is suitable for humans, it has already been clarified that we hold according to Rabbi Shimon, that what is prepared for humans is considered prepared for dogs. However, there is one who says that this is when one intends to give it to dogs, such as if it died, but raw meat would not be given to dogs. If so, even according to Rabbi Shimon, it would be muktzeh (as brought by the Taz, section 20). 

I do not see this as necessary, for are we forced to give it to dogs, since it is only suitable for dogs, it is not muktzeh. I have seen that other versions of the Gemara on this matter have been brought (see Eliyah Rabbah, section 69 and Drisha), and if so, we cannot determine their exact intention. 

However, in practice, for us, all raw meat is muktzeh, because we do not eat raw meat at all, not even wild goose, and it is not given to dogs because people are compassionate about it. This reasoning was also written by the Baal HaMaor and the Rosh (see Magen Avraham, section 156). 

An egg that was laid yesterday seems to me not to be muktzeh, as many people drink them raw. Cold raw fat is also not eaten and is therefore muktzeh (there). If a non-Jew slaughtered an animal on Shabbat, it is permitted to move it (there), and also, one does not consider it set aside from their mind at all.

A kameah (amulet), even though one may not go out with it into a karmelit (semi-public domain) (as stated there, section 157), nevertheless, it is not considered muktzeh (an object that cannot be moved on Shabbat) and is permitted to be carried. The reason appears to be that inside the house and courtyard, if one wishes to carry it, who will prevent him? And there are those who permit even into a karmelit (as stated there in the name of the Rashal). And even for those who prohibit it (as stated there), nevertheless, in the courtyard and house it is permitted, and there is no concern to decree that one might carry it into a public domain, since there is no decree on something that is used for healing.
