In any case, it is far from being considered muktzeh. It is obvious that all types of medicines are permitted for a healthy person to carry when he needs to give them to a sick person.

Any filthy item, such as excrement, vomit, or feces, whether from a person, chickens, or similar, as well as from animals, dogs, and pigs, and even a dead mouse or rat, or even a dead chicken, and all kinds of carcasses—however, the feces of horses appear not to smell and are not considered like a chamber pot of excrement. It is possible that a fastidious person might still be disgusted by it. If all these items are placed in a house or courtyard where people commonly use, it is permitted to remove them by hand to the garbage or to the bathroom. It is obvious that if it can be done by a non-Jew, it should be done by him, and similarly, it is preferable for a minor to do it rather than an adult. The reason it is permitted to remove them by hand is due to the great respect for human dignity. Similarly, if they are in an alley where people walk, they should be moved to the sides. However, if they are placed in a courtyard where it is not used, and all the more so if they are placed in a garbage area within the courtyard or in another courtyard, it is forbidden to carry them. Similarly, in the bathroom itself, if the place where one needs to sit is not clean and it is impossible to sit there, it is permitted to clean the area. If the place is not where people sit, but there is a concern that a child might get dirty, it is forbidden to remove it by hand unless by a non-Jew, but one should cover it with a utensil.

There is a doubt regarding a "graf shel re'i" (a container for refuse) that was present from before Shabbat, and it was possible to clean it during the day on Friday, knowing that it would be needed to sit there on Shabbat. If one did not clean it during the day, is it permitted to clean it on Shabbat? The Gemara (121b) clearly implies that this is specifically when it is found on Shabbat, as can be seen there. This also seems reasonable, since it could have been done during the day, we do not permit it on Shabbat unless it is done by a non-Jew. (However, from what will be explained in section 63, it does not seem to imply this way, and this requires further investigation).

And even though it is permitted to remove a "graf shel re’i," which is a vessel that contains something repulsive, and similarly, a chamber pot for urine, nevertheless, returning the vessel to the house is not permitted because it is muktzeh since it is not suitable for use. However, if water is placed in it, and the water is suitable for animal drinking, it can be moved. This applies if, after pouring out the excrement or urine, the vessel is placed on the ground. But if it is still held in one's hand, it is permitted to move it and place it in its designated place, according to the law of all muktzeh, which states that if it is already held in one's hand, it is permitted to move it to another place, as mentioned in section 18. Similarly, if the vessel is a utensil used for pouring waste, it is also permitted to move it, and it is common practice to pour out the waste and return the vessel to its place to use it again for pouring waste. Also, if it is needed for a child's needs, it is permitted in any manner to move it, as anything required for a person’s needs is permitted to be moved.

It is not permitted to create a "graf shel re’i" (a designated place for waste) initially. This means bringing something that will eventually become repugnant so that afterward one would be compelled to remove it. Why should we cause the handling of muktzeh (objects that are set aside and cannot be moved on Shabbat) unnecessarily when there is no need? Nevertheless, if one did create it, it is permitted to remove it. Similarly, in a situation of damage, it is permitted to create a "graf shel re’i" initially in order to prevent damage, as in the case mentioned in the Gemara (Beitzah 36b), where rain was falling in a millhouse and damaging the millstones. They permitted bringing a bed and establishing a permanent dwelling there, which would then allow the removal of the millstones from there, and the same applies to anything similar. Specifically, this is permitted only for establishing a permanent dwelling, but for a temporary dwelling, it is not permitted (see Magen Avraham, section 162, who wrote: the phrase "in order to remove it" is not precise, and I do not know why, as this is also the language of the Tur and the Beit Yosef, and it is necessary to examine this carefully).

A person may bring in a full basket of dirt before Shabbat and use it for all his needs on Shabbat, and it is not considered muktzeh (set aside), since he designated it before Shabbat. And even according to the opinion that requires an action for designation, it is not required here, because dirt is not suitable for an action. All the more so for us, who hold that no action is needed, as stated in section 40. However, it is necessary to designate a corner for the dirt where it will be placed, and from where it will be taken for use, because if no place is designated, it becomes nullified as part of the ground and it is forbidden to move it. For this reason, it does not help even if one says on the eve of Shabbat: 'I am preparing all the dirt in the yard for my use,' and even if it would help in another context, it does not help in this case because it becomes nullified as part of the ground. And it seems to me that in a house with a floor, it is not necessary to designate a corner, because there it does not become nullified as part of the ground, since it is not placed on the ground. And those who pile sand in one place and bury fruits in it, such as radishes and the like, are allowed to take them on Shabbat, because the sand was designated for this purpose and is not considered muktzeh. See also section 498, clause 31.

It has already been explained that the muktzeh (set-aside) status of living creatures is the most stringent form of muktzeh, for even Rabbi Shimon agrees with it. Therefore, it is forbidden to move any animal, beast, or bird. Some women are unaware of this and may handle a chicken on Shabbat, and they need to be informed that this is a serious prohibition. Nevertheless, it is permitted to overturn a basket in front of chicks so that they can climb up and down. We do not say, "How can we move a utensil for the sake of something that is muktzeh?" because we hold that "a utensil may be moved even for something that is not to be moved on Shabbat" (Shabbat 43a; see there). While the chicks are on it, it is forbidden to move the basket. If they were on it during twilight (bein hashmashot), "since it was set aside during twilight, it is set aside for the entire day." However, in the middle of Shabbat, it is permitted to move it once the chicks have descended, for there is no muktzeh for part of Shabbat. One should not argue that since it is forbidden to move the basket while they are on it, how is it permitted to overturn the basket before them, which would render the utensil unusable for its original purpose (mevatel kli mehechano)? The answer is that since it is their nature to descend, this is not considered rendering the utensil unusable. Additionally, it is within one's power to make them fly off by making a noise (Tosafot, there).

All domesticated animals, wild animals, and birds, except for chickens, may be guided in a courtyard. This means holding them by their necks and sides and leading them if necessary, due to the principle of preventing animal suffering. Otherwise, even in such cases, it would be prohibited. However, in a public domain, this is not permitted, as there is a decree lest one lifts them and becomes liable, since we do not say regarding animals that "a living being carries itself," as stated in Siman 301. But in a courtyard, they were not concerned about the prohibition of muktzeh for this. It seems that the same applies in a karmelit, that it is permitted, provided one is careful not to lift their legs off the ground, as they are muktzeh and moving them is prohibited, except for chickens, which are forbidden to guide because they naturally lift themselves off the ground, resulting in carrying them. And the Rambam wrote the reason: "because it slips from the hand and its wings get detached" (end of Chapter 26). It appears to me that he was compelled to this explanation, for if we say that it lifts itself, it would fall under the category of "a living being carries itself." Therefore, it must be for another reason, and it is considered a definite outcome (pesik reisha), as otherwise, there would be no prohibition in the matter, but one may push it with hands until it enters (see Magen Avraham, Siman 69, who questions the Rambam, and according to what I wrote, it is clear).

The woman may support her child even in the public domain, which means when she lifts one foot and places down the other. In such a case, even if she lifts him, it is considered that a living being carries itself. Provided that the child is not so small that he drags his feet, because in such cases we do not say 'a living being carries itself,' and there is a liability of a sin-offering if she lifts him. Therefore, if he is bound or sick, even if he is an adult – it is forbidden. Even in a karmelit (a semi-public domain), it is forbidden to drag him because this is considered as actual carrying. However, when he lifts one foot and places down the other, and he is healthy and not bound – it is permissible, because when he leans on her, one of his feet is always on the ground, and only the other foot is lifted off the ground, and he relies on his mother. (The Maor holds that even when one foot is lifted, one is liable if he does not carry himself, but in any case, due to the distress of the child, they did not decree lest she lift him, and according to this, even dragging would be permissible, as it is the same rule, but this is not so and requires further investigation. His words are at the beginning of the chapter "Notel" and are brought in the Magen Avraham section 371. And what the Magen Avraham wrote regarding a pouch hanging from the child's neck has already been explained in Siman 301, where all the laws of carrying out have been clarified.)

And it has already been explained that muktzeh is permitted to touch but not to move. And it has also been explained that by blowing, it is permitted to move it if it is light and can be moved by blowing, and similarly with one's foot or in an unusual manner it is permitted. However, it seems that all this is for some need, but if there is no need at all - why should one do so?

It is stated in the Gemara (124b): The stopper of a barrel that was broken - it and its fragments are permitted to be moved on Shabbat, as they are suitable for covering a vessel (Rashi). However, one should not cut a piece from it to cover a vessel or to support the legs of a bed. Rashi explained: one should not fix it by removing its protrusions and thorns on Shabbat, as that would constitute making a utensil and would be a final hammer blow (makkah b’patish). But Maimonides in Chapter 26, Law 3 wrote: "A stopper of a barrel that was broken, it and its fragments - are permitted to be moved, but if one threw it into the garbage before Shabbat - it is forbidden to move it. A vessel that was damaged, one should not tear a shard from it to cover with it or to support with it." And he does not explain like Rashi that it is due to fixing the protrusions and thorns, but rather this is its explanation: when are the fragments permitted - when they have already been detached from the vessel. But when they have not yet detached, even though they are so damaged that they are about to separate - nevertheless, it is forbidden to detach them by hand. (And this is also the explanation in Shulchan Aruch, Section 44, and it does not bring Rashi's explanation, because according to Maimonides it is also forbidden regardless, and understand this well.)

The balls that are played with are muktzeh (set aside and prohibited to move on Shabbat), for they are not suitable for any use. They are also not suitable for covering vessels, since they are dirty from the mud and dirt that stick to them during play, and consequently, it is forbidden to play with balls on Shabbat. However, some say that since they are suitable for play, and playing is not prohibited for those who take pleasure in it, therefore they are permitted to be moved and played with. And some permit it only on Yom Tov and not on Shabbat, but this is not the main opinion (Magen Avraham 308:73), and thus the custom is to be lenient. However, in the Jerusalem Talmud, Tractate Ta’anit, Chapter 4 (Halachah 5), it is stated that a city was destroyed because they played with a ball on Shabbat, and similarly, it is mentioned in Midrash Eichah on the verse: "The Lord has swallowed up, He has not pitied" (Lamentations 2:2) — see there.

Silk worms are carried under the armpits, and through the warmth they generate and reproduce. It follows that on Shabbat it is forbidden to carry them for two reasons: because it is a burden, and additionally because it causes reproduction on Shabbat. For this reason, it is also forbidden on Yom Tov. There are some who prohibit moving a garment made of shaatnez (a forbidden mixture of wool and linen) on Shabbat, because since it is not suitable for wearing or covering, it is considered muktzeh (set aside and not to be handled). Others permit it, as it still has the status of a utensil. However, it is certain that it cannot be considered more lenient than a utensil whose primary function is forbidden (on Shabbat), and it is also permitted for its own use or its place (as written by the Magen Avraham in section 374 in the name of the Shelah, and what is written in the name of the Agudah to completely forbid it is astonishing).

It is permitted to move a fan on Shabbat for the purpose of driving away flies, as it is a human need. Similarly, brooms used for sweeping the ground are permitted to be moved. For those who maintain, as discussed in Siman 337, that it is forbidden to sweep the house, such items would be considered as tools whose primary function is for a prohibited use. However, we hold that in our tiled floors, it is permitted, as they are tiled as mentioned there, thus making their use permissible. The Rashba, of blessed memory, permitted moving an astronomical instrument on Shabbat, as it is a tool for studying the stars, because he allows studying wisdom on Shabbat. But according to the Rambam, who prohibits studying anything other than Torah on Shabbat, there is uncertainty regarding this matter. This has already been discussed in Siman 307, Section 11, and we have explained there that the primary halacha certainly permits it. See there.

Our Rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, wrote in Section 51: "Regarding time-telling devices called 'Eriluziv,' whether they are secular or of another type, there is doubt as to whether it is permissible to move them, and the custom has already spread to prohibit it." End quote. The reason is that it is similar to a measuring tool whose primary function is prohibited on Shabbat. Even though by knowing the time one can pray and study, the act of measuring time itself is not a mitzvah. And can one perform a mitzvah through something prohibited (Magen Avraham, section 378, citing Maharil)? Furthermore, there is no necessity to move it by hand, as one can simply come and see what time it is currently.

And this was all in their days when they did not have properly made timepieces. But now that they make small ones out of silver and gold and carry them like an ornament—it is obvious that they are permitted to be carried, and so have the great ones of the world practiced (as written in the Shulchan Aruch HaRav, section 149, citing the Pnei Me'iros, the Chacham Tzvi, and the Gaon Rabbi Naftali, and others, see there). However, this applies to the small ones and not to the large ones that stand by the walls of the house, for these certainly have the status of objects whose use is prohibited, and they are only permitted to be moved for their own use or their place, as well as their keys and weights (see Shulchan Aruch HaRav there).

There are times when an item is fit for use on Shabbat, but the owners are wealthy and consider such an item worthless, not their custom to use it, and it is destined to be thrown away. Consequently, it becomes muktzeh (set aside from use) because it has lost the status of a utensil. Therefore, even a poor person is forbidden to move it since the owners have designated it as muktzeh unless the poor person acquires it before Shabbat and it becomes his, in which case it is permitted to move it. Nevertheless, the wealthy person is forbidden to move it, even if the item previously belonged to the poor person. Only the wealthy who live in the homes of the poor are permitted to move such items, because in this regard, the neighbor is considered subordinate to the homeowner, even if the neighbor is wealthy and the homeowner is poor. All this applies when the item is insignificant to the wealthy person due to his wealth. However, if it is muktzeh due to prohibition, such as wine for a nazirite, it does not become muktzeh for this reason, since others are permitted to use it. Therefore, even the nazirite himself is permitted to move it, and similarly for any other case like this (see Taz 325 and Magen Avraham 379 who elaborate on this; however, the ruling is as stated, and so writes the Gra in his commentary).

Maimonides wrote in Chapter 25, Law 19: "Fruits that are forbidden to eat, such as untithed fruits, even if they are only rabbinically obligated in tithing, or first tithe from which the terumah has not been separated, or impure terumah, or second tithe and consecrated items that have not been properly redeemed - it is forbidden to move them. However, demai (doubtfully tithed produce), since it is fit for the poor, and similarly second tithe and consecrated items that have been redeemed even though the additional fifth has not been given - it is permitted to move them." End quote. All the more so, nevelah (animal that died without proper slaughter) and tereifah (animal with a fatal defect) and anything forbidden even rabbinically, such as wine used for libation, and their milk and cheese - it is forbidden to move them. However, anything fit for an animal is permitted to be moved. Similarly, all utensils that are forbidden for use because they became prohibited through cooking meat with milk or through cooking forbidden foods, even if they have not been used that day - it is forbidden to move them, since they are initially forbidden for use. However, if they are fit to hold food for animals or birds - it is permitted to move them. Similarly, a Jew may move terumah, since it is fit for a Kohen.

Even though muktzeh (items that are set aside and not to be used on Shabbat) is prohibited to move, nevertheless, if one moves the muktzeh by means of another object, it is permitted when there is a need for it. Therefore, we have learned: a person may pick up his child who has a stone in his hand, such as a child who is longing for his father so that if he is not picked up, he will fall ill, and the child is compelled to hold the stone in his hand. If the stone is taken from him, he will cry. They permitted the father to pick up the child even though the child is holding the stone. And even though it is somewhat as if he himself is holding the stone, they permitted this due to the distress of the child. But if the child is not longing in this manner, they did not permit it. 

And even if the child is longing, they only permitted it with a stone, but if the child is holding money in his hand, it is prohibited even to hold the child while he walks on his feet. This is because the money might fall from the child's hand and the father might come to pick it up with his hands. However, some say that in such cases where the child is walking on his feet and the father is holding his hand, it is permitted, since there was never a decree that one should not stand next to a child holding money, and the prohibition only applies when carrying the child with the money in his hands. But to hold his hand is of no consequence. And in a place of danger, everything is permitted.

A basket that had a hole and was sealed with a stone and pressed - it is permitted to move it, for it has become a wall. So wrote one of the commentators on the Shulchan Aruch (Magen Avraham, section 3). But I do not understand, for if so, what novelty is there in this? In my humble opinion, it seems that only with a stone in a vessel, which will be explained, did they say in the Gemara (125b) that pressing is needed, for otherwise it falls into the water. But with a stone in a basket, pressing is not needed, and this is the novelty - that with just placing it, it becomes a wall. (The words of the Magen Avraham are puzzling, and it seems that there is some mistake in the Magen Avraham, and so wrote the Eliyah Rabbah, section 4, that here pressing is not required; see there.)

And similarly, a stone that is in a hollow gourd, which is a hollow gourd in which they hang a stone to weigh it down in order to fill it with water, if it is well-tied so that it does not fall - it is permitted to fill it, since the stone is like the gourd itself and is nullified to it. But if not - it is prohibited, even if it was prepared before Shabbat, because it falls. Now in the Gemara (there) they used the term "tightened," since when it is tightened, it becomes like a wall. However, Rashi of blessed memory explained that the tightening is through tying, see there. But the Ra'avad in his commentary on the Mishnah there wrote that it is well-tightened, see there, and it seems that tying is not required. But the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, section 2, wrote tying, which implies specifically tying. However, in the Jerusalem Talmud on this Mishnah, it is explained not like Rashi, stating: "The stone in the gourd... once it is pressed into it - it is like its body," see there. And 'pressed' is a term of tightening and not tying, as it is stated there in Chapter "Kira" (Halacha 7) that the wick is pressed into the lamp, meaning it is squeezed. Similarly, in the Mishnah, Chapter 9 of Oholot (Mishnah 3) regarding a beehive: "If it is less than a handbreadth and plugged with straw or pressed, what is pressed - anything that does not have a handbreadth from one place," see there. This implies that the term means squeezing, and so it is explained in the Aruch, see there. And it is also explained in the Jerusalem Talmud there that a stone in a basket is not squeezed, see there (not like the Magen Avraham in the previous section), and it seems to me that for practical Halacha, one can rely on the Jerusalem Talmud.

A basket full of fruits with a stone inside it, where the stone is considered muktzeh (set aside for prohibited use), since the basket is not perforated to serve as a side partition, the basket is thus a base for both the prohibited and the permitted items. If the fruits are moist, such as figs and grapes, one is not required to take them out one by one until all are removed and then shake the stone out, because this would be a significant burden. Therefore, it is permitted to carry the basket as it is with the stone inside. However, if the fruits are dry and would not be damaged when shaken onto the ground, one should shake them out and thereby also shake out the stone, and not carry the basket with the stone. Similarly, even with moist fruits, if they are placed in small baskets within the larger basket, one should take them out of the larger basket, shake out the stone, and then put them back in. All this applies when one needs only the fruits or the basket. But if one needs the space where the basket is, one can carry it as it is.

As we have written, so have ruled the Rambam in Chapter 25, the Tur, and the Shulchan Aruch, Section 3. According to Rashi and Tosafot there from the Gemara (beginning of Chapter "Notel"), even with moist fruits, it is not permitted to move the basket as it is, unless it is a damaged basket. But with a complete one, one must remove the fruits from there and shake off the stone, as mentioned there. However, in any case, even for those who are lenient, it is only permitted to move it as it is in a situation of significant hardship, as we have written. From this, we learn that the permission regarding a base for something prohibited and something permitted is not an absolute permission, but only in a pressing situation where it is necessary. (And we must also say regarding the oven (47:), "When we were with Rav Nachman, we would move the stove along with the ashes, even though there were broken pieces of wood on it" - this is specifically in a situation of necessity, and in Or Zarua HaGadol at the end of Section 86, he remains in wonderment about this.)

And similarly, one can move impure terumah together with pure terumah when they are in the same vessel. In what case does this apply? When the pure terumah is at the bottom, and the fruits would become soiled on the ground if the vessel were shaken. But if they are nuts and almonds or similar items, one should shake the vessel and take the pure ones and leave the impure ones, unless the space of the vessel is needed, as mentioned. The same law applies to non-sacred items with impure terumah, or any types of permitted items placed together with prohibited items in one vessel.

If one forgets a stone on the top of a barrel or money on a cushion, the barrel or cushion does not become a base [for the prohibited item]. One may tilt the barrel to its side, allowing the stone to fall off, and one may shake the cushion so that the money falls off. This is specifically permitted when done for the sake of using the cushion, but it is prohibited to do so for the sake of preserving the money from being stolen (Magen Avraham, section 5), because indirect handling (tiltul min hatzad) for the sake of a prohibited item is forbidden, except in the case of a corpse as written in Siman 311. If the barrel is among other barrels in such a way that it cannot be tilted in its place, one may lift it with the stone on it to another location to tilt it there so that the stone falls off, as this is also considered indirect handling for the sake of a permitted item.

And this applies when one forgets, but if one intentionally places it with the intention that it should remain there at the entrance of Shabbat, it is forbidden to tilt and shake, because the barrel becomes a base for the prohibited stone, and similarly the pillow for the money. And in Siman 308, Section 43, we explained why it is not said that when one places it, the stone becomes a cover for the barrel and it should not be muktzeh at all, as we explained three reasons there. Moreover, even if the stone falls off by itself on Shabbat, the barrel is still forbidden to move, because once it is set aside at twilight, it is set aside for the entire day. We already explained there in Section 9 that in this muktzeh, the law does not follow Rabbi Shimon. This is the opinion of Rashi, that if one places the muktzeh intending for it to be on the permitted item at twilight, it becomes a base for the prohibition. But the opinion of Rabbeinu Tam is that it does not become a base unless it is placed with the intention that the muktzeh will be there all Shabbat. However, if one places the muktzeh only with the intention that it will be there at twilight, that is, at the entrance of Shabbat and not for the entire day, it does not become a base for the muktzeh, and it is permitted to tilt and shake it on Shabbat. One can rely on this opinion in a case of loss (Beit Yosef and Magen Avraham in subparagraph 7). It is obvious that if one placed it on the eve of Shabbat with the intention to remove it before the entrance of Shabbat, and then forgot and did not remove it, this is considered a case of forgetting (ibid., subparagraph 6 in the name of Terumat HaDeshen).

And there is a great question regarding this: why is it forbidden to place a stone on the mouth of the barrel, since the barrel contains wine, as explained by Rashi and the Ra'avad? If so, the barrel should be a base for both the permissible and the forbidden (A.R. Section 9). And there is one who answered that because the stone is placed on the mouth of the barrel and it is impossible to access the wine without removing the stone, therefore both the barrel and the wine become a base for the stone (T.S. Section 14). But why did the poskim (halachic authorities) not mention this?

And furthermore, they asked how we can reconcile the first opinion, which is the opinion of Rashi, that when something was placed there during "bein hashmashot" (twilight) it becomes a base and is forbidden for the entire Shabbat, even after the muktzeh item is removed from it. If so, when we place candles on a cloth primarily for the onset of Shabbat, how is it permissible to move the cloth the next day even after the candles were removed by a non-Jew, since it has become a base for the candles (Taz, Siman 310:1, and this remains a difficult question). 

There is an opinion that the reason for the leniency is that, in an incidental manner, it is permitted, as will be explained. Therefore, the candles on the cloth are considered incidental, since his intention is to place them on the table, but he cannot clear a space on the table without the cloth, and therefore the cloth does not become a base (Rabbi Shneur Zalman in paragraph 9). This is not a clear reason, because on the contrary, since he cannot place them except on the cloth, it is not incidental.

It seems more reasonable to me that the table becomes a base for the cloth and the candles, and similarly, the cloth becomes a base for the table and the candles, and it is a base for both a forbidden and a permitted item, and it is permissible to move it when necessary, as explained. Especially since it is customary to place the "lechem mishneh" (two loaves of bread) at the time of lighting the candles – the cloth does not become a base only for the candles. This reasoning is mentioned in Siman 277:10, see there. But according to what is written regarding the barrel, that it is not a base for the wine because it is impossible to reach the wine without removing the stone, and therefore everything becomes a base for the stone, if so, similarly here, since it is impossible to remove the cloth without the candles, everything becomes a base for the candles.

Therefore, it appears to me in my humble opinion that the matter is as follows: Certainly, if at the same moment both the forbidden and the permitted items were placed on a certain location, that place becomes a base for both the forbidden and the permitted, as both exert influence over it simultaneously. However, if the permitted item was placed there previously, and close to twilight the forbidden item was placed upon it, then that place is designated at the onset of Shabbat solely for the forbidden item. Otherwise, in the primary case of a base for the forbidden, why would you assume that the permitted item becomes a base for the forbidden? We could say the opposite, that the forbidden item becomes a base for the permitted. Rather, it is clear that the main consideration is what the place is used for close to the onset of Shabbat. According to this, our custom with the tablecloth makes sense, since close to twilight we place the tablecloth and the candles on the table, making the table a base for both the forbidden and the permitted, and similarly the tablecloth. But with the wine in the barrel, where the wine was already in the barrel and the stone was placed upon it close to twilight, they all become a base for the stone (and the Levush seems to interpret this with an empty barrel, which is perplexing).

There is an opinion that a base (for a muktzeh item) is not made unless one places the muktzeh item on it so that it will sit there properly. However, what one places incidentally, like placing various objects in a box because there is no room to put each object in a different place at the bottom of the box—such cases are not considered placing but rather forgetting (Responsa of Terumat HaDeshen, Siman 193). And there are those who disagree, saying that there is no leniency except in the case of forgetting, but if one intentionally places it, there is no distinction (Terumat HaDeshen, ibid.). And one should not ask why, according to this, a pure terumah should not become a base for impure terumah in Section 7. This is because the basket becomes a base for both of them, and so it is in all similar cases. (The Magen Avraham, Section 6, agrees with the author of the question, but his words are not conclusive, as the Eliyah Rabbah, Section 9, and the Taz, Section 14, wrote. However, the Alter Rebbe in Section 9 ruled like the Magen Avraham. In my humble opinion, it seems that it does not depend on incidental or non-incidental placement, but rather on primary and secondary importance, as will be explained in Section 310, with God's help. This also resolves the proof of the Magen Avraham there from the Rashba regarding a bag with a pocket of money. Nonetheless, one who is lenient in rabbinic matters has not lost.)

If a person places a muktzeh item on someone else's object, we do not say that it becomes a base for something prohibited, because one person cannot prohibit another person's item without their knowledge. After all, even in severe prohibitions involving something that doesn't involve an action, it is established that one cannot prohibit something that isn't theirs, such as someone who bows to someone else's animal, as stated in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 4. All the more so with muktzeh, which is rabbinic. However, in a case where it can be said that the owner is pleased with it, such as Reuven placing Shimon's vessel under Shimon's lamp so that if the lamp falls, it will fall on the vessel and not the table, and the lamp falls on the vessel, there is doubt whether it becomes muktzeh or not. Similarly, there is doubt if he himself did this, and the lamp fell on the vessel at twilight and then fell off the vessel, whether the vessel becomes muktzeh for the entire Shabbat (there, Siman 8, in the name of the Or Zarua). And the Tosafot wrote (44b, s.v. yesh) that if a non-Jew or child placed the item with the knowledge of a Jew, it becomes muktzeh. But there is no proof from this, as it can be explained that the Jew requested them to do it (and the Magen Avraham there wrote that from Tosafot 44b it implies prohibition, and he means this, but there is no proof as I wrote).

And even though we differentiate regarding a base for something prohibited between intentionally placing and forgetting, for if one forgets, it does not become a base for the entire Shabbat, nevertheless, in a situation where one knew that necessarily the muktzeh would fall into the vessel during twilight, it becomes a base and is prohibited for the entire Shabbat. For example, a chicken coop, since it is certain that their eggs will fall there, if an egg with an embryo is found there, meaning an egg containing an embryo, it is considered as intentionally placed and not as forgotten (Tosafot 45b, s.v. 'Dait'). And the same applies to anything similar. And know that it is simple, that even though when forgotten it does not become a base and is permitted to be moved, this is when the muktzeh has been thrown off it, but not when it is still on it; rather, one tilts it to the side and it falls off. Except if it was among the vessels, then one lifts it and tilts it to the side and it falls off, as explained. And similarly, if one needs the space of the vessel to be free and tilting and shaking it off will not suffice, one may move it with the muktzeh on it in order to clear the space, and further explanation will be given in Siman 310, with God’s help.

It has already been explained that we follow Rabbi Shimon's opinion, who is lenient regarding muktzeh. Therefore, in the case of muktzeh due to repulsiveness, such as wood used to hang meat or fish, or an earthenware lamp from their days that was not lit during twilight, and similar items - they are permitted to be moved. Likewise, in the case of muktzeh due to storage, such as types of food and beverages stored in a warehouse, like in stores and cellars for commerce - nevertheless, they are not considered muktzeh. The general rule is that no food that is detached and suitable for eating is muktzeh on Shabbat. Dates, almonds, and other fruits that are designated for commerce - it is permitted to eat from them on Shabbat. Similarly, all types of beverages, even those sealed on top - one may break the seal and eat and drink, as it is stated (146b): "A person may break a barrel to eat dried figs from it." However, there are many details in this law, which will be explained with God's help in Siman 314.

And we have already explained in Siman 308, Section 7, that in the case of muktzeh that was set aside with one's hands, Rabbi Shimon agrees. However, this matter requires clarification, as it does not depend solely on setting it aside with one's hands, but also on the item being unfit during twilight (bein hashmashot), such as a lamp that was lit before nightfall, where the muktzeh was done with one's hands and it is prohibited during twilight because of the fire. Similarly, figs and raisins that were set out to dry, at the moment they were set out, they were still fit to eat, but later they spoiled and were not fit to eat until they were completely dried. In this case of muktzeh, Rabbi Shimon agrees, because since they were set aside with hands and also are not fit to eat in the interim, one's mind is not on them until they are completely dried and taken from there. Therefore, even if they are fit on Shabbat, they are prohibited according to Rabbi Shimon because one has removed his mind from them, and he does not sit and wait for them as he does for a burning lamp, where he sits and waits for his lamp to extinguish (Shabbat 45b). And it becomes like a cup and a bowl, where Rabbi Shimon agrees they are prohibited to move even after they have extinguished, because he does not sit and wait. (And this is the intention of Tosafot, Shabbat 36a, s.v. "heicha" and s.v. "ela," see there. And even though for us there is no practical difference, as even for a lamp that has extinguished we do not hold like Rabbi Shimon, because since it was set aside at twilight, we hold like Rabbi Yehuda, nevertheless, according to Rabbi Shimon, it is the same way).

Therefore, wheat that was planted in the ground and eggs that are under a chicken, as long as they have not spoiled, it is permissible to take them and eat them. For although they were intentionally set aside, nevertheless, since they are fit for eating, Rabbi Shimon holds that one does not completely disregard them, and we follow his opinion. And this is not similar to a burning candle which is forbidden to us, because in that case, during twilight, it was not suitable. However, these were suitable during twilight. And even though they were intentionally set aside, we follow Rabbi Shimon. This is what the Tur and Shulchan Aruch wrote in section 2, that even wheat that was planted in the ground and has not yet taken root and eggs that are under the chicken, it is permissible to move them. Similarly, dates that were picked before they ripened and are stored in baskets and ripen on their own, it is permissible to eat them before they are fully ripened. But dried figs and raisins that are left out to dry are forbidden on Shabbat due to muktzeh, because they spoil before they dry out. Since one knows that they will spoil, he disregards them. And since there are two reasons: they were intentionally set aside and are not fit for use, they are considered muktzeh. And this is the intention as written. And dates, even though they are not fit for eating, nevertheless, they were not intentionally set aside. On the contrary, they were brought closer to being eaten by being stored in baskets. (And the Maharshal disagrees with the Tur as the Bach wrote, and according to what was written, the words of the Tur are clear. The Bach answered his question, and according to what was written, it is straightforward. And the words of the Magen Avraham in section 1 are obscure, and one should delve into them.)

A non-Jew who placed figs and raisins in a designated area to dry, and they belong to him - they are not considered muktzeh. If he gives some of them to a Jew on Shabbat and the Jew can eat them, it is permitted to eat them. This is because there is no concept of rejection (dichuy) with them, and the rule of preparation (hachanah) does not apply to them since non-Jews do not have the prohibitions of Shabbat. Therefore, the concept of muktzeh does not apply to their items. In the Jerusalem Talmud, chapter 3 of Beitzah (halacha 2), there is a disagreement about whether items belonging to a non-Jew require preparation. The law follows the opinion that they do not require preparation, as will be explained in Siman 498. From this, it is also proven that for any item belonging to a non-Jew that is permissible for a Jew to eat during the week, the prohibition of muktzeh does not apply on Shabbat. However, utensils that are muktzeh are forbidden even if they belong to a non-Jew, as is obvious.

We hold that there is no concept of muktzeh (set aside) for part of Shabbat. The explanation is as follows: Regarding something that was set aside during twilight (bein hashmashot), we say, "Since it was set aside during twilight, it remains set aside for the entire day." However, if something became set aside in the middle of Shabbat and during twilight it was suitable, but in the middle of Shabbat it became unsuitable either due to a prohibition of eating or a prohibition of handling, if it later becomes suitable again, it is permitted, as it returns to its permissible status. But something that was set aside during twilight is forbidden, as in this case we follow the opinion of Rabbi Yehuda and not Rabbi Shimon, as we have written.

If the item was not muktzeh (set aside) during twilight but the owners mistakenly thought it was muktzeh, we do not consider it as such, because even though they set it aside with their intention, it was set aside by mistake. Therefore, a lamp that was not lit during twilight, and the owners thought it was lit, is permitted to be moved in their lamps, but our lamps are always prohibited, as stated in Siman 277 and Siman 308. Similarly, figs and raisins that were set aside, and when twilight arrived, they had already dried and were fit for eating, even though the owners did not know at that time that they had dried, and later it became known to them that they had dried during twilight, are permitted to be eaten on Shabbat.

However, this is specifically when they are completely fit during twilight. But if they are sometimes fit and sometimes unfit, as there are people who eat them in this state and some who do not, then they still require the owner's designation: if he designated them, they are permitted; if he did not designate them, they are forbidden. Even if he later designates them, it is of no consequence. It appears to me that even if it is his custom to always eat them in this state, but now he was unaware that they were in this state, they are still forbidden without designation, since there are people who do not eat them. This is not considered an erroneous designation. Similarly, his designation is of no consequence if they are completely unfit for eating, and his designation is nothing, as this is like designating wood and stones for eating. And dates that have water poured over them in a tub on the eve of Shabbat and are not fit, but become fit on Shabbat, are permitted (Taz, subparagraph 4 in the name of Beit Yosef), as there is no muktzeh except for dried figs and raisins (Beit Yosef), because they are completely unfit. But the dates immediately become fit and do not have the issue of rejection.

Any item that is forbidden to move—one is not allowed to place a vessel under it on Shabbat to catch it, because this would render the vessel unusable since it would be prohibited to move. This involves the prohibition of building and dismantling, as explained in Siman 265. However, it is permitted to invert a vessel over it on Shabbat, since a vessel may be moved even for something that cannot be moved, provided that one does not touch it in a manner that might cause it to move, such as an egg or similar items. Even an item that does not move and is muktzeh (set aside) is not prohibited from being touched alone, as explained in Siman 308, when the main intention is for the muktzeh, like here where one inverts a vessel over the muktzeh—it is not proper to touch it. (See Magen Avraham, subparagraph 3, and Taz, subparagraph 5.) There is no absolute prohibition in this, but one should refrain from this, because since the entire activity now involves the muktzeh by inverting a vessel over it, if we permit touching it, it is easy to cause it to be moved from its place (this appears to be my humble opinion).

An item that is permissible to move and had placed upon it before Shabbat an item that is forbidden to move – the lower item also becomes forbidden because of the forbidden item placed upon it. This is called a "base for a forbidden item." The reason why something becomes a base was explained in the previous section, paragraph 12. Therefore, a bed that has money on it during Shabbat, and the money was not there at twilight (bein hashmashot), such as if it was placed there on Shabbat with the knowledge of the owner by a non-Jew or a child – the bed becomes a base for the money and is forbidden to move. If the money is removed, it is permitted to move the bed. However, if the money was placed there before nightfall to remain on the bed during twilight or all of Shabbat, as explained in the previous section, paragraph 9, even if the money falls off the bed, it is forbidden to move the bed, because once it was set aside at twilight, it is set aside for the entire day. The prohibition of being a base applies even for the need of its use or its place, as with the law of muktzeh itself. It is clear that if the permissible item became a base for a utensil whose primary function is forbidden, it is allowed for the need of its use or its place, like muktzeh itself. This all applies when the item was placed intentionally, but if money was forgotten on the bed or placed there unintentionally, the bed does not become a base, and one can shake the bed and the money will fall off, as explained in the previous section, paragraph 8.

And know that in the Gemara (44b) it states: Rav said: A bed designated for money, if one placed money on it even during the week - it is forbidden to move it on Shabbat, because since it was designated for a prohibited use, it becomes muktzeh, similar to a lamp designated for lighting. The Rif and the Rambam in Chapter 25 omitted this, as it is not according to the halacha, for we hold like Rabbi Shimon regarding muktzeh, and Rav holds like Rabbi Yehuda, as it is stated there in the Gemara. According to us, designation neither adds nor detracts, rather the main point is if there is money on it - it is forbidden to move due to being a base for a prohibited item when placed intentionally, or if it was placed on it during twilight - it is forbidden to move due to "migu d’itkatzai," and in this we hold like Rabbi Yehuda, as stated in Siman 308, Section 9 there. And this applies even without designation, but designation alone makes it muktzeh due to inherent prohibition, and in this, we hold like Rabbi Shimon. According to this, a purse that holds money: if it has no money in it and did not have money during twilight - it is permitted to move, and if it is suitable for some permissible use - it is considered a utensil whose primary use is permissible. Even if it is not suitable for permissible use, in any case, it is permitted for its own use or for its space. All the more so for pockets attached to garments, if they have no money in them and did not have money during twilight, they are completely permitted. Therefore, our wallets made to put money in, and our tobacco pouches made to put tobacco in to smoke, if they are empty and did not have money or tobacco during twilight - they are permitted to move, as they are suitable to put some permissible item in them, and they are considered as utensils whose primary use is permissible. Even if their primary use is considered prohibited, for their own use or for their space, they are certainly permitted. (And it seems that all these except the garment pocket are considered utensils whose primary use is prohibited, and only the bed is not like this, because most beds are for lying, which is not the case for these, they are like all utensils whose primary use is prohibited. But from the words of the Rema in Section 7, it does not seem so, as he writes that according to some who forbid, which is the opinion of Rabbeinu Tam that will be explained - the pockets are forbidden and permitted for their own use or for their space as stated there, it is explicitly explained that according to the Rif and the Rambam they are completely permitted as utensils whose primary use is permissible, and this requires further study, and be precise.)

However, the method of Rabbeinu Tam in Tosafot there is that the halacha follows Rav, that if one designated it for money - the bed is prohibited from being moved even if there was no money on it during twilight, as long as there had been money placed on it during a weekday. And it is explicitly stated there in Tosafot that for the sake of its use or its place, it is permitted (see there in the Tosafot beginning with 'a bed'), and so it is written in the glosses of the Rosh there. But the wording of the Rosh there is: "And Rabbeinu Tam explained that Rabbi Shimon agrees regarding a bed that one designated... for a person is particular about it and designates a place for it, just like sieves and sieving tools at the beginning of all utensils" end quote. And seemingly, since it is compared to this - it would be muktzeh due to monetary loss and prohibited even for its use or its place, and so is the opinion of one of the commentators on the Shulchan Aruch (Magen Avraham section 5). But it is very puzzling as to what monetary loss is relevant here, it is understandable with sieves and sieving tools, which are weaving or dyeing tools as explained there, that one is particular about them because of their work so they do not get damaged, like a slaughtering knife, but how would a bed get damaged that it would no longer be suitable for placing money. And it seems clear to me that the opinion of the Rosh is also like that of Tosafot and the glosses of the Rosh, and he only explained the relevance of a bed to money, that since it was designated for money - one is particular about it not being used regularly for any other purpose, and we find something similar with sieves and sieving tools, even though they are suitable for other uses - one is particular about them. But he does not compare the particularity to each other, for there the particularity is due to monetary loss so they do not get damaged, and with a bed this is not relevant. And this is the opinion of Rabbeinu the Rama who wrote in section 7 also according to this opinion that the bed is permitted for its use or its place, see there, and so wrote Rabbeinu the Beit Yosef in his great book, see there. And there is one who disputed them from the words of the Rosh, but in my humble opinion the law is with them as I have written. (See Magen Avraham section 5, and I am puzzled by him that he did not see in Tosafot where it is explicitly as I have written, and also what Magen Avraham wrote in Tosafot page 36. This is more puzzling, for there they wrote so according to Rabbi Yehuda and not according to Rabbi Shimon, see there at the end of the Tosafot beginning with 'Rabbi Yehuda'. And what he wrote from the glosses of Maimonides, also there it is not written like dried figs and raisins, but like dried figs, see there, and its explanation is like I have explained in the explanation of the Rosh. And what he wrote in the name of Ra'avan, I do not have his book, and what he wrote that in this everyone agrees that it is a utensil whose function is prohibited, this is certainly so, although from the Rama it does not seem so as I have written, examine it well).

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote in paragraph 7 that according to the opinion of Rabbeinu Tam, it is forbidden to carry a money pouch even if the money was removed from it before Shabbat, unless one did an act to it and made a hole in its bottom and removed it from its designated use. And this is the custom. However, for its own use or for the use of its place, it is permitted. Similarly, with a pouch sewn into a garment, since the main purpose of the garment is to be worn, if the money was removed from it, it is permitted to wear the garment, as the pouch is considered secondary to it. But if one forgot the money in it, it is permitted to carry the garment, as we do not say that the entire garment becomes a base for the money, since the money is not on the main part of the garment. However, it should not be worn on Shabbat, as we are concerned that one might go out with it, end of quote.

Here is the translation of the passage:

Behold, what is written that according to this view, it is forbidden to carry a money pouch without money unless it is needed for its body or place, and it is explained from his words that according to the view of the Rif and the Rambam - it is completely permitted like a utensil whose primary function is permitted. And regarding pockets sewn into garments, certainly, this is the case. But regarding pockets that are independent, it would seem from logic that everyone agrees that they are considered as having a primary function for prohibition (as the Magen Avraham writes, Siman 307:26). And our Master the Rema holds that since the pouch is suitable for all things, it is not classified as having a primary function for prohibition, and this is not similar to other utensils whose primary function is for prohibition. And what he wrote regarding a pouch sewn into a garment, if the money is removed it is permitted to wear it, because the pouch is nullified to it - his intention is concerning going out with it into the public domain, for if it were due to the prohibition of muktzeh, there would be no need for the reason of nullification, for regarding its body it is permitted as mentioned earlier, but rather he is saying that it does not become a burden in the public domain due to nullification (there, Siman 307:6). And what he wrote that if one forgot, it is permitted to move the garment because the money is not on the main part of the garment, here, for forgetting, there is no need for this reason, for if one forgot, it does not become a base, but rather this is what he meant: if it were on the main part of the garment, even on Shabbat, one would need to shake off the money, but now, this is not necessary. However, there is one who says that even in such cases, one must shake it off (there, Siman 307:7), and even if placed intentionally, since it is not on the main part of the garment, the garment does not become a base (there). And our Master the Rema also holds this, but he uses the term 'forgot' because intentionally placing money there is forbidden, for one might go out with it into the public domain (there), and it is also forbidden to put one's hand into the pocket (there). And if the pouch is independent but tied to the garment, then the garment becomes a base when there is money in the pouch, because since it is independent, it has significance, and similarly, a box in a table when there is money in it - the table is forbidden to move for this reason, unless there is also a permitted item on the table, and it becomes a base for both the forbidden and permitted item (there), and I do not know why the box in the table should not be secondary to the table and it requires further study. (And what the Magen Avraham learned from the wheel mentioned in the Gemara, I am puzzled, for there the primary movement is through the wheel, whether according to Rashi's explanation that it is a wheel or according to Rabbeinu Tam's explanation that it is the stand on which the chest stands or according to the Raavad's explanation that it is a roller, as he wrote in Chapter 3 of the Laws of Utensils, and this is his wording: "all its usage is through the wheel," and the primary movement is the wheel, and how is this similar to a box in a table. Therefore, it seems to me that it is permitted in such cases as well, and examine this well).

It has already been explained that a base for something forbidden and something permitted is allowed. We explained in Siman 309, Se'if 6, that this too was only reluctantly permitted in a pressing situation, as noted there, for otherwise one must shake off the forbidden item. Additionally, the forbidden and permitted items must be on it at twilight, for if only the forbidden item is on it at twilight, it does not help to place the permitted item on it on Shabbat, as the primary basis is at twilight. Conversely, if the forbidden item was not on it at twilight, even without the permitted item, it does not become a base for the entire Shabbat, but only while they are on it. In such cases, one can initially place the permitted item on it and move it (Taz 8) if necessary, because he cannot shake off the forbidden item, or it would cause him a loss to shake off the forbidden item (Bach).

This is the language of the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch in Section 8: "A vessel that has upon it something forbidden and something permitted - it is allowed to move it, such as a pan that has upon it ashes from before Shabbat which is permitted to move to cover saliva or excrement, and it also has upon it pieces of wood which are forbidden to move - it is permitted to move the pan as it is. And this is the case when the permitted item is more significant than the forbidden item, but if the forbidden item is more significant than the permitted item - it is nullified by it and it is forbidden to move it." End quote.

And it is not clarified what the law is when both are of equal importance, and there are those who write that it is forbidden (Taz 318:18). This is not clear to me, because if we analyze from what they wrote: "And such that the permitted item is more significant," it implies that when they are equal it is forbidden. But if we analyze from the end, where it is written: "But if the forbidden item is more significant," it implies that when they are equal it is permitted. Therefore, there is no conclusion from this, as this is the way of the language. And logically, it is clear that when both are equal, they do not nullify each other, and this is also evident from the words of the Hagahot Maimoniot (Chapter 26, Section 7) where it is written that a box that has food and money, if the money is not the primary item - it is permitted to move the box. End quote. It is explicitly stated that if only the money is not the primary item, even though the food is also not the primary item - it is permitted, for if not, it should have said: 'if the food is not primary - it is forbidden to move.' And similarly, from the source of the law in the Gemara (47a), it is proven for one who examines there, both according to Rashi's explanation and according to Rabbeinu Tam's explanation there. (In the matter of 'they taught in Galilee,' according to Rashi's explanation because the prohibition is significant to them and according to Rabeinu Tam because the permission is not significant to them. And know that regarding importance, the Magen Avraham writes in section 9 that it depends on the individual, even if it is not so for the whole world. And the proof is not from Galilee as that is a province, but the proof is from what is written there 'Are the small coins of the house of the Rabbi significant?' and examine this well).

And furthermore, our Rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, wrote there: "The reason for permitting this carrying is because it is impossible to hold the ash alone, even if one discards it from the shovel (when the ash is needed) or if the place of the shovel is needed. And if one only needs the shovel itself, he should not carry it as it is; rather, he should shake off the ash and the wood fragments in their place and then take the shovel. Similarly, if it is possible to shake off the prohibited item alone, he should do so and not carry it along with the permitted item." End quote. And all of this is based on the principle we have written, that the permission granted for a base to both (permitted and prohibited items) was only granted out of necessity. Accordingly, we can understand in every case of a base to both items: if there is a necessity to carry both, such as fear of damage or theft and similar cases, it is permitted to carry them; if not, he should shake off the prohibited item. And it has already been clarified, that if one forgot, the concept of a base does not apply. (And the law mentioned by the Beit Yosef in section 9 is what we brought in the previous section from the glosses of Maimonides) (See Beit Yosef in the name of the Ramban, that if the prohibited item has no importance, the concept of a base does not apply).

The deceased, even though it is the greatest form of muktzeh (an item set aside and not to be moved on Shabbat), nevertheless the Sages were lenient in many ways regarding its handling, both concerning the prohibition of muktzeh and the prohibition of carrying in places where it is rabbinically forbidden to carry, such as a karmelit (an area that is neither fully private nor fully public) and similar places. There are two reasons for this leniency: the first is due to human dignity, so that the deceased should not be disgraced, and the living should not be disgraced by him. The second reason is that the Sages understood that a person is more distressed over his deceased relative than over his money, and if no permissible way is found for him, he might come to violate prohibitions. The primary reason is due to human dignity, for if the reason were distress, it would only apply in situations where greater prohibitions might be violated if leniency is not granted. This is only relevant in the case of a fire, where if leniency is not granted, one might extinguish the fire. But in other cases, such as when the deceased is lying in a disgraceful state or exposed to the sun, the reason of distress does not apply, for what more can one do beyond moving the deceased? In these cases, the reason is due to human dignity, for we hold that "Great is human dignity, as it overrides a rabbinic prohibition," as they also permitted for the sake of wiping, as stated in Siman 312. This is the general principle, and the specifics will be explained further. There is also a great principle that if it is possible to handle it permissibly, we do not permit handling it in a forbidden manner, as will be explained with God's help.

Therefore, if there is a corpse lying in a place where there is fear of fire, if there is a loaf of bread or a baby, one can move the corpse by means of them. This is done by placing the loaf or the baby on the corpse and then moving them, as this is considered a lighter form of handling since one is not moving the corpse alone. If there is no loaf or baby, and the corpse is lying on a bed and there is another bed available, one can move the corpse by transferring it from bed to bed until it is brought to a safe place away from the fire. Although this involves moving the corpse alone, it is still considered indirect handling and thus permitted. If the bed has become a base for the corpse, if the corpse was on it during twilight (bein hashmashot), the bed is forbidden to move even after the corpse is no longer on it, due to the principle: "Since it was designated (muktzeh) during twilight, it remains designated for the entire day." If the corpse was not on the bed during twilight, the bed is permitted to be moved afterward, as mentioned in the previous section. Some say that the bed never becomes a base for the corpse, as the bed is not necessary for the corpse and the corpse itself is meant to be placed on the ground. This is the opinion of the Ba'al HaMaor, but the Rosh disagrees, and this is also implied by other poskim (halachic authorities). If the corpse is lying on the ground or there are no two beds, and there is also no loaf or baby, one may move the corpse in the usual manner, as it is permitted in the case of a corpse, as mentioned.

And in all this, there is no difference whether one takes it out to that courtyard where carrying is permitted, as one must first seek the lesser prohibition as mentioned, or whether one takes it out to another courtyard where they have not joined in an eruv or to a karmelit, for even taking it out to a karmelit is permitted, as will be explained, in the case of a corpse that is close to decomposing. And if they permitted it due to the decomposition, all the more so due to a fire. And also in these cases, one must first seek the lesser prohibition regarding muktzeh. And some hold that in these situations, one should not carry it by means of a loaf of bread or a child, in order not to increase the carrying, and this will be explained later in the law of decomposition. But our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in paragraph 1: All this is within the same domain, meaning that concerning fire, carrying in a karmelit was not permitted, as he holds that decomposition is more disgraceful than burning, and when carrying was permitted, it was only for decomposition and not for burning. And he deduced this from the language of the Rambam in chapter 26, who wrote: "And a fire broke out in a courtyard that has a corpse." And many great authorities disputed him, arguing that it is a fortiori from decomposition, for certainly fire is more disgraceful than decomposition. And what the Rambam wrote: "And a fire broke out in a courtyard that has a corpse" - has a different intention, that it was only permitted when the fire broke out in the courtyard of the corpse, as then the commotion and panic are great. And in this, the Sages said: A person is anxious about his deceased and if he is not permitted, he will come to extinguish, and it is permitted for him to take it out even to another courtyard and to a karmelit. But if the corpse is not in the courtyard where the fire is - he is not so anxious, and it is only permitted by means of a loaf of bread or a child and to a courtyard that is joined in an eruv (and the Magen Avraham in section 3 apologizes for the Beit Yosef, and the later authorities disputed him).

And behold, as clarified, they did not permit [saving] from a fire when the deceased is in another courtyard, and the decisors did not speak of this. The language of the Talmud is also general: "One saves the deceased from a fire." And also the language of the Tur, who wrote: "A deceased lying in a place where one fears fire, etc.," he did not clarify his words, but from the language of the Rambam we deduce this. And logic also dictates that when the fire is not in the courtyard where the deceased is, one is not as agitated, and is obligated to seek out bread or a child, and to bring him to a place where carrying is permitted. However, it is certain that if afterward the fire reaches the courtyard where the deceased is, its status reverts to being as if the fire fell in the courtyard where the deceased is, and all the previously mentioned allowances apply. But until the fire reaches there, it is only permitted through bread or a child and into a courtyard that is joined [by an eruv], and this appears to be the primary ruling.

If there is a corpse lying in the sun and it is not currently decaying but could decay over time, the sages did not permit all these leniencies for it. They only allowed moving it from the sun to the shade using a loaf of bread or a child, and only within the same courtyard. Beyond this, they did not permit. Therefore, if one does not have a loaf of bread or a child, one may not move it at all, not even to turn it from one bed to another, because moving indirectly for a prohibited purpose is considered moving. It has already been explained in Siman 308, Se'if 16, that the leniency of using a loaf of bread or a child was permitted only for a corpse. Even according to those who hold that an object whose primary use is prohibited may be moved with a loaf of bread or a child, in the case of something that is set aside like a corpse, they only permitted it for a corpse, as stated there, and no more. And you might ask, if so, what should be done when there is no loaf of bread or child available? Indeed, the sages provided another remedy in such a case, as will be explained.

And so the sages taught (43b): "A corpse lying in the sun, two people come and sit beside it. If it is hot for them from below, one brings a bed and sits on it and the other brings a bed and sits on it. If it is hot for them from above, they bring a mat and spread it over themselves. One then raises his bed and slips away, and the other raises his bed and slips away, and thus a partition is formed by itself." There, the mat remains spread over the beds, protecting the corpse from the sun. To do this intentionally for the corpse is prohibited, and even though one may move an object for the sake of something that cannot be moved, nonetheless, there is the issue of creating a tent, and even for the sake of the living, they did not permit making a partition or a tent. Therefore, they first bring beds for sitting. This need to wait until it is hot for them below, when they could immediately bring beds for sitting, is actually a stringency that they imposed so it would be very clear that it was for the sake of the living (Tosafot there, 'if it is hot'). Similarly, it is specifically when they first spread the mat over their heads and then, when they slip away, the mat remains on the beds. But to spread it initially over the beds is prohibited because of making a tent (there, 'and spread' and Rashi there). Since at the time of the action it was evident that it was for the sake of the living, they are then allowed to slip away from under the mat and leave it over the corpse (there, 'and slips away'). This permission applies where there is no loaf or child, or there is no shady place, or even if they do not want to move it from its place. Though there is a great effort involved, one may still do so since at the time of the action it is done for the sake of the living, as mentioned. (See Taz, subsection 6, for his resolution of Beit Yosef’s question, which is also the intention of Magen Avraham, subsection 17, and the intention of Tosafot there, 'if it is hot', as we explained. Nonetheless, it is difficult, for if so, what did Rav Sheshet say: 'Go and tell Rabbi Yehuda, who says an object may not be moved except for something that may be moved, Rav Huna already explained... from this law.' And in this law, all agree for the sake of recognition, as we said, and we do not follow Rabbi Yehuda. This is the intention of Beit Yosef in his question. It is a severe question, unless we say that Rabbi Shimon’s intention was not exactly like Rabbi Yitzchak's, and it is forced. Consider well.)

And there is a question about this, for here we said that it is forbidden to make this partition for the sake of the dead, only for the sake of the living. However, in Eruvin (44a) regarding a sukkah wall, it is stated that one may erect a bed and spread a sheet over it so that the sun does not fall on the dead, implying that it is permitted for the sake of the dead. And our Rabbis, the Tosafists, explained that there too the intention is like here, to do it for the sake of the living, and the Talmud did not elaborate there. And in Eruvin, they provided another explanation, that if the dead body in the sukkah would rot, they would need to leave the sukkah, thus it is also for the sake of the living so that they do not have to leave the sukkah. (And it is difficult regarding the Magen Avraham 618:18 who wrote in the name of the Tosafists simply that if they need to leave, it is for the sake of the living and permitted, while the Tosafists wrote this only concerning a sukkah where there is a mitzvah to dwell in it. One must say that he wrote this from his own reasoning, for certainly if one needs to leave his house, it is also considered his need, and the Tosafists wrote about the sukkah because that was the context, but in practice, there is no difference, and so it appears. Investigate and you will find it correct.)

Rambam wrote at the end of Chapter 26: "If a deceased person decays in a house and becomes a disgrace among the living, and the living are disgraced by him, it is permitted to take him out to a karmelit (an area that is not fully public nor private). The dignity of human beings is so great that it overrides a negative commandment in the Torah, which is 'You shall not turn aside from the word which they shall tell you, to the right or to the left.' But if there is another way for them to go out, they do not take him out, but leave him in his place and they go out." This is because, since he has already decayed, he has no further benefit, but the disgrace is when he is together with the living. Therefore, when the living have another way, why should we move the deceased?

From the structure of Rambam's language, it is evident that they only permitted taking out a decayed deceased to a karmelit, but not one lying in the sun. This is also clarified from the words of the Shulchan Aruch, for although we permitted this in the case of a fire in section 3, this is certainly because of the great panic to prevent burning, which is not the case for one lying in the sun, for whom they did not permit even other leniencies, as stated in section 5. 

However, this is not the opinion of Rashi (94b), who in that incident where they permitted taking him out to a karmelit wrote: "because he was lying in disgrace or in a fire or in the sun." This is also the opinion of the Tur, who wrote: "If he is lying in the sun or in disgrace, such as if he is decaying, if there is a loaf or a child, they place it on him and move him, even from a private domain to a karmelit, etc." And similarly, he wrote that without a loaf or a child, they did not permit even to turn him from bed to bed. He wrote this about both: the sun and the decay. To him, both laws are entirely equal. It is surprising that they did not permit indirect handling for decay, but permitted taking him out to a karmelit, and were stricter about muktzeh (items that cannot be moved on Shabbat) than about carrying out (as the Magen Avraham wrote in section 5).

Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in the language of the Rambam, that a dead body that has begun to decompose should be taken out to a karmelit (an area that is neither entirely private nor public), and if there is a way for the living to exit, they should leave. On this, our teacher, the Rema, wrote: "And some say that even if it has not yet decomposed but is close to decomposing," end quote. This implies from his words that even in this case, if there is a way for the living to exit, they should leave and leave the dead body as it is. This is surprising because if it has not yet decomposed, why not find a solution to prevent it from decomposing? In truth, the Tur did not mention this, and according to his opinion, even if there is a way for the living to exit, they should take the dead body out (Magen Avraham, Section 7) to prevent it from decomposing. Only the Rambam and the Shulchan Aruch mentioned this law, and that is when it has already decomposed, as there is no benefit to the dead body in removing it, as mentioned. But from where did our teacher, the Rema, derive that even if it is close to decomposing, we do not consider the dead body itself, as the decomposition is only a disgrace to the living and not to the dead body? It seems he inferred this from the language of the Rambam, who wrote: "And it is disgraced among the living, and they are disgraced by it," from which it is understood that the disgrace is not only to the living, and the disgrace to the dead body is only when it is among the living. Therefore, when the living leave, it is not disgraced. Similarly, the Maggid Mishneh wrote in the name of the Raavad (as the Magen Avraham mentioned in Section 6).

When they permitted carrying him (i.e., a deceased person) into a karmelit (a semi-public domain), the Tur wrote that it requires (carrying) with a loaf of bread or a child. In the name of the Ramban, it is written that, on the contrary, it is forbidden to do so with a loaf of bread or a child, because what was rectified with the prohibition of muktzeh is corrupted with the prohibition of carrying, and why should we carry the loaf or the child into the karmelit. Some of our Rabbis hold that it is permitted to carry him even into a public domain with a child, because there is no Torah prohibition here, as carrying a corpse is considered a labor that is not needed for its own sake, and we hold according to Rabbi Shimon that a labor not needed for its own sake is exempt, contrary to the words of the Rambam who ruled according to Rabbi Yehuda regarding a labor not needed for its own sake, as it is written in Siman 242. Regarding the child, one is also exempt if he can walk on his own due to the principle that "a living being carries itself," and even if he cannot walk, one is exempt because he is secondary to the corpse since he is of the same species. However, with a loaf of bread, it is forbidden, because the loaf is not secondary to the corpse, as it is not of the same species, and one is liable for carrying it. The Rambam did not mention a loaf of bread or a child at all. The opinion of Rashi, Tosafot, and the Tur is to carry him into a karmelit specifically with a loaf of bread or a child, and one may rely on them in practice (as only the Ramban leans towards prohibition, and see the Ran there who disagrees with him).

When they permitted [handling a corpse on Shabbat] due to the dishonor of the dead, it does not specifically mean the dishonor caused by decomposition. The same applies to other forms of dishonor, such as when the corpse is being transported on a ship and idle and frivolous people gather there and mock the dead, or similar situations. Likewise, if the corpse is placed in a small room where the air is difficult for those sitting with it. Similarly, it is permitted to tell non-Jews to move the corpse in the same manner as [one would move] with a loaf of bread or a child, but this is only permitted in a karmelit (a rabbinically defined semi-public domain), not in a public domain. However, regarding matters related to burial, it is forbidden even through a non-Jew, because it is dishonorable to the dead that Shabbat be desecrated on their behalf for the sake of burial.
