But to move the corpse for the sake of honor so that it can be placed in a clean place until after Shabbat, this is certainly agreeable to both the deceased and the living, not matters related to burial, which can be done after Shabbat. (See Magen Avraham, subsection 13. I do not understand why he needed the reason of a rabbinic prohibition without action, because since it is in a karmelit, it is a rabbinic prohibition upon another rabbinic prohibition, and a rabbinic prohibition without action is considered a rabbinic prohibition on a Torah prohibition, as the Tosafot write in Bava Kamma 80a, s.v. "Omer" in the name of the Behag. However, according to Rashi's version in Eruvin 68a, it is understandable. Investigate this matter thoroughly.)

Our master wrote in section 2: that it is forbidden to move a corpse with the aid of a loaf or a child for the sake of Kohanim or another matter, but by a non-Jew, some permit it. And I have seen this practiced for the sake of a mitzvah or a wedding, end quote. And the Maharil ruled that with a loaf or a child it is permitted to move it for the sake of the living (there, subparagraph 14), and he wrote that this is the custom, and it is surprising that he did not mention his opinion at all. And it seems that his reasoning is that it is certainly more lenient with a non-Jew without a loaf or a child than with a Jew with a loaf or a child, for with a non-Jew it is a shevut deshevut (a double rabbinic prohibition) in a place of mitzvah, for this is also considered a mitzvah so that the Kohanim should not be distressed to leave their homes on Shabbat, and all the more so for a wedding or another mitzvah or a significant need. But a loaf and a child were only permitted for the sake of the corpse itself, as explained in the Gemara, and therefore, since non-Jews are available among us, it is better to act through them, and therefore he did not write the words of the Maharil. And perhaps in a situation where it is impossible through a non-Jew, it is permitted with a loaf or a child, since the Maharil permitted it and testified that this is the custom. And there are those who say that moving indirectly, that is, to transfer it from bed to bed, is permitted for the sake of Kohanim, for although it was explained that a loaf and a child is more lenient than indirect moving, and since he forbids with a loaf and a child, all the more so indirect moving is forbidden, however, it is not comparable, for here where the place is needed for the Kohanim, it is considered as for the sake of its place and is permitted as will be explained, for this is indirect moving for the sake of something permitted (there, subparagraph 14).

The kohanim (priests) cannot compel the relatives of the deceased to remove the body for their sake, even if they are unable to enter the synagogue to pray because of the presence of the corpse, even on a weekday. The reason is simple: the relatives can claim that moving the corpse from place to place is a dishonor to the deceased, and if the kohanim are unable to perform a mitzvah because of this, they are exempt by law. Therefore, in a place where the custom is to purify the deceased at the cemetery, since the body must be removed before the burial time regardless of the presence of the kohanim, the kohanim can compel the relatives to immediately remove the body. However, if the relatives wish to remove the body for the sake of the kohanim and do not object to doing so, they may remove the body both on weekdays and on Shabbat according to the leniencies that have been explained, because for the deceased himself, certainly, this is not a dishonor; what difference does it make to him if he is here or in another place. All this applies to healthy kohanim, but if there is a sick kohen who cannot leave, it is obvious that the relatives can be compelled to remove the body to prevent the kohen from violating a Torah prohibition, or they can ensure that the impurity does not reach the room where the kohen is, meaning that there should not be an open space of a handbreadth there, as explained in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 371.

Know that what we have said about a loaf of bread or a child is not specifically required, for the same applies to any garment or other permissible item. There is a question regarding this, for if so, how could we ever find a situation where a loaf of bread or a child would be necessary? Every deceased person is presumably not naked, and therefore they could be moved using the garment that is on them. However, it is possible that the garments on them at the time of death are considered nullified to them, and they themselves are considered muktzeh (set aside and prohibited on Shabbat) as a base for a prohibited item (see Beit Yosef). Nevertheless, there are some great authorities who hold this view, as our master the Beit Yosef wrote in section 4, and this is his language: "There is one who says that they only required a loaf of bread or a child for a naked deceased, but if he is in his garment, a loaf of bread or a child is not necessary." End quote. According to this opinion, it must be said that the garment is not a base for the deceased, which is the case when it is forgotten. Additionally, it can be said that this is better than other bases where there is a connection between them, but what connection does a garment have to a deceased? Only burial shrouds are nullified to the deceased, as stated in Chullin (125a), because burial shrouds are related to the body of the deceased, but the garments in which the person died and will not be buried with him are not nullified to him. (And regarding the objection from David, who required a loaf of bread or a child as it is stated in Shabbat 30a, it has already been answered by the Taz and the Magen Avraham in section 16 that his garments are set aside and forbidden to use, and they are burned, for it is forbidden to use the garments of a king, see there).

And what has been explained, that a deceased person lying in the sun is forbidden to be moved from one bed to another because indirect handling (tiltul min hatzad) is considered handling, this is when the handling is solely for the sake of the deceased, as we hold that indirect handling for the sake of a prohibited item is forbidden. But if the space where the deceased lies is needed for the living, or if the object on which the deceased rests is needed and it did not become a base (as previously explained), or if the person died on Shabbat and since it was not a base during twilight, it is permitted after the muktzeh is removed from it - it is permitted to move the deceased from one bed to another, which is indirect handling, since this is for the sake of a permitted item. And we hold that indirect handling for the sake of a permitted item is allowed. And it has already been explained that the permission through a loaf of bread or a child applies only to a deceased person, and some say also to a utensil whose primary use is prohibited. But for complete muktzeh similar to a deceased person - they only permitted it for the deceased alone, for indeed it is a strained permission to initially make something secondary to muktzeh in order to move it, and how does it become secondary, and only for the deceased did they permit it due to his honor. And also for a utensil whose primary use is prohibited, according to those who hold this, because the muktzeh is lighter, as it is permitted even for its own use and its place, but not for complete muktzeh (see Taz, section 5, and we have already explained the essence of his words with God's help).

According to what has been explained, we learn that if someone dies on Shabbat, or before Shabbat and there was no opportunity to bury them, and they were not placed on the ground before Shabbat—it is forbidden to move them from their place and they should remain in their bed until the conclusion of Shabbat. Even using a loaf of bread or a child to move them is prohibited, unless there is concern that the body will become damaged, such as if it is placed on cushions and pillows and could deteriorate by the end of Shabbat, or if the person was obese, or if it is hot in the house, or if it is difficult for the living to be in the same room, or if there are children who are afraid of the body as children usually are, or if there is a sick person in the house who is troubled by the sight of the body, and similar cases. In such situations, one should place some garment on the body and move it to a cool room or a cellar. If it is possible to move the body by a non-Jew, it is better to do so. And if it is possible to close the room and open a window opposite it to allow the wind to enter so that the body does not deteriorate, it is better to do so. This is also how we guide in practice.

Even though the deceased is prohibited from being moved, nevertheless, the sages permitted anointing the deceased with oil in places where it is customary, as well as washing the deceased with water if it is dirty, since this does not involve moving the deceased but merely touching it. It has already been clarified that touching muktzeh is not prohibited, only moving it. Even according to those who hold that touching muktzeh for the sake of the muktzeh is not clearly permitted, in the case of the deceased, it is allowed out of respect. It is also permitted to remove the pillow from beneath the deceased to prevent it from becoming foul-smelling, and the pillow does not become a base for muktzeh due to the reasons we have explained, provided they are careful not to move any limb of the deceased, because if a limb is moved, it constitutes moving muktzeh. If the deceased's mouth opens, one may tie the jaw with a cloth or belt in a manner that prevents it from opening further, but not to close what has already opened or part of it, because if so, it would be moving a limb, and muktzeh is prohibited from being moved even partially. This is not considered nullifying a vessel from its preparedness since one can remove the cloth or belt whenever desired, as removing them does not move the deceased. Additionally, it is forbidden to close the eyes of the deceased due to the prohibition of moving a limb. (See Magen Avraham 311:24, who wrote that it is prohibited through a non-Jew unless it was arranged before Shabbat, and I am puzzled because is this considered a labor? Also, the Eliyah Rabbah 311:22 disagrees with him, and so is the custom.)

When his limbs are dislocated and need to be straightened, this should be done by a non-Jew, but it is forbidden for a Jew to do so. There are places where a Jew does this, and they say there is danger involved (Eliyah Rabbah 623 in the name of Ma'aseh Rokeach), and if it is a received tradition, we accept it. At the very least, those who do so should place an object on the dislocated area and press with the object until the limb is straightened (ibid.), but we permit this only through a non-Jew. It is stated in the Talmud (Shabbat 151b): they bring cooling vessels and metal vessels and place them on his belly so that it does not swell, and they plug his orifices so that air does not enter, and this is not known to us at all. If he is very filthy with mud and excrement, they wash him with cold water through a non-Jew (see Magen Avraham and Eliyah Rabbah there).

Since it has been explained that indirect handling (tiltul min hatzad) for the sake of something permitted is allowed, for this reason, if one forgot money on a pillow, he shakes the pillow and the money falls off, as stated in Siman 309. Therefore, if one buried a radish in the ground, he may take it even though by taking it he displaces soil from its place, for this is indirect handling for the sake of something permitted. Our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in Section 8 three conditions for this:

1. Only if it has not taken root in the ground, because if it has taken root, it is considered planted, and when one removes it, he is liable for uprooting. But if it has not taken root, even though it added somewhat due to the moisture of the soil, we do not concern ourselves with it, for this is not considered planting.
2. He must not intend to plant it. Even though wheat that was planted in the ground may be taken as long as it has not taken root, as stated in Siman 310, here it is different because since it added somewhat due to the moisture of the soil, it is considered like planting if he intended to plant it (thus resolving the difficulty of the Magen Avraham in subsection 22).
3. Part of its leaves must be exposed, and he removes it by the leaves from the ground. If they are not exposed, even though he can insert a spindle or needle into it and remove it, as is explained later regarding fruits in straw, here it is forbidden because it appears as making a hole. However, some say that here too it is permitted to insert into the soil, and so it is in the Jerusalem Talmud at the end of the first chapter of Kilayim, and we do not fear that he might come to level the hole, for in a field we do not fear this, since why would he need to level the hole in the field? Therefore, in a house or courtyard, it is forbidden in such cases for this reason (as stated in subsection 21).

And what we have said that moving indirectly for the purpose of something forbidden is prohibited - this is referring to moving with the hand. But moving with the body, which is moving in an unusual manner - in these cases it is also permitted. And this is what we have learned: "The straw on the bed, he moves it with his body" (141a). And the straw is muktzeh, as it is generally designated for burning in places where they burn straw, and he moves it with his body so that it will be soft and comfortable for lying (Rashi). And even though he needs the straw to lie on, and it is considered moving for the sake of muktzeh, nonetheless, since he only moves it with his body - it is permitted. And there are those who indeed have reservations that if his intention is for this - it is forbidden, and they only permitted it if he needs the bed and not the straw, but the straw prevents him from lying on the bed (see Rosh there and see Magen Avraham section 24). And if he had intended from the previous day to lie on the straw, and all the more so if he had actively placed a pillow or cushion on the straw from the previous day - he may move it even with his hand, since he has prepared it from the previous day and it is not considered muktzeh, and it has already been explained in section 308, paragraph 40 that preparation of muktzeh is effective in several ways there.

Fruits that are hidden in straw or stubble that are muktzeh, one can insert a needle or spindle into them and take the fruits, and the straw will fall off by itself, for this is considered indirect handling for the sake of something permitted. This is not similar to a radish, which is prohibited in such cases because it appears like making a hole, as mentioned. However, with straw or stubble, the issue of making a hole does not apply, as making a hole only pertains to earth. Fruits that are hidden in sand or earth within one's house, which were piled up before Shabbat and designated for use in a specific corner, are not considered muktzeh and can be taken directly, as mentioned in Siman 308, Se'if 64.

And know that concerning the law of a radish buried in the ground, in section 19, our teacher, the Rema, wrote that it is permitted to take it even if it was left there for the entire Shabbat, as food does not become a base for a forbidden item. His words are perplexing, for the Tosafot explicitly wrote at the beginning of the chapter "Kol HaKelim" regarding fruits buried in straw, that it refers to when they were left with the intention to take them, but if he intended to leave them there for the entire Shabbat, it becomes a base for a forbidden item. There are those who interpret his intention as meaning that he intended to eat them on Shabbat when he wishes to eat them (Taz, section 10), but if so, it is not relevant to say that food does not become a base, and certainly, it does become a base. However, here, since it does not become a base. Similarly, in the source of the law in the Kolbo, it is explicitly explained that since his intention is that the food should not serve the dirt, but the dirt should serve the food, therefore it does not become a base (as stated by the Magen Avraham, section 23). In my humble opinion, it seems certain that food not fully cooked, as in the case of "Kol HaKelim" (123.), where it is stated 'a fig preserved in straw,' and Rashi explained that it is not fully cooked and is buried to cook, and similarly, a cake buried in coals to bake, since it is currently not fit for eating, and the straw is like earth for seeds - in this regard, the Tosafot correctly wrote that for the entire Shabbat it becomes a base. But a radish buried in the ground, which has already been cooked but is buried to prevent spoilage, indeed does not become a base, for the dirt preserves it, and the preserver is secondary to the food, not the food to the preserver. This is a good and proper reasoning, with the help of Heaven.

In the time of the Gemara, their restrooms were in the fields behind the city, and generally, they did not have a permanent place for this, but sometimes it was in one place and sometimes in another. Even those who had a fixed restroom did not designate it for one person, but many would use it. Also, in their days, they did not clean themselves with paper due to its unavailability, and furthermore, they did not clean themselves with something that fire affects, as it is stated in Shabbat (82a): "One who cleans with something that fire affects - his lower teeth will fall out." They would clean themselves with soft stones, which are muktzeh like other stones, because preparing them is not possible. If they prepared them at home, it would be forbidden to carry them to the field, and if they prepared them in the field, others would take them, as even someone who had a fixed restroom did not have it designated for him alone. So what should be done? For the dignity of people is great, and such a necessity is significant.

Therefore, the Sages said: Due to the respect for human dignity, they permitted moving stones that are suitable for wiping. This means that someone who has a designated place for a bathroom can bring in a handful of stones, even though he does not need them all at once; he can save some for another time. And even if someone else takes them, it does not matter, because all of this is for the purpose of the bathroom. It makes no difference whether it is for him or for someone else, since taking them with one hand is considered one effort. Although, ideally, one should not move muktzeh (items that are set aside and not to be moved on Shabbat) for another person, the main point is that he is moving them for himself for another time. We only mentioned that if someone else takes them, it does not matter, but the main permission is because they are suitable for him. Therefore, if he does not have a fixed place, he is not allowed to bring in more than a handful, except for what is necessary for wiping, which is the measure of a small spice pestle. And if it is evident that a stone was used for wiping, it becomes prepared and it is permitted to bring it in, even if it is very large. And if there are many stones and it is evident that they were used for wiping, it is permitted to move even more than a handful, since once they were used for wiping, they were prepared for that purpose. And even if it rained and they became muddy, if it is still evident that they were used for wiping, it is permitted (according to Rashi, there in Shabbat 81a, and practically, there is no dispute in this matter). Even though it is possible that they were not prepared before Shabbat but were used for wiping on Shabbat, and preparation on Shabbat does not usually help, in this matter, it is permitted to be lenient even in doubt, since there was a leniency in this matter.

And it was said in the Gemara there (81b) that they permitted the moving of stones, and even to bring them up to the roof if one went up there to relieve oneself, and we do not worry about excessive exertion (Rashi). And we also do not say that since he went up to the roof, he could have prepared from before Shabbat, as it is a fixed place. Nevertheless, they permitted it (Tosafot and Ran there), and as the Tur wrote, and this is his language: "And it is permitted to bring them up to the roof to wipe with them, and we do not say that since he has a designated place, he should bring them up there from before Shabbat," end quote. And even though in the Gemara there it is proven that the reason for the permission is because he does not have a fixed place and could not have prepared from before Shabbat, and if so, here where he goes up to the roof, why is it permitted? He could have prepared from before Shabbat. It must be said that the roof is not considered a fixed place, and this is explicitly clarified in Tosafot Sukkah (36b, s.v. 'on Shabbat').

Based on this, it is clearly proven that in a place where one has a designated location, like in our case where someone has their own private bathroom, and similarly all our bathrooms are in courtyards where carrying is permitted, and each person can prepare wiping paper before Shabbat - it is forbidden to take muktzeh on Shabbat for wiping. This is also written by one of the commentators on the Shulchan Aruch (Magen Avraham, section 1), and in the glosses of the Maimonides (chapter 26). However, our teacher, the Beit Yosef, in his major work at the end of this section, wrote that there is no distinction, and this is his language: "From the words of the poskim who wrote generally, it implies that just as we permit bringing them up to the roof even though it was possible before Shabbat, similarly for us it is permitted because of human dignity." And so it is written in the glosses of the Rosh in Shabbat there, and the Tosafot in Sukkah there also seem to be uncertain about this. From the words of the Tur, it clearly appears to be permitted, and it needs to be said that he holds that the Gemara means: that which was permitted was because a person does not designate a fixed place for a bathroom, but now that it was permitted - it was completely permitted, because it is impossible to permit for one and forbid for another. And this seems to be the main point according to my humble opinion, that although we say according to the previous opinion that one should have prepared before Shabbat, nevertheless, what should he do now if he did not prepare? After all, human dignity is great. And this seems to me to be the main point of the law, that certainly every person is obligated to prepare, since in our situation it is possible to prepare. However, if he did not prepare - human dignity is great, and he may take from the courtyard something suitable for wiping even though it is muktzeh.

Rabbeinu the Rema wrote in Section 1: "Some say that it is permitted to move stones only in a courtyard, and some say that even from a karmelit to a private domain is also permitted, for this too is only a Rabbinic prohibition, and due to the dignity of human beings they permitted it." End quote. And what he wrote according to the first opinion, "only in a courtyard," is not precise, for their privies were in the fields, but rather it means that in one domain they permitted it, not from one domain to another. And even though they permitted muktzeh, nevertheless, carrying is more stringent than muktzeh, and even if it is not more stringent, they only permitted one prohibition and not two prohibitions. The second opinion holds that muktzeh is more stringent than carrying from one domain to another by Rabbinic law, and since they permitted muktzeh because of human dignity, all the more so they permitted a karmelit (Tosafot Sukkah there), and it holds that there is no difference between one prohibition and two prohibitions. And one should not ask according to the first opinion, if so, what should one do in the field when there are no suitable stones for wiping within four cubits of where he relieves himself, and to carry four cubits in a karmelit is certainly forbidden according to this opinion just as it is forbidden to carry from a karmelit to a courtyard, for one can say that he should relieve himself within four cubits of the stones. And even if he has a fixed place there, nevertheless, if there are no stones within four cubits, he should not relieve himself there, for this was not permitted. And regarding the law, one should be lenient with Rabbinic prohibitions (the Gra, and mainly the first opinion that Rashi cited, I did not find this explicitly in Rashi, see there and scrutinize).

And regarding what was explained in paragraph 2, that if the stone used for wiping is recognizable, it is permitted even if it is more than a handful, there is an opinion that even the other stones around it are permitted, even though they do not bear a mark (Magen Avraham 2, citing Shiltei Giborim). This opinion, however, is refuted as having no basis (Magen Avraham and Eliyah Rabbah). In my humble opinion, his words are correct. If we scrutinize, what benefit is there in the sign if it is discarded and nullified for this purpose? We must necessarily say that this is not similar to discarding remnants of a vessel into the trash, because here it is its specific place designated for it, so it is not nullified. However, it still needs to be understood, for if one wipes with it and prepares it for wiping, must he specifically search for it again when he needs to wipe again? We must necessarily say that he prepared this place from which he will take for wiping, and if so, it follows that he prepared all the stones around it. And it is obvious that if one explicitly designates with his mouth or his thoughts the stones in that place, it is effective, as it is written in Siman 308, paragraph 40, that designation is effective. According to this, it is proper for each person to say during the day: I hereby prepare all that is in the courtyard that is suitable for wiping.

If rain falls on stones and they become embedded in the ground: if they are covered by earth, it is forbidden to dig them out, as this involves digging in the ground. However, if their outline is recognizable on the surface as stones, it is permitted to take them in order to wipe oneself, and there is no prohibition of digging, demolishing, or grinding, as would be the case for someone who separates clods of earth and is liable for grinding. Here, since the stones are distinguishable on their own, they are not considered connected to the ground. A pebble with grass growing on it may be used to wipe oneself, and we do not worry that the grass might be uprooted, as this is not a certainty (pesik reisha). Therefore, even if it happens that the grass is uprooted, it is considered an unintended consequence and there is no prohibition. Even if the pebble is lying on the ground, which according to the law in Siman 336 is forbidden to lift from the ground as it is similar to uprooting, nevertheless, since this is only rabbinically prohibited, as mentioned there, it is not forbidden in a situation of human dignity (Magen Avraham, section 3). It is obvious that this applies when there is no other object available for wiping (and from this it is evident that the Magen Avraham holds like the last opinion of the Rema that we explained in section 5; examine this well).

One should not move a clod of earth to wipe with it, because it is not suitable for wiping, as it crumbles. And it is forbidden to wipe with a shard of pottery, even on a weekday, due to the danger that it might break the teeth of the rectum. However, if on Shabbat there are before him a pebble and smooth pottery shards, since they are smooth, there is no danger - one may wipe with the pottery shard, as it is appropriate to cover the mouth of vessels. And although one should be concerned about sorcery with pottery, as mentioned earlier in Siman 3, nevertheless, for the purposes of Shabbat, it is preferable to a pebble which is suitable for nothing. If there is before him a pebble and grasses - he should wipe with the grasses if they are moist, but if they are dry - one should not wipe with them, because they are sharp and cut the flesh, and also because they are something that fire dominates, which the Gemara was particular about, as mentioned (see Magen Avraham section 5 and Taz).

One may wipe on Shabbat with moist grasses, even if they are still attached, as long as they are long enough to wipe with them while they remain attached, provided he does not move them, meaning he does not pull them from the ground due to the prohibition of uprooting (Tosefta Shabbat). However, there is no prohibition of muktzeh in them while they are attached, for if they were muktzeh, how could it be permitted to wipe with them? Muktzeh is forbidden to move even partially, as stated in Siman 311 (ibid., and the words of the Magen Avraham in subsection 6, who wrote regarding muktzeh, are puzzling). And you should know that this is indeed the case, for it is forbidden to climb a tree lest one climb and detach something, and not because of muktzeh. After detachment on Shabbat, it becomes muktzeh, but not while it is still attached. And there is no issue of using something attached, for this applies only to a tree and not to vegetables, as will be explained in Siman 336, with God's help.

And if he needs to relieve himself and cannot do so, and his remedy is to stimulate the anus by using a pebble, which when manipulated in the anus causes it to open, he should not handle it on Shabbat as he does on weekdays, i.e., by holding the pebble with his entire hand because this may cause hair to be removed from that area. And even though with a shard we do not worry about this, it is because when wiping it is not a certain (inevitable) outcome, unlike with a pebble in manipulation. Rather, he should handle it in an unusual manner, i.e., by holding the pebble with two fingers and manipulating it. And manipulating with a piece of cloth called "kerishtir" in the anus has the same rule as a pebble, that it should only be held with two fingers. And it is forbidden to go out into the public domain with a "kerishtir," even if it is entirely inserted into the body, because since it is constantly being inserted and removed, it is considered a burden, like carrying it in one's mouth, which is its usual manner of carrying, and even in a karmelit it is forbidden.

It is forbidden to relieve oneself in a plowed field on Shabbat, meaning a field that has been plowed and is ready for sowing, because we are concerned that one might level depressions, as one might take a clod from a raised area and cast it into a depression (see Magen Avraham, subsection 9). This applies to one's own field, as in another person's field it is forbidden even during the week, because one tramples the plowed field with his feet and damages the field. And large stones that are arranged in a hollow shape to form a seat and are used as a toilet in fields, as was the custom in their days, may be arranged on Shabbat. And even though it is considered a temporary structure, the Rabbis did not decree against it due to human dignity. Nevertheless, making a tent-like structure is forbidden (ibid.), and in Choshen Mishpat, section 274, it is explained based on Joshua's ordinance regarding the need for wiping, see there.

Building is one of the primary categories of labor. It is mentioned in the Jerusalem Talmud, in the chapter "Klal Gadol" (Chapter 7, end of Halacha 2): What construction was there in the Tabernacle? They would place the boards on the sockets. It raises a question: was it not temporary? Meaning, it wasn't fixed, as they would camp and travel, camp and travel. And it concludes: This tells us that temporary construction is considered construction, and construction from the side is considered construction. The commentators explained: Even though it is not complete construction. In my opinion, the explanation is as follows: Standard construction involves walls with a roof, and here we learn that even without a roof, it is considered construction, as the boards did not have a roof but rather coverings were spread over them. According to Rashi's opinion (125b), a tent is only considered such with a roof, and even according to those who disagree with him, it is only with a partition that permits, as will be explained at the beginning of Siman 315, and a tent is a subset of construction, as will be explained there. Therefore, the Jerusalem Talmud informs us that construction even from the side is considered construction. It further says there: This tells us even if placed upon something else. Meaning, do not say that construction is only when the building is attached to the ground, for here the sockets are attached to the ground, and the boards are placed on the sockets. And it further wanted to prove that construction on utensils is also considered construction, as it thought that the sockets were like utensils, but it was refuted because the sockets are like the ground and not like utensils. And in terms of the law, it seems to me that construction on utensils is considered complete construction, for even on utensils themselves, where we hold there is no construction on utensils, nevertheless complete construction is considered construction, as will be explained in Siman 314, and all the more so construction on utensils. However, incomplete construction is not considered construction, and see in Section 2.

The sages taught in the Mishnah (102b): "The builder, how much must he build to be liable?" The builder—any amount, meaning there is no specific measure. The reason is that if a homeowner has a small hole in his nice building and he is particular about it and seals it, likewise in the Tabernacle when a worm fell and made a small hole, he would drip molten lead into it and seal it (Gemara). Therefore, one who aligns the stone is liable, meaning he sets the stone and aligns it until it settles into the foundation of the building and sets it in the ground, even if he did not apply mortar—it is considered building any amount and is liable (Rashi). I am puzzled that I did not find this law in the Rambam, Chapter 10. It seems to me that the Rambam interpreted the Gemara differently from Rashi. There we say: Shmuel said: One who aligns the stone is liable. The Gemara questions this and concludes: There are three types of building—lower, middle, and upper. The lower requires alignment and dirt, the middle also requires mortar, and the upper just placing. Rashi explained that Shmuel's statement stands as it is, that aligning makes one liable, and what is meant by 'alignment and dirt' Rashi explained as the dirt around it to support it, which is alignment. But the Rambam interprets that Shmuel's statement is dismissed, and alignment alone does not make one liable until he places dirt over it and it is embedded in the dirt, which is a complete building and does not need to be mentioned. Therefore, he wrote in law 12: If one places the stone and another places the mortar—the one who places the mortar is liable (this refers to the middle), and in the upper tier, even if he placed the stone and laid it on the mortar—he is liable, etc., his words end (this refers to the upper). He also wrote that building on vessels is exempt. This is from the Jerusalem Talmud that we brought. And we have explained that it is not a complete building, and even though he wrote it simply, we must say so as explained, that it is no worse than the vessels themselves. (And also the Rambam, who wrote in Chapter 22, Law 26, that there is no building in vessels, holds in Chapter 10 that there is building in vessels, and the distinction is as explained between a complete building and an incomplete one, as the Maggid Mishneh wrote there in Law 13, and so wrote the Geonim, and so wrote the Tosafot at the beginning of 'The Builder', and examine this well). And see in paragraph 10.

Derivatives of Building: The Rambam writes there in Halacha 12 as follows: "One who builds any amount is liable. One who levels the ground in a house, such as by lowering a mound or filling a pit, is considered as building and is liable… Derivatives of building: One who makes a permanent tent, and similarly one who makes earthenware vessels such as an oven or a barrel before they are fired, is considered as engaging in a derivative of building and is liable. Similarly, one who curdles cheese is considered as engaging in a derivative of building, but he is not liable until he curdles an amount equivalent to a dried fig." End of quote. And some say that this is only from the Rabbis (Maggid Mishneh there). And what is the analogy of curdling to building? Because anyone who gathers parts together and bonds them all until they become one body, this is considered a derivative of building (Rambam, Chapter 7, Halacha 6).

And similarly, one who inserts the head of an axe into its handle—this is considered a derivative of building, and the same applies to anything similar. Likewise, one who drives a piece of wood into another piece of wood, whether with a nail or by forcefully inserting it until it becomes one unit—this is considered a derivative of building and is liable. Similarly, one who makes any hole in a chicken coop to allow light to enter is liable due to building. And even though we hold that any opening not made for both entry and exit is not considered an opening (Gemara 146b), nevertheless, in the case of a chicken coop, it is made to let in light and air and to let out foul odors (ibid.). Similarly, one who reattaches a door to a pit, a reservoir, or a balcony is liable due to building (Eruvin 102a), as is one who reattaches the door of a house. However, this does not apply to a wardrobe, a chest, or a tower, as will be explained in section 27.

In the Jerusalem Talmud, it is stated: One who forms a shape on a vessel, one who blows glass, and one who makes a vessel in a mold—all are liable for building. However, in our Talmud (75b), it is said: One who forms a shape on a vessel and one who blows glass are liable for striking the final blow, as it holds that the term "building" does not apply to this. And the law follows our Talmud; therefore, if one was warned about these two actions as building, he is not liable.

Demolition is considered a primary category of labor, but only when it is done with the intention to rebuild. However, demolition done destructively is merely damaging and one is exempt from liability. Demolition was present in the Tabernacle because, as it is the opposite of construction, once there was construction, there naturally had to be demolition. It is impossible not to have damaged some construction and then demolished it with the intention to rebuild it. Note that in the Gemara (Shabbat 31b) it is stated that according to Rabbi Yossi, demolition with the intention to rebuild in the same place is considered demolition, but if not in the same place, it is not considered demolition. The halacha does not follow Rabbi Yossi, hence Rambam did not mention this. There is a question on this from most of the poskim who hold according to Rabbi Shimon that a labor which is not needed for its own sake is exempt. Therefore, when extinguishing a fire with the intention to light it again, one is only liable if the extinguishing improves the lighting more than if there had been no extinguishing, such as extinguishing to make charcoal as mentioned in Siman 278. If so, in demolishing with the intention to rebuild, one should only be liable if the demolition improves the building more than if there had been no demolition, which is inconceivable. According to Rambam, this is fine, as he ruled according to Rabbi Yehuda that a labor not needed for its own sake is liable, as mentioned in the first chapter. The answer to this is that since all labors are derived from the Tabernacle, and in extinguishing, we find that there was an improvement through extinguishing, as they needed to make charcoal to melt gold and silver, hence we also require this. But regarding demolition, even in the Tabernacle it was not possible to have such a scenario, hence we are liable in all cases (Tosafot, Shabbat 31b, s.v. 'and demolition'). The derivatives of demolition are simple; all derivatives of construction in their demolition are derivatives of demolition, and if they are done with the intention to rebuild, one is liable (and the same applies to untying and tearing).

The final hammer blow signifies the completion of any work, as a craftsman strikes with a hammer on the sheet to smooth it out upon finishing the work (Rashi, 73a). And anything that involves the completion of work incurs liability under the category of the final hammer blow (74a), and these are considered derivatives of the final hammer blow. It is stated in the Jerusalem Talmud, chapter "Klal Gadol" (beginning of Halacha 2), that any work for which the sages could not find a basis in any primary category of work, they ascribed to the final hammer blow, as it says there.

This is the language of the Rambam there: "One who strikes with a hammer even a single blow is liable, and anyone who performs an action that completes a task - this is considered a derivative of 'striking with a hammer' and is liable. How so: one who blows glass vessels, shapes a vessel even partially, scrapes even the slightest amount, or makes any kind of hole whether in wood, metal, construction, or utensils - this is a derivative of 'striking with a hammer' and is liable. Any opening that is not made for both inserting and removing is not liable for its creation." End quote. Now, regarding what he wrote: 'scrapes even the slightest amount', this is a Baraita there (103b), and Rashi explained: "one who scrapes wooden beams or hides - is liable for smoothing." End quote. The Rambam interprets it as being liable for 'striking with a hammer'. We must say that he explains 'scrapes' as referring to the final stage of the task where one scrapes the utensil to clean it. Additionally, regarding what he wrote that making a hole is liable for 'striking with a hammer', I am puzzled because he himself ruled in the case of making a hole in a chicken coop that one is liable for building, as stated in section 4, and the Gemara there (102b and 103b) compares these cases. Furthermore, according to the opinion in the Gemara that holds making a hole is due to 'striking with a hammer', the Gemara there establishes that it refers to when one strikes with an iron rod and leaves it inside, which is considered completing the task. Why did he not explain this, and this requires further study.

Additionally, it is written: "One who presses a boil on Shabbat to widen the mouth of the wound in the manner that doctors do - is liable for striking with a hammer, as this is the craft of the doctor. However, if he presses it to extract the pus within it - this is permitted." End of quote. Rashi explains this liability as being due to building, but Rambam does not agree, as this is not considered building, but rather the completion of the doctor's work. However, when it is opened for the pus, it is done many times and is not considered the completion of a task. (And the Maggid Mishneh wrote that although there are those who interpret it at the beginning of the chapter of "Eight Creeping Things" according to Rabbi Shimon, and he [Rambam] decided according to Rabbi Yehuda, he [Rambam] does not hold by that interpretation but rather by the initial interpretation that pertains to hunting, see there. The reason seems to me to be because Shmuel said at the beginning of Shabbat regarding these three cases that one is exempt and it is permitted, and a boil is one of them, and Shmuel indeed holds according to Rabbi Yehuda regarding a labor not needed for its own sake, as we say in the chapter of "Kirah" 42. See there.)

Another wrote: "One who chisels a stone even slightly is liable for striking with a hammer. One who positions a stone in the foundation of a building, adjusts it by hand, and places it in its proper location is liable for striking with a hammer." And it appears that this aligns with what Shmuel said at the beginning of the chapter "The Builder": 'One who positions a stone is liable,' and it concludes that this refers to the bottom stone of the foundation that we mentioned in section 2. And I am puzzled as to how it can be explained as striking with a hammer, for the Talmud considers them together: upper, middle, and lower, the first two are from the prohibition of building as Maimonides himself said, and we brought his words there, and he omitted the bottom one. And for this reason, we wanted to say there that it was dismissed from the law. And how can it be said that this is because of striking with a hammer? Furthermore, striking with a hammer is the final act of labor, and positioning is the beginning of construction. It is understandable that chiseling is not yet involved in building, but rather chisels stones from the mountain. But positioning it in the building, what relevance does it have to the final act of labor? And even if we say that the foundation of the building is considered by itself, surely even in the foundation many stones are needed, and in one stone there is no final act of labor, and it remains difficult. (And the Kesef Mishneh in the name of the Ramach questioned him as to why he did not explain that he should place earth in front of it as it is stated in the Gemara there. Therefore, it seems clear to me that Maimonides did not intend this at all, and here we need to say as I wrote in section 2 that it was dismissed from the law. And here it refers to what is stated in the Jerusalem Talmud, chapter "General Principle," at the end of law 2: 'The builder who sets the stone at the top of the structure is liable,' and the Pnei Moshe explained: at the top of the structure to complete it. And it appears that he is referring to the top corner stone, which is the completion. And take note.)

Another point he wrote: "One who removes burrs from clothing, such as those burrs on woolen garments, is liable for 'striking with a hammer' (a form of finishing work), provided he is particular about them. However, if he removes them incidentally, he is exempt. One who shakes a new black garment to beautify it and to remove the white wool that clings to it, as artisans do, is liable for a sin-offering. But if he is not particular, it is permitted," end quote. We have already brought this in Siman 312, and it is explained there, see there. One who opens a neck hole in a garment on Shabbat is liable for 'striking with a hammer' (48a according to Rashi, see there), and similarly, one who completes the work of ovens. After they have been fired in the kiln, he applies a coating, which is the final act of work, and is liable for 'striking with a hammer' (74b). Similarly, one who makes a reed basket and cuts the protruding reeds after finishing it is liable for 'striking with a hammer,' as this is the completion of its work (there). There are also other items we considered in Siman 312 that involve 'striking with a hammer'.

And know that regarding the primary explanation of "striking with a hammer" in the Mishnah of the primary labors, Rashi explained, and these are his words: "It is the completion of any labor, as a craftsman strikes with a hammer on the anvil to smooth it at the completion of the work," end quote. And at the beginning of "the builder," Rashi explained, and these are his words: "That he strikes the stone from the rock after he has quarried the stone around it and separates it a bit from the mountain, he strikes it with a big hammer blow and it breaks off and falls, and this is the completion of the labor of stonecutters. And anyone who completes a labor on Shabbat - this is the derivative of 'striking with a hammer'," end quote. And this is the essence of "striking with a hammer." However, in the Mishnah of the primary labors, he changed his explanation, because in the Tabernacle there was no work with stones, and we need to find each labor in the Tabernacle. Therefore, he explained: as a craftsman strikes with a hammer, etc., and this was in the Tabernacle (Tosafot Yom Tov).

From the language of Rashi, it is somewhat implied that for any type of labor completed on Shabbat, one would be liable for "striking with a hammer." According to his interpretation, it must be said that what they stated in some places that one is liable for striking with a hammer is difficult to understand—what is the novelty? However, the novelty is that even if the completion is something that does not involve labor at all, such as removing lint from a garment and the like. Similarly, it is explained from the language of the Ran, who brought the explanation of Rabbeinu Chananel, and this is his language: "Striking with a hammer - the craftsman strikes with a hammer on the vessel to straighten its curvature... and in the same manner, even though it is not a labor in and of itself, one is liable for it because it completes the work." End quote.

But if so, it is not understood what the Gemara says (75b): "Rabbah and Rav Zeira both say: Anything that has a completion of work is liable due to striking with a hammer." This is difficult, for in every craft there is a completion of work, so what does it mean "anything, etc.," which implies that there are crafts without a completion of work? And if we say that the intention is even though there is no work at all in this, but in truth there is striking with a hammer in all crafts, if so, it should not have said it in this language. Rather, it should have said: "Every completion of work is liable due to striking with a hammer, even in something that has no work in it." But from the language "anything, etc." it clearly implies there are crafts that have a completion of work and there are those that do not.

In truth, it seems to my humble opinion that this is indeed the case, and its explanation is as follows: Any labor that does not have a separate action at its completion from what preceded it - does not involve a completion of labor, for all the work is one, and the completion is not separate from what came before. However, in labors where the completion occurs after the main work is finished, such as a tailor who removes threads from a garment or one who removes a stone from a mountain, who, after completing his work, strikes it with a great blow, or strikes with a hammer on an anvil to smooth it, or collects burs from the clothes after weaving, or removes the white wool to beautify it - this is called striking with a hammer (makeh b'patish).

And I have a clear proof for this from the explanation of the Mishnah by the Rambam, who writes: "And striking with a hammer... Therefore, any final improvement and completion of work, like polishing and smoothing and beautification - all are derivatives of striking with a hammer, and they said: 'Anything that involves the completion of work - one is liable for striking with a hammer.'"

And this is as we have stated. (Regarding the main act of striking with a hammer, he wrote: "And striking with a hammer even at the time of completing the work, as those who strike with hammers do, for their custom is to strike blows on the anvil at the time of the strike." This requires further examination of the language 'even etc.', for it only involves the completion of work, and it can be resolved. Pay close attention.)

One who makes a permanent tent is liable for building. Therefore, one should not make a temporary tent initially, nor should one dismantle a temporary tent, lest one come to make or dismantle a permanent tent. However, if one made or dismantled a temporary tent, one is exempt. It is permitted to add to a temporary tent on Shabbat (Rambam, Chapter 22, Halacha 27). Therefore, a window shutter, which is a board or any other object used to close a window, can be used to close it even if it is not tied to the window, for it appears as a separate item. This is not considered a temporary tent, which is prohibited to make initially, but rather is considered an addition to a temporary tent and is permitted. Even with a chimney on the roof, it is permitted for the same reason (Magen Avraham, subsection 1).

To explain: we do not say that this is like an addition to a building and no less than a temporary tent, for this is not the case. This is not considered an addition but rather is similar to adding to a temporary tent, which is permitted. If it had already been closed, there would be no novelty in this; however, even if it had not yet been closed, one can close it if one had intended to do so before Shabbat, like all things where intention is effective, as stated in Siman 318, Section 40.

And in some cases, thought alone does not suffice. Even though for the preparation of muktzeh, thought is enough, in this case, since it involves the prohibition of building, thought alone does not suffice unless some action is taken. For example, a reed that is prepared to be used for locking, meaning it is inserted by the door in the wall. This appears more like building than a window shutter, which is not against the ground, whereas the reed is against the ground. Therefore, an action is required during the day before, and it is not sufficient to merely think about it the day before. It needs to be prepared for this purpose. 

There is also a dispute regarding this. According to Rashi (Shabbat 126b), it is not enough to prepare it for this specific use of locking the house, but it must also be suitable for another use so that it has the status of a utensil and is not considered as adding to the building. For example, a reed that is suitable for turning olives or similar uses. According to Rabbeinu Tam, it is sufficient if it is prepared for this specific use of locking the house. In the words of the Rambam, there is no clear decision, as he wrote that it needs to have the status of a utensil, as stated in the Gemara. However, if it was used the day before for locking the house, that is sufficient, as once it has been used, it has the status of a utensil (Ran there).

For this reason, some say that even for a window shutter, thought alone is not enough and some physical preparation is required. However, since a window shutter is usually used the day before, and a reed is not usually used (there), the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch did not mention this opinion at all. 

Regarding the dispute between Rashi and Rabbeinu Tam, it seems that since it is a rabbinic matter, one can rely on the opinion of Rabbeinu Tam to be lenient, meaning it does not need to be suitable for another use. As long as it was prepared and some action was taken to designate it for this use, that is sufficient. According to this, this would be considered a utensil whose primary use is permissible, since locking the door is allowed on Shabbat. But according to Rashi's opinion, that it needs to be suitable for another use, if that other use is something prohibited on Shabbat, such as a reed for turning olives, it would be considered a utensil primarily used for a prohibited purpose. However, it is allowed to lock with it as with a utensil primarily used for a prohibited purpose, which is allowed for its function or space as stated in Siman 308.

And behold, even though we were stringent with a reed, in any case, we only required that it have the status of a utensil, but we did not require that it be tied to the door. There is something that we do require to be specifically tied to the door from before the onset of Shabbat, but otherwise, even if one intended and also performed an action with it before Shabbat and designated it for this use, or even for another use—it does not help, because this item enters into the threshold and appears more as part of the building. Therefore, a bolt, which is a peg used to lock the door by inserting it into the threshold below, and resembles more a part of the building—it is not sufficient in this case, and one may not lock with it unless it is tied from before the onset of Shabbat.

And how should the tying be done? If there is a knob at the end, meaning that it is thick at one end and suitable for crushing with, which resembles a utensil, we are lenient with it such that even if it is tied with a thin rope that is not suitable for carrying with, if one were to lift it with the rope, it would break—nevertheless, it is still recognizable. And even if it is not tied to the door itself but to the door bolt, and even if the rope is long and not suspended in the air at all, making it appear as though it is a tool associated with locking the door but is dragged on the ground, and even if it is entirely placed on the ground. And without any tying at all—the knob does not help, even though it resembles a utensil, since it is embedded in the ground, it resembles a building.

And if there is no "galostera" (a knob or handle) on it: If it is tied to the door itself, it is sufficient even with a thin rope that is not suitable for carrying, and even if it is entirely lying on the ground. But if it is not tied to the door but to the bolt of the door, the knot must be strong enough to be suitable for carrying. Even so, it does not need to be hanging, but even if it is entirely lying on the ground it is permitted, for the prohibition only applies when one pulls it off and places it in a corner. It appears to me that if it is hanging, it is permitted even with a thin rope, because there is certainly more recognition in it being hung with a thin rope than in it lying on the ground with a strong rope.

The Tur and Shulchan Aruch, in section 2, write that all the bolts we mentioned refer to when the threshold is high, and when the bolt is inserted into the threshold, it does not pierce the ground. However, if the threshold is damaged in such a way that when the bolt is inserted, it pierces the ground beneath it, this is considered building and it is forbidden to lock with it. And if a handle is made for it and it resembles a hammer, it is evident that it is a utensil and is permitted. Note that this does not refer to a case where it was originally made to pierce the ground, for if it was originally made with a hollow in the ground to insert the bolt, as it is customary with us in small houses, it is certainly permitted, like a bolt inserted into the threshold, as the threshold is also attached to the ground. The prohibition only applies when it was originally made to be inserted into the threshold, without any hollow made in the ground, and now the threshold is damaged, so that the insertion is into the ground, piercing it—this is certainly like building. This is the intention of the Taz in section 2. And it seems to me that in such cases, it is forbidden even with a handle. However, in any case, with us, since the bolts are attached to the door with nails and move up and down by means of a hinge and are inserted on Shabbat into the same place they were inserted on weekdays, it is permitted to raise and lower them on Shabbat, and this is the common custom. All the more so with bolts in windows, there is no doubt about this at all.

And know that at the end of Tractate Shabbat (157a), it is said: an incident occurred where they plugged a window on Shabbat to prevent impurity from entering the house, as there was a corpse in the other house. And there are those who say that this permission is only to seal it before the person dies, but after death, since it provides the benefit of preventing impurity from entering, it would be considered as fixing (Magen Avraham 1:1 in the name of Rabbi Yehuda Halevi). And there are those who disagree, as the vessels that were already there have become impure, and the benefit is only for the vessels that will come afterward, and this is not fixing but indirectly saving from impurity (ibid.). And indeed, Rashi explained there that they plugged it before the person died, because afterward, there would be no benefit for the vessels in the house, as the impurity would immediately enter (ibid.).

There are matters for which neither thought nor action nor tying is effective, unless they are elevated from the ground; otherwise, it is as if one is adding to the building. This is what we have learned in Eruvin (101a): "A door that is in a storage area, thorn bushes that are used to fill a breach, and mats - one may not lock with them unless they are elevated from the ground." This means that certainly, a door made for regular entrance and exit can be locked with, even if it never had a hinge and drags on the ground. But a door in a storage area, which is the back of the houses and is not regularly used, and the homeowner does not care to make a proper door and to fix it in place, but rather props it against the entrance and when opening it, places it on the ground; and there are those that are hung but drag on the ground (Rashi). Similarly, thorn bushes used to fill a breach, which means thorn bushes bundled together and prepared to close a breach, and sometimes it is opened, and a mat of reeds (there) used to close a breach and sometimes opened. Since all these are not regular openings and do not appear in the form of a regular doorway, therefore, one may not lock with them on Shabbat, because it is considered as building. Even if one thought and took action, tying it, but it drags on the ground when lifted over the lintel, it appears as building (there). The Gemara explains there that this applies when they do not have a hinge, which is something the door is inserted into and the door revolves around, called by us as "krokaas." If they have a hinge, it is evident to all that it is a door, and tying and hanging it is sufficient even if it drags on the ground. Moreover, even if they do not currently have a hinge but previously had a hinge, it is also permitted, because even though the hinge is lost, there is still some indication that it is a door. However, the requirement for them to be hanging is when they never had a hinge, and the reason we are stricter with them compared to a bolt, is that a bolt is a minor issue, as is a reed or a window plug. But these doors, which are large in size and significantly appear as a building, therefore, we are stricter with them until they are elevated from the ground. They are not comparable to other doorways regularly used, but these are not regularly used, and when they are closed, it is for a long time, making them appear as a building due to their large size.

And behold, according to what has been clarified, a recognizable hinge is preferable to all of them. Nevertheless, there is a type of door for which even a recognizable hinge does not help, and this is what they said there: 'A widow's door that drags - one may not lock it.' And what is a widow's door? It is a door made of a single board that has no pair, or even if it is made of several planks but does not have a lower threshold, and when they open it, they remove it and place it on the ground - and it does not help even if it has a hinge. Because it does not have the form of a door like other doors and they also remove it and place it on the ground, it clearly appears as a building, and it is worse than all the things that have been clarified, due to its large size and the fact that they remove it and place it on the ground. It is more stringent than everything that has been clarified (see Taz 4 and Magen Avraham 8 who labored on the reasoning, and according to what I have written, it fits well; pay attention and understand).

However, a door made of many planks is permitted even though they remove it when they open it if it has a threshold. The same applies in a place where they lock with many planks and there is a carving above and below where they insert the planks - their status is like a door since they are not a single board like the entire door. And there are those who permit even a single board if it is made for regular entry and exit (Bach and Magen Avraham 8), and one can rely on this, for according to the Rambam it is more lenient as will be clarified.

According to what has been explained, a door made of a single plank does not suffice, even if it has a lower threshold. And if it does not have a threshold, it does not suffice even if it is made of several planks. However, according to Maimonides in Chapter 26, Law 9, the prohibition applies only if it is made of a single plank and does not have a threshold. But if it has one of these, it is sufficient. And this is the language of Maimonides: "A door that is made of a single plank, which they remove and lock with: if it does not have below it something like a threshold that indicates it is a vessel prepared for locking - one may not lock with it. But if it has a threshold - one may lock with it," end quote.

It further becomes clear to me from the words of Maimonides, contrary to the words of the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch, who believed that all these laws are prohibited due to the reason of building, which is the opinion of Rashi. But from Maimonides, it appears explicitly that only the shutter of the window is prohibited due to the addition of building, and he wrote this in Chapter 22, where he deals with this. However, the rod and bolt and these doors that were explained are not prohibited due to building, since everyone sees that they are made for the opening, but the prohibitions are due to muktzeh, for without preparation, each one according to its measure is muktzeh. Therefore, he wrote them in Chapter 26, where the entire chapter deals with the laws of muktzeh. The matter is that although with any muktzeh item, thought is effective, as it is written in Siman 305, Section 40 - this is for general uses. But for uses attached to the ground, we require a status of a vessel for each one according to its matter. Additionally, it seems to me from the precision of his language that all these things are when one comes to use them now for the first time, but if they have already been used for doors, then they are not muktzeh and are prepared and ready. This is not the case according to the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch, which follow the opinion of Rashi, where there is no distinction. Therefore, there is a significant practical difference in the law, and the poskim did not write anything about this, and it requires further study, for thus it seems to me clearly from the words of Maimonides and his arrangement.

It has already been explained in Siman 308 that the doors of a house and those of a pit or a cistern, and all that is attached to the ground, are prohibited to be either removed from their hinges or replaced on their hinges, due to the prohibition of building and tearing down. However, the doors of utensils, such as those of a chest, box, and tower, are permitted to be removed, because there is no building in utensils and no tearing down in utensils. But to replace them is forbidden, because we decree that one might come to fix them firmly, and that would be considered complete building, and in complete building, there is also building even in utensils. And it is explained there that the window openings of houses and the doors are prohibited both to remove and to replace, and there are some common people who are not aware of this prohibition, and they must be informed. Even through a non-Jew it is prohibited, for in building that is attached to the ground, it is a complete prohibition, and instructing a non-Jew is a rabbinic prohibition (Taz, subparagraph 5).

And behold, a standard chest, box, or tower has its openings at the top, and thus there is no difference between the upper hinge and the lower hinge. However, those that have openings from the side, like the doors of a house, and have two hinges, one at the top and one at the bottom, the main support is on the upper hinge, for if the upper hinge is removed, the door will necessarily fall, but if the lower hinge is removed, it will still stand on the upper hinge alone. And since it has been clarified that returning it is forbidden due to the concern that one might drive it in firmly, therefore, if even the entire lower hinge comes out of its place, it is forbidden to return it due to the concern that one might drive it in firmly. But if part of it comes out, one may press it back until it is returned to its place. Since the upper hinge remains in place, it is easy to return the lower hinge. However, if part of the upper hinge comes out, it is forbidden to press it and return it to its place, for since it is the main support, we are concerned even for part of it that one might drive it in firmly. And similarly, when the hinge is in the middle, it is forbidden, as a decree for the middle hinge because of the side hinge. And even though on Yom Tov we do not make this decree, as it is written in Siman Taktin, this is because of the joy of Yom Tov as explained there, but on Shabbat we do make this decree.

And behold, this is all regarding their hinges which were made of wood, and the hinges were part of the wood of the doors, with one protrusion at the top at the upper edge and a second protrusion at the bottom at the lower edge. Corresponding to them was a hole at the top in the lintel into which the upper protrusion was inserted, and a hole in the threshold corresponding to the lower hinge into which the lower protrusion was inserted. However, our hinges, which are made of iron, and the irons are attached with nails to the doors, and corresponding to them are thick irons called "kroka'as" which are made hollow, and the irons are inserted into them. And similarly, in utensils, there are also small ones of this kind, and all are made of iron - and in this case, it seems that there is no concern that it might become stuck, since the hole is wide and hard and pressing on it will not help at all, and this will be explained, with God's help, in Siman 314, Seif 17.

A bed made of sections, meaning it is constructed in pieces, and travelers carry it with them. When they come to rest, they set it up and connect all the sections at their joints, placing each joint into its corresponding section until it is extended and suitable for lying down. It is forbidden to set it up and tighten it because this resembles building, and in tightening it there is a form of the prohibited act of striking with a hammer. If one tightens it strongly, they are liable to bring a sin offering. It appears that the tightening alone is only a rabbinic prohibition, but if one secures it with pegs, they are liable to bring a sin offering (as the Ran wrote at the end of the third chapter). If it is customary for it to be loose, and they are not particular if it is not tightened strongly and it is somewhat close to shaking, it is permitted (see Magen Avraham, subsection 11. In my opinion, the Raavad and the Sefer Mitzvot Gadol do not disagree, and their intention is as I have written, and consider this carefully). This law does not apply to our iron beds, which are unfolded at night and folded in the morning, for this is entirely permitted since they are always complete, and we do not dismantle each section separately. It is no different from a door made of multiple pieces and constructed on joints; when it is opened, it folds, and when it is closed, it extends. The same is true here, and this is the custom of the world, and no one is concerned about it.

And a cup made of segments—it is permissible to disassemble it and reassemble it on Shabbat, since it is not typically tightened very much (Tur). Accordingly, if it is made of sections and they are tightened—certainly it is forbidden (Magen Avraham, section 12). Some say that the law for the cup is like that of a bed; if it is typically tightened, even though it is currently loose—it is forbidden, unless it is typically loose. The same law applies to a shtender in the synagogue if it is made of sections, and similarly to all utensils. However, utensils for eating that are made of segments, like we have spoons, forks, and knives that are a single utensil but during eating are disassembled and then reassembled, and similarly drinking utensils—in such cases, it is permitted to disassemble and reassemble them, because only a cup and similar items that do not need to be disassembled at all times and are considered as made to last, are subject to the prohibition of building and demolishing. This is not the case with eating and drinking utensils, which are typically used this way—they do not fall under the category of building at all and it is considered like a key (this is explicitly stated in Taz, section 7 and Magen Avraham, section 12).

A beam that has broken may be supported with the long boards of a bed, which are considered utensils, and similar items. However, if it is not a utensil but merely a piece of wood, even if it was prepared for this purpose before Shabbat and is not considered muktzeh (set aside), nevertheless, one should not support it with such an item, as it appears like building (Magen Avraham, section 14). Nonetheless, if it was supported in this manner before Shabbat and it fell on Shabbat, it seems to me that it is permitted to replace it. When supporting with the long boards of a bed, one should not support it so firmly that the beam rises slightly, for that certainly appears like building. The support should only be such that it prevents further falling. Additionally, the support should be somewhat loose so that it can be removed from there, for if not, it is forbidden due to rendering a utensil unusable, and therefore, one should be careful not to tighten it there. It has already been explained in section 308 that if a bench breaks and one of its legs is displaced, it is forbidden to return it to its place. To place the displaced side on another bench, there are those who are stringent and forbid it, but if it is broken, it is permitted, as stated there in paragraph 37.

A courtyard that was damaged by rainwater - one may scatter straw in it, and it is not considered as adding to the building, because his intention is not to leave it on the ground but to later take it for animal feed or for mortar. However, if his intention is truly to leave it on the ground, it is a complete prohibition, as it is considered adding to the building on the ground, and even leveling pits is a Torah prohibition, and all the more so in such cases. Even when his intention is to take it from there, he should not do it in the usual manner he does on a weekday, but rather make a change, meaning he should not scatter it with a basket or a container but with the bottom of the container by turning it over and bringing the straw on its bottom, that is through a change. However, with the hand – it is forbidden, and through a non-Jew – it is permitted (Taz, section 10), and it is good to refrain from this on Shabbat, and among us, it is not the norm at all to do so even on weekdays. And to cover spit or excrement – it is permitted with straw that is not muktzeh. And we have already explained in the name of the Rambam that one who drives a nail into wood, whether a nail or the wood itself until it becomes one – this is a derivative of building and is liable for a sin offering, and similarly one who drives the wood into the axe and dismantles it from the axe is considered demolishing, and see Section 4.

This statement from the Gemara (beginning of the chapter "Kol HaKeilim"): "There is no building with vessels, and there is no demolition with vessels," is not to be taken literally. If it were, there would be no Torah prohibition against making a vessel on Shabbat. Rather, they said this only in regard to the stringencies that the sages imposed in this matter, like in the case where it refers to the taking off and putting back of doors. Similarly, in Eruvin (35a), they said this concerning the Mishnah where the key to the tower was lost and the eruv was inside, allowing one to break it and take the eruv, as it is taught: "A person may break a barrel to eat dried figs from it," because this is a way of destruction. This will be further explained. Likewise, in the first chapter of Beitzah (10a), they said this in regard to removing the shutters, and later there (22a) concerning setting up a lamp, as mentioned there. All these matters do not involve a Torah prohibition of building at all, but the Rabbis prohibited them as a safeguard against building and demolishing. In this context, they said: "There is no building and no demolition with vessels," and beyond this, we do not find such a statement.

And so it is explained from the words of the Rambam, that in Chapter 10, where he counts the primary categories of work and mentions building, he does not differentiate between utensils and buildings. On the contrary, he writes there in Law 13: "And similarly, one who makes an earthenware vessel - this is a derivative of building and is liable, and similarly one who curdles cheese... one who inserts the handle of an axe... and one who drives a peg into wood... - this is a derivative of building and is liable." Thus, one is liable for utensils just as for buildings, and even for curdling cheese, according to his view, one is liable for a sin-offering. And where did he mention this? In Chapter 22, for from Chapter 21 onward, he deals with rabbinic prohibitions, as he began there by saying: 'It is said in the Torah "you shall rest",' see there. And he writes there in Law 25: "One who drives a peg is liable because of building; therefore, all doors attached to the ground are neither taken off nor put back, as a decree lest one drives a peg. But the door of a closet, a chest, and a tower can be taken off... but the parts of a lamp cannot be reassembled... because it appears like building, and if he reassembled it - he is exempt, because there is no building with utensils and no demolition with utensils." Thus, he wrote this only regarding something that appears like building, but with actual building - the law for utensils is the same as for a building attached to the ground.

And so wrote our Rabbis, the authors of the Tosafot, in Eruvin (34b, s.v. 'v'amai hu'): "Additionally, one who uses a tool is also subject to the laws of building and dismantling, as stated in the tractate Bava Batra: 'One who inserts a handle into a hoe is liable for [the prohibition of] building.' And regarding what is said nearby that one Master holds it is a tool and there is no building with tools, this refers specifically to those cases where it is said one may take apart but not put back, as this is not considered complete building or dismantling, or as explained in the conclusion with a lock and key tied with a string, and only in such a case is it permitted. But to break a tool and damage it is prohibited, as it indeed falls under the category of building and dismantling with tools. And regarding the permission to break a barrel, it is explained in Beitza (33b) with 'mustaki,' meaning pieces joined together, etc." End quote. Thus, it is explicitly as we have stated. And behold, this is the general principle of the matter, but the details of what is permitted with tools and what is not will be clarified in this section with the help of God.

And know that there is a contradiction in the matter of constructing utensils in the Rambam. For in Chapter 10, Law 14, he wrote: "One who makes any sort of hole in a chicken coop so that light can enter is liable for building," end quote.
