But at the beginning of Chapter 23, he wrote: "One who makes a hole that is meant for both entry and exit, such as a hole in a chicken coop that is meant to bring in light and expel vapor, this person is liable for the final hammer blow. Therefore, they decreed against any hole, etc.," end quote. There are those who say that he is liable for both: for building and for the final hammer blow (Lechem Mishneh on Chapter 10). According to this, he should have written both in one place. And there are those who answered that in Chapter 23, it is discussing a coop that is not attached to the ground, where there is no issue of building (Magen Avraham, Section 3). This too is not correct, for in any case, why in Chapter 10 is he not liable for the final hammer blow, and furthermore, it has already been clarified that in building according to Torah law, there is no difference between building on the ground or with utensils. 

I do not understand why the great ones have labored over this, for the Rambam explains his words well. In Chapter 10, he wrote "any sort of hole" because it is for the light, and for light, even a small hole suffices, even for a person, as explained in Bava Batra (59a), see there. This is the dispute between Rav and Shmuel at the beginning of Chapter HaBoneh, and he ruled according to Rav. In Chapter 23, it is discussing a large hole since it is also for expelling vapor, and a small hole is not sufficient. This is the final act in the coop, and there is no issue of building, for the building is already completed, and the liability is only for the final hammer blow. The source of this law is from elsewhere, in Chapter HaChavit (Shabbat 146a): "Rabbah said: By Torah law, any opening that is not made for both entry and exit is not an opening, and it is the Rabbis who decreed because of a chicken coop that is made to bring in air or light and to expel vapor, etc." This is the foundation of the entire Chapter 23, see there. (And I have seen that the Chayei Adam wrote similarly, see there).

The Sages taught in the Mishnah (146b): "A person may break a barrel to eat dried figs from it," and Rambam in Chapter 23, Law 2 wrote in the language of the Mishnah. It is explained that even with a whole barrel one can do this, because any act of destruction that is not intended for construction is not a Torah prohibition, as it is considered damaging and its prohibition is rabbinic. Therefore, they did not decree regarding utensils when one wants to eat the fruits, and in such cases, there is no destruction of utensils as mentioned. We only learned there: "Provided he does not intend to make a vessel," meaning that he should not meticulously create a neat hole, for if so, it would be like destroying with the intention to build, which is prohibited even with utensils as mentioned. This is also what Rambam wrote.

And there is a question about this: If so, regarding the Mishnah in Eruvin (34b) that if one placed the Eruv in a tower and locked it with a key, and the key was lost – it is still considered an Eruv. The Talmud goes to great lengths to find reasons for this, as one cannot access the Eruv. And now it is difficult, as one could break the tower and take the Eruv, just as one breaks a barrel to take the dried figs. Indeed, the Jerusalem Talmud there says about this Mishnah that it is referring to a stone tower which cannot be broken, but if it is a wooden tower, one breaks it and takes the Eruv, just as one breaks a barrel to eat the dried figs. Therefore, the Jerusalem Talmud goes to great lengths to find another reason for the permissibility, as does our Talmud. Also, our Talmud says there: "We are dealing with a brick tower, etc.," and therefore it goes to find another reason. And when it says: "Here we are dealing with a brick tower," it is not because initially it did not think this, but rather its explanation is: in a brick tower without mortar between them, as explained there (see Rashi, which resolves the Tosafot’s difficulty there). And some have explained that only with a barrel, which is not common, is it permitted because there is no demolition of vessels, but a tower which is large in quantity and resembles a building, they did not permit breaking it (Ran on the barrel there).

Indeed, our rabbis, the Tosafists, derived from this difficulty regarding a tower, that it does not refer to an intact barrel, for with an intact one it would certainly be forbidden to break it just as with a tower. And here it refers to a "musteki," meaning a broken barrel that has been glued with pitch, as the Talmud establishes in Beitzah (33b) according to Rabbi Eliezer who disagrees there about the tower, see there. And we say that even according to the Rabbis we need this establishment, and so wrote the Rosh. And this is the ruling of the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, section 1, and they brought no other opinion at all. And I do not know, since it is a matter of Rabbinic decree, why they did not bring the opinion of the Rambam and the Ran to be lenient, especially since the Jerusalem Talmud also agrees with this, and this is also the opinion of Rashi and the Ra'avad who wrote: "A person may break the barrel - because there is no prohibition in causing damage," end quote, meaning therefore they permitted it with a barrel so that one can eat (Ran). And since Rashi, the Rambam, the Ran, and the Ra'avad permit it, why did they not bring their opinion at all? This requires further investigation.

And this is the language of the Tur and Shulchan Aruch: "There is no [prohibition of] building or dismantling regarding vessels. And these words [apply] when it is not actual building, such as a barrel that does not hold forty se'ah and broke, and one glued its shards with pitch—one may break it to take what is inside it, provided that one does not intend to make a nice hole that would serve as an opening, for if so, it would be considered as fixing a vessel. But if it is whole—it is forbidden to break it even in a manner that does not make it a vessel, and even making a simple hole in it is forbidden. And even if it already has a hole, if one intends to widen it—it is forbidden, provided that one intends to do so."

And know that this [stipulation] of not holding forty se'ah was added by our teacher, the Rema. According to this, I am very puzzled by him, for since he distinguishes between a large vessel and a small one, permitting it in a small vessel and forbidding it in a large one, which is like the last answer in section 6, then it would follow that this is not similar to a tower, and the difficulty raised by our rabbis, the Tosafists, is resolved. If so, why did he not bring the opinion of those who permit breaking even a whole barrel?

And I have heard that there are those who practice breaking the head of a bottle containing wine or other beverages if they cannot open the seal. According to the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, this is forbidden. However, in my humble opinion, one should not reprimand them, because according to many of our rabbis, it is entirely permissible as I have written. And I have found that even the Rashba in Shabbat there disagrees with the Tosafot and concludes that even a whole barrel may be broken. According to this, it is obvious that those who do so have upon whom to rely, based on five pillars of the world, and so ruled one of the great later authorities (the Gra, section 2).

And this is what they wrote: if one intends to make a proper hole, it constitutes "making a vessel." Certainly, if the hole is large enough to allow for both insertion and extraction, it is a Torah prohibition. If it is small, it is prohibited by rabbinic decree (see Taz, subparagraph 1). This statement that even making a mere hole is prohibited is puzzling, as making a hole is certainly forbidden even to those who permit breaking (as noted by Rabbi Akiva Eiger). It must be said that their intention is regarding a hole made through breaking, where the usage is minimal, whereas with breaking, the usage is substantial. They do not mean making a hole properly. Their statement that even widening it is prohibited does not mean actually widening it, as it is obviously more forbidden than breaking. Rather, their intention is that one uses it, and through this it will naturally widen slightly. However, if one does not intend for this – it is permitted, as it is not a "certain outcome." Therefore, they wrote: "provided that he intends for it," meaning that in using it, he intends for it to widen, as with intention, it is forbidden (and this resolves the question of the Magen Avraham, subparagraph 4).

If a knife was stuck into a barrel before Shabbat, it is permitted to remove it and reinsert it even though this might slightly widen the hole. Since the knife was firmly stuck, removing and reinserting it causes the hole to widen. And since this is not a Torah prohibition, the Sages were lenient when the knife was inserted before Shabbat. However, some say this leniency applies only if the knife was also removed once before Shabbat, for then the second removal will not widen the hole as much. But if the knife was not removed even once before Shabbat, it is prohibited to remove and reinsert it on Shabbat, because it is a certainty (psik reisha) that the hole will definitely widen, and this is forbidden, as it creates a hole and an opening in the barrel. Some authorities say that in a great need, it is permissible even if the knife was not removed before Shabbat (Taz, sec. 2; Magen Avraham, sec. 5), and one can rely on this in a case of necessity. See also what I wrote in section 26.

If there was a hole in the barrel and it was sealed, if it is below the sediment – it is forbidden to open it, because since it is below and all the weight of the wine is on it, it was certainly sealed well and the sealing is considered as if there was never a hole at all, and if it is opened now it would be like making a new hole, and even if the spigot was here – it is forbidden. But if the hole was above the sediment and it was sealed – it is permitted to open it, because certainly this is not a good sealing and it is not like making a new hole. And it is permitted to open it even with a drill that is called a "kreiyeitzer," because in the place of an old hole one can drill even with a drill, such as in the place of the stopper when it is broken or in another place. Therefore, the common custom is to open the sealing of a glass bottle even with a drill when there are no letters on the sealing, because this is not like opening a hole, since it is above and its sealing is not a sealing, and it is not like a new hole in a barrel. Therefore, if the spigot of the barrel broke and it cannot be removed – one can drill it with a drill, and all the more so it is permitted to take another spigot and strike the stuck spigot until it comes out if one needs to drink the wine on Shabbat, provided that it is not opposite the sediment.

And there are those who disagree with everything that has been explained, and they hold that the permission granted by the Sages (146a) to open an old hole applies to a clay jug, where the sealing is not perfect. But for a wooden barrel, where the sealing is good and they tighten it a lot, if they sealed it with the intention that it should never be opened again—such as cutting off the top and leveling it with the barrel—it is considered as creating a new hole and is forbidden. However, in a case of necessity, one may rely on the first opinion. And know that even according to those who disagree, this has no relevance to opening a glass bottle, for here, even according to those who disagree, it is permitted, since they seal it with the intention of opening it.

It is permitted to place a hollow reed into a barrel to draw wine through it, even if it was never used for this purpose before. We are not concerned that it might not fit properly and that one might adjust it, since one is not allowed to make a utensil on Shabbat. Additionally, inserting the reed is not considered making a utensil, as the barrel is already prepared for this. However, it is forbidden to place a myrtle leaf or any other type of leaf on the barrel to use it as a spout for the wine to flow through, because if we permit this, one might think it is allowed to make a spout, as the leaf is being used like a spout. Although this is not truly making a utensil, since it is not permanent, we still decree against it so that one does not say: "Just as it is permitted to make a spout from a leaf, so it is permitted from other materials." But a hollow reed does not involve any craftsmanship, as it is simply inserted. Another reason given in the Gemara (there) for forbidding the leaf is the concern that one might pluck it from the tree. Some authorities hold that the primary reason for the prohibition is this concern, and therefore, if one has many prepared leaves, there is no concern of plucking, and it is permitted. This is the opinion of the Rosh and the Tur. If the leaf was placed on the barrel before Shabbat, it appears to be permitted.

It is permitted to chop off the head of a barrel with a sword, and even to chop off the body of the barrel along with the stopper is permitted when the barrel is broken and sealed with pitch (Magen Avraham, subsection 7), because he does not intend to open it, since he is removing its head. Consequently, according to the Rambam and his followers that we mentioned, it is also permitted with a whole barrel. And to chop off the top of the stopper is permitted even according to the Tur and Shulchan Aruch regarding a whole barrel, because the stopper is not considered part of the barrel. But to pierce it on the side, whether of the barrel or the stopper, is forbidden, because on the side, it is certainly intended for opening, and opening is forbidden even with the stopper, although it is not part of the barrel, because opening is forbidden in any case. And even with a spear that makes a large hole, it is forbidden from the side, even though it does not resemble an opening, because in the end, he intends to make an opening. But to pierce the stopper on the top is permitted, because he does not intend for an opening, as it is not customary to make an opening on the top of the stopper but rather to remove it entirely, and even with a whole barrel, it is permitted according to all opinions. The reason is: from the side, it is worthwhile for him, as the stopper is as in the beginning and will not have dust fall into it, but from the top, dust will fall into it, and it is better for him to remove the entire stopper, and therefore he does not intend for an opening. This is not the case with the barrel itself, where he intends for an opening even from the top, as it is better for him to have another opening in the barrel besides the stopper. And there is one who permits even at the top of the barrel (Taz, subsection 6) because dust will fall into it, but this is not the main reason, for he will make a stopper for it like for the original stopper, but from stopper to stopper there is no benefit (and also the Magen Avraham, subsection 8, and the Eliyah Rabbah, subsection 8, ruled similarly, see there).

Baskets or sacks that contain fruits and their openings are tied with ropes, not only is it permissible to untie the ropes, since this is not a permanent knot, as they were tied to be untied, but even if it is difficult to untie them, one can cut the rope with a knife or break the strands of the rope. This is not considered labor, as it is exactly like breaking the shells of nuts and almonds for the food inside them. This is not considered destructive work that is prohibited initially, as this is destructive labor, but here it is not labor. And so it is said in Shabbat (146a): 'Baskets of dried figs and dates - one may untie, unravel, and cut,' and similarly in Eruvin (35a, see Rashi and Tosafot s.v. 'asked'), and also in Beitzah (31a): 'Seals that are on the ground - one may untie the knot but not unravel or cut, as this is like dismantling a building. But seals that are on vessels - one may untie, unravel, and cut, as there is no dismantling of vessels in this manner. According to the Rambam, it is forbidden to break the strands of the rope, but he permits cutting it.

And this is the wording of our Rabbi, the Beit Yosef, in section 7: Seals on utensils, such as a chest, box, or tower, where their cover is tied to them with a rope - one can untie it, cut it with a knife, or undo its braid. And specifically something like the tying of a rope or similar, but wooden or metal locks - it is forbidden to break or shatter, for with utensils, complete construction and complete demolition are also relevant. And for this reason, it is forbidden to remove the hinges that are called "gonzish" and in our language "zawiyeses" that are behind the boxes if the key is lost, and some permit it in this case. And breaking the locks of boxes - some permit and some forbid, and it is permitted through a non-Jew. End of quote, and this requires explanation.

And the explanation of the matter is: It has already been clarified that complete construction and demolition apply also to utensils. Therefore, since a door is a complete utensil, breaking it constitutes complete demolition and is forbidden. Regarding the hinges of utensils, it has been explained in the previous section (paragraph 28) that the prohibition applies only to reattaching them due to the concern that one might drive them in forcefully. However, removing the door of a chest, box, or tower is not prohibited, and this is explicitly stated in the Talmud: "The door of a chest, box, and tower — one may remove it but not reattach it" (Shabbat 122b), and in its simple sense, it implies removing them from the hinges. 

Nevertheless, not all agree with this. The Mordechai, in the name of Rabbeinu Peretz, holds that this applies when there are no hinges. However, removing the hinges from them, or them from the hinges, constitutes complete demolition similar to breaking a door and is forbidden. But the opinion of Rabbeinu Yitzchak of Corbeil, as cited in the Mordechai, is that it is not comparable to a door that needs to be broken, as removing the hinges does not involve breaking, but is considered minor demolition and is permitted. Moreover, this does not constitute nullifying the utensil, as it remains a utensil even without the hinges.

However, it is clear that it is forbidden to place them back on the hinges and secure them with nails, as this constitutes repairing the utensil (as noted by the Magen Avraham, Subsection 10) and is close to a Torah prohibition, unlike removing the hinges, which is considered a destructive act.

And what we have written that breaking off hinges is certainly prohibited, this is the opinion of the Rosh, of blessed memory. However, in the Sefer Mitzvot Katan (SeMaK), it is written that even in this matter the great authorities disagree, and there is one who permits (Tur), who holds that the hinges of utensils are not considered demolition. And it is possible that even the one who permits, permits only the hinges of small boxes, but not of a chest, box, or tower, which appear like a building. And in this matter, certainly the primary law is according to the Rosh, and only through a non-Jew is it permitted, and similarly, the removal of the hinges is only permitted through a non-Jew, and even this only when there is great necessity in this, and so should be ruled (as from what is written, you will understand the words of the Beit Yosef at the end of section 7, where the Taz, section 8, is puzzled by this, refer there and examine well).

Additionally, our master the Beit Yosef wrote in section 8: "Bundles of dates and dried figs: if the covering is tied with a rope - one may untie and unravel the rope’s knots, and even cut it with a knife, and even cut the actual bundles themselves, for all this is like breaking nuts or almonds to take the food within them," end quote. In this, he did not innovate anything, except for what he wrote that even the actual bundles can be cut when cutting the rope, which is certainly puzzling to permit the destruction of a complete vessel. Therefore, it has been written that these bundles are not complete vessels (Magen Avraham, section 12, and Elya Rabbah, section 15). It appears that they are made of reeds and are perforated, and are only made so that the dates can cook within them. 

It seems to me that this is only according to the Tur and Shulchan Aruch in section 7, which states that breaking a barrel to remove dried figs is only permissible with a broken barrel that has been glued with pitch. However, according to the Rambam and his followers, as we wrote there, even with a complete barrel it is permitted, since it is a manner of destruction; therefore, it would similarly be permitted even with bundles that are complete vessels. Nonetheless, this requires careful consideration, as one might differentiate that in the case of the barrel, opening it is necessary, while here one only needs to untie the rope. Therefore, it is possible that here, according to all opinions, it is forbidden with a complete vessel, and thus should be instructed. We have already written that according to the Rambam, it is forbidden to unravel the rope’s knots.

It is further written in section 9: "It is permitted to untie and cut the knots of the spit that are tied to a roasted lamb or chicken," end quote. This means that the ends are tied with a string or some other material, similar to our practice of tying the ends with a string when stuffing thin pieces so that the stuffing does not fall out. This is also analogous to breaking nuts and almonds. Even though cutting is one of the primary categories of work and involves something detached, this applies when cutting measuredly for some purpose. Here, however, it is purely destructive, and destructive cutting of something detached for the sake of Shabbat is permitted even initially (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 14). However, if it is tied to some utensil, it is rabbinically forbidden to destructively untie it, as with a utensil that has bands called "reifen" (hoops), to remove the bands from it to open the utensil and take what is inside, such as small barrels, is forbidden (there), and it is only permitted through a non-Jew (there). It is taught in the Tosefta, chapter 9: "A person may tear the leather off the mouth of a wine barrel, etc.," see there. This is akin to cutting the strings from the knots of the spit, as the leather is also not a utensil. One must be careful not to tear it in a way that creates a nice opening, as concluded in the Tosefta: "As long as he does not intend to make a spout," see there, meaning to make it like a wineskin, as this is like making a utensil and is forbidden. Rather, one should tear it in a long tear so that it does not have the shape of a wineskin, and similarly in all such cases.

Additionally, it is written in paragraph 10: Seals that are on the ground, such as the door of a pit with a rope tied to it - one can untie it, for it is not a permanent knot, as it is meant to be untied. However, one should not unbraid or cut it, because that would be considered demolition (since it is attached to the ground). This is specifically when it is made to remain with the intention not to remove it on Shabbat, but if it is not made to remain at all - it is permitted. For this reason, it is permitted to remove a board placed in front of an oven and plastered with clay, as it is not made to remain (according to the end of his words). When it is not made to last even for one day - it is not considered building, and since it is not considered building - it is not considered demolition. And even though at the beginning of section 313 we brought from the Jerusalem Talmud that temporary building is considered building, see there, this refers at least to one day and not less. The proof is that it is derived from the Tabernacle as explained there, and their encampment was not less than a full day, as explained in the Torah in the portion of Behaalotcha. And even though it is written there: "And sometimes the cloud would be from evening until morning, etc.," but presumably at night they did not set up the tents nor dismantle the loads until the morning, and in any case, this requires further investigation. (And there are those who say that when it is written that it is not a permanent knot, this is specifically when he intended to untie it after Shabbat, for otherwise it would be somewhat of a permanent knot. In my humble opinion, this is not so; regarding food items, even according to those who say in section 317 that even for one day it is considered somewhat of a knot - this applies to things that do not necessarily need to be untied, and not to food items, for otherwise, there is also from one day to the next until after Shabbat, and pay attention).

Now, it has been explained that it is forbidden to make a hole in a barrel on Shabbat. What is the law if there is already a hole in the barrel and one wishes to plug it on Shabbat? The Rambam writes in Chapter 23, Law 3, as follows: "Just as it is forbidden to open any hole, so too it is forbidden to plug any hole. Therefore, it is forbidden to plug a hole in a barrel even with something that does not smear or cause squeezing, such as plugging it with a splinter or a small pebble. However, if one places food there to store it and the hole is thereby plugged, it is permitted, and it is permitted to employ a subterfuge in this matter." This means that one can take some food and say that he wants to store it in the hole, and thus the hole gets plugged by itself. The Tur and Shulchan Aruch, in Section 11, write that only a Torah scholar is allowed to employ such a subterfuge, as stated there. It is also explained in the Gemara (139b) that this is a Rabbinic subterfuge, and a Torah scholar will not come to do it initially, as stated there. However, the Rambam interprets that the Gemara refers to the other matter of crossing in a ferry, as it is a noticeable matter, and not to the matter of storing in a hole, as there is no publicizing involved. According to the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, only a Torah scholar can do this. It seems that although for many matters there is no status of Torah scholar in our times, nevertheless, regarding this matter where the Rambam permits it for everyone, we can say that even according to the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, there is a status of Torah scholar in our times (Magen Avraham, Section 16).

And know that the Rambam there later in Law 11 wrote: "One who smoothes a bandage on Shabbat is liable for erasing the leather. Therefore, one should not seal a hole with wax or similar substances lest he smooth it. And even with fat, one should not seal the hole, as a decree because of wax." End quote. It is not understood why this is due to smoothing, as it is forbidden to seal with anything. The Maggid Mishneh answered that there it is referring to a complete sealing, meaning that the sealing material fills the entire cavity of the hole, and in this case, it is related to building and is forbidden with any material. Here, it is referring to sealing only the opening of the hole from above, in which case it is not related to building and is permitted. Only with a substance that involves smoothing or the concern of smoothing is it forbidden, but other substances are permitted in this manner, see there. And there is one who explained that it means that indeed it is forbidden with any substance, and only with a substance that involves smoothing, an additional prohibition of smoothing is added. In my humble opinion, it can be explained that the intention is that with a substance involving smoothing, even if the intention is to store it, it is forbidden, such as placing a piece of wax or thick fat there. (However, it is difficult for me because wax is considered muktzeh and is forbidden to handle anyway, and with fat, one could say it is fit for eating, and this requires further investigation.) (And the Magen Avraham in subsection 16 wrote that the wax was prepared from the previous day, see there. However, it is difficult to understand what relevance preparation has for an item that is not fit for any permitted labor, and if he prepared it to seal the hole, he should have sealed it before the day began.)

The Tur wrote: "It is forbidden to place wax or thick oil in the hole of a barrel, because it is considered smoothing. If a barrel has a hole and wine is leaking from it, it is forbidden to place a garlic cloth in it to seal it. If he deceives and says that he places it there to store it: it is forbidden for an ordinary person, but permitted for a scholar." So are his words. From his words, it seems that he is stating two matters: at first, he is not referring to a hole from which wine is leaking, but rather that there are merely cracks which could possibly become a hole over time, but currently, building is not relevant, and only something involving smoothing is forbidden. And this is also inferred from Rashi's explanation (146a) where he wrote that the wax is spread around the hole to adhere to the walls of the vessel, and he did not write "within the hole" but "around the hole," as is done with cracks. In the second ruling, there is an actual hole from which the wine is leaking, and Rashi also explained this ruling (139b) there.

Our master, the Beit Yosef (Rabbi Yosef Karo), wrote in section 11: It is forbidden to put wax or thick oil into the hole of a barrel to seal it because this involves smoothing. However, with other materials that do not involve smoothing (since the wine does not come out through there) – it is permitted. If the wine was coming out through the hole, it is forbidden to seal it, even to place anything there in a deceptive manner by saying he only intends to store it there. But if he is a Torah scholar, it is permitted to use such a subterfuge. This is the end of his words. He differentiates between when the wine comes out through the hole, which is regarded as fixing, and when it does not come out, it does not appear as fixing. This has been contested, saying that since the hole is there, what difference does it make if the wine is coming out or not (Taz, subsection 10, and Magen Avraham, subsection 15). It seems to me that his intention was that the hole is small and the wine does not come out through it, and this is similar to what we have explained. (In the gloss of the Rema, it is written: 'since the wine does not come out then,' and it should be understood that it cannot come out, and the word 'then' may be an error. And what the Magen Avraham wrote in the name of the Bach, that it is permitted to seal with wood, the intention is in a stopper-like manner so that it can be removed from there. Refer to the Taz who elaborated, and his words require further study; see there and examine well.)

It is further written in section 12: "A knife that is stuck in a wall before Shabbat - it is prohibited to remove it on Shabbat, since it is considered something attached. But if it is stuck in a bench or any other detached item - it is permitted to remove it, and if he loosened and withdrew it before Shabbat in the wall - it is permitted." These are the words of our master. And this matter of loosening it was written by our master the Rema, and according to what he wrote himself at the end of section 1, even in a detached item, it is only permitted in such cases, as he wrote in section 10. And our master the Beit Yosef does not differentiate except between detached and attached items, as can be seen from his language. However, since according to the primary law of the Gemara, even in an attached item, if he loosened and withdrew it before Shabbat, it is permitted, and in a detached item, there is no need since there is no building in utensils in these cases, as he wrote in his great book. But the custom of the world is to prohibit even in utensils without loosening and withdrawing, and therefore our master the Rema wrote here according to the primary law, and at the end of section 1, he wrote according to the custom of the world (this seems to be my humble opinion).

Just as building constitutes a primary category of labor (Av Melacha), so too the making of a tent constitutes a derivative category (Toladah) of building, as the Rambam writes in Chapter 10, Law 13: "One who makes a permanent tent - this is a derivative of building and he is liable ... one who demolishes a permanent tent - this is a derivative of demolishing and he is liable, provided he intends to improve" (end of quote). We have already explained this in Siman 313, Section 3. The Torah obligation is specifically for a permanent tent, but by rabbinic decree, they prohibited even a temporary tent, as the Rambam writes in Chapter 22, Law 27, and this is his wording: "One who makes a permanent tent - is liable for building. Therefore, one should not make a temporary tent initially, nor should one dismantle a temporary tent, as a decree lest he make or dismantle a permanent tent. If he made or dismantled a temporary tent – he is exempt. It is permitted to add to a temporary tent on Shabbat, how so, etc." (end of quote). This is the general rule of tent laws. One should not ask, since making a tent is a derivative of building and their liability is the same, both punishable by stoning and a sin offering, why then is one liable for building with even the smallest amount, as stated in Siman 313, whereas for a tent we require specifically a permanent tent, and not just any temporary tent like any minimal building? Indeed, this is not a question, for building even the smallest amount is still considered building because it lasts for a long time, which is not the case for a tent when it is not permanent as it lasts only for a short time and does not have the status of a tent. And even though we brought from the Jerusalem Talmud that even building for a short time is considered building, at the very least it is fit to last many days, but he made it for a short time, which is not the case for a temporary tent that is not fit to last at all.

The Tur wrote: "It is forbidden to make even a temporary tent on Shabbat and Yom Tov." Rashi explained that the prohibition of making a tent applies only to a roof and not to walls. Rabbeinu Tam explained that even with a wall, if it is made to permit the usage of a sukkah or for carrying, it is forbidden. But if it is made only for privacy, it is permitted.

Now, there should not be a question as to why a tent is different from building, since building obviously includes walls and all manners. This can be explained by the fact that the term "tent" implies that it provides cover for a person, and therefore it only applies to a roof because walls do not provide cover for a person. An indication of this is the impurity of a tent regarding a corpse, as is well known, and this is Rashi's opinion. However, Rabbeinu Tam holds that even with walls, if there is a benefit for some mitzvah purpose, it is considered as providing cover for the person, meaning that it serves a purpose like a roof does, which protects a person. Here too, it protects a person for some purpose when it is from the side. But if it is only for privacy, it does not serve a useful purpose and therefore does not provide cover, meaning it is not considered a tent. See also in Section 18.

And most of the decisors agree with Rabbeinu Tam, and thus is the opinion of the Rambam and the Raavad in Chapter 4 of Sukkah, Law 16, see there. Therefore, our Rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, brought only this opinion in Section 1. And it appears to me that what is permitted with a partition when it is merely for modesty is when it is temporary, even if it stands firmly without shaking, or even if it is permanent but does not stand firmly without shaking, for these are included in the addition of a temporary tent and are permitted, as stated in Siman 313. But when it stands permanently and without shaking, it is considered the addition of a permanent tent and is forbidden (and this is the intention of the Magen Avraham in Subsection 1, see there and understand well).

It is explained in the Mordechai, Chapter "Kira," that it is permitted to make a partition between men and women during a sermon (see Taz, section 1). This means even if the partition stands without moving, because it is only temporary. And our master, the Rema, wrote that therefore it is permitted to hang a curtain in front of a doorway, even though it is fixed there, because it always moves and does not hinder those passing through. However, in cases where it stands as a partition and without moving, it is prohibited, because this constitutes an addition to a permanent tent (Magen Avraham there). Similarly, it is permitted to hang a parochet (curtain) in front of the Ark, even though it is fixed and it is a mitzvah for the honor of the Torah. This can be compared to the walls of a sukkah and an eruv. Nevertheless, it is permitted because there are doors in front of the parochet, and it is not considered a partition at all, as long as one is careful not to make a roof of one handbreadth. Similarly, it is permitted to make a partition to block the sun or the cold or to prevent the wind from blowing, according to the details explained, and also to protect candles from being extinguished by the wind and similar cases.

And Rabbeinu the Rema wrote: "But it is forbidden to make a partition in front of the light of the candle in order to engage in marital relations, and similarly in front of books in order to engage in marital relations or to attend to one's needs, unless it was a handbreadth (tefach) in place from before the commencement of Shabbat, in which case it is permissible to add to it on Shabbat" - end quote. The reason is that since this partition permits marital relations or attending to one's needs, it is akin to partitions for a sukkah or an eruv. And even though on Yom Tov the Talmud explicitly states in Beitzah (22a) that it is permissible to make a partition, this is because on Yom Tov the labors necessary for food preparation are permitted, and there is even a doubt there whether extinguishing a candle is permitted on Yom Tov. And even though in conclusion it was prohibited, nonetheless a light partition was not prohibited, which is not the case on Shabbat (and this resolves the question of the Darkei Moshe brought by the Magen Avraham in section 3). And to cover books with two covers - it is obvious that it is permissible on Shabbat, and similarly if a partition less than ten handbreadths is sufficient to cover the candle or the books - it is also permissible, because less than ten handbreadths is considered merely a cover (Magen Avraham there), as less than ten handbreadths is not considered a partition. And similarly, if there was a partition protruding from the side that is a handbreadth wide - it is permissible to hang a sheet on it, as this is considered adding to a temporary tent and is permissible (there).

Since it has been explained that adding to a temporary tent is permitted, and it is considered an addition when there is already a tent with a width of one handbreadth, it is permitted to add to it. Therefore, in small boats where it was customary to place ribs, which are called "reifin," and these are thin wooden beams that are bent and made into a half-circle, with one end inserted into the right side of the boat and the other end into the left side. Several such beams are used, and a mat is spread over all of them to provide shade. If one wishes to do this on Shabbat, if one of the beams is one handbreadth wide, or even if it is not one handbreadth wide but the beams are placed close to each other with less than three handbreadths between them, which is considered as if they are joined together and thus have a width of one handbreadth, it is permitted to spread the mat over them on Shabbat, as this constitutes an addition to a temporary tent. However, if none of the beams are one handbreadth wide and they are more than three handbreadths apart, it is prohibited to spread the mat over them on Shabbat, as making a temporary tent is forbidden. The same applies to a baby's cradle where ribs are placed, and a sheet is spread over them. Similarly, if the mat that is spread on top is never removed but is rolled up to the end, and when shade is needed, it is unrolled over the entire area, if one handbreadth is left spread apart from the roll, it is permitted on Shabbat to spread it out, as this is considered an addition. If not, it is prohibited. The rolled-up part is not counted as part of the handbreadth, since the roll is not considered a tent, as is obvious (see Taz, section 3).

The general rule of a tent (ohel): Anything that does not require the space beneath it is not considered a tent, as the definition of a tent is something that covers what is beneath it. Therefore, it is permitted to place one book here, another book there, and a third book on top of them, even if there is a space of a handbreadth, and similarly, a table with four legs without a board on top is permitted to place a board on it on Shabbat, and this is not considered a tent, because there is no need for the space beneath it. And it will be explained that a bed has the status of a tent because the air space beneath it is needed to place shoes and sandals. 

Regarding a table, there is another leniency because we hold that a temporary tent (ohel arai) does not exist without partitions, as what is it covering if there are no partitions? Even though a mat is prohibited without partitions, as will be explained, this is because it is considered significant and its primary intention is for shade, which is not the case with a table, which is a temporary tent and does not exist without partitions (Magen Avraham 306:7 in the name of the Rosh). And some say that in reality, it is one matter, meaning that the conditions of a tent require usage of the space beneath it, and consequently if there are no partitions, the space beneath it is not used (Taz 306:4 in the name of the Ran). 

The partitions need to reach the ground (there), and four partitions are required, but in any case, with two opposite partitions and usage beneath it, it is considered a tent (there), but without any partitions at all, it is not called usage. Only in the case of a mat, which we mentioned is significant usage, does it not require partitions. And when there are four partitions, it is certainly suitable for some usage. Therefore, in the case of a table with four sides reaching the ground, it is forbidden to place a board on it on Shabbat (there), unless there was a space of a handbreadth with a tent spread out from before Shabbat (and the opinion of the Rashba is that the main point depends solely on whether there is a need for usage beneath it).

Constructing a tent involves first making the walls and then spreading the roof over the walls. However, if one first makes the roof and then places the walls underneath it, it is not considered a tent. The reason, as it appears to me, is that since a tent is a derivative of building, and just as in building it is impossible to make the roof before the walls or the foundations of the walls, so too with a tent, if one makes the roof first and then places the walls underneath it, it is not considered a tent. Therefore, a bed that is assembled from pieces—it is forbidden to place the legs first if they have walls that reach the ground, and then put the boards for the cover on them. Rather, one should hold the boards in the air first and then insert the legs underneath them. A bed that does not have walls, like our beds, is permitted in any manner, and the same applies to a table, as we explained in the previous section.

Therefore, a bed frame made of sides that does not have boards but is instead enclosed with ropes, and on them the bedding is placed—if there is a gap of three handbreadths between one rope and another, it is forbidden to place bedding on it on Shabbat due to the prohibition of making a tent. Similarly, it is forbidden to remove the bottom bedding from it on Shabbat because it is considered dismantling a tent. What should one do? He should place a pillow, cushion, or sheet with a width of one handbreadth on it before Shabbat, and then it is permissible to arrange the bedding on Shabbat as he wishes, since it is considered an addition to a temporary tent, as we have explained. However, he must be careful to arrange the bedding while the pillow is still on it, for if he removes the pillow, it is considered dismantling a tent, and it will also be forbidden to arrange the bedding afterward, as we have explained. If there is not a gap of three handbreadths between one rope and another, it is permissible in all situations, because we say "lavud" (the gap is considered closed), and thus there is already a roof made before Shabbat.

A chair made of sections, where when one wishes to sit on it, it is opened and the leather is spread out, and when it is removed, it is folded up and the leather is folded - it is permitted to open and close it initially, as there is no concern of making a tent, since it is all made as one, and this is solely for sitting and not for stretching out a tent. Similarly, our iron beds - we open and close them, as this is not done in the manner of making a tent by first setting up the walls and then the roof in the manner of building, especially since they have no walls at all. Likewise, it is permitted to set up and remove the chuppah (wedding canopy), and also the shelf that is by the wall in the synagogue - it is permitted to set it up and remove it (Magen Avraham, section 8). Some are concerned about spreading a cloth on the table when the ends of the cloth hang from the table to the ground, due to the making of a tent, and this is a mistake. Firstly, since there is a board on the table and the cloth on the table is not called a tent, it follows that even for what hangs down it is not called a tent. Additionally, it has already been explained that when one does not need the air beneath it, it is not called a tent (Taz, section 7). Similarly, it is permitted to spread a cloth on the stander in the synagogue for this reason, even though the ends of the cloth hang down from the sides, and one who is stringent in this matter is merely among the perplexed.

When arranging barrels one on top of the other, one on top of two, grasp the upper one with your hand and arrange the lower ones underneath it. But do not arrange the lower ones first and then place the upper one on them, so that it does not form a tent when air is needed underneath, and it is presumed that air is needed to prevent mold (see there, sub-paragraph 5). And it is obvious that opening and closing the smoke outlet in our ovens with a metal tool called a "yuska" does not constitute a tent, since there are no walls around it, and besides, the surroundings are mostly covered and it is only considered an addition to a temporary tent. And only when there is fire in the oven is it forbidden because of kindling and extinguishing, but not because of the tent. (And what the Magen Avraham wrote in sub-paragraph 7, that it is forbidden to seal the stoves with thick cloth, it seems that in his days it was different from what we have, and pay attention to this.)

There is a significant question here: according to what has been explained regarding the conditions for a tent, which specifically requires partitions and that it be needed for use underneath the tent, if so, what is the explanation in Siman 301, Section 109, according to the opinion of R"T, that a hat which extends a handbreadth from the sides is considered a tent and it is forbidden to wear it on Shabbat because of making a tent? Similarly, the Rambam writes at the end of Chapter 22, and this is his language: "A hat... and if it extends from the garment... it is forbidden, because he makes a temporary tent." And yet, there are no partitions underneath it, and it is also not needed for use underneath it. However, the Rosh, of blessed memory, in Chapter 4 of Beitzah (Siman 11) explained to us that an item which a person intends to make into a tent, i.e., for shade, does not require all these conditions, because since its initial making was for a tent, it is forbidden. And this is also the intention of the Rambam there, who wrote: "A hat that is made on the head and has a brim surrounding it, which provides shade like a tent, etc." It follows from this that when it is made to provide shade from the sun or protection from the rain, it does not require all these conditions, and these conditions apply in other matters, where it incidentally becomes a tent, as we have already mentioned in Section 7. Also, the parasol, which is called an umbrella, is considered a full tent, and it is forbidden to carry it on Shabbat even in a courtyard, because it is made solely to protect and provide shade from the sun or rain, as explained there in Section 113.

A slanted tent is considered a complete tent, for the slopes of tents are regarded as tents, and one is liable for constructing a tent, which is like building. This is specifically when the roof has a width of a handbreadth (tefach), or even if the top does not have a handbreadth, but within less than three handbreadths from the top it has a width of a handbreadth, like the "parasol." However, if its roof and within less than three handbreadths from the roof do not have a width of a handbreadth, it is exempt from Torah law but forbidden by Rabbinic decree, according to the Rif and Rambam. This applies specifically if it was not prepared for this purpose before Shabbat, but if it was prepared for this purpose, there is not even a Rabbinic prohibition. Therefore, the sages said (Shabbat 138a) that a wedding canopy which does not have a width of a handbreadth at the top or within three handbreadths from the top, since it is designed for this purpose, it is permitted to spread and to fold, provided that it does not hang down a handbreadth above the bed. However, with our beds, where the sheets hang down considerably, it does not matter, and similarly, tablecloths on tables are not considered tents, since the roof is already established, as mentioned. Nevertheless, a wedding canopy is considered a tent for shade, and the bed is regarded as the roof since the bed stands in the middle of the canopy. But our beds are not made for shade or as tents, and there are no tent laws here since the roof is already made, as mentioned. Some say that any slanted tent that does not have a width of a handbreadth at the top and within less than three handbreadths is permitted from the outset, like a canopy (see Magen Avraham, subparagraph 11), but our master the Beit Yosef in paragraph 8 did not bring this opinion, so we follow the first opinion. Note that for the condition that its roof and within less than three handbreadths from the roof do not have a width of a handbreadth, another condition is required, namely that after the slope ends, it should not descend a handbreadth vertically without a slope, because if not, the entire slope would be considered a roof, and the handbreadth descending vertically would be like walls (see Taz, subparagraph 8).

A strainer that is hung on a vessel to put dregs in it to filter them, and its mouth is stretched in all directions - is considered a tent, and it is forbidden to spread and stretch it if it was hung with the dregs from before the day began. And even though it has already been explained that a roof without walls is not considered a tent, and therefore it is permitted to hang a jar on a peg, nevertheless, in the case of a strainer, the Sages forbade it so that one does not do as he does on a weekday (Gemara 138a), in order not to desecrate the Sabbath. And specifically dregs they forbade putting in it, but it is permitted to hang it to put fruits or other things in it, and likewise to filter clear wine and water that is permitted to be filtered on the Sabbath, for there is no desecration in this as there is with dregs.

A folded tallit, meaning that it is folded and placed on the pole, with half of it hanging on one side of the pole and the other half on the other side of the pole, and its two ends reaching the ground, and a person enters to sleep there between its two ends to protect himself from the sun, as the garment is spread over him like a tent to be under its shade – it is forbidden to hang it on Shabbat, even though its roof does not have a width of a tefach (handbreadth) nor is it within three tefachim close to the roof. Since his main intention is for shade, it is considered a tent. However, if it was hung on the pole before Shabbat and was prepared for this purpose, it is permitted to spread it and permitted to dismantle it, as we explained in the case of the canopy bed for grooms. This is only considered an addition to a temporary tent if it was hung before Shabbat. Consequently, it is also permitted to dismantle it, because as long as there is no prohibition in building, there is no prohibition in dismantling. And if it has a roof that is one tefach wide or within three tefachim close to the roof, even if it was hung before Shabbat, it is forbidden to spread it, as this is a complete tent, unless it was a tefach wide tent from the top during the day, then it is only considered an addition to a temporary tent. Similarly, a curtain does not have the status of a tent at all, and its law has already been explained in section 4, and it is even more lenient than a folded tallit.

And one who hangs a curtain or something similar on Shabbat must be careful not to create a tent while hanging it. That is to say, since it is common for the curtain, while being hung, to fold slightly from its width, if it folds a handbreadth, it constitutes a tent. And even though in the Gemara (138b) there is a question in this regard phrased as a wonder, and this is what it says there: "But from now on, if one were to extend his cloak a handbreadth, would he also be liable?" meaning, if one wraps his tallit over his head and the tallit extends a handbreadth from his head, should we say it is also considered a tent? However, it is not comparable, because with his cloak, he is not engaged in making a tent, so it is nothing. This is not the case with a curtain, where he is indeed engaged in making a tent, which means to cover in front of the Torah scroll. Yet, according to the law, this does not constitute the prohibition of making a tent for the reasons explained. Therefore, if it folds a handbreadth from its width, it will be considered a tent. Hence, if it is a large curtain, one person should not hang it, because it will certainly fold a handbreadth. Instead, two people should hang it, for when two are holding it, one at each end, they can hang it in such a way that it will not fold. For this reason, some are careful not to hang the curtain on Shabbat (Magen Avraham, section 19).

And our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 12: "If it is a canopy that has a roof - it should not be spread even if it is ten [handbreadths high], because it is impossible for it not to be raised slightly above the ground and form a temporary tent." This is the language of the Rambam at the end of chapter 22. His intention is for a canopy whose roof is a handbreadth wide, for otherwise it is not considered a tent. And how is the roof recognized? For example, if it is sewn with a border around the top that is a handbreadth wide, in this way the roof is recognized (see Magen Avraham, subparagraph 20, and it seems this is his intention). However, the phrase 'it is impossible for it not to be raised slightly above the ground' is not understood at all, and the main matter is not understood. Therefore, in my humble opinion, the 'mem' (letter) in 'above the ground' is a mistake, and it should say: 'it is impossible for it not to be raised slightly on the ground.' And this is the explanation: It has already been explained that a canopy which does not have a handbreadth is permitted to be spread, but when it has a handbreadth it is forbidden to spread it. Here, it does not discuss spreading it but rather stretching it like a curtain, for in this there is no prohibition since it is made like a curtain, and it is like a veil. However, due to its large size, it will necessarily fold slightly on the ground and become a tent, and this is the meaning of 'it is raised,' meaning it will fold.

A garment that is spread over the mouth of a barrel to cover it when there are liquids there—one should not spread it over the entire surface because it would be considered a tent (ohel). Instead, one should leave part of it uncovered, as in such cases it does not appear like a tent. And if one asks why it is forbidden to cover the entire surface, since it has already been explained that a roof without walls is not considered a tent, it has also been clarified that in a situation where one’s intention is to create a tent, walls are not necessary. Here, the intention is to create a tent to cover the wine inside so that nothing falls into it. Therefore, when one leaves part of it uncovered, it does not serve the purpose of a tent, and thus it is not considered a tent. This is also different from covering a pot, where there is no concern of it being a tent, because the pot is typically used in this manner for cooking, and it is small in size and does not appear like a tent. However, the barrel is very large and does appear like a tent. We are discussing a large barrel similar to a vat. Specifically, when the barrel is not full of wine up to the top but is missing a handbreadth (tefach) in height, since a tent applies to a space of a handbreadth. But when there is no space of a handbreadth, it does not constitute a tent, as less than a handbreadth does not count as a tent. This is regarding the prohibition of a tent, but there is another concern of a different prohibition due to wringing (sechitah), which will be explained, with God's help, in Siman 320.

Trapping is one of the primary categories of labor. When someone traps something that is typically trapped—meaning that it is customary to trap it—he is liable, if done intentionally, to stoning and karet, and if done unintentionally, he is liable to bring a sin offering. Trapping was performed in the Tabernacle, as they needed the chilazon for its blood to dye the blue, and they would trap it. Similarly, they would trap the tachashim, as they needed their skins to cover the Tabernacle, and they also needed to trap the quail. In the Gemara (Shabbat 75a), it is clear that trapping applies to the chilazon, but in the Jerusalem Talmud, in the chapter "Klal Gadol" (end of halacha 2), there is a dispute about this, as some hold that trapping does not apply to the chilazon. The reason appears to me to be that since it is merely a worm, it is considered not typically trapped, but the law is that trapping does apply to it. (And the commentators of the Jerusalem Talmud explained there that they hold that trapping does not apply to the primary categories of labor at all, but their words are difficult to understand, and so wrote the Tosafot (Shabbat 75a, end of s.v. 'HaTzad'), and this is their language: "It requires investigation, as in the Jerusalem Talmud it implies that one who traps the chilazon is not liable for trapping." End quote. And this is like our words, only the Tosafot wrote it decisively, but indeed there is a dispute in the Jerusalem Talmud. See there.)

The derivative category of trapping is not explicitly found in the Talmud or the Jerusalem Talmud. Only Maimonides in Chapter 10, Law 22 wrote: "One who sends dogs to trap deer, rabbits, and similar animals, and the deer flees from the dog, and he chases the deer or stands before it and frightens it until the dog comes and captures it – this is a derivative of trapping and he is liable. Similarly, one who does this with birds." End quote. According to his words, it is considered a derivative when he commands the dog to trap and assists the dog in its work, but if he does not assist it and only sends it to trap – it is not a Torah prohibition but only a rabbinic prohibition. This is what our Rabbi the Rema wrote in Section 2: "One who incites a dog after an animal on Shabbat – it is considered trapping, and some say that even on weekdays it is forbidden because of 'the seat of scoffers.'" End quote. If his intention is to assist the dog in its work – it is a Torah prohibition, and if he does not assist it – it is rabbinic (see Magen Avraham, section 4). What he wrote that some say it is forbidden even on weekdays, his explanation is that this is specifically with dogs, but by himself – it is permitted to trap if needed for his work, sustenance, or food, and with dogs, it is considered 'the seat of scoffers' and he will not merit to see the joy of the Leviathan, as it says in the Midrash on Parashat Shemini (section 5), and see section 5.

And the Rambam wrote there: "One who traps something that is typically trapped – is liable, such as a wild animal, birds, and fish, provided he traps them into a place where they are not in need of further trapping. How so? For example, if one chases a deer until he brings it into a house, garden, or courtyard and closes it off, or if he causes a bird to fly into a tower and closes it off, or if he takes fish from the sea into a vessel of water – he is liable. But if he causes a bird to fly into a house and closes it off, or drives a fish and removes it from the sea into a pool of water, or chases a deer until it enters a large hall and closes it off – he is exempt, as this is not considered complete trapping, since if he wants to take it, he would need to chase after it and trap it from there. Therefore, one who traps a lion is not liable until he brings it into its cage where it is confined. Any place where, if he runs, he reaches the animal in one stroke, or where the walls are close enough so that the shadow of both walls falls in the middle together, that is considered a small place, and if he drives the deer or similar into such a place – he is liable. And a place larger than this, if one drives an animal or bird into it – he is exempt." End of quote.

The Rambam does not differentiate between different types of birds, as he generalizes that for birds there is no concept of catching (trapping) within a house. Similarly, the Tur does not differentiate. And even though the Gemara (106b) differentiates between a free bird and other birds, stating that other birds can be considered caught even in a house, while a free bird, which does not accept authority and flits from corner to corner, is not considered caught in a house until it is brought into a tower, as our master the Beit Yosef wrote in Section 1: "One who catches a bird into a tower where it is trapped, and other birds into a house, etc." Nevertheless, the Rambam and the Tur do not agree with this. Also, the Rif and the Rosh do not rule this way, because they believe that this is merely a preliminary explanation, but the final conclusion is not so. (For later it says: "Now that you have come to this point, here in a large enclosure, here in a small one, what is the case: anything that runs and reaches in one leap, etc.”, and consequently in all matters, and also for birds in a very small house, it is considered catching. And since the Rambam wrote this, there is no need for the specific case of a free bird. Similarly, in the Jerusalem Talmud, there is no distinction regarding a free bird. And the Bach wrote that they did not concern themselves with the Talmud's explanation, and this is not correct. According to our explanation, it fits well. On the contrary, it is surprising regarding the Beit Yosef, since all our rabbis do not agree with this, why did he see fit to disagree with them? This requires further investigation and examination).

It seems to me that although capturing a bird in a house is not considered trapping, and similarly, a fish in a pool or a deer in a hall, nevertheless, once they have been trapped from there, one is not liable by Torah law. For although regarding the first person, the trapping was not completed in its entirety, it does not seem that this can be called trapping from here, since they cannot escape from here. And it is possible that if the first one captured them and then someone else trapped them from there, he would be liable since, in any case, he did an act of trapping, and this requires further investigation. However, our Rabbis, the Tosafists, wrote in Beitzah (24a, s.v. 'and it was taught') that wherever it is considered lacking trapping, one who traps from there is liable by Torah law, which is not in accordance with our view, as they elaborated there. And similarly, it is explained in their words in Shabbat (106b, end of s.v. 'and there is no'). According to their opinion, it is possible to call this a derivative of trapping, for complete trapping is the act of trapping itself, and a derivative is called so even though they are in a place where they are considered trapped, meaning that they cannot leave from there. Nevertheless, if they are not completely prepared in the hand of the person and one still needs to chase after them in that place, it is considered a derivative of trapping. But from the language of the Rambam, who wrote: "about a bird in a house, etc., that this is not complete trapping," it implies as we said that it is trapping but not yet complete trapping. Consequently, it is clear that one who traps from there, it is not considered complete trapping. See Section 10, and see what I wrote below in Siman 597 for proof of our words.

One who traps a deer that is asleep or blind is liable, because its way is to escape when a person touches it, and this constitutes trapping. But if it is lame, sick, or old, one is exempt, because they do not tend to escape and are considered already trapped. This is the ruling of the Rambam and the Shulchan Aruch. The Rambam also added that one is exempt for trapping a small one, and I do not know his source; perhaps he wrote this based on logical reasoning. And it appears that this does not apply exclusively to deer; it is the same for all animals and all birds. But regarding fish, it seems to me that this does not apply, because being lame does not pertain to them, and being old also does not apply, because for them, as long as they age, they increase in strength. And being small does not apply either, because as soon as a fish is born, it swims on the surface of the water and requires trapping. Also, being sick does not apply to fish, because they always swim in the water until they die.

And know that in the Gemara (106b), a distinction is made between different types of illness. According to Rashi's explanation, if one is ill due to heat, he is liable, but if one is ill due to fatigue, he is exempt. The Rambam, however, had a different explanation for this, as the Maggid Mishneh writes there, and therefore did not make this distinction. Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, also did not distinguish according to Rashi’s method, because since it is rabbinically prohibited in any case, he did not see the need to differentiate between a Torah prohibition and a rabbinic prohibition. This is also the reason of the Tur, because their way was not to explain this, as they only clarified what is prohibited and what is permitted, and therefore they only wrote in the language of the Baraita. (And in the Turim we have before us, there is a printing error that states: "One who is asleep, blind, lame, etc.," and it should say: "One who is asleep, blind – liable; lame, etc.," and before the Beit Yosef, the Bach, and the Derishah, it was written correctly there.)

All creatures that are typically hunted - one is liable for capturing them. However, any creature that is not typically hunted, such as flies and mosquitoes and similar - one is exempt from Torah liability even if they are captured for a purpose, because they do not fall under the category of trapping. Nevertheless, it is rabbinically prohibited to capture them even if it is without a purpose. Therefore, flies, although they are not typically hunted, it is forbidden to trap them, whether by hand or by covering them with a vessel. Consequently, one should be careful not to close a small box if there are flies inside, but with a large box, there is no concern, as it is not possible to capture them there either. And although, in cases where a creature is typically hunted, it is forbidden even in these manners, with creatures that are not typically hunted, the Sages were not stringent in such manners, and only with a small box or a small vessel should one be careful not to seal them, because it would be a certainty (pesik reisha) that they will be trapped there. Some are lenient in cases where if the vessel is opened, the flies would immediately escape. Regarding the law, certainly, if one sees flies in the vessel or the box, they must try to drive them away as much as possible, but one is not obligated to check if there are flies (Taz, Subsection 4), since there is no Torah obligation in any manner in this regard.

One may spread a mat over a beehive, in the sun to protect from the sun and in the rain to protect from the rain, provided that he does not intend to trap [the bees]. This means that if he leaves a large hole in such a manner that the bees can see the hole and can comfortably exit from there, it is not relevant to say that he does not intend to trap, because even if he does intend, there is no trapping at all in this case. And even if he does not leave any hole at all, in such a way that they cannot exit at all, it does not help even if he does not intend to trap, since they are inevitably trapped, and this is a 'psik reisha' [an inevitable consequence]. And although trapping them is not their usual manner and does not constitute a biblical prohibition, there is nevertheless a rabbinic prohibition, and a 'psik reisha' is also forbidden in rabbinic law. This is not comparable to flies according to the one who permits it, because in the trapping of flies he has no benefit at all, and it is possible that on the contrary, they may ruin what is in the box, which is not the case with bees in a hive, where it is beneficial for him. However, here we permit it if he does not intend to trap, and he also leaves some kind of hole on the side in a way that it is not inevitable that they will be trapped, so that it will not be a 'psik reisha', or he does not spread the mat tightly but loosely, and then it is permitted if he does not intend to trap, because if he does intend, it is certainly forbidden, as this is not a proper opening from which they can exit. (This is the reasoning of the Beit Yosef in section 4, which answers the difficulty of the Eliyah Rabbah, and this is the intention of the Magen Avraham in subparagraph 9; see there and consider it well).

It is taught in the Tosefta of Shabbat (Chapter 13, Halacha 5): "One who traps a domesticated animal, wild animal, or bird from a pen that is in a person's possession, if they require trapping – he is liable. From a pen that is in a person's possession, if they do not require trapping – he is exempt. One who spreads a net over domesticated animals, wild animals, or birds, even though they enter into it – he is exempt; for domesticated animals, wild animals, or birds, if they enter it – he is liable. One who releases a domesticated animal or bird from a net – he is exempt." End of quote.

And it appears to me that the explanation is as follows: An "efer" [pen] is a wide grazing area that is fenced all around, and one who traps from there, even though they cannot escape, still to catch them there requires chasing them because the area is wide. Therefore, one who traps from there is liable, and this follows the opinion of the Tosafot as we wrote in Section 5. However, even according to what we inferred from the words of the Rambam, that one is not liable there, still an "efer" is a very large area, and it is indeed considered trapping when one traps from there. And if one traps from an efer – he is exempt by Torah law, as this is like a bird in a house or a deer in a hall, for which one is exempt, as we wrote in Section 3.

And one who spreads a net over domesticated animals, wild animals, or birds, meaning that he spreads a net so that domesticated animals, wild animals, or birds will enter it, since at that moment they are not there, even though they enter it afterward – he is exempt by Torah law but prohibited by rabbinic law. Therefore, it is forbidden to set up a net on Shabbat for mice (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 9), and also the net is considered completely muktzeh and it is forbidden to move it even for its own use or for its place, as it is not used for anything and is like pebbles and stones.

And afterward, the Tosefta says: 'For domesticated animals, wild animals, or birds,' meaning if the animal stood there by the net at the time of its spreading and entered it – he is liable, as this is considered actual trapping and he is liable for a sin offering, and even if done intentionally there is no liability for stoning, as he did not know it would enter immediately, and it is only considered inadvertent (as explicitly stated in Tosafot in the first chapter 17: 'Ain' see there). And one who releases a domesticated animal, wild animal, or bird from the net, meaning they were already trapped and he came on Shabbat and opened an opening for them to escape, or dismantled the net – he is exempt but it is forbidden, like all destructive acts on Shabbat which are prohibited by rabbinic law, and all the laws of this Tosefta are applicable.

The work of trapping is different from all other labors, for in all other labors one must actively perform the work. However, causing the work indirectly does not incur liability from the Torah, as it is written: "You shall not do any work", indicating that direct action is prohibited; indirect action (grama) is permitted (120:). Yet, in the case of trapping, even indirect action incurs liability, as it is stated (106:): "If a deer enters a house and one locks the door before it, he is liable." This is considered indirect action, for he did not bring the deer into the house, but the deer entered on its own, and he merely caused the trapping by locking the door. The reasoning is that in trapping, this is not considered indirect action, as Rashi explains, "this is its trapping," meaning the essential trapping act is the final act of locking the door before the deer. If he did not lock the door, even though he chased it himself and brought it into the house, if he did not lock it, he has done nothing. Therefore, the essence of trapping is the locking. If two people locked the door together, both are exempt, for in all Shabbat labors, if two people perform it together, they are exempt, as it is written: "in doing it," implying that one person should perform the labor when he can do it alone. However, if one person cannot lock it and two lock it together, both are liable, for neither can do it alone, thus both are liable. If one can do it and the other cannot, the one who can is liable, as stated in Siman 301 regarding carrying, and the second one is merely assisting and is not considered significant. However, if the door is already half-closed, making the deer effectively trapped, it is permitted to lock the door with a lock, even though this adds security to its trapping, for regarding the matter of trapping, he has done nothing, since the trapping was already completed. Refer to what is written in paragraph 16.

A deer that enters a house with an open door, and someone comes and sits at the door, filling the doorway in such a manner that the deer is thereby trapped, another person can come and sit beside him, either in front of him or behind him. Even if the first person stands up and leaves, and now the deer cannot exit because of the second person, nevertheless, the first person is liable and the second person is exempt. It is permitted for him to do so initially, for this is considered merely like guarding a deer that was trapped the day before, which is not considered doing anything significant, and so it is in this case as well.

And know that there are those who say that when the second person is exempt, it is specifically in cases where the second person was sitting in front of the door and the first person entered the house, such that the door was never open, even for a moment (Tosefot Yom Tov there and Eliyah Rabbah section 16). The same applies if the second person was sitting behind the door, and the first person stood up and went outside. But if he was sitting beside the door, and the first person stood up and left, and the second person moved from his place and occupied the first person’s place, then the second person is also liable. Since at that moment the place was left vacant and the deer could have escaped, it turns out that the second person, by sitting, performed the act of trapping at that moment. And there are those who say that even in such cases, it is permitted for the second person initially, because the deer is already trapped, similar to someone who has a chicken inside his house, and the door opens; is it forbidden for him to close the door? (Magen Avraham section 11 and Turei Zahav section 11).

In the Tosefta, it is explicitly implied like the first opinion, as it states: "One who traps a deer in a courtyard that has two openings is exempt (even if he closes one). If the first person closes one opening, and a second person comes and closes the other opening, the second person is liable and the first is exempt. If the first person then comes back, opens the opening, and closes it again, he is liable for the second trapping," end quote. It is clear that even after the deer has already been trapped, if one opens the opening afterwards and then closes it again, he is liable because the deer could have escaped. According to this, in the case of a chicken in a house, if the door is opened, it is forbidden to close it. Additionally, it is taught there in the same context that if the second person sits next to the first, and this is the language of the Tosefta: "If one person sits at the opening, and another comes and sits inside, and another comes and sits outside, the one sitting at the opening is liable, and the other two are exempt," end quote. This clearly implies like the first opinion, that when it says "and the second comes and sits next to him," it means in front of or behind him, as we explained, and not directly next to him. However, it is certain that even according to the first opinion, if the second person sits next to him and does not leave even a moment's gap, but the first person stands and the second immediately fills his place, it is also nothing, as is evident. Similarly, with a chicken in a house, if one opens the door and immediately closes it, it is nothing. The prohibition only applies when the door is open for a short time, as then the first trapping is nullified and a new trapping is created. However, in the case of chickens in a house, trapping does not apply at all, as will be explained in Siman 497 (Aruch HaShulchan there), and also in this Siman, it will be explained that a wild animal or bird in one's possession is not subject to trapping.
