Even for one who forbids trapping them on Shabbat, there is still no liability. Therefore, there is no concern in opening and closing the door for our domesticated birds.

It is further explained in the Tosefta there: "If one sat at the entrance and another one came and trapped it from inside – the one who sat at the entrance is liable, and the one who trapped it from inside is exempt." This means that even if the second person actually trapped it inside the house – nevertheless, he is exempt because it was already considered trapped due to the first person sitting at the entrance. However, it seems to me that in such cases, the second person is exempt but it is still forbidden. And we also learned there: "If one sat at the entrance and found a deer inside, even if he intended to sit there until it gets dark – he is exempt, because the trapping preceded the intention. One is only liable if he intended to trap, but if the trapping preceded the intention – he is exempt." This means that since when he sat at the entrance he did not know at all that there was a deer in the house, but once he realized it and then sat intentionally until nightfall so that it would remain there – he is exempt, because the trapping preceded the intention. It appears that he is exempt and permitted, and so it is in the Gemara (107a): "If a bird entered under his wings – he may sit and guard it until it gets dark," thus it is initially permitted to guard it until it gets dark.

It has already been explained in Section 11 that when one can and the other cannot, the one who can is liable. Our Rabbis, the authors of the Tosafot (93a, s.v. "Amar"), wrote that "cannot" here means even if he is very strong, but he is carrying the beam in such a way that without another person he would not be able to carry it alone, such as with a finger or holding it in a manner that he cannot carry it alone. For what do we care about his strength, since at this moment he cannot carry it alone. This is what is said in the Jerusalem Talmud (Chapter 13, Halacha 6) regarding the Mishnah about a deer that entered a house, if two people locked it in, they are exempt; if one could not lock it and two locked it, they are liable. The Jerusalem Talmud says: "If one was healthy and the other was weak, and the weak one locked it completely, but the healthy one did not lock it completely - the weak one is liable and the healthy one is exempt." This means not only if both are equally healthy and each one can lock it alone, but one of them locked it with weak strength in a manner that he alone would not have been able to lock it with that strength, he is exempt and the other is liable. Even if one is healthy and the other is sick, but the healthy one locked it with weak strength and the sick one with all his strength - the healthy one is exempt and the sick one is liable (this is how it is explained in the gloss of the Shas there, and in the Pri Megadim there, and the Ketzot HaChoshen explained it in a strange and puzzling manner).

It is also stated there in the Jerusalem Talmud: "If a deer was running in its usual manner and one intended to lock the door for himself, and he locked it for himself and also for the deer - it is permitted" (end quote). Some explain that even if he knew that the deer was inside, but his intention was solely to lock his house, and the deer was consequently trapped - it is permitted. They contested this, asking how it is possible to say this, for it is a case of "inevitable consequence" (Ran, end of chapter 13). Rather, the explanation is that he was occupied with locking his house and was entirely unaware that the deer was inside, and afterward he found the deer inside - it is permitted and he is not obligated to open the door to let the deer out (there). I do not understand, for if so, what new insight does the Jerusalem Talmud provide beyond the Mishnah, for the Mishnah also states: 'To what is this similar? To one who locks his house to guard it and finds a deer guarded inside.' In my humble opinion, the explanation is as follows: He is engaged in locking his house and is at the completion of the locking, and in the meantime, the deer enters - he is not obligated to refrain from locking. This is not considered a case of "inevitable consequence" since he has no interest whatsoever in trapping the deer (and perhaps this is the intention of the Rashba cited there by the Ran and the Magen Avraham, section 11).

The Tur and Shulchan Aruch wrote in Section 7: "One who traps snakes and scorpions on Shabbat or other harmful creeping creatures, if for healing purposes – is liable, and if to prevent them from biting – it is permitted," end quote. This is a Mishnah in the second chapter of Ediyot, and it is brought in Shabbat at the end of chapter 13. It is explained there that even though in the Mishnah it says 'exempt,' this exemption is an exemption that permits, and the reason is that this is a labor not needed for its own sake, and in the case of potential harm, the Rabbis did not decree. And if there is definite harm, such as if they are chasing him – it is also permitted to kill them as will be explained, but here we are dealing with a case where the harm is not definite, therefore a Torah prohibition cannot be done for this reason, but a Rabbinic prohibition, which is a labor not needed for its own sake – the Rabbis did not uphold their words in the case of potential harm. And if for healing purposes – one is liable, because when trapping for healing, he intends to trap them, and it is a labor needed for its own sake, therefore he is liable. This does not apply to a dangerously ill person where the healing is certain, for if so, it is permitted to desecrate Shabbat, but we are dealing either with a non-dangerously ill person, or with a dangerously ill person where the healing is not certain.

And behold, this is correct according to the opinion of the poskim (decisors of Jewish law) who hold like Rabbi Shimon regarding a melacha (forbidden work on Shabbat) that is not needed for its own sake. However, according to the Rambam in Chapter 1, who rules like Rabbi Yehuda that a melacha that is not needed for its own sake is liable, it is impossible to explain that the permission for preventing a sting is due to it being a melacha that is not needed for its own sake. Indeed, the Rambam writes at the end of Chapter 10 as follows: "Harmful creatures, such as snakes and scorpions and the like, even though they do not kill, since they bite - it is permitted to trap them on Shabbat, provided that one intends to be saved from their bite. How does one do this? He covers them with a vessel or ties them so that they do not cause harm." This is his exact wording. And the clause "if for healing, one is liable" he omitted, because he previously wrote that creeping creatures that are typically trapped, if one traps them whether for a need or without a need or to play with them - he is liable, since he intended to trap them. Consequently, even for healing, one would be liable. This is what he wrote "since he intended to trap them," which needs clarification, for even if one did not intend to trap them, it would be a case of "inevitable result" (psik reisha). However, the intention is this: in the case of trapping, when one did not intend to trap but rather to protect oneself from being bitten - this is not considered trapping at all, for the main intention of trapping is to bring the creature into one's domain, whereas here the main intention is to distance it, which is the exact opposite of trapping. Therefore, the concept of a melacha that is not needed for its own sake does not apply here, since this is not considered a melacha at all, as it is the opposite of the main intention of the melacha as explained. This is why it says: "provided that one intends to be saved from their bite... covers it with a vessel," meaning that in such cases it is not considered trapping at all. (And what the Magen Avraham wrote in Sk 12 that these creatures are not typically trapped is puzzling, and the Eliyah Rabbah already challenged him on this, and in the Taz he wrote that it is a printing error and it should say "that these creatures are typically trapped," and see Machatzit HaShekel and Pri Megadim, and there is no practical difference in this, and the Rambam's intention is as explained.) (And this resolves the difficulty posed by the Baal HaMaor in Tosafot at the beginning of Shabbat, and see there and examine thoroughly.)

And this is regarding the trapping of harmful creatures, and how the law rules on killing them, as follows: Any beast or creeping thing that certainly bites and kills may be killed on Shabbat even if it is not pursuing you, for if it is merely seen, it is considered a matter of saving a life (pikuach nefesh) and overrides Shabbat. Other harmful creatures, such as snakes and scorpions, in places where they do not certainly kill: if they are pursuing you, it is permitted to kill them, because this is a matter of saving a life. If not, there is no life-threatening danger, and it is forbidden. However, it is permitted to trample them incidentally, even intentionally but appearing as if unintentionally, as is the language of our teacher, the Beit Yosef, in section 10. This is only according to those who hold that a melacha (forbidden labor) not needed for its own sake is exempt from Torah liability, and the prohibition is rabbinic; they permitted this where there is a concern of harm. But according to the Rambam, it is certainly forbidden intentionally. And what is stated in the Gemara (121b): "A snake and a scorpion, one tramples them incidentally," this is its meaning: when one is walking incidentally and a snake or scorpion is in front of him, he does not need to avoid them but continues walking as usual, and if they die by his trampling, they die, since he did not intend to kill them, as Rashi explains there. Consequently, even according to Rabbi Yehuda, it is permitted, for this is not a case of certain outcome (psik reisha), and an unintentional act, even according to Rabbi Yehuda, is only rabbinically prohibited, and due to the concern of harm, it is permitted. And I have seen someone who exerted effort to reconcile the words of the Rambam, who wrote at the beginning of chapter 11 that it is permitted to trample them incidentally even intentionally to kill them (Magid Mishneh there), and the reason is because snakes and scorpions generally kill in most places, and there is danger to life. But with other harmful creatures, it is forbidden (Magen Avraham, section 23), and these are perplexing matters, as we will explain with God's help.

And this is the language of the Rambam in chapter 11, law 4: "A wild animal and a creeping thing that bite and certainly kill, such as the fly in Egypt, the hornet in Nineveh, the scorpion in the mountains (in the Gemara the version is 'in Hadaib') and the snake in the Land of Israel, and a mad dog anywhere - it is permissible to kill them on Shabbat when they are seen. And all other harmful creatures: if they are running after him - it is permissible to kill them, but if they are sitting in their place or fleeing from him - it is forbidden to kill them. And if he tramples them unintentionally while walking and kills them - it is permissible." End of quote. And if so, it includes all harmful creatures, and does not specify a snake and a scorpion. Furthermore, how is it possible to say 'that they usually kill', when he wrote: 'or fleeing from him', and since they are fleeing from him, how is it permissible to desecrate Shabbat? Furthermore, from the words of the Rambam it appears explicitly like Rashi, since he wrote: 'And if he tramples... and kills them', why does he conclude 'and kills them'? Since he trampled on them to kill them, it is obvious that he killed them. Rather, the explanation is: he trampled them unintentionally while walking, and it is not necessarily that through this they will be killed, hence he says 'and kills them', meaning if he kills them it is permissible. (And it is difficult to understand the Maggid Mishneh who wrote that Rashi explained according to Rabbi Shimon, but in Rashi it is explained even according to Rabbi Yehuda, and I do not know if this is from the Maggid Mishneh, and perhaps a mistaken student wrote it).

According to what has been explained, it is permitted to kill a mad dog on Shabbat, as it is a clear danger. However, there is a doubt if it is not clear that this is a mad dog but there is uncertainty, whether it is like any doubtful situation of saving a life that overrides Shabbat, or if it is not similar, as even if it is certainly a mad dog, it is still only a doubt, for who says it will necessarily bite someone it encounters? And since there is doubt in its madness itself, perhaps it is not permitted to desecrate Shabbat. And even though in saving a life we desecrate Shabbat even for many doubts, as it is written in Siman 329, nevertheless this is all when the saving of life is apparent. But when there is doubt in the main issue, perhaps it is not permitted, and this needs to be carefully considered. However, it is certain that one must tell a non-Jew to kill it. And to kill a lizard called a shefin on Shabbat is completely prohibited and one is liable for a sin-offering, for it does not harm, and even if it falls into food, who says it is dangerous? And also, the food can be covered. There are some common people who kill it on Shabbat, and they must be informed that it is forbidden by Torah law (Magen Avraham there).

The Sages taught in the Mishnah (Chapter 14, Mishnah 1): "The eight creeping creatures mentioned in the Torah: one who traps them or wounds them is liable. As for other abominable creatures and creeping things: one who wounds them is exempt; if one traps them for a purpose, he is liable; if not for a purpose, he is exempt." The eight creeping creatures are specified in Parashat Shemini: the weasel, the mouse, the tortoise, the gecko, the monitor lizard, the wall lizard, the skink, and the chameleon. Regarding trapping, the distinction between them and other abominable creatures and creeping things is that people generally trap these for their skins, hence one is liable for trapping them as it is a task needed for its own sake. But for other abominable creatures and creeping things, trapping them is usually not for a purpose other than to prevent harm, which is considered a task not needed for its own sake. Therefore, only one who traps them for a purpose is liable, but if not for a purpose, and usually it is not for a purpose, they are exempt (Ran there). Therefore, Rambam, who ruled that a task not needed for its own sake incurs liability, ruled not according to our Mishnah. And this is Rambam's wording in Chapter 10, Law 21: "Whether the eight creeping creatures mentioned in the Torah or other abominable creatures and creeping things that have a type for trapping, one who traps any of them, whether for a purpose or not for a purpose or to play with them, is liable, since he intended to trap and trapped, as a task not needed for its own sake incurs liability." And this that he ruled regarding harmful creeping things that it is permissible to cover them with a vessel, is because there it is not considered trapping at all, as stated in Section 19. Therefore, the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, who ruled according to Rabbi Shimon, wrote the Mishnah in its form. And the general rule: that for a purpose is a task needed for its own sake, and not for a purpose is not needed for its own sake. And this applies to all types, only in general, the eight creeping creatures are for a purpose, and other abominable creatures and creeping things are not for a purpose.

And regarding injury, the explanation of the matter: One who inflicts a wound on Shabbat is liable when he causes a bruise, and this requires two conditions: The first is that he causes a bruise on a living being that has skin and blood comes out of it, or the blood is trapped under the skin. The second is that he intends with that bruise to benefit from the blood or the flesh, for healing purposes or to feed an animal. But if he only intends to harm or cause pain - he is merely causing damage and is exempt (Rambam in his commentary on the Mishnah there). And the eight creeping creatures mentioned in the Torah all have skins like animals, beasts, and birds. And even though regarding impurity, some of them have skins like their flesh, nevertheless regarding Shabbat they have skin, and therefore, one who inflicts a wound on them is liable even if the blood has not yet come out but is trapped under the skin. But for other creeping creatures and reptiles, one who inflicts a wound on them is exempt until the blood comes out, because for them, one cannot say that the blood is trapped under the skin as they do not have skin. It does not mean they have no skin at all, but their skin is thin and soft, and the blood is quickly trapped there even without a bruise, and if there is a bruise, the blood will immediately come out.

And to which primary category of labor does injuring belong? The Rambam writes in Chapter 8, Law 7 that injuring is liable because of "extracting," which is a derivative of "threshing," as injuring also extracts blood from the flesh. And even though he rules there that threshing only applies to products that grow from the ground, this excludes only creatures in water such as fish and worms, which do not involve injuring. However, animals, wild animals, birds, and humans who grow on land are considered products that grow from the ground (as indicated there). And since the prohibition is due to "extracting," he writes that one is not liable until the amount of blood extracted is the volume of a dried fig (k'grogeret). If the blood has clotted, the clotted area must be the size of a dried fig, as the measure for food on Shabbat is the size of a dried fig, since "threshing" and "extracting" apply to food. 

Rashi, at the beginning of Chapter Eight of the Tractate Shabbat, gives two explanations for the liability of injuring: one due to "dyeing," and the other due to "slaughtering," which means taking life, as the blood is the life-force. The Tosafot and all the early authorities agree that the liability for injuring is due to taking life, and the primary category of labor is "slaughtering." According to this, it is not necessary for the blood to be the volume of a dried fig; even a small amount of blood incurs liability.

The Rambam wrote there that what was explained about one who intends to cause damage being exempt because he is causing a loss, this applies to animals, wild animals, birds, and the like. However, one who inflicts injury on a person, even if he intended to cause damage, is liable because it satisfies him, as his mind is calmed and his anger subsides, and this is considered as if he is correcting, even though he does not need the blood he extracted—it is still considered fixing, and he is liable. This aligns with his opinion that one is liable for a labor that is not needed for its own sake. But according to most authorities, he is exempt, as he does not need the injury itself, and this is explicitly in the Gemara (105b) that this depends on the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon. The Rambam also rules in Chapter 10, Law 10, regarding tearing that it is considered a loss, but if one tears to calm his anger, it is considered as fixing and he is liable. Similarly, at the beginning of Chapter 12 regarding burning to destroy, if one burns his neighbor's stack or house to take revenge and thus calms his anger, he is liable. However, the Raavad and several other early authorities disagree with him, stating that in such cases, even according to Rabbi Yehuda, he would not be liable. The Talmud initially states according to Rabbi Yehuda that this is considered fixing because he satisfies his desire, but then questions this: "In such cases, is it permitted? For it was taught: One who tears his clothes in anger or breaks things... should be regarded as one who worships idols, as this is the practice of the evil inclination, etc." Thus, it rejects the initial statement that this is considered fixing. The Rambam holds that this does not reject the law, but rather that it is certainly forbidden to do so even on weekdays. Nevertheless, regarding Shabbat, it is considered a labor, as in any case, it is fixing for his filthy desire, and it is also forbidden on weekdays (see Maggid Mishneh there).

And know that in several places in the Talmud, there is a dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon regarding causing injury and kindling a fire destructively. Rabbi Yehuda exempts, and Rabbi Shimon obligates. Their positions are switched: Rabbi Yehuda, who obligates in a task that is not needed for its own purpose, exempts in causing injury and kindling destructively, and Rabbi Shimon, who exempts in a task that is not needed for its own purpose, obligates. Rashi of blessed memory (106a) explained these matters, and this is the introduction to the discussion: From where do we know that the Torah obligates for causing injury? For circumcision is an injury, and the Torah permitted it on Shabbat. And if you would think that causing injury is not prohibited by the Torah, why did it need to permit circumcision, as there is no prohibition at all from the Torah? Similarly, with kindling a fire, the Torah prohibits it for the daughter of a priest who commits adultery, as her punishment is burning, and the Torah prohibits burning her on Shabbat (Yevamot 6b). And why is it prohibited, for it is a destructive act? Rather, it implies that destructive kindling is obligated. Rabbi Yehuda holds that there is no destruction here because since there is a mitzvah in both, it is considered constructive. And although this is a task that is not needed for its own purpose, as the purpose of the task is only to fulfill the mitzvah, Rabbi Yehuda obligates in a task that is not needed for its own purpose. Similarly, in any constructive act, Rabbi Yehuda obligates, such as causing injury when one needs the blood for his dog, or kindling when one needs the ashes, even though it is not needed for its own purpose - he is obligated. All this is according to Rabbi Yehuda. But according to Rabbi Shimon, who exempts in a task that is not needed for its own purpose, none of this is considered constructive for the task itself, and it is considered a task that is not needed for its own purpose. And despite this, the Torah obligates - implying that destructive injury and kindling are obligated.

Therefore, the Rambam, who rules according to Rabbi Yehuda regarding a "melacha she'eina tzericha legufa" (a labor not needed for its own sake), thus rules that in cases of wounding where one needs the blood, and in kindling where one needs the ash, one is liable. However, if one does not need the blood or the ash, one is exempt, because it is considered an act of destruction. Now, according to this, for other halachic authorities who rule according to Rabbi Shimon regarding a "melacha she'eina tzericha legufa," they would have had to rule the opposite, that one is always liable for wounding and kindling even if one does not need the blood or the ash. Yet we do not find anyone who rules this way. And it is true that the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch do not delve into these liabilities, because even though a destructive act is prohibited rabbinically, they do not distinguish between a Torah prohibition and a rabbinic prohibition, as is well known. Nevertheless, from a legal standpoint, we need to understand how this view applies.

Certainly, here's the translation:

And behold, according to Rashi's opinion, it is certainly so, that according to Rabbi Shimon one is liable for wounding and kindling even though he does not need it for any specific purpose. However, our teachers, the Tosafists, innovated there that according to Rabbi Shimon himself there is a dispute in the Gemara about this. Rabbi Abahu holds that according to Rabbi Shimon one is liable even without any constructive purpose, while Rabbi Yochanan holds that even according to Rabbi Shimon one needs at least some constructive purpose or a mitzvah-related purpose, or that he needs it for his dog or for its ashes, and this is called needing it for its own sake. That is, since the mitzvah itself is done in this manner, the work must be for the purpose of the work itself in order to perform the mitzvah. However, wounding and needing the blood for his dog, and kindling and needing the ashes – this is certainly called not needing it for its own sake, like digging a pit and needing only its dirt. And one only finds this in the case of wounding and kindling with items that are forbidden to derive benefit from, thinking he can give it to his dog or cook with it, for with items that are forbidden to derive benefit from and are not fit for any purpose – this is called needing it for its own sake. And our teachers proved there that even according to Rabbi Shimon who obligates for destructive acts of wounding and kindling – nonetheless, he requires that the work be needed for its own sake. And according to this, according to the Tosafists, for wounding and kindling – he is exempt, except for wounding and kindling with items forbidden to derive benefit from to use the blood and ashes – he is liable.

It has already been explained that one is not liable for trapping a creature that is not typically trapped, but it is rabbinically prohibited, as we have learned in the Baraita (106b): "One who traps a creature that is typically trapped is liable, but one who traps a creature that is not typically trapped is exempt." This is also the language of the Rambam at the end of Chapter 10: "One who traps a creature that is not typically trapped, such as grasshoppers, lice, hornets, mosquitoes, and fleas, and the like, is exempt." All exemptions on Shabbat mean exempt but prohibited, as we decree lest one come to trap a creature that is typically trapped. Therefore, a flea, which is the small black jumping insect called "flea" and in Arabic "bargut," it is prohibited to trap it rabbinically, but biblically there is no trapping, as it is not typically trapped. However, if it is on one’s flesh and biting, it is permitted to remove it and throw it away, for in a case of pain, the Sages did not decree. One must be careful not to kill it; one who kills it is liable because it reproduces and does not come from sweat, therefore it is considered a creature like all other creatures. It is also forbidden to crush it with one's hands, lest one kill it; only removing it is permitted due to the pain. When it is on one's garment and not biting, it is forbidden even to remove it. Some say that when it is inside one's shirt, trousers, or socks and jumping around there, one is permitted to remove it and throw it away, and so is the custom. There are those who are stringent even when it is on one’s flesh and not biting, but the custom follows what I have written (see Magen Avraham 318:18 and Taz 308:8). However, the creeping lice found on the head and in the seams of clothing may be killed, as they are not considered creatures and they come from sweat.

Nevertheless, one who removes lice from his clothing should not kill them, but rather should roll them between his fingers and throw them away. This is because fleas are also commonly found there, and we are concerned that if we permit killing lice, one might also kill fleas. Therefore, one who removes lice from his head is permitted to kill them, because fleas are not commonly found on the head. And these are the words of the Rambam in Chapter 11, Law 2: "Creeping creatures that reproduce from male and female or their formation is from the dust, like fleas, one who kills them is liable as one who kills an animal or beast. But creeping creatures that come from dung or from rotting fruit and the like, such as worms in meat or worms found in legumes, one who kills them is exempt... And it is permitted to kill lice on Shabbat because they come from sweat," end quote. And there are three disagreements: liability for a sin-offering, exemption but forbidden, and permitted from the outset, which will be further explained in Siman 318 with the help of Heaven.

Just as it is permitted to kill a snake or a scorpion when there is a concern of harm by stepping on them inadvertently, as stated in section 20, so too there is another matter where it is permitted to step inadvertently, because a person cannot tolerate them. It is known that leveling a hole is prohibited by Torah law, as this is considered building, as stated in Siman 313, and consequently it is prohibited to rub saliva on the ground with one's foot because it levels holes. However, the Sages permitted stepping on saliva inadvertently while walking due to its repulsiveness, provided that one does not intend to spread it out and level the holes. Even though it will be spread out incidentally, it is permitted since there is no intention to do so, as long as it is not a ‘פסיק רישא’ (an inevitable outcome), as explained with the snake and the scorpion. This is according to the Rambam, who rules that a labor not needed for its own sake is liable, but according to other authorities, it is permitted even if it is a ‘פסיק רישא,’ because it is a labor not needed for its own sake. This applies where there is no paved floor, but on a paved floor, it is permitted to spread it out, as there is no issue of leveling holes, and spreading does not apply here since spreading only applies when smearing one substance on another, not when one wants it to be absorbed into the ground or the floor such that it is not noticeable at all, which is the main intention (Magen Avraham, section 24). Some have written that nowadays we are not particular about saliva due to its repulsiveness, and therefore it is forbidden to rub it, only to place one's foot on it without rubbing. But mucus that comes from the mouth or nose is certainly repulsive to everyone and it is permitted to rub it (there, section 25), and on a paved floor, it is permitted in any manner.

The Sages taught in a Mishnah (107a): "An animal and a bird that are in one's possession — capturing them is exempt." Similarly, the Rambam writes at the end of Chapter 10: "An animal and a bird that are in one's possession, such as geese, chickens, and pigeons from the dovecote — capturing them is exempt, and all exemptions on Shabbat mean it is exempt but forbidden." It seems to me that this is why this law is not found in the Tur, because since it is rabbinically forbidden, he did not consider it necessary to explain that it is biblically exempt, as this is not his usual method. Our Master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in Section 12: "An animal and a bird that are in one's possession — it is permitted to capture them," and he follows his reasoning in his great book where he wrote that this is what was said at the beginning of Shabbat, that all exemptions on Shabbat mean it is exempt but forbidden, except for these three: capturing a deer, etc. His words are perplexing, as this applies to the law where one person sits at the entrance and fills it, and another comes and sits beside him, as this statement is at the end of "HaOreg" (and also the Magen Avraham in Section 326 was puzzled by this). A clear proof that this is exempt but forbidden is from the Tosefta (Chapter 13) which states: "Geese, chickens, and pigeons from the dovecote, and anything that does not require capturing — exempt," and anything that requires capturing is a bird in the house and a deer in the garden or courtyard, as explained in the Mishnah, and there it is obvious that it is forbidden, as our Master the Beit Yosef wrote in Section 1.

It is stated in the Jerusalem Talmud on this Mishnah that if one captures a domesticated animal or bird that is in his possession, he is exempt. They only said this regarding animals that are in a person's possession. However, if they are not in a person's possession, he is liable. Rabbi Yissa said: This implies that if an ox rebels and one captures it on Shabbat, he is liable. Some interpret that it is one matter: that it is not in a person's possession means that it has rebelled, and if so, what is the meaning of the phrase "this implies"? Some interpret "not in a person's possession" to mean that he cannot control it, and if so, this is like an ox that has rebelled. In my humble opinion, it seems that the explanation is as follows: Specifically when they are in his possession, in his house or courtyard, but if they are not in his possession, such as if they have gone to another courtyard as animals do and have not rebelled, and when the owner whistles, they come back to their pen, nevertheless he is liable, because since they are not in his possession and he needs to bring them into his possession, it is considered trapping. Therefore, Rabbi Yehudah said: This implies an ox that has rebelled, meaning that it does not allow itself to be captured, even though it is in the owner's possession, it is considered trapping. Therefore, if there is a rebellious chicken that flies from corner to corner when one tries to capture it, the one who captures it is liable for a sin-offering.

And this is the language of our teacher the Beit Yosef: "A wild animal and bird that are in one's possession - it is permitted to trap them, provided they do not rebel. But if they do rebel - it is forbidden to capture them even in a courtyard, if the courtyard is large enough that if they were not raised among people, they would require a trap." End quote. And our teacher the Rema wrote on this: "And there are those who say it is forbidden to trap a wild animal and bird that are in one's possession, and if one traps them - they are exempt. But a cow and a horse, and certainly other wild animals and birds that rebel, if one traps them - they are liable for a sin offering, and this is the main ruling." End quote, and certainly this is the law. And according to what we have explained in the words of the Jerusalem Talmud, even if they do not rebel, if one traps them from another domain - they are liable for a sin offering. However, in any case, the law is that it is forbidden to engage in trapping animals, wild animals, and birds on Shabbat.

However, with all this, the matters need clarification. If so, it would be forbidden to bring a cow and a horse into a stable or a chicken into a coop. Yet, it is explicitly taught (128:): "One may guide an animal, a beast, and a bird in a courtyard," and even a chicken, which is prohibited due to muktzeh and not due to trapping, as it is stated in Siman 308. However, the matter of trapping does not at all apply to domesticated animals and birds that are accustomed to entering their pens on their own. Therefore, if the owners whistle to them and they go to their pens without resistance, this is not considered trapping at all, as is evident. And in this case, it is taught: "One may guide, etc." The matter of trapping that we mentioned regarding an animal and bird that are in one's possession and is permitted to trap them or one is exempt but it is forbidden, pertains to those that are not yet accustomed and require some effort to bring them into their pens, such as blocking their way, and similar actions. These are all the distinctions that were explained (and similarly, I saw in Chayei Adam, General Rule 29 in Nishmat Adam, Section 2, see there).

Behold, livestock and horses are always domesticated, and the matter of trapping does not apply to them unless they have rebelled, which is uncommon. However, regarding chickens and hens, every homeowner must supervise their household members. If the birds are accustomed to the house and are easy to bring into the house or their coop, meaning that when whistled to or called, they come immediately, then it is permitted. However, if they are not accustomed and some of them fly here and there and escape from the owner's hand to the point where one needs to stand in front of them to block their path, if they are outside, it is forbidden for a Jew to bring them into the house or their coop by intervening and blocking their path, but it should be done by a non-Jew. In this case, there is a rabbinic prohibition in any situation. And if they rebel like crazed birds, as is sometimes the case with chickens, it is close to a Torah prohibition, and one must be very, very careful about this. Regarding geese and turkeys, it appears that they are docile and do not involve trapping. Nevertheless, even with them, one must be meticulous to avoid desecrating the Sabbath, Heaven forbid. It is better to have a non-Jew bring them in if they do not come easily by whistling. As for pigeons, it appears that in any case, it is forbidden, as it is evident that trapping certainly applies to them.

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote: "A cat is considered like any other wild animal, and it is forbidden to capture it on Shabbat." This is not a novelty, for certainly its species can be trapped. His intention is that even a domestic cat that has gone out – it is forbidden to stand before it and block its way until it enters the house. However, if one whistles to it and it enters because it is accustomed to this house – it appears to be permitted. And what he wrote 'to capture it' is not precise, as it is muktzeh, but rather to do something until it enters, as mentioned. And bees that have left the hive – it is considered trapping and it is forbidden to return them (see Shulchan Aruch, section 318).

Tying is one of the primary categories of labor, and similarly, untying the knot. And where was it found in the Tabernacle? Because the hunters of the chilazon would tie and untie (Shabbat 74b), as the nets used to catch the chilazon were made with many knots, and these were permanent knots (Rashi), and they were also the work of a craftsman. Sometimes, it was necessary to take threads from one net and add them to another, so they would untie here and tie there (ibid). And in the Jerusalem Talmud in the chapter "Great Principle" it is mentioned that in the sewing of the curtains and the weaving of the Tabernacle's curtains, there was tying and untying, but our Talmud does not agree with this (see there). The derivative labor of tying is twisting ropes from fibers and from halaf, which is a type of soft wood from which ropes are made, or from woolen threads or linen threads or hair threads and the like - this is a derivative of tying. Braiding and spinning do not apply here, as this is only with thin threads for making garments, and therefore it is only tying. The measure for liability is that the rope remains twisted without tying, so that its work is lasting. Similarly, separating the twisted fibers - this is a derivative of untying and one is liable, provided that the intention is not solely to ruin. Its measure is the same as that of twisting, as written by the Rambam in Chapter 10, Halacha 8, see there.

Our Rabbis, the authors of Tosafot (Shabbat 73b, s.v. 'The one who ties'), were uncertain whether we require untying with the intention to tie again, specifically as we require tearing with the intention to sew, or not. Their opinion leans towards requiring specifically the intention to tie again. This is also the opinion of the Rosh, and it appears somewhat in the Jerusalem Talmud. However, Rashi, of blessed memory, later in the beginning of the chapter "These are the Knots" where it was taught, "Just as one is liable for tying them, so too one is liable for untying them," explained that the hunters of the chilazon (a type of snail) sometimes need to untie the established knots of the nets in order to shorten or lengthen them. Hence, one is liable merely for untying, and it is forced to say that his intention is to tie them afterward. He also wrote this in "Klal Gadol" regarding the curtains of the Tabernacle. This also seems to be the opinion of the Rambam that we brought in the previous paragraph, who wrote: "One who separates the wick is liable," and that his intention should not be to ruin. If we were to think that it is specifically with the intention to tie again, it would not be appropriate to say that his intention should not be to ruin, as it is obvious. Therefore, one is certainly liable for merely untying if it does not involve ruining. This is the difference between tearing, which is certainly a ruin, thus requiring the intention to sew, and untying, where the act of untying itself is a correction. Hence, this law is disputed: according to Rashi and the Rambam, one does not need the intention to tie again when untying, while according to Tosafot and the Rosh, one does need the intention to tie again, and this also seems to be the opinion of the Ra'avad in his commentary on the Mishnah.

There are three categories regarding tying knots: liable for a sin-offering, exempt but prohibited, and permitted ab initio. According to the Rambam: any permanent knot that is tied forever and is the work of a craftsman, which an ordinary person cannot make such a knot - is liable for a sin-offering. Any permanent knot that is not the work of a craftsman, which an ordinary person can make, or the work of a craftsman but not permanent, tied temporarily - is exempt but prohibited. Any knot that is neither permanent nor the work of a craftsman - is permitted ab initio.

And this is the language of the Rambam at the beginning of Chapter 10: "One who ties a permanent knot which is the work of a craftsman is liable, such as the knots of camels, the knots of sailors, and the knots of straps of shoes and sandals that the leather workers tie at the time of their making, and all similar cases. However, one who ties a permanent knot that is not the work of a craftsman is exempt. And a knot that is neither permanent nor the work of a craftsman is permitted to be tied ab initio. How so: If one's strap broke and he tied it, if a rope broke and he tied it, or if he tied a rope to a bucket or tied a bridle to an animal – he is exempt, and similarly, all these knots that are the work of an amateur and anyone ties them to last. And any knot that is not permanent but is the work of a craftsman – this is forbidden." End quote. And there is no need to explain what is 'not permanent' nor 'the work of a craftsman,' because most knots in the world are such. (And it is necessary to say, according to the Rambam, that what is said at the beginning of Chapter 'These are the knots' – that the knot tied with a belt and the knot tied with a rope are forbidden – this is also a craftsman's knot, but it is not permanent.)

The view of the Tur, which is the view of Rashi, is not so. There is no distinction between professional knots and non-professional knots, but rather between a permanent knot and a non-permanent knot. However, there are two types of non-permanent knots: a knot that is untied every day is permitted ab initio, a knot for a certain period is exempt but prohibited, and a permanent knot incurs a sin-offering even if it is not a professional knot. Moreover, within the category of time, there are differing opinions, as will be explained, with some permitting ab initio even for more than one day. Nevertheless, this is the essence of this view.

And this is the language of the Tur: "Any knot that is meant to last forever - one is liable to bring a sin-offering for tying and untying it, whether it is a craftsman’s knot or a layman's knot. And if it is meant to last seven days - one is exempt but it is forbidden… And a knot that is meant to be untied every day - is permitted initially." End of quote. His words require analysis, as he first says that if it is meant to last forever - one is liable, which clearly implies that if it is not meant to last forever - one is exempt but it is forbidden. Then he says that if it is meant to last seven days - one is exempt but it is forbidden, which implies that for longer than this one is liable. Also, from the fact that he says meant to last seven days - one is exempt but it is forbidden, it clearly implies that for less than this it is permitted initially. And then he says that if it is meant to be untied every day - it is permitted initially, implying that for more than this it is forbidden. The commentators have struggled with his intention (see Beit Yosef, Bach, Taz section 1, and the one who examines will see how much difficulty there is, as it is stated there).

In my humble opinion, it appears that the Tur dealt with a definitive matter: that for something left indefinitely, one is certainly liable to bring a sin offering; for something left for seven days, one is certainly exempt but it is prohibited; and for something that is untied every day, it is certainly permitted ab initio. However, between seven days and indefinitely, there are differing opinions as will be explained, and similarly between one day and up to seven days, there are differing opinions. The Tur did not delve into deciding on these cases. When he came to rule on the law, he ruled that only what is untied every day is permitted, and no more, because of the differing opinions on the matter. And Rashi explains similarly, that a knot left for a week or two is exempt but prohibited, and one that is tied and untied every day is permitted ab initio, as explained there. Some have written that for more than seven days, it is considered permanent and one is liable to bring a sin offering (Beit Yosef in the name of the R"F), and some have written that for half a year it is considered permanent and one is liable to bring a sin offering (ibid. in the name of the R"I), and some have written that for more than one day it is prohibited rabbinically (ibid. in the name of the Mahara"i and the Or Zarua).

And this is the language of our teacher, the Rema: "There are those who say that any knot not made to be untied on that same day is considered permanent, and there are those who are lenient and say that up to seven days it is not considered permanent." End quote. His intention is not that it is considered permanent to the extent of liability for a sin-offering, but rather that it is prohibited though exempt from a sin-offering. Those who are lenient believe that up to seven days it is permitted ab initio (Magen Avraham, sections 1 and 2), and this is the opinion of our teacher, the Beit Yosef, in his major work according to his understanding of the words of the Tur, see there. However, this is not conclusive. And there are those who disagree with this (Taz, section 1) and believe that it depends on his intention at the time of tying (ibid. and Bach), and this too is not conclusive. The main ruling according to halacha is that any knot not made to be untied every day, like knots in garments, shirts, pants, and similar items, which are typically tied for several days or more than one day, is in any case forbidden to tie on Shabbat as well as to untie, for wherever tying is forbidden, untying is also forbidden.

Rabbeinu the Rema wrote: "And there are those who say that one should be careful not to untie any knot that consists of two knots one on top of the other, because we are not proficient in determining what constitutes a craftsman's knot, as even if it is not permanent, it is forbidden to tie it, and the same applies to untying it, and this is the practice. Nevertheless, it seems that in a case of distress, one need not be concerned and it is permitted to untie it, as it is only a rabbinic prohibition, and in a case of distress, they did not decree. And when we require two knots one on top of the other, this means when tying two things together. But if one makes a knot at one end of a thread or string, its rule is like that of two knots." End quote. And this follows the opinion of the Rambam, that any craftsman's knot is prohibited even if it is not permanent, and we are not proficient in what constitutes a craftsman's knot. Perhaps it is because the craftsman ties it very tightly and two knots are very tight, and in the case of one thing, even one knot is tight. (See Magen Avraham subsection 4, who writes in the name of the Shiltei Giborim, but it seems from the language of the Rif that it is a knot that is tied very tightly, end quote, which implies that the Shiltei Giborim does not agree with the Rema, and on the contrary, the Shiltei Giborim himself concludes that therefore two knots one on top of the other are forbidden, and so writes in the Machatzit Hashekel, and there is some error here in the Magen Avraham, and investigate thoroughly).

However, the core matters are puzzling, for if it only depends on strength, what is meant by "skilled work"? After all, it does not depend on craftsmanship but on firmness and looseness. Furthermore, since they said a lasting knot and skilled work, and any lasting knot is presumably firm, how could they make a lasting knot loosely, and skilled work is an addition to this. And it is obvious that skilled work means that in the very making of the knot there is some craftsmanship, which an ordinary person cannot do. It also does not seem reasonable to say that what the Rambam wrote, that a craftsman's knot that is not lasting is exempt but prohibited, refers to a knot made to be untied every day. In my humble opinion, it seems that the main intention of our teacher the Rema is towards those who are lenient, who permit up to seven days initially, and when there are two knots one on top of the other, it is close to making the knot similar to skilled work, and similarly with a knot at one end of a thread or string, or when it breaks in the middle and they tie it firmly to be lasting (Sh.G.). But those who untie it every day, certainly there is no concern, and in a place of discomfort, even with two knots they were not concerned, and even when tied for a few days, for in a place of discomfort they did not decree. And all the more so in a place of mitzvah, they explicitly wrote that knots in such cases are exempt but prohibited, but in a place of mitzvah, it is permitted initially.

Regarding the matter of shoe and sandal straps, the Gemara (111a) discusses several legal distinctions. This was based on the shoes and sandals of their times, which had many ties and loops, whereas in our times these are not known at all. Also, Maimonides only mentioned shoe and sandal straps made by craftsmen at the time of their making, which are permanent, and one who ties or unties them is liable for a sin-offering. He also mentioned shoe and sandal straps that are tied on the foot when putting them on, which is permitted from the outset. In the Gemara, there are also straps for which one is exempt but it is still prohibited, referring to those straps where the shoe can be removed from the foot even without untying the straps, and they are only untied occasionally. Such straps did not exist in the days of Maimonides, which is why he did not mention them. The Tur did not mention them at all, as in his days there were no straps on shoes like in our times. If there are places where they make straps on their shoes, they should be understood based on the details that have been explained.

And the Rambam wrote there in Halacha 4: "If the straps of a shoe or sandal came loose, or if most of the foot came out - it is permitted to return the straps to their place, provided that one does not tie them." These are his words, and it is a Tosefta in Chapter 13. And our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote it in Section 2 (and it is surprising about the Taz in Subsection 3 that he did not see the words of the Rambam and the Tosefta there). And the explanation is as follows: If the straps that go through the holes around the shoe came completely loose, or even if they did not completely come loose but most of the foot came out - it is permitted to return them to their place. For although it is forbidden to insert the straps into a new shoe on Shabbat, as it is considered fixing a vessel (according to the Magen Avraham in Subsection 7), nevertheless, if they came loose - one is allowed to return them. However, if one wants to tie them at the ends so that they do not come loose again – it is forbidden, as it would be considered a permanent knot. And even if only most of the foot came out, necessitating the return of only one end, if one wants to tie this one end – it is also forbidden. And the Tosefta further states: "If the noseband (of the sandal) came loose – one may return it, provided that one does not tie it."

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote about this: "Specifically, this applies when one can return it without effort, but if it requires effort, it is forbidden, because we are concerned that he might tie it" (end of quote). This means that the act of returning itself is not prohibited since the straps were inside it, but when returning it involves effort, we are concerned that he will be reluctant to exert the effort and will tie them at their ends, so they will not slip out again and cause him trouble. The commentators on the Shulchan Aruch have criticized him, saying that the Tosafot and the Rosh at the beginning of Chapter Four explicitly wrote that in a place where there is a concern of tying, even if the hole is wide and there is no effort, it is forbidden, and where the hole is narrow and there is effort, it is forbidden due to the effort even without concern of tying (Taz, subsection 4; Magen Avraham, subsection 9; Eliyah Rabbah; and Taz). But I say there is no contradiction from there, as the Tosafot and the Rosh wrote about a coat, which is an outer garment and large in size, so when there is effort, it is certainly not appropriate to exert so much effort on Shabbat. This is not the case with shoes, which are small in size. And what they wrote about the concern of tying being forbidden even in a wide hole without effort, this applies where it is customary to tie, as evident from their language where they wrote: "In a manner that it is customary to insert and tie," etc., meaning this is the way of the world, and our teacher, the Rema, is not dealing with such cases. And in the notes of Mordechai, Chapter Four, I found explicitly like his words, and this is his language: "Our teacher Shmuel bar Natronai ruled that straps of a coat that have come loose may be returned on Shabbat, and so ruled the Geonim... provided that it is in such a manner that we do not need to worry that he might insert them, such as if the hole is large, so he can return it without effort" (end of quote). This is clearly like the words of our teacher, the Rema. And even if we say that they argue with the Tosafot and the Rosh, since this is a rabbinic issue, we follow the lenient opinion, and thus it seems to me that this is the main opinion.

It has already been explained that with a new shoe, it is forbidden to insert the laces on Shabbat, as this constitutes making a utensil. The same applies to a garment or pants (Magen Avraham, subsection 7). However, a belt is permitted to insert into pants in a place where it is customary to do so, because it is not permanently fixed there and will be removed again, and therefore, it is not considered making a utensil (ibid.). But a thread or a string is forbidden to insert, as it is permanently fixed there. And if it was already there and came undone, it has already been explained in the previous section.

And know that in the Tosefta regarding all those that it teaches "one should not tie," it further states: "A string of a date-palm and a rope of a date-palm and a rope of dried figs - one may tear it and eat, provided that he does not tie. This is the rule: Any knot that is permanent and can be untied with one hand, or is not permanent and cannot be untied with one hand - one is not liable for it, until it is a permanent knot and cannot be untied with one hand." End quote. And none of the poskim (decisors of Jewish law) brought this Tosefta. According to the Rambam, it can be interpreted simply, that a craftsman's knot is presumably one that cannot be untied with one hand, and from this we have a definition of what constitutes a craftsman's knot. And according to Rashi, it can be interpreted that a permanent knot is not called permanent until it cannot be untied with one hand.

It is explicitly apparent that the poskim (decisors of Jewish law) rejected this Tosefta from halacha because it reflects the opinion of Rabbi Meir, who stated in the Mishnah at the beginning of the chapter "These are the knots" (Shabbat 111b) that any knot that can be untied with one hand does not incur liability. However, the halacha does not follow Rabbi Meir, as explained by the Ra'avad and Rambam in their commentaries on the Mishnah, because the halacha follows the Sages. They hold that this Tosefta was taught according to Rabbi Meir and is not the halacha. Nevertheless, we learn from this that a permanent knot does not need to be very tight, for even if it can be untied with one hand, one is liable for it. Based on this, it is necessary to warn women who have many knots in their clothing, and these knots are not made to be untied daily and are made to beautify the clothing but can easily be untied with one hand, that it is forbidden to untie and tie them, and they are close to coming to the prohibition of stoning. Similarly, for men with the knot behind their pants, which is a permanent knot but occasionally is loosened or tightened, it is forbidden on Shabbat to untie or tie it, even if it can be untied with one hand. This knot and similar knots are a Torah prohibition unless they are made as a bow, in which case it is permitted to tie and untie them.

Sewing is a primary category of labor, and its measure [of prohibition] is two stitches, where one inserts the needle twice, pulls through the thread, and ties the two ends of the thread, for otherwise it is not lasting. With three stitches, it is not necessary to tie, for even without tying it is lasting. In the Tabernacle, sewing was done with the curtains that were sewn. 

Tearing in order to sew two stitches is also necessary in certain cases, such as when a garment was not sewn evenly and protrudes somewhat, necessitating tearing the garment below and smoothing it a bit so that the sewing will settle properly (Gemara and Rashi, beginning of chapter "HaOreg"). In the Tabernacle, this was done with a curtain when a worm fell into it and made a small, round hole, requiring tearing below and above the hole so that the sewing would not be wrinkled (Gemara and Rashi 75a).

We have already written in Siman 313, section 6, that even though in extinguishing in order to ignite, it is specifically required that through the extinguishing the ignition is better than without the extinguishing—otherwise it is considered a labor not needed for its own sake—nevertheless, in demolishing in order to build, this is not needed, for the reason explained there. Similarly, we must say regarding tearing in order to sew and untying according to those who require it to be in order to tie, for the same reason explained there.

Derivative of sewing: One who glues papers with adhesive or hides to each other, or other types of materials when he glues them to each other—it is a derivative of sewing and liable, for what difference does it make whether the connection is through sewing or through adhesive? And even though sewing sheets of a Torah scroll does not work with glue, as stated in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 278, that is different because it is a law given to Moses at Sinai that specifically requires sewing, as we brought there from the Jerusalem Talmud in Megillah, see there. And indeed, even sewing with threads is invalid, but only with sinews, as stated there. But in general, sewing and gluing are the same matter, in matters of mixtures of species and similar cases. And if you ask, if so, then tying and sewing are the same, since tying also connects things to each other. It is not so, because a connection by tying is meant to be undone and returned to its original state, which is not the case with sewing and gluing, where if one wishes to return them to their original state, it is necessary to ruin and tear them from each other, which is not the case with tying.

And the derivative of tearing, the Rambam also wrote in Chapter 10, Law 11, and this is his language: "And similarly, one who separates glued papers or glued skins and did not intend merely to spoil - this is a derivative of tearing and is liable." End of quote. And regarding tearing, he previously wrote: "One who tears with the intention to sew, but one who tears to destroy - is exempt," as stated there. However, regarding separating papers, he did not use this language. It seems to me because all tearing inherently involves spoiling, and necessarily requires the intention to sew. But in the case of separating papers, not every separation involves spoiling, and therefore, if it does not spoil - it does not require the intention to re-glue, just like untying does not require the intention to re-tie according to his opinion, as he wrote in Section 2, as stated there. However, in Tosafot, it is explained differently as stated there.

And the Rambam wrote there: "One who tears [his garments] in his anger or over someone he is obligated to tear for – is liable, because this action calms his mind and his inclination rests, and since his anger is soothed by this – it is considered as if he has repaired something and he is liable." This follows his opinion that an act not needed for its own sake (melacha she'eina tzricha legufa) is liable. However, according to those who rule like Rabbi Shimon – he is exempt. And so it is in the Gemara (105b) that according to Rashi, of blessed memory, Rabbi Shimon exempts even in the case of a deceased for whom one is obligated to tear, because Rabbi Shimon does not consider the fulfillment of a mitzvah to be an act needed for its own sake, as we wrote in the previous section, paragraph 27. But the Tosafot there wrote that for his deceased – even according to Rabbi Shimon he is liable, because this also repairs the garment, meaning that through the tearing it is permitted for him to wear it, and Rabbi Shimon exempts only one who tears in his anger. And we already wrote in the previous section, paragraph 26, that the Raavad and other early authorities disagree with the Rambam, because even according to Rabbi Yehuda he is not liable for calming his inclination since this is a great transgression, and the Rambam does not agree with this as we wrote there.

In the Gemara (48a), it is stated: "One may untie the neck opening of a garment on Shabbat, but one may not open it, and one who opens the neck opening of a garment on Shabbat is liable to bring a sin offering." Rashi and Tosafot explained that this refers to creating a new neck opening that was completely sealed, tearing the neck opening and opening it. Therefore, Rashi explained that the liability is because of the melacha (prohibited labor) of 'striking the final blow' (makeh b'patish), as this completes the garment's making. And "untie the neck opening" refers to untying it after it was tied during washing, which is a knot meant to be untied, and therefore it is permitted to do so initially.

The Rambam there wrote simply that one who opens the neck opening is liable to bring a sin offering, without explaining the reason for this liability. According to the Rambam, we can say that the liability is due to tearing (kore'a), since there is a repair in the tearing, as explained in Section 19. 

Some explain that opening the neck opening does not mean creating a new opening initially, but rather it was already opened on a weekday and then closed with light sewing using a thread or cord, and on Shabbat, one opens this thread or cord, and is liable because of completing a utensil (gmar keli) (as explained by the Ritva in the name of R' Chananel, and similarly I have seen in the name of the son of the Rambam in the book Ma'aseh Rokeach. According to this, the Gemara's question there "What is the difference between this and the stopper of a barrel?" is well answered, and it resolves that this is a connection because it was sewn, and pay attention to this).

And this is the language of our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, in Section 3: "One may untie the collar of a garment from a knot that a launderer tied, since it is not a permanent knot, but one may not open it anew, for this is considered fixing a vessel, even if it was already opened and then the craftsman retied or sewed it together in the manner that craftsmen do." End of quote. Some have written that this permission to untie the collar is only when it is customary to untie it on the same day (Taz, subsection 5 and Magen Avraham, subsection 11). However, I am puzzled by this, for if so, what is the novelty and what is the Talmud teaching us with this statement that one may untie the collar? And if the purpose is to teach us that it is not a craftsman's knot, this would be satisfactory according to the opinion of the Rambam, but not according to Rashi and Tosafot. Furthermore, the language 'not permanent' used by the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch does not imply this. In my humble opinion, it seems that this knot lasts for several days while the laundering process continues, and nonetheless, it is permitted from the outset because it is meant to be opened after the laundering. This is what the Talmud, the Tur, and the Shulchan Aruch are teaching us. Meaning, since it is not permanent to the extent that it would be a Torah prohibition, the sages did not prohibit it for the reason we mentioned. (And the Rambam omitted this case of untying the collar, because since he wrote that any knot that is not a craftsman's knot is permitted, it follows that everything is included. Nevertheless, this requires some further investigation, and pay close attention.)

And this that they wrote, that when the craftsman returns and ties or sews it, it is forbidden to open it, the intention is not that the knot is a craftsman's act, but rather that he cannot untie it unless he cuts the threads, and therefore it is forbidden (Magen Avraham, section 11), for they permitted untying but not cutting the threads. And even though it is destructive, it is still forbidden by rabbinic decree. Furthermore, when the craftsman returns and ties or sews it, when one now comes to open it, it is considered a new act. And they further wrote: Therefore it is forbidden to separate or cut a pair of shoes that are sewn together in the way craftsmen do, even though the sewing is not permanent, for there is no distinction in sewing between permanent and non-permanent. And some permit sewing that is not permanent, but one should not permit it in the presence of an unlearned person.

It would seem that the first opinion, which prohibits detaching or cutting, is based on the reasoning that detaching or cutting was never permitted, even though it causes damage. However, this is not the truth, for only in matters that a craftsman performs was it not permitted, even if it is not a craftsman’s work, it is still considered a new thing, as per the second explanation that we wrote in the previous section. And even in this, there are those who permit it, because it has no relation at all to the work of a shoe. But in the case of a shirt or pants or another garment where the ties have become knotted and cannot be untied, which is called "pair knippel," the great authorities have ruled that it is permitted to detach them according to all opinions, for it is only made to be untied whenever one wishes, but even this should not be done in front of an unlearned person, but rather in private (Magen Avraham there in the name of the Maharshal and Bach). And only in the knots of a craftsman is it forbidden to detach, but in other knots, it is permitted. And if one is not accustomed to untie the knot of the shirt except from one Shabbat to the next, there are those who say it should not be untied on Shabbat (there). And it seems to me that this is when one is particular not to untie it, but if one is not particular and sometimes unties it every night and sometimes does not, it is permitted to untie it on Shabbat, and so is the common custom.

We hold that a bow is not considered a knot and is permissible in all circumstances, even two bows one on top of the other, and even if they are intended to last a long time, because it is not considered a knot. And our teacher, the Rema, wrote in section 5 that even if one makes a single knot below, it is customary to permit it. However, in the Mordechai, this is written as a prohibition, and this seems correct, because what benefit is there from the bow above if there is a complete knot below it? And it is written that the intention of our teacher, the Rema, is specifically with a knot that is intended to be untied within the same day (Magen Avraham section 16 and Taz section 7), and this is not understood, because if so, there is no need for the permission of the bow, and if to teach us that it is not a craftsman's work, what relevance does this have? And perhaps because he already wrote that two knots one on top of the other are prohibited because this is like a craftsman's knot, as stated in section 9, it comes to teach us that with a bow on top of a knot, it is not so. Therefore, with a bow on top of a knot intended to last several days, like with a lulav and similar, it is forbidden on Shabbat and Yom Tov, and one should only make a bow or a bow on top of another bow.

A bucket that is situated by a well and one wishes to draw water with it by tying a rope to it – it is forbidden to tie the rope to it, because it is likely that one will leave it tied there permanently, and it becomes a permanent knot. Even if at the time of tying it one does not intend to leave it there, we are concerned that afterwards he might reconsider and leave it. Thus ruled our master, the Beit Yosef, in his great book in the name of the Kolbo, and this is his wording: "Any knot that one might sometimes reconsider and leave it there forever, even though at the time of making it, it was not intended to be left there – it is forbidden. Therefore, it is forbidden to tie the strap of trousers (at the back), because sometimes one might reconsider and leave it there forever until it wears out." End of quote (Magen Avraham, section 20).

And even if one wants to tie a valuable rope, such as a craftsman's rope which certainly would not be discarded with the bucket, it is still forbidden because we decree against this type of rope due to the common rope. However, it is permitted to tie the bucket with a strap or a sash and similar items, since these are not types of ropes that we decree due to the common rope, and therefore it is permitted to tie with them. But with a bow, it is permitted with a rope, and we do not decree a bow due to tying, because a rope with a rope can be confused, but a bow with tying cannot be confused (113:). And all of this applies to a bucket that is at the well, but a bucket that is used in the house and is taken to draw water - it is permitted to tie it with a rope, since it will certainly be untied immediately. However, if this bucket is designated for drawing water - even if it is in his house, it is forbidden, as is evident.

It is permissible to tie a rope across the entrance where the animal stands so that it does not go out, because this rope is not considered a permanent fixture, as it is necessary to untie the rope when the animal needs to be taken out, and animals go out every day. Furthermore, one is even allowed to tie two ropes, one above the other, and we are not concerned that one might untie one and leave the other and bring the animal out with difficulty. Moreover, it is even permissible to tie the rope at both ends of the entrance, and we are not concerned that one might untie one end of the rope and leave the other tied, as the animal would still go out easily. In any case, we are not concerned about this because it is not the usual practice for people to do so, as generally, there are doors, and this situation is an exceptional case where there are no doors or the doors have fallen off, and this is done only occasionally. Therefore, we are not concerned.

However, it is forbidden to tie a rope around the cow's neck and tie the other end to the trough where it eats, because it is very likely that one end will be untied and the other end will remain tied, since this is needed every day. However, with a craftsman's rope, where it is certain that both ends will be untied, it is permitted, and we do not decree a prohibition due to ordinary rope as we do with a bucket, because even ordinary rope is not usually durable, and therefore it suffices to prohibit ordinary rope. And even with ordinary rope that is forbidden, it is only when tying both ends now to the trough and the animal. But if one end was already tied to the trough and one wants to tie it to the cow, or if it was tied to the cow and one wants to tie it to the trough, it is permitted with any rope, because it is assumed that the recently tied end will be untied and not the other one. And the general rule about knots is: one must be careful to make them with a bow, which is permitted in all cases, because there are types of knots in women's jewelry boxes that remain tied for a long time, and care is required with these and similar cases. And it is obvious that the knots of tzitzit are forbidden.

Cooking is a primary category of labor, and it was present in the Tabernacle where they cooked the spices. The Tanna in the Mishnah that lists the primary categories of labor mentions baking, and baking was not present in the Tabernacle. The reason it does not mention cooking is because it follows the order of bread-making (Pesachim 74b). That is, since it begins with sowing, etc., it ends with kneading and baking; see there. In practice, there is no difference. The derivative of cooking is baking and cooking related to derivatives of fire, such as placing an egg beside a kettle near the fire so that it roasts with the residual heat of the fire—it is considered as if one cooked with the fire itself. Similarly, melting any type of metal to any extent or heating the metal until it becomes a coal is a derivative of cooking and one is liable. Likewise, melting wax, fat, tar, pitch, sulfur, and similar substances is a derivative of cooking and one is liable.

In the Gemara (there): "One who throws a peg into a furnace is liable for cooking," and Rashi explains that he threw a moist peg into a hot oven to dry it so that it hardens. And the Rambam in Chapter 9, Law 6 explains that this refers to cooking an earthenware vessel until it becomes pottery - liable for cooking. The rule is: whether one softens a hard body with fire or hardens a soft body - this is considered cooking. And in the Jerusalem Talmud in the chapter "Klal Gadol" it says that baking is a derivative of cooking, and similarly roasting, frying, boiling, and smoking - all are liable for cooking. And in the Jerusalem Talmud in Nedarim (Chapter 6) it remains in doubt whether smoking is included in cooking for the matter of Shabbat, see there, but here it is clear to him, and this is the law. However, one who cooks with the hot springs of Tiberias or with heat derived from the sun, and one who cooks with the sun itself - these are not derivatives of cooking, and their prohibition is rabbinic, and with the sun it is permitted as stated in Section 17, see there.

And what is its measure for one to be liable? The Rambam writes at the beginning of Chapter 9: "One who bakes the size of a dried fig (grogeret) is liable. This applies whether one bakes bread, cooks food, or dyes ingredients, or heats water. It is all one matter. The measure for heating water is enough to wash a small limb, and the measure for cooking ingredients is enough to make them suitable for that which they are being cooked for." End of quote. And the Ra'avad wrote: "Enough to dye a small garment the size of a hairnet." There he ends, and we do not know the source, but it seems that he wrote this based on logical reasoning.

Maimonides wrote: "If one person kindled the fire, another placed the wood, another placed the pot, another added the water, another added the meat, and another added the spices—they are all liable for cooking, for anyone who contributes to the process of cooking is considered to have cooked. However, if one person placed the pot first, another added the water, another added the meat, another added the spices, another kindled the fire, another placed wood on the fire, and another stirred the pot—only the last two are liable for cooking." Explanation: When they all acted simultaneously, with the first one kindling the fire and everyone else performing their tasks at the same time, all are liable, because as soon as the wood is placed on the fire, cooking begins, and all are liable. Even the one who kindled the fire is liable, because the moment he kindled the fire, someone else placed the wood, and it is considered a single act by all, making them all liable. But in the latter case, where the tasks were performed sequentially, until the fire was kindled, nothing significant had occurred. The kindling of the fire alone is not significant, for a fire without wood will extinguish. The liability falls on the last two, the one who placed the wood and the one who stirred the pot. The Tosefta (Chapter 12) follows this approach. In the Gemara (Beitzah 34b), it states that the last person is liable, implying that the one who kindled the fire last, i.e., on the wood, is liable. Therefore, only the one who kindled the fire is liable (as I learned from the words of Rabbi Yosef Caro, who cited this in Kesef Mishneh). The Gemara also states that one who sets up the pot is only liable if it is a new pot, requiring tempering to strengthen it. Regarding the liability for stirring, some say that only the first one who stirs is liable, while subsequent stirrers do not contribute significantly to the cooking, and their liability is Rabbinic. This is the opinion of Ramban and Rashba (as cited by the Maggid Mishneh). (There is a difficulty in Chapter 1, 18a, where it questions: "Should we be concerned that someone might stir it?" What kind of question is that, since we could say that it was stirred once before Shabbat? One could explain that the liability there is due to dyeing, as Tosafot wrote, and dyeing occurs each time it is stirred. Pay close attention.)

From Menachot (57a), it is explained that if one placed meat on coals on Shabbat, if it was fully cooked - he is liable even if it was only cooked on one side, meaning the side on the coals. And if it was only cooked to the extent of "Ma’achal ben Drusai," which is one-third cooked according to Rashi and Tosafot - he is only liable if he turned it and it was cooked on both sides to the extent of "Ma’achal ben Drusai." And what is the measure of cooking: the size of a dried fig, and even if the dried fig is not in one place but a bit here and a bit there - it combines to make one liable. This is the conclusion from the discussion according to the interpretation of Rashi and Tosafot there.

However, the Rambam wrote there: "If one placed meat on top of coals, if it roasted to the extent of a dried fig (grogeret), even in two or three places, one is liable. If it did not roast to the extent of a dried fig but cooked entirely to half its usual cooking, one is liable.
