If it cooked to half its usual cooking on one side, one is exempt until he turns it and it cooks to half its usual cooking on both sides." This is the end of his words. Now, the Rambam holds in every place that "food of Ben Drusai" is half-cooked. The beginning and end are like the explanation of Rashi and Tosafot, but what he wrote: "But if it cooked entirely to half its usual cooking, one is liable" is not understood. If his intention is that for half-cooking, one is not liable for a dried fig's worth but for the whole portion, where did he get this from? It seems he deduced this from the language of the Talmud, as it says: 'from one side like the food of Ben Drusai, and from both sides, etc.', and afterwards it says: 'and if it roasted to the extent of a dried fig' there, meaning that for the food of Ben Drusai, a dried fig's worth is not sufficient because it is not complete cooking. Nevertheless, it is a wonder (and it seems this is the intention of the critique of the Ra'avad that the Maggid Mishneh brought there, and the Maggid Mishneh understood his critique was because he did not know its source, and it is a wonder to say so there, and scrutinize well).

We say at the beginning of Tractate Shabbat (4a): "If one attached dough to the oven, he is permitted to remove it before he comes to the prohibition of stoning." And even though removing bread from the oven is a rabbinic prohibition, nevertheless, in order to prevent him from coming to a Torah prohibition, they permitted him to remove it before its surface hardens in the oven. This applies whether it was done unwittingly or intentionally; for in the case of intentional, it is obvious that he will not heed even if we do not permit him (Tosafot 4a s.v. 'before'), and in the case of unwitting, to prevent him from becoming liable for a sin-offering. And even though once he remembers, he would not become liable for a sin-offering, for all those liable for sin-offerings require that the beginning and end be unwitting, as stated in Siman 342, nevertheless, a prohibition is still being performed by him. And so wrote Maimonides there: "If one forgot and attached dough to the oven on Shabbat and remembered, he is permitted to remove it before it bakes and he comes to perform a labor," end quote.

Maimonides wrote in Chapter 6, Law 23: "A Jew who performed labor on Shabbat, if he did so intentionally - it is forbidden for him to ever benefit from that labor, but other Jews are permitted to benefit from it immediately after Shabbat, as it is said: 'You shall keep the Shabbat because it is holy to you' – it is holy, but its actions are not holy. How so? If a Jew cooked on Shabbat intentionally - after Shabbat, others may eat it, but he may never eat it. And if he cooked unintentionally - after Shabbat, both he and others may eat it immediately, and similarly in all such cases." End of quote. 

And there are some of our sages who ruled that if it was unintentional, it is permitted even for him on that very day, and if it was intentional, it is forbidden for others on that day but permitted for him in the evening, as the Tur wrote in the name of Rabbi Yitzchak of the Tosafists (who ruled according to Rabbi Meir, while Maimonides ruled according to Rabbi Yehuda). 

And Nachmanides decided according to the words of Maimonides, and so did the Geonim, and our master the Beit Yosef. Also, the pot is forbidden, but if one cooked for a sick person, the pot is permitted. 

And the reason they did not require waiting after Shabbat for the time it takes to perform the labor is because this only applies to a gentile who did it for a Jew, as it is lighter for him, and if we do not require waiting, he might come to tell him to do it for him. This is not the case with a Jew himself who did this, as there is no concern that he will come to do it again. 

And even according to Rashi, who says the reason for waiting the time it takes to perform the labor is so as not to benefit from Shabbat labor, there is no difference, and in any case, they did not decree in such instances because it is uncommon for a Jew himself to perform labor, and they did not decree in this matter (Magen Avraham, Section 2). 

Only if the end of Shabbat was a holiday - it is forbidden due to preparation, as Shabbat does not prepare for a holiday (ibid.), and if it was done according to the instruction of a sage - it is considered unintentional (ibid.).

In Yoreh De'ah, at the end of Siman 102, it is clarified that an action done on Shabbat is not considered "a matter that has a permissible alternative" (davar sheyesh lo matirin) with regard to mixtures. Despite the fact that for others, since it is permitted after Shabbat, it would be relevant to say "a matter that has a permissible alternative," nevertheless, since for oneself it is always prohibited, it is not relevant for him to say "a matter that has a permissible alternative," similar to a mixture of terumah with chullin, which is not considered a matter that has a permissible alternative for an Israelite because it is permitted for a Kohen, as stated in Yevamot (perek 2). The same applies here. Even though this is not an exact comparison, because for the Kohen it is also permitted now, but here it is prohibited on Shabbat even for others, and since for others it is considered a matter that has a permissible alternative, one could say that for him it is also considered a matter that has a permissible alternative (Magen Avraham, Siman 2). Only on the concluding of Shabbat, when it gets mixed, can it be said that for him it is not considered a matter that has a permissible alternative since it is now permitted for others, but not when it gets mixed on Shabbat (there). Nevertheless, this is the ruling, that since it is clarified in Yevamot that from one person to another it is not relevant, and we judge each one according to his situation, thus here as well, we do not judge from others to oneself (this appears to me in my humble opinion, and also the Taz argues with the Magen Avraham for another reason, see there). And know that even for someone for whom it was cooked, it is permitted after Shabbat, and we do not say that it is like someone who cooked for himself, as in mixtures in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 99, because it is not similar. There, there is a concern that they might increase cooking for him, but here there is no concern that the Israelite will cook for him (there).

Slaughtering is considered a primary category of labor, and its liability is due to the taking of a life. In the Tabernacle, it was relevant for the red-dyed ram skins needed for the Tabernacle's construction, and they would slaughter or kill them. This is the language of Maimonides at the beginning of Chapter 11: "One who slaughters is liable, and not only slaughtering but anyone who takes the life of any type of animal, beast, bird, fish, or creeping creature, whether by slaughtering, by stabbing, or by striking – is liable. One who strangles a living creature until it dies is a derivative category of slaughtering. Therefore, if one takes a fish out of a bowl of water and leaves it until it dies – he is liable for strangling. And not only if it dies, but as soon as it dries up on a rock between its fins – he is liable because it can no longer live. If one extends his hand into the entrails of an animal and dislodges a fetus within its womb – he is liable." Thus is the conclusion of his words.

Creeping creatures that reproduce from male and female or their origin is from the dust – one is liable [for killing them on Shabbat], but if they originate from sweat – one is exempt. We have already explained this in Siman 316 regarding trapping, and there we also explained the labor of wounding, and that in this there is also the taking of life, refer there. If so, it [wounding] is a derivative of slaughtering. Know that in the Jerusalem Talmud, Chapter 2, Halacha 5, there is a dispute: one says that slaughtering is the primary category and wounding is a derivative, and another says that wounding is the primary category and slaughtering is a derivative, refer there. And the Jerusalem Talmud in the chapter "General Principle" holds this as fundamental, refer there. I do not understand what practical difference this makes, unless we say that one must specifically warn [a transgressor] regarding the primary category, but in truth, this is not so as I have written in Siman 242. It seems to me that the practical difference is that if wounding is the primary category, then anyone who damages through wounding is liable even without any improvement, as most wounds are like this. But if slaughtering is the primary category, and in slaughtering there are several improvements even when a tereifah (an animal with a fatal defect) is found, such as correcting to remove it from the status of a limb from a living animal and correcting to remove it from impurity as it says in Pesachim (73a), refer there, then according to this, we also need some improvement in wounding. We have already explained in Siman 316 that there is a dispute regarding damaging through wounding whether one is liable or exempt, and we have elaborated there. This dispute is not found in the Jerusalem Talmud, and therefore, according to the one who holds that wounding is the primary category of labor, everyone agrees that damaging through wounding is liable. But our Talmud, which says there is a dispute about this, necessarily means that slaughtering is the primary category. And indeed, according to the one who holds that damaging through wounding is exempt, one who kills an animal, beast, or bird, where the meat is not permitted for eating and it also becomes carrion impurity, and the only improvement is removing it from the status of a limb from a living animal, thus according to the one who holds that damaging through wounding is exempt even when blood is needed as I have written there, then in such cases – one is exempt, unless we say that the improvement from a limb from a living animal is a significant improvement, which according to everyone is considered fixing and one is liable, as it implies in Pesachim there, and this requires further investigation.

One who cooks for a sick person on Shabbat or performs other prohibited labor—it is forbidden for a healthy person or a sick person who is not in danger to eat from this food or benefit from this labor. Even though it was not done for them, we still decree that if we permit it for them, they might increase the amount for their benefit. This means that after placing the pot on the fire, they might add more food for them, resulting in a Torah prohibition for the healthy person or the sick person who is not in danger, as this constitutes an independent act of cooking. Even if they increase the amount for them before placing the pot on the fire, which is considered one act of cooking, there is certainly a rabbinic prohibition in such cases. Some authorities hold that this also constitutes a Torah prohibition (see Beit Yosef and Magen Avraham, subsection 6), as increasing the amount beyond what is necessary for the sick person incurs the liability of cooking (this is the opinion of the Ran, as mentioned by the Beit Yosef in Siman 311). Even cooking by a non-Jew is forbidden for a healthy person on Shabbat, but on Motzei Shabbat (after Shabbat ends), it is immediately permitted without waiting the time it would take to be cooked, because the non-Jew cooked it permissibly (see there, subsection 7). The prohibition of gentile cooking (bishul akum) does not apply here, as stated in Yoreh De'ah, end of Siman 113, where they did not decree in this manner. However, for a sick person who is not in danger, it is certainly permitted, as it is initially allowed for his sake by a non-Jew, as stated in Siman 328.

However, if one slaughters an animal for a sick person on Shabbat, it is permitted for a healthy person to eat from it. In the case of slaughtering, there is no concern that one might come to do more work than necessary, because even for an olive-sized piece of meat, the entire animal must be slaughtered (Chullin 15a). The Raavad in Chapter 2 and the Ran wrote that this only applies if the animal was unwell from before Shabbat and thus is not muktzeh (set aside and forbidden), since it was fit to be slaughtered between sunset and nightfall (bein hashmashot). However, if it became unwell on Shabbat, it is forbidden for a healthy person due to muktzeh. The Rosh and the Maggid Mishneh wrote that even if it became unwell on Shabbat, it is permitted, for we follow Rabbi Shimon who holds that muktzeh only applies in cases of active rejection (dachiyah beyadayim). This is also the opinion of the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch in section 2, which states: “whether it became unwell yesterday or today, etc.” This also appears to be the view of the Rambam, who makes no distinction in this matter. At first glance, this is difficult to understand, for Rabbi Shimon agrees regarding the muktzeh of living animals, and it has already been explained in section 308 that concerning muktzeh because of “since it was set aside during bein hashmashot, it remains set aside for the whole day” we follow Rabbi Yehuda and not Rabbi Shimon. Here too, it was set aside during bein hashmashot since it became unwell on Shabbat.

However, the clarification of the matter is as follows: In this case, it is not relevant to speak of muktzeh of living animals or “since it was set aside during bein hashmashot.” This only applies to something that has now become fit, like a candle that was extinguished or dried figs and raisins that were not fit during bein hashmashot but are now fit. But this type of muktzeh was never fit, except that the Torah permits slaughter due to the principle of saving a life (pikuach nefesh), and all the more so it permits muktzeh. If the person had been sick between sunset and nightfall as he is now, the muktzeh would have been removed then as well. And now it is removed, except that according to Rabbi Yehuda, we would say in any event that he had no intention regarding this, and it is considered light muktzeh, where Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon disagree, and we follow Rabbi Shimon (and this is also the intention of the Taz in subsection 2, which resolves the difficulty posed by the Magen Avraham in subsection 4).

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote: If one cut fruits from what is attached (to the ground) on Shabbat for a sick person, even if the person was already sick before Shabbat—it is forbidden for a healthy person to eat on Shabbat, because it grows and continues to grow on Shabbat, and there is an issue of muktzeh (set aside) with it. And this is not understood at all, for the animal also grows on Shabbat, and we have explained that there is no issue of muktzeh here, even if the sickness occurred on Shabbat, and certainly if the sickness was there before Shabbat. And if it is because of the picking on Shabbat, the same applies to slaughtering an animal on Shabbat. And fundamentally, the matter is difficult, for cutting fruits would be anyway forbidden for a healthy person lest one increase for him, similar to cooking. And if we say it is such that one cut one fruit and the sick person did not eat the entire fruit, in such cases there is no concern that one would increase for him, similar to slaughtering; if so, if one cooked one piece, we should also say it is permitted for a healthy person. Rather, it is certainly a concern that one might increase for him to cook another piece, if so, also with fruits there is concern that one might cut another fruit. And furthermore, they challenged him that the growth on Shabbat should be nullified by the majority (Magen Avraham section 8), and so wrote the Tosafot in Bava Kamma (69a). See there.

The source of the law is in the great book of our master, the Beit Yosef, in the name of Orchot Chaim, and this is his language: "One who cuts fruit that has not finished ripening for a sick person on Shabbat – it is forbidden for a healthy person because of muktzeh, etc." End quote. According to this, it can be somewhat reconciled that because it has not finished ripening, it is considered muktzeh, but not when it has finished ripening, and so the commentators have explained. However, if so, the main point is missing from the words of our master, the Rema, and why did he omit the case of it not having finished ripening? However, this is also not understood, for what difference does it make in the prohibition of muktzeh whether it has finished ripening or not? And if we say that it was his intention from the previous day to pick them on Shabbat for the sick person, then even if it has not finished ripening it should not be muktzeh and should be nullified by the majority. Furthermore, why did he not pick them the day before, and it is forced to say that the medicine was specifically when they would be picked on Shabbat. Moreover, even if they have finished ripening, what does preparation have to do with something attached [to the ground], and if so, even if a non-Jew picked fruits on Shabbat and the Israelite intended for them to be picked on Shabbat, we would also say that it is permitted. Clearly, this is not implied later in section 325, see there. In conclusion, this law is difficult to understand, and it has no correct reasoning, and it requires further investigation.

And know that I have heard from those who wish to say that nowadays when one sets up a samovar for a sick person on Shabbat, it is permissible for a healthy person to drink from it, similar to the case of slaughtering. Just as it is impossible to obtain an olive's bulk of meat without slaughtering, likewise, it is known that it is impossible to cook a small amount of hot water in the samovar without filling it entirely; otherwise, the copper will melt. Similarly, the herb known as tea also cannot be limited to prepare for one person alone, as is known, and one is compelled to put in more than the sick person's needs, as otherwise, it is impossible, as is known. Therefore, there is no concern here that one might increase for the healthy person. 

And if the concern is that when they drink and want to drink more, they will pour more water and add more herbs, we do not worry about this. After all, they did not worry that another pot might be cooked but only that they might add to the same pot. However, to start a completely new cooking, why should we worry? And if the concern is that for the sick person himself, one would set up a small samovar, and now one sets up a large one, where is the basis for this concern? If so, we should worry that one might slaughter a larger bird, and besides, every householder always sets up the samovar that is designated for his household.

Nevertheless, it does not seem permissible, as it is very likely that if we permit it for the healthy, many people will drink, and in this, we indeed should worry that they will increase the tea herb and put in much more than if they had only prepared for the sick person alone. And we have never practiced leniency in this matter. And even if it was set up by a non-Jew, it is forbidden, as explained, for there is no difference in this matter.

We have already written that one who cooks with heat derived from fire (toldot ha'ur) is liable, for just as it is forbidden to cook with fire itself, so too it is forbidden to cook with heat derived from fire. Therefore, it is forbidden to place an egg next to a hot pot or to break it on a cloth that has been heated by fire so that it will roast or cook. Even with heat derived from the sun (toldot hachama), such as a cloth heated by the sun, it is forbidden, as a precaution lest one come to use heat derived from fire. Similarly, it is forbidden to bury the egg in sand or road dust heated by the sun, and it is even forbidden to do so before Shabbat, for burying is forbidden even before Shabbat, as we wrote in Siman 256 (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 10). However, with the sun itself, such as placing an egg or water in the sun to heat, it is allowed, because the sun and fire are not confused with each other. But heat derived from the sun can easily be confused with heat derived from fire, since an observer does not know whether it is heat derived from the sun or from fire, which is not the case with the sun itself. It is forbidden to roast an egg on a rooftop heated by the sun, as we decree this as a precaution against heat derived from fire, and similarly, it is forbidden on sand for this reason, contrary to those who wish to permit it. One may place a cooked dish into a pit to keep it from spoiling, and we do not decree that one might come to level the ground to position it properly (Shabbat 146a). This is also taught in the Mishnah (ibid.): one may place a cooked dish into a pit to keep it, good water into bad water to cool it, and cold water in the sun to heat it, for we do not decree sun on account of fire as we explained. (See Bach and Magen Avraham subparagraph 10, and their words require examination, as they follow the opposite approach, and the Machatzit HaShekel struggled to reconcile them with forced explanations. However, in practice, they agree with all that has been explained. The difficulty raised by Magen Avraham regarding Rambam's words in Chapter 9, where he wrote that melting metals incurs liability for cooking, and in Chapter 12, he wrote that heating iron to temper it incurs liability for kindling, and in melting there in Chapter 9, he wrote: or heating metals until they become a coal, has already been resolved by Lechem Mishneh, that initially, it softens and is liable for cooking, and when it becomes a coal, it is considered kindling. In my humble opinion, there is no difficulty at all, and Rambam was precise in his words, as in Chapter 9, he wrote: 'until it becomes a coal,' which is like cooking that transforms from raw to cooked, and in Chapter 12, he wrote: 'to temper it,' which is much less than a coal, and therefore, it is not related to cooking but rather to kindling. Pay attention.)

And know that the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch wrote all the laws of cooking in this section, while the Rambam divided them into two places, in Chapter 9 and Chapter 22. The reason is that in Chapter 9 he explained Biblical cooking, and in Chapter 22 he explained Rabbinic cooking, as he began there in Chapter 21: "It is stated in the Torah, you shall rest… which the sages prohibited due to a rabbinic decree," and in these chapters, he explained all the laws of rabbinic decrees. The Tur and the Shulchan Aruch do not have the practice of explaining what is a Biblical prohibition and what is a Rabbinic prohibition, as is written in Section 242, therefore they included everything in one place. And it is essential to know and understand this, because there is a practical difference in cases of doubt, as a doubt regarding a Biblical law is treated stringently, while a doubt regarding a Rabbinic law is treated leniently. Therefore, the scholar must understand which type of cooking we are discussing. And with our limited understanding, we will explain with the help of Heaven to the best of our ability, and may You, O Lord, assist us.

And this is the language of the Rambam in Chapter 9, end of Law 3: "One who cooks on a fire something that was already fully cooked or something that does not require cooking at all – is exempt," end quote. For example, oil, which is debated in the Gemara (40b) whether it is subject to cooking, and the conclusion is that it is subject to cooking. However, when there is something that does not require cooking – one is exempt. Now, the Rambam does not distinguish between something dry and something liquid, nor whether it has cooled down or not, as he states a general rule that something that has been fully cooked – there is no further cooking, for there is no cooking after cooking. But this is on the condition that it was fully cooked; if it was not fully cooked, even if it was cooked to the level of Ma'achal Ben Drusai (partially cooked, but edible) – it is still subject to cooking. And from his words, it implies that even if it improves upon further cooking, it is not subject to cooking. The opinion of the Rashba, the Ramach, and other commentators is that once something has been cooked to the level of Ma'achal Ben Drusai, it is no longer subject to cooking by Torah law (according to the Maggid Mishneh and Kesef Mishneh). This all pertains to Torah law. However, by Rabbinic decree, there is still a concern of cooking, as they prohibited returning food to the stove on Shabbat even if it deteriorates upon further cooking, as the Rambam writes in Chapter 3 (there). Accordingly, when the Rambam writes 'exempt,' he means exempt but forbidden, as is the case with all exemptions on Shabbat.

In Chapter 22, Law 8, it is written: "An item that was cooked before Shabbat or soaked in hot water before Shabbat, even though it is now cold – it is permissible to soak it in hot water on Shabbat, etc." End quote. And one should not question that we wrote that it is rabbinically forbidden, for indeed this is true. Therefore, he was precise to say it is permissible to soak it in hot water, meaning and not to cook it. And the language of the Mishnah is also thus (145b): "Anything that came into hot water before Shabbat – we may soak it in hot water on Shabbat." And it did not say 'cook', for cooking is certainly forbidden. And also, one should not ask since they said generally to soak in hot water, it implies even in a primary vessel (kli rishon), for if not so, it should have clarified so that we do not err in the halacha. And if so, we hold that a primary vessel cooks. However, indeed, one who is precise in his words there will find that even a primary vessel does not cook according to Torah law, and according to Torah law, there is no cooking unless the pot is standing on the fire.

And this matter is explained in the Jerusalem Talmud in Tractate Kira (Halacha 5) where it states: "There is no clear scalding, there is no clear cooking except when the fire is underneath it," see there. And before this (Halacha 4), it says: "They made a restriction for a kli rishon (first vessel) but did not make a restriction for a kli sheni (second vessel)," see there. This means that the Sages prohibited a kli rishon because of the restriction. And from our Talmud, it is also explained similarly, as it says regarding the Mishnah of the frying pan and the pot (42b): "Rabbi Chiya taught: Salt is not like spices, for even in a kli rishon it does not cook. And this is what Rav Nachman said: Salt needs as much cooking as the meat of an ox," see there. And there is much wonder, for if so, it is permitted by Torah law to cook ox meat and salt, astonishingly. Rather, it is certain that in a kli rishon it does not cook, but when it is on the fire, it does cook. And the Rambam clarified this there in Halacha 6 in concise words, and this is his language: "And similarly, a boiling pot, even though it was removed from the fire, one should not put spices into it, but one may put salt into it, as salt does not cook except over a great fire," end quote. This clearly supports our words. (Also in Yoreh Deah, Siman 68, we explained this, see there. And a bit of this was noted there by the Pri Chadash, see there. And it is a new matter, but the truth is so. And with this, you will understand why the Rambam wrote many laws of cooking in Chapter 22 and not in Chapter 9, and examine this well).

According to what we have explained following the opinion of the Rambam: Any item that has been cooked or baked, if it has been fully cooked, even if it improves when simmered, is permitted by Torah law in terms of cooking, but rabbinically it is prohibited to cook it. However, placing it in a boiling vessel, even if it is a primary vessel, is permitted. But heating it in an oven, if the oven is hot and suitable for cooking, is prohibited, and the same rule applies to items that do not require cooking. 

And it seems that based on this, placing onions and garlic in dishes on Shabbat morning is permitted, because they are not usually cooked. And even though they are placed into the dish to be cooked, those added at the time of eating are ruined by cooking, and our intention is that they should not be cooked, as is known. Therefore, even when the dish is hot, since it is not by the fire, there is no Torah prohibition of cooking, and there is also no rabbinical prohibition, because this is something unintentional, and on the contrary, we intend the opposite. Furthermore, it is not a "psik reisha" (an inevitable outcome), because we can sense in taste that most of the time they do not have a cooked taste at all. And even "psik reisha d'lo nicha lei" (an inevitable outcome that he does not desire) is permitted according to many authorities, and even according to Rashi, as long as he intends the opposite, it is permitted, as we have written in Siman 242. Therefore, for all these reasons, there is no prohibition here, and some great authorities who objected to this did so without reason (so it seems in my humble opinion). See also sections 25 and 44.

And this is the wording of the Tur: "Even a dish that has already been cooked is subject to the prohibition of cooking if it has cooled down, but while it is still hot – it is not. And if it has not been fully cooked, and even if it has been cooked to the level of Ma'achal Ben Drosai – it is still subject to cooking even while it is still hot. And this applies to a dish that has liquid, but a dry item that has already been cooked – it is allowed to soak it in hot water on Shabbat, as it says: 'Anything that comes into hot water, etc.'” end quote. And in this language, our Rabbi the Beit Yosef wrote in section 4. They wrote that this is the opinion of Rashi, that there is no cooking after cooking for a dry item, but for a liquid item that has cooled down, there is cooking after cooking. This is not like the Rambam, who holds that even with a liquid item, there is no cooking after cooking. Nevertheless, it is possible to say that they do not disagree, for the Rambam also forbids it rabbinically as he wrote, and they did not explain that this is from the Torah. However, the distinction between liquid and dry was not heard from the Rambam (for they explain the Mishnah that anything that comes into hot water before Shabbat can be soaked in hot water on Shabbat, for this is cooking, and to the Rambam, we explained that it is only allowed to place it in hot water and not to cook, and this will be further clarified with G-d's help).

However, afterward, the Tur wrote, and this is his language: "Rabbi Eliezer of Metz wrote: Even though there is no cooking after cooking with a dry item, there is cooking after baking or roasting if it is subsequently cooked in liquids. Therefore, it is forbidden to put bread even in a secondary vessel that is still hot enough to cause the hand to recoil. And it is a wonder why it is forbidden in a secondary vessel... and it does not seem reasonable to forbid it in a secondary vessel... and even according to his opinion, there is no baking after baking, and no roasting after roasting," end of quote. Similarly, our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in paragraph 5, and he brought both opinions regarding placing bread in a secondary vessel. And our teacher, the Rema, wrote that there are those who are lenient even with a primary vessel, but the custom is to be cautious initially not to put bread even in a secondary vessel as long as it is still hot enough to cause the hand to recoil, end of quote. 

And the explanation of the matter is: Rabbi Eliezer of Metz introduced that it is true that there is no cooking after cooking with a dry item, this is when the dry item was cooked, like meat in a pot and similar things, in which case we have learned: anything that has come into hot water etc. But a baked item, like bread or meat roasted over a fire - there is cooking after baking and after roasting. And his proof is from Pesachim (41a) that one does not fulfill the obligation with matzah that was cooked after baking, which implies that cooking nullifies the baking. However, this is not a clear proof, for with matzah the issue is that we require the taste of matzah and it is lacking, and thus the Raaviah refutes it. Nonetheless, the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch were concerned about this.

Regarding placing bread into boiling gravy, those who prohibit it in a primary vessel (kli rishon) base their reasoning on the principle that since there is cooking after baking and a primary vessel cooks, even according to what we explained that this cooking is rabbinic - it is still prohibited rabbinically. Additionally, it appears that these rabbis do not differentiate between a primary vessel and being on the fire, and they hold that a primary vessel cooks according to Torah law. Therefore, since there is cooking after baking - it is prohibited, but a secondary vessel (kli sheni) does not cook. Those who are stringent even in a secondary vessel do so because any item that cooks in a secondary vessel is also prohibited in a secondary vessel, as will be explained, and they hold that bread is likely to cook even in a secondary vessel. Our teacher, the Rema, who permits even in a primary vessel, does so because he follows the opinion of the Ra'avyah that there is no cooking after baking, and it is entirely permitted. According to these opinions, placing onions and garlic into a primary vessel is certainly prohibited, since in their view this constitutes cooking according to Torah law and it is considered certainly cooking, which would be a "psik reisha" (an inevitable outcome). However, it seems to me that if one does not desire them to be cooked, it would be a "psik reisha delo nicha lei" (an inevitable outcome that one does not desire), and it would be permitted. In a secondary vessel, it seems to me that even according to those who prohibit placing bread in a secondary vessel, this is because it is likely to cook, but onions and garlic certainly do not cook in a secondary vessel. How can one assert that they cook in a secondary vessel? Therefore, the common practice is justified even according to these opinions. However, I have seen someone who is stringent with onions even in a secondary vessel (Taz, section 8), and I do not know on what basis he is so stringent.

And know that, as explained, regarding a liquid matter, there is cooking after cooking when it has cooled even if it was fully cooked. Our teacher, the Rema, wrote in paragraph 4 that some say this is specifically if it has shrunk and improved (i.e., thickened and become better), but in the case of something that has shrunk and deteriorated, there is no cooking after cooking. They were perplexed by this, asking what relevance this has to cooking; rather, this distinction applies to the concern that one might stoke the coals, as in the case of shrinking and deteriorating, one would not stoke the coals, as stated in Siman 253. However, regarding what constitutes cooking in all aspects, it is still considered cooking, and therefore his words were rejected (Bach, Taz, Sk 4, and Magen Avraham Sk 8).

In my humble opinion, the primary view is as Rema said, and its explanation is as follows: Since it has shrunk and deteriorated, he does not intend to cook but rather to warm it slightly, and even if it is a "psik reisha" (an inevitable consequence) and it must cook, it is a "psik reisha d'lo nicha lei" (an inevitable consequence that he does not desire) and is permitted. Especially since according to the Rambam, the Rashba, and the Ramech, there is no cooking from the Torah at all in this case, as we explained. And in general, I am astonished that our teachers, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, did not mention the view of the Rambam at all, and his view is the most clarified according to the Talmudic and Jerusalem Talmudic discussions as we stated.

And we learned in the Mishnah that anything that was in hot water, etc. (145b), that anything that was not in hot water before Shabbat, one may rinse it in hot water on Shabbat, except for old salted fish and Spanish mackerel, because rinsing them completes their preparation and it is considered cooking (Rashi), since they only need a little, and their rinsing completes their preparation. The rinsing is in a secondary vessel, meaning that hot water is poured on them from a secondary vessel. However, it is forbidden to soak them even in a secondary vessel, because it appears like cooking (Magen Avraham, section 15), and for old salted fish, even pouring on them is forbidden. From this we learn regarding our herring that it is forbidden to pour hot water on them from a secondary vessel, but it is permitted to soak them in cold water. And perhaps soaking appears like a labor, but rinsing them in cold water is certainly permitted (Taz, section 5). And similarly, it is permitted in lukewarm water, and only in hot water that the hand recoils from is it forbidden.

And since it has been explained that anything for which washing constitutes the completion of its preparation is considered cooking and one is liable for it on Shabbat, according to this, the herb called tea on which hot water is poured, and it is known that its cooking is easy, and it even cooks in a second vessel as we can see with our own eyes, one who pours hot water on it on Shabbat even by means of a second vessel is liable for a sin-offering. Many are mistaken in this with senseless claims: some say that the tea has already been cooked at its place of origin and there is no [prohibition of] cooking after cooking. This is a great error, even if it were true, since there the cooking is not to cook it but to make it suitable for cooking, and how can we say about this that it is already cooked, when they sell it now at full price to cook it. And I have also heard that this is not true, that they do not cook it at its place of origin. Some prepare it using a second vessel, which means they pour hot water from the first vessel into a container, and then place the tea into it, and afterwards they put the water and tea into the teapot, and then pour hot water on them from a first vessel, and in any case they are liable for a sin-offering, especially since we see with our own eyes that it cooks in a second and third vessel, as its cooking is easy. Some have the custom of pouring boiling water from a first vessel on it before Shabbat, letting it stand for a little while, and then pouring out the water, leaving the tea dry. The next morning they pour hot water from a first vessel on it, since it has already been cooked from the previous day and there is no cooking after cooking with a dry item. However, in this manner, the hot water must remain on the tea for a little while before Shabbat to cook it and not just be poured on the tea and immediately poured out, because in one moment it will not cook. The proper way is to prepare the essence before Shabbat, and this is our custom, and the same law applies to coffee and other such types of cooking like chocolate and cocoa.

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote in section 4 that the same law applies to any hard item that is not fit to eat at all without soaking—it is forbidden to soak it on Shabbat, as this constitutes completing the work, end quote. This means that even in cold water, if it is not fit to eat without soaking, it constitutes completing the work and one is liable for "striking the final blow." Similarly, a salty item that cannot be eaten without rinsing and one rinses it—one is liable. Many have interpreted that his intention is specifically to soaking in hot water, but in my humble opinion, it seems that even in cold water it is forbidden when this completes its preparation. However, we do not know of such foods that are not fit except through soaking.

And know that all the laws that have been explained as forbidden due to cooking – it is forbidden even to place [the food] on the stove or oven before kindling, as stated at the end of Siman 253 (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 11). And even if a non-Jew kindles the oven, nonetheless, the Jew who placed [the food] on the stove or oven is liable, as this is like one who places the pot and another who brings the fire, for both are liable (Machatzit HaShekel). However, according to this, the liability only applies if the non-Jew kindled the oven immediately, and they were both involved in the same act. But if he kindled it later – the first one is exempt, as stated in subparagraph 4, see there. But in truth, this is also forbidden by Rabbinic decree, unless the non-Jew places the pot on the oven according to the details explained at the end of Siman 253, and see there what we wrote at the end of that Siman.

And since with a dry item there is no cooking after cooking, therefore something that has been fully cooked and is dry, without any liquid, even if it has already cooled down, it is permitted to place it opposite the fire, even in a place where the hand recoils. And why are we not concerned that one might stoke the coals, for which reason it is prohibited to leave [food] on a stove or oven, even in something hot, as stated in Siman 253, Section 32? This is not comparable, for it has already been explained there that leaning against a stove is permitted, as stated there in Section 7, and here it is like leaning and not like leaving. And even though it is not exactly the same, for there leaning has the separation of the wall and it is recognizable and one will not come to stoke, and here there is no separation between the pot and the fire, in any case, since it is only permitted opposite the fire and not on the fire itself, meaning a bit distant from the fire, there is a recognizable difference and one will not come to stoke (Magen Avraham, Section 38 in the name of the Rosh). However, on a stove, it is forbidden because of leaving, as stated there. This is regarding a dry item, but regarding a liquid item, it is forbidden if it has cooled down. If it has not cooled down, meaning the hand still recoils, even with a liquid item it is permitted, for if it has not cooled down, there is no cooking after cooking even with a liquid. And Rabbeinu the Rema wrote in Section 15 that there are those who are lenient and say that as long as one does not place it on the fire or on the stove directly, but rather near it, even if it has cooled down, it is permitted, and the custom is to be lenient in this if it has not entirely cooled down, end quote. This is according to the opinion of the Rambam that we explained, that there is no cooking after cooking even with a liquid that has cooled down, but placing it directly on the fire is prohibited rabbinically, as stated in Section 19, and placing it directly on the stove is considered leaving. And what he wrote, that the custom is to be lenient if it has not entirely cooled down, does not have a correct reason, but if it has entirely cooled down, they were concerned about the opinion that there is cooking after cooking with a liquid, but with a dry item it is permitted. (And the Maharshal, Section 39, wrote that even with a dry item it is forbidden if it has entirely cooled down, because it is considered as placing initially and it is forbidden lest one stoke as in Siman 253, see there. And I am puzzled, for there it discusses inside the oven, as stated there in Section 32, see there, and what comparison is there to here, and investigate carefully).

Our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, wrote in section 16: "It is permissible to place an 'infanda' (which is like our kugel) near the fire in a place where the hand recoils, even though the fat within it that has congealed becomes liquid again. All the more so, a pot that has congealed sauce, when the fat melts it is not visible, and it is permitted. There are those who are stringent, and the custom is to be stringent, but in a case of need, one can rely on the first opinion." End of quote.

The explanation of the matter: Since there is no cooking after cooking with a dry item, it is therefore permissible to place it near the fire. The fact that the fat becomes liquid again is not prohibited due to the concept of "nolad" (something newly created), because it happens naturally. This is similar to placing snow and hail in a cup, which is permitted, as well as placing sugar in a cup of hot water or fat in food. And all the more so in a pot where the fat is not distinguishable when mixed with the dish. And even though 'infanda' is considered frying, and according to this opinion there is cooking after frying, nevertheless, even now it is not considered cooking but frying, and there is no frying after frying.

However, those who are stringent prohibit it because the fat melts and it is considered "nolad," and it is not comparable to snow, hail, sugar, and oil that are placed into dishes or hot water, because there it dissolves and is not noticeable, whereas here the fat is noticeable on its own and is prohibited. But in a pot, it is indeed permitted because it is not distinguishable on its own. And even according to this opinion, 'infanda' itself is not prohibited.

In practice: Initially, the custom is to be stringent, but the main opinion follows the first opinion, and in a case of need, one can rely on this opinion. All of this does not pertain to returning [food] to the oven or stove, as there is a prohibition there due to the concern that one might stoke the coals. However, placing it near the foods is permitted, as written in Siman 253, and see what is written in Siman 318, section 23.

Therefore, it is permitted to place in the cooked dishes meat and fish, and dried figs and dried kashas, and dry rice, and kugel, and similar items. However, one must be careful that there is not too much fat such that the fat alone starts dripping. If a lot of fat is needed for this, then it is permitted, even with fat. But into the oven – it is forbidden, unless the oven does not have much heat and coals to the point that it is close to cooling down, then even in the oven it is not prohibited, as is written in Siman 253, Section 32, see there. (And in the Shach (Se’if Katan 35), it is brought in the name of the Maharit that in the city of Constantinople, the maidservants would place the stuffed chicken to warm in the oven on Sabbath morning before eating, and the Maharit permitted it because our ovens, which open from the side, are like being opposite the firewood, see there and it requires further study).

According to the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, when it comes to a liquid that has cooled down, there is a concept of cooking after cooking, and it is forbidden to place a vessel containing a hot item that is not hot enough to cause one’s hand to recoil on top of a pot that is so hot that it can heat the upper vessel to the extent that one's hand would recoil from it, as this constitutes cooking, for the derivatives of heat are like the heat itself. However, for a dry item, it is permitted, and similarly, for a liquid that is still at a temperature causing the hand to recoil, it is permitted to place it on top of such a hot pot to maintain its warmth so that it does not cool down, as there is no cooking involved since it has not cooled down and remains at a temperature causing the hand to recoil. Some say that even if it has not been fully cooked, in such cases there is cooking after cooking even if it has not cooled down, as mentioned in section 23; nevertheless, placing it on top of a pot is permitted because on top of a pot it cannot come to complete cooking (Taz, subparagraph 9). I do not understand the source for saying this, and many great authorities have disputed this, and this is the primary view, as mentioned in section 36. Even if the pot is insulated in something that adds heat, it is still permitted to place on top of it a vessel containing a liquid that is at a temperature causing the hand to recoil and has completed its cooking, as this is not considered insulation. All of this follows the opinion of the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, but according to the Rambam, there is no cooking after cooking even for a liquid, and our teacher the Rema mentioned this opinion in section 15 as stated in section 31, it is permitted even when the upper vessel is not at a temperature causing the hand to recoil (and this is the intention of the Magen Avraham in subparagraph 21, and see also the Magen HaChaim).

Some interpret that the permission to place a utensil containing liquid that is still hot on top of an insulated pot applies even if the pot is on the fire. Others interpret that if the pot is on the fire, it is always forbidden, as it is akin to placing it on a stove on Shabbat initially. The first opinion holds that since the pot acts as an intermediary, it is not like placing it directly on the stove, since the stove is directly on the fire. The primary ruling follows the first opinion, as the prohibition of the stove is due to the concern that one might stoke the coals, and here, since it is placed on the pot, there is a noticeable difference. However, it is certain that it must be distant from the fire if it has not been fully cooked (Taz, Siman 311:11), which applies to those who permit it in the previous clause when it is not fully cooked, but as we have explained there, this is not so. Also, even according to the latter opinion that prohibits, if the upper pot was removed from the stove after nightfall, it is permitted to place it on the pot, as it is stated in Siman 253, that in such cases, there is no prohibition of leaving it on when returning it to the stove, and consequently, the same applies to placing it on the pot (Magen Avraham, Siman 253:24).

And this which was explained, that if it is "yad soledet" (a temperature at which the hand recoils), it is permitted to place it on top of a pot, our teacher Rabbi Joseph Karo wrote in section 6: that one can seal its mouth with dough if there is dough that was kneaded from the previous day, end quote. And we are not concerned about spreading (the dough), for certainly spreading also applies to dough, since it is not sealed tightly but only that it should not be exposed, and one does not spread it well but only adheres it a little bit, and spreading only applies when one spreads it well with his finger so that it is smooth (Taz, subparagraph 10). But if he spreads it well, it is forbidden, and likewise with any other spreadable substance (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 22). And the reason they were not concerned that one might spread it is because, since it is only for a short while, one will not spread it, and this has already been explained in section 258 (and it is explicitly mentioned in the Gemara at the end of "Bameh Tomnin," see there. And they were not concerned that the dough might bake due to the heat, since he does not intend for this, and it is not a "psik reisha" (an inevitable result), and this somewhat supports the Taz in subparagraph 9, and pay attention).

It has already been explained that a dry item that has been fully cooked is permitted to be placed opposite the fire, as there is no further cooking after cooking for a dry item. Consequently, it is also permitted to place a dry and cold item that has been fully cooked on top of a kettle that is on the fire, for anything that is permitted opposite the fire in a place where the hand recoils (from the heat) is also permitted on top of a kettle that is on the fire. However, some say it is forbidden, because this is similar to placing it initially on a stove, which is forbidden lest one stoke the coals, and even if it has been fully cooked and is drying out and becoming worse, it is forbidden to place it initially on the stove on Shabbat. And how is a kettle different from a stove? Nevertheless, the main ruling follows the first opinion, that it is not similar to a stove where there is no separation between it and the fire, but on top of a kettle, the pot serves as a separation. And just as there is no concern about stoking the coals when it is opposite the fire because there is a noticeable distance from the fire, so too here there is a noticeable distinction, as stated in paragraph 31.

And our Rabbi, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 8 regarding this law that has been explained, and this is his language: "Nevertheless, if it is a dish that has sauce and benefits from further cooking – it is forbidden according to all opinions." End quote. That is to say, as it has been explained that it is forbidden to place a vessel containing something liquid that is not so hot that the hand would recoil from it on top of a covered pot, similarly it is forbidden to place it on top of a samovar, even though the heat of the samovar is not as strong as the heat of the pot. Nevertheless, it is somewhat more lenient, as it is only forbidden if the dish benefits from further cooking (this seems to be his intention in my humble opinion, and this resolves the great difficulty of the Magen Avraham in section 26, see there, and this law applies only to the samovar, and scrutinize this well).

It has already been explained that a primary vessel (kli rishon) cooks, and we have clarified in section 20 that from the words of the Rambam it is understood that this is by rabbinic decree, and according to Torah law it only cooks when it is on the fire. This is also evident from the Talmud Bavli and Yerushalmi, as referenced there. However, from the words of the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch it does not seem so; and even though they did not meticulously differentiate between Torah law and rabbinic law, nevertheless, from the straightforward reading of their words, it appears to be complete cooking according to Torah law. This is also the implication from the words of our Rabbis, the Tosafists, in Shabbat (42b, s.v. "but", see there), and similarly in other places. But from the words of Rashi there it is clearly understood like the Rambam (as he wrote in s.v. "in a vessel": "It is permissible to place even in a primary vessel once it has been removed from the fire," end quote, thus distinguishing between them). The Ran there wrote that the Yerushalmi holds this way and not our Talmud, see there. In my humble opinion, this needs further examination, for it is also clearly implied in our Talmud, as I wrote in section 21, see there.

A primary vessel (kli rishon) cooks even after it has been removed from the fire as long as it is still at a temperature at which the hand recoils (yad soledet bo). If it is not at such a temperature, it is permitted. And even though, with regard to the laws of forbidden and permitted foods, there is reason to say that it still absorbs and releases flavors afterward, nevertheless, regarding cooking, it certainly is not so (Magen Avraham 318:28). The reason is straightforward: regarding absorption and release of flavors, from a Torah perspective, it absorbs and releases in a primary vessel, as we have written in Yoreh De'ah, siman 68. Therefore, there is reason to say that it also continues to absorb and release by rabbinic decree. Some hold that even a secondary vessel (kli sheni) absorbs and releases when the hand recoils there, as we have written there, and all for this reason. But regarding cooking from a Torah perspective, it does not cook in a primary vessel, as we have explained. And even for those who hold that from the Torah there is cooking, they agree that the Jerusalem Talmud (Yerushalmi) does not hold this, as we have written. Therefore, we do not need to be stringent neither with a secondary vessel in which the hand recoils, nor with a primary vessel in which the hand does not recoil.

There are those who want to say that in the Jerusalem Talmud it is stated that they made a separation for a primary vessel (kli rishon) even if it is not hot enough to cause the hand to withdraw (yad soledet bo) (there), but this is not so. The Jerusalem Talmud refers to when it is hot enough to cause the hand to withdraw. And the reason it is called a "separation" is because according to the Jerusalem Talmud, a primary vessel does not cook at all, but the Rabbis made a separation for it. And this is the language of the Jerusalem Talmud, first chapter of Ma'aserot (halacha 4) and Kira (halacha 4): "What is the difference between a primary vessel and a secondary vessel? Rabbi Yosa says: Here the hand controls (meaning it does not withdraw) and here the hand does not control. Rabbi Yona says: Here and here the hand does not control, but they made a separation for the primary vessel and did not make a separation for the secondary vessel." And we have explained this further in Yoreh De'ah, and the Magen Avraham, because he ruled that a primary vessel cooks by Torah law, was forced to explain that it is when the hand does not withdraw, and he does not read "controls" but "withdraws," but this is not so, and the matter is clear with God's help.

Therefore, it is forbidden to place spices in a primary vessel as long as it remains at a temperature where the hand recoils, nor onions, nor garlic, nor anything that requires cooking. However, the Sages permitted salt (Mishna Berura 39:2), because salt requires extensive cooking similar to that of ox meat, which only cooks over a fire. Nevertheless, ox meat remains forbidden for the reason written by the Tur, that although the meat itself does not cook, its fat and moisture do cook, and further reasons for this will be explained.

Know that in the Gemara there are two opinions regarding salt: one as mentioned, and the other to the contrary, that the cooking of salt is very easy, such that it even cooks in a secondary vessel when the hand recoils there. Therefore, some forbid placing salt even in a secondary vessel. The primary ruling, however, is as mentioned earlier, but one who is stringent in this matter shall be blessed. If one transgresses and places salt in a pot while it is near the fire, thus committing a Biblical prohibition, nevertheless the food does not become prohibited, because the salt is nullified in relation to the food. And even though it adds flavor and is something that has a permissible alternative, since it is not discernible in the pot, it does not have the power to prohibit because the cooking is not noticeable at all. Additionally, this is a case of "this and that causing," since the meat was salted before Shabbat. And although this is debatable, the primary ruling is that it is permitted, contrary to those who wish to forbid, and so have written the great later authorities, and this is the main ruling. (See Taz, subparagraph 14, and those who disagreed with him. Also, see what the Magen Avraham wrote in subparagraph 31, that if the salt added now has enough to give flavor without the salt from before, it is forbidden. This is not so clear. He also wrote that sea salt does not involve cooking because there is no cooking after cooking, and according to this, sugar would have the same rule. However, some dispute this—see Tosefet Shabbat and examine it carefully.)

We have already written that even though the Talmud states that salt is needed for cooking like the meat of an ox, and therefore it is permissible to put salt into a primary vessel, nevertheless, for ox meat it is forbidden, as the Tur wrote, because the moisture in it cooks. The Rosh wrote another reason: if it is old salted meat, it cooks quickly. Therefore, the Tur did not mention this reason, as it does not apply to new salted meat.

Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 9 regarding a primary vessel: that some say it is forbidden to put salted meat into this vessel, even if it is ox meat. This refers to the words of the Rosh. It is not understood, as the Rosh only wrote about old salted meat. Our teacher the Rema wrote: "It seems to me that even without salting, it is also forbidden, but he mentioned salting because otherwise it is forbidden due to the blood." This means that the main reason is as the Tur wrote, but he mentioned 'salting' because it must be salted, otherwise it is forbidden due to the blood. This is quite forced: if so, why mention salting, and why not write the reason of the Tur. Therefore, it appears to me that our teacher the Beit Yosef spoke a great matter. For according to the Tur's reasoning, what shall we do with meat that has dried and has no moisture, and according to the Rosh's reasoning, what shall we do with new salted meat, shall we permit it, heaven forbid? Therefore, he cleverly reasoned that all salted meat cooks, for the Talmud only stated that salt is needed for cooking like the meat of an ox, meaning that their nature in cooking is the same, requiring strong cooking, and it is not dealing with prohibition and permission but with the nature of their cooking. But when are they the same? When the meat has not been salted, but when it has been salted, the salt softens it and it suffices with cooking in a primary vessel. Therefore, it is automatically forbidden to do so on Shabbat, for how can one do it, if one salts it, it will cook, and if one does not salt it, it is forbidden because it was not salted. Perhaps this was also the intention of our teacher the Rema. (And indeed, I do not know what compelled the Rosh and the Tur not to explain it this way, and according to what I have said, there is no need for the lengthiness of the Taz in section 13, and the Magen Avraham in section 30 is clear, and pay attention).

In a secondary vessel (kli sheni) - it is permitted to place spices even though the hand recoils from it, because a secondary vessel does not cook. And although regarding absorption and emission some prohibit, nevertheless, cooking in a secondary vessel is not an issue according to all opinions. Furthermore, even regarding absorption and emission, we do not hold this way, as written in Yoreh De'ah, siman 105. Therefore, it is permitted to place spices, onions, and garlic on Shabbat morning in a secondary vessel. There are those who are stringent with onions in a secondary vessel because we see that they sweeten from their bitterness after being placed there for some time (Taz 14). This is an excessive stringency, as they sweeten due to the sauce and fat. On the contrary, we see during weekdays that when onions are added to a dish, they are added at the height of cooking, indicating that they require much cooking. And in the beginning of chapter 10 of Terumot, it is explained that onions are hard to absorb, even though there it discusses onions in their peel. Nevertheless, we learn from there that they are harder to absorb than other things, so how can we say that regarding cooking they are easier? This is perplexing. Therefore, it is permitted to place onions in a secondary vessel on Shabbat morning without any hesitation, and even though it is a solid item, it disperses on the plate. All the more so if the onions are placed in a tertiary vessel (kli shlishi), where there is no room for doubt. For those who enjoy this, it is a delight of Shabbat, and preventing this prevents the delight of Shabbat, and this is the common custom.

Pouring from a primary vessel onto spices when the hand recoils from them is prohibited, because pouring cooks to the extent of a thin layer. Therefore, it is forbidden to put spices in a bowl and pour from a primary vessel onto them, and if one did pour, they are forbidden to the extent of a thin layer. And even though regarding immersion we are stringent that it is not like a primary vessel, as will be explained in Siman 491 because there are those who hold that pouring is not like a primary vessel, in any case, regarding Shabbat we are stringent according to the opinions that prohibit. Nevertheless, it seems to me that the dish should not be forbidden because of the spices that were forbidden to the extent of a thin layer, and in Yoreh De'ah Siman 91 it is explained that in a case where a thin layer is required, if it was not peeled and cooked like this, it is permissible after the fact, see there. And similarly, when it is difficult to peel, it is permissible, unlike those who are stringent in this matter.

Maimonides wrote in Chapter 22, Law 5: "A bathhouse tub that is full of hot water — one may not add cold water to it because it heats them significantly, nor may one pour a flask of oil into it because it is as if cooking it. However, one may pour hot water into a tub of cold water. A boiling pot from which hot water has been removed — it is permissible to add cold water to it in order to warm them, and it is permissible to pour hot water into cold water or cold water into hot water, as long as it is not in a primary vessel, because it heats them significantly." End quote. (And the language of the Gemara 42: Beit Hillel says: Whether hot water into cold water or cold water into hot water. What are we discussing? A cup, but in a bathhouse tub, hot water into cold water and not cold... Rabbi Yehuda thought to say a bowl is like a bathhouse tub, Abaye said to him: Rabbi Chiya taught a bowl is not like a bathhouse tub).

There are those who interpret that an "ambati" (bath) is a primary vessel (R"an and Beit Yosef), therefore it is forbidden to place cold water into it so that it should not be heated by the heat of the primary vessel. However, from it into the cold water – it is permitted, for one reason being that the lower (cold water) prevails, and another being that generally the vessel into which water is placed has a larger quantity of water (Tosafot there), which means that the reverse is permitted – from cold to hot, and therefore the Rambam specifically stated "a bath of the bathhouse that is filled with hot water," indicating that in such a case, the cold water is indeed minimal. Subsequently, he states the law regarding a kettle from which hot water was removed – it is permitted to place cold water into it to warm it, implying that a significant amount of cold water is being added. However, a small amount is forbidden, and this law is a separate Mishna there (Mishna 41a). And even though the conclusion of the Gemara there is that it was emptied along with the water, this is according to Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that an unintentional act is forbidden, but we follow Rabbi Shimon, so this is not necessary (and although one might infer from the language "it was emptied," the Rambam did not use this language, and you should understand this well). He then states that it is permitted to pour hot water into cold water or cold water into hot water in a secondary vessel since a secondary vessel does not cook. The reason he did not use the Talmud's term "cup" is to include also a bowl, as the conclusion is that it is not like a bath. (And even though a bowl is certainly a secondary vessel, since otherwise why wouldn't it be like a bath, in any case, a bath is a primary vessel. And if you ask, if so, how could it be thought that it is like a bath, it can be said that because it is for bathing, they were stringent according to Rashi's interpretation. And it concludes that it is not so, that there is no difference, and therefore the Rambam also mentioned "bath" to teach that even for bathing, it is forbidden only in a primary vessel, not in a secondary vessel. And thus, we have resolved this approach against all objections, see Beit Yosef and Taz section 18, and understand this well).

And there are those who interpreted his intention that this bathtub is a secondary vessel (Magen Avraham and Bach and Taz there, and so wrote Tosafot there). The reason they forbade pouring cold water into hot water is because since the water is meant for bathing, it heats it up significantly, meaning the sages decreed on this. But in other secondary vessels, it is permitted, and even in a bowl which is also for washing, they were not as stringent as with a bathtub, because it does not contain a large amount of water. But a bathtub which is a primary vessel – it is forbidden even to pour hot water into cold (Taz there), because they were stringent with bath water. And there are those who say that in a primary vessel even a large amount of cold water into a small amount of hot water is forbidden (Bach), but this is not the opinion of our teachers, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, as will be explained. And it cannot be said that just a thin layer cooks immediately when it falls into the hot water, because this does not apply to water which mixes together immediately. But with a dry item, this is certainly the case, even with hot into cold, for example to put a piece of boiling meat into cold sauce, because while it cools down, it cooks a thin layer, as is mentioned in Pesachim at the beginning of the chapter "How to Roast" and in Yoreh De'ah, Section 91 (Magen Avraham, subsection 35).

And the words of the Tur are very puzzling regarding this matter, as he wrote: "A cup from which hot water from a primary vessel was poured for drinking - it is permissible to mix cold water with it, whether you pour the water from it into the cold water or pour the cold water into it. But a bowl that contains hot water for washing, even if it is a secondary vessel - it is forbidden to put cold water into it, because since it is for washing, the hot water is generally very hot, and the cold water mixed with it will cook. But pouring from it into cold water - is permitted, because the lower element prevails. And similarly, the law for a primary vessel used for drinking is that it is permissible to pour from it into cold water, but it is forbidden to pour cold water into it. And this applies to a small amount of cold water, but if there is a lot of cold water and it cannot cook but only reduce its chill - it is permitted."

And his words are puzzling, for the Talmud explicitly concludes that a bowl is not like a bath and it is permitted to put cold water into it. Many things have been said about this, but none of them provide a satisfactory resolution. (See Taz, section 17, who is puzzled by the explanations of the Beit Yosef and the Bach, and he wishes to distort the words of the Tur, which is even more puzzling. As for the difference in the Tur between the use of the singular and plural forms, I am puzzled because for the vessel it uses the singular form and for the water it uses the plural form, and indeed even in the case of a cup it uses the plural form with them, but this is because it refers to the waters. And what the Derisha explains is clearer, that the Tur holds that according to the conclusion, the law follows Rabbi Shimon ben Menasia that in a bath it is forbidden to put hot water into cold water, see there in Tosafot, and in this, a bowl is not like a bath, but cold into hot is forbidden, see there. However, this also does not work well, for if so, why did he not write the law regarding a bath, and investigate further.)

In my humble opinion, it appears that the words of the Tur are correct. Indeed, it is difficult to understand: if a bathtub is considered a secondary vessel whose prohibition is due to its use for washing, as stated, why isn't a basin considered like a bathtub? And the explanation we gave, that a basin does not contain much water, is strained, for what measure is there for this? 

Therefore, the Tur interprets: either the basin is a tertiary vessel from which water is drawn from the bathtub, and therefore it is not like a bathtub, or it is not used for washing. And it is explicitly stated in the Song of Deborah: "He asked for water, she gave him milk; she brought him curds in a lordly basin," which implies that a basin is used for drinking. Similarly, in Shabbat (129b), there are references to oil basins. 

And based on this, one might think to be stringent, considering the basin like a bathtub because it contains a large amount of water, but it concludes that this is not so. However, a basin used for washing is indeed similar to a bathtub.

And as he wrote that with a primary vessel for drinking it is permitted to pour from it into cold [liquids], it implies even into a small amount of cold [liquid], as it says that it is forbidden to pour cold [liquids] into it, and this applies to a small amount of cold [liquid], but a large amount is permitted. We learn from this that when it is permitted to pour from it into cold [liquid]—even a small amount of cold [liquid] is permitted. The reason is that although the cold [liquid] is in small quantity, nevertheless, we hold that the lower [temperature] prevails, and whatever is poured into the cold [liquid], the cold [liquid] cools it little by little and it does not cook the cold [liquid]. Therefore, he mentioned at the beginning the reason that the lower [temperature] prevails. According to his words, when drinking hot [liquids] on Shabbat morning from a primary vessel, and the [little bit of] cold water is cold, and one puts a little cold water in a small container and pours the boiling [liquid] from the primary vessel over them—it is done correctly, and there is no need to first pour the hot [liquid] into the small container and then put a little cold water into the small container, which is a secondary vessel (and so we practice).

But our Rabbis, the authors of the Tosafot, did not write this in the same manner in that passage, and this is their language: "One may pour hot water into cold water even in a primary vessel... and not because the lower substance prevails, for if so it would be difficult for the one who says the upper substance prevails, and even for the one who says the lower substance prevails, it would cook a thin layer. Rather... pouring hot water into cold water implies that the cold water below is more abundant, as it is customary to place the lesser amount into the greater amount, and therefore the small amount of hot water does not cook at all, etc." End quote. It is clear that if the cold water were lesser, it would be forbidden to pour hot water from a primary vessel into it. And it cannot be said that this was written according to the opinion that the upper substance prevails and we hold like the opinion that the lower substance prevails, for according to their words, even the one who says the lower substance prevails holds that it cooks a thin layer.

However, the Tur does not hold this way, as this only applies to a dry item, and not to water which mixes immediately. And the Tosafot themselves in Pesachim (40: 'the pan') write this, that a mixture does not cook a thin layer, and so writes the Ran in our passage, see there (and this is what the Magen Avraham hinted at in Siman 35). According to this, based on the Tosafot in Shabbat, one should be careful not to pour hot water from a primary vessel onto cold food. Nevertheless, in practice, if one does so, we do not object, since the Tur, the Ran, and the Tosafot in Pesachim permit it. Additionally, one can rely on the opinion of the Rambam, the Rashba, and the Ramach, which we wrote in section 19, that there is no cooking after cooking even in a liquid, see there.

(And see Beit Yosef who writes that according to the Tur, even for bathing with a primary vessel it is permitted to pour hot water into cold water, and the Rema in Darkei Moshe, section 6, disagrees with him. However, for us, there is no practical difference because we do not have water for bathing. But I am puzzled that in Shulchan Aruch, section 11, his words do not imply this, as he glosses on a bath even though it is a secondary vessel, see there, and it implies that the same applies to a primary vessel, and he says there that one pours hot water into cold water, see there, and it requires further study and attention).

This is the language of our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, in Section 12: "A kettle from which hot water has been removed – it is permissible to place a large amount of cold water into it to warm them. And it is permissible to pour hot water into cold water or cold water into hot water, provided that it is not in a primary vessel, because they heat a lot. And if the water is so much that it is impossible for them to cook but only to lose their chill – even in a primary vessel it is permitted, as long as it is not on the fire." End of quote. For on the fire or the coals where it can cook – it is forbidden even if the water is completely cold and they are removed immediately, since it is a place where it can cook as will be explained, with God's help. And know that in a kettle from which hot water has been removed or still has hot water – they only permitted a large amount of water, for a small amount will cook. And it was explained in the Gemara that the permission for a large amount of water, even though it strengthens the kettle. That is, a kettle made of iron, and hot iron when cold water is placed on it strengthens, and this is a craft and this is the completion of the craft of smiths (Rashi 41a). Nevertheless, they permitted it, because he does not intend to strengthen it, and there is no "inevitable result" here, as it is not clear that it will lead to strengthening because of this. (Magen Avraham, section 146, and the words of the Meiri who brought that wherever there is no intention, there is no "inevitable result," and there is no craft here at all, as he contradicts several passages, and the Meiri himself in Chapter 22 regarding strengthening wrote: because it is possible that it did not reach strengthening, and the Lechem Mishneh already wondered about him in Chapter 12 there, and examine carefully).

It is permissible to place a pitcher of water or other liquids in a second vessel that contains hot water, but in a first vessel – it is forbidden, for a first vessel cooks. However, a second vessel, even though it is still hot to the touch – it is permissible because its walls are not hot and it gradually cools down (Tosafot 40b: s.v. "And we learn"). And one should be careful not to immerse the entire pitcher within the vessel, as this constitutes insulation and is forbidden on Shabbat, even with something that does not add heat, as stated in Siman 259, rather the pitcher should remain uncovered from the top (Taz, se'if 19). And there is an opinion that if one draws liquid with a vessel from a first vessel – it takes on the status of a first vessel stringently (ibid), and this is explained in Yoreh De'ah Siman 92. And it is clear that if it remained in the first vessel until it boiled – it is considered like a first vessel (Acharonim and Tashbetz).

It is permitted to place a pitcher of water or other beverages opposite a fire to remove their chill, provided that they are placed far enough from the fire so that they cannot become heated in that location to the point where the hand recoils from it, meaning that it would scald a baby's belly. It is difficult to measure with the hand since some recoil from a minor boil and some only from a strong boil. When it stands near the fire in these conditions, it is also permissible to place it until it becomes lukewarm, as this is included in the category of removing the chill (Tosafot 48a, s.v. "Mai"). However, it is forbidden to bring it close to the fire to a place where it can become heated to the point where the hand recoils from it, and even to leave it there for a short time just to remove the chill is forbidden because it could come to heating. It seems to me that the same applies to placing it near a stove or an oven, and similarly with our ovens (kikkalim), the same law applies: if it is impossible for it to come to cooking, it is permitted, and if it can come to cooking, it is forbidden.
