The same law applies to fruits that are eaten raw, such as apples and similar things that are eaten raw, which are very cold, and one places them opposite the fire or in the ovens to remove their chill – it is forbidden to place them where they can come to cooking. Even things that are not eaten raw, if placed in a place where they cannot come to heating, it is permitted. It is also permitted to place it even in a lead vessel, even though the lead heats up a bit, we are not concerned with this, since he does not intend for this (see Magen Avraham, section 37).

Rabbeinu the Beit Yosef wrote in Section 17: "It is forbidden to place cold [food] on a kettle, even to thaw it, as long as the kettle is hot enough that if it were left there for a long time, it would come to cooking, that is, it would reach the temperature at which the hand recoils. The law of placing [food] on a kettle is the same as placing it near a fire. If it is not that hot, it is permitted." End quote. It is clear that his intention is regarding cold, dry food that has not yet been cooked, for if it had been cooked, it would be permitted in any case, as it has already been clarified that with dry food, according to everyone, there is no cooking after cooking. Therefore, it is obvious that it is permitted to place cold meat or fish to remove their chill on a boiling pot. However, his intention is regarding something that has not yet been cooked, whether roasted or fried, for those who hold there is cooking after roasting or frying. Therefore, something like "taygeachatz" which is fried, is forbidden to place on top of a boiling pot if it can come to cooking there. But what we call roasted meat "gibratins," this is only cooked, and roasting is only meat that is roasted on a spit over the fire, which we do not know of, and among us, all meat is considered cooked.

The frying pan and the pot that were removed from the fire while still boiling, if they have not yet fully cooked - it is forbidden to stir them, because stirring incurs liability for cooking. Therefore, one should not take from it with a spoon, as this is considered stirring and involves cooking. However, if it is fully cooked – it is permitted, as stirring no longer involves cooking. But wool in a dyeing pot, even if it has absorbed the dye – it is forbidden to stir it, because for dyeing, the more one stirs, the better the dyeing process. And our teacher, the Rema, wrote in section 18: that initially, one should be cautious with a pot in any case, meaning not to stir in a boiling pot even if it is fully cooked. According to this, when taking the cholent on Shabbat morning from the oven while it is boiling, it should not be taken with a spoon. However, the common practice is to permit taking out the legumes or the potatoes or the cassia with a spoon, and there is no concern in this, because even stirring is permitted according to the law, and it suffices to be initially cautious with stirring and not with taking with a spoon (Taz 23 and Magen Avraham 144). And our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 19: that it is forbidden to spread oil and garlic on the roast while it is still opposite the fire, even if it was roasted before Shabbat, because in any case, the garlic and oil will cook. And it is clear that even after it has been removed from the fire while still boiling - it is forbidden to spread it, as this is complete cooking. Therefore, one must be cautious not to spread roasted goose with garlic while the goose is boiling (Taz 24). And some say that with fat that has already been cooked - it is permitted to spread it, as it no longer involves cooking (Magen Avraham 145), and there is no concern of "newly created" since it is not in its original form (there), and it is like crushing snow in a cup. And one should not say that the fat is fried, and according to some authorities, there is cooking after frying. This is not so, because even now when spreading it, it is considered frying, and there is no frying after frying. One should not crush it by hand but place the fat on the meat, and it will be absorbed. (However, regarding those who are stringent, as the Rema wrote in section 16 that this is considered in its original form, and as stated in section 32, it might not be correct. But even there, the Rema wrote that in a case of need, one can rely on the first opinion, as it is the main one as mentioned there).

Separating food from waste is considered a principal category of work, as is winnowing grain with the wind to separate the grain from the chaff, which is also a principal category of work. We do not say that the wind completes the task and not the person, because on Shabbat, the Torah prohibits thoughtful work. When one causes the wind to assist him in winnowing, it is considered thoughtful work, and therefore one is liable for causing this winnowing. Even though in matters of damages this is called causation and one would be exempt, nevertheless, regarding Shabbat, this is called an action and not causation, because this is the method of winnowing and his intention is fulfilled, as he benefits from the wind, and it is included in the prohibition of "you shall not do any work" (Bava Kamma 60, and Rashi and Tosafot there). Therefore, even though we also expound on Shabbat: "It is the action that is prohibited, but causation is permitted" (Shabbat 120b), this is not considered causation on Shabbat, because this is the method of the work, and on Shabbat, the Torah prohibits thoughtful work, which is considered work among people. Similarly, sifting flour to separate the bran from the flour is a principal category of work. These three are considered principal categories of work, and all of them were in the Tabernacle in the work of the spices, where they would separate, sift, and winnow with the wind.

And even though these three, when we scrutinize them, are all one labor, separating the food from the waste, in truth, the Gemara (73b) raises this difficulty, and this is the language of the Talmud: "This is winnowing, this is selecting, this is sifting. Abaye and Rava both said: Any labor that was in the Tabernacle, even though there is something similar to it, it is considered." Meaning, since we derive the labors of Shabbat from the Tabernacle, therefore, any distinction in the labors, even though their essence is the same, each is considered on its own. And this means that selecting is done by hand, winnowing is done by wind, and sifting is done with a sieve, and they are considered three separate labors. And it is necessary to specifically warn by name, and if they warned for selecting because of winnowing or sifting, he is not liable to stoning, and similarly for all of them because they are divided into three primary categories.

The derivatives of these labors: the one who churns, who places congealed milk in a vessel and the whey, which is the liquid part, drips out, and this is called "serawetka" - is liable for selecting (Borer) (page 95a). And it seems to me that when they make butter and the liquid called "mashlinka" remains, and they pour it out from the butter or take the butter out from it - they are liable for selecting. Similarly, those who make cheese using rennet, and the waste remains, and they remove the waste - this is a derivative of selecting. And one who filters dregs, this is either a derivative of selecting or a derivative of sifting, and in the Gemara (138b) there is a dispute: Rabba said it is due to selecting, and Rabbi Zeira said it is due to sifting, and it is not clarified to us whom the law follows. And it seems that even Maimonides was not clear on the law, as he wrote in Chapter 8, Law 11: "And similarly, one who selects dregs from liquids - this is a derivative of selecting or a derivative of sifting and is liable," end quote. According to this, when they come to warn him, they should either warn him for the act of filtering itself, as we have already clarified in Siman 242 that even when warning for a derivative - one is liable. However, if they want to warn for the primary category, they need to warn him for both. This is not called a doubtful warning, and moreover, Maimonides ruled that a doubtful warning is considered a warning in Chapter 16 (Law 4) of Sanhedrin. And the measure for all of them is like a dried fig, and for filtering it seems to me that the measure is a quarter-log, like most liquids (and according to Rashi 138b, warning for sifting is sufficient).

In the Jerusalem Talmud, in the section on the principal rule regarding the Mishnah of the primary labors, it says: "Rabbi Yudan said: There are instances where one separates pebbles all day and is not liable, and there are instances where one takes the size of a dried fig and is immediately liable. How is this? If one was sitting on a pile and separating pebbles all day, he is not liable. But if he took in his hand the size of a dried fig and separated, he is liable." End quote. We learn from this that anyone who separates or winnows, as long as they have not completed the separation or winnowing of the heap before them, is not liable. However, by rabbinic law it is certainly forbidden, and therefore the decisors did not mention this. However, in the case of sifting, this does not apply, as in sifting, the good flour falls through the sieve holes, and the flour with the waste remains in the sieve. Once a dried fig's worth of good flour has fallen, one is liable. Similarly, in separating food from waste, once one has separated a dried fig's worth, one is liable. In winnowing, this also does not apply, as the wind only removes the chaff, and when winnowing with a fan, it is a derivative of winnowing and one is liable. Note that in the language of the decisors, as well as in the Tur and Shulchan Aruch in this section, they included everything under the term "separating," as the specific names do not make a difference except regarding a warning, but regarding the prohibition, it is all one. And so it is in the Gemara (74a), where it says "One should not separate with a sieve or strainer," as mentioned. And it is stated in the Jerusalem Talmud that in the case of chaff, sand, and dirt, one is liable for sifting, as in every matter there is a liability for sifting.

There is no difference in selecting between separating food from waste or separating waste from food – in both cases, one is liable to bring a sin offering. And so it is explicitly stated in the Talmud: in one place it says (138b), "What is the way of selecting? One selects the food and leaves the waste," and in another place it says (74b), "One should not select waste from food, and if one does, one is liable to bring a sin offering." According to our Rabbis, the authors of the Tosafot there, the matter is as follows: one always selects the lesser quantity from the greater quantity. When the waste is greater, it is customary to select the food, and when the food is greater, it is customary to select the waste. However, according to the law, it is all the same, even according to the Torah. According to the Rambam, there is a distinction: separating waste from food is always liable, even if done by hand to eat immediately – one is liable. And in separating food from waste: to eat immediately – it is permitted, as will be explained with God's help. And similarly, in sifting we say there: "What is the way of sifting? Waste is on top and food is at the bottom," and if the sifting is the opposite, food on top and waste at the bottom – one is also liable, for what is the difference.

The obligation of selection (Borer) is not specifically about food and waste, as the same law applies even to two types of foods mixed together, such as figs and grapes, and if one selects one type from the other, he is liable. For when he selects the type he desires, the other type that he does not desire becomes like waste regarding the type he desires (Tosafot 74a, s.v. 'Hayu'). Similarly, the Rambam wrote, and in the Jerusalem Talmud there is a dispute about this, and it ruled according to the one who obligates. And it says there that this only applies to two types, but in one type, to select large from small or vice versa, or black from white and similar cases, it is not considered selection. And this is the language of the Jerusalem Talmud: "Selecting foods from foods: Hezekiah said - liable... According to Hezekiah's opinion, even selecting circles from among circles, even pomegranates from among pomegranates, or similar cases, even people from among people." And this is its explanation: he asks if according to Hezekiah's opinion, it is also forbidden in one type to select one from the other, and it rejects this: 'or similar cases, even people, etc.', meaning that if so, you would say that even selecting people from among people would be considered selection, in astonishment, and he strongly rejects this matter. And I saw one of the great ones who wrote that even in one type selection applies (Taz, sub-section 2), and his words are astonishing. (Also the Taz criticized him, and the Elya Rabbah seems to have grasped in the Jerusalem Talmud, that he says this straightforwardly that according to Hezekiah, even this is considered selection. And his words are astonishing, for the Jerusalem Talmud asks this as a question and rejects it, and so explained the Pri Megadim. And what the Taz brought from the Mahari"l regarding crushed matzah, certainly flour from crumbs is considered selection even in one type, and similarly separating egg white from yolk or vice versa, as the Magen Avraham wrote, sub-section 16, and similarly in the Rambam and Shulchan Aruch specifically two types of foods, and examine this thoroughly).

The obligation of selecting is not limited to types of food, for we say in Shabbat (74b): "Rava said: One who makes a barrel is liable for seven sin offerings, one who makes an oven is liable for eight sin offerings, one who makes a basket is liable for eleven sin offerings." And Rashi explained: regarding the barrel, he selects the coarse pebbles from among them—thus there are two; and regarding the oven, he explained similarly; and regarding the basket, he wrote: 'a basket of reeds… he selects the good ones, thus this is selecting, etc.' See there, thus selecting applies to everything. And this is logical, for in the Tabernacle they performed selection with spices, and they were not for eating (and so wrote the Taz, section 12).

According to this, a significant question arises: How do we find our way in several matters, such as when forks, knives, and spoons are mixed together, and we need knives at the moment, so we select the knives from among them, or the forks or spoons? Similarly, when many garments are hanging on the wall and we need two or three garments, we take all the garments from the wall, select the necessary garments, and hang the rest back on the wall. Likewise, if many books are piled up together and we need certain books at the moment, we select and take them. Similarly, at the table of the wealthy, there are various types of small and large plates, and for each dish, different plates are selected. In such cases and many similar matters, if selection (berira) is involved in everything, we would find ourselves in great difficulty in many matters.

The answer to this matter is twofold: The first aspect is that in cases where the distinction is very evident to the eye, it is not relevant to speak of "selection" (berira), as this is merely a matter of taking, not selecting. All these items we have mentioned are visible to the eye, such as clothing, utensils, and books, obviously. And one should not argue that two types of fruits, like figs and grapes, are also visible to the eye, for this is not the case. Due to their small size and abundance, they require selection from one another, which is not the case with clothing, utensils, and books. 

The second aspect is that it will be explained that during the time of eating, one can take the food from the waste and eat it, as this is not considered a method of selection but rather the normal way of eating. Consequently, in all matters where we currently need to wear the clothing, use the utensils, and study with the books, it is akin to the time of eating, and selection is not relevant here. (Certainly, selecting books from one another to place them in their proper location, or separating clothes to hang them, as well as utensils, is not permissible based on this reasoning. However, according to the first reasoning, there is no prohibition in this matter. This requires further examination, and take note.)

During a meal, one is permitted to separate the food from the waste and eat, for otherwise, how would it be possible to eat on Shabbat? Indeed, every person, when taking food to eat, must necessarily take the food and leave the waste. And in many types of food, there is waste. Therefore, it is certain that during the time of eating, it is not considered sorting. However, this is specifically when done by hand, but if done with a sieve or a sifter, it is considered sorting. Similarly, it is specifically when one takes the food and leaves the waste, but if one takes the waste and discards it, and then eats the food, it is considered sorting and one is liable for a sin-offering. The same law applies to two types of food: if, during the meal, one takes what he desires to eat and leaves what he does not desire to eat, it is permitted. But if one takes what he does not desire to eat and sets it aside, and then eats what he desires to eat, it is considered sorting and one is liable.

This is the language of the Rambam there: "One who selects food from waste, or if there were two types of food before him and he selected one type from another: with a sieve or a sifter - he is liable; with a tray or a dish - he is exempt. And if he selected with his hand to eat immediately - it is permitted. But one who selects waste from food, even with one hand - is liable... One who selects food from waste with his hand to set it aside even for later that day - it is considered as if he selected for storage and he is liable. If two types of food were mixed before him - he may select one from another and set it aside to eat immediately, but if he selected and set it aside for later, even for later that day, such as if he selected in the morning to eat in the evening - he is liable." End of quote. And we learn from his words that anything not for immediate consumption is considered selection and he is liable, and if he intends to eat immediately - it is permitted to select food from waste with his hand and eat it, but with a sieve or sifter - he is liable, and with a tray or dish, which are types of utensils like a wide tube in the front and narrow in the back, and he puts legumes with waste in the wide part and shakes it, and the legumes, being round, fall through the narrow mouth and the waste remains inside (Rashi on that) - there is no liability for a sin-offering, as this is considered selection in an unusual manner, and the primary selection is with a sieve and sifter (there). And when selecting waste - even with his hand, he is liable, and the same applies to two types of food as explained.

And what is called "immediately"? Our teacher, the Rema, wrote in paragraph 1: That which one selects for the purpose of the meal in which he is currently sitting - this is called "immediately," and even if others are eating with him, it is permitted. Therefore, it is permissible to select the greens called "salatin" from the spoiled leaves within it, as much as is needed for that meal. And we learn from his words that all that is prepared before the meal for all the people of the meal - selection does not apply to it, specifically selecting the food from the waste, and not the reverse as was said. Therefore, they should be careful not to select the spoiled leaves, even if they are fit to eat under duress, since he does not want to eat them now - they are considered waste (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 3), for even with two types of complete foods it is thus as was said. (And regarding what he said that it is also permitted for others, it is explained in the Gemara there: 'selects and eats immediately, selects and sets aside immediately,' and Tosafot wrote: selects and sets aside for the sake of others there.)

Behold, the language of our master, the Beit Yosef, in the Shulchan Aruch is like the language of the Rambam, and from their words, it is clarified that whether [it involves] selecting food from waste or food from food: when one selects by hand the food he wishes to eat immediately at the meal prepared before him - it is permitted from the outset. But if he selects for a later time - it is considered as selecting for storage and he is liable. However, I have a significant question about their words: Why, in the case of selecting food from waste, do they write: 'one who selects food from waste to set it aside even for later that day - it is considered as selecting for storage and he is liable,' and in the case of selecting food from food, they write: 'and if he selected and set it aside for a later time, even for later that day, such as selecting in the morning to eat in the afternoon - he is liable' end quote. Why did they not write this language earlier regarding selecting food from waste?

It appears to me, in my humble opinion, that our teacher, the Beit Yosef, addressed this matter in his great work. He wrote that from this language it seems that when one selects food from waste, even if he selects it to eat in three or four hours, he is liable. Whereas when selecting food from food, he is only liable if he selects it in the morning to eat in the evening. However, he does not know from where the Rambam derived this distinction, and if he did not intend this, why did he change the language? His opinion is that one is only liable after an hour, and so wrote the Mordechai there. According to this, I am puzzled: if so, why did he himself also write this language in the Shulchan Aruch? Thus, it appears that it was not conclusive to him.

Therefore, it appears to my humble opinion that indeed it is so: when separating food from food, the obligation only applies from morning until evening, unlike when separating food from waste. This is proven from the Talmudic discussion regarding the Baraita of two types of food, where Ulla interprets it as follows: one separates and eats on the same day, one separates and sets aside on the same day, and for the next day, one should not separate, and if one did, they are liable to bring a sin offering. Rabbi Chiyya questions this: is it permitted to bake on the same day, is it permitted to cook on the same day, until Abaye later explains: one separates and eats immediately, one separates and sets aside immediately, and on the same day one should not separate, and if one did, they are liable. 

One must understand Ulla's opinion, for surely he knew it is forbidden to perform work on the same day. However, the matter is indeed thus: certainly, in the case of separating food from waste, which is the essence of the act of selection, Ulla also held that if one separates for later, they are liable. But here, when separating food from food, since both are complete foods, yet we call the unwanted ones "waste" because one does not desire to eat them, Ulla thought that only when there is no intention at all to eat on Shabbat, but rather for the next day, is it considered as food and waste. But when separating to eat on the same day - it is nothing, for perhaps later one will decide to eat the other as well. However, Rabbi Chiyya did not agree with this reasoning, and Abaye explained that even for the same day one is liable. Nevertheless, we do not establish this as a significant dispute, and the reasoning is also thus: we require at least from one meal to another, namely from morning until evening, and it is appropriate to call this "food," as it will be eaten at the morning meal, and "waste," as it will not be eaten. But up to an hour or two or three later, it is not appropriate to call the other "waste," for perhaps by the next meal one will decide to eat the other as well (and the term "immediately" in the Gemara is not necessarily literal, as we find in Gittin 27, see there).

And know, that according to the Rambam, one who removes waste from food is liable. This is not the opinion of the Tur, who holds that if the food is greater in quantity, one removes the waste. Moreover, if the food is greater, one removes the waste, but if the waste is greater, it is forbidden even to move it, because the food is nullified by the waste. When does one remove the food and leave the waste? When the food is essentially greater, but the effort of separating is greater in removing the waste, such as when it is fine, in such cases one takes the food and leaves the waste, as mentioned there, and this is the approach of the Tosafot there. However, the legal decisors did not agree with this, and this is what our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, wrote in section 4: "One who removes waste from food, even by hand, is liable. And even if the food is greater and there is more effort in separating the food, nonetheless, one should not remove the waste, even in order to eat immediately," end quote, and this is to exclude the words of the Tur. Additionally, what the Tur wrote, that if the waste is greater, it is forbidden to move it because it is nullified by the majority, was also omitted. Their reasoning is clear, for how can food be nullified by waste, since it is inevitably not nullified, as it is meant for eating, and especially if the waste is suitable for animal consumption, then it is permitted to move it.

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote in section 3: Two types of fish are considered two types of foods, and it is forbidden to separate one from the other except by hand to eat them immediately, even though the pieces are large and each one is distinct on its own. However, if it is one type, even if one separates large pieces from small ones, it is not considered separating (borer). Even if there are two types and one separates large pieces from small ones or vice versa, it is permitted since one is not separating one type from another. His source is from the Terumat HaDeshen (Siman 57). 

He explained there that even though, at first glance, separating only applies when they are mixed and indistinguishable, as is evident from the language of Mordechai, and if so, since the fish are large pieces and each is distinct on its own, separating should not apply, nevertheless, one should not be lenient without clear proof. Therefore, Rabbi Moshe Isserles ruled simply. 

In any case, it seems to me that this only applies when there are many pieces, but if there are four or five pieces and one takes one or two, it is not considered separating. This is a daily occurrence when meat and chicken, which are certainly two types, are brought to the table, and the housewife takes the chicken from the plate to save for the Sabbath morning. Similarly, with fish, when two types like akht and salayan are taken, and one takes a piece or two or three pieces from the plate to save for the Sabbath morning and unintentionally takes from one type, is there any concern of separating? Certainly not, as we have said.

Know that it is obvious that even with one type, if some pieces are hard to eat for some reason, they are considered waste (Magen Avraham section 5). Sour and sweet apples, when both are edible, do not seem to be considered two types. But apples and pears are considered two types. Similarly, when there are many pieces of bread from grain and wheat on the plate, they are considered two types. However, grain and grain, even if one is sifted more, called sitnitsah, are considered one type. 

(And indeed, if we were to judge the law of separating with any two foods even if they are few, you wouldn't leave anyone alive, and heaven forbid to say so. In my humble opinion, separating only applies when one does it meticulously to separate one from another, but with casual taking, it is not considered separating).

The poskim (decisors of Jewish law) have written that one who selects lupines from their waste is liable. This means that even though selecting food from waste is permissible when one wants to eat immediately, in the case of lupines, it is considered as if one is selecting waste from food. The reason is that their waste sweetens them when they are boiled together, and it is considered as if one is selecting waste from food, which is prohibited.

We have not clarified this law because we do not know what lupines are. From what appears in the Gemara, lupines are inherently bitter, and their waste sweetens them. Therefore, selecting lupines is considered as selecting waste from food and is prohibited. In places where this species exists, it is necessary to do this (select them) before Shabbat.

I have seen someone who raises a general question regarding the obligation of selecting waste from food, which incurs liability: isn't it a labor that is unnecessary for its own sake, since one does not need the waste at all and his intention is merely to remove the waste from himself, which is similar to carrying out a corpse for burial (as brought in the Mishna Berura in the name of Yeshuos Yaakov)? This comparison astonishes me, for with a corpse, there is no need for the labor at all, but in selecting, one does need the food and cannot eat it without separating the waste from it, therefore it is necessary for its own sake. And should you say that it would have been better if the waste had never been mixed in at all, then we could say the same about many labors. Moreover, our Rabbis, the Tosafists, have already taught us (Shabbos 31b, s.v. “and dismantling”) that we are liable for all labors as they were in the Tabernacle, even if they are not necessary for their own sake, such as dismantling in order to build, even though the construction is not improved by the prior dismantling, and similarly tearing in order to sew and extinguishing in order to kindle, where it is necessary that the kindling is better because of the extinguishing, meaning to make charcoal. If not, it would be a labor that is unnecessary for its own sake. Nevertheless, in dismantling and tearing, this is not required, because it was so in the Tabernacle. Therefore, also in selecting, since it was so in the Tabernacle – one is liable. And we have already written this in Siman 313.

It is stated in the Jerusalem Talmud that there is a major principle: one who grinds garlic, that is, someone who crushes garlic, first violates the prohibition of threshing, and when he separates the peels, he violates the prohibition of selecting, etc. And it appears to me, in my humble opinion, that the explanation is as follows: he takes many garlic cloves and crushes them together, and through this, the heads fall off them, and only the peels of all the garlic cloves get mixed with the garlic, and he selects the peels from the food. Therefore, he is liable for the heads due to threshing, which is a derivative of threshing. And when he selects all the peels from the garlic, he is liable due to selecting. But one who peels each garlic clove individually and cuts off the head and peels the peel, as is done with onions, is not liable for threshing or selecting, just as we do every Shabbat when we peel onions and garlic one by one, just as we eat nuts and almonds, where we discard the peel for each nut. This is the normal way of eating them.

And our teacher, the Beit Yosef, brought this Jerusalem Talmud at the end of Siman 321 in his great book, and this is his language: "The Sefer Mitzvot Gadol (SeMaG), Sefer Mitzvot Katan (SeMaK), and the Terumah wrote that even so, it is not prohibited to peel garlic and onions to eat immediately, for that passage in the Jerusalem Talmud is discussing peeling to set aside, etc. And Rabbeinu Yerucham wrote that what the Jerusalem Talmud forbade in removing the peel is specifically in order to chop it, but if he removes the peel to eat it as is - it is permitted, and the same law applies to small onions. And Rabbeinu Peretz wrote that specifically a little at a time, but to peel a large amount together - appears as selecting and is prohibited", end of Rabbeinu Yerucham's words there. And based on this, our teacher the Rema wrote there: "It is prohibited to peel garlic and onions when peeling to set aside, but to eat immediately - it is permitted, and see above Siman 319", end of quote.

Seemingly, it appears from their words that peeling many garlic and onions would be considered selecting (borer) and is forbidden if it is not for immediate consumption. Besides the fact that it is not understood what relevance selecting has here, it is also against an explicit Gemara in Beitza (13b) regarding peeling barley, where Rav and Rabbi Chiya’s wives would peel them handful by handful. And what difference is there between peeling barley or peeling onions and garlic? Moreover, this is related to extracting (mifarek), as Rashi explained there, and not to selecting (borer). Therefore, it seems to me that this is the explanation: their intent is not when one peels them and leaves the peels separately, but rather peels them and the peels are mixed with them, as we explained in the Yerushalmi, and in this case, it indeed relates to selecting. And for this reason, they said that for immediate consumption, it is permitted, whether to select the food to eat or even to remove the waste according to the opinion of the Tosafot and the Tur, which we wrote in Section 16 when the food is greater in quantity. And Rabbeinu Yerucham permits even when not for immediate consumption, since the Yerushalmi deals with peeling to grind it, where selecting is difficult. But to eat it as is, it is not mixed, and there is no selecting involved. And Rabbi Rabbeinu Peretz forbids in a large gathering, and this is all when mixed together, and also the intention of Rabbeinu the Rema is so when mixed together, even though he did not write it explicitly, and if not so, there is no selecting involved. (And I have elaborated on this because it is the custom of Jewish women to prepare the legs for Shabbat morning, and some place this for the third meal, and peel many onions and garlic for it, and the Mishnah Berurah raised an issue regarding this, and therefore we have come to teach a justification that they act according to the law, and examine this carefully).

In ancient times, they would eat ears of grain as it is written: "And you may pluck the ears with your hand," which means they would take stalks of grain, extract the food from the stalks, and eat it, similar to how we extract legumes from their pods. This extraction is considered a derivative of threshing. Therefore, the Sages stated in Shabbat (128a) regarding various types of spices, that one may rub them between his fingers in an unusual manner, but not with his palm as he does on weekdays. He should rub them between his fingers so that the food falls out. They did not decree that one might rub them in the usual manner with his whole hand, because even if he does, he is not liable for a sin-offering, since the primary act of extraction is when one takes the food and extracts it directly with his hand. But when one rubs and the food falls out, its prohibition is rabbinic even if done with the whole hand. Therefore, when they permitted only to rub with the tips of his fingers, we are not concerned, and this is the opinion of the Rif and the Rambam in Chapter 21. Some of our Rabbis entirely forbade rubbing grain and legumes on Shabbat, as it appears in Beitza (13b) that it was only permitted on Yom Tov and not on Shabbat. And that which they permitted on Shabbat was only to soften the food.

The main opinion follows the view of the Rif and the Rambam, and this is also the ruling of the Tur. And this is what our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, wrote in Section 6: "One should not rub grains, but one may rub them with a slight change using the tips of his fingers. And even though he is separating the food from the husks, since he is only separating in an unusual manner in order to eat immediately – it is permitted. There are those who are stringent, and therefore it is forbidden to remove the nuts or large walnuts from their green shells, and it is good to be stringent since one can eat them without removing the shells." This means breaking them and eating them without removing the shells. However, when breaking them, it is permitted to peel the thin shell on the food, as this is not considered separating. Separating only applies to the outer shell. Similarly, with all kinds of legumes, the thin shell on the actual fruit – it is permitted to peel according to all opinions (the Gra), but one should be careful to peel only what is needed for that meal he wants to eat now, and not to store them for later (ibid.).

According to what has been explained, it is forbidden according to all opinions to manually separate the food from the stalks. Therefore, there is a need to protest against those who eat legumes like arbas (peas) and babas (beans) while they are in their pods, and they break them open and eat the food, which is considered a complete act of threshing. They do not rub them, but break them and extract the food. It appears not only to be forbidden, but it incurs liability for a sin-offering, for this is an act of threshing. Regarding the legumes called arbas, some have argued that since the pods are also fit for consumption, this is not considered threshing. But what can be done about babas, whose pods are not fit for consumption? And even with arbas, not all the pods are fit for consumption. Therefore, it is necessary to inform the public that there is no permit for this, and one who does so is liable unless they were detached from their connection to the pods before Shabbat, and on Shabbat, they can be taken out one by one to be eaten immediately. The great sages have already protested against this, and there is no permit for it. (See Magen Avraham, section 8, Taz, section 4, and the Alter Rebbe in section 9. Also see Eliyah Rabbah, section 12, who brings an opinion in the name of Rabbi Shimon, the teacher of Maharil, that threshing only applies to grain, where the food is merely placed in the stalks and not adhered. But legumes are attached to the pods like fruit to a tree, and in this case, it is considered detaching and not threshing. Therefore, the pod is like a branch detached from the tree, from which it is permitted to pluck the fruit, as stated in section 336. This seems to be the explanation of the matter in my humble opinion. Perhaps this is what the Taz meant when he referred to section 336, paragraph 8, where this law is explained. All Torah scholars and God-fearing individuals do not eat from the pods on Shabbat, and from the beginning of section 510, it is also clear that it is forbidden.)

If one has wheat that was threshed before Shabbat but is still mixed with its chaff, one should not sift it with a sieve or a large plate, and certainly not with a sifter or a sieve, as this constitutes sorting and incurs a sin-offering. Additionally, one should not blow the chaff away using both hands, meaning transferring it from hand to hand until the chaff is removed, as this is considered a weekday activity. Rather, he should blow it away with one hand and with all his strength, meaning he should take it in one hand, raise the hand, and lower it until the chaff passes, in order to perform it in an unusual manner. Blowing it with the mouth, however, seems to certainly be permitted.

Food mixed with waste that is prohibited to separate - it is also forbidden to put them into water so that the waste remains at the bottom, such as if the waste is earth, or so that it floats to the top, such as if it is straw, because this is also considered separating and is prohibited. Similarly, karshinim, which is a type of vegetable found in the Land of Israel and in Babylon that contains waste - one should not soak them in water to make the waste float to the top, nor should one rub them by hand to remove the waste, because this is like separating. However, one may put them in a sieve, but should not sift. And even though the waste will naturally fall through the holes of the sieve, and thus be separated, since he did not perform an action but merely placed them in the sieve as one places something in a location and the waste falls away naturally - this is permissible, and it is not known to us what this is.

A strainer used to filter dregs, even if it was hung from before Shabbat on the vessel where the dregs are dripping, although it is permitted on Yom Tov in such cases, nonetheless on Shabbat, it is forbidden to place dregs in it to filter, and one is liable for a sin-offering. This is considered a derivative of selecting or sifting (Gemara 138a). However, if one placed the dregs in it before Shabbat, and the nature of the dregs is not to come out immediately, one may on Shabbat pour water on them so that they remain clear. And so we learned in the Mishnah (139b): One may pour water over dregs so that they will become clear, and one may filter wine through a cloth or an Egyptian basket, meaning, so that the dregs will become clear and drip well.

The explanation for filtering wine is as follows: Water, wine, and all kinds of beverages that are generally drinkable by most people, even though delicate individuals will not drink them unless they are filtered again, such as when there is a small amount of flour or some fine pieces – this is not considered selecting (borer), since they are fit to drink without filtering. If they are completely cloudy – it is certainly forbidden, but it is not called selecting for the sake of a few individuals who do not want to drink it without filtering. However, there are distinctions in the method of filtering: Water and white wine – it is forbidden to filter them with cloths for another reason, and that is because of the prohibition of laundering, as soaking the garment is considered washing it, as stated in Siman 302. With these, it is only permissible to filter with a designated strainer, even if it is made of cloth, since it is made for this purpose, one is not concerned about squeezing it and also not concerned about laundering it at all. Therefore, laundering is not considered significant to prohibit even if we say that soaking it is washing it. With a cloth, the primary prohibition is that one might squeeze it since one is particular about it, and it becomes laundering. Consequently, with it, we say soaking it is washing it, but not with a designated strainer. According to this, red wine, beer, and other beverages that do not involve laundering and there is no concern about squeezing them, as will be explained in Siman 320, since they dirty the cloth and it is considered a way of soiling, as explained in Siman 302, it is permissible to filter them with a cloth. However, when filtering with a cloth, the sages warned not to fold the cloth inside it like a sieve as a change, so it is not done in the usual way on weekdays. Wherever filtering with a cloth is permitted, it is also permissible to filter with an Egyptian basket, which is a basket made of reeds and willow branches, provided that the basket is not raised from the lower vessel for the sake of change, not that it should not be raised at all, but that it should not be raised a handbreadth, and less than a handbreadth is permitted. A utensil made like a sieve that is used for filtering – its law is like a designated strainer, since it is made for this purpose (Magen Avraham 13). The Tur wrote that the reason for raising a handbreadth is because of a tent, as anything raised a handbreadth is considered a tent. According to this, even with a cloth, there is a concern because of a tent. Therefore, some say it is only permissible with a cloth if it does not cover the entire mouth of the vessel, as in this case, it would not be considered a tent. But if it covers the entire vessel, it is forbidden because of a tent (Taz 11), and see what is written in Siman 320, paragraph 30.

And know that Rambam, of blessed memory, completely prohibits the use of a strainer. For in Chapter 8, Law 14, he wrote: "One who strains wine or oil or water, as well as other liquids, using their respective strainers is liable, provided he strains the amount equivalent to a dried fig. However, one may filter wine that has no dregs or clear water through cloths or an Egyptian basket in order for it to be exceptionally clear, etc." End quote. And in Chapter 21, Law 17, he wrote: "Although it is permitted to filter clear wine and clear water through cloths or an Egyptian basket, one should not make a hole in the cloth, so as not to act as he does on weekdays and come to strain using a strainer. Similarly, it is forbidden to hang the strainer as he does on weekdays, lest he come to strain." End quote. Thus, he completely prohibits using a strainer. The Tur and the Shulchan Aruch, Section 10, also wrote that according to the Rambam, it is forbidden to use a strainer, even for clear wine and water. The reason seems to be as we learned in the Mishnah: "One may put wine into cloths or an Egyptian basket," implying only these and not a strainer, for with a strainer, there is a decree that one might also use it for unclear liquids, as he usually does on weekdays.

However, the words of the Rambam contradict an explicit Gemara (139b): "Ze'iri said: A person may pour clear wine and clear water into a strainer on Shabbat and does not need to be concerned." Moreover, it is taught there: During the wine-pressing season, when all wines are turbid and are drunk with their sediments, one may mix a barrel of wine with its sediments and pour it into a strainer on Shabbat and not be concerned. Look there, and how could he rule against the Talmud? It is even more perplexing that he wrote this law in chapter 8 as follows: "Similarly, wine from the press, as long as it is fermenting, one may mix a barrel with its sediments and pour it into cloths, for the sediments have not yet fully separated from the wine, and all the wine is like one entity, and the same applies to mustard and similar items." He changed the Talmud's language from strainer to cloths. Some wrote that the Rambam interpreted these strainers as cloths (Lechem Mishneh). Certainly, he interpreted it this way, but it is puzzling where he got this interpretation. It seems he was compelled to do so from what we learned earlier: "One does not hang a strainer on Yom Tov, nor does one place it to hang on Shabbat, but one may put water on the sediments so they will pass through and strain the wine with cloths, etc." From the fact that he omitted the strainer, which was the subject, and should have said: 'and strain the wine with it and with cloths,' we understand that with a strainer, not at all, and thus he was compelled to interpret the strainer in the Gemara as cloths.

According to what has been explained, any drink that can be consumed as it is may be filtered. Therefore, all types of pickled vegetable brine, such as cucumber brine, can be filtered, since they can also be consumed without filtering. Similarly, a drink that has straw or splinters or flies in it—one can blow the waste to one side and drink, since it can be consumed without this action (as cited in the Eliyah Rabbah in the name of the Lechem Chamudos, section 10). Likewise, a drink made from ground almonds prepared before Shabbat may be filtered, since it can be consumed without filtering (Magen Avraham, section 12). Similarly, vinegar that is slightly thick may be filtered, unless it is very thick and cannot be consumed without filtering, in which case it is prohibited to filter it (Taz, section 10). Any cloudy drink that is impossible to drink—it is prohibited to filter it, and any drink that can be consumed—it is permitted to filter it (Magen Avraham, section 12).

It is not considered selecting (borer) unless one selects and then drinks, but if during drinking one prevents the waste from entering their mouth, it is not considered selecting (borer). Therefore, our teacher the Beit Yosef wrote in section 16: "Water that contains worms may be drunk through a cloth on Shabbat, as selecting (borer) and straining only apply when preparing the matter before eating or drinking. But if during drinking one prevents the waste from entering their mouth, it is not considered a form of labor and is permitted." This is not considered laundering with a small amount of water on a cloth that has no dirt, as stated in section 302, and therefore, according to those who forbid it in the name of laundering, it is prohibited (as per Magen Avraham 17). This applies to water, but with other liquids, laundering does not apply, as explained. It seems to me that even with water, one who relies on the first opinion mentioned is not at fault, since our teacher the Beit Yosef ruled leniently. Furthermore, it seems to me that in this case, even according to the last opinion mentioned, it is permitted, as this is considered a manner of dirt, as it is known that one who drinks in such manners will get dirt on the other side of the cloth. When flies fall into a cup, one should not remove the flies alone even while drinking, but should remove them with a bit of liquid (Taz 13), and this is the custom. Similarly, all types of waste that are discarded during eating and drinking should be discarded with a bit of food and a bit of liquid.

A vessel used to pour wine from the barrel – one should not place twigs and splinters tightly in its mouth, for there is no greater strainer than this. So wrote our teacher, the Beit Yosef, in section 13. It was questioned against him that in the Gemara (139b) it says: "A person should not tightly insert a twig into the mouth of a wine barrel, because it appears like a strainer." And the Ran explained that it is not actually a strainer, for sediments pass through it, but since there are twigs and debris that do not pass through, it resembles a strainer. How then did he write that there is no greater strainer than this? This requires investigation (Magen Avraham, section 14). However, Rashi also explained there that there is no greater strainer than this. And indeed, it is not difficult at all, for a strainer is a vessel made for straining, and this is what the Talmud means when it says that it appears like a vessel made for straining, but it is not actually a vessel made for straining. But regarding the essence of the law of the prohibition of straining – there is no greater strainer than this.

It is permissible to pour gently from one vessel to another, provided one is careful that when the stream stops and small droplets start to fall, which are the remnants from the sediment, one should stop and leave them with the sediment. Similarly, when drinking tea or coffee, the sediment remains at the bottom, and one should not pour until the very sediment, because if one does not do so, these droplets and this sediment indicate that one is selecting (borer), and when the sediment is not noticeable, it is not considered selecting. However, when drinking tea or coffee at the time of drinking, there is no concern, because just as we hold that one selects food from waste and eats, for that is the way of eating, so too this is the way of drinking. However, when one is not drinking oneself and is pouring from vessel to vessel, one needs to be careful about this. Similarly, with beer and other beverages: at the time of drinking, one does not need to be careful about this, but only when pouring not at the time of drinking, one needs to be careful.

The fat that floats on the cooked dish, and one wishes to remove the fat and eat the dish - it is forbidden to pour it all out, because they are two types and there is selection, and the dish that one wishes to eat immediately is called food, and the fat that one wishes to leave is called waste, and there is selection in this. Therefore, one should be careful not to remove all the fat, but to leave some with the dish. However, milk that is placed in a container, and on top is the cream called "smetana," and below is the sour milk - it seems to be one type and selection does not apply here. However, if we consider this to be two types and one does not intend to eat both immediately, one should be careful to leave a little smetana with the sour milk. It is obvious that one should not even take a little smetana unless it is needed to be eaten on Shabbat, because if it is not needed for Shabbat - it is forbidden to exert effort on Shabbat for the weekday, and if there might be a loss, it should be done through a non-Jew (the Alter Rebbe).

It is permitted to elevate the barrel on something so that the wine flows well from it, and even though by doing so the wine also comes out from the dregs, this is not considered as selecting (borer) as long as the sparkles do not start descending from the dregs, as explained. Similarly, it is permitted to pour water over the dregs in the barrel so that they absorb the taste of the wine, and there is no issue of selecting (borer) in this. However, one must ensure to drink from it on the same day (according to the Gra), as it is forbidden to exert effort on Shabbat for something not needed on Shabbat.

Mustard, which is called mustard seed, contains a small amount of waste, but it is not completely waste, as it is also fit for consumption. They had a sieve through which they would strain the mustard, and therefore, although by Torah law this does not constitute separation, it is nevertheless rabbinically prohibited because it appears like separating food from waste, since he discards the waste outside. They had a practice of preparing mustard with an egg, where the yolk would sink to the bottom and the egg white would remain on top with the waste. The sages permitted this if the mustard was placed in the sieve before Shabbat; it is permitted to put an egg in it on Shabbat to improve the appearance of the mustard. This is not considered separation even though the egg white remains with the waste, even if we consider the egg white and yolk as two different types, because this is only to improve the appearance, and certainly since in truth, it is one type, and it has already been explained that in one type, separation does not apply. However, if the straining was for the purpose of eating the egg itself, the egg white could rabbinically be considered waste, since it is not fit for consumption as it is raw. Therefore, certainly breaking an egg and separating the egg white to eat the yolk is rabbinically prohibited, as it appears like actual separation. But with mustard or other foods where the yolk is not needed except for the appearance, we do not worry about separation in such cases. Nevertheless, it is strictly forbidden to manually separate the egg white from the yolk, but if one places it into something, and the egg white automatically separates from the yolk, this is permitted when the yolk is only needed for appearance. (This seems to be my humble opinion on this matter based on the words of the Rambam and later authorities. See Magen Avraham, section 16, and what the Taz wrote in section 12 that even with one type of food, separation applies; his words have already been refuted. And from the words of the Gra it also seems as I have written, see there and ponder it well.)

Maimonides wrote in Chapter 7, Law 6: "Similarly, one who takes milk and adds rennet to it in order to curdle it is liable for the derivative of selecting, since he has separated the curds from the whey. And if he curdles the milk and makes it into cheese, he is liable for building, for anyone who gathers parts together and joins them until they form a single body is comparable to building." End quote. And he similarly wrote in Chapter 8 that one who curdles is liable for the derivative of selecting, and this is explicitly stated in the Talmud (95a). And Maimonides wrote in Chapter 21 at the end of Law 17 as follows: "Similarly, one who curdles is liable for the derivative of selecting, therefore even though one puts sesame seeds and nuts into honey, he should not curdle them by hand." End quote. And in the Tosefta it is explained that the liability is due to kneading, and Rashi explained curdling as making a kind of reed vessel and placing the curds in it, with the whey dripping out. End quote. The words of Maimonides refer to the cheeses called "Holland cheese," and Rashi's words refer to our simple cheeses, and in both cases the liability is for selecting, as we have already explained in Section 3.

It is forbidden to put dregs into a drink in order to clarify it, even though it is fit for drinking on Shabbat, because by doing so the dregs of the drink itself also settle at the bottom of the vessel, and this is like churning, which is a derivative of selecting (Magen Avraham, section 14). And we do not know what this is, nor do we understand what is meant by mixing sesame seeds and nuts with honey.

I have seen someone who wrote in this manner: "The Rambam wrote in Chapter 21: It is forbidden to hang the strainer in the way one does during the week, lest he come to strain through it." This implies that even to hang it for another purpose is forbidden. However, the simple understanding of the Gemara and the decisors implies that there is no prohibition in this. And I do not know any implication [to support their claim], and on the contrary, it is explicitly stated at the beginning of 'Toluyin' that it is rabbinically forbidden to hang it, so as not to do as he does during the week. Consequently, the hanging itself is considered a weekday activity even though his intention is for another purpose.

Rabbi Moses Isserles wrote at the end of this section: "One who spits into the wind on Shabbat and the wind disperses the saliva is liable for winnowing," end quote, and it is from the Jerusalem Talmud in the chapter "Klal Gadol" which says there: "If one spat and the wind scattered it, he is liable for winnowing," see there. But it is a puzzling matter, for he does not benefit at all from this winnowing, and a "pesik reisha" (inevitable outcome) that one does not benefit from is exempt, as stated in Siman 342. Furthermore, what connection does winnowing have to this? In winnowing, there is a separation of food from waste, whereas here it is all waste. It seems more likely that it is a printing error and should say: "because of throwing," meaning when the wind carries it four cubits.

Threshing, dyeing, and bleaching are primary categories of labor. Threshing was present in the Tabernacle since they would sow the herbs, and consequently, they would thresh them (see Tosafot 73b, s.v. 'Mefarek'). Dyeing was done since they would dye the blue wool, and in the Jerusalem Talmud on the chapter "Klal Gadol" it says that dyeing in the Tabernacle involved marking the hides of rams with redness, meaning they would prepare the animal with a rod so that the hide would turn red (see there). This is surprising, as it overlooks the dyeing of the blue wool and mentions such a minor form of dyeing. It seems to teach us much, for it says there: "One who reddens a lip is liable," meaning if one adds redness to a naturally red lip, they are liable, because it constitutes dyeing. And how do we know to say this, since it is not similar to dyeing the blue wool, which is complete dyeing? Thus, it says they would mark the animal, indicating that even such a minor form of dyeing is still considered dyeing. Bleaching involves bleaching wool or flax or anything that requires bleaching, and it was done in the Tabernacle with the curtains made of twisted linen and the garments of the priests. The measurement for threshing is the size of a dried fig for food measurements, as threshing applies only to things that grow from the ground (Shabbat 75a), and this is also written by the Rambam in Chapter 8, Law 7.

The measurement for dyeing and whitening: The Rambam writes in Chapter 9, Law 10: "One who whitens wool, flax, or crimson or similar materials that are normally whitened is liable. And what is the measure? Enough to spin a single thread whose length is the full width of the double sit, which is a length of four handbreadths." End quote. And in Law 13 he writes: "One who dyes a thread whose length is four handbreadths or something from which such a thread can be spun is liable." End quote. This means that it is not specifically required that the threads have already been spun, but even wool and flax that have not yet been spun, if one dyes an amount from which such a thread can be spun, he is liable. Therefore, this was not written regarding whitening, because whitening is only after spinning, as it is taught at the beginning of the chapter "Reishit HaGez": 'Whitened enough to make a small garment from it.'

And their derivatives: The derivative of threshing, as written by the Rambam in Chapter 8, is that separating is a derivative of threshing, because threshing involves separating the grain from the husks. Therefore, any act of separating one thing from another is a derivative of threshing. And it is taught (Shabbat 73b): "Threshing, combing, and carding - they are all one type of labor." And Rashi explained: Combing refers to flax in the stalks, and carding refers to cotton, separating the seeds from it. And the Aruch explained in the name of the Gaon: Combing refers to separating the food from its associated particles, and carding refers to rubbing the husks. The Rambam wrote that milking an animal incurs liability because of separating, and it must be said that an animal is considered a product of the ground (see Tosafot 73b, s.v. "separating"; delve deeply). He also wrote that wounding incurs liability because of separating, and we have explained this earlier in Siman 316, see there. Similarly, squeezing fruits incurs liability because of separating, and there are many laws and details about this that will be explained in this Siman.

In the Jerusalem Talmud, in the "Great Principle" section, it states: "One who crushes rice, barley, or split beans - is liable for threshing," meaning that one who crushes rice, barley, or split beans to remove their husks - is liable for threshing. "A woman who rubs wheat heads - is liable for threshing," meaning that by rubbing the wheat heads with her hands, she removes their husks. "One who beats flax in a mortar," striking the flax to separate it from the husk - is liable for threshing. "One who grinds garlic when removing its heads - is liable for threshing," and this we explained in the previous section. "One who crushes the soft part around the bark of trees - is liable for threshing," meaning that he crushes it to separate it from the bark - is liable for threshing.

The derivatives of dyeing, Rambam writes in Chapter 9, Law 14: "One who creates a dye is considered a derivative of dyeing and is liable. How so? For example, if one placed qankantum into gallnut water, turning all of it black, or if one placed istis into turmeric water, turning all of it green, and similar cases." End quote. The Ra'avad disagrees with this, asserting that making the dye is not considered dyeing until it is used to dye an item. Otherwise, one who cooks dye substances would also be liable for dyeing. The Maggid Mishneh explains that according to the Rambam, indeed, one is liable for cooking dye substances for two reasons: for cooking and for dyeing. Similarly, one who whitens a wall with lime also appears to be a derivative of dyeing. It was explained earlier in Siman 303 that a woman who applies makeup to her face is considered to be dyeing, and likewise when she spreads dough on her face to make it red, and there it was explained in detail.

Maimonides wrote there: One is not liable for dyeing until it is a dye that lasts. But a dye that does not last at all, such as [if someone] applied rouge or sang over iron or copper and dyed it – is exempt, for you can remove it immediately and it does not dye anything. And any labor that does not endure on Shabbat – one is exempt.

It is established that there is no dyeing with foods, and therefore it is permitted to put saffron into a dish, and there is no concern of dyeing, even if his intention is for appearance. This is specifically when the intention is to eat it himself. But a merchant who dyes types of foods or drinks to show their beautiful appearance to people, it is possible that there is a concern of dyeing (Pri Megadim at the end of this section). Therefore, one should be careful not to do this on Shabbat if his intention is to show them to people. There is an opinion that someone who eats strawberries or other colored fruits should be careful not to touch his colored hands to a garment or a cloth, due to the prohibition of dyeing, but there are those who permit it because it is a manner of soiling (Magen Avraham subparagraph 24 in the name of Radbaz). It is proper to be careful about this and not to be lenient (there), because certainly in laundering it is not relevant when it is a manner of soiling, but in dyeing perhaps even a manner of soiling is considered dyeing. However, when it comes to dyeing his hands or spreading something on his face – there is certainly no concern about this, because since it is not customary to dye – this is not considered dyeing. This is not similar to a woman in section 303, because a woman's way is to dye (there). Certainly there is no concern about dyeing his bread with fruit juice, because there is no dyeing with foods. And one whose wound is oozing blood should be careful not to place a cloth on it, according to the opinion that prohibits dyeing even in a manner of soiling. Wiping a stain of some color that fell on a garment, there are those who prohibit (there), because in this it is considered fixing the garment. Others permit it (Eliyah Rabbah) and this seems correct, that this is not considered fixing.

The derivative of laundering, the Rambam writes there: "One who washes clothes - this is a derivative of laundering and is liable. And one who wrings out a garment until the water comes out - this is laundering and is liable, for wringing is a requirement of laundering, just as stirring is a requirement of cooking. And there is no wringing with hair, and the same applies to leather, that one is not liable for wringing it." End of quote, and this will be further explained with God's help. And in the Jerusalem Talmud, it says about laundering: "One who smokes sulfur on clothes," meaning one who smokes sulfur on clothes, "that woman who smears her face with serk or smears her thread with serk to whiten it," meaning a woman who smears her face with serk or smears her thread with serk to whiten it, "that tailor who puts the thread into his mouth," meaning the tailor who puts the thread into his mouth to stiffen it so it can go into the needle, as tailors do, and the belt makers - are liable because of laundering. And regarding the mei'niton (a type of belt), it also seems that they whiten it with the saliva in their mouth. And know that in all these, a length of a double sit (like a double span), as explained, which is the length of four handbreadths, is required.

Maimonides wrote in Chapter 8: One who squeezes fruits to extract their juices is liable for the prohibition of extracting (mifarek), and one is not liable unless the amount of liquid squeezed is equal to the volume of a dried fig (grogeret). One is only liable by Torah law for pressing olives and grapes alone. It is permitted to squeeze a cluster of grapes into food, for a liquid that comes into food is considered food itself, and it is as if one is separating food from food. However, if one squeezes into a vessel that does not contain food, this is considered pressing and one is liable. One who milks into food or directly into the mouth is exempt, and is not liable unless they milk into a vessel. Concerning one who milks where the milk will be wasted, this is also considered extraction.

In Chapter 21, Law 12, it is written: "One who presses is liable for threshing, and one who squeezes olives and grapes is liable for pressing. Therefore, it is forbidden to squeeze mulberries and pomegranates, since some people squeeze them like olives and grapes, lest one come to squeeze olives and grapes. However, other fruits, such as quinces, apples, and crab apples, are permitted to squeeze on Shabbat because they are not generally squeezed." This is the end of the quotation.

And we find in the Rambam three distinctions regarding the squeezing of fruits: For olives and grapes, one is liable to bring a sin offering because most of them are designated for pressing to make oil and wine. This is what our Sages said (145a), "By Torah law, one is only liable for treading on olives and grapes," as fruits specifically designated for liquids are only olives and grapes, as we learned in Chapter 11 of Terumot: "All fruits do not change their state in terumah and ma'aser sheni except for olives and grapes alone. They do not incur the penalty of orlah (the prohibition of fruits from a tree's first three years)... and one does not bring first fruits (bikkurim) of liquids except from what comes out of olives and grapes, and they do not become impure because of liquids... and one does not offer on the altar except what comes from olives and grapes." See there.

However, mulberries and pomegranates, since it is customary for people to squeeze them, are forbidden to be squeezed by rabbinic decree, as a precaution because of olives and grapes. And all other fruits are permitted to be squeezed initially, as there is no custom to squeeze them at all.

And know that regarding the matter that they permitted squeezing other fruits from the outset, so have ruled also the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch in section 1. And even though in the gloss of the Sefer Mitzvot Katan it is written that squeezing other fruits from the outset for the sake of their juice is also prohibited, and it is only permitted if his intention is to sweeten the fruit, and if juice comes out it is permitted, but squeezing initially for the juice is prohibited, they did not consider this solitary opinion against all those rabbis. And there are some of the great authorities who wrote that also the opinion of Rashi and Tosafot is like this, as they wrote (144b): 'One can squeeze to sweeten the fruit, etc.', and therefore they wrote that one should be stringent in this (Bach and Taz, section 1). And I am astonished, even if it were so that there is a dispute in this matter, it is only regarding a rabbinic prohibition, and we follow the lenient opinion, and indeed our master the Beit Yosef has already explained in his great book that according to the conclusion it is not interpreted this way. (For they explained according to the opinion of Rav Nachman, but according to the resolution of Rav Pappa there is no need for this. And what the Bach questioned, what is different about pickled and boiled foods that their liquids are prohibited, I am astonished, for if so, this would be a difficulty on the Rif and the Rambam. However, the Rambam was precise in his language 'they are not subject to squeezing', but pickled and boiled foods are subject to squeezing, except that there is no law of squeezing regarding them. And indeed, if it is customary to squeeze that fruit - it is prohibited like strawberries and pomegranates as will be explained, and pickled and boiled foods are customarily squeezed. And what the Taz wrote about the intention of the Rif, it does not require refutation, as explained by the words of the Rambam. And what he questioned, that according to Rav Pappa the question of the Gemara would remain, as if the house of Menasheh is the majority of the world, I am astonished, as if without Rav Chisda it would be impossible to explain that an important custom does not need the majority of the world, as Tosafot wrote in 'Hamotzi' 92b regarding the people of Hutzal, and this matter is proven in many places as Tosafot wrote in Eruvin 28. And proof from strawberries, and investigate well).

However, if there is a place where it is customary to squeeze certain fruits to drink their juice, it is indeed forbidden to squeeze them on Shabbat, as our teacher the Rema wrote in Section 1, and this is his language: "In a place where it is customary to squeeze certain fruits to drink their juice out of thirst or pleasure, their law is like that of strawberries and pomegranates." This implies from his language that it is forbidden only in that place. But our teacher the Beit Yosef in his great book wrote: that if it is known to us that in any place they squeeze a certain fruit, it is forbidden to squeeze it, as we find with pomegranates, which are forbidden to be squeezed because of the people of Beit Menashe who used to squeeze them, and therefore they are forbidden everywhere. This means that in the Gemara it is said that strawberries and pomegranates are forbidden to be squeezed because there were places where they were squeezed, and therefore it is forbidden in all places. 

And it seems to me that both are true according to the words of our Rabbis, the Ba'alei HaTosafot in HaMatzni'a (92b), that an important custom in one place drags the whole world, but not so with an unimportant custom. That is, strawberries and pomegranates were forbidden because there are those who squeeze them, and the reason why not everyone squeezes them is because they do not have many of these fruits. But when in all places there are many of these fruits and yet they do not squeeze them, it is not an important custom and it is forbidden only in its place. 

Therefore, our teacher the Rema is referring to fruits that are found everywhere, like apples and the like, and then the prohibition is only in the place where it is customary to squeeze them. And our teacher the Beit Yosef is referring to fruits like strawberries and pomegranates, where in that place there are many, and therefore they squeeze them, and if there were many of these fruits in all places, they would also squeeze them, and therefore they are forbidden everywhere. (This seems to me clearly correct, and the Magen Avraham in Section 1 delves into this and leans both ways. And what he wrote that even in a place... their opinion is nullified when the whole world has them and does not squeeze them, see there, and his foundation is on the words of the Tosafot there, but in truth this is not similar to an unimportant custom, and behold Rabbi Chananel held that even for an individual, since he considers it important, it is considered a beverage, and all the more so in a place where everyone agrees, that for them it is like a beverage. And what he wrote that in Bernas, where in Ashkenaz they make a beverage from them because they have many, and therefore it is forbidden to squeeze them everywhere, this is certainly true, but in our times we do not know of this.)

And Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote: All this specifically refers to squeezing, which is forbidden, but it is permitted to suck the juice from grapes with one's mouth, and all the more so with other things. However, some forbid sucking with the mouth from grapes and similar items. The explanation of the matter is: Squeezing according to Torah law is only with the hand, and not with the mouth, which is considered a form of eating. Nevertheless, it is still rabbinically forbidden, just as it is forbidden to suck milk directly from an animal’s udder with one's mouth, as stated later in section 328. They did not decree in cases of distress, as mentioned there. What is the difference between this and that? This is the reason for those who forbid it. The first opinion holds that it is not analogous, because in the case of the udder, the sucking is also apparent with the mouth, as it is the natural way of sucking, similar to an infant nursing from its mother's breast, and therefore it is forbidden for a healthy person. However, with sucking grapes, the squeezing is not at all apparent with the mouth, and it is not the usual way of squeezing, and therefore it is permitted to suck with the mouth (this is the intent of the Magen Avraham, section 2, and examine it well). All the more so with other items, such as placing meat in broth or bread in wine and sucking the broth or wine with the mouth, this is not considered squeezing, for even complete squeezing of them is permitted by Torah law, as the liquid does not come from their body. Even those who forbid do not forbid these items, only grapes and not broth and wine, nor other fruits. Some are stricter with broth and wine than grapes, because the liquid previously had the status of a beverage (Bach in the name of Rashal), but Rabbi Moshe Isserles holds the opposite, and this appears to be the main opinion and is agreed upon by the great authorities (Magen Avraham, section 4, and Eliyah Rabbah, section 3). Even with grapes, one who relies on the first opinion has not lost, but whoever wishes to be stringent should be stringent with grapes, but not with broth and wine and not with other fruits.

Olives and grapes that have had juice ooze out of them on their own on Shabbat – it is forbidden to drink from them until after Shabbat, as a decree lest one intentionally squeeze them on Shabbat, even if the grapes and olives are intended for eating. As for strawberries and pomegranates from which juice has come out on Shabbat: if they are intended for eating – it is permitted; but if they are intended for juice – it is forbidden lest one squeeze them. And even though their squeezing is prohibited by rabbinic decree, nonetheless, they decreed regarding those intended for juice because it is likely that they will be squeezed. Regarding other fruits – it is obvious that it is permitted even according to those who are stringent about squeezing them directly, and even if they are intended for juice, because such a decree is not applicable.

And this applies to whole olives and grapes, but olives and grapes that were crushed before Shabbat – the liquids that come from them are permitted. In this case, we do not decree against it lest one come to squeeze them, because even if one does squeeze them, there is no Torah prohibition since they were already crushed before Shabbat, as has already been explained in Siman 252. Furthermore, even if they were not crushed before Shabbat, but are placed in a vat with wine and whole grapes, even though the grapes burst there on Shabbat and their juice mixes with the wine – it is permissible to drink them on Shabbat, because all the wine that comes from the grapes is nullified by the wine in the vat, which is much more than the wine coming from the grapes. And although this is something that has a permissible state after Shabbat, and we hold that something which has a permissible state later is not nullified, this applies when the prohibition was initially recognizable on its own. We say that such a prohibition is not nullified. But when the prohibition was never recognizable on its own, it is not applicable to say that something which has a permissible state later is not nullified. In Yoreh De'ah, at the end of Siman 102, we have further explained this. Nevertheless, to initially place grapes into the wine so that they burst is forbidden on Shabbat. There are those who permit even the initial placement on Shabbat, comparing it to placing snow into a cup.
