However, this is not a valid comparison (Taz, Sk 3), because there, it is customary to drink it that way, as we put sugar into hot water, which is not the case with grapes. Even if one put grapes on Shabbat without the intention of bursting them and they burst – it is also forbidden until after Shabbat (there, and it is surprising about the Magen Avraham, Sk 5, who wrote in the name of Bach that it is permissible to place them so they burst, and it is not so in Bach, but rather as the Taz wrote in his name, and examine it well).

It is permissible to squeeze a cluster of grapes directly into a pot that contains cooked food in order to improve the food, as this is considered a liquid that comes for the purpose of food and is deemed like food itself. However, if there is no cooked food in the pot, it is prohibited. We have already brought this in section 9 from the words of the Rambam. Even though some of our sages have said that this is not the law, that this was only permitted on a holiday and not on Shabbat, nevertheless the majority of the poskim have permitted it even on Shabbat, and this is also ruled in the Shulchan Aruch, section 4.

However, Rabbeinu Tam prohibited doing so with grapes that are still unripe. For with ripe grapes, it is considered like food within food, but with unripe grapes, which are not fit for eating, it is like selecting food from waste. There are those who permit it even with unripe grapes, and there is one who says that even according to Rabbeinu Tam who prohibits with unripe grapes, since the prohibition is due to selecting food from waste, it is permitted at the time of eating, as stated in the previous section (Taz, sub-section 4). And there is one who prohibits, for this was only permitted by hand, selecting food and eating it, and not by placing it into a utensil and then drinking it, as this is considered actual selecting, just as it was not permitted with a sieve and a basket (Magen Avraham, sub-section 7).

It has already been clarified that it is permitted to squeeze other fruits aside from mulberries and pomegranates, and therefore, our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 6 that it is permitted to squeeze lemons. And it seems that even according to those who are stringent with squeezing other fruits for their juice, as mentioned in section 11, there is no concern with lemons, for it is not customary at all to squeeze them for their own juice to drink by itself, but rather either for flavoring food, or into water and other beverages, but not to drink them alone. Therefore, they are not considered to be subject to the prohibition of squeezing at all. Even those who are stringent with other fruits are only stringent when making juice from the fruits themselves, similar to grapes, mulberries, and pomegranates. And even though there are those who are stringent with juice that comes into food, and into beverages it is forbidden to everyone, nevertheless, the juice squeezed from lemons is not considered a beverage, and it is like food that comes into a beverage. And all the more so, it is permitted to suck the lemon in one's mouth and then discard it after sucking. And it seems that the same applies to oranges, which are like lemons.

And know that it seems that regarding the permission of squeezing other fruits, a question arises: even though squeezing does not apply to them, they should be prohibited due to nolad (a new entity created on Shabbat) like an egg that was laid. The answer is that, as we have already explained in Siman 318, Section 6, the Rambam, the Tur, and the Shulchan Aruch ruled according to Rabbi Shimon on Shabbat, that nolad does not apply unless it is a complete creation, as explained there. And indeed, regarding eggs, they do not hold the prohibition of nolad, as it is clarified from their words later at the beginning of Siman 322, that they prohibited an egg laid on Shabbat because of the decree concerning a festival following Shabbat, and because of preparation and not because of nolad, as explained there. The Tur also clarified this later in Siman 495. However, it requires examination, as the Tur wrote there that Rabbeinu Tam ruled according to Rabbi Yehuda that nolad is prohibited on Shabbat, and in Section 16, we wrote that Rabbeinu Tam prohibits bosa (unripe grapes), and it is explained that for fruit that has ripened, he allows squeezing it into food, and this is nolad. But indeed, into food it is not considered nolad, as this is like food mixed with food, and indeed on a festival it is permitted to do so, and on a festival, everyone agrees that nolad is prohibited. (But what we hold at the beginning of Chaviot that Rabbi Yehuda says: 'if it is for food, that which comes out is permitted,' and Rabbi Yehuda prohibits nolad. And one cannot say that this is not called nolad, for even date pits are called nolad, as mentioned in Chapter 2:29. And certainly, liquids that come out of fruits are more so. I found that the Tosafot in Eruvin 46b, 'Kol' wrote that liquids in fruits are not considered nolad, since initially, they were also food, it is food that has separated, as mentioned there. And date pits are worse than them, as the pits are not fit for eating at all, and therefore they are nolad.)

Squeezing pickled vegetables, which refers to types of vegetables pickled in water or vinegar, as well as squeezing types of boiled foods, like boiled meat in water or boiled vegetables to squeeze them: if one does not need the water that comes out of them but rather the pickled or boiled food itself to prepare it for eating - it is entirely permitted. Since one does not need what comes out of them, this is not considered extraction at all. This is not similar to olives and grapes, or even strawberries and pomegranates, because the liquid does not come from their essence, and it is permitted to squeeze them even into a bowl that does not contain food. However, if one needs their liquids - it is prohibited to squeeze them, and they are worse than other fruits, which are permitted to be squeezed even for their liquids because they are not considered beverages at all. This is not the case with pickled and boiled foods, which had the status of a beverage beforehand. Therefore, it is only permitted to squeeze them into a pot that contains food, as liquid that comes into food is considered separating food from food. Even with olives and grapes, this is permitted as explained, but if there is no food in the pot - it is prohibited. 

Rabbeinu Chananel holds that if one needs their liquids, one is liable for a sin offering even if one squeezes into a pot that contains food. He also holds this for olives and grapes, and one who squeezes a cluster into a pot, even if it contains food, is liable for a sin offering. He does not agree with the permission of squeezing into food, which is only relevant on Yom Tov and not on Shabbat, as stated in section 16. Most authorities disagree with him, as mentioned there. Rabbeinu Chananel himself prohibits it even on Yom Tov, rejecting the statement about milking into a pot as mentioned by the Tosafot 145, s.v. "and Rabbi Yochanan" and as mentioned by the Taz, section 6. However, Rabbeinu Tam holds that it is permitted on Yom Tov. This resolves the Taz's question there on the Shulchan Aruch, which in section 505 rules according to the permissive opinion, because there Rabbeinu Chananel's opinion is unique, but on Shabbat it seems that even Rabbeinu Tam agreed with him. However, there is no proof of this, and on the contrary, with a cluster, he only prohibited unripe ones, and one should examine this carefully.

Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote in Section 8: "One who squeezes a fish for its brine - the law is like one who squeezes olives and pickles for their liquids," end quote. This means that a fish that has been cooked or soaked in water or other liquids and one squeezes it - the law is like one who squeezes olives and pickles. Similarly, a fish that has been soaked in salt until it becomes brine - the law is the same. Even though when eating it as it is, it is entirely food, nevertheless, since the liquid comes to it from elsewhere, if one squeezes it for its liquids – it is forbidden, unless it is into a pot that contains food. And for its substance, it is permitted, just like with olives and pickles.

Snow, hail, and frost—one may not crush them by hand, meaning to break them into small pieces so that their water flows out, as this would be considered creating something new (nolad). However, one may place them into a cup of water or wine, and they will melt on their own, and there is no concern. Some of our rabbis permit crushing them by hand into the cup, as they hold that the prohibition is due to the concern that one might squeeze fruits that are designated for their juice, and once mixed with water, the decree does not apply. This is also clarified in the words of the Rambam in Chapter 21, Law 13—see there. He holds that there is no prohibition of nolad in this case. However, Rashi, Tosafot, the Rosh, and Sefer HaTerumah wrote that the reason is due to nolad. According to this, crushing by hand is prohibited even into a cup, because at the moment of crushing, it is considered nolad (see Magen Avraham, subparagraph 13).

And it is puzzling regarding our teacher, the Beit Yosef, in Section 9, where he wrote: "Snow and hail should not be crushed... but one may place them into a cup... and similarly, if one left them in the sun or near a fire and they melted, they are permitted." These are his words. Now, since he wrote "but one may place them into a cup" and did not write that even crushing them by hand into the cup is permitted, it implies that he holds like Rashi's opinion, that the reason is because of 'nolad' (a new entity being created). If so, how could he permit leaving them in the sun and they melted, for according to the reason of 'nolad' it is certainly prohibited, as it is written in Siman 318 regarding congealed fat that when it is melted again, it is prohibited there, for those who hold of the concept of 'nolad' (and similarly, the Magen Avraham wrote in Subsection 14 that according to the reason of 'nolad' it is prohibited). And perhaps when he wrote 'place them into the cup,' he also intended to include by crushing, and he used the language of the Gemara at the end of the chapter "With What May One Insulate," but the language of the Rambam is: 'crush into the cup,' there, and he intentionally wrote this as mentioned.

And know that there is a question regarding those who prohibit because of Nolad (a category of creation), and likewise earlier in Siman 318, section 32, regarding fat that melted for those who prohibit because of Nolad, as it says there. However, we explained in section 18 that most authorities do not hold the prohibition of Nolad on Shabbat, only Rabbeinu Tam. And this is explicitly written by the Tur later in Siman 395. The answer is either to say that those who prohibit also hold like Rabbeinu Tam, that Nolad is prohibited on Shabbat. But it is difficult to say this because the Rosh also holds in this matter that there is no grinding (melachah) due to Nolad, and at the beginning of Beitzah, it implies that he leans not like Rabbeinu Tam. Also, from the Tur’s words there, it implies that Rashi holds permissively regarding Nolad, see there. And Rashi at the end of the chapter "Bameh Tomnin" regarding not crushing snow explains it is due to Nolad. Rather, certainly it must be said, as we have already written, that in a complete Nolad everyone agrees, as the Tosafos wrote in Eruvin (46a) that in a complete Nolad even Rabbi Shimon agrees. And the general Nolad in the Gemara at the beginning of Beitzah is about an egg, and in this, Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon disagree. Therefore, these opinions hold that crushing snow and hail, as well as the dripping of fat, is called a complete Nolad, and further study is needed.

And know, according to what has been explained, those who drink hot beverages on Shabbat and put sugar into the cup, this is permitted just like putting snow and hail into a cup. However, according to this, it is forbidden to crush the sugar with a small spoon inside the cup, and the public is not careful about this. Now, according to the opinion of the poskim (decisors) in section 21 who permit crushing into the cup - there is no prohibition in this, but for those who prohibit - it seems it is forbidden. And it is possible that even for those who prohibit, they only prohibited when crushing outside and then putting it into the cup, but inside the cup itself it is permitted, since it is never distinguishable by itself, especially as sugar is initially cooked, and therefore it should not be prohibited. See in Siman 321, section 13.

In the winter, when the water has frozen, it is permitted to break the ice and take the water from underneath it. This is not like crushing snow, because the water beneath the ice has not frozen. And regarding breaking the ice, they have even said a greater leniency: a person may break a barrel to eat dried figs from it. Our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in paragraph 11: "One must be careful in the winter not to wash their hands with water that contains snow or hail, and if one does wash, they should be careful not to crush them between their hands so as not to crush them," end quote. The Tosafot wrote similarly, and this is their language: "And water that is freezing and has hail mixed in it—one should not wash with it, as it is impossible not to crush the hail," end quote. I am uncertain about the language of our rabbis, as it clearly implies that they were only strict about crushing snow and hail, and not about crushing ice. Perhaps because the ice was originally water, there is neither an issue of 'nolad' (newly created) nor a decree concerning squeezing fruits. This needs further consideration, as it seems that this should be considered 'nolad,' similar to fat that congealed in Siman 318, paragraph 32. Those who permit it say the reason is because it is not being crushed by hand, but if done by hand, it is indeed 'nolad.' However, the language of the Talmud and the decisors does not imply this, and the matter requires further study for a definitive ruling.

One should be careful not to rub one's hands with salt, as it dissolves and becomes water. With our salt, it seems that it does not turn into water through rubbing, and one should investigate this, for if it becomes water, it is forbidden. Regarding sea salt, there is a doubt similar to the doubt we had in the previous section about ice. A person may trample snow with his feet and does not need to be concerned, even though it is inevitable that some snow will melt slightly through his trampling. Nevertheless, since this is the normal way of walking, it should not be prohibited, for otherwise, we would have to stay indoors all winter, and they did not decree this. Similarly, urinating on snow, even though the urine causes it to melt, is permitted because it is a human need and it is almost unavoidable to be cautious about this during the winter, and thus they did not decree against it. Rabbeinu Meir of Rothenburg permitted urinating on snow, although the Rosh was cautious about it because it certainly melts and he is performing an action. We do not refrain from this because, in our region, everywhere is full of snow in the winter. (The Magen Avraham in section 15 prohibited breaking the ice in a river or well, and his words are puzzling as explained by the Taz).

And know that the prohibition of squeezing is divided into two primary categories: the first, as explained, is the squeezing of fruits, which is a derivative of "mefarek" (extracting), and its primary category is "dash" (threshing). The second is the squeezing of garments from water and other liquids, which is a derivative of "melaben" (whitening). This is what the Rambam wrote in Chapter 8: "One who squeezes fruits is liable because of 'mefarek,'" and all the laws have already been explained. And in Chapter 9, Law 11, he wrote: "One who washes garments is a derivative of 'melaben' and is liable, and one who squeezes the garment until the water comes out is like washing and is liable, etc." And in Chapter 22, Law 15, he wrote: "One who washes is liable because of 'melaben,' and one who squeezes a garment is liable because of washing. Therefore, it is forbidden to press a cloth or sponge or similar into the mouth of barrels and the like to seal them, lest one come to squeeze. And one should not wipe with a sponge unless it has a handle, so that it will not be squeezed. And one should not cover a barrel of water or similar with a garment that is not prepared for it, as a decree lest one come to squeeze." And this will be further explained.

Our rabbis, the authors of the Tosafot, also divided the wringing of a garment into two categories: when one wrings out water, it constitutes laundering. However, when one wrings out wine, oil, or other liquids that do not cleanse the garment and, on the contrary, dirty it—since the smell remains on the garment—this is not considered laundering. The prohibition in this case is due to extracting, as one extracts the liquid from the garment, similar to the pressing of olives and grapes. Therefore, the concern that one might wring out applies only to water, as one might wring it to clean the garment. But with wine and oil, we do not worry that one might wring them out. Additionally, with wine and oil, when they are wrung out, they are lost and thus extracting does not apply here. Even though it is a "pesik reisha" (an inevitable result), it is a "pesik reisha de-lo nicha lei" (an inevitable result that one does not desire) and is permitted (Tosafot Ketubot 6a, s.v. 'this' and Shabbat 111a, s.v. 'this').

The Maggid Mishneh wrote in Chapter 9, Law 11, that the Rashba agreed with their words, and the Ramban disagreed with them. And this is the language of the Ramban: "It is appropriate to say regarding all fruit squeezing that it is a derivative of 'extracting' when one needs the liquids, and its measure is like a dried fig. There is no 'threshing' except in things that grow from the ground, meaning fruits and similar items. One who squeezes a garment - it is a derivative of 'dyeing' just as 'whitening' is, and it is the same whether one launders with water or with wine, as we say: 'For eating and not for soaking and not for laundering' (Sukkah 40a regarding fruits of the Sabbatical year). This is when the garment is slightly laundered by it, and its measure is the width of the warp thread doubled in the threads, and in weaving 3 by 3, as its measure is for carrying out. Similarly, the Rambam wrote, etc." End of quote. And regarding what he wrote 'a derivative of dyeing,' it is not precisely so, but it is because whitening is similar to dyeing, but it is only a derivative of whitening (Lechem Mishneh).

And I am astonished by our teacher, the Beit Yosef, for in Siman 319, Section 10, he wrote that it is forbidden to filter water through a cloth because of laundering, but wine and other beverages are permitted, as laundering does not apply to them. We explained this in Section 29 there, see it there. This follows the opinion of Tosafot and their supporters. 

However, in this Siman, Section 15, he wrote: "It is forbidden to spread a cloth over the mouth of a barrel and place the vessel used for drawing on it, lest one come to wring it out. But a garment made for spreading over it is permitted, as one is not concerned with wringing it out," end quote. He should have clarified that this only applies to water, for with wine, we are not concerned that one will come to wring it out according to the Tosafot, as we wrote, and a barrel is usually filled with wine.

And it is surprising that Rambam specifically mentioned water, as he wrote at the end of Section 27, and his reason is that in the original source of the law in the Gemara (48a), the incident involved water, see there. And we must say that our teacher, the Beit Yosef, did not consider this, but his intention was solely regarding water.

In section 16, it is written: "It is forbidden to tighten cotton wadding at the mouth of a flask that contains liquids, because of squeezing," end quote. Now, according to the Rambam and the Ramban, this is understandable because it is due to laundering. But according to the Tosafot, it is only forbidden if one needs the liquid that is squeezed out, for if it will be lost, it is permitted with wine and oil and all liquids except water, as we have written. And in section 17, it is written: "A sponge cannot be used for wiping unless it has a handle, as a decree lest one come to squeeze it," end quote, and this is from the language of the Rambam that we brought in section 27. According to the Rambam, this is understandable, but according to the Tosafot, it is only forbidden with water or wine and oil and if one needs the liquid that is squeezed out, as we have written. But even according to the Rambam, it is difficult, since he himself wrote that in something specifically designated for that purpose, we are not concerned that one might come to squeeze. And we must say that a sponge is inherently likely to be squeezed, but if it has a handle, it is not necessarily going to be squeezed. And the Raavad wrote there that when it has a handle, even though it is squeezed, it is like emptying from a flask, meaning it is not the usual manner of squeezing (see Magen Avraham, subparagraph 19).

Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in paragraph 18: "A barrel that is sealed with a flax stopper to close a hole in its side from which wine is drawn, there is one who permits removing it even though it is impossible not to squeeze it, provided there is no vessel underneath it. Since he does not benefit from this squeezing, it is considered a 'psik reisha d'lo nicha lei' (an inevitable result that he does not desire), and it is permitted. However, others disagree and say that even though he does not desire it, since it is a 'psik reisha' (an inevitable result), it is forbidden. The common custom is to permit this, and there is a reason to justify their practice: since the spout extends beyond the flax and the hand does not touch the flax, it is permitted, similar to a sponge that has a handle. However, since this reasoning is not strong and there are grounds for doubt, it is better to instruct them not to place a vessel under the barrel when sealing the hole." End of quote.

Explanation of the matter: It is stated in the Gemara (111b): "This wine-barrel stopper - it is forbidden to press it... because it is a certain outcome (psik reisha)," meaning that they wrap a cloth around the spigot, and therefore, when they press it into the hole of the barrel, it will inevitably result in squeezing. Now, according to Ramban and Rambam, the prohibition is clear, since it constitutes laundering. However, according to Tosafot and their supporters, for wine, it is a matter of extracting (mefarek), and if the wine is wasted, extracting does not apply. Therefore, the Aruch indeed wrote in the entry "saver" as follows: "This hole is above, and therefore the Sages prohibited pressing it... because of squeezing, as it is desirable for him that the wine drips into the jug. But for a hole on the side, they did not prohibit it... because since it will be wasted, it is not desirable for him" (end of quote). And Rabbi Yitzchak of the Tosafot in Ketubot (6a) disputes this, arguing that even though it is not desirable for him and there is no Torah prohibition, it is still rabbinically prohibited, as mentioned there. The Tur also brought this dispute, as mentioned there.

The common practice is to permit using a spigot (beraza) in a situation where the wine is not wasted, and they hold that the opinion of the Aruch is that "pesik reisha d'lo nicha lei" (an inevitable outcome that one does not desire) applies even when the wine is not wasted. And since it is not desired, it is not considered a melacha (forbidden labor). This is also implied by the Tosafot in several places. However, this is certainly surprising, as it is obvious that in any case, there is a rabbinic prohibition. Therefore, some have justified the leniency because the spigot is long and similar to a sponge. Yet, this is questionable, as we see that it gets squeezed out, and it is not comparable to a sponge. Therefore, it is at least advisable to guide people not to place a vessel underneath so that the wine will be wasted. And even though Rabbi Yitzchak of the Tosafot disagrees with this, nevertheless, we rely on the Aruch, but without this, even the Aruch would agree that it is rabbinically prohibited. (And also the Ran there disagrees and holds like Rabbi Yitzchak. And from all this, it is clear that the Shulchan Aruch follows the opinion of the Tosafot, because according to the Rambam, in any case, it is forbidden as he wrote. And the words of the Taz in subparagraph 12 are difficult regarding what he wrote, that the Shulchan Aruch in section 319 holds that wine is like other liquids, and here he wrote that it whitens, look there. And if because of paragraph 15, we have already explained it. And what he differentiated between white and red, what compelled him to this? Are they not two different opinions? And it seems that he did not consider the opinions of the Rambam and Ramban that the Maggid Mishneh brought, and what the Beit Yosef wrote in his large work there, he brought all the opinions, examine it well.)

We have already written in the name of the Rambam that there is no squeezing with hair, and Rashi explained (Shabbat 128b, s.v. 'ein') that the reason is because it is hard and does not absorb. And I am perplexed, for there, Rabba and Rav Yosef hold this view, but Rav Ashi said: "Even if you say there is squeezing with hair, etc.", and the law follows Rav Ashi as he is later. One must say that Rav Ashi expressed this by way of rejection, and it is also possible that the law follows Rabba and Rav Yosef as they are the majority. Nonetheless, in any case, there is a rabbinic prohibition, and therefore those who go to the mikveh on Shabbat morning must be careful not to squeeze their hair.

Maimonides wrote in Chapter 22, Law 21: "If there are two purifications one above the other, one may remove the plug from between them, let the waters connect, and then return the plug to its place, because this does not lead to squeezing, as it is intended for the waters to flow out. One may plug a drain with cloths or any movable object to prevent the waters from spilling over the food and the vessels, but one may not plug the drain to let the waters flow into a pit, lest squeezing occur while pressing, as the plug is soaked in water." This is the wording of the Tosefta in Chapter 8 of Eruvin. 

And the explanation of the matter is: Since at first he intends to connect the waters, he will necessarily plug it loosely so that the waters can connect, and also when he wants to remove it to let the waters truly connect, he will easily take it out. Conversely, in the latter case, where he plugs the drain to let the waters descend, he plugs it well, and the plug is soaked in water, and squeezing will occur. 

But the middle case is difficult because, to prevent the waters from overflowing, one also plugs it well. Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in his great book that even here, one is not concerned with plugging it well, as mentioned there, which is not understood. It seems to me that the middle case refers to plugging in a dry place to prevent the waters from overflowing here, and this is why Maimonides concludes in the latter case: 'as the plug is soaked in water,' meaning, unlike the middle case where the plug is in a dry place.

Grinding is a principal category of labor, and it was performed in the Tabernacle by grinding spices. The derivatives of grinding, as written by the Rambam at the end of Chapter 8: "One who grinds an amount equivalent to a dried fig - is liable. Anyone who crushes spices or herbs in a mortar - this is considered grinding and they are liable. One who cuts detached vegetables - this is a derivative of grinding. Similarly, one who saws wood to benefit from its sawdust or one who files a metal tongue - is liable once they file any amount. However, one who cuts wood is not liable until they cut it finely enough to cook an amount equivalent to a dried fig from an egg." End of quote. And what he wrote 'for its sawdust', implies that if not, they are exempt due to performing a labor not needed for its own purpose, and it is impossible to say this, because the Rambam obligates even for a labor not needed for its own purpose. Rather, the intention is because it is destructive, such as when they do not need the wood to be sawed in this measure, for otherwise, it is not considered destructive (Lechem Mishneh). And the measure of a dried fig is for grinding for eating, like all food measures, and for wood, it is the measure for carrying out, which is equivalent to a dried fig from an egg as stated in Siman 301. And that which he wrote: 'until they cut it finely etc.', means that if they saw it, there must be enough sawdust to cook an amount equivalent to a dried fig from an egg, and if they cut it, there must be pieces of that measure. And know that cutting is not a derivative of grinding, but a principal category of labor in its own right. And it was said in the Gemara (74b) that when one cuts wood and is precise about the measure - it is a derivative of cutting, and if not precise - it is a derivative of grinding, see there, and similarly, in anything related to grinding.

And regarding what is written that cutting vegetables is liable because of grinding, this is from what was said there: "One who cuts beets is liable because of grinding." But the Tosafot wrote there that only with beets is grinding applicable, but with other foods—it is permitted. And their intention is that even other vegetables besides beets are permitted, as explained in the Hagahot Asheri there. And the Rosh completely questioned those who prohibit cutting, and this is his language: "And Rashi's explanation is puzzling, for how is grinding applicable to something that is food and is cut finely, and the explanation of beets is as Rabbi Hananel explained, that they are palm trees, etc., that when fibers are separated, it comes out like fine flour, therefore, one who crushes it is liable because of grinding." And I am astonished at the Tur who wrote: "It is forbidden to cut vegetables finely, as it resembles grinding," not like his father the Rosh of blessed memory, and he did not bring his opinion at all. And it seems from his language that he holds that although there is no liability of a sin offering in this, as the explanation in the Gemara is like his father, nevertheless, since Rashi and the Rambam prohibited it—he did not have the heart to permit it, and therefore he wrote that it resembles grinding.

The Rashba and the Ran wrote that the case of "parim silka" refers to preparing it to be eaten the next day or at a later time. However, to eat it immediately is permitted, just like in the case of selecting, where one selects and eats during the meal itself, as stated in Siman 319. And it is not specifically at the exact time of eating, but rather to eat immediately, and even one person can cut for all the members of the meal, just like in the case of selecting there (Beit Yosef).

In the words of the Rambam, there is a matter to analyze. At first glance, it appears from his words similar to the explanation of Rashi, that cutting vegetables makes one liable for grinding, meaning cutting them into small pieces. For if it were large pieces, we find that they would prepare vegetables on Yom Kippur from the afternoon and onwards (Tosafot 114b, s.v. 'Ela'). However, in Chapter 21, Law 18, he wrote: "One who cuts vegetables finely in order to cook them - this is a derivative of grinding and is liable. Therefore, one may not crush hay or carob before an animal, but one may cut gourds and carcasses, for there is no grinding with fruits," end quote. Here it seems that one is liable only if cutting the vegetables finely to cook them, but to eat them raw – it is permitted. And so wrote our teacher the Beit Yosef in his great book, that this is the opinion of the Rambam. And afterwards, he wrote that perhaps it is prohibited rabbinically, and from his words, it appears that even in Chapter 8, the version in the Rambam he had was "to cook them," see there. However, in my humble opinion, this is very puzzling, for what difference does it make in the labor of grinding whether it is to cook or not to cook. And should you say because the main grinding is with flour and it is in order to bake, but in the Jerusalem Talmud in the chapter "General Principle" it says: "One who grinds salt, one who grinds pepper – is liable for grinding," and is all salt for cooking? And further, it says there: when one grinds garlic in a mortar – is liable for grinding, and similarly, one who beats flax – is liable for grinding, and indeed one is liable also for wood and metal when they are filed, which is called filing, as the Rambam himself wrote. And if not for the words of our teacher the Beit Yosef, I would say that what the Rambam wrote "to cook them" does not specifically mean to cook them, but rather that he cuts them finely enough to be able to cook them, for one who cuts for cooking cuts very finely.

And also what the Rambam wrote that one may cut gourds because there is no grinding with fruits, but the Jerusalem Talmud obligates concerning the grinding of pepper as it says, and pepper is considered a fruit as it is stated in Berachot (36a): "And you shall consider it uncircumcised, its fruit" - to include a tree whose wood and fruit taste the same, and what is that - pepper." See there. Moreover, I do not understand, since he ruled that there is grinding with vegetables but not with fruits, therefore it is permitted to cut gourds. Yet, gourds are a type of vegetable as is evident in the Tractate Kilayim, and also in the words of the Rambam in Chapter 3 of Kilayim where he wrote: "If his field was sown with vegetables and he wished to sow another vegetable, even gourds." See there. And it must be so, for they are neither a type of grain nor a type of seed. Additionally, from where does he know that there is no grinding with fruits?

It appears to me, in my humble opinion, that there is another intention in his words. Grinding applies only to things that are customarily chopped finely, regardless of what type they are. However, fruits are not customarily chopped finely, and this is also true for gourds, as is well known. It is not specifically gourds, but the same rule applies to any type of vegetable that is not customarily chopped finely, like cucumbers with us, which are not chopped finely. Beets and cabbage, which are customarily chopped finely when cooked, are an exception. Fruits, however, are never chopped finely. Therefore, radishes, which are called "rettach," are also known not to be customarily chopped finely. But onions and garlic are customarily chopped finely.

And now, to clarify the law according to Rashi and the Rambam, every type of vegetable is subject to the prohibition of grinding (tochen), but according to Rabbeinu Beit Yosef's understanding of the Rambam, it only applies when one wants to cook it. According to Tosafot and the Rosh, there is no grinding prohibition for vegetables, except for beets according to Tosafot, which is not common among us. According to the Rashba and the Ran, the prohibition only applies if it is to be used later, but if it is before eating - it is permitted, as mentioned. It is surprising that Rabbeinu Beit Yosef in Shulchan Aruch, Section 12, completely ruled in favor of the prohibition without qualification. His words are: "One who cuts vegetables finely is liable for grinding," end quote. This does not align with the Rambam, Tosafot, or the Rosh, nor with the Rashba and the Ran, but rather with Rashi's opinion. However, it is not definitively clear from Rashi, as he only explained that "preparing" means cutting finely, and maybe he also agrees with Tosafot. This proves that his explanation of the Rambam's opinion is lenient, as mentioned, and therefore he wrote simply that one is liable for grinding, which requires further investigation.

However, our teacher, the Rema, wrote the following: "It is likewise forbidden to cut figs and carobs before the elderly. Specifically, fruits and the like are prohibited, but it is permitted to crumble bread before chickens, since it has already been ground, there is no concern, as there is no grinding after grinding. All this applies only when cutting and leaving it, but if it is to eat immediately - everything is permitted, similar to selecting to eat immediately which is permitted, as stated above in Siman 319.” End of quote. And behold, in this matter of immediate consumption, he ruled like the Rashba and the Ran, and according to the Rosh, it is obvious that it is permitted, and similarly according to the Tosafot. And even according to Rashi and the Rambam according to our interpretation, there is no proof that they do not agree with this. Therefore, our practice on Shabbat morning to finely chop onions to mix with fat or to add them to the cholent is not prohibited, because since it is done before the meal, even an hour before the meal is considered "immediate," as stated above in Siman 319, sections 12 and 15. And even though selecting (borer) is only permitted by hand, that is because the act of selection is by hand, but the act of grinding is only with a utensil, and when it is permitted to eat immediately, it is also permitted with a utensil since this is the manner of eating (as also written by the Pri Megadim).

And I have seen those who are skeptical and forbid cutting onions with the “hakmesser,” and this does not seem correct to me at all, for this is also a knife. And in the Rivash (Siman 184), there is concern about forbidding grating cheese with a “morg charutz,” which is called a “rib eisen,” as this is made to grind finely like flour, and in this case, it indeed falls under the category of the labor of grinding. But the knife called a “hakmesser” is a knife made in the shape of a half-circle, and it is like any other knife, and why should we say that Jewish women are acting improperly? And I have also seen someone who wrote that if one cuts onions two or three hours before the meal, it is close to a liability for a sin offering (Chayei Adam, Klal 17). And I am astonished: Are there not our Rabbis who permit it entirely? Tosafot, the Rosh, and the Rambam according to the view of Rabbeinu Beit Yosef, that it is only forbidden to cook. Moreover, anything done before the meal for the sake of the meal is considered immediate, and it is impossible to be precise, and as I wrote above in Siman 319, it is called not immediate from morning until evening, but anything for that meal—there is no concern. And certainly, it is more proper to do it close to the meal, but when there are many people at the meal, it is necessary to prepare some time in advance for everyone.

However, what our teacher, the Rema, wrote that it is forbidden to cut dried figs and carobs before the elderly, this is a Tosefta in the first chapter of Beitza. And in the Tosefta it states: "One may not crush, etc., but one may crush with the handle of a knife or with a wooden spoon and need not worry," end quote. This means that by making a change, it is permitted, as will be explained regarding salt and pepper. And our teacher, the Rema, who wrote "to cut," did so because here we are discussing cutting, and it is all the same; what difference does it make if it is crushing or cutting (see Magen Avraham, subsection 14). And there are those who say that it is only forbidden for the elderly, but for someone who can eat it as it is, it is permitted (ibid.). This is astonishing, for if there is a prohibition of grinding, what difference does it make whether the person can eat it or not? If so, we should say the same regarding vegetables, and we have not heard this distinction from the legal decisors (the Mishnah Berurah also wonders about this), and see in the next section.

However, the basic text of the Tosefta is difficult for me, as the Rambam wrote that there is no grinding with fruits. And it is true that the Maggid Mishneh found this difficult and wrote that he found a version that stated there is no grinding except with fruits. However, our teacher, the Beit Yosef, in his book Kesef Mishneh, rejected this version with both hands, arguing that there is grinding even with dust, wood, and iron as stated in paragraph 1. However, according to what is written in paragraph 6, it is understandable, as his intention is that it is not customary to cut fruits very finely, as mentioned there. According to this, the Tosefta is correct in saying that for the elderly who must have their food cut very finely, it is prohibited. And according to this, the law stated by "some say" in the previous paragraph, that if one can eat it as it is, there is no grinding with fruits, stands. And it is clear that before eating, it is permissible for the elderly as with vegetables. (And if not for the words of the Rema, I would say that the reason of the Tosefta is not because of grinding but because of smoothing, as the Rema himself wrote in paragraph 19, that it is permitted to smooth food on Shabbat and it is not considered smoothing, since it is possible to eat it without this action. Therefore, for the elderly who cannot eat without this action, it is prohibited because of smoothing. And for those who can eat it, it is permitted, as the Magen Avraham wrote in subparagraph 14, which we brought in the previous paragraph. Pay attention and understand.)

Our teacher, Rabbi Yosef Karo, wrote in paragraph 7: "It is permissible to grind pepper, even a lot at once, as long as it is ground with the handle of a knife in a bowl." This means that even though grinding pepper incurs a sin-offering, the Sages permitted it with a modification (141a), because with a modification it is not considered a [forbidden] labor, but rather a labor performed in an unusual manner, and therefore they permitted what is needed for that meal. The modification is that it should be ground with the handle of a knife and not with a mill, and in a bowl and not in a mortar. Some say that one modification suffices: either with the handle even in a mortar, or in a bowl even without the handle (Magen Avraham, paragraph 9). However, from Rashi it is apparent that two modifications are required, as he wrote: "Since he changes both not using a mill and not using a mortar," it is explicitly written that two modifications are needed, and this is the main ruling. And not just pepper, the same applies to all kinds of spices (ibid.). Care should be taken not to place the pepper or the spices inside an object and grind on it, because the fragrance is absorbed into it and it creates a new fragrance, which is also forbidden on Yom Tov as written in section 511 (Taz, paragraph 7). However, we have already explained that Shabbat is more lenient than Yom Tov regarding the issue of creating a new thing, and most authorities permit creating a new thing on Shabbat, as the Tur wrote in section 495. Nevertheless, it is certainly forbidden initially, because Rabbeinu Tam holds that creating a new thing is forbidden on Shabbat, as the Tur wrote there, and we have explained this in section 308 and section 322.

Even with salt, one should not crush it in a mortar, even if it is made of wood. However, one may crush it with the handle of a knife or with a wooden spoon and need not be concerned. This applies specifically to coarse salt, but salt that was initially fine and cooked and became crumbly - it is permissible to cut it with a knife as one cuts bread, for there is no grinding after grinding. Therefore, it is permissible to crumble bread before chickens. Nevertheless, in a mortar - even this salt is forbidden to crush, as this would be a weekday activity (and the Pri Megadim writes that the same applies to sugar, see there, and see what I wrote in section 321, paragraph 24).

It is permissible to cut cooked or roasted meat into very small pieces with a knife. And not only according to the opinion of Tosafot and the Rosh, who hold that there is no prohibition of grinding (טוחן) with vegetables, but even according to those who believe there is grinding with vegetables, in any case, we require something that grows from the ground. But with the meat of animals, the category of grinding does not apply, obviously. Therefore, it is permitted even if not for immediate consumption, and even for someone who cannot chew it as is, it is permitted (Magen Avraham, section 10), since it does not fall under the category of grinding at all. However, it is forbidden to cut raw meat very finely for birds, because since they cannot eat it without cutting, it is considered preparing food for the chickens, and it is forbidden to prepare food for animals on Shabbat. And even though it will be explained in section 324 that it is permitted to prepare food for animals, in any case, with very fine cutting, it is forbidden. There is no satisfactory explanation for this, and indeed there are those who disagree and permit it (Taz, section 9). And what the Magen Avraham wrote in section 10 in the name of the Shiltei Giborim, that regarding separating (מפרק), an animal is considered something that grows from the ground, I do not understand the comparison, because there it is about separating milk from meat, and what relevance does it have to grinding? Consider this carefully.

Rabbeinu the Beit Yosef wrote in section 10: It is forbidden to grate cheese on Shabbat with a serrated grater that has double blades, which is called a "Ralin" or in our language, a "Rib Eisen" or "Tarteki." This is not because there is grinding involved with cheese, as it is similar to meat, but because this tool is specifically designated for grinding, since radish and horseradish, which are called "Krin," are ground on it - therefore, it is forbidden to use it for anything else. However, it is permitted to cut cheese into small pieces with a knife, and even if it is hard cheese, it is permitted (Magen Avraham, section 12). But with a tool designated for grating, even a small tool - it is forbidden (ibid). Similarly, it is permitted to cut cheese with a hatchet or a saw, as it is stated in the beginning of chapter "All the Utensils" (Shabbat 122b): "A hatchet to cut dried figs, a saw to saw cheese" (ibid).

It is clear that one who crumbles a piece of rotten wood into powder is liable for the prohibition of grinding (tochen). Similarly, one who crumbles a clod of earth is liable for the prohibition of grinding, as well as one who crumbles clay or dry manure, or who crumbles coal or food peels and anything similar. And clay that sticks to a garment - it is forbidden to scrape it off, because this constitutes grinding, and this is explained in detail in Siman 302, see there.

Kneading is a primary category of labor, and it was performed in the Tabernacle in the preparation of the spices. It is stated in the Jerusalem Talmud that there is a fundamental rule: "One who kneads gypsum, bran, dirt for a salve, or dyes - is liable because of kneading. Kneading, shaping, and arranging - all are due to kneading." Before this, it says: "One who crushes garlic and adds liquids to it - is liable because of kneading," and similarly with red dye when water is added to it - one is liable because of kneading, as it is a type of dye. This is when one kneads and makes the garlic or the dye into a cohesive mass. And what are its derivatives? Shaping, which means that after kneading, one shapes the bread to give it form, and applying liquid, which means spreading liquid on it after shaping (Rashi Pesachim 36a). Maimonides, at the end of Chapter 8, writes that a derivative of kneading is mixing dirt, meaning that the primary category of labor is kneading with dough. Dirt and everything else mentioned are derivatives. The measure for liability for kneading is the size of a dried fig with dough, which is fit for human consumption, and with dirt, the measure is enough to make the opening of a goldsmith's crucible, like the measure of carrying out that was explained in Section 301, and similarly, each one is according to the measure of carrying out.

Rambam wrote there: "There is no kneading with ashes, nor with coarse sand, nor with bran, nor with similar substances. But one who places sesame seeds or flax seeds or the like in water is liable because of kneading, because they mix and cling to each other." End quote. The Raavad objected to his statement that there is no kneading with ashes, arguing that on the contrary, adding water alone to ashes constitutes kneading and one is liable just as with sesame seeds and flax seeds, see there. Their disagreement hinges on the discussion in the first chapter (18a), see there. Tosafot, Sefer HaTerumah, and the SeMaG wrote like the Raavad. One should not question Rambam's ruling that there is no kneading with bran based on the Jerusalem Talmud we brought, because it can be said that bran and coarse bran are different, and coarse bran is thicker than bran as explained in the second chapter of Challa, and it is also explained at the end of the chapter "Klal Gadol," see there. Also, there is a dispute regarding coarse bran and it will be explained in Siman 324.

Rambam wrote in Chapter 21, Law 33: "Mixing is forbidden due to the prohibition of kneading. Therefore, one should not mix a large amount of roasted flour, lest one come to knead regular flour. It is permitted, however, to mix a small amount of roasted flour at a time. But grain that has not reached a third of its growth, which was roasted and then coarsely ground, and is like sand and called 'shatitah'—it is permitted to mix it with vinegar or similar substances in large quantities at once, provided it is soft. If it is hard, it is forbidden because it appears like kneading. One must make a change, as follows: first put the 'shatitah' and then add the vinegar." End quote. 

Explanation of his words: Both roasted flour and 'shatitah' involve some form of mixing, and 'shatitah' is also roasted flour. The difference is that roasted flour comes from fully grown grain, whereas 'shatitah' comes from grain that has not reached a third of its growth. What is roasted flour? It is flour from grain that was dried when it was roasted in the oven. This flour is always sweet and is mixed with oil, water, and salt (Rashi, Shabbat 155b). Therefore, roasted flour from fully grown grain, although it doesn’t mix well because it was dried in the oven, is still subject to a decree against mixing large quantities, only allowing small amounts due to the similarity in appearance to regular flour. However, roasted flour from 'shatitah,' where the grain did not reach a third of its growth and does not resemble regular flour—it is permitted to mix even in large quantities. Nonetheless, if it is hard and appears like kneading, a change must be made.

However, the Tur has a different approach to this. This is the language of the Tur: "If the dish called 'shitita' is thick, it is forbidden to knead a large amount at once, only a little at a time. If it is thin, it is permitted to knead a large amount at once with a change. And what is the change? That one places the flour first and then the vinegar, whereas on a weekday one places the vinegar first." End quote. He does not differentiate between 'kali' and 'shitita', and everything is included in 'shitita'. Thick is completely forbidden in large amounts, and thin requires a change. Our master, the Beit Yosef, in section 14, copied the words of the Rambam, except that our master the Rema, in the place where he wrote that with a change it is permitted in large amounts, corrected: 'and even with thin', which means that even with thin requires a change, but with thick, a change does not help, and it is forbidden to knead except a little. Now, the matter of 'kali' is not known to us at all, but we can learn from this about crushed matzah that returns to flour, which is called 'matzah meal'. Certainly, its law is like 'shitita', and therefore it is forbidden to knead it on Shabbat in large amounts, and even in small amounts requires a change like 'shitita'. There are those who forbid even with a change (Taz, section 11), but this is not so, and so ruled in Terumat HaDeshen (section 53) in similar cases. He wrote that the change that the Sages mentioned is sufficient: to place the flour first and then the liquid, and only that its mixture should be thin. This is according to the Tur as mentioned. (In my humble opinion, it seems that crushed matzah is lighter than 'kali', since it has already been kneaded once, and just as there is no grinding after grinding, so maybe there is no kneading after kneading, and this requires further study).

And know that in the Gemara there is a dispute among the Tannaim regarding adding water to flour: whether one is liable immediately, as this constitutes kneading, or whether one is not liable until it is actually kneaded. Rabbi holds that one is liable immediately upon adding the water, whereas Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Yehuda holds that one is not liable until it is actually kneaded. The Rif, Rambam, and Rosh rule in accordance with Rabbi Yosei, and the opinion of the Raavad also seems to align with this. However, the author of Sefer HaTerumah rules in accordance with Rabbi, and this also seems to be the opinion of the SeMaG and SeMaK (see Beit Yosef). According to this, based on the Jerusalem Talmud we brought in Section 17, which states that there is an element of kneading in the grinding of garlic, care should be taken when grinding garlic on Shabbat not to add a bit of liquid to it. Instead, one should grind it and add it to the food. Additionally, grinding is prohibited on Shabbat unless it was ground before Shabbat, and if not, one should cut it with a knife and add it to the food.

Our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, wrote in sections 15 and 16: "Mustard that was kneaded on the eve of Shabbat—on the morrow, one may mix it, whether by hand or with a utensil, and add honey to it. But one should not beat it to mix it (i.e., with force), but rather mix it little by little. Cress that was pounded on the eve of Shabbat—on the morrow, one may add wine and vinegar, but should not beat it, only mix it. Similarly, garlic that was pounded on the eve of Shabbat—on the morrow, one may add beans and grits, but should not beat it, only mix it. And some say that one should not mix with a spoon but with a hand, and some say that the permission to mix a liquid with mustard is only if it was added before the day (i.e., before Shabbat); but on Shabbat, it is forbidden to add liquid to pounded mustard or garlic because of kneading. However, if one first adds the food and then the vinegar or wine and mixes it with one's finger—it is permitted, as it is considered a change, like the case of 'shatita' mentioned above. And thus is the custom to permit it by way of change, and in a place where it is customary to do so on weekdays, one should add the vinegar first and then the food on Shabbat." End quote.

Explanation of the matter: According to the poskim (decisors) who ruled according to Rabbi Yossi that simply adding water to flour is not considered kneading, therefore, in these matters of mustard, cress, and garlic, since the mustard was kneaded before Shabbat and the cress and garlic were crushed before Shabbat, it is permissible on Shabbat to add liquids to them. However, one should not stir vigorously, as this is their kneading, but rather mix a little at a time gently. The addition itself is negligible, as it is not considered kneading according to Rabbi Yossi. Nevertheless, some say that the slight stirring should not be done with a spoon but with one's finger, or by shaking the container itself. If the mustard was not kneaded before Shabbat, and the cress and garlic were not crushed before Shabbat, although the addition of the liquids is negligible, one must still knead or crush a little, for otherwise, they are not fit for consumption. Even if they were kneaded and crushed before Shabbat, a complete kneading on Shabbat is forbidden, and there is a liability of a sin-offering. Even for mustard that was already kneaded, its primary kneading is when mixed with liquids, and vigorous stirring constitutes its kneading. Therefore, it is only permitted to add a little at a time and mix with a finger or by shaking the container, and according to the first opinion, also with a spoon, but one must be careful to stir lightly. There are those who hold according to Rabbi, and therefore the addition of liquids must be done before Shabbat, for otherwise, the addition itself is considered kneading according to Rabbi. If the liquids were not added before Shabbat, it is completely forbidden. However, if they were added before Shabbat, it is permitted to add more liquids on Shabbat. Nevertheless, even according to this opinion, adding liquids with a change (shinui) is permitted, as with the dish "shatita" mentioned above. And although it is not similar, since "shatita" does not involve kneading by Torah law as stated, therefore it is permitted with a change, which is not the case with these items. It can be said that they hold that even with a Torah prohibition, it is permitted with a change, or it is possible that they hold that even these items do not involve a Torah prohibition. (See Magen Avraham 322:22, who wrote that according to some opinions, even with roasted flour, it is necessary to add the liquid before Shabbat, which does not seem to be the case from the Tur and Shulchan Aruch. According to what I have written, it makes sense, as there the kneading is not by Torah law. What was forbidden with bran in Siman 324 can be explained that with animal food, they were stringent because it is in large quantity and appears like kneading. Pay attention and understand this well.)

According to this, for us, with mustard that is called "zanafet," everything must be prepared before Shabbat. Similarly, with "karein" into which vinegar or "rasil" is put, it must be added before Shabbat. On Shabbat, it is permitted to add more. However, if it was not added before Shabbat, it can only be added with a change. There are those who say that for us, since it is not made like a thick mixture, there is no concern at all (Bach in the name of Rashal), but nevertheless, it is difficult to rely on this, and one should be careful to do it with a change. This means that on a weekday, they put the "karein" in a vessel first and then pour vinegar or "rasil" over it; on Shabbat, it should be done in the opposite order. And it should not be mixed vigorously but gently, and all similar cases apply (Taz, comment 12).

According to the opinion of the poskim (legal decisors) who follow Rabbi, that placing water constitutes mixing—it is forbidden to urinate on clay or dirt, for when the urine mixes with the clay or dirt, it constitutes mixing (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 19, and Eliyah Rabbah). And it is very difficult to be cautious about this. However, it seems that the primary legal ruling follows Rabbi Yosei, as the Rif, Rambam, and Rosh have ruled, as I have written. And perhaps even according to Rabbi, it would be considered an unintentional act, and even if it is a "psik reisha" (an inevitable outcome), it would be a "psik reisha d'lo nicha lei" (an inevitable outcome that one does not desire).

The one who skins the hide – this is a principal category of labor, and it was in the Tabernacle, where they skinned the hides of the red rams and the tachash hides. And its measure is that if one skins enough to make an amulet, he is liable. And its derivative category: one who removes the parchment layer from the klaf (Rambam, Chapter 11, Halacha 6). And it appears to me that also skinning the hide of a bird or a fish is considered a principal category of labor, as it is explicitly stated in Shabbat (108a) that they have hides. And one should not say that according to this, after cooking it would also be forbidden to skin their hides and eat them, for it is common practice every day that during a meal, someone who likes the skin peels it little by little and eats it. One could say that during a meal, skinning does not apply, similar to the labor of selecting which does not apply during a meal, as we hold that one selects food and eats in Siman 319, and here too with skinning. Additionally, after cooking, they are considered like meat. But before cooking, it seems to me that even for those whose hides are like their flesh regarding impurity, nevertheless regarding skinning on Shabbat, it is a principal category of labor.

Tanning leather is a primary category of labor, and it was done in the Tabernacle as when skinning [animals], as we have written. Its measure [of prohibition] is also sufficient to make an amulet. Both salting [the hide] and tanning it incur liability, as salting is also a type of tanning. A derivative of tanning includes pressing on the leather with one's foot until it hardens or softening it by hand and stretching and smoothing it as leather workers do—this is considered a derivative of tanning and incurs liability (Rambam, there). Be aware that in the Mishnah of primary labors, salting and tanning are counted as two separate labors. The Gemara questions: "Isn't salting the same as tanning?" and answers: "Remove one and include scoring [the skin]." This explains the Jerusalem Talmud which states: "What tanning was done in the Tabernacle? They would score the hides." Scoring means marking them. It is not clear what the question "What tanning was done in the Tabernacle?" means, as there were tachash and red-dyed rams' skins. However, since tanning included scoring, which was done on all four sides to even them out, scoring is called a primary category of labor (and the commentators were puzzled by this, but it is clear as we have explained, and we have mentioned this in Siman 242). See also Siman 327.

And this is the language of the Rambam at the end of Chapter 11: One who engraves in order to write two letters beneath that engraving is liable. Wood craftsmen who pass a chalk line over a beam so that they saw it evenly—this is a derivative of engraving. Similarly, stonemasons who do this with stones so that the stone will split evenly. And whether one engraves with color or without color, they are liable. Therefore, one must be very careful not to engrave with a fingernail as well, for it is a primary category of labor. And see later in Siman 340 that if the engraving does not endure, it is not considered labor. It is known that on paper, the engraving endures, and it is appropriate to inform the public who do not know that this is a primary category of labor.

The Rambam rules there that there is no tanning (processing) with food, and it is explicitly stated in the Gemara (75b) that tanning is only relevant to hides, which are preserved for a long time, and not to foods. Therefore, salting meat, even for a long time with a lot of salt, does not constitute tanning according to Torah law. According to Rashi and Tosafot there, although by Torah law there is no tanning with food, rabbinically there is tanning with food (Tosafot there). Therefore, later (108b) where it is forbidden to make strong brine and salt radishes, Rashi explains that it is because it is like tanning or appears like tanning, and similarly, the Ra'avad writes this in his commentary on the Mishnah. However, the Rambam in Chapter 22, Law 6 does not hold this way.

And these are the words of the Rambam: "A person may mix water, salt, and oil and dip his bread into it or put it into the dish, provided he makes a small amount. But making a large amount is forbidden because it appears as if he is performing the labor of preparing a dish. Similarly, one should not make a strong brine, which is two-thirds salt and one-third water, because it appears as if he is making fish brine. It is permitted to salt an egg, but salting a radish or something similar is forbidden because it appears as if he is pickling vegetables on Shabbat, and pickling is forbidden because it is akin to cooking. However, it is permitted to dip a radish or something similar in salt and eat it." Thus, it is evident that this prohibition is not due to the issue of tanning, but rather because it appears as if he is performing labor, making fish brine, or pickling vegetables.

But the Tur holds that the prohibition is due to the reason of tanning, like Rashi and Tosafot, and this is the wording of the Tur: "One should not make a lot of saltwater at once to put into vegetables, because since it is made to preserve, it resembles tanning, as the salt preserves them. But one can make a small amount to put into a dish. And if one puts two-thirds salt into it, it is forbidden to make even a small amount of it. It is forbidden to salt four or five pieces of radish together, but one should dip each one individually and eat it. However, it is permitted to salt eggs. The Rash wrote that one should not salt many beans and lentils together that were cooked in their shells." End of quote, thus it is written that the prohibition is due to the reason of tanning.

And behold, our master the Beit Yosef in Section 2 in the laws of salted water copied the language of the Tur, that this is because of tanning, and in Section 3 in the laws of radish copied the language of the Rambam, that this is like pickling vegetables, see there. And it seems that he believes there is no difference in the law. However, in my humble opinion, there is a difference, for the Tosafot there wrote that when there is fat, there is no prohibition of salted water, as the fat sweetens the salt, see there. And so ruled the great later authorities (Magen Avraham, Sections 6 and 7). And so is the custom among us when cutting many radishes or onions, we only salt them after first putting oil or fat on them, and then salting them. This is based on the reason of tanning, for in such cases there is no tanning. But according to the Rambam, whose reason is that it appears like doing work or like pickling vegetables, it seems that even in such cases it is forbidden. And you should know that this is so, for he wrote: "water and salt and oil, etc.", and he forbids making much even when there is oil. Besides this, I am surprised at the Tur and Shulchan Aruch for not mentioning the permission of fat that the Tosafot wrote, and also the Mordechai wrote this permission, see there. And why do we need the Tosafot and Mordechai, for it is explicitly stated in the Mishnah itself, for it is taught: "these are permitted: putting oil at the beginning, etc." However, if so, it should also be permitted according to the Rambam, and if so, it is difficult why they omitted this and it requires investigation. (And one cannot say that he holds that only Rabbi Yossi holds this and we hold like the Rabbis, and on the contrary, Rabbi Yossi is stricter, and since it is permitted for him, all the more so for the Rabbis. And it is possible that he holds that this permission is only for a small amount of salted water which Rabbi Yossi forbids, and for a large amount this does not help. And according to this, they properly omitted it, for a small amount is anyway permitted by the Rabbis. And this we can explain for the Rambam, but not for the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, as the Tosafot and Mordechai explicitly wrote that for us it is permitted, and pay attention).

Our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in Section 4: "There is an opinion that permits dipping several pieces of radish one by one, and placing them together before him to eat them immediately one after the other." This is based on the annotations of the Maimonides (Chapter 22, Note 10) according to the Jerusalem Talmud in the Great Principle, which states: "One can dip radish in salt, provided he does not leave it [to sit]." Thus, the prohibition is only if they are salted and left for some hours, but if he intends to eat them immediately, it is permitted. This is also stated by the author of the Terumat HaDeshen (Siman 53). According to this, what the Gemara says: "One does not salt radish, Rav Nachman said, 'I do not salt, but I do dip,'" means that salting a lot together and leaving it is forbidden, but dipping during the meal is permitted even for many pieces one by one. However, according to Rashi, it seems that only one piece is permitted to be dipped in salt and eaten, and therefore the commentators on the Shulchan Aruch were stringent in this matter (Taz Note 1 and Magen Avraham Note 6). But there are those who agree with the Beit Yosef (Gra Note 4), and from Rashi’s words, it is not conclusive (ibid.), and according to Maimonides, it is certainly permitted. Therefore, in my humble opinion, in such a minor prohibition, one who relies on the Beit Yosef has not lost. However, our simple custom is not to salt beforehand until we add fat or oil to them.

It has already been explained in the name of the Tur that one should not salt a large quantity of beans and lentils that have been cooked in their shells, because since salting is effective, it is like radish. Rather, one should dip each one in salt and eat it. Similarly, one should not salt a large quantity of raw cucumbers together, because they are usually pickled and it is like radish (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 7). Rather, one should dip each piece in salt and eat it. However, with oil and fat, everything is permitted, and similarly with salad, one can first put the salt and then add oil and vinegar. Our custom is to put vinegar into green onions or raw cucumbers, and there is no prohibition in this, only one should be careful to do it right at the time of eating. This is not similar to salting, even according to those who prohibit putting salt on many radishes during the meal, because in this case it is only a matter of pickling, and at the time of eating it does not appear as pickling. There are those who prohibit putting wine or other liquids into vinegar, because this is like pickling pickles (Taz, subparagraph 3), but this is an excessive stringency, as we do not find that there is a concept of pickling with a liquid in a liquid. And so, the custom is to put vinegar in wine or water to drink them, especially since the vinegar is less than them.

It is forbidden to salt raw meat or raw fish on Shabbat to prevent them from spoiling, and even in a situation of financial loss, it is prohibited (Magen Avraham section 7). However, placing cooked meat in vinegar to eat immediately is permitted (ibid.). As for meat that has not been rinsed, if the third day falls on Shabbat and if it is not rinsed today it will be forbidden to eat it cooked, as explained in Yoreh De'ah section 69, it is prohibited to rinse it on Shabbat since it is not needed for that day. However, through a non-Jew, it is permitted because of the financial loss. Some prohibit this because there is no financial loss, as it can be eaten roasted (ibid.). This is not the case, as it is known that among us, who are not skilled in roasting meat, it would almost entirely be a loss. Some permit it by washing one's hands over the meat when he needs to perform hand washing, and as a result, the meat is rinsed incidentally, and this is correct. It has already been explained in section 308 that raw meat, even if not salted, is permitted to be moved on Shabbat.

And our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 5: "It is forbidden to salt cooked meat or cooked eggs to leave them" [end quote]. This prohibition is not clear, for it certainly does not pertain to pickling, and if it is because it appears as tanning, even those who prohibit it in the Gemara (75b) only prohibit salting that is done extensively, and in this case, the halacha does not follow their view. Therefore, even if we say it is rabbinically prohibited, it is only in such cases. Hence, it can be said that "to leave them" means for the next day, which is considered unnecessary labor for weekday purposes (as explained explicitly by the Gra). Some interpret it as leaving it for another meal (Taz 5 and Magen Avraham 7), reasoning that why should one salt it now when it can be salted when needed. Therefore, if there is a benefit in salting it now, it is permitted, such as when the meat is currently hot (Taz there). This is also implied in the original ruling in the responsa of the Geonim, who wrote: the reason for the prohibition is that the meat does not spoil without salt (Beit Yosef), as if to say why trouble oneself now unnecessarily. The custom of the world is when they cook tsimmes for the evening meal and leave the meat, called tsimmes fleish, for the next morning, they salt it with a little salt and add some pepper, and in this way, the taste is better the next day. There is no prohibition in this, since it is better for him to salt it now, especially since the salting is not extensive and does not fall under the category of tanning.

Erasing (Memachek) is a primary labor category. What constitutes erasing? Removing hair or wool from a hide after the animal's death until the surface of the hide is smooth. This was done in the Tabernacle with the red-dyed ram skins. The measure of liability is the removal of hair from an area of hide sufficient to make an amulet. Derivatives of erasing include: plucking feathers from a bird, which is a derivative of erasing and incurs liability. Similarly, smoothing any amount of a bandage, wax, or tar—materials that can be smoothed until their surfaces are even—incurs liability for erasing. Additionally, rubbing one's hand over a stretched hide between posts incurs liability for erasing. Likewise, scribes who stretch parchment and rub it with chalk to smooth its surface incur liability for erasing.

It has already been explained in Siman 252 that garlic, unripe grapes, and crushed grains that were crushed before Shabbat - it is permitted to drink the liquids that come out of them on Shabbat. However, if they still require pounding, and have not yet been pounded - it is forbidden to finish pounding them on Shabbat, as this is the labor of juicing. If they only require grinding - it is permitted to finish grinding them on Shabbat. Therefore, it is permitted to finish grinding the "ripot" which are called "gagelach" with a wooden pestle, which is called "ka'k laffel" in a pot on Shabbat after taking it hot out of the oven, and there is no obligation of stirring, which is considered cooking, since it has already been fully cooked, as explained there and in Siman 318, that stirring only applies before the cooking is completed. There is also no issue of smoothing, as it is permitted to smooth food on Shabbat, since it can be eaten without this. Therefore, it is permitted to smooth food on bread to spread it, or in a bowl, even to transfer it from a full place to an empty place, in the manner of smoothing and spreading boiled potatoes, which is called "tzvibene kaas." And even though with mustard and horseradish we prohibited beating them vigorously, this is because the liquid is made in them on Shabbat, which is not the case with food without liquid (Taz, Sk14). And there is one who says that stirring vigorously and hitting with the wooden pestle against the sides of the pot or bowl until the "ripot" and the meat and the water are mixed until it all becomes one entity - is forbidden on Shabbat like with mustard and horseradish (Magen Avraham, Sk28), but Rambam in his responsa permitted this.

And all this is in a case where one can eat without crushing and spreading, but if without this one cannot eat—it is obvious that it is forbidden. For although it is possible that there is no smearing in food, there is also no tanning in food, and nevertheless, it is forbidden by rabbinic decree as explained (there, Section 29). However, according to the opinion of the Rambam, even there, there is no prohibition due to tanning as we explained, but still, one should be stringent. And besides this, our master the Rema wrote in Section 19 that in any case, one who is stringent with food like apples and the like, which are usually treated this way, will receive a blessing, end of quote. And it is customary in the world to permit crushing and spreading cooked potatoes in a tzolent, and similarly, legumes in a tzolent. However, light smearing is permitted according to all opinions. Our master the Rema further wrote that it is forbidden to peel garlic and onions if peeling to set aside, but for immediate consumption, it is permitted, end of quote. The reason is because of selecting, as explained in Section 319.

Cutting is a primary category of labor. This is the language of the Rambam in Chapter 11, Halacha 7: "One who cuts leather to make an amulet is liable, provided he intends to cut it to a specific length and width, and cuts with intention, as it is considered a craft. But if he cuts it in a destructive manner or without intention for its measure, rather as one who is occupied or playing, he is exempt (but it is forbidden). One who trims the wing is considered a derivative of cutting and is liable. Similarly, one who scrapes the tops of cedar poles is liable because of cutting. And so too, any cutting that a wood craftsman does from wood or a metal craftsman from metal – he is liable because of cutting." End quote. In the Tabernacle, there was much cutting of the skins, the boards of the Tabernacle, the stones, the silver, and the gold. One who saws wood, if he cuts it to measure, is liable because of cutting; and if he intends for the sawdust, he is liable because of grinding. One who tears paper to cover a vessel or for wiping is liable because of cutting, and similarly, one who tears a type of merchandise intending to tear it to a specific measure is liable because of cutting, and so too for anything similar. Even one who tears in general in a destructive manner – it is forbidden by rabbinic decree, as is the rule with all who perform destructive actions, they are exempt but it is forbidden.

It states in the Gemara (128b): Bundles of hyssop, thyme, and savory (types of tough vegetables): if one brought them in for firewood - one may not use them on Shabbat (as they are considered muktzeh), but if for animal feed - one may use them on Shabbat. And one may rub them with one's fingertips and eat, as one rubs the pods that contain the seeds (Rashi), provided one does not rub a large amount with his hand as he would do on a weekday. And this has already been explained similarly in Siman 319, and generally it is considered as if specified for animal feed (Tosafot). And before rubbing, when coming to cut off a piece of them - one cuts with his hand and eats by the means of the rubbing that was explained. And one should not cut with a utensil as he does on a weekday, and also it somewhat appears as cutting. And if one intends to measure - it is considered complete cutting, as the pods are like regular wood.

Just as we said regarding smoothing, when something can be eaten without it, there is no prohibition of smoothing. Similarly, it is permissible to water detached vegetables, meaning detached greens, so they do not wilt, since they can be eaten without this – it is not considered anything.
