But when it is impossible to eat without this – it is forbidden (Magen Avraham 13). And if there is a need for it today, some permit it (ibid.), and it requires investigation. It is clear that the plants in the houses are considered as if they are attached, since they are perforated and stand on the ground, and one who waters them is liable for a sin-offering as if he sows, and this will be explained in Siman 336 with God’s help.

It is forbidden to extract honey from a beehive on Shabbat because it resembles detaching something from its place of growth. Even though a beehive is not considered like the ground, as it is stated at the end of the tractate Shevi'it: a beehive is not like the ground, and one who extracts honey from it on Shabbat is exempt from a sin offering, nevertheless, all exemptions on Shabbat mean that it is prohibited by rabbinic decree. This prohibition applies specifically when the honey is still attached to the hive. However, if the honeycombs were detached from the hive before Shabbat, it is permitted to take the honeycombs to eat the honey that is around them, but crushing them is prohibited, as stated in Siman 320, unless they were crushed before Shabbat, in which case it is permitted to take the honey that flows out of them. It is also prohibited to take the honeycombs to eat them entirely because of the prohibition of selecting (borer), as you are selecting the honey from the wax (see Magen Avraham, section 16).

It is forbidden to beat eggs in a bowl, which is called "Zwei Schlagen Eier" in Yiddish, because this resembles a weekday activity, as it appears as if one intends to throw them into a pot to cook (see Magen Avraham, section 24). There is an opinion that something unfit for consumption is prohibited to chew with one's teeth because of the prohibition of grinding (tochen) (see Magen Avraham, section 12), but this opinion is strange and not acceptable. (And the proof cited is from Talmud Shabbat 133 regarding chewing cumin with one's teeth, which Rashi explains is permissible because any possible alteration is done; however, if this was not considered grinding, why would an alteration be necessary, as explained by the Machatzit HaShekel. But this is not the case, since chewing with one's teeth itself constitutes an alteration, and from a legal standpoint, it is permissible to desecrate Shabbat for the sake of a mitzvah, as explained by Tosafot in the Talmud. Study this well.)

Rabbeinu the Beis Yosef wrote in section 17: "It is permitted to make yinomlin, which is aged wine, honey, and pepper, because it is for drinking. But one may not make aluntis, which is aged wine, clear water, and balsam oil, because it is for medicinal purposes," end quote. And this is in the Gemara (140a). At first glance, this is not understandable, as all foods can be eaten for medicinal purposes and all beverages can be drunk for medicinal purposes. However, Rambam in Chapter 22, Law 11, clarified this by writing that it is not suitable for consumption by healthy individuals. Therefore, it is only for medicinal purposes. And we do not know what this is.

It is also written in paragraph 18: "One may not soak asafetida in lukewarm or cold water, as it is customary to soak it for medicinal purposes. However, one may place it in vinegar and dip bread into it. If it was soaked from the previous day, it is permissible to soak it on Shabbat (for without the medicinal aspect, it is still a beverage). If one drank from it on Thursday and Friday and needs to drink from it also on Shabbat, it is permissible, for that is the customary way of its treatment to drink it seven days consecutively. Therefore, it is permissible to soak it in cold water and place it in the sun, because it is dangerous if one does not drink from it." End of quote. And if there is no sun, it is permissible even by a fire because of the danger (Magen Avraham subparagraph 27). This too is not known to us at all, and this too is mentioned in the Gemara there. And there it is explained that it is not referring to a sick person but to someone with a discomfort, who has heaviness of the heart, and this is not an illness, and it was forbidden to drink it on Shabbat. But since he started beforehand, he is compelled to finish, for otherwise there is danger in the matter. Therefore, if this situation arises among us, it is also permissible to permit it.

An egg that was laid on Shabbat is prohibited even for handling. And it is not because of the prohibition of nolad (something newly created), as we have already explained in Siman 318 that most poskim (decisors of Jewish law) hold that nolad is permitted on Shabbat. Rather, the reason is explained at the beginning of tractate Beitzah, and the Rambam also wrote in the first chapter of Hilchot Yom Tov that this is due to the decree regarding Shabbat that follows Yom Tov. Meaning, it is established that a weekday may prepare for Shabbat, but Yom Tov does not prepare for Shabbat. And any egg that is laid today was completed yesterday, which implies that Yom Tov prepared for Shabbat. Therefore, they decreed to prohibit any egg laid on Shabbat due to the decree concerning Shabbat following Yom Tov.

It is forbidden even to touch it, and although generally all muktzeh is permitted to touch, as written in Siman 308, nevertheless, in the case of an egg which is round and can easily move from its place, touching it is forbidden, because touching it will cause it to roll. However, it is permitted to place a vessel over it so that it does not break, because we hold that a vessel is allowed to be moved even for the sake of something that cannot be moved on Shabbat, as written there. If the egg gets mixed in, even with a thousand other eggs, they are all forbidden and there is no nullification, because we hold that something which will become permitted later, even in a thousand, does not get nullified, and this egg will be permitted after Shabbat. This applies even to a rabbinic prohibition. Even if there is doubt whether it was laid on Shabbat and it got mixed in, it is also not nullified, as written in Yoreh De'ah Siman 102. However, if it is mixed with something not of its type, it is nullified in sixty, as written there. Therefore, an egg that was laid on Shabbat, if it was broken and either the white or the yolk or both got mixed into a dish such that they cannot be separated and removed, it is nullified in sixty.

And when Shabbat and Yom Tov are adjacent to each other, if an egg is laid on one, it is forbidden on the other. The reason is that since Yom Tov cannot prepare for Shabbat and Shabbat cannot prepare for Yom Tov, an egg laid on Shabbat is forbidden on that day as we have stated, and similarly on Yom Tov. Therefore, if Yom Tov falls on the eve of Shabbat, if we permit it on Shabbat, it would mean that Yom Tov prepared for Shabbat. That is to say, since it was forbidden on Yom Tov and will be permitted on Shabbat, it means that Yom Tov prepared the permission for Shabbat, and Yom Tov does not prepare for Shabbat. Similarly, Shabbat which precedes Yom Tov (see Tosafot Beitzah 4a, s.v. 'Ela').

Fruits that fell from the tree on Shabbat or were plucked from the garden are forbidden on that day due to the decree that one might ascend and pluck them. This is what the Rambam wrote in Chapter 21, and it is also found at the beginning of Beitzah. Certainly, even without this reason, they are forbidden due to muktzeh, since they were attached (to the ground) between sunset and nightfall. Even Rabbi Shimon agrees with this type of muktzeh that involves something attached, as it is considered an active rejection, similar to dried figs and raisins (Tosafot at the beginning of Beitzah in the name of Rashi). However, sometimes there is no issue of muktzeh, such as when the tree stands in the courtyard and he has ravens that are accustomed to pluck, and he intended from before Shabbat that they would pluck on Shabbat, in which case there is no muktzeh issue (there). Sometimes there is no decree of "lest he ascend and pluck," as this decree only applies to a tree from which one can pluck in a moment and immediately forget it is Shabbat. But for fruits buried in the ground, like garden seeds that require a spade and a hoe to dig up, this decree does not apply, for during the process, he will remember that it is Shabbat. Therefore, the reason of muktzeh is still needed (there). In the evening, the fruits are permitted immediately and there is no need to wait the time it would take to perform the act, because no prohibited labor was done on them, as they fell by themselves. Therefore, there was no decree to wait the time it would take to perform the act, and see Siman 325.

It is stated in Beitzah (33b): "Items used as animal fodder do not involve the prohibition of making a utensil." This means that there are times when making something that is essentially insignificant can still be considered creating a utensil, and one who does so is liable for a sin-offering. For example, if one takes a splinter and shapes it to clean one's teeth, even though it is not much, it is still considered a utensil because it is being used for cleaning teeth. This is the case with a splinter, but straw or stubble suitable for animal fodder is not subject to the prohibition of making a utensil. It is permissible to shape straw or stubble to clean one's teeth, and it is permissible to cut it even with a knife to make it suitable for this purpose. The reason is that any item that is designated for consumption is prepared for any need (Levush), since I can eat it in any manner I choose, whether to cut or break it. The same applies to animal fodder, and it is not considered making a utensil. However, using a splinter to clean one's teeth is forbidden, even if it does not need shaping, because one might come to shape it for this purpose and become liable for a sin-offering if he cuts it for this. This is in accordance with the ruling of the Rambam in Chapter 11. If one invites a guest for a meal on Shabbat and did not have time to prepare a splinter for cleaning teeth, they permitted him, for the sake of human dignity, if in his place it is considered disgraceful not to clean the teeth, to take a splinter and clean with it as it is (Magen Avraham, subsection 4, as it is stated in the Gemara, Chapter 1). However, creating a utensil with food items is certainly forbidden.

And similarly, with items that are meant for smelling, there is no concern of making a utensil, and therefore it is permitted to move fragrant woods to smell them and to wave them before a sick person, and even for a healthy person it might be permitted to wave them (see Magen Avraham, subparagraph 5), and one may break them and fix them by hand, but not with a tool (ibid., subparagraph 6). And even though animal feed is permitted even with a knife, they were stricter with fragrant woods since they are not meant for eating (see Taz, subparagraph 3). And one may rub them by hand to smell them, whether they are hard or soft fragrant woods, and it will be explained in Siman 511 that it is only permitted to add fragrance, but to create fragrance is forbidden, as there are specific laws regarding this.

Members of a group who eat together, each from their own portion, and cook together, and at the time of eating they divide the portions among themselves: if they are particular with each other that one does not leave anything for his fellow - it is forbidden for them to eat together on Shabbat, because it is likely that due to their exactness they will come to weigh or count, and based on the counting they will come to a calculation, and they will come to measure, and if we do not know that they are particular - it is permitted. However, if they come to cast lots to decide who gets which portion - even in general it is forbidden, for we see that they are particular, and therefore such people should not join together on Shabbat to eat together. But ordinary neighbors - are permitted, for certainly they will not be particular and will not cast lots (see Magen Avraham section 7), but with lots - it is forbidden. And the Sages said (Shabbat 148b): that a householder with his children and household members may cast lots for the portions, because since everything belongs to the householder, there is no concern of exactness that will lead to prohibitions, but he does this to avoid jealousy at the meal. And specifically if the portions are equal, but if one portion is large and one small - it is forbidden to cast lots to decide who gets the large and who gets the small even with his children and household members, for this is like the game of dice which is certainly forbidden on Shabbat, as it is like commerce. And even on weekdays some prohibit dice, as we explained in Choshen Mishpat section 207, paragraph 23, which is the opinion of the Rambam there.

However, the Rambam in Chapter 23, Law 17 wrote: "It is forbidden to cast lots and play with dice on Shabbat, because it is like buying and selling. But a person may cast lots with his children and the members of his household for a large portion against a small one, because they do not mind," end quote. He permitted it with one's children and household members even for a large portion against a small one, since everything belongs to him and it is merely play and amusement. But the Tur prohibits this in such cases, as mentioned in the previous section, and it depends on the Talmudic discussion as referenced there (see Beit Yosef and Taz, sub-section 4). And it states in the Talmud (149b) that they cast lots in the Temple over portions of the sacrificial offerings that fell to them, because consuming sacrificial offerings is a mitzvah, and they did not prohibit casting lots for a mitzvah. Therefore, it is permitted to cast lots over consecrated items or other mitzvah matters, but for non-mitzvah matters it is forbidden to cast lots, as it is akin to buying and selling. And even through a non-Jew, it is forbidden to cast lots on Shabbat, because the matter itself is like buying and selling. (And the Magen Avraham, sub-section 9, holds that even for a mitzvah, if one could have cast lots the day before, it is forbidden, see there. However, the proof he brought from there regarding non-sacred portions, that it is forbidden to cast lots in the Temple, is not a proof, because there truly the lot is not according to law, since sacrificial offerings are not divided against other sacrificial offerings, as Tosafot wrote there in the comment "they cast lots," and it is only to settle a dispute. Therefore, they did not permit it for non-sacred items, see there and be precise.) (And the permitted lot for a mitzvah is not with notes, where each one picks a note, as this is certainly forbidden, but rather a lot by opening a book and seeing the letters as is customary) (And why there was no lot for the showbread, as hinted by the Magen Avraham, and he prohibits casting lots on Shabbat, according to what is written it is clear, see there and be precise).

It is well known that buying and selling are prohibited on Shabbat and Yom Tov, whether one sells verbally or gives an item in the manner of a sale, meaning that he pulls the item on Shabbat. And it appears that even if the transaction was made before Shabbat, the money was given, and the item was pulled on Shabbat, it is also prohibited since the main part of the acquisition is the pulling, even if no words were spoken. There is no difference in the matter of buying and selling between objects and food and drink. Only by way of borrowing can one ask his friend for what he lacks on Shabbat, such as food and drink. Even from a storekeeper, one can simply request, 'Give me this food or that drink,' even though both know that after Shabbat he will pay for it. Nonetheless, at this moment, it is not considered buying and selling. And it is permissible to say to his friend, 'Fill this vessel with wine or other drink,' even if it is a vessel specifically used for measurement and is sold with it during the week. Nevertheless, since he does not mention any payment, it is not considered measuring, and it is not buying and selling. (And I have seen in the Shulchan Aruch of the Gaon Rabbi Zalman that he wrote: "It is permitted... fill for me... and I will pay you," and I do not know where he derived this from, and it is certainly forbidden to mention payment, as is implied from the Rambam, Chapter 4 of Yom Tov and all the poskim.)

When we permitted him to say, "Fill this vessel for me" and it is specifically designated for measurement, it is only when he takes this vessel and brings it to his house. But he should not bring a vessel from his house and have his friend pour from his measuring vessel into his own vessel, because this is the way of buying and selling. Rather, he should say, "Fill this vessel for me that I brought from my house," or he should fill it in a vessel that is not for measurement and then pour it into his own vessel, because when it is not for measurement, it does not appear like buying and selling. And our teacher, the Rema, wrote: "Some are lenient to say that as long as he does not intend for an exact measure, adding or subtracting a little, it is permitted," end quote, meaning he reduces slightly from the measure. And there is no theft in this, as it is known that this is the practice on Shabbat and Yom Tov. And some place into the measuring vessel a ring or another non-muktzeh object and fill the measure, as this is a sign that the intention is not for an exact measure, since the space of the ring is missing, and through this, he can also pour from it into the purchaser's vessel. And he further wrote that the simple custom is to measure with a vessel designated for measurement and then pour into the purchaser's vessel, end quote, and the great Acharonim protested against this (see Taz, subparagraph 1). And in truth, this is not our custom, and we do not give at all with a measuring vessel. Rather, the purchaser takes with his own vessel and after Shabbat, they measure it, and this is the correct practice, and it should not be changed.

It is permissible to say to one's friend: "Fill this vessel for me, and tomorrow we will measure it," even though this implies that it will be measured and payment will be made according to the price. Nevertheless, since it is not explicitly stated, it is possible that the intention is also in the manner of a loan, as if saying: "Tomorrow we will measure it to determine how much to return to you." However, it is certainly forbidden for the buyer to say to him: "Give me such-and-such a measure," because although he can say: "Give me this vessel," he should not mention the measure by name. For by mentioning the measure, it is clearly like buying and selling, which is forbidden. Instead, he should say: "Fill this vessel for me," as this language is also used in the context of borrowing.

A person may go to a shopkeeper with whom he regularly deals and say to him: "Give me eggs and nuts by number," meaning, give me ten eggs, twenty nuts. This is not considered a hint at buying and selling, as it is normal for a homeowner to count even within his own house to know how much he needs. And when they permitted saying this to the shopkeeper, as mentioned, one must be careful not to mention the price, for example, not to say: "Give me eggs for one coin" or similar, because mentioning the price is only for buying and selling. Additionally, one should not mention a measure, for example: "Give me a log of nuts," and certainly not a sum of measures, meaning to make an account of measures from before and what is being taken now - it is obvious that this is forbidden. Also, not a sum by number, meaning even though they permitted saying: "Give me eggs by such and such a number," nevertheless, a sum by number, meaning to say to him: "You already have fifty nuts with me, give me another fifty, and I will owe you one hundred" - this is indeed the manner of buying and selling.

And know that our Rabbi, the Rema, wrote in paragraph 4: "Similarly, in the matter of monetary sums, it is only forbidden in such cases where one says, 'Give me this amount of money, and it will be considered as such and such for you,' but otherwise – it is permitted. And similarly, in the matter of measurements, it is only forbidden in such cases, but otherwise – it is permitted. And even though it is forbidden to mention money at all, that applies to something whose price is not known, but in a case where the price is known and he merely says how much he needs – it is permitted, unless he mentions a specific amount, in which case some are stringent in this matter. However, the common custom in these countries is to be lenient, in accordance with the aforementioned opinion." These are his words. This opinion holds that mentioning money and mentioning measurements are not considered as buying and selling, but rather as saying how much he needs, meaning: 'I need eggs for a coin, I need a log of nuts.' However, the great Acharonim have already disputed this, and it is a complete prohibition for the buyer to mention the name of money or the name of measurements, and this is not the custom among us, and Heaven forbid to do so. (Also, what the Magen Avraham wrote in section 5 to make notes or holes as a sign of how much he takes, this too is questionable, and such leniencies are highly doubtful. In my humble opinion, it seems that since the source of the law is in Beitzah on Yom Tov, and even the Rambam did not mention these laws regarding Shabbat, where do we get the permission at all on Shabbat? For perhaps on Yom Tov, when one cooks on Yom Tov itself, it may be that he does not know precisely from the day before how much he needs, and therefore they permitted it with the explained leniencies, but on Shabbat everything is prepared from the day before. However, since the Tur and Shulchan Aruch wrote this also regarding Shabbat, we do not have the power to dispute them, but Heaven forbid to add more leniencies to this, and it is enough for you with what is explicitly permitted.)

One who brings jars of wine from place to place should not carry them in a basket or a container in the usual weekday manner. Rather, he should carry them in front of him or on his shoulder or in a similar fashion, to differentiate from the weekday manner. Even if this change does not make the load lighter, he should still make a change. And even though he is bringing them for the purpose of drinking what is needed for today, if not, any exertion would be completely forbidden. Still, he needs to carry them with a change to be recognizable. If it is not possible for him to make a change, such as if he invited many guests and needs to hurry to bring the wine before them, it is permitted even without a change. This is the opinion of the Tur, as it is stated in the Gemara (at the beginning of the fourth chapter of Beitzah): "He should not bring them in a basket or a container," which also applies to Shabbat. However, the opinion of the Tosafot is that this only applies to Yom Tov when carrying in the public domain, therefore it is better not to appear as if carrying in a weekday manner. But on Shabbat, where carrying is only in the courtyard, it is better to minimize walking, and it is better to bring them in a basket or a container all at once rather than bringing each one individually. (And the Magen Avraham in section 7 writes that the Tur also holds this way, referring to when he carries them through a lane that has an eruv, where many people see him, and this is puzzling. The Ran also writes like the Tur, see there and examine it well.)

It is self-evident that it is forbidden to undertake any effort on Shabbat for the sake of a weekday. Therefore, the utensils that one has eaten with, if it is clear that they will not be needed again that day – it is forbidden to wash them on Shabbat, for why would one exert effort for the sake of a weekday? They should be washed at night, and this is the custom. However, if it is possible that they will still be needed that day, such as if one still needs to eat another meal or something similar, or drinking cups since there is no fixed time for drinking – one may wash them throughout the entire day. And even if one only needs one or two, nevertheless, one may wash as many as they wish so they can drink from whichever they choose. Nonetheless, if one has plenty of utensils or cups available, it is not proper to wash them at all on Shabbat. Generally, after the third meal, it is assumed that no more eating or drinking will take place, and it is obvious that it is permitted to wash from Friday night for use on Shabbat day.

Washing dishes on Shabbat when one needs them for Shabbat is permitted, even if washing off something prohibited, such as wine used for idolatry left inside, or other prohibited substances. This is not considered fixing a utensil, like the prohibition of immersing (as will be explained), because there is no fixing here—the utensil itself is permitted, and when one washes off the prohibited substance, it is like washing any unclean utensil. Even if there are breadcrumbs present, it is permitted to handle the utensil as one would handle a chamber pot (a vessel that is allowed to be moved despite containing waste). The utensil does not become a base for the prohibited substance and the crumbs, even if they were in the utensil during twilight (between sunset and nightfall), because they are not significant enough for the utensil to be nullified to them; rather, they are nullified to the utensil (Magen Avraham, Section 14). 

It is forbidden to nullify a prohibition on Shabbat, as there is no greater form of fixing than this. Even though it is generally prohibited to nullify a prohibition, as stated in Yoreh De'ah, Section 99, there are instances where it is permitted to add and nullify, as stated there, or in the case of dry with dry, as stated in Section 109. However, on Shabbat it is forbidden due to the concept of fixing. But dry with dry in a ratio of one in two, where one must discard one piece, as stated there, is permitted on Shabbat, because from the outset it is permitted according to the law, as explained there. Similarly, measuring sixty (times the prohibited substance) is permitted (there).

The Rambam wrote in Chapter 23, Halacha 8: "It is forbidden to immerse impure vessels on Shabbat because it is like repairing a vessel. However, an impure person is permitted to immerse, as it appears like cooling off, and sprinkling (purifying) water on him is not done on Shabbat. If someone immerses vessels on Shabbat: if done unintentionally, they may be used; if done intentionally, they may not be used until the conclusion of Shabbat. It is permitted to immerse impure water on Shabbat. How should this be done? Place them in a vessel that does not receive impurity, such as a stone vessel, and immerse the vessels in a mikveh until the mikveh waters cover them and they become purified." End quote.

Here, he wrote the reason is that it is like repairing a vessel, and in Chapter 4 of Yom Tov, Halacha 17, he wrote the reason: perhaps one will leave the vessel in its impure state until Yom Tov. And in Beitzah (18a) there is a dispute among the Amoraim about this: Rav Bibi said perhaps one will leave it, and Rava said because it appears like repairing a vessel. And why did he rule on Shabbat like Rava and on Yom Tov like Rav Bibi? Furthermore, on Yom Tov, he distinguishes between a vessel that became impure from a primary source of impurity and a secondary source of impurity, where in the case of a secondary impurity, immersion is permitted on Yom Tov as stated in the Baraita there. Why did he not distinguish similarly on Shabbat? Perhaps he believes that repairing applies also to secondary impurity, and the concern of delay does not apply to secondary impurity, as we do not decree in this case, for even if delayed, it is pure by Torah law. The reason he ruled on Yom Tov according to Rav Bibi's rationale is because the Baraita supports him, and the Baraita explicitly refers to Yom Tov. And on Shabbat, he wrote the reason of repairing a vessel because in many matters on Shabbat, actions are prohibited due to repair, but this still requires further investigation. I am puzzled by the commentators who did not notice this (and the Sha'agat Aryeh in Siman 56 questioned this).

The Tur wrote that it is forbidden to immerse a new vessel. And certainly, this is the case, as there is no more complete act of fixing than this, and similarly, there is the concern of delaying just like with the immersion of vessels from their impurity. And I am very perplexed by the words of our master, the Beit Yosef, in his great book, where he wrote that according to the Rambam, it is permissible to immerse new vessels. Based on this, he wrote in section 7: "It is permissible to immerse a new vessel that requires immersion, and some forbid it. A God-fearing person should fulfill both opinions by giving the vessel to a non-Jew as a gift and then borrowing it back, and it does not require immersion." End quote. His intention in the first opinion is to the Rif and the Rambam, as explained in his great book. And I am very perplexed, for even if regarding the Rif, who wrote only the reason of concern for delaying, one could say this, as the Rosh wrote, that according to this reason, it is permissible to immerse new vessels (and even this is difficult as the Shagat Aryeh wrote in Siman 56). But the Rambam, in Shabbat, wrote the reason of fixing a vessel, and he only brought his words in Yom Tov and not what he wrote in Shabbat, and this is difficult (and also the Maggid Mishneh wrote there in the laws of Yom Tov that the immersion of vessels is forbidden, see there, and so wrote the Shagat Aryeh, and this is the main ruling).

And that which is written about giving a gift to a non-Jew and then asking to borrow it back, even though some are concerned about giving gifts on Shabbat as mentioned in Siman 307, nevertheless, for the sake of Shabbat it is certainly permitted. And if one transgressed and immersed it on Shabbat, it appears that it should not be used on Shabbat. However, it is possible to be lenient after the fact since there are those who permit it even initially (Magen Avraham, Siman 11). And our teacher, the Rema, wrote that if it is a vessel suitable for filling with water - one should fill it with water from the mikveh and its immersion is valid. This is only when the water is fit for drinking, as it then appears as though one is drawing water for drinking, but if it is not fit for drinking, it is clear to all that it is being immersed. And when one fills it in this manner, no blessing is necessary (there, Siman 13). And it is obvious that when one gives it to a non-Jew as a gift and then asks to borrow it back, after Shabbat it needs to be immersed without a blessing, because it was given to a non-Jew. This is explained in Yoreh De'ah Siman 120 (and see Taz, Siman 6).

When cleaning utensils on Shabbat, when it is necessary to use them on Shabbat as explained, it is permitted to clean them with anything, even with sand prepared before Shabbat, and even silverware and copperware, and we do not worry about the sand smoothing or polishing, because this is something unintentional and not a definite occurrence. Except for silverware in its tarnished state, which is dried and hardened wine sediment, because this definitely polishes the silverware which is soft. Similarly, one should not scrub them with salt, because the salt dissolves when scrubbed vigorously and melts into water, and this constitutes "creating a new entity" (nolad), and certainly with various kinds of soap it is forbidden. Also, with dirt and ashes it is forbidden due to kneading (gibul). One should be careful not to put clothing into the water, so as not to come to wringing (schita), and also the cloth used to dry the utensils after washing them should not get into the washing water. With us, women are careful when cleaning utensils on Shabbat to clean only with their hands and not with what they use during the week, such as a scrubbing brush called "voyageetz" (brush), and every homeowner should warn their household about this, because it is easy to come to the desecration of Shabbat, heaven forbid.

Any animal, beast, or bird whose sustenance depends on you, that you raise in your home – you are obligated to provide them with their sustenance and to prepare for them what they need, as will be explained. However, those whose sustenance does not depend on you, which you are not raising – you are not required to trouble yourself for them. Therefore, one does not place water or food before bees, or before doves of a dovecote, or before roof doves, because their sustenance is not dependent on a person but they roam around and gather their own food, nor before a pig. But one does place food before geese, chickens, domesticated doves, and also a dog whose sustenance depends on you. This is the language of our master, the Beit Yosef, in section 11. And the language of the Tur is: "One places food before a dog but not before a pig." (In my humble opinion, this hints at the poor and the wealthy, as our sages said: There is none poorer than a dog, etc.)

And know that the Levush wrote: One gives food to a dog that one raises in one's house, see there. It is explicitly explained that if the dog is not his, one does not give food to it. And there are those who wrote that from the Gemara it implies that even if the dog is not his, it is a mitzvah to give it food. And his intention is from what they said at the end of Shabbat: "A righteous person knows the soul of his animal," which refers to a dog, and it says there that it is proper to throw a bone to a dog, see there (Magen Avraham, section 7). And there are those who reject this, for it says there that this is in the wilderness, but in the city, it will become accustomed to come (Tosafot Shabbat and Machatzit HaShekel, see there). And I say that it is also implied from the Tur, as he wrote: "One gives food to a dog but not to a pig," and certainly a pig cannot be his, for it is forbidden to raise pigs. And it is forced to say when he inherited it, rather certainly it is similar with a dog, that one gives even if it is not his. Also, there is proof from Rashi in the first chapter (19a): "One gives food to a dog in the courtyard and gives food to etc.," and Rashi explained: "A dog is obligated to be fed," see there. He did not write: "A dog that is obligated," which implies that every dog is obligated to be fed because it lacks food. And what they said in the city not to, it means not to accustom it regularly, but occasionally it is permitted. And "His mercies are upon all His works" is written, and from the Beraita itself, it is implied so for one who scrutinizes there. (And see Tosafot there who wrote: Since we support their poor due to the ways of peace, it is considered somewhat their food upon you, see there. And certainly for a dog when it is hungry. And in my humble opinion, any living creature that I know is hungry – it is a mitzvah to give it food even on Shabbat, for "His mercies are upon all His works" is written. And see what the Ran wrote there in the name of the Ra'avad and scrutinize well).

Some criticize the custom on Shabbat Shirah to throw wheat before the birds, arguing that their sustenance is not your responsibility (Magen Avraham). However, it seems to me that the custom of Israel is Torah, for we are not exerting ourselves for them but for ourselves. It is commonly said among the people that the birds sang a song at the sea, and therefore we show them gratitude. Thus, the intention is to remember the joy of the Song of the Sea, and there is no issue with it. There are those who wrote that since our intention is for a mitzvah, it is permitted (Taz). It is also permitted to feed silkworms, for since they have nothing to eat except what a person gives them, their sustenance is considered your responsibility (Taz). Similarly, a cat raised in the house must be given its food on Shabbat, for certainly, its sustenance is your responsibility.

And even for those whose sustenance is upon you, the Rambam writes at the end of Chapter 21: "One does not feed animals, wild animals, or birds on Shabbat in the same manner as one feeds them on a weekday, lest one come to grind legumes or knead flour or similar actions. How so: one does not feed a camel on Shabbat with food for three or four days, nor make a calf lie down and open its mouth and place beans and water into it simultaneously, nor place food into the mouths of pigeons and chickens in a place where they cannot return it. However, one may feed an animal while it is standing and give it water while it is standing, or place water in its mouth separately and beans separately in a place where it can return them, and similarly, one may feed a bird by hand in a place where it can return the food. Needless to say, one can place food before them and they will eat." Thus wrote the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch in Chapter 9. The reason for this prohibition, the Rambam explains, is lest one come to grind. Some wrote that it is due to excessive exertion (Levush and Taz), and this also seems to be the implication in Rashi (155:). It is puzzling why the Rambam did not write this reason, as it also appears from the Mishnah there that the reason is due to exertion (for it is also taught there that one does not place water before bees, etc. - and examine this well).

It has already been explained that sifting is one of the principal categories of labor. Therefore, one may not sift straw using a sieve, nor place a sieve containing straw in a high place so that the chaff will fall out, because this is akin to sifting. However, one may take straw in a sieve and carry it to the feeding trough, even though the chaff falls out during the carrying, since he does not intend for this to happen. And this is not a case of "inevitable outcome" (pesik reisha), because even if some chaff falls out, there will still be much chaff left in the sieve. A person should not measure barley to place before his animal, because measuring is forbidden on Shabbat. Instead, he should estimate with his mind. For example, if he needs to give his animal a kav of barley, he should approximate a kav, which may result in slightly less or slightly more, and there is no concern in this since estimating the amount is not considered measuring (see Beit Yosef and Bach, and not with a measuring vessel).

The Rambam also wrote there: "Even though bran is not suitable for kneading, one should not knead it, lest one come to knead earth or similar substances. One may pour water over the bran and stir it with a spoon in a criss-cross pattern, but not knead it with the hand, so that it does not appear as though one is kneading. If it does not mix well, one may pour it from one vessel to another until it mixes, and then place it before the chickens or the oxen. It is permissible to mix the bran in this manner in one vessel and then distribute it into many vessels and place it before each animal. One may mix even a large measure such as a kor or two kors in one vessel." End quote. 

And regarding what he wrote about stirring with the spoon in a criss-cross pattern, it implies even many times. But from the words of Rashi (156b), it is explained that it is only permitted to stir once in a criss-cross pattern. Refer to there. The law of bran is like that of toasted grain in Orach Chaim 321:19, and as explained there, it is permissible to knead a little at a time, so too with bran (Magen Avraham 1 quoting the Ramban, refer to there). The reason why the Rambam did not explain it this way is because for a person, a small amount of toasted grain is sufficient, but for an animal that needs a lot of bran, it would take too long to do a little at a time. And know that it is only permitted as much as needed for one's animals for that day and no more, and this is obvious. And what we permitted even a large measure such as a kor or two kors, this is when one has many animals.

And all this is according to the opinion of the Rambam, but according to the opinion of the Raavad, which we wrote about there, that in the case of ashes there is kneading, also in bran there is kneading. And this is also the opinion of the Tosafot, Sefer HaTerumah, and the Sefer Mitzvot Gadol (SeMaG). On the contrary, according to them, the addition of water constitutes kneading, and according to their opinion, it is forbidden to add water to bran on Shabbat. And what they said in the Gemara about moving it back and forth, this applies when the water was already added before Shabbat. And the Rosh ruled according to the opinion of the Rambam, as the Tur wrote in his name there, and it seems that this is the custom of the world, to add water to the bran and move it back and forth. However, certainly, it is proper for someone who fears God to be cautious in this matter because according to the opinion of these Rabbis, there is a primary category of labor involved. In any case, one should be careful to do it through a non-Jew.

It is established for us: We prepare food but do not exert excessive effort for food (Shabbat 155a, according to Rabbi Yehuda). The explanation is as follows: There are types of animal feed which, if given as they are, the animal would not be able to eat, such as stalks of grain tied in two or three places. It is necessary to untie these knots so that the animal can eat them, and this is called "preparing food," for otherwise, the animal would not be able to eat. However, there are cases where the animal can eat the food as is, but if we add some effort, the animal would eat it better, such as rubbing the stalks well by hand. This is forbidden to do on Shabbat, because since the food is already suitable for eating, we do not exert effort to improve or prepare it further. The reason we permit untying the knots is that it does not constitute a permanent knot, as they are untied every day. Nevertheless, some say that it is only permitted to untie if it is not a permanent knot, such as a simple tie. But if it is tied with two knots one on top of the other, it is forbidden to untie them on Shabbat, as this could be considered a permanent knot, perhaps intended to remain for a long time.

And similarly, wood that was cut from a tree, and there are those who feed it to animals while it is still moist - they permit and scrape it to feed them. In this case, scraping is also permitted, because without this it is not suitable for consumption, and it is considered preparing food, which is allowed. Similarly, one may cut gourds before the animal, because without cutting, it cannot eat. This applies to hard gourds (Magen Avraham 503:3), for soft ones can be eaten as they are. This is only if they were detached from the tree yesterday, because if not, it would be considered muktzeh like dried figs and raisins, even Rabbi Shimon agrees to this since they were attached during twilight, and it is similar to an active rejection as explained in section 308, where even Rabbi Shimon considers it muktzeh.

And one may cut up a carcass before dogs when they cannot eat it without cutting. And regarding a carcass, even if it became a carcass today—it is permitted, for we hold like Rabbi Shimon who does not consider "muktzeh" (an item set aside and not to be used on Shabbat). And it is not only if it was sick during the day, in which case one's mind was on it that it might die and one would place it before the dogs, but even if it was healthy during the day—it is permitted according to Rabbi Shimon, for this is not considered as actively rejecting it. And this specifically applies to a hard carcass that they cannot eat without cutting, and even if it can be eaten with difficulty—it is permitted to cut it. But if it was fit for them without cutting, but cutting makes it better for them—it is forbidden to cut it, for we do not exert ourselves with food that is already fit. And above in Siman 321, se'if 14, it is explained regarding fine cutting before birds. (See the Taz, subparagraph 4, who wonders about the words of the Rema there, and the law agrees with him as written there. And from the Magen Avraham, subparagraph 5, it seems due to grinding, see there. And the Rema wrote there because of preparing food, see there.)

One does not cut vegetables before an animal, whether small or large, and similarly carob, because even without this they are fit for eating. And it has already been clarified that it is permissible to place food into the mouths of chickens, and it is permissible to crumble bread for them so they can eat, and there is no grinding prohibition involved, as there is no grinding after grinding, as stated in Siman 321.

A person may place his animal on attached grasses to eat, and we do not worry that he himself might come to pluck and feed it. And the reason that it is permissible for an animal to eat from what is attached, we have explained in Siman 305, see there. And why do we not worry that he might pluck and feed it himself? Because since it is a primary labor prohibition, he will not come to stumble in this. Therefore, when it comes to grasses that are muktzeh and were plucked today, it is forbidden to place the animal there, as we are concerned that he might take them in his hands and feed the animal, since it is a minor prohibition. And it is specifically forbidden to stand directly over muktzeh, but it is permissible to stand in front of it so that the animal cannot turn except through that place, meaning he stands a little distance away from where it is eating. In such a case, we are not concerned that he will take it in his hands and feed it, since he is not standing directly over it.

You may take food from in front of a donkey and place it before an ox, for the ox will eat the leftovers of the donkey. But you may not take food from in front of an ox and place it before a donkey, because the donkey does not eat the leftovers of the ox. This is because when the ox eats, it drools, and the food becomes repulsive due to the drool, and the donkey will not eat it. Therefore, it is considered moving something that is not fit for use, which is prohibited on Shabbat. Even though the donkey might eat it in pressing circumstances, that is not considered proper eating. Some are also stringent with other types of animals, not to take from one and give to another that is not its kind, because generally, they will not eat from each other's leftovers. Therefore, if one knows that the animal will eat it, it is permitted. 

It is forbidden to scrape the trough before an ox being fattened, as it is customary to scrape the trough for it during the week, but on Shabbat, it is forbidden even if the trough is a utensil because we decree against it due to the possibility of scraping a trough that is part of the ground. This involves the concern of leveling holes, which is a form of building and is prohibited. It is also forbidden to move the straw aside from before the ox, because the straw becomes repulsive and unfit for eating, rendering it muktzeh (set aside) and prohibited to move. 

Nowadays, we do scrape the trough of a horse, because the scraping is minimal and not comparable to that of a fattened ox. Additionally, we do not have ground troughs, so there is no decree concerning those (as stated in Tosafot, Shabbat 29b, s.v. 'decree').

It is permissible to invite a non-Jew on Shabbat to eat with him at his table, even though on Yom Tov it is prohibited to invite him unless he comes on his own, as stated in Siman 512. This is because on Yom Tov we are concerned that one might cook extra for him, but on Shabbat, he is only inviting him to eat from what was prepared the day before, and there is no concern of performing labor. And if the concern is due to exertion - it is permitted for the sake of peaceful relations (see Ran, Chapter 7, regarding providing sustenance, where he cites the Raavad, and this requires further examination).

It is permissible to give bread to a non-Jewish poor person who is standing in the courtyard, for it is a mitzvah for us to support their poor. And even though there is a concern that he might carry it out to the public domain, thus causing the Jew’s property to be transported on Shabbat from a private domain to a public domain, nevertheless, he is not giving it to him with the intention that he should carry it out. For in such cases, it is forbidden as explained in the Jerusalem Talmud (Chapter 1, Halacha 8): “One does not give to a non-Jew with the intention that he should go out; if he took it and went out, it is not our concern.” Since he went out on his own, we have no issue with it, for now it belongs to him and not to the Jew, and when he gave it to him, he could have eaten it here in the courtyard. Therefore, if it is known that he will not eat it here, or he gave him so much that it is impossible to eat it here, or an object that is not for eating and he will necessarily take it out from here – it is forbidden to give it to him on Shabbat.

It has already been explained in Siman 246, Section 6, that on Shabbat itself it is forbidden to lend any utensil to a non-Jew. The Rambam in Chapter 6 explains the reason: that when the non-Jew leaves the house of the Jew, people will say that he sold it to him on Shabbat. According to this, even in a city that has an eruv, it is forbidden. However, our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote there the reason: that the observer will think that the Jew commanded him to carry it out on Shabbat. According to this, the prohibition only applies in a city that does not have an eruv. And there we explained why he rejected the Rambam's reasoning. Therefore, what is ruled here in Section 1, that even if the non-Jew is standing in his courtyard, and even if the objects belong to the non-Jew, it is forbidden to hand it to him when he takes it out, because the observer will think that the objects belong to the Jew, meaning they will suspect that he commanded him to carry it out on Shabbat, and this is in a city that does not have an eruv. Therefore, our teacher the Rema wrote that even if he designated a place for him before Shabbat, one should be stringent. And this is due to suspicion, as stated. Also, what our teacher the Beit Yosef wrote that even regarding food, if the non-Jew is standing outside and extends his hand inside, knowing that he will take it out - it is forbidden to give it to him, all for the reason that people will say that he gave it to him to take it out. Additionally, there is a prohibition even without this reason when it is given into his hand, because he is performing an act of lifting in a private domain, and the non-Jew is performing the act of placing it in a public domain. There is someone who is stringent that even if he is standing in his courtyard, one should not give it into his hand out of concern that he might immediately go out to the public domain, and it will turn out that the Jew performed the act of lifting (Magen Avraham, Section 2). But this is not the case, as there is no act of lifting by the Jew at all, for when the non-Jew uproots himself to leave the courtyard, he is the one performing the act of lifting and not the Jew (Eliyah Rabbah), as the uprooting of the body is like the uprooting of an object.

There are those who write that when the object belongs to a non-Jew, it is only forbidden if the non-Jew is standing outside and extends his hand inside, and the Jew hands him the object, because anyone who sees the Jew giving it to him would assume that the object belongs to the Jew. And it is not just about handing it to him, because that in any case is forbidden due to the prohibition of uprooting, but even if the non-Jew takes it from the Jew's hand, in which case the non-Jew is also performing the uprooting, it is forbidden due to the appearance, as mentioned. However, if the non-Jew is standing in the courtyard, it is permissible to give him his own object, because anyone who sees the non-Jew leaving the courtyard will assume that the object belongs to the non-Jew, which is the truth, and it is only forbidden with the Jew's object (Magen Avraham, subsection 4). And if the object is pawned to the Jew, it is forbidden even if he designated a place for the object before the day began, because rental does not acquire ownership and the Jew's domain is not removed from it. However, if he declared it ownerless before the day began, it seems to me that it is permitted. All these matters apply where there is no eruv, but where there is an eruv, it is obvious that it is permitted, and even where there is no eruv, it is possible to permit it for us since we do not have a public domain (Taz, subsection 1). And he should place the object in front of him, and he will take it, and not hand it to him directly, because of the prohibition of uprooting, as even in a karmelit it is initially forbidden, and it seems to me that this is the custom.

Even in a place where it is forbidden to give to him, if the non-Jew is a violent person or if it is due to maintaining peaceful relations, it is permissible to give to him, but one should be careful not to give it directly from hand to hand because of the prohibition of transferring. Similarly, it is permissible to send it to him via a non-Jewish messenger. The same rule applies to a mitzvah matter, such as removing chametz from one's house - it is permissible. Know that this law is written in Tosafot (19a, s.v. 'notnin' in the Tosafot Yeshanim there), and it concludes: 'Since we do not have a public domain,' which clearly implies that in a public domain it is forbidden even in such cases. Similarly, our teacher the Beit Yosef wrote in his great book. If so, it is surprising why he wrote it in general terms in Shulchan Aruch, section 2, and this requires further investigation.

It has already been explained that even if the object belongs to the non-Jew, such as a pawned item, it is forbidden for reasons that have been explained. However, when the non-Jew comes to exchange his pawn for another item and can leave with it by wearing it as a garment, it is permitted, as it is not noticeable at all. Just as he came with the garment he is wearing, so too he leaves with the garment he is wearing. And there is no prohibition of commerce in this case, as it does not involve commerce; he is not discussing any payment, but only requesting from the Jew: "Exchange this for another one that you have." It is also permitted for a Jew to do so, to exchange his pawn on Shabbat if the Jew needs to wear it on Shabbat. It is preferable that the non-Jew take the pawn himself and place another in its place, and that the Jew does not touch it, so it does not appear as commerce. However, if the pawn is placed in a hidden location and the Jew must bring it, it is also permitted. The Jew brings it here, and the non-Jew removes the garment he is wearing and takes this one, and the Jew stores the garment that was left. But he must be careful not to discuss any accounting. Similarly, if the non-Jew comes on Shabbat and leaves his money and takes his pawn without the Jew saying anything to him, there is no need to object, as the Jew is doing nothing. As long as there is no accounting, for accounting is certainly a complete prohibition. (See Magen Avraham, section 8, who disagrees with the Sema who permits acting as a guarantor on Shabbat, and we have already explained this in Choshen Mishpat, section 131, paragraph 6. Also, the Taz and Urim V'Tumim there disagree with the Sema, see there.)

The Tur wrote: "Bread of a non-Jew that was baked on Shabbat – Rabbeinu Tam forbids it, because it might have been ground today, making it muktzeh, since between sunset and nightfall it was not fit for use. And in the Sefer HaTerumot, reasons are given both for prohibition and permission. And my master and father of blessed memory wrote: It seems to me to permit it, because even if it was flour or dough between sunset and nightfall – it is not muktzeh, since it was completed by a person. The grinding and baking do not prohibit it, since it is for the sake of a non-Jew." End quote. Based on this, our master the Beit Yosef wrote in section 4: "Bread that a non-Jew baked for himself on Shabbat – some forbid and some permit, but in a time of need or for the sake of a mitzvah meal, such as a circumcision or for the blessing of Hamotzi, one may rely on those who permit." End quote. And our master the Rema wrote: "But it is forbidden to give him money on Friday and to receive the bread on Shabbat, for then he is doing it with the intention for a Jew." End quote. It must be said that this non-Jew is a baker, and in a place where people eat baker’s bread as stated in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 112, because homeowner’s bread is not permitted as stated there (see Taz subparagraph 3). And it seems that the law leans towards permission, but not in a time of need they were concerned with Rabbeinu Tam's words. And indeed, Rabbeinu Tam's words are not understood, why he was concerned with the grinding more than kneading and baking, and further how is this different from all other labors when a non-Jew does it for himself and a Jew uses it as will be explained, and many commentators have labored over this.

It appears that Rabbeinu Tam follows his own reasoning that "nolad" (something that came into being on Shabbat) is forbidden on Shabbat, as he wrote in Siman 318. He agrees with the opinion of the Ba'al Halachot Gedolot (Ba'al HaMaor) cited by Tosafot (Avodah Zarah 66b, "Amar") that grinding constitutes "nolad" there. According to this, it makes sense to say that perhaps it was ground today, meaning it would be "muktzeh" (set aside) as "nolad", and since it was set aside during "bein hashmashot" (twilight period), it remains set aside for the entire day. In this case, we also follow Rabbi Yehuda's opinion, as we wrote there (see Beit Yosef who wrote this). According to this, according to most poskim (halachic authorities) who also hold by Rabbi Shimon regarding "nolad", and there are also those who disagree with the Ba'al Halachot Gedolot and hold that grinding does not constitute "nolad", as Tosafot wrote there, therefore for us, the halacha is that our Rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, ruled leniently and permitted it for the sake of a mitzvah or in a pressing situation.

Furthermore, we can explain the reasoning of Rabbeinu Tam as follows: When we scrutinize what the Rosh wrote, that this is not considered muktzeh (set aside and therefore prohibited) since it is prepared by human hands, his intention is that since a person can prepare it — meaning grind, knead, and bake — then it is not muktzeh. However, fruits that are plucked from the tree are also within human capability to pluck, yet we say that this is comparable to figs and raisins that have been actively set aside by not being plucked the day before (as Rashi explains in Beitzah 24b). If so, we should say the same about bread, and what difference is there in this case? 

We must say that the reasoning is as follows: Plucking is a simple task, and one could have plucked them the day before but did not, which indicates that he diverted his intention and actively set them aside. For if he had intended to use them, he would have plucked them. This is not the case with other muktzeh items like bread, which require significant preparation: grinding, kneading, and baking. We can say that he did not divert his intention, and what he did not do the day before was because he did not find an appropriate time for it yet, and as soon as he finds an appropriate time, he will do it. Therefore, when a non-Jew bakes it, the bread is permitted, as he did not divert his intention. This is the reasoning of the Rosh (see Beit Yosef and Drisha, and according to what we have explained, everything fits well, and scrutinize this well).

But Rabbeinu Tam holds that this is considered an active rejection, like the plucking of fruits, since it was not started before the Sabbath. Therefore, if indeed it was ground before the Sabbath, it is not comparable to the plucking of fruits, since the work had already begun. Consequently, when the non-Jew kneads and bakes, there is no issue of muktzeh (set-aside), as his mind was on this, unlike if the grinding was not done before the Sabbath, in which case it is indeed comparable to the plucking of fruits. This is what the Tur states in the opinion of Rabbeinu Tam, who prohibits it, lest it was ground today and would be like dried figs and raisins. For if it had been ground from yesterday, his mind would not have been diverted from it, and it is permitted when the non-Jew bakes. There is no difference in this regard whether the Jew ground it before the Sabbath or the non-Jew ground it before the Sabbath, as we follow the matter itself. If it was ground before the Sabbath, it is not comparable to the plucking of fruits, but if it was not ground, it is comparable (so it appears in my humble opinion, and see Beit Yosef and Derisha).

Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 5: "A non-Jew who catches fish or gathers fruits for himself - it is forbidden for a Jew [to benefit from them], and even if it is uncertain whether he gathered or caught them today - it is forbidden on that day. But in the evening - they are permitted immediately, even if it is certain that he gathered or caught them today. If he gathered or caught for a Jew or for both a Jew and a non-Jew - one must wait until the evening for the amount of time it would take to do the work [before benefiting]. If it is uncertain whether he gathered for a Jew or it is known that he gathered for a Jew but it is not known if they were gathered today or not - it is forbidden on that day, and in the evening, one must wait the amount of time it would take to do the work, and some say that in the evening it is permitted immediately." End of quote, and it is necessary to explain the reasons for these laws.

Even though any labor that a non-Jew does for himself is permitted for a Jew to use, why did they prohibit the catching of fish and the picking of fruit? The Tur wrote: "If a non-Jew catches fish, picks fruit, bakes bread, or cooks for himself, the Sefer HaMitzvot states: some permit it just like other labors he does for himself, and some prohibit it like fruits that fall by themselves, because they were more stringent with food-related matters, etc." End quote. For us, this reason cannot be said, for if so, why do we permit bread that he bakes for himself as explained? Some say the reason is as written later in section 507, lest he climb and pluck (Magen Avraham, note 12). I am puzzled by this, for that case is when the fruit fell by itself, as stated at the beginning of Beitzah, but for something a non-Jew did for himself, we do not find this decree anywhere that he might climb and pluck. Rather, it can only be said that they were stricter with food matters as mentioned, and this reasoning is also written by the Tosafot in one place (Shabbat 122b, s.v. 'uses'), where they wrote about the candle lit by the non-Jew for himself that the Jew may use its light, why don’t we decree lest he light it, as we decree with fallen fruits lest he pluck, and with liquids that flow out lest he squeeze, because they are easy to do and one is eager for them since they are food-related, etc., end quote. The main reason is because it is food-related as brought by the Tur, for due to ease alone, there is nothing easier than lighting a candle. According to this reason, we should also prohibit bread as mentioned. Some wrote the reason is that catching fish and picking fruit do not seem like labor to people, and there is room to decree lest he do it with his hands (Taz, note 4). These are puzzling matters, for they permitted when he filled water for himself as will be explained, and this certainly does not seem like labor and yet they permitted it. (And the Taz himself rejected this there, bringing the Tosafot from Shabbat. And we already wrote that if so, bread too, even though one could say their intention is that we need both: ease of labor and desire for food, but this is not necessary as will be explained with G-d’s help. Furthermore, it is difficult for me, for if so, why did they not prohibit drinking water after him when he filled it from the public domain, for this is very easy and when a person is thirsty, he desires to drink, and examine this matter carefully.)

However, the true reason was written by Rashi in Beitzah (24b), and this was brought by the Rosh there, as well as by Tosafot at the beginning of Beitzah. And this is the language of Rashi: "Even according to Rabbi Shimon, there is 'muktzeh' (set aside) with figs and raisins, and something attached is like figs and raisins, because if it was not picked yesterday, he set it aside from his mind. And do not differentiate between something attached whether it belongs to a Jew or to a non-Jew." End of quote. And this is the reason also concerning trapping, but with bread, this reason does not apply, as we explained in section 9. And plainly it is not comparable to bread, for the wheat or flour exists in the world and is detached and can be used, and he did not set it aside from his mind, which is not the case with fruits attached to a tree and fish that were submerged in the river. Therefore, all the work that a non-Jew did for himself - it is permitted for a Jew to use it, for all the work is similar to bread that existed in the world, like a candle or making a ramp to descend, for the candle itself and the wood or stone from which the ramp was made existed in the world and were detached, and it cannot be said about them 'he set it aside from his mind', and furthermore, it is not being moved. Similarly, the water in a well existed in the world, and one could descend into the pit and drink, which is not the case with fruits attached to a tree and fish in the river, which he set aside from his mind.

And they only required waiting the time it would take for the item to be produced after Shabbat when it was made for a Jew, because there is a concern that he might tell the non-Jew to do it, and also to ensure that he does not benefit at all from Shabbat labor in something made specifically for him. This is not the case with something that was not made for him (see Tosafot Beitzah 24b s.v. 'u'le'erev'). Even in cases of doubt whether it was prepared today or hunted today, it is also prohibited, even though it is a rabbinic doubt, they were stringent because it is something that will become permissible later (Hilchot Yom Tov 2:7). According to the Rashba, there is another reason for this, which will be explained in Siman 497. Similarly, if there is doubt whether it was picked for him, we are stringent even regarding the time it would take to be produced, for the reason stated. Some are lenient regarding the time it would take, saying that there is no need to be so stringent. If the non-Jew brought it to the Jew’s house, we say it was certainly picked for him, and this is not a doubt (Magen Avraham 319:13), but this is when it was brought as a gift. However, if it was brought to sell, it remains a doubt.

An item that does not involve the concern of trapping and is attached, or if it is known that it was trapped and detached yesterday and was only brought from outside the boundary, if the non-Jew brought it for himself - it is permitted for a Jew even on Shabbat, both in terms of handling and eating or drinking. However, if it was brought for a Jew, the Jew for whom it was brought is forbidden to eat it on Shabbat, so that he does not instruct the non-Jew to bring it. But another Jew is permitted to eat it on Shabbat. Consequently, handling is also permitted for that Jew, as it cannot be considered muktzeh, since it is permitted for another Jew. In the evening, one must wait the amount of time it would take to perform the task, so that he does not benefit by instructing the non-Jew to bring it for him. Some say that one must wait one day for the amount of time it would take, and the night of Motzei Shabbat is not included in the calculation because it is not customary to bring from afar at night, and this is an additional stringency (Magen Avraham 318:18 in the name of Yam Shel Shlomo). The amount of time to wait is according to the time it takes to bring it, for if it was brought by riding a horse, where the time is less than walking on foot - he should wait accordingly and no more. And if it was brought on foot - he should wait the time it takes to walk. Some say that for an item brought from outside the boundary - there is no need to wait the amount of time it takes, for this only applies to a Torah-prohibited labor. And know that if it was brought by ship - it is permitted, as there is no boundary limit on a ship. However, if it was on land during twilight - it is forbidden to move it beyond four cubits as will be explained in Siman 405. And when two items are brought before two Jews - both are forbidden, and it is forbidden to exchange what was brought for Reuven with what Shimon will eat and Shimon's with Reuven's (Magen Avraham 318:16). It seems to me that this is when the same non-Jew brought it, but if one brought for Reuven and another for Shimon - they are permitted to exchange. And know that the members of a person's household are considered as himself, that if it is forbidden for him - it is also forbidden for his household members, but guests he has are considered as others and are permitted, as stated in Siman 415.

Later in Siman 401, it will be explained that something brought from outside the Shabbat boundary is forbidden to be carried beyond four cubits, except within a city that is surrounded by a wall intended for dwelling—meaning that it was first settled with houses and then enclosed by a wall. Generally, towns are enclosed for dwelling, while fortresses are generally not enclosed for dwelling, and it will be explained there, with God's help. Therefore, fruits that were brought from outside the boundary for one's own sake, which are permitted for an Israelite to eat as mentioned, must be taken care not to carry them beyond their four cubits, unless within a city enclosed for dwelling (see Magen Avraham, subparagraph 19, who disagrees with the Beit Yosef, and with God's help it will be explained there).

If there is a doubt whether it was brought from outside the Shabbat boundary or whether it was brought for a Jew - it is prohibited for the reason explained, that it is considered something that will become permissible later (davar sheyesh lo matirin). There is no need to wait after Shabbat for the amount of time it would take to do it, as there is no need to be stringent in such a doubt. When does doubt apply regarding a non-Jew: when he does not live in the same city or if he does live in the city and these fruits are not available in the city. But when he lives in the city and the fruits are available in the city - one should not create doubt that they may have come from outside the city. And it is not specifically about a city, as the same applies if he lives within the boundary. And even if he has two houses, one within the boundary and one outside the boundary, we assume it came from within the boundary. And even though there are those who are hesitant about this, because this too is a doubt, nevertheless there is no need to be stringent about this, and it is permissible to eat even for the one for whom it was brought.

The Sages taught in a Mishnah (122b): "If a non-Jew lights a candle, a Jew may use its light; if he fills water to water his animal, a Jew may drink afterwards; if he makes a ramp to descend, a Jew may descend after him. There was an incident with Rabban Gamliel and the elders who were coming on a ship, and a non-Jew made a ramp to descend, and Rabban Gamliel and the elders descended after him." And in a Beraita there regarding gathering herbs and filling water, it is taught: "When are these matters said? When he does not know him, but if he knows him, it is prohibited lest he increase for the sake of the Jew." And it questions: Rabban Gamliel knew him, so how did he descend on the ramp? Abaye answered: It was not in his presence, meaning if the work was done not in his presence, it is permitted even if he knows him, as how could he increase for him since he does not see the Jew at all. Rava answered: Even if you say in his presence, a candle for one is a candle for a hundred, meaning the act of Rabban Gamliel was with a ramp, and this concern of increasing for him does not apply. And certainly, Abaye also agrees with this; rather, Abaye thought that if it was in Rabban Gamliel's presence, certainly the entire act was only for Rabban Gamliel, who was the Nasi (leader) (Tosafot). And Rava did not worry about this, for since he also needed it, he did it for himself.

The Rashba and the Ran wrote that even Rava agrees with Abaye's reasoning, that in the absence of the Jew, even if the non-Jew is known to him, there is no concern that the non-Jew will increase the work for the Jew's sake, even in something that can be increased, such as herbs and water. However, Rava says that with meat, it is permitted even in his presence, as mentioned there. The Maggid Mishneh also writes similarly in Chapter 6, Law 3, and this is his language: "Certainly, even if he is known to him, as long as it is not in his presence, there is no concern that he will increase the work for him – it is permitted, like Abaye's opinion. And perhaps this is included in our master's words, that wherever there is no concern that it will be done for the sake of the Jew, it is permitted," as mentioned there. I have proof for this from the language of the Rambam in his commentary on the Mishnah, where he wrote: "And know that when the non-Jew and the Jew are together and he knows and recognizes him, he is forbidden to water his animal after him, because due to his recognition, he might increase the drawing of water for him." Thus, it is written that when they are together. The language of the Mishnah also proves this, as it states: 'He waters after him,' 'He feeds after him,' 'He descends after him.' What does 'after him' mean? It implies that this language is used when they are together, and initially, one acts and the other follows. Otherwise, it should have said: 'He filled water to water his animal – it is permitted for the Jew to water his animal.' According to this, it seems clear to me that the Rif, the Rambam, and the Rosh, who did not explicitly write this, omitted it because by copying the language of the Mishnah, it automatically indicates they are together, and this is the intention of the Maggid Mishneh. It seems that to our Rabbis, the Rashba and the Ran, this matter was simple, for if not, they would not have ruled against the Rif and the Rambam. At the very least, they should have mentioned that the Rif and the Rambam do not hold this view and refute their words, especially since the Ran explains the words of the Rif. Rather, it was clear to them that there is no dispute in this matter (see Rashi on the term 'after him').

And our master, the Beit Yosef, in his great book, rejected the words of the Maggid Mishneh and the Ran with the argument that the Rif and the Rambam did not mention Abaye’s statement. Based on this, he established his words in his pure table and did not mention that the Rashba also wrote like them, as did the Ra'avan of blessed memory. And I am astonished, since it is clear that the Rashba and the Ran did not interpret the words of the Rif and the Rambam differently, as they did not mention them, as we have explained and from the reasons we have elucidated. Why did our master the Beit Yosef disagree with them? (And also the Magen Avraham in section 128 leans towards this, see there). And our master the Beit Yosef brought a Tosefta that is according to his words, which is in chapter 14, which is the Baraita brought by the Talmud. And it concludes there: "But if he is familiar with him - it is forbidden, because he will become accustomed to him and will do so with him on another Shabbat," see there. And since the concern is for the coming Shabbat, it follows that this concern also applies even in his absence (and the Magen Avraham struggled with this there). And in my humble opinion, it seems that since the Talmud brought this Tosefta and did not bring the end of its words, and did not mention throughout the entire discussion a concern for the coming Shabbat, it implies on the contrary that the Talmud was not concerned with this. And also in the explanation of the Tosefta, it seems to me that on the contrary, its intention is that the Jew is with him together, and just as he does with him on this Shabbat, so he will do with him on the other Shabbat. And its intention is that although for this one time it is not forbidden due to the concern that he might increase for his sake, nonetheless, there is a concern that he will do so again in the future and it will become a constant problem. But all this is when they are together, as the language 'with him' implies.

And I have elaborated on this because it is the custom of many Jews to visit their non-Jewish acquaintances on Shabbat to drink hot beverages, and they are close and familiar with each other. According to our teacher, the Beit Yosef, they are committing a prohibition. Therefore, we have explained that since the four pillars of the world permitted this, we have a basis to rely on, particularly in a rabbinic concern, and thus our custom is proper, as the non-Jews prepare the hot beverages not in the presence of the Jew. However, even according to our teacher, the Beit Yosef, the custom can be justified, as in a samovar it is not relevant to worry that they might increase the quantity on behalf of the Jew, as we have written this reasoning in regard to preparing for a sick person in Siman 318, section 16. The concern we wrote there about increasing the amount of tea leaves does not apply here, because since only one or two Jews are drinking with him, they will not increase the quantity, as we wrote there.

A non-Jew who filled water for his animal, and the cistern is located in the public domain while the cistern itself is private domain, and he filled the water from the cistern which is private domain and brought it to the public domain, since he filled it for himself, it is permitted for a Jew to use it and give it to his animal. Provided that he is not acquainted with him, so there is no concern that the non-Jew will draw extra water on his behalf. According to what we have explained, even if he is acquainted with him, the prohibition only applies if he filled it in his presence. And if he filled it for the sake of the Jew's animal, the water is forbidden for any use, even for another Jew, because anything done as a Torah prohibition for the sake of a Jew is forbidden for all Jews. However, if the cistern is in a karmelit (an area that is neither public nor private domain) and he filled water from the cistern to the karmelit for the sake of a Jew, it is only forbidden for the one for whom it was filled, but for another Jew, it is permitted, as explained in section 15 regarding bringing from beyond the techum (Sabbath boundary).
