Some of our great rabbis have said that from the statement of our Sages, "to water his animal," we learn that it is specifically for his animal that it is forbidden if the gentile filled the water for the sake of the Jew, because he could not bring the animal into the pit to drink, and therefore the transfer from private to public domain was beneficial for him. However, if the gentile filled water for the Jew himself to drink, it is permitted for the Jew to drink it, because even without transferring it to the public domain, the Jew could have descended into the pit and drunk. And since there is no benefit to him from transferring it to the public domain, we cannot forbid him the water that was permitted to him, and he did not need it to be transferred to the public domain at all. Also, regarding the rule of gathering grass that was explained, if it was for the Jew - it is forbidden, and the Jew could have stood his animal over the grass; this also means when he could not stand it there, such as when a river separates them or the like, but otherwise - it is permitted (Rabeinu Tam in Tosafot there, s.v. ‘Mashkeh’, and Rabbi Yitzchak disagrees, see there). And it is clear that only when he could obtain that particular water and grass is it permitted according to this opinion, but if he could not obtain these, even though he could obtain other water and other grass – it is forbidden, because ultimately, regarding these, it was done in a forbidden manner for him (Magen Avraham 324), contrary to those who are lenient even in this according to this opinion.

And behold, according to this opinion, all the more so if the non-Jew brought food or drink for the Jew through a karmelit, and the Jew could have gone there and eaten or drunk - then it is also permitted for the Jew for whom the non-Jew brought it to eat or drink it, for the reason explained. And this is what our teacher, the Rema, wrote in section 10: "And there are those who are lenient and say that even if it was brought for the Jew through a public domain - it is permitted to drink from them, since it is possible to go there and drink. And some permit even initially, and so is the custom to say initially to a non-Jew to bring beer or other things through a karmelit or without an eruv. And even though it is preferable to be stringent in this matter, nevertheless one should not protest against those who are lenient for the sake of Shabbat and in times of need, for indeed it is permitted to be lenient in instructing a non-Jew for a need, as stated in Siman 307, and all the more so in such cases."

His words are not understood at all, for even according to this opinion, the permission is only when the non-Jew brings it on his own, as in that case there is no prohibition on the Jew since he did not need it, as was mentioned. But to initially tell the non-Jew to bring it, who permitted this? And also in his book Darkei Moshe he himself wrote this. And it appears to me that he was referring here to the words of the Hagahot Maimoniot (Chapter 10, letter 5), who wrote that Rabbeinu Tam permitted telling a non-Jew: "Bring a burning candle," as this is only a prohibition of muktzeh, and through indirect handling, a Jew himself could have done it. And since there is a way for a Jew himself to have done it, we are not concerned if the non-Jew does it in a prohibited manner, as mentioned there (and the Magen Avraham brought this in Siman 276, subsection 11). And if so, here too, since there is a way for a Jew to go there and drink, we are not concerned if the non-Jew does it in a prohibited manner with a rabbinic prohibition. And afterwards, he says: "Even though one should be stringent in this matter," because this is not a complete analogy, as there, when telling the non-Jew: "Bring the candle," he can bring it through indirect handling, and the prohibition is not explicit in his words, which is not the case here when telling him to bring, as he is telling him to bring it through a karmelit. Nevertheless, one should not protest against those who are lenient, as in this case we can combine another leniency explained in Siman 307, that it is permitted to tell a non-Jew to do a rabbinic prohibition due to slight illness or a mitzvah or when there is a great need, as mentioned there. And here, when telling him to bring beer, there is a need for it, especially for the honor of Shabbat, and therefore one should not protest against those who follow this leniency. However, one who guards his soul should distance himself from this leniency. (As I wrote, this resolves the difficulty of the Taz, subsection 10, and the astonishment of the Magen Avraham, subsection 25, as mentioned. And what was written that giving him money on Shabbat is forbidden, it seems there is a printing error, for what is the novelty in this, rather it should be stated: that giving money, etc., meaning that even if the non-Jew pays from his own, it is forbidden, as this is essentially a sale and purchase through his non-Jewish agent, and scrutinize this).

If a non-Jew gathered herbs for his own animal by plucking them from the ground, a Jew may feed his animal with these herbs afterward. It has already been clarified in the previous section, paragraph 12, that if one places his animal on muktzeh (an object that is set aside and cannot be used on Shabbat), it is forbidden to stand by it, lest one move the muktzeh and place it in the animal’s mouth. Instead, one should stand a bit farther away, only to guide the animal so it does not stray from there. And indeed, the herbs are considered muktzeh since the non-Jew plucked them today. It has also been clarified that this applies when the non-Jew is not known to him, but if he is known to him, it is forbidden. According to what we have explained, this prohibition is only in the presence of the non-Jew (and so wrote the Magen Avraham, Subsection 128). Similarly, in any situation where there is concern that the non-Jew might do extra work for the Jew, it is forbidden if the non-Jew is known to him. However, if there is no concern that the non-Jew might do extra work, such as if a non-Jew lit a candle for himself or made a ramp to descend, and similar cases, then if he did it for himself, it is permitted even if he is known to the Jew and even in the Jew’s presence.

Even though he does not know him, if he explicitly says that he is doing it for the sake of a Jew, or even if he does not explicitly say but his actions indicate that he did it for the sake of a Jew, such as lighting a candle and leaving without using its light at all, and the Jew was there, or even if the Jew was not there but it is clearly evident that he lit it for him — it is forbidden for any Jew to use its light. Similarly, in the case where we permitted if he knows him but he is not present, if the non-Jew knows that the Jew needs it (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 28) — it is forbidden when it is apparent to the eye that he increased the act for the Jew. And know that in the case of knowing him, where we forbade it, there is no need to wait the time it takes to do the same act after Shabbat (ibid.).

If the non-Jew performs a task for both himself and the Jew in something that requires two people rather than one, such as filling water or gathering herbs, it is obviously forbidden. However, regarding a candle or a lamb, some say it is also forbidden (Magen Avraham, Siman 276:6). But we have explained there that it is permissible, as the Rashba has written. In the Jerusalem Talmud at the end of chapter 16, there is a discussion on this, and in the conclusion, there are different versions. (See Magen Avraham 276:28 who elaborates on the reason of the Tosefta, that the concern is for the coming Shabbat, and therefore, even regarding a candle, there is a need to be cautious, although he struggles to differentiate there. We have already explained in section 20 that the Talmud does not hold by this Tosefta, and the Tosefta is only referring to when the Jew is present. According to this, indeed, according to the Tosefta, the same rule would apply to a candle. However, according to the Talmud, we are not concerned at all about the coming Shabbat, as it is not mentioned in the entire discussion. Examine this well.)

From everything that has been explained, it is necessary to protest against some of the wealthy who keep in their homes a servant or maid who is not Jewish and have them set up the samovar on Shabbat, with the foolish claim that the non-Jew also drinks from it, and their main intention is for themselves and not for the Jew. This is an affront to Heaven, as they are trying to deceive God, as it were. Who does not know that even if the intention of the servant or maid is for themselves, their main intention is for the Jewish household members, just as it is throughout the week. There are those who teach them to lie and say that their intention is for themselves. Moreover, even if this were the case, we are concerned that they might increase the quantity for the sake of the Jew. It is obvious that more tea leaves are required, and this is a complete prohibition, desecrating Shabbat, and their sin is very great. Some foolishly say that nowadays everything is secular when it comes to hot water, and it is permissible to tell a non-Jew to set up the samovar. The mouths of those who speak falsehood should be stopped. It is possible to prepare it before Shabbat and place it in the oven or on the stove, as all Jews do. Just because it does not taste as good as hot water from the samovar, we should not permit desecrating the holy Shabbat. Such a thing should not happen in Israel, and their sin is very great. May a blessing come upon those who prevent this.

If the non-Jew does it on his own accord, such as drawing water from a private domain to a public domain and giving it to the animal of a Jew to drink, or plucking grass and feeding it to the animal, the Jew is not obligated to prevent him from doing so. However, if the non-Jew regularly does this and deceives by saying that he is drawing and plucking for himself and afterward gives it to the Jew's animal, it is forbidden. This is because it is only when done occasionally that there is no need to protest in matters where the Jew himself does not benefit directly, like with a lamp where it is forbidden to use its light. But regarding his animal, what difference does it make? Nevertheless, when it is done regularly, it is considered as if the non-Jew is the Jew's agent, and it is forbidden. (See Magen Avraham, section 31, who holds that the Mordechai disagrees with the Rosh. In my humble opinion, both intended the same thing, that when the deception is even from the non-Jew, it is assumed to be under the Jew's deception, and take note.)

If a non-Jew made a coffin or grave on Shabbat for himself, meaning for his relative, and it later turned out that it was not needed, it is permissible for a Jew to be buried in it if the place is suitable for the burial of a Jew, and similarly with the coffin. But if it was made for a Jew, he may never be buried in it. And even though with other kinds of work done for a Jew it is permissible to use it after Shabbat, regarding a grave and a coffin, which are matters that are public, it is forbidden forever. And so, for anything public, the prohibition is eternal. This is specifically when the grave is in a public place and the coffin is above ground, where everyone knows it was made for a particular Jew, and it is disgraceful for him to be buried in a publicly known grave where Shabbat was desecrated for him. But if it is in private, it is permissible after waiting the amount of time it would take to do the work. And even when it is public, the prohibition applies only to the Jew for whom it was made, and it is forbidden for him and his household. But for another Jew, it is permissible, provided he waits the amount of time it would take to do the work. And even though the other Jew did not need to wait the amount of time it would take to do the work, since the reason is so that he does not tell the non-Jew to do it, and this does not apply to another Jew, nevertheless, they did not differentiate in a matter where a complete work was done for a Jew. See above in Siman 244.

A gentile who brought flutes on Shabbat to eulogize the dead: if he brought them for a Jew, neither he nor others should eulogize with them until waiting until the evening for the time it would take to bring them from a nearby place outside the Shabbat boundary. This applies when it involves a Torah prohibition, such as bringing them through a public domain. But if the prohibition is only due to being outside the boundary: for others, it is permitted immediately as explained, and for himself, some say he does not need to wait the time it would take to bring them, as mentioned in paragraph 15. If he brought them through a well-known place, they are forbidden to him forever, similar to a grave. If it is known for certain that they were brought from a distant place, one must wait the time it would take to bring them from that place. Even if it is something commonly found in a nearby place, since these were brought from afar, one must wait the time it would take to bring them from that place (Beit Yosef). Some say that if they were not brought through the public domain, he is permitted to use them immediately in the evening, without needing to wait the time it would take to bring them according to all opinions. This is unlike food brought from outside the boundary, where some say one must wait the time it would take to prepare it, because the enjoyment is not as significant, hence they did not require waiting the time it would take to prepare (Magen Avraham, Siman 344 and see Taz, Siman 315). Know that in all labors where one must wait the time it would take to prepare, this applies even if the Jew instructed the non-Jew to do it for him, as it is not possible to prohibit more than this (Magen Avraham, Siman 342). Regarding flutes, if there is doubt whether they were brought from within the boundary, we are concerned that they might have been brought from outside the boundary, as in paragraph 17, and everything explained there applies here as well.

It is stated in the Gemara: Initially, they would bathe in hot water that was heated before Shabbat, as there is no prohibition in this since the water was not heated on Shabbat, and the bathing itself is not a labor. The bathhouse attendants began to heat the water on Shabbat and claim it was heated before Shabbat. They prohibited the hot water and permitted the steam. Still, they would bathe in hot water and say they were just sweating. They then prohibited the steam and permitted cold water and the hot springs of Tiberias.

Therefore, it is forbidden to wash one's entire body or the majority of one's body with hot water that was heated on the eve of Shabbat, even if one washes limb by limb and not the entire body at once, whether the hot water is in a vessel or in the ground, and even if the hot water was not heated in a bathhouse. And even to pour water on one's body to rinse, which is not the usual way of washing, nonetheless, since washing the body is prohibited, the Sages did not differentiate regarding the manner of washing. However, it is permitted to wash one's face, hands, and feet or any other limb with hot water that was heated on the eve of Shabbat, as long as it is not the majority of the body. But with hot water that was heated on Shabbat, even if it was heated by a non-Jew for his own use, it is forbidden even to dip one's hand in it. And it is not similar to other things that a non-Jew does for himself, which are permitted for a Jew to use when he is not aware, as mentioned in the previous section. Nevertheless, washing is completely prohibited. Washing the face, hands, and feet is only permitted if the water was heated on the eve of Shabbat, as is explicitly proven in the Gemara (there), and the prohibition is not because of the labor performed on them but because of the washing itself, as the Sages decreed.

Since it is permissible to wash a minority of one's limbs with hot water that was heated before Shabbat, therefore, a woman who begins counting the seven clean days from the first day and needs to wear white garments on Shabbat towards evening and wash her thighs, may wash her thighs with hot water that was heated before Shabbat. However, she must be careful not to wash with a cloth, lest she come to wring it out, but rather washes with her hands the lower part of her body and between her thighs, as stated in Yoreh De'ah, section 196. And there it is explained that the washing is not an absolute requirement, as mentioned there. And going to the mikveh on Friday night after nightfall is forbidden when the mikveh is very hot, since washing the entire body is prohibited. Rather, they should ensure that the water is lukewarm or slightly warm, because the prohibition of washing only applies when the water is very hot, close to the temperature at which the hand recoils. Otherwise, it is not considered hot water but lukewarm. In any case, it is not clear to us what the exact measure is, and we did not find this clarified. It seems to me, in my humble opinion, that anything considered hot by common standards is forbidden.

And that which the hot springs of Tiberias are permitted - this is specifically on the ground, for everyone sees that this is the hot springs of Tiberias and not water heated by fire, but in a vessel - it is forbidden, as it can be confused with water heated by fire. And this is not like a decree upon a decree, for it is one decree, that all hot water in a vessel is forbidden. And similarly, the steam that is forbidden makes no distinction between steam that comes due to fire or that comes due to the hot springs of Tiberias, and therefore when the hot springs of Tiberias are permitted, it is only when the place is not covered, for then there is no steam. But when the place is covered - it is forbidden, as it leads to steam. And some say that the steam of the hot springs of Tiberias is permitted, for it is not logical that the water itself is permitted and the steam that comes from it would be forbidden. And the first opinion does not consider this, as we find that the derivative of the sun is stricter than the sun itself, as stated in Siman 318, because it can be confused with the derivative of fire as stated there, and here too the steam is stricter than its source for this reason. Therefore, those traveling to the hot baths, if there is steam there - they should beware of this, and in the water itself they are permitted to bathe, for there everything is from the hot springs like the hot springs of Tiberias. And it is permitted to go to these baths of such waters, as they are known, and only if there is steam should they beware as stated (see Shulchan Aruch), and in a pressing situation one can rely on those who permit.

The water channel of the hot springs of Tiberias - it is forbidden to continue a stream of cold water into it even before Shabbat, because the mouth of the stream exits outside the channel and spills into a pit in the ground. Why do they do this? To heat the cold water as it passes through the pipe submerged in the hot springs of Tiberias. This is similar to insulating with something that adds heat, which is forbidden even before Shabbat as stated in Siman 257. Therefore, this water is forbidden both for washing and drinking until the end of Shabbat, like water heated on Shabbat, which is forbidden even for washing one limb, as stated. If this stream was continued on the eve of a festival - its status is like that of water heated on a festival, which is permitted for drinking and for washing the face, hands, and feet, but not for washing the whole body as will be explained in Siman 511. This is when the pipe is enclosed and the hot water does not mix with the cold water, which is similar to insulating. But when the cold water falls into the hot water, and the waters mix together - this is not a form of insulating. Therefore, if the process began before Shabbat, even if it continues all of Shabbat and they mix together - it is permitted, like all actions that begin before Shabbat and are completed on Shabbat, as stated in Siman 252. It is permitted to wash the whole body in them, as with the hot springs of Tiberias (and Rashi in 38b believes that this too is considered insulating, but the Tosafot reject this, see there).

A person should not rinse their entire body with cold water and then warm up in front of a fire, because it melts the water on them and it turns out that they are effectively washing their entire body with warm water. And even though lukewarm water is not forbidden, in this case, the water becomes hot (see Rashi 40a: it melts and warms, and analyze this well). However, if one first warms up by the fire and then rinses with cold water, it is permitted, for in this manner, the water on them does not become heated, but rather, only loses some of its chill. Washing one limb in such a manner, for example, washing one's hands with cold water and then warming them by the fire, if it is not considered a full washing, it is permitted (Magen Avraham, section 5), and this also seems to be implied from the language of the Rambam in Chapter 22. However, there are those who say that this is considered a full washing, and therefore, one should be cautious not to warm their hands by the fire after washing, unless they first dry them thoroughly. But from a distance, where the hand does not get scalded, it is permitted to hold them by the fire (Beit Yosef), because in this case, it cannot lead to full heating. And there are those who forbid it even in a place where the hand does not get scalded (Magen Avraham, section 6 and its commentary, Maharshal), and in the Jerusalem Talmud, Tractate Kira (Halacha 4), it is explicitly stated otherwise. (And this is what is stated in the Jerusalem Talmud: "One descends and immerses in cold water and warms up by the fire, the words of Rabbi Meir, and the Sages forbid it. What is the reason of the Rabbis? As Mar of Rav Zeira said: It is permitted to melt in a place where the hand can tolerate, etc." There, it is clear that even in a place where the hand gets scalded, this is neither the way of washing nor the way of heating, as is evident, and therefore what the Magen Avraham stated in section 5 is not clear to me. And it also seems that they understood the Gemara's statement 'because it melts the water on them,' meaning lukewarm water itself, and even so, it is forbidden. And I am astonished, because lukewarm water was never forbidden, and all the more so in such washing that is not considered washing at all, and therefore we explained that the water becomes hot, and this is clear from Rashi's language. And what the Rambam wrote that this is not a full washing, certainly this is so, even in a place where the hand gets scalded, that this is not considered washing at all; analyze this well).

It is permitted on Shabbat to heat a garment and place it on one's stomach, but specifically a dry garment. It also appears to me that it is allowed to place a pan in a spot where it is not hot enough to cause one's hand to recoil, to warm it slightly, and then place it on the stomach. However, it is forbidden to place on the stomach a vessel containing hot water that was heated on Shabbat, lest it spill on him and he ends up washing on Shabbat. According to this, if the water was heated before Shabbat, it is permitted, for it does not constitute washing one's entire body even if it spills on him. However, in the Gemara there, this was prohibited even during the week due to danger, as sometimes the water is boiling and if it spills on him, he could get burned. The Tosafot there wrote that on Shabbat the prohibition is due to healing, which was prohibited because it might lead to grinding of herbs, but with a garment, they did not decree this because it does not appear as healing to such an extent, as it is stated there. And this applies when it is not a serious illness but just a minor discomfort, for with a serious illness even if there is no danger, one can perform all remedies through a non-Jew, as stated in Siman 328.

One who bathes in a river must thoroughly dry his body when he comes out of the river, so that the water does not remain on him and he ends up carrying it four cubits in a karmelit (an area that is rabbinically prohibited to carry in on Shabbat), since when one comes out of bathing, there is a lot of water on his body. However, when one walks in the public domain and rain is pouring on his head and clothes, they did not insist on this, for the water is minimal, and even if it is abundant, what can he do, he is compelled. Additionally, this is considered as a case of an inevitable outcome which he does not desire (פסיק רישא דלא ניחא ליה), unlike the one who bathes in the river by his own will and for his pleasure; any minor action that is done in this case is considered as done willingly. Furthermore, one must be careful in the river not to swim, and it is also forbidden to push the scattered twigs on the water from one place to another in order to clean the water in the place where one is standing. It is also necessary to be cautious not to wring out one's hair, and even though wringing hair is not considered wringing according to Torah law, it is forbidden by rabbinic decree (according to the Gr"a). This is very common when one submerges his head under the water and comes up, placing his hands on his head, and without realizing, wrings the hair, as is well known and perceptible.

And because there are great obstacles in bathing in the river, therefore our ancestors instituted that one should not wash their entire body in cold water on Shabbat. And so wrote the Maharil in his responsa (Siman 150). Moreover, he wrote that even women refrain from immersing not at their prescribed time on Shabbat (Magen Avraham, Siman 308). Similarly, the author of the Terumat HaDeshen wrote that it was customary to forbid washing in cold water (Siman 295), and this custom has been accepted by our forefathers and their forefathers for many hundreds of years. And one who seeks to breach the fence set by the early authorities, upon him it is said, 'One who breaches a fence will be bitten by a snake,' for we have accepted this as a severe prohibition to not bathe in rivers, lakes, and springs on Shabbat at all.

Nevertheless, to immerse in a mikveh on Shabbat morning is permitted, especially for someone who is accustomed to immerse for purification. This is not considered as "fixing" because, according to the law, the immersion has been nullified, as stated in Siman 88. However, one must be careful about squeezing the hair and ensure that the mikveh is not very hot, as this would be a clear prohibition due to bathing in hot water. Instead, the water should be cold or lukewarm. Nevertheless, an unlearned person should refrain from this, as they may easily come to transgress the prohibition of squeezing the hair, as I have seen with my own eyes. Although there are those who question even immersion in a mikveh, this concern is not heeded, and this is the common custom among all Jewish communities (and it is explicitly stated in Beitzah 17b that a person is permitted to immerse, as it appears like cooling off).

It is permissible to wash one's face, hands, and feet with substances that do not remove hair, and even if they are mixed with substances that do remove hair, provided that the majority is not composed of hair-removing substances, for then it would inevitably remove hair and would be a "pesik reisha" (an inevitable prohibited outcome). However, if they are the minority, it is not a "pesik reisha," and even if hair is removed, it is considered an unintended consequence and is permitted. Our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, wrote in Section 10: "It is permissible to wash one's hands with bran, for kneading in an unusual manner is permitted, but it is forbidden to wash one's hands with salt, and even more so with soap called 'zeif' or other fats that dissolve in one's hand, as this constitutes 'nolad' (a creation of a new entity)." This is the end of their words.

The explanation of these matters: it is not only because of the change (i.e., the unusual manner), for if so, it would also apply to flour. Rather, it is clear that concerning a Torah prohibition, one cannot initially rely on a change where there is no great need. The primary reason for permitting bran is because Rambam ruled that bran is not subject to kneading (as stated in Section 321:18), and for this reason, we permitted in Section 324 to put bran in water for animals. Those who prohibit it still prohibit it here. However, since the opinion of those who prohibit it is not brought here as it is elsewhere, one can say that here it is permitted according to all opinions because he is not putting the bran into water but rather taking it with wet hands (Magen Avraham 10). Nevertheless, our women customarily prohibit it, and this is proper, for it is known with certainty that if we permit it, they will pour water on the bran in their hands. According to the Raavad, as we brought there, this constitutes a primary labor and incurs a sin-offering. Furthermore, even Rambam only exempted bran and not chaff, as he wrote there, and who can distinguish between chaff and bran? Similarly, ashes have the same status as bran. According to the Raavad at the end of Chapter 8: putting water into ashes incurs liability for kneading, but coarse sand may be used for cleaning, as all agree there is no kneading involved, as stated there. With salt, soap, and fats, it constitutes 'nolad' and is prohibited. However, some prepare melted soap before Shabbat, called 'moliyanis,' and it is permitted to clean hands with it. Similarly, it is permitted to clean with crushed brick dust (Tur). Some permit anointing with soap (see Magen Avraham 11), but these matters are questionable and certainly prohibited.

Rabbeinu the Beit Yosef wrote in section 11: "A bathhouse whose vents were sealed before Shabbat - one may bathe in it immediately after Shabbat. But if its vents were not sealed, even if it heated up by itself on Shabbat - one must wait until enough time has passed after Shabbat to account for the heating, because it is forbidden to do so due to a decree lest one stoke the coals." Their bathhouses were heated from underneath, and there were vents at the bottom of the bathhouse through which the heat entered. When the vents were plugged, the heat did not enter the bathhouse. Therefore, if the vents were plugged before Shabbat, the heat did not enter on Shabbat, and thus one may open the vents and bathe in it immediately after Shabbat. But if the vents were not plugged and the heat entered by itself on Shabbat, there is no intrinsic prohibition in this case. Nonetheless, it was forbidden in such a situation due to the concern that one might stoke the coals beneath the ground to increase the heat, and therefore one must wait the time it would take to heat up. However, one should not derive from this that it is forbidden to open a small vent of a winter stove after it has been kindled in a manner that does not involve a concern of kindling or extinguishing by opening it, for we do not find a prohibition against opening a vent to allow the heat to enter another room. The reason it was forbidden in the bathhouse is that the usual manner of heating the bathhouse involves opening and closing vents, and there is a concern lest one stoke the coals. But opening a vent merely to allow warmth to enter - there is no reason to prohibit this. (And this is what the Magen Avraham wrote in section 12: "From here there is a difficulty regarding winter houses... However, I have seen that they customarily permit it," and the permission is clear for the reason we have explained. Reflect on this thoroughly.)

It has already been explained that they also decreed concerning sweat, and therefore, in a small bathhouse that is full of sweat, it is forbidden to pass through it. However, in the bathhouses of cities, one may stroll in them without concern, because they do not have much steam. And in a city where Jews and non-Jews live together and there is a bathhouse that is heated on Shabbat: if the majority are non-Jews, it is permitted to bathe there immediately after Shabbat, but if the majority are Jews, it is forbidden to bathe there after Shabbat until the time it takes to heat the water, because presumably it was heated with the majority in mind. And even if it is half and half, it is forbidden until the time it takes to heat the water, because certainly the intention was for both. Any doubt regarding this matter is forbidden, because this is a matter that will eventually become permitted, as was stated in the previous section regarding something brought from outside the Shabbat boundary, see there (and it is explicitly stated in the Gemara 151a according to Rav, who the law follows in prohibitive matters, see there and examine it well).

Anointing is not prohibited on Shabbat, but it is forbidden to anoint with substances that dissolve due to [the prohibition of] Nolad (creating something new), or with substances that spread due to [the prohibition of] Memareach (smearing), and also not with substances that produce a fragrance. Most of their anointing was done with oil, which does not involve any of these prohibitions. Even if his intention is for healing due to some ailment he has, and it is prohibited for one with an ailment to perform healing on Shabbat due to the decree of grinding herbs, as will be explained in the next section, nevertheless, with things that healthy people also do, it is permitted even for the ill, since it is not evident that he is doing it for healing, as will be explained there.

And so the sages taught in the Mishnah (111a): "One who feels pain in his loins should not anoint with oil and vinegar, but he may anoint with oil alone." For with vinegar, healthy people do not anoint, and it is evident that it is for medicinal purposes, but with oil, they do anoint. And also with rose oil, one should not anoint, because it is very expensive and healthy people do not anoint with it, making it evident that it is for medicinal purposes. However, if it is a place where rose oil is common and people use it even not for medicinal purposes, it is permitted. And in our regions, where it is not customary at all to anoint on weekdays, it is forbidden to anoint on Shabbat for medicinal purposes. Therefore, it is forbidden to anoint the head with scabs (Taz, section 2). There is a doubt nowadays if someone wants to anoint themselves on Shabbat and they are healthy, whether we say it is permitted, or perhaps, since healthy people do not customarily anoint themselves, people will assume that they are ill. And in several places, we find that they were concerned about appearances even with rabbinic prohibitions, and this requires further investigation to determine the law.

There are seven types of rubbing oil into the body, and it is beneficial for the oil to be absorbed by the body. The sages taught in the Mishnah (Shabbat 147a): "One may anoint and rub, but not exercise or scrape." The Gemara explains that one should not do as they do on weekdays, meaning that on weekdays, one first anoints and then rubs. On Shabbat, one should anoint and rub simultaneously. Additionally, one should not rub with force but with gentle hands. Similarly, one should not scrape the body with a utensil made for that purpose unless their hands or feet are soiled with mud or filth. If one has a special scraper designated for Shabbat use, it is permitted (Gemara there). Nowadays, we are not familiar with any of this.

Maimonides wrote in Chapter 23, Law 10: "Tanning is one of the primary categories of labor, and softening leather with oil in the manner that tanners do is considered tanning and is forbidden. Therefore, a person should not oil their foot while it is in a new shoe or sandal, but they may oil their foot and then place it into the shoe or sandal, even if they are new. Similarly, one may oil their entire body and rub it on a new leather cushion without concern. When does this apply? When the amount of oil is minimal, sufficient only to polish the leather. However, if there is a significant amount of oil on the body that would soften the leather, this is forbidden because it is akin to tanning it. This applies to new items, but with old ones, it is permitted."

Nonetheless, even with the amount sufficient only to polish, it is prohibited to intentionally aim to polish (141:), for if one intends to do so, there is a decree lest they come to tan it (Rashi). And with the act of tanning, even without intention, it is forbidden, as it is a 'certain outcome.' It is prohibited to clean shoes on Shabbat, and if one cleans them with wax, it is a primary category of labor due to smoothing and one is liable for a sin-offering. Only with one's hand or foot is it permitted to clean, or with a cloth to remove dust and no more; any kind of polishing is prohibited on shoes.

Saving a life overrides Shabbat, as it is written, "and live by them," and not die by them (Yoma 85b). Even the possibility of saving a life overrides Shabbat (Mishnah Yoma 8:3), as there is nothing that stands in the way of saving a life except for idolatry, sexual immorality, and murder (Yoma 82a). It is forbidden to hesitate in violating Shabbat for a dangerously ill person, for the laws of the Torah are meant to bring mercy, kindness, and peace to the world, as it is written, "which a person shall do and live by them" (Rambam, beginning of Chapter 2). And one who is prompt in saving a life is praiseworthy. It is stated in the Jerusalem Talmud (Yoma 8:5): "One who asks [whether to violate Shabbat] is reprehensible," for one should not ask questions in a situation of saving a life, as by the time one asks and receives a response, the patient could be in danger. "And one who is asked [a question about saving a life on Shabbat] is considered a shedder of blood," for he should have publicly taught that saving a life overrides Shabbat.

I have learned from the responsa of the Ritzba brought in the Or Zarua HaGadol (Siman 108), that which has been clarified, that one who asks is disgraceful and the one who is asked sheds blood, this applies to a patient whose time is urgent, who is in great danger and every moment is critical for him. In such a case, certainly there is no question and no answer, and they do everything within their ability without being meticulous, and the Sabbath is treated exactly like a weekday. However, for a patient whose time is not urgent, there certainly are questions, as it was said in Menachot (64a): Rava asked: A patient who was assessed to need two figs and there are two figs on two stems and three on one stem, which should he bring? And it concludes that he should bring the three. This shows that there can be doubts in matters of saving a life, and it is necessary to ask and for the one who answers to respond, but this applies to a patient whose time is not urgent. Therefore, in the case of a patient who is in great danger and time is urgent, it is forbidden to ask any question, and they should act according to what seems right without any concern or hesitation, and the one who is quick is praiseworthy. However, for a chronically ill patient, one can deliberate and ask questions, and thus is the custom of the world (this seems to me in my humble opinion), and see at the end of paragraph 13.

If Shabbat is overridden or permitted in the case of saving a life, the opinion of the Rashba in his responsa (Siman 629) is that it is overridden, and the Ran also wrote this in the second chapter of Beitza. It appears that this is also the opinion of the Rambam at the beginning of the second chapter of Shabbat, and this is his wording: "Shabbat is overridden in the case of danger to life like all other commandments, etc." But from the words of the Rosh in the eighth chapter of Yoma (Siman 14) it seems that it is permitted, as he wrote: "And Rabbeinu Meir brought an analogy from food preparation on Yom Tov... since the Torah permitted food preparation on Yom Tov, it is like a weekday, and here too, since the Torah permitted saving a life, all work is like on a weekday," and from this wording, it is clear that it is permitted and not overridden. Additionally, since he compares it to food preparation on Yom Tov, and in that case, it is not appropriate to say it is overridden since it was never forbidden, and also in the responsa of the Rashba there, it is explained that according to Rabbeinu Meir, it is permitted and not overridden. (And the Ran in the second chapter of Beitza also wrote the difference that Shabbat is overridden in the case of danger to life, and food preparation on Yom Tov is permitted, as mentioned there. And since Rabbi Meir compares these, it implies that he holds that in both cases it is permitted. And it seems that whoever learns in Yoma there from circumcision that saving a life overrides Shabbat would certainly say it is permitted, for it is impossible to say that circumcision is overridden, as it is stated in Yoreh De'ah Siman 266, Se'if 25. And there we explained that even in the case of saving a life, what the Rambam wrote that it is overridden, his intention is not that it is truly overridden, as mentioned there. But since the Rashba and the Ran explicitly hold that it is overridden and not permitted, there is no necessity to interpret the Rambam’s words out of their plain meaning, and perhaps they would also hold that circumcision is overridden. Or even though they learn from circumcision, there is no proof that they are completely equal. Examine this thoroughly.)

In the Talmud Yoma (6b) regarding the matter of impurity, whether it is overridden or permitted, it states that there is a practical difference concerning seeking out pure individuals. If pure individuals are readily available, even according to the opinion that impurity is permitted, the pure individuals should perform the service and not the impure ones, according to the first interpretation in the Gemara there. Only if pure individuals are not present and need to be sought out, then according to the opinion that impurity is permitted, the impure individuals perform the service, and according to the opinion that it is overridden, we seek out pure individuals. Therefore, similarly with a sick person, if the prohibited and permitted items are both readily available, certainly we feed him the permitted item and not the prohibited one. Only if the prohibited item is readily available or easily obtainable, and the permitted item is not readily available or is difficult to obtain, it depends on the dispute: if the Sabbath and all prohibitions are permitted in the case of saving a life, we use the prohibited item; if they are only overridden, we seek out the permitted item. This would seem to be the case, but it is a novel idea and we have not found this in the decisors, and on the contrary, they urged to hasten with zeal everything the sick person needs. Although according to what we have explained, this might apply to a patient whose condition is urgent, as we mentioned in section 2, nevertheless, it appears from all the decisors that this is not the case.

In truth, it appears to me clearly that even if it is considered "pushed aside," there is no need to wait for the permissible option. This is unlike [the laws of] impurity, because since the Torah commanded to desecrate the Sabbath for him and to feed him all the prohibitions, if we say that we should wait, it could lead to danger. Therefore, according to this, there is no difference between "pushed aside" and "permitted" in matters of saving a life in this regard. However, there is a difference according to the "there are those who say" in the Talmud, for according to the opinion that it is "permitted," even if there are impure and pure individuals before us, the impure should perform [the task] on the Sabbath. Thus, there is a significant practical difference: for example, if both a permissible and a forbidden option are before us, according to the opinion that holds "pushed aside," it is forbidden to give him the forbidden option, while according to the opinion that holds "permitted," it is allowed. Nevertheless, for us, even in this case, there is no practical difference, as the first opinion is not so, as I have written. In any case, there is a practical difference between carrion and slaughter, which is when a sick person needs meat on the Sabbath, we slaughter for him, as will be explained, and we do not feed him carrion for reasons that will be explained. However, if the carrion is prepared before us, according to the opinion that holds "permitted," we slaughter for him on the Sabbath and do not feed him the carrion, while according to the opinion that holds "pushed aside," we feed him the carrion in order not to desecrate the Sabbath with a primary labor, as explained by the Rashba there (this is how it appears to me in my humble opinion).

And our Sages said there, that when it is necessary to desecrate the Sabbath for a sick person whose life is in danger, what needs to be done for him should not be done by a non-Jew, nor by women, nor by minors, but by adult Jewish men. The reason is that observers might say that it is only allowed with difficulty to desecrate the Sabbath for the sake of saving a life, and it is not permitted by those obligated in commandments. This could lead to a stumbling block, as perhaps there will be a time when they cannot find a non-Jew, minors, or women, and adults will not want to desecrate the Sabbath, leading to danger (Ran, and similarly explained by the Rosh). The Tosafot further wrote that even when it is possible to have a non-Jew do it, it is a mitzvah for a Jew to do it, as the non-Jew might become lazy and this could lead to danger. Consequently, the same applies to women and minors, as women are generally lazy, and all the more so minors. According to their opinion, this might be the reason why the Sages prohibited doing it through them.

We must be astonished at our master, the Rema, in paragraph 12, regarding what our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote on this law. This is his wording: "When one desecrates Shabbat for a dangerously ill person, one should strive not to do so through non-Jews, minors, and women, but rather through adult men of understanding." And on this, our master, the Rema, wrote: "And some say that if it is possible to do so without delay and without postponement, one should do so with a change. And if it is possible to do so through a non-Jew without any delay at all, one should do so through him, and this is the custom. But in a place where there is a concern that the non-Jew will be lazy, one should not do so through him."

And how is it possible to say such a thing? For according to the first reason we wrote, that the concern is for another time, it is obvious that it is forbidden. Even according to the second reason, due to concern for laziness, since the Talmud was concerned about this, how can we say that we are not concerned about it? This is astonishing. According to the Rambam, what the Talmud said that it should be done by the great ones of Israel, it means the truly great ones of Israel, those great in Torah and fear of Heaven. This is to show everyone that the Torah commanded us, and the Holy One, blessed be He, who commanded us about the Shabbat, also commanded us to desecrate the Shabbat for a dangerously ill person.

(The Taz also wondered about this, and it seems that the one who holds this opinion does so due to the concern of laziness. And what the Talmud said, "and one does not do this through etc.," it means that one is not obligated to do so through them. But this is against the majority of the decisors, and therefore, in practice, it is certainly proper to do so specifically through a great one of Israel.)

Anyone who is zealous to desecrate Shabbat for something involving danger is praiseworthy, even if they perform another prohibited labor along with it. How so? The Rambam writes in Chapter 2, Law 16: "If one sees a child fall into the sea, they spread a net and lift the child out, even if they catch fish with it. If one hears that a child has drowned in the sea and spreads a net to lift them out but only lifts fish, they are exempt. If one intended to catch fish and lifted both fish and the child, they are exempt even if they did not hear that the child had drowned, because they lifted the child along with the fish. If a child falls into a pit, one removes a section of the wall and lifts them out, even if they are building steps while removing it. If a door is locked in front of a child, one breaks the door and lifts them out, even if they break it into pieces suitable for work, lest the child be frightened and die. If a fire breaks out and it is feared that there is someone inside, they extinguish it to save them from the fire, even if they clear a path and fix it while extinguishing. Anyone who rushes to save is praiseworthy, and one does not need permission from the court in any matter involving danger." End of quote.

There is a need to scrutinize the breaking of the door: who forces them to break it in a way that constitutes labor? They should break it in a destructive manner, which would only be considered damaging. It seems to me that the explanation is as follows: there is concern that the child will be frightened by the sound of the breaking if it is done destructively, so they break it in a way that splits it, so the child does not notice the breaking. This is what is meant by "lest the child be frightened," meaning if it is broken in a simple destructive manner, and certainly if the child is left there, they will surely be frightened. (And this is what the Talmud says in Yoma there: "Even though they intend to break it into splinters." And the Kesef Mishneh asked how it is permitted with intent, while in all other cases intent is not mentioned. According to what I have said, it makes sense, because here one must intend so that the child is not frightened, and you should understand this well).

A dangerously ill person who, according to medical estimation on Shabbat, requires a known remedy that involves violating the Shabbat for eight days — we do not say that we should wait until nightfall so that only one Shabbat will be desecrated on their behalf. Rather, it should be done immediately, even if it means that two Shabbats will be desecrated. Extinguishing a candle so that the patient can sleep is clarified in Siman 278, where it is permitted for a dangerously ill person if needed. Even if it is clear to the doctors that the person will die, but with the treatment, they can live a few more hours — it is permitted to desecrate the Shabbat for them, as even for a few hours of life we desecrate the Shabbat. This will be further explained in Siman 329.

If one needs meat or chicken broth, they are obligated to slaughter for him. The slaughterer is not permitted to say: "Why should I desecrate the Sabbath with a primary labor? Let him eat carrion," meaning through the killing by a non-Jew or a minor. For even for the sick person himself, it would be better to transgress the prohibition of eating carrion, which is a lesser prohibition compared to slaughtering on the Sabbath, which incurs stoning, excision, and a sin offering. Nevertheless, this is not so. There are several reasons for this: the first reason is that we are concerned that the sick person may be repulsed by carrion (Rosh there, and similarly written in Or Zarua the Great); the second reason is that the prohibition of the Sabbath has already been overridden by kindling and cooking, whereas the prohibition of carrion has not yet been overridden (there in the name of the Raavad); the third reason is that with carrion, one transgresses with every olive-sized piece, whereas with slaughtering, it is only once (Ran there). And even though it is evident from there that they do not worry about this, as they argue there regarding untithed produce and terumah (priestly dues), where some hold that terumah is stricter than untithed produce and would feed him untithed produce rather than terumah, even though with untithed produce there is a prohibition for every olive-sized piece, this is because to avoid creating a new prohibition with one's hands and feeding it to him, they feed him the lesser prohibition as it is, despite the multiple prohibitions it contains. However, this is not the case with slaughtering, where we are creating a permitted state for him, meaning that at the time of eating, it is completely permissible. Therefore, this reasoning is valid. The fourth reason is that the Torah permitted a sick person prohibitions that hinder his healing, and since carrion does not prevent his healing, for he can be healed with kosher meat, this prohibition was not permitted to him. Whereas the Sabbath prohibition, which stands in his way, whether for slaughtering, kindling, or cooking, was permitted to him by the Torah (see Ran in the name of Raavad and Rosh in the name of Ran, and scrutinize well). See what I have written on this in Yoreh Deah, section 85, paragraphs 45 and 46.

It is obvious that if the non-kosher meat (neveilah) is readily available and slaughtering requires a delay, and the sick person needs it immediately, we feed him the non-kosher meat. If he does not need it immediately, according to those who hold that Shabbat is entirely set aside to save a life, we slaughter for him. But for those who hold that Shabbat is merely overridden, we do not slaughter for him; instead, we feed him the non-kosher meat that is readily available. Since he has meat, we do not permit the overridden Shabbat to be set aside (Rashba in his responsa there). It is also obvious that if a slaughterer is not available, we feed him non-kosher meat. Similarly, if they slaughtered for him and he needs it immediately, it does not need to be salted. (See Magen Avraham paragraph 9, who wrote about slaughtering that Shabbat is set aside, and it is surprising, for everyone agrees we slaughter, and only in the case we mentioned is there a difference between overridden and set aside, and there is no difference whether the sick person is an adult or a child).

If one needs to heat wine for him, a Jew should fill the vessel, and a non-Jew can heat it. This is not similar to the laws of slaughtering, as it is a minor prohibition, and one would not be stringent about it. According to Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) in his responsa (Siman 124 in the Hanau edition), even a sick person who is not in life-threatening danger is permitted to drink their ordinary wine (see Magen Avraham there). Some say that this leniency applies only to a sick person in life-threatening danger. Even on Shabbat, a Jew should heat the wine and not a non-Jew, lest the Jew transgress for each drop (Bach and Taz, subparagraph 6). Refer to Yoreh De'ah, Siman 155. When slaughtering a bird on Shabbat, one should not cover its blood until nightfall if its mark is noticeable, as mentioned in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 28.

The Sages said in Menachot (64a): "If the doctors say that a sick person needs one fig for his recovery, and ten people each pluck one fig and bring their fig to the sick person, they are all exempt [from liability] and receive a good reward from God, even if the sick person is healed by the first fig. For they are all performing a mitzvah (commandment), since, due to the need to be quick in saving a life, they are not required to ask each other if they are also going to do this matter. And if the doctors estimate that he needs two figs, and there is one cluster with three figs and other clusters with one fig each, it is better to minimize the plucking of clusters and pluck the one cluster with three figs. Even though he plucks three figs and the sick person only needs two, it is still better to pluck one cluster of three than two clusters of one each. It is obvious that if there are two figs in one cluster and three in another, he should only pluck the cluster with two figs. And all this applies to a sick person whose condition is not urgent and there is time to be precise. But in the case of a sick person whose condition is urgent, he should not be precise at all. Whatever he can quickly obtain will suffice. This is evidence for what we wrote in Section 2, see there."

Any illness that doctors state is dangerous, even if it is external on the flesh, permits the desecration of Shabbat. And even if one doctor says it is necessary [to treat] and another doctor says it is not necessary, we desecrate [Shabbat], for this is a case of doubt regarding life-threatening situations which overrides Shabbat. There is no difference between a Jewish doctor and a non-Jewish doctor. If one doctor says it is necessary and two say it is not necessary, we do not desecrate [Shabbat], for one cannot stand against two. 

This applies when all the doctors are of equal wisdom. However, if the one who says it is necessary is exceedingly wise, we listen to him to be lenient, such as when he says it is necessary, but not to be stringent when he says it is not necessary, even against another who says it is necessary and is much less knowledgeable. If two say it is necessary, even if a hundred say it is not necessary, we desecrate [Shabbat]. 

If the patient himself says it is necessary, we desecrate [Shabbat] even if all the doctors say it is not necessary, for "the heart knows the bitterness of its soul." But not the opposite: if the doctor says it is necessary and the patient says it is not necessary, we compel the patient to accept the treatment and desecrate Shabbat for him. All of this we learn from the laws of a sick person on Yom Kippur, which will be explained in Siman 618.

And behold, all this applies when there are differing opinions among doctors. But a layman against a doctor, it seems that his words neither add nor detract. For example, if a doctor says there is no need to desecrate Shabbat for him, and a layman says there is a need – it is not considered a doubt at all, and Shabbat is not desecrated. However, there is an opinion that in cases of potential danger to life, one should be lenient even in such situations, and Shabbat is desecrated if it is known that this person is knowledgeable about illnesses and says that, in his understanding, the patient is in a life-threatening condition. Therefore, this is considered a doubt.

And know that what we have written appears to me to explain what the Tur wrote: "And similarly, if one doctor says [that we need to desecrate Shabbat], and another says that it is not necessary, we desecrate [Shabbat]." And Rabbi Yitzchak wrote that a specialist is not necessary, because all people are considered somewhat knowledgeable, and in matters of life and death, we are lenient." The intention of Rabbi Yitzchak is regarding the earlier statement that every person is somewhat knowledgeable and is considered a doubt against the doctor who says it is not necessary. And this is also the intention of our master, the Beit Yosef, in section 10, who wrote in the language of the Tur, and he brought the words of Rabbi Yitzchak in the name of some who say, and his intention is as stated. But I have seen someone who wrote that against a doctor – it is obvious that their words are nothing, and the intention of Rabbi Yitzchak and those who say is when there is no doctor at all, then we rely on ordinary people to desecrate Shabbat when they say it is necessary (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 7). And I am very astonished, for if so, what has Rabbi Yitzchak innovated and who would dispute this? For in a place where there are no doctors, would we not desecrate Shabbat for the sick? Would we wait for the sick person himself to say it is necessary, which is an uncommon matter? Therefore, it seems to me in my humble opinion as I have written. And it is obvious that in a place where there are simple doctors called Feldshers, and doctors called Doctors, we consider the opinion of the simple doctor against the opinion of the Doctor to be lenient and not stringent. Only our master the Rema wrote that for ordinary people, we specifically need Jews who know the severity of Shabbat and not non-Jews who are not doctors, for we do not consider them knowledgeable regarding the matter of desecrating Shabbat. (And one who is being forced to commit a great sin, whether we desecrate Shabbat for them, is explained in Siman 307, see there.)

A general rule regarding illnesses on Shabbat: For a sick person whose life is in danger, Shabbat is desecrated for them, as explained. For a sick person whose life is not in danger, Shabbat is not desecrated directly by a Jew, but they are permitted to have a non-Jew perform a rabbinic prohibition for them. Thus, the sages said: "For a sick person whose life is not in danger, one tells a non-Jew and they do it." They are also permitted to eat food cooked by non-Jews, and there is a dispute regarding their wine. 

Regarding whether it is permitted for the sick person or another Jew to perform a rabbinic prohibition by hand on Shabbat: the Rosh was uncertain about this. According to the Tur's understanding of the Rambam's words, the Rambam permitted this, whereas according to Rabbi Yosef Karo's understanding in his main work, he did not permit it. The Ramban ruled that doing it in the usual manner is forbidden, but doing it with a change (in an unusual manner) is permitted.

There are those who differentiate in such cases: if there is a connection to a Torah-level prohibition, such as applying eye salve which is like writing, or making a medicine where there is concern for grinding herbs, it is forbidden. If there is no connection to a Torah-level prohibition, it is permitted. Rabbi Yosef Karo, in section 17, agreed with the Ramban to permit it with a change, and this is the ruling to be followed.

And if the patient has a danger to one limb but not a danger to the entire body, almost all the authorities agree on one opinion: that a rabbinic prohibition may be done by hand for him, and all the more so instructing a non-Jew to do a Torah prohibition is permitted for him, as it is much lighter than a rabbinic prohibition done by a Jew himself, as is evident from the previous law. In the Talmud, this is called "a rabbinic prohibition without an action" (Eruvin 68a, according to the explanation of Tosafot Gittin 8b). But to perform a Torah prohibition by a Jew is forbidden for the danger of a limb when there is no danger to the entire body. However, if through the limb the illness would spread to the entire body, this is considered a danger to the body, and one may desecrate the Shabbat for it by a Jew, even with a Torah prohibition.

All these matters apply to a sick person who is bedridden or sitting on his bed, unable to leave his house. There is a distinction between whether there is danger to his life or not, as explained. But someone who merely has a minor ailment, such as a headache, stomachache, heart pain, or similar, and he strengthens himself and goes about as usual, like those who are weak due to ailments like a cough and still go, travel, and conduct all their affairs—such a person does not have the status of a sick person at all. It is forbidden to administer medicine to them, even through a non-Jew, due to the decree against grinding herbs. However, if someone has an ailment that weakens his entire body, and although he strengthens himself and goes about, he does so with difficulty and weakness—his status is like one who has fallen ill without danger to life.

A child who is not yet able to eat like everyone else is considered as a sick person who is not in danger, for whom it is permissible to tell a non-Jew to cook for if necessary, and it is permissible to feed him muktzeh (items that are not to be handled on Shabbat) by hand if needed (Magen Avraham, section 315). Therefore, if the child only wants to eat from his mother, it is permissible for the mother to feed him from what was milked and cooked today, but she must be careful not to put the food into the pot herself; rather, the non-Jew should put it into the pot. Similarly, for a sick person who is not in danger, one should be careful about this. See also section 318. And know that in all laws regarding a sick person, there is no difference between the sick person himself and another Jew; whatever is permitted to be done for him is also permissible for another Jew, and whatever is forbidden to be done for him is also forbidden for the sick person himself, except for providing slight assistance when the non-Jew is performing the work for him, which is permitted. For example, if the non-Jew is applying eye ointment and the sick person opens and closes his eyes during the application, such assistance is considered insignificant. Even earlier, when the sick person provides some slight assistance, it is permitted, as our teacher the Rema wrote in section 3: If one has tooth pain and is suffering from it, he can tell a non-Jew to extract it for him. And even though he has to open his mouth wide before the non-Jew places his hand in his mouth to remove the tooth, it is still permitted, because this is considered merely assisting and is insignificant. Some of the great authorities indeed disagreed with this ruling, arguing that assistance provided beforehand is not permitted at all, only during the actual act (Taz, section 1), but their words were refuted by many great authorities (Eliya Rabba, section 4, and Turei Zahav, section 5, and similarly the Shach in Yoreh Deah, Nekudat HaKesef, section 198, who also wrote this in the name of the Ritva and the Rama).

The Sages said (Avodah Zarah 28b): Any wound that is in the internal body cavity, where one of the internal organs is damaged due to a wound it has or due to an internal abscess, and it is from the lips inward, whether in the mouth, intestines, liver, spleen, or other places within the body cavity – this is considered a dangerously ill person, and there is no need for an assessment that the illness is severe. Therefore, one may desecrate the Shabbat for him immediately without an assessment (Rambam, Chapter 2). And how do we know that there is a wound there? If there is a doctor who says so, then there is no need for signs, as it has already been explained that if only the doctor says that he is dangerously ill, one may desecrate the Shabbat for him, and the doctor does not need to say if there is a wound there. Rather, this applies even without a doctor, and regarding this, we said that no assessment is needed. So, how do we know this? Only from the pain and suffering that the patient feels in one of the internal organs, we estimate that there is a wound there (and according to what we have written, there is no disagreement among the poskim, and see Beit Yosef, Bach, and Magen Avraham, Section 2, and it is not understood there, and investigate thoroughly).

And similarly, regarding the teeth themselves, in the case of general pain, it is merely a minor discomfort, and it is forbidden to do anything, as has been explained. However, if the pain is very severe to the extent that the entire body becomes ill from it, even if one does not become bedridden, this is considered a dangerously ill person. Similarly, if the area around the teeth, referred to as "yaslas", becomes severely painful to the extent that the whole body becomes ill, as mentioned, this is considered a condition affecting a vital organ, and one may desecrate the Sabbath. All the more so for the illness referred to in the Gemara (there) as "tzafidna," which begins in the mouth and ends in the intestines, and the sign is when one puts something in the mouth and blood comes out from between the teeth; this is a dangerous illness.

And it has already been clarified that a mere discomfort is nothing, and this is what our teacher the Rema wrote in section 3: "However, one who feels pain in their teeth and suffers from it to the point of needing to remove it - tells a non-Jew to remove it," end quote. This applies when the pain causes the whole body to become ill (Magen Avraham section 3). Nevertheless, it is not considered a danger, such as when the pain is not very severe, and its status is as though there is no danger. It is permitted to be done by a non-Jew but not by a Jew, as removing a tooth is a primary category of labor, which involves uprooting something from its growth. There are those who prohibit even through a non-Jew because the patient needs to open their mouth and thus assists. However, we have already written in section 20 that this is not the case and it is permitted, see there.

Any internal injury does not require an expert assessment, as stated, and even if there are no experts there, and even if the patient says nothing, and even if he is not constantly bedridden, one does for him everything that would be done on a weekday. And even if by withholding the thing that is to be done for him, he would not come to danger, nonetheless, one acts according to the regular weekday practice. However, from Rashi it appears that only when the treatment saves him from danger, and without it, he would remain in danger, is it permitted for a Jew to desecrate Shabbat. But without this, it is not permitted to desecrate Shabbat for a Torah prohibition, and it is proper to be careful about this. However, if they know and recognize that the illness can wait and it is not necessary at this moment to perform the treatment that requires desecrating Shabbat and it can wait until nightfall, it is forbidden to desecrate Shabbat for it, even though it is an internal injury. Therefore, someone suffering from a heart condition, which is dangerous, and his treatment is to drink milk - one does not desecrate Shabbat with a Torah prohibition such as milking the cow on Shabbat himself, because it is known that missing one time of drinking will not make him dangerous, so have ruled the early authorities (Ramban in Milchamot, Chapter 22, and Rashba in Ketubot 61).

A wound that is not internal – we consult an expert and the patient, and we do not desecrate Shabbat for it until one of them says that it requires desecration of Shabbat, or until one of them says that at the very least there is a potential danger to life, which also overrides Shabbat. But otherwise, it is forbidden to desecrate Shabbat for it, because generally, any external wound on the body does not involve a danger to life, unless they say it does. And our sages said (Shabbat 109a) that a wound on the back of the hand or the back of the foot, meaning the area of the hand and foot behind the fingers on the side of the nails – this is considered like an internal wound and we desecrate Shabbat for it, because a wound in this place is severe and dangerous to the whole body.

And similarly, one who is bitten by a rabid dog or one of the deadly creeping creatures, even if it is doubtful whether it is deadly or not, and similarly with a rabid dog if there is doubt - this is considered like a mortal wound. And one desecrates the Sabbath for any wound that is caused by iron due to the force of the blow on any part of the body. There are those who are uncertain whether this applies only with force or even without force (the Gaon Rabbi Akiva Eiger), but it seems to me it is specifically with force, as the language of the Gemara (Avodah Zarah 28a) is: "This wound is dangerous, etc.," and Rashi explains it as a sword wound. And the Targum on 'wound for wound' translates: 'a wound for a wound,' and on the verse 'a maul, a sword, and a sharp arrow' in Proverbs (25), he translates: 'a wound and a sword and a maul,' which is a large hammer that strikes with force, and the Sages called it 'a wound,' indicating that it is with force. Similarly, for an abscess that comes at the opening of the anus - it is a danger and one desecrates the Sabbath for it, and for a fistula which is called "plonker" in the vernacular, and I do not know what this is, and for one with a very high fever, or with chills called "shviderin" where cold and heat come simultaneously - one desecrates the Sabbath. This excludes a common fever where the cold comes first and then the heat - there is no danger in this, and its law is like a sick person without danger. And similarly, one who is seized by blood - they let blood even by a Jew, for it is a danger, even if he walks on his feet and even on the first day, because of the danger. And if he is seized by blood in part and it is clear that it is just a minor discomfort - he is forbidden any treatment until the evening, unless the doctor says it is necessary. And know that a sick person lying in bed with a high fever - is considered a sick person with danger, as it is known that until the sweat breaks, he is in danger. And even afterwards until he rises from his bed, he is considered sick, and if it appears that his sweating is not yet complete - he is considered as having danger.

Even though it has been clarified that for a limb-threatening situation, one does not desecrate the Shabbat by performing a Torah prohibition through a Jew, nevertheless, if an eye has become inflamed—which means there is pain in both eyes or even in one eye, and there is pain in the eye, or tears are flowing due to the pain, or there is bleeding, or there is discharge, and it is at the beginning or middle stages of the illness—one desecrates the Shabbat for it. This is because the veins of the eye are connected to the heart, and it poses a danger to the heart. This excludes if all these symptoms are at the end stage of the illness, for then there is no danger due to these signs. Certainly, administering medicine to enhance vision is definitely forbidden on Shabbat. However, if a doctor says the situation is dangerous, it has already been clarified that one desecrates [the Shabbat].

If one has undergone bloodletting and has become chilled—it is a danger, and one may make a fire for him even in the summer season. Similarly, any sick person who has become chilled—it is a danger, and one may make a fire for him. However, if it is possible to do so through a non-Jew, it is better to do so through him, since there is no urgent need and it is not immediately necessary, unless the doctor says that warmth is needed immediately. In such a case, it is a mitzvah for a Jew to light the fire and not to wait until a non-Jew can be found. It has already been clarified that for a sick person who is not in danger, it is permitted to have cooking done by a non-Jew, but in the evening it is forbidden even for himself. Regarding the utensil in which the non-Jew cooked, some say it requires kashering, and some say it does not. One may rely on the lenient opinion, as our teacher the Rema ruled at the end of Yoreh De'ah section 113 that even the food itself is permissible after Shabbat, even for others, because cooking on Shabbat for a sick person has a distinct sign, and they did not decree against it. Although there is disagreement on this matter, in any case, the utensil is certainly not to be forbidden post facto for one who wishes to rely on the lenient opinion (see Magen Avraham section 17, who disagreed).

It is stated in the Gemara (108b): Wine inside the eye is prohibited, for it is evident that it is for medicinal purposes, as it tightens and opens (Rashi). On the surface of the eye, it is permitted, for people will say it is merely for washing (there). And this is specifically when one does not open and close [the eye], but if one opens and closes [the eye], it is prohibited, for it is evident that it is for medicinal purposes, and inside the eye, it is impossible not to tighten and open. And unsavory saliva—even on the surface [of the eye]—is prohibited, for it is a repulsive thing, and it is evident that it is for medicinal purposes. But if it is difficult for him to open his eyes, he may moisten them with unsavory saliva, for it is evident that he intends to open them (Taz, subsection 15), and not for medicinal purposes. Unsavory saliva is when one rises from his bed in the morning and has not yet tasted anything (see Magen Avraham, subsection 19). And regarding wine: nowadays, when it is not customary to wash with wine—it is prohibited (there), for it is evident that it is for medicinal purposes. Conversely, with water, when one rinses his mouth and then passes it over his eyes—it is permitted (there), for this is the common practice of many people always.

A person may soak a collyrium before Shabbat and place it on the eye, as it only appears as if he is washing, provided he does not open and close his eyes tightly, so it does not clearly appear to be for healing purposes, as a collyrium alone does not seem to be for healing. This is specifically when it is thin, but if the collyrium is thick, it appears as a remedy. And even though a thin one also somewhat appears as a remedy, nevertheless, they did not decree a prohibition in this case, and we do not worry about grinding herbs, since they only allowed soaking it from before Shabbat, which provides a distinction (this is how it seems to me to explain it). The main reason is that in their days even healthy people would do so for pleasure, and in Tosafot (Shabbat 18a, s.v. 'u-mitrapat') it is written that it refers specifically to a healthy person, but from Rashi (Shabbat 108b, s.v. 've-noten') it does not seem that way. It appears that for us it is certainly forbidden, as healthy people are not accustomed to this, and it is done only for healing.

One may remove the scabs that have formed on a wound on Shabbat and anoint it with oil, but not with fat, because fat melts and is considered creating a new substance (nolad). Even when the wound has healed to the point where there is no pain, and the anointing with oil is done purely for pleasure, it is still permitted, as anointing was never prohibited, as stated in Siman 327. This does not appear to be for medicinal purposes. Therefore, one should not apply a mixture of oil and hot water on it, as this clearly appears to be for healing purposes. It is also forbidden to place oil and water on a cloth due to the prohibition of squeezing (sechita), and even water alone is forbidden for this reason. However, applying oil alone, since the prohibition of squeezing only applies when one needs the liquid that comes out, as stated in Siman 320, is permitted to put on the cloth. The prohibition of applying hot water and oil is specifically on the wound itself, but it is permitted to apply it outside the wound so that it drips down onto the wound. It seems to me that according to our custom, where we do not anoint with oil on weekdays, it is forbidden to anoint the scabs of a wound with oil, as it is obvious that this is for healing purposes, as mentioned in the previous Siman, paragraph 2.

One may place a sponge and pieces of new dry cloth on a wound because they are not for healing but to prevent the clothes from scratching the wound. However, one may not use old cloths because they have a healing effect on the wound. A sponge, even if old, is permitted. It seems that a sponge is permitted even if it is of a type that absorbs water within it, as well as a wool sponge, as stated in the account of the death of Rabbi Chanina ben Teradyon: "They brought wool sponges and placed them on his heart."
