It is possible that wool sponges have the same status as cloth, and this requires further study. Regarding the prohibition of using old cloths, this applies only if they were never placed on the wound before. But if they were already on the wound, even if they are old, they are permitted because they no longer have a healing effect.

And one may place a leaf on a wound on Shabbat, because it does not heal but rather protects it from being irritated by his clothes, except for grape leaves which are for healing. Similarly, other leaves, if they are known to be for healing, are prohibited, and certainly it is forbidden to place a salve on the wound. Likewise, one may not place papyrus on the wound, because papyrus heals. And all of this concerns a typical wound that does not pose any danger and is not considered an illness. However, there are wounds that are dangerous according to the doctors, and if the danger is to the whole body, it is considered like a sick person in a life-threatening situation. And if there is a danger to a limb, it should be done by a non-Jew, and a rabbinic prohibition may be performed by oneself as explained, and all of this depends on the doctors' assessment.

If a bandage was placed on a wound before Shabbat, and the bandage is a piece of cloth that has been smeared with ointment for healing purposes and it fell off on Shabbat from its place, if it fell on the ground - it is forbidden to put it back. This is not due to the prohibition of healing, since it was on him before Shabbat, but rather the reason is because we decree that he might smear it when he sees that the smearing has deteriorated, and smearing is liable because of smoothing, as it is written in Siman 321. But if it fell on a vessel – he can put it back, because this is considered as if it slipped from its place, and it is certainly permitted to put it back in its place, as they only prohibited lifting it from the ground since it is considered as a new placement, as the original action has been removed and it is considered as placing it anew (Rashi Eruvin 102b), but not if it fell on a vessel, and he should be careful when putting it back not to tie it but to fasten it with a bow. And this permission of putting it back if it fell on a vessel is only if it fell by itself, but if he intentionally removed it – it is forbidden to put it back. Some disagree and permit it, and if he is in great pain – he may place it through a non-Jew even initially. And this is with a bandage made before Shabbat, but instructing a non-Jew to make a bandage on Shabbat, meaning to smear it on part of a garment which constitutes a complete rabbinic prohibition – is forbidden even if he is in pain, unless he is ill throughout his whole body from the wound, even though there is no danger – in any case, it is permitted to tell a non-Jew to make a bandage for him and place it on his wound or bruise, and similarly if there is danger to a limb.

A bandage that is placed on a wound from before Shabbat – on Shabbat, one may uncover part of the bandage and wipe the opening of the wound, and then return that part to its place and uncover another part, wipe there as well, and return it to its place. However, the bandage itself is forbidden to be wiped, because it constitutes smoothing (mimareach), and only the wound itself may be wiped. A wound that has healed – it is permitted to place a bandage on it that was prepared before Shabbat. There was no concern to prohibit this, because since it is not needed for healing but only for protection, we do not fear that one might come to the prohibition of grinding (shachikat samemanim). Not only is it forbidden to initially place a bandage on a wound that has not healed, but even ashes from a hearth, which are ordinary ashes, are forbidden to be placed on a wound because they heal. Only through a non-Jew was it permitted if one is in much pain and needs it. Know that in the Temple, it was permitted to initially place a bandage, because there is no rabbinic prohibition (shvut) in the Temple. (Mishnah Eruvin 102b, and there it states: "One may replace a bandage in the Temple," but in Rambam, Chapter 21, Halacha 27, it is written as I stated. Raavad objected, and the Maggid Mishneh wrote that it is a mistaken text. In my humble opinion, it is a correct text, as the meaning of "replacing" in the Mishnah is placing it initially, as Rashi explained there, that it is removed during the service and then placed again. Pay attention and understand.)

One who lances a boil on Shabbat in order to widen the opening of the wound, as doctors do when they intend to widen the opening for medical purposes, is liable for the prohibition of striking the final hammer blow (makeh b'patish), as this is the work of a doctor. Rashi explains (107a) that it is because of building an opening or repairing a vessel, but the Rambam wrote that it is due to striking the final hammer blow (makeh b'patish). However, if one lances it only to release its pus and does not mind if it immediately closes up again, this is permitted initially, as this is not considered completing a task at all. All the more so, according to those who hold that a task not needed for its own sake (melacha she’eina tzericha l’gufa) is exempt, although initially forbidden, in any case, it is permitted due to the suffering involved, and it is preferable to have it done by a non-Jew if possible (Magen Avraham, Siman 32). It is permitted to remove a thorn with a needle (Mishnah, Chapter 17), provided one takes care not to draw blood, to avoid creating a wound on Shabbat (ibid.).

People who have an aperture on their hands for medical purposes, meaning that it is always perforated and when the hole closes, they place legumes inside it to open it, there is a question if it is permitted to place the legumes inside the hole on Shabbat to open it, as the intention is that it should always remain open, and it is like creating an opening which is forbidden. However, there are those who say that since the hole was already there, it is permitted (ibid.). In my humble opinion, this is similar to removing phlegm, as the closure is due to the phlegm, and the legumes remove the phlegm and prevent it from accumulating. Despite this, it occasionally becomes closed again, so why is this not like lancing a boil to release phlegm? Placing a bandage on the aperture is like any other wound, where for healing it is forbidden, but for protection it is permitted (see Magen Avraham ibid. and scrutinize carefully). Releasing phlegm is permitted, and even though a little blood may come out with the phlegm, it is not blood absorbed by the body but blood from a wound that was already there (ibid. in the name of Sefer HaTerumot). If a piece of cloth is placed on the wound, it is permitted to replace it with another one if the first one becomes dirty (ibid.), provided there is no healing bandage on it. It is forbidden to scratch a boil on Shabbat until it bleeds, as this blood is from the body (ibid.) and not from a pre-existing wound. (See Magen Avraham ibid. who wrote that from the language of the Shulchan Aruch it implies that the obligation regarding lancing a boil to create an opening is even if there was already a hole and it is being expanded. Certainly, this is the opinion of the Rambam that the obligation is due to "striking with a hammer," but according to Rashi that the obligation is due to building or creating an opening, the obligation is only when it was sealed. This is also clarified from Rashi’s language in Shabbat 107. See there and scrutinize carefully).

If someone's hand or foot is injured, it may be soaked in wine to stop the bleeding, but not in vinegar because it is too strong and has medicinal properties. Certainly, it is forbidden to use strong alcoholic beverages or other sharp substances. If the person is delicate or sensitive, even wine is considered like vinegar for him and is prohibited. It is obvious that this applies when there is no danger from the injury, only general discomfort, and therefore medical treatment is not permitted on Shabbat. However, there are injuries in locations that are dangerous, such as an injury at the juncture of the tendons, and it is obvious that one is allowed to seek medical treatment according to the detailed laws that have been explained, and this depends on the doctor's directive as stated. If someone's hand or foot joint has been dislocated, meaning the bone has come out of the joint but there is no danger, he should not rub it excessively with cold water, which is its treatment, but should wash normally, and if it heals, it heals.

And know that this law is written by the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch in section 30, and in section 47 it is written: a bone that has dislocated, it is returned to its place. These two statements contradict each other. In truth, there are those who dispute this, for in the Gemara (148a), they only permitted it for a broken bone, not for one that has dislocated. This is the language of the Gemara: "The law is: a fracture may be set" (Magen Avraham 161). In my humble opinion, the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch are correct when we scrutinize why they altered the language of the Gemara. Certainly, it is because for a true fracture, the term "return" is not applicable, but rather "joining," as it is customary in the language of the poskim (decisors of Jewish law): "fracture to fracture they will join together," and the term "return" is only applicable to a bone that has dislocated. Indeed, these are two separate laws: certainly, returning it to its place is permitted, for how is it possible to leave it dislocated? And the matter of section 30 is a different issue: that one should not rub the area with water after it has been set back in place, and what does this have to do with the other? I have seen someone who differentiates between a bone that has completely dislocated and one that has only partially dislocated (Mishnah Berurah in the name of Sha'ar HaTziyun), but this is mere speculation, and it is clear as I have explained with the help of Heaven. It is surprising that Rambam omitted these two laws entirely, even though both are explicitly stated in the Mishnah and the Gemara there.

It appears to me that the reasoning of the Rambam is as follows: In the Mishna (147a), it is taught: "One does not set a broken bone, and if someone’s hand or foot is dislocated, one should not immerse it in cold water, etc." And in the Gemara, Shmuel says: 'The law is: One sets a broken bone.' In the case of a dislocated limb, Rav Avya also thought to say the opposite of our Mishna, and Rav Yosef told him that where it was stated, it was stated, etc. See there. We need to understand how Shmuel knew to rule against the Mishna, and Rashi explains that Shmuel believed it was taught that one sets the bone. This is difficult because, if so, he should have said in the language of 'it was taught' rather than 'the law is'. Additionally, it is difficult to understand why Rav Avya thought to contradict even the latter part of the Mishna. Therefore, in my humble opinion, the matter is as follows: Shmuel was known to be a physician, and he knew that according to the nature of the people of his generation, if they did not set the bone, it would be dangerous. Therefore, he says: the law is that one sets a broken bone, meaning that now it is a danger. Consequently, Rav Avya thought that the latter part of the ruling also changed according to the nature of the generations, and Rav Yosef told him that there is no proof, meaning that although Shmuel says that the matter of setting the bone has changed, there is no necessity that the matter of immersing in cold has changed; it could be that it has changed, or it could be that it has not changed, and there is no definitive ruling on the matter. Since Rambam saw that these laws depend on the nature of people, it is impossible to establish a fixed law, and it depends on the statement of the physicians. Perhaps Rambam himself was a physician and knew that sometimes there is danger in this, and it is necessary to use medical treatments, and thus he did not establish a firm rule and included it in what he wrote in Chapter 2: "If a physician says it is necessary – we desecrate [the Sabbath]." And it seems to me that even now they consider this a danger, and therefore if such a situation arises, God forbid, they should consult physicians and act according to their words.

One who removes a fingernail using a tool, such as a knife or any other instrument, is liable for a sin-offering, as this is considered a derivative of shearing. Using one's hand, which is considered an atypical manner, is exempt but still forbidden, as explained in the Gemara (94b) and by the Rambam in Chapter 9, and it will be further elucidated in Siman 300. Therefore, if a fingernail has partially detached and is causing discomfort, or if there are small pieces of skin around the nail causing discomfort: if most of it has not detached, it is not considered significant discomfort and is completely forbidden. Even if most has detached: if it is detached downward, it is not considered significant discomfort. However, if it is detached upward and causes significant discomfort, it is permitted to remove it entirely by hand. As for the definition of "upward," there is a dispute between Rashi and Rabbeinu Tam. Rashi explains "upward" as towards the tips of the fingers, where the detachment begins towards the nail, and it is called "upward" because they are above when the hand is raised. Rabbeinu Tam explains it in the opposite manner, as towards the body, which is called "upward" when the fingers are pointed downward. Therefore, due to the uncertainty of the two interpretations, one should not act at all, but rather bandage the finger and wait until night.

We learned in the Mishnah (111a): "One who feels pain in his teeth should not rinse them with vinegar, but he may dip [his food] as usual, and if he is healed, he is healed." The Gemara establishes: One should not rinse and spit out [the vinegar], but he may rinse and swallow, for if he spits it out, it is evident that it is for healing purposes (and it is difficult because if so, what is the Mishnah teaching us by saying he may dip as usual). And this is regarding minor discomfort, but if he is in great pain to the extent that his body is weakened from it, it has already been explained in section 22 that this is considered a danger (see there). (And see Tosafot there, s.v. "who wrote," who stated, "and the same applies..., and it is difficult to understand what is relevant about 'and the same applies,' since one might err that it only refers to dipping and not swallowing without dipping, and examine this well).

One who feels discomfort in their throat, merely as a mild ailment, should not gargle with oil, meaning to hold the oil in their mouth, as it is evident that this is being done for medicinal purposes. Even by means of anigron (a mixture of oil and water), as explained in Siman 282, it is forbidden for this reason. However, one may swallow the oil, and if they are healed, they are healed. There are those who prohibit this nowadays, since it is not the custom of healthy people to do so. Certainly, it is forbidden to tell a non-Jew to perform a medical treatment for them. Similarly, in the previous law concerning one who feels pain in their teeth, in the case of a mild ailment, it is not permitted to instruct a non-Jew.

The Tur wrote: "A person who groans from heart pain, whose remedy is to suck milk from an animal - it is permissible to suck from it on Shabbat. However, if he is in distress due to hunger - it is forbidden on Shabbat and permissible on Yom Tov." And in Ketubot (60a), the reason is explained: because sucking is considered an unusual way of extracting, and in a situation of distress, the Rabbis did not issue a decree. And in Yevamot (114a), it is said that due to distress, it was only permitted on Yom Tov and not on Shabbat. The Rif dismissed the statement in Yevamot in favor of the one in Ketubot. The Tosafot distinguished that in Ketubot, it refers to the distress of illness, which is permitted even on Shabbat, whereas in Yevamot, it refers to the distress of hunger, which is only permitted on Yom Tov. This is the opinion of the Tur. 

Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 33: "A person who groans - it is permissible to suck milk from an animal because in a situation of distress, the Rabbis did not issue a decree. Some say that if he only has the distress of hunger - it is forbidden to suck from the animal on Shabbat." 

The explanation of his words: The first opinion is that of the Rif, who believes that since the Rif does not differentiate between the distress of illness and the distress of hunger, it implies that they are the same, and it is also permissible on Shabbat even for the distress of hunger. The Gemara, which mentions a person who groans, speaks in a common manner, as the person who groans specifically needs milk, but hunger can be satisfied by eating or drinking other foods and beverages, and it is uncommon for one to need specifically milk. However, if this does happen, it is permitted. 

He then brings the opinion of "some say," which is the opinion of the Tosafot and the Tur. (This resolves the question of the Magen Avraham in section 39, and what the Ramban wrote that for the sake of desire, it is not permitted, as he criticized the Maor who permitted it for the sake of desire. See there and analyze well.)

A woman should not express milk from her breasts into a cup or a pot and then nurse her child because why should she commit a prohibition for something that is not necessary for the child, as he can nurse directly from her breasts like all other infants. However, there are some infants who will not latch onto the breast until a little milk is expressed onto it – this is permitted, as it is necessary for the child so that he will latch on and nurse. Similarly, if doctors have instructed her to express milk from her breasts for a patient who is in a life-threatening situation – this is also permitted. But for a patient who is not in a life-threatening situation – it is forbidden, as this is a Torah prohibition of "extracting." Certainly, it is forbidden to express her milk for someone who has been affected by an evil spirit, as there is no danger in this. There are those who say that in a case of great distress – it is permitted, because this is a labor that is not needed for its own sake (Magen Avraham, Siman 141). However, I am puzzled, for according to Rambam, one is liable for a labor that is not needed for its own sake, and we have never heard of this being done, and it should not be done.

One should not chew "metzachei," which is an insect from which tar is made, and no healthy person chews it, and it is evident to all that it is for medicinal purposes. Nor should one rub it on the teeth for medicinal purposes. However, if one does this for bad breath, it is permitted, since it is not for medicinal purposes. And even though it is possible that someone who does not know that he has bad breath might suspect him of doing it for medicinal purposes, nevertheless, it is impossible to prevent him from doing something necessary for him to be among people, due to baseless suspicion.

All foods that healthy people eat and all beverages that healthy people drink—those with minor ailments are permitted to eat and drink them for medicinal purposes. There is no concern of violating the prohibition of grinding medicinal ingredients, since it is food for healthy people. Moreover, even if these are items that are beneficial for some conditions and harmful for others, such as spleen which is good for teeth but bad for intestines, and leeks which are bad for teeth but good for intestines (Berakhot 44b), it is still permitted to eat them even if it is evident that one is eating them for medicinal purposes, because ultimately, healthy people do eat them. Know that in Berakhot (38a), it is explicitly understood that if one intends to eat for medicinal purposes, it is forbidden, as it says there regarding the principle that one may eat any food for medicinal purposes: "The individual intends to eat, and healing happens incidentally." See there. And Rambam in Chapter 21, Law 22 wrote: "A person may eat... and eat them to be healed by them—it is permitted." See there, and it implies that even if the primary intention is for healing. Similarly, the language of the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, Section 37, which states: "It is permitted to eat and drink them for medicinal purposes," implies that the primary intention is for healing, and this requires further study.

And anything that is not food or drink for healthy people - it is forbidden to eat or drink it for medicinal purposes, even if it is sweet to the palate. In any case, since healthy people do not eat this, it is evident that it is for medicinal purposes. Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 37: "This applies only to someone who has a minor ailment and strengthens himself and goes about as if he is healthy, but if he has no ailment at all - it is permitted," end quote. This means that if he is completely healthy and wants to eat them - it is permitted. The reason must be that it is impossible to forbid him because of what onlookers might think, since he is healthy, who can object to him. But the wording of the Tur is: "But if he eats and drinks it because he is hungry or thirsty and has no illness - it is permitted," end quote. This implies that it is only allowed if he is hungry or thirsty, but otherwise - it is forbidden. Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, holds that this is the normal practice. However, one of the great later authorities explained that it is specifically this way, and he brought several proofs that it is specifically for hunger or thirst, but otherwise - even for a healthy person, it is forbidden (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 143), and this also seems to be the ruling. It appears to me that there is no disagreement here, and our teacher, the Beit Yosef, also means this: for a healthy person, it is permitted to eat them in general, meaning that he wants to eat them and is not eating them explicitly for medicinal purposes, that is to strengthen his powers more. But for someone with an ailment, even in these cases, it is forbidden.

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote about this: "And similarly, if he fell ill and is bedridden, it is permissible." End quote. The explanation of his words: A sick person who is bedridden but not in danger is permitted to have a "Shvut" (a rabbinic prohibition) of telling a non-Jew to do work for him. There is a dispute about whether a Jew can perform a rabbinic prohibition directly for him, as stated in section 17. However, regarding eating things that healthy people do not eat but are good for consumption, it is certainly allowed according to all opinions, as it is not worse than telling a non-Jew. We do not decree against this due to the grinding of herbs (a rabbinic prohibition), because since we forbid him or others to do any act involving a rabbinic prohibition, there is a noticeable difference, and eating is not similar to work and is more similar to telling a non-Jew. (And this is the intention of the Beit Yosef as brought by the Taz in section 25, and the words of the Taz are not understood at all. And what the Magen Avraham wrote in section 44 that even another Jew is permitted to do for him, etc., his intention is that since there are opinions in section 17 that even a real act is permissible, all the more so that eating is allowed. And although there are those who disagree regarding actions, nevertheless, regarding eating, all agree. The Maharshal struggled with his intention, and the Primagadim remained with a question, as stated there, and his intention is as I have written, and consider this carefully.)

It is permitted to eat sweet sap and to swallow a raw egg to enhance the voice, even though it is not customary to eat them this way. Nevertheless, since this is not for healing a sick person, but rather for enhancing the voice, it is considered a Shabbat delight and is permitted. However, making beaten egg yolks with sugar is forbidden to beat them on Shabbat, just as it is forbidden to beat honey with mustard and wine with rue as mentioned in Siman 321, section 22. Additionally, this has the appearance of a weekday activity. If one needs this, they should prepare it before Shabbat, and on Shabbat, they should stir it lightly with a spoon, as mentioned there.

It is prohibited to induce vomiting on Shabbat, which involves taking some substance to vomit the food in order to eat more. Even on a weekday, it is forbidden to do so in this manner due to the waste of food. However, if one is suffering from overeating on a weekday, it is permitted even with a substance. On Shabbat, it is forbidden with a substance because it is taken for medicinal purposes, which is prohibited. By hand, however, it is permitted, meaning that one can place their hand deep into the throat to induce vomiting, as it does not involve any substance and there is no decree against grinding herbs.

For someone who has abdominal pain, it is permitted to place a cup from which hot water was poured over it, even though there is still some steam. Even though this provides relief, it is not considered a medicinal act that would warrant a decree against grinding herbs. This is all when there is no concern of illness, but if there is concern of illness, one should follow the regulations discussed earlier.

Similarly, if someone is intoxicated and their remedy is to rub their hands and feet with oil, it is permitted to do so on Shabbat. Reducing intoxication is not considered a medicinal act, and people do not usually use ground herbs for this purpose. (See Taz, section 27, who prohibits placing crushed herb ash into the nose of an intoxicated person because it is considered a medicinal act and there is a decree against grinding herbs. However, tobacco, which everyone smells, is permitted.)

One should not engage in physical exercise, that is, pressing on the body with force to the point of fatigue and sweating. According to the Rambam, if one does not intend to sweat, it is permitted, for the prohibition is due to sweating, which serves as a remedy for most ailments, and sweating is induced by medicinal substances. Therefore, all forms of sweating are prohibited, even those not induced by medicinal substances (Taz, subsection 28). It is forbidden to press a baby's stomach to induce a bowel movement, lest one come to administer laxative substances. All of this applies where there is no illness, but in the case of illness, the specific laws have already been clarified above.

It is permissible to place a cup of warm water on the navel and elevate it, which is called heyiv motar. Similarly, it is permissible to elevate the ears, whether by hand or with an instrument, meaning the veins of the ears, which sometimes descend and cause the ears to dislocate (Rashi on Avodah Zarah 28b). Rashi explains there that this poses a danger, but from the words of the Rambam in Chapter 21, Law 31, where he writes: "It is also permissible to elevate the ears... since they do not use medicinal substances to be concerned with grinding," it implies that if it were a danger, it would also be permissible to desecrate Shabbat. In the Jerusalem Talmud (Chapter 14, Law 4), it is considered among the matters of danger, and similarly, it is explained in the Midrash Ha'azinu: "A person who feels pain in his ear... and this is an ear wound, if it is dangerous - one may treat it on Shabbat."

It appears to me that Rashi and the Rambam do not disagree in practice, but rather in the interpretation of the term "raising the ears." Rashi explains it as the tendons of the ears, which sometimes descend and cause the cheeks to dislocate, necessitating lifting them. This involves a Torah prohibition of construction. The Jerusalem Talmud calls it "daughters of the ears," meaning that the tendons are secondary to the ears, which involves danger, and thus, the Sabbath may be desecrated for it. However, the Rambam explains that the ears themselves have slightly loosened, and tightening them does not involve the prohibition of construction. This is what the Midrash says: "If it is a danger," meaning that if the tendons have descended, it is dangerous. But if it is the ears themselves, there is no danger, and no medicinal procedures are performed. Similarly, it is permitted to lift the "unkali," which is the lobe opposite the heart that obstructs breathing when bent inward. These do not involve the use of remedies that might lead to grinding, and they cause discomfort. Therefore, they permitted it, for otherwise, we would need to prohibit it even though there is no labor involved; nevertheless, it would be considered a weekday activity.

Rambam writes in Chapter 21, Law 21: "How so? One should not eat things that are not food for healthy people, such as Greek hyssop and madder root, nor things that induce diarrhea, such as wormwood and similar items. Likewise, one should not drink things that healthy people do not typically drink, such as water in which herbs and plants have been boiled. One may eat foods and drinks that healthy people typically consume, such as coriander, hops, hyssop, etc., and one can drink Egyptian olives anywhere." And in Law 29 he writes: "One should not bathe in water that induces diarrhea, nor in mud in which one sinks, nor in foul-smelling soaking water, nor in the Sea of Sodom, nor in the bad waters of the Great Sea, as all these cause discomfort, and it is written: 'And you shall call the Sabbath a delight.' Therefore, if one did not linger in them but ascended immediately, even if he has sores on his head - it is permitted." End quote. And before this, he wrote that it is forbidden to stand on the Demusit ground in the Land of Israel, because it causes fatigue and heals, end quote. There are many things we do not know, but from this we can learn about things known to us. The reason it is not forbidden to not linger in bad waters is that it appears as if he is cooling off. And one may bathe in the waters of Gerar, the waters of Hamat, the waters of Tiberias, and the good waters of the Great Sea, even though they are salty, because it is common to bathe in them and there is no indication that it is for healing purposes. And one may chant incantations over snakes and scorpions so that they do not harm, and there is no issue of trapping, as it is merely an incantation.

One may place a vessel over the eye to cool it, provided it is a vessel that may be handled on Shabbat, for this is a remedy for one who has eye pain and this remedy involves no medicinal substances, therefore it is permitted. Similarly, one may surround the eye with a ring to prevent swelling, and it is also permitted to press a wound with a knife to prevent it from spreading, because in these cases there is no concern of grinding medicinal substances.

It is forbidden to place a garment on a wound from which blood is oozing, because the blood will dye the garment. Even though this spoils the garment, it is nevertheless prohibited by rabbinic decree. All the more so if the garment is red, as it does not spoil it. Therefore, one must first wash the wound with water or wine to clean the blood, and only then place the garment or the rag prepared before Shabbat on it. Some say to wrap spider webs, which are called 'savetina', on the wound, covering all the blood and the entire injury, and then wrap a rag over it, so that it will not be stained by the blood. This is only when the web is prepared, for if not, it is considered muktzeh (an item prohibited to be moved on Shabbat). It is forbidden to press on the wound with one's hands, because pressing will cause blood to flow, and one is liable for extracting (blood). Therefore, one should not bandage it tightly for this reason. All the more so, it is forbidden to apply leeches on Shabbat, unless in a case of life-threatening illness, and certainly to perform bloodletting.

It is forbidden to place a wick in the anus, which is called a "crystir," as is customary for someone who is constipated, because this is considered a form of healing. However, it may be done with a change, by holding it with two fingers and placing it gently. It is obvious that the wick must be prepared before Shabbat. Certainly, it is forbidden to perform "crystir" with a tool called a "canna," as this is close to a Torah prohibition, and therefore it should only be done for someone who is in danger. A simple "crystir" can be done with a change, as mentioned. Note that some forbid placing spider webs on a cut because it heals. In my humble opinion, it does not heal but rather stops the bleeding, and I do not know if this is called healing, since the bleeding from a cut is not life-threatening but merely unpleasant. The spider webs stop the bleeding, but the webs are muktzeh (set aside, and thus forbidden to move on Shabbat). Through a non-Jew, it seems to me that it is permitted, meaning that the non-Jew should take the web and place it on the bleeding area.

It has already been explained that any situation involving danger to life overrides Shabbat, and one who acts swiftly is praiseworthy. Therefore, the Sages said (Yoma 84:): "One extinguishes and creates barriers in the face of a fire." This means that if a fire breaks out in a courtyard where there is a potential danger to lives, such as if there is a sick person or children there, and due to the panic, it would be very difficult to remove them without harm, and perhaps bodily harm might befall them, it is permitted to extinguish the fire. Additionally, it is permitted to bring vessels filled with water through a public domain to create barriers against the fire (Tosafot there). It is also permitted to do both acts, extinguishing and creating barriers, if there is doubt that one action alone might not suffice (this seems to me). Moreover, even if the fire is in another courtyard, but there is a concern that it might spread to this courtyard, and in this courtyard, there is a sick person or children as mentioned, it is permissible to extinguish and create barriers as mentioned. Even if it is possible to remove the sick person and the child, but the removal would be through a public domain, it is better to extinguish the fire, as this is a labor that is not needed for its own sake and is exempt according to most authorities from the Torah, rather than removing them through a public domain which is a primary category of labor (Magen Avraham 1). In a case of removal to a karmelit (an area that is neither private nor public domain), the prohibition is equal as both are rabbinic prohibitions, and only according to the Rambam who rules that labor not needed for its own sake is liable, extinguishing would be a Torah prohibition.

Maimonides wrote in Chapter 2, Law 20: "If there is a courtyard with both non-Jews and Jews, even if there is one Jew and a thousand non-Jews, and a collapse occurs, we clear away the debris for everyone because of the Jew. If one of them moved to another courtyard and a collapse occurred there, we clear the debris because perhaps the one who moved was the Jew. If all of them left this courtyard to go to another courtyard, and during their departure one of them moved to another courtyard and a collapse occurred there, and it is not known who it is, we do not clear the debris. Since they all left, there is no Jew here, and anyone who leaves the group while they are walking is assumed to have left from the majority. Therefore, if the majority were Jews, even if they all left, and one of them moved to another courtyard and a collapse occurred there, we clear the debris." End of quote.

The explanation of his words: The principle that we do not follow the majority in matters of saving lives applies only when the situation is fixed, and this is also true for all prohibitions; anything fixed is considered as if it is half and half. Even if one separated from the fixed group and the doubt arose regarding the one who already separated, as in the case of nine stores where we rule that if found, we follow the majority, here we do not clear the debris. However, if they all left this courtyard to disperse each to his own place, and during their walking one separated and came to his place in another courtyard and a collapse occurred there, we do not clear the debris, because since the fixed group has completely disbanded, we follow the majority. Nevertheless, if the majority were Jews, even if they all left, we clear the debris. It is not necessarily the majority; the same would apply if it were half and half, as I wrote in Chapter 15 of the Laws of Forbidden Relations. However, since this law is not discussed here, the language of majority and minority is used (this is how it seems to me to explain, and this is also implied by the Maggid Mishneh. This is also implied in his response to the sages of Lunel, cited by the Kesef Mishneh. The difficulty raised by the Lechem Mishneh regarding the foundlings in Chapter 15 of the Laws of Forbidden Relations has already been explained by us in Even HaEzer, Chapter 4, Section 55. See there and pay attention).

According to Rashi and Tosafot in Yoma (84b), if everyone leaves this courtyard, and one of them separates and enters another courtyard and a collapse falls upon him, we clear the debris, because since among those who have separated there is an established presence of a Jew, we do not follow the majority even when they have separated, unlike in all other prohibitions. However, if only some of them have left this courtyard, and one of those who separated enters another courtyard and a collapse falls upon him, we do not clear the debris, since a Jew has not been established among those who separated, unless most or half of them have separated, in which case we say that it is as if a Jew has been established among those who separated, and we follow the majority. And half and half is considered like a majority regarding the saving of a life, and this is also explained by Raavad and Ramban as Maimonides has written there.

And the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch in paragraph 2 wrote like the Rambam, and I am astonished at our master, the Beit Yosef, who began with the phrase "we do not follow the majority in matters of saving a life," see there, for this is not a general rule as has been explained, and in truth, neither the Rambam nor the Tur began with this phrase. And in his responsa, the Rambam clarified that we do not hold like the one who says "we do not follow the majority in matters of saving a life" (see Kesef Mishneh who holds that in this, there is a dispute between Shmuel and Rabbi Yehudah, and the law follows Rabbi Yehudah).

And it appears to me that the reason for this law is that the majority is from the Torah, but the Torah said: "And you shall live by them and not die by them," so that no situation should lead to the death of a Jew (Tosafot Yoma 85a). And against this, it is impossible to nullify the Torah's law that we follow the majority. Therefore, the Sages said that as long as the majority remains in place, or due to the principle of "established" (kavua), which is considered as half and half, and half and half is certainly like the majority because of the verse "and you shall live by them," then everything that deviates from this majority or from this established status - it all has the law of the majority, even though for other laws it is not so, and for this reason, the verse "and you shall live by them" applies. Therefore, when a part of them is separated - we act to save a life, but when this majority or established status is nullified, such as if all separate - its law is like all the Torah where we follow the majority, and this is according to the opinion of the Rambam (Maimonides), the Tur, and the Shulchan Aruch. According to Rashi and his supporters, the reasoning is this: as long as the majority or the established status remains as one, meaning if all separate, the previous status is not yet nullified, and we do not follow the current majority but the previous established status, and for this, the verse "and you shall live by them" applies. But when their status is divided, meaning some separate and some remain established - the previous status is nullified and we follow the current majority, and we do not act to save a life. If they all were uprooted, meaning one after the other, if they were all uprooted at once, this is also considered established (Magen Avraham 3). However, it can also be that if they were uprooted at once and dispersed here and there, the established status is nullified, as known in the laws of "established" in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 110. (Therefore, if a child is found in a city where the majority are non-Jews - we do not violate the Sabbath, because since every day people separate here and there, it was never established, as the Magen Avraham 2 states).

And just as we do not follow the majority in matters of saving a life in various situations, as mentioned, likewise we do not follow the principle of double doubt (safek sefeka), even if there are three or more doubts. Therefore, if a person is buried under a collapsed building, whether they are alive or dead is uncertain, and it is further uncertain whether there is a person there at all or not, and even if it is assumed that there is someone there, it is uncertain whether they are a non-Jew or a Jew – nonetheless, we clear away the debris and desecrate the Sabbath for them, as it is said, "And live by them," so that one should not come to die in any manner, as mentioned. However, for someone who is sentenced to death or a burglar tunneling in, we do not clear away the debris, as such a person is considered already dead (as stated in section 4).

When they dismantle a heap of debris and find someone alive, they continue to remove the debris until they can extract the person and provide all necessary medical care without any delay, as is the law concerning the saving of a life. If they find the person dead, they stop removing debris and do not move the body until evening. If they find the person crushed, such that they can only live for a few hours if the debris is removed, otherwise they will die immediately, we are concerned for the short-term life and continue to remove debris. This too is included in the principle of "and live by them." 

And what is said in Avodah Zarah (27b) that we are not concerned for short-term life refers to a situation where seeking treatment has a risk that it might hasten death. However, the matter is as follows: we are concerned for the person's benefit in both scenarios. Here, we are concerned that they might live a few more hours, and there we are concerned for their benefit to receive treatment, which might completely heal them. And if one argues that the treatment could also shorten their life by a few hours, since they will die either way, we do not worry about the hours. It is better to endure this uncertainty for the other possibility that they might be completely healed, because without the treatment they would certainly die, as explained there (Tosafot).

And how is this done: When they find him crushed, they check up to his nose, and if they do not feel life in his nose, then he is certainly dead. There is no difference whether they encountered his head first or his legs first, for in all cases, the examination to determine if he is alive or dead is only at the nose, as it is written: "All in whose nostrils was the breath of the spirit of life" (Gemara there). And if the rubble fell on many people, they uncover until they find all of them. Even if they found the upper ones dead, they should not say that certainly the lower ones are also dead and why should we desecrate the Sabbath—it is forbidden to say so, because it is possible that the upper ones died and the lower ones are alive, and such an incident indeed occurred (there).

Robbers who besiege Jewish homes: if they come for the purpose of stealing money - one does not desecrate the Sabbath because of them, as it is forbidden to desecrate the Sabbath for the sake of money alone. But if they come with the intention of killing and destroying, or even if they come without clear intention and it is unknown why they came, it is also considered as if they definitely came with the intention to kill, because ordinary robbers are typically killers - one goes out against them with weapons and desecrates the Sabbath because of them. And in ancient times, when the Holy Temple was standing, if they came to a city on the border, even if they came only for the sake of straw and hay - one desecrates the Sabbath because of them (Eruvin 45a), for such a city, if it is captured, it is easy to capture the entire land (Rashi). And even if they have not actually come yet but are preparing to come - it is considered a potential life-threatening situation and one desecrates the Sabbath because of it.

There are those who say that nowadays, if bandits come even just for monetary matters, one may desecrate the Sabbath because it is well-known that many people will not stand by and let their money be taken. They will resist, and it is known that if bandits are not allowed to rob and plunder, they will kill. Thus, it becomes a matter of life and death. Therefore, when they come to an individual, he is obligated to allow them to take the money and not desecrate the Sabbath, and the Holy One, blessed be He, is trusted to repay him manifold. This all depends on the situation. And know that this law cannot apply in a city where there are government authorities, for the world is not lawless, but it can apply in a village.

One who sees a ship in distress during the day with people on board, or a river that is flooding and could sweep away people, or an individual being pursued by bandits—it is a mitzvah for every person to desecrate the Sabbath to save them. And earlier at the end of Siman 306, it was explained whether one desecrates the Sabbath for someone who is being coerced; see there. And it was taught in Eruvin (45b): "All who go out to save may return to their place." This means that the law is that one who goes beyond the techum (Sabbath boundary) has only four cubits, but when they go out to save people, they are permitted to return to their place even from outside the techum. And some do not permit this, but rather allow them two thousand cubits in every direction, and this matter will be explained in Siman 407 with the help of Heaven.

And know that any doubt concerning life-threatening situations overrides the Sabbath, such as needing to bring medicine from a distant place for a patient whose life is in danger, even if there is doubt whether the medicine is available there and also doubt whether it will heal - the Sabbath is violated. However, it is possible that if there is doubt whether it will heal, the Sabbath is not violated, and this seems to be indicated from the Mishnah in Yoma (chapter 3), which states that only when the medicine is certain do we violate the Sabbath. And even though there are several doubts in this matter, nevertheless, since the medicine is certain, the Torah commands us to violate the Sabbath, but not in a case where the medicine itself is not certain. See there.

The Rambam wrote in Chapter 2, Law 11: "A woman in labor, as she crouches to give birth, is considered in mortal danger, and one may desecrate the Sabbath for her. We call a midwife for her from place to place, cut the umbilical cord, and tie it. If she needs a candle while she cries out in her labor pains, we light a candle for her, even if she is blind, because her mind is calmed by the candle even though she cannot see. If she needs oil or similar things, we bring them to her, and whenever it is possible to make a change, we change the way we bring them, such as if her friend brings her a vessel hanging in her hair. If it is not possible, we bring it in the normal manner." End of quote.

Explanation of his words: Even though for any sick person who is in danger we do not require conditions if they need a candle, as Maimonides himself wrote at the beginning of chapter 2, where he wrote: "and we light a candle for him and extinguish a candle for him," without writing "if needed," and he also did not write there that if possible to make a change, we should change. The matter is as follows: Even though when a woman is about to give birth she is in a dangerous situation, nevertheless, it is not similar to a typical sick person in danger because this is the nature of the world and the essence of creation, and we are not afraid of it. She also is not afraid, and most women endure the labor pains with peace of mind, knowing that they will pass soon, as she saw in her mother. Therefore, indeed before the birth, there is generally no desecration of Shabbat for most women. And for this reason, Maimonides says: "if she needs a candle," and this is also the language of the Gemara (128b), meaning when we see that she is more fearful and worried than other women, then it is necessary to light a candle for her even if she is blind, so that she will feel secure that people are looking after her and doing all that she needs, because otherwise, the fear itself could harm her. Therefore, also when bringing oil, if it is possible to do so in an unusual manner, we do so, since in truth it is only necessary because of her fear. And why did he not write also: "extinguish the candle for her" as with a sick person? Because with a sick person, sometimes they need to sleep and the light will disturb them, whereas with a woman in labor, it is not a time for sleep, and there is never a need to extinguish the candle for her. However, if a situation arises where she needs it, we do it. The Tur and Shulchan Aruch wrote simply: "we light a candle for her," which is not the language of the Talmud, but their intention is the same as written (and according to what is written, the two questions of the Magen Avraham in section 2 are answered, see there and consider well).

Pious and righteous individuals, when a woman reaches her ninth month [of pregnancy], prepare everything necessary on the eve of Shabbat, as perhaps she will go into labor on Shabbat, so that they will not need to desecrate Shabbat (as mentioned there, subsection 1, in the name of the Sefer Chasidim). And for an Egyptian woman, they do not assist her in childbirth on Shabbat, even in matters that do not involve Shabbat desecration, and they call her Egyptian companion to do what is necessary for her (see Magen Avraham subsections 5 and 6, and it is impossible to explain further on this matter).

And from when is a woman considered to be in labor such that it is permitted to desecrate Shabbat for her needs? From the time she sits on the birthing stool, meaning when she is seized by labor pains and contractions, or from the time blood begins to flow and drip from her, or from the time her companions support her in their arms because she lacks the strength to walk. Once one of these things appears, it is permitted to desecrate Shabbat for her needs. This applies to other matters, such that if she needs something, we can do it immediately. However, to call the midwife, it is permitted even before these times; rather, from the moment she feels some discomfort, it is permitted to call her even from outside the Shabbat boundary, for if she needs her, we will not be able to obtain her immediately (Taz, section 2).

After childbirth, a woman is considered in complete danger for up to three days, and it is obligatory to do for her everything that is done on a weekday without any delay and with urgency, and by prominent Jews, as explained in Siman 328 regarding a sick person who is in danger. We cook for her what she needs, heat water for her, and clean her just as on a weekday, and we do not ask either a doctor or the woman who gave birth. Even if she says she does not need to desecrate the Sabbath for her – we do not listen to her and desecrate it, and similarly, if the doctor says she does not need – we do not heed his words, and he is considered an unskilled doctor. The sages decreed that during the first three days, the woman who gave birth is considered in danger, and we desecrate the Sabbath for her. This is the opinion of the Sheiltot, and it also appears from the Rambam who wrote: "Whether she says she needs or she says she does not need," and this is also the language of the Talmud. Since we do not listen to her, the same applies that we do not listen to the doctor or anyone who says she does not need. However, the Ramban disagrees with this and holds that if the doctor and the midwife say she does not need, and she herself also says so – we do not desecrate the Sabbath, because there are many women who do not need hot water and are satisfied with cold. But if one of them says she needs or women beside her say she needs – we do not pay attention to those who say she does not need and we desecrate the Sabbath for her, even if we see that she eats like other people, as they say she does not feel it at the moment (Magen Avraham, subsection 8). In practice, it seems that it is forbidden to be stringent in this matter, and if we see even some suspicion that she needs – we desecrate the Sabbath for her with urgency (see Rashi 129, s.v. "whether" and examine well).

And from the third to the seventh day, it is stated in the Gemara (129a): "If she says, 'I need [it],' we desecrate [the Sabbath for her]; if she says, 'I do not need [it],' we do not desecrate [the Sabbath]." And in a general sense, Rambam and the Tur wrote that we desecrate [the Sabbath] for her, for she is still considered a dangerously ill person, especially if a doctor says she needs [it]. There are those who wrote that if her companions say she needs [it], it is meaningless if she herself says she does not need [it] (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 9), but I have seen someone who disagreed with this (the GRaYBi). And it seems to me that women are more knowledgeable in this matter, and even if it is only a doubt, it is forbidden to be stringent in a case of potential danger to life. 

From the seventh to the thirtieth day, her status is like a sick person who is not in danger, and we do not desecrate the Sabbath for her unless she develops an illness, in which case her status is like any other illness. Some women are weak to the extent that their danger persists for a long time, and this depends either on herself or on the doctor, as the law was explained in Siman 328.

It is obvious that the three, seven, and thirty days are counted from the time of birth and not from when she sits on the birthing stool, as the Rambam wrote there, and this is his language: "A birthing woman, from the time the blood begins to flow until she gives birth, and after she gives birth until three days - we desecrate etc.” end quote. And I have seen someone who wishes to say that this is its interpretation: that it refers to what was mentioned earlier, and this is from the time the blood begins to flow until three days after she gives birth from the flow of blood (M.B.). It is forbidden to say so and to be stringent regarding the saving of a life (and so wrote the Lechem Mishneh), and it is also explicit in the Ra'avad at the end of chapter 18, and this is his language: "From the time she sits on the birthing stool and the blood begins to flow until all three days after she gave birth etc.” end quote. And what the Rambam wrote in his commentary on the Mishnah, and this is his language: "But we do not begin to desecrate the Sabbath until she sits on the birthing stool and the blood begins to flow, and from that time until the completion of three days we desecrate etc.” end quote, also means this: until the completion of three days after the birth, because if he intended from that time for three days, what is this language 'until the completion', and he should have said from that time for three days, but certainly as I have written, and because it is an obvious matter he did not feel the need to explain this, and on the contrary he wrote it to indicate that the three days are in addition to the time before the birth from the time of the birthing stool.

If a woman is in labor and dies, one brings a knife on Shabbat, even through a public domain, and cuts open her belly to remove the fetus, as it may be found alive. Even though the fetus does not yet have a presumption of life, they desecrate Shabbat for it even on the chance it might be alive. Some say this applies specifically to a woman in labor, as the fetus has already been dislodged, and thus there is a possibility it is alive. But if she dies before this, they do not desecrate Shabbat since the fetus is certainly already dead. Others say there is no distinction (see Magen Avraham section 10 for both opinions).

However, in practice for us, there is no difference in this regard, as even on a weekday we do not do this, because we are not knowledgeable about the exact moment of the mother’s death close to her actual passing. The certainty of death for us extends for a long time after she has already truly died, and therefore the fetus would already be dead. Among us, the custom for any pregnant woman who dies is to make every effort to extract the fetus from her. We do not know the reason for this practice, and the common people hold this as a necessity.

We make a bonfire for a woman who has given birth for the entire 30 days, even during the summer season. This is the language of our master, the Beit Yosef, in section 6. However, the language of the Gemara there is: "We make a bonfire for a woman who has given birth on Shabbat, etc." And also in the Rambam there, it is written similarly: "We make a bonfire for a woman who has given birth, even during the summer, because the cold is very difficult for her in cold places. But we do not make a bonfire for a sick person to warm up, etc." This is the conclusion of his words. The Tur wrote: "We make a bonfire for a woman who has given birth or for another sick person… even during the summer." This is his conclusion. And even though in the Gemara it does not mention 30 days, nevertheless, it is clear to our master, the Beit Yosef, that it is 30 days, because for the entire 30 days she is called a woman who has given birth. If not, what would be the reason? And so the Maggid Mishneh wrote in the name of the Raavad there. And it is obvious that the intention is even through a Jew, because regarding cold, she is considered in danger for the entire 30 days. If it were through a non-Jew, what would be the reason? For any sick person who is not in danger, one tells a non-Jew and he does it. And although one might say that it comes to teach us that it is permitted through a non-Jew, and we do not say that it is possible to wrap her in clothes and she will be warm, and we do not permit it even through a non-Jew, this is not reasonable at all. For this is an obvious matter that for a sick person who is not in danger, anything that appears to be good for him is permitted through a non-Jew. And that which the Rambam wrote: "because the cold is difficult for her in cold places," does not mean that it is only permitted in cold places, for the Talmud permits even during the summer. Rather, he was telling the truth that in cold places, the cold is very difficult for her, as can be seen clearly. Therefore, when she becomes cold in any place and at any time, it is permitted to desecrate Shabbat for her, since we see that the cold is very difficult for her. (And he did not use the expression "summer season" because in the Gemara it refers to bloodletting, and regarding a woman who has given birth, they used the term "during the summer," and for bloodletting, the term "summer season" is used. The Tur did not concern himself with this because it is all the same).

In the dispute between the Tur and the Rambam regarding a sick person, the Rambam prohibits making a fire for a sick person, reasoning that quilts and pillows are sufficient. However, for a woman who has just given birth, due to her weakness, this would not be tolerable. The Tur permits it even for a sick person, which is also the opinion of the Rif and the Rosh. This disagreement hinges on the Talmudic discussion there and variant texts, as explained by the Maggid Mishneh and the Beit Yosef. Our master, the Beit Yosef, did not mention this at all; in section 328, he only wrote: "If one has bloodletting and becomes chilled, one may make a fire for him," and not for a sick person, because he leans towards the Tur's view and did not want to rule against the Rambam. Therefore, he omitted this issue. Additionally, in his main work, he writes that this law is unclear: whether it applies to a sick person in danger or not in danger. Therefore, he did not mention it at all.

As for the practical law: it seems that this should be done by a non-Jew. And if a fire was made for a woman who has just given birth or a sick person, whether healthy individuals may warm themselves by it is explained in section 276, where it is permitted. When it is very cold, one may initially tell a non-Jew to light the oven on Shabbat, because everyone is considered sick when it comes to cold, as stated there.

The Holy One, blessed be He, rebuked Israel through the prophet Ezekiel (16) and said: "As for your birth, on the day you were born, your navel was not cut, nor were you washed with water to cleanse you; you were not salted, nor swaddled at all." It is evident from this that a newborn suffers if these actions are not performed for him. Therefore, because of the newborn's suffering, the sages permitted performing these actions for the newborn on Shabbat, since there are no Torah-prohibited labors involved, only rabbinic prohibitions and weekday activities. This is what they said at the end of Chapter "Mefanin": "As for your birth, on the day you were born" – from here we learn that a child may be delivered on Shabbat. "Your navel was not cut" – from here we learn that the umbilical cord may be cut on Shabbat. "Nor were you washed with water to cleanse you" – from here we learn that the newborn may be washed on Shabbat. "You were not salted" – from here we learn that the newborn may be salted on Shabbat, as salting hardens his flesh (Rashi). "Nor swaddled at all" – from here we learn that the newborn may be swaddled on Shabbat, meaning wrapped in bands and cloths (there), which in our language is called "wickeln." Additionally, the placenta is buried to warm the newborn, as this is a special practice; burying the placenta brings warmth to the newborn. On weekdays, it was buried in the ground, but on Shabbat, this is obviously forbidden, so their practice was to bury it on Shabbat in wool, cotton, or straw.

The Rambam wrote: "Because it is dangerous for him if these things are not done for him," see there. According to this, if one needs even a Torah prohibition, such as bringing a knife through a public domain or similar, it is also permitted. However, Tosafot at the end of the chapter "Mipanin" wrote that this is only general discomfort, and only rabbinic prohibitions are permitted in this case, as none of the things listed involve a Torah prohibition, see there. It appears to me regarding the law: since the Rambam wrote that it is a danger, even though Tosafot disagrees, there is a potential danger since the law might follow the Rambam. In any case of potential danger, it is permitted to desecrate Shabbat. Therefore, if these things require a Torah prohibition, they should be done by a non-Jew. If that is not possible, then they should do it themselves, as in cases of doubt regarding life-threatening situations, we are lenient (this seems to be my humble opinion).

The Tur and Shulchan Aruch write in Section 7: "This applies to one who is born after seven or nine months, but one who is born after eight months or if there is a doubt whether he is a seven-month or eight-month baby – we do not desecrate the Sabbath for him unless his hair and nails are fully developed." This is their wording, and without this, we consider him a miscarriage, and even if there is doubt, we do not desecrate the Sabbath. Even though in any case of doubt regarding saving a life, we desecrate the Sabbath, and even if he does not have a presumption of being alive, like in the case in Section 8 where we bring a knife through public property for a fetus, nevertheless, here we do not desecrate the Sabbath because it appears defective if his hair and nails are not fully developed, and it clearly seems like a miscarriage (Magen Avraham, Section 15). And there is an opinion that in Section 8 we need to specifically know that his months are complete (there), and this is surprising because at the end of the first chapter of Arakhin it teaches in this law: 'She sat on the birthing stool,' and is it possible that without the completion of her months she does not sit on the birthing stool? Therefore, it seems as I wrote that in a case of doubt and there is a defect in the actual fetus, we certainly do not desecrate the Sabbath.

A baby born in the eighth month with certainty, or one who is possibly a seventh-month or possibly an eighth-month baby whose hair and nails have not fully developed, is prohibited to move because of muktzeh. However, the mother may bend over him to nurse him, due to the discomfort of the milk that causes her distress when her breasts are full. Similarly, she herself can express the milk by hand if it causes her distress. And even though one who milks is liable because of extracting, this is only when the milk is not wasted, but when it is wasted, it is only a rabbinic prohibition, and due to distress, they did not decree. All the more so, according to most authorities who hold that a labor not needed for its own sake is exempt, just like one who lances a boil, they did not decree because of distress.

And we straighten the limbs of the newborn that were dislocated due to the pain of birth, but only on the first day. After that, it is forbidden (Tur), because it appears like building (Magen Avraham, note 18). It is sufficient to straighten them on the first day, and if they become dislocated later, there is no danger if they wait until nightfall, as the Rambam wrote in Chapter 22, Law 26, that the vertebrae of the spine of a child should not be adjusted side by side because it appears like building. I did not find in the Rambam in Chapter 2 that it is permitted on the day of birth, and in his opinion, it is also forbidden on the day of birth because there is no concern in this matter. The Tur and the Shulchan Aruch derived this law from the beginning of the chapter "Kol HaKeilim": "Rav Sheshet permits adjusting the limbs of a child" as explained by Rashi and Tosafot, therefore they were compelled to distinguish between the day of birth and afterwards, as Tosafot wrote there. But it seems to me that the Rambam interprets it according to the Aruch's explanation, and this is the law that our teacher the Beit Yosef wrote in Section 11: If the newborn's throat membrane falls, it is permissible to put a finger in his mouth and place the membrane back, even though sometimes he might vomit. Therefore, according to the Rambam, straightening the limbs is forbidden even on the day of birth. It is permitted to wrap the newborn in clothes so that his limbs don't become crooked and to arrange and straighten his limbs, as this is customary and is considered like feeding and giving him drink, but dealing with the vertebrae of the spine is forbidden even by wrapping in clothes (Bach). And know that what was explained in the previous section that it is forbidden to carry a doubtful seven-month-old infant, some permit carrying all doubts, and this is the custom (Magen Avraham, note 16 in the name of Agudah), and this is also the implication of the Talmud and the poskim (there), that one should not be stringent regarding the carrying of a muktzeh person due to doubt, unless it is known for certain that he is a nefel (non-viable infant), such as when he was born and separated, but in doubt, it is permissible to carry (there).

It has already been explained in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 266, that circumcision at its proper time overrides Shabbat, but if it is not at its proper time, it does not override Shabbat. And we explained there in Section 25 that circumcision is permitted on Shabbat and not merely pushed aside, see there. And all the needs of circumcision are done on Shabbat: they circumcise, uncover, suck, and place ground cumin prepared before Shabbat on it. And it was explained there that there is no difference between one circumciser and many circumcisers, and that initially, even on Shabbat, three circumcisers can perform the circumcision: one cuts, one uncovers, and one sucks, unlike those who are stringent and say that on Shabbat only one circumciser should perform the circumcision, see there.

As long as one has not removed his hand from the circumcision, he may return even for small pieces of skin that do not prevent the circumcision from being valid, to cut them. And even if he has removed his hand from the cutting, as long as he or another is engaged in the uncovering of the glans (priah), it is considered as if he has not removed his hand. However, after the priah, it is considered that he has removed his hand, as the suction (metzitzah) is only due to the danger (of infection). 

What is considered small pieces of skin that prevent the circumcision from being valid? Flesh that covers most of the height of the glans in one place, even if it is very thin. Flesh that covers a minority of the height of the glans is considered small pieces of skin that do not prevent the circumcision. Similarly, if the priah was not done correctly, one returns to correct it even afterward. Also, regarding metzitzah, if it was not done properly or there is even a doubt whether it was done properly, one returns and performs it, as in the case of any doubt concerning danger, which overrides the Sabbath.

It appears to me that even in cutting, if there is a doubt whether this is one of the small pieces of skin that prevent the circumcision from being valid, for example, if it is difficult to determine if the flesh covers most of the glans or not, similarly with priah when there is doubt, one returns. For since the Torah permits the Sabbath violation for the sake of circumcision, it permits it until the doubt is removed from his heart whether he circumcised properly or not. If he did not circumcise properly, it would be a desecration of the Sabbath not in the context of a mitzvah. 

There is even a dispute in the Gemara (Shabbat 133b) concerning small pieces of skin that do not prevent the circumcision, with some holding that one returns even for them. However, we do not hold that way. Nevertheless, in a case of doubt, certainly one returns. It is also obvious that even for small pieces of skin that do not prevent the circumcision, one returns to them after the Sabbath.

Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 3: "An eight-month-old infant: if its hair and nails are fully developed, we circumcise it on Shabbat (for this is a sign that it was delayed), but if they are not fully developed, even if there is doubt whether it is a seven-month-old or an eight-month-old, we do not circumcise it, and certainly not if it is definitely an eight-month-old. If it is definitely a seven-month-old, even if its hair and nails are not fully developed, we circumcise it." These are his words. There are many complexities in these matters, and similarly, there are contradictions in the words of the Rambam regarding this issue. We have explained this, with God's help, in Yoreh De'ah, section 266, from paragraph 21 to paragraph 24, and in Even HaEzer, section 156, from paragraph 5 to paragraph 13. See there.

"And on the eighth day, the flesh of his foreskin shall be circumcised," and we expound: on the eighth day – even on Shabbat, for the word "on the day" is superfluous. It should have written "on the eighth," since the time is already specified, as it is written earlier: "and she shall be unclean for seven days" (see Shabbat 132a). The word "foreskin" is also superfluous, as the location of the circumcision is already explained in the portion of Lech Lecha, and it should have written: "and on the eighth day he shall be circumcised." We expound "from the flesh" concerning a leprous spot (133a), that one can perform the circumcision at the site of the leprous spot, and this is explained in Yoreh De'ah. From "his foreskin" we expound that only a definite foreskin overrides Shabbat, not a doubtful foreskin, such as an androgynous, who is doubtful whether he is male or female – he is not circumcised on Shabbat. Similarly, not when the time is in doubt, such as when born at twilight, meaning after sunset, for immediately after sunset the doubt begins. But before sunset, even if Shabbat has already been accepted, it does not pertain to the time of circumcision. Now, if born on Shabbat at twilight – it is obvious that he is circumcised on Sunday, for even on weekdays in such a case, he is circumcised the next day, for perhaps it is not yet his eighth day. Rather, even if born on Friday at twilight – he is not circumcised on Shabbat, for perhaps it was daytime and his time is on the eve of Shabbat, and on Shabbat it would be a non-timely circumcision that does not override Shabbat. Sometimes, due to doubt, he is circumcised on the twelfth day, and this is explained in Yoreh De'ah. Also, one born circumcised – is not circumcised on Shabbat, and this is also included in "his foreskin," meaning a complete foreskin and not one born circumcised, for even if obligated to draw covenant blood, it does not override Shabbat (135a). The main verse refers to an androgynous and one born circumcised, for regarding doubtful time it is not necessary, for we do not desecrate Shabbat in doubt with our hands (Tosafot there). But an androgynous, since he is obligated to be circumcised, and one born circumcised who needs to have covenant blood drawn, I might say they should be circumcised on Shabbat – the verse teaches us that they are not circumcised on Shabbat. And the Rif wrote that one born circumcised is a doubtful law if Shabbat is desecrated for him or not, therefore it is not appropriate to say that we expound from the verse, and it must be said that the verse refers only to an androgynous. (And it is a query, for Rabbi Yehuda holds in the Mishnah 134a that an androgynous overrides Shabbat, and the Gemara 137a explains that he expounds from the verse "every male" that an androgynous is obligated in circumcision from the Torah, and the Sages hold that he is not obligated, if so, for an androgynous it is also not necessary. And Tosafot 135a at the end of the statement "and not" wrote that the main verse refers to one born circumcised, therefore, according to the Rif, it is difficult and requires investigation and precise understanding).

A baby born circumcised is considered circumcised if it appears circumcised even without an erection, for if it only appears circumcised with an erection, that is not significant. It is surprising that we do not have the custom to examine a baby born circumcised on Shabbat, as it may be forbidden to circumcise him on Shabbat. It might be because it is uncommon for a baby to appear circumcised even without an erection. However, if it is found to be certain, it is forbidden to circumcise him on Shabbat or a festival. Similarly, a baby delivered by caesarean section or born to a non-Jewish woman who later converted (in ancient times) – their circumcision does not override Shabbat. In the Gemara, this is derived from verses, see there. Also, one who has two foreskins, which means either two layers of skin one on top of the other or two penises (Rashi 135b). Some explain two layers of skin on the area of the uncovering (Pri Megadim), which is a surprising explanation because it is not noticeable at all. Many children have two thin layers of skin on the area of the uncovering, and this is not a significant difference. Rather, it means a thick layer of the actual foreskin that has another layer (see Maharshal, sect. 4).

Circumcision overrides Shabbat, but the preparations for circumcision that could have been done before Shabbat do not. Therefore, if one did not bring the circumcision knife before Shabbat, one may not bring it on Shabbat from a public domain, and even from a karmelit it is forbidden to bring it, even though this means that the circumcision will not take place today. For the Sages upheld their decrees even in cases of karet. To instruct a non-Jew to perform a task or bring the knife, our teacher the Beit Yosef ruled in section 6 that if it is something that, if a Jew did it, would only be a rabbinic prohibition, it is permitted to tell a non-Jew to do it, as this is a "shvut d'shvut" (a double rabbinic prohibition) in the context of a mitzvah. But if it is something that would involve a Torah prohibition if done by a Jew, it is forbidden to instruct a non-Jew to do it, for we do not override the prohibition of instructing a non-Jew for the sake of a mitzvah. However, according to what our teacher the Rema wrote earlier in section 276, that it is permitted to tell a non-Jew to light a candle for the Shabbat meal, certainly it is permitted for the sake of circumcision. And indeed, there we do not hold this way, as we wrote there, but for circumcision, one can rely on this opinion to instruct a non-Jew to bring the knife through a public domain or to fix the knife if necessary (see Magen Avraham section 65). However, for a Jew himself, it is forbidden in any form of rabbinic prohibition, and certainly to fix a nail, as this involves a derivative of a primary labor. It is also forbidden to bring the baby to the synagogue even by a non-Jew through a courtyard that is not enclosed by an eruv, and certainly not through a karmelit, since the circumcision can be done at home (there). There is also an opinion that if the mohel took the knife out of his hand, it is then forbidden for him to carry it and hide it, as it is muktzeh (there), and it is also forbidden to wash the blood off the knife (there). We have explained with G-d's help in Yoreh De'ah there in sections 14 and 15 that it is permitted, see there.

If one did not have ground cumin prepared before Shabbat, or in our case, if one did not grind the rotten wood called "pulver" before Shabbat, it is forbidden to grind it on Shabbat. Instead, one should chew it with a change, meaning with one's teeth. Similarly, in places where it is customary to put wine and oil on the circumcision, where they mix the wine and oil together and beat them strongly, if they did not beat them before Shabbat, it is forbidden to beat them on Shabbat. Likewise, if they did not mix them together before Shabbat, they should not mix them on Shabbat. Instead, they should place each one separately or, if they place them together, they should do so with some change. Know that all this applies before the circumcision, but if the circumcision has already been performed and they see that there is no cumin, oil, or wine, it is obvious that they desecrate the Shabbat for this, as after the circumcision, the child is in danger.
