Some make a covering after the circumcision in the form of a division, like a tight pouch that covers the head of the organ until the glans, and they tie it there so that the skin does not return to cover the organ. If this was not prepared before Shabbat, it is forbidden to make it on Shabbat. Instead, one wraps a cloth around it, and if he does not have a cloth in his house, he wraps it around his finger as a garment to change the usual manner of carrying on weekdays, and he brings it through another courtyard even if they did not make an Eruv together. However, through a public domain, it is forbidden (Magen Avraham, section 8). This is forbidden even after the circumcision, because this is not done for healing but so that the skin does not return to cover the organ. If it is not done today, it can be done tomorrow, so it does not matter.

The Tur wrote: "It is forbidden to tell a non-Jew before the circumcision to heat water for the circumcision, because since there is a Torah prohibition involved, they did not permit instructing a non-Jew. However, for a rabbinic prohibition, such as bringing it through an alleyway where there was no partnership or in a courtyard where they did not make an eruv, it is permitted to tell a non-Jew to bring it. Similarly, if a non-Jew had water that he heated on Shabbat for himself, or if a Jew violated and heated them, it is permitted to wash him with them. And even though they forbade washing the entire body even with water that was heated before Shabbat, they permitted it for circumcision." End of quote. It is explained from his words that bringing hot water by a non-Jew through a public domain is forbidden, but according to what we wrote in paragraph 6, it is permissible, see there. And this is all before the circumcision, but after the circumcision - it is dangerous and everything is permitted, like the law of a sick person in danger.

The Rambam in Chapter 2, Law 15 wrote: "One bathes him before the circumcision and after the circumcision and on the third day of the circumcision with hot water that was heated on Shabbat, due to the danger involved." Similarly, he wrote in Chapter 2 of the Laws of Circumcision, Law 8, and this is his wording: "In a place where it is customary to bathe the child - one bathes him on Shabbat on the day of the circumcision, whether before the circumcision or after the circumcision, or on the third day of the circumcision when it falls on Shabbat, whether it is the entire body or just the area of the circumcision, whether with hot water that was heated before Shabbat or with hot water that was heated on Shabbat, because it is a danger for him." End of quote.

And his words are puzzling, for before the circumcision there is no danger involved. However, he himself explained in his responses to the sages of Lunel that his intention was only for the third day of the circumcision (see there in several places). And moreover, even after the circumcision, if there is no hot water prepared, they should not circumcise and should not heat water, unless the water spilled after the circumcision, in which case it is necessary to heat it. And what he wrote 'before the circumcision' refers to the permission to bathe the entire body.

And this is the text of our Rabbi, the Beit Yosef, in paragraph 9: "In the time of the sages of the Talmud, if they did not wash the infant before the circumcision and after the circumcision and on the third day after the circumcision with hot water, it was dangerous. Therefore, they needed to describe its procedure when it occurred on Shabbat. And nowadays, it is not customary to wash at all, and its rule is to wash on Shabbat if they wish, like the rule for any person's washing." End of quote, meaning it is forbidden to wash his entire body, even with hot water that was heated before Shabbat.

But our teacher, the Rema, wrote about it and this is his language: "And in these regions, the custom is to wash the infant before the circumcision with hot water that was heated from the day before, and after the circumcision on the night following Shabbat. And if the third day after the circumcision falls on Shabbat and they see a need to wash him, they prepare hot water from the eve of Shabbat and wash him on Shabbat. All of this is generally assumed, but if they see there is a danger if he is not washed after the circumcision, it is certainly permitted to wash him and desecrate Shabbat, just as we do for any other dangerously ill person." End of quote.

The explanation of his words: Our custom is not like the words of the Gemara, which permits the desecration of Shabbat for washing after the circumcision and on the third day, because we do not consider this a necessity for the infant. Nevertheless, we do not follow the words of our teacher, the Beit Yosef, who forbids washing entirely, even with hot water heated from the eve of Shabbat. Rather, even before the circumcision, we wash the entire body with this hot water, because we believe that although washing is not necessary, it is still beneficial for the infant.

Therefore, we wash the entire body before the circumcision, and only after the circumcision do we wait until the night, because we hold that since he was washed before, he does not need to be washed again until the night, and it is forbidden to wash the entire body. Similarly, on the third day, we do not consider it a great necessity, but only a general benefit, and we wash the entire body with hot water that was heated from the eve of Shabbat. All of this is assumed, but when there is a necessity, we desecrate Shabbat. It is obvious that care should be taken not to wash with a cloth, but with hands, to avoid squeezing.

It has already been explained in Yoreh De'ah there, that a person who has never performed a circumcision should not perform his first one on Shabbat, and similarly, someone who has never done the priah (uncovering) should not do his first one on Shabbat, lest he make a mistake and cause a wound that is not in the place of the mitzvah. But if he has performed a circumcision or priah once, it is permitted for him to do so for the second time on Shabbat, even if he is the father of the child. See there. Also, many laws of circumcision on Shabbat are explained there. See there.

The Sages taught in the Mishnah of Shabbat (128b): "We do not assist an animal in giving birth on a festival, but we do assist a woman in giving birth on Shabbat, etc." It seems to me that the explanation is as follows: The Tanna is clarifying for us the significant difference between a woman and an animal. For an animal, we do not assist even on a festival, whereas for a woman, we assist even on Shabbat. Therefore, this was taught in Tractate Shabbat and not in Tractate Yom Tov. According to this, the statement that "we do not assist on a festival" is as if it says, "and all the more so on Shabbat." Based on this, there is room to question whether the rule of assisting applies only on a festival, or perhaps since the primary context of the tractate is Shabbat, the mention of the festival is to emphasize the point, as I have explained. However, in truth, it is as if it were taught regarding Shabbat, and consequently, the rule of assisting applies also on Shabbat.

And this is the opinion of the Tur who wrote: "One does not assist an animal in giving birth on Shabbat, but one may support it, etc.," and the Rosh was uncertain about this in the name of the Ri, see there. However, for the Tur, it was clear, especially since this is a rabbinic prohibition and in cases of doubt, we are lenient, particularly in instances involving animal suffering. Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, in section 1, omitted this, writing: "One does not assist an animal in giving birth on Shabbat," end quote. There are those who say that he also forbids supporting (Magen Avraham, section 1), but this does not seem correct, for if that were the case, he would have explained it. Rather, it is because he was uncertain, as he wrote in his larger work, and he did not want to rule against the Tur. Therefore, he completely avoided this issue. It seems to me that one who relies on the opinion of the Tur has not lost out (and similarly, it appears to be the opinion of the Bach, the Pri Chadash, the Taz, and the Shach, see there. According to what I have written, the words of the Tur are clear in their reasoning, and the difficulty raised by the Beit Yosef is resolved, without needing the forced interpretations of the commentators, see there and examine thoroughly).

How do we assist: We hold the newborn so it does not fall to the ground, blow into its nose, and give it something in its mouth so that it will nurse (Gemara), because its nostrils are blocked by mucus. Blowing into its nose opens the passages, and we place its mother's breast into its mouth (Rashi). The Rambam, in his commentary on the Mishnah, wrote: 'We do not deliver,' meaning the pulling of the newborn from the womb, and 'assisting' means helping the animal by loosening its legs, shaking it, and similar actions. He believes the Gemara did not detail all matters, and the general rule is that anything which assists is permitted. In the Jerusalem Talmud, it says the assistance is: bringing wine and blowing into its nose, placing a hand below to receive it, and inserting the breast into its mouth. The Rambam did not mention this law in the laws of Shabbat. (In the Gemara, it states: "We have compassion for a pure animal on Yom Tov," etc., and the Tur writes this later in Siman 523, but does not mention it here. It is questionable if this is similar to assisting. The reason for mentioning 'on Yom Tov' is because the whole matter applies on Yom Tov for the reason we wrote, or perhaps everyone agrees it is not done on Shabbat. In my humble opinion, the effort is the same, and there is no difference between this and that. The Tur relied on what is written later, since the law for animals is the same for Shabbat and Yom Tov, and he did not want to elaborate. Consider this well).

It is prohibited to remove scabs from an animal's wound on Shabbat, meaning to remove the scabs, and one may not anoint the wound with oil, as all this is only for the animal's pleasure, and one does not trouble oneself on Shabbat for the animal's pleasure. Therefore, the prohibition only applies to a wound that has healed, as then it is only a matter of pleasure. But at the beginning of a wound, where there is suffering if nothing is done for it—it is permitted, for it is allowed to trouble oneself to remove its suffering. Therefore, if the animal has eaten a lot of vetch and is suffering from overeating—it is permitted to make it run in the courtyard, meaning it should run, exert itself, and be healed, for one may trouble oneself for its suffering. And specifically in the courtyard, but in a public place—it is prohibited, as it appears like a weekday activity. And even though this is its remedy, and if so, why is it not forbidden due to the grinding of medicines, since grinding of medicines does not apply to animals (Taz, section 2). Similarly, if the animal is seized with blood, one can place it in water so that it cools down, because it is suffering. And if it needs bloodletting—it is prohibited even to tell a non-Jew to let blood, but if there is a doubt that it might die if not let blood—they permitted saying to a non-Jew to let blood, for since he is anxious about his property, if you do not permit it, he will do it himself (Magen Avraham and Taz, section 3). Therefore, one who knows himself that he is not so anxious as to desecrate Shabbat, it is proper for him to refrain from this, and the Holy One, blessed be He, will reward him.

Maimonides wrote in Chapter 26, Law 15: "A storehouse of grain or wine barrels, even though it is permissible to take from it, it is forbidden to start emptying it except for a mitzvah purpose, such as emptying it for hosting guests or to establish a study hall there. And how should it be emptied: each person fills four or five containers until they finish. They should not sweep the floor of the storehouse; rather, one should enter and exit and make a path with his feet as he goes in and out." End of quote.

Explanation of his words: According to the Maggid Mishneh and Kesef Mishneh, it is so because we hold according to Rabbi Shimon that there is no prohibition of muktzeh due to setting something aside as a storehouse and diverting one's attention from it. And this is what he says: "Even though it is permissible to use it for eating and drinking," since we do not have the prohibition of muktzeh, nevertheless, to clear it all out is forbidden due to exertion, except for a mitzvah. And even for a mitzvah, one should not clear out more than four or five baskets until they are finished. Nevertheless, one should not sweep the floor of the storehouse, lest he come to level the holes, which would be a Torah prohibition because of building. And this that he wrote: "But instead, he enters and exits and makes a path with his feet" does not refer to the previous statement, but rather to a matter of permission. For regarding a matter of permission, he is not allowed to clear it at all. Rather, when he wants to enter there, he enters and makes a path with his feet (and this requires further study, as the language seems to clearly indicate that it is all one matter).

And in my humble opinion, it appears that there is another intention in the Rambam. For although, according to the Talmudic discussion (127a), the case of creating a path with one's feet refers to a matter of permission, as is stated there, nonetheless, the Rambam explained his words based on the Jerusalem Talmud, which asks: "What is the ruling on clearing out from the storehouse in this manner? We learn from this: They agree that one should not touch the storehouse, but he may make a path and enter and exit." End quote. It is not understood what this question is, as in the Mishnah it is taught 'one may clear out,' and furthermore, how can it say 'they agree that one should not touch the storehouse,' and how can one not touch it since clearing is permitted? Rather, the explanation is as follows: in the Mishnah it is taught that one may clear out even four or five baskets, etc., but not the storehouse, meaning one should not finish clearing out the storehouse because of leveling the ground, as was mentioned. Thus, it turns out that the term 'storehouse' refers to the ground of the storehouse. And this is the question: what is the ruling on clearing out from the storehouse in this manner, meaning perhaps what was taught, but not the storehouse, means that one person should not finish clearing the ground of the storehouse. However, in this manner, meaning each person clearing the area of four or five baskets, it is permitted, or is it entirely prohibited? And it brings a Baraita: they agree that one should not touch the storehouse, meaning the ground of the storehouse. However, if so, even though they cleared the produce, still much remains on the ground and it is difficult to walk there. Therefore, he makes a path with his feet to clear them here and there and enters and exits. And this is also the intention of the Rambam, and this does not contradict our Talmud, which does not deal with this (and the Kesef Mishneh and the Perush Mishnayot labored in explaining the Jerusalem Talmud, as mentioned there).

The Tur and the Shulchan Aruch wrote: "And how does one clear it out? If the storage is large, he clears out five baskets from it. If there were only five baskets, he clears out four, but he does not clear it all out, lest he come to level the holes." End of quote. And there is such a case in the Gemara there, and the Rambam ruled according to another case. And what is the measure of a basket? It is stated in the Jerusalem Talmud: three seahs, as each basket holds three seahs. And they wrote that even though it is forbidden to start clearing out the storage for a non-essential matter due to the effort involved, nevertheless if he started to clear it out before Shabbat, it is permitted to clear it on Shabbat even for a non-essential matter (Beit Yosef and Magen Avraham). And there are those who disagree with this, arguing that if the prohibition was due to muktzeh, it would make sense to differentiate between starting before Shabbat and not starting, but what relevance does effort have, for even if he started before Shabbat, the effort remains (Taz). And in my humble opinion, it seems like the first opinion, for is effort forbidden on Shabbat? If one carries a heavy table, is there no effort? Rather, the issue is that even though we do not have the concept of muktzeh, nevertheless it is separated from this, and one should not start with something separated when there is effort involved. But when he started before Shabbat, it is not considered separated, and it is like all the efforts within the house.

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote: Any rabbinic prohibition that was permitted due to the necessity of a mitzvah, is also permitted for the sake of guests. However, they are only considered guests if they are staying at his house or if he invited guests who are staying at others' houses. But if he invited his friend to eat with him, it is not considered guests, and it is not a mitzvah meal but rather a permissible meal. And if he invited his friend in honor of the guest staying with him, it is considered a mitzvah meal (Taz). Even with guests, the mitzvah is for the host and not for the guests, and for them it is considered a permissible meal (Magen Avraham, section 5). And if he invited his friend because his friend is a Torah scholar, it seems to me that it is considered a mitzvah meal.

When moving these four or five baskets, one can move them to any place he desires: to roofs, to attics, and even climb ladders to place them there (see Beit Yosef). However, he should be careful when moving them not to divide them into smaller baskets to carry them many times to lighten the load, because doing so increases the number of trips, and this makes more noise. See what is written in Siman 323, Section 6. These four or five baskets that are moved are for one guest, and if many guests come, he moves this amount for each and every guest. Provided that one person does not move for all of them, as this would cause excessive exertion; rather, each person should move for himself or another should move on his behalf (see Tosafot at the beginning of the chapter "Mipanin" where it implies that each person moves for himself, and see Rashi and scrutinize well).

Our teacher, the Rema, wrote: "Barrels of wine that were brought on a wagon - it is forbidden to unload them on Shabbat, unless it is for the honor of guests or for a mitzvah, as it resembles clearing out a storage room." This means that as long as they have not been unloaded from the wagon, it constitutes excessive exertion and resembles a storage room. And if a single barrel holds more than fifteen seahs, it is forbidden to take it, since it is more than five baskets, as mentioned. And if the wagon arrived before Shabbat, for if it arrived on Shabbat from outside the boundary, it is forbidden for the one for whom it was brought, as mentioned in Siman 325.

Extinguishing and kindling are among the primary categories of labor, and they were present in the Tabernacle, where fire was kindled to melt the metals for the vessels of the Tabernacle, and extinguishing was done when they extinguished coals to create embers needed for melting gold and silver. The derivative of kindling, as Rambam writes at the beginning of Chapter 12, is that heating iron to temper it in water is considered a derivative of kindling and is liable. The derivative of extinguishing is that blacksmiths heat the iron until it becomes a coal, and extinguish it in water to harden it, and this is to temper it, and one who does so is liable for extinguishing. In Chapter 9, Law 6, Rambam writes that heating metal until it becomes a coal is a derivative of cooking. The Raavad disagrees with him on this. However, Rambam's words are correct, that heating to temper is not kindling until it becomes a coal, and therefore it is a derivative of kindling, and heating it until it becomes a coal is a derivative of cooking, like cooking that is cooked until it softens completely. The Raavad holds that tempering is a rabbinic prohibition, but Rambam believes that tempering is forbidden by Torah law, as it appears from the plain reading of the Talmud in Shabbat (41b). And although in Yoma (34b) it says: 'Tempering is rabbinic,' Ramban already explained that in Yoma, it refers to an iron lamp that they would immerse in the mikvah for the High Priest, which does not involve tempering at all. Also, Rashi and Tosafot hold like Rambam.

The Rambam wrote (there): "One who kindles even a small amount is liable, provided he needs the ashes. But if he kindled for the purpose of destruction, he is exempt, because he is causing damage. However, one who kindles his neighbor's stack of grain or burns his house is liable, even though he is causing destruction, because his intention is to take revenge on his enemy, and his mind is settled and his anger is appeased. This is similar to one who tears his garment over a deceased relative or in his anger, who is liable, and to one who injures his fellow during a quarrel, because all these actions provide satisfaction to their evil inclination. Similarly, one who kindles a lamp or wood, whether for warmth or for light, is liable." These are his words. 

And we have already written in Siman 316, Section 26, that this, which holds one liable based on the intention to take revenge, follows his opinion that one is liable for a labor that is not needed for its own sake. But according to those who rule that one is exempt for a labor that is not needed for its own sake, he is also exempt in this case, since he does not need the result of the labor. Nonetheless, we have further explained that many of the earlier authorities disagreed with him, as even according to Rabbi Yehuda, who holds one liable for a labor not needed for its own sake, one would be exempt in this case, for the conclusion of the Talmud is not in accordance with this view. We have clarified there the Rambam's opinion on this matter.

And also in what he requires for needing the ash, it is only according to his opinion that one is liable for something not needed for its intrinsic purpose, for according to Rabbi Shimon, even something needed for its ash is considered a melacha she’eina tzericha legufa (a labor not needed for its intrinsic purpose). However, opposite to this, there is an argument that according to Rabbi Shimon, one is liable even if he does not need the ash because he holds that one who causes damage through burning is liable, whereas Rabbi Yehuda holds he is exempt, for in this matter, their opinions are reversed. And in Siman 316, sections 27, 28, and 29, we explained that according to Rashi, this is indeed the case, that according to Rabbi Shimon, one is liable in all situations. But the Tosafot disagree on this, holding that according to Rabbi Shimon, some rectification is still needed: either for the sake of a mitzvah or when one needs the ash, as stated there.

Extinguishing (a flame): The Rambam wrote in Chapter 1, Law 7: "Anyone who performs a labor on Shabbat, even though he does not need the result of the labor itself, is liable for it. How so? If one extinguished a candle because he needed the oil or the wick so that it would not be lost, or so that it would not burn, or so that the ceramic of the lamp would not break, since extinguishing is a labor and he intended to extinguish, even though he does not need the extinguishing itself... he is liable." End quote. And most of the poskim (halachic decisors) rule according to Rabbi Shimon that a labor which is not needed for its own sake is exempt, and one is not liable for extinguishing unless he extinguishes the wick in order to improve it, because by extinguishing it, it lights better than if he had not extinguished it, as was done in the Mishkan (Tabernacle) where they extinguished to make coals (Shabbat 31b and Tosafot there). But other extinguishings that are not needed for the extinguishing itself are exempt from the Torah.

At the beginning of Chapter 12, it is written: “One who extinguishes even a small fire is liable, whether one extinguishes a candle or a wooden coal. However, one who extinguishes a metal coal is exempt, but if one intends to harden it, they are liable, for this is what blacksmiths do: they heat the iron until it becomes a coal and then extinguish it in water to harden it. This is considered hardening, and one who does it is liable, and it is a derivative of extinguishing. It is permitted to extinguish a metal coal in the public domain to prevent harm to the public.” End quote. The Raavad and Remach were puzzled by this, for since one is liable for extinguishing when it is not needed for its own sake and is liable for hardening, why is one exempt for extinguishing a metal coal, as it inevitably hardens it, and even though one does not intend it, it is a case of 'inevitability'? The Magid Mishneh answered: when one does not intend it, it is not considered a labor at all, since one does not want to make a utensil from it, it is considered nothing. And it appears that this is similar to the reasoning of the author of the Aruch, as brought by the early authorities, that an 'inevitability' that one does not desire is not considered an inevitability, and we brought this in Siman 242 (but according to the Tosafot 102a 'that makes' this only applies according to Rabbi Shimon and not according to Rabbi Yehuda).

In my humble opinion, it seems that if this was indeed his intention, he would not have been so vague. Rather, the explanation is as follows: for tempering, a substantial amount of water is required until the iron hardens and tempers. The first waters, although they extinguish it, still they themselves become heated due to the intense heat, and afterward, it requires a washing of water over the first waters to cool them. This is what is said: "One who extinguishes a metal ember is exempt," because with metal, extinguishing does not apply, as Rashi explains. If one intended to temper, meaning he poured a lot of water until it tempered, he is liable. And it is explicitly explained in the Gemara that for tempering, there is a measure, but for cooling, there is no measure, and it is understood that extinguishing is like cooling, as even when they are lukewarm, they extinguish. And there it discusses a vessel, but the matter is the same, as is evident.

He also wrote: "A fire that breaks out on Shabbat, one who extinguishes it to prevent monetary loss is liable, for the loss of money does not override Shabbat, only the loss of life does. Therefore, people should leave so that they do not die, and let the fire burn, even if it consumes the entire city." These are his words. And what he wrote, that one who extinguishes is liable, this follows his view that a labor not needed for its own sake is liable. But according to most poskim (decisors), who hold that a labor not needed for its own sake is exempt, there is no Torah liability here, only a rabbinic prohibition. And this is what the Ra'avad wrote in his glosses, and this is his language: "There is no liability here according to Rabbi Shimon, because he does not need the charcoal." These are his words. This means that according to us, who hold like Rabbi Shimon, there is no liability for extinguishing unless one needs to make charcoal, and in the case of extinguishing a fire, one does not need charcoal.

And we should be meticulous in understanding what the Rambam is teaching us with this law, for he has already explained that anyone who extinguishes a fire is liable. And if he is informing us that the destruction of life overrides Shabbat, he has already clarified in Chapter 2 that even a doubt regarding saving a life overrides Shabbat. It appears to me that he is teaching us a significant law: because earlier he wrote that one extinguishes a metal ember in the public domain so that the public is not harmed by it, which is a rabbinic prohibition permitted due to harm to the public, as he wrote. And generally, in fires, the flames and embers spread into the public domain, and there is a public hazard if the fire is not extinguished. I would say that it is permissible to extinguish it – he informs us that it is not so, for extinguishing a fire involves a Torah prohibition. It is permitted only in cases of saving lives, not merely for preventing harm. Only with a metal ember is there no Torah prohibition of extinguishing, not with a wooden ember, because he holds like Rabbi Yehuda that a labor not needed for itself is liable, as he wrote.

Therefore, indeed, the Tur and Shulchan Aruch at the end of this section wrote: "A burning coal placed in a location where many people can be harmed by it can be extinguished, whether it is made of metal or wood, though the Rambam forbids extinguishing a wooden coal." Their reasoning is that most authorities hold like Rabbi Shimon, that a labor not needed for its own sake is exempt, and is only a rabbinic prohibition, which is waived due to public harm, and the law follows this opinion (A.R.). The Tur did not mention the Rambam's opinion at all. According to this, it seems to me, in my humble opinion, that there is an additional allowance in our times, in addition to the permissions clarified at the end of this section regarding extinguishing fires on Shabbat. Since nowadays houses are built adjacent to the public domain, unlike in the time of the Gemara when houses were within courtyards and not adjacent to the public domain, now the houses are adjacent to the public domain. Consequently, many coals from a fire fall without number into the public domain, and we hold that one may extinguish a coal in the public domain even if it is made of wood to prevent public harm. It is well known that if we were to try to extinguish every coal where it falls, it would be impossible, because the wind scatters them to many places without limit, and we would not be able to extinguish them all. Therefore, because of public harm, there is a permission to extinguish the fire itself to prevent public harm. Further reasons will be explained, with God's help, at the end of this section.

However, due to financial loss, even a rabbinic prohibition was not permitted, and furthermore, even in a situation where there is no prohibition at all, they did not permit saving more than what is necessary for three meals. The reason, as the sages said (117b) on the Mishnah that permits saving for three meals, and they asked: Since it is permitted to exert effort for something that is allowed to be carried and into a courtyard that has an eruv (Rashi), why not save more? Rava answered: Because a person is anxious about his property, if you permit him, he may come to extinguish the fire. And Rashi explained: If you permit him to start saving to such an extent, because he is anxious, he may forget about Shabbat and come to extinguish the fire.

This is the language of the Rambam in Chapter 23, Law 20: "If a fire broke out in a courtyard on Shabbat, one may not save everything that is in the courtyard to another courtyard in the same alley, even if they made an eruv, as a decree lest he extinguish the fire in order to save [his belongings], because a person is anxious about his property. Therefore, they decreed that one may only save the food he needs for that Shabbat, and the utensils he needs to use on Shabbat, and the clothes he can wear, so that he becomes resigned to losing everything and does not come to extinguish [the fire]. And if they did not make an eruv, he may not even save his food and utensils. And what may he save for his food: if the fire broke out on Friday night, he may save food for three meals, what is appropriate for a person for a person and what is appropriate for an animal for an animal. If it broke out in the morning, he may save food for two meals; in the afternoon, he may save food for one meal." End quote. And this is all before eating, and he can save the meals he needs for Shabbat for all his household members. Thus, they were very stringent in this matter.

And one cannot say that this is only according to Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that a labor that is not needed for its own sake incurs liability; therefore, they were stringent lest one come to extinguish and transgress a Torah prohibition. Hence, Rambam, who rules according to Rabbi Yehuda, wrote this law, and not according to Rabbi Shimon. This is not so, for the Tur and Shulchan Aruch rule according to Rabbi Shimon, and they nonetheless wrote this law like Rambam. They are compelled to do so, for it is Rava who states this reasoning: that since a person is agitated about his property, he will come to extinguish it, as stated. And Rava indeed holds at the beginning of the chapter "Notel" according to Rabbi Shimon regarding a labor that is not needed for its own sake, see there. And even though the Sages permitted, for the sake of monetary loss, a rabbinic prohibition, as it is found in Ketubot (60a): “A gutter that accumulated scales – one may crush them with his foot in private on Shabbat. What is the reason? It is a repair done in an unusual manner,” and due to the loss, they permitted it, see there. This is because the matter is done in private, and not extinguishing a fire, which is in public (Ran in the chapter "Haviot," see there well). And if other examples are found where they permitted, it is all in private.

However, regarding the main reasoning given by the Talmud that if you permit him [to save items from a fire], he will come to extinguish [the fire], we have great questions about this. For in the case of a deceased person, they said the opposite (Shabbat 44a): that they permitted saving a deceased person from a fire because, since a person is distressed over their deceased, if you do not permit it, they will come to extinguish [the fire]. And Tosafot there explained: "Because a person is not as distressed over their property as over their deceased, and if you permit it, since they will be preoccupied with saving, they will forget that it is Shabbat and come to extinguish inadvertently. But over their deceased, they are more distressed, and if you do not permit it, they will come to extinguish intentionally," end quote. But in truth, we also find the opposite reasoning regarding property in the Gemara, specifically in the chapter "With What May a Woman Go Out" (Shabbat 65a), regarding the ruse of cracking a nut to carry it out on Shabbat. It says there: "It should be asked of the one who says one may use a ruse in the case of a fire to wear as many garments as possible because if you do not permit it, they will come to extinguish," see there. This is precisely the opposite reasoning. And similarly, in the very topic itself, in the discussion of saving three meals, in the Mishnah that permits making a partition with any vessels, whether full or empty, so that the fire does not spread, and Rabbi Yose forbids using new earthenware vessels because they crack and extinguish [the fire]. And the Gemara (Shabbat 120a) states that Rabbi Yose's reasoning is that although indirect causation is permitted, nevertheless, if you permit it, they will come to extinguish, see there. And the Rabbis disagree with him, and the law follows the Rabbis, showing they were not concerned with this reasoning that if you permit it, they will come to extinguish. If so, why are we concerned with it here? Similarly, at the beginning of the chapter "One Who Was Overtaken by Night," it says: "The Rabbis established that a person does not restrain themselves regarding their property, and if you do not permit it, they will come to carry four cubits in the public domain," see there. This shows that we also say the opposite reasoning regarding property.

In truth, regarding the main reasoning: When is one more likely to sin, if we permit him or if we do not permit him, this is a dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis in the first chapter of Pesachim (11a) concerning a firstborn animal that has a blood condition. Even if it would die, one may not let its blood, according to Rabbi Yehuda. And the Sages say: One may let its blood, provided he does not cause a blemish. And the Talmud there says: Rabbi Yehuda holds that since a person is anxious about his property, if you permit him to let blood in a place where it does not cause a blemish, he will come to do so in a place where it does cause a blemish. And the Rabbis hold, on the contrary, that if you do not permit him at all, he is even more likely to do so in a place where it causes a blemish, since once he transgresses your words, he will no longer heed them. But if you permit him in a place where it does not cause a blemish, he will not transgress your words and will do it only there (Rashi). Thus, they disagreed on this very reasoning. And the law follows the Rabbis, as we say: 'If you do not permit him, it is worse,' as in the case of the deceased. And if so, how do we rule here in the case of a fire the opposite? However, since the Talmud does not say on this matter of Rava "let us say it is a dispute of Tannaim," as the Talmud says everywhere, one can infer that here all agree, and the reason is hidden from us.

In my humble opinion, it appears that Rashi, of blessed memory, with his sweet language, corrected all of this when he wrote about the statement of Rava: "If you permit him to begin with rescue to such an extent" (see there). The matter is as follows: Indeed, in monetary matters, when the Sages prohibited a Jewish person from engaging in rescue, he should not transgress the words of the Sages and should justify upon himself the judgment of Heaven. However, this is when he is not excessively involved in the rescue. But when he is greatly involved in the rescue permissibly, it naturally follows that due to the preoccupation, he might forget about Shabbat and perform the rescue in a forbidden manner. Therefore, on the contrary, it is necessary to permit him everything that we can possibly permit, because if we do not permit him, it will be worse, and he will forget and extinguish (the fire). But when we permit him, he is not so anxious, since he knows he can rescue permissibly. Thus, the reasoning is as follows: Indeed, there are arguments both ways, but the law is as follows: If he does not begin at all with the rescue, it is certainly better to close off the path entirely. However, if he begins with the rescue - the second way is better, as we will explain with the help of Heaven.

Therefore, we only permitted him the food for three meals, for this is not considered a rescue, as it is a minor matter and does not involve confusion and panic. Hence, we closed the way for him to start rescuing, as Rashi explained. This is not the case with making a barrier with vessels to prevent the fire from spreading—for all vessels, you permit him this. The sages did not consider closing the way for him to prevent the fire from passing. If you forbid him new earthenware vessels and he is engaged with other vessels, when those are insufficient and he is troubled and panicked, he might extinguish the fire entirely. But when you permit him, he will not panic and will not extinguish it. Similarly, with the subterfuge involving garments, since you have to permit him all his garments, if you do not permit more, he will panic and extinguish the fire, as we said. Similarly, with someone who is overtaken by darkness on the road and holds his purse, it is necessary for him to hold his purse before nightfall, and you do not influence him to perform an action to throw it away. Therefore, they sought a permissible way. Similarly, with the case of the firstborn whose blood flows, he is engaged in healing him by placing him in water and seeking a non-Jewish expert, as stated in Siman 332, which is permitted. If we close the way for him, he will panic and act in prohibition. According to this, it is also understandable why some prohibited rescue even through a non-Jew, as will be explained. This seems puzzling, but according to our explanation, it makes sense. They purposely did this to distance him from trouble, as explained.

Tosafot and the poskim wrote in the name of Rabbeinu Tam: Since the reason the Sages prohibited saving [items from a fire] is due to panic, as one might become so preoccupied with saving that they forget it is Shabbat and extinguish the fire, this only applies to the house where the fire is, where the confusion is great. But in a house adjacent to the house where the fire is, where they are merely afraid that the fire might spread to them, they can save whatever they want, because in their case, it is unlikely they will forget it is Shabbat, as the panic is not as great. And some say that this leniency is only permitted in another courtyard, but other houses in the same courtyard have the same rule as the house where the fire is (Bach). And this reasoning makes sense: in the whole courtyard, the panic is great, and there is concern they might forget it is Shabbat, unlike in another courtyard. And this is also implied from the language of Tosafot, where they wrote: "Rabbeinu Tam says... when a fire falls in that house or that courtyard...," meaning even in that courtyard, [the rule applies] to another house.

Rabbeinu, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 2: There are those who permit moving money and other muktzeh items to save them from a fire or from thieves coming to steal them, for in a situation of loss, there is no need to be concerned about the prohibition of muktzeh. However, others prohibit this. And even instructing a non-Jew to move merchandise that is being damaged by rain, there is one who prohibits this. The explanation is: The Tur brought from the Sefer HaTerumah that they permitted the prohibition of muktzeh due to financial loss, such as in the case of a fire or to save from theft, just as we find in the case of one who is overtaken by darkness on the road, that it is permitted to move his money, for in a situation of loss, they did not uphold the prohibition of muktzeh. Therefore, neighbors, as explained, who can save whatever they want – can even save money and other muktzeh items. And what was prohibited in the house where the fire is, even permitted items, is due to the concern that one might come to extinguish, as explained. But in other houses where this concern does not exist, as mentioned – it is permitted to save even muktzeh items.

Even according to this opinion, it is only to save [items] to a courtyard that is enclosed (eruv), but to one that is not enclosed—they did not permit, and certainly not to a karmelit (semi-public domain). And regarding this, it is taught: One may save a book cover with the book even though there are coins inside, but coins without a book—it is forbidden (Beit Yosef in the name of Sefer HaTerumah). And even though they permitted [the violation of] the prohibition of muktzeh, nonetheless, the prohibition of carrying to a courtyard that is not enclosed is more stringent. And even though with regard to a corpse they were stricter about the prohibition of muktzeh than the prohibition of transferring (as explained above in Siman 311), this is because there is a remedy for the prohibition of muktzeh by means of a loaf of bread or an infant (and this is the intention of Rashi, Shabbat 94b, s.v. "to exclude," see there). And that which they permitted transferring to a karmelit in the case of a corpse is because the honor of the dead is more stringent than monetary considerations. And that which is clarified in Siman 267 that one who forgot a purse in a courtyard is not permitted [to violate] the prohibition of muktzeh, this is because it was due to negligence in forgetting. But in the case of a fire or other unavoidable circumstances, where there was no negligence, they permitted the prohibition of muktzeh, and this is the opinion of Sefer HaTerumah, the Sefer Mitzvot Gadol, and the Sefer Mitzvot Katan.

The Tur disagrees with this, and this is the position of those who prohibit. The Tur wrote the reason: that the permission given to someone who was overtaken by nightfall on the way to carry muktzeh less than four cubits at a time was in order to prevent him from violating a Torah prohibition of carrying four cubits in the public domain. But in cases of coercion, this concern does not exist, for he fears to carry them out because of them, and furthermore, even if he does carry them out, there is no Torah prohibition for us since we do not have a public domain. Similarly, in the case of a fire, there is no concern of extinguishing, since it is in another house, as explained there. And the Tur could have also said regarding fire that we have no concern of extinguishing, for according to what he ruled like Rabbi Shimon regarding a labor that is not needed for its own sake, there is no Torah prohibition of extinguishing, and I wonder why he did not write this. The leading later authorities agreed with the ruling of the Sefer HaTerumah (Beit Yosef and Magen Avraham, section 3), that indeed, besides carrying, there are no other Torah concerns, for he can dig in the ground and bury them or similar actions (there).

Even according to the Sefer HaTerumot, it is only permissible in cases of bandits or fire, because the situation is urgent and one might transgress a Torah prohibition. But if rain falls on merchandise that is muktzeh (set aside), it is forbidden according to all opinions to have a Jew do anything, because in this case, the urgency is not such that we fear he will come to a Torah prohibition. However, through a non-Jew it is permitted, as we mentioned earlier in Siman 307, that for merchandise that is being ruined, it is permissible to call a non-Jew for assistance, as it says there. The Tur wrote that even to instruct a non-Jew to move merchandise that is being damaged by rain, there are those who forbid it. And earlier in Siman 307, when we permitted it, we did not permit explicitly instructing him to save it, but rather to call him, and he will see for himself, or to say: "Anyone who saves will not lose," as we wrote there, and there we explained it in detail with God's help.

And behold, according to what we have explained, even the permission granted by Sefer HaTerumot is only for houses adjacent to the fire in another courtyard, and not in the house where the fire is. For in that house, only three meals are permitted to be saved, and all the more so other items. However, there are those who interpret that the intention of Sefer HaTerumot is even in the house where the fire is, and although they only permitted saving food for three meals, this applies to simple items where there is no concern that one might intentionally desecrate the Sabbath, but rather the concern is due to forgetting it is the Sabbath. Therefore, they did not permit saving a lot. But for money and valuable items, where the concern is that one might intentionally desecrate the Sabbath because a person does not restrain himself regarding his money, as in the case of one whose way was darkened, on the contrary, they permitted it so that he would not come to a Torah prohibition. And with this reasoning, the contradictions we brought in section 13 can be resolved. (This reasoning is found in Beit Yosef in the name of Rabbi Yosef Ibn Abuhav, as implied by the Ran, and in Taz subparagraph 2 there, and the Bach rejected it with both hands. It is questionable whether one can rely on this opinion, but we practice according to this opinion.)

We have already written that one can save three meals for each member of his household. There is one who wrote in these words: "It appears to me that even if he saved a lot of bread, each member of his household is permitted to save three meals' worth of food, as each person is allowed three meals" (Magen Avraham, Section 4). And it seems to me that this is only the case when he saved a lot, not for his household but for himself, and thereby violated the decree of the Sages. However, if he saved for his household, why would we permit them to save for themselves? After all, it has already been saved for them. And it was said in the Gemara that if he saved coarse bread, he can later save fine bread. But if he saved fine bread, he is not permitted to later save coarse bread. Similarly, if he saved meat, he can save fish afterwards, and likewise with other types of food. And for drinks, he can prepare for the entire day.

One may rescue (food) from Yom Kippur for Shabbat, if Yom Kippur falls on Friday, but not from Shabbat for Yom Kippur if Yom Kippur falls on Sunday, because the eating of Yom Kippur is at night, and he can prepare then. Now, this law does not apply to us, since Yom Kippur does not fall on either Friday or Sunday, and this could have been the case when the months were sanctified based on sighting (of the new moon). However, there is a practical difference for us when Yom Kippur falls on Thursday, and one knows that on Friday he will not be able to obtain anything, he is allowed to rescue (food) for Shabbat (Magen Avraham, section 6). And from Yom Kippur to the night after Yom Kippur, one may rescue one meal. And for a sick person, an elderly person, or someone with a great appetite, one may rescue as for an average person, since we do not follow his individual needs but rather the majority of people. (And the reason they did not permit rescuing from Shabbat to the night after Yom Kippur is because they did not want the burden of Shabbat to fall on the night after Yom Kippur, unlike Yom Kippur which is the usual practice).

And that which we only save food for three meals, this is specifically when saving with two vessels. But when saving with one vessel, one can save even a lot, since it is all considered one burden and one effort, and there is no concern that he will forget about Shabbat and come to extinguish. Not only that, but even if he had many vessels filled with food, and he spread out his cloak and poured from the vessels into the cloak and saved them all – this is also permitted, since they are carried in one load, and they are all in one vessel, which is the cloak. But to place the vessels in the cloak and carry them together is forbidden, since they are in separate vessels, they are considered as multiple loads.

It is permitted to save all his utensils needed for meals, as well as cups and jugs necessary for drinking for the entire day. He may wear as many clothes as he can, take them out, and remove them, and then return to wear and save more clothes, and then remove them again, and keep doing this. However, with food, they did not permit doing this multiple times, each time for three meals, due to the concern of extinguishing, as we have written. But with wearing clothes, there is no such concern, because since it is only permitted through wearing, he will naturally remember that it is Shabbat and will not come to extinguish (Taz, section 5, in the name of the Rashba). Nonetheless, there is an opinion that even with wearing, they only permitted it once, meaning to wear and take out, as this seems to be the implication from the language of the Rambam (Beit Yosef).

And he says to others: 'Come and save for yourselves,' meaning that it should be for yourselves, and each person saves food for three meals and wears as much as they can. As explained in the Talmud (120a), there are three levels among those who save: someone who wants to completely keep it for themselves can do so, since by saying 'save for yourselves' he has rendered it ownerless. If he had not said this, he would not be able to keep it, as this is not like saving from a river, bandits, or fire, where the owners could have saved it through a non-Jew or others who would not take it for themselves (Magen Avraham, subsection 11). Saving from a fire is considered when saving it directly from the fire, where there was no time to save it otherwise. However, someone who is pious and waives his own rights does not benefit from this at all, and returns the items to the owners without any compensation, not even for their effort, as it appears like payment for Shabbat. 

There is, however, a middle path for someone who fears Heaven: not wanting to keep it completely, knowing that the statement 'save for yourselves' was made out of necessity and not willingly, yet not wanting to toil for nothing - he returns it to the owners and receives his wages. This is not considered payment for Shabbat, since by law it entirely belongs to him (Rashi), and furthermore, initially, he did not intend to take a wage (there). Therefore, if he returns it, he cannot later demand his wages against the will of the owners, as the owners might say to him: 'Didn't you give it to me, and presumably, you saved it to return it to me, not intending for a wage?' However, if the owners give them compensation for their effort, they can accept it, and this is also derived from the words of Maimonides, as explained there. (This seems to me to be the correct understanding, as explicitly stated by the Maharshal, and the Magen Avraham in subsection 13 differentiates between saving with permission and saving with prohibition, comparing this to the laws in Choshen Mishpat, section 183, but this is not a valid comparison as explained by the Eliyah Rabbah. What Maimonides wrote, that the reason this is not considered payment for Shabbat is that there is neither labor nor prohibition involved, is not the main reason; the main reason is as explained by Rashi. The explanation is: if there were labor and prohibition, we would not allow him to receive payment, as who requested this of him? And understand this well).

Our teacher, Rabbi Yosef Karo, wrote in section 10: "All rescue that we mentioned is only to another courtyard that is merged, but not to one that is not merged." And Rabbi Moshe Isserles wrote on this: "And there are those who are lenient even to one that is not merged." They did not explain their words, for certainly there is no opinion that permits rescuing food, drink, and utensils to a courtyard that is not merged. Rather, it certainly refers to wearing clothes, where Rabbi Isserles held that the first opinion prohibits even wearing clothes to a courtyard that is not merged, and so held the commentators (Bach, Taz, section 7, and Magen Avraham, section 14). Their reasoning must be that even though it is in the manner of wearing, since it is a manner of rescue, it is not permitted to a courtyard that is not merged. And it is surprising to say this because what is stated in the Mishnah there: "and he wears all that he can wear" does not refer to the earlier case, to rescue to a merged courtyard. For only with food, drink, and utensils that he carries in his hands is it called rescue, but this is called wearing, for since he is wearing them, their rescue is not noticeable at all.

And I have seen that they have held that this is the opinion of the Rambam and the Tur, but I say that from the Rambam it is clearly proven not so, for he wrote: "Therefore, they decreed that one should only save the food necessary for Shabbat, and the utensils needed for use on Shabbat, and the clothes that one can wear... And if they did not establish an eiruv - even his food and utensils should not be saved," end quote. It is clearly written "his food and utensils" and clothes are not mentioned, from which it is inferred that clothes are permitted even without an eiruv. And also the Tur, who wrote: "And one does not save except to a courtyard with an eiruv," was not referring to clothes, for they are not in the category of saving, and this is also the intent of our master, the Beit Yosef, for he did not mention this in his great work. And it is obvious that carrying not in the manner of clothing is forbidden even for clothes and for anything (Magen Avraham there). And in the Sefer HaTerumah, it is explicitly written that clothes are permitted also without an eiruv (and all the words of the Bach need investigation, see there).

The Tur writes that the author of the Sefer HaTerumah wrote that any rescue effort we spoke of, beyond which one is not permitted to rescue, applies to courtyards and alleyways adjacent to public domains and also not covered, as they are similar to public domains. Therefore, it is not permitted even if there is an eruv, except to rescue food for three meals and the utensils needed for Shabbat. However, to rescue to a house in his fellow’s courtyard, where there is an eruv, he can carry out whatever he wants. Even in a courtyard, he can only carry to his fellow's courtyard, but to his own courtyard, which does not require an eruv, he can carry whatever he wants. 

The Tur disagrees with this, arguing that since the reason is so that one should not be preoccupied with rescuing and come to extinguish the fire, it makes no difference whether it is to a house in his fellow’s courtyard or to his fellow's courtyard, and similarly, whether it is his own courtyard or his fellow's courtyard. There is an opinion that the Tur does not disagree regarding his own courtyard, because since it is adjacent to his house, there is no preoccupation and he will not come to extinguish (Taz, subparagraph 8). 

The reason of the Sefer HaTerumah for permitting in his fellow's house seems to me that since he permits in the house and not in the courtyard, there is a noticeable difference, and he will not come to extinguish, as we said regarding changing clothes many times, as stated in paragraph 26. (And concerning the Taz's difficulty on the Sefer HaTerumah from Rav Huna, it is true that the Sefer HaTerumah would rule according to Rabbi Abba, who differentiates between this courtyard and another courtyard, as explained by the Eliyah Rabbah, subparagraph 8, where it is clear that the Sefer HaTerumah ruled according to Rabbi Abba, and also the Smag, Smak, and Mordechai ruled like Sefer HaTerumah).

The Sages taught in the Mishnah: "All sacred writings may be saved from a fire," meaning even to a courtyard that has not been combined [with an eruv]. However, they should be carried through an alleyway that has three walls with a side post, but without a side post, it is forbidden. And know that in the Jerusalem Talmud it says that according to Rabbi Shimon, who states that an act not needed for its own sake is exempt from Torah prohibition, one may even extinguish the fire to save the sacred writings, as there is nothing that is a rabbinic prohibition that stands before sacred writings. And the decisors wrote that since this is not mentioned in our Talmud, it implies that they hold that even according to Rabbi Shimon, extinguishing the fire is forbidden, and only carrying them to a courtyard that has not been combined [with an eruv] is permitted.

It is known that, according to Torah law, oral teachings are forbidden to be written down, and written texts do not have sanctity unless they are written in Ashurit script and in the Holy Tongue (Hebrew). Therefore, if they are written in another script or another language, they are not saved from a fire, even to a courtyard where an eruv has been made. Even on a weekday, it is forbidden to read from them; rather, they should be left to be destroyed on their own (Rambam, ibid.). However, if they were written in ink or red dye, even though it is not a permanent writing, since they are written in Ashurit script and in the Holy Tongue, they are saved from a fire. The margins of books, whether above, below, between sections, between pages, at the beginning, or at the end of the book, are not saved. Similarly, blessings and amulets, even though they contain letters of the Name and many matters of Torah, are not saved from a fire (ibid.).

A Torah scroll from which one can gather eighty-five letters from complete words, meaning if the collection of letters is not from complete words - it is nothing. However, if one can gather eighty-five letters from complete words, where the total number of words will contain these letters - one can save it from a fire. And why do we need this number: corresponding to the section "And it came to pass when the ark set forward" which is considered as a book by itself, and therefore it has the inverted nun symbols and it contains eighty-five letters. Therefore, this number is considered as a complete book regarding saving it from a fire. And even if among the words there are Aramaic words, like 'Yegar Sahadutha' - one can also save it. And even a section that does not have this total but contains divine names, which are sacred names - one can also save it. Therefore, the section "And it came to pass when the ark set forward" even if it is missing words, since it has divine names - one can save it from a fire. All the more so if one wrote laws and legends which are forbidden to save, since it is forbidden to write them at all.

All of this applied in their times, but nowadays, when it has been permitted to write down laws, homilies, and all of the Oral Torah due to "It is time to act for the Lord," for otherwise the Torah would have already been forgotten by Israel, Heaven forbid — we save all holy books from a fire. Nevertheless, the Written Torah takes precedence in rescue, and similarly, a Torah scroll takes precedence over other books, even if they are written in any language and even if written with ink or red dye and not in the Assyrian script, because not everyone can write in Assyrian script. Likewise, printed holy books are saved, as well as prayer books and texts of blessings whether written or printed. Even translations that include scriptural verses, like 'Yegar Sahadutha' written in the sacred tongue, or 'Thus you shall say unto them' in Jeremiah, and sacred writings in other languages familiar to the people are saved. This is specifically when they were written and printed for the sake of holiness and not for any other purpose, for those written for other purposes are not to be saved even on weekdays.

There are those who say that the Megillat Esther, since it does not contain the name of God, if it is not written in its proper form, i.e., in Assyrian script on parchment and with ink, does not possess sanctity that would require saving it from a fire. But this is not understandable, for since nowadays it is permissible to read and write it in any language, why should it not be saved from a fire? Therefore, it seems that it should be saved even if written on paper and not in the Holy Tongue, but not when written with other substances like sap or red ink, for ink is readily available and it can be written with ink. This seems to be the main ruling (Magen Avraham, section 118). As for amulets that contain verses, they should not be saved from a fire because they do not possess sanctity and are not made for reading, thus the reasoning of 'It is time to act for the Lord' does not apply to them. However, some say they should be saved, since permission was given to write due to 'It is time to act,' so there is also permission to write amulets (Taz, section 12). The primary opinion follows the first view (Magen Avraham).

One may save a Torah scroll case along with the Torah scroll, even if there are coins inside it, and similarly, one may save a tefillin bag along with the tefillin, as well as other sacred writings. One is not obligated to shake out the coins, for out of respect for the sanctity which is for the sake of Heaven, we also allow the saving of coins, which are for mundane use, even from a house that is on fire, and even to a courtyard that is not enclosed by an eruv. Even if one placed tefillin in a purse full of coins, one can save them from the fire or from thieves and robbers, to a place where one can save the tefillin. Some say this applies only if they were placed there before Shabbat, but if they were placed there on Shabbat for the sake of saving them, it does not help. In truth, there is no disagreement: before Shabbat, it is permitted even if placed there for the sake of saving; on Shabbat, if placed there for the sake of saving, all agree it is forbidden. However, if they were not placed there for the sake of saving, it is certainly permitted. (Magen Avraham 320:20 and Turei Zahav 320:13, and it is difficult with the Turei Zahav who wrote that this is in a house where there is a fire, for in another house it is permitted as muktzeh even for the coins themselves, and there is a practical difference regarding saving to a courtyard that is not enclosed by an eruv, that by themselves it is forbidden, but with tefillin it is permitted. Delve into this matter.)

Some permit rescuing a purse full of money by means of a loaf of bread or a child, even in a place where rescuing money is forbidden, such as from a house where there is a fire, as stated in Section 18. Nevertheless, by means of a loaf or a child, it is permitted, and even to place them initially now in order to rescue the money, even if the money is more valuable than the loaf. And although it was said that they only permitted a loaf or a child for a corpse, nevertheless, in the case of a fire, they permitted it, but only to a private domain, not to a courtyard that is not enclosed, and certainly not to a karmelit (a type of semi-public domain). This ruling does not follow the opinion in Section 22, which holds that muktzeh (items that are set aside) is permitted even in a house with a fire, for according to that opinion, there is no need for a loaf or a child. And it has already been explained that books can be rescued even to a courtyard that is not enclosed and to an alley that has not been merged, provided it has three walls with a side post.

And they wrote in the name of a Gaon that it is permissible to tell a non-Jew to save books even through the public domain, for there is no rabbinic prohibition of speaking that stands in the way of saving holy texts. And everything that is permissible to save from a fire is permissible to save from water and other things that destroy. And it has already been clarified that the blank pages of books are not saved from a fire, for they lack sanctity. Therefore, bookbinders cut off the blank pages and discard them, but once they have been studied upon, it is forbidden to cut off the blank pages, and the earlier authorities instituted a penalty for this (Magen Avraham section 24), even though they are not saved from a fire. And it is obvious that heretical books, books of apostates, and books of idol worship that have sacred writings in them are not saved from a fire even though they contain divine names, and even on weekdays, it is forbidden to read from them, and they should be burned along with the mentions of the divine names.

The verse states: "You shall not do any work." It is the doing that is forbidden, but causing indirectly [grama] is permitted. Therefore, it is permissible to make a barrier with vessels filled with water in front of a fire, even with new vessels that will certainly break and the water will extinguish the fire, for this is only indirect causation [grama] and is permitted in a case of loss. All the more so, if a box has caught fire on one side, one may spread a goat skin on the opposite side to prevent it from burning, for here it is not even an indirect extinguishing, but merely preventing the fire from spreading further. Similarly, if a garment has caught fire, one may spread it out and cover oneself with it, and if it gets extinguished, it gets extinguished, and there is no concern, for this too is only indirect causation [grama], as one is not directly engaged in extinguishing it. Therefore, some say that one should not intend for this to happen, meaning one should not perform actions for this purpose, such as running, jumping, or shaking to extinguish it, but rather cover oneself with it in the usual manner. Likewise, if a Torah scroll has caught fire, one may spread it out and read from it, and if it gets extinguished, it gets extinguished. It is also permitted to cover a candle with a bowl so that it does not catch onto a beam, as stated in Siman 277.

And although causing extinguishment is permitted, nevertheless, some say that if a garment has caught fire, it is forbidden to place liquids on it away from the fire so that when the fire reaches the liquids, it will be extinguished, because causing extinguishment is only permitted through an interruption, like with pots full of water, but not without an interruption, as this appears like direct extinguishing (see Tosafot at the end of [the tractate] Kira). And some permit it, arguing that this too is considered causing extinguishment. And some permit all liquids except for water, due to the issue of laundering, which is a derivative of whitening [the garment], and this seems to be the main ruling.

A non-Jew who comes to extinguish a fire, a Jew does not need to prevent him, because he is acting on his own intention. And even though he knows that the Jew benefits from this, in any case, he is doing it for his own will and benefit, as he knows he will not suffer a loss. This is not similar to lighting a candle for a Jew in Siman 276, which is forbidden for the Jew to benefit from the light, because in that case, the Jew's body itself enjoys it. But a minor who comes to extinguish - we do not allow him, and we need to prevent him, because he is acting based on the intention of his father or the elder over him. And even a Jew's hired worker has the same law as any other non-Jew.

Our Sages said (121a): "In the case of a fire, it is permitted to say: 'Anyone who extinguishes it will not lose,'" meaning one may stand among non-Jews and say in their language, 'Anyone who extinguishes will not lose.' And even though it appears as if they are his messengers, since he did not explicitly command them, they are not considered his messengers, just as in the case of one who is forbidden from deriving benefit, who can say: 'Anyone who feeds [the person] will not lose' (Ketubot, beginning of Chapter "Hamadir"). And even if the non-Jew is not present, one can call him to come and say this to him, even though he will certainly extinguish it when he arrives. Similarly, in any sudden damage, such as if a barrel of wine breaks, one can call a non-Jew even though he will certainly fix it. Indeed, according to most authorities who follow Rabbi Shimon, who holds that a labor not needed for its own sake is exempt, we should permit explicitly telling a non-Jew to extinguish, as it is a double rabbinic prohibition in a case of great loss. However, they nevertheless prohibited it because a person is anxious about their property and, if permitted, might come to extinguish it themselves out of distress, forgetting it is Shabbat, as explained. Therefore, in such a case, calling him or saying: 'Anyone who extinguishes will not lose,' or both together, the Sages did not see fit to forbid. It is obvious that holy books are the first to be saved before other items, and they precede even sacred writings, and this applies even on weekdays.

And there is no need to question after it has been clarified that it is forbidden to extinguish a fire on Shabbat, and even the act of saving [possessions] was prohibited as a decree lest one come to extinguish [the fire], and even to explicitly tell a non-Jew to extinguish it is forbidden. If so, from where did the custom arise among us to extinguish the fire on Shabbat? However, this matter has been explained by our early authorities, that among us every fire is considered a danger to life, and therefore, on the contrary, it is an obligation for us to extinguish it, even when the fire is at a non-Jew's place. This is explained in the Or Zarua HaGadol and in the Mordechai, chapter "Kol Kitvei," and in the Hagahot Ashri, chapter 4 of Eruvin, and in the Terumat HaDeshen, siman 58, and our teacher the Rema brought them in brief (and in section 9 we have written another valid reason, see there).

And this is his wording: "All the laws mentioned regarding the laws of a fire: these apply in their times, but in our times, since it is a concern for danger to life, the earlier and later authorities, of blessed memory, have written that it is permissible to extinguish their fire on Shabbat, because there is a danger to life, and one who is quick to act is praiseworthy. Nevertheless, everything depends on the situation: if they are certainly safe and there is no danger involved - it is forbidden to extinguish; but if there is a questionable danger - it is permissible to extinguish, even if the fire is in the homes of non-Jews, and this is the practice. And specifically to extinguish the fire, which is a work that is not needed for its own sake and there is danger if it is not extinguished, but it is forbidden to desecrate Shabbat to save money. And if one transgresses and desecrates - he must fast for 40 days, on Mondays and Thursdays, and should not drink wine or eat meat, and should give 18 simple coins to charity instead of the sin-offering. And if he wishes to redeem the fast, he should give 12 simple coins to charity for each day." End of quote. And regarding what he wrote about not eating meat, his intention is for the night following the fast.

And this need for repentance is when one desecrates the Sabbath, even in a rabbinical prohibition. But regarding the actual extinguishing itself, since we consider it a matter of danger, there is no need for repentance. On the contrary, we prevent him from doing so to ensure they do not become lax in rescuing [from fire], and unfortunately, we see in many fires that lives are lost. And for handling muktzeh, there is no need for repentance (as stated in Shulchan Aruch in the name of Magen Avraham), since it has been clarified that handling muktzeh is permitted in a case of loss. And it is mentioned in the Gemara (Shabbat 12b) about someone who erred on the Sabbath by tilting a lamp, who wrote in his notebook: When the Temple is rebuilt, he will need to bring a sin offering, as mentioned there. And the value of simple coins we do not know today, and we are accustomed to consider this as a perutah, and a perutah is one-sixth of a kopek in our country Russia, and eighteen simple coins are three kopeks. We do not have an accurate tradition regarding this, and from the coins mentioned in the books, we do not know what they are. (Nevertheless, every God-fearing person should deeply contemplate the sanctity of the holy Sabbath, for it is holy, and not be lenient in trivial matters, and pay close attention.)

A barrel of wine or oil that broke on Shabbat—the Sages decreed that one should not save all that they can, but rather food for three meals before the evening meal, food for two meals before the morning meal, and food for one meal before the third meal, similar to a fire in the previous section. And the reason is also the same as there, that we are concerned that due to the urgency of saving, one might forget that it is Shabbat and bring vessels through the public domain to save. And even now that we do not have a public domain, we are concerned that due to the urgency, one might repair the barrel. And even if the barrel is completely broken and the liquids have fallen to the ground, one should not gather from the ground more than what is needed for Shabbat, for we decree that one might soak it up. This means placing a sponge in the liquids to pour them back into a vessel. And even if the sponge has a handle, so there is no concern that one might wring it out, it is still forbidden, because using a sponge is a weekday activity and it is forbidden to do so on Shabbat. Additionally, there is a concern that one might forget it is Shabbat and intentionally wring out the sponge, and therefore, with a sponge, it is forbidden even for what is needed for Shabbat.

And similarly, it is forbidden to smear oil, which means inserting one's hand into the oil and having a lot of oil stick around his hand, then wiping it off into a vessel so that the oil drips from his hand into the vessel, in order not to act as he would on a weekday. And just as the law regarding a conflagration is that one can save a lot with one vessel – so too here, it is considered one act of saving as we mentioned there. And similarly, he can tell others, "Come and save for yourselves," following all the laws explained regarding a conflagration as mentioned there. And as we wrote there in the name of the Sefer HaTerumah, the prohibition applies only to his friend's courtyard, even if they made an eruv, because it is exposed, but not to the house within his friend's courtyard. And similarly, it is permitted in his own courtyard, as mentioned there. So too here, if the saving is to his own courtyard or to the house within his friend's courtyard, he can save as much as he wishes. And even the Tur, who disagrees there, might agree here because the urgency is not as great as in a conflagration (and according to this, the Taz's difficulty in subparagraph 2 is resolved, see there and examine it well).

Some say that all of this applies when the vessel is significantly broken or cracked, as the alarm is great, and we are concerned that one might forget it is Shabbat and carry the vessel through a public domain or fix the vessel or mop up as mentioned. However, if it is merely cracked and drips drop by drop, which does not cause such alarm, it is permitted to save with many vessels, and also to catch and combine when it is broken at the top of the roof as will be explained regarding catching and combining, which is prohibited in the case of a break, but allowed when it drips drop by drop.

And if the barrel breaks on the roof of his house, how can he save the three meals? For ascending to the roof is certainly forbidden because it is considered a weekday activity. He brings a vessel and places it on the ground beneath the barrel so that the contents can flow into it. This vessel can hold even a large amount, as it has been explained that with one vessel, he can save as much as he wants, provided he does not bring another vessel to catch the wine or oil spilling from the air, or to attach the vessel to the roof so that the wine or oil spills into it. For if you permit him another vessel, there is concern that he will become frantic and bring many vessels. But with one vessel that he is permitted to use, he can save even through catching or attaching.

And know that there is a dispute among the great authorities regarding whether a single vessel placed on the ground is insufficient for three meals, if it is permissible to bring another vessel to collect and combine. There are those who permit it (Taz, Orach Chaim 325:7), and there are those who forbid it (Pri Megadim, Mishbetzos Zahav 325:7). It appears that the primary opinion is that it is forbidden, for otherwise, what is the Talmud teaching us by stating that one should not collect and combine? For without this, it is already forbidden to save with two vessels more than for three meals (and what the Tosafot Shabbat writes that it is the usual practice is forced). Nevertheless, it seems to me that it is permissible, if we are diligent in understanding why the Talmud (Shabbat 117b) says, "provided that he does not bring another vessel to collect and combine." It should have said, "provided that he does not bring another vessel," as it is stated regarding a fire, where saving is permitted only with one vessel.
