Therefore, it appears in my humble opinion that certainly, if one can position two or three vessels opposite the spout of the barrel, it is permissible, for there is no concern of an increase in vessels, since he is only permitted to use the spout of the barrel and no more, and it is not analogous to a fire, obviously. And this is what the Talmud states, that another vessel by means of collecting and combining is forbidden, for he is not permitted two types of saving: one with the vessel on the ground and one with the vessel in his hand collecting or combining. But this is all when it is sufficient for three meals, but when it is not sufficient, it is permitted also by means of collecting and combining, as will be explained regarding guests.

If guests arrive and he needs a lot of beverage, he is permitted to bring another vessel and catch the beverage in a different vessel and combine them. However, he should not catch and combine the beverage and only then invite guests; rather, he should first invite guests and then catch and combine the beverage. He should not deceive by bringing guests who do not need to eat, but there is an opinion that according to the Rambam, it is permissible to do so (Magen Avraham, section 2), since deception in rabbinic matters is allowed, as we say in Tractate Shabbat (139b). Therefore, if he transgressed and did this, catching and combining the beverage and then inviting guests, it is certainly permitted.

If grape juice flows from a vat of grapes that have not yet been trodden, the liquid that comes out of them is prohibited on Shabbat because it is considered muktzeh. How can one place a vessel underneath it? When the liquids fall into the vessel, the vessel becomes a base for a prohibited item and it is forbidden to move it, thereby nullifying the vessel's preparedness. One should not question this by saying that it is forbidden to save it for another reason, namely that they only allowed saving what is needed for Shabbat, and this liquid is prohibited due to muktzeh. It can be said that we are dealing with a case where it drips drop by drop and not in a continuous flow, as it has been explained that in such a case one can save even more than what is needed for Shabbat. Therefore, due to the essence of the rescue, it would be permitted. But how should one handle the vessel? (This is the intention of the Magen Avraham section 3, which has puzzled many, as the Magen Avraham himself explained).

And this is what should be done: Place there his bed or his table and establish his place of sitting there, and then the leaking water will be in front of him like a "chamber pot" because it dirties the ground and creates mud. He can place a vessel there to collect the leaking water so that it does not make mud. He does not nullify the vessel from its preparedness since when it fills up, he will pour from it into another vessel in order to return it under the leak so that it does not make mud. This is such that the other vessel is attached or very large, making it impossible to place it under the bucket. With a "chamber pot," there is no prohibition of moving muktzeh, as stated in Siman 308. And even though it is forbidden to intentionally create a "chamber pot" as stated there, here it is permitted due to the potential loss of his property. However, in truth, one cannot pour into another vessel, for if so, he nullifies it from its preparedness. And even though one might say that when it is attached, there is no issue of nullifying a vessel from its preparedness, as stated in Siman 265, where the reason is due to building, since it is already built. However, there is someone there who holds that the prohibition is due to dismantling, as stated there. Therefore, they wrote that the solution is to pour into a basin, which is already prohibited because of the liquids it contains. This is what our master the Beit Yosef wrote in paragraph 4, as stated there. But I do not understand, for the basin overflows, so how can one pour into it? This requires further investigation. There is another solution: to place under it a vessel with water, and the wine will be nullified in the water progressively, and it will be permissible to move. And even if the wine increases over the water, there is no concern of muktzeh prohibition, for regarding yayin nesekh there are those who are lenient, as stated in Yoreh De'ah Siman 134, and all the more so in the matter of muktzeh one may rely on this. And regarding something that has a permitted use, there is no prohibition, for this applies only to its own kind and not to a different kind, as stated in Yoreh De'ah Siman 102, as stated there.

If fruits were scattered in a courtyard, one here and one there, and they are spread over a large area of the courtyard - he may gather them little by little and eat. But he should not gather them and put them into a basket or a container, so that he does not act in the manner he does on a weekday. However, if they fell in a non-scattered manner - he may put them even into a basket or a container, unless small stones and dirt from the courtyard got mixed with them, in which case, he may only gather them one by one and eat, due to the prohibition of selecting, and how can he gather them and place them into a container and a basket when he is selecting them from the dirt, as is explained in Siman 319 there, and also his intention is not to nullify the prohibition.

Sowing is considered a principal category of labor, and it was performed in the Tabernacle where they planted the herbs needed for the anointing oil and to dye the blue wool. Whether one sows seeds, grain, or vegetables, or whether one plants trees, layers, grafts, or prunes—meaning to cut some branches so that they will grow—all of these are principal categories of labor, and they are all one principal category. The only difference is that one involves seeds and the other involves trees, but they are essentially the same because in each case the person's intent is to promote growth. This is the essence of sowing. 

In the Jerusalem Talmud, in the chapter "Klal Gadol," it says: "Anything that promotes the growth of fruit is liable for sowing. This includes planting, layering, grafting, pruning, trimming, thinning, shaping, fertilizing, dusting, fumigating, worming, cutting, applying oil, watering, perforating, and making holes—all these actions are intended to promote growth, and therefore one is liable for sowing." All these activities apply to trees, as explained in the tractate Sheviit.

The derivatives of planting: One who waters plants and trees on Shabbat - this is a derivative of planting or of sowing, and similarly one who soaks wheat and barley and the like in water - this is a derivative of planting and one is liable (Rambam, Chapter 8). And what is the measure: One who plants any amount – is liable, and similarly for one who plants and in all cases, and similarly for one who soaks wheat and barley in any amount – is liable (there), for even regarding carrying out we learned at the beginning of the chapter "One who stores away: 'For planting… and he takes it out - he is liable for any amount,'" and all the more so for planting itself. And although regarding plowing the Talmud asks (103b) about what is taught: one who plows any amount – is liable, for what use is it, as will be explained, but regarding planting this question does not apply, for a single seed is suitable for planting, and similarly for planting trees and all matters.

Plowing is a primary category of work, and there is no difference between plowing before sowing and plowing after sowing, such as in the Land of Israel where the ground is hard and after sowing it is necessary to plow again. This too is considered plowing (Gemara 73b). The Jerusalem Talmud states a general principle: just as plowing was done in the Tabernacle, where they would plow to plant herbs. Both the one who plows, and the one who digs, and the one who makes a furrow—they are all considered one category of work (Gemara ibid). Each of these is a primary category of work, as they all serve the purpose of loosening the soil (Rashi), and each one involves digging in the ground (Rambam ibid).

The derivatives of plowing: The Rambam writes at the beginning of Chapter 8: "One who weeds around the roots of trees, or trims grasses, or prunes shoots in order to improve the land - this is a derivative of plowing. Similarly, one who levels the surface of a field, such as by lowering a mound and smoothing it, or filling a valley - is liable because of plowing, as is one who smooths out holes." And in the Jerusalem Talmud there: Rabbi Chiya taught: Digging, trenching, planting - these are derivatives of plowing. And the Gemara implies that this is a principal category, as it is written. The Jerusalem Talmud further states: Anything that benefits the land is liable because of plowing: digging, trenching, planting, hoeing, weeding, fertilizing, sweeping, watering clods, clearing the fields, cutting small trees in the forests so they thicken and grow, lighting a fire in thickets of reeds to burn them so they do not hinder plowing, similarly in a palm grove where bad palm trees are burned so they do not hinder plowing, preparing the sides of a water channel for planting, meaning fixing the sides, removing stones, building terraces in the land itself, filling depressions under olive trees, making basins for grapevines, and anything that benefits the land - is liable because of plowing. End quote.

The measurement for plowing is stated in the Mishnah (103b): "One who plows, even any small amount is liable." And the Gemara asks: "For what purpose is this small amount fit?" It answers: "For planting a single pumpkin seed," as Rashi explains, similar to the Mishkan where it was fit for planting a single stalk of spices. In the Jerusalem Talmud, it says: "How much must one plow to be liable? Rabbi Matanya says: enough to plant a leek. Rabbi Acha says: enough to plant a wheat seedling," and this, too, is any small amount. Its explanation aligns with the Gemara's interpretation. The wheat seedling is the head of the wheat without a crack, and the leek is also a small seed. Similarly, for all its derivatives, any small amount makes one liable, as we learned in the Mishnah: "One who weeds, prunes, or removes small branches, any small amount makes one liable. One who gathers wood or herbs: if to improve the ground, any small amount." Maimonides also wrote there about leveling the field's surface, filling a valley, or leveling pits, that their measurement is any small amount.

Reaping is a primary category of labor, and it was performed in the Tabernacle when they harvested the herbs. One who reaps grain or legumes, or one who picks grapes, or one who harvests dates, or one who gathers olives, or one who plucks figs—all these are considered one primary category of labor, since each of these actions involves removing something from its place of growth. Anyone who removes something from its place of growth is liable for reaping. The derivative form of reaping is plucking by hand, as reaping is typically done with a sickle or a knife, but when one plucks with their hands or with another instrument, it is considered a derivative form of reaping and one is liable.

The Rambam wrote there: "Therefore, if a rock has grass growing on it, or if hops have grown on a bush, or if grass has grown on a barrel, one who plucks them is liable, because that is their place of growth. However, one who plucks from a non-perforated pot is exempt, because that is not its place of growth. A perforated pot, even if it has a small perforation, is considered like the earth, and one who plucks from it is liable." These are his words, indicating the measure for qualifying seeds, as explained at the end of the chapter "HaMetzni'a." 

And know that there is a question about whether there is a difference between a wooden pot and an earthenware pot. In Menachot (84b) regarding the laws of Bikkurim, there is a difference between them: according to Rashi, an earthenware pot does not need to be perforated, and according to Rabeinu Tam, a wooden pot does not require perforation, and a non-perforated pot is considered as if it were perforated. 

Regarding a tree planted in a utensil, concerning the laws of Orlah, it is always considered as if it were perforated, because a tree penetrates deeper, as stated in the Jerusalem Talmud, the first chapter of Orlah, and as written by the Rambam in the tenth chapter of Ma'aser Sheni. Therefore, concerning Shabbat, one who plucks from it is liable.

In the second chapter of Uktzin it is taught: "A cucumber planted in a pot that grew and extended outside the pot is pure," meaning that even if the pot is not perforated, whatever extends outside the pot into the air of the earth is considered connected to it. How is the law regarding Shabbat if one plucks from there, whether one is liable or not, requires further investigation.

However, in practice, there is no difference, because even from a non-perforated pot it is forbidden to pluck on Shabbat, as it is taught (Shabbat 95a): "One who plucks from a perforated pot is liable, and from a non-perforated pot is exempt." All exemptions on Shabbat mean exempt but forbidden. This is also ruled by the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch (see Beit Yosef and Maggid Mishneh, chapter 2 of Bikkurim), though they did not address how this applies to Shabbat.

The measure for reaping is the size of a dried fig, similar to the measures of food regarding carrying, as stated in Siman 301. And it is mentioned in the Gemara (73b): one who prunes the branches of the vine so that they will grow more and he also needs the wood, is liable for two [transgressions], one for reaping and one for planting. But if he does not need the wood, he is only liable for planting. And even according to Rabbi Yehuda, who holds one is liable for a labor that is not needed for its own sake, and thus even if he does not need the wood, he should be liable for reaping, nevertheless, when he does not need the wood, it is not considered reaping at all (Tosafot there). And there is proof for this from the words of the Rambam there, who wrote this law that if one prunes and needs the wood, he is liable for two, see there, and he ruled according to Rabbi Yehuda regarding a labor that is not needed for its own sake. Therefore, it appears to me the opposite: when he needs the wood and his intention is not for the vine to grow more, he is liable for two, and not only according to Rabbi Yehuda, but even according to Rabbi Shimon, since this is a case of an inevitable outcome that he desires.

They also said there: One who cuts alfalfa, which is harvested as fodder and then regrows, is liable for two [transgressions]: one for reaping and one for planting. And one who cuts beets, which is a type of vegetable, is liable for two [transgressions]: one for reaping and one for sowing. Here, they did not say that it must be for fodder or for beets. Similarly, the Rambam wrote there: "Any seed whose harvesting causes it to grow and flourish, such as alfalfa and beets, one who reaps it inadvertently is liable for two sin offerings, etc." End quote. 

It appears that even if there is no need now for the fodder or the beets, nevertheless, since he performed the act in the manner of their harvesting, he is liable even according to Rabbi Shimon, for the reason explained. This is not comparable to trees, for when one prunes and does not need the wood, there is no harvesting issue at all, which is not the case with seeds and vegetables. The reason is that most trees are for fuel from trees that do not bear fruit, as is known. Therefore, when one harvests from a fruit-bearing tree, he must intend it for wood. But for grain and vegetables, which are typically harvested and also improve their growth, one is liable in any case.

The Rambam wrote there: "A mound of dirt upon which grass has grown, if one lifts it from the ground and places it on stakes, one is liable for uprooting. If it was on stakes and one places it on the ground, one is liable for planting. Figs that dried on their trees, and similarly a tree whose fruits dried on it—if one plucks from them on Shabbat, one is liable, even though they are considered as detached regarding impurity." End of quote. According to Rashi and Tosafot at the end of the chapter "HaMotzi Yayin," this mound is only a rabbinic prohibition. See there (refer to the Mishna and Kesef Mishneh and Lechem Mishneh). He further wrote: "One who plucks chicory or twigs, if for human consumption—the measure is like a dried fig; if for an animal—the measure is like a goat's mouthful; if for fuel—the measure is enough to cook an egg." End of quote. Note that chicory is a type of vegetable, and twigs are a type of reeds. When they are still soft, they are for human consumption; when they harden a bit, they are for animals; when they dry, they are for fuel (Rashi 103).

It is stated in the Jerusalem Talmud there: "One who shears sponge, gum, or caroline wood - is liable for reaping and for planting." These are types of trees, and it does not specify that it is only when needed for wood. According to this, it disagrees with our Talmud, and the law is not like that, or it is possible that these are types of trees that are used for fuel, and it is like the grain we explained, that one is liable in any case. And it is not necessarily for fuel, for the same is true if their shearing is usually for another purpose, as is obvious. It also says there: "One who shears coriander, leeks, or celery - is liable for reaping and for planting,” and these are types of vegetables, and it is clear that this is similar to lucerne. It also says there: "One who places a perforated pot on top of another perforated pot - is liable for reaping and for planting,” because the lower one gets blocked and ceases to grow, and the upper one grows from the ground, and this gives some support to the Rambam's opinion in the previous section. And one who reaps sycamore beams - is liable for reaping and for planting, for it is used for building and is like lucerne. And one who smooths - is liable for striking with a hammer, meaning that he smooths and polishes it to be fit for building, and this is the completion of its work.

It also says there: "Those who hunt fish or any creature that you remove from its life source - are liable for harvesting." Refer there. This is a novel idea, and even Maimonides did not mention this. If so, for any act of hunting fish, one would be liable for two transgressions. The commentators explained that it was already caught before Shabbat and was in a vessel of water, and one is only liable for uprooting something from its growth. This is also not understood, for he should be liable for taking a life, as indeed stated in Section 316. I found in the novellae of the Rashba in the chapter "Eight Creeping Things" that this Jerusalem Talmud does not follow the method of our Talmud. Refer there. And in the Gemara (107b): "He inserted his hand into the womb of an animal and detached the fetus inside her - he is liable for uprooting something from its growth," which seemingly is for the reason of harvesting. But Maimonides at the beginning of Chapter 11 considers this among the liabilities for taking a life, refer there. Similarly, the Rashba wrote there in the name of the Ramban, of blessed memory, that this is also the intent of the Gemara, meaning that he separates it from its life source and is liable for taking a life. Refer there.

The sages decreed that one should not climb a tree on Shabbat and Yom Tov, nor use it in any manner while it is still attached to the ground, whether the tree is moist or dry. One should not hang onto it, as a decree lest one might climb and detach [something]. And even though it is explained in Eruvin (100a) that with a dry tree there is no Torah prohibition of detaching, and even its fruits when it is dry, Rashi there explains that there is no Torah prohibition of detaching. And what Rambam wrote, which we brought in section 10: that a tree whose fruits have dried, one who detaches from them on Shabbat is liable, and it is explicitly stated in the Gemara Chullin (127b), this is when the fruits have dried and not the tree, and since the tree draws from the ground, one is liable for detaching its fruits. But when the tree itself has dried, it is entirely considered as detached. (There is a difficulty with the Magen Avraham in section 1 who created a dispute between Rashi and Rambam there, and the Macha Shekel elaborates there, but it is unnecessary. And indeed, the language of the Gemara there: 'figs that shriveled on the tree,' and it can be said specifically shriveled and not dried, and so it appears from the words of Raavad in chapter 2 of Tum'at Ochlin there, but Rambam does not differentiate. However, that which is in Eruvin is a different matter as we said, and so wrote Tosafot in Shabbat 150a s.v. 'attached', that with dry there is no prohibition of detaching, and that which is in Chullin specifically shriveled and not dried according to the opinion of Raavad there, and examine well.)

And perhaps you will ask, if so, why indeed did they prohibit climbing and using a dry tree? However, in this regard, it is stated in Eruvin there that during the rainy season it is certainly prohibited, as one cannot distinguish between a moist tree and a dry one. Additionally, during the summer, there is a concern that one might break off branches from it, which refers to the limbs. This is prohibited by Torah law even with detached branches due to the prohibition of cutting (mechatech). And even if the branches have fallen off, the Sages did not differentiate (Magen Avraham there). 

One should not ask why it is prohibited to use a tree but permitted to walk on grass, as will be explained. They are not comparable; with grass, one will not pluck it with his hands since it has no fruits. The prohibition is due to the concern that one might inadvertently pluck it while walking, which is considered an unintentional act. This is not the case with a tree, where there is a concern that one might intentionally pluck with his hands. Therefore, all trees are prohibited, even those that do not bear fruit, as the Sages did not differentiate. I have not found any decisors who address this issue. (See Jerusalem Talmud, Beitzah chapter 5, halacha 2, and there is a difference between the interpretation of the Korban HaEidah and the Pnei Moshe. Examine it thoroughly).

If one climbed a tree on Shabbat, they penalized him not to descend until nightfall, if he ascended intentionally. However, if he ascended unintentionally, he is permitted to descend. And if he ascended on the eve of Shabbat, even intentionally and even if his intention was to remain there on Shabbat, nevertheless, since he ascended while it was still day, they did not penalize him, and he may descend. And there are those who say that this is specifically if he ascended with the intention to descend while it was still day, but if he ascended with the intention to stay there on Shabbat, they penalized him just as if he ascended on Shabbat. And in the Jerusalem Talmud, Beitzah there, it says, why did they not penalize him similarly with an animal, meaning when one ascends an animal on Shabbat or Yom Tov that he should not descend from it all day as they penalized with a tree? Because a person is commanded regarding the rest of his animal from the Torah, and it turns out that every moment he is transgressing from the Torah, which is not the case with a tree.

And when do we say that if one ascended unintentionally or on the eve of Shabbat, they may descend? It is in the case of a person who finds it difficult to remain in the tree for the entire Shabbat. But if one placed an object on the tree, it is forbidden to take it from there on Shabbat, even if it was placed there before the onset of Shabbat. This is not due to a penalty but because, at the moment of taking it, one would be using something attached to the ground. Therefore, what difference does it make to us if it remains on the tree until the end of Shabbat? However, the Rosh wrote in the fifth chapter of Shabbat (end of section 2) that taking something from a tree or an animal is not considered using something attached to the ground. He brings proof from what is written in section 317 that it is permissible to tie a rope to the mouth of a cow. According to the first opinion, there is no proof from there, as it is not customary to use an animal in that manner, but it is customary to use a tree to take from it and place upon it. (See Magen Avraham section 2, and what he questions on the Rosh from section 528, and it is not difficult at all, as the Tosafot wrote in Shabbat 154: "two" that in the case of a sukkah which is high and one cannot ascend to it unless he uses the tree, as explained by the Korban Netanel there. And what he questioned from Eruvin 33, it will be explained at the end of this section, that if a basket is hanging from a tree, it is forbidden even to take from the basket, all the more so from the tree itself. It seems to me that it is not difficult at all, for there, when one needs to take from the depth of the basket, it is inevitable that he will lean on the sides of the tree, and in such a case, it is certainly forbidden. But in the mere act of taking from the tree, it could be that it is permitted. See Tosafot in Eruvin there, "And Rabbi," where they wrote that the eruv is at the bottom of the basket, and study this well.)

And our master, the Rema, wrote that all of this applies to a tree and similar items, but soft reeds, which are like vegetables, are permitted to be used even though they are attached to the ground, for it is not forbidden to use vegetables. And there are those who disagree with him, and they wrote that since the Rambam wrote that one should not use what is attached to the ground, it implies all things attached, even vegetables (Bach and Taz, section 4). But their words are puzzling, for it is explicitly clarified above in section 312 that they did not decree regarding vegetables as they did with trees, see there. And this is what will be explained in section 409, that with a soft and easily breakable reed, it is forbidden to place the eruv there. This is certainly correct, for a soft reed that has hardened indeed poses a concern that one might break it, as explained in Eruvin (34b). But with truly soft reeds, it is permitted. And so wrote the Rashba in the book "Avodat HaKodesh", and these are his words: "It seems to me that reeds that are meant to harden – even when they are soft, are like trees and are forbidden. But reeds that grow in a marsh and never harden – are permitted like grasses, whether large or small," see there (and so wrote the Ateret Zekenim, section 3, and the Tza"sh, section 4).

Since the Sages forbade using a tree, even a tree that has been cut down, if three handbreadths of the root remain from the ground - it is considered a tree and it is forbidden to use it. Now, I did not find this law explicitly stated, but it seems to me that since it will be explained that up to three handbreadths it is considered a tree even if only the root remains without branches, then even if it is cut down, what difference does it make, since there are still three handbreadths. Although it can be differentiated that this explanation applies when the tree is whole, thus the root is also forbidden, which is not the case when it is completely cut down, nevertheless, it does not seem appropriate to differentiate in this way. In any case, it seems that this is when it was cut down so it could grow again, since then it is considered a tree when three handbreadths remain, but if it was completely cut down, even if three handbreadths remain - it is just an ordinary piece of wood and it loses its status as a tree (this appears to be my humble opinion and I did not find a clear ruling on this matter).

It is taught in Eruvin (99b): "If its roots are raised three handbreadths above the ground, one may not sit on them." From Rashi's commentary, it is implied that this applies to any tree, meaning that the primary prohibition concerns the branches lest one pluck them. Therefore, if the branches start close to the ground, the prohibition applies to the entire tree. However, if the branches start at a height of three handbreadths from the root, it is prohibited to make use of them, but if they are lower, it is permitted. And from Rabbeinu Yonatan, it is explained as follows: For example, if a root extends from the side of the tree, as is common with old trees, and if it is three handbreadths high, it has the same status as the tree itself; if it is less than this, it is considered as the ground. However, regarding the root of the tree itself, according to this explanation, it might be prohibited to use even if it is less than three handbreadths. Nevertheless, according to Rashi's explanation, it is permitted as long as there are no branches there. And stalks of cabbage are also like tree roots, and if they are three handbreadths above the ground, it is prohibited to use them and their leaves (Yam Shel Shlomo).

If these roots protrude to a height of three handbreadths and then bend down below three handbreadths, coming from above and descending below: in the place where they are three handbreadths high, it is forbidden [to use them], and in the place where they are not three handbreadths high, it is permitted. If they are three handbreadths high, but on one side they are level with the ground because the earth is elevated on that side, it is forbidden to use even the side that is level with the ground, because since it is three handbreadths high on three sides, this side is considered nullified to its three sides. However, if it is three handbreadths high on two sides and level with the ground on the other two sides, it is permitted to use the sides that are level with the ground (Magen Avraham, Subsection 4). Note that even if the entire tree is level with the ground but there is a hollow of three handbreadths beneath it within the ground, it also has the status of a tree, for it makes no difference whether the hollow is above or below the ground. Regarding the sides as well: if there is a hollow on three sides and none on the fourth side, it is forbidden there too. But if there is a hollow on two sides, it is permitted on those sides as mentioned.

It is permitted to walk on grass on Shabbat, as the prohibition was only decreed regarding trees, and we are not concerned that one might inadvertently uproot some of the grass while walking, since it is not inevitable that the grass will be uprooted. Therefore, even if some grass is uprooted, it is considered an unintentional act and is permitted. There is no difference whether the grass is long or short, whether one is walking with shoes or barefoot, or whether one is walking normally or running. I have seen someone who is stringent regarding running and when the grass is tall, but we should not create new prohibitions from our own reasoning. Since the Sages said it is not a definite occurrence (פסיק רישא), in any situation it is not a definite occurrence, and common sense confirms this (the Beur HaLacha wants to innovate based on a puzzling statement found in the Sefer Mitzvot Gadol, but we are not responsible for this).

But to pour water on grass is a Torah prohibition, because through this they grow, and it constitutes a derivative of sowing, as one who waters seeds is liable (beginning of Moed Katan). Therefore, those who guard gardens should be careful not to wash their hands over the grass, and hence should not eat there on Shabbat and Yom Tov, as they would need to wash their hands over the grass, which is a Torah prohibition, even though it is unintended, as it is a "pesik reisha" (an inevitable result). And concerning "pesik reisha" that is not desirable to him, there are opinions on this as written in Siman 242, and furthermore, who says it is not desirable to him? Therefore, they should be very, very careful about this. However, it is permissible to urinate on them or pour other liquids that do not promote growth, although it is proper to refrain from other liquids as well (Magen Avraham, Subsection 7), for who says they do not promote growth? And I have also seen someone write that nowadays it is said based on experience that urine is good for fertilizing the soil (Tiferet Yisrael in the introduction to Seder Moed). Nevertheless, in any case, one should refrain from eating in gardens, as it is difficult to avoid water there, and one who is careful about this, the merit of Shabbat will protect him.

One must also be careful not to throw seeds in a place where rain falls, as they will eventually sprout. If one throws them to chickens, he should only throw as much as they can eat in one or two days, for sprouting occurs on the third day. However, if thrown in a place where people walk, it is permitted, since they will not sprout. A clod from which grass has grown or grass that has grown on the earthenware due to its moisture is considered attached to the ground, and one who plucks it is liable for reaping, as mentioned in section 7. This is not similar to an unperforated pot, from which one is exempt by Torah law, because planting there is not the usual way, but through human effort, whereas here they grow on their own. Grass that is stuck in the ground during the day to keep it moist is permitted to be held by the leaves and removed, even if the soil falls off them, as this is indirect handling for a permitted purpose, and it is allowed as mentioned in Siman 311. This is only if they have not taken root and when placed, it was not intended for planting but for covering, for if intended for planting, it is forbidden.

And it has already been explained that by rabbinic decree it is forbidden to detach even from an unperforated pot or from any container, and it is also forbidden to take an unperforated pot from the ground and place it on stakes, or conversely to take it from the stakes and place it on the ground, whether it is made of wood or of earthenware. The reason has already been explained in section 7, that one of them, even if it is unperforated, is considered like a perforated pot regarding several matters, see there. However, a branch of a tree that has been severed, that is, detached from the tree and has fruits on it – it is permitted to detach the fruits from it on Shabbat, because they are considered already detached. Specifically, it is forbidden to detach from the tree itself, because that would be considered cutting, but the fruits do not have any attachment to the branch except when it is connected to the tree. Thus, we eat grapes and various types of berries that cling to small branches as is known (Chullin 124b). Additionally, there is no issue of extracting in this case, because that only applies to stalks or nuts in their green shells where the food is enclosed within them, and not to fruits that hang on branches. This is a separate matter (and there is a question on the Taz in subparagraph 8 who raised this issue, and perhaps he also intended this answer, but his wording is difficult, see there).

The Sages said in Ketubot (60a): If there is a drainage pipe that pours water from the roof, and straw and grass have accumulated in it, blocking it and preventing the water from flowing, and the water then spreads on the roof and drips into the house, one may crush the blockage with one's feet discreetly. Since the remedy is done through a change, meaning he does not fix it with his hands but with his feet, the Rabbis permitted it in a situation of potential loss, as there is no concern of a Torah-prohibited labor but merely a rabbinic prohibition. Therefore, in a situation of potential loss, they did not decree a prohibition. However, if there is no potential loss, such as when it is not dripping into the house, it is forbidden. And even though anything forbidden due to appearance’s sake is prohibited even in private, this applies to matters that are Torah prohibitions, not to those that are rabbinic prohibitions (Taz, subparagraph 9).

Since we decree that one might come to pick the fruit, therefore any fruit that is fit for eating and has a good fragrance – it is forbidden to smell it while it is still attached to the tree, lest one picks it and eats it, or bites it with their mouth, for this too is considered picking. And there is one who wishes to say that biting it with the mouth is not a biblical prohibition but rather rabbinic, because it is not the usual manner of picking (Magen Avraham, Siman 511). However, it appears to me that this is indeed a biblical prohibition, as it is a normal way of eating, and the picking happens as a result. (Also the Tvuot Shor in Bekhor Shor challenges him, and so Rashi explicitly writes in Sukkah 37b. The Maharshal is forced into a difficult explanation there, and who compelled him to this? Many transgressors relied on this, and it is clear without any doubt that eating from something attached is a primary category of labor. And see Menachot 70a, and there is a distinction if one bends down, and examine thoroughly.)

Therefore, they said (Sukkah 37b): A myrtle branch that is still attached [to the ground]—it is permitted to smell it, because it is primarily meant for smelling and not for eating, and for smelling, on the contrary, it is better when it is attached, as its fragrance spreads more. Hence, there is no decree lest one pluck it. But an etrog or an apple—it is forbidden to smell it while it is attached, because since they are meant for eating, we are concerned that one might cut it off or bite into it to eat it.

We have already written the words of the Rambam in Section 2, where he rules that soaking wheat, barley, and the like in water is considered a derivative of planting (zore'a) and one is liable for any amount. Our master, the Beit Yosef, also wrote this in Section 11. It is obvious that this refers to placing them in water, where they will soak for several days, as the term "soaking" implies. Therefore, the Rambam wrote at the end of Chapter 8: "One who places sesame seeds or flax seeds in water is liable for kneading (lisha), since they mix and cling to one another," end quote. Our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote similarly in Siman 300. They were careful to say "one who places," indicating that even just placing them causes them to stick together immediately, which is not the case with wheat and barley, as mentioned in Zevachim (94b). However, when it comes to being liable for planting, it requires several days for the seeds to sprout, hence the term soaking is used. But when one places wheat and barley in water for animal feed, this is not included in this at all. (This also resolves the difficulty raised against the Rambam from Zevachim, where it says: "If so, wheat and barley as well," which clearly implies exemption. See Magen Avraham, Subsection 12, and the Gra, Subsection 12. The question was further raised that if so, one should be liable for both kneading and planting with flax seeds. Some have answered that this is indeed the case, and the passage there is not discussing planting. See Chayei Adam in Nishmat Adam, General Rule 11, where the difficulty is explained. According to what we have written, it is clear that there, for immediate action, one is only liable for kneading. Pay attention.)

Based on what has been explained, one must be careful not to place any type of grain or seeds into water to soak for several days, as this constitutes the primary labor of planting. All the more so, one who places barley to make malt, this is considered a complete primary labor. Consequently, if one places them to soak for several days, they are immediately liable from the moment they place them, as with all Sabbath labors that we explained in Siman 242. However, if one immediately removes them from the water, they are exempt, as in the case of placing bread in the oven and immediately removing it, as stated in Siman 318. And seeds that stick to each other are completely forbidden due to kneading, but placing wheat and barley and any other that do not stick together before one's animal is permitted, as it is only temporary, as we have stated. Similarly, it is permitted to place raisins and other dried fruits in water on Shabbat, but placing them there for pickling to stay for many days is forbidden, as this is like pickling vegetables (Peri Megadim), and is only permitted if one intends to eat them immediately or after a short while.

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) writes in section 11: "It is permissible to place tree branches in water on Shabbat, provided they do not have flowers and roses that open due to the moisture of the water." Explanation of his words: Tree branches that were placed in water before Shabbat so that they would not wither, and were removed from the water on Shabbat or before Shabbat - one may return them to that water, but it is forbidden to add to the water. Certainly, one must not replace the water with other water, and this is explicitly stated in the Mishnah in Sukkah (42b) regarding the lulav, see there. Rashi explains the reason, that it is considered an effort to prepare a vessel, see there. And when there are flowers and roses - it is forbidden in any manner when placing them to remain there, as this constitutes planting, for the flowers and roses open and grow. Certainly, it is forbidden to pour water on Shabbat into vessels where branches called "vases" are standing, as this would be considered the primary category of work of planting, whether they have holes or not, for it is clear that planting is liable even in an unperforated pot and is not comparable to detaching, as every type of planting is considered a primary category of work.

The Rosh in his responsa (klal 2, siman 4) innovated that the issue of a non-perforated pot only applies to a movable vessel, like a pot or something similar, but with something fixed, like a roof filled with soil in which something is planted—if one detaches from it, he is liable. And he brought proof from a Mishnah in Ma'aserot, chapter 5: "Onions that took root in an attic—became purified from impurity," implying that they are considered connected [to the ground]. And they challenged him, as the Rash brought a Yerushalmi that this is only regarding impurity because the Torah included it, and not for all matters. And some reconciled (Tosafot Yom Tov and Magen Avraham sk 14) that the Yerushalmi says there because he does not want their rooting, but if he wants their rooting, for all matters it is as if they are connected. And I am astonished, as the Yerushalmi explicitly rejects this, saying there that regarding Shabbat there is no distinction. However, the Rambam in chapter 1 of Ma'aserot also ruled regarding tithe that it is considered connected, because he holds that what the Yerushalmi says—that only regarding impurity it is considered connected—is not the halacha. It is Rabbi Shimon who holds this, that the Torah included it regarding the purity of seeds, and also in our Talmud in Shabbat (95b) it says this, that it says there: "For all matters, Rabbi Shimon considers it detached," and it is different regarding impurity because the Torah included it regarding the purity of seeds, etc., as mentioned there. But the Rabbis do not make a distinction, and for all matters they consider it connected, and this is also the opinion of the Rosh (in the same place).

And we have already brought the words of the Rambam that figs that have dried up on their branches, meaning on their twigs, and similarly a tree whose fruits have dried up on it - one who detaches them on Shabbat is liable, even though they are considered as uprooted regarding impurity. And we explained in section 13 that this is when the fruit has dried up but not the main part of the tree, for if the main part of the tree has dried up, there is no liability for detaching by Torah law. And the reason the Rambam specifically mentioned figs is because the Rambam is known for preserving the language of the Talmud, and in the Gemara (Chullin 127b) only figs are mentioned. And to avoid the misconception that this law applies only to figs, he wrote: "And similarly a tree," meaning that all trees are equal in this law. And dried herbs - are certainly considered as if they are detached (as the Magen Avraham there).

Some say that one must be careful with clothing made from animal skin not to pull out hair from it, as this incurs a sin-offering liability, as stated in the Jerusalem Talmud, Chapter "Klal Gadol": "One who pulls hair from a dead animal is liable, as pulling it is like shearing it." Furthermore, one must be careful not to pull hair from one's own skin by hand or from other places, as it is considered like something attached to the ground, and it is also implied at the beginning of Sanhedrin that a person is considered like the ground (Taz, Subsection 10). According to this, one must be careful in winter when wearing fox furs called "piks" or "tsavil" or any kind of animal hair called "putar varg," as well as in hair hats, not to pull out even a single hair, as this incurs a sin-offering liability and, if done intentionally, stoning. Similarly, one should be careful not to pull cuticles around the nails, as it is considered like pulling from something attached and incurs a sin-offering liability.

And I am astonished at the first ruling, besides the fact that logically just as with plucking from the ground, the obligation only applies when it is attached, similarly plucking from animals should only apply when they are alive. Additionally, this is explicitly stated in the Mishnah regarding the primary labors: "the one who smooths," and Rashi explained that it refers to scraping the hair from the hide. Similarly, Rambam wrote in Chapter 11, Law 5: "What is considered smoothing? It is the removal of hair or wool from the hide after death until the surface of the hide is smooth." And if you think that plucking hair from the hide of a dead animal incurs liability for plucking, then even for one [hair] he should be liable, so why do we require that the surface be smoothed? And it cannot be said that for smoothing he is liable for two [violations], as it should have been explained. Furthermore, it is explicitly stated in the Gemara (74b): "The Rabbis taught: One who plucks the wing, trims it, and smooths it is liable for three sin-offerings: plucking for shearing, trimming for cutting, and smoothing for scraping." And this is its explanation: that one who plucks a wing from a living animal during its life is liable for plucking, and after he has plucked it, if he trims and smooths it, he is liable for cutting and scraping, but not for plucking.

Even if we explain that "plucking the wing" refers to after death, as the Ran writes in the chapter "Klal Gadol," it still refers to birds and not to animals. This is explicitly stated in Bechorot (25a) that "plucking" is not the same as "shearing," and only for birds is one liable for plucking, as this is their manner, but not for animals. This is also the ruling of the Rambam in the first chapter of Me'ilah, that plucking is not the same as shearing. The Jerusalem Talmud, which states that one is liable for plucking from a dead animal, means that this plucking is considered shearing. However, in the Jerusalem Talmud, it does not refer to animals but to birds. This is what is stated in the Jerusalem Talmud: it raises a question on Reish Lakish who exempts one who plucks in the case of consecrated items, yet he says that one who plucks a wing from a bird is liable for shearing. The Talmud answers that it is not the same, for in birds, where there is no shearing, this plucking is considered shearing, unlike in animals. 

Know that this is so, for it is taught: "If one plucks from a dead bird, he is liable; this plucking is considered shearing." The commentators explain that "plucking from the dead" means even from an animal, and I am puzzled by this from the case of erasing that we mentioned. Therefore, it seems to me, in my humble opinion, that it refers to birds, and this is its explanation: Know that plucking is not the same as shearing, for it is taught that even plucking after death one is liable, and after death, there is certainly no reason to say that in animals plucking is considered shearing. Even though one is liable for shearing after death, as it is taught in the Tosefta and ruled by the Rambam in chapter 9, law 7, that one who shears wool or hair from an animal or beast, whether alive or dead, is liable, nevertheless, to say that after death plucking is considered shearing is not reasonable. Only in birds, where there is no shearing, is there a reason to say this, for in birds, plucking is considered shearing, and shearing applies even after death. But plucking only applies during life, like plucking from a tree that is attached, and after death, it is considered detached. 

(This seems to be my humble opinion, and the Rambam in chapter 9 ruled that plucking a wing from a bird is a derivative of shearing, and in chapter 11 he ruled that plucking a feather is a derivative of erasing, as it is explicitly stated in the Gemara on 74a, as we have written. But for plucking, one is not liable, and also in the Jerusalem Talmud it is so. If after death one is liable for plucking, how is he liable for erasing, which would be contradictory, and this needs further examination.)

We learned in Oholot (Chapter 3, Mishnah 8): "A shoot of a fig tree that was split but is still attached by its bark, if it can live – it is pure, because it is considered connected. But if not – it is impure, because it is considered detached." And we learned from this Mishnah concerning Shabbat as well, that a branch that is broken: if it is still partially attached, and it can definitely live – one who detaches it on Shabbat is liable. Similarly, with all types of vegetables and seeds, even if they have been separated from the root, if a minority of them is still attached – one who detaches it is liable. And similarly with skin and flesh growths on a person that we wrote about in Section 33, even if the majority is separated, as long as a minority is still attached – it is considered entirely connected, and this is also proven from the case of a nail on Shabbat (94b). Refer there, and it will be explained in Siman 300, with God's help.

Just as it is forbidden to use a tree, it is likewise forbidden to use the sides of a tree. However, it is permitted to use the sides of the sides. Therefore, it is forbidden to lean a ladder against the sides of a tree and climb it, because when one climbs it, one is using the sides. But if there is a peg inserted into the tree on its sides, it is permitted to lean a ladder on the peg and climb it, because the peg is considered a side, and the ladder is considered the side of the sides. Similarly, if one inserts a peg into the tree and hangs a basket on the peg, the peg is considered a side and the basket is the side of the sides. And it is permitted to take an object from the basket, but the basket itself is forbidden to be taken from the peg because one would be using the peg, which is a side. And if the basket is hanging directly on the tree itself, it is forbidden to take from the basket because it itself is considered a side. Sometimes even if it is hanging on the peg, it is forbidden, for example, if the mouth of the basket is narrow, and when taking an object from the basket, one must push their hand in and thereby shake the tree – it is forbidden (Magen Avraham, section 15, based on the discussion in Eruvin 33b). And it is stated in the Jerusalem Talmud, Chapter 5 of Beitzah, that leaning on a sturdy tree is permitted because this is not considered using the tree but merely touching it, which was never forbidden, just as touching muktzeh was never forbidden. But with a weak tree, it is forbidden because leaning on it will cause it to move, and thus one is using the tree. And just as it is forbidden to use a tree, it is likewise forbidden to use animals, and similarly, the sides are forbidden but the sides of the sides are permitted, as already explained in Siman 305 (and some say that "sturdy" and "weak" refer to a person, and this will be explained in Siman 339).

Even though it is forbidden to use a tree because one might climb it and detach something, nevertheless, with a pit, we do not decree that one might uproot the ground in the process of ascending and descending. Therefore, a pit, even if it is one hundred cubits deep, is permitted to descend into and ascend from. The reason is that it is not as easy to uproot the ground as it is to detach something from a tree, and in the meantime, one will remember that it is Shabbat. This is not the case with detaching, which can happen in an instant; we are concerned that one might forget it is Shabbat and detach something (see Rashi on Eruvin 100a, s.v. 'pit,' where it implies that there is no concern with a pit at all, only the effort involved; refer to it and study it well).

It has already been explained several times that an unintended action is permitted even if it involves a biblical labor, as long as it is not a 'psik reisha' (inevitable result). That is, if the labor is necessarily performed, one is liable according to the Torah. And not only according to the opinion that holds one is liable for a labor that is not needed for its own sake, but even according to Rabbi Shimon - one is liable for a 'psik reisha'. And even though whenever one does not intend, it is automatically considered as not needed for its own sake, we have explained in Section 242, Paragraph 32 in the name of the Tosafot that whenever it is evident to us that he desires it, it is as if he intended and it is needed for its own sake. And in the name of the Rambam, we have explained there in Paragraph 34 that whenever one does not intend for something else, it is automatically as if he intended for this, see there. And not only with a biblical prohibition is it forbidden in a 'psik reisha', but even with a rabbinic prohibition, it is forbidden in a 'psik reisha', unlike those who are lenient with rabbinic prohibitions (see Magen Avraham, Section 314, Subsection 5).

And it has already been explained that any type of digging in the ground and any type of trench is considered a derivative of plowing, and similarly, any type of leveling of mounds, such as removing a mound or raising a low area to level it, is considered a derivative of plowing. This applies in a field, but in a house, one is liable for building. And so the Sages said (73b): If he had a mound and removed it, or if he had a ditch and filled it: in a house, he is liable for building; in a field, for plowing. Except for when one digs a ditch and only needs its dirt—he is exempt even according to Rabbi Yehuda who holds one liable for a labor not needed for its own sake, because it is considered destructive (there), and it is prohibited by rabbinic decree, like all exemptions of Shabbat which are exempt but forbidden.

Therefore, the Sages said (29b) that a person is permitted to drag a bed, chair, and bench on the ground, whether they are large or small, provided that he does not intend to make a furrow. For if a furrow is made, it is considered an unintentional act and is not a definite outcome (pesik reisha), since it is possible that no furrow will be made. Therefore, if they are very large and will definitely make a furrow, it is forbidden, even on a marble floor, because we decree [against dragging on marble] lest one come to drag on a place without a floor (Magen Avraham, sk 1). However, if the entire city is paved, we do not make a decree for this city because of another city (Tosafot 29b, s.v. "Gezeirah"). And even though digging by dragging is certainly not a Torah prohibition, as proper digging is done with a spade and pickaxe and not by dragging, and it is only a rabbinic prohibition, nevertheless, a definite outcome (pesik reisha) is forbidden even in rabbinic prohibitions, as we have written (Magen Avraham there).

And I have a question regarding this: What prohibition is there when one makes a furrow in a house? For in a field, it is understandable as it resembles plowing, but in a house, it is similar to building as it is written. However, this only applies when one levels the depressions, such as removing a mound or filling a hole, as it is written. But when one makes a furrow in a house where the ground is level, on the contrary, it is considered damaging and not building. And it is explicitly proven in the Gemara there that we are discussing a house. We must say that we are concerned lest one make the furrow in a place where there is a depression, or perhaps we are concerned that afterward, one will fill the furrow.

And it is permitted to sprinkle water on the floor to prevent dust from rising, as one does not intend at all to level the depressions, but only to prevent dust from rising, and there is no "inevitable result" (psik reisha) that the depressions will be leveled, even on an unpaved floor. However, sweeping the house with brooms known as "b'azim" is a matter of dispute among the authorities: The Rif permits it completely, even on an unpaved floor, as he holds that it is not an "inevitable result" that by doing so, the depressions will be leveled. The Rambam, in Chapter 21, permits it on a paved floor but prohibits it on an unpaved floor, as he considers it an "inevitable result" that by sweeping, the depressions will almost certainly be leveled. Nevertheless, on a paved floor, it is permitted, and we do not decree against it because of the unpaved floor. And although he himself wrote there: "One does not smear the ground, nor wash it, nor blow it even if it is paved," as we decree because of the unpaved floor, as explained in the Gemara there, in any case, sweeping, which is greatly necessary, was not decreed against (according to the Magen Avraham). And the opinion of Rabbi Yitzchak of the Tosafot and the Rosh is that sweeping is prohibited even on a paved floor, as we decree because of the unpaved floor. And Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote in Section 2 that this is the custom and one should not change it. However, among us, we sweep based on the reasoning that all our floors are paved, and it is not relevant to decree because of the unpaved, as even one city is not decreed because of another city, as it is written, and certainly nowadays, where all places have paved floors. And there is no difference between wooden pavements and stone pavements, nor do we worry about the gaps between stone and stone, for regarding sweeping, this concern does not exist, as the gap between layer and layer is minimal. And although Tosafot (Chullin 95a, s.v. 'shari') wrote this reasoning, it was written concerning washing, because the nature of water is to enter every narrow place, which is not the case with sweeping.

However, through a non-Jew it is certainly permitted to sweep, and even though if we say it is a "psik reisha" (an inevitable outcome), it would be considered telling a non-Jew to perform a rabbinic prohibition which is forbidden, nevertheless, since he does not intend for this - it is permitted to tell a non-Jew even in a "psik reisha," as stated in Siman 253. And there are those who forbid it even through a non-Jew (Magen Avraham, Subsection 3, in the name of Yeshuot Yaakov), but the custom is to be lenient (there). Similarly, it is permitted to sweep oneself with something light, such as a garment or a cloth or a goose feather, which are light and do not create grooves. And even if there are nutshells on the ground which are muktzeh - it is permitted to sweep them for two reasons: the first is that it is considered like a "graf shel re'i" (a repulsive item), and the second is that it is indirect handling for the sake of something permitted, and it is allowed as stated in Siman 311.

And our Rabbi the Rema wrote that it is forbidden to clean clothes using a broom made of twigs, so that their twigs do not break. From this, it is clear that the actual cleaning of clothes is permitted on Shabbat, as stated in Siman 302, and only with a broom made of twigs is it forbidden. However, with a pig's hair brush, where there is no concern of breaking, it is permitted to clean the clothes from feathers and similar things, as our Rabbi the Rema wrote there, that it is permitted to clean clothes from feathers on Shabbat, see there. Also, regarding cleaning the house, one should be careful with items that have a concern of breaking (Magen Avraham, Subsection 5). And earlier in Siman 302, Clause 9, we brought that there is an opinion that forbids removing feathers, and we explained there that they do not disagree, see there.

Our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 4: "It is forbidden to tilt a barrel on the ground, because since it is heavy, one will certainly come to level the holes, and this constitutes a 'psik reisha' (an inevitable outcome)." This means to tilt it forcefully, but merely placing it - we have no issue with it. And on a floor - in any manner it is permitted. Similarly, when one needs to pour from a barrel, one should not tilt it on its side to press it against the ground, but rather lift it and pour, for the reason explained.

The Rambam wrote in Chapter 23, Law 4: "Anything that constitutes the completion of a task incurs liability for striking with a hammer. For this reason, anyone who scrapes even a little bit (to finish a vessel) or fixes a vessel in any way is liable. Therefore, it is forbidden to produce musical sounds on Shabbat: whether with musical instruments such as lyres and harps or with other things. Even to tap with a finger on the ground or on a board, or one against the other like singers do, or to rattle a nut for a child or play with a bell to quiet him—all of this and similar actions are forbidden, lest one come to fix a musical instrument." (End of quote)

Explanation of the matter: In the Gemara at the end of Eruvin (104a), there is a disagreement: Ulla holds that all types of sound are prohibited on Shabbat, even sounds not associated with music, such as knocking on a door to open it and the like—which is forbidden. Rava, however, holds that only musical sounds, those resembling a melody and sung pleasantly and gently (Rashi), are prohibited. Some have ruled according to Ulla, and if so, all types of sound are forbidden. However, the Rif, Rambam, and Rosh ruled according to Rava, that only a musical sound is prohibited. This is what our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in paragraph 1: "Producing sound with a musical instrument is forbidden, but knocking on the door and the like, when it is not in a musical manner, is permitted," end quote. According to this, in large places where bells are hung above the door, in such a way that when the door is opened the bell rings, and it is made so that people inside can hear who is entering the house—it is permitted to open the door even though the bell rings, since the intention is not for music, it is like knocking on the door. And even though the ringing is a pleasant sound, nevertheless, since the intention is not for music—there is no prohibition. Similarly, if the bell is inside the house and from outside someone pulls a metal string causing the bell to ring and they open the door for him—it is also permitted for the same reason, because it is not made for music. And similarly, if someone pushes from outside and the bell rings inside and they open the door for him—it is also permitted for the same reason.

And similarly, the bells on the curtain at the opening of the ark make noise, and the bells that hang on the Torah scroll make noise when it is carried. Since the intention is not for music but merely to produce sound to inform the congregation that the Torah scroll is being taken out or that it is being carried to the bimah, this is not considered musical sound which the sages prohibited (as also written by the Magen Avraham in section 1 and the Eliyah Rabbah). There are those who are stringent in this matter (the Taz in section 1 based on the reasoning of the Rema which will be explained), but this is not the main opinion as explained with the help of Heaven, and this is the simple custom throughout the world.

The general principle according to this is: Any matter where the intent is for the pleasantness of the song, whether they are joyous songs, mourning songs, or licentious songs, and this is done with an instrument or even with his hands, as Maimonides writes: "To tap with a finger on the ground or on a board or one against another in the manner of singers," meaning that there are types of melodies where tapping with the finger enhances the song, since he is performing an action with his finger—it is forbidden just like with musical instruments. Similarly, to shake a nut for a child or a bell so that he will be quiet or sleep, because he shakes it pleasantly and produces a sound like a hum (Gemara), which is a type of flute, and he intends for the pleasantness of the song, because through this the child will be quiet and sleep—it is forbidden. Similarly, if one puts water in a vessel full of holes and drips it into a metal vessel to produce a pleasant sound like the hum of a flute—it is forbidden (Magen Avraham from the Gemara there).

Regarding matters where the intent is not for the pleasantness of the song, and there is neither joy nor mourning nor frivolity involved, but merely to produce sound, even if the sound is loud, such as a person striking a wall with a hammer to call people to the synagogue or striking something hard on the bimah, and similarly, even if it makes a sound like a bell, which has some pleasantness, such as the bells on the Torah scroll or the curtain, or the bells on the door as I have written, since the intent is not for pleasantness but merely to produce sound – this is not considered a musical instrument and is not forbidden for this reason. Similarly, playing with nuts, where one nut strikes another, even though it produces sound – this is nothing (Talmud), except on the ground, where it is forbidden due to leveling the ground, as will be explained. Therefore, it is permissible to set up before Shabbat an instrument that makes a sound at certain hours, like a clock that is arranged and prepared before Shabbat with a weight to chime every hour all Shabbat day, for this is not considered a musical instrument, since the intent is not for pleasantness but to know and hear what time it is, and therefore, even though it chimes pleasantly – it is permitted, and the reason is as explained, since the intent is not for a song but merely to produce sound. There is someone who wishes to forbid this for some reason, but this is not the main opinion (see Taz, subsection 2), as ruled by our teacher, the Beit Yosef, in subsection 3. And it seems from this that setting up a musical instrument before Shabbat that will play by itself on Shabbat is also forbidden, and this is reasonable, since the prohibition is due to the concern that one might fix a musical instrument, so it does not matter whether it plays by itself or with assistance, as there is still the concern that if one sees it not playing well, one might fix it (and setting it up on Shabbat is forbidden due to making a vessel).

And know that regarding what our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote that it is permissible to knock on the door when it is not done in a musical manner, our teacher, the Rema, wrote the following: "And likewise, if no action is performed, it is permitted. Therefore, those who call their friends and whistle with their mouths like a bird - it is permitted to do so on Shabbat," end quote. This is not understood at all—what is he teaching us? For singing with the mouth is not prohibited at all, only singing with an instrument or using one's body by snapping fingers, as he wrote. And regarding this, he himself says that if no action is performed, it is permitted, meaning that one sings only with his mouth without the action of an instrument. If so, what is he teaching us that it is permitted to whistle with one's mouth like a bird? Indeed, any kind of song is permitted with the mouth.

In the source of the law (Shu"t HaRashba, attributed to the Riaz, end of Eruvin, see there) it is written in this language: "Even though in that whistling they are also accustomed to enhance with song, here, etc." end of quote. And it is explained that this is the novelty, that even with instrumental song they are accustomed to this whistling. This also is not understood, for what does it matter, after all, vocal song was never forbidden. And if his intention is not about instrumental song but rather that in this whistling they enhance with song, it is obvious that it is permitted, for all vocal song is permitted. Therefore, it appears to me that the explanation is as follows: In this whistling, they are accustomed to place their finger into their mouth between the lips and the teeth, and thereby the sound comes out like a bird. And this is the novelty, that even though with the hand it is forbidden, as Maimonides wrote that it is forbidden to strike with the finger, etc., as mentioned in section 1, nevertheless - here it is permitted, because with his hand he is not making a musical act, and his song is with his mouth, and the hand is only to make the whistling in the mouth come out nicely, therefore it is permitted.

And know that according to what we have explained, there may be some justification for what, due to our many sins, has spread among the cantors for some ten years, that they hold in their hands a small fork made of silver or iron, which they call a "tuning fork" when standing before the prayer stand on Shabbat and festivals. It is made to maintain the pitch of the melody; they place the fork between their teeth, and the sound of the melody is heard in their ears, enabling them to assess the tune. This is essentially a musical instrument made for singing. 

We are unable to protest, as they claim that without it they cannot sing. And due to our many sins, the generation is lax, and the masses support them. Not only is it impossible to protest, but anyone who tries to leave the synagogue because of this causes a known dispute. Perhaps because the sound of the melody is only heard from mouth to ear and is momentary, and its purpose is for vocal singing, which was never prohibited, it might not be considered a musical instrument that the sages forbade, as we have written regarding the sound made by placing the hand in the mouth. It is necessary to find a merit, for Heaven forbid to say that the entire Jewish people would stumble on a rabbinic prohibition, especially while standing in prayer before the King of Kings, the Holy One, blessed be He.

(And also regarding the repetition and tripling of words and the spreading of the notes before the prayer stand to sing according to musical rules, all God-fearing individuals are distressed by this and cannot protest, as the masses are unruly and do not listen to the words of the sages, claiming that this is their enjoyment of Shabbat and festivals. Perhaps there is indeed no prohibition in this, and it is good for the one who fears God to avoid it. We have come to find merit for the holy seed, the blind ones. Perhaps because the sages only silenced someone for repeating "Shema, Shema," it implies that for other words, there is no issue if they are repeated and tripled. And regarding the spreading of the notes before the prayer stand, we do not have a clear reason to prohibit it. Therefore, leave Israel alone; it is better that they err unknowingly, etc.)

It is also written: It is forbidden to knock on a door on Shabbat using a knocker that is fixed to the door, even though one does not intend to produce music. Nevertheless, since the instrument is designated for this purpose, it is forbidden. Therefore, it is prohibited for the synagogue attendant to use an instrument designated for this purpose to knock on the door to call people to the synagogue; rather, he should knock on the door with his hand. Hence, in some places, the attendant uses a different instrument to knock on the door on Shabbat (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 3). The reason for this prohibition is not entirely clear, since it is not a musical instrument. Some say that since the instrument is designated for this purpose, we are concerned that one might intend to produce music (Beit Yosef), but it is not understandable why we would decree such a matter, and furthermore, this would be a decree upon a decree. It seems that the prohibition is due to it being a weekday activity. (The Taz, subparagraph 1, wrote that it is similarly forbidden to hang a strap with bells on the curtain; see there. I do not understand the comparison, especially according to what was written. Study this well.)

And there are some of the early authorities who permitted telling a non-Jew to play musical instruments at weddings on Shabbat, as it is considered a double rabbinic prohibition (shvut deshvut), and in the context of the mitzvah of bringing joy to the bride and groom, the Sages did not decree against it. And our teacher, the Rema, wrote in section 2: that even to tell a non-Jew to fix a musical instrument is permitted, for the honor of the bride and groom, but otherwise, it is prohibited. However, in our times, it has become customary to be lenient, for reasons that will be explained in the next section regarding clapping and dancing. This is certainly puzzling, to permit telling a non-Jew to perform a Biblically prohibited action (Magen Avraham, sub-section 4), and it is possible that he follows his own reasoning in section 276 where he permitted telling a non-Jew to light a candle for the honor of the Shabbat meal, and it has already been clarified that this is not the law. And also in our times, we have not heard of this leniency, even to tell a non-Jew to play an instrument on Shabbat for the honor of the bride and groom, and in all countries, it is customary to prohibit this, and all the more so to tell him to fix a musical instrument. If the non-Jew comes on his own to play an instrument, one does not need to protest (there), but one should not tell him to play. And even on the eve of Shabbat, one should not tell him to come on Shabbat to play an instrument, and this is the simple custom, and it should not be changed. (And what he wrote for reasons that will be explained in section 339, this is because we are not experts in fixing musical instruments, as mentioned there, this is concerning clapping and dancing but not actual playing, and heaven forbid to permit this).

One who guards his fruits and seeds from animals and birds should not clap his hands to frighten them away, nor should he slap his hands on his thigh, nor should he dance to scare them away. And even though this does not involve the decree against clapping and slapping which will be explained in the next section—where they decreed against it lest one come to repair a musical instrument, which applies only to clapping and slapping out of joy and song and not in these manners—nonetheless, this too is forbidden, as a decree lest when he sees that he cannot frighten them away in this manner, he will take a stone and throw it from the private domain to the public domain to scare them away (Rashi Eruvin 104a). Therefore, it is possible that for us, who do not have a public domain, it may be permitted to clap and slap, for even if he throws a stone, he will not come to a Torah prohibition (Magen Avraham 6).

One may not play with nuts on the ground nor with apples, due to a decree lest one come to level the holes, which would incur liability for building in the house and for plowing in the field. It is prohibited to play with all kinds of fruits for this reason. However, on a table or in a house with a floor, it is permitted because there is no concern of leveling holes in these cases, and there was no decree made for playing on the ground, similar to what some hold regarding sweeping the house in the previous section. Playing is not a fixed activity that would warrant such a decree (which resolves the difficulty raised by the Magen Avraham in subsection 7). Likewise, it is permitted to play with bones called "tchik" and in our language "myliskas," and although they make a sound when struck together, since it is not the sound of a musical instrument, it is permitted as explained.

And know that types of games are only permissible when they are played merely for amusement, but if they are played to gain profit—it is forbidden, as this is like buying and selling. Even those who play the game called "Um Grad"—this is forbidden for this reason, and similarly, those who play with nuts to gain profit—it is forbidden. And regarding women and children who play, our teacher the Rema wrote in paragraph 5: that one should not protest against them, as it is better that they err unintentionally than intentionally, end quote, meaning that they certainly will not listen, and in matters of rabbinic law, we say it is better [that they err unintentionally], as stated in Beitzah, the beginning of chapter 4, see there. And perhaps according to the current custom where there is no obligation in this play for anything except what they play for, for example, if someone's nut strikes his friend's nut, he wins his friend's nut, and if it does not strike, his friend wins his, and similarly in the simple and deficient game, where one takes several nuts in his hand and closes his hand and asks his friend "simple or deficient," and he responds "simple" or "deficient," and he opens his hand and counts: if it is as the second said, the second wins them, and if the opposite, the second must give him as many nuts as were in his hand, and in this play there is only a conditional commitment and not like buying and selling, and for those who hold that a conditional commitment does not acquire—it is not obligatory to pay. Therefore, what is paid is merely a gift, and there is no decree of buying and selling in this (so it seems in my humble opinion to judge favorably), and playing with a ball is explained in Siman 338.

We learned at the end of Eruvin: One may fill from the Exile Pit and the Great Well using a pulley on Shabbat in the Temple, but not in the provinces, due to a decree lest one fill for his garden or ruins, because since one can fill without effort, he may come to water his garden or ruins on Shabbat (Rashi), or he may fill to soak flax. And it is explained in the Gemara there that if there was neither a garden nor ruins nor a pool to soak flax, it is permitted, and they did not decree on account of other places, because this is a distant decree, and it suffices to decree in its place. And some of our rabbis explained that it does not refer to a regular pulley, for in such cases it is not relevant to decree, and they only prohibited a large pulley that draws much water at once without effort. This is a large pulley with many buckets fixed around it that fill and pour out together. But our pulley, which does not fill so much, is permitted, for there is nothing to be concerned about, and this is the main ruling according to this opinion (A”R).

If one has fruits on the roof and sees that rain is coming, it is forbidden to lower them into the house through a skylight on Shabbat.
