The Sages taught in the Mishnah (beginning of Chapter 5 of Beitzah): "One may lower fruit through a skylight on Yom Tov but not on Shabbat," because it constitutes a significant exertion that is not necessary for Shabbat. However, it is permitted to cover them with mats or similar items. Although this also involves some exertion, it is allowed in order to prevent loss. This applies not only to fruits that are fit for eating but even to bricks, which are muktzeh and one fears that the rain will damage them - it is permitted to cover them to prevent loss.

There is an opinion that forbids even covering them, including fruits, because all forms of exertion not necessary for Shabbat are forbidden (Magen Avraham 311:11 in the name of the Shelah). However, we follow the ruling of our master, Rabbi Yosef Karo, in Shulchan Aruch 301:7, who permits even covering bricks.

It is permitted according to all opinions to place a vessel under a leak, and when it fills up, to pour it out and return it to its place. This is specifically when the water is at least fit for washing, and it is permitted to move the vessel with the water. But if the water is not fit for washing, such as if it is dirty water, it is forbidden to place a vessel under such a leak because it renders the vessel unusable, as it becomes muktzeh. Although when the vessel fills up and becomes repulsive, it is permitted to pour it out as one would with a chamber pot, it is nonetheless forbidden to create a chamber pot situation initially. Consequently, he would be forced to agree not to move it, resulting in the vessel becoming unusable.

However, if one did place a vessel under such a leak and it is in a place where he sits, it becomes like a chamber pot and it is permitted to remove it, but he should not return it to that place under the leak. This applies when there is no significant damage from the water leaking from the ceiling. But in the case of significant damage, it has already been explained in Siman 338 that one may create a chamber pot situation initially to avoid significant damage (see the Tur, who permits this initially, and see Beit Yosef, Bach, and Taz, and according to what we said, it can be understood that they do not disagree in principle, and examine this thoroughly).

It is forbidden to ride on an animal, and it is prohibited to use an animal for any purpose, even on the sides of the animal. However, on the sides of the sides, it is permitted. These laws have already been explained in Siman 305 and Siman 336. There, in Siman 336, Section 15, it is explained that if one mounts an animal, he must immediately dismount. This is not similar to a tree, where one is penalized to remain there until nightfall, because with an animal, there is a Biblical prohibition of resting one's animal, which does not apply to a tree. At the end of Siman 336, we clarified that it is permissible to lean on a sturdy tree, but it is forbidden to lean on a weak tree. This is based on the Jerusalem Talmud, Tractate Beitza, Chapter 5, Halacha 2.

But according to our version in the Jerusalem Talmud there, it appears to have a different intention—not referring to a tree, but to a person, distinguishing between when he is weak and when he is strong. A healthy person, when he leans on an animal or a tree, leans slightly and stands on his own strength, and this is not considered using animals or a tree. However, a weak person, if he leans entirely on the animal or the tree—it is forbidden. And even a healthy person is only permitted to lean slightly, not with all his weight.

And this is the language of the Jerusalem Talmud: "There is a Tanna who teaches that one may lean on an animal, and there is a Tanna who teaches that one may not lean on an animal. Rav Chisda said: The one who says one may lean refers to a healthy person, and the one who says one may not lean refers to a weak person." There is also another explanation there: "The one who says one may lean refers to someone who leans lightly, and the one who says one may not lean refers to someone who leans with all his weight," meaning with a strong support, and both refer to a healthy person. Both explanations are true according to the law, and therefore a weak person is completely forbidden to lean on an animal, and the same applies to a tree. A healthy person is permitted to lean lightly but not with all his strength, and this is the law. Also, in our Talmud in Chagigah (16a) it is clearly implied that the prohibition of using animals only applies when one uses them with all his strength, as mentioned there, and the poskim did not mention this at all.

One should not float on water because of the decree lest one makes a floating barrel to learn how to float on it. And if the river is not in a courtyard but is like ordinary rivers which are considered a karmelit, there is an additional prohibition, lest one splashes water with his feet beyond four cubits (Rashi 40: s.v. "Even" see there). And we have already written in Siman 326 that one who bathes in a river needs to be cautious of this, and for this reason, it is customary among us to prohibit bathing in a river on Shabbat, see there. It is not prohibited to float in a vessel like in a bathtub if it is located in a courtyard, where there is no concern of splashing water beyond four cubits. However, if it is not located in a courtyard – it is prohibited for this reason. Similarly, a pool in a courtyard is treated like a bathtub, because it is not similar to a river since it has a surrounding edge, meaning that even if the water is displaced, the edge returns it to its place, and it is not similar to a river, where the water is pushed out beyond it, and it is similar to a vessel. They did not decree here lest one makes a floating barrel, because this does not apply to a vessel. Therefore, if the pool does not have an edge around it but is level with the ground outside it – it is similar to a river, because when the water is displaced, it flows outside the pool like in a river, and it is prohibited to float in it like in a river.

And our teacher Rabbi Yosef Karo wrote in section 6: "It is forbidden for a person to float an object on water to move it from himself or to bring it to himself. Therefore, it is prohibited to scatter sticks on the surface of the water to move them here and there in order to clean the water so that it becomes clear." End quote. Just as it is forbidden to swim with one's body, it is likewise forbidden to float an object on the water. Therefore, it is permitted with a vessel, as floating is permitted with a vessel as explained. Now, the source of this law is from the Mordechai, chapter 5 of Beitzah, and its source is from the Jerusalem Talmud there. There is a difficulty with this, as the conclusion of the Jerusalem Talmud permits it, stating that if it is for drinking, it is allowed, just as one may break a barrel to eat dried figs from it (as this was questioned by the Pri Megadim there in his commentary). This is not difficult at all, as the Jerusalem Talmud does not contradict the previous prohibition. If one does not want to drink now, it is forbidden to scatter. But if one wants to drink, it is permitted. And our teacher Rabbi Yosef Karo does not refer to a case where one wishes to drink, as he did not mention this. (This is also the intention of the Mordechai and the glosses of the Rema that bring this law, indicating that one does not wish to drink now but only wishes to clean it for later. And on Shabbat, there is also the prohibition of selecting, so consider this well).

It has already been explained in Siman 248 regarding the laws of boarding a ship before Shabbat, but on Shabbat – it is obviously forbidden to board a ship for the reasons explained there. However, if the ship is docked near the shore and is resting on the seabed or riverbed and is not sailing at all – it is permitted to board it, as this is akin to entering a house. Similarly, even if it is floating on the water but is securely tied to a post or bridge as ships are in the harbor – it is also permitted to board it, for it is not fit for sailing as long as it is tied. And know that in the Gemara (139b) there is a permit for a learned scholar to board a ship to sleep there, and the ship is resting on the ground, even though he knows that a non-Jew will come later and sail it to the other side, because it is considered a ruse in a rabbinic prohibition, and a learned scholar will not come to do so initially, see there. Nowadays, we do not have the status of a learned scholar, and it is forbidden. Some permit it due to great harm to travel by ship on Shabbat, and some hesitate and forbid it (see Magen Avraham 12 and there 13 who requires two ties, and I do not know why). By some ruse – it is obviously permitted, and also one who relies on the permit has something to lean on, and similarly for a passing mitzvah some want to be lenient. A ferry that is called a "parom" is considered like a ship (see Shulchan Aruch 308).

It is taught in Beitzah (36b): One may not clap, nor slap, nor dance for joy and song. Clapping refers to striking one hand against the other, slapping refers to striking a hand against the thigh, and dancing refers to moving the feet. The reason is that since these actions occur when singing with musical instruments, and because they decreed against musical instruments on Shabbat and Yom Tov lest one come to repair a musical instrument, they similarly decreed against these actions because they are also associated with musical instruments. Even to strike a finger on the ground or on a board or to strike one finger against another finger as singers do, or to shake a nut for a child in a musical manner or to play with a bell to make it quiet – all of this and similar actions are forbidden due to the concern that one might repair a musical instrument. However, clapping in an unconventional manner is permitted; this is how the Sages decreed.

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote in section 3: "The reason we clap and dance nowadays and we do not protest against it is because it is better that they act unintentionally rather than intentionally. And there are those who say that in this time everything is permitted, for we are not experts in making musical instruments, and there is no need to decree lest one repair a musical instrument, for it is an uncommon matter. And perhaps because of this, the custom has become lenient in everything," end quote. These matters are perplexing: Firstly, the tying of the strings of the harp is quite common, as well as winding them on the pegs, which means turning the peg until the string becomes properly tuned. In both actions, there is a liability for a sin-offering: for tying and for fixing a vessel, as Rashi explained in Eruvin (103a, s.v. 'af' and s.v. 'meshal'shel,' see there). Furthermore, God forbid to nullify a rabbinic prohibition for such reasons.

In my humble opinion, it appears to me that there is a simple reason: Our clapping and dancing were never forbidden. In the time of the Sages, this occurred when musical instruments were played, and they would clap, beat, and dance in accordance with the rhythm of the song, as implied in the Jerusalem Talmud. However, nowadays this does not happen at all when musical instruments are played, but rather when people sing joyous songs with their mouths, they clap their hands together merely as an expression and not in accordance with the rhythm of the song. The practice of clapping one's hand on one's thigh is entirely unknown to us, and the dancing during times of joy is not like their dancing in an orderly manner as women dance, but rather people dance without orderly steps. There is no concern here that one might repair a musical instrument, as these actions have no connection to each other at all, and this is not what the Sages decreed upon. Therefore, even on Simchat Torah, when we dance and clap before the Torah scroll, and some say the reason is that it is permitted to dance in honor of the Torah (Magen Avraham, section 1), it is difficult for me to nullify a rabbinic prohibition for this reason. But according to what we have written, it makes sense, as this is not the type of dancing and clapping that the Sages forbade, and many times we have seen that great individuals clap their hands during joyous occasions. (And this also makes sense regarding the snapping of fingers on the night of Yom Kippur by the High Priest, even if we do not say it is because there is no rabbinic prohibition in the Temple, and it is also not considered the sound of a musical instrument as the Magen Avraham wrote in section 2).

It is not permitted to adjudicate cases on Shabbat. The Rambam writes in Chapter 24: "One does not administer punishments on Shabbat, even though the punishment is a positive commandment—it does not override Shabbat. How so? If someone is liable for death or lashes, they are not lashed, as it is stated: 'Do not kindle a fire,' and similarly for other punishments." This is the end of his words. The prohibition of "do not kindle a fire" is expounded regarding the burning of a priest's daughter, which is forbidden on Shabbat (Sanhedrin 35b). And in the Mekhilta on Vayakhel, it is stated: "'Do not kindle a fire'—burning was included and was singled out to teach: just as burning, which is one of the death penalties by the court, does not override Shabbat, so too all other death penalties by the court do not override Shabbat." This is the end of the passage. From this, we only know about the death penalty, but the Rambam holds that lashes also involve a desecration of Shabbat, because certainly with thirty-nine lashes, a wound would be made (see Magen Avraham in subparagraph 3). The reason monetary cases are not adjudicated is because, as stated in Beitzah, the reason is that it was decreed lest one write down the claims and the judgment. However, in the Yerushalmi Sanhedrin (Chapter 4, Halacha 6) it is stated: "From here, the courts should not adjudicate on Shabbat. What is the reason? It says here 'in all your dwellings,' and it says there 'these shall be for you a statute of judgment for your generations in all your dwellings'—just as there it speaks of the court, so too here it speaks of the court." And even though it learns there in regard to the death penalty, from this comparison, we can learn about all types of judgment, just as we do not burn on Shabbat, so too all statutes of judgment. Therefore, the Sanhedrin also did not sit in the Chamber of Hewn Stone on Shabbat as they did on weekdays, but rather in the Temple Courtyard, as explained in the Tosefta, and we have already brought this in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 5. Therefore, it is forbidden to set a place for chalitzah on Shabbat, as this is considered like sitting in judgment (Magen Avraham there).

And it is certainly forbidden to send a warning (hazmana) on Shabbat, as this is akin to being involved in a legal matter. All the more so, it is forbidden to accept testimony on Shabbat, except in a case of a mitzvah, such as for an agunah (a woman whose husband is missing and cannot remarry) where after Shabbat it would not be possible to accept the testimony, and similar cases, for in matters of a mitzvah, speech is permitted on Shabbat. Similarly, it is not proper for a litigant to arrange his claims on Shabbat. However, a judge who had a Torah law case on the eve of Shabbat and did not complete it, and reviews the matter on Shabbat, it is permitted, for this is considered Torah study, just as one studies the laws of prohibitions and permissions, so too one can study monetary laws. But the court should not sit in their usual place and deliberate, as this appears like a legal proceeding. And our master the Rema wrote that therefore it is forbidden to seize and imprison (with government permission) someone who has been sentenced to some punishment so that they do not escape, and all the more so it is forbidden to flog them, and if they escape, it is not our concern. However, in the case of a transgression, they can be guarded in a house so that they do not escape. Similarly, all public needs may be announced on Shabbat, as stated in Siman 306.

The Sages prohibited betrothing a woman on Shabbat, and certainly marrying her, and likewise, it is forbidden to perform chalitzah (release from levirate marriage) and yibbum (levirate marriage) on Shabbat. The Gemara states the reason: lest one come to write. I am puzzled as to why they did not state the reason as being due to acquisition, for a woman is acquired by her husband through betrothal and marriage, and similarly, the yevamah (widow) to the yavam (brother-in-law). It seems to me that this is because Rambam in Chapter 23, Law 12 wrote: "It is also forbidden to buy and sell or rent and lease, as a decree lest one come to write." Therefore, why should the Talmud state the reason of acquisition, since this itself involves the decree of prohibition just like acquisition? (However, I do not understand Rambam's words, for at the beginning of the chapter on borrowing, they stated the reason of lest one come to write regarding a loan and its repayment, but the essence of buying and selling is a significant rabbinic prohibition in itself, not due to a decree, as explained in Nehemiah, and as I wrote at the beginning of Siman 243 that it is almost like a biblical prohibition, for otherwise Shabbat would be like a weekday, and we brought this in the name of Ramban. It seems to me that Rambam did not mean this literally, but did not want to elaborate, and wrote some reason briefly. Study this well.)

Know that in the Gemara, it questions why one cannot betroth on Shabbat: "Isn't it a mitzvah?" And it answers: "It is only needed when he already has a wife and children." Rashi explains that the question is not on the fundamental law, for certainly even if he does not have a wife and children, it is forbidden to betroth. Rather, the question is on the language of the Mishnah, which calls it optional. This is also clarified by the words of the Rif, Rambam, Rosh, and Tur, who did not write that it is permitted to betroth if he does not have a wife and children. However, Rabbeinu Tam in the Tosafot there explains that the question is indeed on the fundamental law, for certainly if he does not have a wife and children, it is a great mitzvah and a matter of heavenly concern, so it should not be forbidden to betroth on Shabbat. And it answers that it refers to when he already has a wife and children, but if he does not have them, it is indeed permitted. Even according to this, there is doubt whether marriage (i.e., entering the chuppah) is permitted, because it is a complete acquisition where he acquires her for her work, her findings, and to inherit her, and it is not similar to betrothal. Or it is possible that this is also permitted, for betrothal is also an acquisition where he acquires her as a wife, and nevertheless, it is permitted. Therefore, it is possible to say that marriage is the same (see there in the Tosafot and Ran).

And behold, regarding the law, we certainly follow the majority of the decisors, and even Rabbeinu Tam himself wrote in a responsum that one should only perform a wedding under great duress. Even if one consecrates the marriage before Shabbat, it is forbidden to conduct the wedding ceremony on Shabbat (Ran there). Nevertheless, our Rabbi, the Rema, wrote as follows: "There are those who permit the wedding where he has no wife and children, and it is possible that the same applies to entering the wedding canopy. And although we do not hold this way, in any case, we rely on this in pressing situations because the honor of people is significant. This is as it is customary that sometimes they could not arrange the dowry on Friday until nightfall, so they perform the wedding canopy and the consecration on Friday night since they are already prepared for the meal and the wedding. It would be embarrassing for the bride and groom if it were not to happen then. Nevertheless, ideally, one should be careful to avoid this situation." These are his words. And with our Rabbi, the Rema, himself, such an event occurred in Krakow when he was the head of the beit din there, with an orphan where it extended about two hours into the night, and he himself arranged the consecration and the wedding canopy as he wrote in a responsum. The entire city criticized him, and he elaborated there to explain that the honor of people and the distress of the bride and groom are significant. We have heard that from this incident, they made a decree in Krakow not to perform any weddings on Friday evening, and it is a good decree because there are many problems that arise from this, leading to the desecration of Shabbat, especially in the winter days when the days are short. In any place where this can be instituted, their reward is great from Heaven. In any case, even where it is impossible to institute this, it is incumbent upon all God-fearing individuals to try to arrange the wedding ceremony as early as possible.

Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote in Section 5: "One who marries a widow should not have the first intercourse with her on Shabbat or Yom Tov," end quote. This is from the Jerusalem Talmud. The explanation is as follows: In Even HaEzer, Section 64, it is explained that a virgin has a chuppah (bridal canopy), but a non-virgin does not, as mentioned there. The reason is that the chuppah is the bridal canopy (hinuma), which involves leading the bride and groom under the canopy with festive celebrations, and this is only for a virgin. According to this, a widow does not acquire through the chuppah, and the acquisition is through intercourse; therefore, it is forbidden on Shabbat. They explained that what is stated in the Jerusalem Talmud at the beginning of Ketubot: "Those who marry widows must consummate the marriage during the day," means to have intercourse, because she does not have a chuppah. However, there are those who disagree and hold that even a non-virgin has a chuppah, which is defined as seclusion suitable for intercourse, and this applies equally to both virgins and widows or divorcées (Gra, Section 16, and there in Even HaEzer). The Jerusalem Talmud that says: "Those who marry widows" means because a virgin, in any case, is forbidden to have first intercourse on Shabbat, as this is the opinion of the Jerusalem Talmud, and the intention of the Jerusalem Talmud is seclusion suitable for intercourse. Also, for us, it is the same for a virgin, as we hold that it is permitted to have first intercourse with a virgin on Shabbat. We have already explained this in Even HaEzer there, and there in Section 55, we elaborated on what constitutes a chuppah. In Section 14 there, we explained that the poskim (decisors of Jewish law) do not disagree at all, as mentioned there, and there in Section 64, Section 17, we explained that there is no disagreement even for a widow. If there was seclusion suitable for intercourse during the day, it is permissible according to law to have intercourse with her on Shabbat. Also, for a virgin, some require specifically seclusion suitable for intercourse during the day (Magen Avraham, Section 11, in the name of Magen David). However, specifically for a widow, Maharil wrote that there is danger in having first intercourse with her on Shabbat (there), and in Even HaEzer, we mentioned an incident where this happened, and she immediately died, as mentioned there. Therefore, we are accustomed to warn about this very much. This applies only to a widow and not to a divorcée. For a divorcée, if there was seclusion suitable for intercourse during the day, one can have intercourse with her on Shabbat. The seclusion during the day must be such that no one else is in the room (there). If she was not suitable for intercourse during the day, such as if she was impure, she is forbidden to immerse on Shabbat, as it is forbidden to have intercourse with her on Shabbat, since before that, he had not acquired her at all, because there was no seclusion suitable for intercourse (there, and he disagrees with the Chelkat Mechokek, and also the Beit Shmuel there disagreed with the Chelkat Mechokek, as mentioned there).

It is obvious that it is forbidden to perform a divorce on Shabbat, even if the get (divorce document) was written beforehand and there is no issue of it being "pre-dated," such as when done through a messenger or if the date written is only the month and not the specific day, which is also valid. Nonetheless, it is forbidden to divorce just as it is forbidden to betroth, since in the act of divorce she removes herself from his domain, which is akin to a transaction. However, in the case of a get for a deathly ill person who is on the verge of death and it appears that he might die immediately, leaving her in need of chalitzah or yibbum, it is stated in Gittin (77b) that the Sages permitted him to transfer ownership of the room where the get is placed to her, and she establishes possession through opening and closing the door, thus transferring the get to her domain.

The Rambam wrote in Chapter 23, Law 9: "We do not separate tithes on Shabbat, because it appears as if one is fixing something that was not corrected," end quote. And even to give them to a Kohen on that day is forbidden (Ra'avad). And even during twilight, it is forbidden to tithe definite produce, but doubtful produce (demai) may be tithed during twilight, as it does not seem like fixing, for most of the common people do tithe (Rashi 34a). Nevertheless, on Shabbat itself, it is forbidden, because since they decreed to tithe, it is ultimately a form of fixing. And for meduma, which is teruma mixed into a hundred times its amount in chullin, where one portion is taken and the rest is permitted, it is not allowed to be separated on Shabbat, as this constitutes fixing (and the halacha is not according to Rabbi Yehuda at the beginning of 'Notel'—see there). Any form of fixing is forbidden on Shabbat due to the prohibition of fixing a utensil (Rashi Shabbat 142a, s.v. 'ha'), meaning that they will say what difference is there between this fixing and the fixing of a utensil? And even Rabbinic tithes are forbidden to separate on Shabbat, as well as during twilight, except for demai as mentioned.

The Rambam further wrote in the laws of Yom Tov: "We do not judge cases... nor do we consecrate or evaluate or anathematize (whether for the Temple treasury or for the priests, see Taz section 4 which is quite perplexing), because it is like buying and selling. We do not separate tithes, as this resembles consecrating the fruits that are separated, and also because it is like fixing them on Shabbat (he added this reason to the previous one, and perhaps due to second tithe, investigate further). We do not tithe animals, due to the decree lest one mark them with red dye (not because of fixing, as it was initially permissible, and not due to buying and selling, as he eats it himself). A person may consecrate his Passover offering on Shabbat and his festival peace-offering on a festival, as this is a commandment of the day. Just as we do not consecrate, so we do not sanctify the water of purification." End of quote. I did not find his source, and I also do not know why we do not sanctify the water of purification, as there is no fixing without the sprinkling. Perhaps because sprinkling does not override Shabbat as stated in Pesachim (65a), therefore why trouble in vain. And perhaps even moving it is prohibited, because it is muktzeh since it is holy, and it is forbidden to do anything with it on Shabbat, as it is taught in the Tosefta of Shabbat (Chapter 15): "We can move new produce on Shabbat, and we can move second tithe in Jerusalem but not in the provinces," meaning because in the provinces it is forbidden to eat it and it is forbidden to benefit from it due to its sanctity. Unlike new produce, although it is forbidden to eat, it is still permitted to benefit from, since it does not have sanctity. Therefore, the water of purification and the ashes of purification are also prohibited to move.

One who separates tithes on Shabbat or Yom Tov: if done unintentionally, he may eat from what he has prepared; if done intentionally, he may not eat until after Shabbat. In either case, the produce is considered tithed. Similarly, one who consecrates, valuates, or donates something as cherem on Shabbat, whether unintentionally or intentionally, what he has done is valid, and this is certainly true on Yom Tov. Likewise, if one transfers ownership to his fellow on Shabbat, the transaction is valid, as we hold that a sale done in a prohibited manner is still a sale, as explained in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 208, where we elaborated on why we do not say in this case: "If it is done, it does not take effect." (See Magen Avraham, subsection 10).

Maimonides wrote in Chapter 23, Law 16: "One who designated Terumat Ma'aser (tithe of the tithe) from Demai or Ma'aser Ani (poor man's tithe) from definite produce should not take them on Shabbat, even if he designated their place before Shabbat and they are known and placed beside the fruits. But if a priest or a poor person is accustomed to eating with him, they may come and eat, provided that he informs the priest that this which I am feeding you is Terumat Ma'aser, and the poor person that this is Ma'aser Ani." These are his words, and this is a Mishnah in Chapter 4 of Demai (Mishnah 4). And this is its explanation: "One who designated," meaning that he said, "The Terumat Ma'aser that I am obligated to give from this pile should be placed on its north or south side," but he did not separate it. And the same applies to definite produce, except that with definite produce, the Israelite does not separate the Terumat Ma'aser but the Levite does. However, with Demai, where the tithe belongs to himself, he separates the Terumat Ma'aser to give it to the priest. Therefore, even though it is already as if it were separated, nonetheless, he should not give it to the priest or the poor person because it is forbidden to give priestly gifts on Shabbat. Only those accustomed to eating with him may come and eat, provided he informs them; otherwise, they might think he is feeding them from his own. And the reason it does not say "one who designated Terumah of definite produce" is because it is not customary to delay the Terumah, since the large Terumah is separated immediately when the threshing floor is cleared (Rash). And the reason it does not say "one who designated Ma'aser of definite produce" is that even if he gives it to a Levite on Shabbat, it is of no benefit, as the Levite has to separate Terumat Ma'aser (Tosafot Yom Tov).

However, the words of the Rambam are perplexing, for in the Jerusalem Talmud there, they interpret this Mishnah according to Beit Shammai, who say in the first chapter of Beitzah (12b) that one cannot bring challah and gifts to a Kohen on Yom Tov, but according to Beit Hillel, it is permitted to take them on Shabbat. And there it explains that there is no difference between Yom Tov and Shabbat (and the Tosafot in Beitzah there brings the Jerusalem Talmud). And the Rambam himself in Chapter 4 of Yom Tov, law 26, ruled that one can bring them, and this has already been questioned about him (gloss in Kesef Mishneh). 

It seems to me, on the contrary, that the Rambam ruled according to this Jerusalem Talmud, which says there: "This is learned from that in teaching etc.," meaning that what Beit Hillel permits in Beitzah is not to bring to the Kohen, but rather in teaching, to eat there, they may come and eat there. And even though our Talmud in Beitzah does not hold this way, as the Rambam himself wrote in Chapter 4 of Yom Tov, the Rambam holds that this is in reference to terumot that were completely separated before Yom Tov, as he explains there. But in merely naming it [declaring it as terumah] — they agree with the Jerusalem Talmud that the permission is only in teaching, etc. (And this is not in accordance with the words of the Tosefot Yom Tov there in Demai, that the Mishnah is not according to the halacha, and I am puzzled that this is not mentioned in the words of the Rambam).

And know that there is someone who was uncertain whether, since acquisition is prohibited on Shabbat, one can acquire something from ownerless property on Shabbat if it is not muktzeh, for in this case as well, one acquires from the ownerless property. Or perhaps, since there is no buyer and seller, this is not considered acquisition (Rabbi Akiva Eiger). In my humble opinion, it seems clear that it is permitted, for if not, how is it permitted to bring challah and gifts to a priest on Yom Tov (Beitzah 12b)? Granted, he is allowed to give what is not his, but nonetheless, the priest acquires it on Shabbat and Yom Tov, and this is not his, for he could give it to one priest, and necessarily this priest acquires it as an acquisition. Rather, since there is no seller, as the Israelite is not transferring ownership but the Torah grants it to him – it is permitted, and the same applies to ownerless property. Additionally, according to the reason written by the Rambam regarding buying and selling, lest one write, it does not apply to ownerless property. Furthermore, even for a gift, we have explained in Siman 306, Section 17, that it is not comparable to buying and selling, and therefore they permitted it for a mitzvah purpose there, and all the more so for ownerless property, which is permitted in all cases. (And there is a bit of proof from Bava Metzia 9b: "If he lifted a purse on Shabbat, etc.," see there, and if it is forbidden to acquire from ownerless property on Shabbat, even if it is not a purse, consider this carefully.)

Gathering is one of the primary categories of work, and its definition is gathering detached produce into one place. This is part of the labor of harvest, to collect them into one place and to make them into bundles, sheaves, and piles. Its measure, as written by the Rambam in Chapter 8, Halacha 5: "Gathering food: if for eating, the measure is a dried fig; if gathering for an animal, the measure is a mouthful for a kid (young goat); if for fuel, the measure is enough to cook a dried fig from a chicken egg." Gathering only applies to things that grow from the ground. Therefore, one who gathers salt from a salt field, meaning collecting salt from evaporated seawater, where water is drawn into a trench from the sea and the sun evaporates it, turning it into salt - this does not constitute the primary category of gathering, since it does not grow from the ground (Gemara 73a. See there, the law follows Abaye and not Rava, and the Ra'avad challenged the Rambam because he read it as Rava; see there in Kesef Mishneh).

The Rambam wrote there: "One who gathers figs and makes them into a round shape, or who threads figs on a string until they form one body - this is a derivative of the labor of gathering and is liable, and similarly for anything similar to this." And it is obvious that when one gathers any type of vegetable in a garden to one place, or similarly various types of fruits when they are gathered detached to one place, such as apples and all types of tree fruits - this is the primary labor of gathering. And it is necessary to warn those who sit in orchards not to gather two fruits to one place on Shabbat, and this prohibition is entirely hidden from the eyes of the public. Therefore, it is necessary to inform them that there is a prohibition of stoning for this, and one who does it unintentionally is liable to bring a sin offering. Gathering was done in the Mishkan as mentioned in section 10, and see section 8.

In the Jerusalem Talmud, in the chapter "Klal Gadol," it states: "What is the derivative of 'gathering'? ...Those who spread out grapes to dry into raisins on the roof - they are liable for 'gathering.' Anyone who touches the food - is liable for 'gathering.' With the peel - is liable for 'threshing.'" From this, we learn that when one spreads out fruits with the intention that the fruits should be together - they are liable for 'gathering.' However, if the intention is to remove their peel - the liability is for 'threshing.' It is clear that 'gathering' applies only to grains and fruits that have not been baked or cooked or ground, as they are still like they were when harvested and picked. Otherwise, it would be forbidden on Shabbat to place several loaves of bread in one place or to put different kinds of fruits next to each other. Rather, the prohibition applies only to collecting them from the field, gardens, and trees, and not when they are in the house. Certainly, this is even more so after grinding, baking, and cooking. See section 8.

Shearing is a primary category of labor. This is the language of the Rambam in Chapter 9, Law 7: "One who shears wool or hair, whether from a domesticated animal or a wild animal, whether from a living creature or from a dead one, even from their tail – is liable. What is the measure [that renders one liable]? Enough to spin a thread whose length is the width of a doubled sit. And what is the width of a sit? Enough to stretch from the thumb of the hand to the first finger when they are opened with all one's strength, which is close to two-thirds of a span. Plucking a feather from a bird - this is a derivative of shearing. Spinning wool from a living creature – one is exempt, because this is not the usual manner of shearing, nor is it the usual manner of combing, nor is it the usual manner of spinning." End of quote. We have already explained in Siman 336, Clause 35, that one is liable specifically for shearing from the dead, but plucking is not considered shearing for animals, see there.

And know that the Rambam ruled regarding one who shears: the measure is the width of a doubled sit, and he did not write any other measure. However, in the Jerusalem Talmud of "Klal Gadol" it says: If his intention is for spinning, the measure is as stated; but if his intention is for weaving, he is liable for the measure of a sit. Afterwards, it inquires about the general case of shearing, concluding leniently that the measure is doubled. And it can be said that the Rambam is referring to the general case, but if one shears for weaving, he is liable for the measure of a sit. This must necessarily be so, for we have learned in the Mishnah (105b) that the measure for spinning is the width of a doubled sit, and the measure for weaving is the width of a sit. Hence, it follows that for shearing, if it is for spinning, the measure is the measure of spinning, and if for weaving, the measure is the measure of weaving. Thus, certainly as stated. And shearing was in the Mishkan, as explained in section 10.

One who cuts their nails, hair, mustache, or beard - this is considered a derivative of shearing and is liable. This applies when using a tool, but if done by hand: whether for oneself or for another – one is exempt. And this liability when using a tool applies when there is a need for the hair or nails. But if there is no need for them - it is considered a labor not needed for its own sake and one is exempt, according to the authorities who follow Rabbi Shimon (Magen Avraham, siman 1), while the Rambam rules according to Rabbi Yehuda, as mentioned several times. One who cuts hair with a tool, how much must be cut to be liable: two hairs, and if one plucks white hairs from among black ones - even one hair makes one liable. This matter is forbidden even on a weekday, due to the prohibition of "a man shall not wear a woman's garment." And if a woman forgot to cut her nails before immersion on Shabbat, it is explained in Yoreh De'ah siman 198, see there. And the law regarding a nail that is mostly detached is explained above in siman 328, paragraph 41, see there.

The Rambam writes there: "Similarly, one who cuts off a wart from his body, whether by hand or with a utensil, is exempt, whether for himself or for another. It is permissible to cut off a wart in the Temple by hand but not with a utensil, and if it is dry, one may cut it even with a utensil and continue performing the service." The Maggid Mishneh questions this exemption for cutting with a utensil, as at the end of Eruvin it is clearly proven that the law for a moist wart is like that of a fingernail, that for cutting with a utensil one is liable. Rashi also explains there (103a) that cutting with a utensil constitutes a primary category of labor. Further, if using a utensil is only a rabbinic prohibition, why did they not permit it in the Temple just as they did by hand, for using the hand is also a rabbinic prohibition? All the measures explained, even regarding hair, are only for liability to bring a sin-offering, but rabbinically, even the slightest amount is forbidden, even by hand, and yet they permitted it in the Temple. Therefore, it stands to reason that this is a printing error in the Rambam, as the entire discussion there explicitly shows that using a utensil is a Torah prohibition.

A fundamental principle must be known: regarding all primary categories of labor, their measurements, and their details—meaning in this manner one is liable and in that manner one is exempt—this exemption is only from Torah law. However, from Rabbinic law, it is prohibited, for a fundamental principle of Shabbat is that all exemptions of Shabbat are "exempt but prohibited," except where it is stated that it is permitted. Therefore, even for gathering (ma'amer) that has been explained, there is no gathering except with things that grow from the ground and not with salt, as stated in Section 1. The intention is not that it is permitted with salt, but that with salt it is exempt but prohibited. And this is what our master the Beit Yosef wrote in Section 9: "It is forbidden to gather salt from salt pans, as it resembles gathering, etc." See there, and the prohibition is from Rabbinic law. However, what we have written in Section 3 is categorically permitted, as the Kesef Mishneh wrote there in the name of the Remaḥ concerning the law of one who gathers figs and makes them into a cake, that he is liable for gathering. And this is his language: "Specifically if he gathered them from the place where they fell from the tree, but if he gathered them in the house—no, as we say in Beitzah, etc." End quote. And similarly, Tosafot wrote in Beitzah (31a, s.v. 'from there'), that gathering is only relevant in the place where they grow. See there. And concerning the measurements explained for gathering and shearing—even less than their measurements is prohibited, as with any half-measure that is prohibited even by Torah law, and all the more so by Rabbinic law, and so it is with all primary categories of labor that have been and will be explained. (The Magen Avraham, in his commentary, questioned regarding gathering figs, etc., why one would not be liable for building as with cheese-making. This is not a comparison, as with cheese-making the form changes from before the cheese-making to after, similar to building a house from wood, but not so with figs. Perhaps this is also the intention of his answer, but there is no basis for this question.)

Beating (Menapetz) is one of the primary categories of work. What is beating? It refers to separating wool or flax that is stuck together by beating it with a stick or combing it with a comb, which in our language is called "treaflen." This is the language of Maimonides in Chapter 9, Law 12: "One who beats wool, flax, or silk and the like is liable. And what is the measure for liability? Enough to spin one thread four handbreadths long. And one who beats sinews until they become like wool to spin them is considered a derivative of beating and is liable." This is the end of the quotation. And in the Jerusalem Talmud, in the chapter "Klal Gadol," it is stated: "One who beats fibers of palm leaves, rushes, or bulrushes is liable for beating," meaning one who beats fibers that grow around the palm tree, rushes, or bulrushes, which is a long grass, with the intention of making them thin in order to weave them, is liable for beating. And in the Jerusalem Talmud, the version is "menafes," and it was done in the Tabernacle as will be explained.

Spinning is a primary category of labor, and it was in the Tabernacle as it is written: "They spun the goats' hair." Also, combing was in the Tabernacle, for the flax and wool that were needed for the work of the Tabernacle necessarily had to be combed. Similarly, shearing was in the Tabernacle, as they sheared wool from the sheep for the needs of the Tabernacle. Gathering into bundles was also present in the planting of herbs, as when they grew, they gathered them into one place. And its measure, it is taught (105b): like the full width of a double stitch. According to Maimonides, it is four handbreadths, and this is his language in Chapter 9, Law 15: "One who spins a length of four handbreadths from any spun material is liable, whether one spins wool, flax, feathers, hair, tendons, and anything similar. One who makes felt – this is a derivative of spinning and is liable, provided that one makes felt from something from which it is possible to spin a thread of four handbreadths in moderate thickness." End of quote.

And the Raavad objected to him, and this is his language: "I do not recognize spinning in the making of felt, for he takes white and combed wool and spreads it on a garment, and puts tuft upon tuft until it becomes thick, and wets it with water and rolls it with the garment and presses it until it binds and hardens and becomes felt. And if this connection is called spinning, I do not know, and it seems more that it is like cheesemaking, and it is a derivative of building, and its measure I do not know. And perhaps in length and width like those braids that poor girls make on their foreheads." End of quote. And it seems to me that in the Jerusalem Talmud of "Klal Gadol" it is explicitly like the Rambam, who says there: "Those who make ropes, those who make mats - are liable for spinning." And a mat seems to be a mattress, as it is stated in the 19th chapter of Kelim: "A mat that comes out from the bed, any amount," and it is explained in the Aruch under the entry 'Mat': that it is a woolen garment that the important people place on their beds under all the bedding, and in the foreign language it is called "tapeta," and in the Ishmaelite language "mizar." And it is translated there in our language "kabritz," and some call it "kaviar," and this is felt, for felt is wool that is beaten without spinning and weaving as the Raavad said at the end of Kilayim, and in our language it is "filz."

Weaving is considered a primary category of labor. What constitutes weaving? Stretching the warp threads on the weaver's frame from the upper beam to the lower beam. This is the wording of Maimonides in Halacha 17: "The way of the weavers is that they first stretch the threads lengthwise and widthwise of the fabric. Two people hold, one from here and one from there, and one beats the threads with a rod and aligns them side by side until the entire fabric is composed of warp threads without the weft. The stretching of the threads in the manner of the weavers is called 'stretching the warp,' and the one who stretches is called a 'weaver.' When they fold it and begin to insert the warp into the weft, this is called weaving. The person who stretches the warp is liable, and it is a primary category of labor. Beating the threads until they are aligned is considered a derivative of stretching the warp. The measure is when one has adjusted the width of two fingers." This was performed in the Tabernacle with the work of linen and sky-blue wool for the curtains.

And in the Jerusalem Talmud of "Klal Gadol" (Great Principle): "One who makes a sieve, a basket, or a mat is liable for [the labor of] weaving." A sieve and a mat are well known, and a basket is a type of sack made from reeds. When one performs the weaving labor described, he is liable for [the labor of] weaving. "A woman who drinks from a sieve is liable for weaving," and this refers to when she places the warp into the holes. "One who makes a basket from twigs is liable for weaving," and this refers to one who makes baskets from reeds and fibers. When he begins to weave the braid around the basket at its base, he is liable for weaving. "One who makes beds from 'milin' lengthwise is liable for weaving," and this refers to making beds from a type of wood called 'milin.' When he begins to weave them lengthwise, since the wood is soft and can be stretched, it is like the labor of wool and flax.

The one who makes two heddles—this is a principal category of labor. This also applies during weaving if one made or fixed two loops or two knots, where one thread is inserted into each loop or knot. It appears that liability is incurred both for making the heddles themselves (see Lechem Mishneh) and for inserting two threads into them. And this is the wording of the Rambam there, Law 16: "One who makes two heddles is liable. One who makes a sieve, a sifter, a basket, a mesh, or who weaves a bed with ropes—these are derivatives of making heddles, and once one makes two heddles in any of these—one is liable. And anyone who makes two heddles in an item that is made with heddles like these—is liable." End quote. And this was in the Tabernacle in the weaving of the curtains and the screens. And in the Jerusalem Talmud there: "This woman, when she sets the threads before her—it is because she makes heddles," meaning when she inserts the threads into the holes before her. "One who makes 'milin kanklatin'—it is because he makes heddles," meaning, from a wood called 'milin' that makes small rooms during weaving—is liable because he makes heddles. It further states there: "Two threads in one loop and two loops in one thread." It appears that the explanation is: This liability applies whether one inserts two threads, meaning two threads into one loop, or one thread into this heddle and its other end into another heddle—one is liable (and see there in the Kesef Mishneh and the Perush Mishnayos).

Weaving is considered a principal category of labor, and weaving is defined as when one inserts the warp into the weft. It is obvious that this was present in the Tabernacle, as they wove the curtains and hangings. The measure for this, as the Rambam wrote in Halacha 18: “One who weaves two threads the width of two fingers is liable, whether he weaves them initially or adds to an existing woven section, the measure is two threads. And if he weaves one thread and completes the garment with it, he is liable. If he weaves two threads on the edge of the curtain the width of three warp threads, he is liable. To what is this similar? To one who weaves a small belt the width of three warp threads.” This means that even though it does not have the width of two fingers, since it is like a small garment in itself, one is liable with the measure of two warp threads. Note that the measure the Rambam gave for weaving the width of two fingers is seemingly puzzling, because in the Mishnah (105b) it states: one who weaves two threads, the measure is the full width of a sit. And since the Rambam himself wrote that the width of a sit is double, which is four handbreadths as he wrote in Section 10, then the full sit is two handbreadths. So how can he obligate for two fingers? However, the understanding of the Rambam from not saying ‘the full width of the sit’ but rather ‘the full sit’ is that this is another measure which is two fingers. But Rashi did not explain this way, rather he explained it as half the measure of spinning.

The Rambam writes there (Halacha 19): "One who meticulously arranges the threads and separates them during weaving - this is a derivative of weaving, and similarly, one who braids threads - this is a derivative of weaving. The measure for liability is when one makes a braid the length of two fingers." End quote. According to Rashi, it requires two handbreadths, and in the Jerusalem Talmud: even one who makes an item from wood called milin, which is soft, is liable for weaving when they insert the weft over the warp. See there.

Tearing is also considered a primary category of labor (Av Melacha). What is tearing? It is the removal of the woof threads from the warp threads or the warp from the woof for the purpose of weaving (Ra'avad). Rashi, of blessed memory, wrote in the Mishnah regarding the primary categories of labor, and this is his wording: "Tearing – separating, sometimes there are too many threads and one separates them and makes them thinner for a purpose." And the Rambam wrote in the ninth chapter: "One who tears two threads is liable. Tearing is separating what was woven, whether he removed the woof from the warp or passed the warp over the woof - this is tearing and he is liable. However, he should not be damaging but should intend to repair, as those who stitch delicate clothing do, who tear and then stitch again and weave the threads they tore until they make two garments or two pieces of fabric into one. And one who undoes weaving to fix it - this is a derivative of tearing, and its measure is like the measure of tearing." And the Ra'avad explained there that tearing is a term of cutting, that one cuts two threads, that after completing his weaving, he cuts the woven part from what remains on the loom. And even if he only cut two threads - he is liable for this cutting. And according to all interpretations, it was certainly present in the Tabernacle, as it pertains to the work of weaving.

Writing and erasing are considered primary categories of work (melachot). One is only liable for erasing if it is done with the intention of writing again. However, erasing with the intention to spoil or destroy is exempt from liability but still forbidden. The measure for liability is writing two letters. As it is taught in the Mishnah (104a): "One who writes two letters in one lapse of awareness is liable." This was done in the Tabernacle where they would mark the boards of the Tabernacle to know which ones paired together (Mishnah 103a). Since they would dismantle it, and when reassembling it, they would not mix up the order of the boards, they would write letters on the boards as a sign (according to the first Tanna, there were letters by necessity, and according to Rabbi Yosi, they would engrave them; pay attention).

And their derivatives, Maimonides wrote at the end of Chapter 11: "Marking is a derivative of writing. How so? One who makes marks and designs on a wall or on marble, or similar surfaces, in the manner that artists make marks—this person is liable because of writing. Similarly, one who erases a mark in order to correct it—this is a derivative of erasing and he is liable." End quote. And know that in the Mishnah (103a) it is taught: "One who writes two letters is liable… Rabbi Yose says: They only obligated [for writing] two letters because of marking, etc." And Rashi explained that even if one did not write but rather made two simple marks, he is liable. See there. And from the fact that Maimonides wrote that marking is a derivative, we learn that the law is not in accordance with Rabbi Yose, because according to Rabbi Yose it would be a primary category. Furthermore, according to Rabbi Yose, why would one need marks of designs, for even simple marks would make one liable? And Maimonides and the Ra'avad in their commentary on the Mishnah wrote that the law is not in accordance with Rabbi Yose. See there. However, in the Jerusalem Talmud, it seems that the law follows Rabbi Yose. See there (refer to the Pnei Moshe in the Mareh HaPanim who wrote that Maimonides ruled according to Rabbi Yose, but it is not a primary category, and his proof is from the fact that he makes one liable for marks. See there. His words are perplexing, for this refers to marking of designs and not simple marking. Furthermore, in his commentary on the Mishnah, he wrote that the law is not according to Rabbi Yose. Therefore, it is certain as we have written, and carefully consider this).

Maimonides wrote in Chapter 11, Law 9: "One who writes two letters is liable. One who erases writing with the intention of writing two letters in the place of the erasure is liable. One who writes a single large letter equivalent to two is exempt. One who erases a single large letter and in its place can write two letters is liable. One who writes a single letter and completes a book with it is liable. One who writes with the intention of damaging the parchment is liable, for the liability is not on the place of the writing but on the writing itself. However, one who erases with the intention of damaging is exempt. If ink falls on a book and one erases it, or if wax falls on a notebook and one erases it, if there is enough space to write two letters in the place of the erasure, one is liable." End of quote.

And this is what he wrote: "Ink fell on a book, etc.," meaning that ink fell not on the writing but on a blank parchment or paper, and similarly wax on a blank notebook. And this is the language of the Rosh in the chapter "Klal Gadol" (Siman 9): "One who writes one large letter which is as two—he is exempt; one who erases...—he is liable, and this is a stringency in erasing over writing. And the reason is that sometimes a mistake was written in the Mishkan on one board, and one would erase it in order to write another in its place. And by law, one should be liable even for erasing one letter to write another in its place, except that it is not appropriate to be more stringent about the intention of writing more than about writing itself. And it appears that one is not liable for erasing a smudge of ink even to write several letters, because in the Mishkan there was only erasing letters to write in their place. And after I wrote this based on reasoning, and also from the fact that the Baraita specifies: 'erased one letter,' I saw in the Tosefta it is written: "Ink fell on a book and he erased it, wax on a notebook and he erased it; if there is enough space to write two letters—he is liable." And the reason is not clear to us, and it can be said that the reason is that a letter written by mistake is considered as if it does not exist, and the main liability is for the intention of writing, and therefore even a smudge of ink as well. And the reason the Baraita specifies: 'erased one large letter,' is because it taught: 'wrote one large letter.' And similarly, it can be explained in the words of the Rambam. And what was written earlier: "erased a letter, etc." is not precise, because in erasing we do not require a letter, and one can add in reasoning that this is a purposeful act, when one erases the ink on the paper in order to write on it.

The Tur also wrote: "One who erases ink smears on the parchment or wax on the notebook, if the space created is large enough to write two letters – is liable," and similarly is the language of the Shulchan Aruch, Section 3. Certainly, even if the space created is not large enough to write two letters, it is prohibited by rabbinic decree. Therefore, care must be taken when wax drips on a book not to remove it, even if it drips on only one letter or an area the size of one letter. If it drips on two letters or an area the size of two letters, one is liable for a sin offering (Bach, Taz, and Magen Avraham, Subsection 4). Some dispute this ruling, and it is also discussed earlier in Siman 143. Nevertheless, the primary ruling is that on Shabbat it is strictly forbidden to remove wax that has fallen on letters. Similarly, when pages stick together due to wax at the location of the letters, it is forbidden to separate them (Pri Megadim). One must be very careful about this, as it can easily lead to a prohibition (see Magen Avraham, Subsection 18).

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote in paragraph 3: It is forbidden to break a cake upon which letters are written, even though one's intention is only to eat it, as this constitutes erasure. And even though it is not with the intention to write, nevertheless, there is a rabbinic prohibition involved. According to this, it would also be forbidden with mere drawings, although people are not careful about this. Perhaps because all the drawings or letters made on sweets are from the dough itself or from spices, and in this case, it is certainly not considered writing, as it is also food and is completely permitted (see Magen Avraham, subparagraph 6, who wrote this in the name of Knesset Hagedolah). And the intention of our teacher, the Rema, is when the letters are written with ink or paint. Similarly, if the letters are written with honey mixed with water, there is also no concern. There are those who completely permit it even with writing from other substances (Dagul Mervavah), as it is not considered writing at all, it is destructive, and done in an unusual manner, and there is no prohibition whatsoever. And the source of the Rema's ruling concerns when it was written as a charm, so that the child would eat it to become wise, as that was their custom. Nevertheless, it is good to give the place of the letters to the child since it comes from the mouth of our teacher, the Rema, and fundamentally, there is no prohibition in this (also the Taz, subparagraph 2, permits this, see there). Likewise, there are those who prohibit opening a book whose edges of the pages have letters written on them, as when it is opened it constitutes erasure (Levush), but others disagreed with him (there). And our teacher, the Rema, wrote in a responsum (Siman 119), that since it is made to open and close, there is no issue of erasing or writing, and it is nothing, and it is like a door that is always opened and closed, where there is no issue of building and demolishing, and here too there is no issue of writing and erasing.

One who writes a double letter twice, and it is one name, like "rar," "tat," "gag," "dad," "shesh," "sas," "chach," and similar – is liable. But if one writes two identical letters without the intention of forming a word – is exempt (Mishnah Torah, Hilchot Shabbat 11). And one who writes in any script and any language – is liable, even if with two different inks, as we learned in the Mishnah there. Rashi explained: even one with ink and one with red ink (sikra), and the Rashba wrote in the name of the Gaon that it refers to the forms of the letters, such as making reversed letters like the reversed "nun" in the section "And it came to pass when the ark set forward," that anything that has the form of a letter, even if it is reversed – one is liable.

The one who writes one letter near a written letter, meaning that he places a second letter close to an already written letter, or writes over writing, i.e., he traces over already written letters with the quill – is exempt, because he has not created anything new. This is specifically when the writing was done with ink, for then, whether he traces over the writing with ink or with paint, he is exempt, because he has degraded it. But if the original writing was with paint and he traces over it with ink – he is liable for two [transgressions]: one for erasing, as he has erased the paint, and one for writing, as he has enhanced it, for ink is superior to paint. However, when he traces over it with paint, even if it is a different type of paint – he is exempt, because there is neither erasure, since the paint remains, nor writing, since it was already written beforehand (nevertheless, if paint is applied over ink, he is not liable for erasing, since there remains writing, but he has degraded it. And with ink over paint, since he is liable for writing, he is also liable for erasing, and with paint over ink, it is considered damaging, as explained in Gittin 19b).

And similarly, one who intended to write the letter "chet" but wrote two "zayin" letters instead, and similarly in other such cases with other letters - is exempt. Similarly, if one wrote one letter on the ground and one letter on a beam, since they do not function together. Likewise, if one wrote on two walls or on two pages of a notebook that are distant from each other - is exempt. But if one wrote on two walls of a corner or on two pages of a notebook, one at the end and one at the beginning, and thus they are adjacent to each other - is liable. And know that there is no distinction in writing whether one wrote on paper, parchment, wood, or any material, as long as the writing is recognizable and durable - one is liable.

It states in the Gemara (104b): "If one wrote one letter in Tiberias and one letter in Sepphoris - he is liable, for it is considered writing, but it requires bringing them close." And Rashi explained (s.v. 'requires'): that he wrote one letter on the edge of one board in Tiberias and one on the edge of another board in Sepphoris, and when they are brought together, the letters will be near each other. But the Rambam wrote there (Halacha 12) as follows: "If one took parchment or something similar and wrote one letter on it in one city, and went on the same day and wrote another letter in another city on another scroll - he is liable, for when they are brought close, they join together and do not require any further action to bring them close." And according to his opinion, with soft paper or thin parchment, even if they are distant from each other, one can fold the paper and bring them close. This is how the Maggid Mishneh wrote. In my humble opinion, I do not understand why we should not interpret the Rambam's words similar to Rashi's explanation, and his intent is that he wrote on the edges of the parchment.

One who writes one letter, even though a whole word can be read from it, is exempt. How so? For example, if one wrote the letter "mem" and everyone reads it as "ma'aser" (tithe), or if it was written in place of a number, like forty — this person is exempt. However, if one corrects one letter and makes it into two, such as splitting the roof of a "chet" and making it into two "zayins" — they are liable, and similarly in all such cases. Additionally, if by correcting a single letter in a minor way the book is fixed, such as when a "resh" was needed but a "dalet" was written, and one removed the "tag" of the "dalet" turning it into a "resh" — they are liable (Gemara), since this is considered fixing the book and is akin to completing the book (Rashi), as explained in Section 20, see there.

One who writes with his left hand, or with the back of his hand, with his foot, mouth, or elbow, which means with the upper arm – is exempt, because this is not the usual way of writing. Similarly, a left-handed person who writes with his right hand, which for him is like the left hand for everyone else – is exempt, but if he writes with his left hand – he is liable. One who is ambidextrous and writes with either hand – is liable. It is taught in the Tosefta: "If a minor holds the pen and an adult guides his hand and writes – he is liable. If an adult holds the pen and a minor guides his hand and writes – he is exempt," because the main aspect is who is actually writing, not who is holding the pen. (And similarly, in the case of an inadvertent act, see there in Chapter 12).

A person is not liable for writing unless they write with a substance that leaves a permanent mark, such as ink, black dye, red dye, gum, or vitriol, and the writing must be on a material that sustains the writing, such as leather, parchment, paper, wood, etc. However, if one writes with a substance that does not leave a permanent mark, such as liquids or fruit juice, or if one writes with ink or similar on leaves or any other non-durable material, they are exempt. One is only liable if they write with a permanent substance on a permanent material. Similarly, one is not liable for erasing unless they erase writing that is permanent on a permanent material (Rambam, ibid.). If one writes on their own skin, they are liable because it is considered like leather, even though the warmth of the skin eventually causes the writing to fade, which is similar to writing that is later erased. However, if one scratches a form of writing into their skin, they are exempt. Tearing a form of writing on leather incurs liability for writing, but inscribing a form of writing on leather does not. This is what Rambam wrote there, and it is based on the Tosefta (Chapter 12). However, in our version of the Tosefta, the text is reversed, stating that inscribing incurs liability and tearing does not. The correct version follows Rambam, as it also appears in the Jerusalem Talmud, Chapter 12, Halacha 4. The Tosefta also states: "If one wrote two dots and another came and completed them into two letters, the latter is liable."

Our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, wrote in Section 4: "One should be careful not to write with one's finger on a table using liquids or dust, but it is permissible to trace letters in the air." This means that even though one is exempt when using something that does not last, as has been stated, it is still forbidden to do so initially. However, in the air, it is nothing at all since it is not discernible. Similarly, one who moves his finger on a dry table is also permitted for this reason (Taz, subparagraph 3). And tracing on windows when they are wet with moisture is forbidden, as it is like writing on a table with liquids.

Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote in paragraph 5: "It is permitted to inscribe with a fingernail as a sign, since this is not something that endures." And even though lechatchila (initially) it is forbidden even with something that does not endure as mentioned, this applies to writing letters and not to mere inscriptions, for we have already written in paragraph 19 that the law does not follow Rabbi Yose who obligates even for inscriptions, as mentioned there. And there are those who toiled in this matter (Taz section 4, who questions from the inscription in the Mishnah), but it is clear as stated. Therefore, for inscriptions, it is sufficient to prohibit with something that endures. However, some say that specifically on parchment it does not endure, but on paper it endures and is forbidden (Magen Avraham section 10 in the name of Rashal), and there are those who forbid even on parchment (Bach), and their reasoning is based on Rabbi Yose's opinion. But we have already written that the law does not follow this, and therefore the main opinion is the previous one, that on parchment it is permitted and on paper it is forbidden. However, writing letters, even on parchment, is forbidden (Levush). And writing with a pen made of a feather, called a "blay feder" - one is liable from the Torah.

And know that there are those who wish to say that writing in a non-Hebrew script does not incur a Torah obligation, and we have already written in Siman 306 that it is forbidden to say this, and Maimonides explicitly writes that for any writing one is liable, as we have written. And it appears in Gittin (20a) that if one inserts silver letters onto a garment, it is considered writing, and if so, it might be forbidden to do so on Shabbat (as the Magen Avraham writes there). However, upon careful examination, it appears that on the contrary, it is clarified there that it is not considered writing (and the Magen Avraham struggled greatly and did not succeed, see there carefully).

Our master, Rabbi Yosef Karo, wrote in sub-section 6: "A thread of sewing that has come loose—it is forbidden to stretch it, because this constitutes sewing. And those who tighten their garments around their arms using a thread that they stretch and tighten—it is forbidden to stretch it unless the holes are somewhat wide and properly sewn and rounded," end of quote. For if not, it is considered sewing. But when they are properly sewn, even if the thread is threaded through a needle with an eye—it is permitted (there in sub-section 13). And this applies when they tighten every day, but if they sometimes leave it that way for several days—it is forbidden to tighten it on Shabbat (there in sub-section 12), because it is considered a permanent knot. And a needle that has bent, even slightly—it is forbidden to straighten it on Shabbat (there in sub-section 11), because it constitutes fixing a utensil. And stuffing that has fallen from the pillow—it is permitted to return it, but it is forbidden to put it in the pillow initially, because now he makes it into a utensil, and also we are concerned that he might sew (there in sub-section 14). All the laws of sewing and tying we have explained in Siman 317, see there (and also the law concerning the one who glues papers in the Shulchan Aruch, sub-section 14, we have explained there).

Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote in section 11: "Even though one may put sesame seeds and nuts into honey, one should not knead them by hand. And one who puts flax seeds or sesame seeds or similar into water is liable for kneading, because they mix and adhere to each other." End quote. The first law we explained in Siman 319, section 39, and the second law we explained in Siman 336, section 28, see there. Additionally, he wrote in section 13: "One may not break pottery or tear paper, because it is like repairing a utensil." End quote, and this is from the Rambam, chapter 23, law 6, see there. And I am perplexed as to what relevance this has to Shabbat, for this is a Mishnah in Beitzah (32b): "One may not break, etc.", and Rashi explained: "When roasting fish, etc.", and similarly the Rambam wrote in chapter 4 of Yom Tov, law 8: "One may not break pottery or cut paper to roast upon them," see there. And what relevance does this have to Shabbat, for on Shabbat, all breaking and cutting is forbidden, and it requires further investigation.

It is taught at the end of Shabbat (157b): "One may annul vows on Shabbat, and one may ask for the annulment of vows that are for the sake of Shabbat." This means that, by law, it would have been forbidden to annul vows on Shabbat, as this is not considered a heavenly matter and is prohibited due to 'seeking your own affairs.' However, in the case of a husband annulling his wife's vows or a father annulling his daughter's vows, if he does not annul them on the day he hears them, the vow is upheld, and he can no longer annul it. Thus, it is permitted to annul any vow on Shabbat. But regarding the annulment by a sage, one may only ask if the vow pertains to the needs of Shabbat, such as if one vowed not to eat meat or drink wine, and all the more so if one vowed not to eat or drink at all. Even if one vowed not to wear fine clothing, it is considered a need for Shabbat. The same applies to a vow related to other mitzvah matters; if annulling it will allow him to perform a mitzvah, it is permitted to annul it on Shabbat. There is an opinion that forbids this (Maharsha at the beginning of Eruvin). The primary view seems to be the former one, that since it pertains to a mitzvah matter, it is considered a heavenly matter. And the Mishnah, which taught 'for the sake of Shabbat,' speaks in the usual manner, and all the more so for a complete mitzvah matter, one may ask even if it was possible to ask before Shabbat (Rambam, Chapter 24).

In Yoreh De'ah, section 234, it is explained that when annulling a vow on Shabbat, one should not say to her, "It is annulled for you" as one would on a weekday, but rather say to her, "Take, eat; take, drink," and think of the annulment in his heart. However, the release by a sage must necessarily be verbalized with "It is permitted to you," for otherwise, it is not considered a release. One of the great authorities wrote: "If there is an excommunication in a dream, we acted and released it on Shabbat (Keneset HaGedolah and Eliyah Rabbah)." And know that sometimes one might need to ask a sage even not for the sake of Shabbat, such as a husband who upheld his wife's vows, and it is established that he can ask to annul his upholding of it, as mentioned there. Some authorities hold that this is only on the day of hearing, so if he does not ask today, he will not be able to annul it. If so, it is considered as if it is the annulment itself (Taz).

It is obvious that if the husband does not yet know about his wife's vows, they should not tell him on Shabbat. When he hears about it tomorrow, he will annul it on the day he hears it, unless the vow concerns the needs of Shabbat. Similarly, if she is betrothed and her father has already heard her vow, then it is necessary to inform the betrothed as well so that both can annul it together, as we hold that they must both hear it on the same day. And know that according to what is explained in Yoreh De'ah, section 323, regarding challah that fell into a dish and is not nullified, that one can seek to annul the challah and remove its sanctity—it is certainly permissible to ask and annul it on Shabbat, for this is a need of Shabbat.

If someone took an oath to perform a specific task and specified that it should be completed on a certain day, but he was unable to perform it until the last day of that period, and that day falls on Shabbat, and at the time of the oath, he did not consider that it would fall on Shabbat, for example, if he was thinking about the days of the month or a number of days - it is necessary for him to request the annulment of his vow on Shabbat, and it is permitted to annul it on Shabbat through a "petach" (opening) or "charata" (regret). (In the Shulchan Aruch it is written: 'and he has openings to annul his vow' see there, and it is not strictly necessary, for we hold in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 228, that we can annul through regret. And what is written in the Shulchan Aruch that communal bans are customarily annulled on Shabbat even if not for the sake of Shabbat, it has already been explained in Siman 306 that all communal needs are considered matters of Heaven, see there).

Rambam wrote in Chapter 24, Law 10: "All activities that are prohibited due to 'shevut' (rabbinic prohibitions) were not decreed for the time between sunset and nightfall (bein hashmashot), but only for the actual day itself are they prohibited, and not during bein hashmashot, provided there is a matter of a mitzvah or pressing need. How so: it is permitted during bein hashmashot to climb a tree or to float on water to bring a lulav or shofar, and similarly to lower from the tree or take out from the karmelit an eiruv that was made. Likewise, if one was preoccupied and hurried and needed something which is a 'shevut' during bein hashmashot – this is permitted. However, if there is no pressing need or matter of a mitzvah – it is prohibited. Therefore, one may not tithe definite produce during bein hashmashot even though the prohibition of separating tithes on Shabbat is due to 'shevut,' but one may tithe demai (doubtfully tithed produce)." End quote.

Explanation of his words: For the sake of a mitzvah, it is always permitted to perform a rabbinic prohibition (shvut) during twilight (bein hashmashot). Even for a non-mitzvah purpose, if he was preoccupied and hurried and could not do it beforehand, it is also permitted for his needs. Indeed, from the language of the Talmud in several places, which states that rabbinic prohibitions were not decreed during twilight, it implies that this applies even to non-mitzvah matters. This is also implied by Rashi’s language (8a: s.v.
