'and Rabbi') who wrote that the rabbinic prohibitions decreed by the sages for Shabbat were only decreed for definite Shabbat, etc. However, since we do not find this everywhere but only regarding Eruv Techumin (boundary extension for Shabbat), and we hold that one may only make an Eruv for the sake of a mitzvah, and even if not for a complete mitzvah but to greet his friend or even to stroll, as written in Siman 415. We also hold that if one made an Eruv for a non-mitzvah purpose, his Eruv is valid. Therefore, the Rambam, in his great wisdom, ruled that it is always permitted for a mitzvah purpose, and for a non-mitzvah purpose if he was hurried and preoccupied. But for a non-mitzvah purpose in a relaxed manner where he could have done it beforehand, it is certainly not permitted.

And this is the language of the Tur: "Any rabbinically prohibited activity (Shvut) is permitted during twilight for the sake of a mitzvah, such as taking one's eiruv placed in a karmelit or climbing a tree to get it, or taking a lulav placed on it, or if one was preoccupied and needed to tithe fruits during twilight. Similarly, Rabbi Yitzchak wrote that it is permitted to tell a gentile to light a candle for him during twilight." End of quote. From his words, it is implied that it is only for the sake of a mitzvah, but for a non-mitzvah purpose, it is not permitted under any circumstances. He also holds that the permission to separate demai during twilight is only if one was preoccupied, but certainly, in any other case, it is forbidden. According to the Rambam, however, it is also permitted in such cases. The Tur holds that tithing is not considered a mitzvah at all, since one can eat other things on Shabbat. However, it is certain that if one has nothing else to eat, even the Tur agrees that he can tithe during twilight. And even for a yahrzeit candle, it is permitted to tell a non-Jew during twilight to light it for him (Taz in the name of the Maharshal, and in explaining the words of the Tur, see Beit Yosef, Bach, Derisha, and Taz, and I have written what seems right in my humble opinion, examine it carefully).

And know that there are those who are uncertain whether on the night following Shabbat, during twilight, we also say that no decree was made for twilight, or whether, since Shabbat has been established, it is forbidden (Magen Avraham). And from Tosafot in Eruvin (34b, s.v. "ve'amai") it appears that there is no distinction there (Tosafot Shabbat), and also from the fact that the Talmud and the decisors are generally silent on the matter, it is clear that there is no distinction. This is also explicitly evident from the language of Rashi and the Rambam that we have brought, who wrote: that they only decreed concerning the actual day and a definite day, and thus, by extension, they did not decree concerning twilight at the conclusion of the day.

Maimonides wrote at the end of the Laws of Forbidden Foods: "A minor who ate one of the forbidden foods or performed work on Shabbat - the court is not commanded to separate him, because he is not of sound mind. What are we talking about? When he did it on his own, but to feed him with one's hands is forbidden, even things that are forbidden by rabbinic decree. Similarly, it is forbidden to accustom him to desecrate Shabbat and festivals, even in matters that are rabbinically prohibited. And even though the court is not commanded to separate the minor, it is a commandment for his father to reprimand him and separate him in order to educate him in holiness, as it is said: 'Train a child…' etc." This is the end of the quotation. And there are those who want to say that one is not obligated to educate his daughter, and similarly, the mother is not obligated to educate her son (see Magen Avraham, section 1). And we have already clarified elsewhere that this is not the case, and that the mother is also obligated in educating, and one is also obligated to educate the daughter. However, Maimonides is referring here to a minor who has not yet reached the age of education, for when he reaches the age of education, he is certainly obligated to educate him in mitzvot, and all the more so to prevent him from transgression; and so wrote our Rabbis, the Tosafists, in Shabbat (121a). See there.

This is what Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote in this section: "Some say that all this applies to a minor who has not reached the age of education, but if he has reached the age of education, we must separate him. And some say that education is only relevant to the father, not to the court." Certainly, for an orphaned minor, education is relevant to the court. And what is the measure of education? Every minor according to his sharpness, and generally when he understands the matter. But as long as he does not understand the matter, he is not included in education, and this is also evident from the language of the Talmud at the end of the third chapter of Sukkah, where it says: "A minor who knows how to wrap himself is obligated in tzitzit." And the law regarding a minor priest becoming impure through contact with the dead we have explained in Yoreh De'ah, section 373. And know that in matters that could lead to destruction, such as the sounding of the shofar whose sound is heard from afar, therefore when a minor blows the shofar on Shabbat, the court is commanded to separate him, and similarly in all such cases (Magen Avraham).

It is stated in the Talmud (Shabbat 90b) that it is forbidden to give a child a live impure grasshopper to play with, lest it die and he eats it. Even something that only has the prohibition of "Do not make yourselves abominable" (Lev. 11:43) is forbidden to give to him (Shulchan Aruch, Yoreh De'ah 116:3), for feeding him something by hand is forbidden even if it is a rabbinic prohibition, and "Do not make yourselves abominable" is a rabbinic prohibition, as stated by the Rambam at the end of Hilchot Ma'achalot Assurot. When giving it to him, it is as if feeding him by hand. However, it is permitted to give him an impure bird to play with, for when it dies, it is not fit for eating. The same applies to anything similar (ibid.).

Rabbeinu Yerucham wrote that one should not protest against non-Jews who feed a child forbidden food, but it is forbidden to tell them to give the child forbidden food, unless the child needs it and is somewhat ill; in that case, it is permitted to ask them to feed him. Therefore, it is customary on Passover, if a child refuses to eat matzah and becomes weak because of this, to ask a non-Jew to take him to his house and feed him chametz (ibid.). It is clear that whatever the child needs, the Jew can give him by hand, like feeding him on Yom Kippur or similar situations (ibid.).

It is proper to accustom a child to a mitzvah and to distance him from sin, especially from speaking lashon hara (slander), gossip, and falsehood, so that he does not become accustomed to it. Later, when he grows up, it will be difficult for him to separate from it. This is all the more so in our times, where it is necessary to pay attention to children so that they do not break boundaries, for if they are left unchecked in their youth, they will certainly do so in adulthood in our degraded generation where we have no power to protest. When he is young, he can still listen to us, and naturally, he will then train himself in the good and upright path.

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote: A minor who struck his father or committed other transgressions during his minority, even though he does not need to repent when he grows up, nevertheless, it is good for him to accept something upon himself for repentance and atonement, even though he transgressed before he became liable for punishment. End of quote. (See Rashi in Bava Kamma 98 regarding the case where Rafrām coerced Ravina, and see Taz, subparagraph 2).

And know that the Rambam in Chapter 24 of Shabbat, Law 11, wrote: "A minor who did on Shabbat something that is a rabbinic prohibition (shvut), such as plucking from an unperforated flowerpot or carrying in a karmelit - the court is not commanded to prevent him, and similarly if his father allowed him, they do not protest against him." End of quote. And the Maggid Mishneh and the Tur have already questioned him, asking how he only wrote about shvut, since it is established for us that even if a minor eats non-kosher, we are not commanded to prevent him, as he himself wrote at the end of Forbidden Foods as stated in Section 1. Furthermore, regarding Shabbat itself, he wrote in Chapter 12 about a fire, that if a minor extinguishes it on his own accord, there is no need to prevent him as mentioned there. And according to the Rambam, extinguishing on Shabbat is a Torah prohibition. And even though it is a labor not needed for its own sake, he ruled in Chapter 1 according to Rabbi Yehuda that one is liable for a labor not needed for its own sake. And our teacher, the Beit Yosef, explained that what he wrote about shvut, this pertains to the conclusion that if his father allowed him, they do not protest against him, and in this matter specifically concerning shvut, but with a Torah prohibition, they do protest against him as mentioned there.

Based on this, our master the Rema wrote regarding what our master the Beit Yosef wrote, that a father is commanded to rebuke and separate him, saying: "from a biblical prohibition," to indicate that from a rabbinic prohibition, it is not necessary to separate him. And these words are perplexing, for we have explicitly brought the words of the Rambam in section 1 that a father is commanded to rebuke and separate him. And there are those who wrote that his intention is that the Bet Din does not protest when he does not rebuke him (Magen Avraham, section 2), and this is even more perplexing, for our master the Beit Yosef did not mention at all that they do not protest, and furthermore, on what basis do we make such a distinction. And there are those who wrote that here the Rambam is referring to a minor who has reached the age of education, and in all other places, he is referring to one who has not reached the age of education (Bach). And it is astonishing to make such a distinction in similar languages, and furthermore, if he has reached the age of education, why should we not separate him also from a rabbinic prohibition.

Therefore, it seems to me, in my humble opinion, that in the case of a minor who eats non-kosher food, as stated in Yevamot (114a), there is no need to prevent him, and we do not distinguish between whether he acts on his own accord or on his father's accord. This is also the opinion of Maimonides there. Why then does the Talmud in Shabbat (121a) and Maimonides in Chapter 12 make a distinction when it comes to extinguishing a fire on Shabbat between acting on his own accord or on his father's accord? Surely, in all prohibitions, this distinction should apply. However, the common practice is such: in matters of eating, where there is certainly a desire, it is assumed he acts on his own accord. This is not the case with the work of Shabbat, which does not involve such desire; thus, we need to investigate on whose accord he acts. Therefore, regarding extinguishing a fire, the Talmud and Maimonides instruct us to investigate. This applies to a Torah prohibition, but for rabbinic prohibitions, we do not need to investigate and assume he acts on his own accord. This is what Maimonides innovated here that a minor performing a rabbinic prohibition on Shabbat does not need to be restrained by the court, meaning we do not need to investigate whether he acts on his father's accord. Therefore, he concludes: "And if his father allows him - we do not protest," meaning that if his father allows it, it would seem he acts on his father's accord, for if not, his father would certainly protest. Nevertheless, since this is only a rabbinic prohibition, we are not required to investigate this, and we assume he acts on his own accord.

And so it appears, in my humble opinion, that the principal ruling in the case of a minor who has not yet reached the age of education and is performing a prohibited labor on Shabbat, and we do not know if he is acting on his own accord or on the instruction of his father or others: if it is a biblical prohibition, we admonish him, assuming that he is acting on the instruction of his father or others, unless we clearly know that he is acting on his own accord. However, if it is a rabbinic prohibition, we assume that he is acting on his own accord, and we do not admonish him unless we clearly know that he is acting on the instruction of his father or others, in which case we do admonish him. (And with this, we can resolve the difficulties raised by the Beit Yosef and the Bach against the Rif and the Rosh, who omitted the entire Talmudic discussion regarding a minor who comes to extinguish [a fire], because they hold that we generally assume that he is acting on the instruction of his father, and we admonish him. Reflect on this.)

The Sages said (Shabbat 69b) that if someone is traveling in the desert and forgets the days and does not know when Shabbat is, what should he do? He counts seven days from the day he realizes his forgetfulness and sanctifies the seventh day with Kiddush and Havdalah. For him, the day he forgot becomes the first day, and he counts six days and observes one day. Thus, the Sages said that he has no other recognition of Shabbat except through Kiddush and Havdalah. Regarding work, all the days are the same for him because he must refrain from work every day, lest it be Shabbat. In this case, the principle of nullification by majority does not apply because each day is considered separately, and moreover, Shabbat is definitely included, even if he does not know which day it is. He is forbidden to perform even rabbinically prohibited work. The principle of "doubt regarding a rabbinic prohibition is lenient" does not apply here, because any doubt due to lack of knowledge is not considered a doubt, as explained in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 110. Moreover, this is not a case of doubt, because necessarily, there is a Shabbat among the days, and it stands alone and is not mixed with the other days.

However, if he has no bread to eat, he is permitted to do whatever is necessary to provide for his sustenance each day because it is a matter of life-saving, which overrides Shabbat. Even on the day he considers to be Shabbat, he should do so, because it cannot be said that he should prepare two days' worth of provisions the day before, as that previous day might have been Shabbat. Regarding his travel, he may walk as much as he wants every day because otherwise, he would never reach civilization. Although on the day he rests, he could refrain from walking beyond the Shabbat boundary (techum Shabbat), since boundaries are a rabbinic prohibition, the Sages did not impose this restriction on someone lost in the desert (Ran and Maggid Mishneh, Chapter 2). Even if boundaries are a Torah prohibition, according to those who hold that twelve mil is a Torah boundary, since there is no penalty of stoning, the Sages did not impose this restriction on someone lost in the desert (ibid.), in order to hasten his exit from the desert (Tosafot and Rosh), so that he may observe Shabbat properly. Therefore, we said that Shabbat is only recognizable to him through Kiddush and Havdalah.

And if he knows the number of days since he left, such as knowing that today is the fourth or fifth day since he left, but he does not know on which day he left, he is permitted to do work on every eighth day since he left, for it is certain he did not leave on Shabbat. Similarly, he is permitted to do work on the fifteenth day since he left and on the twenty-second day, and so on indefinitely. And if he knows for certain that he did not leave on the day before Shabbat, he is permitted to do work for two days, the seventh and eighth days since he left, and so on indefinitely. And if he is able to prepare his food for the entire week at that time, he is obligated to do so, and it is forbidden for him to do work on the other days entirely.

Our Rabbis taught (Shabbat 6a): "There are four domains for Shabbat: a private domain, a public domain, a karmelit, and a place of exemption." This is only a general classification, as there are many specifics. In general, according to Torah law, there are two distinct domains, namely a private domain and a public domain, where it is forbidden to carry or throw from one to the other. If one carries or throws intentionally, they are liable for stoning, and if done unintentionally, they are liable to bring a sin offering. Besides these two domains, it is permitted to carry from them to a private domain and a public domain, and from them into these domains. However, the Rabbis instituted two additional domains, namely a karmelit and a place of exemption. From a karmelit, it is forbidden to carry into a private domain and a public domain and likewise from them into it, but from a place of exemption, it is permitted. In specific details, even in a complete private domain, it is rabbinically forbidden to carry more than four cubits, and from it to a private domain is forbidden, as well as from a private domain into it, such as a courtyard and an alleyway that have not made an eruv, and similarly an enclosure larger than two seahs that was not enclosed for dwelling, and similar cases as will be explained with the help of Heaven. (This is the intention of Tosafot there, s.v. Arba', see there).

What is a private domain? The Rambam writes at the beginning of Chapter 14: "Anything that is ten handbreadths high and four handbreadths wide by four handbreadths or more, (meaning - a mound that is ten handbreadths high and four by four wide) and similarly a trench that is ten handbreadths deep and four handbreadths wide by four handbreadths or more, and similarly a place that is surrounded by four walls each ten handbreadths high and within them four by four or more, even if it extends several miles - if it was enclosed for dwelling, such as a city surrounded by a wall with gates that are locked at night, and alleyways that have three walls and a side post on the fourth side, and similarly a courtyard, pen, or stable that are enclosed for dwelling - all of these are considered a complete private domain. Even vessels, such as a ship, tower, or beehive and the like - if they have four by four in height of ten or more, they are considered a complete private domain." - End of quote.

And regarding what he wrote, "if it was enclosed for residential purposes," this does not pertain to a Torah-level private domain (reshut hayachid). Similarly, with a courtyard, pen, or enclosure that he wrote "which were enclosed for residential purposes," from the Torah there is no distinction. Rather, because he wanted to say it is a complete private domain, meaning that carrying within it is permitted rabbinically, he required it to be enclosed for residential purposes. Similarly, what he wrote about alleyways that have three walls and a sidepost (lechi) on the fourth side, this also seems to be the case. From the Torah, a sidepost is not needed since three partitions constitute a Torah-level private domain. However, in truth, although this is the opinion of most of our Rabbis and it appears so throughout the tractate Eruvin, nevertheless, the Rambam himself holds that three partitions without a sidepost is not a Torah-level private domain but rather a karmelit. And regarding the definition of a karmelit, he wrote there, "an alleyway that does not have a sidepost or a crossbeam," see there. And in chapter 17, law 9, he wrote explicitly as follows: "An alleyway that was made permissible with a crossbeam, although it is permitted to carry within it as in a private domain, one who throws from it to the public domain or from the public domain into it is exempt, because the crossbeam is made for recognition purposes. But if it was made permissible with a sidepost, one who throws from it to the public domain or from the public domain into it is liable, because the sidepost serves as a partition on the fourth side." End quote. Although this has been disputed, this is still his opinion, and there is evidence for his words from the chapter "All Roofs" (Eruvin 94a), where it is taught: "A courtyard that was breached into the public domain... and the Sages say: One who brings something from it to the public domain or from the public domain into it is exempt, because it is considered like a karmelit." This indicates that three partitions are considered a karmelit. But in truth, the conclusion of the Gemara there concludes that this is only regarding the place of the partition, meaning that now there is no partition there and it is like the sides of the public domain, see there (and this is also written by the Tosefot Yom Tov, see there). And it is explicitly explained there in the Jerusalem Talmud (and this is its wording: "Rabbi Eliezer only said this about the place of the partitions when the corners were removed, etc." that regarding this, Rabbi Eliezer holds it is a public domain and the Sages disagree, but regarding the entire courtyard, everyone agrees it is a private domain).

However, I have examined his words, and he did not say this about all matters. He also believes that three partitions constitute a private domain (Reshut HaYachid) according to Torah law, but this is only if they stand in a place where there is no public domain (Reshut HaRabim) in front of them. Only in a place where there is a public domain in front of them, it is impossible to make it a private domain according to Torah law unless it is enclosed by some interruption like a side post (Lechi), a beam (Korah), or projections (Gipufin), because the public tends to enter it, and how can we call it a private domain? Therefore, it is also considered a karmelit according to Torah law. 

This is what he wrote here (Halacha 4) in the context of a karmelit, and these are his words: "And similarly, a corner adjacent to a public domain – which is a place surrounded by three partitions, and the fourth side is the public domain, such as an alleyway that does not have a side post or a beam, etc." End of quote. 

And similarly, in his commentary on the Mishnah at the beginning of Shabbat, he wrote, and these are his words: "And also places that have three walls and the fourth side is opposite the public domain are considered a karmelit." End of quote. 

It is clear that he was precise because the fourth side is the public domain. The reason is as we explained, and its source is from the matter of all roofs that we brought – even though the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and the Sages there is only about the place of the partition as we said, nevertheless, since it says there in the Gemara, "So said the Rabbis to Rabbi Eliezer: Don't you agree with us that if one transferred from it to the public domain and from the public domain to it, he is exempt because it is a karmelit?" So too, etc. 

And Tosafot (93b, s.v. obligated) struggled to explain – 'that is when the side partitions fell,' see there. But the Rambam explains it according to its plain meaning. According to this, even according to the Rambam, an alleyway that has three partitions, and the public domain does not go in front of the open side, but in front of one of the partitions, he agrees that it is a private domain. And if one threw from it to the public domain through a door or window, he is liable. (And I found support for this in the Rambam – brought by Kesef Mishneh in Chapter 17, Halacha 9, see there, it seems that this is his opinion, and investigate thoroughly).

It is clear that when we require four handbreadths in length and width in a private domain, this refers only to the empty space, and we do not measure the thickness of the partition within the four handbreadths. This is explicitly clarified from the language of the Rambam that we have cited, where he wrote, "and between them four by four." Similarly, Rashi wrote in Eruvin (5a, s.v. u'man de'amar) as follows: "There are no partitions unless there is within the space four [handbreadths]." This is also evident from the language of the Tur and all the poskim (and the Magen Avraham wrote similarly in section 1). There are those who wrote that the partitions are also measured within the four handbreadths (Bach and Taz, section 2), and they derived this from what Tosafot and the Rosh wrote in the first chapter of Shabbat, regarding a beehive, that the sides join together with the hollow space of the beehive to make up the width of four [handbreadths]. This is puzzling, for certainly in a private domain – of a vessel that is not used within it as a domain, and it is a private domain because something is placed on it and used, like the case of a pit and its rim in Eruvin (78a) – we say that it joins together to make up the width of four [handbreadths], as Tosafot wrote there. And the reason is explained – because something is placed on it and used, and it is like a rock that is ten handbreadths high and four handbreadths wide. But between partitions, where the usage is between the partitions, it is obvious that we require the width of the empty space to be four [handbreadths]. There is no doubt about this, and this is the fundamental ruling, as mentioned in section 45.

And know that I saw one of the great ones (Ba'er Hetev 3) who brought what the Rashba wrote in the book Avodat HaKodesh - that partitions combine to four [cubits], but he differentiated - that this is only for strong partitions, such that if he wanted to cover it, he could cover and use it, but weak ones do not combine. Refer there. And behold, this book is not in my possession, yet if he wrote so - his intention is regarding 'vessels', as he wrote in the first chapter of Shabbat regarding a beehive, where he brought the words of the Tosafot that the partitions of the beehive combine to four [cubits], and he wrote about this, and this is his language: "And I am astonished at their words... but necessarily they only said this about thick walls made to cover and use, which is not the case for a beehive and mat," end quote.

And aside from this, the matter is puzzling, to say regarding partitions that stand on the ground that one places something upon them and uses them, for the usage is meant for its inside. This is specifically regarding the rings of a pit, where it is customary to place a board over the pit and use it, or on a vessel, as it is written in Samuel (II 17:19), "And she spread the covering over the well's mouth and strewed ground corn upon it," but not on partitions that are on the ground. Furthermore, a width of four [handbreadths] and more than four are equal, and just as one does not say placing something upon it and using it with a large width, so too with a width of four. Moreover, in the Jerusalem Talmud, in the chapter "The One Who Throws" regarding the Mishnah of the rings of the pit and the rock, it says there, "The standing part and the hollow part combine to four [handbreadths] provided that the standing part is greater than the hollow part." If so, you would need to say the same for partitions on the ground, and do you have something as puzzling as this? (And further examination is needed regarding Tosafot and the Rosh in the case of the beehive as they did not mention this Jerusalem Talmud. And apparently, it is not so in the case of the beehive. And the Rashba there mentioned it. And perhaps his intention was to challenge Tosafot. Nevertheless, in any case, the Rashba does not hold this way regarding partitions, unlike what was written by the Eliyah Rabbah, and examine it thoroughly).

And even regarding utensils, not everyone agrees that the thickness combines with the width to make up the four handbreadths, as we have brought. For the Rashba disagrees with this, and similarly, Tosafot (8a, s.v. Rechava) quotes in the name of R’ Chananel regarding the beehive that there must be an airspace of four handbreadths within the beehive. And the Tur and Shulchan Aruch in section six wrote: "Even a utensil, such as a box or a tower or a beehive, if it has a width of four by four handbreadths and is ten handbreadths high, it is considered a private domain." Their words are unclear whether the thickness combines or not. And from the Jerusalem Talmud that we brought, it is also evident that the thickness does not combine. Regarding the practical law, one should be stringent.

Specifically, the status of a private domain applies to vessels, but the status of a karmelit does not apply to vessels, such as a vessel that is four [handbreadths] wide and not ten [handbreadths] high, which is the definition of a karmelit as will be explained. There is no karmelit status for vessels, as the Rabbis did not decree to nullify the status of a vessel since it is a vessel (Rashi, Shabbat 8a, s.v. Pachot). It is nullified to the domain in which it stands, and all the more so if it is less than four [handbreadths]. If the vessel is attached to the ground, it becomes a karmelit (Magen Avraham, section 4), because since it is attached to the ground, it loses its status as a vessel (Tosafot, there 11b, s.v. Ela). This is not related to the laws of 'detached and then reattached - whether it is considered detached or not,' for even if for other matters it is considered detached, regarding the carrying on Shabbat, its status is as if it is attached, since it cannot be moved like a vessel.

Specifically, when the vessel is in a public domain or a private domain, it does not have the status of a karmelit, but a vessel standing in a karmelit is judged with the status of a karmelit. Therefore, a ship in the water is considered a karmelit, as will be explained in Section 355, as mentioned there. The reason is simple: even if it is nullified to the domain in which it stands, it is still a karmelit, since the sea and the river are considered a karmelit, as will be explained.

The walls that enclose a private domain, even their tops are considered as a private domain, even if they are not four [handbreadths] wide. It is an a fortiori argument: if for others they create a private domain, all the more so for themselves. (Shabbat 99b) Similarly, the airspace of a private domain extends up to the sky and does not have the same status as a public domain or a karmelit, which only extend up to ten handbreadths, as will be explained. Therefore, if one plants a pole in a private domain that is one hundred cubits high, and throws [an object] from a public domain and it lands on top of it, one is liable. 

If one plants a pole in a public domain and places a basket on its top that is ten [handbreadths] high and four [handbreadths] wide, the basket is considered a private domain, but what is beneath it is not considered a private domain. If the basket is not ten [handbreadths] high, even though it is four [handbreadths] wide, it is not considered a private domain, and we do not say "extend and lower the partition" because it is a partition that young goats can breach. This is a law given to Moses at Sinai: any partition that young goats can breach, we do not say "extend and lower the partition," and its measure is three handbreadths from the ground.

Similarly, a pillar that is ten [handbreadths] high and four [handbreadths] wide but not four handbreadths at its base, even if there is no breaching by young goats, what is beneath it is not considered a private domain, only what is on top of it. Specifically, if the narrow part is three handbreadths thick, then with one handbreadth there is no breaching by young goats. But if the narrow part is only slightly thick, it is considered like the basket on the pole, and there is breaching by young goats, so it is not a private domain. (Tosafot there 101, s.v. "and there is").

We maintain that the holes in a private domain are considered like the private domain itself, meaning holes in the wall on the side of the private domain, whether they are large or small, high or low, have the status of a private domain because the owner of the courtyard uses them for his purposes, and they are like the courtyard itself. However, the holes in the wall that face outward are judged according to their height and width, as will be explained in section 36.

And our master the Rema wrote in section 2: "There are those who say that we require in these four handbreadths by four handbreadths - they and their diagonal, as is written later in section 349" end quote. That is to say, it will be explained later that every person has four cubits in the public domain within which he can carry, and these four cubits are measured with their diagonal - meaning according to the measurement of four cubits with the diagonal. And since every cubit in a square is a cubit and two-fifths in its diagonal, it follows naturally that to four cubits eight-fifths are added, and one is not liable until he carries in the public domain five cubits and three-fifths. Similarly, regarding the width of four handbreadths, the width is required with the diagonal, which is five handbreadths and three-fifths of a handbreadth, because this opinion holds that in all the measurements of Shabbat we must also consider the diagonal.

I am astonished at our master, the Rema, for this is only the opinion of Rabbeinu Tam in Eruvin (51a, s.v. Kaze). Rashi there, the Rashbam, the Tosafot there, and in Yoma 67b, refuted this matter. Also, from the words of the Rambam at the end of Chapter 12, it is clear that this is not so, as he wrote regarding the four cubits in the public domain, 'Since it is permissible for him to walk and carry within this entire square area, and consequently, he can carry also along its diagonal, therefore one is not liable for transferring until he transfers along the diagonal as well.' See there, and this has no relation to domains. It seems to me that even our master, the Rema, only said this to be cautious of this opinion if there is any stringency found, such as regarding a beehive, as it is said in the Gemara (8a), 'If one threw a beehive into the public domain – if it is ten high and not six wide – he is liable. If it is six wide – he is exempt, because it is its own domain.' See there. For this reason, we need to be stringent both for its area and its diagonal. But to be lenient in a place that is ten high and four wide, not to consider it a private domain but rather an exempt area, heaven forbid to say so, for the law follows the majority and most of the decisors do not hold this way.

What is considered a public domain? We learned in a Baraita: "A main street, a large plaza, and alleyways that open into a public domain - this is a complete public domain." The main street - this refers to a road, and Rashi explains that it is a path that people use to travel from city to city. In other words, it is like our thoroughfares. The large plaza, Rashi explains, is the main square of the city where people gather for commerce. Alleyways that open into a public domain, Rashi explains, are those that are sixteen cubits wide and open at both ends to the main street. In their times, the streets and buildings were not like ours. The residential areas were within courtyards, and many courtyards opened into an alleyway with three walls. Only in the middle of the city was there a large street called the main street, to which all alleyways led. This street was completely open and used for travel between cities. There was also a large area like our market, completely open, where people gathered for commerce, and it was called the plaza. There were alleyways with both ends open to the main street, and they too had the status of a public domain. According to this, in their times, the courtyards with all the alleyways would combine together or each alleyway on its own, and they would carry within them. But the main street, the plaza, and the alleyways that opened into the public domain could not be enclosed with an Eruv using a symbolic doorway, only with doors, as will be explained further with God's help.

One of the conditions of a public domain is that the street must be sixteen cubits wide. We derive this from the wagons in the wilderness, as two wagons that went side by side were sixteen cubits wide, as stated in the Gemara (Shabbat 99a), where it is established that the width of a public domain is sixteen cubits, which we learn from the Tabernacle. Based on the measurements of our country, Russia, this is twelve arshins, which are four sazhen, as we explained in Choshen Mishpat, siman 218. Additionally, it must not be roofed, for a roofed public domain is not considered a public domain since it does not resemble the encampment in the wilderness (ibid. 5). Also, the city must not be surrounded by a wall, or a mountain, or a ditch ten handbreadths high or deep and four handbreadths wide. Even if there is a wall surrounding it, if the gates are aligned from gate to gate, and the gates are directly opposite each other and do not have doors, or even if they have doors but are not locked at night, it is considered a public domain, and any road aligned from gate to gate is a public domain (Magen Avraham, sk 6). Even if only one gate is locked at night, it also nullifies the public domain status, since it is not open through and through (Taz, sk 5). Only locked doors nullify the public domain status, but not a doorway structure, for what benefit is a doorway structure if it is still open through and through? And indeed, with doors, there is certainly a doorway structure, yet if they are not locked, it is nothing. Thus, our Sages said in Eruvin (6a): "Jerusalem, if not for its doors being locked at night, would be liable as a public domain." And although it is written 'Jerusalem is surrounded by mountains,' it must be said that there were many places where the mountains did not surround them, for if not, they would not have needed doors.

And our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in Section 7: "There are those who say that any place where six hundred thousand do not pass through every day is not considered a public domain." End quote. And similarly, the Tur wrote and this is his language: "A public domain is streets and marketplaces that are sixteen cubits wide, (and marketplaces) and open from gate to gate where six hundred thousand pass through." End quote. And this is the opinion of Rashi in Eruvin (59a), that since all matters of Shabbat are learned from the Tabernacle, we require it to be similar to the encampments in the desert, where there were six hundred thousand. And even though there were many more, as six hundred thousand were only the males from age twenty to sixty, nonetheless we only learn from what is explicitly stated in the verse. And there are some early authorities who agreed with this view and many who disagree with it, and also the Rif and the Rambam did not mention this, and even in the Babylonian and Jerusalem Talmud this is not explicitly mentioned.

According to this approach, all the permissibility of the Eruvin in our country is due to the fact that in all our cities, there are not 600,000 people passing through, and they are not considered as a public domain. Therefore, the form of a doorway is effective for them. According to the first approach, since our streets are sixteen cubits wide, there is no permissibility because they are considered a full public domain, and doors are needed that should be locked at night, as mentioned. Now, the commentators of the Shulchan Aruch wrote that most of the authorities hold this view (Taz, section 6, and Magen Avraham, section 7). However, one of the great authorities of the previous generation caused a commotion about our Eruvin and clearly showed that those who prohibit are much more numerous than those who permit. However, the commentators of the Shulchan Aruch did not see them because they were not printed in their time. Those who permit are Sefer HaTerumah, the SeMaG, the SeMaK, Rabbeinu Meir of Rothenburg, the Rosh, and the Tur, who follow the approach of Rashi of blessed memory. Those who prohibit are the Rif, the Rambam, Rabbeinu Tam, the Rashbam, the Ra'avan, the Ramban, the Rashba, the Ritva, the Ran, the Maggid Mishneh, the Rivash, and many of the Tosafists: the first Rashba, the Riva, Rabbi Yehuda HaLevi, Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yitzchak of Dampierre (as mentioned in Mishkenot Yaakov, section 109), and also the Maharshal in Yam Shel Shlomo on Beitzah (chapter 3, section 8) ruled not according to this approach.

And besides this, they elaborated to explain that even the intention of Rashi is not that sixty myriad (600,000) should constantly be passing through it, for this is something impossible. If so, when Nehemiah cried out about the desecration of Shabbat due to their bringing all sorts of merchandise to Jerusalem on Shabbat, and they decreed decrees and enacted ordinances, the entire assembly was only forty myriad (400,000). Would he have made such a commotion and decreed ordinances for a rabbinically prohibited domain (carmelit)? Rather, the intention of Rashi is that it should be a thoroughfare for the public, such that it is possible for sixty myriad to pass through it, excluding small paths that are only for one city and not for the entire world. If so, all our roads are considered public domains. (This is in the name of the Ritva). However, in any case, what benefit is there in this elaboration after the eruvin have spread throughout most cities of Israel many hundreds of years ago, relying solely on this leniency? It is as if a heavenly voice proclaimed that the law follows this opinion. If we come to object, not only will they not listen, but we will appear as madmen, for this practice has spread throughout all of Israel and the decisors, that nowadays we have no public domain except in a few large cities in the world - like royal cities that have sixty myriad, but not in our cities. And since it is a commandment and an obligation to find merit for the entirety of Israel, therefore, I have set my heart to find some leniency, as we will explain with the help of Heaven.

And it appears in my humble opinion, when we scrutinize the beginning of the chapter "Hazorek" (Shabbat 96b), where the Talmud asks: "Where is the prohibition of carrying [on Shabbat] written in the Torah?" Rabbi Yochanan says, "The verse states: 'And Moses commanded, and they proclaimed throughout the camp, saying: Let neither man nor woman do any more work for the offering of the sanctuary. So the people were restrained from bringing.'" Where was Moses situated? In the Levite camp. And the Levite camp was a public domain, as everyone would gather around Moses our teacher, (Rashi) and he told the Israelites, "Do not carry and bring from your private domain, that is, from your tents, (there) to the public domain." We need to understand why it specifically mentions the Levite camp as a public domain, as the entire Israelite camp was a public domain. The Israelite camp was three parasangs by three parasangs, (Eruvin 55b) and the entire camp was organized around the banners, some to the right and some to the left, as explained in the Torah. The entire camp was arranged in a square, and if so, the entire camp was a public domain. Why specifically mention the Levite camp?

One cannot say that the intention is indeed that as soon as they brought items out from the tents, they transferred them from a private domain to a public domain, because if so, why is there the need for the preamble that the Levite camp was a public domain? Furthermore, what differentiates the Levite camp from the Israelite camp, as within the tents themselves, it is obvious that the tent in which Moses sat was not a public domain, and on the street, it was entirely a public domain.

Therefore, it seems that the matter of a public domain is as follows: there should be in the city only one public domain extending to the two sides of the city, east and west, and similarly, one public domain extending to the north and south. And its name reflects its nature, as this place is a domain where all the inhabitants of the place turn to and not to another place. This is similar to how their cities were comprised of alleyways, and within the alleyways there were many courtyards, and in each courtyard many houses. The alleyways were enclosed on three sides. However, in the middle of the city was a large main street (seratya) to which all the alleyways opened, and it was open on both ends. Anyone who needed to travel to another city necessarily exited through this main street, as there was no other route available, obviously. There was also a large plaza (platya) where everyone gathered for commerce. This is what we learned in the Baraita: "What is a public domain?" Meaning, the one place where the public turns to — the main street and the plaza. But if the city is not comprised of alleyways, but instead all the streets are open to the four directions of the world, and one who lives on this street exits to another city through this street, and one who lives on another street exits through his respective street, and so on with all the streets, then there is no place that can be called a public domain, because there is no place where everyone gathers.

And according to this, it makes sense, because in the desert encampments there were no alleyways but rather streets like we have, and each tribe exited through a different place from the other tribe. Therefore, there was no place within the camp that could be called a public domain where everyone walked, except for the Levite camp, since all of Israel needed to go to Moses our teacher. Thus, it turns out that only the Levite camp was a public domain. After the incident of the Golden Calf, the Levite camp was outside the camp of Israel, as it is written (Exodus 33:7), "And Moses took the tent and pitched it outside the camp, far from the camp, and called it the Tent of Meeting." And there the entire Levite camp, the Tabernacle, and the wagons were located. Therefore, only there was a public domain and not in the entire camp.

And according to this, in our case, since we do not have alleyways but rather open streets, and in every city, there are many streets, some people exit the city through one street, and others through another street, and there is no main thoroughfare where everyone must pass through, it turns out that there is no public domain here. Also, we do not have a plaza, for although every city has a market and shops, nonetheless, there are many shops and trading places that are not in the market area, so it turns out that there is no plaza here either. Their status is only like open courtyards or open alleyways, and we have the ability to establish an eruv in them. This is not considered a public domain which cannot be enclosed except with locked doors. Furthermore, it appears to me that even if we say that regarding carrying in and out, they are not considered a karmelit but rather a public domain – according to the authorities who do not require sixty myriads [600,000 people], nonetheless, regarding this matter that a public domain cannot be enclosed, it only applies to a single public domain, like their main thoroughfare, where there was one main thoroughfare in the entire city, and not in our case where there are many main thoroughfares. If so, this is not considered a main thoroughfare. However, it seems more likely as I stated earlier, as is evident from the Talmud at the beginning of the chapter "Hazorek" as I have written.

In truth, in the Jerusalem Talmud at the beginning of Shabbat, it says: "From where do we know that carrying out is called a labor? Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachman in the name of Rabbi Yonatan [said], 'And Moses commanded... and the people were restrained from bringing'—the people refrained from taking [items] out of their homes and giving them to the treasurers. Rabbi Hezekiah in the name of Rabbi Ila said—even bringing in, you can derive from this, just as the people refrained... so too the treasurers refrained from accepting from their hands and bringing into the chamber." End quote. And the Jerusalem Talmud does not mention that 'Moses was sitting' etc. According to the Jerusalem Talmud, it is possible to say that indeed the entire camp was a public domain. According to the Jerusalem Talmud, it needs to be said as the second opinion in the previous section, that in any case, regarding not combining a public domain, it is only like a single street. But it seems more reasonable to say that the intention of the Jerusalem Talmud is like our Talmud, that the treasurers were presumably in the Levite camp with Moses our teacher, and so it implies from the language 'to bring into the chamber,' and the chamber was in the Tabernacle.

And know that I have proof from Ba'al Halachot Gedolot (BaHaG) that there is a type of public domain where an eruv is effective, as he wrote in the laws of Eruvin: "It is forbidden to carry anything on Shabbat four cubits in a public domain, as it is said, 'And Moses commanded, etc.' - 'from doing' is not stated but 'from bringing,' which teaches that they would bring through the public domain. And not only a public domain that is a royal road, where it is forbidden to carry within it four cubits without an eruv. But even from one alleyway to another, etc." End of quote.

And it is difficult - how can he say 'where there is no eruv,' which clearly implies that with an eruv it is permitted, while it is known that one cannot make an eruv in a public domain? And one cannot say that his intention is regarding locked doors, for doors are not considered an eruv but complete partitions, as proven from Eruvin (6a), where it is taught: "How does one make an eruv in a public domain…" and it raises the question - "And can a public domain be made into an eruv?" And afterward, the Talmud says - "And if you say that by locked doors it is not made into an eruv, but with doors it is made into an eruv, and Rabbi Yehuda said about Jerusalem, if its doors were not locked, etc."

And it is difficult - what is the question, let us say that 'how does one make an eruv' - the intention is about locked doors. Rather, certainly, locked doors are not called an eruv, and if so, how does BaHaG say 'where there is no eruv,' and this language BaHaG also wrote at the beginning of the laws of Shabbat, see there. Rather, certainly, there is a type of public domain where an eruv is effective, and that is as we said.

And know that in the Gemara, regarding the four domains, the wilderness is considered a karmelit, and it raises a difficulty from another Baraita – which considers the wilderness a public domain. And it resolves: there is no contradiction, here it refers to the time when Israel dwelled in the wilderness, here it refers to the present time. And Rashi and all the early commentators explained that when Israel dwelled in the wilderness, it was a public domain, but in the present time, it is a karmelit because it is not a place where the public traverses, as travelers in the wilderness are uncommon. (Rashi) 

And they raised a difficulty on the Rambam who wrote there: "What is a public domain? Wildernesses and forests, marketplaces and roads that lead to them, provided that the width of the road is sixteen cubits and it does not have a roof over it." And the Kesef Mishneh wrote in the name of Rabbi Abraham, the son of the Rambam, that the interpretation in the Gemara is the opposite: that when Israel dwelled in the wilderness and their camps were arranged there, it was like a valley and a field and what is similar to them, and in the present time, when anyone who wishes goes there, it is like a public domain.

And it must be said that his intention was that in the time when Israel was in the wilderness, the entire wilderness was like a valley and a field, but the place where Israel stood, it is clear in the Gemara that Moses's place was a public domain. And he further wrote that forests are superior to a valley and a field because the public does not go there, unlike a forest where everyone needs wood. And in the wilderness, it must be said that there are always caravans. And all the poskim did not agree with him, and they hold that wildernesses and forests are considered a karmelit, and so wrote the Rashba.

The path that goes from city to city, according to most authorities, is considered a public domain (reshut harabim). However, those who require sixty myriads (600,000) passing through do not consider it a public domain. Based on what we have explained, it is a public domain, since it is only one path, and any path where many people pass is considered a public domain. This applies only to an open path through which people travel to any place, but a side path that is designated only for a specific village or courtyard does not appear to be a public domain.

There is a question in our time, where most travelers travel by railway, which is certainly a public domain according to all opinions, since certainly 600,000 pass through it within a certain period of time. According to Rashi's interpretation in Eruvin (6a), which requires that there be 600,000 in the city, it is not necessary to say that 600,000 pass through at once or in one day, as this is impossible. Rather, it means that 600,000 pass through over time, and with railways, this is certainly the case.

However, there is a question regarding the previous paths that now have fewer travelers if this is considered a public domain according to the authorities who do not require the condition of 600,000. This requires further investigation. The Tur and the Shulchan Aruch wrote according to Rashi that 600,000 passing is required, and the Shulchan Aruch added "every day." According to this, even railways would not be a public domain. But I do not understand, as Rashi did not mention "passing," only that there should be 600,000 in the city.

In the Nimukei Yosef at the end of the laws of Tzitzit, it is written in the name of the Ritva that one whose tzitzit strings were torn in a complete public domain that is sixteen cubits wide and open, and where 600,000 occasionally pass through, etc. From here, it does not require "every day." According to this, the railway path would be a public domain according to all opinions, and it seems to me that what is written "every day" is not literal.

The requirement of sixteen cubits in width for a public domain - even if in some parts it narrows and there are not sixteen cubits in width, we do not concern ourselves with it, as it is still considered a public domain. This is because even alleyways that open to the public domain on both ends are considered a public domain, even though they are not sixteen cubits wide. We only require that they be thirteen and a third cubits wide, as we find with the partitions of wells. (See Tosafot Eruvin 6b.) Therefore, alleyways that extend along the length of the public domain and are sixteen cubits wide, even though in some parts they narrow and are not sixteen cubits wide, are still considered a public domain since they are along the length of the public domain. (This is in Shulchan Aruch, Section 8, and the previous statement in Section 9, and the Gra in Section 12 made them into two opinions. See there. In the Shulchan Aruch, no disagreement is mentioned, and they are separate laws. Here, it is referring to those that go along the length of the public domain, and the previous one refers to those that open to the public domain. Consider this well.)

A mound that is sloped—if the slope is significant, such that rising four cubits on the mound results in a height of ten handbreadths, it is not suitable for walking and is considered a private domain. However, if it does not reach a height of ten handbreadths until one has ascended five cubits, it is convenient for use and suitable for walking and is considered a public domain. Similarly, the corner posts of wells, which consisted of four pairs of double posts, meaning a double post at each corner with a height of ten handbreadths and a width of six handbreadths, are considered a private domain by Torah law, for any area enclosed by four partitions is by Torah law considered a private domain. (Magen Avraham) This matter is explained in Eruvin (20a). Even if the opening is very wide, such that the breaches are greater than the standing sections, it is still considered a private domain. Although breaches greater than the standing sections do not constitute a partition even by Torah law, this applies when poles or boards are placed close to each other, but where there are four complete partitions, it is considered a partition even if the breaches are greater than the standing sections. (Tosefot at the beginning of the chapter "Osin Pasin" (Eruvin 17b); see there) And see Siman 362, Section 29.

And I was uncertain whether the corner posts (diomdin) that are each less than six handbreadths (tefachim) wide are still considered as forming four partitions, thus creating a private domain (reshut hayachid), or perhaps if they are less than six handbreadths wide, they are considered a public domain (reshut harabim) when the gaps are greater than the standing sections. And it is clear to me that if they are less than four handbreadths, they are not significant at all, as it is not a significant place. Even if they were four handbreadths, it would not be a private domain unless the openings were small enough that the standing sections are greater, or at least equal to the gaps. But if the gaps are greater, it appears to me that it would be a public domain. And the proof is that in the case of the corner posts surrounding wells (passi biriot), they were lenient to uphold the Torah law, and even so, they did not permit less than six handbreadths. This is also explained in the Jerusalem Talmud there, which states, "Since the gaps are greater than the standing sections, they required corner posts, etc." And the reason is that the air from this side and that side nullifies it. But when there are two corner posts next to each other, each being six handbreadths, they are significant, and the air cannot nullify them (as is also explicitly stated in the Yerushalmi there).

Any object that is in the public domain, if it is not three handbreadths high, even if it is an object that the public does not trample on, such as excrement or thorns and the like, nevertheless they themselves have the status of the public domain. If one takes an item from a private domain and places it on them, he is liable, because it is impossible for the public domain to be perfectly level, and there must necessarily be slight elevations and depressions. Therefore, anything less than three handbreadths is considered as if it is level (with the ground), meaning it is not considered a separate domain but rather as part of the public domain itself. If it is three handbreadths high or more, and has an area of four by four handbreadths, it is considered a karmelit, provided it is not a vessel but a mound or a stone, for vessels do not constitute a karmelit as we wrote in paragraph 9. If it is ten handbreadths high and four handbreadths wide, it is considered a private domain even if it is a vessel, as we wrote there. If it is less than four handbreadths wide, even if it is ten handbreadths high, it is considered a makom patur, as will be explained.

And know, it is stated in the Gemara (8a) 'A pillar nine handbreadths high in a public domain, and the public leans on it'—meaning that in their walking, they lean on it and adjust their loads—it is considered like a public domain. Rashi explains (s.v. nine) that it must be exactly nine, neither less nor more, and this applies whether it is wide or narrow. Similarly, the Rambam writes in Chapter 14 (Halacha 8) that the reason is that the sages assessed that if it is slightly higher, it is not suitable for leaning, and only when it is nine handbreadths high—whether it is four handbreadths wide or not. The opinion of the Rosh and the Tur is that up to ten handbreadths, it is suitable for leaning and it is considered a public domain, but if it is higher than ten handbreadths, if it is four handbreadths wide, it becomes a private domain, and if it is not wide, it is considered an exempt place, even if there is enough space to carve and complete it to four handbreadths. Meaning, this is a hole in the wall facing the public domain (it is not) [and it is not] four handbreadths wide, and towards the private domain, it is four handbreadths wide. Therefore, there is room to say 'we carve to complete,' and it is as if it is also four handbreadths wide outside—we do not say so, as we do not say 'we carve to complete.' What has been clarified regarding the public leaning on it is that it is considered like a public domain, this is when we see them leaning on it, but what is suitable for leaning on, does not help if they are not accustomed to lean on it. (Beit Yosef and Magen Avraham section 8) and see in section 36.

A hole in a public domain - if it is not three handbreadths deep, it is considered as part of the public domain, as we mentioned. But if it is three handbreadths deep, the following applies: up to a depth of ten handbreadths, but not including ten, it is considered a karmelit if it is four handbreadths wide. If it is ten handbreadths deep and more, it is a private domain. If it is not four handbreadths wide, it is a makom patur. (Tur) It seems to me - this applies if it is three handbreadths wide, but less than three is considered as lavud, since people step over it and it has the status of a public domain. However, this applies to the area above, but within the hole itself, if something is placed there, it does not have the status of a public domain, since it is not convenient for use there. For this reason, we do not apply the rule of 'the public leans' as with a post. It also seems to me that even if the hole is very wide, if a board that is four handbreadths wide is placed from one end to the other, and people walk on the board, the board has the status of a public domain. But if it is less than four handbreadths, since it is not convenient to walk on it, it is not considered a public domain. (This is my humble opinion and see Magen Avraham, section 14).

A pit in a public domain that is ten handbreadths deep and four handbreadths wide, which constitutes a private domain, even if it is filled with water, remains a private domain because water does not nullify the partitions. However, if it is filled with fruits - even fruits that can be moved on Shabbat - nevertheless, as long as they are there, they nullify the partitions, and it is not similar to water where one can look through and see the partitions. All the more so if it is filled with straw, hay, or pebbles. And it is obvious that the pit we mentioned is one that does not slope but rather is uniform. However, a valley that slopes is judged like a mound in Section 28, where if it rises ten handbreadths within four cubits, meaning if within four cubits it rises ten handbreadths in height, it is a private domain. If it rises ten handbreadths within five cubits, it is a public domain. Such pits, when filled with water, are considered a karmelit, because they are not convenient for use.

And stagnant water in the public domain that is not ten [handbreadths] deep—it is nullified with respect to the public domain if people typically walk through it, because walking under pressure is still considered walking. (8:) And even if it is not four [handbreadths] wide, such that people do not walk through it but rather leap over it, it is still considered a public domain since they break through it and pass over it and do not circumvent it. Therefore, when they circumvent it, it becomes a karmelit. Similarly, a board placed over the stagnant water or over a pit is considered a public domain since many people break through it. And it appears to me that this is specifically when the board is four [handbreadths] wide, because if it is less than this, people are afraid to walk on it. And stagnant water that people do not break through but rather circumvent, even if it is not ten [handbreadths] deep, its status is like that of a karmelit as stated.

The airspace of a public domain only extends up to ten handbreadths in height, but above ten it is considered a "place of exemption." This is unlike a private domain, which extends upward to the sky, and this is a law given to Moses at Sinai. There is also a logical reason for this: a domain belonging to an individual is controlled by him even above, and he can build above ten handbreadths and do as he pleases. However, the public domain is only controlled by the public below, to walk and temporarily place their items there. But above, they do not have control to build and arrange, and therefore the public domain only extends as high as the measure of a partition, which is ten handbreadths.

However, this only applies to airspace, such as when one catches something from the air above ten handbreadths, it is permissible to bring it into a private domain through the space above ten handbreadths. Or if a sticky fig adheres to a wall above ten handbreadths, where the fig faces the air. But a hole in the wall or the top of a pillar, if it does not measure four by four handbreadths—even below ten handbreadths—it is considered a "place of exemption." And if it does measure four by four handbreadths—even above ten handbreadths—it is considered a private domain, as the private domain extends upward to the sky.

Holes in the walls that face the public domain and do not penetrate inward to the private domain are judged according to their measurements. If they are not three handbreadths wide, they are nullified regarding the public domain and are considered as the public domain. If they are three handbreadths wide up to four (but not including four), they are considered a "makom patur" (an exempt area) whether they are below ten handbreadths or above ten handbreadths. If they are four handbreadths wide, if they are below ten handbreadths, they are considered a "karmelit" (an intermediate domain), and if they are ten handbreadths or higher, they are considered a private domain. If the holes penetrate inward, it appears that their status is that of a private domain. (This is explicitly stated in Tosafot, Eruvin 7b, "and the law" - see there.) And what we wrote in section 31 - regarding a hole that faces the public domain and is not four handbreadths wide, and on the side of the private domain is four handbreadths wide - does not mean that the hole extends all the way through, for if it did, it would entirely be a private domain. Rather, it means that there is a hole on the side of the private domain and a hole on the side of the public domain with a separation in between. And know that a hole that is below three handbreadths from the ground, in any case, has the status of the public domain, for anything below three handbreadths is considered as part of the ground. (See Taz, Orach Chaim 345:22, who questions the Magen Avraham 345:9, and according to what we have written, it is clear, and the intention of the Magen Avraham is as we have written - see there and examine it well.)

What is a karmelit? It is a place that is not a public thoroughfare and is also not enclosed by proper partitions. Therefore, even if the area belongs to an individual, since it does not have partitions, it is not considered a private domain. One should not ask: we have established that an enclosure larger than a beit se'ah that was not enclosed for residential purposes has the status of a karmelit, even though it has partitions. However, this is not a question, because, by Torah law, it is definitely considered a complete private domain, and one who throws from a public domain into it is liable. Rather, by rabbinic decree, it is forbidden to carry within it more than four cubits, similar to a courtyard where they did not make an eruv. And we are dealing with a karmelit by Torah law, meaning that by Torah law, it is neither a private domain nor a public domain. This is the meaning of the term "karmelit," akin to "armelit" (a widow) – who is neither a virgin nor married. By Torah law, any karmelit is considered an exempt area, and it is permitted to carry from a karmelit to a public domain or a private domain, and likewise from them into it. However, by rabbinic decree, it is forbidden in a karmelit and permitted in an exempt area, as will be explained with the help of Heaven.

And these are the characteristics of a karmelit: A place that is four by four [handbreadths] and is not ten handbreadths high and is not surrounded by partitions. Likewise, a mound or pillar that is four by four and not ten handbreadths high, and a trench that is four by four and not ten handbreadths deep. Also, seas, rivers, forests, deserts, fields, and valleys—which are groups of many fields, gardens, alleys, the sides of public domains, and lakes. This is unlike what we said in section 33, where water does not nullify partitions. That refers to a small ditch within a settlement where many people use the area, not to large seas and rivers which are significant places by themselves and are not used [regularly]. Therefore, they are a karmelit. Some have disagreed, arguing that it does not ascend ten [handbreadths] within four [cubits], and therefore is not a private domain (as mentioned by the Magen Avraham, subsection 14). There is no need for this argument, for how can we consider seas and rivers, which span hundreds of parsangs, as a private domain? Certainly, if there is a deep ditch that is ten [handbreadths] deep and four [handbreadths] wide in the sea, it would be a private domain as stated in the Gemara (100a), because it is a separate ditch. But we do not make seas and rivers into a private domain. Even a ditch in the sea is only a private domain according to Torah law, but rabbinically it is forbidden to carry there (as mentioned by the Magen Avraham there), for everything in the sea is considered a karmelit. (And what the Magen Avraham wrote, "like a karpef and a mound"—this is not exact, for there it is more than two beit se'ah, as explained by the Alter Rebbe in his last booklet. However, the Magen Avraham's intent can be understood as stating that this is also the case, for the ditch is open to the sea which is more than two beit se'ah, and one should examine this thoroughly).

In their locales, there were platforms in front of the shops—a place where the merchants would sit, and it was called an "istavanit." Similarly, they had columns in the open space where traders would hang their merchandise, and in front of them were platforms on which the merchants would sit. Therefore, these "istavanit" and platforms are considered a karmelit (a semi-public domain), because it is not convenient to use them. However, between the columns is considered a public domain, even if the distance between the columns is not the measure of a public domain, and even if it is not thirteen and a third cubits, nevertheless, since many people pass through them, they are secondary to the public domain. (See there, Section 11). And the platforms are considered a karmelit when they have the dimensions of a karmelit, meaning their width is four handbreadths and their height is from three to ten handbreadths. For if their height was ten handbreadths—they are a private domain, and if their width was not four—they are an exempt area.

It is stated in the Gemara (7a) that the corner of a wall adjacent to the public domain is considered like a karmelit. Rashi explains that this refers to a case where someone extended their house into their property and left part of the ground in the public domain. Even though at times many people might press into it and enter there, since it is not convenient for use, because it does not align evenly with the entire public domain, it is considered like a karmelit. Rashi offers another explanation: a house whose front is angled, where one corner is adjacent to the public domain and the other corner is set back from the public domain, and the protruding corner prevents the public from entering directly into the entrance of the other corner. The Rambam, there, explains: 'For example, alleyways that have three walls but lack a side post or crossbeam on the fourth side.' This is according to his view that three walls constitute a karmelit from the Torah, as he wrote, but according to all other authorities, this is not included in a Torah-level karmelit, as from the Torah it is considered a private domain. Therefore, I am puzzled by the Tur and Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) in section 14, who brought his explanation for the corner of a wall, which has no relevance to the laws of a karmelit as he wrote. It seems they did not differentiate between Torah and Rabbinic law, and Rabbinically it is forbidden to carry. However, if so, they should have also included courtyards and alleyways that were not joined in an eruv, as it is forbidden to carry from one courtyard to another or from one house to another. It has already been explained that a covered public domain is not considered a public domain, and it is also included in a Torah-level karmelit, since it has no walls and is neither a private domain nor a public domain.

A house that does not have a height of ten handbreadths but is very wide is considered a karmelit. If one digs into the ground of the house within three handbreadths of the walls and completes the height to ten handbreadths—such as if it was eight handbreadths high and he digs two handbreadths into the ground—it becomes a private domain. However, this is only if the excavation is within three handbreadths of the walls, for if it is further than three handbreadths, the partitions will not join to it, as it is written in Siman 733 regarding a sukkah. But a house that does not have an interior height of ten handbreadths, and its roof completes it to ten handbreadths—since the roof is considered a private domain because it is ten handbreadths high, and inside it is a karmelit—if he digs, even far from the walls, if the excavation is four by four handbreadths, which is a significant area, the entire house becomes a private domain. This is because the outer partitions have a height of ten handbreadths, and only the inside does not have ten handbreadths. Therefore, when he makes a place of four handbreadths that is ten high, the whole becomes a private domain since what is from the excavation to the walls is considered like the cavities of a private domain. (Gemara 7a: and I have written according to the words of the Rosh brought by the Magen Avraham in Siman 13. From Tosafot there, it seems that in any case, the excavation that is not near the walls is effective. See there and analyze thoroughly.)

Even though a private domain cannot exist without partitions, nevertheless roofs are considered a private domain because we say "extend the partition upward"—meaning, we view the walls of the building as if they extend upward, and this is a law given to Moses at Sinai. However, when do we say this? When the roof is aligned with the walls and does not extend beyond the walls, so that the partitions are noticeable to someone standing on the roof. But roofs that extend beyond the walls of the house, like our roofs which are called "caps," we do not say "extend the partition upward" because the partitions are not noticeable to those standing on the roofs. Therefore, the status of these roofs is like a karmelis, even if they are very high and wide. However, if there is an open window and the window is four by four handbreadths, the entire roof is considered like the holes of a private domain and has the status of a private domain. One should not ask why it is considered a karmelis, since the public does not frequent it and it is difficult to use, and it should be considered a place of exemption. The reason is that we do not find a place of exemption that is four handbreadths wide. (Rosh, Chapter 9 of Eruvin, see there) And even though it will be explained that a karmelis does not exist above ten handbreadths, and the roof is very high, this applies to the ground, since due to the ground, the air above ten handbreadths is not a karmelis. But here, the roof is considered like the ground, and up to ten handbreadths in height from the roof becomes a karmelis (ibid.).

And similarly, projections that extend from walls - if they are not four handbreadths wide, they are considered a makom patur (an exempt area). If they are four handbreadths wide, they are considered a karmelit, since they are not ten handbreadths high, and they must be four by four handbreadths. If a window of four by four handbreadths opens to them from the house, such that one can use the projections from the window, they are considered like the holes of a private domain and are governed by the laws of a private domain. Know also that the holes of a karmelit do not have the status of a private domain, but rather like the holes of a public domain, and they are judged according to their dimensions, as mentioned in section 36, see there.

The definition of a karmelit is that it should not be less than four by four [handbreadths], and it should not be higher than ten [handbreadths]. It does not extend upwards beyond ten handbreadths, similar to a public domain but not like a private domain. Above ten handbreadths, it is considered a makom patur (exempt area), just like in a public domain. Seas and rivers, the ten handbreadths measurement starts from the water. Therefore, from the water up to ten handbreadths above the water is considered a karmelit, and above that is a makom patur. (If) [If] we were to start measuring from the ground beneath the water, then the water above would be a makom patur, but this is not the case. Taking from the water's surface up to ten handbreadths above is a karmelit, and above that is a makom patur. A pit located in a karmelit, even if it is a hundred cubits deep, is considered a karmelit if it is not four [handbreadths] wide. It is not considered a makom patur, because there is no makom patur within a karmelit. Since the karmelit surrounds it, it inevitably becomes a part of the karmelit. However, if it is four by four [handbreadths] wide, it is considered a private domain. The authority of the karmelit is nullified regarding a private domain, for even a pit in a public domain that is ten handbreadths deep and four handbreadths wide is considered a private domain, and all the more so in a karmelit.

Which is considered a Makom Petur (exempt area)? An area that does not measure four by four handbreadths and is elevated from three handbreadths and up to the sky. Or a trench that does not measure four by four and is deeper than three handbreadths, even if it is very long; since it does not have a width of four, it is considered a Makom Petur. We do not say that if you calculate the total volume, it would be four by four, because the total calculation is irrelevant since it is not convenient for use when it is not four wide. Similarly, walls that are higher than three handbreadths and above, and there is no four by four space between them, i.e., the space between them, and the walls do not combine, as stated in section 5 (and this is also written by the Magen Avraham in sub-section 16).

And know that this applies to a Makom Petur in a public domain. However, a Makom Petur in a private domain is considered a private domain, because even a Karmelit (semi-public domain) within a private domain is considered a private domain.
