The reason for this is that in a public domain, we require that it be conveniently usable for the public, for the public domain is meant for walking and using as they walk. Therefore, anything that is elevated above three handbreadths is not convenient for walking or use, and thus it is either a Karmelit or a Makom Petur. But in a private domain, we do not require convenient walking or use, because since the public does not interrupt it, everything is convenient for use, and everything is considered a private domain.

A Makom Petur within a Karmelit, some say its status is like a Makom Petur in a private domain, and it is also considered a Karmelit, since 'one type finds its kind and awakens.' That is, even in a Karmelit we do not require convenient walking or use, and all the laws of Makom Petur apply only in a public domain. Others say that even in a Karmelit it is a Makom Petur. The reason is that a Karmelit cannot be more stringent than a public domain, for regarding above ten handbreadths, it is considered like a public domain and not a private domain. (This seems to be the reasoning behind the opinions, and both opinions are brought by the Ran in the first chapter of Shabbat, regarding 'a Karmelit is not less than four,' see there. And in Eruvin 9, it clearly follows the first opinion, see there and examine thoroughly).

Maimonides wrote in Chapter 14, Law 9: "A pillar in the public domain that is ten handbreadths high and four handbreadths wide is considered a private domain. If one places a peg of any size on top of it, even if it is not three handbreadths high, since it is suitable for hanging something on it and using it, it reduces the height of the pillar and it becomes a 'karmelit' (an intermediate domain). We only measure the height from the peg upward, and even if the entire top is filled with pegs, it reduces the height because things can be hung and used on those pegs." This is according to the Talmudic discussion in Eruvin (78a). According to the version of Rashi and Tosafot there, the conclusion of the Talmud is the opposite, that even if the peg is three handbreadths high, it does not nullify the status of the private domain, because it is suitable for hanging things. Even if it is completely filled with pegs, one can place something on it and use it. Therefore, none of the later authorities brought Maimonides' ruling, and it seems he had a different version of the text.

There are four types of transferring from one domain to another that are from the Torah: transferring out (hotza’ah), bringing in (hachnasah), throwing (zorek), and handing over (moshit). They all share the same law, except for handing over, which has a stricter aspect than all of them, as will be explained. This is the language of the Rambam in Chapter 13, Law 16: “One who throws from a private domain to another private domain with a public domain in the middle, even though the object passed through the airspace of the public domain, is exempt (because we do not say ‘caught is as if placed’), provided it passes above three [handbreadths]. But if it passes within three handbreadths close to the ground and rests on something, even if it was later uprooted or rolled from one private domain to another private domain, it is considered as if it remained in the public domain, and therefore he is liable." End of quote. And Rosh and Ramban ruled that below three [handbreadths] there is no need for it to rest on something, for anything within three handbreadths of the ground is considered as if it rested on the ground. In the Gemara (97a), there is a dispute about this, see there. And one should not ask, since we consider it as if it rested, then he should be liable for two [violations], for there is here both transferring from a private domain to a public domain and bringing into a private domain from a public domain. Indeed, this is so, but one is not liable for a derivative [category] in the place of a principal [category] (there), and as it is taught in the major principle 'one who performs many labors of a similar kind is liable only for one sin-offering,' as explained in Siman 242.

He further wrote: "Similarly, one who throws an object from a public domain to another public domain with a private domain in between is exempt. However, if the object passed within three handbreadths of the ground and rested on something, even though it then rolled and exited to the second public domain, it is considered as if it remained in the private domain and therefore one is liable." This means that one cannot be liable for throwing in the public domain, as it refers to a case where he did not throw four cubits, and even together with both public domains it does not amount to four cubits. Therefore, the liability is only for placing it in the private domain, as explained later in Halacha 17: "One who carries four cubits in a public domain combined with another public domain is liable, because four cubits in the two public domains are combined since the object did not rest in the domain between them." And it is obvious that the same applies to one who throws, and the reason he wrote 'carries' is to emphasize that even if he himself carried the object through the private domain, we do not say 'walking is like standing', and all the more so for throwing. Therefore, when it was previously written 'one who throws from a public domain to a public domain with a private domain in between is exempt' - it must be in a case where there are not four cubits between the two public domains. And it is clear that according to Rabbi Chanina and Ramban, even if it did not rest on something, as stated in the previous section. And know, that this liability for passing within three handbreadths and resting on something is due to transferring from a public domain to a private domain, and this is when he intentionally threw it close to within three handbreadths, intending for it to rest briefly in the private domain. For if his intention was to throw it to the other public domain, he would not be liable for transferring, as he did not intend for it, and this is not considered a deliberate act, as is explicitly proven in the Gemara there. (Where it questions 'if he intended for it here... saying wherever it lands is fine, but otherwise exempt').

And this applies to throwing and passing, but handing over is more stringent, as the Rambam wrote there: "One who hands over from a private domain to a private domain with a public domain in between is liable, even if he handed it over above the airspace of the public domain, as this was the practice of the Levites in the Tabernacle - they would hand the planks from one wagon to another with the public domain between the two wagons, and each wagon is a private domain. When does this apply? When the two private domains are in the length of the public domain, as the wagons travel in the public domain one after the other. But if the two private domains are on opposite sides of the public domain, even if one hands over from this private domain to the opposite private domain, he is exempt." End quote. 

And it turns out that there were two stringencies in handing over: the first is that one is liable from a private domain to another private domain through a public domain when they are on the same level, even above ten [handbreadths], which is not the case with throwing. But with passing, one is also liable above ten, as this was the load of the sons of Kehat, (92b) as all derive from the Tabernacle. 

And the concept of handing over, as explained by Rashi and the Ra'avad at the beginning of the chapter "One who throws," is that one hands over the load to his fellow, and his fellow to his fellow, as the Levites would hand the planks to each other. And it appears that even for a light load, one is liable for handing over, for although the planks were heavy, nevertheless, we do not derive from the Tabernacle in specifics, for otherwise, we would only be liable for planks. Rather, certainly, for any type of handing over, one is liable, and this seems to be the primary ruling in law. (And from Tosafot 4a, s.v. 'and what,' it is explained that handing over applies even not to a fellow, see there).

In Chapter 14, Law 14, it is written: "One who carries from a private domain to a private domain or from a public domain to a public domain with a karmelit in between is exempt. Similarly, one who passes or throws from one to the other with a karmelit in between is exempt," end quote. This means that even in the case of passing, one is exempt because the work of the Levites was only from a private domain to a private domain through a public domain, not through a karmelit. And regarding what is written 'from a public domain to a public domain with a karmelit in between - exempt', this applies when there are not four cubits in the second public domain, but if there are four cubits, it has already been written that they combine and one is liable, as walking is not considered like standing still (nevertheless). And he further wrote: "One who takes an object from a public domain to a karmelit and places it there, and then takes it from the karmelit and places it in a private domain, or who takes it from a private domain to a karmelit and places it there, and then takes it from the karmelit and places it in a public domain - this person is exempt," end quote. This is obvious, because there was a placement in the middle in the karmelit. But if there was no placement in the middle, one would be liable even if they passed through a karmelit, because walking is not considered like standing still, and certainly in the case of throwing in such instances one would be liable.

And this is what he further wrote (Halacha 15), and this is his language: "One who transfers an object from a private domain to a public domain and passed through an exempt area in his path is liable, for walking is not considered as standing. And it goes without saying that if one throws an object and it passes through an exempt area, it is not considered as if it rested there." End of quote. This is the case when it did not pass close to three handbreadths from the ground and did not rest there at all, for in such situations, one who throws is exempt. According to Rach and Ramban, even if it did not rest at all, as they wrote. And when he wrote 'exempt area' - it is the same as a karmelit, for according to Torah law, a karmelit is also considered an exempt area. And when he wrote 'exempt area' - it is for a novelty. (Maimonides) meaning, even though it passed through an area where even rabbinically it is permitted to transfer initially from there to a public domain or a private domain and from them into it, nevertheless, one is liable, and all the more so through a karmelit. And he further wrote: "But if one was standing in an exempt area and took an object from a private domain or from a person standing there and placed it in a public domain or in the hand of a person standing there, he is exempt. Similarly, if he brought it from a public domain to a private domain and stood in an exempt area, he is exempt." End of quote. And the same applies to a karmelit, as I wrote, and see in section 8.

It is stated in the Gemara (8b): Rava said, "One who transfers an object from the beginning of four cubits to the end of four cubits in a public domain, even if he transfers it through the airspace above ten handbreadths, is liable." And Rashi explained, "Through the airspace above ten handbreadths"—meaning he lifted it above ten handbreadths—but nevertheless, he is liable because when he places it down, it is as if he walked, since walking is not considered standing. This law has already been clarified, and there is no novelty in it. It is also evident from the words of the Rambam in Chapter 12, the end of Law 14, and this is his wording: "One who transfers an object from the beginning of four cubits to the end of four cubits in a public domain, even if he transfers it above his head, is liable." These are his exact words. This is similar to Rashi's explanation. However, Tosafot (s.v. Leima) interpret there in the name of Rabbi Chananel that "transferring through the airspace above his head" means he transfers it in front of him from his right to his left, opposite his body. I would have said that when it reaches opposite his body, it is considered as if it has been placed down, and it turns out that he did not transfer it four cubits together. The Gemara teaches us that this is not so, and he is liable. This is also written by the Ra'avad and the Rashba. And if he paused momentarily opposite his body, it is obvious that he is exempt. 

Know that all this which has been clarified, that "walking is not considered standing," applies when walking without pausing. But when one stands still for a moment, it is considered as if the object was placed there, for we hold that the lifting of one’s body is like the lifting of an object, and the placing of one’s body is like the placing of an object. This will be explained in Siman 347, with God's help.

From the Torah, there is only an obligation regarding one who takes out, brings in, throws, or passes an object from a private domain to a public domain, or from a public domain to a private domain. However, from a karmelit to a private domain or to a public domain is permitted, and likewise from them to it. But from a rabbinic perspective, it is forbidden to carry, throw, or pass from a karmelit to a private domain or to a public domain, and from them to it. But a makom patur, even rabbinically, it is permitted from a makom patur to a private domain or to a public domain, and from them to a makom patur. The reason they forbade in a karmelit is because it resembles a public domain, but a makom patur does not have the appearance of a domain. Nevertheless, it is initially forbidden to carry an object from a private domain to a makom patur and pass through a public domain, lest one might place it down in the public domain (Bach and Taz section 2). Similarly, it is initially forbidden to throw from a private domain to a makom patur through a public domain, lest it fall in the public domain or remain there briefly. Likewise, it is initially forbidden to carry an object from a private domain to a private domain through a public domain, lest one pause slightly in the public domain, and similarly, throwing is forbidden.

It has already been explained that one who stands in a private domain and transfers, brings in, extends, or throws an object into a public domain via a place of exemption or a karmelit is liable, for walking is not considered the same as standing, and an object caught in mid-air is not considered as if it has been placed down. Similarly, one should not stand in a place of exemption and take an object from someone standing in a public domain and give it to someone standing in a private domain, or vice versa. If one did take and give the object, they are exempt by Torah law, for standing in a place of exemption is considered somewhat like placing it down. However, initially, it is forbidden, for it is a disrespect to the prohibition of Shabbat to cause an object to be taken from a private domain to a public domain (Rashi 6, beginning of the section "Ubilevad"). This has already been explained in section 5. Initially, it is forbidden even if the place of exemption stands between domains that are rabbinically prohibited, such as two courtyards that did not make an eruv together. It is forbidden to stand in the place of exemption and take an object from a person in one courtyard and give it to a person in the other courtyard. This is the opinion of the Rosh and the Tur, but the Rif and the Rambam permit initially exchanging in such manners between rabbinic domains. See what is written in Siman 355, section 10.

Based on what has been explained, a private domain and an exempt area - it is permissible to carry in all of them. Even if the private domain is very large and the exempt area is very long, carrying and throwing are permitted. However, in a public domain and a karmelit, one may not carry more than four cubits. If one carried, threw, or extended beyond four cubits, in a public domain - one is liable, and in a karmelit - one is exempt, since the prohibition of a karmelit is rabbinic, lest it be confused with a public domain. The Rambam wrote in Chapter 14, the end of Law 11: "Therefore, if one did not need the essence of the carrying, such as removing a thorn from a karmelit so that the public would not be harmed by it - this is permitted, even if he carried it several cubits, and likewise in all similar cases." End of quote. And from domain to domain it is forbidden, except from a private domain to another private domain and from an exempt area to all domains and from all domains to the exempt area. And know that there are several types of karmelit, as stated in the previous section, and it is permissible to carry within four cubits from one karmelit to another karmelit, but in the Jerusalem Talmud, Chapter 11, Law 5, it is explained that this is forbidden. See there.

Therefore, a "karpaf"—an area enclosed by four partitions without a roof, like a courtyard, and larger than a "beit se'atayim" (approximately 5,000 square cubits) that was not enclosed for the purpose of dwelling—according to Torah law, it is considered a complete private domain. However, rabbinically, it is regarded as a "karmelit" and it is forbidden to carry within it more than four cubits. It is permitted to carry from it to a complete "karmelit," such as a valley passing in front of it, as long as it is within four cubits. Therefore, gardens adjacent to a "karmelit" (like a valley) or on our streets, where we do not have a public domain, and the garden is locked with a key, it is permitted to take the key from the "karmelit" in front of the garden to unlock and lock, and then return the key there. Although the garden is considered a complete private domain according to Torah law, since rabbinically it is forbidden to carry within it more than four cubits, it is permitted to carry from it to a complete "karmelit" within four cubits, provided there is no private domain between them. That is, a threshold that is ten handbreadths high and four handbreadths wide, which is forbidden to carry into from the "karmelit" in front of it. Similarly, from the garden to the threshold it is forbidden to carry, as per the laws of carrying from a "karmelit" to a complete private domain.

And this is the language of our teacher, the Rema, in paragraph 3: "Therefore, it is permitted to take a key from a karmelit (an area with intermediate status) that is in front of a garden... provided that there is no threshold between them that is a private domain, or that has two partitions on the sides that are four [handbreadths] wide with a lintel above that is four [handbreadths] wide, for then it would be considered a private domain even though it is not ten [handbreadths] high. However, it is forbidden to transfer from the threshold to a private domain or vice versa, because we are concerned that the roof might not be four [handbreadths], and if the threshold is not three [handbreadths] high, it has the status of the area before it. And even if it is three [handbreadths] high, since all our domains are considered karmelit, we say 'a kind finds its own kind and is awakened,' as it is written in section 345. Similarly, if the roof is very wide and does not have partitions on the sides - it has the status of the area before it, and likewise with roofs that protrude in front of houses, like our roofs - they have the status of the area before them." End quote. His words require explanation.

And this is its explanation: that it requires that there should not be a private domain between them. This refers to a threshold that is ten handbreadths high and four handbreadths wide, which constitutes a private domain by virtue of the edge of the roof. This is when there are two partitions, each four handbreadths wide, with a beam on top that is four handbreadths wide. We say regarding the two open sides, "the edge of the roof descends and seals." But when they are not four handbreadths wide, we do not say "it descends and seals," because any partition that does not have a space of four handbreadths between the partitions is not considered a partition. (Rashi 9a, s.v. "opening") And as we say "it descends and seals," it automatically means that there are four partitions, each ten handbreadths high and four handbreadths wide, making the threshold between them also a private domain, even if it is not ten handbreadths high. And even though it will be explained later in Siman 361 that for the condition of "the edge of the roof," the two partitions must also be connected, meaning like the shape of a "dalet" and not facing each other, nevertheless, there is concern that this is merely a stringency. Essentially, we say "the edge of the roof" also in the case of facing each other. However, in any case, even though this is a complete private domain, it is still forbidden to transfer from it to a private domain or from a private domain into it, because we are concerned that the roof might fall and there will not be four handbreadths left, nullifying the "edge of the roof." And then, if the threshold is not three handbreadths high, it is clear that it becomes like the domain in front of it, and even if it is three handbreadths high, there is reason to say "it found its kind, etc.," and the threshold also becomes a karmelit, even though it is really a makom patur (exempt area) like an exempt area adjacent to a karmelit, as some say "it found, etc." as it is written in Siman 345, Se'if 45, see there. And similarly, a roof without partitions or protruding roofs are considered like the domain in front of them. Therefore, our protruding roofs are like the street, and similarly, when a small roof is made in front of an entrance, suspended on iron rods, and there is no partition under it that is ten handbreadths high and four handbreadths wide, or a small bridge that is ten handbreadths high and four handbreadths wide, the roof and bridge have the same status as the street, because they are nullified to it, and "it found its kind and was aroused." (This is the explanation of his words, and what the Magen Avraham wrote in Siman 4 that at the opening of an alley we say the edge of the roof even if it is not entirely covered, this is explained in Rashi and Tosafot 9a in the discussion of the threshold, see there. But it is not relevant to this Siman. And what he wrote in Siman 3 in the name of the Maharil that we must be concerned about the explanation of the Ri, meaning that even with three partitions we do not say the edge of the roof as explained at the end of the chapter "all roofs," is very puzzling, because there it is according to Shmuel and we hold like Rav, see there. And the Maharshal strains himself with difficult words, see there, and the law is clear like the Rama. And also what the Taz wrote in Siman 7 that a roof without partitions has the status of the domain in front of it, we have already explained, and be precise).

One who transfers an object from one domain to another is not liable according to Torah law unless there is both an uprooting and a placing down, meaning he uproots it from a private domain and places it in a public domain or vice versa. But uprooting without placing down or placing down without uprooting—he is exempt. This is not comparable to any incomplete measure which is forbidden by Torah law, and the reason for this is explained in Siman 242:35, and according to Rabbinic law, it is forbidden. Similarly, when one carries [an object] four cubits in the public domain, it also requires both uprooting and placing down. We explained there that less than four cubits is even permitted according to Rabbinic law, see there for the reason. Additionally, the uprooting must be specifically from a place that is four by four handbreadths, and similarly, the placing down must be on a place that is four by four handbreadths, because the uprooting must be from a significant place and so must the placing down. It seems to me that it must be specifically four by four and not in a long and narrow manner, even though in total it has the measure of four by four, because since it does not have a width of four, it is not convenient for use and is not considered a significant place, as we wrote regarding a place of exemption in Siman 345:45, see there.

Even though a space of four by four [handbreadths] is required, nevertheless, our Sages said (5a) that a person's hand is considered as four by four, for there is nothing more important than a person's hand, with which all tasks are performed. There is no difference between the right hand and the left hand, for even the left hand is considered more significant than any other space of four by four, as it is taught (92a), "One who carries an object, whether in his right hand or his left hand, is liable." Therefore, if one moves an object from the hand of a person standing in one domain and places it in the hand of another person standing in a different domain, he is liable. There is a question whether only the hand of a person is considered as four by four and not any other limb, such as if one moves an object from a person's head or the upper part of his arm or his leg, none of which have four by four. It seems that this does not apply. (And this is explicitly stated in section 4, see there.)

And this is the language of the Rambam at the beginning of Chapter 13: "A person's hand is considered... Similarly, if he was standing in one of these two domains, and he extended his hand to the second domain and lifted an object from it or from the hand of a person standing there, and then brought his hand back to him - he is liable. And even though he did not place the object in the place where he is standing, since it is resting in his hand, it is as if it is resting on the ground." End of quote. There is a novelty in this, that even though his body is in this domain and his hand is extended to the other domain, we do not say that his hand follows his body and consider the hand as if it is in the domain where the body is, and therefore there is no transfer from one domain to another. This teaches us that it is not so. Similarly, there is a novelty that even though there is no change between the lifting and the placing, since the hand in which he lifted is also the hand in which he placed, nevertheless the lifting of his hand is like the lifting of the object, and the placing of his hand is like the placing of the object. Hence, it turns out that the lifting was in this domain and the placing in another domain - and he is liable.

And so we say (at the end of the chapter "Hazorek" (Shabbat 102a)): 'His intention designates it as a place.' In other words, even though we require placing on an area of four by four [handbreadths], nevertheless, if he intended it to rest in a particular place, he is liable, even though it is not an area of four [handbreadths]. For example, if he threw [an object] intending it to rest in a dog's mouth and it rested in the dog's mouth, he is liable, even though there is not an area of four [handbreadths] there. Similarly, if he was eating and passing from one domain to another, and he intended to transfer the food from one domain to another, he is liable, because his intention designates his mouth as an area of four [handbreadths]. And even though he did not transfer it in the usual manner of transferring, he is liable because transferring while eating is considered a normal manner of transferring. Similarly, if he is standing in one domain and urinates or spits into another domain, it will be explained in section 160, with God's help, that the reason is because his intention designates it as an area of four [handbreadths], and there in subsection 5 the reason will be explained as well, see there.

It is stated in the Gemara (5a): 'Rava said: Water on top of water – this constitutes placing.' And if one lifts from the water or places on the water – it is considered lifting and placing in a four-handbreadth area. And specifically when one lifts water and places water, but a nut on top of water – this does not constitute placing, and if one places the nut on the water, it is not considered placing in a four-handbreadth area. Similarly, if one lifts a nut from the water, it does not constitute lifting. And it is not specifically a nut, as the same applies to any item. And it seems to me that an item which is naturally on the water, like a ship, is considered placing, and lifting it from there is considered lifting, and see paragraph 6.

And we say there: 'Rava asked: A nut in a vessel and the vessel is floating on the water - do we follow the nut and it is considered at rest, or do we follow the vessel and it is not considered at rest because it is moving - it remains unresolved.' And since it is a doubt, one is not liable, and so wrote the Rambam there. And the Tosafot (s.v. Aguz) questioned this from what we say regarding the acquisition of a ship that it is considered at rest and it is the water that moves it. (Bava Metzia 9a) And they answered - that acquisition is different, since there it is considered as at rest. But regarding Shabbat we derive from the Mishkan, and in the Mishkan they stored things in the way people typically store them, see there. And in my humble opinion, it seems that surely in a ship it is considered at rest, and this is the way of people. And Rava only spoke about a vessel that is not typically on the surface of the water. And similarly, if there was oil floating on the surface of the water and one collected from the oil and took it out - he is exempt, because they are not connected to each other, (there) and it is like collecting from a place that does not have four by four [handbreadths]. And it appears to me that this is specifically for oil that does not mix with any liquid, but other liquids, since they mix with the water, are considered as one entity.

Maimonides wrote in Chapter 13, Law 5: "We have already said that one who transfers an item from one domain to another is not liable unless he both uproots and places the item down. However, if he uproots but does not place it down, or if he places it down but did not uproot it, he is exempt. Therefore, if someone is standing in one of two domains and extends his hand into the other domain with an object in his hand and another person takes it from him, or if another person places an object into his hand and he then retracts his hand - both are exempt, because one performed the uprooting and the other performed the placing down. When is this the case? When his hand is above three handbreadths from the ground. But if his hand is within three handbreadths of the ground, it is as though he placed it on the ground and he is liable." End quote. In such cases, it appears that even if another person places an object into his hand which is within three handbreadths and he then retracts his hand, he is liable, since we hold that his hand is not considered part of his body, as stated in section 3, and the uprooting of his hand is like the uprooting of an object. Therefore, it is as though he uprooted it from the ground, and when he retracts his hand it is considered placing it down, even though it was not placed on the ground as stated there. (This is explained in Tosafot, s.v. 'kegon,' see there). And there are those who say that even below three handbreadths it is not considered as though it were placed on the ground (Ra'avad in Hilchot Shabbat, and "there are those who say" in the Mishneh Torah).

It is simple that when we said both are exempt, when one did the lifting and the other the placing – nonetheless, it is prohibited by rabbinic law, like all exemptions on Shabbat which are exempt but prohibited, and so it is explicitly stated in the Gemara at the beginning of Shabbat, see there. However, in a case where one did both the lifting and the placing and the other did nothing, such as when one was standing in one of these two domains and his friend extended his hand from the other domain and took an object from the hand of the one standing in this domain and brought it to himself, or he took an object from himself and placed it in the hand of the one standing, the one standing did nothing, for he either placed the item in his hand or took it from his hand. The other is liable, for he did the lifting and the placing. And in the Gemara there it says about the one standing – “exempt and permitted,” and so it is explained from the language of the Rambam who wrote about him – “he did nothing,” see there.

The early authorities asked why he is exempt and permitted, for he is aiding those who commit a transgression and is thereby transgressing "Do not place a stumbling block before the blind." And even if we say that the second person would have taken and placed it even without him, there is still at least a rabbinic prohibition. And even if we say that the second person is a non-Jew, it is still forbidden to give him the property of a Jew to carry into the public domain, as stated in Siman 325. We must say that the case refers to when the object also belongs to the non-Jew (Tosafot). Others have answered that the Talmud only states that regarding Shabbat, he is exempt and permitted, but there remains another prohibition, because some hold that even with the property of a non-Jew, it is initially forbidden to give it to him to carry out due to observers (Rosh), as stated in Siman 325. And based on this, the words of the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch are understood. In my humble opinion, it seems that these laws refer to inadvertent acts - regarding the obligation of a sin-offering. And indeed, all obligations and exemptions on Shabbat generally refer to inadvertent acts, as is evident from the Mishnah in "Klal Gadol" which teaches "he is only liable for one" or "he is liable for each one," and this is only regarding sin-offerings and inadvertent acts, as it does not apply to deliberate acts since we do not punish him twice. And since in inadvertent acts "Do not place a stumbling block" does not apply at all, it is understood that we only say that in such cases one is completely liable and the other is completely exempt, and in such cases both are exempt but have committed a rabbinic prohibition inadvertently. But this does not relate to "Do not place a stumbling block." (The laws written by the Magen Avraham in subsection 4 have no connection to the laws of Shabbat as stated there.)

In the Jerusalem Talmud, at the beginning of tractate Shabbat, it says that one is liable when placing an item into the hand of another person who is standing in a different domain - specifically when the other person's hand is below ten handbreadths. However, if it is above ten handbreadths, it is considered an exempt area in the public domain, and therefore, in such cases of transferring, one is not liable if it is above ten handbreadths. This is also written by Tosafot (5a, s.v. "kan" - see there) and the Rashba. The language of the Jerusalem Talmud is as follows: "provided that the hand of the poor person standing in the public domain is within ten handbreadths from the ground" - see there. And even though we maintain that in the case of passing an item, even above ten handbreadths one is liable, as this was the method of carrying of the sons of Kohath, still, when placing it there, it is certainly exempt. (See the Mishneh Torah, beginning of Chapter 13, where it is written that there are those who disagree, and so wrote the Magen Avraham. However, I do not know who these dissenters are).

We hold that the movement of one's body is like the movement of an object, and the resting of one's body is like the resting of an object. (3) That is to say, if someone was standing in one of two domains, and his friend placed a load on him, either in his hand or on his shoulder, and he went out with that object to the other domain and stood there - he is liable, even though he did not move the object or place it down, because by moving his body after being loaded, it is considered as if he moved the object, and when he stood in the other domain, it is considered as if he placed the object down. Therefore, if his friend did not load him while he was standing but did so while he was walking, it is not considered a lifting. Similarly, if he did not stand in the second domain but kept going in and out all day until it got dark and did not stand, there is no placement. And even if he stood to adjust the load, that is not considered standing unless he stood to rest.

Therefore, our Sages said (5:): "Within four cubits—if he stopped to rest, he is exempt; if he stopped to adjust his load, he is liable. Beyond four cubits—if he stopped to rest, he is liable; if he stopped to adjust his load, he is exempt." This means that within four cubits, when he stopped to rest and it constitutes a placement, he did not carry four cubits at once. But if he stopped to adjust his load, which is not considered a placement, he is liable because this does not constitute an interruption. And beyond four cubits, when he stopped to rest, it is considered a placement, and he is liable because he carried four cubits. But to adjust his load, he is exempt as stated. Additionally, they said (153:): "If his bundle was resting on his shoulder before Shabbat and Shabbat began while it was still on him, he should run with it until he reaches his house, and there he should throw the load in an unusual manner." This is specifically if he runs, but if he walks slowly, he is close to violating a Torah prohibition, meaning he may stop momentarily without realizing it, which would constitute a placement followed by a lifting. But when he runs, there is a noticeable difference. (From Maimonides, Chapter 13, Law 9, it is clear that if he walks slowly, he is certainly liable; see there. But the language of the Talmud does not imply this, and Rashi also explained this way. Perhaps Maimonides was not being precise; consider this carefully.)

Maimonides wrote in Chapter 13, Halacha 11: "If a rod or a spear, or something similar, is lying on the ground, and one lifts one end while the other end remains on the ground and throws it before him, and then returns and lifts the other end which was on the ground and throws it before him in this manner, until he has moved the object several miles - he is exempt, because he did not uproot the entire object from the ground. But if he drags the object along the ground, from the beginning of four [cubits] to the end of four [cubits] - he is liable, because rolling is considered uprooting." End quote. This means that dragging and rolling is itself considered as uprooting and placing down. Therefore, if one rolls a barrel four cubits in a public domain or rolls it from one domain to another - he is liable. (Tosafot 8: s.v. 'lo') The same applies to a round box, but if it is square - he is exempt, because it is impossible that part of it is not resting [on the ground]. (ibid.) And even though it is customary to transport it in such a manner, and similarly with a rod or a spear, even though it is customary to transport it in such a manner due to its weight - nevertheless, he is exempt (ibid.).

He further wrote: "One who moves an object from one corner to another within the same house, and this initial movement is permissible, but then changes his mind along the way and takes it out to another domain - is exempt, because the initial lifting was not intended for that purpose, and thus this is a placement without a corresponding initial lifting. Similarly, one who lifts an object and places it on his companion while he is walking, and when his companion decides to stop, he takes it from his companion - he is exempt, because this is considered a lifting without a corresponding placement." And this is exempt but prohibited, as written in section 8.

Additionally, he wrote: "One who throws an object from one domain to another, or from the beginning of four cubits to the end of four cubits in the public domain, and before it comes to rest, another person catches it in his hand, or a dog catches it, or it gets burned – he is exempt, because this is not the intended placement. Therefore, if he intended at the time of the throw for this to happen – he is liable. One who throws an object from one domain to another, and it is tied by a rope and held in his hand, if he can pull the object back to him – he is exempt, because it is not considered a complete placement, and it is as if he uprooted it but did not place it down. One who throws and it comes to rest in his friend's hand, if his friend stood in his place and received it – the thrower is liable, because he uprooted and placed it. But if his friend moved from his place and received it – he is exempt. (Since he did not intend for this) One who threw and then ran after the object and received it in his hand in another domain or beyond four cubits – he is exempt (as if) [as if] another person had moved and received it, because the complete placement is not until the object comes to rest in the place where it was intended to rest at the time of uprooting." End of quote. And it did not come to rest as the object ran to the place where it was intended at the time of uprooting. And in the Gemara (5a) this was a question that was not resolved. And it appears that if from the beginning he intended, at the time of the throw, to run and receive it – he is liable. (And so it is explicitly stated in Rashi there, s.v. 'as two', see there, and there is indeed a placement according to the thought at the time of uprooting).

The Rambam wrote in Chapter 14, Law 19: "If one throws a stick or spear from a private domain and it gets stuck in the public domain while standing – he is exempt, because part of it is in an exempt area. (Above ten handbreadths) If one throws a vessel from a private domain to a public domain and that vessel is large and has four by four handbreadths with a height of ten – he is exempt, because this vessel is considered a full private domain, and it is as if he transferred from a private domain to another private domain." End quote. But if it was less than ten – he is liable, and we do not say it is a karmelit, because there is no karmelit with vessels as stated in Siman 345. And it seems to me that even with a large vessel, one is only exempt when throwing, for it is like throwing from one private domain to another private domain through a public domain. But if one passes such a vessel to his friend – he is liable when they both stand along the street. For when passing, one is liable from a private domain to a private domain through a public domain in such cases, as stated in the previous Siman. (And this is explicitly stated in Tosafot, s.v. 'Rechava' – see there carefully) And it is clear that if it is not four by four handbreadths wide – he is liable even if it is ten handbreadths high, for it is not considered a domain. But when it is higher than ten – he is exempt, for the upper edge is in the airspace of an exempt area. Therefore, the Sages said (there) that if the vessel was made of reeds, such as a beehive and the like, even if it is ten handbreadths high – one is exempt, for it is impossible for the reed tips not to go above ten handbreadths – see there, and I do not know why the Rambam omitted this.

He also wrote: "A pit of nine [handbreadths] in the public domain, and one removed the rim from its edge and completed it to ten [handbreadths], (and left it in the public domain) even though the removal of the object and the making of the partition occur simultaneously - he is exempt, because the partition was not ten [handbreadths] initially. If the pit was ten [handbreadths], and he threw a rim into it and reduced it from ten [handbreadths] - he is exempt, as the placing of the object and the removal of the partition occur simultaneously," end quote. And in the Talmud (99b), there was a question that was not resolved, see there. Specifically a rim, because it is fixed there and will always be in the pit - it is considered the removal of the partition. But another object - one is liable, because he will take it away from there and there is no removal of the partition. (Talmud there) (And it is not similar to the case in Gittin 77b where we say 'her bill of divorce and her courtyard come simultaneously' and it is a valid divorce, because here we require the domain from the start of the removal and also at the end of the placing itself, and it is not similar to there. Study this well).

He also wrote: "If someone throws a sheet and it lands on top of stakes in the public domain and thereby creates a private domain, even if there is a vessel on top of the sheet, he is exempt, for the construction of the partition and the placement of the vessel occur simultaneously." End of quote. This is also in the Gemara there. There is a question regarding what this refers to. If the stakes are very close to each other, with a height of ten and a width of four, then there is no creation of a partition, as it was already a private domain. Therefore, it must be that the stakes are distant from each other. If so, how is a private domain created by the sheet, as it would be a partition that young goats can breach? (Maimonides in the name of Rashba) It is possible to say that up to three handbreadths from the ground, there are complete partitions and no more, so there is no breaching of young goats. (And perhaps this is the intention of Tosafot there in the entry 'threw', see there) Nevertheless, it is not a private domain beneath it. (there) It must be said that there are two complete partitions of stakes, and when the sheet is thrown, we say 'the edge of the roof descends and closes off' (there) and it becomes a private domain. Rashba wrote that it refers to being adjacent to a private domain and is considered as the cavities of a private domain, where the breaching of young goats does not nullify it, see there, and it requires further study. In my humble opinion, it seems that the stakes are close to each other but are not ten high. Through the thickness of the sheet, they become ten high, and this is what is meant by the simultaneous creation of the partition and the placement.

He also wrote: "A pit that is ten [handbreadths] deep and eight [handbreadths] wide in the public domain, and [someone] threw a mat into it (this is the correct wording) and divided [the space of] the pit in its width into two - he is exempt, for with the placement of the mat, the partitions are nullified, and each section is made less than four by four [handbreadths]." End of quote. This is specifically when he nullifies the mat to remain there permanently. And similarly, if he threw it on the floor of the pit and reduced it from ten [handbreadths] (ibid).

If one is standing in his courtyard and extends his hand full of fruits through a window or an opening into the public domain—if he did so unintentionally, he is permitted to bring his hand back. However, if he did so intentionally, he is prohibited from bringing his hand back. He is penalized such that he must remain in this position until nightfall. This penalty is because he began with a transgression; for if he had placed the fruits in the public domain, he would have transferred from a private domain to a public domain. Therefore, he is penalized. This applies specifically when he extended his hand to below ten handbreadths, but if he extended it above ten handbreadths, there is not considered to be public domain airspace there, and even if he extended it below, he is permitted to bring it back through an area above ten handbreadths (Tosafot 3a, s.v. "kan," see there). 

There is another stipulation in the Gemara (3a) that if he extended it on Shabbat, he is permitted to bring it back, but if he extended it during the day before Shabbat, he is prohibited from bringing it back. The reason is that, generally, it would be difficult for him to keep his hand extended until nightfall, and he might throw the fruits away. Therefore, on Shabbat, when throwing the fruits would lead to a liability for a sin offering, they did not want to penalize him. But if he extended it during the day before Shabbat, even if he throws the fruits there would be no liability for a sin offering since the initial act of lifting did not occur on Shabbat, thus, he is penalized, and if he throws the fruits, it does not matter. (See Magen Avraham, who explains that liability for a sin offering is not necessary, as in the case of intentional transgression, the person would throw them anyway, thus it is considered a prohibition).

There is another explanation in the Gemara, which is the final one, that they did not impose a penalty at all, and it is permitted to return it. However, the permission is only to return it to the same courtyard where it is currently located, but if there is another adjacent courtyard, it is forbidden to return it so that his intention to transfer it from this courtyard does not succeed. Therefore, when he returns it to another courtyard, his intention is fulfilled, and they decreed that perhaps another time he might permit himself to transfer it to the public domain. (Rashi, s.v. 'his intention' and see Tosafot there, s.v. 'and what', who wrote that if a public domain interrupts between them, he is liable for transferring when they are on the same level. According to this, it is proven that he does not hold as written in Siman 346, Section 3, that transferring is only to his friend).

The distinction is only in the case of inadvertence, but in the case of intentional violation, it is forbidden to return [the object] even to the same courtyard. And this is the language of the Rambam in Chapter 13, Law 20: "If one forgot and stretched out his hand, and it was full of fruits, and he took it out from this courtyard intending to bring it into the adjacent courtyard, and then remembered before bringing it in, and his hand is now suspended in the airspace of the public domain - it is permitted to return it to his courtyard. But to bring it into that second courtyard - it is forbidden, so that he does not fulfill his intention that he had during the inadvertence. But if he extended his hand intentionally, it is forbidden to return it to him, rather they penalize him that his hand should remain suspended until it becomes dark" (end of quote). And he did not differentiate between before nightfall and after nightfall, because he holds that according to the last interpretation, he does not agree with the previous interpretation. But there are those who disagree and hold that after nightfall there is no penalty for the reason we explained in Section 1, and our teacher the Beit Yosef brought both opinions. And it is clear that the Rambam is referring to below ten [handbreadths], as he explicitly mentioned, since he wrote 'suspended in the airspace of the public domain,' and there is no public domain above ten [handbreadths], and so wrote the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch there.

However, from the words of the Rambam, it is clear that it is specifically when his intention was to bring it into the courtyard next to it, in which case it can be said that his intention was fulfilled. But from Rashi, it is not clear, as he interprets "his intention was fulfilled" to mean that he intended to remove them from this courtyard, and similarly, it is explained in the words of the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch. And our teacher the Beit Yosef wrote: "What are we speaking of? When he took it out to the public domain. But if he took it out to a Karmelit, he is permitted to return it in any case" (end quote). For if not, it would be a decree upon a decree (Beit Yosef). And this is specifically in a case of inadvertence, but if it was intentional, since the reason is due to a penalty, they also penalized him in a Karmelit (Magen Avraham). And from Tosafot there it seems that even in a case of inadvertence and in a Karmelit they decreed (similarly, it seems from the Talmud's resolution 'here during the day,' and in such cases there is no Biblical prohibition, yet they still penalized, see Magen Avraham paragraph 3 and examine well).

The Rambam wrote (there): "One who intended to throw eight cubits in the public domain, and the object came to rest at the end of four cubits, is liable, since the act of labor was completed to the prescribed measure and his intention was fulfilled. It is known that this object would not reach the end of eight cubits without passing through each and every part of the eight cubits. But if he intended to throw four cubits and threw eight, and the object came to rest at the end of eight cubits, he is exempt, since it came to rest in a place where he did not intend for it to pass through, let alone come to rest. Therefore, if he intended at the time of throwing that the object may come to rest wherever it will, he is liable." So are his words. According to Rashi’s version and interpretation (97b: 'And this is not'), even if he intended to throw eight and threw four, he is exempt unless he said, 'Let it come to rest wherever it will,' since he intended for it to rest precisely at the end of eight cubits, as mentioned there. And the Rambam holds that this is not a strict requirement, as long as it passed beyond the end of four cubits. Perhaps even according to the Rambam, liability only exists if it passed within three handbreadths of the ground, for it is considered as though it has come to rest. However, the Rambam also requires it to come to rest within three handbreadths on something, as he wrote there. And Rav Hai Gaon’s opinion aligns with Rashi (according to the Maggid Mishneh)."

He also wrote: "If one threw (an object) within four cubits and it rolled beyond four cubits, he is exempt. If he threw it beyond four cubits and it rolled within four cubits, if it rested on something outside the four cubits and then rolled and entered within four cubits, he is liable; but if it did not rest at all, he is exempt." So it is written. And if the wind held it even slightly, it is considered as if it rested on something. (Gemara 100. See also the Mishneh Torah, where it quotes the Rashba, which requires further study).

Rambam writes in Chapter 12, Law 15: "A person is permitted to carry within a four by four cubits area in a public domain, as long as he stands within it, and he may carry anywhere within this square. The measurement is based on his own cubit. If he is a person with unusually short limbs, he is given four cubits as per the average person. And from tradition, it is taught that what is said in the Torah 'each person is to remain in his place'—this means that he should not carry outside this square but only within this square, which is the length of a person when he stretches out his hands and legs, and only within this can he carry." End quote.

This teaching comes from Eruvin (48a), and Rabbi Meir says that a cubit is measured by the length a person can stretch out his hands and legs. But Rabbi Yehuda says that the fourth cubit is to allow a person to retrieve an object from his feet and place it by his head. It is stated there that according to Rabbi Meir, the four cubits are expansive, and according to Rabbi Yehuda, they are precise. And even though the law follows Rabbi Yehuda, Rambam only cited Rabbi Meir's words because they are more straightforward, and for practical purposes, it does not make a difference whether it is for this reason or that reason. Even though it is said there that according to Rabbi Yehuda, the four cubits are precise and according to Rabbi Meir, they are expansive, this is certainly correct. Since Rambam did not mention expansive, it implies they are precise. (See Kesef Mishneh, who wrote that Rambam's interpretation is the opposite, that according to Rabbi Meir, they are precise. I do not understand why we should force the interpretation that he ruled like Rabbi Meir against the general principles of the Talmud. Even though the Rif holds like the Kesef Mishneh, nevertheless, for Rambam, it is more comfortable to say like Rashi, and as written. For the Rif, indeed, they need to be expansive, and examine this well.)

According to the Rambam, it is permissible from the outset to carry within these four cubits. This is also evident from the language of the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch, who wrote: "Every person has four cubits in the public domain within which he can carry." However, the Ra'avad disagreed with him, arguing that this is only permitted in the case where one has gone outside the boundary and is not allowed to move from his four cubits, or if he established his residence there, making it a fixed place for him. Without this, it is not permitted. His reasoning seems to be that it is easy to come to a Torah prohibition by carrying outside the four cubits. In the Mishnah of Eruvin (45a), this law is mentioned regarding someone who did not establish residence and only has four cubits. The Rambam holds, from what the Sages said at the beginning of "One Who Became Dark," that carrying less than four cubits over a long distance was only permitted in a case of loss. From this, we learn that within his four cubits, it is entirely permitted, and we are not concerned that he will carry outside the four cubits, because since he has only this one area, he is very careful about it.

And this that he wrote - 'that he stands beside them,' his intention is that the four cubits are not two on each side with him in the middle, as there is in the Mishnah there someone who holds so, but rather four cubits to whichever side he chooses. And when he selects for this side, he cannot then select for another side, unless he leaves this place and goes to another place, for in every place he is, he has these four cubits. And this that he wrote 'we measure with his own cubit' - this is from the elbow, which they call "alynboygn," to the tip of the middle finger, which is the longest of all the fingers and is called a cubit, and after it this measure is called a cubit. And if he is a dwarf in his limbs, meaning that the measure of his limbs is small relative to the measure of his body, and his own cubit would not be sufficient for him, they give him a medium cubit. And we have already explained, that according to the measure of our country Russia, it is twelve "vayerskes," and four cubits are the measure of the "sazhen" or "klafter" of our country, and three "arshins" of our country are the four cubits of the Gemara as we explained in Choshen Mishpat section 218 see there. And in Yoreh De'ah beginning of section 241 we explained, that the measure of an average person which is three cubits as we wrote, this is according to our measure two "arshins" and four "vayerskes," and similarly the government assesses until today, and that this measure is with the head see there. (The Tosafot in Eruvin 48b s.v. 'his body' wrote that this is without the head, but the Ramban and the Rashba disagreed with them, and there in Yoreh De'ah we explained this with God's help).

And he further wrote: "Therefore, it is permissible for a person to move an object from the public domain and give it to his friend who is within four cubits of him, and likewise from his friend to another friend next to him, even if there are a hundred people, and even if the object travels several miles on Shabbat—it is permitted, because each person has only carried within his own four cubits." End quote, and so wrote the Tur. And also in this matter, the Ra'avad wrote that they only permitted this in a case of great necessity, and certainly this is so, as it is a significant matter. And it is necessary to understand that the Rambam also intended this, for this is only done due to a great necessity. However, some of the poskim (decisors) completely disagree with this ruling and say that this is not the halacha. (The Razah and the Rosh according to the Rif in Eruvin 95.) And know that even according to those who permit it, care must be taken that the object does not leave the owner's domain or in the case of an ownerless object which does not acquire a place of rest, as stated in Siman 401. According to all opinions, it is forbidden to carry an object less than four cubits and less than four cubits again, even during twilight and even in a karmelit, because a person is very likely to make a mistake and carry it beyond the four cubits. With many people, each one will remind his friend, but not with one person. Therefore, they decreed this even during twilight. And there is someone who says that in a karmelit and during twilight, where there are two leniencies, it is permitted. (Taz) And it is obvious that all of this applies in the public domain itself or in a karmelit, but from a private domain to a karmelit and certainly to a public domain, the concept of within four cubits does not apply, for as soon as one takes out from one domain to another, he is liable. And because there are those who err in this matter, I have written it. (There)

If there are two people, each of whom has four cubits, and part of the cubits of one overlaps with part of the cubits of the other, such as if there are six cubits between them, then both are allowed to carry within the two middle cubits. They can bring and eat in the middle, provided that neither brings from his own area into the area of the other. The novelty here is that we do not decree that since they are together, one might use the place of the other because he sees the other using it and they are eating together. Nevertheless, we do not decree. 

If there are three people and the middle one overlaps with the others, such as if there are eight cubits between the two outer ones, and thus the middle one has two cubits in the area of each of the outer ones, the middle one is allowed to use the two cubits that overlap with each of the outer ones. This is an even greater novelty because, even though he uses the space of both, and the two outer ones are forbidden to use each other's space, and there are more people and more uses, and it would be appropriate to decree that one of them might err and use a prohibited area, especially the middle one who uses both areas and might easily err, nevertheless, we do not decree. Even though in courtyards we do decree in such cases, as stated in Siman 378, that is because there are more people, but here, they did not decree. (Gemara 48.)

And the Rambam wrote: "Since a person is allowed to carry within the square which is four cubits by four cubits, one ends up carrying along the diagonal of this square five cubits and three-fifths of a cubit. Therefore, one who carries or throws is not liable until he carries beyond five cubits and three-fifths of a cubit. Anytime we mentioned 'from the beginning of four to the end of four,' or 'one who carries four cubits in the public domain is liable' - it is from the beginning of the diagonal of four cubits to its end, and if one carries less than this, he is exempt. Here we find three measurements. How so? If one moves an object from this place in the public domain and places it in another place in the public domain, if the distance between the two places is up to four cubits - it is permitted. If the distance between them is more than four cubits but still within five cubits and three-fifths of a cubit - he is exempt. If the distance between them is exactly five cubits and three-fifths of a cubit - he is liable, because he has carried the object beyond the diagonal of the square." End quote.

Many have challenged him, questioning the basis for making these distinctions. However, the truth is that from what is said in the Gemara that "one who carries four cubits in the public domain is not liable until he carries both the distance and its diagonal" (Eruvin 51a), it is clear that regarding liability, this is indeed the case. But regarding prohibition, the diagonal is not required. Consequently, the view of the Rambam is also shared by Rashi, Rabbeinu Tam, and the Rashba, of blessed memory. Some poskim (halachic authorities) believe that the phrase "both the distance and its diagonal" only applies when one carries along the diagonal of the world, but for a straightforward distance, one is liable for four cubits. This is the view of the Rashbam in Tosafot there and the Ramach. According to the Rambam, this has no relevance to the measurements of four handbreadths in a private domain, where the diagonal does not apply. Rabbeinu Tam holds that the diagonal is also necessary in this case, and we have already written about this in Siman 345, Section 12. In Eruvin there, it is explicitly understood that the reason is due to corners - "like this shall be the measurement for all who observe the Sabbath," as Rashi interprets there. The Rambam provides a different reason, which may be an explanation for the verse.

It has already been explained in Siman 347, Section 7, that a person's hand extended into another domain is considered as part of the domain where the hand is extended, and we do not say that the hand follows the body to be considered as part of the domain where the body is standing. Therefore, a person standing in the public domain can move items within the private domain by extending his hand as much as he wants, or a person standing in the private domain can move items within the public domain, taking from one place and putting it in another. Provided that he does not transfer [an item] four cubits, and if he transfers four cubits, he is liable. And in the beginning of Chapter 15 in the Rambam, it is written: "And if he takes it out, he is exempt, because he is in another domain." This is puzzling, what difference does it make that he is in another domain, since his hand is considered as the domain it is extended into. And if it is because he transfers it through his body, behold it is also established that he is liable, as the Rambam himself ruled at the end of Chapter 12, Law 14, and the Talmud in Eruvin (99a) compares this to it. And the Raavad has already challenged this, and the Maggid Mishneh wrote that it is an error, and found in some of his books the version 'liable'. (And according to this, it must be said, even though it is in another domain).

The previous law is from a Mishnah in Eruvin (98b). It also teaches there: "A person should not stand in a private domain and drink in a public domain, or stand in a public domain and drink in a private domain, unless he inserts his head and most of his body into the place from which he is drinking." It is proven in the Gemara that the reason for this is due to a decree lest he bring the vessel to himself in the domain in which he is standing, thereby transferring from one domain to another. The Talmud questions why the previous law did not decree this and how it permitted standing in one domain and moving objects in another domain without requiring the insertion of head and most of the body. The Talmud answers that, concerning items necessary for him, such as water or other beverages, they decreed lest he bring them in, unlike ordinary items as in the previous law, where they did not decree this. This applies between a private domain and a public domain or vice versa, but from either of them to a karmelit or from a karmelit to them—it is permitted to stand here and drink in the other domain by inserting just his head, even if he has not inserted most of his body. In a karmelit, they were not concerned lest he bring them to himself, because even if he does so, there is no Torah prohibition, and they did not decree one decree upon another. However, his head must be inserted into the place of his drinking because if not, it would be placed in his mouth while standing in the other domain, and he would be directly transferring from a public domain to a karmelit, or from a private domain to a karmelit, or vice versa.

And there are some of the poskim (halachic decisors) who explained that items which he needs are not only because of the beverage alone, for if it were solely for this reason, we would not be concerned lest he bring them to himself. Rather, it refers to fine vessels in which he also drinks; in this case, they decreed that he might bring them to himself. However, concerning fine vessels in which he does not drink, or if he drinks in vessels that are not fine, they were not concerned and did not decree, and it is sufficient for him to cover only his head and not his entire body, unless he drinks in fine vessels. And this is the opinion of the Rambam who wrote: "In what case are these words said? When he drinks in fine vessels, etc." See there. (And his reasoning appears to be, for if not, he would have said 'drinking is different.' And if it depends only on fine vessels, why did he depict it with drinking? Rather, certainly, we need both. And the first opinion is the opinion of Rashi, Tosafot, the Rosh, and the Tur, and according to their words, we can say that this is what we are saying, that items needed for him, like water or other items needed for him, and pay close attention).

And there is a question here: Why does the Talmud compare the second law to the first law, when in the second law one is required to insert his head and the majority of his body into the place where he drinks, since the liquids enter his intestines? And if the intestines were not in the domain where the water is, then he would be performing an uprooting in a private domain and placing in a public domain or vice versa. The answer to this is that if the liquids were to go straight to the intestines, it would not be difficult. However, the liquids are first in his mouth, and from his mouth they go down to the intestines, and the mouth is considered a neutral area (makom patur) that does not have a width of four handbreadths. This means there is an uprooting in a private domain and placing in a neutral area, and afterward an uprooting from a neutral area and placing in a public domain. And although it is initially forbidden to do so, as written in Siman 347, this is because we are concerned that perhaps he will not place it in the neutral area. But in drinking, it is impossible to be in any other manner. From this, the Talmud derives that the reason for the prohibition is only that he might bring them to himself, and therefore it questions what is the difference from the previous law. (Rashi, see there) And even though we do not consider his mouth a neutral area, since it is significant as written in Siman 347, paragraph 4, this is when his mouth is in the same place as his whole body. But here, where his mouth is in the place where he drinks and his body is in a different domain, his mouth is considered a neutral area (Rosh there, Siman 6) as will be explained.

Behold, that which we say 'one's intention designates a place' - the meaning is because that item is nullified to the domain it stands in, and it is considered as part of the domain itself which has a space of four [cubits]. And this applies to something that has no fixed place, such as a person, other living creatures, or portable vessels. But something that has a fixed place - we do not say that one's intention designates a place, because it is not nullified to the domain due to its fixed nature. Therefore, at the beginning of the chapter "HaZorek" we say, regarding those who weave large curtains who threw a shuttle in the curtain, and we ask, isn't it going to a place of exemption? Look there. And the difficulty is, doesn't one's intention designate a place? However, the answer is, since it is something fixed, this does not help as we have said. (Tosafot at the end of the chapter "HaZorek" s.v. "VeHotzi'u" and Maharsha there)

According to this, it is understood that if his mouth is in the same domain as his body - we rightly say that 'one's intention designates a place.' But when his mouth is in a different domain from his body, it is impossible to say that it is nullified to the place it is in, because the body which is in another domain does not allow it to be nullified to the domain where his mouth is, and thus it becomes a place of exemption. (This is the intention of the Rosh and see the commentary there) Therefore, regarding the law that one should not spit, it will be explained that 'one's intention designates a place,' because his mouth and body are in the same domain. (See Magen Avraham section 2) And even though, with his hand extended into another domain, we consider it as a space of four [cubits], even though his body is in another domain, as we wrote in section 347, his hand is different, as it is itself considered as four by four for the reason we explained there, and so our sages said (Shabbat 5a), "a person's hand is considered as four by four," and not because of 'one's intention designates a place.' (And the Magen Avraham section 2 makes this difficult and strives to differentiate because the object was in his hand previously, look there, and his words are perplexing, what is the relevance of this, examine it carefully) (See Tosafot Eruvin 20. And this is before we conclude that the hand is considered important).

And since a person stands in a private domain and transfers to a public domain or vice versa, therefore it is permissible to stand in a public domain and extend his hand into a private domain to take a key in order to open a door, and we do not worry that he might bring the key to himself. Similarly, when he wants to lock his house, he can go out to the public domain and lock his house with the key, and place the key somewhere in the private domain, and we do not worry that he might take it to carry it in the public domain. (And do not ask that in Siman 346, paragraph 10, we only permitted this in a karmelit, that is concerning bringing the key to himself, as explained there, but here it is only to lock and open and leave the key there.)

A person should not stand in a private domain and urinate into a public domain, nor stand in a public domain and urinate into a private domain, and similarly, one should not spit. If he urinates or spits, he is liable to bring a sin offering, since he has transferred from a private domain to a public domain or vice versa. Even though the place of the urine is not a space of four [handbreadths], and similarly, his mouth is not a space of four [handbreadths], his intention makes it a significant place, as stated in Siman 347, Se'if 4. Since his mouth and the place of the urine are in the place where his body stands, we say his intention makes it a significant place, as stated. Similarly, one should not stand in a karmelit (a semi-public domain) and urinate into a private domain or a public domain, or from them into a karmelit, for he is transferring from a karmelit to a private domain or public domain or vice versa. Even if he extends his mouth and member outside, it is forbidden to urinate or spit, for they have been detached from his body which stands in another domain. This is not comparable to drinking, where the item is placed in his mouth initially and then enters his intestines. But urine does not remain in the mouth of the member at all, rather it goes directly from his body outside, and similarly, spit. However, in this case, he is not liable to bring a sin offering since it is a matter unresolved in Eruvin (99a). Similarly, one walking in a public domain with spit collected in his mouth, some say he should not walk four cubits until he spits it out, since he needs to discard the spit, it is considered a burden. This is the opinion of the Tur. However, the Rambam in his commentary on the Mishnah there ruled that the law is not so, and similarly, the Ra'avad wrote there. It appears from the Talmud there that with phlegm and mucus, it is certainly forbidden when they are detached and placed in his mouth, as stated there. (However, this is not a complete proof, as there everything follows Rabbi Yehuda, and they ruled not in accordance with Rabbi Yehuda. Though phlegm and mucus are not mentioned in the Mishnah, who can say that the sages did not also dispute him in this case. Nevertheless, one should be stringent, since the Tur rules according to Rabbi Yehuda even regarding spit, and in the Shulchan Aruch this opinion is brought, certainly one should be cautious. However, in our regions where there is no public domain, perhaps all agree, and one should examine this carefully.)

The Tur and the Shulchan Aruch wrote: "A person should not stand in the public domain and extend his hand to a gutter, which is a long pipe placed along the length of the roof within three handbreadths of the roof, to receive water from it, because since it is within three handbreadths of the roof, it is considered as the roof. And it is forbidden - whether it is above ten handbreadths or below ten handbreadths. However, it is permitted to catch water from the air, even if his hand is within three handbreadths of the gutter. If the gutter protrudes three handbreadths from the roof, and likewise any pipe that protrudes three handbreadths, he can extend his hand to it and receive the water. This is as long as they do not have four handbreadths by four handbreadths, and they are below ten handbreadths. But if they have four handbreadths by four handbreadths, or even if they do not have four handbreadths by four handbreadths and they are above ten handbreadths - it is forbidden." End of quote. The explanation of the matter is as follows:

For the large gutter placed along the wall close to the roof, spanning the entire length of the roof, and it is less than three handbreadths from the roof, it is considered part of the roof and is a private domain. If one were to collect water from it, it would be akin to transferring from a private domain to a public domain or to a karmelit (an area that is neither fully private nor fully public). There is no difference whether the gutter is above ten handbreadths or below, since it carries the same status as the roof; therefore, even below ten handbreadths, it remains a private domain. This applies when one directly connects their hand to the gutter and collects the water, but if one does not connect their hand to it and instead collects the water from the airspace, they are not collecting from the private domain but from the airspace. If this airspace is above ten handbreadths, it is considered a place of exemption, and if it is below ten, it is a public domain, and one is transferring within the public domain over a distance of less than four cubits. Even collecting close to within three handbreadths of the gutter does not invoke the principle of 'lavud' (which treats spaces less than three handbreadths as if they are closed), and thus it is not considered as if collecting from the gutter itself, since in any case, one is not transferring directly from a private domain. Obligations for transferring only apply when one transfers directly from a private domain. (Taz, section 1) Some authorities forbid collecting within three handbreadths, considering it as if one is collecting directly from the roof. (ibid, in the name of the Ri) There is no distinction regarding the size of the gutter; whether it is less than ten handbreadths high and four handbreadths wide, it is forbidden to collect from it as it is considered part of the roof, but collecting from the airspace is permitted even if it is ten handbreadths high and four handbreadths wide.
