Similarly, water dripping directly from the roof may be collected from the airspace, whether it is above ten handbreadths or below, as the airspace above ten is a place of exemption, and below is a public domain or karmelit. (the Gra) Only within three handbreadths of the roof is forbidden according to those who prohibit it. (The opinion of those who prohibit is not brought in the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, see there).

And this is all when the gutter is close to the roof within three handbreadths. But if it is three handbreadths away from the roof, and similarly a pipe that extends three handbreadths from the roof - they do not have the status of a roof at all, and are considered a separate domain. Therefore, if they do not measure four by four handbreadths - it is a place of exemption, and one can extend their hand to it and take water. But if they measure four by four - it is considered a karmelit, and it is forbidden to receive from it if in front of it is a public domain. However, if in front of it is a karmelit, it is permitted. But when is it permitted, when it does not measure four by four and it is below ten handbreadths, but above ten - it is forbidden, even though above ten is also a place of exemption, nevertheless above ten we decree lest it be also four handbreadths wide and one will carry from it to the public domain, which would then be carrying from a private domain to a public domain. And it is possible that in a karmelit they did not decree in such cases, because it is like a decree upon a decree and requires further study, and one should deliberate on this.

And one should not ask, "Even if it is ten handbreadths high and four handbreadths wide, it should not be considered a private domain because it is in the air, and it would be like a 'partition that young goats can breach'." This can be explained by saying that since it is subordinate to the roof, even though it is three handbreadths away, it is nevertheless considered like the cavities of a private domain, which are deemed like the private domain itself. In the cavities of a private domain, the concept of 'young goats breaching' does not apply because it is subordinate to the private domain, as we explained in Siman 345. And know that all this follows the opinion of Rashi and Tosafot and their version in Eruvin (99b), but the Rif and the Rambam in Chapter 15, Law 3 have a different version, as will be explained with God's help.

And this is the language of the Rambam: "A person stands in a public domain and catches water from the air, from water flowing from a pipe or from a wall, and drinks, provided that he does not touch the pipe or the wall and catches from above them. If he touches — if the place he touched is above ten handbreadths and within three handbreadths from the roof — this is forbidden, because it is considered as if he uprooted from the roof, which is a private domain. Similarly, if the pipe is four by four (handbreadths), whether the pipe is within ten or above ten handbreadths, and he catches water from it — this is forbidden. And why is he not liable? Because the water did not come to rest, rather they are flowing and moving." End of quote. 

And it turns out that the Rambam disagrees with the approach of Rashi and Tosafot on three points: 
1. According to the Rambam, there is no biblical prohibition in any case, because the water does not come to rest.
2. Below ten handbreadths, it is permissible to combine, even within three handbreadths of the roof.
3. When the pipe does not measure four by four handbreadths, even above ten handbreadths, it is permissible to combine. 

I am astonished at our teacher the Beit Yosef for not bringing his words at all in the Shulchan Aruch. And perhaps for us, since we do not have a public domain, we can rely on the approach of the Rif and the Rambam and fulfill all opinions, with our pipes that run horizontally and vertically along the wall near the roof and the wall, as they are attached to the roof and wall, but at the end there is a protrusion. If the protrusion is three handbreadths long — it is permissible to place one's hand on it to receive the rainwater, and if it is not three handbreadths long — one should not place his hand, but rather keep it distant from it, and have his hand in the air opposite the mouth of the pipe, so that the water descends from the pipe into the air and from the air into his hand.

Maimonides wrote at the end of Chapter 15: "One who reads from a scroll in a karmelit, and part of the scroll rolls into the public domain while part remains in his hand—if it rolls out beyond four cubits, he should turn it over onto its writing and leave it there, as a precaution lest he drop the entire scroll from his hand and carry it four cubits. If it rolls within four cubits, he may roll it back to himself. Similarly, if it rolls into a private domain, he may roll it back to himself. If he was reading in a private domain and it rolls into the public domain, if it rests on the ground, he should turn it over onto its writing, but if it does not rest, rather it is hanging in the airspace of the public domain and has not reached the ground, he may roll it back to himself." End of quote.

Explanation of his words: Their books were made in a scroll form like our Torah scroll. If one was reading in a karmelit (an area that is not a public or private domain), such as on a threshold that is four handbreadths wide and not ten handbreadths high - if the end of the scroll rolled into the public domain at a distance of four cubits, even though if he were to bring it back to himself now there would be no carrying of four cubits in the public domain (since the first part of the scroll is still in his hand, and he is not carrying the whole scroll), nevertheless, they prohibited bringing it back, out of concern that he might drop the entire scroll from his hand and bring it back to himself, thus involving carrying four cubits in the public domain. However, within four cubits, even if he were to drop the entire scroll from his hand, it would only involve carrying from the public domain to a karmelit - they did not prohibit it when the first part of the scroll is still in his hand, due to the respect for holy writings. But for other items, it is prohibited even in such cases. (Maimonides in the name of the Rashba) And what should one do if he cannot bring it back to himself - he should turn it over on the writing, so it will not be so disrespectful. But if it rolled into a private domain - it is permitted, even beyond four cubits, because in a private domain there is no distinction. But if he was reading in a private domain, such as a threshold that is ten handbreadths high and four wide, or if he was sitting in his house or courtyard and it rolled into the public domain - even within four cubits, he should turn it over on the writing, because from domain to domain one does not need four cubits, and there is no permission to bring it back to himself, unless the other end has not yet rested on the ground but is still suspended in the air, then he may roll it back to himself because in such cases where there is no resting at all, even if he were to drop the entire scroll from his hand, he would not be liable. And even beyond four cubits in such cases - it is permitted, and we do not decree that he might drop the entire scroll from his hand and it will rest on the ground, because we do not issue two decrees. And it seems that if it has not rested, even for other objects it would be permitted.

The Rosh and the Tur wrote that if the first part of the scroll is still in his hand, even if it rolled outside of four cubits in the public domain while he is reading in the private domain, he can roll it back to himself if he is reading in a low place, such as on a threshold, even if it is ten handbreadths high and four handbreadths wide. Since the public domain passes in front of it and it is dragged to a place where many people tread, they did not decree concerning sacred writings in such cases, due to the disgrace of sacred writings. The Tur also wrote: "If he was reading from it on a roof and one end of it rolled out of his hand, if it did not reach the lower ten handbreadths close to the ground, he can roll it back to himself. If it reached the lower ten handbreadths, if the wall is sloped in such a way that it rests upon it, it is forbidden to roll it back to himself, and to avoid it being in a disgraceful state, he should turn it over onto the writing. If it is not sloped, as long as it has not reached the ground, he can roll it back to himself." This is when the sloped wall is considered a public domain, such as when many people lean on it. But if many people do not lean on it, and it is considered a karmelit, he can roll it back to himself. (Beit Yosef) And if it did not reach the lower ten handbreadths, even if it rests on a sloped wall, he can roll it back to himself, since it is a place of exemption. (ibid.) On this matter, the Rambam does not disagree; rather, he shortened the language, but the intention is the same, and they only disagreed on the previous matter. Our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, concluded according to the opinion of the Tur to permit this. (Since the Rif also holds this opinion, as the Beit Yosef wrote, and in our scrolls, these laws are not relevant at all, as it is obvious that in a Torah scroll, there is no way to read alone).

Two houses on two sides of a public domain: If one throws an object from one to the other above ten handbreadths, he is exempt, provided that both houses belong to one person or to two people who have made an eruv between them. And even though it is generally impossible to make an eruv when a public domain separates them, it can be said that this applies when the houses are at the edge of the public domain and their sides are adjacent to an alleyway that has been corrected, and each house has a door opening to the alleyway, in which case they can make an eruv. (Magen Avraham, Section 1) It is permitted to throw any item, even clothing and metal utensils that do not break. However, if the houses are not directly opposite each other, but one is higher and the other lower, it is initially forbidden to throw from one to the other, because since the throw is not level, we are concerned that the object might fall and he might come to carry it. It is only permitted to throw breakable items, such as earthenware and glass utensils, because if they fall to the ground, they will break and be of no use, and he will not come to carry them. And even though it is possible that they might not break, we are not concerned to such an extent. This applies specifically above ten handbreadths, which is considered an exempt space. However, below ten handbreadths, which is within the airspace of the public domain, it is initially forbidden to throw from a private domain to a private domain through the airspace of the public domain. This applies when the public domain passes between them, but if a karmelit (a semi-public domain) passes between them, it is permitted in any manner, because the Sages did not decree that he might come to carry, since even if he does carry, it would not be a Biblical prohibition. (See Magen Avraham at the beginning of Section 1, and there is a question about this since it refers to placing in an exempt space. See Eliyah Rabbah who challenges this, and the Taz resolves it there.)

Maimonides wrote in Chapter 15, Law 4: "A ledge in front of a window that extends into the airspace above a public domain, if it is above ten handbreadths - it is permitted to use it, as a public domain only extends up to ten handbreadths. Therefore, it is permitted to use the entire wall up to the lower ten handbreadths. In what case are these words stated? When there is one ledge extending into the airspace. But if there are two ledges extending from the wall, one below the other, even if both are above ten handbreadths, if the upper ledge in front of the window has a width of four by four [handbreadths] - it is forbidden to use it, because it is a domain unto itself, and the ledge below it is another domain, and they prohibit each other, as two domains cannot use one domain." End quote. 

It must be said that his intention is when the two ledges belong to two different people, and therefore they prohibit each other, because if they belong to one person, why should he not have control over both? And so wrote the Maggid Mishneh in the name of the Rashba. Even though there is a point to scrutinize here, for the ledge is certainly considered as the recesses of a private domain, why should one prohibit the other? It can be said that since they are exposed to each other without partitions, they prohibit each other (see Lechem Mishneh), even if the lower ledge does not have a width of four by four (Maggid Mishneh). The prohibition specifically applies to utensils that rested inside the house, as will be explained in Siman 372 (there), and it will be explained later that a ledge of four handbreadths is considered a domain unto itself, and is not called the recesses of a private domain.

And if neither the upper nor the lower has four [handbreadths] - both can use it. (Thus in the Rambam) The reason is that a domain that does not have four [handbreadths] does not qualify to be called an exclusive domain, since it lacks significance. Only if one has four [handbreadths], then the designation of ownership also applies to the other, even if it does not have four [handbreadths], because by virtue of one being called an exclusive domain, the other is also called such. The rationale is correct, for one that does not have four [handbreadths] is forbidden to use the ledge that has four [handbreadths], and consequently, he can also prevent the other from using his ledge. However, if neither has four [handbreadths], both can use the ledges and the entire wall up to ten handbreadths from the bottom as stated.

And he further wrote: "If the lower one has four [handbreadths] and the upper one does not have four, one may only use the upper one corresponding to its window alone. But regarding the rest of the ledge on both sides of the window - it is forbidden to use, because the one below it has made a separate domain for itself." End of quote. The reason why it is permissible to use the area corresponding to the window, it appears to me, is because it is considered like the holes of a private domain, meaning it is secondary to the window. But when it has four [handbreadths], it is not secondary to the window, and it is forbidden to use even the area corresponding to the window, if they prohibit each other. (So it seems to me according to the opinion of the Rambam). And from his words, it is implied that the ledges prohibit each other, even if they are not directly opposite each other. And the opinion of the Rashba is that they only prohibit each other if they are directly opposite each other. (Maggid Mishneh). And the Rashba also disagrees with the permission to use the area corresponding to the window. (As mentioned in the Maggid Mishneh, see there).

He further wrote: "Any projection extending into the airspace of a public domain, where it is permissible to use it, when one uses it, one may only place or take from it earthenware and glass vessels or similar items, because if they fall into the public domain, they will break. However, other utensils and foods are prohibited." This is the end of his words. From the generality of his language, it implies that this applies even to a projection that is four handbreadths wide, and this is also the opinion of Rashi (Eruvin 98b). The Tosafot questioned this, arguing that if so, even if it is much wider, one should not use utensils that do not break. It seems to me that the prohibition applies only when it is called a "projection," and if it is very wide, it is not called a projection but rather a board or a bridge. It appears to me that this is the opinion of our Rabbi, the Rema, in section 3, where he wrote: "Specifically a projection or something similar, but if it is something wide like a roof where the user stands with the utensil, it is permitted to use all utensils." This is the end of his words. The opinion of the Tosafot and the Rosh is that with a projection that is four handbreadths wide, it is permitted to use all utensils. (And the Rema did not intend this, for if so, he would have said 'a projection that is four handbreadths wide,' but rather as he wrote, 'much wide' and extending from it is a projection).

And all this applies to projections extending into the public domain. But projections extending into a karmelit, if there is no division of domains or a single projection extending over the airspace of a karmelit, as long as it is ten tefachim high, which is always considered an exempt area - it is permitted to use it, whether it is wide or narrow, and even for items that are not fragile, because they did not decree regarding a karmelit. Therefore, in our location where there is no public domain, it is permitted to use the projections. And we have already explained that if they do not measure four by four tefachim, they do not create a division of domains, and most of our projections do not measure four by four. (See Magen Avraham, subsection 4, who questions what is written above regarding above ten tefachim, for regardless, if the window is open to them, even below ten tefachim it is considered as the cavities of a private domain. And if the window is not open to them, even above ten tefachim it is considered a karmelit, as stated in Siman 345, section 17. And his intention is to what is written there that there are no cavities in a karmelit. In my humble opinion, it is not difficult at all, for a projection of four by four is not considered as the cavities of a private domain, but as a domain in its own right. And since it is not ten tefachim high, and stands above ten tefachim in the public domain or in a karmelit - it is an exempt area. And when it does not measure four, it is called 'cavities' only opposite the window, as we have said. But not when it is not opposite the window, and this is evident from the words of the Rambam, and consider this well.)

A pit in the public domain that is adjacent to a private domain, and the pit is ten handbreadths deep and four handbreadths wide — it is permitted to carry from it to the private domain, as one is carrying from one private domain to another private domain. And this is not noteworthy at all, rather, even if the pit is not right next to the private domain, if it is not four handbreadths away — it is permitted to carry from it to the private domain, and it is permitted to draw water from it to bring inside, even though the public domain separates them. However, since the area is not four handbreadths wide, and it is between the pit and the public domain, it is not convenient for the public to use that space, and since it is less than four handbreadths — it is considered a place of exemption. But when there is an area of four handbreadths between them, that area is considered a public domain, and it is initially forbidden to carry from one private domain to another private domain through the public domain. And only because of the disrespect to sacred writings did we permit it in such cases, as discussed in Siman 352 (see Beit Yosef and Taz), but not for other matters, because there is concern that it might fall in the public domain and one might come to carry it (there).

And there is no permissibility in these manners, except that one makes a rim around the pit, such that the rim is ten handbreadths high, and the bucket goes from one private domain to another private domain through an exempt place, since above ten handbreadths is considered an exempt place. Some say that this is specifically when the pit stands opposite the private domain, on the side of the other street. But if they are on the same level, there is a Torah prohibition in passing from one private domain to another private domain through a public domain, even above ten handbreadths, as it is written in Siman 346, Section 3, see there. (Magen Avraham, Subsection 3) And this does not follow the method we explained there, that passing is specifically to his fellow, see there. According to this, when bringing water to the private domain, one must bring it through a window that is ten handbreadths high.

And know, that the requirement that the rim itself must be ten [handbreadths] high is so that the drawing of the bucket will be through a height of more than ten [handbreadths], as has been stated. However, concerning the requirement for the pit to be considered a private domain, even if the pit itself is not ten [handbreadths] deep but combined with the rim it is, the pit is considered a private domain. And so it is said in the Gemara (Shabbat 99a): "A pit and its rim combine to ten [handbreadths]." And even though outside the pit the rim is considered a carmelit when it is not ten [handbreadths] high, nevertheless, within the pit it is a private domain, and one who draws water from it to the public domain is liable, even though the bucket is held in his hand, because the water was indeed removed from a private domain and placed in a public domain.

A garbage heap in the public domain that is ten handbreadths high and four handbreadths wide: if it belongs to the public, it is permitted to throw onto it from a private domain that is very close to it, even within ten handbreadths and even if it is somewhat distant, provided there are not four handbreadths, as is stated regarding a pit. If it is four handbreadths away, one must throw through a window above ten handbreadths, and we are not concerned that it might roll from the heap into the public domain and one might come to carry it, because it is not customary to throw anything onto a garbage heap except for disgusting items and things that are of no use at all, like broken pieces of vessels and the like. However, if the garbage heap belongs to an individual, it is forbidden to throw onto it, because an individual’s garbage heap is intended to be cleared, and out of habit, people might come to throw and pour even after the heap has been removed, resulting in carrying from a private domain to a public domain. It appears that nowadays, when the government is strict about not having garbage in the public domain and forces people to remove it, it is obvious that it is also forbidden for public garbage heaps.

The Sages taught in the Mishnah of Eruvin (7:1): "A balcony that is above the water - one may not draw water from it on Shabbat, unless they made a partition ten handbreadths high for it, either above or below." 

And this is its explanation: Behold, seas and rivers are considered a karmelit, as stated in Siman 345. Consequently, it is forbidden to draw water from the river passing by the wall of a house, where there is a window in the wall, and to bring the water into the house through the window, because one would be transferring from a karmelit to a private domain. 

And if there is a balcony projecting from the wall by the window, which is a board or structure extending over the water, and if it were not by the window, it would also be a karmelit (as per Magen Avraham 1) if it is four handbreadths wide, and it is permitted to transfer from it to the water, and certainly if it is not four handbreadths wide, it would be a makom patur (an exempt area). 

However, now, when it is by the window and one makes use of it from the window, it is considered like the holes of a private domain, and its law is like that of a private domain. Therefore, it is forbidden to transfer from it to the water and from the water to it. And certainly, if it itself is ten handbreadths high and four handbreadths wide, it is itself a private domain. But most often, the balcony is not ten handbreadths high, and it is considered a private domain only because of the window.

And the sages said, how should one act to permit drawing water from it and bringing it into the house through the window? They instructed to make a barrier ten handbreadths high around the balcony, or to make an opening in the balcony of four by four handbreadths, for less than this is not effective, because any barrier that is less than four handbreadths in length and width is not considered a barrier. The reason is simple: a barrier needs to create a domain, and less than four handbreadths is considered an exempt area. It is commonly stated by the decisors that there is no barrier less than four handbreadths. Consequently, when they make such a barrier ten handbreadths high and four handbreadths wide, the entire area becomes a private domain, including the water that is against the barrier, and it is permitted to transfer from it and draw water through the balcony into the house through the window, as one is transferring from a private domain to a private domain.

If you ask, how can the water beneath the partition be considered a private domain, since any partitions that do not reach the ground within three handbreadths are considered a partition through which goats can pass, and are therefore not considered a partition? Especially here, where the partition is much higher than the water. However, in truth, regarding this matter, the Sages said (Eruvin 86b): "The Sages were lenient with water, allowing a suspended partition to permit." Since it is impossible to make a partition that reaches the ground beneath the water, they were lenient to allow just a partition of ten handbreadths in height, even if the partition is suspended in the air. Since a karmelit is a rabbinic domain, they (the Sages) made the prohibition against carrying from a karmelit to a private domain, and they also permitted it through a suspended partition.

And this is what we have learned in our Mishnah: "whether above or below," and Rashi explained - 'above' means literally above, above the opening of the balcony, 'and below' means below the opening of the balcony. And the reason is simple, for even if it is made below, it is also far from the water, but we say 'extend and lower the partition,' and we see it (as if) the partition reaches down to the end of the water. If so, even if it is made on the balcony, what of it? Indeed, in such cases, we can also say 'extend and lower the partition,' since we permit a suspended partition over water. However, the Rambam did not explain it this way, but rather 'above' means below the balcony according to Rashi's explanation of 'below,' and 'below' means below on the water opposite the opening of the balcony, and we say 'extend and raise the partition' (and as if) the partitions rise up to the balcony, and the Tur and Shulchan Aruch wrote according to Rashi, see there.

And they further wrote that since they made a partition, it is also permitted to pour from it, meaning to pour the waste water from the house into the hole of the balcony. This has even more of a novelty than drawing water, for the waste water is poured with force and falls into the water opposite the balcony, and inevitably spreads out over the water far from the place of the balcony. Nevertheless, this is not like pouring from a private domain into a karmelit, for he is not directly pouring into the karmelit, but rather into the private domain, and only through his force does it end up in the karmelit, and they did not decree against his force in the karmelit (Shabbat 100a). And some wrote that even though it is close to a puddle, which is a public domain, it is permitted since his intention is not to pour out (Magen Avraham 4, Eliyahu Rabbah 2, and Tosefet Shabbat 4). And indeed, this is implied by Rashi and Tosafot in Eruvin (88a, "there" and Tosafot "these"), but it is not understood what benefit there is if his intention is not to pour out, since it is a definite outcome (psik reisha). It is necessary to say that it is not a definite outcome, as it is possible that it will not flow out. However, from the words of the Rambam in Chapter 15, Law 15, who explained this law, it is clearly as we have said, for he wrote: "And just as they draw water, so too they pour, for they are pouring into the karmelit" (end quote). And the Magid Mishneh wrote that this is because they did not decree against his force in the karmelit, and so too wrote the Ritva in Eruvin there in the name of his teachers.

And there is a significant question to ask regarding this fundamental law: How can we say that the water opposite the balcony is considered a private domain? After all, this water beneath the balcony is connected to the water beyond the balcony, which is a karmelit (a semi-public domain), and they mix completely without any separation between them. Therefore, the water beneath the balcony is fully open to the karmelit, meaning the water beyond the balcony, and open to a prohibited area. The answer to this is that this is also one of the leniencies that the sages applied to water, not to be concerned with their mixture or with the interruption of their partition. It suffices with what we say, "extend and lower the partition," and it is as if the partition descends to the depths. The reason for this, it seems to me, is that even if a partition of iron were made down to the ground beneath the water, it would be impossible for the water not to enter beneath it. (Rashi Eruvin 48a, s.v. 'partition') According to this, it is impossible to distinguish between waters that they should not mix with each other, and therefore a partition of ten handbreadths in any form suffices. (See Tosafot Eruvin 12b, s.v. 'here', and this is what we learned in the Tosefta of Eruvin at the end of chapter 6: "A balcony... unless they made for it a partition of ten handbreadths below the water, even though the water floats atop it, etc." See there, and it argues with the Mishnah. However, we brought it concerning the mixture of waters, that we are not concerned, and this is a fundamental principle in all laws of water partitions).

For those traveling by ship, the sages were even more lenient. This is because the ship is considered a private domain, being ten handbreadths high and four handbreadths wide, while the sea and the river are classified as a karmelit (a semi-public domain). If we were to demand that they make a partition like that of a balcony, it would be impossible, as one cannot do on a ship what one does at home. Therefore, the sages said (Shabbat 100b) that one makes a space of four by four handbreadths and draws water from there. This means attaching a board of four by four handbreadths to the outside of the ship, making a hole in it, and drawing water through that hole. There is no need to make partitions; rather, we say "bend the sides and consider the partition as if it descends ('gud achit mechitzta')"—meaning, we view it as if the sides are bent into partitions. The Rambam, at the end of Chapter 15, states: "A person should not draw water from the sea while inside the ship unless he has made a space of four by four handbreadths extending from the ship over the sea." The Beit Yosef added the expression "bend and consider" (kof vegud) there.

In my humble opinion, this language is not precise. If we need to say 'bend and extend,' then we would require that the board be large enough in length and width to be suitable for bending on all sides to a height of ten handbreadths for the partitions and four by four in the middle. It would need to be twenty-four handbreadths by twenty-four handbreadths—twenty handbreadths for both sides regarding 'bend,' and four in the middle. And indeed, this is found in Eruvin there, in the case of the balcony, where Rabbi Chananiah ben Akavia disagrees and holds that partitions are not required and instead we say 'bend and extend.' He says that a balcony that is four cubits by four cubits—one carves out four by four and fills it in. And four cubits are twenty-four handbreadths, and here we only require a board of four handbreadths by four handbreadths. Indeed, none of the decisors mentioned this language of 'bend,' because the sages were lenient in this matter, and this is what we said that the language of 'bend' is not precise and not specifically required.

Indeed, this is the Rambam's opinion, but the Tur wrote: "Similarly, one who is on a boat can only draw water if he makes a board four by four [tefachim] and surrounds it with partitions, makes a hole in it, and draws water through there." This is the opinion of Rashi and Tosafot in Shabbat, except that Rashi did not require partitions of ten [tefachim]. And this is Rashi's language there: "A place of four - a space of four [tefachim] surrounded by small partitions, and a suspended partition permits in water." From his language, it is proven that small partitions are sufficient, as long as there is a semblance of partitions. And in similar language, the Ran writes there in the name of the Gaon, and this is his language: "This place of four, we carve around the hollow like a kind of partition, like a basket whose bottom has been removed, and draw water through that hole, and we say 'Gud Achit' with these partitions, even though they are not ten [tefachim]." And our teachers, the Tosafot, wrote there that partitions of ten are required. Similarly, the Rosh wrote there, and this is the opinion of the Tur. It is astonishing that our teachers, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, did not bring these opinions at all, for although this is a Rabbinic matter, since most of our teachers disagree with the Rambam, they should have ruled like them or at least mentioned their opinion, and this requires investigation.

All of this applies if the ship is moving in deep water, such that from the surface of the water to the top of the ship's side, there are ten handbreadths, which would be considered as the airspace of a karmelit (a rabbinic public domain). But if there are ten handbreadths remaining, and it turns out that the bucket is above ten handbreadths, which is a makom patur (an exempt area), it has already been clarified that the airspace of a karmelit does not extend beyond ten handbreadths. Therefore, there is no need for any correction according to the law, since one is drawing water from a karmelit to the private domain via a makom patur. However, earlier in Siman 346, Se'if 8, we explained that even when standing in a makom patur, some hold that it is forbidden to transfer from one domain to another, even in rabbinic domains. And certainly, if one is standing on the ship and transferring from the sea, which is a karmelit, to the ship, which is a private domain. This is what the Sages said in Shabbat there: to extend even a small ledge and draw water, meaning that the ledge serves merely as a sign, and through this, they permitted one to draw water from the sea to the ship via a makom patur, even not in the place of the ledge. They were lenient in this due to the difficulty, since he is not in his home. And our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote: "Extend even a small ledge, make a hole in it, and draw water through there." (This is his exact language). They critiqued him, as it is clear that it is permissible to draw water anywhere in the ship (Taz, Se'if Katan 5, Bach, and similarly, the Magen Avraham in Se'if Katan 4, and the Eliyah Rabbah in Se'if Katan 6, and the Tosefet Shabbat in Se'if Katan 7). And even if one fills the bucket and carries it along the side of the ship to the top, which would be considered like placing it in a makom patur, this is a complete permission, but in any case, we need the sign of the ledge. (And this is the intention of Rashi there, and see Magen Avraham Se'if Katan 7, and examine carefully).

And one may pour on the sides of the ship from the outside and they descend into the sea, for he is pouring on the ship, and this is completely permissible. And what descends to the sea is due to his force, and it has already been explained that they did not decree against one's force in a karmelit (a type of domain). Similarly, one can throw bones and peels on the side of the ship from the outside for the reason that has been explained. But to throw directly into the sea is forbidden, even if it is above ten handbreadths, for from a private domain to a karmelit via a place of exemption, it is forbidden to throw. And know that a small ship whose walls are not ten handbreadths high is considered a karmelit if its width is four handbreadths, and it is permitted to move directly from it into the sea or river and from them into it, since both are karmelit, but only within four cubits as is the rule of karmelit, and this is obvious. (Magen Avraham, Section 6)

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote in Section 1: "Two ships next to each other - it is forbidden to transfer items from one to the other, unless they are tied together or they are at least ten handbreadths above the water. And they need to make an eruv (joining of domains) together if they belong to two different people." His words seem to mean that, as stated in the Mishna in Shabbat (100:), "Ships that are tied together - one can transfer items from one to the other. If they are not tied together, even if they are enclosed, one cannot transfer items from one to the other." The Gemara concludes that this refers to the laws of eruv: when they are tied together, the eruv is effective, but if they become untied, the eruv is nullified, which is when the ships belong to different people. Rambam wrote this law concerning eruv at the end of Chapter 3 of Eruvin, and it seems that when the ships belong to one person, this law does not apply. (This is also explicitly stated in Magen Avraham, Section 9.) Therefore, this law does not apply here, and Rema comes to clarify that even if the ships belong to one person, it is forbidden to transfer items from one to the other if they are not tied together, even though it is transferring from one private domain to another private domain. The reason is that the item might fall into the water, and one might transfer it from a private domain to a karmelit (a semi-public domain), which is forbidden. (Tosafot there, 101:, s.v. 'Peshita') Also, because they are likely to drift apart, the airspace of a karmelit would separate them. (Elya Rabba, Section 9, in the name of Ravyah and Pri Megadim) This is what Rema means by "Two ships... it is forbidden to transfer, etc.," meaning even if they belong to one person, unless they are tied together or are above ten handbreadths, transferring through a place exempt from carrying rules. He then says they need an eruv if they belong to two people, and the eruv is only effective if they are tied together. (If they become untied on Shabbat, there is a dispute whether we say "since it was permitted, it remains permitted," as Magen Avraham mentioned, and this will be explained in Siman 374, with God's help. Additionally, even when tied, there should not be more than four handbreadths between them.)

It is stated in the Talmud, Shabbat 101a: "These Misha eggs" - small boats that are narrow at the bottom up to the edge of a knife, one may not carry within them except within four cubits. This means that even if they are ten handbreadths high and four wide at the top, since they are narrow at the bottom, their partitions are not considered partitions and their status is like a karmelit (an area that is neither a private domain nor a public domain). This applies only when there are not four handbreadths within three handbreadths from the bottom, meaning that until the height of three handbreadths, there is not a width of four handbreadths. But if within less than three handbreadths there are four handbreadths, meaning that until the height of three handbreadths there is a width of four handbreadths, it is not a problem, and it is considered a private domain. And if one fills it with reeds and willow branches - it is not a problem, meaning that if one places reeds and thin willow branches inside the narrow part and nullifies them there, we do not consider the narrow part, even if it is three handbreadths high or more, and we consider it based on the wider part. And if it is ten handbreadths high - it is considered a private domain, and this is according to Rashi's explanation. The Tosafot question this, arguing that if due to the narrow part it loses the status of a private domain, then it should also lose the status of a karmelit, as a karmelit cannot be less than four handbreadths, and it should be considered a makom patur (an exempt area), as the Rashba also questions there. The Rif, Rambam, Rosh, Tur, and Shulchan Aruch did not mention this at all, indicating that they do not agree with Rashi but rather with Tosafot, who explain that these are boats made with hollow sections filled with water, and naked people sit in them there, and this is not common among us, so they did not need to mention it. But according to Rashi's explanation, it is very common among us, as the small boats that stand on the banks of the rivers are made in this way, very narrow at the bottom. Therefore, if they are not ten handbreadths high with a width of four - they are considered a karmelit. But if they are ten handbreadths high with a width of four - they are considered a private domain, and we do not consider the narrow part. (And I am astonished at the Gra in section 7 who wrote this law according to Rashi's explanation, as the Tosafot and all the poskim disagree with this, and the law follows the majority, especially in rabbinic matters, as mentioned there).

A toilet that stands over water and is a private domain, and when one goes there to relieve oneself, the waste falls directly from the private domain into a karmelit (semi-public domain). The partitions of the toilet itself do not help in this matter because, although partitions generally do not need to be made for a specific purpose, here the partitions are not complete but suspended. The Sages only permitted partitions that were made specifically for this purpose. Therefore, one should make partitions of ten tefachim (handbreadths) around the toilet for this purpose, and the water that is opposite the partitions is also considered a private domain, and it is permissible to go there to relieve oneself. If one makes a board or a rod within three tefachim of the hole, so that the waste falls on it before it falls into the water, no special permission is needed because the board is considered like an extension of the private domain, and what falls from there into the water is considered an indirect action, and indirect actions in a karmelit were not prohibited, as mentioned. The same law applies if the setup is such that the waste falls on a wall and from there into the water; this is also permissible for the same reason. Regarding the permission with the board mentioned, even if the board breaks on Shabbat, it is still permitted because human dignity is great, which overrides a rabbinic prohibition, as mentioned in Siman 312 regarding moving stones for wiping, see there.

In ancient times, the latrines were situated outside the city walls, and there was a large trench surrounding the city that was more than two seahs in area, which is considered a karmelit. Waste would fall there. Now, not only do the walls of the latrine itself not help, as they do not work even for water as we have stated, but even creating hanging partitions for the latrine does not help, as a hanging partition is only permitted for water. Therefore, it is prohibited to relieve oneself there on Shabbat. However, the leniency of the board that we mentioned is effective here as well, as rabbinic decrees were not applied with the same stringency in all karmelits. If the latrine is more than ten handbreadths high, some say that nothing is needed, as one is transferring from a private domain to a karmelit through an exempt place, and in Siman 346 there is a dispute about this. Some also say that if there was excrement there before Shabbat, it is completely permissible when relieving oneself on the excrement, as it is an exempt place since the public does not tread there, and even though it later falls into the water, it is considered indirect action as we mentioned. However, in Siman 345, it is explained that some hold there is no exempt place in a karmelit, and certainly if the excrement is within the partitions of the latrine, which is a private domain, all agree that there is no exempt place in a private domain as explained there. Therefore, this leniency does not apply.

And since there is no exempt area within a private domain, therefore, a restroom that stands between two houses belonging to two different people who did not make an eruv together - it is prohibited to relieve oneself there, as its status is like a karmelit. One must make the necessary correction as explained regarding the board, so that if the excrement falls on the ground, it is considered as if one exerted force in a karmelit, and it is permitted, since a courtyard that is not joined by an eruv is not better than a karmelit. All this applies only initially, but after the fact - it is permitted to relieve oneself there, because the honor of human beings is great, as stated. And those who travel by ship customarily relieve themselves from the oar into the sea or river, since the oar is not ten handbreadths high, even though it is four handbreadths wide - it is only a karmelit, and one is transferring from one karmelit to another karmelit. We hold that it is permitted to transfer from one type of karmelit to another type of karmelit, unlike the Jerusalem Talmud in the eleventh chapter of Shabbat, as stated in section 346, clause 9.

Our Rabbi, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 4: "Water that is not ten tefachim deep does not have the status of water to permit pouring into it with a suspended partition. All the more so if the water has dried up, even though it was once ten tefachim deep." End quote. The leading later authorities disagree with him based on the words of the Tosafot in Shabbat (100b, s.v. 'oseh'), from which it is clear that it is effective (see there). (Bach and Magen Avraham, subparagraph 16)

In my humble opinion, the words of our Rabbi, the Beit Yosef, are correct. The Tosafot only wrote regarding a river or the sea, where it certainly works, even in a place that is not ten tefachim deep, because it is impossible to separate them from each other, and immediately it will be ten tefachim deep, as is the nature of rivers and seas. But our Rabbi, the Beit Yosef, intended it for a mere puddle, where since it is not ten tefachim deep, why should we permit a suspended partition? After all, it is possible to extend it to the ground, which is not the case with seas and rivers. (And with this, the proof of the Magen Avraham from the case of the ledge is also resolved, see there and scrutinize.)

Two balconies from which water is drawn – if they are one above the other, even if they are significantly elevated from each other, if they are precisely aligned, such that the residents of the upper balcony cannot draw water unless the bucket passes through the lower balcony, if both have partitions of ten handbreadths – then both are considered a private domain, and their domain extends up to the sky according to the law of a private domain, and both are prohibited from drawing water unless they made an eruv, for each prohibits the other. The lower balcony prohibits the upper one, as its domain extends up to the sky and enters the domain of the upper one. And the upper one prohibits the lower one since it has usage through the lower one against its will, as it dominates there. Therefore, if they are separated from each other by the width of the wall more than four handbreadths – they have no connection with each other, and each uses its own space. And even though the upper one extends through the lower one, nevertheless, since the usage is by throwing the bucket through an airspace of four handbreadths, which is a usage by force, and in the air, one does not prohibit another through an airspace of four handbreadths, because it is not a convenient usage, and it is not considered as having control over the lower domain, and the lower one certainly has no connection with the upper one.

And if they are slightly separated from each other, such that there is not a continuation of four handbreadths, it does not matter how high one is from the other, whether there are ten handbreadths from one to the other or not. If each one made a partition for himself, one does not prohibit the other, since each can use his own without the other's. Therefore, even if one uses the other’s partition, it does not matter, because even on a weekday he can object to it, and all the more so on Shabbat. Therefore, even if he does not object, it does not concern us. The reason we needed to provide in the previous section that a person does not prohibit another through airspace is just an additional preference, and it is not necessary for this, for as long as each one made for himself, and they are not directly one under the other, they have no connection to each other when each one made for himself.

But if they made a partition in the upper one in partnership, and in the lower one they did not make any partition at all - both are forbidden to draw water through the hole until they make an eruv, since the partition belongs to both of them, and they are within four handbreadths of each other, which prohibits through such an airspace. And even though in height, the upper one is higher than the lower one by ten handbreadths, and the lower one needs to use it by throwing upwards and lowering downwards, which is obviously not a convenient use, nevertheless it prohibits, as will be explained in Siman 375, that only through an airspace of four handbreadths does it not prohibit, but through throwing and lowering it does prohibit.

And in the lower one – it is obvious that they are forbidden, since it does not have partitions. All the more so if they made a partition for the lower one from both of them, where the upper domain also exercises control over it, as its use is only through lowering, which is an easy usage. This is the case when they made it in the lower one and not in the upper one, but if they also made it in the upper one, even if both projections were made through partnership, nevertheless, since each one has a place to use his own, he does not have the power to forbid his fellow. And what they made in partnership is not in order to forbid him, but to ease the carrying, as it is cheaper to make for two than for one, and each one uses his own. All the more so if each one made for himself, they have no connection to each other, as I have written (all this is from Levush, see there).

It is taught in Eruvin (7:1): “A water channel that passes through a courtyard – one may not draw water from it on Shabbat unless a partition ten handbreadths high is made at both its entrance and exit.” The explanation is that the water channel extends from afar and passes through the courtyard from one side and exits through the other side, continuing further. Therefore, if it is ten handbreadths deep and four handbreadths wide, it is not nullified in relation to the courtyard, unlike other objects in the courtyard which are considered as a private domain, as mentioned in Siman 345, because this is only if it does not have an external connection. Hence, its status is like that of a karmelit, and it is forbidden to carry and draw water from it into the courtyard and from the courtyard into it. However, if it is not ten handbreadths deep or not four handbreadths wide, it is not significant, even though it is connected to the outside, and it is nullified in relation to the courtyard, and its status is that of a private domain. Similarly, with the correction that will be explained, it separates what is in the courtyard from what is outside it.

The correction is to make a partition of ten [handbreadths] at the entrance and exit, which means either nine handbreadths outside the water and one handbreadth within the water, or nine within the water and one above the water, in order to separate between water and water. And even though in the previous section regarding the balcony, we did not require even that the partition be close to the water, and certainly not within the water, why do we require here that part of the partition be within the water? It is not similar, for we have already explained there that the permission of a suspended partition in water requires a distinction that it was made for the purpose of allowing [the carrying]. Therefore, the partitions of the privy do not help, as explained there. According to this, it makes sense: regarding the balcony, where the partitions are around the hole of the balcony from which water is drawn, everyone sees that the partition is made for the purpose of allowing [the carrying], and therefore it does not need to reach the water, and certainly not within the water, because partitions do not help for the essence of the water, as they mix from below. However, regarding the actual water passing through the courtyard, if a partition is made above the water, there will be no distinction, for these are the partitions of the courtyard like all courtyards. Therefore, it is required that part of the partition be within the water, to make it recognizable that it was made for the purpose of allowing [the carrying]. (I learned this from Rashi’s words there in the commentary 'They made' as explained there).

And know, in this ruling there is no difference whether the stream of water enters the courtyard with a width of ten cubits or less, and whether it enters fully, meaning that no part of the courtyard's walls remain on the side, or whether it does not enter fully, and some parts of the walls remain and it is less than ten cubits wide. In any case, it is forbidden to draw water from it into the courtyard. And do not ask why it will be explained in this section, in the language of the sea entering the courtyard, that it is only forbidden to draw water from it into the courtyard if the breach is more than ten cubits, or if it enters fully, but otherwise it is permitted to draw water from it into the courtyard - it is not similar, because there the breach is only on one side of the courtyard, and it is judged like all breaches, where less than ten cubits and remaining sidewalls are considered like a doorway and do not prohibit. This is not the case with a stream of water that flows through the courtyard from both sides, and it is evident to all that it flows from a distance from both sides, and it is considered by itself, and we cannot judge it as a doorway, since it is open from side to side. Therefore, even if it is less than ten cubits and does not enter fully - it is forbidden to draw water from it into the courtyard. (I learned this from the words of the Ritva) Nevertheless, when it is not ten handbreadths deep or not four handbreadths wide - it is not considered significant, and it is nullified to the courtyard as stated. (there)

If the water channel enters the courtyard with a width of less than three handbreadths - no correction is needed, (Ritva) as anything less than three is considered as if it were closed. And even if it enters in several places, as long as in each place it is less than three handbreadths - it is not considered significant. Therefore, even if one started to make partitions on each side but did not complete them, leaving them unconnected in the middle to allow the water to enter and exit through that space, if there is less than three handbreadths between them - it is permitted, but if there are three handbreadths - it is forbidden. Likewise, initially, it is forbidden if the gap is more than three handbreadths. And even though less than four handbreadths is not considered a significant space, nonetheless, if the channel itself is four handbreadths wide and ten handbreadths deep, the breach is forbidden even if it is less than four handbreadths. (And in Taz, subparagraph 4, it is written that if the width is four, partitions are needed, which is perplexing, and perhaps it is a printing error, and it should say three, as the Pri Megadim wrote).

And know, all of this is regarding carrying water from the water channel. But for the water channel to prohibit the entire courtyard from carrying within it - it does not prohibit. And it is not only in a case where it is less than ten [cubits] and there are still walls remaining, but even if it is breached more than ten [cubits], or if it is fully breached - it does not prohibit, because since the water channel is ten [handbreadths] deep and four [handbreadths] wide as mentioned, the water channel itself automatically becomes a partition. (Magen Avraham, section 2, in the name of the Raavad) And even if at its beginning it is not ten [handbreadths] deep, if it rises to ten within four [handbreadths] - it is a partition, but if not - it prohibits when it is more than ten [cubits], or fully breached. (ibid.)

The Tur and Shulchan Aruch wrote in Section 2: "A courtyard that was breached, and a river passes through the breach, if it is not entirely breached and the breach is not more than ten [cubits] - it is permitted to draw water from it and bring it into the house. If it was entirely breached, or if the breach is more than ten [cubits], if there remains at the place of the breach a ten [cubits] high embankment and the water covers it - it is permitted to draw water from it in the courtyard, but it is forbidden to bring it into the house, unless they made a ten [cubits] high partition on the water. If no embankment remains - it is forbidden even to draw water in the courtyard." End quote.

Explanation of the matter: When a courtyard is breached on one side and a tongue of the sea enters it, if it is less than ten handbreadths and not in its entirety, it is considered an entrance, and the water that enters is like a pit in the courtyard. The walls of the courtyard divide it from the sea water before the courtyard, and it is not similar to a stream that is breached from two directions, as it was explained. However, if the breach is more than ten handbreadths or in its entirety, it completely prohibits the courtyard, even to carry within it, since it is breached to a prohibited area. But if ten handbreadths of the walls remain and are visible, it is completely permitted, both to carry in the courtyard and to draw water from the sea to bring into the house, since there is a complete partition. If these remaining walls are not visible and the water passes over them, it is permitted to fill water in the courtyard because it is considered a partition even though it is covered, since sometimes the water will recede, revealing the partitions. However, to bring the water into the house is forbidden, because in the house the partitions are not visible at all. Nonetheless, if the tongue of the sea is ten handbreadths deep, it does not prohibit carrying in the courtyard, as it is considered a partition itself, as was mentioned in Section 5 regarding a stream. However, it is forbidden to draw water from it because there is no partition to separate it from the external water, since it is breached entirely or more than ten handbreadths, and the sea is considered a karmelit (an intermediate domain). Do not ask why, even when there are remaining walls, we do not worry that the sea might raise a bank, as we are concerned in Siman 363. This can be explained that it is speaking where the remaining walls are very high, or it is far from the shore of the sea. (Tosfot Eruvin 12b, s.v. 'Here') All this is the opinion of Rashi, Tosfot, and the Ra'avad in Chapter 15, as well as the Tur and Shulchan Aruch. The Rambam has a different opinion there, as explained.

It was taught in Eruvin (p. 88): "A courtyard that is open on four sides - one may not pour water into it on Shabbat unless a pit with a capacity of two seahs is made from the hole and below, whether outside or inside. However, if it is outside, it must be covered, and if it is inside, it does not need to be covered." The explanation of the matter is that certainly pouring water into the courtyard, where the water then flows out into the public domain, is a complete prohibition, since by his force it goes out into the public domain. Specifically, his force in a karmelit (semi-public domain) was not decreed upon, but in the public domain, it is forbidden, and it is possible that it is also forbidden by Torah law when he intends for it or when it is inevitable that it will go out into the public domain, as his force is considered like his body (Tosafot Shabbat 99: 'or'). According to this, in a small courtyard adjacent to the public domain, when one pours into the courtyard and the water flows out into the public domain, he transgresses a Torah prohibition, and for this, they found a remedy as will be explained.

The Sages said that every day a person spills two se'ah of water in his house for washing and other needs. This amount of water can be contained in a vessel that is half an amah by half an amah with a height of three-fifths of an amah. Furthermore, they said that a courtyard that is four amot by four amot has enough space to absorb this amount of water, so it does not need to flow out into the public domain. And if it occasionally does flow out, it is considered an unintentional act, and no correction is needed at all. However, if the courtyard is smaller than this size, they required him to make a pit that can hold this amount, so that the water will go into it. This pit is considered a private domain, whether it is made in the courtyard or even outside the courtyard adjacent to it. The size of the pit we mentioned is a karmelit, as it is four handbreadths wide and not ten handbreadths high. Therefore, they required it to be covered with boards or something else, and it is considered like the holes of a private domain even if it is ten handbreadths deep, and it is poured from a private domain to a private domain.

(The Tur and Shulchan Aruch wrote that it is a makom patur and so did Rashi. See Magen Avraham and Taz in section 1. I do not understand, as it is four handbreadths wide and is a karmelit, and as we have said, the Ritva also wrote so. And the Rambam in chapter 15 wrote that the covering is so that the people of the public domain would not see it, and his intention is also to distinguish it from the public domain, as he wrote in his commentary on the Mishnah. That is to say, if we consider it as standing in the public domain, it is a karmelit. And also the R"Y wrote that it is a karmelit, and when it is covered, it is considered like the holes of a private domain. So it turns out that they do not disagree. See Beit Yosef, and what seems correct to my humble opinion I have written, and examine it well.)

And since one makes a ditch, he can pour whatever he wants into the courtyard, and even if it fills up before Shabbat, he can pour into it because since there is a rim, it means that at the time of pouring, the water will first settle in the rim before it goes out to the public domain, and there is never a situation of a biblical prohibition. And since it is uncommon for it to be full before Shabbat, since one can pour it into the public domain before Shabbat, and even when it is full, it could be that it gets absorbed in its place, and he can also pour some in the courtyard and some in the rim - the sages did not decree (a prohibition), and they permitted pouring waste water into the rim even if it filled before Shabbat. (Beit Yosef in the name of the R"I)

But if it does not have two se'ah (a measure of volume), it is forbidden to pour even a little into it, lest he pour a lot. And what has been explained, that a courtyard of four by four is permitted, it is not specifically when it is square, but the same applies if it is long and narrow, since in total it has the area of four by four, and therefore the water is absorbed there. And furthermore, it was said in the Gemara, that the courtyard and the portico combine to make four cubits, so if one of them does not have four cubits, but combined they do - it is also permitted, since there is a place for the water to be absorbed. And a portico is a place with three walls and the fourth side completely open, which goes together with the courtyard and is used for unloading loads. Similarly, two balconies in front of two upper stories, with a soft roof that can absorb water, if they are close to each other within four handbreadths, they combine. (See Magen Avraham section 2 who wrote that the reason if it filled before Shabbat one can pour, is because they decreed a reminder for Shabbat so that he will not forget and throw into the public domain. And this is very puzzling, for the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch and also the Rambam in Chapter 15 ruled according to Rabbi Zeira, that the prohibition is because the water does not get absorbed, so it is not because of a reminder not to throw into the public domain but from the basic law. And his words are taken from Rabbeinu Yonatan who wrote them later, and earlier he wrote the reason we explained. And this is correct according to Rabbi Zeira whom we follow, and also what the Magen Avraham wrote in section 1 needs further study, and examine it well).

And know that the Tur and Shulchan Aruch wrote that during the rainy season, even in a courtyard, one may pour and repeat without hesitation, and it is permitted to pour anything there that one wishes. The Rosh also wrote this. I do not understand these words, for it is true that the Gemara states this, explaining the reason being that one wishes the water to be absorbed in its place, since damaging the courtyard is not relevant during the rainy season, as it is all filthy, and due to the concern that people will not say that so-and-so's pipe is flowing water on Shabbat — all pipes generally flow during the rainy season. This is clear according to the reason of sprinkling. But according to what we have established — that the water does not get absorbed in less than four cubits, what difference is there between the summer season and the rainy season? According to this reasoning, there is also a difference, but in another manner, as Rav Nachman says there — in the rainy season the reservoir holds two seahs, etc., as Abaye concludes there. Nevertheless, a reservoir is required even in the rainy season, and this is the opinion of the Rambam in Chapter 15, Law 19.

And this is the wording of the Rambam: "If the pit is less than two seahs, one may pour into it in its entirety. If it holds two seahs, one may pour even sixty seahs into it, even though the water will overflow and spread out over the surface of the ground. What does this apply to? During the rainy season... But during the dry season, if it holds two seahs, one may only pour two seahs into it. If it is less than two seahs, one may not pour into it at all." End of quote. However, the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch, who did not require a pit at all during the rainy season, and wrote that the reason is that the water is absorbed, require further examination.

All these matters pertain to courtyards adjacent to a public domain. However, in courtyards adjacent to a karmelit, even if they are very small, and even in the summer, nothing is required, because one pours into the courtyard, and what flows into the karmelit is considered his indirect action in a karmelit, and the Rabbis did not decree against this, as we have mentioned several times. And if you ask, if so, why do we need to cover the basin in the public domain adjacent to the courtyard, since it is considered a karmelit as we have said, and therefore one could pour into the courtyard and it would flow there, as indirect action in a karmelit is permitted? This is not a question, firstly because we have indeed permitted pouring directly into the basin. (And it is also possible to say that this is what the Rambam wrote 'so that the people of the public domain do not see,' as mentioned in section 2, and this is merely for recognition. The reason given by the Taz in subsection 5 is not clear to me, and examine this carefully).

In their days, they used to make a trench in the public domain near the courtyards, which they called a "beiv," and it was covered. The waste water from the courtyards would be poured there, and the water would flow through the beiv into the public domain or a karmelit. Therefore, any beiv that is covered for four cubits along the length of the public domain, thereby constituting a separate domain unto itself, and has the dimensions of four cubits by four cubits—which is sufficient to absorb the water within it, as explained—one is permitted to pour even at the mouth of the beiv, even during the summer months, even though the water immediately flows from there into the public domain, because there is a place for the water to be absorbed. However, this is provided that the pipe is not made of wood, which is not suitable for absorption, but rather of earth. They further permitted that even if it is made of stones, like a pavement, it absorbs and is permitted. It seems to me, specifically like a pavement, where there is some space between the layers and the water can be absorbed there, but a pipe made of stones certainly does not absorb and is forbidden.

In what case are these words stated? When the water flows into the public domain. But if the water flows into a karmelit, it is permissible in any case to pour, even onto the surface of the drain, and even during the summer, for the Sages did not decree against one's force in a karmelit. And know that according to the Rambam there, when the water flows into the public domain, even if the drain is one hundred cubits long and made of earth, it is still forbidden to pour onto its opening during the summer; rather, one must pour outside the drain and the water will flow into the drain, for when one pours onto its opening it clearly appears as if pouring into the public domain, and it may lead to suspicion. And know that some say that regarding the laws in this chapter, there is no difference between a public domain and a karmelit, for although one's force in a karmelit is permitted, nevertheless a karmelit within the city itself, like we hold that we do not have a public domain, can be confused with an actual public domain, such as a city that is certainly a public domain. Therefore, in a karmelit that is outside the city, or a courtyard that is not enclosed, or where the water flows to a river like with our underground channels in large cities - it is permitted. Similarly, if the city is surrounded by a wall, even if it does not have an eruv, it is considered like an unenclosed courtyard. Also, if the pipes pass through an exempt area, such as above ten handbreadths, and the water flows into a karmelit - it is also permitted. And in the large cities of our time, where there are underground channels leading from the river outside the city to each house and courtyard called "pravodina," and in each house the pipe continues, and they made a device called a "kran," from which they take the water and into which they pour the water - it is obvious that there is no concern with this, for the excavations beneath the ground are very high and very wide, and it is considered transferring from private domain to private domain, and the water flows to the river, which is considered one's force in a karmelit and is permitted. (And this is not decreed in a boat within a karmelit in the city, because a boat does not travel in the public domain, as written by the Taz subparagraph 9. According to this, the same would apply to a balcony, and see Magen Avraham subparagraph 13, and there is no need for this. See there and understand well.)

It has already been explained that according to the Torah, any place that has four walls is considered a complete private domain according to Torah law. However, the Sages prohibited carrying in it as if it were a karmelit until the enclosure is made for residential purposes, as then it is like a person's house and courtyard. But if it was not enclosed for residential purposes, it is considered like a field stringently, and one may not carry within it more than four cubits. However, this applies when the enclosed area is larger than two beit seah, which is an area that contains seventy cubits in length and seventy cubits in width with a few extra handbreadths that the Sages did not concern themselves with. In the language of the Gemara, it is seventy cubits and a bit. Up to and including this measurement, it does not need to be enclosed for residential purposes, but beyond this size, it must be enclosed for residential purposes, and if not, it is forbidden to carry in it more than four cubits.

The reasoning behind this matter is already known, as all matters of Shabbat are learned from the work of the Mishkan (Tabernacle). The courtyard of the Mishkan was one hundred cubits long and fifty cubits wide, as it is written: "The length of the courtyard shall be one hundred cubits, and the width fifty by fifty." The straightforward understanding of the verse is that the Torah commanded to set up the Mishkan, which was thirty cubits long and ten cubits wide, at the edge of the fifty, so that there would be fifty cubits in front of it and twenty cubits on each side. According to the interpretation accepted by our Sages, the Torah said to take fifty, wherein the length exceeds the width, and surround the fifty, making it square. When you cut a piece of fifty by fifty into five pieces, each piece will be fifty cubits long and ten cubits wide. You place four pieces on the four sides, resulting in seventy by seventy, except that the corners are deficient by ten by ten cubits each. You take from the fifth piece four pieces of ten by ten and fill the corners, leaving one piece of ten by ten. When it is cut into strips and surrounds the entire perimeter, which is two hundred and eighty cubits, it adds a small amount to the length and width but does not reach a cubit in any case, as in this piece we have only one hundred pieces of one cubit by one cubit.

The courtyard of the Tabernacle was not enclosed for residential purposes, as no person resided there, but rather sanctity hovered there. Therefore, they said that for an enclosure of this size, it does not need to be enclosed for residential purposes, but for anything larger, it does need to be enclosed for residential purposes. And know that this measure of seventy cubits is not exact, as it is seventy cubits and four handbreadths by seventy cubits and four handbreadths, and this is the remainder, with a small amount left unspecified. (See Rashi there, and you will find the calculation precisely.) According to the measurements of our country, Russia, it is forty-eight arshin in length by forty-eight arshin in width, as every four cubits in the Gemara is equivalent to three of our arshin. According to the sazhen measurement, it is sixteen sazhen in length by sixteen in width, as each of our sazhen is equivalent to four cubits in the Gemara, and each handbreadth is two vershoks, as we explained in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 218. Therefore, such a place does not need to be enclosed for residential purposes, but anything larger does.

This area that we said does not need to be enclosed for dwelling, there is no difference in what shape it is, whether it is square or circular, whether its length is greater than its width, even double, such as if its length is one hundred and its width fifty. But if its length is more than double its width, it needs to be enclosed for dwelling. The reason is because in the courtyard of the Tabernacle, its length was not more than double its width. And specifically if it is more than an amah (cubit), but less than an amah is nothing. A full amah prohibits, even if in total it is not more than a Beit Sa'atayim (area sufficient to sow two seahs of seed). (Rashi there 103, s.v. 'im') And it seems, that even if in total it is less than a Beit Sa'atayim, for less than a Beit Sa'atayim and a Beit Sa'atayim are the same in law, and if it is enclosed for dwelling - even if it is several miles, it is permitted.

In an area enclosed for dwelling purposes, we require that the enclosure be made for the sake of dwelling. However, if the enclosure was not initially made for dwelling purposes, and only afterward was a dwelling place opened there, it is not valid. This is called "enclosed and afterward opened," meaning that the enclosure was initially made not for the sake of dwelling, and only afterward was a dwelling place opened. We require "opened and afterward enclosed." However, if it was "enclosed and afterward opened," there is a remedy: to make a breach larger than ten [cubits], which is considered as nullifying the enclosure, and afterward to close up the area larger than ten [cubits], which is then considered as "opened and afterward enclosed." More details on this will be explained with G-d's help.

And what is called "enclosed for dwelling" and "not enclosed for dwelling"? Behold, gardens and orchards and watchtowers - this is not considered enclosed for dwelling, and even though there is some building where the guard lives inside - this is not made for dwelling but for guarding. And even if one wants afterward to make there a complete dwelling house - it does not help, because it was enclosed and then opened. Similarly, it appears that a synagogue and a study hall and a bathhouse, if there is no dwelling place for the attendant or the bathhouse guard - it is not considered enclosed for dwelling, because praying and studying there is not considered dwelling, just as the Tabernacle is not called enclosed for dwelling. Similarly with the bathhouse, and similarly an enclosure behind the city where they place wood (Mishnah beginning of Chapter 2) or other merchandise - it is not called enclosed for dwelling.

A space enclosed for dwelling purposes refers to courtyards in front of houses and designated areas, such as the open space behind houses. Even places where no one actually resides, but are made for regular entry and exit, are considered enclosed for dwelling. For example, a livestock pen used in fields, moving from place to place to fertilize with animal manure (as mentioned in the Mishnah). Similarly, a city’s livestock enclosure. For this reason, the partitions around wells are also considered enclosed for dwelling, because people frequently enter and exit to drink (as noted in the Mishnah and Rashi, s.v. 'courtyard' and Tosafot, s.v. 'even').

It has already been explained that even for an enclosure intended for dwelling, the dwelling must precede the enclosure. But if an enclosure is made and then a dwelling is established, it is not valid. Therefore, it is explained later in Siman 401 that typical cities are enclosed for dwelling, while typical fortresses are not, because in most cities, houses are built first and then the city is enclosed. In most fortresses, the area is enclosed first and then houses are built (see Rabbeinu Yonatan who wrote about a pen where there is a dwelling house for the guard).

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote in section 1: "There are those who say that the typical enclosures (karpifot) we have nowadays are considered to be enclosed for residential purposes, because it is customary to make an entrance first and then to enclose.
