And there are those who say further that any enclosure adjacent to one's house is considered to be enclosed for residential purposes, because one's intention is upon it, but there are those who disagree." End of quote. He shortened his words. The first ruling is from the Mordechai there, who wrote that nowadays our enclosures are considered to be enclosed for residential purposes, and it is customary to make an entrance first and then to enclose, end of quote. This means that even though it has been clarified that an enclosure behind the city where wood is placed is not considered to be enclosed for residential purposes, this is because people did not enter and exit it regularly. But nowadays, people enter and exit it regularly. And if it is because we require an entrance first and then an enclosure, our enclosures are also like this, as first an entrance is made for this residence, and then it is enclosed. He also wrote that an enclosure adjacent to one's house within the Shabbat boundary is considered to be enclosed for residential purposes, because one's intention is upon it, but there are those who disagree. Now, according to what appears, this is entirely superfluous, because since he initially wrote that our typical enclosures are all considered to be enclosed for residential purposes, which is not similar to the enclosures in the time of the Gemara, what relevance does this dispute, which pertains to the time of the Gemara, have? It must be said that he brought this even for those who do not agree with the previous ruling. (See Magen Avraham section 4, who wrote that regarding a guardhouse and a residence, even the Tosafot agree that it is effective. And the Elya Rabbah section 12 already contested him, as it is explicitly proven that even in this case they disagree, as seen in Beit Yosef. And what Rema did not mention, it seems to me, is because it was obvious to him according to the opinion of Tosafot that it is not effective, and only adjacent to the city, since in any case according to the previous opinion it is effective nowadays for any enclosure, he also brought the opinion of the glosses of Asheri. But in the main matter, I do not know if the glosses of Asheri disagree with Tosafot, because it seems to me they only wrote this to explain the words of Rabbi Yochanan ben Broka, and this is also explicitly explained in Or Zarua HaGadol, section 130, see there and examine it well).

It appears to me that the courtyard of a prison is considered enclosed for the purposes of residence, even though it is very large and there is no residence for the prison guard, because it serves as the residence for the inmates. And even though it is not pleasant for them to live there, and they are forcibly placed there, nevertheless, it is ultimately a residence. This is proven in the first chapter of Yoma (10a), where it states that a residence, even one that is forced, is still considered a residence according to the sages, whose opinion is the halacha. (Additionally, it is obligated in a mezuzah if it belongs to a Jew, as stated in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 286, end of Se'if 4.)

And know, that even though we have said that a space of two seahs, and certainly less than this, does not require enclosure for the sake of habitation, and it is considered as more than two seahs that were enclosed for habitation, this is regarding carrying within it or to a courtyard and alleyway. However, regarding carrying to a house, there is a distinction, which will be explained in Siman 372. And it has already been explained that for an enclosure for habitation, we require that first the habitation be built and afterwards it be enclosed, or that it be enclosed close to his house and first he opens a door from his house to this place, and afterwards he encloses the place, and this is a case of a door first and then enclosed. And it has also been explained that even if it was first enclosed and then a door was made, there is no need to break down the entire fence, rather he breaks a breach larger than ten [cubits], and it turns out that the house is open to it without an enclosure, and then he rebuilds the entire breach, or the measure exceeding ten cubits, and the ten cubits remain as a door, and this is a case of a door first and then enclosed. And even if he did not break it down all at once, rather he broke down one cubit and rebuilt it, and again broke down one cubit next to what he rebuilt, and continued doing so until he completed more than ten [cubits] – it is permitted, because throughout this process, new entities have come here. (Gemara 24.)

And if it is difficult for him to break the wall, some say that he can make another correction, namely to place a lot of earth next to the wall on both sides. The length of the earth along the wall should be more than ten cubits, and the width of the earth should be four handbreadths, so that it is considered a significant area. He should fill the earth until there is not more than ten handbreadths of earth left to the top of the wall, making it as if the partition is nullified by more than ten cubits. Not only if the height of the earth is ten handbreadths, which would then be considered a new partition, making it an entrance that was later surrounded, but even if the height of the earth is not ten handbreadths, nonetheless, the original partition is nullified, since there are not ten handbreadths from the earth to the top of the wall. It is impossible to make the earth and the wall as one partition, since the width of the earth is four handbreadths—it is considered a separate entity. Consequently, when the earth is removed from both sides of the wall, the wall becomes like a new partition, making it an entrance that was later surrounded. Since the partitions were nullified for one Shabbat, they are considered new partitions. Even though he intends to remove the earth, the partitions are nullified, because even a wallet can nullify a partition, as stated in Siman 372. Nevertheless, some disagree with this correction, holding that earth does not nullify unless he does not intend to remove it from there, and this specific law will be explained in Siman 372 with God's help.

A mound that is ten handbreadths high - its status is that of a karpef (an enclosed area). Up to two beit se'ah (a specific measure of area), it is permitted to carry within the entire area. If it holds more than that, it is forbidden to carry within it, except for four cubits. If one made partitions on the mound that are ten handbreadths high, and created a dwelling there with an entrance, and it was enclosed afterward - it is permitted to carry within the entire area (as stated in the Gemara 105; see there).

There is a doubt regarding a pit, a ditch, and a cave that are larger than two beit se'ah, whether it is permitted to carry within the entire area or only four cubits. Seemingly, they are similar to the mound, but in the Mishnah (23), there is an opinion that they serve as a dwelling for others (see there). Although we do not rule according to this opinion, nevertheless, they themselves are certainly considered a dwelling. There is also no proof that the law is not so, and the pit of Pasei Biraot demonstrates this, as they make a dwelling between the partitions. However, this is not a proof, except for a well that has water, but not for a pit, ditch, and cave that do not have water. (This matter requires further investigation; see the end of the chapter on "How to Form an Eruv" and study it well).

A courtyard larger than two se'ah, and one wishes to reduce its size by planting trees within it, so that excluding the area occupied by the trees, it will not be larger than two se'ah – this does not constitute a reduction, for trees do not nullify the airspace, as it is customary for a courtyard to have trees. Even if one planted seeds in the remaining area, which will be explained later that seeds nullify human habitation, nevertheless, it is clear that it does not reduce the courtyard, for it itself is a courtyard, and it is worse than a courtyard, and the entire area is considered a long courtyard. And if one built a pillar to reduce its size from more than two se'ah, and it was thereby reduced, if the pillar is three handbreadths wide – it constitutes a reduction, but if it is less than three handbreadths wide – it is nullified to the courtyard and is not a reduction. And even though in all places a significant measurement is four handbreadths, nevertheless, since three handbreadths is significant, as it removes it from the halachic principle of "lavud" (connected), it constitutes a reduction. (Talmud) And know, that the trees we mentioned that do not reduce the courtyard, even if they are many, and even if each tree is ten handbreadths high and four handbreadths wide. This is not comparable to a pillar, because trees are an adornment for the courtyard, and how could they reduce it? And our teacher the Beit Yosef wrote in section 4: that the same law applies if one dug a pit in it – it does not reduce it. The reason is that a pit is a utility for the garden to water it. (Magen Avraham section 9 in the name of Rashba) From this, it seems that a pit without water, or if it is not in a garden but in a courtyard – the pit does reduce it. But from the language of our teacher the Beit Yosef, it is clear that even in a courtyard it does not reduce, for he is referring to a courtyard, and the Ritva also wrote that a pit does not reduce in a courtyard. One could say the reason is that a courtyard is suitable for planting, and the pit is suitable for water. (And see Turei Zahav section 18 who questions this).

If one built a new partition more than ten cubits away from the first partition, thereby nullifying the first one so that it becomes as if it does not exist, this new partition would then be considered an entrance, and thus it was enclosed afterward. For example, if at this moment an opening from the house was made before the second partition was built, if it was distanced from the first by three handbreadths - it is permitted. However, if it is less than three - it is merely considered an addition to the first, and it is one partition, and it is nothing. Similarly, if one plastered the first partitions with clay to reduce their airspace, meaning that through the thickness of the clay the space that is more than two seahs is reduced, and after plastering, there is no longer more than two seahs, if the clay is so thick that if the partitions were removed, the plaster could stand on its own - it is considered a reduction because it is something that can last. If not, it is as if it is not there and is not considered a reduction. 

One should not question why, even if it can stand on its own, it does not require being three handbreadths away from the wall as in the previous ruling. This is because it is not similar; in the previous ruling, there is still more than two seahs, and the permission is due to the entrance being enclosed afterward. Therefore, the first partitions need to be completely nullified, which only happens if the second partitions are three handbreadths away. This is not the case in this ruling, which is about reducing the airspace; it does not matter for the first partitions, and we only require that the second partitions be something permanent. (However, according to the Talmudic discourse, it is difficult, as in the previous ruling the Tur and Shulchan Aruch ruled according to Raba, and in the second ruling according to Rava. It must be said that they hold like Rav Shimi and according to Rashi's explanation. And indeed, the Rambam ruled even in the case of plastering with clay like Raba, that even if it cannot stand on its own, it is considered a reduction. See Beit Yosef, Bach, and Taz.)

Building partitions upon the original partitions to surround it by them is not effective, as they are redundant. However, if the lower partitions fell and the upper ones remained by themselves, it becomes permissible through them, since now he dwells between the lower partitions. This applies to partitions upon partitions, but for a mound larger than two seah (an area measurement) where he made partitions, even if they are on its edge, and from the outside the height of the mound is noticeable, which makes them partitions by themselves, and he surrounded it for dwelling purposes according to the law, it is certainly effective, as he dwells between the partitions he made. And since within them there is an entrance and only afterwards it was enclosed, it is permitted.

It has already been explained that trees do not nullify a person's residence, as, on the contrary, trees are planted for beauty. But seeds, such as garden plants and field crops, do nullify a person's residence, as it is not customary for people to plant within their residence but rather outside of it. When one plants, they nullify the residence, even if it was a complete residence. When the planting is done after the enclosure, the seeds nullify it, and the place becomes like any garden which is considered a karmelit. However, there are details to this. If the majority of the courtyard is planted, the minority is nullified in relation to the majority, and it is forbidden to carry throughout. If a minority is planted, if the minority is only two se'ahs, and certainly if it is less, the minority is nullified in relation to the majority, and it is permitted to carry throughout. However, if the planted area is more than two se'ahs, it cannot be nullified, as it is considered a full karmelit. And though the courtyard itself is not nullified due to being the majority, nonetheless, the entire courtyard is breached into a forbidden area, and therefore it is forbidden to carry in the entire courtyard.

As we have written, so it is in the Gemara (24a), and in the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, except that they differentiate between a karpef (an enclosed area) and a courtyard, as will be explained. The words of the Rambam in Chapter 16, Law 6 are puzzling in this matter. He wrote: "An area larger than two beit seah that was enclosed for dwelling purposes—if two beit seah of it were planted, it is permitted to carry in the entire area. But if the planted area was more than two beit seah, it is forbidden to carry in the entire area. [If] most of it was planted, it is like a courtyard and carrying in the entire area is permitted." End quote. He did not differentiate between whether most or a minority of it was planted. And it is even more puzzling, for he wrote, "An area larger than two beit seah—if two beit seah were planted, it is permitted," and an area larger than two beit seah includes even a little more, and when two beit seah are planted, it is the majority, so how is it permitted to carry in the entire area? (And it is surprising that the commentators did not address this.)

And what appears in my humble opinion is that the words of the Rambam are clear in their reasoning, and he interprets the Gemara there differently. This is because it is difficult [to accept] that if the majority is sown it is forbidden, even if it does not exceed the area of two se'ah, since the Mishnah there explains that a garden and a karpef that do not exceed the area of two se'ah do not require an enclosure for dwelling. If so, why would the remaining part of the courtyard be forbidden, since even for themselves they are permitted? Rather, it is certainly so, and more than two se'ah, even if they are a minority, would inevitably render the courtyard forbidden because it is fully breached. And since this is the case, it follows that there is no difference between the majority and the minority, but rather between exceeding two se'ah and not exceeding two se'ah. (And in the Gemara there, this is the explanation: 'This minority is permitted; we only said this when it is two se'ah, etc.' – meaning not because it is a minority, but in response to what is stated there – 'a karpef that is more than two se'ah and was enclosed for dwelling and the majority of it was sown – is forbidden,' and more than two se'ah includes much more, even up to a hundred se'ah. Therefore, the explanation that we deduce 'the minority is permitted' only applies when it is just two se'ah. In such cases, it is truly not because it is a minority that it is permitted. Pay close attention.)

The reason for the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch is that they hold that if the majority of an area has been sown, it is considered as if the entire area has been sown, as the minority follows the majority. If the entire area exceeds the size of a Beit Seah, it is considered as if an area larger than a Beit Seah has been sown. The first version in the Gemara explicitly states this. Therefore, they hold that even in the second version, this principle applies in this particular detail. The Rambam, however, holds that according to the second version, this reasoning does not apply at all. According to the Rambam, if it is less than an area exceeding a Beit Seah, it is insignificant. According to the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch, if the majority of a karpef or courtyard is sown, the minority follows the majority, and the entire area is forbidden. Furthermore, their words explain that if the majority has been sown, even if the sown area together with the rest of the courtyard is only a Beit Seah, it is forbidden to carry from within it to the house and from the house into it, because the seeds nullify the dwelling, even if it is less than a Beit Seah. (The Alter Rebbe also wrote this in section 17.) And if it is more than a Beit Seah, it is forbidden to carry even more than four cubits within it.

And this is the language of our Rabbi, the Beit Yosef, in section 9: "A courtyard (karpef) larger than two se'ahs that was enclosed for dwelling, and most of it was planted with trees, even if they are not planted in rows, does not nullify its status as a dwelling. But if most of it was sown with seeds, the seeds nullify the dwelling, even if there are only two se'ahs of them. If a minority was sown, if it is only two se'ahs, it is permitted. More than two se'ahs is forbidden." End of quote. 

And this is its explanation: When the majority is sown, the minority follows the majority, and it is considered entirely sown, and it is forbidden. (Magen Avraham section 11, and what is said about more than two se'ahs is an independent phrase and was printed in error). The intention is that if, in total, there is more than two se'ahs, it is forbidden to carry throughout it more than four cubits, even if in total there is not more than two se'ahs, because it nullifies the dwelling, and it is forbidden to carry from there to the house. However, within the courtyard itself, it is permitted to carry throughout it, as is the rule for a courtyard that is not larger than two se'ahs. But if a minority of it was sown, if it is only two se'ahs, it is permitted to carry throughout it, for even though in the sown area the dwelling is nullified, there are not more than two se'ahs. And the rest that was not sown is not nullified by the sown part, since the sown part is the minority. However, it is forbidden to carry from this courtyard to the house and from the house into it, for in the sown area the dwelling is nullified, and it is as a courtyard not enclosed for dwelling, which is forbidden to carry from it to the house. Consequently, also from the permitted part it is forbidden, because it is entirely open to the sown area. (Gra"z) And some permit carrying from the permitted part to the house, as entirely open is only considered when it is open to a complete karmelit, where even within it, it is forbidden to carry more than four cubits. This is if the sown area is more than two se'ahs, but in these cases where even in the sown area it is permitted to carry throughout it, and only to the house it is forbidden, it is not considered entirely open to the extent that it forbids the permitted part. (there) And if the sown area is more than two se'ahs, it is forbidden to carry throughout it more than four cubits, for the sown area is a complete karmelit, and the permitted part is entirely open to it. Therefore, if there is a fence between them, they have no connection to each other. This is in a courtyard when it is sown, but in a yard, the Rosh is uncertain if the seeds have the power to nullify the dwelling of the yard, as the Tur wrote there, and in the name of Rashi, it is written that they certainly do not nullify, and see the end of the next section.

And this is what our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 10: "If one has a garden in his courtyard, if it constitutes the majority of the courtyard, even if it only contains an area of two seah, one may not carry from it and from the courtyard to the house. And if it is more than two seah, one may only carry within four cubits in both it and the courtyard. If it constitutes a minority of the courtyard, whatever exceeds two seah forbids the entire courtyard. And if it contains two seah or less, it is forbidden to carry from it to the house." These are his words. The explanation is as follows: In the previous section, the rule regarding a karpef (an enclosed area) that was sown was explained, and here, the rule regarding a courtyard that was sown is explained. A courtyard is less stringent than a karpef, for in a karpef, if the majority is sown, even if it contains only two seah or less, if the total exceeds the area of two seah, it is forbidden to carry in them more than four cubits, as stated in the previous section. However, in a courtyard, this prohibition only applies if the sown area is more than two seah. But if the sown area is not more than two seah, even if the total exceeds the area of two seah, the prohibition is only on carrying from there to the house, but within the courtyard itself and within the sown area, it is permissible to carry throughout, because the sown area does not have the power to nullify the residence of the courtyard unless it constitutes the majority and also exceeds two seah. There is also a distinction between this and a karpef when it constitutes a minority of the courtyard or karpef and does not exceed two seah, for in a karpef, in such cases, it was explained that it is forbidden to carry from the entire karpef to the house according to the first opinion in the previous section, but in a courtyard, everyone agrees that it is only forbidden to carry from the sown area to the house, but from the rest of the courtyard to the sown area, it is permitted. And when we said "everyone agrees," it is not literal but rather to say that our teacher, the Beit Yosef, ruled permissively here and did not bring two opinions as in the previous section regarding a karpef. (This seems to be my humble opinion, and the Gra did not follow this path, see there and examine carefully.) The Tosafot and the Rosh are in doubt, for perhaps the seeds nullify the residence only in a karpef and not in a courtyard and an open area, and the Tur also brought this. And perhaps in the case of eruvin of an entire city in pressing circumstances, one may rely on this. And perhaps regarding a city, it is considered the minority of the minority. And now there are those who do not allow making a symbolic doorway (tzurat hapetach), and in such cases, there is the ability, and to such an extent, perhaps, and this requires further study.

And behold, nowadays, anyone who has a garden in their courtyard - makes a fence between it and the courtyard. Consequently, for the courtyard itself, the garden neither adds nor detracts. Regarding carrying from the garden into the courtyard: if it is larger than two seahs, it is entirely forbidden; if it is not larger than two seahs, it is permitted to carry from it into the courtyard and from the courtyard into it. But as for the house, it is forbidden to carry from the garden, and likewise from the house to the garden. Therefore, it is also forbidden to carry utensils that spent Shabbat in the house from the courtyard into it, as will be explained in Siman 372. (Taz, Sk 5) And when there is no fence, we have already explained. (See Magen Avraham, Sk 14, who differentiates between two seahs and less than two seahs and disagrees with the Shulchan Aruch as explained in the Machatzit HaShekel there, but this is not conclusive, and the main ruling follows the Shulchan Aruch as we have explained. Investigate and understand).

A courtyard more than two se'ah in size that was enclosed for dwelling purposes and filled with water: if the water is fit for drinking, it does not nullify the dwelling status, even if the area where the water has spread is more than two se'ah, and even if it is very deep. If the water is not fit for drinking, it is treated like planted seeds, provided it is ten tefachim deep, as less than ten tefachim is considered like mud and mire and does not create a separate domain. (Magen Avraham, section 15) And when it is ten tefachim deep and not fit for drinking, it does not prohibit the courtyard, as the water itself forms a partition since it is ten tefachim deep. (ibid.) It appears that the water must be fit for human drinking as well. But if it is not fit for human consumption, even though it is suitable for animals, it nullifies the dwelling status and is treated like planted seeds. This is because even the wells with boards around them were fit for human drinking, as Rashi and Tosafot explain in the Mishnah regarding making boards.

A backyard of three seah (a measure of land) where a roof was made over the area of one seah - the backyard is permitted, because the roof serves as a partition, as we say "the edge of the roof descends and seals," leaving only two seah. Even if the roof is slanted like our roofs, meaning it slopes down - nevertheless they were lenient in this matter as well, saying "the edge of the roof descends and seals." And a backyard that is exactly two seah and a courtyard that opened fully into each other - the backyard is forbidden, because it is now more than two seah, even though the air of the courtyard does not cause it to be considered more than two seah, since it was enclosed for dwelling, and anything enclosed for dwelling has no limit to its airspace. Nevertheless, when the partition is breached, it causes it to exceed (and makes it) more than two seah. The courtyard is permitted, because there is no limit to its airspace. And it is clear that for this reason the courtyard is permitted, but for another reason - it is forbidden, because it was fully breached into the backyard. Therefore, if no remnants of the partitions remained on either side - it is forbidden. And what the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch wrote, that only the backyard is forbidden and the courtyard is permitted, this is when remnants of the partitions remained in the courtyard. (Magen Avraham section 15 and therefore the Beit Yosef generally concealed it and did not mention the permissibility of the courtyard, see there in section 13).

And know that what was explained in Section 14, that when one makes a new partition along the length of a wall more than ten cubits and extends it three handbreadths from the old wall, the enclosed area is permitted to be made into an entrance and subsequently enclosed—that is only as long as the new partition exists. However, when it falls, it returns to its prohibition, for as long as it exists, it nullifies the first one, which was not made for residential purposes. But now, against one's will, we rely on the first partition, and the prohibition returns to its place.

Know that in the time of the Talmud, their buildings and courtyards were arranged differently than ours. With us, the houses stand at the edge of the public domain, and the courtyard is behind the house. But with them, the courtyard was in front of the house, as the houses were built within the courtyard, and the area in front of the houses was called the courtyard, and that was their main area of use. The area behind the houses was called a "rechava" (open space), and it was similar to a "karpef" (an enclosed area not primarily for residential use). Sometimes a threshing floor would separate the house from the rechava, and there they would use it to store wood and merchandise. Sometimes it was much larger than two beit se'ah, and in such cases, it required a "petach ul'v'sof hukaf" (an entrance and then enclosure) like a karpef. It appears that a karpef was distant from the courtyard, while a rechava was adjacent to the courtyard, as Rashi wrote in Eruvin (7a, s.v. "um'sayeim"), and this is his language: "Rechava - the enclosed area behind the houses is called a rechava, surrounded by four walls," end quote. With this, we can understand the words of the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch as we will explain, with God's help.

And this is the language of the Tur and Shulchan Aruch: "A courtyard behind houses, larger than a Beit Satayim and not enclosed for dwelling purposes - one may not carry within it except within four cubits. But if he opened an entrance from his house to it and then enclosed it, even if there is a threshing floor between the house and it – it is considered enclosed for dwelling purposes." End quote. And we do not say that this entrance is open for the sake of the threshing floor and not for the sake of the courtyard, and therefore, there is no entrance to the courtyard, but rather it is considered a proper entrance to the courtyard. (Tur) But when it is a Beit Satayim, and all the more so if it is less - it does not have the status of a Karpef, and it is permissible to carry from it to the house. (Magen Avraham and Beit Yosef in Siman 358) And the reason seems to me, that a Karpef which is very far from the house, and has no connection with the house – they are considered as two separate domains, and one may not carry from one to the other. But a courtyard which is adjacent to the house, when it is not larger than a Beit Satayim – it is like a courtyard, if the entrance was made first and then it was enclosed. And do not be surprised, because logically if the courtyard had the entrance first and then was enclosed, the same applies to the courtyard, and what difference is there between the courtyard and the courtyard behind the house. The matter is thus, that initially they would designate a courtyard and build a house within the courtyard, and then they would fence the courtyard, and afterwards they decided to designate the area behind the houses for a courtyard. Therefore, regarding the courtyard – it is considered 'an entrance first and then enclosed', because the main building was after they designated the courtyard. But the courtyard behind the house – they did not designate it at the time of building, and afterwards when they designate a place for the courtyard, it does not have a building that permits it, because the house was not opened for its sake. Therefore, they need to first open an entrance from the house to the courtyard, meaning towards the courtyard, and then they fence it, and it is considered 'an entrance first and then enclosed'. And this is what our Rabbi Rema wrote and this is his language: "And the reason we are not careful to avoid carrying in courtyards behind the houses, is because in our time, their usual state is to be enclosed for dwelling purposes, as mentioned above regarding a Karpef" End quote. This was necessary in his time, but according to our current custom – they do not have the status of a courtyard or a Karpef at all, and all of them are courtyards, as all our courtyards are behind the houses. (Only a Karpef made on its own behind the city and the like, in a separate place within the city – they have the status of a Karpef. But all that is adjacent to the houses – all of them have the status of a courtyard, and only in villages is there a need to consider their manner of dwelling).

In Siman 362 it will be explained that partitions can be made with vertical without horizontal, and horizontal without vertical. The explanation of this is that since it is a tradition from Moses at Sinai that anything less than three handbreadths is considered as if it is closed, therefore, the partition that needs to be ten handbreadths high can be made using this principle. This means placing reeds that are ten handbreadths high, and each reed is placed less than three handbreadths apart from the next one—this is called vertical without horizontal. It is also possible to make a partition using three ropes, one above the other, and the distance between each rope is less than three handbreadths, and similarly from the first rope to the ground. Thus, there are three gaps that are each less than three handbreadths. Therefore, if the combined thickness of the ropes is somewhat more than one handbreadth, it constitutes a partition of ten handbreadths, and this is horizontal without vertical.

Nevertheless, the Sages said that even though, according to Torah law, these enclosures are considered complete partitions, rabbinically it is forbidden to carry within such partitions if they enclose an area larger than a Beit Se'ah, similar to the prohibition regarding enclosures in karpifot. However, in the case of karpifot, the prohibition is because they are not surrounded for the purpose of dwelling, whereas here it is forbidden even if they are surrounded for the purpose of dwelling. For example, if someone is traveling and wishes to establish a dwelling place on the way, and he sets up a tent and leaves an opening to the air, and then surrounds the area with such partitions because he does not have the materials to make complete partitions, and indeed there is an opening and it was subsequently enclosed, since he enclosed it to dwell in it on Shabbat, (as explained by Rashi on Eruvin 16b, s.v. 'not'), the prohibition, however, is due to the inferior quality of the partitions. The general principle is that the Sages prohibited all types of enclosures that do not resemble the enclosures of a courtyard and a house, whether because they are not enclosed after opening the house to them, or because of the inferior quality of the partitions themselves. If we permit carrying within all such large areas enclosed by inferior partitions, people will not distinguish between these and a full-fledged karmelit like a valley, field, forest, or garden, because in the eyes of the people, even in such cases, it is not considered a complete private domain. Therefore, they prohibited carrying within them entirely, and one is only allowed to carry within them up to four cubits and no more, and they are included in the prohibition of a karmelit.

Nonetheless, it is not entirely comparable to an enclosure that was not made for residential purposes, for in such an enclosure it is never permitted to carry within an area greater than two seah. However, with these partitions, they permitted a caravan to carry within the entire area, even if it is very large. Three people are considered a caravan, provided that none of them is a minor or a non-Jew, for these are not counted among the three. It appears to me that the same applies to a deaf-mute and an imbecile; they are not counted in the number, and similarly, a man and his wife are considered as one. The reason seems to me that the sages were concerned about a caravan with many burdens when they are on the road, for it is necessary not to restrict their way by giving them a fixed space, and it is also impossible to forbid them from carrying more than four cubits, for this would cause them loss, as is evident. Only for an individual did the sages estimate that an area of two seah is sufficient. And since there is no fixed number for a caravan, therefore the sages said that three people have the status of a caravan, for three are called many, as we expound regarding a discharge: "days" means two, "many" means three.

And this is what the Tur and Shulchan Aruch wrote in Section 1: "An individual who observed Shabbat in a valley and enclosed it with inferior partitions, such as vertical without horizontal or horizontal without vertical, up to an area of two seah - it is permitted to carry within the entire area. From two seah and onward - one may not carry within it except for within four cubits. The same law applies if there are two people. If there are three Israelites - they are considered like a caravan, and it is permitted to carry throughout the entire area, even if it is very large, provided that they do not enclose more than necessary, so that there does not remain an area of two seah that they do not need for use. But if an area of two seah remains unused - it is not permitted to carry in the entire enclosed area, only within four cubits."

However, less than two seah - we do not concern ourselves with this, because it is impossible to be precise, and therefore, as long as no significant area remains unused, it is considered like the courtyard of the Tabernacle, and we do not worry about it. And even though in every place an area of two seah and less than two seah have the same law, this is regarding an enclosure for residence as it is written in Section 358, and also from what we derive from the courtyard of the Tabernacle as mentioned there. But here, regarding a significant area that should not remain unused - certainly, only an area of two seah has significance, and not less than two seah.

Know that the words of the Rambam regarding this matter are very puzzling. He wrote in Chapter 16, Law 12: "An individual who rested in a valley and made a partition around himself, if it encompasses up to an area of two seah, it is permitted to carry within it entirely. But if it was more than two seah, it is only permitted to carry within four cubits. However, three people are considered a caravan, etc." End quote. And he did not mention at all that this applies specifically to inferior partitions, such as a vertical without a horizontal or a horizontal without a vertical, contrary to the words of the Talmud and all the decisors. I am astonished that the commentators did not address this.

It seems clear to me that the Rambam had a different approach to this matter. In the chapter "Kol Gagot" (Eruvin 93a), it is stated: "Rav Yehuda said: Three courtyards are next to each other, and the two outer ones are enclosed while the middle one is not enclosed, and an individual is in this one and an individual is in that one—they become like a caravan and are given all their needs, etc." There, it does not mention dilapidated partitions but simply says enclosed. Indeed Rashi explains there: "that they enclosed with vertical or horizontal poles," but the Talmud does not specifically refer to these types of partitions. Therefore, Rambam interprets that indeed this is the case, that even with good partitions, the law is the same. The reason is that these are temporary partitions because when they travel from there, they will dismantle them, and therefore they are not like a complete residential area. Consequently, they only permitted an area of two seahs for an individual or two people, and only for a caravan did they permit more.

(In the Mishnah in the first chapter, 16b: The main dispute is whether such a partition is completely permitted, and Rambam and Ra'avad explain it this way. Even according to Rabbi Yehuda who says in the Gemara that this pertains to more than two seahs, this is all while traveling, but in a settled area, such partitions were only permitted by the later sages who said one of two things. The Gemara concludes in 17a that this permits an individual in a settled area, and the halacha follows them. However, according to all other Tannaim in the Mishnah, such partitions were not permitted in a settled area. Consequently, according to the later sages, there is no difference between these partitions and complete partitions. Since this is the case, even with complete partitions, more than two seahs were not permitted for an individual. It also seems to me that everyone agrees with this because Rabbi Yehuda says—all Sabbath partitions were not permitted for an individual more than two seahs; he is referring to all partitions. Rashi explains there that he refers to these partitions, but if so, what does he mean by "all partitions"? Therefore, Rambam interprets it simply. This is also evident in the Tosefta at the beginning of the second chapter, which states: "A caravan that encamped on a mound ten handbreadths high or in a trench ten handbreadths deep...as long as they fill the entire area and do not leave an area of two seahs," and these are complete partitions. There is also evidence for this from the Jerusalem Talmud on this Mishnah, which asks if there is a difference between an individual and a caravan according to the Rabbis, and it resolves this from the Tosefta. Thus, it is clear that the law is the same for all, and be precise in this).

If there were three people and they enclosed a large area as a caravan would, and one of them died on Shabbat — nevertheless, they are permitted to carry within the entire enclosed area on that Shabbat, because we say that since it was permitted at the entrance of Shabbat, it remains permitted for the entire Shabbat. And likewise, in the opposite case, if there were two people who enclosed more than the prescribed area, and an additional person or more joined them on Shabbat — nevertheless, they are forbidden to carry, since the Shabbat began with a prohibition, we say that since it was forbidden, it remains forbidden. This is a great principle in all the laws of Eruvin: that if an Eruv becomes invalid on Shabbat, it does not become prohibited, and if it becomes valid on Shabbat, it does not become effective, for the main consideration depends on the entrance of Shabbat, and we say, "since it was permitted, it remains permitted," and "since it was forbidden, it remains forbidden." This applies specifically in cases where the actual partitions have not changed, but if the partitions themselves have changed, we do not say this, and any partition made on Shabbat is considered a partition (Shabbat 101b) and will be explained in Siman 374, with God's help.

And regarding this law that was explained with a caravan, that when an area of two seah is left empty, it is forbidden to carry, our master the Beit Yosef wrote in paragraph 1 that this is specifically when they enclosed more than six seah. But if they did not enclose more than six seah, even though there is an area of two seah empty, since they are three people, it is permitted. And Rashi explicitly wrote the opposite, and this is his language: “Even though they are three, if they only need up to two seah, and they enclosed four seah, the partitions are also nullified.” Hence, even for four seah it is nullified, and certainly for six. And this is also explained from the words of the Rif on the law in the previous paragraph, where he wrote: “If there were three people and they enclosed six seah, and one of them died, it is permitted… the Sabbath causes etc.” And why does he not teach us that with six seah, even if two seah are empty of utensils, it is permitted, since before this he was discussing this law. And indeed, the Rambam and other poskim did not mention in the law regarding one of them dying about six seah, but rather they enclosed as much as they needed, which implies even a lot. But the Rif, who mentioned six seah, and taught us to permit when one of them dies, it would be necessary to inform us also about the permission of an area of two seah being empty. Therefore, it is certain that he agrees with Rashi. And it is true that the Mordechai in the name of the R”I ruled like our master the Beit Yosef at the end of the first chapter, but one can say that he holds that each person is given an area of two seah, and for two people - four seah, and for three - six seah, as there are those who hold this way.

If there were three people, and each one enclosed an area for himself next to the other to reside there on Shabbat, and they are open to each other and made an eruv together so that they can carry from one to the other, if each area is only a "Beit Se'atayim," it is obvious that they are all permitted to carry from one to the other. However, if one of them has more than a "Beit Se'atayim," they are all forbidden. This is evident from the Gemara (Eruvin 93a). It seems to me that this is the case when they are not equal in width, and necessarily there are partitions from one to the other or from the second to the third, or even if they are equal in width but one of them made partitions, then they are considered separate even though they made an eruv together, and they cannot be considered a "camp." But if they are equal in width and there are no partitions at all, and each one is completely open to the other, then they are considered a "camp" and are given all their needs, since there is no indication that they are three separate dwellings. But when there are partitions, even though the openings are more than ten cubits wide, it still does not make them one, because for stringency, more than ten cubits is considered as fully open to prohibit carrying from one to the other, but not for leniency. There is someone who says that even for leniency, more than ten cubits is considered as fully open, and it is as if they all reside as one and are considered a "camp" (Magen Avraham, Section 7), but this does not seem correct. (Taz, Section 18 disputed this with clear proofs, and the Maggid Mishneh brought it. According to our explanation, you will understand what the Talmud depicted there specifically with partitions, because otherwise, they would become a "camp," and examine this well).

In Siman 55 it was explained that when there are two adjacent courtyards, one large and one small, and the small one is entirely open to the large one, while the large one has remnants of walls on either side, we say that the residents of the large courtyard extend into the small one, but not vice versa. This means that the small courtyard is considered subordinate to the large one, as if the owner of the large courtyard also occupies the small one, but not the reverse. Therefore, in the case of three courtyards side by side that made an eruv among them, if the outer courtyards are wide and the middle one is narrow, such that the middle one is entirely open to the outer ones, and the outer ones have remnants of walls extending beyond it on both sides, it is considered as if the outer courtyards extend into the middle one, and they become a caravan, and we give them all their needs. Hence, even if the middle one is very large, it is permitted. Consequently, even in the outer courtyards, we give them all their needs, because since they are considered a caravan in the middle, the outer courtyards become like a courtyard to the middle one. However, some say that in this case, the concept of a courtyard to the middle does not apply, as we only find this in the context of making a gatehouse, and this is not a fixed place. Additionally, how can the outer courtyards become subordinate to the middle one to act as its courtyard, since they are larger than it? Therefore, in them, there is no allowance beyond an area of two seahs. If one of them exceeds an area of two seahs, the middle one is also prohibited because it is entirely open to each of the outer ones.

And if it is the opposite, where the middle area is larger than the outer areas, and the outer areas are completely open to the middle, and the middle area is enclosed on both sides and has a single person in each - we only give each one a space of two Beit Se'ah. Here, even if we say that the larger area controls the smaller one and it is as if the middle area stands in one of the outer areas, in the end, it is still only two areas. And if one of the outer areas is more than two Beit Se'ah - it alone is prohibited and the middle area is permitted, because it has enclosures and is not completely open, provided that it is not more than ten [cubits], for more than ten cubits is considered as completely open. And even though necessarily it is more than ten cubits according to the calculation, for more than two Beit Se'ah when we are precise about this, it can be said that it has many openings, and each opening is less than ten cubits. (And in Taz, he struggled with this; see there.) And if the middle area is more than two Beit Se'ah - the outer areas are also prohibited, since they are completely open to a place that is prohibited to them. This all applies when there is one person in each of the three enclosures.

But if there are two people in the middle section and one in each of the outer sections, or two in each of the outer sections and one in the middle, and the middle section is large and enclosed while the outer sections are small and completely open - we allocate to the two outer sections all their needs, for the owners of the middle section control [the outer sections]. Therefore, when there are two in the middle and one in the outer section - there are three in the outer section, and similarly in the second outer section. And when there is one in the middle and two in each of the outer sections - when the middle person turns to this outer section, there are three, and similarly to the second outer section. And do not wonder how we turn here and there, the two middle ones or the single middle one, how we turn them here and there, for this is not difficult at all, for we say that the middle ones have their dwelling in the entire circumference here and there. And according to the first opinion in paragraph 10 - even the middle one is permitted more than a Beit Sa'atayim, for it is considered as a courtyard for them, (Magen Avraham, Siman 6), and when the middle is small, all this is not necessary.

And know that what has been explained, that whether one is enclosed and one is fully open, the one that is fully open is forbidden. As will be explained later in Siman 374, where it appears externally and is even internally, it is considered both a post and a partition. Similarly, this partition that is enclosed is also visible from the outside to the one that is fully open, as is clear. It is only found when the walls of the smaller one enter the larger one by three handbreadths, for then everyone sees that the partition of the enclosure of the larger one is three handbreadths away from it. Otherwise, it would be considered as if they were all enclosed, and each would only have a Beit Satayim (an area of two seahs). In that place, these details will be explained with the help of Heaven.

A roof adjacent to the public domain, meaning that the house is not situated in a courtyard away from the public domain, but rather on the edge of the public domain like our buildings. And the roof on three of its sides is ten handbreadths high, as roofs usually are, but on the side facing the public domain it is not ten handbreadths high, such as when the street level is higher than the courtyard level. From the Torah, it is considered a private domain. Nevertheless, since it is within ten handbreadths of the public domain, and many people use it by placing their hats and scarves on it when they are tired on hot days, they take off their hats and scarves until the wind blows on them (Rashi, Eruvin, Chapter 4). Therefore, the owner of the roof is forbidden to use it from the courtyard until he sets up a permanent ladder from his courtyard, thereby indicating that he has removed this roof from the control of the public and intends to use it himself. But a temporary ladder does not indicate removal, because since it will eventually be taken down, it is as if it does not exist. And what is considered a permanent ladder? One that is fixed there both on weekdays and on Shabbat. But if it is fixed only for Shabbat and not for weekdays, or for weekdays and not for Shabbat, it is not considered permanent. And it appears to me that a permanent ladder is larger than a temporary ladder, as it explicitly implies in Eruvin (76b) and it implies in Avodah Zarah (58b) that a permanent ladder must have no fewer than four rungs, meaning steps, as mentioned there.

And if the roof is ten [handbreadths] high also from the side of the public domain - no ladder is needed. But if it is not ten [handbreadths] high from any side - a ladder does not help, (and in the Magen Avraham section 1 there is a printing error as the Machatzit Hashekel wrote) and even though the house within it is ten handbreadths high, it is not considered a private domain on the roof but rather a karmelit. (The Gra) And if from the side of the public domain it is ten [handbreadths] high, and from the side of the courtyard it is not ten [handbreadths] high - no ladder is needed either. (The Taz section 1 in the name of the Hagahot Asheri, and this is not found in the Hagahot Asheri, yet it seems correct according to the law. And all this is when many people use the roof to shoulder burdens, but if they do not shoulder burdens - nothing is needed. And the Beit Yosef wrote that from the Tur it implies even when they do not shoulder burdens, but the Bach wrote that this is also the intention of the Tur, see there, and according to Rashi in Eruvin 44a: there is another opinion on this, but what we wrote is the opinion of the Rambam and Tosafot there).

A courtyard that has been breached entirely or by more than ten cubits into a public domain - the area of the partition is considered a karmelit, which is treated like the sides of a public domain, and the sides of a public domain are not considered like the public domain itself. Additionally, in the courtyard itself - it is naturally forbidden to carry within it more than four cubits, as it is entirely breached or more than ten cubits. However, according to Torah law, the entire courtyard, aside from the area of the partition, is considered a complete private domain (as mentioned by Tosafot on Eruvin 93b, s.v. "Chayav"), and this is also stated in the Jerusalem Talmud there. But the opinion of the Rambam is that the entire courtyard is, by Torah law, considered a karmelit, as he wrote at the beginning of Siman 345, see there.

However, if the breach is only ten cubits, and certainly less than that—it is considered a doorway, and it is permissible to carry within the entire courtyard. This is when the breach is along the length of the wall, but when the breach is at the corner—even if it is less than ten cubits, it is prohibited, because people do not make doorways at corners, as our Sages have said. However, if he made it like a doorway, with doorposts and a lintel—it is indeed considered a doorway, even at the corner. But along the length of the wall, even a complete breach without any repair with doorposts or a lintel—is considered a doorway if it is ten cubits, and certainly less than ten. In such cases, it does not help at the corner to be considered a doorway. The Tur and Shulchan Aruch did not mention this because it is obvious, as it is not a law given to Moses at Sinai that a doorway cannot be at a corner, but rather it is the way of the world. Since he made an effort to make it a doorway, why should we care?

A house that stands on the border of a public domain or a karmelit and the wall adjacent to the public domain is breached—if the roof remains as it was before, even if the breach is wider than ten cubits, and even if the entire wall is missing—it is not considered significant because we say "the edge of the roof descends and seals." It is as if the wall stands in its entirety, and this is a law given to Moses at Sinai. Even if two walls that are adjacent to each other, such as the east and south walls or the east and north walls, and similarly the west and south walls or the west and north walls, are breached, we say "the edge of the roof descends and seals." However, if two walls opposite each other are breached, we do not say "the edge of the roof descends and seals" because this is considered as if the space is open. The roof must be at least four by four cubits, for less than four, we do not say "the edge of the roof," etc., as stated in Siman 358. Another condition for "the edge of the roof" is that the roof must be level, but if it is sloped, we do not say "the edge of the roof" because it does not have an edge. Although in Siman 358, Section 24, concerning a courtyard of three seahs and a roofed area of one seah, it is explained there that we say "the edge of the roof" even if it is sloped—the reason for leniency is because a roofed area is not considered a courtyard. And the phrase "the edge of the roof descends and seals" stated there is not precise but means that it reduces the area. However, where the main reason for permission is due to "the edge of the roof," we do not say "the edge of the roof descends and seals" if it is sloped (see Tosafot, s.v. "Ela," and similarly written in the Taz). There is an opinion that if the width is four cubits, we say "the edge of the roof" even if it is sloped (Taz, Siman 2), but this is not conclusive, and Rabeinu Beit Yosef ruled otherwise at the end of Section 2. It is obvious that we say "the edge of the roof" even if the height is more than twenty cubits. This is not comparable to a beam across an alleyway, which is invalid above twenty cubits because it is only one tefach wide and serves merely as a marker, and above twenty cubits, it is not noticeable. But for "the edge of the roof," there is no maximum height limit. As we said concerning a courtyard, where an opening at a corner is not typical, similarly, in a house where a corner is breached, even if the breach is less than ten cubits and the roofing is also breached so that it remains diagonal, we do not say "the edge of the roof" permits carrying in the house that is open to the public domain or karmelit because we do not say "the edge of the roof" at a corner. The reason for "the edge of the roof" is also because of an opening. Since we say "the edge of the roof descends and seals," it is only like an opening. And since an opening is not made at a corner, it follows that we do not say "the edge of the roof" there. There are other opinions on this matter, but what we have written is the opinion of the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch based on the words of our Rabbis, the Tosafists, at the end of Perek Kol Gagot. The words of the Rambam on this matter are ambiguous in Chapter 16.

Earlier, at the beginning of Siman 358, it was explained that an enclosure not made for dwelling purposes, such as one that was enclosed and only later opened, is not permissible to carry within it more than a Beit Se'atayim, because the enclosure was not made for dwelling purposes. It is akin to a valley when it is larger than a Beit Se'atayim. Additionally, there are partitions in such cases that are not for the sake of proper dwelling, and it is forbidden to carry within them when they are larger than a Beit Se'atayim. Thus, our Sages said (Eruvin 26a), "A partition of builders"—builders who make a partition for shade around them when they build in the sun—"since it is made for modesty"—to protect themselves from the sun—"it is not considered a dwelling, and similarly, a partition made for storage,"—not to dwell there but to guard what is placed there (Rashi)—is not considered a partition.

And this is what the Tur and Shulchan Aruch wrote in Section 1: Any partition that is not made for dwelling within it but for modesty, or to guard what is placed inside it, or to sit in it to guard the fields, is a valid partition for carrying within it. However, it is not a valid partition to make what is inside it considered enclosed for dwelling if it is more than a Beit Satayim (an area of approximately 5000 square cubits). Therefore, a tree whose branches hang down, if they are not higher than three handbreadths from the ground, and the base (of the branches) where they connect to the tree is ten handbreadths high (and four handbreadths wide, and similarly, if at their top they are not four handbreadths wide but in the middle they become four handbreadths wide, and from there downwards it is ten handbreadths) – it is considered a partition, and it is permitted to carry within the entire area. This is provided that the space between the branches is filled with wood or straw (so that the wind does not move them) and the branches are tied so that the wind does not sway them, for any partition that cannot withstand a common wind is not considered a partition at all. This is specifically up to a Beit Satayim, but more than a Beit Satayim – it is not allowed, even if it was planted for this purpose, since it is not made for dwelling within it but to seek its shade to guard the fields. Thus, it is clear from their words that a partition that cannot withstand the wind is not considered a partition at all, and it is as if it does not exist. But partitions for modesty or guarding are complete partitions, and only for carrying within an area greater than a Beit Satayim is it forbidden, as they are considered not enclosed for dwelling.

The words of the Rambam on this matter are very remarkable, as he wrote in Chapter 16, Law 15: "Any partition that cannot withstand an ordinary wind is not a partition. And any partition that is not made for rest is not a partition. And any partition that is made only for modesty is not a partition. And any partition that is not ten handbreadths high or more is not a complete partition." End of quote. And behold, his version in the Gemara is 'not made for rest,' meaning it is not made to rest in or to dwell in. And the intention, according to our version, is made for rest. (Maimonides) But from his words, it is clear that for rest and modesty, they are not partitions at all, just like a partition that cannot withstand an ordinary wind, and like one that is not ten handbreadths high. (there) And this is a great wonder, for are such partitions worse than a post ten handbreadths high and four handbreadths wide or a mound ten handbreadths high and four handbreadths wide, which certainly are not places for dwelling, and because of this, they are not considered partitions?

And it is true that the language of the Gemara implies like the Rambam, for the language of the Gemara is: "The partition of architects is not considered a partition, a partition made for rest is not considered a partition." And if it is as our Rabbis say, that the intention is regarding an area larger than a beit se'atayim, what language is it that "it is not considered a partition"? Therefore, it seems to me that the Rambam explains that these partitions are made only for a short time and afterwards they are dismantled. And so Rashi wrote regarding the partition of architects, and this is his language: "Since it is for modesty and tomorrow they demolish it," see there. And so the Rambam explains regarding a partition for rest. And according to his version "that it is not made for rest" as he wrote, the interpretation is that it is not made to remain permanently, but temporarily, and tomorrow they demolish it, and it is a temporary partition, and we require permanent partitions. Therefore, they are not similar to a post and a peg, for they are permanent, and therefore their law is like a partition that does not stand in the wind, which is also temporary. And this is what he wrote regarding it not being ten handbreadths high, the language "it is not a complete partition," because it is a partition for a karmelit if it is four handbreadths wide, or for a place of exemption if it is not four handbreadths wide (and so it is explicitly stated in the Maggid Mishneh).

And it seems to my humble opinion to bring proof for the Rambam from the Jerusalem Talmud, Shabbat, beginning of the chapter "The Builder" (Chapter 12, Halacha 1), which states there: "What construction was there in the Tabernacle? That they would place the boards upon the sockets." And it questions, "Wasn't this temporary, and why is it considered construction?" And Rabbi Yose answers, "Since they would travel and encamp by divine commandment, it is as if it were permanent." And Rabbi Yosi bar Bon answers, "Since the Holy One, blessed be He, promised them that He would bring them into the Land, it is considered as if it were permanent." Thus, even regarding the labor of building, the Jerusalem Talmud says that anything temporary is not considered construction, and certainly, it should not have the status of a partition. And even according to the Jerusalem Talmud, in the general rule at the end of Halacha 2, with a different version, where Rabbi Yosi bar Bon refutes Rabbi Yose and says, "Since the Holy One, blessed be He, promised to bring them into the Land, it was temporary construction." And it concludes, "This says that temporary construction is considered construction," as we ruled above in Siman 313, Section 1. Nevertheless, since the Jerusalem Talmud was perplexed about the labor of building, and Rabbi Yose and Rabbi Yosi disagreed about this, it follows that even if it is temporary, it is construction and one is liable for building. However, it is certainly impossible to attribute to it the status of a partition, because we do not establish distant disputes. And it is possible that all the decisors agree with the Rambam in this matter; in any case, the words of the Rambam have a solid foundation.

A mound that is five handbreadths high, and one completed it to ten by making a partition five handbreadths high on it - it is considered a valid partition for carrying and for all purposes. This is the ruling of the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch in section 2, and also the ruling of the Rambam in chapter 15. This is explicitly stated in the Gemara in Eruvin (93b). According to this, if there are two courtyards, one above the other, five handbreadths apart, and the upper one made a partition five handbreadths high - it is considered a partition for both the lower and the upper. (See there, where it says that according to Rabbi Chanina, it is only a partition for the lower one, and since we do not follow Rabbi Chanina, it is a partition for both. And Tosafot wrote there: "And it is questionable if there is a mound in the public domain five handbreadths high and four handbreadths wide, and they made a partition of five on it, whether one who throws from the public domain into it is liable, and from it to the public domain is exempt," end quote. This is only according to Rabbi Chanina and not according to the halacha, and so wrote the Ritva there, that all the discussions in the Gemara regarding the upper one are not according to the conclusion of the Talmud. See there and scrutinize well.)

A partition that stands by itself, not made by human hands, is considered a partition. Therefore, any mountain, hill, or mound is considered a partition, even though it was not made as a partition, because this is not a commandment that requires specific intent. And behold, even with a lechi (a vertical post used in an eruv), which is a rabbinic enactment, we hold that a lechi that stands by itself is valid, all the more so a partition. And although for a lechi we require it to be relied upon before Shabbat, otherwise it is not considered a lechi as will be explained in Siman 363, nevertheless for a partition we do not require this, because a lechi, being a rabbinic enactment to allow carrying there, requires reliance before Shabbat, but not a partition which is a Torah law. And all the more so a partition made by a non-Jew on Shabbat is considered a partition, and even if a Jew transgressed and made a partition on Shabbat, it is considered a partition. However, if it was done unintentionally, it is permitted to carry within it, but if a transgressor made it intentionally, although it is a partition by Torah law and one who throws into or out of it is liable, nevertheless regarding carrying, the Sages penalized and prohibited carrying within it, and even another Jew is prohibited from carrying within it more than four cubits, just as food cooked on Shabbat intentionally is prohibited to others as well, as stated at the beginning of Siman 318, so too here. (And the poskim did not explain this, but it is obvious that this is the case).

And know that the opinion of Rabbeinu Tam in Tosafot (Shabbat 101b, s.v. 'Ki') is that sometimes even intentionally a partition can be effective to permit carrying within it. However, our Rabbis have disagreed on his intention. The Ran, of blessed memory, explained in the chapter "Hazorek" that this applies specifically when there was never a partition here before. But if there was a partition and it was destroyed on Shabbat and he made it on Shabbat — it is considered a partition even to permit carrying, even if done intentionally. However, the Rosh, of blessed memory, explained there that certainly, a biblical partition is not allowed to permit carrying, even if it existed previously. It is only regarding rabbinical partitions, such as two courtyards with a partition between them, where each courtyard had its own eruv and the partition between them was destroyed on Shabbat, thus prohibiting each other. In this case, if they reestablished the partition on Shabbat — even intentionally, they revert to their original permissibility, and each courtyard is allowed to carry within it and from it to the houses. See there.

Here is the translation of the passage:

And this is the language of the Tur: "But if it was done intentionally, it is considered a partition to be stringent… and these words apply only when there was no partition initially. But if there was a partition, and it was removed and then reinstated, even if intentionally - it returns to its original permissibility. For example, if two or three individuals surrounded their area with mats in a private domain, and also separated between themselves with mats and made an eruv together, allowing them to carry from one to another, and the mats were rolled up on Shabbat - it became prohibited. If they were spread out again, even intentionally - they return to their original permissibility." End of quote. And in this language, our teacher the Beit Yosef wrote in Shulchan Aruch, section 3. And it is not understood at all, for if they made an eruv together, why was it necessary to state that they also separated between themselves with mats. And our teacher the Beit Yosef in his larger work, held that the opinion of the Tur is like the opinion of the Ran, that even with partitions that are Torah-based, they return to their original permissibility, and this is also his intention in Shulchan Aruch, that the outer mats were rolled up and it became a public domain, and afterward, they were spread out again and it became a private domain. And it is very perplexing, for if so, why did he need to describe that they made an eruv, what difference does it make to us about the eruv. In short, he should have said that the partitions between the private domain and the public domain fell, and they were reestablished.

There is an opinion that explains that the intention of the Tur is like the Rosh, that specifically with partitions that are rabbinic, they reverted to their original permissibility. He explains that the mats are in a private domain, and even when they are rolled up, the outer partitions remain, and therefore they reverted to their original permissibility (Bach). However, aside from the difficulty we raised, why do we need the mats between them, since they made an eruv together? Additionally, it is difficult because according to this, why did he need to elaborate? He could have briefly described that when the partition between the courtyards fell when each had made an eruv for itself, and when it fell, they became prohibited. If it was re-established, they reverted to their original permissibility. (Also, the Drisha elaborated to reconcile the words of the Tur with many forced explanations, that what he said 'and they made an eruv together' is a dividing 'vav', and he described it in two ways, see there, and they are forced and perplexing. The Taz in Siman 1 merely rejected the words of the Bach and also the words of the Beit Yosef, who wanted to say that the intention of the Rosh is like the Ran, but he did not explain the words of the Tur, see there. And the Magen Avraham in Siman 1 wanted to say that the Rosh and the Ran do not disagree, except that the Rosh is referring to partitions that fell before Shabbat, and then specifically with rabbinic partitions, they reverted to their original permissibility. And the Ran is referring to partitions that fell on Shabbat, and then even with biblical partitions, they reverted to their original permissibility, see there. This is very perplexing, because the Rosh wrote that each one made an eruv for itself relying on the mats between them, and if so, they were extant at the entrance of Shabbat and fell on Shabbat, see there, and with biblical partitions, even in such cases it is forbidden, and this is explicitly stated in Tosafot there. And what the Magen Avraham wrote, why does the Rosh not explain that Rav Nachman is referring to the end of the Baraita, etc., is very perplexing, for the Rosh explained his reasoning in this, that if so, Rav Nachman would have brought this at the beginning of the Baraita taught in Eruvin. And he has already been challenged on this by the Taz in Siman 8 and the Machatzit Hashekel elaborated, and there is no resolution in it, see there).

And behold, regarding the halacha, we certainly hold stringently like the opinion of the Rosh, that only in rabbinic partitions do we revert to their initial permissibility if they were intentionally dismantled. For the Rambam in Chapter 16 completely generalized his words, writing that if it was intentional, it is not considered a partition regarding carrying, and this is also the opinion of the Rif, and this is the opinion of Rashi in the Gemara there. And if so, it suffices for us to be lenient with rabbinic partitions, for in this case, another leniency can be said, that since they fell on Shabbat, we say 'Shabbat, since it was permitted, it remains permitted,' as it says in Siman 360, section 7, see there. And with biblical partitions, we certainly do not say 'since it was permitted, it remains permitted,' as will be explained in Siman 374. But with rabbinic partitions, it seems that even if they fell, we can say 'since it was permitted, it remains permitted.' And this is hinted at by our Rabbis, the Tosafists, at the end of Chapter "Hazorek" (Shabbat 101a) when they brought the opinion of Rabbeinu Tam and wrote like the words of the Rosh: "And this needs examination in the teaching regarding residents who come on Shabbat, that it is said 'Shabbat, since it was permitted, it remains permitted,'" end quote. Meaning, if so, it is difficult according to the opinion of Rabbeinu Tam, why specifically if they were re-erected, they go back to their initial permissibility, when even if they fell, they should need to be permitted due to 'since it was permitted, it remains permitted.' It is necessary to say, according to this opinion, that even for complete rabbinic partitions, we do not say 'since it was permitted, it remains permitted,' and this is not according to what we hold later in Siman 374, that we say for rabbinic partitions 'since it was permitted, it remains permitted.' (And this opinion holds that specifically if one made an eruv through a doorway and the doorway was sealed, or through a window and the window was sealed, we say 'since it was permitted, it remains permitted,' but not for a complete partition. According to this, the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch who ruled later in Siman 374 that we say for complete rabbinic partitions 'since it was permitted, it remains permitted,' cannot uphold the words of Rabbeinu Tam according to the interpretation of Tosafot and the Rosh except when the partitions fell before Shabbat, and examine this well.)

It is permitted to carry throughout an entire ship, even if it is larger than a "Beit Satayim" (a specific measurement), because it is considered enclosed for the purpose of dwelling, as it is a proper dwelling for those who travel on seas and rivers. If the ship is turned upside down to dwell underneath it, the top of it also becomes a private domain, as we say "extend and raise the partitions." It appears to me that this applies when the bottom of the ship is not rounded, because in a rounded object, it does not seem appropriate to say "extend and raise the partitions." If this is the case, carrying is only permitted within four cubits on the top if it is larger than a Beit Satayim. If the ship is turned upside down only to repair it or to tar it, carrying is not permitted even underneath it except within four cubits, if it is larger than a Beit Satayim, because its partitions are now nullified for the purpose of dwelling. (Eruvin 90b) As long as it is turned upside down, it is fit neither for dwelling above nor for dwelling below, and it is considered merely like a platform. (Rashi there) A ship that has many rooms and many Israelites, with each one dwelling in a separate room, requires an Eruv, which will be explained in Siman 382.

It is stated in the Gemara (Shabbat 101b): Ships that are tied together – one can make an eruv and carry from one to the other, if they belong to two different people. If they become untied – it is forbidden, because the eruv is nullified. If they were retied, whether inadvertently, intentionally, under duress, or by mistake – they return to their original permissibility. Everyone agrees that it cannot be said here ‘since it was permitted, it remains permitted,’ because the water separates them. It seems that this is specifically if they became untied on Shabbat, for then when they are retied, they return to their original permissibility, since the eruv was valid at the entrance of Shabbat. But if they became untied during the week and were retied on Shabbat – it is forbidden to carry from one to the other, because the eruv was not valid at the entrance of Shabbat. And even if one made an eruv for many Shabbats, nevertheless, since the eruv was not valid at the entrance of Shabbat – it cannot take effect on Shabbat.

In all matters, one may construct a partition, even with vessels or even with foodstuffs (Tur). Even if the partition is made from many vessels, such as placing saddles one on top of the other, and the like, it is valid as long as the partition is not something that the wind can easily remove, like thin sheets. In the Talmud (Eruvin 86b), we find that they made a partition with sheets. This must mean either that they were thick and the wind would not move them, or they were tied with pegs, as will be explained later in Siman 630 regarding the walls of a sukkah. It is clarified there that initially, it is not correct to do so because the ties might come undone and it would not be noticed. One can make a partition from straw, hay, or grass, and the animal can eat from it. We do not worry that the height of the partition will be reduced below ten handbreadths because the animal cannot eat that much. However, one should not place food into a basket to feed the animal, as one might place so much food that the height of the partition will be reduced below ten handbreadths (as is made clear from the Mishnah and Talmud Eruvin 79a).

There is room for doubt whether a partition made of snow, frost, and ice is effective during the winter months.
