It would appear at first glance that it is not effective, as we say in Bava Batra (20a) that they do not diminish the size of a window concerning an opening of a handbreadth that brings impurity, because since they dissolve by themselves, they do not diminish the opening of a handbreadth, as explained there. All the more so, this cannot be considered a partition, and it is like ordinary water. However, this is not a proof, because in the closure of an opening of a handbreadth, we need a permanent nullification, as the Rambam writes at the beginning of Chapter 15 of the Laws of Impurity of the Dead, that we require something that is not typically removed. But for partitions, it suffices for the moment, like the partitions in a caravan, and for the moment, snow is considered a permanent thing in the winter. And although we wrote in section 4 that according to the Rambam a temporary partition does not help, that applies to an hour or a day. But for several days, it certainly helps, and snow in the winter lasts for many days. And also, there is no proof from Bava Batra there, which says that a partition of grease, meaning something greasy, is not effective, as explained there. This is because it melts immediately in the heat of the sun, which is not the case with snow in the winter. There is some proof that it is considered a partition from what the Mordechai wrote in the chapter "Covering the Blood" in the name of a Gaon, that one covers with snow, as it is written, "For to the snow He says, ‘Fall on the earth,’" indicating that snow is likened to the earth. And although our teacher, the Beit Yosef, rejected this in Yoreh De'ah section 28 in his great book, this is because for covering we require earth, as explained there. Nevertheless, it is a hint that snow is similar to the earth. And although concerning a mikveh, snow is like water, as explained in Chapter 7 (Mishnah 1) of Mikvaot, that this is when it is placed into the water and melts, as explained there, and also in Niddah (17a) it is said that snow is not a liquid until one considers it as such, as explained there, and as long as it is not considered, it is like all things, and why should it not be suitable for a partition? In practice, this requires further investigation.

It is stated in Bava Batra (20b) that one does not make a partition with grease, but with salt one does make a partition. And this refers to Sodomite salt, which means that it is drawn from the sea and is hard. But with Astarkanite salt, which is soft salt, one does not make a partition, except under the beam in an alleyway, where the beam holds it in place so that it does not scatter, see there. And this is no proof regarding snow, that it is not a partition, for surely snow is softer than salt. The reason for salt is not because it is soft, but because it consists of small pieces and scatters, as Rashi explains there. But snow in the winter lies well and does not scatter. And I am perplexed about the Rambam in Chapter 16 and the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, who did not bring either the law of grease or the law of salt, and this requires further investigation.

It has already been explained in section 360 that one may make a partition of vertical posts without horizontal ones, like a partition of reeds spaced less than three handbreadths apart from each other, as it is considered like a solid partition. Similarly, one may make a partition of horizontal ropes without vertical posts, such as with three ropes stretched horizontally: the first within three handbreadths of the ground, the second within three handbreadths of the first, and the third within three handbreadths of the second. The ropes themselves need to be more than a handbreadth thick so that together they reach a height of ten handbreadths. This is permitted for an individual up to an area of two beth se'ah, and not only while traveling, but even in a city, as these are complete partitions. However, for an area larger than two beth se'ah, it is only permitted for a caravan, as explained there. 

Additionally, one is permitted to make a partition out of living animals, provided they are tied so that they do not move around or escape. If there is a space between their legs greater than three handbreadths, it must be fenced, or their bellies should not be more than three handbreadths above the ground. It is also necessary to ensure that even if the animal falls, the partition will still be ten handbreadths high. And what we said about the animal being tied also applies if it can be made stationary, as we explained in section 630 regarding the wall of a sukkah. (Magen Avraham, sub-section 8). And although without tying, the animal might move itself, we are not concerned about this. This is not similar to the swaying of tree branches, which does not constitute a valid partition, because there the wind moves them, making it a partition that cannot stand in the wind. However, if the animal moves of its own will, we do not consider this an issue.

It is also permissible to make a partition out of people, but there is a condition: the people who are being used for the partition must not know that they are being made into a partition. Even if one of them knows, it is forbidden. This is what our Sages said in Eruvin (44b) that it must be without their knowledge. The reason for this is not clear. Some say it is because if they know, it would be considered a partition made on Shabbat, and if they do not know, it is like an inadvertent action (Beit Yosef in the name of the R"I). But this is not understood, for if so, how is it permissible for the one making the partition with them? (Taz, section 3). Therefore, one must say that there is no prohibition in making a partition with them since nothing is actually being done, and if so, what difference does it make if they know or not? Others say the reason is so that they do not come to be lenient with the prohibition of Shabbat (ibid., in the name of the Rashba). This too is not understood, for if so, how is it permissible for the one who intends to make them into a partition? It seems to me that the intention of the poskim (decisors of Jewish law) is this: when the individuals used for the partition know about it, they will certainly stand perfectly still next to each other and be careful not to move, making it similar to a proper partition, which is forbidden. But when they do not know, they move or stand naturally as people do, and it does not resemble a partition at all – thus, it is permitted.

And even if he did not inform them that he is now making a partition from them, if it is likely that they will notice it, for example, if this person once made a partition from them and they later found out about it - he is prohibited from making a partition with them another time, even if he does not inform them, because it is likely that when they see him among them, they will understand this. And if another person is permitted to make a partition with them - it is a doubt, (Beit Yosef) but with other people, he may also do it, since they will not notice. And know, that if initially they were not aware of this, and this person intending to do so walks among them, even though they later noticed - there is no concern, since the beginning of the action was without their knowledge. And the reason we forbid him with these people another time is because they will notice immediately from the start.

Our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in Section 7: "There is one who says that a person should not position them [people] if he intends to use this partition, but rather someone else should position them without his knowledge." End quote. And this is the opinion of the Rambam at the end of Chapter 16, see there. And there is no clear rationale for this. The Rashba, of blessed memory, disagrees with him, for it is implied in the Gemara there: "A person can make his friend a wall so that he may drink, eat, and sleep," see there. And the Rambam interprets that the act should be done by another person. His reasoning seems to be that if he himself does it, they will immediately notice, but if another does it and he subsequently comes to use it, they will not notice as much. Our master, the Rema, wrote that one should only make human partitions in times of necessity and distress. And if one forgot an item in a public domain, it is preferable to bring children there to retrieve the item without a partition, rather than to make a partition of people and have an adult bring it. End quote. Meaning that the children should intend for their own benefit, that they see the item and pick it up and bring it home. For if they act on their father's command, it is forbidden, as written in Siman 334 and Siman 343, see there.

However, I have a fundamental question regarding this matter: since the people are not supposed to know that they are there for the sake of forming a partition, and they are walking innocently, it is known that a human foot does not have a width of three handbreadths, and the distance from one foot to the other is a half cubit, which is three handbreadths. The height of the foot is certainly three handbreadths or more. If so, how can it be considered a partition, since such a partition is invalid? And our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 5: "Even if people are standing next to each other with less than three handbreadths between them, and even when they are walking, they are considered a partition, and the area between them is a private domain." End quote. It is perplexing how they can be considered a partition when they are walking. It must be said that there are many rows of people, one row behind the other, so that the feet of the second row are opposite the gaps between the feet of the first row. In such cases, it is possible that there will not be three handbreadths between them. (See Magen Avraham, section 9, and it is puzzling why he did not address this issue. What he wrote at the end of his words, "This refers to feet that are bound," refers to animals, as the Machatzit Hashekel wrote, because with people, it is impossible, since they must not know, and also because they are walking, as was mentioned. Pay close attention.)

A law given to Moses at Sinai regarding all partitions is that when the breaches are equal to the standing portions, it is permitted, but if the breaches are greater than the standing portions, it is forbidden (Eruvin 16b). This matter requires explanation. A gap less than three handbreadths is not included in this, since it is considered as if it is closed (lavud) and is completely permitted. Similarly, a gap that is more than ten cubits is completely forbidden, even if the standing portions are greater than the breaches, because this is considered an opening. But this principle applies to gaps from three handbreadths up to ten cubits. For example, if the length of the partition is thirty cubits and it contains multiple breaches, if all the breaches together do not exceed fifteen cubits, it is permitted, even if the standing portions include segments less than three handbreadths (lavud). However, if the breaches exceed fifteen cubits, it is forbidden. This only applies to breaches without openings that have the form of a doorway, which will be explained; for if the breaches have openings with the form of a doorway, which includes side posts and a lintel above, they are not considered breaches, even if they do not have doors, as will be explained with God's help.

There is a question regarding when the partitions are on two sides, or on three, or on four sides: should we consider the standing and the breached parts for each partition individually, or should we consider them collectively. For example, if on the east side the breaches are greater than the standing parts, and on the north side the standing parts are greater than the breaches, and if we consider them collectively, the breaches are not greater than the standing parts, what is the status of such partitions? However, from the language of the Mishnah (15b): "A caravan that camped in a valley and surrounded it... and the breaches should not be greater than the standing parts," it appears that it is speaking about an enclosure on four sides, and it says that collectively the breaches should not be greater, for if not, it would have said "and there should not be breaches in each partition, etc." Similarly, in the Gemara (16b), it says: "These partitions that have many openings and windows are permitted, provided that..." This also indicates that it considers the partitions collectively. And logically, this is also correct, for since the Holy One, Blessed be He, told Moses at Sinai that the breaches should not be greater, it certainly refers to the collective enclosure, for why would you differentiate between one side and another, is it not all one entity? And this seems to be the main point. (And Rashi, of blessed memory, explained "breaches equal to the standing parts" - the entire enclosure is made this way." His intention can be understood to mean that we consider according to the entire enclosure. It cannot be said that it refers to each partition individually, and thus according to Rav Huna, who forbids breaches equal to the standing parts, even one partition would be entirely forbidden. Rather, certainly, it is as we said, and further proof will be brought in section 29 and in chapter 363, section 17).

When there is a breach equal to the standing portion, it is permitted even opposite the breach. However, when the breach is greater than the standing portion, it is forbidden even opposite the standing portion. This is taught in a Baraita in the Talmud (16a), where sometimes it is forbidden opposite the breach and permitted opposite the standing portion. This applies to kilayim (the prohibition of mixing different species) and not to Shabbat, as explicitly stated in the Jerusalem Talmud (Chapter 1, Halacha 8). Furthermore, the Jerusalem Talmud explains there that the standing portion should not be aligned with the standing portion and the breach with the breach, but rather the breach with the standing portion and the standing portion with the breach. This means that in the wall opposite another wall, if the breach aligns with the breach in the other wall, it appears as if it is entirely open. Therefore, the standing portion of the western wall should align with the breach in the eastern wall, and the breach should align with the standing portion, the same applies to the north and south. This is not mentioned in our Talmud, nor do the poskim (decisors of Jewish law) mention it, but certainly, this is the halacha since there is no contradiction from our Talmud. There is also a dispute there: when the standing portion is greater than the breach, and for us, a breach is like the standing portion, if there is not a place where the standing portion is ten tefachim (handbreadths) together, some prohibit it because there isn't a significant standing portion in one place. The conclusion there is that Rabbi Yossi bar Bun in the name of Rav states that since the standing portion is greater than the breach, it is permitted, and for us, even if the breach is like the standing portion, it is permitted. (The Jerusalem Talmud holds that only when the standing portion is greater, but in our Talmud, the halacha is decided that a breach like the standing portion is permitted).

And there is a great question to ask here: How can we say that it is a law given to Moses at Sinai that if the breaches are greater than the standing parts, it is forbidden by Torah law, when in the case of the corner boards surrounding wells, the breaches were greater than the standing parts? The standing parts were two cubits on each side, and the opening was thirteen and a third cubits. Yet, the corner boards surrounding wells are considered a private domain by Torah law, as one who throws into the area between the corner boards is liable (Shabbat 20b). And in the Gemara (Shabbat 11a), it is said: “What about more than ten?... You will say regarding breaches being greater than the standing parts, as you permitted this by the corner boards surrounding wells, etc.” However, our rabbis, the Tosafists, at the beginning of the chapter "Making Corner Boards," addressed this and wrote as follows: "One makes four double posts, and as for what was said earlier that the Merciful One taught Moses not to have more breaches than standing parts, this applies where there are not four partitions like here, since there is a cubit on each side, it is considered an entrance." This is their language. And the Ritva, in the discussion of breaches being equal to standing parts, further explained, saying: "Since he set up boards that are a cubit wide, they are considered complete partitions by Torah law, similar to what is said about a ceiling that 'descends and seals.' And here we are dealing with something made with breaches, breaches."

And we learn from the words of our sages that whenever there are four partitions with an opening between them, even if the opening is exceedingly large, it is not considered a breach but rather an entrance. For according to Torah law, there is no set measure for an entrance. The prohibition against an opening larger than ten cubits is not from Torah law but from Rabbinic decree. For example, in the case of wells surrounded by partitions, the opening could be larger than ten cubits, but this was permitted by Rabbinic decree. The halacha from Sinai concerning a breach being greater than the standing partition applies when it is not considered an entrance but merely breaches. However, Rabbinically, this distinction is not made, and the Gemara states that in the case of wells surrounded by partitions, we permit a breach greater than the standing partition. That is to say, the Rabbinic prohibition is waived in this case. This is also implied in the Jerusalem Talmud at the beginning of the tractate on partitions, which states: "Since the breach is greater than the standing partition, one makes corner posts but not simple posts." This means that with simple posts, a breach greater than the standing partition is prohibited by Torah law, as they are merely breaches, but with corner posts, it is considered an entrance. Furthermore, it states there: "Rabbi Yose said, since everywhere else the standing partition is greater than the breach, but here you have permitted the breach to be greater than the standing partition, you have made a stricter requirement in another respect: everywhere else, one makes a post of four handbreadths, but here one makes a post of six handbreadths." (The post of four handbreadths is for a courtyard, as mentioned in Siman 363).

The Tur and the Shulchan Aruch wrote in section 9 that a breach equal to the standing part is permitted, whether in a vertical or horizontal direction. This is in the Gemara (16b). The meaning of "vertical" is straightforward, as explained, that it does not refer to less than three handbreadths, which is considered entirely closed, but rather to more than three handbreadths. Now, how can we illustrate this in a horizontal direction? According to the ropes mentioned, any rope less than three handbreadths is not considered a breach equal to the standing part, but entirely standing, as it is considered like solid (Lavud). (Rashi) The Talmud illustrates this with a mat that is seven handbreadths and a little bit more, and he carved out three handbreadths and left four and a little bit more. This means he left four complete handbreadths at the top of the mat and a little bit more at the bottom, and placed the complete part of the mat at the top and the little bit more at the bottom within three handbreadths of the ground. There is a little bit from this until the four complete handbreadths, making three handbreadths breached, and the standing part of the four complete handbreadths is greater than the three breached handbreadths. (Sometimes we say "the air of this side and the air of that side cancel it out," and this matter will be explained in section 363, see Magen Avraham sub-section 16).

It has already been explained that a breach larger than ten [cubits] invalidates the entire enclosure, whether in a courtyard or an alleyway. The sages based this on the entrance of the Temple, which is called a 'door,' as it is written: "And they shall slaughter it at the entrance of the Tent of Meeting," and it was ten cubits wide. If the term 'door' could apply to more than ten [cubits], they would have made it more than ten. (At the beginning of Eruvin, see there). It is explained there in the Mishnah that if the opening has the form of a doorframe, it is permissible even if it is much wider than ten [cubits], and we will explain the form of the doorframe later. However, in what manner the doorframe permits - whether also when the breached part is greater or only when the standing part is equal to the breached part - there are different opinions on this matter. The Rambam, in Chapter 16, Law 16, requires specifically that the standing part be greater, while the Tur disagrees with him, as we will elucidate with God's help.

This is the language of the Rambam: "If this breach had the form of a doorway, even though it exceeds ten [cubits] - it does not invalidate the partition, provided that the breached part is not greater than the standing part." End of quote. For the Rambam holds that more than ten with the form of a doorway is equivalent to less than ten without the form of a doorway. And just as for partitions where the breaches are less than ten, the breached part must be equal to the standing part, so too for more than ten with the form of a doorway. (And do not ask about the fourth wall of an alleyway, where a side post or a beam suffices, for there no partition is needed at all. But one could ask, for an open alleyway we hold that one side has the form of a doorway and the other side has a side post or a beam, and the Rambam himself ruled this way at the beginning of chapter 17, and according to him, the form of a doorway does not help when the breached part is greater, and here in the third wall it is entirely breached, so how does the form of a doorway help there? However, based on what we explained in section 23, that we consider all the sides together - it works out well, for from all of them together it is breached as much as it is standing, and not more.

However, the opinion of the Tosafot, the Rashba, the Rosh, and the Tur is that if there is a "tzurat hapetach" (form of a doorway) - even if the open space is greater on all four sides, it is effective. And this is the language of the Tur: "Even if he only placed four posts on the four sides and made a 'tzurat hapetach' above them – it is permissible. And this applies in a courtyard or alleyway that has residences, but in an open valley where one wants to make an enclosure to carry within it – it is not effective. And specifically when all four sides are made with a 'tzurat hapetach' – in this case, we say that it is not effective in an open valley. But if the enclosure is properly made, except that it has breaches larger than ten [cubits] – a 'tzurat hapetach' is effective, even if the open space is greater." End quote. 

And the reason is that according to Torah law, even in an open valley it is effective, but because there are no residences and partitions and it appears like a public domain or a "karmelit" (semi-public domain), the sages prohibited it. But when there is a proper enclosure, it does not appear like a public domain or a "karmelit." And according to the Rambam, it is clear that it is effective even in an open valley, as long as the open space is not greater. And in practice, we certainly follow the opinion of the majority of the poskim (halachic authorities), and this is also evident from the words of our master the Beit Yosef in section 10, who brings the opinion of the Rambam as a singular opinion.

The form of the doorway - there should be a post on this side, ten handbreadths high, and a post on this side, ten handbreadths high, and a post over them. It does not necessarily have to be a post over them; even a rope or reed is sufficient. And so it is stated in the Jerusalem Talmud: "A post on this side, a post on this side, and a reed over them." And it is not necessary for the posts on either side to touch the top post, and even if there are several cubits between them, it is permissible, as long as they are directly aligned under the top post. It is stated in the Talmud (11b): a form of a doorway made from the side - it is not considered anything. And this is the language of the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch in section 11: if the top post is connected to the two posts, or to one of them from the side - it does not help, because it does not resemble a doorway where the lintel is placed on two doorposts. (Beit Yosef) Therefore, if they do not touch the top post, they must be directly under it. If they are not directly under it, it is considered from the side, and one must set up other posts opposite it. It is appropriate to remove the invalid post for the sake of onlookers (Magen Avraham, subsection 20), but if it is not removed, there is no invalidation. Note that when they are distant, even a small amount invalidates it, and this is obvious. (The Rif and the Rambam did not write this law because they interpret "from the side" differently. However, they possibly do not disagree on this matter. (Beit Yosef) The Tur wrote that we require the recognition of a hinge, as the Rosh ruled, and according to this, all our forms of doorways are invalid. But all the decisors, including the Rif and the Rambam, did not write this, and it is not brought in the Shulchan Aruch. It is clear that even though Reish Lakish said so, it is later stated in the Talmud there: "Rav Acha found the students of Rav Ashi, and asked them, did the Master say anything about the form of a doorway? They said no, he did not say anything." This means that a hinge recognition is not required, and the Rosh himself wrote this. There is also a dispute in the Jerusalem Talmud on this, and the conclusion is that a hinge recognition is not required. In my humble opinion, it seems that those who require a hinge recognition would not accept merely a post, and therefore, those who say a post on this side, etc., do not require a hinge recognition. This explains the Jerusalem Talmud there and also the discussion in our Talmud. Study this well.)

It is obvious that if the beam placed on top is supported by the beams from both sides, even if the beams on either side extend significantly above the beam on top, such as when one carves into the beams and places the top beam into the carved space on both sides, it does not matter that the beams extend much higher. There are those who mistakenly say that this too is called "from the side," based on Rashi's language that states: "From the side - when the vine is stretched in its middle from this one to that one and not from its head," which they interpret to mean that even if they are placed in the middle of their width, it is still invalid because they are not placed directly on top. This is a mistake, and Rashi's intention is that in the middle, from the side, it is naturally so, that when it is placed on the top of this one and that one, it is not from the side, but when it is placed in the middle, it is from the side. Certainly, if one carves in the middle of the width and places the top beam there, it is valid. However, Rashi was not discussing this, and similarly, the language of the gloss of the Rosh, which states: "It should not be inserted between them in their middle," means that it should be inserted from the side in their middle.

(Some rely on the language of the Taz who wrote that if the rope is wound around the top end from the side and does not extend above the beam from the rope, it is valid. On the contrary, the Taz is more lenient, that at the very top, even from the side, it is valid. According to his view, the invalidation from the side only applies when the side beams extend above the beam on top, as the Taz wrote, and he objected that we do not permit so much, that anything from the side, even at the top end, is invalid, as stated by the Acharonim, who agreed with his words. But certainly, like what we do, that the top beam is of iron wire called "draat," which is wound around the beams until it is inserted in the middle of the width of the beams, and it is exactly in the middle of the width, it does not matter that the beams extend above).

It is a simple matter that even though the side branches do not need to touch the branch above them, as we have said, this refers to height. However, in terms of length, the top branch must extend to align with the branches on either side. If it is distant by even three handbreadths on one side, it is invalid. Additionally, the side branches must stand opposite each other. Further laws regarding this will be explained in the next section, with the help of Heaven.

There is no concern if one post is much larger than the one opposite it, as long as each post is at least ten handbreadths high. The posts on the sides must be strong enough to support a door, but it does not need to be able to support a heavy door; even any type of door, such as one made of straw or reeds, suffices. However, the post on top can be of any size, and even one made of rushes is acceptable, as mentioned.

It is obvious that the doorways of our gates and houses are complete forms of doorways, for they have doorposts on both sides and a lintel above them. Even if it is a rounded arch, if its legs, meaning before it starts to curve, have a height of ten handbreadths and a width of four handbreadths, it is permitted because it is considered a form of a doorway. And if one might question that the upper lintel, which is even after the curve, does not touch these sides before the curve - we hold that it does not need to touch, as we have stated.

I saw one of the great authorities who wrote that the side posts of the form of a doorway should not be more than three handbreadths away from the walls. (Taz at the end in Be'er Hetiv) And there is someone who wrote that on one side it should be so, but on the other side it can be distant from the wall. (Sha'arei Teshuva in Siman 363, Sif-katan 12, in the name of Beit Ephraim). These statements are puzzling, because the form of a doorway is really like a wall, and therefore it is valid even on four sides, as explained. What does it matter if one wall is far from the other, and it becomes like a breach, for up to ten cubits it is permitted? Another clear proof is that Rabbeinu Yonatan wrote that if the side post is distanced three handbreadths from the wall, it is invalid, because the air from both sides nullifies it. (Brought by Magen Avraham in Siman 363, Sif-katan 5). But this does not apply to the form of a doorway. Furthermore, what connection does the form of a doorway have to the wall? Even in an open field, the form of a doorway is valid. Moreover, if one were to think that the form of a doorway has the same rule as a side post, that it should not be three handbreadths away from the wall, why did the Talmud (14b) specifically teach us about the side post? Let it teach us about the form of a doorway, and all the more so about the side post. Certainly, the second law mentioned, 'if raised three handbreadths from the ground,' applies also to the form of a doorway, for even a complete partition is invalid if it allows goats to pass through. But not if the form of a doorway is distant from the wall, which is like the distance between one wall and another, for up to ten cubits it is considered a doorway. And although a side post is also considered a partition, nevertheless, it is a light partition and therefore invalid if it is more than ten cubits or in a thoroughfare or courtyard. This is not the case with the form of a doorway, which is considered a complete partition in all the laws of the Torah, both for Shabbat and for mixed seeds. Therefore, it seems to me in my humble opinion that there is no concern in this matter. (And the proof brought by Taz from Tosafot 11a, s.v. 'Ipecha', where Rabbeinu Tam questioned why the height of the form of a doorway matters, since it is valid with one post because of the side post, and he questioned that there is a difference if it is three handbreadths away from the wall. And I am puzzled because Tosafot indeed explain this way in a place where a side post does not work, such as in a thoroughfare, etc. And what is the advantage of this explanation over that explanation, and also Taz in Siman 363, Sif-katan 10 rejected this).

The Mordechai writes in the first chapter that a form of a doorway is sufficient with a rod on top, provided it is not completely removed by the wind. He did not write that it shouldn't sway in the wind, because that is impossible, as it is thin and elevated and surely the wind will sway it a bit. It is not comparable to a partition that is completely moved by the wind, like tree branches, which sway entirely and have no stability at all. But here, the swaying is minimal, and it remains in its place since it is tied at both ends. His intent is that it should not fall completely due to the wind, for then it is not considered a partition, even if there is no wind. The Rokeach writes that the rods on either side, if one does not have rods, they can be made with ropes, and this is also written by the Kolbo. (Beit Yosef) And it seems to me that this is only if the ropes are fastened with nails to the walls; otherwise, they would certainly sway a lot in the wind, and it would not be considered a partition.

It has already been explained in Siman 345 that, according to Torah law, any place surrounded by three partitions is considered a private domain. According to the Rambam, as we explained there, if the fourth side that is open faces a public domain, it is considered a karmelit by Torah law because many people crowd there, and it is not a private domain. However, if the fourth side that is open does not face a public domain, it is considered a private domain by Torah law. The Tur also seems to hold this opinion. (As the Taz wrote in subparagraph 1. And with this, you will understand the words of the Rambam, who sometimes calls a place with three partitions "a private domain by Torah law," as at the beginning of chapter 17, and sometimes calls it "a karmelit." The great commentators struggled with this, as the Maggid Mishneh wrote at the beginning of chapter 17, and the words of the Maggid Mishneh are strained. According to our explanation, it is simple, as we have written. Investigate this well.)

And this is from the Torah, but the Sages forbade carrying within an area enclosed by only three partitions until a correction is made on the fourth side as well. And that is, in an alleyway it suffices with a side post or a crossbeam, and in a courtyard, they required either a board of four handbreadths on one side or two thin boards on two sides, as will be explained. The reason they were more stringent with a courtyard than an alleyway is because anything that is made more for dwelling and modest uses requires more of a boundary. And in courtyards, many people eat there and use it and do modest things, which is not the case with an alleyway. (Beit Yosef in the name of the Rashba) And further, it seems to me that anything closer to the houses requires a nicer boundary so that it somewhat resembles a house. Because the main reason the Sages decreed was so as not to confuse it with a public domain, and therefore what is entirely close to the house, if a proper correction is not made, the great difference between it and the house will be visible, and people will err also in the public domain. Therefore, a courtyard that is adjacent to the house needs a good boundary to resemble the house, and an alleyway adjacent to the courtyard suffices with a lesser boundary, and even in this it will resemble the nearby courtyard.

And all these corrections are valid when the width of the fourth breached side is no more than ten cubits. But if it is more than ten cubits, these corrections do not help, whether in an alleyway or a courtyard, unless they make a form of a doorway as stated at the end of the previous section. Therefore, a courtyard that is entirely breached, meaning the entire fourth side is breached, and it is ten cubits or less - it can be permitted with a board four handbreadths wide placed on one side of the breached area. And it should be placed close to the wall within less than three handbreadths, for if it is three handbreadths away, it is ineffective. And if one wishes to correct it from both sides of the breach, it suffices with two boards of any width, placing one next to one wall within less than three handbreadths, and one next to the opposite wall within less than three handbreadths from the wall. The same law applies if the fourth wall is not entirely breached, leaving a stretch of four handbreadths in height ten on one side, or leaving two small amounts on both sides. Some say that leaving two small amounts is not effective unless they are a handbreadth wide, for when one makes two small amounts, there is a recognition due to their creation, but when left, they do not help unless there remains a handbreadth here and a handbreadth there. (Tosafot 10, end of 'Rabbi' and the Beit Yosef ruled this way. See Taz section 3, and so wrote the R"Y in the Rif, and so wrote the Rema in Darkei Moshe section 1. But from Rashi 12, in the explanation of 'with the boards' it does not appear so, see there and examine it closely).

The Tur and Shulchan Aruch, Section 1, write that even if the breach is less than four handbreadths, since it is fully open, it requires repair until it is less than three handbreadths wide. And although regarding a mavoi (alleyway), the Tur later rules that it specifically needs to be four, and the Shulchan Aruch, Section 28, brings two opinions on this matter in a mavoi, nevertheless, for a courtyard, they are stringent as per the first explanation in the Gemara (12a). This stringency in a courtyard, more than in a mavoi, is due to the reasons we explained in Section 2. There is an opinion that says this is referring to a courtyard that is very wide inside but narrow at its end (Magen Avraham, Section 1), but if the entire courtyard is not four handbreadths wide, nothing is required. These words are perplexing, as a courtyard requires repair in any case (Eliyahu Rabbah, Section 3), and indeed, according to the Rambam, this is also the case for a mavoi. The Tur and Shulchan Aruch differentiate between a mavoi and a courtyard. Additionally, the main consideration is the width of the end, and this is the primary ruling in practice (as also written in the Mordechai). If it is wider than ten cubits, or the breach is more than ten cubits, even if it is not fully open, only a form of a doorway is effective, as stated at the end of the previous section.

An alleyway (מבוי), which is derived from the term "entrance to the city" (Judges 1:24), and here it refers to the entrance to the street. This is because their setup was not like ours, where one goes from courtyards to the street. Rather, in front of the courtyards was an alleyway, which was enclosed on three sides, and several courtyards opened into it. The entire city was arranged this way, and people would enter from the courtyards into the alleyways. All the alleyways opened into a main street, which was called 'seratia,' and it was considered the public domain. People would go from the courtyards to the alleyways, and from the alleyways to the main thoroughfare, which was the seratia, as explained in Siman 345. Since the alleyway was completely open on the fourth side, the Sages forbade carrying within it unless a corrective measure (tikun) was made for the sake of recognition, so that people would not come to confuse it with the public domain. For in the eyes of the common people, it is all the same; since many people turn into the alleyway, they would say, "What difference is there between an alleyway and the public domain?" Therefore, a corrective measure (tikun) was required.

And what is its remedy? A side post (lechi) or a crossbeam (korah). And what is a lechi? It is a board or a reed that is ten handbreadths high, with any width or thickness, even less than a fingerbreadth (Beis Yosef, Bach, Magen Avraham). It should be placed at the entrance of the alleyway next to the wall. Any material is suitable, even living creatures, as long as it is tied with ropes to the walls of the alleyway with pegs extending from the walls, so that it does not move from there. Additionally, it must be ensured that the creature does not sit down and reduce its height below ten handbreadths. A person is also suitable for a lechi if he stands there the entire day until the conclusion of Shabbat, even if he knows that he was placed there for the purpose of being a lechi. This is not comparable to a human partition, which requires unawareness, as mentioned in the previous section, because that requires many people and is noticeable, unlike a lechi. Therefore, a person must also be tied there, for otherwise, he certainly will not remain in one place the entire Shabbat, which would result in carrying being done in a prohibited manner. (This appears to be my humble understanding of the words of the Rema at the end of section 3. The words of the Magen Avraham in subsection 3 seem difficult, as according to his opinion, a lechi also requires unawareness. How could it be tied without the person noticing? The Taz in subsection 7 also disagrees with him. Study this carefully.)

And the same law applies if there is a small section of a wall on the fourth side that is ten handbreadths high—it can serve as a lechi (side post). However, it must be at least one handbreadth wide. Even though, when placing something specifically as a lechi, any amount is sufficient because it is recognizable when one places it, this is not the case for a remaining part of a wall. If it is less than one handbreadth, it is not recognizable, as stated in Section 3 regarding a courtyard. Nevertheless, a lechi that stands by itself, which is valid as will be explained, does not need to be one handbreadth wide. Since it stands on its own, it is recognizable. Additionally, because it is required to rely on it from before Shabbat, as will be explained, it is considered as if it has been placed there intentionally (in my opinion).

A side post (lechi) that, if a strong wind blows on it and it becomes uprooted, is not considered a valid side post. This is specifically referring to a common wind; however, if a common wind does not uproot it, even though an uncommon wind would uproot it, we do not concern ourselves with that. (In my opinion) It is not just if it becomes uprooted, but even if it sways due to the wind, it is not considered a valid side post. (Magen Avraham, Section 4) This is specifically referring to a strong swaying, like the branches of trees that sway back and forth without stopping. But slight swaying - we do not concern ourselves with it (in my opinion). (What the Magen Avraham mentioned in the name of the Magen Katan is not relevant to this section).

The side-post must not be more than three handbreadths away from the wall. Some say the reason is so that the airspace on either side does not nullify it (Sham, Se'if Katan 5, in the name of Rabbi Yitzchak). According to this, if the side-post is wider than three handbreadths, it is permitted, since the standing portion is greater (Sham). However, others say the reason is that if it is far from the wall, it is not noticeable. Even though the side-post serves as a partition, as will be explained, it certainly also serves as a marker (Sham). According to this, even if it is very wide, it is invalid if it is three handbreadths away from the wall, and this is the main opinion, as the Tosafot wrote (Eruvin 10a, s.v. 'and makes')—see there.

Since a lechi does not require a specific measure for its thickness and width, even if it is made from fragments and shattered pieces, it is valid. Similarly, stones that protrude from the wall one above the other, less than three handbreadths apart, are considered a lechi (Talmud, Eruvin 15a), provided they are ten handbreadths high, even if there are gaps between them.

Rabbeinu the Rema writes in paragraph 7 that this is why a lechi is often made from lime plastered to the wall, as long as one ensures that it does not erode more than three handbreadths above the ground. Not precisely three, but less than three is required, as any lechi that is three handbreadths high from the ground is invalid because a lechi is considered a partition, and this would be a partition that young goats can breach.

It appears that the lime must have some thickness, for otherwise, it is just like paint. I found in the Mordechai, in the first chapter, that it requires the thickness of a finger, and this is the language of the Mordechai: "Rabbeinu Meir wrote that making lechis from lime or a form of a doorway is properly done, for we have learned: 'One can make lechis from anything.' And lime or gypsum when applied to the wall with a thickness of a finger is much stronger than a cord or reed" (end quote).

The Terumat HaDeshen (section 74) explains further that the requirement for the thickness of a finger applies to lechis and not to the rods of a form of a doorway. It also clarifies from the Mordechai that any lechi needs to be at least as thick as a cord.

It is obvious that those who make lechis from lime must ensure that dogs or pigs do not rub against the wall, for if they remove three handbreadths of lime near the ground, it will invalidate the lechi (and there is a difficulty with the Taz in subsection 4, who wrote that lime is only for a form of a doorway and not for a lechi, but in the Mordechai and Terumat HaDeshen, it is explicitly stated otherwise).

A side post (lechi) made from Asherah wood is valid. Even though a crossbeam (korah) would be invalid, that is because it requires the measure of a handbreadth. But a side post, where it is valid even if it is made from fragmented pieces, what difference does it make if it is made from Asherah wood, since its measure is considered as if it is crushed (i.e., it does not need a specific measure). And even though the height requirement for a side post is ten handbreadths, nevertheless, since no thickness measurement is necessary, it is a minor matter and is permitted (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 7, in the name of Tosafot). Furthermore, a side post can have its fragments attached to the wall (Tosafot there). And one should not question that Asherah wood is forbidden in benefit, as it can be said that this is not a bodily benefit but a commandment, and commandments were not given for benefit (Sukkah 31b).

Ideally, the lechi (side post) should be placed in a way that it is recognizable as a lechi both to those standing inside the alley and to those standing outside. This means it should be positioned with its width along the length of the alley and extended slightly outward. However, if it is not extended outward, those standing behind the alley will not notice that there is a lechi, because the extra thickness of the lechi over the wall's thickness will not be noticeable at all. They will think it is just part of the wall’s thickness, and only from the inside will it be noticeable as its edge protrudes from the wall. Similarly, there are times when it is visible from the outside but not from the inside, such as when the entire lechi is extended outward from the alley, and only its inner edge is within the thickness of the wall. From the inside, it looks like an extension of the wall’s length, but from the outside, it is noticeable as it extends beyond the wall’s thickness either to the right or to the left. Nevertheless, if it is made this way, it is valid, because we hold that whether it is visible from the inside and flush with the outside, or visible from the outside and flush with the inside, it is considered a lechi. Tosafot and the Rosh ruled that being visible from the outside is not effective unless it is visible to those standing outside opposite the alley’s opening. This means it should be extended outward, and its inner edge should be placed at the edge of the thickness at the back of the alley. In this way, it is not noticeable from the inside, but to those standing outside opposite the opening, it is noticeable as its thickness is not the same as the wall's, and it is a lechi. There are other scenarios regarding this, and as we have written, this is the main principle.

If they raised it three handbreadths from the ground, it is invalid because the side post is like a partition, and young goats can breach it. However, if they raised it less than three handbreadths, it is valid, even if the post is only seven and a bit handbreadths, since anything less than three is considered as though it is attached (to the ground), and it is as if it extends to the ground. It has already been explained that it must also be close to the wall by less than three handbreadths.

A side post (lechi) that stands by itself, meaning it was not placed there intentionally as a lechi but happened to be there for some other reason, is valid. Since a lechi serves as a partition, and a partition that stands by itself is valid, as mentioned in the previous section. Nevertheless, it is required that they rely on it from before Shabbat, for we have already written that although it functions as a partition, it also serves as a marker. If they do not rely on it from before Shabbat, there is no marker at all. However, if there was no other lechi there, it is assumed they relied on it from before Shabbat. But if there was another lechi and it fell on Shabbat, and now they come to rely on this one, it is forbidden. Sometimes it can happen that they did not rely on it even when there was no other lechi, such as if they truly did not carry on the previous Shabbat; thus, they did not establish it as a lechi. Therefore, explicit reliance from before Shabbat is necessary if they want to carry using it. If they did not explicitly rely on it, it is forbidden to carry. One should not ask, regarding a lechi that fell on Shabbat, why we need another lechi, for we hold 'once permitted, always permitted.' This is not so, for when a partition between a private domain and a public domain or between a private domain and a karmelit falls, we do not say 'once permitted, always permitted.' Therefore, when the lechi or the crossbeam falls on Shabbat, it becomes forbidden to carry, as this is like the collapse of partitions since the fourth wall remains completely breached to the public domain or the karmelit. See also section 374.

A lechi (vertical post) that stands on its own and protrudes into the alleyway with a width of four amot (cubits), even if they relied on it before Shabbat, is not considered a lechi. The reason is that four amot is the measure of an alleyway, as will be explained, and there is no indication that it is a lechi. For although a lechi serves as a partition, we also require a visible indication, as we have said. Therefore, another lechi is needed to permit this alleyway, and it should be placed on the opposite side of this lechi. If one wishes to place it next to it, it should be made a bit thicker or thinner than the original, so that it is recognizable that it is a lechi and not merely an addition to the first one. This applies when the alleyway is more than eight amot wide. But an alleyway that is only eight amot wide does not require another lechi to permit it, even if they did not rely on it before Shabbat. It is permitted by the principle of "standing as breached," meaning that the lechi which is four amot wide is treated as if it is a breach from it to the other wall, and "a breach as standing" is permitted, as stated in the previous section. This applies to a lechi that stands on its own, but if it was placed there specifically as a lechi, it is permitted even if it is four amot wide in a large alleyway, because it is known that it was placed there as a lechi, and it serves as a visible indication. However, this is only when it was placed there as a lechi; mere reliance on it is not sufficient.

A Lechi (side post) that extends in its width along the length of the alleyway's wall, with its edge placed against the thickness of the outer wall, where its edge does not cover the entire thickness of the wall but only part of the thickness on the side of the alleyway's interior, or part of the thickness on the rear side of the alleyway, according to the opinions explained in section 12. If this Lechi is four cubits wide, it is considered as part of the alleyway itself and loses its status as a Lechi, even though it was placed there for the purpose of being a Lechi. This is unlike the previous law concerning a protruding Lechi, which is within the width of the alleyway and blocks it; therefore, if it is placed as a Lechi, it is not considered part of the alleyway. However, in this case of a Lechi extending along the length of the alleyway and not blocking it, it is worse, for even if it was placed as a Lechi, it is considered part of the alleyway and not a Lechi. But if it is less than four cubits wide, it retains its status as a Lechi (Tosafot 5:). One may only use the space up to its inner edge, for beyond that point there is no wall opposite it; and when it is four cubits wide, there is no Lechi, and it is forbidden to use the entire alleyway.

Another solution for an alleyway is to place a beam across it that is a handbreadth wide. Our sages said (12b): "A side post acts as a partition, and a beam acts as a marker." This makes it clear that a beam does not serve as a partition at all, and the principle of 'the edge of the beam descends and seals' does not apply to it, since it is not four handbreadths wide. For any partition whose roof is less than four handbreadths, we do not say 'the edge of the roof descends and seals.' But the statement that 'a side post acts as a partition' is not understood. How can a thin pole like a needle be considered a partition, especially since even a breach wider than the standing parts nullifies the partition, all the more so a thin pole?

I found in the Tosafot Yeshanim (ibid.) the following: "And if you say, how can it be thought that a side post acts as a partition, since the Torah taught Moses not to have more breaches than standing parts. Perhaps for a partition of three or four handbreadths, this was not taught." These words are not understood at all. It seems to me, in my humble opinion, that based on what we wrote in the previous section, paragraph 23, that a breach equal to the standing parts is considered valid for all partitions, it makes sense. Namely, that according to Torah law, three partitions are required, and within them, the breaches can be equal to the standing parts. However, there needs to be a minimal standing part in every partition, because if it is entirely open, it is not considered a partition at all. Therefore, they said there: 'An alleyway that is not suitable for merging,' meaning it is completely open (Rashi), 'was made valid with a side post, and one who throws into it is liable, because a side post acts as a partition.' This means that overall, the standing parts are greater, and even if there are some breaches in the side partitions, it will still be considered equal to standing parts. If indeed it is more, according to the calculation of three partitions, it is not a private domain.

Perhaps this is the intention of the Tosafot Yeshanim, that for a partition of three or four handbreadths, this was not taught, for this reason of overall calculation. Therefore, even for the fourth side, which the sages required a marker, a side post, or a beam, the main purpose of the side post is as a marker, just like the beam. But when it is said that 'a side post acts as a partition,' it is indeed true, since for an open alleyway, it makes it a private domain. Accordingly, it makes sense what the poskim said, that a side post always acts as a partition, and still, some marker is needed. This seems unclear, and many have struggled with it, but according to what I have written, the matter is clear with God's help.

The beam must be placed in order to permit the alleyway. But if it was not made for the purpose of permitting, even if it was relied upon from the eve of Shabbat, it is invalid. This is not similar to a side-post, whose primary function is like a partition. However, a beam, which serves merely as a marker, requires a proper marker. It must be made for the purpose of permitting the alleyway; otherwise, it is not a complete marker. This beam must have a width of a handbreadth. Therefore, if it was made from wood of an Asherah tree, it is invalid, because its measurement is considered as if it were reduced, since it is designated for burning. This is not comparable to a side-post, which does not have a required width measurement.

The measurement of the beam is that its width should be one handbreadth and its thickness can be anything, as long as it is strong enough to support a half-brick, which is half of a brick that measures three handbreadths, along the entire length of the beam, so that it resembles the setting of bricks upon it for building. (Rashi 13:) They were lenient with the requirement for supporting a half-brick because it represents the minimal form of construction, as is evident at the beginning of Bava Batra, see there. If the beam is four handbreadths wide, it does not need to have the capacity to support a half-brick. The reason appears to be that when it is four handbreadths wide, we say 'the edge of the roof descends and closes off,' and it is considered a complete partition. It seems to me that if it is four handbreadths wide, it does not need to be made for the purpose of permissibility, and perhaps it also does not need to be leaned upon from before Shabbat, since it is considered a complete partition. Nonetheless, it seems that it does need to be leaned upon, since even a side post is considered a partition, and still it is explained in section 14 that it needs to be leaned upon from before Shabbat.

If it is difficult to place the beam, it can be placed on other supports, meaning it can be placed on pegs that protrude from the wall, even though their width is not a handbreadth. As long as their length is not three handbreadths but less than three, it is considered as if it were directly on the walls, since less than three handbreadths is regarded as if it were attached (Lavud). Otherwise, it has no connection to the walls. The supports do not need to be so strong as to be able to hold both the beam and the bricks, but only strong enough to hold the beam alone, since in reality, it is not being built upon, but it itself is needed for this, and this does not pertain to the supports of the beam. Some say that they need to be able to hold both the beam and the bricks, for if not, the beam itself does not appear permanent. If the beam is made of straw or reeds, it is invalid (Tur), even though they can hold a brick, nevertheless, because they are soft and thin, they can be compressed (Taz, subsection 11, and the Magen Avraham, subsection 16, who writes that for holding bricks, any side less than three handbreadths can be used; see there, and it is clear).

And know that although we permitted placing the beam on supports, nevertheless, this is only when it is within the boundaries of the walls. But it is not permissible to place supports outside the alleyway and place the beam on them, even though its other end is close to the walls of the alleyway, because we require the beam to be within the walls of the alleyway. Otherwise, it is not a valid recognition for the alleyway. This is not similar to a side post extending from the wall of the alleyway which is valid, because a side post is always a recognition to permit the alleyway. But a beam is only a recognition when it is within the space of the alleyway, as no ceiling beam is placed except on the walls. (Ritva 8:) Furthermore, the side post is recognized while walking, and everyone sees it. But the beam is only recognized when one raises their head to look, and it is not the way to raise one's head while walking, except when standing in the alleyway, one might raise their head and look. Therefore, we require the recognition to be within the walls of the alleyway.

If the crossbeam was round, it must have a circumference of three handbreadths, so that its width is one handbreadth. And even though the calculation is not exact according to the mathematicians (Tosafot Eruvin 14a, s.v. "v'ha'ika"), nonetheless this is how the Torah decreed to measure. And we derive this from the sea of Solomon (there), as it is written: "Ten cubits from one brim to the other; it was round all about, and a line of thirty cubits did compass it round about" (1 Kings 7:23). This is what the Gemara asks, "From where are these words?" It is difficult—let us bring a string and measure. Rather, this is itself the question: the calculation is not precise. And it answers that the Torah commanded thus, and this resolves Tosafot's question there. See also what I wrote in Yoreh De'ah, siman 30, se'if 13.

If the crossbeam is bent and its bend extends outside the alleyway, or if the bend rises above twenty cubits or falls below ten handbreadths—both of which are disqualifying for an alleyway, as will be explained—we view it as if the bend were removed, and if the distance between the segments is less than three handbreadths, it is valid because we invoke the principle of "lavud" (considering gaps less than three handbreadths as closed). If not, it is invalid. (See Rashi, Eruvin 8b, end of 'According to the one who permits' who wrote: "And here it is not a real partition to permit through 'lavud'"—this is outside the walls, but within the walls, we use many 'lavuds' with the crossbeam. This is also clearly explained in Tosafot, Eruvin 9a, end of 'There is not', see there and examine well.)

If the beam is less than three [handbreadths] away from the walls, it is valid (Magen Avraham, section 17) because of "lavud," since it is within the walls. Similarly, if it extends from one wall and does not touch the other wall by less than three [handbreadths], it is valid, provided it stands on pillars. Also, if one beam extends from one wall and another beam extends from the opposite wall, and they meet in the middle of the alley but do not touch completely, if there are less than three [handbreadths] between them, it is valid. If there are three [handbreadths] between them, it is invalid.

Ideally, there should be one beam with a width of one handbreadth. Nevertheless, if one placed two beams side by side, each with a width of half a handbreadth, since together they are able to support a brick placed across them — meaning even if they are slightly separated, as long as there are not three handbreadths between them — there is no need to bring another beam. If there is more than that distance between them, another beam is required, or they must be brought within three handbreadths of each other, provided they are strong enough to support a brick. However, some say that in this context, we do not follow the principle of "lavud" (considering gaps of less than three handbreadths as closed), and we require the measure of a beam, meaning they must be within one handbreadth of each other, which is the measure of a beam. If they are more than one handbreadth apart, they are invalid, as there is no beam here. Furthermore, even if there were many such beams close to each other but more than one handbreadth apart, even if together they measure four handbreadths or more, it is still nothing, because we do not have a beam to place a brick on. (See Magen Avraham, section 10).

For the first opinion that validates two beams when they are not separated by three handbreadths from each other, even if they are not placed evenly next to each other, but one is higher and one is lower — if there are not three handbreadths between them, neither in height nor in length — we consider the upper one as if it is lowered and the lower one as if it is raised. This means that less than three handbreadths is considered as "joined," and therefore we see (as if) one has descended to the other or the other has ascended to it, provided that the upper one is not higher than twenty cubits and the lower one is not less than ten handbreadths. And there are those who say that in the previous clause, this is also invalid, and they only validate with a measure of one handbreadth. (And this is the opinion of the Tur, that the law is not according to Rabbi Yosi the son of Rabbi Yehuda, as mentioned. Regarding this seeing concept, look there).

If one spreads a mat over the crossbeam and it does not touch the ground, if the mat is not higher than three handbreadths from the ground, the alleyway is valid. For even though there is no crossbeam, since it is covered and there is no visible distinction, nevertheless, there is a partition due to the mat. But if it is higher than three handbreadths from the ground, the alleyway is invalid, for there is neither a crossbeam nor a proper partition, as a partition that is three handbreadths above the ground is invalid. And even if it is not higher than three handbreadths from the ground, one must ensure that it does not sway in the wind.

Even though there is no specific measurement for the thickness of the crossbeam, if its thickness is ten tefachim (handbreadths), Rabbi Shlomo ben Aderet (the Rashba) of blessed memory invalidates it. This is because, since it has the measurement of a partition, the crossbeam is nullified, similar to when a mat is spread over it. However, it does not form a partition since it is not within three tefachim of the ground. Rabbi Asher ben Jehiel (the Rosh) of blessed memory disagrees, arguing that it is not comparable to a mat, which covers it. But if it is extended significantly, its designation as a crossbeam is not nullified due to its thickness. Note that the Rosh brings the Rashba's ruling in the first chapter (Siman 18) and disputes it as mentioned. However, it is written that it is extended below ten tefachim, and it is not understood; if it was for the sake of a partition, ten would suffice. (This is also questioned by the Ketzot HaChoshen.) In my humble opinion, it appears that it is not precise, and often the poskim use such expressions regarding three tefachim and ten tefachim, meaning it is not exactly ten. The Rashba would not invalidate it due to exactness, as there is a difference between a precise measurement and an approximate one, as will be explained.

But there is someone who interpreted and said that the intention is even if the lower edge is below ten handbreadths from the ground, and any beam that is placed below ten is invalid, here it is valid, as the lower part is disregarded. (Taz, subsection 13) Based on this, the words of our teacher, the Beit Yosef, at the end of section 24, which he wrote: "But if he placed a wide beam and it extends slightly below ten [handbreadths] - it is valid," should be interpreted to mean below ten from the ground. And this has no connection at all to this law, as is evident, but certainly as I have said, that the intention is regarding the height of the beam being ten handbreadths, which is the measure of a partition. (And this also appears from the Bach and the Magen Avraham, subsection 20).

And even regarding the fundamental ruling itself—that if the beam extends down to less than ten handbreadths from the ground, it is valid—it appears to my humble opinion that this is not so. The proof is from what we say at the beginning of Tractate Sukkah (4a): If it (the sukkah) is ten handbreadths high, and the foliage descends within ten, Abaye thought to validate it, similar to a height above twenty, where it is valid in such situations. But Rava said to him, "This is a repugnant dwelling, and a person does not dwell in a repugnant dwelling," and this is the accepted ruling later in Siman 733. Therefore, it is clear that below, we require ten handbreadths to be completely clear. There is no distinction to be made between a sukkah and an alleyway in this matter, for in an alleyway also, a proper passageway is required, just as in a sukkah a pleasant dwelling is required. (Therefore, although the Taz there validates it, and the Eliyah Rabbah also wrote so, in my humble opinion, it is invalid. And I found that the Acharonim also rejected the words of the Taz, and the Vilna Gaon explained like the Taz and rejected the words of the Rosh.)

If one inserted two bent pegs into the two walls of the alleyway from the inside, and the bends are directed into the alleyway, and placed the crossbeam on them, and the pegs do not have a width of a handbreadth, which is the measure for a crossbeam to be considered as such on its own, if they are not higher than the walls of the alleyway by three handbreadths, and also if the bends do not extend three handbreadths, and it turns out that the crossbeam is not distanced from the walls by three handbreadths, whether in length or in height, it is valid. For we see it (as if) [as though] they extend to the walls of the alleyway and (as if) [as though] they are lowered to the walls of the alleyway. But if it exceeds three handbreadths, it is invalid. There is a significant point in this law, as we say there are two types of "lavud" (considered connected) at once: "lavud" in length, and "chavut rami" (lowering) in height. And even though in Sukkah (22a) we say regarding a sukkah and impurity that for a length of a handbreadth we say "chavut rami" even for more than three handbreadths, and so the law was given to Moses at Sinai, nevertheless, here in an alleyway we do not say this. For we require that the crossbeam be within the walls of the alleyway, and if it is distanced by three handbreadths even in height, it is not within the walls of the alleyway. (Tosafot 9a, s.v. "She'ein," and this is the intention of the Magen Avraham, section 21).

Know that there are measurements of tefachim (handbreadths) and amot (cubits) that are precise and those that are more generous, and the difference between them is half a finger for every cubit. (See there, note 22.) And this is the language of the Rambam at the end of Chapter 17: "The finger used for measurement everywhere is the width of the thumb of the hand, and the tefach is four fingers. And any cubit mentioned anywhere, whether in relation to Shabbat, Sukkah, or kilayim (forbidden mixtures) – is a cubit of six tefachim. Sometimes they measure with a cubit of six tefachim that are tightly measured, and sometimes they measure with a cubit of six tefachim that are loosely measured, and in both cases, it is to be stringent. How so? The length of a mavoi (alleyway) is measured with four loosely measured cubits, and its height is twenty tightly measured cubits. The width of a breach is ten tightly measured cubits, and similarly for sukkah and kilayim." End of quote. According to this, in the Shabbat boundary, which is two thousand cubits, there is a difference of a thousand fingers, which are 250 tefachim, close to 42 cubits. And behold, the Rambam mentioned that it is so everywhere, and he did not need to mention it in the context of boundaries. But the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, section 26, wrote to be stringent here, and did not mention this at all regarding boundaries. And even more puzzling, in section 396, the Tur and Shulchan Aruch wrote regarding the four cubits given to each person – they are given generously, so why do they not follow the stringency to give only the precise measurement? This requires further investigation.

The Ba'al HaMaor, the Rosh, the Tur, and the Shulchan Aruch ruled like the Rambam, while the Rashba (Ba'al HaKoteret) and the Ritva ruled that all measurements concerning kilayim (mixed species) are always generous, and all measurements concerning sukkah and alleyway (mavoi) are always exacting. This is because in most laws concerning kilayim, generous measurements are a stringency, and in sukkah and alleyway, exacting measurements are mostly a stringency. Therefore, we are not concerned if in some laws of kilayim the generous measurement leads to leniency, and in some laws of sukkah and alleyway the exacting measurement leads to leniency. This also appears from Rashi's words at the beginning of Eruvin (3a, s.v. 'these'), see there. The Rif completely omitted this, and the Ba'al HaMaor wondered about this, and the Ramban did not respond at all. Also, I do not understand, for in the case of kilayim and sukkah, which are from the Torah, it is proper to be stringent, but in the case of an alleyway, which is rabbinic, in every case of doubt we are lenient in rabbinic matters, as is common in the Talmud and poskim that a doubt in their [rabbinic] matters is lenient. And it is obvious that the reason we follow this way here and that way there is because of doubt. For if it were clear to us that it was stated to Moses at Sinai that the measurements are generous or exacting, we would not have permission to follow the opposite even as a stringency. Rather, it is certain that it was stated in a general manner, and if so, it is a rabbinic doubt and lenient, and this requires further examination.

What appears to me in my humble opinion regarding this matter is that there is no doubt at all. It was said to Moses at Sinai that whether the measurements are broad or exact, they are valid in any case. The reason is that the Torah was not given to the ministering angels, and it is impossible for the measurements of all people to be exactly the same. There are healthy individuals who can press their fingers together very tightly, resulting in a narrow measurement, and there are weak individuals who cannot press as tightly, resulting in a broader measurement. Regarding such matters, it is said that "it is impossible to be exact." Certainly, everyone must measure according to their own ability and habit. Certainly, when a person measures a place where they can walk, they measure generously for their own benefit. Therefore, the four cubits that the Torah grants each person on Shabbat to carry, as mentioned in Siman 349 from the verse "each person should remain in their place," are presumably measured generously. This is why it was ruled in Siman 396 that the measurements are generous. Also, when measuring the limit within which a person can walk, the measurement is generous to allow for movement, which is why it was not mentioned that the measurements should be exact. 

However, in a public alleyway, which is used by many, it is impossible to rely on the measurement of an individual alone, and there is no loss in being stringent. The sages said we should measure stringently because there are certainly people for whom that is their exact measurement, and we cannot be lenient for some at the expense of others. On the contrary, we should be stringent for some for the sake of others. Only Maimonides and his supporters hold that every law should be scrutinized in detail, while Rashbam and his supporters hold that one should follow the majority of laws. Similarly, in the case of a sukkah and kilayim (mixed species), where the matter also affects many others—whether it concerns the prohibition of kilayim or the fulfillment of the mitzvah of sukkah—we are compelled to be stringent for some because it is fundamentally their measurement. Therefore, the Rif omitted this entirely because, fundamentally, the measurement is valid either way, and he did not consider it necessary to mention it at all. (This is how it seems to me in my humble opinion.)

And it also appears to me in my humble opinion that in the case of a single alleyway, even according to the Rambam, the measurement should be done in only one way, either precisely or generously. And even though from the language of the Rambam it slightly implies that we should follow each specific rule stringently, perhaps the Rambam's intention was regarding separate alleyways, because it does not make sense to say that in the same alleyway sometimes we do it one way and sometimes another way. However, since we explained that both measurements are valid, it can be said that even in a single alleyway this is the case, and this requires further investigation. (And the Gaon Rabbi Akiva Eiger is certain that this is due to doubt, and he wrote that in a single alleyway it should be done in one manner, and he brought proof from Tosafot. See there. And there is no proof from Tosafot, as it seems they hold like Rashi and the Rashba, that in an alleyway and a sukkah, all are precise as we wrote. However, according to his words that it is a doubt, it is certainly so, but according to our words, it requires further investigation, and pay attention to this).

It is explained from the Talmud and the poskim (decisors of Jewish law) that a mavoi (alleyway) must be longer than it is wide, and a courtyard must be square. A mavoi that is as long as it is wide is considered a courtyard, and a courtyard that is longer than it is wide is considered a mavoi. This is the language of the Gemara: "If its length is greater than its width, it is a mavoi... and if not, it is a courtyard." (Eruvin 12b). The reason, it seems to me, is that a courtyard typically belongs to one person, and usually, every courtyard is square, as are most buildings. However, a mavoi, which passes by courtyards, necessarily needs to be very long, and its width is not allowed to expand much into the street, as we see with our own eyes that every street's length is much greater than its width. Therefore, they also said that a mavoi must be at least four cubits long (according to Abaye, and this is the halacha). In a courtyard, we do not find this measurement, and the reason is also that a courtyard, being for an individual, can be made small or large as desired, unlike a mavoi, which is for the public. If it is not at least four cubits long, it does not allow for public passage. This is regarding length, but in width, it can be less, even down to four handbreadths or even three, as will be explained with G-d's help.

From the conditions of an alleyway that can be permitted with a side post (lechi) or a crossbeam (korah), the walls should not be lower than ten handbreadths, and the width of the open fourth side should not be more than ten cubits, and its length should not be less than four cubits. Regarding its height, if it is permitted with a side post, there is no limit to its height, for even if the walls are as high as the heavens, it does not concern us, since the permission and recognition are at the ground level. However, if it is permitted with a crossbeam, the space beneath the crossbeam should not be more than twenty cubits high. On this, it is taught at the beginning of our tractate: "An alleyway that is higher than twenty cubits is invalid," because since the recognition is the crossbeam which is above, our Sages have determined that higher than twenty cubits the eye does not notice it, similar to the sukkah. And we conclude in the Gemara (Eruvin 3b) that it refers to the space of the alleyway, meaning that the crossbeam can be exactly at twenty cubits and above, for only the space should not be more than twenty cubits.
