If one of the conditions is missing, it cannot be permitted with a side post or crossbeam but only with a doorframe (tzurat hapetach), for a doorframe is effective for everything, as it is almost like a complete partition. (This is the opinion of the Rambam in Chapter 17, who also holds that for a height of less than ten handbreadths, the doorframe is effective. But the Rashba disagrees, holding that less than ten handbreadths does not have the status of a partition. See there in the Mishneh Torah. In my humble opinion, it seems that the Rambam also agrees that the doorframe needs to be at a height of ten handbreadths, and it is only the side partitions that we do not worry about if they are not ten handbreadths high. According to this, it can be said that there is no disagreement between the Rambam and the Rashba, and examine this well).

The sages of blessed memory said at the beginning of the tractate (there), that a beam that is higher than twenty cubits, if he made an "amaltara" for it, which means decorations and carvings that cause everyone to look at it - it is valid. Because the disqualification, as we said, is that there is no recognition above twenty cubits, but when there are decorations - there is recognition. And it seems that it specifically requires protruding decorations, like those made of wood and the like, for indeed the heichal (Temple) had amaltaras, as we learned in the third chapter (Mishnah 7) of Middot, and Rashi explained that they were made of wood there. And in Shulchan Aruch, section 26, it says that a decoration made of plaster is acceptable, but in my humble opinion, this is not so, and indeed it is clearly stated in the Gemara there, where it says: "What is an amaltara? One said bird nests, and one said cedar wood" there. And in the Aruch, it is written that in Greek, a beam is called an amaltara. Also, what is written there, that even a decoration on the wall is effective, I do not know from where this is derived. (And this is a certain gloss in the Shulchan Aruch and it is not from the Rema, and see the Mishneh L'Melech chapter 17, halacha 15, what he wrote in the name of the Rashba, and it requires further study and scrutiny).

There is another solution: to elevate the area beneath the beam so that there is not more than twenty cubits from there to the beam. And this is the language of the Rambam in Chapter 17, Law 16: "If its height is more than twenty cubits, and one comes to reduce it with a beam placed below, it needs to have a width of one handbreadth like the beam." Since the recognition needs to be beneath the beam, it suffices to elevate only there, so that anyone standing on it will see the beam. From the language of the Rambam, it appears that it specifically needs a beam below, and similarly, the language of the Tur and Shulchan Aruch is that if it was higher than twenty cubits and one built a structure beneath the beam, a width of one handbreadth is sufficient. They used the term "building." Some have written that the same applies to earth, but there is a concern that when trodden upon, it might diminish from the required measure (Magen Avraham, section 24). And indeed, Rashi explained this in the Gemara (Eruvin 4a: "And he comes to reduce it by making a structure or earth"), but from their language, it appears that it specifically refers to a beam of wood or stone. The reason is that earth will certainly diminish, and it is mentioned at the beginning of our tractate that people rely on each other and do not mention [this concern]. However, if it is not ten handbreadths high, and one excavates the ground to complete it to ten, one needs to excavate four cubits in length along the entire width of the alley. Here, one handbreadth does not suffice, since these are not actual walls, we need the measure of walls like the length of a valid alley (Rashi 5a). And it seems that even if the excavation is less than three handbreadths from the wall, it is valid, as we say at the beginning of Sukkah regarding a sukkah.

A courtyard is not permitted with a side post or a crossbeam unless there are houses and courtyards open to it—two courtyards to the alley and two houses to each courtyard. The reason for this leniency with an alley as opposed to a courtyard, allowing a single side post or crossbeam, is due to the multitude of inhabitants, and the usage is minimal, so it does not need as much enclosure, as mentioned in paragraph 2. Therefore, if there are not two courtyards and two houses to each courtyard, there is not a multitude of inhabitants, and it is similar to a courtyard (Magen Avraham, section 25, in the name of the Rashba). Also, none of the entrances of these courtyards and houses should be less than four handbreadths, as less than four handbreadths is not considered at all. Additionally, the people living there must need an eruv, such as if they eat there, since we hold that the place of eating determines the need for an eruv, as will be explained in section 370. For example, even if one house belongs to the father and the other to the son, and the son receives his sustenance from the father, if he eats on his own, they need an eruv if the father eats in his house and the son in the other house. All this is to ensure a multitude of inhabitants with a multitude of usages, thereby reducing the usages in the alley. Therefore, some require that the eruv be specifically through the alley, meaning when the courtyards are not open to each other. If they are open to each other, they can make an eruv together through the courtyards without the alley, and it is considered as one house and one courtyard. The Rosh, the Tur, and the Mordechai argue on this, holding that even if they are open to each other and make an eruv through the courtyards, it is permitted, as this is also considered a multitude of inhabitants. In this, everyone agrees that we do not require specifically Jews in both courtyards and both houses of each courtyard; even if one side is non-Jews and the other side Jews, it is permitted, as there are usages. If there are no houses and courtyards open to it, its law is like that of a courtyard, and it requires a four-handbreadth board or two boards. Similarly, if any of the previously stated conditions are lacking, it is not permitted.

However, an alleyway that does not have an entrance width of 3 handbreadths, even though its interior is very wide but narrows at the fourth wall so that the entrance is not even 3 handbreadths wide, does not require any permit, as it is not considered an open side but rather as closed. And some say that up to 4 handbreadths, no permit is needed. This is the opinion of the Ra'avad, the Rosh, and the Tur, and the first opinion is that of the Rambam. It is clear that the same law applies to a courtyard according to the first opinion, but according to the second opinion, there is a difference between an alleyway and a courtyard. In a courtyard, even if it does not have 4 handbreadths, it requires a correction, as this is explicitly implied in the Gemara. (12. And so writes the P"Y)

The definition of a courtyard has already been explained: its length should be equal to its width. But if its length is greater than its width, it is considered like an alleyway and can be permitted with a side-post or a cross-beam. This is the ruling of the Rambam, the Tur, and the Shulchan Aruch in section 27, as derived from the Gemara, as I have written.

There is a question regarding this: How can it be considered like an alleyway, for there are no houses and courtyards opening into it? Our teacher, the Rama, answered that since it is not close to the public domain but opens into an alleyway, and the alleyway opens into the public domain, it is sufficient. This means that the stringency applied to an alleyway, which if it does not have houses and courtyards opening into it, it is not permitted with a side-post and cross-beam, is due to its proximity to the public domain. But a courtyard considered like an alleyway, since it is not close to the public domain, we do not apply this particular stringency of requiring houses and courtyards.

(And so wrote the Tosafot in Eruvin 12b, end of "Houses": "Because an alleyway is closer to the public domain than a courtyard, it requires houses and courtyards." This means, although in all other aspects we are stricter with a courtyard, as written in section 2, in this particular aspect, it is not so. There is no specific measure for its length being greater than its width, even if it is slightly longer, it is considered greater. Be aware that the Maggid Mishneh in chapter 17, halacha 8, brings a dispute regarding whether its width being greater than its length makes it like an alleyway or a courtyard. From the Gemara in Eruvin 7a, it seems clear that both are the same. See Turei Zahav, section 162, and "length" is defined by its entrance, and note this well).

Rabbi Moshe Isserles wrote in Section 26: "And there are those who say that nowadays the practice is to correct all alleyways with a 'tzurat hapetach' (a form of a doorway), because all our alleyways have the status of courtyards. The common custom in all these countries is to correct it by using a rope tied across the width of the alleyway. The law of this rope is not as a beam, since it is not a handbreadth wide, and it is only effective as a 'tzurat hapetach,' which is valid above even with a reed. Therefore, care must be taken to place two posts under the rope, each ten handbreadths high, aligned under the rope, and then it is effective even in an open alleyway as a 'tzurat hapetach,' or even in a courtyard, and in any place where a 'tzurat hapetach' is effective, as we wrote above at the end of Siman 362." End quote.

Behold, it is hidden from us how the configuration of the streets was in the times of our master, the Rema, and generations before him, for even with them, it was not as in the time of the Talmud. Therefore, they wrote that [the streets] do not have the status of an alleyway, and they were stringent to treat them like a courtyard, and even more stringent than a courtyard, since the courtyards were adjacent to the public domain. They were stringent to make a form of a doorway. Some wrote that all the cities were surrounded by a wall, and were settled and then surrounded. According to this, if the entrance is not wider than ten cubits or more, two side-posts like a courtyard are sufficient. Others wrote that even if they were not surrounded by a wall, their status is like a courtyard. Nevertheless, they require a form of a doorway (see Magen Avraham, subsection 27) even if it is less than ten [cubits].

In earlier times, Jews used to reside in a section of the city designated for them, which was called the Jewish Quarter, as is still the case today in the country of Morocco. However, nowadays in our countries, we are scattered throughout the city together with others, and we do not have alleys but only houses and courtyards, and from the courtyards, we go out to the public domain. In the country of Lithuania, there are hundreds and thousands of houses without any courtyard at all, and they exit their homes directly into the public domain. Most of our streets are much wider than ten cubits, and therefore it is necessary to make the form of a doorway at all the corners. In every city, there are places where the small street at the edge of the city is not ten cubits wide, and it requires two side-posts, as we do not have alleys for various reasons explained, and we make the form of a doorway at all corners of the city. We place them at the very edge of the city so that there is no gap from the place of the form of the doorway to the houses or fences greater than ten cubits. Even if it is less than ten cubits, it still requires two side-posts. The beam of the form of the doorway extends to the side-post, and it is necessary to place a second side-post opposite it near the houses. Since it is at the edge of the city, it is not included within the general city, which the forms of the doorway encompass. Similarly, in all the edges of the city where there is a breach leading outside the city less than ten cubits wide, two side-posts suffice. If it is more than ten cubits, it requires the form of a doorway. The measure of ten cubits according to our country's (Russia) measurement is two and a half sazhen. All this is based on the principle that we do not have a complete public domain, as we elaborated on in Siman 345. According to the Magen Avraham in Siman 327, even less than ten cubits requires the form of a doorway, but we do not practice this way, as we consider it like a courtyard even leniently, as discussed later in Siman 365, Paragraph 6.

And it has already been explained that in the case of a "tzurat hapetach" (a symbolic doorway), the crossbeam above does not need to touch the side posts. Therefore, if there are some protrusions coming out of the walls that are ten handbreadths high from the ground, and they are not three handbreadths high from the ground, one can rely on them for the posts of the "tzurat hapetach" on either side. Similarly, for partitions less than ten cubits wide, as mentioned. Certainly, the reeds used to fence gardens are suitable for partitions and for the sides of the "tzurat hapetach," and the upper beam should be stretched directly opposite the protrusions or the reeds themselves, so that it is not to the side. 

There is an opinion that one must be careful when stretching the upper beam over the roof of a building and stretching it opposite the side posts placed at the sides of the wall, that the roof's protrusion, known as "kapaz," should not extend below the upper beam. If it does, the protrusion interrupts between the upper beam and the sides. (Taz, Subsection 19) 

However, there is an opposing opinion which brings proof from a dome, where the curvature interrupts between the upper part and the sides, and yet it is permitted, as proven in the Gemara (11b). From this, it is proven that the interruption does not matter. (Taz, Subsection 64) 

Although one could differentiate, saying that this applies to a single construction, whereas here the roof is a separate construction and thus an interruption, still, what basis do we have to make such a distinction? 

Whoever wishes to satisfy the first opinion should make a hole in the protrusion opposite the side posts, so that they align directly under the upper beam without interruption. (Taz, ibid.)

And we have already written at the end of Siman 362 that there is an opinion that prohibits if the side posts are three handbreadths away from the wall, similar to a side post which is invalid in such cases, and we have explained there that this is not so. (And also the Taz in this Siman, Subsection 10, disagrees with the Taz Beit Yosef who was stringent in this matter, see there.)

Rabbeinu the Beit Yosef wrote in Section 29: "An alleyway where one side ends at the sea and the other side ends at a public trash heap requires nothing, because a public trash heap is not usually cleared, and we are not concerned that the sea might recede and expose dry land." And Rabbeinu the Rema wrote: "There are those who disagree and hold that we do worry that the sea might recede and expose dry land, and thus there would be no partition."

However, if there remains a slope that rises ten handbreadths over four cubits at the place where the sea's edge was, it is clear that this itself constitutes a partition. (Taz, end of Section 20) There are those who prohibit even in such cases, arguing that people might carry up to the sea's edge as they were accustomed to, and thus it would be considered a karmelit even if there are partitions from the sea, since they were not made for residential purposes. Therefore, even the form of a doorway does not help in the place that was previously the sea’s edge, but a complete partition is required because people might carry beyond it. (Magen Avraham, Section 131)

This is an excessive stringency, and we only worry about the sea receding and not rivers. (ibid.) It is only necessary that the riverbank be very close to the end of the alleyway. If it is far from there, the breach must be repaired. If it is less than ten cubits, boards suffice, but if it is more than ten cubits, a form of a doorway is required. (ibid.) It is clear that rivers that tend to dry up in the summer are forbidden, (ibid.) and if the shore rises ten handbreadths over four cubits, it is permitted as stated. When there are bridges, a form of a doorway is needed if they are more than ten cubits, and if less, two boards suffice.

And know that rivers in the winter when they freeze—certainly the partition is nullified, as people walk on it as if it were land. (There) And there are those who wish to prohibit also in the summer, because of the freezing in the winter, (Taz there) and many disagree with this, and there are even those who wish to permit in the winter. But the main ruling is that in the winter it is prohibited and in the summer it is permitted. And in the winter, besides being prohibited because of the nullification of the partition, even if we say that this is not a nullification of the partition, since it is used for public walking, we say ‘the public comes and nullifies the partition’, for although it is explained in the Gemara (22b) that the Rabbis do not hold ‘the public comes and nullifies the partition’, our Rabbis, the Ba’alei HaTosafot, have already written there, (end of s.v. 'dilma') that a partition made by Heaven, even the Rabbis agree that we say ‘the public comes and nullifies the partition’. And if it is difficult, for if so, how do we consider the sea a partition, since ships pass through it, there are those who say that indeed it refers to a place where ships do not pass, (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 30) and this is a clear difficulty. However, the reason is that ships do not nullify the partition and it is not comparable to public walking. (Rabbi Shimon Aelian in Responsa Knesset Yechezkel, chapter 2, and so wrote Magen Avraham himself in chapter 345, subparagraph 14). And some of the great ones said that Tosafot did not mean to say that in a partition made by Heaven, even the Rabbis agree that we say ‘the public comes and nullifies the partition’, for it is clearly proven there in the Gemara that even in a partition made by Heaven, we do not say ‘the public comes, etc.’, (for it is asked there in the Tel) rather, the intent of Tosafot is to say that this is not a complete partition regarding more than two se’ah, for this is not called surrounded for dwelling. (Knesset Yechezkel there and Rabbi Shimon Aelian there). And there are those who say that in a place where it is not convenient for use, we do not say ‘the public comes and nullifies the partition’, and therefore in the Tel that is gathered there in the Gemara, we do not say this for this reason. (Rabbi Shimon Aelian there and see Chatam Sofer, chapter 189).

Furthermore, it appears to me, in my humble opinion, that even if we understand the words of Tosafot literally, that in the case of a partition made by Heaven we say "the public comes and nullifies the partition," nonetheless, with one partition, they agree that we do not say this. This is clear from their earlier words (22a, s.v. "Kashe"), where they wrote that even according to Rabbi Yehuda, who holds "the public comes and nullifies partitions" even for partitions made by man, and this is their language: "Alternatively, even if he holds that three partitions are from the Torah – the public does not come and nullify the third partition, since there are two complete partitions," end quote. Thus, they wrote this even according to Rabbi Yehuda, and certainly according to the Rabbis. Furthermore, there is proof from the words of the Ba'al HaMaor there, who wrote, and this is his language: "Rabbi Yochanan holds like Rabbi Yehuda, that the public comes and nullifies the partition, and two partitions are from the Torah… because there are not even two partitions, since the public breaches them in all directions, and there was not even one partition that the public did not breach," end quote. Thus, it is explicit that even according to Rabbi Yehuda, if there were one partition that the public did not breach, we would not say "the public comes and nullifies partitions," and certainly according to the Rabbis. (And with this, it resolves what was questioned on Tosafot regarding a mound that gradually slopes, and consider this carefully.)

It appears to me, in my humble opinion, that the principle "the public comes and nullifies the partition" (אתי רבים ומבטלי מחיצה) applies only when it is open to a public domain and not when it is open to a karmelit (a semi-public domain). Since we hold in our times that we do not have a true public domain (רשות הרבים), there is thus no concern for "the public comes and nullifies the partition" in our case. A proof for this is from the words of Rabbeinu Yonatan, who wrote in the Mishnah regarding the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis in the case of the partitions around wells (פסי ביראות). Rabbi Yehuda held that the public comes, etc., while the Rabbis held that the public does not come, etc. This is his language: "And the Sages say it is not necessary, meaning that the public does not come and nullify the four partitions of the well enclosures… for if not for the partitions, the Rabbis would agree that the public nullifies the partition, as we see in the previous dispute where one has two houses on either side of the public domain, etc." End of quote. It is thus clear that the reason the Rabbis prohibit in the case of two houses on either side of the public domain is due to the principle "the public comes and nullifies the partitions."

Now, in the first chapter (6b), the Sages taught: How does one make an eruv in a public domain? One makes a form of a doorway here, etc. And it asks, can one make an eruv in a public domain? But it was taught: If one has two houses on either side of the public domain… one cannot make an eruv in a public domain like this. And it concludes: How does one make an eruv for alleyways that are open to a public domain? Clearly, any area that is not a complete public domain, even if it is open to a public domain, can be merged by means of a form of a doorway and a side post or a crossbeam. And according to Rabbeinu Yonatan, the reason the Rabbis prohibit is because the public nullifies the partitions. In any case, regarding alleyways that are open, the public does not nullify the partitions, and certainly not in a complete karmelit.

While it is true that the Tosafot do not explain the case of the two houses as he does, but rather due to the Torah law of three partitions, still according to him, this is certainly the law. And we do not find anyone who disagrees with him on this particular point. And from the very essence of the discussion there (22b), it is explicitly clear that this concern only exists in a public domain and not in a karmelit. (And we have proof from the Jerusalem Talmud, chapter one, halacha one, that with one partition we do not say that the public comes, etc., for it says there: "And this mound of Rabbi Chanin does not require a form of a doorway, as it gradually rises ten handbreadths within three handbreadths. They made an enactment to allow the houses below." End of quote. It is explicitly permitted on this mound, although the public walks there, and this is due to the one partition. The commentators are pressed there, and study this well.) (And from Mahari there is no proof at all that whenever there is a form of a doorway, we do not say the public comes, etc.)

A passageway that has one long side and one short side, even if the long side does not exceed the short side by four cubits as the measure of a passageway, nevertheless, he should not place the crossbeam on the long side but rather opposite the short side. And he should not place the crossbeam diagonally, intending to use it up to the end on this side and up to the end on that side, because the crossbeam serves as a marker, and diagonally it is not a marker. One who sees that the residents of the passageway extend beyond the short wall will say that it is permitted to use the public domain or a carmelite, because this extra part does not appear to be part of the passageway. And even if he sets up two side posts, one next to the long side and one next to the short side, and the side post serves as a partition, nevertheless, it is forbidden, as we have already explained that even with a side post there needs to be a marker, and diagonally it is not a marker, although some permit with side posts. (Bach and see Magen Avraham Section 32) But with a form of a doorway, it is certainly permitted, and he can extend it diagonally, and use up to the end on the short side and up to the end on the long side, because it is considered a complete partition, and even diagonally it is a partition. And what we have said, that one should not place the crossbeam diagonally, this is in such cases of long and short sides, but within the passageway, he can place it diagonally if he wishes, and use up to the end of the crossbeam on this side and up to the end of the crossbeam on that side, since there is a wall opposite a wall - it serves as a marker even diagonally, and there is no stumbling block in this.

If one places a side post (lechi) in the middle of an alley, and outside this side post towards the entrance of the alley there are courtyards open to the alley, and they also made a side post at the entrance of the alley, the inner side post does not serve to divide the alley into two separate alleys, such that these courtyards and those courtyards would each make their own eruv (joining of domains). Rather, they prohibit each other until they make an eruv together. For the statement that a side post is considered a partition (mechitza) does not mean it is a complete partition to entirely separate them from each other. Rather, it serves as a partition in terms of completing the fourth side (of the alley), but it is not a complete partition to divide one half of the alley from the other half. And if there is no courtyard at all beyond the inner side post, one may carry up to the inner side post and no further, for it is evident that they made this side post the primary one. Even if they placed another side post at the end of the alley, if they did not explicitly remove or nullify the first one, who says they rely on the outer one? Perhaps they rely on the inner one. (This is my opinion.)

If there are houses beyond the inner side post, and they did not place a side post at the end of the alley, the houses beyond the side post are certainly prohibited from carrying, since they do not have a side post. However, they do not prohibit those who live before the side post, and the inner residents are permitted to use the area from the side post inward if they made an eruv among themselves. Since the outer ones did not make a side post and cannot carry in the alley, it is as if they have withdrawn from the alley and do not prohibit the inner residents. This is not similar to two courtyards, one within the other, where sometimes the lack of an eruv in one can prohibit the other, as will be explained in Siman 378. There, too, it only prohibits if one has the right of passage over the other, like an inner courtyard over an outer one, but not the reverse. Additionally, this applies to courtyards, but in an alley, those who did not make a side post are not considered as residents of the alley, and it is as if they have withdrawn from it, and the end of the alley is considered to be at the side post.

But if they made two side-posts (passim) in the middle of the alleyway (mavoi), one on each side of the alleyway, or a four-handbreadth post (pas) on one side, or if it is wider than ten cubits and they made a form of a doorway (tzurat hapetach), even if there are courtyards beyond the correction and they also made an outer correction at the entrance of the alleyway with a side-post (lechi) or a crossbeam (korah) - they are divided from each other, and each part makes an eruv for itself, and they do not prohibit each other. The reason for this is that since a side-post (lechi) would have sufficed, and they added to the correction with two side-posts, or a four-handbreadth post, or a form of a doorway, it is understood that their intention was to completely separate from each other. And this is effective in these cases, for are they not permitted to separate? However, with the necessary correction, this does not constitute separation unless they added to the correction. (See Taz, section 23, and see further in Siman 392).

And just as the law applies to a side post (lechi), so too does it apply to a crossbeam (korah). One can place a crossbeam in the middle of an alleyway, and carrying is only permitted up to the crossbeam. If there are residents beyond that point and they also placed a crossbeam at the end of the alleyway, they prohibit each other from carrying until they join in an eruv. If they did not make a crossbeam, they are removed from the alleyway, and those who remain make an eruv for themselves. 

And know that all these matters apply when that half of the alleyway qualified with a side post or crossbeam has all the characteristics of an alleyway, meaning its length is greater than its width, and its length is not less than four cubits, and there are houses and courtyards opening into it. But if this is not the case, this half does not have the status of an alleyway but rather the status of a courtyard, and it requires either a side post of four cubits or two small side posts on either side.

From the laws that have been explained regarding an alleyway (mavoi), we learn that the same applies to a single courtyard (chatzer) that has many houses, and they want to divide from each other, with each half of the courtyard making its own eruv. They need to make an enhancement beyond the necessary correction. The necessary correction is a board (pas) of four cubits or two small boards, so now they need to make two boards of four cubits each or a doorway structure (tzurat hapetach). In our cities, which are enclosed by a doorway structure on all sides, there is nothing to divide them into two, since the doorway structure is the necessary correction, and they need to make a complete partition to divide from each other, or if there is a breach of less than ten cubits, they need to make a doorway structure there, as this is not the necessary correction, since it would suffice to have two boards or a board of four cubits. It is possible that even with a breach wider than ten cubits, they can divide from each other with a doorway structure, because it is like a complete partition, and therefore, even though it is necessary, it is effective, and this requires further consideration. (And see Magen Avraham, section 34, regarding a city surrounded by a wall and gates, that they can only divide from each other with a partition, and it implies that a doorway structure does not suffice, and perhaps he did not delve into this, and the doorway structure is like a partition, and further investigation is needed.)

A courtyard that is twenty cubits wide at its entrance and one wishes to divide it into two, so that each part will not exceed ten cubits and necessitate the form of a doorway, it does not suffice to divide it in the middle with a rod or any partition, even if it is four handbreadths wide, because we say 'the air from this side and the air from that side nullify it', and it is as if it does not exist. Rather, the sages said - one makes a post ten handbreadths high along four cubits and places it lengthwise along the courtyard. Since it has the length of the measure of a courtyard, the airspaces do not nullify it, even when each side of the airspace is greater than it, like here, where each side has an airspace of more than four cubits. The reasoning behind this is that with complete partitions, it is not applicable to say 'the air from this side and the air from that side nullify it', because partitions are a law given to Moses at Sinai in their general and specific aspects, and just as we do not say there is a break less than three between rod and rod, because it is a halachic tradition that it is considered as joined, so too in all matters of partitions. Only when making a gap between partition and partition do we say that the airspaces nullify the gap. Therefore, it is required that this post of four cubits be placed lengthwise along the courtyard, for if it were placed widthwise, the airspaces would nullify it. But now, having placed it lengthwise along the courtyard and made it into two courtyards, this post serves as the third wall for each courtyard, and with a partition, the airspaces do not nullify it. Consequently, each part must have the status of a courtyard with houses and courtyards open to it, and all conditions of a courtyard. Therefore, if one validates them with a side post - a side post must be placed in each one, and if one validates them with a crossbeam - a long crossbeam of twenty cubits can be placed over both, provided that the crossbeam is not more than three handbreadths away from the dividing post, since it is considered a partition for each one. (This seems to be the explanation of the matter in my humble opinion, and it also seems to me from the words of the Rashba in the holy city brought by the Acharonim in Siman 39, and this is his language: "From now on, the air from here and there does not nullify, as the air does not nullify the walls of the courtyard" - end quote, and examine well).

And it is written in the Tosafot, the Rosh, the Tur, and the Shulchan Aruch, section 33, that from the board to the middle wall of the alleyway, it has the status of a crooked alleyway, for these two alleyways bend, and in the middle, they are open at both ends to the public domain. End quote. The explanation of the matter is that it is true that we said that this board divides the alleyway into two alleyways, but this is if the board reached the middle wall, such as if the entire length of the alleyway is not more than four cubits, or if the board is longer than four cubits. But when the board is four cubits and the length of the alleyway is more, then it only divides it until the end of the four cubits of the length of the board. And this is certain, if the residents from there and beyond do not worry about the permissibility of carrying - these alleyways can be divided, each one by itself. But if they also want the permissibility of carrying and to be included in the eruv, and for them, the entire alleyway is one, it is considered like a crooked alleyway. Therefore, they must make a form of a doorway at the bend, and on the other side a sidepost or a beam, as will be explained in the next section.

But there are some of our rabbis who say that this does not at all have the status of a bent alleyway (mavoi akum), as a bent alleyway only exists when there are two sides facing the public domain, such as the east and south, and similar cases, making it open through. But if both openings are on one side, like here - we have no concern with it. And even though it will be explained in the next section that even when bent like the shape of the letter "ח" it is considered a bent alleyway, it must be said that one opening exits to another side. (Ritzba in Tosafot there) And the opinion of our teacher, the Rema, in paragraph 33, is that even according to the earlier opinion, this only applies when there is more than ten cubits from the post to the middle wall. But within ten cubits, and certainly less - it is only considered a regular opening. And even though in a completely bent alleyway, even within ten cubits it is considered like an open alleyway, this applies to two complete alleyways, but not in cases like these. (And the Magen Avraham in section 136 wrote that this applies to two sides of the public domain. And I am puzzled, as this is the opinion of the Ritzba that we wrote, who wrote explicitly even with more than ten cubits, but the Tosafot and the Rosh do not hold this way. Therefore, it seems to my humble opinion as I have written, and it also seems clearly from the Taz in section 126, and the words of the Magen Avraham require further study).

And the Ritva in his novellae disagrees with everything that has been explained, for he interprets that this side post (pas) does not make it into two alleyways at all, and it is only to reduce the width which is more than ten [cubits], and we do not say that 'the air of this side and that side comes and nullifies it,' for with a side post that is four cubits long, we do not say this reasoning as with partitions. And according to this, it remains one alleyway (as before), and one side post suffices, and similarly if the beam is much higher than the side post, since the side post is not considered a partition. And he wonders about the Raavad who requires that the beam not be higher than three handbreadths from the side post, see there. And the reason of the Raavad is that he holds like Tosafot and the Rosh, that it is divided into two alleyways, and therefore the Rosh brought his words, see there.

There is another solution for an alleyway that is twenty cubits wide, which is to distance two cubits from the wall and make a strip that is three cubits wide, and do the same on the other side, leaving an opening that is ten cubits wide. Another side post is needed, for these do not suffice since they are far from the wall, and the side post must not be more than three handbreadths from the wall. Similarly, one can distance one cubit and make a strip of one and a half cubits, then distance another cubit and make a strip of one and a half cubits, and do the same on the other side, with two strips of one and a half cubits and two spaces of one cubit. Similarly, one can distance two cubits and two handbreadths and make a strip of two cubits and four handbreadths, and do the same on the other side, and so on. Another side post is needed for the reason explained. The general rule is that the strip must be more than the space between the wall and the strip because otherwise, the airspace from both sides will nullify it, as the two airspaces will exceed it, and each airspace is equivalent to it. Therefore, it must be greater than the airspace on one side, for in such cases, the two airspaces do not combine to nullify it, as it is stronger than each of them individually.

This board that we mentioned does not need to be a single plank or one continuous piece to reduce the width of the alleyway's airspace. Even if it is made of several reeds, each less than three handbreadths apart, it is still permitted, because any gap less than three handbreadths is considered as if it is closed (lavud), and it is as if it were a single, continuous piece. How much more so if one places two or three boards next to each other or more. One must only be careful not to leave the large entrance of the alleyway and walk through the smaller ones, for if they do so, the correction of the alleyway is nullified, and the side post that was set up there is nullified, and this alleyway is found to be without correction (Rashi 10: s.v. dilma).

The Ritva wrote that if the alleyway is corrected with a crossbeam, and the crossbeam extends from wall to wall, it does not matter if they walk through here or there. However, we are discussing a case where the crossbeam does not reach the wall but only the distant plank from the wall, and the two cubits that are free from the wall to the plank do not have a crossbeam over them. Therefore, we are concerned that if they walk through these two cubits, there is no recognition of the crossbeam. And although, according to this, the crossbeam is not on both walls of the alleyway, it can be said that since it is on the plank, it is considered as if it is on the wall. According to this, with a side post, it should also be said that they should not walk in the airspace where there is no side post. Generally, we are not concerned that they will leave the large entrance and walk through the small one, for why would they do so, since it does not shorten the walk. This concern only arises when there is a gap in the side walls, as then it shortens the walk, and this will be explained in Siman 365.

An alleyway that is level from within and slopes toward the public domain, or is level with the public domain and slopes inward, if the slope gradually rises up to ten handbreadths within a span of four cubits - it is considered as if it were fully vertical, and this itself constitutes a partition, requiring no other correction. However, if it rises within a span of five cubits - it is not considered a partition, but rather like the rest of the public domain or a karmelit, since it is easy to traverse and not vertical. (See Magen Avraham section 140, who writes that it must not be frequently traversed by the public, for if it is, it nullifies the partition. He later wrote that the general understanding of the poskim does not support this view, and suggested that perhaps it requires traversing by sixty myriads. His words are puzzling, and as I have explained in paragraphs 49 and 50, this is not necessary. See there for further detail, which supports our position, and examine it thoroughly).

Even though a "form of a doorway" (tzurat ha-petach) is considered like a partition, nonetheless, for a bona fide public domain (reshut ha-rabim), a "form of a doorway" does not help to turn it into a private domain (reshut ha-yachid) to allow carrying there. The reason for this is that although from the Torah's perspective, making a "form of a doorway" on one side of a public domain, and certainly on both sides, would prevent someone who throws from within it to a private domain from being liable, nevertheless, rabbinically, they did not permit making an eruv in an actual public domain by using a "form of a doorway." This is not surprising, for we also did not permit an enclosure for a valley (bika’ah) using a "form of a doorway" on all sides, as stated in Siman 362, Section 30. The correction for a public domain requires complete partitions and doors, and they must be locked every night. Thus, the Gemara (6a) says: "Jerusalem, if not for its doors being locked at night, would be liable as a public domain." 

The Rambam in Chapter 17 rules that it does not have to be actual locking, but rather that it should be possible to lock, meaning that the doors should not be embedded in the ground. If they are embedded, it is necessary to remove the dirt and fix them so that they can be locked. Even if the city ruler does not allow them to be locked, this does not matter, as the doors make the opening a valid partition. After fixing the doors, the entire area is considered like one courtyard, and its alleyways do not need the corrections of a side post (lechi) or a crossbeam (korah).

(Note that when it says "Jerusalem, if not for its doors being locked, it would be liable as a public domain," even though there are still partitions and "forms of doorways" at the openings, this is because of the principle that 'the multitudes come and nullify the partition.' The opinion in the Gemara is Rabbi Yochanan's, who holds like Rabbi Yehuda on page 22. But we follow the Sages, who do not say 'the multitudes come and nullify the partition,' as stated in the previous Siman. Even without locking, Jerusalem is only considered a karmelit, and the Sugya in Eruvin 101 regarding the 'butcher's market' and the Gemara there also follow Rabbi Yehuda, as the anonymous Sages there are Rabbi Meir, who is Rabbi Yehuda. Otherwise, Rav Papa's answer there would not suffice. And examine this thoroughly.)

(One may be lenient like the Rambam and the Tur, who do not require actual locking. See Pri Megadim.)

And specifically, for the public domain itself, a tzurat ha-petach (form of a doorway) does not help. But a courtyard that is open to the public domain on both of its ends, or if one side is open to the public domain and the other side to a karmelit (semi-public domain), or if it is open on both sides to a karmelit, it requires a tzurat ha-petach on one side and a side post or beam on the other side. For when one makes a tzurat ha-petach on one side, it now has three partitions and is considered like any other alleyway, where on the fourth side one makes a side post or beam. This applies if it has all the requirements of an alleyway as explained in the previous section. Otherwise, it is considered a courtyard, and a side post or beam on the fourth side does not help, but rather two posts or a post of four handbreadths as explained there. However, on the side that requires a tzurat ha-petach, there is no difference. 

And the reason we require an adjustment on the fourth side is when this side is open to the public domain or karmelit. But if it is open to a courtyard, even if it is not joined with an eruv, and even though one side is open to the public domain, there is no need for a tzurat ha-petach. Instead, on both sides, side posts or beams are sufficient – a side post on this side and a side post on that side, or a beam on this side and a beam on that side. The reasoning is that the side open to the courtyard is considered as closed, because the partitions of the courtyard on the other side count for it, and it is like an alleyway closed on three sides, which only requires a side post or beam on the fourth side. 

And the requirement for a side post or beam on the side of the courtyard is only for recognition, because it is open to the courtyard. For this reason, there is an opinion that a beam does not help on the side of the courtyard, only a side post, because it serves as a partition and is considered as if it is closed. (Bach)

And know, there are some of our teachers who hold that a mavoi (alleyway) which is open to the public domain at both ends requires a door that is capable of being locked on one side. (Rashba and Maggid Mishneh in Chapter 17, in the name of "some disagree" there). And there are some of our teachers who hold that a mavoi which is thirteen and a third cubits wide, like the measure that was used for the wells, and is open at both ends to the public domain - its rule is like that of the public domain itself. (Tosafot 6b). However, the first opinion is the view of the Rif, the Rambam, and the Rosh, and this is the law that we follow. (And in the Shulchan Aruch, only this opinion is brought, see there).

And know that the requirement for doors in a public domain is because doors are clearly considered a complete partition even in the eyes of people, and it is not comparable to a doorway form. Therefore, if even on one side there is a proper door, which can be locked or is suitable for locking, it suffices on the other side to have a side post or a crossbeam, as in all alleyways. And this is indeed the opinion of the Rashba, as stated by the Maggid Mishneh in chapter 17. However, our Rabbis, the Tosafists (Eruvin 6b, s.v. "Veha'amar") wrote that if the third partition is through a door, the fourth also requires a door, as explained there, and so it is elucidated by Rashi there (s.v. "Chayavin"). However, according to the words of Rabbeinu Yitzchak of the Tosafists, it seems that he holds like the Rashba, as stated there, and according to this, it would be a dispute among the authorities. (And the Magen Avraham 362:2 wrote that the opinion of Rabbeinu Yitzchak is like the Rashba, and I am astonished, why did he not bring from the Tosafists before the words of Rabbeinu Yitzchak, which explicitly state the opposite, and from Rabbeinu Yitzchak there is no proof. And one should not ask that this is the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel according to Chananiah, and Beit Hillel holds that one door is sufficient, for it can be said that according to the conclusion, this applies to alleyways open to the public domain, but in the public domain itself it can be said that even Beit Hillel agrees with Beit Shammai, see there and analyze thoroughly.) (And know that I heard regarding the law of suitable for locking, that if the government insists on locking, it is considered not suitable for locking, and this is not clear, as it appears from the Talmudic discussion, see there.)

A crooked alleyway shaped like a "Dalet" (the Hebrew letter "ד"), meaning that it does not run straight but bends to the right or to the left, and it turns out that from one side it opens to the public domain in the east or the west, and from the other side it opens to the public domain in the north or the south. Therefore, just like a straight-through alleyway that runs straight requires a symbolic doorway on one side and a side post or a beam on the other side, so too here. However, in this case, there is an obligation to make the symbolic doorway at the bend, because there it appears open on both sides, and this opening is considered as open to the public domain. And on the other side, a side post or a beam is required on both sides specifically, since they are considered as two separate alleyways due to the bend. It is obvious that one can make two symbolic doorways on each of the two ends, and at the bend, a side post or a beam, as it is all the same, of course. Consequently, each alleyway can make its own eruv and the other does not prohibit it, since by making their own eruv they have revealed their intention to separate from each other. And even though in a straight alleyway this does not help, as stated in the previous section, but in a crooked alleyway it does help, as they clearly appear as two separate alleyways. And one can force the residents of the second alleyway not to walk through this alleyway on this Shabbat, because if they do, they will prohibit it for them. And even though later in section 378 it will be explained that a permissible footstep in its own place does not prohibit it in another place, this applies to courtyards where each one has its own courtyard. But in an alleyway, everyone has control, and therefore it is necessary to compel them not to walk through here. (Magen Avraham, subsection 3, in the name of the R"Y). And know that this requirement for a symbolic doorway at the bend applies even if the bend is no more than ten cubits, (Gemara 6.), because since it is like an opening to the public domain, there is no difference between less than ten cubits and more than ten cubits.

There is an opinion that when we require a "Tzurat HaPetach" (a form of a doorway) for a bent alleyway, it is only when the openings lead to a public domain. However, if both openings lead to a karmelit (a semi-public domain), no correction is needed for the bend, only a side post or a crossbeam at each entrance (Taz section 2 in the name of the Mahari"v). According to this, in our case where there is no public domain, it would be the same (ibid). Even though for a completely open alleyway there is no difference between a public domain and a karmelit, still, for an alleyway that bends, which is not completely open, there is a difference (and this answers the question of the Taz there). There is an opposing opinion that holds that it is all the same (Taz ibid), but the primary view is the first opinion (and this is also the ruling of the Eliyah Rabbah section 5, and it is explicitly understood from the Magen Avraham, section 363, subsection 27, see there).

A crooked alley in the shape of the letter "Chet" (ח), meaning that it bends towards the south and then bends towards the west, thus has two bends and two openings to the public domain. (Rashi 6: 'in the alley of Nehardea') Therefore, it requires two [forms of] doorframes at the two bends, and two side posts or beams at the two openings. Or conversely, [the forms of] doorframes at the openings, and the side posts or beams at the bends, and their ruling is like two crooked alleys, as is apparent. And we have already written in the previous section, paragraph 59, that some of our Rabbis hold that when two openings go out to one public domain, it does not have the status of a crooked alley requiring a form of a doorway, and only when there are two openings to two sides of the public domain, such as east and south, does it resemble an open alley. But when they go out to one public domain, they are like all alleys. However, Rashi did not explain it this way, and this is also clarified from the words of the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch, paragraph 3, see there. (And we wrote there that according to this opinion, we must say that even though it is like a "Chet" shape, nevertheless, one of the openings leans towards another side).

And know that the law of a crooked alleyway applies even when there are many alleyways open to each other, and one goes to the east and another to the south, and then one to the west and then to the north, and so on. Consequently, all of their crookedness is only relative to each other, and similarly, their intersections are with each other and not with the public domain. Nevertheless, if the first and last alleyways are open to the public domain, all the alleyways are considered open to the public domain on both sides. Therefore, each alleyway requires a "tzurat hapetach" (a form of a doorway) at its bend, and either a side post or a beam at its intersection with the other alleyway, or vice versa, a "tzurat hapetach" at its intersection and a side post or a beam at its bend. Each alleyway is considered as if it is open to the public domain. (What is stated in the Shulchan Aruch in singular form is not precise.)

An alleyway constructed like a centipede, which is a creature with many legs – two rows of legs on the right and left, and they are not aligned with each other (Tosafot 8: s.v. 'Mavoi'). Similarly, this large alleyway, which has small alleyways opening into it from both sides, either directly opposite each other or not directly opposite each other (Bach and Magen Avraham 4). Each of the small alleyways, apart from the fact that each one opens into the large alleyway, also opens on the other side into the public domain. Consequently, each one has the status of a crooked alleyway, having two openings into the public domain, one of its own and one of the large alleyway, which also opens inevitably into the public domain. And it has already been clarified that an opening into an alleyway, which itself opens into the public domain, is considered as if it directly opens into the public domain. Therefore, each of the small alleyways needs at its opening into the large alleyway a form of a doorway, and at its other end that opens into the public domain, a side-post or a cross-beam, or vice versa. And the large alleyway, if it has only one opening into the public domain, can use a side-post or a cross-beam at its head and that is sufficient. Although it is also considered a crooked alleyway due to the small alleyways, it has a form of a doorway at each of the small alleyways where they open into it, and this form of a doorway serves both the small alleyways and it. However, if it is open on both ends into the public domain, and thus it has three openings into the public domain – two of its own and one for each small alleyway – it needs a form of a doorway on one of its sides and a side-post or a cross-beam on the other side. (This seems to me to be the explanation of 'an alleyway constructed like a centipede', see Beit Yosef and Bach and scrutinize it carefully).

The Tur writes: "An alleyway that has been breached on its side—if many people frequently pass through the breach, even if the breach is only four handbreadths wide, it is not considered an entrance and requires repair. If many people do not frequently pass through it, it does not require repair until it reaches ten handbreadths, even if there are no remaining fragments. This applies if four handbreadths remain towards its head. But if four handbreadths do not remain, even if the breach is only three handbreadths, it requires repair. If it is less than three handbreadths, it does not require repair. And if it is breached at its head, the breach is considered significant at four handbreadths." End of quote.

Explanation of his words: Although up to ten cubits in any place is considered an entrance, in the case of an alleyway, it is different. And it is not because it is not an entrance, but for another reason: we are concerned that those who pass by will leave through the large entrance, where there is a noticeable marker of the side post (lechi) or the crossbeam (korah), and they will go through this breach, where there is no side post or crossbeam, and it will be like an alleyway without a side post or crossbeam. The primary reason for allowing the side post and the crossbeam is because those who pass by will see the marker, and therefore, if they do not pass by there, the marker is nullified. Therefore, if the breach in the alleyway is from the side wall, it prohibits even a breach of four handbreadths if many people pass through there, for the reason explained. Hence, if many people do not pass through it, up to ten cubits does not need any correction, like all entrances. He wrote “even if there are no remnants” because some hold according to the Gemara (6a) that it is specifically when remnants remain, meaning that a small height of the wall’s foundation remains along the entire breach, a few handbreadths high, so that it is not possible to walk through there. But when no remnants remain, even if many do not pass through it because it opens to a dirty or ruined place, we are concerned that the dirt might be removed and people will start to pass through it. The Tur informs us that this is not the case. And even if many do not pass through it, this is only if from the breach to the end of the alleyway there are no less than four handbreadths. But if less than four handbreadths remain, the breach invalidates it anyway, as there is no wall next to the side post or crossbeam. The reason for four handbreadths is because we hold that the length of an alleyway is four cubits, as written in Siman 363, and this is at the beginning of the alleyway. But at the end, so that it does not lose its status as an alleyway, the sages said (5a) that four handbreadths are sufficient. This is what they said: when four handbreadths of the wall remain, the side post and crossbeam are not nullified, as they are placed on the wall of the alleyway that is four handbreadths long at its end, as stated. But if four handbreadths do not remain, it is invalid, unless the breach is less than three handbreadths, which is considered as closed according to the principle of lavud.

And this is all when it was breached from its side, but if it was breached from its head, meaning for example, if the alley was twenty cubits wide and they made a wall of ten cubits, and afterwards they placed a side post or a crossbeam, the wall does not count as part of the side post as it is stated in Siman 363, and this wall was breached, the Tur wrote that from its head, within four. That is, if it was only breached four handbreadths, it invalidates. And the words of the Tur are puzzling because clearly, it is questioned in the Gemara (6a): What is the difference between its head and its side? And it answers that at its head, it is dealing with when it was breached at the corner, because people do not make an entrance at the corner, as it says there. But if not at the corner, it is all the same. And since the Tur did not mention this, his words are puzzling. And indeed, the Rambam in Chapter 17 did not mention 'from its head,' because it is all the same, and similarly, it is not mentioned in the Shulchan Aruch.

However, in truth, the words of the Tur are correct, and so it appears to me in my humble opinion, that the Tur found it difficult to understand the differentiation between "from its side" and "from its head," and the intention is between a corner and not a corner. Therefore, the Tur explains that the meaning of "from its side" is not the walls that are on the side, and "from its head" is not on the fourth wall, and we would need to interpret it as being wider than ten [cubits] as explained. The Tur interprets it that according to the answer, the explanation is that everything refers to the side walls, and the fourth wall is open like the manner of alleyways. Here, the explanation is from the very head of the side wall, which is the head of the wall. Consequently, the opening is like a corner, obviously, because the head of the fourth wall does not have a partition anyway. Therefore, when the Tur says "from its head," it also means from its very head, and it is like a corner. (See Bayit Chadash, Drisha, and Magen Avraham, Section 3; each offered various forced explanations, see there.)

A lane that is much wider than ten cubits, and it was enclosed with a permissible barrier and then a breach was made in it, as we wrote that its law is like that of the side — this is when the beam is not placed from wall to wall, but from the edge of the partition to the other wall. Then, when a breach is made and they walk through the breach, there is no beam there. Therefore, the breach invalidates it according to the measurements that were explained from the side. But when the beam is placed from wall to wall, what difference does it make if they walk through the breach? Similarly, if its validity is with a side post, the law is like that of the side, because the side post stands only at one end. And when they do not walk through there, the side post is nullified. Refer to what is written in Siman 363, Se'if 62 in the name of the Ritva. And know that at its end, a breach of less than four handbreadths is never invalid, even if less than four handbreadths remain close to the wall. In this, it is more lenient than from the side. The reason for this is that in this case, there is no concern that they will walk through here and nullify the side post or the beam, because what difference does it make to us, since a lane that is less than four cubits wide does not require correction, as is written there. (And this is the intention of the Magen Avraham in Siman 363, Se'if Katan 3. See there and understand well.)

And all of this applies to a breach in an alleyway, but for a breach in a courtyard, it is always [permitted up to] ten cubits, and less than ten does not invalidate it at all. And so it is stated in the Gemara (5a): "What is the difference between a courtyard, whose breach [is permitted] up to ten, and an alleyway, whose breach [is permitted] up to four?" The Ritva wrote the reason: because a standard courtyard has four walls, they were lenient regarding its breaches up to ten cubits. But an alleyway, which only has three walls and a minimal side post, even though there is a courtyard that has only three walls and the fourth side is entirely open but less than ten cubits, and it has only a strip of four or two strips of minimal size, nevertheless, this is not comparable to an alleyway, which has only one side post, and this is also implied in Tosafot there (s.v. "You might say").

According to this, in our eruvin, where we treat our cities as courtyards, as stated in Siman 363, their breaches are up to ten cubits. (The Magen Avraham in subparagraph 4 was uncertain about this, and follows his reasoning in Siman 363 subparagraph 27, that for stringency, we treat it as a courtyard and not leniently. And it is explained there from his words that we always need a form of a door, even for breaches of less than ten cubits in a city that is not surrounded by a wall, since we consider it as open to a karmelit; see there. But our custom is not like this, and we treat them as actual courtyards. And for breaches of less than ten cubits, we make two strips of minimal size, and thus their breach is always up to ten cubits, and this is also explained in Siman 363, paragraph 45; see there.)

Maimonides wrote in Chapter 17, Law 18: "If an alleyway is entirely breached into a courtyard, and the courtyard is breached opposite it into a public domain - it is forbidden, because it is considered an open alleyway. However, the courtyard is permitted, for if a courtyard that many people pass through, entering from one side and exiting from the other - it remains a complete private domain." End quote.

This means that the alleyway is entirely breached, but in the courtyard, there remain protrusions on both sides, both in the wall between it and the alleyway, and in the wall between it and the public domain. Therefore, the breaches do not forbid the courtyard, as long as they are less than ten [cubits]. But for the alleyway, since the breaches are opposite each other, and one standing in the alleyway sees a clear opening straight to the public domain - the alleyway becomes forbidden. And if one would ask, should the protrusions between the alleyway and the courtyard not also benefit the alleyway, due to the principle of 'visible from the outside and flush on the inside'? Indeed, this is true, but here we are dealing with a case where the walls of the alleyway enter the courtyard in such a manner that everyone sees that these protrusions are not from the walls of the alleyway, but from the walls of the courtyard, as these laws are explained in Siman 363, Section 12, see there.

The Rambam does not differentiate between whether the residents of the courtyard made an eruv with the residents of the alleyway or not. In the Gemara (7b), there are various specific laws about this, which the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch in Section 3 explain. The reason the Rambam did not explain them here is because this pertains to the laws of eruvin, such as whether the courtyard and the alleyway prohibit each other, and in what manner they prohibit. The Rambam wrote these laws separately in the laws of eruvin, whereas here we are dealing with the laws of partitions. Conversely, the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch combined the laws of partitions with the laws of eruvin, as is evident to anyone who studies them.

And the difference between when the residents of the courtyard made an eruv with the residents of the alleyway and when they did not is as follows: If they did not make an eruv, the courtyard is permitted even if the breaches are opposite each other, because of the side walls. However, the alleyway is prohibited even if the breaches are not opposite each other, because once it is fully breached to the alleyway, the residents of the alleyway prohibit it, since they did not join in an eruv together. But if they made an eruv and the breaches are not opposite each other, both are permitted because they joined in an eruv together, and the breaches are not aligned opposite each other to be considered like an alleyway breached to the public domain. If the breaches are aligned opposite each other, the courtyard is permitted and the alleyway is prohibited. The residents of the alleyway are prevented from going to the courtyard, even though the eruv accustomed them to be together, so that they do not prohibit it. (Similarly, the Magen Avraham wrote in section 7 regarding when the walls of the alleyway do not enter the courtyard, that the alleyway is also permitted because of "visible from the outside," as the residents of the courtyard are prevented from passing through there to the public domain, and they will go through their breach, see there, and all the more so that the residents of the alleyway are prevented from going into the courtyard.)

However, even if they combined and the breaches are not directly opposite each other, sometimes the alleyway is still forbidden. This is when the breach between the alleyway and the courtyard is not in the middle of the courtyard wall but rather on the side, i.e., at the beginning of the wall. Since the wall of the alleyway continues evenly with the wall of the courtyard, it appears as a long alleyway that extends to the public domain opposite it, making it open and thus forbidden. But if the breach is in the middle of the courtyard wall, it is clear to everyone that from the breach to the public domain is not part of the alleyway. However, even in such cases, if the courtyard belongs to an individual, the alleyway is forbidden, because there is a concern that over time, the owner of the courtyard may decide to build structures in the space wider than the alleyway, aligning the walls with those of the alleyway, and it will then appear as if the alleyway is open to the public domain. In the case of a courtyard belonging to the public, this concern does not exist, because when the courtyard is public, they will not allow an individual to build so extensively. (These laws are not found in the Rambam, and it seems to me that the reason is that all these laws in the Gemara are according to the initial understanding that Rav and Shmuel disagree whether they combined or not, as explained there. But according to the conclusion, we do not say these laws at all, as it seems from the plain reading of the Gemara. See there and examine it well.)

A passageway that is breached into an open area, and the open area is behind the courtyard. If the open area is less than two seahs, or even if it is more than two seahs but was enclosed for residential purposes, as explained in Siman 358, it is considered like a courtyard, as if it were breached to a courtyard. But if it is more than two seahs and was not enclosed for residential purposes, it is obvious that the open area prohibits the passageway as if it were breached into a karmelit. And if the passageway does not have remaining side posts, or if the breach is more than ten cubits, it is forbidden to carry in the passageway until the breach is fixed.

In the Gemara (24b), there is an incident involving an alleyway that was open to a courtyard which was not enclosed for dwelling purposes. The courtyard was open to a vineyard path where there were no inhabitants, yet the residents of the alleyway used it. (Tosafot, s.v. 'Let them make') The courtyard had fencing, so the path did not prohibit its use, (Magen Avraham, sec. 9) and the vineyard path extended to the riverbank, which was ten handbreadths high and served as a partition. Rava instructed to place a side post between the entrance of the alleyway and the entrance of the courtyard, thus permitting both. Even though the courtyard was not enclosed for dwelling, nevertheless, since the side post was effective for the alleyway, it was also effective for the courtyard, rendering it as if it were enclosed for dwelling, thereby allowing carrying from the alleyway to the courtyard. However, it was forbidden to carry in the path, and it did not prohibit the courtyard because it had fencing. Why not place a side post between the path and the courtyard, since the path has the status of an alleyway because the residents of the alleyway use it? Because we decree concerning another path that is not used, and people might say that a side post permits it as well, whereas for an ordinary path, a side post is not effective. (See Magen Avraham, sec. 9)

It is permitted to use the area beneath the beam and opposite the side-post, as they are considered part of the alleyway. However, this applies when the alleyway opens to a public domain. When it opens to a karmelit (a semi-public domain), it is forbidden. Although the public domain is stricter than the karmelit, in the case of a karmelit we say "like kind attracts like kind and is aroused." This means that the areas between the side-posts and beneath the beam, which do not have the measure of a karmelit (as a karmelit is not less than four cubits, as stated in Siman 345), meet the karmelit outside and are strengthened by it, thus becoming a karmelit as well. But when opposite a public domain, it cannot become a public domain since it is not of the same type, and therefore it is included in the alleyway. However, when of the same type as a karmelit, they are related since they do not have the public traffic like a karmelit but are just missing the measure. 

If the beam has a width of four handbreadths, even if it opens to a karmelit, it is permitted to carry beneath it because we say "the edge of the roof descends and seals," making it a complete partition. But less than four handbreadths, we do not say "the edge of the roof descends and seals," as stated in Siman 363, section 17, and only if it is sturdy enough to support a layer of plaster. According to the Magen Avraham in the name of the Rashba, and according to Rashi at the end of the chapter "Kol Gagot," we say "the edge of the roof" even for four sides according to Rav, whose opinion is the law. But according to Tosafot and the Rosh, we only say "the edge of the roof" with two walls forming a right angle, not opposite each other, as that would be like an open passage. Therefore, roofs and projections extending from houses into the street, even if they are wide, we do not say "the edge of the roof" as stated at the end of Siman 346. But for a portico with three walls and a roof, if it is four handbreadths wide, we say "the edge of the roof." I have seen in the name of the Maharil that even in such cases he was stringent, which is surprising as we explained at the end of Siman 346, and there is no doubt that in such cases it is permitted.

Even though it is permitted to make use of the area under the beam, one should not sit at the entrance of the alleyway with an object in hand, lest the object roll out of his hand into the public domain and he will bring it back, since there is no distinction between him and the public domain. However, if it opens into a karmelit, it seems to be permitted. But at the entrance of a courtyard, whether it opens into the public domain or a karmelit, it is permitted, since there is a distinction, either a four-handbreadth board or two boards. But a side post on one side does not constitute a distinction. However, a doorway frame seems to be a distinction, and it is permitted to sit there. There are those who prohibit this as well, even if it opens into a karmelit, like in our days when we do not have a public domain. (Magen Avraham, section 11) Women sitting at the entrance of the alleyway with their jugs in their hands, the first time they are told that it is forbidden to do so, and if they do not listen, they are not admonished further, for it is better that they be inadvertent sinners rather than deliberate sinners. This is even said regarding a Torah prohibition, as we say at the beginning of chapter 4 (30a) of Beitzah concerning the additional sanctity of Yom Kippur, and all the more so regarding a rabbinic prohibition. (Regarding what the Beit Yosef wrote in section 6, because it is a rabbinic prohibition, and the Magen Avraham questioned this in section 12, saying that even with a Torah prohibition it is so, it can be explained according to what the Ran wrote there, that the Gemara at the beginning of chapter 23 of Shabbat does not hold this way, as mentioned there. However, our version is like in Beitzah, and furthermore, they wrote there that regarding something explicitly stated in the Torah, we do not say better they be inadvertent, etc.)

A mavoi (alleyway) whose crossbeam or side post was removed on Shabbat, even though it was permitted for part of Shabbat, is forbidden from that point on. We do not say, "Since it was permitted for Shabbat, it remains permitted," because we do not say this when the partitions have changed, as explained in Siman 362. For these purposes, a side post and crossbeam are considered like a partition. Similarly, if the markers of a courtyard were removed on Shabbat, whether it opens to the public domain or to a karmelit (semi-public domain), it is forbidden. Some say this applies in a city not surrounded by a wall, but in a city surrounded by a wall and intended for dwelling, such as one that was first settled and then surrounded by a wall, it is permitted. Since there are outer partitions, this is not considered a change in partitions, as explained there regarding mats that are spread out. One may rely on this to permit. All this applies when they were fit to stand all day on Shabbat, but a reason occurred that caused them to be removed or to fall. However, if they were not fit to stand the entire day on Shabbat, such as if it was known that non-Jews would damage them, it is forbidden after they fell or were removed, even in such cases. If there is doubt whether they were removed on Shabbat or before Shabbat, in a situation where it would be permitted if it happened on Shabbat, we follow the doubt leniently, since in rabbinic matters, we rule leniently.

Our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in Section 8: "If a courtyard joined in an eruv and the beam [of the alleyway] broke, the courtyard where the eruv is placed and the courtyards that open into it are permitted [to carry], but the courtyards that do not open into that courtyard are forbidden." The explanation is that if all the residents of the alleyway placed a single eruv and put it in one courtyard, and since the beam broke, the connection through the alleyway is nullified, and the connection is only through the courtyards. Consequently, the courtyards that open into the courtyard where the eruv is placed benefit from the eruv, but those that do not open into it are necessarily cut off from the eruv, as will be further explained in Siman 374. Therefore, in our cities where the eruv is placed in the synagogue, if the alleyway arrangement of the synagogue is disrupted, the entire city is forbidden to carry from house to house or from room to room if two homeowners reside there, even if their alleyways are properly arranged, because they cannot bring the eruv to them due to the disruption of that alleyway. (Magen Avraham, Section 15) And if the synagogue where the eruv is placed is closed by government officials and sealed, and it is forbidden to break the seal, the eruv is nullified, and a new eruv should be made on Friday in another place. (Regarding what the Magen Avraham wrote at the end of Section 15, see its explanation in the Machatzit Hashekel, and this does not apply to us.)

The sages permitted "Pasi Biraot" (boards around wells) in the Land of Israel at the time when the Temple was in existence, so that water would be readily available for pilgrims to water their animals. What are "Pasi Biraot"? It is a well situated in a public domain or a karmelit (an area with intermediate status), and they did not burden people to make complete partitions around it. Instead, they placed eight boards around it, each board being one cubit wide. They placed two boards at each corner, joined together: east and south, east and north, west and south, and west and north. The space between each board could be up to thirteen and a third cubits wide. They were lenient in this case as well, for in other openings we do not permit more than ten cubits, but here we permit more because this is only rabbinic law. And even though there is more open space than standing partitions, it is a law given to Moses at Sinai, and here there is more open space than standing partitions. Our rabbis, the Tosafists, have already written at the beginning of "Osein Pasin" that whenever there are four partitions as here with an opening between them, it is considered a partition by Torah law. We have explained the reasoning for this in Siman 362, section 26.
