And so it is explained in the words of the Rambam, Chapter 17, Law 33, who wrote: "One who throws from the public domain into the area between the partitions is liable, since each corner has a complete partition, which has a height of ten [handbreadths] and more than four by four [handbreadths], and the square is noticeable and visible, and everything between them becomes a private domain, even if it is in a valley and there is no well between them, since on every side there is a partition here and a partition there. And even if many people pass and traverse between the partitions, the partitions are not nullified, and they are like courtyards through which the public passes, and one who throws into them is liable. And it is permitted to water the animal between them, if there is a well between them," end quote. And this is the explanation: even though the open area is greater, nevertheless it is considered a partition by Torah law, and therefore it was permitted for the pilgrims.

If there is in one of the corners, or in every one of the four corners, a large stone, or a tree, or a mound that rises ten handbreadths within four cubits, or a bundle of reeds, we consider all of these as if they were divided, and if there is one cubit here and one cubit there at a height of ten handbreadths, it is regarded as a corner with two partitions. Similarly, a partition of reeds, where there are no three handbreadths between each reed, and they are placed one cubit here and one cubit there, is also valid. It is permissible to bring the partitions close to the well, provided that the cow's head and majority are inside and it drinks, which is two cubits. For if its head and majority are not inside, we are concerned that one might follow his animal with the vessel in his hand to give it water and bring it out to the public domain or to a karmelit. It is permissible to distance the partitions as much as one wishes, provided that the gap is not more than thirteen and a third cubits, and this is considered as surrounded for dwelling. If it is more, one should place additional partitions in the middle to reduce the airspace so that it is not more than this measure. (As mentioned in the Mishnah about making partitions there) And it can be more than a "beit satayim" (an area of approximately 5000 square cubits), since it is considered surrounded for dwelling (there).

The measure that we required of two cubits, this applies even to a camel whose neck is long. Likewise, conversely, when there is no measure - it is forbidden to water even a kid (a young goat) whose entire body fits within one cubit, because the Rabbis did not differentiate. This is true for all rabbinic decrees. And thus it is stated in the Jerusalem Talmud. Similarly, there is no difference in watering it whether one holds the vessel without the cow, or whether one holds both, or whether one does not hold them at all - less than this measure is not permitted, and it is all because of the principle of 'the Rabbis did not differentiate.' Conversely, with this measure - one can act as they wish, even to hold the vessel and not the cow, since it can exit through its rear - in any case, we do not worry that it will drag the vessel after it.

And it has already been explained that this was only permitted in the Land of Israel during the time of the Temple, and only for those who made pilgrimage, and only for watering animals, but a person can descend into it and drink. However, if the well is very wide, such that a person cannot descend into it, one can draw water and drink between the partitions. And this permission was granted only for a well of living waters and of the public, but a public pit or a private well was not permitted, unless there were partitions all around it ten handbreadths high, and with an opening like all partitions. And likewise in other lands, a person can [descend] into a pit and drink, but if one draws water outside, partitions and an opening are required like all partitions.

If one fills water for his animal within the partitions - he may fill the water and place it in a vessel in front of the animal or hold it in his hand, as explained. If the trough is situated in the public domain and the head of the trough enters within the partitions, and the trough itself is ten handbreadths high and four handbreadths wide, thus making it a private domain, it is forbidden to fill the vessel and place it on the head of the trough or to hold it in his hand. This is because we are concerned that one might see that the head of the trough, which stands in the public domain, has become damaged, and he will go there with the bucket and transfer from the private domain to the public domain. Although in such cases one is not liable, since the initial lifting was not intended for this purpose, we are concerned that afterwards he will place the bucket in the public domain, and after fixing the trough, he will bring it back from the public domain to the private domain. (Gemara 20:) Rather, he should fill the vessel and pour the water into the trough. And even if he wants to water the animal with the vessel and not hold the vessel in his hand - it appears from there that it is forbidden, as explained by Rashi there, and it is also clear from the Rambam there, Law 32. (Also from Tosafot there, s.v. “Amar”, even though they wrote not to fill etc., "and hold it in his hand" is not precise, as they concluded "but rather pour it in front of it" there).

The Rambam wrote (there): "A courtyard where one end enters between the upright boards [used to construct a partition for a well] - it is permissible to carry from it into the area between the boards, and from the area between the boards into it. If there were two courtyards - it is forbidden until they make an eruv." This means, if there is an opening between them, as it is in the Gemara. (21a) There is a doubt whether carrying is only what is necessary for watering the animal, or since it was permitted for the animal, it becomes like a complete private domain, and it is permissible to carry anything. And from the words of the Ritva there, it implies that since it was permitted for the sake of the animals of those who ascended for the pilgrimage - it was then permitted for all animals, see there. Nevertheless, this matter was not explained, and requires further investigation.

If the water dried up on Shabbat, it is forbidden to carry between the partitions, as they are only considered a partition because of the water. We do not say "since it was permitted, it remains permitted," because this principle only applies to complete partitions. (Tosafot 20a, s.v. 'Mechitza') If the water came on Shabbat, it is permitted to carry between them, as any partition made on Shabbat is considered a partition, and here it was made permissibly, as the water came on its own.

Translation:
A house that has many neighbors, and each one lives in his own room, and similarly, a courtyard that has many houses, where each one lives in his own house, according to Torah law - all are permitted to carry from the courtyard to the houses, and from the houses to the courtyard, and from room to room, and throughout the entire courtyard, because all of this is considered a private domain and not a public domain. Similarly, an alley that has a side post or a crossbeam, according to Torah law - it is permitted to carry throughout the entire alley, and from the alley to the courtyards and houses, and from them to the alley, since it is not a public domain. Similarly, a city that is surrounded by a wall and was enclosed for residential purposes - it is permitted according to Torah law to carry throughout the entire city, as long as it has doors that are locked at night, or are capable of being locked according to the Rambam, as stated in Siman 364, and this is the law according to the Torah.

However, by rabbinic decree, it is forbidden for neighbors to carry in an area that has separate dwellings until all the neighbors make an eruv before Shabbat. They must combine their food into one and place it in one of the houses to show that we are all mixed together and have one food for all of us. It is as if we all live in this place, in this room where the eruv is placed, and no one has a distinct domain separate from his neighbor. Just as we all have equal rights in this place, so too we have equal rights in the places that each one has taken for himself, and thus we are all one domain. This was instituted by Solomon and his court (Shabbat 14b), and when he made this enactment, a heavenly voice proclaimed, "My son, if your heart is wise, My heart will also rejoice" (Proverbs 23:15). Regarding this, it is stated at the end of Ecclesiastes: "And more than being wise, Kohelet also taught knowledge to the people and pondered, sought out, and set in order many proverbs" (Ecclesiastes 12:9), meaning he made safeguards for the Torah (Eruvin 21b). That is, he erected fences around the commandments of the Torah to prevent breaches. Just as vineyards, orchards, and gardens situated in public pathways, if not fenced properly, will be trampled by passersby leaving nothing behind, so too the commandments of the Torah, if not safeguarded, will ultimately be entirely nullified, as we see and hear that the breaches made by the degenerate of the generation eventually led to the complete uprooting of our holy Torah from them. Therefore, a person must be exceedingly cautious with rabbinic decrees. Concerning this, it is said, 'Beloved are the words of the Sages,' and we, the people of Israel, are obligated to stand firmly for all the enactments and decrees of our Sages, ensuring that no breach whatsoever occurs.

And why did they establish this? So that the people would not err and say - just as it is permitted to carry from a house designated for one person to a courtyard where many have a share, and from a courtyard to a street in a city surrounded by a wall, where all the city's inhabitants have shares, so too it is permitted to carry from a private domain to a public domain. For now they are carrying from a domain designated for one to a domain designated for many people. Therefore, Solomon decreed that any domain controlled by an individual is forbidden to be carried into a domain controlled by another, like from one room to another within one house, and similarly from houses each controlled by an individual to a courtyard controlled by all, and similarly to an alleyway and to a city surrounded by a wall.

And the Rambam wrote in Chapter 1 of Eruvin, Law 3: "Similarly, those who dwell in tents or booths, or a camp that is surrounded by a partition – they may not carry from one tent to another until they all make an eruv. But a caravan that surrounded themselves with partitions does not need to make an eruv; they may carry from one tent to another without an eruv, because they are all considered mixed, and those tents are not permanent for them." End quote.

And that which is taught at the end of the first chapter: 'Four things were exempted in a camp,' and one of them is the eruv of courtyards, this refers to a camp that goes out to war, as explained in the Gemara there. But an ordinary camp that remains for many days in one place is obligated in an eruv. A caravan is defined as those who rest only for the Sabbath day, which is considered a temporary tent, as explained by the Rambam, and this is clarified in the Jerusalem Talmud there. And the Tur wrote that those who travel in deserts are exempt from the eruv of courtyards, and this is similar to a war camp, or because their tent is considered temporary since they do not stay long in one place.

(In the Tosefta, Chapter 2, Law 4, the version is the opposite, that a camp is exempt and a caravan is obligated, as mentioned there. And so wrote the Ritva at the end of the first chapter, that this is how it should be stated in the Jerusalem Talmud. And see the explanation of the Gra, subsection 6).

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote in section 2: "Houses on a ship require an eruv, even though the ship has partitions. And if the ship does not have partitions, it is forbidden to carry on the ship except within four cubits." End of quote. This is because a ship is considered a fixed dwelling for those who travel the seas and rivers, like houses on land. The novelty here is that even though the ship has partitions that are ten handbreadths high within it, and even though it sinks deeply into the water, and there are not ten handbreadths from the water's edge to its top, nevertheless, since within it there are ten handbreadths, it is considered a private domain. One might have said that the houses are subsidiary to it and are included in the ship, and are not considered a separate entity since they are movable - it comes to teach us otherwise. And if it does not have partitions of ten handbreadths, it is considered a karmelit, and it is forbidden to carry within it more than four cubits, and certainly from the houses to it and from it to the houses. And from it to the sea and the river, it is permitted within four cubits, as both are considered a karmelit. And an eruv does not help in such cases from house to house, unless the houses are close to each other and there is an opening between them. For if they are far apart, with the ship intervening between them, an eruv does not help due to the interruption of a complete karmelit. (The laws written by the Magen Avraham in section 5 regarding a ship, we have explained above in Siman 355, section 13, see there.)

The eruv that the residents of a courtyard make with each other is called an "eruv chatzerot." When all the residents of an alleyway make an eruv together, it is called a "shituf" or "shitufei mavot." Even when courtyards make an eruv together among themselves without involving the alleyway, such as when they open to each other, it is also called a "shituf." There is no practical difference in these terms except to understand the language for the laws that will be explained, whether one can rely on a shituf in place of an eruv or an eruv in place of a shituf, or not. One must know that an eruv is called for one courtyard when they make an eruv, and a shituf is called for many courtyards with a common alleyway. Another practical difference is that an eruv chatzerot must be made specifically with bread, while a shituf mavot can be made without bread, as will be explained with God's help.

In the Gemara (49a), there is a dispute regarding whether the concept of an eiruv (joining of domains) is based on acquisition—meaning that the house where the eiruv is placed is transferred by the homeowner to the others. According to this view, an acquisition can even be made with a handkerchief (symbolic act of acquisition), and a minor's house would not be valid since a minor cannot transfer ownership. Similarly, a minor cannot create an eiruv for others, and it requires an item of at least the value of a perutah (a minimal coin).

Or, it might not be based on acquisition but rather on residence—meaning that through the eiruv, it is as though all are residing there, and there is no actual transfer of ownership. Therefore, an acquisition with a handkerchief would not be effective, and it specifically requires bread, as a person's main residence is where their bread is placed. Additionally, a minor's house is permissible, and a minor can collect the eiruv, and the bread does not need to be worth a perutah. 

Certainly, a house where the eiruv is placed does not require giving bread, since the person already resides there, and even according to the acquisition rationale, it is unnecessary. We hold that the concept is based on residence and not on acquisition (as per Tosafot on 49a, s.v. 'u'katan', since this is Rabbi Yochanan's opinion). All the legal authorities ruled this way (see Taz, section 62, but it is not necessary as clarified by Tosafot on Sukkah 3a, s.v. 'v'ain', examine there carefully).

One does not place the Eruv in a courtyard, nor in a house that is not fit for dwelling, such as a gatehouse, portico, or balcony, and likewise not in a house that does not have four cubits by four cubits. And if it has enough area to square off four by four, such as a long and narrow house, there are those who say it is valid (Magen Avraham section 6 in the name of Ralbach), but according to what is explained in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 286 regarding a mezuzah, it seems it is not valid. (For at the beginning of Tractate Sukkah, this is equated with the law of mezuzah, and the Rosh ruled there that it is exempt from a mezuzah, and this is the intention of the Magen Avraham there who referenced this, as explained by the Maharshal.)

If it is customary to always place the eruv in a particular house, it should not be changed to another house for the sake of peace, even if there is some reason to change it, unless there is a significant reason. And even if the owner of the house dies or sells the house to someone else, it appears that it should not be changed, because the reason is due to suspicion that people may say they are carrying without an eruv (see Magen Avraham 7), as it is stated in the Gemara (Gittin 60). Even if the second person wants to give money for a mitzvah in exchange for having the eruv placed in his house, it should not be changed (Magen Avraham 8). However, if from the outset it was stipulated that they have the ability to change it, it is permitted (ibid.). Similarly, if the first person demands money, it can be changed (ibid.). And if after the fact the eruv was placed in another house without any reason, it is not to be removed from there (ibid.). But if the first person makes a fuss and complains about this, it is taken from there and placed in the first location. (This seems correct to me.)

However, nowadays the custom is to place the eruv in the synagogue, which was also the practice of the ancients. And even though the synagogue is not a dwelling place, since our eruv encompasses the entire city, it is considered like a partnership, which does not need to be placed specifically in a dwelling, as even a courtyard suffices, as stated in Siman 366. And one must ensure that it is permissible to carry from the synagogue to the entire city, so that there is no interruption of a karmelit, such as gardens or similar places, for if not, the eruv is nullified. This applies to any place where the eruv is placed, and it is clear. (Taz 3)

If there is no Eruv in the city, the synagogue is treated like a courtyard of many people without homes designated for each individual, where carrying within it is permitted. Similarly, it is permitted to carry from the synagogue to the synagogue courtyard, assuming there are no residents in the courtyard. This is not considered carrying from a house to a courtyard, but rather it is all considered as one courtyard without any designated private domain. Even though there may be specific places designated for each person, since there are no partitions between them, it is not considered a dwelling place as explained. Even if an individual built and dedicated it as a synagogue, he has nevertheless relinquished his ownership and it is open to all.

The Magen Avraham (section 10) quotes the Maharil, who prohibits carrying from the synagogue to the courtyard. The reason for this prohibition is unclear, as ostensibly there should be no prohibition. Even if there are guests eating in a room adjacent to the synagogue, guests do not prohibit carrying, as stated in Siman 370. However, it is possible that this applies when there is a permanent homeowner, but in a synagogue where there is no permanent homeowner, even guests would prohibit carrying. This matter requires further study.

Generally, there are residents in the synagogue courtyard, and therefore it is prohibited to carry from the synagogue to the courtyard when there is no Eruv. However, within the synagogue itself, from the men's section to the women's section, and to the rooms adjacent to the synagogue where there are no residents, as well as the vestibule of the synagogue called a "foyer," all are considered part of the synagogue itself. Carrying from one to the other is permitted, since there are no residents, and they are all treated like a public courtyard.

It is stated in the Gemara (49a): One who divides his Eruv - it is not an Eruv. However, if he filled one vessel and there was overflow - there is no issue if it is in two vessels. And it seems to my humble opinion that this language indicates when one intentionally places it in two vessels, for some specific concern. But if it was placed in two vessels unintentionally, or his intention is that it would be placed better in this way or something similar - it is permitted. And this conclusion that "if he filled one vessel and there was overflow" - is a definitive statement, and it is also derived from the language of the Rambam who wrote in Chapter 1, Law 18: "If they divided the Eruv - it is not an Eruv," which implies they divided it intentionally. However, the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, Section 4, wrote: "One must place the entire Eruv in one vessel. If they divided it and placed it in two vessels - it is not an Eruv, unless one was filled, then it is permitted, provided the vessels are in one house," which implies that it is an obligation to place the entire Eruv in one vessel. Nevertheless, it seems that their intention is also that the obligation is to place it in one vessel and not to be particular to divide it specifically into two vessels, but without particular insistence - it is permissible. And it also appears so, for the reason is due to particular insistence, as we say there: "One who is particular about his Eruv - it is not an Eruv, for the name 'Eruv' implies mixing," that they should all be mixed and agreeable in it, so that one does not object to another, but rather a pleasant and agreeable partnership. (Rashi) And since he places it in two vessels with insistence, this is not a pleasant and agreeable Eruv. But without insistence, what difference does it make to us.

And based on this, it seems to my humble opinion that neighbors who each live in their own room or in their own house, and only share a common kitchen that they call a "kitchenette" - do not need an eruv. Since all their Shabbat food is in one room and in one oven, it is as if they all live there, because the place where the bread is stored determines residency. And even though they do not eat there, they are able to eat there, for in a complete eruv, not everyone eats in the same place, but because it is fit to eat there, it is considered as such. However, there may be an objection to this because they do not share one utensil, but according to what we have explained, only if the eruv is divided with strictness is it not valid, but without strictness, it is considered an eruv, and here too it is not done with strictness, but rather in their usual manner. Additionally, this is similar to "filling a vessel and there is leftover," which is allowed in two utensils. Furthermore, this is only in a general eruv, but here since all their eating is done on Shabbat and weekdays only in this room, there is no need for the condition of one utensil, since this is considered a real residence.

(And a support for our words is from Tosafot on Eruvin 72b, s.v. "And they agree," where they wrote: "Since they all use... for baking and cooking - it is considered as if they eat and sleep in one place." And I have seen in Chayei Adam, General Rule 73, Section 11, where he wrote that since there are two reasons, they use the homeowner's house and the house is only lent to them, etc. These are two reasons, as explained in Tosafot there, that borrowing is itself a permissive factor, see there and analyze deeply.) (And another proof from Section 24, see there.)

It is necessary that none of them should be particular about their portion of the eruv, if another eats it. If one is particular, it is not a valid eruv. Therefore, care must be taken not to make an eruv with something prepared specifically for Shabbat. This means that when one makes an eruv from his own property for all the residents of the courtyard and grants it to them through another person, he should not use an important item prepared for Shabbat. For when the residents of the courtyard come to request it from him, he may be reluctant to give it to them, and thus the eruv would be invalidated. Therefore, it seems to me that one should not make an eruv with the large loaves designated for Shabbat meals, but rather with smaller bread that is not so important. (This rule is elucidated in the Gemara 68a, in the case of Abaye who said, "If he granted them bread...but it is not possible to give it to them," etc., as well as in Tosafot there, and in the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, Section 5, where they wrote about this regarding an eruv, where each person contributes. This is not so relevant here, see there and examine it well.)

One may only establish an eruv with bread, even with bread made of rice or lentils. However, not with millet bread, as it is not considered bread at all. Any bread that is permissible to eat, even if it is forbidden for the one establishing the eruv, may be used for the eruv. Therefore, one may establish an eruv for a Jew with terumah, and a partnership for a Nazirite with wine. Similarly, if one vowed not to eat a certain food or swore not to eat it, one may still use it for an eruv or partnership, because even though it is not suitable for him, it is suitable for others, as we do not require that it be suitable specifically for him. The Sages were lenient in this matter, because as long as it belongs to him, such as if he inherited the terumah from his maternal grandfather who was a priest, or if he paid the priest for the terumah, or if the priest gifted it to him, it is considered as his own property. The Sages did not require that he himself be able to eat it specifically. See what is written in Siman 386, Section 12.

But something that is forbidden to everyone, such as untithed produce (tevel), even tevel of rabbinic origin, or first tithe from which the proper terumah has not been taken, or second tithe and consecrated items that have not been properly redeemed - one may not make an eruv or join in a partnership with them. However, one may make an eruv or join in a partnership with demai, because it is fit for the poor, as we give demai to the poor, and with first tithe from which the proper terumah has been taken, and with second tithe and consecrated items that have been redeemed, even if the additional fifth has not been given, because the additional fifth is not essential. And in Jerusalem, one may make an eruv with second tithe, even if it has not been redeemed, because it is fit for consumption there, but not in other areas unless it has been redeemed. And second tithe that was brought into Jerusalem and then left - redemption does not help it. There is a doubt, since an eruv of courtyards is only made with bread, whether it requires specifically bread upon which the blessing of Hamotzi is recited, or even bread upon which the blessing of Mezonot is recited. And I found in the Darkei Moshe in the name of Rabbeinu Yerucham that one may make an eruv even with small rolls, and this is bread that comes in a pocket for which the blessing is Borei Minei Mezonot, as I wrote above in Siman 168.

When each person contributes bread to the Eruv, they should not give a piece, even if it is very large, but rather a whole loaf, even if it is small. The reason is to prevent animosity, as one might say, "I am giving a whole loaf and you are giving a piece." Even if everyone agrees to give pieces, it is still prohibited, lest the situation deteriorate. (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 11) This means that on the following Shabbat, one might want to give a whole loaf and another a piece, and they will argue with each other. However, to require that all the whole loaves be of equal size is impossible and not much of a concern. Each person should simply ensure to give the required amount, which will be explained in section 368 regarding how much is needed altogether. 

Nevertheless, although a whole loaf is required, if part of it was taken as challah, it is acceptable, as this does not create animosity. Therefore, even if the loaf is missing the amount of challah taken by a baker, which is one out of forty-eight, we are not concerned, as they will assume the missing part is due to taking challah. Thus, even if the dough was not subject to challah at all, such as if it was kneaded in a quantity less than the challah requirement, it is still acceptable. If a piece was used and two pieces were joined together with a skewer, inserting the skewer into both ends to join them, if it is not noticeable that they are pieces and it appears whole, it is permitted, as this will not cause animosity since it appears whole.

The Tur and Shulchan Aruch write that all this applies when each person contributes to the Eruv. However, if one person makes the Eruv on behalf of others through an act of acquisition, he may use a piece, as animosity does not apply here since no one else is contributing with him.

And Rabbi Rema wrote in section 6: "Some explain that the requirement to use a whole loaf for the Eruv means that the entire Eruv together should be a whole loaf. Therefore, the custom is to collect a small amount of flour from each household, make one whole loaf from it, and use it for the Eruv. This is the widespread custom in all these lands. One must be careful that the loaf has the required measure specified later in section 368. Even if some of the flour remains and not all of it was used to make the loaf, it is still considered a valid Eruv, as it is no less valid than when one person acts as an agent for everyone, and the flour was given with this understanding from the outset." 

In our community, they make a large matzah or several matzot from the communal flour or from an individual's flour. When the sexton makes it from his own, he designates it for the entire city through another person. If the flour belongs to an individual, the sexton designates it on behalf of all the city's residents. The reason for using matzah is that it lasts longer (see Magen Avraham, commentary 13, that it is good to merit others). In our community, it is kept in a small closed box with a glass window, and it is hung in the synagogue so that everyone can see it and ensure it does not become moldy or infested with ants. If such issues do occur, another matzah is baked, and the sexton oversees this.

If one of the members of the courtyard or the city wants to give his own bread for everyone, it is acceptable, provided that he grants it to them through another person. He himself cannot grant it to them, as any item belonging to a person cannot be transferred to the domain of others until it is removed from his own domain. When the other person acquires it, he lifts it one handbreadth from the ground when he takes it from the ground at his command. When he takes it from the table, he lifts it one handbreadth from the table. When he transfers it from hand to hand, he lifts his hand one handbreadth in the air. Even though in all acquisitions, when acquiring by lifting, three handbreadths are required according to several legal authorities, as stated in Choshen Mishpat, Chapter 198, nevertheless, in the case of an eruv, which is rabbinic, they were lenient (Tosafot 79b s.v. "requires" see there). Additionally, lifting through one’s force is considered lifting, meaning if it was placed on a board and he moved the board until it was elevated by one handbreadth, it is considered lifting even in acquisitions, as we explained there in Section 8. It appears that one can also acquire through a kinyan sudar (symbolic act of acquisition) and through a kinyan agav (acquisition of land that includes movable property), as in all acquisitions.

And the one who acquires [the eruv] must acquire it on behalf of all the residents of the courtyard, or the alleyway, or the city, and for anyone who will be added from this day onward. One should not question how it is possible to acquire it for those who will be added, since they are not currently aware of this, and how can one acquire it on their behalf? This is not a question, because since it is a benefit for them to be able to carry, we can acquire a benefit for a person even without their knowledge. And there are those who say that even if one does not explicitly acquire it for those who will be added, the court's intention includes them as part of the eruv. If additional residents join after the eruv has been reduced from its required amount for the previous residents, it is not necessary to add more, since the remnants of the eruv are sufficient in any quantity, as stated in Siman 368. But for the newly added residents, it is necessary to add more, because for them it is the beginning of the eruv when they join after it has been reduced.

(It seems to me that for a slave who has been freed, or a non-Jew who has converted (in ancient times), one cannot acquire for them when they are added, because they are considered as something that did not exist at the time, as they are essentially a different entity. However, it is possible that according to what Tosafot wrote in Ketubot 58a, "afterwards," one can acquire it, see there. And for a minor who has reached adulthood, it is obvious that one can acquire it, because we can acquire a benefit for a minor, and scrutinize this carefully.)

Since the bread needs to leave the owner's domain, as mentioned, when one grants it through another, he should not do so via a person whose hand is considered like the owner's hand, for if so, it is as if he granted it through himself, which is ineffective. Therefore, he should not perform the granting through his minor son or daughter, even if they are not dependent on his table, because their hand is like his hand, nor through his Canaanite servant or maidservant, whose hand is like his hand. However, he can grant it through his adult son or daughter, even if they are dependent on his table, for although regarding found items they belong to their father, as mentioned in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 270, this is a rabbinic decree due to enmity, as explained there. But their hand is not considered like his hand, and since he wants them to acquire it on behalf of others, they can acquire it. Similarly, he can grant it through his Hebrew servant or maidservant, even when they are minors, because their hand is not like his hand. 

One might ask how a minor can acquire on behalf of others. The answer is that while in matters of Torah law he cannot acquire on behalf of others, in rabbinic matters like eruv, he can acquire on behalf of others, as explained in Gittin 64b. Similarly, he can grant it through his wife, even though he provides her with sustenance, for although a wife's hand is like her husband's hand, since we hold that if another gives her a gift on condition that her husband has no rights to it, it is effective according to several authorities, as mentioned in Even HaEzer, Siman 85. Therefore, when he grants it through her, it is as if he wants it to leave his domain. Therefore, even though she does not have a house in the courtyard, it is effective. (We must say that his minor son is worse than other minors because he is connected to his father. And in the Jerusalem Talmud, Eruvin, Chapter 7, Halacha 6, it differentiates between whether he has understanding or not, see there and examine it carefully.)

All of this is according to the opinion of the Rambam in the first chapter of Eruvin. However, the opinion of Rabbeinu Tam in the Tosafot (79b, s.v. "umazakeh") is that this law is similar to the law of found objects: a person cannot acquire on behalf of his grown son or daughter who are dependent on his table. He also cannot acquire on behalf of his daughter as long as she has not reached maturity, even if she is not dependent on his table, because the Torah has placed her under her father's authority regarding betrothal and other matters. Similarly, he cannot acquire on behalf of his wife if he provides her sustenance, or if he has said to her, "Take your earnings for your sustenance," even if she has a house in the courtyard, because we maintain later in Siman 370 that she does not require an eruv, and therefore it is of no use. If she herself required an eruv, I might say, "Since she acquires for herself, she can acquire for others," but since she does not require an eruv, it is of no use at all, and all the more so if she does not have a house in the courtyard. However, another person who is dependent on his table can acquire on his behalf. It also seems to me that grandchildren are not like children in this regard, and he can acquire on their behalf even if they are dependent on his table, as their hands are not considered his at all.

Initially, it is preferable to be stringent and consider both opinions where possible. However, in hindsight, one can rely on the more lenient opinion regarding the eruv. Similarly, an adult who has a wife and they are both supported by his father’s table can act on his behalf even initially if he provides for them based on an obligation, since in such cases, even found items do not belong to him, as stated in Choshen Mishpat. (This is the intention of the Rema in Section 10.) According to what we have explained in Choshen Mishpat, if the period of obligation ends and he continues to support them at his table, their found items belong to him, as written there. According to this, Rabbeinu Tam holds that one cannot act on their behalf, and according to our practice, initially, one should not act on their behalf. 

Know that when making an eruv, there is no need to inform the neighbors before Shabbat; rather, one informs them on Shabbat, as one can act in a person's interest without their presence. Once they are informed, they are permitted to carry on Shabbat. Even though they were not aware at the onset of Shabbat and did not intend to establish their residence there, nonetheless, this matter is agreeable to them even on the eve of Shabbat, and they assume that if someone makes an eruv on their behalf, they are content to establish their residence where the eruv is. (This must be the intended meaning of the Rema in this ruling; examine it thoroughly.)

Members of a group who were reclining at a meal and the day became sanctified (i.e., Shabbat began) - the bread on the table is relied upon for the purpose of an Eruv. This is provided that they are reclining in a house in a place where it is appropriate to place an Eruv, but if they are reclining in a courtyard - it is not valid. This is stated in the Gemara (Pesachim 86b) and by the Poskim (decisors of Jewish law), but it is not clear what the novelty is in this ruling. 

There are those who write that even if the bread belongs to the host, since it is placed on the table for everyone to eat from - it is considered shared by all, as if he explicitly granted them a share. (Taz, Section 334) However, this is not clear, because the term 'members of a group' implies that they joined together to eat, as is evident from the end of Chapter 7 of Pesachim. Furthermore, from our teacher the Rema in Section 11, who wrote regarding this law: "And similarly, if they have bread in partnership in one of the houses - they rely on it for the purpose of an Eruv," it is clear that each person has a portion in it. 

And when they are relying on the table of others, who gave them permission to establish an Eruv? The host only granted them the bread to eat and nothing more. Indeed, a guest is forbidden to give from the table even to the host's son or daughter, as stated in Chullin (94a). 

And it is true that the Maggid Mishneh wrote this in Chapter 1, Law 19, quoting the Rashba, and he wrote that the Rambam does not explain it this way. According to the Rashba, we must say that for the mitzvah of Eruv, the host certainly agrees, but according to the Rambam, it is necessary to understand what the novelty in this ruling is.

It appears to me that this is its explanation: Since at the time of the Kiddush, everyone was sitting in one room, and on the table was bread belonging to everyone—this itself constitutes the eruv, even though they did not explicitly establish an eruv. This is the meaning of 'relying on it,' meaning that they rely on this alone, since the essential acquisition of the eruv is that they live together. And the essential acquisition of the eruv is at the entrance of Shabbat, and they indeed live there at that time. And our master the Rema informs us of an even greater novelty, that even if they themselves were not together, but only their bread was together in one room, they can also rely on this alone, and there is no need to explicitly make an eruv. This is a strong proof for what we wrote in section 12, see there. And even though they did not recite the blessing, the blessings do not prevent [the eruv from taking effect], and even in such cases, a blessing is not necessary.

It is a mitzvah to seek out the practice of eruv chatzerot, and one blesses "upon the mitzvah of eruv." When should one recite the blessing? Either when collecting it from the members of the courtyard or when bestowing it upon them. And one says: "With this eruv, it shall be permitted for us to carry out and bring in from the houses to the courtyard, and from the courtyard to the houses, and from house to house among all the houses in the courtyard, for all the Sabbaths of the year." Some wish to add "for Yom Tov" as well, but this is not the custom. If the eruv was collected but the blessing was not recited, the blessing does not prevent the eruv from taking effect, and it is permissible to carry, as blessings do not prevent the mitzvah from being fulfilled. This is unlike the eruv tavshilin mentioned later in Siman 527, where the blessing is essential, as the main purpose is the blessing, to ensure a portion is chosen for Shabbat, and without this, it is nothing. But here, the main aspect is the participation or bestowing of ownership. 

One should not say that the blessing is not considered "over la'asiyatan" (before performing the mitzvah) because it is not so; before Shabbat begins, it is still considered "over la'asiyatan." Another person who is not from the courtyard should not recite this blessing since he has no connection to this eruv and is not performing any act that would warrant a blessing. Therefore, this is not similar to other mitzvot where another person can recite the blessing.

If Yom Tov falls on a Friday, whether it is permissible to bestow ownership on Yom Tov will be explained in Siman 528, where it is forbidden. Note that there are texts that include "from roof to roof" in this formula. However, it is unnecessary, as it is permissible to carry from roof to roof regardless, as stated in Siman 372. A guardian of a minor can make an eruv on his behalf, meaning to give a portion in the eruv for the minor. We do not say that since the minor can carry without an eruv, as a minor eating non-kosher is not something the court is commanded to prevent, as stated in Siman 343. Nevertheless, initially, we do not allow him to act in a prohibited manner, and also so that his household does not prohibit all the residents of the courtyard by not having a portion in it. (See Magen Avraham Siman 326, where the Ari z"l would bless and then bestow ownership on the members of the courtyard, and the Magen Avraham was puzzled by this. One can say that he did this so that the blessing would be "over la'asiyatan" and he would bless, bestow ownership, and say the formula. This explains the phrase "after making the eruv for himself, he should bestow it on others"—meaning when he makes the blessing over the bread, his intent is on the eruv, he bestows it on others as well, completing the eruv, and consider this well.)

It is stated in the Gemara (Eruvin 80a): One of the residents of an alley who customarily participates in the merging of alleyways but did not participate, meaning he does not want to participate, the residents of the alley may enter his house and take his portion of the merging against his will. Consequently, the same applies to one of the residents of a courtyard who customarily participates in the merging of courtyards and does not want to - the residents of the courtyard may come and take his portion of the merging against his will. Tosafot (s.v. "ragil") and the Rosh write that, in any event, the consent of his wife is required, as it is said there, "A man's wife can act on his behalf for the merging without his knowledge," and without his knowledge means even if he objects. But without the knowledge of his wife - certainly it does not work. Their reasoning is, how can one’s merging be effective against his will, since the main reason for the merging is that it is as if all are dwelling together, and he does not want to dwell there. But when his wife's consent is present, or one of the members of the household as will be explained - there is then someone from this household who is considered to dwell there. We do not concern ourselves with the fact that he does not want to, since, in any event, this house is included in the merging with a person from there.

However, the Rif and the Rambam do not interpret it this way, and this is the wording of the Rambam at the beginning of Chapter 5 of Eruvin: "One of the residents of an alleyway who is accustomed to participate with the residents of the alleyway but did not participate — the residents of the alleyway come into his house and take the contribution from him against his will. And one of the residents of the alleyway who does not want to participate at all with the residents of the alleyway — they compel him to participate with them." End quote. And its explanation is as follows: When he is accustomed, they can take his contribution themselves from his possessions. But when he is not accustomed, they cannot do so themselves; rather, they compel him through the court to give his share. (Maggid Mishneh) And the second ruling is from the Jerusalem Talmud, (end of Chapter 7) as written by the Maggid Mishneh and our teacher, the Beit Yosef, in Shulchan Aruch, end of Section 11.

And I am astonished, for in the Jerusalem Talmud it is explicitly the opposite, and this is the language of the Jerusalem Talmud: (there and at the end of the first chapter of Bava Batra) "One may establish an eruv for a person against his will." And in Bava Batra (chapter 1, halacha 7) the language is: "If someone does not want to participate in the eruv, they enter his house and establish it for him against his will." And it raises a difficulty from a Baraita, that it is specifically when he does not explicitly object, but if he explicitly objects, they do not take it against his will. And it answers that this 'objecting' refers to someone who is a Sadducee and does not acknowledge the eruv. But if he objects out of stinginess, they take it against his will. See there, as the version in Bava Batra is correct and in Eruvin there is a printing error. And behold, from this Jerusalem Talmud, there is clear proof for the opinion of the Rif and the Rambam, that it is not necessary to have the consent of his wife, as this is not mentioned at all in the Jerusalem Talmud. However, at any rate, we learn that the compulsion is not through the court, but that they take it themselves. (And the Pnei Moshe there in his commentary wants to explain this intention in the Rambam at the end of his superfluous words, that his intention is specifically when he does not want because he is stingy. But if he is a Sadducee, it is not an eruv. See there. And I am astonished, for the main point is missing, and what does it teach us?)

Therefore, it appears to me that the Rambam's intention is as follows: Since the wording of the Talmud implies that we only compel someone to contribute if they were accustomed to participating, but if not accustomed, we do not. And there are those who explicitly read in the Gemara, "Accustomed - yes, not accustomed - no," but the Rambam does not have this version (as stated in Kesef Mishneh there). This is also evident from what supports it from a Baraita, that we compel him to make a side post and crossbeam for the alleyway, as mentioned there. And here, it is not about being accustomed. Similarly, in the Jerusalem Talmud, it states generally, "We establish an eruv for a person against his will," and does not specify "accustomed." And the reasoning also supports this, for since he prohibits them, what difference does it make if he is accustomed or not? The Talmud's resolution on the support from the side post and crossbeam is merely a superficial dismissal, as is the way of the Talmud. And as proof, the Jerusalem Talmud also brings a proof from the Baraita of the side post and crossbeam and does not dismiss it. Therefore, the Rambam indeed ruled that there is no distinction between accustomed and not accustomed, and when he says "accustomed," it is not specific and is merely stating the common scenario. And this is what the Rambam is teaching us: After he transcribes the Talmud's ruling about accustomed, he says that even one of the residents of the alley who does not want to participate at all, even if he was not accustomed, we also compel him. In this case, it is not relevant to say "we enter his house and take," which is suitable for a one-time refusal, not perpetually. Therefore, we compel him by various means of coercion until he continually gives his share in the partnership. And if they wish to enter his house each time to take, they can do so, and who will prevent them? All this applies in an alleyway that prohibits them, such as when it does not have an entrance to another alleyway. This ruling the Rambam explains later, and in such cases, he holds that we do not compel even if accustomed, as clarified from his words there.

It turns out that the approach of the Rif and the Rambam is completely opposite to the approach of the Tosafot and the Rosh. According to the Tosafot and the Rosh, they themselves cannot take [it], even if it is regular, and it is forbidden for them unless it is with the consent of their wife or one of the household members. But according to the Rif and the Rambam, even if it is not regular, as long as it is forbidden for them, they can take it themselves, or according to the Maggid Mishneh and Rabbeinu Beit Yosef - through a court. And in a case where it is not forbidden for them, the Tosafot and the Rosh are lenient, for according to their opinion, even if it is regular and it is not forbidden, they can take it through their wife. But according to the Rif and the Rambam, if it is not forbidden at all - not at all, for even if it is regular, they cannot force him, for according to their words, there is no advantage to regularity at all, as is explained from the Rambam and the Yerushalmi that we brought.

And similarly in the case of his wife, the Rambam's opinion differs from that of the Tosafot and the Rosh, for according to their view, this is the law: A man's wife can make an eruv for him without his knowledge, even if he objects to her making it, and even if he does not usually make an eruv with them. And these words apply when he imposes restrictions on them, such as when the house is open only to that courtyard. But if the house is open to two courtyards, one in which he usually enters and exits and thereby imposes restrictions on them, and one in which he does not usually enter and exit. Therefore, in the courtyard in which he usually enters and exits and thereby imposes restrictions, she can make an eruv without his knowledge, even if he does not usually make an eruv with them. And in the courtyard where he does not usually enter and exit, even though he does not impose restrictions, if he usually makes an eruv with them, she can make an eruv without his knowledge. But if he does not impose restrictions and also does not usually make an eruv with them, she cannot make an eruv without his knowledge. This applies when he objects to it, but as long as he has not explicitly objected, even if he does not usually make an eruv with them and does not impose restrictions, she can make an eruv without his knowledge, for it is generally assumed that he consents.

According to the Rambam, a woman has no power when her husband objects, and only as long as he does not object does the woman's hand equate to her husband's hand, as stated by the Tosafot and the Rosh. However, when he objects, she does not have the authority to give even in a case of prohibition and regularity; rather, they themselves take it from him against his will. The Rambam's language there is: "A man's wife can make an eruv for him without his knowledge, provided that it does not prohibit his neighbors. But if it does prohibit, she cannot make an eruv for him or join him without his knowledge. How does it prohibit? For example, if he said, 'I do not join you in the eruv' or 'I do not share with you.'" End quote. Clearly, according to the Rambam, the power of his wife is less than theirs, as their power is greater than hers, because she does not have the authority to act against her husband's will, whereas according to the Tosafot and the Rosh, it is the opposite.

And even according to the opinion of Tosafot and the Rosh, she has no authority except to contribute his portion to the eruv or the partnership. But she cannot transfer ownership of his property to others without his knowledge, even if he did not protest. It appears to me that if he regularly transfers ownership to others, then she can also do so by default, as long as he did not protest. Likewise, she can transfer ownership from her own sustenance. (Magen Avraham, section 1)

And similarly, if the husband and wife are not in town, if the house opens only to this courtyard and it prohibits others - the household members can make an eruv without his knowledge. And even if it opens to two courtyards, and he is accustomed to using one - they can include his portion in the eruv. But if he is not accustomed and does not prohibit - they do not have permission to include his portion without the owner's knowledge, and in this, it is worse than a wife. In any case, the members of the courtyard do not have permission to take against his will, according to Tosafot and the Rosh. And our Rabbi the Rema wrote: "One who is not accustomed to making an eruv and made an eruv with the members of the courtyard, and then retracted his eruv - he needs to re-establish it. But if he is accustomed to making an eruv - the eruv stands against his will," end quote, meaning if he retracted before Shabbat. And it seems to me that this even according to Tosafot and the Rosh, the eruv stands against his will if he is accustomed to making an eruv, since he has already handed over the eruv, and this is his intention. That is, he handed it over for many Sabbaths and then retracted, and consequently, the eruv is nullified, for they did not acquire it for themselves but for the eruv, and by retracting, it is nullified. (And the Magen Avraham in subparagraph 5 seems to hold that he still needs to give the eruv, and therefore he questioned the Rosh at the beginning of chapter "Hadur," from which this law is derived, on this Rosh in chapter "Chalon," which are the previous laws, see there, and they do not come close to each other, as I have written. And also what he wrote in subparagraph 4 on the law of the courtyard members according to the opinion of those who say, which is the Rambam, that the same law applies to his wife, see there. And this too is puzzling, for in the Rambam it is explicitly stated that his wife does not, as I have written, and pay close attention.)

If the eruv has become diminished from its required measure, as will be explained, if one Shabbat has not yet passed over it, it is necessary to add to it until it reaches its required measure. But if one Shabbat has passed over it, even if part of it remains, it is valid. For it is taught: (Perek 80:) that the remnants of an eruv, any amount is sufficient. And anything over which one Shabbat has passed is called the remnants of an eruv, since it is no longer its beginning, as it has already been used for the first Shabbat. If one Shabbat has not yet passed, it is called the beginning of the eruv. And it seems to me that "any amount" is not literal, for it is not reasonable at all that if less than an olive's bulk remains it should be considered an eruv. Certainly, an olive's bulk is required. And from the Jerusalem Talmud there it seems to me that two-thirds must remain, as it says there: How much are the remnants of an eruv? "As Rabbi Yosi said, a hyssop that has been used once is valid; from then on, it is called its remnants. So too here." End quote. And the language is not proper, for can it be that a hyssop cannot be used even several times if it is lacking? And it is explicitly taught in chapter 11 of Parah: "The mitzvah of a hyssop is three stalks, and its remnants are two." There. Rather, the explanation is that one time it must be completely valid, that is, three stalks, and from then on it is called remnants. So too here, its remnants are two-thirds. (So it appears to me in my humble opinion.)

In the name of Maharil, they wrote that if the eruv is broken, even before the first Shabbat, it is permitted, since at the time of its placement it was intact (Magen Avraham, subsection 3). However, this does not seem to be the opinion of the other authorities. Nevertheless, it is certain that if it was intact at the commencement of Shabbat, we are not concerned if it breaks on Shabbat. There is an opinion that even if it breaks after the first Shabbat, it is good to make another, because the validity of the remaining eruv is only when at least one whole piece of bread remains (ibid. in the name of R. Menachem Mendel). This too is explained by the authorities in the opposite manner, that even a fragment is valid (ibid. and Beit Yosef). There is also an opinion that this is specifically when there is a joining of courtyards (shitufei mevo'ot) as well, then the remnants of the courtyard eruv are valid even in any amount. But when there is no joining of courtyards, the remnants of the eruv are not valid at all (Magen Avraham, ibid.). This seems to be the meaning of the language of the Mishnah there, which says: "The remnants of an eruv, any amount," because they did not say to make an eruv in courtyards after joining in an alleyway except so that the children do not forget, and therefore they were lenient with the remnants of the eruv. But otherwise, no. However, if so, it is very puzzling about the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, who wrote this law simply regarding courtyard eruvin. And Rabbeinu Yonatan explicitly wrote that a courtyard without an alleyway does not have the law of remnants of an eruv, see there. And I did not find this law of remnants of an eruv at all in the Rambam, for the truth is that he rejected it as law, as he wrote in the commentary on the Mishnah, that the law is not so, and so wrote the Ra'avad (who holds that the first Tanna disputes R. Yose as written by the Tosefot Yom Tov, and the Tur and Shulchan Aruch hold that R. Yose does not dispute the first Tanna, and they hold that "and they did not say to make an eruv in courtyards, etc." is an independent statement and not the words of R. Yose, and this is also evident in the Rambam Chapter 5, Halacha 13, see there. And this is certainly puzzling, that the Beit Yosef did not bring the opinion of the Rambam at all, and pay attention).

And what is the measure of the eruv initially? When there are eighteen householders or fewer, it suffices to have a fig-size amount (grogeret) for each one. If they are more than eighteen, even if they are a thousand or more, its measure is the food of two meals, which is eighteen fig-size amounts, which are about six eggs, and some say they are about eight eggs. This is what Rambam, the Tur, and the Shulchan Aruch wrote. And this is very surprising, as an olive-size amount (k’zayit) is half an egg, and it is explicitly stated in Shabbat (91a) that a fig-size amount is larger than an olive-size amount. How then can the calculation be twelve olives equaling eighteen fig-size amounts? The truth is, therefore, that our Rabbis the Tosafists (Pesachim 80: s.v. 'Agav') wrote that the calculation of two meals is not according to the calculation of eggs but rather large loaves, as mentioned there. But according to the Rambam, the Tur, and the Shulchan Aruch, it is puzzling. Some have resolved that here the six eggs are with their shells, and the olive is half an egg without its shell, and the shell is significantly large in volume. According to this, it is possible that a fig-size amount is larger than an olive-size amount (as the Gra writes later in Siman 426 and the Taz in Sk 6). 

Furthermore, it should be added that in Chapter 17 of Keilim, it is taught that there are large, small, and medium-sized eggs, and all the measures of the Sages are with the medium-sized ones, as it is taught there. And regarding two meals for an eruv, it is said that they are large ones. Although according to the Mishnah in "How to Join" (Eruvin 82b), it is difficult to interpret this way, nevertheless, there is room to stretch the interpretation. Likewise, regarding fig-size amounts, it is taught there in Keilim that there are large, small, and medium ones. We can say that here it is with the small ones, and the statement that a fig-size amount is larger than an olive-size amount refers to the large ones. Combining all these points together, the difficulty can be resolved, as is evident.

They made an Eruv, and afterwards the Eruv became defective. One of the residents of the courtyard came to repair it. Even though the remnants of the Eruv are valid, here it became defective before the first Shabbat (Taz, subsection 1), or when there is no alleyway according to those who invalidate the remnants of an Eruv in a courtyard without an alleyway, as stated in subsection 2. Even without this, one could say that they want to repair it so that it does not become entirely defective. If he comes to make the Eruv from the same type as the first, such as if they made it with wheat bread and now he also repairs it with wheat bread or something similar, even if he makes it from their own share, he does not need to inform them, as it is presumed they would agree. There is an opinion that says he needs the consent of one of the household members (Taz, subsection 2), which follows the opinion of Tosafot and the Rosh in the previous section. In my humble opinion, it seems that there is no need for this. According to their view, this is only necessary at the beginning of the Eruv, as stated there, but not when it has already been placed and has become defective, even if it has completely ceased.

And if one wishes to establish an eiruv with a different type, for example, if initially they established it with wheat bread and now wish to establish it with barley bread, or vice versa, if it has completely run out and they wish to establish it with their own – they need to inform them. And even according to the opinion of the Rif and the Rambam there, who say one can establish an eiruv against their will – nevertheless, perhaps they do not want a different type but prefer the previous type. However, when establishing it with one's own – there is no need to inform them, as it is presumed they would be agreeable. And if the first type has not completely run out but has diminished, even if establishing it with their own – there is no need to inform them, because as long as some of the first type remains, they will not mind if the correction is made with a different type.

And all of this applies if one comes to add because it has become damaged. But if one comes to add because new residents have joined, and there was not enough food for two meals sufficient even for a thousand residents, for them this is considered the beginning of the Eruv. Therefore, if they have only one entrance to this courtyard, and it results in them prohibiting the residents of the courtyard from carrying, they do not need their consent at all according to the Rif and the Rambam in the previous section, even if they are making an Eruv from their own (food). However, according to the Tosafot and the Rosh, the consent of one of the household members is required. But when they have two entrances, one to this courtyard and one to another courtyard, they must inform them, even if making an Eruv from their own (food), because perhaps they do not wish to join in an Eruv with this courtyard but rather with the other one. And although if they made an Eruv with both courtyards, they would be permitted to carry in both, as will be explained in section 378, nevertheless, perhaps they do not prefer the increase in residents. Some say that when making an Eruv from their own (food), there is no need to inform them. (The Rosh) The reason being that he holds it is permitted to carry in both courtyards, and if so, they certainly agree, and the reason that perhaps they do not prefer the increase in residents is a weak reason, and it suffices when making an Eruv from their own (food) and not from theirs. (And needlessly did the Magen Avraham wonder about this in section 1, as also written in Tosefet Shabbat section 4) And it is also explained in Mordechai, who wrote: "If new residents who have not yet joined them are added, they add and grant merit if making an Eruv from their own (food), and they must inform if making an Eruv from theirs," end quote. Thus, it is explicit that when making an Eruv from their own (food), there is no need to inform them.

If the city's eruv becomes moldy and is no longer fit to eat, or if many worms or ants fall on it, it is as if it has completely ceased to exist, and a new eruv must be made. Therefore, the custom is to make the eruv from a challah of matzah, which does not become moldy quickly, and also because it can be preserved during the days of Passover and can be preserved all year round. They should see to it that it is kept in a place without moisture and under glass, so that ants will not fall on it. This is better than making an eruv every Shabbat, lest they forget one Shabbat. However, if they want to make an eruv every Friday and eat the eruv on Shabbat, they are permitted to do so, as the eruv only needs to be in place at the onset of Shabbat, as stated in Siman 394. Some prefer to make an eruv every Friday because the eruv that is meant to last all year is prone to spoil. (Taz Sk 4, and he wrote there that it is also good to make an eruv every Friday without a blessing. However, this requires further examination, for if so, there would be an eruv in two places, and the residents would be divided and would prohibit each other unless they make an eruv on the condition that if the synagogue eruv is invalid, their eruv is valid, and if the synagogue eruv is valid, theirs is not an eruv. This requires further examination. And what was stated not to rely on an eruv that has diminished and to make another - this is certainly the case, and this is the common custom.)

Maimonides wrote in Chapter 6, Law 20: "A person can give a coin to a homeowner so that he will acquire bread and establish an Eruv for him with it. But if he gave it to a shopkeeper or a baker and said to him, 'Acquire [the bread] for me with this coin,' it does not constitute an Eruv. If he said, 'Establish an Eruv for me with this coin,' the shopkeeper or baker buys bread and establishes the Eruv for him. Similarly, if he gave him a vessel and said, 'Give me food with this and acquire it for me,' the shopkeeper or baker takes food and establishes the Eruv with it." End of quote. This is in the Gemara (Eruvin 81b). The explanation is that when one gives a coin to a homeowner to acquire bread for the Eruv, the homeowner becomes his agent to establish the Eruv, and an agent of a person is like the person himself. However, if he gives it to a shopkeeper or a baker and says, 'Acquire it for me,' he did not make him an agent but rather purchased bread from him, and since he did not take possession (pull the bread), it does not belong to him. But if he said to him, 'Establish an Eruv for me,' he made him an agent. Similarly, through a vessel (used for acquisition), it becomes a symbolic acquisition, and the bread is acquired through this act. However, there is no difference between a homeowner and a shopkeeper or baker, as even with a homeowner, if he says 'Acquire it for me,' it is ineffective, and with a shopkeeper or baker, 'Establish an Eruv for me' is effective. Consequently, Maimonides should have differentiated in the language, not between a homeowner and a shopkeeper or baker.

In truth, the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch wrote that for a homeowner, it is effective even if he says 'acquire for me,' because it is not customary for a homeowner to sell bread. Therefore, even with 'acquire for me,' his intention was not in the manner of a sale, but in the manner of agency, as is mentioned there. However, according to the Rambam, it is difficult. It seems to me that the Rambam also agrees with this, but he is speaking in the usual manner. For a shopkeeper and a baker, it is customary to say 'acquire for me,' meaning from your bread that is for sale. But for a homeowner, how could he say 'acquire for me,' since he is not selling his bread but is asking him to buy it on his behalf, and the term 'acquire for me' is not appropriate; rather, he is requesting him to buy bread for him.

And behold, the Rambam wrote this law in the context of Eruvei Techumin, see there. And we can say that in the case of Eruvei Chatzerot and Shitufei Mavo’ot where there are many people, and one says to a baker or a grocer, "Acquire for me with this coin," and he acquires for everyone from his own resources - it is a valid eruv, for just as he acquired for everyone from his own resources, he also acquired for this person from his own resources. But the Tur wrote that even in such cases it does not work, because even though he acquired for everyone from his own resources, since he took a coin from him, his intention was in the manner of a sale and not in the manner of acquisition, and he did not acquire, see there. And this is the approach of Rashi, see there. And the Tosafot wrote further, that even if the baker intended to acquire it for him from his own resources - it does not help, since he gave the coin and intended only to buy him bread, and the acquisition is nothing, see there. And the Rosh rejected this, arguing that since his desire is for an eruv, why would he not consent in such cases. And the Tur and Shulchan Aruch ruled according to the opinion of the Rosh, and the reasoning of Tosafot is also acceptable, for it is preferable for him to perform the mitzvah with his own money rather than having someone else acquire it for him. (Taz, subparagraph 4) And the Rosh holds that indeed this reasoning is valid, but since he cannot acquire with his own money without pulling it (an act of acquisition), it is obvious that it is better for him that there should be an eruv and not with his money, rather than not having an eruv at all. (See Magen Avraham, subparagraph 1, who questioned from Choshen Mishpat, Siman 199, where a judge for kiddushin acquires with money alone, because it is a matter of a mitzvah. And why not acquire also in the case of eruv with money alone, see there. And in truth, we brought there in Choshen Mishpat, section 5, that there are those who question this, see there. However, even without this, it works out well, for indeed in the Mishnah there is a dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and the Sages, where Rabbi Eliezer holds that for the sake of the mitzvah of eruv, one acquires with money alone. And the Sages disagree with him, and hold that this mitzvah is not so significant that for its sake we would nullify the rabbinic enactment that requires pulling, as what is the superiority of the enactment of eruv over the enactment of pulling. And they only nullified this enactment for a matter of Torah significance, like during the four periods, where the joy of the festival is a Torah obligation, and similarly, the essence of kiddush is a Torah obligation, and examine this well).

The sages taught in the Mishnah (Eruvin 5:7): "One who places their Eruv in a gatehouse, a portico, or a balcony - it is not a valid Eruv, and someone who lives there does not impose restrictions on the other residents. A storage house for straw, a cattle shed, a woodshed, or a storage room - this is a valid Eruv, and someone who lives there imposes restrictions." This means that an Eruv for courtyards must be placed in a house within the courtyard, as stated in Siman 366. A gatehouse, which is a passageway to the rooms in the house, even though it has four walls, and similarly a portico and a balcony - are considered like a courtyard, and the Eruv is not effective there. Therefore, someone who lives there does not impose restrictions on the residents of the courtyard, since it is not regarded as a house. However, a storage house for straw, etc. - is considered like a house, and placing the Eruv there is like placing it in a house. Therefore, someone who lives there and eats there imposes restrictions on the residents of the courtyard. But if someone has a storage house for straw, etc., and does not eat there, even if they sleep there - they do not impose restrictions, because we hold that the place of one's bread determines their residence. Similarly, a sukkah during the festival of Sukkot does not impose restrictions on the residents of the courtyard, even though one eats there, because it is a temporary dwelling and not considered like a house (Yoma 10a). Consequently, one should not place the Eruv there either. Nevertheless, it seems to me that a sukkah built like a house, but with the roof removed and covered with something suitable for a kosher sukkah - is called a house.

And it is stated there in the Gemara: "Wherever they said that one who lives there does not prohibit the carrying, the one who places the Eruv there, it is not considered an Eruv, except for the gatehouse of an individual," meaning that only one person passes through it, and a typical gatehouse is passed through by many, and therefore it is not like a house at all. But the gatehouse of an individual is not like a house except in the sense that one who lives there does not prohibit, since it is not a fixed dwelling. However, if they placed the Eruv there, it is valid, as it is considered like a house. And the Rambam ruled the opposite, that in the first chapter regarding placing the Eruv, he ruled that even in the gatehouse of an individual, it is not considered an Eruv. And in the fourth chapter regarding dwelling, he ruled that only in the gatehouse of many does one who dwells there not prohibit, but not in the gatehouse of an individual. His version in the Gemara was: "Wherever they said that one who places the Eruv there, it is not an Eruv, one who lives there does not prohibit, except for the gatehouse of an individual." And the reason is that since it is somewhat of a dwelling, they were stringent in this matter. The Tur and the Shulchan Aruch did not mention this at all, and I do not know why, and this requires further investigation. As for the practical Halacha, it seems that the law follows the lenient opinion regarding the Eruv, and one may rely on the version of Rashi and Tosafot to be lenient. But Rabbeinu Beit Yosef in his great work ruled like the Rambam, and he also inclined the opinion of the Tur to his view. And this is regarding a gatehouse, but in the case of a portico and a balcony, there is no difference between an individual and many. (Our foyer does not prohibit).

A homeowner who has many houses in his courtyard and lends or rents them to others - they (the renters or borrowers) prohibit him and prohibit each other (from forming a single eruv), since for the time being, each one is considered as his own house. Nevertheless, the Sages said that if the homeowner has access or control in all the residences, he does not prohibit (the formation of the eruv), since it is considered as if the homeowner dwells with them. The reason appears to me to be because borrowing and renting are not like selling, and in any case, since the borrower or renter controls the house, it is considered as his. And since the homeowner also has access or control - the homeowner is considered to be in control of the house.

And what is "Tefisat Yad" (possession or holding a place)? Rashi explains that it is where the homeowner has a place in the residence of another, where he puts his utensils to store. And we conclude in the Gemara that we require something that cannot be moved on Shabbat. And so wrote the Rambam in Chapter 4, Halacha 14, and this is his language: "A homeowner who rented out his courtyard houses to others and left his utensils or merchandise in each and every house of them - they do not prohibit him, since he has 'Tefisat Yad' in each house, they all become like guests to him. In what case are these words said? When he left there something that is forbidden to move on Shabbat, such as untithed produce (tevel) and lamps. But if he left in each house utensils that are permitted to be moved, since it is possible he could remove them today and no longer have 'Tefisat Yad' there - they prohibit him, until they make an Eruv." End quote. And any item that is permitted to be moved for its place, like a utensil whose primary use is forbidden, is not called 'Tefisat Yad.' Specifically, like untithed produce and lamps that are forbidden even for their place - this is called 'Tefisat Yad.' (Mishneh Torah) And the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch wrote that even something that cannot be moved due to its weight is considered as something that cannot be moved - and is considered 'Tefisat Yad,' such as large boxes and similar items. (And from the words of the Magen Avraham, Section 3, it appears that the Rambam disagrees with this. And I am astonished, since follow the reason. And what he wrote about the measure of weight, surely there is a measure in things that our eyes see that they always remain in their place.)

It is uncertain from the words of our Rabbis whether the intention is that the homeowner had a condition in this, that he is able to place his utensils there, but without a condition it is not effective, or even without a condition. And from the language of Rashi it is clear that it is specifically when he has a condition in this, for he wrote: "The homeowner has a place in the dwelling of this one where he places his utensils," end quote. And the expression "has a place" clearly indicates that this was his condition with him. And we must also say that what Maimonides wrote, "and he placed his utensils there, etc." means that this was their agreement, and this is the logical view, for without a condition, how can he be considered a homeowner and the residents as guests. And it is also explained in the Mordechai, who wrote: "It is not considered an act of possession unless the homeowner rents out his house and retains for himself one of the corners of the house to place his utensils there, etc." end quote, which clearly supports what we said.
