(And the Bach questioned what it matters that the homeowner can remove them from there on Shabbat, since the neighbors cannot, etc., see there. And it is not understood, for since the homeowner can remove them on Shabbat, it is not a permanent arrangement, and it is not called an act of possession, and he is not considered the homeowner there, and they are considered guests. And understand well.)

Therefore, when he has control, and they are considered as his guests—they are also permitted to carry from their homes to the courtyard, even though they did not make an eruv. And there are those who say that this applies in a situation where there are no other residents in the courtyard, for in all the dwellings, the owner has control. But if there are other residents in the courtyard, where the homeowner does not have control and they need to make an eruv—these too must contribute to the eruv and are not considered as guests of the homeowner, for just as those prohibit, these also prohibit. And this is when they bring their eruv to the others who prohibit. But when the eruv is brought to them—they rely on the homeowner's eruv, and the reasoning for this will be explained in section 12.

It is obvious that possession (seizure) of the house is only effective from the owner of the house to his neighbor. In other words, if Reuven is the owner of the entire courtyard, whether it is entirely his, or he rented it all, or borrowed it all from the owners who are not present, and then he rented or lent it to neighbors. But from one neighbor to another neighbor, the possession of the house does not help to consider both as one, and they need an eruv. Similarly, if two people bought a courtyard or rented or borrowed it together, they prohibit each other, and possession of the house does not help, even if one has a designated corner. (See Taz, subsection 1, who wrote that even if the owner has a designated corner, it is still called possession, see there. And some mistakenly interpret that a designated corner is effective without utensils, but this is a mistake. The intention is the opposite, even if he only has a corner with utensils and not the whole house, it is called possession, see Beit Yosef.)

Rabbeinu the Rema wrote: "One who rented a house from a non-Jew and rented one of the rooms to his friend. If at first he did not rent it with this intention - it is considered as if the entire building is his, and he rented one of the houses to his friend. But if he rented it initially with this intention - it is considered as two houses, and it does not help, even if one of them has some control over the other's house." End quote. Meaning, even though he alone rented it from the non-Jew, and the non-Jew does not know the second person at all, and he did not speak with the landlord at all about renting it for another person, nevertheless, since they agreed between themselves that one would rent and both would live there - neither has an advantage over the other, and having some control does not help. Only when he rented it for himself alone, and afterwards rented out a room or house - he is considered as the homeowner, and having some control helps.

The sages taught in a Mishnah: Five groups that observed Shabbat in one hall require one eruv for all of them. But when some of them reside in separate rooms or upper stories, each group requires its own eruv. The Gemara explains that we are dealing with partitions between each group that do not reach the ceiling, though they are ten handbreadths high, but do not reach the ceiling; therefore, one eruv suffices for all of them. However, if the partitions reach the ceiling, or are less than three handbreadths away from the ceiling, which is considered as if they reach the ceiling, each group requires its own eruv. This is not the same as what is taught: "when some of them reside in separate rooms or upper stories," since here the partitions are not complete but temporary partitions like curtains. Nevertheless, since they reach the ceiling, each group requires its own eruv (Tosafot, 72b, s.v. 'with partitions'), as is also explained in the Jerusalem Talmud there.

And the explanation of the matter is as follows: This hall belongs to someone who is not present here and does not render it prohibited, because a dwelling without its owner is not considered a dwelling. Therefore, these five groups that rested in it, even though they are guests, they prohibit each other, since there is no owner, and each group made between themselves and the other group a light partition from curtains ten handbreadths high, but they do not reach the ceiling. For if they were less than ten handbreadths high, they would all be considered as one room. And there is no significance in this, rather even if they are ten handbreadths high, since they do not reach the ceiling, they are all considered as one room. And it is dealing with a case where they do not pass through each other's areas, for if they did, it would all be considered like a gatehouse, but each one has a door to the courtyard. (Rashi) And in the Jerusalem Talmud it is stated that the hall is considered for them like a courtyard, and certainly, this is so, as in the hall, they all have authority over it.

And this is the language of Maimonides, Chapter 4, Law 7: "Five groups that stayed in one hall, if there were partitions between each group that reached the ceiling, then each group is considered as if they are in a separate room or a separate upper story. Therefore, they need bread from each group. But if the partitions do not reach the ceiling, one loaf suffices for all of them, as they are all considered like members of one household." End of quote. And it refers to when there are inhabitants in the courtyard, because otherwise, one loaf for all of them would not be relevant, as there would be no need for an eruv at all. And it is not understood according to this, for why does the Mishnah need to state "when some of them reside in rooms or upper stories," it should have taught a greater novelty, that even with partitions reaching the ceiling, there needs to be an eruv for each group.

But our Rabbis, the authors of the Tosafot, deduced from the discussions in the Talmud (s.v. 'But') that there is a distinction between them. If the partitions reach the ceiling, the law is that the groups do not need a separate eruv unless they bring their eruv to a house in the courtyard. However, if the eruv is brought to them, they do not need a separate eruv for each group, since they are considered as one house. Since it is established that the house where the eruv is placed does not need to contribute bread, as stated in Siman 366, therefore, they are all like one person, as the entire hall is considered one house. But in the case of complete rooms and upper stories, even if the eruv is brought to them, each group needs its own eruv. This is the way the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch in Siman 3 follow, see there.

Consequently, if there are no other residents in the courtyard, for partitions that reach the ceiling, no eruv is needed at all. But for complete rooms and upper stories, even in such cases, an eruv is needed. They also wrote that if everyone passes through each other's area, only the innermost two need an eruv, and all those before them are considered like a gatehouse. The one before the innermost needs an eruv because it is like a gatehouse for an individual, and according to the Rambam’s opinion we brought in Siman 2, a gatehouse for an individual prohibits, see there.

But if each one has an entrance to the courtyard and does not pass through each other's area, or if each one has an entrance open to the gatehouse in front of them, and the gatehouse is open to the courtyard, then each group needs an eruv for partitions that reach the ceiling. If some of them made partitions that reach the ceiling and some did not, those that reach the ceiling are considered separate and need an eruv for each one, and those that do not reach the ceiling are considered like partners, and they all give only one eruv. (See Taz Seif Katan 2 and it requires further study. In my humble opinion, the words of the Bach are correct, see there and consider it carefully).

And we have a significant question regarding this: Why did the Tanna need to describe this law with five groups residing in one hall? Since the primary distinction is between partitions that reach the ceiling and those that do not, he should have taught it with five people living in one house. If the partitions do not reach the ceiling, no eruv is needed, and if there are other residents, one eruv suffices for all of them. And if they reach the ceiling, each one needs an eruv. Certainly, this is not without reason. 

It appears to me, in my humble opinion, that this is specifically when they are only dwelling temporarily. But for actual residences, even partitions that do not reach the ceiling require an eruv for each one. For only in temporary dwellings and temporary partitions are they considered as one. But in permanent residences with temporary partitions, it is like temporary dwellings with permanent partitions, where an eruv is required for each and every group, as it is taught there.

We learned in the Tosefta (Chapter 5): "Five groups, some residing in rooms, some in upper stories - their common hall is like a courtyard for the houses" (end quote). This means that in the common hall, all of them have a share, and therefore, if they did not make an eruv among themselves, they are prohibited from carrying from their rooms to the common hall, just as from a house to a courtyard if they did not make an eruv. We can learn from this for our cities, where each one lives in their own rooms and there is one large room like a common hall, which they call a salon, that everyone uses. If they did not make an eruv among themselves, they are prohibited from carrying from their rooms to the large room, and from their rooms to the room of their friend. However, if they eat in one place, or if they have one kitchen, which they call a kitchen, it is permitted as mentioned in Siman 366.

The Tur and Shulchan Aruch wrote at the end of Section 3: "But if one has a teacher or a scribe in his house, as well as students who study before the rabbi and live in his house, each in his own room, even if each has an entrance to the courtyard and eats and sleeps in his room - they do not prohibit [the carrying]." This means that the homeowner who gives permission to a teacher or scribe to be in his house, and lends him a room and provides him with food, and he eats in his room, and uses the homeowner's utensils for baking and cooking - does not need an eruv. Similarly, students in their rabbi's house in such cases, because they use the entire house for baking and cooking, are considered as if they all eat in one place. However, this is a weak reason, but there is an additional reason, that he does not lend them his property to prohibit him, for the homeowner does not take rent from them but gives them accommodation for free, and it is like a loan, and he does not lend it to them to prohibit him, and they are nullified to him, and they are all considered as one. Therefore, if they indeed rent a room from him and pay money, and eat and drink by themselves, even though they use the household utensils for eating and drinking - they prohibit him, and an eruv is required. (This is the intent of Taz in Subsection 6 and Magen Avraham in Subsection 8) and see what is written in Section 382, Subsection 27.

Residents of a courtyard who all eat in one room, even though each individual has his own separate house, do not need an eruv because they are considered as members of one household. If they need to make an eruv with residents of another courtyard, one eruv suffices for all of them; this means that they bring only one piece of bread to the place where the eruv is made. If the eruv comes to them, meaning that the eruv is placed in this courtyard, they do not need to contribute bread at all, just like the house in which the eruv is placed does not need to give bread. All these houses are considered as one house, because with an eruv, the main factor is the place of eating.

And similarly, if many householders eat in one room, each at his own table, even though each one sleeps in a separate room and also regularly drinks and eats light meals there, nevertheless, an eruv is not required, since they eat their regular meals in one room. And even though each one eats there at his own table, and sometimes a light partition is put up between the tables for privacy – it is not considered a partition, since the partition is not permanent. All the more so when the partition does not reach the ceiling, it is like 'five who rested in a hall,' where it is explained that this does not constitute a partition or separation, since it is not permanent, and is only made when they want to perform an act of privacy or the like.

According to what has been explained, if someone eats in one place and sleeps in another, the place where he eats is primary, and there he causes a prohibition, but in the place where he sleeps, he does not cause a prohibition. Therefore, brothers who eat in their father's house and sleep in their own homes do not cause a prohibition, and all are considered as one. If they receive sustenance from their father's house, meaning that he gives them bread or money to buy bread and they eat in their own homes, they are neither considered as one nor as separate. This applies when there are no other residents in the courtyard, or even if there are residents but they place the eruv with them, they do not need to contribute to the eruv, as per the law of a house where the eruv is placed, since all are considered as one. However, if they take the eruv to another house, each one must contribute his part to the eruv. The same applies if they join with another courtyard for the eruv. The reason is that for one who receives sustenance, there is a perspective that he eats from the provider and is nullified to him, and there is a perspective that since he eats independently, he is considered as a separate domain. It is clear that this applies only to a son who receives sustenance, as well as to one who has five wives and five servants who receive sustenance from him and each eats in his own home, and similarly a student who receives sustenance from his teacher and eats in his own home, they do not cause a prohibition on each other if there are no other residents with them, or when the eruv is placed with them, as explained. However, a stranger who receives sustenance for his work or for another reason is considered as a homeowner in his own right, and they cause a prohibition on each other.

A guest who stays up to 30 days does not prohibit the homeowner and the courtyard residents. If he stays for more than 30 days, he is considered one of the courtyard residents. (Bava Batra 8a) Therefore, if someone stays in a courtyard, even if he stays in a separate house, as long as his stay is not permanent and does not exceed 30 days, he does not prohibit the homeowner and the courtyard residents, and both he and they are permitted to carry objects, whether from their house to the courtyard or from his house to the courtyard, and from his house to their house and from their house to his house. In a city where there is a general eruv for the entire city, even if guests come to the city and stay for more than 30 days, no eruv is needed, as the heart of the Beit Din (rabbinic court) stipulates on their behalf, as stated in Siman 366. (Taz, Subsection 10)

And this matter that a guest does not prohibit until thirty days, this applies when there is a permanent homeowner who owns or rents the lodging, for then even if there are many guests, they do not prohibit each other nor on the homeowner, because they are all subordinate to the homeowner. However, when there is no homeowner, such as when the homeowner lives in a different courtyard, the guests prohibit each other, and this is the law of 'five who stayed in a hall' as explained - they prohibit each other immediately if each one has a separate room where he eats. But if they all eat in one room, they do not prohibit each other. And if there is a non-Jew in the courtyard, they need to rent the right of way, and a non-Jewish guest does not prohibit until thirty days, as will be explained in Siman 384. (The Even HaEzer elaborated in disagreement with the Shulchan Aruch and holds that the guest immediately prohibits the homeowner. See there. However, we follow the words of the Shulchan Aruch and this is how we rule in practice).

Ten houses, one within the other, and they all pass from one to the other and exit through the outermost one to the courtyard or the street—only the two innermost houses need to contribute to the Eruv, and the rest are exempt, as they are all considered like gatehouses. The reason for this we have already explained in section 12.

A dwelling without an owner is not considered a dwelling and does not cause a prohibition for the residents of the courtyard. Therefore, if one of the residents of the courtyard leaves his house and goes to another courtyard, and leaves no one in his house, he does not prohibit the residents of the courtyard, whether he left on Shabbat or on the eve of Shabbat. There is, however, a difference between leaving on the eve of Shabbat and on Shabbat itself. If he left on the eve of Shabbat, even if he returns on Shabbat, he does not prohibit, because he was not present at the onset of Shabbat, which is the time when the eruv is established. But if he left on Shabbat and returned on Shabbat, he does prohibit, since he was present at the onset of Shabbat.

Rabbeinu the Beit Yosef wrote in Section 2: "A Jew from this courtyard who went to spend Shabbat in another courtyard, and did not intend to return on Shabbat, but then decided on Shabbat to return, does not prohibit." This is when he left during the day (before Shabbat), and since he was not present at the onset of Shabbat, we say, "Once Shabbat was permitted, it remains permitted." However, if he initially intended to return on Shabbat, he certainly prohibits, because this is not considered as if he left the place. It is like someone who leaves his house for a few hours; does this mean he is not considered to be living there?

And if he left on Shabbat and returned, even if he did not initially intend to return, nevertheless, when he returns, he does prohibit. In this case, we cannot say, "Once it was permitted, it remains permitted," because this only applies at the onset of Shabbat, which is the time of acquiring the eruv. (And the matter of prohibiting or not is relevant when he did not join the eruv with the residents of the courtyard, or if there are only two residents, meaning when he leaves, only one remains, and no eruv is needed.)

Even if he went to his nearby courtyard, in any case, if he only removed it from his mind and does not intend to return on Shabbat, this does not cause a prohibition on them. And the Tur wrote that this is specifically when he went to his daughter, but when he went to his (son-in-law), it causes a prohibition, because it is likely that his daughter-in-law will quarrel with him, and he will return home on Friday evening. And so it is in the Gemara (86a), and the Rambam in Chapter 4 of Hilchot Shemitah, holds that the law is not so. For the one who said it, only said it regarding what the Tanna mentioned "that he went to his daughter," because it is not customary to go to one's son because of his daughter-in-law, and therefore he mentioned daughter. But when he went, he went and does not cause a prohibition (and this is the intention of the Maggid Mishneh there). And also, our Rabbi the Beit Yosef did not bring this in Shulchan Aruch, and the law follows the lenient opinion regarding Eruv.

When do these words apply? To a Jew. But a non-Jew who left his home, even if he went to be in another city on the Sabbath day, he prohibits [carrying] until they rent his domain from him, as will be explained in Siman 382. And this is when he went to a nearby place within a day's journey from here, so that he has the ability to return here. But if he went to a distant place, he does not prohibit [carrying], even if he left several days before the Sabbath, since he has the ability to return and leave his place before the Sabbath. Nevertheless, we only need to be concerned about the Sabbath day if he could return to his home. (Magen Avraham, Subsection 2) And it is obvious that this is only if he left before the Sabbath. But if he left on the Sabbath, it does not make any difference at all, because in any case, if they rented from him before the Sabbath, they are permitted to carry; and if they did not rent, they did not make an Eruv before the Sabbath, and even if they made an Eruv, it is of no consequence. And some say that even a non-Jew has the same status as a Jew, and even if he went to his neighbor in the city, if he did not intend to return on the Sabbath, he does not prohibit and they can make an Eruv before the Sabbath. And if he settled and returned to his home, he then prohibits. (Tur) And we do not say "since it was permitted, it remains permitted," since from the beginning the Eruv was not fit to last the entire Sabbath, due to the concern that he might come and it turns out that it was not permitted at all. (Tosafot, Eruvin 65b, s.v. "d'asa") However, as long as he has not come, the Eruv is valid, and Rabbeinu Rema ruled according to this opinion. And there are those who say that even with a non-Jew, if it was clear that he did not intend to return on the Sabbath and he later settled and returned, we do say "since it was permitted, it remains permitted." And what the Tur wrote that he prohibits, and similarly later in Siman 382, this is in a general case. (Taz, Subsection 1 and Elya Rabba) But this does not seem to be the case from the decisors, as his intention is of no consequence. (And so wrote the Taz, Subsection 7. And what the Elya Rabba wrote that the Tur hinted that he does not prohibit, in our version it is written that he does prohibit, see there)

The Tur and Shulchan Aruch write in Section 3: "If someone from the marketplace had a house in the courtyard and died, and he left his property to one of the residents of the courtyard, if he died while it was still daytime, the inheritor does not cause a prohibition, as the eruv which was made for his house permits also what he inherited. But if he died after nightfall, he causes a prohibition, even though the inheritor participated in the eruv, it does not help for what he inherited afterward on Shabbat." End quote. The explanation is as follows: This individual from the marketplace, who had a house in this courtyard, would eat in this house. The reason he is called "someone from the marketplace" is because he did not live there permanently, but only to eat. Therefore, if he did not join in the eruv, he prohibited them. Hence, if he died on Shabbat, even though one of the courtyard residents inherited him, nevertheless, the eruv given on Friday does not help for what he inherited on Shabbat. But if he died during the day, even though this inheritor had already given his portion in the eruv, nevertheless, at the time of the acquisition of the eruv, this house was included in his portion. However, if this person from the marketplace did not eat there and did not prohibit them, even if he died on Shabbat, he does not cause a prohibition, because "once it is permitted, it remains permitted." The same law applies if one of the courtyard residents who did not join in the eruv died. It is usually the case that a courtyard resident likely gave his eruv, and therefore it is always permitted. But this is not so for someone from the marketplace, even though he is obligated to join in the eruv, sometimes he forgets because he is not regularly in the courtyard. (And this is the intention of the Magen Avraham in Section 4 and the Taz in Section 3.) From this we learn that if there are five residents in one courtyard, and four made an eruv, and one did not and he died on Shabbat, it is permitted to carry, and we do not say that the eruv did not take effect at the onset of Shabbat because of the one who did not join, and how can it take effect in the middle of Shabbat. It is not so, because the eruv takes effect at the onset of Shabbat, and these four become like residents together, and only one person prohibits them, and since he died, his prohibition is nullified. The proof of this is that the one who did not join in the eruv can relinquish his rights to them, as will be explained in Section 380, and what does relinquishing rights help if the eruv did not take effect. Rather, certainly the eruv takes effect, as we have written.

If one of the residents of the courtyard dies on Shabbat and did not leave any household members in his house, if he had made an eruv, even if someone from outside the courtyard inherits the house and comes to live in it on Shabbat, it does not prohibit [carrying], even though the inheritor did not join in the eruv, because "once permission is granted, it remains granted." This is because even if a resident of the courtyard inherited it, this reasoning would still be necessary, since the eruv made the previous day does not apply to the inheritance that occurred on Shabbat.

However, if the deceased had not made an eruv and someone from outside the courtyard inherited it, as long as the inheritor did not come to live in it, it does not prohibit [carrying]. If the inheritor comes to live in it on Shabbat, it does prohibit, because in this case, "once permission is granted, it remains granted" does not apply, since the permission had not been granted at the onset of Shabbat. If someone from within the courtyard inherits it, it prohibits [carrying] even if the inheritor did not come to live in it, since, as a courtyard resident, the inheritor prohibits the other residents by virtue of this house, which had not joined in the eruv before Shabbat.

This applies only if the inheritor had not been living with the deceased. But if the inheritor had been living with the deceased and had contributed his share to the eruv before Shabbat, then this house is automatically included in the eruv, since not all residents of the same house need to each contribute to the eruv. If the deceased died before Shabbat and someone from outside the courtyard inherited the house and came to live in it on Shabbat, it prohibits [carrying]. If the inheritor did not come to live in it, it does not prohibit. If someone from within the courtyard inherits it, it is permitted, because when he contributes his share to the eruv, this house is also included, since he inherited it before Shabbat. See Siman 381, where it is discussed that an inheritor can renounce his right.

A Jew and a convert who lived in a courtyard and made an eruv together, and the convert died while it was still daytime, and another Jew took possession of his property and moved in there, even if he did not enter until after nightfall – he still prohibits it for him. And we do not say: 'Since it was permitted at the onset of Shabbat, it remains permitted,' even though when he entered after nightfall, it was allowed at the onset of Shabbat, as in the case of a residence without an owner. Nevertheless, we do not say this, since it was possible for him to enter it on Shabbat. And it is not comparable to someone who left his house, where he left with the intention of not returning; whereas here, on the contrary, at any moment he is prepared to enter it. Moreover, even if he took possession of it on Shabbat and moved in there to live – we also do not say 'since it was permitted, it remains permitted'; because it was possible for him to acquire it during the day, and the permit was not clear, but rather pending. However, if he died on Shabbat – the one who takes possession does not prohibit it even if he enters there, since at the onset of Shabbat it was permitted due to the eruv of the convert, and we say 'since it was permitted, it remains permitted.' However, he can renounce his rights if he died during the day, like any other heir. And if the convert did not make an eruv – it has been explained in the previous laws that there is no difference in this matter between a convert and anyone else, as is evident.

If one of the residents of the courtyard is in a dying state (goses) at the onset of Shabbat, he still prohibits [the carrying] as long as he has not died, for a goses is considered alive in all respects. Therefore, they should transfer ownership of bread to him before Shabbat and establish an eruv on his behalf. Nevertheless, if he dies on Shabbat and one of the residents of the courtyard inherits his property, this person now prohibits [the carrying], and we do not say "since it was permitted, it remains permitted," because the eruv was not fit to last the entire Shabbat, as he was certainly expected to die on Shabbat since he was a goses before Shabbat. Therefore, if one of the residents of the courtyard or someone from the marketplace inherits his property and comes to live there on Shabbat, this person prohibits [the carrying]. However, everything that was explained earlier, that it is permitted by virtue of the eruv established before Shabbat, applies when he was not a goses before Shabbat but merely ill, as most sick people survive, and the eruv was fit to last the entire Shabbat, so we say "since it was permitted, it remains permitted." A minor who has a house and did not join in the eruv prohibits the residents of the courtyard, even if he cannot eat an olive's bulk of food. A guest does not prohibit [the carrying] for up to 30 days, as stated at the end of Siman 370.

Know that when Solomon and his court decreed the laws of Eruvin, they only decreed regarding carrying from house to house, as these are used regularly and each person's dwelling is distinct from the other's. However, roofs, courtyards, and enclosed yards (karpifot), which are not used regularly but only occasionally, do not have distinctions of domains regarding objects that were within them at the onset of Shabbat and not in the house. It is permissible to carry from Reuven’s roof to Shimon’s roof even without an Eruv, and similarly from this one's roof to that one's courtyard or to that one's enclosed yard, and so on. This is what the sages taught in the Mishnah: "Whether roofs, courtyards, or enclosed yards - they are all one domain regarding objects that were within them, but not for objects that were within the house.” And this is the law, as stated in the Gemara. The general principle is that any place that is a complete private domain, like those we mentioned, as well as an alleyway permitted by a side post or a beam, it is permissible to carry from one to the other for objects that were within them at the onset of Shabbat. But objects that were within the house - the house's rule applies to them. This means that even if the object is now in the courtyard, it is forbidden to carry it to a neighbor's courtyard, roof, or enclosed yard, or to the alleyway, because at the onset of Shabbat, when it was in the house, the prohibition applied to it, and once the prohibition applies at the onset of Shabbat, it applies for the entire Shabbat. Conversely, an object that was in the courtyard at the onset of Shabbat, and was later brought into the house and then taken back out to the courtyard, it is permitted to carry it to a neighbor's courtyard, roof, or enclosed yard. This is the general principle.

In the Gemara there, there is a dispute. Some hold that when we say that all of these are considered one domain, it is when the houses in the courtyard did not make an eruv, and it is forbidden to carry from the house to the courtyard. In such a case, household utensils are not commonly found in the courtyard. But if they made an eruv, and household utensils are commonly found in the courtyard, if we permit carrying from one courtyard to another, they might also carry household utensils that are in the courtyard. Therefore, it is entirely forbidden to carry from one courtyard to another, even utensils that rested in the courtyards. And some hold that there is no difference between whether they made an eruv or not, and even if they made an eruv, it is permitted. We do not decree concerning courtyard utensils because of household utensils, as this would be like a decree upon a decree. Most of the poskim ruled this way, and so it is ruled in the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch.

And this is the language of Maimonides in Chapter 3, Law 18: "All the roofs of the city, even though this one is high and that one is low, together with all the courtyards and all the enclosures that were surrounded not for the purpose of dwelling and none of them is larger than a 'Beit Se'ah,' together with the thickness of the walls between the courtyards, along with the alleyways that have a side post or a crossbeam - all of these are considered one domain, and one may carry within all of them without an Eruv utensils that were within them at the onset of Shabbat. However, utensils that were within the house at the onset of Shabbat may not be carried unless an Eruv has been made."

How so? A utensil that spent Shabbat within the courtyard, whether the residents made an eruv or did not make an eruv – it is permissible to bring it up from the courtyard to the roof or to the top of the wall, and from the roof to another adjacent roof, even if it is higher or lower, and from the other roof to a second courtyard, and from the second courtyard to a third courtyard's roof, and from the third roof to the alleyway, and from the alleyway to a fourth roof, until he transfers it throughout the entire city via roofs and courtyards, or via roofs and enclosures, or via courtyards and enclosures, or through all three from one to another and from this one to that one. However, one should not bring this utensil into a house unless all the residents of these places made a single eruv. Similarly, if the utensil spent Shabbat in a house and was taken out to the courtyard – one should not transfer it to another courtyard or another roof or the top of the wall or an enclosure unless all the residents of the places where this utensil is being transferred made a single eruv. This is the end of the words of the Rambam, of blessed memory. And see what is written in Siman 88, Section 4.

It is obvious that from all these places it is forbidden to carry to a karmelit. Therefore, it is forbidden to carry from a courtyard to an alleyway that does not have a side post or crossbeam, as it is considered like a karmelit, and similarly from a roof and an enclosed area (karpef). Regarding the enclosed area that we mentioned, it is permitted to carry from it to a courtyard and to a roof - this is in an enclosed area of two beit seah that was not enclosed for dwelling, or more than two beit seah and was enclosed for dwelling. But more than two beit seah that was not enclosed for dwelling is considered like a karmelit, and it is forbidden to carry from it even to another similar enclosed area, except for two cubits in this one and two cubits in that one. And within it as well, it is forbidden to carry more than four cubits, just like in a complete karmelit, such as the sea and a valley. All the more so, it is forbidden to carry from it to a courtyard, and to a roof, and to an enclosed area of two beit seah that was not enclosed for dwelling, or to more than two beit seah that was enclosed for dwelling, even two cubits in this one and two cubits in that one. (And in Rashi on Shabbat 130b, s.v. 'enclosed areas,' he wrote: "And if it is more than two beit seah and was not enclosed for dwelling - it is called one domain regarding its fellow or regarding the courtyard, to carry two cubits in this one and two cubits in that one." End quote. And certainly, these three words 'or regarding the courtyard' are a printing error, for how could it be permitted from a karmelit to a courtyard? Rather, it is certainly an error, and pay attention carefully.)

There is one who says that vessels that rested in the house are forbidden to be carried from a courtyard to an unfenced area less than two se'ah, even if they belong to one person. (Magen Avraham, Comment 1) And what Rambam wrote, which we brought in Section 3, that roofs, courtyards, and unfenced areas are considered one domain for vessels that rested within them, but not for vessels that rested inside the house, unless they made an eruv, his words imply that if they made an eruv it is permissible – does not refer to unfenced areas, because an eruv does not help for them. Even if they belong to one person, it is forbidden. (ibid.) For anything that was not fenced for dwelling is not included in the eruv and is considered its own domain regarding vessels that rested inside the house, even if they belong to one person who does not need an eruv. And so wrote Rashi (23b, s.v. 'that it is taught,' see there) and Tosafot at the beginning of the chapter of 'Window' (s.v. 'provided'). And one should not ask according to this, that an eruv does not help for unfenced areas that were not enclosed for dwelling, even if they are less than two se'ah. And if so, when they make an eruv for an alley or the entire city, the courtyards are open to the unfenced areas and it should be considered an open place that is forbidden to them. For one could say that since for vessels that rested within them they are considered one domain, it is permissible to carry from one to the other – it is not called a forbidden place in regard to what is forbidden to carry vessels that rested inside the house.

And in my humble opinion, it seems forced to interpret the words of the Rambam as not referring to enclosed yards (karpeifot). In truth, when they are included in an eruv, all enclosed yards less than two seah are nullified and do not count towards the eruv for the city. Proof of this is from what we established earlier in Siman 358, that a garden less than two seah, which is a minority of the courtyard, it is permissible to carry from it to the house (the Magen Avraham himself wrote there in subsection 14) because it is nullified in relation to the courtyard, as mentioned there. A garden is considered like an enclosed yard that was not surrounded for residential purposes, as explained there, because the seeds nullify the residential status. And if so, although an enclosed yard, even if it is a minority of the courtyard, is not nullified in relation to the courtyard like a garden, because it is considered a separate entity and is not similar to a garden that was a courtyard and became a garden, nevertheless, through an eruv it is nullified and included in the general eruv. According to this, the Rambam also refers to enclosed yards. (See in the Ritva 23b, who wrote in the name of his teacher, the Ra'ah, of blessed memory, that according to Rabbi Shimon, it is permissible to carry from a house to an enclosed yard that was not surrounded for residential purposes if it is less than two seah when they belong to one person. In this, Rabbi Shimon is more lenient than the Rabbis even regarding vessels that rested in the house. And he brought those who disagree with this, as mentioned there. However, in any case, according to an eruv, one can certainly say it is permitted, and examine this carefully).

Two courtyards that wish to make an eruv together in order to permit carrying from the houses—if each courtyard has already made an eruv for itself, there is no need for a new eruv. Rather, the residents of this courtyard bring their eruv into a house in the other courtyard where the eruv of the other courtyard is placed, and then all are permitted to carry from the houses and it is considered as one domain. Not everyone needs to bring their eruv; rather, one person from the courtyard brings it on behalf of all, as he acts as their agent. It seems to me that one must ask all the residents of the courtyards if they wish to make an eruv together, even though for the eruv of each courtyard alone, there is no need to ask, as one can benefit a person in his absence. However, with another courtyard, perhaps they do not wish to increase the number of residents. It also seems to me that when each courtyard has made its own eruv and now they combine their eruvin together as explained, a new blessing is required, and they do not fulfill their obligation with the previous blessing, as this is a different eruv. The blessing is recited, saying: "With this eruv, it will be permitted for us to carry from the houses of the two courtyards from house to house, and from houses to courtyards and from courtyards to houses."

And if they have not yet made an Eruv for each courtyard by itself, they collect bread from all the houses in both courtyards and place one Eruv. And if one of the residents of the courtyards wants, he can acquire [the Eruv rights] on behalf of everyone from his own [bread], just as in the Eruv of a single courtyard. Nevertheless, there is a distinction between them: he cannot go to the other courtyard and acquire [the Eruv rights] from his own [bread] for both courtyards and make the Eruv, because he has not yet been appointed as an agent from his own courtyard to make an Eruv with the other courtyard. Rather, he first makes an Eruv for his own courtyard through acquisition [of bread], and afterward for the other courtyard, he indeed becomes their agent, since the Eruv is made with their [bread]. Similarly, if his own courtyard does not need an Eruv, such as when they all eat in one place, as stated in Siman 370, one of them can initially go to the other courtyard and make an Eruv for everyone together from his own [bread] through acquisition. This is the intention of our master, the Rema, in Section 3, as mentioned there, provided he informs them as stated.

Two courtyards cannot join in an eruv unless there is an opening or a window between them that is four by four [handbreadths], and part of the window must be within ten handbreadths from the ground. Then, if they wish, they can join in one eruv, and it is permissible to carry even through the holes in the walls or over the walls. If they wish, each courtyard can make its own eruv. If the opening is more than ten [handbreadths] and does not have the form of a doorway, they must make a single eruv for both courtyards, for if not, they will render each other prohibited. Know that the window must be four handbreadths wide, even if it is very long, for if it is not four handbreadths wide, it is not a sufficient space for use. If the window is circular, it must have a circumference of seventeen handbreadths without a fifth, and a handbreadth and four-fifths of a handbreadth and a bit must be within ten handbreadths from the ground. (See Talmud, beginning of [Tractate] Eruvin).

And that which we require in a window that part of it be within ten [handbreadths from the ground] – this is in a window between two courtyards. But if two houses wish to join together through a window between this house and that house – they can join even if the entire window is above ten [handbreadths], as a house is considered as if it is filled [up to the ceiling], and it is not comparable to a courtyard. The reason is that a house has a roof while a courtyard does not. Therefore, a window between two houses, even if it is above ten [handbreadths] – if they wish, they may join together. The same is true for a chimney between a house and an upper story, even if there is no ladder to ascend from the house to the upper story – it is permissible to join together through the chimney if it is four by four [handbreadths wide]. And there is no question of how they ascend to the upper story without a ladder, as it can be said that they ascend with a ladder through the courtyard. And our teacher the Rema wrote in paragraph 5 that if they made a lattice before the window – it nullifies it from being considered a window. And a lattice is an iron grid with holes. It seems to me that this is when they set it and fixed it there permanently. But if they did not fix it – it does not nullify it from being considered a window.

It is a simple matter that the requirement for an eruv between houses applies when they did not make an eruv in the courtyard. If they made an eruv in the courtyard, then all places are permitted, and one can carry through any place he wishes. There are those who want to say that when they made a partnership in the alley, if there is no window or door between the courtyards, it is forbidden to carry through a hole between them, only through the alley. Similarly, in a courtyard and houses, when they made an eruv in the courtyard, and there is no door or window between the houses, it is forbidden to carry from house to house through a hole between them, only through the courtyard. (Magen Avraham, section 3) These words are perplexing and cannot be accepted, for if so, one should not be able to carry from room to room within a house through a hole between them by means of the house's eruv. How could it be said that in a place where an eruv is made, it would be said to someone, 'Through here you are permitted to carry and through here you are forbidden'? Therefore, this law does not hold. (The Gaon Even HaOzer disagrees with this, see there, and the Taz and Pri Megadim mention this, and it seems they agree with his words. The Magen Avraham, according to his reasoning, wrote in section 6 'through the courtyard,' and the Taz wonders at this, but according to his reasoning it is understandable, and delve into this matter.)

If there is a wall between the courtyards that is ten handbreadths high without a door or window, or if the ground of one is ten handbreadths higher than the other, or if one is five handbreadths higher and a partition of five handbreadths is made on it to complete it to ten, and there is no door or window – they cannot make an eruv together, but each one makes an eruv on its own, unless there is an alleyway and they make an eruv through the alleyway with a partnership of alleyways. And this will also be explained in Siman 387, if one can rely on the partnership in place of the courtyard eruv, see there. Similarly, if the courtyards are completely open to each other or more than ten cubits – they cannot make an eruv each on its own, for they prohibit each other, but they make one eruv together. Especially if there is no partition of ten handbreadths between them, they only make one eruv together. If there is a partition of ten handbreadths between them with a doorway not more than ten cubits, they have the choice – if they want, they make one eruv, if they want, they make two eruvin, each on its own. It is obvious that if there is a form of a doorway between them, even more than ten cubits and even entirely open – they can make an eruv each on its own. And know, that less than ten and not completely open – nevertheless, it needs to leave either a four-handbreadth strip or two small strips as per the law of a courtyard.

A wall between two courtyards without a window or door, which requires each courtyard to make its own eruv, or if there is a door or window and they chose to make separate eruvin, and there were fruits or other items that can be handled on Shabbat on top of the wall – the residents of both courtyards can lower them into their courtyard, and also raise fruits or objects from the courtyard onto the wall, as the wall and courtyards are considered one domain, as explained. However, they should not lower them into the house, or from the house onto the wall, and also objects that were in the house from before Shabbat cannot be placed on the wall from the courtyard. Nevertheless, there is a distinction based on the width of the wall on top: if it is four tefachim wide, which has the measure of a karmelit, it is prohibited to lower from it into the courtyard objects that were in the house from before Shabbat. But if it is not four tefachim wide, it is considered a makom patur and is permitted, as long as they do not exchange as stated in siman 346.

And if the wall is ten tefachim high for one courtyard and not ten tefachim for the other, where the ground level of one courtyard is higher than the other and the wall is four tefachim wide, the courtyard where the wall is not ten tefachim high is permitted to use it even with objects that were in the house when they made an eruv for themselves. The courtyard that is ten tefachim high is prohibited to use it even with objects that were in the courtyard. Because for the neighbor it does not have the status of a roof, since for him it is not ten tefachim high, it has the status of a courtyard, and it is permitted to carry on it even objects that were in the house when they made an eruv for themselves. Therefore, if the second one uses it with objects that were in the courtyard, it will be treated as a roof, and consequently, the first one will be prohibited from using it with objects that were in the house, and it is not just that he should be prohibited.

And if you question, why should we give the entire wall to the first one and not part of it to the second one? This is the law, that anything which is easier for one to use, like this case where it is not ten tefachim high, and difficult for the other – we give it to the one for whom it is easier to use. (Gemara Avodah Zarah.) However, if the wall is not four tefachim wide, which is a makom patur – both are permitted to use it, even with objects that were in the house, as stated. (And this is the intention of the Magen Avraham, section 12)

A house situated between two courtyards, where each courtyard made its own eruv, and the homeowner made an eruv with both courtyards – he may carry items to and from both courtyards. And one should not question how a person can reside in two places, because this is not an issue, as anyone has the right to live and eat in multiple places, and all of them are considered his residences. However, the residents of the courtyards cannot carry utensils that were in the house at the onset of Shabbat from one courtyard to the other via this house that opens to both courtyards; only he is allowed to do so, since his residence is in both places, but theirs is not.

The Sages said (Avoda Zara 2b) that a ladder is considered a doorway. Meaning, when there is a wall between two courtyards without a door or window, if a ladder is placed on each side, it is considered as if there is a doorway, and they can join in an eruv, since one can ascend this ladder and descend the ladder on the other side. The ladder must be four handbreadths wide, meaning the rungs should be four handbreadths wide, and it should be a fixed ladder, which means it must have at least four rungs. If it has fewer than this, it is considered temporary and does not help unless its rungs and side supports are heavy, making it stable and fixed. The ladder must be placed opposite the ladder on the other side or within three handbreadths of distance so that one can ascend on this side and descend on the other. But if the distance is three handbreadths or more, it does not help if the wall is less than four handbreadths wide, as this is not proper passage. However, if the wall is four handbreadths wide, even if the ladders are distant from each other, one can ascend the ladder, walk on the wall to the ladder on the other side, and descend into the courtyard, since a width of four handbreadths is suitable for walking.

And the ladder must reach the top of the wall, or be less than three handbreadths from its top. It is not necessary to set the ladder at an angle; even if it is upright, it serves as an entrance, similar to a platform, which is also not set at an angle. Therefore, sometimes a ladder ten handbreadths high is not required. For example, if the wall is only ten handbreadths high, one can place a ladder that is seven handbreadths and a bit high next to it, and place another ladder on the other side. The ladder should be four handbreadths wide, as mentioned, and the ladder serves both for using the top of the wall, allowing one to use it comfortably while standing on the ladder, and for combining the two areas when placing a ladder on the other side as well, since there is not three handbreadths left to the top of the wall. Then, regarding use of the wall, both sides are considered equal, of course.

If the wall of earth is higher than ten handbreadths, and one removes a clod from the top of the wall to reduce its height from ten handbreadths, if this removal covers a length of four handbreadths, it is effective to make it like an entrance for the purpose of joining [domains] together, whether the removal is across the entire width of the wall from one side to the other, or if it is not from side to side, this person can use the entire wall, because for him, its use is convenient. But if the removal does not cover a length of four handbreadths, it is not considered an entrance to join [domains] together, and it also does not allow using the entire wall; one can only use the area directly decreased. And even though with a ladder that is not four handbreadths wide, it is not effective even to use directly opposite it, this is because a ladder less than four handbreadths wide has no permanence and can be moved. But with the removal of a clod, at least directly opposite it, its use is convenient. However, for the entire wall, it is not effective, because it is not convenient to stand there, but directly opposite, one stands on the ground and uses it.

If one builds a platform next to the wall to reduce its height from ten handbreadths, if it has a length of four handbreadths along the wall and also projects four handbreadths, making it four by four, it is effective for using the entire wall. And even though with a ladder or a mound we do not require it to be four by four, nevertheless, with a platform we do require it, because a platform is not convenient to stand on if it is not four by four. With a ladder, one can hold onto the sides of the rungs, and with a mound, one can hold onto the sides of the wall. But a platform, which is like a separate structure, if it is not four by four, it is nothing. In any case, even if it is four by four, it is not considered an opening to join together (for an eruv) unless it reaches the top of the wall or is within less than three handbreadths. The same applies to a ladder. Only with a mound did we not require anything more than reducing from ten (handbreadths), because it is part of the wall itself, and it is considered a complete opening. And if it is not four by four, it is not effective even to use against it, for the reason I have written.

If one inverts a bowl that is four by four and of any height, whether small or large, and reduces thereby the wall's height from ten [handbreadths], it is permitted to use the space opposite the reduction, but not the entire wall. This is less effective than a bench because it is not fixed, as it can be removed since it is a utensil. (Magen Avraham, section 17) Some say that its law is like that of a bench, and one may use the entire wall. (Bach and Taz, section 7) Know that with a bowl, it does not help unless it is attached with mortar, for if not, it is nothing, as it can immediately be taken away. It must be firmly attached, so it cannot be removed from its place without digging it out with a spade. But if the mortar is only placed on it, it is permitted to take it, and it is not considered a base for something prohibited, as the mortar is muktzeh. For his intention is not that the bowl should serve the mortar and be a base for it; rather, the mortar serves the bowl. Therefore, the bowl is not considered a base for the mortar, as we have explained similarly in Siman 259. (Magen Avraham, section 18) Therefore, it has no permanence until it is firmly attached, as mentioned.

If one builds a platform on top of another platform, if the lower one has four by four [handbreadths] and reduces the height from ten handbreadths - this indeed reduces, as there is no need for the upper one at all. Even if the lower one does not have four by four but the upper one does, and there are not three handbreadths between the lower and the upper - it also reduces, as they are considered as one. And even though this reduction is short from below, since its measure is completed from above and there are not three handbreadths between them - it is considered a reduction. But when there are three handbreadths between them - it is considered a reduction in the air, and it is not considered a reduction. (Rashi on Avodah Zarah) This only helps for using it, but it does not help to make an opening to combine them in an eruv, even if the other person also did the same on the other side, unless the platform reaches the top of the wall or less than three [handbreadths]. This is according to the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch, section 11. But according to the Rambam, chapter 3, law 5, it is explained regarding a platform on top of another platform that if they wish, they can combine into one eruv, and perhaps his intention is when it reaches the top of the wall. (See Beit Yosef and see Maggid Mishneh there, law 13, who wrote that all reduction is until the top of the wall with less than three, and pay close attention).

A projection extending from the wall between two courtyards, which is like a board and measures four by four [handbreadths], and one placed any type of ladder on it, even if it does not meet the required measurement of a ladder as previously defined, is sufficient to permit the use of the wall, provided that the distance from the projection to the top of the wall does not exceed ten handbreadths. This allows one to stand on the ladder, ascend to the projection, and use the wall. Even though the ladder is temporary, since it is adjacent to the projection, it will not be removed from there. However, to create a joint eruv, if the other party also has a similar arrangement, it will not be effective unless it is placed at the top of the wall or within three handbreadths of it. This arrangement is only effective for usage, as it is considered convenient for this purpose, as previously discussed. Additionally, this is specifically when the bottom rung of the ladder is not more than three handbreadths from the ground, making it easy to climb, and similarly, the rungs should not be more than three handbreadths apart. Although this condition was not stipulated for a permanent ladder, as a permanent ladder is easy to climb even if the rungs are more than three handbreadths apart because the foot stands firmly. However, for a temporary ladder, if the rungs are more than three handbreadths apart, it is not easy to climb.

According to what we have explained, so it appears to me from the wording of the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch, that in a fixed ladder they did not write this condition, and in a ladder next to the beam they clarified this condition. But according to what appears from the words of the Talmud, it is not dependent on this reason. And this is what is stated in the Gemara: "A ladder whose rungs are spaced... and there is not three [handbreadths] between one and the other - it reduces." And Rashi explained that a standard ladder is a ladder with steps, similar to those we have permanently for ascending to attics, and they are like steps. And a ladder whose rungs are spaced is like our ladders, where the rungs are spaced one above the other and there is air between them. If so, the distinction is clear: a ladder with steps that are wide, even though there are three [handbreadths] between the lower step and the ground and between each step - it is easy to ascend, not so with a standard ladder. And the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch, who mentioned this detail in a ladder that is under the beam, I do not know their reason, and indeed Maimonides did not mention this in a ladder that is next to the beam. However, the one whose rungs are spaced - they all omitted, and the reason is hidden from me and requires investigation.

In the case of a ladder adjacent to a projection, the ladder must rest upon the projection, meaning the top of the ladder must lean on the projection so that they function as one unit. However, placing the ladder merely near the projection is ineffective because the ladder does not serve the projection but rather expands it, whereas we require a ladder for the projection itself.

If the wall is not higher than twenty handbreadths, one projection is sufficient, positioned in the middle of the wall, so that there are not ten handbreadths from the ground to the projection, nor from the projection to the top of the wall. The ladder is placed beneath the projection as stated, allowing one to climb to the projection and use the wall.

If the wall is twenty handbreadths high, two projections are needed: one within the lower ten handbreadths and one within the upper ten handbreadths. A ladder is also placed on the lower projection, allowing one to climb to the upper projection and use the wall. Therefore, care must be taken that the projections are not aligned directly above each other, as it is impossible to place a ladder in such a manner. Instead, the upper projection should be offset along the wall from the lower projection, and the ladder should be angled towards the upper projection.

Even though we have stated that with a fixed ladder, even if it is not placed at an angle, it still serves as a reduction, this applies to a fixed ladder and when it is against the wall. However, for a temporary ladder adjacent to a projection, if it is not slightly angled, one cannot climb it. Therefore, when one projection is offset from the other along the wall, the ladder can be placed at a slight angle, as is evident. (This is my humble opinion.)

Regarding a ladder that is next to a wall, if one does not have a ladder that is four handbreadths wide and places two ladders together such that their combined width is four handbreadths, and arranges it so that it is easy to climb—meaning that he spaces the ladders slightly apart and fills the gap between them with straw, intending to hold onto the ladders with his hands and climb on the straw with his feet—it is not effective. This is because it is not convenient to climb on the straw. It does not permit one to use the wall, and certainly not to establish an eruv together if the other person does the same on the other side, because the place for the feet is in the middle of the ladder, and it is not suitable to climb on straw.

However, the reverse is effective: placing the ladder in the middle and the straw on the sides, holding onto the straw with the hands and climbing the ladder with the feet. Therefore, even if the ladder is not four handbreadths wide, it is effective both to permit using the wall and to establish an eruv together if both sides do the same, because this is a proper way of walking. This is on the condition that the ladder reaches the top of the wall, as stated in paragraph 17. (Magen Avraham, section 22)

If the ladder is not four [handbreadths] wide, and he carved into the wall on either side of the ladder to complete it to four [handbreadths], such as when the wall is thick and projects on the side of the ladder (Tosafot 78b, s.v. 'chakak'), it is sufficient for him to carve four [handbreadths] in the height of ten [handbreadths]. And even if the wall is very tall, since the ladder reaches the top of the wall, and even though it is not four [handbreadths] wide, nevertheless, since at the height of ten [handbreadths] there is a width of four [handbreadths], it is considered as an entrance. If he did not place a ladder at all but instead carved the wall in the manner of ladder rungs to climb it, he must carve [the width of four handbreadths] throughout the entire height of the wall. This is not comparable to a ladder, which does not need to be four [handbreadths wide] up to the top of the wall, because a ladder is easy to climb, which is not the case with carvings in the wall. Therefore, it needs to be four [handbreadths wide] up to the top or less than three [handbreadths apart] (Gemara 78b). And the Rambam in Chapter 3, Halacha 11, diverted this law to a completely different matter, see there.

Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote in Section 15: "If there was a tree beside the wall and it was made into a ladder to the wall - if they want, they can make one eruv. But if an Asherah (idolatrous tree) was made into a ladder to the wall - they cannot make one eruv, because it is forbidden to ascend it by Torah law, as it is forbidden to derive benefit from it. And the Rosh, of blessed memory, wrote the opposite, that a tree does not work but an Asherah does work, provided it is dry." This is the end of his words. The reason for the first opinion regarding the tree is that even though it is forbidden to use a tree, nevertheless, since this is only a rabbinic prohibition, and the time of acquiring the eruv is during twilight, and for any matter that is a rabbinic prohibition, they did not decree during twilight, even though we need the entrance for the entire Shabbat - nevertheless, the main point is during twilight. Therefore, the Rosh's opinion is that it is certainly forbidden, because the entrance needs to be permitted for the entire day. Regarding the prohibition of the Asherah, the Rosh holds that since it is a secondary prohibition and not from the prohibitions of Shabbat - we are not concerned about it. And if it is because there is also a rabbinic prohibition, because one is using a tree, we are dealing with it when it is dry. And even though above in Siman 336 we also forbade it when it is dry, nevertheless, the primary prohibition is when it is moist, and they were stringent with dry because of a safeguard as explained there, but the primary decree of the Sages was only for moist. (See Magen Avraham Section 26 who raised this difficulty, and according to what we have explained, it is resolved, as explained in Eruvin 100b, that they decreed regarding dry because it is not distinguishable, as stated there.)

A trench between two courtyards that is ten handbreadths deep and four handbreadths wide, and runs along the entire separation between the courtyards, and does not leave a space of four handbreadths together without a trench - is considered a separation like a wall, and each courtyard must make its own Eruv and not a joint one. Even if it is filled with straw and hay - it is not considered a seal, as long as they have not explicitly nullified them to remain there permanently, and certainly not with fruits. But if it was filled with earth and pebbles, even if it was not filled with the intent to nullify but rather it got filled up on its own - it is generally considered nullified, unless it was cleared from there, and they must make an Eruv together. And nullification for one Sabbath does not help to nullify the partition, for although it works for other matters, it does not work to nullify the partition. (There, section 127, in the name of Tosafot, Chapter 4: 'Bor')

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote in section 16: "There are those who say that if it is filled with fruits in a regular manner, they are nullified, for it is customary to make a storehouse there," end quote. This means that they disagree with the first opinion, which requires a permanent nullification, and it is sufficient to nullify for this Shabbat. And even though one can also take from there on this Shabbat, as stated in Siman 333, nevertheless, it is not customary to use it extensively until it is nullified from its regular state. (See Magen Avraham section 28, who raised this difficulty on the Rema, but the Eliyah Rabbah section 24 already answered it as I have written. And what the Gemara established in chapter 4 regarding untithed produce [tevel], the same applies to a storehouse, as mentioned there.)

If part of the trench is sealed with dirt or something similar, which permanently nullifies it, if there is a length of four handbreadths in the trench, it is considered an entrance, and they may choose to make an eruv together or separately. This applies up to a length of ten cubits. Beyond this, it is considered a breach greater than ten cubits, and they make one eruv and cannot make two. (This is the intention of Rabbi Yosef cited by the Taz, subsection 9). Similarly, if a board four handbreadths wide is placed over the trench like a bridge from one edge to the other, it is considered an entrance, and if they wish, they can make an eruv together or separately, and this applies up to ten cubits, which is considered an entrance. Beyond this, it is considered a breach, and they make one eruv and cannot make two. If the board is placed lengthwise along the trench, reducing its width so that it is less than four handbreadths wide, if it covers the entire length of the trench, the partition is nullified, and they make an eruv together. If it does not cover the entire length, it is considered an entrance up to ten cubits, provided it has a length of four handbreadths within the trench; otherwise, it is nothing, and they make two eruvin. If the trench for one courtyard is ten handbreadths deep and for the other is not ten handbreadths deep, or if it is level for both, its law is like that of a wall as detailed in sections 13 and 14.

A stack of straw between two courtyards, if it is ten handbreadths high - each one makes an Eruv for itself, as it is considered a complete partition. And even though over time they might remove it, nevertheless, even a temporary partition is considered a partition. The same law applies to a stack of grain or seeds. If it decreases during the week to less than ten handbreadths - they need to make a joint Eruv, but if it decreases on Shabbat - we say 'since it was permitted, it remains permitted', and if it decreases to ten cubits - it is considered an entrance. As long as it has not decreased, it is forbidden for either of them to place straw from the stack into his basket on Shabbat to feed his animal, because we are concerned that he might take so much that it decreases from ten handbreadths. And even though on Shabbat 'since it was permitted, it remains permitted', it is still forbidden to do so initially. (See Taz section 195) And even placing it there so that the animal can eat is forbidden, because there is also a concern of muktzeh (set-aside). But he can stand at a distance in front of it, so that it does not move to another place. There is no concern of diminishing the partition because of its eating, since it will not eat so much that it decreases from ten handbreadths to more than ten cubits. This law is similar to the law explained in section 325 regarding a gentile gathering herbs, see there. (And this can resolve the Taz’s question in section 10 on the Beit Yosef, see there, and the Beit Yosef does not imply this, see there and understand well).

According to the Rosh, even on a weekday it is forbidden to put it into his basket, and similarly to place an animal there by hand, because we are concerned that it might be reduced to less than ten handbreadths on the eve of Shabbat and he will not notice. However, due to the issue of muktzeh (set-aside objects) - the Rosh does not hold this concern, as this is not considered an act of dismantling a tent. (Magen Avraham, section 30)

In what case are these words said? In the case of a stack of straw between two courtyards. But a stack of straw between two houses, where each one makes an individual eruv (joining of domains) - it is permitted to place it into his basket and to feed from it to his animal by hand. Because since there is a roof and a partition - it will be noticeable if it gets reduced to less than ten handbreadths over a length of more than ten cubits. And it is not necessary to say if the stack reaches up to the roof, it will be noticeable when it is taken, but even if it does not reach the roof - it will still be noticeable if it decreases significantly. 

(And what the Magen Avraham wrote in section 31, that one house is open to this courtyard and the other to another courtyard and the two courtyards did not join together in an eruv - it is certainly possible to say this, but it is not necessary, for it can be said that they are open to one courtyard, but on this side, there are two homeowners in two rooms who made an eruv together, and similarly on the other side. And when it is reduced to less than ten handbreadths - they will prohibit each other, and pay attention to this matter).

There are times when two houses can make an eruv together, even though a public domain separates them. For example, two people living in two upper stories facing each other, with the width of the public domain separating them. From each upper story protrude two balconies facing each other, and they are wide boards that protrude from the walls of the upper stories facing each other, and are more than ten handbreadths above the ground, and the two balconies do not touch each other. If one places a board that is four handbreadths wide from one to the other, it becomes like a doorway. If they wish, they can make one eruv together, and if they wish, each can make their own eruv, as this is like two courtyards with a doorway between them. The board must be fixed with nails so that it does not wobble and cannot be removed on Shabbat. (See Magen Avraham 1:1) And if you ask, isn’t the public domain separating them? However, above ten handbreadths, it is not considered a public domain, as stated in chapter 345.

And specifically when the balconies are directly opposite each other. However, if they are not directly opposite each other, with one extending to the east and the other extending to the west, they cannot combine to form an eruv. Even if a plank four handbreadths wide is placed from one to the other, since the plank would go from one corner to the other, and people do not make an entrance at a corner. (See there, subsection 3) And even though this is not a similar case, and in the previous section it was explained regarding a wall with a ladder, that since the wall is four handbreadths wide, we do not worry if the ladders are not directly opposite each other, nevertheless here, in the case of height in the air, if the paths are not directly opposite each other, it is not a proper path even if it is four handbreadths wide, because one would fear falling. The same applies if one is higher than the other. This is when they are three handbreadths apart or one is three handbreadths higher than the other. But if they are within three handbreadths of each other, whether in distance or in height, it is considered a proper entrance, as anything less than three handbreadths is considered as if it is joined together, and it is as if they are placed equally.

And Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote: "If the distance between them is not four [handbreadths] - even without a board, the law is the same." This means that the reason we require a board is because they are significantly separated from each other. However, if they are close to each other, no board is needed. Even if they don't actually touch, as long as the distance between them is less than four handbreadths, one can stride over and they can combine into one eruv. If they actually touch or are less than three handbreadths apart, it seems that they can only make one eruv and not two. This is also taught in the Tosefta at the beginning of Chapter 8, which states that even if the separation is less than four [handbreadths], they make one eruv. The language of the Tosefta is: "Two balconies opposite each other in the public domain, if there are four handbreadths between them, they make two eruvs and not one. Less than this, they make one eruv and not two." This is referring to without a board.

(It is a great wonder that the versions of the Rif and the Rosh in the Mishnah (Eruvin 78b) are the same, for they wrote: "And similarly, two balconies opposite each other - they make one eruv and not two. Less than this, they make two eruvs and not one," as mentioned there, and so it is in the Rema's notes. It is astonishing that the Tur and the Beit Yosef did not mention this at all, and this 'less than this' has no reason. If I were not afraid, I would emend their words to match the Tosefta. And in the Jerusalem Talmud on this Mishnah, it says: "Some say they make two eruvs and not one, some say they make one eruv and not two. The one who says two, less than this [requires] a board; the one who says one, less than this [requires] a gap." Both versions are mentioned, and it needs explanation. Investigate further.)

According to this, the laws regarding balconies are as follows: If they are close to each other, or less than three [handbreadths apart]—one joins them in one eruv, not two, unless some are close to each other and some are not, and where they are close, it is not more than ten cubits. In that case, if they wish, they can create one eruv, and if they wish, they can create two. If they are four [handbreadths] apart and no plank is placed between them—they create two eruvin and not one. If they are less than four [handbreadths] apart, according to the Tosefta—they create one eruv and not two. However, our rabbis, the Tosafists, wrote (Eruvin 78b s.v. 'and so on') that if they are less than four [handbreadths] apart—if they wish, they can create one eruv, and if they wish, they can create two. When a plank is placed from one to the other, if the plank is less than ten cubits or exactly ten cubits and does not fill the entire space of the balconies—if they wish, they can create one eruv, and if they wish, they can create two. But if the plank fills the entire space or is more than ten cubits—they create one eruv and not two. (And this is also found in Magen Avraham 382:2, and the words of Taz 382:2 are very difficult, and similarly wrote Eliyah Rabbah—examine well).

It has already been explained several times that regarding Shabbat, once something is permitted, it remains permitted. Meaning, if at the onset of Shabbat something was permitted, even if later the permission is compromised, we say, "since it was permitted, it remains permitted." It is understood that this does not apply to complete changes in partitions, such as if the partition between a private domain and a public domain falls; in such a case, can we also say, "since it was permitted, it remains permitted"? It is obvious that it is unreasonable to say so. Rather, we say this in a situation where there is no significant change in the partitions, or where it does not concern partitions at all, as will be explained with God's help, and as is explained in the Gemara. (At the end of the first chapter regarding this matter of "since it was permitted, it remains permitted," it says there that Rabbi Yochanan said this only when the partitions are not there, etc., see there.)

Therefore, if there were two people with a doorway or a window between them and they made an eruv together, and then the doorway or window was sealed on Shabbat, and they are no longer open to each other — nevertheless, they are permitted to carry from one to the other through holes and cracks between them, because once it has been permitted, it remains permitted. Similarly, they are permitted to carry over the top of the wall.
