Also, if there was a wall between two courtyards and each made an eruv for itself, and the wall was breached on Shabbat — each is permitted to carry in its own courtyard, even objects that were in the house when Shabbat began, because once it has been permitted, it remains permitted. And even though this is a change in the partition, it is not a partition that separates between distinct domains, like between a private domain and a public domain or between a private domain and a karmelit, but rather between one private domain and another private domain, and it is as if there is no change in the partitions. However, if the courtyard was truly breached into the public domain or a karmelit, it is forbidden, and we do not say in this case that once it has been permitted, it remains permitted, and if the courtyard was breached into a karmelit, it also becomes like a karmelit. Nevertheless, there is a lenient aspect to this, that one is permitted to carry two cubits in the courtyard and two cubits in the karmelit. Some say that even this is forbidden, because to be stringent, the courtyard's status has not been lost (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 3), and our teacher the Beit Yosef in his great book wrote that it is permitted (see there). (And in the Turei Zahav, subparagraph 6, he wrote that this is a dispute between Rashi in Eruvin 24 and Tosafot in Shabbat 9, see there).

And know that in the case where they made an eruv through a doorway and the doorway was sealed, it has been explained that it is permitted to carry (as before) from courtyard to courtyard through holes and cracks and over the wall. Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 1 that according to the Rambam, it is only permitted to carry within each courtyard itself, but not from courtyard to courtyard. The novelty here is that even though one courtyard does not have an eruv, since the eruv was placed in the other courtyard, it is still permitted to carry. And this is the language of the Rambam at the end of chapter 3: "Two courtyards that made one eruv through a doorway and the doorway was sealed - each one is permitted by itself, since part of Shabbat was permitted, the whole Shabbat is permitted," end of quote. The Ra'avad objected, saying that for themselves, it doesn’t need to be said, but even from one to the other as before the sealing, see there. In my humble opinion, the Rambam does not mean this, for if so, he would not have said 'each one is permitted by itself,' since the novelty is only in the courtyard that does not have the eruv. And the Rambam's intention is according to the essence of the matter, that they placed the eruv to carry from one to the other and now the doorway was sealed, and there is no place to carry from one to the other. Nevertheless, the eruv remains valid, and each one is permitted by itself, meaning as before the sealing, to do all their needs in both courtyards. And if one finds any crack through which they can carry to the other courtyard, it is certainly permitted, and the Rambam did not differentiate except because they were forcibly separated, and his intention is not to prohibit carrying from courtyard to courtyard.

If one made an eruv for the year and the entrance was sealed during the weekdays, the eruv is nullified, since it was not open at the onset of Shabbat. However, if it was reopened during the weekdays, the eruv remains valid. We do not say that since it was sealed, the eruv is completely nullified. Moreover, even if it was sealed during the weekdays and reopened on Shabbat, it is permitted to carry, as the essence of the eruv is not nullified. Even if it was intentionally sealed to nullify the entrance, the eruv remains valid, and whenever it is reopened, it returns to its valid state. There is an opinion that if the entrance was breached, the eruv is completely nullified, and a new eruv would be required when it is reopened. (Bach) However, this is not the main opinion, as in this matter, the issue is not dependent on the intent revealed by sealing the entrance, but rather on the time of the making of the eruv. (Taz 1 and Magen Avraham 1)

And there are those who want to say that in a standard situation with intent, it only works when it was opened on a weekday, for then we say that at the entrance of Shabbat, he reverted and intended for it to be an Eruv. But if it was opened on Shabbat, and he intentionally closed the entrance, then he did not want at the entrance of Shabbat for the bread to be for Eruv. (Magen Avraham there) For it is understandable if it was closed automatically, one could say he thought about the Eruv, that when it would be opened, it would be an Eruv, and he did not divert his mind at the entrance of Shabbat. But not when he himself closed it. (there) However, from the words of our master the Rema in section 1, who wrote after 'and it was opened on Shabbat' - 'and even if he intentionally closed it', it is explicitly implied that even in such cases, it is permitted. And one could say in his reasoning, that his closing the entrance was not intended to nullify the Eruv, but rather he did not want this entrance until he decided to open it or make another entrance. But the partnership of the bread - he never nullified.

A small courtyard that was breached entirely into a larger one before Shabbat, and the breach is not more than ten cubits wide - the larger courtyard is permitted to carry objects that were inside a house into its courtyard if it made an Eruv for itself, but the smaller courtyard is forbidden to carry objects that were inside a house into its courtyard unless they made an Eruv together. This is specifically when the walls of the smaller courtyard enter into the courtyard of the larger one, so that everyone sees that the projections of the larger courtyard are not from the smaller one. Otherwise, the smaller courtyard would also be permitted due to "appearing from the outside and flush on the inside," as someone standing outside behind the smaller courtyard will see the projections that are also from the smaller one. This is specifically when the walls of the smaller courtyard are three handbreadths away from the larger one, for less than three handbreadths is considered as if they are joined (lavud), and they are permitted by "appearing from the outside." These laws have already been explained in Siman 363 and in Siman 365.

And similarly, a small roof that was breached before Shabbat entirely to a large roof – it is forbidden to place on the small roof any utensils that were in the house, unless they made an eruv together, but the large roof is permitted if it made an eruv by itself. The Tur and Shulchan Aruch (in section 4) write that this is specifically when the walls of the house of the large one are recognizable to someone standing on the roof, meaning that the roof is aligned with the walls, for we say 'extend and raise the partition'. However, if they are not recognizable, such as when the roof protrudes beyond the walls – it is considered a karmelit, unless there is a window from the house that is four by four [handbreadths]. And why is the roof considered a karmelit, for it is fully a private domain, except that we are dealing with a protrusion of four handbreadths which is the measure of a karmelit, and if so the entire roof is breached completely to a karmelit, and it too becomes a karmelit. (Magen Avraham section 5) And if it protrudes a little bit – we do not say 'extend and raise', but if it does not protrude – it is fully a private domain, like a pillar in a public domain that is ten handbreadths high and four handbreadths wide. (ibid.) In any case, when the two roofs are open to each other – they prohibit each other (ibid.) if they do not have partitions. (And the Maharsha at the beginning of the chapter 'All Roofs' in the commentary 'by the partitions' wrote that not because of the protrusion itself is it a karmelit, but since it protrudes a little, there is no 'extend and raise', and automatically it becomes a karmelit, and this requires further study.)

A courtyard that has many houses and many dwellings in the upper stories, and before the upper stories there is a balcony called a gallery, and on the balcony there is a ladder of steps from the courtyard to the balcony, and the residents of the upper stories go out from their house to the balcony, and from there they descend via the ladder to the courtyard, and from the courtyard they go out to the public domain—their status is like that of two courtyards. It has already been explained in Siman 372 that a ladder has the status of an entrance, and it is like two courtyards with an entrance between them. These can make an eruv for themselves, and those can make an eruv for themselves if they wish, and the residents of the upper story are forbidden to carry from the balcony to the courtyard utensils that were in the house over Shabbat, and certainly from their house to the courtyard. Similarly, the residents of the courtyard are forbidden to carry from the courtyard to the balcony utensils that were in the house over Shabbat, and certainly from their house to the balcony. Nevertheless, if the residents of the courtyard made an eruv for themselves and the residents of the balcony did not make an eruv at all, the residents of the balcony prohibit the residents of the courtyard for another reason: since their movement is through the courtyard, and they are forbidden in their place, and we hold later in Siman 378 that a foot that is forbidden in its place prohibits in another place. But if the residents of the balcony made an eruv for themselves and the residents of the courtyard did not make an eruv, it does not matter to them, because the residents of the courtyard do not pass through the balcony. And if the residents of the upper stories have no movement at all through the courtyard, such as if the balcony is towards the public domain and the ladder stands in the public domain, they have no connection with each other at all, and they cannot make an eruv together, since they do not have an entrance to the courtyard. Nor can it be done through a window, for the windows in the upper stories are obviously above ten handbreadths. (According to Rashi, even a foot that is permitted in its place prohibits in one courtyard, and so it appears from the Rambam and the Ra'av.)

From these matters we have learned that in cities where each courtyard has many dwellings, and the buildings are lower, middle, and upper levels, and each has its own balcony, and each one exits to the courtyard through its own balcony - the residents of the lower levels can make an eruv for themselves and the residents of the upper levels for themselves, and the courtyard will belong to the residents of the lower levels. However, if the residents of the upper levels do not make an eruv for themselves, they will prohibit the residents of the lower levels from using the courtyard, as per the law of "a foot that is forbidden in its place." It is good and proper for the entire courtyard to make an eruv together, or one person should acquire it for them and make an eruv for everyone, and this is the common practice and should not be changed. (And if there are dwellings that do not open to the courtyard at all but rather exit through a balcony to the public domain, they cannot have a part in the eruv, but this is generally not found as they would usually have an entrance to one of the houses or to the courtyard.)

In a courtyard and a balcony, it has been clarified that the courtyard belongs to the residents of the courtyard, and the balcony belongs to the residents of the upper floors. However, they are not similar in every respect. Specifically, regarding the balcony—everything found on the balcony belongs only to the residents of the balcony; this is not the case in the courtyard. That is, sometimes there is a high mound or a high pillar in the courtyard, and it belongs to the balcony and not to the residents of the courtyard. Sometimes it belongs to the residents of the courtyard and not to the balcony residents, and sometimes both are prohibited from using it, as will be explained. The reason for this is as follows: The Sages said (Eruvin 83b) that if an area is accessible to two domains, and it is easily used by one and difficult for the other, it is given to the one for whom it is easily used. We already mentioned this above in Siman 372:14. Therefore, elevated areas in the courtyard, if they are easily used by the courtyard residents and difficult for the balcony residents, they are given to the courtyard residents. If they are easily used by the balcony residents and difficult for the courtyard residents, they are given to the balcony residents. If they are easily used by both or difficult for both, they prohibit each other from using it, and both are forbidden to use it. Now we will explain what is considered easy and what is considered difficult.

If there is a pillar in the courtyard that is not ten handbreadths high from the ground, and the balcony is not ten handbreadths higher than the pillar, then both the courtyard and the balcony have equal ease of access to it, and they prohibit each other from using it. Even though for the balcony it involves lowering from above to below, and for the courtyard it involves throwing from below to above, and it is known that it is easier to use by lowering than by throwing, nonetheless, this does not suffice to give preference to one over the other, and it is considered equally accessible to both, and both are prohibited from taking objects that rested in the houses to there.

However, this applies when the pillar is close to the balcony within four handbreadths. But if it is removed by four handbreadths, according to the Tur, it is not considered easily accessible to the balcony residents because they need to use it by extending a distance, and it is given to the courtyard residents. However, our master the Beit Yosef, in his large book, prohibits even in such cases. He wrote that since the use of the courtyard residents is by throwing, the balcony residents can also use it by throwing. Even though it is not exactly the same, because for the courtyard, which is less than ten handbreadths, it is not considered throwing at all, whereas extending four handbreadths is considered throwing, nonetheless, this is his opinion. (And the Magen Avraham in subsection 1 leans towards the opinion of the Tur, see there.)

If the distance from the pillar to the balcony is ten handbreadths, and for the residents of the courtyard it is less than ten handbreadths, the usage is assigned to the residents of the courtyard, even if it stands close to the balcony. If it is ten handbreadths high for the residents of the courtyard and less than ten handbreadths from the balcony, and stands within four handbreadths of the balcony, it is assigned to the residents of the balcony because their usage is easier and for the residents of the courtyard it is difficult. But if it is four handbreadths away from the balcony, both are forbidden to use it because both need to throw to use it. Therefore, both are forbidden to place on it utensils that were in the house until they make an eruv. If for the courtyard it is ten handbreadths high and also ten handbreadths from the balcony, both have difficult usage and it is forbidden. But when it is four handbreadths away from the balcony, and thus the balcony has two disadvantages, a height of ten and a distance of four, it is assigned to the residents of the courtyard. (Taz 2 and similarly from Magen Avraham) If there is a pit ten handbreadths deep in the courtyard, and now if it is also fenced ten handbreadths high, the usage for the residents of the courtyard is by throwing and lowering, as they need to lift above the fence and lower into the pit. For the balcony, it is just lowering. The Rosh wrote (Chapter 8, Section 3) that it is assigned to the balcony. And even though he did not write this explicitly, it is evident from his words. The Gemara does not imply this, and so is written in the Rosh's glosses there - and it must be said that the Rosh also holds this view and did not bother to explain it. (He only wrote that the law follows Rav regarding lowering and throwing and did not bother to explain that the same applies to both together for one. The Magen Avraham assumed that the Rosh did not agree with this, but it cannot be said so. Check it and see) (And the Rambam in Chapter 4 was very brief about this, see there).

Our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in Section 3: "If there is a barrier of four tefachim (handbreadths) in front of the balcony, the balcony does not prohibit the residents of the courtyard because it separates them," end quote. The reason is that since he made a separation in front of the balcony, he revealed his intention to withdraw himself from the courtyard (Taz, Subsection 3). This is from the Rambam, Chapter 4, Law 16, see there. And the Tur does not mention this. In truth, I do not understand what relevance this has to these laws, as in the Gemara (60a), it is mentioned in a different context, when the balcony itself is not ten tefachim higher than the courtyard, and they prohibit each other. And regarding this, they said that if they made a partition of four tefachim, it shows they have withdrawn from here, and they do not prohibit the residents of the courtyard, and the residents of the courtyard can make an eruv for themselves, see there. But here we are dealing with a case where the balcony is much higher than the courtyard, and they do not prohibit each other at all. What need is there for a partition of four tefachim, and what benefit does it provide? Even without it, they have already withdrawn from here. We must say that the Rambam holds that even here the partition helps to permit everything in the courtyard to the residents of the courtyard, even what is easily accessible to the balcony. (And it is clear that for this reason the Tur did not write this law).

Projections in a courtyard that extend from the walls, if they are below ten handbreadths - are considered part of the courtyard, and the residents of the courtyard are permitted to use them, but not the residents of the balcony. And anything within the top ten handbreadths close to the upper floors - the residents of the upper floors use them, and not the residents of the courtyard. And the space between the lower ten handbreadths and the beginning of the upper ten handbreadths, for the projections that extend there - both are prohibited from using them, and they cannot use them with utensils that were in the houses during Shabbat, unless they made an eruv together.

It is stated in the Gemara (60a): Residents of a courtyard and residents of a balcony—if the balcony is within ten handbreadths of the courtyard but they made a fence around it, ten handbreadths high, and left an opening up to ten cubits—nevertheless, they cannot make separate eruvin and need to make a joint eruv. If not, they prohibit each other [from carrying], since it is within ten handbreadths. And it is considered like one of the houses of the courtyard that has an entrance to the courtyard—it indeed prevents the eruv. However, if they made a partition in front of the entrance, four handbreadths wide and ten handbreadths high—they have revealed their intent to separate themselves from here, and the residents of the courtyard can make their eruv for themselves. I am astonished at the decisors who omitted this law, and it appears that specifically here a partition of four handbreadths is effective, but in a house within the courtyard it is not effective. See further in Siman 392.

It has already been explained in Siman 355 that the sages were lenient regarding partitions over water, allowing a suspended partition to be permissible, and we view the partition as if it extends down to the depths. We are not concerned that the water mixes beneath the partition, and we only require a recognizable partition. Therefore, if there is a pit or well between two courtyards, and there is no doorway or window through which they can join together in an Eruv, or if there is one and they did not make an Eruv, one may not draw water from it on Shabbat using vessels that were brought into the house, or bring the water into the house, since both domains have control over it. However, if they draw water using vessels that were in the courtyard and drink the water in the courtyard, or water the animals in the courtyard and not in the barn, no correction is needed, as it has already been explained in Siman 372 that courtyards are considered one domain for vessels that were in them, even if each courtyard made its own Eruv.

And how should they make a partition to permit bringing water into the house and drawing it with vessels that rested in the house? They should make a partition of ten handbreadths, or it should be above the water with only one handbreadth descending into the water and nine handbreadths above the water, or it should be entirely within the water with one handbreadth above the water, so that one domain is distinguishable from another, and the bucket does not cross into the domain of the other. As for the water mixing below, we are not concerned with it, as stated. But an upper partition on top of the pit is not effective, because it is not made for the recognition of the water, and also because it needs to be near and partially within the water. Although earlier in Siman 355 regarding a balcony, we did not require that the partition be within the water, that is because one stands above on the balcony and lowers the vessel straight through the hole, and we are not concerned that the bucket will go beyond the partition. This is not the case here, where one stands by the pit and lowers the bucket, we are concerned that the bucket might go diagonally into the domain of the other. Therefore, we required that part of the partition be within the water, to prevent the bucket from going to the other side. This one will stand here and fill from his half, and the other will fill from his half.

And this is with a standard partition. However, if they wish to place a beam four tefachim wide over the well - there is no need for any partition, because we say 'the edge of the roof descends and seals.' This is effective even on dry land, as it has been explained several times that with a width of four tefachim, we say the edge of the roof descends and seals, but not with less than that. In such cases, one person can draw water from one side of the beam and another from the other side, and we do not worry that the bucket will go to the other side, because the sages assessed that a bucket does not go more than four tefachim. And even if the bucket goes under the beam - it does not appear so much like it is in the domain of the other, just as they were not concerned about the mixing of the water. This is one of the leniencies they allowed regarding water, because it is not possible otherwise, as mentioned in Siman 55.

All that has been explained applies when the pit is close to the two courtyards. However, if it is four handbreadths away from each courtyard, for example, if there is a narrow path between the two walls of the courtyards and the pit is within it, and neither courtyard has direct access to it except by drawing water through windows that open into the pit from both courtyards, and if the windows are ten handbreadths above the water, making this usage difficult, involving both a distance of four handbreadths and a descent of ten handbreadths—then both are permitted to draw water from it on Shabbat without any correction, and they do not prohibit each other, even if the pit belongs to both of them. Since they only use the pit by casting the bucket through an airspace of four handbreadths, we hold that one person does not prohibit another through an airspace in such cases (as per the Gemara in Eruvin 85, according to Rashi's opinion), because this is not considered a significant usage unless it is within ten handbreadths. However, if the courtyards open onto the path through a gate, then both have control over it and they prohibit each other until they make the correction explained, and this is like the law explained in the previous section regarding a courtyard and a balcony, where if both have equal control, they prohibit each other. This is according to Rashi's opinion there.

But the Rambam, of blessed memory, wrote in Chapter 3, Law 23: "A well that is in the middle of a path between two courtyard walls, even though it is four handbreadths away from this wall and four handbreadths away from that wall, both [courtyard owners] may draw water from it, and they do not need to extend projections over it, because one person does not prohibit another through airspace." This is the end of his words, and so wrote Rabbeinu Beit Yosef in Section 2. The Maggid Mishneh explained that the Rambam's intent is also that there is no door open to there, but they use it through windows. And so wrote Rabbeinu Rema on Rabbeinu Beit Yosef's words, that they are according to the Rambam. However, the Rambam mentioned "even though it is four handbreadths away from this wall, etc.," indicating that all the more so if it is less than four handbreadths. And "through airspace" means through airspace that is ten handbreadths deep or ten handbreadths high. And even though in the previous section regarding a courtyard and a balcony, they prohibit each other if it is ten handbreadths high or low, this is different because a courtyard is a permanent usage, unlike drawing water from a well or in a ruin, where it will be explained that there is no permanent usage there either. (Taz Section 2) And furthermore, in an actual courtyard, they certainly prohibit each other even through airspace, because even in this well, the permission is only when it stands in the path. But if it stands between the courtyards, half in this courtyard and half in the other courtyard, they would prohibit each other. Only when it stands in the path, which is a domain in its own right, and its usage is through airspace, they do not prohibit each other. Additionally, "through airspace" means that the usage is only by drawing water like from a well, or by throwing as in a ruin, which will be explained. But in a courtyard and balcony, even if they are ten handbreadths high, isn't it possible to use them by carrying back and forth, and it is not necessary to use only by throwing.

Indeed, regarding what the Rambam wrote, "Even though it is distanced four tefachim" – it is not understandable, as it implies that with less than four tefachim, there is more allowance. However, on the contrary, with a distance of four tefachim, it is less convenient to use than when it is not distanced four tefachim. For this reason, according to Rashi's opinion, the allowance is only specifically when it is distanced four tefachim, as mentioned. And it must be said that this is the reason: when it is within four tefachim to the courtyards, since it certainly belongs to the domain of the courtyards, it is obvious that one cannot prohibit another through the airspace of something that belongs to him. But even if it is distanced four tefachim, and it is not considered as his, why should they not prohibit each other? Therefore, it informs us that even in such cases, one does not prohibit the other. (Mechatzit Hashekel, comment 4) And with less than four tefachim, it could be that even if they are open with actual openings, they are permitted for the reason explained. (Magen Avraham, comment 4, and there is no need to correct it, and see Mechatzit Hashekel) And one of the great authorities did not bring the Rambam's opinion at all, only Rashi's opinion. (Shulchan Aruch HaRav, section 2)

It appears to me that if this pit is close to one person within four cubits, and to the other, it is more than four cubits or exactly four cubits, we give it to the one who is closer, according to the principle explained in the previous section: that if one person can use it with ease and the other with difficulty, we give it to the one who can use it with ease. Similarly here, for the one who is farther away, using it would require throwing and distance, whereas for the one who is closer, it only requires throwing. This is exactly like the law we explained in the previous section, paragraph five, regarding a courtyard and a balcony, see there. Additionally, it appears to me that this is only when the pit belongs to both of them. But if it belongs to only one of them, we give it to him in any case. Even if on weekdays he permits the other to draw from it, he can still forbid him on Shabbat, because it is unreasonable that by doing him a favor on weekdays, he should incur a loss on Shabbat. (A proof for this is from the laws of Eruvin explained in section 370, paragraph 15, see there.)

It is stated in the Gemara (85a): Two houses with three ruins between them, and generally there is no open entrance from the house to the ruin, because it is not used regularly, but rather they use it through windows - each one is permitted to use the ruin next to him by throwing through the windows, and his neighbor does not prohibit him, because it is more convenient for him to use than for his neighbor who is farther from it. (Rashi) And the middle ruin is permitted for both of them, since they can only use it by throwing, and the airspace (the outer one) separates each one, and no one prohibits his neighbor through airspace in such an inferior usage, as stated in section 4. And this is when the middle one stands between the two outer ones. But when it stands without the outer ones interrupting, such as when they stand like a triangle, and it turns out that the middle one is also close to the houses, standing opposite the two like three heads of a jug - each one is permitted to use the ruin next to him, and the third one close to both courtyards is prohibited for both of them, since both use it only by lowering, and they prohibit each other. And even though regarding a pit we permitted in such cases, that is because a pit has only one use, drawing water. But a ruin has many uses, and they prohibit each other. (Rashi there, s.v. 'And the middle one') And Ba'al HaMaor wrote the reason, that since it stands alone close to the public domain - we are concerned that it might fall into the public domain and come to carry [on Shabbat]. And the Tur wrote that these ruins, even if they belong to other owners, do not prohibit, since no one lives in them, and a dwelling without owners is not considered a dwelling. And a bathroom between two houses that did not make an eruv together - they prohibit each other, since the domain of both has control over it, and the laws of a bathroom were explained earlier in Siman 55.

Earlier in Siman 357 it was explained that a courtyard less than four cubits (amot) is prohibited from having water poured into it on Shabbat unless a cistern (uka) is made in the courtyard for the water to fall into, otherwise the water would flow into the public domain. This is a Mishnah in the end of the eighth chapter of Eruvin (88a), and it is taught there: Similarly, two balconies opposite each other, these being two upper stories in a courtyard that are not aligned in a row but opposite each other, some made a cistern and some did not make a cistern, those who made a cistern are permitted to pour their water, and those who did not make a cistern are forbidden. The Gemara explains this is when they did not make an eruv between them, for if they had made an eruv between them, then both would be permitted to pour, for as long as there is a cistern, even many homeowners are permitted to pour there, but when they did not make an eruv, those who did not make a cistern are forbidden.

And if it is difficult to understand, for when they did not make an eruv, what benefit does the trough provide, since they are prohibited from carrying in the courtyard? However, the meaning is that those who are permitted do not pour [the water] into the courtyard, but rather pour it onto the platform, and the water flows down to the trough adjacent to them. And even though by their action the water goes into the courtyard where carrying is prohibited, they did not decree [against] indirect action in a courtyard that is not joined [by an eruv]. But those who did not make a trough - it is prohibited [for them], for we are concerned that since the trough is far from them, they will not want to pour [the water] onto the platform, from where the water will go to the courtyard and from the courtyard to the trough, as it will spoil the courtyard, and they will take it with their vessels and go to the trough to pour it out, and it turns out that they will carry in a prohibited courtyard. (Tosafot, Rosh, and Ritva)

According to the opinion of our Rabbis, we are dealing with a courtyard that is smaller than four cubits, for if it is four cubits, then there is no need for a drainage pit, as stated in Siman 157. However, this does not appear to be the view of the Rambam, who wrote the law of a drainage pit in a courtyard that does not have four cubits in Chapter 15 of Shabbat, and this law is written at the end of Chapter 4 of Eruvin, without mentioning at all when the courtyard does not have four cubits. And this is the language of the Rambam: "Two balconies opposite each other, and a courtyard below them into which they pour water - they should not pour until they both make one eruv. If some of them made a drainage pit in the courtyard to pour water into it, and some did not, those who made a drainage pit may pour into their pit, and those who did not make a drainage pit - may not pour into the courtyard until they make an eruv. And if these made a drainage pit and those made a drainage pit - each one can pour into their own pit, even if they did not make an eruv together." This is the end of his words, and he did not mention any difference whether the courtyard holds four cubits or not.

It appears to me that Tosafot, the Rosh, and the Ritva, according to their version of the Mishnah, "and similarly two ledges" – were compelled to explain it in this manner, as it refers to the earlier case, where there are not four cubits. However, from the language of the Rambam in his commentary on the Mishnah and the Ra'avad, it is clear that they did not have the version "and similarly" (and so the Tosefot Yom Tov also wrote), and also in the Mishnah of the Jerusalem Talmud, this is not mentioned. According to this, it is a separate matter and does not pertain to the concern that the water will go into the public domain, but rather due to the prohibition of carrying within the courtyard itself. Therefore, when they have not made an Eruv, neither of them is permitted to pour water into the courtyard, and in this, there is no novelty at all. And how the law is when they pour onto the ledge and from there it goes into the courtyard is not addressed at all, and the main novelty is when they made a basin. Even though the basin is in the courtyard, nevertheless, since it is adjacent to the wall of the house, it is considered as part of the house, and it is permitted to pour from the window of the house into the basin. Consequently, the one who did not make a basin is compelled to carry through the courtyard, which is prohibited. And if each one made a basin near their house, each one pours into their own basin, as the status of the basin is like the status of the house. And it can also be said that when the basin is ten handbreadths deep, it is a private domain by itself and does not belong to the courtyard at all. In his commentary on the Mishnah, the Rambam added another reason why the one who did not make a basin is prohibited, due to the concern that they might use the courtyard from the dwellings. And it can be said according to his intention, that even if they want to pour from a distance into the basin, which would be permitted because it is a domain by itself, nevertheless, it is prohibited for this reason. However, from his language in his code, it seems like the first reason we mentioned.

The words of the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch are not entirely clear, and this is their language: "Two upper floors that open into this courtyard opposite each other, and one made a pit in the courtyard to pour into it because it does not have four cubits of space for its water, and the other did not make a pit. If they made an eruv together, both are permitted to pour their water. If they did not make an eruv together, and one made an eruv for itself and the other did not make an eruv at all, the one that did not make an eruv is forbidden, and the one that made an eruv is permitted. Provided that it does not pour directly into the pit, but pours in the upper floor and it flows down into the pit, because the force of its flow in the courtyard that is not joined by eruv is permitted." End quote. And our teacher, the Rema, wrote that the same applies if the courtyard is more than four cubits—both are permitted in such cases, and they do not need a pit. End quote.

The commentators (Bach and Taz) have already wondered what benefit the eruv provides when this courtyard makes an eruv for itself. What benefit does the eruv provide? It is prohibited in the courtyard because of the second apartment, and since the permission is only due to its power—what is permissible in a non-eruv courtyard, why does it need an eruv? Furthermore, the reason for the prohibition of the second apartment is because it did not make a gutter; if so, what is meant by the conclusion 'the prohibition is due to not making an eruv'? Some have written that the intention is that since it did not make an eruv for itself, even if it made a gutter, it would be prohibited because it is forbidden to carry to its porch without an eruv. Therefore, even if it wants to pour from its house, it is forbidden because we are concerned that it might carry to the porch. (Magen Avraham, section 1) It is difficult, for if so, why do they say that 'one made a gutter'? Let them say that both made a gutter. And the main issue is also puzzling according to the Tosafot, because since the main prohibition of the second is due to the concern that it might carry the vessel with the water to the gutter through the courtyard, what permission is there when the courtyard is more than four cubits? This concern always exists. (See Beit Yosef and Taz. The words of the Levush are completely puzzling, as the Taz wondered about him there. And the Magen Avraham, section 2, wrote that if the second made an eruv for itself, the first could carry in the courtyard and pour directly into the pit. But when it did not make an eruv, it is considered 'a foot that is prohibited in its place' there. And it is surprising, as this pertains to the residents of the courtyard and the residents of the porch, not to two porches, for in any case, the courtyard belongs to both. Furthermore, who will force them to say that this one is permitted to pour by its own power? Let us indeed say that it can pour into the pit and that each made an eruv for itself. The main point of the law is only that the second is prohibited, and the Magen Avraham himself remains in doubt, and his previous words are also in doubt there, and examine well.)

Therefore, it seems to my humble opinion that the explanation is as follows: The Tur found difficulty with the approach of the Tosafot and the Rosh regarding the issue we raised – what is the relevance of four cubits here? Additionally, the main concern the Tosafot wrote about, that this is the reason why one who did not make an eruv is forbidden to pour water onto the platform, lest the water flows through the courtyard to the drainage pit, because they might be concerned about damaging the courtyard and thus carry a vessel to the drainage pit as they wrote – we do not find this decree. Therefore, the Tur explained it differently, that a courtyard without four cubits requires a drainage pit, and without a drainage pit, it is forbidden. When there is a drainage pit, it is permitted even for a thousand residents. This is the reason for the prohibition here for one who did not make a drainage pit nor made an eruv for herself, while the one with the drainage pit made an eruv for herself. Under this circumstance, they are completely separate from each other, and she is like the owner of another courtyard that does not have a drainage pit – it is forbidden for her to pour into the courtyard because the water might go into the public domain. Therefore, the Tur did not mention the Tosafot's concern that she might be concerned about the courtyard and carry with the vessel, but since she did not make an eruv nor a drainage pit, her status remains like a courtyard without four cubits and without a drainage pit. However, if she had also made an eruv for herself, in any case, she would be considered as one entity with the owner of the drainage pit, which is not the case when she did not make an eruv at all. (This seems to be my humble opinion, and with this, all difficulties are resolved, and examine it well).

Three courtyards that open to each other, and all of them also open to the public domain or an alleyway, in such a manner that it is not necessary to pass specifically through the previous courtyard— in such cases, they are considered one inside the other and have different laws, as will be explained. If all three made an eruv together, they are all permitted to carry within each other, even with utensils that were in the houses. If they did not make an eruv with each other at all, but rather each made an eruv for itself or did not make an eruv at all, it is forbidden to carry utensils that were in the houses from one courtyard to another. If two made an eruv and one did not join them, the two are permitted, and the one is forbidden; also, they are forbidden to bring utensils that were in the houses into its courtyard.

However, if the middle courtyard made an eruv with each of the outer courtyards, since a person has the right to reside in two places, as stated in Siman 372, Paragraph 15, see there, but the outer courtyards did not make an eruv with each other – it follows that the outer courtyards are prohibited from transferring objects that were in their houses at the onset of Shabbat from one to the other via the middle courtyard. Nonetheless, the middle courtyard is permitted to transfer objects with each of them, and they are permitted to transfer objects with it. And we do not worry that, since many objects of both outer courtyards are commonly found in the middle courtyard, the owners of the outer courtyards might forget and transfer objects from one to the other through the middle courtyard – we do not worry about this, just as we do not worry in the above Siman 349 concerning three people each having four cubits of space, where the middle person's space is embedded between them – we do not worry that one of the outer people might transfer objects from the other outer person into his space. This is the same case here. (Gemara 48a, according to Rabbi Shimon, and the law follows his opinion).

In what case are these words stated? When the middle one placed her Eruv in this one and her Eruv in that one, then the middle one has two dwellings in the two outer courtyards, and the outer ones do not have dwellings in the middle one, since they did not place their Eruv in the middle one. And even if they placed their Eruv in the middle one, but they placed it in two houses, it turns out that the outer ones do not connect to each other, for this one dwells in one house and the other in another house. But if both placed their Eruv in one house in the middle courtyard, then they are all connected, and all three are permitted with each other. This is the case when they placed them all in one vessel, or if they did not fit in one vessel and placed them in two vessels. And according to what we explained above in Siman 367, Se'if 11, that if there is no strictness, we do not worry at all about two vessels - this works out simply. (And so it appears from the straightforward reading of the Sugya in Eruvin 41, which only mentions two houses, see there).

Seemingly, when the two outer courtyards place their Eruv (collective Shabbat boundary) in the middle courtyard in two separate houses, it is as if all reside in the middle courtyard. If so, the Eruv should be entirely invalidated since the Eruv is divided into two houses, making it like a courtyard where some have made an Eruv among themselves and some among themselves, thus prohibiting one another. However, the Gemara (there) responds: "If they spoke of residents to be lenient, should they speak of residents to be stringent?" Meaning, certainly, if one or two members of the courtyard did not contribute to the Eruv, they prohibit the other members of the courtyard. But here, the outer courtyards do not actually reside here; rather, the Eruv brings them into it, and they are not considered actual residents to impose stringency on the members of the courtyard and invalidate their Eruv. However, this is not an absolute rule, for sometimes they also impose stringency, where there was negligence on their part, as will be explained with two courtyards, one inside the other. (When one from the inner courtyard forgot and did not make an Eruv, the outer courtyard prohibits on it because of the Eruv, as the Tosafot wrote there in 'Yomru'.)

Two courtyards, one inside the other, with the outer courtyard open to an alleyway or a public domain, and the inner courtyard open to the outer courtyard but not to the alleyway or public domain. Consequently, the inner courtyard must have passage through the outer courtyard, as it has no other way. It has already been explained that a foot (i.e., a right of passage) that is permitted in its place does not prohibit in another place, and a foot that is prohibited in its place prohibits in another place, as stated in section 375 regarding the residents of a courtyard and the residents of a balcony. Therefore, even if these two courtyards did not make an Eruv together, but each made an Eruv for itself, the inner courtyard does not prohibit the outer courtyard through its passage, since it is permitted in its place. However, if the inner courtyard did not make an Eruv for itself, or made an Eruv but one of the residents forgot and did not join the Eruv, thereby invalidating the Eruv, it prohibits the outer courtyard because it is a foot that is prohibited in its place. But the outer courtyard can never prohibit the inner courtyard, since it does not have passage over the inner courtyard. Therefore, if the inner courtyard made an Eruv for itself and the outer courtyard did not, or made an Eruv and one of its residents forgot and did not join the Eruv, the inner courtyard is permitted and the outer courtyard is prohibited. 

One should not ask why we say that if one from the inner courtyard forgot (to join the Eruv), it prohibits the outer courtyard because the inner courtyard is prohibited in its place, when it could be permitted in its place if the one who forgot to join the Eruv renounces his rights, as will be explained in section 380. One can say that this is indeed the case, and if he renounces his rights, the outer courtyard will become valid, and it seems that they can even compel him to renounce his rights.

If these two courtyards made an eruv together and placed their eruv in the outer courtyard, and one person, whether from the inner or outer courtyard, forgot and did not join the eruv, both courtyards are forbidden until he nullifies his domain, for even if the neglect was from the outer one, the inner courtyard cannot separate itself, since its eruv is not with it. And the outer courtyard is automatically forbidden, even if the neglect was from the inner one, since the inner one has the right to walk through it, and it is forbidden in its place. But if they placed the eruv in the inner courtyard, and one person from the outer courtyard forgot and did not join the eruv, the inner courtyard can close its gate and prevent the outer courtyard residents from entering, even though through the eruv they became like one courtyard. Because they can say, "I joined with you to improve, not to worsen." And since the neglect is yours, you have no connection to me. But if one from the inner courtyard did not join the eruv, both are forbidden until he nullifies his domain, because since the inner courtyard is forbidden by default, it also forbids the outer courtyard, as it has the right to walk through it. And if the inner one who did not join the eruv wishes to nullify his domain only to the inner courtyard and not to the outer one, he cannot do so, because then the outer courtyard residents would be forbidden, as the eruv makes it seem as if they have the right to walk through it, since the error stems from the inner courtyard as mentioned at the end of section 4. (According to those who hold in the Gemara that "nullifying domain from one courtyard to another is not possible," both remain forbidden. However, we hold that nullifying domain from one courtyard to another is possible, as mentioned in Siman 381. Therefore, in such cases, one should be careful to nullify his domain to both courtyards' residents) (From Rashi's commentary in Siman 60 and Chapter 3, it is explained that in one courtyard, even a permitted domain can forbid, see there).

If an individual who does not need an eruv lives in the inner courtyard and another individual lives in the outer courtyard, or if two people live in the outer courtyard and they made an eruv, the individual in the inner courtyard does not prohibit them since he is a leg permitted in his place. Similarly, if many people live in the inner courtyard who are like an individual and do not need to make an eruv among themselves, such as a father and his son or a master and his disciple who receive sustenance, as mentioned in Siman 370, and similarly, if there are three courtyards within each other and an individual in each one, even though the two inner courtyards pass through the outer one, nevertheless, they do not prohibit it because each one is a leg permitted in its place. However, if there were two in the innermost third courtyard and they did not make an eruv, they prohibit the middle and the outer courtyards since they are prohibited in their place. And if two are in the middle courtyard and did not make an eruv, they prohibit the outer courtyard, and so forth in all similar cases.

Two courtyards with three houses between them: one house opens to this courtyard and one house opens to that courtyard, and the middle house opens to the two houses on either side. They want to make an eruv together. A resident of this courtyard goes through the house that opens to him and places his eruv in the middle house, treating the house that opens to him as a gatehouse to pass through to the middle house. Similarly, a resident of the other courtyard treats the house that opens to him as a gatehouse and places his eruv in the middle house. In this case, none of the three courtyards needs to contribute bread. The two outer courtyards are exempt because they are considered gatehouses, and the middle house is exempt because it is the place where the eruv is placed, as stated in the Gemara (end of the chapter "Hadur" in the Tur and Shulchan Aruch).

It is not understood, for if so, there would be no need for an eruv at all, and how could they be connected without an eruv? Rather, the explanation is that there are many houses in the courtyards, and all of them placed their eruv in this middle one, and therefore these three do not need to contribute to the eruv. This is also clarified by the words of the Rambam in Chapter 4, Law 10, where he wrote: "Two courtyards with three houses between them... and the residents of this courtyard brought their eruv through the house that is open to them and placed it in the middle house, and likewise the residents of the other courtyard... those three do not need to contribute bread, etc." End of quote. The language of the Tur and Shulchan Aruch is concise. (This is also written by the Ritva).

And there are those who say that even if they placed their Eruv in one of the other houses of the courtyard, and these three do not need to contribute bread. For example, if the residents of one courtyard, when bringing their Eruv to another courtyard, are compelled to pass through these three houses - they are all considered like a gatehouse. (Tosafot there) And it appears to me that this is when they have no other way except through these three houses, but if they have another way - why should they be considered like a gatehouse? Therefore, they too must contribute bread.

And know that any house that serves as a gatehouse, as explained, is not considered a gatehouse for this purpose. For example, there are two courtyards and two houses between them, and they did not make an eruv together but each one made an eruv for itself. If a resident of one courtyard goes through the house next to him and places his eruv in the house next to the other courtyard, and similarly, the second resident places his eruv in the house next to the other courtyard, the eruv is not valid. For, in any case, if we consider each house as a gatehouse, then placing the eruv in a gatehouse does not constitute a valid eruv. And if we consider them as houses, then there is an interruption of a house between the courtyard and the house where the eruv is placed. Rather, you would have to say that for one person, the house next to him is considered a gatehouse and the second house is considered a full house, and for the other person, the opposite. If so, this is a contradiction. And even though in the laws of eruvin we sometimes say contradictory things, as will be explained in Siman 393, this applies to matters that are not so noticeable. But in a noticeable matter, it would be laughable and not to be given to the Sadducees to mock. (Rashi, end of the chapter "HaDār" [Eruvin 76a])

And know, in the cases discussed in the previous sections, where a leg that is prohibited in its place renders prohibited elsewhere, we need to investigate: if so, in a city where the entire city is combined like our cities, and people who live outside the city come to the synagogue, and the eruv does not encompass them – why do they not prohibit the entire eruv for us, like a leg that is prohibited in its place that renders prohibited elsewhere. This is not analogous, for only in an inner courtyard that has no entrance except through the outer one, it is relevant to say this, since there is no other place to exit to the public domain or the alley. But here, the whole land is before them, except for the combined city which is like a large courtyard. And if it is because they wish to come to pray in the synagogue, and perhaps they also have places in the synagogue – what concern is it of ours what they wish, and they are like general guests to us. (See Shulchan Aruch, section 378, what is stated in the name of the Nodah B'Yehudah, part 2, Orach Chaim, section 44, and the responsa Chinnuch Beit Yehudah, which agree to permit this).

Residents of a courtyard, if one of them forgot to contribute to the eruv, or intentionally refused to contribute, and all the other residents made an eruv, he thereby prohibits them [from carrying], and it is forbidden for all of them to carry from their houses to the courtyard or from the courtyard to their houses. What is their remedy? The Sages instituted that he can renounce his rights to them, and that suffices. He can say, "My rights are relinquished to you" or "My rights are acquired by you," and no formal acquisition is necessary. It is permissible to renounce one's rights on Shabbat, as this is not considered a sale but merely a relinquishing of rights. If there are many residents in the courtyard, he must renounce his rights to each and every one.

And this is the language of the Rambam at the beginning of Chapter 2: One needs to nullify explicitly for each and every one, and says: "My authority is nullified to you and to you and to you," end quote. And the Tur wrote that one should say: "My authority is nullified to you and to you" or say "to all of you" collectively, end quote. And there are those who wish to say that according to the Rambam, "to all of you" does not suffice, as perhaps he means only the majority, since the majority is like the entirety and not everyone. (Taz, Siman 1) And this is indeed puzzling, as even in the case of a woman's get (divorce document), the phrase "to all of you" includes everyone, (end of Chapter 6 of Gittin, see there) and certainly the Rambam also holds this view, except that it is not his style to elaborate much. And regarding the language of the Gemara (69b): "My authority is acquired to you, my authority is nullified to you," and it says there (70a) that one needs to nullify for each and every one, he wrote this language "to you and to you and to you" to preserve the language of the Talmud as is known. And just as we say that the Talmud's intention is not specifically for each one individually, so too we say regarding the language of the Rambam, and this is the primary ruling in practice, and so have ruled the great later authorities. (Eliyah Rabbah and Taz, and there is a printing error in the Eliyah Rabbah) And if he did not nullify to all of them - it does not help, and even though for those to whom he nullified, they have already made an Eruv, and it would seem that this authority is also included in the Eruv, it is not so, for at the time of the Eruv, this authority was not included.

And one might question whether it is effective for someone to annul [the possession of chametz] afterwards only for those who did not annul it beforehand, or whether, since he did not perform the act as prescribed by the Sages, partial annulment is not valid, and he must now annul it for everyone, including those for whom he had previously annulled it. It appears that it is not effective, for logically, since he initially gave it to those, how can he give it to others? We are compelled to say that he retracts his initial annulment, because he is able to retract it, as will be explained. If so, by logical necessity, the previous annulment does not stand, since he retracted it. Therefore, he must specifically annul it for everyone together.

It further appears to me that the nullification must specifically be in their presence. For it is understandable that one can acquire ownership through another not in their presence, since 'one can act in someone's interest without their knowledge.' But here, it is merely verbal, only that the Sages ordained it to be effective, and they only ordained it in their presence, as is evident from the phrasing 'my domain is nullified to you.' And if he wishes to transfer ownership through a formal act of acquisition, who says it is permissible to perform such an act on Shabbat? Surely, it is forbidden. However, prior to Shabbat, when he does not wish to join the eruv, or is unable to join the eruv, it appears that he can transfer his domain to them through an act of acquisition via another, as is evident from the language of the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, which state that one can nullify even after it gets dark, implying that all the more so it can be done before Shabbat. And despite the fact that the Mishnah (Eruvin 69b) states, 'When can one give up their domain? Beit Shammai say: Before Shabbat, and Beit Hillel say: After it gets dark,' they did not say 'even after it gets dark,' and there is substantial reason to prohibit nullification before Shabbat, for why would one nullify if they can join the eruv. Nevertheless, our Rabbis decisively interpret Beit Hillel to mean 'even after it gets dark,' and all the more so before Shabbat. (This is also evident from the explanations of the Rosh and the Rashba, and it is explicitly implied in the Jerusalem Talmud. See there, and from Rashi on Eruvin 69b s.v. 'lo,' it is implied that nullification through an agent is effective. See there.)

The Tur wrote that if one does not want to annul his ownership (of the courtyard) to them but rather rent it to them, it is effective just like annulment. This is the opinion of the Rosh (in the chapter "HaDar," siman 13) who brought it in the name of the RaM, that among Jews, annulment is specifically required and not renting, but he disagrees, stating that renting is also effective among Jews. However, the Mordechai there ruled that renting is not effective among Jews, and this is also clarified in the words of the Rambam at the end of chapter 2, who wrote concerning a Sadducee that one does not rent from him because he is not like a non-Jew. It is thus explained that renting is not effective among Jews, and this is also clarified by Rashi's language in the Mishnah in "HaDar." The Beit Yosef says that their reasoning is that the renting permitted by the Sages for a non-Jew is a weak rental, as explained in siman 382, and the decree was only for a non-Jew where annulment is not possible. To make a complete rental is certainly forbidden on Shabbat due to the prohibition of buying and selling. However, making a complete rental on the eve of Shabbat seems to be agreed upon by all as permissible. This is indicated by the Magen Avraham and see also the Taz. In the Jerusalem Talmud (HaDar 5:3), the opinion of the prohibitors is clarified, stating there: "The law is that a Jew annuls and a non-Jew rents." And our master the Beit Yosef in section 3 brought two opinions on this matter, and it appears that the majority opinion is for prohibition, and this is also the opinion of the Jerusalem Talmud. However, for a complete rental on the eve of Shabbat, there is no proof from the Jerusalem Talmud for prohibition, as it does not address this matter. And there is no question that, if so, Rabban Gamliel in the Mishnah in "HaDar" who made an effort with the Sadducee, should have rented from him on the eve of Shabbat with a complete rental, as it can be said that the Sadducee did not agree to this, and this should also be said according to the opinion of the Rosh and the Tur. (From Rashi it is also implied like the Rosh).

In the case of renouncing one's rights, if one wishes to renounce only his share in the courtyard and not his house, he may do so. If he wishes, he can also renounce his house. If he renounces without specifying, saying "My rights are renounced to you," he has only renounced his rights in the courtyard and not his house. The reason is that the primary necessity for them is in the courtyard.

And what is the law when he renounces? If he renounces to them only his share in the courtyard, or generally, which is interpreted as only his share in the courtyard, they are permitted to transfer items from their houses to the courtyard, and he is also permitted because he is considered only as a guest since he has no rights in the courtyard. However, from his house to the courtyard and from his house to their houses, it is forbidden for both him and them.

Therefore, some say that he must lock his house so that he does not come to transfer items unlawfully, for out of habit he may forget and transfer items. He should only open it when he wants to go out and come back, and he should lock it immediately after going out and coming back. And even though in a courtyard that is not joined by an eruv, we did not require him to lock his house, that is because everyone is forbidden. But here, since everyone else is permitted to transfer items from their houses to the courtyard, we are concerned that out of habit, he too might transfer items. Therefore, we required him to lock it as a reminder that it is forbidden to transfer items from his house to the courtyard.

If he renounced to them also the rights to his house, they are permitted to transfer items both from his house to the courtyard and to other houses, and he is also permitted since he is considered as a guest. However, he is only permitted after they have taken possession of the courtyard, as will be explained in the next section. (And one should not ask, when he renounced only his courtyard, why it should be forbidden to transfer items from his house to the courtyard since he is considered a guest. One could say that since he did not renounce the rights to his house, he is not considered a guest regarding his house).

Just as an individual who did not join in an eruv can nullify his domain to the many who also did not join in an eruv, similarly, the many can nullify their domain to him when necessary, for example, when he must move items from the house to the courtyard. And thus it is taught in the Tosefta (Chapter 5): "The residents of a courtyard, if one of them forgot and did not join in the eruv, he must nullify his domain. If it was a house of mourning or a wedding feast and they wished to nullify their domain, they have the right to do so." Even though when he nullifies his domain of the courtyard and his house, he can carry from his house, as explained, it can be argued that it is difficult for him to nullify his house domain so that many do not frequently enter and exit. (And earlier in the Tosefta it states: "It is a mitzvah for a person to nullify his domain; if he is a prominent person, he has the right to do so." That is to say, if he is a prominent person and it is not fitting for him to nullify his domain to them, they will nullify theirs to him. And even though in the Gemara (68a) it says that Rava nullified his domain, it can be argued that there it was necessary because of a child who needed hot water for a circumcision, as explained there.)

However, there is a difference between the nullification of an individual to a group and the nullification of a group to an individual. In the case of an individual nullifying to a group, we said that even the individual is permitted to carry, because he is considered like a guest with respect to them. But a group nullifying to an individual is not the same, because a group does not become guests with an individual. The reason is that everyone knows that they are not guests, and only in the case of an individual with respect to a group is it not noticeable. But a group with respect to an individual, or even an individual with respect to another individual, such as if there were only two in the courtyard and they did not make an eruv, when one nullifies his domain to the other, he does not become like a guest with him. Therefore, if the residents of the courtyard who made an eruv nullify their domain to the one who did not make an eruv, he is permitted to carry from his house to the courtyard, but not from their houses unless they also nullified their house domain to him. If they did nullify, he can carry also from their houses to the courtyard, but they are forbidden to carry even from his house to the courtyard. We do not say that they become like guests, because a group does not become guests with an individual. Even if they nullified the domain of their house, they are forbidden to carry even from his house to the courtyard, and even if he first took possession of the courtyard, it does not help. The same law applies if there were only two, and one nullified to the other: the one who nullifies is forbidden even in the domain of his companion, and his companion is permitted even in his own domain, and also in the house of his companion if he nullified to him also the domain of his house. All of this is because, as explained, an individual with respect to another individual does not become like a guest.

It is clear that just as the annulment of property rights (bitul reshut) is effective for one person who did not participate in the eruv, so too, two or more people who did not participate in the eruv can annul their property rights. This means that each of those who did not participate in the eruv can annul their rights to any one of the residents of the courtyard who did participate in the eruv. They can also all annul their rights to even one person who did not participate, if necessary. However, they cannot annul their rights to two people who did not participate, as this would be pointless since they would still prohibit each other from carrying, just like two residents of a courtyard who did not make an eruv and thereby prohibit each other. Even if one person says to another, "I annul my rights to you on the condition that you in turn annul your rights to my companion," this is also not effective. We do not say that he made the other a messenger to transfer his rights (Rashi, s.v. "lo"), because at the time he transferred his rights, it was not permissible to carry. Therefore, they must annul their rights only to one of those who did not participate in the eruv. Just as we said that many people cannot become guests with one, the same applies to many with many. Therefore, if many who did not participate in the eruv annul their rights to many who did participate, the ones who annulled are not allowed to carry in the courtyard even from the houses of those who made the eruv to whom they annulled their rights, in accordance with all the laws explained. It seems to me that two can become guests with more than two, but three are considered many. It also seems to me that an individual, whom we said can become a guest with many, even if he is not alone in his house and has a large family, is still considered an individual. Conversely, many, whom we said cannot become guests, are considered many even if they are individuals, as we follow the number of houses.

The Tur and the Shulchan Aruch wrote: "If someone nullified their domain and then subsequently brought something from their house to the courtyard, if it was done unintentionally - it does not prohibit, but if it was done intentionally - it prohibits, since they have retracted their nullification. If others have already established possession, by bringing things from their houses to the courtyard or from the courtyard to their houses - they cannot retract their nullification. According to Rashi, possession is only effective if it was established after dark," end quote. During the day, possession is not relevant, since on a weekday there is no prohibition of carrying, as even without nullification, they could have brought things out. (Taz and Magen Avraham, section 3) And it seems to me, in my humble opinion, that for this reason, even if the one who nullified brought something out during the day - it is not considered a retraction of their nullification, unless they brought it out after dark. (And this is evident from Rashi and Tosafot, Eruvin 69, s.v. 'brought out', where Rashi explains that it is because they are desecrating the Sabbath and cannot nullify, and Tosafot write that in an incidental case, they are not considered a transgressor and can nullify, see there, and this only applies on the Sabbath, and pay close attention).

The reason he can retract his nullification is because there was no formal acquisition involved, only a mere removal of his ownership. Therefore, when he reclaims it, it becomes his. However, if the others had already taken possession of it, they acquire the ownership, just like any acquisition through possession. There's a question here: why don't we say "since it was permitted, it remains permitted" as we do in other matters, and why should we care if he reclaims it? The Rosh, of blessed memory, answered (Chapter 8, Section 6) that since he reclaimed it intentionally, it implies that he did not truly nullify his ownership, and he never really diverted his mind from it, so it turns out it was never permitted. Some explain that we only say "since it was permitted, it remains permitted" in matters dependent on the onset of Shabbat, and then we say since it was permitted at its onset, it remains permitted for the entire day. This is not the case with nullification of ownership, which is effective even after nightfall and is not dependent on the onset of Shabbat. Therefore, it must be sustained for the entire Shabbat, and if it is nullified, it remains nullified. (Taz, Section 1, mentions that he did not recall the words of the Rosh at all, and from the fact that the Rosh did not answer this way, it implies that even if the permission occurs in the middle of Shabbat, we say "since it was permitted, it remains permitted." However, from our ruling that there is no Muktzeh (an item that is set aside and not to be used on Shabbat) for part of Shabbat, there is evidence for the Taz's opinion. According to the Rosh, we must say that Muktzeh is different, as it depends only on twilight, "since it was set aside, etc." See Eliyah Rabbah, who does not agree with the Taz's opinion, and he also did not mention the words of the Rosh. In my opinion, the Taz's opinion is correct, and examine this carefully.)

There are those who say that 'return' is only considered an act of taking out, where the one who nullified his domain took it out from his house to the courtyard and established possession in the courtyard. But if he brought it from the courtyard into the house, it is not considered a return unless he also nullified the domain of his house, for then bringing it in is also considered a return. (This is the intention of the Magen Avraham in section 1, as explained by the Machatzit HaShekel.) The reason is simple, for when he brings it from the courtyard into his house, even though it is forbidden for him to do so when he has not nullified the domain of his house, nonetheless, by not leaving the utensils in the courtyard and bringing them into the house, it is actually evidence that he wants to withdraw from the courtyard. But if he also nullified the domain of his house, then by bringing it into the house, he re-establishes possession in the house, thereby automatically nullifying the entire nullification. However, our Rabbis, the Tosafists, explicitly wrote (Eruvin 68b, s.v. 'and took out'), and this is their language: "And that which is taught later, one who gave up his domain and took out, makes it forbidden—not specifically taking out, but even bringing in," end quote. It is forced to say that their intention is when he also nullified the domain of his house, for where would they know to say this? The reason appears to be that since it is forbidden for him to bring in and he still brought in, it implies that he has reverted from his nullification. And even though he is currently also committing a prohibition, nonetheless, if he had not reverted from his nullification, he would not have done so. (And I saw in the Tosafot Shabbat that he brought from great authorities who refuted the words of the Magen Avraham because of this, and the Tosafot Shabbat seeks to reconcile it, see there, and the Gaon Rabbi Shneur Zalman ruled like the Magen Avraham and did not bring the words of the Tosafists, see there.)

We have established that there is a concept of relinquishing one's rights from one courtyard to another. This means that not only within a single courtyard, when one resident forgets to join the eruv (joint ownership of the shared space) and can relinquish his rights in the courtyard to the other residents, but even a resident of one courtyard can relinquish his rights in his courtyard to a resident of another courtyard, if necessary. Whether both courtyards made an eruv together, such as in the case of two courtyards, one inside the other, that made an eruv together and placed their eruv in the outer one, and one of the inner courtyard residents forgot and didn't participate, as explained in Siman 378, where both courtyards are prohibited from carrying, the resident of the inner courtyard who forgot to participate can relinquish his rights to any of the residents of the inner courtyard, and also to any of the residents of the outer courtyard. He alone will be prohibited from carrying, while everyone else will be permitted. And once they take possession of the area, he will also be permitted to carry, like a guest, according to the laws explained in the previous Siman.

And behold, in the matter that was explained, it is not such a significant novelty, since when they prohibit each other, it is possible to annul it. Rather, even in a place where they do not prohibit each other, they can annul. For example, two courtyards with an entrance between them, and each has an entrance to the public domain, so they do not prohibit each other. And each one made an eruv for itself and did not make an eruv together, nonetheless, each one can annul its domain to the other. This means that all the residents of one courtyard will annul their domain in their courtyard to the residents of the other courtyard, so that they will be permitted to carry from their house to the other courtyard, while the residents of the courtyard will be prohibited. Similarly, two courtyards, one inside the other, and only the outer one made an eruv, while the inner one prohibits it, as explained in Siman 378, the inner one can annul its domain to the outer one. This means that the right of passage that the inner one has over the outer one is annulled to the outer one, so that it does not use or pass over it except when it needs to exit, and the outer one will be permitted. This is a significant novelty, that even the right of passage, which is necessarily unavoidable, can still be annulled, and this means minimizing the right of passage as much as possible.

There is also the nullification of ownership in a ruin, meaning if there were two houses with a ruin between them, and each house belongs to a different person, but the ruin belongs to both of them, and they forgot and did not make an eruv, and it is forbidden to carry from the ruin to the house and from the house to the ruin — one can nullify his part in the ruin to the other. The one who nullifies would be forbidden to carry, and the one to whom it was nullified would be permitted to carry. And there is an additional novelty here, that even something that is not entirely usable — the nullification is effective.

The Tur and Shulchan Aruch write in Section 4: "There is annulment of domain from house to house, for if there were two houses with an opening between them and they did not make an eruv, one can annul his domain in favor of the other. Even the one who annuls is permitted to carry from his house to his friend's house, but he cannot carry from his friend's house to his own house, for then he would be reasserting control over the domain he annulled. Similarly, if he has a room that opens into his house, and he annulled the domain of his house, he is forbidden to carry from the room to his house." This is based on the principle explained, that an individual in relation to another individual is not considered a guest, and therefore it is forbidden to carry from his friend's house to his own. What is permitted to carry from his house to his friend's house is explained in Section 3 regarding the annulment of a courtyard, that one is not considered to be reasserting control unless he brings items into the courtyard, which would be like reasserting control, but not when he carries items out of the courtyard into his own house. Similarly, when one annuls his house, he is forbidden to bring items into his house or to carry items out from it.

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote: "There are those who say that one should not nullify from house to house unless he leaves for himself one room that is not nullified, and then it is permitted to bring even from his friend's house to his own.
