And it is good to be stringent initially." End quote. The reason for this opinion is that they hold that in all nullifications, it is necessary to leave one thing not nullified, such as nullifying his courtyard but not his house, and when he nullifies his house as well, he should leave one room not nullified. And the reason for this is that since we hold that through nullification, he is also permitted to carry, because he becomes like a guest among them, if so, the law of eruv will be completely forgotten. (Tosafot 64, s.v. 'If so') But these matters are perplexing, for it has been explained that an individual relative to another individual is not considered a guest, and how is it permitted to bring in and out. (Magen Avraham section 7) And even if we say that it refers to an individual nullifying to many, if so, we must say that these many have made an eruv among themselves, for if not, the nullification would not be effective, and how will the law of eruv be forgotten. (ibid.) This requires further study.

And behold, these difficulties also apply to the words of Rabbeinu Yitzchak the Elder in Tosafot. What appears to me, in my humble opinion, is that he holds that the principle that many cannot become guests with one, nor one with one, applies to a courtyard in which all were partners. Now, when the many nullify their domain to one, it cannot be considered as if they are guests, because the situation remains as before, and everyone knows that the courtyard is shared, as stated in the previous section, paragraph 8. However, when it comes to nullification from house to house, where each house belongs to an individual and they never shared ownership of the house, it can be said appropriately that even if many nullify to one, and all the houses become like his, they all become guests with him. This is because the situation does not remain as before, since now the individual uses the houses, which was not the case previously, and everyone sees that the houses are his, and they are all like guests with him. Similarly, an individual can become a guest with another individual for the same reason. Consequently, they are all permitted to carry in and out from all the houses, and he is also permitted to carry even into his own house. It does not appear as though he is retracting his nullification, because it is clear that he is not, since they also carry into his house. It is not similar to a courtyard, where previously everyone carried from their houses to the courtyard, and now they do the same, thus it appears as though he is retracting his nullification. But in the case of a house, it does not appear as a retraction, since there is a change from the previous situation. Additionally, the concern of retraction is only before they have taken possession and not afterwards, as stated in paragraph 1. Now, if we permit nullification from house to house, they would not make an eruv at all and would nullify to one, and everyone would carry. Therefore, it is necessary to leave one room that is not nullified, and it will be forbidden to carry from it to the houses, and thus there will be a distinction between nullification and eruv, and these are the words of Rabbeinu the Rema. And since these reasons are only according to Rabbeinu Yitzchak of Tosafot, the Rema wrote that it is "better to be cautious initially," meaning that certainly many of the poskim disagree with these reasons, but initially, one should fulfill the opinion of Rabbeinu Yitzchak of Tosafot. (So it appears in my humble opinion).

Nullification (of domain) is effective only in a place where an Eruv could have been made before Shabbat. But in a place where, before Shabbat, it was not possible to make an Eruv, they cannot subsequently nullify (the domain) on Shabbat. For example, two houses on opposite sides of the public domain, and non-Jews came and enclosed them with a partition on Shabbat. A partition made on Shabbat is considered a partition, as we have written above in Siman 362. Nevertheless, one cannot nullify his domain to the other, since they could not have made an Eruv between them before Shabbat. Nullification was only established as a remedy for the Eruv, and where the essence of the Eruv does not exist, it is not applicable to remedy it with nullification. However, an heir can nullify his domain. If the bequeather did not make an Eruv before Shabbat and died on Shabbat, and the heir comes to reside there on Shabbat, which makes it forbidden for them as we have written in Siman 371, he can nullify his domain. It is not said that he could not have made an Eruv before Shabbat, because this is not so, for an heir is considered an extension of his father, and his father could have made an Eruv, and therefore he can also nullify.

One can nullify and then nullify again. That is to say, since the nullification is done for the sake of a rectification, in order to enable one to manage his needs, therefore if there were several people who did not make an eruv and it is only possible to nullify for one person, as explained in the previous section, what should be done if the one who nullified now needs to carry his utensils? And even though it has been clarified that the one who nullified can also carry, as he is considered like a guest among them, this applies to an individual among many, but not many among an individual, nor an individual among individuals, and in a courtyard everyone agrees that this is the case. Therefore, the Sages permitted that everyone nullifies to this person so that he can carry what he needs, and afterward, they nullify to the one who originally nullified so that he can carry, and so on to a third person, and so on indefinitely. Whether in this courtyard or in two courtyards, initially this courtyard nullifies to the other courtyard until they manage their needs, and afterward, the first courtyard nullifies back to the original. And we do not say that this is a mockery and jest, for it is not so, for thus did the Sages establish.

The Sages taught in the Mishnah (61a): "One who lives with a Kuti in a courtyard does not prohibit him [from carrying within the courtyard] until there are two Jews living in two houses, and they prohibit each other." The Gemara explains that this is the matter: According to the basic law, the residence of a Kuti does not prohibit a Jew, but the Sages were concerned that he might learn from his actions. Therefore, if there is only one Jew in the courtyard, there was no need to enact a regulation, since it is an uncommon situation, as the Jew would be afraid of the Kuti, who is suspected of robbery, and would therefore leave and not live there. However, when there are two Jews living in two houses, and this situation is common, since being two, they are not afraid of him, the Sages said that their Eruv is of no effect until they rent the Kuti’s right. That is, the right he has in the courtyard must be rented from him, and without that, the Eruv is ineffective. They only prohibited it when two Jews live in two houses and prohibit each other. But if they live in one house, even though in such cases they would not be afraid of him, and it is common for them to live there, still, they did not decree in such cases, since it is itself uncommon for two householders to live in one room. For if they live in two rooms, it is considered as two houses, and they prohibit each other, as I wrote in Siman 366 and Siman 370.

And perhaps you will say, what benefit is there in not learning from his actions in order to leave there, since you allowed it through rental? It is explained in the Gemara (62b) that this will not easily befall an Israelite, because the Gentile fears witchcraft and will not want to rent it to him. And Rashi of blessed memory explained there another reason (in the commentary 'but') and this is his language: "Perhaps he will learn from his actions - the sages troubled and caused loss to the Israelite living with him, so that it would be difficult in his eyes to pay rent every Sabbath and he would leave there." And Rabbeinu Yonatan on the Rif wrote in this language: "In order that he will not learn from his actions - they were stringent and required that the Israelite rent from them, and he will not want to rent to him because he fears witchcraft, and he will say in his heart, 'I want to give him my portion as a gift and even so he does not want to carry it until I rent it to him for less than a perutah, he certainly intends witchcraft,' and he will not rent to him. And from this, the Israelite will leave his house and not learn from his actions." And all these matters seemingly contradict each other.

Indeed, all the words of the sages are upheld, and everything is one matter. We need to understand why the Kuti (Samaritan) would be concerned about sorcery. Is rental something that is not customary among people? Rather, the matter is as follows: the sages permitted this rental under the conditions of a shaky rental and for less than the value of a perutah, as will be explained. The Kuti knows that less than the value of a perutah is not considered money by the Israelite, and nonetheless, the Israelite's intention is only for this rental and not for a gift. The Israelite does not want a gift because the sages decreed that it must be specifically a rental. However, the Kuti does not understand why this is so, for less than the value of a perutah is like a gift. Why would the Israelite not desire a gift but only a rental for less than a perutah? Therefore, the Kuti suspects that there is an element of sorcery involved. (This is the intention of Rabbi Yehuda) However, this is understandable when he rents it for less than the value of a perutah – he would be concerned about sorcery. But what can we do if he rents it for a perutah or more than a perutah? From now on, he would not be concerned about sorcery. And for this, Rashi of blessed memory comes to explain that this would be difficult for the Israelite to give full payment every Shabbat, and consequently, he would leave. Meaning that the Kuti, when he sees that full payment is being given for it, would not rent it to him for a long time but only for one Shabbat. And the following Shabbat, he would ask for more money, and consequently, it would be difficult for the Israelite, and he would leave. (So it appears in my humble opinion)

In the Jerusalem Talmud (Hadrian's Law 3), it is stated: the law is that a Jew annuls and a Kuti (Samaritan) rents. It raises the question, why does the Kuti not annul? It answers that we are concerned that he might retract, for after annulment, he can indeed retract, as mentioned in the previous section. The Kuti would definitely retract, and there would be no reliance here. However, when he rents from him, he cannot retract, because renting acquires, as mentioned there. From this, there appears to be clear evidence for the view of the Rashbam and Tosafot, which we brought in Choshen Mishpat at the beginning of section 194, that the Kuti acquires land with money, contrary to the Rambam in the first chapter of Zechiyah, who holds that he only acquires land with a deed, as mentioned there. However, we explained there in section 7 that in the rental of land, even the Rambam agrees that it can be acquired with money, as mentioned there. And we learn from the Jerusalem Talmud that after he rented, he cannot retract, and this will be further explained in section 14. (And there is no proof, for the Jerusalem Talmud does not agree with our Talmud, which holds that the reason is due to concern about witchcraft. It can be said that it does agree. And the reason it questions why annulment does not work is because in annulment, there is definitely concern about witchcraft, as the matter of annulment is not familiar to him at all, and be exact in this matter).

The nullification of ownership does not help without rental. For example, when many Jews live in a courtyard, each in his own house, and they did not make an eruv, or they made an eruv but one of them forgot to contribute his share, or even if they all made an eruv but did not rent from the non-Jew, if they all wish to nullify their ownership to one person so that they will be considered as one individual in relation to the non-Jew, it is forbidden. Some say the reason is that since in these circumstances it is common for people to live there, the concern returns that one might learn from the non-Jew's actions. However, this reason is rejected in the Gemara (63b), because the nullification of ownership to one person is an uncommon situation, and the Sages did not decree in such a case. Rather, the reason is that if so, the law of eruv will be forgotten, and in the Gemara there, it is about a non-Jew who did not want to rent, and necessarily the law of eruv will be forgotten. However, even if he is willing to rent, and only this Shabbat there was some reason they did not rent from him, in which case certainly the law of eruv will not be forgotten, since next Shabbat they will rent from him – nevertheless, it is forbidden to nullify ownership, because if he were not willing, the nullification would not help, there is no difference between willing and not willing, for does his statement cause the nullification? But when they rented from him and need nullification – they can nullify. (And in Magen Avraham section 4 there are brief and fragmented words, and so wrote the Turei Zahav)

There is no need for rental except in the case of a non-Jew who lives with him in one courtyard and prohibits him, or even if he lives in another courtyard, but the courtyards are one within the other, and there is no way to the inner courtyard except through the outer one, then rental is also necessary according to the details that will be explained. But in two courtyards that are open to each other, and each has an entrance to the public domain or to an alley, and in one courtyard the non-Jew lives and in the other courtyard live two Jews, even though sometimes he passes through their courtyard, in any case, since he does not have the essential right of passage, rental is not necessary. They can carry and transfer items from this courtyard to that courtyard through the entrance and through windows, even items that were in the house on Shabbat, and there is no need to rent from him. They did not decree in this case lest one learn from his actions, since they do not share one essential path, and there is not so much closeness between them. See also Siman 370, Section 3.

But regarding courtyards, one within the other, the Rambam wrote in Chapter 2, Law 11, and this is his language: "Two courtyards, one within the other, and a Jew and a Kuti (Samaritan) reside in the inner one, and a Jew resides in the outer one, or a Jew and a Kuti reside in the outer one and a Jew in the inner one - this prohibits the outer one until he rents from him, because the feet of two Jews and a Kuti are found there, and the inner one is permitted in the inner courtyard," end quote. In the inner courtyard, he is alone in the place of the Kuti, but in the outer one, another Jew and a Kuti always tread upon him, and it is like two Jews and a Kuti in one courtyard. And in Chapter 4, Law 22, he wrote: "And if there was a Kuti in the inner courtyard, even though he is alone - he is like many, and prohibits the outer one until they rent his place," end quote. And the intent is even if the Jew is also alone in the outer one - in any case, it is prohibited. So explained our master, the Beit Yosef, in his great book, that this is worse than one courtyard, because not everyone knows that the Jew is alone, and in one courtyard, they know more.

However, Rashi of blessed memory explained in the Gemara (75b) that the intention is when there are two Jews in the outer courtyard, and the novelty is that even though no Jew lives with him in his courtyard, his mere right of passage forbids them. This is also written by the Tur. Therefore, our teacher the Beit Yosef in section 17 brought the opinion of the Rambam and the opinion of the Tur. But all the great later authorities disagree with our teacher the Beit Yosef and hold that even the Rambam does not mean when there is one Jew in the outer courtyard, for in such cases it is obvious that it is permitted, and this is the main ruling. (Taz section 18, Magen Avraham section 14, Eliyah Rabbah section 20, and Taz section 29) On the contrary, there are those who are even more lenient, that even when there is a Jew and a non-Jew in the inner courtyard and a Jew in the outer courtyard, the owner of the outer courtyard is also permitted, since the Jew is "a permissible foot in his place" (Magid Mishneh in chapter 2 there, citing some who disagree). However, the Rambam, Tur, and Shulchan Aruch do not hold this way and forbid it, because this does not relate to "a permissible foot in his place," as the reason is lest they learn from his actions, as mentioned, and this is the main ruling.

A courtyard where a Jew and a gentile live, and the Jew is alone with the gentile, it is permitted, as we said. However, next to the Jew's house, there was another Jew's house that did not open into the courtyard, and between the Jew who owns the courtyard and the other Jew, there is no entrance between them, only windows between them through which they can make an eruv. The sages prohibited making an eruv through the windows. And even though it is permitted to make an eruv through windows, as we said in Siman 372, here it is forbidden for another reason, because it is forbidden to be alone in a place with a gentile. This means that the sages were concerned that one might learn from the gentile's actions, and only with one person did they not prohibit it, because it is uncommon for one to dwell alone. But when they make an eruv through the windows, they will use it together, and he will not be afraid to live there. Therefore, they prohibited it, so that they do not use it together, and he remains truly alone, and leaves from there. (Rashi there s.v. 'forbidden')

And the opinion of Rashi, of blessed memory, is that the same rule applies even if there is a door between one Jew and another Jew – they are also forbidden to make an Eruv between them, for the reason that was explained. And the fact that the Gemara mentioned 'windows' is because it is not customary to make a door between one house and another, but for the law, there is no difference. However, Rabbi Yitzchak (the Tosafist) wrote – it is specifically when there is no door between them, but if there is a door between them – they are permitted to make an Eruv. And the reason is that if there is a door, the Jew will not fear living there, since the other Jew can always come through the door – the non-Jew will be afraid and will not harm him. Therefore, there is no benefit in prohibiting the Eruv. And if you ask, in that case, we should require renting from the non-Jew – this is impossible, because in any place where there is an individual among non-Jews, the sages permitted it, and they did not differentiate between whether he has a door from another house or not. Since he is alone in the courtyard – they permitted it for him. And only when there is no door, but just a window – in this case, the sages saw fit to prohibit the Eruv, because in this case, it would be beneficial for him to leave, as explained. But in the case of a door where there is no benefit – they did not prohibit the Eruv.

And the Rambam, may his memory be blessed, in Chapter 2, Law 15, wrote this law in one style, and this is his language: "A courtyard where Israelites and a Samaritan reside, and there are windows open from one Israelite's house to another Israelite's house, and they made an eruv through the windows, even though they are permitted to carry from house to house through the windows, they are forbidden to carry from house to house through the doorways because of the Samaritan, until they rent (the space from him). For many people do not become as one in an eruv in a place of a Samaritan." End of quote. And behold, according to this, on the contrary, the Rambam has a significant leniency, that even though the Sages prohibited making an eruv in a courtyard where two Israelites and a Samaritan reside without renting the space from the Samaritan, this is when they make an eruv through the doorways to carry in the courtyard. But through the windows, they can make an eruv to carry from house to house through the windows, and not through the doorways.

In my humble opinion, it seems clear that the Rambam does not hold by the previous ruling. For according to his view, even in a place where an eruv does not work without renting, nevertheless, they permitted making an eruv through windows without renting. All the more so in the previous case where it is truly an individual, and the second Jew has no connection at all to this courtyard, that the Jews are permitted to make an eruv among themselves through the windows. It is certainly logical, for if in a prohibited place we permitted an eruv through windows, all the more so in a permitted place. However, our teacher, the Beit Yosef, brought in section 19 the ruling of Rashi, and in section 20 he brought the ruling of the Rambam there, implying that he holds that these do not contradict each other. Also, the commentators on the Shulchan Aruch were silent on this, and I do not know their reasoning. Indeed, the Tur did not bring the ruling of the Rambam, and this requires further investigation.

The rental that one needs to rent from the non-Jew – it is not necessary to explain to him that one is renting from him in order to permit carrying, rather one rents from him without specifying, and carrying is permitted automatically. It is not necessary to write any document regarding the rental. One can rent from him even for less than the value of a perutah, as for him it is considered money. It is permissible to rent from him on Shabbat, as this is not considered buying and selling, for the rental is a weak form of acquisition, and it is merely like requesting permission to permit them to carry. The sages were very lenient regarding the essence of the rental and did not want to be stringent in this matter.

We have already written in section 4 that it is explicitly stated in the Jerusalem Talmud that after one has rented from a non-Jew, he cannot retract. Similarly, Rashi wrote in the Mishnah of Hador, and this is his language: "For if he rented from him, how can he retract, since he has already taken the money?" End quote. However, the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch in section 6 wrote: "As long as the non-Jew does not retract, the rental is effective, even for a long time," end quote, indicating that he can retract. There is an opinion that this is when he rented it without specifying and retracted before the first Shabbat, as the Jew has not yet taken possession. But once Shabbat has begun and the Jew has taken possession, he cannot retract. And if he rented for a specified period, he cannot retract until the end of that period (Magen Avraham, sub-section 6). According to this, we must say that what Rabbi Rema wrote on this: "He cannot retract from his rental until he returns the money," end quote, refers to when he retracts before the first Shabbat. And when he retracts before the end of the period, he cannot retract even if he wants to return the money. And if he rented without specifying and retracts after the first Shabbat, he can retract without returning the money, as he can say that the rental was for the past Shabbat.

But there are those who say that one can retract even within the time period if he returns the money (Taz, section 8). This is also evident from the language of Rabbi Rema, as it is forced to interpret that it refers to retracting before the first Shabbat as mentioned. The language of Rashi, which we brought, also implies this when he wrote: "since he holds the money," indicating that if he returns the money, he can retract. This is also the intention of the Jerusalem Talmud which states there that if he retracts, he is a robber, but if he returns the money, he is not a robber. And the reason he can retract is that it is considered a weak rental as mentioned. Nevertheless, there are some poskim (Jewish legal decisors) who wrote that before the first Shabbat and even within the time period, he cannot retract, even if he returns the money (Bach and Eliyah Rabbah, section 8), which does not follow Rabbi Rema. It is possible that since this is a rabbinic ordinance, one can rely on the lenient opinions. Additionally, in the name of the Ramban, it is written that within the time period, one cannot retract at all, even if he returns the money (Taz, section 11, in the name of the Responsa of the Ramban). The Tur and Mordechai wrote that it is not necessary to rent specifically every Friday, contrary to an opinion from one of the early authorities who required renting specifically every Friday (Hagahot Maimoniot, beginning of chapter "Hadar" from the Or Zarua).

Our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 7: "If one rented from a non-Jew for a specific period, once that period ends, one must rent again. And one must also make a new eruv, for the first eruv does not automatically become valid again." End quote. This is very puzzling. Why should the eruv be invalid? For if one made an eruv through a doorway, and the doorway was sealed during the week and reopened on Shabbat, the eruv becomes valid again, as stated in Siman 374. And in his larger work, he brought this in the name of the Ramban. Perhaps he holds that since this is a rabbinic ordinance, that an eruv without renting is not considered an eruv at all, it is as if the eruv is completely nullified. And it is not similar to the case of a sealed doorway, where the rabbinic ordinance does not apply. Another distinction can be made: in the case of a sealed doorway, one has the power to reopen it, which is not the case with renting. If the non-Jew does not wish to rent, it cannot be rented from him against his will. It appears to me that even our master, the Beit Yosef, only stated this if a Shabbat passed without renting. In that case, it is considered a nullification of the eruv. But if during that week they rented again from him, it is not considered a nullification of the eruv.

If one rented [a property] from him for a specified time, and within that period he rented his dwelling to another non-Jew, the first rental does not become void, because the first landlord is still considered the owner, as after the second rental period ends, it will revert to the first [tenant]. (Taz, Subsection 10) According to this, even if the second [tenant] objects and even if he wants to return the money, we do not listen to him, because the original owners are the first [tenants]. According to this reasoning, it is not only when it is rented for a specified time, but even if it was rented without specifying the time. However, this does not seem to be the implication of our master the Beit Yosef's language in Section 8 regarding this law, where he wrote: "that it was rented for a specified time." Therefore, the primary reason seems to be as stated by the Levush, that since it was rented for a specified time and he cannot retract without returning the money, it is (as if) the first [tenant] stipulated with the second [tenant] that he cannot retract until the time [ends], see there. Therefore, in a situation of unspecified rental, one must rent from the second [tenant]. (And so wrote the Taz in Subsection 14. Also, the Ateret Zevi in Subsection 9 disagrees with the Taz and wrote that whether he rented to another or sold to another within the period, the second [tenant] is obligated to uphold the condition of the first [tenant]. And it is obvious that if the non-Jew rented to an Israelite, he gives a portion in the eruv and that suffices.)

There are those who say that if one rented from a non-Jew for a specific period of time and the non-Jew died, the rental is nullified, and one must rent from the heir. (Taz, subsection 9) They bring proof from the laws of Eruv in סימן שע"א, where if the non-Jew dies, the heir must make a new Eruv, and the father's Eruv does not suffice. (There) But this is not a valid comparison, as the reason for an Eruv is due to residence, and the heir did not reside there. What relevance does this have to rental, where it is upon the heir to uphold what his father sold or rented, for it is not in his power to inherit what his father gave to another. And it is not only according to the opinions explained in סעיף ט"ו that he himself could not retract, but even according to those who hold that he could retract by returning the money, nevertheless, as long as he has not retracted, it belongs to the renter, and there is no need to rent from the heir until the end of the period. Certainly, if the heir did not object, they can continue to carry until the time agreed upon with the original owner.

Five people living in one courtyard do not each need to rent separately from the non-Jew; rather, one person rents on behalf of all of them. It appears to me that it is not necessary to inform the non-Jew that he is renting on behalf of everyone, for even if he were to rent solely for himself, what difference does it make, since the courtyard is currently entirely Jewish-owned. The rental must be done willingly. If they compel him to rent, it is not effective. Even if he had rented until now and now does not wish to rent, they are not allowed to force him. This is not similar to the case of an eruv, where someone who usually participates and then retracts can be compelled, as stated in Siman 367, because this applies to a Jew. But it is forbidden to compel a non-Jew (Taz, sub-section 12); one may only rent from his wife, servant, or laborer as will be explained.

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote in section 1: "A Jew who lends or rents his house to a non-Jew does not prohibit him [from carrying], because he did not lend or rent his house to him in order to prohibit him. But if the house belongs to the non-Jew and a Jew rents it from him, and he lives in the house with him, the rental does not help concerning the rental for the eruv." End quote. The reason is simple, because the rental for the eruv means that he rents his part in the courtyard to him. But through renting the house, does the non-Jew not still have a part in the courtyard? And there are those who questioned Rabbi Moshe Isserles from what will be explained in Siman 384, that a guest who enters with permission immediately prohibits, and why does the renter or borrower not prohibit? (Elya Rabba and Taz there) And it seems to me that there is no difficulty at all, because there it deals with those whom he is compelled to allow, like the king's soldiers, and it will be explained there with God's help.

Additionally, he wrote: "A Jew who rented or lent a house to his fellow Jew, and there a gentile lives, even though the Jew has possession in the house - it does not help, and they need to rent from the gentile." End of quote. This means that even if the Jew who rented the house lives there, and since there are two Jews - they need to rent from the gentile when the gentile lives in his house and not a rented one from a Jew, and the Jew who rented the house has possession, meaning items that cannot be moved on Shabbat in the other Jew's house, one might think that in such a case it is considered as if the renter also lives there, and it turns out that both are living in one room, and there is no need for renting. It comes to teach us that it does not help, for just as an 'eruv' does not work without renting, possession does not help either.

The sages permitted renting from the wife of a non-Jew, even though he objects—she can still rent it out. Similarly, one may rent from the servant or the harvester of the non-Jew. A "servant" refers to someone employed for the entire year, and a "harvester" refers to someone hired for the days of harvesting and gathering (Rashi, 64). One may rent from them even if the non-Jew objects. There is an opinion that in the case of the servant and harvester, if the non-Jew objects, they cannot rent it out (Beit Yosef). However, from the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, section 11, it is clear that they are considered the same as his wife, and this is the main ruling (Taz, sub-section 13). It seems to me that also from his son, daughter, son-in-law, daughter-in-law, and similar people, if they live in the same courtyard, they can rent it out like his wife, as they are no less than his servant and harvester. Furthermore, the servant and harvester of the servant and harvester are also considered like the servant and harvester of the non-Jew himself, for the sages were lenient in this matter to consider it just a rental.

Our Sages also said (S.A. 64) that if [the non-Jew] does not want to rent [his property], one of the residents of the courtyard should approach him until he grants permission to place his belongings in the courtyard, which is considered as if he has lent him his property, and he becomes like his hired worker or agent, and rents it to them without his knowledge. And some say that he does not even need to rent, because since the Jew is his hired worker or agent, it suffices for him to contribute to the eruv. This is the opinion of the Tur, and Rashi also explained (there) that this is implied by the language of the Talmud, which says that his hired worker or agent contributes to the eruv and it suffices, because he is considered as if he resides together with the non-Jew, and the house and courtyard are his for this purpose, so no rental is needed. But Maimonides ruled that even if he is his hired worker or agent, they still need to rent from him. Maimonides would explain that the Gemara is referring to the hired worker or agent of a Jew (see Beit Yosef), and this can apply even to a Jew who is not a resident of the courtyard. (Levush)

When one lends his property to another to place his belongings there, even if he doesn't place them there, it is still acceptable, since he has permission. However, in such cases, some form of legal acquisition must be made. (Magen Avraham section 8) Additionally, he must give him permission to place his belongings anywhere he wishes in the house, for if he designates a specific place in the house for him, since he is not considered his agent in the entire house, it does not suffice for him to be regarded as his employee and laborer. There are those who write that even in such cases, when the gentile also has permission to place his belongings in that location, the situation reverts to considering the Jew as his employee and laborer. (Bach and Magen Avraham section 9) Since both have permission in one place, the Jew is regarded as the gentile's employee and laborer. Moreover, even if the gentile does not have permission to use the place but has the authority to remove the Jew from that place at any time, it is also considered that the Jew is his employee and laborer. (Bach and Machatzit Hashekel there) This is called that the Jew is under his authority, and thus, he is deemed his employee and laborer.

If one hired a non-Jew as a tenant or laborer for a set period, and during that period the non-Jew was dismissed from his position as a tenant or laborer, nevertheless, the rental agreement remains in effect until the end of the agreed period. This is because, at the time of the agreement, the non-Jew had the authority to rent out the property, so all actions taken at that time are valid. However, if the arrangement was made without a specified time, then once the non-Jew is dismissed, the rental agreement is nullified, as it is assumed that he rented it only for the duration of his tenure as a tenant or laborer.

The same rule applies if one rented the property from the treasurer of a nobleman and the treasurer is subsequently entirely removed from his position. If the rental was for a set period, it remains valid until the end of that period. If it was an indefinite rental, the agreement is nullified. However, this is only if the treasurer is completely removed from his position. If he is merely dismissed from the treasury but still receives a salary from the nobleman, he is still considered a tenant or laborer, and one can rent from him. Consequently, the initial rental agreement also remains valid, even if it was an indefinite arrangement.

According to what has been explained, in places where the entire city establishes an eruv and it is necessary to rent the rights from the city official, if a Jew holds any official position in the city, he is considered a tenant or laborer. One may rent the city rights from him for many years to ensure that even if he is later removed from his position, the rental agreement remains valid, as explained. It is advisable to rent from him for fifty years or similar. However, if the rental was indefinite and he is removed from his position, the rental agreement is nullified as mentioned, and one must rent from another official who takes his place or from a non-Jew who holds an official position in the city.

Our Rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, wrote in Section 15: "If a Jew and a non-Jew live in one house, it is necessary to rent from the non-Jew and to make an eruv with the Jew, if each one has a separate dwelling. The same law applies if there are two non-Jews living in such a manner in one house—it is necessary to rent from both of them." End quote. It is obvious that the intention is that each one lives in a separate room (and so wrote the Gra"z). If so, what is the innovation in this? We must say that we do not consider the Jew to be the servant or the agent of the non-Jew, nor the non-Jews living in such a manner each to be the servant or agent of the others, and it is sufficient to rent from one of them, and in the case of a non-Jew and a Jew to rent from the Jew or that the eruv of the Jew would suffice—this comes to teach us that it is not so. Since each one has a room designated for himself, they have no connection to one another. However, if there are no separate domains, but rather they are all partners in the entire house, then certainly the Jew is considered as the servant or the agent, and similarly among the non-Jews, each one is considered as the servant of the others. This is why they were precise in saying 'if each one has a separate dwelling.' (And this is also clarified from the source of the law in Tosafot 66a, s.v. 'merav,' which brings this from the Jerusalem Talmud. It is surprising that it is not found in our version of the Jerusalem Talmud, but there is another statement in the Jerusalem Talmud, end of chapter three, similar to this. Look there and examine it carefully.)

It is stated in the Gemara (64a) that Abaye asked Rav Yosef: If a Samaritan had five Jewish tenants and five Jewish laborers, what is the law? Rav Yosef responded: If they said that a tenant or laborer can be lenient, they would also say that a tenant or laborer can be stringent. Rashi explained that the question was whether a tenant or laborer, who can rent and thus be considered like an owner, requires each of them living in a separate room to contribute to the eruv if it was their own domain. Now that it is the domain of the Samaritan, do they need an eruv? Similarly, if there are residents in a courtyard, do they need to contribute to the eruv? Rav Yosef answered that we do not say a tenant or laborer to be stringent, and they are considered as not present and nullified in regard to the Samaritan, who is the homeowner.

Based on this, the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch wrote in section 16: "If a Samaritan has five Jewish tenants or five Jewish laborers living in his house, their residence is not considered significant enough to prohibit one another." The Rema concludes with the following language: "A tenant (this is the correct wording) of a Samaritan does not prohibit, if he rented from the homeowner." This means that if there are residents in a courtyard and they rented the space from the Samaritan or one of the tenants or laborers, they do not prohibit, even though each one lives in a separate room.

In truth, the Ritva wrote there that this applies only if they do not eat or sleep there, but otherwise, they are obligated in the eruv. However, the Tosafot (82a) brought proof from this law to what was explained in section 15, regarding one who hosts a teacher or a scribe in his house and uses all the homeowner’s utensils—that he does not prohibit, as discussed there. The same applies to a tenant or laborer. Our master, the Beit Yosef, in his major work, added another reason: "Since it is possible that tomorrow the homeowner may decide to switch their rooms… it is not called a designated place." The same is said regarding a teacher or scribe, and it is further explained that the homeowner did not lend his domain to prohibit him, as discussed there. It seems to me that this reason does not apply here, as the homeowner does it entirely for free, but with a tenant or laborer, he is performing his work. However, the main reason for this law is as we said: this is not considered a designated and fixed place. But when a Samaritan or a Jew rents a room to a Jew, it is not in the category of a tenant or laborer and does prohibit, requiring a contribution to the courtyard eruv.

A Kuti who rents his house to another Kuti, if he retains any hold in the house, such that he has permission to leave his belongings there - it is permissible to rent from him, since the house is his and he still has a hold in the house. And even if he has no hold, but if he has the ability to remove the tenant from the house at any time he wishes - it is also considered that the house is still his, and it is permissible to rent from him. But if he has no hold and also cannot remove the tenant until the end of the lease term - it is only effective if rented from the tenant. Similarly, if there is a Jew who has a hold in the Kuti's house - it is permissible to rent from him, as it is no less than his tenant or worker. So ruled our teacher the Rema in section 18. And it seems to him that the law is not only for a landlord, but anyone who has permission to place his belongings anywhere in the house is considered like his tenant or worker, as the Rivash wrote in his responses. (Siman 428) And specifically, he can place his belongings anywhere he wishes, but if he has a designated corner for this - it is not considered like his tenant or worker, as detailed in section 24. (And I do not know what the Rema added, as this was already explained in section 12)

And know, that in a courtyard of gentiles where no two Jews reside, it is permissible for anyone who comes there to carry on Shabbat throughout the entire courtyard, and from the houses to the courtyard and from the courtyard to the houses. And our teacher, the Rema, wrote at the end of this section: "A ship that has many Jews on it, and they have designated rooms, they need to make an eruv and rent the domain from the gentile owner of the ship, or include it in the rental of the ship" (end quote). This means that the rental of the ship itself does not cover the rental needed for the eruv, as stated in section 20. However, in the name of the courtyard, we wrote the reason is because of the courtyard, but here too, the entire length of the ship is considered like a courtyard. It is obvious that this applies when they do not assist him in the business of the ship, for if they did, they would be considered his employees or hired hands. (And among us, it is not customary to make an eruv on large ships, because usually a Jew does not have a designated room. And if some of them do have designated rooms, the rooms of the gentiles separate them. However, if there are only two designated rooms on the ship for two Jews, they are forbidden to carry from room to room, and we are not careful about this. And this requires further examination, for certainly one should be careful about this. Pay attention and understand.)

The Tur and the Shulchan Aruch wrote: "A Cuthean (Samaritan) who lives with two Jews, and the Cuthean is not in his home - does not prohibit, and they (the Jews) can make an eruv and be permitted. If the Cuthean comes on Shabbat - he prohibits, and the eruv is nullified. However, they can rent (his space) from him on Shabbat and afterwards one (Jew) can nullify to his friend, and the individual will be permitted. And certainly, if the Cuthean dies on Shabbat - one (Jew) can nullify to his friend, and the individual will be permitted." End of quote, and their words need explanation.

And this is its explanation: What is written that when he is not in his home, he does not prohibit - this is only according to the opinion of the Tur at the beginning of Siman 371. But according to the Rambam there - he prohibits, because he is likely to come on Shabbat and cancel the eruv, unless he was more than a day's journey away, as written there. And what is written, that after he comes, the eruv is nullified, even though in the case of ships that were permitted and then reconnected, the eruv returns to its original state, as written in Siman 362, this is because there it was likely to be maintained the entire Shabbat since they are not likely to separate. But here it was never likely to be maintained the entire Shabbat, since once his intention was to come on Shabbat, it was destined to be nullified. And for this reason, we do not say 'Shabbat, since it was permitted, it remains permitted.' And according to what is written in the previous Siman, section 16, it works out fine even without this reason, see there. And what is written, that afterwards one can nullify to another, before the rental - nullification is forbidden, as written in the previous Siman, section 5. And what is written, that the individual will be permitted, even though in Siman 380 it is explained that also the one who nullifies is permitted, but this is between an individual and many - he becomes like a guest among them, and not an individual to an individual, as written there. And if indeed the one who nullified needs this - the one who was nullified to can later nullify to the previous nullifier, for we hold 'one can nullify and return and nullify,' as written at the end of Siman 381. And what is written, that all the more so if he died on Shabbat - this is when they did not rent from him initially. But if they rented from him and he died on Shabbat, and they had an eruv which was only nullified at his death, according to the opinion mentioned in the previous Siman, section 18 - in any case, they can rent from the heir, (Taz) since the eruv was likely to be maintained the entire Shabbat, since it was possible for him to live, and it is similar to a ship and not to a gentile coming on Shabbat. (there) However, according to what is written there, the eruv is not nullified at all by his death, see there. Therefore, it must be said that here it refers to when they did not rent from him, as written. (See Magen Avraham, Siman 371, and his words are not clear to me, see there and examine well).

It is stated in the Jerusalem Talmud (Hadra Halacha 2): There is a teaching that the "koster" (like "kasdor," a royal official appointed by the king) prohibits immediately, and the "aksanya" (military lodging) after thirty days. Another teaching states that the "koster" prohibits after thirty days, and the "aksanya" never prohibits. The one who says the "koster" prohibits immediately refers to when it is common, and the "aksanya" after thirty days refers to when it is uncommon. And the one who says the "koster" prohibits after thirty days refers to those who enter with permission, and the "aksanya" never prohibits refers to those who enter without permission. End quote.

And this is its explanation: It has already been clarified in Siman 382, Section 20, in the name of our teacher the Rema, that when one lends or rents his house to a non-Jew, it does not create a prohibition, as he did not lend or rent it to prohibit himself, see there. And this is regarding a regular non-Jew. But for a king's officer (kestor) - the law of the kingdom is the law, and he has permission to reside in any house he desires, and the house is considered his. From the moment he enters the house, it is considered his, and it creates a prohibition. However, this applies to one who habitually comes; but if he does not habitually come, he is like a guest and does not create a prohibition. But if he resides for thirty days, the house is considered his, and it creates a prohibition. This is the first Baraita, and when he does not habitually come, he is referred to as a guest, meaning this kestor is a guest. In the second Baraita, which states that a kestor creates a prohibition after thirty days, this applies to one who does not habitually come, as stated earlier. However, this is when he enters with the king's permission, as the law of the kingdom is the law. But if this kestor enters without the king's permission, he is merely considered an intruder and does not create a prohibition even after thirty days. (This is the explanation of the Jerusalem Talmud, and the Korban HaEdah posed many questions, see there in the Shiyarei Korban, and he wanted to alter the text; according to what we have explained, the text is accurate and the explanation is clear, with God's help.)

According to this, what the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch wrote: "A non-Jew who enters for accommodation, if he enters without permission – he never causes a prohibition. If he enters with permission, if he is accustomed to come – he causes a prohibition immediately, and if he is not accustomed – he does not cause a prohibition until after 30 days," the intention is also whether it is with the king’s permission or without the king’s permission, as the source is from the Jerusalem Talmud. (See Beit Yosef) And what our teacher the Beit Yosef wrote in section 2: "King’s soldiers who entered Jewish homes either forcibly or willingly, if the homeowners in those places have items that are forbidden to move on Shabbat – they do not cause a prohibition for them," this is akin to seizure mentioned in the previous sections. But otherwise – they do cause a prohibition, as the law of the kingdom is the law, since they entered by the king’s permission. And what he wrote "either forcibly or willingly," meaning whether the Jew wanted it or not – because every Jew is obligated to obey the king’s orders. (And with this, the questions of the Taz and the Magen Avraham are resolved. And what the Magen Avraham wrote in subsection 1 that one who enters for a debt is considered to have permission – this is certainly so, but this is when it is done with the permission of the courts according to the law of the kingdom).

A Sadducee is considered like a Jew and can renounce his domain, and even though he desecrates the Sabbath in matters of rabbinic law, they are considered coerced because they follow the customs of their ancestors (Magen Avraham 385:1). However, his eruv is not effective since he does not acknowledge the eruv, as the essence of the eruv is that one should resolve in his heart that his residence is in the place of the eruv, and he does not acknowledge this. The Samaritans are considered as non-Jews entirely, and there is no remedy except through rental. A Jew who is a transgressor in idolatry or who publicly desecrates the Sabbath, even if he only desecrates it in rabbinic prohibitions, is considered like a non-Jew, and there is no remedy except through rental and not through renunciation, and certainly not through an eruv. If he desecrates privately and not publicly, even if he desecrates with a biblical prohibition, he is considered like a Jew and can renounce his domain. However, his eruv is ineffective if he does not acknowledge the eruv.

A Jew who becomes a transgressor and has houses in a Jewish neighborhood where an eruv has been established for the entire year—if he has no other entrance at all except through the Jewish neighborhood, then he invalidates the eruv for every Sabbath that falls after he becomes a transgressor. However, if he has another entrance to a non-Jewish neighborhood, even if the entrance is small and was not used previously, nevertheless, we direct him to use this entrance to the non-Jewish neighborhood so that he does not invalidate the eruv. This was the case in earlier times when Jews lived in separate neighborhoods. But nowadays, he cannot invalidate the entire city’s eruv since we rent the rights for the entire city. However, his own courtyard where he resides certainly invalidates the eruv, and it is necessary to rent his rights in the courtyard if the courtyard has its own eruv. But when it is included in the whole city's eruv, nothing is needed, because in any case, we rent the rights, and consequently, everyone who needs their rights rented is included, and he is nullified to the general community of the city against his will. (So it seems in my humble opinion)

The alleyway (mavoi) to the courtyards is like the courtyard to the houses. According to Torah law, it is permitted to carry from the houses and courtyards into the alleyway, even items that were in the houses when Shabbat began, but the Sages prohibited it. This prohibition also stems from the enactment of Solomon and his court, because the alleyway is considered a shared domain in relation to the courtyards, and they decreed this to prevent confusion with carrying from a public domain to a private domain. They permitted it through an arrangement called a "shittuf" (joining), just as an "eiruv" of courtyards combines all the houses in the courtyard, so a "shittuf" of alleyways joins all the courtyards of the alleyway. Why is it called "eiruv" in the courtyards and "shittuf" in the alleyways? To shorten the terminology and provide a sign for what we are discussing. Otherwise, we would need to say "eiruv of courtyards" and "eiruv of alleyways" each time. Therefore, they established the term "eiruv" for courtyards and "shittuf" for alleyways. When we say "eiruv," we know we are talking about courtyards, and when we say "shittuf," we know we are talking about alleyways. Additionally, the term "shittuf" is more inclusive than the term "eiruv," and therefore, in an alleyway, which is larger in quantity than the courtyard, they called it "shittuf."

In general, all the detailed laws are the same for an Eruv and a Shituf, and there are only two differences: an Eruv can only be made with bread, while a Shituf can be made with either bread or any other food or drink, as will be explained. Additionally, an Eruv can only be placed in a house within the courtyard, whereas a Shituf can be placed either in a house within the courtyard, in the courtyard itself, in a space without four cubits, or in a gatehouse, provided it is in a protected place. The reason is straightforward: the Eruv unites all the houses in the courtyard into one house, thus it must be placed specifically in a house. The Shituf unites all the courtyards in the alleyway into one courtyard, thus it is sufficient for it to be placed in a courtyard. One collects bread or other types of food or drink from all the courtyards and places it in one of the courtyards, as mentioned, and this will be explained in Siman 395.

And know that according to Rashi's opinion, it is permissible to place the partnership contribution in the courtyard, but certainly, it is effective in the house. And Tosafot wrote there that the partnership contribution is specifically for the courtyard and not for the house because in the courtyard it is more noticeable as a partnership, as it is more connected to the alley, and the uses are closer to each other, as stated there. And from the language of the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, which wrote that they can place it in the airspace of the courtyard and do not need to place it in the house, as stated there, it is explicitly implied that they can place it in the courtyard. But in the house, it is certainly better. And similarly, it is explained from the language of the Rambam in Chapter 1, Law 17, who wrote: "How do they form a partnership in an alley? They collect food... and place everything in one vessel in the courtyard of the alley courtyards or in one of the houses, even a small house or a portico or a balcony, etc." End quote. He explicitly wrote "even a small house," and all the more so a large one. And it is explicitly explained in the Jerusalem Talmud (end of Halacha 8) that says there: "It is obvious, an eruv requires a house, does a partnership require a house?" And it concludes that it does not require a house, as stated there. Thus, it is explicitly stated that all the more so a house, and this is the essential law. (Tosafot there brought this from the Jerusalem Talmud in 'Whoever was taken out,' but we do not have it there except in 'Eruvin.' And see Tosafot 70a s.v. 'they form a partnership' who wrote that it slightly implies that initially, using wine is more of a mitzvah than using bread because it is more noticeable as a partnership, as stated there, but the decisors did not bring this.)

The Tur and the Shulchan Aruch write that one should not place the partnership (shituf) in the airspace of an alleyway (mavoi), and similarly, Rambam writes that if it was placed in the airspace of the alleyway, it is not a valid partnership. This is also stated in the Gemara, which says that in any place where the Sages said one may not place an eruv, one may place a partnership, except for the airspace of an alleyway. In the Jerusalem Talmud that we referenced, Rabbi Yochanan says that one may place it either in the airspace of a courtyard or in the airspace of an alleyway, but the law does not follow this; rather, it follows our Talmud. Even though one might argue that the reason in the Gemara is because it is not guarded in an alleyway—as it implies somewhat when it says, "in an alleyway it is not guarded"—and likewise, it seems from the language of the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch, who wrote that it should be placed in a guarded location, thus it should not be placed in the airspace of an alleyway, one could say that the Jerusalem Talmud refers to placing it in a guarded location within the alleyway. However, this does not seem to be the opinion of Rambam, and in the Gemara, the explanation is that because it is not guarded, it does not work in an alleyway at all, even if placed in a guarded location. This is also apparent from Rashi there, and this is also the intention of the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch, and this is how we rule—that a partnership placed in an alleyway is invalid.

The measure for the partnership is the same as for the Eruv: more than two meals is not necessary even if there are a thousand people. Consequently, less than this is also not effective. For although with an Eruv, if there are not eighteen people, a fig-sized portion is sufficient, in the case of a partnership, it is assumed there are eighteen or more. All other matters, their judgments, and their laws are the same as all the laws and statutes of an Eruv of courtyards. One's wife can participate on his behalf, and one can include another in the partnership without his knowledge if his courtyard has no entrance except to this alleyway. A minor can collect the partnership contributions, and the partnership can be placed in the courtyard of a minor, and another can acquire the partnership for everyone. If they were all partners in some type of food or drink and it was placed in one location, there is no need to establish a partnership. Even if it was divided among neighbors, with wine for one and oil for another, there is no need to establish a partnership, provided it is in one vessel. Although with an Eruv, we permit it when the vessel becomes full and the excess is placed in another vessel, this is only when it was collected for the purpose of an Eruv. But here, since it was not placed for the purpose of a partnership, it specifically requires one vessel. (Rashi and Tosafot, 71a). I have seen in the name of the Rashba who wrote that anything that is not fit to be mixed together is not considered a connection, even if they are in one vessel (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 4), and this seems to be the plain meaning of the discussion there (which says that wine and wine are fit to be mixed, etc. see there).

Our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, wrote in Section 2: "Israelites who dwell in three separate places, and the doors of each of these places are locked at night, and the sexton collects flour from all of them - it does not help them to participate together, because an alleyway merging (shituf mevo'ot) needs to be placed in a courtyard within the alleyway. Those who are separated from each other and distant - their merging is not considered one, and their alleyways are not considered as one. And if they made an eruv in one place, the others who did not make an eruv do not prohibit them, since they do not have the right of passage one over the other, because the whole city is not considered one alleyway, even though they reside within one wall enclosure." End of quote.

The explanation is that their city layouts were not like ours. Their city was divided into many sections, and each section had its own alleyways, with their gates closing at night in such a way that they were not connected to each other. The entire city was surrounded by a wall. Therefore, the sections could not all join together as one, since the eruv would be placed in one of the sections. Consequently, the other sections would not have the eruv, because they are locked at night and are distant and separated from each other by the locking. Rather, each section would make its own eruv. If one section makes the eruv and another section does not, it would be considered a "foot that is forbidden in its place" and people would walk through them. Nevertheless, they do not prohibit them, since it is not necessary to walk through them, as there is another way. They are not like two courtyards, one within the other. This is what is meant by "they do not have the right of passage," meaning necessarily, since they have another way. Therefore, even when they walk through, they do not prohibit. And even though they sit within one surrounding wall, they are still not considered as one, since each section is closed off by itself. (See Magen Avraham, subsection 3, and Machatzit HaShekel, and it will be explained with God's help in section 392.)

One may form an eruv with all types of food, and even four or five different types of food can combine to the amount of two meals. One may form an eruv with any food or drink, except for water alone or salt alone. However, if one mixes water and salt together, one may form an eruv with this, as it becomes like brine in which bread and meat are dipped, and it is considered a condiment. Similarly, truffles and mushrooms cannot be used for an eruv even if cooked, because they are not considered as food (according to Rambam, Chapter 1), since one can only form an eruv with something that is suitable for a meal or to accompany bread. Truffles and mushrooms are not used for a meal nor to accompany bread, and those who eat them are not considered normal people (according to Ritva at the beginning of Chapter 3). Someone who eats them as a condiment is considered to have an unusual opinion compared to everyone else (ibid). However, there is someone who disagrees with this (Gra, note 18), as it is said that they brought this to Shmuel at the end of the meal (Berachot 47), implying that it is considered an important food (ibid) and it is served on the tables of kings (ibid). What is stated in the Gemara (beginning of Chapter 3) that truffles and mushrooms cannot be used, refers not to the eruv but to the redemption of second tithe, as it is taught there: they cannot be purchased with second tithe money, since we require produce from produce and something that grows from the ground, as explained at the beginning of Torat Kohanim (ibid, and it is written that in the Gemara a word is missing, and the meaning refers to the end of the Mishnah. According to the Rif, Rambam, and all the poskim, we must say that while it is true that they are important food, nonetheless they are not to accompany bread nor to be the main part of a meal by themselves, which is a condition for the eruv. Study this carefully).

Any food that is eaten as it is, such as bread made from grains and raw meat, if they are included in the partnership - the measure is enough for two meals. And anything that is a condiment and people customarily eat with their bread, such as cooked wine, roasted meat, vinegar, brine, olives, and onion bulbs - the measure is enough to eat with two meals, meaning the condiment should suffice for two meals of bread. If they partnered with raw wine - the measure is two revi’it for everyone, and similarly with beer - two revi’it. Eggs - two, and they can partner with them even if they are raw. Pomegranates - two, etrog (citron) - one, walnuts - ten, and five peaches. A liter of vegetables - whether raw or boiled. If it was cooked but not fully cooked - they do not partner with it, because it is not fit for eating. The Raavad disagrees with this, stating that this law applies only to beets and not to other vegetables. Half a revi’it of spices, a kav of dates, a kav of dried figs, a maneh of pressed figs, a kav of apples, hops - a handful, fresh beans - a handful, and a liter of chaziz, which is a type of vegetable. And beets are included among vegetables - and they can partner with them. Onion leaves - they do not partner with them unless they have softened, and each leaf has become a span long. But less than this - it is not food. All these items are considered condiments, and therefore these measures were given, and similarly for all similar items. It has already been explained that all foods combine to measure, and the Raavad disagrees on this, holding that this applies only to eruv techumin and not to shitufei mevo'ot, and most of the poskim disagree with him. It seems that in partnership - they can even partner with a piece, as it is not worse than other food. And similarly, any food that is not whole - they can partner with it, and all measures are according to the opinion of the Rambam in Chapter 1.

The opinion of the Rosh and the Tur is that one cannot make an eiruv with spices, because these are condiments for roasted meat, and roasted meat itself is considered a condiment. Therefore, it is sufficient to eat two meals with it, as stated, and we do not say that a condiment is for a condiment. (Beit Yosef) The Rosh also considers that one cannot make an eiruv with unripe dates, which are not fully ripened, nor with lentils, wheat, or barley. The Rambam did not need to enumerate these, because since they are not suitable for eating as they are, it is understood that one cannot make an eiruv with them. (Beit Yosef) It is written that one can make an eiruv with water and salt together, but this is not the opinion of the Tosafot (27: s.v. 'but') which holds that this is only when oil is added to them. And if one asks, why not just use oil itself, the answer is that if the oil alone does not meet the required measure for two meals, then the water and salt are combined with it. (ibid.) Regarding the ruling that one cannot make an eiruv with lentils, this refers to raw lentils, but cooked lentils can be used for an eiruv. (Beit Yosef)

The general rule is: anything that is commonly used as a condiment for bread—the measurement is enough to accompany bread consumed in two meals. And anything that is not used as a condiment for bread—the measurement is enough to eat by itself for two meals. Raw meat is not considered a condiment, and therefore, we require it to be enough to eat for two meals. But roasted meat is considered a condiment, and it suffices to accompany two meals. Even if there are places where, due to the abundance of meat, they eat it without bread—their opinion is nullified by the majority. Meaning, certainly for them, the measure is enough to eat the meat for two meals, but for the rest of the world, this is not the case. This is clearly proven in the Gemara (29b) and Tosafot (28a s.v. 'and Bavel'), and this is the primary ruling. (And the Magen Avraham 6 is very brief.) Vinegar is considered a condiment, and its measure is enough to dip vegetables for two meals. Similarly, cooked wine is considered a condiment, but raw wine is not, nor are other beverages. It is written that cooked wine is used for finishing a meal, not for dipping, and its measure is as much as they bring cooked wine to finish two meals. (Magen Avraham 8 in the name of the Meiri) And we do not know this, because wine is not common among us, and similarly, there are several things we do not know.

One may participate even with food that is not suitable for him, if it is suitable for any person, such as wine for a Nazirite, or terumah for an Israelite. Similarly, if one has vowed not to eat a particular food or has sworn not to eat it, he can still participate in it, as stated in Siman 366, Section 14, regarding the Eruv of courtyards. Some say that this applies specifically if he swore or vowed not to eat it. However, if he vowed or swore not to benefit from it, he cannot participate in it, and the same law applies to the Eruv of courtyards. Even though it is permissible in the case of limits (techumin), this is because limits apply only for the sake of a commandment, as stated in Siman 415. But an Eruv and participation, although also somewhat a commandment, is nevertheless optional. Some have written that it is permissible because his intention was not to prohibit benefiting in this manner but rather through direct benefit, not through an Eruv and participation. (There, Subsection 10, in the name of the Maggid Mishneh) And our teacher, the Rema, wrote in Section 8 on the words of our teacher the Beit Yosef, who prohibits one who vowed or swore not to benefit, and wrote in this language: "And if he said, 'Konam, its benefit or eating it is forbidden to me,' everyone agrees that he cannot participate in it," end quote. His intention is not that 'Konam' is more stringent than 'not to benefit' for everyone, but rather the explanation is that in 'not to benefit' there are those who disagree and permit, like in limits. But in 'Konam,' even in limits it is forbidden, because it resembles consecration, and this is the opinion of the Tur. However, according to the Rambam, even in 'Konam' it is permissible in limits. And those who hold that an Eruv and participation are similar to limits also permit 'Konam.' (See Magen Avraham there, and the Rema abbreviated as is his way)

If one said about a loaf on Friday evening: "This loaf - today is secular and tomorrow is holy" - one may use it for an Eruv. The same applies to a vow, even for someone who prohibits with a vow. However, if he said: "This loaf - today is prohibited to me by a vow, and tomorrow is secular" - one may not use it for an Eruv according to the one who prohibits. Similarly, if he said: "Today it will be holy, and tomorrow it will be redeemed on money that is in my house" (see Rashi 36a, s.v. "today"), the reason being that the time of acquiring the Eruv is between sunset and nightfall, which is a doubt whether it is day or night. Therefore, when he said "today is secular and tomorrow is holy," when the time of acquiring the Eruv arrives, the holiness has not yet descended upon it due to the doubt. Conversely, with "today is holy and tomorrow is secular," the holiness does not depart from it due to the doubt, as we always maintain the previous status in a situation of doubt. The procedure for partnership and its blessing will be explained in Siman 395.

A courtyard that opens into two alleyways, and has joined in partnership with each of them, as we have already explained that one person can reside in multiple places, therefore he is permitted to transport items with each of them from the houses in the courtyard to the two alleyways, and from the alleyways to the houses in the courtyard. However, they are prohibited from transporting items that were in the houses in one alleyway to the other alleyway via the courtyard. But their belongings – it is permitted to bring them to this courtyard. And we do not worry that because there will be an abundance of items from this one and that one in the courtyard, they will come to swap, transporting an item from one alleyway to the other via the courtyard – we do not worry, as in the case in section 378 with courtyards, where we did not enact decrees in such instances, see there. And if he did not join in partnership with either of them or with any of them, and each alleyway joined for itself, if he customarily goes in and out with both of them on weekdays through their paths – then automatically he prohibits on both of them as the law of the inner and outer, where the inner prohibits on the outer due to his foot traffic as we have mentioned there. And there is a question on this: why do we not say here that 'a foot that is permitted in its place does not prohibit outside its place' as mentioned there. One could say that this applies from one courtyard to another, because since he has a courtyard that is permitted in its place – he cannot prohibit the courtyard he passes through, since he has his own courtyard. But the alleyway – he prohibits, even though he is permitted in his own courtyard, since this does not relate to the alleyway, as every courtyard owner needs the alleyway. (So it seems in my humble opinion.)

And if he is familiar with one and not familiar with the other, the one he is familiar with prohibits, and the one he is not familiar with does not prohibit. However, this is when he did not join at all, but if he joined with the one he is not familiar with and did not join with the one he is familiar with, the one he is familiar with is permitted to himself, for he has removed himself from him by joining with the other. All the more so if he was familiar with both and joined with one of them, the second one is permitted, for he has removed himself from him. And if it was otherwise, meaning he did not join with either of them and the alley he is familiar with joined among themselves, and if he has a foot on them, he will spoil their partnership and prohibit them, and the second one he is not familiar with did not join together. If he is pushed to them, it will not spoil them, for they did not join anyway. The sages said (Menachot 49a) that against his will, they push him to the unfamiliar one this Shabbat, so that he does not spoil the familiar one, for in such a case we compel him to follow the measure of Sodom, for these benefit and he does not lose, and he will be removed this Shabbat from the familiar one.

The eiruv and the shituf have the same purpose, for the eiruv unites all the residents of the courtyard, and the shituf unites all the residents of the alleyway. They share the same law, as mentioned in the previous section, except that they differ in two matters. Regarding the substance of the eiruv, in a courtyard, one may only use bread, while in an alleyway, one may use even wine or any other item. Regarding the place where the eiruv is placed, in a courtyard, it must be placed only in a house within the courtyard, whereas in an alleyway, it can even be placed in a courtyard. The reason is that the eiruv is due to residence, to combine their residences and make them one, and a person's residence is associated with bread, not wine. The shituf of an alleyway is only to unite the domains of the courtyards, and a courtyard is not a residence, hence bread is not required. (Rashi 71a) This is also the reason for the difference in their placement, for the eiruv, which is due to residence, a person only resides in a house, and therefore the eiruv must be placed specifically in a house. The shituf, which is merely to unite the courtyards, is sufficient if placed in a courtyard.

There is a question regarding this matter: since ultimately their intention is the same, to treat them all as if they are in one place, why do we need two [separate actions]? And it makes sense that when each courtyard makes its own eruv, they then need a joining of the alleyway to permit carrying within the alleyway and from one courtyard to another. But when they have made a joining of the alleyway, why is an eruv of the courtyards necessary? After all, ultimately they are all considered as being in one place, so why is the eruv of the courtyard also needed? And it's not only when they made the joining with bread and placed it in one of the houses—as is our custom, to make an eruv for the entire city and place the matzot in the synagogue—that there is no need at all to make courtyard eruvs afterward, since they are all already considered to be dwelling in one place. Rather, even if they made the joining with wine and placed it in the courtyard, which in such cases the eruv does not work, still, ultimately all the residents of the alleyway are already considered to be in one place.

However, the sages have said (71a): "We make an eruv in courtyards and join in alleyways so that the concept of eruv is not forgotten by the children." And this is the wording of the Rambam in Chapter 1, Law 19: "Those who join in an alleyway need to make an eruv in the courtyards so that the children do not forget the obligation of eruv, since the children do not recognize what is done in the alleyway. Therefore, if they joined in the alleyway with bread, they rely on it and do not need to make an eruv in the courtyards, as the children recognize the bread." End quote. And this is what he wrote in Chapter 5, Law 14: "If they joined in the alleyway and all of them forgot to make an eruv in the courtyards, if they are not particular about their piece of bread, they rely on the joining for the first Sabbath only. And they permit this matter only out of necessity." End quote. And this is from the Jerusalem Talmud (Eruvin 5:9). This is when they made the joining with wine or another item, and not with bread. And this matter was forbidden so that the children do not forget the obligation of eruv. Therefore, they only permitted it for the first Sabbath, and on the condition that they are not stingy and particular about their piece of bread, and there is no concern that they will not make an eruv for the following Sabbath. But if they made the joining with bread, it is also permissible from the outset.

And the Tur is more lenient, for even if they made the partnership with wine or with another item, there is no need for an additional eruv, as this is his understanding from the Talmudic discussion, that we are not concerned that one might forget the obligation of eruv. And this is the language of the Tur: "We rely on the eruv in place of the partnership and on the partnership in place of the eruv. For if there were five courtyards open to each other and open to an alleyway, and the courtyards made an eruv through the doorways between them, they do not need a partnership in the alleyway. Similarly, if they made a partnership in the alleyway, even with wine which is not suitable for making an eruv in courtyards, they do not need to make an eruv in the courtyards. And the Rambam, of blessed memory, wrote that one does not rely on a partnership in place of an eruv unless they partnered with bread, and my master, my father the Rosh, of blessed memory, did not write this."
