End of quote. And the first distinction was not mentioned by the Rambam at all, and it requires further investigation.

And our master, the Beit Yosef, after writing the words of the Rambam, wrote: "And there are those who say that if each courtyard did not make an eruv for itself, one cannot rely on the shituf. But if each courtyard made an eruv for itself, and then made a shituf for the alleyway, and did not make an eruv through the openings between them, they are permitted to use the courtyards of the alleyway through the openings between them, as they rely on the shituf in place of the eruv. And if they made an eruv through the openings between them and did not make a shituf for the alleyway, the courtyards are permitted to use the alleyway, as they rely on the eruv made through the openings in place of the shituf." End of quote. And they were astonished by him, as this opinion is not found at all. (See Beit Chadash and Taz who raised many objections against him and the Perisha who elaborated greatly to reconcile his words, see there).

And our master, the Rema, wrote: "And there are those who say that one can rely on a shituf (partnership) in place of an eruv, even if they only partnered with wine, and similarly, one can rely on an eruv in place of a shituf. And above in Siman 366, I wrote that we customarily only make one shituf with flour. And it seems to me the reason is because our eruv, where each member of the courtyard contributes to the shituf, is like both an eruv and a shituf together, and initially, one should not do more. And that which required both a shituf and an eruv was in the time of the Gemara, when the members of the courtyard did not contribute to the shituf, but rather the courtyard made an eruv together, and one member of the courtyard would contribute to the shituf. But in this case, everyone agrees that only one shituf is made. And if one does more and blesses on it, it would be a blessing in vain." End of quote.

They also wondered about him, why he seeks reasons, since we make the partnership with bread – it is permitted according to all opinions. (Taz, subparagraph 2; Magen Avraham; Bach) However, his intention is regarding those who say, as written by the Beit Yosef, that with partnership alone – one does not fulfill the obligation at all, even with bread. Therefore, he says that when each member of the courtyard contributes to the partnership – it suffices even according to those who say that partnership alone is enough. I say that all of this was to investigate according to the structure of their cities, which had courtyards and alleyways. But for us, who do not have alleyways, only courtyards, and when we make an eruv for the entire city – the whole city becomes like one large courtyard, for which we therefore rule in our place that the law of the courtyard requires two side posts, and not like an alleyway where a single side post suffices, as explained in Siman 363. Hence, it is necessarily impossible for us to have anything but one eruv, specifically with bread, and it must be placed in a house. Nowadays, it is placed in the synagogue, which is no worse than a house. Consequently, in our case, we only have eruv courtyards, and we do not have alleyway partnerships at all. Therefore, those people who are stringent upon themselves and make an eruv also in their courtyards without a blessing – in my opinion, they are causing a problem and it is forbidden to do so, for it is like someone dividing his eruv in one courtyard – the eruv becomes nullified, unless they make a condition – if the city eruv is valid, then our action is null, etc. (This seems to be my humble opinion.)

If the courtyards did not make an eruv and did not join together at all, it is clear that from the houses it is forbidden to carry both to the courtyards and to the alleyway, and similarly, utensils that rested in the houses are forbidden to be carried even from a courtyard to an alleyway, and likewise from a courtyard to another courtyard. However, utensils that rested in a courtyard are permitted to be carried from one courtyard to another, and from a courtyard to an alleyway. And similarly, utensils that rested in an alleyway are permitted to be carried throughout the entire alleyway, and from the alleyway to the courtyards, as it has already been explained at the beginning of Siman 372 that roofs, courtyards, enclosures, and alleyways are all considered one domain for utensils that rested in them before Shabbat.

And behold, in the Gemara (91a), there is a dispute about this matter. Rav holds that when is it permissible to carry from one courtyard to another and to an alleyway utensils that were in them during Shabbat? It is when none of the courtyards made an eruv at all, not even each courtyard for itself, because then household utensils are not commonly found in the courtyard. But if each courtyard made an eruv for itself, then household utensils are commonly found in the courtyard, and therefore, even utensils that were in the courtyard during the onset of Shabbat are forbidden to be carried to another courtyard or an alleyway, because we fear that one might also carry utensils that were in the house, since with an eruv, they are very common. However, Shmuel and Rabbi Yochanan disagree with Rav, and they hold that whether an eruv was made or not, it is permissible because we do not decree that one might carry utensils that were in the house. Rashi, Tosafot, the Rosh, the Raavad, and most of the authorities rule according to Shmuel and Rabbi Yochanan, and not like Rav, and it is permissible in any case to carry utensils that were in them during the onset of Shabbat from one to the other. We have already mentioned this in Siman 372.

Therefore, the words of the Rambam on this matter are very surprising. He wrote in Chapter 5, Law 15: "A lane (mavoi) in which the residents have not joined together in an eruv, if the courtyards made an eruv with the houses - one may not carry within it except within four cubits, as in a karmelit, because once the courtyards made an eruv with the houses - the lane becomes as if it were only open to houses without courtyards. Therefore, one cannot carry in the entire lane. However, if the residents of the courtyards did not make an eruv - one may carry throughout the entire lane objects that were there before Shabbat, just like a courtyard in which an eruv was not made." End quote. 

He wrote this based on the Gemara in Shabbat (130b) where it also brings a statement of Rav. The Gemara first explains Rav's reasoning, that since the courtyard made an eruv with the houses, the lane becomes like houses without courtyards. And we hold that the proper arrangement of a lane is only when it is open to both houses and courtyards, as stated in Siman 363. 

And it makes sense that when everyone made an eruv and it is permitted to carry in all of them, they all become as one unit, and it is properly considered houses and courtyards open to the lane. But when they did not join together in an eruv for the lane, and the courtyard made an eruv with the houses separately, and the lane is separate from them, the courtyard with the houses is considered as one unit - it appears as if there is only one thing in the lane, houses without courtyards. 

Now, Rashi and Tosafot explained there that in the conclusion, this reasoning is nullified, and so wrote the Raavad. However, this is not so difficult, as the Rambam interprets this reasoning even according to the conclusion, as the Maggid Mishneh wrote there. (Rav Ashi explains: 'What causes the courtyards to be prohibited? - The houses, and they are not there.' Rashi and Tosafot explained this is because household items are commonly found in the courtyards, as discussed there. 

And the Rambam would explain that the meaning is, without an eruv they are considered two separate entities, and there are houses and courtyards. But this is not the case when an eruv is made, as the Maggid Mishneh wrote. And examine this well.)

However, the main issue is very puzzling, as all of this pertains to Rav, but according to Shmuel and Rabbi Yochanan in Eruvin, it is not so. And the law follows Rabbi Yochanan over Rav, and certainly so when Shmuel is with Rabbi Yochanan. In my humble opinion, the ruling aligns with the Rambam, as it is truly difficult to understand why the Talmud in Shabbat goes to the trouble of seeking a reason for Rav's ruling, when in Eruvin the reason is explained as a decree lest one come to carry objects from houses. However, it is certain that the two sugyot (sections of the Talmud) do not contradict each other at all. The reasoning in Shabbat is universally accepted, and there is no dispute about it. The matter in Eruvin is a different issue. The reason in Shabbat applies only if all the courtyards have merged with the houses, leaving the alleyway without courtyards. But if some merged and some did not, there are still houses and courtyards from those that did not merge. In such cases, Eruvin discusses the matter, and the Rambam's intention is also when all have merged, as is clear from his wording. But if some merged and some did not, the Rambam agrees that carrying is permitted, and we do not worry that one might come to carry objects from houses, like Shmuel and Rabbi Yochanan. A clear proof of this is that in Chapter 3, Law 19, he explicitly rules like Shmuel and Rabbi Yochanan, that whether they merged or not, carrying is permitted, as we have quoted his wording above in Siman 372, Section 4. (I am very puzzled by the Tur, Shulchan Aruch, and the later authorities, for according to them, the Rambam would contradict himself from Chapter 3 to Chapter 5. And know that according to the Rambam's reasoning, if the alleyway is permitted with a doorway form, it is allowed. And so wrote the Magen Avraham, that with a doorway form, there is no need for houses and courtyards. But what the Magen Avraham wrote, that even with two beams it is allowed, I do not understand, for if its length exceeds its width, it is not considered a courtyard but an alleyway, and requires a doorway form. Investigate this thoroughly.)

It is well-known that a Kuthi (a Samaritan) who lives in an alleyway causes a prohibition for the residents of the alley until they rent his right of way, and if not, he prohibits all the residents of the alley. The Sages have said (67a) that if the Kuthi has another entrance from his courtyard that does not lead to the alley but to some open field or enclosure, he does not prohibit the residents of the alley, because it is more convenient for him to use that entrance than the alley entrance, as there he is alone and has more space. And even if it is a small entrance that is only four by four [cubits], nonetheless, this entrance is better for him than the alley entrance, and it is as if he has no foot traffic in the alley. Not only that, but even if we see him bringing in and out camels and wagons all day through the alley, he does not prohibit, because certainly it is more convenient for him with the other entrance where he is alone, and we say that his using the alley was incidental. However, this is only when the place where the entrance opens is more than a beth se’ah (a specific measurement), as he has ample space there. But if it is only a beth se’ah, and certainly if it is less than that, he does prohibit, because it is not convenient for him in that place, and the alley is better for him, even if the alley itself does not hold much, because it is a well-trodden path. (This is my opinion)

And so too, an Israelite who lives in an alleyway and did not join in the merging of courtyards with the others nor relinquished his rights, thereby prohibiting the alleyway, if he has another entrance not towards the alleyway, even though he also has an entrance to the alleyway, he does not prohibit it, for the reason that has been explained. However, regarding an Israelite, the situation is the opposite: if this area is larger than a "beit se'atayim" and was not enclosed for the purpose of dwelling, it prohibits, for this area is not suitable for him at all, since it is forbidden to carry in it more than four cubits. This is not the case with an alleyway, where it is permitted to carry within it any objects that were in it when Shabbat began, and it is more convenient for him to use the entrance to the alleyway. But when it is less than a "beit se'atayim," where it is permitted to carry within it, in this case, it is more convenient for him to use that entrance and he does not prohibit it, as it is as if he does not regularly use the entrance to the alleyway. And even though we said regarding a non-Jew that a "beit se'atayim" is not a spacious area for him, this is because he has many uses, but the Israelite does not have many uses on Shabbat, and less than a "beit se'atayim" suffices for him.

If it was enclosed for residential purposes, even if it is more than a Beit Satayim (a specific area measurement) - it does not prohibit [carrying], since it is possible to carry within it. And some say, on the contrary, that an area enclosed for residential purposes is not counted at all, and even if it is less than a Beit Satayim - it prohibits, because since it was enclosed for residential purposes - it is like his courtyard, and it is not considered as surplus space, and he does not wish to remove himself from the alleyway because of it. This is the opinion of our rabbis, the Tosafists. The first opinion is that of Rashi, of blessed memory. And know, that what we said regarding a Jew, 'more than a Beit Satayim' - is not precise, for the same applies to exactly a Beit Satayim - it is like more than a Beit Satayim, as stated at the beginning of Siman 372, that it is forbidden to transfer from a house to a Karpef (an enclosed space) of a Beit Satayim. (See the Magen Avraham who questioned this, but the Gemara and the Tur Shulchan Aruch used familiar terminology, and see Eliyah Rabbah, and it requires further study).

And know that in the Gemara there it is said that they have another entrance not towards the alleyway, and so wrote the Rambam in Chapter 5, Law 17, see there. And the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch wrote the term 'window', that even if there is a window, it does not prohibit [carrying], see there. And I am puzzled, because an entrance, even a small one, is still fit for entry and exit. But a window is not fit for entry and exit, only for general usage. And who told our Rabbis that 'entrance' is not specifically [required]? And indeed we see that in a place where a window is effective, the Gemara used the term 'window' as in the case of an alleyway where one side is Jewish, etc., (74b) which will be explained in the next section, and likewise the language of the Mishnah at the beginning of Chapter 7. But here, the sages said 'entrance', and from where do they know that a window is also permitted? This requires further investigation. (The Rif did not bring this law and this requires investigation).

The Tur wrote: "An alleyway where one side is owned by a non-Jew and the other side by a Jew, and there is a house of a Jew adjacent to the non-Jew's side that opens to the public domain and not to the alleyway, with a window between them and the Jew. The one dwelling in the alleyway cannot establish an eruv through the window between them to carry his belongings into the alleyway through the Jew’s house that opens to the alleyway. But if there is a doorway between them, it is permitted according to Rabbi Yehuda, but according to Rashi, even if there is a doorway between them, it is forbidden." End of quote. And this law has already been clarified in the courtyard in Siman 382, and the reason is the same, that it is forbidden to make a private domain in a place with a non-Jew. We have also explained there the reason for the difference between a window and a doorway, according to Rabbi Yehuda's view. (And the Beit Yosef wrote that even though this alleyway has only one courtyard of a Jew and we require courtyards, nevertheless the courtyard of the non-Jew is also considered a courtyard in this matter, see there.)

And the Rambam in Chapter 5, Law 18 wrote this law in a different manner, and this is his wording: "An alleyway, one side of which is inhabited by non-Jews and the other side by Jews, and there were windows open from courtyard to courtyard of the Jews, and they all made an eruv through the windows. Even though they have become like members of one household and are permitted to carry in and out through the windows, they are still forbidden to use the alleyway through the entrances until they rent [the rights] from the non-Jews, for many do not become like one in the presence of non-Jews." End quote. We also brought this in Siman 382, Paragraph 11, and we explained there that in my humble opinion, the Rambam disagrees with Rashi, who explained in the Gemara like the Tur, that the previous ruling is a significant stringency, and according to the Rambam it is a significant leniency. All the more so, the Rambam does not hold by the Tur's stringency, which is Rashi's opinion. And I am astonished at our teacher, the Beit Yosef, who brought both laws as if they do not contradict each other, and here too he brought both laws, and it requires further study.

We have already explained in Siman 382, Section 6, that a Cuthean (non-Jew) only prohibits (carrying without an eruv) when he resides in the same courtyard as the Jews, or in two courtyards where one is inside the other, where inevitably there is a right of passage from the inner to the outer. But if there are two courtyards open to each other, and each courtyard has its own entrance to the public domain or to an alleyway, and a Cuthean lives in one courtyard and two Jews live in the other courtyard, they do not need to rent the rights from him, even though he sometimes passes through their area, because he has another way (to exit), and he only prohibits in an alleyway when his entrance opens into the alleyway. However, in courtyards, they can make an eruv between themselves (the Jews), as mentioned there. According to this, even if the Cuthean's courtyard is situated between the two courtyards, they can make an eruv through the entrances between them to carry through the Cuthean's courtyard, as it is not considered an interruption since he does not prohibit it. However, there are those who disagree with this and hold that only if the Cuthean does not have an entrance to the alleyway or to the courtyards of the Jews, but only a window above ten tefachim (handbreadths) does he not prohibit. But if he has either an entrance or a window below ten tefachim, he does prohibit. In my humble opinion, the primary view follows the first opinion.

There is nullification of domain in an alleyway (mavoi) just as in a courtyard (chatzer). All the laws of nullification that were explained in Siman 380 regarding a courtyard for someone who forgot and did not join the eruv in his courtyard, similarly, any courtyard that forgot and did not join the alleyway, or intentionally did not join, nullifies its domain to the other residents of the alleyway. It can nullify only its domain in the alleyway and not its domain in the courtyard, and then they will be prohibited from carrying from their courtyard to the alleyway. However, if they want, they can also nullify their domain in the courtyard, and then they can carry also from their courtyard to the alleyway, and to their courtyards and houses. Just as in a courtyard, the one who nullifies can also carry because he is considered as a guest among them, so too in an alleyway – the courtyard that nullifies its domain can also carry. Even though they are many, and it was explained there that many do not become guests, regarding a courtyard in relation to an alleyway, all the residents of the courtyard are considered as one, like a house in relation to a courtyard, where even if there are two people in one room, they are considered as one, similarly a courtyard in relation to an alleyway. And just as there, all the residents of the courtyard can nullify to the one who did not join the eruv if there is a need for it, as explained there, so too, all the courtyards can nullify their domain to this courtyard that did not join the alleyway. Then, if they made an eruv in the courtyard, they can carry from the courtyard and their houses to the alleyway, and the other courtyards are prohibited, because many in relation to one do not become guests. But if they did not make an eruv in the courtyard, there is no benefit in nullification for them, for they prohibit each other. However, when they made an eruv in the courtyard, they can nullify for them. Even though they did not join the alleyway, and they should be considered many who did not join, and nullification does not apply to two who did not join as explained there – we do not say so, for a courtyard in relation to an alleyway is considered as one. They can also nullify to it only their domain in the alleyway, or also their courtyards, and the law will be as explained there regarding a courtyard. (The Taz in Sif-Katan 1 struggled with what was said, "even though they are many," and his explanation is puzzling, for what is he teaching us? But the truth is that regarding an alleyway, it should be considered many who did not join, and nullification does not apply to two who did not join. He teaches us that they are considered as one, and so wrote the Eliyah Rabbah in Sif-Katan 1.)

And just as the laws that apply to a courtyard shared with a Gentile, where it does not prohibit until there are two Jewish homes that prohibit each other, so too with an alleyway and a city. If there are two Jewish courtyards that prohibit each other, then the courtyard of the Gentile prohibits, and they must rent the rights from him. But if there is only one Jewish courtyard, it does not prohibit. Even though there are many houses in the courtyard and it is common for people to reside there, and it should have been prohibited, nevertheless, they are considered as one, just as a house is to a courtyard, so too a courtyard is to an alleyway and a city, for the Rabbis did not differentiate in their ordinance. And when renting the rights from the Gentile's courtyard, it appears to me that one must rent specifically from the owner of the courtyard, or from his servant, agent, or wife, but not from one of the neighbors in the courtyard. Even though in a house, in such cases, when they live in one room, they are considered as his servant or agent, as explained in Siman 380, and we have a principle that a courtyard regarding an alleyway is like a house regarding a courtyard, nevertheless, in this case, it cannot be compared, for how can we consider them as his servant or agent, since they have no connection with him. Rather, certainly, the rental must be from the owner of the courtyard or his wife or the one appointed over the courtyard, who is certainly considered as his servant or agent. And if the owner of the courtyard does not reside there, and his wife and household members are also not there, and he has no appointed person over the courtyard, it appears to me that one must rent from all the householders in the courtyard, who rented the courtyard from the owners.

In a city entirely inhabited by Cutheans, it is permitted to carry throughout the entire city if there is a wall around the city and it is surrounded for residential purposes. This means that the city was first settled and then the wall was built around it, as opposed to being walled first and then settled, which is not considered surrounded for residential purposes, as stated in section 358. The early authorities wrote that most towns are surrounded for residential purposes, as houses are first built and then the city is encircled. However, most fortresses are not surrounded for residential purposes, as they are first encircled and then the houses are built. If there are two courtyards of Jews in the city, they need to rent the city's domain, as will be explained. This was in their times, but now cities are not surrounded at all, and it is forbidden to carry in any city, large town, or village in the streets and marketplaces. Only in the courtyard of a Cuthean is it permitted to carry. Nowadays, in cities where we rely on the form of a doorway (tzurat hapetach) for an eruv, and there are many houses and courtyards of non-Jews, it is necessary to rent the city's domain, and it will be explained from whom we rent the domain.

The Tur wrote: One must rent from every courtyard of a non-Jew, and it is not sufficient to rent from the city official, end quote. Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, explained this as follows: "When is this said? When the official does not own the houses, and also does not have permission to use the houses of the city at all, even not during peacetime. But in a place where all the needs of the city are only carried out by the official or his appointed representative, certainly renting from him or his agent is effective, for he has the authority to place his people in the houses of the city inhabitants without their consent, when needed," end quote. According to this, nowadays, by the decree of His Majesty the Emperor, every city has administrative offices, overseeing city matters and all its needs, called the "Upravva", and by their decree, the construction of houses and courtyards is carried out, and they own the markets and streets - one can rent from the head of the city administration or his agent, but not from the courts or the police. Our teacher the Rema wrote that the words of the Tur only apply to carrying in and out of the domain of a non-Jew, but to carry within an alleyway - one can rent from the official, since the alleyway is under the control of the official, and he has the power to remove all residents from there, end quote. Nowadays, this does not apply, and therefore one rents from the city administration. In small towns, there is always some official from the government to whom all city matters are referred, and he forwards them to the provincial city – and one rents from him or his agent. And when there is a Jew who is his agent – one rents from him, and then it is permitted to carry throughout the city and even in the courtyards of the non-Jews, as the entire city becomes like one courtyard.

Israelites dwelling in a courtyard alone in a city where all the inhabitants are non-Jews, and it is surrounded by a wall in a manner that permits carrying throughout the city, as explained, and several Jews passed through there on the eve of Shabbat and stayed there, lodging in another courtyard—they do not restrict them, for a guest does not impose restrictions, and it is permitted to carry throughout the city. And until when is one considered a guest? Until thirty days, as stated at the end of Siman 370. (What the Magen Avraham wrote in the name of the Rashal regarding the fair in Lublin, and what the Shach wrote in the name of several responsa concerning Jewish streets—is not applicable in our times, as is evident; therefore, we have not discussed it and have explained according to the prevailing custom. Examine this thoroughly.)

In this section, it will be explained that although the sages permitted creating an eruv for an entire city, nevertheless, there are cities where some houses must be excluded from the eruv and should make their own eruv if they wish. However, they would be prohibited from carrying from there to the city and from the city to there. The reason for this exclusion is to ensure that people understand that it is the eruv that permits them to carry, and the proof is that the houses not included in the eruv are forbidden to carry to and from. If they do not make this exclusion, people might completely forget that it is forbidden to carry and transfer on Shabbat from a private domain to a public domain and vice versa, and they might forget entirely about the prohibition of transferring. This applies specifically to a public city and not to a private city, as will be explained. According to the Rif and the Rambam, a "public city" is one that is collectively owned and does not belong to an individual. A "private city" is one that was built by an individual for himself, who then rented it out to many or sold it later to many, or built it to house residents while reserving paths, streets, and plazas for himself. (Magen Avraham, section 1, quoting the Mishneh Torah, chapter 5) According to this, a private city is not commonly found among us at all.

Many have wondered why we do not act in this manner, and we make an eruv for our cities without any exclusion, which is contrary to the Mishnah (59a), the Gemara, and all the poskim. Some have explained that we rely on Rashi's interpretation, who explained that a 'large city' means it has 600,000 inhabitants. (Magen Avraham 362:2) Others have written that we rely on the opinion that non-Jewish houses are considered an exclusion (Eliyahu Rabbah 362:2), which is a strained interpretation. 

In my opinion, there is no basis for this question. The requirement for an exclusion by the Sages was in their cities, which were surrounded by a wall around the city, and only the eruv was lacking, thus requiring an exclusion for recognition, as mentioned. However, in our cities that are not surrounded by a wall, and it is forbidden to carry in the city unless we make it as if it were surrounded by using doorframe structures, and when one of these doorframe structures is damaged, it is announced that it is forbidden to carry—therefore, there is no greater recognition than this. Everyone sees the doorframe structures at all the boundaries of the city, and immediately beyond the doorframe structure, it is forbidden to carry. There is no greater recognition than this. (Moreover, without a surrounding wall, there is no specific house at the edge of the city, and therefore there are houses beyond the doorframe structure, and they serve as the exclusion.)

The sages taught in the Mishnah: (59a) A city that was private and became public, meaning even if it became public – one can make an eruv for the entire city without leaving a portion out. This applies when it is surrounded by a wall, even if the wall has many openings. For a city that was private – there is no concern of mistakenly carrying out [on Shabbat]. But a city that is public, even if it later became private – one cannot make an eruv without leaving a portion out. This is specifically when the surrounding wall has at least two openings, one in the east and one in the west, or in the south and north, for since it has two openings where people can enter from one and exit from the other – it resembles a public domain, and people might come to err. However, if there is only one opening in the entire wall – there is no need to leave a portion out, for there is no risk of error, as everyone sees the entire city as one courtyard.

And how much is the remainder? Even just one house and one courtyard, from which place one cannot carry to the city, and consequently there is a distinction, and the entire city is joined. And everyone is permitted throughout the city, except for that place of the remainder. And if there were many houses and courtyards in the remainder, they can form an Eruv among themselves through the doorways between them, and they may carry from courtyard to courtyard through the doorways between them, but in the city, they are prohibited. And the people of the city are permitted throughout the city, but prohibited in their area.

The enactment of this matter is due to recognition, so that it will be known that the eruv allows them to carry within this city where everyone traverses. The proof of this is that the place which remains and is not included with them – they do not carry from it, but rather these carry for themselves and those for themselves. And if they wish to create an eruv for each alleyway by itself – all the more so it is effective, for there is no greater exclusion than this, for they will see that from one alleyway to another they do not carry. And our master the Rema wrote that in this case, they need to make between them two posts of any small size if it is ten cubits wide. And if it is more than ten – it requires a doorway frame, end quote. That is to say, even though for an alleyway a side post or a crossbeam is sufficient – this is in a city that only has alleyways and public domains. But in such a city that is surrounded by a wall, which can be fully enclosed by an eruv – it is considered like one courtyard, and in a courtyard two posts are needed. However, what he wrote that for more than ten cubits it requires a doorway frame – he mentioned this incidentally, for more than ten cubits – even in an alleyway a doorway frame is needed, as is known. (The Magen Avraham questioned that Rashi explained that this is only in a private city where they were accustomed to being together and would make an eruv for the entire city, and how could he write this about a public city. And it seems to me that indeed the Tosafot there questioned Rashi regarding this, about making a side post for half an alleyway, that this half is permitted even though they were accustomed to being together. Therefore, he explained that this is also the case for a public city, that if they can enclose the entire city excluding something – its law is like a courtyard. And this is explicitly implied from the Rosh and the Tur who wrote similarly regarding the exclusion. And what the Magen Avraham wrote, that this is when the exclusion is in the middle of the alleyway – I do not know from where he derived this. And Rashi who explained this, because the statement about each alleyway by itself was said in the Gemara regarding a private city, but it is obvious that this is also the case for a public city, and follow the reasoning and be precise.)

According to what has been explained, there is no need for an exemption when dealing with a public domain, except when the wall surrounding the entire city has two gates. But if there is only one gate, no exemption is required. Based on this, according to what is stated in Siman 372, that a ladder is considered a gate, one might say that if on one side of the city there is a gate and on the other side a ladder that is four handbreadths wide, and another ladder that is four handbreadths wide on the other side, it would be considered as having two gates and would require an exemption. However, this is not so, as it has already been explained there that the ladder is considered a gate only to be lenient, not to be stringent. Therefore, even if many ladders are placed side by side up to a width of ten handbreadths or more, it is not considered a gate, and no exemption is required. Similarly, even if there are two gates, but in front of one gate there is a pile of trash ten handbreadths high, it is as if the gate is sealed, and no exemption is required. Even if the trash belongs to an individual, and we are concerned that it might be removed, as stated in Siman 363, nevertheless, in this case, regarding the exemption, which is merely a concern, it is permitted without an exemption as long as it stands. If it is removed, then an exemption should be made. Or it is possible that since it was permitted, it remains permitted, as there is no change in the partitions. (See Magen Avraham, Subsection 6)

The houses that are left as a remnant, even though their entrances do not face the city but their backs are to the city and their fronts face outwards from the city, still they are considered a remnant. Even when only one house is left in this manner, it is considered a remnant. And even if it is not a residential house, but a cow shed or a hay store that does not require an eruv, it is still considered a remnant, and the entire city can be included in the eruv, because the sages decreed this only for the sake of a recognizable marker, and they were lenient regarding the quality of the house, as for recognition, any house suffices. However, this is only when it has a courtyard, as a house without a courtyard is nothing, and it does not serve as a recognizable marker at all.

Some say that the remaining area must only contain Jewish homes (Magen Avraham, Section 3, in the name of Rabbi Yehuda ben Levi). This reasoning is sound, for otherwise, it would not be apparent that those people would not carry within the city, as is obvious. Others say that it is effective (ibid., in the name of the Responsa of the Ran), and the Jerusalem Talmud clarifies according to the first opinion. It must be said that the distinguishing factor is that the residents of the city will not carry into that area. However, if the remaining area comprises Jewish homes, a distinct marker must be made there so that it does not prohibit the city's residents (Ba'er Heitev, in the name of Ginat Veradim), specifically a small partition, as will be explained concerning the remaining area of an alley. The Tur writes to make a form of a doorway or two side-posts, see there.

The Rambam writes at the end of Chapter 5: "A city where all the residents, except for one alley, joined together [in an eruv]—this one alley prohibits [carrying] for all of them. However, if they built a barrier at the entrance of the alley, it does not prohibit [carrying] for them. Therefore, a city cannot be divided in half for an eruv, but either the whole city or each alley individually, and each alley builds a barrier at its entrance, if it wishes to separate its domain from the rest, so that it does not prohibit carrying in the other alleys." This is the end of his words. 

And dividing in half is not effective even with a barrier, because it does not help where the public pass through (Ra'avad). The reason is as we explained, that even though in each alley individually no additional measures are needed—this applies to a city entirely made up of alleys, with a public domain within it, and not surrounded by a wall. But in a city surrounded by a wall, where it is all like one courtyard—each alley prohibits the other, as it is like half a courtyard. Therefore, a light barrier is needed to show that they have separated from the rest of the alleys. 

And it is possible that even two posts or a doorway frame would suffice, and certainly that is the case, as our teacher the Rema stated, which we brought in Section 5. The Gemara and the Rambam mentioned 'a monument' [barrier] as an example, which is merely a light barrier four handbreadths high, as explained in the Rif and the Rosh, and all the more so that posts ten handbreadths high would be effective, even if they are only slightly thick. (And this is clearly understood from the Magen Avraham, subsection 7, see there.)

The Rambam does not mention any distinction between a city of an individual and one of many when they make an eruv for the entire city by leaving a part out. Now, regarding what our master the Beit Yosef wrote in section 4: "A city where all its inhabitants joined in an eruv except for one alleyway - this alleyway prohibits the entire city. But if they erected a marker at the entrance of the alleyway, it does not prohibit them. Therefore, a city that was privately owned and became public - they do not make an eruv for part of it, but rather for the whole, etc.," end quote, which is in the language of the Rambam. But what compelled him to add to the language of the Rambam, implying it refers to a privately owned city, when the Rambam does not mention this at all? And from the Tur, this is also not evident, as seen there, and there is also no reason for it.

It seems to me that our master the Beit Yosef only intended to correct the language in the statement 'they do not make an eruv for part of it.' In the case of a public city, they are forced to make an eruv for part of it since they need to leave a part out, and there is no measure for this left-out part, so they are compelled to divide it. Therefore, he corrected the language, indicating that this applies to a privately owned city even if it becomes public. But aside from the part left out, the law is the same for both, and we have explained that even for the left-out part, some recognizable sign is required.

And our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 5: "In what case are we saying that it is not permissible to create an eruv for half of [the area]? In a city surrounded by a wall ten tefachim high, and it has gates. But if the entire city was not properly enclosed with partitions, and they want to enclose half of it and make an eruv - they are permitted to do so." End quote. The reason is simple, for the main reason for the prohibition is that it is like one courtyard, as mentioned, and this only applies when there is a surrounding wall and gates.

He further wrote in section 6, that when we say it is not permissible to create an eruv for half [the area] - this means that a lechi (side post) and korah (cross beam) do not help to separate them from each other. But with a partition of four tefachim or with two minimal partitions - they can be separated from each other, and an eruv can be made for half [the area]. And if it is wider than ten amot - a form of a doorway is made. End quote. Also, a matzevah (standing stone) does not help in separating into halves, as mentioned in section 9. And our teacher, the Beit Yosef, did not bother to mention it, for it is understood by itself, and certainly, if he makes a partition ten tefachim high at the entrance of the alleyway - it is effective, for this is better than all other methods.

And our teacher the Rema wrote in section 6: "Some say that the prohibition of dividing a private city applies only to its length, since both sides need to access the public domain within it. But regarding its width, where these exit through one gate and those through another, and they do not tread upon each other’s paths - they may create separate eruvs and establish a partition between them, as stated in Siman 363, that up to ten [amot] a side post or beam suffices, and for more than ten - a doorway structure" (end of quote). This is the opinion of the Tur, and this matter is found in the Gemara there. 

The explanation of the matter is that the reason we prohibit dividing them is not merely because it is considered as one courtyard, for that alone would not be a reason to prohibit. Rather, the main reason is because necessarily, in the middle of the city there is a public path, which is not a true public domain, since it is surrounded by a wall and has doors, for if not - in any case it would be permitted to make an eruv for part of it, as stated. Consequently, when they are divided along its length, one side will be on the right of the public path and the other on the left, and they will both need to use the public domain and will thus prohibit each other. 

And even though each side is 'a permitted path in its own place' and does not prohibit outside its place, like an inner courtyard to an outer courtyard in Siman 378, this is because the main part of the outer courtyard belongs to the outer residents, and therefore the inner does not prohibit when it is permitted in its place. But this public path, which is not designated for either of them, causes them to prohibit each other. (Magen Avraham, section 10) But along its width - these will keep away from this side of the public path, and those from the other side.

However, the Rif and the Rambam disagree with this, because in the Gemara there are two versions, and according to one version even along the width it is prohibited, because it is impossible to avoid the public path. Additionally, they hold that the main reason is that it is considered as one courtyard, and if so, there is no difference between its length and its width. (And what the Rema wrote 'public domain', he meant a public path).

And know, all have questioned our teacher, the Rema, who wrote to make a side post or a cross beam, whereas here it discusses a situation where there is an enclosure and doors, and if so, there is no need for the ends of the alleyways to be fixed, except in the place where they divide. The Tur wrote that they should make a form of a doorway (Magen Avraham section 11 and Eliyah Rabbah and Taz), and they rejected his words. In my humble opinion, it seems that he spoke well, and his intention is not for the place where they divide, which requires a form of a doorway, but his intention is that if they divide widthwise, and there they also want to make separate alleyways - in this case, it certainly needs a side post or a cross beam to separate one alleyway from another alleyway. And know, that there is someone who is unsure regarding a city of the many whose doors are locked at night, if it has the status of a city of an individual (there section 9) regarding the matter of leaving a portion unjoined. And in my humble opinion - there is no doubt that it certainly requires leaving a portion unjoined, because since the reason is so that it should not be forgotten that the eruv permits them, what does it matter if they are locked at night or not locked?

It is stated in the Gemara there that a city of many people that has been reduced to fifty households – its law is like that of an individual, and it does not require a remainder. (Rashi and Tosafot explained that a city of an individual is not the property of an individual, and a city of many is not the property of many. Rather, a city of an individual is when there are not six hundred thousand people there, and a city of many is when there are six hundred thousand people there. Refer to there. This is not understood according to this, as they said in the Gemara that even on the morning of Shabbat it is common, refer to there. Is it possible that there are six hundred thousand? Likewise, by the head of the exile, were there six hundred thousand? Refer to there. We must say that this was stated only as an example. Refer to there thoroughly.)

One who grants a partnership to all the residents of the city, if they all made one eruv together, it is not necessary to inform them, as it is considered a merit for them. However, when they are divided, they need to ask where they wish to belong. And the law regarding someone who forgot and did not join in the partnership with the residents of the city, or someone who went to spend Shabbat in another city, or a non-Jew who is among them in the city—all have the same law as a courtyard and an alleyway.

One does not establish an Eruv Chatzerot (an eruv for courtyards) or Shitufei Mavo'ot (an eruv for alleyways) on a Yom Tov that falls on the eve of Shabbat. And even though on Yom Tov itself there is no Eruv Chatzerot, and in this respect, it is like a regular weekday—nevertheless, it is forbidden to establish an eruv on Yom Tov, as it is considered like preparing something on Yom Tov (Rashi, Beitzah 16b), and there is also an issue of preparation, as one is preparing on Yom Tov for Shabbat the permissibility of carrying, and Yom Tov does not serve as preparation for Shabbat (Tosafot, Eruvin 38a, s.v. 'v'R. Eliezer'). Therefore, one must establish the eruv before Yom Tov. If one did not establish the eruv before Yom Tov and remembered on the first day of Yom Tov, if Yom Tov falls on Thursday and Friday, one may establish the eruv on the first day of Yom Tov conditionally, by taking the bread in his hand and saying: If today is a weekday, this is my eruv, and if today is holy, my words are of no consequence. And the next day, he takes the bread again and says: If today is holy, I established the eruv yesterday, and if today is a weekday, this shall be my eruv. This applies to the two days of Yom Tov observed in the Diaspora, such as Pesach, Shavuot, and Sukkot. But on Yom Tov of Rosh Hashanah, it is forbidden even conditionally, as it is considered like one long day, and both days have a single sanctity. However, for the Yom Tov of the Diaspora, only one day is inherently holy, and we observe two days out of doubt, as is known.

In the Tur, it is written that on the next day, one should take the bread that was taken the previous day. Certainly, this is not precise, for what difference does it make whether it is this bread or another bread (Beit Yosef)? Rather, it is good advice, for it is forbidden to eat it until Shabbat begins, so why be careful with two loaves (Magen Avraham)? Moreover, since the mitzvah was performed with it yesterday, it should be done with it today as well (Taz). It is also obvious that "with this eruv" should be said on both days, for on the first day he said, "if today is holy, my words mean nothing," so how can he rely on this tomorrow? And a blessing should not be recited neither on the first day nor on the second day, for how can he bless on the first day when he says, "if today is holy, my words mean nothing," what would he bless over? And the same applies to the next day. And if we say that he should bless conditionally: "Who has sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us to make an eruv conditionally" – we do not find such a blessing anywhere, and so it is further on in Siman 527 regarding the eruv tavshilin. There are those who wrote there that one should bless (Magen Avraham there, Siman 25), but these things seem strange to me.

And know that the Rambam in Chapter 6 of Yom Tov, Law 15, wrote: Nowadays, when we are knowledgeable in the fixing of the months, and the first day of Yom Tov is definitely a Yom Tov, this second day of Yom Tov that we observe is merely a custom, as they sent from there, "Be careful with the custom of your ancestors," as explained in the Gemara (Beitzah 4b). One cannot establish an Eruv on a condition, saying "If today is a weekday, etc.," for we know that today is holy. The Ra'avad, the Rosh, and the Ran disagreed with him, for even in the time of the Gemara they were knowledgeable in the fixing of the months, and nevertheless, they were instructed to establish the Eruv on a condition, and the Rif also brought this as law. On the contrary, according to his opinion, why don't we establish the Eruv on the second day of Yom Tov, since we know it is a weekday? Rather, it must be because we are commanded to treat it as a Yom Tov, it is forbidden to show that it is a weekday. Therefore, the original ordinance remains in place, and the Shulchan Aruch does not bring his words at all.

Both eruv chatzerot (an eruv for courtyards) and shitufei mevo'ot (an eruv for alleyways) - one may establish them during twilight, for since it is a rabbinic requirement, the uncertainty is treated leniently. And even if one has already accepted the additional sanctity of Shabbat, in essence, it is still considered a weekday, and one can establish the eruv. However, there are those who prohibit it if one has accepted the additional sanctity of Shabbat, for since the sanctity of Shabbat has taken effect for that person, how can he treat it as a weekday? And even if another person were to establish the eruv, it seems that according to this opinion, it would not be effective for him. From the Tosefta in the last chapter of Sukkah, there is evidence for this opinion. (The Gra and the Taz's question are not understandable; see there and examine it carefully.)

If one made an Eruv for two people: for one person, he made the Eruv for him while it was still day, and it was consumed during twilight; for the other, he made the Eruv for him during twilight, and it was consumed after nightfall. The sages have said (Shabbat 34a) that both have acquired the Eruv. For the one whose Eruv was consumed during twilight, we consider it night; and for the one for whom the Eruv was placed during twilight, we consider it day. This is not a contradiction, since it pertains to two different people, and a doubt in rabbinic law is ruled leniently. Even though it was done by the same agent, it does not concern the agent but rather the principals. However, if he made the Eruv during twilight and it was consumed during twilight, it is not a valid Eruv. Even though one could say that at the time it was placed it was day, and at the time it was consumed it was night, nevertheless, the entire twilight period is a single doubt, and for one person, it is impossible to apply such a contradiction. The rabbis did not go so far as to consider part of the time as day and part of it as night for the same person. (Beit Yosef in the name of the R"Y)

A doubtful case of an eruv (a ritual boundary), such as if one placed the eruv and it was consumed: if it is doubtful whether it was consumed before the onset of Shabbat, in which case it is not a valid eruv, or if it was consumed after the onset of Shabbat, in which case it is a valid eruv. Similarly, if one placed terumah (a type of offering) and it became impure: if it is doubtful whether it became impure before the onset of Shabbat, in which case it is not a valid eruv, or if it became impure after the onset of Shabbat, in which case it is a valid eruv. In all such cases, we say that a doubtful eruv is valid. This is specifically in situations where the eruv had an initial presumption of validity—then we uphold its presumption. But if it did not have an initial presumption of validity, such as if it is doubtful whether it was placed at all, or if it is doubtful whether the terumah was impure or pure, or if it is doubtful whether it was terumah or untithed produce and the like—we do not say that the doubt permits leniency. All the more so when there is a presumption to the contrary, such as if one made an eruv with produce from which terumah and tithe were separated, but it is doubtful whether they were separated before or after the onset of Shabbat, we uphold the presumption that it is untithed. (Gemara 36)

The reason for this matter is that the principle of "a doubt in a Rabbinic law is ruled leniently" only applies when the matter has been performed but there is a doubt about it. However, if there is a doubt whether the matter was performed at all, it does not apply. This is why if one placed an eruv during twilight, it is valid because the act was performed, though there is a doubt about the time. But when there is a doubt whether the eruv was placed at all, there is no basis to say "a doubtful eruv is valid." Similarly, if there is a doubt whether it was placed with impure terumah or pure terumah, it is like a doubt whether it was placed at all, as impure terumah is considered as if it was not placed. This contrasts with a doubt whether it became impure before nightfall or after nightfall, or a doubt whether it was eaten before nightfall, as the eruv definitely exists – we rely on the presumption that it was certainly fit during the day, and for an eruv, we need a meal that was fit during the day. (See Magen Avraham section 1, and this is his intention, examine it well)

The eruv must be in a place where it can be accessed during twilight. Therefore, if a pile fell on it and it cannot be accessed without a shovel or pickaxe, which involves a Torah prohibition, it is not a valid eruv. However, if it can be accessed by a rabbinic prohibition, it is a valid eruv, because any prohibition that is rabbinic in nature was not decreed during twilight in the case of a minor mitzvah or great need, as stated in Siman 342. Therefore, if one placed it in a tower and locked it, and the key was lost before nightfall, if it is impossible to access the eruv without performing a Torah-prohibited labor during twilight, it is considered as if it is lost and is not a valid eruv, since it cannot be eaten. But if it can be accessed by a rabbinic prohibition, it is permitted, for the reason explained. The Tur holds that dismantling a structure, even if it involves a rabbinic prohibition, does not constitute a valid eruv, because dismantling a structure appears to be a Torah prohibition, and this requires further study (see Taz and Magen Avraham, section 2). If the key is found on Shabbat in a place where it could have been brought during twilight without a Torah-prohibited labor, it is a valid eruv, even though it was not in hand during twilight. Since it is likely to be found, it is as if it was in hand during twilight (Tur).

The eruv (ritual enclosure) does not need to exist except during twilight (bein hashmashot). And even though the eruv is for the purpose of residence, and the residence is for the entire Shabbat day, nevertheless, the main aspect of the residence needs to be during twilight, the time when the eruv is acquired. And we hold that the beginning of Shabbat acquires the eruv, and therefore, when it is certainly dark, one can eat the eruv. And Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote that one should break bread over it on Shabbat morning, since it was used for the mitzvah of eruv, it should be used for another mitzvah, to break bread over it during the Shabbat meal and recite the blessing "Hamotzi" over it. And this was according to their custom, where they would eat the evening meal before nightfall, but for us, it is obligatory to break bread over it during the nighttime meal. All this applies if one makes an eruv every Friday, but it has already been explained in Siman 368 that it is better to make an eruv for the entire year.

It is a mitzvah to pursue the establishment of partnerships in alleyways (shitufei mevo'ot) just as one does with courtyard eruvin, so that people do not stumble into the prohibition of carrying on Shabbat in the alleyway. One collects bread or another item from each homeowner in the alleyway, or he sanctifies it for them from his own property through another person, and that person lifts it a handbreadth and acquires it on behalf of all the residents of the alleyway. He then recites the blessing, “Who has sanctified us... regarding the commandment of the eruv.” And even though we refer to this as 'shituf' - this is to differentiate it from the courtyard eruvin, as stated at the beginning of Siman 386. However, the actual name is 'eruv' - because it unites all the residents of the alleyway to dwell in one place. He then declares: "With this eruv, it shall be permitted for us and for all the residents of the alleyway to carry from the courtyards to the alley, and from the alley to the courtyards and houses, and from the houses to the courtyards and to the alley." It is necessary to mention 'houses' because we rely on the partnership in place of the eruv. And all the more so for us, since we only set up one eruv for the entire city. It seems to me that in our case, we need to say, "from the houses to the courtyards and to the streets and markets, and from them to the courtyards and houses, for us and for all who dwell in this city."

And when does one recite the blessing? The Tur and the Shulchan Aruch wrote that it is said when gathering from the residents of the alley. Or if one person grants it on their behalf, the blessing is recited at the time of granting. That is to say, not before, but afterward, one can still recite the blessing. The general rule we have is that the blessings do not prevent the action from being valid, therefore if they collected for the purpose of an Eruv and forgot to recite the blessing, the blessing does not prevent the Eruv from being valid. It seems to me that the declaration "with this Eruv" is essential, because otherwise how is it recognizable that this is an Eruv? However, according to our custom, where the sexton makes the Eruv from the community's funds and grants it to all the residents of the city, and places the Eruv in the synagogue, which is a significant indication that this is an Eruv, then even the declaration "with this" is not essential. The Levush wrote that their custom was to collect flour from each household, and the sexton would bake from it for the Eruv, and the remainder was eaten. If they forgot to recite the blessing, it is not an Eruv because there is no granting and not all of it is included in the Eruv. The Taz disputed this, arguing that since each person gives a small amount of flour for the entire community to benefit from, it is considered an Eruv even without the blessing.

Every person has a Sabbath boundary. Additionally, beyond the boundary, even someone who goes outside of the boundary is given four cubits, as it is taught (Shabbat 48b): "Let each person remain in his place"—like his place, which is the measure of a person when he stretches out his hands and feet. And behold, Moses told those who went outside the boundary to gather the manna. (Tur) And one measures for each person according to his own cubits, and if he is a dwarf in his limbs, he is given four cubits of an average person, as already explained in Siman 349. These cubits are measured loosely and not precisely, and earlier in Siman 363, section 34, we explained the reason for this. See there.

The Tur wrote that the Rif ruled that he only has four cubits, and he stands in the middle, meaning two cubits on each side. The Ra'avad ruled that he has four cubits in every direction, which is (eight) [eight] by (eight) [eight]. And this applies to walking, but for carrying, he only has four cubits, end quote. But Maimonides in Chapter 12, Law 15 wrote that he has four cubits at his side, and then he wrote that if there were two people, part of the four cubits of one enters into the four cubits of the other... if there were three and the middle one is surrounded by them, see there. And so, the Tur and Shulchan Aruch wrote above in Siman 349, it is clear that they do not hold that he is in the middle, for if so, it would not be possible for the middle one to be surrounded by them. Rather, they hold that he has four cubits in whichever direction he chooses. According to this, one must wonder about the Tur and our teacher the Rema who brought his words, for they do not hold this way. (Magen Avraham note 1) It must be said that indeed they do not hold like the Rif but like the Ra'avad, and the Ra'avad does not hold that he is in the middle, but there are those who say that this is also not the opinion of the Rif. (Taz)

Any area enclosed for residential purposes is considered as if it were four cubits. If someone was there at the onset of Shabbat, they may walk throughout this entire area, even if it is very large. Therefore, if Shabbat began in a city surrounded by a wall, even if it is as large as Antioch, they may walk throughout the entire city, as it is considered like four cubits, even if the area is now ruined and uninhabited. However, if it is not enclosed for residential purposes and is an independent area, such as a high mound or a karpef (an enclosed area) that was not enclosed for residential purposes, or a field where the crop has been harvested and the remaining stalks enclose it, and one constructs a fence of palm branches and myrtle to prevent the wind from scattering them, if the enclosed area is less than or exactly two seahs, it is considered as four cubits. If it is more than two seahs, one is limited to four cubits.

Every person is permitted to go out on Shabbat beyond the city limits up to two thousand cubits, and this is the Shabbat boundary. The Rabbis based this on a verse, as it is written: "Let no man go out of his place"—this refers to two thousand cubits. (Talmud, Eruvin 51a) It is written regarding the borders: "And you shall measure from outside the city on the east side two thousand cubits," and similarly in all directions, "and the city shall be in the midst"—as explained in the portion of Masei. Consequently, two thousand cubits are considered the surroundings of the city, and this is "let no man go out of his place"—from the city's place. Two thousand cubits is a mil (a measure of distance). According to the measurement in our country, Russia, it is a Russian verst, which they call a viorst, which is five hundred sazhenes. Each sazhen is four cubits of the Talmud, as we have explained in Choshen Mishpat, section 218.

According to the opinion of the Rambam at the beginning of Chapter 27, there is also a biblical domain limit, which is three parasangs - twelve mil. And this is the language of the Rambam: "One who goes beyond the domain limit of the city on Shabbat - receives lashes, as it is stated: 'No man shall go out from his place on the seventh day.' This place is the domain limit of the city, and the Torah did not give a measure for this domain. But the sages transmitted that this domain is beyond twelve mil, corresponding to the camp of Israel, and so Moses our teacher said to them - you shall not go out beyond the camp. And by rabbinic decree, a person should not go out from the city except up to two thousand cubits. But beyond two thousand cubits - it is forbidden, for two thousand cubits is the city's outskirts." End quote. And this is the method of the Jerusalem Talmud in Chapter 3, Halacha 4, see there. And if this measure also applies to vessels according to the Torah, it will be clarified in Siman 404. However, most of our Rabbis agree that in our Talmud it is explicitly proven that there is no biblical basis for domain limits, and it does not follow the Jerusalem Talmud. (And also the Rif at the end of Chapter 1 who brought this Jerusalem Talmud, the Ramban elaborated to explain that on the contrary, the Rif's intention is that our Talmud does not hold this view, see there, and this is the opinion of most of the poskim).

If one finds himself sanctifying (welcoming) the Sabbath while in a valley and does not know the Shabbat boundary, he may walk two thousand medium steps. This is the length of two shoes: one shoe is the length of the foot, and one shoe is the space between one foot and the other (as stated in Magen Avraham). This is the Shabbat boundary, as each step is half an amah (cubit). Note that the walking is measured in a straight line, and any curving of the path is not taken into account. Sometimes, walking according to the path may result in a distance far greater than the Shabbat boundary, but in a straight line, it will still be within the Shabbat boundary. Most paths curve, and the measurement of boundaries will be explained in the next section, with God's help.

And know that even though the laws of Eruvei Chatzerot (joining of courtyards) and Shitufei Mavo'ot (joining of alleyways) do not apply on Yom Tov (festivals), the laws of techumin (limits of travel) are the same for Shabbat and Yom Tov. The reason for this seems to me to be that the purpose of eruv and shituf is because of the prohibition of carrying, and on Yom Tov there is no prohibition of carrying, and they also did not want to restrict carrying on Yom Tov since it is necessary for food preparation. However, regarding techumin, it seems that the sages did not want a Jewish person to walk excessively on Shabbat as on a weekday, and instead engage more in Shabbat delight and Torah study. This reasoning applies also on Yom Tov, and therefore in all the laws of techumin, Shabbat and Yom Tov are the same.

And just as a person is not permitted to walk on Shabbat and Yom Tov more than two thousand cubits, so too his utensils and animals—it is prohibited to take them outside the owner's domain, for the animals and utensils follow the movement restrictions of their owners. (Beitzah 37.) And if their owners made an Eruv to one direction, no one else can take them in another direction, not even one step beyond where the owners themselves are permitted to go. It was explained earlier in Siman 405 whether it is permissible to hand over an animal to a non-Jew, where there is a concern that he might take it outside the domain—see there.

If one entrusts his animal to his son, it follows the feet (i.e., movement restrictions) of the father, because it is customary for people to place their belongings in the care of their children without intending to transfer ownership. This applies unless it is explicitly stated that the ownership is being transferred. There is no difference whether the son is an adult or a minor, whether he is dependent on his father's table or not. Certainly, this is the case when one entrusts it to his wife or any member of his household; it follows the feet of the owner.

If one entrusts his animal to a shepherd, it follows the feet of the shepherd, even if he gave it to him on Shabbat or Yom Tov (festive day), because it is assumed that this was the arrangement from before the commencement of Shabbat or Yom Tov, even if the shepherd is not Jewish. However, if one entrusts it to two shepherds, even from before Yom Tov, it follows the feet of the owner, since neither of them acquired it. Even if he declares on Yom Tov that his primary intention was for one specific shepherd, it still follows the feet of the owner, because he did not clarify his intentions before Yom Tov. (Magen Avraham, section 5)

An ox that is fattened and prepared for slaughter follows the domain of the one who acquires it for slaughter on Yom Tov, as this was the intention of the owner on the eve of Yom Tov: that whoever acquires it on Yom Tov, it will be in his domain. It is obvious that it was acquired not through a sale, or the price was fixed on the eve of Yom Tov, or the price was known, for on Yom Tov it is forbidden to conduct a sale. Furthermore, even if the owner slaughtered it on Yom Tov and divided the meat among buyers, each buyer can take his portion to the place where he is permitted to go, as this was the owner's intention on the eve of Yom Tov.

Nevertheless, if two people bought an animal in partnership on the eve of a festival and slaughtered it on the festival, even though they divided the meat between them, all the meat is still subject to the rules of both of them. This means that neither of them can take the meat to a place where the other is prohibited to go. The reason is that during twilight, the domains of each partner are absorbed into each other, as each part of the animal draws from the other. This is not similar to the previous law, where on the eve of the festival, everything was under the owner's control, and we say that his intention was that whoever buys from him on the festival, the meat will now be in the buyer's domain. However, it is not applicable to say they draw from each other since no specific owners were designated on the eve of the festival. This is not the case with two people who bought on the eve of the festival, where the owners were designated. If they bought an animal on the festival from the city's animal herder, for example, if he has permission to sell the meat, it is subject to the city's domain. Even if this herder made an eruv (joining of domains) of 4,000 cubits in another direction, it does not prevent one of the city's residents who bought from him from taking it in the opposite direction. From yesterday, it was established in the domain of the city's residents, as they are accustomed to buying from him, and it is not in the herder's domain except for an ox that is intended for grazing, not one intended for sale and slaughter. Since all the city's animals are there, they all intend that they will have the city's domain of 2,000 cubits in every direction. See Section 17.

Utensils that are designated for one of the brothers in the household are considered as having the status of that brother's domain. However, utensils that are not designated for any specific brother are considered communal property, and thus they can only be taken to places where all brothers have the right to go. This applies to brothers after the death of their father, when they jointly hold the property of their father's household. While their father was alive, everything was under his authority and within his domain.

Two individuals who borrowed a garment from one person on the eve of a festival, one to wear it in the morning and the other to wear it in the evening – the area of movement for both of them applies to the garment, and they can only take it to a place where both are permitted to go. If one made an eruv to the end of two thousand cubits to the east and the other to the end of two thousand cubits to the west – they should not move it beyond four cubits, or in a city – they should not move it beyond the city wall. And if one borrowed a utensil from his fellow on the eve of the festival, even if he did not take it until nightfall – it follows the movement area of the borrower, since he was promised it on the eve of the festival – it is considered in his possession at the time of the establishment of the eruv. Therefore, even if he returned it on the festival day – it remains in the possession of the borrower. But if he agreed on the eve of the festival to return it on the festival day – it is in the possession of both of them, as it is no less than two borrowers. However, if he borrowed it from him on the festival day, and did not agree on the eve of the festival, even though he regularly lends it to him – it remains in the possession of the owner, as it is not comparable to a partnership, which inherently belongs to both.

If a woman borrows water and salt from her friend for her dough, or spices for her pot on a Yom Tov (Jewish festival), the dough and the dish follow the movement restrictions of both of them. We do not say that the water and salt are nullified in the dough, or the spices in the pot, because since they came to enhance the dough and the pot, it is considered a mixture of like items, and it is not nullified in something that will eventually become permissible, even rabbinically, since by nightfall it will be entirely permitted. However, if the food will spoil by nightfall, or if it was on the first day of Yom Tov and it will spoil by the next evening, then they are nullified, and we do not apply the rule of 'something that will eventually become permissible,' as explained in Yoreh De'ah, section 102. If she borrowed some cooked dish on Yom Tov and mixed it with her own dish, the dish follows the movement restrictions of both of them, and we do not follow the majority and minority. (Rashi in Beitzah 39a explained: something that will eventually become permissible - tomorrow she can bring it or eat it here today. According to this second reason, it does not apply if it will spoil by tomorrow. However, it seems to me that the primary reason is the first one, because according to the second reason, this cannot be called 'something that will eventually become permissible,' since it was never forbidden here, and it is like the case in Yevamot 82a: if it is permitted to a Kohen, it is permitted. Refer there carefully and analyze it well).

If one takes a coal from his friend on Yom Tov, he may only carry it as far as the one who gave it. However, if one lit a candle or wood from his friend's flame, it follows the limits of the one who lit it, since a flame has no substance. In all matters, a flame is considered insubstantial, except for prohibitions of benefit, where they were stringent regarding the flame, as it is written in Yoreh De'ah, section 162, see there.

The Sages taught in the Mishnah (Beitzah 39a): A private well is limited by the movements of its owner, because since the water belongs to him, it follows his movement restrictions. A well owned by the city is limited by the movements of the inhabitants of that city, extending two thousand cubits in any direction (Rashi). This implies that even if one of the townspeople made an eruv, he cannot carry the water beyond the two thousand cubits, as the Tur writes. However, the Rashba and the Ran wrote that if some of the townspeople made an eruv, one to the north and another to the south, each may carry the water to their respective direction, as this well is like a partnership well, and there is retroactive clarification in rabbinic law. We say it was clarified that the water drawn the day before was designated for each individual's share. If someone drew water and gave it to another, it follows the movement restrictions of the drawer, as he acquired it. If an outsider, not from the city, drew the water for himself, he cannot move it from its place, because the townspeople make eruvs in different directions—some to the north, some to the south, some to the west, and some to the east (see Beit Yosef). This is certainly puzzling, as most of the city likely did not make eruvs, so why shouldn't the drawer have two thousand cubits in any direction? This requires further investigation. A public well is limited by the movements of the drawer. Note that this applies to a well with collected water, as a spring well does not have a fixed place of rest because its water continuously flows. Anything that moves does not establish a place of rest, as will be explained.

Rivers that flow and springs that gush forth follow the movement of the one who draws from them, for they do not have their own place of rest since they are constantly moving, and how can they acquire a place of rest if they do not rest? Even though they do not go beyond the place from which they emerge to flow further, unlike our wells, they still do not rest in their place. Therefore, they follow the movement of the one who draws from them, like an ownerless pit, even if they have owners. And it does not apply the rule of the movement of the owners, because if the owners themselves were moving, they would not acquire a place of rest, and their vessels are not better than the owners themselves. And since they do not have a place of rest, even if they flow from outside the city's boundary and come within the boundary, one may draw from them on Shabbat, and certainly on Yom Tov, and they follow the movement of the one who draws from them. Therefore, rainwater that falls near the city, and all the more so within the city, follows the movement of the people of that city, for it does not acquire rest in the ocean or in the clouds, since there it is constantly moving. And near the city is considered within the boundary. And why do they follow the movement of that city? Because the people of the city have their minds on them, and it seems to me that this is only during the rainy season. And rainwater that falls outside the city's boundary follows the movement of the one who draws from it. (And from the Gemara, it is clear that on Yom Tov, the rainwater follows the movement of any person, and so wrote the Achronim and the Machatzit Hashekel. But in the Yam Shel Shlomo and the Magen Avraham it is as I wrote, and according to what I wrote, it is clear, and examine it carefully.)

If one draws water from a public well for the use of another person, the water follows the feet (i.e., the Shabbat boundaries) of the one who drew it. Even though we hold that "one who lifts a found item for another, the other acquires it," and therefore it should follow the feet of the person for whom the water was drawn, nonetheless, this is not the case. The reason the other acquires it in the case of the found item is based on the principle "since he can acquire it for himself, he can acquire it for another" (Baba Metzia 10). However, since he did not acquire it except through the effort of the one who drew it, it follows the feet of the one who drew it. (Magen Avraham, Siman 14, citing Tosafot)

One who has fruits deposited in another city far away from him, and the residents of that city have established an eruv in a way that they are permitted to come to him – nevertheless, they may not carry his fruits with them to bring them to him. For any deposited item is considered under the ownership of the depositor, and they are placed outside the boundary of the owner, and it is forbidden to move them from their place.
