This is not similar to borrowing, where the item is considered within the boundary of the borrower, since the borrower borrows it for his benefit to use it, therefore it is under his jurisdiction for the entire duration of the loan. But a deposit is for the benefit of the depositor, and hence it remains under his jurisdiction. However, even a deposit is not like the owner regarding boundaries, except when a specific corner is designated for the deposit at the place of the depositee, where the deposit is laid down, for in such cases the responsibility of guarding does not fall on the depositee. But otherwise, since the responsibility of the deposit is on the depositee, it is necessary that the deposit be under his jurisdiction regarding boundaries, as how could he guard it if he does not have the right to take it to the place where he goes? Therefore, it is within the boundary of the depositee.

If one invited guests on Yom Tov, they should not carry portions [of food] to a place where the host cannot go, unless he designated their portions for them through someone else on the eve of Yom Tov. For otherwise, even if he intended from the eve of Yom Tov to invite them, all the food and drink remains under his domain, and it follows the domain of the owner, not the domain of the guests. And know that what was explained in section 8 regarding two people who bought an animal in partnership - the meat follows the feet of both of them, this only applies to living creatures, because their domains are intertwined. But with other items that were taken in partnership on the eve of Yom Tov and divided on Yom Tov, like wine, flour, and anything that does not have a living spirit - each one can carry his portion to where he is permitted to go, and we say it has been clarified that from the eve of Yom Tov it was prepared for this half to be his portion, for in rabbinic matters we hold there is retroactive clarification, and the laws of domains are rabbinic.

The two thousand cubits of the Sabbath boundary – this is in addition to the four cubits of the place of his residence. This applies when he resides in a field. But if he resides in a city, he has the entire city in addition to the two thousand cubits, even if it is as large as Antioch. Whether it is surrounded by a wall or not, he has the entire city in addition to the two thousand cubits. According to the Tur, an extension is given to the city, meaning that one does not start measuring the boundary immediately at the end of the city; rather, an additional seventy cubits and a fraction are added, as stated in Siman 398. This is called 'the extension of the city,' and it is considered like the city itself. After the seventy cubits, one begins measuring the two thousand cubits, which is the Sabbath boundary. However, the Rambam ruled that an extension is not given to the city unless there is some house or building within the seventy cubits, or at the end of the seventy cubits. In such a case, it is considered part of the city, and the boundary is measured from there onward. Similarly, if at the end of the seventy cubits from this house there is another house, it is also considered part of the city, and this continues indefinitely as will be explained. This is according to all opinions. But when there is no house at the end of the seventy cubits, no extension is given to the city, and one begins measuring the boundary immediately. And since the boundaries are rabbinic, we rely on the Tur to be lenient in this matter, and so ruled our master the Rema in section 5.

And sometimes the boundary starts beyond the houses for another reason, as it is taught: "A new city - we measure from its settled area, and an old city - from its wall. And what is a new city? One that was surrounded [by a wall] and then settled, and an old city - one that was settled and then surrounded." The explanation of the matter is that it has already been clarified in Siman 58 that "surrounded for residence" is only called so if first the houses were built and then the wall was surrounded. This is called "settled and then surrounded." But if it was first surrounded and then settled - it is not called "surrounded for residence." And now, in a city surrounded by a wall where the houses are far from the wall, if it was settled and then surrounded - we measure the boundary from the surrounding wall even though it is far from the houses. But if it was surrounded and then settled, it is not considered surrounded for residence - we measure from the end of the houses and not from the surrounding wall unless there is a residential house in the wall.

According to this, anyone measuring the Shabbat boundary, if they establish their residence in a field, should measure the boundary beyond four cubits. If they establish their residence in a house, they should measure beyond the courtyard. If they establish their residence in a city, large town, or village, they measure from the end of the houses of the city. In a city surrounded by a wall, if one settled and then it was enclosed, they measure from the wall. If within seventy and two-thirds cubits there is another house, they measure from that house. According to the Tur, even if there is no house, they start measuring seventy and two-thirds cubits from the city. This is what we have learned: "They give a karpef (an open area) to the city, according to Rabbi Meir, but the Sages say they do not give [a karpef] etc." And the Rambam rules according to the Sages, while the Tur rules according to Rabbi Meir, because the law follows the lenient opinion in matters of eruv, even if it is an individual opinion against the majority. See Beit Yosef.

They square the boundaries as will be explained, and it is taught at the beginning of Chapter 5: "How do they extend the cities? A house that juts out and a house that recedes, a ruin that juts out and a ruin that recedes... they extend the measurement opposite them." And Rashi explained that when one comes to measure the boundary and the houses are not aligned, one protrudes more than the other. And if it was surrounded by a wall with protruding towers, and some protrude more than others, this is what is meant by a ruin that juts out and a ruin that recedes—they extend the measurement opposite them, meaning they stretch a cord from the house that protrudes at the southeast corner to the northeast corner, as if it protrudes there as well, and from there they begin to measure the boundary. The same applies to the ruins.

This is what the Tur wrote: "When one comes to measure the two thousand cubits of the city's boundary, if the entire wall is not straight but has places that protrude from it, we consider it as if a string is stretched over the entire length opposite the outermost part that protrudes from it, and measure from the string outward. Even if it has a protrusion to the east and to the west, we consider it as if a string is stretched over them on every side." These are his words. Now, the Rambam in Chapter 28 did not mention this at all, and similarly, our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, did not mention this at all. It seems to me that the Rambam follows his approach in his commentary on the Mishnah, where he explained how to extend the city's boundaries – a house that goes in and a house that goes out – which refers to the seventy cubits and the remainder of the city's extension. And this is his language in the commentary on the Mishnah: "The matter of 'extending' – that they add something to the city, like the embryo which is an addition... Because if there is a house outside the city and a house inside the city, we measure outside from the house that extends, in order to add seventy cubits, etc." These are his words, and he did not explain like Rashi. And the law of the seventy cubits, indeed, they explained, as explained in the Rambam and Shulchan Aruch.

In truth, I do not understand the words of Rashi and the Tur, for what are they informing us, that we measure opposite the house that protrudes? Even if it stands as far as seventy cubits away, we measure opposite it, all the more so for a house that protrudes more than other houses. It seems to me that there is a significant practical difference in this law, namely that it will be explained that we make the city square, and consequently, if the protrusions extend from one side and according to the protrusions the length on this side will be greater than the width, meaning for example that the city's width is one hundred cubits and its length is also one hundred cubits, but according to the protrusions, an additional ten cubits are added to the length - we are compelled to also add ten cubits to the width, in order to make it square. This is not the case with the seventy cubits extension, which is only on the side where the extension is, and not on the other sides. Even though according to the Tur, even without a house, we add a seventy cubits extension on every side as he wrote, nevertheless, if there is a house and beyond it another house within seventy cubits - it will add much more on this side, and not on the other sides. Therefore, there is a significant practical difference in this law according to Rashi and the Tur, and certainly also according to the Rambam. And this that we learned in the Mishnah there: "And they make it like a square tablet" - does not refer to the beginning, but it is an independent statement, as is explained there. This is not the case according to Rashi and the Tur - it refers to the beginning, as we will explain in section 8.

According to this, we can clarify a significant difference in the law between the Tur and the Rambam. For the Tur, all the protrusions extending from the houses outside the city, in addition to extending the measurement correspondingly on that side, are also added on all sides to make it squared. According to the Rambam, the squaring only applies to all the inner houses and not to those protruding outward. The outward protrusions only have the status of an "extension" of seventy and a fraction cubits, where the measurement is extended correspondingly on that side as if it were a house situated seventy cubits away, but it does not pertain to the squaring of the city. I am astonished that none of the decisors have pointed this out.

And know, that which we said according to the Tur that we should add to the width according to the length – this is when, based on the protrusions on one side, it forms the image of a circle or triangle, or some other kind of image, then one must add from all sides until it becomes square. But if, due to the protrusions, it has equal angles – we do not worry that the length is greater than the width, for this too is considered as square, as will be explained with God's help. However, if due to the protrusions it has the image of a circle, such as when there are many curved and circular protrusions on two or three sides of the city, then we are forced, when we wish to make it into the image of a square, to add from all sides until it takes on this shape, because when it needs to be adjusted, it should be adjusted into a perfect square. But according to the Rambam, this only applies in the context of the seventy cubit extension, where we are not concerned with the image of a square. (So it appears in my humble opinion)

The one who comes to measure the two thousand cubits of the city's boundary, whether it is long and narrow, meaning its width is not like its length, or it was quadrilateral but not aligned with the cardinal directions, since it has four equal corners - we leave it as it is and measure two thousand cubits from its four sides. For behold, what requires us to have a quadrilateral form, we learned from the borders mentioned in the Torah, where it states 'corner,' and a corner means an equal angle. And since it has equal angles, we do not worry if its width is not like its length.

But if it (the city) is round, they create a corner for it, and consider the entire city as if it is within a square. They then extend the lines of the square to all directions of the city, and measure two thousand cubits from there in every direction, thus gaining the corners that the square extends beyond the circle within it. Similarly, if the city is triangular or pentagonal, or has many sides, they square it, and then measure two thousand cubits from outside the square in every direction. Consequently, since they need to make a square, they align the square with the cardinal directions, so that each side of it aligns with one of the directions of the world. If the city is wide on one side and narrow on the other, they consider it as if the entire city is wide, and extend the line until the narrow side is as wide as the long side, and from there they measure the two thousand cubits. If they needed to create a square and did not align it with the cardinal directions, they can change it to align with the cardinal directions. However, as long as they have not changed the boundary markers, they must follow this configuration, and an individual cannot separate from them and say, 'I will make my own configuration according to the cardinal directions,' since this is not a requirement as stated.

A city that is shaped like a gamma (Γ), which is a Greek kappa (Κ), or like an inverted dalet (ד), or a city that is shaped like a bow, meaning in a semicircle, with houses around the circle, Rambam wrote in Chapter 28, Law 8, as follows: "If there is less than four thousand cubits between the two ends, we measure it from the string, and consider the entire width between the bow and the string as if it were filled with houses. But if there are four thousand cubits between the two ends, we only measure it from the bow." The reason is that if there is less than four thousand cubits between the two ends, the boundaries overlap, and it is considered all as one. But if there are four thousand cubits, each side has its own boundary, and thus we do not consider the empty space as if it were filled with houses, since they are not connected to each other. However, it is certain that we do not measure them as they are, for a city shaped like a bow does not have the form of an angle, obviously; rather, we make an angle on each side, but we do not consider the entire empty space as if it were filled with houses. But in the case of a gamma, no correction is needed, as it has angles. And it seems to me that any city shaped like a bow, and there is not four thousand cubits between the two ends, is considered all as one, and we see it as if it were filled with houses. However, on the outer sides of the bow, one must add until it forms a rectangle, as this is necessary, as explained. The Rambam only intended to teach us about the place of the string, whether we measure from there or not, and that depends on the overlapping of the boundaries. But a rectangle is obviously necessary. (So it appears to me in my humble opinion)

The Tur wrote: "If it is shaped like a gamma or like a bow, we consider it as if it is squared and filled with houses, and we measure from the chord. This is only applicable if the distance between the chord and the bow is less than two thousand cubits, such that one can reach there. In this case, we measure from the chord, even if there are four thousand cubits between its two ends. If the two ends are not four thousand cubits apart, and the two domains overlap, even if there is more than two thousand cubits between the chord and the bow. However, if there is more than two thousand cubits between the chord and the bow, and four thousand cubits between the two ends, we do not measure from the chord, but from where the bow does not extend beyond two thousand cubits, or if it has been shortened so that there are not four thousand cubits between them." End quote. According to the Tur, just as the overlap of the sides' boundaries makes them one, so too if one can walk from the bow to the chord without exceeding the Sabbath limit, they are considered one. The Rambam does not hold this way, for if it is a matter of walking, each person in the bow can walk around the bow, even if it is several thousand cubits, as is the rule for the city itself which has no size limit. Therefore, the walking permission is insignificant, and the main factor is the overlap of the boundaries. The Tur believes that walking within the inhabited area is certainly insignificant, but walking outside the inhabited area, such as from the bow to the chord, is significant. Their disagreement depends on the Talmudic discussion (Eruvin 55b, whether the law follows Rav Huna or Rava the son of Rabba, see there). The Beit Yosef ruled like the Rambam, the Rema like the Tur, and he abbreviated the Tur's words. What the Magen Avraham wrote in section 2 in the name of the Meiri, that those who rested in the bow can walk its entire circumference and square to the ends of the bow, and from there two thousand cubits - it is certainly correct. What he wrote in section 4 is very puzzling and has already been refuted as mentioned in the Machatzit Hashekel in section 12.

Any dwelling that is located outside the city, if there is a distance of seventy and two-thirds cubits between it and the city, which is the side length of a square area of two seahs, or less than that - it is considered part of the city and is included in its boundaries. When measuring the two thousand cubits in every direction for the city, we measure from outside this dwelling. However, without a dwelling, we do not extend the city's boundary, and this is the opinion of the Rambam. But according to the Tur, we do not begin measuring immediately from the houses, but rather we stretch a line across the width of the city opposite the house, and from there we distance seventy and a bit cubits, and then we begin measuring. This is also the ruling of Rabbeinu the Rema in section 5, and we have already mentioned this in section 1.

If there is a house close to the city within seventy cubits, and a second house close to the first house within seventy cubits, and a third house close to the second house within seventy cubits, and so on for several days' journey, it is all considered one city. When measuring, they measure from outside the last house. This is provided that the dwelling house is at least four cubits by four cubits or more. Similarly, a synagogue that has a residence for the cantors is included. But the synagogue itself, since it is not made for dwelling, is not considered an extension of the city. It appears to me that a study hall (Beit Midrash) is called a dwelling house, because people study there, and someone who studies eats and sleeps there, it is called a dwelling house. A bathhouse is not called a dwelling house unless there is a dwelling place there for the bathhouse owner. A house of prayer (Beit Tefillah) that has a residence for their priests, as well as stores of wine, oil, and other goods, when there is a dwelling place for the store. But the store itself is not called a dwelling house. Similarly, a bridge that has a residence for the bridge-keeper, and a grave that has a residence for the grave-keeper.

All these cases apply when there is a place suitable for residence, even if no one actually resides there—it is still considered a residential property, and an extension can be made for it (this is implied in the Gemara Eruvin 55b and Rashi there). Similarly, a place surrounded by three walls, even if it has no roof, as long as it measures four by four cubits, is considered a residential property. Likewise, two walls with a roof and overlay, or a house built by the seaside intended for storing ship equipment—all these require four by four cubits. If it does not have four cubits in width, even if it has significant length, it is not suitable for residence. Similarly, a cave with a built entrance that serves as a residential property—the cave and the house combine to make up four cubits (Gemara), with the majority needing to be from the house. Measurement begins from the end of the cave to the seventy cubits, even if the house itself has four cubits (Magen Avraham section 8).

All these combine with it if they were within seventy and a fraction of cubits. And from that house that extends, we see (as if) [as though] a string is stretched over the entire width or length of the city, and we measure two thousand cubits beyond that string. And if there were two such houses opposite the city, one to the north and one to the south, its law is like a city made in the shape of a bow. This means that if there were many houses like these opposite each other at a distance of less than two thousand cubits from the city, their law is like a city made in the shape of a bow. And if it extends from one side and not from the other, it seems to me that its law is like a city made in the shape of a gamma (Γ), for this is the shape of a dalet (ד). (See Magen Avraham, section 9, and it is necessary to say that this is his intention.)

And know, from the Tur, it seems to me that the case of three walls without a roof and two with a roof is when they come from a house that was destroyed, see there. But two walls without a roof, even though they live there, and the bridge and the grave and their prayer house and the treasure that do not have a residential house, and the pit and the trench and the cave and the dovecote and the house on a ship that does not have permanence—all these and similar ones do not combine with it. And similarly, the huts that garden watchmen and city watchmen make are not measured with it, because they are temporary, specifically in a place where thieves or torrential rains are common. (Beit Yosef in the name of the Rashba.) And it seems to me that this applies to city watchmen, but garden watchmen—in any case, it is considered temporary, since it does not have permanence and is for a short time.

And there is someone who wants to say that huts that combine with it also exist even if they do not have four cubits by four cubits, (Shulchan Aruch, section 5, in the name of the Geonim) and this is astonishing. (And what the Shulchan Aruch mentions, from the beginning of Sukkah, there is no indication of this, and the novelty is because it is a light building from a hut and similar to this. And what we wrote regarding garden watchmen—this seems to me correct, and it is not similar to field and fruit watchmen, for this is constant.)

If there are two towns close to each other at a distance of 141 and one-third cubits, so that each has seventy cubits and a bit to its side, they are considered as one town. Thus, each town can walk to the other and beyond it for two thousand cubits. Similarly, if the city wall is breached on both sides opposite each other and the houses between them are destroyed up to 141 and one-third cubits, it is considered as sealed. However, a single house, even a very large one, does not have the status of a town to grant it seventy cubits and a bit unless it stands within seventy cubits of the town. It is obvious that this does not only apply to a city; the same law applies to a village that has its own name, but not to individual houses.

If there are three villages arranged in a triangular formation, and the distance between the middle village and each of the outer villages is two thousand cubits or less, and the distance between the two outer villages is 283⅓ cubits in addition to the width of the middle village, meaning the middle village is aligned between the two outer villages such that they all stand like a sigol (∴), and if the middle village stands between the two outer villages, the distance from the middle to each of the outer villages will be 141⅓ cubits, then all three are considered as one city, and they measure two thousand cubits outside of them. However, if the distance between the middle village and each of the outer villages is more than two thousand cubits, they do not combine with each other since it is more than the Shabbat boundary, as stated regarding a city shaped like a bow with the distance between the string and the bow, according to the Tur in section 12. And that which we permitted there when there is up to four thousand cubits between its two ends is because there are houses throughout the bow, which is not the case between the middle and outer villages. (Gemara 57:) And between the two outer villages can be even more than four thousand cubits if the middle village is so large that if it were placed between the outer villages, only 141⅓ cubits would remain for each of the outer villages. And this is not similar to the two ends of the bow because here we fill the space with the middle village. (See Tosafot s.v. 'there' and Magen Avraham section 12, and examine it well.)

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote on this law in paragraph 8: "And some say that we do not measure from the middle one but only from its walls." End quote. This means that when we say 'we see the middle one as if it stands between the two outer ones,' this is to measure for the outer ones from one to the other, as we have said. But the middle one itself, we only measure from it. Because if we measure from the outer ones, it would lose on the other side where it stands. And so wrote the Tur. And the Tur further wrote that we do not say 'we see the middle one as if it stands between the two outer ones' except when it fits between the two outer ones. But if it is so large that it does not fit between them, we do not say 'we see' there. And our teacher, the Rema, does not agree with this, and therefore he did not bring this opinion. (And this depends on the two answers of the Tosafot there, see there in the Tosafot, s.v. 'Hatam.')

A city that sits on the bank of a river, which most of the time is dry and people use it, and it only fills up during the rainy season, if there is a barrier in front of it with a width of four cubits on the riverbank so that people can stand on it and use the river—the river is considered part of the city, and we measure two thousand cubits from the other side of the riverbank, making the entire river included within the city limits. This is not only because of usage but also because of the barrier built beside it, which reveals their intention to include it within the city limits, and it is considered as if it were built and the river as their courtyard. But if there was no barrier, we only measure from the end of the houses, even though they use the river without the barrier. This is like any other land outside the city, where even though they use it, it is not reasonable to include it in the boundary measurements. Thus, the river is measured within the Shabbat boundary.

(The Magen Avraham in section 13 is uncertain about any place used outside the city if it is included in the boundary measurements. I am puzzled because it is explicitly stated that this is due to the barrier, for otherwise, why without a barrier would it not be fit for use? This is as we have explained. However, in the Gemara 61a, it is said that it is difficult to use, and it could be that without a barrier, it is not fit for use. Nonetheless, from the language of the Rambam and the Shulchan Aruch, section 9, which state that it is included in the city because of the barrier, it implies that without a barrier, it is nothing. Pay close attention.)

And know that what we have explained is according to the words of the Rambam and the Shulchan Aruch, who interpret the statement in the Gemara there: "A city that sits on the bank of the river, etc." However, Rashi of blessed memory interpreted it differently, and it is not a river of water but rather just a valley, and the houses are up to the valley, and the establishment of the partition is to separate between the valley and the city so that they shouldn't be afraid to use it. Therefore, when there is a partition, we measure the boundary from the end of the houses, as with all cities. But when there is no partition, their status is like those who dwell in huts, and we measure for each person from the entrance of his house, not from the edge of the city, as it says there, and so wrote the Rosh. And the Tur also wrote similarly, except he interpreted "river" as a stream, meaning that the city sits in a valley with a stream in front of it. If it is surrounded by a wall four cubits high, we measure from its wall, and if not, it is not considered a city, and we measure for each person from the entrance of his house, since it sits in a valley with a stream in front of it, as it says there. And I do not know what compelled him to deviate from the interpretation of Rashi and the Rosh. And in terms of the law, it seems to me that all the interpretations are true, as they only disagreed regarding the interpretation of the Talmud, not the law. (And the Shulchan Aruch only brought the words of the Rambam, and see the Jerusalem Talmud there).

Residents of huts, meaning those who dwell in tents made from reeds and willow branches and who do not have a fixed place, as they stay in one place for some time and then move to another place, do not have the status of a city. Therefore, the measurement of two thousand cubits is measured for each person from his house. However, if they have an enclosure of a fence ten handbreadths high, or a ditch ten handbreadths deep, they are considered as a city, and the measurement is taken from the edge of the houses from the fence or the ditch, as this indicates permanence. Similarly, if there are three courtyards with two permanent houses each made of stone or planks, it establishes all the huts as permanent, and they all have the status of a city. In this case, the city is squared off and given two thousand cubits in all directions like other cities. It has already been clarified that for a city that was enclosed and then settled, the measurement is taken from the edge of the houses. If it was settled and then enclosed, the measurement is taken from its wall, even if the wall is far from the houses, as clarified in Section 2. If the wall has a dwelling house, the measurement is always taken from the wall. (Magen Avraham, Section 15)

The boundary of the city is measured only with a flax rope of fifty cubits. Not shorter—because it stretches too much, and not longer—because it becomes heavy and does not stretch properly. And why don't we measure with iron chains, which are the most suitable for measurement? Because the prophet Zechariah said: "And in his hand was a measuring rope" (Zechariah 2:1), indicating that measurement should be done with a rope. A flax rope is better for measurement than all other ropes. In Ezekiel (40:3), it is written: "And a flax cord was in his hand" (Jerusalem Talmud). The reason for fifty cubits is that it is written: "The width shall be fifty by fifty" (Exodus 27:18), meaning the Torah said to measure with a rope of fifty cubits (Talmud).

If there is a river in front of him at the end of 75 cubits, there is a dispute in the Jerusalem Talmud (Eruvin 5:3). One says that he measures 50 cubits, and the remaining 25 he measures with a rope of 4 cubits. And another says that after measuring the 50 cubits, he goes back 25 cubits and measures with the rope until the river. And since in our Gemara it is not mentioned about this 4 cubit rope, therefore, we hold that he goes back. (Tur and Beit Yosef) And our Rabbi the Beit Yosef wrote that it refers to a river that is wider than 25 cubits, for if it is only 25 or less, he can measure with a 50 cubit rope and reach the other side of the river. (Magen Avraham 401:1) And from this it is clear that the river is included in the measurement of the boundary. And in the Jerusalem Talmud it says that up to 50 cubits, it is regarded as if it is filled with earth and stones, meaning it is measured as flat ground. And more than 50 cubits, you see it as if it goes up and down, and it seems that this is similar to 'measuring across mountains' which will be explained. And I am astonished that the Tur and Shulchan Aruch did not mention at all the manner of measuring the river when it is within the boundary. And know, that when we say 'it holds such and such' – it is only by estimation, for if we knew clearly how much it holds, there would be no need to measure. (Perisha)

The measurement is done by two people, one holding one end of the rope and the other holding the other end. The Sages ordained that they should hold the rope opposite their hearts, because if no specific place for holding the rope was established, one person might hold it opposite his heart and the other opposite his feet, causing the rope to shorten and the boundary to diminish. Therefore, they established a fixed place for holding the rope, which is opposite the heart, and they should stretch the rope with all their strength, because if not, it will not be stretched properly, and the boundary will be shortened.

One should measure only directly opposite the city. Even if there are mountains and valleys opposite it, one should not measure from the sides as if opposite the city, where the terrain is flat, and measure there, and then return to opposite the city according to the measurement taken there in order to absorb the mountains and valleys. Rather, one should measure directly opposite the city itself. If one encounters a mountain, and if the mountain is so steep that it is not suitable for walking, such that if a builder's plumb line is dropped from the top of the mountain to its base, the deviation of the plumb line from the top to the bottom is not more than four cubits in a straight line, then there is no need to measure the slope of the mountain either downward or upward. Instead, if there is flat ground at its top, one should measure there. If there is no flat area at the top, there is no need to measure it at all, since it is not suitable for walking at all. However, if the slope is not so steep, such that the deviation is four cubits from the top, and it also rises ten handbreadths within five cubits, meaning that in walking five cubits on the slope, it rises ten handbreadths in height and not before, then we see if the distance from edge to edge is only fifty cubits, we absorb it with a measuring rope that is fifty cubits. This means setting a tall stick at one edge and a tall stick at the opposite edge, stretching the rope from one to the other, and measuring the exact distance.

And if according to visual estimation it is not possible to measure with a rope of fifty cubits, they said, "We measure the mountains," meaning that he measures with a rope of four cubits. One person stands at the bottom of the mountain and another four cubits above him. The one below holds the rope against his heart and the one above against his feet. Then the one below moves to the place where the one above stood, and the one above moves four cubits further up as before. They measure again, with one holding the rope against his feet and the other against his heart, and so they continue until the whole mountain is measured. However, if the slope is steeper, that is, if the rope distances four cubits from the foot to the head, but it does not rise ten handbreadths within five cubits but within four cubits—in such a case, they were lenient and did not require him to measure with a rope of fifty cubits by erecting poles. Instead, if by estimation it does not exceed fifty cubits, he should estimate it well and consider it accordingly. But if by estimation it exceeds fifty cubits, he must measure it with a rope of four cubits as mentioned, because since the rope distances four cubits, it is fit for walking.

He reaches a valley. If the plumb line deviates from the upper to the lower part by four cubits, and thus it is suitable for walking, then we assess: if it can be spanned with a fifty-cubit rope, we span it. If not, we are compelled to measure it with a four-cubit rope. And with the spanning of a valley, there is no difference whether it rises ten handbreadths within five cubits or within four cubits, because even if it rises ten handbreadths within four cubits, it requires precise measurement. This is explained according to the interpretation of Rashi (58a) and the Rambam in Chapter 28. The Rashba holds that there is also such a distinction in a valley, and the Magid Mishneh already questioned him on this matter there.

However, regarding a valley, there is a different matter. This applies when the valley is not deeper than two thousand cubits. But if it is deeper than the limit of the Shabbat boundary (techum Shabbat) – there is no leniency through overlapping, but one measures the descent and ascent as if it were flat ground, and the entire slope needs measurement. And why did they not say the same about a mountain? It seems to me because there is another leniency regarding such a height in a mountain, that there are no boundaries above ten handbreadths, which is not the case in a valley. And if the plumb line does not distance four cubits, then if it is possible to overlap it with a fifty-cubit rope – one overlaps it; if not – one does not measure the slope of the descent and ascent at all, but rather the flat ground at the bottom, even if it is deeper than two thousand cubits. And see what is written in Siman 404, Section 5.

And know that according to the Rambam (Laws of Shabbat, Chapter 28, Law 11), even when the plumb line descends opposite it, which we have said measures only the lower plane when it cannot be leveled, and even if it is deeper than two thousand cubits - in any case, it should not be deeper than four thousand cubits, see there. The Tur and the Shulchan Aruch did not bring this. However, in principle, I do not understand the statement that whether on a mountain or in a valley, when the plumb line distances the lower part from the upper part by four cubits, it is considered walkable. It is very puzzling, in a valley when its depth is two thousand cubits, how can it be considered walkable with a distance of four cubits over the great length of two thousand cubits, and similarly on a mountain when it is very high. And indeed in the Rambam, there is no measure of four cubits at all, when the plumb line does not descend opposite it, see there. And what is stated in the Gemara there: "And when the plumb line does not descend opposite it, until when - until four", he does not interpret it as until four cubits, as Rashi and Tosafot explain, but to the depth of the valley, which should be up to four thousand cubits, and from this he derived his ruling. But when it does not descend opposite it - it should be interpreted that the slope should be walkable, and the deeper or higher it is - the more the lower part needs to be distanced from the upper part. (And according to Rashi and Tosafot, and even more according to the Rashbam there in Tosafot, beginning with 'And when', it is difficult to understand)

The Sages further permitted a leniency regarding the spanning (of a valley) of fifty cubits, which was explained concerning a mountain or a valley. If one cannot span it, meaning it is much wider than fifty cubits, it requires measurement with a rope of four cubits. The Sages said that if even on the side opposite the city one cannot span it, but further on it can be spanned—such as if the mountains and valleys are to the east, and opposite the city it cannot be spanned, but beyond the city and outward, turning to the north and south, it can be spanned—one should span it there, and measure from its edge and onward, until opposite the place where the width of the valley ends opposite the city. Then, he returns to his measurement opposite the city and completes the measurement of the boundaries. (Rashi on the Mishnah, 57b) This is specifically within the two thousand cubits on the side of the city to the north and south. But if it cannot be spanned within these two thousand cubits, one should not distance oneself further on the side of the city to span it, so that people do not say that the measurement of boundaries comes until here.

One may only rely on the measurement of an expert who knows how to measure land, as this requires wisdom and knowledge on how to measure. The measurement must be done on level ground and not according to the path, as most paths bend and turn. If we had established Shabbat boundaries and an expert came and altered them, increasing in one place and decreasing in another, we listen to him, especially in the place where he decreased. We say that over time, one side became a mountain and another side became a plain or valley and so forth, and we do not say that the previous ones made a mistake. It seems to me that the reason an individual is believed to change the previous established status is that it is possible to verify, and anything that can be revealed, people do not lie about it.

It is clear that the equalization of sides applies only to the houses of the city and their extensions, but not to the boundaries. That is to say, it has already been explained in the previous section that if one house extends beyond the city houses, the measure is extended also to the other side to equalize it. Similarly, with houses that are within seventy and a bit cubits, the measure is extended on the other side as well to consider it as an extension of the city, and the boundary is measured from there onwards. However, this is not the case with boundaries. For example, if in the northeastern corner there were no mountains and valleys, and the boundary was long, but in the southeastern corner there were mountains and valleys, causing the boundary to be shortened, we do not equalize this side with the northeastern side. Rather, in the northeastern corner, the boundary is measured according to its own measurement, and in the southeastern corner, according to its own measurement, and similarly in all such cases. (And I have seen those who erred in this matter.)

And this is what the Tur wrote: "If one measured and found that the northeastern corner was greater than the southeastern corner opposite it, he should stretch the boundary line from one to the other diagonally." This is the opinion of the Rosh. However, Rashi of blessed memory explained that the measurement should be extended from the shorter side to the longer side. Our teacher, the Rema, brought both opinions in section 8, see there. This does not mean that Rashi holds that in the case of a boundary one should extend the measurement against the longer side, as he clearly explained in the Mishnah that the reason is due to the assumption of an error, perhaps the rope was not stretched properly at this corner. The Rosh holds that we do not assume an error, rather we assume that on the shorter side there were mountains and valleys. And if one asks, isn't it possible to clarify this? One can answer that it is difficult to clarify, as it requires an expert. And if indeed an expert comes and clarifies it, we act according to his words.

If two experts came and measured the boundary, one increased it and one decreased it, and they left without clarifying the matter with each other to know which measurement is correct - we follow the more lenient opinion, and we listen to the one who increased it because the laws of boundaries are rabbinic. Since they measured on one side and at one corner - we say the one who decreased made a mistake in the law. We say that the one who decreased measured from the very corner of the city and measured diagonally and not along the side, and therefore his measurement was decreased, because by measuring along the side it would be less than two thousand [cubits], and the one who increased measured along the side as per the law. But more than this - we do not assume the first made a mistake. Therefore, if the difference between them is the measure of the city's diagonal or less - we attribute it to a mistake, but more than this - we do not attribute it to a mistake, and this measurement is a little more than 280 cubits. (Magen Avraham section 6)

The boundaries are made like a squared board, meaning that one measures the entire length outward to the east two thousand cubits, and similarly to the north. Then, one considers it as if it were a squared board at the corner to complete it, and thus the boundary at the corner is two thousand cubits and their diagonal, which is two thousand and eight hundred cubits. But one should not measure from the corner itself two thousand along the diagonal, and similarly at the opposite corner, and stretch the string from one to the other, for if so, one loses the eight hundred cubits at the corner. The boundary will not be opposite the city but rather one thousand and eight hundred cubits, and so on each side of the city. This being like a squared board applies to a city that is squared two thousand by two thousand. But for a city whose length exceeds its width, if it only has equal angles, there is no squaring in the boundaries, obviously. Even in a squared city, the boundaries are only squared on flat ground, where there are no mountains and valleys, for if on one side there are mountains and valleys, which shorten the boundary, and on the other side there are none, it will not be squared. Even on the other side, one does not draw the measure from corner to corner, if on one side there are mountains and valleys and on the other there are none, as explained in section 11.

And know that the opinion of Rabbeinu Tam in the Tosafot (Eruvin 51a, s.v. "Kazeh") and the Rosh is that the measurement of the Shabbat boundary is two thousand cubits with their diagonal, which means two thousand and eight hundred cubits. Consequently, through an eruv, it becomes five thousand six hundred cubits, and there are those who rely on this, but it requires further investigation.

Even a male or female servant is trusted to say, "This is the Shabbat boundary." However, a minor is not trusted, as a minor is only trusted regarding something within his capability. (Magen Avraham, subsection 7) But an adult is trusted to say, "I remember that we used to come to this point on Shabbat when I was a child," and we rely on his testimony. The Mishnah (58b) explains the reason why these individuals are trusted is because the Sages did not want to be stringent regarding the testimony of boundaries.

The two thousand cubits that every person has from their place of residence apply even without a declaration or intention. Moreover, we learned in the Mishnah (45a) that if someone sat down on the road and stood up, finding himself near the city without intending to enter, he may enter. An incident occurred where Rabbi Tarfon entered without intent. Rashi explains that someone who sat on the road to rest because he was tired and did not know he was within the city's boundary, and it became dark there, and when he stood up, he saw that he was near the city and within its boundary. When it became dark, he did not intend his residence to be in the city but at his location. Nevertheless, he has the city's boundary. Similarly, the Rif wrote: "Since if he had known that the city was close, he would have established his residence together with the city's inhabitants, it is as if he had established his residence with them, and he is permitted to enter the city and walk throughout it and beyond it for two thousand cubits." His residence was established mistakenly, and therefore, he has the city's boundary. In the following Mishnah, it is explicitly stated that even if he was sleeping when establishing the residence, he acquires the residence and has two thousand cubits in every direction. This will be explained in the next section, with God's help. The Tur and the Shulchan Aruch wrote similarly, and see paragraph 4.

And this is when he intended to enter the city, but it was hidden from him that he was within the city's boundary. However, if he did not intend to enter the city, he establishes his residence where he is, and he has two thousand cubits in every direction from his place of residence. If the two thousand cubits end in the middle of the city, he may not go beyond that point. If they end at the edge of the city, the entire city becomes like four cubits for him, and he completes the two thousand cubits beyond it. The reason for this will be explained in Siman 408. Similarly, even if while traveling, he intended to enter the city and knew he was within its boundary, and he said, "My residence is in my place," since he willingly abandoned the city's residence and established his residence in his place, he has two thousand cubits from his place. If the two thousand cubits end in the middle of the city, he may not go beyond that point. If they end at the edge, it becomes like four cubits for him, and he completes the two thousand cubits beyond it, as stated.

And this is the language of the Rambam in Chapter 27, Law 9: "Someone who was on the way to enter a city, whether he was coming by sea or by land, if he entered within two thousand cubits close to the city before Shabbat began, even though he did not reach the city until Shabbat, he may enter and walk throughout the city and outside it for two thousand cubits." End quote. He further wrote: "If someone was coming to a city and slept on the way and did not wake up until Shabbat, and when he woke up he found himself within the boundary, he may enter the city and walk throughout it and outside it for two thousand cubits in every direction, because his intention was to go to this city. Therefore, he established his residence with the people of the city like them, since he entered the boundary with them." End quote.

In the first ruling, it teaches us that establishing one's residence (for the purposes of Shabbat boundaries) is not necessarily where one is currently standing; one can establish residence even not at their current location, anywhere within two thousand cubits from where they are standing. This is on the condition that they declare it as such, which will be explained in Siman 409 with the help of Heaven. And if one is within the boundary of the city to which they are traveling, even if they did not say anything, they have the boundary of the city, because it is assumed that their intention is for the boundary of the city. Then, it teaches us that even if they were not aware at all that they were within the city's boundary, and even if they were asleep and woke up to find themselves within the city's boundary, they have the boundary of the city. However, this point was not clarified, that even though they intended to establish residence at their location because they did not know they were close to the city, this is considered a mistaken establishment of residence, and they have the residence of the city, since nothing was mentioned about this. Additionally, this ruling is not explicitly mentioned in the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, but it is explicitly stated in Rashi and the Rif, and similarly, the Ritva writes so.

If someone falls asleep on the road and night falls upon him, he establishes his residence (for Shabbat) in his place, and he has two thousand cubits in every direction, for we do not require a statement or intention to establish residence. Moreover, even if he was near his city within the boundary and intended to enter the city, he has the city’s boundary, as stated in the previous section. However, if he did not intend to enter the city before he fell asleep, even if afterward, upon waking up after nightfall, he decided to enter the city, he does not have the city’s residence but rather the residence of his place, since at the time of establishing residence, his intention was not so.

We have established that ownerless objects do not acquire a place of rest (Shvita), meaning that ownerless items do not have a designated place of rest because they have no owners. Instead, the first person to acquire them can carry them to any place he can go. Seemingly, the reason they do not acquire a place of rest is that they have no intention for rest. If so, why does a sleeping person acquire a place of rest, since while sleeping, he has no intention? However, this is not comparable, for a person who was awake and acquired a place of rest continues to have it while sleeping, which is not the case with objects. (Gemara 45b) And if someone acquires it on behalf of another, it follows the latter's movement, as stated in Siman 397.

The property of a non-Jew - according to the law, they are not subject to the prohibition of resting, since their owners are not obligated in resting. Nevertheless, it was decreed that they should rest, because of the property of Jews. For if it were said that they do not need to rest, the same would be said about Jewish property. This is not considered a decree upon a decree, as it is all one single decree, that property acquires the requirement to rest. For if not for this - the other would not stand. Therefore, they have the rest of their location, two thousand cubits in every direction. If a non-Jew brought them on Shabbat or Yom Tov into the city from outside its boundaries, if the city is surrounded by a wall and is inhabited and then enclosed, it is permissible to move them throughout the entire city. If it was enclosed and then inhabited, they may only be moved within four cubits. If they were brought into a courtyard, they may be moved throughout the courtyard. Generally, cities are enclosed for habitation, where the houses are built first and then the city is enclosed. Generally, fortresses are not enclosed for habitation, as stated in Siman 398. If the city is joined by an Eruv through a form of a doorway, they may be moved throughout the entire city, and the same applies to an alleyway. Therefore, one must be careful if a Jew lent his utensils to a non-Jew before Shabbat and they were returned on Shabbat, not to move them beyond four cubits if the city is not enclosed, or is not enclosed for habitation, since the utensil is considered to be in the possession of the borrower regarding the rest, as stated in Siman 397. (See Taz, subparagraph 1, whose words are perplexing, as stated by the Ateret Zekenim and Turei Zahav, while the words of the Shulchan Aruch are correct according to the law, and consider this carefully.)

The Tur and Shulchan Aruch wrote: "A trench filled with gathered water that is between two Shabbat domains, part of it within the boundary of one city and part of it within the boundary of another city - both cities are forbidden to draw water from it, even within the boundary, because the water within the boundary acquires the rest of the city's Shabbat restrictions, and they mix with each other. It is necessary to make a partition at the end of the boundaries to separate them, and even if it is suspended, not reaching the bottom of the trench and made merely of reeds, it suffices. But if the water is flowing, no correction is needed, as they do not acquire Shabbat restrictions, and they follow the person drawing the water."

And this is why they needed to say that part of it is within the boundary of another city, for even if it is not within the boundary of another city, they are outside of this boundary. And the water within the boundary mixes with the water that is outside the boundary - for this there is no prohibition at all, for the water that is outside the boundary is ownerless and does not acquire a place of rest, and it follows the feet of the one who fills it. And one should not ask that if so, all water has no place of rest, since it has no owner, for the truth is that the people of the city within the boundary are considered its owners, because their intention is upon it. And the partition needs to be either nine handbreadths above the water and one handbreadth within the water, or nine in the water and one out of the water, as it is written in Siman 356, and they did not bother to explain, relying on what was written there. And for flowing waters, no correction is necessary, because since they move - they do not acquire a place of rest, as it is written in Siman 397, and it is explained there that even standing springs, like our wells, are considered moving and do not acquire a place of rest, and they follow the feet of the one who fills them, as it says there.

It is stated in the Gemara (Eruvin 79a) that if there is a stack of straw or a bundle of straw standing between two Shabbat boundaries, each group can feed their animals from their respective sides, and we do not worry that one might take from what is beyond their boundary. It appears from the Gemara there that this is specifically for allowing the animals to eat directly, but to place it into a basket is forbidden. The reason for this is explained in Siman 372 regarding a stack of straw between two courtyards.

It has already been explained in Siman 396 that the place where one resides is not included in the two thousand cubits of the boundary, even if one resides in a large city like Antioch, it is not counted. And earlier in Siman 362, it was explained that a partition made on Shabbat is considered a partition. According to this, if it happened that someone resided in a large valley, and non-Jews came and surrounded the valley with partitions on Shabbat, and the enclosure was made for the purpose of residence, such as if there were scattered houses and they enclosed them for the sake of the houses, which would be considered an enclosure for residence - then it would follow that he may walk throughout the entire valley and an additional two thousand cubits outside it.

Nevertheless, it is not so, for our sages of blessed memory said (Beitzah 37b) that it is only when one rested within the airspace of the partitions before Shabbat that this area is considered as four cubits, but if one did not rest within the airspace of the partitions, it is counted in the calculation. The reason seems to be that since the time of acquiring the resting place is at the onset of Shabbat, when the boundaries of the domains are established, therefore, if one rested within the airspace of the partitions at that time, it is considered as four cubits. However, if at the onset of Shabbat one was not within the airspace of the partitions, and this place was part of the domain calculation, it cannot change during Shabbat. This is similar to what we say: 'Shabbat, since it was prohibited, remains prohibited.' And even though for someone who went outside the domain and only has four cubits, if they were placed within the airspace of the partitions on Shabbat, it is only considered as four cubits, as will be explained in Siman 405, this is due to their confinement to only four cubits, thus it is treated as four cubits. But for someone who has a full domain, it is not considered as four cubits if they did not rest within the airspace of the partitions. (Magen Avraham) Furthermore, according to what we have explained, this is not a comparison at all, for here the main reason is that this place itself was established at the onset of Shabbat within the domain calculation, which is not the case there.

And what is the law regarding carrying? Since a partition made on Shabbat is considered a partition, it is permitted to carry within the entire area, as it is a complete private domain that was enclosed for dwelling, as mentioned. However, if this enclosed area is more than two thousand cubits, and one is not permitted to walk more than two thousand cubits within it, how can one carry throughout the entire area? The sages said (there) that one may carry throughout the entire area by means of throwing. That is, it is permitted to throw objects there throughout the entire area, but to carry them by hand is only permitted within two thousand cubits, due to the prohibition of walking beyond that limit. It is clear that when it comes to throwing, it specifically means not with one's belongings, as it is forbidden to take one's belongings outside of their boundary, as explained, since animals and utensils follow the owner's boundary. (Magen Avraham) This is the opinion of Rashi there, but Tosafot disagree, as will be explained with God's help.

And our master, the Rema, wrote that even to carry something physically is prohibited beyond four cubits, even within the two-thousand cubit boundary, see there. And this is the view of the Tosafot there, because since it is forbidden to carry beyond two thousand cubits, it is considered "completely breached to a prohibited area," see there. But Rashi holds that this is not called "breached to a prohibited area," since even there it is permitted by throwing, therefore it is a place allowed to him, and the reason he is not permitted to carry is because of walking, not because of carrying. (And even though in the Gemara there it presents this reasoning, it is according to the one who prohibits carrying entirely even by throwing, due to a decree lest he pursue his object, and therefore it is completely forbidden beyond two thousand cubits to carry - it is indeed called breached, etc., but not according to what we hold like Shmuel, that it is permitted to carry entirely by throwing, so wrote the Taz and he rules like Rashi) (And so wrote the Maharshal there, and so wrote the Perisha, and so the Eliyah Rabbah and the Taz agreed with the Taz).

In the Gemara (Eruvin 43a), there is a doubt whether the laws of boundaries apply above ten handbreadths or not. The reason for this doubt seems to be because there is no public domain above ten handbreadths, nor is there a karmelit above ten handbreadths, as stated in Siman 345. Only a private domain extends up to the sky. Most boundary laws apply only in the public domain and karmelit, for a private domain, which is an area enclosed for residential purposes, is not measured in terms of boundaries, as it is considered like four cubits, as explained. Therefore, above ten handbreadths, where there is neither a public domain nor a karmelit, boundaries might not apply, or perhaps it makes no difference. Another reason for this doubt will be explained in section 7.

And behold, the Rambam in Chapter 27, Law 3 also wrote: "One who walks beyond the boundary above ten handbreadths, etc., it is uncertain whether there are boundaries above ten handbreadths or not" end quote. And why did he not decide the law definitively as is his usual manner? Because according to his view, the twelve mil boundary is from the Torah, there are boundaries from the Torah and there are boundaries from the Sages of two thousand cubits. Therefore, for twelve mil, it is a Torah-level doubt and we are stringent, and for two thousand cubits, it is a rabbinic doubt and we are lenient. Thus, the Rambam did not want to elaborate on this, and he wrote similarly in a response. This is what our masters, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, wrote: "One who walks beyond the boundary above ten handbreadths... it is a doubt... and what is rabbinic, its doubt is lenient. However, if he was walking... from within twelve mil to outside twelve mil - we are stringent, according to the opinion that the twelve mil boundary is from the Torah" end quote. And according to most poskim who do not hold this twelve mil view, it is always lenient.

The Tur wrote that there are boundaries above ten handbreadths because the Rosh wrote that this question was not resolved, and we act stringently. Many great scholars have already questioned him on this, and some have explained that since this doubt remained unresolved for the Talmudic sages, therefore, he was stringent. (Bach and Kenesset HaGedolah there) I am puzzled by this, for this is acceptable regarding the principle 'the law follows the lenient opinion in matters of eruv,' where here no one is lenient, and the doubt is for everyone. But this is not relevant to 'a rabbinic doubt is treated leniently,' as in many places in the Talmud, in a doubt that remains unresolved in rabbinic matters, we go leniently. In my humble opinion, it seems the reason is because the Rif did not bring up this question at all, and if he had considered it lenient, he would have mentioned it. But since he did not bring it up, it is implied that he holds there are boundaries. Their reasoning appears to be because in the Gemara there, they wanted to resolve that there are boundaries from the Mishnah about someone taken out [of the boundary], as Rabban Gamliel and his colleagues came from the sea, and he said, "I was observing that we were within the boundary before nightfall," implying that there are boundaries, as the sea is above ten handbreadths. And the Gemara answered that the ship was traveling in shallow water, where the water is less than ten handbreadths deep. And the Rif and Rosh hold that this is merely a rejection, and generally, it is not so. Also, it is clear from the Jerusalem Talmud, which explains Rabban Gamliel's ship simply, as stated there, and this is also the Rif's view. I saw someone write that the Rif’s opinion seems to be lenient (Beit Yosef in the name of the Rivash), but I do not know where he got this from. However, the law follows the majority of the decisors leniently, as ruled by the Shulchan Aruch. (And what the Rif wrote in the first chapter of Shabbat is in the name of "some say," and he rejected this for another reason, as stated there, and examine it well).

And even more so, our teacher the Rema wrote, that even if there is a doubt whether it is above ten [handbreadths] or not, we go leniently. And even though in such cases there is a double doubt to be stringent, for perhaps it is below ten, and if you say it is above ten, perhaps there are boundaries above ten, nevertheless, since it is a rabbinic matter and concerning an eruv, we are lenient even in such cases.

What is considered "above ten handbreadths"? The Gemara explains that this is, for example, if one jumps onto pillars that are ten handbreadths high and not four handbreadths wide, or onto a single pillar of such height, part of which is within the boundary and part outside the boundary. However, a pillar that is ten handbreadths high and four handbreadths wide is not considered "above ten"; rather, it is like solid ground because it is convenient for walking, thus it is deemed like the earth. Similarly, places that are elevated, such as rooftops, mountains, and hills, are not considered "above ten."

However, it seems to me, in my humble opinion, that if a mountain is very steep and difficult to climb, it should also be included in the category of "above ten," as per the reasoning we wrote in Siman 99, Section 7. This requires further consideration and investigation. (See Tosafot, Shabbat 66b, end of the entry "Kishurei")

And also regarding seas and rivers, it is proven in the Gemara that there is no prohibition of boundaries if there are no boundaries above ten [handbreadths]. Since the waters are ten [handbreadths] deep, they are considered ten handbreadths above the ground, meaning from the ground beneath the waters. And one should not ask that if so, why did we explain in Siman 397, Section 13, that there is a prohibition of carrying beyond the boundary in water. However, the truth is that this is a different matter, as there it concerns the waters themselves, which are all connected as one. Just as the waters up to ten handbreadths have boundaries, so too the waters above ten, since they are all connected as one. This is not the case with a ship that floats on the surface of the waters; since it travels only above ten [handbreadths], there is no prohibition of boundaries, as it has no connection to the lower waters. (Tosafot 45b, s.v. 'Liknu')

And the reason that there is no prohibition of techum (Sabbath boundaries) in days and rivers, even within twelve mil, is explained by the Rambam in his responsa (Siman 310) as follows: "Because they are considered a karmelit (a rabbinic domain), and carrying within them is only prohibited by rabbinic decree, it is not logical that one who traverses over water would be prohibited by rabbinic decree, while one who walks would be liable by Torah law." End quote. Additionally, he provides another reason, that the twelve mil correspond to the encampment of Israel, and this does not apply to water. The explanation of his words is that since it is definitely only a rabbinic prohibition even within twelve mil, it is more lenient as a rabbinic doubt. Now, the first reason can also apply on land above ten handbreadths, where throwing above ten handbreadths is considered a makom patur (an exempt area). And one should not question that if so, the same should apply within twelve mil, as one who passes over ten handbreadths is liable, as stated in Shabbat (92a), and as written in Siman 346, Section 3.

And since there is no prohibition of Techum Shabbat (Sabbath boundaries) by Torah law in the case of seas and rivers according to all opinions for reasons that have been explained, therefore, one who arrives at a port on Shabbat while on a ship may disembark without hesitation, and he has two thousand cubits in every direction, as he did not establish a Shabbat residence while on the ship. However, this is only when the ship was traveling more than ten handbreadths above the water. But if it was traveling less than ten handbreadths, meaning that from the bottom of the ship to the ground there were not ten handbreadths, even though he was above on the ship, he established his residence there. And if he goes out beyond two thousand cubits from that place, he is considered to have gone beyond the Shabbat boundaries and has only four cubits. If it is uncertain whether he was below ten or above ten handbreadths, we are lenient. If he once exited after dark onto the land and then re-entered the ship, when he arrives at a place on Shabbat, he has only four cubits, because he established his residence at the first place where he exited onto the land, even if he exited after dark, not during the time of establishing the residence. The general rule is: if on Shabbat he was at any moment on land or below ten handbreadths in the water, that is where he established his residence, and when he returns to the ship and it reaches the port, it is forbidden for him to go beyond four cubits. If this happens, he must wait there until nightfall. However, if he is forced to leave the four cubits, such as if it is raining or the sun is shining on him and he cannot bear it, or he needs to relieve himself and must enter the city, then the entire city is considered as four cubits because "since he entered, he entered," and the details of this law will be explained in Siman 405 and Siman 406, and it is not appropriate to elaborate here. It is only necessary to know that in such a case of traveling beyond the boundaries, it is considered as being forced and not as intentional, as there are distinctions in this as explained there. The laws of entering a ship on Shabbat and on the eve of Shabbat are explained above in Siman 248 and Siman 349. (See Magen Avraham, Subsection 5).

The sages taught in the Mishnah (at the end of Chapter 4): “One who goes beyond the boundary, even by one cubit, may not re-enter.” This is also the ruling of the Rambam in Chapter 27, Law 11, and the Tur and Shulchan Aruch. There is a significant question regarding this: do we not hold that every person has four cubits beyond the boundary, as stated in Siman 396? And in Siman 407 it will be explained regarding one who goes beyond the boundary for the sake of a mitzvah, in cases of saving a life, and similar situations — that the sages granted him a boundary of two thousand cubits from the place where he is. And we hold that if the new boundary overlaps slightly with the old boundary, he may return to his original boundary. This is the common language in the Talmud (44b): “the overlapping of boundaries is significant.” If so, even here, when he went out by one cubit, he still has three cubits within his boundary, so why should he not be able to return to his boundary through overlapping?

Now, the Ra'avad and Rabbeinu Yonatan explained that this Tanna does not accept the concept of "absorbing the boundaries," see there. According to this, the law does not follow this Mishnah. However, from the words of Rashi of blessed memory, a different understanding is clarified for me, as he explained: "One who went outside the boundary - intentionally and knowingly, not for the sake of a mitzvah," end quote. His intention is clear: we do not say "absorbing the boundaries is a valid concept" except in the case of someone who went out by coercion or for the sake of a mitzvah, but not intentionally and not for the sake of a mitzvah.

And the Rambam, of blessed memory, resolved the question in another manner, and this is his language: "One who has gone out... shall not enter, since the four cubits that a person has are measured from the place where he stands. Therefore, once he has gone outside his boundary by a cubit or more, he must sit in his place, and he may only walk four cubits from where his feet are standing and no further." End quote. His words were questioned, (by the Maggid Mishneh and the Kesef Mishneh) for it is explicitly taught (Eruvin 45a) regarding one who sleeps on the way and did not establish a residence—that he has four cubits, and in whichever direction he wishes. In my humble opinion, it seems that there is no difficulty at all, for we hold that even one who is asleep acquires a residence, as it is written in Siman 401, and even according to the one who holds that one who sleeps only has four cubits and can choose in which direction he wishes—this is certainly so, for what difference does this make in this law? But one who walks outside the boundary, how can we permit him to return and enter his boundary? On the contrary, we tell him: ‘Go on your way.’ (And perhaps this is also the intention of the Maggid Mishneh, see there.) According to this, it could be that according to the Rambam, the law is the same even in a case of coercion, or it could be said that in a case of coercion he agrees with Rashi, and this would not be considered coercion.

The Ra'avad, of blessed memory, wrote there that this is considered a case of duress, allowing one to step slightly beyond the boundary. In truth, he can choose any direction he wishes and enter his original boundary completely. The Mishnah refers to a case where he has already designated his four cubits. Similar to this, it is explained in the Hagahot Maimoniot (section 7) in the name of the Ri: "He should not enter as if he had not gone beyond the boundary, but he has four cubits in all directions, and it is permitted for him to enter within his original boundary up to his four cubits." And it seems to me that the explanation is as follows: I do not consider him as having not left the boundary, but he is certainly outside the boundary. However, he has four cubits, and he has the right to choose any direction he wishes. If he indeed chooses the direction of his boundary, he will walk his four cubits, and consequently, he will then be able to walk the entire boundary. (We have explained all the opinions with God's help, and see Magen Avraham section 1 and examine carefully.)

And similarly, one who has established their residence for Shabbat (eruv techumin) while being outside the city's boundary even by one cubit (ama) - they may not enter to be considered as one of the city's people, as explained in Siman 70, and they are only permitted to walk two thousand cubits in any direction from the place where they established their residence for Shabbat. In this case, it is obvious that the concept of the four cubits does not apply, for they acquire their Shabbat residence at their location like all who establish residence for Shabbat. The Sages stated that if one foot is within the boundary and one foot is outside the boundary - it is considered as if the entire person is within the boundary, and they supported this with a verse from the Gemara. (There it states "If you turn away your foot from the Sabbath" - see there.)

One who went outside the Shabbat boundary unknowingly, meaning not intentionally but either because he made a mistake or was preoccupied— it is permissible to make a partition of people for him, as stated in Siman 362, since an enclosure of people constitutes a partition. This can be done using people who eruv-ed in that direction and can walk there, surrounding him like a partition. This will be beneficial because if the partition extends into his original boundary, he can re-enter his boundary. It will be explained that one who goes outside the boundary due to coercion and enters within partitions can walk within the entire enclosed area, even if it is very large and more than two thousand cubits. This leniency is granted because he otherwise only has four cubits, as stated in Siman 403. This is contingent on the fact that those forming the partition do not know that they are being positioned to form a partition, as explained in Siman 362. This applies when he went out due to coercion. However, if he went out knowingly, it is forbidden, and this method will not help him. Even if he is brought within a partition, he is forbidden to walk within it because he did not reside within the partitions before Shabbat began, as will be explained, God willing.

If someone goes beyond the boundary, they only have four cubits. There is no difference whether they went out intentionally or unintentionally, even if bandits took them out or if they were overcome by a fit of madness—they only have four cubits. This is what we learned in the Mishnah at the beginning of Chapter 4. Similarly, if someone went out because of other compulsion or unintentionally, and then they were brought back within the boundary, it is as if they never went out. If they were brought back into the city, the entire city is considered as four cubits for them, and beyond it, they have two thousand cubits in every direction. This applies specifically if they went out due to compulsion and returned due to compulsion. However, if they went out intentionally, even if they returned due to compulsion, or if they went out due to compulsion and returned intentionally, they only have four cubits.

However, if one left intentionally and was forcibly returned to the city where he observed Shabbat, and the city is surrounded by walls and inhabited, and he first lived there and then it was surrounded by walls – the entire city is considered as if it were within four cubits for him. But beyond the city limits, he is not allowed to walk even a single cubit. Within the city, he is permitted because he observed Shabbat within an area enclosed by walls from before the onset of Shabbat, and in such cases, even if he left intentionally and returned intentionally, it is impossible to prohibit it. However, beyond the city, it is forbidden because he lost his boundary if one of his actions (leaving or returning) was intentional. If he went out under duress and was returned under duress, even if he was brought back within his original boundary to a city where he did not observe Shabbat, the entire city is considered for him as if it were within four cubits, and his boundary is restored as before. And even though he did not observe Shabbat within the area enclosed by walls from before the onset of Shabbat, since he was under duress both in leaving and returning, the entire city is considered for him as if it were within four cubits, because they were lenient with him in this matter.

Similarly, if bandits took him outside the boundary and placed him in a pen, a stable, a cave, or a city surrounded by a wall and designated for residence, even if they are outside the boundary, all these places are considered for him as four cubits, and he may walk throughout them.
