But if he went outside his boundary intentionally and entered one of these places, he only has four cubits and is forbidden to walk through the entire area. How can these be considered as four cubits when they are entirely outside his boundary? Rather, in cases of coercion, they were lenient with him, and in these circumstances, we consider it as four cubits, but not if he went out intentionally. However, if they brought him into the outskirts of a city, it is not considered as four cubits (Magen Avraham, subsection 6) even in cases of coercion, for in terms of calculating boundaries, it is like a city, but not to make it as four cubits, since it is not surrounded at all.

Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote in section 7: "One whose ship sailed in the sea - he may walk throughout the entire ship, since he observed the Sabbath within the walls. And if the walls of the ship were breached on the Sabbath, if it is moving - he may walk throughout the entire ship, but if it is stationary - he may only walk within four cubits." End quote. Now, the Rambam did not mention this law at all, because there are no boundaries above ten handbreadths, and the Tur mentioned it because he ruled in the previous section that there are boundaries above ten handbreadths. However, Rabbeinu Beit Yosef, who ruled there that there are no boundaries above ten, did not need this at all, and why, when it is stationary, can he only walk within four cubits? But his intention is thus, that he entered it before the Sabbath, but it went several times below ten, or he went out twice to the dry land, and consequently his status is like one who went outside the boundary and is not considered forced, and therefore when the walls are intact - he may walk throughout the entire ship, since he observed the Sabbath within the walls from the previous day. But if he went to another ship or an enclosed place, since he did not observe the Sabbath within the walls from the previous day - he has only four cubits. And when the walls of the ship were breached while it is stationary - consequently his status is like one who went outside the boundary, having only four cubits. But when it is moving - it is permitted to walk throughout the entire ship, because with every leap it is more than four cubits, and the ship always takes him from these four cubits and places him in another four cubits. (Gemara 42b: "Rabbi Zeira said, since the ship takes him, etc." see there, and see Maggid Mishneh 7 and his words are difficult, and scrutinize well.)

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote: "If in the middle it has partitions of ten [handbreadths], but at its end it does not, we follow the middle. And even if it does not have [partitions] at all, but it is possible to carve out ten [handbreadths], we say we carve to complete." End of quote. And this is referring to 'the sides of the ship that have been breached,' for those at the end are considered like the holes of a private domain, and we require that it not be breached more than it is standing, and that the breach should not exceed ten cubits. (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 10). And what he wrote, 'we say we carve to complete,' is puzzling, for our established ruling is that we do not say we carve to complete, as stated in Siman 345, and it is explicitly explained in Shabbat (7b) that Rabbi Meir holds we carve, but the Rabbis hold we do not carve, and the law follows the Rabbis. (There, subparagraph 11). And it seems to me, in my humble opinion, that this is not ordinary carving, but this is its interpretation: that if under the ground of the ship upon which they stand there is additional space, this space combines with the partitions that have been breached and remain less than ten [handbreadths], to complete them as if they themselves are ten handbreadths. This is merely an example of carving to complete.

Furthermore, it is written in Section 5: "Similarly, if one boarded a ship and the ship sailed beyond the permitted boundary, and then returned to the port from which it had departed - it is as if he never left, for it is as if robbers took him out and brought him back." This means, for example, that the ship was docked outside the boundary, and he boarded it on Shabbat to sit and not to sail, thereby boarding it permissibly. If the ship's owner then sailed it beyond the boundary to a place where the water is not ten [handbreadths] deep and then returned - it is considered as if he was taken out and brought back by force. And this teaches us that even though he boarded the ship willingly, since he boarded it to sit, which is completely permissible, he is judged as if he was coerced. (See Magen Avraham, Section 5, which also describes such cases where it was below ten [handbreadths] during twilight and he acquired residence there, and then sailed on Shabbat and returned.)

Fruits that were taken outside the boundary and brought back—even if it was done intentionally—do not lose their original status, because the fruits themselves are considered to be coerced. Therefore, if it is a festival, when carrying is permitted, the entire city is regarded as four cubits for them, and beyond that, they have two thousand cubits in every direction, as originally. If it is Shabbat, they are permitted to be eaten in their place, even for the Jew who intentionally brought them back for his own use, since the fruits themselves are coerced. This is not comparable to one who cooks on Shabbat, which is forbidden, as that is a biblical prohibition. And even though they penalized someone who immerses their vessels or tithes on Shabbat, which is also a rabbinic prohibition, nevertheless, regarding boundaries, since no change has been made to the fruits themselves and now they are back in their place, they did not impose a penalty. In several matters, they were more lenient with boundaries than with other prohibitions, such as someone who comes from outside the boundary for the sake of one Jew is permitted to another Jew, as discussed later in section 415, and similarly with regard to "the time it takes to perform an action," as the Tosafot write in Eruvin (39b, end of the "If" entry, see there). The Magen Avraham in subparagraph 14 made an effort to establish it as a case where there are no other fruits available, see there. All such cases should be explained, and see the Eliyah Rabbah and Taz, and to me, it appears as I have written, and examine it well.

And as long as the fruits have not been returned and they are outside their place, if they were taken out unintentionally—they are permitted to be eaten but prohibited from being moved beyond four cubits. And who may eat them? Those who made an eruv in that direction. But if they were taken out intentionally—they are forbidden to be eaten even by those who did not take them out. However, some permit them to be eaten by those who did not take them out, and this is agreed upon by the later authorities. (A”R Section 16) But in the Jerusalem Talmud, Chapter 4 of Eruvin (Halacha 1), it appears according to the first opinion. (And through a non-Jew, it is certainly permitted.)

One who has gone beyond the Shabbat boundary (techum), who has only four cubits, and needs to relieve himself – he can go out from there until he finds a modest place to relieve himself. And this applies even if he went out intentionally, since he is now in a state of compulsion. And if he went out unintentionally, it was explained in the previous section that if they brought him back within the boundary, it is as if he had not gone out. The sages gave him advice when he needs to relieve himself – he should approach the side of his boundary, and if he does not find a modest place until his boundary, he may enter his boundary, and after he has entered, it is as if he had not gone out, since he entered with permission, and it is like they brought him back. This is when he did not find a modest place before his boundary. But if he found a modest place before his boundary, he should not enter his boundary; rather, he should relieve himself there, and distance himself from the place where he relieved himself until the smell dissipates, and there he has four cubits. And if he distanced himself due to the smell towards his boundary and entered his boundary, it is as if he had not gone out. This applies when he went out under compulsion, but if he went out intentionally, it does not help that he enters his boundary, as he still only has four cubits, as stated in the previous section.

This which we have said regarding the need for bodily functions, some say that this applies even when one needs to urinate. And some say it specifically applies to defecation, but for urination, one may do so anywhere and does not need a private place, since it is absorbed on the spot, and people urinate in public. (Bekhorot 44b) And perhaps when one needs to pray or recite the Grace After Meals, and it is not possible within four cubits of the urine, one should find a private place.

It is well known that there is nothing that stands in the way of saving a life, for which one desecrates the Sabbath. All the more so, one is obligated to go beyond the Sabbath boundary, even the boundary of twelve mil (18,000 cubits). Regarding boundaries, the sages made an additional decree for this, granting two thousand cubits in every direction from the place one reaches, even if one did not establish residence there beforehand. If one is in a city, they are considered like the inhabitants of the city and have the whole city and an additional two thousand cubits beyond it. Therefore, anyone who goes beyond the boundary with permission, such as a midwife coming to deliver a baby, and similarly in all such cases, they have all the laws that have been clarified. The sages did this so that it should not be a burden on them.

Not only that, but even if one was originally permitted to leave to save a life, and while on the way, he was informed that the matter he was going to address has already been resolved, and there is no longer a need for him to continue — and thus he must remain in his place and is forbidden to desecrate the Sabbath further — the sages still granted him, from the place where he was informed, a radius of two thousand cubits in every direction. Moreover, if part of the domain from which he initially set out with permission overlaps within the two thousand cubits of his current location, he may return to his original place, as if he had never left, because the overlapping of domains is significant, as stated at the beginning of Siman 405.

All those who go out to save lives from robbers, or from the river, or from a collapse, and the like – they have two thousand cubits in every direction from the place where they saved. And if the hand of the robbers is strong, and they are afraid to stay in the place where they saved for the entire Sabbath – they can return even with their weapons to their place, for any potential threat to life overrides the Sabbath. And as a general rule, witnesses who testified about the sighting of the new moon, at the time when the sanctification was done based on sighting, as it is taught in Rosh Hashanah (23b) and as Rambam wrote at the end of chapter 27.

Just as the Sages instituted an eruv for courtyards and alleyways to permit carrying within them through the use of an eruv, making it as if all residents live in one place, so too they instituted eruv techumin. This means that if someone needs to go beyond two thousand cubits on Shabbat for a mitzvah or some necessity, they can make an eruv on Friday afternoon for an additional two thousand cubits, allowing them to travel four thousand cubits on Shabbat. This eruv can be made in two ways: the primary way is by foot, meaning that one goes on Friday afternoon to the end of the two thousand cubits, sits there at the time the Shabbat rest is established, and declares that they want their Shabbat residence to be there. Consequently, they have two thousand cubits in every direction from that spot. They then return home and spend the night there, but their Shabbat residence is considered to be where they were at the time the Shabbat rest was established. The second way, which the Sages allowed for a wealthy person who finds it burdensome to establish their Shabbat residence by foot, is to stay at home and send food for two meals through a messenger to the end of the two thousand cubits, and declare that they establish their Shabbat residence there. The details of this matter will be explained in Siman 409, with God's help.

Therefore, someone who left the city on Friday and placed enough food for two meals at a distance within the city's boundary up to the end of the boundary, and established his residence there, even if he returned home during the day and slept at home—it is still considered as if he had established his residence at the place of the two meals, and he may walk two thousand cubits in any direction from the place of his eruv. Therefore, when he walks two thousand cubits towards the city, he may only walk within the city up to the end of his measure. If the city is encompassed within his measure, the entire city is considered like four cubits, and he may complete his measure of two thousand cubits minus the four cubits outside of it.

How so? If one placed his eruv (an object establishing a symbolic boundary for permitting movement on Shabbat) one thousand cubits east of his house in the city, he may walk from his eruv two thousand cubits to the east the next day, and he may walk from his eruv two thousand cubits to the west: one thousand from the eruv to his house, and one thousand cubits from his house within the city, but he may only walk within the city up to the end of that thousand. If the distance from his house to the end of the city is less than a thousand, even by one cubit or less, so that his measured distance ends outside the city, the entire city is considered as four cubits, and he may walk outside it nine hundred and ninety-six cubits to complete the two thousand. Therefore, if he placed his eruv two thousand cubits away from his house in the city, he loses the entire city, and he may walk from his house to his eruv two thousand cubits, but he cannot walk from his house in the city to the west even a single cubit. All of this is the opinion of the Rambam in Chapter 6 of Eruvin, and this is also the ruling of Rabbeinu Beit Yosef in Section 1.

But the opinion of the Tur is not so, as he holds that even if one's measure ends in the middle of the city, the city does not become like four cubits for him. This only applies in the sense that we do not extend for him outside the city the remainder [of the distance]. However, in any case, regarding walking through the entire city, it becomes like four cubits for him, since he stayed there overnight. This specifically applies to a city that becomes like four cubits only due to the measurement of the boundary, meaning a city that stands within two thousand cubits and he did not stay there overnight. In such a case, we properly say that if his measure ends in the middle of the city, he only has half the city. But not in a city where he stayed overnight. Otherwise, the eruv would cause a great stringency for him, as without the eruv, it would be considered like four cubits, and the eruv is meant to be lenient, not stringent. And our master the Rema agreed with this. And know that what we said, that when one's measure ends at the end of the city, the whole city is like four cubits, this applies even if it ends before the extension, which is seventy cubits, for we do not say that the extension of the city is like the city itself to be stringent.

It has already been explained in Siman 398 that the boundaries of a city are measured in every direction as two thousand cubits, including the filling of the corners, as stated there. One measures along the length to the east and west, and similarly along the width to the north and south, according to the length and width of the city, which means opposite the city. Similarly, when one places an Eruv and measures for it two thousand cubits in every direction, it is also opposite the place where the Eruv was set. Consequently, it is forbidden for him to walk to the north and south, only opposite the width of the place where he established his residence and the corners. If it is only four cubits, such as when the Eruv is not in a private domain enclosed for dwelling, he is forbidden to walk in any direction two thousand cubits, only opposite the four cubits, and one fills its corners to make it in the form of a squared tablet, as stated in Siman 398.

Nevertheless, our master the Rema wrote at the end of Section 1 as follows: "Nevertheless, if the measure ends at the end of the city and the entire city is like his four cubits, it is permitted to walk its entire width, and he has two thousand cubits outside the city to the north and to the south, even though he does not have such width corresponding to the place where he established his eruv." End quote.

They were puzzled by him, questioning what relevance the north and south have to the city, as the two thousand cubits in any direction are relative to the place of his residence, and the corners fill the entire two thousand cubits to the north and south, as well as to the east and west. However, the city is not part of the measure of the boundary at all. (This is the intention of the Magen Avraham, subparagraph 3.)

But our master the Rema holds that since the city is considered like four cubits, then it is also included within the boundary. For we subtract four cubits from the boundary due to the city being considered as four cubits, so then even relative to the city, it is like relative to the boundary. (Elya Rabba on Orach Chaim 408:2)

If opposite part of the width of the city in some direction there is a city that completes the two thousand cubits at the end of the city, then the whole city is considered as four cubits, and the remaining distance is completed outside the city. And opposite the other part of the width of this direction there is no city, or there is a city whose measure ends in the middle of the city - the sides are not equalized, but one goes here according to its measure, and here according to its measure, and it is clear. (And so it is written in Shulchan Aruch HaRav in the name of the Nodah B'Yehudah) And one who places his eiruv in the city, even a large one (like Nineveh), [like Nineveh] and even a ruined city or a cave suitable for dwelling - he can walk all of it and outside of it two thousand cubits in every direction. And one who places his eiruv within the city in which he rested - we do not measure from the place of his eiruv but he is like all the residents of the city, who have two thousand cubits in every direction outside the city. And similarly, if he placed his eiruv in places joining to the city, such as houses standing within seventy cubits, or according to the Tur within seventy cubits from the city - he has done nothing and he is like the residents of the city, for this is exactly as if he placed it in the city. And if he placed his eiruv outside the boundary - it is not an eiruv, and he has the boundary of his house. And we do not say that he removed his intention from his house, because his intention is that if the eiruv does not work - he will not lose the boundary of his house, and this will be explained in Siman 141. (See Magen Avraham, Subsection 4)

One who places their Eruv in a cemetery, meaning on the grave of a structure that is forbidden to benefit from, as stated in Yoreh De'ah, siman 364, it is not an Eruv. Even though at the time of establishing the Eruv we have no issue because mitzvot were not given for benefit, nevertheless, since it is preferable for the Eruv to remain valid afterward, as it is food or drink, there is benefit derived from it. And even though we do not have to be concerned with what will happen after establishing the Eruv, since the intention is to establish residence there and it is like one's home, it is forbidden to acquire a home through forbidden benefits (Gemara Eruvin 31a). Consequently, this residence is nullified, and the Eruv is nullified. This is according to the opinion of the Rambam in chapter 6 and Rabbeinu Beit Yosef in section 1. However, the Tur actually ruled that only for a Kohen is it not an Eruv, because he cannot reach his place of residence, but not for an Israelite. (And what is in the Gemara is not according to the conclusion there). But if one placed the Eruv in a Beit HaPras, which is a field that had a grave plowed over and its impurity is rabbinical, even for a Kohen it would be an Eruv, because he can enter it in a flying tower, meaning a tower that has forty se'ah and is carried on animals, or by blowing, in accordance with the law of Beit HaPras, where one blows and sees that there is no bone the size of a barley grain and proceeds, and a Kohen can also reach the Eruv and take it with simple wooden utensils that do not become impure. Similarly, a grave of soil is not forbidden for benefit as stated in Yoreh De'ah there, and for those who forbid the soil placed on the grave, it is not an Eruv, and these laws are not to be explained here.

In the place of the eruv, he establishes his residence. Therefore, he and his eruv must be in the same place during twilight, which is the time of establishing the eruv, so that it would be possible for him to eat it there during twilight. But if they are in two different domains, it is not a valid eruv. Therefore, if one intends to establish residence in a public domain and places his eruv in a private domain, or if he intends to establish residence in a private domain and places his eruv in a public domain, it is not a valid eruv, because he cannot transfer it during twilight from a private domain to a public domain or from a public domain to a private domain.

However, if one intends to establish residence in a private domain or in a public domain and places his eruv in a karmelit, or if he intends to establish residence in a karmelit and places his eruv in a private domain or in a public domain, it is a valid eruv, because at the time of establishing residence and the eruv, which is during twilight, it is permitted to transfer between a public domain or a private domain to a karmelit. This is because one only makes an eruv for the sake of a mitzvah, and anything that is a rabbinic prohibition (shvut) is not decreed upon during twilight for the sake of a mitzvah, as stated in Siman 342.

And even though one could also bring the eruv from a private domain to a public domain or vice versa by means of a non-Jew, which is only a rabbinic prohibition (shvut) - nonetheless, how can we say that his residence is established through the two meals by something he cannot bring himself to his residence? Since the essence of his residence is the meal, it is as if he is bringing his residence through others, and that is not considered his own residence.

If [the eruv] is placed at the top of a reed or a vine that grows from the ground, for which there is a prohibition to use on Shabbat similar to a tree - it is not a valid eruv. For even though this too is only a rabbinic prohibition, nevertheless, they decreed against it even during twilight, because they are soft and easy to pluck, and one might easily come to a biblical prohibition, and they decreed even in the case of a mitzvah. However, if they are detached from the ground but are stuck into the ground - this is a valid eruv, because in such cases, there is no biblical prohibition of plucking, as explained in Siman 336. Similarly, if one places the eruv in the public domain and also intends to establish their residence in the public domain, but the eruv is eight cubits away from where they intend to establish their residence - this is also not a valid eruv, even though one can carry less than four cubits at a time, because this too is close to leading to a biblical prohibition. (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 7) However, if it is less than eight cubits - it is permitted, because one can carry less than four cubits at a time, and the eruv will be within four cubits of the place of residence, and in one instance, one will not transgress. Similarly, if one places the eruv in a tower and locks it, and the key is lost before Shabbat or a pile falls on it, if it can be retrieved without performing a biblical labor - it is a valid eruv. Provided that the residence is in the same domain where the tower is located, meaning that if the tower is in a private domain - the residence should also be in a private domain or a karmelit, and if the tower is in the public domain and the tower is ten handbreadths high and four handbreadths wide - the residence should be on the tower or in a karmelit.

Anyone who places his eruv in a location - he has four cubits in that location in addition to the two thousand cubits, since he establishes his residence there as if it were his home, and a home is no less than four cubits. One should not ask, therefore, that we should require placing the eruv specifically in a dwelling house, as in the case of eruv chatzerot, for we can say that they did not want to burden him in this way. If so, if he does not have a house at the end of the boundary, he would not have an eruv, and the entire ordinance would be nullified. Therefore, since the eruv techumin is only for the purpose of a mitzvah, the sages said that one can establish a residence in any place whatsoever.

And since he has four cubits, therefore the Sages said (Eruvin 35b) that if one places his Eruv Techumin at the end of the boundary, and it rolls outside the four cubits before twilight - it is not a valid Eruv. And even though he could bring it within the four cubits during twilight by carrying it less than four cubits at a time, as mentioned in Section 3 - nevertheless, it is not effective, for if he had established his resting place where the Eruv is, he would now be outside the boundary. Therefore, the Rabbis decreed that an Eruv is valid only if it is within the boundary (Tosafot there), because it is impossible for the power of the Eruv to exceed its own power. And if it rolls within four cubits - it is a valid Eruv. And although someone who goes outside the boundary - even by one cubit - may not re-enter, as stated at the beginning of Siman 405, this is not comparable, for in that case, he has the resting place of his house and it is like his four cubits of rest, so he does not have an additional four cubits. This is not the case with the place of his Eruv, for he has the resting place of four cubits, so he is still not outside the boundary (Beit Yosef). Similarly, if he did not place the Eruv at the end of the boundary but within the boundary, and it rolls afar but is still within the boundary, even though he intended for those specific four cubits and how can he be given another four cubits - this is because we testify that his intention was that if it rolls afar, that place would be his resting place, since it is still within the boundary, which is not the case outside the boundary - his intention does not help.

If the eruv was lost or burned, or if it was at the edge of the boundary and rolled beyond four cubits, or if it was terumah (a portion of food designated for priests) and became impure, in all these cases, if it happened while it was still daytime, it is not a valid eruv. But if it happened after dark, it is a valid eruv, because the acquisition of the eruv takes place during twilight. And if there is doubt, it is valid, because the doubt concerning an eruv is a rabbinic doubt, and we tend to be lenient. This is specifically when the eruv had a presumption of validity, such as in a case where it was placed there and then a doubt arose. But if it did not have a presumption of validity, such as in a case where there is doubt whether it was placed there or not, we do not say 'a doubtful eruv is valid,' because in such cases there is a presumption of stringency — we assume the person remains within the boundary of his home and did not make an eruv. When the eruv has a presumption of validity, we maintain its presumption against the presumption of the boundary of his home, and in rabbinic doubts, we are lenient. (See Rashi 36a, s.v. 'ha'amad,' and see what I wrote in Siman 394). If one made an eruv with a doubtful tereifah (an animal with a condition that will cause it to die within a year), it is not a valid eruv, because we require a meal that is fit from before the onset of Shabbat, and this one is certainly not fit due to its doubtful tereifah status. (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 9).

All those we mentioned where 'it is not an Eruv' - they have their residence established at their home, and we do not say 'Behold, he has uprooted his intention from his residence at home,' and this is similar to the law that will be explained regarding someone who is traveling and recognizes a tree or a fence and says, 'My residence is under it,' but was unable to reach there at the time of acquiring the Eruv - he only has four cubits, because his residence was uprooted from here and there is no Eruv, as it will be explained in section 14. Similarly, here too, since his residence was uprooted from his home and the place of the Eruv is not an Eruv, he should not move more than four cubits. But this is not the case, for there he was traveling, but here he is at home and made an Eruv in a place that is not an Eruv - he has his residence at home, because presumably he is content for his residence to be acquired at home if his Eruv is not an Eruv. (Rashi 60: s.v. 'And he forbade' see there, and see Magen Avraham, siman 411, sk 1)

How is an Eruv established? If one wishes to go to the edge of the boundary or within the boundary and remain there until dark, with the intention of establishing a place of residence there, this is the primary way to fulfill the mitzvah. Even if he did not say, "My residence is in this place," but merely stayed there until dark and remained silent, as long as his intention was to establish his residence there, it is considered an Eruv. However, if his intention was not to establish residence there, it is not considered an Eruv unless he explicitly said, "My residence is in this place." 

There is no difference in this matter whether one left his house to establish residence there and went to stay until dark at the boundary or whether one was traveling and it became dark for him – he acquires a residence within two thousand cubits without saying anything. When traveling, no specific intention is needed because he automatically acquires residence at the place where he was between sunset and nightfall, as even if he was sleeping, he acquires residence, as mentioned in Siman 401, and certainly if he was awake. 

It seems to me that even if he was walking the entire time between sunset and nightfall and did not stay in one place, as explained in Siman 397 that anything which is mobile does not acquire residence, like flowing rivers, nevertheless, a person acquires residence in his location because he has the ability to stop or sit down. We do not find anywhere that a person who is walking does not acquire residence. We say: "Since he could stop and acquire residence, while walking he also acquires residence," similar to one who sleeps there, as we say in such cases.

And behold, this is the essence of the eruv, which is an eruv made by walking. But the Sages were lenient with one who does not want to exert himself and stay there until nightfall. He can go during the day or send a messenger and place there food for two meals, each person according to his own food. And even in this, they were lenient, as the average person needs two medium meals, which are about six eggs' worth of bread, and even if he is very hungry, the medium amount suffices. However, if he is sick and does not need as much as two meals, less will suffice for him. And it is not specifically bread, for the same applies to any item with which one participates in the merging of alleyways. And even if one has sworn not to benefit from a loaf of bread, he can still make an eruv with it, for an eruv is only made for the sake of a mitzvah, and mitzvot were not given for benefit. (Magen Avraham, section 12) And if it is a cooked dish, it suffices with the amount of cooked dish that one eats for two meals.

And with such an eruv, a declaration is specifically required, since it is not at the place of his residence. And he should say at the time he places the eruv: 'With this eruv, it will be permitted for me to walk two thousand cubits from the place of this eruv tomorrow.' And he should recite the blessing as will be explained at the end of Siman 415, and then he returns and sleeps in his home. And his techum (Shabbat boundary) is measured from the place of his eruv, as we consider it as if he resides there, since it is evident (that if) he had a place to live there, he would live there. (Talmud 73a)

And for this reason, students who eat in the homes of householders, whose houses are in the field, and they go and sleep in their teacher's house, even though regarding eruvin the place of eating is primary, nevertheless for the students, the techum is measured from their teacher's house where they sleep, because it is evident (that if) they would bring their food there, it would be more comfortable for them, since their main residence is in their teacher's house. (ibid)

If he desires, he can send the eruv by means of an agent, and the agent should say at the time of placing the eruv: 'With this eruv, so-and-so will be permitted to walk tomorrow two thousand cubits from the place of the eruv.' And he should recite the blessing, for a person's agent is like himself. However, the agent should not be a deaf-mute, an imbecile, or a minor, as they are not fit for agency, and also not a violent person who is not capable of setting the residence. This is not similar to an eruv for courtyards, which can be collected even by a minor, as stated in Siman 366, because there, speech and intention are not required, unlike in the case of the eruv for boundaries. Also, one should not appoint as an agent someone who does not agree with the concept of the eruv or a non-Jew. If any of these were made the agent, the eruv is invalid, even if the person stands from a distance and sees that the eruv has been placed—it is nothing.

And this is when they appoint them as agents to place the Eruv. But if they appoint one person to receive it from them on behalf of the Eruv and place it for them, and they are not agents except to hand over the Eruv to this person, it does not matter to us. In such cases, one can even send it through a trained animal, like an elephant or a monkey. However, even in this case, they are not trustworthy, and one must stand at a distance and see that they handed it to him. And although in a rabbinic matter they are considered trustworthy, nevertheless, in the case of Eruvei Techumin, which has a basis in Torah law, they are not given this trustworthiness. Moreover, it is a bothersome matter, and we are concerned that they may not fulfill their agency. But someone who promised to place the Eruv is trusted, and it is not necessary to see if he fulfilled it, for there is a presumption that an agent performs his agency. And although there are those who hold that in Torah matters one should not rely on this presumption, in rabbinic matters we certainly rely on this presumption. And in a matter where another could fail, even in Torah matters we say this presumption, as we explained in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 182, Seif 7. (See Magen Avraham, Siman 17) Similarly, many who joined in Eruvei Techumin can all send through one person who will make the Eruv for all of them.

Ideally, when appointing a messenger, one should explicitly say to him, "Go and make an Eruv for me to the east or to the west," according to his preference. For if he tells him in general terms, how will the messenger know in which direction he wishes to make the Eruv? Nevertheless, if an individual or a group tells someone, "Go and make an Eruv for us" without specifying further, and he goes and makes an Eruv in one of the directions, the Eruv is valid. We assume that their intention was that they are fine with whichever direction he chooses, and it will be revealed retroactively that they preferred that direction. This is because we hold that there is retroactive clarification in rabbinic matters, and Eruvin are rabbinic. It is obvious that if they told him "Make an Eruv to the east" and he made it in another direction, it is not a valid Eruv. Even regarding the type of Eruv, if the messenger deviated, it is not valid. For example, if he said to him, "Make an Eruv for me with dates," and he made it with dried figs, or "with dried figs," and he made it with dates. If he said, "Place my Eruv in the tower," and he placed it in the dovecote, "in the dovecote," and he placed it in the tower, "in the house," and he placed it in the upper room, "in the upper room," and he placed it in the house, it is not a valid Eruv, even if the messenger used his own items. However, if he said, "Make an Eruv for me" without specifying further, and the messenger made it with dried figs, dates, placed it in the dovecote, the tower, the house, or the upper room, it is a valid Eruv, even if the items used belonged to those who appointed the messenger.

If someone is traveling and sees a tree or a fence from a distance and recognizes them, and they are at the end of two thousand cubits from where he currently stands, and he fears he will not reach there before twilight, which is the time of establishing the eruv, he can declare at his current location: 'My residence shall be under that particular tree at its base,' or 'under that particular fence on its eastern side,' or similar statements that specify the place. In such a case, he acquires his residence there by declaration, and he has two thousand cubits in every direction from that point. This is also one of the leniencies applied to the eruv. However, we require that he must be able to reach there by some form of walking before twilight, even if he would need to run very fast. Therefore, even though he might not reach there by normal walking, it does not matter to us, and we consider it as if he is standing there at twilight. But if under no circumstances could he reach there by twilight, this is not a valid eruv, because how can he establish his residence there if he cannot reach there at the time of establishing the residence? In such cases, he has not established his residence at all, and he only has four cubits from the place where he is at twilight, since he has uprooted his residence from here and has not acquired it there. This is not comparable to someone who stays at home, for if he does not establish an eruv, he still has the boundary of his home, as explained in Section 7, see there.

And this also applies when he designates his place of residence explicitly, as we have said. But if he did not designate his place of residence, such as if he said: "My residence is under the tree" or "under the fence," and the entire tree or fence does not stand within two thousand cubits from his location – he has not acquired the residence, because perhaps he intended a place beyond the two thousand cubits. Therefore, he should not move from his place and he only has four cubits, as we have said. And if the entire tree or fence stands within two thousand cubits, and he did not specify his place of residence, saying "My residence is under it" – he has two thousand cubits from his location towards the tree or fence, subtracting the length of the tree or fence. For example, if their length is twenty cubits – he has two thousand cubits minus twenty because of the uncertainty, as we do not know where he intended to establish his residence, and perhaps he intended at the beginning, and thus the boundary will reach twenty cubits less.

According to the Rambam, there is a different opinion on this matter: if someone establishes their place for Shabbat rest at a distant location but does not specify the exact place, even if the entire area is within two thousand cubits, they do not acquire a place for Shabbat rest there but only at the spot where they are standing during twilight. Similarly, in his opinion, if someone says, "My place for Shabbat rest is at such-and-such a location," and that place is more than two thousand cubits away, they acquire the place for Shabbat rest at their current location, just as if they were sitting in their home.

Therefore, one who says, "My residence is under such-and-such a tree," if there are eight cubits under it, he has not acquired residence, because we do not know to which four cubits he was referring. But if it is less than that, there is a central cubit, which in any case his residence is within, and part of his place is recognizable, and he has acquired the eruv. Therefore, in such cases, one needs to intend to acquire residence at the base of the tree, or within the four cubits to its north or its south, and the like. This is also the opinion of the Rif, of blessed memory. If there were two people walking on the way, and one recognizes the place of residence and the other does not, the one who does not recognize entrusts his residence to the one who recognizes, meaning he relies on him, and the one who recognizes says, "Our residence is at such-and-such a place." This leniency of saying "my residence is at such-and-such a place" without bread was only permitted for someone who is traveling, but not for one who is sitting at home. One who is sitting at home must either go and sit at the place during twilight where he wants to acquire residence, or send bread there, as has been explained.

This was explained at the end of the previous section, that only someone who is on the road is permitted to establish a "Shvitah" (residence) at a distant location, for example by saying "My residence is in such-and-such place," and not someone who is sitting in his home. However, there are times when someone sitting in his home is considered as if he is on the road. For example, if someone was at home and wanted to establish a residence in a certain place, and he went there to designate that place as his residence by saying "My residence is in this place," and he set out on the road and met his friend at the beginning of the journey, and his friend said to him: "It is a hot time, it is a cold time, return to your home," or if he himself decided to return because of the heat or cold, or he was delayed there for some reason - his status is like that of someone who is on the road, and he can say "My residence is in such-and-such place," and return to his home to sleep, and the next day he has two thousand cubits in every direction from the place of the residence he designated. Since he had resolved in his heart to establish his residence there and set out on the road - it is as if he stood there or placed his Eiruv there.

And know that this statement we wrote, that one should say, "My resting place is in such-and-such a location," this is the opinion of Rashi (note: see another version there). However, from the words of the Rambam in Chapter 7 and the Shulchan Aruch, Section 1, it is clear that it is not necessary to say at all "My resting place is in such-and-such a location." For since he resolved in his heart to go and acquire a resting place and began to go, it is as if he is actually standing there, and there is no need for a verbal declaration. The Tur brought both opinions there, and the Rashba ruled according to Rashi, that in such cases where he is not at the location, the verbal declaration is essential (Beit Yosef). However, the Rambam explicitly explained at the end of Chapter 7 that no verbal declaration is needed, and these are the words of the Rambam: "Anyone who acquires a resting place from a distance does not need to say, 'My resting place is in such-and-such a location,' but once he resolved in his heart and set out on the way, he has acquired a resting place there. And certainly, one who sets out on foot and stands at the resting place does not need to say anything, but once he resolved in his heart, he has acquired it." End quote. Accordingly, we must say that what is written at the beginning of the chapter: "One who set out on the eve of Sabbath... and said, 'My resting place is in this location,' etc." end quote, is teaching the usual manner of things, or that he did not leave his house with this intention, but along the way decided to go there to acquire a resting place.

And our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote at the end of Section 1: "In what case are these words said? In the case of a poor person who is not troubled to set an eruv, or if he is at a distance, such as if he was on the road. But if he was neither poor nor at a distance – no." These are his exact words, and this is from the language of the Rambam there. And I am puzzled, because from this language it is clear that for a poor person, they permitted him to say, "My residence is in such-and-such place" even without having embarked on the road. And while it is true that the Rambam holds this opinion, our teacher, the Beit Yosef himself, wrote at the end of the previous section that they did not permit this for one who is sitting at home, and he did not differentiate between a poor person and a wealthy person. And this is indeed the opinion of the Tur there, and also the Rashba holds this view, as the Maggid Mishneh wrote there. Therefore, our teacher, the Beit Yosef, ruled there like the Rashba and the Tur, but here like the opinion of the Rambam, which requires further study.

And what we have said, that someone who establishes residence at a distant place, this is when they have initiated the journey—not that they must leave the city and walk in a field specifically, but even if they just came down from the upper floor to go to that place, and before they left the courtyard gate, their friend called them back—this is considered as having initiated the journey, and they have established residence. And anyone who establishes residence at a distant place does not need to say 'My residence is in such-and-such a place,' but as soon as they decided in their heart and initiated the journey in any way—they have established residence there. And it goes without saying that someone who went out on foot and stood in the place where they establish residence—they do not need to say anything, but as soon as they decided in their heart—they have established residence. This is how our teacher, the Beit Yosef, ruled in section 2, and it is from the words of the Rambam in chapter 7, and we have already written in section 2 that Rashi and the Rashba disagree on this matter. (And if one recognizes a tree or a fence—all agree that a declaration is necessary).

The residents of the city who sent one of them to carry their eruv to a specific place, and he started on the way but then his companion brought him back and he did not carry their eruv — they did not establish their residence in the specified place, since their eruv was not placed there, and they remain within the boundaries of their original location, with two thousand cubits in every direction. And he — he established his residence there, since he started on the way and intended to reside there. Therefore, he is permitted to go to that place the next day and travel from it two thousand cubits in every direction. According to Rashi and the Rashba, this is only when he said, "My residence is in such and such a place." But for them — it does not help even if he said it on behalf of all of them, since they wanted an eruv with bread and not an eruv with walking.

If someone told his agent during the day, "Make an eruv for me to the west of my house," and the agent went and made the eruv for him, but the person himself later went to the east of his house for his own purposes, and was there during twilight, which is the time of the acquisition of the eruv, then if the agent placed the eruv so far to the west of his house that the distance from the eruv to the place where he is standing to the east of his house is more than two thousand cubits, it is understood that the eruv is nullified, and he remains within the boundary of his house. However, if the distance from the eruv to the place where he is standing is not more than two thousand cubits, even though he is within two thousand cubits of his house, he still has the boundary of his eruv. We do not say that since he is now standing to the east of his house, he does not benefit at all from the eruv which is to the west of his house; we do not say this.

And we have already written in Siman 409, Section 7, that opposite the boundary of his house, we do not say that he should not move from his place, as we do for someone who recognizes a tree or a fence, because one never loses focus on their home, as mentioned there. And this reasoning was written by Rashi, of blessed memory, there. And some say the reason is not because of this that the boundary of his house is not lost, but because the agent made a mistake, as he should not have made an Eruv so far away, and therefore the agency is nullified. (Rashi) But in Siman 408, it appears explicitly like Rashi, there. (See Taz, who notes a practical difference between the reasons if he himself did this, placing the Eruv to the west and going to the east, there.)

If someone made an error in halacha, thinking that he could establish an eruv (boundary for carrying on Shabbat) for half a day in one direction and for the other half of the day in another direction, and he placed two eruvin, one to the north for the first half of the day, and one to the south for the second half of the day, or if he told two people to establish the eruv for him, and one established it to the north and the other to the south, and each placed his eruv at the end of two thousand cubits — he is not permitted to move from his place, because it is not known which eruv has taken effect. This means that it is certain that once he realizes his mistake, he will say that his intention was that only one of them should take effect, and not the other. However, this itself is not known, neither to him nor to us, which one should take effect and which one should not. Therefore, he must necessarily remain in his place, and he has only four cubits, which is necessarily given to every person.

And if he set two Eruvin, or his two messengers set them, and they were not at the end of the domain, he can go as far as possible by the virtue of the two Eruvin. How so? If each Eruv is at the end of a thousand cubits from his house, he has a thousand cubits from his house for each of the Eruvin. And if one Eruv is to the east at the end of a thousand cubits, and the other to the west at the end of five hundred cubits, he goes to the west a thousand cubits by the virtue of the Eruv placed to the east, and to the east, he goes a thousand and five hundred cubits by the virtue of the Eruv placed to the west, and so on in similar cases. But we do not say that the two Eruvin are nullified, leaving him only four cubits.

One who establishes an eruv for the public using his own resources says: "Behold, this eruv is for all the residents of the city," provided that there is enough food for two meals for each individual. This is not comparable to an eruv chatzerot (courtyard eruv), where two meals suffice for everyone, even if there are a thousand people, as stated in Siman 365. There, the purpose is to prevent residents from prohibiting each other and to make them as if they are mixed together, so two meals are sufficient. But here, each person retains their own residence, and therefore, each one needs two meals. Additionally, the laws of techumin (boundaries) are more stringent as they are based on Scripture. And even though there is leniency regarding bread, it seems to me that this is because, concerning techumin, the primary form of eruv is by walking, and thus it cannot be said that only bread is required. Moreover, it appears to me that the reason is straightforward: since regarding techumin, one uproots his residence entirely from his house, courtyard, and city to another place entirely, therefore two meals are required for each person. And when establishing it for all the residents of the city, one must acquire it on their behalf through another person, as is the case with eruv chatzerot in Siman 366.

And this is also not comparable to the case of "Eruvei Chatzeirot" (joining of courtyards) and "Mavot" (alleys), which can be done without their knowledge. But for "Techumin" (boundaries), it can only be done with their consent, because it is not merely a benefit; it can also be a disadvantage, as it causes a loss in another direction, as has been explained. Therefore, one who makes an eruv for an individual or a group must notify them beforehand. However, for anyone who was notified beforehand, even if they did not finalize their decision until nightfall, it is still considered an eruv. For regarding techumin, we apply the principle of "brerah" (retroactive clarification), meaning it is retroactively clarified that they had established their dwelling at the place of the eruv. But if they were not notified at all beforehand, on what basis would the principle of "brerah" apply, since they were entirely unaware of the eruv?

And similarly, one who set aside an eruv for all the Sabbaths of the year, and said, "On whichever Sabbath I wish, I will rely on it," even if between sunset and nightfall he did not decide in his heart until the next day — he can rely on it, based on the principle of retroactive designation (bererah) that we have explained. Similarly, if someone heard that a certain sage would come on the Sabbath, but did not know from which direction he would come, and he set aside two eruvs and said: "If the sage comes from the east, my eruv is to the east, and if he comes from the west, my eruv is to the west, and if two sages come, one from here and one from there, I will go wherever I choose, and if no one comes from either direction, I will be like the residents of my town" — he can do so, and his eruv is valid. And even the next day, he can choose, if two sages come, one from here and one from there, to which side he wishes to go, all based on the principle of retroactive designation, and all according to his condition. Similarly, if he said to two or three people: "I am setting an eruv for whichever one of you I choose tomorrow," or if he said generally: "For whichever one of you I choose," and did not specify whom he chose until nightfall — the eruv is valid, all based on the principle of retroactive designation as we mentioned.

It has already been explained that for Eruvei Techumin (boundary extensions), one can only establish an eruv with the consent of the person involved, as perhaps he does not wish to establish an eruv at all, so as not to lose the boundary of his home, or he wishes to establish it in a different direction. However, the sages said: A person may establish an eruv for his minor son and daughter, even if they are not dependent on his table, in order to educate them in the mitzvot, as one may only establish an eruv for the sake of a mitzvah, and their consent is not required since the obligation of education falls on the father. Even if the children objected to the establishment of the eruv, or even if they established an eruv in a different direction, their opinion is of no consequence, and we consider the father's decision. Similarly, one may establish an eruv for his Canaanite servant and maidservant.

However, his grown son and daughter, even if they are reliant on his table, and his Hebrew servant and maidservant, and his wife — he does not establish an Eruv for them except with their knowledge. Nevertheless, there is a distinction between them and others, for with others, it is impossible for him to establish an Eruv on their behalf until they explicitly consent. But here, even if they do not explicitly consent but do not object, and they have not made another Eruv and remain silent — they fulfill their obligation with his Eruv, as it is presumed that they are satisfied with what he has done. However, if they object or they made their own Eruv — his Eruv does not serve for them.

A child of six years goes out with the Eruv of his mother, and all the more so if he is younger, and it is not necessary to set aside two meals for him. However, after six years, it is forbidden to take him outside the boundary, for we do not have the authority to impose a prohibition on them. But a six-year-old who cannot be without his mother is compelled to go with her. And if he is an intelligent child and does not need his mother even at the age of five, she should not take him with her. (See Magen Avraham, Subsection 7; the primary explanation is as the first answer mentioned there).

One may only establish an eruv techumin for the sake of a mitzvah. Some want to say that this applies to an eruv made with bread, but with walking, one can make an eruv even for a discretionary matter (Beit Yosef and Rosh, chapter 88). In a pressing situation, one may rely on this (Eliyah Rabbah). In retrospect, if one made an eruv for a discretionary matter, according to Behag, it is not a valid eruv, but Rambam in chapter 6 rules that it is a valid eruv. Rashba wrote to differentiate between making an eruv with bread and making an eruv by walking: with bread, it is not a valid eruv; but by walking, it is a valid eruv (Beit Yosef). Our master, the Beit Yosef, ruled like the Rambam. Certainly, if one made an eruv for the sake of a mitzvah, one may also walk for a discretionary matter. The reason one may only establish an eruv for the sake of a mitzvah is straightforward: for eruvin of courtyards and partnerships in alleyways, the eruv itself is a mitzvah, to prevent transgressing the prohibition of carrying. But with techumin, there is no concern about coming to a prohibition, and it is only permitted for necessity. Therefore, they permitted it for a mitzvah necessity, but not for a discretionary matter. In truth, the intention is not only for an absolute mitzvah but even if it provides pleasure on Shabbat or Yom Tov, it is also considered a mitzvah, as will be explained. The sages also permitted this because it is a mitzvah to "call the Shabbat a delight," and on Yom Tov, we are commanded to rejoice.

Therefore, one may only make an eruv to go to a mourner's house or to a wedding feast, or for a circumcision or other mitzvah, or to meet one's teacher or friend who has come from a journey, or to oversee communal affairs, or if one was outside the city and needs to return home, as it is a mitzvah to be with one's wife and children. And our teacher, the Rema, wrote: "Or if one wants to stroll on Yom Tov or Shabbat in an orchard, which brings joy and the like – this is considered a mitzvah matter," end quote, and this is for the reason we have explained. Similarly, for reasons of fear, if one wants to escape from coercion or robbers – this is considered a mitzvah matter, and so too in all similar cases.

Even though one may ideally set an Eruv Chatzerot (courtyard eruv) during twilight, as stated in Siman 393, setting an Eruv Techumin (boundary eruv) is not ideally done during twilight (Shabbat 34a), because this is considered a significant establishment, and they based it on scriptural verses (Rashi). However, post-factum, the eruv is valid. Therefore, if two people told someone, "Go and make an eruv for us," and he made an eruv for one of them during the day and for the other during twilight, and the eruv set during the day was consumed during twilight, while the one set during twilight was consumed after dark, both eruvim are valid. The reasoning for this ruling was already explained in Siman 393. However, there are those who disagree and hold that for techumin, even post-factum, it does not work during twilight (opinion of Rabbeinu Tam in Tosafot there, whereas Rashi there and the Rambam in Chapter 6 ruled according to the first opinion).

When placing an Eruv Techumin, one blesses: "Who has sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us concerning the commandment of Eruv. With this Eruv, it will be permitted for me to walk from such-and-such place two thousand cubits in every direction." And if one is making the Eruv for many people, he blesses and also says: "With this Eruv, it will be permitted for so-and-so and so-and-so, etc." or he should say: "It will be permitted for all the residents of the city." The blessing is not indispensable, but if he did not say "with this, etc." it is indispensable (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 5). And even though for an Eruv made by foot one does not need to say anything, as stated in Siman 410, that is because he is standing in the place of his residence. But for an Eruv with bread, if he did not say it, in what way is it recognizable that it is an Eruv? And it appears to me that if he blessed and did not say "with this," it is still an Eruv.

We have established in Eruvin (38b) that when Shabbat and Yom Tov are adjacent to each other, such as when Yom Tov falls on the eve of Shabbat or on Sunday, they are considered two separate sanctities. This means that the two days of Yom Tov during Pesach, Shavuot, and Sukkot, which are referred to as the "Yom Tov of the Diaspora" because in the Land of Israel only one day is observed, are considered two separate sanctities, since only one of them is actually sanctified and the second is observed out of doubt. However, Yom Tov of Rosh Hashanah is considered one sanctity and is like one long day, for a reason that will be explained elsewhere. Regarding Shabbat and Yom Tov, there is a dispute in the Gemara there, but the halacha has been decided that they are two separate sanctities, and therefore, they have no connection to each other.

Therefore, on a festival adjacent to Shabbat, whether before it or after it, and likewise on the two festival days of the Diaspora, a person can make an eruv for two directions: the first day to the east of his house, and the second day to the west of his house. He relies on whichever one he wants on the first day, and on the eruv in the other direction for the second day, and he places both on the eve of the festival. Similarly, he can make an eruv for the first day, and on the second day he will be like the residents of the city, or on the first day like the residents of the city, and on the second day the eruv will take effect. On the day he is like the residents of the city, he has two thousand cubits in every direction from his city, and on the day the eruv takes effect, he has two thousand cubits in every direction from the place of the eruv. He blesses both and says: 'With this eruv, it will be permitted for me to walk on one of the two days in this direction,' and likewise with the second eruv, and tomorrow he will decide in which direction he wants to go, for we have already written that in matters of boundaries there is retroactive clarification, because it is rabbinic.

And this applies to Shabbat and Yom Tov, and to the two days of Yom Tov in the Diaspora. But on Rosh Hashanah, where the two days are considered as one day, one can only make an eruv for both days together. If one makes an eruv for only one day, it is as if one is making an eruv for half of Shabbat, and it is not a valid eruv. Similarly, one can make a condition on the eruv and say: 'My eruv is for this Shabbat and not for another Shabbat,' or 'for another Shabbat and not for this Shabbat.' Likewise, 'My eruv shall be for Shabbatot and not for Yomim Tovim,' and 'for Yomim Tovim and not for Shabbatot.' If he wishes, he can make one eruv for both Shabbat and Yom Tov, and for the two days of Yom Tov in the Diaspora, for both days in one direction. However, there is a stringency in this, as each day requires a separate acquisition of residence (keniyat shevita), since they are distinct from each other, and how can one acquire residence from one day for the other? This is like acquiring residence on Thursday for Shabbat, which is not the case on Rosh Hashanah.

Therefore, on Yom Tov, Shabbat, and the second day of Yom Tov observed in the diaspora, when making an eruv with bread, the eruv must be complete also during twilight of the first day. If it is lost, there is no eruv for the second day. Therefore, one who makes an eruv with bread does as follows: He takes it on the eve of Yom Tov or the eve of Shabbat and remains with it until it darkens, then takes it in his hand if it was the night of Yom Tov, and brings it to his house. The next day, he takes it to the same place and leaves it there until it darkens, and eats it if it was the night of Shabbat, or brings it back if he wishes when it was the night of Yom Tov. If it was eaten on the first day, it serves as an eruv for the first day but not for the second day.

If one established an eruv by walking there, he must establish an eruv on both the first and second days. This means that on the first day, he should be there during twilight and have in mind that he is establishing his residence there. However, he should not say anything, because it is forbidden to make any preparation from Yom Tov to Shabbat, or from Shabbat to Yom Tov, or from the first day of Yom Tov to the second, even merely by speech. All the more so, he cannot establish an eruv with bread that he did not use on the first day, because it would have required a declaration of eruv, which would imply preparing from one day to the next. If he did establish an eruv, it is not considered an eruv. However, if he made the declaration, it is considered an eruv. (Magen Avraham, section 2)

This is the rule: If one made an Eruv on the first day with food, and he wants to make an Eruv with his feet on the second day, this is considered an Eruv. He should do it with intention; and if he verbalizes it, it is not an impediment. But if he wants to make an Eruv with bread also on the second day, he needs to use the same bread he used for the Eruv on the first day, and he does not need to say anything, since it has already been designated as an Eruv, and thus he is not preparing anything new. If he used different bread, it is not an Eruv. Also, the leniency to make an Eruv with his feet on the second day applies only if he made an Eruv on the first day, either with bread or with his feet. But if he did not make any Eruv at all on the first day, it seems to me that it is forbidden to make an Eruv with his feet on the second day even without verbalization, because this would be considered complete preparation and something entirely new. This is explicitly implied by the language of the Talmud (Eruvin 39a), which states: "If he made an Eruv with bread on the first day, he can make an Eruv with his feet on the second day." Meaning, even though it is a change from an Eruv with bread to an Eruv with his feet, since at any rate it was designated as an Eruv on the first day, the preparation is not so noticeable. However, if he did not make any Eruv at all on the first day, he cannot make an Eruv on the second day in any manner, and if he does, it is not considered an Eruv, because this is significant preparation. (This seems to me correct.)

And all this applies to Shabbat and Yom Tov and the two days of Yom Tov in the Diaspora. But regarding the two days of Rosh Hashanah - one sets an eruv for both days from the eve of the first day of Yom Tov, and even if it is consumed on the first day, it serves as an eruv for the second day. Similarly, if one sets an eruv with his feet on the first day, he does not need to set an eruv with his feet on the second day. This is the opinion of the Rambam in chapter 8. However, the Raavad disagrees with him and maintains that the concept of "one sanctity" is stated only as a stringency, not as a leniency. Therefore, he holds that one needs to set an eruv with his feet on the second day as well. And if one set an eruv with bread on the first day and it was consumed, he does not have an eruv for the second day. However, most authorities agree with the Rambam, that the Sages entirely equated the two days as one extended sanctity. Since this is not a Torah prohibition, and the laws of eruv techumin are rabbinic, the Sages established the mitzvah of eruv techumin and stated that the two days have one sanctity, both for leniency and for stringency. This is also the ruling of the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch.

And know, that which they have said that one can establish two eruvs for two directions for the two days - this is specifically when he is able to reach each of the two eruvs on the first day. But if he cannot reach the eruv for the second day on the first day - it is not considered an eruv for the second day, for we require that the eruv be a meal that is suitable from before the day. And even though on the two days of Yom Tov in the Diaspora, in any case, if the first day is a weekday - he can go to his eruv, and if the first day is holy - the second day is a weekday and does not need an eruv, nevertheless, since in the end he cannot reach the eruv on the first day due to the doubt - it is not an eruv (Magen Avraham, section 3).

Therefore, one must be careful not to place the Eruvin too far from each other. How so? If one placed an Eruv for the first day at the end of two thousand cubits to the east, and placed the second Eruv for the second day to the west, it is not a valid Eruv even if placed closer, since he cannot reach it during the daytime, as nothing remains for him to the west. But if he placed the Eruv for the first day one thousand five hundred cubits to the east, then he has five hundred cubits remaining to the west – he can place the Eruv for the second day up to five hundred cubits to the west and no more, because within this measure he can reach the Eruv of the second day on the first day. Yom Kippur is like Shabbat both regarding Eruvei Chatzeirot and Eruvei Techumin, and one can make an Eruv with bread. Even though he cannot eat it – nonetheless, it is suitable for a child, as we do not require a meal that is specifically suitable for him, as stated in Siman 409. Yom Tov observes Eruvei Techumin but not Eruvei Chatzeirot, as we explained the reason in Siman 397, section 4, see there.

Maimonides wrote at the beginning of the Laws of Sanctification of the New Moon: The months of the year are lunar months, as it is stated: "A burnt offering of the new moon in its month." Thus far his words, meaning: The month of the moon appears as something new. In the first half, it grows and increases, and in the second half, it wanes and diminishes until it is entirely dark, and then it renews itself. This is not the case with the solar months; no change is visible to the eye. And since the Torah says "in its month," it is explicitly clear that the renewal must be visible, and this refers to the lunar months. And it is stated: "This month shall be for you the beginning of months" – as the sages said (Rosh Hashanah 20a): The Holy One, blessed be He, showed Moses the form of the moon and said to him: "Like this, see and sanctify."

The years that we calculate are solar years, as it is stated regarding Passover: "the month of spring"; and regarding Shavuot it is written: "the Festival of Harvest"; and regarding Sukkot it is written: "the Festival of Ingathering." The growth of the crops, their harvesting, and their gathering depend only on the solar months, for the changes of the seasons—cold and heat, summer and winter—depend on the sun. The solar year exceeds the lunar year by nearly eleven days. Therefore, when this excess accumulates to approximately thirty days or slightly less, we add one month to the year, making that year have thirteen months, with two Adars: "First Adar" and "Second Adar." This year is called a "leap year." In a cycle of nineteen years, there are seven leap years, and this cycle is called a "small cycle."

And this is also the reason why sometimes we observe one day of Rosh Chodesh, and sometimes two days. Because the lunar month is twenty-nine and a half days, plus 793 parts (of an hour). Therefore, it is necessary that one month be twenty-nine days and one month be thirty days, in order to balance the missing half day. If not for the 793 parts, every month would be alternately full and deficient. But the advantage of the 793 parts accumulates over time to a complete day, and therefore we have Cheshvan and Kislev – sometimes both full, sometimes both deficient, and sometimes one full and one deficient, in order to balance the calculations.

And one should not ask: Why do we need all this effort, both with the years and the months? Since the years follow the solar months, let each year be eleven days longer than the lunar year, and we will not need to intercalate the years. These eleven days of that month will belong to the past year, and the remaining days of the month will belong to the next year. Similarly, with the months: let each month be twenty-nine and a half days and 793 parts, and let the first of the month always be one day. The thirtieth day, which is half and 793 parts, will belong to the past month, and the remaining part will belong to the next month.

The answer to this is as follows: Our sages of blessed memory expounded in the Megillah (5a): From where do we know that we do not count days to make up a year? As it is said, "for the months of the year" — you count months to make up a year, but you do not count days to make up a year. Consequently, if we were to make each year have eleven additional days over the lunar months, the next month would have some days belonging to the previous year and some to the next year — thus you would be counting days to make up a year, which the Torah forbids. Therefore, we wait until the days accumulate to a month, and we add a month, and we count the year by months. Similarly, they expounded: From where do we know that we do not calculate hours to make up a month? As it is said, "until a month's days" — you calculate days to make up a month, but you do not calculate hours to make up a month. Consequently, if we were to make each month twenty-nine days and a half and 793 parts, and the thirtieth day would be twelve hours and 793 parts for the past month, and twelve hours less 793 parts for the next month — thus you would be counting hours to make up a month, which the Torah forbids. Therefore, we wait another month, so the hours accumulate to a full day, and we make the first two days of the month, and the month is accounted for by days. I learned all this from the words of the Rambam. And it is taught in Arakhin (8b) that we do not reduce from four intercalated months in a year, nor add more than eight, see there. Also, in the early days of the prophets, we find that they made the New Moon two days. (In I Samuel 20:27, it is written: "And it came to pass on the morrow of the second day of the month," which is the second day of the New Moon. And so wrote Radak.)

There is a positive commandment from the Torah upon the Great Court, which is the Sanhedrin that was in Jerusalem during the time of the Temple, to sanctify months and years, and to calculate according to the wisdom of astronomy whether it is possible for the moon to be seen today or not, and to accept the testimony of the month, as it is stated: "This month shall be for you the head of months." And we have learned through tradition, passed down from person to person until Moses our teacher, who received it at Sinai from the Almighty, that its interpretation is: This testimony shall be entrusted to you, to Moses and Aaron, and to all who stand after you in your place. This mitzvah is not entrusted to every individual as is the Sabbath, where each person counts six days and rests on the seventh day. Rather, the New Moons and Festivals are established by the Great Court. Months are not sanctified, nor years determined, except in the Land of Israel, as it is written: "For out of Zion shall go forth the law…"

And this all applied when the Sanhedrin and ordained sages were still in the Land of Israel. But now we rely on the calculations from the calendar of Rabbi Hillel the Prince, the great-grandson of our holy Rabbi [Judah the Prince]. When he saw the great dispersion of the Jewish people, who were scattered to the four corners of the earth, and the abolition of the Sanhedrin and the ordination [of new sages]—he and his great court calculated the months and years according to the laws of the Torah and the wisdom of the constellations, and sanctified the months until the end of time. As a remembrance of this, we stand and bless the month: "The new month of such-and-such is on such-and-such day." Our main reliance is on the calculation of Rabbi Hillel the Prince and the ordained sages of his time. They sanctified all the months and festivals and intercalated all the years that needed intercalation, until the end of time. When the righteous redeemer comes, we will once again sanctify each month individually, as in ancient times. All of this was explained by Maimonides in his great book and in the enumeration of the commandments, commandment 153. (And Nachmanides there also holds this view, and he discusses it there with Maimonides. This is his conclusion, and this is also the intention of Maimonides, as the author of the "Megilat Esther" wrote there. Look there and you will find it clear.)

And therefore our custom is to stand when we bless the new month, similar to the sanctification of the month which was done standing. It seems that the reason for the custom to know the molad (the time of the new moon) when blessing the month is because the Beit Din (rabbinic court) would not sanctify the month without knowing the molad. The reason this is done on the Shabbat before Rosh Chodesh is because there is a larger congregation, allowing everyone to be informed when Rosh Chodesh will occur. I found a support for this in the Jerusalem Talmud, Sanhedrin (Chapter 5, Halacha 3), regarding the Mishnah that states one knew about the leap month and the other did not. Rabbi Yose says: "For example, like me, who from the day I did not know when the month was, did not pray the Musaf prayer." The commentator explains that this is referring to the Musaf of Rosh Chodesh, which is puzzling: since he knows he needs to pray Musaf, it is obvious he knows that today is Rosh Chodesh. Some explain that this refers to the knowledge of the molad (Tzion Yerushalayim), which is also puzzling: where is the molad mentioned here? Therefore, it seems to me that it refers to the Musaf of Shabbat, consistent with our custom.

In Tishrei, it is not customary to bless the new month on the preceding Shabbat. The hint for this is: "On the throne, for the day of our festival." Additionally, how can we mention Rosh Chodesh Tishrei on a specific day without mentioning Rosh Hashanah? And if we mention Rosh Chodesh and Rosh Hashanah on a specific day, it would be different from all other Shabbatot when the blessing for the new month is recited. Furthermore, this Rosh Chodesh is not called "Rosh Chodesh" at all but rather "Rosh Hashanah." In leap years, we say for the first Adar: "Rosh Chodesh Adar Rishon," and for the second: "Adar Sheni." It is customary to say: "He who performed miracles" and "May He renew it." This is not a prayer on Shabbat but a good sign and a hope for redemption, that just as the month is renewed, so too will Israel be renewed.
