However, regarding the custom of saying the "Yehi Ratzon" beforehand, I wonder how it is permissible to pray a new prayer on Shabbat, which is not part of the established blessings but a separate prayer? We ask for sustenance and other needs, and how is this allowed on Shabbat? This prayer is Rabbi's prayer throughout the year in the blessings (Berachot 16a). It begins with "That You grant us long life," and here they added at the beginning "That You renew for us this month for good and blessing." Therefore, some prayer books include at the end "by the merit of Rabbi's prayer." But this is nonsense: what does "by the merit of Rabbi's prayer" mean? It seems that the printers made a mistake, as the one who noted it indicated it was Rabbi's prayer, and they did not understand the meaning and added the word "by the merit of." Nonetheless, who permitted us to establish a new prayer on Shabbat? And if I had the power, I would abolish it. However, it is difficult to change a custom, and this requires great consideration.

Rosh Chodesh is permitted for work. And the women who have the custom not to do work on Rosh Chodesh – it is mentioned in the Jerusalem Talmud, the first chapter of Ta'anit, and in Pirkei DeRabbi Eliezer (chapter 44) that it is a good custom, because they did not want to give their jewelry to their husbands for the making of the Golden Calf. Therefore, they were given an additional festive day on Rosh Chodesh. And if there is a custom to do some work and some not to do – we follow the custom. And specifically when it is known that the custom has been so from long ago. But in general – women are forbidden in all work. And behold, among us, the women of householders do not work, and women who are engaged in a craft do work. And it must be said that they did not accept upon themselves to lose their livelihood.

There are pious individuals who have the custom to fast on the eve of the new month, due to the diminution of the moon. Significant matters are dependent on this, which relate to our situation. In the future, the moon will be renewed like us, as we say in the blessing of the sanctification of the moon. Therefore, some of the Kabbalists fasted until the new moon. Among those of us who fast, we fast until the evening, and refer to it as "Minor Yom Kippur." If there are ten people, we read "Vayechal" and say "Aneinu," as on any public fast. When it falls on Shabbat or Sunday, we fast on the preceding Thursday. If someone was accustomed to fasting and then becomes concerned for their health, they need an annulment. If they are truly not in good health, they do not need an annulment, as it is forbidden for them to fast. Among us, we recite the liturgical poems and confessions after the Mincha prayer, although some question this practice, and have written that it is preferable to say them before Mincha (Magen Avraham). Nevertheless, this is not the custom.

The New Moon is forbidden for fasting, as it is stated in the Jerusalem Talmud (Chapter 2, Halacha 12) of Tractate Ta'anit: "One may fast on any day, except for Sabbaths, festivals, the New Moon, intermediate days of the festival, Chanukah, and Purim." In the Babylonian Talmud, Tractate Ta'anit (17b), it is mentioned regarding the Scroll of Fasts that the New Moon is considered a Torah commandment. Some support this from what is written: "And on your joyous occasions, your festivals, and your new moons," where the New Moon is equated with festivals. The New Moon itself is called a "festival," as it is written: "He has declared a festival against me to crush my young men," referring to the New Moon of Av. In any case, our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in his major work that it is not reasonable to say that the prohibition to fast is strictly from the Torah; rather, it is very stringent and has support from the Torah, but is not strictly a Torah commandment. See there. Furthermore, there is no obligation to eat bread, only that one should not fast. Therefore, if one forgets to say "Ya'aleh Veyavo" during the Grace after Meals on the New Moon, one is not required to repeat it.

It is not decreed to fast for the community, for any trouble that may arise, on Rosh Chodesh, Chanukah, and Purim, to begin the fasts on those days. If they had already started beforehand, such as if they had previously decreed to fast for a certain number of days, and they began before Rosh Chodesh, and when they decreed, they did not specify "except for Rosh Chodesh"; therefore, if they even began one day – they do not interrupt, but rather continue and complete the fast because the decree of the court and the community is very stringent. It is considered a complete vow, and it is not a Biblical prohibition that a vow should not apply to it. Furthermore, vows can apply to a mitzvah matter. This applies to the community. But an individual who accepted upon himself to fast for a certain number of days, and Rosh Chodesh occurred, or he accepted upon himself to fast on Rosh Chodesh; if he accepted it in the manner of accepting a fast in general terms – it does not require annulment. For it is not considered a complete vow, as I wrote in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 215. If he accepted it explicitly as a vow, or if he said "it is upon me," which is like a vow – it requires annulment by a sage. And in Yoreh De'ah there it is explained in this context.

If one took an oath to fast for a certain number of days, and during those days a Rosh Chodesh (New Month) occurs—the oath certainly applies to him, even if it is a Torah commandment, due to the principle of inclusion. And if he explicitly swore to fast on Rosh Chodesh, Rabbi Yosef Karo wrote in Section 3, and this is his language: "It appears to me that the oath applies to him, since it is only rabbinic in origin. However, from the words of the Rambam, it seems that it is a Torah commandment." Until here is his language. And it will be explained in detail in Siman 491, see there. And one who fasts on Rosh Chodesh or during Chanukah and Purim as a dream fast—needs to fast another fast for his fast.

The Tur wrote: "It is a mitzvah to increase in the meal of Rosh Chodesh. For we learn in the first chapter of Megillah (in the Jerusalem Talmud) regarding the Mishnah that we advance and do not delay: but the meal of Purim and the meal of Rosh Chodesh – we delay and do not advance. Meaning: when Rosh Chodesh falls on Shabbat, since there is already a Shabbat meal – we make the meal of Rosh Chodesh on Sunday, similar to Purim that falls on Shabbat. And from the fact that it is compared to Purim – we understand that it is an obligation. Additionally, it is juxtaposed to a "festival" in the verse "and on your days of rejoicing". And it is written regarding David: "for there is a family sacrifice for us", and it was Rosh Chodesh, as it is written "and it was on the morrow of the second new moon". And in the Pesikta it is stated: all of a person's sustenance is determined for him from Rosh Hashanah, except for what he spends on Shabbatot, festivals, Rosh Chodesh, Chol HaMoed, and what children bring to their teacher. If he adds – they add for him, etc.", until here is the language of the Tur.

And so too it is written in the Rokeach (Siman 228). He also brought a verse, "And it shall be, from one New Moon to another, and from one Sabbath to another," and the verse, "Why are you going to him today, it is neither New Moon nor Sabbath," see there. And similarly, the Kolbo wrote that the meal is due to the honor of the day, which is an atonement for Israel, etc., a remembrance of the meal that they would make for the witnesses of the moon during the Temple times, etc. Thus far his language. And it seems that his intention is the meal they would make for the intercalation of the month, as it is written in the Jerusalem Talmud. And this also appears from our Talmud in Sanhedrin, regarding the rebellious and wayward son, that if he ate during the intercalation of the month – he does not become a rebellious and wayward son (70a). The great wonder is: why is it not practiced among us at all to have a meal on Rosh Chodesh? And all the more so when Rosh Chodesh falls on Shabbat, that they do not make a meal on the first day? And perhaps the world has grasped this because in our Talmud there is no mention of this. For example, the Pesikta which enumerates Rosh Chodesh among the expenditures of Shabbat and holidays – is not in our Gemara at the beginning of the second chapter of Beitzah. And also: concerning the rebellious and wayward son, it implies that the intercalation of the month is not a mitzvah, for it states: if he ate in a mitzvah group, if he ate during the intercalation of the month – we understand from this that it is not a mitzvah. And also, our teacher the Beit Yosef in his great book rejected all the Tur’s proofs, see there. Nevertheless, it is proper to be concerned about this, but what can we do, as the hand of time has been severe upon us? Even so, those who are meticulous add some food on Rosh Chodesh, and similarly on Shabbat Rosh Chodesh they add a dish in honor of Rosh Chodesh. (And what the Magen Avraham wrote regarding if one's meal extended until night, concerning the mention of "Retzeh" and "Ya'aleh VeYavo" – we explained above in Siman 188.)

The Tur wrote that it is forbidden to deliver eulogies on Rosh Chodesh, as it is taught (at the end of Moed Katan) that on Rosh Chodesh, women would wail and clap. "Wailing" means that they would all wail together, and "clapping" means clapping hand to hand. However, they would not lament, and after the deceased was buried, they would neither wail nor clap. "Lamenting" refers to when one person speaks and all respond after her, see there. 

There is a doubt regarding the intent: whether it is specifically after the burial that eulogies are forbidden, similarly to how after the burial they do not wail or clap, but before the burial it is permitted. Or perhaps it is also forbidden before the burial, since eulogies resemble lamenting. And this seems likely, because during a eulogy, the eulogizer speaks and stirs people to weep, which is similar to lamenting. 

Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, did not mention anything about the issue of eulogies. However, for a sage in his presence, it is obvious that it is permitted, and it is a mitzvah and an obligation as well. For even during Chol HaMoed, the Gemara there states: "There is no festival in the presence of a sage," and all the more so on Rosh Chodesh.

Regarding the matter of the Tziduk HaDin (the prayer recited at a funeral), the Tur brought that there was a disagreement between the people of Worms and the people of Mainz. And our teacher, the Beit Yosef, ruled that they recite the Tziduk HaDin and Kaddish. However, this is not the custom, as our teacher the Rema wrote. And it is not specifically on Rosh Chodesh, as the same applies to all days when Tachanun is not recited. And similarly, on the eve of Shabbat and the eve of a festival after midday, Tziduk HaDin is not recited. Kaddish can be recited over a Psalm, and it is our custom to recite Psalm 49 and then recite Kaddish. However, it is obvious that for a great person, one must recite the Tziduk HaDin and Kaddish, as they are also eulogized. This is also what the Tur wrote (and it has been testified about the Rema, of blessed memory). And at night, neither Tziduk HaDin nor Kaddish is recited.

In Ashkenaz, it is customary to recite the portion "U'V'Roshei Chodsheichem" (And on your New Moons) during the morning service after the portion of the daily offering. In Sephardic communities, this is not customary, because it will later be read from the Torah scroll. Specifically on Shabbat, the verses "U'V'Yom HaShabbat" (And on the Sabbath day) are recited, because they are not read from the Torah on Shabbat. This is not the case with Rosh Chodesh, which is treated like a Yom Tov, where the additional offerings of Yom Tov are not recited after the daily offering because they are read from the Torah. The same applies here for Rosh Chodesh. The reason for the Ashkenazi custom is to publicize that it is Rosh Chodesh. Yom Tov is recognized from the previous day that it is Yom Tov, but Rosh Chodesh is not recognized at all, and one might forget to say "Ya'aleh V'Yavo" in the prayer. Therefore, the verses are recited before the prayer to remind everyone (see Magen Avraham).

On Rosh Chodesh, during Maariv, Shacharit, and Mincha, one prays the Shemoneh Esrei (Eighteen Blessings) and says "Ya'aleh V'Yavo" in the blessing of "Retzeh." The sexton announces "Ya'aleh V'Yavo!" after the Half Kaddish during Maariv, and this is not considered an interruption because it is necessary for the prayer. If one did not say it during Shacharit and Mincha, they must repeat the prayer, whether it is the first or second day. During Maariv, however, one does not repeat the prayer, whether it is the first or second night, because the month is not sanctified at night (Berachot, end of the fourth chapter). Therefore, during Maariv, once one finishes the blessing "Hamachazir Shechinato L’Tzion," they should not say it again, as I have written in Siman 294 regarding "Atah Chonantanu." In Shacharit and Mincha, if one finished and has not yet begun "Modim," they should say it there. If they already started "Modim," and they remember before completing their prayer, they return to "Retzeh." If they do not remember until after completing their prayer, they must start from the beginning, even if they have not yet stepped back.

If one is accustomed to recite supplications after his prayer, as long as he has not finished the supplications, it is not considered that he has "completed his prayer." When he has finished the supplications, even if he has not moved his feet, it is still considered that he has "completed his prayer" and must return to the beginning [if he needs to repeat it]. However, there is an opinion that for this matter, supplications are preferable, and even if he has finished the supplications, as long as he has not moved his feet, he returns to "R'tzei" (Magen Avraham, subsection 2). The reason is that there is no fixed rule for supplications, and he can still say more supplications. Even though he is not accustomed to saying more than he has already said, he can still say more. Nevertheless, it is difficult to say this, and it appears from the Jerusalem Talmud, chapter five of Berachot, that once he has diverted his mind from praying further, it is considered as if he has moved his feet. It seems to depend on the recitation of "Yehiu l'ratzon" (there), meaning: if he is accustomed to saying "Yehiu l'ratzon" also after the supplications, or if he says it only after the supplications, before saying it, it is considered "he has not moved his feet." After saying it, it is considered "he has moved" (Eliyah Rabbah, subsection 5, and Machatzit HaShekel questions this, and I do not know why). And so should one instruct. (And regarding the evening prayer, which we have written that once he finishes "Who returns His presence to Zion," he should not say it again – the same applies even if he only said "Blessed are You, Lord." There is an opinion that he should say "Teach me Your statutes," and then say "Ya'aleh V'yavo," see Sha'arei Teshuvah, subsection 4. This is not clear. And so writes Sha'arei Teshuvah in the name of Magid Mishneh, see there.)

In the earlier Siman 126, it was explained that a prayer leader (Shaliach Tzibbur) who forgot to say "Ya'aleh Veyavo" during the repetition of the Amidah is not required to repeat it, due to the burden it would place on the congregation. This is because the Musaf prayer follows, in which Rosh Chodesh is mentioned, as discussed there. Based on this, several prominent authorities deduced that an individual who did not say "Ya'aleh Veyavo" during Shacharit and did not recall until after Musaf is not required to repeat the Shacharit prayer, as the individual’s status, after the fact, should not be worse than that of the prayer leader from the outset (see Magen Avraham there in the name of Rem"a and Keneset HaGedolah). Therefore, if this occurs, he is not required to repeat the prayer. If he wishes, he may pray Mincha twice, one as the obligatory prayer and the second as a compensatory prayer, intending the latter as a voluntary prayer (see Sha’arei Teshuvah, subsection 3). If he stood to pray Musaf and within the first three blessings remembered that he forgot "Ya'aleh Veyavo" during Shacharit, he should complete the first three blessings, then start from "Atah Chonen" and complete the Shacharit prayer, and afterward, pray Musaf (as stated there).

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote in section 1: If there is a doubt whether one mentioned "Ya'aleh V'Yavo" or not—one does not need to repeat [the Amidah]. Thus are his words, and it is very puzzling: for certainly he did not say it, according to his custom. And his words were rejected, and they ruled that he needs to repeat [the Amidah] (Bach and Magen Avraham, subsection 4). However, it seems his intention is: Certainly, if one did not know at all at the beginning of the prayer that today is Rosh Chodesh; or even if he knew, but at the start of the Shemoneh Esrei it did not occur to him at all that today is Rosh Chodesh—certainly he needs to repeat [the Amidah]. But if at the start of the Shemoneh Esrei he knew that today is Rosh Chodesh, and after the prayer it left his mind, and he did not remember whether he said "Ya'aleh V'Yavo" or not—in this case he said that one does not need to repeat [the Amidah]. For it is more likely that he did say it, since at the beginning he knew it was Rosh Chodesh, and therefore it is more likely that he said it (Taz, subsection 1). And this is the primary ruling.

According to Rashi of blessed memory at the end of the fourth chapter of Berachot: An individual praying with the congregation, who forgot "Ya'aleh Veyavo" – can rely on the prayer of the prayer leader, see there. The Tur wrote that the language in the Gemara does not imply this. However, regarding the law – one can certainly rely on this. And if he knows that he can concentrate and hear the entire repetition of the prayer leader – he should listen and not interrupt, and only answer "Amen" and no more, and he fulfills his obligation with this.

Reciting Hallel on Rosh Chodesh is merely a custom and not a strict law. For Hallel by law is only on Yom Tov and Chanukah, on days when miracles and salvations occurred. The custom was also in the days of the sages of the Talmud, as it is stated in Taanit (28b). And the Geonim offered an allusion: in the last psalm "Praise God in His sanctuary" there are twelve instances of "praise," corresponding to the twelve months. The repetition of the verse "Let every soul praise God" corresponds to the leap month (Beit Yosef). The primary reason seems to be that the renewal of the moon hints at our situation, as we say in the blessing of the moon. Therefore, we consider this as a partial salvation and instituted the recitation of Hallel. (The Pri Chadash questioned the allusion: in Tishrei there is no Hallel, see there. And it is not difficult at all, for the intention of the Geonim is that the matter of Rosh Chodesh involves praise. Investigate and you will find it easy.)

And since it is merely a custom, therefore, we skip "Lo Lanu" and "Ahavti," to signify that it is not an obligation. According to Rashi and the Rambam, one should not recite a blessing over it at all, whether individually or in a congregation. However, according to the Rif, it appears that the congregation recites a blessing, but not an individual. In the Land of Israel and its surroundings, the custom follows Rashi and the Rambam, and no blessing is recited, neither at the beginning nor at the end. But Rabbeinu Tam's opinion in Tosafot Berakhot (14a) is that even an individual can recite a blessing. Many customs have a blessing, and this is the common practice in these regions. The blessing at the beginning is "to recite Hallel," and at the end "King who is praised with praises."

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote in Paragraph 2 that, in any case, a person should be careful to recite (Hallel) with the congregation, in order to recite the blessing over it with the congregation. And some say that when an individual reads (Hallel), he should tell two others to recite the main parts with him, for then it is considered as if it were with many. And the custom is to do so in "Hodu" but not in "Ana." Thus far his words. The explanation of his words: Since there are many opinions that an individual should not recite the blessing, and there is a concern for a blessing in vain, therefore every person should endeavor to recite Hallel of Rosh Chodesh with the congregation. And similarly on the intermediate days of Passover and the last two days of Passover, for with the congregation, in any case, there are several opinions to recite the blessing. Therefore, even if one has not yet prayed, one should not pray but should first recite Hallel with the congregation, and afterward pray. And even if one is in the middle of the verses of praise, one should interrupt and recite Hallel with the congregation, to avoid reciting the blessing as an individual. And some offer another advice for this: that one should tell two others to recite the main parts with him, for it is considered as if it were with many and he can recite the blessing. And the custom is to do so in "Hodu." But our custom is not so. And all this is for Rosh Chodesh, the intermediate days of Passover, and the last two days of Passover. But when the Hallel is completed, none of this is necessary, as the individual is obligated to recite the blessing. And it seems to me that on Rosh Chodesh and the intermediate days, etc., those who pray with the congregation – I do not understand why they would recite the blessing by themselves, as they can respond "Amen" to the blessing of the prayer leader at the beginning and end? And the one who responds "Amen" is as if he recited the blessing, so why should we increase blessings in a place where for our great rabbis it is considered a blessing in vain? And this is also my practice.

It is a clear matter that when one recites Hallel individually, one should not say "Hodu l'Hashem" after "Yomar na Yisrael" and "Yomru na Beit Aharon" and "Yomru na Yir'ei Hashem" — "Hodu l'Hashem ki tov." This is only done in a public setting, or at least when there are three people, where one says "Yomar na" and the other two respond. This does not apply when one is alone, and even two people do not suffice unless there are three, where one says and the other two respond. The custom of Hallel among us in all countries is the same, except that some say the Psalms section by section, and some say up to "Hodu" in one go. Each should follow their custom. (And regarding the interruption of "Ana... Hoshia Na," "Ana... Hatzlich Na" into two parts, even though it is only one verse — reasons have already been written about this. The most accepted reason is that when Hallel was established, it was said in this manner, as it is stated in Pesachim 118a. Similarly, the Song at the Sea was said section by section, as stated in Sotah 30a. Therefore, those who recite Hallel divide the verses. See what I wrote above in Siman 51.)

Regarding interruptions during Hallel on days when it is completed – its laws are like those of the blessings of the Shema and the Shema itself. But on Rosh Chodesh and Chol HaMoed, etc., when it is not completed, our master the Beit Yosef wrote in section 4 that even in the middle, one may greet a person to whom he is obligated to show honor, and respond to anyone's greeting. But for other matters – he should not interrupt. Thus are his words. And it appears that his intention is according to the custom of his place, where they did not recite the blessing on Hallel on Rosh Chodesh, as I wrote earlier. But in a place where they do recite the blessing – certainly it is forbidden to interrupt, just like during the Shema, because ultimately there are blessings at the beginning and end. And if you ask: if without a blessing, why not interrupt for other matters? One could say that indeed it is so, that even without a blessing, why should one interrupt needlessly?

This is how it seemed to my humble opinion to explain. But if so, why did our Rabbi the Rema not correct it, for according to our custom, where we bless – it is forbidden to interrupt?! Rather, it is certain that he holds that even when we bless, the interruption is light, and I do not know why. But also from the Tur it is proven like our Rabbi the Rema, who wrote as follows: "And since it is not completed – it is not as severe regarding interruption as the Shema." But even in the middle...until here is his language. And if it enters your mind without a blessing – why did he depend more on the fact that it is not completed? He should have depended on the fact that it is without a blessing! Moreover, the Tur previously brought the conclusion of his father the Rosh, of blessed memory, that we bless, see there. Rather, it is certain that even though there is a blessing – the interruption is light. And we find something similar in the verses of praise according to the Ari, of blessed memory, as I wrote above in Siman 51. But the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch were stringent there like with the Shema, see there. And we must say that they hold that here it is even lighter. And this requires further investigation.

And if one interrupted and paused during it, even if the pause was long enough to complete the entire [Hallel] - he does not go back to the beginning. And even according to the one who holds earlier in Siman 65 that if one was forced to interrupt, he goes back to the beginning, in any case, since they read it in a fragmented manner - he does not need to (Beit Yosef). And it implies that when they finish Hallel - he needs to go back to the beginning in such a case. But there are those who say that in Hallel, which is only Rabbinic, even when they finish - he does not need to go back to the beginning (Darkei Moshe and Bach, and Magen Avraham section 9). And one who wishes to be stringent - should go back to read without a blessing (ibid), and this should be the instruction.

The one who recites Hallel out of order has not fulfilled his obligation, for it must be recited in order. In Megillah (17a), they derive this from the verse "From the rising of the sun to its setting"—meaning it progresses in order, see there. Therefore, if one recited and made a mistake, he should go back to the place where he made the mistake and continue from there to the end. But he should not say what he skipped at the place where he stands and then continue from there, because if so, it would be considered out of order. And if he does not remember the place where he made the mistake, he should return to the place where the doubt arose in his mind, similar to the reading of the Shema above in Siman 64. 

And the mitzvah of reciting Hallel is to be done standing. A scriptural hint to this is "Praise the servants of Hashem, who stand in the house of Hashem..." It is obvious that someone who is not in proper health can sit. Even though during the Amidah (the Eighteen Benedictions) he exerts himself to stand, nevertheless for Hallel we are not stringent, since on the nights of Pesach we recite it sitting. Leaning is not considered standing. (The Magen Avraham in subparagraph 11 critiques the Rema in Choshen Mishpat Siman 17 who wrote that leaning is considered standing. See what I wrote there in Choshen Mishpat.)

And after Hallel, one recites "Kaddish Titkabal," for whenever there is Musaf, "Kaddish Titkabal" is recited after Shacharit. The Torah scroll is taken out, and four people are called up to read from it, one more than on Mondays and Thursdays, due to the additional Musaf offering. Therefore, we do not call up fewer than four. However, neither do we add more than four, as the sages were concerned about the interruption of work. Hence, we also do not recite the Haftarah. After the Torah reading, half-Kaddish is recited.

The reading consists of the section of the Tamid offering, which is eight verses, and the section "On the Sabbath day," which is two verses, and the section "On your New Moons," which is five verses, and this is for the fourth reader. The first two sections are for three readers. Now, how should it be done? If we call the Kohen for three verses, and the Levite for three verses, then the Levite will finish less than three verses before the end of the section, and the third reader will begin less than three verses before the end of the section. Both of these are forbidden due to the decree concerning those who enter and exit, as I have written in Siman 138. Therefore, out of necessity, we read three verses up to "the lamb": "And the Lord spoke," "Command," "And you shall say." The Levite then repeats "And you shall say" with two more verses: "the lamb," "and a tenth of an ephah" up to "a continual burnt offering." Even though there is a concern that those entering might say that the Kohen only read two verses, it can be said that they will ask and be informed. But if the Levite begins from "the lamb" and reads three verses, leaving only two verses remaining, we are concerned that those exiting will say that the third reader only read two verses, and those exiting will not ask.

And if you ask: If so, should the Kohen and Levi each read the entire section of the Tamid, which is eight verses; and the third should read two verses of "And on the Sabbath day" and two verses from "And on your New Moons," leaving three verses for the fourth. And now those who leave would not question it, for they heard that the third read four verses. And if because those who enter during the fourth would say that the third only read two verses – we have said that those who enter should ask and be told, just as now those who enter during the reading of the Levi ask about the Kohen. This is not analogous, for regarding the Kohen, it makes sense to ask why he did not read more, since the Levi has a gain. But regarding the third, they would not question it at all, because they would assume he had to leave three verses for the fourth. And the blame will remain on the third, that he only read two verses.

All our Rabbis have ruled thus: the Rif in the fourth chapter of Megillah, the Rosh there, the Rambam in the thirteenth chapter of Tefillah, the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch. However, one of our later Rabbis disagrees and says that the Talmud states this in the context of the Ma'amadot, where the passages are no more than five verses. But on Rosh Chodesh, which has eight verses, we have a proper method to neither start with fewer than three verses nor leave any over. This means: the Kohen reads three verses, then the Levi reads five verses until "and on the Sabbath day." Then the third begins from "the continual burnt-offering" which is three verses before the passage, and reads them along with the passage "and on the Sabbath day" (Gra). In many places, this practice has been instituted, as it is a clear method. The Ramban also holds that the Talmud's statement applies only to Ma'amadot. But on Rosh Chodesh, it is unnecessary, since it is impossible to avoid starting with two verses from the passage. Therefore, what difference does it make whether one starts from the beginning or the end? They should read sequentially: the Kohen and Levi read six verses, and the third reads the remaining two along with the passage "and on the Sabbath day" (Ran in his name). But according to the method explained, it is not necessary at all to start with fewer than three verses near the passage. (I have seen in the Chasam Sofer and Mishkenos Yaakov attempts to reject the Gra's method. Anyone who examines it will be amazed, as his method is clear. See there.)

Afterwards, we recite "Ashrei" and "Uva L'Tzion." We do not say the psalm "Ya'ancha" because Rosh Chodesh is not a day of distress; it is a day of joy. The Torah scroll is then returned to its place. In our country, we recite "Ashrei" and "Uva L'Tzion" after the Torah is returned. We recite half-Kaddish and remove the tefillin. There is no clear reason for removing the tefillin before Mussaf, but this is the custom, as I wrote earlier in Siman 25, and it should not be changed. We then pray Mussaf. It is necessary to say "Rashei Chodashim le'amecha natata" with a kamatz. Some say "u'se'irei chatat," while others say "chataot," and we say: "zecheron l'kulam yihyu," meaning the sacrifices they offered then should also be a remembrance now. Some say "le'kulanu," and the intention is the same. Some say "hayu," referring to the past. Everyone should follow their custom. In a leap year, we add "u'lechaperet pesha." Some do not say this addition until after the second Adar, but this does not seem correct, as it should be said all year. We say "u'chukei rashei chodashim lahem kavata," meaning: among all nations, there is no uniform calculation for everyone, as it is known, because human intellect is too limited to make an equal calculation for all the days of the world. Our calculation comes from Sinai, from the Holy One, blessed be He, who conveyed it to Moses. As the ancient sages of the nations admitted, the calculation of the intercalation of months and years of Israel testifies to prophecy. In the repetition of the Shaliach Tzibbur, we say "Nekadesh" as in Shacharit. The Sephardim say "Keter." Nevertheless, the additions for Shabbat and festivals are not said. After the repetition of the Shaliach Tzibbur, "Kaddish Shalem" is recited. Some say the psalm "Barechi Nafshi," because it says there: "He made the moon for appointed times." It seems this was the song of the Levites in the Temple for the Mussaf sacrifice. I am puzzled: in Tractate Sofrim (Chapter 18), where the songs of the Mussaf offerings are listed, the one for Rosh Chodesh is not mentioned. See there. In the next section, we will resolve this with the help of Heaven. (The Magen Avraham wrote: If one prayed the Shacharit prayer instead of Mussaf, they have not fulfilled their obligation, even if they mentioned "Ya'aleh V'Yavo." This is straightforward.)

We mention "Ya'aleh V'yavo" in the Grace After Meals, before "and rebuild Jerusalem." If one did not say it, they are not required to repeat [the Grace]. This is not comparable to the prayer, which is obligatory. Nor is it comparable to "R'tzei V'hachlitzeinu" on Shabbat, where one must repeat [if omitted], because on Shabbat it is obligatory to eat bread, unlike Rosh Chodesh: although it is forbidden to fast on it, nevertheless, eating bread is not obligatory. And since it is optional—if one wishes, they eat; if not, they do not eat—therefore, one does not need to repeat [the Grace]. This is also not comparable to the Grace After Meals itself, where if one makes a mistake and forgets a blessing, they must always repeat—this is because it is a Torah obligation "and you shall eat and be satisfied and bless." But mentioning Rosh Chodesh in the Grace After Meals is a rabbinic obligation, and the rabbis did not establish to repeat except in a situation where it is obligatory to eat bread. Nevertheless, if one remembers before starting "HaTov V'HaMeitiv," they should say with the name [of God], "Blessed is He who gave new months to His people Israel for remembrance." This matter is explained at length above in Siman 188, see there.

It is stated in Massekhet Soferim, Chapter Nineteen (Halacha 9): On Rosh Chodesh, groups of elders, and of prominent individuals, and of students should sit from the afternoon onwards until the sun sets. And it is necessary to recite in the blessing over the wine: "Who creates the fruit of the vine. Blessed are You, Hashem, our God, King of the universe, Who in the cycle exalted His seekers, elevated them and taught them times, good months, the moon in its fullness, from it understanding ones; He arranged the times, our Rock adjusted the moments, in which He established those months and festivals. As it is written: 'He made the moon for festivals; the sun knows its setting.' And one says: 'For as the new heavens…' and concludes with: 'Blessed are You, Hashem, Who sanctifies Israel and the beginnings of the months.' And one says: 'Give thanks to Hashem for He is good. On this day in Jerusalem, we are all joyful and happy, Elijah the prophet will quickly come to us, the King Messiah will sprout in our days, and with the building of the Temple, joys will increase.' And the people will respond and say 'Amen! May there be many good tidings in Israel, may there be many good days in Israel, may there be many Torah students in Israel! Sanctified is the month, sanctified is Rosh Chodesh! Sanctified in its time, sanctified in its leap year! Sanctified in Torah, sanctified in Halacha! Sanctified in the upper realms, sanctified in the lower realms! Sanctified in the Land of Israel, sanctified in Zion! Sanctified in Jerusalem, sanctified in all places of Israel! Sanctified by the mouths of our Rabbis, sanctified in the Beit Midrash! Give thanks to Hashem for He is good, and all of you are blessed, blessed…” Up to here is his wording. And it appears that this was at the time of the sanctification of the month, fortunate is the eye that saw all these. And may Hashem grant us to see all these speedily in our days, Amen.

In the previous section, we were puzzled as to why the Musaf song for Rosh Chodesh is not mentioned in Tractate Sofrim. It seems to me that at the beginning of chapter nineteen it states: "On Rosh Hashanah one says: 'Clap hands, all you nations.' On Yom Kippur: 'Bless the Lord, O my soul' and 'Out of the depths, I have called you.' On Sukkot: 'Known in Judah...'" Refer there. It is not understood: what relevance does "Bless the Lord, O my soul" have to Yom Kippur (the Gra deleted this)? And further, regarding its beginning, where it says: On Rosh Hashanah. Therefore, it seems to me that it should be said as follows: On Rosh Chodesh "Bless the Lord, O my soul", on Rosh Hashanah one says "Clap hands, all you nations", and on Yom Kippur "Out of the depths...". According to this, it appropriately mentions the Musaf song for Rosh Chodesh.

Rosh Chodesh that falls on Shabbat: during Ma'ariv, Shacharit, and Mincha, one prays the seven blessings and says "Ya'aleh V'Yavo" in the Avodah (service) blessing, which is in the "Retzei" blessing before "Ve'techezena." One does not mention Shabbat in "Ya'aleh V'Yavo" since Shabbat has already been mentioned in the fourth blessing (Tur). Additionally, in Shabbat Ma'ariv, if one forgets to say "Ya'aleh V'Yavo," he is not required to repeat the prayer. Although the Ma'ariv prayer on Shabbat is obligatory in order to sanctify Shabbat, and unlike weekday Ma'ariv which is optional, nonetheless, since the month is not sanctified at night, this is the reason he is not required to repeat it, as I wrote in Siman 422. Therefore, it makes no difference whether it is a weekday or Shabbat. In Musaf, we say "Ata Yatzarta" and mention both: Shabbat and Rosh Chodesh, and we conclude with "Mekadesh HaShabbat V'Yisrael V'Rashei Chadashim" (Who sanctifies Shabbat, Israel, and the New Moons). For Shabbat is inherently sanctified, but Rosh Chodesh and festivals depend on Israel, as I wrote in Siman 417. If one concluded only with "Mekadesh HaShabbat" or only with "Rosh Chodesh," it seems to me that he has not fulfilled his obligation and must repeat it. However, I have seen someone write that he has fulfilled his obligation (Eliyah Rabbah in the name of Knesset HaGedolah), but I do not understand the reasoning for this, as the main part is the conclusion. (And the Magen Avraham in Siman 487 remains in doubt about this. In my humble opinion, there is no doubt about this. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

And know that I have always wondered about our text, that at the end of "Ata Yatzarta" after "Mechilat Avon" we say: "For You have chosen Your people Israel... and Your holy Sabbath..." – why don't we say "Sanctify us with Your commandments and give us our portion... and grant us... and let Israel, who sanctifies Your name, rest on it, for You have chosen Your people Israel..."? For every festival that falls on Shabbat, and Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur that fall on Shabbat, we say this text at the end of the middle blessing, as this is the essence of the sanctity of Shabbat. So why not say this on Rosh Chodesh that falls on Shabbat? And in the Sephardic text, this text indeed exists. And in my humble opinion, in the Ashkenazi text this is missing from the print, and I make it a practice to say it, and there is no reason not to say it. And I have not found anyone who has commented on this.

Two Torah scrolls are taken out, and in the first, seven or more are called up for the weekly portion. The second Torah scroll is placed on the table, and Kaddish is recited over both of them. The first Torah scroll is then lifted and rolled up. In the second Torah scroll, the Maftir reads "On the Sabbath... and on your New Moons." The regular Haftarah of the week is set aside, and the Haftarah "The heavens are My throne" is read, since it mentions "From one New Moon to another and from one Sabbath to another." In the blessings of the Haftarah, only the Sabbath is mentioned, not the New Moon, because there is no prophet specifically for the New Moon, unlike other special days that have specific prophetic readings. Therefore, the concluding blessing is "Who sanctifies the Sabbath, Israel, and the festivals," which is not the case for the New Moon. If the New Moon falls on a Sunday, the Haftarah "And Jonathan said to him, Tomorrow is the New Moon" is read. If the New Moon is two days, on the Sabbath and Sunday, Rabbi Yosef Karo wrote that "The heavens are My throne" is read, and it is customary to also read the first and last verses of "Tomorrow is the New Moon" as a reminder that the next day is also the New Moon. This is his language. However, Rabbi Moshe Isserles wrote that some say not to interrupt from one prophet to another, and only the Haftarah of the Sabbath and New Moon is read, and this is the prevailing custom. This is his language. This is also our custom, not to mention. However, if such a case occurs with the same prophet, they would do so. Similarly, in some places, it is customary to read for a groom "I will greatly rejoice," and if this occurs on the New Moon or one of the other Sabbaths of the year, the "I will greatly rejoice" is set aside and said at the end, if the Haftarah was from the same prophet, i.e., Isaiah. It is explained later in Siman 428 that other Haftarot are deferred for it, see there. However, we do not know of this custom at all.

The Haftarah of Shabbat Rosh Chodesh is deferred in favor of the Haftarah of one of the Four Parshiyot, which are: Shekalim, Zachor, Parah, and HaChodesh. This is because these have a greater obligation than Rosh Chodesh. Additionally, the one who reads the Maftir portion reads from the Torah in the Four Parshiyot. Therefore, also on Chanukah, when Rosh Chodesh Tevet falls on Shabbat, we read the Haftarah of Chanukah, as will be explained in Siman 684. All the more so, the Haftarah of "Machar Chodesh" is deferred in their favor.

And if Shabbat coincides with Rosh Chodesh during one of the seven weeks of consolation, such as Rosh Chodesh Elul that falls on Shabbat – our master, the Beit Yosef, holds that "The heavens are my throne" is also deferred, and "O afflicted, storm-tossed" is recited. However, our master the Rema holds that it is not deferred, and on the contrary, the one from the consolations is deferred for two reasons: One: Even in "The heavens are my throne" there are consolations for Jerusalem (Taz). Furthermore, since the maftir reads from the Torah for Rosh Chodesh – it is necessary to also read the Haftorah for Rosh Chodesh. And similarly, during the three weeks of affliction, such as Rosh Chodesh Av that falls on Shabbat – some say that the Haftorah for Rosh Chodesh is deferred, and some say that "Hear" is deferred, and "The heavens are my throne" is read. And this is the main ruling in places where there is no contrary custom. And so they practiced in Pozna (Levush and Magen Avraham), and so we practice because this is the main ruling. However, the Haftorah of "Tomorrow is the new moon" is definitely deferred, whether for "Hear" or for "O afflicted, storm-tossed," since there is no Torah reading for it.

We learn in Sanhedrin (42a): Anyone who blesses the new month at its proper time is as if they received the Divine Presence. It is written here: "This month" (Exodus 12:2), and it is written there: "This is my God, and I will glorify Him" (Exodus 15:2). And the school of Rabbi Yishmael taught: If the Israelites merited only to greet their Father in Heaven once a month, it would suffice. Abaye said: Therefore, we should say it while standing. It is thus explained that the sanctification of the moon is a great and awe-inspiring matter, like receiving the Divine Presence. Certainly, there are great and awesome secrets in this, as the Kabbalistic sages have elaborated: the matter of the diminution of the moon and the matter of the sin of Adam are interconnected. In the future, when the sin of Adam is rectified, the diminution of the moon will also be rectified. Concerning that time, it is said: "And the light of the moon will be like the light of the sun" (Isaiah 30:26).

In its simple understanding, the reason why we bless the moon more than all the stars, even though it is smaller than almost all the stars (except for one star), is because it is closer to the Earth than all the stars. It is only approximately 43,000 parasangs away from the Earth. In it, we perceive the greatness of the Holy One, Blessed be He, every night through its observable movement and its monthly orbit around the Earth. Therefore, it is called "Yareach" (moon), as it is written: "He made the moon for appointed times," because it orbits the Earth every month, and its waxing and waning is noticeable. And Israel, who count by the moon, are compared to the moon: just as the moon has no light of its own but illuminates from the light of the sun, so too Israel has no light except for the light of the Holy One, Blessed be He, which shines upon us through the holy Torah, as it is said: "For the Lord God is a sun and shield." And just as the moon darkens and then illuminates, so too Israel, as we say in its blessing: "And to the moon He said that it should renew itself as a crown of glory for those borne from the womb, who are destined to renew themselves like it." And just as the moon, even in its days of deficiency when it appears dark on the Earth, still illuminates in the heights, so too Israel. And for all these reasons, Israel accepted this commandment with joy.

Therefore, one who sees the moon in its renewal blesses: "Blessed... Who with His word created the heavens...". The reason why the firmament is called "heavens" here is because it is said in Chagigah (12b): "Heavens" - where mills stand and grind manna for the righteous. However, Rav Yehuda, who states this saying about the blessing of the moon in Sanhedrin (42a), holds in Chagigah there that there are two firmaments: "heaven" and "heavens of heavens". And it is possible that the two are firmament and heavens, and his intention is: even though it is clear that there are seven firmaments, they are nevertheless included in two. For in the Bible, we find only these two names for the firmaments: "firmament" and "heavens", and they are "heaven" and "heavens of heavens". And this is what it means: "With His word He created heavens, and with the breath of His mouth all their host" - because David said: "By the word of the Lord the heavens were made, and by the breath of His mouth all their host". And it says: "He gave them a statute and time, that they should not change their function". The "time" is all the days of the world, and they are six thousand years, happy and rejoicing to do the will of their Creator, as it is written: "He rejoices like a strong man to run his course". And it says the phrase "joy and gladness", just as this phrase is destined for Israel, as it is said: "Joy and gladness will be found therein, thanksgiving and the voice of melody". "Workers of truth whose work is truth" - this is Rashi's version, and it refers to the sun and the moon, which do not change their function. And the Tosafot version is "Worker of truth whose work is truth", and it refers to the Holy One, Blessed be He, who justly and truly diminished the moon. "And to the moon He said that it should renew..." - this refers to the future, when it will be completely renewed. And for the present - it renews every month. And it is a sign for Israel, who are "those burdened from the womb", as the prophet said: "Those burdened from the womb". Meaning: burdened with troubles. And it concludes "Blessed... Who renews the months".

Afterwards, the custom is to say: "Blessed be your Creator..." in reference to Jacob. Some begin: "Blessed be your Maker" according to the order of the worlds. He then dances three times on his toes and says: "Just as I... fall...", and three times in reverse. It is customary to say: "David, King of Israel, lives and endures", referring to the descendants of David. The kingdom of the house of David is compared to the moon, as it is written in Psalms: "His seed shall endure forever... it shall be established like the moon." This means: even though it darkens, it will shine again afterwards. Afterwards, they say to each other: "Peace be upon you...". "The voice of my beloved... resembles my beloved...", "A song of ascents...", "Praise God in His sanctuary...", "The academy of Rabbi Yishmael taught, if not for...", and the "May it be Your will" as written in the prayer books. Rabbi Moshe Isserles (the Rema) wrote: Therefore, the custom is to say "David...", as his kingdom is compared to the moon and is destined to be renewed like it. And the community of Israel will once again cling to the Holy One, blessed be He, similar to the moon which renews with the sun, as it is said: "The Lord God is a sun and a shield...". Therefore, they make celebrations and dances at the sanctification of the new moon, similar to the joy of a wedding. Thus far his words. The main thing is the blessing, which is essential. If one did not say the other things, it does not invalidate the process. (And he should shake the hem of his garment.)

One should only sanctify the moon at night, at a time when it is shining and one can benefit from its light. Not before nightfall, because we need its shine to be noticeable on the earth, meaning that it casts a shadow. At the time of the blessing, one should straighten one's legs, lift one's eyes to the moon, and bless while standing. Some have written that one should lift one's eyes to look at it only before the blessing, but during the blessing, one should lower one's eyes and not look at it. And thus is the custom according to the Kabbalah.

It is stated in Masechet Soferim (beginning of Chapter 20): One should only recite the blessing over the moon on Saturday night, when one is fragrant and in fine clothing. This is the version of the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch, Section 2. Some have the version: One should not recite the blessing over the moon until it is fragrant, meaning until it is dark and one can benefit from its light, similar to the previous rule (this is the version of the students of Rabbeinu Yonah in the fourth chapter of Berachot). And they do not have the version: on Saturday night, for what relevance does Saturday night have here? Even according to our version, it is not meant to be an absolute requirement, but merely an enhancement if possible. It is written that when one sanctifies on Saturday night, there will be success (Magen Avraham, subsection 2).

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote: Specifically, if the night of the conclusion of Shabbat is within the first ten days of the month, then we wait until the conclusion of Shabbat. But if it is after that, we do not wait until the conclusion of Shabbat, lest there be two or three or four cloudy nights, and the moon will not be seen, and the time will pass. And when sanctifying it during the week, one should wear nice clothes. Thus far his words. And in our regions during the winter months, particularly in Cheshvan and Kislev, one should not wait until the conclusion of Shabbat. For in most years in our country, the skies are overcast all the time during these months. And we also do not have the custom of wearing nice clothes, because usually the sanctification is done in the synagogue courtyard after the evening prayer, and how can one go home to change clothes? This is obviously impossible. And it seems to me that the intention is not for expensive clothes, like those worn on Shabbat and festivals, but clean clothes, since one is receiving the Divine Presence. Therefore, it follows that the clothes in which one prays are considered nice. For indeed, one also needs clean and respectable clothes for prayer, as I wrote above in section 91, see there.

He also wrote: One does not sanctify the moon before Tisha B'Av, nor before Yom Kippur. And on the night after Yom Kippur, one sanctifies it, for then one is in a state of joy. But not on the night after Tisha B'Av, nor on other fast days. Thus far his words. The reason one does not sanctify before Tisha B'Av is because they are in sorrow over the destruction [of the Temple]. Therefore, also a mourner during the seven days of mourning should not sanctify, unless the time will pass, then it is necessary to sanctify. And before Yom Kippur, it is because they are in sorrow over the atonement of sins.

There are those who completely question these delays, as we are concerned that one might die. Furthermore, the diligent perform mitzvot early (Eliyah Rabbah in the name of Beit Yaakov). And there are those who reject this, arguing that for a short time we do not fear death. And delaying a mitzvah for the sake of beautification is permissible (ibid.). However, in our countries where clouds are frequent, it is not advisable to wait, and so the great ones have practiced not to wait.

If the new moon was not sighted until the last night, and they are in the midst of prayer and the moon is sighted, and it is likely that by the time they finish the prayer the time will have passed, if they are in the middle of the Shema and its blessings, they need to interrupt, even in the middle of a section. If they can finish until the end of the section, all the better. Similarly, in such a case, they need to interrupt during the reading of the Megillah (Shaarei Teshuva in the name of Noda Bihudah). However, such an occurrence is rare, and there is no need to elaborate on this.

Our teacher, the Rema, also wrote: that one should not betroth on Motzei Shabbat that coincides with a Yom Tov. This is his wording. And certainly, one should not betroth on Shabbat (Magen Avraham, Siman Katan 7). The reasons provided for this in the halachic discourse are not convincing. The truth is that according to the law, there is no concern about this, but there are mystical reasons according to Kabbalah. Therefore, it is obvious that if there are several more nights, one should not betroth on Shabbat. And if Shabbat is the last night, it is obvious that one should betroth. However, even if there is one more night, it seems that in our country, which is prone to clouds, one should betroth on Shabbat. And there were times we acted accordingly, and it happened that on the subsequent Motzei Shabbat, the skies were covered with clouds. However, it is clear that if one betroths on Shabbat, only the blessing should be recited, and not the prayers and verses. For it is certain that one should shorten as much as possible, and only the blessing is essential.

Until when can one recite the blessing on it? Until the sixteenth day from the new moon, but not including the sixteenth. This is the ruling of the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch, section 3. Similarly, the Rambam in the tenth chapter of Berachot writes: until the sixteenth, and his intention is: up to but not including the sixteenth. For in the Gemara there it is said: until its blemish is filled, and when the fifteenth day is completed, its blemish is filled, and afterwards it begins to wane. Therefore, our teacher the Ramah wrote: one should only sanctify it until half of twenty-nine days, twelve hours, and 793 parts from the new moon; for this is the time of the moon's cycle, as I have written in section 417. Therefore, at half of this time, its blemish is filled. He did not write in the language of "some say," because he believes that the intention of the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch is the same, and they did not concern themselves with the extra hours. Additionally, the extra hours are only when the new moon occurs at the beginning of the day, which is a rare occurrence, and usually, the new moon occurs many hours into the day. Thus, when half of twenty-nine days, twelve hours, and 793 parts are completed, the fifteen days will be completed as well. On the contrary, sometimes the fifteen days will be completed and yet the half of twenty-nine days, twelve hours, and 793 parts will not be completed, such as when the new moon falls within the second half of the day. Indeed, it is impossible to be precise to the exact hours, because at that time its waning is not noticeable at all. Therefore, the Talmud and the legal authorities did not concern themselves with a few hours here and there. Thus, our teacher the Ramah says that one should initially be careful not to delay beyond half of twenty-nine days, twelve hours, and 793 parts. There is no practical difference in the law. (This seems to be my humble opinion. With this, all the doubts of the Magen Avraham in subsection 12 will be resolved, see there. Be precise and you will find it easy.) (And what the Tur wrote: from the time of the new moon – he does not mean from day to day, as the Magen Avraham wrote, but as I have written, not from the beginning of the month.)

And I have seen someone who brought in the name of a great authority: that even on the sixteenth day from the new moon, it is permissible to sanctify the moon (Shiyarei Knesset HaGedolah). He explains that what the Gemara says "until the sixteenth" means up to and including the sixteenth. And there are those who bring proof to this, since in the Gemara there is a dispute between Rav Yehudah and Nehardea. Rav Yehudah holds up to seven days, and Nehardea up to sixteen. And the halachah follows Nehardea. If so, just as for Rav Yehudah it is up to and including, so too for Nehardea (Eliyah Rabbah, section 8). However, this is not a proof at all. For even in one Mishnah, in adjacent statements, we find that the first is "up to and not including" and the second is "up to and including." This is in the nineteenth chapter of Keilim: A rope coming out of a bed—up to five handbreadths is pure. From five to ten—it is impure, see there. The Gemara in Chullin (55a) explains that "five" is like the higher measure, and "ten" is like the lower measure, see there. All the more so with two Amoraim. Furthermore, it is explicitly stated at the end of the chapter "HaRoeh Ketan" that all measurements of the Sages regarding this matter of "up to and including" or "not including" are stringent, see there. If so, here it follows that in cases of doubt regarding blessings, we are lenient. The stringency is due to the concern of a blessing in vain. Especially since this is against the reasoning that the blessing "Renewer of the months" should be recited when the moon is deficient. Therefore, Heaven forbid to rely on this against all our early authorities, the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch. (And there are those who in Marcheshvan, when the moon is not visible due to the abundance of clouds in this month, say it is found in Tana Devei Eliyahu that when the moon is not seen in Marcheshvan, it is a bad sign, and they wish to rely on this opinion. But "You shall be wholehearted with the Lord your God," and do not enter into a blessing in vain. And indeed in Tana Devei Eliyahu it is not about the absence of the moon, but about the eclipse of the moon. This is in Tana Devei Eliyahu Zuta, chapter sixteen, see there.)

From when is it permitted to recite the Kiddush Levanah (sanctification of the moon)? The Rambam in the tenth chapter of Berakhot, law 17 wrote: If one did not bless it on the first night, one may bless it until... its blemish is filled. Thus are his words, clearly implying that even on the first day from the new moon one can bless. Similarly, Rashi wrote in Sanhedrin there, and these are his words: If one did not bless today, one blesses tomorrow until the seventh... until the sixteenth, see there. And the students of Rabbeinu Yonah wrote at the end of the fourth chapter of Berakhot that on the second or third day one can bless. However, on the first day, due to its smallness, the light is not sweet, and one does not derive pleasure from it. And there are those who wrote after three days (Bach). And it is surprising about Rabbeinu Beit Yosef in section 4 who wrote: One does not bless on it until seven days have passed over it. Thus are his words, and he wrote in his larger book that thus wrote R. Yitzchak Giqatilla, see there. And it is puzzling: how did he leave the opinion of our rabbis and adopt a singular opinion? And this is not his usual way. Additionally, they challenged him: for in the Gemara, there is one who holds that after seven days one should not sanctify, and how can one say it is forbidden to sanctify before (Bach and Taz section 3)? Therefore, the great later authorities agreed that after three days one can bless without any hesitation, and so is the practice. (And the Beit Yosef based his words here on the Kabbalists. And they interpret the Gemara as not disagreeing, and the one who says until the seventh refers to the beginning; and the one who says until the sixteenth refers to the end. Meaning: from the seventh until the sixteenth. And even now many practice thus, and it is good in countries where clouds are not common. But in our countries, and especially in the months of Marcheshvan and Kislev, it is difficult to practice thus. And be precise and you will find the truth.)

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote: "One should not sanctify the moon under a roof." This is his language, and we do not know the reason. Some have written the reason: so that no impurity should overshadow it (Magen Avraham, section 14, in the name of the Maharil). Others have written: because one goes out into the street, as one goes out to greet the king (ibid., in the name of the Bach). However, all this applies where it is possible. But if one has some ailment, or it is difficult in that place to stand outside and sanctify, or he is sitting in an assembly—he opens the window and sanctifies it from his house, and sees the moon through the window. And so did the Maharshal conduct himself (ibid.). There are those who wrote that one who sees the moon through glass should not recite the blessing on it (Be'er Heitev, section 1, in the name of Devar Shmuel). This is surprising: for we hold that seeing nakedness through glass—it is forbidden to recite the Shema opposite it, because it is considered as seeing, as I have written above in section 75. And since it is considered seeing—he sees the moon. Indeed, the great authorities have disputed this (as written by the Sha'arei Teshuvah, section 11). Some have written that a blind person is obligated to sanctify the moon (Magen Avraham, beginning of this section, in the name of the Rashal). One must say that this is compared to the blessing "Creator of the lights" which a blind person blesses, as I have written at the end of section 69. However, the term "the one who sees" does not fit well for a blind person, as he does not see. And so I found that one of the great authorities questioned this (Rabbi Akiva Eiger, in the name of the Rikash). Women have not adopted the practice of reciting the birkat halevana (blessing of the moon), because it is a positive time-bound commandment, and they are exempt. And although in several positive commandments they have adopted the practice, such as shofar, lulav, and sukkah—nevertheless, in this they have not adopted the practice. And in the Gemara, it is explicitly implied that in their days, women also recited a short blessing: "Blessed is He who renews the months," see there.

When Rosh Chodesh (the new month) is two days, the days of the month begin to be counted from the second day, except for Tishrei, where the counting begins from the first day because Elul is not extended. The reason we observe two days of Rosh Hashanah is specifically because of Rosh Hashanah, as will be explained in its place. However, for the other months, when there are two days of Rosh Chodesh, the first day belongs to the previous month, due to the reasons explained in Siman 417. Therefore, the Tur and Shulchan Aruch ruled here regarding documents, and in Even HaEzer Siman 126 regarding divorce documents, that when one writes a document or a get (divorce document) on the first day of Rosh Chodesh, they write, "on the first day of Rosh Chodesh of such and such month, which is the thirtieth day of the previous month." And for documents, it is acceptable to write at the outset "on the first day of Rosh Chodesh of such and such month," and no more. However, for a get (divorce document), there is a stricter requirement. And even if written otherwise, it is valid after the fact. See what I wrote in Even HaEzer there.

When the year is a leap year, one writes "Adar" simply in the first [month], as this is the main opinion according to most decisors. In the second [month], one writes "Second Adar." If one wrote "Adar" simply in the second, it is invalid. Similarly, when blessing the month. And so ruled our master, the Rema. However, some are concerned based on what appears from the words of Maimonides in the tenth chapter of Nedarim, that the main [Adar] is the second. Therefore, even in the first, one should write and announce "First Adar," and this is the custom. But the main ruling is that the main [Adar] is the first. And similarly, one should act regarding a yahrzeit. In Yoreh De'ah, Siman 220, we elaborated on this, see there.

These are the days on which the festivals are not set: Rosh Hashanah does not fall on Sunday, Wednesday, or Friday; Yom Kippur does not fall on Sunday, Tuesday, or Friday; the 14th of Adar (Purim) does not fall on Monday, Wednesday, or Friday; Passover does not fall on Monday, Wednesday, or Friday; Shavuot and Hoshana Rabbah do not fall on Tuesday, Thursday, or Saturday; Hanukkah does not fall on Tuesday; the Fast of Esther does not fall on Sunday, Tuesday, or Friday; and the 17th of Tammuz and the 9th of Av do not fall on Monday, Wednesday, or Friday. And it is always the case that the day of Purim determines the day of Lag BaOmer, as a mnemonic: "PeLaG" (which means "split" or "divided," and indicates the relationship). And the day of Shavuot determines the day of the following Hanukkah if the months are in order or lacking; but when the months are full, it will fall on the second day of Shavuot.

These are the days on which Rosh Chodesh (the New Moon) is established, and not on other days: Nisan [falls on] 1, 6; Iyar [falls on] 2, 7; Sivan [falls on] 3, 4, 6; Tammuz [falls on] 1, 6; Av [falls on] 2, 7; Elul [falls on] 1, 4, 6; Tishrei [falls on] 2, 7; MarCheshvan [falls on] 3, 5, 7; Kislev [falls on] 1, 2, 3, 4, 6; Tevet [falls on] 1, 2, 3, 4, 6; Shevat [falls on] 2, 3, 4, 6; Adar [falls on] 1, 2, 4, 6. In a leap year: the first Adar [falls on] 2, 5, 7, and the second Adar [falls on] 1, 2, 4, 6. When Rosh Chodesh is two days, the signs are for the second day, as the days of the month begin from it, as I wrote in the previous section.

A sign for the determination of the festivals: א"ת ב"ש ג"ר ד"ק ה"ץ ו"ף. Explanation: On the first day of Passover – it will always be Tisha B'Av, and the sign is: "On matzah and maror they shall eat it." On the second day, Shavuot; on the third day, Rosh Hashanah; on the fourth day, the Reading of the Torah, meaning Simchat Torah; on the fifth day, the Fast of Yom Kippur; on the sixth day, the Purim that has passed.

The Torah portion "Tzav" is always read before Passover in a regular year, and "Metzora" in a leap year; except when Rosh Hashanah falls on a Thursday and the year is a leap year, in which case "Acharei Mot" is read before Passover. The portion "Bamidbar" is always read before Shavuot. Tisha B'Av occurs before "Va'etchanan." "Nitzavim" is read before Rosh Hashanah, and therefore, when Rosh Hashanah falls on a Monday or Tuesday, with two Shabbatot between Rosh Hashanah and Sukkot, "Nitzavim" and "Vayelech" are split so that "Vayelech" is read between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, and "Ha'azinu" is read between Yom Kippur and Sukkot. The mnemonic for this is: "B"G Hamelech Pat Vayelech," meaning: "B"G" - when we say "Hamelech Hakadosh" on Monday and Tuesday, "Pat Vayelech" - from the phrase "Patot Ota Patim." But when Rosh Hashanah falls on a Thursday or Friday, there is only one Shabbat between Rosh Hashanah and Sukkot because Yom Kippur falls on Shabbat. "Ha'azinu" is read then, and thus "Nitzavim" is read together with "Vayelech" before Rosh Hashanah. The mnemonic for a regular year is: "Pakdu U'Paskhu," indicating that "Tzav," which means command, is read, and then Passover is celebrated. For a leap year: "Sageru (the metzora) U'Paskhu, Manu ("Bamidbar" which is a census) U'Atzaru (Atzeret), Tzomu U'Tzalu (Va'etchanan which is prayer), Komu (Nitzavim) U'Tik'u."

The Torah portion "Ha'azinu" – the portions are divided as they were in the Temple: "Ha'azinu," "Zachor," "Yarkivehu," "Vayar," "Lu Chachamu," "Ki Esha," until the end of the song. And these are: "Ha'azinu," "Zachor," "Yarkivehu," "Vayar," "Lu Chachamu," "Ki Esha," until the end of the song. The seventh reader reads from the end of the song until the end of the portion. According to Rashi, instead of "Lu Chachamu," "Ki Esha" – they read "Lulei," "Ki Yadin." The custom follows the first opinion. No additional readers are added on this Shabbat. This applies to the Shacharit service on Shabbat, but at Mincha and on Mondays and Thursdays – they may read as they wish. Similarly, on Rosh Chodesh Tevet or Adar that falls on Shabbat, and when three Torah scrolls are taken out – no additional readers are added, because the seventh must read from the Rosh Chodesh portion, and it should be counted among the readers (as explicitly clarified in Megillah 29b).

The curses in the Torah portion of Leviticus should not be interrupted; rather, one person should read them all. One should begin with the preceding verses and end with the verses following them. The third reader must read the admonitions. However, the third reader should not read up to the admonitions and then have the fourth reader start again from the portion the third reader read, as this would be a disgrace to the Torah, Heaven forbid. But the curses in Deuteronomy can be interrupted according to the law, yet the custom is not to interrupt them. Similarly, one should begin with the preceding verses and end with the verses following them. Our master, the Rema, wrote in Section 5 that one should not call someone by name to read the admonitions; instead, anyone who wishes may come up. In our custom, we do not practice this. If someone does not want to go up for the admonitions, they should leave the synagogue beforehand. However, if they are in the synagogue and do not go up, it is a disgrace to the Torah, Heaven forbid. The custom is that the reader himself goes up for the admonitions. Similarly, the last eight verses of the Torah should not be interrupted; rather, one person reads them all. Likewise, in the forty-two journeys in the portion of "Masei," one should not interrupt during the Sabbath morning service because they correspond to the forty-two-letter name of God (Magen Avraham, Section 8).

From the seventeenth of Tammuz onwards, we read three haftarot of calamity: "The words of Jeremiah," "Hear," "Vision"; and seven of comfort: "Comfort," "Zion said," "Afflicted, storm-tossed," "I, I am He," "Sing, barren one," "Arise, shine," "I will greatly rejoice"; and two of repentance: on the fast of Gedaliah at Mincha "Seek," and on the Shabbat between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur "Return." And if Rosh Hashanah falls on Monday and Tuesday, so that there is a Shabbat between Yom Kippur and Sukkot when we read "Ha'azinu," we then read "David spoke" as the haftarah. Some say that in such a case, we read "Seek" between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur and "Return" between Yom Kippur and Sukkot, but this is not the custom. And throughout the year on Shabbat, we read a haftarah related to the parsha. When two portions are read, the haftarah is from the second portion, except for "Acharei Mot" and "Kedoshim," when we read "Are you not like the children of Cushites," which is the haftarah of "Acharei Mot." In Siman 428, we explained that on Shabbat Rosh Chodesh, these haftarot of repentance and comfort are postponed, and we read "The heavens are My throne," but not for "Tomorrow is the new moon," see there. It is written to read "I will greatly rejoice" at a wedding. We do not know of this custom at all. It has already been clarified there that we do not skip from one prophet to another. We did not trouble to write the calendar calculations, as they are printed in the thousands and tens of thousands every year and are known to everyone, and everyone has a calendar. And with this, we have concluded, with God's help, the laws of Rosh Chodesh. May the Merciful One grant us the coming of our Messiah, and then we will offer our obligatory sacrifices: the daily offerings in their order and the additional offerings of Rosh Chodesh according to their laws. Amen. With the help of Heaven, the laws of Rosh Chodesh are concluded.

Nisan is the head of the months. Because of its greatness, even though the years are counted from Tishrei, nonetheless the months are counted from Nisan, as it is stated: "This month shall be for you the head of the months; it shall be the first for you of the months of the year." That is to say, because it is the head of all the months, it remains the first in the counting of the months. And what is the greatness of the month of Nisan? Because in it was the Exodus from Egypt. Through this, God's providence over His creations was revealed, and His signs and wonders; and that He repays the wicked according to their wickedness, and repays good to those who love Him. Just as He struck Pharaoh and Egypt, and redeemed Israel.

And why was this month chosen? Because the Egyptians worshipped the ram, which is the chief of the constellations in the circular zodiac, and the constellation of the ram serves in the month of Nissan. And Pharaoh relied on its power and constellation. Therefore, even though in the plague of hail his stubborn heart was broken, to the point that he said, "The Lord is righteous, and I and my people are wicked," nevertheless, afterwards, in the plague of locusts, he raised his head, as it is written: "And he drove them out." And in the plague of darkness, he acted with great audacity, to the point that he said to Moses our teacher: "Do not see my face again." And the reason is because the days of Nissan were approaching, and he relied on his constellation in this month. And this is what the Holy One, blessed be He, said to Moses: "This month shall be for you the head of the months," meaning: this month that Pharaoh is waiting for – it shall be the head of the months for you, through which it will become clear that there is no substance to the constellations. And the Lord is the God, in the heavens above and on the earth below, there is no other; and Israel is His chosen people. Therefore, it is the first for you of the months of the year.

Because of the greatness of this month, the Tabernacle was also erected on the first of Nissan, as it is written in "Pekudei": "And the princes brought" their offerings day by day for the dedication of the altar, as it is written in "Naso", and each prince made his day a festival. Similarly, in the future, the Temple is destined to be built in Nissan, as it is taught in the last chapter of Tractate Sofrim. It also says there that, therefore, we do not recite supplications all the days of Nissan, and we do not fast until Nissan has passed, except for the firstborn who fast on the eve of Passover. We do not say "Tzidkatcha Tzedek" at the Mincha service on Shabbat, and we do not deliver eulogies. We also do not recite "Tziduk HaDin". 

From the words of our teacher, the Beit Yosef, it is clear that only public fasts are forbidden. But an individual by himself may fast. He wrote: "We do not fast to make mention in public." But our teacher, the Rema, wrote that the custom is not to fast at all during Nissan, even on the day of one's father's or mother's passing. A groom on his wedding day may fast, as I wrote later in section 573. As for a fast due to a bad dream, it is obvious that one may fast, and it is not necessary to observe another fast for having fasted on Shabbat or a festival. 

There is no need to question the significance of the days after Passover, as one can say that since most of the month has passed in holiness (Magen Avraham, small section 3). In truth, this is not necessary, as the whole month of Nissan is holy due to the reasons we have explained. If one fasted on Shabbat within Nissan due to a bad dream, and needs to observe another fast for having fasted, he should fast the following day, even if it is still Nissan (ibid, small section 6). However, if it was close to the tenth of the month, he should delay the fast to that day, as it is a fast of the righteous, for reasons that will be explained in section 580. Similarly, regarding Rosh Chodesh itself, it will be explained in section 573 that some do fast, see there (ibid).

And we do not recite "Mizmor LeTodah" (Psalm of Thanksgiving) on the eve of Passover and throughout the entire Passover, because the thanksgiving offering includes chametz (leavened bread). Similarly, in the Mishnah of the thanksgiving offering in "Eizehu" – one should not say "as if I had offered a thanksgiving offering" for this reason. Likewise, we do not recite "El Erech Apayim" and "Lamnatzeach Ya'ancha," and the Sephardim do not recite these throughout the entire month. Additionally, we do not say the "Yehi Ratzon" prayer that follows the Torah reading on Mondays and Thursdays. We do not hold memorial services throughout the entire month of Nisan. It has already been clarified that we do not recite "Tziduk HaDin" (justification of the Divine decree), and consequently, the Kaddish prayer is also not recited (as mentioned in that section, small clause 5). However, it is permissible to recite a psalm and say Kaddish over it. The custom is to recite Psalm 49, and then say Kaddish. When a sage passes away, it is obvious that we must eulogize him, for there is no festival in the face of a Torah scholar, and certainly not in Nisan. Refer to what I wrote above in Siman 430.

And it is customary to increase somewhat in eating and drinking on the day after the holiday, which is called "Isru Chag." The custom is not to fast on this day, as it is considered somewhat like a festival day.
