For the Isru Chag of Shavuot was certainly a festival day, as it was the day of the sacrificial offering, and they extended this festival status to the Isru Chag of both Passover and Sukkot. In Sukkah (45b), it is said: Whoever makes an "Isru" for the festival through eating and drinking, it is as if he built an altar and offered a sacrifice on it, as it is stated: "Bind the festival offering with cords to the horns of the altar." Rashi explains in one interpretation that "Isru Chag" refers to this, see there. It seems to me that this is the explanation: the joy of the festival, when done for the sake of Heaven, primarily comes from the sacrificial offerings, the peace offerings of joy. If, in the fervor of his soul bound to God, one also rejoices on the day after, and eats from the peace offerings of the previous day, as peace offerings are eaten for two days and one night, this additional joy is as if, besides the sacrifices, he also built the altar.

It is stated in Pesachim (6a): One inquires and expounds on the laws of Passover thirty days before Passover. They raised a difficulty from the end of Megillah where it is mentioned that Moses instituted for Israel to inquire about the laws of Passover during Passover and the laws of the festival during the festival, implying only during Passover itself. Several resolutions were offered for this. One resolution is that if one person inquires about matters not related to Passover and another about Passover laws, the latter takes precedence; there are other resolutions as well. The truth is that in the Jerusalem Talmud, the first chapter of Pesachim (end of Halacha 1), it states: This applies to the study hall, meaning in the house of assembly, the place where sages gather – it is thirty days. But for each individual personally – only during Passover (Chayei Adam). Currently, the custom is for the rabbi to give a sermon on Shabbat HaGadol and on Shabbat Shuva. One should preach on relevant topics to inspire the people towards Torah and fear of Heaven. However, regarding Passover inquiries, it is not applicable, as each person asks about what he is uncertain of unless they are general matters, and each person expounds according to his capacity (see Magen Avraham, subsection 1).

All of Israel has the custom of providing "wheat money" to purchase Passover flour for the poor or to give them money so they can buy it themselves. Everyone who has lived in a city for twelve months is obligated to contribute to this. Nowadays, the custom is that even someone who has lived there for thirty days must contribute. Even a Torah scholar must give, as this is considered charity and not a tax. 

If someone comes to live in a city temporarily, the period is either twelve months or thirty days. However, if someone comes to settle in the city permanently, they are required to give immediately. Similarly, a poor person who has lived in the city for thirty days is entitled to receive Passover flour. If someone has not yet been in the city for thirty days, the community is not required to give them flour but only matzah for each day, as per the rule for someone passing from place to place, which is explained in Yoreh De'ah, section 256. 

A poor person who comes to settle in the city must be given Passover flour immediately. Why should the poor recipient be worse off than the wealthy giver? If their intention is to settle, they are immediately considered as part of the city.

It is permitted to make an announcement in the synagogue due to a great need throughout the month of Nissan, but not in Tishrei, for reasons that will be explained in Siman 472. It is customary from the beginning of the month to read the portion of the Nasi (leader) for that day, and on the thirteenth day, to read from "This was the dedication of the altar" until "Thus he made the menorah," which corresponds to the tribe of Levi. On the eve of Passover after midday, one reads the portion of "This month shall be for you," and all portions that speak about the matter of Passover. After the Mincha (afternoon) prayer, the order of the Passover offering is recited, which is printed in the prayer books. On the eve of Passover, one prays Shacharit (the morning prayer) early, because one must finish their meal by the tenth hour, which is four hours into the day. The Maharshal would instruct that everyone should take a little of the Passover flour and eat it before Passover in some dish or bread, so that if there is any concern of chametz in this flour, it would be nullified by the small amount eaten before Passover. This is merely a stringency, as we do not presume a prohibition. Moreover, flour with flour is considered a mixture of like substances, and in any case: if there is sixty times the amount, it is nullified. If not, it does not help (Magen Avraham in Siman 430). However, it seems he was concerned for the opinion that flour with flour is considered a dry mixture, and it would reawaken on Passover (Chayei Adam). It is customary to make the "round bread" on Shabbat HaGadol from Passover flour.

The Shabbat before Passover is called "Shabbat HaGadol" (the Great Shabbat) because of the great miracle that occurred on it. For the Passover in Egypt, the lamb was acquired on the tenth day (of the month), and the Passover when they left Egypt was on a Thursday (Shabbat 87a). Therefore, the Shabbat before it was the tenth of the month, and each person took a lamb for their Passover offering and tied it to the legs of their bed. The Egyptians asked them: What is this? They replied that the Holy One, Blessed be He, commanded them to slaughter it. The Egyptians worshipped the lamb, and their teeth were dulled, and they were silent. Furthermore, the Israelites informed them that the Holy One, Blessed be He, was going to kill their firstborn, and the firstborn of Egypt went and fought with Pharaoh and their fathers. This is what is meant by the verse: "To Him who struck Egypt through their firstborn," as explained in the Midrash. Because of that miracle, it is called "Shabbat HaGadol."

And perhaps you will say: if so, it should not have been connected to Shabbat, but rather to the tenth of the month? One can say: since Miriam died on the tenth of the month, they did not want to associate it with that day, to make it a day of joy. Additionally, on the tenth of the month, they crossed the Jordan, as it is written in Joshua, and I might have said that the commemoration is for the miracle of the Jordan – therefore, they established it on Shabbat, because the crossing of the Jordan did not occur on Shabbat (Bach). And perhaps you will say: what does it matter to us if it is connected to the Jordan? One can say: that these days are connected to the miracles of Egypt, which are greater than the miracles of the Jordan.

And there are those who wrote: Because the miracle occurred through Shabbat. Since the Egyptians knew that they observed Shabbat, they asked them: What do you need the lamb for on Shabbat? And their response was as explained (Levush). Furthermore: They saw them tying the lamb on Shabbat, and tying is forbidden on Shabbat. They asked them about this, and they responded as I have written (Perisha). And one should not ask: If so, the miracle lasted all four days until Passover, that the Egyptians were unable to prevent them from this, and they waged wars, and if so, all of them are called "great"? One can say: The main point is the beginning (Beit Yosef).

And furthermore, it can be said: The truth is that Shabbat depends on Pesach, and Pesach depends on Shabbat. For Shabbat is a sign of the creation of the world, and Pesach is a sign of Divine Providence and the love for Israel. One without the other is meaningless, as is understood. Therefore, immediately upon the Exodus from Egypt, the Holy One, Blessed be He, gave us Shabbat and did not wait until the giving of the Torah, because Pesach is necessary for Shabbat, and Shabbat is necessary for Pesach. Therefore, this Shabbat is called "HaGadol" (the Great), for on it the Holy One, Blessed be He, was exalted, as besides the creation of the world, His Divine Providence was clarified. And we were also exalted, as He chose us from all nations. And therefore it is truly called "HaGadol." And see what I have written above in Siman 242.

The custom is to interrupt on this Shabbat from reciting "Barchi Nafshi." Instead, we recite "Avadim Hayinu" until "lechaper al kol avonoteinu." There are those who question this practice, as it is taught: Can it be from Rosh Chodesh? The Torah says: "on that day," referring to the verse "vehigadeta levincha" (the Vilna Gaon). It has already been explained that we give a sermon on Shabbat HaGadol. Some have written that when Erev Pesach falls on Shabbat, we give the sermon on the preceding Shabbat (Chayei Adam). This is according to them, who would discuss the laws of Pesach in the sermon and needed to inform the people before Pesach about what to do. But for us, anyone who has a question asks the rabbi, and our sermon is on other matters, so we give the sermon on the Shabbat of Erev Pesach. All the laws are mentioned in the piyut of Shabbat HaGadol. The Haftarah "VeArvah" is read only when Erev Pesach falls on Shabbat, as it is written: "Bring the tithe to the storehouse," and Erev Pesach was the time for the removal of the fourth-year tithe and the seventh year, as taught in the fifth chapter of Maaser Sheni. Some say the opposite: that on Shabbat it is impossible to remove, and we do not read "VeArvah" on it, but in other years we read "VeArvah" in memory of this (in the name of the Vilna Gaon). And so is the custom among us, to read "VeArvah" on every Shabbat HaGadol, except when Erev Pesach falls on Shabbat, then we read the Haftarah of the weekly portion.

There are three positive commandments and four negative commandments regarding Passover, and according to the Rambam, there are five. The positive commandments are: to eat matzah on the first night, to recount the Exodus from Egypt on that night, and to remove chametz and leaven on the fourteenth day. The four negative commandments are: not to eat chametz all seven days, not to eat mixtures containing chametz all seven days, that chametz should not be seen all seven days, and that chametz should not be found all seven days. According to the Rambam, there is also a prohibition against eating chametz on the afternoon of the eve of Passover from midday onward. However, according to other authorities, it is only a positive commandment, which is the commandment of "removing chametz." The prohibition of chametz and the prohibition of leaven are the same because leaven is what causes fermentation. If one eats chametz or leaven during the seven days of Passover, if he eats an olive-sized portion intentionally, he is liable to karet, as it is stated: "For whoever eats chametz shall be cut off." If he eats it unintentionally, he is liable to bring a sin offering. This applies to both eating and dissolving chametz and drinking it. However, for a mixture containing chametz, one is not liable to karet but only to a negative commandment. (Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon disagreed regarding chametz before and after its time. Rabbi Yehuda holds that it is a negative commandment, while Rabbi Shimon disagrees. For after its time, Rava in Pesachim 30a ruled according to Rabbi Shimon. Most authorities hold that even before its time, the law follows Rabbi Shimon. The Rambam holds that before its time, the law follows Rabbi Yehuda.)

Chametz (leavened bread) on Passover is prohibited for any benefit, as it is stated: "Chametz shall not be eaten"—there shall be no permission for eating it, meaning: there shall be no permission that leads to eating it. And general benefits usually lead to eating, as one takes money for food (Rashi Pesachim 21b). This we need according to the opinion that "you shall not eat" is only a prohibition of eating. However, the Rambam has already ruled in the eighth chapter of Forbidden Foods, law 15, according to the opinion that wherever the Torah states "you shall not eat," it implies both a prohibition of eating and a prohibition of benefit, unless the text specifies a permission, as it specified with a carcass for the stranger: "You shall give it to the stranger in your gates, and he shall eat it." And with chametz, there is no specification for permission of benefit, and consequently, it is prohibited for benefit. (And what the Rambam wrote at the beginning of Chametz and Matzah, giving Hezekiah's reason: there shall be no permission for eating, the reason for the change, as it is written "it shall not be eaten" with a tzere and a kamatz, as explained in the Gemara there. And according to Rabbi Abbahu, with whom we hold, there is no need for this. But he took the simple interpretation and did not want to elaborate, as is his way in several places.)

This is the language of the Rambam in the first chapter, law 8: It is forbidden to eat chametz on the fourteenth day from midday and onwards, which is from the beginning of the seventh hour of the day. And anyone who eats during this time is liable to lashes according to the Torah, as it is stated: "You shall not eat chametz over it," meaning over the Passover sacrifice. From tradition, they learned: Do not eat chametz from the time fit for the slaughtering of the Passover sacrifice, which is in the afternoon, and this is midday. Up to this point is his language. And even though the Passover sacrifice was offered after the daily afternoon offering, which is brought after midday, and if so, the time for the Passover sacrifice extends beyond midday – this is not relevant to the validity of the Passover sacrifice. For certainly also the Passover sacrifice, when slaughtered immediately after midday, is valid, for it is also said regarding Passover "in the afternoon." But the daily offering is brought first for the reason explained in Pesachim (59a), because regarding Passover it is also said "in the evening" – therefore it is delayed until after the daily offering. Additionally, the daily offering is more frequent (Tosafot there). However, if in retrospect they offered it before the daily offering, it is valid, as the Rambam wrote in the first chapter of the laws of the Passover sacrifice. If so, when the Torah said not to eat chametz from the time of the slaughtering of the Passover sacrifice – it means from midday, which is the primary time. The Raavad and other poskim disagreed with him, and they hold that there is no Torah prohibition of lashes after midday, but rather a positive commandment of "you shall remove" [the chametz], as I have written.

According to the Rambam, even after midday it is forbidden to derive benefit from chametz, because since there is a verse that states "you shall not eat," it implies that deriving benefit is also forbidden, as he himself wrote at the end of the eighth chapter of Ma'achalot Assurot, which we mentioned in section 2 (Kesef Mishneh at the beginning of the first chapter). However, according to those who disagree with him, it is not forbidden to derive benefit until the night, and this is the opinion of most of the poskim. Nevertheless, rabbinically it is forbidden to derive benefit, as will be explained later in section 443. Regarding nullification, even according to the Rambam, it is more lenient on the eve of Pesach after midday than during the rest of Pesach; for during the rest of Pesach the prohibition is in any amount, but on the eve of Pesach, it is nullified in sixty, since there is not yet a prohibition of karet, as will be explained in section 447 with the help of Heaven.

And the Rambam wrote in the first chapter, law 7: One who eats any amount of chametz (leavened bread) on Passover – this is prohibited by Torah law, as it is stated: "It shall not be eaten." Nevertheless, one is not liable for karet (spiritual excision) or a sacrifice unless it is the measure, which is an olive's bulk. And one who eats less than an olive's bulk intentionally – they are given lashes of rebelliousness. Thus is his language. And the Maggid Mishneh explained: because half a measure is prohibited by Torah law. But if so, it is puzzling: why did he need to clarify this specifically for chametz? Is this not the case for all forbidden foods? Furthermore, the verse he brought would be the opposite, for eating is by an olive's bulk (Kesef Mishneh). And there are those who want to say: because chametz is only prohibited during the days of Passover, I would say it is not included in all prohibitions where half a measure is forbidden by Torah law – the Rambam needed to specify chametz with its own verse (Mishneh Lemelech in the name of Ralnach). But this is not understood, for at the beginning of the last chapter of Yoma (74b), the Talmud brought the matter of half a measure regarding Yom Kippur, and Yom Kippur is also only prohibited on its day. Furthermore, the verse would be the opposite. And there are those who say that standard eating is any amount, and the measure of an olive's bulk is from the law given to Moses at Sinai (there in the name of Ra'am). And this is even more puzzling, for throughout the Talmud, standard eating is by an olive's bulk. And the truth is that measures are a law given to Moses at Sinai, but nevertheless, the halacha revealed that the Torah's intention with the term "eating" – is by an olive's bulk. Therefore, it is customary for the Talmud to say standard "eating" by an olive's bulk.

And in my humble opinion, the intention of the Rambam seems to be that regarding chametz (leavened bread), there is a specific verse for a half-measure (chatzi shiur). For according to Chizkiyah in the Gemara (Pesachim 21b), we learn the prohibition of deriving benefit from chametz from the verse "it shall not be eaten" written with a tzere and kamatz. And Rabbi Abbahu holds that any expression of "eating" includes also deriving benefit. And the Rambam rules according to Rabbi Abbahu, as I wrote in Section 2. If so, it is difficult according to Rabbi Abbahu: why did the verse need to change the expression to "it shall not be eaten" regarding chametz? To this, he answers: it comes to include a half-measure. And the intention of the Rambam, who says "it shall not be eaten" – this refers to the change in expression, which implies an inclusion. And if you ask: what is specific about chametz, since this is the case for all prohibitions?! There is indeed a significant difference, for the reason for the prohibition of a half-measure – we say in Yoma because it is fit to combine. Accordingly, when one eats a half-olive size at the end of the seventh day, it can no longer be combined, since then it is permitted to eat chametz. But when there is a specific verse for this – even in such a case, it is forbidden by Torah law. Nevertheless, there is no karet (excision) or chatat (sin-offering) for this. Since this is only from an inclusion of the verse, and not from its plain meaning – it is considered like any other half-measure of other prohibitions.

The Ra'avad wrote in the third chapter, law 8 in his glosses, and this is his language: "Perhaps this author holds that one transgresses 'You shall not see and you shall not find' from six hours and onward. But this is not so, for it is written 'seven days.'" Until here are his words. It is thus clear that according to the Ra'avad, one does not transgress 'You shall not see and you shall not find' until nightfall. 

And the Maggid Mishneh wrote that the Rambam also holds this way. However, one of the great authorities (Noda BiYehuda, First Edition, Orach Chaim, Siman 20) has already elaborated that this is not the case, and certainly, the Rambam holds as the Ra'avad stated in his words. According to the Rambam's view, it is definitely so, because since he believes that there is a prohibition on eating after midday, it follows that after midday is also included regarding 'You shall not see' during the seven days just as it is for eating and nullification - it is similar to eating; although the nature of the punishments is not the same - nevertheless, in the end, there is a prohibition after midday, just as for all seven days of Passover. 

And according to the Ra'avad, that there is no prohibition on eating - it is obvious that there is no 'You shall not see' here. And since most of the poskim (decisors of Jewish law) hold in eating like the Ra'avad, it follows that also regarding 'You shall not see' we hold that there is no prohibition of 'You shall not see' until nightfall.

Maimonides wrote in the first chapter, law 3: One is not liable to lashes for "it shall not be seen nor found" unless he bought chametz during Passover, or his chametz was such that he performed an action with it. But if he had chametz before Passover, and Passover arrived and he did not destroy it, but left it in his possession, although he has transgressed two prohibitions, he is not liable to lashes from the Torah because he did not perform an action with it. However, he is given rabbinic lashes. So are his words, for any prohibition that does not involve an action does not incur lashes. And so it is taught in the Tosefta of Makkot (Chapter 4, Law 5): One who retains chametz or maintains kilayim (mixed species) does not receive lashes, because there is no action involved.

And they raised a difficulty against him: Even if one acquired chametz (leavened bread) during Passover or caused it to become chametz, thereby committing an act, why should he be liable to lashes? For it is explicitly stated in Pesachim (95a) that "you shall not see" is a prohibition that is corrected by a positive command. And Rashi explained that throughout the days of the festival, it is in a state of "stand and remove," and so wrote the Tosafot (29b). And the great ones exerted much effort on this question and did not find a clear answer (see Mishneh LaMelech there in the name of several great ones). And in my humble opinion, it is not difficult at all. For behold, it is known that there is a dispute in Makkot (16a) whether we require "he fulfilled and did not fulfill," or "he nullified and did not nullify." And the Rambam in chapter eighteen of Sanhedrin ruled according to the one who holds "he fulfilled and did not fulfill." And we explained in Choshen Mishpat, section 97, paragraph 5, that according to the Rambam, when it is not within his power to fulfill the positive commandment, even if he did not nullify it with his hands – he is liable to lashes, see there. And if so, it follows naturally that when the seventh day of Passover arrives, at the last moment of the end of the day when there is no longer time to destroy it – then it is not called "corrected by a positive command" and he is liable to lashes, for nullification is not effective on a festival. And any type of destruction, such as burning or crumbling and scattering to the wind, requires a little time. And at the last moment – it is impossible for him, and therefore he is liable to lashes. (And I found in the Sha'agat Aryeh, section 80, that he wrote something similar. And he rejected it, saying that if so, it should have been explained, see there. And this is not a rejection.)

It seems to me that even if one derives benefit from chametz on Passover, he does not receive lashes, since he did not eat it. Although benefit is included in the term "eating," nevertheless, there are no lashes involved, as the Rambam wrote in Chapter 8 of the Laws of Forbidden Foods, Halacha 16, and this is his language: "Any food that is prohibited regarding benefit, if one benefited but did not eat... he does not receive lashes... until here is his language." The reason for this matter is explained in the Sefer HaMitzvot, Negative Commandment 187, but it is not understood there either. The Ramban in Shoresh 2 wrote that lashes are given for benefit, and this is also implied by Tosafot in Chullin (102b, beginning of "Ela") and by the Semag, Negative Commandment 259, and similarly wrote the Shiltei Giborim in the name of the Riaz (Pesachim 82). The great ones have already labored over the reason of the Rambam (Pri Chadash later in Siman 442, and Mishneh LaMelech in Chapter 5 of Yesodei HaTorah). We have explained, with the help of Heaven, the Rambam's reasoning in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 88, Paragraph 37, because benefit is a part of the mitzvah, as every eating includes benefit, and the main verse refers to eating. The Rambam's position in the Sefer HaMitzvot, Shoresh 12, is that lashes are only given for the main mitzvah and not for a part of it. There he wrote that one should not consider a part of the mitzvah as an independent entity, and consequently, there are no lashes for it, see there. The other laws concerning the eating of prohibition are explained by the Rambam in Chapter 14 of the Laws of Forbidden Foods, and we have explained them with the help of Heaven in Yoreh De'ah there. It is clear that the prohibition of "not being seen" does not apply to less than a kezayit. Similarly, there is no distinction between chametz and se'or. The laws of mixtures of chametz and hard chametz, whether they involve the prohibition of "not being seen" or not, and other related laws, will be explained with the help of Heaven in Siman 442 and Siman 447.

Maimonides wrote at the beginning of the second chapter: It is a positive commandment from the Torah to eliminate chametz before the time of its prohibition for consumption, as it is stated: "But on the first day you shall remove leaven from your houses." And through tradition, it was learned that this "first day" refers to the fourteenth day [of Nissan]. Evidence for this is from what is written in the Torah: "You shall not slaughter the blood of My sacrifice with chametz," meaning: you shall not slaughter the Passover sacrifice while chametz still exists. And the slaughtering of the Passover sacrifice is on the fourteenth day after midday. So far are his words. And our sages of blessed memory accepted that "but" signifies a division, meaning it divides the day: for until midday, chametz is permitted by Torah law, and after midday, it is prohibited. Consequently, since the elimination must occur before the time of its prohibition, the elimination must be before midday. And by rabbinic decree, there is an additional precaution, as will be explained with the help of Heaven.

And what is the removal mentioned in the Torah? Our sages of blessed memory said (Pesachim 4b) that from a Torah perspective, mere nullification is sufficient. And Rashi explained: from the fact that it is written "tashbitu" (you shall remove) and not "tav'iru" (you shall burn), it implies that nullification in the heart is considered removal. This is his language. And Onkelos translated: "you shall nullify." And in the Sifrei it is taught: "leaven shall not be seen by you" – nullify it in your heart. And our teachers, the Tosafists, wrote there that once one has nullified it, it is considered ownerless property and has left his domain, and it is permitted. From the fact that it says: "yours" you shall not see, but you may see that of others and that of the Most High. And what we say in Nedarim: ownerless property in front of three – from a Torah perspective, it is not required. This is their language. And similarly, it is written in Sefer Mitzvot Gadol, negative commandment 78, see there. However, the opinion of the Rambam in the second chapter of Nedarim is that even from a Torah perspective, it is not effective if done privately; rather, it needs to be declared ownerless in front of one person, and rabbinically, in front of three, as we explained in Choshen Mishpat, section 273, paragraph 7, see there. Therefore, this nullification does not work by means of declaring it ownerless when one nullifies chametz privately. Additionally, ownerlessness in the heart is not effective, as thoughts in the heart are not considered significant (Ran at the beginning of Pesachim). Moreover, there are those who hold in Nedarim (53b) that ownerlessness is like a gift, and until it reaches the domain of the acquirer, it remains in the domain of the one declaring it ownerless. Therefore, the chametz remains in his domain (ibid.).

However, the intention of our Sages is this: Certainly, in other matters, nullification is not like renunciation, for the reasons we have explained. But chametz (leavened bread) is different, because chametz on Passover is not in a person's possession. It is a royal decree that forbids its benefit, and against his will, it is removed from his possession. But regarding the prohibition of "it shall not be seen" (bal yera'eh), the Torah considers the chametz to be in his possession, as it is said in the Gemara (Pesachim 6b): "There are two things that are not in a person's possession, and the Scripture treats them as if they are in his possession: a pit in public domain and chametz from the sixth hour and onward." Therefore, a mere expression of intent is sufficient. Since he expresses his intent that he does not want it to be in his possession and nullifies it to be like the dust of the earth, it automatically leaves his possession completely. This is what is commonly expressed in the language of the Sages: he nullifies it in his heart, and that is enough. Meaning: for it is not in his possession as the Torah has forbidden it to him. Therefore, even with nullification in his heart, it leaves his possession and becomes like renunciation.

And also, one cannot say that the Torah only permitted nullification and not searching, for this is not logical at all. In the case of all forbidden items of benefit, such as Asherah trees and idolatrous objects, the Torah commanded only searching, as it is written: "You shall surely destroy..." Therefore, it is certain that the Torah came to be lenient regarding chametz, allowing nullification to suffice. However, it is clear that searching is also included in "you shall remove," for someone who does not wish to nullify or cannot properly intend the nullification should search all places where chametz is brought and remove it from the world, either by burning or by other means, as will be explained with Heaven's help. And after he has searched all the places, even if chametz is later found, he does not transgress a Torah prohibition, since the Torah relies on presumptions (Ran there), and he did everything required, making him essentially like one who is coerced. Therefore, from the Torah's perspective, one can fulfill the obligation by doing either of the two actions: searching or nullification.

However, the Sages required both actions: searching and nullification. They did not want to rely solely on nullification because this nullification depends on a person's intent, and not all minds are alike. It is possible that some may take this lightly and not completely remove it from their thoughts (as mentioned there). Therefore, they required searching. Concerning this, it is taught: on the night of the fourteenth, one checks for chametz, meaning not to rely solely on nullification. Nevertheless, they also required nullification even after searching, as it is stated in the Gemara (6b): "One who searches must also nullify," due to the concern that one may later find chametz. Though biblically speaking, one does not retroactively transgress, as we explained, still, there is an immediate need to destroy it. We are concerned that perhaps one might find a nice piece of chametz and hesitate a bit to destroy it, thereby transgressing the prohibition of "it shall not be seen" (bal yera’eh).

As we have explained, the majority of our rabbis hold that from the Torah, either nullification or searching is effective; whether it is known chametz to a person or unknown chametz. And from the Rabbis, both things are needed: whether it is known chametz or unknown chametz. However, in the words of the Rambam at the beginning of the second chapter, there is room for inquiry, as he wrote: "And what is this destruction mentioned in the Torah? That he should nullify it in his heart and consider it as dust. And he should place in his heart that there is no chametz in his possession at all, and that any chametz in his possession is as dust, and as something that has no need at all. And from the words of the Scribes, one must search for the chametz in hidden places and holes, and check and remove it from all his boundaries." Until here is his language. And seemingly his intention is that from the Torah, only nullification is required. But this is not a logical conclusion, as I have written. Rather, his intention is that from the Torah, nullification suffices, and from the words of the Scribes, searching is required. He did not elaborate his intention here. And a proof: for from his language it implies that from the words of the Scribes, searching suffices, for he did not write "and from the words of the Scribes, one also needs to search...". And indeed it is not so, for it was explicitly stated: one who searches must also nullify, and so the Rambam himself wrote in the third chapter, law seven, and this is his language: "And when he finishes searching... he must nullify...". Until here is his language. But he did not bother to elaborate, and his opinion is like that of all the poskim.

And know that there is a version in the Rambam, quoted by the Kesef Mishneh in the following language: "And what is the 'removal' mentioned in the Torah? That he should remove the known chametz from his possession. And what is not known - he nullifies in his heart..." This implies that only for unknown chametz is nullification effective. But for known chametz, even according to the Torah, nullification is not effective, only searching. And the Kesef Mishneh has already rejected this version, as it is clearly proven in the Gemara that nullification is effective for all types of chametz, for the language of the Gemara in several places is: "according to the Torah, mere nullification suffices," which clearly means it applies to all types of chametz. There are also clear proofs, and it is clear that this version is mistaken. Or if this version existed, the Rambam later corrected it. A clear proof is that the Maggid Mishneh did not mention it, and who was more proficient in the Rambam's words than him? Therefore, even though this opinion is also found in the Kol Bo in the name of a Gaon, nevertheless, we do not innovate something that most of our Rabbis do not agree with. And the Talmud does not imply this, as I have written (and so wrote the Pri Chadash). There are some great authorities who wanted to uphold these words through many forced explanations, and I do not know what compelled them to do so. And if there is a distinction to be made between known and unknown chametz, it is not a Torah distinction but a Rabbinic one, as we will explain with the help of Heaven.

For in section 15 we wrote that the sages required inspection because they did not want to rely on the nullification that depends on the heart, lest one not nullify it properly. This is from the words of the Ran, at the beginning of Pesachim. According to this, even if one does not have known chametz, nullification does not help if chametz is later found. This is also evident from the language of the Rambam, who wrote that by rabbinic decree one is obligated to search for chametz in hidden places and holes. However, our teachers, the Tosafists, wrote at the beginning of Pesachim that the sages required inspection lest one come to eat the chametz, see there. If so, this only applies when the chametz is before us in a known place. But in an unknown place, there is no concern that one may come to eat it. Therefore, according to this, a person who does not have known chametz suffices with nullification. And perhaps this is what the Gaon mentioned, as cited in the Kolbo, that for known chametz, nullification does not help, meaning by rabbinic decree. I do not have the Kolbo to examine it. However, even according to the Tosafists, in places where chametz is brought in and out, it is obvious there is a concern that there may be chametz there and one might come to eat it.

And I have also seen a dispute regarding whether one transgresses the prohibition of "bal yera'eh" (not seeing leaven) with chametz that is not known. There are proofs for both sides. In my humble opinion, it appears that there is no dispute, and there are two categories of unknown chametz: The first is in places where it is customary to bring chametz, but it is not known if there is currently chametz there. In this case, one certainly transgresses "bal yera'eh" if chametz is found there. The second category is places where chametz is not brought, but chametz is found there by chance. In such a case, it is clear that one does not transgress "bal yera'eh," as from the Torah one is certainly not obligated to check there at all. And in the Mishnah of "Or le-arba'ah asar" it is taught: Any place where chametz is not brought does not require checking. And it is clear that one does not transgress "bal yera'eh" if chametz is found there.

And some bring proof from Rashi’s commentary (6a) on the case of one who sets out on a journey and intends to return - that he is obligated to check for chametz even if he left at the beginning of the year. Rashi explains that when he returns during the days of Pesach, he transgresses, and at that time it is not within his control to nullify it... And when he sees it, he transgresses it. Thus are his words, which imply that as long as he does not see it, he does not transgress. It is unthinkable to say this, for certainly if he knows there is chametz in his house, he transgresses even if he does not see it. Here it is referring to someone who departed from his house without checking, and he does not know if there is chametz there or not. Therefore, it does not apply that he transgresses until he sees it - and certainly, he transgresses retroactively once he sees it. Rashi’s intention, of blessed memory, is that when he becomes aware of it, he transgresses, and this is the common way of speaking: when he sees the chametz. Similarly, some bring proof from Tosafot at the beginning of the chapter "Kol Sha'ah," regarding what is stated in the Gemara: that therefore it needs to teach that at all times when it is permitted to eat, one can feed it to animals and beasts. If it had taught us about wild beasts, it is because they store it away. Tosafot wrote: there is no transgression of "not to hide," for we derive from "it shall not be found," and this is not considered found since its location is not known. Thus are their words. And Rashi also wrote that if it is hidden, there is no transgression of "it shall not be seen," see there. They deduced from this that they hold the view that when it is not seen, one does not transgress. I am puzzled by this proof, for here it is referring to someone who checked properly, but it teaches us that we are not concerned about it being hidden in its usual manner (as the Pnei Yehoshua also wrote). And if it were necessarily hidden, he would certainly transgress. However, Tosafot themselves have already written there that there is a difference between a wild beast and a weasel, and a wild beast does not hide it to the same extent, see there. And it is like a place where chametz is not brought in, where one does not transgress even if chametz is found there, as I wrote in the previous section.

Regarding the variation in language in the Torah, in the portion "This month shall be," it is written, "For seven days leaven shall not be found in your houses," and in the portion "Sanctify to Me every firstborn," it is written, "And no leavened bread shall be seen to you, nor leaven, in all your borders." The differences are that by "shall not be found" it only mentions "leaven" and does not say "to you," and it says "in your houses." Whereas by "shall not be seen" it mentions both "leavened bread" and "leaven," it says "to you," and it says "in all your borders." 

Now, according to the law: Leavened bread and leaven are considered the same, for we find two verses that begin with "leaven" and end with "leavened bread," as it is written: "But on the first day you shall remove leaven from your houses, for whoever eats leavened bread..." And it is written: "For seven days leaven shall not be found in your houses, for whoever eats anything leavened..." This indicates that they have the same law. Both are necessary because from leavened bread we would not know about leaven, since it is not fit for eating, and therefore regarding eating it is written "leavened bread" and not "leaven." And from leaven, we would not know about leavened bread, since leaven's fermenting power is strong and can ferment other doughs, unlike leavened bread. This is also expounded in the Mechilta, and Rashi brings this in his commentary on the verse "shall not be found in your houses," see there.

The reason for the differences: It appears to me, in my humble opinion, that in the Gemara (5b), we derive "houses" from "borders" and "borders" from "houses," see there. And the verse regarding leaven, "it shall not be found in your houses" – we derive there regarding the leaven of a non-Jew which was deposited with a Jew, and the Jew accepted responsibility for it, that he transgresses "it shall not be seen" and "it shall not be found," see there. Therefore, it is not written "yours," because even if it is not yours – it is considered as yours. Therefore, it is written "in your houses," because it is customary to deposit something in a house, in a guarded place. And therefore, it is written "it shall not be found" and not "it shall not be seen," because it is customary to hide a deposit in a place where it is not visible. And therefore, it is written "leaven," because leavened bread which is needed for eating is not usually deposited with others, unlike leaven. And so as not to err and think that the prohibition of "it shall not be seen" and "it shall not be found" applies only in houses and not in borders, therefore it is written: "and it shall not be seen in... all your borders." Meaning: if it is yours – it is forbidden not only in your houses, but in any place within your borders, wherever it may be. And what is yours you shall not see, but you may see what belongs to others and what is consecrated – even in your houses, if you did not accept responsibility. For we learned this from each other. And so that you should not say: that it is specifically dependent on seeing, therefore it is written "it shall not be found" – that even if you do not see it, but it is present within your borders, you transgress. And by law, there is no difference between leavened bread and leaven, and between houses and borders, it is all the same. The laws of deposits will be explained in Siman 440 with the help of Heaven. (And with this, the Torah explained all the laws of the prohibition of leaven. Therefore, in "Mishpatim" and "Ki Tisa" and "Emor" where the festivals are mentioned – the matter of leaven is not mentioned at all. Only in Deuteronomy, which is a repetition of the laws, it is briefly written at the end of "Re'eh": "you shall not eat leavened bread with it, and leaven shall not be seen with you," and both are mentioned, the prohibition of eating and the prohibition of "it shall not be seen." And that in the Gemara and in the Mekhilta they prefaced "it shall not be seen" before "it shall not be found," even though "it shall not be found" is written first, but this is the method of "not only this but also that": "it shall not be seen" even "it shall not be found." And with this, we have explained with the help of Heaven all the laws of "it shall not be seen." Examine carefully and you will find it easy.)

Here is the translation of the provided passage from the Aruch Hashulchan:

"In Section 18, we explained two reasons for the necessity of searching for chametz: one, because one might not annul it properly; and the second, because one might come to eat it. One should not question this reason by asking: If so, why did they not worry about this with other prohibitions? It is not comparable, because with chametz, since one does not abstain from it all year, there is more reason to be concerned. Additionally, because the Torah was stringent with chametz, making one liable for 'bal yera'eh' (it should not be seen), the Sages were more concerned about this (Tosafot at the beginning of Pesachim). There is a practical difference between the reasons: for the reason that one does not abstain from it, one must search even for chametz that one is not liable for 'bal yera'eh', like hard chametz and mixtures, according to the opinion that holds this, as will be explained in Siman 442. But for the reason that one is liable for 'bal yera'eh', and also for the previous reason that one might not annul it properly, one only needs to search for chametz that one is liable for 'bal yera'eh'. However, the Gemara (10b) clearly proves that there is a concern for eating, see there, and therefore the main ruling is that all types of chametz require searching. However, one could say that they were only concerned about chametz for which one is liable for karet (excision), and not for chametz which only incurs a prohibition without karet. And what we say in Yevamot (82a), that there is no difference between a prohibition with a simple negative commandment and one with karet, Rashi (there 119a) already explained that this is in regard to doubt. But in regard to Rabbinic precaution, it is reasonable to say that they made a precaution for karet and not for a simple negative commandment, see there in Rashi who explained this clearly."

When is the time for the search [for chametz]? The Sages taught in the Mishnah: On the evening of the fourteenth [of Nisan]—we search for chametz by the light of a candle. And the Gemara explains the reason: Although the prohibition begins from midday, and if so, it would have been sufficient to search in the morning, as zealous individuals perform mitzvot early, as it is written: "And Abraham rose early in the morning"—and not the night before. However, the reason is because the candlelight is suitable for the search. And although, according to this, one could search at night whenever he wishes, why did they require it at the beginning of the night? Because at that time people are usually at home, as they come home from their work to pray Ma'ariv and eat, and it is a set time for the search (see Taz, subparagraph 1).

The Raavad, of blessed memory, inferred from the term "light" that the inspection must take place while there is still some light, meaning at the beginning of the night, but not during twilight (Chaye Adam Section 1 and Eliyah Rabbah Section 5). Some say that the time for inspection is before the appearance of the stars (Bach and Magen Avraham Section 5), but the primary opinion follows the first view (Mekor Chaim Section 1, and so wrote the Taz Section 5, and the Raavad himself wrote similarly in Sefer Tohorat HaDeshen). Therefore, at the beginning of the night of the fourteenth of Nissan, one inspects for chametz by candlelight in holes and cracks, and in all places where chametz is typically brought.

Every person should be careful not to start any work at the end of the thirteenth day, which is a half-hour before night (Magen Avraham, subsection 3). Similarly, it is forbidden to eat a meal until he has checked [for chametz]. However, tasting fruits or up to the size of an egg in bread is permitted (ibid.). This refers to bread upon which "mezonot" is recited. But to wash his hands and eat bread upon which "hamotzi" is recited, even the size of an olive is forbidden. Even the bread upon which "mezonot" is recited is only permitted up to the size of an egg, as it is considered a temporary eating concerning the sukkah. But more than the size of an egg is forbidden. And this is only regarding bread, but fruits and other foods can be eaten in larger quantities. Certainly, drinking is allowed, as all of these are considered temporary concerning the sukkah. Similarly, it is forbidden to enter the bathhouse and all other things forbidden before Mincha, as I have written in Siman 232.

Even to study Torah is forbidden once the time for the inspection arrives, but not before the time. This is not similar to eating, as the same law applies to the evening prayer, as explained in Berachot (4b). Even if he has a fixed time for study, he should not study until he performs the inspection. Some say that it is even forbidden to study half an hour before [the time], unlike the evening prayer (Taz, subsection 2). However, this is not the main opinion, for how is it possible to forbid the study of Torah before the time arrives? (Chayei Adam, subsection 5, and Magen Avraham, subsection 6). And what the Rambam wrote at the beginning of the second chapter, that one should not establish a study session at the end of the thirteenth day, and similarly, a scholar should not begin reading at this time, lest he be drawn and prevented from inspecting for chametz at the beginning of its time. His words are as follows: This does not mean that regular study is forbidden before its time, for if so, he would have said briefly that it is forbidden to study at the end of the thirteenth day. Rather, the explanation is: study that prepares oneself for a long time is forbidden. This is the establishment of a study session where they learn in public and debate with each other, which takes a long time. Similarly, a scholar teaching students is forbidden, for this takes a long time. But to study individually, there is no prohibition except when the time arrives. (And the Gra in subsection 5 wrote like the Taz, and it seems that they understood the Rambam's words as such. But according to what I have written, on the contrary, it is evidence to the opposite, and one should not interrupt Torah study until the time arrives. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

There are those who wrote that those people who say a halachic lesson in the synagogue after prayer are permitted to say the lesson. For only someone who studies at home is prohibited, as he is not compelled to rise from his place. But this person will certainly go home. And specifically, it refers to a halachic matter without debate, but with debate it is forbidden to engage even if not at home, for in this case, there is certainly concern that it may lead to prolonged study (Magen Avraham, subsection 5). And in my humble opinion, it seems this is contrary to the words of the Rambam that we brought, for this is the fixed study session that the Rambam prohibits. And it must be said that the Rambam's intent is at home and not in the study hall. But this does not seem correct, for the term "fixed study session" implies the study hall. (And it seems to me that the Rambam was precise from the language of the Talmud in Berachot 4a: "This student of the sages should not open..." And why did it not simply say it is forbidden to study? Rather, this is a fixed study session, or the discourse of the sage before students, for in this there is concern for prolonged study.)

And our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote that if one began studying while it was still daytime, he does not need to interrupt. And our master, the Rema, wrote that some say he does need to interrupt, and this seems to me to be the main opinion. Thus far his words. And even though if he started permissibly, he also does not interrupt with secular matters, as I wrote in Siman 235; nevertheless, with Torah study, which has no end, and there is no concept of completion, he will inevitably need to interrupt, and therefore he should interrupt now (Chayei Adam). And according to this, it seems to my humble opinion that there is no disagreement at all. For certainly by law, he does not need to interrupt, all the more so with secular matters in Mincha. However, the opposite is true with secular matters, there is completion, and with words of Torah, there is no completion, and he will inevitably need to interrupt. Therefore, if he needs to finish until the chapter or complete the topic, it seems to my humble opinion that everyone agrees he does not need to interrupt.

And if one began learning once its time arrived – they certainly need to stop, for they began in prohibition. And if they began with a permissible activity while it was still day – some say they need to stop (Magen Avraham, Section 6). And even though in the case of Mincha one does not stop, that is because it is frequent and there is no concern that they will forget. This is not the case with the search for chametz, which occurs only once a year – there is a concern that they will forget (Bach). And even though with the lulav we also hold that if one began they do not stop, as I wrote in Siman 672 – it is not comparable. For the lulav is in any case for seven days a year. Additionally, the time for the lulav is all day, while the primary time for the search for chametz is at the beginning of the night (Magen Avraham). Furthermore, the lulav involves a momentary action and one fulfills the obligation, and there is no concern as it is certain they will do so, which is not the case with the search for chametz. Nevertheless, there are those who say that one does not need to stop, just like with Mincha (Chaye Adam). It seems to me that one should tell their wife or another person to remind them to search for chametz, and they can complete what they started. For even without this, there are those who say that if one appoints someone to remind them to search – all activities are permitted (Eliyah Rabbah, Section 8, and Mekor Chaim, Section 8). Therefore, in such a case – it is obvious that one can rely on this.

And one who did not pray the evening prayer with the congregation – some say that he should check, and then pray; if he is not accustomed to praying with ten in the synagogue – he should pray first, because it is a burden to gather them afterwards. And one who always prays the evening prayer at home – he should check and then pray (Magen Avraham, subsection 5). But there are those who say that the evening prayer always precedes (Chaye Adam), and this is the main ruling (Mikra Kodesh, subsection 6). For there was never an ordinance to check before the evening prayer.

Before beginning the search [for chametz], one should recite a blessing, just as we bless over all commandments. Here, there is a Torah-commanded positive mitzvah of "However, on the first day you shall remove leaven…" and a Rabbinic positive mitzvah instituted to search on the night of the fourteenth. The mitzvah extends from the search until the next day after the burning [of the chametz]. The blessing is: "Blessed are You... who has sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us concerning the removal of chametz." If one blessed "to remove chametz," he has fulfilled his obligation, but ideally, the blessing established is "concerning the removal" (Pesachim 7b). The term "removal" was chosen because it encompasses both the search and the removal, and it also includes the nullification that one performs immediately after the search for chametz that was not found, as will be explained (see Taz, subsection 1). If one began searching without a blessing, he may bless as long as he has not finished his search, for as long as he has not finished, it is still considered "before the performance" [of the mitzvah]. If he finished without blessing, he should bless the next day at the time of the burning, and the nullification on the next day which also nullifies the chametz he sees, as will be explained, since this is the essential completion of the mitzvah. It is proper to wash one's hands before the search. However, if one searches immediately after Maariv, he does not need to wash his hands, as he already washed them before the evening prayer. The nullification after the search will be explained in section 434.

It is forbidden to speak between the blessing and the beginning of the inspection, just as with all blessings for commandments or for enjoyment. If one spoke about matters related to the inspection, there is no need to repeat the blessing, as it is similar to saying "bring salt" after the "Hamotzi" blessing, where there is no need to repeat the blessing. However, if one spoke about matters not related to the inspection, one must repeat the blessing. However, once one has started the inspection, there is no prohibition according to the law if one spoke in the middle of the inspection. This is similar to interrupting a meal with speech, which is not an issue since one has started the activity for which the blessing was made. Nonetheless, it is proper to be cautious even in this, and not to interrupt with speech until after the inspection is completed. This is not due to concern about interruption, but so that one focuses on inspecting all the places where chametz might be found.

And there is someone who wants to say that from a legal standpoint, it is forbidden to interrupt even after one has started checking. And it is not similar to a meal, where there one can stop and not eat anymore. But with checking – one is obligated to check the entire [area]. And if so, regarding what remains – it would be considered an interruption (Taz, section 1). However, this does not seem correct, for should one have to bless for every part of the checking? And one can fulfill the blessing even for several houses. Therefore, just as in a meal the blessing of "Hamotzi" remains valid for what one eats after the interruption, so too with checking.

And with one blessing, one can inspect several houses. If the homeowner wishes, he can have members of his household stand by him at the time he recites the blessing, and they will answer "Amen" and then disperse, each to his place to inspect, relying on the blessing the homeowner recited. For ten people performing one mitzvah, one blessing suffices for all. If the homeowner instructs another person to inspect, that person should recite the blessing, even though the mitzvah is not incumbent upon him, for nonetheless, his agent is like himself. Just as with circumcision, where the obligation is upon the father of the son, the mohel recites the blessing (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 6). And it is preferable for the person himself to perform the mitzvah rather than his agent. Nevertheless, if he makes an agent, he should appoint an agent who is obligated and knowledgeable, not minors. Going from house to house does not constitute an interruption (Chayei Adam). It is customary to place pieces of hard chametz so that the inspector will find them, to prevent his blessing from being in vain. If he did not place them, it does not invalidate, for everyone’s intent is to remove whatever is found. It is customary to place ten hard pieces of chametz in the windows. We do not recite “Shehecheyanu” for the inspection of chametz, as it is not a mitzvah that involves joy. Additionally, since it pertains to the essence of Passover, the “Shehecheyanu” will be recited over the cup of Kiddush (see Tur and Beit Yosef).

And know: There are those who ask, according to our custom, where the women clean the rooms, the cupboards, and all the places where chametz was used, several days before Passover; and on the night of the fourteenth, no chametz is found, except for what is left to eat that night and the following morning, and these are guarded. If so, what is the purpose of the search [for chametz] for which we recite a blessing? After all, all the places have already been checked?

However, this is not a question. Firstly, we have already explained that the blessing also includes the nullification and the burning [of chametz] the next day. Additionally, until tomorrow before midday, there is still chametz that needs to be destroyed, whatever remains from the night's and morning's meals. Therefore, it is as if one is in the middle of the search. And we have already explained that when one is in the middle of the search, one can recite the blessing, as I wrote in section 1. And see in the next section, paragraph 13.

The inspection must specifically be done by the light of a candle, and not by the light of the moon. And even though on the night of the 14th the moonlight shines brightly, nevertheless the inspection must specifically be by the light of a candle because the light of a candle is good for inspection. And thus the prophet said (Zephaniah 1:12): "At that time I will search Jerusalem with candles." And not only is it preferable over the light of the moon, but even over the light of the sun. For example, if one did not inspect at night and needs to inspect during the day, he should not inspect the rooms by the sunlight, but rather light a candle and inspect by its light, because the candle can be brought into holes and cracks. And only a portico, which has ample light because one of its sides is completely open (see Tosafot Eruvin 25a), can be inspected by the sunlight. And the Rambam and the Shulchan Aruch wrote: if one inspected by the sunlight, it is sufficient, which implies after the fact. And in the Gemara (Pesachim 8a) it is explicitly stated that even initially, and so wrote the Tur. And there are those who say that their intention is that initially one should inspect at night (Magen Avraham, section 3). And this is not sufficient, for we are dealing with a case where one did not inspect at night. Therefore, it seems to me: because in the Jerusalem Talmud at the beginning of Pesachim it was questioned whether even in places with ample light a candle is specifically needed, see there. And therefore, even though according to the halacha we follow our Talmud, nevertheless the Rambam was concerned for the Jerusalem Talmud and wrote it in a manner that implies after the fact. And similarly, opposite a skylight in the roof where the sunlight shines a lot, it is like a portico. And according to the Tur, also opposite a window in the wall the law is the same, and there are those who disagree with this (see there, section 4 in the name of the R"I). And through glass it is forbidden (see there).

One does not check [for chametz] by the light of a torch, but by the light of a candle. This is because a torch is feared to be brought into holes and cracks, and its light is behind it. Even after the fact, it does not suffice as the light of the moon (ibid., subparagraph 5). There are those who say that after the fact, one fulfills [his obligation] (Taz, subparagraph 3), but this is not the opinion of the later authorities (Eliyah Rabbah and Mekor Chaim). What is a "torch"? When two candles are twisted together or joined together. Only a single candle [is valid], and the candle must be made of wax, not of tallow or fat, as there is a fear that it might drip onto utensils and clothing. After the fact – one fulfills [his obligation]. Therefore, if one does not have a wax candle – he should take a tallow one, and similarly not use oil. And there are those who say that one does not fulfill [his obligation] with oil, due to the fear of bringing it into holes and cracks, lest the oil spills (Magen Avraham ibid.). This is an excessive stringency (and this is implied by the Chayei Adam, and so wrote the Magen HaElef). Certainly, with petroleum that is now lit in glass – one fulfills [his obligation] after the fact. But with wood – certainly, one does not fulfill [his obligation], as it is like a torch.

And one is obligated to check all places where chametz might have been brought, as well as places where there is concern that one might have come there with his bread while using those areas. Therefore, all the rooms of the house and the upper floors need checking, as well as cellars that contain wine, beer, oil, and other beverages, and different types of foods, since one might sometimes enter them with his bread. Similarly, wood sheds, straw houses, coal houses, and the like need checking. However, wine and oil storage rooms, where one does not regularly take from them, or if he takes in one go what he needs and does not take little by little, do not need checking. Similarly, a straw storage room which is not frequently entered does not need checking, and the same applies to similar cases. Also, in our homes: under beds, under large chairs, and under large boxes and cupboards, if there is a space between them and the floor, need checking because chametz often rolls there. Similarly, small boxes within large cupboards and within large boxes need checking, because sometimes people hide pastries and the like in them.

The holes in the house, and the protrusions from the walls that are not very high, where a person's hand can reach while standing on the ground, and are not very low close to the ground – require checking. But those that are high where a person's hand cannot reach, and those that are less than three handbreadths from the ground – do not require checking, as it is uncommon to use those places. However, if children are found there – the lower places require checking, as they play on the ground and might hide chametz there (Magen Avraham, subsection 8). Similarly, the roof of a porch and a tower, whose roofs are slanted; or in our case, where all our roofs are slanted – they do not require checking, because they are not used, as they are not suitable for any use. Even if there is such a roof inside the house, such as a tower with a slanted roof – it does not require checking. But if its roof is flat – it requires checking, even though it is very high, because in the house people often stand on a chair and use it. And so it seems to me that in our case, regarding the flat roof that is beneath the slanted roof, which we call "attics", and one ascends there by ladder; if it is used occasionally throughout the year for various purposes – it requires checking, but if not – it does not require checking.

A cattle pen does not require inspection, because if there were chametz there, the animals would eat it. Similarly, a chicken coop does not require inspection, because if there were chametz there, the chickens would eat it. Likewise, the ground of the house where chickens are present does not require inspection (there, subsection 9). Nevertheless, under the beds does require inspection, because perhaps a large piece was dragged there which they cannot eat. Therefore, sweeping is sufficient, and it does not require inspection (there). However, when there are no chickens, inspection is necessary, because perhaps it was dragged into a hole or a crack, and the chickens would dig it out from there. When there are no chickens, it remains there. It is obvious that one needs to inspect under chairs and benches (there).

Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 6: Similarly, the middle of a courtyard does not require inspection because, if there were chametz there, the crows and other birds that frequent the area would eat it. This is only in a case of doubtful chametz. However, in the case of definite chametz, it does not apply. Thus far his words. Our teacher, the Rema, wrote on this, and these are his words: But later on, in section 3 of Siman 448, it is explained that it is permissible to throw chametz in a place where birds are frequent. All the more so that there is no need to destroy it from there, even definite chametz, until after the time of its prohibition. Thus far his words. Some have answered that here it refers to one's own courtyard, and there it refers to a street or a public courtyard (Bach and Taz, sub-section 5). Others have answered that certainly before the time of inspection, we rely even on definite chametz that the birds will eat it. However, if one sees chametz at the time of inspection, one is certainly obligated to check. We do not rely on the fact that the birds will eat it because doubt does not remove certainty (Chayei Adam, and this is also the intention of the Magen Avraham in sub-section 10, and the Levush, as written by Eliyah Rabbah). Some differentiate between the night of the fourteenth, when we do not rely on the fact that the birds will eat it, and before the fourteenth (Mekor Chaim, sub-section 7). In my humble opinion, the primary opinion seems to be the first answer, for what is stated in the Gemara (Pesachim 9a), that doubt does not remove certainty, applies to one's own property in places that one is obligated to inspect. In such a case, even several days beforehand, if chametz is established, one is certainly obligated to check and destroy it. However, later in Siman 448, the Beit Yosef explicitly wrote, and these are his words: Before the time of its prohibition, one can throw it in a place where crows are frequent. If chametz is found after the time of its prohibition, even if the place is public, one should not leave it there but should destroy it. Thus far his words. It is clear that he is referring to throwing it in a public place, and this has no connection to the previous matter. This is the main ruling in law. (And regarding the difficulty raised by the Magen Avraham: If so, what is difficult from Rava, perhaps here it refers to definite chametz? His intention is to page 8. This is not difficult at all: Every inspection is to see if there is chametz, and therefore, light is needed. Thus, by necessity, it refers to doubtful chametz. All his objections to the Bach, the reader will see that the law is with the Bach. The Gra, in section 28, wrote according to the Magen Avraham, but in my humble opinion, the main opinion is like the Bach and the Taz. Be precise and you will find light.)

And similarly, in a barn or chicken coop as explained, it is only a matter of uncertain chametz. But when it is definite chametz, even if it is many days prior, as long as it is in his possession, one cannot rely on the animals and chickens eating it, and he is obligated to check and eliminate it. And the sides of the courtyard, even if it is uncertain chametz, require checking; only the middle of the courtyard, where ravens are commonly found, does not require checking for uncertain chametz, but not the sides of the courtyard. And for us, we do not customarily check the courtyard at all, because we are not accustomed to eating in the courtyard. Additionally, with us, dogs and pigs rummage through the holes and eat. Furthermore, we are accustomed to sweeping the courtyard. Moreover, by the time of Passover, it is still typically winter in most years, and it is not common at all to find chametz in the courtyards because we do not eat in the courtyard due to the cold.

A hole between a Jew and his fellow – each one checks as far as his hand can reach, and the rest he nullifies in his heart, and that suffices. However, nullification is necessary, for perhaps a small amount of chametz (leavened bread) has rolled there. But between a Jew and a non-Jew – no checking is necessary at all, for perhaps the non-Jew will say that the Jew is performing sorcery against him, and this could lead to danger. Therefore, nullification suffices. And although those engaged in a mitzvah are not harmed, where harm is common, it is different (Chullin 8b), and we do not rely on miracles. Nevertheless, if there is certainly chametz, it must be removed during the day (Orach Chaim 16:6). And it seems that nowadays one is obligated to check, for in our times, the non-Jew will not say that the Jew is performing sorcery, and they know that he is practicing his religion.

A wall that was used for chametz in its holes and fell and became a heap; even if it is not three handbreadths high and a dog can search there – nevertheless, it does not need to be checked underneath, because there is a danger of scorpions. This is true in their hot climates. In our regions, where this danger does not exist, one is obligated to check. And in a place where snakes are found but not scorpions – one is also obligated to check (Magen Avraham, subsection 13), because there is not as much danger from a snake as from a scorpion. The reason we are concerned about danger, despite the principle that those performing a mitzvah are not harmed, is that this is not similar to the previous law where harm is common; this pertains to a person and not to a scorpion, as a scorpion is not considered a common danger. However, here we are concerned that perhaps he lost a needle there earlier, and after completing his inspection, when he is no longer engaged in the mitzvah, he might search for the needle and then be bitten by the scorpion, resulting in danger. This only applies to doubtful chametz. But when there is definite chametz, if it is not covered by three handbreadths, one is required to remove it using a hoe and shovel, in a way that does not bring danger. If it is covered by three handbreadths, one nullifies it in his heart and that suffices, as it is considered as if it has been burned. There is an opinion that even in the case of doubt, one is obligated to remove it, but there is no obligation to use a candle and perform a meticulous inspection (Bach), rather one should inspect as much as possible by daylight. Certainly, one must inspect at night and by candlelight, and all using a hoe and shovel (Kesef Mishneh in Magen Avraham at the end of subsection 12). It is also explained in the language of Rashi (Pesachim 8a, s.v. "denafal") who wrote: "He is not obligated to inspect a heap of stones except for what is visible, but not to insert his hand among them." This is his language, explaining that one is not exempt from inspection entirely.

And if one transgresses the prohibition of "bal yera'eh" (not seeing chametz) when a mound fell on the chametz and he did not nullify it: if there are not three handbreadths over it, it is clear that he transgresses. However, if there are three handbreadths over it, some say he does not transgress, as it is considered as if it were destroyed. And some say that since he can remove it with a shovel and pickaxe, it is not considered destroyed, and he transgresses "bal yera'eh." According to this, if he did not nullify it until after the prohibition time, when he can no longer nullify it, he is obligated to remove the mound to destroy it. It is obvious that if a large mound fell on it, which he cannot remove, he does not transgress, as it is not considered "yours" (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 17). Therefore, some say that in such a case, if it is found after Passover, it is permitted to eat. This requires further study. (See Magen Avraham there, Chayei Adam subparagraph 2, and Taz subparagraph 8.)

A wine cellar, from which wine is taken for use at a meal, and it is arranged in rows of barrels next to each other until it is completely filled, and then other rows are arranged on top of the lower ones up to the beam – it is only necessary to inspect the top row and the one below it, that is, the row along the width of the cellar. And not the entire area of the cellar, but the top one that faces the beam and the entrance, and the one below it, meaning when the entrance is opened – the upper row and the one beneath it. For in these two rows, it is customary to use the wine for the meal, and there is a concern of chametz, and no more.

Synagogues and study halls – it is certain that children bring chametz (leavened bread) into them throughout the year, and they are considered places where chametz is brought in. The sexton is obligated to check them by the light of the fourteenth, with a blessing. He should check all the hiding places, and all the cabinets and shtenders. If he did not check at night, he can check during the day by sunlight, because there are many windows and it is like a portico that is well-lit (Ch. 10, small section 22). It seems to me, in my humble opinion, according to the Tosafot, who wrote at the beginning of Pesachim in one resolution, that the reason for requiring checking is so that one does not transgress "bal yera'eh" (the prohibition of chametz being seen) – there is no need for a blessing when checking a synagogue or study hall, as they do not have specific owners who would transgress "bal yera'eh." In this regard, it is like an ownerless house. And it cannot be said that the treasurer or sexton would transgress "bal yera'eh," because he can say, "I do not wish to acquire this prohibited item," as we say in the Gemara (Bava Metzia 96b). The chametz found is completely ownerless. And according to all opinions, it is obvious that the sages did not institute the inspection for such cases. Therefore, it appears to me that the sexton should not recite a blessing but should inspect without a blessing. Additionally, he does not need to recite "Kol Chamira" (the declaration nullifying chametz), as this chametz does not require nullification, and nullification would not help since it does not belong to him (this is how it appears to me in my humble opinion).

The Tur and Shulchan Aruch write in Section 11: "One who sweeps his room on the thirteenth of Nisan, with the intention to search for and destroy chametz, and is careful not to bring in more chametz, nonetheless must still check on the night of the fourteenth." This is their language, and this is similar to what I wrote at the end of the previous section: even though they have already checked, as is our custom, they are still obligated to perform the primary search which was ordained for the night of the fourteenth. It is written that one must check thoroughly at night, and not just to fulfill the obligation of checking, because through sweeping, what is in the cracks is not destroyed, and one must now check with the light of a candle in the cracks, holes, and crevices (Magen Avraham, Subsection 20). This does not apply to us, as we check thoroughly before Passover. There is an opinion that says: specifically if one checked on the day of the thirteenth. But if one checked on the night of the thirteenth, they do not need to check again on the night of the fourteenth (Chayei Adam, Subsection 23). And I am astonished: since it was not done according to the enactment of the sages, it certainly does not help, and one is obligated to check on the night of the fourteenth. Unless one checked on the night of the thirteenth with a blessing, then certainly they cannot bless again, and the mitzvah was not performed in the most preferred manner (and perhaps this is the intention of the Chayei Adam).

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote: Every person needs to clean their rooms before the search. This is his language because they cannot be properly checked without cleaning. For this reason, it is customary to use feathers for the search for chametz, in order to clean (Magen Avraham, Subsection 21). And with us, where we wash and scrape – this is preferable to cleaning. And the pockets or sleeves of clothes, where chametz is sometimes placed – they need to be checked at night, and the next day, and shaken out thoroughly.

After the inspection, one should be careful with the chametz that is left to eat at night and the next morning; to store it in such a way that he will not need another inspection, such as if a mouse takes it in front of him. And such as if his bread is missing, that he left ten and found nine. But if he stores it – no harm will come. And it is not only another inspection that will be required, but also another nullification if it is missing. For when he nullified after the inspection – his intention was not on the chametz that he left to eat (Chapter 10). Therefore, if he will be compelled to inspect it, he will also be compelled to nullify it again. And he should not make another blessing (ibid.).
