And not only after the examination should he hide it, but during the examination and before the beginning of the examination he should hide the chametz (leavened bread), because perhaps in the middle of the examination he will lack from what he set aside, and he will need to examine again what he already checked (Magen Avraham and Chayei Adam, and see Taz). Therefore, the custom is that before the examination, they place the chametz that they are setting aside into one container, and place it in a special designated place to hide it. (And what the Magen Avraham wrote in subsection 1, that the people only hide the chametz they find during the examination, and the rest of the chametz they carry here and there, and they do not act properly. Until here his words – we do not know of this custom.)

And specifically, when it is known that some chametz (leavened bread) is missing from that which was set aside – another inspection is required. But in a standard case – there is no concern that perhaps a weasel dragged chametz from place to place, and perhaps after we inspected this room – it dragged it from another place into this room. For if we begin to worry about this – there would be no end to the matter. Additionally, even if there is a concern that the weasel dragged it, one can also say that it dragged it and ate it. However, if it is certain that the weasel dragged it – it is not possible to permit it on the grounds of "perhaps it ate it," for a doubt does not override a certainty (see Gemara 9a).

The Tur writes: If one covered it with a utensil and did not find it, no further inspection is necessary; since it is impossible for a weasel or mouse to take it, we can assume with certainty that a person took it. However, if it was not covered with a utensil and was not found, further inspection is required. Therefore, it is good to suspend it in the air or place it in a box, a place where a mouse cannot reach. This is the end of his words. Explanation of his words: Behold, we said that one should hide the chametz, and one must know the manner of hiding. What should we do if we hid it and it is missing? He explains that there are three levels in this matter: The first and best manner of hiding is to suspend it in the air or place it in a box, where a mouse cannot reach. In this way, no mishap can occur at all. The second level is to cover it with a utensil. Even though this is not entirely secure, as perhaps a person might come and remove the utensil, and then a weasel or mouse might come and drag away the chametz, nevertheless, we do not worry about this. And even if the chametz is missing, we assume that a person took and ate it. The third level is when it is placed somewhere without a cover – certainly if it is missing, further inspection is required. Therefore, the Tur did not initially prescribe covering, because this is not a proper guarding method except as a last resort, as I have written. But our teacher, the Beit Yosef, in section 1, wrote: Therefore, one should cover it with a utensil or suspend it in the air, etc. – for he holds that covering with a utensil is also a proper guarding method initially. And we are not concerned about uncovering, because it is not customary for people to uncover, but rather to cover, as explained in Tractate Parah, Chapter Eleven; see there. And even though in Siman 460, regarding finding chametz on Yom Tov, covering with a utensil is not sufficient, as will be explained there – this is due to the concern that one might come to eat it (Magen Avraham, subsection 4), and not due to the concern of uncovering. And this applies specifically to a wide utensil, which a weasel or mouse cannot uncover. But covering with a cloth or something similar is not effective, because they tend to uncover, as stated in Chullin (10a there).

After completing the search for chametz at night, one should immediately nullify the chametz. The reason is that now, even if there remains chametz in the house that was not found, one will not transgress the prohibition of "bal yera'eh" (not seeing chametz), since it has been nullified. One nullifies the chametz that was not seen, because it is impossible to nullify also the chametz that one sees, as one plans to eat it that night and the next day. For how can one nullify it while keeping it to eat? Therefore, one only nullifies the chametz that is not seen, so as not to transgress "bal yera'eh" if chametz is later found in any place. And one says: "All chametz and leaven that is in my possession, which I have not seen and have not destroyed, shall be nullified and shall be like the dust of the earth." This formula is established in Aramaic because that was their language, and it is also close to the Holy Tongue. One may nullify in any language one wishes. Moreover, if one is unlearned or if a woman is nullifying, it is better to say it in a language that is understood. One must specify "chametz" and "se'or" (leaven), and the term "chamira" includes both. In our prayer books, the text reads: "All chamira and chamia," and at the end: "and shall be ownerless like the dust of the earth." There is no difference in this, but the main point is that one understands what is being said, for if one does not understand, it is not a valid nullification and amounts to nothing (Magen Avraham, small section 6).

And it is good to annul it again the next day, a second time, in the sixth hour at the time of burning the chametz. The reason is that the annulment at night does not include the chametz that was set aside to eat, as we have explained. If so, there is a concern that some of that chametz might remain and he will transgress "bal yera'eh" (the prohibition of owning chametz during Passover), since it was not included in the annulment. In the second annulment, he can also annul the chametz that he sees. For at night, when he set it aside to eat, it was not possible to annul it, as I wrote. But the next day, at the sixth hour, when it is forbidden to eat and benefit from it, he can annul everything. And they say: "All chametz that is in my possession, whether I have seen it or not, whether I have destroyed it or not, shall be annulled…" The annulment is before the sixth hour, for in the sixth hour it is forbidden to benefit from it by rabbinic decree, and he cannot annul it. And he should perform the annulment after burning the chametz, for if he does it before, the chametz he wants to burn will be annulled, and he will not fulfill the mitzvah of burning his chametz. However, if he annulled it before the burning, what he has done is done. And one should not say, "Since he annuls during the day, why is the night annulment needed at the time of checking for chametz?" It is not so, for what if he forgets to annul during the day and will transgress "bal yera'eh" if chametz is found? But at night, he will not forget, for he has a specific time during the checking of the chametz. And even though there is also a specific time during the day, at the time of burning the chametz, it is not the same; for he might forget to burn it until after the time of its prohibition, and then he cannot annul it (Magen Avraham, section 7).

And know: The reason we wrote that the purpose of nullifying [the chametz] after the search is so that one does not transgress "You shall not see [leaven]" if any chametz remains, as the Tur wrote. And this is his language: "And after the search, one should nullify it... so that even if some chametz remains in the house that he did not find, he does not transgress it...". But this is not understandable, for how could he transgress "You shall not see" after he has searched with all his ability? The Torah was not given to ministering angels, and he is completely coerced! And there are those who wrote in this language: "If he did not nullify it, he transgresses, even though he does not know, similar to one who ate forbidden fat unknowingly" (Magen Avraham, Small Paragraph 5). And I am astonished: This certainly transgresses, even though he does not know of the chametz, but that is when he did not search! But when he did what the Torah commanded him and searched, this is not inadvertent but coerced. And in the Gemara (6b), which states: "one who searches needs to nullify" – it did not say so because perhaps there is chametz that he does not know about and he will transgress, but rather perhaps he will find a beautiful piece of bread and spare it from burning, and then he will transgress "You shall not see." See there. But if he does not find it – he does not transgress. (And even according to the Tosafot's interpretation there, that it is not nullified by itself – all this is when he finds the chametz. And it is forced to say that the Tur's intention is also that there remains chametz and he finds it, for if so, the essence of his words is lacking. And the Bach also wondered about this, and they are also against the words of the Rosh, see there. And be precise, and you will find it light.)

And it appears to me that the intention of the Tur is as the Rambam wrote in Chapter 3, Halacha 7, and this is his language: "And when he finishes checking... he needs to nullify... Therefore, if he did not nullify before the sixth hour, and from the sixth hour and onward he finds chametz that he had in mind, and it was in his heart, and he forgot it at the time of the burning and did not burn it – he has transgressed 'Bal Yera'eh'... until here is his language." And he was precise in saying "chametz that he had in mind... and he forgot it," in this it is clear that he transgresses, because he saw it and had it in mind, and it is close to intentional. And there are those who interpret the Rambam's intention that any chametz he was initially unaware of – he does not transgress it at all. And they created a dispute between the Rambam and the Tur (Magen Avraham there). But this is not so, for certainly in a place where chametz is brought in, and chametz is found there – he transgresses 'Bal Yera'eh', even though he was not aware of it at all. But this is when he did not check and did not do what the Torah commanded him. But when he checked, and this chametz he did not find, and he was completely unaware of it – certainly he does not transgress, as he is completely coerced. And this is also the intention of the Tur, who wrote: if chametz remained in the house that he did not find... and this is the chametz he saw when he began to check, and he had it in mind... (and the Rambam explains in the Gemara: perhaps he will find a nice piece of bread and have it in mind, meaning: perhaps he will find that chametz which he had in mind previously. And this is not like the explanation of Rashi and Tosafot. Be precise and you will find the truth.)

The Tur and Shulchan Aruch ruled that one can appoint an agent to nullify his chametz. Several other authorities have also ruled this way. Just as one can appoint an agent for the search (for chametz), so too for the nullification. And even though it is merely verbal, this is not considered "matters that cannot be entrusted to an agent." This applies when one appoints an agent to delegate the matter to another agent. However, for the agent himself, one can appoint him even for verbal matters (see Gittin 29a). According to this, to tell Reuven to appoint an agent on his behalf to Shimon to nullify (the chametz) – this is not possible, for this is considered "matters that cannot be entrusted to an agent."

And specifically when it is explicitly stipulated that he will nullify [the chametz]. But if he appoints someone solely for the search – he cannot nullify [the chametz] (Magen Avraham, small section 9). However, it seems to me that nowadays, when someone is asked to search for chametz – the intention is also for nullification. For the entire process of searching and nullifying is referred to as "the search for chametz," as is known. And there are those who say that one needs to stand next to the agent (there in the name of Maharil). This is not understood. The reason for those who are stringent about this is because they hold that a mitzvah that is incumbent upon the person’s body cannot be delegated to an agent (as written by the Machatzit HaShekel and the Magen Avraham in Siman 437). If so, what does it help that he stands next to him? And furthermore, this is not the custom.

When the agent nullifies the chametz, he needs to say, "The chametz of so-and-so shall be nullified." He can nullify the chametz wherever he is. If he is not accustomed to doing so, his wife can nullify the chametz. Even though it is without his knowledge, it is certainly agreeable to him, and it is beneficial for him so that he will not transgress "You shall not see [leaven]." The current custom is that if the head of the household is not at home, the wife asks a man to perform the search for chametz. This includes both the search and the nullification according to the law, as we are witnesses that it is agreeable to the owner. There should be no doubt about this, but it is necessary to say: "All chametz that is in the domain of the law." (What is written in the Ba’er Hetev regarding this is puzzling.)

Some of the early authorities completely forbade nullification [of chametz] through an agent, reasoning that since nullification is akin to declaring something ownerless (hefker), and just as one person cannot make something belonging to another ownerless, similarly, they cannot nullify it (Ran, first chapter, in the name of some authorities). However, this comparison is not valid, because chametz, in any case, is not considered to be in a person's possession. The Torah only considers it to be in one's possession for the purpose of the prohibition of "it shall not be seen" (bal yera'eh). Therefore, a mere expression of intent (gilui daata) is sufficient (Beit Yosef), as I have explained this reasoning regarding the nullification itself in Siman 431, Section 13. See there. This is the primary ruling in practice. And a guardian (apotropos) of orphans must inspect and nullify the chametz of the orphans (Chayei Adam).

If one did not check on the night of the 14th, he should check during the day whenever he remembers. If he remembers before the sixth hour, he should check and nullify. During the sixth hour, he should check and burn. He should not nullify, as it is no longer in his possession, since it is forbidden to benefit from it. One must check by candlelight as at night. If one did not check on the 14th day, he should check throughout the days of Passover, even on Yom Tov itself, even if he nullified before Passover. He does not transgress "bal yera’eh" (the prohibition against seeing leaven), nevertheless, we decree lest he come to eat from it. On Yom Tov, when it is forbidden to burn, he should cover it with a vessel until the night, and then burn it (Magen Avraham and Taz). Why do we not decree that he might come to eat during the checking? Because there is no concern for this, since he is occupied with its removal, he will remember and not eat. Even on the last day of Yom Tov, one must check (ibid.). There is an opinion that on Yom Tov one should not check (Bach), but this is not the main opinion.

And if one did not check during the intermediate days of the festival, he is required to check even after Passover so that he does not stumble upon chametz that has passed through Passover, which is forbidden for benefit. This checking also needs to be as the Sages ordained, by the light of a candle (Taz). And if he nullified [the chametz] before Passover, thereby not violating "You shall not see [chametz]," some say, according to the Ba'al Ha'itur, that he does not need to check, for if he nullified it, it is permitted for benefit (Chayei Adam). However, we do not hold according to the Ba'al Ha'itur.

When one checks for chametz on the eve of Passover, and during Passover itself, one must recite a blessing, even if one has nullified the chametz. However, after Passover, since the checking is only to prevent the prohibition of chametz that has passed through Passover, it is not appropriate to recite a blessing. How can one bless over the removal of chametz while consuming chametz? Even if one did not nullify it and violated the prohibition of "it shall not be seen," in any case, a blessing is not appropriate for this. If one checked and nullified the chametz properly and then found chametz during Passover, or if dough became chametz during Passover, some say one must bless at the time of removal (Chayei Adam and Mahara"m Chaviv). Others are uncertain about this (Turei Zahav and Magen Avraham). It seems to me, in my humble opinion, that in cases of doubt regarding blessings, we are lenient, and the blessing recited on the eve of the fourteenth (of Nissan) applies to all subsequent searches (as written by the Gaon Kereiti u'Pleiti in Sefer Shar HaElef). If one did not check for chametz and died at the sixth hour, the heirs should not recite a blessing. They should check without a blessing, as they do not inherit the prohibition, and the deceased is no longer required to check (Chayei Adam and Mahara"m Chaviv). It is obvious that one should not recite a blessing for a tiny amount of chametz, only for an olive-sized amount (Chayei Adam). (Mahara"m Chaviv wrote that one can appoint an agent to handle chametz that will be acquired later, as an act of removal, by distancing oneself from the chametz. For chametz, an explicit declaration of intent suffices.)

Maimonides wrote at the end of the second chapter: One who sets sail on the sea or goes out in a caravan, within thirty days [before Passover] is obligated to perform the search [for chametz]. If it is more than thirty days [before Passover], he is not required to perform the search. However, if he intends to return before Passover, he must perform the search and then depart, lest he return on the eve of Passover at twilight and not have time to eliminate [the chametz]. If he does not intend to return, he is not required to perform the search. Thus far his words.

The reason for the thirty days is because from that time, since we begin expounding the laws of Passover thirty days before Passover, as I have written in Siman 429, the obligation of the search falls upon him, as it is stated in the Gemara (6a). One should not ask: if so, anyone who travels from his home after Purim should be obligated to perform the search. This is not so, as this concern applies only to someone embarking on a distant journey, such as by sea or through deserts. But for a regular journey, there is no concern (Magen Avraham, subsection 1).

However, for sea and desert journeys, even if he plans to return several days before Passover, he is obligated to perform the search, because on a distant journey delays can occur. Nevertheless, everything depends on the situation. Even on a nearby journey, if he plans to return one or two days before Passover, he must perform the search, as even in a short time delays can occur (ibid.). It is obvious that all this applies when he does not leave a wife and children at home. If he leaves them, they will perform the search (Beit Yosef), and this is the ruling in the Tur and Shulchan Aruch.

And behold, regarding this stringency, that even if one's intention is to return before Passover, one is still obligated to check, lest he comes on the eve of Passover during twilight – Rashi and the Tur did not rule this way. And this is the language of the Tur: One who sets out from land to sea or departs with a caravan and does not leave anyone in his house to check, and does not intend to return during Passover, if it is before thirty days prior to Passover – he does not need to remove [the chametz]. And when Passover arrives – he will nullify it in his heart. And if it is within thirty days – he must remove it, for the obligation of removal has already fallen upon him, since we are expounding on the laws of Passover. And if his intention is to return during Passover – even from the beginning of the year, he must remove it. And if he forgot and did not check – he will nullify it when Passover arrives. Thus far his language. So, it is clear that he did not require checking before thirty days if his intention is to return, except when his intention is to return during Passover, for then he cannot nullify it and will transgress "You shall not see [chametz]." But if he returns before Passover – he does not need to do anything, for upon his arrival he will check. And if you ask: Even if he does not intend to return, why does he not need to remove it before thirty days, since he will transgress "You shall not see [chametz]?" The Tur indeed wrote: "And when Passover arrives – he will nullify it in his heart," meaning: where he is. And although the Rabbis decreed checking, this applies to the place where he is, where there is concern of eating [chametz]; not when the chametz is elsewhere. And even according to the reason we wrote in Siman 431:15, that the Sages did not want to rely on nullification, because it depends on a person's thought, and perhaps he will not nullify it properly, see there – this is in general. But in a specific case where he is far away – it is necessary to rely on nullification. And it is a simple matter that if he did not nullify – he will transgress "You shall not see [chametz]" even if he did not see the chametz, if there is chametz in places that require checking (Magen Avraham, small section 11). And we have already written this in Siman 434:8, see there. (And the Magen Avraham there, small section 5, made a dispute about this. And we have explained there that it is not so, as the Magen Avraham himself wrote here plainly, and there is a need to examine his words there. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

And behold, from the words of the Tur, it is explicitly clear that if one intends to return before Passover, even within thirty days, one is not required to perform the search [for chametz]. And this is necessarily so, because according to this opinion, we are not concerned that one might come [back] on the eve of Passover during twilight. If so, what difference does it make whether it is within thirty days or after thirty days? And so wrote one of the commentators on the Shulchan Aruch (Taz, subsection 5). But from the words of our Rabbi, the Beit Yosef, who wrote in subsection 2: "And some say that before thirty days, one does not need to check, meaning when one does not intend to return during Passover. And even if one intends to return before Passover or after it, one does not need to check, as long as it is before thirty days...," this is his language. And this is the opinion of Rashi and the Tur. He was meticulous in saying "before thirty days," but within thirty days, one is obligated to check even if one intends to return before Passover, because the obligation to check has already fallen upon him. And so agreed the great later authorities (Chayei Adam, subsection 10, and Machatzit HaShekel, subsection 9, not like the Taz. And this also appears in the Jerusalem Talmud, as we will explain with the help of Heaven).

And know that the opinions of the Rambam and the Tur are according to our Talmud, that their view is that returning [to one's home] is more stringent. However, they differ in their interpretation: the Rambam holds that even if one intends to return before Passover, and the Tur interprets that it is specifically within Passover, as I have written. But in the Jerusalem Talmud, it is explained in this language (Jerusalem Talmud, Pesachim, Chapter 1, Halacha 1): One who goes out to sea before thirty days does not need to check [for chametz]. Within thirty days, he needs to check. This is said when he intends to return, but if he does not intend to return, even before thirty days, he needs to check. And in doubt, but certainly, even from Rosh Hashanah. Rabbi Ba said: And even if he intends to return, he needs to check, lest he change his mind and not return. Thus far is the language of the Jerusalem Talmud.

According to the opinion of Rashi and the Tur, one should align the matters as explained in our Talmud, and this is its explanation: This statement applies when one intends to return before Passover. But if one does not intend to return before Passover, but rather during Passover – even before the thirty days, one needs to check. According to the Rambam's interpretation, the Jerusalem Talmud disagrees with our Talmud (Ran there). In my humble opinion, it seems that the Rambam interprets our Talmud as referring to definite chametz, as the Jerusalem Talmud itself says that one is always obligated to check. However, if one does not intend to return at all – the Jerusalem Talmud would agree that one can nullify it in its place, and that is sufficient. There is evidence from the language of our Talmud that it is referring to definite chametz, since it says "obligated to remove" and does not say "obligated to check" as the Jerusalem Talmud states. "Checking" applies to doubt, and "removal" applies to certainty. And even though the Rambam himself used the term "to check" – he did not concern himself with this detail to change his language from other chapters. But in cases of doubt – it is possible that the Rambam agrees with Rashi and the Tur, and the Rambam rules like Rabbi Ba, that in certainty, even if one intends to return before Passover – one is obligated to remove. According to this, our sages would not differ in practice, only in the interpretation of the Gemara. For Rashi and the Tur interpret it in a case of doubt, and the Rambam interprets it in a case of certainty. However, in any case, for us, in practice, one should be stringent in all matters regarding certainty, and in cases of doubt, one should rule according to Rashi and the Tur, since the Jerusalem Talmud supports them. (And the commentators of the Jerusalem Talmud struggled greatly to interpret it according to the Rambam, and according to my interpretation, it fits well in simplicity. Examine it and you will find it easy.)

And know that in a situation where one is required to check (for chametz) – one must check on the night before (Passover) by candlelight (Magen Avraham, subsection 1). And at the time of checking, one should also nullify (the chametz) (ibid). Some say that the nullification should be left for the eve of Passover (Taz and Eliyah Rabbah, subsection 3). In my humble opinion, the primary view is the first one (and so wrote the Ma'aseh Choshev, subsection 2), that wherever the Sages instituted checking, nullification is required, as they said: "One who checks must also nullify." (And what the Rema wrote – this applies to before thirty days, see there.) However, one should not recite a blessing, as the blessing was only instituted for the time of checking for chametz. Similarly, in a place where we said one needs to check, and he forgot and did not check – he should nullify (the chametz) when Passover arrives. And he should not recite a blessing on the nullification, because the essence of nullification is in the heart, and we do not recite blessings on matters of the heart (Magen Avraham, subsection 13).

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote regarding these laws, and this is his language: "Also, his wife should check and annul [the chametz] in his house, because he might forget to annul it where he is." Until here is his language. And his words are puzzling: for it has already been explained that these laws only apply when one has not left someone in his house to check and annul. But when he has left someone – he does not need to do anything (there, subsection 14). And it must be said: that which has been explained – is when he left a man in his house, but one should not rely on a woman (Bach). And therefore, it says that in any case, she should check and annul. And there is one who says that which has been explained, that when he left someone in his house he does not need to check – this is when he instructed that they should check in his absence, and here we are dealing with a case where he did not instruct, and therefore he should not rely on the checking of his house (Magen Avraham there). And therefore, it says that in any case, she should check and annul. And there is one who explained such as when he has a separate room, and his wife and household have their own separate rooms (Chayei Adam, subsection 14). And it seems to me that he holds that only checking was not required when he left someone in his house, because they will check on the night of the fourteenth. But the annulment – it is always upon him even when he is far away on the road, for in every place he can annul. And his annulment is much better than theirs, for the chametz is not theirs. Therefore, the one who goes on the road – they will check on the night of the fourteenth, and he will annul wherever he is, and they do not need to annul. And therefore, it says that in any case, his wife should check and annul in his house, because he might forget to annul where he is, meaning: that at the time of the checking she should also annul.

And similarly, one who makes his house a storage, meaning: all year he used chametz there, and now he wants to make it a storage for wood or another item (Magen Avraham, Small Section 4) – within thirty days, he is required to check, and afterward he can place his storage inside it. If he did not check beforehand – he must remove the storage and check (ibid., Small Section 5). And even if he does not intend to clear it before Passover, which is akin to rubble falling upon it, nevertheless, since it is within thirty days – the obligation of checking applies to him. If it is before thirty days, if he intends to clear it before Passover – he must check, and afterward make it a storage, because we are concerned that he might clear it until only three handbreadths remain, and then he will be preoccupied and not check (ibid., Small Section 6). If he does not intend to clear it before Passover – he does not need to check, as it is akin to rubble falling upon it. This is according to the Rambam. But according to the Tur, if he intends to clear it before Passover – he also does not need to check, as he will check then, as he holds regarding one who is traveling and intends to return before Passover (Beit Yosef). And what is stated in the Gemara (ibid.) that if he intends to clear it, he is obligated to check – this is if he intends to clear it during Passover.

And this applies to a standard inspection. But if there is known chametz there, in any case, one is obligated to remove it (Magen Avraham, subsection 7). This is not comparable to chametz upon which a collapse has fallen, as that is considered as if it has already been removed; for this applies when it has fallen, not when it is intentionally placed upon it, like in the case of a storage house, which is considered as intentionally concealing it from the outset. And we have already written that all matters regarding someone going on a journey do not pertain to known chametz. Only according to the Rambam have we innovated that it pertains to known chametz, as I wrote in subsection 5. (And I am puzzled by the Magen Avraham, who wrote here that it does not pertain to known chametz, and in subsection 1 regarding someone going on a journey, he wrote that it does pertain to known chametz. And in the Gemara, it compares someone going on a journey to making one's house a storage house, see there. This requires further examination.)

And Rabbi Moshe Isserles (the Rema) wrote: Regarding a storehouse of wheat, if there are leavened grains at the bottom of the pit, if the storehouse was set up thirty days before Passover, one is not required to remove them; it is sufficient to nullify them in one's heart. However, after Passover, when cleaning out the storehouse, it is forbidden to benefit from those grains. And if there is no known chametz, only a doubt, it is permissible to sell the storehouse as is. Thus far his words. And there are those who disagree with him, for in the case of known chametz, it has been clarified that in all instances one is obligated to check (Taz, subparagraph 4). Furthermore, in this law where there is a concern of leavening in the storehouse itself, there is no difference between within thirty days or before thirty days. For only when the concern of leavening is due to what was previously under the storehouse is there a distinction, because it is like chametz upon which a collapse fell, which is considered as removed. Therefore, before thirty days, there is no need to remove. But if there is a concern of leavening in the storehouse itself, what difference does it make whether it is within thirty days or before thirty days (ibid.)?

And behold, there is no proof from our teacher, the Rema, that his intention is there is a concern of chametz in this storehouse. For if so, certainly there would be no difference between within thirty days and before thirty days. Rather, he is dealing with bringing in good wheat that has no concern of chametz, and the chametz was there beforehand. And that which he permitted even known chametz, even though known chametz is certainly forbidden—this is initially. But after the fact, there is no concern, for it is like a collapse (Magen Avraham, subsection 8). And there is one who says that even initially it is permitted even with known chametz, for the reason of a collapse, and for the reason that before thirty days we do not care, and when the time arrives, it will be nullified (Chayei Adam, subsection 8). And this is a very lenient position. And from the Jerusalem Talmud it is explicitly clear that known chametz must be removed even before thirty days, as I wrote in subsection 5.

One who places good wheat in a clean pit, and there is no concern of leavening there, but afterwards, due to the moisture, the wheat becomes slightly leavened—he does not need to remove it, even if it happens within thirty days. Since at the time he placed it there it was not leavened, later when it becomes leavened, it is as if a collapse fell on it, and it is considered as if it has been removed. All the more so if there is doubt whether it has become leavened, as no one would empty their pit (Magen Avraham, subsection 8, in the name of the Responsa of the Rashba).

Our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, wrote in Section 3: A Jew who leaves the house of a non-Jew within thirty days, and enters another house in this city, or goes to another city, does not need to search and remove the chametz from the non-Jew's house, for he will fulfill the mitzvah of search and removal in that other house. However, if he is traveling on a ship or going in a caravan, and will not enter a house during Passover, there is an opinion that he is obligated to search and remove the chametz, since it is within thirty days. He needs to search and remove the chametz from the non-Jew's house that he is leaving in order to fulfill the mitzvah of search and removal, even though the non-Jew will enter the house during Passover. And there are those who say that he does not need to do so if the non-Jew will enter the house. Thus far is his language. At first glance, the first opinion is puzzling, for is the search an obligation upon the person? The obligation of searching within thirty days applies when he has something to search. But in this situation, where the non-Jew enters the house and the chametz remains with the non-Jew, why should the Jew need to search? Moreover, if so, even one who leaves the house of a Jew within thirty days would need to search if it were a personal obligation. And indeed, there are those who have rejected the first opinion for this reason (Taz, Subsection 7).

It appears to me that the intention is as follows: Certainly, if the non-Jew enters the house before Passover, it does not require inspection. However, if he enters during Passover and there is Jewish-owned chametz found there, even though it is considered ownerless since it was left there, nevertheless, the obligation to inspect this house for chametz still applies. This is because all chametz is not under a person's control during Passover, yet the Torah commanded to inspect, and if not, one violates the prohibition of "it shall not be seen." Therefore, here too: although one does not violate "it shall not be seen," nevertheless, the mitzvah of inspecting for chametz has not been fulfilled, because even when the first hour of Passover arrives, it is still considered his chametz. And it would be acceptable if a Jew were to enter and fulfill the mitzvah of inspecting this chametz, or if the non-Jew were to enter before Passover, the chametz would be considered the non-Jew's. But if he enters during Passover, he must inspect. However, if he has another place to inspect, we do not worry about this, because the Jewish ownership of this chametz is nullified when he has another house and other chametz. It is clear that if no one enters the house, one is obligated to eliminate it if it is within thirty days (Magen Avraham, subsection 17).

It is proper that for the entire thirty days before Passover, when one performs any action, they should ensure that no chametz (leavened bread) remains stuck, which would be difficult to remove, or hidden chametz in a crevice. Therefore, one who studies a book while eating should examine it from Purim onwards to ensure that no chametz remains in it, so that it is not found on Passover. And similarly for all similar cases (see Magen Avraham there and Bach).

If a person rents a house to his friend for the purpose of (starting) the fourteenth (of Nisan) and beyond, meaning he rented it to him before the fourteenth, and the renter has already acquired it through one of the methods of acquisition that apply to the rental of land: through money, a document, physical possession, or a symbolic act of acquisition, and the landlord has already left the house, but the keys of the house are still in his hand, and the renter does not enter the house until after the beginning of the night of the fourteenth, when he receives the keys. Therefore, the obligation to search for chametz (leavened bread) falls on the landlord, since the chametz is his; even though he nullified it and will not transgress "you shall not see" (the prohibition of owning chametz during Passover), and he will not be in the house at all during the days of Passover, and the renter has already acquired it; nevertheless, since the keys were with him at the beginning of the night of the fourteenth, and the chametz is his, the obligation to search for chametz applies to him, and it does not transfer from him when the renter enters afterward, even on that same night. The nullification also applies to him (according to the Gra). The renter also needs to nullify it, since he is also nullifying his own chametz. But if the landlord handed over the key to the renter during the day, the renter is obligated to search and also nullify it. Even though the chametz is not his, the landlord certainly renounced ownership of it when he left, and therefore it is considered the renter's chametz, and he can nullify it. This applies when the renter has acquired the house. But if he has not yet acquired it, it does not help that the key is in his hand. The obligation falls on the landlord, as this is similar to someone who has deposited his key with another person; the obligation to search falls on the depositor and not on the depository. (The Magen Avraham writes in subparagraph 3 that if the key was handed over, the renter is obligated to search and also nullify it. Nevertheless, the landlord also needs to nullify it. He wrote that this is implied in Tosafot. There is no proof from Tosafot, as the Chayei Adam wrote. The Machatzit HaShekel in subparagraph 3 raised the difficulty: This implies that the chametz becomes the renter's, and in the Gemara, it says that the chametz belongs to the landlord. See there for a lengthy discussion. It is not difficult at all. What the Gemara means is: Or perhaps the renter must search, as the prohibition is in his domain – the explanation is: He acquires the chametz for this reason, since the landlord renounced it, and he accepted the house, he accepted everything in it. This is Rashi's intention, see there. Even though the chametz itself is not his, and perhaps he does not want to acquire it, it is still considered "found in your possession" and he transgresses "you shall not see." The Pnei Yehoshua also wrote this, see there. This is not related to the general statement that renting does not make it (the house) his, as this concerns making the house his in essence. But for the time being, it is his house, and we call it "it shall not be found in your houses." See Pnei Yehoshua there, analyze and you will find it clear.)

And this applies to a renter. But if one sells a house to another, and he leaves the house on the thirteenth and locks it, and the buyer acquires it with a complete acquisition, even if the key remains with the seller at the beginning of the night of the fourteenth – nevertheless, the obligation of searching for chametz is not on the seller, since he has completely removed himself from the house. And the buyer, whose house it is – is obligated to search when he obtains the key (Ch. 10, sub-section 2). However, if the seller retains the key all night – it is obvious that the obligation to search is on him, since the buyer is unable to enter the house.

The Tur and Shulchan Aruch write in section 2: If someone rents a house from his friend on the fourteenth (of Nisan), and he does not know if it has been checked (for chametz), if the landlord is in the city, he should ask him if he has checked it. If the landlord is not in the city, it is presumed to be checked, and he nullifies the chametz in his heart, and that is sufficient. So far is their language. 

The intention is that he rented it on the morning of the fourteenth. For if he rented it at night, even in the middle of the night, even though the obligation of checking is on the landlord, as has been explained, and certainly when at the beginning of the night it was entirely in his possession, nevertheless we would not say that it is presumed to be checked if he is not here. For perhaps he was not among the diligent, and he thought to check it at night, and when he rented it and handed over the key, he relied on the tenant. Therefore, without asking, the tenant is obligated to check. 

Therefore, Rashi explained that he rented it on the morning of the fourteenth, and so it is in Or Zarua (Siman 245). However, some have written that even if he rented it at night, since at the beginning of the night it was in the landlord's possession, he certainly checked it. Therefore, when the landlord is not available to ask, we assume it was checked. 

So too, the Tur wrote in hints, see there (Ch. 18 and the Gra). But from Rashi and Or Zarua it is evident as I wrote. (And the words of the Taz in sub-section 2 are not understood, and see Pri Megadim.)

And why, when he is in the city, do we need to ask him and not rely on a presumption? Since the whole year he is presumed to have chametz, and based on the presumption that he presumably checked – would you come to remove him from the presumption of chametz? Therefore, wherever it is possible to clarify, we clarify. And similarly, if his wife and household members are in the city – we can ask them. Only when there is no one to ask, do we rely on the presumption that it was checked. This is the ruling of the Rambam, the Tur, and the Shulchan Aruch. Some ruled stringently (the Or Zarua and the Hagahot Maimoniyot), but this is not the opinion of the majority of decisors. (Even though in the Gemara there they straightforwardly rejected the reasoning of Rabbi Nechemiah bar Yitzchak, nevertheless, the law is like this, and since this is a rabbinic matter, we rule leniently.)

If someone rents a house to his fellow with the assumption that it has been checked for chametz (leavened bread), such as renting it to him on the morning of the fourteenth of Nisan, or if he explicitly told him that it has been checked, and afterwards it is found that it has not been checked, this is not considered a mistaken transaction (mekach ta'ut). Even though any condition regarding monetary matters is valid, in this case, we assume that his intention was not to make it a hindrance, since it is a matter of a mitzvah (commandment). And even if there are some minor expenses involved, a person would be willing to spend a small amount of money to fulfill a mitzvah. Therefore, he should check it himself or hire someone to check it, and the transaction remains valid. Some say that the cost of the checking should be deducted if he has to spend money on it, provided that it was explicitly stated that it would be checked. Certainly, he would be willing to fulfill the mitzvah but not to incur expenses for something explicitly mentioned. This is not similar to the case of a mezuzah in Yoreh De'ah, siman 291, where one does not need to return the cost of the mezuzah because the mezuzah itself has monetary value. This is not the case here, where the money is lost (Magen Avraham, subsection 6). There is no difference regarding when it was rented, whether on the thirteenth or on the fourteenth. (And in the Gemara, it says it is only assumed to be checked. It could be that this is in a general sense, but when explicitly stated, it is a mistaken transaction. However, the Ran wrote there that even if it was explicitly stated, it is not a mistaken transaction, and the Maggid Mishneh wrote similarly in the second chapter.)

Everyone is considered trustworthy regarding the searching for chametz, even women, servants, and minors. Since the searching for chametz is of rabbinic ordinance, as biblically mere nullification would suffice—the rabbis deemed them trustworthy. And although women are also considered trustworthy in biblical matters, such as slaughtering, removing forbidden fats, tithing, and separating challah, nevertheless, searching for chametz, which involves great effort, if it were not rabbinic—they would not be considered trustworthy. And in the Jerusalem Talmud, it says: Women are lazy. (See Tosafot 4b, s.v. “he’emanu.” And perhaps the Jerusalem Talmud is referring to a case where there was no nullification, and in the Jerusalem Talmud, minors are not mentioned. The version of the Jerusalem Talmud we have is corrupted; see there in the first chapter, law 1).

Even if this house is known not to have been checked, such as when we know that the owners did not inspect it, nevertheless, these individuals are believed when they say, "We have checked it." All of this is based on the rationale that has been explained. A minor needs to have the understanding to inspect. It is obvious that all of this is when the chametz has been nullified, for otherwise, they are not believed. However, even when the chametz has been nullified, it is not advisable to initially rely on the inspection of women (Magen Avraham, subsection 8). Nowadays, our women inspect even better, searching diligently for any trace of chametz, washing and cleaning all areas, and being more meticulous than men.

The Rambam wrote in the second chapter, law 7: We do not worry that a weasel might drag chametz (leavened bread) to a place where chametz is not usually brought. For if we were concerned about one house to another, we would have to be concerned from city to city, and there would be no end to it. If one checked on the night of the fourteenth... up to here is his language. For if we worry about a weasel dragging chametz, then how would we ever find a place where chametz is not usually brought that does not need checking? We would have to worry that a weasel dragged it there. However, this is not a definitive proof, for one could say that we are discussing a place where a weasel cannot go. But from the reason of "there would be no end to it," there is no need to be concerned even in a place where weasels are common (Tosafot, Pesachim 10a, s.v. "we do not worry," see there).

And this is when we did not see a weasel take a piece of chametz. But if we saw it take it – a new examination is required. And why do we not assume that it ate it? Because the doubt of eating does not remove the certainty of chametz (Talmud there). And even though it is a common doubt that it presumably ate it, nevertheless it does not remove the certainty of chametz (Tosafot there, beginning with "And if"). There is a doubt whether this is specifically when one did not nullify the chametz, making it a biblical doubt, but if it is a rabbinic doubt and one nullified the chametz – we do not need to be so concerned. Or perhaps: even in a rabbinic doubt we say that a doubt does not remove the certainty. (And the Chayei Adam, section 1 wrote: that even in rabbinic matters we say this, see there. But for me, it requires investigation, for the Talmud there is referring to the Mishnah of "we do not worry," and at the time of the Mishnah, it was not yet said that one who checks must nullify. And the cases of the person who died and the case of the fallen item brought there are biblical. And it requires investigation.)

Not only that, but even if we see a mouse entering a checked house with a loaf of bread in its mouth, and we follow it and find crumbs, even if the crumbs amount to the entire loaf – we must recheck the house for the loaf that the mouse brought in, because it is not the way of a mouse to crumble (the bread). These crumbs came from elsewhere and not from that loaf, and certainly if the crumbs are less than the amount of the loaf. One must check the room into which the mouse entered, and no more. The other rooms are doubtful, as will be explained in the next section (Magen Avraham, subsection 1). For this is a doubt upon a doubt, and not definitive. There is no difference whether the loaf is large or small. Likewise, if a dog or a chicken took it, it is also not their way to crumble (the bread). Therefore, if they took it and we find it even whole, if it is crumbs – it is not from that loaf, but from another, and rechecking is required, even if the chametz was nullified (Chayei Adam, subsection 1).

However, if a child enters a checked house, and he does not have the awareness that we can rely on his statement that he ate it, and crumbs are found after him—there is no need to check again, for the presumption is that he ate it. And these crumbs are from him—because it is the nature of a child to crumble. Therefore, these crumbs fell from him while eating. There is no difference whether the crumbs are the amount of the entire piece of bread or not. If they are the amount of the entire piece of bread, we say that he did not eat anything and crumbled it. If they are not, we say he ate part and crumbled part. Only if no crumbs are found at all, do we not assume that he ate it all and it is necessary to check again. Some say that this applies specifically when the crumbs amount to the entire piece of bread. But if they do not, we do not assume that he ate the permitted part, for a doubt regarding eating does not remove the certainty of chametz. It appears to me that in all this, there is no difference whether one has nullified (the chametz) or not. For when we assume (he ate it)—we assume even if he has not nullified it, because it is considered as certain. And when we do not assume— we do not assume even if he has nullified it, if we say that a doubt does not remove the certainty even in rabbinic matters (as I wrote at the end of section 2 in the name of the Chayei Adam).

A mouse entered the house with a loaf of bread in its mouth, and afterward we saw a mouse leaving with a loaf of bread in its mouth – we say it is the first mouse that entered, which is the same as the one that left. And there is no need to check. But if the first mouse was black and the second one was white, or if it is recognized that this is not the mouse that entered – checking is necessary. We do not assume that the first mouse dropped the loaf and the second mouse picked it up, because a doubt does not override a certainty. Moreover, even if a mouse entered with a loaf of bread in its mouth, and afterward a rat exited with a loaf of bread in its mouth, since generally the mouse would be afraid of the rat and would drop it, and the rat would take it; still, we do not assume this, because we did not see the mouse in the rat's mouth. Therefore, if a rat exited from there with a mouse and a loaf of bread in its mouth – there is no need to check, because it is certain that this is the loaf that was in the mouse's mouth. So ruled the Rambam in Chapter 2, Law 13, see there.

And we must understand, for all of these are questions in the Gemara (Yoma 10b). And for the previous ones, the Talmud says, "And if you wish to say," and the method of the Geonim is that every "if you wish to say" is considered as a resolution. But the last law regarding a mouse with bread in its mouth, this remains unresolved in the Gemara with a "teiku" (unresolved question), see there. So how did he rule leniently? The Maggid Mishneh wrote that every "teiku" of Rabbinic origin is ruled leniently, see there. That is to say, it refers to when one has nullified the chametz. And the Rambam did not need to explain this, as he writes the law for us according to the Halacha, that one who checks must nullify. And the Tur also wrote that all these are questions, and if one has nullified, we rule leniently, and if one has not nullified, we rule stringently, see there, because the Tur does not agree that the earlier questions were resolved. But according to the Rambam, in the earlier laws, even without nullifying, we rule leniently, since the questions were resolved. (And from the Rambam, it is clearly implied that all are equal in law, and this requires further examination.)

The Rambam wrote (there): A snake that enters a hole with bread in its mouth – one is not obligated to bring a snake charmer to remove it. Thus ends his words, and the reason: since it requires expenses to hire a charmer – the Rabbis did not impose this burden (Gemara there). And even though regarding the search for chametz we say: a person is pleased to perform a mitzvah with his money – this is certainly true for chametz. But here it is a doubt, for perhaps the snake will take it outside or eat it (Tosafot there). And this is also an unresolved issue, and it must be said as well that it refers to where he nullified (the chametz), and it is a Rabbinic (obligation), and in cases of doubt we are lenient.

Additionally, it is written: If there is an olive-sized piece of chametz in the rafters, he is obligated to bring a ladder to remove it, for sometimes it may fall from the rafters. If there is chametz in a pit, he is not obligated to bring it up; rather, he nullifies it in his heart and that suffices. Thus are his words, and similarly, it is written in the Shulchan Aruch, Section 2. Now, according to our version of the Gemara there, based on the rule of the Geonim that "if you say" indicates a resolution, even in a pit, one is obligated to bring it up, for it is stated there: "If you say, sometimes he will descend there and come to eat it," see there. However, the Rambam had a different version (Magid Mishneh). And I am puzzled by our teacher, the Beit Yosef, who should have brought that according to our version, it is not so. It seems to me that in this matter, he relied on the Tur, who wrote that even in the rafters it is doubtful, and if he nullified it, he does not need to remove it, and all the more so in a pit. Therefore, our teacher, the Beit Yosef, even though he was stringent like the Rambam regarding the rafters, nevertheless, in a pit, since according to the Tur, even according to our version, he does not need to bring it up, he left the matter as it is.

And know that the reason the Rambam needed to explain here "he nullifies it in his heart and it is sufficient," and indeed in all the laws that were clarified, nullification is specifically required, as I wrote in the name of the Maggid Mishnah in paragraph 6; rather because there it deals with an incident after the inspection where a mouse entered, etc., and he had already nullified after the inspection. But here it deals with the time of inspection, hence he says "he nullifies it in his heart," meaning he relies on the nullification he will perform afterward and also intends for this piece of bread. The Raavad in his glosses wrote that even here it deals with after the inspection and nullification, and then he found it, see there. But at the time of inspection – in any case, he is obligated to remove it, as it is like storing it in a pit. And his reason seems to be: because since this law was stated along with the laws of the mouse, it is presumably referring to the same context. (The Maggid Mishnah was puzzled by the Raavad, and according to our explanation, it fits well. And delve deeply.) And if it fell into a well of water – the chametz is considered as destroyed (Mei’kat HaChim).

If there were nine piles of matzah and one of chametz in front of us, and a mouse came and took a piece of bread from one of the piles and entered a house that had already been checked for chametz, and we do not know if it took chametz, requiring us to check the house again, or if it took matzah, in which case we do not need to check; even though the majority is matzah, we do not follow the majority, and we must check again. For anything that is fixed (kavua) is considered as if it is half and half, since we saw the mouse take from a fixed place. But if the piece of bread was separated from its fixed place, and from there the mouse took it, we do not need to check, as we follow the majority. This is similar to the law of nine stores in Yoreh De'ah, section 110. Check there. And fixed (kavua) is a decree from the Torah, as explained there.

According to our Rabbis, the Tosafists (Pesachim 9a, s.v. "hainu"), this only applies when one has not nullified the chametz, which is a Torah prohibition. But when one has nullified it, which is a Rabbinic prohibition, and since it is considered as half and half – a Rabbinic doubt is ruled leniently. This is also the opinion of the Raavad in Chapter 2, Law 9, and so wrote the Tur; see there. According to this, it seems to me that even if there are nine piles of chametz and one of matzah, and we saw someone take from a fixed place and enter a checked house – it does not require checking if one has nullified the chametz. For something fixed is considered both leniently and stringently, as explained in Yoreh De'ah there.

And our masters, the authors of the Tosafot, themselves wrote that even without nullification, there is no fixed law here at all, regarding the requirement to check when a mouse enters a checked room. It is not comparable to the case of the nine stores, where there is no presumption of permissibility. But in a checked room, there is a presumption of permissibility, which is the presumption of having been checked. Therefore, they explained that this law is not about checking, but rather about whether it is permissible to eat this loaf, see there. And according to the Ra'avad and the Tur, and similarly to the Rambam and other poskim who interpreted this law regarding checking, it seems to me to say that because in a fixed situation we do not follow the presumption, just as we do not follow proximity. As we explained in Yoreh De'ah there with complete proofs, that the Torah decrees not to follow proximity in fixed situations, see there. And similarly, we do not follow the presumption. The Torah's decree is that everything fixed is considered as half and half, whether near or far, whether there is a presumption or not.

And the Rambam in the second chapter ruled this law even when he nullified (the chametz), for this is the implication of his words, and the entire chapter there deals with a case where he nullified. And the Magid Mishneh wrote in the name of the Ra'ah the reason: since the Sages instituted the search for chametz due to doubt, they were stringent with this doubt more than with any other doubts of their decrees, see there. And even though in all the cases of doubt in the Gemara, with the mouse and the snake and all the laws explained in the previous section, the Rambam was lenient in cases of doubt, as I wrote there; this is when there is doubt in the law - certainly we go lenient, for the search remains in its place. But in doubt regarding the essence of the matter, where the search has not yet been properly performed. Since the search is due to doubt about the matter, whether there is chametz or not, and there is still this doubt about the essence of the matter - we are stringent in this, which is not the case with doubt concerning the law (Lechem Mishneh and Mishneh Lamelech there).

The Tur writes that if the piece of bread is small, even without nullification, one may be lenient. And we say that it was consumed based on a double doubt: perhaps it was matzah, and if you say it was chametz, perhaps it was eaten. And even though in the previous section, where a mouse entered and a mouse exited, we did not permit a small piece of bread based on this double doubt — namely, perhaps it was eaten, and if you say it was not eaten, perhaps the second mouse took it out — this is because both doubts there are essentially one doubt, meaning: there is a doubt if the chametz remained in the house or not. What difference does it make if it did not remain because it was eaten or because the second mouse took it out? In the end, it is one doubt, as is explained in the principles of double doubts in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 110. But here, the first doubt is whether it is chametz at all or matzah, and if you say it is chametz, perhaps it was eaten, which constitutes a complete double doubt (Magen Avraham, small section 3).

And know that in the general rules of "safek s'feka" (a double doubt) in Yoreh De'ah there, we require that the two doubts come simultaneously. But if they come one after the other, it is not considered a double doubt, see there. And if so, here the doubts come one after the other. For when the mouse enters the house, there is a doubt regarding what it brought in, whether it was chametz or matzah; and there is still no doubt as to whether it ate it, since it is whole before us. And afterwards, the second doubt arises, whether it ate it. And this is not a double doubt, because here the matter concerns all the days of Passover, and when the days of Passover arrive, both doubts have already taken effect (see Magen Avraham there). Additionally, as long as the bread is in the mouse's mouth, there is no doubt. And when does the doubt arise which necessitates checking? After we no longer see it in the mouse's mouth, and by then both doubts have already taken effect (there). Besides this, the doubt of eating is considered a doubt close to certainty, and we combine it with a double doubt in all cases (Mikdash Me'at, small section 3). For so the Tosafot wrote there (Pesachim 9a) concerning impurity, where we say "safek s'feka," and they questioned: Isn’t the doubt of impurity in a private domain not effective as a double doubt? And they answered that eating is better than other doubts, because it is a frequent doubt and close to certainty, see there. (But this is not a complete proof, for there it deals with meat, and the Talmud distinguishes there between meat and bread. And perhaps according to Rava, there is no need to differentiate, see there thoroughly. And be precise and you will find it easy.)

And all of this is according to the opinion of the Tur. But according to the Rambam, who was stringent about checking even for rabbinic prohibitions, one could say that he was stringent even in many cases of doubt; and even for a small loaf of bread, one must go back and check. And so it appears from the words of our master the Beit Yosef, that according to the Rambam there is no difference between a large loaf and a small loaf (and so wrote the Gra"z). For the Rambam's reasoning is that the inspection must be clear, as this was the enactment of the sages. (And the Taz in subsection 1 challenged the Tur, that if so, even with a large loaf there is a double doubt, perhaps it called other mice to eat it, as Tosafot wrote in Bava Metzia 40a in the name of the Jerusalem Talmud, see there. But this is not analogous, for if they said this regarding extracting money, and in a heap of grain where many mice are present – we would say the same regarding one loaf and one mouse, and regarding prohibition. Investigate and you will find it easy.)

According to the laws that have been explained, if there was a single container with a mixture of chametz (leavened bread) and matzah, and a mouse came and took from it, we follow the majority. If the majority is chametz, one must check (for chametz), and if the majority is matzah, there is no need to check. For as long as the permitted and prohibited items are not distinguishable from each other, it is not considered a fixed (prohibition). And although it is explained in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 110, that if the mixture consists of large, respectable pieces, it is treated with a fixed prohibition by rabbinic law, nevertheless, this does not apply here, because regarding mixtures of prohibitions, there are other reasons, as explained there.

Two piles, one of leavened bread (chametz) and one of unleavened bread (matzah), and two houses before us, one that has been searched and one that has not been searched; and two mice came into the two houses, one taking chametz and the other taking matzah, and it is not known into which house the one that took the chametz entered. Similarly, if there are two houses that have been searched and one pile of chametz, and a mouse came and took some, and it is not known into which house it entered, or if it is known that it entered one of them and someone followed it and searched but found nothing; or if part of the house was searched and a loaf was found – there is no need to search again. This is the ruling of the Rambam in the second chapter, and the reason is: since we are dealing with a case after the nullification of chametz, it is a doubt of Rabbinic origin and we are lenient. And even though the Rambam was stringent regarding a fixed doubt of Rabbinic origin, as explained, in any case where there is a possibility that there was no prohibition at all – we are lenient even in the search for chametz. For this possibility is something we find with terumah and stains, and therefore even here we assume that the chametz entered the unsurveyed house. And in the case of two surveyed houses – each one assumes the other has the chametz, and even though with terumah and stains we do not assume this way when they are of equal status. Indeed, the Tur differentiates here between when they come to ask at the same time, in which case both need to be searched, and when one after the other, they do not need to be searched, similar to the case of the two paths known in the Talmud, see there. And the Rambam does not distinguish in this way, and his opinion seems to be that since there is doubt whether the mouse entered this house at all, and a doubt of entry does not negate the certainty of the search, and any doubt of entry in the search for chametz in a surveyed house, and after nullification we assume leniency, unlike in a fixed case which is considered a definite entry – therefore we are stringent even in a doubt. (And even though in the Gemara 10a it is compared to the two paths, the Rambam will explain that it refers to when nullification has not occurred. In any case, this needs examination, who compelled him to this? And the Maggid Mishneh, Kesef Mishneh, and Mishneh Lamelech have already labored over his words. And the Mishneh Lamelech brought proof from Ketubot 27 that in Rabbinic matters we do not judge like the two paths. But what he wrote about being lenient in the doubt of entry – it must be said specifically with two houses, for in one house he is stringent, as will be explained in section 12. And the words of the Tur are as in the Talmudic discussion. And see Taz small section 3, and Mekor Chaim, and according to what I have written, it fits well. Examine and you will find ease.)

The Tur wrote: If one placed nine loaves and found ten, he must check all nine. Similarly, if one placed ten and found nine, he must check all ten, for we say that what he placed was taken and these are different loaves, even if he nullified [the chametz]. And that which we say when he placed ten and found nine, he must check all ten, is specifically when they are tied together. But if they are not tied together, he needs only to check one. Up to here are his words, and it implies that when one placed nine and found ten, even if they are not tied together, he must check all nine. However, the commentators wrote that his intention applies to both cases. (Bach and Maharlach. But the Magen Avraham in subsection 7 wrote as we have stated.)

And the Rambam in Chapter 2, Halacha 7 wrote: If one checked on the night of the 14th and placed ten loaves and found nine, he must be concerned and must check again, for certainly a weasel or mouse took one. Thus are his words. And later in Halacha 12, he wrote that if one placed nine and found ten, he must check again, and he included it in the law of placing in one corner and finding in another corner. It seems clear from the fact that he divided them into two places that they are not similar. For if one placed ten and found nine, he only needs to check for the one missing. But with the surplus of placing nine and finding ten, we say that they are entirely different ones, as with placing in one corner and finding in another corner, and he must check for all of them. He did not mention tied loaves at all. And our Rabbi the Beit Yosef in Section 3, who brought the opinion of the Rambam, also wrote that if one placed ten and found nine, he must check for all ten, see there. And I do not understand, for if so, the Rambam should not have divided them into two places. Furthermore, in Beitzah (10b), it is established regarding tied loaves that then one must check for all of them. But if they are not tied, he does not need to. And he did not mention tied loaves at all, so certainly, only one needs to be checked. Therefore, as I wrote in Section 10, that if one placed nine and found ten, even the Tur agrees that one must check for all of them—the Rambam and the Tur do not disagree. And this seems primary. And there is no difference in these laws between whether one nullified or did not nullify.

And the Rambam wrote: If one placed chametz in this corner and found it in another corner, or he placed nine loaves and found ten, or a mouse came and took the chametz and it is uncertain whether it entered this house or not – in all these cases, he must check. Thus are his words, and it also appears in the Gemara: that if there is a doubt about a doubt, checking is not required, see there. But if so, why is he lenient with two checked houses, and a mouse with chametz entered one of them, as I wrote in paragraph 9? One must say that he distinguishes between one house and two houses. But it is not understood what the difference between them is. Therefore, it seems to me that also there, what the Rambam wrote about two checked houses and a bundle of chametz, and a mouse came and took it, and it is not known into which house it entered, or it is known that it entered one of them, and someone entered after it and found nothing, or he checked and found a loaf... – the phrase "and someone entered after it" applies also to the first division of two checked houses. But otherwise, checking is required, just like here where there is a doubt upon a doubt. And although the commentators did not explain it this way, nevertheless it seems to me that this is the main explanation (and all the difficulties are resolved).

Maimonides wrote at the beginning of the fourth chapter: It is written in the Torah: "No chametz (leaven) shall be seen by you" – one might think that if he buried it or deposited it with a non-Jew, he would not transgress? The Torah teaches: "Leaven shall not be found in your houses" – even if he deposited or buried it. One might think he would only transgress if the chametz is found in his house, but if it was far from his house, in a field or another city, he would not transgress? The Torah teaches: "Throughout your borders" – in all your domains. One might think he would be obligated to remove from his domain chametz that belongs to a non-Jew or to the sanctuary? The Torah teaches: "It shall not be seen by you" – you do not see your own, but you do see that of others and of the sanctuary. Thus, you learn that chametz belonging to a Jew, if he leaves it in his domain, even if it is buried, even in another city, and even if it is deposited with a non-Jew, he transgresses "it shall not be seen" and "it shall not be found." Chametz belonging to the sanctuary or a non-Jew that is with a Jew, even if it is in his house – it is permitted, because it is not his. And even if the Jew has control over it – he is not compelled to remove the chametz from his domain on Passover. However, he must make a partition ten handbreadths high in front of the chametz of the non-Jew, lest he come to use it. But for that of the sanctuary, he need not, because everyone distances themselves from the sanctuary's property, so they do not come to misuse it. Thus far the words of Maimonides, of blessed memory.

And we need to understand: From where do we derive that chametz (leavened bread) owned by a Jew that is deposited with a non-Jew – he transgresses the prohibition of "it shall not be seen"? For here there is neither "your house" nor "your borders." And there is someone who wrote from the perspective of a kal vachomer (a fortiori argument): Since chametz owned by a non-Jew deposited with a Jew, where the Jew accepted responsibility, transgresses "it shall not be seen," as will be explained – all the more so his own chametz in the possession of a non-Jew (Maggid Mishneh). And this is not understood: For there, since he accepted responsibility – it is considered as his own, and under his domain. This is not the case with his chametz in the possession of a non-Jew – it is his, but not under his domain. Additionally: the Rambam says "from this you learn…", indicating his intention that we learn this from a verse, not from a kal vachomer. And there is someone who wrote that the place where the non-Jew places his chametz – it is considered like the Jew's house (Kesef Mishneh). And this too is problematic, for if so why do we need the verse: "you shall not see [that which is] yours," but you may see that which belongs to others? For the place where the chametz is placed would be considered like the non-Jew’s house, and do we need a verse to teach that one does not transgress on the chametz of a non-Jew in the non-Jew's house? Additionally: it is obvious that the place is not considered the depositor’s, unless he explicitly granted him the place, or designated a specific place, as I wrote in paragraph 14, see there.

Furthermore: What is this that he wrote: One might think he does not transgress unless the chametz is in his house, but if it was far from his house, in a field or another city, he would not transgress? The Torah says: "in all your borders" – in all your domain. Thus far is his language. But another city is not "your border." Furthermore, a field is also not "your border," for one cannot say it refers to his own field, for if so, it should have said "in his field."

And in truth, the Ramban of blessed memory wrote in his commentary on the Chumash that one does not transgress “bal yera’eh” (the prohibition against owning chametz during Passover) except with chametz that is his and within his possession (as brought by the Maggid Mishneh there). However, his chametz that is not in his possession—he does not transgress “bal yera’eh.” Similarly, the Ran wrote in the first chapter, and this is his language: For even the chametz of a Jew, as long as it is in the possession of a non-Jew, he does not transgress it. And so it is in the Mekhilta: Just as “your house” means in your possession, so too “your borders” means in your possession: this excludes the chametz of a Jew that is in the possession of a non-Jew... However, these matters are from the Torah, but rabbinically, the chametz of a Jew that is in the possession of a non-Jew requires removal… until here is his language. Behold, their opinion is explicit that as long as the chametz is not in his actual possession, he does not transgress the Torah prohibition of “bal yera’eh,” and only rabbinically is he obligated to remove it. (And this is not related to the words of the Geonim that the Rosh and the Tur brought, that when the custodian took responsibility, the depositor does not transgress, as will be explained. For this is because of responsibility, but otherwise, they agree with the Rambam. And see Shagat Aryeh, Siman 83, who critiques the Beis Yosef and the later authorities, who conflated two opinions into one matter, and it is not so, see there.)

And it seems to me, in the intention of Maimonides, that his words are clear, and this is their explanation: in the Torah, four terms are written regarding this matter: "shall not be seen," "shall not be found," "your house," and "your borders." The difference between "shall not be seen" and "shall not be found" is understood: if it only stated "shall not be seen," I would say that the matter depends on visibility, but if it is hidden, one does not transgress. Therefore, it is written "shall not be found." However, between "your house" and "your borders" – if you would think that "your borders" means literally your domain, meaning it is your property, then what difference is there between the domain of your house and the domain of your field or your courtyard? After all, it is all the same: his house is his, and his field and courtyard are his. And there is no difference between them for all laws of sale, gift, and acquisition. Rather, certainly "in all your borders" – the intention is not that the border is his and the domain is his, but it refers to the chametz, that the chametz should not be "in all your borders," meaning: any place where the chametz is yours, that is, the chametz belongs to you, and it is placed wherever it is placed. And this is what Maimonides wrote "in all your borders" – in all your domain, this is an explanation that the chametz should be under his control, meaning that the chametz is his, and he can do with it whatever he wishes. And this is what he wrote "one might think he would not transgress unless the chametz is in his house..." meaning: he would not transgress unless the chametz is placed in his domain, whether in his house or in his field or in his courtyard. The Talmud states: "in all your borders" – in all your domain, meaning: we do not require that the domain be yours, but that the chametz be in your domain, meaning: you have control over the chametz, that it is in your domain to do with it whatever you wish. It is clear in his intention with the help of Heaven.

For in truth, the term "boundary" does not refer to what belongs to a person specifically, and the entire Tanach is filled with this usage, such as: "the boundary of Israel," and similarly "He makes peace in your borders," and similarly "from the end of the boundary of Egypt," and similarly "the boundary of the land of Edom" – which means the entire country.
