And here too, the straightforward meaning of the verse "shall not be seen throughout all your borders" – means "throughout the entire country." A clear proof of this is from the Mekhilta, Parasha Bo (Chapter 10), and this is its language: "In your houses" – why is this stated? Because it says "throughout all your borders" – I might understand it literally. The verse teaches us: "in your houses" – just as your houses are under your control, so too your borders are under your control... It is clearly explained that the meaning of "your borders" is not "under your control." And this is as I wrote, that "throughout all your borders" means "throughout your entire country." And the interpretation of the Mekhilta is: just as your houses, etc. – excluding the chametz of a Jew that is in the possession of a non-Jew. This means: just as in your houses the chametz is under your control, where you have the ability to do whatever you want with it – so too your borders are under your control, where you have the ability to do whatever you want with it. And that is: even if it is in the hands of others but you do not receive money for it. Excluding the chametz of a Jew that is in the possession of a non-Jew. Meaning: that the chametz is under his control, where he receives money. (And also the Rosh in the first chapter, sign 4, wrote that the Mekhilta is dealing with a loan, see there. And in the Gemara 5b, the interpretation is: I only have in houses, in pits... from where? The verse teaches us: throughout all your borders, meaning: I would say only in houses where he regularly sees the chametz, and not in pits. The verse teaches us: "throughout all your borders." And since it is forbidden even throughout the entire boundary, which is distant from him and is not under his control, all the more so in pits. And still, I would say in houses... in your borders you shall not see..., meaning: I would say that in the houses of others it is also forbidden, the verse teaches us "leaven"-"leaven" by a verbal analogy... And be precise and you will find it light.)

And behold, all the decisors align with the opinion of the Rambam, that chametz of a Jew entrusted to a non-Jew is subject to the prohibitions of "bal yera'eh" (it shall not be seen) and "bal yimatzeh" (it shall not be found) from the Torah, to the extent that the Rosh wrote that no proof is needed for this, see there. Except for the Ramban and the Ran of blessed memory, who hold that from the Torah, one does not transgress, as they interpret "in all your borders" to mean within one's own domain, and only rabbinically it must be destroyed. And all this is without acceptance of responsibility. But with acceptance of responsibility, there are different laws, as we will explain with the help of Heaven. And in the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, the opinion of the Ramban and the Ran is not brought at all, see there. The reason is that the halacha follows the majority of the decisors. Additionally, even according to their view, rabbinically one is obligated to destroy it, and they did not delve into differentiating between Torah law and rabbinic law, but rather between what is forbidden and permitted, as I wrote at the beginning of the halacha of Shabbat.

Our sages, of blessed memory, derived from the term "shall not be found" that even the chametz of a non-Jew that is deposited with a Jew, and the Jew accepted responsibility for it, he transgresses "it shall not be seen" and "it shall not be found." For the term "shall not be found" implies that it is present with you, and this is present with you. Because without responsibility, he does not need to pay attention to it, and it is placed with him without concern. But when he accepts responsibility, he must take care of the chametz so that it is not lost or spoiled, so he does not have to pay for it. This is called "present with you" and regarding the prohibition of "it shall not be seen" it is considered as his own. There is no difference whether the chametz is in his house or elsewhere within his domain. Even if he does not see it, and even if he subsequently deposits it with another non-Jew who is not its owner, this is like depositing his chametz with a non-Jew, and he transgresses (Magen Avraham, subsection 1). However, if he subsequently deposits it with the first non-Jew with whom he initially deposited it, he does not transgress. Even though the responsibility for theft and loss remains with the Jew, it is still permissible, as it is like accepting responsibility for a non-Jew's chametz in the non-Jew's house, which is permitted (ibid.). There are those who disagree, arguing that since the chametz was under the Jew's responsibility and considered as his own, when he deposits it again, even with the first non-Jew, it is like depositing his own chametz with him, and he transgresses "it shall not be seen" (Chayei Adam, subsection 6). The primary opinion follows the first view (Machatzit HaShekel, subsection 4).

And if this non-Jew's chametz, for which he accepted responsibility, was deposited with another non-Jew, and the other non-Jew accepted all responsibility – some say that the Jew does not transgress (Magen Avraham there). And some say that he does transgress (Chayei Adam, small section 5). The main opinion follows the first view (Mekor Chaim there), that whatever responsibility he had, he transferred. And there are those who say that chametz of a non-Jew that was deposited with him, and he accepted responsibility – nullification does not help him (Sha'agat Aryeh, Siman 77). This also seems logical. For if it were his own chametz – he has the authority to renounce ownership and nullify it, because during Passover it will be completely forbidden and a mere declaration of intent suffices, as I wrote in Siman 431. But this chametz which is not his, and when Passover arrives it will not be forbidden to the owner, and only the Torah decreed that he transgresses the prohibition of "it shall not be seen" – in what capacity can he renounce ownership or nullify it? He must, against his will, return it to its owner, and if the owner is not in his house – he should sell it or destroy it and reimburse the non-Jew. And if a non-Jew deposited his chametz in another non-Jew's house, and the Jew accepted responsibility – it is permitted, since the chametz is not in his house (Mekor Chaim there). This is because accepting responsibility for a non-Jew's chametz in his house is permitted. What difference does it make if it is his or another's?

And if one transgressed the prohibition of "bal yera'eh" (owning chametz during Passover) with this chametz – in any case, he can return the chametz to the non-Jew after Passover. This is not considered as benefiting from forbidden items, for it is established that if one stole chametz and Passover has passed over it, he can tell the owner, "Here is yours," even if the owner is a Jew, as I have written in Choshen Mishpat, section 363. All the more so, he can return it to the non-Jew (Magen Avraham there). It is possible that even during Passover, he can leave it for the non-Jew to take the chametz (there). However, there is a concern that the non-Jew might sell it to a Jew after Passover, causing the Jew to violate the prohibition of chametz that has passed over Passover (there). In any case, he does not need to be concerned about this, since he is returning what belongs to the non-Jew – he does not have to pay for this concern (Chayei Adam, section 4).

And under what responsibility does one transgress "bal yera'eh" (the prohibition against seeing chametz during Passover)? The Tur wrote in the name of the R"i that it is specifically when he is a paid guardian, who is liable for theft and loss. And in the name of the Bahag, it is written that even if he is an unpaid guardian, and is only liable for negligence, it is still considered responsibility. See there. And from the Rambam it is clear like the first opinion, for he wrote, "If the Israelite accepted upon himself responsibility, that if it was lost or stolen…" See there. The Rosh's opinion is like that of the Bahag. And as the Tosafot wrote in Bava Metzia (82b) in the name of Rashi z"l, he does not transgress unless he accepted responsibility for unavoidable accidents. See there. And it is surprising that in the Bahag we have, it also states theft and loss, and this is his language in the chapter "Kol Sha'ah": "Certainly, if a Gentile deposited chametz with an Israelite, if the Israelite accepted responsibility, since if he was negligent and it was stolen or lost, he is liable to pay, he must destroy it," etc. Until here is his language. And if his intention is negligence, why does he conclude with theft and loss? Rather, certainly he meant: responsibility for theft and loss, and this too is from lack of guarding. Therefore, he said if he was negligent with it. And the Rosh seems to explain that his liability is for the negligence, and through the negligence it was stolen or lost. And if so, he should not have said "stolen" but "lost," as loss is closer to negligence. This requires further study. And regarding the law, it seems from Rabbeinu the Beit Yosef like the first opinion. For the opinion of the Bahag and the Rosh he wrote as "some say," and most opinions are like R"i, Rashi, Tosafot, Rambam, and SeMaG. And in practice, one should be stringent like the Bahag and the Rosh in a Torah prohibition.

Maimonides wrote: If a coercer deposits his chametz (leavened bread) with an Israelite, and the Israelite knows that if it gets lost or stolen, the coercer will compel him to pay for it, even though he did not accept responsibility for it – he is obligated to destroy it, since it is considered as if it is his own, because the coercer holds him responsible. Thus far his words. And the Raavad disagrees with him, asking how one can transgress "you shall not see" (the prohibition of owning chametz during Passover) in a situation where he is being coerced? And several of the early authorities disagree with him, stating that what is mentioned in the Talmud (5b) in such a case – this applies when it is the law of the kingdom, for the law of the kingdom is the law, and not in the case of a coercer (Maggid Mishneh). In my humble opinion, it seems that the intention of Maimonides is that accepting the chametz depends on his will, and if he wishes – he need not accept the chametz. And on this, the coercer will not coerce him, but if he accepts it – he will be coerced to pay when it is stolen or lost, and according to this, he rightly transgresses "you shall not see." And it is also clear from his words that the deposit was with his consent. Therefore, when he willingly put himself in this position, it is considered as accepting responsibility. And according to what we have explained, it is possible that the authorities are not in disagreement at all. (And this resolves the difficulty raised by the Taz, subsection 1, see there. And similarly, I found in the book Magen HaElef, see there.)

There are those who say that according to the opinion of the Rambam, who holds that one transgresses "Bal Yera'eh" (the prohibition of possessing chametz during Passover) even in a case of coercion, therefore in our sale of chametz, where the money is noted as a loan and the non-Jewish buyer receives only a small amount, it is clear that if the chametz is lost, the buyer will not pay for it – thus, it is as if the responsibility for the chametz remains with the Jew, and they transgress "Bal Yera'eh" (Magen Avraham, small section 5). Therefore, it is necessary to specifically sell the room where the chametz is located, as this would be considered as transferring responsibility to the non-Jew's residence (ibid.). However, in our practice, where we appoint a Jewish guarantor for the buyer (as per the enactment of the Alter Rebbe) – there is no concern in this matter. For if the buyer does not pay, we demand payment from the guarantor. Nonetheless, we also customarily sell the room, as will be explained in Siman 498, due to the acquisition process, as I will write there (and see Magen HaElef who refutes the words of the Magen Avraham).

The Tur wrote: If one deposited with him, and he accepted responsibility – he is obligated to remove it. But if he designated a place for it, saying "Here is the house before you, place it wherever you want" – he is not required to remove it. Rashi explained: this is when he did not accept responsibility. And Rabbeinu Tam explained: even if he accepted responsibility, since he designated a place for it – it is not considered to be in his house. And my master, my father the Rosh, of blessed memory, agreed with this. Up to here is his wording. The explanation of the matter: The reason the Torah obligated a Jew to violate "bal yeira'eh" (the prohibition of seeing leaven) with a non-Jew's deposit based on accepting responsibility – this is a decree of the Torah only concerning chametz. For this matter is merely a cause of monetary loss, that when it is destroyed – he will have to pay money. And in all laws, we hold: causing monetary loss is not considered as actual money, as I wrote in Choshen Mishpat section 386. But regarding chametz, where the Torah wrote "it shall not be found" – that which is found in your possession you transgress, and therefore based on responsibility, it is considered found in your possession, as we explained in section 8. Therefore, if he accepted responsibility for the chametz of a non-Jew in the non-Jew's house – he does not transgress, because it is not considered found in his possession. And therefore, also when he designated a house for it – it is like the house of a non-Jew, and it is not considered found in his possession. And from the Rambam, it clearly appears that he holds like Rashi. However, this is when he says to him only "here is the house before you." But if he designated a specific corner – certainly even according to Rashi and the Rambam, he does not transgress "bal yeira'eh" with accepting responsibility, for this is exactly like the house of a non-Jew (Beit Yosef).

The Ran wrote in the first chapter: The matter of liability for "bal yera'eh" (prohibition of leavened bread being seen) is not specifically when one explicitly accepts responsibility. Rather, even if someone deposits it with him without any specification, he is obligated to destroy it. This is because accepting a deposit without specification is considered as if he explicitly accepted responsibility, as we say in Bava Kamma (48a): "Bring your ox into my domain" - he is liable for its safeguarding. I am puzzled that the Ran, of blessed memory, also wrote this in the name of Rashi, of blessed memory, that without specification it is considered as accepting responsibility, see there. However, in our version of Rashi (6a) it is explicitly the opposite, where he wrote: "He deposited it with him and he accepted responsibility for it," see there. Thus, it is explained that explicit acceptance of responsibility is required. Similarly, from the language of the Rambam, it is clear that explicit acceptance of responsibility is required, as the Levush also wrote.

And the reason can be explained: Even though it is certainly so, that in a general sense he accepted the responsibility, as I wrote in Choshen Mishpat, siman 291, nevertheless, this applies to a Jew. But with a non-Jew, it is clarified there in siman 94 that there is no law of guardians, and consequently, explicit acceptance of responsibility is required. However, according to the Rambam there, for negligence, they are liable in all cases, and according to the Bahag and the Rosh here, even for accepting responsibility for negligence, they violate "bal yera'eh" as I wrote – it could be that here too, it applies in a general sense (Chayei Adam, section 1). According to the Ran, explicit wording is needed to indicate that he does not accept responsibility. (And according to the law, it is clarified in Choshen Mishpat there that most poskim disagree with the Rambam, see there.)

However, without responsibility [for the non-Jew's chametz] – one is not required to destroy it, even if the non-Jew is under his control and resides with him in the courtyard. He merely needs to erect a partition ten handbreadths high in his presence, so that he does not forget and eat it. And although for other prohibitions we do not require a partition – chametz is different, since it is eaten all year long, and there is concern that he might forget and eat it. But from other prohibitions we are always separated. If a non-Jew left chametz in the house of a Jew on Yom Tov, and it is impossible to make a partition – he should cover it with a vessel. And even though it is possible to use a sheet – this does not count as a noticeable partition. During Chol Hamoed, a proper partition is needed. However, if he deposited it for a short time, like for half a day – no partition is needed, and covering it with a vessel suffices (Magen Avraham Section 5, and this is also implied by Rashi's commentary on Pesachim 6a, "he makes", see there).

A non-Jew who enters a Jew's house on Passover and has chametz in his possession – there is no need to make him remove it. For even though one sees the chametz, the prohibition is only regarding your own chametz, not that of others. And there is no concern about eating it, as the non-Jew is watching over it and will not allow the Jew to eat from his bread. However, it is forbidden to place it on the table with him, even with a separation of a cloth. And even though when one person eats meat and another eats cheese, it is permitted with a separation of a cloth, as I wrote in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 88 – chametz is different. Its prohibition is even in the smallest amount, and it is inevitable that some small amount will transfer from one to the other. Therefore, if the Jew is not eating, it is permitted to allow the non-Jew to eat there (Magen Avraham, Siman 7). And similarly, when he eats on a separate table, there is no concern.

The Rosh writes at the beginning of Pesachim: There are some of the Geonim who said: If a Jew deposited his chametz with a non-Jew, or with another Jew, and the custodian accepted responsibility for it – the custodian is obligated to destroy it and not the depositor, even though it belongs to the depositor, since it is not in his possession. And they brought proof from the Mekhilta… and Rabbeinu Yonah says that it always remains in the possession of the depositor, and he is obligated to destroy it according to the Torah… And it seems to me that it is simple: Even though the custodian accepted responsibility, nonetheless, the principal ownership remains with the owner… up to here is his language, and so wrote the Tur. And the opinion of the Geonim is not like that of the Ramban and the Ran, whom we brought in section 4, that as long as the chametz is not in his possession, he does not transgress "bal yera'eh"; for if so, there would be no need for responsibility. Furthermore, according to the Rabbis, he still transgresses, as I wrote there. Rather, their reasoning is that the responsibility of the custodian removes it from the prohibition of "bal yera'eh." And what the Rosh questioned – that the principal ownership remains with the owner – it can be said that this is not called "found in your hand," since the chametz is not with him and he is also secure with the money, it is called that the chametz is not found in his hand. And this is what they wrote: since it is not in his possession – because if it were in his possession, responsibility would not help. And the law is according to Rabbeinu Yonah and the Rosh. And if a Jew deposited with another Jew, and the custodian accepted responsibility – both transgress "bal yera'eh," and so ruled Rabbeinu Beit Yosef in section 4. (The Pri Chadash and the Shach took the opinion of the Geonim like the Ramban and the Ran. In my humble opinion, it does not seem so, and see Mekhilta. Practically, there is no difference. And what seems in my humble opinion we have explained with the help of Heaven.)

And know: One who forgot to sell his chametz (leavened products) until midday has no remedy, and is obligated to destroy it immediately. If a non-Jew who knows him comes and takes it for himself after the chametz has been put out in the street in a manner of abandonment, and the non-Jew intends to return it to him after Passover, he may take it back, for the non-Jew acquired it through abandonment, and it is considered the chametz of a non-Jew that has passed through Passover, which is permitted even for eating. However, if he sells or gives it to an idolater, it is of no benefit at all, and he transgresses "bal yera'eh" (the prohibition of seeing chametz), for his sale or gift is of no consequence. He still transgresses "bal yera'eh" because concerning "bal yera'eh," the Torah places it in his possession, and he is obligated to destroy it after Passover. (Chatam Sofer, Siman 113; and Mekor Chaim, Siman 442 in the explanations, in the middle of sub-section 5; and the Gaon Rabbi Akiva Eiger, in the notes at the beginning of Siman 442 on the Magen Avraham, sub-section 1, see there. And the words of the Noda B'Yehuda, Tanina, Siman 63, are very puzzling, and Heaven forbid to act accordingly. See there, and scrutinize, and you will find it easy.)

A non-Jew who lent money to a Jew with chametz as collateral, and the chametz was placed in the possession of the non-Jew, and he said to him: "From now, it will be yours if I do not repay you by a certain time," and the time came and he did not repay – it is permitted, even if the time did not come until after Passover; for once the time came and he did not repay, it is retroactively acquired by the non-Jew, and it is considered the chametz of the non-Jew. However, if he did not say "from now" – it is prohibited even though the collateral is in the possession of the non-Jew, because a non-Jew does not acquire collateral from a Jew, and it is as if it belongs to the Jew. Similarly, if he said "from now" and it is in the possession of the Jew – it is also prohibited; since the responsibility is on the Jew – it is prohibited even with the chametz of the non-Jew, as I wrote in the previous section, all the more so in such a case. Similarly, if the time came and he repaid – it is prohibited even if he said "from now" and it was in the possession of the non-Jew, because since he repaid, it reveals that the chametz belonged to the Jew. But when all three conditions are met – it is permitted.

And the Rambam, of blessed memory, wrote in Chapter 4, Halacha 5: A Jew who pawns his chametz with a non-Jew, if he says to him, "If I do not bring you money by such-and-such a day, this chametz is yours from now" – then it is considered in the possession of the non-Jew, and that chametz is permitted after Passover. This is provided that the set time is before Passover. But if he does not say "it is yours from now" – then the chametz is considered as if it is a deposit with the non-Jew, and it is forbidden to derive benefit from it after Passover. So far are his words, but the Raavad, the Tur, and most of the poskim disagreed with him. For if the time arrives before Passover – why do we need "from now"? Even without saying "from now" the chametz would already be decided as belonging to the non-Jew. And one cannot say that it is an asmachta (a conditional commitment), and he did not acquire it because every conditional commitment is an asmachta, for the Rambam ruled in Chapter 11 of the Laws of Sale that in the case of a pawn there is no law of asmachta. Rather, the reason of the Rambam is because we hold that a non-Jew does not acquire a pawn from a Jew (according to the Maggid Mishneh), and therefore it is still considered as the Jew’s. But when he says "from now" – it is considered a sale from now even if the time does not arrive before Passover, since until that time it is not permitted, it should have said in the Gemara "when the time arrives it is permitted." And from the fact that it says "after Passover it is permitted" – it implies that it is immediately permitted, and necessarily the time arrived before Passover. And one cannot say that the set time was during Passover or immediately after Passover, because it is not customary for a Jew to set such a time for chametz (there). And the halacha follows most of the poskim, that if the time arrives before Passover – it is permitted even without "from now." And in the Shulchan Aruch, the opinion of the Rambam is not mentioned at all, see there.

And one should not question according to the opinion of most poskim (halachic authorities) that even if the time (for repayment) arrives after Passover, and without saying "from now" (at the time of the loan) – since the Jew did not redeem it, and the collateral was decided for the non-Jew, it retroactively becomes clear that the chametz (leavened bread) belonged to the non-Jew during Passover. This is not the case, for we hold: a creditor collects from the time of repayment onward. That is to say, when he collects a field for his debt that was mortgaged to him – the field does not belong to him retroactively from the time of the loan, but from the time of repayment. And since this is the case, automatically the chametz during Passover belonged to the Jew and not to the non-Jew. And know that sometimes, even if the chametz was in the possession of the Jew – it is permitted. For example: if the Jew transferred ownership of the chametz to the non-Jew through a legal transaction or by means of land, and it is not under the responsibility of the Jew – it is permitted even if it was left in the Jew's possession (Magen Avraham, Siman 1).

And since the primary basis for the permissibility is because of "from now," therefore, even without the matter of a loan on collateral, such as if one said to a non-Jew, "If I do not do such-and-such for you by Nisan, the chametz will be yours from now," and the chametz is in the possession of the non-Jew, and the time arrives and he did not do it – the chametz belongs to the non-Jew and is permitted after Passover. And if one is concerned about it being an 'asmachta' (a form of conditional commitment that might not be binding), it has already been clarified in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 207, that with "from now" there is no 'asmachta.' However, according to the opinion that holds that "from now" is effective only with collateral and not with other matters – it returns to being an 'asmachta.' Yet, the Raavad holds that with a non-Jew there is no 'asmachta.' And also, since in their laws it belongs to the non-Jew – we follow them, so that the Jew does not transgress "bal yera'eh" (the prohibition of owning chametz during Passover), as will be explained in Siman 448 (see Magen Avraham, subsection 2).

And there is a question about this: How do we permit [ownership of chametz] through "from now," even if the time comes after Passover? Behold, one could redeem it before Passover, and we could say: Since he could have redeemed the chametz, he would transgress "bal yera'eh" (the prohibition of owning chametz during Passover), as we say in a similar case regarding dough that was kneaded on a festival, and he separated challah and the challah became chametz, that he transgresses "bal yera'eh" because: Since he could nullify the designation of challah, it would become his. Therefore, even though the challah is not his and he does not transgress "bal yera'eh," nevertheless, since he could make it his, he transgresses. Similarly, here: he could redeem it, and it would be his, and he would transgress "bal yera'eh." This will be explained in Siman 457. However, this is not comparable, because in that case, he would not lose money through this; but here, he would need to pay money to the non-Jew if he redeems the chametz from him, and he does not want to do this. Therefore, we do not say that he could redeem it in a case that involves monetary loss (as stated in subsection 3 in the name of the Ran, of blessed memory). Additionally, here it requires an action, that he must pay the non-Jew and take the chametz to his house, for he would not want to leave it in the possession of the non-Jew after paying him. And regarding something that requires an action, we do not say "since." (According to Rashi, we do not say "since" at all in such a case, see there.)

All of this applies after the fact. However, initially, it is certainly forbidden to borrow against chametz (leavened products) from a non-Jew and to set the repayment time after Passover, and to say to him, "If I do not repay you by such-and-such time, it will be yours from now." For in such a case, the chametz remains dependent and standing in his possession during Passover. However, if the repayment time was set before Passover, and a reason arose causing the repayment to extend until after Passover, he is not obligated to exert himself to redeem it before Passover. But when the time was initially set for after Passover, he is certainly obligated to exert himself to redeem and destroy it before Passover (Kesef Mishneh on Tur, subsection 2). And one should not ask: Since ordinarily a collateral is not subject to the lender’s responsibility for accidental loss, as I wrote in Choshen Mishpat, beginning of Siman 72, if so, concerning accidental loss, the chametz still stands in the possession of the Jew, and if so, he would transgress "you shall not see" because of the responsibility? This is not a question: even if it entails responsibility, in any case, the chametz is in the hands of the non-Jew and is considered as his. And it has already been explained in the previous Siman that accepting responsibility in the house of a non-Jew for the chametz of a non-Jew is permitted (Magen Avraham, subsection 3).

If someone borrows money from a non-Jew using their chametz (leavened bread) as collateral, and does not specify "from now" (i.e., that the transfer of ownership is immediate) – they are obligated to redeem it before Passover and destroy it, so that they do not violate the prohibition of "having chametz seen." If they do not do so, the chametz is forbidden for benefit, and no one is permitted to purchase it from the non-Jew after Passover, as the person has transgressed the prohibition of "having chametz seen." There is no financial loss, as the non-Jew accepts it as repayment for the debt. However, it is possible that one is obligated to redeem it and throw it into the river or burn it, and then pay the non-Jew with money. For if not, they would be repaying their debt with something that is forbidden for benefit. And perhaps since this happens automatically and the person does not actively do anything, it is impossible to obligate them in this regard. And in the Jerusalem Talmud (Pesachim, Chapter 2, Halacha 2), it is explained that even in a situation where one transgresses the prohibition of "having chametz seen" – nevertheless, we do not compel them to incur a loss because of this, see there (brought in the Beit Yosef, Siman 448, subsection 4, see there).

A Jew who lent money to a non-Jew on the security of his chametz, and the chametz was deposited with the Jew, and the non-Jew said to him, "If I do not repay you by such-and-such a time, this chametz shall be yours from now"; even if the chametz was in no way the Jew's responsibility, and even if the time did not arrive until after Passover, nevertheless, if the time arrived and he did not repay - this chametz is forbidden to benefit from, since it has become clear that this chametz retroactively belonged to the Jew. And even if it was stored in the non-Jew's house throughout Passover, such as if the Jew entrusted it back to him, it is considered as chametz of a Jew that was deposited with a non-Jew, and it is forbidden to benefit from it. But if he did not say "from now," and the responsibility for the chametz was not on him - it is permitted, as we hold: between a Jew and a non-Jew, and a non-Jew and a Jew - a pledge is not acquired (Magen Avraham, small section 6). And even if it seems from the non-Jew's intention that he plans to keep the chametz, nevertheless he does not violate anything as long as he has not explicitly sold it to him. But a Jew who pledges chametz to another Jew, the trustee violates "bal yera'eh" (the prohibition of chametz being seen), since between Jews, a pledge is acquired (there). And also the depositor violates "bal yera'eh."

And know: There is one who says regarding the case of "from now" that was explained, that the chametz is forbidden for benefit. Nevertheless, during Passover, one is not obligated to destroy it, since it is still under the ownership of the non-Jew; for perhaps the non-Jew will redeem it because the time is after Passover (there, subsection 4). And there are those who disagree with this, and hold that one is obligated to destroy it (Taz, subsection 3, and Chayei Adam, subsection 7), because afterward, when it remains with him, he retroactively transgresses "it shall not be seen." Nevertheless, if one did not destroy it and the non-Jew comes during Passover to redeem it – it is permitted to accept the money from him and allow him to take the chametz. However, one should not hand the chametz to him directly, as this is forbidden, but rather he should take it by himself. And this is not considered benefiting from forbidden items, because since he is redeeming it, it turns out that it was never truly owned by the Jew (Magen Avraham there and Chayei Adam).

If the Jew did not take possession of the chametz before Passover, and the chametz was left in the non-Jew's house, but it was pledged that if the debt was not repaid by a certain time, the chametz would belong to the Jew, and this time is after Passover, and the debt was not repaid – it is permissible for the Jew to take the chametz, even though he said "from now." Since he did not take possession of the chametz, it turns out that the acquisition is only through the money of the loan. And it is established law that between a Jew and a non-Jew, and a non-Jew and a Jew, acquisition is only through physical possession, as I have written in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 194 (the Gra).

However, according to Rashi's opinion, as brought in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 330, that acquisition is only through money, one transgresses "bal yera'eh" (the prohibition of chametz being seen during Passover). Nevertheless, most authorities do not hold this view, as explained there. Therefore, according to what will be explained in Siman 448, that in exigent circumstances we rely on Rashi's opinion that acquisition occurs through money, see there. Hence, it appears to me that if this very person who sold his chametz to a non-Jew for money, the non-Jew should mortgage his chametz, so that if he does not repay him after Passover, the chametz will belong to the non-Jew – it is forbidden to take it. How can we rule two contradictory things for him: that here he acquires through money and here he does not acquire through money? And it is simple that if the time arrived before Passover and he did not repay him, even if the chametz was left in the non-Jew's house – the chametz belongs to the Jew, and he transgresses "bal yera'eh," and it is forbidden to benefit from it.

Regarding a mixture that contains chametz, there is a dispute among the Tannaim in Pesachim (43a), as it was taught: For complete chametz of grain – one is liable for karet, for its mixture – one violates a negative commandment; these are the words of Rabbi Eliezer. And the Sages say: For complete chametz of grain – one is liable for karet, for its mixture – one is not liable for anything. That means: there is no negative commandment, only a general prohibition. And it is stated there in the sugya that when there is an olive's bulk (kezayit) of chametz within the time of eating a pras (half a loaf) from the mixture – all agree that one is liable. And when there is a dispute between an individual and the majority, the law follows the majority. And so Rambam wrote in his commentary on the Mishnah there, that the law does not follow Rabbi Eliezer. And likewise wrote the Ra'avad, see there.

And so the Rif ruled there, and this is his language: Even though the Sages said that the mixture is as if it is nothing - this means that one does not receive lashes, but there is still a prohibition. And when the Sages said that one does not receive lashes - this only applies when there is not an olive-sized amount (kezayit) within the time it takes to eat a portion (kdei achilat pras), such as Babylonian kutach and the like. But when there is an olive-sized amount within the time it takes to eat a portion - even according to the Sages, one would receive lashes. This is his language; and so wrote the Rambam in the first chapter, law 6, and this is his language: One is only liable for karet (spiritual excision) for the consumption of actual chametz. But a mixture of chametz, such as Babylonian kutach and Median beer and the like, if one eats them on Passover - one receives lashes but there is no karet, as it is stated: "No leavened substance shall you eat." In what case are these matters spoken of? When one eats an olive-sized amount of chametz within a mixture in the time it takes to eat three eggs - then one receives lashes from the Torah. But if there isn't an olive-sized amount within the time it takes to eat three eggs, although it is forbidden to eat, if one ate - one does not receive lashes, but rather receives disciplinary lashes (makkat mardut). This is his language; hence, his words are like those of the Rif, and like the Sages. And although he wrote "an olive-sized amount within the time it takes to eat a portion" regarding "Babylonian kutach," and in kutach there is not an olive-sized amount within the time it takes to eat a portion, and on this matter the Raavad critiqued him, and this is his language: The Rabbi ruled in these matters according to the Sages, because there isn't an olive-sized amount within the time it takes to eat a portion. This is his language. However, the Rambam did not go into these details of the food items, and he generalized, that when there is an olive-sized amount within the time it takes to eat a portion - one is liable for lashes. And if not - it is merely a prohibition (and so wrote the Maggid Mishneh, see there).

And this that he brought a verse, "No leavened bread shall be eaten," even though in the Gemara Rabbi Eliezer derives from this verse when it does not contain the volume of an olive's bulk within the time it takes to eat half a loaf, and not according to the Rabbis, for in the case of an olive's bulk within the time it takes to eat half a loaf, a verse is not needed, as this is the law with all prohibitions. And already Ramban in the Sefer HaMitzvot (negative commandment 198) and the Maggid Mishneh have questioned him, for since there is an olive's bulk within the time it takes to eat half a loaf, it is obvious that there is also the penalty of karet (spiritual excision), for this is complete chametz. And behold, with all prohibitions it is so, that when there is an olive's bulk within the time it takes to eat half a loaf, one is liable just as if the prohibited matter were not mixed at all, see there.

However, the truth is that according to the Rambam's approach, this applies to all prohibitions that incur karet (excision). Regarding a mixture containing a forbidden substance, even if it contains an olive-sized portion within the amount of time it takes to eat a pras (half a loaf of bread), it only incurs lashes and not karet. This matter is explained at the beginning of chapter fifteen of Forbidden Foods, and this is his wording: "How is its substance defined? For example, if there was an olive-sized portion of forbidden fat within three eggs' volume of the mixture, if one ate a volume equal to three eggs of this mixture, since it contains an olive-sized portion of forbidden fat, he is lashed, for the taste and substance of the prohibition are present." This is his wording. And forbidden fat incurs karet, yet even so, one only receives lashes. We have already explained his words in Yoreh Deah, at the beginning of section 98; see there (and in this regard, the Kesef Mishneh also disagrees with the Maggid Mishneh; see there). His source is from the Talmud in Avodah Zarah (67a): "Anything whose taste and substance are forbidden incurs lashes upon it"; see there. And it appears to the Rambam, from the fact that he does not say "and one incurs karet for prohibitions of karet" – we can infer that for a mixture, there is never karet, even if there is an olive-sized portion within the amount of time it takes to eat a pras. However, we need to explain from where he deduces this.

In my humble opinion, it appears that all prohibitions are derived from chametz (leavened bread). Rabbi Eliezer derives from "kol machmetzet lo tocheilu" ("you shall not eat any leavened product") that a mixture (of chametz) incurs a prohibition even if there is not an olive's bulk (kazayit) within the time it takes to eat half a loaf (k'dei achilat pras). He further states: "kol machmetzet lo tocheilu" – this includes Babylonian kutach (a type of dip)... Could it be that one would be liable for karet (spiritual excision)? The Torah states: "For anyone who eats chametz will be cut off" – implying that for pure chametz of grain one incurs karet, but for its mixture, only a prohibition applies; these are the words of Rabbi Eliezer. Therefore, the Rambam believes that the Rabbis also derive from this verse regarding a mixture that contains an olive's bulk within the time it takes to eat half a loaf. The teaching is not about the obligation of the prohibition, as that is not necessary; chametz is not less severe than other prohibitions, but it exempts from karet according to the verse "For anyone who eats chametz will be cut off," which applies only to pure chametz, not a mixture, as Rabbi Eliezer holds for less than the time it takes to eat half a loaf. The explanation, in my humble opinion, is as follows: In the section "This month shall be for you" (Exodus 12), three warnings regarding chametz are written. First, it is written "For anyone who eats chametz will be cut off..." (Exodus 12:15), and afterward, it is written "For anyone who eats a leavened product will be cut off" (Exodus 12:19). The Gemara explains that this refers to chametz that fermented because of another substance, not necessarily by itself. Then it is written "You shall not eat any leavened product" (Exodus 12:20), indicating that there is a type of chametz that only incurs a prohibition, not karet. It cannot be said that this verse comes as a warning like all punishments, where the scripture does not punish unless it has warned, as another verse in the section "Sanctify to me every firstborn" (Exodus 13:3) states "and chametz shall not be eaten." Therefore, it is certain that "You shall not eat any leavened product" comes to teach that there is a type of chametz that only incurs a prohibition. And which type is this? A mixture of chametz – according to Rabbi Eliezer, when there is less than an olive's bulk within the time it takes to eat half a loaf, and according to the Rabbis, when there is an olive's bulk within that time. And from chametz, we learn about all prohibitions. (The Tur assumes that the Rambam rules according to Rabbi Eliezer, as does the Ra'avad. The Kesef Mishneh elaborates greatly and concludes that he rules according to Rabbi Eliezer. The Pri Chadash and the Mechaber also elaborate and get entangled in the Rambam's words. In my humble opinion, it seems clear as I have written, and in this, the Maggid Mishneh also assumes that he rules according to the Rabbis, and he explicitly writes this in his commentary on the Mishnah. Analyze this, and you will find it simple.)

And even though it is explained in the Gemara (Pesachim 43a) that the Rabbis do not derive anything from the term "kol machmetzet" (any leavened), and only Rabbi Eliezer derives from it, see there, and from this the poskim deduced that Rambam rules like Rabbi Eliezer – it seems to me in my humble opinion that this is indeed the case: Rabbi Eliezer derives from the extra word and the term "kol" (any), as explained in the Gemara. But according to the Rabbis, it is from the term "machmetzet," which implies not completely leavened, meaning through a mixture. And clear proof of this is that Rambam in the fifteenth chapter of Forbidden Foods, where he rules that something which has a permitted status (davar sheyesh lo matirin) is not nullified even in a thousand; and he wrote there that chametz is also prohibited in any amount, because it will become permitted after Pesach, see there. And he further wrote: the law of something which has a permitted status only applies to its own kind and not to a different kind, and he wrote in this language: "And do not be astonished about chametz on Pesach, for the Torah said 'any leavened substance you shall not eat,' therefore they were stringent with it." End quote, meaning that even in a different kind it is not nullified. And it is not understood, for according to him, the prohibition is with an olive's volume within the time it takes to eat a half loaf – there is no greater stringency in chametz from the Torah than in other prohibitions. And it cannot be said that his intention is about what the Torah was stringent with when it comes to something leavened due to another substance – in the end, it is completely chametz. Moreover, something leavened due to another substance – we do not derive it from this verse, rather from "for anyone who eats leavened shall be cut off," as explained in the Gemara. Rather, certainly this is the explanation: the term "kol machmetzet" implies any kind of chametz, such as a mixture of chametz. Even though there is no karet (excision), there is still a prohibition. And also included is something leavened due to another substance, but for this, the second verse "for anyone who eats leavened shall be cut off" comes, for even karet is liable for this. And it seems reasonable to establish it only in this case and not in a mixture, for it is unreasonable to impose karet on a mixture even with an olive's volume within the time it takes to eat a half loaf. And it is explicitly proven in the Yerushalmi at the beginning of the third chapter, where it says there: it is resolved with chametz and matzah that were mixed. And it challenges: what are we dealing with? If the majority is chametz, karet is liable…? See there. Thus, only with the majority being chametz is karet liable, because the minority is nullified by the majority, and not with an olive's volume within the time it takes to eat a half loaf. (And what is taught in Challah Chapter Three Mishnah 7: one who makes dough from wheat and rice, if it has the taste…, see there – this is because rice tends to be like it, as it is stated in the Yerushalmi there, and it is explained in Yoreh De'ah there.)

It follows that according to the Rambam, the term "machmetzet" includes anything that is not completely chametz. And because the Torah explained this regarding chametz, even though it applies to other prohibitions as well, nevertheless, our sages were stringent about mixtures involving chametz in terms of nullification, because the Torah mentioned mixtures in relation to chametz. But Rabbi Eliezer derives it from "kol" (all), while the Rabbis do not derive "kol," as stated in the Gemara. I am puzzled by the Ramban and the Magid Mishneh, who criticized the Rambam for saying that there is no karet (excision) for a mixture containing an olive's bulk within the time it takes to eat a pras (half a loaf). For it is also explicitly stated in the Rif that one incurs lashes for an olive's bulk within the time it takes to eat a pras, as I wrote in section 2. And since he did not write that one is liable for karet, it implies that he holds like the Rambam. Moreover, it is known that the Rambam always follows the approach of the Rif.

However, the Ramban, the Maggid Mishneh, and most of the poskim (decisors of Jewish law) wrote that in a mixture containing chametz where there is an olive's bulk within the time it takes to eat a piece of bread, one is liable for karet. And similarly, with all prohibitions that result in karet, because an olive's bulk within the time it takes to eat a piece of bread is a law given to Moses at Sinai regarding the consumption of a prohibited item, that one should not delay more than the time it takes to eat a piece of bread. And here too, it applies to mixtures. But the Rif and the Rambam hold that this applies to the prohibition itself in terms of extending the time, and not to mixtures. And when there is not an olive's bulk within the time it takes to eat a piece of bread, some of the poskim ruled according to Rabbi Eliezer, because the unspecified case of "these pass over" follows Rabbi Eliezer, and there is a prohibition here. And some ruled according to the Sages, and there is no prohibition here, according to the Rif and the Rambam, and there is the law of half a measure, which is forbidden by Torah law but does not incur lashes.

And all this applies to a mixture where the chametz does not impart flavor to the mixture, such as dry with dry. But when it does impart flavor, it depends on the dispute in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 98: whether the principle of "taste as substance" is from the Torah or Rabbinic. It is explained there that Rashi and the Rambam hold that "taste as substance" is Rabbinic, and Rabbeinu Tam holds that "taste as substance" is from the Torah. This is also the opinion of the Rosh and the Tur, see there. Therefore, the Tur writes here, and these are his words: "Specifically when there is no chametz flavor in the mixture... but if there is chametz flavor, one is liable for it, for 'taste as substance' is from the Torah." Thus are his words. And also regarding the measure of an olive's volume within the time of eating a half loaf, he agrees with the Ramban and the Maggid Mishneh, who wrote: "This also applies where there is no olive's volume within the time of eating a half loaf. But if there is an olive's volume within that time, one is liable." Thus are his words.

There is a significant practical difference between these opinions regarding nullification. Chametz on Pesach prohibits even the smallest amount, and the Rosh wrote in the second chapter (section 5) that on the eve of Pesach after midday, it is nullified because it does not carry the penalty of karet (excision), see there. If so, any type of chametz that does not carry the penalty of karet is nullified in sixty! According to this, for the Rif and the Rambam, in a mixture of chametz, even if there is an olive's bulk within the time it takes to eat a portion, and even if the taste is primary, it is nullified in sixty since there is no karet. For this reason, the Mahari”l permitted chametz nuksheh in sixty, because there is no karet (Magen Avraham, section 447, subsection 5). However, the Rosh at the end of Avodah Zarah wrote: the reason for the stringency of chametz that is not nullified in sixty is because people do not avoid it all year, see there. According to this, any type of chametz is prohibited even in the smallest amount. Similarly, the Rambam in the fifteenth chapter of Forbidden Foods wrote: the reason for the stringency of chametz in the smallest amount is because it is something that will become permitted – so too, any type of chametz is prohibited. However, according to his opinion, there is another leniency when the mixture is in a cooked dish, that until after Pesach it will spoil, and we do not apply the rule of something that will become permitted, as explained in Yoreh De'ah, section 102. Later in section 467, it will be explained that we are stringent in mixtures, see there. It will be further explained with Divine assistance in section 447 and section 467.

The prohibition of "chametz noksheh" (imperfectly leavened bread) is not mentioned by the Rambam at all. However, it can be inferred from his words that there is a prohibition for chametz noksheh. In the Gemara (Menachot 53a), it is stated that "se'or" (sourdough) is considered chametz noksheh. And in the Mishnah (Pesachim 48a), it is taught: What is "se'or" according to the Sages? Anything that has turned pale like the face of a person whose hair has stood on end. And the Rambam in Chapter 5, Halacha 13 wrote: Similarly, if it has turned pale like the face of a person whose hair has stood on end – it is forbidden to eat it, but one is not liable for karet (spiritual excision). Thus are his words. And since he wrote that there is no karet, it implies clearly that there is a prohibition; otherwise, he would have taught us a greater novelty. And from where do we learn this prohibition? It can be said from the term "machmetzet," which means that it is not completely chametz according to the Rambam, as I have written. However, the Tur in this section wrote: And the Rif ruled according to the Sages that there is no prohibition, neither for a mixture of chametz (where there is not an olive's bulk within the time to eat half a loaf), nor for chametz noksheh, but only a rabbinic prohibition... Thus are his words. And behold, the Rambam also rules according to the Sages, as has been explained. And it is also difficult to say that the Rambam would disagree with the Rif, as is known in most laws. And so wrote the Ran that the Rif ruled thus. And he brings proof: for a mixture is more stringent than noksheh, as is evident in the Gemara; and since one is exempt in a mixture – all the more so in noksheh, see there. Consequently, the Rambam also has this proof. And although in the Gemara there, some say that noksheh is more stringent than a mixture, nevertheless, the poskim (decisors) have followed the other opinion, that a mixture is more stringent than noksheh. If so, we must say that the Rambam's intention is also that even a prohibition does not exist. And what he mentioned about karet is because he was previously discussing that if it remained for the time it takes to walk a mil – it becomes complete chametz; meaning: and is liable for karet. To this, he says that in such a case there is no karet; but it is the same even that there is no prohibition. And so agreed the Rosh and the Tur that there is no prohibition in noksheh.

Regarding the issue of "bal yera'eh" (not to be seen) in mixtures, the Rambam writes in Chapter 4, Law 8: One transgresses the prohibition of "bal yera'eh" and "bal yimatzeh" (not to be found) with a mixture of chametz... This is his language. The Magid Mishneh explains that he is presumably referring to a case where there is an olive's bulk (kezayit) within the amount of food that can be eaten in the time it takes to eat a loaf (kdei achilat pras). He relies on what he wrote in the first chapter. He also brought that Rabbi Moshe HaKohen explained the words of the Rambam, saying that his intention is also in a case where there is not an olive's bulk within the time it takes to eat a loaf. The Beit Yosef in his book Kesef Mishneh, and all the poskim (decisors), agreed with this. They wrote a logical explanation: For in the case of eating, if there is not an olive's bulk within the time it takes to eat a loaf, he is not eating the amount of food that was given to Moses at Sinai. But regarding "bal yera'eh," since there is an olive's bulk of chametz, he transgresses "bal yera'eh." And this is also the opinion of Rashi at the beginning of the third chapter, that there is "bal yera'eh" in a mixture. But Rabbeinu Tam wrote in Tosafot that there is no "bal yera'eh," because without the verse "kol machmetzet" (any leaven), we would not even know the prohibition of eating. If so, how do we know about "bal yera'eh"? Look there. And one can say according to Rashi and the Rambam: For in the case of eating, a verse is needed because he eats it in a mixture. But regarding "bal yera'eh," since there is an olive's bulk of chametz, why should he not transgress "bal yera'eh"? Similarly, we find regarding impurity with two half-olive bulks of a carcass, if he joins them with a stick, in contact he is pure because the contact is not at once, but in carrying or moving he is impure because he moves them as one (Chullin 124a). Here too, when the olive's bulk of chametz is scattered in the mixture, in eating, he is exempt because he does not eat it as one. But in "bal yera'eh," he is liable, for he keeps an olive's bulk of chametz, similar to carrying in impurity. For here too, he sees the entire olive's bulk as one, just as he carries the entire olive's bulk as one.

Regarding the prohibition of "Bal Yera'eh" (the prohibition of possessing chametz during Passover) with respect to hardened chametz – in the Rambam, he does not mention at all that there is a "Bal Yera'eh" concerning hardened chametz. It is almost explicitly stated in his words that it is not subject to "Bal Yera'eh," for concerning se'or (leaven) which we brought in paragraph 11, he wrote: "It is forbidden to eat it, but one is not liable to karet." And if you would think that there is a prohibition of "Bal Yera'eh" – he should have said "and one is obligated to destroy it." And although according to Rashi's interpretation, it seems that there is also a "Bal Yera'eh" concerning hardened chametz, for in the Mishnah of "These must be removed," there is mention of hardened chametz, and Rashi explained there that one transgresses "Bal Yera'eh" with all of them – nevertheless, according to the Rambam, it clearly seems that this is not the case. However, in truth, there is no conclusive proof from Rashi, for he interpreted this according to Rabbi Eliezer. But if we follow the sages, there is no prohibition of "Bal Yera'eh" at all, as the Tur wrote, that according to the Rabbanan, it is permitted to keep them during Passover. See there (and these are the general principles of the laws).

Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote in Section 1: A mixture containing chametz is subject to the prohibitions of "bal yira'eh" (it shall not be seen) and "bal yimatzeh" (it shall not be found); for example, moriyas (a type of fish brine), Babylonian kutach (a type of dip), Median beer, and all similar food items. However, a mixture containing chametz that is not fit for consumption is permitted to be kept during Pesach, such as a tanner's vat into which flour and hides were placed. Even if they were placed there an hour before the time of removal (of chametz), it is permitted to keep it. If the hides were not placed and only flour was put in, if it was done three days before the time of removal, it is permitted to keep it because it has become spoiled and ruined. But within three days, it must be removed. Similarly, eye salve, plasters, bandages, and theriac (a type of medicinal compound) into which chametz was placed are permitted to be kept during Pesach, because the chametz has lost its original form. So far are his words, and all of this is from the language of the Rambam at the beginning of the fourth chapter.

Here is the translation of the passage:

Now, "murias" is not mentioned in the Mishnah of "These are to be removed," and nowhere is it mentioned that "murias" contains chametz (leaven). "Median beer" is mentioned in the Gemara, where they added barley water; and Rashi explained: because their beer was from dates, and in Media, they made beer from barley water similar to ours, therefore it is called "Median beer." So far his words. And I am puzzled: if so, this is not a mixture of chametz, but complete chametz, as our teacher the Beit Yosef wrote in section 5. And it must be said that Rashi says "similar to ours," not exactly "like ours," and there are also other kinds in it. And we have already explained that the opinion of most authorities is that even if there is not an olive's bulk in the time it takes to eat a piece, one is obligated to remove it. And this is specifically in a mixture of different kinds. But a mixture of the same kind, such as chametz flour in Pesach flour, since by Torah law it is nullified in the majority, as I wrote in Yoreh Deah, section 98, although rabbinically, liquid in liquid requires sixty, and flour is considered like liquid in liquid, nevertheless – it is permitted to keep it (Magen Avraham, subsection 1).

And behold, the Tur wrote that any item not prohibited by the Torah for consumption is permitted to mix and keep initially, see there. However, the Tosafot at the beginning of Pesachim wrote that the Sages did not differentiate, and even something that is only rabbinically prohibited is forbidden to keep. And so it appears the opinions of our Rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch in Siman 447, who ruled that chametz noksheh (hardened chametz) is forbidden to keep, and there is no transgression of "bal yera'eh" (it shall not be seen), and consequently, it is also not prohibited by the Torah for consumption. Nevertheless, it is forbidden to keep it, but if one did keep it, it is not forbidden for benefit, see there. And all the more so, if it imparts flavor, it is forbidden to keep it, and if one did keep it, it is permitted for benefit (Chayei Adam and Machatzit HaShekel). However, an item that is forbidden due to absorption from a chametz utensil is permitted to keep (there), and pickled items are forbidden (there).

And what is "imperfect chametz"? This refers to something that from the outset is not completely chametz, such as those substances that scribes use to glue their papers, which are made from flour and water, or dough whose surface has turned white but has not become chametz, or chametz that is initially bad for eating. However, if it was initially complete chametz and good for eating, it does not lose its status as complete chametz until it becomes unfit even for a dog's consumption (Magen Avraham, ibid.). And this is what our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in paragraph 2: bread itself that has become moldy and unfit for a dog's consumption, and a mixture that has become spoiled – one is not obligated to remove it. This is his exact wording. But for eating – it is forbidden. And if the bread became moldy after the time of prohibition – one is obligated to remove it (ibid., minor paragraph 3), because since it was fit for eating at the time when the prohibition began, it violates the prohibition of "it shall not be seen." And it appears to me that this applies to those who hold that one violates "it shall not be seen" after six hours; but those who hold that one does not violate "it shall not be seen" until nighttime – it is possible that one is not obligated to remove it. This requires further investigation.

Clothing that has been washed with wheat starch, or clothing that has been soaked in bran with water – it is permissible to wear them, as they do not have the status of chametz at all. Similarly, papers that have been glued with chametz, in the manner that bookbinders do – it is permissible to keep them during Pesach. Certainly, this chametz mixture, if the papers were not glued with it – it is forbidden to keep it, as it has the status of chametz. But after the papers have been glued with it – it is permissible. This is what we have learned in our Mishnah: "The glue of scribes" – this is before the papers have been glued (Magen Avraham and Taz, subsection 2). Therefore, it is permissible to glue papers in a window within thirty days before Pesach. There are those who are strict within thirty days if the glue is visible from the outside, as then the form of the chametz remains. But before thirty days – it has already hardened. There is someone who is stringent to spread clothing washed with wheat starch on the table, and also to wash women's scarves with them (Magen Avraham, subsection 5). There is no sense in this, for our eyes see that there are no crumbs in them at all, so there is no concern that a crumb might fall into the food. Perhaps in their days crumbs remained, but now it is clear that it is permissible without any doubt (Chayei Adam, subsection 11).

Something that has mixed with chametz, and is not fit for human consumption at all, or is not fit for all people, such as theriac which is made for medicinal purposes and similar items, even though it is permitted to keep it – nevertheless it is forbidden to eat it until after Passover. And even though it contains only a minimal amount of chametz, it is still forbidden for consumption and benefit (Magen Avraham). Later in Siman 447, it will be explained that there are those who disagree and permit any amount of chametz even for eating, when it has already been nullified before Passover, and this seems correct. And with Heaven's help, it will be explained there. (The Taz in subsection 3 is stringent, and the Chayei Adam in subsection 14 disagrees with him, see there.)

Barley beer is considered complete chametz, and one is liable to karet for consuming it. This is not due to the principle of "taste as substance," as there are opinions that "taste as substance" is not a Torah prohibition. Nor is it because there is an olive's bulk of chametz within the time it takes to eat a pras, for according to most authorities, one is liable to karet. Rather, even according to the Rif and the Rambam, whom we explained hold that there is no liability for karet with an olive's bulk within the time it takes to eat a pras, as I wrote in section 2, here it is entirely chametz, because the essence of the barley enters into the water. This is like dissolving chametz and drinking it, for which one is liable to karet (Chullin 120a). Similarly, distilled wine made from grain is considered complete chametz, and one is liable to karet for consuming it. All the Geonim agree on this. Anyone who claims that it is merely a vapor is making a great error, for the essence of the grain is dissolved into it, leaving only the waste. Even distilled wine made from potatoes but also containing some grain, if it has an olive's bulk of grain within the time it takes to eat a pras, one is liable to karet according to most authorities. Furthermore, the primary fermenting agent is the barley malt, which is complete chametz.

Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote in Section 5: Similarly, if one curdled cheese with vinegar made from barley or wheat beer – one is obligated to destroy it. This is his language, for the curdling agent is not nullified even in a thousand. The same law applies if one poured chametz, or beer, or distilled wine into it to make it sharp; even though the cheese was already made and curdled with rennet – nevertheless, this is done for flavor, and is not nullified (Eliyah Rabbah, Subsection 11). And even though a curdling agent and something made for flavor are only rabbinic prohibitions – nevertheless, they are considered as if the substance is present, and even post facto it is forbidden (Chayei Adam, Subsection 16). And even if one delayed it until after Passover, it is still forbidden (ibid.). There are those who are lenient in cases of significant loss, by throwing the value of the prohibition into the Dead Sea (Eliyah Rabbah, ibid.). Similarly, if one leavened dough after Passover with yeast that was present during Passover – the entire dough is forbidden because it is a curdling agent (ibid., in the name of the responsa of Maharam of Lublin, see there). Some of the great authorities wrote that a curdling agent is nullified, and it is permitted to keep it (Yam Shel Shlomo, Chullin, Chapter 8, Siman 6). This is against the opinion of all the early authorities (Magen Avraham, Subsection 9). The Rashba explicitly wrote in a responsum (Part 1, Siman 455) that vinegar fermented with beer yeast is forbidden to keep.

Even if the substance causing the fermentation was fourth or fifth in the sequence, it is forbidden. For example, honey water that they call mead, which was fermented with beer sediments and honey water sediments. This made the second honey water, and with the sediments of the second they made the third honey water, and from the third to the fourth, and from the fourth to the fifth—one is obligated to remove even the last honey water. If this extended past Passover, it is prohibited for benefit, as the substance causing the fermentation is considered like actual chametz (leavened bread) (this is stated in the name of the Ramban, see there). And we have already written that in a case of significant financial loss, it is permissible to nullify the benefit by throwing it into the Dead Sea or selling it to a non-Jew, except for the value of the forbidden part within it, without concern that the non-Jew might sell it back to a Jew (the Gra, section 10). There are those who permit the fourth honey water (there), because after three times the fermenting power is exhausted. One can rely on this leniency in a case of significant financial loss since the prohibition of causing fermentation is rabbinic.

Both this and that which causes [a prohibited result] are permitted even in the case of an agent, such as when it is established with permissible honey dregs together with beer dregs – it is permissible, as I have written in Yoreh De'ah, end of Siman 87 (Magen Avraham and Chayei Adam there). There are those who question this, arguing whether it is worse than the second or third setting. Certainly, those are better than this, and this causes [a prohibited result], as the primary component is permissible (Mikdash Me'at, Siman Katan 6). In my humble opinion, it appears that this is not comparable. Although in the second or third setting the agent has less power than this, and this causes [a result], nevertheless the root and essence of the permissible item also come from the prohibition, and this is its power that is never nullified. This is not the case with "this and that which causes," where the root and essence come from both the permissible and the prohibited. It is explicitly explained in the Mishnah of Orlah (Chapter 2, Mishnah 14) that even in prohibitions of benefit, such as mixed vineyard produce (kilayim), this and that which causes is permitted. See there, it is permitted even for consumption.

Cheese that was curdled in a stomach (rennet) that had been in a chametz vessel – it is forbidden to eat it, but it is permitted to keep it (Magen Avraham there in the name of Radbaz). This is specifically when the stomach had been in the chametz vessel for twenty-four hours (there). Even though after twenty-four hours it becomes spoiled, it must be said that this is like a sharp item (Eliyah Rabbah there). And it is difficult to say this (there). Those who cook honey water in a beer pot, if within twenty-four hours – it is completely forbidden, and after twenty-four hours – it is permitted to keep, as it gives a spoiled taste (Taz, subsection 4). And in a doubt whether it is within twenty-four hours or after twenty-four hours – one may be lenient, as the general rule is that vessels are not "a day old" (there). Some people drink on the last day of Pesach from honey water of the whole year, and this is not the main practice. One should not be lenient in this, and one who guards his soul should stay away from this (there).

And they wrote that it is customary to scrape the walls and chairs that have some kind of chametz stuck to them. And even though it has already been nullified, nevertheless, they have something to rely on, for perhaps a crumb might fall during Passover. And if there is chametz in a crack that one cannot dig out, one should place a little clay over the crack to ruin its appearance. And now, people clean extensively, washing and scrubbing and searching for any trace of chametz to remove it. Dough that remains in the cracks of a kneading trough, if there is an olive-sized amount in one place, one is obligated to remove it and transgresses the prohibition of "it shall not be seen." Less than an olive-sized amount, if it is there to reinforce the cracks of the trough or to plug a hole, it is nullified by its minority. If not, one is obligated to remove it. And an olive-sized amount, even in a place meant to reinforce, one is obligated to remove it. This is the opinion of the Rif in the third chapter and the Rambam in the second chapter.

And the opinion of Rashi (Pesachim 14b) is that regarding the dough residue in the kneading trough – even if there is an olive's bulk, it does not need to be removed. But on its upper edge – even if there is less than an olive's bulk, it must be removed. And on its sides, if there is an olive's bulk in one place – it must be removed; if less than an olive's bulk in one place – it does not need to be removed. According to Rabbi Yitzchak of the Tosafists: in the place of kneading, meaning the entire trough except for its upper edge, if there is an olive's bulk in one place – it must be removed, even if it is meant to reinforce. And similarly, less than an olive's bulk, when it is not meant to reinforce – it must be removed. But less than an olive's bulk in a place meant to reinforce – it does not need to be removed. And not in the place of kneading – it never needs to be removed, unless there is an olive's bulk in a place that is not meant to reinforce. But less than an olive's bulk, even if it is not meant to reinforce, or meant to reinforce even an olive's bulk – it does not need to be removed. And the reason we are not concerned about less than an olive's bulk in a place that does not need to be removed lest one eat it – is because in dough, this concern does not exist at all, as it is not fit for consumption. And the concern that it might be baked and then eaten – we do not find this concern. And it also appears that it is not fit for baking, because of its age and hardness. Nevertheless, it is considered chametz. (And with this, the difficulty of the Taz, paragraph 5, is resolved; see there.)

There are those who say that in any case where we have obligated one to remove less than an olive's bulk (kazayit), this is when their accumulation together would be an olive's bulk. But otherwise, in any situation, he is not obligated to remove it (Magen Avraham, subsection 10, in the name of the Sefer Mitzvot Katan). And there are those who disagree with this (ibid.). The first opinion seems more correct, and there is proof from the law that will be explained in the next section. Also, with half an olive's bulk, it must be clean, but if it is somewhat dirty, there is no need to remove it (ibid.). And with an olive's bulk, there is no distinction unless it is very dirty to the extent that it is unfit for a dog's consumption. All this is according to the law. However, the custom is to remove and search even for the slightest amount, as I have written.

In a case where an olive-sized amount is specifically required, if there were two half-olive amounts in two different places, and a thread of dough connects them, we consider that if, when the thread is removed, the halves are also removed with it – one is obligated to destroy it. If not – one is not required to destroy it. What are we discussing? A kneading trough. But in a house, even if when the thread is removed the halves are not taken with it – one is obligated to destroy it, because sometimes they are gathered together when sweeping the house. If there was half an olive in the house and half an olive in the attic, or half an olive in the house and half an olive in the portico, or half an olive in this house and half an olive in the inner house – in all these cases, it was a question in the Gemara (Pesachim 30b) and was not resolved. Therefore, if one nullified the chametz – the inspection is a rabbinic doubt, and leniency is applied. If one did not nullify – it is a biblical doubt, and stringency is applied. Therefore, if it is before the sixth hour – one nullifies it in his heart, and that suffices. If it is during the sixth hour, and certainly afterwards, and one did not nullify – one is obligated to destroy it. (From this it is clear that there is no half-measure in prohibition, Beit Yosef.)

According to Rashi's interpretation there, the question arises when half an olive is placed here and half an olive is placed there, and this is also evident from the words of the Rosh and the Tur. However, from the words of the Rambam in the second chapter, who wrote: "Since these half-olives are stuck to the walls, or to the beams, or to the ground – one is not obligated to remove them, but rather nullifies them in his heart and that is sufficient," until here are his words; and so wrote our Rabbi the Beit Yosef in section 8 – we learn from this that they interpret the question specifically when the half-olives are stuck. But otherwise – we certainly worry that they might come together. And in one house, even if they are stuck, we worry that perhaps when one cleans the house, he will remove them from their attachment, and bring them close to each other.

Leaven that became moldy before the time of its prohibition and became unfit for a dog to eat, or that was burned in fire before its time and charred to the point of being unfit for a dog, or that was designated for sitting and smeared with clay – it is permissible to keep it during Passover. However, eating it is forbidden; since it was designated for eating, it is considered as food. It is clear that the prohibition is not from the Torah, for would its designation change its status? Rather, it is forbidden by rabbinic decree, since it was originally leaven (Taz, subsection 8). And why do we require leaven to be unfit for a dog, and it is not sufficient that it is unfit for human consumption, like with all other prohibitions? Because leaven is different, for even sourdough is not fit for human consumption, and yet one is liable for karet for it, because it is fit to leaven another dough. Similarly, with leaven: even when it is not fit for eating, it is fit to leaven another dough; which is not the case when it is unfit for a dog – it is not fit for anything.

The Rosh wrote at the beginning of the chapter "Kol Sha'ah": The murias that they make nowadays, which they call almad'i, in which they put roasted bread – some say it is permitted after Passover, because chametz through a mixture that has passed through Passover is permitted for benefit. Additionally, since they roasted it before its time, it is permitted for benefit after its time. However, we do not hold this way, because Rabbi Shimon only permits it when it was mixed unintentionally. But for intentional mixing and retention – no. And because it was roasted, we also do not say that it was roasted perfectly well, as the thought of Passover did not arise at the time of its making. Additionally... but murias which is customarily eaten in this manner – is forbidden. This is his exact wording, meaning: that it is only permitted when it is not fit for eating at all. But murias that they eat – there is no permission in the matter. This is also the opinion of the Rambam, who considers murias among the prohibitions of "bal yera'eh" (it shall not be seen), as I wrote in Section 14. And from the language of the Rosh, even though he forbids it after Passover, it does not seem from his words that one transgresses "bal yera'eh" because of it. And even more so from the language of the Tur, who wrote that almad'i is forbidden to eat after Passover, see there, it explicitly implies that it is only forbidden to eat. It is surprising regarding the Tur, for from the language of the Rosh it is clear that it is also forbidden for benefit (Magen Avraham, Section 14). However, the Tur is consistent with his view at the end of Siman 447, that it is permitted to mix initially and retain it, see there.
