However, for eating – it is forbidden (see Korban Netanel there).

Ink that is cooked with barley beer – it is permissible to write with it on the intermediate days of Passover. This is specifically if it was made before Passover, but making the ink on Passover is prohibited. We do not worry that during writing one might put the quill into his mouth. Even though it is unfit for a dog to eat, nevertheless, it is still forbidden to eat it, as explained, because it is not the norm to put the part of the quill with the ink into one's mouth. Furthermore, the prohibition of eating it is because one considers it significant, as I have written, but in this case, it is not considered significant.

And what has been explained regarding the dough in the cracks of the kneading trough—this refers to a trough where bread is merely stored. However, a trough used for kneading bread—not only must all chametz (leavened bread) be removed from it, but even washing it with hot water and scraping out all the chametz within it is not sufficient, because it is impossible to scrape it without leaving behind a kezayit (olive-sized amount). The utensil combines them, since it is made for kneading, and everything inside the utensil is considered as one piece. Not only is it forbidden to use it during Passover, but one is also likely to transgress "bal yera'eh" (the prohibition against seeing chametz). Therefore, it must be given as a gift to a non-Jew or sold until after Passover, as will be explained in Siman 448, or it should be plastered with clay. And although this is a stringent measure, it should still be done. However, this applies to a trough made of boards with cracks. But a small trough like ours, which is made from a single piece and has no cracks, can certainly be washed and scraped of chametz, and can be kept. But using it is forbidden, as this is the "house of leaven" mentioned in the Gemara (Pesachim 30b), which is forbidden to use. Similarly, for dough in a utensil made of boards, if one cannot remove the chametz from them, it should be given as a gift to a non-Jew. It is also advisable to do the same for utensils where flour is stored all year round if the utensil has cracks—certainly, there is chametz flour between the cracks. Similarly, for utensils where bread is stored all year and there are cracks, and it is made of wicker, which is hard to clean, and for a cloth placed on a flour sack—shaking it out is not sufficient, and it should be washed with hot water if one wants to use it during Passover. It requires washing with hot water, ashes, and pounding (Magen Avraham, section 19). But ordinary tablecloths used all year round only need washing. This will be explained further with Divine help in Siman 451.

It has already been explained in Siman 431 that according to the Rambam, one who eats chametz on the eve of Passover after noon transgresses a prohibition. The Rosh and the Tur agreed with him, and this is also the opinion of the Geonim (Magid Mishneh, Chapter 1). Although the Raavad, the Meor, and the Itur did not rule this way, nevertheless, this is the halacha. And so the prohibition spread throughout all the communities of Israel, that after noon, chametz is forbidden for benefit by Torah law (Beit Yosef). Regarding "Bal Yera'eh" (the prohibition of chametz being seen), the Raavad also holds that one does not transgress until nightfall, whereas the Rambam holds that one transgresses "Bal Yera'eh" from noon, as I wrote there. And so Rashi explicitly explained in Bava Kama (29b), see there.

And because chametz (leavened bread) is accessible to everyone, men and women, adults and children – our sages of blessed memory made a safeguard to prohibit it even two hours before midday, as will be explained. And they differentiated between the prohibition of eating and the prohibition of benefit: for benefit, they only prohibited it one hour before midday, while for eating, they prohibited it two hours before. And the reason for this matter: because between the sixth hour and the seventh hour, mistakes are very common – therefore they prohibited it for benefit. But between the fifth hour and the seventh hour – it is only possible to make a mistake on a cloudy day, for when the sun is shining – everyone knows and sees that at five the sun is in the east, and at seven it is in the west. Therefore, it is sufficient to prohibit eating, but not benefit (Bach). And this is explained in the Talmudic discussion (12b), see there. And even the chametz of a non-Jew – it is forbidden to benefit from it. And even chametz through a mixture, and even unfit chametz – this is the same law (Chayei Adam, section 3).

Therefore, it is forbidden to eat chametz from the beginning of the fifth hour. Throughout this entire hour, it is permitted to derive benefit from it. One is allowed to sell it to a non-Jew, even a large quantity of chametz together, as it is certain that he will not consume it before Passover. He is not obligated to ensure that his chametz is destroyed from the world after selling it to a non-Jew. There is no concern that the non-Jew will sell it to a Jew, as a Jew would not purchase chametz in the fifth hour. Even a type of chametz that is associated with its owner, like kutach (a type of dip) that is referred to as "this is So-and-so's kutach," may also be sold. We do not worry that people will suspect him of having sold it during Passover. This is according to the opinion of Rashi and the Rambam. However, according to the Tosafot at the beginning of the chapter "Kol Sha'ah," it is forbidden to sell it thirty days before Passover. See there. Nevertheless, no halachic authority brought their opinion at all (and the Bah was concerned about this, while the Chayei Adam disagreed with him).

During the fifth hour, one can feed chametz to animals, wild animals, and birds, provided that one stands over them to see that they do not hide any of it, and one must destroy whatever remains of it. And even though it is the way of wild animals to hide things, nevertheless, we do not worry that they will hide it since one is standing over them. And regarding domesticated animals, even though it is not their way to hide things, nonetheless, one is obligated to stand over them (Kesef Mishneh on the Gemara there). From the beginning of the sixth hour and onward, it is forbidden even to derive benefit from it. The Tur writes that if one betrothed a woman with it, she is not betrothed, since deriving benefit from it is forbidden to all of Israel, see there. And this is regarding actual chametz. But regarding chametz nuksheh, which according to Rashi is rabbinically forbidden, it is like chametz that is biblically forbidden. And according to Rabbeinu Tam, since there are two rabbinic factors, the hours which are rabbinic and the chametz which is rabbinic, we are concerned about the betrothal. This is explained in Even HaEzer, Siman 58, see there.

And our Rabbi the Rema wrote that in a leap year, when the day is long, these four hours are according to the proportion of the day, and it is permissible to eat chametz until a third of the day. And some say until two hours before noon, thus his language. Meaning: that those who say this hold that we do not go after a third of the day, but rather it was decreed that it is always forbidden to eat chametz two hours before noon. However, the great ones rejected this, and the main law is that we consider a third of the day. And there are those who calculate from dawn until the stars come out for a third of the day, and there are those who calculate from sunrise until sunset, and so is the law according to the majority of the later authorities (the Vilna Gaon and the Alter Rebbe). And so we calculate in regard to the time for reciting the Shema and prayer, as I wrote above in Siman 58. And so we rule in practice. (As the Vilna Gaon elaborates on this later in Siman 459, and the Alter Rebbe in his Siddur regarding the time for reciting the Shema, see there). And the hours are proportional hours, such as if the day is fifteen hours long – one hour is an hour and a quarter. And this is always the calculation.

If a Jew has another Jew's chametz (leavened products) in his possession as a deposit, he should hold onto it until the fifth hour [on the day before Passover]. If the owner does not come to claim it by then, he should sell it to a non-Jew. If it is something that cannot easily find buyers in the fifth hour, it is permissible to sell it earlier. Even if he must sell it at a loss, he should sell it, because otherwise, it will become completely forbidden. However, if he can sell it to a non-Jew who knows to return it after Passover, in the manner of our chametz sales, as will be explained in Siman 448, he is obligated to do so and not to sell it completely (Magen Avraham, small section 4). Even if he sells it at its proper value, a person prefers to retain his own property (Machatzit HaShekel).

And if he did not sell it – he is obligated to destroy it at the time of its prohibition, even if he is not responsible for the chametz. And even though he does not transgress because of it, nevertheless, he must destroy it so that the depositor will not transgress "bal yera'eh" (the prohibition of chametz being seen). And even though it is possible that the depositor sold it to a non-Jew where it is located, nevertheless, uncertainty does not override certainty (Magen Avraham, subsection 5). And even though it is assumed that the depositor nullified the chametz and does not transgress "bal yera'eh," nevertheless, since according to the decree of the Sages, nullification does not suffice without destruction – he is obligated to destroy it. And the custodian does not need to pay him, as it is the owner's responsibility to take care of his chametz (Chayei Adam, subsection 8 and Even HaEzer). And there are those who obligate the custodian to pay (Magen Avraham there), but this is not the main opinion. And even if it was a pledge in his hand and he did not sell it and the chametz became prohibited – he can say to him, "Here is yours before you." And the borrower needs to pay him his debt, for since he is the owner of the chametz – it is his responsibility to take care of it (Taz, subsection 4, and Chayei Adam there, and see Magen Avraham there who is uncertain about this). And all the more so with a general deposit, that when the chametz is intact, he can say to him, "Here is yours before you," even according to those who hold that the custodian must pay when he destroys it (Magen Avraham there). And all this is after the fact, but initially, the custodian is obligated to see to it that it is sold before the time of its prohibition, as explained.

Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote in paragraph 3: If one purchases anything with chametz after six hours, it is permitted because chametz does not retain its monetary value. End of his words. This is not understood: it is true that, according to Torah law, all items that are forbidden for benefit do not retain their monetary value in prohibition, except for idolatry. However, from a rabbinic perspective, it is forbidden for the owners themselves to sell or exchange such items, as written by Rashi and Tosafot at the beginning of Chullin, see there. One could say that his opinion is that chametz is more lenient because after Passover its prohibition is only rabbinic due to a penalty, and perhaps they were not stringent about retaining its monetary value. However, in the Tur it is mentioned only when a maidservant purchased without the knowledge of the Jew, in which case Rabbeinu Tam ruled permissively, see there. But when a Jew buys or exchanges, it is completely forbidden for him, because otherwise we would find monetary value for chametz on Passover. And this is the main ruling. In the case of indirect exchanges, they are permitted, and there is no difference whether it is exchanged for money, clothing, or utensils. Some distinguish in this matter (Chayei Adam), but this is not the main view (as written by the Gra in his notes). Some say that if the non-Jew first pulled the chametz and then gave the money, it is permitted even for the Jew who sold it to him (Magen Avraham, paragraph 6); for this is how we rule even with wine used for libation in Yoreh De'ah, section 132, because since he pulled it, he acquired it, and the money is not considered the value of the exchanged chametz. And although with libation wine it is forbidden for the Jew, as I wrote there, nevertheless with chametz it is lenient, since the prohibition of exchanges for libation wine is from the Torah. And in this manner, it is permitted for everyone. Certainly, with chametz, which is only a rabbinic prohibition for him, it is permitted in such a case. (In the notes of the Magen Avraham, paragraph 7, he elaborates on the words of the Magen Avraham, and I do not know why, since his intention is clear as I wrote. See Chayei Adam, paragraph 9, regarding grain that became leavened during its growth and passed over Passover, which is permitted; for its growth is considered as exchanged items, see there. And see Pri Chadash who ruled completely leniently regarding retaining its monetary value, that it is permitted even for the exchanger himself or the seller, see there. This is difficult to say. However, in a case of significant loss, the Gra in paragraph 12 wrote that one can rely on this, see there. And especially since this seems to be the opinion of the Beit Yosef. Be precise and you will find leniency.)

The sages taught in the Mishnah (Pesachim 49a): If the fourteenth [of Nisan] falls on Shabbat, all chametz must be removed before Shabbat, according to Rabbi Meir. But the sages say it should be done at its proper time. Rabbi Eliezer son of Rabbi Tzadok says: Terumah must be removed before Shabbat, but ordinary (chametz) at its proper time. Because terumah does not have many who can eat it, but ordinary chametz will find many who can eat it (Rashi). And it is better to remove it at its proper time on the fourteenth. And the removal should not be by burning, which is forbidden on Shabbat, but rather by scattering to the wind or casting into the sea. Therefore, we should rule according to the sages, as the law follows the majority over an individual.

But this is not the ruling of the Rambam in Chapter 3, Law 3, and this is his language: "If the fourteenth [of Nisan] falls on Shabbat, one checks for chametz on the night of [the preceding] Friday, which is the night of the thirteenth. One leaves some chametz to eat until the fourth hour on Shabbat day and keeps it in a hidden place. The rest is burned before Shabbat. If any chametz remains after the fourth hour, one nullifies it and covers it with a vessel until the conclusion of the first day of the festival, and then burns it." So far his language. The Tur and the Shulchan Aruch also ruled this way, and this is the simple custom. And even though it goes against the Mishnah, they relied on what is stated in the first chapter (13a), where it is taught: "If the fourteenth falls on Shabbat, one burns everything before Shabbat..." These are the words of Rabbi Elazar ben Yehuda of Bartota, who said in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua... They said: They did not move from there until they established the law accordingly. See there. And although one does not derive halacha from a Mishnah and a Baraita (Niddah 7b, and see there Rashi and Rashbam in Bava Batra 130b), and so it is stated in the Jerusalem Talmud (Peah, Chapter 2), nevertheless, here the Talmud brought the Baraita and said "they did not move from there until they established the law accordingly" – meaning that it is clear halacha. (However, the Rif has a different approach in this matter, and he rules like Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Tzadok that chametz is disposed of in its time, which is like the Sages. He wrote because Rabbi Elazar of Bartota agrees with him. See there. The Ran, Beit Yosef, and Taz Section 1, and the commentators struggled with his words. With Divine assistance, we explained in the introduction to the Haggadah that his words are simple, that he rules like the Sages. And what he wrote like Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Tzadok – because in the case of terumah, the halacha is not like the Sages but like Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Tzadok, because he agrees with Rabbi Elazar of Bartota, and the halacha was established like him. And although the Rif does not rule halacha in terumah, nevertheless, he could not write the opposite ruling, so he cleverly ruled like Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Tzadok. This is also the intention of the Ran, of blessed memory, and all the difficulties raised against him are resolved. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

According to the Tur, I have another reason why it was necessary to reject this Mishnah as halachah. Rabbi Yehuda states that the only way to dispose of chametz is by burning, which is impossible on Shabbat. However, the Rambam rules according to the Sages who say that burning is not required, whereas Rashi rules according to Rabbi Yehuda, as the Tur writes later in Siman 448. But the Rosh writes that even according to Rashi, this applies only on the eve of Pesach; before that, burning is not required. The Tur disagrees with him later and writes that according to Rashi, even before the eve of Pesach, burning is specifically required. Accordingly, by his reasoning, one must search and dispose of chametz by burning on the eve of Shabbat. This is what the Tur wrote in this Siman: "And so Rashi instructed to dispose of everything before Shabbat." Why did he attribute this to Rashi’s instructions? His intention is that this supports his view in Siman 448, that even before its time, burning is specifically required according to Rashi. (But the commentators explain that the Tur is referring to what comes later, see there.)

Therefore, when Erev Pesach (the day before Passover) falls on Shabbat, we check for chametz (leavened bread) on Thursday evening with a blessing. We recite "Kol Chamira," and we set aside chametz for the meal of that night, for the meal on Friday evening, and also for the two Shabbat meals. However, the third meal (Seudah Shlishit) does not take place because the third meal needs to be after midday, and at that time it is forbidden to eat chametz. Similarly, it is forbidden to eat matzah on Erev Pesach. Only matzah ashira (rich matzah) kneaded with fruit juice can be eaten on Erev Pesach, and one fulfills the obligation of the third meal with it. The prohibition of matzah on Erev Pesach applies only to matzah that one fulfills the obligation of eating matzah on the first night. And with matzah ashira, one does not fulfill that obligation, as we require "lechem oni" (bread of affliction). One must be careful to eat it before the tenth hour, for from then onward it is forbidden to eat so that one will eat the kezayit (olive-sized portion) of matzah with an appetite at night, as will be explained in Siman 471.

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote: In these countries where it is not customary to eat rich matzah, as mentioned later in Siman 462 - one should fulfill the third meal with fruits or with meat and fish. These are his words. And it seems that the intention is not that one should also refrain from eating rich matzah on the eve of Passover according to the custom, as there is no reason for this. Rather, the intention is that since it is not our custom to eat rich matzah on Passover, consequently, we do not prepare rich matzah, and to prepare it only for the third meal - people do not trouble themselves for such a small amount of food. And behold, with us as well, one can make the third meal with cooked matzah, and many among us do so. He preceded "fruits" to "meat and fish" even though meat and fish are preferable to fruits for the third meal as I wrote above in Siman 291, nevertheless, on the eve of Passover, fruits are preferable so that one does not become full and can eat matzah with appetite. And perhaps for this reason, he did not also mention cooked matzah, because it is very filling, as is well known by experience. And some say to divide the morning meal into two, as some say one fulfills [the obligation] with this (Magen Avraham).

And in the Zohar, it is written that Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai was engaged in Torah study during the time of the third meal (there, subsection 2). This needs to be understood: was Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai unable to fulfill the third meal with any of the items that were explained? It seems to me, in my humble opinion, that all of this is an additional matter. For on this Shabbat, we are compelled to say that we were not commanded at all regarding the three meals, since it is impossible, as it coincides with Yom Kippur that falls on Shabbat. The same applies to Shabbat that is the eve of Passover concerning the third meal. Even if we say that the prohibition of eating matzah on the eve of Passover is rabbinic, nevertheless, we find that complete positive commandments are deferred by rabbinic decrees, such as the shofar and lulav on Shabbat. All the more so, the mitzvah of the third meal is deferred. Since this is the case, the mitzvah of the third meal is nullified on this Shabbat. And since a complete meal is impossible, it follows that it is not relevant to fulfill it with fruits, or with meat and fish, which are not needed at all. Furthermore, it is certainly a Torah obligation to eat an olive-sized piece of matzah with appetite. This is the reasoning of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, who engaged in Torah study, because there is no mitzvah at all on this Shabbat to eat the third meal.

Even though one can burn the chametz any day on the eve of Shabbat, it is still good to do it as in other years and burn it before midday, so that people do not come to err in other years and burn it after midday. However, one should not nullify the chametz again at that time, for how can he say "that I have seen and that I have not seen" – after all, he still needs to eat? Just as we do not say this at night during the search, as I wrote in section 434. Therefore, this nullification should be said on Shabbat after the morning meal. And even though no chametz remains in the house, it is still necessary to nullify it in the same manner as one nullifies during the burning of the chametz in other years.

One may not cook this porridge or similar items on this Shabbat, as it is complete chametz and it sticks to the utensils. One would need to wash them with hot water on Shabbat and scrub them thoroughly, which is considered excessive labor on Shabbat and is forbidden since it is not necessary for Shabbat. Therefore, even dry bread in a bowl, which is called "soaked bread," and soaking them in hot water — this is not done on this Shabbat. It is already customary not to cook any dough on this Shabbat. Only on the eve [of Shabbat] do they cook rice or legumes or potatoes, and likewise in the morning. They make the round loaf from matzah flour and store it in new pots that are suitable for Passover and pour it into chametz bowls. However, if one went ahead and cooked, and the food is stuck to the pot and cannot be cleaned — it is necessary to wash it a little to remove the chametz, and this is considered "necessary for Shabbat" since it is forbidden to leave it like that on this day.

After they have eaten the morning meal on Shabbat, they should shake out the tablecloth on which they ate. Technically, they can shake it out inside the house, because the crumbs stick to the feet and are trampled, and they are insignificant and nullified. Nevertheless, it is not proper to do so, and they should shake out the tablecloth in the courtyard in a place that is not clean and where people do not walk. As for the dishes, even though they do not have chametz, it is still improper to leave them as they are. Therefore, one can wipe them with his fingers, as this is not considered a burden, and hide them from sight along with other chametz utensils. If there is leftover bread, one can give it to a non-Jew. If it is in a place that does not have a public domain, and certainly in a place with an eruv, it is permissible to tell him not to eat it here and to take the chametz with him. However, in a place with a public domain, it is forbidden to tell him to leave with the bread, as I wrote in Siman 325. Even without explicitly telling him, it is forbidden to give him a large amount of chametz that he cannot finish eating there. What should one do? Give him a small amount at a time in a manner that appears as if one does not care if he eats it there, and if he takes it out on his own, he does so of his own accord. When there is no non-Jew to give the chametz to, he should nullify it in his heart and cover it with a utensil until the end of the first day of Yom Tov and then burn it.

And know that on this Shabbat, if one forgot to separate challah on the eve of Shabbat, even though we hold that in the Diaspora one may eat and continue eating and then separate [the challah], nevertheless, it is not possible now, as how can one leave chametz? Therefore, the great authorities have written that if one forgot to separate challah, it is forbidden to eat the bread (Magen Avraham in Siman 506). And some say that since there is no remedy for this, one can designate a portion of the challah in one's mind as challah, without a blessing, and call a minor Kohen who has not seen a seminal emission to eat it (Shaarei Teshuvah in the name of Pnei Moshe and Yaavetz, see there). And it is necessary to rely on this, since there is no other remedy. And they have written not to prolong the prayer on this Shabbat, so as not to delay the time of eating (Chayei Adam, small paragraph 9 in the name of Sefer Chassidim).

And when the Temple will be rebuilt, how will the disposal of chametz of terumah be handled on Shabbat that falls on Erev Pesach? In the case of terumah, even the Rif agrees that it is burned on Erev Shabbat, and only leaves over enough for two meals. But how is it burned? Rambam writes in the third chapter, law 4, and this is his language: If he had many loaves of terumah and needed to burn them on Erev Shabbat, he should not mix the pure with the impure and burn them, but rather burn the pure by itself, the impure by itself, and the doubtful by itself... until here are his words. This implies that he holds that specifically on Erev Pesach that falls on Shabbat, and he burns them on the 13th before they become prohibited, each one is burned separately. But on any other Erev Pesach, he can burn the pure and impure together. In the Gemara (14a) it is not so, and this requires further investigation (Kesef Mishneh). Even more difficult is: if so, why did he not explicitly state that on any Erev Pesach, they are burned together? Therefore, it appears to me in my humble opinion that the matter is as follows: although the plain reading of the sugya implies that even on any Erev Pesach they are burned separately, nevertheless, this is not according to everyone. And there is proof, for Rabbi Yochanan says there (15b) that in the seventh hour, since it is forbidden by Torah law, everyone agrees they are burned together, as the prohibition is like impurity, and even the pure ones are considered impure. And further, it is said there that piggul, notar, and impure are burned together according to Beit Hillel, even though piggul and notar are only rabbinical impurities, it is permitted to burn them with Torah-level impurity. According to this, even when burning them in the sixth hour it is a rabbinical prohibition, and it is like a Torah-level prohibition and therefore permissible to burn them together. Therefore, Rambam could not write this explicitly, that on any Erev Pesach they are burned together, because it is not his way to bring a law that is not explicitly in the Gemara. But nevertheless, his opinion leans this way. Therefore, he only wrote this law for Erev Pesach that falls on Shabbat and they are burned on the 13th. (In the introduction to the Haggadah, we elaborated on this, as it depends on the dispute of Rabbi Eliezer, Rabbi Yehoshua, and Rabbi Yosi in the Mishnah there. Analyze and you will find it simple.)

We learned in the Mishnah (Pesachim 49a): One who is going to slaughter his Passover offering, or to circumcise his son, or to eat the engagement meal at his father-in-law's house, and he remembers that he has chametz in his house, if he can return, remove it, and then go back to his mitzvah, he should return and remove it. If not, he should annul it in his heart. To save from bandits, from a river, from thieves, from a fire, or from a collapse, he should annul it in his heart. And to observe an optional rest, he should return immediately. The Tanna divided it into three parts: For a mitzvah, if there is enough time, he should return. For saving from a life-threatening situation, even if there is enough time, he should not return. And for an optional matter, even if there is not enough time, he should return.

According to this, in the case of a mitzvah, if it is the sixth hour and it is impossible to nullify, one must return against his will even though there is no time to avoid violating "Do not see" (Magen Avraham, subsection 12). Only if it is possible to nullify, even though rabbinically he is obligated to destroy it, in the case of a mitzvah, it stands as a Torah obligation (there). Similarly, someone going to save a life, if it is impossible to nullify, and he is certain that he can save even afterward, he should return and destroy it. But if there is doubt, the doubt of saving a life overrides all commandments (there). Certainly, a deceased with no one to bury him overrides everything (there). 

One should not ask: why do we say that someone going for the sake of a mitzvah, if he cannot nullify, he should return immediately? According to the opinion that until nightfall one does not transgress "Do not see," and here there is only a positive commandment of "You shall remove" – what is the superiority of this positive commandment over that positive commandment? One can say that the positive commandment of "You shall remove" is more stringent because every moment one transgresses it (there). Even though circumcision is also transgressed each day, in the continuation of the day there is no difference when he circumcises, and it is only a matter of being zealous in performing mitzvot. Therefore, he can circumcise later until nightfall. (And the Machatzit HaShekel struggled with this in subsection 11, and the matter is clear as I have written.)

And behold, the Tanna enumerates the engagement feast. And earlier in Siman 249, it was explained that it is forbidden to hold an engagement feast on the eve of Shabbat. Refer there, and it is based on the Yerushalmi. Therefore, there is an opinion that this applies when the engagement did not occur on that day, but if the engagement took place that day, the feast is permitted (Magen Avraham there, and see what I wrote here in subsection 9). However, we have already explained there in subsection 8 that if there is no necessity, it is forbidden. But when there is a necessity, such as a groom going to his father-in-law's house and it is impossible to postpone until after Shabbat, it is permitted. And here, it refers to such a scenario, as the Mishnah specifies: "and to eat the engagement feast in his father-in-law’s house," meaning he goes to his father-in-law’s house and then returns to his own home. Specifically, this applies to the groom, but others need to return. (See Magen Avraham subsection 10, who wrote that it does not seem to be the Rambam's opinion. I do not see any indication of this, as it is obvious that it refers to the groom. And I have seen that both the Chayei Adam and the Mekor Chaim wrote like the Magen Avraham. In my opinion, this requires further investigation.)

And what has been explained, that for a matter of personal choice one should return immediately, the Tur wrote that even going to learn Torah from one's teacher is considered a personal matter regarding the removal of chametz. And so it is in the Yerushalmi on this Mishnah: What is considered a personal matter? One who goes to his teacher, or to someone greater than him in wisdom. Here Rabbi taught: Deed is greater than study. This is the language of the Yerushalmi. And it concludes there that a mitzvah that can be done by others – study is greater than deed, but if it cannot be done by others – deed is greater than study, see there. According to this, if he left someone in his place to remove the chametz – he may go and study. And there is no novelty in this ruling, for even in our Gemara it is forbidden to study when the time for the search for chametz arrives, as I wrote in Siman 431. And this is how we hold in Yoreh De'ah Siman 246. (And there is a need to examine the Magen Avraham in subsection 13, who questioned: did they not permit passing through a beit hapras to study Torah? See there. And it is puzzling: what is the relevance of this? There, the Sages permitted their prohibition for the sake of constant Torah study, and what relevance does this have to study at the specific time when the mitzvah arrives? And I found that the Magen HaElef also wondered about this.)

In a case where we obligate him to return, how much chametz must he have in order to be required to return? Up to the quantity of an egg (kebeitza), which is a significant measure. But less than this, he annuls it in his heart and that suffices, for the sages did not trouble him for less than a kebeitza. And less than the quantity of an olive (kezayit), even after the time of its prohibition, when he can no longer annul it – he does not need to return, as he does not transgress the prohibition of "it shall not be seen" (see Magen Avraham, subsection 14).

It is stated in the Gemara (Pesachim 7a) that if one has dough in his house and is preoccupied elsewhere and fears that it might become chametz (leavened), he can nullify it in his heart before it becomes chametz. However, if it has already become chametz, the nullification is only effective before the sixth hour and not afterward, and therefore he is obligated to go and burn it. This is also the ruling of all the poskim (halachic authorities). It seems to me, in my humble opinion, that before it becomes chametz, a full renunciation is required according to what we wrote in Siman 331, as the reason nullification works for chametz is that the chametz is not in his possession, see there. If so, when it has not yet become chametz, how can nullification be effective? Indeed, in the Gemara, it does not mention nullification in the heart; only Rashi explains it this way. Similarly, this is the language of the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch in paragraph 8, and it is also the language of the Rambam in Chapter 3, Law 10. This requires further examination. Perhaps, since it is on the verge of becoming chametz, it is considered like chametz, and the revelation of his intention not to acquire it is effective.

It is taught at the beginning of the chapter "Kol Sha'ah" (Pesachim 21a): Rabbi Yehuda says: There is no disposal of chametz except through burning. And the Sages say: One can also crumble it and throw it to the wind, or cast it into the sea. Rashi and Tosafot ruled according to Rabbi Yehuda, while the Rambam and the Geonim ruled according to the Sages. And all of Israel are accustomed to burning the chametz. The reason of Rashi and Tosafot is because, at the end of Temurah, the Tanna lists chametz on Pesach among those things that are burned according to Rabbi Yehuda, and it is considered a dispute, and then a general ruling is given that the law follows the general ruling. (According to the Rambam, this is not a difficulty, as in two different tractates there is no order for the Mishnah. See Tosafot Yom Tov there. And Tosafot 27b, in the beginning of the discussion "Ein," brought another proof that the law follows Rabbi Yehuda, as Rabbi Yehuda derives it from notar by analogy on 28a. And the Sages refuted him according to their method, but according to their method, it was a valid derivation. And the Rosh there refuted this, see there.)

According to our text, which states "The Sages say: even crumbling...", there is no need for scrutiny. But according to the version of the Rif, the Rosh, and the Tur, which states "The Sages say: crumbling...", it implies specifically crumbling. Therefore, we must scrutinize their view, as they ruled according to the Sages: how is it permissible for us to burn chametz? For at the end of Tractate Temurah (34a) it is taught: All that must be buried should not be burned, because that which is burned has its ashes permitted, and that which is buried has its ashes prohibited. And also, the Rambam, who ruled according to the Sages and ruled that it is permissible to burn chametz, wrote in the third chapter, law 11: How is the destruction of chametz done? One burns it or crumbles it..." – how is it permissible to burn it, for its ashes are prohibited? Therefore, some have written that indeed his intention is to caution against using its ashes (Magen Avraham, subsection 1).

However, in truth, there is no need for this, and this does not apply to chametz (leavened bread). For the Tosafot in Temurah there are meticulous inquiring as to why the ashes of items that are meant to be buried are forbidden, while the ashes of items that are meant to be burned are permitted. They wrote that for items to be burned, since the Torah commanded to burn them, the commandment is fulfilled, and the prohibition ceases. But for items to be buried, the prohibition continues indefinitely, see there. And now, regarding chametz, even with burial, the commandment of "you shall remove" is fulfilled, and therefore its ashes are permitted (and so wrote the Mekor Chaim). Furthermore, Rabbi Yehuda holds at the end of Temurah that if one wishes to be stringent upon himself to burn items that are meant to be buried, he is permitted to do so. And although the Sages disagree with him, nevertheless regarding chametz, they agree with him (and this is the intent of the Rosh in the second chapter, section 3, see there). Additionally, regarding chametz, the permissibility of using the embers and ashes and their prohibition depends on the time of their destruction, as will be explained. And chametz is not included at all in this matter within all other prohibitions.

Indeed, even according to Rashi and Tosafot, who ruled according to Rabbi Yehuda that specifically burning (is required), it was taught (12b): "When? When it is not at the time of its destruction. But at the time of its destruction – its nullification can be done in any manner." And Rashi explained "when it is not at the time of its destruction" – this is the sixth hour and "at the time of its destruction" is from then onwards, and he calls "at the time of its destruction" from the time that chametz is forbidden by Torah law. According to this explanation, one is indeed obligated to burn the chametz, for we burn it in the sixth hour. But Rabbeinu Tam explained the opposite, that "at the time of its destruction" is the sixth hour, and "when it is not at the time of its destruction" is from then onwards, and he calls "at the time of its destruction" the time when people burn the chametz. According to this explanation, even according to Rabbi Yehuda, it is not specifically required to burn it when we are destroying it in the sixth hour. And even according to Rashi, based on what the Rosh wrote there, according to Rashi, it is specifically in the sixth hour that burning is required, but in the fifth hour or earlier – burning is not required. Therefore, even according to Rashi, if we destroy it before the sixth hour, and as is the custom of the world not to wait precisely until the sixth hour, burning is not required. 

However, the Tur rejected this, because Rashi explicitly wrote (27b, starting with "if") that one who sets out on a journey within thirty days – must specifically burn, see there. Therefore, our custom is according to Rashi and Tosafot, and according to Rashi's explanation. And this is also not against the opinion of the Rambam and the Geonim, for they agree that burning is also permissible, but according to them, we could also fulfill the obligation without burning, but by crumbling and scattering to the wind or throwing into the sea. According to this, our custom aligns with the opinion of all the authorities.

And this is the language of our Rabbi, the Rema, in section A: "And the custom is to burn it. And it is good to burn it during the day, similar to leftover sacrificial meat which was burned during the day." So far his language, meaning: Since Rabbi Yehuda learns the law of burning chametz from leftover sacrificial meat, just as the latter is burned, so too chametz is burned, as it is stated in the Gemara (27b), therefore we also learn from leftover sacrificial meat that it must be done during the day, as all sacrificial burnings are done during the day. And he further wrote: "But if one wants to burn it immediately after the search, so that a weasel does not drag it away – he has permission to do so." So far his language, as this is not a requirement. For sacrificial items, all their actions are only during the day, but this does not apply to chametz. And even though it is also proper to fulfill the mitzvah of "destroying" chametz close to the time of "removal," nevertheless, even if one burns it at night and the time for "removal" arrives and he has no chametz – he has fulfilled the mitzvah of removal. Nevertheless, the Mahari”l was particular to burn it specifically during the day, and so do we. And there are those who wrote to burn the chametz with the willows of Sukkot, but we are not able to preserve them until the burning of chametz.

Maimonides wrote in Chapter Three: How is the removal of chametz done? One burns it, crumbles it and scatters it to the wind, or throws it into the sea. If the chametz is hard and the sea will not break it apart quickly, one should crumble it first and then throw it into the sea. So far his words, and similarly wrote Rabbeinu the Beit Yosef in Section 1. But the Tur wrote in the name of the Geonim that all types of chametz need to be crumbled when thrown into the sea, see there. And this also appears explicitly from the Talmud (28a to Rabba, as the halacha follows him over Rav Yosef). The Kesef Mishneh asked: How did Maimonides rule according to Rav Yosef? And the Taz struggled with this, see there. In my humble opinion, it seems that this is not like the usual disputes between Rabba and Rav Yosef in the Talmud, where one says this and the other says that. Here, Rav Yosef said to Rabba: On the contrary, the opposite makes sense…, and Rabba did not respond to him. This implies that Rabba conceded to him. However, the Maggid Mishneh explained that wheat requires crumbling, as the Magen Avraham wrote in subsection 2, that it should be cut into pieces, and bread does not require crumbling. The Beit Yosef explained the opposite. Consequently, according to both, crumbling is required. However, if one throws it into the toilet, crumbling is not necessary. This is what the Magen Avraham wrote there.

There are those who write that it is forbidden to perform work from the time the period for burning chametz begins, which is from the beginning of the sixth hour, until the chametz is burned (Magen Avraham, section 2). And this is specifically in work that is not related to Passover. But if it is related to Passover, it is permitted, because since one is engaged in Passover matters, one will not forget to burn the chametz. (Similar to what the Gemara says in 11: "He himself...", see there.)

If one gives chametz to a non-Jew before the sixth hour, he does not need to destroy it, for he no longer possesses chametz. He can also give it to his Canaanite servant or maidservant. This applies to a small amount of chametz that they can consume immediately. However, a large amount of chametz that would last them through Passover is forbidden, because since he must provide their sustenance, it appears as though he is repaying a debt with items forbidden for benefit (Ba'er Heitev, subsection 3, quoting the responsa of the Bach). If they are hired by him for a year or more and he must provide their sustenance, it is forbidden to give them a large amount of chametz. If he does not provide their sustenance, but rather gives them money and they buy their own food, it is permissible to give them even a large amount, provided he does not deduct the value from their wages. Further details on this will be explained in Siman 450 with the help of Heaven.

And our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in paragraph 2: If one burned [the chametz] before the sixth hour, it is permitted to benefit from its ashes during Passover. However, if one burned it from the sixth hour and later, since it is forbidden to benefit from it, one may not heat an oven or stove with it, nor cook with it. And if one cooked or baked with it, that bread and that cooked dish are forbidden to benefit from. Similarly, its ashes are forbidden to benefit from, since it was burned after it became forbidden to benefit from. Thus far his words. And the flame of chametz is also forbidden to benefit from. For just as we learned in Beitzah (31a) that the flame of consecrated items is not to be benefited from, because one does not separate from it, see there – all the more so chametz, from which one does not separate all year (Chot Yair, subsection 6, and not like the Beit Hillel).

Some say that with bread, the prohibition only applies when the torch is directly opposite it. For then, since the heat of the wood enhances the bread, it is as if the leaven itself baked the bread. But when the torch is not opposite it, although the leaven causes the bread to bake, nevertheless, the oven also contributes to the baking. This is considered a combination of causes and is permitted. However, with cooked food, it is prohibited because the food does not need the oven (Kesef Mishneh). There are those who disagree: they hold that only for something that can be nullified, like orlah which is nullified in two hundred parts, such a combination of causes is permitted. But with chametz, which cannot be nullified, since its prohibition is in any amount, even the smallest amount is significant (Magen Avraham, subsection 5). We have already elaborated on this in Yoreh De'ah, section 142, from paragraph 10 to paragraph 18; see there. It is also explained there regarding deriving benefit by sending it to the Dead Sea, and selling to a non-Jew except for the prohibited value within it; see there.

He further writes in Section 3: Before the time of its prohibition, one can throw it to a place where crows are present. If it is found after the time of its prohibition and the crows did not eat it, even though the place is ownerless, one should not leave it there but must burn it. These are his words. The intention is not that he threw it in the street in an ownerless place, because if so, even if it is found after the time of its prohibition, what of it? It has already been declared ownerless before the time of its prohibition, and there is no greater act of renunciation than this. Rather, the intention is that he threw it in the middle of his courtyard where crows are present, as we say (Pesachim 8a): A courtyard does not need checking because crows are present there, as I wrote in Siman 433. Therefore, when it is found, he is obligated to burn it since it is lying in his domain. And when it says "even though the place is ownerless," it means: that he threw it in his courtyard in a place designated for the crows (Magen Avraham, Section 7). 

One should not ask: How is it permitted to do this? In Siman 438, it is explained that when a mouse drags something in front of us, we are obligated to check after it, because a doubt of eating does not override the certainty of chametz, see there. How then can we permit throwing chametz into one's domain relying on the crows' eating? This is not comparable, for only a mouse, because it drags things into holes and crevices, requires checking, which is not the case with crows (Chayei Adam, Section 10, which also answers the question of the Taz). This all applies before the time of its prohibition, not afterward. It is forbidden to throw it even to dogs that do not belong to him, as we say in the Jerusalem Talmud at the beginning of the chapter "Kol Sha'ah," and these are its words: One should not feed chametz even to dogs. What are we dealing with? If to his own dog—there is a prohibition of benefit. Rather, even to another's dog. This means it is forbidden to feed it to someone's ownerless animal. These are its words. 

(The Rema writes that if one did not find chametz during the checking, he should burn the utensil he used for the checking, so as not to forget the obligation of burning. These are his words. And it has already been explained in Siman 432 that therefore it is customary to place pieces of chametz during the checking so that his blessing will not be in vain, see there, and consequently, he will have something to burn.)

It is stated in the Gemara (6a): One who finds chametz in his house on a festival should overturn a vessel on it. Rashi explained: because it is not fit to be moved or removed. However, he does not transgress the prohibition of "bal yera'eh" (not to be seen), because he nullified it in his heart from yesterday. But in order not to forget and eat it, he must overturn a vessel on it. Up to here is his wording. It is clear from his words that if he had not nullified the chametz from yesterday and thus transgresses "bal yera'eh", overturning a vessel is not sufficient. This is the opinion of the Tur in the name of his brother Rabbeinu Yechiel, who wrote that one can burn it on a festival; since there is some mitzvah in burning it, we say "since kindling is permitted for a need, it is also permitted without a need." Therefore, if he did not nullify it, he should take it out and burn it, so that he does not transgress intentionally, because until now he has only transgressed unintentionally. So too it is written in the Sefer HaMitzvot. Up to here is his wording.

And this is the language of the Sefer Mitzvot Gadol (Positive Commandments 39): "Cover it with a vessel" – This means: it is referring to when it has been nullified, because if it had not been nullified, it could have been burned on Yom Tov... Since it was permitted... it was also permitted not for a necessity, but there should be some necessity for Yom Tov. Up to here is his language, and similarly, the Ra"n of blessed memory wrote, see there. And even though chametz is considered completely muktzeh (set aside), as it is not fit for anything since it is forbidden to benefit from it, nevertheless, due to the prohibition of "it shall not be seen" (bal yera'eh) – we do not worry about rabbinic muktzeh.

However, the Tur wrote: One who finds chametz in his home... and if it is a Yom Tov (holiday) there are those who say that he should cover it with a utensil until the night when he can remove it (and burn it). But on Yom Tov he cannot move it in order to remove it. And it is not only if he nullified it... but even if he did not nullify it, which involves a Torah prohibition, even so he should not remove it, since he cannot destroy it in the proper manner, which according to Rabbi Yehuda is by burning. And the same rule applies to chametz that remains in his home on the fourteenth [of Nisan] when it falls on Shabbat after five hours. But my brother... thus far his words. And he holds that we do not say "since burning was permitted for a necessary purpose, it is also permitted for an unnecessary purpose," except for something that has some necessity for the essence of Yom Tov. But what pertains to a prohibition is considered entirely unnecessary.

It is explained from the words of the Tur that because one cannot burn it on Yom Tov, it is impossible to destroy it. This follows his reasoning that he rules according to Rabbi Yehuda that the destruction of chametz is only by burning, as I wrote in Siman 448. But according to the Rabbis, who say one crumbles it and scatters it to the wind or throws it into the sea, he should indeed destroy it on Yom Tov. And even though according to Rashi, after the sixth hour, one can nullify it in any manner, the Tur holds like the interpretation of Rabbeinu Tam that on the contrary, after the sixth hour, burning is specifically required, as explained there. However, from the words of the Rambam in Chapter 3, Halacha 8, it does not seem this way, as he wrote: “Therefore, if one did not nullify before the sixth hour, and from the sixth hour and onward, found chametz – he has transgressed the prohibition of ‘bal yera’eh’… and must destroy it whenever he finds it. And if he finds it on Yom Tov – he covers it with a vessel until the evening and then destroys it.” Thus are his words. And the Rambam rules there according to the Rabbis, that burning is not specifically required, as I wrote in Siman 448, and nonetheless, he prohibits destroying it on Yom Tov. And he is referring to a case without nullification, as is clear from his words which begin with “if one did not nullify.” And so wrote the Maggid Mishneh, see there. And a reason is needed for why he should not destroy it on Yom Tov.

And I have seen that they wrote the reason is because of muktzeh, that it is forbidden to move it (Taz, section 3, and Magen Avraham, section 2). And even though muktzeh is rabbinic, since this is a case of "sit and do not act" – they prohibited it. And he does not transgress "bal yera'eh" (the prohibition of owning chametz during Passover), since he is compelled by a rabbinic ordinance (Magen Avraham there), or because it was not at the time, meaning that at the time he moves the muktzeh – it is not yet the time for destruction (there). 

And this is very puzzling: While it is true that we find in several matters that the sages upheld their words out of concern that one might come to a Torah prohibition, such as with the shofar and lulav on Shabbat lest one carry them four cubits in the public domain. But to say that due to the prohibition of muktzeh alone, he should be left to transgress "bal yera'eh" – it is astonishing to say so! Also, regarding "at the time," we only find this in cases where a positive commandment overrides a negative commandment, not in the context of muktzeh prohibition.

It seems more reasonable to say that it is because breaking and scattering to the wind can come close to a Torah prohibition. Breaking, since it is not for eating, could be liable due to grinding, and scattering is also a primary category of work, and throwing into the sea also requires breaking for hard chametz, as I have written in section 448. And when one finds chametz – it is presumed to have dried and requires breaking.

And know that dough that became chametz on Yom Tov, even if he nullified it before the sixth hour – it does not help, since it was not included in the nullification, and he transgresses "bal yera'eh." And this is obvious. (Also, it is not similar to the shofar, which is a nullification of a positive commandment, and not "bal yera'eh," which one transgresses every moment.)

They further wrote a reason: that by covering the chametz with a vessel, one does not transgress "Bal Yera'eh" according to the words of the Tosafot (Pesachim 29b). This is because someone who keeps chametz with the intention of destroying it does not transgress "Bal Yera'eh," since the prohibition of "Bal Yera'eh" is considered to be rectifiable by a positive commandment (Magen Avraham there). However, it is impossible to say this, because the Rambam does not hold that "Bal Yera'eh" is rectifiable by a positive commandment, as he requires lashes for one who purchases chametz during Pesach in the first chapter, as written by the great scholars there (Mishneh LaMelech, first chapter, citing several great authorities, see there). But according to what we wrote in Siman 331, Section 9, it is possible to say that even the Rambam holds that it is rectifiable by a positive commandment, see there (see Machatzit HaShekel).

And by a non-Jew, there are those who permit him to remove it from his house, even when the chametz has been nullified, because since it is rabbinically required to destroy it, the positive commandment of "you shall remove" from the Rabbis comes and overrides the rabbinic prohibition of instructing a non-Jew (cited there in the name of the Shlah). However, by removing it from his house, he has not yet fulfilled the rabbinic positive commandment of "you shall remove" (cited there). Nevertheless, to throw it into the river by a non-Jew is permitted, as it is a double rabbinic prohibition in the place of a mitzvah (cited there). But to scatter it to the wind is close to a biblical prohibition (cited there). And it seems to me that even to throw it into the toilet is permitted by a non-Jew. The custom of the world is to destroy chametz found on Yom Tov itself and to throw it into the river or into filthy places. And even a grain of wheat found in a dish – one should take the dish out and throw it into a filthy place. And in Siman 447, it will be explained further with the help of Heaven. (See the Magen Avraham there, what he wrote in the name of the Bach. And he wrote that in a place where there is no custom – it is better to sit and do nothing, see there.)

If one finds chametz in his house during Chol HaMoed, he is immediately obligated to remove and destroy it. He should not keep it even for a moment, even though he has already nullified it. Certainly for those who hold that the destruction of chametz must be by burning, and according to the opinion of Rabbeinu Tam in Siman 440 that this applies after the time of its prohibition, one is obligated to burn it. Some say that one must recite a blessing upon the destruction of chametz (see there, subsection 1). Others are uncertain about this. We have already written in Siman 435, subsection 3 that in cases of doubt concerning blessings, we are lenient, and the blessing recited on the fourteenth [of Nisan] covers all the days of Pesach, see there. During Chol HaMoed, even a small amount of chametz must be removed and destroyed, as well as on Erev Pesach after midday. However, on Yom Tov, if it is less than a k’zayit, it is obvious that one should cover it with a utensil until the evening, as well as on Shabbat Erev Pesach after the fifth hour. Some say that even in the fifth hour, when it is forbidden to eat, it is also forbidden to handle it. This is also implied in the Rambam in the third chapter, where he writes that on Erev Pesach on Shabbat after four hours, one should cover it with a utensil, see there. And it requires investigation: why should this be worse than a carcass that became non-kosher on Shabbat, which is permitted to be handled because it is suitable for dogs? Here too, in the fifth hour, it is allowed for benefit (see there, subsection 3). We must say that it is referring to a case where he has no one to give it to at this time (see there). That is, the Rambam is not specifically referring to this hour, but wrote that after four hours one should cover it with a utensil, see there, and consequently, if in the fifth hour he has someone to give it to, it is also permitted to handle and remove it.

There are those who say that the second day of Yom Tov (holiday) has the same status as Chol HaMoed (the intermediate days of a festival) in this regard. Since the second day of Yom Tov is of Rabbinic origin, we permit moving muktzeh (items that are set aside and cannot be moved) and burning it. Nevertheless, it is not permitted to burn it, and it suffices to cast it into the river (Magen Avraham and Taz, subsection 4). And even though according to Rabbeinu Tam it requires burning, we can rely on the opinion of Rashi that after its time of prohibition, its nullification can be done in any manner (there). All the more so according to the Rambam and the Geonim who hold that burning is never specifically required, as I have written. And according to what I have written, that even by crumbling and winnowing there is a concern of a Torah prohibition – one should cast it into the toilet. However, from the language of the Tur it is explicitly clear that only on Chol HaMoed should one burn it, but on Yom Tov there is no difference between the first day and the second day. This is also implied by the language of the Talmud, and some of the great later authorities have ruled this way in practice (Chayei Adam, subsection 5, and Eliyah Rabbah, subsection 3).

It is stated in the Jerusalem Talmud (Chapter Two, Halacha 2): If the roof of a non-Jew is adjacent to the roof of a Jew, and chametz rolls from the roof of the non-Jew to the roof of the Jew, he should push it away with a stick. If it is Shabbat or a Yom Tov, he should cover it with a vessel. This means that even during Chol HaMoed, he should not take it with his hand, but rather push it away with a stick, because we fear that he might come to eat it. This is not comparable to finding one's own chametz during Chol HaMoed, where one would take it and burn it, because since he is engaged in burning it, he will not come to eat it. But this is not the case with chametz that does not belong to him, which he is not burning; therefore, we decree against it. Even though on Yom Kippur it is permitted to take food with one's hand and we do not decree that he might come to eat it, as I wrote in Siman 612, it can be said that the awe of Yom Kippur is upon him, and we are not concerned that he will forget that today is Yom Kippur. This is not the case with Pesach, where he might forget that today is Pesach. From this we learn that it is forbidden to take chametz of a non-Jew by hand on Pesach, or if one sees chametz in the street, he should not touch it for this reason. On Shabbat and Yom Tov, if it rolls to his roof, he should cover it with a vessel, because it is forbidden to move it even with a stick because of muktzeh. Although this is indirect handling, it has already been explained in Siman 311 that indirect handling for the sake of something forbidden is prohibited. See there.

It seems clear to me that this rule applies only to their roofs, which were not sloped and were used for various purposes. However, with our roofs – we do not care, and it does not concern us at all. Only in the case of a courtyard adjacent to the courtyard of a non-Jew, or a house adjacent to the house of a non-Jew, and chametz (leavened bread) rolled from one to the other – one should act as previously explained.

If one finds bread in his house during Passover and does not know if it is matzah or chametz, such as chametz wafers that resemble matzah, it is permitted even to eat it. This is because we follow the principle of "going after the majority." In other words, typically, people use food containers by taking the top items first to prevent spoilage. All the more so, it is assumed that the house was checked for chametz on the fourteenth of Nisan, and this piece is the last one and is matzah. This matter is considered a certainty. Even if it is found in a hidden place, it is permitted because it is assumed the house was checked properly (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 6). 

However, if the bread is very moldy, to the extent that it could not have become so moldy within the days of Passover, it is certainly chametz. If Passover has already passed, and it is possible that the bread became moldy from the beginning of Passover until now, and in his household they customarily bake fresh bread every day during Passover, we lean towards leniency even if it is very moldy. We assume that fresh bread was baked every day and placed on top, hence it became very moldy. It is not surprising that we rely on this leniency even in the case of a severe prohibition like chametz, because this matter is considered a certainty, as every Jewish person checks their chametz before Passover. It is obvious that this does not refer to finding the bread on the ground or in some open place, as this would certainly be forbidden. Rather, it refers to finding it in a container where food is stored. In our community, this law does not apply because it is easy to distinguish between chametz and matzah, and we have never heard of anyone doubting whether a piece of bread is chametz or matzah.

It is a clear law that although all prohibitions are nullified in sixty, nevertheless, chametz (leavened bread) on Passover is prohibited in any amount, whether it is mixed with its own kind or with a different kind. There are three reasons for this: The Rambam (Maimonides) in the fifteenth chapter of Ma'achalot Asurot explained the reason: because chametz is considered something that has a permissible alternative, it is not nullified even in a thousand, since this chametz will be permitted after Passover when it is in its mixture. And although anything that has a permissible alternative is where the prohibition itself will become permitted, and here the chametz when it is present is forbidden as a penalty because he transgressed "you shall not see" (the prohibition of owning chametz on Passover) as will be explained, and indeed there are those who disputed him for this reason (the Ran as the Kesef Mishneh wrote in the first chapter), nevertheless the Rambam holds that this also is called "something that has a permissible alternative." And although anything that has a permissible alternative that is not nullified is only with its own kind and not with a different kind, as I wrote in Yoreh De'ah, chapter 102, the Rambam wrote there that with chametz they were stringent even with a different kind. See there.

The Rosh in the chapter "Kol Sha'ah" (Siman 5) wrote the reason for the stringency regarding chametz: Because the Torah was stricter with chametz more than with all other prohibitions that incur karet, they were stringent with its nullification even in a minute amount, see there. And this reason is not sufficient, for fat and blood also incur karet, yet they are nullified in sixty. It must be said that his intention also includes the prohibition of "Bal Yera'eh" (Chametz shall not be seen), which does not exist with other prohibitions. And in the fifth chapter of Avodah Zarah (Siman 29) he wrote the reason: because one does not separate from it the entire year, see there. It is perplexing that the Rosh would contradict himself. Therefore, it seems that both reasons are necessary: the main reason is because it incurs karet, and even though fat and blood also incur karet, one separates from them, but from chametz one does not separate. (Now, there is no need for the reason of "Bal Yera'eh" that we mentioned. And this is also explicitly stated in Rashi 29b, s.v. "Shelo B'mino," and this is his language: Rav decreed on chametz in its time, even if not in its kind, because it incurs karet. And even though he did not decree on fat and blood, there one separates from it. But... until here is his language. Thus, it is clearly as the Rosh said in both places.)

It appears to me that there is a practical difference in the law between the reason given by Rambam and the reason given by the Rosh. According to Rambam, even chametz nokshah (leavening that is not fully leavened) that becomes mixed in during Pesach is not nullified by sixty times its volume, because it has a permissible use after Pesach. Similarly, if chametz becomes mixed with matzah before Pesach in a way that it does not have sixty times its volume, and there is also not an olive-sized portion within the time it takes to eat a peras (a specific measure of time), and this mixture then becomes mixed during Pesach, it is also not nullified by sixty times its volume for the same reason. However, according to the Rosh, since the reason is because of the penalty of karet (spiritual excision), nokshah should be nullified by sixty times its volume, and so should this mixture, since there is no penalty of karet. Most of the poskim (decisors of Jewish law) mention only the reason of the Rosh, because Rashi also holds this way as I have written, and it will be further explained with divine assistance. (See Taz, subparagraph 1, who only brings the words of the Rosh from the end of Avodah Zarah, and according to this, even chametz nokshah and mixtures are treated this way, as is evident, and nothing is mentioned about the words of the Rosh in Pesachim, which is the main reason as explained by Rashi. Analyze and you will find it easy.)

There is another practical difference between the reasons: according to the Rambam's reasoning, the prohibition is due to it being something that will eventually become permitted. If it gets mixed into a dish and the dish spoils before Passover ends, it is permitted, as explained in Yoreh De'ah, siman 102, that something which will become permitted does not apply when the food spoils before it becomes permitted. See there. However, according to the Rosh's reasoning, it is prohibited in all cases. Thus, each of the reasons presents its own leniencies and stringencies. Most of the poskim have accepted the Rosh's reasoning, as I have written.

And know that according to the opinions of the Raavad, the Ramban, and the Rashba of blessed memory, the prohibition of chametz on Passover, even in the smallest amount, applies only to eating and not to deriving benefit (see the Rashba's responsa, Siman 53 and Siman 1377). However, these opinions were not accepted by the poskim (decisors of Jewish law). For according to Rashi, Tosafot, the Rif, and the Rambam, chametz is also forbidden to derive benefit from, even in the smallest amount, as written by the Rosh and the Ran (in the fifth chapter of Avodah Zarah). They also brought that the opinion of the Sheiltot and Rabbeinu Tam is that chametz on Passover is nullified in sixty (parts), but this was rejected as halacha. And even Rabbeinu Tam himself did not rely on his own opinion to rule accordingly. The text in our version of the Sheiltot reads "in the smallest amount." The Mordechai writes in the chapter "Kol Sha'ah" that in any situation where there is another reason to permit, although we generally prohibit even the smallest amount, in such a case we rely on their words to permit with sixty (parts) (this is brought by the Rema in Darkei Moshe, note 1, see there).

The Mordechai also wrote at the end of the third chapter of Avodah Zarah, and the Ran there (chapter five), that with all prohibitions of benefit that their mixture is forbidden in any amount – the value of the forbidden portion must be destroyed, and the rest is permitted for benefit. And so it is written in the name of the Rashbam (Beit Yosef in the name of Hagahot Maimoniot). However, the conclusion of the Mordechai in the chapter "Kol Sha'ah" is that this does not help. And so wrote the Terumat HaDeshen (Siman 164) that if a grain of wheat is found inside a chicken – everything must be burned. And this is the wording of our Rabbi the Rema in Section 1: One must burn everything. It is not sufficient to redeem the value of the chametz and sell the rest. However, utensils that were cooked with it – are permitted after Passover and do not require breaking or purging. This is his wording. And it is permitted initially to keep them until after Passover, as I wrote in Siman 552 (Magen Avraham Section 1. And the AriZal wrote: Whoever is careful with even a tiny amount of chametz on Passover – is assured not to sin all year.) And since it is forbidden to destroy the value of the forbidden portion, it follows that it is forbidden to sell it to a non-Jew except for the value of the chametz within it. And the reasoning is understandable, since the main reason for the stringency is to distance from the prohibition of karet (spiritual excision), which is not separated from it all year, if you give him these leniencies – the distancing is nullified, obviously. And if a chametz utensil is mixed with Passover utensils – it is not nullified, as it is something that will become permitted (Beit Yosef). And all are left until after Passover. And it is possible that if it is not used that day, according to the opinion that imparts a bad taste, it is permitted as will be explained. Therefore, regarding utensils, it seems one can rely on the principle of one in two being nullified as dry in dry (Pri Chadash elaborates to disagree that it is permitted to sell to a non-Jew except for the value of the prohibition within it. This is against all the later authorities. And the Chok Yaakov Section 2 also agrees in a great loss to destroy the value of the chametz, and the rest is permitted for benefit but not for eating. The Eliyah Rabbah Section 2 disagrees with him. And the Machatzit HaShekel Section 2 wrote that regarding hard chametz or fruit juice with water – there is room to be lenient, see there. And so should be ruled.)

They were not more stringent with chametz than with other prohibitions except in the quantity needed for nullification, for while other prohibitions are nullified in sixty, chametz forbids even in a tiny amount. But regarding the quality of the prohibition, they were not more stringent. For example, in other mixtures where sixty is not needed but only a peel or removal of the place, the same applies to chametz. And just as with other prohibitions, when hot touches hot without liquid, such as when hot non-kosher meat touches hot kosher meat, it requires peeling or removal of the place according to the laws explained in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 105. This applies when there is nothing that causes spreading, such as lean meat. However, with fatty meat, even if the permitted part is fatty and the prohibited part is lean, the prohibition spreads because the prohibition absorbs from the permitted part and spreads throughout it. The same applies to chametz.

Therefore, a hot matzah wafer that touches a hot leavened wafer requires [removal of] a peel. And if one did not peel it off and cooked it as is, it appears that despite the fact that in all other prohibitions it is permitted, as I wrote there, in the case of leaven it is forbidden. The reason in all other prohibitions it is permitted is because there is nothing that does not have sixty times [the volume] against the peel, as explained there. This is not applicable to leaven, whose prohibition applies even to the smallest amount (as also written by the Or Zarua). There is someone who wrote that it is permitted for benefit (Chapter 10, subsection 9), but I do not understand why.

However, when there is fat that spreads, such as a chametz pastry that contains fat, or even if the matzah is a pastry or smeared with oil or fat, it is completely forbidden, because the fatty matzah spreads and absorbs the chametz, and it permeates everything. And even though with other prohibitions we require, as stated in Yoreh De'ah 105, that the prohibition itself can permeate, but a lean prohibition absorbed from fat that is not prohibited in itself does not permeate, since the prohibited item can only prohibit in a place where the prohibition itself can go, and here the chametz cannot permeate. Nevertheless, with chametz, which is prohibited in any amount, even in this case it is forbidden, because in any case it permeates in any amount (so it appears to me according to the opinion of the Magen Avraham, subsection 2, and see Chayei Adam, subsection 8). 

However, this is when the matzah touched the fatty chametz. But a piece that is half matzah and half chametz, like a double matzah which is considered chametz, and it is entirely smeared with oil, and another matzah touched this matzah in a place where it was not doubled – it is permitted. We do not say that the fat permeates from the doubled area to the non-doubled area, making it as if it touched chametz, that is, the doubled area, since prohibition does not transfer from piece to piece without liquid. And even though we said that even the permissible can permeate the prohibited, and if so, the prohibited should also permeate the permissible even without liquid, making the permissible like the prohibited and prohibiting the second matzah, nevertheless it is not so. For only when the permissible touches the actual prohibition do we not require liquid, but when the permissible touches the permissible, and that permissible touches the prohibition – we do not prohibit without liquid. However, the entire doubled matzah is forbidden when it is fatty, for this is the touching of permissible with prohibition. (So it seems to my humble opinion. And it is possible that according to the one who prohibits two small amounts – in this case it is also prohibited, and it requires further study. From the words of the Magen Avraham there, it seems his intention is to permit in this case. But from his conclusion, like in salting – it seems his intention is to prohibit that piece. His intentions are unclear. Study and you will find clarity.)

Chametz is only prohibited in minute quantities during Passover itself, but not on the eve of Passover from midday onward: since there is no [punishment of] karet (spiritual excision), it is nullified in sixty [parts]. All the more so if it became mixed before Passover, it is nullified in sixty. This is the consensus of all the halachic authorities. Therefore, if a grain of wheat is found in a cooked chicken on the eve of Passover – it is permitted, as it is nullified in sixty. This is when the grain has been removed from it. But if the grain is left inside it and it is reheated on Passover – it reintroduces its flavor into it, and then it is prohibited in any amount. It cannot be said that it was already nullified, for that would be the case if it was reheated without the grain. But reheating with the grain – this is a new absorption. Even according to the opinion that does not hold by "reawakening" (chazarah v'ni'ur), as will be explained – it is prohibited, for this is not a reawakening from before, as I have written.

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote in section 3 regarding this law, and this is his language: "However, with the heating of a secondary vessel (kli sheni) – there is no concern. Yet, some are stringent with a secondary vessel on Passover. It is good to be stringent if the hand recoils (from the heat), for otherwise, it is not considered a secondary vessel." Until here is his language. And it seems clear that his opinion leans towards the ruling that it is not prohibited in a secondary vessel, for since we are not stringent with chametz except in cases where other prohibitions are nullified in sixty – chametz is prohibited in any amount. But a secondary vessel, which does not prohibit with other prohibitions, consequently also does not prohibit with chametz. However, he wrote that it is good to be stringent because according to the Rashba, a secondary vessel also prohibits with other prohibitions when the hand recoils from it. And though we do not hold this way, as I wrote in Yoreh De'ah there, nonetheless, regarding chametz, it is good to be stringent. And it seems to me that also with pouring (irui), which with other prohibitions it only prohibits a thin layer (kedei kelipah) – so too with chametz. However, since he wrote that it is good to be stringent with a secondary vessel, all the more so with pouring. Nevertheless, from the essence of the law, it is permitted, and in cases of great loss and the honor of Yom Tov, perhaps one can rely on this. And this requires further consideration.
