However, there is cause to wonder about our master, the Rema, for in Siman 452 he unequivocally writes to prohibit in a kli sheni (secondary vessel), and in Siman 467 he prohibits even in cold, and he does not mention at all that there are two opinions on this matter. However, it can be said that he relied on our master, the Beit Yosef there, who brings two opinions regarding cold, see there. Yet, how distant is the comparison from cold to a kli sheni! All the commentators have labored over his words, as well as the words of the earlier authorities where there are contradictions in their statements on this matter (see Magen Avraham, subsection 9, and Chayei Adam and Eliyah Rabbah, subsection 15). There are those who say that here he was lenient because it concerns "chozer v'ne'or" (reactivated leavening) (Eliyah Rabbah there). But this is not clear: for when it is heated while the wheat is still inside it during Pesach – it is not called "chozer v'ne'or", as I have written. Now, from Siman 452, it can be explained: for there he does not speak about the prohibition of a minuscule amount, but rather regarding a vessel that was used for chametz, and it is a kli sheni as I wrote there in subsection 1. If so, the entire vessel is absorbed with chametz, and it is not comparable to the prohibition of a minuscule amount. But from Siman 467 it is difficult, for there in subsection 12 he also speaks about the prohibition of a minuscule amount, see there.

It seems that specifically here, with a grain of wheat in a roasted chicken without sauce, the opinion leans towards not prohibiting it in a second vessel. For there are those who say that with roasting, it never prohibits more than the amount that needs to be removed. And there are those who prohibit it entirely, on the grounds that during roasting the spit is turned on all sides, but otherwise – it does not prohibit entirely, as Rabbeinu the Beit Yosef wrote in (section) [siman] 467, section 15, see there. And there it deals with lean meat, for with fatty meat it is entirely forbidden as will be explained there. However, in any case, roasting is much lenient compared to cooking in water. And here, even though it deals with a cooked chicken, nevertheless it deals with when it was heated on Pesach without water, and therefore it is lenient in a second vessel, but it is good to be stringent. This is not the case in siman 467 which deals with water, and therefore it prohibits in section 12 from scalding in a second vessel, even with cold. And it appears that with cold, it only prohibits if it remains there for a long time, like two or three hours, but not for a short period. However, in a second vessel when it is yad soledet bo (the temperature at which the hand recoils) – it is prohibited immediately, which is not the case with roasting in a second vessel. (And this is the intent of the Magen Avraham in subsection 9.)

Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 4: If chametz was mixed before Pesach and was nullified in a ratio of sixty, it does not reawaken during Pesach to prohibit even in the smallest amount. However, there are those who disagree. This is his language. This is similar to a grain found in a chicken on the eve of Pesach, which was removed, and the chicken was cooked on Pesach – the prohibition does not reawaken. Likewise, any type of chametz that was nullified before Pesach, if the chametz is not recognizable by itself during Pesach but is completely mixed, even dry with dry, for example, crumbs of chametz mixed with many crumbs of matzah – it does not reawaken. This is the ruling of the Rosh and the Tur and other poskim. They bring proof from what is taught in Kilayim (Chapter 9): camel wool and sheep wool that were spun together, if the majority is from camels – it is nullified. And it is permitted to later combine it with linen, as we do not say the prohibition reawakens. In my humble opinion, it seems even this proof is unnecessary. For it is understandable when something additional is added after nullification which is prohibited with the mixture, like after the nullification, the camel wool is joined with linen, which together with the sheep wool is prohibited – it makes sense to require the reasoning that it does not reawaken. But here, nothing additional is added and it was already nullified. However, one could argue that the arrival of Pesach is considered an addition of prohibition, meaning an additional prohibition, albeit a minimal one, is added to the previous nullification of sixty.

And there are those who disagree, bringing proof from Bekhorot (22a), that blood which was nullified in brine, if it subsequently comes into a pot of water – the water that was nullified concerning impurity reawakens. And the same applies to prohibitions, as Tosafot writes there. Similarly, it is explicitly stated in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 99, that a prohibition which was nullified, having sixty [times its volume against it], and then additional from the original prohibition was added – it reawakens, whether it is of the same type or a different type. And there is no difference between liquid and dry, and whether the prohibition was known in the interim or not, see there. In my humble opinion, I do not understand the comparison. For there, additional prohibition was added, but here, nothing additional was added. And if you say that the arrival of time is considered an addition as I have written, nevertheless, in the end, it was already nullified. This is very similar to what is written in Yoreh De'ah there: an olive-sized portion of forbidden fat that fell into water and was nullified in sixty, and afterward, some of the water fell into a pot of meat – it is permitted, even though there is not sixty times the amount of meat against the forbidden fat, since it was already nullified in the water, see there. And here too: even if we say that the arrival of time is considered an addition of prohibition, there the meat is certainly prohibited, and nevertheless, since it was already nullified – it is nullified. And here too, it is the same. And we have explicitly said that we do not treat chametz more stringently than other prohibitions except in the amount required for nullification, and not in other matters (as they are prohibited in Mordechai, second chapter). And see in section 17.

And those who prohibit it provided another reason: that before Passover, nullification (bitul) is not applicable at all, since the time of prohibition has not yet arrived. This is not comparable to other prohibitions where the prohibition existed previously and then was nullified, which is not the case here: there was no prohibition to say that it could be nullified (Sham in the name of Raaviah). And I do not understand this reasoning. For when the eve of Passover arrives at the sixth hour, the time of prohibition has arrived and it becomes nullified in sixty as I have written, unless it is believed according to this opinion that even on the eve of Passover it is prohibited in any amount. But we do not hold this way. Furthermore, on the contrary, when the time of prohibition has not yet arrived, it is even better. For this reason, we hold in Yoreh De'ah there that milk is nullified in water, and the meat does not prohibit it, because it was nullified while it was not yet a prohibition. And in Mordechai, it is brought that Rabbeinu Tam, the Ri, and Sefer HaTerumah ruled that it does not reawaken, and so wrote Rav Paltai Gaon. Only Raaviah disagreed with them, and he is a single opinion against many. Additionally, if so, for what purpose did the poskim say that before Passover and on the eve of Passover it is nullified in sixty, since you say that when Passover arrives, it will be prohibited? And you would have to say it is regarding eating them before nightfall, meaning from the sixth hour until night. And this is merely a puzzling statement, and see in section 17. Moreover, according to this opinion, how would we ever be able to cook from the matzah on Passover? Certainly, there are some sprouted grains that were nullified, and now if we cook on Passover, it will reawaken? Rather, certainly the main ruling is according to the first opinion, that it does not reawaken. And this is also clarified from the words of Rabbeinu Beit Yosef, who wrote the first opinion as the standard, and the second one as "some disagree." (However, the practice is according to the ruling of the Rema, as will be explained. And the main proof of Raaviah from Nedarim 68a about immersing an impure vessel to purify it... was refuted by the Gra in subsection 21, and he wondered that on the contrary, according to the conclusion, it is the opposite, see there. And also our proof from Yoreh De'ah, section 99, from milk is a refutation to him. Study and you will find an easy solution.)

And our master, the Rema, wrote that we follow the first opinion in all mixtures that are liquid with liquid. However, in the case of a dry item that got mixed, or where there is concern for a mixture, such as bread that fell into wine, even if it was removed from there, it is prohibited on Passover, because we are concerned that perhaps crumbs remained, which impart flavor on Passover. These are his words. From his words, it is proven that even those who believe in "Chozar Veneir" (the reawakening of the flavor) only apply this to a substance of tangible matter, like a mixture of beer in wine. But in the absorption of the flavor of chametz, even this opinion agrees that it does not reawaken. According to this, they hold that what we said that it was nullified before Passover refers to the absorption of flavor. Additionally, based on this, what we wrote about the warmth of the chicken after the wheat was removed from it, according to the first opinion it is permitted, is not so, because even in mere flavor, this opinion agrees that it does not reawaken (and so wrote the Magen Avraham, subsection 7). And there are those who permit bread that fell into wine by means of filtration (Magen Avraham, subsection 13, in the name of the Shach). Specifically, when it was filtered before Passover, but on Passover, it should not be filtered (there). Also, when the liquid is thick, filtration does not help (there). And there are those who say that filtration does not help, because there might be very fine particles that pass through the sieve holes (Taz, subsection 6). This is not the main opinion, for why should we be stringent on remote concerns when, according to the fundamental law, it is entirely permitted even according to concerns? For it has already been clarified that the main law follows the first opinion (and also the Chayei Adam, subsection 17, rejected his words, see there). (And what the Magen Avraham wrote at the end of subsection 13 in the name of the Rashba, that if after removing the bread, one took wine from this barrel and mixed it with other wine, all of it is prohibited, see there – this is certainly an excessive stringency, for we hold the primary opinion as the first opinion. And the Rashba holds that it reawakens, as he wrote there in the name of the Shach. And also the Noda BiYehuda Kama, Orach Chaim, Siman 24, testified that in all of Poland and Ashkenaz, the halacha is ruled that it does not reawaken. And also the Gra in his response wrote that the primary law is that it does not reawaken even dry with dry, see there.)

Regarding the matter of "two somethings," meaning a pot that has been forbidden by "something" (a minute amount), and a "something" from that pot fell into another pot—there are those who permit it (Taz in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 92, and later in Siman 467, Seif Katan 17). However, many disagree with this (Magen Avraham in Siman 467, Seif Katan 13, and Pri Chadash in Siman 447, Seif Katan 5, and the Mekor Chaim in Siman 467, Seif Katan 17). Even those who permit do not allow it in the case of a liquid that was forbidden by "something" and spilled into another liquid, for in such a case it is clear that the second item also contains "something." But in the case of a solid item, such as a piece of meat that absorbed chametz and was forbidden by "something," and a "something" from this piece fell into another pot, the forbidden "something" does not have the power to forbid others by "something." Those who disagree prohibit even in this manner and have written that all the authorities follow this practice. (And the Eliyah Rabbah in this Siman, Seif Katan 1, agrees with the Taz that a piece that was forbidden by "something" and fell into another dish where there is a majority against it—he removes the piece from the dish, and the dish is kosher. Refer there.)

Regarding the issue of aroma (reicha) and whether it causes a prohibition with chametz, our teacher the Rema wrote as follows: "Regarding the issue of aroma in a dish that contains chametz with other dishes, there are those who are lenient in a case where it would be permitted with other prohibitions. And there are those who are stringent, as even a minute amount (mashehu) is present. This only applies in a situation where aroma is relevant, but with other prohibitions, it is not significant, as I have written in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 108." This is his language, meaning: For example, in a small oven that does not hold twelve esronim and is sealed, and both the chametz and the matzah are uncovered inside the oven, in this case, we permit it post facto with other prohibitions as I wrote there – in this case, there are those who are stringent with chametz. But in a large oven, even when the dishes are uncovered, or in a small oven and one of the dishes is covered – there is no concern even with chametz (Taz, subsection 3). And regarding bread, the poskim wrote that aroma is not relevant at all. Therefore, if matzah and chametz were baked in the same oven, even if the oven is small and sealed – it does not cause a prohibition (ibid.). And it seems to me that if they were baked on the same rack – it is prohibited for another reason, as the rack absorbs from the chametz bread, and the matzah absorbs from the rack. And although with other prohibitions we do not worry about this, nevertheless there is at least a minute amount (mashehu). Similarly, the steam rising from the chametz to the matzah is at least a minute amount and causes a prohibition. See Yoreh De'ah, end of Siman 92, where it is explained that with other prohibitions, there is no concern for this.

And know that our master, the Rema, in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 108, ruled that in a case of loss, one may rely on those who are lenient regarding the smell of chametz, see there. Meaning: even in a small and uncovered oven. And there is someone who says specifically when it is slightly open where the smoke escapes, but if it is completely closed – it is explained there that even in other prohibitions one should not be lenient except in a case of loss. Therefore, with chametz even in a case of loss – it is forbidden (Magen Avraham, Siman Katan 4). However, this is regarding roasting directly in the oven, without a vessel. But in cooking, even if the pot is uncovered – it is allowed, except in the case of the Shabbat dish where we see clearly that it has a smell (there) because of the wrapping. And there are those who are lenient in all this (Pri Chadash and Chayei Adam, Siman Katan 10). And an incident occurred where they sealed the oven on Passover with the cover they use all year before chametz, and they permitted the cooked dishes (there). And since the whole main doubt regarding the smell is whether it is at least something or not, it seems to my humble opinion a clear proof from Shabbat (62b) that the smell is not even something, and it is as if it is not there. (As it says there: but if it has no fragrance, she is liable for the vessel. Meaning: one who carries food less than the required amount..., since it has no fragrance – it is considered less than the required amount because of the smell, as Rashi explains in the commentary beginning with "since it has no fragrance". And Rav Ashi refutes: here it is different, as there is no substance at all, since the smell has no substance, see there in Rashi. Hence, it is nothing. However, with something pungent, one should prohibit, when the matzah is pungent, as Chayei Adam wrote there. And Pri Chadash is lenient even in this. And this is an excessive leniency, as something pungent certainly absorbs. And if the prohibition is something pungent – it is permitted, as Chayei Adam wrote, see there. And with chametz, there is something pungent like in arset, as Magen Avraham wrote there. Be precise and you will find leniency.)

Regarding the matter of "noten ta'am lifgam" (imparting a detrimental taste), there are also differing opinions. Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 10 that "noten ta'am lifgam" is permitted even on Passover. Our teacher, the Rema, wrote that there are those who are stringent, and this is the custom in these countries. In places where the custom is to be stringent, even "noten ta'am lifgam" and even a tiny amount is forbidden. This is his language. If there is also an addition of smell, it is permitted. However, in places where there is no custom, one who is lenient with "noten ta'am lifgam" has not lost out (Magen Avraham, section 41), and even less than sixty is permitted (Chayei Adam, section 45), as this is the fundamental law. According to this, cooking on Passover with a chametz pot that has not been used for more than a day is permitted, just as with other prohibitions. Nevertheless, one should only rule this way for a poor person and not for a wealthy person. And with a pot that has not been used for twelve months, it is permitted for everyone, as its taste and smell have already deteriorated. On the eve of Passover after midday, it is permitted everywhere. Similarly, if the chametz has been completely spoiled to the point that it is like dust, it is obvious that it is nothing even on Passover itself (Chayei Adam there). Regarding hardened chametz, some say it is nullified in sixty (Magen Avraham, section 5). See also in section 462.

And similarly, with a mixture of dry with dry, there is a dispute among the authorities. The Rif, of blessed memory, at the end of Avodah Zarah rules that it is prohibited in any amount, just like liquid with liquid. For although with other prohibitions, it is nullified by a majority when it is not a piece that is significant or an item counted individually – this applies to prohibitions that impart flavor, not to prohibitions in any amount. Therefore, even in a ratio of one to a thousand, it is not nullified. However, the opinion of Rashi, the Rosh, and the Tur is that it is nullified by a majority like other prohibitions. For only with liquid with liquid, where other prohibitions are forbidden by imparting flavor, is chametz forbidden in any amount. But regarding nullification by a majority, there is no difference. And Rashi, of blessed memory, required one to throw one piece into the river. The Rosh disagrees with this, as the Tur writes. And if it is a whole loaf – it is certainly not nullified even with other prohibitions, as I have written. And the consensus of the major authorities in practice follows the opinion of the Rif (Chapter 10, subsection 44). And on the eve of Passover until nightfall – according to all opinions, it is nullified by a majority, and it is permitted to eat them until nightfall (Magen Avraham, subsection 40). And if one of them fell into the river – it is permitted on the eve of Passover even if it is a whole loaf (Machatzit HaShekel), as I have written in Yoreh De'ah, section 110.

It has already been explained in paragraph 13 that we prohibit even in a second vessel if the hand recoils from it, particularly with a liquid like water, and all the more so with pouring from a first vessel. But with pouring from a second vessel, there is no need to be stringent at all. And all the more so, there is no need to be stringent with a third vessel (as per Magen Avraham, paragraph 9). However, if hot meat that absorbed chametz was placed on it, one should be stringent, as I wrote in Yoreh De'ah, section 94, that a solid item is always considered like a first vessel because it retains a lot of heat (there). And although there, some are lenient, nevertheless, with chametz it is certainly forbidden. (And what Magen Avraham wrote in section 318 that there are things that cook in a second vessel—I do not know if there is such a case with chametz. Similarly, what he wrote there regarding meat with cracks being forbidden even when cold, as I wrote in Yoreh De'ah, end of section 91—I also do not know if this applies to chametz. Examine and you will find leniency.)

Rabbeinu the Beit Yosef wrote in Section 5: Dry meat, cheese, and fish that were salted before Passover, even if caution was not taken with them – it is permissible to eat them on Passover. However, salted fish that are soaked in water on Passover in a chametz vessel – one should be stringent and avoid them, because they absorb from the vessel's emissions on Passover, and chametz on Passover is prohibited even in the smallest amount. These are his words. 

Explanation of the matter: Regarding being salted before Passover and not taking care to select salt free of chametz, there is no concern at all, not even a stringency. Not only according to those who hold in Section 14 that if it was nullified before Passover, it does not reawaken. This opinion is fundamental in law, as I wrote there. But even according to those who hold that it reawakens – this is only when we know that there were chametz crumbs. However, we do not know this, and we do not assume the presence of prohibition. (This law was brought by the Tur in the name of Rashi, based on the reasoning that it was nullified before Passover, and he holds that it does not reawaken, for this is what he stands on, see there. However, we explained that even according to the opinion that it reawakens – it is permissible. Otherwise, since the Beit Yosef in Section 4 also brought this opinion that it reawakens, he should have explained that according to this opinion it is forbidden. Therefore, certainly, as I wrote. Investigate and you will find it easy.) (And this is the intention of the Taz in Subsection 7.)

And this is what is written: "However, salted fish soaked in water on Passover in a chametz vessel – one should be stringent…”, which clearly implies that according to the letter of the law it is permitted, but one should be stringent. And indeed, this is the truth, for even though the vessel is chametz, nevertheless, it is not a ben yomo (used within 24 hours), for generally, vessels are not ben yomo, and certainly if we know that it is not ben yomo. And our master the Beit Yosef ruled in Section 10 that a taste that has become foul is permitted, as I wrote in Section 21. However, nevertheless, one should be stringent, for perhaps salted fish is considered like a pungent item, which is forbidden even if it is not ben yomo. Or perhaps since the water nullifies the strength of the brine, it is of no consequence. Therefore, if they are soaked during Passover itself, one should be stringent. But if they were soaked before Passover – there is no need to be stringent at all. For what should we be concerned about? If it is because of the pungency of the brine – the water nullifies the strength of the brine. And if it is because it was soaked for 24 hours and is considered pickled, and pickled is like cooked, still, it is not ben yomo? Additionally, before its time, it is permitted, and the rule of pickled being like cooked does not apply (Magen Avraham Section 16). And similarly, if they are soaked on Passover but not in a chametz vessel – one should also not be stringent out of concern that there might be chametz crumbs, as I wrote in the previous section.

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote about this: "There are those who disagree and are stringent. And in these countries, the custom is to be stringent from the outset, not to eat cheeses, fish, and dry meat. But if the meat was washed three times before Passover, they customarily eat it. In regard to sausages, washing does not help, therefore one should not soak the dry meat in water. But after the fact, one should not be stringent with these. However, in the case of fat that has been rendered in a chametz utensil, it is forbidden by law if they were not careful during its preparation to avoid chametz, and it was not rendered in a chametz utensil that had not been used within the past 24 hours. Similarly, anything cooked in a chametz utensil, such as cooked wine or preserves, is forbidden on Passover. But on the last day of the holiday, one may be lenient in this regard. The same applies if a small amount of these things got mixed into the food – one should not be stringent to forbid the mixture. Thus far his words, and they require explanation."

And this is its explanation: It disagrees with the two rulings of our teacher, the Beit Yosef. Regarding the first ruling, that items salted before Pesach, where care was not taken to remove the salt, are permitted, our teacher the Rema ruled that one should be stringent due to the concern that according to the opinion which holds that in a dry item, chametz reawakens. Therefore, there may have been chametz crumbs in the salt, which reawaken on Pesach. Hence, the custom is to be stringent and not consume anything that was salted before Pesach if care was not taken to remove the salt from chametz crumbs. However, if it was rinsed three times before Pesach, the concern is alleviated. The three times are for beautification purposes only, to rinse very well. It is permitted to rinse even in a chametz utensil, as cold does not cause absorption. However, initially, the custom is to rinse in a non-chametz utensil (Taz, subsection 9). Some say further that this applies specifically to meat, which is not usually eaten without rinsing, and similarly to dry fish. But cheese and fish, even if one wants to rinse them, are forbidden, lest one eats them without rinsing. Therefore, the custom is not to eat any salted items (Magen Avraham, subsection 18 and Bach). Consequently, pickled lemons not designated for Pesach are not eaten without removing the salt (ibid.). As for stuffed items, rinsing does not help, since they are stuffed with very thin pieces, and rinsing only affects the outside. It is understood that these are merely stringencies, and in a pressing situation, there is no concern for all of this. However, if there are garlics in the stuffed items, it is certainly forbidden, as they were cut with a chametz knife. Garlic is considered pungent, and it is forbidden to eat them on Pesach. It is permitted to keep them until after Pesach (Chayei Adam, subsection 26). And what has been clarified, that they should be rinsed before Pesach, the Mahari"l permitted, in a pressing situation, if they were not rinsed before Pesach, to rinse them even on Pesach (ibid., subsection 24).

He also disagrees with the second ruling regarding salted fish that are soaked in water in a chametz vessel on Passover. Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote that one should be stringent. It implies that according to the basic law it is permitted, and if they were soaked before Passover – there is no need to be stringent at all. However, our teacher the Rema does not hold this view and ruled that fat melted in a chametz vessel before Passover is prohibited by law. For regarding Passover, we do not say that vessels are assumed not to have been used within the past day. Additionally, there are those who prohibit even when the taste is spoiled, and in a chametz vessel there is not sixty times the volume against the vessel. Similarly, anything cooked in a chametz vessel. However, if it is known for certain that the vessel was not used within the past day – it is permitted post facto, for regarding a spoiled taste post facto, one should not be stringent (Magen Avraham, subsection 23). According to his words, even with salted fish soaked in water in a chametz vessel for twenty-four hours – it is forbidden due to the principle that soaking is like cooking, even before Passover, since regarding Passover, we do not assume that vessels are not used within the past day. Concerning the leniency before its time, it is not considered soaking – there is no proof for this reasoning. However, one might say another reason to permit soaking, as it only becomes considered soaked after twenty-four hours, and by then the taste is spoiled. But it is possible that regarding Passover, we do not say this reasoning. However, on the last day of the holiday, one can be lenient, but with a spicy dish, one should not be lenient (Taz, subsection 10).

And know: Seemingly, regarding something cooked in a chametz pot before Passover – there is a leniency based on the principle of 'noten ta'am bar noten ta'am' (a secondary imparting of taste). While during Passover it is impossible to permit due to this principle, as the reason for 'noten ta'am bar noten ta'am' is that the taste weakens, concerning even a small amount (mashehu) this is not a leniency, as there is still a taste of something, albeit minor. But before Passover, why should it be prohibited?

However, regarding chametz, there is no leniency at all, as it is explained in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 95, that 'noten ta'am bar noten ta'am' is permissible only when it pertains to something that is permissible, and not for something that is forbidden. See there. And regarding chametz, it is considered as if it is forbidden, as the Magen Avraham (section 24) states, meaning that everything is considered "chametz." Only on the last day of the festival do we not worry about this. Also, if something falls from one vessel into another – it is subject to the laws of 'noten ta'am bar noten ta'am.' However, even in this case, it is permitted only if a small amount fell from this pot. And it is surprising: Why do we not permit even more than a small amount? 

There is an opinion that indeed it is so, and what was written "a small amount" refers to the melting of fat, where there is concern for tiny crumbs of chametz remaining in it. But regarding boiled wine and similar items, even if it is mixed in a large amount – it is permitted (there, section 26). But if so, what difference is there between a small amount and a large amount (Magen Avraham, section 13)?

But indeed, it is as I have written, that during Passover itself, the law of 'noten ta'am bar noten ta'am' is not applied at all. Therefore, even if it falls into another pot – it is permitted only if it is a small amount. And what was written "a small amount" – refers to Passover itself. And see what I have written in Siman 452, section 9, regarding 'noten ta'am bar noten ta'am.'

From all the matters that have been explained, it is clear that there is no concern with our herring (erring). For what should we be concerned about? The vessels are new, as is known. And to worry about crumbs of chametz, since the merchants place them in their locations by the hundreds and thousands of barrels, and obviously, the merchants are particular about cleanliness. Indeed, it has never happened that a piece of chametz was found in the barrels of salted fish. And if it should happen – it would be one in a thousand. And when they salt them, they are salted in a large storeroom by the thousands, where chametz is not found at all. And I have heard people say that perhaps the workers do this while they are eating, and chametz falls there. This is a mistake, for it is clear that in such a large operation, workers are not allowed to eat while working. When the time for eating arrives, the workers go to the eating area, and the storeroom is closed. Certainly, an open barrel standing in a shop should not be used, for there, chametz can easily fall into it. But a whole barrel has no concern. Nonetheless, we have the custom to follow the words of our master the Rema, to rinse them three times before Passover. And if what was prepared before Passover is not enough – we rinse them also during Passover, as I wrote in section 27. And those who are stringent not to eat any herring at all on Passover – there is no basis for this stringency, given how they are made nowadays.

And our Rabbi, the Rema, wrote in section 5: There are those who are stringent to be concerned about wine vinegar that is used throughout the year, for we worry that perhaps some of the leftovers from the meal were put into it, and sometimes there are bread crumbs in it. In those places where wine vinegar is not common, I have not seen people being stringent about this. Until here is his language, meaning that we are not speaking about a case where one takes a little bit at a time for each meal, for if that were the case, even without this concern it would be forbidden, because we worry that perhaps someone went in the middle of the meal to take from it, and crumbs of chametz fell into it. For even the search for chametz is required there for this reason, as I wrote in Siman 433. Rather, we are speaking about a case where one takes from it for many days, and there is no concern of chametz falling in. The only concern is that since it is good for the vinegar to strengthen it by putting in leftovers from food, like kvass in Russia, therefore, we worry about this. This is in places where wine vinegar is common, and people are accustomed to doing so. But in places where it is not common, they are not accustomed at all to putting food leftovers into it. Therefore, they were not stringent about this. (See Magen Avraham, sub-section 27, who wrote for the reason that it is difficult to obtain another. According to our explanation, it fits well and simply.)

It is further written that some are stringent from the outset not to fill wine and wine vinegar into a chametz (leavened) vessel within thirty days before Passover. And if they did fill it within thirty days, the custom is not to drink it on Passover. However, one who is lenient has not lost out, especially in a place where wine and vinegar are not readily available. Thus far is his language. And if the vessel is scoured and rinsed, it is certainly permitted (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 29). There are those who say that strong vinegar, which easily absorbs and releases, is certainly forbidden, and the principle of "a secondary taste imparting a secondary taste" does not apply to something sharp (ibid., subparagraph 28). Even if it is not a day-old vessel, this principle does not apply to something sharp (Chayei Adam, subparagraph 34). There are those who are stringent only with a day-old vessel (Magen Avraham, ibid.), for even though it is established in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 96, that the sharpness enhances even a non-day-old vessel, nevertheless, since there are those who dispute this there, one should not be stringent based on a mere concern (Machtzit HaShekel). All of this applies when the liquid remains in the vessel until it is placed on the fire and begins to boil, as this is the measure of pickling in brine. But less than this, there is no concern at all (ibid.).

Additionally, he wrote: A barrel of wine whose staves are glued with dough, if it is within two months before Passover, the dough is still soft and imparts flavor during Passover, and it is forbidden to drink it. But if the dough was applied earlier, it has already dried and does not impart flavor during Passover, and it is permitted. However, if there is an olive-sized piece of dough in one place, it must be removed even though it was used for reinforcement, as I wrote in Siman 442. This is the end of his words.

This two-month measure, even though in the case of glued papers thirty days are sufficient, nevertheless, regarding imparting flavor, two months are necessary, contrary to those who argue that thirty days are also sufficient here (Chayei Adam, Siman 36, unlike the Taz). Furthermore, the cases are not comparable at all, for in the case of papers there is nothing to moisten them, whereas here the wine moistens the dough, and it does not dry quickly. And indeed, the measure here is also thirty days, meaning thirty days until it stops absorbing moisture, and thirty days for drying.

And what he wrote that it is forbidden to drink, but permissible to keep, even though the wine absorbs the taste of chametz, nevertheless it only imparts a minimal amount of flavor and is considered 'weak chametz.' And there is no proof from here that 'weak chametz' prohibits even a minimal amount, for here it was done intentionally, unlike 'weak chametz' that fell into a dish, which only prohibits if it imparts a noticeable flavor (Magen Avraham, Siman 30). And when there is an olive-sized piece in one place, and it is covered with clay, it does not need to be removed, as I wrote there (Siman 31). All this applies after the fact, but initially, it is certainly forbidden to glue a barrel with dough, even long before Passover. And this is the simple custom, and it should not be changed.

Salt that has been placed in a mortar used for chametz, but the salt has not been ground in it, is permitted to be used for salting meat on Passover, because it does not absorb [the chametz] in a cold, dry state. And even though it is explained in Yoreh De'ah, at the end of Siman 95, that it is preferable not to place salt that has been in a meat bowl into milk, nevertheless, in a mortar it is permitted even initially. And all the more so with our mortars, which are not typically used for chametz at all. However, if the salt has been ground in them, it is prohibited to use this salt on Passover, because due to the pressure of the grinding, it absorbs some chametz (there, Siman Katan 32). And if it was ground before Passover, it is permissible with our mortars that have only a minimal concern, and it becomes nullified before Passover (Chayei Adam, Siman Katan 38). Initially, it is prohibited even before Passover to grind salt in it for Passover use. This is the common custom, and one should not deviate from it.

Unripe fruit, which refers to grapes or other fruits that have not ripened and have a certain tartness, if they were ground before Passover in mortars that had been used for chametz – it is permissible to eat them on Passover, because they do not absorb flavor from cold and dry substances. The mortars should be clean. Even though unripe fruit is considered like a sharp substance, nevertheless, regarding absorption, and in a mortar used infrequently for chametz, before Passover there is only a minimal concern, and it is nullified before Passover. Our teacher, the Rema, wrote in section 7 that even if this was done during Passover – it is not prohibited if the utensil was clean. These are his words. However, it is surprising: because in truth, it seems from the authorities that unripe fruit is considered a sharp substance. And although one may be lenient before Passover, but during Passover itself, when there is both sharpness and the pressure of the knife – how can it be permitted? And even without sharpness, certainly with the pressure of the knife and if it is slightly moist – it absorbs a little. This requires significant investigation. (The Magen Avraham in section 33 prohibits even before Passover. The Chayei Adam permits, as does the Maharitatz. But during Passover itself, it is surprising. From the words of the Taz in section 13, it appears that it was not written in the Shulchan Aruch that even during Passover it is not prohibited, see there. And this is the main ruling. Be precise and you will find leniency.)

And unripe grapes that were cut with a chametz knife during Passover are prohibited, because a regular knife is not assumed to be clean, and we must be concerned about the chametz that adheres to it. Nonetheless, if some of it got mixed into a cooked dish, our Master, the Rema, ruled there that one should not be stringent and prohibit it out of doubt, because he holds that unripe grapes are not sharp. And even though, in any case, there is at least a small amount, since the knife is not clean, he holds that this applies to grease that adheres to the knife. But chametz does not adhere, and it is considered as if it were clean regarding this mixture. In any case, this requires further examination in practice, because, in any event, there is at least a small amount present (as noted by the Magen Avraham, sub-section 37). Additionally, we see that even bread adheres to the knife. Furthermore, many hold that unripe grapes are considered sharp, and even if cut before Passover, and even with a clean knife, further examination is needed. However, before Passover with a clean knife, one may be lenient, as I wrote in the previous section. But during Passover, one should not be lenient at all according to the opinion of the eminent later authorities.

And regarding items that are definitely not pungent, if they were cut with a chametz knife during Passover and the knife was not cleaned, even if the knife was used that day, it is permitted to eat the food on Passover by thoroughly washing and scraping slightly at the place of the cut. If the knife was cleaned, it is permissible even without washing. For although there is pressure from the knife, it does not transfer in a dry substance. If what was cut was slightly moist, washing is required. If the item is pungent, such as radish, onion, garlic, or similar, it is forbidden even if it was cut before Passover, even if the knife was not used that day, and even if it was cleaned, because pungency and the pressure of the knife definitely transfer (as stated by the Gra in section 59). However, in pressing circumstances, if it was cut before Passover, there is room to be lenient, as I wrote regarding unripe fruit, because at most it is only a small amount, and it has already been nullified. During Passover itself, it is always forbidden.

All of this applies to a homeowner's knife in his house when he cut with it during Passover, which is an incidental occurrence. However, something that was cut with a chametz knife regularly by a non-Jewish shopkeeper, such as pieces of fish called "lox," or other types of fish sold during Passover — and Jews buy from them, such as unsalted fish, because salted fish is anyway forbidden to buy from them during Passover due to the salt — but even if they are unsalted, if the shopkeeper cuts them with his knife that he also uses to cut bread, it is proper to be stringent and not eat [the fish] even after rinsing. But if it was cut before Passover, there is no need to be stringent, and it is permissible to eat it after rinsing (according to the Gra"z). Similarly, if he has a designated knife for this purpose, it is permissible even during Passover.

Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote in Section 8: Olives that were careful to cut them with a new knife, even if they were not careful to pickle them in a new pot, if it is not "ben yomo" (used within the day) – are permissible according to all opinions. Until here is his wording. That is to say: Olives are certainly considered sharp. And if they were cut with an old knife, even if it is not "ben yomo" – they are forbidden even if they were cut before Passover. And although in all olives there is sixty times against the knife and it is nullified before Passover, similar to onions that were cut with a knife of prohibition in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 96 – it is not comparable. There, the onions were cooked in a sauce, and the taste was mixed in entirely, and in the entirety, there is sixty times against the knife. But here, each small piece stands on its own, and each one absorbed a little from the knife, and in each one, there is not sixty times against the absorbed taste. Therefore, the combination does not help (Taz, Section 14, and Magen Avraham, Section 38). Therefore, it is also not comparable to unripe grapes in a mortar, where the pounding mixes them all together. And if indeed after cutting them one pickled them all in water before Passover – they are permissible, because the water transfers the absorptions from one to another, and they become as one, and it is like the onions. And see in the next section.

However, if one cut them with a new knife but pickled them in a chametz pot before Pesach, and the pot is not a "ben yomo" (i.e., it has not been used within the past 24 hours) – it is permitted. And even though with a sharp food item, an "aino ben yomo" (a pot not used within the past 24 hours) is considered as if it were "ben yomo," nevertheless, since they are pickled in water – the water nullifies the sharpness (Tur), and it is considered as giving a detrimental taste before Pesach and is permitted. But during Pesach itself, it is forbidden. And know that what we wrote in the previous section, that if after cutting them with a chametz knife, they were pickled in water before Pesach, they are permitted, there are those who disagree with this. They hold that only if they were cooked are they permitted, because cooking transfers the taste throughout, not pickling (Taz there). And there is one who prohibits even if they were cooked (Magen Avraham there), and only the water is permitted, whether in pickling or cooking, because in water the emissions are certainly mixed and nullified in sixty. And one may be lenient according to the first opinion (the Gra), that even pickling is an excessive stringency, as why wouldn't the taste transfer from one to the other when they are pickled in water? However, this is evident from the words of the Tur; see there. And it suffices to be stringent in pickling and not in cooking.

Just as chametz (leavened bread) before Passover is nullified in sixty (parts), so too after Passover, it is nullified in sixty. Whether the chametz was mixed before Passover and remained until after Passover, in a manner that did not transgress "bal yera'eh" (the prohibition against seeing chametz) according to the details explained in Siman 442, Se'if 12. And although rabbinically one was obligated to destroy it, as I wrote there in Se'if 16, nonetheless, since from a Torah perspective they did not transgress, it is permitted after Passover. The great authorities agreed that it is permissible ab initio to mix before Passover and let it remain until after Passover, since it does not transgress "bal yera'eh" (Magen Avraham, Se'if Katan 42; Taz, Se'if Katan 17; Chayei Adam, Se'if Katan 47). This is not considered as nullifying a prohibition ab initio, since there is not yet a prohibition. However, during Passover itself, or after Passover, it is obvious that it is forbidden to mix. Nonetheless, if it was mixed during Passover in sixty, and it remained even intentionally, if it did not transgress "bal yera'eh," for example, less than a kezayit (olive's bulk) or if it was hardened, it is permitted after Passover (there). Similarly, if one nullified his chametz, and also after Passover when it was mixed, it is nullified in sixty, even though he transgressed "bal yera'eh" and its law is like during Passover. However, if one mixed intentionally during Passover or after Passover, it is not nullified at all. Specifically, if it was mixed unintentionally and remained intentionally, we permitted it, but not if it was mixed intentionally.

Many authorities hold that after Passover, if chametz (leavened bread) is mixed in, it does not require a ratio of sixty to nullify it; rather, it is nullified by a majority. This is explicitly implied in the Gemara (Pesachim 30a), which states that Rabbi Shimon imposed a penalty that chametz which has passed through Passover is prohibited for benefit. But when he imposes a penalty, it applies only to chametz in its original state, not in a mixture. Refer there for further details. The penalty is because one has violated the prohibition of "it shall not be seen." Thus, anything not in its original state is permitted. Therefore, if there is a majority against the chametz, it is permitted even for consumption. Even in a liquid mixture, a majority suffices, for in a dry mixture, certainly even the first opinion agrees that a majority nullifies, as it is not stricter than other prohibitions. And although during Passover itself we are stringent even with a dry mixture, after Passover, it is certainly nullified by a majority. 

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote in section 11 that if there is less than sixty, it suffices to cast the prohibited benefit into the Dead Sea. This is his language: "It implies that this is even according to the first opinion which requires sixty, for this opinion is the basis." (This is also found in the Alter Rebbe's Shulchan Aruch, section 61.) And when there is sixty, nothing further is required. According to the latter opinion, a majority suffices for nullification, and nothing further is required. In cases of significant financial loss or pressing need, one can rely on the lenient opinion, as this is the primary view (Alter Rebbe). All of this applies after Passover. But before Passover, according to all opinions, sixty is required. It has already been explained that one may nullify before Passover with a ratio of sixty. Therefore, if one has chametz grains, one can add to them until there is a ratio of sixty, and this is the common custom (as agreed by the Magen Avraham in subsection 45).

But dough that became leavened with beer yeast that has passed over Passover – the entire dough is prohibited for benefit, even if there is sixty times [the amount of permissible substance]. For a substance that causes fermentation – even in a ratio of a thousand, it is not nullified. And neither discarding the value of the prohibited substance into the Dead Sea nor selling it to a non-Jew except for the value of the prohibition helps, because we consider the entire dough as if it is yeast. Similarly, if one set cheese with leavened vinegar that has passed over Passover, or set mead that is called mead with beer yeast that has passed over Passover. And there are those who disagree with this and hold that discarding the value of the prohibition into the Dead Sea is effective even for a substance that causes fermentation, and similarly to sell it to a non-Jew except for the value of the prohibition within it. And in a case of significant loss, one may rely on their opinion (the GRaZ, section 62, and likewise the Chayei Adam wrote in section 442). And if it became leavened also with permitted yeast, this and that together cause it to be allowed.

And know that in all this, there is no difference between someone who nullified their chametz on the fourteenth and someone who did not nullify it. For in a case where we permit it through a mixture, it is permitted even without nullification, as explained in the Talmud, that the law follows Rabbi Shimon that chametz which has passed over Pesach is not subject to a prohibition of a negative commandment, but is rather prohibited for benefit due to a fine imposed because he transgressed "you shall not see [chametz]." However, they did not impose a fine in the case of a mixture, as I have written. And in a case where it is prohibited, it is prohibited even if one nullified the chametz and did not transgress "you shall not see," since he did not destroy the chametz. And this is true even if he was inadvertent or coerced. The reason for this will be explained with the help of Heaven in Siman 448 based on the Jerusalem Talmud.

Rigid chametz (chametz nuksha), even in its pure form without any mixture, is not prohibited for benefit after Passover, because one does not transgress "bal yera'eh" (the prohibition of seeing chametz) with it. It is also permitted for consumption, but rigid chametz is not fit for eating (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 46). And even though we said that nullifying chametz does not help, and there also one does not transgress "bal yera'eh," this is not comparable. There, the primary form of chametz is subject to "bal yera'eh," and therefore it is penalized in all forms. This is not the case with rigid chametz, which is never subject to "bal yera'eh." Rav Rema writes at the end of this section that some refrain from playing with cards (kartiyn) on the table during Passover, fearing that some of their rigid chametz might fall into the food. So far his words. Rav Beit Yosef writes in paragraph 12 that "pideyosh" are considered completely chametz and are prohibited for benefit after Passover. So far his words, and we do not know what this is.

Chametz (leavened products) owned by a non-Jew that has passed through Passover is permissible even for eating. A Jew may buy it from him and eat it in a place where they eat their bread, or if a Jew threw a toothpick during its baking, as I wrote in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 112. However, chametz owned by a Jew that has passed through Passover is forbidden for benefit by rabbinic decree, and they penalized him because he violated "You shall not see [leaven]." Even if he nullified the chametz, it is still forbidden for the reason that will be explained in section 6. Even if a Jew is a transgressor and has cast off the yoke of commandments, and it is not recognizable at all that his chametz came from a Jew, it is forbidden for benefit to all Jews. If he sold the chametz to him, it is considered as if he sold it to a Jew, for even if he sinned, he is still a Jew. Except if he was born from a Jew who had relations with a non-Jewish woman, then the child is like her and is not considered a Jew at all.

A Jew and a non-Jew who have chametz in partnership, and Passover has passed without them dividing it before Passover, and they divided it after Passover— the portion of the non-Jew is permitted. For in rabbinic law, we hold that there is retroactive clarification (yesh bereirah), and we say that it is retrospectively clarified that this is his portion. However, the portion of the Jew is forbidden. 

There is an opinion that wants to say that even the portion of the Jew is permitted, on the grounds that the rule that there is retroactive clarification in rabbinic matters is lenient, and not that through this, there will be a stringency, through which the portion of the Jew would be forbidden. Rather, to the contrary, we say there is no retroactive clarification, and perhaps the Jew's portion is in the possession of the non-Jew, and the non-Jew's portion is in the possession of the Jew (Shagat Aryeh, Siman 90). 

I wonder about this: Is it really the case that by saying there is no retroactive clarification there would be a clear allowance? For it still remains a doubt. And should you say that a rabbinic doubt is treated leniently, nevertheless, in any case, half of this is certainly forbidden, and how can we permit both portions through this reasoning? 

Even though in rabbinic matters we do say two contradictory principles can coexist, as I wrote above in Siman 493 regarding two people who placed an eruv, where for one it is considered day and for the other night—this is not similar at all. For there, there are two people and two actions, and likewise with the two paths mentioned in the Talmud. But here, there are two people and one action, and we are discussing all of this chametz, half of which belongs to the Jew, and how can we say that there is no portion of the Jew in it?

And similarly, the chametz (leavened bread) of two Jews, where one sold his chametz to a non-Jew and the other did not sell, and after Passover they divided it between them – the portion belonging to the one who sold his chametz is permitted due to the principle of retroactive clarification, whereas the portion belonging to the one who did not sell his chametz is prohibited (Orach Chaim 91). And it is stated in the Jerusalem Talmud (Pesachim, Chapter 2, Halacha 2): If a convert died and his property was distributed, and in it was found chametz that had passed through Passover – the chametz is permitted, see there. This is when the convert died before the time of prohibition, so he did not violate "You shall not see" (the prohibition against owning chametz during Passover). But if he died after the time of prohibition – it is prohibited, since he violated "You shall not see." However, if someone stole it, and there was chametz in the stolen property, even if the owner died before the time of prohibition – the chametz is prohibited to the thief, since it was in his possession when the owner died, and he acquired that chametz, thus he violated "You shall not see." Moreover, even if the owner sold all his chametz before Passover and did not despair of the chametz, nevertheless – this chametz is not included in the sale, since the chametz was under the control of the thief, and we hold that stolen property, where the owner has not despaired, neither can consecrate (Bava Kamma 69a). The same law applies that he cannot sell.

If a non-Jew brings a Jew a gift of chametz on Passover, even on the last day of Passover, he should be careful not to accept it. And if he does accept it—it is forbidden to derive any benefit from it. He should also be careful not to make it apparent through his actions that he desires it. And then, even if the chametz is left in the Jew's house, even on the first day of Passover—it is permitted, because he never acquired the chametz, and when he acquires it after Passover—it is considered chametz of a non-Jew that has passed through Passover, and it is permitted. 

And if you ask: If he does not want it, why does he allow the non-Jew to leave the chametz with him? It can be said that he does not want to provoke the anger of the non-Jew who brings him a gift and he rejects it. According to this, when the non-Jew brings him chametz to purchase from him—he is certainly obligated not to allow the non-Jew to leave the chametz in his house. Because he can say: I do not need this, and I do not want you to leave the chametz in my house. And if the non-Jew is a strong person and he is afraid to protest against him—his status is like that of a gift. Whether it is a gift or a forced sale like with a strong person—it is good for him to say with his mouth that “I do not want to acquire it willingly.” And if he did not say this—it is not a hindrance, because it is certain that he does not want to acquire something forbidden (Bava Metzia 92b).

Maimonides wrote in the first chapter, law 4: Chametz (leavened bread) that has passed through Passover is forever prohibited for benefit. This is a penalty from the Sages, because he transgressed "You shall not see" and "You shall not find" [chametz during Passover], they prohibited it. And even if he left it unintentionally or under duress, so that a person would not leave chametz in his possession during Passover in order to benefit from it after Passover. This is his language, meaning: even if he left it unintentionally or under duress, and did not transgress "You shall not see," since one under duress is exempted by the Torah, nevertheless, they made a prohibition for another reason. The main penalty is because he transgressed "You shall not see," but because of this, they also prohibited it even if he did not transgress "You shall not see," "so that he would not leave..." According to this, even if he nullified the chametz and did not transgress "You shall not see," nevertheless, since the Sages decreed destruction [of chametz], therefore, in any case where he did not destroy it, it is prohibited for benefit, for the reason of "so that he would not leave..."

And these are the words of the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, Section 5, which state: "Chametz found in a Jew's house after Pesach is prohibited, even though he nullified it." This is their language, and its source is from the Jerusalem Talmud (there). The reason is given: so that one will not deceitfully say he nullified it even though he did not, as the Tur writes, see there. This is also included in the words of the Rambam who wrote: "So that he will not leave...", meaning: that he should not engage in some form of deceit to benefit from it after Pesach. Previously, the Rambam wrote the reason from the Gemara (30a) that the fine is because he transgressed "it shall not be seen," and afterward he added the reason from the Jerusalem Talmud. The Talmud Bavli and the Jerusalem Talmud do not disagree, as we have explained. He added: even if he was mistaken or coerced, for this is a greater novelty, for what could he have done? Certainly, if he nullified but did not destroy it.

(It is difficult for me regarding the Jerusalem Talmud: why is there a need for the reason of deceit? Let it say because he did not follow the Sages' enactment to destroy it. It appears in my humble opinion that in the Jerusalem Talmud it states "he declared his chametz ownerless on the thirteenth," see there. And so is the version in the book Or Zarua the Great, Section 246, and not as the version of the Rosh in the second chapter, Section 4: "he declared it ownerless on the fourteenth." According to this, it is not related to nullification on the fourteenth, for which they required inspection, but rather a complete declaration of ownerlessness before the fourteenth, making it like declaring it ownerless in the middle of the year, and indeed the reason of deceit is needed. The Tur brought the language of "nullification," but this is not the case in the Jerusalem Talmud. A perplexing matter is found in Or Zarua there, and this is his language: it is permitted to declare chametz ownerless in the seventh hour with the intention to reacquire it after Pesach. And so it is in Hagahot Ashri there. And he explains there that the Jerusalem Talmud forbids when one does not intend to reacquire it after Pesach, but when he intends to reacquire it, it is permitted, see there. This needs great examination, for if so, the requirement to destroy it is nullified. However, in the end, this is rejected from the first chapter of Chullin, see there. Investigate and you will find it easy.)

And know: Even though the reason for the prohibition is because of the penalty for violating "bal yera'eh" (the prohibition of owning chametz during Passover), nevertheless, it is forbidden for all Jews (Ran, there). And even though in many penalties, the penalty only applies to the transgressor alone, nevertheless, with chametz, which is necessary every year, the sages saw that if they did not forbid the chametz to all Jews, there could still be some loopholes. And the proof for this prohibition for all Jews is from what they said at the beginning of Chullin: Chametz of transgressors after Passover – is immediately permitted, because they exchange it. And if the prohibition were only for him alone – then without the exchange, it would be permitted. (From this, the Or Zaru'a rejected the ruling that we brought: Why do they exchange? Because they do not leave the permitted and eat the forbidden. And if it were permitted to renounce ownership with the intent to reclaim it after Passover – why would they transgress the prohibition? See there.)

One may question whether, if someone nullified the chametz (leavened bread) but was unintentionally negligent or forcibly prevented from destroying it, the penalty still applies or not. It appears to me that it is permitted. The proof for this is from the words of the Tur and Shulchan Aruch. In Section 3, they wrote: "Even if it was unintentional or due to coercion, it is forbidden." And in Section 5, they wrote that it is forbidden even if it was nullified. They did not write both laws together, i.e., even if it was unintentional or coercion, and even if it was nullified—implying that in such a case, it is permitted (and this also seems clear from the Chayei Adam, Section 20). There is someone who forbids even in such a case (the Magen Avraham, Section 14), but this is an excessive stringency in a rabbinic prohibition. (And regarding the extensive discussion in the Biur Halacha, Section 9, in explaining the Jerusalem Talmud, see there. According to what is written in Section 6 to explain specifically on the thirteenth, most of the difficulties are resolved. And I saw at the end of his words that when he rendered it ownerless three days beforehand, it is not considered deceit. This is based on the discussion at the end of the fourth chapter of Nedarim, and it is not related to the Jerusalem Talmud, see there. Be precise and you will find ease.)

And I found similarly in the Tashbatz (Part Two, Siman 199), and this is his language: Reuven stored grain underground, and on the eve of Passover, he found it soaked in water, and he did not have time to sell it... If it became leavened, it is forbidden to eat it, but it is permissible to sell it to a non-Jew, for it is only prohibited as a penalty. And in this case, we do not impose a penalty, for what could he have done? He was coerced, and he has already nullified it... Thus far his language, and it seemingly contradicts the Rambam and all the authorities. Heaven forbid to say so, rather, it is as we have said that in both cases, with nullification and coercion, it is certainly permitted to benefit from it.

It has already been explained in Siman 448, based on the Jerusalem Talmud, that it is forbidden to feed chametz even to an ownerless animal or to someone else's animal, and similarly after Passover, chametz which has passed through Passover (Section 18, subsection 24). And our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in Section 7: It is forbidden to give one's animal to a non-Jew to feed it during the days of Passover if he knows that he will feed it barley waste which is chametz. Thus are his words. And there are those who say that it is specifically when he explicitly told him to give chametz that it is forbidden, but in an unspecified manner it is permitted, because he acts on his own discretion (Section 18, subsection 23, in the name of the Agudah). In my humble opinion, there is no disagreement here, for surely even our teacher, the Beit Yosef, agrees that in an unspecified manner it is permitted. However, this is when it is not certain that he will feed it chametz, for he has the option to give it non-chametz food, in which case, even if he gives it chametz, we have no issue. But our teacher, the Beit Yosef, said "if he knows that he will feed..." meaning there is no doubt that he will certainly feed it chametz, in which case, what use is an unspecified manner? It is equivalent to explicitly stating. And if the non-Jew has a share in the animal, for example, if he was given to raise it for half the profit, even if he knows that he feeds it chametz, we have no issue, for he does it for his own benefit (Ba'er Hetev, subsection 17 in the name of Pnei Moshe, Siman 10). The same applies if he is a partner in this animal, similar to the laws of Sabbath work. However, it seems that in any case, the Jew needs to renounce his benefit to the salt sea, so that he does not benefit from chametz. Even though he did not commit a prohibition, nevertheless even incidental benefit is forbidden with chametz (so wrote in Section 18, subsection 24). And from Terumot, Chapter Eleven (Mishnah 9), there is proof for the rule that has been explained; see there.

It is taught in Tractate Terumot (ibid.): If a priest rents a cow from an Israelite, even though he is responsible for its sustenance, he should not feed it terumah carrots, see there. It is evident that even though the cow is with the renter, it is still considered entirely as belonging to the owner. According to this, if a non-Jew rents an animal from an Israelite for all the days of Passover, even though he is responsible for its sustenance, it is forbidden for the Israelite to allow him to feed it chametz, if he knows for certain that he will feed it chametz. I have seen someone who permits it, reasoning that he does it for his own benefit. If he did not feed it chametz, he would need to feed it something more expensive (Sha'arei Teshuvah, sub-paragraph 17, in the name of Pri Megadim). To me, it seems to be an absolute prohibition. The previous law, where he gave it to him for half the profit, is different because the non-Jew has a share, as it is taught in Tractate Terumot (ibid.): A priest who measures a cow from an Israelite may feed it terumah carrots, but not a renter. (And an animal that eats chametz permissibly, such as the animal of a non-Jew, or as previously explained, it is permitted to drink its milk on Passover. We have already explained this in Yoreh De'ah at the end of Siman 60, see there. I have seen those who are stringent in this matter, but this is not the main opinion.)

One of the great authorities wrote that even according to our custom, where we sell all the chametz to a non-Jew on the eve of Passover along with the animals, it is still forbidden to feed chametz to the animals via a non-Jew. The reason is that since this sale is considered a legal fiction, as everyone knows that the non-Jew will return after Passover and sell it back to the Jew. Therefore, regarding chametz that was in possession during Passover, the prohibition is rabbinic because everyone nullifies the chametz – the sale is effective. However, regarding feeding chametz to animals, which is a Torah prohibition – the sale is not effective (Taz in Ba’er Heitev on Pesachim). Many disagreed with this, as it is explicitly stated in the Talmud that legal fiction is permitted even in matters of Torah law, such as circumventing the law of the firstborn. (See Sha’arei Teshuvah section 17, and Magen Avraham section 11. The Chayei Adam objected to this. And similarly, it is written in the name of the Noda B’Yehuda.) Based on this, many have the custom to feed their animals chametz on Passover through a non-Jew by means of this sale.

In my humble opinion, it is clear that this is a complete prohibition, and the words of that great authority are explicitly stated in the Gemara. His intention is not to say that in matters of Torah law (d'oraita) subterfuge does not work, but rather he means to say as follows: In Shabbat (139b) it is said that one may use subterfuge on a sieve on a festival to hang pomegranates on it, and then hang dregs on it. And this is only if he actually hung pomegranates on it. And it questions: What is the difference... subterfuge...? And it answers there: It is not evident... see there. Thus, there is a difference between evident subterfuge and non-evident subterfuge. Furthermore, it is stated there: Rabbi... and he saw them in a boat, and he said: I intended for their kind. He said to them: Are you talking about subterfuge? Subterfuge is only in rabbinic law... see there. From this, it is explained that there is a difference between types of subterfuge. Non-evident subterfuge is permitted even in matters of Torah law. But evident subterfuge is only permitted in rabbinic matters. Now, our sale of chametz is evident subterfuge to everyone, and therefore that great authority correctly said that in matters of Torah law it is prohibited. And we have already prohibited in our community giving chametz to animals through a non-Jew, and we have already mentioned this in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 241, end of Section 9. And even if we say that this is not considered evident subterfuge, for the Jew surely desires that if the non-Jew pays him according to the purchase price, he will take it for himself—it is in the case when the animal is with the non-Jew, like the animals standing on the non-Jew's property, or in the non-Jew's courtyard. But when the animal is in the Jew's domain—there is no more evident subterfuge than this. It is obvious that there is no permission for this, and it is prohibited to feed chametz to animals during Pesach.

Maimonides wrote in Chapter Four, Law 6: A Jew and a non-Jew who were on a ship, and the Jew had chametz, and the fifth hour arrived—he should sell it to the non-Jew; or give it to him as a gift, and then take it back from him after Passover. Provided that he gives it to him as a complete gift. The Jew says to the non-Jew: "Instead of taking it for one hundred, come and take it for two hundred. Instead of taking it from a non-Jew, come and take it from a Jew, as I might need it and take it back from you after Passover." Up to here is his wording, and this is from the Tosefta and Jerusalem Talmud, Chapter Two. Similarly, the Tur and Shulchan Aruch wrote in Section 4, and they added to say: But he should not sell it or give it to him on condition, and if he did so, he transgresses "it shall not be seen" and "it shall not be found." Up to here is their wording.

And behold, that which is permitted to sell and give as a gift before its prohibition time – there is no novelty in this at all, and there is no need to inform us of it. And why should one not be permitted to sell and give? Rather, the novelty is that even though the non-Jew understands that the intention is not because he wants to sell, but to escape the prohibition of chametz, and understands from the Jew’s intent that he plans to buy it back from him after Passover, and presumably will give him a profit, and if so, it is merely a trick and should be forbidden – we are informed that nevertheless, it is permitted. And this is what they warned regarding giving as a gift, that it should be given as a complete gift. Meaning: that in a sale where he receives money and performs an act of acquisition – it is naturally considered a sale. But in the case of a gift where he does not receive money, and it could be that in his heart he did not intend it as a complete gift at all, and he would transgress “you shall not see” – for this reason, they warned that he should intend it as a complete gift.

And the second ruling informs us of a greater novelty: For in the first ruling, he does not mention at all that he might buy it back from him after Passover; rather, it is understood by themselves according to the context that this is his intention. And in the second ruling, it teaches us that he can even tell him this and persuade him to buy more than he needs, and to buy only from him. Only that he should not tell him explicitly that it necessarily has to be so, for this is certainly forbidden. And even though when he says to him, "Take it for two hundred, take it from a Jew, perhaps I will need it and I will take it..." – this is also considered explicit, nonetheless, it is not absolutely explicit, and regarding the law, it is considered a valid sale. According to this, our sale of chametz has a solid basis from the Tosefta, the Jerusalem Talmud, and all the poskim (decisors of Jewish law).

This is the wording of our teacher, the Beit Yosef, in paragraph 3: Chametz of a Jew that has passed through Passover is forbidden for benefit, even if it was left inadvertently or under duress. However, if it was sold or given to a non-Jew outside of his home before Passover, even if the Jew knows him and knows that he will not touch it at all, but will keep it for him until after Passover and then return it to him, it is permitted, provided it was given as a complete gift without any conditions, or sold to him as a complete sale for a small amount. But a gift on condition to return it does not help. Thus far his wording. And his main intention is that even if the buyer also understands that this sale is a subterfuge, and the Jew is only doing it to escape the prohibition of chametz, nevertheless, if the sale is according to the law of the Torah, we have no issue with it.

And this requirement of "to a gentile outside his home" – the intention is regarding the chametz, that the buyer should take the chametz out of the Jew’s home. For if not, even though the chametz is sold to him, since the chametz is placed in the Jew’s possession, it is as if a gentile deposited chametz with a Jew. And if the Jew accepted responsibility for it, he transgresses "bal yera'eh" (the prohibition of chametz being seen or found in one's possession during Passover). And now, when the gentile leaves the chametz with the Jew, it appears as though the Jew is accepting responsibility for the chametz (Magen Avraham, subsection 4). But according to the strict law, there is no issue, only he must be careful not to accept responsibility (ibid). And also, he should designate a specific place for it, like a corner or something similar, because then he is not required to destroy it, as I have written in Siman 440 (Taz, subsection 4). And by designating a corner, it has been clarified there that even if he accepts responsibility, he does not transgress, see there.

And if the chametz is very abundant, such that it is impossible to remove it from the house – he should sell him the room in which the chametz is placed (Magen Avraham there). And in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 194, it is explained that a gentile does not acquire land with money according to the Rambam, but only with a deed. And even according to the Rashbam and Tosafot, who hold that he acquires with money, nevertheless in a place where deeds are written, he does not acquire with money without a deed. Therefore, if he is unable to write a deed, he can stipulate with him that he acquires only with money, as explained there. The reason he does not acquire with money is because his mind is not settled without a deed, see there. Therefore, when he speaks with him and he relies on this – indeed, his mind is settled, and it is effective according to all opinions. (And this is the intent of the Magen Avraham there, who wrote: stipulate with him at the beginning of the transaction that he acquires it with money alone, see there.)

The translation of the passage:
        
It is not specifically about selling the room, as the same rule applies if he rents him the room or the place where the chametz is located, for the rental of land is also acquired with money, as explained there. Particularly if the place where the chametz is located does not belong to the Jew, but he rents it – he cannot sell it, but rents it out with all the rights and authority that he has. Similarly, if there are non-Jewish workers in the business – he rents out the workers to him so that they are on the buyer's account, meaning they are his workers and not the Jew’s workers. And the rental of the workers and contractors does not require an acquisition or a document, but merely a verbal agreement, as I have written in Choshen Mishpat, the beginning of Siman 339. And even though it is explained there regarding a homeowner who rents workers, and here the Jew rents out the workers to the non-Jew, nevertheless, it is all the same: for the workers it does not matter whether their wages are paid by this one or that one. And we do not say there is no agency for a non-Jew, and how can the workers be the agents of the buyer? However, we have already explained in Choshen Mishpat Siman 188 that a worker can become a non-Jew for a Jew, and a Jew for a non-Jew. All the more so a non-Jew for another non-Jew, as even in agency there is an opinion that they become agents for one another, as I have written there. And we have also explained there that agency for a fee is like a worker. And if there are horses and animals involved in the business – he needs to sell the horses and animals to the non-Jew for such and such a price.

And how does one acquire chametz? It is known that Rashi of blessed memory holds that one acquires movable property with money and not by pulling. Rabbeinu Tam of blessed memory holds that it is specifically by pulling and not with money, and most of the poskim support this. The Rambam in the first chapter of "Acquisition" rules that one acquires both with money and by pulling, see there.
