In Choshen Mishpat, Siman 194, Section 10, we explained that there are some great authorities who hold that according to all opinions, if it is impossible to perform the act of pulling, one can acquire with money, see there. Therefore, one receives a coin from the buyer and transfers the chametz to him. However, one should not rely on this alone. Now, pulling is not possible with a large amount of chametz, and one can transfer it with a kinyan sudar. This means that the non-Jewish buyer gives him a garment and holds it in his hand. We have already explained there that a kinyan sudar works with a non-Jew. Rabbeinu Tam actually did this in practice (Tosafot Kidushin 3a). And regarding what is written in Ruth about the kinyan sudar, "And this was the attestation in Israel" – it means that they used to acquire with this kinyan, see there. However, since one leases him the place where the chametz is placed, as explained – he can transfer the chametz to him with a kinyan agav, as we explained there in Section 11 that it works with a non-Jew, and not like one of the great authorities who questioned this, see there. Also, the non-Jew acquires the chametz when he rents the place by the law of chatzer, as I wrote there in Section 12; although one of the great authorities questioned this, it is nevertheless effective. This is the opinion of the great early authorities, as I wrote there. It is good to perform all the kinyanim: kinyan kesef, kinyan sudar, kinyan agav, and kinyan chatzer. And among us, we also write a bill of sale. Although movable property is not acquired with a document, we have already explained there in Siman 190, Section 16 that since merchants customarily write contracts for the sale of goods, and with this document, he obligates himself, creating a personal obligation, and a person’s status is like land. Additionally, since this is the custom – it is considered a valid form of acquisition (situmta), as I wrote in Siman 201. Other reasons are also explained there. Similarly, horses and animals are acquired like movable property.

And know that the acquisition through money is the deposit that the buyer receives for the chametz, and all the transactions they call "Oph Gab" or "Zadatak," and the money for all the chametz, and other matters – he sets it as a loan upon him. For the acquisition through money does not require giving all the money but only a portion, and that the deposit is given as the beginning of the payment, as we explained in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 190. And there are those among the great ones who said that partial money does not suffice, and they established that the buyer should appoint a guarantor for the money. And we have already explained there in paragraph 3 that there is no concern in this, and all our earlier and later rabbis hold that partial money acquires, see there. Nevertheless, it is also good to appoint a guarantor, and so we practice. And there is also to make the "Anat Shalok" (a merchant's custom). (And know that what I wrote about the acquisition through a courtyard is not possible in the sale of much chametz, for we require that the courtyard be guarded with his knowledge or that he stands beside it, as I wrote in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 200, see there.)

It is obvious that the chametz must be placed in a location where the buyer can enter by himself (Taz, subsection 4, and Magen Avraham, subsection 4). For if he cannot enter and the key is held by the Jew, it is merely a deceit. Therefore, they wrote that the key must be handed over (ibid. and Bach), and this was the custom in previous generations. However, nowadays this is impossible in any manner, as is well known. Especially since the primary chametz in our possession is distilled wine and beer, which are under government supervision, and cannot be handed over to another. But indeed, this does not invalidate the sale at all, specifically if one intends to hide the key. Additionally, according to their laws, one can take possession of it even without handing over the key (Chayei Adam and Ba'er Heitev, subsection 8). Furthermore, the great authorities wrote that the stringency applies only at the time of the sale, but afterwards, if one locks or seals it, it is permitted (Chayei Adam, subsection 14, and Mekor Chaim, subsection 8), although it is not appropriate to do so. But if done without the intention against the buyer, there is certainly no stringency, as handing over the key is not a form of acquisition. Our custom is to instruct in this manner, telling the non-Jew to whom the chametz was sold, or the non-Jew who works in the house and is considered the buyer's employee, as I wrote: "See that the key is placed here and here, and whenever you wish to take the chametz, take the key from here, go and take it, and return the key to this place so it is not lost." And in the place where the chametz is kept, there should be some utensils and items needed during Passover. When the non-Jew goes there, either he or one of his household members will also go to take some utensil or item, ensuring that the non-Jew does not steal. However, it is forbidden to discuss the matter of chametz with him.

And this which our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote that "a gift on condition to return" does not work with chametz – the reason is not known, for in all other places we maintain that a gift on condition to return is considered a gift. And the Levush indeed wrote that this is only an extra stringency, see there (and so wrote the Beit Yosef and the Magen Avraham, subsection 5, in the name of the Terumat HaDeshen). According to this, after the fact, we need not be concerned (Eliyah Rabbah, subsection 11). And there are those who wrote that it is forbidden according to the law, for the reason that as long as the condition is pending – it is considered as a deposit. And before the condition is fulfilled, one has already violated "bal yera'eh" (the prohibition of owning chametz during Passover). Therefore, even though once the condition is fulfilled it retroactively becomes clear that it belonged to the non-Jew, nevertheless, one has already transgressed (there, in the name of Radbaz). And this is not understood at all, for in several laws we say regarding chametz "it becomes clear retroactively…" (there). And there are those who tried to forcefully maintain these words (see Machatzit HaShekel, subsection 6), and it is not so.

And what appears according to my humble opinion: The source of this law is in the Hagahot Maimoniot (Chapter 6 of the Laws of Shabbat, Note 2). This is inferred from the Tosefta that we brought in section 14 regarding a Jew and a non-Jew who were on a ship..., provided that it is given as an outright gift. From this, it is inferred that a gift on condition to return is not effective. And he questioned this: after all, isn't it effective everywhere else? And he wrote that perhaps because of the stringency of Passover, see there. Therefore, I say that the Rambam and the Tur, who brought the Tosefta as it is, apparently did not infer this at all. The intention is a complete gift without any trickery. However, if one were to infer this, one could say the simple reason is that any gift given on the condition to return – the recipient takes the gift into his hand, and then returns it. But here, when they are on a ship, and the chametz is not moved from its place – therefore, if it is given as an outright gift, it is a gift, but on condition to return – there is neither a gift, nor a condition, nor a return, but merely empty words, for he does not take it and does not return it. And this indeed seems to me to be the law: when one takes the chametz into his house – it certainly works. But when he does not take it into his house, like our modern sales – a gift on condition to return does not work for the reason I have written. However, in practice, even if he takes it into his house, since the early authorities said that because of the stringency of chametz one should be stringent – we should not deviate from their words.

There was an incident involving Reuven who sold his chametz to a non-Jew along with the room, as per the law. Shimon, however, had chametz which he did not sell to the non-Jew. Instead, he placed his chametz in this room, thinking that by doing so he fulfilled his obligation. It was ruled that his chametz is prohibited for benefit. It is obvious that even if he had told Reuven, "I placed my chametz in your room," it would not be effective unless he appointed him as an agent to sell it, or he transferred ownership of the chametz to him as a gift. But merely stating it – is of no consequence (see Chayei Adam, Section 10, Subsection 15).

And behold, the sale of our chametz, which has been customary for many, many generations before us, is as follows: All chametz owners sign an authorization. They write: We, the undersigned, give power and permission to Rabbi [so-and-so] to sell our chametz, all types of chametz. They specify in detail all the types, such as wheat bread, barley bread, wheat flour, as well as all types of beverages in detail. Also, other types of chametz, such as vinegar and yeast... And we, the undersigned, authorize the aforementioned Rabbi to sell it at any price that seems appropriate to him, and we do not have the right to say "I sent you to improve, not to ruin." Also, to sell and lease the places where the chametz is stored. And also to sell our animals and horses at any price that seems appropriate to him. And we also give permission to lease our mills and the courtyard, with all rights and authorization. And all the workers involved in our businesses will be at the expense of the buyer, and we have no connection to them. Also, all types of chametz that will be acquired until the fourteenth of the month of Nissan of this year, until the tenth hour – we give him power and permission to sell them. And they sign themselves.

And one should not ask: How is it possible to appoint an agent for something that he does not yet have? It is explained in Nazir (12b) that anything that one cannot do personally, one also cannot do through an agent. However, chametz is different, because since it is not within a person's domain, but the Torah considers it as if it is in his domain to transgress "bal yera'eh" (the prohibition of seeing chametz) by expressing intent, it suffices. And one can appoint an agent both to sell and to nullify even chametz that is not yet in his domain (see Magen Avraham at the end of Siman 434). And we have the custom to add for this reason that we write that they accept upon themselves with an oath not to nullify the agency, and that they will agree to everything that the agent will do. Therefore, they are compelled by the oath to uphold the agency, and it is as if they make the agency on the eve of Passover at the tenth hour, where the agent can act on their behalf. The rabbi makes a bill of sale with the non-Jewish buyer, and he calculates for him all the types that he is selling, each type at such-and-such a price, or as they are sold in the market here in such-and-such city. And even if the buyer does not know the exact measurement, it does not invalidate the sale, for we hold that pulling without measuring acquires. He receives from the buyer a deposit, which is called "iof gaba" or "zadatek." It is appropriate to receive enough so that there is a small amount for each of the signatories. The money is recorded as a loan until after Passover. The buyer appoints a guarantor for him. The rabbi speaks with the buyer and explains the matter to him, and they make a kinyan kesef (acquisition by money) and a kinyan sudar (acquisition by exchange), and also a bill of sale and a document of transfer. He rents to him all the places where the chametz is located, and along with them, the chametz is acquired. Similarly, with animals and horses, he transfers to him the places where they stand, and along with them, the animals and horses are acquired. To strengthen the matter, we make many types of acquisitions. He also rents him the businesses specifically, this one for such-and-such an amount, and that one for such-and-such an amount. Each one adds whatever he can, but this is the essence of the sale that is customary among us. After Passover, he buys it back from him. It is proper to buy it back from him immediately after havdalah on the last day of Passover, so that the homeowners do not open their businesses before the repurchase. See Aruch Hashulchan Orach Chaim Siman 460, Paragraph 15. (And we only deal with the buyer according to our laws. See Bava Metzia 71b and Bava Kama 113a. There is no concern in this matter, see Chatam Sofer Orach Chaim Siman 111. Be precise and you will find ease.)

The Tur writes: If a store belongs to a Jew and the merchandise sold therein is his, but the workers who assist there are non-Jews, chametz found there after Passover is permitted even for consumption, as we attribute it to the workers. However, if the store and merchandise belong to a non-Jew and the workers are Jews, it is forbidden, as we attribute it to the Jewish workers. This is the version of Rabbeinu Chananel. Rav Hai has the opposite version, that it follows the owner of the store, and this is also the version of Rashi. These are his words, and it is found in the Gemara (30b).

Seemingly, this is not understood at all, for certainly it is referring to a case where everyone eats there all year round. If this were not so, it would be obvious that we follow the one who eats. And if we say that none of them eat there, then it does not apply at all to say whom to follow. Rather, it is certain that they all eat there. If so, why should we follow this one? Let us follow that one! And indeed, according to the first version that we follow the workers, one can say the reason is that we follow the majority. For this is the implication of the language, that the shop owner is one person, and the workers are many. But according to the second version, it is difficult. It seems that this is why Rashi explained there that it is referring to merchandise that is chametz, for he explained: bread and wine sold within it. See there. According to this, it makes sense that we follow the merchandise from the shop, which is more than what the workers eat. According to this, it is possible to say that the versions do not disagree in practice, but according to Rabbeinu Chananel's version, it is not referring to chametz merchandise, and therefore we follow the workers who are the majority. (See Beit Yosef, Bach, and Taz, and in my humble opinion, it is as I have written.)

The Rif, the Rambam, and the Rosh did not mention this law at all. The Ra'avad in the book Tamim De'im (Siman 245) wrote that the reason for the Rif is that since there are different versions, we go stringently; see there. And it is not understood, for if so, it is obvious that he should have brought it and ruled stringently. And there are those who say the opposite, that both are lenient, since it is a rabbinic doubt (Chayei Adam). And this certainly cannot be said, for how could they disagree with the Baraita that the Talmud brought based on their own reasoning?

In my humble opinion, it seems that this Baraita was dismissed from the halacha. For according to what we have established in Siman 446 that we follow the latter, if so, here too we should follow the non-Jews, whether he is the shop owner or a worker, since he is the last to consume chametz, having eaten it throughout the days of Passover. And if chametz is found on the road after Passover, if it is possible to assume that it was made after Passover – it is also permitted for eating. If not – it is forbidden for eating but permitted for benefit (Bach and Magen Avraham). And there are those who say that we follow the majority of passersby (Chayei Adam). I am puzzled by this, because in any case: even if it belonged to a Jew, certainly he threw it away or lost it before Passover, and it would be considered ownerless and permitted. And if the reason is that perhaps it is chametz of a Jew who passed over Passover and then discarded it, which is forbidden for benefit, nevertheless there is still a double doubt: doubt if it belongs to a non-Jew, doubt if it belongs to a Jew; and if you say it belongs to a Jew, perhaps he discarded it before Passover (see Machatzit Hashekel who raised some of these points).

A Jew who borrowed a loaf of bread from his friend before Passover must repay it after Passover. If he does not repay it, it is considered theft. This is not considered an exchange for chametz (leavened bread), because although we hold that even though its monetary value is not retained, it is nevertheless initially forbidden, as I wrote at the end of Siman 443. This is not considered an exchange for chametz, because an exchange is only called such when the chametz is still in existence at the time he gives him the exchange, which is not the case when the chametz has already been consumed. According to this, even during Passover itself, he can receive other items in exchange for the loaf, except that after Passover he can also receive chametz (Chayei Adam, Section 1). However, in truth, in the case of a loan, it is permissible to repay a loaf after Passover, even if the original loaf is still in existence, as this has no connection at all to the exchange for chametz. A loan is given to be spent, and the borrower already acquired it before Passover and became obligated for its value (Maharam Chaviv, Section 1). Similarly, he can repay him with other items during Passover, as he is taking what he is owed. The rule we explained that it is only permissible when it is not in existence applies only to actual exchanges. (And it is not similar to the case of Shemitah in the beginning of the fifth chapter of Avodah Zarah, where Shemitah retains its value, which is not the case with chametz. Study this and you will find it easy to understand.) Certainly, for someone who buys chametz before Passover, he must repay it.

A Jew who receives a loaf of chametz (leavened bread) every week from a non-Jew as interest, which was stipulated at the time of the loan, what should he do during the week of Passover? He should tell him before Passover that during the week of Passover he should give him flour or money. Since he stipulated this with him, even if he gives him a loaf of chametz after Passover, it is considered an exchange for the flour or money and is permitted. And after the fact, even if he did not tell him, but the non-Jew brought him a loaf after Passover for the week of Passover - it is permitted, because the Jew did not acquire it during Passover (Bach and Magen Avraham, subsection 2). There is an opinion that it requires specifically a stipulation, and without a stipulation, it is forbidden (Taz, subsection 1). However, one should not be so stringent in this matter, as the entire prohibition of chametz that has passed over Passover is only due to a penalty (Chayei Adam, subsection 3). The same law applies to those who purchased the servants' ration, who receive chametz, that it is permitted to take after Passover what they lacked during Passover (ibid.), as in this case, the penalty does not apply at all, obviously.

Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote in section 3: If a Jew and a non-Jew have a joint ownership of an oven, the Jew should tell the non-Jew before Passover, "You take the oven for Passover, and I will take it afterward." Up to here is his wording. And even though regarding Shabbat, this method does not work unless they stipulated initially before forming the partnership, as I wrote earlier in section 245, because in that case, since both are obligated to use the oven every day, it would be like renting out for Shabbat, since the non-Jew bakes on Shabbat because the Jew bakes on Sunday. But here, there is no prohibition in the act of baking itself, and indeed one can bake matzah in it. The Jew is not telling the non-Jew during Passover, "You bake chametz, and I will bake chametz after Passover," which would certainly be forbidden. Rather, he says simply, "You bake this week, and I will bake another week." Therefore, it is certainly forbidden to say, "However many loaves you bake during Passover, I will bake afterward." (And so wrote the Magen Avraham in section 3). This seems to me to be the rationale for the permission. The great authorities have struggled with this, and in my humble opinion, it appears as I have written (and this is the intention of the Magen Avraham in section 3).

And it is obvious that on the Shabbat that falls during Passover, it is forbidden, as stated earlier in Siman 345. There are those who wish to prohibit this even on the four days of the festival as on Shabbat, but this is not so. For on a festival, the preparation of food is permissible. And even though baking for Gentiles is forbidden for us on the festival, nevertheless, he does not tell him to bake for them, and he can bake for those who are permitted. This then becomes similar to the reasoning we wrote regarding chametz in the previous section (and legally, the Chayei Adam in subsection 4 agrees with this). There are those who say that even regarding chametz, the Jew must receive payment from him for his portion before Passover, but this is not obligatory (see Magen Avraham there, and analyze and you will find it easy).

It is further written in Section 4: A Jewish person who had an oven, and non-Jews baked chametz in it during Passover—even receiving money as payment for its use is prohibited, as this would be considered deriving benefit from prohibited items. However, if he has already received the money, it is permitted to benefit from it. This is his exact wording, meaning: It is not only if they brought him loaves after Passover, which would be forbidden to benefit from since he acquired them during Passover as payment for his oven, thus making it chametz that belonged to a Jew over Passover; but even if they brought him money, this is also prohibited because he is benefiting from prohibited items. This is not similar to the case of a partnership oven discussed in the previous law, where he does not benefit during Passover itself, as the week of Passover is for the non-Jew. And even if he takes another week in exchange, we have already explained the reason, because he does not tell him "bake chametz." But here, where the oven entirely belongs to him and chametz was baked in it, how can he take payment for chametz and benefit from prohibited items? However, if he received money, it is permitted after the fact, because chametz does not retain its monetary value. And even though exchanging it itself is forbidden, as I wrote at the end of Siman 443, this applies to directly exchanging chametz, not in this manner. (The Taz in Section 3 is puzzled that the two laws in Section 3 and Section 4 contradict each other. According to what I have written, there is no contradiction. This is also implied by the Magen Avraham in Section 4, see there. Similarly, it is written in Tosafot, Avodah Zarah 62a, "What is the reason?").

The Tur wrote that it is permissible to rent one's oven to a non-Jew on the condition that he bakes matzah in it. Even if he bakes chametz in it, the owner does not need to worry and can collect the rental fee. Although with yayin nesekh (wine used for idolatrous purposes), it is not so. If he rented it to do other work and ended up using it for yayin nesekh, the payment is forbidden, as I have written in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 133. There, if he did not do the work, he would not receive any payment; hence, when he receives payment, it is considered payment for yayin nesekh. This is not the case with an oven rented for a day or a week; even if no baking occurs at all, the tenant must still pay the rental fee. Therefore, it does not matter if he bakes chametz, as the agreement was for matzah (Magen Avraham, Sif Katan 5). Thus, if the stipulation was explicit that payment only occurs if baking happens, and no payment if not, it is forbidden. 

One should not question what benefit the condition provides since we are certain chametz will be baked, similar to the case in Siman 246, where one cannot rent a horse to rest on Shabbat because it will certainly not rest. This was raised as an objection (Taz, Sif Katan 4). However, this is not analogous, as there, he is commanded concerning the rest of his animal, and since it is known that it will not rest, it is forbidden. Here, he is not commanded regarding the rest of the oven from chametz, only that he should not benefit from chametz. Since he rents out his oven not specifically for chametz but generally, he is not receiving payment for chametz (Chok Yaakov, Sif Katan 8). All the more so if he explicitly states that it is to bake something other than chametz.

And when one rents a house to a non-Jew during Passover or on the eve of Passover, it is forbidden to explicitly rent it out for the purpose of bringing chametz into it. Rather, one should rent it out without specifying, and if afterwards the non-Jew brings chametz into it, it does not concern us, since the rent is not for the chametz, but for the dwelling. However, before Passover, it is permitted to rent it out even if it is explicitly rented for bringing in chametz, since it is not specified to bring it in during Passover, and the rent is taken for what is brought in before Passover (the Gra, section 11). There are those who are stringent even for the thirty days before Passover (Pri Chadash). However, it is obvious that if the Jew must guard the chametz, it is forbidden during Passover even if the chametz belongs to the non-Jew. Although it is permitted to see it, as we say, "You shall not see your own, but you may see that of others," guarding it is forbidden, even if guarding it for free, because one desires its existence. And any desire for its existence is forbidden in all prohibitions of benefit, like in the case of idolatrous wine in Yoreh De'ah there (section 18, subsection 9). (The Pri Chadash elaborates that with chametz there is no prohibition of "desire for its existence," see there. And he is against the Tur and the Posekim.)

It is forbidden for a Jew to purchase chametz during Passover on behalf of a non-Jew, even with the non-Jew’s money, because this involves three prohibitions: desiring the existence of chametz, which is prohibited as I have written; furthermore, he might come to eat it; and additionally, there is no agency for a non-Jew, so it is considered as if he is purchasing it for himself (Magen Avraham, subsection 10). Similarly, it is forbidden to assist in matters related to chametz, such as loading a non-Jew’s chametz onto a wagon, as the non-Jew will feel grateful to him, which is considered as deriving benefit from prohibited items (ibid.). Even in his absence, where there is no feeling of gratitude, it appears to be forbidden, as it is akin to desiring its existence. However, in a case of animal suffering, such as if his animal is burdened with chametz and is lying under its load, where it is a mitzvah to unload it, he is obligated to do so due to the positive commandment from the Torah. In such a case, we do not worry about the non-Jew feeling grateful, as it is considered a situation of "impossible and not intentional," which is permitted (ibid.), as stated in Pesachim (25b).

It is forbidden to rent a utensil to a non-Jew for cooking chametz (leavened food) during Pesach (Passover), as this would involve deriving benefit from prohibited substances. However, renting it out without specifying its use is permitted, as it is not exclusively meant for chametz. But in the case of an oven, this is forbidden, as an oven is typically used for baking chametz. Therefore, one must stipulate that it be used for baking matzah, as I wrote in paragraph 6. However, the Tur prohibits renting out a utensil for another reason, namely because one desires the utensil to be preserved through its use, so it does not break. This means that one wants the chametz to remain inside it; otherwise, the utensil would crack from the fire, hence deriving benefit from the chametz. Additionally, it is written that since the utensil itself is forbidden for benefit due to the absorption of chametz, it is forbidden to rent it out initially. However, it is permitted to rent out a donkey or a horse to carry a load, and even if it carries chametz, it does not concern us. But explicitly for carrying chametz, it is forbidden. (All of this is based on the words of the Magen Avraham, subsection 11, and it is true according to the law.)

There was an incident involving Jews who sold their chametz to non-Jews on the eve of Passover, and the chametz was placed in a room not far from the river. During Passover, the waters overflowed and neared the room, threatening to destroy all the chametz. They permitted the Jews to go to the non-Jew who bought the chametz and say to him, "Look and save your merchandise." If the non-Jew is not present, they can say to another non-Jew, "Look, the merchandise of so-and-so is about to be lost," and through this, the chametz will be moved to another location (Shaarei Teshuva, section 13, quoting Sh"Y). However, it is forbidden for a Jew himself to save chametz on Passover.

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote in Section 7: "There are those who permit heating water in a chametz utensil and washing with it, as well as other uses for enjoyment with a chametz utensil. And this is the custom." This is the end of his words. Such as placing cold items in it temporarily when dry, or moist items that are not edible, such as washing and the like (Chayei Adam, Section 14). It is clear that this applies to a utensil that has not been used for chametz within the past 24 hours. And know that according to the second reasoning of the Tur in Section 9, which forbids renting the utensil due to the absorbed chametz – it is certainly forbidden to use it. There are those who forbid it for this reason (see Magen Avraham, Section 12). Nevertheless, the main ruling is that it is permitted. Perhaps the Tur's intention is regarding a utensil that has absorbed a significant amount of chametz and is within 24 hours. This requires further study. And now, in our times, we do not use any chametz utensils. Even if the chametz was used cold in them, like water containers – we do not use them on Passover.

When a person has a non-Jewish servant in his house, it is permitted to say to him during Passover: "Here is this coin, go and buy and eat," even though he knows that the servant will buy chametz (leavened bread) and eat it. For he does not derive any benefit from this, and he also does not tell him to buy chametz. However, the servant should not eat in his house because of suspicion, lest people say that he gave him the chametz. But one should not say to him, "Go and eat, and I will pay you back," when he knows that he will definitely feed him chametz. This is the ruling of the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch in section 6, and their words are puzzling. For they themselves ruled in Yoreh De'ah, section 132, regarding yayin nesekh (wine used for idolatrous libations) in such a case, that it is permitted unless he gave a coin to the shopkeeper in advance, in which case the prohibition is acquired by him. But if he did not give a coin in advance, it is permitted, because how is the prohibition acquired by him? And when he pays, the prohibition is no longer in existence. And at the time when they eat or drink the prohibited item, it belongs to the shopkeeper, not the house owner. And indeed, the Mordechai also does not forbid it here with chametz, unless he gave a coin to the shopkeeper in advance, or he handled the chametz and gave it to them. This is the opinion of the "yesh omrim" (some say) brought by the Beit Yosef; see there. And so ruled the great Acharonim (later authorities) (Magen Avraham, section 9, and Pri Chadash). The first opinion, which is the opinion of the Tur, is puzzling.

And there is one who wrote that due to the stringency of chametz, they were stringent (Chayei Adam, Small Section 11, and Eliyah Rabbah), but there is no reason for this. And there is one who says that the Jew acts as a guarantor for them regarding the chametz, that if it is lost from the time they receive it until they put it in their mouths, they become liable for its responsibility, and it is like the chametz of a non-Jew for which the Jew accepted responsibility, which transgresses "you shall not see" (Magen Avraham, Small Section 4). And this too is nothing, for in what way did he accept responsibility?

And in my humble opinion, the words of the Tur are correct and necessary, that the prohibition is because he wants the chametz to exist. For if not, he would have to feed them other food. This is not the case with yayin nesech (wine used for idolatry), where he does not want it to exist, for even if they do not drink it, he will not give them another, as there is no delay in drinking wine like there is in eating bread, as is evident. Therefore, he does not want it to exist and it is permitted.

And someone who has a baby, and the baby cries to eat chametz, and it is impossible to stop him, the great authorities have written that it is permissible to tell a non-Jew: “Feed him or give him chametz to drink, and I will pay you” (Magen Avraham there). And this follows their view, which rejects the words of the Tur. But according to how we have explained his words – it is forbidden to say so, rather he should say: “Give him food,” and consequently he will give him chametz. Or he should give him a coin and say to him: “Feed this baby with this coin.” And all this is in the case of a baby who is not in danger if he does not eat chametz. But when there is danger – everything is permitted (there). And one is obligated to feed him himself, as with any life-threatening situation that overrides all prohibitions. Therefore, in our case where there are many nursing infants, who from birth are accustomed to being fed soaked dry bread called "sukharyakes" made from wheat flour, and if they do not receive it even for one day they will become ill and are likely to die – one is obligated to prepare these dry breads before Passover, and to store them in a hidden place, and to have a special vessel and spoon for this. And whenever needed, they should be mixed with hot water or milk, and placed in the baby’s mouth, taking care with the crumbs. And if it can be done through a non-Jew – it is better.

The great Acharonim have delved extensively into the matter of "arendas" and those who hold mills, from the nobles who receive a measure of grain for grinding a certain amount. Some grind complete chametz, like malt. How can a Jew receive these measures even after Pesach and profit from chametz during Pesach? And also, since the chametz is his, he has violated "bal yera’eh" (the prohibition against chametz being seen in one's possession during Pesach). It is obvious that the arenda or the mill should be sold before Pesach, similar to the sale for Shabbat (as mentioned in Bach) and as we do, as I wrote in Siman 448. 

Some have questioned: How does the sale take effect? It is a matter that has not yet come into existence (Taz, subsection 6), since before Pesach the chametz has not yet come, so how can it be sold? However, this is not a difficulty, because if so, the Jew has also not acquired it from the noble (Magen Avraham, subsection 8). Moreover, renunciation is effective even for something that has not yet come into existence, and he is renouncing his involvement in the business (Pri Megadim). 

In truth, all these acquisitions are based on the custom of merchants and the law of the kingdom, just as we sell goods that are not yet in our possession according to a contract, as I wrote in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 201, subsection 16. See there. The same applies here. Therefore, the Jew acquires from the noble, and the non-Jew acquires from him. There is no reason to doubt this at all, and this is also our practice concerning Shabbat and Yom Tov.

Pots made of earthenware, or bowls and frying pans made of earthenware, that were used for chametz throughout the year, even those used for porridge and various flours, which are all chametz and stick around the pot – should be thoroughly scrubbed so that no chametz is visible on them, and it is permissible to keep them after Passover and use them, whether for its kind or for a different kind. This is not similar to chametz that got mixed in, which is forbidden to keep as I wrote in Siman 447, for there the chametz is visible but not recognizable. This is not the case here: the chametz is absorbed in the vessel and is not recognizable. Moreover, what is absorbed becomes a foul taste after twenty-four hours. And even though during Passover itself we prohibit a foul taste as I wrote in Siman 447, nonetheless after Passover, since the prohibition is only due to a penalty – it was not prohibited. And even though for all other prohibitions we prohibit the vessel even after twenty-four hours, as I wrote in Yoreh De'ah Siman 122, and there is no difference between a Torah prohibition and a rabbinic prohibition, for even a vessel that absorbed poultry and milk, which is a rabbinic prohibition, is also forbidden, nonetheless for chametz, the pot is not prohibited. The reason may be said: because chametz was absorbed when it was permissible, during the time of absorption, it was not a prohibition. This is not the case with prohibited substances, which were absorbed when prohibited. Moreover: there it is an accident, but chametz happens every year, and it is impossible to destroy all the pots in the world. (See Tosafot Pesachim 30a, s.v. "and let them remain", and Ran there. And they wrote for the Master who ruled according to Rabbi Yehuda, and we hold according to Rabbi Shimon.)

There is an opinion that although on Passover itself, if one cooked in a pot that has not been used for a day, the food would be forbidden, as I wrote in Siman 447, nevertheless, if twelve months have passed since the pot was used for cooking chametz, its taste has completely dissipated, and the food is permitted (Chatzot Siman 75). The proof is from yayin nesach (wine used for idolatry), where aging for twelve months is effective, as I wrote in Yoreh De'ah Siman 138. However, in the responsa of the Rashba (Siman 515), it is explicitly written that this is not the case, and this is his language: A pot that has not been used for a day in which something was cooked… the vessel remains prohibited. And it is clear that aging is only effective for wine vessels... until here is his language. Therefore, one should not rely on this (see Sha'arei Teshuva, small section 1). However, it can be combined with another leniency if there is a situation that permits it.

And these chametz utensils should be stored away during Pesach in a concealed place where one does not usually go, so that one will not come to use them during Pesach. And it is good to lock them in a room and hide the key. Some people place these utensils high up on the walls, where the hand cannot reach. Some of the great authorities have protested against this and brought proof from the law of studying by the light of a candle on Shabbat, which is forbidden even if the candle is two stories high (Beit Yosef). However, this is not a valid proof because there the concern is that one might tilt the candle and come to a Torah prohibition. This is not the case here, where it is a minor rabbinic prohibition, as the utensils are not used within the day, and there is no proof to forbid it. Certainly, regarding utensils used in a secondary vessel (Magen Avraham, subsection 2), there is no reason to object. Therefore, according to the strict letter of the law, there is no need to protest, and one who is stringent will be blessed.

The Sages stated (Pesachim 30b) that earthenware vessels are unique in that boiling does not help them, and even burning does not help. Even if one fills them with coals, which would certainly expel the prohibition, it does not help. The reason is that we are concerned that one might have pity on them so that they do not crack, and thus reduce the coals, and not perform the heating properly. Therefore, no heating by fire helps for them, nor for any earthenware vessels that were used with hot substances, even if not directly on the fire but by pouring boiling liquids into them, because pouring also absorbs much into earthenware vessels. As it says in Zevachim (95b) regarding the verse "And any earthenware vessel into which it is cooked shall be broken" – this teaches only about cooking in it; from where do we know about pouring boiling liquid into it? The verse states, "it shall be broken," see there. There are those who prohibit even in a secondary vessel, meaning if one poured from the pot into a secondary vessel, and then placed this vessel into it. This is according to the Rambam in Chapter Five (according to the Maggid Mishneh and the Beit Yosef). However, the opinion of the Tur is not like this. And some say that the Rambam does not hold this either, and his intention is only regarding pouring from a primary vessel (Magen Avraham, small paragraph 3). However, the Rashba holds that in all prohibitions, a secondary vessel also forbids, and therefore the custom is to be stringent with a secondary vessel for chametz as with a primary vessel (ibid.). But with a tertiary vessel, one should not be stringent post facto.

And this which was explained that heating does not help for earthenware vessels, our master the Beit Yosef wrote in Section A, and this is his wording: However, if one returned it to the kiln where new earthenware vessels are fired - it is permitted, because since it is subjected to such intense heat - surely he is not concerned about them lest they crack. But in our ovens - no. Until here is his wording, for there is concern that he might be careful with them and remove them from the oven before they become white-hot (Taz, Section 2, in the name of the Rosh). And specifically earthenware vessels, but metal vessels that do not crack from the fire - one can fill them with coals from the inside (Tur), and leave the coals there until if one touches the outer side of the vessel - his hand recoils from it because the vessel has become white-hot from the coals. Then surely all the chametz absorbed in it is burned, even though it has not become so white-hot that sparks fly from it, for metal vessels are purified by boiling, and this light heating is not worse than boiling, and it is thus purified (Gra, Section 10).

And know that nowadays we use pots made of a type of metal which are called "Praysisah Tap," and they are made of metal, with some kind of coating inside. The custom is to burn these pots for Passover if they were used for chametz. Some people are not pleased with this because it is known that they can crack. However, truly there is no concern for several reasons: Firstly, we do not find this concern in the Talmud except regarding earthenware vessels. Furthermore, the way they are burned is as follows: they are placed inside the walls of the oven, and many pieces of wood are put into the oven, and the pots are filled with ash and the oven is heated, and the pots remain there for twenty-four hours and more until they cool down. Their nature is such that if they are removed from the oven before they cool down, they will break. The burning is like in a kiln, and consequently, there is no concern that they will crack, as we have explained that this concern is due to the possibility of removing them from the oven before they are fully heated, and here, on the contrary, care is taken to remove them only after they have fully cooled down, otherwise, they would crack. Additionally, since it suffices to kasher them through boiling, there is no need to be overly concerned about the burning, as in any case, it is not worse than boiling.

And for an oven, it is obvious that libun (burning out) is effective, contrary to the opinion of some who are stringent based on the words of the Tosafot, which state that even repeated heating does not help for an oven (Bach). However, this is incorrect, as that pertains to matters of ritual purity and impurity, where if it was impure, it would not become pure through this method. But regarding matters of prohibition and permission (Magen Avraham, subsection 4), the Gemara states that filling a pot with coals does not help because the pot is always heated from the outside, see there. But an oven is heated from the inside. Additionally, our ovens are not like their ovens, which are the type of oven mentioned in the Torah, which is small and portable, similar to a pot. Our ovens are more like actual buildings, and it is obvious that libun is effective.

And our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in Section 2: A "kobia," which is a utensil made from bricks and earth, used for baking and frying, and similarly, a small oven called a "pidlyah" that is heated from the outside – it is forbidden to bake in it on Passover, because the leaven within it is not expelled in this manner. However, if it is filled with coals from the inside – it is permitted. Thus is his wording, for in this case, there is no concern that it might crack, since it is made from bricks and earth (Taz, Subsection 4). And a "kobia" made from bricks that were fired in a kiln – it has the same status as earthenware vessels, for its nature is exactly like earthenware vessels except that it is much thicker, and if something boiling spills on it – it has no remedy except through intense heating (Magen Avraham, Subsection 4). We do not know these utensils. And a brick that has been dried in the sun – has the status of an earthen vessel (ibid.). And it is written in the Tur that Rav Hai Gaon's opinion is that dung vessels and stone vessels – have the same status as earthenware, and scalding does not help them, only intense heating. However, the Rif disagreed with him and ruled that they are like wooden and metal vessels, and scalding helps them, and this is the main ruling (Tur). And our "kalkalin" – they fill them with many coals and they are fit for Passover.

And know that new pots obtained from non-Jews, as well as all types of utensils obtained from them, whether earthenware, metal, or glass, if they are sold in the market and appear new – we do not need to be concerned that they might have been used, for those intended for sale are not used. However, utensils found in [a non-Jew’s] home – one should only take a new utensil that is certainly unused. But if there is doubt – one should not take it unless the seller casually mentions that it has not been used. As for glass utensils, they may be permitted even without a casual mention, if they appear clear and new, indicating they have not been used (Gra”z, section 5). And glass utensils used for drinking hot beverages – certainly do not absorb any prohibition other than hot beverages and sugar. And the proof is: we drink from them when we are with them, and it is known that all glass utensils designated for drinking hot beverages are not used for anything else, except for Passover one should not purchase them. Additionally, we do not drink hot beverages with them during Passover, because occasionally they soak dry bread in them. But for the rest of the year – there is no concern, for even if something else might enter them by chance – we follow the majority of their use.

Chametz knives, according to the basic law, are like all utensils used with hot foods and require immersion in a primary vessel (kli rishon). However, it is a pious practice to elevate the treatment of knives since they are frequently used with chametz and may have unnoticed cracks. Additionally, there are times when pieces of bread are inserted into the knife's tip to roast over the fire, or it is used to cut a pastry on the fire, which requires burning (libun), as some require for knives used with prohibited substances as I wrote in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 121. Therefore, one who can obtain new knives is praiseworthy. If this is not possible, one should burn the metal in the fire and immerse the handle in boiling water. If this too is difficult, such as if the metal will be damaged, then the entire knife should be immersed in boiling water, as we follow the majority of its use, which is with hot chametz. If the handle is made of wood and is attached with small nails, there is an opinion that immersion does not suffice because there may be hidden crevices (Bach). This is merely a stringency. Our custom is that if the metal is well attached to the handle and there are no cracks between them, we immerse it. Rust must be removed beforehand. (I saw in Atret Zekeinim, section 1, that one should not place anything on a winter oven, nor on kachelin. Even if it is plastered with clay as thick as a finger, some prohibit and some permit. So far his words. It is clear that if one places burning coals in the kachelin, it is permitted. Regarding the winter oven called lizanaka, which is very large, one may use it covered with a layer of clay according to those who permit. If a new sheet is placed on it, it is certainly permitted to use it on Passover. As for the oven used all year round, it should not be used on Passover, as it is difficult to kasher. See section 44.)

Any utensil that requires libun (burning) or hagalah (boiling) – it is forbidden to use it even for cold things without kashering it. If one used it temporarily – it is permitted after the fact, if it was clean or if it was washed beforehand. Any item that requires libun, if one performed hagalah instead of libun and used it with something hot – it is forbidden even after the fact, because it has not been fully purged by the hagalah, and as long as it is used – it releases small amounts (Ch. 10, small section 10). And the sheath of knives, which is a case where the knives are placed all year – hagalah is not effective for it, because it is impossible to clean it thoroughly from the visible chametz that is stuck to it. Therefore, on Passover, one should not place the knives into it. If one wishes to open the stitches and scrape it well, it does not even require hagalah (the Gra”z, section 23), since it has never been used with heat.

Immersion in a primary vessel is defined as a vessel that was heated by the fire; even though it is now removed from the fire, it is still considered a primary vessel as long as it retains heat that would cause the hand to recoil. Any vessel, before its immersion, must have all its rust removed. If a knife has rust, it must be thoroughly polished with a grinder or a stone. If a knife or any other vessel has crevices and cannot be properly cleaned, immersion will not be effective, and it requires heating in those crevices. This means placing burning coals there. This specifically refers to rust that has substance. However, mere blackness or redness, such as found on pots and pans, where even after removing the rust, a mark remains, is not a concern. Otherwise, it would be nearly impossible to find any vessel that could be immersed (Taz, subsection 6).

Utensils that are used with fire without water, such as spits and grills that are used for roasting over fire and similar items, require libun (burning). Hagalah (purging by boiling) is not effective for them, for what is absorbed through water, like cooking, is purged through water. But what is absorbed through fire cannot be purged through water, only through fire. Therefore, trays used for baking bread or pastries require libun. However, a frying pan used to fry bread with fat, oil, or butter is considered like cooking, and hagalah is sufficient. For what difference does it make whether it’s water or fat? And even though fat is much less than water in a pot, there is no measure for this matter. Some say that the frying pan requires libun because sometimes the fat dries up, and the dough bakes directly on the pan. However, a light libun is sufficient, and it suffices when a straw burns on it from the outside. The custom is to perform libun initially. However, if hagalah was performed, it is acceptable post facto if there are no cracks in it. We do not trouble the person to do libun afterward, as the primary ruling is that hagalah is sufficient. See section 52.

Complete libun (purging by fire) is until sparks fly from it. Some are lenient and say that it is sufficient until straw burns on it from the outside. Specifically regarding chametz, which was absorbed when it was permitted – some say that such libun is sufficient. Others hold that chametz is considered "absorbed prohibition," since chametz is considered prohibited concerning Pesach even before Pesach (see Magen Avraham, subsection 11, and Taz, subsection 8). The custom follows the first opinion. However, this applies to an item that definitely requires libun. But for an item that one is only stringent to perform libun on, such as a frying pan or similar, or if there are cracks, grooves, or rust in the utensil necessitating libun – light libun, as explained, suffices. The tripod, which is a utensil with three legs used to support a pot, requires libun, as sometimes something spills from the pot onto it. If there is dough in the pot and a piece of dough spills, it is like a spit and requires libun. However, it seems that light libun, where straw burns on the outside, is sufficient.

All kashering is according to its usage: if its usage is in a primary vessel (kli rishon), such as a spoon that stirs in a pot, or a vessel that draws from a primary vessel (Chayei Adam, section 27) – it requires kashering in a primary vessel. And know that it seems clear that an item whose usage is directly on the fire, such as a pot in which food is cooked – immersing it in a primary vessel does not suffice, rather it must be directly on the fire. For it has already been clarified above in Siman 318 that a primary vessel is of a lesser degree than that which stands on the fire, as explained in the Jerusalem Talmud and elucidated by the Rambam, see there. Therefore, since the general rule in kashering is "as its usage, so is its kashering," if its usage is by standing on the fire – its kashering must also be the same. And this is implied by the language of the Rambam, who wrote in Chapter 5, Halacha 23: Metal and stone vessels that were used for chametz with boiling water in a primary vessel, such as pots and pans – one places them into a large vessel of water, fills it with water, and boils it until it expels [the absorbed chametz]. Afterward, one rinses them with cold water and uses them for matzah. Thus far his language, indicating that he wrote regarding pots that "one boils them in it," meaning: he boils them on the fire.

However, from the words of the Tur and Shulchan Aruch in section 5, it does not seem so, as they wrote: "If they are used in a primary vessel, such as a spoon that stirs in a pot – it needs to be purified in a primary vessel." This is their language. And indeed, the spoon is used when the pot is on the fire, and the purification is in a primary vessel. And the Levush wrote explicitly: "such as a metal pot or a spoon," see there. And if we say that he holds that a primary vessel expels even what was absorbed by the fire, where do we get this from? And in any case, they should have explained this. Therefore, it seems to me that according to what we have explained in Yoreh De'ah, section 68 and earlier in section 318 – the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch did not go into the difference between this and that, and all are included in the term "primary vessel." Therefore, here too, their intention is the same. And in practice, certainly it does not help for a pot, or a spoon that stirred the pot, to be purified in a primary vessel, unless it is standing on the fire. Or as they place heated stones into the water, which is also like on the fire, as will be explained. However, it is possible that this too is only like a primary vessel, as there is someone who holds that even as a primary vessel it is not (Bach, brought by the Magen Avraham, section 18).

According to this, a utensil that is used directly on the fire must be kashered through fire. A utensil that is used in a primary vessel after it has been removed from the fire must also be kashered similarly. A utensil that was used in a secondary vessel, such as a spoon inserted into a bowl into which something was poured from a pot, must be kashered in a secondary vessel. A utensil that is used through pouring, like a bowl into which something is poured from a pot, must be kashered through pouring from a primary vessel, but not from a secondary vessel. This means that even if the bowl is put into a secondary vessel in which one's hand would recoil from the heat (yad soledet bo), it does not suffice (see Taz, Section 9, who also did not differentiate between on the fire and in a primary vessel). And it has already been explained that any utensil that has cracks, crevices, or rust, in such a way that it cannot be scrubbed and cleaned, immersion does not suffice. Rather, one must place coals on that area.

All utensils are determined by their primary use. Therefore, bowls, even though sometimes they are used as a primary vessel on the fire, nevertheless, since their primary use is by pouring from a primary vessel onto them, this is how they are made kosher. Some are stringent to immerse even the bowls in a primary vessel, and this is the common custom and should not be altered, because the masses do not differentiate between them. All the more so with spoons and forks, which are often inserted into the pot. The custom is to be stringent with all drinking utensils, to immerse them if they are fit to be immersed, even though they are used with cold, because sometimes they are used with hot. Additionally, bread crumbs are soaked in them for a full day, and what is soaked is considered as cooked. In a pressing situation, rinsing them thoroughly is sufficient, as I wrote in section 49, see there.

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote in paragraph 6 that for large bowls that cannot be inserted into a primary vessel, one should place a heated stone on them and pour boiling water from a primary vessel over them, and this is considered like a primary vessel. Similarly, for anything comparable to this. And one should move the stone over the entire vessel so that the entire vessel is purged. Until here is his wording. And even if perhaps in some place the stone did not touch, the boiling water touched there. There are those who say that this is not considered like a primary vessel and does not help at all, as by law it requires purging (Magen Avraham, section 18, in the name of the Bach). Similarly, if the vessel has grooves or protrusions where it is impossible to move the stone, this does not help (ibid.). And now the custom is to thoroughly heat small stones in the fire and place them in the water, and then the boiling increases greatly, and one pours the water over the places and also moves the heated stone. And this certainly helps even in places that by law require purging, as it is better than a primary vessel, as we see with our own eyes.

One who has utensils made of wood, stone, metal, or bone - their law is to purify them through immersion in boiling water. There are those who say that spoons made of horn cannot be purified through immersion in boiling water, because since they get damaged in hot water, we are concerned that the person may be lenient and not immerse them properly. Similarly, the handles of knives that are partially made of horn, or if the handle is glued together, we are concerned that it might come apart. It seems to me that all these are stringencies, and after the fact, immersion in boiling water is effective.

Baskets in which meat is salted - some require them to be immersed in boiling water. Even though the meat itself is permissible, as I wrote in Siman 467, this is because even if there was some chametz (leavened bread) in the salt, it was nullified before Pesach. However, for the utensil, nullification does not apply. There are those who disagree and say they do not need immersion in boiling water, and their words seem correct. Nevertheless, it is good to immerse them or to buy new ones. There are those who say that immersion in boiling water is not effective at all, because perhaps there is visible chametz in the crevices (Taz, Siman 15). All this is for the outset, but after the fact, if they salted meat on Pesach using baskets that were used all year - it is permitted without any purification, because the salt is not assumed to contain chametz. Additionally, salting is not effective in causing utensils to absorb, as I wrote in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 105 (Magen Avraham there). Similarly, if they soaked the meat in a soaking vessel used all year, and rinsed it after salting in that vessel - it is permitted, and there is no concern. Similarly, if they salted on the board used all year for salting.

And with a frying pan, we have already written in section 13 that it is sufficient with immersion in boiling water (hag'alah), but there are those who are stringent and require heating until red-hot (libun). And the custom is to heat it until red-hot initially, and after the fact, immersion in boiling water is sufficient. And know that any immersion in boiling water where it is not possible to immerse the entire utensil at once due to its size, such as a frying pan and the like, one can first immerse one half and then turn it over and immerse the other half. And if it is very long such that the middle cannot enter the immersion vessel, one heats the middle until red-hot and immerses the sides. And one who immerses before the fifth hour can immerse a primary utensil and a secondary utensil together, and similarly utensils that absorbed a lot of chametz with utensils that absorbed a little chametz. And one can also immerse the utensil twice. All of this does not apply when immersing after the fifth hour. The reason for this will be explained with the help of Heaven in section 452. And there are several details in this; refer there.

All handles of all utensils require immersion in boiling water (hagalah). This is not because they also absorb chametz, as absorption does not spread throughout the entire utensil, as I wrote in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 121. Additionally, if absorption spreads, it would be expelled in the same manner as it was absorbed. Rather, the reason is that the handle surely absorbed some chametz flavor over the course of the year, and now, during Pesach, it will come into contact with matzah. However, if one did not immerse the handles, it does not render the utensil forbidden post facto, as this is merely a concern. Nonetheless, the entire spoon must be immersed because it often gets entirely immersed in the pot, and even post facto it is problematic. Similarly, with a knife, one should be stringent even post facto, since the Gemara (30b) requires the handle to be koshered, and we should not be lenient (Taz, Siman 17). However, it is certainly sufficient to kosher the handles by pouring boiling water over them, since their absorption is not even equivalent to pouring. There are those who say post facto leniency applies only if the utensil has already been used, but if it has not been used, it is forbidden even post facto until the handle is immersed (Magen Avraham, Siman 24). This is not conclusive, and one may permit the utensil even before use (see Chayei Adam, Siman 40). A utensil that was used in its entirety and was partially koshered, and then used again on that part, is permitted. But if used on the part that was not koshered, it is forbidden (Magen Avraham, ibid.).

A vessel that has a patch, such as a metal or copper vessel that, when it has a hole or crack, they place a patch there, and therefore the boiling water (used for koshering) does not extract the absorbed (non-kosher substance) that is under the patch. However, if the patch was fused with fire onto the place – there is no concern about this, because at the time of placing the patch, all the forbidden substance was burned away (Taz, subsection 18; and Magen Avraham, subsection 41). However, a patch made with nails, meaning they place a piece of metal on the spot and fix it with nails – in this case, there are detailed laws, as will be explained. And among us, most patches are made by fusing with tin, and therefore we do not have all these laws. And some are mistaken about this.

Patches that are attached by nails: if the patch was placed before the utensil absorbed the forbidden substance, meaning the patch was placed while the utensil was still new, or if it was boiled before the patch was placed – there is no need to remove it now. For if it absorbed anything while the patch was on it – it will release it the same way it absorbed it, and before that it did not absorb anything. And if there is a concern that there might be small holes where crumbs of chametz could have entered – they should be cleaned. And if it is truly impossible to clean – place a little bit of coals there. However, if the absorption of the forbidden substance preceded the patch, then the absorbed substance under the patch will not be expelled through boiling, and it will be released little by little; therefore, either remove the patch before boiling, or place coals on the area of the patch, such that sparks fly from it, ensuring that the forbidden substance, if present, is definitely burned. After that, boil the entire utensil. There are some who want to say that even if the patch preceded the absorption, one should always perform a light burning (libun kal) on that area (Magen Avraham, subsection 27). This is an excessive stringency and is not necessary (Chayei Adam, subsection 42). And this is the main ruling in practice.

And old vessels that have been coated with tin, which is called "whitening," where the coating is done with heat using molten lead – some have been stringent and required immersion afterward as well. And some have said that this whitening alone suffices, and this is the main ruling. For even if it is a light form of whitening – it is preferable to immersion. And one of the great early authorities (Rabbi Eliyahu Mizrachi) proved that this is necessarily the case, for otherwise, what would the immersion accomplish? The coating interrupts between the absorbed matter and the immersion, and it is like before absorption to a patch. Furthermore: since the tin interrupts – it is considered as a new vessel. (Magen Avraham there. And it is also explained from the Taz, subsection 18, who wrote: when a piece of tin is dripped – it burns all the absorbed matter, see there. And it is also visible to the eyes, that the heat is as intense as actual fire. Especially since they are not used within a day. And there is no reason to be stringent in this matter, and thus we rule in practice.)

The markings that craftsmen make on utensils, which include engraved letters, do not have the same status as cracks and crevices that would require libun (intense heating). This is because they are made anew before their use, and they are also made smooth, thin, and straight, so that hagalah (boiling) can cleanse them effectively, and they can be cleaned thoroughly as needed. If it is impossible to clean them, it is necessary to place a few coals there. Similarly, it is necessary to scrape well around the ears of the utensils, for there are sometimes fine indentations there. Likewise, when the handles of utensils are attached with nails, such as with shovels, it is necessary to scrape well around the nails, for there are sometimes fine indentations there as well. And the same applies to all similar cases.

A metal cover used to cover a pot requires hagalah (boiling), because it constantly sweats from the heat of the pot and from the steam rising from the food, and this gets absorbed into it—its status is like that of the pot itself. Indeed, concerning a cover, we are even stricter in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 93, where we treat a cover that is not used within a day as if it were used within a day. And although many disagree there and even those who are stringent only do so for a deep and short cover, as explained there, nevertheless, regarding Passover, where the prohibition is severe even with a tiny amount, and since there are those who forbid even when the taste is spoiled, as I wrote in Siman 447, we certainly should be stringent. And if one covered a pot on Passover with a chametz cover, the entire dish should be forbidden because the sweat from the cover mixes with the dish. However, everything depends on the specific circumstances; if a lot of time has passed since the cover was used with chametz and it was completely dry, the dish should not be forbidden. This is for a pot cover, for which hagalah is sufficient. But a metal cover that is placed on chametz bread requires libun (burning). Certainly, metal trays or other metal vessels in which chametz was baked require libun. If matzah was baked in them before libun, even if they were subjected to hagalah, and the same applies to their covers, all the matzah becomes forbidden, even if they were not used within the day, because they absorb a lot.

A mortar, whether made of wood, stone, or metal, in which chametz is sometimes placed to pound together with garlic and onions, requires hagalah (purging) even though its usual use is with cold substances. However, pounding with sharp items causes absorption as if it were cooking, and through hagalah, it becomes permissible. One must also scrape out any holes and cracks. If, due to its large size, it cannot be immersed in a cauldron, one should pour boiling water into it and then place heated stones inside, causing the boiling to reach all its edges. This acts as a primary vessel, and perhaps even more so, as can be observed from the different types of boiling.

Some say that a mortar is like a leavening house and requires libun (burning). This is the opinion of Rashi, as written by the Tur. However, even minimal libun suffices, which means to burn straw on it from the outside. Our teacher, the Rema, wrote in section 16 that one should ideally perform libun. However, it is sufficient to perform hagalah (boiling) if there are no cracks. If the mortar is made of wood, it should be peeled with professional tools, as we are concerned about cracks, and then it should be boiled afterward. Thus far are his words. 

This was in their days, but in our times, we have not heard of using a mortar for chametz. Our mortars are only used for grinding salt, pepper, and similar items. Even if on rare occasions bread was ground in it, it is incidental, and at most, hagalah would suffice (Magen Avraham, section 31). Regarding spices and salt ground in our mortars before Pesach without hagalah, there is certainly no reason to forbid them, as there is no concern according to our mortars. Even if there was possibly some chametz, it was nullified before Pesach. However, if they ground chametz in a mortar on Pesach, it is certainly forbidden to put them into food. Nevertheless, if it was added to the food, it is not forbidden post facto, as it is a mere concern, and there is no need to forbid it post facto (see there and Taz, section 19).

The board on which dough is kneaded throughout the year, as well as the trough in which it is kneaded, requires boiling. For although their use is with cold, nevertheless, due to the constant kneading and rolling, and the leaven, much absorption occurs. Therefore, it is forbidden even after the fact without boiling if they were used with hot items on Passover, or if matzah was kneaded or rolled in them. Peeling with a professional tool does not help because the absorption has spread throughout. And similarly, for any item that requires boiling, peeling does not help, and this is clear. This is the law. However, the custom is not to use the board and trough of chametz on Passover at all, even through boiling, because there are cracks and crevices, and it is impossible to avoid even a small amount of chametz. Additionally, they resemble a sourdough container, for which according to one opinion, boiling does not help, as will be explained. It is forbidden to use them even with a cloth barrier. They are stored away as chametz utensils, and this practice should not be changed, for this is the main ruling.

And for this reason, we are careful not to kasher (purge) a barrel that was used to store flour throughout the year, or a barrel in which beer or kvass with bran and bread crumbs was stored, because it is inevitable that some chametz (leavened substance) will be trapped in the cracks. However, if before Passover they stored water in it for some time, it is permitted to kasher it, as the water would have washed out all the cracks (Taz, section 20). But a barrel that was used to store water throughout the year does not need anything, because there is no concern. Even if occasionally they drew water from it with a vessel that contained chametz, when drawing water, there is no chametz in it. And even if a little chametz fell into it, it would have been nullified before Passover. Nevertheless, one cleans it for Passover, and that suffices. However, barrels that belong to a baker, where he often washes his dough-filled hands into it and sometimes flour dust falls into it, cannot be permitted without kashering or a three-day soaking process, which will be explained.

Our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 21: A clay barrel that had barley beer put into it can be rendered permissible through boiling or through pouring water over it for three days. This is his language. The Tur explained the reason: Even though boiling does not help for clay vessels – this is when it absorbed through hot, not through cold. Refer there. However, this is not understood: since it was left for a full 24-hour period, it is considered as if it was pickled, and pickling is like cooking. However, they have written that in cold, even if it was pickled, it does not absorb like it does in hot, as regards to the absorption of the vessel it is not considered as cooked (refer to Taz section 22), and even in clay, it only absorbs a little. They brought from the Jerusalem Talmud at the end of the chapter "Kol Sha'ah" that Rabbi Ami instructed regarding these barrels of kutach, that they should be filled with water for three days and poured out, like the law of wine used for libations, that pouring helps for vessels. This means to fill it with water for three days, each 24-hour period, and to change the water each 24-hour period, as I wrote in Yoreh Deah, section 135. And even if the three days are not consecutive, and even for clay vessels as explained there. It is established that the barrels are made of clay.

And since pouring (irui) is effective, all the more so immersion (hag'alah), for immersion is preferable to pouring (Tur). And how does one perform immersion on a barrel? One should heat stones and place them in the barrel, then pour boiling water over them, and roll the barrel so that the immersion reaches every spot, and the boiling water must be from a first vessel (kli rishon). They further wrote that if, after the fact, one placed wine or honey in the barrel without immersion, but merely washed it thoroughly beforehand, it is permissible to drink them on Passover if it was placed there before Passover. This is because the taste of chametz is nullified in sixty, as the absorption does not spread throughout the entire vessel through cold, even in an earthenware vessel, and even if it remained there for many days. Additionally, the taste it imparts is detrimental since it is not a day old. Furthermore, beer in wine results in a detrimental taste (Magen Avraham, sub-section 40, in the name of the Mordechai).

All of this is according to the strict letter of the law. However, we have already adopted the custom not to kasher beer barrels because they often have crevices, and it is impossible to clean between the staves to ensure that no chametz remains (as stated in the Shulchan Aruch, Bach, Rashal, and Levush). Similarly, we do not kasher any wooden utensils that have crevices. It is all the more so that it is forbidden by law to kasher a whiskey barrel, because its odor is strong and pungent. Even if it stood in water for some time, it does not help for whiskey. But for beer, if it stood in water for some time, it is permissible to kasher it, as I wrote in section 31. It appears to me that for a whiskey barrel, if twelve months have passed without holding whiskey, it is permissible to kasher it. Know that we only find the concept of pouring boiling water (irui) for items used with cold, as I wrote in Yoreh De'ah there. They wrote that utensils used with cold, such as pitchers and cups, it is better to pour boiling water over them than to kasher them with utensils used with hot (Magen Avraham, subsection 39). This is when the kashering is done within twenty-four hours of their usage. But afterwards, we have no concerns. And so is the custom to kasher together, because we kasher long after their usage. And we also kasher before the time of the prohibition of chametz.

One must be very meticulous with the sieve to clean it from any crumbs of chametz that may adhere to it, and get entangled and stuck in the sieve's mesh and its wooden parts, and they should rub it very well with water. The same applies to all other kneading utensils, where rubbing them is very important. If water comes in contact with the sieve, even partially, it cannot be used on Passover (there, subparagraph 34). One should not sift Passover flour on it, even if there is no new sieve, and it is better not to sift at all (there). It is customary not to use the sieve even after boiling it, and this should not be changed. Similarly, with any other such utensils, such as the utensil called a "rib eizen" where sometimes bread is crumbled on it, or horseradish called "kren" is grated on it, which was cut with a chametz knife and some chametz remains inside it. If it was grated on Passover, even post facto, it is forbidden. However, if it was grated on the eve of Passover, it is permitted, as it is nullified in sixty (there, subparagraph 35). It seems to me that with our "rib eizen," where only horseradish is grated, and the horseradish is clean from anything, and when it is cut, it is done with a clean knife - even on Passover itself, it is permissible if Passover horseradish is grated on a chametz "rib eizen."

And know that regarding what we have written, that it is better not to sift the flour than to sift it using a chametz sieve, there are those who disagree and say that flour for Pesach which has not been sifted is forbidden even after the fact, because they have often found broken wheat grains in the flour (Chayei Adam, Section 51). Their words are puzzling, for what of it? For explicitly, the Tur writes in Siman 467 that there is no concern in this matter, that if the dough has not fermented, all the more so the wheat. And the Tur is only concerned there that perhaps the wheat came into contact with water, see there. But when it comes from the flour – it is obvious that it is of no consequence (Magen Avraham, Section 9). However, if one went ahead and sifted even on Pesach – it is permitted after the fact if no water came upon it. And before Pesach, even in such a manner, it is permitted after the fact (there), for it has already been nullified.
