And similarly, baskets that are used with chametz are treated like a sieve. But with old sacks, it is customary to permit them through washing. And one must undo all the stitches before washing. There is an opinion that even if one undoes the stitches, washing does not help, because the chametz sticks to them, and it is impossible that some chametz will not remain inside (Bach). In Terumat HaDeshen (Siman 147) it is written explicitly to be lenient, and one only needs to scrape well the dry places on the sacks (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 36). And certainly for us, who bake everything before Pesach, there is no concern. However, the washing must be thorough, and not just a simple rinse. And in a pressing situation, it is not forbidden even with a simple rinse, since the prohibition is cold (ibid). Similarly, tablecloths used for making matzot should not be used again, because of the dough that sticks to them (ibid). It is not our custom to prepare matzot on tablecloths, but there are those who prepare matzah shemurah on paper. Even so, only one matzah should be prepared on each piece of paper, because it sticks a lot. It is better to prepare it on a smooth wooden table that does not stick, and if it does stick, it can be easily scraped off. All the more so if it is prepared on iron – how good this is. Some prepare it on a type of iron called blach, and this is good and proper, as long as it is nailed to the table. If not, it wobbles back and forth and is not good for preparing the matzah. There are those who do this, and they shall be blessed.

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote in section 18 that for the sack of the mill, immersion in boiling water does not help, see there. It appears that his intention is for the iron and perforated sack which they call a "shateka," through which the flour descends. The silk sack, they customarily remove it and cut the stitches, wash and clean it, and sew it anew. And other items there such as boxes and the like, they clean them very thoroughly. The first grinding is left until after Passover. And now, with steam mills, extra caution is needed because there is much heat from the steam, and care must be taken that moisture does not rise there. This is not in our locale, and I am not familiar with them and their names. And one of the great authorities wrote (K.N. 82, note 125) that in Prague they established the practice of removing the top cover, because through the cover, moisture increases and it leads to leavening, see there.

Rabbeinu the Beit Yosef wrote in section 19: The spatula which they call "palhe" or "shoybel" or "lapete," upon which they place the loaves to set them in the oven – some say that immersion in boiling water does not help, and it must be purchased anew. Thus are his words, because this is considered usage by fire and requires burning out, and for wooden ones that cannot be burned out – they are not purified by immersion in boiling water. And a matzah spatula that is stored for the following year – does not need anything. Only they should be careful to scrape it well, and see if it was scraped properly. And some have the custom to immerse it in boiling water for the following year, and they should be prevented from doing so, for by this they do not properly observe the scraping. Additionally, one who sees might say that he is immersing a chametz spatula, and he will do the same (Taz, subsection 21). And similarly, any Pesach utensils that are stored for the next Pesach – do not need anything.

There are those who say that in the following year, it requires kashering, lest some chametz (leaven) adheres to it (Magen Avraham, subsection 37). However, the first opinion, which holds that it does not require kashering, seems more plausible (Chayei Adam, subsection 54). A chametz shovel does not help even with peeling and kashering (Magen Avraham there).

There was an incident where matzah was placed in a chametz shovel, and it was permitted through peeling even when it was taken out hot (there, from the Mahar”m of Rothenburg), for even actual chametz that touches hot matzah – it suffices to remove the place of contact, and certainly, this is true for absorbed chametz and when it is not within a day of use. It is understood that with our matzot, which are thin, it is impossible to peel them.

It seems to me that if one baked one or two matzot in it, they should not be eaten on Pesach. But if many matzot were baked in it, all the matzot are permitted, since it is dry and not within a day of use. Before Pesach, there is no reason to prohibit them, and one who prohibits them causes a loss of Jewish property for no reason. Especially with us, where we only scrape the matzot from the oven with a shovel. But to place them in the oven, we use sticks, and the scraping is momentary – it is permitted without any doubt. 

And it is obvious that with doubled or puffed matzah, which is merely a stringency, if it was scraped with a shovel, the shovel does not become forbidden. (See Magen Avraham there, that if one scraped actual chametz matzah, it is forbidden to scrape with it again. And if they did scrape again, those matzot are forbidden. And if they got mixed with previous ones, they are nullified. See there, that one in two is nullified in dry with dry. And even those who prohibit in Siman 467 agree with this, that the prohibition is absorbed and minimal. And the intent of the great bakers like the Eliyahu Rabbah is that they got mixed with the previous ones. And in vain did the Magen Avraham wonder about this, see there and the Chayei Adam. Examine and you will find it easy.)

Tables and boxes where chametz is stored, and benches on which pots are placed, as well as the table of the kitchen where hot pots are placed, according to the law – they do not require kashering by boiling, since the pot acts as a barrier between the chametz and the surface on which the pot stands and does not absorb at all (Ch. 10, Subsection 55). However, there is a concern that chametz broth may have spilled on the surface, and therefore it is customary to pour boiling water from a primary vessel over them. Nowadays, it is also customary to pass a heated stone, called a "kashering stone," over them, though this is not necessary. (It is also not necessary to place boards on the tables. The Maharil wrote to cover them with cloths after kashering, in case there is some visible chametz, as the Magen Avraham wrote in Subsection 38. Nowadays, people clean, scrape, and scour them, and there is no need for this.)

All utensils, even those made of earthenware, that were used with chametz (leavened bread) in a cold state – it is permissible to use them with matzah even in hot conditions. Therefore, boxes and cabinets where chametz bread was placed – it is permissible to use them for matzah even in hot conditions without any koshering process. Nonetheless, they need to be washed in cold water, cleaned, scraped, and scoured, because there are certainly chametz crumbs there. Once they are properly cleaned, it is permissible to place even hot items in them. This excludes a sourdough container, which is the utensil in which sourdough is made to leaven the dough, and a charoset container, which is where pungent items are placed with the chametz. Even if chametz was only used in them in a cold state, it is forbidden to use them for matzah in hot conditions. However, it is permissible to place baked matzah in them in a cold state. This is permissible in a temporary manner. But in a permanent manner, it is forbidden, lest one come to use it in hot conditions. Even in a temporary manner, it is not proper initially, as I wrote in section 11, see there.

According to the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch (section 22), hagalah (purging through boiling) is effective for utensils used with sourdough or charoset, since the boiling will certainly expel them, even though their leavening is sharp and tough, because their absorption was in a cold state. This is the opinion of the Ri and the Rosh. However, Rashi and the prominent authorities of his generation prohibited even through hagalah, because since its leavening is constant, sharp, and tough, the boiling will not expel them, except through libun (purging through heating) if they were made of metal. And this is the common practice. Nowadays, we refrain from using any kind of old earthenware vessels even in a cold state, and we completely store them away until after Passover. And even good earthenware vessels coated with sand and some lead, and glass called 'faliwa' are completely forbidden. All the more so, earthenware utensils used with sourdough or charoset are forbidden to use even in a cold state, and even through hagalah. Some mistakenly say that earthenware vessels coated with lead can be purged through hagalah. This is an error, firstly because the coating is thin, and the primary absorption is in the earthenware. Additionally, the coating is not entirely lead, there is only some lead there, and the main substance is sand and glass (and what Mordechai wrote was in their times).

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (the Rema) wrote in paragraph 22 that the oven of the winter house – its law is like that of earthenware, and it is forbidden to place anything on the oven during Passover. Thus are his words. Meaning: inside the oven, heating and libun (intense heating) are effective, but the heating of its interior will not expel the chametz that is on its surface. Like the ovens of the winter houses in earlier times which had a place on top for use and sitting, and they called it lizanqa, and all year they placed pots of hot chametz there. And certainly, if one wants to perform libun, such as placing coals on it like we do with the kachalon, as I wrote in paragraph 10 – certainly it is permitted. But it is not customary to do so because of the large area, as I wrote there. And there it is explained whether plastering with clay helps, see there.

And know that there are those who prohibit, even after the fact, placing a hot pot on the stove of the winter house or into the kakhalin on Passover, because sometimes actual chametz is used there, such as placing a piece of bread or kreplach and similar items (Bach and his mentor). However, the great authorities disagreed with this, stating that it is similar to what is explained in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 92, regarding placing a hot pot of meat on a place where cheese pastries were baked, which is permitted because the pot serves as a separation. The same applies here, as it is like two pots touching one another, and certainly if matzah was placed directly on that spot it would be forbidden, but not if it is in a pot (Taz, subparagraph 28, and Magen Avraham, subparagraph 44, and Chayei Adam and Machatzis HaShekel). And see what I wrote in paragraph 10.

Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote in Section 23: Earthenware vessels coated with glass glaze are considered as earthenware vessels. Thus is his language, and this refers to our glazed earthenware. Rabbeinu the Rema wrote that in some places the custom is not to use glazed earthenware vessels, even new ones, and one should only be stringent in places with this custom. Thus is his language. The reason for this custom is written because they are reinforced with bran. And even though they are put into the fire, they are only placed in an oven that has been heated, not in kilns. There are also other weak reasons. Among us, we do not have this custom, and all our usages are with glazed earthenware vessels, and as far as is known their manufacture nowadays, there is no concern at all.

It is also written that wooden vessels coated with substances called "barnis" have the same status as earthenware vessels. This is the end of his statement. We do not know what this is. And our teacher, the Rema, wrote that in some places, they are stringent not to use painted vessels, even if they are new, as well as those coated with tin. And one should only be stringent in places where it is customary to prohibit it. This is the end of his statement. The reason for this custom is because we are concerned that perhaps someone coated old vessels or painted them (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 47). Similarly, vessels painted with saffron, or what is called "blach malat" (ibid. and Chaye Adam, subparagraph 65). And among us, we use painted "faliyo" vessels, as they do not have this concern. Anything that comes from the factory is new. However, earthenware vessels coated with tin should certainly not be used, but they are not common among us. And it is written that in some places a Jew stands during the work process (Ba'er Heitev, subparagraph 52, and Machatzis Hashekel).

All drinking vessels used for water or wine, whether flasks or cups, require only rinsing, whether they are made of glass, wood, metal, or earthenware. Even though hot bread is sometimes placed in them, since their primary use is with cold, rinsing is sufficient. The rule for all vessels follows their primary use. However, there are those who are stringent and require immersion in boiling water, and this is the practiced custom. When using them for beer or distilled wine, it is obvious that they require immersion in boiling water. Therefore, this applies only to wooden and metal vessels, and this is clear.

And our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 26: Glass vessels, even if they are used for long-term storage, and even if one uses them with hot liquids, require no form of kashering. Mere rinsing suffices for them. Thus are his words. And even though glass is made from sand, nevertheless, because they are very smooth, they do not absorb. And this is our ruling in Yoreh De'ah, siman 135, regarding yayin nesech (wine used in idolatrous libations). And even though there it concerns absorption in cold, nevertheless, even in hot they do not absorb. However, I am uncertain even according to this opinion, for those who store distilled wine in them, if one may be lenient with them? And it appears that they are forbidden, for our eyes see that the smell persists in them even afterward, and therefore they require a three-day immersion.

And our master, the Rema, disagrees with this, and this is his language: "There are those who are stringent and say that glass vessels—even boiling does not help them. And this is the custom in Ashkenaz and these countries." End of his language. The reason: since they are made from sand, their law is like earthenware vessels. According to this, even pouring (hot water) does not help, as pouring is not better than boiling. 

And it seems that this is only when they were used with hot (substances), for if they were used with cold, why was there no stringency regarding yayin nesekh (forbidden wine) in Yoreh De'ah there? According to this, certainly all drinking vessels made of glass benefit from three days of pouring, for those who use them with hot (substances), chametz (leaven) does not enter them. And even if it may enter occasionally—it is not significant. And so we rule in practice. And even glass cups that are used to drink strong wine, since the usage is only for a short period—it is not significant. 

But glass bottles in which strong wine is placed—we do not permit with pouring, because they are used for storage, and they remain for many days, and it is very strong—it is not similar to yayin nesekh.

He also wrote: Similarly, a silver vessel that has within it a glass coating, which is called "gishmaltz" – it should not be subjected to hagalah (purging through boiling). But from the outside, it does no harm. This is the end of his words, because from the outside, the absorption does not penetrate the entire vessel. However, according to what I wrote in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 92, we hold that it does penetrate the entire vessel. But here they wrote another reason, because these vessels are not used with hot items (see Magen Avraham, sub-paragraph 50). And such vessels are not known to us in these times.

In section 13, it is explained that a spit requires libun (a form of kashering through intense heat). This applies to a spit that has been used to roast chametz (leavened products), such as a pastry or the like, but if it was only used to roast meat, there is no chametz involved. Even if it was used to roast salted meat with salt that was not checked for chametz, what of it? If there was any chametz, it would have been nullified before Passover, and at most, boiling water (hagalah) is sufficient (Taz, subsection 8). If it was used to roast meat and poultry on Passover without any prior kashering, they are permissible to eat. However, this leniency is only post facto; ideally, kashering is required. 

Regarding the willkaes (implement used to handle pots in the oven), which are used to place the pots in the oven and to remove them, they require hagalah because spills from the pots often occur on them. The wooden handles inserted into them do not require any kashering since they are distant from the pot. Nevertheless, the custom is to make new ones. The willkaes are kashered through burning. The board used to close the oven requires hagalah or should be completely new. 

The spigots of a wine barrel are permitted to be used if they were used for chametz wine. The custom is to rinse them off, as they might have been handled with chametz-covered hands. However, spigots used for beer or distilled wine need to be new or kashered because they have absorbed a strong chametz odor. Similarly, the wooden rods used to handle drinking vessels, called pravkas, need rinsing to be used with Passover utensils. All covers have the same ruling since they are not used directly. However, covers used for beer or distilled wine require kashering or new ones due to the strong chametz odor they have absorbed, and it is proper to be stringent with them.

In the previous section, the laws of kashering vessels for Passover were explained, which are the same as for other prohibitions: vessels used with fire, such as spits and grills, require libun (heating until red-hot), and those used for cooking, like pots and similar items, require hagalah (boiling). The early authorities questioned the end of Tractate Avodah Zarah, where it differentiates between holy items and other prohibitions. Regarding holy items, it is taught: spits and grills that absorbed leftover sacrificial meat after its permitted time for consumption, and the absorbed substance became leftover, which is a prohibition punishable by karet, it is taught that spits and grills are kashered by immersion in hot water and do not require libun. The Talmud answers that holy items absorbed permissible matter, and although it later became prohibited, at that time the prohibition is not present, unlike other prohibitions, where the absorption is of forbidden matter. This is the conclusion there. According to this, they questioned that chametz (leavened bread) should also be considered as absorbing permissible matter like holy items. Indeed, the opinion of the Ra'avad is that chametz also does not require libun, as the Ran wrote there. However, the Rif and the Rambam ruled that libun is necessary, which is difficult. The Ran explained that they hold that chametz is not considered "absorbing permissible matter," since it had the status of chametz beforehand, unlike leftover sacrificial meat, which did not have the status of "leftover" initially. Although this is not entirely clear, since the name "chametz" matters because it was permissible at that time, nonetheless, since the name did not change, it is considered "absorbing forbidden matter." We do not have the authority to dispute the early authorities on this matter.

According to this, the Ran, of blessed memory, wrote there that the reasoning of "noten ta'am bar noten ta'am" (secondary transferred taste) does not apply to chametz, because in the case of a prohibition, "noten ta'am bar noten ta'am" is not relevant. This reasoning only applies to meat and milk, because each one on its own is permitted and the taste is weakened, but not in the case of a prohibition, as I have written in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 95. According to this, there is a difficulty with the Rosh, who used the reasoning of "noten ta'am bar noten ta'am" in the case of chametz, as will be explained in this Siman. This implies that he holds that chametz is considered "absorbed in a permitted manner." However, he ruled in the chapter "Kol Sha'ah" like the Rif and the Rambam, that libun (burning) is required. This presents a contradiction. (Pri Chadash and Knesset HaGedolah there, note 38. And what he wanted to say, that according to the reasoning of "absorbed in a permitted manner," a strong taste is also required, see there—it is puzzling, because the explanation of "absorbed in a permitted manner" resolves the issue before the explanation of a strong taste was raised, and likewise in the conclusion, see there. Also, the main reasoning does not apply to chametz, see there. Examine and you will find it easy.)

In my humble opinion, it seems that the Rosh holds that there is no difficulty here. When we say that where permissible absorption is sufficient with hagalah (purging through boiling), it applies to prohibited substances that are nullified in sixty. This is not the case with chametz, whose prohibition is in any amount. And sanctified items (kodashim) are nullified in sixty, as it is stated in Zevachim (97a): "If one cooked sanctified items with non-sacred items, if there is enough to impart taste..." It is clearly stated that with kodashim we follow the imparting of taste. How can this be compared to chametz? However, in the case of "giving taste to something that gives taste" (noten ta'am bar noten ta'am) which is weakened, and the taste is completely gone, one should not be more stringent with chametz than with other prohibitions. It has already been explained that chametz is only stringent in cases where other prohibitions are forbidden with sixty, chametz is forbidden in any amount. But in cases where sixty is not needed for other prohibitions, chametz is also not forbidden, as I wrote in Siman 447, Section 7. And this is clear with the help of Heaven.

The Tur wrote: The procedure for hagalah (purging of utensils): Take a large pot full of water and bring it to a boil, and immerse all the utensils in it. For a large utensil that cannot be immersed in the pot, fill it with water and bring it to a boil, and make a clay rim around its mouth so that it is completely filled and the water touches its rim. If he wishes, he can take a hot stone or a burning torch and throw it into the boiling water, which will cause the water to boil more and overflow its rim. This is the end of his words, meaning that in such a case, it is not necessary to make a clay rim around its mouth. And so wrote our teacher, the Beit Yosef, in section 6. And even though in this case the purging is only through the sparks that the boiling water raises to its rim, it is still permissible, as the absorption is expelled in the same manner it was absorbed. For the absorption also travels through the sparks (Talmud). Without this, it could happen that during this process no sparks would rise at all. Even with a clay rim, it is only like raising sparks, as the water seeps through the clay, but raising sparks is necessary (Magen Avraham, subsection 11). Therefore, for a utensil whose rim is used directly, like bowls that are sometimes placed upside down on the pan, or used to draw from the pot, this method is not effective, as it would only raise sparks, and it is necessary to place it inside a large pot (ibid and Taz, subsection 11). Furthermore, when drawing from the pot for another reason, it is necessary to place it inside the large pot, as the outside also absorbed, and it needs to be purged in the manner it was absorbed, meaning that the outside should also be inside the hagalah water. Therefore, it is necessary to place it in the large pot (ibid).

A vessel with a narrow opening, which cannot be scrubbed inside, or one that has tubes that cannot be scrubbed – is forbidden to be kashered by boiling (there). And this applies to vessels that are used with chametz. But if they are used only with hot water, like our copper kettles which by law do not need any kashering – we are accustomed to kasher them in a pot or to fill them with water until it boils. And similarly, our samovar – we kasher them, although by law they do not need anything. However, the samovar has a wide cavity, and even if chametz was placed in it, such as strong arak or spirits occasionally – boiling is effective for it, because it can be cleaned. And we place coals and water in it up to the top, and when it starts to boil – necessarily the water will rise to the top and spill out as well, as our eyes see. And it does not need “gedenfa,” meaning a clay rim around, for this is better than a fiery torch.

And this is the language of the Tur: The Rif wrote: One should leave the utensils in the pot until they expel [their absorbed taste]. That is to say, one should not place the utensil in the pot and immediately remove it, for perhaps it will not expel [the absorbed taste] in such a short time. Therefore, it must be left there for a little while. The specific duration is not explained, but it is left to one's discretion (Rashba, Part One, Siman 479). And in the name of Avi HaEzri, the Tur wrote: Who knows how to estimate the duration of expulsion, and perhaps they will remain inside and reabsorb. Therefore, a God-fearing person who wants to kasher many utensils together should leave them for a full day from their use, for since their taste is impaired, they do not prohibit [other items]. However, one should perform the kashering during the permissible time, before the fifth hour [of the day], for after the prohibition takes effect, their impairment does not permit [the kashering]. And my master, my father, the Rosh, of blessed memory, wrote that before the time of the prohibition, one can even kasher a utensil used within the day, even if there is not sixty times [the volume of water] to nullify it. However, after that time, and similarly throughout the year when one comes to kasher a utensil that has absorbed a prohibition, one should not kasher it unless the utensil is not used within the day, or there is sixty times [the volume of water] to nullify it. And the custom is to insert and immediately remove them. Thus far is his language.

It seems to me that they dispute whether chametz [leavened bread] is considered "absorbed permissibility" or "absorbed prohibition." For the Avi HaEzer holds that it is considered "absorbed prohibition," following the opinion of the Ran that we wrote in Section A, and therefore, even before its time [of prohibition], it must not be used if it is a day-old. The Rosh, however, holds that it is considered "absorbed permissibility," and therefore, even if it is day-old, it is permissible due to "a flavor that imparts a flavor." For the chametz imparted a flavor to the vessel, and the vessel to the water, and it is reabsorbed into the vessel, and still, all of it is permissible. But after the time of its prohibition, "a flavor that imparts a flavor" does not apply, for in prohibition, "a flavor that imparts a flavor" does not exist. Therefore, it must not be a day-old. And even according to those who prohibit "a detrimental flavor" on Passover, in any case, regarding absorption, they were not concerned.

The Tur further writes, and this is his language: The Rashbam wrote that one must first kosher the large pot in which other vessels are koshered. Similarly, Rashi and the Riva instructed. It is also mentioned in the responsa of the Geonim: One should rinse the large pot, kosher it in boiling water, purify it, rinse it in cold water, and initially purge it from chametz. After that, he boils water in it without measure. He must ensure that the water does not stop boiling, for if it does, it is forbidden to kosher vessels in them. He then takes them out and rinses them in cold water. Afterward, he fills the large pot, surrounds its rim, and koshers it as in the first procedure, then pours it out and rinses it. And my master, my father, the Rosh, of blessed memory, wrote that the law regarding the large pot is the same as for other vessels: If it has not been used for a day, or even if it has been used within the day but it is before the fifth hour, it does not need to be koshered first. However, if it is from the fifth hour onward and it has been used within the day, it needs to be koshered first, because in the first koshering the water becomes forbidden, as there is not sixty times the amount to nullify the absorption of the pot, since we measure it all together. It turns out that all the water becomes forbidden and is absorbed into the vessels being koshered in it, if they remain there until their absorption is complete. But before the fifth hour, even though it is reabsorbed into them, there is no concern, as it is the time of its permissibility, and it is similar to "imparting a secondary flavor." Until here is his language. And this that he wrote: "if they remain there," for otherwise, as long as they are busy expelling, they do not absorb. And also here the main point of their dispute, for our Rabbis hold that chametz is considered "absorbed in a forbidden state," and the Rosh holds that it is considered "absorbed in a permitted state," as I have written.

And behold, according to what has been explained, many of our rabbis hold that chametz is classified as "absorbed forbidden substance," except for the Rosh. Nevertheless, our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, ruled in accordance with him, because his reasoning is compelling. And even though in Siman 447 we did not permit items cooked in a chametz vessel before Pesach due to the principle of "imparting a secondary flavor," and we held the view that chametz is classified as "absorbed forbidden substance," as I wrote there in Section 29 (see there) – that certainly, regarding eating on Pesach itself, due to the permissive principle of "imparting a secondary flavor," we do not rely on this against all those great authorities. However, this is not the case with regard to purging before Pesach. There are many reasons why until it releases into the food – in this, we properly rely on this reasoning (see Magen Avraham, Subsection 1, and Chayei Adam, Subsection 2).

And this is the language of our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, in paragraph 1: One should be careful to perform the process of kashering before the fifth hour, so that there will be no need to be precise about whether the utensils were used within the last 24 hours or not, or whether there are sixty times the volume of water against the utensil being kashered. Similarly, when kashering utensils that absorbed a small amount together with those that absorbed a large amount (because after the time of prohibition, one must be concerned that the utensil that absorbed a small amount may absorb from the utensil that absorbed a large amount before it has finished expelling). Similarly, if one leaves the utensils in the pot for too long (there is a concern that after the utensil has expelled, it will reabsorb). One should not leave them for too long. (That is to say: because one fears leaving them for too long, they should not be left at all, even for the necessary amount of time). Similarly, so that one does not need to be careful that the water does not stop boiling (as long as it is boiling, it expels and does not absorb, but afterwards, it absorbs). And the utensil should not be put in until the water is boiling (also for this reason). Similarly, so that one does not need to kasher the large pot in which they kasher both at the beginning and the end. Until here is their language, which is not in accordance with the opinion of the Geonim that we brought, but in accordance with the opinion of the Rosh, that it suffices either at the beginning or the end.

And know that regarding what was written that the water should not cease from boiling, our teacher the Rema wrote, and this is his language: "However, many disagree and hold that hagalah (purging) does not help at all if the water is not boiling. Therefore, one must be careful, even before the time of prohibition, that the water should not cease from boiling the entire time of the purging." Until here is his language. And it is entirely not understood: Who is disagreeing on this? The first opinion also holds that hagalah is only at the time of boiling, and they only say that before the time of prohibition, the water can cease a bit from boiling and it will not prohibit the utensils. But after the time of prohibition, if the water ceases from boiling, the utensils will absorb the prohibited emissions. But it is obvious that hagalah is only at the time of boiling, and the commentators (Magen Avraham, subsection 3, Chayei Adam, and Eliyah Rabbah) have already contested him. And the Levush holds that according to the previous opinion, hagalah is effective even if the water ceases from boiling because in any case, the taste is weakened. See there. And these things are puzzling (and in the case of wine used for libation, there are those who hold this opinion).

It seems to me that what he says is correct, and he has taught us something significant. For it has already been explained that one must limit the time that the utensil is in the water: not a brief moment, because there is no time for expulsion, and not too long a time, because then it reabsorbs. And even though when one immerses before the time of prohibition, we do not worry if it reabsorbs, especially if the utensils are not used that day, nevertheless, initially, why should we do this? After all, it will eventually absorb chametz, and it is not proper to do so. But who can limit the time precisely? And usually, the utensils are in the pot more than the required amount of time. However, as long as the pot is boiling and bubbling, there is no concern, because then it only expels and does not absorb. This is not the case when it stops boiling. And this is what he says regarding the previous opinion: that before the time of prohibition, one does not need to be meticulous if the water stops boiling. To this, he says that there are those who disagree and hold that immersion is ineffective if the water is not boiling, meaning it is as if it was not immersed, because it reabsorbs. And although it is still permitted, what benefit is there in the immersion if it reabsorbs? Therefore, one must be careful that throughout the immersion, the pot does not stop boiling, and this is how one should act and be cautious.

If one did not perform hagalah (purging of utensils) before the time of prohibition, he can perform hagalah until Passover. However, on Passover itself, one should not do hagalah because at that time even a tiny amount of chametz (leavened substance) is significant, and the hagalah would not be effective, as it is almost impossible to avoid some reabsorption. However, it is permissible to perform libun (purging by fire) on utensils during Passover, because the fire extracts all absorbed substances and does not allow for reabsorption. It is clear that this applies to Chol HaMoed (the intermediate days of the festival), as on Yom Tov (the festival day) it is prohibited due to the prohibition against labor, as I wrote in Siman 509. 

Know that when one performs hagalah on the eve of Passover after the time of prohibition, he must be careful about things that he did not need to be careful about before: the utensils should not have been used within the past 24 hours (not "ben yomo"), and if they have been used within 24 hours, there must be sixty times the volume of water to the absorbed substance, as this nullifies the absorption in the water. Even though one should not nullify a prohibition intentionally, in this case, his intention is not to nullify the prohibition but to perform hagalah. For utensils not used within 24 hours, it is permitted even without sixty times the volume of water. Even though one should ideally not use something that imparts a detrimental taste, here, since the absorbed substance is involved and it is not possible in another way without great difficulty, it is permitted.

There is another matter to be cautious about after the time of its prohibition, and that is not to kasher a utensil piece by piece, for it is inevitable that part of the kashered section will not enter the boiling water again, and thus it will reabsorb. Rather, one should kasher it all at once (Taz, subsection 5). Nevertheless, after the fact and in pressing circumstances, one should not prohibit all these things that have been explained, since the primary prohibitions are due to the concern that they will reabsorb. Some hold that even with food, it does not reawaken, and certainly not with the absorption in utensils (Magen Avraham, subsection 6).

First, one should purge utensils that have absorbed a small amount, and afterward those that have absorbed a large amount. Do not leave them in the boiling pot for too long, and ensure that the water does not stop boiling. The pot itself should be purged first and last. If the pot has not been used that day, it does not need to be purged first and last. However, it is customary to be stringent with all stringencies even before the fifth hour. Some have questioned the benefit of purging, arguing that the utensils will inevitably absorb some of the purging water, which will then reawaken during Passover. Nevertheless, it has already been clarified that with absorbed substances, we do not say "it reawakens."

When purging a small utensil, such as a forbidden knife, in a pot that has sixty times its volume, one can even purge it in a kosher pot (Taz, end of subsection 5), and the water remains kosher. This is not considered nullifying a prohibition from the outset, as the intention is to purge and remove the prohibition. Certainly, if the pot has not been used that day, there is no concern. Note that we customarily purge utensils before Passover in a public bathhouse, where there is a very large pot and a strong fire. It is appropriate to appoint a learned individual to oversee the public purging to ensure it is done properly (see subsection 19, where it is stated that if the pot has been used that day, the water should not be used).

One must be careful not to kasher meat and dairy utensils together, unless one of them is not used within the last 24 hours. For if not, they will absorb from each other. And after the fact, this is considered a secondary flavor as explained in Yoreh De'ah, section 95. All the more so, forbidden utensils must not be used within the last 24 hours, and here the concept of secondary flavor does not apply, as I wrote there. And it has already become customary not to kasher any utensil when it has been used within the last 24 hours, even if only one utensil is being kashered.

And also the tables and benches in the dining room, which require pouring boiling water on them as has been explained, the common custom is that first they are scrubbed very well and left for twenty-four hours, and afterward boiling water is poured on them. One should pour quickly, and pour from the pot in which the water was boiled, not from another vessel. If one pours into another vessel, heated stones are placed in it. If one places a vessel into the pot in which the water was boiled and leaves it there, and then takes it out with the water, it is considered as a primary vessel (Magen Avraham, subsection 9). Some have written to kasher three days before Passover (ibid). However, the custom is not to be meticulous about this.

One should not place many utensils one inside the other to put them in a pot and immerse them together unless there is space between them so that the water can reach every utensil inside and outside all around. In our practice, we place many small utensils into a sieve with large holes and place the sieve into the pot, leaving the sieve in the pot until the boiling water rises over each utensil all around. One must ensure that in the sieve each utensil is placed separately, and they should be loose and not stuck to each other or to the sieve. If one is using tongs to immerse the utensil, they should rotate the utensil because otherwise, the water will not reach the place where the tongs are holding it. Know that women customarily do not use for Passover the pot from which they pour hot water onto tables and benches because of the steam that rises. This custom has no basis or reason. Additionally, it is customary to have a special pot for cooking eggs on Passover and for cooking potatoes. This is not a valid custom, and the women themselves have adopted it.

One may not perform hagalah (purging of absorbed taste) using the hot springs of Tiberias, meaning hot water that descends from the mountains or a hot spring, even for utensils that are treated as a secondary vessel, because their absorption occurred through fire, and thus their purging must also be through fire-heated water, for “as it absorbed, so it releases.” Even post facto, it seems that this does not help. Additionally, even with fire-heated water, purging is effective only with water and not with other liquids. Similarly, water mixed with ash is not effective for hagalah. However, post facto, if one performed hagalah with other liquids, it is acceptable. If one purged many utensils in a pot to the extent that the water became like brine due to the many expulsions from the utensils, one should not perform further hagalah in that water. However, post facto, it does not invalidate the process. (See Chayei Adam, small section 18 in the name of Or Zarua, that one should not use hagalah water even if there is sixty times the volume. It seems to me that if the utensil is not used within a day and there is sixty times the volume, it is permitted, as I have written in section 15 that even if it was used within a day, it is permitted. This is also written regarding a utensil not used within a day.)

Maimonides and the Geonim cited by the Tur require rinsing the vessel with cold water immediately after immersion in boiling water. This is also the custom. The reason is not clear, for if it is due to concern that the vessel might reabsorb from the boiling water on it, then immediately upon removal from the boiling water it would absorb, as it is impossible to be precise with moments (Rosh, end of Avodah Zarah). Moreover, when it is in the boiling water, this concern also exists (ibid.). However, since there is sixty times the amount of water, or it is not a day old, we do not worry about it. The same applies here. Nevertheless, this is the custom, and it should not be changed. We find support for this in the context of sacrificial offerings: "and rinsed in water" – immersion in hot water and rinsing in cold. It is clear that if it was not rinsed in cold water, there is no issue. It seems to me that this custom is only practiced during Passover, perhaps as a remembrance of the Temple.

The Sages taught in the Mishnah (Pesachim 35a): These are the items with which a person fulfills his obligation on Passover due to the obligation of matzah on the first night, as it is written, "In the evening, you shall eat matzot" (Rashi): with wheat, barley, spelt, rye, and oats. It is clear that an olive-sized portion from all of them can combine. And even though regarding challah, they only combine when kneaded together, as I wrote in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 324, this is because one does not separate from one type on behalf of another type. But regarding an olive-sized portion of matzah – all of them are considered bread.

Similarly, the prohibition of chametz applies only to these five species, as Rambam wrote at the beginning of the fifth chapter: only the five species of grain are prohibited as chametz on Pesach, and they are the two types of wheat, which are wheat and spelt, and the three types of barley, which are barley, oats, and rye. But legumes, such as rice, millet, beans, lentils, and similar items are not considered chametz. Even if one kneads rice or something similar with boiling water and covers it with cloths until it swells like dough that has leavened, it is permitted to eat, as this is not chametz but spoilage. This is the end of his words. Therefore, also regarding fulfilling one's obligation on Pesach, it is the same, as it is written: "You shall not eat chametz with it; for seven days you shall eat matzos with it" – items that come to leavening, one fulfills his obligation with them in matzah, excluding those that do not come to leavening but to spoilage (Gemara there). Consequently, it is permitted to make a dish from them.

And similarly, buckwheat, which is called gri'ka or retzka, is not a type of grain. And corn kernels, which are called tarkes'ka wheat, or kakaruz'a or kikes, are also a type of legume. Similarly, white beans, which are called fasolyes or bablach, are also a type of legume. 

Regarding our types of groats, some of them are completely chametz, such as gerstena and havern'a, which are made from barley and oats and ground in small mills called zarnes. They are not made except after soaking them in water, making them completely chametz. But what is called peril groats, which is also made from peeled barley and produced in large mills called kropernia, by their nature do not require water for their production, and on the contrary, water spoils them. Therefore, they are like barley itself. However, for some years we have heard that water is poured on them, making them completely chametz. Similarly, wheat and barley that have had water poured on them are completely chametz and it is forbidden to keep them during Passover.

Also, groats that are pounded in a mortar have water added to them, and since they are barley, they become completely chametz. Know that the type called saga is completely chametz because it is made from wheat flour (Sha'arei Teshuvah, subsection 4).

And know that even though according to the strict law it is permissible to eat rice and all kinds of legumes on Passover, nevertheless, our rabbis and ancestors instituted many hundreds of years ago, and accepted upon themselves as a prohibition, not to eat rice and kinds of legumes on Passover. This is because it is well-known that many grains of wheat are found among them. Additionally, since both grain porridge, such as barley and oats, and legume porridge are cooked in a pot, and the common people who are not knowledgeable might confuse one for the other (Hagahot Maimoniot). Moreover, since it is possible to make dough from kinds of legumes, like in some countries where corn flour is eaten in place of bread, the common people would not distinguish between one dough and another (Bach and Taz). And this prohibition, since our ancestors accepted it as a protective measure, it is forbidden for us according to the Torah law to nullify it. Those who doubt and are lenient in this matter testify about themselves that they lack fear of Heaven and fear of sin, and they are not knowledgeable in the ways of the Torah. (The Pri Chadash brings a proof for this custom from Pesachim 40b: Rava said: Is there anyone who would permit such a thing in a place where servants are common?)

And I bring clear evidence for this custom from the Jerusalem Talmud "Kol Sha'ah" (Chapter Two, Halacha 4), where Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri disagrees and says that rice is a type of grain, and one is liable for kareis (spiritual excision) for its leavening, because he holds that rice flour also comes to leavening. And the Rabbis hold that it does not come to leavening but rather to spoilage. The Jerusalem Talmud questions: "Let it be examined?" Meaning, let us make dough from rice and examine whether it comes to leavening or spoilage. And it answers: they dispute the very basis of the examination. Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri holds that they examined it and found that it comes to leavening, while the Rabbis hold that they examined it and found that it does not come to leavening. See there. 

And now, it is evident: if among the greatest of the Tannaim (Mishnaic sages) there was a dispute about something that sensory perception testifies to, this one saying sensory perception testifies one way and that one saying the opposite, then all the more so it is clear that ordinary people, thousands of them with lesser understanding, can make a mistake in this, saying that this too comes to leavening! And yet, the Sages permitted it. If so, the same applies to this or that type of grain that resemble each other. This is conclusive evidence for the words of our holy Rabbis who decreed this, and they knew the reason for which they decreed. 

And although there are countries that did not adopt this stringency, nonetheless, all the countries of Ashkenaz, France, and Russia (and Poland) have upheld and accepted upon themselves and their descendants this good stringency, which has a substantial reason. And one who breaches the fence will be bitten by a snake. However, they explicitly accepted that if there should be a year of famine, Heaven forfend, where the poor are hungry for bread, then all the sages of the city, headed by the local rabbi, permit the eating of legumes in that Passover. And now that potatoes have become abundant, even this is not necessary, as is known.

However, it is clear that we do not prohibit the dish if a small amount of legumes fell into it. One should remove them and can eat the dish. Similarly, it is permissible to light with oils made from them, and they do not prohibit the dish if they fall into it. And the Maharil wrote not to use oil in a place where there is a concern that it might fall into the dish, because they crush them in a mortar where barley is soaked. However, even in this there is no concern, as it was nullified before Passover, and it is not a sharp substance (Magen Avraham, Subsection 2). And now we do not know of this at all.

And our master the Rema wrote at the end of Section 1: "And similarly, it is permitted to keep various types of legumes in the house. And it is also permitted to benefit from them" (there in Subsection 3). Consequently, it is permitted to sell them to a non-Jew during Chol HaMoed and to profit, as well as to purchase them. Similarly, it is permitted to buy and sell rice. But other types of groats are considered complete chametz, and one transgresses the prohibition of "it shall not be seen." However, grain, wheat, barley, and oats – it is permitted to buy and sell them on Passover, and their flour needs to be checked whether it came in contact with water – if it did, it is forbidden; if not, it is permitted. And much wheat flour has come in contact with water, but not rye flour, which is called "karin." The main thing is to know whether they came in contact with water or not.

It is also written that the seeds of akliza, anise, and alendor are not types of kitniyot (legumes), and it is permitted to eat them on Passover. Thus is the text. However, we do not know what these are. Some have written that it is good not to eat anise and cumin until the last day, because it is impossible to clean them well (there). And there are those who differentiate between kram cumin, where there is a concern, and peeled cumin, where there is no concern (Taz, Section 1). One should not be overly stringent in these matters (Magen Avraham, Section 9). All that we have written, where it is not forbidden if it falls into a dish – even if there is not sixty times its volume, it is permitted (there), as long as it does not constitute the majority of the dish (there). And even though in a dish it does not prohibit, nevertheless, if found in baked matzah – it prohibits that matzah (Taz, there), and the reason will be explained in Siman Tets.

It is taught in the third chapter of Challah: One who makes dough from wheat and rice, if it has the taste of grain – he fulfills his obligation on Passover. And in this language, the Rambam wrote in the sixth chapter, law five. The Raavad wrote that this is specifically when there is an olive-sized piece of grain within the amount of a pras (half a loaf), and similarly wrote the Rashba. And this is logical, for if it were only because "taste is like the essence" – even in prohibitions, many authorities say one does not receive lashes for this, as I wrote in Yoreh De'ah, section 98. And even if "taste is like the essence" is from the Torah, in any case, it is not reasonable to fulfill a positive commandment of eating matzah with it. However, the Ramban and the Rosh wrote based on the Jerusalem Talmud there, that even if there is not an olive-sized piece within the amount of a pras. And this also appears from the words of the Tur, as the Jerusalem Talmud says that the wheat drags along the rice, so it has the taste of wheat itself, and the rice turns into being like the wheat itself. Therefore, this law applies only to wheat and rice, and not to other types. And in the Jerusalem Talmud there is a dispute about this: one says until there is a majority of grain, and one says it does not require a majority. And the reason of dragging is not mentioned there, except at the beginning of Tractate Challah. Look there, as there are also different versions. Practically, one should be stringent. (See Pri Chadash, and his words need examination, as written by the Makom Chaim.)

The Tur, citing Rabbeinu Peretz, writes that some have the custom to inspect wheat kernels one by one to ensure they have not been nibbled by mice. Others say this is unnecessary, as it is akin to fruit juice. However, it is not similar to fruit juice because saliva causes leavening, as it is taught: a person should not chew wheat and place it on a wound. Therefore, one should not be lenient. The Tur writes that it seems there is no need to be concerned about this at all, as it is a far-fetched concern to say that hard wheat would leaven with a small amount of saliva from a mouse's mouth... Furthermore, even if there are nibbled kernels, they are less than one in a thousand and become nullified when ground. This is not considered nullifying a prohibition from the outset, as the grinding is not done for the purpose of nullification. Until here is his wording. And I am puzzled by the comparison of human saliva to mouse saliva, which contradicts the Mishnah in Makhshirin, Chapter Five, which teaches: "Derivatives of water include those that come from the eye..., and from the mouth: urine...". And we have learned in the Tosefta: specifically human, even with urine, but from other animals, it is like fruit juice. So too the Rambam writes in Chapter Ten of the Laws of Food Purity, see there. Furthermore, if so, there would be no wheat or any kind of grain in the world that has not been susceptible to impurity. Rather, it is certainly because they are similar to fruit juice and do not render susceptible. See Siman 466.

And so wrote the Rashba in a response (Siman 488), even though he did not bring this proof, and this is his language: It seems reasonable that there is no concern of chametz here, as they only said this regarding a person who chews wheat. But regarding the biting of mice – there is no concern of chametz. For if it were so, we would not find any wheat that would be permitted on Pesach, as there is no storage house from which mice have not eaten... until here is his language. According to this, even if there is not sixty times against it – it is permitted. But according to the second reason of the Tur – sixty times is needed. And one should not ask that according to what Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote in Siman 467, that dry with dry reawakens on Pesach – what does it help? For we can say that flour with flour is called "moist with moist," since it is not recognizable in itself. And therefore, since it was ground before Pesach – it is already nullified, and one can bake it also on Pesach itself. All the more so if it was baked before Pesach, as it is already nullified. This is not similar to flour that became damp and then dried, which we say reawakens as I wrote in Siman 467, there the crumbs are visible as will be explained there. And similarly, it is not necessary to check the wheat, perhaps there is grain that sprouted, when we do not know that there is a lot of them in such a way that there would definitely be sixty times against them, because when they are ground – they will be nullified before Pesach. And this is moist with moist, as I wrote. It is better to bake it before Pesach (see Taz, subsection 2, and Magen Avraham, subsection 6, and in Siman 467, subsection 9). And see in Siman 466.

The Tur wrote, and this is his language: Rav Alfas wrote that one must guard the wheat used to fulfill the obligation of matzah from the time of harvest, so that no water comes upon them. And my master, my father, the Rosh of blessed memory, wrote that it is only necessary from the time of grinding, because it is then that they come close to water, as they grind in water mills. Similarly, it is written in the Sheiltot: One does not fulfill his obligation except with matzah that has been guarded from leavening, from the moment water falls upon it. And if a non-Jew, deaf-mute, imbecile, or minor handled the wheat – one does not fulfill his obligation with it. Thus far his language, meaning: if such people brought it to the grinding, it is invalid, because we require "for its sake," meaning "for the sake of the matzah of the commandment." As it is stated in the Gemara (Menachot 42a) according to Rava, who holds that the guarding must be from the time of harvest, as he said to those who harvest and bind the sheaves: When you turn them over, turn them over for the sake of the commandment. And Rashi of blessed memory explained there that for the matzah of the commandment, guarding for its sake is required. Thus far his language. And consequently, anything that requires "for its sake" – needs an adult Jew. However, they differed: the Rif ruled according to Rava that the guarding "for its sake" is from the time of harvest, and the Rosh holds like those who disagree with Rava, and he believes that guarding from the time of harvest is not required.

And it is perplexing: for in the Gemara it only mentions for Rava "from the time of reaping," and for those who disagree with Rava it is from the time of kneading. For it explicitly states there that the guarding at the time of kneading is considered guarding. If so, from where did the Rosh and the Tur derive that guarding is required from the time of grinding? After all, this guarding is not mentioned in the Gemara at all. And one cannot say that this is not for the sake of "for its sake" (lishma) but rather out of concern that water might fall in, for if that were the case, why would it be invalid if handled by a non-Jew, a deaf-mute, a fool, or a minor? Clearly, it is required "for its sake" from the time of grinding. It is therefore necessary to say that our sages definitively concluded that the guarding is certainly from the time of grinding, since they are close to water. And the Gemara that states "from the time of kneading" is because in their days most people ground with hand mills, or mills operated by animals, or wind mills. For in several places in the Gemara it implies that water mills were not common among them, only hand mills, as is explained at the end of the fifth chapter of Gittin and the beginning of Chullin, and similarly it is implied in Makhshirin (chapter three, mishnah five). Consequently, the proximity to water is from the time of kneading and thus requires guarding. However, when grinding with water mills, guarding is needed from the time of grinding.

And one should not ask: If so, why did they not mention the primary requirement of guarding from the time of kneading? The truth is that the Tur abbreviated their words, and the Rosh concludes there in the name of the Sheiltot, and this is his wording: Alternatively, if a non-Jew, a deaf-mute, an imbecile, or a minor kneaded the dough, since they are not obligated in the commandment of guarding. And even though a Jew of sound mind baked it and performed the guarding at the time of baking, nevertheless, one does not fulfill their obligation. Until here are his words, showing that guarding "for its sake" is required from the time of grinding until after baking.

Furthermore, it seems to me, in my humble opinion, to resolve the words of our rabbis who required guarding from the time of grinding: because they interpret in the Talmud that even those who disagree with Rava—nevertheless, guarding from the time of kneading is not considered guarding. And it is a way of rejecting to say "perhaps there was guarding from the time of kneading," but in truth, guarding is needed before kneading, which is from the time of grinding. And this is also explained from the words of the Ran there, who wrote about the words of the Rif that require guarding from the time of harvesting, and this is his language: "However, it is possible that even if he did not do so, but instead took wheat from the market and guarded it for the sake of matzah—he has fulfilled his obligation. And in the Talmud, it explains that guarding from the time of kneading is not considered guarding. That is to say: before kneading, guarding is required, but as long as he guarded the wheat before kneading—he has fulfilled his obligation." Thus far his language. Therefore, the Sheiltot and the Rosh say from the time of grinding.

The Ran, of blessed memory, wrote that one of the Geonim said that one who buys flour from the market in a pressing situation—it is permitted, and he fulfills his obligation with it. And it seems that he holds that when the Gemara says that guarding from kneading is not considered guarding—that is only ideally. Thus far his words. And also the Tur wrote a response to the Gaon that buying flour from the market in a pressing situation—it is permitted and one fulfills his obligation with it, for we do not assume it to be prohibited. But ideally—guarding is required. Thus far his words. In my humble opinion, it seems that this Gaon explained the Gemara that guarding from kneading is considered guarding for those who disagree with Rava. And what he wrote "in a pressing situation" is because ideally, guarding is required from the time of reaping according to Rava.

And this is what our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in Section 4 briefly, and this is his language: The wheat used for making matzah for the mitzvah—it is good to guard it so that water does not fall on it from the time of harvesting, and at the very least from the time of grinding. And in times of pressing need, it is permitted to take flour from the market. Until here is his language. And there is one who wrote in this language: thus is the meaning of the verse "And you shall guard the matzot"—every guarding that can be done should be done. If it is not possible from the time of harvesting since one buys from the market—one should guard from the time of grinding. And if one cannot find wheat to buy from the market—they guard from the time of kneading. And according to this, the Geonim do not disagree at all (Bach). And it is obvious that in places where they wash the wheat before grinding—it becomes complete chametz, and it is forbidden even in times of pressing need to buy flour from the market (Magen Avraham, Small Section 8). And there is one who wrote that perhaps it did not become chametz, and Heaven forbid to say such a thing (see Taz, Small Section 3).

And behold, in any case, all of these our Rabbis hold that the primary obligation of supervised matzah is for eating an olive-sized piece on the first night, as this is the matzah of the mitzvah, as stated by our teacher, Rabbi Yosef Karo. But what one eats throughout the days of Passover does not need any supervision at all, and so wrote the Ran, of blessed memory, and this is his wording: "But these words refer to the matzah of the mitzvah, but other bread that a person eats on Passover does not require supervision for the sake of matzah at all, but it must be known with certainty that it did not come to leavening, as it is taught: 'The flour and dough of a non-Jew, a person may fill their stomach with them, such as kneaded before us, etc.' up to here is his wording." Similarly, our teacher Rabbi Yosef Karo wrote in his larger work, and this is his wording: "And that which we require supervision specifically for the matzah of the mitzvah, but other matzah, etc., does not require supervision at all, etc." up to here is his wording.

And this is what Rashi explained in Gittin (10a, s.v. 'and a person fulfills') regarding the matzah of the Cuthean, the obligation of the first night that one is obligated to eat matzah that is supervised, and even if we know that it did not leaven, one does not fulfill the obligation unless it was made with supervision for the sake of the mitzvah of matzah, as it is written (Exodus 12:17), "And you shall observe the matzot," up to here is his wording. According to this, this required supervision is for its intended purpose, like the intention required for all mitzvot, as Rava said, "he turned it over for the sake of the mitzvah," as Rashi explains there. Therefore, it is invalid if done by a Cuthean, a deaf-mute, an imbecile, or a minor, as they are not considered capable of having the proper intent. Similarly, the great Or Zarua wrote (Siman 249), and this is his wording: "It is clearly implied that a person does not fulfill their obligation even with complete matzah unless it was baked for the sake of the obligation of matzah, etc. And a regular Israelite is presumed to have proper intent, for regarding sacrifices we require slaughtering with intent, and we hold that the general intent is considered proper intent, etc." up to here is his wording.

And in this manner, all the early and later authorities have ruled. According to this, there is no requirement to eat "shemura" matzah all the days of Passover, as guarding (the matzah) is only necessary for the first night, as written by one of the great later authorities (Pri Chadash in Siman 396, cited in Sha'arei Teshuva, Subsection 8), and these are his words: Those who are accustomed to eat matzah all Passover from the time of harvest – this is not called a "safeguard" but an unnecessary stringency. And if one wants to eat matzah that is not guarded from the time of harvest all the days of Passover, except for the first night – he does not need an annulment (of vows). Thus far his words. And there are those who wrote that an annulment is necessary (see there in Sha'arei Teshuva).

In my humble opinion, it is not so. For it is true that this is the opinion of Rashi, Tosafot, the Rosh, and other early authorities. But the opinion of the Rif and the Rambam is not so, and according to them, the obligation is to eat guarded matzah (matzah shemurah) throughout all the days of Passover. They do not interpret "guarding" as for the sake of the mitzvah, but rather as "guarding from chametz," and they do not have the version in the Gemara where Rava said to them "turn it for the sake of the mitzvah," but rather "for the sake of matzah." For this is the version in the Rif, and this is the language of the Rif there: "And a person must guard the flour for Passover from the time of harvest, as it is written 'and you shall guard the matzot' (and this verse applies to all seven days, see there). And Rava said to those who turn over the sheaves: When you turn them - turn them for the sake of matzah. Meaning: be careful with them that water does not come upon them." Thus far is his language. He did not mention the first night, and he reads "for the sake of matzah" and not "for the sake of the mitzvah." And he explained explicitly "meaning..." - so that you should not err and think there is some "for its sake" here, rather the guarding is from water causing chametz, and this applies to all the days of Passover.

And also Maimonides in the fifth chapter, law 8, explained this explicitly, and this is his language: "A dish that was cooked... and if it did not split..., the grain that did not split is not considered complete chametz from the Torah. It is only from the words of the Scribes, because it is stated, 'And you shall guard the matzot,' meaning: be careful with matzah and guard it from any aspect of leavening. Therefore, the Sages said: a person must be careful with the grain from which he eats on Passover, that no water comes upon it after it has been harvested, so that there will be no aspect of leavening in it." Until here is his language. It is explicitly clear that the guarding is for all the days of Passover equally, that the guarding is from leavening and not because of the matter of "for its sake" of the mitzvah. Therefore, the Rif and Maimonides omitted the issue of the doughs of the Cutheans, as a person fills his stomach with them. Many have labored over this, and the matter is simple that they rejected this from halacha because of the matter of Rava, who required guarding for every matzah on Passover from the time of harvesting, to guard them from leavening. (However, since this is only rabbinic, therefore the Rif and Maimonides wrote at the end of the order that if it is impossible to obtain guarded [grain] for all the days of Passover, at least one should obtain it for the first olive-sized piece to eat matzah properly according to the enactment of the Sages, see there. But when it is possible to obtain, one is obligated to eat guarded [grain] all the days of Passover.)

And I say that this is also the opinion of Rav Hai Gaon, as brought by the Rosh there, and this is his language: "And Rav Hai Gaon, of blessed memory, wrote: 'Matzah that was baked by a non-Jew in the presence of a Jew, with proper supervision, is permitted for a Jew to eat.' And the Rosh wrote about this that pious individuals are strict upon themselves like the stringent Geonim, and they knead and bake by themselves." Thus far his language. And there has already been an effort to understand the words of the Gaon, for since it requires 'for its sake' — how is it permitted in such a manner? However, it is clear that he holds that there is no issue of 'for its sake' at all, only supervision from becoming chametz, and therefore, it does not matter who does it. (And it is very surprising about the Tur, who wrote in the name of the Rif that one must guard the wheat that fulfills the requirement of matzah...— where did he see in the Rif 'wheat that fulfills the requirement of matzah'? For the Rif discusses all the days of Passover. Rather, because it was obvious to him that it is only for the obligation of the first night, thus he wrote so. Also, the words of the Ran need some examination. However, the Maggid Mishneh wrote, and this is his language: 'And no distinction is mentioned in the laws or in the words of our Rabbi between the matzah of the first night and the matzah that a person eats on the other days of Passover.' Thus far his language, and he made an effort in this, and according to what I have written, the matters are explained. Be precise and you will find it light.)

And it turns out that, according to practical halacha: One who wishes to fulfill the obligation of eating matzah on Pesach properly must eat "shmurah" matzah, which means that the wheat was guarded from the time of harvesting for all the days of Pesach, in accordance with the opinions of the Rif, Rambam, and the Gaon. Additionally, a portion must be harvested "for the sake of" matzah mitzvah for the first night, and it must be ground "for the sake of," and kneaded and baked—all "for the sake of" by a competent Jew. This is the approach of Rashi, Tosafot, the Rosh, the Tur, the Shulchan Aruch, most of the early authorities, the Sheiltot, and the Baal Halachot Gedolot. However, there are those who rule according to Rava, that specifically from the time of harvesting. And there are those who rule according to the dissenting opinions, that it suffices from the time of grinding until after baking. And there are those who rule that it suffices from the time of kneading and onward, as we have explained with the help of Heaven. (And it seems to me that even in the Mekhilta in Parashat Bo there is this dispute. For it says there "And you shall guard the matzot"—guard it so that it does not become invalid. From here they said: If it starts to rise, knead it with cold water. [This is like the Rif and Rambam, that the guarding is because of chametz.] Rabbi Yoshiya says: Do not read it so, but "And you shall guard the mitzvot..." [This is like Rashi and Tosafot.] And what it says afterward "Just as you do not let the matzah become chametz, so too do not let the mitzvah become chametz, but if a mitzvah comes to your hand, do it immediately—this is another interpretation, see there.)

During the time of the Gemara, they were proficient in washing the wheat, meaning to rinse it with water and guard it so that it would not become leavened. However, already in the days of the Rabbanan Savoraim, who resided in the Yeshiva, it was stated that we are not proficient in washing, and it is forbidden for us to wash, whether it be wheat or barley. Barley is also forbidden according to the law of the Gemara, because it is softer than wheat and becomes leavened more quickly. Therefore, all of Israel customarily bake matzah only from wheat, because it is harder and the flour is tough, and the dough does not stick together as much. Nowadays, if water falls on wheat, we consider it to be complete chametz. All the more so other types of grain, such as rye, which is called karyin, and barley, and oats.

Sacks that are used to store flour throughout the year, and even if they were used only once for flour, and one wishes to wash them and use them for Passover flour – it is necessary to first undo all their stitches before washing them, including at the edges. Additionally, if they have patches – the patches must be removed before washing, and then they should be washed very thoroughly, and afterwards the sacks can be re-stitched and the patches replaced. Certainly, it is better to make new ones if possible, because there are some who wish to forbid their use even after washing and unstitching, due to the strong adherence of the flour to the sacks (Taz, Subsection 5). However, the law is not in accordance with this stricter opinion, nor is the custom, as it is common to scrub them thoroughly by hand (Chayei Adam, Subsection 20). Nevertheless, in any case, one must be very careful in washing them. If the stitches were not undone – even post facto, the washing does not help. It is obvious that the same applies if they contained Passover flour this year and one wants to wash them for next year; the stitches must be undone to fulfill the requirement.

When transporting sacks from the mill on the back of an animal, not in a wagon, one must be careful not to place them directly on the animal’s body. Rather, one should place a saddle, or a thick leather, or a thick garment under the sack. Otherwise, the sack will become damp from the animal’s sweat. Although the sweat of an animal might not be considered like water, as is evident from Tractate Machshirin, Chapter Six, nevertheless, one should not be lenient. Even if this is compared to fruit juice, when water comes into contact with it during kneading, it will become a mixture of fruit juice and water and will hasten fermentation, as I wrote in Siman 462. And although one might say that this sweat, since it dried by nightfall, does not reawaken during kneading, and there is no mixture of fruit juice and water; necessarily, we must say so. Otherwise, why did the Tur permit, in the name of Rabbeinu Peretz, the case of mice biting, due to fruit juice, as I wrote there? Wouldn't there be fruit juice and water during kneading? Therefore, one must say, as I wrote, that it has already dried. Nevertheless, it is forbidden to do so initially. 

In our situation, this does not apply at all, since we transport in a wagon. However, one must be very careful, as during that time there are often snow and rain, to place mats or sacks under the Passover flour sacks in the wagon, and also to cover the sacks well on top. Especially now that we transport on long journeys on railways, with many loadings and unloadings, one must be extremely careful in covering the sacks. Anyone who is not careful in this causes many to stumble, and the sins of the community are upon him, and his sins will be upon his bones. However, one who is careful in this matter will be blessed from Heaven (see Chayei Adam, Section 22).

And our master, the Rema, wrote in section 7: "And similarly, one should be careful from the outset not to place many sacks of flour on top of each other where possible." Until here is his language. But now this is impossible in any way. And in truth, there is no concern in this, for the reason for the stringency is that due to the warmth from lying one on top of the other, and kneading immediately, they will warm up and come to leavening (as the Chayei Adam wrote in section 23). And with us, when the sacks are brought, it will still be days until the time of kneading. Additionally, we see clearly that our sacks, where the flour is placed firmly and the sacks are smooth, there is no warmth at all. Furthermore, from the time the flour is taken to the baker's house, many hours will pass. Therefore, we do not need to be careful about this at all.

It is customary to clean the millstones, because sometimes grain is placed in them to be ground into fine flour. It is also customary to set aside the first flour ground after cleaning until after the festival. Pious individuals customarily go themselves to the mill, since it is a greater mitzvah to do it oneself than through an agent, and they observe the grinding of their flour personally. If one cannot go himself, he should ensure that at least a Torah scholar and God-fearing person is present during the grinding. 

There is an opinion that if one grinds grain in a mill for the purpose of making fine flour, one should not grind for Passover in that mill, even with another set of millstones, because the dust can transfer from one to the other. A minor should not oversee the mill (Magen Avraham, section 11). If there is no dust, it is permitted. 

We have already written in the previous section several laws and precautions regarding mills, and in general it is impossible to explain everything in writing, especially in our times where several new devices for mills have been developed. An expert in these matters must take care to guard all areas from which chametz could arise, whether from moisture, dough that collects there, or from heat. A wise person will listen and increase in learning. All this requires the supervision of a Torah scholar and God-fearing person.

One must grind the wheat a day or days before kneading, so that the flour cools down. Some say three days, and some say that leaving it overnight is sufficient. The main opinion is that it requires a full 24 hours, not less (see Magen Avraham, sub-paragraph 23 and Chayei Adam, sub-paragraph 26). Ideally, it should be two full days (there), but after the fact, it is not a strict requirement. However, if one ground the wheat on the eve of Passover, some say that it is prohibited even after the fact to knead on the day of the eve of Passover, because the flour is hot at the time of grinding and heats the water, making the dough prone to fermenting.
