Some have written that even this is not a strict requirement after the fact, because the flour is sifted before kneading and cools down (there, sub-paragraph 14). Know that from the words of the halachic authorities it is clear that heating without water does not lead to fermentation. According to this, we must say that what is stated in the Jerusalem Talmud, third chapter, end of halacha 1, where Rabbi Abbahu instructed the grinders not to place the sieves one on top of the other so that they do not heat and ferment, does not refer to heating by itself, but rather heating with the subsequent water. (This is also explained from the words of the Agur, cited by the Beit Yosef. See Magen Avraham, sub-paragraph 15.)

The Tur wrote: One makes matzah from fine flour, even if it is as good as the matzah of Solomon or from the bread of the derah. Rashi explained: even if it is entirely made of bran. But the Rambam, of blessed memory, forbade matzah made entirely of bran, as he wrote in the sixth chapter: one does not fulfill the obligation with bread of bran or bread of coarse bran. However, if one kneads the dough with its bran or coarse bran, one fulfills the obligation. This is also the opinion of the Rif. Thus far his words. The explanation of the matter: do not say that since it is written "bread of affliction" it must not be made of fine flour. The text informs us that it is permitted. And "bread of affliction" pertains to the kneading, the shaping, and the baking, that only flour and water should be used, and it should be baked immediately. And so it is in the Gemara (36b). Similarly, on the contrary: even the derah, meaning coarse bread, one should not say that this is not called "bread." The text informs us that it is not so, for many poor people eat this way.

However, according to Rashi who explained that it is entirely bran – this is certainly perplexing. For this does not qualify as bread at all concerning the obligation of separating challah, and the law is the same for them (Ran). According to the Rif and the Rambam, it works out well. It must be said that Rashi's intention was not entirely bran, but that he mixed a lot of bran with it, and even so, it is still suitable for human consumption (Bach). Also, from the words of the Rif, it seems that he wrote "bread of deraa is bran bread," and although the Rosh explained the Rif's words like the Rambam, the Ran of blessed memory explained his intention according to Rashi, for if it were like the Rambam, he would have said "bread with bran," and his intention was for a lot of bran.

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote in section 1: "It is preferable, initially, not to make the matzah excessively wide, as it would be like an 'ashisha' (a large cake). Thus far his words, meaning, in the Gemara it is taught: 'Bread of affliction' – excluding scalded bread and an 'ashisha,' see there. It is very surprising why all our Rabbis omitted this 'ashisha.' And even our teacher, the Rema, wrote 'it is preferable…' – is it not an explicit Baraita? 

And it is possible to say that they rejected it from the halacha, because since even a matzah like that of Solomon is valid – all the more so this is valid. Or it is possible because it is said there that an 'ashisha' is one-sixth of an ephah, see there. And the measure for challah is one-tenth of an ephah, as it is written 'and the omer is one-tenth of an ephah,' and an omer is the measure for challah. If so, the 'ashisha' would need to be close to twice the measure of challah, and this is entirely impossible, for we do not knead more than the measure of challah, as will be explained in section 460. Therefore, there is no need to write this law. Therefore, our teacher, the Rema, said 'it is preferable…', meaning: that even with our matzahs – it is preferable to do so, so that part of it does not resemble an 'ashisha.' And this is not from the law. And so we customarily make the matzahs for the seder not very large. And this is not an obligatory restriction.

It was taught in the first chapter of Challa: Dough intended for dogs, if shepherds eat from it, is obligated in challa..., and a person can fulfill his obligation with it on Passover. If shepherds do not eat from it, it is exempt from challa..., and a person does not fulfill his obligation with it on Passover. The Rambam explained that if one kneads it with bran and intends to feed it to dogs and not to people, it is exempt from challa, as it is written, "When you eat of the bread of the land"—those that people eat, and not what animals eat. Therefore, one does not fulfill the obligation of matza on Passover with it, since matza is dependent on challa. However, if shepherds do eat from it, meaning that in that place it is customary that even though it is made to feed dogs, nevertheless shepherds usually eat from it, then it is indeed called "when you eat of the bread of the land."

And Rabbeinu Shimshon explained that this is its meaning: "Dog dough" – for example, if it contains a lot of bran. Therefore, when the shepherds eat it, meaning it does not contain so much bran that they cannot eat it – it is obligated in challah and can be used to fulfill the obligation of matzah, since it is called "bread." But if it cannot be eaten – this is not bread. The Ramban, of blessed memory, explained based on the Jerusalem Talmud that even if it were made from fine flour, if its kneading and making do not have the form of bread – it is called "dog dough," for this is how they make it for dogs without the form of bread. And we have already written in Yoreh De'ah, at the end of Siman 3, that they do not disagree with the Rambam in practice, only in the explanation of the Mishnah. Also, in the Jerusalem Talmud there, there is a dispute about this, see there. And this, too, is not in practice but in the explanation of the Mishnah, see there.

And know: Even though flour from which bran and pollard have not been removed combine to make up an olive's bulk (kazayit) as I have written, nevertheless, if the bran or pollard is removed from the flour and then returned to it, they do not combine. There is someone who is uncertain about this (Magen Avraham, Subsection 2). However, there is no doubt here, as this is also the case regarding challah, and matzah depends on challah as I have written (Chapter 10, Subsection 2).

And know that Rashi of blessed memory at the end of the seventh chapter of Shabbat explained that "subin" (bran) is the outer shell that falls off during grinding, and "morsan" (pollard) is what remains in the sieve. The Ra'avad in the second chapter of Challah explained the opposite; see there. The Arukh under the entry "morsan" explained that "subin" is the fine waste of the flour, and "morsan" is the coarse waste; see there. According to him, the shell is insignificant. And it seems that this is what the world assumes, for when a shell is found in a dish on Pesach, we do not forbid the dish. According to Rashi and the Ra'avad, it would lead to fermentation. According to the Arukh's explanation, it is clarified in the Rambam's commentary on the Mishnah in the eleventh chapter of Terumot (Mishnah 5), and this is his language: "Morsan" is what rises from the bran, and "subin" is known. His language means the coarse waste that rises from the fine waste. This is also the explanation of the Rosh there, who wrote about "morsan" that it is the coarse waste; see there. And in the Mishnah there it is explained that in new grain there is more bran than in old grain; see there thoroughly.

The Sages taught: "Lechem Oni" – excludes scalded dough. For if the flour was decided with boiling water, which prevents it from leavening – nonetheless, one does not fulfill their obligation with it on Passover, as this is considered bread of the wealthy, not bread of poverty. The Tur wrote: dough that is mixed softly and scalded with boiling water – is not called "bread" to bless "Hamotzi" on it. And if it was baked afterwards in an oven – it is called "bread" regarding "Hamotzi" and challah, and one fulfills their obligation with it for matzah. And if its mixture is thick and scalded and baked – it is considered "bread" regarding challah and "Hamotzi", but one does not fulfill their obligation with it on Passover. According to Rav Hai – one fulfills their obligation with it on Passover. All this is according to the Talmudic law, but the Geonim prohibited all scalding. Thus far his words. And similarly, the Rif and the Rambam wrote that in our times, there is no one who knows how to properly scald. Therefore, all forms of scalding are prohibited. Nonetheless, if a wheat grain, or barley, or a piece of dough fell into a boiling dish – it is possible to permit the dish, and in any case to join it to some leniency (see Magen Avraham and Chayei Adam section 4).

A person does not fulfill his obligation with stolen matzah. This is the language of the Rambam in Chapter 7, Law 7: A person does not fulfill his obligation with matzah that is forbidden to him, such as if he ate untithed produce, or first tithe from which the terumah has not been taken, or if he stole it. The rule is: Anything upon which one recites the Grace after Meals – he has fulfilled his obligation with it. And anything upon which one does not recite the Grace after Meals – he has not fulfilled his obligation with it. This is the end of his language. And the Rosh in the chapter "Kol Sha'ah" (Siman 18) also writes that one does not fulfill his obligation with stolen matzah, because it is not "yours." For matzah, we derive from challah in the Gemara (35b) that it must be from your own, see there. But borrowed matzah is considered properly "yours," and one fulfills his obligation with it (Taz, subparagraph 3). And also with stolen matzah: specifically if he stole matzah. But if he stole wheat or flour and made it into matzah – he fulfills his obligation with it, because he has acquired it through a change, and he is only liable for the monetary value. And this is according to the reasoning of the Rosh because of "yours."

However, according to the Rambam, who attributes the reason to the blessing, and based on what we establish later in Siman 649 regarding the lulav, that even if one acquired it through a change (shinui), he should not recite the blessing over it—if so, here too, one does not fulfill the obligation of matzah according to the Rambam. There are those who differentiate between a change in name and a change in action, but this is not the main opinion (Ch. 10, Small Section 6). This is also evident in several places in Tosafot. And one cannot argue that for Birkat Hamazon, which is a Torah obligation, one must recite it, since the Rambam explicitly rules at the end of the first chapter of Berachot that one does not recite Birkat Hamazon over something prohibited. The Rosh disagrees with him, as I wrote in Siman 196. Therefore, I am puzzled by our master the Beit Yosef, who in one place rules according to the Rambam, and here rules according to the Rosh. However, the Maggid Mishneh also wrote that with a change (shinui), one fulfills his obligation, implying that this is also according to the Rambam. See there for further study. And see Magen Avraham there, Small Section 1.

Seemingly, why did our Rabbis not say the reason is because of "a mitzvah that comes through a transgression"? However, it appears to be because they hold that a mitzvah that comes through a transgression is only a rabbinic prohibition, and there are varying opinions among the Rishonim on this (Tosafot, Sukkah 9a). In the Jerusalem Talmud, the first chapter of Challah (halacha 9 [5]) states: A stolen matzah - it is forbidden to recite a blessing over it. Rabbi Oshaya said: Because it is stated, "The robber who blesses has blasphemed the Lord" (Psalms 10:3). This is said initially, but at the end – he owes the value of the matzah. The Rosh explained there that the intention is initially and post facto, that post facto one fulfills the obligation with stolen matzah. The Maggid Mishneh explained that "at the end" means after a change has occurred, see there. In my humble opinion, it appears that "initially" refers to the first blessing, as it is still in his power to return it. And "at the end" refers to the Grace after Meals, as he has already eaten it, and he owes the value. Therefore, he recites the blessing, for what has happened has happened.

Afterwards, the Jerusalem Talmud states: Rabbi says: "There is no sin – [only] a mitzvah." Rabbi Yossi says: "There is no mitzvah – [only] a sin." Rabbi Ila said: "These are the commandments; if one performs them as commanded – it is a mitzvah, and if not – it is not a mitzvah." Thus far his words. And the Rosh wrote: "It is possible that these Amoraim are in disagreement, and they hold that since one did not perform them as commanded – it is not a mitzvah, and he does not fulfill his obligation." Thus far his words. Their reasoning is because of a mitzvah that comes through a sin, only they express it in different terms. According to this, it implies that a mitzvah that comes through a sin is considered a Torah prohibition.

The Kohanim fulfill their obligation of eating matzah with challah and terumah, even though it is matzah that is not suitable for everyone. Similarly, one fulfills the obligation with matzah of ma'aser sheni in Jerusalem, as we hold that ma'aser sheni is considered personal property in Jerusalem, but not in the provinces (we conclude like the sages against Rabbi Meir). This is what Rambam decides in the third chapter of Ma'aser Sheni, that it is sacred property, but here in the sixth chapter, he rules that one fulfills the obligation of matzah with ma'aser sheni in Jerusalem (Lechem Mishneh). However, one does not fulfill the obligation with matzah of bikkurim even in Jerusalem, as it is stated: "In all your dwellings you shall eat matzot" – meaning matzah that can be eaten in all dwellings, excluding bikkurim, which can only be eaten in Jerusalem. But ma'aser sheni has a permit in the provinces through redemption.

Loaves of thanksgiving and wafers of a Nazirite that he made for himself – he does not fulfill his obligation with them, as it is stated, "And you shall guard the matzot" – matzah that is guarded for the sake of matzah alone is what one fulfills one's obligation with, excluding this which is guarded for the sake of a sacrifice. However, if he made them to sell in the market – he fulfills his obligation with them. For one who makes them to sell in the market, his intention is that if he does not sell them for the sake of a sacrifice, he will eat them for the sake of matzah, and it turns out that they were made for the sake of matzah (Lechem Mishneh 28). And even though if so, we come to the matter of retroactive clarification (bereirah), to say that afterwards it is clarified that it was done for the sake of matzah, and with Torah laws there is no retroactive clarification – it can be said that this is not like other cases of retroactive clarification, for he baked them for the sake of a mitzvah, and afterwards it was clarified for which mitzvah it was done. (And this is similar to the words of the Ran at the beginning of the fifth chapter of Nedarim. See there thoroughly. Be precise and you will find light.)

It is clear that hot water, when used to knead dough, will cause it to leaven, even if its heat is only comparable to that of saliva. Therefore, it is forbidden to knead matzah for all the days of Passover with anything other than cold water. And although in the Temple all meal offerings were kneaded with lukewarm water and were watched to ensure they did not leaven (Menachot 55a), the priests were diligent. However, this is not the case with us, and it is forbidden for us to knead with lukewarm water, only with cold water. Even with cold water, our Sages of blessed memory were stringent at the end of the chapter "Kol Sha'ah" and said: A woman should only knead with "our water," meaning water that was drawn and left overnight after being drawn. There are various reasons for this.

Rashi of blessed memory explained that because in the month of Nisan the springs are still warm as in the days of winter, it is therefore necessary to cool them for one night after they have been drawn from their source. Similarly, river waters also need to be cooled for one night, because the sunlight has struck them during the day. According to this reasoning, the main concern is that the water remains detached all night long, and they should be drawn before nightfall. One can draw them at any time during the day, as long as they remain detached throughout the night. Before dawn, it is prohibited to knead with them. Some have written that the main concern is from midnight, because then the northern wind blows and cools. Therefore, in a situation of pressing need, if they were drawn at night, but before midnight – it is permitted to knead with them the next day. Thus, according to this view, there is no impediment to drawing the water during twilight, but this is only for an ideal situation. In pressing need, even if the water was drawn during the day or at the beginning of the night – it is permitted. However, according to this view, there is a stringency that the water needs to be cooled for one night.

However, Rabbi Eliezer of Metz wrote the reason: Because at night all the springs and rivers are warm, since the sun moves beneath the visible horizon of the earth, and therefore it heats the springs and rivers at night. And therefore, at dawn, one can see something like smoke over the rivers. Hence, water should not be in the spring or river at night, even at the beginning of the night, but should be drawn before the night begins. And even though during the past night they were in the spring and river, during the day they cooled while being in the source. But when they are drawn at night, even if they are left until the next day or for several days – it does not help, because they were drawn warm. And cooling does not help them unless they are in the river or spring for a whole day, so they cool from the heating of the night. Hence, just as it is forbidden to draw them at night – so too during the day, because we require a whole day for cooling while they are in their source. According to this opinion, the drawing is only during twilight, when it is neither day nor night. Correspondingly, there is a leniency in this opinion, that immediately after drawing them, one can knead the dough with them, and they do not require waiting overnight as per Rashi's opinion.

Therefore, ideally, in order to fulfill both opinions, one should draw the water during twilight, so that it cools for twelve hours in its source. Since it is difficult to precisely time twilight, it should be close to twilight. One should not bake with this water until the morning light, whether it is well water, spring water, or river water. It is permissible to draw water on one day for use over many days. If the weather is hot, the water should be placed in a cool cellar. If the weather is cold, the water should be placed in the air, as the cellar will then be warm. In our region, the weather is generally cold. Nevertheless, the water should not be left outside, as the sun may shine on it. Therefore, the custom is to place the water in a "firahuviz" (a storage room), where there is no heating and it remains cool. A small amount is brought into the house for kneading, and when it is used up, more is brought from the "firahuviz". However, the "firahuviz" should have a roof to prevent the sun from shining on the water.

Initially, it is better to immediately bring them into the house, to the place where they will stay overnight, as I have written. However, if one takes them to a house under the open sky, they should be covered. And not because of the sun, for the sun has already set, but so that nothing falls into them. Nevertheless, if they were not immediately brought into the house but were left outside, one must rise early and bring them into the house before the sun rises, even on a cloudy day, for the sun's rays penetrate through the cracks in the clouds. Thus it is said in Yoma (28b): "A cloudy day is entirely sunny," see there. Nevertheless, if one did not bring them in early, and they remained under the open sky, even uncovered, as long as they did not remain so long that they became heated, it is not harmful, even if they stood in the sun (Magen Avraham, subsection 2). This depends on one's observation. There is also an opinion that when they are inside the house, it is actually better not to cover the water, so that the air can have an effect (Chayei Adam, subsection 2).

If one did not bring them [the water] in during twilight but rather at night or while it is still fully day, and he has no other water – it is permitted after the fact (bediavad) after twelve hours (Chayei Adam, small section 1) according to Rashi's view. And since it is impossible to precisely determine the exact time of twilight – it is better to draw the water a little earlier than a little later (there, in the name of the Maharil, and see Taz). And when baking on Sunday – it is necessary to prepare the water initially on Thursday during twilight, because on Friday evening and Shabbat it is not possible to do so during twilight. And this is what our teacher the Rema wrote: "And when Passover falls on a Sunday, one should draw the water on the night of the thirteenth, which is Thursday night." This is his exact wording. And this was like in their times, when they would bake on the night of Passover when it fell on a Sunday. And if one forgot to draw the water on Thursday – he should draw it on Friday before it gets dark, or instruct a non-Jew to draw it during twilight (Magen Avraham, small section 4). It seems to me that this applies when Passover falls on a Sunday, as I have written. But for us, who bake several weeks before Passover in bakeries, if one did not prepare the water on Thursday – one should not bake on Sunday at all, but rather on Monday. And he should draw the water on Sunday during twilight as per the law. And there are those who are lenient (Shaarei Teshuvah, small section 4).

Ideally, one should draw water from rivers and not from wells, because in Nisan the sun travels beneath the earth, and the waters in the wells are warm. However, when the rivers swell from melted snow and rain, it is better to draw from wells, as river water is always warm due to the snow and rain. And since in our countries it is always like this, we always draw from wells. This is not mandatory, for in a place where there is only a river, one always draws from the river. And in a place where there are only wells, one always draws from wells. And know that even though the custom is to pour out water at the time of a death or during the solstice, one should not do this with our water, as it should not be poured out, for "a keeper of the commandment shall know no evil thing." And among us, during the solstice, there is no custom to pour out water; rather, some place a piece of iron. Therefore, one should be careful not to place the iron in one's hand into the water, as the hand warms it.

Ideally, one should be meticulous that the drawing of the water for matzah, and especially for the matzah of the mitzvah, be performed by an adult Jew. And at the time of drawing the water, he should say "for the sake of the matzah of the mitzvah." It should not be drawn by a non-Jew or a minor in order to enhance the mitzvah. For the matzah of the mitzvah, special water is taken, and in a special vessel. Our master, the Rema, wrote that it is customary to take new earthenware vessels, and this custom should not be changed. With wooden vessels, there is no need to be particular. Thus far is his language. Among us, we draw with wooden or metal vessels. And metal pails that are painted – there is no concern, as there is no worry of leavening in our times. Furthermore, since it is cold and for a short period – there is no concern in any case.

Rabbeinu the Beit Yosef writes in section 2: There are those who say that water collected in a cistern may be used for kneading dough immediately after drawing it. However, one should not be lenient in this matter except in a pressing circumstance. Thus are his words. This refers to water gathered in a large structure, from which the water flows through pipes to other places. This structure is built with a roof, floor, and walls, and sunlight does not enter it. Therefore, they said it is permissible to knead with this water immediately. But one should be lenient only in a pressing circumstance. However, sometimes the water is not cold, and it is forbidden to knead with it. Similarly, the water that comes through pipes in large cities has the same status as well water and must be drawn at twilight. The small amount of water at the beginning should be poured out, as it is not cold. Similarly, in pumps, some of the previous water should be poured out for this reason, as it has warmed slightly from remaining there.

Further, he wrote in section 4: Water that was not left overnight, which was nullified one in two with our water – one may knead with it. Thus is his language, for in this manner – surely they also cooled significantly. And it is not specifically one in two, but the majority should be from our water (Magen Avraham, subsection 15). And some permit even initially mixing water that was not left overnight with our water, for this is not like nullifying a prohibition initially, as there is no prohibition here but rather a need for cooling, and in this manner, it has cooled (ibid). And nowadays, many are lenient regarding this matter of mixing water that was not left overnight with our water, because many loaves of Passover flour are baked in one day, and our water has decreased, and it is necessary to mix them. Additionally, because in our northern regions, we see clearly that the water is very cold before Passover, and therefore they are lenient in the mixture.

If one kneaded dough with water that was not left overnight, the Rif and the Rambam in Chapter 5, Law 14 forbid it even after the fact, and so wrote the Behag. However, Rashi and the Rosh permitted it after the fact. Some say that if done unintentionally, it is permitted, but if done intentionally, it is forbidden. And in a pressing situation, such as if one has no other water, it is permitted to knead with such water if it was done unintentionally. If one already kneaded with water that was not left overnight unintentionally, it is permitted even not in a pressing situation, meaning if one has other matzah. However, it is certain that one should not use these matzot for the mitzvah of matzah on the first night, as they are not considered optimal. Additionally, some of the early authorities say that the entire prohibition of water that was not left overnight applies only to matzah for the mitzvah, as the Tur wrote in the name of the Riatz Gaot and the Eitur; see there. And know that rainwater is not mentioned at all in this law. It appears to me that rainwater certainly requires a twelve-hour wait, as we often see that they sometimes have a bit of warmth.

It is obvious that it is forbidden to knead with hot water, even if it was only warmed by the sun. And even hot water that has already cooled down—it is forbidden to knead with it (Magen Avraham, subsection 12), because it still retains some degree of heat. Similarly, it is forbidden to knead with water that has been placed in a large copper pot with thick walls, even if it is not currently being heated—nevertheless, cold water that is placed in it becomes lukewarm, since it retains heat for several days. If one transgresses and kneads with such water, even inadvertently, or even under pressing circumstances, and even not for the purpose of a mitzvah, it is forbidden after the fact. This is not comparable to water that has not rested, which is merely a stringency. But here, there is a significant concern of actual leavening, and therefore, there is no allowance under any circumstance. The same law applies if one kneads with lukewarm water; it is also forbidden after the fact.

It is forbidden to put salt in matzah, because salt heats the dough, and the same applies to pepper. This is the established custom and should not be changed. Even after the fact, it is prohibited. The Mordechai also writes that one who eats salty matzah is like one who eats chametz. However, if a grain of salt falls into the dough, it does not render it forbidden, because this grain does not cause fermentation, but one must be careful to bake it immediately. If one kneads the matzah with some spices or sesame seeds that are not sharp, the matzah is not forbidden since it still has the taste of matzah. Nevertheless, one does not fulfill the mitzvah of matzah with it, as it is not "bread of affliction." Ideally, no spices should be added to the dough because they have a certain sharpness and heat the dough. Salt and pepper even after the fact are forbidden. Some say that even a pinch of pepper heats the entire dough, and the same applies to lime (Magen Avraham, Small Paragraph 19). This is when it is kneaded into the dough, but if it falls onto the dough, it should be removed. Similarly, ginger, cloves, and saffron, which are very sharp, render the dough forbidden even if a small amount is kneaded into it.

One should not knead for Passover a dough larger than the amount requiring the separation of challah, which is an "omer" (a tenth of an ephah). This is equivalent to the volume of forty-three and one-fifth medium-sized chicken eggs. How should one measure this? One should take a vessel filled with water and pour the water into another empty vessel. Then, place the forty-three eggs into the first vessel, and afterwards pour the water back from the second vessel into the first. The water remaining in the second vessel is the measure of the eggs. A small amount should be added to this to account for a fifth of an egg. This measure—namely, a vessel that holds the amount of the remaining water—is the measure for challah. According to our tradition, three liters of flour is the measure for challah. More details on this can be found in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 324; see there.

The reason for this matter is because, although there is a time limit for dough left unattended to become chametz, as will be explained in Siman 459, nevertheless, initially, one should not leave the dough without working it even for a moment, as I wrote there. The sages estimated that dough of a quantity greater than the amount requiring challah cannot be sufficiently worked by hand all at once, and inevitably part of the dough will remain unattended. However, with an amount equal to the requirement for challah, it is possible to work all the dough at once. And even though with the showbread they would knead two esronim at once, since each loaf was of this measure as explicitly mentioned in the Torah, we do not derive from the Temple practice, as the priests are diligent. Therefore, after the fact, if they kneaded more than this measure, we do not prohibit it, because although part of it was unattended, it would not reach the measure of chametz. Some knead more than the measure initially, and this is forbidden. Although the sages of France prohibited even after the fact, as the Tur wrote, nevertheless the Rambam, the Rosh, the Tur, and the Shulchan Aruch permitted it after the fact. And this is the law. (Regarding the Magen Avraham’s critique of the Rosh in Siman 6, see Chayei Adam Siman 9 which refutes it).

The Tur wrote that one of the great early authorities used to say that this measure only applied in their days, when the ovens were small. But now that the ovens are large, it is preferable to knead a large dough. However, they did not agree with him; see there. This means that he holds that the reason for this decree is not because of the kneading, but because a large dough would not fit into the oven, and they would have to wait with part of the dough until the previous batch is baked, and in the meantime, it would become leavened. But with a large oven, it is preferable to have a large dough so that the oven will be full of bread and bake well (Beitzah 17a). And perhaps this is the reason for those who initially knead more than the measure, as we mentioned in the previous section. But his words were rejected because the reason is due to the kneading, as we explained.

The measure that holds the prescribed amount for challah should be filled with flour without heaping, as it needs to be level and not heaped. If it is heaped, it will contain more than the prescribed amount for challah. And its measure: Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote that the measure from Egyptian wheat flour is approximately five hundred and twenty Egyptian dirhams. We do not know this measure. The flour should not be packed into the measure, for if so, it will not knead well, and the flour will turn into dough and ferment. Rather, it should be measured loosely, in the manner of sellers, without pressing his hand on the flour. And one should not do so even if it does not exceed the prescribed amount for challah, for otherwise it is forbidden initially. It is good to say at the time of adding the flour, as well as at the time of adding the water to the flour: "For the sake of the mitzvah of matzah."

Even though it is forbidden to measure flour on Yom Tov for kneading, nevertheless, if one is baking on Pesach, it is permitted to measure to ensure that one does not bake more than the amount required for challah. This is considered a measurement for the sake of a mitzvah. However, some prohibit this, arguing that the measurement is not essential, as a slight deficiency or excess does not impede the process. Therefore, one should estimate, and this is the customary practice.

Since it is forbidden to bake more than the amount required for challah, one would naturally bake a little less. Consequently, no single dough has the required amount for challah, and it is forbidden to separate challah from it. You might suggest: Let us separate without a blessing due to the doubt. However, this is also not possible, because perhaps later he will place matzah from several doughs into one vessel, and the vessel will combine them for challah, and they will become obligated in challah by law. He will think that he has already taken challah, and if each one did not have the required amount, then the challah he took is nothing, and it turns out he will eat tevel (produce from which tithes have not been taken). Therefore, one should not separate from each dough individually. What should one do? If there are many people involved, and they are making several doughs – he should take two doughs and attach them slightly to each other, as is explained in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 325. If the doughs are hard – he should place the edge of one on the edge of the other, and cut challah from both and make a blessing, and throw it into the oven. However, this is impractical to separate from the dough, because the time is pressing, lest the dough becomes chametz. Therefore, although ideally there is a commandment to separate from the dough, nevertheless, regarding matzah, all of Israel has the custom to separate after baking, for the reason explained.

And how should he proceed? He should place several doughs, that is, the baked matzot from several doughs, into one basket or other vessel that has rims. And this is our established rule that the basket combines them for the purpose of challah just like kneading, and he should take challah from one matzah, and it will cover all of them. He should be careful that they do not extend beyond the rims of the vessel, for those that extend – the basket does not combine them, unless he places a sheet over them from above, which encircles all the matzot. And this also counts as combining by means of a vessel. And by placing a sheet, a vessel is not necessary. And even if each dough has the required amount, and he wants to separate from one on behalf of all – he can do so. In such a case, even a vessel combination is not needed, but they should be close to each other. And although challah outside the Land (of Israel) does not require surrounding, for our established rule is that challah outside the Land one eats and then separates – this is for one dough, but not for two doughs.

According to this, there are three levels: If there is enough dough to require separating challah and it was baked, he can eat and then separate. This applies outside the Land of Israel and not in the Land of Israel, as I wrote in Yoreh De'ah there. If there were two or more doughs and he wants to separate from one for all of them, he is not allowed to eat until he first separates, joining all the matzot together and separating from one for all. He does not need a single vessel for combining. If each dough does not have the required amount for challah, he needs a single vessel or a sheet covering, as I wrote. Before combining them in one vessel, he is allowed to eat from each one since they are exempt from challah. But after placing them in one vessel or covering them with a sheet, he is not allowed to eat from them until he separates challah. A general rule is that the challah of the Diaspora does not need to be within the same boundary, but this is only when they were kneaded as one dough.

According to this, since we do not bake a quantity of dough that requires separating challah in each batch, we must be very careful to combine all the doughs in one vessel, and not in two vessels. If they do not fit in one vessel, place the two vessels next to each other, spread a cloth over both vessels, and separate one portion of challah for all the dough. Be careful to separate the challah immediately and not to delay until the eve of Passover, for one might forget, and it is prohibited to separate on Yom Tov. Additionally, this could lead to spoilage. This is how modest women conduct themselves.

According to this, if it happened that the matzot were divided into two containers, and challah was taken from one container and not from the other, the second container has no remedy. This is because it is impossible to separate from the second container, as one might take from the dough that was already tithed in the first container, and it is therefore exempt since it was already tithed. This results in separating from the exempt for the obligated. However, if only one matzah was taken from the first, there is a remedy. This means that one should take from the second container from multiple matzot in a way that includes at least one matzah that is definitely not from the first dough. For example, if each dough produces ten matzot, one should take from eleven matzot, and similarly in other such cases. But if one took from several matzot, the second container has no remedy until a small additional dough is baked and combined within the second container, making it obligated in challah, and then one should take from it for the entire second container.

However, if one wants to take from each and every matzah, it is obvious that he does not need to bake a new dough. Similarly, the law applies if many doughs were baked, and some had challah taken from them and some did not, and afterward they all got mixed together. It is impossible to separate from one or two or more, because perhaps he will separate from those that already had their challah taken, and he will be separating from exempt dough for obligated dough. Therefore, all the regulations that were explained are necessary. In this case, there is no difference whether each had the measure of challah or not. This is what our teacher the Rema wrote: If he took from some of the doughs and from some he did not take, and they got mixed together, he needs to take challah from each and every one, or knead another dough and take from it also for those that got mixed. And if he recognizes one matzah that is obligated in challah, he takes from it for the others. Until here is his wording, and it is obvious.

Therefore, when one collects matzot from all the householders before Passover, some of whom have already separated challah and some who have not yet separated it, because some wait until the eve of Passover—it is therefore impossible to separate challah from the gathered matzot, as one might separate from those already exempt, which would be separating from the exempt for the obligated. Therefore, it is necessary to bake another dough and combine it with all the matzot, and separate from it for all of them. And this is the common custom among us when collecting matzot for the wheat money from all the householders—two or three matzot.

And know that there is an opinion that just as with a single dough one may eat and continue to eat and then separate [challah], so too with doughs that each individually did not have the required measure but became obligated through combining in a basket, one may also eat and continue to eat and then separate, for combining in a basket is exactly like kneading together (the opinion of the GRa"Z, section 10, in the name of the Ba"Ch and Pri Chadash). However, there are those who disagree, and they hold that in this case it is forbidden to eat before separating, and one must separate specifically from the adjacent dough. Only when kneaded together is there no need for adjacency, and not when combined through a basket (ibid. in the name of the Chayei Adam). And this seems to be the main opinion, as it appears from Tosafot and other early authorities that combining in a basket only obligates in challah but does not make it exactly like a single dough regarding "eating and continuing to eat and then separating."

And behold, when they forgot to separate challah before Passover, on Yom Tov it is forbidden to separate challah if the obligation to separate challah occurred before Yom Tov, as I wrote in Siman 506. Therefore, if the combining of the basket occurred on Yom Tov and not before – it would be permissible to separate challah on Yom Tov, since the obligation came on Yom Tov when there was not enough dough in each piece to require separating challah, and until Yom Tov they were scattered and on Yom Tov they placed them in one vessel. However, this is uncommon, and usually after baking they place them in one vessel. If so, they became obligated from the eve of Yom Tov, and how can one eat on Yom Tov according to the last opinion in the previous section, which holds that through the combination of the basket, we do not say "eat and continue and then separate." And even according to the first opinion, it is only valid when all the matzot were placed in one vessel, but if they divided them into two vessels – even according to this opinion, there is no solution to eat on Yom Tov from one vessel, and on the evening after Yom Tov to combine the vessels and cover them with a cloth and then separate challah, as perhaps he will then separate from the second vessel, and it did not exempt what they ate, as they were not in one vessel. However, in this case, one must be careful to separate challah from the vessel they ate from on Yom Tov. Nonetheless, we have already written that the primary opinion is like the last opinion.

Therefore, the ordinance for this is that on Yom Tov, they shall eat whole matzot and leave part of each matzah. It is not necessarily required to be whole, but rather large pieces, leaving a small part from each piece. On the night after Yom Tov, the remnants should be placed among all the matzot, so that they are all in one vessel or covered with a cloth. One should take challah from the remnants, and this is similar to the practice outside the Land of Israel where one eats and then separates [challah]. Since something is left from each matzah that is eaten, it is not obligatory to take specifically from the remnants, but it is preferable to take from the remnants.

Indeed, what should be done with the crushed matzah to eat from it on Yom Tov (festival day)? After all, it consists of several doughs, and perhaps what one eats will be from one dough that he consumes entirely. And when he takes challah (a portion of dough) on Motzaei Yom Tov (after the festival), it will not exempt what was eaten on Yom Tov from the crushed pieces. And to bake dough on Yom Tov and combine it, as I have written – we are not accustomed to baking matzah on Pesach itself, and among the masses, this would seem strange. Therefore, if it is possible for him to borrow crushed matzah from his neighbor on Yom Tov and repay him during Chol Hamoed (the intermediate days of the festival) when he takes challah, that is best. If not, it is necessary to eat and leave some of the crushed pieces, and combine them on Motzaei Yom Tov with the matzot and take one challah from all of them. And even though there is a concern we mentioned, that he might eat from one dough, it is necessary to rely on the opinion that mixing exists in a fine matter, and all the crushed pieces are considered as one piece (so it seems in my humble opinion).

And know that there is a dispute regarding the joining of a basket, whether the matzot need to touch each other, or if they can even be placed separately without touching one another. The simple custom is that they all touch each other. However, from the fundamental law, it seems that they do not need to touch. This applies when none of them have the required measure, but if some of them have the required measure for challah – they need to touch according to the law (see Chayei Adam, small section 7). There is no difference in the blessing of challah between Passover and the rest of the year. One always recites: "Who has sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us to separate challah." Some, on Passover, recite "to separate the offering of challah," but this is not our custom (see Magen Avraham, small section 1, in the name of Drisha).

One who kneads dough on Yom Tov of Pesach, how should he handle the separation of challah? If he separates from the dough – behold, it is forbidden for him to bake it on Yom Tov, because it is not fit for consumption by the Kohen, as we are all presumed impure in these times. And to burn the challah – this too is forbidden on Yom Tov, as one does not burn consecrated items on Yom Tov. And to leave it as is – it will become leavened. Therefore, one should not separate challah from the dough until after baking, since he can take a small piece from each loaf, and consequently, all are permitted for baking. And then even if afterwards he takes a whole loaf as challah for all the bread – it is acceptable (Rashi 46a). And if he forgot and designated it while it was still dough – he should place it in cold water so that it does not become leavened, and the water should remain in the cellar. (See Magen Avraham, subsection 6, who writes that this requires further investigation whether to rely on this in our times. And Chayei Adam questions him in subsection 11.)

And our master, the Rema, wrote in Section 2 that if there is a minor Kohen who has not experienced a seminal emission, or an adult who has immersed for his seminal emission – it is permissible to bake the challah for him. And there are those who say that in this time, one should not feed challah to any Kohen. Thus are his words, and the explanation of these matters is found in Yoreh De'ah, Section 322. And we do not practice this, therefore there is no need to elaborate on this. He also wrote that there are those who say it is permissible on Yom Tov to knead less than the required measure, in order to exempt oneself from the obligation of challah. Thus are his words, and we do not bake on Yom Tov.

The Tur wrote: "One should not begin to engage with bread on the fourteenth [of Nisan] until after six hours." And it is stated in a responsum: "There was an incident with someone who baked beforehand... and our Rabbis forbade the matzah. For it is compared to the Paschal offering ('on matzot and bitter herbs'), and since the Paschal offering is not slaughtered until after six hours, so too with matzah." However, Rabbeinu Eliezer HaGadol and Rabbeinu Shmuel HaKohen permitted it. But ideally, one should be cautious because "a mitzvah is cherished at its proper time." And Avi HaEzri brought in the name of a Tosefta that one can fulfill the obligation with old matzah... and he wrote that the Yerushalmi disagrees... and since the Yerushalmi forbids it, it is proper to be stringent... and if Shabbat falls on the eve of Passover, they should bake on Saturday night... and my master and father, the Rosh, of blessed memory, would bake on Friday... until here are his words. And similarly, the Mordechai wrote at the end of the first chapter of Pesachim and the Or Zaru'a HaGadol (Siman 250). And they concluded leniently, see there.

And it is very, very puzzling the opinion of those who prohibit, as the analogy to Passover is only for eating, not for preparation. For if it were not so, it would override Shabbat like Passover. Furthermore, there is an explicit Mishnah that states one fulfills their obligation with the loaves of thanksgiving, and it is forbidden to bake the loaves of thanksgiving on the eve of Passover because of the chametz in them. And also in the Jerusalem Talmud, it is explicitly stated to the contrary, in the second chapter (halacha 4), which says: because he was not precise with the matzah. But if he was precise, it is valid. And these arguments have already been answered to those who prohibit. And it is somewhat possible to reconcile that the analogy is only for Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah, who holds that the Passover offering is only eaten until midnight. And at the end of Pesachim, it is said: Rava said: According to Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah, one who eats matzah after midnight has not fulfilled his obligation, because it is analogous to the Passover offering; see there. And according to this, it is possible to say that the Mishnah of the loaves of thanksgiving, the Tosefta, and the Jerusalem Talmud follow Rabbi Akiva, who holds that the Passover offering can be eaten all night. And according to this, there is no need for an analogy for the time of eating, as it is written "in the evening you shall eat matzot," implying all evening. Therefore, according to Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah, who requires an analogy, we also make an analogy for baking. But according to Rabbi Akiva, this is not so. And Rambam in the sixth chapter ruled according to Rabbi Akiva, and Tosafot at the end of the second chapter of Megillah and the end of the fifth chapter of Zevachim ruled according to Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah. According to this, it can be said that these geonim held like Tosafot, and therefore Rambam did not mention this at all. And if you ask: if so, should not baking also override Shabbat? There is no difficulty at all, because even the loaves of thanksgiving and all the meal offerings do not override Shabbat.

In my humble opinion, it appears that the reason for this is well-known: in ancient times, they did not bake all the matzot before Passover. Rather, they would bake bread each day of Passover for that day. The Tur even wrote a novel idea, and this is his language: "And I saw in Barcelona, among the meticulous ones, that they would bake everything they needed for the festival before the festival, so that if any chametz mixed with it, it would be nullified before it became prohibited." This is his language, and this is like our custom. He wrote this as a novel idea. Therefore, when they would bake every day to eat warm bread, why should the matzah for the mitzvah be any less, such that they would not bake it close to the time of eating, which is after midday? Especially considering that it is written that maror (bitter herbs) contains poison and the heat nullifies the poison (Or Zarua there). Therefore, they would bake close to the evening, and also because "a mitzvah is beloved at its proper time." Additionally, so that they would enjoy the matzah in the evening, as warm bread is much better than cold bread. They would bake thick matzot, not like ours, and cold bread is hard to eat. This was considered beautifying the mitzvah. The comparison they made was merely a mnemonic aid and a reminder of the Passover offering. And the prohibition for someone who baked before the sixth hour was to prevent issues, as the ancients were diligent in observing mitzvot and careful with the customs of Israel. But for us, who bake before Passover, the custom has no reason. Therefore, in truth, nowadays only a few meticulous people observe this, and the rest of Israel are entirely unaware of it (so it seems to me in my humble opinion).

And this is the language of our Rabbi, the Beit Yosef: It is customary not to knead the matzah for the mitzvah on the eve of Passover until after six hours, which is the time of the offering of the Passover sacrifice. And on the fourteenth that falls on Shabbat, they knead on the eve of Shabbat after six hours. Thus far his language. They had other customs: they would bake the three matzot for the Seder from one-tenth of an ephah, and they would mark them to know which is the first and which is the last, as I wrote in Siman 475. They would also bake additional matzot, called "doubtful ones," meaning that if the first ones became invalid, these would replace them. When they baked on Yom Tov, it was forbidden to bake from the first Yom Tov day for the second. And because with us, these customs do not apply, there is no need to write them. (See the Shulchan Aruch of the Gaon of Zal, who explained them. Perhaps in his days there was still a remembrance of this, but not so now.)

One should not knead matzah dough outside, in a place where the sun shines, because the heat of the sun warms the dough, and it can easily become chametz. However, in a shady place, it is permitted to knead even under the open sky. This applies when it is not a cloudy day. But on a cloudy day, it is forbidden, because a cloudy day is entirely like a sunny day (Yoma 28a), as the sun breaks through all the cracks in the clouds. If someone transgressed and kneaded under the sun, and it appears that the dough has warmed slightly, it is forbidden even post facto (see Bach). In my humble opinion, on a cloudy day in our northern countries, it is permitted post facto, as we can perceive that there is no warmth there. Especially before Passover, when the weather is still cold here.

One should also be careful not to knead dough in a house opposite an open window. This is not only when sunlight enters through the window, but even if sunlight does not enter through the window, because we are concerned that the sky might become overcast and one might not notice, as it has already been explained that a cloudy day is entirely sunny. However, outside we are not concerned about this, because one would certainly notice when the sun becomes covered. This is not the case indoors, where one might not notice. They have written that this applies specifically to an open window, but if the window is not open, even if sunlight enters through the window glass, it is permissible to knead the dough (Chapter 18, Subsection 3). And even though earlier in Siman 455 regarding water, we forbade in a similar case, water is different because it heats up quickly. This is not the case with dough, which does not heat up in this manner (there).

And it appears to me that the laws regarding windows that have been explained are not absolute. This is not mentioned in the Gemara, and the poskim (decisors) wrote according to the climate of their regions. And in our region, we know from experience that sometimes the sun strikes the glass of the windows, heating the dough on the table where the women knead it. Therefore, it is necessary to cover the glass of the windows with something, either by hanging a cover over the window or by closing the shutters from the outside, which are called "laddins." Conversely, we also observe that when the room is small and due to continuous heating the warmth in the room increases, causing those working to sweat and weaken, making it difficult for them to continue their work. When a window is opened, the wind blows and cools the air, strengthening those who are working. The breeze will also pass over the dough and cool it, provided that the sun does not shine directly on them. And this is the custom.

If one kneads the matzah in this place, and carries it to bake in another house far from this place, he should not carry the matzot uncovered under the open sky but should cover them with some light material. If there is a concern that some dough might stick to the covering, he should not use the same covering repeatedly (Magen Avraham, subsection 2). Similarly, water or flour should not be carried under the open sky without a cover. One should not knead close to the mouth of the oven due to the heat rising from the oven's mouth. Also, near the side of the oven, if heat rises from the oven’s wall, it is forbidden to knead there. If not, for example, if the wall is thick and the outer side of the wall is not very hot, it is permitted. Everything depends on what he sees with his eyes (see Chayei Adam, subsection 9). Similarly, we must be careful when placing the matzot into the oven using thin sticks to quickly place the matzot into the oven, and not leave them on the sticks, which might be warm, as this may easily lead to leavening. It is also obligatory to prepare many sticks, so that if one starts to warm up, he should place it in a cold place to cool and take another cool stick until it warms up slightly, then place it in a cold place and take another stick. Thus, he should continually switch until the stick does not become warm. They should also be cautious that the rollers used for kneading, called "velgerin," and the small rolling pins called "redlen," should not be near the oven. It is preferable that the matzah work be done in a large room where the air circulates well.

Ideally, one should not leave the dough without working it, even for a single moment. As long as one is working the dough, even all day, it will not become chametz. "Working" is defined as kneading and shaping. If the "stoplan" is done vigorously, it is considered "working." If done weakly, it is not considered working. One should be careful not to touch the matzah excessively, as the hand contains warmth. 

How long can the dough remain without working before it becomes chametz? Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 2 that it is a quarter of an hour and a twentieth of an hour, which is eighteen minutes. His reasoning is from the Gemara (Pesachim 46a) which states: the measure of walking a mil and an average person walks ten parasangs by day, which is forty mils, each parasang being four mils. The day is twelve hours, and thus it reaches three and a third mils per hour. A mil is two thousand cubits, and each hour has sixty minutes, reaching approximately one hundred and twelve cubits per minute. This amounts to two thousand twelve cubits in twelve minutes, according to the calculation of one hundred and twelve cubits. These are not exact but approximate, being around two thousand cubits precisely. The measure of an hour is a twenty-fourth part of a full "day and night" cycle, which is a full day and night.

However, Maimonides and the Ra'av (Rabbi Ovadiah of Bartenura) in his commentary on the Mishnah, Pesachim, Chapter Three, wrote that the measure of a mil is two-fifths of an hour, which is twenty-four minutes. Since a fifth of sixty minutes is twelve, two-fifths are twenty-four. They calculated from sunrise to sunset as twelve hours, and the walking distance is thirty mil, as ten mil are walked before sunrise and after sunset, as it is stated in Pesachim (94a). Therefore, if you divide thirty mil by twelve hours, which are sixty-fifths of an hour, each mil results in two-fifths of an hour. Similarly, the Mahari"l (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 3) wrote this. And the prominent authorities have agreed that this is the main interpretation. The first opinion is refuted by the senses (Chayei Adam, subparagraph 10, the Gra, subparagraph 5, and the Alter Rebbe, subparagraph 10), but nevertheless, one should be stringent initially according to the first opinion (Alter Rebbe). Here, the last opinion is a leniency, but regarding the salting of meat, it is a stringency, since the measure of salting is the time it takes to walk a mil. Therefore, according to the first opinion, eighteen minutes are sufficient, while according to the last opinion, twenty-four minutes are required. Refer to what I wrote in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 69.

It is proper to be stringent and swift regarding the performance of mitzvot. For there is an opinion that it is forbidden to delay the time it takes to walk a mil (approximately 18 minutes) from the beginning of kneading until baking, meaning until placing it in the oven. This calculation includes the time spent working on the dough (Bach in the name of Riaz). And although the halacha is not in accordance with this opinion, nonetheless, it is appropriate to be stringent with matzah. Moreover, according to the law, it is certain that it is not necessary for the dough to remain idle for the entire duration of a mil continuously; rather, even if it was idle for a short period and then worked on, and again idle for a short period, these idle times are combined if together they amount to the time it takes to walk a mil. Especially if the dough is left in a warm place, as it ferments according to the law in much less than the time of a mil. Similarly, after the dough has been worked on and warmed by hands, it ferments faster than the time it takes to walk a mil. Therefore, one should be quick and diligent in baking the matzot. One should not begin to arrange the matzot until the oven has been properly stoked, so that the dough is not left idle.

Great care must be taken with matzah. Specifically, the kneading trough used, if it is made of earthenware, requires a new trough every quarter-hour because it is impossible to clean it properly. Therefore, we knead with copper or gilded copper, which is smooth and easy to wash and clean. It should be ensured that there are no patches, as a small amount of dough can get stuck in the cracks of the patches. When making two or three batches of dough, they should switch to a different trough, and the first one should be cleaned. Additionally, care should be taken that the person who adds the flour from the sack into the measuring vessel should not add the water, and the water should not be kept near the flour sack. The woman kneading the dough should constantly clean her hands. While kneading, she must keep her eyes on the dough and not converse with other women in a way that would make the kneading inattentive. She should be careful to knead very well so that no flour remains in the dough.

And be careful when the dough is soft—not to add flour to it, because that flour will not mix well and might not bake properly, and when it falls into the soup, it will become chametz. It is only permitted to add flour as long as the mixture has not yet been blended, but once it has been mixed and becomes dough, it is forbidden to add more. So what should one do when the dough is soft? Knead another hard dough and mix it with the soft one, for it is permitted to mix dough with dough since both are well-kneaded. It is obvious that someone else should make the hard dough, but the woman who kneads should not make two doughs at once, as her hands cannot manage it. However, she can make two small doughs at once, one with her right hand and one with her left hand. They should be careful not to leave the dough or the rolling pin, which they call "katsilke," under the armpit, where it is warm. They should also be careful to constantly clean the table where they roll the dough, as well as the rolling pin and hands from any dough crumbs stuck to them. It is customary to pierce the matzot with an iron roller called "radel," and the matzot are placed on a metal sheet called "blach." Those involved should be careful not to eat chametz bread while working with the matzot and should eat legumes or potatoes and similar items. And the one who comes to purify will be helped.

If one added flour to the dough, it is not prohibited after the fact; however, one should be careful to knead it well together (see Chayei Adam, Section 27). If it appears that flour dust has fallen on any matzah, one should be careful to eat it dry, so that it does not come into contact with water. If the matzah is already made and there is no room in the oven to bake it, and it must wait for several minutes, it is good to break it again, knead, and roll it, so that the matzah does not remain without activity. However, initially, one should not break the matzah, knead, and roll it again.

This is the wording of our teacher, the Rema, in section 4: The utensils used in the preparation of the mitzvot, and the knife that cuts the dough – should always be scraped during the preparation to prevent dough from sticking to them. After the preparation, they should be washed and dried well, to be used again for a second time. This is preferable to the custom of scraping, because it is impossible to clean them thoroughly by scraping alone. The meticulous will scrape them and then wash them. Thus far his wording. Among us, we scrape with pieces of glass, which scrape well. And we do not practice washing with water at all.

And it is further written that on a festival (Yom Tov), it is permissible to scrape (dough) through a non-Jew, as the act of scraping is a rabbinic prohibition (shvut), and instructing a non-Jew is also a rabbinic prohibition, and it is considered a "shvut of a shvut" (a double rabbinic prohibition) in the context of a mitzvah and is therefore permitted. If there is no non-Jew available, one should place them (the utensils) in cold water, or put them in the oven so that the dough on them bakes. It is permitted to wash the kneading bowls oneself, as they are fit for some use related to food preparation, which is permitted on a festival. And this applies to all similar cases. It is further written that one must be careful with the kneading bowl used for kneading, ensuring that there is no hole or crack that cannot be cleaned after kneading, lest it ferment, and afterward, when kneading again, it mixes with the dough. And one should not place the kneading bowl on a cushion or woolen pillow during kneading, as it heats the bowl. But placing it on a leather cushion is permitted. Thus far his words. And among us, we do not bake on a festival. However, when baking on a festival, and similarly on the eve of Passover after midday, one must nullify the crumbs of chametz before they ferment. And the custom is to say: "The crumbs are ownerless." And this must be done specifically before they ferment, for afterward they are no longer in his possession. See also in Siman 460, section 5.

The roller, which is called a "katzilka," among us is made of smooth wood. Some are coated with metals, some are made of stones, and some are made of glass. They are smooth and cooling. Similarly, the table on which one rolls – care must be taken that it is of a single board, so that there is no crack. And it should be smooth. Some people roll on metal, and some on stones, and this is good and proper as is known. However, one should not roll on paper, because the paper wobbles and is not suitable for rolling. For those who roll on paper – it is forbidden to roll another matzah on that same paper, because the dough sticks significantly to the paper. A new paper is needed for each matzah, or to use the other side of the paper. However, it is better to roll on the table over the paper. (And the Magen Avraham wrote in subsection 13: A vessel that got cracked at its edge, and Maharil ordered to widen the crack and scrape it well, to boil it and seal the cracks and smooth them, see there. One should distance oneself from a bowl or a paddle that has a crack. And regarding what he wrote about a “sedin” – we do not know what it is. See there).

And know that even though there is a specific time for leavening, which is the time it takes to walk a mil (approximately 18-24 minutes), as I have written, nevertheless, if signs of leavening are seen in the dough, it is forbidden by Torah law, even if the specified time has not passed. These are the signs of leavening: If cracks appear in the dough, even if the cracks do not intersect, but one goes this way and the other goes that way, it is considered complete chametz, and one is liable for karet (spiritual excision). If there are no cracks but the surface has turned pale, meaning the appearance has changed as a person whose hair stands on end, this too is considered chametz, but one who eats it is exempt from karet. Similarly, if two doughs were started at the same time and one of them became leavened, the second one is also forbidden, even if no signs of leavening are visible and even if it has not been left for the time it takes to walk a mil, because it is certainly leavened. Care should be taken not to place one matzah on top of another, for this hastens the leavening process. In summary, great care and diligence are required with matzah.

Our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, wrote in Section 3: If a woman who is kneading needs to cool her hands with water, she should not use the same water with which she cools her hands to moisten the dough, because the water becomes warmed and causes the dough to leaven. Instead, she should have a separate vessel filled with water for moistening the dough. However, if she did not cool her hands, it is permissible. And if she kneads dough after the time when chametz is prohibited, she should not pour this water, along with the other water used for washing the kneading trough, in a place where it can collect, lest it leaven. Instead, she should pour it in a sloped area so that it does not gather in one place and leaven. This is their language. But before the prohibition time, we do not worry about this (see Taz, sub-section 5). Nowadays, we do not know at all about moistening water. On the contrary, the women are careful not to let water come into contact with the dough, and this is done due to their lack of knowledge regarding this law. In fact, cold water prevents leavening. It seems to me that because our matzot are thin, they do not need moistening water.

And know that if two homeowners are baking in one oven, and it is possible that their matzot might get mixed up, it is proper for them to say: "Whoever receives my matzah, it will be a gift to him" (Beit Yosef and Magen Avraham, Siman 452, Subsection 5). Similarly, if there is a concern at the mill or in a store that they might get mixed up, they should also say this (ibid.), to avoid the concern of stolen matzah, as I wrote in Siman 454. However, after the fact, even without this declaration, it is assumed that they forgive each other. Nevertheless, among us, two people do not bake in one oven.

The Tur and the Shulchan Aruch wrote: One should not knead the matzah for the mitzvah, nor bake it, through a non-Jew, nor through a deaf-mute, an imbecile, or a minor. This is their language. We have already explained this in Siman 458 that the reason is because of "for its sake" (lishma). And even if one tells him, "Do it for such and such a purpose," he does it based on his own understanding. So too wrote the Rashba in a responsum (Siman 26). And the grinding and harvesting also require "for its sake," as I wrote in Siman 458, although there are opinions on whether it is needed from the time of harvesting. There is a dispute about this in the Gemara. (And the words of the Taz in subsection 1 are perplexing, as I wrote there.)

And similarly, none of these individuals should assist in any of the labors related to this matter. However, the poskim (decisors of Jewish law) have written that if it is impossible without the non-Jew, a Jew should stand over him and say to him, "Do it for the sake of the mitzvah of matzah," as the Rosh ruled regarding tzitzit in a previous section (Beit Yosef and Magen Avraham). Nevertheless, the Jew should try to assist a little. And know that a minor is preferable to all of these, as he will come to the fulfillment of mitzvot (ibid.). All these matters apply only to matzah for the mitzvah, and not for matzah for all the days of Pesach. And we have already written in section 453 that the Rif and the Rambam have a different approach regarding the guarding of matzah. According to them, there is no difference between matzah for the mitzvah and matzah for all the days of Pesach; see there in detail.

A "deaf-mute" is one who neither hears nor speaks. A "fool" (shoteh) is as the term implies, and the definition of a fool is explained in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 1. A "minor" (katan) is as the term implies, one who has not reached thirteen years and one day. There are those who say that a "minor" is considered as such when he lacks understanding, but if he has the intelligence to comprehend what is instructed to him to do for the sake of a mitzvah – it is permissible from the outset (Taz, subsection 1). In my humble opinion, it seems clear that for anything requiring "intent" (lishma) – one needs to be thirteen years and one day old (as also written by the Eliyah Rabbah). It seems to me that a blind person (suma) and a drunk person (shikor) are prohibited from engaging in kneading matzah and its preparation, even for matzah that is not for a mitzvah. This is because a blind person will not see to gather all the dough together, and thus it may come to leavening. As for the drunk person – it is obvious that he does not know well what he is doing, even if he has not reached the drunkenness of Lot.

Even though one can bake the mitzvah matzah through a messenger, nevertheless, if it is possible for him to do it himself—it is a greater mitzvah for him than through his messenger. The Rosh, of blessed memory, would personally oversee their making, and he would diligently involve himself in the mitzvah matzah, encourage those engaged in it, and assist in their preparation. Similarly, it is proper for every person to involve himself and engage personally in this great mitzvah. (And in the name of the Arizal, the Taz wrote that it is a great rectification to toil in this mitzvah until one sweats; see there.)

After the time when chametz is forbidden, one should say at the time of kneading: "All crumbs that fall during kneading and rolling, and also dough that sticks to utensils – I nullify them," so that it is found that he nullifies them before they become chametz. For after they become chametz, he cannot nullify them, since it is after the time of their prohibition. And after finishing the kneading and rolling, they should clean the place where they kneaded and rolled. And even though crumbs are generally considered ownerless (hefker) anyway, still we are concerned that all the kneading crumbs might gather together and become significant, and therefore they need to be nullified. This is not similar to bread crumbs which do not stick together and are not significant (Magen Avraham, subsection 2). People customarily say "crumbs are hefker." However, it has been written that this does not help, as this expression implies that they become hefker by themselves. This is not the case; rather, one needs to say "they shall be hefker" (ibid., see Taz, subsection 3). But in truth, the custom is correct, for with chametz, revealing one's intent is sufficient, as I have written in Siman 334 regarding the essence of nullification, especially concerning crumbs which are in any case considered hefker (see Chayei Adam, subsection 7, who explains that hefker is like a vow. But we have already explained in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 273, subsection 4, that there is no connection between hefker and vows, see there).

In ancient times, it was customary to make markings on the three matzot for the Seder. They would call the first one "Kohen," on which they recited the blessing "Hamotzi." The second one was called "Levi," for "Yachatz." The third one was called "Yisrael," for "Korech." Nowadays, this practice is not followed because it is not appropriate to delay the matzah before baking to make the markings. We do not make decorated designs on matzot for Pesach, meaning we do not make drawings on the matzot, because the time taken to create them could lead to leavening. Even using a mold is prohibited. There is no distinction between a homeowner and a baker, even if the latter is accustomed to making such designs and does not delay in doing so; still, the sages made no exceptions and forbade all designs. However, if the matzah is already made with such designs, it is not prohibited if there was no delay in making them, and it is permissible to eat them initially. The perforations made in matzot, known as "radlein," are not considered designs. On the contrary, they are made quickly and help prevent the dough from leavening and the matzah from puffing up in the oven. It is good and proper to make them.

One does not make matzah thick to the extent of a tefach (handbreadth), because when it is so thick, there is concern that the fire will not quickly penetrate its middle, and it will come to leaven. However, after the fact, they are permitted to be eaten (Magen Avraham, subsection 4 and Chayei Adam, subsection 14). Less than a tefach is permitted, as the sages have established that the fire penetrates it. Nevertheless, we have the custom to make matzot thin and crisp, and not thick bread like other bread, because thin matzot do not quickly come to leaven.

The early authorities prohibited making "molyotot" on Passover, which means filling the dough with meat and eggs in the manner of a pie, as it delays the baking and is close to becoming chametz. Additionally, the moisture that comes out of them is like fruit juice, and fruit juice with water hastens the leavening process, as I wrote in Siman 462. Even after the fact, it is forbidden. However, if seeds are placed inside it, even if they are not crushed, it is permitted to eat after the fact, as this does not delay the baking. But initially, it is forbidden. And in our times, we have neither heard nor seen anyone doing this (and the Taz in subsection 6 also forbids it even after the fact).

An oven in which chametz was baked requires thorough libun (burning) to make it suitable for Passover use. One must be careful when heating it to bake matzah, ensuring that the coals spread over the entire surface from beginning to end, including its edges. It is not sufficient for the flames alone to dominate there; as it absorbed, so it expels, and since the absorption was through coals, the expulsion must also be through coals. The entire oven must have sparks flying from it. Even if it was heated several times before Passover, it is ineffective if the intention was not for Passover preparation, as surely he did not ensure the coals spread over the entire surface, and it is possible they did not. Nevertheless, after the fact, if matzah was baked, it is permissible in this manner if it was heated several times, even not for the sake of preparation, as it is likely that at least once the coals spread over the entire surface. However, if it was heated once without the intention of preparation, it is ineffective even after the fact. (Magen Avraham, subsection 1.
