And regarding the comparison to milk during Shavuot, I am puzzled, as there they bake and cook in utensils and not in the oven itself, which is not the case with chametz and matzah. This requires further study. Deliberate and you will find it easy.)

The fundamental law is that when one heats the oven for the purpose of kashering, it is permitted to bake matzah with this heating. However, the custom is not to do so; rather, after the heating for kashering, they do not bake in it but perform another heating for the matzah after the oven has cooled down. This is a good and proper custom, and it is right and proper to do so, for perhaps there was visible chametz there that was burned, and that fire benefits the matzah, and it turns out that one is deriving benefit from chametz. However, this reason only applies after the time of prohibition, as I wrote in section 448. There is also another reason: if one were to bake with this heating, there is a concern that one might not heat it thoroughly to avoid scorching the bread. And although these decrees are not found in the Gemara, nevertheless, since they have adopted this practice on their own, it is a proper and upright custom. (See Magen Avraham, subsection 3, who also raised the issue regarding meat and milk, see there. This is also from the reason we wrote in the previous section. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

Some have the custom to make a new floor in the oven, and it is a good custom. With this, there is no need for burning out. And even though there is absorption of chametz on the top and the sides, the burning that is done to bake the matzah is sufficient, as the flame will rise there and expel it (Magen Avraham, subsection 2). Therefore, for the usage on top of the oven and on the sides of the oven, this does not help. How thick should the new floor be? The Levush wrote that it should be the thickness of a finger. His reasoning appears to be that even with food, absorption does not go in more than the thickness of a finger, like I wrote in Yoreh De'ah, siman 105. And with chametz, there is no greasiness that would permeate entirely.

A new earthenware baking pan, which is a utensil that is heated from below and used for baking on top, and is not common among us – it is permitted to bake matzah on it. Since the fire heats it from below, it becomes thoroughly heated, even though the flame does not reach its top. The bread bakes immediately and does not become chametz. However, one must be careful to heat it well first, until it is very hot, and only then adhere the dough on it. Similarly, when baking in a frying pan without liquid, one must be careful to heat it well first, until it is very hot, and only then place the dough inside. If the dough is placed first and then the pan is heated, there is concern that before it becomes thoroughly heated, the dough might become chametz. Even after the fact, one should be stringent unless there is no other bread available (see Chayei Adam, Section 7). Similarly, it is forbidden to place matzah in an oven on paper. However, after the fact, there is no need for concern, as the fire certainly reaches it through the thin paper.

It is good to be stringent and protest against baking a cake in embers or baking in the sun, as there is a concern that it might become leavened before it starts to bake. However, if one transgressed and baked in embers, it is permitted to eat, and one fulfills their obligation on Passover with it. But if it was baked in the sun, one does not fulfill their obligation, since what is baked in the sun is not called "bread." And the Torah states "bread of affliction." It is only called "bread" if it is baked with fire in an oven or on a griddle without liquid, not if it is baked in the sun. To eat it is permitted after the fact, because once the heat of the sun is strong enough to bake it, it certainly does not allow it to become leavened. (According to the opinion of the Gra).

And similarly, if it was baked in the ground, such as "troknin," which is a hole made in the ground of the stove, and one places there mixed flour and water and it is baked there, even though its mixture is very soft and it does not have the form of bread; therefore, one does not recite "Hamotzi" over it unless one establishes it as their meal, as I wrote in Siman 168; nevertheless, one fulfills their obligation with it on Passover even initially, because this is "poor man's bread," like a poor person who does not have an oven and bakes his bread in the ground. And one recites "Hamotzi" and Birkat Hamazon over it, for on Passover, it is considered establishing a meal.

Matzah that is baked to the extent that if it is broken, no threads are drawn from it – one fulfills the obligation with it. Even if it crumbles when handled, one fulfills the obligation with it, as long as no dough threads are drawn from it. However, if threads are drawn from it, one does not fulfill the obligation with it, as it is not considered bread but dough. The sign for this is that its surface has crusted. One must be careful not to remove it from the oven before this time and return it, as it could become leavened. But after this time, one can remove and return it, as it is then considered baked. If there is doubt whether threads are drawn or not, one should be stringent. Note that this can only be recognized when the bread is hot and not when it is cold. However, one must see the crusting, which is also recognizable when cold. If one inserts a finger and it does not stick, this is a sign that threads are not drawn (Ch. 18, Sec. 10). Some say that if it is removed from the oven before the threads are drawn, it is immediately forbidden (Taz and Ch. 18), as it can become leavened immediately due to the heat. However, in the doubt of threads being drawn, one can be lenient (ibid.). In our matzot, it is not common at all for threads to be drawn from them.

A person can fulfill their obligation with matzah that has been soaked in water, but only if it has not disintegrated. However, if it has disintegrated, they have not fulfilled their obligation, as we say in Chullin (120a): if one melts matzah and swallows it, they have not fulfilled their obligation. Similarly, if one cooks it, even if it has not disintegrated, they have not fulfilled their obligation. Therefore, one should not place it in a first vessel that cooks, and even in a second vessel, it is best to be stringent unless necessary (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 8), because cooking nullifies the taste of matzah. And although we hold that if one swallows matzah, they have fulfilled their obligation and do not need to taste the flavor of matzah, as I wrote in Siman 475, it means that one does not need to taste the flavor of matzah in their mouth like maror (bitter herbs), as I wrote there. Nevertheless, the taste of matzah must be present in one's stomach, and cooking renders it as if it is not matzah at all (Taz, subparagraph 2). Regarding soaking, some say it is specifically with water and not with wine, as wine nullifies the taste of matzah (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 7), unless absolutely necessary. Others say that it is all the same, as wine also does not nullify the taste of matzah, and the same applies to broth, provided it is not hot from a first vessel. Know that even soaking in water is only permitted for the sick and elderly who cannot eat dry matzah, or for those whose teeth are damaged. But for someone who can eat matzah dry, soaking is not permitted, as the main taste of matzah is in its dryness.

If one baked matzah and chametz in the same oven, it is not forbidden unless the matzah touched the chametz. The matzah is not forbidden due to the smell of chametz, even according to those who prohibit the smell of chametz on Passover as stated in Siman 108, because only the smell of something fatty is considered a smell, not the smell of bread (Magen Avraham, subsection 9). If they did touch each other, one must remove the part that touched, which is the thickness of a finger. This is because, at most, it does not absorb more than this measure, since there is no fat here to penetrate deeply. 

It seems to me that if they were baked in the same pan, the entire matzah is forbidden, because the entire pan absorbs from the chametz, and the absorbed substance enters all the matzah. Therefore, one needs to remove from all of it, and in the entire thickness, there is not the thickness of a finger. Hence, it appears to me that even in the same oven, which does not prohibit as explained, this is when they were not on the same level, and it is considered as two vessels. But if they baked chametz and matzah on the same level, the entire matzah is forbidden. Therefore, if the entire oven is just one stone, it is forbidden.

Rabbeinu the Rema wrote in Section 5: A matzah that doubled over in the oven and stuck together, to the extent that the fire cannot reach it, is forbidden during Passover. However, other matzot in the oven are permitted. Before Passover, only the place where it is stuck is forbidden. This is his wording. This applies specifically when it is actually stuck together, meaning part of it folded over another part and it is truly stuck, since then the fire doesn't penetrate between them. But if they are merely close without being stuck, there is no concern at all (Taz Section 3 and Magen Avraham Section 11 in the name of Mahari"l). There are those who forbid it if its surface did not crust over (ibid. in the name of Bach), as this is a sign that it did not bake there. This applies to a folded matzah that shows a defect, but for a regular matzah, there is no concern if its surface did not crust over (ibid.), since sometimes there is dough that does not crust over. Before Passover, only the stuck place is forbidden, and it is discarded. Even if there is not sixty times the amount of the entire matzah against the stuck place, since it is not considered complete chametz, it is not something that dissolves and blends, and it has not spread throughout the entire matzah. Some require sixty times, but the primary opinion is the first one, as agreed upon by the prominent authorities (Taz Section 5, Chayei Adam Section 18, and see Magen Avraham Section 12). A doubled matzah that touched another matzah at the place of the fold – it forbids up to the amount that needs to be removed, but not at the place of the fold – it does not forbid (ibid.).

And I have a question about this: a double and actually stuck matzah, which we prohibited because the fire does not penetrate between the stuck parts, what logic is there in this? For if the matzah were twice as thick as it is now, we would not prohibit it if it were not thicker than a handbreadth. And now that it is doubled, why should we care? On the contrary, when it is completely stuck, it is like one thick matzah. And indeed, in the Gemara, there is no law found at all about double matzah. And it must be said that there was a tradition among the earlier authorities that two lumps of dough stuck together – the fire does not penetrate between them properly. And in my humble opinion, it would seem the opposite, that when they are stuck together, there is no concern at all, for they are one dough. And when they are not stuck together, the fire does not penetrate between them. But since our rabbis did not say so, our humble opinion is nullified before their great opinion.

He also wrote: A matzah that is puffed up in its middle is forbidden. But if a crust formed on it, as happens with bread during baking, it is permitted. Thus are his words. There are two explanations for this: one is that the matzah is puffed up in its middle and split into two with a hollow space between them. The second explanation is that the entire middle of the matzah rises upward like a mountain. Some have written that only according to the second explanation is there a concern of leavening, because it is the way of leavened bread to rise up due to the strength of the leavening. But if it is split into two, this happens because it was not properly perforated, and this is nothing to worry about (Taz, subsection 6). Some, however, forbid it also according to the first explanation, that if it is very puffed up in its middle, there is a concern of leavening (Magen Avraham, subsection 13). However, only that matzah should be forbidden, and no more. And with our matzot, there is no concern at all of puffing up, because they are thin. Sometimes they puff up a little due to insufficient perforation or because of the strength of the fire affecting their thinness, causing them to rise, as is evident by observation. And in our time, we have never forbidden because of puffing up, and only if they are stuck together, we remove the part that is stuck along with a bit from the surrounding area and discard it. It does not require burning because it is not chametz (see Magen Avraham, subsection 12).

He also wrote: If two matzot lie on top of each other in the oven before baking, they are forbidden because it is like a double matzah. Similarly, one must be careful that they do not touch each other in the oven while they are still moist, because the fire does not penetrate the place where they touch, and they come to leavening. Thus far his words. But after the fact, if they touched each other and both are in contact with the oven below, then the heat of the fire controls well from below and they bake nicely, and it is permitted (there, subsection 14 in the name of the Rashal). (The Magen Avraham subsection 13 elaborates on the matter of a hole in the matzah, that this is forbidden, as it is a sign of leavening, and also in small pieces, see there. And we did not know at all about the matter of the hole, and also small pieces are necessarily present in all the matzot.)

It is a clear law in Pesachim (35b) and Menachot (57b) that fruit juices do not cause leavening. And even though it is taught (Pesachim 36a): One should not knead dough with wine, oil, or honey, and if one kneads it, it must be burned immediately, these are the words of Rabban Gamliel—because it is impossible to guard it from leavening. And the Sages say it can be eaten, as it is possible to guard it from leavening. However, in any case, we see that fruit juices cause leavening. Rashi explains that it does not become complete chametz, but it becomes a type of chametz known as "chametz nukshah." See there. Accordingly, the law is that fruit juices are like water, only without the punishment of karet.

But our Rabbis, the Ba'alei HaTosafot, the Rosh, and most of our Rabbis disagreed with him and hold that fruit juice does not cause leavening at all. And what appears in the Beraita that it causes leavening – this is with fruit juice mixed with water, for then it hastens the leavening, and it is not full leavening but rather chametz noksheh (a lesser form of chametz). And this is also the opinion of the Rif and the Rambam in the fifth chapter. And likewise, it is found in the Yerushalmi at the beginning of the chapter "Elu Ovrin" that it says: "And all of them through water." Meaning: all those listed in the Mishnah of "Elu Ovrin": Babylonian kutach, Median beer... – specifically when they contain water. And this is how the halacha is decided in the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, that fruit juice without water does not cause leavening at all. And fruit juice with water is chametz noksheh. And it is difficult to guard them from leavening because they hasten to leaven, and therefore they are prohibited on Pesach. And one should not knead with fruit juice and water. And even though the Rif ruled that it is permitted because one can guard it from leavening, nevertheless the Rosh and others among the Rishonim disagree with him. And such is the law. And if one kneads – it will be explained in section 9.

And there is a great astonishment regarding this Jerusalem Talmud that we brought, for prior to this it is found in the Jerusalem Talmud at the end of the chapter "Kol Sha'ah": Rabbi Shmuel had kosses wine, and he put barley in it so that it would ferment. Meaning: so that it would become chametz. He asked Rabbi Ami. He said to him: you need to eliminate it. Rabbi Chanina had honey mixed with fine flour. He asked Rabbi Mana. He said to him: you need to eliminate it… It is clearly like Rashi, that even fruit juice alone causes fermentation. And the Rosh (Chapter 2, Sign 13) wrote that they hold like the one who says in our Gemara that fruit juice ferments, and the law is not so, see there. And I am astonished: here Rabbi Ami ruled, and in the third chapter Rabbi Ami also says this, and how can he contradict himself? Therefore, we must say that here it also refers to a mixture with water, but if so, he should have explained it. And indeed, according to Rashi's explanation, it can be said that "those who transgress" – his intention is regarding the obligation of karet. (And so the Pnei Moshe wrote there concerning the Mefaresh, see there. But this is also difficult, for in the Mishnah it concludes that there is no karet in these cases. And this requires great examination.)

I wrote this not to disagree with the words of our Rabbis, but regarding our custom that we do not bake "rich matzah" for Passover, which means using only fruit juice. As our teacher, the Rema, wrote in section 4, and this is his wording: "In these countries, the custom is not to knead with fruit juice. And even to smear the matzot, it is only customary to do so after baking while they are still warm. And this should not be changed, except in pressing circumstances for the needs of a sick person or an elderly person who requires it." Until here is his wording. And the same applies to someone whose teeth are damaged and cannot eat hard things. The reason for this custom is because fruit juice with water hastens fermentation, and it is impossible to guard it from leavening. Therefore, they were concerned lest water would also be mixed in. This seems to be the reason for the custom.

And behold, now in our times, due to our sins, this custom is treated with disdain. They knead with egg water and even healthy people eat it. Behold, besides that they are destined to give an account, for they are transgressing a custom that our ancestors and their ancestors practiced for many hundreds of years, and it is like a vow; and besides this, according to Rashi, it is considered "chametz nokesh" (hard chametz) when it is left to sit, and from the Jerusalem Talmud that we brought, there are several Amoraim who ruled this way in halacha. How can a base desire awaken to transgress the custom and the words of Rashi and the Jerusalem Talmud, who ruled this way in law? Therefore, one who guards his soul will distance from this, except for the sick, the elderly, and those with bad teeth. And one who is cautious about this will merit the great good that is reserved for the righteous in the Garden of Eden.

And likewise, one does not fulfill the obligation of matzah on the first night with matzah that was kneaded with fruit juice, as it is written "bread of affliction" – just as the way of a poor person is to eat flour mixed only with water, and not kneaded with fruit juice, as this is considered "rich matzah." Similarly, fruit juice mixed with water is not called "bread of affliction" (Chayei Adam, small section 2, and Magen Avraham in Siman 471, small section 5). And know that Rambam wrote in Chapter Six, Law 5: Matzah kneaded with fruit juice – one fulfills their obligation with it on Passover. But one should not knead it with wine or oil or honey or milk because of "bread of affliction." And if one kneaded and ate it – they have not fulfilled their obligation. Thus are his words, as he holds that "rich matzah" is only called these four items he considered, and not fruit juice.

It appears that the ruling is based on the Gemara (Pesachim 36a) which states: "Lechem Oni" (bread of affliction) excludes dough kneaded with wine, oil, and honey. Regarding milk, it is mentioned there that Rabbi Yehoshua said to his son: On the first day, do not knead for me with milk, see there. However, this is puzzling: according to this, it appears that it is not specifically wine, oil, and honey, but even milk is called "rich matzah". If so, then all other liquids as well. And if it is due to the precision, then Rabbi Yehoshua should have said "On the first day, do not knead for me with fruit juice," why did he not say wine, oil, and honey? Rather, it is certain that because he was used to dough kneaded with milk, he instructed that on the first day, they should not do so for him. If so, all fruit juices as well. 

Moreover, it is puzzling, for we expound "You shall not eat chametz with it; for seven days you shall eat matzot with it" – that anything that can become chametz fulfills the obligation of matzah, and anything that cannot become chametz does not fulfill it, as I wrote in Siman 453. If so, since fruit juice does not cause leavening, how can one fulfill the obligation of matzah with it? However, this can be explained that Rambam holds that from this verse, we exclude only species that do not become chametz, like rice and legumes; otherwise, why do we need the verse of "Lechem Oni"? Even without it, one would not fulfill the obligation since it does not become chametz. Rather, it is certain that the verse excludes only species that do not become chametz. 

Regarding the first question, it can be said that Rambam holds that "rich matzah" is only called something of importance, like wine and oil, as first fruits are only brought from the produce of olives and grapes, and not from other fruit juices, as it is taught in chapter eleven of Terumot: first fruits are only brought from the produce of olives and grapes. Hence, other fruit juices are not considered important at all. Milk and honey, because the Land of Israel is praised for them, as it is written "a land flowing with milk and honey" – therefore, they are considered important and called "rich matzah", but not other things. 

Nevertheless, the majority of our Rabbis disagree with him and hold that one does not fulfill the obligation with any fruit juice. And so is the law, for the law follows the majority.

Egg water and other liquids – all of these are classified as fruit juices. Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 5: One who kneads dough with fruit juices – it is best to make it less than the size of an omer, so that it will not be obligated in challah. This is his language because there are those who say that the obligation of challah only applies when the dough is kneaded with water, as I have written in Yoreh De'ah, section 329. But it is not understood: so what? He should separate challah without a blessing. Furthermore, he himself ruled there that dough kneaded with fruit juices is obligated in challah. It seems to me that the reasoning is: because he wrote there that one who kneads dough with fruit juices should mix in one of the seven liquids, because if not, it is forbidden to burn it since it has not been prepared to receive impurity, see there. And among the seven liquids, there is also water, and if so, one should be concerned that water will be mixed in, which is common, and fruit juices with water are forbidden on Passover, as I have written. Therefore, even if he kneads with wine and oil…, which are among the seven liquids and do not need a mixture of water, for us, they are all considered fruit juices, and they will knead with fruit juices as well. And if so, from whichever perspective, it will lead to prohibition: either he will burn pure challah, or he will mix water and eat tough chametz. And among the common people, all are considered fruit juices, and if so, it is likely to lead to a great mistake. Therefore, it is best to avoid the measure of challah. (See Magen Avraham, section 5, Taz, section 2, and Chayei Adam, section 9, who remain in need of study. And according to what I have written, it fits well with good reasoning. Be precise and you will find ease.)

All fruit juices, even sour fruits like sour apples and pomegranates, are considered fruit juices and do not cause leavening (Magen Avraham). It has already been explained that fruit juices mixed with water cause leavening faster than other doughs. Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in paragraph 2 that if one kneads fruit juices with water, it should be baked immediately, meaning without any delay at all. In the Talmud and among the poskim (decisors of Jewish law), there is a dispute about this, and the Bahag (Ba'al Halachot Gedolot) ruled that it should be burned immediately, but the Rosh disagreed with this. The Beit Yosef ruled according to the Rosh. The Tur brought both opinions; see there. It is not specifically when kneading together fruit juices with water, but even if one first kneads with fruit juices and then with water, or vice versa, it is considered fruit juices with water (Chayei Adam, paragraph 3). A small amount of fruit juice mixed with a lot of water is not considered as fruit juices with water, but as water alone (Magen Avraham, paragraph 1). It seems that the same applies in reverse: a small amount of water and a lot of fruit juice is considered as fruit juice alone. Likewise, regarding fulfilling the obligation of matzah. Some require that there should be sixty times the water against the fruit juices, then one fulfills the obligation of matzah, but not with less than this (Chayei Adam, paragraph 2. See Magen Avraham, paragraph 3, and it requires further study).

And know that since it has been explained that fruit juice with water is considered chametz noksheh, and in Siman 467 it is explained that chametz noksheh is nullified in sixty, therefore there are those who want to say that if a grain of wheat is found on Passover in a charamzel or in "knaydlech" which are kneaded with fat, and egg water, and the charamzel is also kneaded with honey – it should not be forbidden by even a small amount, since this is fruit juice with water and it is nullified in sixty (a certain sage in the responsa of Noda BiYehuda Siman 22). And there are those who want to reject this because it is proven in the Talmud Menachot (57a) that it is impossible to say both. Meaning, if noksheh is rabbinic – it must be that fruit juice with water is complete chametz. And if it is noksheh – it must be that noksheh is from the Torah (Noda BiYehuda there). And his words were rejected, for the Rosh and the Tur ruled in Siman 442 that noksheh is rabbinic, and in this Siman they ruled that fruit juice with water is noksheh (Mishna Berura 1 and Magen HaElef 3). Furthermore: even if noksheh is from the Torah – it is also nullified in sixty, since it does not incur karet like chametz on the eve of Passover (Magen HaElef there). However, with a small amount of fat, it should not be considered as fruit juice with water. But when there is significant fat and egg water, and certainly in a charamzel which also has honey – one can be lenient in cases of great loss and preventing the joy of the festival by a small amount of rabbinic prohibition, and forbid only that specific piece of charamzel and not more. Certainly, if there are additional leniencies according to the situation. And similarly, if a grain is found in a dish called "tzimes," if there is a proper amount of fat and honey, and in this there is a small amount of water, as it is known that a lot of moisture comes out from the tzimes itself, and this is fruit juice, one should not be stringent in this matter (so it seems in my humble opinion).

And all the more so if additional kernels are found in the honey or the fat, and the honey was boiled before Passover, and the fat was fried before Passover. We say that the kernel came from the honey or the fat, and it has already been nullified before Passover in fruit juice, and it no longer causes leavening (Noda B'Yehuda and Magen Avraham, Section 9). And for cake or tart that was kneaded with honey or sugar without water, but it was not kept from being kneaded on a chametz surface, and it was not sold before Passover – it is permissible to keep it until after Passover and to eat it (ibid.).

Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote in section 6: A wheat grain found in honey, wine, or vinegar is permitted, provided no water has been mixed with them. Thus far his language. And in section 3 he wrote: It is permitted to knead with wine, even though it is impossible without a drop of water falling during the vintage. And initially, it is customary to add water during the vintage to permit pouring (as explained in Yoreh De'ah, see Magen Avraham subsection 2). Nevertheless, there is no concern for them since the water has already been nullified in the wine before the dough was kneaded. Thus far his language. And they questioned him: If so, why did he require in section 6 that no water be mixed? It has already been nullified. And they answered that in section 3, since the wine ferments, it is as if it has been cooked and the water has become like wine, which is not the case in section 6 (Magen Avraham subsection 6). And some explain that in section 6, his intention is that no water be mixed while the wheat is in the honey, as it would be considered mixed during kneading and is forbidden. This is not the case in section 3—it has already been mixed (the son-in-law of Magen Avraham in his gloss). And some explain that indeed a small amount of water does not cause leavening. However, the dough still requires guarding, and without guarding, it will leaven. Therefore, in section 6, we are concerned about leavening (Chayei Adam subsection 12). In my humble opinion, it seems simple that in section 3, the water was during the vintage before Pesach, and it has already been nullified. Which is not the case in section 6—it is during Pesach. (And so it is explicitly implied in Taz, section 263, subsection 1, see there. And so it is implied by the language of the Levush. And he omitted this from section 3, see there.)

In paragraph 9, we explained that a small amount of fruit juice with a lot of water is not considered as fruit juice with water, but rather as water alone. We also wrote that the same applies in the reverse situation. However, the commentators (Magen Avraham, subsection 6, and Chayei Adam) did not write this way. They hold that even a small amount of water with a lot of fruit juice is considered as fruit juice with water, and therefore, one must bake immediately. Consequently, great caution is required with matzah kneaded with egg water, ensuring that the container called a "bekin" has no moisture of water. Therefore, it is necessary to wash and clean it between each dough, and they should ensure it is dry.

The great authorities wrote in the name of the Tashbatz: raisin wine or raisin honey, which are made by water that has completely changed its taste, are considered like pure fruit juice (Mishnah Berurah, small section 9). Therefore, there are those who are uncertain about honey water, which is called mead, if it contains a seed, whether it is called "fruit juice" since it changed through cooking (Magen Avraham, small section 6). And there are those who wrote that raisin wine is like fruit juice with water, which is only like diluted wine (Mishnah Berurah there in the name of the Chacham Tzvi). However, if a seed is found in boiling goose fat, it is permissible without question, even though it was rinsed in water, but the water has already dried up (Magen Avraham there). And similarly, if found in solidified fat, even though there is water there, it is permitted because it solidified before Passover, so there is no concern of pickling during Passover. But when the fat is soft, there is a concern (Mishnah Berurah there). And the law of whether we establish a prohibition from place to place or from time to time will be explained with Divine help in section 467.

And our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 7: One should sift the salt before Passover to remove grains of wheat that might be in it. For when the salt becomes moist, it penetrates the grains bit by bit and causes them to leaven. Thus far his words. Before Passover, even if it becomes moist, it is already nullified, which is not the case on Passover, where even a minute amount is significant (Magen Avraham, subsection 7). And if, after the fact, a grain is found in the salt during Passover, one should remove an amount sufficient for removal, and the rest should be set aside until after Passover. And if the salt was put into a dish during Passover, it should not be prohibited (there). And it appears from the Tur that salt dug from the ground has no concern, as he wrote that brine is considered like fruit juice, see there. This applies to ground salt, but sea salt seems to be considered like water. (See Magen Avraham, subsection 7. And the Tur criticized the M'Ch, see there. And it can be said that they do not disagree, and examine and you will find it easy.)

It is permissible to toast two ears of grain together. Similarly, it is permissible to fill a pot with ears of grain to dry them in the oven, and there is no concern that moisture might come out from one ear and fall onto another due to the heat, since this moisture is considered fruit juice and does not cause leavening. Even though our custom is not to knead with fruit juice, as I wrote in the previous section, still we are not concerned about this, for the exuding of moisture from the ears is not so common. However, the primary practice of toasting ears of grain is not common among us at all, and it seems that this was done in the Land of Israel where the wheat was very oily. Similarly, roasted grain is not common among us because our wheat is lean and not suitable for this.

And the ears of grain and the wheat that were roasted in the oven or by fire, if one ground them – one should not cook them in water, lest they were not properly roasted and they come to leaven. And even if the flour itself was roasted in the oven – we are concerned that it was not properly roasted, and when it comes into contact with water – it will leaven. However, there are those who permit cooking roasted flour (Beit Yosef), for the heat of the fire affects it more than it affects the wheat grains. And in a situation of ex post facto, one can rely on this opinion, but this matter is not common among us at all.

And this is the language of the Tur: "But with baked and ground matzah, it is permitted, and we do not worry that it might be confused with flour... And the Rif and my master, my father the Rosh, wrote simply to permit baked matzah. And in the Gemara, it says that even baked matzah is forbidden where there are servants who are negligent in mitzvot or similar situations, because there is concern that they might come to permit even flour." Thus far is his language. And the commentators (Beit Yosef and Bach) wrote that from the Gemara it is not difficult, as there is another version in the Gemara that permits it; see there. And I am astonished at the Tur and the commentators, for in the Gemara there is no mention at all of baked matzah. And this is the language of the Gemara (Pesachim 42b): "Rav Papi permitted the household of the Exilarch to cook a dish with toasted flour. Rava said: Is there anyone who permits such a thing in a place where servants are common? Some say: Rava himself cooked a dish with toasted flour." And Rashi explained "toasted flour" as flour from roasted grain. This is flour made from roasted grains as explained, like the Tur himself wrote. If so, what relevance does this have to baked matzah? And even according to the Tosafot, who explained it as flour from lentils, nevertheless, it is all made from roasted grains, and we issue a decree because of roasted wheat. But what connection is there to baked matzah? This requires significant investigation.

Vatika, which is a dish made from oil and salt with flour, is permitted to make on Pesach if there is no mixture of water at all. And even salt that comes from water, nevertheless, since it is minimal and its form has changed from its original watery state, it does not have the power to act against the oil. But when there is a large amount of salt, one should be concerned and prohibit it, similar to the law of fruit juice mixed with water. This is also not common among us. And when seasoning new pots, which are cooked with flour, water, and vinegar to harden and strengthen them, one should not season them on Pesach except with flour from baked matzah. This too is not known to us.

Mustard, which is called "zaneft," is very sharp and strong, and it is used to season meat. It contains vinegar or other types of acidity, and a bit of water is also added to it. It is customary to add a little flour to it as well – this is forbidden to do on Passover. For although the vinegar and the juice from the mustard are considered fruit juices, nevertheless, since there is also water in it – it becomes a mixture of fruit juice with water and is forbidden, as I wrote in Siman 462. And if one did add it – he should eat it immediately, before it has a chance to leaven. Just as we ruled regarding kneading that one should bake it immediately, here too one should eat it immediately.

In what case is it stated that it is permissible to eat it immediately? In the case of mustard, which is sharp and strong, and will not allow the flour to leaven quickly, and meanwhile, he can eat it. But other types of seasonings, in a case where flour is added to them, are completely forbidden, because since they are not as sharp, and it is necessary to wait a bit while eating, perhaps during this time it will leaven. Therefore, there is no remedy for this, and one is obligated to burn it or throw it into a filthy place. And even if it seems to him that this seasoning is as strong as mustard, nevertheless, it is forbidden, for we only rely on what the sages said (Mishnah 39b).

And this is according to the law. But it has already been explained in Siman 453 that we do not eat types of legumes. Mustard is also considered a type of legume; therefore, we do not eat mustard on Passover. And even though it was explained there that through a mixture it is permitted, and with mustard there is indeed a mixture, nevertheless, the primary ingredient is mustard. And it is forbidden to eat it on Passover even if it was prepared and arranged before Passover, and this is the custom.

It is well-known that just as it is forbidden for a person to eat chametz on Pesach, it is likewise forbidden to give it to one's animals. For chametz on Pesach is forbidden for benefit, and one also transgresses "bal yera'eh" (it shall not be seen) and "bal yimatzeh" (it shall not be found). Therefore, one who gives chametz to an animal, wild beast, or bird on Pesach transgresses three prohibitions: the first is "You shall not eat chametz," which includes deriving benefit. The second is "it shall not be seen." And the third is "it shall not be found." There is no difference whether one gives it oneself or through a non-Jew, and whether it is in one's courtyard or not – one transgresses all three prohibitions. We have already explained in Siman 448, Section 13, that for an animal that is in one's possession in one's courtyard, no sale is effective. One must give it on Pesach things that are not chametz, such as potatoes or types of legumes and buckwheat. It is also permissible to cut straw for it, which is called "shatzka." And even if some grain might be found there, this is not one's intention. Similarly, the chaff of grain, which is called "makenna." However, if one wishes to cook them, they should be cooked by a non-Jew and in a different oven, for perhaps some grain might be found there. This is how we conduct ourselves in our locale.

And if one wishes to give them grain, he should give them dry grain such as flour or dry bran, and in a place that is not moist. After they eat, he should sweep with a broom so that no grain remains, in order that it does not become moist and come to leavening. Thus, the sages taught in the Mishnah (Pesachim 39b): One does not soak bran for chickens. And even if he wishes to soak it and feed them immediately, before it comes to leavening – it is forbidden, for it will certainly come to leavening. Additionally, it is initially forbidden to leave the dough without working it even for a moment, as I wrote in Siman 459. And this prohibition applies from the eve of Passover, from the sixth hour and onward.

Blanching in boiling water is permitted by law. However, the Geonim prohibited it, as I wrote in Siman 452. And if one places dry grain before them, it is proper to be careful not to give them water to drink while the food is still in front of them, because certainly in the middle of drinking or at the end of drinking, they will turn to eat, and the water from their lips will drip onto the grain and cause it to ferment. Rather, when they have finished eating, one should first clean that place well, so that no grain remains. Only then should one give them to drink.

We also learned in the Mishnah (there): A woman should not soak bran to take with her to the bathhouse, but she may rub it on her body dry. This means that it was their custom to rub their bodies in the bathhouse with bran for medicinal purposes. Therefore, it is forbidden to soak it on Passover, and on the eve of Passover from the sixth hour. However, rubbing it on her dry body is permitted even though her body is full of sweat from the heat of the bathhouse, because sweat is not considered water regarding fermentation, as I wrote in Siman 466. Therefore, if she washed her body with water, it is forbidden in any manner. Additionally, when she rubbed it on her dry body, if she wants to wash, she should remove the bran from her body and discard it in a dirty place, and then wash in hot or cold water. And nowadays, since we are not proficient in this, it is forbidden in any manner.

Their custom was to rub a moist goose with bran. If one did so on Passover or on the eve of Passover after the sixth hour, the entire goose is forbidden because the skin of the goose has small pores, and since chametz on Passover is forbidden even in the smallest amount, we are concerned that some bran might remain in these cracks. Therefore, on the eve of Passover, if one wishes to eat it, it is permitted because on the eve of Passover it is nullified in sixty. Similarly, one must be careful not to singe birds with straw on Passover, lest there be a grain among the straw, and it imparts flavor to the bird during the singeing. However, after the fact, it is permitted. Even if fermented grains are found in other places among this straw, we do not assume there is a prohibition regarding the straw used for singeing (see Magen Avraham, Taz, and Chayei Adam).

Just as water leads to leavening, so too dew, hail, frost, and ice, when they melt and become water, are considered like water. In the Mishnah of Makhshirin (Chapter Six), it is taught: derivatives of water include what comes from the eye, the ear, the nose, the mouth, and urine, whether from an adult or a child. This means that sometimes it also comes from the rectum as water. And it is taught in the Tosefta that the urine referred to is specifically that of a human, and so rules the Rambam in the tenth chapter of Tum'at Okhlin. It seems to me that all the more so, what comes from the eye, the ear, the nose, and the mouth is specifically of a human, as I wrote earlier in Siman 553, Section 10, see there. For we see that the urine of animals is like water itself, and yet it is not considered like water, all the more so these other things. Additionally, in the Tosefta of Shabbat (Chapter Nine), it is stated: from where do we know that the tears of the eye are a liquid? Because it says: "And you gave them to drink with tears by measure." From where do we know that the fluid of the nose is a liquid? Because it says: "And our eyelids flow with water," see there. This is written about humans, not animals. I have seen that many do not write this, but in my humble opinion, it appears as I have written (see the Gra, Section 1). But human excrement, and that of all living creatures, human sweat, milk, fat, and bile are all like fruit juice and do not cause leavening. When mixed with water, they hasten leavening, and it should be baked immediately. If they fall on flour and are dried, it is nothing and is not like fruit juice with water. Blood is also like fruit juice. But if one spits blood and it is mixed with saliva in the mouth (Ch. 18, Section 2), it is considered like fruit juice with water because it is impossible for it not to have traces of saliva, as we say concerning the spitting in the Chalitza ceremony. (Nevertheless, it requires investigation whether we learn from Makhshirin, for there milk renders susceptible. And there are distinctions in blood, see there. Here, it is considered fruit juice, and similarly, honey and oil render susceptible, but here they are fruit juice. However, the Tanna calls them "derivatives of water," see there. Be precise and you will find clarity.)

And since saliva causes fermentation, the sages taught in the Mishnah (Pesachim 39b): A person should not chew wheat and place it on a wound, because it will ferment. However, there is an opinion that says it is permissible to chew and swallow it, as it does not ferment immediately (Magen Avraham, Section 1). But it seems to me that it is forbidden, as it is impossible that something does not remain between the teeth, as we say at the end of the seventh chapter of Chullin, and that residue will ferment. And regarding a wound, even if the dressing was placed before Passover, it must be removed on the eve of Passover at the sixth hour if it has not become spoiled and is still fit for a dog to eat. It is obvious that all this applies to a sickness that is not life-threatening. But for a life-threatening illness, even eating chametz is permitted, as nothing stands in the way of saving a life.

And know: What is taught that it is forbidden to chew wheat to place on a wound – this is with one's own wheat, and when it becomes leavened, one transgresses "You shall not see [leaven]." But with the leaven of a non-Jew – it is permitted to place on a wound, even though one benefits from the leaven that heals, nevertheless, this is not in the usual manner of benefiting and it is permitted, as Rambam wrote in the fifth chapter of the Laws of the Fundamentals of Torah, and this is his language: In what case is it said that one may not be healed with prohibitions? When it is in the usual manner of benefiting, such as feeding him creeping things or leaven on Passover. But if it is not in the usual manner of benefiting, such as making a poultice or a plaster from leaven – it is permitted for a sick person. Until here is his language, and you are compelled to say that his intent is for a sick person who is not in danger, for if he were in danger – it is permitted and obligatory to feed him leaven for healing (Magen Avraham, small section 2). Therefore, we feed leaven to nursing infants, if it is necessary due to danger.

The Tur and the Shulchan Aruch wrote: One who gives barley to his animal and finds saliva on it must destroy it. For they believe that the saliva of an animal causes fermentation. This is specifically when he finds saliva on it. But if there is no visible saliva, there is no need for concern, because at the time of giving the barley, he nullified and abandoned ownership of it in his mind, and it is not considered his chametz. Nevertheless, when he clearly sees it, he should not rely on this. (This is the intention of the Rema, as the Chayei Adam wrote in section 4, and the Magen Avraham's perplexity on this in section 3 was unnecessary.) However, some are stringent and require destroying all that remains from the animal, even if no saliva is visible on it. And there are those who are meticulous to give them a small amount at a time, so that nothing remains.

The sweat (moisture) of houses, pits, ditches, and caves – it is taught in Mikvaot (beginning of the second chapter) that it does not render [food] susceptible [to impurity], and it is not considered like water. According to this, a sack full of flour that became moist from the sweat of a house or wall – does not become leavened. This is the opinion of the Rosh (chapter two, section 22), and similarly written in the glosses of Maimonides, chapter five. However, the Rokeach prohibits it and writes that it is not similar to the case of susceptibility, as I wrote at the end of section 1. The Rosh compares it to human sweat, which does not cause leavening. (Refer to Magen Avraham, subsection 5, who writes that this requires investigation, since on the contrary, most authorities prohibit it; see there. I do not know who they are, and the Mishnah supports those who permit it. The Beit Yosef did well to write the opinion of those who permit it as the main opinion. Additionally, what he wrote that the wall sweats due to the water, see there – it is difficult, for if so, why does it not render susceptible? However, one could say that we see with the sweat of houses, that when the weather is humid, they sweat more, and then certainly it is due to the rains. Therefore, during Passover, which is the season of rains and thawing of snow, when the air is humid – it could be that it certainly causes leavening. The Rosh, who was in Spain, where it was then the summer season, was lenient in this. But in our northern countries, it seems that it is certainly prohibited. Examine and you will find the leniency.) (Sweat of the flesh – is considered like water.)

Flour upon which water has dripped all day, when it falls continuously drop after drop, does not become chametz (leavened), because the dripping itself prevents it from fermenting. However, when there is an interval between the drops, it does become chametz. Therefore, if there is some doubt whether the dripping is continuous or not, it is forbidden. Even when the dripping is continuous, it must be baked immediately, because if it is left for a short time, it will quickly become chametz. If the dripping is not continuous, all the flour is forbidden, even in cases where it is not visible that it has absorbed water, because the flour absorbs it and it is not noticeable. Indeed, we have never heard this law being practically applied, for who can testify that it was drop after drop? (See Taz, subsection 5.)

And behold, this law that we have written is in the Gemara (39b) in a baraita: Flour into which drips have fallen all day long – it does not become leavened, as long as it drips drop by drop. And Maimonides in the fifth chapter, law 10, wrote: Grain upon which drips have fallen, as long as it is disturbed drop by drop, even all day long – it does not come to leavening. But when it stops, if it remains for the time it takes – it is forbidden. Thus far his words. And I am puzzled: What benefit is there for grain with drop after drop? Until it is ground and kneaded, it will become leavened. And I have seen someone write that it must be ground immediately (Gra"z, section 16). And it is puzzling: Even though during the grinding it will not leaven because of the activity, nevertheless, after the grinding until the kneading – it will leaven?! And if we say to knead immediately, behold immediately after the grinding it is forbidden to knead, as explained at the end of section 453. Therefore, it is clear to me that Maimonides' intention also is regarding flour. And his manner throughout that chapter is to call "grain" flour, as he wrote earlier there: These five types of grain, if kneaded with fruit juice..., one must be careful with the grain he eats on Passover... – and the intention is regarding the flour from the grain. And here too it is the same.

The Rosh (there) wrote in the name of the Rokeach: If water falls on flour, or the sack becomes damp – the flour should be sifted, and the rest is permitted. The Rosh objected to this, and this is his wording: It is a great leniency to do this during Passover when chametz in any amount is forbidden, because perhaps even a small amount of chametz will pass through the sieve with the flour. And I have seen those who rule in practice that one should hold the entire damp area of the sack in his hand until all the flour in the sack is emptied. Thus is his wording, and the Tur brought it. And it is explained that he was stringent only during Passover, but before Passover, it is permissible to sift because it will be nullified before Passover. And regarding "it reawakens" – the Rosh and Tur ruled in Siman 467 that we do not say "it reawakens." And they also do not differentiate between wet and dry, as I wrote there. And in the Mordechai in the chapter "Kol Sha'ah," it is also stated that during Passover it is forbidden once it has dried, see there. But before Passover, he also holds that it does not reawaken.

And behold, our master the Beit Yosef in Siman 447 ruled that it does not reawaken, but he wrote that there are those who disagree, see there. And the main opinion holds according to the law that it does not reawaken, whether in liquid or in dry. And our master the Rema differentiates there in this matter, but our master the Beit Yosef does not agree with this. And there we explained that this is the main point according to the law. And our master the Rema also only wrote this because of custom, but according to the law we explained there that the main point is that it does not reawaken.

Based on this, we can understand the words of our teacher, the Beit Yosef, in section 4, where he wrote: If water fell on flour, or the bag became moist – one should hold the entire moist area of the bag with his hand until he can empty all the flour from the bag. And if it is not possible to do so (such as if it has become moist in many places) – he should sift the flour, and the rest is permitted. And this is specifically while it is still moist. But if the moisture has dried – sifting does not help, because it crumbles and mixes with the rest. And it is forbidden to eat it on Passover; rather, he should sift it and guard it until after Passover. And if it dried on Passover – it is forbidden to keep it. Up to here is his wording, which implies that he is referring to before Passover. And it is difficult: before Passover, why should we care, since we do not say "it reawakens"? (And it is difficult to say that he wrote according to the opinion of "there is one who forbids" in Siman 467. If so, he should have explained this, since there he took the opinion of the permissive ones as primary.)

In my humble opinion, this is its explanation: Certainly, if one wishes to bake it before Pesach, we do not mind, because once it has already been mixed and kneaded together, we do not say "it reawakens." Rather, the intention is if one wishes to bake it on Pesach, then certainly, even if it does not reawaken, since on Pesach the crumb stands by itself, it is considered as if it were dry with moist, where the dry stands by itself, and one nullifies it on Pesach in sixty. This is obviously forbidden, for chametz on Pesach is forbidden in any amount. But if he bakes it before Pesach, it is permitted in any case, even if the moisture has dried up, since it does not reawaken and has already been mixed and nullified. (And this is what the Magen Avraham means in sub-section 9, where he writes about the reason of reawakening, see there. And this is when he bakes on Pesach. And this appears to be the understanding of the Gra in section 9, see there carefully. Examine and you will find it easy.)

According to this, it seems clear to me, in my humble opinion, that although we are stringent according to the words of our master, the Rema, that in the case of "dry on dry" we say "it reawakens," nevertheless, if it happens that the moisture has dried up and everything was sifted before Passover, and it was baked before Passover, it is permissible in a significant loss, because the main ruling is that it does not reawaken, as I wrote in Siman 447. And I also saw one of the great authorities (the Gra, at the end of section 10), and this is his language: Therefore, if it was baked before Passover, it is permitted. And one can rely on their words in pressing circumstances… Nevertheless, it is proper to be stringent and to take from the flour before Passover and eat it, to attribute the crumbs to what was already eaten. This is his language until here, meaning: to take from the matzot that were baked and eat a little before Passover. (And in section 15 it will be explained that even according to the Rema it is permitted.)

And according to this, the practical halacha is as follows: If the sack becomes moist in one place, hold that moist spot with your hand until all the flour empties out. In any case, sift it afterward (Magen Avraham, subsection 6 and Taz). This is merely a stringency. This remedy of holding the moist spot is effective even when the moist spot has dried up, because once you take all the spot where there is doubt, we no longer have any concern (Taz, subsection 4).

If there are several moist spots in the sack, making it impossible to hold the moist spot with one's hand, there is a distinction between wet and dry. If the moist spots are still wet, sift all the flour in the sack. Consequently, the moist flour will become like dough and remain on top (Magen Avraham, subsection 8). If all the flour is sifted, it is a sign that the moisture only affected the sack from the outside and did not enter the flour at all; hence, all the flour sifted. 

It appears to me that when sifting, one should not sift the flour by hand within the sieve, because in such a case, the wet flour may be crushed and pass through the sieve's holes. Instead, shake the sieve with your hands, and then necessarily, the wet adhering flour will not pass through the sieve's holes.

And this pertains to moist (dough), for in such a case, even on Passover itself, it is permitted. However, on Yom Tov, if one does not need all the flour, one should not sift it oneself, because it is not necessary for Yom Tov. Instead, one should have a non-Jew sift it, in order to eliminate any chametz that may be present. And even though sifting is a Torah-prohibited labor and instructing a non-Jew is rabbinically prohibited, here, since there is no waste matter, it is not considered a primary labor (Magen Avraham, subsection 8). Similarly, if it has not yet become chametz, but will become chametz if left, one can give the flour as a gift to the non-Jew before it becomes chametz, and thus not violate "You shall not see" (chametz) (ibid.). Now, in our practice, we do not bake on Yom Tov; everyone bakes before Yom Tov, so we do not need this ruling.

However, when one of the places has dried, in such a case it is impossible to hold it because there are many places in the bag that have become wet, and even sifting is of no benefit, for the moist flour that has dried and crumbled goes out from the holes of the sieve. Therefore, this flour has no remedy for those who hold that "it reawakens on Passover." But according to the fundamental law that it does not reawaken – it is permissible to knead and bake it before Passover. Therefore, even according to Rabbi Rema, who does not say "it reawakens" in the case of wetness but does say it in the case of dryness – it is still permissible to bake it initially before Passover, for since it is blended and kneaded together – it is considered like wet with wet, and is nullified before Passover, as I wrote in section 447, that flour with flour is considered wet with wet. However, to bake it on Passover – it is forbidden even if we do not say "it reawakens," because it would be considered actual chametz on Passover, as I wrote in section 11. Accordingly, what we wrote in section 12, that when it has dried and was baked before Passover, the leniency is only in cases of significant loss, due to the words of Rabbi Rema – this is not so. For even according to his words, it is permissible initially, as this is like wet with wet. And the authorities who wrote to forbid it when dried – this is concerning baking on Passover, or for those who hold that even in the case of wet with wet, we say "it reawakens." But for us, according to the ruling of Rabbi Rema – it is permissible initially (this seems to be my humble opinion).

If mice ate from the flour, there is an opinion that one should take that spot and its surroundings thoroughly, and the remainder may be used and eaten on Passover. This is no worse than water that fell on flour in one spot, and in such a case, even on Passover it is permitted, just like water in one spot (Taz, subparagraph 4). However, there is an opinion that challenges this, arguing that these mice are nefarious and move around the entire sack, eating as they go. All the more so if the flour is in a barrel, as they traverse the entire contents. This is not comparable to flour that became damp in one spot (Magen Avraham, end of subparagraph 9). In my humble opinion, this challenge is not valid, for even if the mice traversed the entire flour, it is still not clear to us that they deposited saliva there, and this remains a rabbinic uncertainty, and we should not be so stringent. Moreover, there is doubt whether their saliva causes leavening, based on what we wrote in paragraph 1. Therefore, we only need to be concerned about the spot where we see the mice ate.

There is someone who wrote in this language: Mice that ate from flour, if it dried before Passover – sift it and keep it until after Passover. And if found like this on Passover – everything is forbidden for benefit. And if the sack is placed in its place without moving, and the flour did not get mixed – then hold by hand the place that was bitten, tie there under the bite with some flour, shake out all the flour in the sack and sift it, and it is permitted to keep it but forbidden to eat it on Passover. And all this is when it is evident that the mouse ate some of the flour. But if it only bit the sack, and there is doubt whether it ate from the flour or not, even if found on Passover – it is permitted to keep it... (Magen Avraham, subsection 9 in the name of the Bach). And he was very stringent with excessive stringencies. And this is good to be stringent for oneself, but not to instruct others.

The main ruling is as written by one of the great authorities (Maharam of Lublin in Magen Avraham there), and this is his wording: Regarding sacks that were bitten by mice and were danced upon, there is a concern that certain areas may have dried out, crumbled, and mixed with the flour... they should take other flour that has been guarded for the first two nights, and that flour should be baked before Passover. There is no need to be stringent about it, and it is permissible for all days of Passover. Until here is his wording. This is similar to the first opinion, except that he was stringent regarding the olive-sized piece of matzah for the first two nights. And so it should be ruled.

Wheat that has been submerged in a river or had water fall upon it, and the leavening is not evident in them, for if the leavening were evident, we would have no concern that a Jew might purchase them for Passover since he sees the leavening. Even though, in times of need, people buy flour from the market, this is not common. However, since the leavening is not evident, there is a concern that a Jew might purchase them for Passover when the wheat is sold to a non-Jew. And if we tell him to leave them until after Passover, he would transgress "bal yera'eh" (the prohibition of owning leaven during Passover), and he does not need to eat them so much. Therefore, the sages said (Pesachim 40a) that he should sell them to a Jew, informing him that they are leavened, and he should eat them before Passover or sell them to a non-Jew in small quantities so that each one eats them before Passover. There is no concern that he will resell them to a Jew because even if he does sell them to a Jew, they will be consumed before Passover. Some are stringent that even to a Jew, he should not sell them except in small quantities so that they are consumed before Passover. But in large quantities, even if he informs him to eat them before Passover, he might come to a stumbling block (Bach in the name of Rashal, see Taz). And now that we are accustomed to selling chametz, if such an incident occurs, he should not sell them at all before Passover but should sell them with his chametz, and he will sell them after Passover. And know that if such an incident occurs with a non-Jew, where his wheat fell into water or had water fall upon it, and there is a great concern that he will sell them to a Jew for Passover, it is necessary to announce in the synagogue and study hall that no one should buy this wheat for Passover. Even though with a Jew in such a case, we do not rely on announcements, as we require that he sell them in small quantities before Passover (see Magen Avraham, subsection 1), nevertheless, with a non-Jew, it is necessary to do so.

There is a question regarding this matter: How do we find a case for this law? After all, the sign of fermentation in wheat is when it cracks open. Therefore, logically, if it has cracked open, a Jew should not acquire it for Passover. And if it has not cracked open, then it is not chametz. The answer to this is provided by the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, section 2. These are the grains that were submerged or had water fall on them. Since they are lying idle, they will ferment even without cracking open. Although in the case of dough it is stated in the Gemara that if it has not cracked open, it is permitted, that is because he is actively kneading it, and the activity prevents it from fermenting. But without such activity, as in this case, they ferment even without cracking (Taz, subsection 3). Some differentiate between wheat and barley: wheat, which in any case is as if it is cracked, does not need to crack open, unlike barley (Ran in the name of the Ra'ah). Others differentiate between a large amount of liquid and a small amount, and with a large amount, they do not need to crack open (Hagahot Maimoniyot in the name of Ra'am). The Tur and Shulchan Aruch follow the first opinion. This also seems to be the view of the Rif and the Rambam, as the reason is because they are lying idle.

Accordingly, our teacher the Rema wrote in paragraph 2 that one must be careful that water or rain does not sprinkle on the wheat, because then, even if they have not split, they are prohibited. This is his language. And one should not ask, according to this, how we buy wheat from a non-Jew in a year when there is rain at the time of the harvest? And in our countries, it is very common for rain to fall during the harvest. It is not similar to rain that falls on heaps, as will be explained, that we do not worry because there we say that the rain did not penetrate inside, as will be explained. This applies to large heaps. But at the time of harvest, when it is known that they are scattered little by little across the field, and they leave them for a long time until they make heaps – it is obvious that the rain affects every stalk. One might say that certainly if we know that this wheat was rained on at the time of harvest – it is definitely forbidden to take from it for Passover. But in a situation where it is not known – we do not assume a defect, because the majority of the majority do not harvest on a rainy day, even non-Jews, due to the spoilage of the produce. They strive to harvest when the sun is shining, and then, even if it rains, they stop harvesting until the rain passes. The small amount that is harvested – they bring it into the threshing floor or another place. Therefore, we are not concerned about an unknown situation, because it is certain that even during the rainy season, there is a lot of time when the rain does not fall, and during that time they harvest. This is different from heaps that remain in the field for a long time – there is a concern. Therefore, we need the reasons that will be explained.

Additionally, it is written: Grain that was stored in an attic, and rain came down through the roof in several places and moistened it—those grains that became moist are forbidden. However, the other areas are permitted to keep due to a double doubt: perhaps rain did not fall on them, and even if you say it did, perhaps they did not become leavened. But to eat them on Passover is forbidden, and the double doubt does not help. This is his language. And even though a double doubt is effective everywhere, it seems to me that his reason is because the second doubt is not a complete doubt, since it is more likely that through the rain they became leavened, and only in regard to keeping them, which is rabbinic—since he nullified them by burning on the fourteenth—do we consider it a double doubt, but not for eating, which is a Torah prohibition. According to this, we would say that this law applies only before Passover, but during Passover, the previous nullification does not help. The commentators wrote that even for eating, the double doubt helps, but since there is no loss here, they were stringent. However, when there is a loss, it is permitted even for eating (Taz, subsection 4 and Magen Avraham, subsection 10). In my humble opinion, it seems as I have written. And if a little snow or water fell on a pile of grain, one should remove the top ones, and the rest are permitted for eating (Tur, section 466), as certainly only the top ones were affected. (And in the ruling of the Rema, the Beit Yosef brought in the name of the Agur that Ra'avan and Riva were stringent, and Raavyah permitted eating some of them before Passover, and eating them on Passover due to the double doubt, see there. And since the Rema did not mention eating some of them before Passover, we deduce that he ruled like Ra'avan and Riva. He only permitted keeping them for the reason I have written. This is proof for our words, and examine and you will find it easy.)

There was an incident involving a Jew who bought wheat from a non-Jew. Another Jew came and also asked him to sell him wheat, and he replied, "I don't have any wheat, for the first Jew was my friend, and I sold him the wheat that I had washed for my household needs. Out of love for him, I sold it to him." The second Jew does not need to be concerned about this, as the seller is not believed in what he says once the wheat has left his possession, as I have written in Yoreh De'ah, section 16. However, if he does believe him, it is certainly forbidden (Magen Avraham, subsection 4). In my humble opinion, it seems proper to be stringent in all matters, because this is akin to speaking innocently—who compelled him to say that he had washed them? And even though it is possible that he said it out of boasting, to show how much he loves him, nonetheless, it is difficult to be lenient in matters of chametz in such a case (so it appears in my humble opinion).

Soured wheat that got mixed with kosher wheat: if the soured wheat is not distinguishable, its status is like dry mixed with dry, which is nullified by the majority, and it is permissible to keep them until after Passover. But if they are distinguishable, it is forbidden to keep them, since nullification does not apply to something that is recognizable on its own. If one wishes to grind them before Passover and add enough to make a ratio of sixty to one, he may do so, as before Passover it is nullified in sixty, and it does not reawaken, since flour mixed with flour is considered a liquid with a liquid, as we ruled in Siman 467 that it does not reawaken. He can also bake them during Passover, as they have already been nullified. This is not considered nullifying a prohibition from the outset, as before Passover there is no prohibition. But if he did not grind them before Passover and wishes to grind them during Passover, even if they are not distinguishable on their own, it is forbidden, as this is dry with dry, and it reawakens according to the ruling of our master the Rema there, that with dry it reawakens. Even if some of it was eaten before Passover, it is still forbidden, as definitely some amount of chametz is present. (I learned all this from the Magen Avraham, subsection 4, see there. And what he wrote that if it was mixed dry with dry during Passover, and one of them was eaten, it is permitted, as I wrote in Yoreh De'ah Siman 109, see there. It requires investigation if we say this with an issur of any amount, and see Machatzit HaShekel, subsection 9. One should be stringent.)

Wheat that arrived on a ship: if it is dry and hard and its appearance has not changed, we do not assume it is prohibited, and it is permitted. But if it is soft or its appearance has changed, it is forbidden to eat it on Passover. However, regarding storing it, it seems there is no concern. Yet, the Tur wrote in the name of the BeHaG: wheat that arrived on a ship, if it is moist or its appearance has changed, it is known that water has come upon it, and it is forbidden to store it. This is his language. In my humble opinion, it seems that this applies specifically if it is moist or its appearance has greatly changed. But if it is not moist, just slightly softened, and its appearance has not greatly changed, there is no concern to store it. Nevertheless, in practice, this requires further investigation. And if it is known that water has come upon it, then even if its appearance has not changed at all and it is hard, it is forbidden to eat it. Regarding storing it, it might be permitted because it is hard and its appearance has not changed at all.

A year in which rains fell during the harvest season upon the sheaves in the fields, to the extent that some of the stalks on the sheaves began to sprout, nevertheless, there is no need to be concerned about the wheat of that year, to say that most of it became leavened. For if this were the case, we would never be able to eat matzah, as there is no year in which rains do not fall on the sheaves. Rather, according to Torah law, we follow the majority, and the majority do not become leavened (Rashba in his response, siman 102). Even those sheaves upon which we saw rain fall—we assume leniently that perhaps the water only entered the upper stalks, but not those in the middle of the sheaf. And this is also known and evident to the eye. And even if the water did enter, perhaps it did not have enough time to cause leavening (there). The main reason for leniency is because it is certainly so, as it is evident to the eye that leavening did not occur there, since there are no sprouts on them.

Therefore, wheat that has been found to be cracked, which is a sign of fermentation – we do not say that all of it has fermented. Rather, those that are not cracked are permitted, because it is common that during heavy rains the top and bottom of the pile ferment and crack, and the water does not touch the middle part at all. If it is difficult to separate the cracked ones, if there is a ratio of sixty to one – it is permissible to grind them before Passover and eat from them during Passover. Most years, inspection is hardly needed, as it is obvious that there is a ratio of sixty to one against the sprouted ones. However, in a year when there was an abundance of rain at the time of harvest – it is clear that inspection is needed to see if there is a ratio of sixty to one. If there is not a ratio of sixty to one – one can add until the ratio is reached. But without inspection, it is forbidden in that year. The common practice among us is to bring several handfuls of wheat, and the rabbi inspects them to see if there is a ratio of sixty to one against the sprouted ones, and he gives his certification. Without certification, Passover flour is not used. The certification is given for the wheat and for the grinding. Now that wheat is brought from afar by railroads, there is an obligation to supervise also during transportation to ensure the sacks are properly covered. This is our obligation, and this is proper for us. The certification is obtained from the local rabbi where the grinding takes place.

In the Gemara (33b), it is stated: for example, if it became leavened while still attached (to the ground). From this, it is clear that even while attached, it can become leavened. This happens when the wheat has completely dried and no longer needs the nourishment of the ground. At that point, it is like it is placed in a vessel and will become leavened if rain falls on it. The signs of leavening are well known among us: when they sprout, a small ear emerges at the top, or they soften and split open. This requires understanding, as is known. Therefore, it is customary to harvest the specially supervised wheat before it has fully grown. But those who harvest it while it is still really green, it seems to me that they are not doing well, because it is difficult to grind and knead, and it also contains a lot of moisture, making it more susceptible to becoming leavened. Rather, it should not be harvested until it has completed its growth and turned white. However, they should not wait until it has completely dried, and after harvesting, they should immediately gather it to the threshing floor.

A Jew who has pits filled with wheat and is concerned that there might be cracked wheat at the bottom or on the walls of the pit due to the saltiness of the pit and the earth—mere nullification suffices, for even the cracked ones do not have complete leavening but rather spoilage and deterioration, as the Rashba of blessed memory wrote in his responsa (Volume 10, section 15). And in our practice, we sell all types of grains on the eve of Passover during the sale of chametz, as I wrote in Siman 448, and this is appropriate.

The Tur and Shulchan Aruch wrote in Section 8: Honey of non-Jews – we do not presume it to be prohibited by saying it is adulterated, and it can be eaten on Passover. Thus is their wording, meaning: because some prohibit it, as they mix it with flour or semolina. To this, they said there is no concern, for even if they mixed it – it is considered fruit juice. And to be concerned that perhaps water was mixed in as well, making it fruit juice with water and causing it to leaven immediately – we do not concern ourselves with a distant suspicion of mixing two things. Additionally, the Rosh wrote in a response in the name of Rabbi Yitzchak that honey transforms anything mixed with it into honey, and therefore, should we all year round be concerned that they mix it with non-kosher meat and completely prohibit it? Rather, even if they mix the honey – it transforms into honey (Beit Yosef). However, the Rosh himself wrote in the sixth chapter of Berachot (Siman 35) that this requires proof, see there. And in the Jerusalem Talmud, at the end of the chapter "Kol Sha'ah," it is explicitly forbidden, as it says there: Rabbi Chanina had honey adulterated with semolina. He came and asked Rabbi Mani. He said to him: You must remove it, see there. And perhaps specifically semolina, because it is roasted and becomes complete chametz. (And this contradicts Rabbi Yitzchak's opinion. And perhaps it takes a long time until the honey transforms it, and in the case of Rosh Chodesh, it was close to Passover. Also, perhaps they had date honey. This requires investigation, and be precise and you will find clarity.)
