And therefore, our master the Rema wrote that the custom in these lands is not to eat honey, except for that which is brought in a barrel from the beehive, from which they make a beverage called mead. Thus far are his words. Meaning: that from this honey, it is customary to make a beverage. And this honey is permitted to eat even in its raw form (Taz, small section 6), although there are those who prohibit eating any kind of honey, because it might be confused with that which is mixed, as written in the Mordechai. And there are those who want to interpret the words of our master the Rema as intending to permit only making the honey beverage called mead and not eating it raw, for this reason that it might be confused (Magen Avraham, small section 7). And it is astonishing to impose stringency upon stringency and to enact decrees from our own reasoning. The primary opinion is as I have written, that it is also permitted in its raw form (Chayei Adam, small section 17).

And now, even though we have clearly heard that flour is not mixed, in any case, we do not buy honey from a non-Jew unless it is still mixed with wax and made like small chambers, as it is taken from the beehive. Similarly, what they call "lipetz," which is the good honey that drips by itself and has no mixture, because even a small mixture would spoil it, and they would not sell it even at half the price as it is pure, and the experts know this well. But ordinary honey we forbid for Passover. However, if it got mixed during Passover in food – we do not prohibit the food, even if there is not sixty times as much. And likewise, with all dried fruits which we have accustomed to prohibit – we do not prohibit if they fell into food. And this is like legumes in Siman 453. And to make mead – we make it before Passover from all types of honey, because even if there is something leavened – it is nullified before Passover. But on Chol HaMoed (the intermediate days of Passover), one should only cook water with honey from the beehive.

As far as we know, the production of sugar nowadays does not involve any concern of chametz, as everything is made through steam. Nevertheless, it is customary to designate sugar for Passover that is produced under the supervision of a learned scholar who oversees the factory and certifies it. It is also permitted to sell sugar to a non-Jew, even sugar produced throughout the year. Similarly, all types of dried fruits are permitted to be sold. However, sugar cubes that contain a mixture of flour are prohibited from being sold, for even though this is fruit juice, these sugar cubes are plain, and it is likely that they also contain some water mixture, and they are sold as chametz. (And regarding what the Rema wrote that sugar is forbidden even to keep, but sugar candy is permitted, it has already been written that the opposite is true. There is no need to elaborate on what the latter authorities have written about hot sugar and sugar in barrels, as all this was in their times. Nowadays, everything is made in large factories through steam power, and there is no concern of chametz.)

Additionally, it is written that dried figs and dried grapes known as raisins, whether large or small, depend on local customs. For there are those who are stringent and do not eat them, and there are those who are lenient. Therefore, in these countries, the custom is to be stringent and not eat any dried fruits unless it is known that they were dried in a manner that does not raise concerns of chametz. These are his words. The early authorities wrote that flour was sprinkled on figs, and who knows the method of drying all dried fruits? Indeed, we see that dried apples and pears are dried in an oven after baking bread. Therefore, we do not eat any types of dried fruits on Pesach, except for prunes, which are known to be dried in the fields due to their abundance. Nevertheless, the custom is to bring special ones for Pesach. Almonds, even those without shells, are not considered dried fruits because they are not dried, but are as they are naturally. As for oranges, it seems that the good ones do not have a concern, as they are not dried in ovens. However, there are simple ones that are peeled from lemons, and those are dried in ovens, and who can distinguish? Therefore, they should not be eaten on Pesach. 

(See Magen Avraham, subparagraph 8, who wanted to say that even what is baked in an oven after bread is permitted because of "notein ta'am bar notein ta'am" (secondary imparting of flavor), see there. His words are puzzling, for there is visible flour in the oven, which is placed under the bread during baking. The Noda BiYehuda already challenged him, as written in Sha'arei Teshuva, subparagraph 14, see there. And it is absolutely forbidden.)

The custom in these countries is not to eat saffron, which is called "zafferan." Even the type called "LND zafferin," which has no concern – we don't eat it, because due to its high cost, people are not knowledgeable enough to separate it (Taz, small section 9, and Magen Avraham, small section 10). Likewise, "nagalach" is not eaten on Passover. However, pepper, even though it is dried – there is no concern, because it is produced in large quantities where it grows, and there is no concern that it was dried in an oven. Similarly, what is called "English pepper" – there is no concern. And know that for several years we have heard from the city of Warsaw that it was discovered that pepper was adulterated with flour in the middle. However, since the vast majority is not adulterated – we do not need to be concerned with regular pepper. Additionally, the government imposes severe punishment on counterfeiters, so it is certainly not common among us. (The Magen Avraham there wrote about tobacco that it is sprinkled and soaked in beer. And now it is known that this concern does not exist.)

Ginger, which is called "Ingever," and cinnamon – we eat on Passover, and presumably there is no concern about them. And "Septalins," which is a type of plum – these are dried fruits, as even plums are specially prepared for Passover. And "Zoyer Salt" – it is permissible to use on Passover, as there is no concern of leavening with it. It is a great benefit to the poor, who add this to the dip they call "Burekas," as the main food for the poor on Passover is this dip, and they cannot afford to prepare it in a vessel before Passover to ensure it has a sharp taste, as is well known. When a little of this is added – it has a good taste. Those who are stringent – should be stringent for themselves and not for others. Similarly, the sand called "Soda" – is permissible on Passover, and there is no concern with it. It is known that in the factories, where they make the "Zoyer Salt" and the "Soda" – they have special utensils for these, and there is no concern with them. Similarly, it is permissible to drink on Passover the water called "Selzine Water," which is made in special utensils, and there is no concern of leavening with it. Similarly, lemon water which contains lemons and sugar, when specially prepared for Passover – provided they do not add the usual "Alk" of the whole year. But since there is no concern, and this "Alk" is added one drop to many bottles and is done before Passover, and even if there was any concern – it is already nullified in a thousand and more than a thousand. It is not a significant factor, especially according to our investigation, there is no concern at all. Those who are stringent – should be stringent for themselves and not for others. And carobs called "Baksar" – we also eat on Passover, as there is no concern of leavening with them. It is obvious that dried fruits dried by Jews are permissible to eat.

We learn in the Gemara (Pesachim 40a): The Rabbis taught: One may not soak barley on Passover. If one soaked them and they split – they are prohibited; if they did not split – they are permitted. Rabbi Yosi says: Soak them in vinegar. The vinegar constricts them and does not allow them to become leavened (Rashi). Shmuel said: The halacha is not like Rabbi Yosi. And we learn from this that even if they split – they are not yet fully leavened, for if they were, what benefit would there be in vinegar according to Rabbi Yosi? And so Rashi explains that if they split – they quickly become leavened, see there. And so wrote the Ran. And it says there: Mar Ukva said: They did not literally split, but if one were to place them on the mouth of a barrel, they would split on their own. And Shmuel said: They literally split. Shmuel acted according to this, that they literally split, see there.

And the Ri"f wrote: Since the law is not explicitly decided, we act stringently like Mar Ukva, as it is a biblical doubt. And this applies to eating these barley grains in their entirety. But if they are found with cooking and they have not split, since the prohibition is only a small amount by rabbinic law – we do not prohibit that cooking in which two or three grains are found, unless they have split, as per Shmuel, since it is a rabbinic doubt and we are lenient. And some say that the law follows Shmuel, as Mar Ukva was his student. Furthermore, Shmuel performed an action… up to here is his wording.

The Rambam in Chapter Five, Law 8, writes: A cooked dish in which barley or wheat is found, if they have split open – the entire dish is forbidden, for chametz has mixed into it. If they have not split open – they are removed and burned, and the rest of the dish may be eaten. This is because grain that has been mixed but not split open is not full chametz by Torah law, but by the words of the Sages, as it is said: "And you shall guard the matzot." Meaning: be careful with matzah and guard it from any leavening. This is his language, and it seems he rules like Mar Ukva stringently. He believes that Mar Ukva prohibits it rabbinically (and so wrote the Lechem Mishneh and the Beit Yosef). There are those who wish to differentiate between wheat and barley, that wheat, even if not split open, is considered full chametz (Ran in the name of the Ra'ah). This is disputed (Ran there), as there is no distinction. Likewise, the Rambam equates them, for he wrote "wheat or barley" – thus equating their laws.

Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in paragraph 9 using the language of the Rambam that if [the grains] have not split open – the dish is permitted. And our teacher, the Rema, wrote about this: "This is not the custom, but we prohibit everything with even a tiny amount, even if they have not split open." Thus are his words. The reason for the custom is based on two reasons written by the Mordechai in the chapter "Kol Sha'ah": The first is because of something that has a permissible condition. And the Mordechai himself rejected this reason, as the condition of permissible does not apply when the food becomes spoiled. Furthermore, it would return to its prohibition the following year, and all the more so with something that is merely a flavor, see there. The second reason is because we are not proficient in what is called "fit to split open." And he wrote about this: "And one who is lenient because of the joy of Yom Tov – has not lost." See there.

It is clear that our master, the Rema, did not state this as a strict law, but rather because this was the custom to prohibit everything: the cover, the spoon, and everything that got mixed with that dish (Magen Avraham, subsection 13). Similarly, the Mordechai wrote, and this is his language: "And because of the custom, I prohibit out of doubt. And one who is lenient for the sake of the joy of the festival has not lost." This is his language. And it implies that even for eating, it is permitted (Chayei Adam, subsection 27). And even according to the custom, it is only if it softened in any case, but if it did not soften, it is nothing (Taz, subsection 10). And even if three grains were found, we do not say that there is a presumption that there are many more, since it is possible to check. And the Rif explicitly says: two or three grains, as I wrote in subsection 20. Furthermore, there is one who says that we do not say this presumption with worms that come from outside, as I wrote in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 84. And here too: the grains come from outside. And even though there are those who disagree with this, as I wrote there, nevertheless, here it is permitted for the first reason, because it is possible to check. (See Magen Avraham, subsection 12, and Chayei Adam, subsection 26. And what the Magen Avraham wrote, why do we not say that since it is placed, it will come to chametz? And he answered with difficulty, see there. And in my humble opinion, it seems that in a pot during cooking, and even after cooking during the great heat, it does not rest because it is boiling.)

But if it cracked open, all the cooked food is forbidden by law, as well as the first vessel, the bowl into which it was poured from the first vessel, the spoon that was inserted into the pot, and the cover. Some are stringent even with the second vessel, as I wrote in Siman 447. However, on the seventh day of Passover, one can cover the food and wait until the conclusion of the festival, and then eat the cooked food, and the kernel should be burned (Eliyah Rabbah in Siman 440, subsection 3, and Chacham Tzvi Siman 86, brought in Sha'arei Teshuvah in this Siman, subsection 18). And certainly on the last day of Passover. If a non-Jew comes to take them on the seventh day of Passover, it is forbidden to protest, but on the last day of Passover, one can protest (as stated in Sha'arei Teshuvah there). See the next section.

According to the fundamental law, when a kernel is found in a cooked dish, or a cooked chicken is found to have a split grain inside it on Passover, it is permitted to sell it to a non-Jew. This is not considered deriving benefit from chametz (leavened product), since the payment received is for the chicken and not for the grain, and the chicken is not sold at a higher price due to the grain found inside it. Nonetheless, in these countries, the custom is to burn everything or to throw it into the toilet, because they consider the whole dish or the whole chicken as chametz. However, on the last day of Passover, our master the Beit Yosef wrote in Section 10 that if the grain is found on this day, it is permitted to keep it until after Passover, since a minuscule amount, which is rabbinically prohibited, does not warrant stringency on the last day of the holiday regarding keeping it. Certainly, when it imparts a detrimental taste, there is leniency regarding keeping it (Taz, Section 11). In the previous section, we mentioned that even on the seventh day of Passover, it is permissible to cover the utensil and wait until the end of the holiday. Some have the custom that on the seventh day of Passover, when such a question arises before the authority, he will tell the questioner that he finds it difficult to answer now and that he should return at night, which is already the last day of Passover. He will then permit him to keep it until the next night and eat it.

If matzot were baked on Passover and a split grain of wheat was found in the dough or in the baked matzah, the Rosh ruled that one should remove the area around the grain, and the rest is permitted. For at most, the taste of the wheat did not permeate more than the area removed, as this is not something fatty that would spread extensively. However, some prohibit the entire dough or the entire matzah, as the Rashba wrote in a responsum (Siman 176), arguing that the wheat did not touch only one spot but rather came into contact with the entire dough as it was kneaded. Therefore, it is not applicable to say "here it was found, here it was," because necessarily, as it was kneaded, it spread throughout the dough. Since this occurred during Passover, when even the smallest amount is forbidden, the entire dough is prohibited. Additionally, the water in the dough carries the taste throughout the entire dough. Rabbi Yosef Caro wrote in section 11 that it is appropriate to be concerned about this opinion unless it involves significant loss or in pressing circumstances, in which case one may rule in accordance with the Rosh. The reasoning is that it is not necessarily the case that the taste spread throughout the entire dough, even if it was kneaded through it all. Therefore, we say "here it was found, here it was," meaning that the taste was imparted only in that specific place. Furthermore, even if it was split, it is not fully chametz but rather close to becoming chametz (Tur), as I wrote in section 19.

And our master, the Rema, wrote about this that the custom on Passover is to prohibit that matzah in which a grain of wheat was found, but permit the others, whether it was found baked or raw. We say, "Where it is found – there it was." And if it is found in the dough – the entire dough is prohibited. This is specifically during Passover, but before Passover – only the amount that needs to be removed is prohibited, and this is the custom. Thus far his words. Meaning: When found in the matzah – we do not say that the grain was in the dough and the whole dough is prohibited, but we say "where it is found in the matzah – there it was," and we do not assume prohibition from one place to another. Accordingly, if it appears that the grain is filled with water from one side to the other, implying it was in the water – the entire dough is prohibited. However, it can be argued that it was filled with water somewhere else and then fell into the matzah (Magen Avraham, subsection 16).

Here is the translation of the provided passage from the Aruch Hashulchan:

And behold, among us, we do not bake on Passover. And what was baked before Passover, even if a grain of wheat is found in the matzah during Passover – it only prohibits the amount that can be removed. And in this case, the principle of "reawakening" does not apply, since during Passover, it did not impart flavor. Therefore, one throws away the grain of wheat along with a finger's breadth of matzah adjacent to it, and consumes the rest. And during the kneading before Passover, if a grain of wheat is found in the dough – one removes the amount that can be taken. Therefore, we do not have any practical difference in the previous law. However, in any case, it is proven from the words of our Rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, that even in a cold state, there is a prohibition, for the one who forbids the entire dough during Passover – it is because the grain of wheat was in the water. And the one who permits it holds that it was not in the water, as we have explained. But if it certainly was in the water – it would prohibit. On this, the Levush objected that the cold state does not prohibit.

And so it is explicitly stated in the Rosh and the Tur, and this is their language: There was an incident where a wheat grain was found cracked in a vessel of water, and a dish was cooked with that water, and they permitted the dish. And we do not say that the water is forbidden and therefore the dish is forbidden. And similarly, the Avi HaEzri permitted wheat that fell into a well..., since the water is cold – the wheat does not impart flavor into it. And even if complete chametz fell into a well – it is permitted for this reason. Thus far is their language. It is clearly evident that cold does not cause prohibition. And our master, the Beit Yosef, in his great book, challenged this regarding the Rosh, who forbade dough if a wheat grain was found in the water, and he himself ruled that cold does not cause prohibition? And he answered that here it refers to before Passover, and therefore it does not cause prohibition when cold, see there. And others objected to him, asserting that certainly this also refers to Passover itself (Levush, Bach, and Taz, subsection 12). However, dough is different, because as it is kneaded and rolled and pressed, the dough and the wheat grain are pressed and mashed by his hands, and it is inevitable that some flavor is squeezed out from it when it was in the water and softened (Taz there). According to this, both the Rosh and the Rashba do not prohibit in the case of cold, but dough is different as I have written.

Accordingly, what our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in Section 12 that if a split grain of wheat or leavened bread is found in a vessel of water, and it does not impart flavor to the water because the water is cold, and one cooked a dish with that water or kneaded dough with it — it is permitted. And there is someone who prohibits it if it is during Passover. Thus are his words. And he wrote this based on his distinction between before Passover and during Passover. But according to what all the great later authorities have rejected his words — there is no distinction, and even during Passover, it is permitted with cold.

And in practical law, it appears to my humble opinion that even though there are those who prohibit [it] when cold, nevertheless, since most of our later authorities agreed not to prohibit [it] when cold—one should not cause a financial loss to a Jew over a minor prohibition, which is rabbinic in nature. And there are those who wish to prohibit [it] in the case of meat that was soaked in water, where there was a kernel in the water, because in meat there are crevices (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 19). His words are puzzling, for since we say that when cold it does not impart flavor, what do we care about the crevices (Chayei Adam, subparagraph 31)? And only when the wheat was in dough should it be prohibited for the reason we mentioned, if it was during Passover. But other cold [situations] do not prohibit, as with all prohibitions.

However, all of this applies when the seed has not remained in the water for twenty-four hours. But if it remained for twenty-four hours – it is prohibited, because soaking is like cooking (Magen Avraham there, and Taz section 17, and Bach in the name of Rashal). And it seems to me that if there is a doubt whether it was in the water for twenty-four hours or not – it is permitted, because the prohibition of something minute is rabbinic, and we are lenient in cases of rabbinic doubt. According to this, if seeds are found in water pits, even if it is clearly known that they drew from the pit while the seeds were in it, nevertheless, if there is a doubt whether they were there for twenty-four hours – it is not prohibited. All the more so if there is a doubt whether at the time of drawing the water, the seeds were not there, and even more so if the seeds have not cracked, it is not prohibited. And even if there is a doubt whether they cracked or not – it is a rabbinic doubt and we are lenient. (And earlier in section 462:10 it was explained that when a seed is found in knaidlach or charamzloach, when there is fat and eggs there, it is considered fruit juice. And in charamzloach there is also honey, in cases of great loss and the joy of a festival – one can be lenient so that it is not prohibited by something minute. And similarly with turnips, see there. And see section 47 regarding the doubt of soaking.)

And know that it appears to me, in my humble opinion, that what is found in the Mordechai and other early authorities regarding the law of chametz that fell into a pit—whether the water is prohibited or not—this all pertains to a pit of gathered water, as is evident from the language of the Tur, who wrote that Rabbi Eliezer permitted wheat that fell into a pit... the leavened water descended into the pit... see there. But concerning a well that is a spring, it is puzzling to say that the water would become leavened, for they are constantly flowing and connected to the waters beneath them, just as we do not prohibit a river. Even though the water stands, nevertheless it does not rest, and it is connected through the veins of the ground to the waters outside of them, as our Sages said in Chagigah (22a): "The entire earth is porous." And Rashi explained that the water flowing here comes from a large river, see there. (Only for a mikveh are they not considered connected, but otherwise, they are connected. And that which is found in some places using the term "well"—they were not precise about this.)

The great authorities have agreed that we establish a presumption of prohibition from one time to another, but not from one place to another. In other words, for example, if one took from the barrel mostly into a bowl, and later chametz was found in the bowl, we do not prohibit the cabbage that is in the barrel. We say "here it was found, here it was," meaning it was found in the bowl and it was in the bowl, and not in the barrel. For we do not establish a presumption of prohibition from one place to another. But if chametz is later found in the barrel, then even what is in the bowl is prohibited. For although we say "here it was found, here it was," nevertheless, the cabbage in the bowl was also there. We do not say that the chametz fell into the barrel after the cabbage was taken into the bowl. For from one time to another, we establish a presumption of prohibition, and we say, "just as the chametz is found there now, so too it was there previously" (Magen Avraham, subsection 16, in the name of the Maharam). And similarly, in all matters, for example, if one poured sauce from the pot into several bowls and a kernel was found in one bowl, only that bowl is prohibited, and we do not establish a presumption of prohibition from the bowl to the pot. But if it is found in the pot, all the bowls are prohibited. And so in all similar cases.

And such a ruling is explicitly found in the Mishnah at the end of the ninth chapter of Taharot regarding olives, where first they are placed in a matan, which is a type of vessel, and from the matan they are brought up to the roof. And it is taught: if a sheretz (creeping creature) is found on the roof, the matan is pure. We do not consider that the impurity from the roof extends to the matan, and we say that the sheretz fell on the roof and not in the matan. If it is found in the matan, the roof is impure, and we do not say that the sheretz fell after the olives were taken to the roof, because we assume continuity from one time to another. (And the Tosefot Yom Tov there questioned: why don't we say that the sheretz fell after the olives were brought to the roof? See there. According to the Magen Avraham, there is no difficulty at all. And although we should scrutinize this in the Mishnah there, chapter four, Mishnah four regarding filling ten buckets, there are different interpretations there, see there thoroughly. Also, this does not apply to all impurities at the time they are found, as this pertains to life and death. Furthermore, the Tosefot in Eruvin 35b, in the discussion starting with "Kol," wrote that this applies only to terumah and holy things like "from time to time" in Niddah, see there.)

And this is what our master the Beit Yosef wrote in section 12: If one scalds a chicken by placing it in boiling water to remove its feathers and then finds a split wheat kernel in the water, the chicken is forbidden. This is his wording. And we do not say that the wheat came after the scalding, because we assume continuity from time to time. And this applies specifically to a split kernel, but if it is not split, the chicken is permitted because it is a case of double doubt: perhaps it did not become leavened, and if you say it did become leavened, perhaps it fell in afterward (Taz, sub-section 15). Therefore, even though our master the Rema was stringent even with an unsplit kernel, as I wrote in section 22, nevertheless, here there is another doubt, so we do not need to be stringent (Chayei Adam, sub-section 34, and see Taz there). Furthermore, as we have already written in section 23, it is not a strict law but rather due to custom, see there.

And our master, the Rema, wrote, and this is his language: "There are those who permit [consumption] even in the case of scalding a chicken, because we say that perhaps it fell in there afterwards. And there are those who prohibit other meat but permit chicken due to a double doubt. Regarding the custom, it seems that one should prohibit other meat or whole wheat, even chicken. And specifically if they were blanched, meaning the water was hot. But if the water was cold and the chickens were soaked there – one should not prohibit due to doubt. And in cases where there is reason to say that perhaps the wheat was digested in the chicken, for example, if it is broken – even in blanched cases, it is permitted due to a double doubt. However, if the mixtures were mixed, and there is a significant loss and deprivation of the joy of the holiday – one can be lenient in all this in the case of a doubtful rabbinic prohibition, which is minimal. And one should permit other dishes that have a mixture from that dish of the meat that was soaked in water or blanched. So it appears to me. Until here is his language, and it requires further explanation."

Here is the translation of the given halachic passage from the Aruch Hashulchan:

"And this is its explanation: There are those who permit it, because they do not hold that we maintain a presumption of prohibition from one time to the next, but rather we say: it just fell now. And although in the Mishnah of Taharot it is not so, as I wrote in Section 35, if so, why when a creeping creature is found in the water channel does it render the roof impure, why not say it just fell now? It can be said that indeed Rambam in Chapter Seventeen of the Laws of Impurity ruled this way, that even if found in the water channel of the roof – it is pure, see there. He wrote: if found in the water channel of the lower part – it is impure. And it is clear that in the roof it is pure, even if we do not know his source. The Kesef Mishneh wrote that he ruled according to the sages of the Tosefta in Taharot (Chapter Eleven), as it is stated in the Tosefta: he was cutting from the water channel and bringing it up to the roof, and a creeping creature was found on the roof – the water channel is pure. It was found in the water channel – the roof is impure, according to Rabbi. And the sages say: if found on the roof – only the roof is impure. If found in the water channel – only the water channel is impure. And although we usually hold that an anonymous ruling in the Mishnah and a dispute in the Baraita follows the anonymous Mishnah (Yevamot 42b), nonetheless, in any case, Rambam ruled this way. (And it can be said that he held like some of the commentators wrote, that all the general rules of the Talmud apply only to the three orders in practice in our time. Additionally, since Rabbi himself is the one who disagrees, it is possible that we do not say this rule.)"

And behold, according to this opinion, in all similar questions we say "now it has fallen" as with a chazakah (presumption) that has been undermined, where we say "now it has been undermined." The third opinion, which differentiates between meat and chicken, is because it follows the first opinion that we assume continuity over time. However, with chicken, an additional doubt arises: perhaps the grain was in its intestines and got digested, as we say concerning impurity. The first opinion holds that we do not derive prohibition from impurity, as the Tosafot wrote in Bechorot (7b). Additionally, it can be said that a doubt due to lack of knowledge is not considered a doubt (Bach); but since it is impossible to know, it is considered a doubt (Taz, subsection 17). He also added that "regarding custom," meaning that it is not decided according to the law but according to the custom to be stringent, and we assume prohibition over time. Also, with chicken, when there is no indication that it is digested, such as if it is broken, one should be stringent. And this stringency applies specifically when it was soaked in hot water, but not in cold. Meaning, even for those who are stringent with cold, nevertheless, regarding the principle that we do not assume continuity over time, one should not be stringent with cold, and we say "now it has fallen."

And all this pertains to the matter itself. However, regarding mixtures, such as when some of this has mixed into other dishes – it is obvious that one can be lenient with cold mixtures, even when it is not possible to say "it just fell in now." For example, if it is certain that the wheat was together with the meat in the water, or even in hot water and it is not certain – we say regarding mixtures "it just fell in now," and we permit it in cases of significant loss and to prevent the loss of Yom Tov joy. According to this, the law that we mentioned that we do not establish a prohibition from one place to another but do establish from one time to another – some entirely disagree, saying that even from one time to another we do not establish a prohibition. And proof for this opinion is from the words of the Rambam that we brought in paragraph 38. However, even according to the custom to be stringent, in any case with cold mixtures, we certainly do not establish a prohibition from one time to another. Therefore, if water was taken from a vessel for a pot and then cooked in it, and afterwards chametz was found in the vessel – the cooked food is permitted, and we say "it just fell in now." And similarly regarding mixtures, even in hot water. (And the Bach exaggerated in stringency in this matter, and his words were already rejected by the Magen Avraham in subparagraph 25, and the Taz in subparagraph 17, and the Chayei Adam. And in the case of wheat that did not soften – even the Bach agrees that there is no reason to be stringent at all.)

There was an incident where someone took a piece of matzah and a piece of chicken into his mouth and ate them both together. He felt a grain of wheat in his mouth, spat out the food, and found the grain. It was not known whether the grain was inside the matzah, and the matzah is only prohibited to the extent of the piece that was taken, as it is certain that the grain was inside the dough during baking. If it had fallen onto the matzah when it was cold, it would have rolled off. However, the chicken and the cooked dish are permitted. Alternatively, if the grain was in the chicken, the chicken may be permitted due to a double doubt (safek sefeika): perhaps it was in the matzah, and even if it was in the chicken, perhaps it was digested or fell in when cold. Concerning a double doubt, we certainly say "now it fell," and we do not maintain a prohibition from one time to another. Even with meat, it is permitted in such a case. Furthermore, even according to those who are stringent from time to time, certainly from place to place we do not maintain a prohibition. Therefore, even if we assume it was in the meat or the chicken, we say it fell in here, and not when they were in the pot or large bowl (see Magen Avraham, subparagraph 25). If a grain of wheat is found on the table and it is not known where it came from, we say it fell on the table and do not maintain a prohibition from place to place (see Shaarei Teshuvah, subparagraph 33).

There was an incident involving a servant who brought a vessel with honey water, which is called mead, to drink, and a wheat grain was found in it. They said that in cold [liquid] it does not render it forbidden even though it became chametz, as the Tur wrote that it does not render it forbidden in cold [liquid]. And perhaps you will say that it was at the time when they cooked the honey water before Passover, if so, it was already nullified and does not reawaken. And even though the wheat grain is still in it, nevertheless, it is cold and does not render it forbidden (Taz, subparagraph 18). And even according to those who are stringent with cold [liquid] and also hold that it reawakens, as I wrote in Siman 447, nevertheless, only what is in the vessel is forbidden and not the entire barrel, for we do not assume [the impurity] transfers from place to place, and we say that it fell into the vessel and not the barrel. (And one who relies on the Taz to be completely lenient has not lost, for there are several doubts here. Be precise and you will find leniency.)

Rabbeinu the Beit Yosef wrote in Section 13: If one purged a pot with vinegar that was used within the last 24 hours, and the vinegar water flowed into a cistern during Passover, it is prohibited to drink the water from that cistern during Passover because it has mixed with chametz. This is his exact wording. He specifically mentioned "during Passover" because if it had occurred before Passover, it would have already been nullified and would not reawaken, as I wrote in Siman 467. However, initially, it is certainly prohibited, since one can take water from another cistern (Taz, Section 18, and Magen Avraham, Section 27). And this is why he specifically said "because it has mixed," meaning: even according to the opinion that it does not prohibit when cold, this applies to wheat or bread that fell into the water. However, when it comes to water mixing with water, it is indeed mixed, and it is prohibited during Passover (there). 

Know that if the vinegar is noticeable and remains distinct by itself even while in the cistern, such as when there is a substance like rust or something similar, it prohibits the water even retroactively, even if it fell before Passover, because when the chametz is noticeable by itself, it is never nullified (Taz, there). And since this ruling is not common at all, there is no need to elaborate on it.

And regarding salting on Passover, there are many opinions. The Tur, quoting the Rokeach, wrote: A grain of wheat found on a salted chicken, and other chickens were salted with it, the one that the grain was found on is forbidden, because chametz on Passover is forbidden even in the smallest amount. The others are permitted. And Rabbeinu Eliezer of Metz ruled that even that chicken is not entirely forbidden, rather one removes the area where it has spread, which is the measure of removal. And this is agreed upon by the Rosh and the Smak. Both opinions hold that although salting is like boiling, nevertheless it does not transfer from piece to piece without liquid. And even though with fatty prohibitions we are stringent as in Yoreh De'ah, section 105, nevertheless with chametz there is no prohibition of fat. And some forbid all the pieces in salting (Bach quoting Issur VeHeter and Rashal). And it can be said that the reason is: Since meat has fat - the prohibition spreads from piece to piece even without liquid, as chametz on Passover is forbidden even in the smallest amount. And some require peeling the other salted meat (Kol Bo quoting the Raavad). And this is when it is found on the chicken, where there is a doubt that it might have touched all of them. But if it is found inside the chicken – the others require nothing according to this opinion (Magen Avraham, small section 31). And some are completely lenient, that even that piece itself only requires peeling (Beit Yosef quoting the Rashba).

And this is the language of our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, in Section 14: If a split wheat kernel is found in a chicken before salting – rinsing is sufficient. If after salting – peeling (the outer layer) is sufficient. There are those who are stringent and say to deeply cut around it and discard it. If other chickens were salted together with it – peel all of them. There are those who are stringent and forbid everything that was salted together. The primary ruling is to forbid the entire piece on which the wheat kernel was found, and permit the others through slight peeling. If one wishes, he may sell everything to a non-Jew as I wrote in Section 447, even though this is not customary with other chametz mixtures. This appears to be my opinion. Until here is his language. If the others were cooked without peeling – it is permitted, as this is merely an additional stringency, as I wrote in Yoreh De’ah Section 91 (Magen Avraham Subsection 33). Nevertheless, even after cooking – one should peel, but the peeling does not prohibit the rest of the piece (there). There are those who permit initially even without peeling (there in the name of the Mishnah Berurah). This is when there is no concern that it might have touched the other pieces (there). And it seems to me in my humble opinion that even in doubt, if it is certain that it did not touch – one may be lenient among us, as the peeling is very difficult as is known. And indeed, the opinion of some of our rabbis is that even this piece itself is not entirely forbidden, as I have written. However, the practical halacha in salting is that only that piece is forbidden and no more.

And that which they wrote that before salting, washing is sufficient – it is obvious that if it is cold without any liquid, it does not prohibit according to all opinions (Magen Avraham, subsection 29). Similarly, if a piece of wheat is found on the meat after salting and washing – it is also permitted for this reason, as it certainly was not there during the salting; for if it had been there, it would have fallen off during the washing. However, this is if it is found on the outside, but if it is found inside the chicken – it certainly was there beforehand (ibid., subsection 30). And women customarily check very thoroughly inside the chicken before soaking and salting to ensure that no grain remains inside. In my humble opinion, one can rely on this presumption, such that if a grain is found later, we can say that it fell in afterward since it had been checked beforehand (and there is proof from Pesachim 7a and Niddah 4a; see there and analyze, and you will find it easy). And if a grain is found in the crop, even after salting – it is permitted, as the crop serves as a barrier, and one should discard the crop. There is also a doubt that perhaps it was digested, which is likely since it was found in the crop (this seems correct to me, and see Shaarei Teshuva, subsection 36). And if after salting and washing, the meat was placed in a vessel, and afterward a grain is found there, if the meat was not salted in the vessel – discard the grain, and the meat is permitted. If it was salted there a little – discard the piece on which the grain was found, and the rest are permitted even without peeling. Although in complete salting we require peeling, here, since it is only slight salting – it is sufficient to prohibit that piece alone. If there was a small amount of salt – it is sufficient to prohibit the amount of removal even on that piece, because sometimes a small amount of salt is added. Similarly, if a grain is found in the soaking water before salting – the meat is permitted. Even according to those who prohibit with cold – that is only when it has been there a long time. But meat, before salting, is not soaked in water for more than half an hour – there is no need to be stringent and prohibit. Especially since the main halacha is that cold does not prohibit, as I have written. (And know that "cold" is defined as anything where the hand does not recoil. Similarly, a third vessel does not prohibit. Regarding a second vessel, there are those who are stringent, as I have written in Siman 447, and that is when the hand recoils.)

If a kernel is found in a barrel of pickled cabbage, all the cabbage is forbidden, for pickling is like cooking. This applies when the brine covers it, but if the brine does not cover it, it is treated like salting, and one must remove a few fingerbreadths deep and wide and discard it, and the rest is permitted (see Magen Avraham, subsection 33). Similarly, if a kernel is found in a container of "Borikass" that has a lot of water, since there is no salt like in cabbage, it depends on the opinions whether it is forbidden in cold or not. However, if it was there for twenty-four hours, it is clear that pickling is like cooking. In a case of doubt whether it stayed for twenty-four hours, it appears that doubtful pickling is permitted. I have seen that great authorities disagree on this, whether doubtful pickling is permitted or not (see Shaarei Teshuvah, subsection 34, where the Biur Halacha permits, and the Magen Avraham forbids). It seems to me that it is permitted, because since the prohibition of something small is rabbinic, we rule leniently in cases of doubt regarding rabbinic laws. The reason we do not permit in salting except by a double doubt is in a case where the prohibition is clear, such as in hot, but you want to permit it. However, in cold, there is no prohibition before us unless it was pickled in it for a whole day, and it is permitted in doubt. And even though those who forbid in cold consider it a double doubt for prohibition: a doubt whether cold forbids, and if you say it does not forbid, perhaps it was pickled in it for a whole day, and it is considered pickled. But we have already explained that the primary ruling is that cold is permitted, as agreed by our early authorities. Therefore, in a case of significant loss and prevention of holiday joy, such as a container of "Borikass" which is the main food of the poor on Passover, and even wealthy households mostly eat it as is known, if a kernel is found in the container and it is not clear that it was in it for twenty-four hours, one discards the kernel, and the "Borikass" are permitted to be eaten on Passover. If a kernel is found in a barrel of salted fish, one removes that layer and eats the rest. The fish on which the kernel was found should be discarded in a despicable place, and that layer should be set aside until after Passover, and the rest is completely permitted. (The Magen Avraham, subsection 33, brings in the name of Rabbi B. of Posen to discard the entire layer into the river, see there. I do not know why. And if it is because of the brine, then all of them should be forbidden. Therefore, in my humble opinion, it seems as I have written. Be precise and you will find it lenient.)

A roasted chicken on a spit that is found with a split grain of wheat inside it during Passover, and it is clear that it was there during its roasting: if the chicken is lean, one cuts out the area around the wheat according to an estimation. Some prohibit the entire chicken, since when it is turned on the spit during roasting, the flavor spreads throughout the whole chicken. And this is the main ruling. Even though in other prohibitions we do not say this reasoning, as is evident from Yoreh De'ah, siman 105, this is because turning the spit does not cause the flavor to spread, and it is nullified in sixty. But in the case of a minuscule prohibition – it is clear that turning the spit causes it to spread. Some have gone to the extent of being stringent and even prohibiting all the chickens that were roasted with it if they touched it, because by turning the spit, it spreads from one to the other. However, if they did not touch, they are permitted, and we do not say that the prohibition spreads throughout the spit, causing the other chickens to absorb from the spit. We only say this when the chicken with the wheat inside is fatty, as then the prohibition spreads through the entire spit (Magen Avraham, siman 36). If the wheat is found in the chicken afterward and it is split, even though it is explained that we assume the prohibition from the time it was roasted, and this chicken is prohibited, in any case – regarding the other chickens, we may be lenient straightforwardly, as we were lenient in mixtures in siman 40, see there.

And our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 16: Wheat or barley found in the crop of a bird, after the bird has been scorched – it is permitted. And the wheat and barley – they need to be burned, because they are not considered as digested. Thus far his language. And the reason: because roasting does not prohibit more than the peel, and the crop itself is considered the peel. And even though according to our custom we prohibit the entire bird when roasted, in any case, scorching is not the same as roasting (Magen Avraham, subsection 37). And even in complete salting, it appears to me in my humble opinion to permit the bird when the crop is found inside with several grains, as I wrote in section 46. And it is true that according to custom we prohibit the entire piece in salting, as I wrote in section 45, but in the case where it is found in the crop, where it is likely to say it has been digested – one can rely on our rabbis that peeling is sufficient in salting, all the more so in scorching. (See Magen Avraham, subsection 37, where he wrote that there are women who customarily remove the gizzard prior to scorching. We do not know of this custom. And what he wrote, that all matters of Passover should only be done by a Jew – it is certainly correct, and this is the common practice.)

It is taught (Pesachim 50a): In a place where the custom is to do work on the eve of Passover until midday, one may do so. In a place where the custom is not to do work, one may not do so. And why did they adopt the custom not to do work? So that one should not forget to eliminate their chametz, to slaughter the Passover offering, and to prepare the matzah for the night (Rashi). Until midday, it depends on custom, but after midday, it is prohibited by law, as explained in the Jerusalem Talmud there, because from midday is the time of the Passover offering for all of Israel, and it is considered a holiday. For anyone on the day they offer a sacrifice, it is a holiday for them, and work is forbidden. Therefore, even in our times, the holiday has not been nullified (Rosh). Additionally, something that has been prohibited by a count (i.e., a formal decision) cannot be permitted even if the reason is nullified, and it requires another count to permit it (Ran there). And when it was prohibited, it was prohibited for all of Israel, even those living outside the Land, because it is a general holiday for all of Israel. And one who does work on the eve of Passover after midday, besides not seeing a sign of blessing in this work, will be cursed and denounced.

There is no differentiation in the prohibition of work whether it is done for payment or for free – it is all forbidden. Regarding having a non-Jew do the work, there are differing opinions: the Rokeach permits it, while the Mordechai forbids it (Beit Yosef). One could say that the one who permits it holds that the prohibition is rabbinic, and therefore it is not relevant to prohibit instructing a non-Jew. The one who forbids it holds that the prohibition is biblical, as the Tosafot wrote there, and this is their language: "It is implied from the Jerusalem Talmud that it is forbidden by Torah law," end quote. If so, it is relevant to this case "instructing a non-Jew is a rabbinic prohibition." (However, the Rokeach wrote that "instructing a non-Jew is a rabbinic prohibition" only applies on Shabbat, Chol HaMoed, and Yom Tov. Therefore, it is permitted to have a non-Jew do it even in one's home. See Beit Yosef.)

The custom follows the opinion of the lenient position. Therefore, getting a haircut after midday is forbidden if done by a Jew, but permitted if done by a non-Jew (Taz, subsection 2 in the name of R. Shlomo Luria). Even trimming nails is forbidden after midday (ibid). Some permit trimming nails after midday if one forgot to do so before midday (Chayei Adam, subsection 4, and Eliyah Rabbah), as this is not considered a complete act of labor concerning the eve of Passover. There is an opinion that forbids getting a haircut even by a non-Jew after midday, because the person getting the haircut assists somewhat by tilting his head (Magen Avraham, subsection 13). This is not the main opinion, for what difference does it make? For even doing minor adjustments to one's clothing is permitted, all the more so in this case where the assistance is minimal and insignificant (Chayei Adam, ibid). Bloodletting is customarily forbidden all day for another reason, because our sages stated in the Talmud (Shabbat 129b) that there is danger in this on the eve of Shavuot, so they decreed it for all eves of festivals. However, cupping, which is called "bankes" – Mahariv forbids it, and Maharil permits it (Magen Avraham, subsection 15), as it is not like bloodletting since the blood from cupping is not from the internal body like bloodletting. It seems appropriate to be stringent on the eve of Shavuot, but lenient on the eves of other festivals. The night belonging to the eve of a festival – everything is permitted.

And this prohibition of labor is specifically for actual labor, such as sewing clothes or doing work for profit. But one is allowed to repair his utensils for the festival. And even though we do not find this permission for Chol HaMoed, nevertheless, the eve of Passover is less stringent than Chol HaMoed. Therefore, all the types of work that we permit on Chol HaMoed, such as preventing a financial loss and similar cases as will be explained in the laws of Chol HaMoed, are certainly permitted on the eve of Passover. Similarly, someone who writes books for his own study is permitted to do so on the eve of Passover, and certainly to write novel Torah insights. Even with regard to casual letters, the custom is to permit it.

Until midday – it depends on the custom, as I have written. And our master the Rema wrote in paragraph 3 that for us, it is a place where the custom is not to do work. And this applies specifically to complete labors, but other labors – there is not even a custom. So he wrote. And the Levush wrote that it is possible that in his place they customarily refrained from doing work, but in many places I have seen that they do work until midday, see there. The great later authorities (Taz and Magen Avraham, paragraph 6 and Chayei Adam) have quoted him. And so it is now that work is done everywhere, and it would be desirable if they would stop doing work at midday.

One who goes from a place where work is permitted to a place where work is not permitted, even if he intends to return, may perform such work discreetly in other matters. However, work that is difficult to do discreetly should not be done at all in the city, due to the potential for conflict. Outside the city, it is permitted if he intends to return. But if he does not intend to return, it is forbidden. However, if he has not yet entered the city's boundary, even if he does not intend to return, it is permitted (Magen Avraham, subsection 8). 

One who goes from a place where work is not permitted to a place where work is permitted, and intends to return, it is forbidden for him to work, as he retains the stringent practices of the place he left. But if he does not intend to return, he may follow even the lenient practices of the place to which he has gone (Magen Avraham, subsection 9). 

There is an opinion that always one should follow the stringent practices of the place he left, but this is not correct, as I have written in Yoreh De'ah, section 214, paragraph 20; see there. In any case, when one follows the stringent practices of the place he left with the intention to return, he should not appear before the people of the place he is currently in as if he maintains this prohibition, for one should never differ from local practices due to potential conflict. When one needs to observe a prohibition, he should do so without attracting the attention of the local people. 

The general rule is that anyone who intends to return should follow the practices of his original place, whether lenient or stringent, as long as he does not appear before the local people as changing their custom, because of potential conflict. And peace is paramount. There are many detailed laws concerning these matters. Regarding customs, it has been explained with Divine assistance in Yoreh De'ah, and here is not the place to elaborate.

And even in a place where the custom is to do work until midday, nevertheless, one should not begin a new task on the fourteenth of Nissan, even if it can be completed before midday. Only three trades are permitted to start work in a place where the custom is to work, provided they finish by midday. These are: tailors, barbers, and launderers. The reason for this leniency is that these three trades are also permitted during Chol Hamoed (the intermediate days of the festival). In the case of tailors, the leniency allows a non-professional to sew as usual during Chol Hamoed because this is not considered complete work according to his sewing. For barbers and launderers, the leniency is due to those coming from a distance or those released from prison being permitted to have a haircut and launder for the sake of the festival. Therefore, these trades are also permitted on the eve of Passover. However, other trades, if they began before the fourteenth, may be completed on the fourteenth until midday, even if they started on the night of the fourteenth. But to start on the day of the fourteenth is forbidden. This is the opinion of the Rambam at the end of the laws of Yom Tov. See there.

However, the opinion of the Tur in the name of the Rosh is that for these three types of work, it is permitted to start and finish until midday even in a place where the custom is not to do work. And if they started before, they can finish until midday even with other types of work. And in a place where the custom is to do work, it is permitted to start any work if one can finish it until midday. And the custom follows this opinion. And know that all this applies when there is a need for the festival. But if there is no need for the festival, it is forbidden in any case. And there are those who say that a poor person who has nothing to eat is permitted to do work even after midday (Chayei Adam, section 11 in the name of Knesset HaGedolah), for it is no worse than Chol HaMoed, where this is permitted, as I wrote later in Siman 542.

On the fourteenth [of Nisan], one sets up coops for chickens, meaning to prepare a place for the roosters and hens to stand. However, placing chicks on eggs is prohibited all day, unless a hen that has been sitting on the eggs for three days or more dies and the eggs have already begun to spoil. In such a case, another hen may be placed on the eggs so they do not spoil, as this is considered a loss. Some permit, even initially, placing chicks or a hen on eggs (the first opinion of Rashi on the Mishnah in Pesachim 45b), as this is not considered labor with respect to the eve of Passover.

One may remove manure from under the feet of the animal on the day before Passover throughout the entire day and throw it outside into the garbage. But during Chol HaMoed (the intermediate days of the festival), one should only move it to the sides. As for the manure in the courtyard, it should not be taken out but rather moved to the sides even on the day before Passover. Because under the feet of the animal, it is permitted to take it outside for the health of the animal, but in the courtyard, it is sufficient to move it to the sides. However, if the manure accumulates in the courtyard, it is permitted to take it outside even during Chol HaMoed.

One may transport and bring utensils from the craftsman's house all day, even if it is not for the purpose of the festival, as this is not considered a form of labor at all. If one gives an item for repair, and it is needed for the festival, it is permitted until midday. We do not recite "Mizmor LeTodah" on the eve of Passover, nor do we recite "Mizmor Ya'ancha". We hasten the morning prayer in order to finish eating by the third of the day. Some bake "Shmura" matzah after midday. Due to the honor of the festival, it is customary to go to the bathhouse and the mikveh, even though it is not obligatory. After the afternoon prayer, we recite the order of the Passover offering, as a remembrance of the Temple. (See Berachot 22b: Rav Chama would immerse on the eve of Passover. The halachah does not follow his view.)

Know that in the Torah, this holiday is called "Chag HaMatzot" (Festival of Unleavened Bread). In the language of the Sages, it is called "Pesach" (Passover), and so it is in common parlance. Perhaps this is because, in this term, the great miracle that happened to us in Egypt during the plague of the firstborn, when the Almighty passed over the houses of the Children of Israel, is included. Therefore, they named it by this name. Our Sages of blessed memory said (Pesachim 53a): It is forbidden to say "This meat is for Pesach," because it appears as if one is sanctifying his animal and eating consecrated things outside the Temple. That is, although it is our custom to refer to what we prepare and purchase for this festival with the term "Pesach," in any event, with meat one should be cautious not to say this, so that it does not appear as if one is designating it as a Pesach offering, which would make it consecrated outside the Temple. However, with wheat and barley, it is permitted to use this term, since they have no association with the offering. The same applies to all other items, and everyone knows the intention is for the Pesach festival. Even when it comes to meat, if one says it in such a way, it is permitted. It appears that this caution is only for the ideal situation, but after the fact, there is no prohibition in eating it (Taz), because everyone understands that this is the common way people speak.

The Rosh wrote there that it appears that this prohibition specifically applies to the meat of a lamb or kid, from which the Passover sacrifice is brought. But Rashi wrote that the prohibition is because it appears as though one is consecrating it for the money of the Passover sacrifice, meaning to sell it and use the money to buy the Passover sacrifice. And if one would ask: If so, why did they say that wheat and barley are permitted, since we can also say the same about them? One could say: Because wheat and barley need to be guarded from becoming leavened, it is therefore appropriate to say that they are being guarded for Passover (Chayei Adam). According to this, other items would be forbidden. However, it does not seem that way. Rather, it appears that even according to Rashi, the prohibition applies only to an animal fit for the altar, as Rabbeinu the Beit Yosef wrote. And this is his wording: It is forbidden to say about any animal, whether alive or slaughtered, "This meat is for Passover," because it appears as though it was consecrated while alive for the Passover sacrifice, and it turns out that one is eating consecrated offerings outside [the Temple]. Instead, one should say, "This meat is for the holiday." But it is permitted to say, "This wheat is for Passover." Until here are his words.

Seemingly, there is much to wonder about, for since it is written that the reason is because it appears that one dedicated it during its lifetime as a Passover offering, then this should only apply to a goat or lamb. So why are all animals forbidden (Magen Avraham)? Rather, one is compelled to say that his intention is according to Rashi's explanation, that people will say it was dedicated for the monetary value of a Passover offering. However, with other items, there is no concern, for one can say that they were dedicated and then redeemed. This is not the case with an animal, which cannot be redeemed, for anything fit for the sanctity of the body cannot be redeemed, as is known. Therefore, any animal that is fit for the altar is forbidden, but other items are permitted. However, I would have thought that wheat and barley, which are fit for meal offerings, should be forbidden. Therefore, it teaches us that they are permitted (there), because with wheat, everyone knows that the intention is to preserve them for Passover. Some want to forbid any type of bird that requires slaughter, but this is an excessive stringency, since they are not fit for the altar (there, subsection 1).

And know that the Rambam completely omitted this law, and I am astonished that the commentators did not notice this. It seems to me that his reasoning is clear, because Rabbi Shimon holds in Menachot (103b) that anyone who does not make a vow in the standard manner of making vows, such as saying "It is incumbent upon me to bring a meal offering from barley"—his words mean nothing. And in the Tosefta, it is taught in the last chapter of Menachot: One who says "It is incumbent upon me to bring a burnt offering on the condition that I offer it in the Temple of Onias"—Rabbi Shimon says this is not a valid burnt offering. All the more so, one who says "on the condition that I offer it outside [the Temple]" (Tosafot Pesachim 53a, s.v. "Mipnei"). And the Rambam in the seventh chapter of Hilchot Maaseh HaKorbanot ruled according to Rabbi Shimon. Therefore, he omitted this, for in the Gemara it is said that according to Rabbi Shimon, even a roasted kid is nothing for this reason, and all the more so one who says "this meat is for Pesach." However, regarding a roasted kid, since all the Sages of Israel rebuked Todus of Rome with reprimand, as explained in the Gemara, he also ruled accordingly, as will be explained. This is not the case with "this meat is for Pesach."

This is the language of the Rambam in Chapter Eight, Law 11: In a place where the custom is to eat roasted meat on the nights of Pesach, they may eat. In a place where the custom is not to eat, they do not eat, as a decree lest people say it is Pesach meat. And in every place, it is forbidden to eat a fully roasted lamb on this night, because it appears as though one is eating consecrated offerings outside [the Temple]. However, if it is cut up, or if a limb is missing, or if a limb was boiled while it was still attached, it is permitted in a place where it is customary. Thus far his words. And roasted meat means when it is roasted on a spit over a fire, not what we call "braaten" (roast). And a "kid mikulas" (a whole roasted kid), even though it is not explicitly stated "this meat is for Pesach" – it is forbidden to make it, and it will be explained in Siman 471. (The Magen Avraham and the Chayei Adam wrote that saying "this meat for Pesach" is not a concern. For if his intention was for a sacrifice, he should have said "for Pesach", and "for Pesach" – the intention is for the festival. And what was written that in the case of a kid or lamb, one should be stringent even after the fact if he said "for Pesach", see there – the Chayei Adam has already rejected this, for there is no prohibition after the fact according to Rabbi Shimon, see there. And the Rokeach wrote that a person should not say "how much trouble is Pesach", for in the Jerusalem Talmud it says: What does the wicked one say? "What is this service to you, what trouble is this." Thus far his words, and see Chayei Adam.)

It is stated in the Tractate Sofrim (Chapter 21) that one does not fast in Nissan, except for the firstborns on the eve of Passover, and the modest ones because of the matzah so that they enter it with appetite, as stated there. The firstborns do so to commemorate the plague of the firstborn; and the modest ones, it seems, refers to delicate individuals, for when they eat during the day, they do not eat at night with appetite, as it is stated in the Gemara (Pesachim 108a): Rav Sheshet would sit in a fast every eve of Passover because he was delicate. For if he tasted anything in the morning, it would not benefit him to eat at night. And in the Jerusalem Talmud at the beginning of "Erev Pesachim" it is stated: Rabbi would not eat on the eve of Passover... because he was a firstborn. Rabbi Mana said in the name of Rabbi Yonah: My father was a firstborn and he would eat... However, from this: Rabbi was delicate, for if he ate during the day, he would not eat at night. And why would he not eat? So that he would enter the matzah with appetite. Thus far his words. And even though if it were because of delicacy, a fast is not necessary, the Tosafot wrote there and this is their language: Rav Sheshet would sit in a fast—not literally, but he would guard himself from eating. Alternatively, he would actually accept upon himself a fast so that he would remember and be cautious not to eat. Thus far their language. (And further examination is required on the Rosh, who wrote that there is support from the Jerusalem Talmud. However, the conclusion is not so.)

According to the words of the Massekhet Soferim, the Tosafot, the Tur, and the Shulchan Aruch have written that firstborns fast on the eve of Passover, whether a firstborn from the father or a firstborn from the mother. For anyone who is called a "firstborn," either a firstborn for inheritance, like from the father, or a firstborn for the priest, like from the mother, must fast. For in Egypt, all kinds of firstborns were killed, whether from the father or the mother, as Rashi explained on the verse "for there was no house where there was no one dead." Also, the eldest of the household is called a "firstborn," see there in Rashi. And in Psalms (78), it is written: "And He struck all the firstborn in Egypt, the first of their strength in the tents of Ham." And "the first of their strength" is a firstborn from the father, as it is written: "for he is the first of his strength; the right of the firstborn is his." And Jacob said about Reuben: "my might and the beginning of my strength." And with all this, the Holy One, blessed be He, commanded to sanctify the firstborn only from the mother, because he is the "first issue of the womb." And it seems to me that the reason is because the Holy One, blessed be He, sanctified "from the firstborn of man to the firstborn of beast," and in the case of a beast, it only pertains to the "first issue of the womb," as is evident. Therefore, also in the case of man, only the first issue of the womb is sanctified.

There are those who say that even a firstborn female must fast, for surely in Egypt they too were killed in the Plague of the Firstborn. And the proof is that the Midrash says that Bithiah, the daughter of Pharaoh, was saved due to the merit of Moses, implying that the plague also affected the females. Nevertheless, the custom is not so, because the Holy One, blessed be He, did not command the sanctification of the females, only the males. And one who follows a miscarriage must fast, since he is considered a firstborn for inheritance. Similarly, firstborns who are priests and Levites must fast, even though they are not redeemed with five selas, as they are not lesser than a firstborn from the father. If there are ten firstborns, some say the prayer leader should say "Aneinu." However, it is not proper to do so, because then it would be like a communal fast, which is prohibited in Nisan. Instead, the individual says "Aneinu" in the blessing of "Shomea Tefillah." And "Vayechal" is not read.

If the eve of Passover falls on Shabbat, it is customary for the firstborn to fast on the preceding Thursday. Some say that since it is postponed, it is entirely set aside, as it is only a custom. However, the custom is to fast according to the first opinion. One does not fast on Friday, so as not to enter Shabbat while in a state of affliction. When fasting on Thursday and one needs to check for chametz and finds the fast difficult, he may taste food before the search (Magen Avraham). Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote that it is customary that when the father is a firstborn, the mother fasts on behalf of her young son who is a firstborn. If the father is not a firstborn, the father fasts on behalf of his son until he grows up. Thus far are his words. Nowadays, this custom does not exist.

Regarding a brit milah (circumcision) or a pidyon haben (redemption of the firstborn) – the firstborn may eat. And there are those who wrote that only those connected to the mitzvah, like the father of the child, the sandak (godfather), the mohel (circumciser), and similar, may do so (Magen Avraham). And there are those who say that one who is lenient for any person at a seudat mitzvah (festive meal for a mitzvah) does not lose out (Pri Chadash). However, for several generations now, there has been complete leniency regarding the fast of the firstborn, specifically through the completion of a tractate of the Talmud. Not only the one who learns, but the firstborns gather around the one who completes it, finish it with him, and then eat. This has spread to all countries. It is not known from where they derived such leniency, except that perhaps due to the weakness of the generation, the significant effort required on the eve of Passover, and the fact that the consumption of bitter herbs is also not beneficial for health, they consider themselves unable to fast. And since the Talmud does not mention this at all, and in the Jerusalem Talmud the conclusion is that they do not need to fast, and it is only a custom according to the Massekhet Sofrim – therefore, the sages of the generation did not object to this practice. This requires further study.

The sages taught in the Mishnah (Pesachim 99b): On the eve of Passover, close to the time of the afternoon offering, a person should not eat until it gets dark. This is so that one will eat the matzah of the mitzvah with appetite, due to the enhancement of the mitzvah (Rashi). This means that even though someone who eats an olive-sized portion of matzah when they are full—if it is not to the extent of being disgusted by the food due to extreme fullness—has fulfilled their obligation of eating matzah, as we say in Nazir (23a) regarding the Passover offering, and the same applies to matzah. Nevertheless, this is not considered an enhancement of the mitzvah. The enhancement is that one should be somewhat hungry and eat with appetite.

And this "Mincha" is close to the Mincha Ketana, which is from nine and a half hours and onward. Nine and a half hours is the time of the Mincha Ketana, and "close to Mincha" means from the beginning of the tenth hour (Rashbam). This is also the conclusion of the Talmud (107b). There are those who wrote that one should be stringent from close to the Mincha Gedola (Ran there). This is also clarified from the words of Rabbeinu the Rema later in Siman 639 on the eve of Sukkot, where he writes: similar to eating matzah (and this was already questioned by the Magen Avraham there). The truth is that it can be said that his opinion is the same here. The reason he did not correct it here is because, in any case, we do not have what to eat after midday on the eve of Passover, as both chametz and matzah are forbidden. The prohibition is only on rich matzah, and we are forbidden rich matzah as I have written in Siman 462, which is not the case on the eve of Sukkot (Chayei Adam Small Section 1). It appears that everything depends on the person. According to the law of the Gemara, the prohibition is only close to the Mincha Ketana, but there are many people who, if they eat at midday, will no longer eat the kazayit of matzah with appetite as is known, and these are certainly forbidden from midday.

There is no prohibition related to chametz, for it is already forbidden. And matzah that is used to fulfill the obligation of eating matzah is also forbidden on the eve of Passover, for anyone who eats matzah on the eve of Passover is considered as if he has engaged intimately with his betrothed in his father-in-law's house, as stated in the Jerusalem Talmud. The prohibition only applies to matzah ashira (rich matzah), but it is permissible to eat types of delicacies (Gemara there), such as meat and fish, fruits and vegetables, provided one does not fill his stomach with them. If someone is delicate and even a small amount of food harms him, then everything is forbidden. Cooked matzah is considered like types of delicacies. The prohibition applies only to bread-like food, such as matzah ashira or fruit juice with water, which is also considered like matzah ashira (see Magen Avraham, subsection 5).

And wine, it is stated in the Gemara (108a) that Rava would drink wine on the eve of Passover because wine stimulates the appetite. And in Berachot (35b) it is said that when one drinks a lot of wine, it stimulates the appetite. But a little does not stimulate; rather, it satisfies the heart. Therefore, our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote that one should not drink a little wine, but a lot is permitted for the reason explained. And so wrote the Tosafot there. And it is surprising about the Tur, who wrote that one may drink wine, whether a lot or a little, because it stimulates the appetite. Until here is his language. And this is against the Gemara, as I wrote. And the commentators have already addressed this, and some have explained that although it satisfies, it does not satisfy so much that it would be forbidden to drink because of this (Beit Yosef). And some have explained that a little indeed satisfies but only a little (Bach). And some have explained that when adding this little to the first two cups, it becomes a lot and stimulates the appetite. And although this is a long time before the cups, it still stimulates the appetite (ibid. and Taz, subsection 2). But from where did the Tur derive to say this? And it seems to me that his reason is because in Pesachim, regarding the main law, it does not mention a distinction between a lot and a little – implying that there is no distinction. For if there were, the Talmud would not have omitted to say regarding Rava's case: "We only said a lot, but a little satisfies." This implies that there is no distinction except regarding the blessing. And the Rambam did not mention this at all. And drinking a little strong wine certainly stimulates the appetite.

A minor who does not know what is being recounted about the Exodus from Egypt on that night – it is permissible to feed him. But a minor who does know – it is not permissible to feed him, so that he will not fall asleep. One should explain to him the matter of the Exodus from Egypt, as it is said in the Mekhilta, "And the one who does not know how to ask, you should open for him" – it seems to me that this means a minor who does not have the capacity to ask and does not know how to ask, but understands what is being said. Therefore, it is a mitzvah to explain to him the matter of the Exodus from Egypt (see Magen Avraham, subsection 7). 

There are those who customarily do not eat lettuce on the eve of Passover, so that they will eat the maror with appetite. Similarly, on the first day of Passover, so that they will eat it on the second night with appetite. This has no basis, for is maror a good food that should be eaten with appetite? On the contrary, it is a remembrance of affliction. Similarly, there are those who minimize eating matzah on the first day so that they will eat it on the second night with appetite, and similarly minimize drinking wine, unless they drink a lot to stimulate appetite as I have written. Some are stringent not to eat fruits on the eve of Passover, so that they will eat the charoset with appetite. There is no need to be concerned with this custom. Some are stringent not to crumble or break matzot on the eve of Passover, so that they will not come to eat from them. There is no need to be concerned with this either, for this is only in the case of a Torah prohibition. 

Know that matzah that is baked properly and then crumbled and kneaded with wine, oil, and honey, and not cooked – is not called "rich matzah" and it is forbidden to eat it on the eve of Passover. "Rich matzah" is only when the dough is kneaded with fruit juice, but if it is cooked – it is permitted to eat it, and not if it is baked without liquid.
