If one begins eating before the tenth hour and the meal extends until the night – its law is like that of all Sabbaths and festivals, as explained in Siman 271, see there. It is a mitzvah to wash and shave on the eve of the festival, and to wear nice clothes as on the Sabbath.

Even though on Shabbat and Yom Tov we add from the mundane to the holy, and one can make Kiddush and eat while it is still daytime, nevertheless, on the night of Pesach it is not so. As it is written: "And they shall eat the flesh on that night" – we require it to be actual night. And matzah is compared to the Pesach offering (Tur), as it is written: "With matzot and bitter herbs they shall eat it." This is what we learned in the Mishnah in "Erev Pesachim," that one should not eat until it gets dark. Meaning: not like every Erev Shabbat and Erev Yom Tov (Tosafot there). And so we learned in the Tosefta, that the mitzvah of Pesach, matzah, and maror is from when it gets dark. Therefore, also the cup of Kiddush, which is one of the four cups, and also the eating of other vegetables, and other changes made so that the children will ask questions, and certainly the recitation of the Haggadah – all these need to be at the time of eating matzah and maror (Beit Yosef in the name of Terumat HaDeshen). Additionally, since the Kiddush is for the sake of eating matzah just like any Kiddush in the place of a meal, and since the eating of matzah is at night – the Kiddush also needs to be at night (Taz, Seif Katan 1).

Nevertheless, one should set the table while it is still daytime, in the manner of free people whose table is set long before the meal. Additionally, this is so that one can eat immediately when it gets dark, for the sake of the children, so they do not fall asleep. And even if one is in the study hall learning, it is a mitzvah to hasten, get up, go, and arrange the seder. Thus they said about Rabbi Akiva, that he never said "the time has come to rise from the study hall" except on the eve of Passover, for the sake of the children, so they would not fall asleep. And Rabbi Eliezer says there: "We snatch the matzot on the nights of Passover, for the sake of the children, so they will not fall asleep." And Rabbi Akiva would distribute roasted grains and nuts to the children on the eve of Passover, so they would not fall asleep and would ask questions. The reason for this is that we see that the Torah insists on the questions of the children on this night, as it is written several times, "When your child asks you..." The essence of the retelling of the Exodus from Egypt is through the questions of the children and the answers of the father, for through this the pure faith is clarified. Therefore, all actions are done so that the children will be awake and not asleep during the seder. And thus it is an obligation upon us to do. Regarding the snatching of the matzah, Rashi and Rashbam explained that they eat quickly or lift the seder plate. Rambam in the seventh chapter wrote: "They snatch the matzah from one another," see there. (And this is the custom that the children snatch the afikoman from under the cushion. See Chayei Adam, section 2.)

And he should set his table with beautiful vessels according to his ability. For although throughout the year it is good to minimize the use of beautiful vessels as a remembrance of the destruction [of the Temple], nevertheless on the night of Passover we perform all the symbols of freedom. And even if he has silver vessels on loan, if the owners do not object, it is appropriate to place them on the table on the night of Passover. And this is the reason our sages required reclining, because in their time free people would eat in a reclining manner, on cushions and pillows, as a sign of prominence. Therefore, one should prepare his seating during the day, and arrange the seating in a manner of freedom.

Know that the Tur wrote in the name of Raaviya that in our times, in our countries, where it is not customary to eat while reclining, there is no need to recline. See there. However, all our Rabbis do not agree with this. On the contrary, it seems to my humble opinion that since it is a commandment to make changes on this night, as the Rambam wrote in the seventh chapter that one must make changes on this night so that the children will see and ask, there is no greater change than reclining, which we are not accustomed to, and now we do it. And a proof for this is that in the Mishnah (Pesachim 116a), in the question "What has changed," the question of reclining is not mentioned, but in our version, it is included. The reason is that in the time of the Mishnah, it was not a change, and the child had nothing to ask about it. But now, he asks about the change, and therefore the main ruling is according to the majority of the decisors that there is an obligation to recline.

And another clear proof that reclining is necessary is from the Mishnah in "Arvei Pesachim", where it is taught that even the poorest person in Israel should not eat until he reclines. This means: do not say that since he is poor and not accustomed to reclining, he does not need to recline; it comes to teach us that he must. And the same applies to us. And our teacher, the Rema, wrote in paragraph 2 that even a poor person who does not have cushions should recline (this is how it should be stated) on the bench. This is the end of his words, meaning: he should do some form of reclining on the bench, by placing his garment or another object; provided that he does not go without reclining, for reclining is essential. (The Bach wrote that a mourner does not recline, but his words were refuted by the Chayei Adam and the Knesset HaGedolah. However, the Taz and the Magen Avraham mentioned this. In our practice, we do recline, but not with an abundance of cushions. Regarding wearing a kittel, there are differing opinions, and one can do as he wishes. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

When one reclines, he should not lean on his back or on his face, for this is not the proper manner of reclining. Nor is it respectful, but he should lean on his side. And not on his right side, but on his left side. Reclining on the right side is dangerous because the esophagus is on the right side, and when one leans on his right side, the cover of the windpipe may open by itself, and the food is supposed to enter the esophagus. If he leans on his right side, the food might enter the windpipe instead of the esophagus, leading to danger. Additionally, it is the custom of noblemen to recline on their left side. Reclining on the right side is not considered "reclining" (Gemara 108a, refer there and analyze, and you will find it easy to understand). And know that in reclining, there is no difference between a left-handed person and others. Although he is the opposite of everyone else in his hands, this is not so with his internal organs. Therefore, even a left-handed person must recline on the left side like everyone else (and he can lean on the thigh of his fellow).

Our Sages of blessed memory stated (Pesachim 108a): A woman with her husband does not need to recline. But if she is an important woman, she needs to recline. Rashbam explained that because she is subordinate to her husband, she does not need to recline. An "important woman" is considered one whose husband takes pride in her, and who is of higher status than him; thus, she is not subordinate to him and needs to recline. Consequently, a woman who does not have a husband – all women need to recline. Also, if the husband is not at home, all women need to recline. However, in the Sheiltot (Parashat Tzav), it is written: A woman does not need to recline because it is not the manner of women to recline, see there. This applies to all women, as his version did not state "a woman with her husband" but simply "a woman." The same is true for the Rif. The reason is that it is not their custom to lean on their side. But if she is an important woman, meaning prominent in beauty or wealth, like the important woman mentioned in the chapter "Ein Ma'amidin" (Avodah Zarah 25b), whose manner is to recline – she needs to recline like a man. And nowadays, it is not the custom of women to recline at all, and our women do not recline. Our Master the Rema wrote in section 4 that our women are considered important and need to recline. However, they rely on the Ra'avya, who said that in this time, there is no reclining. Thus far his words, and this is from the Mordechai. In my humble opinion, it is difficult to say this, for if so, why did the men not rely on the Ra'avya? Additionally, it is a solitary opinion. Rather, it seems that they relied on the Sheiltot and the Rif according to their version. An important woman is not common, and even if she is important, she does not consider herself so.

A son with his father – he needs to recline, even if his father is also his primary teacher, because presumably the father is not particular about it, unless it is known that the father is particular. A student with his teacher – he does not need to recline, for the awe of one's teacher is like the awe of heaven. He should not recline in front of him, as this would appear as if he is assuming authority for himself. Even if the teacher is not his primary teacher, unless the teacher gives him permission, then if the student wishes, he may recline. But if he does not wish to, we do not force him, for he can say that even with permission, he does not have the audacity to recline in front of his teacher. Moreover, the teacher is not obligated to give him permission, because the way of the Torah is for the student to fear his teacher with a superior fear. If one is sitting with a distinguished Torah scholar of the generation, even if he has not learned anything from him and he is not his teacher, his status is like that of a teacher, and he does not need to recline because he is also obligated to fear him. It is obvious that all this applies when they are eating at the same table. But if he is eating at a separate table, even in the same room, he needs to recline, for in such a manner it does not appear as arrogance in front of his teacher. A servant, even though he is busy with the needs of the household and needs to get up from his place at any time, nevertheless needs to recline while eating and drinking. (And the Kesef Mishneh in the seventh chapter explained the reason: because whoever buys a Hebrew servant is like buying a master for himself, see there. It seems that the reason is because he is subordinate to the homeowner. And I would say that he is exempt and not understand, what relevance is this? Is he worse than other workers who are obligated to recline, as it is stated in the Gemara there about the apprentice carpenter? We do not say this except for a Torah student, not for other types of work. This requires further examination.)

Some have written that anyone who is exempt from reclining during the Seder and still reclines is considered a "commoner," as stated in the Jerusalem Talmud, the first chapter of Shabbat (cited by the Magen Avraham, section 6, in the name of the Rashal and Taz). And some have questioned this: do we not find many stringencies that a person can take upon themselves (ibid.)? One can say that in this context, it is certainly so, for this is only found in a student whose teacher has given him permission, and this is his commonness - that he should not do something that is against the honor of his teacher even if he has been given permission. And similarly in all such instances. (And similarly for a mourner, according to those who exempt him - it is a disgrace towards the deceased.)

Anyone who requires reclining, if he ate or drank without reclining, has not fulfilled the obligation and must eat or drink again while reclining. Our teacher, the Rema, wrote in paragraph 7 that some say that in our times, since it is not customary to recline, it is sufficient to rely on the opinion of the Ra'avyah, and after the fact, one has fulfilled the obligation even without reclining. It seems to me that if one did not drink the third or fourth cup while reclining, he should not drink them again while reclining, because it might appear as if he is adding to the number of cups. However, for the first two cups, he should drink them again without a blessing. Ideally, one should recline for the entire meal. So far his words. After the fact, one fulfills the obligation if he ate the required amount of matzah for "Hamotzi" and for the Afikoman and drank the four cups. From the words of the Rambam, who wrote in the seventh chapter, "For the rest of his eating and drinking, if he reclines, it is praiseworthy," so far his words, it implies that even ideally it is not necessary. But if he did it, it is praiseworthy. (See Chayei Adam, section 15, in the name of the Maharai, that for the olive-sized portion of "Hamotzi" it is not necessary to recline. His intention is what he wrote in Siman 475 that one should eat two olive-sized portions for "Hamotzi." But in my humble opinion, this does not seem correct. He wrote "olive-sized portion of matzah" because according to the fundamental law, only one olive-sized portion is required. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

And here is what is written: There is a concern about adding to the cups in the latter ones and not in the former ones. The reason is that in the former ones it is permissible to add, which is not the case with the latter ones, as will be explained. According to this, nowadays when it is not customary to add even in the former ones – one should not drink again, as it appears as adding (Magen Avraham, Section 7). However, the Rosh wrote that since he drank improperly – it has been clarified that it was not counted among the cups, and what he drinks now is obligatory, see there. And there is someone who says that for all the cups, if he drank without reclining – he does not need to drink another cup (Bach in Siman 479 and Chayei Adam, Section 14). And this seems to be the main opinion, as in the Gemara (Pesachim 108a), the halacha is established that only two cups require reclining, but due to doubt, we require reclining for all of them. Therefore, for each cup, it is a rabbinic doubt, and we are lenient. It appears to me that also our Rabbi, the Rema, his main reason is because of this, and not because he relies on a singular opinion, nor because it appears as adding to the cups. However, for the first two, since it is permissible to add by law – what difference does it make to us if he adds? And now that it is not customary to add even in them – one should not drink again, as I have written. And there is someone who wrote that at the beginning of the Seder, he should intend to drink again among the first ones, and then if he erred and drank without reclining – he should drink again without a blessing (Magen Avraham there).

One must drink the cups in the order established by the Sages: the first for Kiddush, the second after the Haggadah, the third for Birkat Hamazon, and the fourth for Hallel. If one drinks them all at once, meaning he drinks cup after cup until he has consumed four cups, he has not fulfilled the obligation of the four cups. It appears that the same applies if he drinks two cups not in the prescribed order, such as drinking two cups after Kiddush; only the Kiddush cup counts, and after the Haggadah he must drink the second cup. It seems to me that if he drinks the cup in the middle of the Haggadah, he has fulfilled the obligation even before the blessing "Who has redeemed us," because the blessings are not essential. The recitation of the Haggadah has no fixed length, so it is considered as having been drunk after the Haggadah. However, if he drinks in the middle of Birkat Hamazon or in the middle of Hallel, he has not fulfilled the obligation, since the Sages ordained that the cups be drunk after the entire Birkat Hamazon and after the entire Hallel. It also appears to me that if one did not drink one of the cups at its designated time, such as not drinking after Kiddush, he should drink it later, as there is no other remedy for this, and this applies to all the cups (this is what seems correct to me in my humble opinion).

The measurement of the cup: a revi'it, after it has been diluted if one wishes to dilute it, such as their wines which were strong. But with our wines, dilution is not relevant. And the measurement of a revi'it is a vessel that holds two fingers by two fingers, and the height is the width of two and a half fingers and a fifth of a finger (Tur). And its measurement is the capacity of one and a half eggs of water. And there are some of the great authorities who now wish to double the measurements because the eggs have become smaller, and many of the meticulous follow this practice. But we have already explained above in Siman 168, Section 13, and in Yoreh De'ah Siman 324 that this is not the case, see there thoroughly. And also regarding our raisin wine, there is much to discuss. And see what I have written above in Siman 204, Section 15, and Siman 272, Section 7 to teach favorably. And what can we do since in our country wine is not available? And the wine that comes from afar, besides being expensive and beyond the reach of most Jews, has many concerns as is known. And if he does not have wine – he should take mead, which they call mead, for the four cups.

And one must drink all or most of it. If the cup contains many quarter-logs (revi'it), several people can fulfill their obligation with it, each according to the measure of a quarter-log, but not according to the measure of most of a quarter-log, because each person needs a full quarter-log, even though for drinking purposes, one fulfills the obligation with most of it. However, some say that one cup, even if it contains many quarter-logs, can only fulfill the obligation for one person, who is required to drink most of the cup however it is. And this is the primary ruling, as it is the opinion of the Ramban and Mordechai (see Beit Yosef). One must drink the required measure in one go, or at least without a long interruption. And one should drink it in the manner of drinking a quarter-log. After the fact, if one drank with an interruption up to the time it takes to eat a "pras" (half a loaf), one has fulfilled the obligation. But if one waited longer than this measure, one has not fulfilled the obligation and needs to drink another cup. But if less than this, one has fulfilled the obligation. (The Magen Avraham in subsection 11 wrote that for the first two cups, if one waited longer than a quarter-log, one should drink again, see there. In my humble opinion, since the primary ruling is not like the Rambam, as I wrote in Siman 472, see there, one does not need to drink again.)

One who does not drink wine because he dislikes it or it harms him is nevertheless obligated to compel himself to fulfill the mitzvah of the Four Cups with wine, except when he is ill. We find among the Tannaim and Amoraim that wine was very difficult for them, yet they compelled themselves to fulfill this mitzvah of the Four Cups. It is a mitzvah to seek out red wine if the white wine is not superior, as it is written: "Do not look at wine when it is red." One can fulfill the obligation with cooked wine and with konditon (a spiced wine). Among us, this is not commonly found. Even a poor person who is supported by charity should sell his clothing or borrow or hire himself out to obtain the Four Cups, or receive from the charity collectors. If he only has enough for the Four Cups for the two nights, he should use them all on the first night, which is the primary one, since we are knowledgeable about the fixing of the month, and therefore he should fulfill the Four Cups on this first night properly (Magen Avraham, section 14). The candle for his home takes precedence over the Four Cups because of household peace, as I have written in section 263.

Women are also obligated in the four cups and in all the mitzvot related to that night, such as eating matzah and reciting the Haggadah. If they cannot recite it themselves, they should listen to the Haggadah. This is because it is written: "You shall not eat leavened bread with it; for seven days you shall eat matzot with it" – anyone who is included in the prohibition of leavened bread is included in the commandment to eat matzah. Women are included in the prohibition of leavened bread, as prohibitions apply to women just as they do to men. Therefore, they are also obligated to eat matzah, even though it is a positive time-bound commandment. Consequently, since they are obligated in matzah, they are also obligated in Pesach and maror (bitter herbs), as they are linked to each other, as it is written: "They shall eat it with matzot and maror." Even though maror nowadays is rabbinic, everything the Rabbis instituted is similar to the Torah law. As a result, they are obligated in all the mitzvot of the night, as they are all one matter. Additionally, it was in the merit of righteous women that our ancestors were redeemed from Egypt, so it is obvious that they are obligated in all the mitzvot of the night, which are all due to the redemption from Egypt.

Therefore, one must give a cup to each member of his household, both males and females. Even children who have reached the age of education – it is a mitzvah to give each one their own cup. The term "reached the age of education" refers to a child of about five or six years old (Chayei Adam, section 27). If one did not give them a cup, it does not invalidate the obligation (ibid.). One can give them a small cup (see Taz), and they only need to drink a little. Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote in section 15 that one should not use a cup with a narrow mouth like a small flask, because one cannot drink a quarter-log at once from it. For the cup of Birkas Hamazon (Grace after Meals), in any case, one should not use it, and see above in section 183, and likewise for the cup of Kiddush. See above in section 271. Up to here is his wording. For children, there is no strictness. It appears to me that although girls are generally not included in the obligation of education, on the night of Pesach they should also be educated, because the foundation of faith depends on the Exodus from Egypt. It is a mitzvah to distribute roasted grains and nuts to the children so that they see a change and ask questions. The Torah is particular about the questions of the children on this night, as I have written in section 2.

At the beginning of the order, they pour him the first cup. This pertains to their wines, and from the language of the Mishnah (Kiddushin 41a) "they pour for him" – it implies that others pour for him and not himself, as an expression of freedom. He recites the Kiddush over it, first blessing "Borei Pri HaGafen" (Creator of the fruit of the vine), and then he recites the Kiddush of the day and "Shehecheyanu" (Who has kept us alive), and he drinks the first cup. If he did not bless "Shehecheyanu" on the first night, he should bless on the second night. If he did not bless on the second night, he should bless during the entire festival even without a cup, since "Shehecheyanu" does not require a cup (Eruvin 40b). Similarly, if he blessed on the first night but did not bless "Shehecheyanu" on the second night, he should bless afterward (Magen Avraham, subsection 1), because he is obligated to bless due to the doubt of the day. However, if he did not bless on the first night but blessed on the second night, he does not need to bless again for the first night, because in any case: if the second night is a festival, then he does not need [to bless] on the first night, and if the first night is a festival, then the blessing on the second night suffices, as it is no less than the other days of the festival (Chayei Adam, subsection 1). It is obvious that if he did not bless during Kiddush and remembered afterward, he must bless at the place he remembered, even without a cup, as "Shehecheyanu" does not require a cup. Therefore, even if he does not have cups, he blesses "Shehecheyanu." If he did not recite the Haggadah on that night, there is no compensation (ibid.). Similarly, if he did not eat matzah or maror on that night, there is no compensation, as their commandments apply only on that night.

The Tur wrote: "And one does not bless 'Who performed miracles,' because he will say it later in the Haggadah." This is his language, meaning: Just as we bless on Chanukah and Purim 'Who performed miracles,' it is obvious that on Passover one should bless similarly. However, since in the Haggadah we recount the miracles and wonders, and afterwards we bless the blessing of 'Who redeemed us' – it follows that this is like the blessing of 'Who performed miracles,' and why do we need both? In any case, in my humble opinion, this is not sufficient, for in the case of the Megillah we bless at both the beginning and the end, so why should we not do the same for the Exodus from Egypt, whose miracles are greater than those of Purim?

In the name of Maharil, I have seen a reason: because it is a commandment written in the Torah, and we do not bless "Who performed miracles" except on rabbinic commandments such as Hanukkah and Purim (Perisha). At first glance, these words are not understood, but the truth is that the explanation is as follows: The Sages instituted all blessings, and a blessing is only relevant to bless the Holy One, blessed be He, who commanded us in this commandment, like eating matzah, sitting in the sukkah, or blowing the shofar. But it does not apply to making a blessing on the essence of the commandment itself. And since we are commanded by the Torah to recount the miracles on this night, which is a positive commandment, how can we bless "Who performed miracles"? For this is the essence of the commandment, and it would be like one declaration following another. And the blessing of "Who redeemed us" – its main focus is on eating matzah and maror, as we say, "and enabled us to reach this night to eat matzah and maror." But "Who performed miracles" – this is the main commandment of recounting the Exodus from Egypt, and it is only for a rabbinic commandment that they have the discretion, not for a Torah commandment. (Perisha also wrote in the name of R' Akiva because it is a day of salvation, and the miracle is superior. This is his language, but I do not understand his explanation.)

And if [Yom Tov] falls on Shabbat, one says "Vayechulu," and on Motzaei Shabbat [the conclusion of Shabbat] one says Havdalah after Kiddush while seated. Even though other Havdalot [plural of Havdalah] are said while standing, this one which is with Kiddush and in order is said while seated. And there are no spices in this Havdalah, because spices are only to rejuvenate the soul, which is necessary when Motzaei Shabbat falls on a regular weekday and not on a Yom Tov, for on Yom Tov the soul is already in its strength and there are also good foods. The text of the Havdalah is: "He who distinguishes... between the sanctity of Shabbat and the sanctity of Yom Tov, You have distinguished, and You sanctified the seventh day from the six days of work. You distinguished and sanctified Your people Israel with Your sanctity."

Rabbeinu Tam wrote in Tosafot on Pesachim (104a) the reason for extending this Havdalah: because it was taught there, "One who shortens should not shorten to less than three, and one who extends should not extend to more than seven." Therefore, due to the obligation of the day, we mention seven distinctions once, and they are: "Between holy and profane" – one, "between light and darkness" – two, "between Israel and the nations" – three, "between the seventh day and the six days of work" – four, "between the sanctity of Shabbat and the sanctity of Yom Tov, You have distinguished," as on Yom Tov food preparation is permitted – that is five, "You distinguished and sanctified Your people Israel" – two distinctions: between Israel and the tribe of Levi as it is written "At that time the Lord set apart the tribe of Levi," and between Levites and Kohanim as it is written "And Aaron was set apart to sanctify him" – that is seven.

The order of Havdalah is: YaKNeHaZ – wine, Kiddush, candle, Havdalah, time (blessing). And this is the halachic ruling in Pesachim (103a), because Kiddush precedes Havdalah, and the time blessing is always at the end. If one forgot to make Havdalah and only remembered after starting the Haggadah, he should complete the Haggadah until "Ga'al Yisrael" and then make Havdalah. Why not make Havdalah in the middle of the Haggadah? Not because it is forbidden to interrupt, but because Havdalah requires a cup, and what should he do? If he drinks, he adds to the cups, as it is initially forbidden to add even with the first two cups. If he does not drink until the second cup, there is an interruption between Havdalah and drinking the cup (Orach Chaim 18:5). And if he drinks and fulfills the obligation with the second cup, according to what we wrote in the previous section 11, certainly it is initially forbidden to do so. Therefore, he should wait until "Ga'al Yisrael," make Havdalah, and drink. What is the issue? He is not eating or drinking until then, as it is forbidden to eat or drink before Havdalah. Therefore, if he did not remember until he started eating, he should stop immediately and make Havdalah. If he intended to drink wine during the meal, he does not need to bless "Borei Pri HaGafen." If not, he needs to bless. If he forgot until after Birkat Hamazon, he should make Havdalah afterward and drink the third cup, and it will count for both. Similarly, if he did not remember until after Hallel. In the middle of Birkat Hamazon and in the middle of Hallel, he should not interrupt. Even though we do not say two sanctifications over one cup, in a case where it is impossible, it is different (see Magen Avraham 18:2).

One should not wash their hands before Kiddush at all. Even those who always wash their hands before Kiddush, as I wrote in Siman 271, in the case of Pesach it is impossible because it would cause a significant interruption in the recitation of the Haggadah, and one is compelled to wash their hands before the meal. And even though here one needs to wash immediately for the dipping of the Karpas, why not wash before Kiddush? However, this too is impossible, for anyone seeing it would say that washing is required for Kiddush. And truly it is not so, for throughout the year everyone knows that the washing is for the meal, but on Pesach it is not evident that it is for the dipping. And even if his hands are not clean, he should wash a little. If it happens that one washed their hands before Kiddush, they should not wash again for the dipping (Rashal). Some say he should wash (Bach), but the primary opinion follows the first view (Magen Avraham, Siman Katan 3, see also Taz, Siman Katan 1. Study and you will find it easy). And know that when one's hands are not clean, we wrote to wash a little, but one does not recite the blessing "Al Netilat Yadayim". And we already wrote that the head of the household should not pour the wine himself but someone else, as this is the way of freedom. However, we are not particular about this, because it seems arrogant to command one's wife to pour, and the husband is not superior to her. Therefore, the custom is for one to pour themselves, and this is not a strict matter.

And after the Kiddush, one drinks the cup while reclining. No blessing is recited afterward, as we rely on the final blessing after Hallel; since they are all one matter, why should we increase blessings unnecessarily? Additionally, no blessing is needed for the second cup. The reasons for our blessings will be explained in Siman 474. If one drank without reclining, the Tur rules that he should drink another cup while reclining. We discussed this in the previous Siman, refer to it there. If one wishes to drink several cups, he is permitted to do so, as it is taught (Pesachim 117b): "Between these cups, if one wants to drink, he may drink; but between the third and fourth cups, he should not drink." The Jerusalem Talmud explains the reason: so that he does not become intoxicated. However, wine before the meal does not cause intoxication. The Tur wrote that one should have in mind not to need to bless again, so it does not appear as though he is adding to the cups. This is his language: for any situation that requires a blessing constitutes adding. Thus, for us, who bless over each and every cup, it is prohibited to add. The Tur and Shulchan Aruch follow their approach that no blessing is needed for the second cup, as I will write in the next Siman, and not for us. Therefore, for us, there is no permission to drink between the first and second cups unless one had the intention to drink. (Chayei Adam, small section 10). Rabbi Yosef Karo also wrote in section 3 that in any case, it is proper to be cautious not to drink between the first and second cups unless there is a great need, so that one does not become intoxicated and refrain from conducting the Seder and reading the Haggadah. This is his language. Even though wine before the meal does not cause intoxication, this applies to them, but not to us, as our strengths are weaker. Other non-intoxicating beverages should also be avoided. Only water when thirsty seems to me to be permissible, and no blessing is needed, as wine exempts all kinds of beverages. (This seems to me in my humble opinion. Refer to Chayei Adam, small section 11).

Know that the opinion of the Rif, the Rambam, and the Rashba is that only two matzot are needed on the Seder plate. When one is broken, one remains broken and one remains whole. We do not find in the Gemara that three matzot are required. And in the Yerushalmi "Erev Pesachim," as brought by the Or Zarua (Siman 252), it is also so. It also seems this way in Berachot (39b) which states that on Pesach one places the broken piece within the whole one and breaks it, implying that there is only one whole matzah. The Ba'al Halachot Gedolot (BaHaG) distinguishes between Shabbat and weekday, stating that when Pesach falls on Shabbat, three are needed. But the Rosh in "Erev Pesachim" (Siman 30) disagrees and says: "Is Pesach worse than other festivals that require two loaves?" The Tosafot also write this, as does the Or Zarua in the name of the Rashbam. This is in remembrance of the loaves of the thanksgiving offering, which were brought as three loaves from one issaron (measure of flour). Therefore, three matzot are needed for the Seder, and this is the custom of the world.

And they bring before the head of the household a plate with three matzot, maror (bitter herbs), charoset (a mixture of fruits and nuts), karpas (a vegetable, usually parsley or celery) or another vegetable, vinegar or salt water, and two cooked dishes—one in remembrance of the Passover offering and one in remembrance of the festal offering. The common custom is to use meat and an egg. It is appropriate for the meat to be from the forearm, specifically from the arm if possible, in remembrance of the "outstretched arm." However, we are not accustomed to this because it is difficult to obtain, so we take meat with a bone. Our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 4 that the custom is for the meat to be roasted over coals and the egg to be boiled. Our master, the Rema, wrote: "It is also permissible to roast it," and so is the custom in our city. Thus far is his wording. According to this, it would be forbidden to eat the meat at night because roasted meat is not eaten at night. The reason appears to be that the meat is in remembrance of the Passover offering, which is only eaten roasted, so the meat is also roasted. The egg is in remembrance of the festal offering, which is eaten boiled, so the egg is also boiled. The custom of also roasting the egg could be because Ben Teima held that the festal offering is also only eaten roasted. Some have written that it is preferable to cook both the meat and the egg so that they can be eaten at night. If they are left for the second day, they might spoil if roasted on the first night, as one festival day does not prepare for the next. However, a roasted egg is still permitted. In our community, the custom is to cook both the meat and the egg. The reason for choosing the egg instead of the festal offering is because we are accustomed to eating eggs at the Seder. (See Magen Avraham, small section 8, and Taz, small section 4.)

And for Karpas, we customarily take onions, or radishes, or any type of vegetable whose blessing is "Borei Pri Ha'adama" (the Creator of the fruit of the ground), or potatoes. The later authorities mentioned that it became customary to take "petrushka" (parsley), though we do not know what it is. The concept of Karpas serves as a remembrance for the hard labor (avodat perech) that six hundred thousand (Jews) endured, as "Karpas" consists of the letters "sixty perech" (sixty times ten thousand). Concerning the salt water, if Passover falls on Shabbat, it should be prepared before Shabbat, as it is forbidden to make salt water on Shabbat, as I wrote in Siman 321. However, it has been clarified that anything needed for that meal is permitted. Therefore, if it was not prepared on the day before, it may be made on Shabbat, but not in large quantities.

He should arrange the Seder plate before him in a manner that he does not need to pass over any mitzvot, meaning: the karpas should be closest to him, as this is needed first. The salt water should also be closer than the matzah. However, in our custom, we do not place the salt water on the Seder plate. The matzah should be closer than the maror, because eating the matzah precedes the maror. The charoset and the other items should be closer than the meat and the egg, which are only eaten in the middle of the meal. Our custom is to arrange on the Seder plate: the shank bone on the upper right, the egg opposite it on the left, and the maror in the middle, lower than them. Lower on the plate: the charoset on the right, the karpas slightly lower on the left, and the maror used for the "korech" in the middle. This is in accordance with the wisdom of Kabbalah, as explained in "Pri Etz Chaim."

The Sages taught in the Mishnah (Pesachim 39a): These are the vegetables with which a person can fulfill their obligation on Pesach: with lettuce, with tamcha, with harhavina, with chervil, and with bitter herbs.

"Lettuce" is commonly explained to be salad, as the translator in the Arukh interpreted under the entry "chazer." And in the Gemara, they said: What is chazer? Lettuce. In the entry "chas" the translator explained it as lettuce (latich), see there.

"Tamcha" is commonly interpreted to be either kress or horseradish. In the Arukh, it is translated as ein paplanca, but I do not know what this name refers to.

"Harhavina," I do not know, and in the Arukh it is explained as a type of bitter herb. In the Gemara, they said: It is the tender part of the palm tree, and Rashi explained it as a fiber that grows and wraps around the palm tree. The Arukh also explained it this way, and it must be said that it is a bitter herb that wraps around the palm tree (see Tosafot there). And in the name of Rav Hai Gaon, it was explained: It is a very thick plant with needle-like points, see there.

"Chervil" is explained in the Gemara as hindiva. The Arukh explained it in a foreign language that we do not know. However, it is not the same foreign language as Rashi, and perhaps they are two different languages.

"Bitter herbs" are explained in the Gemara as merirata. Rashi explained it in a foreign language, but we do not know its meaning, and I did not find it in the Arukh. The Ra'avad explained: It is a type of coriander, and it is very bitter. We do not know what this is, and I also did not find coriander in the Arukh.

Anything mentioned first in the Mishnah takes precedence over what comes after it. Therefore, lettuce takes precedence over everything else. And thus it is stated in the Gemara there: "It is a mitzvah with lettuce." What is "lettuce"? It is "chasa." What is "chasa"? It means that the Merciful One has compassion on us. And therefore, even though it does not have bitterness, it is still more of a mitzvah. After it comes chicory, and so on in order. And in our country, they take chicory because lettuce is not commonly available before Passover, except in the gardens of the noblemen. And our teacher, the Rema, wrote in section 5 that if one does not have any of these vegetables, he should take wormwood or any other bitter herb. This is his language. And it seems that he holds that what we learned in the Mishnah "and with bitter herbs," and the Gemara explains "marirta," means any type of bitter herb. And there are those who believe that "marirta" specifically refers to wormwood and not any other bitter herb. Therefore, any other bitter herb should be eaten without a blessing. And this is how one should act (see Magen Avraham, subsection 15, and Chayei Adam, subsection 24). And "wormwood" – they wrote that this is what is called "vermit." And a Jew should not uproot the bitter herb from the ground himself, as it might be from stolen land. Rather, a non-Jew should uproot it, and he should take it from him, as this would constitute both abandonment and a change of domain. And see further in section 489 (see Magen Avraham, subsection 14).

These five species combine to make up a kezayit. Therefore, it is common to take a little bit of horseradish with a little bit of tamcha (a type of bitter herb), as it is good to eat them together. When the combined amount reaches a kezayit, one fulfills their obligation. One can fulfill the obligation with any of these, whether it is their leaves or their stalks, but not with the roots, meaning the small roots that branch off here and there. However, the main root from which the leaves grow, even though it is buried in the ground, is considered part of the stalk. Nevertheless, it is better to take the leaves and the stalk that is above ground, since some say that what is buried in the ground is called "root." However, the primary opinion follows the first view (see the opinion of the Gaon Rabbi Zalman, section 28).

Know that there is someone who wanted to say that tamcha, which is called "green," can only be used if eaten whole as it is, and not when it is grated finely, as it is usually eaten with meat. This is a strange thing to say, for on the contrary, its primary way of being eaten is when it is grated, and eating it as it is whole is dangerous, as is known. And this has been the custom of all the great sages. For someone who finds it difficult to eat tamcha because of a weak heart, it is necessary to seek out horseradish, even if it will be expensive. However, one can take the leaves from the tamcha, which are only slightly bitter, as one can fulfill the obligation with leaves as explained. Someone who is ill and cannot eat maror (bitter herbs) should not eat it. We maintain that matzah in our time is a Torah obligation, while maror is rabbinical (Pesachim 120a). For it is written: "They shall eat it with matzot and maror," meaning when there is a Pesach offering, there is maror; when there is no Pesach offering, there is no maror. And if you question: should this not apply to matzah as well? The Torah repeats regarding matzah, "In the evening, you shall eat matzot," even when there is no Pesach offering (ibid).

Leaves can only be used if they are fresh, but not if they are wilted, which is referred to as "tzvielat," and certainly not if they are dry. However, stalks can be used whether they are fresh or dry, and certainly if they are wilted, because since the stalk is thick, its bitter taste is not ruined by drying. But one cannot use a cooked stalk, because cooking completely ruins the bitter taste. And even though lettuce has no bitterness at all, that is because its nature is such. But this, which has bitterness, when its bitterness is ruined—it is no longer maror, because it has changed from its original state. And pickled is like cooked, and one cannot use it. There are two types of pickling: one is pickling in vinegar and brine. The time for this pickling is short, just the amount of time it takes to place it on the fire and start boiling. The second is pickling in water. This pickling requires "a day and a night." Therefore, one must be careful not to leave horseradish in water for a day and a night. Some are pressured to say that horseradish, even if soaked for a day and a night, does not change. This is not the main opinion. Anything soaked for a day and a night cannot be used, and this is agreed upon by the great authorities. (Magen Avraham, small section 14, and Chayei Adam, small section 20, see there where he struggles to justify the custom. His words are strained, and one can remove them before the "day and a night." And see what the Alter Rebbe wrote in section 29. Pay close attention and you will find it easy.)

All the laws that apply to matzah also apply to maror. Therefore, one fulfills the obligation with demai, with first tithe from which the terumah has been taken, and with second tithe and consecrated items that have been redeemed; all as explained in Siman 453. And everything that is explained there regarding what one does not fulfill the obligation with matzah, one also does not fulfill the obligation with maror. And even though matzah is a Torah obligation and maror is Rabbinic, whatever the Rabbis instituted, they instituted in a manner similar to the Torah law, as stated in the Gemara (Pesachim 39b). 

And one should not wonder about the fact that the primary mitzvah is with chazeret (lettuce), and it does not have bitterness, and the Torah said "bitter herbs." However, in truth, the name "maror" includes two aspects: the bitterness of the taste and the toughness, which ultimately becomes hard. The hard labor in Egypt began soft and ended hard, as Rashi explains in the Chumash. And chazeret starts soft and ends hard; therefore, it is the primary form of maror. And this is the intention of the Talmud there (Pesachim 39a, see there, examine, and you will find it easy).

Charoset should be thick, in remembrance of the mortar with which our ancestors were enslaved in Egypt, as it is written: "with mortar and with bricks." Afterwards, it should be softened with liquid, in remembrance of the blood that the Egyptians spilled from Israel, as it is written: "Every boy that is born, you shall throw into the river." And they would also place children in the building, as explained in the legends. The charoset should be made from fruits to which Israel is compared: fig, nut, dates, and pomegranates. And for us, who do not eat dried fruits, we make it from nuts and almonds, in reference to the verse "The LORD watches over the end to perform it." And from apples, in reference to "Under the apple tree I roused you," where they would give birth to their children, as it is stated in the first chapter of Sotah (11b). Something sharp like wine or vinegar should be added, in remembrance of the enslavement which caused the teeth of Israel to become dull from the severity of the enslavement. Spices resembling straw, such as cinnamon and ginger which are called zimring and ingber; which are not ground well and remain somewhat long after grinding, should be added, in remembrance of the straw that was not given to us, as it is written in the Torah. If Passover falls on Shabbat, the charoset should be softened before the day begins, for on Shabbat it is forbidden because it resembles kneading. If it was not softened before the day began, liquid should be added to it, but it should not be mixed with a spoon. And even then, the liquid should be added first.

And after he sanctifies (makes Kiddush) – he washes his hands for the purpose of the first dipping, but he does not recite the blessing “Al Netilat Yadayim” (on the washing of the hands). Even one who is not careful throughout the year to wash his hands for dipping in liquid – on Passover he should wash his hands, for we perform many changes on this night. The purpose of the dipping is so that the children will ask why we dip before eating, which is not the usual practice. For it has already been explained that the Torah emphasizes the children's questions on this night.

He should take a piece of karpas that is less than the size of an olive, dip it in vinegar or salt water, and recite the blessing “Borei Pri Ha'adama” (Who creates the fruit of the ground). He should have in mind with this blessing to also cover the maror (bitter herb), even though according to the basic law, the maror does not require a blessing because it is eaten during the meal and must be eaten – it is considered like things that come during the meal that do not require a blessing. Nevertheless, he should have the intention to cover the maror with this blessing, because perhaps since the maror is for the mitzvah and not for the purpose of eating, it is not like things that come because of the meal.

And that which we wrote that one should not eat an olive's size (kazayit), the reason is so that one does not come to the obligation of the after-blessing. For there are those who say that if one eats an olive's size, he must say an after-blessing. And this is not similar to an appetizer before the meal, for which the Grace after Meals covers it, because here there is a significant interruption with the recitation of the Haggadah. And there are those who say that he does not need to bless, for the Haggadah is not considered an interruption since it pertains to the Seder. Therefore, one should not initially eat an olive's size. But if he did eat, he should not say an after-blessing, because in cases of doubt regarding blessings, we are lenient. And the Rambam wrote in the eighth chapter that one should eat an olive's size, and all those reclining should eat an olive's size each, for a meal is not less than an olive's size (Magid Mishneh). And the Tur and other early authorities argued against him, for since this dipping is only for recognition, why is an olive's size necessary? Additionally, the Rambam wrote that this dipping is in charoset. And the Tur wrote that it does not need charoset, and our custom is like the Tur.

After the dipping, one takes the middle matzah and breaks it into two, giving half to another person to guard for the Afikoman. Our custom is to place it under the cushions of the reclining, as a remembrance of "their kneading troughs bound up in their clothes upon their shoulders." Therefore, some people lift the half of the Afikoman onto their shoulder for a moment. The other half should be placed between the two whole matzot. One then lifts the Seder plate containing the matzot, or just the matzot alone, and recites "Ha Lachma Anya" until "Ma Nishtana." The primary version of the text is "Ha Lachma," as I have written. It should be said in a language understood by the women and children, or the matter should be explained to them. This was the practice of the great ones. Nowadays, with the proliferation of printings and the Haggadah being printed in the vernacular, and since all our women and children read on their own, it is not customary to explain it to them because they know how to read and understand the matter of the Exodus from Egypt on their own.

After reciting "Ha Lachma Anya," the matzah should be removed from the table. This follows their custom, where they had small tables and would remove the table. Nowadays, we cover the bread with a cloth, which serves the same purpose as removing the table. This is also done so the children will see and ask, "Why are they removing the table? We haven't eaten yet!" Immediately, the second cup is poured so the child will ask, "Why are they pouring a second cup? We haven't eaten yet!" Nowadays, this question is not commonly asked; instead, they ask, "What is different?" The phrase "What is different" is similar to the expressions "How great are Your works, O Lord!" and "How goodly are your tents, O Jacob!" – in a manner of amazement. Here too, we are amazed: "How great are the changes on this night!"

In the Mishnah, there is a question about roasted food, but not about reclining, because they ate the Passover sacrifice and were always accustomed to reclining. Now, there is no question about roasted food, but there is a question about reclining because we are not always accustomed to reclining. If the son does not have the wisdom to ask, his father teaches him to ask. If he does not have a son, the daughter should ask. If he does not have a daughter, his wife should ask, or another person sitting at the table should ask him. The Torah insists that the remembrance of the Exodus from Egypt on this night should be through question and answer. However, if there is no one to ask, he should ask and answer himself. When there is someone to ask, he does not need to say "What is different," but begins with "We were slaves." (And he should not say "This night is all bitter herbs," but rather "This night is bitter herbs.")

When the questioner finishes saying "Mah Nishtanah," the matzah is uncovered, and "Avadim Hayinu" is recited aloud with enthusiasm, joy, and happiness. The primary essence of reciting the Haggadah is that through the Exodus from Egypt, we became eternally subjugated to God and His Torah for all generations, and we are His servants. This is a legal principle, for a free person cannot be made a servant against his will, but one who was already a servant to someone and was then acquired by another to be his servant does not require the servant's consent and can be acquired against his will, as explained in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 267. 

Now that we were servants to Pharaoh, and the Holy One, blessed be He, redeemed us from his hand, we are consequently His servants against our will. This is what the scripture says: "For the children of Israel are servants to Me; they are My servants whom I brought out of the land of Egypt." Meaning, the children of Israel are servants to Me against their will because I brought them out of Egypt, where they were servants. Therefore, in every generation, one is obligated to see himself as if he personally came out of Egypt and was acquired by the Holy One, blessed be He, as an eternal servant, and he is not permitted to cast off the yoke of the Torah from his neck. 

A proof is brought from the verse "because of this, God did for me...," which applies to every generation. Since someone who wishes to be obstinate might say that it only applies to the generation that left Egypt, as the wicked son's question implies, "What is this service to you?" meaning, you did not leave Egypt. Therefore, a proof is brought from the verse "and He brought us out from there," which concludes "to give us the land," although all those who left Egypt died in the wilderness. It is certain, then, that it applies to every generation. (And this is what Rava said in the Gemara, Pesachim 116b: one must say "and He brought us out from there." Analyze and you will find it accurate.)

When reaching "this matzah" – one should lift the matzah. The main piece to lift is the broken one, as it represents the "bread of affliction," to show it to those present, so that the mitzvah becomes cherished by them. Similarly, when reaching "this maror" – one should lift the maror. However, for the Pesach offering – one should not lift the shank bone, so it does not appear as if consecrating it for the Pesach offering. When reaching "therefore" – each person lifts their cup in hand until they reach "redeemed Israel." Among us, we place the cup on the table when reaching Hallel, and afterward, during the blessing, we hold it in hand until "redeemed Israel." Similarly, when saying "and it is this that has stood," one holds the cup in hand. The idea is that whenever mentioning salvation – one lifts the cup, as in "I will lift the cup of salvation, and call upon the name of the Lord." For all joys are on wine, as it is written: "And wine makes...". There is also a deep matter related to our pure faith, as it is written: "The Lord is God," and "God" has the numerical value of "nature." The explanation is: even our nature is not natural, but under the providence of the blessed Name. This is a significant principle, as is evident. And "cup" has the numerical value of "God." When lifting the cup – the bread should be covered so it does not see its shame, as in Kiddush. But during the telling of the Haggadah – the bread should be uncovered to show the "bread of affliction."

And when one reaches "Blood, fire, and pillars of smoke," it is customary to throw a little from the cup with a finger, referring to "the finger of God." Likewise, during the Ten Plagues, and similarly at "Detzach, Adash, Beachav." Altogether, there are sixteen spillings, and there is a mystical explanation for this. Some people are accustomed to pouring from the cup itself. Some use the fourth finger, which is called the ring finger. Others use the fifth finger, known as the pinky (see Magen Avraham, subsection 28). Whichever way one does it, it is acceptable.

In the Haggadah, when saying "You might think from Rosh Chodesh" – one should first say "And you shall tell your son," because this verse refers to it as explained in the Mekhilta. Also, one should not say "corresponding to four sons…" but rather "against four sons," as it is a separate matter and does not refer to the previous statement. One should say "and we shall say before Him a new song" with a segol under the nun, because it refers to the past event of the Exodus from Egypt (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 27). One should say "from the sacrifices and from the Passover offerings," because the festival offering precedes the Passover offering, as the Passover offering is eaten when one is already satiated. On the night after Shabbat, one should first say "from the Passover offerings," because the festival offering does not override Shabbat. Some want to say that it refers to the previous year, but this is incorrect, as we have explained in the commentary on the Haggadah with the help of Heaven.

And they divide the Hallel: part of it before eating, and part of it after eating, because we do not recite a blessing over the Hallel. Therefore, we say part of it beforehand, so that the blessing of "Who has redeemed us" also covers the Hallel. And how much is said before the meal? Until "to the one who turns the rock into a pool of water" (Psalms 114:8). The Tosefta explains the reason, and we have elucidated it with Divine assistance in the commentary on the Haggadah. Some have the custom to recite the Hallel in the synagogue according to the Jerusalem Talmud, and it is a good custom. Therefore, they do not recite a blessing over the Hallel at the meal, because they have already blessed in the synagogue. And we, who do not say Hallel in the synagogue, should technically bless the Hallel at the meal, but it is not customary to do so. And this Hallel is said while sitting, even though in the synagogue it is recited while standing.

Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote: One drinks the second cup, and does not recite a blessing over it, neither the initial blessing nor the concluding blessing, because we only recite "Borei Pri HaGafen" over the cup of Kiddush and the cup of Birkat Hamazon. And we only recite "Al HaGefen" after the fourth cup. Thus far his words, for he holds that the Haggadah and Hallel are not considered an interruption. Therefore, the blessing of Kiddush exempts the second cup from a blessing, and the blessing on the third cup, which is the cup of Birkat Hamazon, exempts the fourth cup from a blessing. And why do we not recite a concluding blessing over the second cup? Because it is wine that precedes the meal, and it exempts the wine within the meal, and Birkat Hamazon exempts it from a concluding blessing as it does all year round, as I wrote in Siman 174 (refer to Ba'al HaMaor and Milchamot).

However, our Rabbi the Rema wrote: "The custom among the Ashkenazim is to recite the initial blessing on each and every cup. But the final blessing is only recited after the last one alone. And this is also the opinion of most of the Geonim." Thus are his words. And he holds that the Haggadah and Hallel constitute an interruption. And even though, if so, why not recite the final blessing on the first and the third, since they are not related to each other? Rather, by necessity, one must say that it is not an interruption. If so, why is an initial blessing needed on the second and the fourth? They resolved that since these four cups were instituted by the Sages to be drunk in a manner of freedom, and each one is a mitzvah in its own right; therefore, they do not join together to be exempted by one blessing, but rather a blessing is required on each one individually (Magen Avraham). And this is not sufficient. And some added to say that it is as if one stipulated on each cup that it would not exempt any but itself (Taz). And this is even more puzzling, for where do we get this condition?

In my humble opinion, it seems: Behold, in the Maharil it is written that one must recite a blessing over each and every cup, even though the Rosh ruled that one should not bless. The Tosafot ruled that one should recite a blessing, and it is forbidden to benefit without a blessing, and a doubtful prohibition should be treated stringently. Thus far his words, and it is not understood at all: on the contrary, doubtful blessings are treated leniently (and the Chayei Adam already questioned him and remained in wonderment, see there). Therefore, it seems to me that the explanation is as follows: Behold, it is certain that there is doubt whether the Haggadah constitutes an interruption or not, which is why we ruled in the previous section regarding Karpas that one should not eat an olive-sized portion. And if he ate – he should not recite a final blessing because doubtful blessings are treated leniently, as I wrote there. If so, it is obvious that he should not recite a final blessing. But if so, why should he drink? Out of doubt, he should neither drink nor bless, and why should he enter into the doubt of benefiting without a blessing? Rather, what can you say, that he is compelled to drink due to the mitzvah of the Sages who instituted four cups. If so, how can we tell a person to drink when it is a doubtful prohibition? And behold, he can say: I do not want to enter into a doubtful prohibition, to benefit without a blessing! Rather, we say to him: drink and bless, and it turns out that we permit him to bless. Consequently, according to the Sages' ordinance – it is necessary that the intent was not to exempt the second cup from the initial blessing. But regarding the final blessing, since there is doubt – doubtful blessings are treated leniently.

And after he drinks the second cup, he should wash his hands and bless "Al Netilat Yadayim" (on the washing of the hands). And even though he already washed his hands for dipping, since he interrupted with the Haggadah, we are concerned that perhaps he became distracted and touched an unclean place (Talmud Pesachim 115b). And if not for this reason, the first washing would have sufficed. And even though the first washing was not for sanctity, but rather so that he would not render the liquids impure, nevertheless it would have sufficed, as we hold that washing does not require intent (Tosafot there). And according to this, if he intended with the first washing to cover the entire meal without distraction, and he blessed "Al Netilat Yadayim" and kept his hands clean, he does not need a second washing (see Magen Avraham, subsection 1).

Our master, the Beit Yosef, in his great book, was not pleased with this, and this is his language: "It seems to me that one should not intend for this, so as not to nullify the enactment of the Sages who instituted washing the hands twice on this night." Thus far is his language. And they challenged him: Where did the Sages institute this? For they explained the reason as perhaps he diverted his attention, and if he did not divert his attention, he does not need a second washing (Magen Avraham there and Bach). And it appears to me that the principal is as the words of our master, the Beit Yosef, that since the law was decided in the Gemara there that a second hand washing is necessary, even though the reason is due to the concern of diverting attention, nevertheless, the Sages instituted it as such. And on the night of Passover, we are particular not to deviate from all that they have instructed us. And who knows how many other reasons there are for this. And so is the custom, and it should not be changed.

The Tur brings two opinions: Some say that on the whole matzah one blesses "Hamotzi" as on any other Yom Tov, and on the broken piece one blesses "Al Achilat Matzah" because it is "bread of affliction." Others say the opposite—that "Hamotzi" is recited on the broken piece, as this is the distinction on Pesach. Consequently, "Al Achilat Matzah" must be on the whole piece, because it is not possible to recite two blessings on one piece of matzah, as we do not perform mitzvot in bundles. Therefore, to fulfill all opinions, one should hold both. As our teacher the Beit Yosef wrote, one should take the matzot in the order he placed them, with the broken piece between the two whole ones, and hold them in his hand and bless "Hamotzi" and "Al Achilat Matzah." Then he should break from the top whole matzah and from the broken one, from both together, dip them in salt, and eat them together, reclining, a kezayit from each. If he cannot eat two kezaytim together, he should eat the one for "Hamotzi" first, and then the one for "Al Achilat Matzah." Thus far is his language. It is not understood why he says "eat the one for Hamotzi first," for how can he know which is for Hamotzi? He is holding both together due to the doubt, as I have written (see Taz, subsection 3, who raised this question). It seems to me that fundamentally we hold that "Hamotzi" is on the whole matzah and "Al Achilat Matzah" on the broken piece, as this is the opinion of the majority of poskim; however, out of respect for the other opinion, we hold both.

We have heard from the words of our master, the Beit Yosef, that the enhancement of the mitzvah is to swallow both olive-sized portions together, and at the very least, one olive-sized portion at once. And even though it combines within the time span of eating a half-loaf, nevertheless, the primary mitzvah is indeed like this. And this is what he wrote in section 6: If one ate half an olive-sized portion, and then ate another half an olive-sized portion, he has fulfilled his obligation, provided that he did not delay between the two eatings more than the span of time it takes to eat a half-loaf. Thus far his words, meaning: he should not delay from the start of eating to the end of eating more than the time span of eating a half-loaf. Nevertheless, we do not find that the early authorities required this, to eat it all at once. And the Maharil explicitly wrote that one can eat little by little, provided that he does not delay more than the time span of eating a half-loaf. And I have seen someone write that section 6 contradicts this (Magen Avraham, subsection 4). But it seems to me that these are unrelated matters. For in section 6, it discusses where one eats half an olive-sized portion and pauses, and this is certainly not ideal from the outset. But if one eats consecutively, where do we find that he must eat it all at once? (And what the Magen Avraham wrote from the end of the chapter "Gid HaNasheh" – I am puzzled. For there it concerns the prohibition of eating a limb from a living animal, where a complete limb is required, see there. Nevertheless, since it was stated by our master, the Beit Yosef, one should be careful if possible to do so.)

Some have questioned why it is necessary to have an olive's worth (k’zayit) of the “Hamotzi” blessing. If it were for the mitzvah of eating matzah, its requirement is only a k’zayit, for eating is not considered less than a k’zayit. But for “Hamotzi,” do we require an olive's worth for every “Hamotzi” blessing (Beit Yosef)? It was explained in Siman 210 that it is not necessary to have a k’zayit. However, in truth, there is no difficulty at all, for from the Torah one fulfills the obligation of matzah with whichever matzah one eats. It is only due to beautifying the mitzvah that we say this piece is for “Hamotzi” and that piece is for the obligation of eating matzah. Therefore, it follows that with the first eating, one fulfills the obligation, and thus it is necessary to eat a k’zayit. Afterwards, when eating the second piece with the intention for the obligation of eating matzah, one must also eat a k’zayit from it according to one's intention, as established by our Sages. Therefore, it is necessary to have two k’zayitim. (The Taz in section 2 labored over this, but according to what I have written, it is straightforward and simple.)

Regarding what our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote about dipping in salt, our teacher, the Rema, wrote that the custom is not to dip it in salt on the first night, since clean bread (matzah) does not require salt. These are his words. And not only on the first night, but the same applies to the second night (Chayei Adam section 4). Rather, his intention is for the obligation of matzah on the first night, and for us, it applies to both nights due to the uncertainty of the day. The reason for not using salt is because we customarily dip even clean bread in salt, but this is due to the love of the mitzvah (Maharil). That is, we cherish the mitzvah of matzah and do not want to mix anything else with it. The Levush wrote that the reason is because of “bread of affliction.” I do not understand: does a poor person eat without salt? It seems to me that now we dip it in salt because it tastes better and this is an enhancement of the mitzvah. The Rambam wrote to dip it in charoset, and others disagreed with him, and the custom is not to do so.

Then, he should take an olive-sized portion of maror (bitter herb) and dip it entirely in charoset (a sweet paste), because there is a kind of venom in the maror, and the charoset nullifies it. However, he should not leave the maror in the charoset for too long, so that the bitterness of the maror is not nullified. For this reason, he should shake off the charoset from it. He should recite the blessing "on eating the maror" and eat it without reclining, because it is a remembrance of affliction, and reclining "like free people" is not appropriate. If he ate it while reclining, he has fulfilled his obligation. 

Since there is a dispute in the Gemara, Hillel holds that one must wrap the matzah together with the maror and eat them as one. They do not nullify each other, for even according to the opinion that prohibitions nullify each other, as I wrote in Yoreh De'ah, Chapter 98, commandments do not nullify each other. However, even according to Hillel, this is only in the time of the Temple, when both were of biblical origin. But in our time, when matzah is of biblical origin and maror is rabbinic, the rabbinic maror comes and nullifies the biblical matzah (Pesachim 115a).

Therefore, we first eat matzah alone, and maror alone. Afterwards, we take the third matzah in order to fulfill the mitzvah, and place the maror between the matzah, wrap them together, and eat them while reclining. We say, "This is in remembrance of the Temple according to Hillel." There is a question about this: Why do we eat maror by itself first? Let us eat the matzah, which is a Torah commandment, and then wrap the matzah and maror together; since both are rabbinic, they do not nullify each other. Just as when both are Torah commandments they do not nullify each other, so too when both are rabbinic. Why then do we eat maror by itself?

The answer to this is: Certainly, Hillel could do so. But we are uncertain in the Gemara there whom the halacha follows, and perhaps the halacha is according to the Rabbis that wrapping is not required. If so, the matzah in the wrapping would be optional and not a mitzvah, and the optional matzah would nullify the maror of the mitzvah (as per Tosafot there, starting with "Ela").

And know that regarding what was explained about needing to eat them wrapped and reclining, our master the Beit Yosef wrote that it should be dipped in charoset. And our master the Rema wrote: "And some say not to dip it." And so it is in Minhagim, and so I have seen practiced. Thus far his words. And it is not understood: for the charoset is because of the poison, and how is it possible not to dip it in charoset? And indeed, all the later authorities disagree with him and hold that it must be dipped in charoset. And so we practice. And the reason is not understood, and it must be said that he holds that the matzah nullifies the poison. And we do not bless "Borei Pri Ha'adama" on the maror, because this is something that comes due to the meal. Additionally, the blessing "Ha'adama" on the karpas exempts it, as I wrote in Siman 473. And one must be careful not to interrupt with speech about matters not related to the meal until the wrapping is eaten, so that the blessing "Al Achilat Matzah" and the blessing "Al Achilat Maror" also apply to this wrapping. Since for Hillel the main mitzvah was so, one must bless. However, if one spoke, one does not need to bless again, for we are uncertain as to whom the law follows. Additionally, even according to Hillel, this is only in the time of the Temple and not at the present time, for the obligation of maror is not from the Torah at this time, and the maror would nullify the matzah as I wrote. (See Taz, small section 7, and it requires investigation. Be precise and you will find ease.)

And this is the language of the Rambam in Chapter Eight, Law 6: Afterwards, he blesses "on the washing of the hands"... Afterwards, he wraps matzah and maror together, dips them in charoset, and blesses "Blessed... who sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us concerning the eating of matzah and bitter herbs," and eats them. If he ate matzah by itself and maror by itself, he blesses on this one separately and on that one separately. Afterwards, he blesses "Blessed... who sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us concerning the eating of the sacrificial offering," and eats from the meat of the fourteenth's festive offering first. And he blesses "Blessed... who sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us concerning the eating of the Passover offering," and eats from the body of the Passover offering. The blessing of the Passover offering does not exempt the festive offering, and the blessing of the festive offering does not exempt the Passover offering. And in this time, when there is no offering, after he blesses "Hamotzi," he blesses "on the eating of matzah," dips the matzah in charoset, and eats. And he blesses "on the eating of maror," dips in charoset, and eats... and this is a commandment from the words of the Sages. And he returns and wraps matzah and maror, dips in charoset, and eats them without a blessing, as a remembrance of the Temple. Up to here is his language.

And all his words are not understood at all. Firstly, during the time of the Temple, it was necessary to have all three together: the Paschal lamb, matzah, and maror, as it is written: "They shall eat it with matzot and bitter herbs." Furthermore, according to whom is he ruling? If like Hillel, how can one fulfill the obligation by eating them separately? And if according to the Rabbis, although we might say that even according to the Rabbis one fulfills the obligation with a wrap, as implied by the language of the Gemara there, nonetheless, the main principle is that each should be eaten separately. And this is proven in Zevachim (79a), see there. Additionally, it is difficult: if he rules according to Hillel, why do we need to eat the maror separately in our times, as I have written in Section 7? (See Lechem Mishneh and the commentator, and they did not resolve his words.)

And it seems to me, in my humble opinion, that his words are based on the Yerushalmi in the first chapter of Challah, where it states: Hillel the Elder used to wrap all three together. Rabbi Yochanan said: They disagree with Hillel the Elder. And it questions: But Rabbi Yochanan wraps matzah and maror? And it answers: Here [it refers to] during the time of the Temple, and here [it refers to] not during the time of the Temple. And even if you say both are during the time of the Temple, two things overpower one and cancel it out. Thus far is the language of the Yerushalmi. And this is its explanation: It initially resolves that during the time of the Temple they cancel each other out, since all are from the Torah. And not during the time of the Temple, since maror is not from the Torah—it does not cancel out. And this is the opposite of the reasoning of our Talmud. Therefore, it says: And even if you say both are during the time of the Temple—it is specifically wrapping all three together that is forbidden, as two things overpower one and cancel it out. But two together—the one does not cancel out the other. And it interprets "on matzot and bitter herbs they shall eat it"—that the matzah should be wrapped with the maror and not with the Pesach. Therefore, the Rambam ruled according to Rabbi Yochanan, who holds that the disagreement with Hillel is only regarding wrapping all three together, and not two. And he ruled according to the Rabbis in line with Rabbi Yochanan. And in our time, he ruled according to our Talmud, that the Rabbinic commandment comes and cancels the Torah commandment. Therefore, one must first eat each one separately, and afterward together in a wrap. (And this is the opinion of Tosafot; and also, the sugya in the Talmud there will be well explained, see there. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

If he does not have vegetables for the first dipping except for maror (bitter herbs), he should recite over it during the first dipping "Who creates the fruit of the ground" and "Concerning the eating of maror." During the second dipping, he should dip it in charoset and eat it without a blessing. How could he possibly recite a blessing when he has already filled his stomach with it? Therefore, it is necessary to bless beforehand "Concerning the eating of maror," even though the main mitzvah (commandment) is after the matzah. He does not need a concluding blessing. Since he has already recited "Concerning the eating of maror," he has definitely fulfilled his obligation. Even though it is written "with matzot and bitter herbs," it is not an impediment if the maror is eaten first (Tosafot Kiddushin 2, s.v. "Zot"). 

And if you ask: If so, why does he need to eat it a second time after the matzah? This is for the sake of distinguishing it for the children (Gemara there). And the reason he does not need charoset for the first dipping, even though charoset is because of the poison, what difference does it make whether it is the first or second dipping? The Rosh answered in the name of Rabbeinu Yonah, and this is his language: Because the first dipping is not obligatory but for the sake of distinction, and they are accustomed all year to eat lettuce without charoset, even now the sages did not consider it important.
