But the second dipping, which is a mitzvah, the sages warned that there should be no concern of danger. This is his language. And it is not understood at all: have we not explained that he has fulfilled his obligation with the first dipping? Rather, certainly, the Rosh does not hold as I wrote that one fulfills their obligation with the first dipping, but does not fulfill it. Either because he holds "matzah and maror" – specifically matzah first and then maror. Or because he holds that mitzvot require intention, as he indeed ruled in the fourth chapter of Rosh Hashanah. Therefore, the first is like the dipping of vegetables. And if you ask: If so, how does he bless on the first "Concerning the eating of maror"? One might say that the main intention is for the second dipping. And why does he not bless on the second dipping? Because it would appear as a joke, since he already ate of it and now blesses (Ran there). Therefore, it is necessary to do so. (And the Magen Avraham in subsection 14 wrote: Even though mitzvot require intention – in matters of eating it is different, for he ate and enjoyed it, see there. And the Bach differentiates between Torah commandments and Rabbinic ones, that Rabbinic ones do not require intention, see there. And the Perisha differentiates between whether he knew he ate or not, see there. But from the words of the Rosh and Ran that we brought, it does not seem so. Be precise and you will find ease.)

And since there are doubts about eating maror (bitter herbs) twice, therefore one must strive not to eat maror the first time but rather vegetables. And there are those who say that if he does not have vegetables, he can eat turnip (Magen Avraham, subsection 9). This is astonishing to say, since the Sages only commanded vegetables (and the Eliyah Rabbah also wrote that this requires further investigation). And there are those who say that according to our custom of using horseradish for maror, if he does not have vegetables and uses this for the first dipping as well, as explained, he should not bless "Borei Pri Ha'adamah" (the blessing over vegetables). This is because it is not suitable for eating by itself (Magen Avraham, subsection 10). Rather, he should only bless "Al Achilat Maror" (the blessing over eating maror). And there are those who disagree, saying that since the Sages instituted "and dip it in vinegar or salt water," it is indeed considered suitable for eating, and he must bless "Borei Pri Ha'adamah" (Chayei Adam, subsection 16, and Eliyah Rabbah). Additionally, the blessing over enjoyment (Birkat Ha'nehenin) is similar to the blessing over commandments (Birkat Ha'mitzvot) because it is according to the institution of the Sages. However, among us, it is unlikely that one would not obtain some kind of vegetable.

Ideally, one should chew the matzah with his teeth in order to taste the flavor of the matzah. However, if one swallowed the matzah without chewing it, he has fulfilled his obligation (Talmud, Pesachim 115b). One should not question: since post facto (bediavad) the taste of matzah is essential, as we ruled in Siman 461 that if one cooked matzah he has not fulfilled his obligation because it lacks the taste of matzah, why then has one fulfilled the obligation if they swallowed it? The answer is that it is not comparable, because cooked matzah, even before placing it in the mouth, has already lost its status as matzah and is considered like placing another food in the mouth. This is not the case with swallowing (Magen Avraham, Siman 11). Additionally, in the case of cooked matzah, no matzah reaches the stomach, whereas with swallowing, the stomach does receive matzah. At the end of the "Gid HaNasheh" section, it is explained that eating in the stomach is considered eating. (Reish Lakish said that only eating in the stomach is considered eating, while Rabbi Yochanan believed that even in the throat it is considered eating, but in the stomach it is certainly considered eating. This is why with maror (bitter herbs), one has not fulfilled their obligation because the taste of maror is required, as will be explained with the help of Heaven.)

If one swallows maror (bitter herbs) without chewing, they have not fulfilled their obligation, because one needs to taste the bitterness of the maror in their mouth. When it is swallowed without chewing, one does not taste the bitterness (Talmud there). One might ask: The most preferred type of maror is lettuce (chazeret), and it does not have any bitterness at all. This can be explained by saying that for lettuce, the designation of "maror" applies due to its toughness, as I wrote in Siman 473, Section 16, see there. However, for other types, the designation of "maror" is due to their bitterness; and since one does not taste the bitterness, they have not fulfilled their obligation. Consequently, even with lettuce, one needs to taste its inherent taste, because it is not possible to differentiate between this type of maror and another type. Thus, the Torah commanded to taste the bitterness of the maror in the mouth, whichever type of maror one eats, they must feel in their mouth what they are eating, and not by swallowing. Even if one swallowed matzah and maror together, they have fulfilled their obligation for matzah, but not for maror. The maror does not nullify the matzah since it was not chewed at all. If one wrapped matzah or maror in a fiber and swallowed it, they have not fulfilled their obligation for matzah either. This is not because of the taste, as with matzah there is no need to taste it, but because this is not the way of eating, and we do not call this "in the evening, you shall eat matzot." For maror, one has not fulfilled their obligation certainly, because in addition to it not being the way of eating, there is no taste of bitterness.

Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in Section 4: If one ate matzah without intention, such as if he was forced by coercers or bandits to eat it, he has fulfilled his obligation, since he knows that tonight is Pesach and that he is obligated to eat matzah. However, if he thought it was a regular day or that this was not matzah, he has not fulfilled his obligation. These are his words. He wrote this reasoning to reconcile the words of the Rambam, who ruled here that he has fulfilled his obligation, but in the second chapter of Shofar ruled that without intention one has not fulfilled the obligation, differentiating between eating and other matters. However, even in eating, if he did not know it was Pesach today or that this is matzah, he certainly has not fulfilled his obligation, for mitzvot require intention. And in eating, if he knew, even if it was done under duress, it is considered as intention. This reasoning is mentioned in Tosafot Pesachim (115a). But from the words of the Rosh there and the Tur here, it does not seem so. See there. (See also the commentary of the Achronim there, section 100, where this is discussed at length.)

If someone ate a kezayit of matzah and was an epileptic during his seizure, and afterwards at night he was healed, he is obligated to eat it again when he is healed, because that eating was at a time when he was exempt from all the commandments. This is not related to the principle that "commandments require intention," because even if they do not require intention, nevertheless, one must be alive and conscious, and not when he is completely out of his mind. And know that even if they do not require intention, nevertheless, if one intended not to fulfill the obligation, he has not fulfilled it. And one should not ask: if so, how do we say that if robbers forced him to eat matzah, he has fulfilled the obligation? For since he was forced, he did not want to eat, and thus intended not to fulfill the obligation. It can be said that he did not want them to feed him, but he wanted to eat by himself. And after being forced, he certainly did not intend not to fulfill the obligation (see Beit Yosef in the name of the Riv. Examine this well, and you will find it easy to understand).

It is well known that there is no obligation to eat matzah except on the first night alone, as it is written: "In the evening you shall eat matzot." However, throughout the entire festival, if one wishes not to eat matzah but rather other types of food, he has the option. Only on Shabbat and Yom Tov must one eat bread, but not necessarily matzah. Even on the first night, from the Torah, one fulfills his obligation with an olive-sized portion. And Rabbeinu the Rema wrote in paragraph 7: "It is customary to make three matzot for the Seder from an isaron, as a remembrance of the loaves of thanksgiving. And they make a sign on them to know which is the first, second, or third, placing the first on top, the second in the middle, and the third on the bottom for wrapping. And if one changes this order, it does not invalidate it. They also bake them in this order. If one of them breaks, they use it as the second, since anyway it will be broken." Until here are his words. And now we do not practice this because it causes the dough to be delayed, which is not desirable. And know that I have received this tradition: Even though the obligation of matzah is only on the first night, nevertheless, it is a mitzvah to eat matzah all the days of Pesach, as it is written: "For seven days you shall eat matzot." And the reason it is called "optional" is because, in comparison to an obligation, it is termed "optional," since it is not a positive commandment but rather the will of God that the children of Israel eat matzah all the days of Pesach.

We learned (Pesachim 53a): In a place where the custom is to eat roasted meat on the nights of Pesach, one eats it; in a place where the custom is not to eat it, one does not eat it. Since the Pesach offering is only eaten roasted, meaning on a spit over the fire and not in a pot or with water, there are those who were concerned that people might say they are eating the Pesach offering nowadays, which would be considered offering sacrifices outside the Temple. Therefore, they were stringent and prohibited eating any roasted meat on the night of Pesach, even from animals that are not suitable for the Pesach offering. And those who adopted this prohibition – the prohibition applies to their descendants after them. Regarding this, it is said: "Hear, my son, the instruction of your father..." (Proverbs 1:8). In our regions, the custom is not to eat [roasted meat]. This applies specifically to meat roasted over the fire, and not what we call "braten" (broiled or grilled).

Roasted in a pot, which means placing the meat in a pot without water – it appears to me that it is permitted since for the Passover offering it is invalid in this manner, as stated in the Gemara (41a). And even though there is a dispute there, that is only regarding lashes. But according to everyone, the Passover offering is invalid, because it is not roasted by fire (Tosafot there, s.v. "There is"). And so wrote the Rambam in the eighth chapter of the laws of the Passover offering, see there. Therefore, even if one roasted it and then cooked it, or cooked it and then roasted it – it is permitted to eat, since it is invalid as a Passover offering, as the Rambam wrote there. And the later authorities wrote that even roasted in a pot, and cooked and then roasted – it is forbidden. And even if one cooked it and then made it roasted in a pot – it is forbidden, because it has the name "roasted" upon it (Magen Avraham and Chayei Adam). And I do not know why we should be stringent in a mere custom in something that has no reason. And the proof brought from what our teacher the Beit Yosef wrote in section 2 that even calf and chicken meat, anything that requires slaughter is forbidden to eat roasted in a place where they are accustomed not to eat roasted, until here is his wording – it is not similar. For there, when they accepted upon themselves not to eat roasted, they accepted upon themselves all types of roasted meat. However, in any case, it should be fitting for the Passover offering, and not roasted that is not fitting for the Passover offering. And this requires further investigation.

And even in a place where the custom is to eat roasted [meat] – it is forbidden to eat a whole roasted kid or lamb, that is, when it is entirely roasted as one piece. This clearly appears like the Passover sacrifice, and people might say that he is eating consecrated items outside [the Temple]. Therefore, if it was cut up, or if a limb was removed, or if a limb was boiled while still attached – it is permitted to eat in a place where the custom is to eat roasted [meat]. And it seems that even if only the intestines were removed – it is also permitted, as this does not resemble the Passover sacrifice. And this is explained from Rashi (Pesachim 53a) who wrote: "Roasted whole – its head on its knees and on its entrails," look there.

Even for us, roasted fish and roasted egg are permitted, as they are not considered meat. However, liver, spleen, and all intestines are considered meat and are forbidden when roasted, as is proven regarding vows in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 217; see there. According to this, it is forbidden for us to eat liver on the night of Passover, as it can only be eaten roasted, since salting does not work for liver, and it is only permitted if it is subsequently cooked or fried in fat. There are those who have exaggerated and also forbid roasted eggs, but there is no reason for this (Taz, subsection 3). It is proper not to eat or drink excessively at this meal, so that one does not eat the afikoman in a gluttonous manner, and the eating of the afikoman will not be burdensome (see Magen Avraham, subsection 2). It is customary for us to eat eggs at this meal in remembrance of mourning, because the day on which Passover falls, Tisha B’Av also falls, as is known. It is also in remembrance of the destruction, for they used to offer the Passover sacrifice and now we have lost it due to our sins. There are those who have the custom not to eat any dipping on this night, except for the two dippings of the Seder. Therefore, they eat meat without dipping it in anything. One should be careful not to drink excessively at the meal, so that sleep does not overtake him, and he will be unable to recite Hallel and complete the entire Seder. The wise person has his eyes in his head, knowing that this night is entirely holy, and he should perform the Seder with great joy.

Know that concerning the matter of the Afikoman, there is an explanation: At first glance, it seems clear that the primary fulfillment of the positive commandment "In the evening you shall eat matzot" is accomplished with the first and second olive-sized portions, over which we recited the blessing "Who sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us concerning the eating of matzah." The Afikoman is merely a remembrance of the Pesach offering, which was eaten while satiated. This is also evident from the language of the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch, who wrote that after finishing the entire meal, each person eats an olive-sized portion of the matzah that was kept under the cloth, as a remembrance of the Pesach offering eaten while satiated. It should be eaten while reclining, and no blessing is recited over it. One should be careful to eat it before midnight. This is their exact language. They wrote "a remembrance of the Pesach," and therefore no blessing is recited over it. And regarding the caution to eat it before midnight, although it is merely a remembrance, nevertheless, since it is a remembrance of the Pesach offering, and according to Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah, the Pesach offering is only eaten until midnight, it is necessary to eat the Afikoman before midnight as well.

But Rashi and Rashbam wrote (Pesachim 119b, s.v. "Ein," see there) that the main mitzvah is the afikoman. And this is the language of Rashi and Rashbam there: "Ein maftirin..."—one needs to eat matzah at the end of the meal, as a remembrance of the matzah that was eaten with the paschal lamb. And this is the broken matzah that we eat at the end for the obligation of matzah. And necessarily, we bless "Al Achilat Matzah" initially, even though it is not for the obligation, as it says above regarding maror that after one has filled his stomach with it, how can he go back and bless on it? Here too, regarding matzah... until here are their words. And it also seems to me from the language of the Rambam in Chapter Eight, where he wrote that at the end one eats from the meat of the paschal lamb..., and in our times, one eats an olive-sized portion of matzah..., for their eating is the mitzvah. Until here is his language, thus implying that this is the main mitzvah. And it can be said that his main intention was for the time of the Temple. And the Tosafot (Pesachim 120a) seem to be uncertain about this, see there. But the Rosh brought the words of Rashi and disagreed with him, writing that the afikoman is not for the obligation but as a remembrance of the paschal lamb, see there. According to this, according to Rashi and Rashbam, one should be very, very careful in eating the afikoman, because it is the main mitzvah of eating matzah, as also explained by the Rambam as I have written. Therefore, one should be very careful to eat at least a whole olive-sized portion. (And Rashi's own language requires examination, as he begins with "a remembrance of the matzah eaten with the paschal lamb" and concludes with "for the obligation of matzah." Also, Tosafot there wrote that Rashi's reasoning is compelling, for in the time of the Temple it was necessarily so, see there—I do not understand. For they could have eaten all the meal with rich matzah until they reached the paschal lamb, and then they ate the obligatory matzah and maror, and then blessed on them, and not from the beginning of the meal. The words of our Rabbis are hidden from me, and this requires great examination.)

And they wrote that ideally, one should take two olive-sized portions: one as a remembrance of the Passover offering, and one as a remembrance of the matzah eaten with the Passover offering. At the very least, one should not have less than an olive-sized portion (Magen Avraham in the name of Maharil). And if he does not have an olive-sized portion, he should eat even less than an olive-sized portion. It also appears that for the first olive-sized portion of "eating matzah," if he only has less than an olive-sized portion, he is obligated to eat it, but he should not recite the blessing "on eating matzah." We do not say that less than an olive-sized portion is nothing, because just as with prohibitions, half of the required measure is a Torah prohibition, so too with matzah, it is somewhat of a mitzvah, since he cannot fulfill more. However, if there are two people and they only have one olive-sized portion of matzah, it seems that it is better for one of them to eat the entire olive-sized portion and fulfill the mitzvah properly, rather than each eating half an olive-sized portion. And how should they proceed? They should draw lots. It is obvious that if they have two olive-sized portions, each should eat an olive-sized portion for "HaMotzi," which is the main mitzvah, and they should not eat the afikoman, which is merely a remembrance. If they have three olive-sized portions, each should eat an olive-sized portion for "HaMotzi," and the third olive-sized portion should be divided between them for the afikoman, as a half olive-sized portion is sufficient for remembrance in a pressing situation. (This is my opinion. And see Sha'arei Teshuvah in Siman 475 and 482.)

And regarding what was written that one should strive to eat the afikoman before midnight, our teacher the Rema wrote that one should also strive to recite Hallel before midnight. Thus far his words. I do not know the reason for this, as what connection does Hallel have to midnight (see Tosefta at the end of Pesachim)? The afikoman should be eaten while reclining. If one ate it without reclining, it appears to me that he has fulfilled his obligation, as it is only a commemoration (and so wrote the GRa"Z in section 4). There are those who have the custom to take the afikoman wrapped in a cloth, sling it over their shoulders, walk around the house for about four cubits, and say: "Thus our ancestors went, their kneading bowls bound up in their clothes upon their shoulders." Afterwards, they eat it. In these regions, this custom is not practiced; rather, they take out the afikoman and eat it (Chayei Adam and GRa"Z). There are some who take a piece of the afikoman, pierce it, and hang it around their necks. There is no prohibition in this, but it is an unnecessary action. We do not have this custom (ibid.).

And know that it is a simple matter that if it extends until after midnight, one is obligated to eat the afikoman. For indeed, Rambam, at the beginning of the sixth chapter and in the eighth chapter of Hilchot Korban Pesach, rules in accordance with Rabbi Akiva that the Pesach offering and matzah are eaten all night. This is also the opinion of several of the Rishonim (as noted in the Hagahot Maimoniot in the eighth chapter, see there). This is also the opinion of Beit Hillel at the end of Tosefta Pesachim, see there.

However, there is a doubt regarding this: if one was prevented and did not conduct the Seder until after midnight, should he recite the blessing "on eating matzah" or not? For since our Rabbis, the Tosafot, rule everywhere that the halacha follows Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah, who says that the Pesach offering is only eaten until midnight, similar to the anonymous opinion in "Eizehu Mekoman" which states: the Pesach offering is only eaten at night, and only until midnight. And it is stated in the Gemara (Pesachim 120b): if one eats matzah nowadays after midnight, according to Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah, he has not fulfilled his obligation. Therefore, how can he recite the blessing "on eating matzah" since its time has already passed according to Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah? Therefore, it seems that one should eat it without the blessing "on eating matzah".

If one forgot and did not eat the afikoman, and did not remember until he had washed his hands, or until he had said "Bring the blessing" – he eats the afikoman without the blessing of "Hamotzi." For even though during the rest of the year, if one wishes to eat afterward, it is considered a distraction and requires a blessing, nevertheless on Passover, since we rely on the Torah's command, and we are not permitted to avoid eating it – this is not considered a distraction. And he should wash his hands without a blessing before eating the afikoman, as I have written in section 179 (the Gra"z). However, there are those who disagree and hold that one should not eat the afikoman at all and rely on the first olive-sized portion (Beit Yosef in the name of the Rashal, and see Magen Avraham section 2). But we have only the words of our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, who ruled that one should eat it.

If one remembers after having recited the Grace After Meals, if he remembers before reciting the blessing "Borei Peri HaGafen" – he should wash his hands and recite the blessing "Hamotzi", eat the afikoman, recite the Grace After Meals again, and drink the cup with the blessing "Borei Peri HaGafen". If he remembers only after drinking the cup, or even just after reciting the blessing "Borei Peri HaGafen", since he is compelled to drink the cup so that his blessing is not in vain – then he should not eat the afikoman and should rely on the matzah he ate beforehand. For if he eats, he would need another cup, and it would be as if he is adding to the cups. However, this applies to one who is careful throughout the year to not recite the Grace After Meals without a cup. But for us, who do not recite the Grace After Meals over a cup – he should wash his hands, recite the blessing "Hamotzi", eat the afikoman, and recite the Grace After Meals without a cup (Magen Avraham, sub-section 4). Similarly, if he remembers after starting Hallel – he should finish Hallel, drink the cup, wash his hands, eat the afikoman, and recite the Grace After Meals without a cup.

And this is the language of our masters, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch: If one did not remember until after he blessed "Borei Pri Hagafen" (the blessing over wine), he should not eat the afikoman, and rely on the matzah eaten during the meal, as they are all guarded from the time of kneading. But in a place where it is customary to guard the matzah for the mitzvah from the time of harvesting, even if he did not remember until after Hallel, he should wash his hands, recite the blessing "Hamotzi" (over the bread), eat the afikoman, and bless over the cup again. There is no concern about adding to the cups. Thus is their language. And one should not ask: Did he not eat an olive-sized piece of matzah guarded from the time of harvesting at the blessing "Al Achilat Matzah"? It can be said that we do not rely on that, because the afikoman is a separate matter. Only if he ate the entire meal from the guarded matzah can he rely on the other matzah eaten during the meal, but not on the first matzah. And regarding what they wrote about blessing over the cup again, it seems in my humble opinion that this applies to one who is careful to bless over the cup throughout the year. But one who is not careful does not need the cup. The commentators did not understand this way, but in my humble opinion, it seems like I wrote (see Taz, Magen Avraham, Chayei Adam, and it requires further study. Be precise and you will find it easy). And if the afikoman was lost, he should eat an olive-sized piece of matzah from another matzah, as they are all at least guarded from the time of kneading. All the more so if he has matzah guarded from the time of harvesting, he must eat it even if the afikoman was lost.

Just as after the Passover offering one should not eat anything, so as not to lose the taste of the Passover offering, likewise with the afikoman, which is a remembrance of the Passover offering – one should not eat anything after it, so as not to lose the taste of the matzah. Similarly, drinking any beverage is forbidden (Magen Avraham) except for water, so as not to lose the taste, aside from the two cups that must be drunk as part of the Seder requirements. Just as it is forbidden to eat the Passover offering in two places, so too with the afikoman. It is not preferable if one interrupted with sleep, which is forbidden as will be explained, similarly with two places.

And even in the same room, they should not eat the afikoman at two different tables. But for the rest of the meal, there is no strictness, for we are only stringent with the afikoman, which is a remembrance of the Passover offering. Similarly, if one started to eat the afikoman, and then slept and woke up, he does not return to eat it, as it is considered like two places. And if some members of the group slept in the middle, they can continue eating when they wake up, since the others did not sleep. But if all of them fell asleep and then woke up, they should not eat, as this is considered like two places. If all of them dozed off, meaning they were in a state of light sleep where they could respond when called but were not fully awake or capable of coherent thought, they may eat it, for this is not considered sleep. All this applies only to sleep that occurs after starting to eat the afikoman, and not to one who is stringent throughout the entire meal.

And know that this which we call the matzah that is eaten at the end "Afikoman" – seemingly has no reason, for we have learned: One does not conclude after the Pesach [offering] with Afikoman. That is to say, one should not eat anything else. And "Afikoman" is an expression meaning "bring out delicacies" (Rashbam). If so, how do we call it "Afikoman"? 

We must say that this is its explanation: "Afikoman" – "bring out from", meaning: only this food and no more. Or it refers to after its consumption as "Afikoman", meaning: not to bring out any more food. However, after the fact, if one ate something after the Afikoman – he is not required to go back and eat the Afikoman again. 

Similarly, all types of drink are forbidden after it except for water, which does not ruin the taste. And all types of water are permitted, such as seltzer and lemonade. There are those who permit drinking all beverages, arguing that only eating is forbidden, not drinking (Chayei Adam and as implied in Taz, Orach Chayim 479:2).

However, in any case, it is obvious that all types of prepared waters are permitted to drink after the Seder, as well as licorice water and the like. This will be further explained in Siman 481.

And after eating the afikoman, they should pour for him a third cup, and he should recite the Grace After Meals over it. It is written that the cup requires rinsing and washing, even for one who is not particular about it throughout the year. However, nowadays we clean the cups for the first cup, and with it we drink all four cups. It is customary to seek out a zimun (prayer quorum of three) for the Seder, not because of the Grace After Meals but because of the Hallel for "Hodu" and "Ana," which requires one person to recite and the others to respond, as it is stated in Midrash Tehillim. However, if he does not have a zimun, his wife and sons and daughters respond after him (Tur).

And this is the language of our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch: It is a mitzvah to pursue a zimmun. The most distinguished among them says "Hodu" and "Ana," and the others respond after him. The most distinguished can grant permission to a minor, and he can join them for a zimmun regarding Hallel, even though he did not eat with them. And it is customary that the head of the household recites Birkat Hamazon on the night of Passover, as it is said, "He who has a good eye will be blessed," and he is the one with a good eye who said, "All who are hungry, let them come and eat." Until here is his language. And he can honor a distinguished guest. According to the law of the Gemara, the guest recites the blessing. And the custom is to add in "HaRachaman" (the Merciful One) "He will grant us to a day that is entirely good": "To a day that is entirely long, to a day when the righteous sit with their crowns on their heads, and enjoy the radiance of the Divine Presence."

After the Grace After Meals, one blesses "Borei Pri Hagafen" (Creator of the fruit of the vine) and drinks the cup while reclining. If one drank without reclining, it is explained in Siman 472; see there. One does not bless afterwards, nor does one drink between the third and fourth cup, as explained in the Jerusalem Talmud, lest one becomes intoxicated. It implies that a non-intoxicating drink is permitted (Taz). However, from the third cup, even if it is very large, one can drink multiple times, even if there was an interruption in between, as it is all considered one cup and one drinking. (See Magen Avraham, subsection 1. I do not understand why it requires intention for one cup; this needs further study.) The later authorities elaborated on the practice where one would leave his home and join a zimmun (quorum for Grace After Meals) in another house, which is not correct. Not only for the Grace After Meals, but even for the Hallel, one should not uproot from his place to another place and then return home. Nowadays, we do not hear of this custom, and it is clear that everyone should complete the entire seder in his own home. After finishing the seder, if one wishes to go to another house to respond "Hodu" and "Ana," he is permitted, as none of this is critical. Even an individual can recite Hallel by himself, but in that case, he should only say "Hodu" once and not four times. The same applies to the Hallel of Yom Tov and Rosh Chodesh, and this is obvious (see Taz, Magen Avraham, and Bach).

And after drinking the third cup, it is customary to say "Pour out Your wrath..." and to open the door to remember that it is a night of protection. And through the merit of this faith, the Messiah will come and pour out His wrath on the Babylonians who destroyed the Temple. And because Elijah will come before the arrival of the Messiah, as it is written: "Behold, I send you Elijah the prophet before..." Therefore, the custom is to place another cup in the middle of the table, and it is called "Elijah's Cup." There are those who would customarily stand up from reclining and say "Blessed is he who comes." All this is to strengthen the faith, as we have received the tradition that in Nisan they were redeemed, and in Nisan they are destined to be redeemed, as it is stated in the first chapter of Rosh Hashanah (11a). Therefore, at the conclusion of the Seder, before reciting "Not unto us, O Lord, not unto us, but unto Your name give glory," we are aroused to give glory to His great and blessed name.

And we pour the fourth cup, and begin "Not to us" and complete the Hallel. And when reaching "Yahalelucha," we recite the Great Hallel, which is the psalm of twenty-six "Give thanks" until its end. Afterwards, we recite "Nishmat," which is called "Birkat Hashir" in the Gemara (Pesachim 118a) because on Shabbatot and Yom Tov we say it after Pesukei Dezimra (Tosafot there, s.v. "Mai"). These twenty-six "Give thanks" correspond to the twenty-six generations before the giving of the Torah, during which the Holy One, Blessed be He, sustained them with His kindness (Gemara there). It is called "the Great Hallel" because it is written in it "He gives food to all flesh" (ibid.), indicating that the Holy One, Blessed be He, sits in the heights of the world and distributes sustenance to every creature (ibid.). And because on Pesach we entered under the wings of the Divine Presence, and He promised us that He would never abandon or forsake us forever – therefore, we recite this in the order of the Seder.

Regarding the conclusion of Hallel, there are many opinions: Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote that one should recite "Nishmat" and "Yishtabach" until "For from eternity to eternity, You are God." Afterward, one should say "Yehalelucha" and conclude with "King, praised with praises." The Tur wrote that "Yehalelucha" should be said after Hallel until the blessing, and afterward "Nishmat" and "Yishtabach," and conclude with "Yishtabach"; this is also written in the Tosafot there. And we follow the practice of our teacher, the Beit Yosef. After the blessing, one blesses "Borei Pri HaGafen" on the fourth cup, because there was an interruption with Hallel. Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, ruled without a blessing, but we do not follow this practice, as I wrote in Siman 474. One should drink while reclining, and if one did not recline, this is explained in Siman 472. One should drink it all in order to bless the final blessing "Al HaGefen..." Afterward, one recites the piyutim according to the custom. Some do not drink until after the recitation of the piyutim, and this is also printed in the Haggadot. This is incorrect because the fourth cup should be drunk immediately after Hallel. (The Beit Yosef wrote: if one drank without reclining, one should drink again while reclining. In that case, one must bless beforehand "Borei Pri HaGafen," because one's attention was diverted from drinking again. End of his words. And earlier in Siman 472, we brought opinions that one does not need to drink again while reclining; see there. The Rema wrote that Hallel can even be recited not in the place of the meal; see there. Nevertheless, it is better to say it in the place of the meal and to drink all the cups in one place.)

The Geonim had a tradition that if one wishes to drink a fifth cup, he may do so. Similarly, Rambam wrote in the eighth chapter, and these are his words: "Afterwards, he pours the fourth cup and completes Hallel over it, and says the blessing of the song, which is 'May all Your works praise You, Hashem...'. He then recites the blessing 'Borei Pri Hagafen' and tastes nothing for the rest of the night except for water. He may pour a fifth cup and recite over it the Great Hallel, from 'Give thanks to Hashem for He is good' until 'By the rivers of Babylon'. This cup is not obligatory like the four cups." This is the end of his words, and this was their version in the Gemara (Pesachim 118a): "For the fifth cup, he says the Great Hallel." According to our version, based on the interpretations of Rashi and Rashbam, it refers to the fourth cup. See there. The Tur elaborates on this. Some have said that with the fourth cup, one concludes with the blessing "May all Your works praise You," and with the blessing of the Great Hallel, one concludes with the blessing "Yishtabach." Others have said that one drinks the fourth cup without a concluding blessing. See there. In the glosses of Maimonides: However, we do not know of this, and we only know about the four cups.

And there are some of the Geonim who said that it applies specifically in a case where one is compelled to drink a fifth cup, such as when he is very thirsty, as Rabbeinu Yosef Tov Elem composed in the poem "Elokei Haruchot" for Shabbat Hagadol, see there. And this is what Rabbeinu the Rema wrote, that someone who is delicate or very thirsty may drink a fifth cup and recite the Great Hallel over it. These are his words. However, in our times, we have neither heard nor seen this practice being followed.

And this is what the Rambam wrote, that it is forbidden afterwards to drink wine except for water – so also wrote the Rif. And the Rosh posed a difficulty with this, for it is taught in the Mishnah "One does not conclude after the Pesach [offering] with an afikoman" – but drinking is permitted, see there – however, the custom of the entire world follows the Geonim. And Rabbeinu Yonah explained the reason, because a person is obligated to engage all night in the exodus from Egypt, and to recount the miracles and wonders that the Holy One, Blessed be He, did for us until sleep overtakes him. Therefore, if he drinks more wine – sleep will overtake him immediately. And some wrote that it is to not nullify the taste of matzah in his mouth, and all drinks are forbidden except for water. But for not-milk and ginger water which they call ginger water – it is permitted (Magen Avraham). And similarly, for us, seltzer and lemonade – it is permitted, as I wrote in Siman 478. But apple cider in Germany, which is made by crushing apples in a press, and has a strong taste – is forbidden (there).

All the laws of the first night also apply to the second night. Even regarding not tasting anything after the Seder, those who are meticulous observe this just as on the first night (Beit Yosef). It is customary not to recite on one's bed during these two nights except the Shema passage and the "Hamapil" blessing, and not the other Psalms that are usually recited for protection, because the night of Passover is a night of protection from harmful entities.

Rambam writes at the end of the eighth chapter: If one has no guarded matzah except for the size of an olive, when he finishes his meal with unguarded matzah, he blesses "on the eating of matzah" and eats that olive-sized piece, and he does not taste anything afterwards. This is his wording, and according to Rambam's opinion, which requires guarding from the time of harvesting and throughout all the days of Passover, as I wrote in Siman 453, see there. However, if he does not have such guarded matzah, it is obvious that we do not tell him not to eat all the days of Passover, for the primary guarding is a rabbinic requirement, as Rambam wrote in the fifth chapter. According to Rashi and Tosafot, the guarding is "for its sake," and anything not done "for its sake" is not called "guarded," as I wrote there. And this is only for the first night.

And behold, the Rambam did not specify when to eat the maror and the "korech." The Rif wrote that one should eat the maror after the kazayit of matzah, and also perform the "korech." The Tur, in the name of Rabbeinu Yonah, wrote that after the kazayit, one should not eat anything else; see there. Therefore, it follows that one eats the maror first. And even though one eats the maror before the matzah, we do not concern ourselves with this. This is the opinion of Rabbeinu the Beit Yosef, who wrote: If one only has one kazayit of guarded matzah, one blesses "on the eating of maror" and eats it, and when one finishes the meal with non-guarded matzah, one blesses "on the eating of matzah" and eats that kazayit. And one should not taste anything afterward. Until here are his words. However, if one has two kazayitim, one should eat the first for "hamotzi" and the second for the afikoman, and the "korech" should be done with non-guarded matzah. And a sick person who cannot eat without a cooked dish should eat the kazayit of matzah with the cooked dish. And if one can only eat one kazayit, one should eat it initially without matzah, and afterward eat the kazayit and bless "on the eating of matzah" (Magen Avraham), or eat rich matzah first.

And one who has only three matzot for both nights – should eat one matzah on the first night, and recite “HaMotzi” and “Al Achilat Matzah” over it. And the remaining two should be set aside for the second night, so that he will have Lechem Mishneh (two loaves) for the second night. It is obvious that if one matzah is not sufficient for all the olive-sized portions, the first night takes precedence. (See Taz who explains the opinion of the Rosh, and it requires further study, see there. And nowadays, the law regarding dough of a non-Jew does not apply at all, because we knead with yeast and it becomes chametz immediately. In their days, they used to knead as cakes.)

If one does not have wine for the four cups, he should take mead, which is called "mead," if it is a place where it is customary to drink this beverage, and it is considered the local wine. And even though there are those who say that one should not make Kiddush on other beverages, as I wrote in Siman 272, nevertheless, on Passover, when four cups are required and it is impossible to make Kiddush on bread, one can rely on the opinion that allows making Kiddush on other beverages. Especially since we, throughout the year, also make Kiddush on other beverages. And it is a sacred obligation for every Jew to obtain wine for the four cups. If one only has one cup, he should use it for Kiddush. If he has two, he should use them for Kiddush and for Birkat Hamazon. If he has three, he should use them in order, leaving the Hallel without a cup (Magen Avraham). And if he has a little wine and the rest is mead, Kiddush should still be made first on the wine, then Birkat Hamazon, and then after the Haggadah. And the first night takes precedence over the second night in all the cups.

And if he has no wine nor other beverages at all, there are different opinions on this matter: The Rif z"l wrote that one sanctifies (makes Kiddush) on the matzah, and blesses "Hamotzi" before Kiddush, and after Kiddush, blesses "to eat matzah" and eats. Then he takes the karpas and recites the Haggadah up to "Go'el Yisrael," eats maror, and makes a sandwich ("korech"). The Ri Gaon wrote that after Kiddush, he does not bless "to eat matzah." Instead, he finishes Kiddush, eats matzah, then takes the karpas, finishes the Haggadah, and afterward blesses "to eat matzah," eats matzah and maror, and makes a sandwich. The Ba'al Ha'itur wrote like the Rif to bless "to eat matzah" after Kiddush, but requires eating maror immediately because one should not interrupt between matzah and maror. The Tur wrote that it is better to eat the karpas without Kiddush. Then he should recite the Haggadah, then wash his hands, bless "Hamotzi" and "to eat matzah," and eat maror and make a sandwich. And our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote only the opinion of the Rif, which is the most clear. (Because for the Ri Gaon, it is difficult: after filling his stomach, he blesses? And for the Ba'al Ha'itur, the order is completely reversed. And for the Tur, it is necessary to eat before Kiddush. But for the Rif, it is only an interruption with the Haggadah between matzah and maror, and what of it? After all, maror in our time is rabbinic, and since it is not possible in another way, we do not care about the interruption. Analyze and you will find leniency.)

In my humble opinion, one may make Kiddush on distilled wine for Pesach, as well as on any other cups if he does not have wine, and on honey water, which is also considered a local beverage. Indeed, throughout the year many people make Kiddush on distilled wine. However, it should not be made very strong, so that it is possible to drink the majority of a revi'it. Similarly, on any drink that is suitable for Pesach, like vishnick, which is made from fruit with sugar as is known. (See Magen Avraham on likritz and further in kvass and barst, where he permits it. In my humble opinion, this requires further investigation.)

If someone has neighbors who are unlearned in Jewish law and do not know how to conduct the Seder, and he is compelled to conduct the Seder for them, how should he proceed? He should first conduct the Seder for himself in his own home until after he has eaten and until after he has recited the Grace After Meals. For before the Grace After Meals, it is forbidden for him to leave, even if he wishes to eat there, as this is only permitted due to a fleeting mitzvah, as I have written in Siman 178 and 179. In this case, he may go after the Grace After Meals. After the Grace After Meals, he should go, and he should recite Hallel afterward, because the neighbors wish to eat, and also so that midnight does not pass. When he finishes teaching them the Seder, he should return to his home, recite Hallel, and drink the fourth cup. In this, we are not concerned about interruption, and even if it is after midnight, it is not an impediment, especially since he was engaged in the mitzvah of teaching them the Seder. If he wishes, he can also complete Hallel in his home.

And what should one do with them? For he is forbidden to eat and drink any more, since he has already eaten the afikoman. Additionally, he does not eat in two places, as I have written in Siman 478. He should make Kiddush for them and they should drink the cup, for Kiddush is a blessing of the mitzvah, as we hold that even if one has fulfilled his obligation, he can still fulfill it for others. It is not like the blessings over enjoyment, which require that one also benefits himself, and if not, he cannot recite the blessing for someone else. For with mitzvot, all of Israel are responsible for each other, and it is as if the obligation is upon his own body. Therefore, he can make Kiddush for them, even though he does not need it for himself. And even the blessing of "Borei Pri Hagafen" (Creator of the fruit of the vine), although it is a blessing over enjoyment, since it is necessary for Kiddush, it is considered a blessing of the mitzvah like Kiddush (end of the third chapter of Rosh Hashanah). Similarly, the blessing of "Hamotzi" (who brings forth bread) for eating matzah is considered a blessing of the mitzvah (there), and he can bless for them. And even the blessing of "Borei Pri Ha’adama" (Creator of the fruit of the ground) for karpas, although it is only a sign for the children, nevertheless, since it is an enactment of the Sages, it is considered a blessing of the mitzvah. Some have doubts about this as explained in the Tur, but the Rosh ruled so in practice. However, Birkat Hamazon (Grace after Meals), although it is an obligation, one is not allowed to bless for them unless he ate with them, for it says, "And you shall eat and be satisfied and bless" – and not someone who did not eat. So it is stated in the Jerusalem Talmud, third chapter of Berachot (halacha 3).

And this is what should be done: He sanctifies [the wine] for them and they drink the cup. They wash their hands, and they dip the karpas, and he blesses for them "Borei Pri HaAdama" ("Who creates the fruit of the ground"), and they respond "Amen" and eat. He explains the Haggadah to them in a language they understand until "Ga'al Yisrael" ("Who redeemed Israel"). He blesses over the second cup, and they drink. They wash their hands, and he blesses "Hamotzi" ("Who brings forth bread from the earth") and "Al Achilat Matzah" ("On the eating of matzah"), and they respond "Amen" and eat. Afterwards, he blesses "Al Achilat Maror" ("On the eating of bitter herbs"), and they eat. He makes for them a "Korech" (a sandwich of matzah and bitter herbs) and they eat. They finish the meal, and they bless the Grace after Meals by themselves for the reason that has been explained. If they are unable – he recites for them word by word, and they respond after him. For this is not considered as fulfilling their obligation for them, but rather like a minor who prompts an adult.

And so he goes to all the houses and does so. Afterwards, he goes back to his house, finishes the Hallel, and drinks the fourth cup. Regarding the Hallel, everyone can come to him and listen to it, since the Hallel does not necessarily need to be recited in the place of the Seder. Note that what we have said, that one should first finish his own Seder at his house, is not an absolute requirement. If he wishes, he can first conduct the Seder at their place without tasting anything, and afterwards, he can conduct the Seder for himself. Alternatively, if he wishes, he can first conduct the Seder for himself and then at their place, as I have written. (See Magen Avraham, subsection 2, in the name of the Shiltei Giborim, that what has been explained—that it is forbidden to eat at their place—applies when he has already eaten the Afikoman at his own place. However, if he has not yet eaten, it is permissible, as we do not worry about changing locations for the rest of the meal. But the Tur, in the name of Rav Cohen Tzedek, prohibits eating in two places for the entire meal. See there and see Taz.)

One who swears not to eat matzah on the night of Passover is flogged and eats matzah, for an oath does not take effect to nullify a commandment. Since he is already sworn from Mount Sinai to fulfill the commandment, he has sworn a false oath and is flogged for it, as I have written in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 236. However, if he swears not to eat matzah all year or all month, the oath takes effect on the days before and after Passover, and hence it also applies to Passover inclusively, in a manner that nullifies the commandment through inaction. It seems to me that even if he swears regarding all the days of Passover, the oath takes effect inclusively, for aside from the first night, the oath is effective, and consequently, it also applies to the first night inclusively.

But if one swears not to drink the four cups, which are rabbinic, or not to eat maror in our times, which is rabbinic, or on the second night, which is rabbinic, also eating matzah – his oath takes effect, for the oath takes effect on rabbinic commandments to nullify a mitzvah by passive inaction. Therefore, they should compel him to annul his oath through questioning and regret, to fulfill the commandments of the Sages. Similarly, with a general oath, they should compel him to annul the oath. And know that vows also take effect on mitzvot, as I wrote in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 215. Therefore, if he said, “Eating matzah is forbidden to me as a vow,” he is forbidden to eat matzah. Hence, he should be compelled to annul the vow through questioning and regret, as I wrote there in Siman 228. The reason for the distinction between a vow and an oath is explained there with Divine assistance.

The measurement of an olive’s size (kezayit) – It is taught in Chapter Seventeen of Keilim that it is neither large nor small but medium, see there. And it is known that there is a dispute between Rashi and Tosafot against the Rambam: Rashi and Tosafot hold that a kezayit is about half an egg, and the Rambam holds it is about a third of an egg. Therefore, regarding matzah which is a Torah obligation – it is obvious one should be stringent and eat about half an egg. And for maror, which is a rabbinic obligation – one can be lenient. And regarding the final blessing and Birkat Hamazon – in matters of doubt regarding blessings, one should be lenient and not recite a blessing until one eats about half an egg. And a person should always strive to remove himself from doubt. And even in rabbinic measurements – it is appropriate for one who cherishes the mitzvah to be meticulous and fulfill all opinions. And we have already explained above in Siman 472, Section 12 that there are some great authorities who now wish to double the measurements, but we do not agree with this. And we have explained this also in Siman 168 and in Yoreh De'ah Siman 324. And one who is stringent should be stringent for himself and not instruct others, see there.

One must be careful when estimating the volume of a kezayit of maror with vegetables that fulfill the obligation of maror, to press down the space between the leaves; and ensure that the leaves themselves amount to a kezayit, not including the air between them. Similarly, if there is a hollow space in the matzah – the hollow space does not contribute to the kezayit. However, when there is no hollow space and it is just soft and sponge-like – it does not need to be pressed. It is a mitzvah to eat the entire kezayit of maror at once, and not bit by bit. However, for someone who finds it difficult – they may eat it bit by bit, as long as they do not delay more than the time it takes to eat a peras. And earlier in Siman 475, Section 4, we explained that we do not find in the early authorities that they required eating the entire kezayit at once, but rather that it should be eaten without interruption. See there. And those who eat horseradish for maror – should reduce the bitterness a little, but not so much that there is no bitterness left at all, for if so, they do not fulfill the obligation of maror. Rather, they should reduce it a little.

The order of the day for the first two days: Candles are lit just like on Shabbat, for the honor of Yom Tov, and the blessing "to kindle the light of Yom Tov" is recited. And the women recite the "Shehecheyanu" blessing at that time. We then enter the synagogue and pray the evening service just like on Shabbat, except that we do not conclude with "He who guards His people Israel forever" but with "He who spreads the shelter of peace…". The verse "And Moses spoke…" is recited. We pray the first three and last three blessings, and the sanctity of the day in the middle: "You have chosen us… and with love, O Lord our God, You have given us this Festival of Matzot, the time of our freedom, a holy convocation, a remembrance of the Exodus from Egypt." We do not say "with love a holy convocation" because we already said "with love," except when it falls on Shabbat, in which case we say "this Shabbat day and this Festival of Matzot." We then say "with love a holy convocation" due to Shabbat on its own, which we received with love (see Levush).

And know that the Sephardim say "this day of the Festival of Matzot, and this day of the holy convocation," and on Chol HaMoed "this day of the holy convocation." The Ashkenazim do not say this, and so wrote our teacher, the Rema, later in Siman 490, Section 3, see there. Seemingly, the law is with the Sephardim, for the Torah calls it a "holy convocation." However, in my humble opinion, the law is with the Ashkenazim, for indeed we say "the season of our freedom, a holy convocation," and why do we need both? And if because of Yom Tov, we do not find this term in the Torah at all. This is the intention of our teacher, the Rema, later, who wrote that we do not say "holy convocation" at all. The commentators all objected to him, for on the contrary, we do say it! But in truth, his intention is also thus: that we do not say "holy convocation" at the beginning, when we say "this day of the Festival of Matzot," and on the contrary, the reason is that we say it at the end. And so it is for all holidays. And the Sephardim say "on the Sabbath day of rest." But the language of the Torah is "the day of the Sabbath," as it is written: "Remember the Sabbath day to keep it holy."

We say "Ya'aleh Veyavo," "Vehasienu," and conclude with "Who sanctifies Israel and the seasons." Why don't we mention each festival by itself, for instance, "Who sanctifies Israel and the Festival of Matzot," and similarly for all of them? It seems to me that this is because the Torah encompasses all the times with one sanctity at both the beginning and the end, as it is written in "Emor": "These are the appointed festivals of the Lord, holy convocations," and at the end: "And Moses declared the appointed festivals of the Lord…" — thus, they were all sanctified with one sanctity. Therefore, we say "Who sanctifies Israel" — and sanctifies all the times, as it is written: "The appointed festivals of the Lord, holy convocations, which you shall proclaim in their appointed time." This means: when you proclaim a holy convocation for each of the times, as it is written in the Torah for each festival "a holy convocation shall be for you" — you proclaim them inclusively, by saying "Who sanctifies Israel and the seasons." And this is similar to "festivals."

If he made a mistake in his conclusion due to habit and said "Who sanctifies the Sabbath" and then corrected himself within the time it takes to say a greeting and said "Who sanctifies Israel and the festive seasons" – he has fulfilled his obligation. But if he corrected himself after the time it takes to say a greeting – he has not fulfilled his obligation and must repeat the prayer. 

Some say that this only applies if he knew it was a festival and just stumbled in his speech. But if he did not know at all that it was a festival – he has not fulfilled his obligation. Others say that even in such a case – he has fulfilled his obligation. This depends on the opinions in Siman 209; see there (see Magen Avraham, subsection 2).

All this applies if he did not mention the festival in the middle of the prayer. But if he mentioned the festival, even if he concluded with the Sabbath – he has fulfilled his obligation. Likewise, if he concluded with the festival and did not mention the festival in the middle of the prayer – he has also fulfilled his obligation (there). Similarly, if he concluded only with "Who sanctifies Israel" – he has fulfilled his obligation (there). On the Sabbath, one concludes with "Who sanctifies the Sabbath, Israel, and the festive seasons." If he forgot the Sabbath – he has fulfilled his obligation (Eliyah Rabbah, subsection 7 in the name of Keneset HaGedolah). This is when he mentioned the Sabbath in the middle, but otherwise, he has not fulfilled his obligation. 

Some disagree and say that even if he mentioned the festival in the middle but did not mention it in the conclusion – he must repeat, as the conclusion is determinative (Pri Chadash). Similarly, if he concluded only with "Who sanctifies Israel" – he has not fulfilled his obligation. Likewise, if he mentioned it in the conclusion but not in the middle – he has not fulfilled his obligation (Rabbi Akiva Eiger). This also seems to me to be the main opinion.

If he is in the "Retzeh" blessing and is unsure whether he said "Vehaseinu" after "Ya'aleh Veyavo" or said "Retzeh" as usual on Rosh Chodesh – he should go back to "Ata Bechartanu" (there), as he most likely said it out of habit. If he moved his feet – he must go back to the beginning. If he did not explicitly mention the festival but only said "this holy convocation day" – he has fulfilled his obligation (there). But if he mentioned a different festival – he certainly has not fulfilled his obligation.

One does not recite the Blessing of "Me'ein Sheva," that is "Magen Avot," on the first night of Passover when it falls on Shabbat. This blessing was only instituted because of harmful spirits, and now it is a night of protection. The prayer leader does not make Kiddush in the synagogue, for every poor person has four cups [of wine]. Additionally, the Kiddush cup needs to be part of the order. Even in a place where wine is not readily available in the city, one should not make Kiddush in the synagogue (Magen Avraham, subsection 4).

If one forgets to say "Ata Bechartanu" and instead says "Ya'aleh Veyavo," he has fulfilled his obligation, for he mentions the festival in it. The specific wording is not crucial after the fact. Even if it was Shabbat and he only said "Ya'aleh Veyavo" and mentioned Shabbat in it, he has fulfilled his obligation. Our teacher, the Rema, wrote in paragraph 3 that if one said "Ata Bechartanu" and mentioned Shabbat in it, nevertheless, he needs to mention it in "Ya'aleh Veyavo" as well. However, if he did not mention it in "Ya'aleh Veyavo," he does not need to repeat it. This is his language. From his words, it is clear that on a festival, one must also mention Shabbat in "Ya'aleh Veyavo." And even though on Rosh Chodesh that falls on Shabbat, we do not mention Shabbat in "Ya'aleh Veyavo," as I wrote in Siman 425, this is because one has already concluded with "Mekadesh HaShabbat." Moreover, if it is not Rosh Chodesh, Shabbat is not mentioned in the "Avodah" blessing, unlike a festival that falls on Shabbat, where one is still in the middle of the blessing and has not yet concluded with "Mekadesh HaShabbat," and it is not in the "Avodah" blessing, so it is appropriate to mention it. Nonetheless, the custom is not so, and we do not mention Shabbat in "Ya'aleh Veyavo," neither in prayer nor in Birkat Hamazon. The Levush writes the reason: because the concept of "remembrance" applies only to the festival and Rosh Chodesh, not to Shabbat, as it is written: "And on your days of joy, on your festivals, and on your new moons... and you shall be remembered before the Lord your God." If a Shaliach Tzibur forgot to mention Shabbat in the Shacharit prayer, see above Siman 126.

Our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in Section 4: On the first night of Passover, the Hallel is completed in the congregation with melody, with a blessing at the beginning and at the end. And similarly, on the second night outside the Land of Israel. Thus are his words. We do not have this custom, and we do not say the Hallel in the synagogue at all, because this is not mentioned in the Talmud. But in the Jerusalem Talmud, it is stated that they would recite the Hallel in the synagogue.

In the morning, they enter the synagogue and recite the Psalms of Praise just as on Shabbat. Regarding "A Psalm, a Song for the Sabbath day," some begin with "It is good to give thanks," since it is not Shabbat today. Nevertheless, there is no strictness in this, for Yom Tov is also called "Shabbat," as it is written "a day of rest" regarding Yom Tov as well. Therefore, the custom is to start as on Shabbat. They pray the morning prayer and complete the Hallel. However, they do not bless "to complete the Hallel" but rather "to read," lest one might skip a word and the blessing would be in vain. If there is doubt whether one recited Hallel or not, he does not repeat it out of doubt, as Hallel is of Rabbinic origin, and in cases of doubt regarding Rabbinic matters, we are lenient (Sha'arei Teshuva in the name of Sha'agat Aryeh).

One does not interrupt the recitation of Hallel except in the manner prescribed for the recitation of Shema: in the middle of a section, one may greet one's father or teacher out of reverence, and respond to the greeting of an honored person who greets him. Between the sections, one may greet an honored person and respond to the greeting of anyone. This applies on the first two days when the full Hallel is recited. However, on the other days, the law is like that of Rosh Chodesh, as explained in Siman 422. If one interrupted in the middle and waited even long enough to finish the entire Hallel, one does not return to the beginning but continues from where one stopped. This law is explained earlier in Siman 65. 

Also, know that in the case of Hallel, a knowledgeable person can fulfill the obligation on behalf of someone who is not knowledgeable, who hears it from him and fulfills his obligation. Even if there are ten people reciting it, and he hears it, he fulfills his obligation. For although with the reading of the Torah we say "two voices cannot be heard," nevertheless with Hallel, which is beloved, one pays attention and hears (Gemara Megillah 21a).

After Shacharit, two Torah scrolls are taken out. In the first one, five men are called up and read from the portion "Draw out…" until "from the land of Egypt, by their hosts." Additional readers are not added. Even though according to the basic law it is permissible to add, as I wrote in Siman 282, nevertheless we do not customarily add, following the opinion of "some say" that our teacher the Rema brought there. See there. When they finish, they take the second Torah scroll, place it on the table, and recite Kaddish over both. The Maftir is called from the second scroll, in the Musaf section of "Pinchas." The Haftarah is in the section about Passover from Joshua. Then they pray the Musaf prayer. The congregation mentions the rain, because it is not appropriate to announce not to say the rain prayer, like on Shemini Atzeret when it is announced to say the rain prayer. Since rain is a blessing, it is not proper to announce not to say it, and therefore they say it. The prayer leader ceases to mention it in the Tal prayer, and from then the congregation also does not mention rain anymore in Mincha. The laws of rain are explained in Siman 114. Additionally, the mention of "dew and rain" in the weekday Amidah is also stopped on Chol HaMoed. The custom is to recite the verses of Musaf in the Musaf prayer on every Yom Tov, after saying "From Your mouth as it is said." If one did not say it, he does not go back.

On the second night of Passover, we pray the evening service as we did the previous night. After the prayer, we begin counting the Omer, as it is written: "You shall count for yourselves from the day after the Sabbath." And the Sages taught in Menachot (65b): "You shall count for yourselves" – that the counting should be for each individual. Since it does not say like it does for the Jubilee year, "You shall count for yourself," which refers to the court, but rather "You shall count for yourselves" – we learn from this that it applies to each and every Jew (Tosafot there). And it has been received in tradition that this counting is an actual counting, to say: "Today is one day," "Today is the second day." It is unlike all the other countings in the Torah (Ran at the end of Pesachim), such as the counting of a zav and zavah and similar, where the intention is not an actual counting but rather to know the number. Here, however, it is an actual counting.

Most of the authorities agree that counting the Omer in the present time is only of rabbinic origin, since now we do not have the Omer offering. The counting mentioned in the Torah is to count from the Omer offering until the offering of the two loaves, and now this is not relevant (Ran, there). This is also implied in Menachot (66a), where Amemar says: "Count the days but do not count the weeks," and he said it is a remembrance for the Temple. Rashi explained: This current counting is not an obligation, because we do not have the Omer. Rather, it is a remembrance for the Temple... until here is his language. And in the Haggadah, it is said: At the time when Moses told them, "You will serve God on this mountain," the Israelites asked him: "Our teacher Moses! When will this service be?" He told them: "At the end of fifty days." And each person counted for themselves. From here, the sages established the counting of the Omer. Meaning: In the present time, when we do not bring the offering and not the Omer, we only count fifty days for the joy of the Torah just as the Israelites counted in that time. And this is a homiletic path, for the main point is that this is a remembrance for the Temple. But in any case, all this proves that the counting now is only of rabbinic origin (Ran, there).

However, this is not the opinion of the Rambam in Chapter 7 of Tamidin, Law 22, and this is his wording: "It is a positive commandment to count seven complete weeks from the day of the Omer offering... and this commandment applies to every Jewish man, in every place and at all times. Women and slaves are exempt from it." Thus far his wording, indicating that he wrote it is a positive commandment in every place and at all times. He explains in the Gemara there that the Amoraim disagreed on this: Amemar, who counted days but not weeks, believed that this is a Rabbinic ordinance in remembrance of the Temple. Abaye and the Rabbis of the school of Rav Ashi, who said it is a commandment to count days and a commandment to count weeks as we do, believed it to be of Torah origin (Kesef Mishneh). And he ruled according to the majority. And even though now there is no sacrifice, it can be said that the primary purpose of the counting is for the giving of the Torah, as Israel counted originally according to the Midrash we brought. However, the Holy One, blessed be He, commanded to bring sacrifices at the beginning of the count from the Omer of barley, and at its end from wheat, to indicate that without the Torah, we are likened to animals whose food is barley. As it is said in Sotah (15b) that the offering of a Sotah is from barley: she acted like an animal, therefore her offering is the food of animals. When they received the Torah, they became like a human being, and therefore their offering is from wheat, the food of humans. Thus, the Torah commanded to count for the offering. But the main intention is for the giving of the Torah, and therefore the commandment also applies in our time (so it seems in my humble opinion).

If one forgets to count at the beginning of the night, they should count throughout the entire night. It is a mitzvah for each person to count for themselves and not to rely on hearing it from the prayer leader; just as the mitzvah of taking the lulav applies to each individual, so too does this mitzvah. Only the blessing can be heard from the prayer leader, and one should answer "Amen," but the counting itself is an individual obligation.

One may count in any language, as long as they understand what they are saying. Some say that one fulfills the obligation by hearing it from the prayer leader, as hearing is like responding; this is written in the name of the Rashba (Beit Yosef and Magen Avraham, section 2). However, the true intention of the Rashba is regarding the blessing and not the counting itself (Chayei Adam, section 4). The Rashba himself wrote in a responsum (Siman 126) that he was asked why the prayer leader recites the blessing out loud, as the obligation is on each person to bless themselves. He replied that the obligation is for each person to count for themselves, but they can hear the blessing from the prayer leader; see there. And this is the main ruling in law.

One must count while standing, based on the interpretation of the verse "bekome" (when you stand) as "bekome" (while standing). The primary reason is explained in the Zohar Tetzaveh (page 183), that counting is a significant matter, akin to the Amidah prayer, and therefore must be done while standing. However, if one counted while sitting, they have fulfilled the obligation. Women are exempt because it is a positive time-bound commandment. Nevertheless, they customarily bless and count, as they do with other time-bound positive commandments such as the shofar, sukkah, and lulav.

One recites the blessing "Who has sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us regarding the counting of the Omer." However, one does not recite the blessing "Shehecheyanu," because "Shehecheyanu" is only recited over a commandment that brings joy. Here, on the contrary, we are reminded of the sorrow that the sacrifices have ceased (Rashba there). It is a mitzvah to count the days and it is a mitzvah to count the weeks. One says: "Today is one day of the Omer" or "in the Omer"; "Today is two days" up to seven days. On the seventh day, one says: "Today is seven days, which are one week." On the eighth day, one says: "Today is eight days, which are one week and one day." And so forth. This is not like those who say that one should count the weeks only at the end of each week (see Beit Yosef), as this is incorrect. When reaching beyond twenty, one says "twenty-one," "twenty-two," as the smaller number always comes first. If one altered the order, it does not invalidate. Similarly, if one counted only the days and not the weeks, one has fulfilled the obligation. Likewise, if one counted the weeks alone, one has fulfilled the obligation (Magen Avraham, subsection 4). This is also stated in the Tur, see there. Some disagree and hold that counting the weeks without the days does not fulfill the obligation, especially at the end of the week where there are no days at all (see Eliyah Rabbah and Chayei Adam). In cases of doubt concerning blessings, we rule leniently; however, it is certain that one should count again without a blessing. This should be done in any case of doubt.

And in this manner, one continues counting until forty-nine days. Until ten, one says "days," and afterward, one says "day." If one changes this, it does not invalidate the count. After the counting, one says "May it be Your will that the Temple be rebuilt," or "May the Merciful One restore the service of the Temple to its place." Some also say the Psalm "May God be gracious to us," because it contains forty-nine words. Some add a lengthy supplication, elaborating on hidden matters. Many great authorities have protested against this, as these are matters of great profundity, and such publicity is not appropriate. However, now it has become customary to say it publicly and with great emotional fervor.

If they made a mistake on a cloudy day and counted during the day, and they blessed "on the counting of the Omer" – they must count again after nightfall with a blessing, because counting during the day for the next day is meaningless. Therefore, those who are meticulous do not count until after nightfall, and this is the proper practice. If they counted after sunset during twilight – they have fulfilled their obligation. And the Rosh at the end of Pesachim wrote, and these are his words: And Rabbeinu Yitzchak explained that in a case of doubt regarding nightfall – one can bless, and there is no need to wait until it is definitely night, since it is a rabbinic doubt. Additionally, it is preferable to be close to nightfall because of the requirement of completeness. These are his words. And similarly, the Tosafot in Menachot wrote there and rejected it, saying that this does not seem correct. And all the poskim wrote similarly, that ideally one should count after nightfall. And we do not rely on counting during twilight except for the acceptance of Shabbat, because it is a mitzvah and an obligation to accept Shabbat while it is still day.

Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote in Paragraph 3: One who prays with the congregation while it is still daytime should count with them without a blessing. And if he remembers at night, he should bless and count. End of his words. And not specifically during the day, for if so, how could the congregation recite blessings in vain? And why should one count with them to support those who transgress? Furthermore, why does he say "if he remembers" – is he not obligated to remember, since he has not fulfilled his obligation at all? Rather, the intention is that it is not yet completely night, but twilight, during which it is permissible to count, as I have written. However, he is not accustomed to counting except at night. Therefore, he should count with them without a blessing, intending that if he does not remember later, he has fulfilled his obligation with this count. And if he remembers, he has not fulfilled his obligation. Such a condition is effective in this manner. This is what Rabbeinu Rema concluded, and this is his language: And even if he answered "Amen" to the congregation's blessing, if his intention was not to fulfill his obligation, he should recite the blessing and count at night. End of his words, which align with our explanation. (And this is also implied in Taz, Paragraph 6. The Magen Avraham, Paragraph 7, elaborated on his words, see there. Be precise and you will find it easy.) And that which he wrote "if his intention was not to fulfill his obligation" is because usually, when one counts with the congregation, his intention is to fulfill his obligation. And even according to the opinion that mitzvot require intention – this is considered intention, since he is counting with the congregation. (See Magen Avraham, Paragraph 8. In my humble opinion, it seems as I wrote. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

Regarding the wording "ba'omer" (in the Omer) or "la'omer" (of the Omer) – there is no definitive ruling. It seems more correct to say "la'omer," and that is how we say it. If one counts using acronyms, such as "ז' לעומר" (7 of the Omer), or "ח'" (8), or "י"א" (11), and the like – there are differing opinions on whether one has fulfilled the obligation or not. It appears that one has fulfilled the obligation, as it is no worse than using a foreign language. At most, one should count again without a blessing. 

And if someone wrote in a letter "today is such-and-such of the Omer," if he did not intend to fulfill the obligation, it seems that even according to the opinion that mitzvot do not require intention, he has not fulfilled the obligation; because he did not perform the mitzvah in its proper manner, it is as if he intended not to fulfill it. And even if he intended to fulfill the obligation, it seems that he has not fulfilled it. For even if writing is equivalent to speaking, this is only when the writing is to reveal the thoughts of his heart, not in a case where speaking is the mitzvah itself, similar to one who writes the Shema or prayer, who certainly has not fulfilled the obligation; or one who writes the Grace After Meals. (See Sha'arei Teshuvah, subsection 7, who writes this reasoning. And see the responsa of the Gaon Rabbi Akiva Eiger).

It is customary in the world to count [the Omer] after the evening prayer. However, the counting is not dependent on this, for one can count even before the recitation of the Shema and the prayer if it is night (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 7). And even on the night after Shabbat, if one has not yet performed Havdalah, one may still count, for although performing work is prohibited because of the Torah's decree that one must first perform Havdalah, it is nevertheless considered night (ibid). 

If one has prayed the evening prayer and has not yet counted, it seems that it is prohibited to eat or drink until one counts. This is what our teacher, the Rema, wrote in subparagraph 4: "When the time arrives, it is forbidden to eat until one counts." This is his wording. 

The difficulty is: is it not already prohibited because of the recitation of the Shema and the evening prayer? And even half an hour before, it is prohibited, as I wrote in Siman 235. However, this refers to one who has already prayed. But half an hour before, there is no need to be stringent if one has already prayed, according to the custom of the world to pray before nightfall.
