(See Magen Avraham, subparagraph 11, which questions this.)

Furthermore, he wrote that even if one has started eating, one should interrupt and count [the Omer]. However, if one started eating before the time [for counting] arrived, one does not need to interrupt but may finish eating and count afterward. These are his exact words. And the reason for being stringent about interrupting is because, according to the Rambam, the counting [of the Omer] is a Torah obligation even in our times, as I have written. However, even if it is of Rabbinic origin, since it is a minor matter, it is worth interrupting (Chayei Adam, small section 17). Nevertheless, if one started before the time arrived, one does not need to worry at all. And know that there are those who count the first counting after the seder. This is perplexing: how are they permitted to eat beforehand? This requires further investigation. (It can be said that the Magen Avraham in small section 1 raised a question in the name of the Kesef Mishneh: how are they permitted to count on the second night? This is a disrespect to the second day of Yom Tov, as it implies it is a weekday. And he answered: since by saying it, one is not declaring it a weekday, we do not have an issue with it. See there where he provides another answer. And we can say that those who practice this way hold by this answer, and therefore show that the counting does not interfere, because today is Yom Tov. Examine this and you will find it easy.)

On Friday night and the night of a festival, one recites the blessing and counts [the Omer] after the Kiddush in the synagogue. On Saturday night and the night following a festival, one counts before Havdalah, after the "Tiskabel" Kaddish. This is because the departure of the day [Shabbat or festival] is delayed, so the counting is done before Havdalah. Conversely, to sanctify the day [Shabbat or festival], it is done earlier, so Kiddush is recited before counting.

When Shabbat falls on the eve of Passover, meaning the last day of Passover falls on a Sunday, and there is both Kiddush and Havdalah on that Saturday night, one should count before reciting the blessing over the cup in the synagogue, so that Shabbat is not a burden upon him. The sanctity of Shabbat is greater than that of a festival, thus it is delayed until after Shabbat. This is the practice in the synagogue, but at home, one should count before Kiddush. Furthermore, it is forbidden to eat or drink before counting (Magen Avraham, subsection 14). After Kiddush, one must eat immediately, as Kiddush must be in the place of a meal, which is not the case with the Kiddush in the synagogue.

If someone asks his friend during twilight, "What is the count of the Omer for this night?" and he has not yet counted, he should respond, "Yesterday was such and such." For if he says, "Today is such and such," he is no longer able to count with a blessing. And even though he did not say "to the Omer," he has fulfilled his obligation post facto. Unless he explicitly intends not to fulfill his obligation, for even if commandments do not require intent, if he intended not to fulfill it, he has not fulfilled it. Likewise, if he said "such and such" without saying "today," it also means nothing (there, section 9). Similarly, if it is still before twilight, since it is not yet the time for counting, it means nothing. And if it happened that someone asked him during twilight and he said, "Today is such and such," he should count afterward without a blessing, and he gains that initially he did not intend to fulfill his obligation, and now he intends to fulfill it. And according to the opinion that commandments require intent, the intent is essential, therefore he should count afterward without a blessing. And some say he should count again with a blessing (Taz, section 7).

If one does not know the count and begins with the intention to complete it, such as by hearing it from his friend and remaining silent until he hears from his friend and completes it like him, he has fulfilled his obligation after the fact (bedi'avad). However, initially (lechatchilah), one should not recite the blessing until he knows the count for that day (section 8). If one makes a mistake, for example, if he begins and says, "Blessed are You, Hashem..." intending to say, "Today is the fourth day," but then remembers that today is the fifth day and concludes with "the fifth day," he has fulfilled his obligation. Alternatively, if today is the fourth day and he begins with the intention of the fourth day but mistakenly concludes with the fifth day, he does not need to repeat the blessing. Some say that in such a case, he should repeat the blessing because he has spoken falsely (Levush and Bach). Others say he does not repeat the blessing, but should count again without a blessing, as the initial blessing covers it unless there was a long interruption (Magen Avraham section 12). It is clear that if he corrects himself within the time it takes to say a greeting (toch kedei dibur), he has fulfilled his obligation (ibid.). The main point depends on the rulings detailed in Siman 209; see there (and see Taz section 9 who elaborates on this).

If one forgot to recite the blessing at night, he should count during the day without a blessing, as it is written: "they shall be complete," and a day without a night is not considered complete. The Ba'al Halachot Gedolot wrote that if one forgot to count for an entire day, whether it was the first day or any other day, he should count all the following days without a blessing, because it is not considered "complete." The early authorities were puzzled by this ruling, but since his words are based on tradition, the halacha follows this opinion. If one counted during the day as explained, he should continue counting all the days with a blessing. Similarly, if there is doubt whether one missed a day's counting, he should continue counting with a blessing, because this ruling is innovative, and we should not add to it. A minor who becomes Bar Mitzvah during the counting period, since he counted beforehand due to the obligation of education, it is clear that he should continue counting with a blessing. However, if he did not recite the blessing previously, he should not count with a blessing thereafter. Similarly, one who was ill and did not count, and then recovered, should not count with a blessing. Likewise, a convert who converted during the counting period should not recite the blessing. (See Sha'arei Teshuvah, subsection 5, for certain rulings that require further investigation. Examine and you will find clarity.)

Our Rabbi, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 10: It is forbidden to eat new grain even in our times, whether it is bread, roasted grain, or fresh kernels, until the beginning of the night of the eighteenth of Nisan, and in the Land of Israel until the beginning of the night of the seventeenth of Nisan. Thus are his words. And in Yoreh De'ah, section 293, we have elaborated on the law of new grain with the help of Heaven.

On the second day, we pray as on the first day, and "Mashiv HaRuach" [the phrase added in the Amidah prayer during the rainy season] is already omitted from the afternoon prayer of the previous day. We read from the Torah portion "Emor": "An ox or a sheep" until after "And Moses spoke." The Haftarah is from Kings about Josiah's Passover, from "And the king sent" until "and after him was none like him," which is in II Kings (chapter 23). There are those who have the custom on the second day to add some special food to the meal, and they call this "Esther's Feast," because on this day Esther made the feast for the king, and Haman was hanged. Regarding the piyutim [liturgical poems], each place should follow its custom. And know that the "Maariv" [evening] prayer is not said on Shabbat, and therefore, if the first day falls on Shabbat, the "Maariv" of the first day is said on the evening of the second day. A mnemonic for this is what is said at the end of Sukkah: "Yimotu Yidcheh," see there. However, some say that although this is the rule for other holidays, on the second night of Passover, since the "Maariv" relates to the counting [of the Omer], like the piyut "Or Yom Hanaf," it is not postponed (Magen Avraham, beginning of Siman 489).

On Tuesday, which is Chol HaMoed (the intermediate days of the festival), for the evening, morning, and afternoon prayers, one prays in the usual manner and says "Ya'aleh V'Yavo" in the blessing of "Avodah" (service). If one did not say it, they must repeat the prayer. Similarly, it is mentioned in the Grace After Meals (Birkat Hamazon). If one did not say it, they do not need to repeat it, because eating bread is not obligatory. Regarding the laying of Tefillin, this is explained above in Siman 31. For the Musaf prayer, one prays in the same manner as on a festival. However, Sephardim, who say "V'et Yom Tov Mikra Kodesh Ha'zeh" on Chol HaMoed, do not say "Yom Tov" but rather "Yom Mikra Kodesh Ha'zeh." After "Mipnei Chata'einu," when reaching "Al Yedei Moshe Avdecha Mipi Kevodecha Ka'amur," they begin "V'hikravtem." The same applies to the last days of Pesach. The reason they do not say on the last days "Uvayom Hashvi'i Mikra Kodesh..." as on other festivals is because this verse is stated in the Torah after "V'hikravtem," and they always say this before "V'hikravtem," and after "V'hikravtem" there is no place for it, as is evident. On Chol HaMoed and the last days of Pesach, the complete Hallel is not recited, because on the seventh day of Pesach the Egyptians were drowned. And the Holy One, blessed be He, said: "The works of My hands are drowning in the sea, and you are singing before Me?" And since on the seventh day it is not completed, it is not possible to complete it on Chol HaMoed, as it cannot be better than the festival day itself (Taz, small section 3). This is the reason according to the Midrash. The main reason is that the days do not differ in their sacrifices, unlike the festival of Sukkot. This reason is found in the Gemara.

Our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in Section 3: It is customary on Yom Tov to say "this Yom Tov, a holy convocation," and on Chol HaMoed to say "this day, a holy convocation." Thus are his words. And our master, the Rema, wrote about this that we do not have the custom to say "holy convocation" at all, neither on Yom Tov nor on Chol HaMoed. Thus are his words. And we have already explained in Siman 487 that his intention is that we do not say it close to "this day of the Festival of Matzot," because we say this at the end "a holy convocation in remembrance of the Exodus from Egypt." (And the Taz and Magen Avraham in subsection 2 were puzzled by him, but according to our explanation, his words are correct.)

The sequence of Torah readings during the eight days of Pesach (Passover): "Mashchu," "Tora," "Kadesh," "Bekaspa," "Pesal," "Bemidbara," "Shelach," "Buchra." This is the explanation: On the first day, we read "Mashchu," on the second day "Shor o Kesev," on the first day of Chol HaMoed we read "Kadesh Li Kol Bechor," on the second day "Im Kesef Talveh," on the third day "Pesal Lecha," on the fourth day "Bemidbar" in relation to Pesach Sheni, on the seventh day of Pesach we read "Beshalach" until after the song, and on the last day of Pesach "Kol HaBechor." This order does not change unless Pesach begins on a Thursday, in which case on the first day of Chol HaMoed we read "Pesal Lecha," starting from "Re'eh Atah Omer Elai Ha'al..."; and on the first, second, and third days of Chol HaMoed we read "Kadesh," "Bekaspa," "Bemidbara." On all days of Chol HaMoed, we read from the second Sefer Torah for the fourth Aliyah, from "Vehikravtem" until "Kol Melechet Avodah Lo Ta'asu." Similarly, on the last days, this is read for the maftir. On the seventh day of Pesach, the haftarah is "Vayedaber David" from the end of Shmuel. On the last day of Pesach, the haftarah is from Isaiah: "Od Hayom B’Nov La'amod," because it speaks about Sennacherib, whose plague occurred on the night of Pesach. On the seventh day, we read the song corresponding to the Song of the Sea. During the Kiddush of the last days, we do not say "Shehecheyanu," because it is not considered a separate festival. In the prayers and Kiddush, we say "Zman Cheiruteinu" as on the first days, even though they had already left Egypt. But until after the splitting of the sea and the drowning of the Egyptians, it is still called "Zman Cheiruteinu" (the time of our freedom).

When Shabbat falls during Chol HaMoed, for Ma'ariv, Shacharit, and Mincha, one prays as on every Shabbat, but one says "Ya'aleh V'Yavo" in the "Avoda" section. If one did not say it, they must repeat the prayer. Similarly, in Birkat Hamazon, because it is obligatory to eat bread on Shabbat. In Mussaf, one recites the Mussaf for all of Chol HaMoed and adds "this Shabbat day," and says "You have given us, Hashem our God, this Shabbat day and this Festival of Matzot day." Likewise, in "Umipnei Chataeinu," one says "the additional sacrifices of...," and concludes "who sanctifies the Shabbat, Israel, and the times." However, the Maftir does not conclude except for Shabbat, because without Shabbat there would be no Haftorah on Chol HaMoed (Taz, section 5). For this reason, it is also the same on Shabbat Chol HaMoed Sukkot, but the custom is not so, for on Shabbat Chol HaMoed Sukkot, "the Festival of Sukkot" is mentioned because the additional sacrifices differ, and Hallel is completed, which is not the case on Pesach (Magen Avraham, section 7). The Haftorah is read from Ezekiel "The hand of Hashem was upon me...," because it speaks of the resurrection of the dead, which is destined to occur on Pesach. On Sukkot, the Haftorah is "On the day that Gog shall come," because the victory over Gog and Magog will happen in Tishrei (Tur). It is customary to read Shir HaShirim, because Shir HaShirim speaks of the love between the Jewish people and their Father in Heaven, which began with the Exodus from Egypt. On Shavuot, the book of Ruth is read, and on Sukkot, the book of Kohelet is read. If all of Chol HaMoed is during the weekdays, this is read on one of the last days when Shabbat falls. The custom is not to recite a blessing over them, even if read from a scroll, because we do not find an ordinance from the Sages of the Talmud regarding this. Some of the great authorities wrote to recite a blessing, but this is not the custom (and the Taz wrote that it would be a blessing in vain).

On the night following a festival, whether it is the night following a festival leading into a weekday or the night following a festival leading into Chol Hamoed, we recite Havdalah, because even Chol Hamoed is considered a weekday relative to the festival. We say "Ata Chonantanu" and the order of Havdalah is the same as on the night following Shabbat. And even though at this time it is not appropriate to say "between the seventh day and the six workdays," nevertheless, this is the order of Havdalah, and one proceeds with the order of Havdalah even though it is not applicable at this moment. However, we do not recite a blessing over the candle, since the use of fire was not prohibited on Yom Tov, nor over the spices because on Yom Tov there is no "additional soul" (neshama yeteira). The reason we do not say a blessing over the spices when transitioning from Shabbat to Yom Tov is because there are good foods (Magen Avraham). This matter is further clarified in Siman 473. 

If someone extends their meal on the last day of Pesach until nightfall and then recites Havdalah, they are permitted to eat chametz even if they have not yet prayed Ma'ariv (Magen Avraham). This is because the matter of chametz is not related to the prayer, and since it is night, it is permitted to eat chametz. However, if they have not recited Havdalah, the sanctity of Yom Tov still remains upon them.

On Yom Tov that falls on Motza'ei Shabbat, one says in "Ata Bechartanu": "V'todieinu." For "Ata Chonantanu" cannot be said because it is not a weekday, but rather that the sanctity of Shabbat is more stringent than that of Yom Tov, as we conclude in Havdalah, "between holy and holy." And in the prayer, there is no conclusion in the Havdalah; therefore, it is necessary to precede by stating that Yom Tov is also holy, but Shabbat is holier. For this reason, we say, "And grant us times of joy and sacred festivals... and bestow upon us the sanctity of Shabbat, the honor of the festival, and the celebration of the pilgrimage festival." This is akin to "distinguishing between holy and holy." In the Gemara, this is called "a precious pearl," as it elucidates the elevated status of Israel, Shabbat, and Yom Tov.

The Tur wrote: In Ashkenaz and France, it is customary to fast on Monday, Thursday, and Monday after Passover and Sukkot. They wait until the entire month of Nissan and Tishrei has passed and then fast, as they do not wish to fast in Nissan and Tishrei. They based this on the verse in Job (Job 1:5): "And it was, when the days of the feast had gone round... perhaps my children have sinned...". Because the festival days are days of feasting and joy, perhaps they have sinned. They treat these fasts like a public fast, reading "Vayechal". Thus far his words. There is an allusion in the Gemara: "the end of the year is a festival" (Kidushin 81a). Our Rabbis, the Tosafists, explained this, and this is their language: "The weak point of the year for sin is during the festival days... Therefore, it is customary to fast after Passover and after Sukkot." Thus far their words. After Shavuot, they did not concern themselves, as it is only two days even in the Diaspora, and there is not enough time for sin.

It is customary that on the first Shabbat after Rosh Chodesh Iyar or Marcheshvan, the fasts are announced. And they recite the "Mi Sheberach..." as printed in the prayer books, because we did not accept it as obligatory. For this reason, now, due to the weakening of the generations, the number of those who fast has diminished. And one who answered "Amen" does not need to accept the fast on Sunday and Wednesday during Mincha, as this is considered acceptance. However, the "Amen" does not compel him to fast, as some mistakenly believe, for the "Amen" is merely an affirmation of the blessing for those who voluntarily choose to fast. Nevertheless, this is no less than acceptance during Mincha. And in Siman 566 and 568 these laws will be explained with the help of Heaven. And when there is a circumcision or a wedding, it is announced during Mincha (Magen Avraham).

These days between Passover and Shavuot are firmly established among all of Israel for many hundreds of years as days of judgment and mourning, because in this short period twelve thousand pairs of Rabbi Akiva's students, who were great Torah scholars, died, as it is stated in Yevamot (62b), and they all died from the plague of ascaris (ibid.). Additionally, we have seen that the main days of persecutions in the past hundreds of years in France and Germany occurred during these days, as explained by the liturgical poems composed by our ancestors for the Sabbaths between Passover and Shavuot. These poems are filled with lamentations and woe. There are also other reasons why these days are considered days of judgment (see Chayei Adam, section 3).

Therefore, it has been the custom of all Israel from the time of the Geonim not to marry a woman between Passover and Shavuot. They did not differentiate between a mitzvah marriage, such as one who has not yet fulfilled the commandment of procreation, and others. And even though in cases of complete mourning there are distinctions, nevertheless, here they were stringent upon themselves. However, if someone hastened and got married, we do not punish him since he performed a mitzvah. All the more so if he saw that the match might be nullified. But to betroth and sanctify a woman - that is permissible. And similarly, it is permissible among us to arrange matches and write conditions, lest someone else precede him. It is permissible to make a meal, but without dancing and rejoicing. And all the more so it is forbidden to play musical instruments. Likewise, a non-obligatory meal, such as friendship meals, is permissible as long as it is without dancing and rejoicing.

And so, the custom in these countries is not to have haircuts during these days, which is also a matter of mourning. And someone who gets a haircut is penalized for violating the custom and not performing a mitzvah. It is obvious that if one needs a haircut for health reasons, it is permitted. Similarly, if there is a circumcision during these days, the participants of the circumcision, namely the mohel (circumciser), the sandek (who holds the baby), and the father of the child, are permitted to have a haircut the day before the circumcision, close to the evening, because it is their festival day.

And know that there are different customs regarding this matter: There are those who have the custom to prohibit [marriages and haircuts] from immediately after Passover until Lag BaOmer, and from then on it is permitted to marry and cut hair, because it is stated in the Midrash that fifteen days before Shavuot they ceased dying, leaving thirty-four days [of mourning]. And it would have been appropriate to observe the prohibition until the thirty-fifth day of the Omer count, but we say that part of the day is considered like the whole day, and it is permitted on the thirty-fourth day and not earlier. This is the approach of our teacher, the Beit Yosef, who wrote: "The custom is not to cut hair until Lag BaOmer, as it is said that they ceased dying then. And one should not cut hair until the morning of the thirty-fourth day, unless Lag BaOmer falls on a Friday, in which case one may cut hair in honor of the Sabbath." Thus far his words. And he wrote in paragraph 3: "There are those who have the custom to cut hair on Rosh Chodesh Iyar, but this is a mistake." Thus far his words, meaning: According to this custom, since it is permitted after Lag BaOmer, the prohibition begins immediately after Passover, because they died for thirty-four days after Passover. Therefore, how can they cut hair on Rosh Chodesh Iyar? It would be a contradiction. And the mention of haircuts also applies to marriages, as it is one matter.

And there is another custom where the prohibition continues even after Lag BaOmer until Shavuot, or until the Three Days of Hagbalah (the days of preparation before Shavuot). For according to the simple understanding of the Gemara in Yevamot there, their deaths continued until Shavuot; and only on Lag BaOmer itself are marriages and haircuts permitted, because it is established for us as a day of festivity, and we increase somewhat in meals, and they say that on this day they did not die at all, and afterwards they began to die again. Additionally, it serves as a sign that they died for thirty-three days. And the days begin from the second day of the month of Iyar, and continue until Shavuot. And even Lag BaOmer itself is counted in the calculation, even though they did not die on this day.

According to this custom, it is permitted [to have haircuts] until Rosh Chodesh Iyar. The prohibition begins on the first day of Rosh Chodesh Iyar and continues until the first day of the Three Days of Restriction, with part of the day being considered as a whole day. Therefore, according to this custom, it is permitted until Rosh Chodesh Iyar, and also on Lag BaOmer itself, as well as during the three Days of Restriction. All other days are prohibited. This is also our custom. If Lag BaOmer falls on a Sunday, haircuts are permitted on the preceding Friday in honor of the Sabbath.

These are the words of our teacher, the Rema, who wrote in Section 3: "However, in many places, the custom is to get haircuts until Rosh Chodesh Iyar, and those people do not get haircuts from Lag B'Omer onward, even though it is permissible to get a haircut on Lag B'Omer itself. And in those places that have the custom to get haircuts from Lag B'Omer onward, they do not get haircuts at all after Pesach until Lag B'Omer." This is his language. And what he wrote in Section 1: "However, from Lag B'Omer onward, everything is permitted," this is his language—this is according to this custom, which allows haircuts from Lag B'Omer onward, and no haircuts until Rosh Chodesh Iyar. This is the custom of our teacher, the Beit Yosef, but not for us. And what he wrote in Section 2 about the words of our teacher, the Beit Yosef, that one does not get a haircut on Lag B'Omer but rather on the 34th day, he wrote: "And in these countries, they do not follow his words, but rather they get haircuts on the day of Lag B'Omer and increase somewhat in joy, and they do not say Tachanun." This is his language. And his intention is that regarding Lag B'Omer itself—in every place, they have the custom to permit, whether according to the custom of our teacher, the Beit Yosef, or according to our custom, because they consider this day somewhat of a festival, including the Mincha prayer before it. And they are accustomed to call it "the Hilula of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai," and in the Land of Israel, they increase in prayer and lighting candles at his holy grave. And they say that he passed away on this day, and also that he exited the cave on this day. (And the Magen Avraham wrote in Section 3 and in the Ba'er Heitev that a great individual was accustomed to say "Nachem" every day, and they said it on Lag B'Omer and he was punished. See there.)

And our master, the Rema, wrote that one should not practice part of one custom in one city and part of another custom, because of "lo titgodedu" (do not form factions). All the more so, it is forbidden to act leniently in both. Thus is his language. For one should not adopt the leniency of one custom to allow until the first of Iyar, and the leniency of another to allow from Lag BaOmer onwards, as this would be self-contradictory. And it seems to me that his intention is that even though at the end of the first chapter of Yevamot, we say that in one city with two courts, "lo titgodedu" does not apply, and this is also the conclusion of the Talmud there according to Rava. And it is true that the Rambam, at the end of the laws of idolatry, ruled that in this matter, "lo titgodedu" does apply, like Abaye in Yevamot; though they were puzzled by his ruling like Abaye and not like Rava. However, we have explained his words in Yoreh De'ah at the end of Siman 180, see there. And this is the matter: Rava rejected Abaye, as in matters of prohibitions and permissions, the verse "after the majority to incline" teaches us that we must rule according to the majority view. And if so, for Rava, why would one court in one city need the verse "lo titgodedu"? Rather, Rava truly aimed to reject Abaye, saying that in matters of rulings, "lo titgodedu" is unnecessary. For in one city with two courts, "lo titgodedu" does not apply, and for one court, we know from the verse "after the majority to incline." Rather, the main verse of "lo titgodedu" pertains to customs in general, and even for two courts in one city, it is forbidden. For in rulings, the matter is not handed over to the public, but in general customs, when some do this and others do that, even if it comes from two courts, it is still disgraceful that it appears as if Israel in one city is divided into factions. And these are the words of our master, the Rema, that one should not practice part of one custom and part of another custom in one city, even when it comes from two courts. And this is also the intention of the Rambam, as I wrote there. And the minority follows the majority (see Magen Avraham there).

Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in paragraph 4: Women customarily refrain from work from Passover until Shavuot, from sunset onward. Thus are his words, in memory of the righteous women in the days of Rabbi Akiva who attended to his students (Eliyah Rabbah, section 11, in the name of Tanya). And there are those who wrote that men also should refrain from work at this time (ibid., in the name of Knesset HaGedolah). And this is also implied by the language of the Tur, except that he concluded that women customarily refrain from work, meaning the custom was for everyone because the students died after sunset, but only women accepted this custom. And even they only refrained from work from after sunset until after the Maariv prayer following the counting of the Omer. There is also an allusion to this: "And you shall count... seven weeks," implying "rest from work" (Tur). And even now, there are women who follow this custom.

On the fiftieth day of the counting of the Omer – it is the Festival of Shavuot. This is how the Torah refers to this festival, meaning: the festival that comes after the completion of the counting of the weeks, as it is written (Deuteronomy 16:9): "You shall count seven weeks." Our Sages, of blessed memory, called this festival "Atzeret," and the commentators have already spoken about this. It appears to me that the Targum (Aramaic translation of the Torah) always translates “weeks” as "Shavu'in." In the book of Numbers, regarding the verse "On the day of the firstfruits, when you bring a new meal-offering to the Lord in your Shavu'oteichem" (Numbers 28:26), Onkelos translates it as "in your Atzeret," in the language of the Sages. Perhaps this is because at the chosen event (the giving of the Torah), they were commanded "Do not go near a woman." And regarding David, when he came to Ahimelech, it is written (1 Samuel 21:6): "For women have been kept from us." This alludes to the fact that the Torah was given in purity and sanctity, and in remembrance of this, the Sages called it "Atzeret."

Even though the Torah does not mention the giving of the Torah on Shavuot, this is because the Torah, when it was given, was given forever and for all eternity; and it is not appropriate to designate a specific day for this as with all other festivals where a specific event happened on that day, like the Exodus from Egypt on Passover and the Clouds of Glory on Sukkot which were during a fixed time period during their journey in the desert. However, the Torah is eternal and for all time, and therefore the Torah linked this festival to the offering of the two loaves, which was only on this day. Nevertheless, in prayer we say "the time of the giving of our Torah," because on the day that Shavuot falls for us, that is, the sixth of Sivan, the Torah was given to Israel. As it is taught in Shabbat (86b): The Sages taught: On the sixth of the month the Torah was given to Israel. Rabbi Yossi says: On the seventh of it. And the halacha follows the Sages. And even though Passover, when Israel left Egypt, was on a Thursday, and the Torah was given on Shabbat, therefore according to our calculation that Iyar is always incomplete and Nisan is full, Rosh Chodesh Sivan was on a Sunday, and thus the Torah was given on the seventh of Sivan; it can be said that when they established it based on sighting, Iyar could also be full, and Rosh Chodesh Sivan was on a Monday. (See Chayei Adam for what he wrote. And what the Magen Avraham questioned from what we hold in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 196 regarding a woman who emits semen for six intervals, which is according to Rabbi Yossi as stated there in Shabbat — this is merely a stringency. And indeed, Rambam in the fifth chapter of the Laws of the Fathers of Impurity did not rule thus, as Magen Avraham himself wrote. And Magen Avraham brought from the Rama a hint regarding the Diaspora — it is a beautiful and refined hint. And the Torah was given in the desert and not in the Land of Israel to teach that the Torah is not dependent on place, and the desert is outside the land. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

On the night of Shavuot, one does not recite Kiddush over the cup until it is truly night, due to the principle of "temimot," meaning the counting should be completed in its entirety. The early pious ones used to stay awake all night, as mentioned in the Zohar. Even now, many do so, and in the morning they go to the mikveh. All of this is in remembrance of the giving of the Torah. The matter of the blessing over the Torah has been explained in Siman 47. On the night of immersion, one should not refrain from marital relations.

The order of prayers is like on Passover, except that instead of "the time of our freedom" we say "the time of the giving of our Torah." The complete Hallel is recited. Two Torah scrolls are taken out; in the first one, we read from "Yitro" from "In the third month" until the end of the section. The Ten Commandments are read with the upper cantillation marks, as is known to the readers. Before the priestly blessing, "Akdamut" is recited. In the second Torah scroll, the Maftir is read from "On the Day of First Fruits." The Haftarah is from the vision of Ezekiel's chariot, ending with the verse "And a spirit lifted me" that appears later. On the second day, we read "All the firstborn," and if it falls on Shabbat, we start from "You shall surely tithe." The Haftarah is from Habakkuk: "The Lord is in His holy temple," since the prophecy there is about the giving of the Torah and the Exodus from Egypt, concluding with "For the conductor, on my stringed instruments." The customs of the liturgical poems are followed according to each community's custom, but all of Israel recites the 613 commandments on Shavuot, each in their own version. For in the Ten Commandments, there are 620 letters, corresponding to the 613 commandments of the Torah and seven rabbinic commandments, as all are hinted at in the tablets, beyond what the mouth can speak and the ear can hear. (And we begin the Haftarah with "A prayer of Habakkuk.")

It is customary to eat dairy and honey foods, as it is written, "Honey and milk are under your tongue." There are also other hints regarding the consumption of dairy. They found a hint in the Torah in the acronym of "A new offering to the Lord during your weeks." This is the language of our Rabbi, the Rema: It is customary to eat dairy foods on the first day of Shavuot. It seems to me the reason is similar to the two cooked dishes taken on the night of Passover, one as a remembrance of the Paschal lamb and one as a remembrance of the festival offering. Similarly, we eat dairy foods and then we eat meat foods. We must bring two loaves of bread to the table, which is in place of the altar, and this serves as a remembrance of the two loaves that were offered on the Day of First Fruits. This is his language. Additionally, because through the giving of the Torah they were elevated and transformed from the impurity of Egypt to the purity of holiness, therefore, we eat dairy which is formed from blood, as we say: Blood is transformed and becomes milk. There is also a hint that judgment has turned into mercy. It is also customary to add saffron, which is called "za'afran" in the dishes and cooked foods, because it brings joy and has a good fragrance, as it is written, "The smell of your oils is good" (see Magen Avraham, small section 6, in the name of the Zohar, and this is as I have written). One should not be lenient on Shavuot in the matter of eating meat after dairy or vice versa more than during the rest of the year. Additionally, regarding milk that was milked on that day by a non-Jew – it is forbidden to consume it, just as on any other festival day.

It is written that it is customary to spread grasses on Shavuot in the synagogue and in homes, as a remembrance of the joy of the giving of the Torah. If Shavuot falls on a Sunday, the grasses are spread on the eve of Shabbat, because they are muktzeh (set aside and not to be handled) and it is forbidden to move them on Shabbat and Yom Tov when they are not suitable for animal food. However, if one had intention for them on the eve of Shabbat and the eve of Yom Tov, it is permitted, as I have written in Siman 288 (Magen Avraham, subsection 5). Some have the custom to place trees (there). However, in previous generations, the trees and grasses were abolished for reasons known to the great ones of the generation.

It is forbidden to fast on the day following the holiday of Shavuot, and on any Isru Chag (the day following a festival), one should not fast nor recite Tachanun. However, Isru Chag Shavuot is more stringent because if Shavuot falls on Shabbat, the day for offering the festival sacrifices would be the day after Shabbat, since they do not override Shabbat. Women are permitted to work on Isru Chag, and all the more so men. Tachanun is not recited from Rosh Chodesh Sivan (the beginning of the month of Sivan) until after Isru Chag, because on Rosh Chodesh it is certainly not recited, and the three days before Shavuot are the three days of preparation for the giving of the Torah and are days of joy. Consequently, the day between Rosh Chodesh and the first day of preparation is also included in the joy. Additionally, on that day, Moses commanded the people to sanctify themselves, and it is customary to call it "the distinguished day" because of this. Furthermore, Yom Kippur also falls on this day. (Note that nowadays, Shavuot cannot fall on Shabbat, due to the rule that Passover does not start on Monday, Wednesday, or Friday, so the second day of Passover determines the day of Shavuot. However, when the months were sanctified based on sighting of the moon, it was possible for Shavuot to fall on Shabbat.) With Heavenly assistance, we conclude the laws of Pesach.

Six days in the year, and in the Diaspora twelve days, are holidays. And these are: the first day of Passover, and in the Diaspora two days; and the seventh day of Passover, and in the Diaspora also the eighth day of Passover; and one day of Shavuot, and in the Diaspora two days; and one day of Rosh Hashanah, and in the Diaspora two days, and now also in the Land of Israel it is so; and the first day of the Festival of Sukkot, and in the Diaspora two days; and Shemini Atzeret, and in the Diaspora one more day.

These days, the Torah has forbidden labor, except for work related to food preparation, as it is written in the portion of "Bo" (Exodus 12:16): "No manner of work shall be done in them, except that which everyone must eat, that only may be done for you." Therefore, in "Emor" (Leviticus 23:7) and "Pinchas" (Numbers 28:18), it is written: "You shall not do any servile work," meaning that work related to food preparation is not considered servile work, but work that brings pleasure to the body. And regarding the seventh day of Passover, it is written at the end of "Re'eh" (Deuteronomy 16:8): "You shall not do work" – it did not specify "servile work" because it had already been explained in "Emor" and "Pinchas." Therefore, it was abbreviated in Deuteronomy, as several commandments were shortened in Deuteronomy, as is known.

Therefore, anyone who refrains from labor on any of them fulfills a positive mitzvah, as it says regarding them "a day of rest," meaning: you shall cease from labor. And anyone who performs labor on any of them transgresses a negative commandment of "you shall not do any laborious work." This is what is customarily stated in the Talmud regarding Yom Tov, that it has both a positive commandment and a negative commandment, meaning: one who performs labor transgresses the positive commandment of "a day of rest" and the negative commandment of "you shall not do any laborious work." (And so explained Rashi in Beitzah 8b.)

On all the festivals it is written "It shall be a holy convocation for you." And it is expounded in the Torat Kohanim in Parashat Emor, and in the Mechilta in Parashat Bo: "A holy convocation" – sanctify it. How do you sanctify it? With food and drink, and with clean clothing. And in Rosh Hashanah (32a) it is said: "A holy convocation" – this is the sanctity of the day. And it seems to me that also in the Torat Kohanim and the Mechilta this is the explanation: "A holy convocation" – sanctify it, meaning with the sanctity of the day: with Kiddush, and with prayer, and with Birkat Hamazon. How do you sanctify it? Meaning: how will it be practically evident that this day is holy for you? With food, drink, and clean clothing. You should not eat as on a weekday, nor drink as on a weekday, nor dress as on a weekday. And this is the enjoyment of the festival day, and it turns out that the enjoyment of the festival day is like a mitzvah from the Torah (so it seems to me in my humble opinion).

Even though on Shabbat, if one performs many prohibited labors in one lapse of awareness, one is liable for each and every labor, as it is written in Siman 243, on Yom Tov there is no sacrificial offering for unintentional transgression, since for intentional transgression there is only a prohibition. However, if one performs many labors with one warning, it would be logical that one should receive lashes for each and every labor, just as on Shabbat one is liable for a sin-offering for each labor even if they were done in one lapse of awareness. Nevertheless, it is not so, and one who performs many labors with one warning, such as building, demolishing, planting, weaving, and similar activities, is only lashed once. Thus, our sages of blessed memory said (Makkot 21b): The separation of labors applies to Shabbat, but there is no separation of labors for Yom Tov. For Shabbat, there is a scriptural derivation for this, as written there, which is not the case for Yom Tov.

It is taught at the beginning of the third chapter of Beitzah (23b): One may not trap fish from ponds on Yom Tov, even though slaughtering, baking, and cooking are primary categories of forbidden labor that are permitted for the sake of Yom Tov. The reason is that it is impossible to perform these tasks on the eve of Yom Tov, for with regard to slaughtering, there is a concern that the meat would spoil if left overnight. However, trapping can be done on the eve of Yom Tov, and the fish can be left in the water without dying, and they can be taken the next day. This is the language of Rashi, of blessed memory. The explanation of his words is that the Torah permits the labor of preparing food on Yom Tov because it is better to have fresh bread, freshly cooked food, and freshly slaughtered meat. However, in the case of trapping, even though fish caught on Yom Tov are better than those caught the day before, one can trap them on the eve of Yom Tov, keep them in water, and they will be as good as if they were caught on Yom Tov.

And behold, although there are those who say that Rashi's intention is that the prohibition applies to things that can be done on the eve of Yom Tov and will not be ruined — this is only a rabbinic prohibition (Maggid Mishneh), nevertheless, many agree that his intention is that the prohibition is from the Torah (Yam Shel Shlomo and Pnei Yehoshua, and similarly, the Ran wrote this, see there). And so wrote the Sefer Mitzvot Gadol in the name of Rabbi Yitzchak the Elder, one of the Tosafists. And this is the language of the Sefer Mitzvot Gadol at the beginning of the laws of Yom Tov: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Shmuel says that preparations — it is logical that they should be permitted by Torah law in all respects if not for the fact that the Torah specifically excluded them, because they would be just as good if made yesterday as if made today. But food preparation is certainly prohibited by Torah law, except for something that would spoil if made yesterday. So far his language. And also the Ran wrote that it appears explicitly from the Jerusalem Talmud that they are from the Torah. And even the Baraita in Shabbat (95a), that teaches: One who sweeps, sprinkles water, or removes honeycombs; if he did so intentionally on Yom Tov, he receives forty lashes, see there — implies this.

There is another approach in the Jerusalem Talmud, Tractate Beitzah, Chapter One (Halacha 10). It states: From where do we derive that one should not select, grind, or sift? Rabbi Acha in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish: "No work shall be done on them" until "and you shall observe the commandments." Rabbi Yosi asks: Did they only learn this for cooking? Rather, from here, Rabbi Yose did not say so. Instead, Rabbi Yosi in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish: "Only that which is eaten by every soul, that alone may be done for you" until "and you shall observe the commandments." Hezekiah taught and disagreed: "Only that alone" - these are exclusions, that one should not harvest, grind, or sift on Yom Tov. Thus far are the words of the Jerusalem Talmud. The explanation is: The Torah only permitted from kneading and onward, which is the time of guarding the matzah. But not the preceding labors, which are not typically done immediately before eating, but rather much earlier, like harvesting, grinding, and sifting. And in the case of selection, they argue.

In the Mishnah at the end of the first chapter of Beitzah, Beit Hillel permits the grinding of spices and the sorting of legumes. However, the Jerusalem Talmud there explains that even though grinding is a derivative of the labor of grinding, it is nevertheless permitted because it is grinding in an unusual manner. Regarding the sorting, the Jerusalem Talmud dismisses it, noting that there is a dispute between Rabban Gamliel and the Rabbis. From the words of the Rosh at the beginning of the third chapter, it seems that the Jerusalem Talmud's statement is merely an allusion. It is surprising to say this, as it previously states there: "One who sorts, grinds, and sifts on Shabbat is stoned, and on Yom Tov he receives forty lashes." Refer there. The same is found in the Jerusalem Talmud in the second halachah of the chapter "Klal Gadol." According to the Jerusalem Talmud, it fits well with what is said at the beginning of Beitzah, that it is a decree lest one come to pluck. According to Rashi's explanation, it is somewhat difficult: for it is certain that fruit plucked today is better than fruit plucked yesterday, as the Raavad wrote in his critiques in the first chapter, law 8, and this is his language: "In all these, there is no reason why one should not pluck greens or gather fruits from the tree on Yom Tov, for those freshly picked today are better..." until here is his language. But according to the Jerusalem Talmud, it is satisfactory, since they are not labors done before the meal like kneading. (And the Raavad also wrote there: "And the Jerusalem Talmud relies on the verse 'but that which every soul must eat,'" until here is his language, which also implies that it is an allusion. Yet the Jerusalem Talmud states: "He receives forty lashes." This requires great investigation.)

And this is the opinion of the Maharshal in Yam Shel Shlomo, the beginning of the third chapter, and this is his language: Specifically, these labors which are immediately for eating, such as slaughtering, and similarly kneading and onward. But all other labors which stand for many days…, such as picking fruits and harvesting grain, and even grinding is typically… for many days. And from grinding pepper there is no proof, because it stands for eating as a spice… they lose their flavor. And even though salt does not lose its flavor, nevertheless it is not customary to make a storehouse from it after grinding, rather they grind it for the need of a day or two… And the general principle we derive: harvesting, grinding, picking, trapping, and all similar things that are not immediately for eating like slaughtering and kneading – are prohibited by Torah law. And a change does not help, even if it happened in a way that it was not possible to do them before the holiday. And actual food preparation, even if it is possible to do it on the eve of the holiday – is permitted by Torah law, and prohibited rabbinically. And by means of a change, it is permitted. And if it loses its flavor – it is permitted even without a change. Until here is his language, and this is the way of the Jerusalem Talmud. And from our Talmud there is no contradiction to this, and on the contrary, from the decree at the beginning of Beitzah lest one go and pick, it is clearly implied that picking is a Torah prohibition. And the Tosafot in Beitzah agreed with this view.

Indeed, the opinion of the Rambam, the Rosh, the Tosafot on Shabbat (95a), and several other Rishonim is that, according to Torah law, all labors related to food preparation are permitted, even reaping and grinding. However, many labors are prohibited by Rabbinic decree. And this is the language of the Rambam in the first chapter, law 5: Any labor that can be done on the eve of a Festival without causing loss or deficiency – the Sages prohibited doing it on the Festival itself, even if it is for the purpose of eating. And why did they prohibit this? As a decree lest a person leave tasks that can be done on the eve of the Festival for the Festival itself, and thus the entire Festival would be spent doing those tasks, and one would be prevented from enjoying the Festival… And for this same reason, they did not prohibit carrying on the Festival, even though carrying can be done on the eve of the Festival, in order to increase the joy of the Festival: that one can go and bring whatever he desires, and not have his hands tied. But other labors, since they involve effort – one does not perform them on the Festival. How so? One does not reap, thresh, winnow, select, grind wheat, or sift on the Festival, for all these and similar activities can be done on the eve of the Festival without causing loss or deficiency. Thus far his language.

The Ra'avad questions: If so, why did they not permit the picking of vegetables and fruits, since those of today are better than those of yesterday? The Maggid Mishneh answers: Because in all cases where the main labor does not result in loss, they did not worry about the partial loss. And since the main reaping of grain is equally good whether from yesterday or today, they did not permit the picking of fruits and vegetables even though there is a loss. And although they permitted the grinding of spices, even though it is a derivative of grinding, because it is like preparing food, and they were lenient with preparations; see there. And he concludes: This requires further study. And indeed, why would the Sages be more lenient with preparations than with the food itself? Also, it is impossible to say like the Yerushalmi that we brought in section 9 that only with a change is it permitted, because the Rambam ruled explicitly in the third chapter, law 12, that spices do not require a change. And this is the way of the Rif: that the change mentioned in the Gemara is only regarding the salting, see there. It seems more reasonable to say as the Ran wrote, that the Sages only prohibited labor that is done for many days, like reaping, picking, and grinding, even if it would spoil like picking fruits and vegetables, as they are done as the main labor. But grinding spices, which is not done as the main labor of grinding but in a mortar, and is not done for many days – they permitted, because they spoil from yesterday, see there. In this, the reason of the Rambam that it would nullify the joy of the festival does not apply. And we cannot say that since grinding in this manner is permitted, we should say that because it is permitted for the need, it is also permitted not for the need. This is not difficult at all, as the main labor was not permitted, and this grinding is not the main labor of grinding, as I wrote. And especially according to the Rambam who will be explained, we do not say "since" except regarding carrying and kindling, and not for other labors. (And according to this view, we must say that the one who extracts honeycombs on Shabbat 95a who is liable, it does not refer to this but to sweeping and sprinkling, as the Ran wrote there; or as the Tosafot there, referring to something not fit for eating. And those who expound in Beitzah, lest he come to pick, indeed the Rif and the Rambam did not rule according to this reason, but according to Rabbah's reason of preparation, see there. And furthermore: just as they said there that the entire decree is one, so too we should say the entire decree is one for Shabbat and Yom Tov. And when they decreed for Shabbat – they also decreed for Yom Tov. And investigate and you will find leniency.)

It is stated in Beitzah (12a) that for any labor which is permitted on Yom Tov for the purpose of food preparation, we say, "Since it is permitted for a need, it is also permitted without a need." The reason seems to be: since it is written (Exodus 12:16) "Only that which every person must eat, that alone may be prepared by you," it implies that labor for the sake of eating is permitted on Yom Tov (and this is also written in the Penei Yehoshua, see there). According to Rashi's opinion, even if there is no need at all, it is permitted. This is also clarified from the words of the Rambam there, as we will explain with the help of Heaven. However, Tosafot and the Rosh proved from several sources that it is only when there is some need, but if there is no need at all, it is forbidden by Torah law. They brought proofs from one who bakes on Yom Tov for a weekday, that he receives lashes. And even according to the one who holds he does not receive lashes, this is because of "since" as will be explained. And if we completely say "since," why would he receive lashes and why would we need the reasoning of "since"? Moreover, it is established: "for you" – and not for others, "for you" – and not for animals, since we say "since," why would it be forbidden? However, according to Rashi's opinion, this is not comparable, for baking for a weekday or for others, since the Torah explicitly forbade this – he certainly receives lashes. And it is not similar to something that has no need at all, which the Torah did not explicitly forbid (and this is also written in the Korban Netanel there).

According to the opinion of Rashi, Tosafot, and the Rosh, we say "mitoch" (since) for all labors that are for the purpose of preparing food. However, the opinion of the Rambam is that this is only said about the labors of carrying and kindling a fire. And this is the language of the Rambam there in Halacha 4: Any labor for which one is liable on Shabbat, if he does it on Yom Tov not for the purpose of eating – he receives lashes; except for carrying and kindling a fire, since carrying was permitted on Yom Tov for the purpose of eating – it is permitted even not for the purpose of eating. Therefore, it is permitted on Yom Tov to carry a child, or a Torah scroll, or a key, and similar items from one domain to another. And similarly, it is permitted to kindle a fire, even though it is not for the purpose of eating. Other labors – any that have the purpose of eating are permitted, such as slaughtering, baking, and cooking, and similar activities. And any that do not have the purpose of eating are forbidden, such as writing, weaving, building, and similar activities. Until here is his language, and according to him, the question of Tosafot and the Rosh regarding baking from Yom Tov for a weekday, and cooking for others, is resolved, as in baking and cooking we do not say "mitoch." (And we need to say that in his version of the Gemara Yevamot 12b the phrase "kindling and cooking is not a Mishnah" did not appear, but only "kindling" alone. And this is also implied from what he concludes there: "Similarly, we do not say 'since' kindling was permitted for the purpose…, that if Beit Hillel… since kindling was permitted for the purpose…". And he did not mention cooking, see there.)

The reasoning seems to me to be that we do not find this rationale of "mitoch" (since) in the Gemara except for these two labors. And there is a significant reasoning to distinguish them from all other labors regarding Yom Tov, because even on Shabbat, although they are included in the general prohibition of "do not perform labor," there are specific verses concerning them. For carrying out, we derive on Shabbat at the beginning of the chapter "HaZorek" (Shabbat 96b) from "And Moses commanded and they caused it to be proclaimed throughout the camp" (Exodus 36:6), and as Tosafot wrote at the beginning of Shabbat (s.v. "Yitziot") that since carrying out is a lesser labor, therefore, if there were not a specific verse about it, we would not include it in the general category of labors. See there. And for kindling, there is a verse "You shall not kindle" (Exodus 35:3). And even though from this verse the Tannaim derive whether kindling was excluded to establish a prohibition or to divide, in any case, there is ultimately a specific verse concerning it, which implies specifically on the Sabbath. Additionally, according to the one who holds that kindling was excluded to establish a prohibition, certainly there is no prohibition of kindling on Yom Tov, since it is not included in the general prohibition of "whoever does any labor on the Sabbath day shall be put to death." Moreover, since the labor on Shabbat is punished by stoning and on Yom Tov by a prohibition, if so, kindling, which on Shabbat is a prohibition, on Yom Tov is nothing. Therefore, even according to the one who holds that it was excluded to divide, it is not included in the labors, as there is no dispute about this. (See Maggid Mishneh who wrote about carrying out: because it is also in food and drink. This is not understood at all, for slaughtering and cooking and baking are also in food and drink. See Lechem Mishneh who questioned him. And what Lechem Mishneh challenged, that if so, why do we need "mitoch" for these two labors, since they are not included in the labors, see there—I am astonished, for ultimately they are also included in the prohibition of "do not perform labor" of Shabbat, after we learn carrying out from the verse "And Moses commanded," and for kindling we hold that it was excluded to divide, but we said that therefore they were divided regarding "mitoch" because there is a change in them. Be precise and you will find it easy.) (In Ketubot 7a where it says regarding a wound "mitoch"—it does not apply here. And the explanation is: What is your reasoning to say here also "mitoch," but it is not possible. See section 21).

And what Rambam wrote about carrying out "to carry out a child or a Torah scroll or a key" – it is certainly permitted by Torah law, even with stones and anything that has no purpose at all, according to Rashi's opinion. However, it is prohibited by rabbinic decree. Yet, what he wrote that all other labors that have a need for eating are permitted, such as slaughtering...; and anything that does not have a need for eating is prohibited, such as writing and weaving... – this is not relevant to what he started with. Carrying and kindling are permitted even without the need for eating, and it should have concluded that other labors, like slaughtering and cooking, are prohibited if there is no need for eating. What relevance does writing and weaving have here? And the Maggid Mishneh explained that carrying and kindling are like writing and weaving, but since they are needed for food preparation, they are fully permitted, see there. This comparison is not understood at all. (And the words of the Lechem Mishneh, who wrote that writing and weaving are prohibited even for food preparation, he refuted and elaborated and left it unresolved. All these matters are wondrous. Examine and you will find clarity.)

In my humble opinion, it seems that this is the explanation: This is the difference between carrying and kindling a fire and other forms of work related to food preparation. Carrying and kindling a fire are permitted even if not for the purpose of food preparation, but other forms of food preparation work, such as slaughtering, baking, and cooking, are only permitted for the purpose of preparing food for Jews and what is needed for Yom Tov. However, anything that is not necessary is forbidden, like writing, weaving, and building, which certainly have no connection to food preparation. Similarly, slaughtering, cooking, and baking are also included. And when it says "such as writing and weaving," it means "like writing and weaving," that is to say: slaughtering not for the purpose of food preparation is like writing.

In Pesachim (46b), it is recorded: "One who bakes on Yom Tov for a weekday, Rav Chisda said: he is liable to lashes. Rabbah said: he is not liable to lashes, because if guests were to come, it would be fit for them." And the law follows Rabbah. Therefore, Rambam ruled there that one who cooks on Yom Tov for others, or for an animal, or for a weekday, is not liable to lashes, for if guests were to come, that dish would be fit for them. Thus are his words. 

I have seen that there is a difference between the words of the Rambam and the explanation of Rashi. From the Rambam's language, it is clear that even when one explicitly cooks for others, or for an animal, or for a weekday, he is not liable to lashes, because if guests were to come, it would be fit for them. But Rashi (s.v. "one who bakes") explained: "One who bakes on Yom Tov for a weekday after he has eaten and finished his meal, for it is obvious to us that it is not fit for him now until evening, which is a weekday." Thus are his words. This clarifies that it does not refer to someone who cooked or baked explicitly for a weekday, for in such a case he would certainly be liable to lashes, as well as if he cooked for others or for an animal. Rather, it refers to a case where it appears that he is cooking for a weekday because he has already eaten. In such a case, we say "since..." 

According to both opinions, if he baked or cooked close to nightfall, he is liable to lashes, for in such a case it is not relevant to say "if guests were to come," as they would only come at night. We have already explained why we do not say "from the fact of" according to Rashi, because it is clearly evident that it is for a weekday, or for others, or for dogs, as the Torah explicitly forbids this. This is different from when it is not needed at all, which is lighter because this type of labor was not explicitly forbidden by the Torah. According to Rambam, it is straightforward, because we only say "from the fact of" regarding carrying and kindling. (And what is implied in Ketubot 7a, that "from the fact of" is also said regarding slaughter, will be explained in paragraph 20, as I wrote at the end of paragraph 15).

And know that I have a great wonder about the Rambam, who omitted in the laws of Yom Tov the rule that we require something that is suitable for all people. And in Ketubot 7a it is explicitly stated that the prohibition of incense is because we require something that is suitable for all people. And so explained Rashi and the Ran regarding the prohibition of incense in the Mishnah in Beitza (22b). And likewise in the Mishnah there (21b) regarding the prohibition of heating water for washing the entire body, Tosafot wrote (s.v. "not") that the reason for the prohibition is because it is not suitable for all people but only for the pampered. And the Rambam in Chapter 1, Law 16 wrote that the reason for the prohibition of heating water for washing the entire body is because of the decree of bathhouses, see there. And it is also explained from the words of the Rif there, who wrote that the prohibition is because of a decree, see there. And regarding the reason for incense, the Rambam wrote in Chapter 4, Law 6 that the reason is because of extinguishing, that when one places the incense on the coals, it extinguishes the fire. And nowhere did he mention the reason of being suitable for all people.

And it appears to me in its reasoning, as in Ketubot (7a) there is a dispute between Rav Papi and Rav Papa according to Rava, regarding the initial consummation of a virgin on Shabbat and Yom Tov. Rav Papi says it is permitted even on Shabbat, and this is the halacha as ruled by the Rambam in the thirtieth chapter of Shabbat and the Tur and Siman 240, as this is the conclusion there. Rav Papa permits it on Yom Tov but prohibits it on Shabbat. Rav Papi said to Rav Papa: What is your reasoning that you permit it on Yom Tov more than on Shabbat? Because on Yom Tov we say: Since wounding is permitted for the sake of food preparation, as in slaughtering, it is also permitted not for the sake of food preparation. If so, it should also be permitted to make incense on Yom Tov, since burning is permitted…? And he responded: The verse says "for all people" – something that is necessary for all people. And Tosafot asked: Does Rav Papi not hold the principle of "since"? For this is the reason of Beit Hillel regarding carrying a child and a Torah scroll? And they answered that he thought the reason of Beit Hillel was because there is no prohibition of carrying… until here is his language. And furthermore, I find it difficult what he questioned: If so, it should be permitted to make incense... – what is his difficulty? Indeed, Rabban Gamliel permits it in the Mishnah in Beitzah there, and the Rabbis who prohibit it do so because of extinguishing.

And it seems to me, in my humble opinion, that the explanation is as follows: Thus said Rav Papi: "It is understandable for me, who says that it is also permitted to have intercourse on Shabbat, as there is neither the prohibition of 'opening' nor the concern of causing a wound – it is therefore not necessary to say that we apply the principle of 'since' regarding a wound, for indeed we only say 'since' concerning carrying and kindling. The reasoning behind incense is due to the concern of extinguishing, but from the Torah it is permitted, because 'since' kindling was permitted for a need, it was also permitted even without a need. But according to you, who say that on Shabbat it is forbidden due to causing a wound, and there is also the concern of 'opening', as explained earlier in the discussion – see there; if so, according to you, why is it permitted on Yom Tov? You are compelled to say that we also apply the principle of 'since' regarding a wound, and therefore it is permitted on Yom Tov even though there is a concern of 'opening'. Therefore, it should be permissible to make incense, meaning that since we certainly say 'since' regarding kindling, the sages should not have prohibited incense due to the concern of extinguishing, just as they did not worry about 'opening' in intercourse." And he answered him that incense, according to his opinion, is prohibited from the Torah, because it is not suitable for everyone. And this is all according to Rav Papa. But we, who hold like Rav Papi – we do not apply 'since' regarding a wound, and we do not have the prohibition of something not suitable for everyone. And this is the reasoning of the Rambam of blessed memory in all his words, as we have explained with the help of Heaven.

Regarding the preparation of food-related items, we do not find a clear ruling in the law. Here, in the Gemara (28b), a Baraita is brought where the Sages completely prohibit the preparation of these items, as it is written, "it"—and not its preparatory items. Rabbi Yehuda permits it, as it is written, "for you"—for all your needs. And that which is written, "it"—this refers to preparatory items that can be made on the eve of the festival, which are prohibited. And that which is written, "for you"—this refers to preparatory items that cannot be made on the eve of the festival. And it says there earlier, Rava said to Rav Chisda: Do we teach in your name that the law follows Rabbi Yehuda? And he said to him: May it be G-d’s will that I teach such excellent matters in my name. See there. It is explicitly stated that the law follows Rabbi Yehuda. And it is also made clear from the words of the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch in this section, who wrote: And similarly, preparatory items for food that could not have been made the day before—are permitted. And this is according to Rabbi Yehuda. And similarly, the Sefer Mitzvot Gadol (SeMaG) and the Rosh wrote that the law follows Rabbi Yehuda.

And behold, there in the Gemara it states that Rav Chisda expounded: whether it is a knife that has become notched, or a spit that has been bent, or the sweeping of an oven and stove on a Yom Tov - we have come to the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis. See there. And since we hold according to Rabbi Yehuda - it must be permitted. And similarly, earlier there, regarding the ruling that one may not sharpen a knife on Yom Tov, it says there: Who is the Tanna that forbids with a whetstone? Rav Chisda said it is not according to Rabbi Yehuda. See there. And since we hold according to Rabbi Yehuda, it must be permitted to sharpen the knife. Also, in the second chapter (22a) it says: Abba bar Marta asked Abaye: Is it permissible to extinguish a lamp for the purpose of marital relations...? He said to him: It is forbidden. He challenged him: One does not extinguish a piece of wood to spare it. But if it is to prevent the house or the pot from becoming smoky - it is permitted?! He said to him: That is according to Rabbi Yehuda, when I spoke - it was according to the Rabbis. See there. And since we hold according to Rabbi Yehuda - it must be permitted to extinguish the lamp for the purpose of marital relations. However, the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch ruled entirely prohibitively.

And this is their language in Siman 516: One may not extinguish a burning log, even to prevent the house or the pot from becoming smoky, or in order to engage in marital relations. Thus is their language. And in Siman 509 they wrote: A spit that has been bent may not be fixed, and one may not sharpen a knife on its sharpening stone. See there. And only regarding the sweeping of an oven and stove did they rule in Siman 507 that it is permitted when it is impossible to bake without it. See there. And it is not understood: Why is this ruling permitted when it is different from all other preparations for food? (And this will be explained in Siman 509 with the help of Heaven.)

From the words of our Rabbis, I have learned reasons for all of this: because in the Gemara there it is said that the law follows Rabbi Yehuda, but we do not teach this. Therefore, they all ruled it forbidden, except for the sweeping of the oven and stove, which is a necessity for food preparation itself, as it is impossible to bake without this, and therefore it is permitted. And a proof of this is what the Rambam wrote in Chapter 1, Law 8, and this is his language: "And similarly, preparatory actions for food that have some deficiency, if they are done from the eve [of the festival] – they are done on the festival, such as grinding spices and the like." Up to here is his language. And it is difficult: since he equates grinding spices to preparatory actions for food, how did he permit it? For in all other cases he ruled it forbidden. Rather, certainly when it pertains to the food itself, it is permitted. Therefore, in Chapter 3, Law 10, regarding the sweeping of an oven, he also ruled it permitted when it is impossible to bake without sweeping, see there. And according to this, the Rambam also holds like all the other decisors. And I am puzzled by the Maggid Mishneh in Chapter 4, Law 8, regarding a spit that became bent, which the Rambam forbids, he wrote that the Rambam ruled not like Rabbi Yehuda but like the Rabbis, see there. And the matter is puzzling, for clearly he ruled in the first chapter like Rabbi Yehuda, as I have written. And his opinion is like that of the Rif, but he differentiates between preparatory actions that pertain directly to food and those that do not. And there are more details in the laws we have brought, such as those who hold that a stone sharpener is also forbidden according to Rabbi Yehuda. And they will be explained with the help of Heaven each in its place. (And see Beit Yosef, Siman 509, who elaborates on this. And according to our words, everything fits well. And since it is only that we do not teach this, but the law is according to Rabbi Yehuda – an individual may be lenient in a pressing situation, as the Taz wrote at the beginning of Siman 514 in the name of the Maharshal, see there. And see in Section 34.)

Regarding the issue of extinguishing on Yom Tov for the purpose of food preparation, it is explained in the Gemara (Beitzah 23a) that it is permitted, as it says there: Rava said: It is also permitted on a coal, similar to meat on coals. Rashi explains (s.v. "Rava said"): And if it is due to extinguishing, igniting, or creating fragrance, it is similar to meat on coals, which involves all these actions and is permitted. This is his language. Similarly, the Tur and Shulchan Aruch write in Siman 507 at the end of section 4, and this is the language of Rabbeinu the Beit Yosef there: And even though it extinguishes, it is unavoidable. Just as it is permitted to ignite for the purpose of food preparation, it is also permitted to extinguish for the purpose of food preparation. And this is like placing meat on coals. And this is the custom. This is his language, and similarly, the Maggid Mishneh wrote in Chapter 3, Halacha 10, in the name of the Rashba, and this is his language: And to rake out the oven from ash and coals after heating, it appears to me that it is permitted. And even though it extinguishes, it is unavoidable. Just as it is permitted to ignite for the purpose of food preparation, so too it is permitted to extinguish… This is his language. And that which the Rambam prohibited incense in Chapter 4 due to extinguishing is because it is not actually for food preparation, and the sages did not want to permit it. And a proof to this is that there he permitted smoking under fruits even though it extinguishes, and he wrote the reason that it is similar to meat on coals, see there. But certainly, as I wrote. And there are detailed laws about this, and they will be explained with the help of Heaven in Siman 511. However, in any case, we hear the ruling that for actual food preparation, extinguishing is permitted, and for non-food preparation, it is forbidden; even though it is permitted to do it on Yom Tov, nonetheless, through extinguishing, it is forbidden. And this will be explained with the help of Heaven there.

Regarding the matter of muktzeh on Yom Tov, the Tur wrote, and this is his language: "There are certain things that are stricter on Yom Tov than on Shabbat, such as the prohibition of muktzeh according to the Rif. For although we hold like Rabbi Shimon concerning Shabbat, on Yom Tov he ruled like Rabbi Yehuda because it is more lenient, and they were stringent with it so that people would not come to treat it lightly. This is also the ruling in the Sheiltot, and similarly, Rambam of blessed memory ruled. However, the Ba'al HaMaor, Rashi, the Ri, and Rabbeinu Tam rule like Rabbi Shimon, both on Shabbat and on Yom Tov. Except that Rabbeinu Tam differentiated, saying that the law is like Rabbi Shimon only regarding muktzeh, but concerning nolad, the law is like Rabbi Yehuda. Similarly, Rabbeinu Chananel ruled like Rabbi Shimon even on Yom Tov, except that regarding muktzeh due to prohibition and nolad, he ruled like Rabbi Yehuda on Yom Tov." Thus far the words of the Tur. And see what I wrote above in Siman 308, Section 6, and there. The details of the laws of muktzeh are explained there and in Siman 311, see there.

This is the language of the Rambam in Chapter 1, Law 17: Anything that is forbidden on Shabbat, whether because it resembles a form of labor or it leads to labor, or because it is a form of rabbinic prohibition (Shvut), is also forbidden on Yom Tov, unless it is needed for food preparation or similar matters, or things that are permitted on Yom Tov, as will be explained in these laws. Anything that is forbidden to move on Shabbat is also forbidden to move on Yom Tov unless it is for the purpose of food preparation or similar matters. Anything that is permitted on Shabbat is permitted on Yom Tov. However, there is an additional prohibition on Yom Tov that does not exist on Shabbat: the prohibition of Muktzeh. Muktzeh is forbidden on Yom Tov but permitted on Shabbat. Because Yom Tov is less stringent than Shabbat, they prohibited Muktzeh on Yom Tov, lest people come to treat it lightly. How so? A chicken that is raised to lay eggs, an ox that is used for plowing, dovecote doves, and fruits designated for commerce are all considered Muktzeh and it is forbidden to eat them on Yom Tov unless they were prepared from the previous day and designated for eating. But on Shabbat, everything is considered prepared and does not require preparation. Just as Muktzeh is prohibited on Yom Tov, so too is anything newly created (Nolad) prohibited. Thus far is his language.

The explanation of his words is that this stringency regarding Muktzeh on Yom Tov more than on Shabbat does not apply to all types of Muktzeh. For there are many types of Muktzeh that are more restricted on Shabbat than on Yom Tov, such as the Muktzeh of living creatures, which are forbidden on Shabbat but permitted on Yom Tov if they are intended for eating. Similarly, the Muktzeh of fire, coals, and wood is forbidden on Shabbat but permitted on Yom Tov, since on Yom Tov the preparation of food is allowed, and thus Muktzeh does not apply to them, unlike on Shabbat. The stringency applies specifically to one aspect: the literal meaning of Muktzeh. This means something that is fit for eating but was set aside intentionally. For example, a chicken designated for laying eggs, an ox for plowing, doves for raising, and fruits for commerce are all forbidden on Yom Tov and require preparation. On Shabbat, what is fit for Shabbat, such as fruits for commerce, is permitted without preparation. (The reason is clear: for the Mishnah in Beitzah states that an egg laid on Yom Tov is forbidden, and the Gemara explains that Yom Tov is stricter than Shabbat in that it includes this type of Muktzeh and also Nolad. With a chicken designated for laying eggs, see there. This is like the goat for its milk and the sheep for its wool in the first chapter of Shabbat 19b, where Rav prohibits slaughtering them on Yom Tov unless they were prepared, and the halacha follows him on Yom Tov.)

And know that although in several matters our Sages of blessed memory were stricter regarding Shabbat compared to Yom Tov, as it is taught in the Mishnah (Beitzah, beginning of chapter five): "One may lower fruits on Yom Tov but not on Shabbat." And in Beitzah (21b) regarding consecrated items, it states: "The prohibition of labor (Shvut) of Shabbat is different from the prohibition of labor of Yom Tov," meaning that Shabbat is stricter. And in Yevamot (114a) concerning one who is in distress, where they permitted him to suckle from a pure animal, it says: "Extracting in an unusual manner, on Shabbat which has the penalty of stoning – the Rabbis decreed, on Yom Tov which has the penalty of a prohibition – the Rabbis did not decree." See there. If so, why were they stricter regarding muktzeh of preparation on Yom Tov more than on Shabbat? The reason is as follows: Certainly, in matters that are not constant but happen occasionally, like lowering fruits when it rains, or in the case of consecrated items that were slaughtered not for their sake, or when one is in distress and close to illness and needs healing, where there is a concern of coming to a severe prohibition – it is obvious that they were stricter on Shabbat more than Yom Tov, since Shabbat has the penalty of stoning and Yom Tov has the penalty of a prohibition.
