And although in Yevamot (82a) it says: "In all matters from the Torah, whether it is a prohibition or a penalty of excision (karet), there is no difference," Rashi already explained there (119a, s.v. "What") that this is concerning a doubt, where one must be concerned for a doubtful prohibition just as for a doubtful penalty of excision. But regarding distancing – certainly one must be more cautious of distancing from excision than from a prohibition. See there. And here, where they were stricter on Yom Tov, it is only in a constant matter in the preparation of food for Yom Tov, so that one does not take what comes to hand like on a weekday. And we require that they be prepared from the eve of Yom Tov, to know that today is Yom Tov and not a weekday. For even though the Torah permitted food preparation, it is still not exactly like on a weekday and requires preparation, and in a matter that one has set aside from his mind – it is forbidden. This is to strengthen the observance of Yom Tov, so that it should not be treated lightly by people due to the permission of food preparation granted by the Torah. (See Mishneh Lamelech there who elaborated on this. According to our words, it is simple and clear, be precise and you will find it easy.)

And know that we have a great question on the Rif and Rambam, who ruled that muktzeh (objects that are set aside and not to be used on Shabbat or Yom Tov) is stricter on Yom Tov than on Shabbat. For in the fourth chapter of Beitza (31b), it is taught: "A house that is full of produce and its wall is breached – one may take [produce] from the place of the breach." And the Gemara questions: "But isn't it muktzeh?" And it answers: "This was said regarding Yom Tov and not Shabbat." Meaning, that on Yom Tov they permitted muktzeh because of the need for food preparation for the joy of Yom Tov, but not on Shabbat. It is clear that regarding muktzeh itself, they were more lenient on Yom Tov than on Shabbat. And our Rabbis, the Tosafists, wrote in three places in Beitza (there, s.v. "Amar", and 8b, s.v. "Amar", and 28b, s.v. "Grifat") that muktzeh is permitted due to the need for food preparation.

However, according to what we have explained, it makes sense. Indeed, Yom Tov is much less stringent than Shabbat, but this applies to incidental matters, even with muktzeh, such as a house full of fruits that had its wall breached, which is an incidental matter. Similarly, clearing an oven when it is impossible to bake in any other way, for example, if plaster falls into it and it was not known beforehand (as explained by Rashi on Shabbat 28b s.v. "ve'echad"), which is also incidental. The stringency regarding muktzeh refers to consistent preparation, to not take on Yom Tov from what comes to hand as on a weekday. If one designated something to not be eaten, it is prohibited unless it was prepared from the eve of Yom Tov, as I have written. This is the essence of the sanctity of Yom Tov: to acknowledge that although the Torah permits food preparation on Yom Tov, it still requires preparation from the eve of Yom Tov, and not to take from muktzeh that was designated away from eating as on a weekday.

Regarding the rest of one's animal on Yom Tov, this is divided into two parts on Shabbat: one involves placing a load on it, which is certainly permitted in the public domain. For on Shabbat, the prohibition is in the public domain, and on Yom Tov, even a person himself is permitted to carry in the public domain, as there is no prohibition of carrying in the public domain, and one's animal is not more stringent than oneself. However, there is another type of rest for an animal, which is that it should not perform work. This applies also on Yom Tov. And we have already written above in Siman 246, Se'if 15 that there are those who say this does not apply on Yom Tov, for "so that your ox may rest" is written regarding Shabbat, and not Yom Tov. This is the opinion of our teacher the Rema there. Consequently, the rest of a servant and maidservant does not apply on Yom Tov either, as I wrote there. And there are those who say that Yom Tov is like Shabbat. In the Jerusalem Talmud, Chapter 5 of Beitza, they said that one should not ride an animal on Yom Tov because of the rest of one's animal. And for practical law, we explained there with the help of Heaven. We also explained that leading an animal does not apply on Yom Tov, see there in Se'if 16. Nevertheless, it is forbidden, as I wrote in Se'if 37.

After we have clarified, with Divine assistance, the primary labors of Yom Tov according to the opinions of our early sages, we should now turn to see where the opinions of our sages, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, lean. Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in Section 1: All labors forbidden on Shabbat are forbidden on Yom Tov, except for the labor of preparing food, and except for carrying and kindling a fire. Similarly, preparations for food that could not have been done the day before are also permitted. However, reaping, grinding, pressing, and trapping, even though they are related to food preparation, were prohibited by the sages. This is because these tasks could have been done before Yom Tov without the food deteriorating, and there was a concern that engaging in such large tasks could detract from the joy of Yom Tov, as I have written in Section 11. (Refer to Taz Section 2, and Magen Avraham Section 4. As for what Magen Avraham wrote in Section 1, regarding the shaking of fruits as mentioned in Siman 521, it requires further examination; certainly, the Beit Yosef did not refer to this. The Machatzit HaShekel struggled with the idea that he referred to the Tur, which is also questionable. The Pri Megadim also remained in doubt; see there. The main points are puzzling, as in Beitzah 37a, when it questions, it did not challenge the Mishnah in Megillah as Tosafot wrote there. It does not deal with rabbinic prohibitions, but only questions the Mishnah about rabbinic decrees; see there. Examine and you will find clarity.)

However, it is necessary to scrutinize how it is written that preparatory acts for food consumption that could not have been done the day before are permitted. Did not the Rambam only write this regarding the grinding of spices, but other preparatory acts are forbidden? Moreover, Rabbi Yosef Karo himself rules this way, as we clarified in Section 24. And it seems to me that Rabbi Yosef Karo spoke of a significant matter. For behold, in Section 25 we clarified that from a legal standpoint it is permitted, but we do not instruct this way. If so, an individual for themselves can be lenient in a pressing situation, see there. Therefore, the matters are stated generally here, saying that from a legal standpoint all preparatory acts for food consumption that could not have been done the day before are permitted. However, when he reaches the specific details later, he does not rule permissively but rather restrictively.

And our master, the Rema, wrote about it that there are those who are stringent even regarding food preparation itself, as long as it does not lose its taste at all if it was made on the eve of the festival. However, if it was not made on the eve of the festival and there is a need for it on the festival – it is permitted to make it with a change. Thus is his language. And this follows the opinion of Rashi and the Sefer Mitzvot Gadol (SMaG), who also in the essentials of food preparation, the Torah only permitted what is better on the day itself than if made the previous day, like slaughtering, baking, and cooking. But if it is not better – it is forbidden. Only with a change is it permitted, as I wrote in paragraph 10, see there. And Tosafot wrote at the beginning of Beitzah and the beginning of the third chapter that regarding food preparation itself, there is no difference, for even if it does not spoil – it is permitted. But this is not the opinion of Rashi, the SMaG, and the Maharshal, as I wrote there.

According to this, all types of dried fruits when cooked, meaning all types of compotes, which are better the next day than the same day – it is forbidden to cook them on Yom Tov, except by making a change. And it is permissible from the outset to leave them to cook on Yom Tov with a change (Magen Avraham, subsection 2 and subsection 3). Similarly, all types of preserves, and all types of sugar cakes, such as lekach, tarts, and teiglach, and eingemachts – these should not be made on Yom Tov except with some change. Similarly, grinding almonds to extract milk – it is forbidden to do this on Yom Tov except by making a change (there). And even though this somewhat diminishes the taste, it is still similar to the squeezing of fruits which is prohibited (there). And certainly, it is forbidden to make cheese on Yom Tov, as I have written later in Siman 511, see there.

In paragraph 3, our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote: One may not place a load on an animal on Yom Tov. This is his language. That is to say: even though there is no prohibition of resting one's animal in this manner, as I have written in paragraph 32, nevertheless, it is forbidden because it should not be done in the same way it is done on a weekday. For so ruled the Rambam at the beginning of the fifth chapter; see there. Additionally, there is a prohibition due to the use of living creatures (Magid Mishneh there).

In paragraph 4, it is written: "Muktzeh, although it is permitted on Shabbat, they were stringent about it on Yom Tov and prohibited it." Until here is his language, and he was very brief. He did not explain that he was referring to muktzeh of preparation. And our teacher, the Rema, wrote about it: "And there are those who permit muktzeh even on Yom Tov. But nolad is forbidden according to them even on Shabbat." Until here is his language, he was precise in saying "according to them," meaning: that there are those who permit muktzeh and forbid nolad, but there are those who permit even nolad. He did not consider it necessary to mention their opinion, because most prohibit nolad. And as I wrote in paragraph 27 in the name of the Tur, see there.

He also wrote: Any muktzeh that is not living beings, such as a storehouse of fruits and wood, it is sufficient to say "From here I will take," and there is no need to mark it. And it is permissible to prepare from the first day of Yom Tov to the second, in the two days of the diaspora. So far his words, meaning: for those who permit, no declaration is needed at all, except for dried figs and raisins that are deliberately set aside, as I wrote in Siman 310. However, even for those who prohibit and require preparation, in the case of birds, specific preparation is needed, saying "This and this I will take tomorrow." But if one says "From here I will take tomorrow" without specifying "this and this," it is forbidden, as will be explained in Siman 497. But in a storehouse of fruits, it is sufficient to say "From here I will take tomorrow." And it is also permitted to make this preparation from the first day of Yom Tov to the second, even though all preparations are generally prohibited, nonetheless, such a minor preparation as this is permitted. However, with birds, it is forbidden to prepare from one Yom Tov to the other, as this is considered complete preparation when he says "This and this I will take." Some are stringent and say: even in a storehouse of fruits, it is necessary to mark where he will take from. This is the opinion of the Rambam (Magen Avraham, small section 10). And certainly with fruits that are not yet completely ready to eat, even though they are somewhat ready, it is still necessary to mark that these will be taken tomorrow (ibid). It seems to me that initially, one should follow the stringent opinion. But in a case of minor prohibition like this, one can rely on the lenient opinion for the joy of the holiday.

In the diaspora, where they observe two days of Yom Tov, the second day is as stringent as the first day in all respects, except in matters regarding a deceased person and a sick individual, as will be explained. The one who degrades the second day of Yom Tov, the Rambam considers in the sixth chapter of the Laws of Torah Study, that this is one of the twenty-four things for which one is cursed, see there. And similarly, it is in the fourth chapter of Pesachim (52a). If he is a young Torah scholar, we do not strictly curse him, but rather he receives lashes of rebellion. There is an opinion that he receives thirteen lashes, as a curse is more severe than lashes.

And even though in several places we find that one who transgresses a rabbinic prohibition is given lashes of rebellion, as in the case of Shabbat (40a) regarding one who cooks with the hot springs of Tiberias, see there. However, the matter is as follows: In a case where the primary prohibition is from the Torah, but there are several rabbinic prohibitions involved – lashes of rebellion suffice. This is not the case for something that is entirely rabbinic in nature, and one disrespects it to the point of nullifying it – lashes of rebellion are not sufficient, but rather a curse is warranted, such as the second day of Yom Tov in the Diaspora whose basis is rabbinic. Similarly, with the washing of hands in the fifth chapter of Eduyot, they did so to one who doubted it, because he was undermining the whole matter (Ran in the fourth chapter of Pesachim). Likewise, in Kiddushin (39a) regarding the prohibition of planting mixed seeds outside the Land of Israel for one who holds that it applies outside the Land – it is necessary to do so, because this is entirely rabbinic. However, we do not hold this way, see there. (And this resolves the question of the Chidushei HaRashba).

Except regarding a deceased person: due to the honor of the deceased, they were lenient on the second day of Yom Tov. And thus, the sages said (Beitzah 6a): "The second day of Yom Tov regarding a deceased person, the Rabbis treated it like a weekday." The detailed laws will be explained in Siman 526. Similarly, they permitted applying kohl to the eye for healing on the second day of Yom Tov, even if there is no danger involved. Some say that the same applies to other illnesses that are not life-threatening – one can do whatever is necessary for them through a Jew on the second day of Yom Tov (Ran, third chapter of Beitzah). Others say that it specifically applies to rabbinic prohibitions like applying kohl to the eye, but a complete labor was not permitted (ibid., and Maggid Mishneh, first chapter of Yom Tov in the name of Ramban, see there) through a Jew, only through a non-Jew, just like on the first day of Yom Tov and Shabbat. And this is the law. Only rabbinic prohibitions are permitted for a Jew to do himself, even though on Yom Tov it is only permitted through a non-Jew if it is not a sickness of the entire body. These leniencies do not apply on the second day of Rosh Hashanah, as the two days of Rosh Hashanah are considered one long sanctity, as will be explained in its place. Similarly, a delayed circumcision does not override the second day of Yom Tov in the Diaspora, as I wrote in Yoreh De'ah 266. Even in a doubtful case, such as if on the second day of Yom Tov the newborn is in doubt whether it is the eighth or ninth day. Some say it does override (see there in Shach, and in Tammim De'im, Siman 102 in the name of Rosh of Lunel that it overrides, see there). I saw in Magen Avraham, Siman Katan 3, that someone who fell and blood congealed, needing to draw blood through cupping, and in our language, leeches, it is forbidden even through a non-Jew, because he can wait until tomorrow, see there. These are perplexing matters: who told us that he will not get sicker until tomorrow? In my humble opinion, even on Shabbat and the first day of Yom Tov it is permitted through a non-Jew, as per the law of any illness that is not life-threatening unless the doctor says there is no concern until tomorrow.)

Jews from the Land of Israel who come to the Diaspora, even though they intend to return and are not bound by the stringent practices of the place they have gone to, are nonetheless forbidden to do work on the second day of Yom Tov in a settled area due to potential discord, as I have written in Siman 468. Some say this applies only in public, but in private it is permissible, as there is no discord in private (Taz, subsection 2 and Shach). However, others say that work is forbidden in any case, as it is not possible to do it so privately (Magen Avraham, subsection 4, in the name of Tosafot). Additionally, it is considered a breach of the communal standard accepted by the entire Diaspora, and is therefore forbidden by law (ibid., in the name of the Maor). This is the main ruling.

However, as long as they have not yet reached a settled area, meaning they have not yet entered the city's boundaries, they are permitted in all matters, even if they do not intend to return, since they have not yet been established as part of the local community. If they have reached a settled area, meaning within the city's boundaries, and do not intend to return, even if it is a city not predominantly Jewish, they fully become like the Diaspora residents in all matters, not just regarding work. They are obligated to observe the sanctity of the second day of Yom Tov in prayer, Kiddush, and Birkat Hamazon (Grace after Meals).

A resident of the Land of Israel who comes to the Diaspora, and does not intend to establish a permanent residence in the Diaspora but plans to return to the Land of Israel within a short period – prays the weekday prayers, for since prayer is done quietly, there is no issue of division (machloket). He may cook without an Eruv Tavshilin if the second day of Yom Tov falls on a Friday, but he should wear Yom Tov clothes, as this is like a publicly visible act. If one relocates with his wife from the Land of Israel to the Diaspora, even though they plan to return eventually, their status is like those who do not intend to return, for since he and his household have come, it is considered a permanent residence. Similarly, it appears to me that even if he comes alone, if he does not intend to return within a year, it is considered "not intending to return." Even if someone does not intend to return, although there might be some constraints which could cause him to return, such as his wife not currently agreeing to leave, or similar reasons, even though he might eventually return – since at this time he has resolved not to return, it is considered "not intending to return." There are those who say that a resident of the Land of Israel who comes to the Diaspora is forbidden to eat chametz on the last day of Pesach in any case, even if he intends to return. This is correct, as it is worse than performing labor. A Kohen from the Land of Israel who comes to the Diaspora and intends to return should not go up to the platform (to bless) on the second day of Yom Tov. If he is forced to go up, he should not recite the blessing, but rather say "May He bless you..." without the blessing. A resident of the Diaspora who comes to the Land of Israel and does not intend to return – immediately follows the customs of the people of the Land of Israel. If he intends to return, he follows the customs of the Diaspora on the second day of Yom Tov in all matters (see Sha'arei Teshuva).

It is taught at the beginning of the third chapter: One may not trap fish from ponds on Yom Tov. This means: not only is it prohibited to trap from the river, but even when they are already gathered in a pond, which are pools of water where fish are collected (Rashi), and from which they cannot escape – nevertheless, it is considered trapping, and it is forbidden on Yom Tov. And as we explained earlier in Siman 316, Section 5, according to the Tosafot, any place that is still considered "lacking trapping" – one is liable from there according to Torah law, see there. And similarly, in this pond, they slip away here and there, and therefore, one who traps from there is liable. And so it is explained in Rashi and Tosafot that the reason one may not trap is due to the prohibition of trapping, as is the simple meaning of the language, see there.

And behold, as we have explained in the name of the Rambam, it appears that trapping fish in a pond does not constitute a Torah prohibition of trapping on Shabbat. See there. According to this, on Yom Tov, there is also no rabbinic prohibition of trapping according to the Rambam’s view, since all work related to food preparation is permitted by Torah law, as I have written in Siman 498. And indeed, this is the case, as it is explained from the words of the Rambam in the second chapter of Yom Tov, law 7, that the prohibition of trapping is not due to the prohibition of trapping itself, but because of muktzeh. And this is the wording of the Rambam: Fish in large enclosures, and likewise, animals and birds in large enclosures, if they require trapping such that one would say "bring a trap and let's catch them" – they are considered muktzeh, and one may not trap them on Yom Tov. And if one traps them, they should not be eaten. But if they do not require a trap – they are considered prepared, and one may trap them on Yom Tov and eat them. Thus far his wording; it is clear that the reason for not trapping is due to muktzeh. Similarly, the Rambam wrote in his commentary on the Mishnah that anything requiring trapping is considered muktzeh. See there. (And I am puzzled by the commentators who did not mention this at all.)

And seemingly, according to the Rambam, since the reason is due to muktzeh, if so, if one brought them in on the eve of Yom Tov and said, "This and this I will take tomorrow" – it is permitted, just like with dovecote pigeons and loft pigeons that will be explained. However, it does not seem so. And the truth is, with fish, since they still require trapping in a large enclosure – it is impossible to prepare them, for who knows if these will come into his hand. This is unlike pigeons, where he can take what he desires – his statement is effective. Conversely, anything that does not require trapping, such as when the enclosure is small – they are permitted even without a statement on the eve of Yom Tov, "This and this I will take tomorrow." And it is not similar to pigeons that he designated from his mind. But fish, since he brought them in on the eve of Yom Tov to a place where they do not require trapping – this is their preparation, and they are all ready and available.

And know that the Rambam equates the laws of fish with the laws of wild animals and birds: in both cases, if they require trapping, they are forbidden, and if they do not require trapping, they are permitted. Even though the Mishnah differentiates, with the Tanna Kamma distinguishing between fish and wild animals and birds, the Rambam holds that the law does not follow the Tanna Kamma, but rather follows Rabbi Shimon ben Gamliel, who says there: "Not all enclosures are equal; if it requires trapping, it is forbidden, and if it does not require trapping, it is permitted." The Gemara concludes that the halacha follows Rabbi Shimon ben Gamliel, see there. However, this is not the opinion of the later authorities, who hold that Rabbi Shimon ben Gamliel's statement applies only to wild animals and birds, and in their case, there is a distinction between requiring trapping and not requiring trapping. But regarding fish, it is entirely forbidden, for reasons that will be explained. This is what the Raavad critiques there, see there. And this is also the opinion of the Tur, as will be explained with Divine assistance.

And this is the language of the Tur: "One may not trap fish from a pond..., nor any other animal or bird, and anything that requires trapping such that one needs to say, 'Bring a trap and we will catch it' – it is forbidden to trap them..." Up to here is his language. Thus, regarding fish, even if they do not require trapping – it is forbidden. Some say the reason is because they are covered by water and slip away here and there; therefore, they always require trapping (see Taz). And some say the reason is because since they are hidden from sight – they are considered muktzeh (Taz, small section 1), as it is certain that they were not prepared.

There is a practical difference in law between the reasons, specifically in large places where fish are placed in a large box on the water's surface, and the box has many small openings to the water. According to the first reason, they are prohibited, since the box is large and the fish can slip here and there (Beit Yosef). But according to the second reason, which is due to muktzeh, since they were prepared during the day by placing them into the box, it is therefore permitted to take them on Yom Tov (Taz there, and similarly wrote the Shach at the beginning of the third chapter).

In the Gemara (Beitzah 25a), it is stated: If one blocks a canal on the eve of a festival, and the next morning he finds fish in it, they are permitted. Rashi explains: He blocked it so that fish would not enter it after nightfall, and consequently, the fish found in it the next morning were there from the eve of the festival. Thus, he prepared and designated them beforehand through this action (Rashi). According to the second reason, it is understandable, for he has prepared them, and there is no issue of muktzeh (set aside). But according to the first reason, why are they permitted? Are they not concealed from sight? The answer given is: The canal is small, and therefore, even though they are concealed from sight, they do not slip away from one side to the other. This is not the case with a large enclosure, where even if trapping is not required, it is still large, and they slip away from one side to the other. Hence, they are considered "requiring trapping," which is not the case with the canal.

And this is the opinion of our teacher, the Rema. In section 1, on "one may not trap fish from the reservoirs," he wrote: even in a place where they are not lacking in trapping, because the reservoir is very wide, and the fish slip away here and there. Thus is his language. And in section 5, on the law "if one dammed up the water channel at the entrance and exit before the festival – it is permitted to take fish from it on the festival, because they are considered trapped and standing," he wrote about this: since the water channel is narrow, and it cannot slip away. Thus is his language. Hence, the main point depends: if it is a wide place, it is called "lacking in trapping," and if it is not a wide place, it is not called "lacking in trapping." And one should not say that if so, how did he previously state two contradictory things: that they are not lacking in trapping because the reservoir is wide, and if it is wide, then it is lacking in trapping? For the explanation is as follows: regarding the main law of trapping – it is not called lacking in trapping, since it cannot escape from here. Nevertheless, regarding the festival, even though it is not lacking in trapping, still, it is very wide and they slip away here and there. And its law is like that of lacking in trapping, which is not the case with the water channel.

According to this, it also depends on the containers on the water: if they are very wide, it is forbidden to take from them on Yom Tov. But if they are narrow, like a water channel that is about a cubit wide, it is permitted to take from them on Yom Tov. And it seems that in large places, they are accustomed to permit taking from them on Yom Tov, even from very wide containers. They rely on the second reason mentioned in Section 5, for according to this reason it is permitted to take from them on Yom Tov even from a wide container, as I wrote in Section 6. And also according to our master the Rema, there is a permit, because there is someone who says that if the water is clear and the fish can be seen, it is permitted to take from them on Yom Tov (Magen Avraham, Subsection 1). And although in my humble opinion this applies only to the second reason and not to the first reason, nevertheless, because of the joy of Yom Tov, one could say that even according to the first reason, since they can be seen, it is not called "lacking trapping." And in our containers, the water is clear and the fish can be seen. (And there needs to be scrutiny regarding the Tur, who omitted this about blocking the water channel. See there.)

And with birds, the law is as follows: Geese, chickens, and pigeons that are in the house or in the yard, which are designated for eating (for those that are kept to lay eggs are considered set aside), since they are designated for eating – there is no issue of trapping with them; for they are domesticated and are considered as if they are already trapped. Also, the issue of preparation does not apply to them, since they are considered prepared and ready from the day before, and one may take any of them on Yom Tov and slaughter them. However, if not for the purpose of slaughtering, one should not take them, as I have written in siman 516, see there. Nonetheless, it is written that a God-fearing person should prepare them on the eve of Yom Tov and say "I will take this one and that one tomorrow," to avoid excessive exertion on Yom Tov, such as selecting and setting aside repeatedly. But if he designates them on the eve of Yom Tov, this will not happen (Taz and Magen Avraham, subsection 8).

Know that there is someone who wants to say that it is specifically permitted to take chickens or geese from a house or courtyard, but not from the street, due to the prohibition of trapping. This is not the case. What the poskim (decisors of Jewish law) wrote with the phrase "from a house or courtyard" means that they were raised in the house or courtyard. However, even if they are in the street, since they are accustomed to entering their coop by themselves in the evening, there is no concern of trapping, and it is permitted to take them from the street. However, if they were recently purchased and are not yet accustomed to entering their coop in the evening, it is certainly forbidden to take them from the street due to the concern of trapping (Magen Avraham, subsection 7).

And this is all regarding domesticated birds. However, other wild animals and birds that grow in orchards or enclosures, whether the enclosure is covered or not, if the place is so large that they require trapping, meaning one has to say "bring a trap and we will catch it" — it is forbidden to trap them. And any that do not require trapping — it is permitted to trap them. And it appears to me that they require designation. But those that require trapping, designation does not help them. Therefore, dovecote pigeons, attic pigeons, and birds that have made nests in walls — it is forbidden to trap them, and designation does not help them. And even if they come to their coop in the evening, nevertheless, their sustenance is not upon you, and they are not considered designated. Additionally, because their nature is to evade and flee from humans, it is not easy to catch them (there, small section 11).

And specifically, the large ones that can fly, but the small ones that cannot fly outside their place, but rather walk heavily around the nest and are hopping about – it is permissible to trap them, as there is no prohibition of trapping with them. However, they require designation, because one’s mind is not on them from the eve of the festival. And how this designation is done will be explained before us in paragraph 17. Similarly, a ram or deer that nested in an orchard and gave birth to small fawns there, and they still do not need to be trapped – they are permissible without designation, if the orchard is adjacent to the city within the city’s boundary, which is seventy and a fraction cubits, because it is presumed that his mind is on them. But if it is far from the city – it is presumed that his mind is not on them. And the mother, even designation does not help for her, as I have written, for anything that requires trapping – designation does not help for her. (And what I have written in the previous paragraph concerning animals and birds, that they require designation because it seems that one’s mind is not on them, also here even within the boundary if it is known that one’s mind is not on them – they require designation.)

Since it has been explained that anything that requires trapping is prohibited, therefore even uncertain trapping is prohibited, such as traps for animals, birds, and fish that were set up before the festival and the next day are found to have caught something. We are concerned that they might have been trapped during the night. They are only permitted if it is known that they were trapped before the festival. This is their preparation: by setting up the trap and trapping them before the festival. Similarly, if the traps are found broken, indicating that their entrance caused the breakage, we assume that they certainly entered before the festival. And if you ask: If so, why didn't he see them before the festival? It can be said: such as when the trap is large and he saw at one end that they were broken, and they were at the other end (see Taz section 4).

And there is a question about this: Why is doubtful trapping prohibited? And it is understandable according to those who hold that trapping is prohibited on Yom Tov by Torah law, as I wrote in Siman 498, it makes sense, for a doubt concerning a Torah law is treated stringently. But according to those who hold there that it is Rabbinic, isn't the rule that a doubt concerning a Rabbinic law is treated leniently? One can say: because it is something that will eventually become permitted, and it is prohibited even by Rabbinic law. Moreover, we find several doubts where the Sages wished to be stringent. However, in the evening, there is no need to wait the time it would take to do the action (Magen Avraham, subsection 3). And all this is on the first day of Yom Tov. But on the second day of Yom Tov, doubtful trapping is permitted, because it is a double doubt, since the second day of Yom Tov itself is a doubt. And there are those who prohibit it even on the second day of Yom Tov (ibid. subsection 4 in the name of the Yeshu'ot Yaakov), and this is also implied later in Siman 515.

The Rambam writes in Chapter Two, Halacha 17: Fish, birds, and animals that are muktzeh – one may not give them water on Yom Tov, nor may one place food before them, lest he come to take from them. And anything that is forbidden to eat or use on Yom Tov because it is muktzeh – it is forbidden to move it. Thus far his words. This law is in the Mishnah of "One does not trap," see there. And ostensibly, even on Shabbat one may place food before animals and wild animals whose sustenance depends on you, whether they are impure or pure. And indeed, it is even permitted to exert effort for them to prepare food, so they can eat, as I wrote above in Siman 324, and as it is taught: one cuts up a carcass before dogs. All the more so on Yom Tov. So why is it forbidden to place food before them?

And Rashi, of blessed memory, explained: because fish can live without it, see there. But the Rambam was not satisfied with this, as he concludes in the Mishnah: "But one traps animals and birds and places food before them," which clearly explains that the permission for food is only because of trapping. Therefore, the Rambam explained that the reason is only on Yom Tov, because we are concerned that one might come to take from them. But this concern does not apply to an impure animal, and it is permitted to place food before them. And it is possible that even for a pure animal that is muktzeh, it is also permitted, as we are only concerned about the issue of trapping. And this is the opinion of our teacher, the Beit Yosef, in his great book in Siman 498. And there are those who disagree with this (Magen Avraham, subsection 2). And some say that fish, wild animals, and birds in enclosures are not considered to be at hand for a person, and it is as if their sustenance does not depend on you (Ran, see there). And this is in accordance with the opinion of Rashi that we mentioned. But all other species that are in a person's house and courtyard, whether impure or pure, are considered "their sustenance depends on you," and one must feed them on Shabbat and Yom Tov. However, at the end of Beitzah, it clearly implies that regarding giving them water, one may even provide for those that are not in his house and courtyard, see there (see Magen Avraham, subsection 2).

How does one designate the small birds mentioned in section 13? When one says on the eve of the festival, "I will take this one and that one tomorrow," it is sufficient. He does not need to handle them, as verbal designation alone makes them prepared. However, if he says, "I will take from here tomorrow," it does not suffice. This is not due to the principle of selection, where it is said that it becomes clear which ones he intended, as for rabbinic matters, we do apply selection. Rather, the reason is that since they are small and he does not know them yet, we are concerned that he might take some, find them unsuitable, return them, and take others, thus moving something that is not suitable for him. But when he says, "I will take this one and that one tomorrow," it is assumed that he has examined them and found them good.

Even if the entire dovecote is designated, if one only needs a minority of them, it is not effective due to the concern we mentioned. However, if it is possible that one might need the entire dovecote for the next day, then the designation is effective in such a manner, even though in the end not all will be taken, because one is compelled to designate them all due to the uncertainty, as one might need all of them. The reason we are not concerned about the designation of fish in "blocking the water" as mentioned in Section 7, and do not require one to say, "I will take this and that tomorrow," is because there is no concern that one might take a portion of them, find them unsatisfactory, throw them back into the water, and take others. People do not typically throw fish back into the water after having caught them. Therefore, even if they are found unsatisfactory, one would take others along with those already taken, which is not the case with dovecote pigeons (Taz, small section 7). Similarly, with animals and wild beasts, if they required designation, one could designate them all, and there is no concern of this issue, that one might take and return them and take others. They are recognizable to him, and he knows what he is taking, like geese and chickens with which he is already familiar, unlike young pigeons (see there in Taz).

He designated two, and the next day he found three mixed together, and he cannot recognize the two he designated—[they are] forbidden, in any case: if we say that the two left and these are others—it is obvious that they are forbidden. And even if we say that these are the two he designated—nevertheless, the third one, which he did not designate, is mixed among them, and we do not say it is nullified by the majority, because living beings are significant and not nullified. Moreover, it is a matter that has a permitted state (Tosafot 10b, s.v. "Eika"). However, according to this, if one of them was eaten or fell into the sea—all are permitted, as we assume that the forbidden one was eaten or lost, as I wrote in Yoreh De'ah, section 110. But if we are concerned that these are others, even in such a case, they are forbidden. (See Magen Avraham, subsection 14, who wrote that according to the conclusion of the Gemara there, since young birds are prone to wander, we are not concerned that they are all others; see there. In my humble opinion, this applies only to [the case of] three and found two, and not to two and found three, where there is certainly a prohibition. Therefore, just as the third one is from elsewhere, so too are the two; see there. Be precise and you will find the light.)

However, if one designated three and found two, they are permitted. We do not say that they all left and these are others, because there is no definite prohibition here. It is more reasonable to assume that one left and the two remained in their place, as it is the nature of young birds to waddle away from each other. Even if they were all tied together, we still say that through waddling, the tie became undone, and one left while the two remained in their place. There are those who prohibit in the case of being tied (Siman 7, Se'if Katan 9). However, it is obvious that if the two are found tied together, they are permitted (there). Similarly, if one designated three and found three, and he left them tied, and found them untied, we do not worry about it and say that the tie became undone (there). There are those who prohibit even in such a case (Bach), but it is an excessive stringency, for it is certainly permitted in such a case.

He designated black and white [birds] in nests separated by a partition, and the next day he found black [birds] in the place of the white ones and white [birds] in the place of the black ones, and he does not recognize them – all are forbidden, because we say that all of them left and these are different ones. And we do not say that these [birds] themselves switched places, because why should we attribute it to these [birds]? Let us attribute it to the majority of birds in the world. And even though these [birds] are close and we could attribute it to them – however, [regarding] majority and proximity, we follow the majority even in a case of clear proximity. But if the nests are not separated – it is obvious that we attribute it to the birds themselves, as this is their usual behavior, unlike when they are separated. And similarly, even if separated, if they are all found in one place – we assume that these [birds] went to those [places], and not that all of them left and these are others, because we do not see a deficiency in all of them, unlike when they switched places. And in the case of a deficiency in all of them, we attribute it to the general population (Kesef Mishneh from the Talmudic discussion, see there).

If one designated them inside the nest and found them the next day outside the nest, they are forbidden, because we say that those went away into the world, and these are others. We do not attribute them to those that were inside the nest, even though they are close by, and we attribute them to the majority of the world, as the rule is that when there is a conflict between the majority and proximity, we follow the majority, as I have written. And it appears to me that this is specifically when all of them left the nest, but if some remained in the nest, then these are also permitted, because just as those are from yesterday, so too are these. Similarly, if one designated them inside the nest and found them at the entrance of the nest, they are permitted, because it is evident that these are the same ones. It also appears to me that if one designated them in front of the nest and found them inside the nest, they are permitted, because it is their way to enter into the nest. And although it is also their way to leave, nonetheless, it is also their way to completely leave the nest, and we say that indeed they left, and these are others.

And know that what we have said, that if one designated (birds) within the nest and found them in front of the nest, they are forbidden, there is a distinction between large birds that can fly and small ones that can only hop. Large ones, even if there is no nest within fifty cubits around them, are forbidden because we say they flew off to the world. But small ones, the sages established that any bird that hops does not hop more than fifty cubits. And when they see a nest within fifty cubits, they hop. If not, they do not hop. Therefore, if there is a nest within fifty cubits, they are forbidden, and if not, it is certain that they are from the nest. And even if there is a nest within fifty cubits, if the nest stands in a corner from this nest in a way that the doves cannot see it, they are also permitted, because if they do not see the nest in front of them, they will not hop, and it is certain that they are from those within the nest. (See the Taz, subsection 11, that in the case of flyers it is forbidden in any case because of trapping.)

A non-Jew who brought a gift to a Jew on a festival, young pigeons from his dovecotes in the city – since they do not require trapping, and they were not brought from outside the boundary – it is permitted to eat them on the festival. And even though he did not designate them before the festival, it is stated in the Jerusalem Talmud that for a non-Jew, no preparation is needed, for all are considered prepared to him, as he does not have the prohibition of muktzeh. However, mature pigeons are forbidden, since catching them involves the prohibition of trapping. Similarly, if they came from outside the boundary, as will be explained in Siman 515, only young pigeons from within the boundary are permitted.

One who slaughters an animal on Yom Tov – it is better for him not to skin the hide after the inspection, but before the inspection. For if he waits until after the inspection, it might be found to be a tereifah (an animal with a defect that renders it non-kosher) and it will be forbidden to skin it. Before the inspection, it is permitted, because it is impossible to reach the meat before skinning the hide, and this is also included within the category of "food preparation." However, if it is found to be a tereifah, it is forbidden. If it remains with the hide until the next day, he will lose a lot in selling it to a non-Jew. Why didn’t they permit "the end because of the beginning" here, as they permitted placing the hide before trampling animals, as I wrote in Siman 499? Because that is in a rabbinic prohibition. But skinning, which is a Torah prohibition – they did not permit (Magen Avraham, Siman Katan 18). Similarly, when it is found to be a tereifah, it is forbidden to move it, because it is muktzeh (set aside). But it is permitted to sell it today to a non-Jew, in the manner that they permitted selling to a Jew: not to weigh, nor to mention a sum of money, as I wrote in Siman 517. If he does not trust him, he should take collateral from him. This was permitted because of loss, so that it should not be lost until the next day. There is someone who forbids selling, but this is not the primary opinion. Similarly, it is permitted to sell the hindquarters to a non-Jew in a place where they do not remove the forbidden fats, and there is concern that it will spoil. All this applies when it is slaughtered on Yom Tov. But if it was slaughtered on the eve of Yom Tov, in any case it is forbidden, because he should have sold it on the eve of Yom Tov, unless he did not have time to sell it before the day, or he is compelled to give meat today to a minister or official. He may sell to him without weighing and for a full sum of money (see Magen Avraham, Siman Katan 19).

In Yoreh De'ah, Siman 18, it is explained that every butcher must show his knife to a sage before slaughtering, out of respect for the sage. Our sages of blessed memory said in Beitzah (28b) that on a festival, he should not show his knife. Rashi explained the reason: it appears like a weekday activity, as it is a noisy matter because it implies that he intends to sell in the market; see there. The Rambam in the fourth chapter wrote the reason: lest he finds it defective, and tells him it is defective, and he goes and sharpens it on a grindstone. And the Rif wrote the reason: lest he goes beyond the techum (Sabbath boundary). That is to say, if you require him to show it to a sage, he will follow him even beyond the techum. And the Ba'al HaMaor wrote the reason: this is similar to the inspection of blemishes in a firstborn, and granting permission for it is like fixing something on a festival. The Beit Yosef only wrote the reason of the Rambam.

There is a practical difference in the law based on the reasons: According to Rashi, it seems that specifically a butcher, who customarily does so on weekdays, and it makes noise, but an ordinary person – we do not concern ourselves with this (see Beit Yosef). Similarly, according to the reason of the Rif, it is only a butcher who is accustomed to go to a sage; we are concerned that he may also go beyond the Shabbat boundary, but not an ordinary person. It appears to me that according to Rashi and the Rif, there is no prohibition in this time, since knives are not shown to a sage as explained in Yoreh De'ah there, because nowadays sages have waived their honor. Therefore, there is no noisy activity, and no concern that he will go beyond the Shabbat boundary, since he is not accustomed to doing so. However, according to Rambam and the Me'or, it is forbidden for everyone; and even nowadays it is forbidden, lest he sharpen it on a whetstone, which appears like fixing. However, there is a leniency according to Rambam when the butcher is a Torah scholar, and there is no concern that he might sharpen it. Similarly, according to the Rif, it is permitted, since a Torah scholar will not go beyond the Shabbat boundary. And according to Rashi and the Me'or, it is obviously forbidden.

And how should they proceed? The Torah scholar should examine the knife himself, for there is no concern even according to the opinion of the Maor, since for oneself there is no issue of fixing a utensil but merely clarifying a doubt (Ran). Afterward, he may lend it to others. Our teacher, the Rema, wrote in Section 1 that nowadays, since every slaughterer examines the knife himself, anyone who wishes to slaughter on Yom Tov should inspect his knife on the eve of Yom Tov and not on Yom Tov, lest he come to sharpen it. However, if he did not inspect it on the eve of Yom Tov, and it is a pressing situation, he may inspect it on Yom Tov. This is his language. 

And it seems to me that the explanation is as follows: Certainly, even in the time of the Talmud, there was an obligation to prepare it on the eve of Yom Tov, but the inspection would not have been effective without the scholar’s examination. He was compelled to show it on the eve of Yom Tov, for on Yom Tov it is forbidden for the reason explained. But now that he examines it himself, he can prepare it on the eve of Yom Tov and inspect it on Yom Tov; if it is good, he will slaughter, and if not, he will not slaughter. Therefore, I say that this is not so, as there is still concern nowadays that he might sharpen it if he is not a Torah scholar. Even a Torah scholar, why should he put himself in this situation, perhaps he is not a Torah scholar. 

And he added that in a pressing situation when it was not inspected on the eve of Yom Tov, he may inspect it on Yom Tov. And not only according to all interpretations but even according to the Rambam’s interpretation. And not only if he is a Torah scholar but even if he is not a Torah scholar, one could say that nowadays, since he relies on his own inspection, presumably he prepared it well as usual, and there is no concern that he might sharpen it. It is obvious that after slaughtering, one is obligated to inspect the knife, as I wrote in Yoreh De’ah there. And in Yoreh De’ah, section 6, it is explained that on Yom Tov it is permitted to wrap a cloth around a nick in the knife, see there. (According to my explanation, all the criticisms of the Magen Avraham on the words of the Rema are resolved, and his words are clear. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

And even though it was explained in Siman 492 that according to all opinions it is rabbinically prohibited to perform any act related to food preparation that could have been done the day before, and certainly preparatory actions for food preparation when they could have been done the day before, which are prohibited by Torah law. Accordingly, if one needs to slaughter an animal or a bird on Yom Tov, he should have prepared the knife and the animal or bird in one place on the eve of Yom Tov, and on Yom Tov the slaughterer would come and slaughter them; and not to bring the animal or the knife to the slaughterer. Nevertheless, the Sages permitted (Beitzah 11a) bringing the animal and the knife to the slaughterer, or the slaughterer bringing his knife to the animal. The reason we explained there in the name of the Rambam is that regarding carrying out, they permitted us entirely, so that our hands would not be restricted in enjoying Yom Tov. And we are permitted to carry and bring anything we want without any restriction at all. Therefore, even a kid that needs to be carried on the shoulder is permitted for this reason. (What the Magen Avraham wrote in subsection 3: since it is for food preparation, see there – this needs examination, for it is rabbinically prohibited to all opinions, as I wrote there.)

It has already been clarified in Siman 498 that regarding muktzeh due to preparation, according to the Rif and the Rambam, Yom Tov is more stringent than Shabbat, for on Yom Tov it is forbidden. Therefore, one is only permitted to slaughter animals that were prepared for him from the eve of Yom Tov. This does not only apply to animals that are always with him, but even those that go out to graze beyond the boundary and return to spend the night within the boundary are considered prepared, for he has intention for them, and one may take them and slaughter them on Yom Tov. However, those that graze and spend the night beyond the boundary, if they come on Yom Tov, they may not be slaughtered on Yom Tov, because they are muktzeh, and the people of the town do not have intention for them. Even though they are otherwise forbidden because they came from beyond the boundary, this is not the case, as this prohibition only applies to those for whom they came. But for others, it is permitted, as I wrote in Siman 415. However, due to the reason of muktzeh, they are forbidden even for others. According to this, for the poskim who permit muktzeh, as I wrote there, these animals are also permitted for others. There are those who are stringent even according to these opinions, because there is an establishment in the Gemara (end of Beitzah) that compares them to figs and raisins that were dried by hand. Nevertheless, the opinion of the Rosh is that since there is another establishment in the Gemara that does not compare them to figs and raisins, one may be lenient in rabbinic matters. (See Magen Avraham, subsection 4, where the Shelah is stringent. I do not know why he is stringent in rabbinic matters against the opinion of the Rosh and the Tur. However, the opinion of the Rema also seems to be so, as he did not comment here in subsection 3 on the words of the Mechaber, as he did in Siman 498. This implies that he agrees that here it is forbidden according to all opinions. Examine this well and you will find it straightforward.)

And all this applies to the animal of a Jew. But the animal of a non-Jew is permitted in every case, as it has already been explained there based on the Jerusalem Talmud that theirs does not require preparation, and there is no issue of muktzeh unless it was brought for a Jew on Yom Tov – then it is forbidden for the one for whom it was brought, as is the law of something brought from beyond the techum. But for others, it is permitted. Sometimes it is forbidden for all the people of the city: for example, if the animal was brought from beyond the techum for someone to purchase, and the city is mostly Jewish, as it was brought with the Jews in mind. But when the city is mostly non-Jewish – it is permitted, as will be explained in Siman 515. And if it is uncertain whether it was brought from beyond the techum or not, for instance, if he has animals both within the techum and beyond the techum – it is permitted, even if it was brought for a Jew, since with muktzeh, we are lenient in cases of doubt. And even though we were stringent in cases of doubt regarding preparation in Siman 497, that only applies when there is a concern of a Torah prohibition, like trapping and similar issues, but not in cases of doubt concerning beyond the techum, which is a Rabbinic issue. And there are those who forbid even in cases of doubt concerning beyond the techum (see Magen Avraham, subparagraph 7). And if it is known that it was brought for the needs of a non-Jew – in every case it is permitted. And one should not ask: How can he purchase it from him on Yom Tov? For it can be said that he acquires it without a transaction and without weighing, or that it was given to him as a gift.

Our master the Beit Yosef wrote in section 4: Known animals that sleep outside the boundary and are found in the city on the second day, I say that perhaps they were brought in on the eve and they slept outside the wall—and they are permitted. And certainly, those that were slaughtered in the morning, there is a presumption that they were brought within the boundary on the eve. Thus is his wording. And there are those who wrote that even on the first day it is permitted with a doubt of outside the boundary, as I wrote in the previous section (Taz, small section 1, and Magen Avraham, small section 7 in the name of the Shach). And so wrote the Rashba. And there are those who say that the Beit Yosef holds that on the first day one should be stringent even in a doubt of outside the boundary (Magen Avraham there), and this will be explained in section 515. (And regarding what the Taz wrote that on the second day the "all the more so" does not apply, see there—I do not know why. For someone who came from outside the boundary on the first day is permitted on the second day, as I wrote in section 515. And also the Pri Megadim remains in need of clarification, see there.)

A calf that is born on Yom Tov: If the animal is not designated for slaughter, it is forbidden to slaughter it due to the prohibitions of muktzeh and nolad. However, if it is designated for eating and we know that its months have been completed, meaning it does not need to wait eight days as I wrote in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 13, it is permitted to slaughter it on Yom Tov because it is considered prepared through its mother’s slaughter. For if the mother were slaughtered while the calf was still in her womb, the calf would also be permitted, as in the case of a "ben pekuah" (an animal found alive inside its slaughtered mother), and it therefore never acquires the status of muktzeh or nolad. Even if it turns out that the mother was a treifah (an animal with a fatal defect), and the calf is not permitted together with the mother, it is still allowed because the treifah is considered prepared for dogs, and we hold that what is prepared for dogs is considered prepared for humans (Maggid Mishneh). According to those who hold that muktzeh is permitted on Yom Tov, even if the animal is not designated for eating, the calf is permitted. There is reason to say that it is permitted even if born on Yom Tov is generally forbidden, because in the case of a calf, nolad does not apply since it is sometimes permitted even while in its mother’s womb, that is, when the mother is slaughtered. (Tosafot 2b, beginning with "A calf", and see there in Maharama, Maharshal, in Yam Shel Shlomo, and in Magen Avraham, Siman Katan 8, and in Machatzit HaShekel.)

Even on Shabbat and Yom Tov that are adjacent to each other, if a calf is born on Shabbat, it is permitted on Yom Tov; if it is born on Yom Tov, it is permitted on Shabbat, provided that the mother was intended for consumption and its gestation was complete. And although an egg that is born on Yom Tov is prohibited, even from a chicken intended for consumption, due to the principle of preparation (hachanah), meaning: if Yom Tov falls on Sunday, it is prohibited because of the law of preparation, for any egg that is laid today was completed yesterday, and it turns out that Shabbat prepared for Yom Tov. Therefore, they decreed regarding all Yom Tov, as will be explained in Siman 513. But why is there no law of preparation with a calf? The reason is that preparation does not truly apply to a calf, because it is only an egg that, when inside its mother, is not fit to grow into a chick, and upon its emergence, it becomes fit, making its emergence a complete vessel – thus it is appropriately called "preparation." This is not the case with a calf. It is the same whether it is in its mother's womb or after its birth.

The Tur wrote: A calf that is born on a Yom Tov is permitted to be slaughtered... provided... that its months are complete, and provided that it has trodden on the ground, indicating that it is not suffering from crushed limbs. This is the end of his words. And they questioned him: for it is explicitly concluded in Chullin (51b) that a fetus within the womb does not have the concern of crushed limbs. And the Tur himself wrote in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 58, that if a fetus is born, there is no concern for crushed limbs, even if it shows signs of weakness and cannot stand. And it is permitted to slaughter it immediately if its months are complete. See there (see Beit Yosef, Bach, and Drisha).

And therefore, our teacher the Rema wrote in paragraph five regarding this law, and this is his language: "And it is also required that it spread out on the ground, for we are concerned that it might display a defect in the internal organs, and it will turn out that one slaughtered on Yom Tov unnecessarily." This is the end of his language, meaning: Certainly on a weekday, it does not need to spread out on the ground, and if a defect is found, it will be rendered non-kosher. Therefore, on Yom Tov, when it is forbidden to slaughter a non-kosher animal, it must spread out on the ground to show that there is no defect in the internal organs. And even though with a bird that has been attacked, which requires inspection, it is still permitted to slaughter it, and we are not concerned about defects, as will be explained, this is because it has delayed for twenty-four hours, as will be explained. Therefore, even though it requires inspection, it is still more likely that there is no defect since it has delayed for twenty-four hours. But here, it is likely that a defect will be found. Therefore, one should not slaughter it unless it has spread out on the ground. And all this was in the time of the Talmud. But nowadays, we are not experts in "its months are complete," and we do not slaughter a calf until the night of the eighth day. (And see what I wrote in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 15, paragraph 8 regarding the words of the Tur, see there. And be precise and you will find light.)

If an animal is dangerously ill, and one fears it will die, and he does not need it because he has already eaten his meal, but he slaughters it to avoid losing its value (Rashi 25a) – he should not slaughter unless he can still eat from it an olive-sized portion of roasted meat during the day. If there is enough time for this – he is permitted to slaughter, even though he will not eat, for we say: "Since, if he wanted to eat, he could eat" (Pesachim 46b). Even though we do not initially permit an action based on "since," for it is forbidden to cook on a festival for a weekday, and we do not say "since, if guests happened to come, it would be suitable for them," as is proven from what will be explained in Siman 503, in this case, due to the loss of his money, it is permitted. And even without the "since," he resolves in his mind, due to the loss of his money, to eat an olive-sized portion of meat, and it is impossible to obtain this portion without slaughtering. (This is how it appears to me to explain in Pesachim there, for otherwise, it is difficult even for Rabbah; see there. Examine and you will find it easy.)

And this is the language of the Tur: A dangerously ill animal... unless there is enough time during the day to eat an olive's bulk of it while it is still day. And even if there is not enough time during the day to examine and dissect it – one can eat without examination. Thus far is his language. And some have inferred from this language that the Tur holds that actual eating is necessary and it is not sufficient that one is able to eat (Bach). But it does not seem so, as it is explicitly proven in Pesachim there that for those who hold "since" (ho'il), it is not necessary to actually eat. Rather, the Tur is informing us that if one wishes to eat, one can eat the olive's bulk without examination and dissection. For although it is forbidden to eat before the lung is examined – nevertheless, they permitted it here due to potential loss. And this is also explicitly stated in the words of the Rosh there. They were compelled to this: for if not, how could they permit it even when there is no time to examine, since he cannot eat? Rather, it is certain they permitted him to actually eat as well. And this is also the intention of our teacher, the Rema, in paragraph 6, where he wrote about this law: And even if there is no time to dissect and examine it first. Thus far is his language. (And see the Gra in paragraph 11, and in my humble opinion, it is clear as I have written. Examine it and you will find it easy.)

They only permitted this matter in the case of a dangerously ill person, and not for a healthy person. When they permitted it for a dangerously ill person when there is ample time, they even permitted skinning the animal if the flesh would spoil by the next day. However, to move the hide after skinning—they did not permit due to muktzeh, unless a limb is still attached to the hide, or a bit of flesh, and then one moves the hide because of the flesh. And even though for any slaughtering on a festival they permitted moving the hide, and even placing it before trampling feet, as they permitted the end because of the beginning, as I wrote in Siman 499, that is because the slaughtering is for the joy of the festival—it is necessary to permit, for if not, he will not slaughter. But when the slaughtering is to prevent loss, he will still slaughter even without this permission, and if he does not slaughter, it does not prevent the joy of the festival. Indeed, some say it is forbidden to completely skin in such a manner when the slaughtering is not for the joy of the festival. And so it is appropriate to rule (Rema there).

When one slaughters an animal on Yom Tov in the field, even a healthy animal, and due to the joy of Yom Tov – nevertheless, he should not bring it with a pole or a frame as he does on weekdays, because of the disrespect to Yom Tov. Rather, he should bring it by hand, piece by piece, as it is less conspicuous. All the more so if he slaughters a sick animal to prevent loss. And although this will require him to walk many times and increase his walking, whereas with a pole he could carry it all at once – nevertheless, it is better to increase the walking than to carry it as on a weekday, due to the disrespect to Yom Tov (Magen Avraham, subsection 15).

The Tur and the Shulchan Aruch write in Section 8: A bird that has been trampled upon by feet and there is concern that its limbs have been crushed, therefore it requires a 24-hour waiting period and an examination after slaughtering – it is permitted to slaughter it on Yom Tov. We do not worry that it might be found to be a treifah, even though there is a suspicion of injury. This is their language, for since it had a presumption of fitness – it is permitted to slaughter it, as we rely on its presumption. The presumption is based on the majority, as most animals are fit, just as with any animal that requires a lung inspection and yet it is permitted to slaughter it, because we rely on the majority, and the same applies here. Even though it is not precisely the same since there is a suspicion of injury, nevertheless we do not worry, for as long as the injury has not been confirmed – we rely on the presumption. Even though a calf born on Yom Tov is forbidden to be slaughtered unless it is known that its months are complete – this is a general decree that the Rabbis decreed, that anything that has not lived seven days is considered a miscarriage, and it is also forbidden on a weekday. But in the case of an incidental injury that is permitted on a weekday – it is also permitted on Yom Tov. (And this resolves the difficulty of the Magen Avraham in Section 16 regarding a calf, see there. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

However, there are those who forbid [slaughtering] when a defect is found. Similarly, in places where non-kosher animals are as prevalent as kosher ones – it is forbidden to slaughter on Yom Tov (Taz, subsection 8 in the name of the Ran, and Or Zaru'a and Sheyarei Knesset HaGedolah, and likewise, the Magen Avraham there in the name of the Hagahot Asheri). Indeed, our custom is not to slaughter on Yom Tov (ibid.). Nevertheless, if it is absolutely necessary – one may slaughter (ibid.). To me, it appears that the reason we customarily refrain from slaughtering on Yom Tov is not due to a concern of prohibition, for it is common practice to slaughter poultry on Yom Tov. And even with animals, it is not due to the prohibition of slaughtering, but because the selling process is difficult on Yom Tov, since one must sell without bargaining and without weighing. Furthermore, someone who has never slaughtered before should not do so for the first time on Yom Tov, as they are likely to make a mistake and render the meat non-kosher (Sha'arei Teshuvah). (See Sha'agat Aryeh, Siman 64, where he elaborates to prove that there is no prohibition to slaughter when a defect is found, in accordance with the first opinion.)

A firstborn animal in our times, which is forbidden to be slaughtered without a blemish, and requires a court to permit it, and if they slaughtered it before it was permitted, its meat is forbidden as I have written in Yoreh De'ah siman 311. Therefore, if it was not permitted before the festival, it is forbidden to permit it on the festival, as this would be like judging a case. Certainly, to see the blemish and to think in one's heart whether it is a blemish or not in order to permit it after the festival is allowed, as this is merely instruction. But to permit it is considered as fixing and like judging a case. Not only initially, but even if they transgressed and permitted it on the festival, it is forbidden to slaughter it as it is considered muktzeh. This muktzeh is like dried figs and raisins, as it was not fit for consumption at all from the moment it was born. And even though in its mother's womb it was fit due to its mother if she was slaughtered, as long as it had not come into the world, it is not sanctified. Nevertheless, immediately upon birth, it becomes muktzeh in his mind. Therefore, if it was born with its blemish, and they transgressed and saw it on the festival, they may slaughter based on their observation, as it was prepared due to its mother, as I have written. And this is when it was born on the festival from an animal designated for eating, and its months were completed, as at twilight it was prepared due to its mother. And even though after it was born it became muktzeh, there is no partial muktzeh for half of Shabbat, as muktzeh only applies at twilight, as I have written in siman 308. Also, if they saw the blemish on the eve of the festival and saw that it was a blemish that warranted slaughter, even though they did not say, "You are permitted to slaughter," the muktzeh status was removed on the eve of the festival. And even though they still need to investigate whether the blemish occurred naturally or intentionally, and it is not permitted because of this, such as when the firstborn is in the hands of a priest who is suspected regarding firstborns, this does not prevent the permission. For even if they were to slaughter it before the investigation and examination, it would still be permitted, as I have written in Yoreh De'ah there, siman 314, see there.

A firstborn animal that has fallen into a pit, since it is not fit to be slaughtered today – it is forbidden to lift it out of the pit, as it is considered set-aside (mukzeh), since it is not fit for consumption. Additionally, it is forbidden to exert effort on its behalf on Yom Tov; rather, one should provide for it in its place, meaning he should give it in the pit all that it needs to eat and drink. The same law applies to an animal designated for milking and not for slaughter; since it is not fit for slaughter on Yom Tov, it is also forbidden to lift it out. However, it seems to me that through a non-Jew it is permitted, as it is a double rabbinic prohibition (shvut d'shvut) in a case of animal suffering and potential loss – it is certainly permitted.

Regarding "it and its offspring" that have fallen into a pit, where one of them is fit for slaughter on Yom Tov, and consequently, the other is forbidden to be slaughtered today due to the prohibition of "it and its offspring on the same day" – he can lift the first one with the intention to slaughter it. Afterwards, he can reconsider and decide not to slaughter it, but rather to slaughter the other, and he lifts the second one. Although this is considered deceitful, it is permitted due to the concern for animal suffering and loss. Subsequently, he can slaughter whichever he wishes: if he wants, he can slaughter this one, and if he wants, he can slaughter that one, since each was lifted permissibly. And it appears that if he wants, he does not have to slaughter them at all, for animals designated for consumption, when they fall into a pit – it is certainly permitted to lift them even if he does not slaughter any of them, since they are fit for slaughter. The same applies here. And in the Jerusalem Talmud, it is explicitly explained that in the case of "it and its offspring" – he does not need to slaughter either of them, see there. (And this is the language of the Jerusalem Talmud, third chapter of Beitzah, halacha 4: Even if he did not intend to slaughter either of them – it is permitted, see there.)

An animal that is half-owned by a non-Jew and half-owned by a Jew can be slaughtered on Yom Tov. This is not similar to dough in such a case where it is forbidden, as I wrote in Siman 506, because dough can be divided, and he can bake his portion separately. But for an animal, it is impossible to get even an olive's worth of meat without slaughtering it (Talmud, Beitza 21a). Furthermore, even if they have two animals, he can slaughter both of them. Although it is possible to divide, nonetheless, they are not completely equal, and one might say he wants his portion from each animal. Accordingly, some say that if the non-Jew wants to give him the better and fatter one, it is forbidden for him to slaughter both (Magen Avraham, subsection 21). However, others disagree and say that even so, he can claim, "I prefer to eat from both" (Levush and Eliyah Rabbah, subsection 21). And some say that if both animals are equal, it is forbidden for him to slaughter even one without division, so as not to exert effort for the non-Jew's portion (Taz, subsection 10). But this is certainly not the case, for why should we force him to divide? (And what the Taz wrote from Tosafot there regarding dough is not similar at all, for with dough, there is effort involved in each portion of the dough, which is not the case with slaughtering, where the effort is singular. This is what was meant by saying: it is impossible to get an olive's worth of meat without slaughtering. Meaning, slaughtering for an olive's worth is the same as slaughtering for the whole. Additionally, with an animal, the Jew can claim he wants to taste from each animal, as it is impossible for the tastes to be completely equal, which is not the case with dough. Examine and you will find clarity.)

Rambam writes in Chapter 3, Law 3: If one slaughters an animal on a festival, it is permitted to pluck wool with one's hand from the area of the knife, provided that one does not move it from its place, but rather leaves it entangled with the rest of the wool of the neck. However, with a bird, one should not pluck because this is its usual manner, and thus it would be considered plucking on a festival. This is his wording, indicating that for an animal, its usual manner is shearing, and plucking is not like shearing. Plucking with one's hand is considered shearing in an unusual manner, whereas with a knife it is considered actual shearing and is forbidden. But with one's hand, it is permissible to pluck intentionally, as long as one does not move it from its place so that the plucking is not evident. However, with a bird, its usual manner is plucking, so plucking is a complete act and is considered a primary category of labor, and therefore it is forbidden. Even though after slaughtering, one will indeed pluck all of it, this is permitted because all labor for the sake of food preparation is allowed, unlike before the slaughter which is only considered a preparatory act. Therefore, something that is necessary like the slaughter itself is permitted, but the plucking could have been done the day before (Maggid Mishneh).

And the Ramban, of blessed memory, disagrees with him, and holds that it is permissible to pluck the bird at the place of slaughter, for just as its slaughtering is permitted, so too is its plucking. For all of it is considered preparation of food, meaning that the work is on the food itself, and it is permitted. However, the R”I (Rabbi Isaac) of the Tosafists, the Rosh, and the Tur agreed with the Rambam that it is forbidden to pluck. Moreover, they were stringent even with an animal, stating that it is forbidden to pluck directly, because plucking is considered shearing, and it is only permitted if it is unintended, since we hold that an unintended act is permitted. And so ruled our teacher, the Beit Yosef, in section 12, and this is his language: "One who slaughters an animal on a festival is not allowed to pluck the wool to make a place for the knife, but rather he moves it and pulls it this way and that. And if it gets plucked, it gets plucked." This is his language, meaning it is an unintended act and not a certain outcome. And our teacher the Rema glossed that one should move it with his hand. Not because there is a difference between the hand and the knife, for this is only according to the Rambam who holds that plucking is not shearing, and with a knife it is shearing. But if plucking is shearing, then it is also forbidden by hand as by knife. The permission is because it is unintended, and if so, even with a knife it should be permitted. However, the reason is that with a knife it is a certain outcome, for it is inevitable that it will be plucked. And regarding a bird, he ruled in section 13 according to the Rambam, and this is his language: "One who slaughters a bird should not pluck the feathers to make a place for the knife." This is his language, due to the reasons we have explained. (And their dispute is dependent on the Talmudic discussion in Bechorot 25a. And see what I wrote in Yoreh De'ah, section 24, paragraph 21, that one must be careful that the knife is not covered by feathers, so that it should not be like a hidden defect, see there. And it appears in my humble opinion that if the slaughterer cannot perform the slaughter properly without plucking the feathers, he can rely on the Ramban and pluck.
