For the main reason for the prohibition is that it is not necessary for the slaughter and does not override the festival, as written by the Maggid Mishneh and in the Magen Avraham at the end of section 24, see there. But when it is necessary, it is permitted. Be precise and you will find leniency.)

One who knows that they need to slaughter a bird on Yom Tov, and a bird requires covering its blood with earth, and all earth is muktzeh – therefore, they need to prepare earth from the eve of Yom Tov. If they did not prepare – they should not slaughter, as the Rambam writes at the beginning of the third chapter: "One who had prepared earth or ashes that are permitted to be moved – this person may slaughter a wild animal or bird and cover their blood. If they do not have prepared earth or ashes that are suitable to be moved – they should not slaughter. If they transgressed and slaughtered – they should not cover the blood until the evening." So far his words. In this case, it is not applicable to say that it should be permitted on Yom Tov for the sake of food preparation, as covering is considered a preparatory act for food preparation, and it could have been done yesterday. Therefore, it does not override Yom Tov; consequently, if one does not have what to cover with – it is forbidden to slaughter. Inevitably, this nullifies the joy of Yom Tov, and although one can leave the blood until the evening and then cover it, who says it will last until the evening? Perhaps it will be consumed, and there will be nothing to cover it with, and the positive commandment of covering will be nullified. Therefore, it is forbidden to slaughter. However, if one did slaughter, they should leave the blood until the evening; if it lasts, they should cover it, and if not, the positive commandment of covering is nullified. They did not permit taking unprepared earth, as they upheld their words in a situation where the person is at fault for not preparing from the eve of Yom Tov. All the more so, the positive commandment of covering does not override the prohibition of Yom Tov in a Torah prohibition like digging or grinding the earth, even though a positive commandment overrides a negative commandment. However, Yom Tov has both a positive and negative commandment, and a positive commandment does not override a positive and negative commandment (Gemara Chagigah 8b). Therefore, even though it will certainly dry by the evening – nevertheless, it is forbidden. (So it seems to me from the discussion in the Talmud Chagigah 8b, for otherwise, what purpose does the rule of a positive commandment overriding a negative commandment serve? For it can be fulfilled in the evening. And even if there is a doubt whether it will last, how can one override the negative commandment due to doubt? Rather, it is certain – even if it will certainly dry. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

It is taught at the beginning of Beitzah: One who slaughters a wild animal or bird on a festival, Beit Shammai says: he should dig with a spade and cover [the blood]. And Beit Hillel says: he should not slaughter unless he has soil prepared from before the festival. However, they agree that if he did slaughter, he should dig with a spade and cover [the blood]. And it is stated in the Gemara that this is specifically when he had a spade stuck in the ground from before the festival, and the soil is loose, so it does not require crushing. And even though he makes a hole, we hold that one who digs a hole and only needs the soil is exempt, and here he only needs the soil. And even though it is rabbinically prohibited, here, due to the joy of the festival, they were lenient when there is a spade stuck [in the ground] that was prepared from before the festival. But without preparation, they did not permit it because of the prohibition of muktzeh (as the Tosafot there 8a in the beginning of the discussion "and he does not need"). And this is specifically in a case of ex post facto, when he already slaughtered. But initially, even in such a case, it is prohibited because of digging the hole. Therefore, if there is a lot of loose soil in a way that does not make a hole, it is permitted even initially to slaughter, since there is no prohibition at all. And similarly, ex post facto, even without a spade stuck [in the ground], where there is no preparation, it is permitted if there is a lot of loose soil, for just as they permitted the prohibition of the hole when there is preparation, so too they permitted the prohibition of preparation when there is no hole. (Magen Avraham, subsection 25 in the name of the Yeshu'ot Yaakov. And see Taz, subsection 12, who elaborates on the intention of the master of the Semag, who wrote that if he already slaughtered and does not have prepared soil, he can cover with unprepared soil, see there. And the Beit Yosef understood this according to Rabbeinu Tam's opinion, and the Taz also elaborated on this. But according to the words of the Magen Avraham, it is clear that this is the opinion of the Tosafot, that with a spade stuck [in the ground], they permitted the prohibition of the hole, and when there is no hole, they permitted the prohibition of preparation, and we are not concerned about muktzeh. Examine and you will find it simple.)

However, the Sages did not permit slaughter without covering the blood and leaving the blood until the evening initially, because the blood might get consumed and the mitzvah of covering the blood would be nullified. As we have said, with loose soil and no pit, it is permitted to cover the blood after slaughter even if the soil was not prepared; or even if the soil was prepared, it is permitted initially to slaughter as explained. If it happens that when slaughtering, the blood falls on hard ground, if there is a lot of blood – take some of the blood and place it in loose soil and cover it. For post facto, not all the blood needs to be covered, as I wrote in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 28. But if the blood has dried, it is forbidden to scrape it on Yom Tov, because by doing so one makes a small pit in the house, which is close to a Biblical prohibition (there). It is obvious that when there is prepared soil, one needs to place soil below as part of the mitzvah of covering the blood. We do not worry that since the soil below is placed before the slaughter, there is a concern that one might change their mind and not slaughter as there is no other way. This is also implied in the Gemara there.

In this allowance for when the peg was inserted before Shabbat, our teacher, the Rema, wrote in section 14 that even if one needs to make multiple insertions, it is permitted. This is his language: since the earth is loose and the peg is already inserted, there is preparation, but there is a rabbinic prohibition of making a hole. Therefore, what difference does it make if it is one insertion or many insertions? And some say that only one insertion is permitted, because inserting in a new place is like a new excavation (there, subsection 26 in the name of the Bach, and Taz at the end of subsection 21). But this is not the opinion of the decisors (Magen Avraham there).

The ashes of a stove or oven that was heated on the eve of a festival—one is permitted initially to slaughter and cover [the blood] with it, for it is not muktzeh. And one covers with ashes, as I wrote in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 28. However, if it was heated on the festival—it is forbidden, as it is considered nolad (something newly created), for initially, it was wood and now it is ashes. And in such a complete case of nolad, even Rabbi Shimon, who does not hold by muktzeh, agrees that it is forbidden (see Tosafot Eruvin 46a). However, if the ashes are still hot, such that one can roast an egg with them—they are not considered muktzeh, as their status remains the same as it was permitted on the festival, and consequently, it is also permitted to cover with them. And if one heated today upon the ashes of yesterday and they mixed—the prohibition of today is nullified by the majority of yesterday if there is a majority. And we do not treat ashes as a liquid mixed with a liquid that requires sixty [times the amount], since the prohibition is rabbinic, and the prohibition was never noticeable by itself—it is properly nullified by the majority (see Magen Avraham, Siman Katan 28). However, if one slaughtered and there are no hot ashes—it is permitted to cover even with cold ashes that were heated today, because we have already explained that one rabbinic prohibition was permitted for the sake of covering in a case of necessity when one has slaughtered (ibid, Siman Katan 30).

And regarding this law, when he slaughters, it is permitted to cover [the blood] even with cold ash. Our Rabbi, the Rema, wrote in Section 15, and this is his wording: "However, it is preferable to cover with a spade stuck in loose earth if he has one." Until here is his wording. According to him, the case of digging a pit and only needing its earth is lesser, for it is exempt but forbidden due to the prohibition of muktzeh. And this is muktzeh and nolad of cold ash. And even though both are rabbinic prohibitions, nevertheless, muktzeh and nolad are a comprehensive prohibition, and their prohibition is stricter than a specific rabbinic prohibition. They brought proof for this from the Jerusalem Talmud at the beginning of Beitzah, which says: "It is better to take ash that was heated on Yom Tov, than to dig with a spade and cover," see there. This shows that regarding digging with a spade, which is a Torah prohibition, ash is lighter, but not when the spade is stuck in the ground (Beit Yosef and Taz, Section 16). But there are those who say the opposite, that muktzeh is lighter, since it was permitted for the sake of food preparation, as I wrote in Section 502. And the Jerusalem Talmud refers to the Mishnah, which deals with a spade stuck in the ground, as established in our Gemara. And in this, it says that it is better to take ash (and this is the intention of the Magen Avraham in Section 31). And it seems to me that the primary opinion is the first one, for the Jerusalem Talmud explains there that the reason to dig with a spade and cover is because a positive commandment overrides a negative commandment (see there in Halacha 3). This teaches that it interprets digging with a spade without it being stuck, unlike our Talmud.

If one brought a large amount of soil into his house for the purpose of his garden or ruin, and the soil is loose, not requiring crushing or digging, but rather prepared for his garden or ruin – this is not considered preparation, since the types of work prohibited on Yom Tov are involved. Nevertheless, it is permitted to cover with it, because as long as it remains piled in one place and has not been spread over his garden or ruin, we say that his intention is to use the soil for all necessary uses, and it is considered prepared. In this case, neither digging nor making a hole is relevant since it is not in its original place. However, if the soil is not loose, making a hole is relevant even if the soil is not in its original place, since the clod remains whole as it was in its place. But if the soil is loose, even if it later becomes stuck together with water like clay, it seems to me that making a hole is not relevant in this case, as I wrote in Siman 511. (See Magen Avraham, Subsection 32, who writes that placing a wax candle into hard sand on Yom Tov involves making a hole. According to what I wrote, if it is stuck together by water, there is no concern of making a hole. And generally, this is how it is, as they do on Simchat Torah).

This which we said regarding bringing in a large amount of soil for the purpose of one's garden, that it is permissible to use it, the Tur and Shulchan Aruch wrote in Section 16 that one brings [the soil] into his house for the purpose of his garden. But in the Gemara (Beitzah 8a) it is stated: "If one brings soil into his garden or his ruin, it is permissible to cover with it." This implies that even when one brings it into a garden or a ruin, it is permissible. And it seems that their opinion is that for a garden and a ruin in any manner it is forbidden, because from that point the soil is nullified to them. Therefore, they interpret that he brought it into his house for the purpose of his garden and ruin. And Rambam in the second chapter omitted this law, and I do not know why. And the Rif brought it, see there. And our teacher the Beit Yosef added and wrote: "But if he brought a full basket for the purpose of his garden, it is not [permissible], because since it is a small amount it is nullified." So far his language, and I do not know his source. And his reasoning is that since he brought it into his house, how is it nullified to the garden? And it seems that he learned this from what is said in the Gemara (Beitzah 8a): "A person can bring a full basket of soil and do with it all his needs." And its explanation is that he brought it in without specifying, as will be explained. And so the Tur wrote. And it implies specifically without specifying, and consequently for his garden and ruin it is forbidden. And the reason can be said that since fixing the garden and the ruin are necessary for him, and the soil is small in quantity, certainly he designated it only for that. Which is not the case with a large amount of soil.

A person may bring a full basket of dirt into a house or courtyard and use it for all his needs. We do not say that it is nullified by being on the ground of the house or courtyard. This is provided that he designates a specific corner for it, meaning he designates a place for this purpose. However, if he spreads it on the ground, it is certainly nullified to the ground, even if the ground has flooring. But when he designates a place for it and does not spread it, it is clear that he needs the dirt for his purposes. Therefore, if the dirt is loose, it is permitted to use it to cover things. 

Accordingly, in our practice, we must caution that when some people spread green sand on the floors in houses, it is forbidden to use this sand for any purpose, as it is nullified to the ground. They should use the sand that was placed in a designated corner. It seems that people are not careful about this, and perhaps they think that nullification only applies when the sand is spread on the ground without flooring, but not when there is flooring. One cannot argue that if so, why is a designated corner necessary? It can be said that this applies where there is no flooring. As we wrote earlier in section 308, paragraph 64, when there is flooring, the dirt is not nullified to the ground. See there.

It is stated in the Gemara (8b): Rava said: If one brought in dirt to cover excrement in case a child soils himself, it is permissible to use it to cover the blood of a bird. Since he designated it for the possibility that the child might soil himself, all the more so he designated it for the blood of a bird, knowing for certain that he would need to slaughter on Yom Tov. But if he brought it in specifically to cover the blood of a bird, it is forbidden to use it to cover excrement, as he designated it for the certainty and not for the possibility. The Naharbela'i said: Even if he brought it in for the blood of a bird, it is permissible to use it for excrement, since once he designated it, he designated it for all purposes, whether for certainty or for possibility. Now, the poskim (decisors of Jewish law) did not mention this statement at all. It appears that they hold the halacha (law) like the Naharbela'i, for even though Rava was the master of the entire Talmud, nevertheless, an individual versus many, the halacha follows the many. Moreover, in matters of rabbinic law, we rule leniently. Therefore, since they did not write that if one designated for this purpose it does not help for another purpose, it is inferred that it is all one designation. One does not need to specify anything in the designation, and even if he specified for a certain purpose, it is permissible for all purposes. Nevertheless, they should not have omitted and entirely skipped this matter. (And the Yam Shel Shlomo, section 23, rules like Rava, see there. This is certainly against all the poskim, obviously. Be precise and you will find leniency.)

A "koi," which is an animal that is in doubt whether it is a wild animal or a domesticated animal, and requires covering its blood out of doubt – it is forbidden to slaughter it on a festival, because it is not possible to cover its blood on a festival, as will be explained. And if one slaughtered it – one does not cover its blood, even if he has earth prepared from the day before, for a different reason: we are concerned that the observer who sees the blood being covered on the festival will say, "Certainly it is a wild animal," because if it were not so, they would not trouble to cover its blood on the festival. And they will come to permit its fat like the fat of a wild animal. But on a weekday, we are not concerned about this, for people will say he needs to clean his courtyard (as stated in the Gemara there). Meaning: he is doing it for the sake of cleaning, and not for the sake of covering. But on a festival, they will not attribute it to cleaning the courtyard, for it is not customary to clean the courtyard on a festival. Therefore, when one slaughters it – let the blood remain until evening. And if its mark is still visible – he should cover it, and if not – he should not cover it. And eating is not hindered by this, for the covering is not related to the eating.

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote on this law in section 18: And specifically if one slaughtered in a corner or the like. But if one slaughtered in the middle of the courtyard, even the blood of an animal can be covered if he has prepared earth, because it is like a 'chamber pot of excrement.' And it is necessary to cover it so that his clothes do not get soiled in the courtyard. Thus far his words, meaning: Even though it is stated in the Gemara that on Yom Tov one should not depend on cleaning the courtyard, as I have written, this refers to cleaning the entire courtyard to the extent that even the corners are cleaned—this is not common on Yom Tov. But something repulsive placed in an open area—one must remove it even on Shabbat. For this reason, we say above in Siman 308 that a 'chamber pot of excrement' is permitted to be moved on Shabbat, see there. Therefore, in the middle of the courtyard, it is certainly considered something repulsive, and it is customary to cover it even on Yom Tov, and one should not rely on the mitzvah of covering (the blood). (See Magen Avraham, small section 35, who struggled much with this. Based on what I have written, the matter is clear in its reasoning. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

It is stated in the Gemara (8b): Rabbi Zeira taught: Not only is the case of a koi (a hybrid animal) mentioned, but even if one slaughtered a domesticated animal, a wild animal, and a bird, and their blood mixed together – it is forbidden to cover it on Yom Tov because one would also be exerting oneself for the sake of the domesticated animal (Rashi). Rabbi Yossi bar Yasinaya said: They only taught this when it is not possible to cover it with a single thrust. But if it is possible to cover it with a single thrust – it is permitted, as he is not increasing his exertion for the sake of the domesticated animal. The Gemara questions: Isn't this obvious? And it answers: One might have thought to decree against a single thrust because of two thrusts. Therefore, it informs us that this is not the case. 

From the simple understanding of the language, which states "not only the koi...", it implies that any type of covering is forbidden, even if he has prepared dirt, as Rabbeinu the Beit Yosef wrote in paragraph 19, and this is his language: If one slaughtered a domesticated animal and a wild animal and their blood mixed, and he has prepared dirt or stove ashes, if he can cover it with a single thrust, not needing to increase exertion for the blood of the domesticated animal – he should cover it. If not – he should not cover it. Until here is his language.

But the matter is perplexing: for dust that is completely prepared, why should we nullify the mitzvah of covering because of a slight exertion? And it is true that our Rabbis, the Tosafists, raised this question and explained that "sitting and refraining" (passivity) is within their power, see there. However, it is not understood. It is true that they have the power, but what did they see to establish it this way? Furthermore, what is the meaning of the terms "one stabbing," "two stabbings," as this terminology applies only to an embedded thorn. But regarding the covering of ashes and dust, it should have said "one covering," "two coverings." Moreover, what is meant by "not only for a koy did they say, but even...?" What is the connection between the koy and the slaughtering of domestic and wild animals? For a koy, they decreed because of the permissibility of its fat, as explained, but for domestic and wild animals, it is because of the exertion? One could say that the baraita holds that even for a koy, it is due to exertion.

It seems clear to me that from all this, the Tur wrote, and this is his wording: "It appears that if he can cover it with one piercing, since he has already slaughtered – it is permitted, even if he does not have prepared earth, as long as he has a fixed spade and loose earth. And if he has prepared earth – he can cover it, even with many piercings." Until here, his wording. The Tur holds that this rule applies only to a fixed spade, where there is a prohibition of making a hole. And as I wrote in paragraph 24, where there is a rabbinic prohibition on this, the reasoning of the Tosafot applies, who established their words to nullify the commandment of covering [the blood] by "sitting and not doing" when two piercings are needed? Otherwise, it is permitted even with many piercings, as I wrote in paragraph 26. But when he has completely prepared earth, it is obvious that it is permitted in all cases. The commentators found difficulty in his words, but according to our explanation, his words are necessary. (See the annotations of the Tur, who wrote similarly. And perhaps it can also be said that the Tur holds that even here there was a concern about permitting the fat, for when they see two piercings, they will think that both were vital. And see Beit Yosef and Taz paragraph 21, who elaborated on this. And according to what I wrote, everything is explained well. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

And the Rambam at the beginning of the third chapter explains that it is also forbidden with prepared earth. However, from his words, I have learned a different intention in this, and these are his words: "If one slaughters an animal, beast, or bird and their blood gets mixed together, one should not cover it until the evening. But if he has prepared earth or ashes and can cover it all with one thrust, he should cover it." Up to here are his words, and his intention is certainly not to nullify the mitzvah of covering due to the effort, but because he can leave it until the evening and then cover it. For presumably, since they got mixed together and there is a lot of blood, it will not be consumed until the evening. And according to his words, it makes sense what he said "not only with a koi...," meaning: "not only with a koi should he leave it until the evening, but even...". And it was said in the Gemara there that if one slaughtered a bird on the eve of Yom Tov and did not cover it, it is forbidden to cover it on Yom Tov because of unnecessary effort since he neglected to cover it on the eve of Yom Tov. Therefore, even a small amount of blood like that of a bird, which would certainly be consumed by the end of Yom Tov, is forbidden to cover on Yom Tov, since he neglected to do so himself. And there is no prevention of Yom Tov joy, for the covering does not impede the eating, as I wrote in section 33.

It was taught in Bechorot (33a): One should not skin (an animal) on Yom Tov because it involves excessive labor that is not necessary for him. Rashi explained: "One should not skin" — to remove the entire hide through its legs in one piece, to make a bellows for blacksmiths or water skins, see there. This is also the opinion of the Tur, who wrote that one may skin the hide whole to make a water skin from it. However, the Rambam in the third chapter wrote: What is "skinning"? It is when one removes all the flesh from one leg so that the entire hide comes off whole without tearing, because this type of skinning involves great labor, and it is not necessary for the festival. Thus are his words. They did not worry to permit the end for the sake of the beginning, for if not, one would refrain from slaughtering, thereby diminishing the joy of the festival. Just as they permitted (handling) the hide before those who tread on it, as will be explained, because our sages established that even if this were not permitted, one would still slaughter and not refrain.

Our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in Section A in the language of the Rambam. And there are those who hold that according to the Rambam, it is permitted to skin the hide whole, according to Rashi's interpretation that it is only forbidden when done by way of one leg. Therefore, they wrote that it is proper to be stringent like the Tur (Bach and Magen Avraham Subsection 1). And there are those who question our master, the Rema, as to why he did not correct it according to his usual manner (Taz Subsection 1). In my humble opinion, there is no disagreement here. Even according to the Rambam, any case where the hide is skinned whole is forbidden, because it involves excessive labor. The Rambam stated it according to the practice in his days in his region, and Rashi explained it according to the practice in his days in his region. Therefore, the Tur stated the matter in general terms, to say that whenever the hide is skinned whole, it is forbidden. For if it were not so, he would have explained that in such a case it is forbidden, and in such a case it is permitted, or that even in such a case it is forbidden. Rather, certainly there is no difference, and in all cases it is forbidden when the hide is skinned whole. And there is no difference whether one starts from the leg, the head, or whether it is a large or small animal.

Poultry is permitted to be scalded to remove the feathers, as skinning is not applicable to poultry, and plucking them involves more effort than scalding them. However, any kind of animal, even a small kid where it is possible to skin the hide, since it is easier than scalding, it is forbidden to scald it. And even if his intention in scalding is to eat the hide, for through the hide being soft, it softens even more through scalding and becomes like meat—nevertheless, it is forbidden because it involves significant effort on Yom Tov. Only the head and feet are permitted to be scalded, as I will write in Siman 506, but not the whole body. And our master the Beit Yosef wrote in סעיף ב: it is forbidden to scald a kid unless it is scalded to eat the hide. End quote. They wrote that a corrupted version was found in the Tur (Bach, Magen Avraham, and Taz). And I do not know why they attributed this to a mistake, as the Magid Mishneh in the third chapter brought that there is a dispute among the Geonim about this, and one who is lenient in a Rabbinic matter has not lost. And also in our version of the Tur, the text is the same, see there. And concerning what is stated in the Gemara (34a): "They would scald the head and feet"—this was spoken of as a common practice (Magid Mishneh there), as this was their way. (And regarding what the Magen Avraham wrote in subsection 2, that the Tosafot and the Rosh wrote this—I am perplexed. For the Tosafot did not mention this at all, see there. And the law of scalding is explained in Yoreh De'ah Siman 68).

An animal that was slaughtered on Yom Tov, even though the hide is muktzeh, nonetheless, to lift the hide after placing it on the ground after skinning and to place it in a location where people tread, even though there is no meat on it at all—since in this way the hide is somewhat worked—this is permitted. And the Sages permitted this at the end because of the beginning (i.e., they permitted this end result to ensure people would not refrain from slaughtering on Yom Tov, thereby diminishing the joy of the festival). They allowed this because there is not a significant indication that this is for tanning, as people might say it is to sit on. Moreover, this is not considered tanning at all. 

They further permitted salting meat on the hide, meaning to place the hide at an angle so that the blood from the salting will drip off and the meat will be salted, and thus some salt will remain on the hide, which will benefit the tanning. The Jerusalem Talmud even permits salting a little here and a little there so that the salt spreads over the entire hide, even though this is a form of subterfuge. However, this is only when salting for roasting, which does not require much salt. But for cooking, which requires a lot of salt, it is prohibited as this is akin to complete tanning. It is also forbidden to place the hide on pegs to stretch it, as this clearly shows it is for tanning. There are those who permit this as well, but this is not correct (Magen Avraham, Section 3).

And all this applies when it was slaughtered on Yom Tov, but if it was slaughtered on the eve of Yom Tov, none of this was permitted. It is forbidden to handle the hide on Yom Tov even if it was skinned on Yom Tov, such as when there was no time to skin it on the day because the permission was only for those slaughtered on Yom Tov. But for the eve of Yom Tov – there is plenty of time to do it on the eve of Yom Tov. And even if this one slaughtered close to the eve – there is no distinction between this and that. And some say that if there was no time to skin them before the day, they permitted him all these leniencies: to handle them, to place them before tramplers, and to salt meat on them for roasting (see Beit Yosef and Magen Avraham, subsection 5). And anything that could have been done before the day and was not done, even if he forgot or was forced – they do not permit him on Yom Tov (ibid.). And we who observe two days – the first is considered weekday regarding the second. That if he slaughtered on the first – it is forbidden to handle it on the second. And know that this is regarding a moist hide that is not suitable for sitting. But with a dry one, it is permitted in any case, as it is suitable for sitting and is not muktzeh at all, and on every Shabbat and Yom Tov it is permitted to handle it, as I wrote in Siman 321.

And similarly, a chicken that was slaughtered on Yom Tov—it is permitted to move the feathers after they have been plucked and to store them, even though they are muktzeh (set aside/not prepared for use), since they are not currently suitable for anything. Nevertheless, if we do not permit him to store them, he would refrain from slaughtering, which would lead to a decrease in the joy of Yom Tov. And know that the Mordechai wrote that any form of subterfuge was only permitted for a learned scholar (a disciple of the sages), so that they would not come to be lenient in other matters, but not for everyone. However, not all the poskim (halachic decisors) agree with this (Beit Yosef).

Even though they were lenient regarding the skin, as I have written, nevertheless, they were not lenient regarding the fats. This means that it is customary to salt the fats after removing them from the animal to prevent them from spoiling, and on Yom Tov, it is forbidden because this constitutes full-fledged tanning. One should not even turn them over to spread them on pegs, because in doing so, it is evident to everyone that he is preparing them and he might come to salt them. This is not the case with the skin, as its preparation is not noticeable, as I have written. And even though they were slaughtered on Yom Tov, and it might be that one would refrain from slaughtering because of this, it is still impossible to permit a complete and apparent prohibition. Similarly, it is forbidden to salt meat on top of them in the air directly above them, since it is forbidden to place meat on top of fats, and only in the air above them is it possible, and automatically some salt will fall on the fats. It is forbidden to do so, because it is evident that he is preparing the fats, which is not the case with the skin. Additionally, with fats, even a small amount of salt constitutes tanning, and it is a complete prohibition. There is also an opinion that nowadays, since it is not customary to salt on the skin, it is also forbidden to salt on it, as it is evident (Magen Avraham, subsection 10). This is also the ruling to be followed.

But regarding moving fats, the poskim (halachic authorities) have written that it is permitted, as they are not considered muktzeh (set aside) because they are suitable for lighting. However, there is someone who questioned this, noting that in Siman 501 it will be explained that food pits are forbidden to move even though they are suitable for lighting (there, section 9). This is not comparable, as foods are not primarily intended for lighting, and it is like something new that came into being (nolad). But fats are primarily intended for lighting, and this is not considered nolad. (And it is surprising that the Magen Avraham himself in section 15 wrote this reasoning.) They also wrote another reason to permit it, because one intends to store them so they do not get lost. And since it is not considered complete nolad as I have written – one's intention helps regarding this, similar to a carcass that became unfit on Shabbat, if one intended from before Shabbat to feed it to dogs. There are those who are stringent in all this (Magen Avraham there), but the principal opinion is like the lenient ones. (And with what we have explained, all the difficulties are resolved, see there. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

It is permissible to cut meat even on something that is muktzeh (set aside) due to monetary loss, and it is permissible to move it because of the joy of the festival. For example, a leaf, which is a thick and heavy sheet, is considered a utensil whose primary use is forbidden, as it is made for crushing grains. And it is muktzeh due to monetary loss, which is forbidden to move even for its use or its place, as I wrote in Siman 308. However, they permitted moving it to cut meat on it because of the joy of the festival. But after cutting meat on it, it is forbidden to move it from the sun to the shade. But for its use or its place, they permitted the end because of the beginning. But from the sun to the shade, one can be careful not to come to that, and they did not see fit to permit this. (The Rif in the first chapter wrote this law and concludes as we established in the chapter "All the Utensils." And the Rosh wrote that the Ri disagrees because, according to Rabbah on 123a, this was considered muktzeh due to monetary loss. And the Rif holds according to the explanation of Rava on 124a, that this is only muktzeh due to prohibition. See there. And according to this, it is not related to the end because of the beginning. But in my humble opinion, the intention of the Rif is that Rava does not necessarily disagree with Rabbah. And what he established regarding from the sun to the shade – also means according to Rabbah, that it was muktzeh due to monetary loss. Only for its use and place did they permit the end because of the beginning, and not from the sun to the shade, as I have written. Analyze and you will find it easy.)

It is well-known that buying and selling are forbidden on Yom Tov just as they are on Shabbat. Therefore, when buying meat from a butcher on Yom Tov, one should not set a price for the purchase, such as saying to him, "Give me meat for a sela or for two." This is considered a complete transaction. Even if he says to him, "I am your partner for a sela or for two," which is not the language of a transaction at all, nevertheless, since he mentions a specific amount of money, it is automatically considered a transaction and is forbidden. The general rule is that the mention of money is completely forbidden, even without the language of a transaction or without weighing.

And how does one acquire (meat)? He says to the butcher: "Give me a third or a quarter portion of this animal." Or if there is a known name for the portion in the city, such as calling five pounds a "portion" – he can say to him: "Give me a portion" or "half a portion" or "two portions." And he gives it to him without weighing, but rather by estimation, and without determining a price. After the holiday, he will pay him according to the price that the butcher states, or according to the prevailing price in the city. The butcher can also ease the burden of pricing after the holiday if there are several householders who want to take equal parts of meat from this animal – he sets up two equal animals for them, and says to them "This is like this," and he slaughters one and divides it among them. The next day, they appraise the second one to see how much it is worth, and he collects from them for the first one according to the valuation of the second one. If there is meat left over – they appraise the remaining meat, and the excess they will pay him equally. It is forbidden to say to him: "What you take for this one – tomorrow we will give you for this one," as this is also considered buying and selling (Magen Avraham, subsection 2). Rather, "This is like this" and nothing more.

Some say that these leniencies apply only to a Jew dealing with a Jewish butcher, but it is forbidden to buy from a non-Jew, even without mentioning a specific price, and to say to him "half," "a third," or "a quarter," or to say to him "this for that." The reason is that since it is not customary to partner with him regularly, it appears clearly as a transaction. Similarly, it is forbidden for a Jewish butcher to sell kosher meat to a non-Jew in this manner, also for the reason explained. It seems that not all authorities agree with this, but nonetheless, one should be stringent (see Magen Avraham, subsection 3).

And know that what we said, that it is permissible for the butcher to divide into portions and give each one a portion without mentioning money — this is when they are not particular with each other, lest one portion be slightly bigger than the other, and they divide without a lottery. But if they are particular and divide by lottery — it is forbidden, as I have written in Siman 323, because we are concerned that through their particularity, they will come to weigh (there, subsection 1). And if they are particular and divide without a lottery, if they are neighbors to each other — it is permitted. But if they are just a group — even without a lottery, it is forbidden if they are particular, for with them there is a concern due to their particularity even without a lottery that they will come to weigh, which is not the case with neighbors, as I have written there (there).

And know that the source of all the laws that have been explained is from the Mishnah in the third chapter (27b) where it is taught: One may not form a group to share an animal on Yom Tov from the outset. However, they may form a group on the eve of Yom Tov, and slaughter and divide it among them. And it is stated in the Gemara: What does "one may not form a group" mean? – It means one may not set a price for the meat on Yom Tov, see there. This means that you should not think that on Yom Tov it is forbidden entirely to form a group to acquire meat, even without setting a price, for certainly forming groups to obtain meat is permitted even on Yom Tov. Rather, it is the setting of a price that is forbidden on Yom Tov, only allowed on the eve of Yom Tov. However, in the Jerusalem Talmud it says: But to add [to the group] – one may add; if there were five, they may become ten, see there. It is explicitly explained that it is forbidden to form a group on Yom Tov for the purchase of meat, and the formation of the group must be on the eve of Yom Tov, and only on Yom Tov may they add to the group. This is not the way of our Talmud, but nevertheless, the Rashba was concerned about it (see Pri Chadash).

The sages taught in the Mishnah: One should not use a balance scale at all. Meaning: one should not examine the weight at all. Not only for selling, but even a homeowner in his house who wants to know how much to cook, and is not particular about a slight deficiency or excess, even though it is permitted to measure in such a manner as explained earlier in Siman 323 – nevertheless, using a scale is also forbidden in this case. For in measuring, it is not evident that it is for the purpose of measuring, as one could claim he is simply putting it in a vessel, as if placing it in another vessel. But with a scale, it is evident that it is for the purpose of weighing, and it is forbidden. And even to place meat on a balance scale to protect it from mice, and not for the purpose of weighing – it is forbidden if the scales are hung in their usual place. Similarly, it is forbidden to weigh one piece against another if they are equal, and not to know their weight. This is what we learned: one should not use a balance scale at all, for the sages completely forbade using scales, as it appears like weighing on a festival.

Estimating the weight by hand is permitted. For example, if one takes the meat in his hand, lifts it up and puts it down to know the approximate weight – it is allowed. But it is forbidden to take a weight in one hand and the meat in the other hand to estimate the weight, for whenever there is an actual weight – it is prohibited. A skilled butcher who knows how to precisely estimate by hand is not allowed to weigh by hand for the purpose of selling. However, in his own home – it is permitted. A skilled butcher who cuts the pieces and knows how to cut them to exact weights, such as a litra or half a litra – he may cut as usual and need not be concerned. There is an opinion that says one may say: "Give me a litra of meat," as he is not intending to measure the weight precisely but only to know how much he needs, similar to measuring in Siman 323 (Magen Avraham subsection 6). In my humble opinion, it seems that it is forbidden to mention the term "weight" on Yom Tov, as weight is much more stringent than measurement, as I have written. (And this is also implied by the Eliyah Rabbah subsection 14. This is also brought by the Maggid Mishneh on the Mishnah, see there.)

And know that what we wrote in Section 6, that even the homeowner in his own house is forbidden to weigh to know how much to cook, is explicitly permitted in the Jerusalem Talmud. And so it is stated there (Chapter 3, Halacha 6): Rabbi Shimon ben Gamliel says: A person may appease himself with a pound to know what he has. And also the Rashba, of blessed memory, permits it, as the Tur wrote in his name. And the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch disagree with him, and also with the Jerusalem Talmud, because in the Gemara (29a), Rav permits a woman to measure flour for her dough, and Shmuel forbids it. And we conclude in the Gemara there that in practical halacha, if they ask us – it needs to be forbidden, as I wrote below at the beginning of Siman 506. And consequently, meat is also forbidden in such a manner (Tur). And there are those who want to differentiate between flour and meat: that flour could have been measured on the eve of the festival, and also it is not customary for a woman to measure flour for her dough, but it is not so with meat (see Beit Yosef and Bach). Nevertheless, one should not differ from the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, as the distinction is not so clear, evidently. And also from the language "we do not pay attention to the scales at all" it implies more prohibition. And also from what is stated in the Gemara (28a) that it is forbidden to weigh meat in water, which means that there are marks on the vessel, and they put water and meat in it, and as much as the water rises – it is known by the marks how many pounds there are. And since even in such a manner it is forbidden – all the more so with scales. However, it can be said that this is regarding selling, and so it implies the language in the Gemara: a skilled butcher – is forbidden to weigh meat in water, because the butcher does so for selling. And it is a wonder that the poskim omitted this law. And furthermore: that from the Jerusalem Talmud there is no proof, for even in our Gemara there is a dispute about this between Rav and Shmuel, and it can be said that the Jerusalem Talmud holds like Rav. Nevertheless, it seems to my humble opinion that if someone does so in his house to weigh the meat – one should not rebuke him. But to instruct it as permissible is forbidden. (And so it implies from Tosafot 29b, s.v. "Shmuel". And even though according to the Behag it is not so, see there, nevertheless in a light prohibition such as this – one can rely on the permitters. And be precise and you will find leniency.)

Their custom was that when they would buy meat from the butcher, they would make a hole in the meat with a knife in order to hang the meat on their finger. This is forbidden on Yom Tov (a Jewish festival). Instead, one should make the hole by hand and not with a knife, in order to ensure a change from the way it is done on a weekday, and to be aware that buying and selling is forbidden on Yom Tov. However, if the hole is not for hanging the meat but to make a mark so it would not be exchanged, it is permitted even with a knife, because this hole is not like one made for hanging, but rather some kind of cut as an identification mark (see Gemara 28a).

The head and legs are scalded, singed in fire, and buried in hot ashes, as all these are considered food preparation. However, they may not be smeared with lime, clay, or earth, as this appears like tanning. In our practice, even on weekdays, it is not customary to do so. It is forbidden to shear the hair of the head and legs with scissors, as it appears to be done for the hair rather than for the meat. There is a doubt if it is permitted to cut the hair with a knife, as perhaps only with scissors does it appear to be done for the hair, just like it is permitted to pluck them by hand. Certainly, this is no worse than plucking feathers from a chicken with a knife. Or it is possible that any method of shearing is forbidden, and this requires further investigation.

It is stated in the Gemara (11b): Shmuel said, "A person may salt several pieces of meat at once, even though he only needs one piece." Rashi explained that it is considered one effort for all of them. It seems that this is the explanation: he takes a lot of salt in his hand and, in one motion, spreads it over all the meat. Similarly, when he turns them to salt the other side, he does it the same way. But to do it in two separate actions is forbidden, as it involves unnecessary effort on Yom Tov. Salting is somewhat similar to processing, even though there is no processing in food items; nevertheless, it is rabbinically prohibited. Only what is needed for Yom Tov is permitted, but what is not needed for Yom Tov is forbidden. The language of the Talmud is the same as the language of the Rambam in the first chapter, and the Tur and Shulchan Aruch in section 5.

However, from the language of the Rosh, it does not imply like our interpretation that one salts all at once literally. And this is the language of the Rosh: Because there is no tanning in food, he is lenient with the salting of meat. And even though there is no reason at all for this leniency, as the piece that one needs is not fixed and considered at all by the salting of the other pieces, and one also needs to turn each piece and salt it. Until here is his language. Therefore, he explains that one salts each piece individually, but does so in one sequence. And behold, in the Gemara there it says Rav Adda acts cunningly and salts piece by piece; after salting this one, he says, "I prefer its companion," see there. And the Rif and the Rosh wrote this, but the Rambam, the Tur, and the Shulchan Aruch did not mention this matter of Rav Adda. Many things were said about this (see Beit Yosef, Bach, Magen Avraham, and Taz), and all of them are difficult. In my humble opinion, it seems that the Rambam and the Tur interpreted the matter of Shmuel as we have. And if so, there is more leniency in the case of Rav Adda, and they were stringent like Shmuel. But the Rif and the Rosh interpreted it as the Rosh wrote, and if so, the matter of Rav Adda is a stringency, as it is only permitted to salt each one separately through cunning. (And it seems to me that this is also the position of the Maggid Mishneh, the Rashba, and the Prisha, see there. Be precise and you will find leniency.)

And regarding the wording of our master the Beit Yosef in paragraph 5, where he wrote: "It is permitted to salt multiple pieces even though one only needs one piece"—our master the Rema wrote: "And some say that it is only permissible to employ this subterfuge before the morning meal. And it is permitted to salt meat on a festival, even though one could have salted it on the eve of the festival." This is his wording, and it is not understood at all: for our master the Beit Yosef did not mention at all this matter of subterfuge (Magen Avraham, small paragraph 10). And it seems to me, in my humble opinion, that he holds that this matter of Shmuel is also a form of subterfuge, but he does not clarify the subterfuge. And that is why they permitted him to salt a lot, because he can say regarding each piece, "This one is dear to me." And Rav Adda would explain the subterfuge, and therefore there is no permission except before eating. And this is what he wrote, that it is permitted to salt even though one could have salted it on the eve of the festival, the reason being out of concern that it might spoil if one salts a lot in advance. And if it was slaughtered on the festival—it is permitted to salt even after eating, if one is concerned about spoilage (there). And know that this salting is what one does to prepare the meat and remove its blood (there). And other items like fish and similar things—certainly one must salt them on the eve of the festival (there), and on the festival it is forbidden. And if they came to him on the festival—what is needed for that day is permitted, and the rest is forbidden. And it is not similar to meat where one is compelled to slaughter the entire animal for a small amount of meat, and therefore they permitted salting a lot. And they wrote that the custom is to clean meat on the festival, even though it was slaughtered on the eve of the festival, and it is good to change slightly in some manner if they can change. And there are those who wrote that it is necessary to change, because if not, it is like selecting (see Taz and Magen Avraham who elaborated on this). And we did not have the custom to clean, nor to slaughter animals and birds on the festival where there is no need for cleaning, for all of it is kosher. And regarding rinsing meat after three days—see what I wrote in Siman 321.

One may not chop wood for fuel on Yom Tov from beams designated for building. And this is not limited to chopping; even without chopping, it is forbidden, as they are considered muktzeh (set aside). Even Rabbi Shimon agrees with this type of muktzeh, as it is muktzeh due to significant financial loss, because building beams are not intended for burning due to their expense. Even if a beam broke on Yom Tov, it is still forbidden because it was muktzeh at twilight. However, this is only according to Rabbi Yehuda, who holds by the laws of muktzeh, as per the Rif and the Rambam, who ruled according to Rabbi Yehuda regarding muktzeh on Yom Tov, as I wrote in Siman 498. But according to Rabbi Shimon and those poskim who ruled like him, as I wrote there – it is not considered muktzeh. And these are the words of the Tur: But according to Rabbi Shimon, it is permitted if it is weak and close to breaking. If it is not weak, even Rabbi Shimon agrees. Until here is his wording.

Explanation of his words: Even Rabbi Shimon, who does not hold by the principle "since it was set aside during twilight, it is set aside for the whole day," only applies this when he had intention for it during twilight, like in the case of a candle that goes out on Shabbat, because during twilight one is sitting and waiting for his candle to extinguish (Shabbat 46b). However, if it was lit in a large vessel like a bowl, where one does not sit and wait for it to extinguish, it is forbidden (there), as I wrote in Siman 279, see there. And here too, in the case of building, we say in Beitzah (30b) that the law is the same: if it was rickety and about to break, it is permitted according to Rabbi Shimon, because he had it in mind and is waiting for it to break. But if it was not rickety, he is not sitting and waiting, and it is forbidden.

If the beam broke on the eve of Yom Tov, it is permissible to burn it on Yom Tov. However, the Jerusalem Talmud in the fourth chapter of Beitza (Halacha 3) states: But with a beam that broke on the eve of Yom Tov, it is permissible if it does not have the form of a utensil. But if it has the form of a utensil, even if it broke on the eve of Yom Tov, it is forbidden. And immediately after this, it says: One may burn utensils, but one may not burn broken pieces of utensils, utensils that broke on Yom Tov. But if they broke on the eve of Yom Tov, it is permissible if they do not have the form of a utensil. But if they have the form of a utensil, even if they broke on Yom Tov, it is permissible. Thus far is the text.

And this is its explanation: A beam that was broken before the festival - it is permitted [to use it as firewood], because it was already designated for burning before the festival. This is when it no longer retains the form of a utensil, meaning the form of a beam. But if it still retains the form of a beam - it is still considered a complete beam intended for construction, and it is considered muktzeh [set aside and prohibited to be moved]. Concerning utensils, the law is that one may burn whole utensils but not broken utensils, because it is considered a new entity [nolad], and consequently, the prohibition only applies if they were broken on the festival. However, even if they were broken on the festival, if they still retain the form of a utensil – they are considered like a whole utensil, and one may burn them. Therefore, with utensils, retaining the form of a utensil is an advantage, but with a beam, it is a disadvantage, because one may burn a whole utensil, but not a whole beam. Some have claimed that the Jerusalem Talmud contradicts itself and have suggested there is a textual error here. This is not so, and the Jerusalem Talmud is consistent. (See Magen Avraham, subsection 2, who mentioned that there are two versions and wrote that it is considered nolad, and this is also implied in the Darkei Moshe. The Paneach Moshe also wrote that initially, it is for those who prohibit burning utensils. See there. All these interpretations are puzzling and strained. The truth is as I have written, that the form of a utensil that was previously in the beam makes it forbidden. This is also written by the Karban Ha'edah in Shiyarei HaKarban, see there. Be precise and you will find the truth.)

And a beam that broke on the eve of a festival: if it can be used for kindling without chopping at all, it is forbidden to chop it. But if it cannot be used for kindling without chopping, one may chop it into large pieces but not small ones. The reason is that the act of chopping does not override the festival, since it is a preparation that could have been done yesterday. However, chopping large pieces is not considered a labor but merely an exertion, and due to the honor of the festival, it is permitted. Although cutting wood into pieces incurs liability for grinding, this applies to small pieces, which resemble grinding to some extent. Therefore, it is indeed forbidden to cut small pieces. But large pieces do not fall under the category of grinding. The distinction between large and small pieces is not clear to us. And if one is meticulous about how to chop, one is liable for cutting, as I wrote at the beginning of chapter 321. Therefore, we have never heard of chopping wood on a festival, and one who needs to do so should have it chopped by a non-Jew. There is an opinion that wood is considered like food itself, for it can be used for heating, and since it is permitted to chop wood for heating, it is also permitted to chop for cooking needs (Magen Avraham, subsection 3, in the name of the Ran, see there). This is only when the weather is cold, and for heating, only small pieces are suitable. Otherwise, the festival should not be overridden for this, and it is not common at all (and even according to this, it is only permitted with a change).

And when he splits [wood] – he should not split with an axe, nor with a sickle, nor with a saw, so that he does not do it in the manner he does on a weekday. Rather, he should use a cleaver, which is a butcher’s knife. Some make it with two heads, somewhat resembling an axe. Even with a cleaver, he should not split with its wide side, but with its narrow side. The Tur forbids even with a cleaver, because we are not proficient with such a tool, as it is not common among us. It is only permitted with a knife, because with a knife it is certainly evident that the splitting is not done as it is on a weekday. We have already explained that among us, we do not split wood on Yom Tov at all. Even on Chol HaMoed, the meticulous ones refrain from splitting wood, and prepare everything before Yom Tov, even small pieces of wood for cooking fish (as mentioned there, subsection 4, in the name of Yam Shel Shlomo). However, in a case of necessity, it is obvious that on Chol HaMoed it is permitted. On Yom Tov, it should be done by a non-Jew if it cannot be done otherwise. This should also be done with some variation, discreetly, and in small amounts, because among us, this is considered a desecration of Yom Tov.

Large pieces of wood that are somewhat big and suitable for burning without splitting—one is certainly prohibited from splitting them, and even breaking them by hand is prohibited according to the Tur. However, some permit breaking them by hand, and even inserting them into a hole and breaking them. Only with a stone is it forbidden to break them. And this is taught in the Tosefta (chapter three of Beitzah): A person should not place a stone on top of a log to break it, but one may insert it into a hole and break it. See there. Thus, it is clearly permitted even in a hole, and all the more so by hand (see Pri Chadash who prohibits).

And this is the language of the Rambam in the fourth chapter: And why did they prohibit using an axe and similar tools? So that one does not perform actions in the manner he would on a weekday, for it was possible for him to chop the wood on the eve of the holiday. And why was chopping wood not entirely forbidden? Because it is possible that he will encounter thick wood that he will not be able to ignite, and he will be prevented from cooking. Therefore, they permitted chopping with a change. And all matters similar to this for the same reason – they permitted what they permitted and prohibited what they prohibited. Up to here is his language, and the explanation of his words: For apparently, even if we liken this to food preparation, as is the opinion of some who say in section 5, it is still prohibited by rabbinic law if it could have been done yesterday, as I wrote in section 498, and all the more so if it is considered as a preparation. However, the sages saw that this matter is considered as if it could not have been done yesterday, for even if one prepared wood, it is not possible to precisely determine which will be thick and which will be thin. It is necessary, during the cooking, to observe this, and therefore they saw fit to permit it with a change. And similarly, in all matters like this – one should not question why this was permitted and that was prohibited, for this depends on their great wisdom, to understand and discern which matters are typically done the day before and which are not. And we should not question why this was prohibited and that permitted.

The wood that one uses to fuel a fire on Yom Tov needs to be prepared in advance; otherwise, it is considered muktzeh. Even according to those who do not hold by the concept of muktzeh, gathering wood little by little resembles the prohibited labor of 'me'amer' (bundling). However, some say that 'me'amer' only applies in the place where the items grow (Tosafot). Therefore, one should not bring wood from the field, even if it was gathered there before Yom Tov and is not considered muktzeh, because we should be concerned that one might gather scattered wood, which would be a biblical prohibition if it constitutes 'me'amer'. But one may collect wood in a courtyard from what is in front of him, near his cooking pot. Similarly, if one is cooking in a field, this does not appear as 'me'amer', since his cooking pot proves that his intention is not to store the wood for later, as in the manner of 'me'amer', but for the purpose of cooking. However, some prohibit gathering wood in a field because it always appears as 'me'amer' (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 7, in the name of Yam Shel Shlomo). Additionally, what is in the field is considered muktzeh, but whatever is in the courtyard is considered prepared. According to Rambam, in Chapter 2, Law 14, even in the field, what is in front of him is not muktzeh. See there. One could say that the reason is that he certainly had this in mind from before Yom Tov. Therefore, if it is certain that he did not have this in mind before Yom Tov, it is considered muktzeh and forbidden.

If the wood is gathered in an area enclosed by partitions, even if it was not enclosed for residential purposes, if this area is within the boundary (techum), and it has a framework that is not considered ownerless – it is permitted to take wood from there. If any one of these conditions is missing – it is considered muktzeh (set aside). According to the Tur, any place adjacent to the city within seventy and two-thirds cubits, which is considered the city's outskirts – even if it does not have a framework, it is permitted, because it is like one’s own courtyard. There is no issue of muktzeh, and it does not appear as if one is gathering, since the wood is laid out in an orderly manner in an area enclosed by partitions.

Leaves of trees, as well as leaves of reeds and grapevines, even though they are gathered in a courtyard that is enclosed, nevertheless, since the wind can scatter them, they are considered scattered and are forbidden, either because of muktzeh (set aside) or because of gathering. It appears that if the leaves are hanging on the branches, if they are not light enough for the wind to scatter them, it is permitted when they are gathered, but otherwise, they are forbidden. And one should not ask: if at the time of taking them the wind did not scatter them, what concern is there? It can be said that the concern is that at the time of taking them, the wind might come and scatter them, and he will gather them (Beit Yosef and Magen Avraham). Therefore, if one placed a heavy utensil on the leaves from the eve of the festival, something that is permitted to move, it is permissible to take them on the festival, as the wind cannot scatter them and they are not muktzeh, and it does not appear as gathering. And wood that fell from the tree on the festival, one may not use them for fuel because it is considered nolad (newly created), as initially it was part of the tree and now it is wood. Moreover, we decree lest one might come to climb and detach. And if they fell into the oven, it will be explained in Siman 507 with Heaven's help.

It is stated in the Gemara (33b): The Rabbis taught: One may gather wood from the courtyard and light with it, because everything in the courtyard is considered prepared. Provided that one does not make piles. And so wrote the Tur. When one collects wood in the courtyard to burn, one should not make a pile, but rather bring a little and burn it, and then bring a little more and burn it. So far his language. The Rif and the Rambam did not bring this law, and their reasoning is unknown. Perhaps because they wrote that one only gathers from what is in front of him and lights it, it automatically implies that there are no piles (see Beit Yosef and Perisha). However, some say that this is not related, as gathering from what is in front of him refers only to small pieces of wood, which are nullified by the ground. But for slightly larger pieces, it is not necessary to be from what is in front of him, and for these, one should not make piles (Ran there). In my humble opinion, the distinction between large and small pieces is relevant only to the reason of gathering, which is the reason given by those who say otherwise. But according to the Rif and the Rambam, whose reason is because of muktzeh, there is no difference between large and small pieces. (It requires examination why this is not mentioned at all in the Shulchan Aruch).

It is established that one may use utensils for kindling, but one may not use broken pieces of utensils. This is because utensils are permitted to be handled and are not considered muktzeh (set aside). Therefore, it is permissible to throw them into the fire if this does not constitute wanton destruction (bal tashchit), such as when their value is only equivalent to that of wood. And if it is argued that one thereby nullifies the utensil's status as a utensil on Yom Tov, which would be akin to demolishing it – it can be said that there is no concept of building and demolishing with regard to utensils. Even though it was explained in Siman 314 that complete demolition applies to utensils as well – this refers to actual demolition, but when using it for the purpose of preparing food on Yom Tov, it is no different from other labors permitted for food preparation, as long as one is not demolishing it directly with his hands; rather, he is kindling the fire, and the demolition occurs incidentally (see Magen Avraham, subsection 13, and examine carefully and you will find it easy). However, one must be cautious with this: if one kindles with utensils, he should not stir the fire after some parts have already burned, because then they become broken pieces of utensils and are forbidden to be handled, unless he adds more wood to them as I have written in Siman 507.

And one may not fuel the fire with broken vessels that were broken on Yom Tov, for this is considered "nolad" (a new entity). However, if they were broken before Yom Tov, they are permitted. And we have already brought in section 3 from the Jerusalem Talmud that if they still have the status of a vessel and serve a similar function, even if they were broken on Yom Tov, they are permitted. Anything that is prohibited to be moved is also prohibited to be lit in its place without moving it, for "muktzeh" is forbidden for benefit. But when one lights a whole vessel, even though the benefit comes when it is broken, it comes on its own (Magen Avraham, subsection 12). And in its place, there is a permit when one adds more prepared wood, as I have written in Siman 507. And a non-Jew who made a vessel on Yom Tov, it is forbidden to light it and move it, for it is "nolad."

Almonds and nuts that were eaten on the eve of a festival – one may use their shells for fuel. But if they were eaten on the festival itself – one may not use their shells for fuel, as this constitutes a new entity (nolad), since yesterday they were considered suitable for human consumption. Therefore, even if they are suitable for animal feed – it is forbidden. And even though one had in mind from the day before that he would eat the fruit and use the shells for fuel – it still does not help, because since the shells are needed to protect the food until the time of eating – they are considered like the food itself, and thus are considered a new entity (Tosafot Shabbat 29a, s.v. "Akhlan," see there). And Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote in section 7 that one should also not use the nuts and almonds themselves for fuel, unless they are still in their shells. Thus far his words. They are worse than utensils used for fuel, because utensils are at least a type of wood, and this type is designated for burning, which is not the case with fruits (Magen Avraham, subsection 15). Therefore, this itself is considered a new entity. However, when they are in their shells – it is permitted, because the shells are designated for burning, and when they are together there is no concern. And in the Jerusalem Talmud, Chapter Three (Halacha 3), it states: Rabbi Chiya taught: one may use food for fuel but not their shells and pits – implying that it is permitted. However, it can be said that the intention is when the food is in their shells, and it does not refer to all foods but to fruits, since it says "in their shells" and not "shells" (Magen Avraham there argues from this Jerusalem Talmud but there is no proof). This also seems to be the implication in the Tosefta, Chapter Three, see there.

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote in Section 7 that torches which were left from the first day of Yom Tov and extinguished—it is permissible to relight them even on the second day of Rosh Hashanah or Yom Tov after Shabbat. Thus his language ends. Meaning: torches that were extinguished, and the same applies to wicks which were not completely burned, and this involves preparation from one day of Rosh Hashanah to the other and from Shabbat to Yom Tov, where preparation is prohibited, which is why an egg laid on one day is prohibited on the other. And indeed, the Tur ruled it forbidden, see there. And he (the Rema) ruled it permissible based on the Mordechai's reasoning, that since the substance of the wick exists in the world, preparation does not apply so much here (see Taz, Section 7, and Magen Avraham, Section 16). And there are those who ruled like the Tur (Yam Shel Shlomo). However, with our wicks, there is no difference between whether they were not lit, or they were lit and extinguished, and therefore for us it is simple that it is permitted.

The sages taught in the Mishnah (Shabbat 33a): One may not produce fire from wood, nor from stones, nor from earth, nor from tiles, nor from water. And this is its explanation: Wood and stones, when rubbed together extensively, produce fire. "From earth," Rashi explained: Hard ground, when dug, emits fire, like our flint from its excavation place. And the Ran explained: Calves or sheep are buried in the earth, and when they decompose, fire emerges from them. "From tiles" – this refers to when they are heated. "From water," Rashi explained: They put water in a clear glass vessel and place it in the sun when it is very hot, and the glass emits a flame. They bring a wick, touch it to the glass, and it ignites. Thus far his words.

The reason for the prohibition is because it is considered "newly created" (Rashi and Ran), and so wrote the Raavad at the beginning of the fourth chapter. But the Rambam wrote there: "One does not produce fire from wood, nor from stones, nor from metals, such as by rubbing them together or striking them against each other until a fire emerges. Similarly, very fresh naphtha, which is like water and is agitated until it ignites, or a shiny hard utensil, or a glass filled with water that is placed against the sun's rays until it reflects onto flax or something similar and ignites—all of this and anything similar to it is prohibited on Yom Tov. Only kindling from an existing fire is permitted on Yom Tov, but creating a new fire is forbidden, since it is possible to produce it from the evening before." Thus far his words. This is very perplexing, for the Gemara there explicitly states: "What is the reason? Because it is creating something new on Yom Tov." What did he see to give a reason from his own mind? And he is stringent regarding muktzeh on Yom Tov more than on Shabbat, as I have written in Siman 502, and all the more so regarding something newly created. Why was the reason given in the Talmud not sufficient for him?

And it appears to me in my humble opinion that certainly he also believes the reason is because of "Nolad" (something newly created). However, it was difficult for him to understand: how is it possible to prohibit making fire on Yom Tov, since the Torah permits baking and cooking on Yom Tov, and there is no cooking or baking without fire? If so, it is necessary that the Torah permitted making fire on Yom Tov.

And for this, he says that this is not a necessity, as the Torah permitted using an existing fire, such as from a coal or a candle, and the like, but not to create a new fire. This is similar to the preparations for food ("Machsirei Ochel Nefesh"): what can be done on the eve of Yom Tov is forbidden on Yom Tov by Torah law. And even if it is like the food preparation itself, nevertheless, it is rabbinically forbidden if it could have been done on the eve of Yom Tov. And it is true that regarding kindling (a fire) we say "mitoch" (since it was permitted for food preparation, it is permitted for other needs as well), as I wrote there – this is all from an existing fire. But from a new fire – it is forbidden because of "Nolad" (so it appears to me in my humble opinion).

The Maggid Mishneh explained that with fire it is impossible to prohibit due to "nolad" (a category of forbidden labor on Yom Tov related to new creations), and this is his language: "For this is not like an egg that was laid, which is forbidden because it is not something that is inherently usable, but rather for cooking and baking, and it seems that if he kindled it, it is permitted to use it; they only prohibited it because he should not have kindled it, since he could have done so before the festival." Thus far are his words. According to him, the Gemara's statement: "What is the reason? Because he creates on Yom Tov" does not mean because of the prohibition of "nolad", but rather because he should not have created on Yom Tov. However, the essence of his words is puzzling: How can one say that anything that is not food itself does not have "nolad"? For the prohibition of broken vessels is due to "nolad". Likewise, the prohibition of lighting with seeds is due to "nolad" (Lechem Mishneh), as I wrote in Siman 501. One must say that his intention is not specifically food that has "nolad", but anything substantial. However, fire, which has no substance at all, just as there is no prohibition of carrying it on Shabbat, or deriving benefit from it in consecrated items by Torah law, and similarly many things where the flame is not subject to prohibition (Beitzah 30b), because it is considered something that has no substance, and it is not applicable for a prohibition to apply to it. Even the prohibition of idolatry, which is severe, does not apply to a flame (ibid). If so, how can the prohibition of "nolad" apply to a flame? Rather, surely it is according to the reasoning of the Rambam. And indeed, it is a great logic. (And the Taz, in subsection 1, got entangled in the words of the Rambam and the Maggid Mishneh, and explained their intention due to preparatory acts. He wondered at the Maggid Mishneh who permitted it post facto, and ruled that even post facto it is forbidden, see there. But according to what I have written in his intention – his words are clear and suitable. And so it is proper to rule.)

We also learned in the Mishnah (32a): One does not make charcoal on Yom Tov, which means taking wood and burning it until it becomes charcoal, and then extinguishing it. Rashi explained: because it becomes a tool for goldsmiths. The Ran explained: because it involves extinguishing, as in making charcoal the fire is extinguished (Levush). This specifically applies to making charcoal, but lighting cold charcoal is obviously permitted. And it was taught (34a): One does not blow on a fire with a bellows, as it appears like a craftsman doing work (Rashi). But one may blow with a tube. The Tur wrote that the Rosh permitted a small household bellows, as it does not resemble the work of a craftsman, nor that of blacksmiths, nor of goldsmiths. The Tur wrote that nevertheless, one should not be lenient, as the permission was only for a tube, implying that all bellows are forbidden. The Tosafot there rejected this, arguing that there is no proof, as it only discusses a craftsman's bellows, and they wrote that the world customarily permits using a household bellows by reversing it upside down. Similarly, Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote in section 1. And in our place, household bellows are not found at all. The practice of blowing with hard feathers tied together is certainly permitted like a tube. And mostly we blow with the mouth to ignite the coals. There is no prohibition of "nolad" (creating something new) in this, as we are merely drawing out the flame from the already burning coal, since the flame is already there, and by blowing we bring it out.

And know that it has been about two generations that among us, during the week, we use sulfur wood to produce fire. These have on their ends a substance called phosphorus, in which much heat is stored. When it is struck against something, fire immediately emerges and catches onto the thin wood called a match. It is well known that on Yom Tov (a Jewish festival), this is prohibited due to the principle of "nolad" (something newly created). And we all are careful about this. However, in our youth, a leniency spread permitting one to touch it to a burning coal, and it would immediately ignite. I do not know the reason for this leniency—for after all, one is still producing fire from the sulfur! I heard in my youth that a great scholar permitted this, and his reasoning was that the fire does not come from the sulfur, but rather the fire is drawn from the coal. Since the coal contains much of the fire element, it attracts the flame from the coal. This matter requires proof, for perhaps the coal merely activates the fire potential in the sulfur. And perhaps since, in any case, the flame element in the coal also assists, this is not considered "nolad." Moreover, according to the Rambam's view, who only permitted using an existing fire as I wrote in section 2, this fire from the coal is considered existing. However, in any case, the world has adopted this leniency. (Thus, sulfur wood is not considered muktzeh (set aside) since it is suitable to place near the coal.)

It is permissible to cover a fire with a utensil or prepared earth, as long as it does not extinguish it at that moment. And even if it happens to be extinguished, it is considered an unintentional act and also a labor not needed for its own sake (Magen Avraham, subsection 5, in the name of Yam Shel Shlomo).
