This is specifically for the needs of that day, but if one does this for the needs of the second day of Yom Tov, such as covering in the morning for the evening – it is prohibited, for one should not do anything from the first day of Yom Tov for the second day of Yom Tov, and certainly not on the second day of Yom Tov for the evening, which is a weekday, as this is certainly prohibited. If one increases the covering to the extent that it certainly extinguishes part of it, it is prohibited even for the needs of that day, for extinguishing is not permitted on Yom Tov. The detailed laws of extinguishing will be explained in Siman 514 with the help of Heaven.

A bundle of wood that was ignited in a bonfire, any piece of wood that has not yet caught fire – it is permitted to remove it, and this is not considered extinguishing since the fire has not yet taken hold of it. This is not comparable to oil in a lamp, which is forbidden to use from it because of extinguishing, as I have written in Siman 514, since all the oil is connected. However, the pieces of wood are separate from each other. And know that what we have written "a bundle of wood..." – this is the language of the Rambam at the beginning of the fourth chapter. And the Tur wrote in this language: a bonfire made of thin pieces of wood – it is permitted to remove them as long as the fire has not yet taken hold of them. Thus far his language, meaning those pieces that the fire has not yet taken hold of. And this is also according to the words of the Rambam.

There are those who wish to infer from the language of the Rambam, who wrote "bundle," that when they are bundled together—even those that the fire has caught on to—it is permitted to remove them. And the Tur, who did not mention "bundle," and yet did not permit it except for those that the fire has not caught on to—this refers to thin wood, but with thick wood there is no prohibition except in a bundle (Magen Avraham, small section 10). And this is not understood at all. For how can it be permitted to remove the piece that the fire has caught on to? What difference does it make if it is a big tree or a small tree, or if it is in a bundle or not in a bundle? And in the Rokeach it is explicitly written: wood that is in the fire—it is not permissible to remove, as it would be like extinguishing. And he did not differentiate between one type of wood and another. And the Rambam, who wrote "bundle"—his intention is not specifically that they are tied together, but that they are placed together as if they were tied. For if not, there is no significance at all in permitting to take those that the fire has not caught on to. And the Tur, who wrote "from thin wood"—his intention is also the same, that typically thin wood is gathered together. And the law is clear that any wood the fire has caught on to—it is forbidden to remove it (and this is also the intention of the Eliyah Rabbah, small section 13; see there).

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote in paragraph 2: "It is permissible to take a burning piece of wood from one side of a bonfire and place it on the other side, since there is no intention to extinguish it." This is his language, and it seems to me that the explanation is as follows: It is customary that when one takes a burning piece of wood, it does not extinguish immediately, but after a short time. Therefore, to take it entirely is prohibited, because this is extinguishing, as it will extinguish immediately. However, when one takes it from one side to the other, it will not extinguish. And even if it might possibly extinguish, it is considered an unintentional act, and it is not a certain outcome (פסיק רישא). It is not similar to the law explained later in Siman 514, which prohibits taking a wick from a burning lamp to place it in another lamp, as explained there, because the wick extinguishes immediately. Therefore, they were precise in stating that when one removes it, it extinguishes immediately, as explained there. (And the Taz there in subsection 5 raised a difficulty from here, and wrote that these are two opinions, as explained there. But it is not so. Examine it and you will find clarity.)

Some have written that it is permissible to take a burning ember from the bonfire to provide light at night, as it is merely causing an indirect extinguishing, and one does not intend for that, and sometimes it does not extinguish. However, people are accustomed to being cautious, and this is appropriate (Beit Yosef, Taz, and Magen Avraham in the name of the Hagahot Maimoniyot and the Mordechai). And certainly, it seems evident from what has been explained, that specifically moving it from one place to another or to another bonfire (Taz, subsection 3) is permitted, but not to remove it entirely (Magen Avraham there). In my humble opinion, there is no disagreement here, as certainly a somewhat thick piece of wood – we see with our senses that when it is removed, it does not extinguish immediately. But over many moments it will extinguish, and certainly, it is forbidden to take it to provide light. However, there are very thin and somewhat wide pieces of wood called "kin," which, when lit, burn until they are consumed. And these are certainly permitted, and it is to these that the permissive opinions refer. And so one should instruct.

It is well known that the reason it is permitted to move wood on Yom Tov is because it is suitable for burning. Accordingly, moist wood that is not suitable for burning is forbidden to be moved, as it is considered muktzeh. This is what we have learned in the Mishnah: one may not support a pot with a piece of wood, nor a door. This means to support the pot so it does not fall, or the door, with a piece of moist wood is forbidden. Even those who do not hold by the laws of muktzeh agree regarding wood and stones, as I wrote in Siman 308. However, dry wood that is suitable for burning may be used for all one's needs, since it is not muktzeh. This is the ruling of the Tur, see there.

However, the Rambam wrote in the fourth chapter: "One may not support a pot... for they only permitted moving wood on Yom Tov for burning alone." This is his language, and it is also in the Rif there, and it is likewise the language of the Baraita in the Gemara (33a). The reasoning is perplexing: since it is fit for use on Yom Tov, how can we say it is muktzeh (set aside)? And from the language of the Baraita, there is no proof, for there it says that wood was given only for burning. And this is its explanation: since it was given only for burning, it follows that damp wood, which is not fit for burning, is prohibited to move. And regarding the reasoning of the Rif and the Rambam, it seems to me that therefore the sages prohibited moving wood except for burning: for if not, they would move all the pebbles and all the wood for all uses, even those not fit for burning. For something given over to the entire populace of Israel – it is impossible to explain to everyone that this wood is permitted, and this one is forbidden. Therefore, they necessarily restricted it so that only for burning is it permitted to move, and not for anything else.

It seems to me that the disagreement between the Tur and the Rambam depends on the Talmudic discussion there (33a), which states: "Hazra, Rav Nachman forbids, and Rav Sheshet permits." Meaning: a branch of a tree that is sharp like a thorn, and is suitable for sticking into a roast like a spit and roasting with it (Rashi). And there in the Gemara, there are two versions: one is that in the case of a moist branch, even Rav Sheshet forbids, and they disagree regarding a dry branch. The second version is that in the case of a dry branch, even Rav Nachman permits, and they disagree regarding a moist branch. And the reason for the permissive opinion: since it is suitable for a significant heating purpose, the Talmud concludes that the law is that a dry branch is permitted and a moist branch is forbidden, see there. 

The Tur holds that according to the conclusion – for all uses, this is the rule: that a moist branch is forbidden and a dry branch is permitted. And the Rambam holds that even a dry branch is only permitted to be used as a spit for roasting, which pertains to food preparation, and he ruled this way in the second chapter, see there. But for other purposes, they did not permit it. And the proof is that they disagreed only about this – from which we infer that for other uses, everyone agrees that even a dry branch is forbidden. And the Tur thinks that this is not a precise inference, because the Talmud mentioned something that was common for them on a festival, like making a spit for roasting. And the same would apply to other things.

The words of our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, on this matter are not understood at all. For our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in paragraph 3: "One may not support a pot or a door with a chip of wood." Thus are his words, and he left the matter unspecified, not clarifying whether the wood chip is moist or dry. Our master, the Rema, wrote about this: "But it is permitted to roast with it, and certainly it is permitted to fuel a fire with it along with other woods, even though it is not fit to be used for fuel by itself." Thus are his words.

Now, from what he wrote, "But it is permitted to roast with it," it is obvious that this refers to dry wood, for regarding moist wood, the conclusion of the Gemara is a prohibition, as I have written, according to the Rambam's view. Therefore, how could he write that it is permitted to fuel a fire with it along with other woods, even though it is not fit on its own, which implies moist wood since it is suitable for a large fire? This contradicts itself. Furthermore, according to the conclusion of the Talmud, the reasoning that it is suitable for a large fire is rejected.

However, his intention is clear based on what the Ran wrote there, that even according to the conclusion, it is permitted to place moist wood into a large fire. Nevertheless, it is forbidden to use it for roasting since it is not fit for fuel by itself, see there. The extent of his words is this: "But it is permitted to roast with it if it is dry, and certainly it is permitted to fuel a fire with it if it is moist along with other woods." This is considered to be more lenient, for according to the Rambam's view, even dry wood is prohibited for any use, and yet for roasting, it was permitted, and certainly for the main use of fueling a fire when it is fit along with other woods.

(Know that Rashi wrote there that the ruling of the Talmud that moist wood is forbidden applies to those who hold by the principle of muktzeh. But for us, who follow Rav Sheshet, it is permitted. The Tosafot rejected this, stating that even according to Rav Sheshet, it is forbidden when it is not fit for fuel. It seems to me that their intention is that this is like stones and pebbles. The Rosh, in the name of Rabbeinu Tam, explained that this is a decree for Yom Tov due to Shabbat. Also, the statement that wood was given only for fuel is for the same reason, see there.)

The Tur wrote: One should not cook in new earthenware pots unless they have been boiled first on the eve of the festival, because the first cooking strengthens them and completes their preparation. This is his language. And there are those who disagree, saying that cooking with food does not strengthen the pot (Tosafot 34a, beginning with "here"). However, aside from this, the poskim wrote that this applies to their pots, which were not fully completed by the potter. But ours are fully completed and do not need any strengthening at all (Beit Yosef in the name of the Ra'avyah and the Riva). And this is what our master the Beit Yosef wrote in section 4, and this is his language: For us, it is permissible to cook in new pots on the festival. This is his language, and the reason as I have written. Nevertheless, our master the Rema wrote that some prohibit it, and this is the custom unless in a pressing situation. Therefore, the custom is when buying new pots for Passover, they cook in them before the festival. This is his language. And it is not specifically for Passover, but because on Passover it is necessary to buy new ones due to the prohibition of chametz. But in general, this applies to any festival. And there are those who differentiate between glazed earthenware, which does not need strengthening as it is already strengthened, and unglazed, which needs strengthening (Magen Avraham, section 14). However, it is certain that if one did not cook in them before the festival, and now he has no other pot, it is permissible to cook in it (Taz, section 5, and see Magen Avraham, section 15). And our women – some are careful not to cook in a new earthenware pot on the festival.

Know that there are certain activities on Yom Tov (Festival) that the Sages warned to be cautious of, so as not to perform them in a manner similar to building a structure, which is considered construction. Even though it is temporary construction, it is still forbidden on Yom Tov just as it is on Shabbat, as explained earlier in Siman 314 and Siman 315. These activities are: when making a bonfire, it is customary to place many logs arranged one on top of the other in four directions, with logs on top like a roof, and it is forbidden to do so on Yom Tov because it appears like building. Instead, one should either place the logs in a disorganized manner or arrange them with a modification. How? One places a log on top, then one below it, and then another below that one, until reaching the ground. Similarly, when setting up a pot on four stones, as was their custom – one should not first set up the stones and then place the pot on top, but rather hold the pot and set the stones under it. Similarly with their beds, where they would set up the legs and place boards on top of them. On Yom Tov, this should not be done if the legs also have side panels, but rather hold the boards and insert the legs underneath them. Even with eggs, when arranging them one on top of the other in rows to stand like a tower – it is proper not to do so on Yom Tov. Instead, one should make a change and start from the top downwards. And even though the definition of a tent (structure) is specifically when needing the space underneath it, as I wrote there – here in all these cases, the space underneath is needed: for logs and pots, to place fire underneath them; for a bed, to place shoes underneath; and for eggs as well, when placing fire underneath their space (Tosafot 32b) to roast them. Similarly, anything of this sort requires a change.

And our master, the Rema, wrote in Section 1: Similarly, a table that has walls extending to the ground requires a change. However, it is permitted to set up our table on its legs, and this does not constitute building. Some say that even if it reaches the ground, as long as it does not need the air underneath it, it is permitted. So ends his words. And this is the primary ruling in law, that as long as it does not need the air underneath it, it is not called a tent, as I wrote there. And so wrote the Tur in the name of the Tosafot and the Rashba, see there. And regarding the necessity that the partitions reach the ground, some say that even within less than three handbreadths from the ground, it is considered as if it touches the ground (Beit Yosef). And some say that we do not apply the principle of 'lavud' to be stringent, only to be lenient (Rema in Darkei Moshe, and the Magen Avraham in Section 9 elaborates to prove that we do apply 'lavud' to be stringent, see there thoroughly).

It is well known that it is forbidden to trouble oneself to prepare something on one festival day for another, even if it is not a laborious task. All the more so, it is forbidden to cook or bake from one festival day to another. Since the two festival days observed are due to doubt—perhaps tomorrow is a weekday, it would mean one is preparing or doing work from a festival day to a weekday. Especially now, when the calendar is well established, it is certainly forbidden. Even the two festival days of Rosh Hashanah, which are considered one extended sanctity, this is for stringency and not for leniency; except regarding the matter of an eruv for the two days, which is also a leniency on Rosh Hashanah, as I wrote above in Siman 516, that one can walk on the second day using the eruv of the first day. The reason is simple: if the first day is indeed the primary day, as it truly is, then the second day is a weekday, and no eruv is needed. But here, on the contrary, if the second day is a weekday, it is certainly forbidden to cook from the festival day to a weekday (Magen Avraham, subsection 1). Similarly, it is forbidden to cook from a festival day to Shabbat, unless an eruv tavshilin was set aside. And it is certainly forbidden to cook from the second festival day to the evening, which is entirely a weekday.

The Sages taught (17a): One may not bake from one Festival day for another. However, they said in truth, a woman may fill an entire pot with meat, even though she only needs one piece, and a baker may fill a barrel with water even though he only needs one jug, because the entire task is done with the same effort (Rashi). But for baking – one may only bake what is needed. Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says: A woman may fill an entire oven with bread, because the bread bakes better when the oven is full. Rava said: The law follows Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar. And this is the explanation: The Sages did not permit extra work just for the improvement of the small amount that is needed. They only permit what is done with one effort, even if there is no improvement in the part of the surplus, like the water in the barrel where the small amount of water needed does not improve because of the remaining water. All the more so with a pot of meat which improves, as it is known that the more meat in the pot, the better each piece in it tastes. Therefore, the Sages only permitted cooking and water that are done in one vessel. But baking, where each piece of bread is a separate task – they did not permit. Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar added that even for the sake of improvement, it is permitted, and therefore baking is also allowed, and certainly what is done in one action is permitted. And this is the law, and everyone agrees with this (see Taz, small section 1). And adding water to the pot not all at once – it seems there is no concern, as it is not considered labor. But drawing water from the well several times – it seems this is forbidden.

Certainly:

And all the more so, it is permissible to slaughter an animal even if one only needs a small portion of it, as it is impossible to obtain an olive-sized piece of meat without slaughtering. Similarly, one can cook many pots and eat a little from each one. If there is deception involved in this, it will be explained later. Know that there is a difference between the reason of one effort and the reason that a little improves. In matters where the reason is solely due to the effort of one act, like with a barrel of water, if one places the barrel on the fire, it is forbidden to add more water to it afterward, as this constitutes a new effort. This is not the case with a pot of meat or bread in an oven; it is permissible even to add more meat to the pot or bread to the oven afterward, in order to improve those portions one wishes to eat. Even if one has placed a small pot, it is permissible to transfer it to a larger pot and add more meat (Magen Avraham, subsection 2). Regarding bread, it will be explained in Siman 107 that in our ovens, a small amount does not improve by the oven being full of bread. Therefore, it is forbidden nowadays to bake more than what is needed, see there.

The Tur wrote that some say even if she explicitly states that she wants it for the next day, it is permitted. And there are those who forbid it. It appears that it is permitted, since the reason for the permission is that the addition causes flavor in the dish. If so, even if she explicitly stated it – it is also permitted. Thus far his words. And the Rokeach is the one who forbids it. His reasoning appears to be that although our sages of blessed memory permitted it for this reason, nonetheless, if the main intention is for the next day – it is certainly forbidden. And the Tur holds that we do not concern ourselves with the intention, since it is permitted by law. However, I have seen in the Rokeach that he does not care about the intention, only about the speech, and these are his words (in Siman 298): A woman fills a pot... but one should not say, "These will be for Yom Tov and not these." But when she fills the pot, then the dish is good, and her trickery is not noticeable, like the case of adding salt bit by bit... Thus far his words, and his intention is that the reason for the permission is because the trickery is not noticeable. And when she said it – the trickery is noticeable.

Based on this, we must say that the Tur, who disagrees with the aforementioned opinion, holds that even if the subterfuge is recognizable, it is permitted. However, this cannot be the case because the Tur subsequently wrote in the name of the Itur that one can only increase cooking before the meal, but after the meal, one cannot cook and claim, "I will eat an olive-sized portion from it," because this is clearly a significant subterfuge. This is the end of his words, and the Tur agreed with this. Thus, it is evident that he holds that recognizable subterfuge is forbidden. If so, how did he permit it when she says she wants it for tomorrow? Here, there is clearly recognizable subterfuge. We must say that he holds that recognizable subterfuge is only called such when an observer would understand the subterfuge on their own, such as after the meal. But before the meal, even if she says she wants it for tomorrow, since at the time of cooking there is no apparent subterfuge – we are not concerned about her statement being immediate, and the listener might assume that her desire to save for tomorrow arose afterward. This reasoning is explicitly proven in Tosafot (Yoma 11b, s.v. "Me'arim", look there carefully and you will find it clear). (See Taz, subsection 1.)

And even though after eating it is forbidden to employ subterfuge, even if one wishes to eat a piece of it, nevertheless, if one went ahead and cooked after eating, and ate an olive-sized portion of the food, or if one slaughtered an animal after eating and ate an olive-sized portion – it is permitted to eat it in the evening, even on the festival of Rosh Hashanah. There are those who prohibit this even after the fact, but this is not the main opinion (Magen Avraham, subsection 3). And proof of this: for in the case of someone dangerously ill, they permitted this initially, as I wrote in Siman 498. And if you think that it is also forbidden after the fact, except in the case of someone dangerously ill or with other cooked dishes – it would not have been permitted in the case of someone dangerously ill.

And know that there is a dispute among the authorities regarding the permission to "deceive" before eating by cooking a lot, with the intention to use it in the evening even though at present he only needs one piece as explained, because this piece is better when the pot is full as I have written: whether the intention is only when he genuinely needs this piece for his meal today, but if he does not need it at all for his meal today because he has other foods, and he only wants to eat a bit for the sake of the permission – it is forbidden. Or perhaps, even in such a case, it is permitted. There are those who forbid (Bach and Kenesset HaGedolah in the name of Radbaz), and there are those who permit (Magen Avraham, subsection 2, Yam Shel Shlomo, and Taz at the end of subsection 1), and he can even cook many pots and taste a kezayit from each one (there). And this is also implied by the words of Tosafot, the Tur, and the authorities who forbade after eating, as I have written. Now, after eating, he certainly does not actually need the piece he is eating – from this one can infer that before eating, even in such a case, it is permitted. And this is the custom of the world, that they cook some food for the night and taste a bit of it (there). And it is clear that the manner of tasting only helps to eat a little in the manner of eating. And some say that only from the first day of Yom Tov to the second day is it permitted in such a manner, but not from the second day of Yom Tov to a weekday (there). And I do not understand the distinction in this (and so it is written in the name of the Ri"v that it is permitted).

Even though food preparation that can be done on the eve of a festival is prohibited on the festival itself, whether by Torah law or Rabbinic decree as explained in Siman 527, and certainly for the preparations of food, nevertheless our Sages of blessed memory said (Beitzah 14a) that spices may be ground in their usual manner on the festival, even though grinding is a derivative of the prohibited labor of grinding, and even though they could be ground on the eve of the festival. The reason is that since their flavor deteriorates if prepared the day before, it is considered as if it is not possible to prepare them on the eve of the festival. Therefore, it is permitted to grind them even if they are considered preparatory, and even if one knew from the previous day that he would need those spices.

Therefore, it is forbidden to grind salt in the usual manner, because salt does not spoil if prepared the day before. Hence, it is only permitted to grind salt on Yom Tov with a change, such as grinding it on the table or in a bowl, but not in a mortar. And if it is only possible to use a mortar, it should be tilted to the side during the grinding. Similarly, if there is a type of spice that does not spoil if prepared the day before, like saffron, and one knew the day before that it would be needed, it should only be prepared with a change, like salt. This applies to pepper and similar spices (Magen Avraham, subsection 1, in the name of Yam Shel Shlomo, Bach, and Mahari"l). However, garlic certainly spoils, and it is permitted to grind it on Yom Tov. The same applies to onions and similar items. There are those who hold that even with all this, some change is needed when grinding spices, if one knew from the day before that they would be needed. Some are concerned even if one did not know (see Magen Avraham, subsection 4). It is proper to be cautious about this, so that one remembers not to grind more than is needed for Yom Tov (there in the name of Sefer Mitzvot Gadol). But the main halacha follows the first opinion.

In their time, they had a special mill for grinding pepper and mustard. Even now, we have a small mill for pepper and coffee. It is forbidden on Yom Tov to grind there even with a change, because it is considered a weekday activity and is a detriment to the sanctity of Yom Tov. Rather, one should grind in a mortar or pestle, like all other spices. It is permitted to carry spices and a pestle to the mortar, or the mortar to them, even through a public domain, even though this could have been done on the eve of Yom Tov. The reason for this has already been explained in Siman 498 regarding leading an animal to the slaughterer, because in matters of carrying, the way was entirely permitted. See there, and at the beginning of Siman 499.

Maimonides wrote in the third chapter: One should not crush grains in a large mortar, but in a small mortar it is permitted, as this constitutes a change. However, in the Land of Israel, even in a small mortar it is forbidden, since their grain is of good quality, and if one crushes it before the festival, there is no loss. So far his words. And in the Talmud there, it is explained according to one interpretation that in a place where transgressions are rampant, it is also forbidden to use a small mortar in any place. However, besides this, the Tur and Shulchan Aruch wrote in paragraph 3 that since we do not know what is considered "large" and what is considered "small," therefore, in all cases it is forbidden. And it is clear that now the practice is to completely prohibit crushing groats.

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote there that it is permitted to grate cheese on Yom Tov using a tool that is like a serrated threshing board, and in our language, a grater. However, a slight change is required, like the grinding of salt. The same applies to matzah without any change, because there is no grinding with foods that were initially ground. Until here are his words, meaning: there is no grinding after grinding. And the matzah has already been ground into flour.

There are those who wrote regarding this that it is not similar to mustard, which is forbidden to grind in a millstone, because there it is customary to grind a lot at once and it resembles the activities of a weekday. But here, it is not customary to scrape more than what is needed for the moment. According to this, horseradish, which is called "krein," would be forbidden to scrape on Yom Tov, because it is customary to scrape a lot for two or three days (Magen Avraham, subsection 7). This is very strange, as there is nothing that spoils as quickly as "krein," as is known. It is obvious that it is permitted to scrape it on Yom Tov, and this is indeed the custom of the world (as also written by the Eliyah Rabbah). Additionally, the comparison to the mustard millstone is strange, because this tool called "morag charutz" does not resemble a millstone at all, as is known. In contrast, the millstones for pepper and mustard do somewhat resemble millstones, so what is the relevance of this comparison?

Even though measuring flour is forbidden on Yom Tov, as I wrote in Siman 506, nevertheless, it is permitted for a person to measure spices to put into a pot in order not to ruin the dish, for this is considered like actual food preparation. The same applies to salt and pepper. However, in a place where even on weekdays they do not measure but rather add by estimation, it is also forbidden on Yom Tov. But in a place where they add by measure on weekdays, it is permitted to measure even on Yom Tov.

We learn in the Talmud (Shabbat 145b): A person may milk a goat directly into a pot, but not into a bowl. In a pot, there is food, and the milk that comes into it is considered a liquid entering food and is regarded as food, thus it is like separating food from food. This is not similar to extracting, which is a derivative of threshing. However, into an empty bowl, it is considered extracting. And the Tosafot wrote that this applies specifically on Yom Tov, as the animal is fit for eating and it is considered food that separates, but not on Shabbat since it is not fit for slaughter. Similarly, the Rif wrote that this refers to Yom Tov, and it is surprising that the Rambam did not mention this law at all. (It is impossible to say that he holds like Rabbi Chananel, who rejected this law as stated by the Rif, since the Rambam wrote the law of squeezing a cluster of grapes in the laws of Shabbat, chapter four, and Rabbi Chananel also rejected this law. The Maggid Mishneh already wondered there about his omission of this law in the laws of Yom Tov, see there.)

And this is the language of the Tur: A pot that has food in it – it is permitted to milk an animal into it according to the Rif, even though it is forbidden to suckle from the animal on Yom Tov unless one is in distress – even so, it is permitted to milk into the pot. But if there is no food in it – it is forbidden. Thus far his language, and the reason, as I have written: for when one suckles, it is considered as extracting, like milking into a vessel that has no food in it. However, when there is food in it – it is considered as separating food from food, and it is permitted. Seemingly, this permission is only when the animal is designated for slaughter. But an animal designated for milking – although there is no prohibition of extracting because of the food in the pot, nevertheless there is a prohibition of muktzeh. And the Tur, who did not make this distinction – it is because he holds like his father, the Rosh, of blessed memory, that also on Yom Tov there is no muktzeh, as I have written in Siman 495. But according to the Rif and the Rambam, who hold that there is muktzeh on Yom Tov – this is only with an animal designated for slaughter.

And so it is explained from the words of our master the Beit Yosef, who wrote: An animal that is designated for eating, and one wants to milk it to eat the milk, if it is for a pot that does not contain food – it is forbidden. But if there is food in it – it is permitted... this is his language until here, and it is explicitly as I have written. And one should not question: should it not be forbidden due to "nolad" (something newly created), for initially it was food and now it is a liquid? For this is not a question, since as it comes for food – it is considered as food. Therefore, without food, besides the prohibition of "mefarek" (extracting), it is forbidden due to "nolad", even if it was milked by itself or by a non-Jew.

The world is accustomed to milking on Yom Tov into food, especially on Shavuot. And this is a great wonder: after all, our milking animals are designated for milking and not for eating? It is necessary to say that the world either holds that we do not have muktzeh on Yom Tov according to the opinion of the Rosh, as tends to be the opinion of Rabbi Moshe Isserles in Siman 498; or they hold, as the Ran wrote in Shabbat there in the name of the Ramban, that even those who hold of muktzeh – it is permissible even with an animal designated for milking, since there is no muktzeh in something that comes of its own, such as this, because it was not rejected by human hands since the prohibition was removed, the muktzeh was removed. That is to say: certainly if the milk were also meant to be curdled and dried for cheese – they would be muktzeh. But since the milk is meant for drinking, although when it is inside the animal it is muktzeh, but when it is separated from the animal, the muktzeh is removed. And it is not similar to all muktzeh that a person made muktzeh, like lighting a candle, or placing something to dry, or for commerce, or for storage. But here, the muktzeh is from its own nature, and when it is separated from the muktzeh – it is permitted. And so appears to be the opinion of the Meor, see there. And even the prohibition of nolad (something newly created) is removed for this reason, and even though at the beginning of Beitza it is explained that an egg laid on Yom Tov is nolad. And even those who do not hold of muktzeh hold of nolad, and if so, it is nolad. And the same applies to the milk of an animal: even if muktzeh is permitted – in any case, it is nolad at the very least. And I have indeed seen someone who posed this difficulty (the Gaon Rabbi Akiva Eiger). Nevertheless, it appears that the poskim (decisors) hold that all this is in the Gemara according to the initial understanding of the discussion. But according to the conclusion, it is not so, since the Gemara concludes with other reasons for the egg, and not because of nolad. And the reason for the egg laid on Yom Tov is because of preparation, as I wrote below in Siman 513. And also above in Siman 324 regarding Shabbat, they did not write the reason of nolad, see there (and in any case, it requires further study). And see in Section 7.

When it is permitted to milk directly into food, it is specifically when this milking improves the food, according to what is needed for that food. All the more so if the milk is absorbed into the crumbs of the food. However, if one milks a lot of milk, more than what is needed for the food at all, and his intention is to pour the milk later into another place, this is completely prohibited. And it is certainly forbidden to put some bread in a vessel and milk onto it, and one is liable for lashes. And the unlearned people who practice this way should be rebuked with all kinds of severity. Rather, one should only milk according to what is needed for the food in this pot. (See Taz, subsection 2, whose words are not clear to me. And as we have explained, this seems correct.)

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote that if a non-Jew milks an animal on Yom Tov and a Jew sees him, it is permissible [to use the milk]. However, the custom is to prohibit it, and one should not change this custom. Nevertheless, on the second day of Yom Tov in the Diaspora, it is permitted. Thus are his words. The Levush explained that the animal belongs to the non-Jew, and therefore, even if it is set aside for milking, it is not considered muktzeh, because an item belonging to a non-Jew does not require preparation, as I wrote in Siman 498 in the name of the Jerusalem Talmud, that muktzeh does not apply to a non-Jew's belongings. However, there are those who disagree, arguing that the concept of nolad (something that came into existence on Yom Tov) applies even to items belonging to a non-Jew (Magen Avraham, Section 3), as I wrote in Siman 517 regarding an egg; see there. In my opinion, the intention of the Levush is that certainly, something that comes into existence on its own, like an egg, applies to a non-Jew just as it does to a Jew. But milk, which was extracted by the non-Jew himself and separated from the food, just as it does not fall under the category of nolad for the non-Jew himself, it similarly does not apply when he gives it to a Jew. Since it was permitted for him, it remains permitted and does not acquire the status of nolad.

There is an interpretation that this refers to the animal of a Jew, but it was milked by a non-Jew. The reason that this is not considered muktzeh (set aside and prohibited on Shabbat) is based on the opinion of the Ramban, which we mentioned in section 4 (Taz, small section 3). And even though this is not according to the opinion of our teacher, the Beit Yosef, and he should have written it in the language of "some say" (there), it seems to me that because we can say that when a non-Jew milks it, everyone agrees that the muktzeh status and the issue of nolad (something that came into being on Shabbat) are removed by the action of the non-Jew, since there is no direct action by a Jew. The removal of the muktzeh status was not by a Jew, nor by itself, but by a non-Jew. And be that as it may, the custom of the world is to prohibit it, and one should not change this, as we do not rely on this reasoning in practice. However, milk that was milked on the first day is permitted on the second day, except for the two days of Rosh Hashanah, and except when Shabbat and Yom Tov are adjacent to each other. It is obvious that if Yom Tov falls on Thursday and Friday, milk that was milked on Thursday is permitted on Friday, and certainly on Shabbat. Similarly, if Yom Tov falls on Sunday and Monday, milk that was milked on Shabbat is permitted on Monday. This applies to Yom Tov in the diaspora, but not on Rosh Hashanah. And this is the practical halacha. (There are more laws regarding milking, and they are explained in the laws of Shabbat.)

One does not measure flour on Yom Tov to know how much to knead, but rather one should take an estimated amount. This does not diminish the joy of Yom Tov, even if it is slightly more or less. And even those who permit it in the Gemara (29a) do so only so that one may give challah generously, as explained in the Gemara. This was relevant when challah was given to the Kohen, but now that it is burned, there is no mitzvah in increasing the amount of challah (Tosafot there, beginning with "Shmuel"). And if the concern is to know whether there is the minimum amount required for challah, one can estimate until it is certainly the required amount or certainly less than the required amount. Why should we permit measuring, which is a weekday activity, when it does not add to the joy of Yom Tov?

It appears to me that even partners' flour can be divided by estimation, or by using a non-measuring vessel. The same applies to other similar situations. Some permit measuring when baking on Pesach, to avoid kneading too much and causing chametz. However, the Rif and the Rambam indicate that it is forbidden even on Pesach, as they do not differentiate in their writings, and the Tur also writes this in their names. And Rabbi Yosef Karo did not write this either, because even on Pesach it is not necessary; one can estimate or measure on Erev Pesach. It is permitted to take flour from a container even though it creates a hollow, because the prohibition of creating a hollow applies only to the ground, not to flour. See what I wrote in Siman 498, Section 29.

It is not permitted to sift flour on Yom Tov, since it could have been done before Yom Tov. Even with a change (in the method of sifting) – it is forbidden. This is not comparable to salt, which is permitted with a change, even though it could have been done before Yom Tov, as I wrote in Siman 504, because sifting is a task usually done for a longer period, not just for one day (Magen Avraham, Subsection 2). Additionally, sifting appears more like a weekday activity. It seems that even if one does not have sifted flour, it is forbidden to sift, and one should bake without sifting. The person has only himself to blame for not sifting before Yom Tov. Even if he was forced (and couldn’t sift before Yom Tov) – it is not permitted, because it is possible to eat without sifting. There are some of our Rabbis who permit it with a change (Tosafot, end of the third chapter, beginning with "Agaba"). One can rely on this to permit the initial sifting by a non-Jew with a change. However, we ourselves are forbidden (there).

And this is the language of the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch, Section 2: One may not sift flour initially on Yom Tov, even with a change. But if it was sifted yesterday, and a pebble or a splinter fell into it and one wants to sift it a second time – it is permitted even without a change. If nothing fell into it, but one wants to sift it a second time so that the bread will be fine – a small change is required, such as sifting on a table. However, a significant change, such as sifting behind the sieve, is not required. This is the end of their language. And know that "a second time" is only considered such when there is no intention to remove any waste, but merely to sift generally, as this is the normal practice at the time of kneading (Magen Avraham, Subsection 4, in the name of Yam Shel Shlomo). Or when a pebble fell into it, and it is forbidden to remove the pebble by hand because of the prohibition of selecting, therefore one sifts it so that the pebble remains in the sieve. This is more lenient because sifting a pebble is not considered sifting at all, and therefore no change is required. But when the intention is to remove waste, such as when the bran was removed the first time, and afterwards one wants to sift the semolina from the flour – this is considered "the first time," and is completely forbidden just like the actual first time (Bach).

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote: "There are those who say that it is permissible to take a pebble or a splinter in one's hand. But some are stringent and forbid it." Until here is his language, meaning: According to the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, it is forbidden to take the pebble in one's hand because it is considered selecting, as I wrote. This is the opinion of those who are stringent. But the opinion of those who permit is that it is allowed to take the pebble by hand from the flour, and this is the opinion of the Rashba. According to the Maggid Mishneh in the third chapter, the Rambam also holds this view. Their reasoning could be either that this is not considered selecting because it is like something that is placed by itself and not mixed, or because since it came about on Yom Tov, it is as if it was impossible to do it the day before, so it is permitted to do it today. And if because of muktzeh—it is permitted due to food preparation. Know that it is a change to sift on the table, as I wrote, because every day they sift into the trough. Accordingly, in a place where they always sift on the table, another change is required (Magen Avraham, subsection 5), such as sifting on a sieve and the like. (According to the Raavad in his glosses there, it is the opposite: without a pebble, no change is needed when sifting a second time, but with a pebble, a change is needed. See there, for he ruled like Rabbi Papa and Ribbia at the end of the third chapter. However, that according to him, with a pebble it is worse—requires examination to reconcile the Talmudic discussion there. See Maggid Mishneh and Lechem Mishneh).

Maimonides writes at the end of the fourth chapter: Even though one may not separate tithes on a festival, if someone has tithes that were separated the day before, he may bring them to the priest on the festival. Needless to say, this applies to the dough offering, the foreleg, the cheeks, and the stomach, which may be brought to the priest on a festival. His words conclude here, meaning: it is permitted to separate these on the festival when the dough is kneaded on the same day, for if one kneads dough on a festival, he may separate the dough offering from it. However, if the dough was kneaded on the day before the festival, it is prohibited, for he could have separated it the day before. But regarding bringing it to the priest, it is permitted even if it was separated the day before, as Maimonides wrote. And even on the Sabbath, it is permitted to bring it to the priest when it is baked bread and fit for eating (Magen Avraham, subsection 6), for it belongs to the priest, and one is giving him what is his. And with regards to the other gifts, it is permitted to separate them even if the animal was slaughtered the day before the festival, as I have written in subsection 9.

And what should one do with dough that was kneaded yesterday and challah was not separated from it? If he is in the Land of Israel, where it is forbidden to eat without separating challah, he has no other remedy but to knead another dough today, combine it with this one, and then take challah from both doughs from the dough that was kneaded today. However, outside the Land of Israel, where the rule is that one may eat and continue eating, and then separate challah afterward – he may eat from the bread all day without separating challah, and he should leave a bit of the bread more than the amount required for challah, and in the evening, he will separate the challah and give it to a priest or burn it according to our custom. He does not need to leave any of the dough, as he can bake all the bread. And even though there may be some portion of the challah that is not for eating – it does not matter to us, since the portion of the challah is not specified by itself. This is unlike the opinion of those who prohibit this, comparing it to dough that is half owned by a Jew and half by a non-Jew, which is forbidden to bake. This is not comparable, for it is forbidden to separate challah today. If it occurred that he separated a bit of dough for challah on the eve of a festival – it is forbidden to bake it on the festival, since it is not fit for eating. (And what the Magen Avraham wrote in subsection 8, regarding the eve of Passover that falls on the Sabbath, and one forgot to separate challah – has been explained above in Siman 484 with the help of Heaven, see there.)

The Tur wrote: "When one separates challah on a festival, they should not burn it immediately but should leave it until the night." Similarly, Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote in Section 4, and these are his words: "One who separates challah on a festival and it is impure (such as in our times, when we are all impure) should not bake it or burn it, for one does not burn sacred items on a festival. Rather, one should leave it until the evening and then burn it." These are his words. It is perplexing, for it is prohibited to burn sacred items at night, just as it is prohibited to burn them on a festival, as explained at the beginning of Pesachim and in Zevachim (56a). The great scholars have debated this matter (see Noda B'Yehuda, Second Edition, Orach Chaim, Siman 96). However, in my humble opinion, it is explicitly proven from the Mishnah at the end of Trumot that one may light with impure terumah oil at night, see there. And I found in the Jerusalem Talmud, Shabbat, at the beginning of the second chapter, that it straightforwardly asks whether one may light with burning oil at night, see there. Thus, it is explicitly permitted with terumah, and the same applies to challah. In the Rambam, there is no mention at all of a prohibition against lighting with burning oil on a festival.

It is permitted to bake large loaves on a Yom Tov, and we do not worry that by doing so, one might come to bake more than necessary. If one has flour or dough in partnership with a non-Jew, it is forbidden to bake it on Yom Tov. Instead, he should divide it and bake his portion. Even in one oven, it is permitted to fill the oven with bread because all the bread improves as a result, as I have written in Siman 503. This is because in any case, he can eat from whichever bread he wishes, which is not the case here (Magen Avraham, Siman Katan 15). Similarly, if a person has a lot of fine bread, he should not bake other bread unless he has household members who are accustomed to eating bread of lesser quality, and he needs to bake for them. However, if he has a lot of coarse bread, meaning inferior bread, he may bake fine bread afterward. Additionally, he may even do so initially if there is a need for it. Likewise, if he has yesterday’s bread, he is permitted to bake today because today’s bread is better than yesterday’s.

It is forbidden to make leaven on Yom Tov (a Jewish festival) except by means of a change, because it could have been made on the eve of Yom Tov. And even though there is a distinction in the separation of challah between dough kneaded today and dough kneaded on the eve of Yom Tov, as I have written – nevertheless, regarding the gifts to the priest, it is permitted to separate them even if the animal was slaughtered on the eve of Yom Tov, because there is no delay in eating when they have not been separated, and furthermore, they are recognizable on their own.

Rabbeinu the Beit Yosef wrote in Section 1: One may bake in a "forni," which is our large ovens with the opening on the side, provided it is not new, as we are concerned that it might crack and ruin the bread, thus detracting from the joy of the festival. And one may heat water in an "antichi," which is a large pot. Thus is his wording, and it is in the Gemara (34a). The explanation of the matter is that their ovens were small, and the "forni" is a large oven similar to ours. It teaches us that we do not say it is too much of a burden on a festival, and we are only concerned about a new one lest it crack. In our ovens, this concern does not apply. Additionally, before baking in it, we heat it several times to dry it. The "antichi" also informs us that we are not concerned about such a great burden. The heat also lasts until the next day, and I might have thought that this would be considered preparing for a weekday; it teaches us that it is permitted.

It has already been explained in Siman 501 that wood which fell from a palm tree on Yom Tov is prohibited to be used for kindling due to the prohibitions of muktzeh and nolad. Nonetheless, if this wood fell into the oven, one may add prepared wood to it and nullify it by majority. And even though it is generally forbidden to nullify a prohibition from the outset, here, since the prohibition is destined to be burnt, and the benefit comes afterward, we do not concern ourselves with this, and we nullify it by majority as per the law of dry in dry. For this reason, we do not worry even though it is something that has a permissible alternative, and also the main prohibition is rabbinic. However, one must be careful not to touch it until it has been nullified by the majority. And "touching" is not to be taken literally, for muktzeh is not forbidden by touching, as I wrote in Siman 308, but rather it means not to move it. (Regarding the question of the Magen Avraham in Siman 3 from Tosafot in Pesachim – the Degul Merivavah and the great Rabbi Akiva Eiger have already wondered about it.)

Our teacher, the Rema, wrote that when one adds prepared wood to the prohibited wood, it is required that the prohibited wood not be recognizable. His reasoning is that the entire concept of nullifying a prohibition with a permitted item is that it should not be recognizable. If it is recognizable, it is not nullified even in a ratio of one to a thousand, as I have written in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 98. Nevertheless, there are those who say that even if the prohibited wood is recognizable, it is nullified (Magen Avraham, subsection 2, in the name of Yam Shel Shlomo), since several leniencies have been applied in this nullification due to the fact that the prohibition is destined to be burned. This is also explicitly explained in the Responsa of Rashba, Siman 485; see there. (I also see proof for this from Shabbat 29a; see there. Study it carefully and you will find ease.)

Some wish to say that since the reason for the permissibility is that the prohibition is destined to be burned, and the benefit will come afterward—therefore, it is forbidden to warm oneself against them, as the benefit comes before the burning is completed. And even if we say that the benefit of the heat comes from what has already been burned—still, to use them for illumination, where the benefit certainly comes before the burning is completed, is forbidden. But in truth, there is no basis for this, for is it forbidden to derive incidental benefit from something that is muktzeh? And if a non-Jew lights a Jew’s lamp for his own use, it is permissible for the Jew to use its light. The prohibition is only in moving it. And the reason it is forbidden to use its light when the non-Jew lights it for the Jew is because a labor was performed for him (see Magen Avraham, subsection 3). However, some hold that muktzeh is forbidden for benefit, as I wrote in Siman 501, and this requires further examination.

All the leniencies that were permitted in this matter pertain to the rabbinic prohibition of muktzeh. However, regarding the Torah prohibition of preparation, no leniency was given. Therefore, if [wood] fell into the oven on Shabbat, it is forbidden to light it on the subsequent Yom Tov, even through the principle of nullification by majority. This is because Shabbat does not prepare for Yom Tov, and here, by its detachment, Shabbat has prepared for Yom Tov, as Shabbat itself does not require kindling. Hence, conversely, if it fell on Yom Tov that falls on the eve of Shabbat, and on the next day it is needed for kindling by a non-Jew for a sick person or the like, it is permissible, because Yom Tov did not prepare for Shabbat but for itself, as kindling is permitted on Yom Tov. Some say that Shabbat also prepares for itself, for if there was a dangerously ill person, it would be permitted (Magen Avraham, subsection 4, in the name of the Ran, see there). However, I do not understand: if so, all the muktzeh and all the matters would be nullified, for all things are permitted for a dangerously ill person, and this requires further study. Nevertheless, the halacha is that it is forbidden, as I have written.

There are those who say that it is specifically when the wood falls into the oven, as it can be assumed that there are also permissible woods there, and then it is allowed to add more wood so that the forbidden wood becomes nullified by the majority. But if the wood falls not into the oven, without a mixture of other woods, it is forbidden to add more (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 1). And I am perplexed: even if the wood falls into the oven, since there is not a majority of permissible wood, it still remains entirely forbidden, so how can it be permitted to add more? If so, it should also be the case when not in the oven! Furthermore, is it always the case that there is wood in the oven? The Talmud which states "into the oven" has a different reason, for if it did not fall into the oven, who would compel him to take forbidden wood and nullify it by the majority? He should take non-forbidden wood. But in the oven, it is necessary to do so, since one needs to bake there. And removing them from the oven is forbidden because they are prohibited from being moved. Additionally, if the wood did not fall into the oven, how would one put them into the oven? But to differentiate between whether there was some permissible wood or not is certainly perplexing. (And the proof brought from Yoreh Deah, Siman 99, is not a proof at all to one who examines it there. The Mahatzit Hashekel elaborated and strained, and there is no proof, see there. Examine and you will find it easy. In the Yam Shel Shlomo, Chapter 1, Siman 6, it is explained as our words. But in the Responsa of the Rashba, Part 1, Siman 336, it is explained like the Magen Avraham. And the Ran at the beginning of Beitzah seems unsure about this, see there. This requires further study.)

The Tur and Shulchan Aruch wrote in paragraph 3: It is forbidden to take a piece of wood from among the other pieces of wood to stoke the fire in the oven, as this constitutes making a utensil. This is their language, and it is from the Gemara (33a). At first glance, what kind of utensil-making is involved here, as the wood is like any other wood? The language of Tosafot in Shabbat (143a) is more refined, as they wrote that even though it does not become a utensil, it is still forbidden, as we make a decree lest one come to make a utensil. This is his language. And the Rosh in Beitzah there wrote that it appears like making a utensil, and it is forbidden even if it is dry and suitable for burning, unless it was prepared for that purpose on the eve of the festival. The language of the Tur and Shulchan Aruch seems to me to mean as follows: Certainly, when one selects a piece of wood from among the other pieces, this piece of wood is not like ordinary wood, but is somewhat like a utensil, as it is suitable for stoking the fire. And this itself is somewhat like making a utensil. Similarly, it is forbidden to select a piece of wood from among other pieces to secure the door for this reason, unless it was prepared for this purpose on the eve of the festival (Taz, paragraph 4).

In our ovens, which bake on the floor of the oven, it is clear that without removing the ash and coals, it is impossible to bake, and it is permissible to remove them. Even though one extinguishes some coals during the removal process, it is unavoidable. Just as it is permitted to kindle a fire for the sake of preparing food, it is similarly permitted to extinguish a fire for the sake of preparing food. This is akin to placing meat on coals, and such is the custom. Nevertheless, there is a difference between removing ashes on a weekday and on a festival. On a weekday, one dips the scraper (called a "pamila") in a lot of water and scrapes, but on a festival, this method is certainly forbidden because it involves extensive extinguishing, which is unnecessary. Instead, one scrapes with a dry scraper and scrapes thoroughly. Even in this method, there is some extinguishing, but it is unavoidable. However, if the oven is large and one scrapes part of it, and it is sufficient for the bread that needs to be baked, but he is concerned that the bread might touch the unscraped part and burn, he should not scrape more. Certainly, if he scrapes it all at once, he scrapes it entirely in the regular manner, but if he scrapes part and leaves it, he should not scrape more if there is enough space. Although there is a slight need, as I mentioned, that the bread might touch the unscraped area, we do not apply the principle of "mitoch" (the allowance of work for food preparation extending to non-food preparation) to extinguishing, as extinguishing is not permitted at all on a festival except when it is absolutely necessary (this is the intention of the Magen Avraham, section 8).

And one should not ask: if so, why is roasting meat on coals permitted? After all, it is possible to roast with a spit in the air, so that there is no extinguishing at all. One could say: the Torah did not restrict the manner of our eating, and the choice is in our hands to eat as we desire, and there are those who prefer meat roasted on coals. And this seems explicitly apparent from Rashi and Rambam, that roasting meat on coals involves complete extinguishing, but the Torah permitted it. However, some of our rabbis wrote that roasting meat on coals is not complete extinguishing, because after the extinguishing, it reignites immediately (Ramban in Milchamot and Ran in the second chapter). And their intention is not that if it were complete extinguishing it would be forbidden when there is no other way like with sweeping; for this is not logical at all, for if so, how could we bake on Yom Tov? Rather, they say it in regard to roasting, that it is possible with a spit and the like. (And this is explicitly explained in their words at the end of the second chapter, and this is the language of the Ran: but Rashi... does not scrutinize to say it is possible to roast it in another manner... thus far his language. But according to the version of the Rif, they do scrutinize, and so it is written in Milchamot: for it is possible to roast without extinguishing, see there.) (And the question of the Magen Avraham in subsection 9 is resolved, and his question is puzzling. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

And know that there is someone who wrote in this language in section 502, paragraph 1 in the gloss: It implies that even for the purpose of eating, it is specifically at the time when one is preparing the food that it is permitted to extinguish, and not before (Magen Avraham, end of subsection 8). And his intention is regarding what our teacher the Rema wrote there, that it is permissible to cover the fire with a vessel or prepared earth if it does not extinguish it, see there. But if it extinguishes it – it is forbidden, because it is not at the time of food preparation. However, in my humble opinion, these words are puzzling. For there, if it were touching the food in the oven – it would certainly be permitted. But the covering is so that the fire will last for a long time, as is proven from what is concluded there, that it is specifically for the sake of the first day of Yom Tov, but for the sake of the second day of Yom Tov – it is forbidden, see there. It is explicitly stated that his intention is for a later time, and in this case surely extinguishing is not permitted, as after some time he will light other wood. But when the extinguishing is for the purpose of food preparation – it is obvious that it is permitted even not at the time of food preparation, like sweeping the oven before baking. And this is the main ruling in law.

And in the time of the Talmud when the ovens were small, and the bread would stick to the side of the oven – the law of raking out had different rules. And this is the language of our master, the Beit Yosef, in section 4: An oven into which plaster has fallen, if it is possible to bake and roast in it without raking out, and the bread or roast will not be charred – it is forbidden to rake it out, because it is moving it without necessity. But it is permitted to smooth down the fire and ashes in it, so that it will be smooth and not touch the bread at all, even though if it did touch it, it would not char it. But if there is enough plaster that fell into it to char the bread or roast if it touched them, even though without raking it out it would be possible to bake and roast in it, since it would be charred – it is permitted to rake it out, for it is considered moving for necessity. And specifically in their ovens, where they would stick the bread around them, and it is only necessary to rake out the plaster that fell into it. But our ovens...until here is his language.

Explanation of his words: To extinguish the fire and the ashes—this is permitted in any manner, even if the bread does not get scorched on the side, because the fire and ashes are permitted to be handled on Yom Tov. And it refers to ashes that are hot and are like fire (Magen Avraham, subsection 6). And when they cool down—it is forbidden to extinguish them, as they are muktzeh. And when they become hot again—they return to being permitted (there). And soil, when it is present, it is forbidden to extinguish it because it is muktzeh (there). But plaster that has fallen into the oven, it depends on whether there is no damage to the bread at all, meaning that one can bake and roast on the spit without raking, and also there is no scorching by their contact with the plaster. In such a case, it is forbidden to rake it. But if by touching it, it will get scorched, even though the baking or roasting is possible without raking, and it is not certain that the plaster will touch them—in any case, it is permitted to rake it because it is likely that it will touch them and get scorched, and it is permitted due to the need for food preparation. (And the Taz, subsection 5, explained the words of the Tur differently. The words of the Beit Yosef are clear in terms of the law, see there.)

Their custom was to anoint a new oven and stove with oil in order to polish them, and it is forbidden to do so on Yom Tov because it is considered repairing a utensil. Similarly, their custom was to rub them with a cloth to polish them, and it is forbidden on Yom Tov for the same reason. Their custom was, after the first heating, to place cold water in them, which means cold water, in order to strengthen them, and it is forbidden on Yom Tov for the reason that was explained. However, the initial heating is permitted on Yom Tov, because this is not considered the completion of the work until it is cooled with cold water, and this we have forbidden. However, if they have been overheated, and it is necessary to cool them with cold water in order to bake in them, because without this it is impossible to bake and the bread would burn, it is permitted to cool them with cold water, which means to immerse rags in cold water and to wipe the oven with them, even though this extinguishes the fire directly, since it is impossible to bake at all without this. And even though this strengthens the oven and constitutes repairing a utensil, which is similar to hardening stones that is forbidden later in Siman 508, nonetheless here it is permitted, because this occurs during the process of preparing the baking. Additionally, it is not certain that they will be strengthened in this manner. (See Magen Avraham, subparagraph 11, who explains that this is not comparable.)

And if it has already been swept out, but some small embers remain, it is forbidden to soak the broom in water and then sweep them out, as it can be done without this (there, subsection 12). Similarly, we wrote in section 8 regarding our ovens, that it is permitted to sweep them out, but without soaking in water. Likewise, the broom, after one has finished sweeping out the oven, it is forbidden to immerse it in water so that it will not burn (there), as there is no necessity for food preparation, but merely a loss in that the broom will burn. For this reason, extinguishing was not permitted, and even though he will not have anything with which to sweep further, since this sweeping has been completed, it is forbidden.

It has already been explained in Siman 503 that it is permissible to bake a full oven of bread, even though one only needs a single loaf, because this loaf bakes better when the oven is full of bread. And some say this is specifically when one intends to improve this loaf, but otherwise it is forbidden (Beit Yosef in the name of the Ra'ah). However, this does not seem to be the view of the poskim (Beit Yosef). And it appears that in the case of cooking, it is certainly not so, since it is one effort. But regarding bread, where each loaf is its own effort, it is proper to be stringent (Magen Avraham, subsection 13).

However, this leniency applies only to their ovens, which were small, and they would stick the bread to the walls of the oven. Since the oven was full, there was no room for the heat to spread, and therefore the bread would bake well when the oven was full. But this does not apply to our ovens, which are large, and filling them with bread does not provide as much benefit. Therefore, it is forbidden to bake more than what is needed. However, one does not need to be exact in this matter, because it is impossible to be precise. Some want to permit even in our ovens, but this is not the main opinion. All the more so, trickery is forbidden with bread, and it is not comparable to a cooked dish, which involves only one effort.

It is permissible to seal the mouth of an oven on Yom Tov with clay and mud from the riverbank, as the clay has already been kneaded; for kneading is prohibited on Yom Tov and it must be prepared before Yom Tov. This means: either soften it a little before Yom Tov, or make a mark on it and set it aside, as if it is separate, and this is its preparation. Clay from the street does not need an action, but one must think about using it before Yom Tov (Magen Avraham, subsection 15). And although it is prohibited to knead clay on Yom Tov, it is permissible to soften it, but ash is allowed to be kneaded on Yom Tov, as it is not subject to kneading. And even according to those who hold that there is kneading with ash, as I wrote in Siman 321, subsection 18, since this is for the purpose of food preparation to preserve its heat – it is permitted. And why is it prohibited with clay? Because it appears as if preparing for construction (ibid., subsection 16). But the Tur wrote that according to Rabbi Yitzchak of the Tosafists, it is prohibited unless water was added to the ash before Yom Tov. And according to Rabbeinu Tam, even in this case it is prohibited, and only placing it on the mouth of the oven without kneading is permitted. And so, it is customary to prohibit kneading even with ash, as it is a doubtful Torah prohibition. And I do not understand, for even if we consider it as food preparation – it can be done before Yom Tov. Moreover, this is certainly a preparation for food. (The esteemed Rabbi Akiva Eiger wrote that from Ketubot 7a it is evident that intimacy is somewhat necessary, and we are compelled to say regarding extinguishing "mitoch," see there. And in my humble opinion, this is not considered as some need, see there. Be precise and you will find leniency.)

It was taught (33a): One does not whiten the tiles to roast on them. These are what we call dachuks, and they used to roast on them. They would whiten them in the fire, and thereby they became strengthened, which constitutes making a utensil. And in the Gemara there, it is explicitly implied that this applies only to new ones and not to old ones, as the old ones have already been strengthened. And this is also the ruling of the Rashba and Rabbeinu Yerucham (see Beit Yosef). But Rambam, the Tur, and the Shulchan Aruch wrote this as a general rule, which implies that even old ones are forbidden because they become increasingly strengthened over time. And our rabbis understand from the Gemara that there are two reasons: see there. And according to the reason that they become strengthened, even old ones are forbidden. It is surprising that Rabbeinu Beit Yosef in section 1 wrote: One does not whiten stones to roast or bake on them, because it hardens them. Thus far his words. Why did he change from "tiles" to "stones"? And with "stones," it seems that hardening does not apply (Magen Avraham, section 1). And in Rambam, there are also those who read "stones," as it is in Rambam's commentary on the Mishnah. Presumably, they ruled that there is also hardening in stones, and therefore, it is forbidden according to the law. (And it is surprising that Rambam in his commentary on the Mishnah wrote only "new," and so did the Rosh. This needs further investigation regarding the Tur and Shulchan Aruch.)

We also learned in the Mishnah (32b): One does not break pottery or cut paper in order to roast a salty fish. Rashi explained: When roasting fish on a grill, which is called a "griddel," and it is made like the rungs of a ladder, one cuts reeds or stalks of grain, or breaks pottery or cuts paper, and soaks them in water. They then arrange the paper on top of the grill because the metal heats up and burns the fish. This is his language. And in the Baraita (34a) it is taught: One does not split a reed to roast a salty fish with it, but one may split a nut with a cloth and does not worry that it might tear. Rashi explained: They place the strips of reed under the salty fish on the grill, which makes a utensil, because anything made to be used is considered making a utensil. This is his language. And the Rambam explained that they split the reed to make it like a skewer. "Splitting" is a term for breaking, and the explanation of "splitting the nut with a cloth" seems to be that they wrap the nuts in a cloth and break them. Even though it is possible that the cloth might tear from the breaking, we do not worry about it, because it is a destructive act, and it is not like tearing with the intention to sew (Rashi).

It has already been clarified that the preparations for food that cannot be done before the festival may be done on the festival itself. For this reason, we permitted in Siman 107 to clean the oven when the plaster has fallen, see there. Similarly, a spit used for roasting meat, if its point broke on the festival in such a way that it is not suitable for roasting – it is permitted to repair it. But if it only bent a little and is still suitable for roasting – it is forbidden to repair it, even if he can fix it by hand without a tool. Likewise, if he can borrow from his neighbor – he should not repair it on the festival, even if it is impossible to roast with it (Magen Avraham, subsection 3). And if it broke on the eve of the festival, and he knew about it, and he had time to repair it, even if he forgot and did not repair it – it is forbidden to repair it in any manner. But if he did not know that it broke, or there was no time to repair it – its law is like it broke on the festival (ibid., subsection 2). Similarly, if it broke on the first day of the festival – it is forbidden to repair it on the second day of the festival, for regarding this matter, the first day of the festival is considered like a weekday, even if we are experts in the fixing of the month (ibid.). And even though it was forbidden to repair it on the first day of the festival, such as if it broke after the meal, still regarding the second day of the festival, it is as if it broke on the eve of the festival, and it is forbidden to repair it on the festival.

And even though, according to the essential law, if it was not possible to perform the task before the holiday, it is permitted to do it on the holiday, nonetheless, we do not instruct the masses in this manner, so that they do not come to repair even something that broke before the holiday. For thus the sages said (28b): "The law is such, but we do not instruct the masses in this manner." However, the Rambam in the fourth chapter and the Tur did not bring this ruling, except concerning a whetstone, as will be explained. They hold that this ruling of the Sages applies only to sharpening a knife, because sharpening a knife appears more like a weekday activity, but not to other laws. However, our master the Rema wrote in section 1 that this applies also to a spit and all other implements, as is the opinion of some of the poskim (decisors). It appears from their words that we do not instruct the masses, but an individual teacher can instruct an individual, for otherwise it would have said "and do not instruct others." And even though the language of the Gemara is "and we do not instruct in this manner" – it implies to them that we do not instruct the masses. But our master the Beit Yosef wrote in his great book in chapter 516 that this is not only for the masses, but also for individuals, we do not instruct in this manner, see there.

Indeed, we have already written in Siman 498, Section 22, that regarding the fundamental laws of preparing food on Yom Tov, we do not find a clear ruling among the poskim (legal decisors). For the Rambam prohibits in all matters except for sweeping out an oven, and the same is explained by the Rif. And we explained there in Section 25 that because it is not taught as such, he ruled stringently in all matters, except for those directly related to food preparation itself, such as sweeping out an oven. See there. Similarly, the Ramban wrote in the opinion of the Rif (as brought in the Bach in this Siman). And this is the language of the Ramban: "Even though the halacha follows Rav Yosef, we do not fully rely upon him. Matters that are essential in the preparation of the food itself, such as sweeping out an oven, the halacha and the ruling are in accordance with him where it is certain that the food will burn. But matters that are not essential in the preparation of food but are needed, such as extinguishing to prevent the house from smoking, extinguishing a house fire, or extinguishing a candle for marital relations – these are entirely forbidden both to teach and to perform any action specifically. And matters that are preparatory for food but are not necessary, such as a knife that has become dull and can be asked about, since there are plenty available – it is permitted with a change. But this is not taught because it is common." Until here is his language. And the Ran wrote that this is also the opinion of the Rashba and the Sefer Mitzvot Gadol, and this is also the opinion of the Rambam (Bach there). And we explained in Section 25 the opinion of the Rambam, see there.

But the Tur followed the approach of his father, the Rosh, that the law is according to Rav Yosef and we rule accordingly, except for two things where we do not rule according to Rav Yosef: sharpening a knife and extinguishing a candle for the purpose of marital relations. Therefore, he wrote here regarding a spit that was broken, if it is not fit for roasting – it is permissible to repair it. And regarding a knife that was nicked, he wrote that it is permissible to sharpen it with a wooden whetstone or on another knife, and we rule accordingly. However, with a stone whetstone, even though it is permissible to sharpen with it – we do not instruct to do so. And if it is to remove its fat – even with a stone whetstone we instruct to do so. And in Siman 514 regarding extinguishing a piece of wood, he ruled that if not extinguishing it will cause the pot to smoke – it is permissible to extinguish it, but for the purpose of marital relations it is completely forbidden to extinguish, see there. And his reasoning is simple: regarding the sharpening of the knife, the Gemara says that we do not instruct accordingly. And for marital relations, his reasoning is that this is considered as something that could have been done before the holiday, for he should not have placed the candle in a place needed for marital relations. Additionally, he can take it to another house.
