And even though in the Gemara it asks about this law (22b) when he does not have another house, and the prohibition to extinguish is according to the Rabbis and not according to Rav Yosef, see there – nevertheless, the Tur holds that since with a knife which is for eating purposes they said not to instruct accordingly, all the more so for marital relations which are not eating purposes, we do not rule accordingly. Therefore, he ruled it forbidden.

Behold, our teacher, the Beit Yosef, followed the approach of the Rambam and ruled in all instances to prohibit. Therefore, he wrote in this section, paragraph 1: A spit that was bent, even though it can be straightened by hand, it is not to be fixed. Thus are his words, indicating a complete prohibition. In paragraph 2, he wrote: A spit that one wishes to roast with, and it was too long, it is forbidden to cut it or to burn it. Thus are his words. And even though a wick is permitted to be burned into two in section 514, there it appears as if one is lighting two candles. But here it is forbidden because of fixing a utensil (Mordechai). And some wrote that it must be said that it refers to a situation where it could have been done the day before (Magen Avraham, subsection 4). Meaning: if it could not have been done the day before, it is permitted. But it seems to me that this is not so, for according to the Rambam's approach, all preparatory actions are prohibited, as I have written. And if so, even if it could not have been done the day before, it is forbidden.

Additionally, he wrote: One does not sharpen a knife with its designated sharpener. However, one may hone it on wood, pottery, or stone. Yet, this should not be taught publicly, lest people come to sharpen it with the designated sharpener. When are these matters said? When it can cut with difficulty or it has become slightly damaged. But if it cannot cut at all, one should not sharpen it even on wood, lest one come to sharpen it with the designated sharpener. This is the end of his wording, and these are the words of the Rambam. This is not like the Tur, who permits instructing to hone on wood, and allows using a stone sharpener with the caveat of not teaching it publicly, as I wrote in Section 4. Regarding honing on another knife, its law is like honing on wood (Section 5). Just as one does not teach this to the public, so too, one should not do it in front of the public, unless one can prevaricate and say he intends only to remove the grease. And with a designated sharpener, one should not even instruct to remove the grease (Section 6, in the name of Yam Shel Shlomo and Bach).

In Siman 516, it is ruled that it is prohibited to extinguish the burning wood, even though it is impossible to save the pot in another way; see there. And even for usage – it is prohibited. And all of this follows the Rambam's approach. However, the words of our teacher, the Rema, are perplexing since he follows the Tur's approach and rules there regarding extinguishing the burning wood that if it is impossible to save the pot in another way – it is permitted to extinguish it; see there. And in this Siman in Section 1 regarding a spit that was bent, he ruled that if it cannot be used for roasting, and it broke on Yom Tov – it is permitted to repair it; see there. And this follows the Tur. And even though he added that this is not instructed to the public, and the Tur did not mention this – he followed the approach of Rabbeinu Yerucham, who also states that there is a ruling but it is not instructed to the public. And this is not a contradiction to the Tur's approach, as is evident.

However, according to this, it is puzzling: if so, why did he not correct in Section 2 about the law of sharpening the knife, that with a wooden object it is completely permitted, and with a whetstone it is permitted but we do not teach this as the Tur states? It seems to me the reason is that regarding a whetstone, he did not follow the method of the Tur because although in the whole sugya (28a) it is explained that according to Rav Yosef it is permitted to sharpen a knife with a whetstone, nevertheless, at the end of the sugya it proves that even according to Rav Yosef it is forbidden. For behold, afterwards, it is forbidden to show a knife to a sage on Yom Tov, as I wrote in Siman 498. And according to the Rambam, the reason is that perhaps the sage will say it is defective, and he will go and sharpen it, as I wrote there. And if it would enter your mind that according to Rav Yosef it is permitted – what is the problem if he sharpens it? And if it is because we do not teach this, behold we are not teaching him, but he is doing it on his own, and it is permitted to do so since the law follows Rav Yosef. Rather, certainly even according to Rav Yosef it is forbidden. And this reasoning was written by the Ran in the sugya there, see there. And the conclusion of the law regarding a knife is that there is no permission to instruct. Only to remove its grease – it is permitted to pass it over a stone, but not to sharpen it, for even with a wooden object we do not instruct to permit. But if he does it on his own – it is permitted. And with a whetstone, we protest against doing it. Therefore, the women who pass the knife to sharpen it a bit on the table or the oven – we do not protest against them, for indeed this is permitted even according to the Rambam. However, we do not instruct them so, and we do not teach them, and when they do it on their own – it is permitted and there is no need to protest against them. (And the reasoning of the Ran we mentioned in Siman 492 at the end of Section 25, see there.)

Birds that are stuffed with meat and eggs and need to be sewn, as well as thin stuffed items that need to be sewn at their ends—it is permitted to sew them on Yom Tov, as this is not a lasting form of sewing and is necessary for food preparation. However, it is forbidden to fix the thread on Yom Tov, as this is considered making a utensil, which could have been done before Yom Tov and is forbidden according to all opinions. Therefore, it is also not proper to thread the needle on Yom Tov, because there is concern that one might cut the thread, and it is forbidden to cut the thread on Yom Tov and tie it at its end, as is done in sewing. Some have written that if the thread was not inserted before Yom Tov, it is forbidden to insert it on Yom Tov (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 8). This is an excessive stringency, for there is no prohibition in this. In my humble opinion, it is permitted if the thread was not inserted before Yom Tov, provided one takes care not to cut the thread that remains after the sewing. It is customary to burn the remaining thread after sewing. In truth, there is no difference between cutting and burning, and fundamentally, it is also permitted to cut the remaining thread after sewing, as it could not have been done before Yom Tov, and it is considered a direct necessity for food preparation. However, women have the custom of burning rather than cutting, perhaps to make a distinction from weekday practice. The prohibition against cutting the thread applies before the sewing, as this could have been done before Yom Tov. But after the sewing, it is permitted by law (see Magen Avraham, subparagraph 9). It is permitted to cut on Yom Tov the bindings of kids and trussed birds, and the sewn threads in food. It is also permitted to burn the wick or rag used to tie the bird, as this is a direct necessity for food preparation and could not have been done beforehand, but only at the time of eating or cooking. If a needle has become bent, it should not be straightened, and it is subject to the same rule as a spit, as explained in paragraph 1.

Our Rabbi, the Beit Yosef, wrote in Section 5: It is permissible to heat a metal utensil on Yom Tov that was used to bake cheese pastries, and after the heating, to bake a meat pie in it. This is provided that when it is heated, it is immediately placed on the food. However, if the utensil absorbed non-kosher meat or something similar, it is forbidden to heat it even to bake permissible food in it. This is his language, and the reason is that with the absorption of permissible food, a light heating that causes straw to burn on the outside is sufficient, as I have written above in Siman 452 and in Yoreh De'ah Siman 121. It is not evident that it is being done to make it kosher, and it appears as if it is being prepared for cooking. Therefore, he requires it to be placed on the food immediately after heating, so that it will appear as if one is only engaged in cooking. But with non-kosher absorption, a strong heating is required, such that sparks fly from it, as I wrote there, and it is evident to all that this is not for cooking but for making it kosher. Additionally, it seems to me another reason: when it is of permissible food, it is allowed to be handled, and at any moment one can cook with the previous permissible food, but he desires a different food. The heating is no worse than mere cleaning, desiring to clean the utensil, unlike when the utensil is non-kosher, even though it might be permissible to handle as it is suitable for placing cold food, once it heats up a bit, it is not suitable for anything, and therefore the heating is forbidden. (And the Magen Avraham wrote in Subsection 11, that from this it is evident that it is permitted to make kosher from meat to dairy and from dairy to meat, contrary to what people commonly say that it is forbidden, reasoning that if so, one would only have one utensil and always purify it and come to err. See there. And indeed it is a surprising thing: can we decree rulings on our own accord? Furthermore, in Shabbat 16b, regarding old impurity where the sages decreed something similar, they said it was because of the hedge for the waters of purification or other reasons. See there. But otherwise, it is completely permissible.)

And so it is forbidden to purify a vessel on Yom Tov if it is non-kosher, just as it is forbidden to heat it. I have seen it written that if one can use the water from the purification for some purpose, such as purifying by pouring, or if there is sixty times the amount of water relative to the prohibited substance – it is permitted to purify (Radbaz, Part 3, Siman 402). This is a reasonable argument. Similarly, if the vessel has not been used for a full day – the water is permitted. However, regarding the primary prohibition written by our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, concerning heating and purifying, the prohibition is because this is not food preparation but rather preparation for food preparation (Mordechai, end of Avodah Zarah). Therefore, if they became non-kosher yesterday – it is certainly forbidden, as it was possible to purify them yesterday. And even if they became non-kosher on Yom Tov, if he has another pot, it is also forbidden. But if he does not have another pot – this is considered preparation for food preparation that could not be done on the eve of Yom Tov. And even according to the Rambam, who explained that we do not rule this way, but an individual who does so for himself – it is permitted. Certainly, according to the Tur, who has been explained (this seems correct in my humble opinion).

And our Rabbi, the Rema, wrote in paragraph 5 that it is permitted to heat a spit that was used to roast meat that was not salted, and one wants to roast on it again on Yom Tov. Thus is his language, and it is like the case where the day was mixed up, where it was not possible to do it on the eve of Yom Tov (Darkei Moshe). Also, it does not seem to be a significant correction as in the case of koshering a pan (Magen Avraham, section 12), because according to the fundamental law, it does not need to be heated at all, as its absorption is as its emission, as I wrote in Yoreh De'ah, section 76. According to this, even if it was possible to do it on the eve of Yom Tov, it is permitted (there). One should not make a new hole in a barrel on Yom Tov. If it was not possible to do it on the eve of Yom Tov, it is permitted (there, section 13), but we do not instruct this way. Immersing a new vessel on Yom Tov is treated the same as on Shabbat, as explained above in section 323. Similarly, washing and scrubbing vessels on Yom Tov is like on Shabbat, as explained there.

Rambam wrote in Chapter 4, Law 17: A vessel that became impure on the eve of a festival – one does not immerse it on the festival, as a decree lest he delay it in its impurity. But if he needed to immerse the water within it – he immerses the vessel with its water and does not worry. Until here is his wording, meaning: it is necessary to purify the impure water by submerging it in the water of a mikvah, as this is like planting which nullifies the impurity. And this is certainly permitted, as it is considered essential for food preparation. Incidentally, he also immerses the vessel, since it is done in one act.

A vessel that was pure for terumah but impure for Kodesh due to the stringencies of Kodesh – it is permissible to immerse it for Kodesh on Yom Tov, because this is not considered a complete repair, since it is already pure, but an extra stringency was imposed for Kodesh. Similarly, with other stringencies that Kodesh has over terumah, and that terumah has over chullin, as explained in Chagigah (second and third chapters) – it is permissible to immerse them on Yom Tov for the reason explained. It appears to me that this applies to impurity of rabbinic origin, which does not require sunset. But if it requires sunset – it is obvious that it is forbidden to immerse it on Yom Tov, since it is not fit until the evening – it would be an unnecessary exertion on Yom Tov. (See Tosafot Chagigah 21a s.v. "the mourner," examine there thoroughly, and you will find it easy. And see Tosafot Beitzah 18a).

And the Rambam wrote (there): A vessel that became impure on Yom Tov – one may immerse it on Yom Tov. If the vessel became impure through impure liquids, which are a secondary level of impurity, on the eve of Yom Tov – one may immerse it on Yom Tov, since it is pure according to Torah law. And one may draw water with an impure bucket, and it becomes pure by itself. And a woman in a state of niddah who does not have clothes – she can immerse herself with her clothes. Until here are his words, and it is clear from his words that if it became impure on Yom Tov, even by a primary source of impurity – it is permitted to immerse it, and this is also implied in the Gemara there. And even though with a primary source of impurity it certainly requires waiting until evening (for purity), and if so, it would be a burden not needed for Yom Tov – one must say that he holds like Rashi wrote in Beitzah there (s.v. "secondary"), because it is fit to use for non-sacred purposes that do not require waiting until evening. However, the Tosafot raised a difficulty there: that for non-sacred purposes, immersion is not needed, see there. And it seems to me that the intention is for tithe which does not require waiting until evening and does require immersion, as it is taught in Negaim chapter fourteen (Mishnah 3). And we derive it in Yevamot (74b) from verses regarding a person, and presumably the same applies to vessels. According to this, there is no need to say what I wrote in the previous section that it refers to rabbinic impurity, for even with Torah-level impurity this can be the case. (See Sha'agat Aryeh, section 56, where he elaborates on the laws of immersing vessels on Shabbat and Yom Tov, and concludes with a prohibition, see there.)

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote in paragraph 7 that it is permissible to move muktzeh for the purpose of food preparation and Yom Tov joy. This is his wording. And indeed, our Rabbis, the Tosafists, wrote this in three places in Beitzah (8a) regarding moving the ashes of an oven, which are removed in order to bake a pastry; also regarding cleaning an oven and stove (28b); and also regarding a house full of fruits where a hole is made, allowing one to take from the place of the hole and move the muktzeh stones (31b). The Mordechai also wrote this. But in truth, these matters are puzzling: for the primary instances of muktzeh are on Yom Tov and regarding food preparation, such as in the case of finding white ones when black ones were designated, an egg laid on Yom Tov according to the opinion that the reason is muktzeh, fallen fruits, and fish caught on Yom Tov. The main principle of muktzeh is on Yom Tov, and according to the Rif and Rambam, it is stricter than on Shabbat. Some have written that in cases of great need, they did not decree muktzeh (Yam Shel Shlomo, chapter three, sign 21). These matters are puzzling: are fish and birds not of great necessity (Magen Avraham, small paragraph 15)? Some have differentiated between eating and moving (there). This too is puzzling, for it is explicitly forbidden to move an unprepared egg and birds. They have said other things about this, which were not accepted (see there in Magen Avraham and in the Gra, paragraph 16).

And in my humble opinion, this has a completely different intention. Certainly, in the case of muktzeh food, the sages prohibited moving it as well, as it is taught (Beitzah 3b): "An egg that was laid on Yom Tov – one may not move it…". However, if the food itself is not muktzeh, but through using the food some muktzeh would be affected, such as ashes of a stove preventing the baking of a pastry; or plaster that fell into an oven preventing the baking of bread; or that muktzeh stones are preventing the taking of fruits – the sages did not prohibit this, for the sake of the joy of Yom Tov, since the main food itself is not muktzeh. Similarly, if one has nothing to cover the blood except with muktzeh – it is forbidden to slaughter, as this is considered muktzeh in the essential act of eating since one is obligated to cover the blood, and it is impossible to slaughter without covering it. However, if he already slaughtered – it is permitted to cover it as I wrote in Siman 498, so as not to nullify the positive commandment of covering the blood; and what was prohibited, was already done. So too it is forbidden to cook and light a fire with muktzeh wood, as since the food cannot be made edible without muktzeh – it is considered as muktzeh in the food itself. This is not the case with fallen plaster, ashes of a stove, or muktzeh stones – they are not related to the preparation of the food, but rather prevent access to the food. Therefore, we are not concerned with the muktzeh, for the sake of the joy of Yom Tov. (And with this, all the difficulties in this matter are resolved, as are the words of Tosafot, Mordechai, and the Rema.)

One may rub ears of wheat on Yom Tov, rubbing them by hand when they are soft, even though this involves separating the edible part from the inedible, which is a derivative of threshing. However, this is considered an unusual form of threshing (Rashi 12b) when done by hand, and it is not prohibited on Yom Tov because it is for food preparation. Similarly, one may break open legumes on Yom Tov, which means to break the pods and remove the legumes. Although on Shabbat this requires a change in the usual method, as I wrote in Siman 319, on Yom Tov it does not. There are those who are stringent even on Yom Tov, requiring the rubbing to be done with a change, using the tips of the fingers (Magen Avraham, subsection 1, in the name of the Ra"n, see there), as on Shabbat this would also be forbidden according to this view. However, this is a minority opinion (and the Ra"n himself wrote that this is not the opinion of the Rif, see there). Now, since the sages said that one may break open legumes on Yom Tov, it is clear that this is forbidden on Shabbat. People are not careful about this, and I already wrote about this above in Siman 319, subsection 25, see there.

When they permitted this on Yom Tov, they only allowed it by hand, meaning to rub the grains lightly, little by little, with his hand; or with a small sieve or a small bowl, which are small utensils where one puts a little on one side and the food comes out from the other side, and the waste remains in the utensil. In these, one also rubs lightly, and it is not like the usual manner of threshing. But not with a large sieve or a large sifter, where one puts a lot, which would be considered threshing. And even with his hands, it is forbidden to scatter a lot on the table and to sort from it, because it appears like someone preparing for the next day (Rashi there). And the same applies to sorting legumes, as will be explained. And it is permitted to blow with all one’s strength.

Maimonides wrote at the end of the third chapter: Similarly, one who selects legumes on a festival may select in the usual manner, in his lap or with a dish. But not with a sieve, nor with a tray, nor with a basket. What are we discussing? When the food is more than the waste. But if the waste is more than the food, he selects the food and leaves the waste. And if the effort to separate the waste from the food is greater than the effort to separate the food from the waste, even if the food is more, he selects the food and leaves the waste. This is his wording, and this is its explanation: One selects the waste from the food in the usual selection manner, which is when the food is more, as the effort is minimal in separating the waste. But if the waste is more, he selects the food, as the effort is less than separating the waste. However, if the effort of the waste is greater, such as when the waste is very fine and the food is coarse, then even when the food is more, he selects the food. The general rule: we follow the one whose effort is less. And we also learn from his words that even if the waste is more than the food, the food is not nullified to the waste, so it is not entirely forbidden.

However, this is not the opinion of the Tur, for the Tur holds that when there is a large amount of waste, it is completely prohibited. And this is the language of the Tur: "One who separates legumes or other items, if there is more effort in selecting the food than the waste, such as when there is a larger amount of food, one separates in the usual manner to discard the waste. And if more effort is required to separate the waste, such as when the waste is fine, one takes the food and leaves the waste. And this is specifically when the food is greater in quantity than the waste... But if the waste is greater in quantity, it is prohibited even to move it, for the food is considered nullified by the majority. Nevertheless, almonds and peanuts that have been broken, and are still mixed with their shells, even though the waste is greater than the food, are permitted, because they are not called 'waste greater than the food,' since this is their usual manner, and it is like a protective covering for the fruit. This is not similar to bones and shells, since they have completely separated from the food." Thus far his language. And it is understood from his words that also almonds and peanuts, if they are not mixed with their shells, their law is like all other items: if the waste is greater, it is prohibited to move them, for since they are not mixed, they are no longer a protective covering for the fruit. And if so, they are like all other items, where the minority is nullified by the majority. But Rambam does not hold this nullification, because this is the way of all things, that the food is mixed with the waste. And sometimes the food is greater, and sometimes the waste is greater.

And the law is established according to the Rambam, that since this matter is rabbinic, when selecting in his lap or in a serving dish, we follow the lenient opinion. Furthermore, our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, only brought the opinion of the Rambam in paragraph 2, since in any case, we are lenient in many aspects of selecting on Yom Tov compared to Shabbat. For on Shabbat it is explained in Siman 319 that selecting waste is completely prohibited, but here we permit it when the effort is minimal. And on Shabbat, we only permit selecting food from waste if it is to be eaten immediately, not to be left for later in the day. But here we permit it even to be left for later in the day, as they did not require it to be eaten immediately. The Maggid Mishneh also wrote this, see there. This is what our teacher the Rema wrote at the beginning of paragraph 2: "One may select in his usual manner in his lap or in a serving dish if he wants to eat it later in the day." This is his language, meaning not for the next day or night, because that would be considered work for a weekday. But for the same day, it is permitted even if he does not eat it immediately. (And the Magen Avraham unnecessarily commented in subsection 2 that it should say: "even if he wants to eat it later in the day," see there. On the contrary, his intention is like our words, and it comes out accurately. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

And know that the opinion of the Rashba, of blessed memory, is that even on Yom Tov one needs to sort and eat immediately, just as on Shabbat. However, the Maggid Mishneh disagreed with him, and our Rabbi, the Rema, ruled according to him. And there are some of the great authorities who agreed with the Rashba (Taz, small paragraph 3), but the majority of the great authorities ruled according to the Maggid Mishneh. Nevertheless, one who fears God should be concerned with the Rashba's opinion and eat immediately after sorting (Eliyahu Rabbah, small paragraph 2), as it is ruled in the Sefer Tanya, and in Rabbeinu Yerucham, and it seems this way from the Mahari"l. (And see Magen Avraham, section 504, small paragraph 9, who was stringent like the Mahari"l; see there.)

Rabbi Moshe Isserles wrote at the end of paragraph 2: "And nuts and almonds that have been broken, but are still in their shells – the shells are not considered waste, since it is usual for them to be like this, and they are still mixed." So far his words. The commentators (Magen Avraham, small paragraph 4, and Taz, small paragraph 3) have questioned this, since he only brought the explanation of Rambam – there is no difference between them and other items, since he permits sorting even with a lot of waste. And only the Tur mentioned this, because according to him, when there is a lot of waste it is completely forbidden, he wrote that with nuts and almonds it is not so, but not according to Rambam's opinion. And some have written that even according to Rambam there is a practical difference, that with nuts and almonds one can sort in any manner one wishes (Yam Shel Shlomo). And certainly, even with them, one is obligated to sort in the manner that involves the least effort (Taz and Magen Avraham there). In my humble opinion, it seems that there is another intention in his words, that indeed with all food and waste – it is permitted to handle the waste when it needs to be sorted, but without this reason, they are certainly muktzeh. Therefore, he says that with nuts and almonds it is not so, because even if they are broken, as long as they have not been separated from the food – they still have the status of food, and are permitted to be handled even not at the time of sorting.

The Tur and the Shulchan Aruch write in section 3: One may not strain mustard using its strainer, nor sweeten it using a wooden coal. However, with metal – it is permitted. This is their language, meaning: sorting is prohibited on Yom Tov, whether by Torah law or by rabbinic decree, as it is with something that can be done before Yom Tov, according to the opinions explained in section 502. And this permission with legumes – we did not permit complete sorting, as we prohibited the use of a sieve or sifter; rather, with one's lap or a bowl, in such a manner there are also leniencies on Shabbat, and we were more lenient on Yom Tov as explained. However, in any event, complete sorting is prohibited even on Yom Tov. Therefore, one may not strain mustard using its strainer. And it is not only mustard; the same rule applies to all items; rather, it teaches us a significant point with mustard: that even though the waste is also fit for consumption, and therefore it is not complete sorting that would obligate a sin offering on Shabbat, nevertheless it is prohibited on Yom Tov, since it is sorted in its usual way using a strainer (see Shabbat 134a).

And the reason that one does not sweeten it with a wooden coal is because extinguishing the coal occurs during the sweetening process. But with iron – there is no extinguishing, and the same applies to other metals. And even though extinguishing is permitted for the purpose of food preparation, as is explained regarding meat on coals in the Gemara, where it resolves: "It is not possible there, but it is possible here." And Rashi explains there: With meat, it is impossible to prepare it from the day before the festival, as it is better on the day itself. But mustard will not be spoiled if sweetened on the eve of the festival, and therefore extinguishing is not permitted for it. And this way is the straightforward approach. The early authorities have different versions in the Gemara there, and thus some have written that the reason for the prohibition is because it is not universally necessary (the Maor). And some have written because it is like grinding wheat, which is forbidden on a festival (Ramban there). But Rashi's version and explanation are simpler (see Taz, subsection 5, and Magen Avraham, subsection 6). And know that since with metal there is no extinguishing, it is therefore permitted to place a heated spit into a drink when necessary (Magen Avraham, subsection 7).

And even though we forbade filtering mustard because of the prohibition of selecting, nevertheless, filtering dregs from wine or beer is not the same if what is filtered today is better than what was filtered on the eve of the festival. However, they said that one should not hang the strainer on a festival to filter the dregs because it resembles a weekday activity, and this can be done on the eve of the festival. But if the strainer is already hanging in its place, it is permitted to put the dregs in it to filter them. And if it was not hung on the eve of the festival, they permitted doing it in a roundabout way, meaning that one hangs it not for filtering but to put pomegranates in it (Shabbat 139b). One puts pomegranates in it, as that was their custom, and afterward puts the dregs in it. And why did they permit this subterfuge? Because, in principle, it is permitted, only because of the appearance of a weekday activity, and therefore they permitted this subterfuge. All this applies if the dregs from yesterday are not as good as those from today. But if there is no difference, it is entirely forbidden, like mustard, and the other laws of filtering on a festival are like those on Shabbat, as explained above in Siman 319, see there.

Our sages forbade (Shabbat 134a) making cheese on Yom Tov, as the formation of the cheese is considered like building. This is not only because it is not worse than what was made yesterday, but on the contrary, what was made yesterday is actually preferable. Cheese made the same day does not taste as good, and it is generally made for long-term use, which is akin to harvesting (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 11). Similarly, it is prohibited to make butter on Yom Tov. Even though butter made the same day might be slightly better, it still involves significant effort and is made for long-term use. It is forbidden even through a non-Jew (ibid., subparagraph 13, in the name of the Rivash). It is permitted to skim the fat floating on top, known as "smetana," even on Shabbat. However, when reaching the bottom of the fat, one should leave a bit of the fat with the whey (ibid.), as in this manner it is not considered selecting at all. This is only when it is needed to be eaten that day. But if one does this only to prevent spoilage, it is not to be done by oneself, only by a non-Jew (ibid.). Rabbeinu the Rema wrote in paragraph 5 that one does not set milk on Yom Tov, see there. His intention is not about pouring it into containers where it will naturally set, as is our custom, since there is no labor involved in that. Rather, his intention is about setting it with rennet (ibid.), like the Swiss and Dutch cheeses. This is certainly considered labor and is completely forbidden, contrary to those who are lenient in this matter (ibid., subparagraph 12).

One should not cut detached vegetables with scissors, as it is customary to cut with them from that which is attached, due to the appearance of the matter, as people might say that he cut them today from that which is attached. And one may prepare the kondos and the akaviyot, which are types of vegetables, even though there is effort involved in their preparation—it is still permissible because they will spoil if prepared the day before. And it is permitted to salt many pieces of radish on Yom Tov to eat them, even though on Shabbat it is forbidden in this manner. And there are those who are stringent regarding making many [pieces], as despite the fact that it is certainly permitted, since they would spoil if made the day before, still, since it is possible to salt a little at a time, one should not salt a lot at once. And there are those who are stringent also about letting them stay long in the salt; rather, he should dip them in salt and eat immediately (Taz, section 10), and this was the practice of the Maharil. And there is no reason for prohibition if it pleases him more when they stay in the salt, and the Maharil was stringent upon himself, or he did not like them staying in the salt.

And know that even though carrying is permitted on Yom Tov even not for a specific need, as I have written in Siman 498 in the name of the Rambam, that they did not restrict us regarding carrying, nevertheless, the Sages said that one should not carry large loads on Yom Tov because it resembles weekday activities, and one must make a change. How so? One who brings jugs of wine from one place to another should not bring them in a basket or a large container to carry four or five jugs as he does on a weekday, but rather he should carry them on his shoulder, or hold them in his hands in front of him one or two at a time. In this way, it is evident that he brought them for the needs of Yom Tov, and it will not be considered a weekday activity. This is specifically when he is carrying them from one place to another, as it is noticeable. Therefore, even though he has to make multiple trips, it cannot be done otherwise. But when he carries them from one corner to another or from one house to another within the same courtyard, it is permissible in any manner. And on the contrary, it is better to carry many at once to minimize the number of trips (Magen Avraham, section 15), for multiple trips are more of a burden than carrying a larger load. Similarly, one who carries straw should not sling the container behind him, as this is a weekday activity, but should carry it in his hand. Likewise, one should not bring wood using a rope, a large container, or a mat, but should bring it in a cloth, in his lap, or in his hands. And it seems to me that this is also true in a place where others can see. But in his own courtyard, it is better to minimize the number of trips, as I have written.

And similarly, loads that are usually carried with a pole – he should carry them on his back behind him. And those that are usually carried behind him – he should carry on his shoulder. And those that are usually carried on his shoulder – he should carry in his hands in front of him, or he should spread a cloth over them in a way that it does not lead to a concern of squeezing, such as if there is water, and anything similar in terms of changing the manner of carrying. The general principle is: that in carrying, one must change somewhat from how it is done on weekdays. However, if it is not possible, such as if he has invited many guests and needs to hurry to prepare – he may do as he does on weekdays, for there is no prohibition in this. And know that all of this applies when a person carries the load, but to place a load on an animal – it is completely forbidden to do so on Yom Tov. And although we explained in Siman Taf Tzadi Heh, Section 32 that there is no prohibition on a load on an animal on Yom Tov, nevertheless this is certainly considered a weekday activity. Also, he might come to drive the animal, and this is forbidden as I wrote there. The general principle is: a load on an animal for a person – is completely forbidden on Yom Tov, besides the prohibition of using animals.

We learned in the Mishnah (21b) that it is permissible to make a bonfire and warm oneself by it. Some say that the reason is because we say: since kindling a fire is permitted for a need, it is also permitted without a need (Ran). However, in truth, we do not need this reason, because anything that is for bodily need is considered in the category of food preparation. This is also explained by Rashi's commentary in the Gemara there, and by the Rambam as will be explained. This is the language of the Rambam in his commentary on the Mishnah: “Because what the Lord said ‘which shall be eaten by any person’ includes all bodily enjoyment.” I am puzzled that I did not find this law in the Rambam in all the laws of Yom Tov. And perhaps because he wrote in the first chapter, fourth law, that in all labors we do not say "since," except for carrying and kindling, and it is permitted to kindle even without any need at all — see there — if so, all the more so it is permissible to make a bonfire to warm oneself by it, for even without any need at all it is permitted.

It is permissible to heat water on Yom Tov to wash one's hands and feet, but not one's entire body. This is what is taught in the Mishnah there, and our Rabbis, the Tosafists, and several of the early authorities explained that the reason is that it must be something that is necessary for everyone, and this is only suitable for pampered individuals. However, washing one's hands and feet is necessary for everyone. They also explained this reasoning regarding the prohibition of incense, which will be explained in this section. No one has ever questioned this reasoning, and all the decisors agree that this is a definitive law.

We have already written in Siman 492, Section 19, that in the Rambam, this law is not found at all — that we require something that is suitable for all people. And the reason for the prohibition of washing one's entire body is due to the decree concerning bathhouses. And the prohibition of incense is due to extinguishing, as is evident from the Rif. And we explained there the reasoning in Section 20, that the Rif and the Rambam rejected this from the law, and it is permissible even if it is not suitable for all people. And this is explicitly proven in the first chapter of Ketubot, see there.

This is the language of Maimonides in the first chapter, law 16: Washing and anointing are included in the category of eating and drinking, and one may do them on Yom Tov, as it is stated: "Only that which every person must eat" – for everything that the body needs. Therefore, one may heat water on Yom Tov and wash his face, hands, and feet with it. But washing the entire body is prohibited due to the decree concerning bathhouses. However, water that was heated on the eve of Yom Tov – one may wash his entire body with it on Yom Tov, as they only decreed this on Shabbat. This is the end of his language. However, this is specifically outside of a bathhouse, but in a bathhouse – it is prohibited. But with water that was heated on Yom Tov – it is prohibited to wash the entire body, even limb by limb. Water that was heated on the eve of Yom Tov – one may wash the entire body at once, such as by entering a bathtub or something similar. But Rabbi Yitzhak of the Tosafists and the Rosh ruled that washing the entire body is prohibited even with water that was heated on the eve of Yom Tov, just as on Shabbat. And this is the custom. The rule for the hot springs of Tiberias is the same as on Shabbat, as I wrote in Siman 326. (And it seems to me that they follow their view: for Rabbi Yitzhak and the Rosh, who hold that water heated on Yom Tov is a biblical prohibition because it is not equal for every person – they decreed that water heated on the eve of Yom Tov is prohibited due to Yom Tov. This is not the case for the Rif and the Rambam, who hold that water heated on Yom Tov is prohibited only due to the decree concerning bathhouses – it is impossible to decree against water heated on the eve of Yom Tov due to Yom Tov, as this would be a decree upon a decree.)

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote in Section 2 that it is permissible to bathe a baby in water that was heated by a Jew on Yom Tov. However, it is forbidden to heat water for the baby’s sake, even by a non-Jew. But when the water is needed for cooking or washing dishes, it is permissible to increase the amount of water for the baby. These are his words. This means: even for a baby, where it is critical for him, it is forbidden to heat water unless one is heating it for washing the face, hands, and feet, in which case it is permissible to bathe the baby. But for the baby alone, it is forbidden, even by a non-Jew. Only when the water is needed for cooking or washing dishes is it permissible to increase the amount of water for the baby, and only in one instance. And it appears to me that this applies when it is not so critical for the baby. But if it is critical, it is obvious that it is permissible to heat water for him, because for a baby, it is considered a necessity for everyone. And even according to the Rif and the Rambam, the decree regarding the bathhouse does not apply here, but rather, it is not so critical for the baby, and only if there is already prepared water is it permissible to bathe his entire body, for they did not make a decree regarding his bathing. And indeed, some say that nowadays, since even on weekdays we do not bathe the baby every two or three days, it is forbidden to bathe his entire body on Yom Tov (Magen Avraham, small section 5).

To pour hot water into a mikveh now, when women are unable to go to a cold water mikveh — it is clear that this is considered a necessity for everyone. Additionally, there is no decree concerning a bathhouse, and it is permitted on Yom Tov. However, this is when they heat the water at night and pour it into the mikveh. But to heat on the first day of Yom Tov, for women to go at night — it is clearly forbidden, as even preparation from the first day to the second is forbidden, and certainly a Torah-prohibited labor is not allowed. However, through a non-Jew, since it cannot be done otherwise, as if not, they will not go to immerse today — it is a rabbinic prohibition of instructing a non-Jew in a place of a communal mitzvah, and one can rely on the opinion of Baal HaItur, which Rabbeinu the Rama brought earlier in Siman 276, that it is permitted to tell a non-Jew to light a candle for the Shabbat meal, see there. And although we do not rely on this leniency, as I wrote there, nevertheless, in a situation where the mitzvah of procreation would be nullified, and usually the non-Jew who is with the bathhouse attendant does it on his own — it is necessary to rely on this. It is good for the bathhouse attendant to take some of the water for washing his utensils on Yom Tov, and it seems that this is the custom. And to heat for washing at the beginning of her counting, and she wears white garments — it is certainly not proper, for she can wash in cold water or use water heated for drinking, and similar cases.

Rabbi Moses Isserles (the Rema) wrote in Section 1 that some say it is forbidden to heat a winter house on Yom Tov, because sometimes the cold is not severe and it is only for the pampered, and it is like a bathhouse and incense which are forbidden. However, the custom is to be lenient. Until here is his language. And in truth, there is no reason for this stringency, for what matter is not equal for everyone? Indeed, cold is certainly felt by everyone. And regarding the levels of cold, if the natures are not the same, if we call this "not equal for everyone" – we would forbid drinking hot tea and coffee on Yom Tov, as they are only for the pampered. Rather, it is certain that since the essence of drinking is equal for everyone – we do not delve into details, and it is the same with cold. And it is a daily occurrence on Passover and Sukkot, when the weather is cold, that we heat the winter house’s stoves on Yom Tov.

Although it is forbidden to immerse utensils on Yom Tov due to the prohibition of fixing a utensil, as I have written in Siman 509, nevertheless, a person is permitted to immerse themselves from impurity on Yom Tov, because it appears like mere cooling off. And it is also permitted on Shabbat, as I have written in Siman 326. As for washing in cold water, it is obviously permitted on Yom Tov, for it is also permitted on Shabbat. However, on Shabbat, one must sprinkle the hair when coming out of the river, so as not to carry in a karmelit, as I have written there. But on Yom Tov, this is not necessary, though one must be careful not to come to wringing, neither with their hair, nor with their garment, nor with their towel, or similar items.

It is prohibited to make incense, which means to scatter various spices on coals, whether for the purpose of smelling or to scent the house or utensils. The reason, as written by the early authorities, is because it is not something equally necessary for everyone, but rather for the pampered. However, if one burns incense to impart a good fragrance to fruits to improve their edibility, it is permitted even if he scatters the spices on a coal of wood that extinguishes, for extinguishing is permitted for food preparation, as I have written several times. Additionally, it ultimately results in kindling. There is no concern of creating fragrance, as the intent is not to create fragrance but to make food fit for consumption. Even if the food is good without this, but he wants it to be better, it is permitted, for the Torah did not define the manner of our eating.

And the Rambam in Chapter 4, Halacha 6 wrote: "One may not smoke incense on Yom Tov, because it extinguishes, even if it is for fragrance. And all the more so to fumigate the house and utensils, which is forbidden. However, it is permitted to smoke under fruits..., just as it is permitted to roast meat on the fire...". These are his words. And behold, he did not write about incense the reason of 'equally for all people,' because the Rambam does not hold this law as I wrote in Section 3, but rather he wrote the reason of extinguishing. The explanation of his words is: Even though for actual food, like meat and fruits, extinguishing was permitted for the sake of food preparation, but for something that is merely for fragrance – the Sages did not want to permit it.

And know that there are those who wanted to forbid smoking tobacco on Yom Tov because it is not suitable for everyone. However, many disagree and permit it explicitly. A clear proof for this is from what the Tosafot wrote in Shabbat (39b, s.v. "they permit", see there) that sweating is considered something suitable for everyone because it is for the health of the body, see there. Similarly, smoking tobacco for those accustomed to it is for the health of the body, to digest food and to expel excess. And because there is also pleasure involved, does that make it worse? (Pnei Yehoshua there). 

And there is someone who wrote in this manner: "I am accustomed to drinking tobacco on Yom Tov, as is the custom of the world for health, and especially today it is truly suitable for everyone" (Pri Megadim in this siman, Taz section 2). And there is someone who wrote that he refrained from smoking, and a pious person told him that he was not doing well because he was preventing himself from the joy of Yom Tov (Sha'arei Teshuva section 5 in the name of Chacham Tzvi).

And aside from all this, I say that it is not comparable to incense, which is not suitable for everyone but only for the delicate. But tobacco is primarily for coarse people, like villagers who smoke a lot. And the delicate ones, there are many who cannot even tolerate the smell. And if there is also good tobacco with a pleasant smell – it is a minority, and most of it has a simple and thick smell. Should we forbid it because there is some with a good smell? If so, we should also forbid fruits that have a good smell. And those who on the first day do not smoke, and on the second day they do – they are disrespecting the second day of Yom Tov.

And there are those who want to forbid it because of extinguishing, and it is known that there is no extinguishing unless one presses the coal. Furthermore, on Yom Tov it is actually better to smoke from a flame, even from a candle, and even one who is careful to smoke from a candle all year finds it easier to light on Yom Tov from a candle flame, for with sulfur wood it is certainly forbidden. Only today, with the proliferation of cigarettes, one should prepare them before Yom Tov, for on Yom Tov it is certainly forbidden to make them, as this is considered making a utensil.

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (the Rema) writes in Section 4 that it is forbidden to sprinkle perfumed water on garments, because it imparts a new scent to them. This is his wording. And even though it is permissible to crush herbs, as I wrote in Siman 325, this is because they already have a scent, and by crushing them, the scent is intensified. This is not the case with a garment, which initially has no scent, and thus scent is newly created. Even if the garment already had a scent, it is forbidden to add more, since the scent is not inherent to it, and thus a new scent is being added (Magen Avraham, subsection 11). However, if an etrog (citron) was placed on a garment and then removed, it is permitted to return it, because nothing new is being added (ibid.). Some people add scent to water. If the water is for drinking, to make it more pleasant to drink, it is permitted. But if it is for the sake of the scent, it is completely forbidden. Some people add scent to the water used for the priestly washing, and this is completely forbidden (ibid., Taz, subsection 8). Nowadays, we have not heard of this custom.

It is written: "However, that which every soul may eat, that alone may be prepared for you." The word "for you" is superfluous, and we derive from it: "for you" – and not for a non-Jew, meaning that work on Yom Tov was not permitted for the sake of a non-Jew. Therefore, it is forbidden to cook or bake for a non-Jew. Nevertheless, one does not receive lashes, because we say: since guests might arrive – it is considered suitable for them, as the Rambam wrote in the first chapter, law 15. And why don't we say that since it was permitted for a need – it is also permitted for a non-need? According to the Rambam's view, this is not a question at all, as he holds that we only say "since" regarding carrying and kindling, as I wrote there. And according to the Tosafot, who require some need for a Jew – it is also not difficult. And even according to Rashi's view, that we say "since" even without any need at all, in any case, when one explicitly does it for a non-Jew, which the Torah explicitly forbids – it is not applicable to say "since." And so it is regarding baking from Yom Tov to a weekday, as I wrote in Siman 492, Section 18; see there.

For this reason, our sages said (Ketubot 93b): One may invite a non-Jew on Shabbat, but one may not invite him on Yom Tov, due to the decree that he might cook extra for him. For on Shabbat it is permitted to invite him to one's table, as it is not relevant to say that he will perform labor for him. But on Yom Tov, since it is customary to bake and cook, there is concern that he might cook extra food for him. The Rosh, of blessed memory, deduced from the language "invite" that this is because when one invites him, it is assumed that he is an important person and desires to honor him, and therefore there is concern that he might cook extra for him. However, his servant and maidservant, as well as a messenger sent to him, and also when the non-Jew comes on his own – it is permitted to eat with him. We are not concerned that he might cook extra for him, since he did not invite them and does not desire to honor them, there is no concern for this issue.

And this is the language of the Rambam in the first chapter, law 13: "One does not invite... but if the non-Jew comes on his own, he eats with them what they are eating, for it has already been prepared." Until here is his language. And the Tur objected to this, saying it does not seem correct, for even if it has already been prepared, there is still concern that they might increase the amount for his sake if he is important and it is appropriate to do so. Rather, one should say to him: "If what we have prepared for ourselves is sufficient for you, come and eat." Until here is his language, and in truth, so it is in the Gemara there. However, the Rambam holds that saying this does not make a difference, for what benefit is it to not add for him if he says so, and what detriment is there if he does not say so? The main point of the permission is that since they did not invite him, we do not worry that they will increase for his sake, because the non-Jew will not be offended by the lack of increase for him, since he was not invited and did not know he would come. And what we find in the Gemara, that they said to him "if what we have prepared...", this is for the sake of appeasement and proper manners, to say to him and to ask for forgiveness for not honoring him appropriately (and so wrote the Taz, subsection 4).

It is specifically forbidden to invite him to his home. But to send to the non-Jew to his home - it is permitted, because in this case we do not worry that he will increase in work for him, since he is not present and he is not obligated according to etiquette to honor him. And the sending should be done by a non-Jew if it is a place where carrying is forbidden on Shabbat. And even though carrying is entirely permitted on Yom Tov, this is only for the needs of a Jew (Siman 3). And if it is a place where carrying is permitted - it is allowed to send also by a Jew, as there is no prohibition of invitation in this (ibid.). And if it is due to exertion - the Torah did not forbid this exertion on Yom Tov, for even on Shabbat it is permitted to give food to any person and to go and deliver the food to him. And even in a place where carrying is forbidden, if it is not a complete public domain - it is permitted to send on Yom Tov by a Jew (Magen Avraham, Siman 2). And see what I wrote in Siman 11.

There is an opinion that says that the prohibition to invite a non-Jew on a festival applies before one has prepared all the needs of the meal. But after one has prepared, and it is close to the meal – it is permitted to invite him (there in the name of the Tania). However, this situation is only applicable when it was not originally intended to invite him, for if it was intended – it is obvious that it is forbidden, as there is a concern that one might add extra for him. This situation is uncommon, because logically, if one invites him before the meal, how is it possible that an hour earlier he did not have the intention to invite him? Therefore, it refers to a case where the non-Jew comes close to the meal, at which point one asks and invites him, and initially, there was no intention to invite him at all. (And with this, the words of the Magen Avraham there are understood, see there. The Machatzit Hashekel and the Pri Megadim had difficulty with his words, and according to what I have written, it makes sense. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

We need to understand how we permitted that one's servant and maidservant are allowed to eat with him—how did we permit this? After all, it is necessary to increase the amount of food for them. And if we say that it is allowed to increase the amount in the same pot, because it cooks better when the pot is full, as I wrote in Siman 503—if so, we should also permit inviting a non-Jew and increase the amount in the same pot for him as well. But the truth is that when it comes to inviting, we are concerned that one might increase the amount in another pot for the non-Jew, because he wants to honor him and will make him other delicacies. But for one's servant and maidservant, we are not concerned about this. This is the intention of our master, the Rema, who wrote in Section 1 that it is permitted to increase the amount for one's servant and maidservant in the same pot in which he cooks for himself. But for other non-Jews, it is forbidden in any case. Thus far his words. And his intention is like ours. (And behold, in the Beit Yosef and the Darkei Moshe, they raised the question that some permit increasing the amount for a non-Jew in the same pot, and some forbid it. And see Magen Avraham, subsection 3, and Taz, subsection 5. And according to what I wrote, both are true, for it is certainly permitted. Nevertheless, it is forbidden lest one increase the amount in another pot. This is regarding invitation, but not for one's servant and maidservant. And this is also the intention of the Magen Avraham. And what he wrote here regarding the opinion that it is possible to appease him, see there—in my humble opinion, it does not apply here. And see Taz, subsection 4, who concludes that if he comes on his own and is given to eat, it is permitted, but if he is invited when he comes, it is forbidden, see there. This applies when he comes a long time before the meal is prepared. But close to the meal, it is permitted, as I wrote in the previous section. Analyze this and you will find it easy.)

The Rambam wrote in the first chapter, law 14: "Dough that is half owned by a Jew and half by a non-Jew – it is forbidden to bake it, because it is possible to divide the dough. [This is similar to] soldiers who gave flour to a Jew to make bread for them on a festival day. If, when the bread is given from it to a child, they do not mind – it is permitted to bake it for them on the festival day, as every loaf is fit for a child." This is the language of the Rambam, and it is also found in the Gemara (21a). Rashi explained that these two laws contradict each other, for since it is possible to divide them – it is forbidden. And the Tosafot wrote that they do not contradict, for with dough that is half owned by a Jew – it is indeed possible to divide it before baking, but with the soldiers' dough, which is theirs, it is impossible for the Jew to divide it before baking, as they would not give it to him. And only after baking, when giving it to a child, they are not particular. Thus, it is necessary to bake all the bread, and it is permitted for the portion that the Jew eats. This is also the opinion of the Rambam, who wrote both laws. And this reasoning is also written by the Ran and the Maggid Mishneh. See there.

However, in the Gemara there at the end of the discussion it says: "And this is in disagreement with Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, who said: One should not invite a non-Jew on a festival, lest he increase [the amount of food prepared] for him." Rashi and the Rif explained that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi disagrees with the ruling regarding the soldiers that was explained. Therefore, the Tur actually ruled regarding the soldiers that it is forbidden; see there. The Rambam ruled on both matters, and the Raavad agreed with him, that indeed there is no comparison: inviting a non-Jew is similar to dough where half belongs to a Jew, which can be divided beforehand, and similarly, when inviting, one can cook his portion, which is not the case with the soldiers, as I have written. They wrote that the Rambam did not include the phrase "and this is in disagreement with Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi" in his version of the Gemara, or he included it and explained it differently, as the Maggid Mishneh wrote there. Some of our Rabbis wrote that even the Rif agrees with this, but explains that in the case of the soldiers, the Jew could have taken his portion even before baking (Ran there). According to this, there is no practical disagreement. But the Tur did not hold this way, as he wrote that there is a dispute about this; see there. And our master, the Beit Yosef, in section 2 ruled simply like the Rambam, and so is the law.

There is an opinion that permits giving to slaves and maidservants from what one cooks in the same pot, but with bread, it is forbidden to increase the amount of bread in the oven for them, as each loaf is considered a separate act of labor (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 3, in the name of Yam Shel Shlomo). And certainly, this is correct, as it is explained similarly in Siman 503 that there is a distinction between cooking and baking for this reason; see there. One should only feed them from the leftover bread that he baked for himself. However, it has already been explained there that generally, we also bake on the eve of Yom Tov. And Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote in paragraph 1 that if a Jew bakes in a non-Jew's oven and needs to give the non-Jew one loaf for this, he should not designate one loaf before baking that he will give this loaf, because if he does so, he is baking this loaf for the non-Jew. Rather, he should bake without designation and afterward give him one of them. This is his language, and it is straightforward.

It is forbidden to bake or cook for an animal on Yom Tov, as it is written "for you" – and not for an animal. This is the ruling of the Rif, the Rambam, the Rosh, the Tur, the Shulchan Aruch, and the majority of the poskim. Therefore, even though there are those who ruled according to the opinion that permits it in the Gemara (the Maor and the Raavia, as the Tur wrote) – the halacha is not in accordance with this view. Consequently, it is necessary to caution women not to heat water on Yom Tov for the sake of an animal. This prohibition has greatly spread due to their lack of knowledge, as we have seen and heard. Therefore, they must be warned. They can do it in a permissible way, which is by heating water for the purpose of washing dishes, and from this water, they can give to the animals. It is permitted to increase the amount in the pot that one is cooking for oneself for the sake of the animals, and there is no difference whether one has something to give to the animals or not, for in all cases, it is permitted to increase in that pot.

And just as it is forbidden to cook for an animal, so too it is forbidden to carry for it through a public domain. However, through a karmelit it is permitted, as we do not impose rabbinic restrictions on carrying since carrying is entirely permitted on a festival, as I have written several times. Similarly, it is forbidden to knead bran for birds, except with a change. However, it is permitted to carry food and place it before them, as it is also permitted on Shabbat for those whose sustenance depends on you. And specifically if it is suitable for their consumption. But if it is not suitable, it is forbidden, as it is considered muktzeh; even though it can be made suitable, nevertheless in its current state it is muktzeh. There are those who are stringent even if it can be eaten with difficulty (see Magen Avraham, subsection 5). This is not comparable to a karmelit where we were lenient, as I have written, regarding carrying. (And the difficulty raised by Taz in subsection 8 requires further study, see Eliyah Rabbah.)

An egg that was laid on a Yom Tov – it is forbidden to touch it, meaning to move it. That is to say, even though muktzeh is permitted to touch, as I wrote in Siman 308, nevertheless, an egg which is round – touching it is considered moving it, because it is impossible not to cause it to wobble. And this is what our teacher, the Rema, wrote in Section 1 regarding the prohibition of touching it – meaning moving it, that is, touching it is considered moving it (and so understood the Magen Avraham in Subsection 2). And there is someone who understood that his intention was to say that only moving it is forbidden, but touching it is permitted, and he objected to this (Taz in Subsection 1). But this is not the case. And there is someone who holds that even touching without moving, if it is for the purpose of the muktzeh, is forbidden, and this is clarified in Siman 311, see there.

And since it is forbidden to touch it, all the more so it is forbidden to eat it. Thus we learn in the Mishnah at the beginning of Beitzah that an egg laid on a festival may not be eaten. The reason for this matter: it is not only in the case of a chicken designated for laying eggs, which would be considered muktzeh and nolad (newly created), but even in the case of a chicken designated for eating, which is not muktzeh—nevertheless, it is forbidden for another reason, as it is written: "And they shall prepare that which they bring." We derive from this that a weekday prepares for Shabbat, and a weekday prepares for a festival, but a festival does not prepare for Shabbat, and Shabbat does not prepare for a festival. The sages established that any egg laid today was completed yesterday. According to this, when Shabbat and a festival are adjacent to each other, and an egg is laid on Shabbat following a festival or on a festival following Shabbat, it means that Shabbat prepared for the festival or the festival prepared for Shabbat, and the egg is prohibited by Torah law due to the prohibition of preparation. Therefore, our sages decreed that this applies to every festival because of the festival following Shabbat and to every Shabbat because of the Shabbat following a festival (Gemara at the beginning of Beitzah). Consequently, since it is forbidden to eat, it is also forbidden to handle according to those who hold that muktzeh applies on festivals, as anything not suitable for the festival is considered muktzeh. (And the Magen Avraham at the end of subsection 1 wrote the reason for the prohibition of handling it in the name of the Rashal: because of "lo plug" (no distinctions), see there. And it requires investigation why this was necessary. And in Siman 515 he himself wrote as we have, as the Machatzit HaShekel wrote, see there.)

According to this, on a Yom Tov that follows Shabbat and a Shabbat that follows Yom Tov, the prohibition is from the Torah. On a regular Shabbat and Yom Tov, the prohibition is rabbinic due to a decree, as I have written. One should not ask, therefore, that if an egg is laid on Shabbat or Yom Tov, it should not be eaten the next day on a weekday because the Shabbat or Yom Tov prepared it for the weekday. For if its completion were considered preparation, how much more so its laying. However, this is not a question, because the truth is that its laying is not considered preparation. The proof is that if it were otherwise, an egg laid on Yom Tov before Shabbat would be prohibited on Shabbat due to preparation, and we do not find this in the Gemara, except that they are considered one sanctity regarding an egg, not because of preparation which is a Torah prohibition. Similarly, an egg laid on Shabbat before Yom Tov is not prohibited on Yom Tov due to preparation by Torah law, but because they are considered one sanctity. The reason for this is that preparation is only called what was created in the world, not what emerged into the world. For it was already prepared before, and any egg laid today—its creation was completed yesterday.

However, in truth, regarding a weekday, we do not need this. For necessarily we must say that for a weekday, the concept of preparation does not apply at all. Otherwise, an egg that was laid on a Sunday would be forbidden, because it was completed on the previous day, and it would be as if Shabbat prepared for a weekday. Similarly, an egg laid on the day after a festival would be forbidden. Therefore, our Rabbis wrote that a weekday meal is not significant, and it is not appropriate to say that it involves preparation (Rashi and Tosafot at the beginning of Beitzah).

If this egg got mixed with even a thousand [other eggs] - they are all forbidden, and it is not nullified, because something that can become permitted is not nullified, even by a rabbinic prohibition. And all the more so according to those who hold that an egg is considered an item that is counted and therefore cannot be nullified. However, most decisors do not hold this way, as I wrote in Yoreh De'ah at the beginning of Siman 110, see there. And even if there is a doubt whether it was laid on Yom Tov or on a weekday - it is also forbidden. And even if this doubt got mixed with a thousand [other eggs]. And all this is because it is something that can become permitted, since at night it will be permitted. It can be said that on an ordinary Yom Tov it is permitted, as it becomes a double doubt in a rabbinic matter. For it is a double doubt: a doubt if it was laid on Yom Tov, and if you say it was on Yom Tov - perhaps it is not the one we took from the mixture. But on a Yom Tov that follows Shabbat - it is a double doubt in a Torah matter. However, in Yoreh De'ah there it is explained that any double doubt where one doubt is about the item itself and one doubt is about the mixture - it is not called a double doubt, see there. And perhaps in rabbinic matters even this is considered a double doubt. See Yoreh De'ah Siman 102 and Siman 110 (see Magen Avraham subsection 4). And see what I wrote in Siman 498.

Rabbeinu Beit Yosef writes in section 3: An egg that was laid on Yom Tov and was cooked accidentally with meat and a dish, if there is sixty times [the volume of] the egg against it – everything is permitted except for the egg. But if it was used to color the dish or something similar, since it is used for appearance and taste – it is not nullified. Thus is his language. And the reason why sixty helps is because in a case of a non-like kind, even something that has a permitted use is nullified in sixty, as I wrote in Yoreh De'ah, section 102. And they challenged him: Why do we need sixty? After all, the egg does not impart any taste at all, as I wrote in Yoreh De'ah, section 86, that the liquid from eggs is merely water (Taz, subsection 3). However, his intention is when it was cooked peeled, meaning that first it was cooked and peeled, and then cooked with the dish while the egg was whole, then it requires sixty as explained in Yoreh De'ah there. And there in section 102, Rabbeinu Rema wrote that the taste is nullified even in something that has a permitted use. Therefore, even if it was cooked with eggs, which is of like kind – it is also nullified (Magen Avraham, subsection 6).

And that which he wrote that for appearance and taste it is not nullified, meaning that even in a non-like kind, it is considered like its kind and is not nullified in something that has a permissible alternative, specifically regarding appearance and taste. But without appearance, it is nullified even if it affects the taste, even though it comes to improve the pot (there, subsection 7). And it seems clear that if by the evening the dish will spoil, it is nullified. For it is a great rule regarding something that has a permissible alternative, that it is not called "has a permissible alternative" unless it will not spoil, as I wrote in Yoreh De'ah there. And know that it is permissible to cover the egg with a utensil, for we hold that a utensil can be moved for something that cannot be moved, as I wrote in Siman 310. As long as one is careful that the utensil does not touch it, for if it touches it, it will shake it.

Two Yom Tovs (festival days) of the Diaspora: if an egg was laid on the first day, it is permitted on the second day, for one of them is certainly a weekday. But on Rosh Hashanah, if an egg was laid on the first day, it is prohibited on the second day, because it is considered as one long sanctity (kedusha arichta). Similarly, if Shabbat and Yom Tov are adjacent to each other, if an egg was laid on one, it is prohibited on the other. And even though we hold that they are two distinct sanctities, and preparation (hachanah) does not apply to laying as I have written, nevertheless, rabbinically it is prohibited because of preparation. This means that since it is rabbinically prohibited on the first day, if you permit it on the second day, it would appear that the first day prepared for the second and not for itself (Ran there), and Shabbat and Yom Tov do not prepare for each other. Therefore, this is also considered a kind of preparation. If an egg was laid on Shabbat, and the Yom Tov of the Diaspora falls on Sunday and Monday, it is permitted on the second day if it was laid on Shabbat. Similarly, if Yom Tov precedes Shabbat on Thursday and Friday, if it was laid on Thursday, it is permitted on Shabbat. However, on Rosh Hashanah in such a scenario, it is prohibited all three days. (And regarding why we do not say on Yom Tov of the Diaspora that since it was set aside at twilight... – see what I wrote in Siman 438, Paragraph 5).

An egg that mostly emerged before Yom Tov, and then returned to the hen’s body, and was later laid on Yom Tov – is permitted, because once it mostly emerged, it is considered as born. Therefore, even if one checked the hen's nest before Yom Tov close to nightfall and did not find an egg, and the next morning he found an egg – it is permitted, because our Sages established that a hen does not lay eggs at night. Therefore, it must have laid the egg before nightfall and it was not found, or it mostly emerged and returned. And our Sages said that this applies to a hen that lays eggs from a male. But a hen that lays eggs from the heat of the ground – can lay eggs even at night. However, if there is a male rooster within sixty houses of the hen, and there is no river without a bridge interrupting – we attribute everything to the rooster. But if it is farther than sixty houses, or there is a river without a bridge – it is prohibited if one checked the day before close to nightfall and did not find an egg. But if he did not check – even in this case it is permitted, because we assume it was laid the day before, as most hens lay eggs during the day even without a male. This applies if he checked during the day. But if he checked afterwards – in any case it is prohibited, because perhaps it was laid today. And even if there is doubt – as has been explained, doubt is prohibited (all this is in Beitzah 7b).

Therefore, it is permitted to take eggs from a non-Jew on the first night of Yom Tov, because it is certain that they were laid during the day. Similarly, on the second night of the two Yom Tov days of the diaspora. However, it is not permitted on the second night of Rosh Hashanah, nor on the second night when Shabbat and Yom Tov are adjacent to one another, due to the reasons that have been explained. 

If a non-Jew brings eggs on the first day of Yom Tov and casually mentions that they were laid the previous day, it is permissible to rely on him, since he does not enhance the value of his merchandise by this, as eggs laid on the same day are considered better. Unless he knows that it is forbidden for a Jew to use eggs laid on that day, in which case he is not believed, as he might say so to sell his eggs (Magen Avraham, small paragraph 11). 

If the eggs belong to a Jew, and he casually mentions that they were laid the previous day, he is believed even if he knows the law, since he has no personal interest in the matter. Nevertheless, some prohibit this. A similar case is discussed in Yoreh De'ah, section 69, regarding a non-Jew who says he salted the meat, and it is explained there (ibid).

On Shabbat and Yom Tov that are adjacent to each other, since the prohibition is due to Torah-level preparation - it is obvious that he is not believed when speaking casually. For in matters of Torah law, we do not rely on his words, except in the case of a woman whose husband died, as explained in Even HaEzer, Siman 17, but not in other matters. Therefore, he is not believed on the second day. However, on Rosh Hashanah, he is believed, as it is a rabbinic matter. Nevertheless, if the circumstances indicate that the eggs were already laid, such as there being a large number of eggs with him - it is possible to rely on him even on Shabbat and Yom Tov. And most of the egg sellers are selling eggs that were already laid (see Magen Avraham, Section 13).

The one who slaughters a chicken on Yom Tov and finds in it fully formed eggs—they are permitted. Even on a Yom Tov that falls after Shabbat, since as long as they have not come out, it is not considered "preparation," because they have not yet been fully completed; they are not fit to produce chicks, and their taste is not as good as an egg that has come out (see there, subsection 14), and they are merely like one of the organs of the chicken. A chick that is born on Yom Tov is forbidden. If it is born on Shabbat, it is forbidden on the Yom Tov that follows it. So wrote the Tur in the name of his brother, that this too is called "preparation," because while in its shell it is not fit for eating at all, see there. Meaning: Even though a calf that is born on Yom Tov is permitted if its months have been completed, as I wrote in Siman 498, nevertheless, a chick that is born on Yom Tov is forbidden. For the calf is prepared by virtue of its mother in the act of slaughtering, but the chicken in its shell is not fit even for a dog. And it is considered complete muktzeh even for those who hold that muktzeh is permitted on Yom Tov, as this is like dried figs and raisins. Consequently, since it is forbidden on Yom Tov, if you permit it on the following Shabbat, it turns out that Yom Tov has prepared for Shabbat, since it was not permitted for itself but was permitted for Shabbat, and this is rabbinic preparation. This is similar to the preparation of an egg in subsection 8, which is rabbinic. There are those who want to say that this is a biblical preparation (Taz, subsection 11). The main point is as I wrote, and this resolves all the difficulties raised regarding this matter. (This is also implied in Bach. See Beit Yosef, Taz there, and Magen Avraham subsection 15, who worked to resolve the difficulties. According to what I wrote, everything fits well. Examine it and you will find it easy.)

It has already been clarified that extinguishing a fire is only permitted for the sake of food preparation, such as roasting meat on coals, where it cannot be done in any other way. However, extinguishing a fire not for the sake of food preparation at all is prohibited by Torah law. Extinguishing for the sake of food preparation utensils — when it was not possible to do it on the eve of the festival — we follow Rabbi Yehuda’s opinion that it is permitted, but we do not instruct this way, as I wrote in Siman 498, and we have explained this more extensively in Siman 529. There is a difference between the Rambam's approach and the Tur's approach. The Rambam ruled in all these cases that it is prohibited, because we do not instruct this way. The Tur ruled it is permitted, but wrote that we do not instruct this way. Our Rabbi, the Beit Yosef, follows the Rambam's approach, and our Rabbi, the Rema, follows the Tur's approach, see there.
