And in this very matter of not instructing this way, it applies only in two cases: scraping a knife and extinguishing for intimacy. Only in these cases is it completely prohibited, for the reason we explained there. And with this, the words of our Rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, in paragraph 1, will be understood as will be explained with the help of Heaven.

And this is the language of Rabbeinu Beit Yosef: It is forbidden to extinguish a fire on Yom Tov, even if one sees their house burning, as long as there is no danger to life. One may not extinguish a burning log even to prevent the house or a pot from becoming smoky, or for the sake of marital relations. This is his language. Now, extinguishing a fire—it is certainly forbidden even according to the Tur, since it does not involve food preparation but only financial loss. Only if the burning house would also consume prepared food and drink does it then fall under the category of food preparation. One may not extinguish a burning log even if it would cause the pot to become smoky, because this is considered food preparation, nevertheless, it is forbidden because the ruling is not given as such. The same applies to marital relations. And we have already written in Siman 528 that even according to this opinion, when an individual acts for themselves, they are not reprimanded since the law follows Rabbi Yehuda; see there.

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote: "Some say that this applies specifically if it is possible to save the pot without extinguishing the fire. But if it is not possible to save or cook the pot in another manner, except by extinguishing the fire, it is permitted to extinguish it. And this seems to me to be the primary opinion. Similarly, in the case of a house: if the house will be burned and there will be no place for him to eat there, and he will lose his meal, it is permitted to extinguish the fire. But if he has another house where he can eat, it is forbidden to extinguish on account of financial loss." Thus are his words. And this is according to the Tur, that preparatory activities (machshirei ochel nefesh) are permitted, and this is also how we rule. Therefore, if the extinguishing concerns eating or the place of eating, it is considered preparatory for eating and is permitted. However, with regard to marital relations, they were stringent, because even though the Talmud compares it to preparatory activities, it is still not completely comparable, as I have written in section 509:4, that it is considered as something that could have been done before the festival. See there. And when it is permitted to extinguish, one should not extinguish directly with water, but rather throw the burning log outside, and it will extinguish on its own (Magen Avraham, subsection 3). And the Rokeach wrote that even for marital relations it is permitted to extinguish, because he holds that this too is considered preparatory, according to the plain understanding of the Gemara. (And see Taz, subsection 2, who agreed with this. And Mordechai wrote that for the sake of the pot, even according to the Rabbis, it is permitted, because this is not considered preparatory but actual eating itself. And see Taz and Magen Avraham, subsection 1. According to what we have explained, there is no need for all this, and the matters are clear according to the explanations we have provided. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

It is forbidden to tilt the lamp to distance the oil from the wick, as this constitutes extinguishing, and it is prohibited. Some say this is specifically when his intention is to leave it that way, but if his intention is to momentarily distance it from the oil to extend the wick a bit more, and then the oil will return to the wick so that it will illuminate better – it is permitted. This is not similar to completely extinguishing it to light it better afterward, which is certainly forbidden. However, when he only reduces its light so that it will illuminate better, this is all considered part of the lighting process and is permitted (Taz, subsection 4). According to this, it makes sense with our candlesticks, which are customarily lit and the sleeve is extended downward a bit, and at that moment its light is reduced. Then the sleeve is extended upward and it illuminates much more, and it cannot be done any other way. Some complain about this, but according to what we have explained, it is completely permissible. This is also the common custom, and there is no reason to doubt it at all.

It is also forbidden to take a wick from a lit candle even to place it in another candle, because when one removes it – it immediately extinguishes, and what benefit is there in lighting it again afterward? However, if it truly does not extinguish but only diminishes its light somewhat – it is permitted, as I wrote in the previous section. But usually, it does extinguish, and therefore it is forbidden to do so (see Taz there). However, it is permissible to add wicks to a lit candle so that it will burn more and extinguish quickly. This means: even though one's intention is for it to extinguish quickly, in any case, he is performing an act of kindling and it is permitted; just as one tilts the oil towards the candle, which also causes it to burn more and extinguish quickly. Causing extinguishing is not prohibited on Yom Tov, and even on Shabbat there are those who permit it, as I wrote in Siman 334. And one should not ask: why is it forbidden to take a wick from a lit candle and place it in another, whereas in Siman 502 we permitted taking wood from a bonfire on one side and placing it on the other side? For we have already explained there that the wood does not extinguish completely, see there. (And this answers the question of the Taz in subsection 5, see there.)

A wax candle—it is forbidden to heat it and attach it to any object, because it is easy to come to spread it, and one who spreads it is liable for a sin-offering. Additionally, when one rubs it onto the object to which it is being attached, it constitutes spreading (see Magen Avraham, subsection 6). However, it is permitted to fold a wax candle so that it will light more quickly, as I have written. There is no difference between a wax candle and a tallow candle, except that it is not customary to do so with tallow. Nowadays, some people heat the base of a tallow candle and attach it to a table or a stand. It is forbidden to do this on Yom Tov. This is a Torah prohibition because it certainly involves spreading, as it does not attach quickly like wax and requires rubbing.

And our master the Beit Yosef wrote: A wax candle that one wishes to light on Yom Tov, and is concerned that it should not burn completely - he may place something around it before lighting it that will prevent it from burning, in such a manner that it will be extinguished when it reaches there. So far his language, but it is not understood: why is it required to place it before lighting it? It has already been explained that causing extinguishing is permitted. And indeed, in the Tur, he did not write "before lighting it," but rather he wrote: A wax candle that one wishes to light... And from this, our master the Beit Yosef inferred in his great book that it refers to before lighting. And the commentators have disagreed with him, saying that causing extinguishing in this manner, which does not diminish its light, is permitted even afterward (Bach and Magen Avraham, subsection 7).

However, in truth, there is a disagreement on this matter between Tosafot (22b, "Vehamistapek") and the Rosh (Chapter 17). Tosafot wrote that causing a flame to dim, which does not slightly darken the light, as in the case of drawing oil from the lamp which diminishes its light – is permitted on Yom Tov, for causing a flame to dim is only considered such when it diminishes its light, as in the case of drawing oil. Therefore, they permit cutting off a portion of the candle from below, even though as a result the candle will burn much less than before, see there. The Rosh, however, disagrees and holds that causing a flame to dim is considered so even when it does not diminish its light but merely prevents it from burning as much, and it is prohibited to cut the candle from below, see there. This is not analogous to adding wicks so that it burns faster, as mentioned in Section 5, which is permitted, for it is evident that through kindling it is allowed since one is engaged in kindling. Otherwise, it would be forbidden to tilt the oil towards the wick so that it burns well, as I have written there.

According to this, it becomes clear: Our Rabbi, the Beit Yosef, follows the approach of the Rosh, and therefore requires it before lighting it, and he also explains this in the Tur, that afterwards it would be considered an indirect extinguishing. And even though one could differentiate that even according to the Rosh it is not considered indirect extinguishing unless it prevents the candle itself, such as cutting it from below or removing wax from it, but when the prevention is through something else placed around it, it is not considered indirect extinguishing; and there are those who say this (Magen Avraham there) – our Rabbi, the Beit Yosef, does not agree, as this is not conclusive, as both cases are considered indirect extinguishing. (And this is what the Rosh wrote there, that he does not touch the burning thing, but does something external that causes the extinguishing when the flame reaches there, up to here are his words; and the Magen Avraham and Taz in subsection 6 understood his intention to differentiate between when the prevention is from the body of the candle and when it is from something else around it. And I am puzzled: his intention is clearly not due to this distinction, but rather between when the indirect extinguishing is near the candle, and when it is far from the fire, as in the case of empty vessels in a fire, see there carefully. And this is the opinion of the Beit Yosef, and it is clear. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

And this is according to the opinion of the Rosh. But according to the Tosafot, it is permitted. And this is what our Rabbi the Rema wrote, that some permit cutting a wax candle with fire, meaning that they light it also from below in order to shorten it, and so is the custom. But with a knife, it is prohibited. Thus far his language. Meaning: they light it from below, and it splits into two, and consequently it becomes smaller and burns less—this is not considered causing extinguishment. And certainly, according to the ruling of our Rabbi the Beit Yosef, to place something around it that causes it to extinguish, it is permitted even after it is lit. This is his primary intention. And with a knife, it is prohibited, as it constitutes making a vessel, but through lighting in the middle. And some say that when lighting it in the middle, both halves must burn. But if it is done in a manner that only causes it to split and not burn, it is prohibited. And some permit even in this manner (see Magen Avraham, subsection 8). And it is not similar to what will be explained, that when splitting the candle into two, both halves need to be lit—this is because his intention is to light and make a vessel. But here, where his intention is only that it should not burn much—it is not necessary (there). And it is also permitted to place a lit candle in sand or deep clay so that it extinguishes upon reaching the sand or clay (there and Taz there), since he is not diminishing its light. And it is possible that even according to the Rosh, it is permitted, since this is the manner of lighting. And the law follows the words of our Rabbi the Rema, and so is the custom.

He also wrote: It is permitted to place a candle in a place where the wind blows, so that it will extinguish. But it is forbidden to place it there if the wind is already blowing. Until here are his words. Before the wind comes, it is considered causing an extinguishing, since at the moment of the act it does not diminish the light either. But at the time of the wind, it is like actual extinguishing by the wind. And also at the moment of the act, there is a change, and therefore it is forbidden. And some are concerned to forbid it completely even when there is no wind at all, as a decree lest there be wind, as we decreed above in Siman 277 on Shabbat (Magen Avraham, Subsection 10). But the main ruling is like the words of our master, the Rema, for two reasons: Firstly, according to what we explained above there in Subsection 7, even on Shabbat it is not so (and similarly wrote the Eliyah Rabbah, see there). However, even if on Shabbat it is so, Rashi, of blessed memory, already wrote in Yevamot (119a) that regarding distancing to avoid coming to a Torah prohibition, our sages were rightly concerned with a prohibition carrying the penalty of karet, but not with a prohibition of a negative commandment, see there. And if so, even if on Shabbat they decreed because of the wind, in any case, on Yom Tov, which involves a prohibition of a negative commandment, they were not concerned. (And what the Magen Avraham wrote that the custom is not to take a candle home from the synagogue on Yom Tov—certainly this is so, for usually there is wind. But if there is no wind—certainly it is permitted.)

A candle that has extinguished, and one wants to relight it on the same day – it is permissible to cut the tip of the wick so that it will light more easily. This is not considered as making a utensil, since it can be lit even without this, but cutting it makes it better. Nevertheless, it is preferable not to cut it with a knife, but rather by hand (see there, subparagraph 11). And our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in paragraph 10: It is permissible to remove the coal at the tip of the wick while it is burning. However, one should not cut the tip of the wick with a tool. Thus far his language, and he began with the coal and concluded with the tip of the wick. And it must be said that this is what he means: that with a tool, it is forbidden even to remove the coal, because necessarily – it is impossible to precisely remove only the coal with a tool, and the tool would also take from the tip of the wick (Taz, subparagraph 12). Some explain that his intent is this: that the coal is permitted even with a tool, as this is not considered making a utensil. But the tip of the wick – is forbidden even by hand, because it is customary to do it with a tool. And if so, even by hand it would be considered making a utensil (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 20, based on the words of the Beit Yosef). This explanation is forced and strained, and not reasonable at all (Taz, there). And even according to this explanation, nevertheless, in the first case of a candle that has extinguished – it is obvious that by hand it would not be considered making a utensil, since it has already cooled down a lot, and the coal has been consumed. And also, the tip of the wick has become strong, and it is possible to light it even without this, as I have written. And also with a tool, it is not a complete making of a utensil, but nevertheless, it is not proper with a tool, as I have written (see Magen Avraham, subparagraph 11 and subparagraph 20, and you will understand that according to his explanation in subparagraph 20 – it is necessary to distinguish between this and that. And therefore, he wrote in subparagraph 11: And it is possible that with a tool it is forbidden, see there. Examine carefully and you will find it easy).

And the great authorities have written that the allowance to remove the coal is with an oil wick, where one removes the coal and soot. But with our candles made of tallow and wax, it is forbidden to pinch, which is called "snitzing," because when one takes the wick between two fingers to pinch, he is taking from the body of the wick. Certainly, using a tool, like snitzers, is forbidden (Taz, Magen Avraham, Bach, Yam Shel Shlomo). Additionally, it can extinguish in his hands (Bach). And so the custom of the world is not to pinch with the hands, and certainly not with a tool. However, to tilt the wick slightly so the ash falls off is permitted (Taz there). Some permit even pinching with the fingers, as even if one takes a bit from the wick, it is considered an unintentional act. And the extinguishing is also considered unintentional. This is not a "psik reisha" (certain outcome) (Eliyah Rabba, subsection 30, and Knesset HaGedolah), as several of our Rabbis have permitted it even with a tool. And the Rashba explicitly wrote in the book Avodat HaKodesh: one may pinch the wick, whether by hand or with a tool. However, Rambam and the Tur forbade it with a tool, so by hand, it is permitted to everyone (there). But the custom of the world follows the first opinion.

One may not place a candle on a tree on the eve of a festival because we are concerned that one might take it from there on the festival, and thus use the tree. Even if we say that taking it is not considered "using" the tree, nevertheless, there is concern that one might climb the tree to take it (see Magen Avraham, subsection 16, and be precise and you will find it easy). Certainly, it is forbidden on the festival itself. One may not shape a clay lamp, that is, while it is still soft like the potter's clay, by squeezing it with one's hand to make a receptacle, because this constitutes making a utensil. Similarly, artisans who place straw in the air of the lamp to prevent its sides from falling, and when it dries, they remove the straw – it is forbidden to remove the straw on the festival because this completes the utensil. Likewise, if two vessels were joined together during their manufacture – it is forbidden to separate them on the festival because this also completes their making. However, if they became joined later due to some cause – this is of no consequence, and it is permitted to separate them (see there, subsection 17).

One may not cut a wick into two, unless they insert the two ends into the mouths of two candles and light it in the middle, and they need both candles. Otherwise, it is considered making a vessel. When lighting them, it does not appear as a repair but as intended for lighting. Refer to section 10 (and similarly, the Taz writes in section 10). One may not twist the wick, nor undo the braiding. Similarly, with a wax candle that is braided, it is forbidden to untie the braiding, as twisting is considered building, and untying is considered demolishing. It is also forbidden to singe the wick, as this is considered making a vessel. However, if it is not very stiff, one may knead it by hand to stiffen it. It is permissible to soak it in oil when there is no candle burning in it, because if there is a candle burning, it reduces the oil, and this is considered extinguishing, as it dims the light. Even if it does not dim the light, it is forbidden according to the Rosh, as we have written in section 8. On Shabbat, it is certainly forbidden by all authorities in such a case, even if it does not dim the light (see Magen Avraham, section 19, who writes this, and it is obvious).

Rabbeinu the Rema wrote in section 4 that leftover oil and wicks are permitted even on a Yom Tov that follows Shabbat, or on the two days of Rosh Hashanah. Thus are his words. Meaning: although they are suitable for lighting, we do not say this constitutes preparation, and preparation from a Yom Tov to Shabbat or from Shabbat to a Yom Tov is forbidden, as well as from the first day of Rosh Hashanah to the second day. This is not considered "preparation" and it is similar to the law of torches in Siman 501, which are permitted because the substance already existed in the world, as I wrote there. The same applies here as well, and see what I wrote there.

One who lights a candle for Yom Tov must recite the blessing: "Who has sanctified us with His commandments, and commanded us to light the candle of Yom Tov." Just as we are commanded on Shabbat, so too on Yom Tov because of enjoyment and happiness. And there is no enjoyment without a candle at night. Women are accustomed to recite "Shehecheyanu" at the time of lighting the candles. On Yom Tov, they do not need to light beforehand and cover their eyes and then recite the blessing as on Shabbat, because on Shabbat, the reason is that after the blessing, it is considered as accepting Shabbat, and therefore they light beforehand. And in order for it to be "over le'asiyatan" (before performing the mitzvah) – they cover their eyes. But on Yom Tov, since lighting is permitted – it is better to recite the blessing before lighting, as is the proper way to do before performing the mitzvah (Drisha and Perisha in the introduction).

Seemingly, since extinguishing is prohibited on Yom Tov, it should be forbidden to cover the coals in the oven when they are raked to one side with ashes, as they might be extinguished as a result. This is also written in the Tosafot (22a, s.v. "ein," see there). However, the Agudah permits covering them at night in order to find fire in the morning. Likewise, the great latter authorities (Yam Shel Shlomo and Taz at the end of section 12) wrote that this is a matter of unintended consequence and is not a definite outcome. The primary form of extinguishing here is considered a labor not needed for its own sake. But from morning to evening, it is certainly forbidden to cover. This is the simple custom, and it should not be changed.

Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote in Section 5: An idle candle, that is, one which he does not need, is prohibited to light. However, the synagogue's candle is not considered idle, and it is permitted to light it even on the second day of Yom Tov after Mincha; and there is no concern of preparing for a weekday, since lighting it fulfills a mitzvah at that moment. As for preparing the wicks and lanterns on Yom Tov after Mincha: if he wants to light them on that day - it is permitted, but if not - it is forbidden. This is his language. An idle candle is defined as one that is not needed for illumination at all. But if he wants to increase the light significantly - it is certainly permitted, as this enhances the joy of Yom Tov. And even if his intention is to display his wealth - nevertheless, it honors the day (Taz, subsection 8). Some question this (see Magen Avraham, subsection 12 in the name of Yam Shel Shlomo). The Rashba completely forbids the synagogue's candle, as it is only for honor, and this is not permitted by the Torah. Any mitzvah involved is diminished by "for you" - and not for the sacred. However, the Rosh and the Tur permitted it, writing that this is not an idle candle. Especially according to the Rambam, kindling is entirely permitted, as we say "since" (it is allowed for one purpose, it is allowed for another), and this too is for the honor of the congregation. The world is accustomed to permit it. Nevertheless, it is necessary to caution them not to increase excessively. Especially on Yahrzeit days, when they increase without measure, they should be restrained from this. After Mincha, when they light - there is a need for that moment. However, to prepare the candles and wicks for the night - it is obvious that it is forbidden. Similarly, to set up the candles from day to night - it is forbidden unless they are lit during the day. When lighting in the synagogue, it is permitted, even if people have not yet arrived, since they will come during the day. (This matter of the idle candle is from the Jerusalem Talmud, Shilin. It is not clear to us according to the Rosh and the Tur, for if so, what is an idle candle? Would someone act foolishly and light completely in vain? If for some purpose, like to smoke tobacco in it - it is certainly permitted. If for a non-Jew - it is obviously forbidden. So why is he lighting it? This needs examination.)

We learn in the Gemara (24b): Rav Pappa said: The halachah is that if a non-Jew brings a gift to a Jew on a festival, if that species is still attached to the ground, it is forbidden; and in the evening, they are forbidden until enough time has passed for them to have been prepared. And Rashi explained that they are forbidden due to muktzeh. And even Rabbi Shimon, who does not hold by muktzeh, forbids it, for something attached is like dried figs and raisins. And do not differentiate between that which is attached, whether it belongs to him or to the non-Jew. So far his words. Meaning: Even though regarding being prepared there is a difference between a Jew and a non-Jew, for what belongs to a non-Jew does not need preparation as I wrote in Siman 497 – this applies to other preparations like living creatures and the like, which are under his control. But something attached or the trapping of fish – these are complete muktzeh, and in the evening they are forbidden until enough time has passed for them to have been prepared. That is: on the evening of the first day, for on the second day, in any event, it is permitted, since one of them is a weekday. And the reason for the time needed for preparation is so that one does not benefit from festival labor. And this is also the opinion of the Rambam in the second chapter, law 10, who wrote: A non-Jew who brought a gift to a Jew on a festival, if that species is still attached to the ground, or if he brought a living creature or birds or fish that could be trapped that day – these are forbidden in the evening until enough time has passed for them to have been prepared. So far his words. And this that what belongs to a non-Jew does not need preparation – this is regarding what is under his control but not prepared, but not regarding what was trapped, whether fish, living creatures, or birds.

However, our rabbis, the Ba'alei HaTosafot, wrote that it is also forbidden on the second day [of Yom Tov], until the evening, enough time for it to be prepared. The reason for "enough time for it to be prepared" is not because "one should not benefit from the labor done on Yom Tov" but rather "so that one does not tell a non-Jew to bring something from what is attached [to the ground] or from hunting." Consequently, if we permit it on the second day, one might still come to instruct the non-Jew to bring it so that it can be eaten on the second day. Therefore, they prohibited it until the end of the second day of Yom Tov, enough time for it to be prepared.

Seemingly, there is a practical difference between the reasons: according to Rashi's reasoning, which is so that one does not benefit from the labor of Yom Tov, the law is the same for someone who it was brought for and for others. However, according to Tosafot's reasoning, which is so that one does not tell someone to bring something from what is attached [to the ground], this only applies to this particular Jew and not to another, for no one sins for another, to say to him to bring something for someone else. And so the Rosh wrote there that therefore it is permitted for another Jew immediately after the first day of Yom Tov, and the prohibition is only on the first day because of muktzeh. It turns out that regarding another Jew, this explanation is more lenient than Rashi's, for according to Rashi, one needs the time it would take to perform the action, but according to Tosafot, it is not needed. However, the opinion of the SeMaK is that even according to Tosafot, it is forbidden for any Jew until after the second day of Yom Tov by the amount of time it would take to perform the action, for the Sages did not differentiate in a matter involving a complete labor between this Jew and another Jew, since this prohibition is considered light by people, they made a greater distance, since it was brought for a Jew (Beit Yosef), and a Torah labor was performed for him.

And this is what our master, the Rema, wrote in section 1 regarding the words of our master, the Beit Yosef, which are like the words of Rashi and the Rambam, that the prohibition only applies to the first day and the night following it to account for the work done. He wrote the following: "There are those who are stringent and prohibit it until the end of the second day of Yom Tov, and it is customary to be stringent if it is not for the sake of Yom Tov, such as for guests and similar cases. In such cases, it is customary to be lenient for others for whom it was not brought." This is the end of his words, and this is its explanation: Certainly, ideally, one should be stringent even for others until the conclusion of the second day of Yom Tov. However, for the sake of Yom Tov, such as when the other person does not have anything to enhance the second day of Yom Tov, one can rely on the opinion of the Rosh that for others it is permitted on the second day of Yom Tov. Moreover, even if he himself has invited guests, the guests are considered like himself, like all the members of his household, as will be explained regarding the area beyond the boundary – that we add leniency to consider the guests as others, and it is permitted to cook for them. For even though they are not exactly like others, one can rely on the opinion of Rashi and the Rambam in this matter. He can also eat with them, for it is not proper manners for them to eat while he does not eat. The reason is that the majority of authorities hold like Rashi and the Rambam. However, we are stringent like Tosafot and the SeMaK initially, but in a place of need, we rely on the Rosh, that for others it is permitted even according to Tosafot. In a pressing situation, we consider the guests as others, and he also eats with them based on the opinion of Rashi and the Rambam. Also, regarding the prohibition of carrying on the second day, one can rely on this and carry, and it suffices to prohibit in eating. (This is also evident from the Taz, subsection 2, and also the Magen Avraham, subsection 6, who, although he is uncertain about the Rema's interpretation, still seems to conclude this way. Therefore, the Rema was very precise in his wording. Consider well and you will find leniency.)

Seemingly, even in the measure of "waiting the time it would take to perform the act" (כדי שיעשו) – there is a practical difference between the explanations. According to Rashi's explanation, in order not to benefit from the Yom Tov labor – it suffices to wait the time of plucking or capturing alone, for that is the main labor. But not the time it would take to bring it here. And so wrote the Tur, and this is his wording: "The explanation of 'the time it would take to perform the act' – is only the time of plucking and capturing alone. And it is not necessary to wait the time it would take to bring it here." Thus far his wording. But according to the Tosafot's reason, so that one would not tell him to bring it – one must also wait the time it would take to bring it here. But there are those who say not like the Tur, that even according to Rashi's reason, one must wait the time it would take to bring it. And this is the opinion of our teacher the Beit Yosef, who wrote at the end of section 1, and this is his wording: "The measure of 'the time it would take to perform the act,' that is, the time it would take for the non-Jew to go to the place where he picked, finish the labor, and return here. And if it is uncertain from where he brought them – the measure is as if they came from outside the boundary." Thus far his wording, and he indeed ruled according to Rashi and the Rambam. And the reason is written by the Rashba and the Ran, that even according to Rashi's explanation, this is so, as it is proven in the Tractate Mikvaot (Chapter Two) that in all cases of "the time it would take to perform the act," we do not measure according to the actual performance of the prohibition, which is done in a moment, but according to the entire process, that is, the act and the travel. And if he came riding or traveling by wagon – we measure according to this time, for otherwise – there would be no "the time it would take to perform the act" at all, since the prohibition is done in a moment.

Anything that is forbidden to eat, even if one transgresses and places it in his mouth and chews it, it is forbidden to swallow. And anything that is forbidden to eat is also forbidden to move, since it is not fit for consumption, it automatically becomes muktzeh, because it is not suitable for anything, which is the essence of muktzeh. Consequently, according to the Tosafot, which prohibit even on the second day, it is also forbidden to move on the second day (Magen Avraham, Section 2). Do not be troubled by what we wrote at the end of Section 4 that it is permitted to move, as this is not according to the Tosafot. Rather, we said that regarding moving, we rely on the opinion of Rashi and the Rambam, since in times of need we permit it, as I wrote there. And it might also be according to the Tosafot, since according to the Rosh it is permitted for others, it automatically follows that it is not forbidden to move.

If it was brought on the second day, one must wait until the evening as much time as would allow it to be done. And on the two days of Rosh Hashanah, as well as on Shabbat and a Yom Tov that are adjacent to each other, according to all opinions, it is forbidden until the night after the second day so much time as would allow it to be done. For the two days of Rosh Hashanah are considered one sanctity. And Shabbat and Yom Tov, even though they are two sanctities, nevertheless, if it was forbidden on the first and permitted on the second, it would mean preparing on Shabbat for Yom Tov or on Yom Tov for Shabbat. And this is a rabbinic preparation similar to the preparation discussed in section 513 regarding an egg laid on Shabbat, which is forbidden on Yom Tov; there the matter of this preparation is explained. And there are those who hold that fruits that were detached constitute a biblical preparation, which is not comparable to an egg (Magen Avraham, subsection 8 in the name of Yam Shel Shlomo). Nonetheless, in any case, it is certainly a rabbinic preparation.

And this is when they were picked or caught for the sake of a Jew. But if they were picked or caught for his (the non-Jew's) own sake, and afterwards he decided to give them to the Jew, or if they were picked on their own – according to all opinions, the prohibition applies only on that day due to muktzeh, and in the evening they are allowed immediately. For the principle of "sufficient time to be performed" does not apply here, since it was not done for the sake of a Jew. And only on the two days of Rosh Hashanah are they forbidden on both days, as it is considered one long day. Similarly, on Shabbat and Yom Tov due to rabbinic preparation (hachanah), as I have written. And it is permitted even for the one for whom it was brought if it was brought from within the techum (Shabbat boundary), for if it was brought from outside the techum, it is forbidden for the one for whom it was brought, as will be explained with divine assistance in section 12.

Even if there is doubt whether they were detached or caught today – they are forbidden. Similarly, if there is doubt whether they were detached or caught for the sake of the Jew, they are forbidden even on the second day of Yom Tov according to the Tosafot. The reason for the stringency in all this is because it is a matter that will eventually become permissible (Taz, section 13). There is one who is lenient in the case of doubt whether this was done for the Jew (Bach), but others disagree with him (Magen Avraham, section 11, and Taz, section 4).

However, if it is evident that they were not caught today, or not gathered today, even if the evidence is not very clear – it is permissible. Similarly, if they arrived at the beginning of the night, it is more likely to say that they were caught or detached before the day began. If they were not brought from outside the boundary, it is permissible even for the one they were brought for. And if the non-Jew casually mentions that they were not gathered or caught today, he is believed. Even on Yom Tov after Shabbat, he is believed concerning rabbinic prohibitions. Even according to the opinion that he is not believed for rabbinic prohibitions, nevertheless, in the case of a doubtful rabbinic prohibition, he is certainly believed. Additionally, he does not enhance his merchandise by saying this.

We do not delve into whether he knows the law that it is forbidden for the Jew or not, like in the case of the egg in section 513, where in a case of doubtful preparation, we are lenient (see Magen Avraham, section 13, and Taz, section 5. In my humble opinion, it appears as I have written). There is one who is stringent in such a case, knowing that it is forbidden for the Jew (Taz, there).

And all the matters that have been explained apply when the non-Jew acts on his own, either for the Israelite or for his own sake. But if the Israelite arranged beforehand with the non-Jew before the festival to bring him fish and fruits on the eve of the festival and paid him for this, and he brought them on the festival—this is certainly permissible according to all opinions to use immediately on the evening of the second day of the festival in the diaspora. The prohibition is only due to muktzeh, but it does not apply to waiting the required time. Similarly, on the second day of the festival according to the additional opinion, this is exactly like a non-Jew who did it for himself, as he did it for his own sake to receive his payment. And if he brought it from outside the boundary, and it was caught or gathered on the eve of the festival—it is permitted even on the festival itself, for the prohibition of outside the boundary applies to one for whom it was brought. But when he does it for his own payment, we do not concern ourselves with this. And indeed, in the case of a specified payment, it is permitted even on Shabbat, and even for a complete labor, as I wrote in Siman 252 (Magen Avraham, subsection 3). It is not similar to lighting a candle for an Israelite on Shabbat, which is forbidden even if paid, as I wrote in Siman 276—this is because he explicitly lit it for the Israelite to use immediately, as it is not suitable after some time. But regarding food, it is like a garment that was made, which is permitted if paid for, since it is not designated specifically for Shabbat, as it is also suitable after Shabbat. And here too: the food is suitable for the evening and after the festival (ibid.).

And know that what was explained, that on Yom Tov and Shabbat it is forbidden even according to Rashi and Rambam, when one brought a gift to a Jew from things that are attached or involve the prohibition of trapping, if so, automatically when Rosh Hashanah falls on Thursday and Friday, and they brought it on Thursday – it is forbidden until after Shabbat, because the two days of Rosh Hashanah are considered as one day. Consequently, it is forbidden on Shabbat, because it is adjacent to the second day of Rosh Hashanah, and if you permit it – it turns out that Yom Tov is preparing for Shabbat, as I have written. And this is a rabbinic preparation. Nevertheless, there are those who permit eating them on Shabbat, as we do not say preparation from two days. According to the Tosafot, this dispute also applies to the two days of Yom Tov in the diaspora, as is evident. And our Rabbi the Rema ruled in section 4 that on the two days of Rosh Hashanah, one should be stringent, but on the two days of Yom Tov in the diaspora, one may be lenient on the Shabbat that follows them. And specifically with fruits that do not require preparation from Yom Tov to Shabbat, but something that needs to be prepared from the second day of Yom Tov to Shabbat, such as fish and meat that need to be cooked, which cannot be cooked on Shabbat – it is forbidden since it is customary to forbid on the second day of Yom Tov. If so, they are also forbidden to handle, and how can they be cooked for Shabbat if not for the sake of guests, as I wrote in section 4. However, based on what we wrote there at the end of the section and in section 6, that regarding handling we can rely on Rashi and Rambam, and all the more so according to the opinion of the Rosh there that even according to Tosafot it is permissible for others on the second day of Yom Tov, and if so, there is no issue of muktzeh – it is also permissible with meat and fish. And all the more so that it is permissible to cook them through the handling of a non-Jew, and the Jew stands over their cooking (Taz, sub-section 8, and see Magen Avraham, sub-section 17). And especially in honor of Shabbat, one can straightforwardly rely on the Rosh, and on the opinion of Rashi and Rambam, and cook them oneself for Shabbat.

All these matters that have been explained pertain to activities that involve a Torah prohibition, such as plucking and trapping. However, for matters that do not involve such a concern, or for example, if it is certain that the items were plucked and trapped before the festival but were brought from outside the boundary; for if they came from within the boundary, it is obvious that it is permitted to everyone, even to the person they were brought for, since there is no prohibition here. But if they came from outside the boundary, our sages of blessed memory said (ibid.) that if they were not brought for the sake of a Jew, they are immediately permitted. If they were brought for the sake of a Jew, it is prohibited for the Jew on that day, and also prohibited for all the members of his household and for guests who are dependent on his table. There are those who permit it for guests (Beit Yosef in the name of Terumat HaDeshen). However, for others, it is permitted immediately, since no Torah prohibition was committed for their sake, it suffices that it is forbidden to the person himself and not to others. Similarly, if the reason it was forbidden to him is so that he does not instruct to bring it for him, this also has no relevance to others, even if it was brought from beyond twelve mil, which according to the Rif and Rambam is a Torah prohibition, nevertheless it is not forbidden to others (Magen Avraham, subsection 18). It seems to me that a son or daughter who are not dependent on his table are considered like others, and it is also permitted to himself immediately after the festival, and he does not need to wait the amount of time it would take to bring it. This is the opinion of R. Yitzchak of the Tosafot and the Rosh. However, the Rif and Terumah ruled that one must wait the amount of time it would take to bring it, and so ruled Rabbeinu Beit Yosef in subsection 5. He did not bring the opinion of those who permit, because also the Smag, Rashba, and Ran ruled thus, and therefore this is the ruling. The measure of "the amount of time it would take to bring it" is according to the time it took to bring it, whether by walking, riding, or traveling by wagon. Afterwards, it is permitted, and even according to the Tosafot who were stringent until the second evening, outside the boundary they agree. (See Mishkenot Yaakov, section 125, and it can be reconciled.)

Not only that, but even on the two days of Rosh Hashanah, and on Shabbat and a Yom Tov that are adjacent to each other – they also were lenient regarding items brought from outside the techum (Sabbath boundary), as our master the Beit Yosef wrote in section 8, and this is his language: An item that does not grow from the ground, which was brought to a Jew on the first day of Rosh Hashanah – is permitted on the second day, and the same applies to Shabbat and Yom Tov that are adjacent to each other. Thus far his words, for they were lenient regarding the techum, because in this case there is no prohibition of preparation, nor a prohibition related to sanctity – it does not relate to saying it is one sanctity and preparation, as this is only like a mere penalty, and it is sufficient to forbid it on the first day. And this is the law, although there are those who say that according to the Tosafot it is not so – we do not worry about this (see Magen Avraham section 25, who brought the words of the Yam Shel Shlomo and refuted them with good reasoning, see there). But if it is uncertain whether they were brought from outside the techum or not – our master the Beit Yosef was stringent in section 7, and this is his language: If it is uncertain whether they were brought from outside the techum, if the non-Jew resides with him in the city and the fruits are found in the city – it is permitted. And if not – it is forbidden. Thus far his words. And the reason he was stringent is because it is considered an item that has a permitted alternative. And there are those who disagree with him and permit, and in any case on the second day of Yom Tov when it was brought – there is room to be lenient in the case of doubt regarding outside the techum (there section 24).

Accordingly, if non-Jews bring fish or other food items to the city on Yom Tov, and we know they were caught before Yom Tov but brought from outside the boundary, if the majority of the city’s inhabitants are non-Jews, the food is permitted, as it is presumed they were brought with the majority in mind. However, if the majority are Jews, it is prohibited. Even if the population is half and half, it is prohibited. Certainly, if it is known that they were brought specifically for Jews, or if there is concern that they might increase the amount brought for Jews, it is prohibited. This applies when we observe that the quantity being brought is increasing, but generally, we do not assume this. The decision depends on the discretion of the authority. (See Magen Avraham, subsection 22, who wrote that if a non-Jew living in a village brings fish to a city where the majority are Jews, and there is doubt whether the fish were also caught for Jews or were initially caught for the general population and then decided to bring them to the city, there is room for leniency; see there).

Fish or other food that has come from outside the Shabbat boundary, it has already been explained in the laws of Shabbat that they are restricted to a four cubit area where carrying is prohibited. Therefore, if the city has an eruv, or is surrounded by a wall, or a fortress known to be enclosed for dwelling purposes – it is permitted to carry them throughout the city. However, if carrying in the city is prohibited on Shabbat – they may only be carried within the house and courtyard where they were brought, and it is forbidden to carry them outside the courtyard. In this regard, there is no difference between the person for whom it was brought and others, as it is prohibited for everyone to carry them, as is the rule for something that has come from outside the Shabbat boundary. This has been explained in Siman 405, see there.

Rabbeinu the Beit Yosef wrote in section 9: A Jew who sent a gift to his friend via a non-Jew on the eve of a festival, and the non-Jew was delayed and brought it on the festival from outside the boundary – it is permissible even for the one it was brought for to eat them. However, it is forbidden for any Jew to carry them beyond four cubits, or beyond a city surrounded by a wall, or beyond a fortress known to be surrounded by a residential wall. Thus are his words, for in this case there is no reason to prohibit it for the one it was brought for, as the non-Jew is not bringing from his own, that we should decree lest he say, "Bring for me." And it is permitted according to all opinions, only if it is of a kind that grows attached (i.e., fruit or vegetables), a sign is required to ensure they were not exchanged, if there is reason to suspect this. And if he sent to bring it, and knows it must be brought on the festival – it is obvious that for himself it is forbidden, as the law of something brought from outside the boundary for a Jew, for does it become more lenient because he himself sent it? On the contrary, in this case, it is more appropriate to penalize him (see Magen Avraham, subsection 26, and Taz, subsection 15).

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote regarding this: It is specifically when one had the intention from the day before, that there is no prohibition of muktzeh. But if one did not have the intention from the day before, even though there is no prohibition of techumin, there is still the prohibition of muktzeh. For anything belonging to a Jew requires preparation from the day before. And even for someone for whom it was not brought – it is forbidden. These are his words. And his intention is: since the fruits belonged to a Jew, and they were outside the boundary (techum) – they are considered as muktzeh, and they require preparation from the day before. And they are worse than the fruits of a non-Jew, which do not require preparation as I wrote in Siman 497. Therefore, he required that there be intention on them from the eve of the Festival, and if not – they are forbidden as muktzeh, and they are forbidden to all Jews. The commentators on the Shulchan Aruch (Magen Avraham in subparagraph 27 and Taz at the end of Siman 518) disagree with him, and they hold that this is not muktzeh. And only with animals that graze and do not enter the city for a long time is there a concern of muktzeh, but not with fruits. However, on the second day of Yom Tov it seems that it is certainly permissible.

It is taught at the end of the first chapter of Beitzah (14b): Beit Shammai says: one may not send gifts on Yom Tov except for portions. This means that one may not send a gift from one person to another unless it is something prepared and intended to be consumed that day, such as pieces of meat and fish. But Beit Hillel says: one may send an animal, wild animal, or bird, whether alive or slaughtered. One may send wines, oils, fine flour, and legumes, but not grain. This means they disagree on two matters: First, even something not yet prepared, like live animals that still need to be slaughtered, is permitted, since they can be slaughtered. It is obvious that there must still be time to slaughter, salt, cook, and eat them, because otherwise, they are not fit for Yom Tov. Second, even if it is certain that they will not eat or drink all of it today, as they are meant for many days, like wines, oils, and fine flour, which implies they are in large quantities, it is still permitted as long as some of it will be eaten or drunk on Yom Tov. (This is why they are divided into two clauses.) But not grain, because it is forbidden to grind on Yom Tov, and it is not fit for Yom Tov. And see what I wrote in section 4.

And if there is some food that can be made from grain — some say it is permitted (Taz). And some say it is forbidden, because most grains are meant for grinding (Eliyah Rabbah in the name of the Maggid Mishneh, Chapter Five). According to this, sending an animal that is designated for its milk is forbidden, because it cannot be slaughtered due to the prohibition of muktzeh (there) unless it is milked and sent to be milked. And even on Yom Tov, one can milk into food, as I wrote in Siman 506. Similarly, sending animal food is forbidden because one does not exert effort for an animal (Magen Avraham). However, there are those who permit it (Taz and see Eliyah Rabbah).

And even something that is permitted to send on Yom Tov – nevertheless, it should not be sent in a public manner, that is, by three people walking in a row one after the other or in a group (Elya Rabba), all carrying the same type of item. Rather, each person should walk separately, distanced from one another. And similarly, if each one is carrying a different type of item – it is permitted, because it does not appear as if they are all going to the same place. There is an opinion that says that even if they are carrying different types of items, if they walk one after the other, it is forbidden (Magen Avraham in the name of Yam Shel Shlomo).

And one may send garments even though they are not sewn, because it is fitting to lean on them, and there is a need for them on Yom Tov. And even if they contain shatnez (a forbidden mixture of wool and linen), if they are stiff in such a way that it is permitted to lean on them, as I have written in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 301. But if not – it is forbidden. And one may send tefillin even though they are not needed on Yom Tov, because since on a weekday they are ready to be worn immediately – it brings joy and is permitted on Yom Tov. And according to this, also wines and oils, even if they will not be used on Yom Tov – it is permitted. But animals and fine flour are forbidden, since they are not fit as they are.

The reason for the prohibition of sending something that is not appropriate for Yom Tov is because it involves carrying in a public domain. Even though carrying is permitted on Yom Tov, anything that is only for a weekday purpose and does not bring joy on Yom Tov is prohibited. All the items that were mentioned earlier, even if carried through a public domain, may be sent. However, through a karmelit (an area with semi-public domain status), and for us, who do not have a public domain, everything is permitted as long as it is not muktzeh (set aside for a prohibited use) (Taz).

It is permissible for a person to say to a shepherd who is accustomed to him, whom he trusts and gives him without specifying a price: "Give me a kid or a lamb." And to a butcher: "Give me a shoulder or a thigh." And to a baker: "Give me a loaf." And to a grocer: "Give me five eggs and five pomegranates." And similarly, anything of this sort, as long as he does not mention a price, or a specific measure or number. Therefore, one must be careful not to mention a specific measure, such as: "Give me a kab or two kabim." Nor a specific price, saying "I will take such and such, and I will pay you such and such." Nor a specific number, saying: "You have such and such with me, give me such and such, and you will have such and such with me." And see earlier in Siman 323.

In what case are these words said? Regarding a Jewish storekeeper. But from a non-Jewish storekeeper – it is forbidden to purchase from him anything that is connected to the ground or requires trapping, unless it is clear that they were not gathered or trapped today. Similarly, one should not purchase eggs from him, lest they were laid today. But something that is neither connected to the ground, nor requires trapping, nor is a new entity – it is permitted to purchase from him even if it was brought today from beyond the Shabbat boundary, as long as it is known that it was not brought for the sake of a Jew, such as in a city where the majority are non-Jews and similar cases. Likewise, flour that was ground today in a city where the majority are non-Jews – it is permitted to purchase from him, because it was ground with non-Jews in mind. And there is no issue of muktzeh, because the wheat is fit for roasting. However, to send it on a festival day is forbidden, as I wrote in the previous section, because it is not intended for that purpose (Magen Avraham, Section 2). And it seems to me that in our country it is considered muktzeh, because here we do not make roasted grains, and our wheat is not fit for eating raw. Similarly, it is permitted to purchase from him bread that was baked on that day in a place where they eat baker's bread, and it must be known that it was not ground for the sake of a Jew. And likewise, bread that was baked on the Sabbath before a festival in such a manner.

It is forbidden to call a non-Jew to one's house and show him the money, and say to him: "Take this for the bread, flour, and fruits." Even through a non-Jew it is forbidden to purchase by setting a price or weight. Rather, one should say to him: "Give me a loaf of bread." But mentioning weight or a sum of money is forbidden, even in a place where the transaction is known (and what the Magen Avraham writes at the end of subparagraph 4 requires further study). And if the Jew bought flour or fish from him on the eve of a festival, and left it in his store, and came on the festival to take it – there is no concern that he might have exchanged it if he understands that he will not gain anything by doing so, for he is not suspected of causing a stumbling block.

A Jew who tells a non-Jew on the eve of a festival, "Get me pigeons for tomorrow" – has not acted properly. However, if he has already done so – it is permitted to eat them on the festival, provided there is no concern they were brought from outside the techum (Sabbath boundary), or in a city where the majority are non-Jews. And specifically when they are not mature enough to fly beyond the techum, for if they can fly – we are concerned they might have been caught on the festival itself. Similarly, for any item: it is forbidden to tell a non-Jew on the eve of a festival, "Get me such-and-such for tomorrow." But if the non-Jew has already acquired it – it is permitted after the fact, as long as one does not make a habit of doing so. For if one habitually does this – it is forbidden even after the fact.

A person may say to their friend on a festival: "Fill this vessel for me, but not with a measure." This was explained above in Siman 323 regarding Shabbat, and the same applies to a festival. Similarly, the laws of casting lots were explained there, and the same applies to a festival. Likewise, with members of a group who are particular with one another, see there. One should not measure barley to place before their animal on a festival, but rather give it an estimated amount.

It has already been explained in Siman 498 that regarding carrying, we say: "Since it was permitted for the purpose of food preparation, it was also permitted for non-essential purposes." We have explained the reasoning for this there with the help of Heaven. Therefore, with carrying, we do not treat it like every other Yom Tov labor by prohibiting something that can be done on the eve of Yom Tov, as the Rambam wrote in the first chapter, law 6, and this is his language: For this reason, carrying was not prohibited on Yom Tov. And although every act of carrying is a labor that could be done on the eve of Yom Tov, why was it not prohibited? To increase the joy of Yom Tov. And he may carry and bring whatever he wants, and complete his tasks, and not be like one whose hands are tied. This concludes his language.

According to Rashi's opinion (12a), we say, "Since carrying [items] was permitted for a need, it was also permitted without a need." That is to say, even without any need at all. This also appears to be the opinion of the Rambam. And regarding matters forbidden in the Gemara, the reason is explained as being due to the appearance of weekday activities, as the Rambam elaborates in the fifth chapter regarding large loads, carrying with poles, and moving ladders; see there. However, according to the opinions of our Rabbis, the Tosafists, the Rosh, and most of the poskim (decisors of Jewish law), some need is required: even if it is not a need for eating and drinking, there still must be some need for Yom Tov. But if there is no need at all, it is forbidden in a place where carrying is forbidden on Shabbat.

This is the language of the Tur: Any carrying that has even a slight necessity, even if it is not for one's own need but for a mitzvah purpose, such as a child to circumcise him, a Torah scroll to read from it, or a lulav to fulfill the commandment with it – is permitted. And just as it is permitted to carry out – so it is permitted to return it. Similarly, if one needs to go to the synagogue, or needs to walk for the joy of the festival, and cannot leave a child alone at home – he can take him out with him. Likewise, a key with which he locked up the food, if he is afraid to leave it at home – he can take it with him... And similarly, all adornment needs can be taken out in order to adorn oneself on the festival. But an item that has neither a food necessity nor an adornment necessity, such as a key that locks up utensils, or something similar that has no need at all – it is forbidden to carry it out on the festival. So far his language. And this matter, that a key for utensils is forbidden – is explained in the Jerusalem Talmud, First Chapter, Halacha 7, see there.

And the Rosh brings a responsum from the Geonim in the first chapter (Siman 18) that carrying without the need for food or adornment, such as those who go out with keys tied to their belts – they are acting improperly, and it is forbidden to do so. And thus the law was ruled in the two yeshivot. This is his language. According to this, it is puzzling about our master the Rema, who wrote in Siman 1 that utensils that he needs somewhat, or he fears they will be stolen, or other losses – it is permitted. This is his language. And how did he permit it for fear they might be stolen? For the Jerusalem Talmud and the Geonim forbid carrying a key of utensils. And indeed, they wondered about him in this (Taz, Siman Katan 1, and Magen Avraham, Siman Katan 2 in the name of Yam Shel Shlomo). But on the contrary, it is surprising: since we say regarding carrying "mitoch" (the principle that once carrying is permitted for food needs, it is permitted for other needs too), and we only require some need, why isn't it considered a slight need if one fears they will be stolen? And what the Geonim said that anything not needed for food or adornment is forbidden, where do we derive this from? And further, it is difficult for me from the Tosefta (first chapter) that it is taught, Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel said: Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel agree that one may carry filled utensils to bring empty ones to fill them. On what do they disagree? On empty ones not for a need, that Beit Shammai forbids and Beit Hillel permits. This is his language. And since Beit Hillel permits empty ones not for a need, and even if we say that the intention is that there is some slight need, certainly it is not for the need of food, for in this Beit Shammai does not disagree. Rather, certainly in such a case as fearing they will be stolen, or another matter that is not for food or adornment, and certainly not related to utensils. And yet Beit Hillel permits it.

Therefore, it appears to my humble opinion that the truth aligns with the words of our master, the Rema. The Jerusalem Talmud and the Geonim do not contradict his words. It is known that the Jerusalem Talmud often revolves around the words of the Tosefta, and in the Tosefta it is taught: A person may go out with a key in his hand into the public domain and need not be concerned. We need to understand why it says "in his hand." It means that even though he carries it in his hand and everyone sees it, it is not considered a weekday activity. The Jerusalem Talmud specifies that this applies only to a key for food and not for utensils. This distinction is not due to the act of carrying itself, which is permitted if he fears leaving it at home due to theft or similar concerns. The prohibition is to carry it openly in his hand, as that appears like a weekday activity to onlookers. 

There is proof from the Jerusalem Talmud where it questions: Rabbi Abbahu was sitting and teaching, and he had the key to the palace in his hand? It answers that it contained food, see there. It means Rabbi Abbahu held the key in his hand, which is the main prohibition. The words of the Geonim also support this, as they wrote that those who go out with keys tied to their belts are acting against the law… They were particular about them being tied to the belts because everyone sees it, and it appears like a weekday activity. According to this, the Tosefta regarding empty utensils is understandable. Beit Hillel permits carrying them even openly, even if his intention is not to fill them but for another purpose—since it does not appear as a weekday activity. Onlookers will say his intention is to fill them, which is a festival need, and therefore it is permitted. According to this, the words of our master, the Rema, are valid and established.

(It seems to me that this is why the Talmud mentions "stones," because stones have no use, and theft does not apply to them. But anything with a concern of theft is permitted, as long as it does not appear like a weekday activity. According to this, the Tosefta, the Jerusalem Talmud, and the Geonim do not contradict the opinions of Rashi and the Rambam that it is permitted even without any need. They refer to a case of weekday activity, but otherwise, it is entirely permitted. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

(What the Magen Avraham elaborated at the beginning of this section regarding "mitoch" (since) has already been explained in Siman 498 with Divine assistance. What he questioned from the beginning of Pesachim against the Magid Mishneh is not difficult at all, as the Ketzot HaChoshen wrote in the first chapter, note 89, that Rabbi Akiva necessarily did not agree with the Magid Mishneh's interpretation, see there. His second question is also resolved. What he wrote that even regarding cooking, the Gemara there says "mitoch"—we have already explained there that "cooking" is not the correct version, see there with a reasoned explanation. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

According to this, following the opinion of Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema), it is permitted on Yom Tov to carry in a public domain anything that has some purpose, such as carrying the key to money or tools, because one fears they may be stolen. However, according to the opinion of the great later authorities, it is forbidden. The common practice is to permit it, and based on our reasoning, they have a valid foundation. However, something that is needed for Yom Tov, such as tallit, prayer books, machzorim, and other books, it is certainly permitted to carry them to the synagogue and also to bring them back home. And even though at home they are not needed, it was permitted to carry them back because otherwise, one would not take them to the synagogue at all (Magen Avraham, section 2). And if one can store them safely in the synagogue so they will not be stolen, it is better to leave them in the synagogue (ibid.). Carrying a baby is permitted even for a walk. And anything that has beauty, or an ornament, or a need, such as a handkerchief to wipe the nose, it is certainly permitted.

And there is someone who wrote in this language: "And I have seen that when people go out for a stroll outside the city, they remove the knives which are no longer needed for the day, as they are no longer accustomed to eating. But in the city, outside of the eruv, it is not of such concern" (there in the name of the Yam Shel Shlomo). His intention is to differentiate between a karmelit (a semi-public domain) and a courtyard or alley that are not part of the eruv, as a karmelit is more stringent. And there is someone who refuted this, stating that certainly, knives are permitted all day, as even after eating, if one encounters a fruit, he will cut it with the knife. And there is also no distinction between a karmelit and an area not part of the eruv, as both are considered a karmelit (Taz, subsection 2).

And our master the Rema wrote that it is permissible to play with a ball even in the public domain, even though it is merely for amusement. Thus far his language. And there are those who object to this, saying that this is amusement and play only for children and not for adults (there and Magen Avraham, subsection 4 in the name of Yam Shel Shlomo). But in truth, this is not a valid objection, for since it is enjoyable to him according to his own lowly understanding, how can we prevent him?

Further, he wrote that if one has set an eruv, it is permissible to carry and take out anything that has the status of a utensil, even though it is not needed for the day at all. Thus far his language, as Yom Tov is not superior to Shabbat. But without an eruv, it is forbidden to carry even from one courtyard to another without any need at all (Magen Avraham, subsection 4). And his intention is not to establish an eruv on Yom Tov, for one does not establish an eruv on Yom Tov as I wrote in Siman 528. Rather, his intention is that if one has set an eruv for Shabbat, it automatically works for Yom Tov as well. And it would be proper for every God-fearing person to set an eruv for Yom Tov just as for Shabbat, but one should not change the custom. Nevertheless, it is proper when setting an eruv on the eve of Passover for the entire year to include Yom Tov in it and to say "for the Sabbaths and Yom Tovs of the entire year" (Taz there in the name of Yam Shel Shlomo).

Stones, pebbles, and similar items – it is forbidden to carry them on Yom Tov, and one who does so is liable to lashes. They are also prohibited from being moved due to muktzeh. Likewise, it is forbidden to carry anything for the sake of a non-Jew, and it is also forbidden to carry for a weekday purpose; just as it is forbidden to cook for the sake of a non-Jew and for a weekday purpose, so too is carrying. It is prohibited by Torah law, and one is liable to lashes for it. Although in the case of cooking, one is not liable to lashes due to the principle of "since" (i.e., since guests might come), this does not apply to carrying. Similarly, it is forbidden to carry for the sake of an animal, and one who carries into the public domain is liable to lashes. It is also forbidden to carry into a karmelit or into a courtyard that is not enclosed (with an eruv) for any of these purposes. Additionally, on the first day of Yom Tov to the second day, even on Rosh Hashanah, we do not say they are one single sanctity to be lenient, as I wrote in Siman 503. However, from Yom Tov to Shabbat, if one set aside an eruv tavshilin, it is permitted to carry, just as it is permitted to cook and bake.

Our teacher, the Rema, wrote in Section 2 that although it is forbidden for a Jew to carry out anything for the needs of a non-Jew, nevertheless, it is permitted to send it to him through a non-Jew, such as needing to return a pledge to a forceful non-Jew and the like. Thus far his words. The Levush explained that this is specifically through another non-Jew and not for himself, see there. And there are those who disagree with him, saying that the intention is not through a Jew, but for himself it is permitted just like through another non-Jew (Eliyah Rabbah, subsection 10). And it seems to me that the main opinion is like the words of the Levush. For regarding Shabbat in Siman 325, it is written that it is permitted to give something to a forceful non-Jew, or for the sake of peace, even though he will carry it out of his house, as long as it is not given hand to hand, see there. And to exchange a pledge is permitted through clothing, see there. And it implies that even if he is not forceful. But not through clothing—it is forbidden, see there. And it appears that even with a forceful non-Jew, it is forbidden not through clothing, because it appears as business dealings, as I wrote there. Therefore, I say that on Yom Tov, they permitted even a pledge with a forceful non-Jew, only that he should not give it himself, because it appears as business dealings. But he may send it through another non-Jew, as this does not appear so much like business dealings, and therefore they were lenient on Yom Tov. (And also his critique on the Olat Shabbat is not correct, see there.)

It has already been explained at the end of Siman 509 that it is permissible to move muktzeh for the purpose of food preparation, if the primary aspect of the food preparation is not muktzeh. Therefore, it is permitted to take an ordinary piece of wood that is not specifically designated for use as a spit, and also not suitable for kindling, to roast meat with it. After the roasting, it is forbidden to move it because it is not a utensil, but one can pull it and place it in a corner so that it does not cause harm, even if there is no meat on it at all. And this must be done specifically by pulling, which is considered indirect handling. However, it should not be done by complete handling, even though according to the basic law it is also permitted by complete handling, because of public harm. This is to create a distinction, so that people will know it is muktzeh but was permitted for the purpose of roasting (see Taz, subsection 3).

Rambam wrote in Chapter 5, Law 4: One should not carry the dovecote ladder from dovecote to dovecote in the public domain, lest people say he is taking it to fix his roof. But in the private domain, one may carry it, even though any place the Sages prohibited because of appearance – it is forbidden even in the innermost chambers – here they permitted it because of the joy of the festival. Thus are his words. And according to Ra'avad, it is also permitted in the public domain. But a proper ladder, such as for a loft, it is prohibited to even tilt, as Rambam wrote in Chapter 26 of Shabbat. The same applies to a festival. The Tur wrote like Ra'avad, and these are his words: It is permitted to move the ladder from dovecote to dovecote even in the public domain. And this refers to a small ladder, such as for a dovecote. But a large one, such as for a loft – it is prohibited to move it even in the house. Thus are his words. And our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in paragraph 4 like the Tur, because Rambam's interpretation of the subject (10a) is strained, see there. But he omitted the part "even in the house," and perhaps he holds that in the house it is permitted with a small household ladder. (And see Magen Avraham, Section 7, that one who is lenient with a household ladder in the house has not lost out.)

An animal that died on Yom Tov, if it was in a dangerous condition from the eve of Yom Tov – it is not considered muktzeh, for it was prepared for this. It is permitted to give it to dogs on Yom Tov. And if it cannot be eaten without cutting – one may cut it for them, as I wrote in Siman 324, that it is permitted to prepare food for an animal on Shabbat, and all the more so on Yom Tov. And if it was not in a dangerous condition from the eve of Yom Tov – it is forbidden because it is muktzeh. This is according to the Rif and the Rambam, who hold there is muktzeh on Yom Tov. According to those who hold there is no muktzeh on Yom Tov – it is permitted even if it was not in a dangerous condition. This is explained in Siman 498, see there. It is permitted to remove and return a chamber pot on Yom Tov as on Shabbat, as explained above in Siman 308.

The Sages taught in the Mishnah (30a): One may begin using a pile of straw [for fuel], but not wood that is in a designated area. The Gemara explains this: whether according to Rabbi Shimon, who does not hold by the concept of muktzeh, or according to Rabbi Yehuda, who does hold by muktzeh. According to Rabbi Shimon, the meaning is: one may start using a pile of straw, which is a store of straw set aside for animals, even though it was not designated for fuel. But not wood that is in a designated area, nor unspecified wood, but rather wood designated for building, like cedars and similar, which are muktzeh due to monetary loss, even Rabbi Shimon agrees. According to Rabbi Yehuda, it is explained thus: one may begin using a pile of straw, meaning straw that has rotted and spoiled and is only fit for fuel. And even for mixing with clay it is not fit, for example, if it has thorns in it, and it is only fit for fuel. But not wood placed in a storehouse, designated for the winter, which is muktzeh because it was not prepared. And everything on Yom Tov requires preparation. And straw set aside for animals and not placed in a storehouse is permitted even according to Rabbi Yehuda, since we use vessels for fuel (Magen Avraham, small section 10). And specifically when the straw is dry and fit for fuel. But when it is damp, even though it is fit for large fires, it is forbidden to move it, because large fires are uncommon (there). And it is not similar to damp wood which we permitted in section 502, because wood is designated for fuel. However, it seems to me that if most of the straw is dry and a minority is damp, it is nullified by the majority and it is permitted to use them for fuel. (And according to this, the case with the wood is consistent, see there. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

The Tur wrote: One who makes a sukkah on Shavuot for shade – it is forbidden to take wood from it on Yom Tov, even if it was rickety and fell. But Rabbi Shimon permits taking wood from it if it was rickety and fell. And if, after fixing its walls and roofing, one placed additional bundles near it without attaching them there, or if he threw more onto the roofing – it is permitted for everyone to take them. And if one stipulated to take from it on Yom Tov, and it fell – even the first opinion permits it, even from the main roofing. But in the case of the sukkah for the festival [of Sukkot] – a stipulation does not help. Thus far are his words, and they need explanation.

And this is its explanation: Even if one makes a sukkah merely for shade, not for the sake of the mitzvah of sukkah, and it is constructed during Shavuot, which is a hot season, and he makes a sukkah for shade—one is forbidden to take wood from it, whether from the walls or the roof, because of the prohibition of dismantling a tent. And even if he did not fasten them together with nails, since he set them up as a tent, it is considered dismantling. And even if it was rickety before the festival, and he anticipated its collapse, nevertheless, since it was set aside during twilight (before the festival), it is set aside for the entire day. Rabbi Shimon permits it because he does not hold by the concept of muktzeh. However, if it wasn't rickety, even Rabbi Shimon agrees; since his intention was not for this purpose, it is like dried figs and raisins. And if, after he repaired it, he placed bundles [of wood] without attaching them—they do not have the status of a tent, and it is permitted to take them even according to Rabbi Yehuda. This is specifically if his intention was not to thicken the tent, for if his intention was to make it thicker even after its repair, they are nullified to the tent, and there is an issue of dismantling a structure (Taz, subsection 6). Some say that after its repair, even if he intended to thicken it, it is not nullified to the structure (Shach). The primary ruling follows the first opinion. Some also say that specifically a bundle of reeds that he tied is not nullified to the walls, but reeds that were not tied are nullified, and it is considered dismantling a tent even if he placed them after its repair (Bach). And before its repair, even if he tied them, they are nullified. And for the roof, they are never nullified when tied, because it is not customary to place roofing in a bundle, and certainly, he placed them only to dry (ibid.). Some disagree regarding the walls and hold that even if they were not tied, they are not nullified after its repair (Taz ibid., and so it seems from the Beit Yosef). This is what our Rabbi the Beit Yosef wrote in subsection 8: One may take wood adjacent to the walls of the sukkah and use them for fuel. Up to here is his wording, meaning that he placed them after repairing the sukkah, and even if he did not tie them, and even if he placed them to thicken it (Magen Avraham, subsection 11). Some disagree regarding thickening it, as I have written. And our Rabbi the Rema wrote: The same applies if he threw bundles onto the roof—they are not nullified concerning the roof. And if his intention was to use them for fuel, it is permitted to take them from there.
