Up to here is his wording, meaning that bundles on the roof, even before its repair, are not nullified, as I have written. But without bundles, they are nullified. And when he wrote "if his intention was to use them for fuel," his intention was to exclude if his intention was not to use them for fuel. But in a standard case, they are considered for fuel (and so it seems from Magen Avraham, subsection 13, see there thoroughly).

The Tur further states that a condition is effective if it was stipulated before the festival that it would fall — it is permitted to take from it once it falls. However, our master the Beit Yosef holds that the condition is valid only according to Rabbi Shimon, and it is effective even with a complete item, as he sits and anticipates when it will fall. Therefore, when it falls, it is permitted to take from it. But according to Rabbi Yehuda, a condition does not help even with a defective item, for since it was set aside during twilight, it is set aside for the entire day. Therefore, he did not bring this law in the Shulchan Aruch, because he ruled in Siman 498 according to Rabbi Yehuda that there is muktzeh on a festival. 

And there are those who say that with a complete item, even according to Rabbi Shimon, a condition does not help, and with a defective item, it helps even according to Rabbi Yehuda (Ba'al HaMaor). And it seems to me that this is also the opinion of the Tur, for if not, why did he bring this law at all? And it is true that he is uncertain about muktzeh on a festival, whether the law follows Rabbi Yehuda or Rabbi Shimon, and he brought both opinions in Siman 498 without deciding, and similarly in all places. In any case, since it was set aside during twilight, we hold according to Rabbi Yehuda even on Shabbat, as I wrote in Siman 308, and certainly on a festival where muktzeh is stricter. But if a condition helps according to Rabbi Yehuda with a defective item — he brought the entire law for this reason (and thus resolves the question of the Magen Avraham on the Tur there). And in the festival sukkah during the festival — a condition does not help, for it is necessarily set aside for its mitzvah all the days of the festival. And even if it falls during the intermediate days of the festival, it is forbidden until after the festival because of muktzeh due to the mitzvah. (See Tosafot Shabbat 22a, beginning with "Sukkah.")

The Tur wrote: A house that is not plastered with clay, but rather bricks are stacked one on top of the other, and it is filled with fruits, and it collapses on Yom Tov – it is permissible to take from them where the collapse occurred. And we do not say they are set aside (muktzeh), because since their collapse only involves a rabbinic prohibition, he did not completely disregard them. However, if it was a fully constructed building – even Rabbi Shimon agrees that it is forbidden to take from the collapsed area. So far his words. But the Rambam in the second chapter wrote: A house that is filled with prepared fruits and it collapses – one may take from the collapsed area. So far his words, and it implies that even in a fully constructed building, it is not considered muktzeh. And Ramban, of blessed memory, explained this: Since the muktzeh is not in the fruits themselves, and they are not considered as a base for something forbidden due to their placement there, therefore they are not considered muktzeh even in a fully constructed house. And the Rashba, of blessed memory, holds like the Tur, that it is only permitted in a dilapidated house. The Shulchan Aruch ruled like the Rambam, that even in a fully constructed house it is permitted, and therefore they wrote simply "house". According to this, someone who has beets buried in a pit, and a non-Jew came and opened it on Shabbat or Yom Tov – it is permitted to cook the beets on Yom Tov and on Shabbat to eat them, as long as he did not do it for the sake of a Jew (Magen Avraham, subsection 14). Similarly, fruits that were outside the boundary, and a non-Jew brought them on Shabbat or Yom Tov – they are permitted (Taz, subsection 7). And if he brought them for the sake of a Jew – they are forbidden to the one for whom they were brought, as I wrote in Siman 515.

In their days, there were types of shops that were not attached to the ground, but rather like a tower. They would close it, and when they wanted to open it, they would remove the door and place it in front of the shop, arranging merchandise on it to sell. Afterwards, they would remove it again and replace it. And since there is no building with utensils, and no demolition with utensils, as I wrote in Siman 313, it follows that removing the doors is not considered demolition, and replacing them is not considered building. But with doors of a house and a shop attached to the ground, like our shops – it is obvious that it is forbidden to remove the door on Yom Tov, and all the more so to replace it.

And behold, even in those stores that are like vessels, in any case, if not for the joy of the festival, so that it would be available for buyers to acquire the foods and spices they need on the festival day – we would not permit opening, and certainly not returning, because of the exertion and weekday activities. But due to the joy of the festival, they permitted the removal and return, and consequently, we had to permit it. For if we do not permit the return – they would not want to remove them either, and it would lead to a lack of joy on the festival. And they permitted the end because of the beginning. And this applies to these stores that are outside the house. But similar vessels inside the house – it is permitted to remove them, and forbidden to return them, for inside the house there is no necessity to return them. For indeed, outside the house – there is a fear of thieves. But inside the house, there is no concern for this, as with all the objects in the house.

In what case are these words said? When they do not have a pivot at the top and bottom, but only in the middle. The pivot is what protrudes upward, like a peg, and the door has a corresponding protrusion that is placed on the peg, and similarly at the bottom. In our language, we call this "zaviyuses." If the door is in such a manner, it is forbidden to remove it, and all the more so to replace it, even in such shops. And when is it permitted? When the pivot is only in the middle, and there are holes in the lintel above and the threshold below, and they sharpen the corresponding parts of the door to fit into these holes. The reason for this is that a pivot at the top and bottom resembles building and is forbidden. Additionally, we decree that one might insert it firmly, like building. 

One should not ask: do we not open the doors of utensils, and even the doors of houses we open and close? Indeed, this is when they are on their pivots. But to remove them from their pivots is forbidden. The doors of these shops, which have no pivots at all and only rotate on holes as I wrote, are permitted even in the case of house doors to remove and replace them, because in such a manner they do not resemble building at all, and there is no concern that one might insert them firmly.

And know that all this is explained in Beitzah (11b) on the Mishnah concerning the removal of shutters. And the Jerusalem Talmud there states (in Halacha 5): "Provided that he does not replace them completely." The decisors omitted this, and wrote that since it does not appear in our Talmud, we do not concern ourselves with it (see Beit Yosef). It is perplexing to say so, for we learn many laws from the Jerusalem Talmud. Therefore, there is one who says that the Jerusalem Talmud refers to when they have two hinges (Korban HaEdah there). This, too, is strained, as the Jerusalem Talmud does not mention hinges at all. To me, it seems that the Jerusalem Talmud explains the Mishnah concerning shutters: it is not about doors, but rather many boards that are slotted and inserted into large holes above in the lintel and below in the threshold. When they are removed, the boards are taken out of the holes. When they are replaced, they are put back into the holes. Therefore, it is said that they should not be inserted completely. And the proof: for it says there regarding the law of salting the shutters, and "salting" is a term of adhesion, meaning that the boards are glued to one another. For with hinges, the term "completely" does not apply, as one must necessarily place them on the hinges, and they settle properly. But with boards, one can set them evenly like a building or unevenly. According to this, the law is not different but rather the explanation of the Mishnah. And another proof for this: it says there in the Jerusalem Talmud: when there is no doorway, they permitted it. But when there is a doorway, one should use the doorway, see there. For in our Talmud, shutters mean a doorway. According to our explanation of the Jerusalem Talmud, it makes sense, that there is a doorway by itself, and the removal of the boards by itself. According to this, the law should be ruled according to the Jerusalem Talmud.

Utensils that are not made of one piece and are not joined together but rather separate, such as a lamp made of segments, or a chair and table made of separate pieces—one may assemble them on Yom Tov. This is provided that one does not tighten them strongly. Even if they are not loose, it is permitted. Although on Shabbat it is forbidden even if they are not loose, as I wrote in Siman 313, on Yom Tov it is permitted because there is no building or dismantling of utensils in this manner, as it is not considered complete construction when one does not tighten them strongly. However, tightening them strongly is forbidden. Similarly, if they have letters written on them, and when they are separated the letters are disrupted, and when reassembled the letters return to their place—it is forbidden, as this is akin to writing and erasing. See what I wrote in Siman 340 (Magen Avraham, subsection 4).

To permit, to annul, and to cut seals on utensils and on the ground, and to break locks — their laws on Shabbat are clarified in Siman 314, and likewise on Yom Tov. Similarly, to cut straw, or a splinter, or hay, or aromatic wood — their laws on Yom Tov are the same as on Shabbat, as clarified in Siman 322. And if a non-Jew brought a sealed letter, if there are no letters on it — it is permitted to break it open, but if there are letters — it is forbidden to open it (Taz at the end of this Siman). However, tearing the paper is forbidden, as causing damage is forbidden initially. But breaking the seal is merely a way of opening it. (And this is also the intention of the Magen Avraham, Section 4. The words of the Gr"a need further examination, see there.)

The pleats that women make in the sleeves of their arms and in the hems of their skirts – it is prohibited to make them on Yom Tov, because it is considered as if fixing a vessel. Similarly, it is prohibited to make pleats in the necklace that is on the neck, which is called a "collar." And this prohibition specifically applies to folding with pleats, but general folding – we have no issue with that. Similarly, what was explained earlier in Siman 302 regarding the folding of garments on Shabbat – it also applies in situations where precise folding similar to pleats and the like is required. And look at what I wrote there concerning the folding of synagogue prayer shawls.
To honor the house – its laws on Shabbat apply equally on Yom Tov, as explained in Siman 337. And there it is clarified that for us, who have tiled floors – it is certainly permitted, see there.

If someone has fruits and sees rain coming and fears loss, the sages permitted him to lower the fruits through a skylight in the roof, bringing them down with a rope so they fall to the ground, or to simply throw them down to the ground. Although this involves effort and a weekday-like activity, they permitted it due to the potential loss. However, without the risk of loss, this is not permitted. And even in the case of potential loss, they only permitted lowering them through a roof skylight, which is merely lowering, not lifting, which would be excessive effort. Therefore, it is forbidden to lower them through the windows in the wall, because there one needs to lift them up to the window and then lower them. Therefore, if they were placed at a height near the window, where only lowering is involved, it is permitted. One should not bring them down using ladders or stairs, whether with a rope or without a rope. Nor should one move them from roof to roof, even if they are at the same height, because of the effort involved. And even if they are stored in a warehouse, and even to complete the storage, it is permitted due to the potential loss (Magen Avraham, subsection 1, in the name of the Rashi, see there). Some dispute this (see Beit Yosef). And see what I wrote in Siman 333.

It is permitted to cover fruits, or barrels of wine, or bricks, to protect from leakage. They allowed this to prevent loss. Placing a vessel under the leakage - as its law is on Shabbat, so is its law on Yom Tov, and this is explained in Siman 320.

A blind person should not go out with his cane when he can walk without it in a place where carrying is prohibited on Shabbat; nor should a shepherd go out with his bag. And even though there is no prohibition of carrying on Yom Tov, nevertheless, this would be considered a mundane activity. However, in a place where carrying is permitted, such as in a courtyard or a city with an eruv, it does not appear as a mundane activity. The same applies to a lame person: if he can walk without a cane, it is forbidden for him to go out with a cane in a public domain or a karmelis. But if he cannot, it is permitted. See above in Siman 301 regarding Shabbat.

One may not go out in a chair, whether a man or a woman – that is to say, sitting in a chair carried by people – because it appears as a weekday activity, unless one cannot walk in any other manner. And a person needed by the public is permitted, even if he can walk but it is difficult for him, due to the pressure on the community, or if he is elderly and walking is burdensome for him. He may even be carried on the shoulder, where each person places their hand on the shoulder of the other, and the chair is on them, as this is more of a weekday activity. Even in a canopy-like structure, for a person needed by the public, it is permitted. (See Tur, Taz, and Magen Avraham. Nowadays this is not common at all, and there is no need to elaborate on this.) One whose leg muscles have contracted may go out with a cane. One may not lead an animal with a stick. This is not due to the prohibition of muktzeh, as even with a stick prepared for this purpose from the day before, it is prohibited. The reason is that it appears as if he is leading it to the market to sell, as they lead in this manner.

We conclude in the Gemara (23a) that it is permitted to scrape and scrub an animal. Rashi explains that this refers to dragging the animal with a scraper. "Kirud" refers to a metal scraper, which could potentially cause a wound. Nevertheless, we are not concerned about this because an unintended action is permitted. "Kirutzuf" refers to a wooden scraper, which cannot cause a wound, and it must be done in a manner that avoids the risk of pulling out hair. For if there is a risk, as with our combs, it is obviously forbidden because it constitutes an inevitable result (psik reisha), just as it is forbidden to comb one's hair with a comb. The Tur also writes that with our combs, it is an inevitable result and therefore forbidden, see there, and the Shulchan Aruch writes similarly.

And the Rambam in his commentary on the Mishnah, as well as the Aruch, explained a different interpretation: that we are not discussing the dragging of hair at all, as this is certainly forbidden. Rather, the meaning is as follows: there are flies that stick to the thighs of animals and cling to them. Some of these flies are small, and when they are removed, it is possible that a wound may be caused. There are larger ones that will not cause a wound. Therefore, it is permitted even with the smaller ones because this is an unintended action. I do not know how they permitted handling the flies, as they are muktzeh (set aside, i.e., objects that cannot be moved on Shabbat). It is possible that they permitted it due to the suffering of animals. Or it is possible that they are moved with another object, which constitutes indirect handling for a permissible purpose, namely for the sake of the animal, which is a permitted thing. This seems to me to be the correct interpretation.

One may not assist the birth of an animal on Yom Tov. However, one may support it, by holding the newborn so that it does not fall to the ground. And even though it is forbidden to slaughter it today, and it is considered muktzeh (set aside), nevertheless, they permitted it because of the great suffering. Furthermore, if its term has been completed, one may slaughter it today. One may blow into its nostrils and put a teat into its mouth. If an animal has distanced its newborn, it is permitted to sprinkle its afterbirth water on it and to place a handful of salt into its womb in order that it will have mercy on its newborn. For an impure animal, one may not do this, because an impure animal does not distance its newborn, and if it does, it will not come close again (Shabbat 128a). The afterbirth water is certainly muktzeh. Nevertheless, they permitted it because of the suffering, or possibly through another method, as I wrote in the previous section.

One does not climb a tree on Yom Tov, as a decree lest one pluck [something]. Nor does one ride an animal, as a decree lest one cut a branch. And in the Jerusalem Talmud, it is said because of the resting of one's animal, and we have explained this in Siman 246; see there and in Siman 305 whether there is a requirement for the resting of one's animal or not. Nor does one swim on the water, as a decree lest one make a swimmer's barrel. This is a vessel made of papyrus that is shaped like a barrel, and one learns to swim with it.

And we do not clap, that is, striking the palm on the thigh, nor do we slap, striking palm to palm, whether one does this out of anger or out of joy, as a decree lest one come to repair a musical instrument. And the Rambam explains that it refers to making music by striking a cymbal. Likewise, we do not dance for this reason, but it is customary to be lenient regarding dancing (Levush). And it seems to me that we are also not careful about clapping palm to palm, and perhaps the reason is because we are not proficient in repairing musical instruments.

One does not judge cases, nor impose bans like those of the priests, nor consecrate items, nor evaluate valuations, nor raise tithes. Similarly, one does not betroth a woman, nor bring her into the wedding canopy, nor perform levirate marriage or the chalitzah ceremony. It is forbidden to betroth even if one does not have a wife and children. Rabbeinu Tam holds that in such a case it is permitted, but this is not the opinion of Rashi, Rambam, and the Rosh. One may not divorce even with a get (divorce document) that was written on the eve of a festival and through an agent. However, in the case of a dying person, where we see that the world is pressing upon him, and she might remain bound to the yavam (levir), he can give her a get even on Shabbat, and certainly on a festival. (And what is implied in Ketubot 47a that there is a wedding canopy on Shabbat – this is from the Torah. See Magen Avraham and Eliyah Rabbah).

The Tur writes that in all these cases, whether done inadvertently or intentionally, what was done remains effective. Thus far is his wording. And we do not say in this case "if it was done, it is not effective," as I wrote in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 234 regarding a sale on Shabbat. And see what I wrote in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 230 (and see Taz).

We learn in the Talmud, Shabbat (148b): It was stated: Regarding a loan on a festival, meaning that he loaned him food, drink, or any other item needed for the festival, Rabba said: It is allowed to be claimed in court, because if it were not allowed, people would refrain from lending, and this would lead to a lack of joy on the festival. Rav Yosef said: It is not allowed to be claimed in court, because if you say it is allowed to be claimed, it would lead to writing. And what should he do? He should take a pledge. And privately, he admits that it is allowed to be claimed, and he can seize it. And if the other person comes and takes it back from him, it is taken from him in court, because he has stolen from him, since it was rightfully taken (Ran, see there). And Rabba's reasoning is that even though one can lend with a pledge, nevertheless, perhaps he has no pledge, or he does not want to give a pledge, and the joy of the festival will be nullified. And privately, perhaps it will not be possible for him to seize from him, and based on this, he will also not want to give.

And the law is that the Tosafot ruled according to Rabbah, that it is given to be claimed in a court of law. Similarly, the Rambam in the fourth chapter, see there. But the Rif wrote two opinions: there are those who ruled according to Rabbah, and there are those who ruled according to Rav Yosef. And even though the law usually follows Rabbah over Rav Yosef, the Rif has the version of Rava, see there. And the Rif did not decide, and it is surprising that the Tur wrote that the Rif ruled according to Rav Yosef. Consequently, we hold that it is given to be claimed.

And the Rambam wrote there: Charity collectors may collect from the courtyards on a festival. However, they should not announce it as they do on a weekday but rather collect discreetly, placing it into their bosom, and distribute it to each neighborhood separately. This is his language, and so wrote the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch. This is from the Jerusalem Talmud. And even though one may announce for a mitzvah even on Shabbat, as I wrote in Siman 306 – here it is different since it is possible to do it discreetly (Magen Avraham). According to this, if it is not possible to do it discreetly, it is permitted publicly and with an announcement, for otherwise, the poor would not have the means for the joy of the festival.

A corpse that is awaiting burial: If it is the first day of a festival, since we are knowledgeable about the fixing of the month and the first day is certainly a festival, Jews should not handle the corpse in any way, even if there are no non-Jews available to handle it. Even if the person died on the eve of the festival and they did not manage to bury him, and even if the next day is Shabbat, nonetheless, Jews are forbidden to handle the corpse, even if it will decompose, Heaven forbid. For the burial of the dead does not override the positive and negative commandments of the festival. It has already been explained at the beginning of Siman 526 that the festival involves both a positive and a negative commandment. Therefore, efforts should be made to keep the body in a cool place so that it does not decompose. There is an opinion that permits purifying the body and placing it in a coffin if there is a concern that it will decompose (Sha'arei Teshuva in the name of Shvut Yaakov).

However, we bury him on the first day of Yom Tov through a non-Jew, even if he died today and tomorrow is not Shabbat, and he will not decompose until tomorrow – nevertheless, it is a mitzvah to bury him today through a non-Jew. For this is his honor, that he be buried immediately, and it is forbidden to delay his burial until the second day of Yom Tov so that Jews may handle it. Not all tasks are performed by a non-Jew, but only the digging of the grave, the sewing of the shrouds, and the making of the coffin. But the heating of the water to purify him, the purification itself, the dressing in the shrouds, the removal from his house to the cemetery, and placing him in the grave – these are done by Jews. Afterwards, the non-Jew covers the grave with earth, not the Jew. And it is preferable to purify him using straw, on leather or on a board, and not with sheets and towels, items that might lead to wringing.

The reasoning behind this matter is that it is certainly more respectful for the deceased that Jews should do everything possible for him. And rabbinical prohibitions are waived in regard to the deceased on a festival. Therefore, heating water is permitted on a festival, because once it is permitted for a need, it is also permitted for a non-need. There is certainly some need for the deceased. How much more so for purification and dressing in shrouds, even though the deceased is considered muktzeh (set aside), it is permitted in respect for the deceased. Transporting to the cemetery—here too, we say "since it was permitted" regarding carrying. But digging the grave is a Torah prohibition, as is sewing the shrouds and making the coffin—we tell non-Jews to do it. And instructing a non-Jew is permitted in respect of the deceased. However, returning the earth is a Torah prohibition, for one who fills a hole is liable for "building". Therefore, it should be done by a non-Jew. It seems to me that heating the water should also be done by a non-Jew, because according to the Rambam, as we wrote in Siman 492, we only say "since it was permitted" regarding carrying and kindling, and not other labors. Thus, although kindling can be done by a Jew, boiling the water is forbidden unless the water is also used for washing dishes on the festival, which is a festival need. See what I wrote at the end of Section 12.

And if you ask: if so, why is the deceased not buried on Shabbat and Yom Kippur by non-Jews, and let the non-Jews carry the deceased to the cemetery, since rabbinic prohibitions were permitted for the sake of honor? Indeed, it is not so, for on Shabbat and Yom Kippur, they should not engage with the deceased at all, even by a non-Jew, and even to carry him out by them and place him in a niche prepared from the day before. The reason is that it is not an honor for the deceased that Shabbat should be desecrated because of him, and it is a disgrace to him. This is not the case on Yom Tov, where the Torah permits many types of work. Therefore, there is no disgrace for him even in digging the grave, sewing the shrouds, and making the coffin, which are not permitted on Yom Tov. Nevertheless, since cooking, lighting a fire, and carrying are completely permitted on Yom Tov, there is no disgrace for him in other types of work, as the desecration is not so apparent. But not on Shabbat, and on Shabbat, only moving him from the sun to the shade by means of a loaf of bread or a child is permitted, as I wrote in Siman 311.

And know that there are those who hold that what is stated in the Gemara (Beitzah 6a) that if someone dies on the first day of Yom Tov, non-Jews should take care of the burial, applies only if the deceased has been delayed, such as if he died yesterday or if tomorrow is Shabbat, and there is a concern that the body will decompose. But if someone dies on the first day of Yom Tov and the next day is not Shabbat, they should wait until the next day. This is how they interpret the Gemara (see Beit Yosef). This is also the opinion of Rashi in Shabbat (139a). Therefore, there are those who have written in this manner: In places where there is no established custom, it is proper not to bury on the first day of Yom Tov by a non-Jew, unless the body has been delayed or there will be a need to delay it, or it is swollen. Some of the rabbis wrote similarly. And a small child, even after thirty days, may be kept in a cellar, and it is not considered a disgrace among the living as it is with an adult deceased. Therefore, it is better not to bury him on the first day of Yom Tov. This is the wording of the Magen Avraham (section 4, citing Yam Shel Shlomo). However, the custom is not like this, since according to the Rif, the Rambam, our rabbis the Tosafists, the Rosh, the Tur, the Shulchan Aruch, and the majority of our rabbis, they agreed that even if the body was not delayed, it can be buried on the first day of Yom Tov by a non-Jew. Therefore, the simple custom is to do so, and it should not be changed. And a miscarriage is forbidden even on the second day of Yom Tov, as will be explained in section 17.

If one dies on the second day of Yom Tov, Jews may deal with the burial, for the Rabbis equated the second day of Yom Tov to a weekday regarding a deceased person. This applies even to the two days of Rosh Hashanah (as stated in the Gemara), because we are knowledgeable about the calendar, and it is only a rabbinic ordinance to observe two days of Yom Tov. Therefore, concerning a deceased person, they treated it as a Biblical matter, even if the body has not been left unburied for an extended period. Even non-essential matters, like cutting myrtle from a plant if such is the custom for the deceased, are permitted. Certainly, one may dig a grave, make a coffin and shrouds, heat water to purify the body, and cut the hair if that is the custom. The Rabbis entirely equated it to a weekday. If there is no burial place for Jews in that city, the body can be transported to another city, even beyond the twelve-mile limit and with the use of an animal. Similarly, if it is necessary to cross a river, one may hire a boat to transport the body, and people may travel there, for it is entirely considered like a weekday. Therefore, even if it is possible to use non-Jews, Jews should perform the tasks, except for building the arch over the grave, which is not to be done on Yom Tov as it can be done after Yom Tov. However, it seems to me that one should not desecrate Yom Tov more than necessary; why should many people desecrate Yom Tov if they are not essential? And even if the burial is outside the boundary or involves traveling by boat, only those necessary for the burial should go, and no more. Even close relatives should not desecrate Yom Tov if they are not needed for the deceased. See Section 15.

And all this applies when they want to bury him on the same day. But if they do not wish to bury him until the next day, for some reason, the festival does not override this at all. Even on the second day of the festival, and even instructing a non-Jew is not permitted, except to move him, as moving is permitted in this case, for this is necessary for every deceased. But to heat water is forbidden, as this is not considered a need at all if he is not being buried on the same day. There are those who are hesitant even about moving him, and it is good to move him using a loaf of bread or a child, as on Shabbat. And to carry him into a public domain is certainly forbidden. (See Magen Avraham, subsection 11, that cutting his hair is permitted because it is not considered cutting at all, but it is good to be stringent.)

And know that all things permitted to be done by a Jew – there is no distinction between relatives and non-relatives, between members of the community and other individuals, for once it is permitted, it is permitted for all Jews. And some have written that it is also permissible to be done by many people, even though it can be done by a few (Gra, Section 11). However, I do not understand why we should increase the number of people needlessly. This is not respectful to the deceased, and why should people who are not necessary for this desecrate Yom Tov? And indeed, the second day of Yom Tov – the Rabbis treated it like a weekday, but this is according to the necessity of the deceased, not for what is unnecessary. The laws of the recitation of Shema and prayer on the first and second days of Yom Tov are explained above in Siman 71. The other laws of mourning and bereavement will be explained later in Siman 548 and in Yoreh De'ah Siman 340 and Siman 399. See there, and see at the end of Section 11.

And know that it is stated in the Talmud (Shabbat 139b) that in places where people are not Torah scholars, one should not bury the dead on the second day of Yom Tov by Jews, so as not to treat the second day of Yom Tov with disrespect. It is also stated in Beitzah there that nowadays, when there are oppressors, a nation that forces Jews to do their work, and on Yom Tov they avoid this by saying it is forbidden for us to work; therefore, when they see that Jews bury their dead on the second day of Yom Tov, they will decree that Jews should do their work. Therefore, one should not bury the dead there on the second day of Yom Tov by Jews. Based on these matters, Rabbeinu Tam reprimanded a city that buried on the second day of Yom Tov by Jews, since they were not Torah scholars. And Rabbi Yitzchak of the Tosafot said that in several matters we find that they were concerned for those who are not Torah scholars, such as something that can be eaten raw regarding its cooking. And we do not worry about this and similar things, and we consider ourselves Torah scholars. However, Rabbeinu Tam was also concerned that the authorities would impose some work on the Jews under their control, as now there are those who are enslaved, as explained in Tosafot and the Rosh there. Nevertheless, the Rif and Rambam ruled simply on this law, that on the second day of Yom Tov it is permitted by Jews. And so did most of our Rabbis.

Nevertheless, there are those who are concerned with the opinion of Rabbeinu Tam. And this is what Rabbeinu the Rema wrote in section 4, and this is his language: But in Ashkenaz and these countries, the custom is not so. Rather, wherever it is possible to use a non-Jew, we do so: the grave, the coffin, and the shrouds are made by a non-Jew. The other matters are done by Jews, just like on the first day of Yom Tov. But if it is not possible with a non-Jew, everything is done by Jews. Until here is his language. And they also wrote that it is permitted to purify the body on the second day of Yom Tov with a sheet and towels, and it is not necessary to use straw as on the first day of Yom Tov, since all forms of labor are permitted—we are not concerned that they might wring them out, because even if they do wring them out, there is no prohibition. They should only be careful not to intentionally wring them out (Magen Avraham, subsection 9, in the name of the Yam Shel Shlomo). And this is the proper way to act. And even now, we dig the grave through a non-Jew when it is possible to obtain one. However, sewing the shrouds is difficult for non-Jews, as they do not know how to sew them. But on the first day of Yom Tov, we must show them and have them do it. But on the second day of Yom Tov, it is not worth the excessive effort, and the women sew them themselves.

And know: Even though according to the Talmudic law it is permissible on the second day of Yom Tov to do everything by a Jew, nevertheless, some are stringent regarding returning the soil into the grave and filling it, and they make a small mound above it like the manner of graves. This is forbidden even on the second day of Yom Tov according to Talmudic law by a Jew, because this is not for the need of the deceased. It suffices to fill the grave with soil, and not to raise it above. And this is what our master the Rema wrote there, and this is his language: "But it is permissible to cover it with soil as is done on weekdays." Unlike those who are stringent. Until here are his words, meaning: Our master the Rema disagrees with those who forbid, and it seems to him that it is also permissible to make a small mound on it just like on weekdays (Taz, small section 2), because this is the completion of the burial (Magen Avraham, small section 10 in the name of the Beit Yosef). And on the first day of Yom Tov, it is obvious that it is forbidden (Taz there), only through a non-Jew. And even on the second day of Yom Tov, according to our custom that the digging of the grave is done by a non-Jew, it is also forbidden by a Jew (Magen Avraham there). And the Levush wrote that on the second day of Yom Tov, some forbid and some permit, and it is permissible to be lenient. Until here are his words. And perhaps he believes that there is no biblical prohibition in this (see there in Magen Avraham and it requires further investigation). They also wrote: In a place where the custom is to bury by a Jew, others should not dig, except for members of the group who are accustomed to digging. And all the more so, others should not throw soil to close the grave, because whatever can be minimized in desecration, we minimize. And some permit, because the sages equated it to a weekday (there). And in my humble opinion, the main ruling is like the first opinion, that anything that is not necessary for the deceased, the sages did not equate it to a weekday, as I wrote in section 8.

Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote in Section 5: "One who digs a grave for the deceased on the second day of Yom Tov is permitted to take payment." This is his language, and his reasoning: since the Sages equated it with a weekday, it follows that it is permitted just like on a weekday. However, there are those who are puzzled by this: while it is true that concerning the deceased, they equated it with a weekday, this does not apply to other matters. Therefore, there is someone who prohibits it, and even if one cannot obtain the service for free, he should deceive him in this manner, as with chalitzah (Magen Avraham, Subsection 12, in the name of Yam Shel Shlomo). That is to say: promise him payment but do not give it to him, for it is forbidden to take payment on Yom Tov. In my humble opinion, Rabbeinu Beit Yosef's view seems correct, for if so, when a deceased happens to need burial on another Yom Tov, no one will be found to perform it. And this is the main reason for the allowance: to find someone who is willing to profit and take payment. For without payment, everyone would say: "Why should I dig on Yom Tov? You dig!" Certainly, in a place where there are known gravediggers, Rabbeinu Beit Yosef did not permit it, for it is their duty, and they can be compelled. But in a place where there are no gravediggers, Rabbeinu Beit Yosef permitted it appropriately. Also, there is no Yom Tov payment issue here, for payment for a mitzvah is allowed even on Shabbat, as I wrote in Siman 682 (Magen Avraham there). And even the regular gravediggers are customarily paid after Yom Tov, so as not to close the door on such a matter. However, with us, in any case, the grave is dug by a non-Jew, as explained. And it is clear that to buy shrouds, if from a Jewish storekeeper, one should take without measure and without a fixed price. But if it is necessary to take from a non-Jewish storekeeper, and he will not agree in such a manner, it is permitted and obligatory to buy from him with measure, a fixed price, and payment, if no other way is possible, for the Sages equated it with a weekday. And even on the first day of Yom Tov, it seems to me it is permitted if necessary, for they permitted rabbinic prohibitions on the first day of Yom Tov for the deceased, as I wrote in Section 3. Nevertheless, I am uncertain about this: although they permitted the moving of a deceased who is muktzeh, as I wrote there, perhaps they did not permit the rabbinic prohibition of buying and selling. This requires further study for a definitive ruling. Therefore, it is better to give him a pledge, and after Yom Tov, pay him as he demands. (See Taz, Subsection 3, and this requires further study.)

It is permitted to accompany the deceased on the first day of a festival within the Shabbat boundary, and on the second day of the festival even beyond the boundary, and they may return to their place on the same day. They do not have the same status as those who go beyond the boundary, who are limited to four cubits, because since they acted with the permission that the Sages granted to accompany the deceased, it automatically follows that their status is like all those who go out with permission and can return to their place, as I have written in section 407. And even though there they only have two thousand cubits from their place in all directions, here, even if they are several domains away, it is necessary to permit them to enter the city. Otherwise, they would not want to accompany the deceased, and this would be a shame for the deceased. Even if today they accompany the deceased without knowing that we will forbid them to return to the city, and then we tell them that they are forbidden to return to their homes if they are further than two domains, nevertheless, you are causing them to stumble in the future when another death occurs (and this is the intention of the Magen Avraham, subsection 13). And it is obvious that if they have two paths before them, one permitted and one beyond the boundary, like an archer and a bow as explained in the laws of boundaries, they should take the permitted path (there).

And similarly, it is permitted to return burial tools that were taken outside the Shabbat boundary with them, because if we do not permit them to return the tools, they will not want to take them along, similar to the previous reason (and so wrote the Gra in section 15, see there) that they are concerned lest they be stolen. However, for this reason, it is sufficient to leave them in a house near the city, if they are guarded there against thieves. But the Ramban, of blessed memory, wrote that they are not considered muktzeh, because they might be needed for another deceased person on that same day (see Beit Yosef). And if so, since outside the Shabbat boundary it is necessary to bring them back for the aforementioned reason, because if not, they will not take them along, it follows that it is also permitted to return them to their homes, since they are not muktzeh. (And the wording of the Magen Avraham in section 14 is very perplexing, see there and in Machatzit Hashekel. And the Gra did not mention it at all, see there.)

Those who accompany the deceased are prohibited from riding an animal, even on the second day of Yom Tov, or from traveling by ship (Magen Avraham, subsection 15). Even though these are rabbinic prohibitions, nevertheless, there is a degradation of the sanctity of Yom Tov involved, and it is not respectful to the deceased. It is better not to accompany the deceased than to do so in a manner that degrades Yom Tov. However, those who are burying the deceased, if it is not possible for them to do so without riding or traveling by ship, are permitted to do so on the second day of Yom Tov but not on the first day of Yom Tov. The second day of Yom Tov is considered like a weekday in all matters, which is not the case for the first day of Yom Tov. Even if it is possible that other rabbinic prohibitions were permitted on the first day of Yom Tov, in this case, such a prohibition, which is conspicuous, was not permitted, and the deceased should not be buried today. Even on the second day of Yom Tov, they should not ride within the city if they can walk there. Additionally, it would be a desecration of Yom Tov in the presence of non-Jews. Sitting in a wagon is similar to riding. (As for the question raised by the Taz in subsection 4 on what the Shulchan Aruch wrote, that riding is permitted only when it is impossible otherwise - even when it is possible, since it is a rabbinic prohibition, see there; it is not difficult at all, because riding is different due to the evident degradation of Yom Tov, as I have written and as the Magen Avraham wrote in subsection 15, see there.)

If it becomes known to the inhabitants of a certain city that a Jew has died and his body is lying in a place four or five days away, and it has not been buried, even though they will not be able to reach the body until after the festival, nevertheless it is permitted to set out on the journey on the second day of Yom Tov in order to hasten the burial. And even though it has been explained that any deceased person who cannot be buried on the same day is not treated by the Rabbis as if it were a weekday – this is only when the body is not lying in disgrace. If so, what they wish to do today can be done tomorrow. But when the body is lying in disgrace, the Rabbis treated it as a weekday with regard to hastening the burial. All the more so if there is a concern that dogs might eat the body. There are those who disagree and forbid this, arguing that since the burial cannot take place on the same day, it is not permitted. However, the primary opinion is to be lenient, in accordance with the first opinion (Magen Avraham, Small Section 17).

It is forbidden to bury a stillborn on Yom Tov (a Jewish festival), as its burial does not override Yom Tov, not even the second day of Yom Tov. Rather, one should leave it until the next day, as there is no commandment to bury a stillborn, and Yom Tov is not set aside for its burial needs. This is what our teacher, the Rema, wrote in section 10. And they challenged him: Certainly, one must bury stillborns, as we say in Niddah (57a) that the Samaritans would not bury their stillborns, see there – implying that Israelites do bury them (Magen Avraham, section 20). But to me it seems, on the contrary, that this is proof that there is no Torah commandment to bury it, and therefore the Samaritans were not concerned with this. But rabbinically, there is certainly an obligation, and the Samaritans were not careful with rabbinical laws. Therefore, Yom Tov, which is rabbinic, is not overridden, because the burial itself is also rabbinic – a rabbinic command does not override another rabbinic command (and the passage in Niddah must be reconciled accordingly).

Nevertheless, if an infant dies within thirty days but its hair and nails have fully developed, it is presumed to be viable and its status is like that of an adult who has died, even though we do not know if it completed its months. For most women give birth to viable offspring, as we circumcise him on Shabbat with the presumption of viability. This implies that the Torah considers every infant to be presumed viable, as it commanded circumcision on Shabbat. And even though in any case we circumcise him: if he is not viable, it is merely like cutting flesh, as we say in Shabbat (135a), nevertheless, since the Torah decreed to circumcise him even on Shabbat, if it were not for the presumption of viability, the Torah would not have decreed circumcision specifically on Shabbat. Therefore, even when he dies, he is like an adult who has died. (This seems to me, in my humble opinion, to explain and resolve the serious question raised by the Magen Avraham in subsection 19; see there.) There are those who prohibit. In my humble opinion, the primary view is the first one, since rabbinically, in any case, it is certainly a mitzvah to bury him, as I have written.

Our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in paragraph 10: "Stillborns that have the custom to remove their foreskin with a stone or a reed – it is forbidden even on the second day of Yom Tov in the diaspora." Thus ends his words, meaning: It has been clarified that an infant who dies within thirty days is not presumed to be a stillborn, and we bury him on the second day of Yom Tov by a Jew, or on the first day of Yom Tov by a non-Jew – this is if he died after circumcision. But before circumcision – it is necessary to postpone it until the next day, as the person who circumcises him should not be embarrassed there. And circumcising him on Yom Tov – it is forbidden, as this is not by law, but merely a custom based on the Midrash, and it does not override Yom Tov. And although it involves merely cutting flesh, nevertheless it does not override Yom Tov. Therefore, even with a complete stillborn, whose hair and nails have not finished developing, it is forbidden to bury him, as I have written. But by a non-Jew – certainly, it is permitted. However, with a male who needs to be circumcised – it is necessary to postpone it until the next day because of the circumcision, and it is inappropriate to have him circumcised by a non-Jew, for it is a disgrace to him. (This appears to be my humble opinion, and see Magen Avraham, section 20).

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote in paragraph 8 that it is permissible to bring a deceased person on the second day of Yom Tov from outside the boundary into the city to bury him in a Jewish cemetery, even though it would have been possible to bury him in his place. This is his language: Since there is no communal cemetery there, even though it is possible to bury him there in a field by himself, this is not respectful to the deceased. And even from one city to another, it is permitted to transport him if there is no communal cemetery in the city where he died. However, if there is a communal cemetery there, but he left a will to be buried in his ancestral burial plots elsewhere, even though his will should be fulfilled as I wrote in Yoreh De'ah, section 363, nevertheless, Yom Tov is not overridden in this case, and they should wait until after Yom Tov. But if there is concern that he will begin to decompose, they may bury him here, and after Yom Tov, they may exhume him and transport him to his ancestral burial plots (Magen Avraham, subsection 18 in the name of Yam Shel Shlomo).

One does not tear [their garments] for the deceased even on the second day of Yom Tov, even relatives who are obligated in tearing [their garments] and mourning. Instead, they should tear after Yom Tov. And if [the deceased] passed away on the night of the second day of Yom Tov, they bury him in the morning before the prayer, so that the mourners can pray. And if he passed away during the day, they bury him after the meal. Among us, it is not possible to advance the burial so much before the prayer, but rather after the prayer, even if he passed away at night. And also, if he passed away during the day, they bury him before eating. And according to the custom, so shall they do. The law of "Tziduk HaDin" on Yom Tov is explained in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 340. And the law of mourning will be explained in Siman 548 (see Magen Avraham, section 21).

The matter of Eruvei Tavshilin, as it appears in Pesachim (46b): According to Torah law, the needs of Shabbat may be prepared on Yom Tov, as it is written (Exodus 12:16): "But that which every person must eat." And Shabbat and Yom Tov are considered one sanctity, as both are called "Shabbat." Just as it is permissible to cook on the day itself, it is permissible to cook for the next day (Rashi). The Sages, however, instituted a decree lest people say: one may bake on Yom Tov even for a weekday. Since they required Eruvei Tavshilin, it serves as a reminder, see there. This is also explained in the words of the Rambam at the beginning of Chapter Six, where he writes: "On a Yom Tov that falls on the eve of Shabbat, one may not bake or cook on Yom Tov for Shabbat." This prohibition is rabbinic, so that one will not come to cook on Yom Tov for a weekday. It is a fortiori reasoning: if one may not cook for Shabbat, how much more so for a weekday... so far his language. And one should not ask: we hold that preparation is a Torah prohibition, and Yom Tov does not prepare for Shabbat, as I wrote in Siman 513? Because this is not the case, as this refers to preparation by the hands of Heaven, such as an egg laid on Yom Tov and similar cases, and not to prepared dishes that merely need cooking and baking (Tosafot at the beginning of Beitzah). Additionally, this has no connection to the Talmudic dispute whether Shabbat and Yom Tov are one sanctity or two sanctities, as this pertains to rabbinic matters such as Eruv, muktzeh, and nolad, and similar cases. But according to Torah law, they are one sanctity, and according to Torah law, the needs of Shabbat may be prepared on Yom Tov.

However, some of our Rabbis have said that we do not hold that the needs of Shabbat may be prepared on Yom Tov. This is because the one who says this in the Gemara does not hold of the principle of "ho'il" ("since"). But according to the one who does hold of "ho'il", the permission is because "since guests may come, it is fit for them," as is explicitly stated in the Gemara. And we hold according to the opinion that says "ho'il". Therefore, one who bakes from Yom Tov for a weekday is not liable to lashes. And even though it is due to "ho'il", nevertheless it is still a prohibition. However, through the use of an eruv tavshilin, the prohibition is permitted. (Ran there, and the glosses of the Maimonides there in the name of Tosafot and the Rabbis of France, and the Sefer Mitzvot Gadol in the laws of Yom Tov. And the Rambam holds that in this matter, Rabba and Rav Chisda did not disagree. See Beit Yosef. Examine and you will find clarity.)

There is a practical halachic difference between the reasons: According to the Rambam, it is permitted to cook from Yom Tov for Shabbat even close to nightfall, since, by Torah law, it is permitted, and he has set aside an Eruv Tavshilin. However, according to the reasoning of "ho'il" (since it could be used for guests), it is forbidden close to nightfall because it is not fit for guests. And since it is forbidden by Torah law, what good is the Eruv Tavshilin? This is also written by the Sefer Mitzvot Gadol (SeMaG) and similarly by the Magen Avraham at the beginning of this section. According to this, one should be careful not to cook on Yom Tov in the late afternoon before Shabbat. However, people are not careful about this. But in the Jerusalem Talmud at the beginning of the second chapter of Beitzah, it is explicitly like the Rambam, where it raises the question: "It is forbidden by Torah law, and Eruv Tavshilin permits it (in astonishment)?" Rabbi Abahu said: "In principle, it should be permitted to cook from Yom Tov to Shabbat. If you say so, one might also cook from Yom Tov to a weekday?" This is the same as the Talmud in Pesachim. (Moreover, it is perplexing to me: If you think it is because of "ho'il," how come the Talmud at the beginning of the second chapter of Beitzah did not mention the primary reason of the permissibility of "ho'il"? Especially since there is a dispute concerning "ho'il." But if it is permitted from the outset by law, there is no need to elaborate. And the Talmud that queries "from where do we know this," meaning that an Eruv Tavshilin is required, should have instead questioned: "How is it permitted with an Eruv Tavshilin?" as it questions in the Jerusalem Talmud. But if it is permitted from the outset, this is already stated in Pesachim. But with "ho'il," it is impossible to say this, because there is a dispute about "ho'il," and the Talmud there did not decide the law, so it should have clarified there that the law follows Rabbah, who says "ho'il." And furthermore, it is difficult: If it is permitted by Torah law because of "ho'il," then it should also be permitted for a weekday? And it is explicitly explained in the Rambam, chapter one, that by Torah law it is forbidden, but there is no flogging. See there. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

And the Rabbinic authorities based the Eruv Tavshilin on a Scriptural verse, as explained in the Gemara at the beginning of the second chapter (15b). Regarding its reasoning, Rava and Rav Ashi disagreed. Rava said that it is an ordinance for the sake of Shabbat, so that one should set aside a nice portion for Shabbat just as for Yom Tov, ensuring that everything is not consumed on Yom Tov which precedes Shabbat. Rav Ashi said that it is an ordinance for the sake of Yom Tov, so that people will say: if it is forbidden to cook for Shabbat without an Eruv Tavshilin, all the more so for a weekday. The Rosh wrote there that there is a practical difference between the reasons: according to Rava, it is specifically required to set aside the Eruv Tavshilin on the eve of Yom Tov, to ensure a nice portion for Shabbat. According to Rav Ashi, it can be done even before the eve of Yom Tov. The law follows Rav Ashi, as he is later. This is also the ruling in the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, section 14, such as on Sukkot which falls on Thursday, requiring an Eruv Tavshilin for Sukkot, and for Shemini Atzeret one can set it before Sukkot and rely on it also for Shemini Atzeret, provided the Eruv is intact and fit for consumption. This will be further explained with the help of Heaven.

And what is the meaning of the term "Eruv"? The Rambam writes there, and these are his words: Why is it called "Eruv"? Just as the eruv that is made in courtyards and alleyways before Shabbat is for the sake of distinction, so that one does not think it is permitted to carry from one domain to another on Shabbat, so too this cooked item is for the sake of distinction and remembrance, so that one does not think it is permitted to bake on Yom Tov for what is not to be eaten on that day... These are his words. According to him, the term "Eruv Tavshilin" is merely a borrowed name from "Eruvei Chatzerot." There, the intention is to combine domains to be as one, and this name was borrowed here because the matter is the same, for the sake of distinction. But the Raavad explained that here too it implies mixing, as it mixes Yom Tov and Shabbat to make them together. Similarly with boundaries, it mixes the boundaries that one could not walk, see there. And our Rabbi the Rema wrote in Section 1, and these are his words: The explanation of the matter of "Eruv" is that he cooks and bakes from Yom Tov for Shabbat, with what he has already cooked and baked before Yom Tov for Shabbat. And it turns out that he did not begin the work on Yom Tov, but only completed it. These are his words, meaning: Therefore it is called "Eruv," as it mixes the Shabbat dishes, those from before Yom Tov with those on Yom Tov, to indicate that on Yom Tov it is only the completion and not the start, as starting is forbidden on Yom Tov. And in this way, the prohibition is strengthened for everyone not to cook from Yom Tov to a weekday, for if it is forbidden for Shabbat, all the more so for a weekday.

Therefore, if a Yom Tov (festival) falls on a Friday, and one did not set an Eruv Tavshilin, it is forbidden to initially cook for Shabbat in a separate pot. For in one pot, he can cook as much as he wants, even in a manner of deceit, as I have written in Siman 503, and only in a separate pot is it forbidden. However, he can cook several pots for Yom Tov and say that he wants to eat from each pot, and he can eat from each pot and leave some for Shabbat from each pot. And with an Eruv, he cooks initially for Shabbat, due to the reasons we explained. And he can set this Eruv even at twilight, like the Eruv for courtyards. But if he has accepted Yom Tov, it is forbidden. And "Barechu" (the call to prayer) is not considered acceptance until after the Yom Tov prayer (Taz, Siman 3). And some say that "Barechu" is considered acceptance (Magen Avraham, Siman 1), and see what I wrote in Siman 261. And if he is in the synagogue and has not yet prayed Mincha, and if he goes home to make the Eruv Tavshilin, the time for Mincha will pass, and if he prays Mincha, the time for making the Eruv will pass—it is better to pray Mincha and not set the Eruv Tavshilin, and he should transfer ownership of his flour to others, as will be explained (there).

Maimonides, of blessed memory, wrote that this Eruv is not made with bread but with a cooked dish, see there. And it is explained that a cooked dish alone suffices, and so ruled Rashi, of blessed memory (17b, "like the Tanna"), the Sheiltot, and Rabbi Yitzchak of the Tosafot. For although Rabbi Eliezer says there that one may not bake except upon what is already baked, nor cook except upon what is already cooked, nevertheless Rabbi Yehoshua disagrees with him in the Jerusalem Talmud and says: one may bake and cook upon what is cooked. However, the Ba'al Halachot Gedolot and Rabbeinu Tam ruled that both bread and a cooked dish are required, since in the Talmud only Rabbi Eliezer's words are brought. The Tur and the Shulchan Aruch ruled in paragraph 2 that ideally, both bread and a cooked dish are required, but in a situation of necessity, a cooked dish alone suffices, as the law follows the majority of the decisors.

And the measure of the dish is an olive's bulk (kezayit), whether for one person, for a hundred, or for a thousand, whether at the beginning or at the end. That is to say: to place it at the beginning – an olive's bulk suffices. And if one placed a large amount and most of it was lost, leaving only a small amount – less than an olive's bulk is not sufficient (Talmud 16b). Consequently, for bread, for those who require bread – the measure is also an olive's bulk. Some decisors have brought from the Jerusalem Talmud: that bread is a volume of an egg (kebeitza), and the dish is an olive's bulk (see Beit Yosef). Based on this, our teacher the Rema wrote in section 3 that some require, initially, bread of a volume of an egg, and this is the custom initially. This is the end of his words. This means: that after the fact (bedi'eved), we do not require bread at all. However, we do not find this in our version of the Jerusalem Talmud. On the contrary, Rav says there an olive's bulk, and Rabbi Yochanan holds that even less than an olive's bulk suffices, see there. Also, the Jerusalem Talmud brings the opinion of Rabbi Yehoshua, that a dish alone suffices. However, since the decisors brought this – presumably this was their version in the Jerusalem Talmud, and initially one should be cautious about this. The Jerusalem Talmud speaks according to Rabbi Eliezer, and since we initially follow Rabbi Eliezer as I have written – we should act accordingly. It appears that for the Eruv Tavshilin – even a piece suffices, unlike the Eruv Chatzerot where a whole loaf is required. There, it is because of the concern of neighbors, which does not apply to the Eruv Tavshilin.

And this cooked dish must be suitable to eat with bread, such as meat, fish, eggs, and other types of cooked foods that are eaten with bread. Therefore, one cannot use porridge, which in our language is called kasha, for the eruv. And even if someone eats it with bread, his opinion is disregarded, because this is like eating bread with bread. Similarly, all types of condiments that are not eaten with bread, like preserves and the like, cannot be used for the eruv. It seems to me that a thick dish made of wheat or barley, as well as any types of fried foods made from flour, can be used for the eruv, because even though they are not eaten with bread, they themselves are considered like bread. Therefore, porridge made of wheat or barley can be used for the eruv. This is what seems to me, but Rashi of blessed memory explained in Berachot (36b) that porridge made of crushed wheat is not valid, implying that it doesn't work. We must say that this is because, logically, if it is considered a cooked dish, it must be customary to eat it with bread. And if it is not considered a cooked dish, then it is bread and does not work. According to this, all types of fried foods and all types of kasha do not work for the eruv tavshilin. And this is the law.

This dish that they mentioned: even roasted, even overly cooked, meaning it was not properly cooked or it was overcooked; even pickled in vinegar or mustard, or soaked in water from day to night, and it is good for eating since pickled is considered as cooked; and even smoked if it is good for eating – it is considered as cooked. And even with light cooking like mere rinsing, such as small fish of a type that are rinsed in hot water, and this is their final cooking for eating – one also fulfills the requirement with this, as it is considered cooking. And even things that are eaten raw, when they are cooked and used to accompany bread, such as apples and the like, if they are suitable to accompany bread. And even though regarding their cooking they do not have the status of cooked, and similarly things that are not served on a king's table like small fish, even though regarding their cooking they are not considered cooked – nonetheless for the purpose of Eruv Tavshilin it is considered cooking. And similarly all kinds of fruits and vegetables that are eaten raw, if they have been cooked and are customarily used to accompany bread – one can make an Eruv Tavshilin with them.

Now, pickling is not mentioned in the poskim, and it is explicitly clear that pickling does not work for the Eruv Tavshilin. Therefore, one cannot make an Eruv with it if it has not been cooked or fried. It is worse than soaking, for soaking in prohibitions is considered as cooking, while pickling is only considered as hot. And even though for an Eruv Tavshilin it is enough for it to be merely hot, and even if it is not hot at all, like small fish that through mere rinsing are considered as cooked – that is different, for that is their normal way of cooking. And indeed, one is liable for this on Shabbat, as it is taught in Shabbat (145b). But pickling is considered like raw. Nevertheless, I am puzzled by the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch, why they did not write that one cannot make an Eruv with pickling? For in all matters, when they speak of soaking, they also speak of pickling. And indeed, some of the great ones say that with pickling it is an Eruv, and if one placed an Eruv with pickling, it is valid (Sha'arei Teshuvah in the name of Chacham Tzvi). And furthermore, he wrote that whether with soaking or pickling – one should place it without a blessing, and only say "with this Eruv" (there). And I am puzzled, for it is explicitly proven in the Gemara (16a) that it does not work, for it says there that Rav said: Salted small fish do not have the law of their cooking. Rav Yosef said if a non-Jew roasted them – one relies on them for an Eruv Tavshilin, see there. And why did he not say the novelty that even with pickling one fulfills the Eruv Tavshilin? And it is forced to say that he teaches us that even when roasted they do not have the law of their cooking. Moreover, the Tosafot (chapter "Ein Ma'amidin" 38b s.v. "fish") explain that the term "salted" means if they were cooked afterward, which is a greater novelty than roasting. And in roasting – they do not at all read that a non-Jew roasted them, see there. Therefore, it is clear that one does not fulfill the Eruv Tavshilin with pickling (and so wrote the Magen Avraham, subparagraph 3). And with soaking, one must certainly bless, since it is stated so in the Gemara and in the Rambam, Tur, and Shulchan Aruch. (Although in the Tosefta, the second chapter does not mention soaking, see there, nevertheless since it is explicit in the Talmud – what do we have to do with the Tosefta.)

Eruvei Tavshilin – one does not need to initially cook a dish specifically for Eruvei Tavshilin. Even leftovers from food are sufficient for Eruvei Tavshilin. Thus, our sages of blessed memory (there) said that even relying on lentils at the bottom of a pot is acceptable for Eruvei Tavshilin on the eve of a festival, as long as there is an olive's worth. Similarly, one may rely on the fat stuck to a knife, provided it is fit for eating and there is an olive's worth. Certainly, it is not proper to use such leftovers for a mitzvah initially, but the Talmud speaks of a case where there is no other option. Nevertheless, from this, we learn that a special dish is not required for Eruvei Tavshilin.

And know that most people set aside an Eruv Tavshilin with cooked meat. When a holiday falls on Thursday and Friday, and the Eruv Tavshilin is set aside on Wednesday, it often spoils by Shabbat, and the Eruv becomes invalid. Therefore, everyone must be careful about this. Hence, we customarily set it aside using a cooked egg, as the egg does not spoil. The general populace is not knowledgeable about this, and many times we have seen that when people go on Shabbat to take the cooked meat they set aside for the Eruv Tavshilin, it has spoiled greatly, and they throw it away. Therefore, one must be very careful about this.

It is a mitzvah for every person to make an Eruv for themselves and not to rely on that of their friend. Nevertheless, it is a mitzvah for the leader of the city to make an Eruv for the entire city, because many people are busy on the eve of the holiday and may completely forget about it. Nowadays, we have the custom of posting notices in synagogues and marketplaces that say "Eruv Tavshilin." This way, anyone who sees it will remember and not forget. When making an Eruv for others, one must transfer ownership to them through another person to ensure it leaves their possession, as will be explained. Without this, it is not effective. Therefore, even though the text printed in the prayer books says "with this Eruv… for us and for all who dwell in this city," since the ownership was not transferred through another person, it is meaningless. This responsibility lies with the city's rabbi, and through this, even if someone forgets, or is forced, or if they made an Eruv and it was lost, or if an unlearned person who does not know how to make an Eruv, or women who do not have a husband and do not know how to make an Eruv – they all fulfill their obligation with the Eruv made by the leader of the city.

However, one who did not forget and is able to make an eiruv but intentionally relies from the outset on the leader of the city is called negligent ("poshea") and does not fulfill his obligation with it. This is the ruling of the Tur and Shulchan Aruch in section 7, and this is derived from the words of the Rosh (Chapter 2, Sign 3). This is inferred from the incident involving the blind man (Eruvin 16b) who forgot twice to set an eiruv tavshilin, and Shmuel called him "negligent"; see there. All the more so, one who does not forget and relies on the leader of the city is called "negligent" (this must be the intended meaning of the Rosh, as written by the Ketzot HaChoshen). The Gemara explains that for a "negligent" person, relying on the leader of the city does not work. But Rashi explained there that the intention of the leader does not apply to negligent people. There are those who hold that Rashi disagrees with this law, as he wrote that Shmuel said the leader's intention does not apply to the negligent, which proves that if he did intend, it would work; and thus, he disagrees with the Rosh’s ruling (Taz, section 9). Similarly, the Rashba wrote that if the leader intended for him, it would work (see Beit Yosef). Based on this, they wrote that the Rosh disagrees with them.

And I am puzzled: if the Rosh disagreed with Rashi, he should have presented his words and argued against him. In truth, there is no dispute here, for certainly the Rosh also agrees that if the intent is explicitly stated, it is effective. Why wouldn't it be effective? Where do we find that they imposed a penalty in this case? Rather, the Rosh is saying that one does not fulfill their obligation with the city's leader because, generally, the city's leader does not have the intention to include the negligent ones. And Rashi also explained this, that Shmuel did not have the intention to include the negligent ones. Just as Shmuel did not have the intention to include the negligent ones, so too, the city's leader. And this is what the Rashba wrote, that if the intention was explicitly stated, it is effective. The Rosh only added that, just as forgetting twice is considered negligence, similarly, relying on the city's leader without explicit intent is also negligence. We do not find that Rashi and the Rashba disputed this point. (However, the Ran certainly does not agree with the Rosh, as he explained "negligence" differently, see there. According to this, it makes sense why the Beit Yosef only brought the opinion of the Rosh; if all these great authorities disagreed, how could he not bring their opinions? Even though in the Beit Yosef it seems he holds there is a dispute, as the Taz wrote, nevertheless, in the Shulchan Aruch he retracted. He did not bring the opinion of the Ran because, regarding the explanation of "negligence," neither Rashi nor the Rashba agreed with the Ran, as is evident. Study and you will find it straightforward.)

We need to understand the reasoning of the Rosh: Why shouldn't we initially rely on the eruv (mixture) made by the leader of the city? After all, in many matters we fulfill our obligations through others, such as with Kiddush and Havdalah and similar matters. So why are we called "negligent"? Admittedly, if one forgets twice in a row, it is evident that he is lax in mitzvot, for if it were not so, after forgetting once, he should have taken it to heart and remembered. But why shouldn't we initially rely on the leader?

It seems to me that there are two reasons given for the institution of eruv tavshilin: one is for the honor of Yom Tov (festival), so that it should not be treated with disrespect, and another is for the honor of Shabbat, so that one should set aside a good portion for Shabbat and not consume everything on Yom Tov. According to this, it makes sense: While for the reason of the honor of Yom Tov, so that it should not be treated with disrespect, it is effective even through another person, to know that without this it is forbidden. But for the reason of the honor of Shabbat, to set aside a good portion, what benefit is there in relying on others? After all, he can still consume everything on Yom Tov. However, someone who forgot, or is unlearned, must necessarily rely on at least one reason. But someone who did not forget is certainly called "negligent" for not being concerned with the second reason.

There is a question here: Why did the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch not mention the main concept of "negligence"? In the Gemara, when someone forgot twice, like the case of that blind man, or if there were two consecutive festivals regarding the Eruv Tavshilin, or an interruption by another festival. And in any case, why did they completely omit this matter?

It seems to me, in my humble opinion, that it was clear to our rabbis that nowadays, when distractions have increased due to our many sins, it is impossible to label this as "negligence." Even in the time of the Gemara, perhaps only for a great person, like that blind man who used to arrange teachings before Shmuel, was it called "negligence." Therefore, the Talmud mentioned that he used to arrange teachings, meaning that for such a great person, it was certainly negligence, but not for us. And indeed, our opinion is the same for everyone, even for someone who knew and still did not make an Eruv. Our opinion is the same for anyone who did not make an Eruv, but this is also uncommon for us.

When one makes an Eruv for others, it is not necessary to specify exactly for whom it is made; rather, it is established for all the residents of the city. Anyone who is within the city's boundary is included in it, because the default assumption is that it is intended for the city and its boundary. However, someone who lives outside the boundary is not included in it unless it was explicitly stated that the Eruv is being made for so-and-so who lives outside the boundary. Additionally, it must be possible for them to come through the Eruv, and they must have established their own Eruv Techumin. If it was not explicitly specified, then even if an Eruv was made, it does not suffice, because the default assumption is that it is only for the city and its boundary.

It is obvious that the elder who establishes the eruv must have the intention at the time of making the eruv for the residents of the city. However, the residents of the city, even if they did not have the intention to rely on his eruv at that time, are also included in it. And it must be so, for if they had remembered, they would have made their own eruv. If they remembered and did not make their own eruv, it has been clarified that relying on the elder of the city does not help. Nevertheless, on Yom Tov, he should inform them that he made the eruv for them before they begin to cook for Shabbat. He should not let them rely on the assumption that he probably made the eruv for them (Taz, section 10). However, if they know that it is the elder’s practice to make the eruv for them, they can rely on him if they forgot to make their own eruv, even without his informing them. And the Rambam wrote that the next day he should announce that he made the eruv for them. See there.

It has already been explained that when one sets aside [an Eruv Tavshilin] for others, one must also transfer ownership to them through another person, so that it leaves his domain. He cannot transfer ownership to them through his minor son or daughter, nor through his Canaanite servant or maidservant, but only through another person: either through his adult son or daughter who are not dependent on his table, or through his Hebrew servant or maidservant; but not through his wife. All of this has been explained earlier in Siman 366 regarding Eruvei Chatzeirot. There are those who write that if his wife does not eat with him, he can transfer ownership through her, since she needs an Eruv Tavshilin for herself. This is not comparable to Eruvei Chatzeirot (Magen Avraham, Siman 1, quoting Yam Shel Shlomo), even if she receives an allowance from her husband. However, this situation is not common.

And how should he do it? He should say to the one acquiring (on behalf of others), "Acquire this eiruv for all the residents of the city." And the one acquiring should lift it from the table a tefach (handbreadth), as I have written there in Siman 366. Afterwards, he takes it from the hand of the one acquiring, holds it in his hand, and blesses: "Blessed are You... Who has sanctified us... concerning the mitzvah of eiruv." (Then he says:) "With this eiruv, it will be permitted for us to bake, cook, insulate, and light a lamp, from the holiday to Shabbat, for us and for all the residents of this city." He then places it in a protected place until Shabbat, and on Shabbat, he eats it. Some add to say, "and to do all our needs." And indeed, this alone seemingly suffices, as it includes everything. But this is not so. And one who does not know the holy tongue (Hebrew) may say it in any language he understands. Our women are accustomed to say that they need to hear the blessing of the eiruv and its placement, since they are involved in the needs of Shabbat. This is a beautification of the mitzvah and does not invalidate it by law. This is not mentioned anywhere, and there is no reason for it at all.

Maimonides only wrote "to bake and to cook," and similarly, the Or Zarua (Siman 347) brought this from the Jerusalem Talmud. However, some say that one must specifically mention the lighting of candles, and if it is not mentioned, it diminishes the candles (Ran and Hagahot Maimoniot). And our version follows the Baal Halachot Gedolot. Some have written that one must also say to carry from a private domain to a public domain (Or Zarua and Hagahot Asheri), and they wrote that if one did not mention each specific thing, but only said "to do all our needs," it does not suffice (Or Zarua there). These things are not entirely understood, but since the early authorities have said so, we are compelled to accept it, for their understanding is broader than ours. And so wrote our Rabbis, the Tosafists (Ketubot 22b, beginning with "U'medlikin," see there). Some have written that if one wishes to slaughter on Yom Tov, it must be mentioned in the Eruv Tavshilin.
