This is not the custom, nor is it to mention carrying (see Taz, subsection 11, who elaborates on this). And see subsection 32.

When a Yom Tov (festival) falls on Thursday and Friday, and one set an Eruv Tavshilin on Wednesday, it is forbidden to cook on Thursday for Shabbat, and one may only cook on Friday. This is because we are knowledgeable about the fixing of the calendar, and the first day is certainly Yom Tov. Even without this, why should we permit cooking for Shabbat earlier than the day before? It is sufficient to permit it on the day right before Shabbat. Nevertheless, if one cooked on Thursday for Shabbat, it is not forbidden after the fact (Taz, section 12). However, there are those who wish to prohibit it even after the fact (Rashal), and this is surprising, and the first opinion is the main one. (The Yerushalmi that was brought which requires one to say "from one Yom Tov to its fellow, and from Yom Tov to Shabbat" - this is when the first day is on Friday and the second on Shabbat, therefore it is necessary to mention Yom Tov and Shabbat. See Taz there and Beit Yosef. We do not find this in the Yerushalmi at all, and also the text in the previous section is not found before us.)

The Tur writes that one can set aside the eruv with the intention to rely on it as long as it exists, even for another Yom Tov. So are his words. And our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 14: If one set aside the eruv with the intention to rely on it as long as it exists, even for another Yom Tov, initially one should not rely on it for another Yom Tov, but after the fact, one can rely on it. So are his words. The explanation of their words: We have already explained in section 4 that according to Rava, the reason is that one should choose a nice portion for Shabbat, and it only works on the eve of Yom Tov. According to Rav Ashi, because of the honor of Yom Tov, so it should not be treated lightly, it is permissible even several days before. See there. Therefore, the Tur rules according to Rav Ashi, who is the later authority, and therefore he permits even initially to rely on it for another Yom Tov, and it does not need to be on the eve of Yom Tov specifically. And our teacher, the Beit Yosef, holds that initially we need to be concerned also for Rava's opinion, therefore one should not do so initially, but after the fact, we rely on Rav Ashi.

And we learned in the Mishnah that if the eruv was eaten or lost before it was prepared for Shabbat, one cannot bake or cook unless a kezayit (olive-sized portion) remains. And even though, according to the reasons of Rava and Rav Ashi, once the eruv tavshilin is set, it serves as a reminder for Shabbat and a reminder for Yom Tov, nevertheless, the essence of eruv tavshilin is that it is the beginning for Shabbat, and the rest is the completion, as I wrote in paragraph 5. And this is the language of "eruv" according to Rabbeinu the Rema, as I have written there. Therefore, if it was eaten or lost, there is no beginning of anything. It is obvious that this applies when the dish was eaten or lost; therefore, even if the bread remains, it is not an eruv. But if the bread was eaten or lost, and the dish remains, we have no concern. And even if there is still time on the eve of Yom Tov to set another bread, perhaps we are not concerned since the main thing is the dish, as I wrote in paragraph 7 (and from Magen Avraham, paragraph 14, it does not seem so, see there). And after preparing all the needs for Shabbat, one may eat it. However, it is proper to leave it for the Shabbat meal. And the Maharil was accustomed to eating it at the third meal and to combine this bread with the lechem mishneh (double bread), because since one mitzvah was done with it, it is proper to do another mitzvah with it.

And if one started with his dough, and the Eruv was consumed - he completes that dough. The same rule applies if he started cooking - he completes the dish he began, even if he has not yet placed it on the fire but has only prepared it for cutting or placing it in the pot, and the like. The reason seems simple to me: As we explained in the previous section, because there is no beginning here yet, but here the beginning was when he started preparing for Shabbat. And it is clear that if he prepared for Yom Tov and had not yet eaten, and they wanted to prepare for Shabbat, and the Eruv was consumed or lost - they can place what they prepared for Yom Tov for Shabbat, as this was done permissibly when the Eruv was extant. And what they intended for Yom Tov – what of it? The intention does not invalidate this. And now they will bake and cook for Yom Tov. (And this is the intention of the Ra'avad and the Shulchan Aruch, section 18. And from what is written "baked but did not cook..." - it is the same if he did not bake or cook, and so wrote the Levush. And the Taz in subsection 15 elaborated and questioned the Levush, but his words are not understood. Also, what was written by the Magen Avraham, subsection 17, that it is forbidden to leave it for a weekday, his intention is in such a manner when he cooked for Yom Tov, it is settled that leaving it for a weekday is forbidden, unless it is from a bad food to a good one, as I wrote in Siman 506. And know that what we wrote that the cooked food does not help if the bread remains, I saw in Sha'arei Teshuvah, subsection 13, in the name of the handwritten Pnei Yehoshua, that they rely on the bread, see there. And in my humble opinion, it is not so, according to what we hold like Rabbi Yehoshua in the Jerusalem Talmud, that they bake and cook on the cooked. And it requires investigation. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote in Section 19: One who did not make an eruv is permitted to light the Shabbat candle. And some prohibit it. Thus far his words. Those who prohibit are the Rosh and the Ran, for just as it is forbidden to cook and bake, so too is the lighting of the candle. The one who permits it, Rabbeinu Beit Yosef derives from the Rambam in his great book, who did not mention the lighting of the candle in the context of the eruv, see there. But truly this is not a proof, as he holds that all labors are included in the eruv when he mentioned "to bake and to cook," but without making an eruv at all, it is also forbidden to light the candle (Magen Avraham, Section 18). And according to my humble opinion, it seems to uphold the words of Rabbeinu Beit Yosef for another reason: as it was explained in Siman 516 that it is permitted to light even on the second day of Yom Tov after Mincha. It is not considered as preparing for a weekday because it is needed for that very hour, meaning it will provide light at that hour itself, as the day is close to ending. If so, all the more so that it is permitted to light on Yom Tov for that very hour itself, and consequently, it will also remain for Shabbat. And so it appears to me to be the primary view. And if because one lights many candles, who can object when his desire is that at that hour many candles will provide light? And if because on Erev Shabbat one must light them before sunset, when it is still fully day, nevertheless, one needs them at the time of sunset and afterward until it is night, as explained there.

Someone who did not make an Eruv, just as it is forbidden for him to cook for himself, so too it is forbidden for him to cook for others. And it is not just in his own house, where people may say that it is permissible to cook without an Eruv for those who know he did not make an Eruv and do not know he is cooking for others. Rather, even in the house of others, it is forbidden, for in this case it is worse than in his own house. Those who see him cooking in their house will not think that he is cooking for the homeowner but for himself, and they will assume that since he did not make an Eruv, he is not allowed to cook in his own house, but in others' houses he is permitted. And from this, a transgression will arise (Taz, subparagraph 17).

And similarly, others are prohibited from cooking for him. He has no remedy except to give his flour and cooked food as a gift to others who have made an eruv, and it becomes theirs, and they bake and cook for him. Even in his house, for the observer will understand that it belongs to others, for otherwise, why would they be cooking in his house? The acquisition must be through pulling (meshicha), and not through a symbolic act of acquisition (kinyan sudar), as this appears like a secular act. And it seems to me, in my humble opinion, another remedy is that they can cook a lot in their own pot and give it to him, and after the festival, he will return it to them. For it is permissible to cook a lot in one pot, as I have written in Siman 503.

It is stated in the Gemara (21b): One who did not set aside an Eruv Tavshilin – others may bake one loaf of bread for him, cook one pot of food for him, and light… Seemingly, it implies that others do it for him, not he himself. But in the Tosefta and Yerushalmi, it is explicitly stated that he himself can also do it, and the language of the Gemara "bake for him" refers to the members of his household. Thus ruled the Rosh, the Ran, the Tur, and the Shulchan Aruch. The Rif and Rambam omitted this, and their reason is not known. (See Beit Yosef who wrote that they ruled according to Rava, but from where do we know that Rava disagrees with this law?) Nevertheless, all our rabbis ruled this as law. And some wish to say: specifically when there are no others to whom he can transfer ownership of his flour. And this too is not clear, and thus ruled the great authorities (Beit Yosef, Yam Shel Shlomo, Magen Avraham section 20, and Eliyah Rabbah section 27). For all vital needs were permitted by the Rabbis, since by Torah law it is entirely permitted, either because the necessities of Shabbat can be prepared on Yom Tov, or due to the reason of "since" (ho'il), as I wrote at the beginning of the section.

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote in section 20 that if one set aside an eruv and did not explicitly mention the labors, but rather said "It shall be permitted for us to do all our needs" – it is as if he did not set aside an eruv at all. Thus far his words. And we have already written this in section 23, and that these matters are not understood. And I have seen those who are puzzled by this (Taz, subsection 18). And the Levush wrote that the reason is that this phrase implies he wants to perform all labors as on a weekday, and this is impossible, see there. This too is puzzling, for the cooked dish proves otherwise. 

And there are those who wrote that the main point is the saying of "with this," so that he selects a nice portion for the Sabbath (Magen Avraham, subsection 23), which also is not understood, for we hold that the main point is the reason not to disrespect Yom Tov, as I wrote in sections 4 and 25. Furthermore, he did say "with this," and because he did not say "to bake and to cook" – behold, the eruv is before him, and he will select a nice portion?

And it seems in law that one should not make another blessing (Taz, there), but should say "with this" in the proper formula. And if the entire day before Yom Tov passed and he did not correct this – we must necessarily be concerned with the opinion of those who prohibit, and transfer his flour to others. (And perhaps if this is impossible – one may rely in pressing circumstances on the Taz, and cook for the Sabbath. For in rabbinic matters, one may be lenient in pressing circumstances.)

It is further written that one who fasts on Yom Tov is forbidden to cook for others, even for the same day. This is similar to someone who did not set up an Eruv, who is also prohibited from cooking for others. So says the text. This means that just as on Yom Tov that falls on a Friday, one who did not set up an Eruv is forbidden to cook for Shabbat, both for himself and for others, so too on any Yom Tov. The Torah permits cooking for "that which every person eats," and since this person is fasting and does not need to cook for himself, he is forbidden to cook for others. Consequently, it follows that on Yom Tov that falls on a Friday, even if he set up an Eruv Tavshilin, he is forbidden to cook for Shabbat, because the main permission is based on "since guests might come," and for him, it is forbidden to cook for others on Yom Tov, as I have written (Magen Avraham, subsection 22). And if you ask: Let us say "since," and if he wants, he can annul his vow, we do not permit it initially based on "since" (ibid.), and even if she is a servant, if she is fasting, she is forbidden to cook (ibid.).

In my humble opinion, this is not analogous to someone who did not prepare an Eruv Tavshilin, because by Torah law, one cannot cook from a festival day (Yom Tov) for Shabbat without an Eruv Tavshilin. If not for the concept of "since" (ho'il) and the rabbinic enactment of Eruv Tavshilin, or even if by Torah law the needs of Shabbat could be prepared on Yom Tov, the rabbis still prohibited it without an Eruv Tavshilin. However, on Yom Tov itself, the Torah permits cooking and baking, as it is considered like a weekday in this regard. We do not find that the rabbis required any specific enactment for this. Therefore, what does it matter to us if one is fasting? It is a day on which cooking and baking are permitted. And if one argues from the verse (Exodus 12:16) "only that which is eaten by any person, that alone may be prepared for you," implying that anything not for "you" is not for others—where do we find such an interpretation? Furthermore, if so, where do we derive the interpretation of "for you"—and not for the Temple, "for you"—and not for animals? This interpretation is necessary to derive that one who is fasting is forbidden to cook. This requires further investigation.

One who forgot to set aside an Eruv Tavshilin, if he remembers on the eve of Shabbat before the morning meal – he should cook a large amount in one pot for Yom Tov, and there will be leftovers for Shabbat. For in one pot, it is permissible to cook even more than what is needed for Yom Tov, as I have written in Siman 503. And even for a weekday, it is permissible in such a manner, as I have written there. Likewise, it is permissible to cook several pots and eat from each pot on Yom Tov and leave leftovers for Shabbat, as I have written there. And even if it happens that he did not eat from one type of food – it does not matter, since at the time of cooking he intended to eat part of it today. To what is this similar? To one who cooks several dishes on Yom Tov and later does not wish to eat one dish: should we force him to eat it? Here too, it is the same. Provided that he does not use this as a trick, meaning that at the time of cooking he did not intend at all to eat from this pot (Taz, subsection 20, see there).

If the two days of Yom Tov were on Thursday and Friday, and one forgot to make an Eruv Tavshilin and remembered on Wednesday: if it is Rosh Hashanah, the conditional statement that will be explained is ineffective, because it is considered as one long day. However, if it is Pesach or Sukkot, one can make the Eruv today on condition. He should take the Eruv Tavshilin in his hand and say: "If today is holy and tomorrow is weekday, then I do not need an Eruv, and my words mean nothing. But if today is weekday and tomorrow is holy, then I am making an Eruv with this Eruv...". The next day, he does not need to say anything, because in any case: if yesterday was weekday, he made an Eruv yesterday; and if today is weekday, then he does not need an Eruv. It is obvious that he should leave some of his food for the Eruv, because cooking on Yom Tov for the Eruv is certainly forbidden, as is clear. Some say that we specifically need something that was cooked yesterday, as the law of Eruv Tavshilin requires that it begins on the eve of Yom Tov. However, their words were rejected, because since he is making the Eruv conditionally, today is considered as the eve of Yom Tov.

It seems to me clearly that one who makes an Eruv on condition does not need to recite a blessing. Rather, he should state the condition along with "through this Eruv." However, it is impossible to bless, for how can he bless and say, "If today is holy, my words mean nothing," and it turns out that the blessing is in vain? And if one argues that this is how the Sages instituted it – this is not a fixed ordinance, but rather for one who forgot and for one who wants to make an Eruv on condition. Is this a fixed ordinance from our Sages of blessed memory that we should bless on it? There is someone who says that one needs to bless (Magen Avraham, section 25). In my humble opinion, it is clear that one does not need a blessing. And so I found one of the greats who ruled that there is no need to bless, and this is the main ruling in law (the great Rabbi Akiva Eiger in the name of El-Gazi).

And similarly, regarding the separation of terumah, which is forbidden on Yom Tov: if there were two baskets of untithed produce before him, on the first day of Yom Tov he says: "If today is a weekday – let this be the terumah for that. And if today is a holy day – my words are null." He designates it and sets it aside. The next day he says: "If today is a holy day – my words are null. And if today is a weekday – let this be the terumah for that." He designates it and eats the other one. And it is already known the opinion of the Rambam, may his memory be blessed, that in our times, since we are knowledgeable about the fixing of the new moon – conditional statements do not work for any eruv. His words were not accepted by all the poskim, for why should it be any worse because we know today is holy? Therefore, even now we practice making conditional statements for eruvin.

Maimonides wrote in Chapter Six, Law 10: One who did not set aside an Eruv Tavshilin, and cooked or baked on the festival day and had leftovers, or invited guests who did not come – he may eat the leftovers the next day. However, if he acted deceitfully – it is forbidden to eat it. If he transgressed and cooked or baked for Shabbat – it is not forbidden for him. Why did they impose a strict prohibition on the deceitful person, but not on the intentional transgressor? Because if you permit for the deceitful person, everyone will act deceitfully, and the concept of "Eruv Tavshilin" will be forgotten. But the intentional transgressor is not common. And if he transgressed once, he will not transgress again. So far his words, and similarly wrote the Tur and Shulchan Aruch at the end of this section. Based on this reasoning, if one cooked unintentionally – it should be forbidden. For if we permit it, everyone will claim "We were unintentional," just like with deceit. Indeed, there are those who hold this view, but our Rabbi the Rema wrote that even an unintentional act is equivalent to an intentional one. And the truth is this: In the case of deceit – it is easy for people, and they will come to deceive. But with intentionality – we do not suspect any Jew would act intentionally. (See Magen Avraham, subparagraph 27, and see Lechem Mishneh who raised a difficulty on Maimonides from the Talmudic discussion in Yoma 18b and resolved it.)

A festival does not require an Eruv Chatzerot (joining of courtyards) or Shitufei Mavo'ot (joining of alleyways), since carrying is permitted on a festival. And even though there are those who say it would be proper to do so even on a festival, regarding carrying something that has no necessity at all, as I wrote in Siman 518 – the custom is not so. Only on the eve of Passover, when they set up an Eruv for the entire year, it would be proper to mention the festival as well, as I wrote there. And if it happens that one set up an Eruv for the festival – it is also effective for Shabbat (Magen Avraham, subsection 1). However, an Eruv Techumin (boundary Eruv) is required for a festival just as for Shabbat. And above in Siman 416 it was explained regarding techumin on a festival adjacent to Shabbat, what its law is, whether one needs to set up an Eruv for both specifically or not. See there.

If a Yom Tov (festival day) falls on a Friday, one may not establish an Eruv Chatzerot (an eruv for courtyards) or an Eruv Techumin (an eruv for boundaries), as it appears like one is fixing something. Some want to say that if one has set an Eruv Tavshilin (an eruv for cooking), it is permitted, since all the needs of Shabbat can be done in this manner (Hagahot Ashri). However, there are those who disagree (Ran, Chapter Two), stating that this has no connection to an Eruv Tavshilin, and this is also the ruling of Rabbeinu the Rema. But one can establish an eruv conditionally during the two days of Yom Tov observed in the Diaspora, when they fall on Thursday and Friday, if one remembers on the first day, similar to the conditional eruv mentioned in the previous section. This applies to an Eruv Chatzerot, but establishing an Eruv Techumin is prohibited even conditionally, as it is akin to acquiring a place of residence on Yom Tov, which is forbidden.

Rambam wrote in Chapter Four, Law 16: Just as it is a mitzvah to honor the Sabbath and to delight in it, so too with all the festivals, as it says (Isaiah 58:13): "Holy to the Lord, honored," and it is said regarding all the festivals "a holy convocation." And we have already explained the honor and delight in the laws of the Sabbath. Similarly, it is appropriate for a person not to eat a meal on the eve of a festival from the time of Mincha and onwards, just like on the eve of the Sabbath, as this is part of the honor. And anyone who demeans the festivals, it is as if he is attached to idol worship. Thus far his words. And in Pesachim (118a), they derived it from the verses: it is written "You shall not make for yourself molten gods," and adjacent to it, "The Feast of Unleavened Bread you shall keep," see there. And in Avot, Chapter Three, it is taught that one who demeans the festivals has no share in the World to Come. And the Ra'avad explained that this applies even to Chol HaMoed, see there. The matter is because the foundation of the Torah stands on the Exodus from Egypt, where His strength and His might were revealed, so to speak, and His providence over us, and the miracles and wonders He performed for us. All the festivals are a remembrance of the Exodus from Egypt.

Therefore, it is taught in the Megillah (23a) that on a Yom Tov, people come later to the synagogue in order to prepare the needs of the holiday, and they leave earlier in order to enjoy the joy of the holiday. For the essence of Yom Tov should be "half for God and half for you," as the Rambam wrote there, and this is his language: Even though eating and drinking on Yom Tov is a positive commandment, one should not eat and drink the entire day. Rather, this is the proper practice: In the morning, all the people rise early to the synagogues and study halls, they pray and read from the Torah about the day's topic. They then return to their homes and eat. They go to the study halls and read and study until midday. After midday, they pray the Mincha prayer, and return to their homes to eat and drink until nightfall. This is his language. And the cantors who prolong the melodies—the opinion of the great ones is not favorable towards them, for this is neither "half for God" nor "half for you" (Magen Avraham in the name of Yam Shel Shlomo). However, those who take pleasure in this—it is possible that this is their enjoyment of Yom Tov. But one who does not take pleasure in this—it is not proper for him to waste time on something of no value. This is a matter that the great ones of Israel have already lamented, and the hand of the masses is overpowering them in our many sins. And just as it is a mitzvah to say something that will be heeded…

And what has been clarified, that one should not eat from the afternoon of the eve of Yom Tov and onward—similarly on the first day of Yom Tov, so that one eats with appetite on the night of the second Yom Tov. And if Shabbat falls on the eve of Yom Tov, one should eat the third meal before the minor Mincha, which is up to half an hour into the fourth hour after midday, as I wrote in Siman 233 that this is the time for the minor Mincha according to the afternoon Tamid offering, see there. And if one forgot to do it before, he should do it afterward and eat an olive’s bulk or an egg’s bulk and a bit more, as clarified in Siman 291 that the Shabbat meal requires a bit more than an egg’s bulk, see there, even though from the language of the Talmud in Shabbat (119b) it seems that an olive’s bulk suffices. And on Yom Tov, a third meal is not required. And whether there is an obligation to eat bread on Yom Tov is disputed: Tosafot in Sukkah (27a) and the Rosh there wrote that there is no obligation to eat specifically bread and one fulfills the requirement with other foods. This also seems explicit in the Jerusalem Talmud there. But Tosafot in Berachot (49b) and the Ran in Sukkah there wrote that there is an obligation to eat bread on Yom Tov. However, from the words of the Ran there, it appears that not necessarily bread upon which one recites "Hamotzi," but even something upon which one recites "Mezonot" suffices, see there. And seemingly, this is indeed necessary, for regarding matzah, we say the first night is obligatory, from then on it is optional. And what about the first day during the daytime and the seventh day of Pesach? Rather, it is certain that one fulfills the obligation with enriched matzah, though on the first night one does not fulfill it with this. However, earlier in Siman 188, the Tur and Shulchan Aruch ruled that one who forgot and did not mention "Ya'aleh V'yavo" in the Grace After Meals on Yom Tov must repeat it like on Shabbat, see there—it implies that one must eat bread. And the Rosh of blessed memory, although he wrote in Sukkah that bread is not necessary, still in Berachot there he brought both opinions. And this is certainly so that even with "Mezonot" it suffices, and the reason one must repeat from the beginning is because even in the "Al Hamichya" blessing one must mention Yom Tov. (And so it appears in the Terumat HaDeshen there, who wrote that therefore bread is required on Shabbat for two meals because Kiddush must be in the place of a meal, see there. And certainly in this regard "Mezonot" suffices. And the Magen Avraham at the end of Subparagraph 2 wrote simply that one is obliged to eat bread on Yom Tov. But what he wrote that if one did not eat at night, he should eat twice during the day—I do not know from where he derived this. And what he wrote from Siman 271—there it is about Shabbat where it is written three times "today," and three meals are required by Torah law. However, in any case, it is certain that for one who finds it difficult to eat bread with the "Hamotzi" blessing twice a day, he can fulfill the obligation with pastries and bless "Mezonot." So it seems in my humble opinion.)

It is a mitzvah to knead bread on the eve of a festival in honor of the festival, just as on the eve of Shabbat. One is obligated to break bread over two loaves on a festival just like on Shabbat, and to establish every meal with fish and meat, and wine in places where wine is available. And festival garments should be better than those of Shabbat, because on a festival one is obligated to rejoice. For this reason, it is customary to have more food than on Shabbat (Magen Avraham section 4). It is found in the Talmud (Pesachim 109a) that on the first day of Pesach, Shavuot, Rosh Hashanah, and Shemini Atzeret, one should have a significantly larger meal. Some have written that instead of a third meal on a festival, one should eat fruits. Others prepare an additional dish for the day's meal more than usual, for the sake of the third meal (ibid). And it is customary to distribute nuts to children on a festival.

Rambam wrote that all holidays are prohibited for eulogizing and fasting. A person is obligated to be joyful and good-hearted on these days, along with his children, wife, grandchildren, and all those who accompany him, as it is stated: "And you shall rejoice in your festival… and the Levite, the stranger, and the orphan…". Although the joy mentioned here primarily refers to the offering of peace offerings (shalamim)... it also includes the joy of oneself, one's children, and one's household, each according to what is appropriate for them. How so? To the children, one gives roasted grains, nuts, and sweets; to the women, one buys clothes and nice jewelry according to his means; and the men eat meat and drink wine, for there is no joy except with meat, and no joy except with wine. When one eats and drinks, he is obligated to feed the stranger, the orphan, and the widow, along with other unfortunate poor people. But someone who locks the doors of his courtyard, eats and drinks with his children and wife, and does not feed and give drink to the poor and the bitter-hearted—this is not the joy of a mitzvah but the joy of his stomach. Concerning such people, it is said: "Their sacrifices are like bread of mourners…", "I will spread refuse on your faces, the refuse of your festival…". The Zohar strongly warns about this.

And when a person eats, drinks, and rejoices during a festival, they should not indulge excessively in wine, frivolity, and laughter, for drunkenness, laughter, and frivolity are not joy, but rather frivolousness and foolishness. We were only commanded to engage in joyful service, as it is said: "Because you did not serve the Lord your God with joy..." And it is impossible to serve the Lord except from a state of calmness of the soul, not from laughter, frivolity, and drunkenness.

The court is obligated during the time of the Temple to appoint officers who would patrol and search the gardens and orchards, and by the rivers and in all places of leisure, to ensure that men and women do not gather there to eat and drink, leading to transgression. They should also warn the entire populace regarding this matter, that men and women should not mix in their homes during celebrations and should not indulge in wine. All the more so, dancing and festivities together are great iniquities, and their punishment is exceedingly severe. They should be cautious in such matters, as this is an opening for those who commit transgressions. Our sages of blessed memory said at the end of Kiddushin: The climax of the year is the festival. And we, the people of Israel, must be distinct in such matters, as it is written, "You shall be holy." With the help of Heaven, we conclude the laws of Yom Tov.

In Chagigah (18a), the Gemara brings several expositions that indicate that work is prohibited on Chol HaMoed. Similarly, in the Torat Kohanim on Parashat "Emor" it states as follows: "And you shall do no work" – this comes to teach that the intermediate days of the festival are prohibited in work. One might think they are prohibited in "laborious work"? The verse states "it" – it is prohibited in laborious work, but the intermediate days of the festival are not prohibited in laborious work. There is a printing error, and it should be stated: "It is a solemn assembly; you shall do no laborious work," as the verse "you shall do no work" is not written concerning the festivals. This is the same exposition found in Chagigah, see there. The interpretation from "it" – "it is prohibited in laborious work," meaning the festival day itself, not Chol HaMoed. Otherwise, it would write "all laborious work" for all seven days. What is meant by "laborious work"? This refers to something that would result in a loss, meaning that the Torah permits work necessary for food preparation on Yom Tov, but laborious work in general – absolutely not, even if it would result in a loss. Even what is needed for Yom Tov, such as a garment to wear on Yom Tov, is prohibited, or a house to dwell in is prohibited to build. This is the meaning of "you shall do no laborious work." However, on Chol HaMoed, there are instances where you are permitted to work and instances where you are prohibited. This is what is stated in Chagigah there, that the Torah entrusted it to the sages. This means: since it is necessary that on Chol HaMoed some work is prohibited and some is permitted, it must be that the Torah entrusted it to the sages to understand the Torah's intent, which work is prohibited and which is permitted.

The opinion of our Rabbis, the Ba'alei Tosafot in Chagigah, and the Rosh and the Nimukei Yosef at the beginning of Moed Katan, is that all of this is merely an asmakhta (a rabbinic support), and the primary prohibition is rabbinic. There is proof for this from the Jerusalem Talmud, which states there that labor was prohibited so that people would engage in Torah study. This is also the opinion of the Rambam, who wrote at the beginning of Chapter Seven of Yom Tov as follows: "Chol HaMoed, even though it is not stated 'Shabbaton' (a day of rest), since it is called 'Mikra Kodesh' (a holy convocation) and it is a time of festivity in the Temple, it is forbidden to perform labor, so that it will not be like other weekdays which have no sanctity at all. And one who performs prohibited labor on it is given lashes of rebellion, because its prohibition is by rabbinic decree. Not all types of work are prohibited on it as on Yom Tov, for the end matter regarding the things prohibited on it is so that it will not be like a weekday in all respects. Therefore, some labors are forbidden on it, and some labors are permitted on it." Thus far his words.

But the opinion of the Ramban and the Rashba, as well as what is made clear from the words of the Rashbam (Tosafot there), and this is also the opinion of the Rif at the beginning of Moed Katan, as written by the Tur in Siman 536, is that there are Torah-level prohibitions. And this refers to anything that is neither a matter of loss nor for the needs of the festival. And some have raised difficulties: Are there distinctions in the Torah? And it is understandable according to the one who interprets that the Torah entrusted this to the sages – it is satisfactory. But according to the other Tannaim who derive a general prohibition from the verses – from where do we derive such distinctions (Rosh there)? But indeed, it is well explained, for one is compelled to say so: If we were to say that the prohibition is like on Yom Tov, why is it written only for the first and seventh days? The prohibition must be derived from the interpretations, and consequently, the explanation is: On the first and seventh days, "you shall not do any laborious work." But on Chol HaMoed, it is not "any laborious work," but rather some labors are prohibited and some are permitted. And it is logical that matters of loss and the needs of Yom Tov are permitted, and the rest are prohibited. And this is what was said in the Jerusalem Talmud "so that they will engage in Torah study" – because in any case, there are some labors that are permitted by Torah law because they are matters of loss, but the sages prohibited them due to the considerable effort involved, as will be explained, and about these it was said (Hagahot Maimoni there). And see the beginning of Siman 539.

Chol HaMoed has an obligation to honor it somewhat with food and drink and with clothing that is not mundane. According to the Ra'avad in the third chapter of Avot, the Mishnah that states "one who desecrates the festivals" refers to Chol HaMoed, see there. Even though it is not like Shabbat and Yom Tov, nevertheless, it should be treated better than a regular weekday. And it is customary to have a tablecloth on the table all the days of Chol HaMoed, as on Yom Tov. At the beginning of the fourth chapter of Sukkah (42b), it is said: Hallel and joy for eight days, and it is forbidden to fast on them. There is no obligation to eat bread specifically. Nevertheless, it is proper to eat bread, as it is more respectful (see Magen Avraham). A sage should reinforce the prohibition of work if he has the power to do so. And a sage who prohibited something that would cause a loss because people were lax in all forms of work – another sage cannot permit it for them (there).

Shaving and haircuts are prohibited during Chol HaMoed (the intermediate days of a festival). Although this is for the purpose of the festival, and it is considered disgraceful to walk with long hair, and it is also distressing for someone who is not accustomed to it — nevertheless, one could have shaved before the festival. On the contrary, it is for this very reason that it was prohibited, as it is a mitzvah to shave and get a haircut on the eve of the festival in honor of the festival, and if one were permitted to do so during Chol HaMoed, everyone, due to their pre-festival busy-ness, would postpone it to Chol HaMoed.

And for this reason, they forbade even shaving before the festival, and if by nature he needs to shave again during Chol HaMoed, it is prohibited, so that those who see someone shaving during Chol HaMoed will not be misled. Therefore, even if he was compelled and could not shave before the festival, or if he was ill and shaving was difficult for him, and he recovered during Chol HaMoed, even though according to the strict law it might be permissible for him to shave, nevertheless, because of appearances, it is prohibited. For not everyone knows that he was compelled or ill and thus could not shave, or that he is required to shave again. And they forbade it even in such a case.

Nevertheless, there are instances where the Sages permitted one to shave during Chol HaMoed, and this applies to situations where everyone knows the reason why the person did not shave before the festival, and allowing it would not cause a disruption to others, as we learned in the Mishnah of "these may shave." This refers to those who may shave during the festival: one who has been released from captivity, and one who has been released from prison and did not have the opportunity to shave beforehand. Even if he was in a Jewish prison where they allowed him to shave, nonetheless, everyone knows that someone who is imprisoned is distressed and does not have the presence of mind to shave due to his suffering. Similarly, one who was excommunicated and was prohibited from shaving, and his excommunication was lifted during the festival. Although he could have requested the lifting of his excommunication before the festival, meaning he would comply with the law, but he did not request it until the festival, it is still permitted according to the Rambam. However, the Tur ruled that it is only permitted if it was not possible to lift the excommunication before the festival, such as if the period of his excommunication extended into the festival. But if it was possible to lift it before and he did not request it, it is prohibited. This follows the approach of the Jerusalem Talmud.

And similarly, one who vowed not to shave and seeks annulment of his vow during Chol HaMoed. According to the Rambam, even if he could have sought annulment before the festival, and according to the Tur, specifically when he could not have sought annulment before the festival, for example, if he could not find anyone to permit it for him. But if he found someone and did not seek annulment, he should not shave. It seems to me that this applies when he had the opportunity to annul his vow before the festival. However, if before the festival he had intended to uphold his vow, but during the festival, the vow became burdensome and he annulled it, even the Tur agrees that this is not considered as if he could have annulled it before the festival. But some have written that even in such a case, the Rosh and the Tur hold that it is forbidden (Magen Avraham, subsection 5, and Darkei Moshe in the name of the Ri"v). They wrote that in this matter, the opinion of the Rambam is primary (ibid.). And it seems to me that in such a case, even the Rosh and the Tur agree. And it appears similarly in the Yerushalmi, which discusses when he intended before the festival to seek annulment of his vow, but he sought an opening and did not find one. See there.

And similarly, one who comes from a distant place during Chol HaMoed, where it is well-known. But from a nearby place – it is forbidden for him to shave, because not everyone knows [he has arrived]. And even if he came from a distant place on the eve of the festival before nightfall and did not have time during the day to shave – it is permitted for him to shave during Chol HaMoed. This is specifically when he did not have a settled place before the festival, or even if he had, such as passing through settled areas, but on the eve of the festival he did not have a place where he could shave. But if he had a settled place on the eve of the festival where he could have shaved – it is forbidden for him to shave during Chol HaMoed (Magen Avraham, section 6). And similarly, specifically if he did not travel from the Land of Israel to outside the Land for business, or to see a friend, and certainly not for a mitzvah, but merely for leisure. For leisure travel from the Land of Israel to outside the Land, they did not permit him to shave, because he should not have left the Land of Israel for mere leisure. But from outside the Land to the Land of Israel, or within the Land of Israel, or from outside the Land to outside the Land – even for mere leisure it is permitted for him to shave. And even for those whom it is permitted to shave, nonetheless, they should not shave publicly but privately, for perhaps there are those who do not understand the matter, and they may come to disrespect the prohibition against shaving during Chol HaMoed.

And similarly, a minor who was born on the festival with hair and needs to shave it, or even just an ordinary minor who is less than thirteen years and one day old, since he is not bar mitzvah – it is permitted to shave him even in public, because everyone sees that he is a minor. This is when he has a lot of hair and is distressed, which is considered a need of the festival. But otherwise, it is forbidden. And for a non-Jew, in any case, it is forbidden, unless he has nothing to eat as with all labors, as I wrote in Siman 542 (there, subsection 8). And similarly, a mourner whose seventh day of mourning falls on the Sabbath, the eve of the festival – it is permitted for him to shave during the intermediate days of the festival, and this will be further explained in Siman 548. And similarly, penitents who customarily shave when they repent – it is permitted to shave them during the intermediate days of the festival, because of the commandment of repentance. And this too is something publicly known, and it does not lead to a leniency regarding shaving during the intermediate days of the festival.

A nazirite and a leper, when the time for their shaving has arrived, whether before the festival or during the festival, are permitted to shave, so that their sacrifices will not be delayed. And anyone transitioning from impurity to purity is permitted to shave during the intermediate days of the festival. And the members of the priestly watch in the Temple, whose watch ends during the intermediate days of the festival, are permitted to shave, because they are prohibited from shaving during their watch. And these are also well-known to the public.

Every person is permitted to trim their mustache during Chol HaMoed, whether the hair hinders eating or not, whether with a razor or scissors, as this does not constitute the shaving that is forbidden during Chol HaMoed. It is even permitted to do so publicly for this reason. All the more so, it is permitted to shave for a wound. It is also permitted to wash and comb one's hair during Chol HaMoed, even though it removes hair, as this does not count as shaving in the context of Chol HaMoed.

The Rambam in the seventh chapter ruled that it is permissible to cut nails during Chol HaMoed, even with a tool, in the same manner as cutting them on a regular weekday. The SeMaG wrote similarly. This is also the opinion of the Rif and the Rosh, who explained that what we say in the Gemara (Moed Katan 17b) that using a professional tool is prohibited refers to mourning, not to Chol HaMoed. However, the Tur brought opinions that permit it only with a knife and not with scissors. And there are those who forbid it even with a knife, permitting it only by hand.

Therefore, the custom among us is to be stringent about cutting nails during Chol HaMoed, whether with a knife or with scissors, except for a mitzvah need, such as a woman preparing for her immersion. All the more so for those who were previously mentioned as being permitted to shave during Chol HaMoed. Similarly, someone who cut his nails before the festival, and had nothing to cut on the eve of Yom Tov, and they grew during Chol HaMoed – it is permitted for him to cut them in any manner he wishes (Magen Avraham). In my humble opinion, in a pressing situation, someone who was very busy before the festival – he may cut his nails during Chol HaMoed, since this is the opinion of the four pillars of the world. It is permitted to take all kinds of medicines during Chol HaMoed. And even though by doing so he will not be able to enjoy eating and drinking, nevertheless his healing takes precedence, even if it is not a complete illness. (This seems to me, for it is not because of the prohibition that Magen Avraham in subsection 2 was astonished by the section 492, see there. And this is the language of the Tosefta brought by the Rif and the Rosh in the first chapter of Moed Katan: They drink animal dung water..., see there. Examine and you will find leniency.)

The Rabbis taught (Moed Katan 12b): One may grind on the festival for the needs of the festival. But if it is not for the needs of the festival – it is forbidden. And if one ground for the needs of the festival and had leftovers even after the festival – it is permitted. One may cut wood on the festival for the needs of the festival. But if it is not for the needs of the festival – it is forbidden. And if one cut wood and had leftovers – it is permitted. One may brew beer on the festival for the needs of the festival. But if it is not for the needs of the festival – it is forbidden. And if one brewed and had leftovers – it is permitted, provided that one does not act deceitfully.

It appears to me, in my humble opinion, that the explanation is as follows: when it comes to a situation where something will be lost if not done during the intermediate days of the festival (Chol HaMoed), this is permitted only if the person did not intend to perform this work specifically during the festival, meaning that it was not possible to complete it before the festival. However, if the person intended to perform the work during the festival, and it could have been done beforehand, it is prohibited, as will be clarified in Siman 538. The text teaches us that matters related to eating and drinking are different, for even if one intended to grind grain during the festival when it could have been done beforehand, it is still permitted. This is what the Tur and Shulchan Aruch wrote: "Even if one intended to perform the work during the festival... if it is not for the festival's need, it is prohibited" – this applies even to matters of eating and drinking, unless one ground and had leftovers. Then, it teaches us that even cutting wood not for eating, since it is used to prepare food, is also permitted for the festival's need, even if one intended to perform the work during the festival. Furthermore, it teaches us that even brewing beer from dates or barley, which involves significant effort and is typically prepared for a long time, is nevertheless permitted if it is for drinking, even if one intended to perform the work during the festival.

And our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, wrote in Section 1: However, one does not need to be exact; rather, one should act generously, and if he leaves over – he leaves over. But he should not act deceitfully, to grind or make beer more intentionally. Or if he has old flour or beer – he should not deceitfully make more and say, "This is what I want." But if he has bread – it is permitted to grind for fresh bread, as fresh bread is preferable. And the same applies to beer: if the new beer is preferable – without deceit, it is permitted. This is his language. And if he acted deceitfully – it is permitted to eat and drink it (Magen Avraham, Section 2). For one should not be strict about deceitfulness to such an extent, for even on Yom Tov there are instances where deceit is permitted, as I wrote in Section 503, and all the more so on Chol HaMoed. However, without deceit, if one did any of these not for the sake of the festival – it is forbidden even after the fact. And one should not ask: if so, how is it that among us all those who have mills grind on the festival? And similarly, all those who make beer? It can be said that this is from the laws of commerce which will be explained in Section 539. And wherever there is a loss from his pocket – it is permitted, as I wrote there. And among us, it is considered a loss from his pocket, as he pays rent for the mills, and employs people on salary, and pays for each day. And the Gemara is referring to grinding and beer that each person does for himself.

Know that the Rambam wrote in Chapter Seven that even though one has old wine, he may use a subterfuge and drink from the new wine, as this subterfuge is not noticeable to an observer. The same applies to all similar cases. Thus are his words. The Raavad and other authorities challenged him, as there is a dispute about this in the Gemara, and the one who permits it stands alone, see there. Some have explained that the Rambam permits specifically this subterfuge, namely to drink from the new wine. However, a complete subterfuge, to do something for a weekday purpose and claim "I am doing it for the festival," is prohibited. The dispute concerns such a case (Bach). Although there is a logical basis for this distinction, the Gemara compares them to each other. Some have explained that because in Shabbat (139b) it raises an objection from a Baraita concerning subterfuge against one who says it is prohibited to use subterfuge. It resolves that this subterfuge is not noticeable, see there. This implies that this is the halacha (Magen Avraham, subsection 3). I say that in the sugya itself, it fits well, as the Gemara there brings two Baraitas: in one it states simply that subterfuge is permitted, and in the other that subterfuge is prohibited. It resolves that it is a dispute among Tannaim, see there. Consequently, the Baraita that permits subterfuge aligns with the opinion of the individual who permits it, and the Baraita that prohibits subterfuge aligns with the opinion of those who prohibit it. Since there are conflicting Baraitas, we follow the lenient view in rabbinic matters. Furthermore, since even regarding Shabbat we hold above in Siman 313 that one may use subterfuge to spread a mat over nuts to carry them into a karmelit on Shabbat, all the more so may one use subterfuge on Chol HaMoed for a rabbinic prohibition. In my humble opinion, this is a clear proof for the Rambam. (The Magen Avraham also rules like the Rambam there. So wrote the Eliyah Rabbah, subsection 2, see there.)

Even to perform work in order to cover food items – it is also permitted during Chol HaMoed. As it says there: Rav Yehuda permitted uprooting flax, which means uprooting flax to cover food according to Rashi's explanation. Rambam explains that this is for women for adornment, to wash their faces with it. And even though for this purpose one does not need the entire stalk, only the seeds, nevertheless it is permitted to uproot it all for the sake of the seeds, as it cannot be done in any other way. And so we learn from his words that even for adornment purposes – it is permitted to do work during Chol HaMoed. He also permitted uprooting hops to put them in beer for the needs of the festival. I do not know the novelty in this. And he permitted uprooting sesame during Chol HaMoed, even though most of them are not fit for consumption until they dry, and by then the festival will have passed – nevertheless, there are some seeds that have dried and are fit to eat immediately. And for the sake of these few seeds – one may uproot the entire stalk.

And similarly, fruits that are partially cooked and can be eaten with some difficulty—it is permitted to gather them in order to eat them. We do not say that it is not the way of people to eat them in this manner, because there are some who do eat them this way. Furthermore, if one gathered them, ate some, and had leftovers, and fears that they might become wormy if not pickled to remove their moisture, as is done with fruits that are not fully cooked—it is permitted to pickle them. However, it is forbidden to gather them initially in order to pickle them for after Yom Tov, for a complete act of labor is not permitted for after the festival, even if it will not be available after the festival. But it is permitted to buy them and pickle them if they will not be available after the festival, since there is no complete act of labor involved.

And similarly, one may catch fish during Chol Hamoed (the intermediate days of a festival), as much as he can, and salt all of them during Chol Hamoed, because it is possible that he will eat from them during the festival. And although they need to be left in the salt for several days, if he squeezes them by hand many times until they soften, they will be fit to eat during Chol Hamoed. And even though he initially catches more than he needs for the festival, and in grinding we forbid such a situation, catching fish is not comparable to grinding, because not all fish are alike, and one needs many in order to select those he wishes to eat during the festival. Salting is permitted for all of them, because it is not considered a full-fledged labor, as there is no tanning process in food (Magen Avraham, Section 7). 

It is also permitted to catch them even publicly, because it is evident to all that fish are needed for the festival. And even if there is a custom not to catch fish, one can revert from this custom, because it reduces the joy of the festival (ibid., Section 8). However, for all labors done for the festival's needs, if the homeowner does them for himself – he may do so even publicly. But if craftsmen do them – they should do so discreetly. How? Hunters of animals and birds, and the grinders and vintners who sell in the market, if they do so publicly, it would be a desecration of the festival. However, with fish – everyone knows that fish are needed for the entire city for the festival, and there is no desecration in this. Some are concerned even with fish (ibid., Section 10). In my humble opinion, it seems that everyone agrees regarding fish (and this is the intention of the Rema in Section 5). However, digging a pond so that the water will drain and the fish remain – this is certainly forbidden (ibid.), as it is not done solely for the festival. 

Similarly, milking animals even if it is a lot, where everyone sees that it is not for the festival – is allowed. This is because it is a matter of loss, for if they are not milked, the milk will spoil inside them. Additionally, because of the suffering of animals, for this reason, it is permitted to tell a non-Jew to milk on Shabbat.

It is prohibited to launder clothes during Chol Hamoed (the intermediate days of a festival), for one can launder them before the festival. On the contrary, if we permit laundering during the festival, everyone, due to their preoccupations, would postpone the laundering to the festival, and they would enter the holiday with soiled clothes. Therefore, even if one forgot or was forced by circumstances, it is forbidden. This is because it is impossible to permit it due to the appearance it creates; an observer might say that laundering on the festival is allowed, unless it is publicly known that there is no error, and no transgression will result from it. All of this is similar to the rules regarding shaving discussed in Siman 531.

And these are the ones whom the sages permitted to launder during the festival: one who comes from a distant place; one who is released from captivity and from prison; and the cursed one, whom the sages permitted during the festival to break his curse; and one who vowed not to launder and during the festival asked for and received permission to launder, all according to the details explained regarding shaving. Similarly, a mourner whose seventh day falls on a festival, or if it falls on the eve of the festival which is a Sabbath (Rambam). Also, those with discharges, and women with discharges, and menstruants, and those who have given birth, and all who transition from impurity to purity during the festival – these are permitted to launder (there). Likewise, a woman who finds a stain on her garment during the festival – she is permitted to launder her menstrual garments as she is accustomed to on weekdays. And even though not everyone knows this – nonetheless, it is necessarily so. And also in the case of a woman, this will be attributed to her, since this is her usual practice.

And similarly, hand towels, which everyone knows that even if they were laundered before the festival, they get dirty again. And even many times it is permissible to launder them, because they need to be laundered at all times. Therefore, one who knows that they have enough for the holiday, it is forbidden to launder (see Magen Avraham, subsection 2). And in the Mishnah, there are those who permit "book cloths." The Tur writes two explanations: one is the garment given during shaving, and it must be said that it is needed for those who are permitted to shave during the festival, as the Sages permitted them as I wrote in Siman 531. And it seems more likely according to the other explanation that it refers to cloths for holy books, because out of respect for them, it is permitted to launder them. And it is evident to all that they are cloths for holy books, and it is improper to forbid laundering them during the festival.

And so they permitted washing sponges and towels, which are sheets that they wrap themselves in when they exit the bathhouse, as they quickly become soiled. Likewise, they permitted washing children's clothes, which get dirty all the time, and this is evident to all. Additionally, they permitted washing one's shirt if he has only one shirt, as it is necessary to wash it even if he washed it before the festival, because it quickly becomes soiled since he has no other shirt to change into.

Here is the translation of the passage:

At the beginning of the chapter "And These May Shave," the Talmud questions regarding someone who owns only one shirt: is it not apparent to everyone that he only has one shirt, so how can they permit him to wash it? The Talmud answers: his belt proves it. Rashi explains that someone who owns only one shirt removes it, washes it, wraps himself in his coat, girds himself with his belt, and stands and washes it, thus informing everyone that he only has one shirt. This is Rashi's explanation. The Rif, Rambam, and Rosh did not mention this. Their reasoning seems to be that it is obvious, as everyone sees that he is without a shirt. However, according to this, it is only permitted when he washes it himself, as this serves as a sign. They did not need to mention this, as this is their intention: someone who only has one shirt is permitted to wash his shirt, as it directly implies he himself and not another person. (See Beit Yosef, Bach, and Taz, who elaborate on this. In my humble opinion, it appears as I have written. See Beit Yosef, who explains similarly. The Tur brings opinions on this; see there.)

It seems that anything prohibited from being washed during the festival is also forbidden even if done by a non-Jew when washed in a Jew's home. This must be the case, since the primary reason for the prohibition is to prevent people from entering the festival with dirty clothes, and if we permit it through a non-Jew, the concern will return. I have seen someone write that in Egypt, they are accustomed to permitting washing by maidservants whatever is needed for the festival (Ba'er Heitev, section 3, in the name of R. Yaakov Kastro). This is astonishing, and we do not practice this way. 

Know that the Talmud permits washing linen garments during the festival (Moed Katan 18a), and the reason is that washing them is easy (Rashi), and there is not much effort. The reason they did not worry about people entering the festival in a soiled state is that since other items must necessarily be washed before the festival, they would naturally also wash linen garments. However, in our community, it is customary to prohibit even linen garments. Consequently, since this has become the custom, it falls under the category of things that are permitted but others have taken upon themselves to prohibit, and it is forbidden to permit it in their presence. Nevertheless, according to this, an annulment (of the custom) would be effective, as I wrote in Yoreh De'ah, section 214. But in truth, it is not so, for in the Talmud, there is a dispute about this, with some prohibiting. Perhaps we have adopted the opinion of those who prohibit as the practical law, and therefore annulment does not apply. The main point is that it is forbidden for us to wash even linen garments (Magen Avraham, section 5).

And all those whom the sages permitted to launder – it is permissible to launder them even with neter and ahil, which are types of soap. And it appears to me that ironing is prohibited, as we find in the laws of mourning that a distinction is made between laundering and ironing (Tosafot there, 23a, s.v. "kol"). And since during the intermediate days of the festival we only find that laundering is permitted, from where do we derive that ironing is allowed? However, since they permitted laundering with neter and ahil, it implies that it is permitted in all forms. This matter requires further investigation for a definitive ruling.

And all those whom the sages permitted to launder – it is permissible to launder even publicly by the river. This is specifically when washing by the river, as it is necessarily done publicly. They permitted it because washing by the river is more effective. But when not washing by the river – one should launder in private. There are those who prohibit laundering publicly by the river, except for linen garments (Magen Avraham, subsection 4). However, for small garments – it is certainly permissible even publicly (there, subsection 5). And similarly, for all things that are clearly noticeable. And this prohibition of public laundering is similar to our consideration in permitting shaving: those who come from distant places… perhaps not everyone is aware (this seems to be my humble opinion).

However, even for those who permit it, one should only wash clothes as necessary for the festival. That is, one shirt, and similar garments. However, those garments of small children in which they are wrapped, called "wikklen," and in which they urinate and defecate—these may be washed even four or five or more at one time, because several of them are needed at all times, and it is impossible to set a limit and measure for this. But for small children who wear shirts—this has a limit and measure, and one is not permitted to wash more than this.

One may bring utensils from the craftsman’s house during the festival if they are needed for the festival, such as pillows and cushions, bowls and plates. However, utensils that are not needed for the festival, such as a plow or wool from the dyer’s house, may not be brought, since they are not needed during the festival, and why should one trouble oneself unnecessarily? Additionally, people might say that he gave them to be repaired during the festival and that they were repaired during the festival. This applies even within the same courtyard, from one house to another. Even if the craftsman is not Jewish, it is still prohibited because people will say that the Jew gave it to him to repair during the festival (there, subsection 6). If the craftsman has nothing to eat, one may give him his payment and leave the utensils with him. It is always permitted to pay him, even if the craftsman is wealthy, but if he has nothing to eat, one is required to pay him. Nevertheless, one should not take them to his house. If he does not trust him, he should leave them in a nearby house. If he fears that they might be stolen from there, he should move them to another courtyard. If there is no other place, and he is forced to bring them to his house, he should only bring them discreetly so that people do not suspect him. If there is another place, he should not bring them even discreetly, because no matter how discreetly he does it, some individuals will notice and suspect him.

It is taught in Moed Katan (13a): One may not move from one house to another in a different courtyard. But within the same courtyard – one may move from one house to another. And the explanation of "one may not move" – means to uproot his residence from this place to that place. For it is a great exertion, and his mind will not be settled, and he will thereby neglect the joy of the festival. And it is stated in the Jerusalem Talmud there, and brought in the Tur: One may not move from a nice dwelling to another nice dwelling, nor from an inferior dwelling to another inferior dwelling. And this is when both belong to him, or both do not belong to him. But from one that does not belong to him into one that does belong to him, even from a nice dwelling to an inferior one, it is permitted, for a person is more comfortable in his own, and his mind is more settled. And according to this version, it implies that moving from an inferior dwelling to a nice one is permitted even when both belong to him, or both do not belong to him. And so it is written in the glosses of Maimonides (Chapter Eight).

But the Rambam in Chapter 8, Law 16 wrote: One may not move from courtyard to courtyard during the festival, whether from an inferior courtyard to a superior one, or from a superior one to an inferior one. And indeed, in our version of the Jerusalem Talmud, the text is thus, that even from an inferior courtyard to a superior one is forbidden. However, the end of the Jerusalem Talmud, which permits moving within one’s own property, the Rambam omitted, and the reason for this is unknown. (The Maggid Mishneh wrote: If so, why did the Talmud not resolve as it objected, and indeed the truth is in the beginning... – that the intention is within his own property, see there. And I do not understand: If so, it should have said "But one can move to his own house," as it began with "One may not move from house to house." Therefore, he was forced to interpret it as moving to a house in the courtyard. And it is more reasonable to say that this was not in his version. The Beit Yosef established this as law in Section 2, and he wrote the wording "his own courtyard" and it is more comfortable to say "his own house.")

And just as one should not vacate his residence during the intermediate days of the festival (Chol Hamoed), so too one should not move his merchandise and belongings that are not for the sake of the festival from one courtyard to another, as this would detract from the joy of the holiday. It has been written that the prohibition only applies when moving through a public domain, but moving from one courtyard to another through a doorway that connects them—even through several courtyards—is permitted (Bach and Magen Avraham, subsection 1). If the houses do not open into a courtyard but into an alleyway, some say that moving from one house to the adjacent one is permitted. And if one fears theft in the courtyard where he is staying, it is permitted to move even from one courtyard to another through a public domain, provided the items will be secure in the second location. Even moving from one city to another is permitted in the case of potential loss, as anything that would be a significant loss is allowed during the intermediate days of the festival. However, without the risk of loss, one should not undertake such efforts during the festival, even to transfer money from one city to another.

In my humble opinion, it seems that the allowance from one courtyard to another not via a public domain applies to goods and utensils, so that it should not be conspicuous. But to move one's residence, from one courtyard to another even if not via a public domain, is prohibited, because one's mind does not settle in another courtyard and it is a great burden. However, this does not seem to be the implication from the language of the authorities. (See Magen Avraham and Bach. In my humble opinion, it is clear that this is the case.) Nevertheless, all these laws should be permitted according to the discretion of the teacher (Magen Avraham at the end of subsection 2). For there are times when it is necessary to move, and then it is permitted in any manner. Each teacher should understand the matter in their own place, whether to permit or to prohibit.

Manure in the courtyard – it is forbidden to remove it during the intermediate days of the festival (Chol HaMoed); rather, one should move it to the sides. If it accumulates to the extent that the courtyard becomes like a barn, it can be taken out to the garbage heap. (The Be'er Heitev in the previous chapter brought from Sha'ar Ephraim that it is forbidden to play musical instruments for Jews during Chol HaMoed. These words are perplexing, and Sha'arei Teshuvah has already rejected them in the name of Shevus Yaakov.)

One who needs to ride during the festival, even for leisure, and certainly if it is for the needs of the festival, and has not tried to walk on foot – he may trim the horse's hooves, fix its legs with iron, and repair the saddle and bridle, and all riding necessities. We do not say that he could have done it before the festival, for he did not know if he would need it. Therefore, if he indeed knew he would need it and intentionally left it for the intermediate days of the festival – it is forbidden. Our master the Rema wrote that it is permitted to ride during the festival even from city to city, even for free. And so is the custom, except that it is forbidden to fix all riding necessities if he is not riding for a need or for leisure. Thus is his language. It is not understood: since he desires it – it is leisure for him. It is possible that leisure is in preparation and walking calmly. (See Magen Avraham who wrote that from the Land of Israel to outside the Land for leisure – one should not fix riding necessities.) According to this, also in traveling by wagon – the same law applies regarding fixing the wagon, that if he knew before the festival – it is forbidden. If not – it is permitted.

It is permitted to comb a horse in order to beautify it, as this is pleasurable for it. And even if it was combed before the festival, nevertheless, it needs a new combing. One may not mate animals during the festival, as it is not for the sake of the festival, nor is it a matter of significant loss. However, one may let blood from it, and no medical treatment should be withheld from it, even if it involves labor, as this is a matter of significant loss. Similarly, one should not place a hen on eggs to hatch chicks. But if it was placed before the festival and it fled from them, one may return it, for if it is not returned, the eggs will be spoiled, and this is a matter of significant loss. This is provided it is within three days of its fleeing, as after that, there is no benefit. And it is not only if it had already been sitting on them for three days, for then the eggs are completely ruined. Rather, even if it had not sat for three days, as they are still fit to eat, nevertheless there is a loss involved. And our teacher, the Rema, wrote: But it is forbidden to place another hen, even if the first one died. Until here is his wording, one must say that he holds it will not be beneficial. For if you would think it beneficial, why would they forbid it in a matter of significant loss? (And see Beit Yosef, and Magen Avraham, subsection 3. And I have written what seems correct in my humble opinion.)

It has already been clarified that something which would result in a loss is permitted on Chol HaMoed. Even if there is a doubt about the potential loss (Magen Avraham), and even if it involves significant and strenuous work. However, the obligation is upon the person to minimize the exertion as much as possible. Now, regarding fields, there are two types: one is called a "Beit HaShalchin," meaning it does not suffice with rainwater and must be irrigated. The other is called a "Beit HaBaal," which does not need irrigation and suffices with rainwater. When this type of field is irrigated, it is only for the purpose of enhancing it, to make it even better. Such a field, it is obvious, is forbidden to irrigate on the Festival. But a "Beit HaShalchin," if it was not irrigated before the Festival, one should not begin to irrigate it during the Festival and should wait until after the Festival. However, if it was already being irrigated before the Festival, and if it is not irrigated now the crops or vegetables will be ruined, it is permitted to irrigate it on Chol HaMoed.

And even though they permitted labor and exertion, the sages nevertheless set a boundary for exertion. Specifically, it is permitted to water [a field] from a spring, whether it is an old spring or a new spring, because it is possible that the soil around the spring will collapse, and it would be a great exertion to fix it. All this is when the water flows from the spring and descends by itself to the field or garden. However, they did not permit drawing water with a bucket from a well, cistern, or collected rainwater, because this is a very great exertion. And this the sages did not permit even in a case of potential loss. And from rainwater, it is forbidden even to water by walking it, because it surely will not help, and one will end up drawing with a bucket. Even if there is one vegetable bed, half of which is high and half of which is low, and there is water there – it is forbidden to draw from there to the higher place. For the sages set a boundary that drawing with a bucket for seeds and grains is forbidden during the intermediate days of the festival, because the exertion is very great. Nevertheless, vegetables that one wants to eat during the festival – one may water them even with a bucket, because anything needed for the festival is permitted even with great exertion, if by watering they will be suitable for the festival. But if they will not be suitable for the festival, or one does not want to eat them during the festival – it is entirely forbidden unless it is a case of potential loss and without great exertion, as I have written. But for the festival, even if it is not a case of potential loss, and even with great exertion – it is permitted.

Water channels that flow from lakes, if they do not cease and flow continuously, it is permitted to water from them. But if they cease, it is forbidden, because we are concerned that they might stop, and one will end up drawing water with a bucket. And why are we not concerned that continuously flowing channels might cease? Because since they have naturally always flowed and have not ceased, it is assumed that they will never cease. Therefore, man-made trenches that channel water from the river to the field – it is forbidden to water from them, even if they were filled before the holiday, because it is likely that they will cease. And therefore, if an aqueduct that naturally flows passes between them, and thus the trenches will not cease, it is permitted to water from the trenches, for even if they cease, there is still the aqueduct to water from. And even if the majority of the field should not be watered from the aqueduct, in any case, in such a scenario, it is easy to always water the field (see Taz, subsection 1).

A field irrigated by a spring, where the water drips from it into another field to a deep place, and it gathers there and forms a pool – one can water another field from the pool as long as the spring continues to drip into the pool, and the spring has not stopped. However, if it stops dripping, or the spring ceases – it is prohibited, as we are concerned that one might draw water with a bucket from another spring.

It is forbidden to make furrows around the roots of grapevines during the intermediate days of the festival (Chol HaMoed) to collect water, as this is not a necessity for the festival. However, if the furrows were made before the festival and became somewhat damaged but are still recognizable, one may repair them during the festival. It is prohibited to deepen them more than originally, and it suffices to restore them as they were initially. But if they are completely filled in, it is forbidden to repair them, as this is considered a new creation rather than a repair.

Similarly, a water channel that has become damaged may be repaired. This is specifically when there remains a depth of one handbreadth (tefach) in it; for a furrow, even less than a tefach suffices, and it is still considered a furrow. However, for a water channel, if it is less than a tefach in depth, the water cannot flow through it at all, and it is considered completely blocked. If one tefach remains, one may dig up to six tefachim in depth; if two tefachim remain, one may dig up to seven tefachim, but not more. Even if it is originally three tefachim or more in depth, the Sages have determined that up to seven tefachim is sufficient, and they did not permit deepening it beyond five tefachim because of the significant effort involved. (Refer to Magen Avraham, subsection 5, who wrote that it seems this applies even if it was never more than one tefach deep, see there. And how do we know to say this? It is obvious that it refers to when it became damaged.)

One may draw water from tree to tree, as it is comparable to an irrigated field, where there is considerable loss if not watered. However, one should not water the entire field if it is a non-irrigated field. Nevertheless, if the field is moist and has dried up, it is permitted to water it, for if it is not watered now, it will be damaged. Therefore, it is permitted to water the entire field. It seems to me that this applies only when there are trees in it, for otherwise, the Tanna should have stated: "One may water an irrigated field, and a non-irrigated field when it is moist" (see Gemara 6b and Rashi there).

It is forbidden to open an area in a field to allow water to enter and irrigate it when it is a rain-fed field. However, if one opens a place to catch fish to eat during the festival, such as opening an area above for water and fish to enter, and below opening an area for the water to exit and leave the fish behind – it is permitted, even though the field is also improved by this. This is specifically when an action is performed that makes it evident to everyone that the intention is for the fish. But otherwise, it is forbidden, even if the intention is for the fish, since the action is on the field.
