Therefore, even though in section 533 we were lenient with catching fish, even if not all of them will be eaten during the festival, here, where the main action is on the field – there is no permission unless all or most of the fish will be eaten during the festival (see Magen Avraham, subsection 8).

It is forbidden to level a field for the purpose of plowing. However, if it is evident that the intention is to thresh for the needs of the festival, it is permitted. And what is the sign? The Gemara states: "If one levels a mound with another mound and leaves a dip between them, it is clear that his intention is for threshing." If he takes a mound and throws it into a dip, it is evident that his intention is for the field, according to the versions of the Rif and the Rosh, which prohibit leveling the ground. According to Rashi, the text is reversed, and leveling is specifically permitted. Consequently, for us, it is forbidden in all cases. The Tur and the Shulchan Aruch, section 9, rule according to Rashi's version. (And the Bach ruled that both are forbidden due to the different versions.) 

It is forbidden to collect wood from the field to prepare it for plowing. However, if it is evident that he intends to use the wood, such as if he takes the large pieces and leaves the small ones, it is permitted. Similarly, it is forbidden to cut branches from a tree to improve it. But if it is evident that his intention is for the branches, to feed them to his animals and not to improve the tree, such as if he cuts all from one side, it is permitted, as this is clear to everyone. For if his intention was to improve the tree, he would cut from all around the tree.

Know that in all matters related to land and trees, the intention to permit is only effective if it is evident to all, as I have written. Otherwise, it is forbidden because his actions involve the land and trees. This is not comparable to other matters, where intention alone suffices. (Beit Yosef and Taz, subsection 6. And what the Maharil wrote, that from the Gemara it seems that a distinguished person needs to be careful even in a matter of loss, none of the poskim brought this, as we find in several matters in the Gemara that a distinguished person is different. Nevertheless, this was not mentioned in this law, as we do not consider ourselves distinguished, as the Tosafot and the poskim wrote in several places.) (And so wrote the Eliyah Rabbah.)

It is prohibited to remove worms from trees, meaning to take the worm out of the tree, because it is a great exertion, and also the tree does not suffer damage if they wait until after the festival (Tosafot Pri Yitzchak 50). One may not smear manure on young trees, which is done when the bark has been stripped to prevent the tree from dying. However, one may anoint trees and fruits with oil, as this is a minor exertion. Similarly, one may trap the "ishush," a creature without eyes that digs in the ground (Gemara 6b), and mice when they cause damage to trees. This involves digging a hole and placing a trap in it. It is permitted to even dig the hole because they cause significant damage in an orchard. Even in a grain field, referred to in the Gemara as a "white field," adjacent to an orchard, it is permitted to trap them in the usual manner, because they come from there and harm the trees. If it is not adjacent to an orchard, one may only trap them with a modification: by inserting a spit into the ground and moving it back and forth until a hole is made, and then placing the trap in it. Digging a hole in the usual manner is prohibited. Some are stringent and say that this leniency of trapping with a modification is only permitted in a field adjacent to an orchard, where even there it is prohibited to dig in the usual manner. In a non-adjacent field, even with a modification, it is prohibited, because a "white field" does not cause damage. Having a non-Jew do what is prohibited for a Jew to do himself is also prohibited, as I have written in Siman 543; see there. And it will be explained there in detail with the help of Heaven.

One may not bring sheep into a pen on Chol HaMoed to fertilize the field, as this is akin to the labor of planting or plowing. However, if a non-Jewish shepherd brings them in of his own accord, it is permitted even on Shabbat, since the shepherd is acting independently. Therefore, even if one expresses gratitude to the shepherd for bringing them in, it is allowed, provided no payment is given. Even if only food compensation is given, it is prohibited on Shabbat. On Yom Tov, it is more lenient, and one may give food as compensation, but no other form of payment. This is similar to work related to attached produce, where even stipulating beforehand does not help, as I wrote in Siman 244. However, since this is not considered fully attached, it is somewhat lenient on Yom Tov. On Chol HaMoed, even giving full payment is permitted, as long as the shepherd acts independently, and provided he was not initially hired for this task. Additionally, one should not assist him or provide a guard to move the sheep around the pen to fertilize the entire area. If the shepherd is not a day laborer but rather hired for a year, month, or even a week, one may assist him on Chol HaMoed and provide a guard to move the sheep. However, one should not hire a guard specifically for that day, but use a guard from one's own household or a weekly laborer, and the like. On Shabbat and Yom Tov, even providing a guard is prohibited (Magen Avraham, Section 15).

It is forbidden to harvest a field during Chol HaMoed if it will not be ruined by standing in the field until after the festival. But if it will be ruined, it is permitted. Therefore, during Chol HaMoed Sukkot, when there is a lot of rain, we permit digging up potatoes from the ground, because they are greatly damaged by the rain. The same applies to other things that are damaged by the rain. Similarly, in cases where there is severe cold and frost, we also permit digging them up during Chol HaMoed, because they are greatly damaged by it.

And all this applies to a homeowner who does not need it for his consumption during the festival. But if he is poor and has nothing to eat, he is always permitted to reap for his needs and dig up potatoes. And even if he can buy them in the market and acquire money for this, the sages did not burden him when he does not have it prepared beforehand. He may reap, gather, thresh, winnow, and sort in his usual manner all that he needs for the festival, provided he does not thresh with animals, because it makes noise. According to the Rambam, it is permitted with a change, for example, if it is customary to thresh with cows, he should thresh with horses, and similar variations (see there, small section 16). And this is when he needs it only for himself. But if he needs to thresh for the benefit of many who need it during the festival, he is permitted to thresh even with animals, if it will not suffice without them. Nevertheless, it is appropriate to make a change, as I have written, if it is possible for him.

If someone has a vineyard next to a non-Jew's vineyard, and the non-Jew harvests his vineyard during Chol HaMoed (the intermediate days of a festival), and if the Jew does not harvest his vineyard now, he could incur a loss – he is permitted to harvest and press the wine, and make barrels without any change, because it is necessary to do this immediately after the harvest. If he leaves it until after the festival, the grapes will spoil. He may hire Jewish workers. This is all provided that he could not have done it before the festival, or the time for the harvest had not yet arrived. If he could have done it earlier, but purposely delayed the work for the festival – it is forbidden. And the same applies to grains, gardens, and orchards. Anything that would result in a loss is permitted, as long as one does not purposely delay the work for the festival, as I have written several times.

If someone harvested his olives and brought them to the olive press before the festival, and turned them in such a way that they would spoil if not pressed immediately; or his wine is in the pit and needs to be pressed, and he encountered an unavoidable circumstance that prevented him from pressing them before the festival – he may press his olives and grapes as usual, put them in barrels and seal them, and perform all that is necessary for them in the usual manner without any changes. Provided, however, that he did not intend to carry out this work during the festival, meaning: if he knew from the beginning that it would be impossible for him to finish before the festival, then it is certainly forbidden. Rather, the permission is in one of two cases: either he intended to leave them entirely until after the festival, and then something new occurred that would cause them to spoil if left; or he had sufficient time to finish them before the festival, so he started, and something happened in the middle and they remained until the festival – in this case, it is permitted to finish them during the festival due to the potential loss. Similarly, if he forgot about them before the festival, or was lazy and thought he would do it after the festival – these are also considered unavoidable circumstances, for forgetfulness and laziness are natural human traits.

And one should not ask: Why, regarding shaving, did we not permit it in Siman 531 even if one was coerced before the festival, except in matters that the sages permitted as I wrote there, yet here we permit it due to coercion, even coercion from forgetfulness or laziness? The matter is as follows: There, it only involves temporary bodily discomfort, and they upheld their decree. But here, where there is financial loss, the Torah has compassion on the money of Israel, and they established that since it was due to coercion, it is right that it should be permitted to complete it.

The Rambam writes in Chapter 8, Law 14: One may coat a barrel with pitch so that the wine will not spoil. And one may coat a bottle because it does not involve much effort. And one may seal the mouth of a beer barrel so that it does not spoil. This is his wording, and this refers to the stopper. And one can repair the stopper in its usual manner without any change. This is also the ruling in the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch, Section 1. And even though in the Gemara (12a) there is one opinion that permits coating a barrel but not a bottle, and another opinion that permits a bottle but not a barrel, see there. How did they rule leniently in both cases? It appears to me that it is because the Gemara later says that the one who prohibits only does so initially, see there. And in all the laws of Chol HaMoed, we find that something which would incur a loss is permitted, and anything that does not involve much effort is permitted. Therefore, they ruled leniently in both cases (see Magen Avraham, sub-section 1, who remains in need of further study).

Certainly, here is the translation:

"And all the more so with our barrels – it is permitted to repair the hoops, which are called 'reifen' and the staves. This is certainly considered a loss, for if they are not repaired, all the liquid will spill out. Similarly, one can remove flax from the soaking pool. And know that all these: the sealing, the repair of the hoops, and the removal of the flax – all apply when one did not plan their work for the intermediate days of the festival (Chol Hamoed), meaning when one did not know that they needed repair. But if one knew and could have repaired them before the festival, or removed the flax before the festival, and intentionally left them until the festival – it is prohibited even though it is considered a loss, and the Rabbis penalized him. It is necessary to penalize him, for if not, everyone would leave their work for the festival period, and the prohibition of work on the intermediate days of the festival would be completely nullified. And this will be explained in paragraph 7."

It is permitted to bring fruits inside to protect them from thieves if they are in a place that is not secure. However, one should do this discreetly, such as bringing them in at night. If it is something that would attract more attention at night than during the day, such as requiring torches and noise to bring them in, then it should be done during the day. For something that would result in a loss, it is permitted even if it needs to be done publicly. This applies to Chol HaMoed (the intermediate days of a festival). However, on Yom Tov (a festival day), it is forbidden, as we have learned: one may lower fruits through a skylight on Yom Tov, but lowering them through a window is forbidden, as I have written in Siman 536. All the more so, bringing them in is forbidden. What should one do? He should appoint a guard or have a non-Jew bring them in.

It is forbidden to transport one's possessions from city to city, except in a case of potential loss. Because moving from city to city creates publicity, it is considered like work. Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in Section 4: If one has figs spread out in the field to dry and fears rain, it is permitted to cover them with straw, even with a thick covering. Thus are his words. Covering is permitted even on Shabbat and Yom Tov, as I wrote in Siman 248 and Siman 536, but the novelty is in the thick covering, which is similar to building. He also wrote: If one has merchandise that will spoil if not turned over, it is permitted to turn it over on Chol HaMoed. Thus are his words. Certainly, turning over merchandise is not permitted on Shabbat and Yom Tov. If necessary, it should be done by a non-Jew, for a rabbinic prohibition on another rabbinic prohibition is permitted on Shabbat and Yom Tov in a case of loss.

If someone intentionally plans their work and leaves it for the intermediate days of a festival (Chol HaMoed) and then performs it during the festival, the court destroys that work and declares it ownerless for everyone. This is because the court's declaration of ownerlessness is effective. However, if he is doing work for others such that it is impossible to fine him, such as a tailor or a scribe doing work for others, we separate him and lash him. If someone did their own work and then died, his son is not fined after him, and it is permissible for his son to do that work if it is something that would be lost (if left undone). But for something that would not be lost, if he did the work and then died, his son is fined after him according to those who hold that the work on Chol HaMoed is of Biblical origin (as noted by Magen Avraham and see Taz). This is similar to doing work on Shabbat, which is forbidden for him and his household forever, as I wrote in Siman 318 regarding cooking on Shabbat. However, according to those who hold that the work on Chol HaMoed is of Rabbinic origin, his son is not fined after him, even for something that would not be lost. And there are those who say that according to all opinions, his son is not fined after him (see Beit Yosef).

We learn in Moed Katan (10b): Rava said: Any amount of commerce is prohibited… but in a case of potential loss, it is permitted. Similarly, in the Jerusalem Talmud (Chapter 2, Halacha 3): Lost commerce is permitted… this caravan is permitted on the festival… meaning that in a case of potential loss, commerce is permitted, or when caravans arrive, which is a rare occurrence and is considered a potential loss. Additionally, it permits when after the festival one would need to sell at a loss – one can sell during Chol HaMoed. Furthermore, it permits buying shawls for the needs of the festival. It also permits when one is pressed for holiday expenses, and selling the merchandise would enable him to profit for the needs of the festival. All these matters will be clarified in this Siman with the help of Heaven.

And one must understand: commercial activity, even on Shabbat and Yom Tov, is not prohibited by Torah law but only by rabbinic decree, as it is written "from pursuing your business" (Isaiah 58:13), which refers to the prohibitions of Shabbat. So why did the Sages see fit to prohibit it on Chol HaMoed? Even according to those who hold that the labor of Chol HaMoed is a Torah prohibition, as I wrote in Siman 530, it is obvious that commercial activity is not a Torah prohibition. Furthermore, what is the meaning of Rava's statement that any amount of commercial activity is forbidden? Even complete labors are permitted in some cases, as will be explained in Siman 540, such as repairing cracks in the roof or door hinges, which are permitted to be fixed on the festival. All the more so, small-scale buying and selling should be permitted. How, then, did they impose a stricter prohibition on a rabbinic matter than on a Torah prohibition?

It appears to me: because the main purpose of the festival was given to Israel only to eat, drink, rejoice, and engage in Torah study, as it says there in the Jerusalem Talmud: Rabbi Ba Bar Mamel said: If I had someone to support me... I would permit them to do work on the intermediate days of the festival... Was work prohibited on the intermediate days of the festival for any reason other than so that they could eat, drink, and engage in Torah study? And instead, they eat, drink, and engage in frivolity. That is to say: with various kinds of mockery and jest. According to this, if they were allowed to engage in commerce, they would naturally be preoccupied all day and would not have time to engage in Torah study as they do on regular weekdays. Therefore, the Sages were compelled to prohibit commerce. And they were compelled to prohibit even a small amount, for commerce has no limit, and if you permit a small amount, it will naturally lead to more. And in this respect, it is worse than work. It appears to me: even though the Jerusalem Talmud calls it "work," its intention is commerce. For in this discussion, the Jerusalem Talmud did not mention work at all, only matters of commerce. And it calls it "work" because this too is a weekday activity. (And this is satisfactory for those authorities who hold that the prohibition of work on the intermediate days of the festival is from the Torah, who were challenged by this Jerusalem Talmud, as I wrote in Siman 530. According to what I have written, this is resolved.)

And the Rosh, of blessed memory, wrote there that they prohibited business transactions because of the burden, see there. And his intention is not that this reason alone is sufficient, for there are many burdens undertaken during the festival. Rather, his intention is that through this burden, one will be prevented from the joy of the holiday, as the Rosh himself explains in a responsum (Klal 23), and this is his language (in Siman 4 there): "For in the purchase of merchandise, there is great effort in the precise valuation of the transaction. And because of his preoccupation, he will be prevented from the joy of the holiday." Until here is his language, thus this is the primary reason. And included in the joy of the holiday is engaging in Torah study, for even on a holiday we require half for the Lord, and all the more so during the intermediate days of the festival. And if one will be engaged in business transactions, he will not benefit from the joy of the holiday, and he will also not engage in Torah study.

Therefore, all commerce is prohibited, even the slightest amount, whether buying or selling. Even if one lent money on condition that it would be repaid later with wine or other merchandise for profit—he cannot go and demand it, unless these items are not available after the festival, in which case it would be considered a significant loss if he does not go during the intermediate days of the festival to their location and demand them. However, with a standard loan, where one lent money to another to be repaid in money, it is permitted to demand repayment during the intermediate days of the festival to collect his money. Needless to say, it is permitted to collect his money from a non-Jew who borrowed from him, as this does not involve much effort. Also, the primary act of lending, meaning to lend during the intermediate days of the festival, is also not considered like commerce, as will be explained. Even if he has collateral, he can demand his debt.

There is an opinion that what we permitted on the condition that they give him merchandise, if they are not available after the festival, he can demand it from them – this applies when he did not direct his work towards the festival, as he was unable to demand it before (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 2). In my humble opinion, it seems that regarding the collection of debts, it is not relevant at all to say that he directed his work towards the festival. For certainly, everyone, when able to collect their debt, does so without delay. Furthermore, do they immediately pay him as soon as he demands it? This only applies to work, and similarly to the sale of collateral, when he could have sold it before the festival and directed its sale towards the festival – this is certainly forbidden. But not in the case of collecting a debt. (The Magen Avraham brought proof from the Maharik regarding the sale of collateral, see there. But what is the connection between the two?)

There is an opinion that says that the inability to go and claim [the debt] only applies when one needs to litigate with him in court, as this would be an excessive burden, or if it involves traveling to another city. However, within the same city, and without legal proceedings, one can demand the merchandise (Taz, subsection 1). This is also the common custom. Nowadays, claims are made even in court, not only for loans but even for merchandise, because the failure to repay debts is very common nowadays, and people are becoming impoverished, which makes it akin to a matter of loss (ibid.).

And know that there are some of the early authorities who wrote that the prohibition of commerce applies only in public. But in private, such as in one's home, it is permitted (Beit Yosef in the name of Rokeach, Yereim, and Ran). And their reasoning appears to me to be: since the reason for the prohibition is so that one should not be distracted from the joy of the festival and the study of Torah, as I have written, therefore, when it is in private, one cannot be greatly distracted. However, the Rambam, the Rosh, the Tur, and the Shulchan Aruch did not make this distinction (there). Nevertheless, it seems to follow their reasoning, and this is what our Rabbi the Rema wrote in Section 1, and this is his language: However, if a significant profit happens to come his way during the festival, he may sell in private, and he should spend more on the joy of the festival than he had originally intended. This is his language, and the same applies to buying (Magen Avraham, Section 3).

If one sold merchandise to his friend before the festival, some say it is forbidden to demand payment during the festival unless the buyer is someone who is not usually present in the seller's location and happened to come during the intermediate days of the festival, in which case it is considered a potential loss. However, our teacher the Beit Yosef, in section 3, disagrees with this. Since the money was already established as a debt before the festival, it is considered a loan, and it is permissible to collect it during the intermediate days of the festival even if they reside in the same city. Similarly, it is permissible to file a legal complaint in secular courts for debts that are permitted to be collected if it is not possible to collect them in a rabbinical court, as I wrote in Choshen Mishpat, section 26. It is also permissible to consolidate debts during the festival in order to secure them, meaning to make an account and record them on a reliable document, ensuring that there is power to collect them, as this is all considered a potential loss.

It has already been explained that selling merchandise in a case of financial loss is permitted. And what is considered a "case of financial loss"? It says in the Jerusalem Talmud that if after the festival one will need to sell below the principal, it is permitted to sell it. But if one will not lose the principal, it is forbidden to sell it. The Rosh writes (there) that in any case, if selling it now will result in a profit and one will spend more for the joy of the festival, it is permitted to sell it in any situation, since this increases the joy of the festival. This is also found in the Jerusalem Talmud there. (The Rivash explains that a decrease in profit is also considered a case of financial loss; see Beit Yosef.)

And our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote about this in section 4, and this is his language: "It seems to me that these statements were only said regarding someone who has limited funds and is sparing in spending them for the joy of the holiday. If he had ample funds, he would spend more. But someone who has ample funds to spend on the joy of the holiday as much as he desires, and he does not intend to spend so much, we do not permit him to sell in order to spend more." Until here is his language. And this only applies to someone exceedingly wealthy, who is a prominent rich person. But an ordinary wealthy person is not in the category of "spending as much as he desires," and it is permitted for him if he wishes to add to the joy of the holiday (Taz, Section 2). Especially nowadays, when everything is considered merely for his livelihood (ibid).

And if it is something that is not always available after the festival, such as ships or caravans that have come or are about to depart, and they sell cheaply or buy expensively – it is permitted to buy and sell even not for one’s own use, but to trade and make a profit. The same applies to fairs that are held from time to time, and even from city to city it is permitted to travel in such a manner. Similarly, a special market day that occurs once or twice a year, like those that sometimes fall during the intermediate days of Passover, known as "Krasny Targ" – it is also considered like a fair, and it is permitted to conduct business transactions (Taz, subsection 3, in the name of the Rosh). However, on a regular market day, like in most places where there is a market day once a week – it is not permitted to buy and sell on the market day that falls during the festival, because this is not considered a significant loss; if one does not sell at this market, one can sell at the market after the festival. This applies specifically when it is known that there will be no loss of capital, but otherwise – it is permitted to sell (Magen Avraham, subsection 7).

Spice sellers, or vegetable sellers, and any item that does not last, as well as fruits and other types of food – they may open their stores as usual and sell publicly, because everyone knows they are for the needs of the festival. And sellers of types of fruits that are not known to be for the needs of the festival, or sellers of clothing and utensils, some of which are for the needs of the festival and some are not, and if they were not at all for the needs of the festival it would be entirely forbidden, but since some people buy them for the needs of the festival – they may sell discreetly for the needs of the festival. How so? If the store was open to a corner or alley – they open as usual. And if it was open to the public domain – they open one door and close one door, because usually the store has two doors. And on the eve of the last day of the festival of Sukkot, they bring out and decorate the market with fruits for the honor of the festival. And even for the needs of the second festival day of the last festival day – it is permissible to buy, and we do not say that since we are knowledgeable about the fixing of the month it turns out that one is preparing from the intermediate days of the festival for a weekday. For it is not so, because in the end it is still a festival day. And this necessity for discretion – this applies to a storekeeper. But a homeowner who sells for the needs of the festival – does not need discretion (Magen Avraham, subsection 11). And anything that is not for the needs of the festival – is entirely forbidden. (See Magen Avraham, subsection 12, that even if the store is closed and the door is open – it is forbidden, see there. And I do not know how it is closed and open.)

And know that in what was explained in paragraph 12, that what is incidental is permitted, and an ordinary market day is forbidden – our teacher the Rema wrote on this in paragraph 5, and this is his language: “And a merchant who buys from this one and sells to that one, and then goes back and buys and sells again – it is permitted because it is considered a loss.” So far his language, and it is not understood at all: for if so, all shopkeepers are the same, they buy and sell, and then go back and buy and sell. And if so, shops would be permitted, for this is a loss for everyone (Magen Avraham, subsection 8). And some have explained that for a merchant it is only permitted at home, and not in the shop. And the shopkeeper is also permitted at home, and only in the shop it is forbidden (ibid.). And it is a strain to say this, for an ordinary merchant is in the market in public. And furthermore: if it is because of a loss, where do we find that a loss needs to be done in private?

And even more puzzling to me is the custom in our country, where all the shopkeepers sit in their shops during Chol HaMoed as they do throughout the year. We have already protested vociferously, but no one pays attention to us. Only a few are careful about this. What justification is there for this? Therefore, it seems to my humble opinion that the matter is as follows: complete labors of craftsmen are entirely forbidden, whether by Torah law or rabbinic decree, as I wrote in Siman 530. But commerce is only forbidden in the sense of trade that is not a daily necessity and does not incur a loss if sold on another day. For this, specific conditions must be met as explained in this Siman. Otherwise, it is forbidden.

And this is what we have learned: sellers of fruits, garments, and utensils may sell discreetly; this does not refer to shopkeepers but rather to someone selling his fruits from his field or garments and utensils he made or bought, and would not suffer a loss if he sells them today or after the festival, because once sold, he will not have others to sell. Similarly, sellers of spices or vegetables are in the same category. But someone whose livelihood depends on his shop and from it he earns his daily sustenance—there is no greater loss than this. If he closes his shop, he will certainly cut back on his expenses for the joy of the festival. This is explicitly stated in the Jerusalem Talmud which we brought, that to enhance the honor of the festival, it is permitted to engage in commerce. And it is clear to us that if the shops were closed, it would reduce the joy of the festival.

Similarly, it is implied in the Tosefta in the second chapter, where it is taught: shops open to a portico may open and close as usual; those open to the public domain may open one door and close one door. And in the Gemara at the end of the second chapter, this Baraita is brought in the context of sellers of spices; see there. But in the Tosefta, there is no mention of this specific case but rather of shops in general, see there. It implies that it refers to all shops, as we said, that anyone whose livelihood depends on the shop, it is considered a significant loss and a necessity for the joy of the festival. And these are the words of our teacher, the Rema, regarding a merchant, since his livelihood is dependent on it. They should only be warned to open only one door if they are in a completely public domain. (This is how it seems to my humble opinion to justify the practices of the entire Jewish community. And also, the Eliyah Rabbah and the Machatzit Hashekel have justified this.)

A found object that requires effort—It is forbidden to exert effort and search for it. For example, if a river washes fish onto its banks, it is forbidden to gather them in order to pickle them and eat them after the holiday. However, if one can eat from them during the holiday, and pickling them takes only a day or two, then it is permitted, even if some will remain after the holiday. One should not question why we permit items brought by a caravan, considering it as a loss. Certainly in this case, all the fish will be lost if not taken now. The answer is that we only permit commerce, as that is the way of trade, and the loss of business is considered a loss, but not in the case of catching fish and salting them. In my humble opinion, if one trades in fish, it is permitted, as for him, it is like any other commerce.

The Tur wrote: If someone lends to his friend on condition, and the borrower gives him an item, and stipulates with him that if he does not repay by the end of eight days, the item will be acquired by the lender – some permit this, since the acquisition is essentially after the term. However, it does not seem permissible, for if so, all business transactions would be allowed, as they could scheme to do so. Thus far his words. And these two opinions are brought in the Shulchan Aruch, Section 7. And there is an opinion that this applies specifically to one's fellow Jew, but with a non-Jew, even the Tur agrees that it is permitted, as there is no concern of scheming with him (Bach). And all agree that if the non-Jew pays the Jew with wine or other merchandise for his debt during the intermediate days of the festival – it is permitted to accept it from him, as it is considered a potential loss.

And similarly, one who needs to buy wine at the time of the grape harvest for the entire year, for his own drinking and for the drinking of his household members, and not for any commercial purpose, and if the holiday period passes, he will not be able to find this wine to buy, or at the lower price as he buys it now – it is considered a loss, and it is permissible to buy it. And similarly for other foods and drinks. It is also permissible to buy barrels, repair them, and pitch them during the intermediate days of the festival, as this is considered a loss, provided that he did not intentionally delay the work for the festival, and previously he was unable to buy them. Similarly, he should not buy more than what is needed for his drinking and the drinking of his household members for the entire year, but he does not need to be excessively precise about this. For commercial purposes – it is forbidden, unless it is something that will not be available later to profit from, and if he buys it now, he will profit from it, then it is also permitted for commercial purposes, as this is truly considered a loss. (This is how it appears from the words of the Rema, section 9. And the difference between for drinking and for commercial purposes is that for drinking, even if he can obtain other wine later, he still prefers this wine, but for commercial purposes this preference does not apply. And similarly for purchasing for commercial purposes, even if later he can buy it at a slightly higher price, he should pay the higher price. This preference does not apply to drinking. Deliberate and you will find it easy.)

One should not purchase houses, stones, slaves, or animals except for the needs of the festival, or for the needs of the seller who has nothing to eat, or for the needs of the worker transporting these items who has nothing to eat. The details of this law will be explained in Siman 542. The same law applies to all items one wishes to purchase, as the Tosafot (Beitza 13a, s.v. "Ein") wrote, as well as the Ramban and the Rosh there. Therefore, they were surprised at our teacher the Rema in section 12, who wrote that only these items are allowed to be bought because their purchase is publicized, but other utensils are customarily bought in private. Thus far his words. And indeed, the Maggid Mishneh wrote similarly in chapter seven, law 22, but this is against all our teachers. They wrote that therefore he used the term "customarily," meaning that he does not agree with this (Magen Avraham, section 16, and Eliyah Rabbah, section 20). Therefore, in a place where there is no custom, it is forbidden (there). And from a non-Jew, everything is permitted, as it is taught in the Tosefta, first chapter, see there. And lending to a non-Jew with interest, to those who are accustomed to borrowing from him, is permitted, as it is a matter of loss if they would borrow from someone else. This is not like commerce, which involves meticulous calculation and much effort. Also, for those who are not accustomed to borrowing from him, it is permitted if he does not take interest for this week or if he takes and spends it on Yom Tov festivities more than usual. And it is permitted to take a guarantor during the festival for a loan to be made after the festival, as this is not considered doing anything. And the loans of bankers, who engage constantly in lending and exchanging, are forbidden on the intermediate days of the festival, as this is considered a full-fledged business. It is only permitted in a case of potential loss. See what I wrote in section 15. And any purchase for the needs of the festival is permitted.

Building – is completely forbidden, even a minimal amount, and even for the needs of the festival, and it should have been built before the festival. Even if one has no place to live. There is a doubt if one's dwelling burns down during the festival, and it is possible to rebuild it during the festival and move in during the festival, whether it is permitted like any matter of loss when it was not possible to do it before the festival, which is permitted to be done during the festival. And here too: even though this is not a matter of loss – it should be considered as a need of the festival, since he has no place to live. Or perhaps: since complete building is considered a significant matter and involves great effort – it is forbidden even in such a case, like a water channel in Siman 537. And this seems to be the main ruling that it is forbidden. And proof from what will be explained, that in a place of danger it is permitted to build in the usual manner. And it implies that only in danger is it permitted, and not in any other matter.

If the fence of his garden or the wall of his courtyard that is shared with his neighbor was breached during the festival, it is permitted for him to repair it in a non-professional manner, not in a professional manner. And a non-professional manner is not considered building. How so? He places stones one on top of the other without using mortar, or places wood one on top of the other in this manner, or fences it with reeds and similar materials. And it was taught (11a): One may make a guardrail for a roof or a gallery in a non-professional manner, but not in a professional manner. And it seems to me that if the fence of his garden or the wall of his courtyard was breached, and they permitted a non-professional repair, this applies if it was breached on the festival or before the festival and he was unable to repair it before the festival. Because if he was able to repair it, they did not permit it even in this manner. And this is implied in the language of the Mishnah (6b): One may cover the breach during the festival, meaning it was breached during the festival. But regarding a guardrail, it was taught in a general manner: One may make a guardrail, even if he was able to make it beforehand, because it is a mitzvah and at all times one transgresses "You shall not bring bloodguilt upon your house." And there is some danger involved, but it suffices with a non-professional manner (this is what seems to me in my humble opinion).

And this, that they did not permit in a manner other than a layman's work—it applies to a garden fence or a courtyard wall between him and his neighbor, where the damage from the breach is not so great, as there is no concern for thieves there. Therefore, a layman's work suffices. But a courtyard wall adjacent to the public domain that fell, where the damage is very great that thieves might enter (Rashi 7a), and a layman's work would not suffice—he builds the wall in the usual manner, for there is nothing more at risk of being lost than this. And even if we say that building a house in such a manner is forbidden due to the great effort involved, as I have written, nevertheless the building of a wall is not like the building of a house. And a wall that is leaning and about to fall, if there is no danger involved, such that it can be supported until after the festival—it is forbidden to demolish it, and all the more so to build it. But when there is a danger—he is obligated to demolish it, and afterwards it is permitted to build it in the usual manner with skilled work. And even if it is only leaning towards a courtyard or an alley—it is permitted, for they permitted the end because of the beginning, for if you do not allow him to build it in the usual manner, he will refrain from demolishing it, and it will lead to danger. And likewise, in other matters where there is a concern for danger—he builds and demolishes in the usual manner. And it seems to me that a garden wall is not a place of danger, as it is not a place frequented by the public, and the owner of the garden can be careful not to go there until after the festival.

It is permitted to remove a bump from the roof, even though it is considered a complete act of labor, because it does not involve great effort. Only plowing is prohibited (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 5). Cracks in the roof may be sealed by hand or foot, but not with a craftsman’s tool. Some permit placing a ladder and plastering the roof with clay for the sake of the festival, as this is not a craftsman's task but rather an amateur's task, as proven in Bava Metzia (101b), see there (Taz, subparagraph 1). The Tur and Shulchan Aruch do not mention this. In my humble opinion, it is prohibited because it involves great effort. The proof is from what is taught (Moed Katan 11a): "One may smooth out the cracks," as explained. Typically, they smooth them with clay, as evidenced by the Mishnah’s conclusion, "and roll them with a roller," which is on clay, as is known. As we learn in the beginning of the second chapter of Makot (7a): "He was rolling with a roller," and Rashi and Tosafot explain that they plastered their roofs with clay and used the roller to smooth it, see there. Only the smoothing of cracks is permitted, not the plastering of the entire roof.

We also learned there in the Mishnah: the hinge, which is the leg of the door, and the pipe, which is the hole in the threshold, and the beam, which is above the entrance where the door swings back (Rashi), and the lock, and the key that were broken – one may repair them on the festival, provided that one does not intend to do work on the festival. Whether they are made of wood or of iron. And even if they were broken before the festival – one can repair them without any change, because this is a great loss, for if one leaves the entrance open and the doors broken – one would lose everything in the house. Therefore, they permitted even if they were broken before the festival, provided one does not intend to do work on the festival. This means that if one was unable to repair them before the festival, and not that one intentionally left them until the festival. For if one intentionally left them – it is completely forbidden. Similarly, it is permitted to nail the lintel with nails when there is a concern about thieves. And if not – it is forbidden, and similarly anything like this (Magen Avraham section 6).

And it is permitted to build a makeshift trough for the animal to eat from. For anything that is not for the purpose of food preparation, although it is for the sake of the festival, professional work is forbidden, except in the case of something that would be lost (Siman 537:7). Similarly, it is permitted to build a makeshift platform to sit or sleep on. And a plank to which legs are attached like our benches is considered makeshift work and is permitted (Siman 537:8).

And one may clean the millstones, open a hole in the middle of the millstones, and set them up. And one may build an aqueduct for the millstones. And cut the nails of the donkey of the millstones, which means that this is what the donkey of the mill wheel is called. Because all these things, even if they were fixed before the festival, they deteriorate and need fixing at any time. Similarly, it is permitted to sharpen a knife during the festival, for this is neither work nor a burden. And a knife that broke during the festival and is needed by another – it is permitted to fix it during the festival. And even if it broke before, if he did not intentionally leave the work for the festival, it is permitted (Taz 537:5). And even if he could borrow a knife, he is permitted to fix his own (Magen Avraham 537:10), for he does not prefer to use others' items. But if he has another knife, it is forbidden for him to make a new knife during the festival.

A stove and ovens that can be dried and used for baking during the festival – one may make them. If not – one may not make them, because it is forbidden to exert effort for after the festival. The same rule applies to making pots and pans – it is permitted if they can be used during the festival. And if the weather is cold – it is permitted to make a winter stove to warm oneself if one can be warmed during the festival (there, in subsection 9). Rambam in Chapter Eight and Shulchan Aruch in Section 7 write that in any case, one may build on the clay of the stove, and on their secondary stove. Thus are their words. "Secondary" refers to what the stove or oven stands on, as explained in Chapter Five of Keilim (Mishnah 7). From their language, it seems that their intention is towards the plaster surrounding the stove and oven, meaning plastering with clay to retain its heat (Taz, subsection 3, and Bach). This is also called secondary, as Rashi explained in Shabbat (125a, "they placed it"). And there in Keilim, there is something similar. But it is surprising that it seems this is permitted even if one does not bake during the festival, and how can we permit exertion for after the festival (Taz, subsection 3)? It appears to me that the explanation is: "in any case" means whether one can bake without the plastering, or whether one cannot bake without the plastering – one can do the plastering, because even if one can bake without it – nevertheless, with the plastering, it will be better for baking. But baking in the festival oven that is not damaged at all does not apply to the beginning.

It is permitted to make a fish trap out of willow branches, as this is considered a simple task, and when it is needed for the festival. However, traps woven from threads, which are considered a skilled task, are not allowed. Even though for the sake of the festival it is permitted to prepare items necessary for food, like an oven as mentioned in the previous section, a trap is not considered a necessary preparation (Magen Avraham, subsection 1). This is according to the explanations of the Rosh and the Nimukei Yosef. And Rashi, of blessed memory, (11a) explained that fish traps are not considered a "skilled task" and are permitted, while bird traps are considered a "skilled task" and are forbidden, see there. In the Rambam, I did not find this ruling, and it requires further investigation.

One may intertwine the cords of beds on Chol HaMoed, meaning to say that one can weave ropes for the beds to lie on during the festival. However, one should not make the ropes from scratch, as this involves great exertion, and it is possible to do it using ropes prepared before the festival. It is permitted to press linen garments by hand after washing, in order to whiten and soften them for the festival. However, one should not make sleeve pleats, which means to crimp them, as this involves great exertion. Similarly, it is forbidden to crimp collars with the wooden tools designated for this purpose, as this is skilled labor and involves great effort. One can manage without the crimping. It is permitted to smooth garments with glass as usual, since this is for the sake of the festival and is not considered skilled labor. The same law applies to our practice of smoothing with hot iron tools, which are called a "press."

It is forbidden to repair one's clothes or torn shoes during Chol Hamoed. Similarly, it is forbidden to tell a non-Jew to repair them. Even though they might tear more if not repaired, it is still forbidden, because it is not considered a "davar ha'aved" (a matter of loss) unless the main item is being ruined, and not just a little additional damage (Tur). However, through a change, it is permitted to repair them somewhat for the sake of the festival, even by a craftsman. An amateur does not need to make a change (ibid. section 7), for all amateur work is considered a change. Some say that if they were very torn and damaged, it is permitted to repair them completely, for this is certainly a "davar ha'aved," because if not repaired, they would be completely ruined (Taz, section 1). However, it is preferable to have it done by a non-Jew.

One who needs a garment during the intermediate festival days (Chol HaMoed) because he has nothing suitable to wear outside, if he is an unskilled person not proficient in that craft, he may do the work in his usual manner. However, if he is a skilled craftsman, he must do the work in an unskilled manner, meaning he should make wide stitches, with one stitch above and one stitch below, resembling the teeth of a dog. It does not suffice for a craftsman to sew with a change in how he holds the needle; rather, the actual sewing method must be altered. Even though for writing, it is sufficient to change the way the pen is held, as will be explained in Siman 545, writing is different in that it is not a skilled craft (Taz, subsection 3). And who is called a "craftsman"? Anyone who knows how to draw a full needleful of thread at once or who knows how to align a hem on the edge of a garment (Magen Avraham, subsection 9). According to this, most of our women are considered "craftswomen" because they know how to do this. A child born during the festival is not allowed to have new clothes made for him during the intermediate festival days for the purpose of his circumcision. His father can wrap him in silk (Magen Avraham, subsection 8). If not, there is no need at all to wrap him in a fine garment, for this alone does not permit sewing for him during Chol HaMoed.

Even the labors that are permitted during Chol HaMoed, as explained previously, are only allowed when done by oneself or by others who do not receive payment for the work. However, if done for payment, it is prohibited, as receiving payment during the festival is considered like a weekday activity. Nevertheless, if no fixed payment is given, but the worker is compensated by being provided meals, it is not considered a weekday activity because it is not customary to pay in this manner on a weekday. In a case where there is a potential loss, it is permitted to perform the work even for a fixed payment if there is no other way to accomplish it. For example, if the person himself cannot do it, and without a fixed payment, no one would be willing to do it, there is no prohibition in this case. However, the one who takes the fixed payment has not acted properly. (This seems, in my humble opinion, to explain what the Rema wrote, that in a case of potential loss, a fixed payment is permitted, which refers to the one giving the payment. But for the worker, if he has what to eat, what difference does it make to him whether it is a case of potential loss or not? However, from the Taz at the end of the previous section, it does not seem so, and also from the language of the Rema, it does not appear so. Therefore, we must say that since the work is permitted, the payment is also permitted by law. This requires further investigation. The Eliyah Rabbah in the previous section, subsection 7, completely disagrees with the Beit Yosef and those who prohibit taking payment and brings proof from Daf 12a about the avungari of Rabban Gamliel's house. See there. I do not understand his proof. Also, from Rivash, responsum 226, it is clear that only a poor person who has nothing to eat is permitted to take payment, but not others. See there and analyze carefully.)

Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote: Any type of labor is permitted to be performed by a worker who has nothing to eat, so that he can earn and profit. Thus are his words. And since this labor is permitted to him because he has nothing to eat, he is allowed to even take on much of this labor, but not other labor (Taz). He is not required to sell his house and personal belongings (ibid.). There are those who say that if he only has bread and water, it is considered that he has something to eat (Magen Avraham). Specifically concerning business and writing tefillin, it is permitted for him to fulfill the needs of the holiday with profit, but not actual labor (ibid.). There are those who disagree with this (Elya Rabba), and this is the main opinion, as it is explained in the Jerusalem Talmud (ibid., and I have not found this). It seems to me in my humble opinion that although all labor is permitted by a worker who has nothing to eat, nevertheless, labor that is publicly visible is forbidden. Similarly, shaving and haircutting are forbidden, because the reason for the prohibition is so that people do not enter the festival in a disheveled state. Therefore, if you permit it by a worker who has nothing to eat, the concern returns to its place. And one should not say that this is not common and one would not rely on it, for certainly poverty is common, as the Rosh and Ran wrote in Nedarim (64b) in the name of the Jerusalem Talmud. See there.

Any work that is prohibited for a Jew to do himself on Chol HaMoed—it is forbidden to tell a non-Jew to do it, as we have learned in a Baraita (12a). The general principle is: Anything that a Jew is permitted to do himself, he may instruct a non-Jew to do; and anything that he is not permitted to do himself, he may not instruct a non-Jew to do. The same applies to commerce: anything that is forbidden for a Jew himself is also forbidden through a non-Jew. The reason is simple: since the main reason for the prohibition of commerce and work is so that they should enjoy the joy of the holiday and engage in Torah study, as I wrote in Siman 539 in the name of the Jerusalem Talmud, if we permit him to do so through a non-Jew, he will be preoccupied during the festival just as on weekdays. What difference does it make if he does it himself or his agent does it? In the end, the preoccupation is upon him.

There is an aspect where Chol HaMoed (intermediate days of a festival) is more stringent than Yom Tov (festival day). How so? For example, if a non-Jew is contracted to build a building for a Jew on a task-based basis, within the city limits it is prohibited, and outside the city limits it is permitted, provided there is no other city within the limits of the building, as I wrote earlier in Siman 244. However, during Chol HaMoed, even in such a case, it is prohibited. The reason is that on Shabbat and Yom Tov, where it is forbidden to go beyond the city limits, there is no concern that Jews will see that the house of so-and-so is being built on Shabbat and Yom Tov. This is not the case on Chol HaMoed, when one is allowed to go beyond the city limits; therefore, it is prohibited due to the appearance of impropriety. Hence, there is no difference between within the city limits and outside the city limits.

And the Tur wrote that even after the fact, if the house was built in a prohibited manner by a non-Jew, it is proper to be stringent and not enter it. These are his words. This means that according to the strict law, it is permitted, but it is proper to be stringent (Beit Yosef). There are those who write that according to the strict law it is forbidden (Bach), but this is not so (Taz). However, if he gave the non-Jew work to do on detached items before the festival, to do it during the festival within the non-Jew's house and on a contract basis, and he did not explicitly designate that it should be done during the festival – it is permitted. It is permitted to give any work to a non-Jew, even connected to the ground, on a contract or as a day laborer before the festival, and to stipulate with him that he should do it specifically after the festival. And even during the festival – one can hire him to do it after the festival. However, when hiring him during the festival, he should be careful not to measure, weigh, or count in the usual manner, but rather make a transaction with him only. And even a Jew is permitted in this manner, but with a non-Jew there is a greater leniency, even though there is concern that he may not comply and do the work during the intermediate days of the festival. Nevertheless, if he did the work during the intermediate days of the festival, it is permitted, since he stipulated with him to do it after the festival. And he does not need to protest against him (Magen Avraham). However, in a matter that is public and known to many, he needs to protest. (And Magen Avraham wrote in Subsection 1 that for the sake of a mitzvah, it is permitted to tell a non-Jew to do work during the intermediate days of the festival; see there. And it seems to me that this is with detached items and not connected to the ground. And even a synagogue or a study hall – it is forbidden to build, as this would be a desecration of God's name. But if the non-Jew is a sharecropper in his field, he is permitted to work. See above in Siman 243, and see Magen Avraham Subsection 3.)

We learned in the Mishnah at the beginning of Moed Katan that all public needs may be attended to during Chol Hamoed. This is the language of the Rambam in Chapter 7, Law 10: "All public needs may be attended to on the festival. How so? They repair water sources that are in the public domain, they repair the roads and streets, they dig public wells, cisterns, and caves, they dredge rivers so that people may drink from their waters, they collect water into public cisterns and caves, they repair their cracks, they remove thorns from the roads, and they measure the mikvaot. Any mikvah that is found to be deficient, they bring water to it to complete its required measure."

And the emissaries of the court go out to declare ownerless the mixed species (kilayim). They redeem captives, and valuations, and consecrated items, and sacred items. They give the water to the suspected adulteress (sotah), and burn the red heifer, and break the neck of the calf, and pierce the ear of the Hebrew servant, and purify the leper. And they mark graves whose markers have been washed away by rain, so that the priests will distance themselves from them. For all these are communal needs. Thus far are the words of the Rambam. 

The reason they established this for Chol HaMoed (the intermediate days of the festival), is because it is a time when the leaders of the people have the opportunity to reflect on all the communal needs. And most of these are time-sensitive, because during Pesach (Passover) and Sukkot (Tabernacles) there is a transition from winter to summer and from summer to winter, and then the roads, pits, rivers, ritual baths, and fields become damaged, as there are many changes in the waters. 

And then is the time of the ripening of the crops, and there is a need to clear the mixed species from them. Therefore, many markers are washed away at that time, and they need to be repaired so that the priests do not stumble over them. Therefore, even though there are complete labors involved, since they are communal needs – it is permitted. Also, during the festival, workers can be hired at a lower cost (Gemara 6a). And the other matters mentioned in section two do not involve labor, and generally remain for Chol HaMoed, which is a time of gathering in Jerusalem during the time of the Temple, as most of these matters were done in Jerusalem. Also, the redemption of captives becomes known then, and another reason will be explained.

And know that for communal needs there are two leniencies that do not apply to individual needs: Firstly, for communal needs, even amateur work is permitted, even if it is not needed at all for the festival, which is not the case for individual needs. Secondly, for professional work, if it is needed during the festival, it is permitted even for an individual, provided that they did not intentionally delay the work for the festival. But if they did intentionally delay the work for the festival, it is forbidden, as explained in previous sections. However, for communal needs, even in such a case, it is permitted, even if they intentionally delayed the work for the festival, and similarly for amateur work that is not needed at all for the festival. The reason is that communal needs are like a pot of partners, and no one remembers it, and each person relies on the other. If they do not gather together during their free time to do it, it will never get done. Therefore, they permitted all leniencies for them (Taz, small section 2).

And therefore, pits and springs belonging to the public that have become filled with dirt and stones and have become damaged—it is permitted to repair them, even if the public does not currently need them, since this is not a skilled labor, and even if the work is timed for the intermediate days of the festival (Taz there). Similarly, it is permitted to make a trench in an unskilled manner, so that water will flow freely to the city, even though it is a great effort and done publicly, and the work is timed for the intermediate days of the festival, for the reason we have written (Magen Avraham, subsection 3). But to dig new pits for them, which is skilled labor, if the public needs them now—it is permitted, even if the work is timed for the intermediate days of the festival, and even publicly and with great effort. If they do not need them now—they should not do so.

But pits, ditches, and caves belonging to an individual – it is forbidden to dig them anew, even if he needs them now. And even if he has nothing to drink – it is forbidden, unless there is a danger to life. And this is uncommon, as he can obtain water from a distance. And even if he did not plan this work for the intermediate days of the festival, since this is considered like building which makes noise and involves excessive labor, it is not permitted for an individual. However, if they were already made and became damaged, if he needs them now – it is permitted to repair them. But if he does not need them now – it is forbidden to repair them. But it is permitted to extend water to them even if he does not need them now, meaning receiving rainwater from the roofs and directing it to the pits, as this does not involve much labor. But to bring water through a trench – it is forbidden (there, subsection 5).

And know that there is an opinion that for communal needs, when there is a leader who has the authority to act alone – it is forbidden to do so during the intermediate days of a festival as an individual (there, subsection 3). And I am astonished: for at the time of the Temple and at the time of the Talmud, were there not officials appointed over every matter, and did they not have the authority to act as they saw fit? And behold, we learned at the beginning of the fifth chapter of Shekalim that Nechunya was appointed over the digging of wells, and even so, it was permitted because of communal needs. Rather, it is certain that even for an official who can act on his own, there are many impediments in communal needs. And how did the Sages conclude by saying that communal needs are permitted? They should have said that when there is an official – it is forbidden. And certainly, in ancient times there were officials for all matters. And all the more so now, when no official has the power to act on his own, for in this, disputes would increase, as is known. Therefore, it is permitted in any case (so it seems in my humble opinion).

And one should not ask: Since communal needs are permitted, why do we not build synagogues and study halls on Chol HaMoed? Indeed, our Rabbi the Rema wrote in Section 1, and this is his language: Specifically, communal needs that are required for the physical body. But other communal needs, such as building a synagogue, it is forbidden to do on the festival. And the same applies to other mitzvah needs - it is forbidden to perform skilled labor on the festival. So far his language. And there are those who wrote that in our times it is permitted to build a synagogue, as it is considered a loss, for we worry that they might prevent us from building it (there in sub-section 2, and see Taz sub-section 1). And there are those who wrote that fixing benches in the synagogue is permitted on Chol HaMoed to avoid disputes (Shut). And there are those who wrote that a bathhouse is considered a bodily need, and it is permitted to build it with non-expert work (Magen Avraham sub-section 1). And indeed, one should distance oneself from this. In our days, we have not heard of making any repairs in the synagogue and study hall. Similarly, with a bathhouse, this depends on the discretion of the teachers, according to the situation of the city. In general, one should avoid such permissions, as they show disrespect for the festival.

Writing during the intermediate days of a festival (Chol HaMoed) is like any other work: if it is not for the need of the festival or to prevent a loss, it is forbidden. Even though it is not like other types of work, as it does not involve much exertion and is done in private, it is still considered work. Therefore, one may not correct even a single letter in a Torah scroll if there is no need to read from it during the festival. And even though it is forbidden to leave a Torah scroll uncorrected, since it is not for the need of the festival, it is forbidden to fix it. Writing in a Torah scroll is obviously considered skilled work. Therefore, some say that if there is an extra letter that needs to be erased, it is permitted to erase it during the intermediate days of the festival, as erasing is not considered skilled work, and a Torah scroll is regarded as a communal need. It is permitted to perform unskilled work for communal needs even if it is not for the festival, as I wrote in the previous section (Shaarei Teshuva in the name of Peri Megadim). If the erasure is in the middle of a word, and as a result, one would need to extend the previous or subsequent letter so that there is no gap in the middle of the word, it seems that if this extension involves skilled work, it is forbidden. If not, it is permitted. Similarly, small corrections are permitted.

And this is when they have another Torah scroll. But if they need this Torah scroll to read from during the festival, it is permitted to correct it during the festival, and it is an obligation to correct it in order to read from it in public. And even if he could have corrected it before the festival, this is a communal need that allows for skilled work even if he intentionally deferred the work until the festival, as I wrote in the previous section. There is a doubt if they have another Torah scroll, but the custom is to read the Maftir on a festival from a different Torah scroll, and similarly on the intermediate days of Passover, the fourth person reads from a different Torah scroll, if it is permitted to correct it on the intermediate days of the festival. And it appears from the language of Rabbeinu Beit Yosef in section 2, who wrote that if they do not have a kosher Torah scroll to read from... it implies that if they have a single kosher Torah scroll, it is forbidden. And it is better to roll a kosher Torah scroll from place to place than to correct another one during the intermediate days of the festival.

It seems to me that those who have the custom for the scribe to inspect each Torah portion that needs to be read the next day before any reading, and it is a good custom, are permitted to do so even on a festival. If he finds something that needs correction, he should correct it, even if there is another Torah scroll, because that one would also need to be inspected, and it too might need correction, just as this one needs correction even though it was assumed to be kosher. Therefore, it is permitted to correct it if he finds things that need correction.

And it's not only specifically a Torah scroll, but the same applies to other books: Scripture, Mishnah, Talmud, and Halachic authorities. If one needs to study from them during the intermediate days of a festival (Chol HaMoed), it is permitted to correct them during the festival because it is considered a matter of loss. In other words, if the corrections are not made, it becomes difficult to study from them, and one will not learn. There is no greater loss than this (Magen Avraham, subsection 5). This is when the corrections prevent the study. But common errors found in books, which do not impede the study, seem to be forbidden to correct during the festival. However, this is not the case, for it is well known that this is very common, and if we do not correct it now, the matter will be forgotten, and the error will remain. This is certainly considered a matter of loss, and therefore it is permitted to correct it (Taz, subsection 3). All the more so for us, who correct in our own script, which is considered the work of an amateur, as will be explained, for only Ashurit script is considered the work of a professional – it is obvious that it is permitted to correct.

And our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 2: "If they do not have a Torah scroll at all, if it is possible to write the entire thing during Chol HaMoed through many scribes, they should write it, since it is a need of the festival to read from the Torah publicly during the festival." End quote. And the same applies to other books for learning. And even if it was possible to write it before the festival, it is still permitted since for communal needs it is permitted even if one intentionally plans his work for the festival, as I have written. And from all that has been explained, it is clarified that writing a Torah scroll that is not for the need of the festival, such as when there is another Torah scroll, is prohibited. Therefore, one should protest against an individual who writes a Torah scroll and completes it during Chol HaMoed. This is a complete prohibition, for at the time of completion, the scribe finishes writing the Torah scroll. And behold, there is no need for this Torah scroll for the holiday, as there are others. And people are unaware of this prohibition and think it is a mitzvah and a joy for the festival, but it is a complete transgression.

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote in section 1 that for public needs, some forbid anything that is not for the festival, and some permit it. The custom is to be lenient with our writing, which is not the work of an artisan. This is his language. The explanation of the matter is as follows: As it has already been explained in the previous section, for public needs there are two leniencies: one is that non-artisan work is permitted even if it is not for the festival, and the second is that artisan work is permitted if it is for the festival, even if he planned his work for the festival. But anything that is not for the festival is forbidden in artisan work. According to this, if a community needs to write some document, if it is for the festival like announcements or regulations and conduct, it is obviously permitted. But if they need to send a letter to the rabbi or the cantor or for other appointments, which will occur after the festival, some forbid it because writing is considered the work of an artisan, and anything that is not for the festival is forbidden. And some permit it because all public matters are considered "for the festival" in such a context, since after the festival it will be impossible to gather everyone, and the matter will be nullified. The custom is to be lenient with our writing, which is not the work of an artisan, and it is permitted for public needs even if it is not for the festival. Yet, it is also not clear that our writing is considered "non-artisan work," but this leniency is practiced. And thus, the simple custom is to be lenient, especially in our times when it is known that the intermediate days of the festival are a time for gathering for all. If not during the intermediate days of the festival, no correction will ever be made.

The Tur wrote that it is forbidden to write tefillin and mezuzot for others for a wage. But for oneself, or for others for free, or even for a wage in order to have more to spend on the joy of the holiday – it is permitted even if he has what to eat. For if he does not have what to eat – all work is also permitted. And specifically tefillin and mezuzot because of the mitzvah, for even on Chol HaMoed one must put on tefillin and recite a blessing on them. But other books – it is forbidden, whether for free or for pay, if he has what to eat. And it is permitted to spin the blue wool for his tzitzit, whether by hand or with a spindle, but for others it is forbidden. Thus far is his language. It is explained from his words that anything not needed during the festival – is completely forbidden. And even for one who needs it during the festival, though it is permitted to write for him – nonetheless, it is forbidden to take payment from him, and he is obligated to write for him for free. And if he does not want it for free, this one who needs the tefillin or mezuzah will give him payment, and he has committed a transgression. And one who does not have what to eat – it is like all other labors, and he is permitted to write them even for someone who does not need them during the festival, because he needs to eat. And it is lighter than other labors, for in writing it is permitted even if he has what to eat but wants to spend more on the joy of the holiday, because writing is lighter than other labors for the reason we wrote in section 1. And the opinion of the Rambam in chapter 7, law 13 is not so, but rather that writing is like all other labors, and there is no permission except for one who does not have what to eat.

And all of this is according to the opinion of the Tur that Chol HaMoed requires Tefillin, as I wrote in Siman 31. Therefore, he explains the Mishnah (Yoma 18b) which states that a person may write Tefillin and Mezuzot for himself — meaning when he needs them on Yom Tov, because he does not have Tefillin and Mezuzah. According to this, it is similar to other labors, for anything that is not needed for the festival is prohibited to do. However, the poskim who hold that one should not wear Tefillin on Chol HaMoed, as I wrote there, are compelled to explain the Mishnah that writing for oneself — means when he needs them after Yom Tov, and even so they permitted him to write because it is a mitzvah matter and is not similar to other labors. And one should not ask: if so, why did they prohibit writing books? It can be said that they only permitted a mitzvah matter that involves a personal obligation like Tefillin and Mezuzah, where if one does not fulfill the mitzvah, he transgresses a positive commandment. This is not the case with writing books. Therefore, Techelet (blue dye) also does not compare to them, because with Tzitzit there is also no personal obligation; if one does not wear a four-cornered garment, he is not obligated in Tzitzit. This is not the case with Tefillin and Mezuzah which are obligatory. Therefore, the Tur also did not permit Techelet for others for the reason I wrote (and so wrote the Bach).

And this is what we have learned regarding the blue dye (Techelet) (19:1): "And he spins it on his thigh" – there are those who say this is because a change is required. But from the Rambam and the Tur, it does not seem that a change is required, and the reason it states "on his thigh" is to indicate that spinning with a wheel is forbidden, as it makes much noise and there is a disrespect of the festival (Magen Avraham, Small Paragraph 8). And our master the Rema wrote in Paragraph 3: "And if he writes them in order to place them on the festival – in any manner it is permitted. The prohibition is only on the writing, but their making – is permitted." Thus far his words. And from the arrangement of his words, it seems his intention is that to place them on the festival – it is permitted even for payment. And this is the opinion of the Sefer Mitzvot Gadol (SeMaG), and also in Tosafot according to their explanation in the Jerusalem Talmud, see there. And this is not according to the opinion of the Tur as we have written. And that which he wrote that only the writing is prohibited, but their making is permitted – this is from the words of the Tosafot there, who wrote about why the Mishnah only speaks of the writing of the tefillin and the spinning of the blue dye, and not their making, they wrote in this language: "And perhaps the prohibition is only in the writing and spinning." Thus far their words. And the reason is because it is for the purpose of a mitzvah, and there is not so much labor involved as in the writing and spinning (Levush). And although they wrote in the language of "perhaps," they held this way in practice because it seems so from the language of the Mishnah. Nevertheless, it appears to me that this is only regarding the making of tzitzit, and inserting the scrolls into the boxes and sewing them, and cutting the straps and inserting them into the tefillin – is permitted. But making the boxes themselves – involves more labor than writing the scrolls, and is forbidden (and the making is only for the need of the festival).

And know that everything clarified as permissible regarding tefillin and tzitzit according to the explained methods—some say that this is specifically when one did not intend to perform the work during the intermediate days of the festival (Hagahot Maimoniot there), as is the rule with all tasks. And some say that since these are matters of a mitzvah (commandment), it is permissible even if one intended to perform the work during the intermediate days of the festival (Beit Yosef), and a mitzvah matter should not be considered inferior to communal needs in this regard. However, it is certain that if they are not needed for the festival itself, and one intended to perform the work, there is no permission unless the person has absolutely nothing to eat. But for the sake of profit on the festival—this is prohibited in such a manner even for those who permit profit-making (Magen Avraham, Subsection 10).

It is stated in the Tosefta that one is permitted to calculate one's accounts and expenses and to write them down. The Rambam wrote that the reason is because in such writing there is no concern for the refinement of the script, and it is considered a mundane activity. The Rashba wrote that the reason is that it is a matter of financial loss, meaning that one might forget and lose their money.
