There is a practical difference between these reasons: according to the Rambam, it is only permitted for the needs of the festival, because if it is not for the needs of the festival – even a mundane activity is forbidden, as I wrote in the previous section. According to the Rashba, it is permitted even if it is not for the needs of the festival, as it is considered a matter of financial loss. And in our type of writing, which is not Ashurit script, one can rely on the lenient opinion of the Rashba (Taz, small section 6). However, if it is certainly not a matter of financial loss – it is forbidden if it is not for the needs of the festival (Magen Avraham, small section 11). Similarly, if one's accounts are already written, but one wants to arrange them – it is forbidden, as this is certainly neither a matter of financial loss nor a need of the festival (ibid.). Additionally, in most cases when arranging, one makes a beautiful script, and it is considered a professional activity. Even according to what we hold, that our writing is considered a mundane activity, nevertheless, in neat and clean arrangement as done by managers in commercial offices – it is certainly close to a professional activity. Rabbi Rema wrote in section 4 that the writings made when lending on collateral – are permitted. This is his language: This is certainly also a matter of financial loss, if one does not write down how much was lent and to whom. Also, this is not considered a professional activity. Additionally, it may be considered a "need of the festival," as perhaps the borrower borrowed for the needs of the holiday. (Accordingly, even according to the Rokeach brought by the Taz there, that writing pledges requires a slight change, see the Taz for his reasoning. However, if it is for the needs of the holiday – it is obvious that no change is needed, as the Taz himself wrote, see there. Be precise and you will find leniency.)

We learned in the Mishnah (Moed Katan 18b) that it is permitted to write letters of permission during the intermediate days of a festival (Chol HaMoed). Rashi explains that "permission" refers to government authority, as in "Do not become known to the authorities," meaning government directives. However, the Jerusalem Talmud interprets it as greetings of peace, that is, letters of well-wishing between friends. This is also how the Rif and the Rambam explain it, and the Tosafot write similarly. This is what the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch state in Section 5, that it is permitted to write a letter of greeting that a person sends to his friend, even regarding non-urgent business matters. Up to here is his language. Meaning: even if it is not urgent. And they are called "letters of permission" because they do not involve a mitzvah or an obligation, but are optional. The reason for the leniency is that all these are considered amateur work, where precision in writing is not required (Levush). According to this, we must say that it is considered a need for the festival, for otherwise, it would be prohibited even in this manner, as I have written. Now, a letter of peace can be considered a need for the festival, so that the recipient of the letter may delight in the holiday. Similarly, regarding business matters, the recipient may enjoy knowing the information. However, according to this, the leniency would only apply if the letter reaches the recipient during the festival, but if it is after the festival, it would be prohibited. Why has none of the poskim mentioned this? Also, they do not scrutinize this unless we say that the writer also derives pleasure from it, and it is considered a need for the festival. This requires further investigation. Therefore, it seems more plausible to say that in writing where there is no effort involved and it is done discreetly, they did not insist that it be a need for the festival as with other labors. And even this the poskim did not mention. (And the Raavad wrote the reason: that perhaps after the festival, one might not find someone to send the letter through, see there. Nowadays, when there are established post offices everywhere, this reason does not apply.)

And our master, the Rema, wrote about this, and these are his words: "There are those who prohibit greeting others. And the custom is to be stringent, to change even our writing, which is written with the abbreviation 'ShTi"A.'" Until here are his words, and so it should be said. And what he wrote that there are those who prohibit greeting others, his intention is also regarding business dealings that are not lost (and it is like etc.). For if it is a lost item, it is obvious that no change is needed. (And this is the intention of the Magen Avraham in subsection 20, as the Machatzit Hashekel wrote. And not like the Taz in subsection 10 who was puzzled by this.) And the reason for those who prohibit: they were concerned about Rashi's interpretation. And even according to the Jerusalem Talmud, there is much to deliberate, as I wrote in the previous section. Therefore, they customarily make a change. And even though for other labors, making a change does not permit it if it is not for the need of the festival or something that would be lost, nonetheless, in writing they were lenient for the reasons we have explained. And what is called a "change"? Writing diagonally. And even though a change pertains to the actual script, nonetheless, since by the letter of the law it is permitted, and also because our script is sufficient with this change (Magen Avraham subsection 21). Therefore, what is forbidden to write is forbidden by law, even with a distortion, for this is not a change at all (ibid). And some say that our script is not considered script at all regarding Chol HaMoed (ibid in the name of the Bach), and on this the world relies and writes without any change. And there are those who write the first line with a distortion, and this is nothing (and so wrote the Taz there).

The Sages taught in the Mishnah (Moed Katan 18b): These are the documents that may be written during the intermediate days of the festival: betrothal of women, bills of divorce, receipts, wills, deeds of gift, and prosbols, appraisal letters and letters of sustenance, chalitzah and refusal documents, arbitration documents, and court decrees. "Betrothal of women" – this refers to the betrothal document. Even though it is forbidden to marry a woman during the festival, as will be explained in the next section, it is still permitted to betroth her, lest another precede him (Gemara, there). Consequently, it is necessary to write a betrothal document when betrothing with a document, or even when betrothing with money, documents of evidence of the betrothal are still required. This also includes the agreements on dowries, which is akin to our conditions agreements, and this too is permitted during the festival so that another does not precede him. "Bills of divorce" – the Jerusalem Talmud asks: Isn’t this causing distress? It answers: Since they have decided to divorce, it is no longer distressing. This too is necessary during the festival, so that he does not travel far and she remains an agunah. "Receipts" – this includes all kinds of receipts, whether for debt repayment or for a marriage contract. If the receipt is not given, the payment will not be made, and this would be considered a significant loss.

"Diyatiki" refers to a gift given by someone on their deathbed. "Matana" refers to a gift given by a healthy person. It is necessary to write these during the intermediate days of a festival: for the person on their deathbed, lest they die and the gift is nullified; and for the healthy person, lest they retract, and it will be as if something is lost. "Prozbul" is to ensure that the lender will lend, and without a Prozbul, he will not want to lend, and it will be considered a potential loss. "Documents of appraisal" refer to the appraisal of the borrower's assets for the lender. "Documents of sustenance" refer to the commitment to provide sustenance for his wife's daughter, or when land is sold for the sustenance of the wife and daughters. "Documents of chalitza and refusal" are known from Yevamot. "Documents of arbitration" refer to when each party selects an arbitrator. "Decrees of the court" refer to court rulings. Many of these can be postponed until after the festival. The reason for the allowance is the concern that the witnesses or the court may die or travel overseas, which is considered a potential loss (Tosafot there). Additionally, all these are considered public needs, as anything done by a court is considered a public necessity (see Beit Yosef and Magen Avraham, subsection 17). The Rambam gave the reason that all these are not meticulously written and are considered ordinary work, see there. However, a get (divorce document) is obviously written meticulously, but this is due to the decree concerning agunot (deserted wives). From this, we learn that it is permissible to divorce and perform chalitza during the intermediate days of a festival.

It is prohibited to write promissory notes during the intermediate days of a festival, as they can be written after the festival. However, if the lender does not trust the borrower and will not give him the money without a promissory note, and the borrower needs the money, it is allowed to write it. Similarly, if the scribe writes for a fee and has nothing to eat, it is permitted to write. Even if the borrower does not need the money for the festival itself but for his business and fears that after the festival he will not obtain the loan, it is considered a case of potential loss, and it is allowed. This is the common practice, especially with our writing, which is considered unskilled labor (see Magen Avraham, subsection 23). Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote in subsection 5 that it is permitted to write a marriage contract (ketubah) during the intermediate days of a festival, though some prohibit it. This applies when one marries on the eve of the festival or will marry after the festival, and then there will be no scribe in the city. The reason some prohibit it is that it is considered like a promissory note. However, since the practice is to permit even promissory notes, all the more so for a ketubah. Nowadays, it is uncommon to write the ketubah not at the time of the wedding. Therefore, it seems to me that it is forbidden. However, writing an addition to the ketubah seems permissible during the intermediate days of a festival, as it benefits the woman, lest the husband retract after the festival, and it is considered a case of potential loss (as Magen Avraham also wrote in subsection 18).

Additionally, it is written in Section 6 that it is permitted to write a bill of sale during the intermediate days of a festival. However, it is not permitted to write a sharecropping or contracting agreement that was made before the festival. So are the words written. And it seems to me that the explanation is as follows: A bill of sale can occur during the festival, as a standard bill of sale pertains to houses and lands, and it is permitted to sell them during the festival if they are needed for the festival, as I wrote in Siman 539. Therefore, it is also permitted to write the bill of sale if one of the parties does not wish to finalize the transaction without the written bill of sale. But sharecropping and contracting agreements are certainly forbidden during the festival, as there is no festival necessity involved, and they were agreed upon before the festival. Therefore, it is forbidden to write them during the festival. (And with this, the wonder of the Taz in Subsection 11 is resolved. See Magen Avraham Subsection 24, and study it well, and you will find it clear.)

And our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 7: Anything that is permitted to write even without a change – is permitted. And anything that is forbidden to write – is forbidden to write even with a change. Thus are his words, and this refers to changing the quill or the arrangement of the lines. But changing the letters themselves – is permitted (Taz, subsection 12). And in our script, it is possible that even this is not necessary (ibid). And writing on a wax tablet is permitted, because it is not a permanent writing. And for us, this does not exist at all. However, it is possible that writing on tablets even with ink is not considered writing at all (Magen Avraham, subsection 25), because it is poor writing and lacks order. And similarly, in the various notes that a businessman has, which are written only for memory purposes – the writing is also not elegant. And in our script, if it is not in an orderly fashion – it is possible that it is permitted. And so is the custom.

To ask a question regarding the law of our Torah and to respond with an answer is permitted, a mitzvah, and an obligation, for there is no greater loss than this. Similarly, writing down new Torah insights is permitted and a mitzvah on Chol Hamoed, for if they are not written, they will be forgotten, and this constitutes a significant loss. Furthermore, if these are written, it will enable the creation of new insights. It is not appropriate to suggest that one should postpone this until after the festival, for after the festival, there will be other matters (Taz, section 13). The Bach, of blessed memory, wrote his works on Chol Hamoed (there). Similarly, if one hears a novel idea from another, he is permitted to write it down so that it will not be forgotten. Additionally, if one sees a newly written book, he is allowed to copy it if he will not have the opportunity to do so after the festival. It is also permitted to copy questions and answers, for all of this is considered a "significant loss."

In all matters where writing is permitted, it is also permissible to adjust the quill, make ink if necessary, cut the paper, and do whatever is required for writing (Magen Avraham, subsection 26). However, it is forbidden to prepare a notebook to write on after the intermediate days of the festival (ibid.), as this can certainly be done after the festival. But if one needs to write a little in it during the intermediate days, it is permissible to prepare the entire notebook, because as long as the entire notebook is not prepared, one cannot even write a little.

And they adjudicate on the festival, whether it be monetary cases, capital cases, or cases of lashes. And they punish one who does not comply with the law. And it is permitted to file complaints regarding debts during Chol HaMoed. However, they do not summon someone to court against their will during Chol HaMoed, as I have written in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 5. See there.

The Sages taught in the Mishnah (Moed Katan 1:8): One does not marry women during the festival, neither virgins nor widows, nor perform levirate marriages, because it is a joy for him. However, one may remarry his divorced wife. The Gemara explains four reasons for this: the first is because one does not mix one joy with another, and this is what is meant by "because it is a joy for him." That is to say, the marriage itself is a joy on its own, and one does not mix it with the joy of the festival. Just as one does not perform mitzvot in bundles, for we require that one's heart be free for one mitzvah, so too we require that one's heart be free for one joy. This is derived from the verse about Solomon (I Kings 8) when he completed the building of the Temple and made a seven-day celebration, he did not make it during the Festival of Sukkot. As it is written: "And Solomon celebrated the festival for seven days, and seven days…" And in the Jerusalem Talmud, it is derived from Jacob and Rachel, as it is written: "Fulfill the week of this one, and we will give you the other…" And even though the Jerusalem Talmud itself in the chapter "And These May Shave" (Halacha 5) seeks to derive the seven days of mourning from Jacob, as it is written: "And he made a mourning for his father for seven days," and it questions: Can we learn something from before the giving of the Torah? See there. And how does it learn here from before the giving of the Torah? It seems to me that this is the explanation: Certainly, we learn from before the giving of the Torah, and we derive several teachings from the Book of Genesis. However, there it is by necessity that we do not learn, because it was not according to the law of mourning, as it was still before the burial. But here, it is properly derived. (And see Tosafot 20a, s.v. "What." And see Pnei Moshe who struggles with this, and examine and you will find it easy.)

And one should not ask: according to this reason, we should also forbid marrying a woman six days before a festival, so that the seven days of celebration would be completed before the festival, as Solomon did when he dedicated the Temple seven days before the festival. This is not comparable, because the dedication of the Temple was a communal celebration for all Israel and a great joy, and they were joyous each day as on the first day. This is not the same as the joy of a groom, which is primarily on the day of the wedding itself, as it is written, "on the day of his wedding, on the day of the gladness of his heart," and it is stated, "he is like a groom coming out of his bridal chamber" - from which we learn that the primary joy is only on the wedding day. Therefore, it is only forbidden during the festival, but permissible on the eve of the festival, and certainly before that. (And so it is in the Gemara, Taanit 26b, that the primary joy is one day.)

The second reason is that it is written: "And you shall rejoice in your festival" – and not with your wife. The term "in your festival" is redundant, as it is already speaking about the festival, but it comes to teach that it should not be with your wife. This is a complete teaching, not merely a support (Tosafot there). The explanation is that if one marries during the festival, he will forsake the joy of the festival and engage in the joy of his wife. This is what the Tanna says, "because it is a joy for him," meaning that the marriage is a joy for him, and he will forsake the joy of the festival and engage in this joy. The third reason is because of the effort involved, as a wedding feast requires great effort, and it is not appropriate to exert much effort during Chol HaMoed. The statement "because it is a joy for him" is explained as follows: because the marriage is a joy for him, and due to the greatness of the joy, he makes a large feast, and it will be an excessive burden for him. The fourth reason is due to the nullification of procreation, meaning that if it were permitted to marry during the festival, everyone would wait until the festival to make one feast for both the festival and the wedding (Rashi). This is what is meant by "because it is a joy for him" – he delays the joy until the festival joy, so that the meal will count for both.

And it is obvious that even if he wishes to marry without a meal – it is forbidden, for all the reasons apply even without a meal, except for the reason of effort. And so it is explicitly stated in Yevamot (42b) that marriage without a meal is also forbidden, because there is joy in marriage even without a meal, which is not the case with betrothal, see there. And that which is found in Tosafot Ketubot (47a, s.v. "that he gave") that it is permitted without a meal – this is not referring to actual marriage, but rather to the laws of marriage. And that is when the father hands her over to the husband's agents to bring her to the marriage, or to his hand to bring her to the marriage, from then on she has some of the laws of a married woman; such as her work and her findings, which no longer belong to her father but to her husband. And in this, it is permitted on Shabbat and Yom Tov, see there, but not in actual marriage. (And I am astonished at the Magen Avraham, section 1, who struggled with this, and the matters are clear as I have written. And also the Maharshal and the Maharsha struggled greatly with this, see there, and I do not know why. And in the Talmud itself, it is necessary to interpret this way, see there.)

However, betrothal (erusin) is permitted during the intermediate days of the festival (chol hamoed), lest someone else precedes him. And there is not so much joy in this. As long as one does not make a betrothal feast, the betrothed man in the house of his betrothed at the time of betrothal, meaning that they should not be done consecutively. It is permissible to have dances and celebrations, and to have a feast with the betrothed and his friends, not in the house of his betrothed. Similarly, for the betrothed to eat in the house of his betrothed not at the time of betrothal is permissible, for there is no joy except when the feast is together with the betrothal, as we say in Yevamot (there). And behold, in our place, there is no betrothal except at the time of the wedding ceremony (chuppah), and beforehand they bind themselves with conditions or preliminary agreements, and it is permissible to make them during chol hamoed. There are those who prohibit a feast at the time of the conditions, just like during betrothal (Taz, section 2). In my humble opinion, this is not comparable to betrothal, as she becomes his wife. But conditions are nothing, only a binding through a penalty. And many times the conditions are annulled. And this is only like a friendly meal. (And regarding what was written about circumcision and redemption of the firstborn – indeed, the Magen Avraham wrote in section 5 that there is no joy except in marriage. And regarding the documents of agreement – there, they stood and betrothed. And certainly what was written about the first feast during the festival with the bride after the conditions being prohibited is more surprising, since the conditions were before the festival. Moreover, a "feast" is not called so unless others are also invited.)

And it is permitted to take back one's divorced wife, for there is no new joy in this, and it does not involve effort. One should not delay until the festival. This applies specifically when she is divorced from marriage, but if divorced from betrothal – it is forbidden, because since in marriage it is as if it is the first time for him – it constitutes complete joy. Everyone is permitted to marry on the eve of the festival and to make a feast during the festival, whether virgins or widows, for the main joy is only on the first day. On the first night of the festival, one should not make the feast if the marriage took place on the eve of the festival, for the night follows the day regarding joy, as it starts during the day and finishes at night, as is the way of celebrations (Magen Avraham, small section 4, and Taz, small section 3). But on all the days of the festival – it is permitted to make a feast. It is permitted to marry on the eve of the festival until sunset. It is permitted to make a circumcision feast even on the festival day itself, since its time is fixed. Additionally, there is no joy except in marriage. Similarly, it is permitted to make a redemption of the firstborn son feast during the intermediate days of the festival, for the reasons explained. But on the festival day itself, one should not redeem, even if the redemption falls on that day, and it is postponed until after the festival. (What the Taz wrote in small section 1 in the name of the gloss of the Sefer Mitzvot Katan, not to make two weddings on one day, just as one does not marry during the festival, look there, and he was puzzled by this – it seems to me that his intention was for two brothers or two sisters. And not because of prohibition, but merely a hint that one does not mix joy with joy. Be precise and you will find it easy.)(What Magen Avraham wrote that it is not customary to marry on the eve of the festival – now some do marry.)

A woman may do all her cosmetic adornments for her face during the festival, whether she is young or old (Gemara 9b). This includes applying eye shadow and placing kohl between her eyes to enhance her appearance (Rashi there). She may also part her hair in different directions (ibid.), arrange her hair outside of her scarf (Tosafot there), and apply thin dough threads on her face to redden the skin (ibid. in the name of Riva). She may use rouge on her face and apply lime or similar substances to remove hair. However, this is only permitted if she can remove the lime during the festival, as she derives pleasure from it; while the lime is on her face, it causes some discomfort, but afterwards she is pleased. Therefore, if the joy will be during the festival, it is permitted, but if after the festival, it is forbidden. She may remove hair from her armpits and pubic area, either by hand or with an instrument, and she may shave the hair on her forehead with a knife. All these are difficult to do before the festival without spoiling them. Even without this, it is impossible to be stringent with a woman regarding her cosmetics, as her joy is in her adornments, and this is her festival pleasure. However, a man is forbidden to use any cosmetic adornments that involve labor. Besides, a man should not excessively engage in cosmetics and adornments, due to "A man shall not wear a woman's garment," as I wrote in Yoreh De'ah, section 182.

The intermediate days of a festival (Chol HaMoed) are prohibited for eulogies and fasting. Therefore, we do not place the bier in the street or in the synagogue courtyard in order not to encourage eulogizing. Except in the case of a great Torah scholar who has passed away, as there is no festival observance in the presence of a Torah scholar, as I have written in Yoreh De'ah, Section 340; see there. For this reason, we do not take the deceased to the cemetery until the grave is prepared, so that they do not have to wait for the grave to be prepared, which would increase weeping and eulogizing. 

The women who lament during the festival - they only chant in unison, meaning they all respond as one. But they do not lament with antiphonal chanting, where one speaks and they all respond after her, as this would involve more eulogy and weeping. And they do not clap hands, which means striking hand to hand. And even the chanting is only permitted before the burial, but after the burial, it is completely prohibited, except in the case of a scholar in his presence.

For the thirty days preceding the festival, it is forbidden to eulogize someone who died before these thirty days. However, those who died within the thirty days before the festival may be eulogized, because the bitterness is still fixed in the heart, and the eulogy does not add to the sorrow. Even if someone has one person who died before the thirty days and another who died within the thirty days, the one who died before the thirty days should not be mentioned alongside the one who died within the thirty days, as the latter may be eulogized. Even if someone died on the eve of the festival, it is permitted to eulogize them, but it is forbidden to mention the one who died before the thirty days. The measure of thirty days is because the deceased is not forgotten from the heart for thirty days to be eulogized. In Yoreh De'ah, section 347, we have explained more about this; see there.

And one who received news (of a death) within thirty days before a festival—it is permitted to eulogize even though the deceased had already died, since the bitterness is strong in his heart and the eulogy does not add to the bitterness. And the custom to eulogize the deceased and mention his soul at the completion of the year, as was the custom in Spain—is not included in this restriction, and it is permitted to do so within thirty days of the festival, because this, on the contrary, serves to conclude the mourning, allowing one to then wear white garments. Similarly, the memorials that the prayer leader makes during the Torah reading also do not arouse mourning. However, from Rosh Chodesh Nisan, we stop making memorials, as I have written in Siman 429.

One does not rend their garments for the deceased during Chol HaMoed, except for close relatives for whom one is obligated to mourn: his father, mother, son, daughter, brother, and sister. Additionally, for a sage or a righteous person who was present at the moment of passing. There is a distinction between them: for a close relative for whom one is obligated to mourn and for a sage, one rends their garments even if not in their presence, but rather if the news reached them during the festival if it is within thirty days. For a righteous person, one only rends their garments if they knew between death and burial. However, other types of rending mentioned in Yoreh De'ah Siman 340 are not done at all during Chol HaMoed. This is specifically when the death occurred during Chol HaMoed, which is considered a time of heat (immediate grief). But if the death occurred on a festival, there is no need to rend garments during Chol HaMoed until after the festival, for once the time of heat has passed, why should one rend during Chol HaMoed? Also, for close news (recently heard), one rends garments, even if after the festival it becomes distant news. For distant news (heard after thirty days), one does not rend garments even for his father and mother until after the festival, as I have written in Yoreh De'ah Siman 340, see there.

All of this is from the fundamental law. However, the custom of Ashkenaz is that for one's father and mother, one rends [their garments] during the festival, but for other relatives, one does not rend until after the festival. Their reasoning is that there are those who hold that by law, one does not rend during the intermediate days of the festival, just as mourning is not observed during the festival, so too rending [garments]. This is the opinion of the Sefer Mitzvot Katan (SeMaK). However, many disagree with him and hold that by law, one must rend during the festival, since it is a moment of intense grief. Therefore, the custom of Ashkenaz is to rule that for one's father and mother, one rends, but not for other relatives. And this is the custom. In places where there is no established custom, one should rend for all, as this is the fundamental law. And so the great authorities have written, and so ruled our master, the Rema. And this is the custom in the land of Poland (Magen Avraham, subsection 4).

One does not bare the shoulder except the deceased's relatives who need to mourn for him, or for a sage whom people ask about matters of law everywhere and he answers them. And now the custom of baring the shoulder is not practiced at all, as I wrote in Yoreh De'ah there. And although mourning is not practiced during the intermediate days of the festival (Chol HaMoed), nevertheless, a meal of comfort (Seudat Havra'ah) is provided during the festival. However, this should not be done in a public area, but rather by the deceased’s relatives. The mourner should not be comforted in his house but rather on upright beds, since the custom of overturning the bed does not apply at all during the festival. For a sage, everyone provides the meal of comfort in a public area during the festival, as is the manner of comforting mourners, because everyone mourns for him. And in Yoreh De'ah it is explained that we do not have a public area, nor do we overturn beds. However, when we provide the meal of comfort, the mourners should not sit on the ground, as it is forbidden to sit on the ground during the intermediate days of the festival, but rather they should provide the meal at the table.

One may attend to all needs of the deceased during Chol HaMoed: one may cut his hair in places where it is customary to do so, and wash his clothes if necessary, and make a coffin for him. However, this should be done specifically in the courtyard where the deceased is, so it is evident that it is being done for the deceased and people will not suspect that construction is being done during Chol HaMoed. If they do not have boards, they may bring beams and cut them into boards discreetly inside the house. If it is not possible to do it discreetly, they should do it openly. If the deceased was a prominent person, they may initially do it even in the marketplace openly, as there is no suspicion since everyone knows. However, they should be careful of the public view of non-Jews (as noted in Magen Avraham, subsection 6), so that they do not say that Jews are desecrating the festival. But one may not cut down a tree from the forest to saw boards for a coffin, nor hew stones to build a grave, because people will say that the cutting and hewing are being done for construction purposes (see Beit Yosef). In a place where there are few Jews living together in one area, everyone is considered prominent, as everyone knows there is a deceased in the city.

One does not dig burial niches or graves during Chol HaMoed (the intermediate days of the festival) to prepare them for a deceased person. However, one may adjust them, so if they were long, they may be shortened, or if they were short, they may be lengthened or widened. One should not pull out grass and dirt in the cemetery during Chol HaMoed as is done on regular weekdays. The law concerning the recitation of "Tziduk HaDin" (the justification of the divine decree) during the festival is explained in Yoreh De'ah, Section 401, that it is not recited during Chol HaMoed, see there. It is appropriate to recite Psalm 49 and say "Kaddish" over it, and I believe that this is the customary practice.

One who buries his deceased during the festival or on Chol HaMoed (the intermediate days of the festival) – the mourning does not take effect during the festival, as the rabbinically ordained mourning does not override the festival, which is of Torah origin. Even if the first day of mourning is considered of Torah origin, the individual obligation does not override the communal festival. Instead, after the festival, he begins to count the seven days of mourning and observes them. However, the thirty days are counted from the day of burial, and he observes all the regulations of the thirty days. Shemini Atzeret is considered as seven days in regard to the thirty days, as will be explained. There are those who disagree with this (Magen Avraham, subsection 1, in the name of the Bach and Taz, see there). But the custom follows the first opinion.

In the Diaspora, where two days of Yom Tov are observed, the last day is considered as part of the seven days of mourning, and one completes an additional six days. And even though mourning customs are not observed on it, nevertheless, since it is of rabbinic origin, it counts towards the tally. Even the second day of Rosh Hashanah counts towards the tally. There is an opinion that it only counts when the death occurred on the second day of Rosh Hashanah, or at least if the burial took place on it, but if the burial was on the first day, it does not count (Taz, subsection 1). This is not correct, as it always counts towards the tally (Magen Avraham, subsection 2), and this is the custom.

One who buries his deceased on the last day of Passover, or on the second day of Shavuot, or on Simchat Torah, practices mourning if it was the day of death and burial, since the second day of Yom Tov is by rabbinic decree, and the first day of mourning is from the Torah: a positive commandment from the Torah overrides a rabbinic commandment. But not on the second day of Rosh Hashanah, as both days are considered as one long day. And even though ultimately it is by rabbinic decree, nevertheless, since it was not made due to doubt – its strength is like the first day. However, some of our rabbis completely disagree with this and hold that from the Torah there is no mourning even on the first day, for only "aninut" (the initial period of grief) is from the Torah and not mourning. And since both are rabbinic – a rabbinic commandment of an individual does not override a rabbinic commandment of the public. And thus, the simple custom, which should not be changed, is that no mourning is practiced on it.

And know that what we said, that one who buries his deceased relative on a festival does not observe mourning—this applies to public mourning, but private practices are observed, and he is forbidden to engage in marital relations. Nevertheless, it is permitted for him to sleep in the same room with his wife, and there is no need for supervision, since even in the case of a menstruant, seclusion is permitted, as Jews are not suspected of such matters. Also, he does not change his clothing, for although other mourners change their clothes during a festival, since he has not yet begun his mourning, he does not change (Magen Avraham, subsection 5). This is not considered public. Likewise, he is forbidden from Torah study, except for wearing tefillin, which he puts on even on the first day, for since he is not observing mourning, he does not cover his glory in dust, which is the reason for the exemption of a mourner from tefillin on the first day (ibid.).

Even though mourning practices do not apply during the festival, the state of aninut (intense mourning) does apply. Therefore, the individual is prohibited from consuming meat and wine and is exempt from all commandments, as I have written in Yoreh De'ah, section 340. Aninut is certainly of biblical origin, and the honor of the festival does not override it, as the honor of the deceased takes precedence. Therefore, if a person dies during the intermediate days of the festival, the mourner is prohibited from all things that an onen (one in the state of aninut) is prohibited from. If a person dies on the festival itself, and the mourner does not wish to bury him on that day—for example, there are no non-Jews willing to handle the burial—then the mourner does not assume the status of aninut, as aninut only applies to those who wish to bury the deceased. If the mourner needs to stay within the boundary of the town to prepare for the burial, aninut takes effect from the moment he does so. If he does not need to stay within the boundary, and there is no need to handle the burial preparations, aninut does not take effect until the next morning.

If the person dies on the second day of the festival and the mourner wishes to bury him on that day, or if the person dies on the first day of the festival and the mourner wishes to bury him through a non-Jew, aninut applies until after the burial. As we have explained in Yoreh De'ah, section 15, on the night of the second day of the festival, aninut does not apply, as the Rabbis equated only the day of the second festival day to a regular weekday, but not the night. Therefore, if a person dies on the first day of the festival and is buried the next day, aninut does not take effect until the next morning; at night, the mourner is obligated in prayer, Kiddush, and all other commandments. Similarly, if the person dies on the night of the second day of the festival, and certainly if he dies on the night of the first day of the festival, aninut does not apply at night, even if the burial will be the next day through a non-Jew. However, if the burial takes place at night, aninut certainly applies until after the burial. (This is also the opinion of Magen Avraham, section 8, that aninut does not apply on the night of the festival. Taz in Yoreh De'ah and the Drisha there also wrote similarly, in contrast to Shach, section 9. This is also the ruling of Mahari"l, see there.)

And even though there is no mourning during the festival, nevertheless, they engage in comforting him during the festival if a relative passed away during the festival. After the festival, when the seven days of mourning for the deceased have ended, even though he is still sitting in mourning – nevertheless, his work can be done by others in their homes, and his servants can do work for him discreetly within his house. There is no need to comfort him after the festival for the number of days he was comforted during the festival. In summary: even though he sits the seven days of mourning after the festival, in terms of consolation and the prohibition of work by others – the seven days are counted from the day of the death and burial.

If someone had a close relative who passed away before a festival, and the burial took place before the festival, and they observed mourning for even one hour on the eve of the festival, the seven-day mourning period (Shiva) is nullified for them. It doesn't have to be a full hour, just a short amount of time. The days of the festival count toward the thirty-day mourning period (Shloshim) — thus, fourteen days are accounted for. They then complete the remaining sixteen days after the festival to fulfill the thirty days. This applies specifically if they observed mourning during that time. However, if they mistakenly or intentionally did not observe mourning, or if it was right before nightfall and they couldn't observe mourning, it is considered as if the death occurred during the festival. In this case, they observe mourning after the festival, as the festival does not nullify the seven days of mourning (Shiva).

If one observed seven days of mourning before a festival, and the festival occurred – the festival cancels the decree of thirty days. Even if the seventh day falls on the eve of the festival, we say part of the day is considered as the whole day, and the festival cancels the thirty days. He is permitted to cut his hair and launder on the eve of the festival, as well as to bathe in hot water, according to our custom of not bathing in hot water for all thirty days. However, he should perform all this approximately two hours before the evening, and not earlier. All the more so if his eighth day falls on Shabbat, the eve of the festival, he is permitted to do all these things on the eve of Shabbat, on his seventh day, approximately two hours before nightfall. If he did not shave before the festival, he is permitted to shave after the festival, as the thirty-day decree is already canceled. However, he should not shave during the intermediate days of the festival (Chol HaMoed), since he could have shaved before the festival. If his seventh day falls on Shabbat, the eve of the festival, he is permitted to shave during the intermediate days of the festival, as he could not have shaved before the festival, still being within the seven days. It is obvious that the rule that the festival cancels the thirty days decree regarding hair cutting applies to other deceased relatives. But for one's father and mother, for whom the period is until one's friends rebuke him – the festival does not cancel this, even if he observed thirty days before the festival.

If the eve of the festival is not on the seventh day of mourning, but rather from the previous days, then the festival only cancels the remainder of the seven days, and it does not cancel the thirty days. In any case, due to the honor of the festival, he is permitted to launder clothes, but he should not wear them until the night. It is good to be careful not to launder until after midday, so that it is evident that he is doing so in honor of the festival. However, bathing is forbidden until the night, and at night he should bathe in cold water. There are those who say it is permitted to bathe after Mincha, close to nightfall, and he should pray Mincha first. (The Rema in paragraph 10 wrote that for us, who observe the prohibition of bathing for the entire thirty days, it is forbidden to bathe, since the festival only cancels the decree of the seven days. The same applies to laundering, in places where they observe the prohibition of laundering for the entire thirty days. Until here is his language. And in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 399, paragraph 5, he did not write this. The main point is as I wrote there to permit. And so all the commentators of the Shulchan Aruch wrote. And in paragraph 17 we explained that the Rema relied on the fact that these are the main laws of mourning.)

The holidays of Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur are considered like festivals to nullify mourning. Therefore, according to what has been explained, if one observed mourning for one hour before Passover, that hour is considered as seven days, and the eight days of Passover, and completes another fifteen days to make up thirty. One hour before Shavuot is considered as seven days. Shavuot itself, since its offerings can be compensated for all seven days, is also considered as seven days. This totals fourteen days, and another sixteen days are completed. The second day of Shavuot is counted in the sixteen days. One hour before Rosh Hashanah nullifies the seven days decree because of Rosh Hashanah. Yom Kippur nullifies the thirty-day decree, and it is permitted to shave on the eve of Yom Kippur. The same applies to someone who buries his deceased on the third of Tishrei; he shaves on the eve of Yom Kippur, having completed seven days until Yom Kippur. One hour before Yom Kippur nullifies the seven days decree because of Yom Kippur. Sukkot nullifies the thirty days, and one shaves on the eve of Sukkot an hour before Sukkot. Sukkot is fourteen days, and Shemini Atzeret is considered as seven days - this totals twenty-one days. Simchat Torah is twenty-two days - completing another eight days to make thirty. For a deceased during the festival, Shemini Atzeret is not considered as seven days. There are those who disagree, and we have explained this in Yoreh De'ah there, section 19, see there.

If one hears recent news [of a relative's death] on Shabbat or a festival, and after Shabbat or the festival it becomes distant news, the law follows that of hearing distant news after Shabbat or the festival. However, on Shabbat and festivals, one observes private mourning practices that are observed during the seven days [of mourning], and it is forbidden to engage in marital relations, since if it were not Shabbat or a festival, mourning would have commenced. If one hears distant news on Shabbat or a festival, one does not observe even private mourning practices, but after Shabbat or the festival, one observes for one hour, as is the law for distant news. If one hears recent news on Shabbat, and even after Shabbat it remains recent, then Shabbat counts as one day, and the next day one tears [one's garment], and the sixth day becomes the seventh for mourning. This is further explained in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 401; see there.

If ten days after the holiday one hears that a relative died on the eve of the holiday, even though if one counts an hour before the holiday as part of the seven days, and the seven days of the holiday, and Shemini Atzeret which counts as seven, it would now be considered distant news – nevertheless, this is not the case. For all these calculations apply only when one heard and observed mourning, but not when one did not observe mourning. And certainly, for one who did not hear at all, these days are considered just like any other days, and it is regarded as recent news. And death will be swallowed up forever, and may we merit the coming of the righteous redeemer speedily in our days, Amen. With the help of Heaven, the laws of Chol HaMoed have concluded.

It is well known that it is a positive commandment from the Torah to cry out and beseech for any trouble that may not come, and to fast during them; this will be explained in the laws of fasting. And there are days on which all of Israel fasts because of the troubles that occurred on them, in order to awaken the hearts and open the ways of repentance. And this will serve as a reminder of our evil deeds and the deeds of our forefathers that were like our deeds now, which caused those troubles to them and to us. And by remembering these matters, we will return to improve, as it is written (Leviticus 26:40): "And they shall confess their iniquity and the iniquity of their forefathers" (Rambam, fifth chapter of Fasts).

And there are four days: the third of Tishrei, on which Gedaliah the son of Ahikam was killed, and the remaining ember of Israel was extinguished. This was a cause for the intensification of troubles. And the tenth of Tevet, on which Nebuchadnezzar the wicked besieged Jerusalem. As it is written in Kings (II 25:1) and in Jeremiah (52:4), that in the ninth year of Zedekiah’s reign, in the tenth month, on the tenth day of the month, Nebuchadnezzar and all his army came against Jerusalem. And Ezekiel, who was in Babylon with the exile of Jeconiah, the Holy One, blessed be He, revealed this to him in prophecy on that day, as it is written in Ezekiel (24:1-2): "And the word of the Lord came to me in the ninth year, in the tenth month, on the tenth day of the month, saying: Son of man! Write for yourself the name of the day, this very day, the king of Babylon has laid siege to Jerusalem on this very day." Meaning: He commanded him to write the name of the day, that is, the month and also this specific day, and he wrote "on the tenth day of the tenth month," and the prophet did not know why he was commanded to write so. And after he wrote it, it was revealed to him: Know that the king of Babylon has besieged Jerusalem on this very day, and thereby everyone saw the true prophecy, that in Babylon it was revealed to the prophet that very day and hour. For "this very day" is called the essence of the day, like midday. And because there were false prophets then who misled Israel, like Hananiah the son of Azur and his companions, who prophesied that the Temple would not be destroyed and Israel would not be exiled from their land, and they strengthened the hands of transgressors; and Jeremiah who rebuked them to return to God, and if not, the Temple would be destroyed and Israel would be exiled – they placed him in the court of the guard and put him in a pit of mud, as explained in Jeremiah; therefore, the Lord informed Ezekiel the prophet in Babylon that Jeremiah was a true prophet, and he prophesied in Babylon all that occurred in the Land of Israel, and because the tenth of Tevet was the beginning of the troubles. Therefore, they established it as a fast for generations. And it is found in the name of the ancients that if the tenth of Tevet were to fall on Shabbat – it would override Shabbat, because it is written about it "on this very day" like on Yom Kippur (Beit Yosef in Siman 550 in the name of Abudraham). But we do not hold this way, as will be explained.

On the seventeenth of Tammuz, five events occurred: the tablets were broken, the daily offering was abolished in the First Temple, the city of Jerusalem was breached during the destruction of the Second Temple, the wicked Apostomus burned the Torah, and he placed an idol in the Sanctuary. Similarly, on the ninth of Av, five events also occurred: [1] it was decreed upon the Israelites in the desert that they would not enter the land. [2-3] The Temple was destroyed, both the First and Second. For at the end of the book of Kings (II Kings 25:8-9) it is written: "And in the fifth month, on the seventh day of the month, in the nineteenth year of King Nebuchadnezzar... Nebuzaradan came... and burned the house of the Lord...". And at the end of the book of Jeremiah (Jeremiah 52:12) it is written regarding the same event "on the tenth of the month". It is stated in the Talmud, Tractate Ta'anit: It is impossible to say "on the seventh", for it already says "on the tenth". And it is impossible to say "on the tenth", for it already says "on the seventh". How can this be reconciled? On the seventh they entered the Sanctuary, etc., and on the ninth, close to nightfall, they set it on fire, and it burned continuously through the entire tenth day (Ta'anit 29a). [4] Betar was captured, and there were thousands and tens of thousands of Israelites there. There was a king there, and many thought he was the Messiah. Due to the sins, they were all killed, and they were not even given burial, and it was a great calamity like the destruction of the Temple. [5] And on this day, which is designated for calamities, the wicked Turnus Rufus plowed the Sanctuary, fulfilling the prophecy: "Zion shall be plowed as a field".

And these four fasts are explicitly mentioned in the tradition by the prophet Zechariah (8:19): "Thus says the Lord of Hosts: The fast of the fourth [month], the fast of the fifth, the fast of the seventh, and the fast of the tenth shall be to the house of Judah for joy and gladness." "The fast of the fourth [month]" is the seventeenth of Tammuz, which is in the fourth month; "the fast of the fifth [month]" is the ninth of Av, which is in the fifth month; "the fast of the seventh [month]" is the Fast of Gedaliah, which is in the seventh month; and "the fast of the tenth [month]" is the tenth of Tevet, which is in the tenth month. And all of Israel customarily fast on these days. 

And even though during the First Temple period Jerusalem was breached on the ninth of Tammuz, as it is written in Kings, nevertheless they did not establish the fast on that day but on the seventeenth, as the city was breached on that day during the Second Temple period. And for us, the destruction of the Second Temple is more severe, for since then we have become impoverished and dispersed to the four corners of the earth. And to establish fasting on both the ninth and the seventeenth would be too much for the community. 

(The Beit Yosef brought in the name of Rabbeinu Yerucham that Gedaliah was killed on Rosh Hashanah, and the fast was postponed to the following day, see there. Nevertheless, it does not have the status of a postponed fast regarding a person with a covenant, since it is consistently observed every year. It is not comparable to a fast postponed from Shabbat to Sunday, where everyone sees the postponement, unlike with the Fast of Gedaliah, which is the same every year. And as the conclusion of the Taz, see there.)

In the Gemara there, it expounds from the verses of Zechariah that in the time of the Temple, these fasts were for joy and gladness, and so it will be in the future, God willing. But in the time of destruction, and when the children of Israel are in distress, they are obligated to fast. And this is considered a positive commandment of the words of the Prophets, and all of Israel accepted it upon themselves. And in a time when they are not in distress: if the majority of the community wishes, they fast; if they do not wish, they do not fast. Nowadays, they wished and accepted upon themselves to fast (Tur). Especially now, there is distress. Nevertheless, we did not accept upon ourselves these fasts as a complete communal fast to the extent of refraining from eating already from the previous day, walking barefoot, bathing, anointing, and marital relations, except on Tisha B'Av alone, because then the calamities were intensified for us, and it does not depend on choice. But on the other three fasts, we eat at night and do not observe all the stringencies, but only fast from morning until evening as in the case of a private fast. And nowadays, due to our many sins, these fasts are treated with negligence, and they will have to answer for it. For anyone who is healthy is forbidden to separate himself from the community and transgresses a positive commandment of the words of the Prophets. And even someone who needs to eat due to weakness should not eat his meal as on regular days, but only food and drink necessary to sustain his body. And so we practice.

Everyone is obligated to fast on these four fasts, and it is forbidden to breach this rule. Even those with eye ailments, if the fast will not worsen their eyes. Similarly, anyone with a mild ailment, if it is not one of those ailments for which fasting is difficult, such as heart and head pains – they should fast. Pregnant and nursing women should not fast on the three fasts other than Tisha B'Av. However, healthy women have the custom to be stringent on the three fasts. And even though for a fast for rain they are forbidden to be stringent, as I will write in Siman 574, in any case, for the fixed fasts for all of Israel – they are permitted to be stringent. However, if they suffer greatly, they are forbidden to be stringent, even if there is no danger to her or to the child (see Magen Avraham, subsection 2). Similarly, those who are physically weak should not be stringent to fast, except for Tisha B'Av.

And these three fasts – washing and anointing, wearing leather shoes, and marital relations are permitted. It is not necessary to begin fasting while it is still day, as nowadays a communal fast is only observed on the Ninth of Av. If any of these fasts fall on Shabbat, they are postponed until after Shabbat. Why do we not advance them to before Shabbat, like the Fast of Esther? Because we do not advance calamities. However, according to our calendar, the Tenth of Tevet cannot fall on Shabbat, but it can fall on Friday, in which case we fast and complete the fast, and "Vayechal" is read in the morning and afternoon. Even though the members of the Ma'amad did not read in the afternoon on Friday out of respect for Shabbat, as stated in Ta'anit (26a), that was because they did not fast on Friday, as explained there, which is not the case with a communal fast. Additionally, there it happened every week, whereas here it is a rare occurrence (see Magen Avraham, subsection 6, and in my humble opinion, as I have written). We do not say confessions or "Avinu Malkeinu" in the afternoon, but "Aneinu" is said. If a wedding occurs on the day of the fast on Friday, it is customary to pray Mincha, read "Vayechal," and then hold the wedding ceremony. The bride and groom should not drink from the cup because they must fast until evening, and children should drink the cup. Certainly, when a fast falls during the seven days of celebration, they are obligated to fast. However, for a yahrtzeit, one does not fast during the seven days of celebration (see Taz). And know that the Ninth of Av, the Seventeenth of Tammuz, and the Fast of Gedaliah cannot fall on Friday according to our calendar.

From a legal perspective, there is no prohibition against bathing in hot water on any of the three fasts. Nevertheless, the custom is to prohibit it, except on Friday afternoon when one may bathe in hot water in honor of Shabbat (Beit Yosef). However, there is no custom at all concerning cold water, and one may bathe in cold water. Similarly, sweating in a bathhouse is also permitted, as this is not considered a pleasure, but rather the removal of the discomfort of sweat.

And our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 4 that on Shabbat before the fast, the prayer leader announces the fast, except for Tisha B'Av, Yom Kippur, and the Fast of Esther; and a mnemonic for this is "Akhaf alav piyhu" (A = Av, K = Kippur, P = Purim). The reason is that these three fasts do not depend on the will of the community. But for the Seventeenth of Tammuz, the Fast of Gedaliah, and the Tenth of Tevet, it is stated in the Gemara there: "If they wish, they fast, etc." Therefore, they announce it if they wish to fast. However, according to the ruling that now it does not depend on the will (since we have already accepted these fasts upon ourselves), our master the Rema wrote that the custom of the Ashkenazim is not to announce any of them. This is his language, because now it does not depend on the will (Gra).

It is taught in the Mishnah at the end of Taanit (26b): Once Av begins, we reduce our joy. However, the Tanna does not specify how we reduce it. Similarly, Rambam records this in the fifth chapter of Taanit, and so wrote the Rif and the Rosh. The intention of "reduce" means that one should not engage in any joyful activities at all. It must be said this way, for otherwise, what measure is there for the reduction? (And similarly, the Tosafot wrote in Megillah 5b, see there.) The general matter of joy refers to betrothal with a meal, and marriage even without a meal, as it is prohibited during Chol HaMoed due to joy, as I wrote in Siman 546. And so we find in a Baraita in Yevamot (43b) that one may betroth but not marry, and one does not make a betrothal feast. And so it is in the Tur and Shulchan Aruch. Rambam did not mention this because he relied on what he explained regarding Chol HaMoed, that one does not mix one joy with another, and therefore it is forbidden to marry during Chol HaMoed even without a meal. Betrothal is permitted, but not with a meal. And since he wrote "reduce joy," we automatically understand that it is the same as during Chol HaMoed.

Nevertheless, the words of the Rambam are lacking, for indeed in Yevamot there we have learned in two Baraitot that from Rosh Chodesh until the fast, the people reduce their activities: from buying and selling, from building, from planting, etc. Why did he not mention this at all? Similarly, the Rif and the Rosh did not mention this. But the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch did write this, as will be explained. 

And it is possible to say that since we learned "the people reduce their activities" and we did not learn "it is forbidden to buy and sell," etc., as we learned there in that Baraita: the week in which Tisha B'Av falls - it is forbidden to cut hair and wash clothes on Erev Shabbat, we understand from this that it is not a strict law, but rather a custom that they adopted themselves. And where they have the custom - they follow it, and where they do not have the custom - they do not follow it. According to this, it makes sense that in our times they are not aware of this prohibition at all, and they engage in buying and selling, and building and planting. And indeed, the great ones were perplexed by this (Taz, small section 1, and Beit Yosef). According to our explanation, it fits well. (And see Beit Yosef who wrote similarly, and the Lechem Mishneh wrote that it is a forced interpretation, see there.)

And it seems more appropriate to say that our rabbis found it difficult, because the language of this Baraita is also found at the end of the first chapter of Taanit, regarding the fasts for rain in the last seven [fasts]. And this is what it says in the Mishnah there (12b): If these [fasts] have passed and they were not answered, they reduce business activities, building, and planting, etc. And it is taught there (14b): Building—building of joy; planting—planting of joy, see there. And so ruled the Rambam in the third chapter of Taanit, Law 8, see there. And if you thought that the Ninth of Av is equal in this regard to the fasts, why did the Mishnah change its language? For in the fasts, it specified, but regarding the Ninth of Av, it only said "they reduce joy." Rather, it is certain that regarding business activities they are not the same, for in the fasts, business activities are also forbidden, as the Mishnah concludes there: like people rebuked by God, meaning because they prayed and were not answered. And this only applies to new distress, not to the Ninth of Av, which is an old sorrow and ancient mourning, and it does not make sense to say that we are rebuked, heaven forbid. And why should we forbid business activities, which have no joy at all? Rather, it is certain that ordinary business activities are permitted. And that [which is taught in] Yevamot refers to joyful business activities, and joyful building and planting. And what is joyful business activity? Like buying clothes for the groom or the bride, or buying and sewing expensive clothes for oneself, which is not like the business activities of fasts. And in this, indeed, we are careful. And according to this, our custom is appropriate, that we do not abstain from business activities as throughout the year. (And the commentators want to equate this business activity with that of the fasts, and this is the opinion of the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch, and this is also the opinion of the Tosafot in Yevamot there, in the beginning of the discussion "to marry," see there. But this is not the opinion of the Rif, the Rambam, and the Rosh, and therefore they did not need to mention it, because since they wrote "they reduce joy"—it includes everything, all kinds of joy. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

And this is the language of the Tur, and the Shulchan Aruch, Section 2: From Rosh Chodesh until the fast, one reduces business activities; and joyous building, such as a wedding hall for his son, or decorative building and painting; and joyous planting, such as royal gardens planted for shade to sit under, or types of myrtle, and types of aloe. If his wall was leaning to fall—even joyous building is permissible; this is their language. And even if there is not yet a danger in the leaning of the wall, but there would be a financial loss—it is permitted (Taz, Subsection 2). And it is clear from their intention, that their intention is regarding all business activities being prohibited, since regarding business activities, they did not write "of joy," and it cannot be said that "of joy" in building applies to both. For if so, it should have said "like business activities for weddings," as it said regarding building a wedding hall. (And there needs to be an examination of the Magen Avraham, Subsection 7, who wrote that "of joy" also applies to "business activities," like the needs of a wedding, see there. And what he wrote in the name of the Beit Yosef and Bach—they wrote according to the custom of the world, which is not customary in this matter, as I have written. And not according to the words of the Tur, which are like the words of the Shulchan Aruch, see there. And examine and you will find it light.)

There is one who wrote in this language: In a place where they have the custom to prohibit all business dealings, it requires an annulment (of the vow). But in a place where the custom is only to minimize business dealings, an annulment does not help, because there are authorities who hold this way, and their ancestors have already accepted this opinion (Magen Avraham there). Meaning, an annulment only helps with things that are permitted by law but others have customarily prohibited, as it is written in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 214; but not with things that are forbidden by law. However, if so, even in a place where they customarily prohibit all business dealings, an annulment does not help, because there are also those who hold this way, as it is explained in Tosafot Megillah (5b) which writes that they minimize. By necessity, this means "completely," because it cannot be said that only in abundance it is forbidden, but in small amounts it is permitted, as it would have needed to specify what constitutes a small amount. Refer there. And even though they wrote this regarding joy – it follows that this also applies to business dealings, for the same reason. Therefore, they wrote there that business dealings are a form of joy, refer there. But according to the words of Tosafot in Yevamot there, which rejected this interpretation and explained that it applies to all business dealings, refer there – certainly it is completely forbidden. And you should know that this is so, because the Tanna included them in building and planting for joy, and these are completely forbidden. And this is what Tosafot wrote in Yevamot there, and this is their language: "He prohibited an abundance of business dealings," etc., refer there. And certainly, this is so, because it is necessary to buy and sell the necessities for the meal of the night, and it is obvious that on that fast which lasts seven days – how is it possible without business dealings in food and drink and similar matters? Therefore, they taught the language "minimize," but as for commerce – not at all. And similarly, that which we learned: "When Av enters, we minimize joy" – this is also so, because how is it possible otherwise? And if so, if a male child is born to him – shall he not rejoice? Or if some good news comes to him, or he profits money, and similar situations. Rather, the intention is: "we minimize joy" – in what is within a person's control to do or not to do. And similarly, in business dealings related to commerce. But what is forbidden is completely forbidden, for otherwise, the question of Tosafot in Megillah there remains: What is the measure of the minimization? Therefore, in my humble opinion, for those who follow this custom – an annulment does not help. (And it is true that the Magen Avraham follows the method of the Beit Yosef in his great book, who attributed an error to the people of Budein who prohibited all business dealings. And he wrote that in any case: according to Tosafot in Megillah – it is only concerning joy, and according to Tosafot in Yevamot – it is only minimizing, refer there. But in my humble opinion, it is not so, as we have explained, that their intention is not so. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

The Maharil wrote that brokers should not carry silver vessels for brokering in the city from the beginning of the month, because it brings joy to those who see it (there). And any construction that is merely for profit is considered a construction of joy and is forbidden (there). Even through a non-Jew, it is forbidden, because ultimately it brings joy to him. However, if before the beginning of the month he had contracted with a non-Jew for a construction of joy or for painting and decorating, it is permissible to let him paint his house, because the non-Jew works for his own sake. Nevertheless, if it is possible to appease him with a small amount to paint after the ninth of Av, one should do so (there), and a blessing will come upon him.

And Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote that for the sake of a mitzvah, everything is permitted; thus far his words; such as the construction of a synagogue and a study hall. And it seems that any communal need is permitted, as any communal need is considered for the sake of a mitzvah. There are those who write that the same applies to a wedding hall for someone who has not yet fulfilled the mitzvah of procreation. Similarly, new clothes for the purpose of marriage are permitted for someone who has not yet fulfilled the mitzvah of procreation (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 8). Moreover, even marriage is permitted for someone who has not fulfilled the mitzvah of procreation. The reason that we do not marry during these days is because it is not considered a good sign to marry during these troubled days, and not because it is prohibited (there, in the name of the Ran, see there). And indeed, the Ran wrote in the name of Rav Hai Gaon at the end of the first chapter of Ta'anit, regarding fasts for rain, see there. But from the words of Rabbi Moshe Isserles, who wrote this only regarding labor and not regarding marriages, we can infer that marriages are prohibited in any case before the Ninth of Av, but it is possible that this is because it is not considered a good sign. And indeed, even from the Seventeenth of Tammuz, we do not marry. According to this, it makes sense that preparations for the clothing of the groom and bride are made during these days. And if it is absolutely necessary to marry during these days, it is permissible according to this. However, during the week in which the Ninth of Av occurs, it is certainly prohibited.

Similarly, one does not marry women from the beginning of the month [of Av], even without a feast, whether it is a bachelor and a virgin or a widower and a widow. But remarrying one's divorced wife seems to be permitted, just like during Chol HaMoed. However, it is permitted to become betrothed without a feast, and even on Tisha B'Av itself it is permitted to become betrothed, so that someone else does not precede him. But to make a betrothal feast is prohibited, and in this regard, even in the case of a mitzvah it is prohibited. And it seems to me that although, regarding Chol HaMoed, it is clarified in Siman 546 that a betrothal feast is only prohibited at the time of the betrothal and in the bride's house, in any case, here it is prohibited in all respects, because there the reason is that one should not mix one joy with another. Therefore, when it is not at the time of the act and in the bride's house, it is not considered such a joy to nullify the joy of the festival. But here, where any kind of joy is prohibited, it is obvious that even in such a manner it is considered joy and is prohibited. And even the joy of friendship seems to be prohibited. And the same applies to our engagements: it is permitted to become engaged from the beginning of the month and onwards, but without a feast, and certainly without dancing and celebrations. And even on Shabbat it is forbidden to make a feast for this purpose. And even from the seventeenth of Tammuz, dancing and celebrations are prohibited, as we practice not to perform marriages from the seventeenth of Tammuz until after Tisha B'Av. This is not similar to a circumcision feast or a redemption of the firstborn feast, which are permitted because the time dictates it. And also, there is no joy in these, for there is no joy except in matters of matchmaking, for which one blesses "Who has placed joy in His dwelling." Therefore, anything related to betrothal and the setting of conditions is considered joy, but not circumcision or redemption of the firstborn.

The Sages said in Taanit there: A Jewish person who has a legal matter with a non-Jew should avoid him throughout the entire month, as one's fortune is bad throughout the whole month. And a circumcision that takes place from Rosh Chodesh until the ninth of Av, it is customary that the mohel, the sandak (who holds the baby), and the father of the child wear Shabbat clothes. However, other honorees, even the kvatter (who brings the baby), do not wear Shabbat clothes. But women customarily wear [Shabbat clothes], as this is their main mitzvah, in that they wear fine clothes in honor of the circumcision (Magen Avraham, section 3).

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote in section 1: Even on Shabbat Chazon, one does not change into Shabbat clothes, except for the shirt alone. And it is permitted even if Tisha B'Av falls on Shabbat (Levushe). And anyone who is stringent in this matter is only mistaken, since the shirt is only changed because of sweat (Magen Avraham, subsection 4). However, one spreads the Shabbat parochet (curtain), unless Shabbat falls on Tisha B'Av which is deferred, in which case one does not spread the Shabbat parochet. The tablecloths and coverings have the same rule as the parochet. Only someone who has a wedding on Shabbat Nachamu is permitted to wear Shabbat clothes on Shabbat Chazon. But new clothes are forbidden even for a groom (Magen Avraham, subsection 6). Additionally, the father of the groom may wear an outer Shabbat garment in honor of the groom, as Mahari”l did (there).

And know that for the past two or three generations, our practice on Shabbat Chazon has not been as described, but rather we wear all Shabbat clothes. The great leaders of the generation at that time established this practice, saying that otherwise, it would appear as if we are displaying public mourning on Shabbat. Therefore, even on a Shabbat that coincides with Tisha B'Av that is postponed, we wear Shabbat clothes for this reason. Consequently, in our times, it is almost forgotten that one should not wear Shabbat clothes on Shabbat Chazon. This is surprising to me, as did our ancestors not know this? And yet they practiced this way, even though it is not strictly according to the law; so how can we nullify their practice?

Therefore, it seems to me, in my humble opinion, that this depends on the nature of the clothing. Among the ancients, Shabbat and weekday clothing were similar in form and appearance, with the difference being between expensive and simple goods, and the difference was not so noticeable. After all, the poor also went out on Shabbat in simple goods. Hence, they established the practice to wear weekday clothes. But several generations ago, Shabbat clothes had a completely different appearance, whether for the poor or the rich. For example, during the week, they wore a "kalf" hat, and on Shabbat a "shtreimel." Similarly, other garments were clearly distinguishable as weekday clothes, like "kitay," and Shabbat clothes, like silk for the rich and simple silk for the poor. Therefore, the great leaders established not to follow this practice, because the difference was very noticeable, and it was like mourning on Shabbat.

Thus, I say that in our time, due to government regulations, we have already changed the appearance of our clothes, and Shabbat and weekday clothes look the same, with the difference being only between cheap and expensive – it is certainly correct to uphold the practice of the ancients. (This seems to be my humble opinion. And know that what was explained in section 9, that throughout the month of Av one should avoid certain things, is clarified in the Zohar Yitro 78b that this applies only until the Ninth of Av and not beyond, see there.)

The week in which Tisha B'Av falls – it is forbidden to cut hair and to do laundry, even if one does not intend to wear the clothes now, but rather to set them aside until after Tisha B'Av. And even if one has only one shirt – it is forbidden, except for the honor of Shabbat, as will be explained. Clothes that were laundered beforehand – it is forbidden to wear them or to spread them on the bed. Even handkerchiefs and tablecloths – it is forbidden. And it seems to me that for the honor of Shabbat – this too is permitted, meaning: since we have the custom to observe all these prohibitions from the beginning of the month, therefore for the honor of Shabbat it is permitted to wear a clean shirt and clean handkerchiefs, and similar items.

And know that according to the Talmudic law in Taanit (29b), the prohibition against laundering only applies to their form of laundering, which was clean and beautiful, and not to our form of laundering. Our laundering is only prohibited when combined with ironing, which involves passing a smooth stone over the garments to smooth them. Linen garments, however, are permitted even with ironing. And so it is stated there, that linen garments are not subject to the prohibition of ironing, and they are like our laundering, and therefore permitted. The reason is that they are close to the body and always filled with sweat, and there is no concern to iron them well (Tur). This permission, however, is only for ironing them and setting them aside until after the Ninth of Av. But it is forbidden to wear them during the week in which the Ninth of Av falls, and this is according to the Talmudic law there.

However, we have the custom to prohibit even linen garments, and even with our laundering without pressing, whether to launder and wear, or to launder and set aside. And since our ancestors accepted this as a prohibition, it is consequently forbidden for us according to the law. Besides this, some say that our laundering is forbidden by law, because what is stated in the Gemara that our laundering is permitted – that was in Babylonia, because their waters were murky, for Babylonia is not a land of mountains and valleys like the Land of Israel. Therefore, the waters were murky and did not cleanse well like in the Land of Israel. But in other countries outside of Israel, it can be said that it is forbidden like in the Land of Israel, because our waters are clean and cleanse well. Additionally, there is another prohibition; some say that our laundering includes pressing, for pressing is not done with a heated iron, but with water and ash, whether natron and soap.
