And with us, we launder with natron and soap, and it is found that according to the law it is forbidden, even with linen garments. In any case, to wear them is forbidden by the law of the Gemara, as we have written. Furthermore, we see that our linen garments cleanse well, and on the contrary, with them a complete pressing is done according to all opinions, with natron and soap, and with a heated iron. Therefore, according to our law – all types of laundering are forbidden in the week during which Tisha B'Av occurs.

Our custom is to forbid all forms of laundering from the beginning of the month of Av until after the fast, except for a mitzvah-related necessity. For example, a woman who wears white garments is permitted to launder, wear, and spread them out under her. This is allowed until the ninth of Av. However, on the ninth of Av itself, she should not wear white garments but should instead wear a checked and clean garment. Similarly, in honor of Shabbat, one may wear linen garments and spread out white ones, as on other Shabbatot. Laundering for the honor of Shabbat was also permitted on Thursday, but we have adopted the custom to forbid it. Indeed, we have also adopted the custom to forbid bathing, as will be explained, and certainly laundering. Nevertheless, if one does not have a shirt to change into for the honor of Shabbat, he may launder and wear it (Magen Avraham, subsection 14). Haircuts and shavings are entirely forbidden from the beginning of the month. Only nail trimming is permitted, and certainly for the honor of Shabbat (ibid., subsection 11). All the more so, combing with a comb is permitted every day, as it is even permitted for a mourner within the seven days (Shulchan Aruch, subsection 16). Note that laundering is forbidden even to give to a non-Jewish launderer from the beginning of the month onwards, even if they will return it after the ninth of Av. It is entirely forbidden to engage in laundering from the beginning of the month onwards, except for small children's clothes, which need to be laundered daily. However, if the clothes were given to the launderer before the beginning of the month, there is no need to prevent her from laundering them during these days, but she should be warned not to return them until after the ninth of Av.

And know that even though we are stringent regarding laundering only from Rosh Chodesh (the beginning of the month of Av), we customarily forbid haircuts from the seventeenth of Tammuz, because haircuts are not as common as laundering. Therefore, during the nine days (from Rosh Chodesh Av to Tisha B'Av), the prohibition would not be noticeable, and thus we extend it from the seventeenth of Tammuz. After Tisha B'Av, it is immediately permitted to cut hair and launder clothes. And although there is an opinion in the Gemara that forbids during the week in which Tisha B'Av occurs, whether before or after Tisha B'Av, we do not follow this opinion. Immediately on the tenth of Av, everything is permitted. It seems proper to wait on the tenth until after midday, similar to eating meat, as will be explained in Siman 558.

From the law of the Talmud, when Tisha B'Av falls on a Sunday, or on Shabbat and is postponed to Sunday, all matters are permitted during the two weeks: for before Tisha B'Av, it is not considered the week in which Tisha B'Av falls, and the second week is after Tisha B'Av. The opinion of the Tur is to prohibit the week before, because that too is considered the week in which Tisha B'Av falls, except for Thursday and Friday, when everything is permitted in honor of Shabbat. However, our custom is not like this; rather, we prohibit everything from Rosh Chodesh Av onwards, as we have explained, and haircuts from the 17th of Tammuz. The prohibition on laundering applies even to laundering non-Jewish garments for payment. In this, it is certainly permitted by law, as there is no joy involved; but because of suspicion, lest people say she is laundering her own clothes, it is therefore permitted in private (Magen Avraham, small section 19). Similarly, if it is publicly known that she launders their clothes, or if the garments are recognizable as theirs (there), it is permitted to launder them.

New clothes—whether white or colored, whether wool or linen—are forbidden to wear during this Shabbat and for us from Rosh Chodesh, as the difference between wool and linen applies only to old clothes, not new ones. New clothes bring joy regardless of the material. Especially when they are pressed in a press, making them like ironed clothes, which are forbidden by law even if they are not new. Therefore, ironed Shabbat clothes are forbidden even if they are old (Siman 551:20). Even new shoes should not be worn during this week, and for us from Rosh Chodesh, because any new clothing or shoes, even if they are not significant, still bring some joy and are forbidden. However, from the 17th of Tammuz until Rosh Chodesh, it is permitted to wear new clothes. But if it is a significant garment that requires the blessing "Shehecheyanu," it should not be worn, according to the custom of not reciting "Shehecheyanu" during the Three Weeks. Therefore, on Shabbat when "Shehecheyanu" is recited, as will be explained, it is permitted to wear (Siman 551:21). However, we refrain from wearing a significant new garment from the 17th of Tammuz, even on Shabbat. (The Bach and Magen Avraham in Siman 551:18 wrote that a mourner whose thirtieth day falls on the 18th of Tammuz is permitted to shave, since it is permitted by law, as I wrote, and only prohibited by custom. In such a case, it is considered as if mourning has overwhelmed him. See there.)

Just as it is forbidden to wear new clothes and new shoes from the beginning of the month [of Av] and onward, it is similarly forbidden to repair and prepare them until after Tisha B'Av. It is also forbidden to buy them. However, for a bride and groom, or a young man and maiden, or a widower and divorcee who have not yet fulfilled the mitzvah of procreation, it may be permissible, as I wrote in section 7, that for the sake of a mitzvah it is allowed. (Regarding what the Magen Avraham wrote in subsection 23, that according to the Beit Yosef it is permissible to wear [new clothes], his intention is from the beginning of the month of Av, meaning that only during the week in which Tisha B'Av falls is it forbidden to wear new clothes. Therefore, in the law of wearing [new clothes] in section 6, he did not write that some prohibit it from the beginning of the month, as he wrote in section 7 regarding their preparation. However, for us, there is no difference, as I wrote. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

And so too a Jewish tailor—it is forbidden for him to sew new clothes from the beginning of the month, whether for a Jew or for a non-Jew, because of the suspicion that people will say: "They belong to a Jew." However, the custom is to be lenient in this matter, and even if they belong to a Jew, if he took the job before the beginning of the month, he is allowed to complete it. It seems to me that the custom to be lenient only applies if he is being paid, due to his livelihood, but not if he is doing it for free. And certainly, if it is known and publicized that they belong to a non-Jew, it is permitted. And similarly, the custom is to give new items to non-Jewish craftsmen to repair during this time, so that they will be ready immediately after Tisha B'Av. And even though washing is forbidden, as I wrote in section 15, this is because the prohibition of washing is mentioned in the Gemara, which is not the case with making new clothes. And for the needs of a bride and groom, even on Tisha B'Av itself, a non-Jew can repair (there in small section 25). Nevertheless, it is proper to minimize as much as possible, since even in business dealings one should not increase according to several authorities, as I wrote in section 5, and certainly in such a manner. And among us, we do not give work from the beginning of the month of Av, even to a non-Jew, unless it is for the sake of a mitzvah. And know that what has been clarified regarding new clothes—it is the same law for buying new valuable items of silver, and the like. And similarly, giving a craftsman to make valuable items is forbidden from the beginning of the month.

It is stated in the Jerusalem Talmud at the beginning of the fourth chapter of Pesachim: These women who have the custom not to spin wool from the beginning of the month [of Av] is a good custom, based on the verse "for the foundations are destroyed." And this is the explanation: that women have the custom not to make warp threads from wool from Rosh Chodesh until after the Ninth of Av. And "to spin" is derived from the language of either warp or weft. And why do they do this? Because "warp" is a term signifying foundation, as it is said, "for the foundations are destroyed," and the Temple was destroyed, within which was the Foundation Stone. And they do not make it for themselves nor for others, whether for free or for pay (Taz, subparagraph 7). And this applies only to warp threads, but they do make weft threads and other kinds of spinning. As for the custom being limited to wool, I do not know the reason, for if it is to commemorate the blue and purple wool that were in the priestly garments, the linen garments were even more so. In truth, in the Jerusalem Talmud before us, the word "wool" does not appear, it only states "not to spin," based on "for the foundations are destroyed"; and it is only in the Tur and Shulchan Aruch that it is written "wool."

And our master, the Rema, wrote in section 8 that it is customary not to sanctify the moon until after the Ninth of Av; thus his words end. And there are those who wrote that even after the Ninth of Av, one should not sanctify it after the fast, as is written in section 526 (Taz, subsection 8). But in the name of the Ari, it is written that on the contrary, one should sanctify it on the night after the Ninth of Av, because on that night the son of David was born, as explained in the Midrashim, and so is written in Pri Etz Chaim (page 128a), see there. And there are those who question this ruling entirely, asking how we can forgo a mitzvah that comes to our hand? Additionally, there is concern that one might become ill or die and not fulfill the mitzvah. Nevertheless, where it is customary – it is customary; but in our countries, we do not wait regardless, because the clouds are prevalent in our countries, and who knows if it will not be covered with clouds? Therefore, we sanctify the moon before the Ninth of Av.

According to the Talmudic law, there is no prohibition against eating meat except on the eve of Tisha B'Av and during the final meal before the fast. However, our ancestors accepted many centuries ago not to eat meat and not to drink wine from the beginning of the month of Av until after Tisha B'Av, except on Shabbat, in memory of the sacrifices and libations that were annulled due to our sins. Some have the custom starting from the 17th of Tammuz, when the daily sacrifice was annulled. Some have written that it is only during the week in which Tisha B'Av falls. But now, in all our places of dispersion, the custom is from the beginning of the month. And now, due to our many sins, how much this prohibition is disregarded! Besides the fact that they are transgressing a Torah prohibition due to the vow, since our ancestors accepted this custom upon themselves, it is considered a vow of the entire Jewish people. Besides this, how can we not be ashamed and humiliated? Many nations do not eat meat, milk, or eggs for many weeks, and we, the people of Israel, about whom it is said, "You shall be holy," will not restrain ourselves for eight days a year in memory of our Holy Temple and its glory? Concerning such matters, the prophet said (Ezekiel 36:32): "Be ashamed and humiliated for your ways, O house of Israel," and their punishment is very severe.

Other beverages are permitted, even wine vinegar. The prohibition applies to both the meat of domesticated animals and poultry. However, someone who is weak may eat poultry if necessary. There are those who permit the consumption of meat sauce, but this is not the prevailing custom. Even meat that was in our possession before Rosh Chodesh is forbidden to eat, even if it is leftover from Shabbat. This is not comparable to what the Rosh wrote in the first chapter of Chullin regarding the limbs of slaughtered animals that Jews brought into the land, where there was a question of whether they were permitted or forbidden. The Rosh wrote that the practical difference would be for someone who made a vow regarding something and had some of that item before the vow was made — see there. This applies to a new vow, not one that has been observed for generations, which is considered an old prohibition. Regarding mixtures of meat with other items, it seems that they did not follow the rule of imparting flavor, as they did not make such a decree. Moreover, one who vows not to drink wine is permitted to eat a dish that has the flavor of wine, as stated in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 216 — see there. Even if wine existed during these days and turned into vinegar, it is also permitted (Taz, subparagraph 9). One who vows not to eat meat from the seventeenth of Tammuz is permitted to eat on Shabbat, as anyone who vows does so with the intent of following the custom (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 27). However, there are those who disagree and require an annulment (same source, in the name of Bach). Nevertheless, if the vow was not explicitly stated as a vow but as an acceptance, it is certainly permitted (same source).

And there are those who have the custom to put away the knife used for slaughtering from the beginning of the month (of Av) onward, and they do not slaughter except for the sake of a mitzvah: for a sick person, or for Shabbat, or for a circumcision, or for the redemption of the firstborn, and the like. It is understood, therefore, that in a large city where there are always several sick people and several women who have given birth, and many who are weak in health – it is not applicable to put away the knife. And a Jew who needs to prepare meat for a non-Jewish officer – it is permitted to slaughter for him during the week in which Tisha B'Av occurs, and for us (Ashkenazim) from the beginning of the month, only they should not recite a blessing over the slaughter, since a Jew will not eat from it. And it is good to set aside a piece for Shabbat, or for a sick person or a woman who has given birth and needs meat, and then it will be possible to check and recite a blessing over the slaughter. But if it is not possible for a Jew to eat from it – he should slaughter without a blessing and without checking. However, regarding stunning – there are some of the great authorities who are not pleased with this, and there are those who permit it (Shulchan Aruch, Yoreh De'ah, small paragraph 28). And it is better to stun by a non-Jew rather than by a Jew. And in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 117, this matter is clarified, see there. And in the city, the slaughterers should not slaughter until after Tisha B'Av. However, when Tisha B'Av falls on Thursday – it is permitted to slaughter on Tisha B'Av after midday in honor of Shabbat (Magen Avraham, small paragraph 28). And in places where non-Jews do not eat meat on Friday and Shabbat, and there will be no one to sell the hindquarters to, or perhaps the animal will be found to be non-kosher – they may slaughter on Wednesday, before Tisha B'Av (ibid.). And everything depends on the situation and the judgment of the teacher. For in truth, there is no reason to forbid this, as there is no element of joy here. And it is not relevant to decree that perhaps one might come to eat from it, as some have feared (ibid., in the name of Abudraham). And these are puzzling matters, for it is impossible to eat until the meat is cooked, and one will come to remember. And as for eating intentionally – Jews are not suspected of this.

Our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, wrote in section 10: There is an opinion that those who have the custom not to eat meat on the specified days are permitted to eat a dish that was cooked with meat, but are prohibited from eating salted meat, poultry, and fermented wine. It is permitted to drink wine for Havdalah and Birkat Hamazon. However, the custom is to be stringent and not to drink wine, neither for Birkat Hamazon nor for Havdalah, but to give it to a child. In a situation where there is no child, it is permitted to drink the Havdalah wine oneself; thus is their language. 

We have the custom to prohibit a dish that was cooked with meat (Magen Avraham, subsection 29), and this is the prevalent custom, and one should not change it. Regarding wine for Birkat Hamazon, even without this it is not our custom to use a cup for Birkat Hamazon during the weekdays. It is clear that if there is a cup, it should be of beer or mead. However, for Havdalah, there are those who have the custom to drink, but we do not drink and we make Havdalah on beer. 

The statement regarding giving it to a child means that some infer from their words that it is permitted to give a child meat and wine on these days (there, subsection 31), but this is not our custom. Certainly, if a child needs it due to weakness, it is permitted, and similarly, it is permitted for an adult if he is weak to eat poultry, as I have written. Pregnant and nursing women, if they have difficulty with dairy foods, are certainly permitted to eat poultry. If there is no poultry, they may eat beef, for where there is concern for bodily health, the decree was not enacted. However, for regular children, it is certainly not permitted to feed them meat, and this is the custom, and one should not change it. 

The statement about giving Havdalah to children is because it is permitted for oneself to drink, as we have written, that if there is no child, one may drink it oneself, but when there is a child, it is preferable for the child to drink rather than the adult; it is not because it is permitted to give children meat initially (and this requires examination of the Magen Avraham).

They also wrote that for a circumcision, the redemption of the firstborn, the completion of a tractate, and an engagement feast, all those who belong to the meal may eat meat and drink wine. However, it should be limited and not increased. And during the week in which Tisha B'Av falls, one should not eat meat or drink wine except for a small quorum, and this is permitted even on the eve of Tisha B'Av, provided it is not the concluding meal. And anyone who eats meat where it is customary to prohibit it is breaching a fence and a snake will bite him. And it is permitted to drink any alcoholic beverages, even those called "mead"; thus far his words. And they differentiated between from Rosh Chodesh and the week in which Tisha B'Av falls, that in this week it should not be more than a small quorum, and from Rosh Chodesh it can be more, but only not to add invitees who have no connection to the circumcision. And if it were not for the eating of meat, they would not be invited—certainly it should be prohibited.

And know that there are those who schedule the completion of a tractate for these days in order to eat meat. This is an improper practice, for although it is evident from Moed Katan (9a) that it is permissible to leave part of the completion for the sake of a mitzvah, as it is mentioned there concerning the construction of the Temple—refer there—nonetheless, to initially plan in order to eat meat is neither appropriate nor commendable. There are those who study a tractate from the outset with the intention of making a completion during these days, and this is somewhat acceptable, as it encourages engagement in Torah study. However, only scholars who are dedicated to Torah study should be asked to complete a tractate. We do not have the custom of making a completion, and even if a completion happens to occur during these days, we delay it until after the Ninth of Av, so that we can properly rejoice in the celebration of the completion in honor of the Torah.

And that which is written about an engagement feast is certainly perplexing, for it has already been explained that it is forbidden to make an engagement feast. And indeed, some have erased this (Magen Avraham, subsection 34 in the name of the Shach). And some have written that it pertains to someone who does not have a wife and children, who has not fulfilled the mitzvah of procreation, and in such a case, it is permitted to make a feast. However, according to what I have written in subsection 8, even in such a case, it is forbidden to make a feast. And some have written that it does not refer to the time of the engagement itself, but in any case, it is a mitzvah (there). This is even more perplexing, for what mitzvah is there in this? And we have already written there that it is forbidden. Therefore, the main opinion seems to be the first one, and the Levush also omits this. And some say that this refers to those who do not eat from the seventeenth of Tammuz, for then it is permitted to engage and make a feast (Eliyahu Rabbah, subsection 25). And on the eve of Tisha B'Av at a circumcision, they should do it before midday.

And I have seen that the great authorities have explained who is permitted to eat meat at a mitzvah feast and the criteria for those who are close and related to this (see Magen Avraham subsection 35, Taz subsection 12, and Eliyah Rabbah subsection 25). It is difficult to clarify the details, but in truth, there is one general rule in the matter: anyone who would be eating at this meal even during the rest of the year is permitted to eat meat. However, someone who attends just to eat meat, and would not have been invited to this meal during the rest of the year, is forbidden to eat meat and should only eat dairy foods. This is explicitly evident from the words of Maharil that they brought, see there. And this is the opinion of all the great authorities, and it is the same for women.

Haircuts that the Sages forbade during the week in which Tisha B'Av falls, and for us from the seventeenth of Tammuz: whether it is the head or any other hair on the body—it is forbidden. Regarding the mustache: anything that interferes with eating is permitted. It is forbidden for adults to cut the hair of children, for although there is no mourning for a child, as written in Yoreh De'ah, section 384, this applies to regular mourning. But in communal mourning, which is a remembrance of the destruction of our Holy Temple—it is proper to educate even the children (Magen Avraham, subsection 38). Not because this mourning is more stringent than regular mourning, for on the contrary, there are matters where we are lenient in ancient mourning, as we say in Yevamot (43b), see there. Rather, in this case, it provides education for the fear of God, so that when the child asks about it—they will explain to him the matter of the destruction of the Temple.

Similarly, one should not wash the clothes of children during the week in which Tisha B'Av falls, and for us, from Rosh Chodesh. However, clothes that completely wrap around the children, which they soil and urinate in – these are certainly permitted to be washed. And even for other children's clothes, it is customary to be lenient, and they may be washed discreetly. Regarding nail cutting – some prohibit it (Taz, subsection 13) during the week in which Tisha B'Av falls. And some permit it, since it is done discreetly and is not so noticeable (Magen Avraham, subsection 11). And we are accustomed to be lenient, because also regarding washing hands, it is better when the nails are trimmed.

And our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 15: If one is overcome by mourning for a deceased and for Shabbat, and his hair has grown heavy, he may lighten it with a razor but not with scissors, and he may wash his clothes in water but not with natron or sand; thus far is his language. For us, regarding washing, if the end of mourning falls on Rosh Chodesh, and regarding haircutting, if it falls on the 17th of Tammuz, then even with scissors it is permitted. However, during the week in which Tisha B'Av falls, since the law of the Gemara prohibits it, we do not permit using scissors, nor earlier when we follow the custom out of mere tradition. Similarly, regarding washing from Rosh Chodesh with natron and sand (as per Bach and Taz, subsection 14). There are also those who permit someone who is traveling during the week in which Tisha B'Av falls to wash his linen garments as much as necessary for his journey (ibid.), since linen garments are permitted by the law of the Gemara, as I wrote in section 13 – one should not be stringent in such a case.

And so it appears, in my humble opinion, that all those whom the sages permitted to shave and launder during Chol HaMoed, as we learned in the Mishnah in "These are those who shave," as I wrote in Siman 531, are also permitted to get haircuts and launder during the week in which Tisha B'Av occurs, and certainly before, as this is only a custom. For on the festival, aside from the prohibition of labor, they also decreed so that people would not enter the festival in a disheveled state, as I wrote there. Nevertheless, for these individuals, they permitted it—and all the more so in the case of an old mourning, where it is evident to everyone that they could not shave or get a haircut until now, and it is not worse than when mourning periods overlap. And there, it is explained all those whom the sages permitted on the eve of Shabbat.

Some have the custom not to bathe in hot water from Rosh Chodesh (the beginning of the month), and some refrain only during the Shabbat that falls before Tisha B'Av. Some fast from the Seventeenth of Tammuz. Our custom regarding bathing in hot water is to prohibit it from Rosh Chodesh, but if Rosh Chodesh falls on the eve of the holy Shabbat, one may bathe in honor of Shabbat. We only refrain from the bathhouse on Shabbat Chazon, not for two Shabbats. However, not in honor of Shabbat, our custom is not to bathe even in cold water from Rosh Chodesh onward. Therefore, one should not go to cool off in rivers and springs from Rosh Chodesh onward, except in honor of Shabbat. However, one who goes in the morning before prayer to the mikvah is permitted, even on the eve of Tisha B'Av, for this is not considered bathing but rather a purification immersion. On the eve of Shabbat Chazon, one should not bathe in hot water. This is the language of our Rabbi, the Rema, at the end of section 16: Even on the eve of Shabbat Chazon, it is forbidden to bathe except for one's head, face, hands, and feet in cold water. Some are lenient regarding washing the head with hot water for those who are accustomed to doing so every Shabbat; thus far his words. But it is forbidden to wash with soap (Levush and Magen Avraham, subsection 41). Similarly, washing the entire body is forbidden (ibid.). Concerning immersion in the mikvah: One who immerses every Friday is permitted to immerse even on this Friday; but one who occasionally skips, should not immerse (ibid.).

And know that in our generation, people have begun to be lax about bathing in hot water on the eve of Shabbat Chazon, and it is commonly said: that one who bathes every Friday is permitted also on this Shabbat. But this is not so, for our master the Rema only permitted washing the head, as I have written. And the bathhouses were always closed on the eve of Shabbat Chazon. Recently, people have started to be lax, and they will eventually be held accountable. And it is clear that for medical purposes, it is permitted to bathe in hot water, even on the eve of Tisha B'Av.

For the sake of a mitzvah (commandment) – bathing is permitted. Therefore, a menstruating woman (niddah) bathes and immerses. Even if she immerses on the night after Tisha B'Av, she is permitted to bathe on the eve of Tisha B'Av if she cannot bathe on the night after Tisha B'Av. Similarly, a woman who wears white garments can bathe a little in her usual manner throughout the year, since it is for the sake of a mitzvah, and she is not doing it for pleasure. And all the more so, someone who is not clean in his body – it is permitted for him to bathe even in hot water, so that he may be clean.

Our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, wrote in section 17: It is good to be cautious about reciting "Shehecheyanu" during the three weeks (bein hametzarim) over fruit or new clothing. However, for the redemption of the firstborn son (pidyon haben), one should recite it and not delay the mitzvah. Similarly, for fruit that will not be available after Tisha B'Av, it is permitted to recite the blessing and eat it during the three weeks. This is their language. On Shabbat, some prohibit it, and some permit it (Magen Avraham, section 42). The reason is not due to mourning, as we do not find that a mourner is forbidden to recite "Shehecheyanu," but since this period is a time of calamity, one should not say "Shehecheyanu... and brought us to this time" (ibid). Some permit reciting "Shehecheyanu" (Taz, section 17). Our custom is not to recite "Shehecheyanu" from Rosh Chodesh Av onward, even on Shabbat; but before Rosh Chodesh Av, we do recite it. There are those who recite "Shehecheyanu" even from Rosh Chodesh Av.

They also wrote in section 18 that one must be careful from the 17th of Tammuz until the 9th of Av not to walk alone from the fourth hour until the ninth hour, because during that time the "Ketev Meriri" (a harmful spiritual entity) prevails. Students should not be struck during these days; thus far is his wording, even with a strap. It appears that the concern is about walking on the road and not in the city. This is stated in the Midrash Shochar Tov on Psalms, regarding the verse "A psalm of one who sits in the shelter of the Most High," on the verse "a pestilence that walks in darkness," and this is the language of the Midrash: "Ketev Meriri" – it is made like shells and hairs, etc., and it prevails from the fourth hour until the ninth; and it prevails from the 17th of Tammuz until the 9th of Av, etc. Rabbi Yochanan would instruct the scribes not to strike the children, etc.; thus far is his wording, see there. And know that many follow the custom according to the Ari (Rabbi Isaac Luria) to say Tikkun Chatzot (Midnight Lamentations) during the "Three Weeks" after midday, except for on the eve of Shabbat, the eve of the New Moon, the New Moon, and the eve of the 9th of Av.

We learned in the Mishnah of Ta'anit (26b): On the eve of Tisha B'Av, a person should not eat two cooked dishes, nor eat meat, nor drink wine. It is explained in the Gemara (30a) that this only applies to the meal after which one refrains from eating further, and also after midday. But before midday, even if one refrains from eating further, and after midday if it is not the final meal, meaning that one will still eat the concluding meal – one may eat whatever one desires. And regarding meat and wine, it has already been clarified in the previous section that we do not eat meat nor drink wine from the beginning of the month. Therefore, for us, the distinction in the concluding meal only pertains to the matter of two cooked dishes, which will be explained.

According to the ruling of the Gemara: not all meat and wine are forbidden; only meat that was slaughtered two days earlier. But salted meat, which means it is on the third day from its slaughter, is permitted. Similarly, freshly pressed wine, which means within three days of its pressing, is permitted. And so wrote the Rambam in Chapter Five of Taanit, Law 7, see there. The reason is that since this is in remembrance of the sacrifices and libations, the prohibition only applies in cases where the sacrifices were consumed in this manner. Now, regarding sacrifices: in peace offerings, the longest time for their consumption is two days and one night, as stated in Chapter "Which Place." Therefore, anything not consumed within the peace offerings' time frame is permitted. Also, wine for libations is invalid if more than three days have not passed since its pressing. Therefore, it is permitted to drink it. According to this, also birds, except for turtledoves and young pigeons, and also venison, are permitted to eat, since sacrifices do not come from them. And so wrote the Tur in the name of Ravia and Rashbat, see there.

However, the Tur himself disagrees with this, and this is his wording: "It is not for this reason alone that meat was prohibited, but in order to increase mourning. And know that, for another mourner, it is a mitzvah to give him wine to drink; yet here, wine is prohibited because if he drinks, he will forget his impoverished state, and it is a mitzvah to remember the destruction of the Temple and to feel sorrow over it. Therefore, for this reason, it is proper to forbid even poultry, just like meat." And in the Sefer Mitzvot Katan (SeMaK) it is written: "Now that most of our food is meat, after two days have passed, it appears that it is forbidden. And it is permissible to drink freshly pressed wine, which is only three days from its pressing; thus far his wording." And why was he not stringent with wine as with meat? Because we are not accustomed to drinking wine less than three days from its pressing, and there is no concern that one will drink and forget his impoverished state, as it does not yet have the strength and taste of wine. But our master the Beit Yosef wrote in paragraph 2 that they have the custom to prohibit even freshly pressed wine, see there. (And what is written in the Shulchan Aruch "fish" – it is certainly a printing error, and so too in the Hagahot Asheri. And the Magen Avraham in section 2 strained to sustain the version because in vows it is included as meat. But it is not so except in places where they are accustomed to it, as it is written in Yoreh De'ah, section 117. And also what was written that it is because it is served on the table of kings – what relevance does this have? How many good foods are there that are permitted? And our custom proves this, that we do not eat meat from Rosh Chodesh, but we eat fish. And so too the Gra wrote that it is an error, and so too in the Atteret Zekeinim.)

It is also appropriate to reduce the amount one drinks at the concluding meal, even beverages other than wine which are permitted to be drunk. Additionally, one should not drink beer, unless he is weak. Similarly, one should not eat radishes, salted fish, or other items he usually eats at other times after his meal, so that he behaves with restraint. And these are the words of the Rambam there (Halacha 9): "The early pious ones had this practice: On the eve of Tisha B'Av, they would bring a person dry bread with salt, soak it in water, and he would sit between the oven and the stove and eat it, and drink a jug of water with it, in worry, desolation, and weeping, as if a deceased lay before him. This is what is appropriate for the wise to do, or something close to it. Throughout our days, we did not eat a cooked dish on the eve of Tisha B'Av, even of lentils, unless it fell on Shabbat; thus far are his words."

And it is customary to eat lentils or boiled eggs, which are foods of mourners. Some have the custom to eat hard and cold eggs, which are also foods of mourners. Similarly, it is customary to eat round bread called bagels, as we console mourners with them, due to their round shape—to symbolize that mourning and death is a wheel that turns in the world. Some are stringent to dip bread in ashes after eating and eat it, based on the verse "He has broken my teeth with gravel, He has covered me with ashes" (Lamentations 3:16). This is also mentioned in the Jerusalem Talmud at the end of Ta'anit (Chapter 4, Halacha 6), where Rav did so, see there. One should be careful to take ashes from dairy foods, and not ashes from a mixture of meat and milk, as mentioned in Yoreh De'ah, section 89, see there.

It is customary to sit on the ground during the Seudah HaMafseket, like a mourner for the dead in a state of lowliness; but one should not remove his shoes like a mourner, because mourning does not begin until the night. Therefore, after eating, one should sit on a bench. Care should be taken that three people do not eat together during the Seudah HaMafseket, to avoid the obligation of a zimun; rather, each person should sit alone and recite the blessing individually. If it happens that three ate together, they should recite the zimun. This is the ruling of the Tur. In the name of the R"i, it is written that they should not recite the zimun, and the Tur was astonished by this; see there. Some say the reason is that it is not considered a fixed meal unless they recline or sit at one table, as I wrote in Siman 167. And here, they do not intend to establish a fixed meal, since each one eats at a small table by himself (Magen Avraham, small section 9). Therefore, if it happens that three ate at a small table together, they should certainly recite the zimun.

And what constitutes "two cooked dishes"? Behold, items that are eaten raw, such as fruits and vegetables that are eaten raw, are not considered cooked dishes, and one may eat various kinds of them, for a cooked dish is only what is cooked, as its name implies. And if they are cooked, even if they are normally eaten raw, they are considered cooked dishes. This is contrary to the opinion of those who say that something eaten as it is raw is not considered a cooked dish even when it is cooked, as in the case of the laws of cooked food by idol worshippers. Here, we do not descend into such distinctions, and many good foods are made from these, so they are considered cooked dishes (Tur).

There is a doubt whether pickled and salted items are considered cooked dishes, such as salted fish called herring, or vegetables pickled in vinegar or water for a full day. In my humble opinion, it appears that these are not within the category of cooked dishes, and there are those who prohibit pickled items (Shu”t in the name of the Knesset HaGedolah). The reason seems to be because we hold that pickling is like cooking. However, in my opinion, this is not relevant here, as this principle only applies to absorption and release (of flavors), not to the status of being considered a cooked dish. A proof from Nedarim (vows) is that one who vows to abstain from cooked dishes is only forbidden from roasted, boiled, or cooked dishes— not from pickled or salted items, as is evident in Yoreh Deah, siman 217. Since the Sages prohibited only two cooked dishes, pickled and salted items are not included in this. This seems to be the main ruling. 

Even though for the purposes of Eruv Tavshilin, pickled items are effective (as mentioned in siman 527), this is not analogous. There, a cooked dish that does not accompany bread, like porridge, is not effective, as I wrote there. But here, it is certainly considered a cooked dish. However, this does not relate to our case, as there it depends on what accompanies the bread, and pickled items certainly accompany it. Here, it depends on the significance of being a cooked dish, and pickled items do not have the status of a cooked dish.

Two cooked dishes are forbidden, even two types of cooked dishes in one pot. For example, if one cooks fish and eggs in one pot, it is considered two dishes, and anything similar. When does this apply? To things that are not usually cooked together. But things that are always cooked together, like among us where fish are cooked with potatoes called "bulbes," or when one cooks a type of groats with potatoes, or two types of groats, or groats with legumes, since this is their customary way of cooking, it is only considered one dish. Or according to the earlier times, when they would put onions and eggs inside grains, and anything similar. And there are those who wrote that pancakes filled with cheese are considered two dishes (Magen Avraham, small section 4). And this is surprising, because all pancakes are filled with cheese, or with eggs and onions, as is known. Perhaps in earlier times it was not so. However, in our times, it is certainly considered only one dish. Therefore, it is permitted to eat fried kreplach, or blintzes filled with cheese, or with eggs and onions, and anything similar.

And similarly, it is forbidden to have two different types of cooked dishes in two separate pots, such as one dish that is cooked and another that is fried, where in this pot it was cooked, and in this one it was fried. Or roasted and cooked, such as wanting to eat cooked fish, and roasted or fried fish. But with fried alone, even if fried with butter and milk – it is considered one dish, because that is the usual way. Or if one cooked in two pots the same food with a variation, such as in one pot it was thick, and in the other it was thin; but when they are completely identical – they are not considered two dishes. And one can eat one dish with various types of fruits, seeds, and raw vegetables. Therefore, according to our custom of eating eggs – it is forbidden to eat another dish. And drinking tea and coffee – it seems to me that they are not considered a type of dish at all, as it is merely like drinking water, or other permissible drinks except for wine. Some are doubtful about this, and I do not know why. (See Shaarei Teshuva, that it is a common custom in the Land of Israel and Egypt to drink coffee during the concluding meal.)

All these matters pertain to the meal that concludes the fast, when one does not intend to eat another established meal after it, and it is also after midday. However, if it was before midday, or after midday and one intends to eat another established meal after it, there is no need to be cautious about all the matters that were explained, as I wrote in section 1. Our master the Rema wrote in section 9 that the custom is to eat an established meal before Mincha, and then pray Mincha, and then eat the concluding meal. It is customary to increase slightly in the first meal, so that the fast does not harm them, since they cease eating while it is still day, similar to Yom Kippur. There is some support for this from the Midrash Eicha Rabbati. However, one who is able to afflict himself, knows that the fast will not harm him, and is stringent with himself, is called "holy"; thus far his words.

But many prominent authorities protested this custom, and the Ramban, of blessed memory, cited against them the verse "and the belly of the wicked shall want" (Proverbs 13:25). This is nothing more than a mere deception. And we, Heaven forbid, do not practice this way. Rather, we eat the entire meal on the ground, and we eat bread with some kind of food that is eaten raw, and we eat eggs according to custom. As for the custom of cooking noodles with milk – we do not eat this at the concluding meal, because with the eggs, it would constitute two cooked dishes. This is the proper way to conduct oneself. And our master the Rema – he was a lover of Israel, and he endeavored to justify the custom. But it is not correct. And the source he cited is from the Midrash, in the opening of Eicha Rabbati (chapter seventeen), and this was during the Second Temple period when they had this day for joy and gladness, as it will be in the future. And they would drink and become intoxicated, and despite this, they would read the Book of Lamentations in remembrance of the destruction of the First Temple. Thus wrote the commentators, and it is correct. (And I am astonished at the Magen Avraham: in subsection 11 he alludes to this, so why did he labor over the Midrash in subsection 12?)

If Tisha B'Av falls on a Sunday, or if it falls on Shabbat and is postponed to Sunday – one may eat meat and drink wine at the concluding meal, and he can set his table as abundantly as the feast of Solomon in his time. Nevertheless, he should not conduct himself with joy as on other Shabbatot, nor should he sit at a convivial meal with friends. If a circumcision falls on that Shabbat – they should have the meal before Mincha (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 14). Additionally, he should conclude before sunset.

One who has accepted upon himself to fast on Mondays and Thursdays throughout the entire year, and it happens that the eve of the Ninth of Av falls on a Monday – but on Thursday it is not possible, as the Ninth of Av does not fall on a Friday. However, when the Ninth of Av falls on a Tuesday, the eve of the Ninth of Av is on a Monday – and it is difficult for him to fast for two consecutive days, he should consult a sage about his vow and have it annulled, or he should transfer his fast to another day and fulfill it then. And even though in such a case one should not transfer the fast, as will be explained in Siman 568, nevertheless, when there is no other option, it is necessary to do so. The Geonim wrote that he should fast until after the Mincha (afternoon) prayer, and then eat the pre-fast meal before sunset, observing all the stringencies of the pre-fast meal. And he should not eat twice because of his vow. The same law applies to a fast for a dream or a yahrzeit (anniversary of a death) for one who is accustomed to fasting. And some say that in the case of a vow, one should complete another day (see Taz, subsection 4). The most proper way is to consult a sage about his vow, and so he should do (Magen Avraham, subsection 17).

We do not recite Tachanun (supplicatory prayers) during Mincha (afternoon prayer) on the eve of Tisha B'Av, because it is called a "moed" (appointed time). Similarly, we do not recite "Tzidkatecha Tzedek" during Mincha on Shabbat that falls on the eve of Tisha B'Av. This also applies on Tisha B'Av itself. The reason is to symbolize that we are assured by the Blessed Name that these days will eventually be transformed into festivals, joy, and good days.

Even though one has eaten the pre-fast meal and does not intend to eat any more, nevertheless, if he wants to, he is permitted to return and eat, unless he explicitly accepted upon himself not to eat any more that day; for then it is like accepting a fast, and he is prohibited from eating, drinking, and bathing. Similarly, if he said: "I am fasting tomorrow" – it is also prohibited (Magen Avraham, sub-section 1), because it necessarily means that he is now accepting the fast, for otherwise, why would he need to accept it for tomorrow? After all, without accepting it, he is already commanded and obligated.

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote in Section 1: that accepting [a fast] in one's heart is not considered an acceptance; rather, one must verbalize it with one's lips. These are his words. And there are those who dissent, asserting that accepting it in one's heart is effective (Bach). Therefore, it is good to make a condition at the time of the concluding meal (Magen Avraham subsection 2) that one does not yet intend to accept the fast. Similarly, if one thinks so in his heart, or if it is his usual practice. And this is the simple custom among us, that after the concluding meal, if they wish, people eat and drink, and everyone acts according to the custom.

Tisha B'Av, its night is like its day in all matters, and one does not eat except before the day [begins]. And its twilight is forbidden like Yom Kippur. And even though it is of rabbinic origin – it is not appropriate to say that a doubt regarding a rabbinic matter is treated leniently, because they imposed many stringencies on it, in washing and other afflictions. And it is from the words of the Prophets and is treated strictly like Torah law regarding twilight. However, adding time from before the day does not need to be like Yom Kippur, and until twilight, washing, anointing, and wearing sandals are permitted. But if one accepted the fast upon themselves – it goes without saying that washing and anointing are forbidden, for it is not reasonable to say that they accepted it partially, only for eating and drinking. However, regarding wearing sandals, if they did not remove them – it is compelled that they did not accept [the fast] upon themselves (Taz, Section 1). And when Tisha B'Av falls on a weekday – it is customary to remove the shoes before "Barechu." And when it falls on Motzei Shabbat – only the prayer leader removes [their shoes] before "Barechu," and all the people remove them after "Barechu." And they should be careful not to touch the shoes with their hands, so they do not need to wash [their hands]. And why does the prayer leader remove [their shoes] before "Barechu"? So they are not confused in their prayer if they remove them after "Barechu." And the order of the lamentations will be explained in Siman 559.

Our teacher, the Rema, wrote in paragraph 2: "The custom is not to study on the eve of Tisha B'Av from midday onward, except for those things that are permitted on Tisha B'Av. Therefore, if it falls on Shabbat, we do not say Pirkei Avot. Likewise, one should not take a walk on the eve of Tisha B'Av." These are his words. Consequently, if Tisha B'Av falls on Shabbat and is postponed, one should only study those things that are permitted all day, as private practices are observed (Magen Avraham, subsection 7). There are those who disagree, arguing that since on Shabbat one eats meat and drinks wine, how can we forbid Torah study? Therefore, it is permissible to study all day on Shabbat (Taz, subsection 2). Some permit studying on every eve of Tisha B'Av after midday (as brought in the name of the Rashal), and one can rely on the lenient opinion to avoid neglecting Torah study. There is someone who wrote: one can study those things that are permitted (Magen Avraham, subsection 7). This is not a valid argument, as we see clearly that when one stops their regular study, they do not continue studying. (As the Gra wrote in subsection 9, it is an excessive stringency; see there. Therefore, one who studies on every eve of Tisha B'Av until night does not lose their reward. This seems to be my humble opinion).

On the Ninth of Av, it is prohibited to eat, drink, bathe, anoint oneself, wear leather shoes, and engage in marital relations. It is also forbidden to read from the Torah, Prophets, and Writings, or to study Mishnah, Midrash, Gemara, Halachot, and Aggadot, because it is written (Psalms 19:9): "The precepts of the Lord are right, rejoicing the heart." And the children of the school are idle on this day. 

The reason for the prohibition regarding children requires understanding: if it is because of joy, certainly they do not experience joy when they study. And in the Midrash on the verse "they journeyed from the mountain of the Lord," it says: like a child fleeing from school. Some say that the reason for the prohibition is because the teacher rejoices in the teaching (Taz, section 1). 

This is not understood at all, for how then would we cancel the study of children of the school because of the teacher's joy? We hold in mourning that if the teacher is in mourning, he must still teach the children, because of the cancellation of Torah study for the children, as stated in Yoreh De'ah, section 384. Moreover, it is known that teachers also endure much hardship in explaining to them, and therefore their reward is very great, as it is stated in Baba Batra (8b).

Furthermore, at the end of Tractate Taanit (31a), there is a disagreement between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda: Rabbi Meir permits reading and studying in a place where one is not accustomed, because in such a situation it causes distress to understand, while Rabbi Yehuda prohibits it. And the law follows Rabbi Yehuda. According to the versions of the Rif and the Rosh, they also disagree regarding children in a school setting, where Rabbi Meir permits and Rabbi Yehuda prohibits, and again, the law follows Rabbi Yehuda. We need to understand the reasoning of Rabbi Yehuda, who prohibits studying in an unfamiliar place. It is certainly a cause of distress! Some have written that his reasoning is because afterwards, one will rejoice when he understands (Taanit, small section 2). But if that is the case, what is the rationale for the disagreement regarding children, for children do not experience subsequent joy after understanding? Additionally, how does Rabbi Meir permit it? For the teacher, it would be a joy in the moment, according to the previous reasoning in section 1.

Therefore, it appears to me in my humble opinion that the matter is as follows: Certainly, there is joy in the study of Torah, and also distress in the toil of Torah, even for the greatest scholar. For there is no end to the depth of our holy Torah. Nevertheless, the primary engagement in Torah study brings joy to the Jewish soul, even though there is distress and toil at the time of the act. And Rabbi Meir holds that a new matter, as well as children and their teachers, since they have a bit of distress at the time of the act, are permitted to study. And Rabbi Yehuda holds that the distress does not outweigh the primary joy of the soul when it learns the Torah of God, although the body does not actually experience physical joy, still, the Jewish soul is happy because of this. And this is like what the Rambam, of blessed memory, explained in the second chapter of Divorce, regarding "We compel him until he says, 'I want to'": because every Jewish soul truly wants to do the will of its Creator, although the body does not want to, see there. However, in bad matters, it is permitted to study, because the soul also experiences distress from the troubles of Israel. Therefore, even though in bad matters it is Torah and joy, nevertheless, the distress nullifies the joy, and therefore it is permitted. But the distress of the study itself does not nullify the joy of the soul from the study of Torah.

And according to this, I say that the commentators on the Shulchan Aruch have written that even with negative matters, it is only permitted to read them, but not to delve deeply and analyze them (Taz at the end of subparagraph 2, and Magen Avraham subparagraph 5). In truth, this is very difficult for a learned student, because inevitably the intellect will consider questions and answers, and the like. However, according to what I have written, it is understandable, for certainly the taste and sweetness of Torah exists in all matters of Torah, even in negative matters, except that the distress nullifies the joy. Therefore, even if one derives some new insight, nevertheless the distress of the troubles is not nullified. (And what is noted in the Magen Avraham there, that the Mahari"l wrote so, quite the contrary, the Beit Yosef brought in his name that through delving it is preferable, as one is distressed in his study, see there. Only in the name of the Re"f it is written that in the commentary on Job one should not delve, as it is deeper, and analysis is forbidden, see there. And from this there is no proof, for Job is a deep investigation. And also, none of the poskim mentioned this, and even in the Shulchan Aruch it is ruled the opposite.)

And what are the bad things? The Book of Job, and the bad things in Jeremiah that pertain to Israel; but the words of comfort within them – one skips. Similarly, the bad things concerning Ammon and Moab and other nations – one skips. It seems to me that the bad things in the other prophets – it is permissible to read. And what the Talmud lists only Jeremiah – because in Jeremiah there are many bad things. Similarly, the Book of Lamentations, the Midrash of Lamentations, and the chapter “These may shave,” most of which is about the laws of mourning. And even though there are also laws of distancing and rebuke there – but they too are like mourning. And it is permissible to study the commentaries on Lamentations and Job. There are also those who prohibit studying through contemplation, because even though we hold that contemplation is not like speech – nevertheless, there is joy in it. And one should not question why we conclude after the lamentations with verses of comfort: “Have mercy on Zion…,” “I will return to Jerusalem…,” “My house will be rebuilt…,” “Your cities will yet spread forth goodness…” – indeed, this is like a mere prayer, and not for the purpose of study, and it is like when we pray “May our eyes behold…” and similar things. One should not issue a ruling – only that which is necessary for the time. And it is obvious that one should not adjudicate Torah law on this bitter day. Nevertheless, if the litigants are in urgent need for their way – one can judge for them after midday, and all the more so if it concerns a matter of a mitzvah. And everything is according to the discretion of the teacher.

In the prayer, there is no change, for the Torah is forbidden but not the prayer, except for the blessing "Who has provided me with all my needs," which some say should not be recited on Tisha B'Av and Yom Kippur because people walk barefoot. But the entire order of the prayer should be prayed as on any other day. Even the passage of the Akedah, the passages of the sacrifices, the Mishnah "Eizehu Mekoman," the Baraita of Rabbi Yishmael, and also the Song of the Sea—although they are words of Torah, nevertheless, since they are part of the prayer order, it is not considered as Torah study. However, the recitation of Psalms after the prayer and the Song of Unity, in places where it is customary to say them every day—should not be said. And some say this applies to Mincha, since they are in the form of a request (Magen Avraham, section 6). And our teacher, the Rema, wrote in Siman 554, section 4, that it is permissible to repeat the weekly Torah portion on Tisha B'Av; thus far his words. And if his intention is regarding the weekly Torah portion—it is a wonder, except when it falls on Shabbat, as it would be the order of the day. (And so wrote the Magen Avraham, section 7, and the Eliyah Rabbah, unlike the Taz, section 3.)

Pregnant and nursing women must fast and complete the fast on Tisha B'Av, just as they fast and complete the fast on Yom Kippur. However, for the other three fasts, they are exempt from fasting, and certainly for the Fast of Esther, they should not be stringent on themselves. Nevertheless, it is proper that they do not eat for pleasure, but only to sustain the fetus; this applies to anyone who is unable to fast. Even on Tisha B'Av, if they are weak to the point that they are likely to become ill, even if it is not dangerous, they should not fast. This is the difference between Tisha B'Av and Yom Kippur: on Yom Kippur, one should only eat in a case of danger, but on Tisha B'Av, even if it is not dangerous, the Sages did not decree fasting in cases of illness. Therefore, the Tur writes in the name of the Ramban, and similarly, Rabbeinu the Beit Yosef in section 554, paragraph 6, that a woman within thirty days of childbirth, as well as a sick person who needs to eat, does not need an assessment, but should be fed immediately, for in cases of illness, the Sages did not decree fasting; thus far his words. Even an illness that does not confine one to bed—such a person must fast on Yom Kippur if they are bedridden, as anyone bedridden is in danger, as proven in Shabbat (32a), see there, and it will be explained in section 618 with the help of Heaven. But those with mere discomfort must fast. The general rule is: anyone considered ill does not fast on Tisha B'Av, and anyone not considered ill must fast. Ordinarily, pregnant and nursing women fast unless they are weak and close to illness. Children do not fast at all on Tisha B'Av, not even for a few hours. Someone who was mentally ill and has recovered, and is improving day by day, should not fast on Tisha B'Av and should not abstain from meat and wine (Magen Avraham, subsection 8, in the name of Maharil) until they are fully recovered, for the fast might cause a relapse into their mental illness, as might abstaining from meat and wine, and any other forms of affliction, such as washing, anointing, and wearing shoes, since they need much care. (Less than the prescribed amount does not apply on Tisha B'Av, as it is rabbinic.)

And our master, the Rema, wrote in Siman 554:6 regarding a woman who has given birth and a sick person, and these are his words: "However, they are accustomed to fast as long as they do not experience great discomfort that might pose a danger, and one who is lenient does not lose out." Until here are his words. This means that they are stringent with themselves as on Yom Kippur, that as long as there is no danger, they fast. And there are those who rule this way, that after seven days, a woman who has given birth fasts, unless she says she needs [to eat]. And there are those who disagree with this (see Taz, subsection 4; Magen Avraham, subsection 9; Eliyah Rabbah, subsection 8; and Shaarei Teshuvah, subsection 7). And perhaps this was in their days, when the generations were healthy and strong. But now – Heaven forbid for a woman who has given birth to fast on Tisha B'Av within thirty days, because she is still weak, and she is indeed like a sick person. Therefore, she should not be allowed to fast on Tisha B'Av.

Washing is forbidden on Tisha B'Av, whether with hot or cold water. Even to put one's finger in water is prohibited. Immersing in a mikveh for a mitzvah for a woman is not applicable on Tisha B'Av because marital relations are forbidden. However, in ancient times, when they observed immersion at its appointed time and it was considered a mitzvah, they would immerse. But now there is no immersion at its appointed time due to the uncertainty of zavah status, and therefore, women are forbidden to immerse on Tisha B'Av. A woman who needs to immerse on the night after Tisha B'Av should wash and comb on the eve of Tisha B'Av, and at night, after Tisha B'Av, she should comb a little so that the immersion is close to the combing, and then she should immerse, as I have written in Yoreh De'ah, section 199. They also wash a little on the night after Tisha B'Av, and this is the custom.

And for prayer, it is permissible to wash one's hands, as it is considered like an immersion for a mitzvah. Similarly, anyone who enters a bathroom or urinates must wash their hands for cleanliness, as they are required to recite the blessing "Asher Yatzar." However, one should not wash the entire hand, but only as much as needed to remove the dirt. Even if it is not for the purpose of prayer or a blessing, but merely because one's hands are dirty with mud or excrement, and one washes to remove them – it is permitted. The general principle is: any washing that is not for pleasure is permitted on Tisha B'Av. Therefore, women who are cooking on Tisha B'Av and need to wash some food with their hands – they may wash and need not be concerned, since it is not for pleasure (Eliyahu Rabbah, subsection 10).

A person should wash their hands in the morning when they rise from their bed, because generally hands are considered unclean. However, one should not wash the entire hand, only up to the knuckles of the fingers. After washing the hands, while they are still slightly moist before drying, it is permissible to pass them over the eyes. Washing the face is prohibited, but it is allowed to use slightly moist hands to touch the eyes. However, if there is eye discharge, and it is customary to wash it off with water, one may wash until the discharge is removed, as this is similar to removing dirt or excrement, which is washed off in the usual manner. There is no concern, since this is not for pleasure but to clean the eyes from the discharge.

One who goes to visit his teacher, or his father, or someone greater than himself; or who goes for the needs of a mitzvah – he may pass through water up to his neck if the path requires it, and he need not be concerned since it is not for enjoyment. Even when returning from his journey – it is permitted, for if you do not permit him on his return, he will not go and will refrain from the mitzvah. Similarly, one who goes to guard his fruits so that they are not stolen, or is compelled to sell them, and similar cases, or one who goes for his business – he may pass through water up to his neck, and he need not be concerned since it is not for enjoyment. However, on his return – it is forbidden, because in this case, it cannot be said that if you do not permit him to return, he will not go, for he will certainly go due to the potential loss of his property. And even if he does not go – what does it matter to us? Similarly, one who comes from a journey and his feet are sore – it is permitted to wash them in water, since it is solely to remove discomfort and not for enjoyment. Anything that is not for enjoyment – is permitted, as I have written.

It states in Yoma (78a) about one of the sages, that he had a cloth which he soaked in water on the eve of Tisha B'Av, and the next day he would pass it over his eyes and wipe his face, hands, and feet with it. See there. A similar account is given there regarding Yom Kippur. And Rambam, of blessed memory, brings this practice for Yom Kippur in the third chapter (halacha 5) of Hilchot Shevitat Asor (3:5). However, regarding Tisha B'Av, he does not bring this. But the Tur in Siman 613 in the laws of Yom Kippur does bring this, and he also brings it here. It seems that the Rambam's opinion is because this practice settles a person's mind, and therefore on Yom Kippur, which is a holy day and requires a calm mind, it is proper to do so. But on Tisha B'Av, the more one's mind is agitated, the better, since it is a day of distress. And in the Gemara, the one who did this even on Tisha B'Av was because he was very delicate and could not live without it, not referring to ordinary people. And it also implies from the language of the Tur there that this is to settle the mind. See there. And the Tur holds that even now there are delicate individuals who need this, and so our master the Rema brings in Siman 554, section 14. According to them, one takes it out of the water at night so that during the day it is as if dry, with just a bit of dampness. And they wrote that in this manner, even for pleasure, it is permitted. See there. This is astonishing, how can it be allowed for pleasure on Tisha B'Av? It must be said that it is not actual pleasure but rather to remove boredom. This requires further study.

Anointing is forbidden on Tisha B'Av, whether it be the anointing of the head or the body. All of this refers to anointing for pleasure. However, someone who has sores on their head or leprosy on their body and needs to anoint may do so in their usual manner and need not worry, since the intention is not for pleasure. Similarly, combing one's head with a comb is permitted, as this is also not for pleasure but to avoid the need to scratch the head, as is known. However, it is forbidden to wash the hair even with a small amount of water; rather, it should be combed dry if necessary and indispensable.

Wearing sandals – it is specifically forbidden to wear leather ones. However, those made of cloth, wood, cork (which is the bark of a tree), or reed are permitted. Wooden, reed, or cork sandals covered with leather are forbidden. Similarly, leggings that are partially covered with leather are forbidden. Now, in our region, people wear kalasin, which are made of a type of material that looks like leather but is not leather; it is made from some kind of adhesive. They call this rosin, and it appears to be a type of adhesive. I was concerned that it might often be made from boiled leather, and perhaps it should be considered as leather. However, since it has been boiled, it loses its original status, similar to bread that, once boiled, loses its status as bread. The same applies here. Even though boiling leather usually hardens it, as implied in Shabbat (79a), this applies only to boiling alone. But adhesive is boiled and melts, and thus certainly loses its original status. Indeed, even parchment, which is entirely leather but has been processed and scraped, changes its legal status from that of leather, and all the more so in this case. Nevertheless, shoes made of parchment are certainly forbidden because they are considered actual leather.

And similarly, a mourner and someone who is distant are prohibited from wearing sandals, just as on Tisha B'Av. However, if they are traveling on the road, they may wear sandals because it is difficult to walk on the road without sandals. When they arrive in the city, they should remove them. But for a field near the city or to the cemetery, wearing shoes is prohibited. In a place where Jews live among non-Jews in the city, they should only remove their shoes in the Jewish quarter. This was the custom in ancient times when the Jewish quarter was designated. Now that people live intermixed, if there are many Jews as in large cities, one may be lenient, and nowadays people are often lenient for this reason. However, this leniency applies only to large cities and not to small towns. It is clear that if it rains on Tisha B'Av, one is permitted to wear sandals. Even though on Yom Kippur the permission is granted only to someone who is very sensitive, as will be explained in section 614, in any case, on Tisha B'Av, which is of Rabbinic origin, it is permitted for everyone.

There are those who say that one should not sleep with his wife in the same bed on the night of Tisha B'Av. This is proper, as it is said, "Go, go, we say to the Nazirite." It is proper not to touch her at night, but during the day there is no need for concern. And at night, there is also no need for concern, except for the very young. And it has never been customary to be strict about this, as Israel is not suspected of such things, God forbid. And if Tisha B'Av falls on Shabbat and is postponed, just as eating and drinking are permitted, so too is marital relations. However, there are those who prohibit marital relations, and this is the custom. The sexton announces after the evening prayer: "Private matters are observed." And if it is the night of immersion, one is obligated to engage in marital relations, as this is the primary law (see Magen Avraham, subsection 20, and Eliyah Rabbah, subsection 19). It seems that this is the custom, as this is the opinion of most authorities. "Tzidkatcha Tzedek" is not recited in the Mincha prayer on Shabbat when Tisha B'Av falls on it, or when Tisha B'Av is on Sunday. Regarding "Av HaRachamim," some say it, and some do not, and one should follow their custom.

Greeting others with "Shalom" is prohibited on Tisha B'Av, as it is not a day of peace, similar to mourning, as stated in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 385. There, some say that our form of greeting is not considered a formal greeting. However, from the Jerusalem Talmud cited by the Tur there, it is clearly implied that saying "Shalom Aleichem" is considered a greeting, and therefore, one should not be lenient (Magen Avraham, Section 21). For the unlearned who do not know the law and offer a greeting, one should respond softly and with a serious demeanor. However, to not respond at all is inappropriate, so as not to embarrass them.

Additionally, one should not go out and stroll on Tisha B'Av in the market or street, as strolling itself is prohibited on Tisha B'Av. Besides this, it is easy to come to laughter, frivolity, jesting, and mocking. Instead, on Tisha B'Av, if one does not need to go out, he should sit in a corner of his house in sadness. If he must go out, he should walk with a bowed head, hurry to do what he needs to do, and quickly return home. Also, one should prevent groups from going to the cemetery, as they go in groups, and this is not appropriate, and the pious refrain from this. Similarly, on Tisha B'Av, one should not say "Good morning" in any language, including "Guten Morgen."

It was taught in Pesachim (54b): In a place where the custom is to work on Tisha B'Av, one may work; and in a place where the custom is not to work, one may not work. The reason is so that people do not divert their minds from mourning (Ra’avad). According to this, it is also forbidden at night (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 23). This is also evident from Rashi in Pesachim there, see there. However, in Taanit (13b), Rashi does not explain it this way, see there. And work that does not involve prolonged engagement is permitted (ibid.). In any case, Torah scholars refrain from work, for Torah scholars do not work even in a place where the custom is to work. Anyone who wants to make himself like a Torah scholar in this matter may do so, and we do not say it appears arrogant, because onlookers will say he has no work to do.

And even in a place where the custom is not to do [work] - it is permitted to do [work] through a non-Jew, but not in something conspicuous like construction, and the like (Shaarei Teshuva in the name of Knesset HaGedolah). And trading to make a profit and to gain – is considered like labor, and in a place where the custom is not to do [work] – one does not engage [in it]. Also in merchandise and in keeping shops. And in a place where the custom is to do [work] – it is permitted, but one should reduce business dealings, for even from when the month of Av enters – one reduces business dealings, as I wrote in Siman 551. And even according to what I wrote there that it only applies to joyous business dealings, nevertheless on the Ninth of Av certainly one reduces all business dealings.

In our region, the custom is not to perform work until midday. In truth, the current practice is only until after the recitation of the lamentations, and it would be appropriate to extend it until midday, but it is not possible due to the pressure of making a livelihood. However, since this has become the custom, there is no prohibition because Tisha B'Av depends on custom according to the Mishnah's ruling. Nonetheless, the pious are careful not to work before midday, and also not to open their shops before midday. All this applies to significant work that takes some time, even if it is simple labor. But for work that does not take time, such as lighting candles, tying, and similar activities, there is no issue, even before midday.

Similarly, beds are not made before midday, and the house is not swept on Tisha B'Av. As for milking cows, it is preferable to have it done by a non-Jew, but if that is not possible, one may do it oneself, as this is considered a loss, and work to prevent loss is permitted, as stated regarding Chol HaMoed. The same applies to mourning, where preventing loss is permitted.

For this reason, when market day falls on Tisha B'Av, we allow bakers to bake bread in the morning so that it will be ready for market day, as this too is considered preventing a loss. Similarly, when fairs or caravans arrive, it is permitted to buy from them, even in places where work is not done, and certainly to sell to them. However, whatever can be done discreetly is better (see Magen Avraham, subsection 26).

Our Sages said at the end of Ta'anit (30b): Anyone who does work on Tisha B'Av will never see a sign of blessing. It implies even in a place where it is customary to work. Therefore, everyone should refrain from business on Tisha B'Av as much as they can. They also said there that anyone who does work on Tisha B'Av and does not mourn for Jerusalem, as it is stated (Isaiah 66:10): "Rejoice with Jerusalem and be glad with her, all you who love her; rejoice with her in joy, all you who mourn over her." Therefore, anyone who does not mourn for Jerusalem will not merit and see her joy. And anyone who eats and drinks on Tisha B'Av, it is said about him (Ezekiel 32:27): "Their iniquities will be upon their bones," because it is evident in the bones of the deceased whether they drank wine or water, as stated in Niddah (24a). Likewise, anyone who eats meat and drinks wine during the seudah hamafseket (the final meal before the fast), and for us, from Rosh Chodesh Av onwards. And anyone who mourns for Jerusalem will merit and see and rejoice in the rebuilding of Jerusalem and the Temple, speedily in our days, Amen. One should not write Torah novelties on Tisha B'Av.

Even though in several aspects the laws of Tisha B'Av are like those of mourning, nevertheless, the Sages did not require on Tisha B'Av the practices of overturning the bed and wrapping the head like a mourner. Specifically, regarding the prohibitive commandments of mourning, one is obligated on Tisha B'Av, such as: the study of Torah, washing and anointing, wearing shoes, and marital relations. But the positive commandments of mourning, like overturning the bed and wrapping the head (Tur), do not apply. The matter of not wearing tefillin is not mentioned in the Gemara. The Rosh at the end of Ta'anit was perplexed by this: Isn't it true that even a mourner is only prohibited from wearing tefillin on the first day? Some of the great authorities would put on tefillin in the morning in their homes, recite the Shema, then remove them, and go to the synagogue (Ba'er Heitev in the name of Rabbi Moshe Galanti). And it is said that the Arizal did so as well.

However, all of Israel customarily do not wear tefillin and tzitzit in the morning during prayer. The reason seems clear, as the reason a mourner is exempt from tefillin on the first day is because it is written (Amos 8:10): "And its end will be like a bitter day," and the main bitterness of mourning is on the first day. Therefore, one should not wear tefillin, which are called "glory"; and all the more so on Tisha B'Av, the day of bitterness and mourning for all of Israel, we should not wear the glory of tefillin. Similarly, for tzitzit, as it is written (Lamentations 2:17): "He has cut down in fierce anger." And it is stated in the Midrash (Leviticus Rabbah, Chapter 6) and in the Targum: "He cut down His purple garment" (Tur). Rather, one should wear a small tallit under his clothes without a blessing. In the afternoon, we wear tzitzit and tefillin and recite the blessings on them, and this is the custom of all Israel. As for Rabbeinu Tam's tefillin – they should not be worn on Tisha B'Av, even in the afternoon. Some do wear them (see Sha'arei Teshuvah). And why do we wear them in the afternoon? Because in the afternoon we receive consolation, as we say "Nachem" (comfort).

And although we do not practice the custom of overturning the bed, nevertheless, our custom is to sit on the ground or close to the ground, and not on a bench, until midday. There are those who lie down on the night of Tisha B'Av inclined on the ground and place a stone under their head, although not everyone is able to do so. However, in any case, one should cause oneself some discomfort in their sleeping arrangements on the night of Tisha B'Av. If one is accustomed to sleeping with two pillows, they should sleep with one pillow. Some place a stone under their heads as a remembrance of what is stated (Genesis 28:11): "And he took from the stones of the place," as it is taught in the Midrash that he saw the destruction. However, those who are weak and pregnant women, who are unable to endure discomfort, should not do any of these things. Nonetheless, in general, a person should diminish their honor and enjoyment on Tisha B'Av as much as possible.

When Tisha B'Av falls on a Sunday, how should Havdalah be performed? It is impossible to perform Havdalah before sunset and drink the cup, because once one performs Havdalah, one has accepted Tisha B'Av upon oneself and it is forbidden to drink (Tur).
