Therefore, on Saturday night, when seeing the fire, one recites the blessing "Borei Me'orei HaEsh" (Creator of the lights of fire). On the spices, one does not recite a blessing, because although it is permitted to smell spices on Tisha B'Av, since the spices on Saturday night are intended to restore the soul, it is not appropriate to do so on Tisha B'Av.

On the night after Tisha B'Av, one recites Havdalah over a cup [of wine or another beverage]. However, one does not recite Havdalah over a candle or spices. Regarding the candle, one has already recited the blessing, and spices are only relevant on the night after Shabbat. One should not recite Havdalah over wine, but rather over another beverage, as wine is prohibited on the night after Tisha B'Av, even when Tisha B'Av is postponed to Sunday, as I will write in Siman 559. And know that even for those who hold in Siman 299 that there are no make-up Havdalah blessings except on the first day, in the case of Tisha B'Av, they agree that one may recite Havdalah at the beginning of the second day, since it was not possible to do so before. One who fasts for two days should hear Havdalah from others (Magen Avraham). And one can recite "Borei Me'orei Ha'esh" throughout the night after Shabbat, but no later.

In the Jerusalem Talmud, in the fourth chapter of Berachot (Halacha 3), it states: On the Ninth of Av, one must mention an aspect related to the event. What is it? "Console, O Lord our God, the mourners of Zion," etc. And where should it be said? In the blessing of "Avodah" (Service), as is the case with anything pertaining to the future that we say in "Avodah," like "Ya'aleh Veyavo." However, in this matter, we conduct ourselves not according to the Jerusalem Talmud, but rather we mention it in the blessing of "Boneh Yerushalayim" (Builder of Jerusalem), where before the conclusion we say "Console..." and conclude the blessing with "He who consoles Zion and builds Jerusalem." And the Rif wrote at the end of Taanit that we rely on what is said in the chapter "Before Their Festivals" (8a): that even though it was said that one may ask for their needs in "Shomea Tefillah," if one wishes to say at the end of each blessing something related to that blessing – they may. See there. And here it is related to the blessing, of course.

And in any case, a reason is needed: How did it happen that it was not done according to the Jerusalem Talmud, in that there is no disagreement about it? It seems to me that the matter is as follows: In the Tosefta Berakhot at the end of chapter three, it states that "the sprout of David" is included in "the builder of Jerusalem," and so it is in the Jerusalem Talmud, chapter four there. According to this, these two blessings were one blessing. Therefore, it was not possible for the Jerusalem Talmud to establish the blessing of the consolation of Zion before the blessing of Jerusalem, since the kingship of the house of David is mentioned in it, and in "Consolation" there is no hint of this. Therefore, they established it in the blessing of "He who returns His Presence to Zion." But afterwards, when they established the blessing of "the sprout of David" as a separate blessing, and the blessing of Jerusalem was primarily about Jerusalem, why should it be delayed until afterwards? It is better to precede it. And even though now it is also mentioned in the blessing of "the builder of Jerusalem": "and the throne of David," nevertheless, the main part of the blessing is about Jerusalem, which was not the case when the two blessings were together – its main part was about the kingship of the house of David.

And behold, we only say "Nachem" during Mincha. And the Rosh there is astonished by this: why not say it also at Maariv and Shacharit? However, the reason is that it is not possible to say words of consolation throughout the entire day, as it would be as if the deceased is lying before us. But at Mincha, we can accept consolation (Bach). Additionally, in the evening, they set fire to the Temple, therefore at that time we recall its degradation and plead for its rebuilding (Beit Yosef in the name of Rav Saadia Gaon, see there). One who eats on Tisha B'Av should say "Nachem" in Birkat Hamazon before "Uvene Yerushalayim". If he did not say it, he is not required to repeat it. In the prayer, if he forgot to say it at "Boneh Yerushalayim", he should say it in "Avodah". (And what is written in Beit Yosef and Magen Avraham to say it at "Ve'al Kulam" is a mistake and contrary to the Jerusalem Talmud.) And if he forgot also there, it seems to me that he is not required to repeat it, and he should say it at the end of the prayer without a concluding blessing. Also, "Aneinu" must be said in Mincha in "Shomea Tefillah", and the prayer leader says it in Shacharit and Mincha between "Goel" and "Rofeh", as in any public fast. (And Magen Avraham wrote that one who fasts on the tenth should say it in all the prayers, see there.) (And I have seen someone who wants to say that the prayer leader should not say "Aneinu" in Shacharit, and this is a surprising thing.)

The Tur wrote: It was taught: On the seventh of Av, the idolaters entered the Sanctuary, and they ate, drank, and desecrated it on the seventh, eighth, and ninth days. Towards evening, they set it on fire, and it burned until sunset on the tenth day. And this is what Rabbi Yochanan said: If I had been there, I would have established it on the tenth, for most of the Sanctuary was burned on that day (Taanit 29a). And it is mentioned in the Jerusalem Talmud (Chapter 4, Halacha 6): Rabbi Avin fasted on the ninth and tenth; Rabbi Levi fasted on the ninth and the night of the tenth because he did not have the strength to fast the entire tenth day. And in our time – our strength has diminished, and even on Yom Kippur, which should ideally be observed for two days out of doubt – we cannot manage.

Therefore, it is appropriate and proper not to eat meat on the night of the tenth and on the day of the tenth, and also not to drink wine. Some are stringent until midday, but not beyond that, and this is our custom. If Tisha B'Av falls on Shabbat and is postponed to Sunday, it is permitted to eat meat and drink wine on Monday, but on the night following the fast, it is forbidden due to the mourning of the day. For a mitzvah meal, even if it falls on a weekday, and even on the night following the fast, all those invited are permitted to eat meat and drink wine, for this night is completely lenient (Magen Avraham). However, a meal before a wedding should not be held then, as it is not considered a mitzvah meal (ibid.). Certainly, there should be no musical instruments played there (ibid.). Additionally, one should not bathe, get a haircut, or do laundry on the tenth day until after midday. If Tisha B'Av falls on Thursday, the following day, which is Friday, everything is permitted in honor of Shabbat (ibid.). However, eating meat before midday is obviously forbidden, contrary to what some mistakenly think (see Magen Avraham, subsection 3).

If Tisha B'Av falls on Shabbat or Sunday, we do not say "Tzidkatecha" during Mincha on Shabbat, nor do we recite Pirkei Avot. It appears that if it falls on Sunday, we do recite Pirkei Avot. Additionally, we do not say "Tziduk HaDin" on Tisha B'Av. However, some say that "Tziduk HaDin" should be recited, as it is no worse than other lamentations (Taz, Siman Katan 1 in the name of Rashal). It is permitted to deliver a eulogy for a scholar who has passed away, as the entire day is considered a day of weeping (ibid., Siman Katan 6). We say "Atah Chonantanu" in the Maariv prayer, just as on any other Motzei Shabbat. The reason we do not make Havdalah over a cup is because it is forbidden to drink it. If one forgets to say "Atah Chonantanu," this has been explained earlier in Siman 294; see there.

And one should pray the Maariv (evening) prayer with calmness and in the manner of weeping, like mourners. Similarly, this is done during the reading of Eicha (Lamentations). Throughout Eicha, one raises one's voice more, pausing slightly between each verse, and at the end of each section of "Eicha," pausing a bit more. The last verse of each section of "Eicha" is said in a loud voice. When the reader reaches the end of the verse "Hashiveinu," the congregation says it aloud, then the reader concludes, and the congregation repeats it aloud, as does the reader. Some have written that one should bless before reading Eicha with "al mikra megillah" (Magen Avraham, subsection 1), but this is not our custom. An individual should also recite Eicha during the day. In our practice, the reader reads all of Eicha during the day, after the Kinot (dirges) and the prayer.

On the night of Tisha B'Av, we pray the evening service and recite Eicha (Lamentations) and Kinot (dirges). After the Amidah (the Eighteen Benedictions), the prayer leader says Kaddish with "Tiskabel" (the prayer for the acceptance of prayers). However, after the Kinot, "Tiskabel" is not said. Similarly, the next morning at Shacharit (the morning service), "Tiskabel" is not said; this is written in the Minhagim (customs) (Taz and Magen Avraham, subsection 1). I am puzzled by this: if so, we say "Tiskabel" in the evening like on other days, and what relevance is there to say that "Tiskabel" is not said after the Kinot? Where do we find that "Tiskabel" is said twice in a single prayer service? In my humble opinion, it would seem appropriate not to say "Tiskabel" after the Amidah in the evening service, and this would be the distinction from other days. And our master, the Beit Yosef, in his major work, indeed brought that there are places that do so; see there. And what the Tur wrote that a full Kaddish is recited – it can be said that his intention was not on "Tiskabel," but rather that a half-Kaddish is not said. And see what I wrote in Siman 493. (And the children are not blessed when Tisha B'Av falls on Motzei Shabbat.)

After the reading of Eicha and the lamentations, we recite the order of Kedusha, beginning with "Ve'ata Kadosh". Even if Tisha B'Av falls on a Saturday night, we do not say "Vihi Noam" because there is no pleasantness on this day. Additionally, "Vihi Noam" was established concerning the building of the Temple, and now it has been destroyed due to our sins. Similarly, we do not say "Veyiten Lecha" or "Lamnatzeach Binginot". The curtain is removed from before the Ark, based on the verse "He has torn apart His tabernacle" (Eicha 2:17), which we translate as "He has torn His curtain". On the night and day of Tisha B'Av, we sit on the ground in the synagogue until the Mincha prayer. Our custom is to sit until midday and until after the lamentations, which should be prolonged until midday. It does not have to be directly on the ground; one can place something beneath or sit on a low bench close to the ground. We do not light many candles at night, only one candle for the chazzan so he can read by its light. If this is insufficient for the congregation, they may light candles in scattered places, enough to see, but no more (see Taz, section 5). In places where the congregation does not recite, but only listens to the chazzan, they should not light any candles before them, only an additional candle in case the chazzan's candle goes out, so it can be relit from this candle (Magen Avraham, section 4, in the name of Maharil). In the morning prayer, we also skip the verse "And as for Me, this is My covenant" in "Uva Letzion".

We do not recite Tachanun or Selichot on Tisha B'Av, because it is written: "He proclaimed a set time against me" (Lamentations 1:15). And we do not fall on our faces. We have explained the reason for this in Siman 552; see there. We say "Mizmor LeTodah," but we do not say "Mizmor... Ya'ancha" or "El Erech Apayim" when it falls on a Thursday. We rise early to go to the synagogue, and people come on their own accord without being called. We read from the Torah portion "When you beget children" and the Haftarah from Jeremiah "Gather them up," and we read with the tune of Lamentations, except for the last verses. It is stated in Massechet Sofrim that each person called to the Torah should bless "the true Judge" before ascending, but this is not customary. However, one who wishes to say it should do so without mentioning God's name and kingship. We do not recite "Pitum HaKetoret" after the prayer, for those who customarily do so daily. Some have written that even what is said before the prayer, as well as all the sections of the offerings, should not be recited (Magen Avraham, small section 7). This is surprising, as it is explicitly written in the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, Siman 554, the opposite; see there. It is not necessary to change one's place on Tisha B'Av. After the Maftir is completed, the Torah scroll is returned to the ark, and we sit on the ground and recite kinot (lamentations).

There are different customs mentioned in Masechet Sofrim, and the Tur brought them, and this is his language: Some read the Book of Lamentations in the evening, and some delay until the morning after the reading of the Torah. After the reading of the Torah, one stands and rolls in the ashes, and his clothes are disheveled, and he reads with weeping and wailing. If he knows how to translate it, it is good, and if not, he gives it to someone who knows how to translate it so that all the people, women, and children will understand. For women are obligated like men, and all the more so male children. And the one who reads on Tisha B'Av says "Blessed is the True Judge." And some place the Torah case on the ground and say "The crown of our head has fallen." And they tear their clothes and lament, like a person whose deceased lies before him. And some change their places, and some descend from their benches—and all roll in the ashes. And they do not say "Shalom" to one another, etc.; thus far his language. And it is in Masechet Sofrim, chapter eighteen.

One recites lamentations with weeping and eulogy. During the recitation of the lamentations, one should not speak or go outside, so as not to distract from the mourning. All the more so, one should not converse with a non-Jew. The custom is to recite some verses of consolation after the lamentations, to conclude with positive matters. If there is a mourner in the city, he should go to the synagogue at night and also during the day until the lamentations are completed, even within the first three days. Some say this applies specifically after three days, but this is not correct (see Magen Avraham, subsection 8). It is customary to go to the cemetery immediately upon leaving the synagogue, for even the dead are distressed by the suffering of the living. Therefore, one should only go to Jewish graves. The Arizal was not pleased with the practice of going to the cemetery (see Magen Avraham, subsection 15), except for accompanying the deceased. We have already written that nowadays, when people go in groups and engage in idle chatter, it is better not to go.

If there is a baby to be circumcised, the circumcision is performed after the conclusion of the Kinot (lamentations). There are those who do not perform the circumcision until after midday, but this is not the custom. In places where they bless over the spices during the circumcision, they do not bless now. The sandak (person holding the baby during the circumcision), the mohel (person performing the circumcision), and the father of the child wear their tallit (prayer shawl) at the time of the circumcision, but they do not wear Shabbat clothes. The mohel blesses over the cup, and the mother of the child drinks from the cup if the circumcision is at her home. If not, it is given to the children to drink. When the mother drinks, she must hear the blessing and not interrupt between the blessing and the drinking. Although we wrote that they do not wear Shabbat clothes, the participants in the covenant wear other clothes, but not completely white clothes. The father of the child, the mohel, and the sandak are all called "participants in the covenant" and are permitted to wear other clothes after the conclusion of the Kinot and when they come to perform the circumcision, but not completely white clothes. (What is written in the Rema, section 8: Shabbat clothes. It seems to me that it is not specific, for if so, how can it say "not completely white"? This is also proven in the Mordechai at the end of Ta'anit; see there.)

According to the law of the Gemara (end of the third chapter of Eruvin): When Tisha B'Av falls on Shabbat and it is postponed to Sunday, and a circumcision occurs on that day – those involved in the circumcision pray Mincha while it is still broad daylight, either the early Mincha or the late Mincha (see Magen Avraham, subsection 13). They wash their faces, hands, and feet, and make a feast with meat and wine, and eat, because it is their personal holiday. Nevertheless, we have not seen or heard of anyone who does this. Particularly in our region, where most feasts are held at night. And not only on Tisha B'Av, but even on any fast day, and even a postponed fast – no feast is made, whether for a circumcision or for the redemption of the firstborn, until the night. And this is the common custom, and it should not be changed. And know that no slaughtering or preparation of the feast is done until after midday, unless it is necessary for the meal of a mitzvah, which cannot be adequately prepared after midday, in which case one may prepare even before midday. However, this is not common. Also, beds are not made, nor is the house swept, until after midday. It is appropriate not to sweep the house at all throughout the day.

At the end of the third chapter of Bava Batra (60b), we learned three Baraitot. The first: We do not plaster, we do not paint, and we do not decorate with designs at this time. If someone bought a courtyard that was plastered, painted, and decorated – it remains in its status. If it fell – he does not rebuild it. And this is its explanation: We do not make a house with white plaster because of the mourning for Jerusalem. And we do not paint designs that are engraved in plaster. Some explain that this is plastering, but it is whiter (Rashbam, s.v. “and we do not paint”). And we do not decorate with designs of various colors (ibid.). If someone bought a courtyard that was plastered, etc. – it remains in its status that it was done before the destruction. Therefore, we have no practical difference in this matter. It also teaches: A person should not plaster his house with plaster. If he mixed it with straw or sand – it is permitted.

It was further taught: After the Temple was destroyed, many ascetics arose in Israel who decided not to eat meat and not to drink wine. Rabbi Yehoshua joined them and said: "My children, let me tell you something. It is impossible not to mourn at all... and it is impossible to mourn excessively... Rather, the Sages have said: A person should plaster his house with lime but leave a small part unfinished. And how much should be left? An area of one cubit by one cubit, opposite the entrance."

And behold, to reconcile all the Baraitot so that they do not contradict one another, it seems clear that the matter is as follows: The first Baraita prohibits plastering with lime, and the second Baraita permits it when mixed with sand or straw. The first Baraita also agrees with this, but it is speaking without mixing sand or straw. In such a case, when mixed with sand or straw, there is no need for any reservation at all. And the third Baraita, which requires a reservation of one cubit by one cubit, is speaking without mixing sand or straw. And so wrote the Ran at the end of Taanit, and this is his language: "We learn… one who plasters his house with lime and leaves a small part. It implies that if he mixed it with sand or straw, there is no need to leave any part; thus far his language." And similarly, the Nimukei Yosef wrote in Bava Batra there, and this is his language: "If he mixed it with sand, it is permitted because it darkens it somewhat, and in such a case there is no need for a reservation of a cubit. For in the case of a reservation of a cubit, even with pure lime, it is permitted; thus far his language."

Based on this, we should find merit for the majority of Israel, who are not careful now with this law of leaving an area of one cubit by one cubit unplastered when plastering the walls of the house. This is because it is known that now they mix a lot of sand into the plaster, almost half and half. Therefore, according to the strict law, no area needs to be left unplastered at all. And although the Rif and the Rosh, as well as the Rambam, the Tur, and the Shulchan Aruch, only brought the last Baraita and did not bother to elaborate, it can still be said that in their view, when sand is mixed in, no area needs to be left. A clear proof of this is that the Ran and the Nimukei Yosef, who are commentators on the Rif, did not mention this matter. If it were not the Rif's opinion, how could they not have mentioned it? Rather, certainly, it is as we say. (And also in the Beit Yosef, a similar idea is mentioned, although the Bach disagrees with him; see there. And I am puzzled as to why this is not mentioned at all in the Shulchan Aruch, further study is needed.)

And this is the language of our teacher, the Beit Yosef, in Section 1: From the time the Holy Temple was destroyed, the sages of that generation decreed that one should never build a fully plastered and decorated building, meaning painted like the buildings of kings. Instead, one should plaster their house with clay, coat it with lime, and leave an area of one cubit by one cubit unplastered opposite the entrance. And if someone buys a courtyard that is plastered and decorated, it is presumed to remain in its current state, and he is not required to scrape the walls. Thus far is his wording, and it is from the language of the Rambam at the end of the fifth chapter of Ta'anit, see there. He explains that fully plastered and painted is entirely forbidden. And the Tur disagrees with this, see there. Regarding what he wrote about plastering with clay: it appears that this was his version. And in synagogues and study halls, it is not necessary to leave an area unplastered (Magen Avraham, minor section 2). And "opposite the entrance" means directly opposite, such as if the entrance is on the east, it must be done specifically on the western wall. And if someone does it on the wall where the entrance is, above the entrance, it is meaningless. And the great later authorities wrote that blackening a cubit by a cubit is not effective; rather, one must leave it unplastered with lime (there, minor section 3). And among us, we blacken it, and since it is customary that this is the sign of mourning for the destruction, what does it matter whether it is this way or that way? And those who hang embroidered garments around the walls should also leave a cubit (there). And those who attach beautiful paper to the walls, called "Abayas," should also leave a cubit or blacken the area. And we have already written that with our lime, nothing is needed.

And so they decreed that one who sets a table before guests to make a meal for them should leave an empty space, without placing any of the dishes that ought to be there, and should omit some dish as a sign of mourning for the destruction. But now we do not know about this. It is difficult for us to picture: what is the empty space? And when a woman makes silver and gold jewelry, she should leave out one type of jewelry that she normally wears, so that her adornment is not complete, and she does not wear all her jewelry at once. And when a groom marries, he takes plain ashes and places them on his head where the tefillin are placed. In our practice, instead of ashes, we break a glass at the wedding or place a black cloth or other items of mourning on the head of the groom. All these things are to remember Jerusalem, as it is said: (Psalms 137:5-6) "If I forget you, Jerusalem… if I do not elevate Jerusalem above my chief joy." And know that pleasures are not forbidden, only pleasure that involves joy (Magen Avraham Section 7 from Shabbat 62a). And one must make a sign for the joy.

And so, they decreed not to play musical instruments, or any kind of singing, or any sound-producing devices for joy. It is forbidden to listen to them because of the destruction [of the Temple], as it is said (Hosea 9:1): "Do not rejoice, Israel, like the nations." Some say that this prohibition specifically applies to those who are accustomed to these activities, such as singers who habitually play musical instruments. Similarly, at a banquet, it is forbidden unless it is a celebration of a mitzvah. Even those who are not accustomed to this are also forbidden. However, for the sake of a mitzvah, such as in the house of a bride and groom, everything is permitted. But even there, one should not overly rejoice. At a siyum feast (celebration of completing a tractate of Talmud), it is permitted and it is a mitzvah to rejoice in the joy of the Torah. Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 3: "It has already become the custom of all Israel to say words of praise, or songs of thanksgiving, and to recall the kindness of the Holy One, blessed be He, over wine." Until here are his words. This means that in such a manner, even at a non-mitzvah feast, it is permitted. (See Taz and Magen Avraham, who criticized singing inappropriate things at inappropriate times, see there).

And they also decreed regarding the crowns of grooms, that they should not wear them at all. And a groom should not put any kind of wreath on his head, as it is said (Ezekiel 21:31): "Remove the turban and take off the crown." And they also decreed regarding the crowns of brides, if they are made of silver. But those made of threads – are permitted for the bride. And this is specifically for the groom and bride, but for other men and women – they did not decree. And we do not know at all what these crowns are, as they are not customary among us. And it is forbidden for a person to fill his mouth with laughter in this world, because laughter and frivolity lead to licentiousness. And this is forbidden even during the time of the Temple. This applies when one engages in laughter for a long time with others. But general laughter – we do not object to. And it is obvious that it is forbidden to listen to a woman's singing, as this brings one closer to licentiousness.

One who sees the cities of Judah in their desolation says: "Your holy cities have become a wilderness," and tears [their garment]. One is only obligated to tear when they come close to them, like from Tzofim to Jerusalem. And one who sees Jerusalem in its desolation says: "Zion has become a wilderness, Jerusalem a desolation," and tears [their garment]. When one sees the Temple, they say: "Our holy and beautiful house, where our fathers praised You, has been burned by fire, and all our pleasant things are laid waste," and tears [their garment]. From where is one obligated to tear? From Tzofim. Some say this means from any place where they can see it, and some say this is a specific place from where Jerusalem can be seen (see Magen Avraham, section 3). Afterwards, when one sees the Temple, they tear another tear. Each tear is a tefach (handbreadth). If one comes by way of the desert, where they see the Temple first, they tear a tefach for the Temple, and afterwards, when they see Jerusalem, they add a small tear to the first one. However, in the reverse order, one does not fulfill their obligation by adding, because the Temple is more severe (in its desolation) than Jerusalem.

If one tears (their garment) over one of the cities of Judah, they do not tear again when they see other cities of Judah, except for Jerusalem, for which they tear another tear separately. If one tears for Jerusalem first, they do not need to tear for the other cities of Judah. All these tears must be made by hand and while standing. One must tear all their garments until their chest is revealed, similar to the tearing for one's father or mother, as I have written in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 340. The tear should be made on the left side (Magen Avraham). These tears should never be mended, meaning with a proper sewing, but one is allowed to baste them, gather them, or sew them roughly, like a ladder; this is considered an amateur's sewing, not a professional's sewing. If one was going and coming to Jerusalem within thirty days, they do not tear another tear. After thirty days, they tear again, as with all blessings of sight. The same rule applies to the cities of Judah and the Temple. If one sees Jerusalem within thirty days, they tear for the other cities of Judah, even if they see them after thirty days. Someone who was born in Jerusalem, even if they have grown up, does not need to tear, for in their youth they were exempt, and when they grew up, it was still within thirty days (Magen Avraham). However, if they left Jerusalem and stayed away for thirty days, they must tear upon their return. But for the other cities of Judah, they do not need to tear upon leaving Jerusalem. However, upon returning after thirty days, they are like any other person and must tear in the order as if they were outside the land. With Divine assistance, the laws of Tisha B'Av are concluded.

There are four types of fasts. Two are from the Torah, one fixed and one not fixed. Similarly, two are from the Sages, one fixed and one not fixed. How so? The fixed one from the Torah is Yom Kippur once a year. The one that is not fixed is a fast that one accepts upon oneself through a vow to fast for a day or for a certain number of days. About this, it is said (Numbers 30:3): "If a man makes a vow... he shall do according to all that proceeds out of his mouth." Even if he vows to fast on Shabbat or a festival, the vow takes effect, as I have written in Yoreh De'ah, section 215, see there. The fixed fasts from the Sages are five days a year: the four fasts and the Fast of Esther. The non-fixed fasts from the Sages are for any trouble that may come, as we will explain with the help of Heaven.

This is the language of the Rambam at the beginning of the Laws of Fasting: It is a positive commandment from the Torah to cry out and sound the trumpets over any distress that comes upon the community, as it is stated: "Against the adversary who oppresses you, you shall sound the trumpets." This means any matter that causes you distress, such as drought, plague, locusts, and similar events – cry out and sound the trumpets over them. And this is part of the ways of repentance, for when distress comes and they cry out and sound the trumpets over it, everyone will know that it is because of their evil deeds that this has happened to them, as it is written (Jeremiah 5:25): "Your iniquities have turned away these things…" And this will cause the removal of the distress from upon them. But if they do not cry out and do not sound the trumpets, and instead say: This thing is a natural occurrence that happened, and it is a chance event – this is the way of cruelty, and it causes them to cling to their evil deeds, and the distress will be compounded with other distresses. As it is written in the Torah: "And if you walk with Me in casualness, then I will walk with you in a fury of casualness." This means: When I bring distress upon you so that you will repent, if you say it is a casual occurrence – I will add upon you a fury of that casualness. Thus far his words. And he wrote further:

And it is a rabbinic decree to fast for any trouble that befalls the community, until mercy is granted from Heaven. On these fast days, they cry out in prayers, beseech with supplications, and sound the trumpets alone. If it was in the Temple, they would sound the trumpets and the shofar, the shofar with shorter blasts and the trumpets with longer blasts, for the day's commandment is with the trumpets. They do not blow the trumpets and the shofar together except in the Temple, as it is said: "With trumpets and the sound of the shofar, shout for joy before the King, the Lord…" This means: only before the Lord in the Temple do you sound both, and not in the provinces. Nevertheless, in any case, we learn that for trouble, it is a rabbinic obligation to fast. According to Maimonides, even an individual upon whom trouble has come is obligated to fast, as will be explained in Siman 218. The troubles of the community will be explained in Siman 215 and Siman 216 with the help of Heaven.

And we have a question on this matter: Behold, in this chapter it will be clarified that any fast that was not accepted upon oneself the day before during the Mincha (afternoon) prayer is not considered a fast. This is explicitly stated in the Talmud, Taanit (12a). And this certainly applies only to a fast of a vow. For the established fasts do not require acceptance, for even one who is accustomed to fasting during the Ten Days of Repentance does not need acceptance, as our teacher the Beit Yosef wrote in section 2, and as will be explained. All the more so public fasts due to calamities, they obviously do not require acceptance. Only an individual fast requires acceptance, as the Tur and Shulchan Aruch wrote in section 5, that any fast which an individual did not accept upon himself the day before is not a fast, see there. And this is very surprising: since it is a mitzvah from the Torah due to his vow, what difference does it make whether he accepted it the day before or not? Is this worse than one who vowed not to eat this loaf of bread, or the like? And it is indeed true to say that he is obligated to fulfill his vow, but he does not receive the reward of a fast if he did not accept it the day before. But this explanation is very forced.

However, the truth is that accepting a fast in general is not considered a vow. Here are the words of the Ramban in the laws of vows at the end of chapter nine: "This vow here is not a real vow because it was expressed with the phrase 'it is upon me.' Rather, it is merely the acceptance of a fast. The acceptance of a fast is not as severe as real vows to override a festival, even those mentioned in the Scroll of Fasts... until here are his words." Similarly, the Ritva wrote there, and these are his words: "The reason behind the matter is that the acceptance of a fast is neither a vow of prohibition nor an extension of vows to prohibit food and drink on that day. Rather, it is an affliction that he accepted upon himself to perform the mitzvah of repentance on that day. And it does not imply that this... until here are his words." The Nemukei Yosef also wrote there similarly, and these are his words: "Here it is actually a vow of object prohibition, as he said, 'forbidden upon me is all food...,' but there it is not a real vow, rather an acceptance of a fast that he accepted upon himself to fast. It is only like accepting upon oneself to perform a mitzvah, which does not involve a prohibition of the object. And it is not as severe as real vows. Therefore, they said: 'A person can borrow against his fast and repay it...' This shows that the acceptance of a fast is not a vow, and therefore it is only from rabbinic law due to violating his acceptance. And it does not require the annulment by a sage. Until here are his words." This is also the intention of the Raavad in his glosses in the third chapter of Nedarim, law 9, on what the Rambam wrote that one who vows to fast on Shabbat or a festival is obligated to fast. He wrote in these words: "Specifically when he said 'upon me,' but if he said 'I am fasting today' – it is forbidden to fast. Until here are his words (and the Magen Avraham hinted at this in Siman 810, subsection 2, see there). According to this, according to our rabbis, a fast from the Torah is only when one says 'it is upon me not to eat' or 'I vow upon myself not to eat this day,' and in such a manner, it does not require the acceptance of a fast. But if he said 'I am fasting tomorrow' or 'on such and such a day' – it is only from rabbinic law. And it must be accepted during the Mincha prayer, and if not, he is not required to fast. Now, in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 215, we explained that the Rambam does not hold this way, and according to him, we would need to say as I wrote at the end of the previous section. And see what I wrote in section 20.

Based on this, we derive another new ruling. Behold, regarding the obligation to fast, even on Tisha B'Av, which is very stringent, we ruled in Siman 554 that even a sick person who is not in danger does not need to fast, because the Rabbis did not decree in a place of illness (see there). According to this, in the case of a private fast, which is of Torah origin, one is obligated to fast and is only exempt if there is danger. However, we do not practice this way. For all those who customarily fast on certain days like Yahrzeit, the Ten Days of Repentance, or the eve of Rosh Chodesh, where they have the custom to fast, and the custom is like a vow, we are very lenient with them, even more so than the four fasts. Rather, it is certain that a regular fast is of Rabbinic nature. And if they indeed accepted it with the language of "konam" or "hereby upon me," which would make it a Torah prohibition without danger (so it appears in my humble opinion). However, we have already explained in Yoreh De'ah Siman 214 that a custom is not in the category of a vow at all. And what we hold there, that to annul a custom requires a release, this is merely a stringency (see there).

Based on this, it appears clear that there are several laws pertaining to fasting, such as the law that one does not fast for partial hours as will be explained, or that any fast which does not conclude with sunset is not considered a fast, or that the ruling that a person can borrow a fast and repay it—these only apply to a general acceptance of a fast. However, if one says, "Konam (a type of vow) on me from eating and drinking for such and such hours," he must fulfill his vow, and no more. In this case, it is not possible to defer to another time and fulfill it later, because a vow is separate from a fast. In a vow, there is no language of "fasting," for a vow must prohibit the object to himself, and this does not pertain to the language of fasting. Even if he said, "I vow to fast," this is not considered the language of a vow (Magen Avraham, Siman 568, Section 2); and similarly, if he said, "I obligate myself to fast;" but if he says, "I vow not to eat and drink tomorrow or on a specific day," or "I obligate myself not to eat and not to drink," or "Konam from eating and drinking," then any language of "fasting" is an acceptance of a fast and not a vow. (And this is what they said in Taanit 12b: Rabbi Yochanan said in the name of Rav: A person can borrow his fast and repay it. When I mentioned this before Shmuel, he said to me: Did he accept a vow upon himself, etc. See there. This will also be explained further in Siman 668.)

Any fast that does not extend until sunset, meaning that it is not completed until the appearance of the stars, specifically three medium-sized stars when they are visible, or when the moon shines strongly upon the earth – is not considered a fast. If one's intention is to eat before this time – one does not recite the "Aneinu" prayer. Accordingly, it is also forbidden to eat during twilight. And even though in Pesachim (54b) it is said that only on the Ninth of Av is its twilight forbidden like Yom Kippur, and it is explicitly stated that for other fasts, twilight is permitted – this refers to the commencement of the fast day. However, at the conclusion of the fast day – for all fasts, eating is forbidden during twilight, because out of uncertainty, the sanctity does not depart nor does it enter (Beit Yosef and Magen Avraham).

And it is true that this is what the Mordechai wrote in the name of Yosef in the first chapter of Taanit, and the Rosh there (Siman 12). But the Rosh himself at the end of the second chapter of Shabbat wrote in the name of Rabbeinu Yonah that during twilight it is permitted, see there. And so it seems to me is the opinion of the Rambam, as this law is not found in his writings that any fast that does not end with sunset is not considered a fast. On the contrary, in the fifth chapter regarding Tisha B'Av, he wrote that its twilight is forbidden, which clearly implies that for other fasts, all of twilight is permitted. And this is also implied by the words of the Ran, that the statement "any fast that does not end with sunset" is to be understood literally as sunset. And if you ask: What does this teach us? This refers to the previous discussion of whether one can fast for hours, see there. And it means that any fast that does not end with sunset is not a fast, meaning: and there is no fast for hours. Therefore, when the Rambam wrote the law of fasting for hours, he did not need to mention this. And it is also implied by the words of Rashi, see there. According to this, in my humble opinion, it seems that one who relies on these rabbis to fast only until twilight should not be reprimanded. (And also the Gra, small section 2, wrote so and brought proof from the language of doubt in the Gemara there. And also the Tosafot in Avodah Zarah 34a, beginning with "Metanin," also wrote that this sunset is to be understood literally, see there. And I am astonished that he did not bring proof from the Rambam, Rashi, and Ran whom we explained. And I saw that the Korban Netanel in Shabbat there, wanted to interpret the intention of the Rosh as explicitly stipulated, see there in note 44, and his words are puzzling. Examine and you will find clarity.)

Behold, our master the Rema in Section 1 wrote regarding the words of our master the Beit Yosef, that anyone who does not fast until the appearance of the stars has not completed a fast, he wrote the following: "However, the custom is to pray 'Aneinu' even though they do not complete the fast until the appearance of the stars, and this is also the opinion of some of the rabbis." And it appears to me that this applies specifically to an individual who says 'Aneinu' in 'Shema Koleinu', for in any case, he can add it, as I wrote in Siman 119. But a public emissary should not say 'Aneinu' unless they complete the fast, and so is the custom. Until here is his wording. And there are those among the commentators of the Shulchan Aruch who explained his intention in what he wrote "and this is also the opinion of some of the rabbis" that his intention is regarding the Rambam, who ruled in the matter of fasting for hours as it simply is, even if one ate that day, as will be explained. According to this, the intention of our master the Rema is that one can pray 'Aneinu' even several hours before nightfall. And according to this, he was astonished at him: for this opinion is a rejected opinion. Furthermore, how can one say "the day of our fasting" – for it is not a complete day? Therefore, he rejected his words (Taz, Section 1). And there is one who explained his intention: when he clarified at the time of acceptance not to complete the fast, then even if he prayed the early Mincha – he prays 'Aneinu' (Magen Avraham, Section 2). (And see in Section 28 that even according to the Rambam, 'Aneinu' does not apply in such a case.)

All this is perplexing in my eyes. It is clear in its intention that it refers only to the appearance of the stars, meaning that even if one fasted only until sunset and not until the appearance of the stars, it is considered a fast and one prays "Aneinu." And the few authorities who hold this view are Rabbeinu Yonah in the Rosh at the end of the second chapter of Shabbat, and the Tosafot there. It is written that in a public setting, the prayer leader should not say "Aneinu" because it is a blessing by itself, and most opinions hold that one should fast until the appearance of the stars. It seems to me, in my humble opinion, that according to what we have explained, also the views of the Rambam, Rashi, and the Ran align with this – that even in a public setting, one can rely on these authorities. (And what the markers in the Rema wrote that its source is from the Terumat HaDeshen is a mistake, as it is not found there at all, see there.)

Rabbeinu Beit Yosef writes in Section 2: "There are those who say that someone who customarily fasts during the Ten Days of Repentance, since it is not customary to formally accept these fasts in prayer, does not need to fast until the stars come out, but only until he leaves the synagogue." Thus are his words.

And Rabbeinu the Rema writes: "An individual prays 'Aneinu,' and similarly, a groom prays 'Aneinu' before entering the chuppah, and then he can drink from the cup of blessing. However, someone who fasts from the Seventeenth of Tammuz until the Ninth of Av must complete the fast, even though he does not need to formally accept it. Someone who does not fast all ten days of repentance, but only one or two days, requires formal acceptance and completion. And it seems to me that this is only in general, but if he stipulated not to complete the fast, he may do so, as it is no more stringent than other fasts." Thus are his words.

Explanation of the matter: Behold, in Tractate Ta'anit (12a) it states: Any fast in which the sun did not set upon it is not considered a fast. And it raises a difficulty from the members of the priestly watch, who would fast but not complete the fast. And it answers: there, it was merely to afflict themselves. And Rashi explains: but it is not considered a fast for the purpose of saying the "Aneinu" prayer, nor to establish it as an obligatory fast at all. And whenever one wants to eat, one may eat. Thus far his words. According to this, it is not considered a fast at all, and one can eat in the middle of the day whenever he wishes. According to this, even during the Ten Days of Repentance, which are also merely for affliction to atone for one's sins, so that one's prayer will be accepted and one's decree torn up, if one does not accept the fast from the previous day's Mincha time, it is not considered a fast at all, and one can eat whenever he wishes, even in the middle of the day. And as now, there are those who fast until after midday, pray Mincha Gedola, and eat. And they do not say "Aneinu," because it is not considered a fast at all.

However, the Tur wrote, and these are his words: Avi HaEzri wrote: One who is accustomed to fasting during the Ten Days of Repentance is not required to fast for ten full days until the appearance of the stars, but only until he leaves the synagogue. For he only accepted upon himself a general affliction, as the Talmud raises an objection against Rav Chisda from the case of the members of the watch, who fast but do not complete the fast. And it answers there: It is only to afflict themselves. And Rav Chisda only stated this about one who explicitly accepted a fast. And an unspecified fast is a full day, but during the Ten Days of Repentance, it is not. And it is not customary to accept this in prayer during the Ten Days of Repentance. Thus far his words, and this is the opinion of those who say in the Shulchan Aruch. And he disagrees with Rashi, who wrote that one may eat whenever he wishes, as he required fasting until leaving the synagogue. And he calls this a fast, except that it does not need to be until the appearance of the stars. And since it is a fast, he naturally prays "Aneinu" according to the words of Rabbeinu the Rema. And so it is in Mordechai and the Hagahos Ashri, and not like the words of Rashi who does not pray "Aneinu".

And in my humble opinion, they follow their own reasoning. For behold, we have already explained that Rashi of blessed memory holds that any fast where the sun did not set upon it, it is not the appearance of stars but merely the sunset. And if so, by extension, this statement that one fasts but does not complete it – this applies even before sunset. And if so, there is no limit to it, and even in the middle of the day, and by extension, this is not considered a fast at all. But the Tur and Avi HaEzri hold that any fast where the sun did not set upon it – this refers to the appearance of stars, as the Tur wrote, see there, and so wrote the Mordechai in the name of Rabbi Eliezer of Metz, who is known as Avi HaEzri. According to this, the statement that one fasts but does not complete it – this refers to until the appearance of stars. However, in any case, there needs to be some boundary for the fast: either sunset, or after the congregation prays Maariv, which is from the time of the afternoon prayer, an hour and a quarter before nightfall. And this is what is meant by: until they leave the synagogue (and so wrote the Magen Avraham in subsection 5). And since there is a boundary to this, before which it is forbidden to eat – by extension, one prays "Aneinu".

According to this, the explanation of our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, is as follows: Someone who accepts a complete fast—it's obvious that they must fast until the appearance of the stars, as this is the opinion of the majority of halachic authorities, even according to Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema), as I wrote in section 11. However, the fasts that are accepted and established by custom, such as the Ten Days of Repentance, or certain days among them if there is a custom to fast regularly on those days, like those who fast on the first day of Selichot or on the eve of Rosh Hashanah, which are without formal acceptance—though they are called a "fast" for the purpose of the "Aneinu" prayer, nevertheless, one does not need to complete the fast until the appearance of the stars, but it suffices until sunset or after the evening prayer. Since there is a boundary for this, where it is forbidden to eat beforehand—it is called a "fast." Similarly, a groom on his wedding day, who needs to fast until after the chuppah, and this is its boundary, therefore he should pray "Aneinu" before the chuppah, and then he can drink from the blessing cup. But those who fast from the seventeenth of Tammuz until the ninth of Av—even without formal acceptance—need to complete the fast until the appearance of the stars, since their fast is for the destruction, it is automatically like the seventeenth of Tammuz and the ninth of Av. Also, during the Ten Days of Repentance, those who do not fast always uniformly, but only a day or two, and not consistently on this or that day, but sometimes this day and sometimes that day—it is obvious that they need formal acceptance and completion. And if he accepted a fast without specification—he must complete it until the appearance of the stars. However, if he stipulated at the time of accepting the fast not to complete it—it is obvious that he has the right, and he does not need to complete it. (This is the explanation of the words of the Shulchan Aruch. And this is how the Taz and Magen Avraham understood it, although they were brief on the main points. The words of the Bach in this matter require significant examination, see there. And although the Rema in the previous section wrote that it is customary even in a complete fast not to fast until the appearance of the stars, here there is a novelty that even until sunset is not required, only until some boundary, such as during the Ten Days of Repentance until after the evening prayer, and the groom until after the chuppah, and the like. What the Magen Avraham explained in subsection 6, and the Taz in subsection 3, to differentiate between the Ten Days of Repentance and the Three Weeks, because the Ten Days of Repentance are for the future, and the Three Weeks are for the past destruction—it is hard to visualize. Their words are from the Terumat HaDeshen, and the Bach objected strongly to this, raising a major difficulty from the case of Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Tzadok who did not complete his fast, and he fasted for the past. The Taz and Magen Avraham struggled to answer this, see there. But according to what I wrote, this is not the main point, and it is merely an example. The main reason is that since they are between the seventeenth of Tammuz and the ninth of Av, and the fast has one intention for the destruction—therefore it is automatically completed until the appearance of the stars like those days themselves. Unlike the case of Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Tzadok, who on the ninth of Av itself did not complete his fast. According to this, there is no beginning to the Bach's difficulty. The general rule is: all types of fasts without formal acceptance do not need to be completed until the appearance of the stars, but until some boundary. And similarly, those who fast from the beginning of the month of Elul. Except for the Three Weeks, for the reason we explained with the help of Heaven. Examine this and you will find it easy.)

An individual who accepted upon himself a fast without specification to fast on Erev Shabbat must fast until the appearance of the stars, unless he stipulated at the time of accepting the fast "until the community completes their prayer." Refer above to Siman 249. Similarly, a fast for a bad dream must be observed until the appearance of the stars, even on Erev Shabbat, because the remedy for a bad dream is fasting, as stated in Shabbat (11a) – "a fast for a dream is as beneficial as fire to flax." Consequently, a complete fast is required. Refer above to Siman 249.

Any private fast that was not accepted beforehand is not considered a fast, and one should not pray the "Aneinu" prayer. Similarly, if someone is obligated to fast for some reason, they do not fulfill their vow with this fast. Nevertheless, they are required to complete the fast if they intended to fast and complete it. Additionally, they receive a reward, and it serves as atonement for sin, as it is not worse than one who afflicts themselves by abstaining from meat and wine. (In the Magen Avraham, section 9, there is a printing error. It should say: if one began to fast on this day with the intention to complete it, see there. The Machatzit HaShekel struggles with this and his words are not clear, see there. And even though at the beginning of Siman 603, Magen Avraham wrote that without acceptance during Mincha one does not need to fast at all, he later concludes that it is proper to be stringent, see there. The intention here is that one accepted it verbally, but not at the appropriate time.)

And know that in the Gemara there (10a) it states: Shmuel said, "Any fast that one did not accept upon himself the day before is not considered a fast." And if he did fast, what is it like? Rabbah bar Shila said: "It is like a bellows full of air." And Rashi explained: It is like a bellows of blacksmiths that is filled with air, so too this is filled with air, because he did not eat for nothing. Thus far is his wording. From this it is clear that one may eat even if he accepted upon himself to fast, since he did not accept it the day before. Similarly, Mordechai wrote there, and this is his wording: "Any fast..."—It implies that it is not considered a fast, and it is permitted to eat even though he accepted upon himself after dark to fast the whole day. For since he did not accept it the day before, it is as if he did not accept it. Thus far is his wording. And behold, all the poskim (decisors) have concluded their words and only wrote the language of the Talmud. But it is astonishing about our teacher, the Rema, who wrote in section 5 on the words of the author who wrote in the language of the Talmud that it is not a fast, he wrote, and this is his wording: "It is not a fast to pray 'Aneinu,' but regarding the obligation of the fast... he has not fulfilled his vow..." Thus far is his wording. And why did he not also write that it is permitted to eat? And one of the commentators on the Shulchan Aruch (Magen Avraham, small section 9) wrote explicitly the opposite, that he needs to fulfill his vow, meaning: and he is obligated to fast, as we wrote in the previous section. And this is against the words of Rashi and Mordechai.

In my humble opinion, it appears that our teacher, the Rema, intentionally omitted this. For indeed, there are those who question how it is permissible to eat, as it is still considered a vow (Magen Avraham, beginning of section 603, in the name of the Bach). They answered that a fast and a vow are two different matters (ibid.). This is based on the principle we explained in section 5 in the name of the Ramban, the Raavad, the Ritva, and the Nimukei Yosef; see there. And we have already written there that the Rambam's opinion is not like this, and we have elaborated on this in Yoreh De'ah, section 215, with the help of Heaven; see there. According to this, in the view of the Rambam, it is certainly forbidden to eat due to his vow, but regarding the fast, it does not count for him. And this is what the Talmud asks: "And if he sits, what?" – the intention is not that if he wants, he can eat, but rather the meaning is: "And if he sits, what?" meaning, perhaps it counts for him in retrospect as a fast? And it says that it is not so, but rather it is like a bellows filled with air, meaning regarding the fast: he does not pray "Aneinu," and it does not count as a fast, and he must make it up. Therefore, our teacher, the Rema, did not want to explicitly write that it is forbidden to eat, because according to most opinions, it is permissible to eat. But he also did not want to write that it is permissible to eat, because that would be against the opinion of the Rambam, so he left the matter undefined. (And the Magen Avraham here and at the beginning of section 603, who wrote that it seems appropriate to be stringent – either because he holds like the Rambam, or because he did not delve into the count. And we wrote in the previous section that one must fast, because that is how the words of the Rema lean. However, in practice: one who does not want to fast and relies on the majority of the decisors – he has permission to do so. Be precise and you will find leniency.)

Our teacher, the Rema, also wrote that some say that one should pray "Aneinu." And it seems to me that this is the practice for a private fast. According to everyone, on a fast due to a bad dream, one prays "Aneinu," even if they did not accept it upon themselves the day before. This is his language. And regarding a fast due to a bad dream, it is certainly correct, because since the sages said to fast, it does not require acceptance. But for a private fast, there is a disagreement in the Mordechai that we brought, and this is his language there: However, it seems to R"Y that one prays "Aneinu," as it is no less significant than a fast due to a bad dream. And the Ra'avyah disagreed with this. And R' Mordechai heard from our teacher of blessed memory that if one did not accept it during the day, they do not pray "Aneinu" the next day. This is his language. The comparison to a fast due to a bad dream is not understood. However, their intention is that it is no less significant than a partial fast in which one prays "Aneinu," as will be explained. And the comparison to a fast due to a bad dream means this: Just as on a fast due to a bad dream one says "Aneinu" without accepting it the day before, so too here. For an individual, since he does not establish a blessing for himself, we are not so stringent, as long as he accepted it in some manner. But if he did not accept it at all, but simply did not eat all day, it is nothing, and he does not pray "Aneinu."

When does one accept it? During the Mincha prayer in "Shomea Tefillah," or after he has completed his prayer before he steps back. He says: "I hereby accept upon myself a private fast for tomorrow. May it be Your will that my prayer on my fast day be accepted." If he did not verbalize it but merely contemplated in his heart his acceptance of the fast for the next day, it is considered an acceptance. This is similar to tithes and sacrifices, where an internal decision suffices even if not verbalized, as stated in Shevuot (26b). Only an oath requires verbal expression. However, it must be that he contemplates this during the Mincha prayer and makes a complete acceptance in his heart to fast. If he did not make a complete acceptance but only intended to fast, it is not considered anything. Know that it is not specifically during the Mincha prayer, as this is only the ideal. After the fact, an acceptance is valid at any time during the day, even after the Mincha prayer (Magen Avraham, sub-section 12). It is better to accept it after the prayer before stepping back rather than during the prayer to avoid interrupting the prayer. Nevertheless, he should also contemplate it during "Shomea Tefillah." One should not say: in vows, we maintain in Yoreh De'ah, siman 202, that acceptance in the heart is not effective like an oath, so why is it effective for fasting? One can say that fasting is similar to a sacrifice, where one offers their fat and blood that diminishes due to the weakness from fasting (Eliyah Rabbah, and similarly written by the Taz in sub-section 8).

The acceptance of a fast during the Mincha prayer is effective even if one interrupts with eating, as one eats and drinks throughout the night. Similarly, it is effective even for several days, such as if one accepts during the Mincha prayer on Sunday to fast on Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday – the acceptance applies to all these days, even if one eats and drinks in between. There is no need for another acceptance, and there is no need to accept each fast during the preceding Mincha; the acceptance during Mincha on Sunday suffices for all the days. Even if one says that they accept upon themselves two consecutive days, it does not mean consecutive without interruption by eating at night in between, but rather it means to fast until nightfall the next day, and also the day after that, unless one explicitly states that their intention is truly consecutive without interruption at night. Regarding the "Aneinu" prayer during Mincha, there is no difference between one who fasts only during the day and not at night, and one who does not interrupt with eating at night.

And this is when the days of fasting that one accepts upon oneself are consecutive. But if one accepts non-consecutive days, such as accepting at the Mincha prayer to fast four or five scattered days, like Monday and Thursday over two or three weeks, and the like – there are those who are uncertain whether one acceptance suffices for all of them, or if an acceptance is needed for each individual day. However, the custom is to accept them with one acceptance, and that suffices, and this is also the opinion of some authorities. This is our custom with the BeHaB fasts, where we accept on Shabbat for all three scattered days. But from this, there is no proof, as this is like a communal acceptance. And proof of this is that it does not require acceptance at the preceding Mincha, as I have written in Section 32.

If one accepted upon himself to fast for two consecutive days, including the night in between, and he became weak and ate during the night in between, he has lost his fast, and he does not pray the "Aneinu" prayer, and he needs to complete other days (see Taz in the name of Kol Bo). However, if one accepted upon himself to fast many days with a break of the night in between, meaning that he would eat every night, and he fasted some days, and then did not fast one of the days; nevertheless, when he fasts the subsequent days, he says "Aneinu" each day, because each day is considered a separate fast (ibid.).

All of this applies when one has accepted a fast for multiple days. However, if one has accepted a fast only for one day, such as saying "I will fast tomorrow" and fasted, but on the night after the fast decided to fast again the next day, and even if he continued his fast without eating at night and fasted again the next day — in any case, it is not considered a fast, even though it extends from the first day, because he did not accept it for the second day. Even if he accepts it on the second night — it is meaningless. It is less significant than a partial fast, which was accepted before the hours of fasting. Similarly, for a full day's fast, one must begin before the day. Nevertheless, he can pray "Aneinu" (the special prayer for fast days), for it is at least considered a partial fast, as I wrote in paragraph 21, since he accepted it before beginning to fast on the second day. While it is not considered a full day's fast, it is still not less significant than a partial fast (see Magen Avraham, subparagraph 15).

It is determined in the Gemara (11b): The halacha is that one can fast for a few hours and pray the prayer of a fast day. This is provided that one did not taste anything the entire day. The explanation is as follows: If someone was preoccupied with their business or other activities and did not eat until midday or until the ninth hour, and then decided to fast for the remaining hours of the day, they are considered to be fasting for those hours and may pray "Aneinu" during that time, since they accepted the fast before the fasting hours. This is not comparable to what was previously explained, that if one did not accept the fast during the Mincha prayer, it is not considered a fast even if they accepted it at night. Is accepting it at night worse than accepting it the next day after midday? Surely it is worse, because every type of fast must be accepted before the time it is meant to take effect. Therefore, if one wishes to fast the entire day, they must accept the fast before the day starts, and the day starts from the beginning of the night. Even if one eats at night, since this fast is considered a fast for the day, and the day follows the night, they must accept it before the night. For a partial day fast, one must accept it before the hours of the fast begin. Therefore, if it occurs to someone to fast for certain hours and they accept it before those hours, it is considered a proper acceptance. However, the condition for this is that they did not eat beforehand for any reason, as I mentioned. Otherwise, how can this be called a fast? Indeed, it would not be a fast.

And indeed, the approach of the Jerusalem Talmud is that even if one ate during that day, and then decided to fast for the rest of the day, it is also called a "partial fast." And so wrote the Rambam in the first chapter; see there. However, it has already been questioned: but isn't it the case that our Talmud's approach is not like this? And the Rambam took both approaches: the approach of our Talmud and the approach of the Jerusalem Talmud. In my humble opinion, it seems that the ruling is with the Rambam, as the Talmud which requires not eating all day – this is in regard to the "Aneinu" prayer. For otherwise, how could one say "Answer us on the day of our fast" since he did not fast? Nevertheless, even our Talmud agrees that a partial fast is considered a fast, and one receives a reward, and it is forbidden to eat during those hours. However, he does not pray "Aneinu" (the Jerusalem Talmud is in the eighth chapter of Nedarim).

And this is the language of the Rambam there, Law 13: A person may fast for certain hours, provided he does not eat anything for the rest of the day. How so? If he was preoccupied... – he fasts during those hours and prays "Aneinu"... Similarly, if he ate and drank, and then began to fast for the rest of the day – this is a partial fast. Thus far his language, and he did not conclude that one should pray "Aneinu" because in such a case it is not necessary, and it is impossible to pray "Aneinu." He holds that what the Talmud says "provided he did not taste anything the whole day" refers to what it says "and he prays the prayer of a fast" (so it seems clear to my humble opinion). And know that Rashi there explains that if one accepted upon himself from the previous day to fast until half the next day, and then decided not to eat until night – this is considered a complete fast and not a partial fast. See there.

Here is the translation:

"Now, the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch also wrote in section 11, and this is their language: If one accepted upon himself a fast until midday and then ate afterward, or if he ate until midday and accepted upon himself a fast from then onward – it is not considered a fast to pray 'Aneinu'. However, it is considered a fast in regard to needing to fulfill his vow. Until here is their language. And according to this, I am greatly perplexed by the Tur and the Maggid Mishneh, and also other halachic authorities who rejected the words of the Rambam and wrote that it is an error, and that they heard that the Rambam himself retracted his position (see Beit Yosef). And it is very bewildering: the Rambam also says the same, and indeed the precision of his pure language indicates this, for he first wrote that one says 'Aneinu' and afterward did not write so. And this requires great investigation."

Indeed, according to the Rosh and the Tur, this is not considered a partial fast (Taanit Sha'ot) when we mentioned that one did not eat until midday; rather, even a partial fast requires acceptance from the day before. This means, for example, if one accepted from the day before to fast until midday, and then decided not to eat until nightfall, or if one accepted from the day before to fast the next day from midday onwards, and then decided not to eat until midday as well—this is called a partial fast. However, according to Rashi, this is considered a complete fast, as I wrote in section 29. Therefore, according to the Rosh and the Tur, any fast without prior acceptance from the day before is not considered a fast at all regarding the "Aneinu" prayer. Consequently, all the details we mentioned previously about accepting the fast at night and needing to pray "Aneinu" are not applicable according to the Rosh and the Tur, as it is not less than a partial fast.

A fast that is decreed upon the community—each individual does not need to accept it during the Mincha prayer; rather, the prayer leader announces the fast, and it is considered accepted. Some say that this applies in the Land of Israel, where they had a Nasi (leader) whose decree was binding upon all of Israel. But in the Diaspora, the entire community must accept it upon themselves as individuals, with each person accepting it personally. However, it appears to me that even in such a case, their status is not like an individual who needs to accept it during the Mincha prayer; rather, whenever they accept it, it becomes a fast, because when the community accepts it together, even though each person does so individually, it is like the Great Court. As I wrote in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 2, that the leaders of the city in their city are like the Great Court. All the more so, the entire community together. A proof for this is the BeHaB fasts, where the prayer leader announces it in the morning, and the community answers "Amen," and no further acceptance is needed. (This also resolves the question of the Taz in subparagraph 16. And regarding what he wrote, that an individual who accepted to fast by vow is obligated by Torah law to fast, see there—he did not take to heart that a fast is not a vow by Torah law, as I wrote above. Be precise and you will find the matter easy.)

Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote in section 13: There is an opinion that if someone made a vow and said, "If I do not go to such-and-such a place, I will sit in fasting," since the condition involves a discretionary matter, it is considered an asmachta (a non-binding commitment). However, if he said, "If I do not perform such-and-such a mitzvah (commandment), I will sit in fasting," or if he said, "If God saves me from distress or if He makes my way successful," it is not considered an asmachta. This is the end of his language, meaning: We hold in Choshen Mishpat, section 207, that asmachta does not acquire. This applies when he said, "If it will be so," as any conditional statement is an asmachta, and he did not truly intend to fulfill it. However, regarding a mitzvah, it is explained there that there is no asmachta, as in all matters of mitzvah, he fully intends to complete it. This is explicitly found in the case of Jacob (Genesis 28:20): "If God will be with me and guard me..." 

In this context, the phrase "if He makes my way successful" is also considered like a mitzvah matter, as he fully intends to commit due to the merit of success (see Magen Avraham, subsection 17). Nevertheless, there is room for doubt: although the condition was in a discretionary matter, since he said, "I will sit in fasting," which is a mitzvah matter, it should not be considered an asmachta, similar to charity in Yoreh De'ah, section 258, where it is not considered an asmachta in such a manner, see there. One must say that the opinion holds that the essence of fasting is not called a mitzvah matter, as there is an opinion in the Talmud that one who sits in fasting is called a sinner. Therefore, it is written as "there is an opinion," meaning: but one who holds that in all matters fasting is like charity, even in a discretionary matter, there is no asmachta. (And this resolves the difficulties of Taz, subsection 17, and Magen Avraham, subsection 16, see there. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote: If someone thought in his heart, not during the Mincha prayer, to fast tomorrow – it is not considered an acceptance, for it is no better than verbally expressing the intention to fast tomorrow, which is not considered an acceptance because it was not accepted during the Mincha prayer. This is his exact language. And I do not understand what he is teaching us, for he has already explained this in the previous section, paragraph 6, where he wrote: When does one accept it? During the Mincha prayer... And if he did not verbally express it but only thought it in his heart – it is considered an acceptance, provided he thought this during the Mincha prayer. This is his exact language, so what is he adding here? It is far-fetched to say that because the Tur wrote this law in this section, he also felt compelled to write it here to avoid skipping the section, even though he had already written it. This requires further examination.

We have already investigated in the previous section, paragraph 19, whether if one did not accept the fast during the afternoon prayer: is it forbidden for him to eat, but it does not count as a fast for him, or is it entirely permissible for him to eat. The Mordechai holds the latter view. And there in paragraph 20, we proved that our teacher, the Rema, was uncertain, because according to the Rambam, it is forbidden. See there. Therefore, I say that all this applies to verbal acceptance not during the afternoon prayer, but if he merely thought in his heart not during the afternoon prayer — it is permissible for him to eat according to all opinions. For the reason we forbid eating in the name of a fast is because of a vow. According to the Rambam, a vow and a fast are the same matter, as he wrote there. And if so, in a vow, we hold in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 202, that one must explicitly articulate it, similar to an oath, as it says: "to express with the lips." And if so, it is obvious that it is nothing. (And this also seems to be the opinion of the Magen Avraham, see there. And perhaps this is why the Beit Yosef wrote it here. But if so, why did he write it in a general manner?)

Know that there is a significant difference between a private fast and a public fast. A private fast is only a daytime fast and does not require one to begin fasting before the day starts, as on Yom Kippur. A public fast is defined by starting the fast before the day begins, but the sages did not impose this stringency on every public fast, except for Tisha B'Av, as well as for fasts for rain in the Land of Israel and the later fasts, as I have written in Siman 575. However, for all other public fasts, they did not impose this stringency on us, treating them like a private fast. Therefore, when a person accepts a fast, they should say, "I am accepting a private fast for tomorrow." But even if they simply said "fast" – it is still valid (Beit Yosef in Siman 563). However, if they said "I am accepting a public fast for tomorrow" – they must begin fasting before the day starts (ibid. and Magen Avraham at the beginning of Siman 562).

And our sages said in Taanit (12a): Until when can one eat and drink? Until dawn rises. This applies both to a private fast and to a public fast, except for the Ninth of Av. Even if one has eaten the evening meal, he can still eat more if he wishes. However, if he has slept a regular sleep, it is considered an interruption, and he is forbidden to eat. But if he has slept a brief nap, that is, dozed off for a short while, he can eat again. And during the meal, even if he has slept a regular sleep, he can eat again, but this is uncommon. Likewise, for drinking – some say it is forbidden if he has slept a regular sleep. Others say that drinking is always permitted, because one does not divert his attention from drinking. But for eating, a condition is needed: he must stipulate that he still wishes to eat. For drinking, no condition is needed. And so is the custom, because we are accustomed to drink after sleeping. And some say that for a fast of a dream – it is forbidden to taste anything immediately upon waking (Magen Avraham), for its rectification is that one should immediately begin to fast. And see what I wrote in Siman 288.

The individual says "Anenu" in the blessing of "Shomea Tefillah." This applies whether it is a private fast or a communal fast. And even if one is praying alone and will not hear the blessing from the prayer leader, since the blessing was not instituted as a separate blessing except for the prayer leader, as will be explained in the next section. Even the prayer leader in the silent prayer includes it in "Shomea Tefillah," and says it before "for You hear...". He should not conclude with "He who answers in times of distress," but when he reaches "in every time of distress and trouble," he should say "for You hear...". There are those who say that he should also not say "in every time of distress and trouble" (Eliyah Rabbah), but this is not the main opinion. And this is the simple custom, and it should not be changed. It is obvious that a prayer leader who is fasting a private fast should not mention "Anenu" in the repetition of the prayer leader. (And what the Be'er Heitev wrote in subsection 1 in the name of the Kenesset HaGedolah is astonishing.)

It is obvious that on a public fast day, someone who is not fasting should not say "Aneinu," and this is the widespread custom. There is someone who says that he should say "Aneinu" since it has now become a fixed prayer for the community, but he should not say "on the day of our fast" but rather "on this fast day" (Bach). However, we have never heard of anyone who practices this. And know that apparently, on a private fast, one should not say "Aneinu, Hashem, on the day of our fast," but rather "on the day of my fast," and so the great authorities have written (Bach and Taz, subsection 1). But our teacher, the Rema, wrote in subsection 1 that one should not deviate from the established formula, but should say "on the day of our fast." This is his language, similar to someone setting out on a journey as in section 110 above, who says "that You lead us in peace" since there are several who set out on a journey.
