Here too, it is impossible that there are not others in the world who are fasting (Magen Avraham, subsection 1, and see Taz). And this is the custom.

If one forgot to say "Aneinu" in "Shomea Tefillah" and remembered after saying "Baruch Atah Hashem..."—he should not interrupt in the middle of the prayer, but should say it after his prayer before stepping back. It seems to me that he can also say it before "Yihyu L'ratzon...". It is no worse than other supplications, which some say before "Yihyu L'ratzon". If he did not remember until after he stepped back—he is not required to repeat it, as this is not essential, similar to "Al Hanisim" during Chanukah and Purim. Also, when he says it after his prayer before stepping back—he should not say it with a concluding blessing, but in the same manner as he would say it in "Shomea Tefillah".

The opinion of the Geonim is that an individual does not say "Aneinu" except at Mincha and not at Shacharit, because perhaps he will be seized by a bulmus (a sudden, overpowering hunger) and will need to eat, and it will turn out that he lied in his prayer. And even though according to the law of the Gemara, one also says "Aneinu" at the preceding Maariv, nevertheless, we who are weak must be concerned, but at Mincha there is no concern. And even if one prays Mincha Gedola (early Mincha) – in any case, he must say "Aneinu," for even if he is seized by a bulmus, he has at least fasted until midday (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 4). But the Shaliach Tzibbur (prayer leader) says it also in the Shacharit prayer in the repetition of the Shaliach Tzibbur as a separate blessing, because it is possible that some of the congregation are fasting. Therefore, even if he himself is not fasting, he must say it, for it is the prayer of the congregation.

And our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in paragraph 3, and these are his words: "On the four fasts, even an individual recites it in all his prayers, for even if he is overtaken by a bulmus and eats, it is still appropriate to say 'Answer us on this day of the fast of our affliction,' since the sages ordained fasting on this day." Until here are his words. I do not know if he precisely chose this language so that one does not say "on the day of our fast" since he himself might not be fasting, or if it was just a general choice of words. It seems more likely that he precisely chose this language. However, our master the Rema wrote on this: "The custom on all the fasts is only to say it during Mincha, except for the prayer leader who says it also during Shacharit when praying aloud." Until here are his words, and this is also our custom. The reason could be that since one has to change the wording from "the fast of our affliction" to "the fast of this affliction" as I have written – it is not worthwhile.

And it is good to say in the supplications after the Mincha prayer, after "Elokai Netzor...": "Master of the Universe, it is revealed and known before You that when the Temple stood, a person would sin and offer a sacrifice, and only its fat and blood would be offered. May it be Your will that the fat and blood that was diminished from me today through this fast be considered as if I had offered..." However, this is not the current custom, and I do not know why. It is proper to say it, as it is found in Berachot (17a) and in the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, section 5, see there.

An individual should not recite the Thirteen Attributes of Mercy as a form of prayer and supplication for mercy, as they are considered a matter of sanctity and require a quorum of ten. This is explicitly implied in Rosh Hashanah (17b), where it describes the Holy One, Blessed be He, wrapping Himself like a prayer leader with the Thirteen Attributes. However, if one wishes to recite them merely as a reading, with melody and cantillation, he is permitted to do so. When reciting "He called in the name of the Lord," there should be a pause between "in the name of" and "the Lord," as the tevir (cantillation mark) is on "in the name of." The "in the name of" should have a soft "b," unlike the "He called in the name of the Lord" in the portion "Lech Lecha." Before midnight, the Thirteen Attributes should not be recited, nor any supplications, except on Yom Kippur. Similarly, "Ha'aderet Veha'emunah" should only be recited on Yom Kippur (Magen Avraham, subsection 5). Sephardim recite it on every Shabbat, even individually. An individual should not recite supplications in the middle of the prayer service, but may do so afterward, omitting the sections related to the Thirteen Attributes. Someone who fasts and boasts about it to others will be punished for it. However, if asked, he may respond truthfully, as he is not boasting but rather avoiding a lie (see Taz, subsection 6, and Magen Avraham, subsection 7).

On a public fast day, the prayer leader says "Aneinu" as a separate blessing between "Go'el Yisrael" and "Refa'einu." This is supported by a verse, as it is written: "May the words of my mouth... my Rock and my Redeemer," and immediately following it says, "May the Lord answer you on the day of distress." Since we mention "Go'el Yisrael" (the Redeemer of Israel), we ask "Answer us... for we are in great distress," and conclude: "Blessed are You, O Lord, who answers His people Israel in time of distress." This is the text according to the Tur and Shulchan Aruch. However, Maimonides in the second chapter of the Laws of Prayer wrote: "Who answers in time of distress." It appears that the text of the Tur and Shulchan Aruch is more accurate, for in both "Re'eh Ve'anyeinu" and "Refa'einu" we mention "Go'el Yisrael" and "Healer of His people Israel." So why should we not say here "Who answers His people Israel"? Therefore, it is fitting to correct the prayer books accordingly. And if one forgets to say "Aneinu," this was clarified earlier in Siman 119; see there.

And they read from the Torah "And Moses beseeched" until "to His people." The Levite and the Israelite read from "Carve for yourself" until after "Behold, I make a covenant." And even though it is taught at the end of Megillah (31a): on fast days, [we read] blessings and curses, the Rambam has already written in Chapter 13 of the Laws of Prayer, Law 18, that this is on fasts decreed by the community due to impending troubles, like drought or pestilence and the like, where they are warned to repent. Therefore, they read blessings and curses, meaning that all troubles come because of our evil deeds, as written in the Torah: "If you follow My statutes…" But fasts for past events, and most of them are for the destruction of the Temple – they read "And Moses beseeched," see there. And this is according to the Tractate Soferim Chapter 17, Law 7, see there. And the reading hints that just as God forgave the sin of the Golden Calf and gave us the second tablets – so too, we hope that He will build for us the Temple speedily in our days. Amen.

And they read "Vayechal" both in the morning and at Mincha. Even if it falls on Monday or Thursday, they postpone the weekly Torah portion. The congregation has the custom that when the reader reaches "Turn from Your fierce anger," they cry out "Turn...!" as this is a request that the Holy One, Blessed be He, should turn from His fierce anger. The reader then repeats "Turn...," since we said it orally and without cantillation. Similarly, when the reader reaches "And He passed," the congregation shouts "Hashem, Hashem...," to recall the Thirteen Attributes of Mercy. The reader repeats it. Likewise, when he reaches "And forgive our iniquity," they do the same, as this is also a plea and supplication that He may forgive our iniquity. The Haftarah is read at Mincha and not in the morning. The Haftarah is "Seek the Lord while He may be found" until "to His exiles." The same readers are used for both Mincha and Shacharit, except that at Mincha the third one is the Maftir. It seems to me the reason is because on a public fast day, they confess at the end of the day, as stated in Taanit (12b), and as Ezra and Nehemiah did, as written in Nehemiah (Nehemiah 9). Therefore, they read "Seek the Lord while He may be found" to encourage repentance. On Tisha B'Av, they also read in the morning: "When you beget children." Even on a public fast that falls on a Friday, they read at Mincha. Our master the Rema wrote in section 1 that if they are fasting on Rosh Chodesh, they read the Rosh Chodesh portion in the morning and the fast portion at Mincha. Until here are his words. This was when they would fast during times of decrees, which is not common among us.

When the community decrees a fast due to any trouble that may come upon them, and similarly on the fasts of Monday, Thursday, and Monday after Passover and Sukkot, which they customarily fast, it was the custom of the early authorities that the prayer leader says "Aneinu" between "Go'el" and "Rofeh," and they read the portion "Vayechal." Our teacher, the Rema, wrote in Section 2: However, if they established the fast on Monday and Thursday, they do not displace the weekly Torah portions in the morning. Rather, they read the weekly portion in the morning, and in the evening they read the portion "Vayechal," except for the Monday, Thursday, and Monday after Passover and Sukkot, when they read "Vayechal" also in the morning. This is his language. And now, even on the Monday, Thursday, and Monday fasts, they only read the weekly portion in the morning because in our days the number of those fasting has diminished.

Indeed, it is truly perplexing regarding our custom. As the Rosh mentions at the end of the first chapter, the ancients were puzzled as to why we read "Vayechal" when a fast is decreed due to some calamity. After all, in the Tosefta, the second chapter states that for an individual fast, one does not read from the Torah. And in the Gemara, it is mentioned concerning rain, that even a large city like Nineveh is considered like individuals (14b). All the more so, it is considered like individuals regarding the "Aneinu" prayer to establish it as a separate blessing and regarding the reading of "Vayechal." Similarly, regarding Monday-Thursday-Monday fasts, the Raavad wrote: since some fast and some do not, it is obviously considered like individuals. The Rosh wrote that in Ashkenaz, everyone fasts on Monday-Thursday-Monday, and therefore it is indeed considered a public fast. Refer there. Therefore, in our times, when the vast majority do not fast, and only a very small minority fasts – how can the prayer leader recite "Aneinu," and how can we read "Vayechal"?

The Rosh, however, wrote another reason there, and the Tur brought it: that we cannot learn from Nineveh, because this pertains to the blessing of the rains, which is a fixed formula from the Men of the Great Assembly – individuals do not have the authority to change the formula and to request rain at a time when the entire world does not need it. For so it is stated in the Jerusalem Talmud that the reason is due to altering the prayer formula. But regarding a fast – every community on its own can establish a public fast, and say "Aneinu" and read "Vayechal," see there. And according to this, it makes sense regarding Monday, Thursday, and Monday, that since there are ten who are fasting – they are considered a community, and likewise on the eve of Rosh Chodesh. Similarly, in our country, the members of the Chevra Kadisha customarily fast on the fifteenth of Kislev, and say "Aneinu" and read "Vayechal" – this is also acceptable for this reason. And so it is with any established community fast that the public decrees. And during the Ten Days of Repentance, when the prayer leader does not say "Aneinu" and they do not read "Vayechal" because these fasts are for repentance, and each person's heart is broken within him and he fasts individually – it is not considered a public fast (Beit Yosef in the name of the old Mordechai, see there). And even in this, there are those who say "Aneinu" and read "Vayechal" (there), but most do not practice this way for the reason explained (and all this is included in Shulchan Aruch, section 2).

Rabbeinu the Beit Yosef wrote in Section 3: The prayer leader (Shaliach Tzibbur) does not recite "Aneinu" as a separate blessing unless there are ten people fasting in the synagogue. And even if there are ten people fasting in the city, if there are not ten people fasting in the synagogue – he does not recite it. This is his wording. And it seems clear that this applies only to public fasts that are not fixed for all of Israel, such as Mondays and Thursdays, and the eve of Rosh Chodesh. But for the four fixed fasts, and similarly for the Fast of Esther which is fixed for all of Israel – it is a day obligated for "Aneinu" and the Torah reading. And they read even if there are not ten fasting in the synagogue or the city, and it is sufficient if a few are fasting, and they go up to the Torah and pray "Aneinu." But when there are no fasters at all – it seems that "Vayechal" should not be read nor "Aneinu" recited. (This is my humble opinion, and I have seen one of the great authorities who ruled similarly. Examine and you will find it easy.)(And afterwards I saw in Shaarei Teshuvah that seven fasters are required, and this needs investigation.)

There are those who say the Selichot prayers during the blessing of "Forgive us" before its conclusion. And after the confession when they say "We have acted wickedly and we have transgressed" until "the merciful and forgiving", they conclude the blessing with "Gracious One who abundantly forgives, and compassionate and answer us." And "He who answered" they say after the prayer, since it is not related to the forgiveness of sin. And if one forgot and concluded with "Gracious One who abundantly forgives" — they should not say the Selichot until after the prayer. And there are places where initially they do not say the Selichot until after the prayer, and this is the custom of the Land of Israel. And it is proper, so as not to make a large interruption in the middle of the prayer. And so now the custom in all our countries, except in the synagogue where they say it during "Forgive us", and after the prayer they say "Our Father, our King".

Rabbeinu Nissim (Ran) states in the name of Rav Hai Gaon: The custom of the two yeshivot (academies) regarding a public fast is as follows: In the morning, they recite seven selichot (penitential prayers). In the afternoon, they recite three selichot, and if there is time, they say five. This is his wording. Nowadays, we do not say selichot during Mincha (afternoon prayer), only "Avinu Malkeinu" (Our Father, Our King). Even in the morning, we do not say seven selichot; rather, we say two selichot and a piyyut (liturgical poem), and also "El na refa na..." (Please, God, heal us...), followed by "Zachor lanu brit avot" (Remember for us the covenant of the ancestors), "Shema koleinu" (Hear our voice), the confession, "El rachum" (God of mercy), "Aneinu" (Answer us), "Mi she'ana" (He who answered), and "Avinu Malkeinu."

The Tur also wrote, and this is his language: Rabbi Natan wrote: A prayer leader who is not fasting cannot lead the prayers, because since he is not fasting, he cannot say "Aneinu." And I do not understand why, for he does not say "on the day of my fast" but "on this day of fasting," and the fast is for others. Certainly, if it is possible to have a fasting prayer leader, it is better, but if it is not possible, it seems to me that he can lead the prayers. Thus ends his language. And our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote briefly in Section 5, and this is his language: On a public fast day, a prayer leader who is not fasting should not lead the prayers. Thus ends his language. And it implies that even if there is no other, he should not lead the prayers, as per Rabbi Natan. And he ruled similarly in his larger work, see there. And there are those who wrote that if there is no other prayer leader, it is better for one who is not fasting to lead the prayers than to miss hearing Kaddish and "Barchu" (Magen Avraham, subsection 7). And I say that our teacher, the Beit Yosef, did not mean that the prayer leader should not descend before the ark at all, but only that he should not say "Aneinu." And it seems to me that on established public fasts, certainly one should follow the Tur, and he can also say "the fast of our affliction" since it includes all of Israel.

Our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 6: There are those who say that one who has not fasted should not stand to read the Torah. And if the Kohen is not fasting, he should leave the synagogue, and an Israelite who is fasting should stand to read the Torah. Thus are his words. And if the Kohen was mistakenly called up and went up and blessed, it is necessary to call a Levite after him, even if he is not fasting (Rabbi Akiva Eiger). And if it is a day that requires Torah reading, such as Monday and Thursday, even though they read "VaYechal," nevertheless, one who is not fasting may also be called up (Magen Avraham, subsection 8). And if someone who is not fasting was called up, he can say "I am not fasting" and not go up. And it seems to me that all this applies to public fasts that are not fixed. But on fixed fasts, even one who is not fasting may be called up, since the day requires Torah reading.

On a public fast day, two people should stand beside the prayer leader when he recites the Selichot, one on each side, to recite with him, similar to Moses, where "Aaron and Hur supported his hands." However, this is not the custom. One could say this is because it applies only to a complete public fast day, where the fast begins the day before and all the stringencies of a public fast are observed. And there is no true public fast day outside the Land of Israel. Know that on any public fast day, the Priestly Blessing is recited during the Mincha (afternoon) service, except on Yom Kippur because of the Ne'ilah service, as it is stated at the beginning of the fourth chapter of Taanit. However, in our practice, the Priestly Blessing is only performed on festivals, as is well known.

One who is observing a fast is allowed to taste a dish to see if it needs salt or spices, and he tastes and then spits it out. He may taste up to a quarter of a log, as long as he spits it out. And although the palate derives pleasure from this, nevertheless, there is no prohibition in this matter, for in a fast, one accepts upon oneself not to allow food or drink to enter his intestines, but he does not accept upon himself to abstain from enjoying the taste. This is not comparable to one who vows to abstain from food, for he is forbidden to taste it. There is an opinion that even if one intends to enjoy the taste, it is permitted as long as he spits it out (Magen Avraham, subsection 1). It is surprising to say this. And this is only regarding a personal fast. But on Tisha B'Av and Yom Kippur, it is forbidden, as these are complete public fasts. The other four fasts are treated in this regard like a personal fast. Thus, indeed, our teacher the Rema writes that some are stringent with all public fasts, and this is the custom. So far his words. For in a personal fast, one could say that in such a manner, one did not accept it upon himself, but not in a public fast.

And even for an individual's fast, some say that they did not permit drinking a revi'it (a specific measure of liquid) all at once, but rather little by little. And when one tastes the little bit, one should spit it out. And more than a revi'it, even throughout the entire day, is forbidden (there, subsection 4). For when one tastes a revi'it all at once, it is impossible not to swallow a little. And some say that it is permitted even a revi'it all at once, if one knows oneself that one is capable of restraining oneself from swallowing any. And the custom among us is that the woman who is cooking licks a little with her tongue to know whether it needs salt or not. And in such a case, it certainly appears that there is no concern.

One who is accustomed to rinsing his mouth in the morning on a public fast day – it is not proper to do so, for he is likely to swallow [the water] in his throat. It appears to me that this applies when one puts water deep into his mouth, tilts his head back, and lets the water flow in his throat. But if one takes water into his mouth while bending forward, intending only to clean his teeth, and there is no concern that he will swallow – it is permitted except on Tisha B'Av and Yom Kippur. However, on a private fast, it is permitted to rinse in the usual manner since he spits it out, even if there is more than a revi'it (a specific measure) of water, because he does not intend to taste it and does not derive any pleasure from the water. Therefore, with other beverages – it is forbidden, as one derives pleasure from them. (There in subsection 7, see there that he permits it with vinegar. In my humble opinion, vinegar is palatable to his taste.)

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote that it is permissible to chew cinnamon wood and other spices and sweet wood to moisten the throat, and then spit them out, except on Yom Kippur when it is forbidden. Thus are his words. Since there is no moisture of water in it, we do not concern ourselves with it, for it is only like a mere scent (and this answers the difficulty raised by the Magen Avraham in subsection 8). Swallowing saliva is of no consequence, even on Yom Kippur (ibid.). And it is impossible otherwise, for if not, we would need to stand and spit all day long.

It is stated in the Jerusalem Talmud (Nedarim, Chapter Eight): If one vowed to fast, and forgot and ate – he has lost his fast. This applies if he said "a day" in general. But if he said "this day" – he continues and completes the fast, meaning: undoubtedly on the specific day designated for fasting, such as any public fast day, or a fast due to a dream, or a yahrzeit being the day his father or mother passed away which he is accustomed to fast; or those who fast on the eve of Rosh Chodesh, and on Mondays and Thursdays and the Monday following Passover and Sukkot, or the Ten Days of Repentance, and similar times, and forgot and ate or even intentionally ate, even if he ate a lot – what he did, he did, and he will bear his iniquity. The rest of the day he continues fasting and completes it, for it is not permissible for him to eat further just because he sinned or erred unintentionally. It is not relevant to say that he has lost his fast and should eat and make up the day another time, since the fast is specifically designated for this very day.

However, if this day is not specifically designated for fasting, but rather he vowed to fast for one or two days, and he began to fast, and then he forgot and ate an olive's bulk within the time it takes to eat a half-loaf of bread, or he drank a quarter-log or a mouthful (Magen Avraham, subsection 2) – he has lost his fast, and he is permitted to eat further, but he must fast on another day. This applies when he vowed generally to fast for one or two days. Similarly, if he vowed to fast for two days and one continuous night without eating during the night in between, and he forgot and ate during that night – he has lost his fast, and he is permitted to eat, but he must fast on other days in their stead.

But if he said, "I am fasting on this day," such as if he vowed during the Mincha (afternoon) prayer of the previous day for the next day or for a specific day, and he forgot and ate, or intentionally ate – he should complete his fast. This is not considered a make-up like on a designated fast day, for what difference does it make if the day was already designated or if he designated it himself – in the end, this day is obligatory for him to fast. This is the opinion of the majority of the poskim (halachic decisors). However, the Ra'avad holds that "this day" is like any unspecified day, and he has lost his fast, and he may fulfill it on another day if he wishes, and if he wishes, he may complete his fast, and he is not obligated to make it up. This is the difference between an unspecified "day" and "this day": for an unspecified "day," he is compelled to make it up, but for "this day," it depends on his intention (Kesef Mishneh from the responsa of the Rashba, brought in Beit Yosef, see there). And this is what our Rabbi, the Rema, wrote in section 1, and this is his language: There are those who are stringent that even with a vow to fast "this day," he is obligated to complete it, nonetheless, they are stringent to fast another day. End of his language, meaning: they impose on him the stringency of both opinions: the stringency of the first opinion that he must complete it, and the stringency of the Ra'avad's opinion that he can complete it on another day. And even though we explained that according to the Ra'avad it is not mandatory, nonetheless, in order that he should not be punished for eating on the fast day – they impose this stringency on him, that he should fast another day in its place. For indeed, even for a fixed fast, it is proper to fast another day as atonement for his eating. And it seems to me that if he ate intentionally – certainly it is proper to do so, so that he may have atonement. But not if he did so unintentionally.

It is stated in Taanit (12b): A person may borrow his fast and repay it. Our Rabbis explained that this also applies when one vows to fast for a day or two or many days, and he begins to fast on one of those days, but he was not compelled to fast on that specific day, and a mitzvah event occurred where it was proper to eat; or an important person arrived, and out of respect, it was appropriate to eat; or he was hosted by an important person who requested he eat; or he was distressed by fasting — he is permitted to eat and make up the fast on another day, since he did not specify the days at the beginning of the vow. And even though he accepted it during the previous Mincha, nonetheless, he did not say to fast "tomorrow" or on "a specific day," but rather to fast for "one day." According to the Raavad, even if he said "tomorrow" or on "a specific day," he can still borrow the fast. However, this is not the accepted halacha, as the majority of poskim disagree.

Therefore, if he accepted to fast "one day," but specified "tomorrow" or "a specific day" or on a yahrtzeit, and certainly for a fixed public fast — he cannot borrow and repay the fast on another day. Similarly, with a dream fast (Shabbat 11a), the remedy is to fast specifically the day after the dream. Additionally, if one vowed to fast every Monday and Thursday for the entire year, it is considered as "this day," and he cannot borrow the fast. But if he vowed to fast for half a year on Mondays and Thursdays and did not specify "this year," he can borrow the fast. Therefore, one who vowed to fast a certain number of fasts can postpone them until the winter months when the days are shorter, and he can borrow a long day and repay with a short day, as both are considered "a day."

Some say this applies only for a short period, but for a long period, we are concerned he might die (Magen Avraham, small section 13). However, the language of the poskim does not imply this. (And this is not comparable to a vow that requires immediate action upon its arrival, as a fast is a "sit and refrain," not to eat, and it can be postponed to any time he wishes. If he dies, he has not violated his vow. Examine this thoroughly, and you will find it easy to understand.)

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (the Rema) wrote in section 2: However, regarding the fasts on Monday, Thursday, and Monday that are customary to observe after Passover and Sukkot, or even during the Ten Days of Repentance, if a circumcision occurs – it is permitted to eat. There is no need for annulment, as it is not customary to fast in such a situation. This is specifically if one eats there, but if food is sent to his home – he should not eat. And if he accepted the fast during Mincha – he needs to fast. Some say that if fasting causes him significant distress – he can redeem it with money, and the same applies in other cases of coercion. It appears that this is specifically if he accepted the fast in a general manner, but if he accepted it as a vow – he must fulfill his vow. So far his words, and his words require explanation.

And it appears to me, in my humble opinion, that the explanation is as follows: We have already explained at the beginning of Siman 562 that a fast is not a vow but rather a rabbinic commandment. And someone who has the practice to fast on certain occasions—it is also explained in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 214, that it is similar to a vow. And there, we have explained that even so, it is not considered a vow at all, see there. Therefore, even though on established public fasts or a community that decrees a fast it is forbidden to eat at any festive meal, nonetheless, on fasts that some people observe while most do not; and even those who fast do so not by vow but rather by custom, such as on Mondays and Thursdays, the Ten Days of Repentance, the eve of Rosh Chodesh, and Yahrtzeits—if a festive meal occurs, they may eat without any annulment at all. And we say that they did not adopt the custom with the intention of including a mitzvah-related matter, since a customary fast is much more lenient, and on the contrary, it is a mitzvah to eat. Therefore, if on these days a circumcision, redemption of the firstborn, or completion of a tractate occurs, one may eat without any annulment at all. And for a redemption of the firstborn not at its proper time, one should not eat, and they should hold the meal at night. (Magen Avraham, small section 10. And what he wrote in small section 9, that if one knew before Rosh Hashanah that there would be a circumcision, he should fast another day instead, see there—this is a puzzling matter, and to my knowledge, this is not the custom. Also, what he wrote in small section 5, that one should fast part of the day, see there—this is also not the custom. And what he wrote there to be lenient regarding a festive meal, even though it is not related to it, see there—this is indeed the custom in our times even on the eve of Passover for firstborns. And what he wrote even for a joyous celebration among friends, see there—this is a puzzling matter. And also what he brought from the Gemara: anyone who enjoys a meal in which a Torah scholar is present—it is as if he enjoys the radiance of the Divine Presence, see there, nonetheless, it is difficult to consider it a festive meal. And we have not heard of anyone who rules thus, see there. Examine and you will find leniency.)

These days, when one eats at a meal of a mitzvah, it is only permissible if they are invited to eat there. However, if food portions are sent to their home, they are not permitted to eat. And all this is a mere custom. Even if one responds "Amen" to the blessings of Monday and Thursday and Monday, it is not considered as accepting a fast, for one is not obligated to fast based on responding "Amen". Therefore, it is permitted to eat at a mitzvah meal; and even if they accepted it during the Mincha (afternoon prayer) before, they accepted it based on the custom (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 11). But if one accepted a fast explicitly during the Mincha before, it is forbidden to eat at a mitzvah meal, and they must fast. However, some say that since the acceptance of a fast is not like a vow, if one suffers greatly during the fast, they can redeem it with money, and similarly in other cases of compulsion, we say that they did not intend to accept it under such conditions. Yet, this applies only if they accepted it merely as a fast. But if they accepted it in the language of a vow, although it is not a complete vow without the prohibition of the object, as I wrote at the beginning of Siman 562, nevertheless, since it is in the language of a vow, they cannot redeem it with money. The amount for such redemption is explained earlier at the end of Siman 334, see there (this appears to be my humble opinion in explaining the words of the Rema).

In Yoreh De'ah, Siman 228, it is explained that one cannot annul a vow until the vow has taken effect. For example, if someone vowed not to eat meat from the beginning of the month of Iyar onwards and wants to annul his vow, he cannot annul it before Iyar. Even post facto, it does not help, see there. Therefore, one who vows to fast on Mondays and Thursdays for a year cannot annul his vow until Monday arrives. Similarly, one who vows to fast on the eve of every Rosh Chodesh, or during the Ten Days of Repentance, or on the Mondays and Thursdays following Pesach and Sukkot, and wants to annul his vow, cannot annul it until the day of the eve of Rosh Chodesh arrives, or the first day of Selichot which is considered part of the Ten Days of Repentance, or the first Monday of the Mondays and Thursdays. And similarly for all similar cases. And one who is in the middle of a fast and forgets and blesses over some fruit, and then remembers after the blessing, should conclude with "teach me Your statutes." And if he eats and drinks thinking it is still night, and they tell him that dawn has already broken, he should expel it from his mouth (see Sha'arei Teshuvah).

The early authorities wrote that two consecutive days and nights should be equated to forty non-consecutive days. Some say that for a weak person, two consecutive days are sufficient, but for a healthy person, three consecutive days are necessary. This has no relevance to someone who vows to fast, but rather to the matter of penitential fasting for those who wish to undertake repentance and atonement—this is equal to that, as this suffering is like that suffering. Additionally, it is written that it is better for the fasts to be spread out, so that at all times one’s heart will be contrite, and their sins will always be before them (Magen Avraham, subsection 6). In our times, due to the weakness of the generations, we have not heard of anyone fasting for two consecutive days without eating during the night in between.

However, someone who vowed to fast for forty days must fulfill what he vowed. This is not less stringent than "this day," where one cannot borrow and repay [in fasting]. And even according to the Raavad, who holds that even with "this day" one can borrow and repay, as I have written, here he agrees that he must fulfill his vow. There, we say that he did not accept it with the intention of causing himself suffering, and therefore he can borrow; but here, since ultimately he will suffer, he must fulfill what he accepted upon himself (there, subsection 16). All the more so for the forty days before Yom Kippur, which begin to fast after the 15th of Av, and do not fast on Shabbat and Rosh Chodesh (there, subsection 17), and they fast in remembrance of Moses ascending Mount Sinai; someone who accepted this upon himself has no compensation with consecutive days, and even if he did not accept it as a vow but just as a general fast, he cannot borrow. All the more so to repay with two or three consecutive days.

In the preceding section 288, it was explained that one may observe a fast for a disturbing dream even on Shabbat, and must subsequently observe a compensatory fast to atone for having fasted on Shabbat, as noted there. The same applies to one who fasts for a disturbing dream on a festival, Chol HaMoed, or Rosh Chodesh; they must also observe a compensatory fast. This also applies on Chanukah, Purim, and the eve of Yom Kippur; a compensatory fast is required. However, one who fasts for a disturbing dream on the fifteenth of Av, the fifteenth of Shevat, Isru Chag, or Lag BaOmer does not need to observe a compensatory fast, nor during the three days of restriction. Some say that on Rosh Chodesh Nisan or Rosh Chodesh Av, a compensatory fast is also not required, as it is considered a mitzvah to fast on these days, as I wrote in section 490 (subsection 19).

We hold that there is no public fast in the Diaspora that requires beginning the fast during the preceding day, with all its stringencies, and prohibiting labor—except for Tisha B'Av alone. Therefore, an individual who accepts a fast does not need to be concerned that he has accepted a public fast, and he is permitted in all matters. Nevertheless, it is good initially to say at the time of accepting the fast, "I am accepting a private fast for tomorrow." And if he said, "I am accepting a public fast for tomorrow," he must, against his will, begin the fast during the preceding day until he annuls his vow. And we have already written about this.

Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote in Section 7: When the day on which one's father or mother passed away occurs in Adar, and the year is a leap year, one should fast in the second Adar. This is his language, and his words are puzzling: for it is clearly written in Yoreh Deah, Siman 374, that this is according to the Rambam; but most of the poskim disagree with him and hold that the plain "Adar" is the first Adar. Therefore, Rabbeinu the Rema wrote about him: And some say that one should fast in the first [Adar], unless he passed away in the leap year in the second Adar, then they customarily fast in the second. And so the custom is to fast in the first, however, there are those who are stringent to fast in both. This is his language. And in Yoreh Deah, Siman 402, he ruled straightforwardly to fast in the first Adar and did not mention fasting in both, see there. And indeed it is a puzzling matter: Is there a biblical or rabbinic prohibition in this? For it is merely a custom, so what relevance do stringencies have here? And since according to most of our Rabbis the primary [Adar] is the first Adar – this is the law. And only one who began to practice fasting in both requires annulment.

And I have seen someone who disagrees with our master, the Rema, and holds that the main practice is to fast on both [Adars], based on the reasoning that all the mitzvot that apply to the second [Adar] also apply to the first (the Gra). And I am astonished: Are these mitzvot? Is it not merely a custom! And I am even more astonished: For it is taught regarding the dead that the judgment of the wicked in Gehenna is twelve months, and if so, if one dies in a regular Adar, the twelve months are completed in the first Adar. And according to the custom of stopping to say Kaddish one month prior, we would stop in Shevat. Therefore, it follows that the yahrzeit is in the first Adar, and this has no connection at all to other matters. Hence, it seems to my humble opinion that the main practice follows the words of our master, the Rema, and one should fast only in the first Adar. (And the Magen Avraham in subsection 20 brought a proof from Taanit 18a, where Abaye said: "It is necessary only for a leap month," and his intent was according to Rashi's first interpretation, see there. And this is puzzling: for the Adar adjacent to Nisan is always incomplete. But if you say that the moon was not visible until the thirtieth [day], then why is a second Adar needed? Furthermore, it would have been appropriate to say "for a leap year." Additionally, even according to the first interpretation, it is preferable to juxtapose redemption to redemption, as with the reading of the Megillah, and what relevance does this have to a yahrzeit? The second proof is from the day of Turainus and Nicanor, and his intent is to explain that it refers to a leap year. This is perplexing: is it not stated plainly? And if it is because it makes a difference regarding a leap year, it is stated plainly about Adar. Furthermore, juxtaposing redemption to redemption is preferable, as I wrote. Therefore, the main practice is like the Rema; and also the conclusion of the Magen Avraham is as I wrote in the name of Rabbi Shlomo HaLevi, see there. And so ruled the Eliyah Rabbah in Siman 685, subsection 6, see there.)

One only needs to fast on the day of the death of one's father and mother, not on the day of burial, even in the first year. Some say that if the day of the death of one's father or mother falls on Shabbat or Rosh Chodesh, it should be postponed to the next day. However, the custom is not like this; rather, one does not fast at all, and similarly on other days when Tachanun is not recited. Regarding the months of Cheshvan and Kislev, which can sometimes be full (30 days) and sometimes lacking (29 days), we follow the name of the day. For example, if someone died on Rosh Chodesh Kislev and it was a one-day Rosh Chodesh, and the following year it is a two-day Rosh Chodesh, the yahrzeit is on the second day of Rosh Chodesh. Conversely, if someone died on the first day of Rosh Chodesh and the following year Rosh Chodesh is one day, the yahrzeit is on Rosh Chodesh and not on the eve of Rosh Chodesh. Even though the first day of Rosh Chodesh is the thirtieth day of the previous month, it is still called Rosh Chodesh (see Taz at the end of subsection 4, who did not write this, and many have questioned him), and similarly for other similar cases (and also the Magen Avraham’s words in subsection 20 have been questioned by the Pri Megadim, as noted by the Machatzit Hashekel). Similarly, if someone died in a leap year on the first day of Rosh Chodesh Adar Sheni, and the following year is a regular year, one should fast on the first day of Rosh Chodesh Adar (Magen Avraham there, and there is a printing mistake as noted by the Machatzit Hashekel, see there). And similarly for all such cases.

One who vows to go to the graves of righteous individuals in a certain place, and is delayed for many days, and afterwards is hired to go there – this journey suffices. And so with all similar cases. However, if one vowed to spend a certain amount on this journey – he does not fulfill his obligation until he gives the expenses to charity (see Magen Avraham, subsection 21, and delve into it and you will find it easy). Similarly, one who vows to fast a certain number of consecutive days, and during this period there is a mandatory fast – it counts for him. Likewise, one who fasts a dream fast, or who adds an additional fast to his original fast, and on that day there is a mandatory fast – it counts for him. (And with two vows – one does not count for the other, as written by the Magen Avraham, subsection 22. And see Yoreh De'ah, section 239.)

Anyone who is fasting, whether he is fasting due to his own troubles or because of a dream, or whether he is fasting with the community due to their troubles, should not indulge himself. That is to say, he should not engage in any kind of pleasure. He should not be frivolous, nor should he be joyful and light-hearted. He should also guard himself from anger, quarrels, and disputes, but rather be concerned and pensive, as it is said, "What shall a living man complain about?"

An individual who vowed to fast due to some distress and began to fast, and the distress passed in the middle of the day — nevertheless, he is obligated to complete the fast. Moreover, even if he fasted for a sick person to recover, and the sick person died — nevertheless, he is obligated to complete the fast. Furthermore, even if he accepted upon himself many fasts — he is obligated to fast all of them. We do not say: "Behold, we testify that he only accepted them on the condition that the sick person would recover," for in the end, these are thoughts in his heart and are not considered, since he accepted the fasts without specifying. Certainly, if he said, "I accept these fasts on the condition that the sick person will recover" and the person died — he is exempt from fasting. But if he accepted the fasts without specification — he is obligated.

If someone makes a vow to give charity on behalf of a sick person, and he says, "I hereby vow to give charity on behalf of this sick person on the condition that he recovers," and the sick person dies, he is exempt [from fulfilling the vow], and only what he has already given is given. But if he says, "I hereby vow to give such and such amount of charity on behalf of this sick person," and the sick person dies, he is obligated to pay the full amount he vowed; even though it is evident that he only vowed on the condition that the sick person would recover, nevertheless, these are unspoken thoughts and are not considered valid.

But it is not the same with the community. If the community fasted for a certain matter and were answered before midday, they do not need to complete the fast, as we learned regarding the fasts for rain at the beginning of the third chapter of Taanit (19a): because we do not burden the community excessively. Also, the community fasts with the understanding that if the trouble passes before midday, they do not need to complete the fast. All the more so, if the community fasted for a sick person and he died, they do not need to complete the fast. Nevertheless, if the Torah scholars and the majority of the community wish to complete the fast, an individual is not permitted to separate himself from them. (See Magen Avraham, subsection 1, who wrote that according to the Rosh, if the sick person dies, they need to complete the fast. In my humble opinion, this is not so. It is a fortiori: if they were answered, it implies a similar case as with rain. Moreover, he does not wish to mention a bad matter. But he does not disagree with the Ran. This is also the language of the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch. Pay attention and you will find it easy.)

However, when an error is discovered in the actual acceptance of the fast, even an individual is exempt from completing it. For example, an individual who fasts due to a distressing situation and it becomes known that before the acceptance of the fast the distress had already passed, or the sick person had died, he does not need to complete the fast. Similarly, for the charity vowed for the sick person, because the acceptance or vow was made in error. All the more so for a community, if they hear even after midday that the distress had already passed, they do not need to complete it, for an acceptance made in error is considered nothing.

Maimonides wrote in Chapter Three of Nedarim, Law 9: A person who vows to fast on Shabbat or a festival is obligated to fast, for vows take effect on a matter of a commandment. Similarly, one who vows to fast every Sunday or every Tuesday for the rest of his life and one of these days coincides with a festival or the eve of Yom Kippur, he is obligated to fast. Needless to say, this applies to Rosh Chodesh. If it coincides with Chanukah or Purim, his vow is deferred because of these days; since the prohibition of fasting on these days is by rabbinic decree, they require reinforcement, and his vow is deferred in favor of the decree of the Sages. Up to here is his wording. However, the Tur in Yoreh De'ah 215 ruled that the vow applies even to them, and he can annul his vow. This is when it was accepted in the form of a vow. But if it was accepted in the form of accepting a fast, it does not override Shabbat and festivals, nor Chanukah and Purim, and there is no need for an inquiry at all, see there. This is according to what we explained at the beginning of Siman 562, that there is a difference between a vow and a fast. This is also the opinion of the Ra'avad, the Ramban, the Rosh, and the Ran, as we explained there in Yoreh De'ah in this Siman, paragraph 19, see there.

And this is what our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in Section 1: An individual who accepted upon himself a fast for such and such days, and among them occurred Shabbatot (Sabbaths) and Yomim Tovim (festivals), or Rosh Chodesh, Chanukah, and Purim, or the eve of Yom Kippur, if he accepted it in the general language of accepting a fast - he does not need an annulment. But if he accepted it in the language of "Behold, it is upon me," which is the language of a vow - he needs an annulment by a sage. And he should start with regret, saying to him: "Had you considered that these days would occur, you would not have vowed," and he annuls it for him. According to the Rambam, if he accepted it as a vow, and he encountered Shabbatot and Yomim Tovim, or the eve of Yom Kippur, or Rosh Chodesh - he is obligated to fast on them unless he gets an annulment. But if he encountered Chanukah and Purim - his vow is void and he does not fast on them, because they are from the words of the Sages and require reinforcement. Thus far is his language. The explanation is that when he said "Behold, it is upon me," he must say "Behold, it is upon me, the eating of a certain day is Konam (prohibited as a sacrifice)," or a vow or prohibition. But if he said "Behold, it is upon me to fast" – it is not called a vow (Magen Avraham section 2), because we require an object of prohibition, and fasting is not an object. And it is considered as any acceptance of a fast.

The main ruling follows the opinion of the majority of the decisors. If someone vowed to fast for a certain number of days and said "except for holidays" — Hanukkah and Purim are not included because they are not referred to as "holidays" in common parlance. However, if he said that his intention was to include them, he is believed. The eve of Yom Kippur is included as a "holiday," and certainly Rosh Hashanah and Chol HaMoed are included. But Rosh Chodesh is not included, unless he said that his intention was also to include Rosh Chodesh.

One who vows to fast on Shabbat, and Yom Tov, and Erev Yom Kippur, and Chanukah, and Purim, and Rosh Chodesh—their status is the same as one who vows to fast for a certain number of days and these days happen to fall within those. If one expressed it in the language of a vow, the vow takes effect and requires annulment. However, if one expressed it in the language of accepting a fast, the vow does not take effect and does not require annulment. (See what I wrote in Siman 674 regarding Erev Yom Kippur according to the Rambam's opinion.)

It is well known that although a vow applies to a mitzvah (commandment), an oath does not apply unless it is inclusive, as I have written in Yoreh De'ah section 215. Therefore, if one swears to fast for a certain number of days and those days include days on which one is obligated to fast by a mitzvah, the oath is valid due to its inclusivity. However, if one explicitly swears to fast on Shabbat or Yom Tov, the oath does not take effect. This is considered a false oath, and he is liable to lashes and must eat, as an oath does not apply to a mitzvah. If one swears to fast on Chanukah or Purim, the oath is binding because these are only rabbinic obligations. Nevertheless, one should annul the oath and not fast. The same applies to Rosh Chodesh and the eve of Yom Kippur, which are also rabbinic obligations. However, according to Maimonides, these obligations are from the Torah (as implied in Rosh Hashanah 19a). Some say that Rosh Chodesh is rabbinic, and the eve of Yom Kippur is from the Torah (as per Magen Avraham section 9). In both cases, one should annul the oath to satisfy all opinions.

On fast days that a person is not commanded to observe, there is a dispute in the Gemara (Taanit 11b): One says that anyone who sits in a fast is called "holy," while another says he is called a "sinner." Both of these are the words of the living God. Certainly, if he can endure the fast and it does not lead to neglect of Torah study, he is called "holy," as through this his sins are cleansed. If not, if he is not healthy and strong, he is called a "sinner." All this applies to one who fasts for reasons of asceticism. But someone who is a sinner certainly should fast for his sins, and cry and confess before God, and then he will be healed, unless the fast would bring him to danger, in which case he is forbidden to fast. Similarly, if he is a great Torah scholar, it is better for him to minimize fasts and increase Torah study. Otherwise, a Torah scholar is not permitted to fast, as it reduces his heavenly work. All the more so for teachers of children, as there are two concerns: the neglect of the Torah study of the children and stealing from the employers. Also, any worker is not permitted to increase fasts, as it reduces the work of the employer. However, on public fasts, Torah scholars, teachers, and workers are obligated to fast, and one is forbidden to separate himself from the community. This is the understanding on which they were accepted. And all those involved in communal needs have the same status as teachers. Regarding fasting, a Torah scholar has the same status even in this time. A minor boy or girl who accepts upon themselves a fast is like a vow, as explained in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 234, see there.

There are times when one is obligated and needs to decree a fast, but it is impossible. For example, if they decreed that they should not decree a fast, or if there is a plague and it is impossible to decree a fast because it is dangerous to fast during the plague. Or in a city surrounded by enemies, where it is impossible to frighten the city's inhabitants by decreeing a fast. Similarly, an individual who is pursued by an oppressor, or who is afflicted by an evil spirit, and cannot fast at this time. What should they do? They should accept upon themselves a certain number of fasts to be observed when they are saved or when the decree passes.

The ethical works have written that someone who desires to eat and eats, and in the middle stops his hand from his desire – this is a great thing, a significant repentance, and considered as self-affliction (Magen Avraham, end of subparagraph 1).

According to the Talmudic law, one should not initially decree fasts for the community on Thursday, so as not to raise market prices. When people see that two meals are being purchased, one for the night and one for Shabbat, they might think that a famine has come to the world and will raise the price of grain. Even in a place where there is no concern for this, one should not do so. Nevertheless, nowadays, when price manipulators are not common, it has been written that it is permissible to decree a fast on Thursday. And this is the custom (Magen Avraham, subsection 2).

One does not decree fasts on the community on Rosh Chodesh, Chanukah, Purim, or Chol HaMoed. However, if they began to fast due to a distress, even for one day, and one of these days occurs, they continue and complete the fast on that day. And even though Rosh Chodesh is called a "festival," nevertheless it is not a day of feasting and joy. This applies to communal fasts. But for an individual's fast, one interrupts on these days. And nowadays, all fasts that the community decrees are considered like an individual's fast, and one interrupts on Rosh Chodesh and completes the fast on another day (Beit Yosef and Magen Avraham, subsection 4). And this is the custom (Bach).

It appears to me that for an individual fast, when one has accepted upon themselves to fast for a certain number of days, they should also break the fast on other days where Tachanun is not recited. Since these days are established among us as days on which one should not fast, it is certain that this was also their intention, unless explicitly stated otherwise. Similarly, nowadays for the community, whose status is like that of an individual in this regard, as I have written, the same law applies when they have not explicitly stated an intention to fast even on these days.

A congregation that wishes to decree a fast on Monday, Thursday, and Monday, and they decreed thus, and the first fast coincided with the 15th of Shevat—they should not begin to fast on that day, for certainly their intention was not for it. Rather, it should be postponed to the following Monday or Thursday, because it is the New Year for Trees, and it is not proper to begin a fast on it. However, if they began to fast, they do not interrupt it, for it is not more lenient than Rosh Chodesh or Chol HaMoed. Therefore, nowadays, since an individual fast is considered significant as I have written—they interrupt even if they have begun, as I have written.

And all this pertains to fasting. But an individual who has accepted upon himself not to eat meat for such and such a number of days – he is forbidden to eat even on Shabbat and Yom Tov, since there is no obligation to eat meat specifically, unless he specifies that his intention did not include Shabbatot and Yomim Tovim. And if a community decreed in such a manner – it depends on the intention of the Beit Din (see Magen Avraham, subsection 5). And the same law applies to anything that an individual or the public accepts upon themselves, like wine, beer, fish, and similar items.

In the days of the early Tannaim, there was "Megillat Taanit," which comprised the days on which the Holy One, blessed be He, performed miracles for Israel, and on those days it was forbidden to deliver eulogies or to fast. And it is taught in Rosh Hashanah (19b): These days that are written in Megillat Taanit, whether the Temple is standing or not, are forbidden; these are the words of Rabbi Meir. Rabbi Yose says: (...) When the Temple is not standing, they are permitted. And the law follows Rabbi Yose. And the Talmud rules there that the halacha is that Megillat Taanit is nullified, except for Chanukah and Purim, on which it is forbidden to fast themselves. But before and after them, it is permitted in our time, even though in the time of the Temple it was forbidden. And all of Megillat Taanit – even in these days it is permitted, all the more so before and after them. Similarly, on Shabbatot, Yamim Tovim, and Rosh Chodesh, it is permitted to fast both before and after them. And this was even during the time of the Temple. And the reason for this matter is as follows: The reason they forbade fasting before and after in Megillat Taanit during the time of the Temple was to strengthen the significance of the days themselves. This applies to rabbinic ordinances which require reinforcement, but Shabbat, Yamim Tovim, and Rosh Chodesh, which are from the Torah and it is forbidden to fast on them, do not require reinforcement. (Rosh Hashanah there. And there it is explained that Rosh Chodesh is from the Torah, see there. And see the end of Siman 570, and it requires investigation.)

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote: One who has a wedding during Chanukah should not fast. However, if he has a wedding in Nissan, he should fast on his wedding day, even on Rosh Chodesh Nissan, because it is one of the days on which fasting is customary, as explained later at the end of Siman 580. This is the end of his words. Similarly, on Lag B'Omer, the three days of Hagbalah, and the days between Yom Kippur and Sukkot, one should fast, since it is only a custom. But on Isru Chag, the 15th of Av, and the 15th of Shevat, since they are mentioned in the Gemara, one should not fast (Magen Avraham). The reason for the groom's fast on his wedding day is explained in Even HaEzer Siman 61; see there.

One who travels from a place where they are fasting to a place where they are not fasting, if they were not in their city at the time when the fast was accepted upon themselves – the fast does not apply to them at all. In this case, the stringencies of the place from which they came do not apply, because one does not decree upon someone who is not in the city (see Taz). If they were in their city at the time the fast was decreed, and they also accepted the fast upon themselves – they are obligated to fast and complete it, even if they do not intend to return. However, if they were in the city but did not explicitly accept the fast, it depends: if they intend to return, they are included among them, and the stringencies of the place from which they came apply to them, obligating them to fast and complete it. If they do not intend to return, the fast does not apply to them, just as the other stringencies of the place from which they came do not apply if they do not intend to return. (This clarifies the words of Rashi and Tosafot in Ta’anit 10a. Rashi, in his comment beginning with "to a place," explains it is due to the stringencies of the place. Tosafot, in their comment beginning with "one who travels," explain that it applies even if they do not intend to return. See there. They do not disagree as I have written. See there. Be precise and you will find clarity.)

And one who goes from a place where they do not fast to a place where they do fast, and arrives there on the day of the fast, by law, if they intend to return, the fast does not apply to them at all. Nonetheless, it is forbidden for them to eat while they are there, so as not to separate from the community. However, since they did not accept the fast upon themselves, if they leave the city beyond its boundaries, they are permitted to eat and are not required to complete the fast. But within the city and its boundaries, it is forbidden for them to eat even in private, because they need to participate in the community's distress. However, if the distress has passed, they are permitted to eat in private. And if they do not intend to return under any circumstances, the fast applies to them even beyond the boundary, and even if the distress has passed, according to the stringencies of the place to which they have gone.

And all this applies when he only arrived here on the day of the fast itself, and not earlier at the time of accepting the fast. But if he arrived earlier and was there at the time when they accepted the fast, he is obligated to accept the fast and must complete it, so as not to separate himself from the community. Consequently, there is no difference whether he is within the city or outside its boundaries, whether he intends to return or not, since he accepted the fast upon himself. However, if he did not accept it upon himself and intends to return, the fast does not apply to him, and he is only prohibited from eating in their presence, meaning within the city and its boundaries. In a situation where he has nothing to eat due to participating with the community and not by law, and he forgot and ate, he should not appear before them as if he ate, and he should not indulge himself by saying, "Since I ate a little, I will eat a lot." Rather, he must stop immediately once he remembers. Even outside the boundaries, he should not indulge himself, but should eat only enough to sustain his life. He should not conduct himself with indulgences in eating and drinking and other pleasures (see Magen Avraham, subsection 4).

It is a mitzvah for a person to afflict themselves during a year of famine, in order to share in the suffering of the community. Similarly, in any distress, it is a mitzvah to share in the community's pain. If one is able to help them, they are obligated to do so; if not, they should still share in their suffering. Only if they are in a place of danger is one not obligated to endanger themselves as well, if it does not benefit the community (Magen Avraham, subsection 6). One should not engage in marital relations during years of famine, except on the night of immersion. Someone who has no children and has not yet fulfilled the mitzvah of procreation is permitted. Some say this ruling is not strictly halachic but a measure of piety (Tosafot, Yoma 11a, s.v. "it is forbidden"). Therefore, if it might lead to sin, one is permitted to engage in marital relations. Nowadays, years of famine are uncommon (see Taz, Magen Avraham, and Sha'arei Teshuvah).

The order of fasts that are observed in the Land of Israel for rain is as follows: The time for requesting rain in the Land of Israel is the third of Marcheshvan, as I wrote above in Siman 117. If rain does not fall then, we wait until the seventeenth of the month, because until this time there is no damage to the crops yet. If the seventeenth arrives and no rain has fallen, the scholars alone begin to fast on Monday, Thursday, and Monday. All the scholars are suitable for this, meaning if one knows how to respond to a halachic matter in any place, he is obligated to fast. If he has not reached this level, he is not obligated. Nevertheless, if he wants to, he can include himself among the scholars, and there is no arrogance in this (see Magen Avraham and Taz, subsection 1). But ordinary people cannot fast, because they are not fit to include themselves among the scholars. And although in the Gemara (10b) some permit everyone to fast, we do not hold this way. And even though in Siman 554 regarding work on Tisha B'Av, we hold that anyone can make himself like a scholar, see there—it is not comparable at all. Regarding work, many do not work, and there are also places where the custom is that no one works, as I wrote there. And it is not such a significant matter. But regarding fasts fixed only for scholars, there is arrogance, and also considering oneself worthy that his prayer will be accepted. Therefore, one should not do this. (See Magen Avraham, subsection 1, who raised a difficulty and resolved it. According to what I wrote, it fits simply. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

And these fasts are like the fasts of an individual, without starting them from the previous day, and without the stringencies of a public fast, because the lack of rain has not yet become so severe. But if the month of Kislev arrives and it has not rained, the court decrees three fasts on all the community, on Monday, Thursday, and Monday. And all the people gather in the synagogues, and pray, and cry out, and plead as they do on all fasts: with the reading of "Vayechal," and with "Aneinu" and "Avinu Malkeinu." And they are still not like public fasts that begin from the previous day, because we do not burden the community so much, and there is still a remedy for the crops if it rains from now on.

If these [three fasts] have passed and they have not been answered, the court decrees another three fasts on the community, on Monday, Thursday, and Monday. On these fasts, one must cease eating while it is still day, just like on Tisha B'Av. However, the additional period like on Yom Kippur is certainly not necessary, as it should not be more stringent than Tisha B'Av. Its twilight period is forbidden just like Tisha B'Av. They are prohibited from doing work during the day but not at night. And even though on Tisha B'Av it depends on the custom of the place, in these fasts, which require people to pay attention to their deeds, it is necessary not to work during the day, for if they do, they will be preoccupied and will not pay attention to their actions. They are prohibited from washing the entire body with hot water, thus the bathhouses are closed. However, washing the face, hands, and feet with hot water, and the whole body with cold water is permitted. In this respect, it is less stringent than Tisha B'Av because it is hard for the public to go three days without this. They are prohibited from anointing, except to remove dirt; for anointing, it is like Tisha B'Av since they can endure without anointing. They are prohibited from marital relations like on Tisha B'Av, and also from wearing shoes in the city like on Tisha B'Av. They pray in synagogues and supplicate like on other fasts, and they do not add blessings in the prayer except for "Aneinu" alone.

And if these (three fasts) have passed and they were not answered – the court decrees another seven fasts upon the entire community: Monday, Thursday, Monday, Thursday, Monday, Thursday, and Monday. And it is obvious that everything that is forbidden during the first three fasts is also forbidden during these seven fasts. These seven are stricter than the preceding three in that they blow the shofar during the additional blessings in the Amidah prayer, and they pray in the city square to invoke a cry of distress. They also send down an elder and a sage to rebuke them, if there is an elder and a sage. If not, they send down a sage even if he is not an elder. If not, they send down a person of stature, whose words are respected. He stands and says: "Our brothers! It is not sackcloth and fasting that cause [divine favor]…", as will be explained in Siman 579. The additional blessings will also be explained there with the help of Heaven.

In addition to this, we are stringent with these later ones, closing the stores to increase the grief. And on Monday towards evening, they open a little those stores that sell food and drink, so that people can find something to buy for their evening meal. On Thursday, these stores are open all day because of the honor of Shabbat. If the store has two entrances, one is closed, and one is opened. However, if it has only one entrance, it is opened as usual. If the store has a counter facing the entrance, thereby making the opening less noticeable to the public, it is opened as usual even on Monday (Rashi 14b), and even if it has two entrances. But our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 4 that it is only on Thursday that it is permitted with a counter, as Rambam wrote in the third chapter. And the Tur wrote generally, see there.

Pregnant and nursing women fast during the middle three [fasts]. But not during the first three because they are still light, and not during the last seven because it is not possible to impose so many fasts on them after they have already fasted three fasts. (This resolves the difficulty of the Magen Avraham, subsection 5, see there). And they are forbidden to be stringent and fast, so that they do not come to danger. However, they should only eat enough to sustain the fetus. Similarly, whenever a fast is decreed on the community, the weak are not included. All the more so pregnant and nursing women, as they certainly are not more stringent than the first three [fasts] during which they do not fast, as I have written. And Rambam wrote that pregnant and nursing women only fast during the last seven, see there. This does not align with our version of the Gemara (Taanit 14a) and in the Jerusalem Talmud, it says that they fast during the first and middle ones, but not the last ones, see there. This does not align with our Talmud.

When the Holy Temple was standing, and these fasts were decreed, in the Temple there were the people of the watch (mishmar) whose watch was during that week, and the people of the house of the father (beit av) from that watch were divided into family groups, and each family group served on its day. Now, during the first three [fasts], even the people of the watch did not fast. During the middle three [fasts], the people of the watch would fast for part of the day but would not complete [the fast], and the people of the house of the father, upon whom the work of the day was incumbent, would not fast at all. During the last seven [fasts], the people of the watch would fast and complete [the fast], while the people of the house of the father would fast for part of the day but would not complete [the fast].

And after they decreed these thirteen fasts, no more are decreed, even if they were not answered. And this applies when fasting for rain, because once these have passed, the time for rain has already passed, and there is no benefit. But for other calamities, they continue to fast until they are answered from Heaven.

And when they fast for rain, and these thirteen fasts have passed and they were not answered—they reduce business transactions and building for joy, except if the wall is about to fall. And even business transactions are only forbidden if they are for joy. And what is considered building and business transactions for joy? Those related to betrothals and weddings; and it has been explained above in Siman 551 regarding before the Ninth of Av, look there. And they reduce betrothals and weddings, meaning: they should not betroth or marry unless they have not yet fulfilled the mitzvah of procreation. And they reduce greeting one another. This means minimizing it as much as possible, for to cancel it completely is impossible for the general populace. However, Torah scholars should not greet at all, and should behave as if they are rebuked by Heaven, since they cried out and were not answered. And if an unlearned person greets a Torah scholar, they should respond to him softly and with seriousness. And even though they stopped fasting, nevertheless, the Torah scholars alone fast on Monday, Thursday, and Monday until the end of the month of Nisan of the season, which is thirty days after the season of Nisan. They are permitted to eat at night and are permitted in labor, and they cease on Rosh Chodesh and Purim. And when the month of Nisan of the season ends, which is when the sun reaches the beginning of the constellation of Taurus—they do not fast anymore, because rain at that time is a sign of a curse if it did not rain at all until that time. (What is written in the Shulchan Aruch, section 7: "and they cease on Rosh Chodesh of Chanukah...", is a printing error. For Chanukah has already passed.)

And all this order is when no rain has fallen at all. But if rain has fallen in the first rainfall, as is the usual manner of rain that saturates the earth, and the grasses have sprouted, and then the rain stops and the grasses begin to dry up - they fast and cry out until rain falls, or conversely until the plants dry up completely, God forbid, and there is no longer any benefit. Similarly, if the time of Passover or near it arrives, which is the time of the blossoming of the trees in the Land of Israel, and no rain has fallen - they fast and cry out until rain falls that is suitable for the trees, or conversely until their time passes and there will be no benefit at all. Likewise, if the festival of Sukkot arrives and not much rain has fallen to fill the cisterns, ditches, and caves - they fast until rain falls that is suitable for the cisterns. And if they do not have water to drink - they fast for the rain at any time they do not have water to drink, even in the summer months. And if forty days pass between one rainfall and the next during the rainy season - this is considered a drought, and they fast and cry out until rain falls, or conversely until the time passes.

All of these matters are only stated regarding the Land of Israel and its surroundings, where the rainy season is in Marcheshvan, following the order we mentioned. However, in places where the rainy season is at other times of the year, like in our area where the rainy season is after Pesach, when their time arrives and rain has not fallen, individuals fast on Monday, Thursday, and Monday, and they stop on Rosh Chodesh, Chanukah, and Purim if the rainy season falls then, and then they wait about six days. If rain has not fallen, the court decrees thirteen fasts in the order we mentioned. However, these do not have the severity of the fasts in the Land of Israel, where they stop eating before the day begins. But outside the Land of Israel, it is not so; rather, they eat at night, and their status is like other individual fasts. The severity of a public fast, like on Tisha B'Av and Yom Kippur, only applies in the Land of Israel and for rain, and during those ten fasts which include the three middle ones and the last seven, but not for other decrees. And outside the Land of Israel, even for rain, it is not so.

If they were fasting for rain and were answered, how much rain must fall for them to cease fasting? It must penetrate the dry earth to a depth of one handbreadth, in medium soil to a depth of two handbreadths, and in plowed soil to a depth of three handbreadths. The amount of rain required to make a blessing on it is explained earlier in Siman 221. If this amount of rain falls after midday, they should complete the fast for that day. If it falls before midday, they should not complete the fast but eat, drink, and celebrate. In the evening, they should gather and recite the "Great Hallel," which consists of the twenty-six verses of "for His kindness endures forever." The "Great Hallel" is only recited on a full stomach and when the soul is satisfied. The fact that we recite it on Shabbat and Yom Tov during the verses of praise in the prayer service is not an issue. In places where drunkenness is common, they recite the "Great Hallel" before eating and drinking (Gemara). Likewise, if the majority of the community wishes to complete the fast, they should recite it before eating (Magen Avraham, subsection 11). There are those who disagree with this (Eliyah Rabbah).

It seems clear to me that only when rain falls in the amount specified before midday should they not complete the fast, similar to when it rains after midday. For certainly, if this were not the case, there would be no novelty in the ruling. This is also evident from the language of the Gemara and the Rambam. Based on this, the language of the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch, section 11, which states: "If the rain began to fall before midday," is not understandable, as it implies that only if the rain began to fall before midday, even if the amount was not completed until after midday, they should not complete the fast. This is puzzling: have they not fulfilled the fast without the required amount? And if they were exempted after midday, why should they not complete the fast? Additionally, what compelled them to change the language of the Talmud? Therefore, it seems to me that it is not to be taken literally, and in the term "began," both the beginning and the completion are included, as with "after midday." For certainly, this is the case, but it still requires further analysis.

"The 'Great Hallel' is recited only if they were answered on the day of their fast specifically. However, if they were not answered until the day after their fast, it is not recited, because they were not answered due to the fast, but rather Heaven had mercy on them. Similarly, if rain fell for them on the night of their fast, before dawn, 'the Great Hallel' is also not recited, because the primary answer is after dawn (Taz and Magen Avraham). We do not know the reason for this matter."

Some say that during the recitation of "Hallel Hagadol," one should afterward say: "We give thanks to You for every drop and drop...," as I wrote in Siman 241. Afterward, each individual does not need to recite the blessing for rain as explained there (Magen Avraham, small section 12). In the Piskei Tosafot, it is found that one should begin before "Hallel Hagadol" with: "A Song of Ascents: Behold, bless the Lord... who stand in the house of the Lord at night...," because the song of the rains is at night. And they say "He raises the clouds from the ends of the earth..." (there). It seems to me that this is a mistake, and it should be said: because the coming down of the rains at night is a sign of blessing, as our Sages expounded in Taanit (23a) on the verse "And I will give your rains in their time" – on Wednesday nights and Shabbat nights, see there. And so it is in the Midrashim, that this was the case during the time of the building of the Temple. However, in Pesachim (118a), there is a dispute about this, see there. And in the Jerusalem Talmud, at the end of the third chapter of Taanit, it also implies this, see there that it says "who stand in the house of the Lord." But it seems more that it refers to the Psalm "Hallelujah, praise the servants of the Lord who stand in the house of the Lord," for it says there: "He raises the clouds," and this is in this Psalm. And also in the Piskei Tosafot, it is required to say this verse.
