It has already been explained at the beginning of Siman 592 in the name of the Rambam that it is a positive commandment from the Torah, for any calamity that befalls the community, to cry out and sound the trumpets, as it is written, "When an enemy oppresses you, you shall sound the trumpets." And by rabbinic decree, it is customary to fast, as mentioned there. However, in the responsa of the Geonim, it is stated that they blow the shofar (Ran, first chapter). This is also implied in the Gemara (14a): "With what do they sound the alarm? With shofars." Similarly, it is stated in the Jerusalem Talmud, where it says: "In front of Rabbi Yishmael they blew the shofar on a fast day." Rabbi Yossi inquires: "Shouldn't they blow the trumpets?" And he answers: "Have you not heard that trumpets are used in the Temple, and there are no trumpets in the provinces?" Refer to there. It must be said that what was stated in Rosh Hashanah (26b) that in the provinces, where there is a shofar there are no trumpets, and where there are trumpets there is no shofar, indicates that there are trumpets in the provinces without a shofar only at the time of war (there). And the Rashba, of blessed memory, wrote that they can blow either the shofar or the trumpets (Magid Mishneh).

And in what place do they sound the alarm? As explained in the Gemara (Taanit 16b), during the six additional blessings added in the final fasts for rain. Similarly, for all troubles, they add these six blessings, as the Tur wrote at the beginning of Siman 579, and these are his words: "Each day of the last seven fasts, or other fasts during which they sound the alarm, they follow this order...," see there. And they blow the shofar and sound the alarm at the end of each blessing with a tekiah-teruah-tekiah, as the Tur wrote there. However, the Rambam in the fourth chapter wrote that only in the Temple did they blow after each blessing, but in the provinces, they would blow after the prayer. And they would not blow but sound the alarm with trumpets, and this is the practice for any communal trouble fast. (The Gemara there explains that when the matter was brought before the sages, they said: this custom was only practiced on the Temple Mount, see there, which also refers to the blasts in the order of the blessings. But according to Rashi and the Tur, it only refers to the response "Blessed is the Lord...," see there. This is also seemingly the simple understanding of the sugya, see there.)

There are those who have questioned: since according to the Torah, we are to sound the trumpets or the shofar during times of distress, why do we not do so and sound [these instruments] during times of distress (Magen Avraham)? And [while] we decree a fast, which is of Rabbinic origin, we do not perform the sounding, which is of Torah origin! It appears to me that this is not difficult at all, for we hold like Rashi and the Tur that the soundings are at the conclusion of each of the six additional blessings, as will be explained in Siman 579. And since there is no public fast outside of the Land [of Israel], it follows that these six additional blessings are not present, and there is no place to sound [the instruments]. And even though the blessings are certainly of Rabbinic origin and the sounding is of Torah origin, nevertheless, since the Sages instituted [the sounding] in a specific context, consequently, when that context is not present, it is impossible to sound [the instruments]. For in a "sit and do not act" scenario, it can be done in this manner, as is known.

And furthermore, it appears to me in my humble opinion that the warning (teruah) is not mandated by the Torah except during the time of the Temple. And you should know that this is so, as according to the Jerusalem Talmud we cited, trumpets were only used in the Temple. Therefore, the verse that states "and you shall sound the trumpets" (Numbers 10:9) must necessarily refer specifically to the time of the Temple. Moreover, since in that verse it is written "And when you go to war in your land" (Numbers 10:9), this only applies during the time of the Temple. And all the verses in that section only pertain to the time of sacrifices, as it is written (Numbers 10:10) "On your days of rejoicing... you shall sound the trumpets over your burnt offerings...". Certainly, prayer and crying out to God are mandated by the Torah even outside the Land of Israel, as it is written (Deuteronomy 4:29-30): "When you are in distress... and you will seek...". There are many verses about this, but not regarding the warning (teruah). It seems to me that this is why the Gemara states: How do we sound the warning? With shofars. This is indeed difficult, as the Torah specifies "trumpets". However, it is certainly referring to outside the Land of Israel during the exile, or even in the Land of Israel in present times. The Torah mandated this only during the time of the Temple, and during the period of destruction, it is rabbinic in nature. Therefore, they instituted the use of the shofar as on Rosh Hashanah (this is how it appears to me in my humble opinion).

Just as we fast and cry out in prayer for rain, so too we fast and cry out in prayer for other troubles. For example, during the time of the Temple when Israel had sovereignty in their land, and non-Jews came to wage war against Israel, or to impose a tax on them, or to take land from them, or to decree a trouble upon them even in a minor commandment – they would fast and cry out in prayer until they were shown mercy from Heaven. All the cities around them would fast but not cry out in prayer, unless they blew the shofar to gather for their aid. Even if [the non-Jews] only came to pass through their land, not to wage war against them but against other nations, and they pass through their place – they would fast and cry out in prayer, as it is stated (Leviticus 26:6): "And a sword shall not pass through your land" – even just passing through, and not waging war against you; even a peaceful sword. And since this is included in the blessings, it implies that the opposite is the opposite of a blessing.

And similarly regarding an epidemic. What qualifies as an epidemic? A city with five hundred residents – meaning strong and able-bodied men, which implies that this count does not include women, children, or elderly who have ceased from labor – and three people die from it over three consecutive days, dying in their beds, this is considered an epidemic. This excludes cases where one of them was killed, drowned, or was already ill – these do not count. If they die in one day or over four days, this is not considered an epidemic, as it is just a coincidence (Rashi 21b). Similarly, even if two die on one day and the third on the next day or on the third day. An epidemic is specifically three, each dying on one day (ibid.).

If there are a thousand inhabitants in the city, and six people die from it over the course of three consecutive days—specifically two each day—this is considered an epidemic. If they die on one day or over the course of two days, even if some of them die on the third day, or over the course of four days, this is not considered an epidemic. The same applies according to this ratio. There is a question about this: if so, a city with 250 inhabitants will never have an epidemic, because according to this calculation, it would require one and a half deaths in one and a half days, which is impossible; it has to be either less or more. In such a scenario, it would not be considered an epidemic. This issue arises whenever the number is not a whole number. Additionally, according to the calculation, for 500 inhabitants, three deaths are needed over three days, which amounts to approximately one death per 167 people. So, if there are 150 people in the city and one of them dies, would that be considered an epidemic? It is doubtful. Therefore, we must say that the statement "up to 500 inhabitants" means that fewer than three deaths in three days in any place is not considered an epidemic, even in a small settlement. Similarly, if there are slightly more than 500 inhabitants, it is still not considered an epidemic until there are 1,000 inhabitants, at which point six deaths over three days would be required. This ratio is always applicable.

If there is a plague in the Land of Israel, the other communities in the Diaspora fast for them. For if the mistress (i.e., the Land of Israel) is afflicted, how much more so the others? This applies only if the plague spreads throughout the whole Land of Israel. But if it does not spread throughout the entire land, they do not need to fast, since there are also parts of the mistress that are not afflicted. If there is a plague in one province and caravans travel between there and another province, both provinces fast, even if they are far from each other, because the movement of people from the place of the plague brings the plague to the place they are traveling to.

And it is not necessary to mention if the plague was among Jews, but even if it was among other people – we fast. And there is someone who says that the plague does not rule over two nations (see Ran there), but all the poskim did not write this. If there was a plague among animals – we do not fast unless it was among pigs, because their intestines are similar to those of humans. And they wrote that nowadays we do not decree fasts for the plague, because it has been tested and proven that the air is affected by the absence of eating and drinking. Instead, we increase prayers and the recitation of the Ketoret, and we decree a fast with redemption, distribute to the poor, and increase charity. (In the Zohar Bereshit, page 22b, it is stated that the recitation of Ketoret stops the plague. And they should take forty God-fearing men, ten from each direction of the city, and they should recite the Ketoret, and they should do this three times, and all the people should gather in the synagogue and recite the Ketoret. See there.)

And similarly, one fasts for a city struck by a collapse. How so? If there was a significant collapse of sturdy walls in the city, which are not situated by the river where it could be attributed to the effects of water, this is considered a calamity, and one fasts and cries out in prayer over it. Similarly, for earthquakes and winds that cause buildings to collapse and kill people, one fasts and cries out in prayer over them.

And so too, one fasts for illnesses. How so? For instance, if a certain illness comes to the inhabitants of a city and affects many of them, such as croup or throat disease and similar ailments, and people are dying from that illness even if not in the manner described in section 6 - this is considered a communal distress, and they decree a fast and cry out. Similarly, if the majority of the community is afflicted with a spreading boil, or a moist itch that stings the flesh and causes scratching like a spreading boil, even if people are not dying from it – it is still considered an affliction like the boils of Egypt, and one fasts and cries out immediately, without needing to wait three days. Also, for fatal illnesses – it does not require the sequence of events, but as soon as people die, one fasts and cries out, and the surrounding areas fast but do not cry out. However, for a dry itch – one does not fast or cry out, but only cries out. (What the Rema wrote in section 5, that in these cases it is not necessary for people to die within three days... like in a plague that comes due to a change in the air, but they fast and cry out immediately, until here is his wording – the death does not refer to boils and itch, for in these cases death is not required. Rather, his main intention is on illnesses like croup and throat disease and similar ailments. And scrutinize and you will find it easy.)(In Bava Kamma 81a it is explained that for a moist itch – they cry out even on Shabbat.)

The great authorities have written that when pox, called packin, break out among children and they die, it is necessary to decree a fast. And every person is obligated to remove their young sons and daughters from the city, and if they do not do so, they are liable for their lives (Magen Avraham, section 3, in the name of the Shlah). And in the Gemara it says: "When there is pestilence in the city, gather your feet" (Bava Kamma 60b). However, pox is a contagious disease, and therefore there is an obligation to remove them from the city. Nowadays, this is not common because about one hundred and fifty years ago, doctors invented an inoculation for every child one year old or older, and through this, they are saved from this disease, as is known. Now, a disease called diphtheria is common among children, which is a type of throat strangling illness. And it appears to me that if, God forbid, this disease spreads in the city, it is necessary to decree a fast.

And similarly, concerning a dangerous animal that has been sent forth, even if it has not caused harm but only appeared – we fast and cry out in every place, even in distant ones, because it can also go to distant places. But if it has not been sent forth – it is merely accidental. What is considered "sent forth"? If it is seen in the city during the day – it is considered "sent forth," and it is a decree from heaven since it does not fear humans. If it is seen in the field during the day, if it saw two people and did not run away from them – it is considered "sent forth." But if it ran away – it is not considered "sent forth," as it is written (Genesis 9:2): "And the fear of you and the dread of you shall be upon every beast of the earth." And if the field was near a marsh that is full of reeds and small trees, it is only considered "sent forth" if it chased after them. But if it did not chase, even if it did not run away – it is not considered "sent forth," because being close to its regular place, it does not have so much fear. Therefore, if it was in the marsh itself, even if it chased after them – it is not considered "sent forth" unless in its chase outside the marsh it killed both of them and ate one of them. And if it ate both of them in the marsh itself – it is not considered "sent forth," as it killed them due to hunger, not because it was "sent forth." The general rule is: anything that does not depart from its natural behavior – is not considered "sent forth." And in our country, this is not common, but sometimes a mad dog bites several people. This is not considered "sent forth," and they should hurry to kill it.

Houses built in deserts and desolate lands, since they are places of wild beast incursions, if a wild beast climbs onto the roof and takes a baby from its cradle, which is a small bed – this is considered a calamity. If it does not reach this extent – it is not considered a calamity, as these people have endangered themselves by coming to a place of wild beasts. However, other types of creeping creatures of the earth and flying creatures that have been sent and caused damage, such as the sending of snakes and scorpions that harm but do not kill, and certainly hornets and mosquitoes and similar creatures – we do not fast or cry out for them, as this is the way of the world. And this is specifically in a place where they are common. But if they appear in places where they are not common – it seems to me that this is considered a calamity, and we should fast and cry out.

And so too for yellowing, that is, grain that has deteriorated to the point that its appearance has turned pale, and for blasting winds that strip the seeds from the grain after it has begun to grow, even if it has only started in one place the size of the opening of an oven - we fast and cry out [in prayer]; and even those at a distance, as long as they are in the same province, because it is a spreading affliction. For a non-spreading affliction - we fast but do not cry out. And "the size of the opening of an oven" - this means grain that is sufficient to make bread to fill the oven's opening. (And in the Gemara 22b it is questioned whether it is like the covering of the oven or the size of a loaf. See there.)

And similarly regarding the locust and the grasshopper, even if only one wing is seen throughout the Land of Israel, and even if it does not destroy the produce of the land – we fast and cry out because of them. And for the 'gobai', which is a type of locust, in any amount that it is seen, we fast and cry out. But for the common grasshopper, we do not fast or cry out, but only call out loudly. And now we do not recognize these species, so we cry out for all of them.

And similarly, we cry out [in supplication] for sustenance. How so? If the prices of merchandise that most of the lives of the people of that city depend on have dropped, such as linen goods in Babylon and wine and oil in the Land of Israel, and trade has diminished to the extent that a merchant needs to sell something worth ten for six – this is considered a public distress, and we cry out about it. However, a fast is not applicable for the distress of commerce, but rather prayers and supplications. Even on Shabbat, we cry out in prayer about this, since it affects the public. But we do not sound the shofar on Shabbat. On weekdays, in addition to the prayers, we also sound the shofar. And in the next section, it will be explained that it is possible to fast.

And so too regarding an excess of rain. How so? If there was an abundance of rain to the point that it caused them distress – they should pray about it, for there is no greater calamity than this in places where the houses are made of mud and dirt, and they collapse, and people are killed under the houses. In the Land of Israel, however, they do not pray for a reduction in rain because it is a mountainous land, and their houses are built of stone, and an abundance of rain is beneficial for them. And our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 11 that now in Safed, house collapses are common during the rainy season, and they pray about it. Thus are his words. It is explained that they only pray, and do not blow the shofar. Certainly, they do not fast, because this is not like other decrees from Heaven, and it is merely the poor construction of their houses that causes all this. And indeed, it is beneficial for many places. But in the Gemara (22b), it is clarified that they blow the shofar for this, see there. And the language of the Rambam in the third chapter and the Shulchan Aruch in section 11 is explained as I have written. The Rambam must be relying on what he wrote at the beginning of the second chapter, that for all troubles that will be explained – they fast and blow the shofar. And in the Shulchan Aruch, this is written in section 12. According to this, even for sustenance – they also fast, and not as I wrote in the previous section. However, according to this, the language of the Rambam and the Shulchan Aruch is puzzling, for regarding sustenance they specified blowing the shofar, but for an excess of rain they only mentioned prayer. This requires further investigation.

And this is the language of Rabbeinu Beit Yosef in section 12: Any city that has any of these troubles – that city fasts, cries out in prayer, pleads for mercy, and sounds the shofar until the trouble passes. All the surrounding areas also fast, but do not sound the shofar; however, they do ask for mercy on their behalf. In any case, one does not fast, cry out, or sound the shofar on Shabbat and Yom Tov for any trouble, except for food shortages, for which they cry out on Shabbat. Thus ends his language. And what he wrote "and all its surroundings" – refers to the same province (Magen Avraham, subsection 9).

A city that is surrounded by attackers, or surrounded by a river, and a ship that is being tossed about at sea, and even an individual who is being pursued by attackers or robbers, or an evil spirit, or a seriously ill person whose life is in danger that day – we cry out and beseech in prayers on Shabbat. But we do not blow the shofar, unless we are blowing it to gather the people to help their brethren and save them, for in such a situation, not only blowing the shofar is permitted, but desecrating Shabbat is also allowed to save lives. And above, in Siman 288, it was explained regarding blessing the sick on Shabbat, see there. And all these fasts that are observed due to troubles – pregnant women, nursing women, and minors do not fast on them. That is to say, even if they have reached the age of maturity, as long as they are not yet adults with understanding – they do not fast. This means eighteen years for a male, and fifteen for a female (Magen Avraham, section 10). And those who do fast eat at night, except for the fasts for rain during the last ten days, three and seven, when they stop eating while it is still day, as I wrote in the previous Siman.

A congregation that has two troubles should only request mercy for one of them, as it is stated (Ezra 8:23): "We fasted and sought our God concerning this." And they should say in the prayer: Even though there are many troubles in our hearts, we have come to pray only for this trouble. If they have the trouble of famine and the trouble of plague, they should request mercy for the famine. Consequently, the plague is included in this, because when God gives plenty, it is given for life. And the fact that in several penitential prayers and liturgical poems many troubles are mentioned and prayed for – this is incidental. But the main supplication should be for what the fast was decreed for (see Magen Avraham, subsection 11).

On every fast day decreed upon the community due to troubles, the court and the elders sit in the synagogue and examine the deeds of the people of the city from after the morning prayer until midday. They remove stumbling blocks of sins, warn, expound, and investigate those who are violent and sinful, and separate them. They humble those who are overbearing, and similarly address such matters. From midday until the evening, for a quarter of the day, they read from the Torah and the Prophets. For the last quarter of the day, they pray the Mincha prayer, sound the alarm, confess, and cry out as much as they can. 

The reason we do not do this is because we are unable to protest against sinners, as is known (see Magen Avraham, small section 12). And what do they read? The Rambam wrote at the end of the first chapter that they read the blessings and curses from "If you follow My statutes" and the Haftorah from the Prophets relating to the trouble. From his words, it implies that in the morning they did not read at all. Similarly, Rashi explained in Megillah (30b) that there was no time in the morning to read from the Torah because they were busy searching for sins, see there. 

However, the Tur later in section 579 wrote that in the morning they read the blessings and curses from "Bechukotai" and the Haftorah relating to the troubles, and in the afternoon they read "Vayechal" and the Haftorah "Seek," as on every fast day. He brought that the Geonim wrote this as well. 

The reason is that in the time of the Talmud, the investigation into sins was proper, and it was worthwhile to postpone the Torah reading. This is not the case in the time of the Geonim and certainly not now (see Lechem Mishneh there). And we, on all fast days, read "Vayechal" in the morning and afternoon, and in the afternoon, we read the Haftorah "Seek," since we do not have the order of fasts outside the Land, as has already been explained.

In places where the majority of rains muddy the ground, preventing plowing or causing other damage, and certainly in our country where most rains completely ruin the crops, and for us, a lot of rain is much worse than a drought – they cry out and seek mercy. If the matter is urgent, so that there is no time to proclaim the fasts in the order of the first, middle, and last three, and to spread them out over Monday, Thursday, and Monday, such as when the damage is immediate, and similarly in other troubles when the matter is urgent and there is no time to arrange the fasts, and therefore the public would need to fast many consecutive days, which is impossible because many would become ill from this – therefore, no fasts are decreed at all, since the public cannot fast every day; rather, they cry out every day and in every prayer. And verbal outcry is sufficient and not with the shofar, because since there is no public fast – there is no shofar. And if individual scholars wish to fast many consecutive days and are not concerned about becoming ill, and even if they do not become ill, they might weaken and be unable to work or engage in business and would need to rely on others (see Taanit 22b) – they can do as they wish.

And what is the verbal warning? That is when they say certain supplications and pleadings, and they reach "Answer us, O Lord, answer us" in the order of the Aleph-Bet according to the known version. They then say: "May it be Your will, Lord our God and God of our ancestors, that Your mercy overcomes Your anger towards us, and let Your mercy prevail over Your attributes, and conduct Yourself with Your children with the attribute of mercy, and let them enter before You beyond the letter of the law. And in Your great goodness, have mercy on them, for calamity only comes to the world because of Israel, and they are Your people and Your inheritance, whom You brought out of the land of Egypt. They cannot endure neither great good nor great evil. If You bestow upon them great good – they cannot endure it. If You are angry with them – they cannot endure it. May it be Your will that there be relief in the world, and remember Your mercy." And now the custom is to say this version during "Shomea Tefillah" and no more, when there is an abundance of rain. (And one should be precise about the words of the Shulchan Aruch that we brought, that since it is not possible to decree many fasts on the public, we do not decree fasts at all. And it is difficult: at least decree one fast! Rather, it seems that we do not decree a fast for an abundance of rain. And also among us, the custom is not to decree a fast for an abundance of rain. And what we wrote about the reason that the public cannot fast every day – this is for other troubles, and see Magen Avraham. And indeed, in the name, one should decree one fast, and one should deliberate on all this. Be precise and you will find leniency.)

The Rambam wrote in the first chapter, Law 9: Just as the community fasts for their troubles, so too an individual fasts for his troubles. How so? If he had a sick person, or someone lost in the desert, or someone imprisoned – he should fast for them and seek mercy in his prayer, and he says "Answer us...". He should not fast on Shabbatot, Festivals, Rosh Chodesh, Chanukah, or Purim. Thus are his words. And even if he began to fast – he stops on these days. Only in a public setting are there days when, if they began, they do not stop, as I wrote in Siman 572, see there, but not for an individual (Magid Mishneh). The law regarding if he vowed on these days is explained in Siman 570, see there.

And know that this law, that an individual is obligated to fast due to his troubles, is not explained in the Talmud anywhere. Rather, the Rambam states this from his own reasoning, that since it is certain that every individual is obligated to pray about his troubles, as it is written in the Psalm "Four must give thanks": "They cried out to the Lord…". Consequently, he is obligated to fast, for the annulment of trouble requires fasting, as is evident from the fast for a bad dream. (And perhaps there is a hint to this from this Psalm, as it is written: "Hungry and thirsty…". And though in its plain meaning it refers to those who were lost in the wilderness and therefore had nothing to eat or drink, nevertheless, it is possible that it hints also to fasting. And I do not know why the Rambam did not also include "those who travel by sea". And perhaps because this is the usual way of the world and it is done by his own will – fasting is not relevant to this; rather, he brings a thanksgiving offering afterward, as it is written there: "Those who go down to the sea in ships give thanks to the Lord for His kindness" and not fasting. This is not the case with the other three, the sick, those lost in the wilderness, and those imprisoned, which is not by their will – they indeed fast.)

During each of the final seven fasts for rain or other troubles, when they are conducted in this manner (see Tur, Beit Yosef, and Bach), the following order is observed: they remove the ark, which is the Holy Ark where the Torah scroll is placed. It appears that they remove it along with the Torah scroll. And where do they take it? To the city's main square, so as to be publicly humbled with this modest vessel. Also, for the purpose of exile. Therefore, even if it is not possible to take it to the public square, they take it to another place. All the people gather and cover themselves with sackcloth out of distress, as it is written concerning Mordechai: "He wore sackcloth and ashes." They place burnt ashes on the ark, that is, ashes from something that has been burned, and on the Torah scroll, to increase the weeping and to humble their hearts. Also, so they will remember the ashes of Isaac (15:1).

And one of the people takes ashes and places them on the head of the Nasi (leader). And why does the Nasi not take [the ashes] himself? Because the shame is greater when he is humiliated by others. All this is to increase the sorrow. Similarly, ashes are placed on the head of the head of the Beit Din (court). The ashes are placed on them in the spot where the tefillin are placed, in order to increase their shame; for it is the leaders of the generation who must bear the sins of the generation, because their merits were not sufficient to prevent the calamity. Each and every person should also place ashes on his own head in the spot where the tefillin are placed (see Talmud, Ta'anit 21b).

Afterward, they appoint a wise elder among them, and they sit down. If there is no wise elder, they appoint a wise person, even if he is not elderly. If there is not even a wise person, they appoint a distinguished individual before them. He then speaks words of admonition, saying: "Our brothers! It is not sackcloth and fasting that annul the decree, but repentance and good deeds. For we find that it is not written regarding the people of Nineveh, 'And God saw their sackcloth and their fasting,' but rather 'And God saw their deeds' (Jonah 3:10). And in the words of the prophets, it is said: 'Rend your hearts and not your garments' (Joel 2:13)." He continues in this vein according to his ability until their hearts are humbled and they fully repent. After he concludes these words of admonition, they stand in prayer. Similarly, on any fast day or on the eve of the new month when words of rebuke are spoken, they should be said before the Mincha (afternoon) prayer.

And they appoint a prayer leader who is suitable to pray on these fast days. If the one who delivers the words of rebuke is also suitable to pray, meaning he is capable of leading the prayers, he should pray. If not, another should pray. And who is suitable to pray on these fast days? A man who is accustomed to leading prayers as a prayer leader, so that he does not make mistakes. He should be accustomed to reading the Torah, the Prophets, and the Writings. He should have small children and not be wealthy, so that his heart is humbled within him. He should have labor in the field or another form of livelihood. None of his children, household members, relatives, or those associated with him should be sinners; rather, his household should be free of transgressions. No bad reputation should have been spread about him in his youth. He should be humble and pleasing to the people. He should have a pleasant voice that draws the heart, and his voice should be pleasant. If he is elderly and possesses all these qualities, he is praiseworthy. If he is not elderly, as long as he possesses all these qualities, he may pray. If it is not possible to find someone with all these qualities, they should at least appoint someone who is better in good deeds than others.

The prayer leader stands and begins and completes the prayer until "Ga'al Yisrael" ("Who redeems Israel"). He recites remembrances (zichronot) relevant to the trouble, as well as shofarot (verses about the shofar). The Tur explains that before the blessing of "Selach Lanu" ("Forgive us"), he says Selichot (penitential prayers) and confessions until "Ezra the Scribe", and then he says "Re'eh Be'anyenu... Aneinu..." ("See our affliction... Answer us..."). The Rambam did not mention "Aneinu" because he holds that the six blessings take the place of "Aneinu" (Beit Yosef). For remembrances (zichronot) he says "Atah Zocher" ("You remember") as on Rosh Hashanah, and for shofarot he says "Atah Nigleita" ("You revealed Yourself") as on Rosh Hashanah. After that, he recites from "Shir HaMaalot" these three: "El Hashem Batzaratah Li..." ("To the Lord in my distress I called..."), "Esa Einai El Heharim..." ("I lift my eyes to the mountains..."), "Mima'amakim Keraticha..." ("From the depths I call to You..."). After that, he says "A prayer of the afflicted when he is faint..." and offers supplications as he is able. He says "See our affliction, plead our cause, and hasten to redeem us." He implores and concludes his supplications with: "He who answered our father Abraham on Mount Moriah—He will answer you and hear your cry on this day. Blessed are You, O Lord, Redeemer of Israel." And they answer "Amen." According to the Tur, they blow a Tekiah-Teruah-Tekiah on the shofar here, and say "Hayom Harat Olam..." ("Today the world was born..."). But according to the Rambam, they do not blow the shofar during the prayer at all, rather they sound the trumpets after the prayer. We have already written this at the beginning of Siman 576, see there.

And know that as we have written, it is explained in the Rambam that "Zichronot" (remembrances), "Shofarot" (verses regarding the shofar), three "Shir Hama'alot" (Psalms of Ascents), and "Tefillah L'Ani" (Prayer of the Poor) are said before "Go'el Yisrael" (Redeemer of Israel). This is also clarified in the Mishnah at the beginning of the second chapter. However, the Tur does not write this, but rather states that "Zichronot" are said on the blessing after "Go'el Yisrael," which will be explained, as part of the six additional blessings, and he concludes the first one with "Zocher HaBrit" (He who remembers the covenant). And in this blessing, he says "Zichronot" as on Rosh Hashanah, except that he does not conclude with "Zocher HaBrit" as on Rosh Hashanah, but rather "Zocher HaNishkachot" (He who remembers the forgotten). The second he concludes with "Shome'a Teruah" (He who hears the shofar blast) and says "Shofarot" there. In the third, he says "Shir Hama'alot B'Tzaratah." In the fourth, "Esa Einai." In the fifth, "Mima'amakim." And in the sixth, "Tefillah L'Ani," see there. And it must be said that the Tur interprets that what the Mishnah states about saying "Zichronot," "Shofarot," and four psalms is not before the blessings but rather applies to all six blessings that will be explained. In the first, he says "Zichronot," in the second "Shofarot," in the third "B'Tzaratah," in the fourth "Esa Einai," in the fifth "Mima'amakim," and in the sixth "Tefillah L'Ani." This is also implied by Rashi's commentary, see there.

After completing the blessing "Gaal Yisrael" (Redeemer of Israel), one begins to add the six blessings, and supplicates in each of them with pleas and verses from the words of the Prophets and the Writings. He concludes each of them as will be explained: In the first one, he says before the conclusion, "He who answered Moses and your ancestors at the Sea of Reeds, He will answer you and hear the sound of your cries on this day. Blessed are You, Hashem, who remembers the forgotten." And they respond, "Amen." According to the Tur, they blow the shofar with a tekiah-teruah-tekiah sequence, as I have written. And know that in the Mishnah, Moses is not mentioned, only "He who answered our ancestors at the Sea of Reeds," and this is also what we say in the Selichot prayers. However, in the Rambam and Tur, Moses is mentioned, and this requires investigation: did not Moses our teacher not cry out, and on the contrary, Moses said to them, "Hashem will fight for you, and you shall remain silent" (Exodus 14:14).

In the second blessing, he concludes: "May He who answered Joshua in Gilgal, [answer us]... Blessed are You, O Lord, who listens to the trumpet blast." In the third blessing, he says: "May He who answered Samuel in Mitzpah, [answer us]... Blessed are You, O Lord, who listens to the cry." In the fourth blessing, he says: "May He who answered Elijah on Mount Carmel, [answer us]... Blessed are You, O Lord, who listens to prayer." In the fifth blessing, he says: "May He who answered Jonah in the belly of the fish, [answer us]... Blessed are You, O Lord, who responds in times of distress." In the sixth blessing, he says: "May He who answered David and Solomon his son in Jerusalem, [answer us]... Blessed are You, O Lord, who has mercy on the land." After each blessing, the congregation responds "Amen," and according to the Tur, they blow the shofar as I have written. Afterwards, he says the blessing of "Heal us" until the end of the prayer. According to the Rambam, they then blow the trumpets, but according to the Tur, there are no blasts after the prayers.

And for the Tur, they add in "Shomea Tefillah" this text: "Answer us, Creator of the world, in Your attribute of mercy. Choose Your people Israel to make known Your greatness and the splendor of Your honor. Hearer of prayer, grant dew and rain..." until "for You hear," and it is printed in prayer books for withholding rain. Afterwards, they read the admonition from "If you follow My statutes." And the one who reads the Haftarah reads from Jeremiah regarding the droughts. And after the prayer, they say "To You silence is praise" until Kaddish. It seems to me that the reason for this is that it is in place of the psalm of the day related to the day's theme, because it is written in it "Hearer of prayer, to You all flesh will come" (Psalms 65:3), and it is also written in it "You visit the earth... the stream of God is full of water; You prepare their grain... You bless its growth; You crown the year of Your goodness..." (Psalms 65:10-12).

At Mincha, the Tur writes that we read "Vayechal" and the Haftarah is "Shuva," see there. I do not understand why we do not read "Dirshu" as on all public fasts. The Shaliach Tzibbur (prayer leader) repeats the Amidah as in the Shacharit service, including the confession and the seven blessings... There is no Priestly Blessing at Mincha, see there. It is explained that we also add the six blessings at Mincha. When it says "seven," it means starting from "Goel Yisrael," which is where we begin to add. We recite poems, Selichot, and Psalms until Ne'ilah. During Ne'ilah, we pray the Shemoneh Esrei (Amidah) of eighteen blessings and "Aneinu." After the prayer, each person recites the confession "What are we, what is our life." The Shaliach Tzibbur repeats the Amidah until "Selach Lanu," the confessions, "Ashamnu," "What are we," "You have distinguished," as on Yom Kippur. "Vayaavor," "Ezra the Scribe," "See our affliction," and the seven blessings as in Shacharit. "Retzeh," "Modim," the Priestly Blessing, and "Sim Shalom." The Kaddish Tiskabel, "May your supplications be answered from heaven, your cries accepted, and your prayers heard." Afterward, the Ma'ariv (evening) prayer is recited, see there.

And what we wrote that according to the Rambam, they do not blow the shofar for each blessing—this is in the provinces. But in the Temple, the Rambam wrote there, and this is his language: When they would pray in this order in Jerusalem, they would gather on the Temple Mount opposite the Eastern Gate, and pray in the order that has been explained. And when the prayer leader reaches the point to say "He who answered Abraham," he says, "Blessed are You, O Lord, our God, God of Israel from eternity to eternity. Blessed are You, O Lord, Redeemer of Israel." And they respond after him, "Blessed be the name of His glorious kingdom forever and ever" (for they do not respond "Amen" in the Temple). And the synagogue official says to the shofar blowers: "Blow, sons of Aaron, blow!" And the prayer leader repeats and says, "He who answered Abraham..." and afterwards the priests blow a tekiah (long blast), teruah (short blasts), and tekiah. And similarly, for the second blessing, which is the first of the six blessings, he concludes "Blessed is the Lord, God... Blessed are You, O Lord, who remembers those who are forgotten." And they respond, "Blessed be the name of His glorious kingdom forever and ever." And the synagogue official says to them: "Sound a teruah, sons of Aaron, sound a teruah!" And the prayer leader repeats and says, "He who answered Moses..." and afterwards they sound a teruah, tekiah, and teruah. And so for each and every blessing, in one he says "Blow" and in one he says "Sound a teruah," until he completes all seven blessings. And it turns out that the priests sometimes blow a tekiah, teruah, and tekiah, and sometimes sound a teruah, tekiah, and teruah, seven times. And this order is only done on the Temple Mount. And when they blow and sound there—they blow with a shofar and trumpets together. End of his words. And the Ra'avad wrote that in the Temple they did not blow together, a teruah with a tekiah or a tekiah with a teruah, but only a tekiah alone or a teruah alone, see there. And it seems that he interprets what we say in the Gemara (16b): In one he says "Blow" and in one "Sound a teruah," see there, meaning only a tekiah-tekiah truly, and a teruah-teruah truly. However, in our Gemara there it is explicitly stated "They blow and sound and blow" and "They sound and blow and sound," see there, and this is according to the words of the Rambam. And even in the Temple itself they would blow a tekiah-teruah-tekiah, as explained in the Mishnah of the flute (53b), see there and in the Gemara.

These seven fasts, after praying, all the people go out to the cemetery, and cry and supplicate there. Meaning: you are as if dead, if you do not repent from your ways. Therefore, if there are no Jewish graves – they go to their graves. And in the Gemara (16a) there is another reason: so that they will pray for us, and this is only relevant at Jewish graves (Magen Avraham, small section 11).

The Geonim wrote that these are days on which we fast because troubles befell our ancestors, and it is proper to fast on them. And although some of them occur on Rosh Chodesh, there are those who say that one should fast on it. This is indeed a wonder, and the Geonim themselves responded that one should not fast on Rosh Chodesh (Beit Yosef and Magen Avraham). Therefore, it is good not to complete the fast. In Worms, they would fast on Rosh Chodesh Sivan because of certain decrees (Beit Yosef in the previous section in the name of Rokeach), but we do not learn from them (Magen Avraham in Siman 572 in the name of Rama). And I think I have seen that they would pray Mincha at the third hour after midday and then eat. However, nowadays in our countries, we have not heard of anyone fasting on these fasts that will be explained. The decree from the Geonim was not to fast on them, but rather they wrote that it is proper to fast on them. Moreover, after the sealing of the Talmud, it is not possible to decree for all of Israel. The Tur brought in the name of Ba'al Halachot Gedolot in this language: these are the days on which one fasts from the Torah, see there. And the language is very puzzling (see Beit Yosef and Bach), and it requires further investigation.

And these are the days: On the first of Nisan, the sons of Aaron died. On the tenth of it, Miriam died, and the well ceased. On the twenty-sixth of it, Joshua the son of Nun died. On the tenth of Iyar, Eli the Priest and his two sons died, and the Ark of the Lord was captured. On the twenty-eighth of it, Samuel the Prophet died, and some say on the twenty-ninth (Magen Avraham in the name of Megillat Taanit). On the twenty-third of Sivan, the bringing of the first fruits to Jerusalem was annulled in the days of Jeroboam the son of Nebat. On the twenty-fifth of it, Rabbi Shimon ben Gamliel, Rabbi Ishmael, and Rabbi Hanina the Deputy High Priest were killed. On the twenty-seventh of it, Rabbi Hananiah ben Teradyon and a Torah scroll with him were burned. On the first of Av, Aaron the Priest died. On the eighteenth of it, the western lamp was extinguished in the days of Ahaz. On the seventeenth of Elul, those who spread an evil report about the land died, and some say on the seventh of Elul (there).

On the fifth of Tishrei, twenty people from Israel died, and Rabbi Akiva was imprisoned. On the seventh of Tishrei, a decree was made against our ancestors that they would die by the sword, famine, and plague because of the sin of the golden calf. Although afterwards the Holy One, blessed be He, was appeased, nevertheless the sin is remembered for generations. On the seventh of Marcheshvan, Zedekiah's eyes were blinded, and his sons were slaughtered before his eyes. Some say it was on the sixth of Marcheshvan. On the twenty-eighth of Kislev, Jehoiakim burned the scroll that Baruch had written from the mouth of Jeremiah. Some say it was on the seventh of Kislev, some say the eighth, and some say the fifth of Kislev. Therefore, one does not fast on the twenty-eighth of Kislev, as it is Chanukah. On the eighth of Tevet, the Torah was translated into Greek in the days of King Ptolemy, and there was darkness in the world for three days. On the ninth of Tevet, the calamity that occurred on that day was unknown, but it was later revealed that Ezra the scribe died on that day. On the fifth of Shevat, the elders who were in the days of Joshua died, and some say it was on the eighth of Shevat. On the twenty-third of Shevat, all of Israel gathered against the tribe of Benjamin in the incident of the concubine at Gibeah. On the seventh of Adar, Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, died, and in a leap year, it is observed in the first Adar. On the ninth of Adar, the schools of Shammai and Hillel were divided, which was a difficult event for Israel, and a fast was decreed because of it.

And there are those who say that it was decreed to fast every Monday and Thursday for the destruction of the Temple, for the Torah that was burned, and for the desecration of God's name. Furthermore, it is found among the early authorities that they decreed a fast on the eve of the holy Shabbat of the portion "Chukat," when twenty wagons full of books were burned in France. And they established it based on the day of the week and not on the day of the month, as it was revealed to them in a dream that this is what Onkelos translated on "This is the statute of the Torah" – "This is the decree of the Torah." And the Rambam writes at the end of the laws of fasting: All these fasts are destined to be nullified in the days of the Messiah. Moreover, they are destined to become days of joy and gladness, as it is stated: "Thus says the Lord of Hosts: The fast of the fourth, the fast of the fifth, the fast of the seventh, and the fast of the tenth shall become times of joy and gladness and cheerful feasts for the house of Judah." And love, truth, and peace. Amen and Amen. With the help of Heaven, the laws of fasting are concluded.

It is taught in Pirkei DeRabbi Eliezer (Chapter 46): On the first day of the month of Elul, the Holy One, Blessed be He, said to Moses, "Ascend to Me on the mountain," as this was when he ascended to receive the second tablets. And they sounded the shofar in the camp; Moses ascended the mountain so that they would not err as they did previously with the incident of the Golden Calf. And the Holy One, Blessed be He, was exalted with that shofar, as it is said (Psalms 47:6): "God has ascended with a shout, the Lord with the sound of a shofar." And because the shofar saved Israel from sin, and the month of Elul is designated for repentance, as it is the last month of the year and precedes the Days of Judgment. The ethical scholars alluded to this with the verse "I am my beloved's, and my beloved is mine," whose initial letters spell "Elul," meaning: now is the time for all my thoughts to be for my Beloved, and when I do so, then also "my Beloved is mine," He will look upon me for my benefit. And the shofar is also conducive to repentance, as it is written (Amos 3:6): "Shall a shofar be blown in a city, and the people not tremble?" Therefore, all of Israel have the custom to blow the shofar after prayer throughout this month. They begin from the second day of the new month, as it is the first day of this month. Some blow the shofar both in the morning and in the evening, but we only blow it in the morning. The sequence of blasts is "tekiah, shevarim, teruah, tekiah." Except on Shabbat and the eve of Rosh Hashanah, when we interrupt the blowing of the rabbinic blasts to distinguish them from the obligatory blasts commanded by the Torah.

Therefore, it is customary to increase in selichot (penitential prayers) and supplications during the pre-dawn hours in this month, because this time is one of favor. For the Holy One, Blessed be He, roams through eighteen thousand worlds, and at the end of the night, He roams in this world (Magen Avraham, subsection 1). The Sephardim have the custom to say selichot for the entire month of Elul until after Yom Kippur. However, the Ashkenazi custom is different; they only begin before Rosh Hashanah. That is, they ensure that there are no fewer than four days before Rosh Hashanah. This is because the ten days of repentance are short by four days in which it is impossible to fast, namely the two days of Rosh Hashanah, Shabbat Shuva, and the eve of Yom Kippur. Therefore, they complete these four days before Rosh Hashanah. Those who fast on Rosh Hashanah should only fast for two days before it (ibid, subsection 3). Although the custom has already been to fast for four days, since this is to complete the ten days, once one begins to fast on Rosh Hashanah, it automatically negates two days (ibid). Accordingly, if one begins to fast both the four days and on Rosh Hashanah, one must continue to do so always. However, the main law regarding fasting on Rosh Hashanah will be explained in Siman 597, where it is stated that it is not proper to fast on Rosh Hashanah. See there.

Therefore, our custom is: If Rosh Hashanah falls on Thursday, we begin the Selichot on the preceding Sunday, making it four days. But if it falls on Shabbat, it will be six days; because we always begin on Sunday, which is the first day of creation. Since humanity is the purpose of creation to serve the Blessed God, we thus begin repentance on the first day of creation. When Rosh Hashanah falls on Monday or Tuesday, we start from the Sunday of the previous week. And between each Selichah, we recite the Thirteen Attributes. Therefore, the prayer leader must wrap himself in a tallit, even though it is before dawn, as implied in Rosh Hashanah 17b. See there.

And know that one must be cautious with these Selichot, and those of Monday, Thursday, and Monday, in two matters: First, those who are not fasting, and in the Selichot it mentions the term "fast" or "fasting" – they should not say this, so as not to be speaking falsehoods. Instead, they should say the term "prayer" in place of fasting. Second, in many of the Selichot, it is mentioned that our recitation is at night and before dawn, such as: "when they cry out while it is still night" or "during the watch of the morning," and similar phrases. And now, in many places, Selichot are recited when it is already broad daylight, and this would be speaking falsehoods. Therefore, these words should be omitted. And a mourner is forbidden to leave his house for Selichot, except on the eve of Rosh Hashanah, because many Selichot are recited. Likewise, on the eve of Yom Kippur, in places where many Selichot are recited. Also, a mourner should not lead the prayers during the High Holy Days, nor for the entire twelve months for his father or mother, unless he is a regular prayer leader, or if there is no one else who can lead the prayers.

They are meticulous in seeking out the most esteemed and worthy cantor in Torah and deeds to lead the prayers during the days of Selichot, Rosh Hashanah, and Yom Kippur. He should be at least thirty years old and married, similar to the High Priest, who was forbidden to perform the Yom Kippur service if he was not married, as it is written (Leviticus 16:6): "And he shall make atonement for himself and for his household." However, all of this is not essential, and all Jews are eligible, provided that he is acceptable to the congregation. But if he prays silently, they do not respond "Amen" after him. Rabbi Moses Isserles (Rema) wrote, and this is his language: "He also needs to include everyone in his prayer. If he has an enemy and intends not to include him, even his friends are not included in his prayer." This is the end of his language.

It seems to me that this only applies in places where there are many unlearned people who cannot pray on their own and rely on the cantor's prayer. But in our communities, where everyone prays for themselves, this rule does not apply. And concerning "Kaddish," "Kedusha," and "Barechu," this is not considered fulfilling one's obligation, for any ten Jews respond to matters of sanctity, and whoever is present at the time responds with them. And similarly with the response of "Amen," except for the additional services of Rosh Hashanah, where the primary sounding of the shofar is structured around the blessings. And in our custom, where we do not blow the shofar silently, the main prayer is that of the cantor. The same applies to the additional service of Yom Kippur because of the service. Perhaps this seems to be fulfilling the public's obligation and requires further study.

However, it is certain that the common saying that even one person can prevent someone from being the cantor is mistaken and leads to disputes. It is not so; rather, we follow the majority opinion of the congregation. The Levush has already written this earlier in section 53, and see what I wrote there.

It is customary that someone who has taken on the mitzvah of praying or blowing the shofar, and has not been found disqualified, should not be removed from that role in the future, since they have already taken on the mitzvah. If one person took on the role of blowing the shofar on the first day and another on the second day, and the first day falls on Shabbat, the first person blows the shofar on the second day, and the second person is displaced. This is similar to the rules of Ma'ariv, which will be explained in Siman 642. And even though some have doubts about this (see Sha'arei Teshuvah), this is nonetheless the custom. If someone has an established role but misses one or two instances because they were not at home, they do not lose their established role because of this. However, if they miss three times, it seems to me that they lose their established role. The same applies if they were ill. But if they willingly chose not to pray or blow the shofar even once, they lose their established role. Rabbi Moshe Isserles (the Rema) wrote: "In some places, it is customary that the one who leads the Selichot prayers also leads all the prayers of the day." This is the end of his quote. This includes even Ma'ariv, and this displaces a mourner or someone observing a yahrzeit (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 7). However, our custom is not like this, and in general, one should be very careful not to cause disputes over these matters. Anyone who has the fear of God within them should yield their opinion, even if it seems to them that things are being done improperly, to avoid causing disputes. Usually, the Satan dances in such matters, as is well known. Therefore, someone who makes efforts to prevent disputes earns a great reward.

In the Zohar Vayikra, it strongly cautions the prayer leader who prays on the High Holy Days, and the one who blows the shofar, to separate themselves for three days beforehand, to be careful about any impurity, and to examine their deeds. See there. And now, due to our sins, we are not able to be stringent about this. The prayer leader who wraps in a tallit before dawn to say the Selichot should not recite the blessing on the tallit, and it is better to take someone else’s tallit and not his own, due to the doubt concerning the blessing (Taz, subparagraph 2). Similarly, they should be careful to recite the blessing over the Torah before Selichot (ibid.). And see what I wrote in Siman 47.

It states in the Midrash Vayikra (Chapter 30): On the eve of Rosh Hashanah, the great ones of the generation fast. The Holy One, Blessed be He, forgives them a third of their sins. From Rosh Hashanah until Yom Kippur, individuals fast, and the Holy One, Blessed be He, says to Israel: "What has passed is past, from now on, there will be an accounting." From Yom Kippur until the festival, one is involved with his sukkah, and one is involved with his lulav. On the first day of the festival, all of Israel stands before the Holy One, Blessed be He, with their lulavim and etrogim for the sake of the Holy One, Blessed be He. And He says to them: "What has passed is past, and from now on, there will be an accounting." Therefore, it is said: "And you shall take for yourselves on the first day"; thus far is his language.

Based on this, many have the custom to fast on the eve of Rosh Hashanah. This is not considered arrogance, as if one is considering oneself one of the great people of the generation, because anyone can fast for their sins, especially on the last day of the year, and it is not due to thinking oneself one of the great people of the generation (see Magen Avraham, subsection 9). Some people fast on the first day of Selichot. There are individuals who fast all ten days of repentance, and the four days they are missing they complete before Rosh Hashanah during the days of Selichot. This means: when Rosh Hashanah falls on Thursday, they fast the four consecutive days. When it falls on Shabbat, they fast on Sunday, Monday, Thursday, and the eve of Rosh Hashanah. Similarly, when it falls on Monday, they fast on Sunday, Monday, Thursday, and the eve of Rosh Hashanah. This is also the case when it falls on Tuesday. It has already been explained that those who fast on Rosh Hashanah only need to complete two days before Rosh Hashanah.

All these fasts do not need to be completed until nightfall (tzeit hakochavim), not even on the eve of Rosh Hashanah. "Vayechal" is not recited, and the shaliach tzibur does not say "Aneinu," only each individual includes it in the "Shomea Tefillah" blessing during the Mincha prayer as is done for all fasts. The shaliach tzibur does not say the Priestly Blessing (Birkat Kohanim) during Mincha. If there is a brit milah, or a pidyon haben, or any other seudat mitzvah, even on the eve of Rosh Hashanah, anyone who wishes may eat; and those associated with the brit are obligated to eat, as I have written in Siman 568—see there. On the eve of Rosh Hashanah, the meal should be held before midday (see Magen Avraham, subparagraph 11). For these fasts, it is good that when one begins to fast, they should say or conclude in their heart that it is without a vow, so that if in another year they do not wish to fast, they do not have to. However, if they fasted with the intention of doing so regularly, even if they only fasted once, they need an annulment in the second year if they do not wish to fast (according to the Bach). If they fasted without any specific intention, and they fasted three times, an annulment is required. For two times, no annulment is necessary, as I have written in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 214—see there.

There are those who are accustomed to eat on the eve of Rosh Hashanah before dawn, due to the practices of the Amorites, who would fast on the eve of their holidays. But this is not a correct custom, as one should not eat before dawn. In our times, we have not heard of this custom. And in the Jerusalem Talmud, in the second chapter of Taanit, it is explicitly stated that Rabbi Yonatan would fast every eve of Rosh Hashanah, and this does not fall under the practices of the Amorites. There is proof from the case of Bikkurim on the eve of Passover. And know that one may be lenient with these fasts in cases of minor illness, and no annulment is needed (Magen Avraham, small section 12), as the general custom is that when there is a minor illness, one does not fast.

One does not recite the Tachanun prayer on the morning of the eve of Rosh Hashanah. And although one does fall on their face during Selichot at dawn, and sometimes this extends into the day—nonetheless, during the morning service, one does not fall on their face, as is the case on the eve of any festival. There is no sounding of the shofar on the eve of Rosh Hashanah, to distinguish between the voluntary shofar blasts and the obligatory ones. However, in one's home, for the purpose of practice, it is permitted. At night, one should not sound the shofar throughout the entire month of Elul, even for practice; for one should not create an awakening at night, and the sounding of the shofar arouses the higher attributes. The custom is to annul vows on the eve of Rosh Hashanah. (And the custom of admonition found in the siddurim—one should not do.)(See Sha'arei Teshuvah at the end of section 9.)

It is stated in the Midrash Vayikra (Parsha 30): A person who has a legal case wears black, etc., and does not cut his nails, because he does not know how his judgment will end. But Israel is not like this; rather, they wear white, wrap themselves in white, shave, and cut their nails. See there. Based on this, we have the custom to launder and get a haircut on the eve of Rosh Hashanah. We also have the custom to immerse on the eve of Rosh Hashanah due to impurity. And if one needs to engage in marital relations on Rosh Hashanah, such as on the night of immersion, or if he has returned from a journey, it is customary to immerse in the morning. There are places where the custom is to visit graves on the eve of Rosh Hashanah, increase supplications, and distribute charity to the poor there. One should increase merits on the eve of Rosh Hashanah. (When reciting the thirteen attributes individually, begin from "El Rachum" etc., for according to the Ari, this is where the thirteen attributes begin. And the two names of God can be said in the Atbash cipher "Mem-Tzadi-Pe-Tzadi" "Mem-Tzadi-Pe-Tzadi," as explained in Pri Etz Chaim, Shaar HaSelichot, end of chapter eight, see there.)

In the evening, we enter the synagogue, recite the Shema with its blessings, conclude with "U'faros," and say the verse "Tiku bachodesh shofar." There are places where this is not said. We then recite the "Half-Kaddish" with a melody and pray. The custom is to pray aloud, even though the sages are not pleased with this practice. Nevertheless, this is the custom. We add several things to the prayer, namely: in the conclusion of "Ata Kadosh," we finish with "HaMelech HaKadosh," and if one says "HaEl HaKadosh," he does not fulfill his obligation and must start over. Similarly, in the blessing of "Hashiva," the conclusion is "HaMelech HaMishpat," and if not, he must return, as I have written earlier in Siman 117. Additionally, we add in the blessing of Avot "Zochreinu LeChaim." The word "LeChaim" is pronounced with a shva under the lamed, not a patach, for otherwise it would imply "not for life." It contains eleven words, corresponding to the number of words in the verse "Ha'chefetz Echpotz mot rasha" (Tur), and fifty letters (corresponding to the fifty gates of understanding). In "Ata Gibor," we add "Mi Kamocha Av HaRachamim," etc. It has eight words, corresponding to the verse "Vayizkor ki basar heima," etc. (there). In "Modim," we add "V'chatov LeChaim Tovim," etc., and in "Zochreinu," we do not say "Tovim," as proper etiquette dictates first asking for a small thing, and then a large one (there). In "Sim Shalom," we add "B'Sefer Chaim, Bracha, V'Shalom," etc.

These four phrases: "Remember us," "Who is like You," "Write," and "In the book" – are not mentioned in the Talmud, but are from the tradition of the Geonim. And even though in the first three blessings and the last three blessings one does not make requests, this is specifically regarding individual needs, not communal needs (Tur). And so it is taught in the Tractate Sofrim (Chapter 19, Halacha 8): just as the conclusion of Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur is different from other festivals, so too is their prayer. And one does not mention remembrances in the first three blessings and the last three blessings, except etc.; thus is its wording. And "remembrances" means: what we say "Remember us for life... who remembers His creatures for life with compassion," "remembered and written," etc. According to this, these things have a basis in the Tractate Sofrim, which are Baraitas from the sages of the Talmud.

And behold, Rabbi Yitzchak (the Tosafist) wrote in the first chapter of Berachot (12b) that we repeat these statements if they were not said, just like "HaMelech HaKadosh" (the Holy King). The Rosh was perplexed by this, asking why we should repeat them since they are not mentioned in the Gemara. Refer there. And according to what I have written, Rabbi Yitzchak's opinion is clear because they are mentioned in Masechet Sofrim, as I have written. However, the opinion of most of our rabbis is like that of the Rosh, and it is also evident from the Rambam. And this is our established practice: if one forgets them, we do not make him repeat it, since in the end, they are not mentioned in the Gemara.

In the blessing "Who blesses His people Israel with peace," we do not change it on Rosh Hashanah, Yom Kippur, and the Ten Days of Repentance, but rather keep it as it is throughout the year. The Ashkenazi custom, however, is to change it and conclude with "Who makes peace." Many great authorities have already wondered: How is it possible to change the text on our own? Therefore, many great sages say "Who blesses," etc. And what is found in earlier sources to say "Who makes peace" – their intention was not regarding the blessing, but rather about "Who makes peace" at the end of the Amidah and at the end of Kaddish, because it contains a hint relevant to these days. Nevertheless, it seems to me, in my humble opinion, that one should not rebuke them, for indeed, the blessing "Who blesses" – we do not find its exact text in the Talmud, but only in the Rambam and other halachic authorities. And we find at the end of Tractate Derech Eretz that their text was "Who makes peace," as it says there: Great is peace, for all blessings and prayers conclude with peace; the Shema prayer "and spread over us the shelter of Your peace," the Priestly Blessing "and grant you peace," all blessings conclude with peace "Who makes peace," see there. Thus, that was indeed their text. And the Sephardim do not change the text.

If one did not say "the holy King," or if he is unsure whether he said it, if he did not say it – he returns to the beginning, because it is presumed that he did not say it as per his usual habit. And in this case, saying it ninety times does not help, as it does with "He makes the wind blow" in Siman 114, because he cannot say God's name, and how can he train himself (Magen Avraham, subsection 1)? Similarly, with "the King of justice," if one did not say it, or if he is unsure – he returns. However, since this is in the middle blessings, if he has not yet lifted his feet – he returns to the blessing of "Return us." And if he has lifted his feet – he returns to the beginning. And what is considered "lifting his feet" is explained above in Siman 117. According to our version, where throughout the year we also say "King, who loves righteousness and justice," if one did not say "the King of justice" – some say he does not return, since he mentioned "King," and some say he returns. And in Siman 118, this is explained; see there that it is good to return and pray as a voluntary prayer (Taz, subsection 1).

If one said "the holy God" and within the time span of "toch k'dei dibur" (the time it takes to say a greeting) remembered and said "the holy King," he does not need to go back and he has fulfilled his obligation. The same applies for "the King of justice." Even if he did not know beforehand that these are the Days of Awe, and did not remember until afterwards (Magen Avraham, subsection 2). And on the Sabbath between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, or if Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur fall on the Sabbath, one should say in the blessing of "Magen Avot," "the holy King." However, in this case, if one said "the holy God," he has fulfilled his obligation (see Sha'arei Teshuvah). But he concludes with the Sabbath blessing alone, as this blessing was only instituted for the Sabbath.

It has already been clarified that if one did not say "Zachreinu" and "Mi Kamocha Av HaRachamim," as well as "U'chtov" and "B'Sefer Chaim," he is not required to go back. However, if he remembers before he finishes the blessing, meaning before he mentions the name of the blessing, he should say it there. For example, if he said "Melech Ozer u'Moshi'a u'Magen. Baruch Ata" and then realized he did not say "Zachreinu," he should return to "Zachreinu" up to "Elokim Chaim" and then say "Melech Ozer," etc. But if he already mentioned the name, he does not go back. This applies to all of them, and he is not allowed to go back. He should say "LeChaim" with a shva (shewa) as I have written, and not with a patach. There is stringency specifically on Rosh Hashanah, and not throughout the year. (See Magen Avraham, subsection 4. Regarding what he wrote "Zachreinu," "K'tavenu" with a chataf kamatz, I do not know his intent.)

Some have the custom to pray on Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur while bowing, and they must straighten up at the end of the blessings before saying "Blessed," because it is forbidden to bow in a blessing where the Sages did not institute it. The Sephardim customarily say "Shir Hama'alot Mima'amakim" between "Yishtabach" and "Yotzer" during all ten days of repentance. Similarly, on the evening of Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, after the Amidah, they say "L'David Mizmor LaHashem Ha'aretz U'melo'ah." The Ashkenazim do not have this custom. In Kaddish, they repeat "L'eila L'eila," and they do not say "U'l'eila," only "L'eila L'eila." When they take three steps back, they say "Oseh Shalom," and also at the end of Kaddish. They say "HaShultan" with a kamatz under the second shin. They do not say "B'ahavah Mikra Kodesh," but rather "Zichron Teruah, Mikra Kodesh," because there is no love in judgment. They say "V'davarcha Emet" and not "V'davarcha Malkeinu Emet," since the blessing ends with "King over all the earth." And "Emet" also serves as "King," as I wrote in paragraph 13.

And we add on Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur in the blessing "You are Holy" three times "And so": "And so, grant Your fear," "And so, grant honor," "And so, the righteous," etc. The matter is: Behold, on the twenty-fifth of Elul the world was created, and man was created on Rosh Hashanah, and the purpose of man's creation is that His blessed name should be magnified and sanctified through him. This was the intention of creation, but due to the sin of the Tree of Knowledge, matters were corrupted, and the waste increased over the food, and the peel over the fruit. At the giving of the Torah, it was rectified, and with the [sin of the] Golden Calf, it was corrupted again. Therefore, the world will not be rectified according to the original intention until after the coming of the Redeemer, and for this we pray in all prayers: "May His great name be magnified and sanctified."

Therefore, all the prayers of Rosh Hashanah are established on the sanctification of His blessed name. This is the essence of the middle blessing "Reign over the entire world in Your glory," etc., "Let all that has been made know," etc., "and let everything that has the breath of life in its nostrils say: The Lord, God of Israel, is King, and His kingship rules over all." This is the primary focus of our prayers on Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur. For this reason, the Men of the Great Assembly prefaced the blessing "You are holy" with these three "And so": Because we conclude with "the Holy King," which also has this intention, that His blessed kingship be revealed in actual reality before the entire world. Therefore, it is obligatory for us to mention "King" during these days. And the blessing is for the sanctity of the Holy One, blessed be He. Therefore, we say "And so impose Your fear," etc., "And let all form a single band to do Your will with a whole heart," for this is the purpose of creation and the ultimate hope.

And afterwards, we say "And thus, give honor, O Lord, to Your people" – this corresponds to the exile of the Torah, for there is no honor except for the Torah. When the Torah is elevated, the glory of Israel is elevated, and then "the righteous will see and rejoice." The reason they chose the expression "And thus," the Tur writes, is because it is now the Day of Judgment, and we come before the King of kings, the Holy One, blessed be He. This is the language of the Scripture: "And thus I will come to the king." The word "thus" has a numerical value of seventy-two, hinting at the Name of seventy-two, and the Name of four is intertwined with it; thus far is his language. This means that the Name of the Lord in its full form with Yods equals seventy-two (Beit Yosef). And because the Name of seventy-two rotates three times, straightforward, reversed, and straightforward, as Rashi and Tosafot explained in Sukkah (45a) corresponding to the three verses of "And he traveled," "And he came," "And he stretched out," see there – therefore, we say "And thus" three times. And the Sephardim add another "And thus it will be sanctified." (And it appears to me that because four times seventy-two equals "and he will pass" 216, observe and you will find it easy.)

And we say in the prayer "this Day of Remembrance," as the Torah refers to it as "a remembrance of a blast, a holy convocation," because through the blowing of the shofar and the sounding of the alarms, we are remembered favorably before God, as it is written (Numbers 10:9-10): "And you shall sound an alarm with the trumpets, and you shall be remembered before" etc., "and you shall blow with the trumpets" etc., "and they shall be for you as a remembrance" etc. Thus, the sounding of the shofar and the alarms brings about remembrance, and this is what we seek. Therefore, we call it "this Day of Remembrance," both in prayer and in Kiddush. And we do not explicitly mention Rosh Chodesh on Rosh Hashanah in any overt manner, but only by allusion, as Rosh Chodesh is also included in the Day of Remembrance, as it is written: "And on the day" etc., "and on your new moons" etc., "and they shall be for you as a remembrance." Similarly, in "Ya'aleh Veyavo" we use the language of "remembrance," because the moon is still concealed. And thus it is written: "At the full moon for our feast day," meaning that we conceal the explicit mention of Rosh Chodesh.

If Rosh Hashanah falls on a weekday, we say "Yom Teruah" (a day of sounding the shofar). If it falls on Shabbat, when we do not blow the shofar, we say "Zichron Teruah" (a remembrance of the sounding). On Shabbat, we say "Retzeh Bimnuchatenu" (accept our rest). (As for what the Magen Avraham wrote in Siman 6 in the name of the Levush – that is not the custom, see there.) 

We do not say "Mo'adim L'Simcha, Chagim U'Zmanim L'Sasson" (festivals for joy, holidays and times for gladness), because they are days of judgment. Similarly, we do not say "V'Hasi'enu" (and bring us), because even though Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur are included in the passage of "These are the appointed times of the Lord," the blessing "Moadim" is only for the three pilgrimage festivals when we go up to the Temple. 

In the Musaf prayer, in "U'mipnei Chata'einu" (because of our sins), we do not say "we cannot ascend and see," but rather "we cannot fulfill our obligations," for the reason mentioned. If it falls on Shabbat, we mention Shabbat as on all other holidays, and we conclude "V'Dvarecha Emet" (and Your word is true), and end with "Melech Al Kol Ha'aretz" (King over all the earth), both in prayer and in Kiddush. 

It seems to me the reason is that in the Musaf prayer we combine the sanctity of the day with the verses of Kingship, and then we must conclude with "Melech Al Kol Ha'aretz"; therefore, they established this for all prayers. Consequently, the conclusion is the same for Kiddush and prayer, as on Shabbat and Yom Tov, which is why we also conclude "V'Dvarecha Emet," which is akin to the signature, for the seal of the Holy One, blessed be He, is truth. Therefore, we say "for You are a true God and Your word is true." And truth is like Kingship, so there is no need to say "V'Dvarecha Malkeinu Emet," as this would be redundant.

Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 9: Although throughout the year we pray quietly, on Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur the custom is to pray aloud. And we are not concerned about mistakes, since they have machzorim (prayer books) in their hands; thus far his words. And we have already written that many great authorities are not pleased with this, as prayer should only be quiet. The custom is that on the first night after the evening prayer, each person says to his friend: "May you be inscribed and sealed for a good year," and his friend responds similarly with "yes," or says to him "you too" (see Taz section 4, and Magen Avraham section 8).

We learn in Keritot (6a): Abaye said: Now that you have said that a sign is significant, a person should be accustomed to eat at the beginning of the year fenugreek, leeks, beets, dates, and squash. And when he eats fenugreek, he says: "May it be Your will that our merits increase." Leeks: "May our enemies be cut off." Beets: "May our adversaries depart." Dates: "May our enemies be consumed." Squash: "May the decree of our sentence be torn up and may our merits be proclaimed before You." And it is customary to follow the language of the country in this matter. Therefore, among us, we cook black-eyed peas, beans, and squash, which we regard as squash, and small gourds, which are similar to squash, and other such items. Every place follows its custom. Regarding fish, some seek out a type of fish called "karet," which is like leeks. For everything good, we say the "may it be Your will" for ourselves, and if it is the opposite, we say it for our enemies.

There are those who have the custom to eat a sweet apple in honey and say, "May we have a good and sweet year." One should bless "Borei Pri Ha'etz" (Who creates the fruit of the tree), and the blessing of "Hamotzi" (over bread) does not cover it, as it is not something that comes as part of the meal. It is clear that one should taste it and then say the "Yehi Ratzon" (May it be Your will), and not interrupt between the blessing and the eating.
