Or, one can say the "Yehi Ratzon" before the blessing (see Magen Avraham, subsection 2). Some eat pomegranates and say: "May we increase in merits like a pomegranate." In our country, pomegranates are not common, and the custom is to eat fatty meat and all kinds of sweets, so that our portion may be rich and sweet.

And they eat the head of a sheep, and they say: "May we be a head and not a tail." Additionally, to remember the ram of Isaac. And for the first reason, they eat the head of any kind of fish. They also eat the "hamotzi" (bread) dipped in honey. Some are meticulous not to eat nuts, because "egoz" (nut) has the same numerical value (gematria) as "chet" (sin). Some do not dip in vinegar, and do not eat sour things on the first night, nor bitter things. This does not include peppers that are added to food, as they enhance the dish, like fish which cannot be eaten without pepper. Also, they should not eat things that increase mucus and phlegm, which would cause an interruption in prayer, such as nuts and almonds and the like.

There are those who have the custom not to sleep during the day on the first day of Rosh Hashanah, based on the Jerusalem Talmud. The Arizal said that after midday and after the sounding of the shofar, one may sleep. Sitting idle is considered equivalent to sleeping. There are those who have the custom to go to the river on the first day of Rosh Hashanah and recite verses, "And you will cast all their sins into the depths of the sea." This is called "Tashlich." They caution that women should not go, and in places where they do go, it is better that men do not go at all. In any case, there are those who object to this practice nowadays, and many refrain from it for reasons known to them, and this is proper.

Shacharit: We enter the synagogue early, and arrange the psalms as on every Yom Tov. Our custom is to say "Shir HaYichud" and "An'im Zemirot" and the "Song of the Day" before the prayer. The prayer leader wears the kittel and begins "Adon Olam" with the tune of the High Holy Days. Similarly, the blessings and the Pesukei Dezimra are recited until "HaMelech yoshev" etc. Then another prayer leader goes and chants in a pleasant tune, and finishes "HaMelech" aloud, goes to the podium, and prays Shacharit—all like the Maariv prayer. We recite piyyutim (liturgical poems), and every place follows its custom. After the repetition of the prayer leader, we open the ark and say "Avinu Malkeinu" when it falls on a weekday. We do not say "Avinu Malkeinu chatanu lefanecha," nor "katveinu b'sefer selicha," nor "ki ein banu ma'asim." This is noted in the machzorim, see there. Afterwards, we say the full Kaddish. On Shabbat, we do not say "Avinu Malkeinu." We do not say Hallel on Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur because they are days of judgment (Rosh Hashanah 32b).

One should stand during the recitation of Avinu Malkeinu. We say "kaleh kol tzar u'mashtin" with the kaf in the patach and the lamed in the tzeirei. We say "selach u'machal," because forgiveness (mechilah) is greater than pardon (selichah). We say "machah v'ha'aveir chata'einu u'fsha'einu." Similarly, we say "kera ro'a" together, and not to pause between "kera" and "ro'a" (Magen Avraham, small section 3). Some say that one should say "ro'a gezer" together (Taz at the end of Siman 622), and this seems to be the main opinion. (And perhaps there is a printing mistake in the Magen Avraham. What the Machatzit Hashekel wrote requires further investigation; see there.) It is proper to elongate the prayers and piyutim until midday.

And they read from the Torah with the cantillation of the High Holy Days in the portion "And the Lord visited Sarah" with five readers, and on Shabbat with seven. And the haftarah is from Pinchas: "And in the seventh month," and from the Prophets at the beginning of Samuel: "And there was a certain man from Ramathaim" until "and He exalted the horn of His anointed." Some call the one who blows the shofar to the Torah, and some call the prayer leader. But we cannot practice this because of the financial obligations of the synagogue and the study hall, as is known. And this is what our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 3: People who are imprisoned – do not bring a Torah scroll to them, even on Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur. This is his exact wording; it is explained well above in section 135 paragraph 30.

Circumcision on Rosh Hashanah – the circumcision is performed after the Torah reading and before the sounding of the shofar. And thus responded Rabbeinu Gershom, the Light of the Exile: that if there is no circumcision, there is no shofar. Additionally, it seems to me that circumcision in relation to the shofar is considered frequent. There are those who have the custom that the mohel does not wipe the blood of the circumcision from his mouth and sounds the shofar in this manner, to mix the blood of the circumcision with the mitzvah of the shofar (Taz, subsection 2). However, if it is not possible to bring the infant to the synagogue, and the people do not wish to wait to go to the infant’s house, it is necessary to delay the circumcision until after leaving the synagogue.

There is a positive commandment from the Torah to blow the shofar on Rosh Hashanah, as it is stated (Numbers 29:1): "It shall be a day of blowing the horn for you." And every teruah (a specific shofar blast) is preceded by a tekiah (a long blast) and followed by a tekiah, the reason for which will be explained in Siman 596. We blow the shofar twice: once after the Torah reading, and a second time during the Musaf service following the order of the blessings. This does not constitute the prohibition of "bal tosif" (not to add to the commandments), as this only applies when one adds to the essence of the commandment, such as blowing two shofars simultaneously or adding an extra species to the lulav – in these cases, one would transgress "bal tosif." However, if one takes the lulav, sets it down, and then takes it again, even a hundred times, it does not transgress "bal tosif." Similarly, with the shofar: if one blows it and then blows it again, we have no issue with it (Tosafot, Rosh Hashanah 16b, s.v. "and they blow").

However, why did the Sages require this? Now, it is certain that regarding the shofar blasts of the Musaf prayer, there is no question, for the primary blasts are in accordance with the order of the blessings. But why did they require to blow beforehand? And it was said about this in the Gemara (Rosh Hashanah 16b): "In order to confuse the Satan," see there. From Rashi's explanation (beginning with "in order to confuse"), it implies that this is the meaning: Since the Satan sees how beloved the commandments are to Israel, as they perform and then perform again – he becomes silent from presenting accusations. And the Tosafot in the name of the Arukh explained based on the Jerusalem Talmud: That the Satan becomes bewildered, fearing that it might be the shofar of the future: "And it shall come to pass on that day, a great shofar will be blown," and he has no time to present accusations against Israel, see there. And these matters require further explanation.

And it appears to my humble opinion that its explanation is as follows: behold, why indeed did they institute the recitation of Malchuyot, Zichronot, and Shofarot in the Mussaf prayer? And why did they not institute them in Shacharit, with the shofar being blown in Shacharit? Indeed, the Talmud in Rosh Hashanah (32b) raises this question: since those who are zealous for mitzvot perform them early, it should have been instituted in Shacharit. The Talmud answers: it was established during a time of persecution. The Jerusalem Talmud (Rosh Hashanah 4:8) explains further, saying that originally it was so, but due to decrees from the nations against blowing the shofar, they postponed the blessings from Shacharit to Mussaf. Even after the decrees were annulled, they did not revert to the original practice. It is explained there that when the nations saw that the Jews recite the Shema, pray, read from the Torah, and then blow the shofar, they understood that the Jews were engaging in their religious customs and did not object (see Tosafot, and not like Rashi, see there). According to this, the reason for blowing the shofar beforehand is because they used to blow it in Shacharit in conjunction with the blessings, and afterwards, they would not blow it again. However, due to the decree, they postponed it to Mussaf. Therefore, to avoid distancing themselves too much from the original ordinance and to bring the shofar blasts closer to Shacharit, and to be among those who are zealous for mitzvot, they instituted blowing the shofar after the Torah reading and before Mussaf. This causes confusion to Satan, who sees how zealous the Jewish people are in performing mitzvot, that even though decrees are imposed on them, they strive even more to fulfill the mitzvot with greater strength and vigor. For originally, they would only blow the shofar once, but after the decree, they do it twice. He also becomes alarmed, fearing that the merit of these shofar blasts might bring the great shofar, and he will be unable to accuse, and his accusations will be in vain, since the Holy One, blessed be He, sees how beloved the mitzvot are to the Jewish people and how zealous they are in performing them.

And it is customary to blow the shofar on the bimah, in the place where the Torah is read, since the shofar blasts were instituted after the Torah reading. The one who blows the shofar must recite the blessings and blow the shofar while standing, and should not lean on anything. However, if he blew while sitting, he has fulfilled his obligation, for this is not a requirement that invalidates the mitzvah. The congregation, ideally, may also sit (see Magen Avraham, subsection 1). The custom is to say the Psalm "All the nations, clap your hands" seven times before the shofar blasts. There are some unlearned people who, if they have not completed saying it seven times, continue to say it during the shofar blasts. It is necessary to inform them that this is forbidden and they are obligated to listen to the shofar blasts and not say anything during them. The recitation of "Lamnatzeach" is not a strict halachic requirement, and there are places that do not say it at all to avoid this problem.

The one who blows the shofar blesses "Blessed are You..." etc. "...Who has sanctified us with His commandments, and commanded us to hear the sound of the shofar," because the commandment is the hearing. If one blew the shofar but did not hear it, he has not fulfilled his obligation at all. He also blesses "Shehecheyanu," and the congregation answers "Amen" to both blessings. They should be careful not to say "Blessed is He and blessed is His name," as this would interrupt the blessing. Even if the one blowing the shofar has already fulfilled his obligation, he still recites these two blessings to fulfill the obligation for the listeners. It would be better if the listener recites the blessings instead of the one blowing the shofar, since the latter has already fulfilled his obligation, especially for the "Shehecheyanu" blessing, but this is not the custom. Nevertheless, if the one blowing the shofar is blowing for an individual, such as someone who is ill, it is better for the listener to recite the blessings (see Magen Avraham, subsection 3). Particularly if one is blowing for a single woman or many women, who are exempt from the shofar, as it is a positive commandment dependent on time and women are exempt, though they obligate themselves – it is certainly appropriate that they themselves recite the blessings, and not the one blowing for them, unless he has also not yet fulfilled his obligation.

And he shall blow: a tekiah-shevarim-teruah-tekiah sequence three times, a tekiah-shevarim-tekiah sequence three times, and a tekiah-teruah-tekiah sequence three times. The reason for this will be explained in Siman 590; see there. The congregation should not interrupt with "Yehi Ratzon" between the Tashrat, Tashat, and Tarat sequences, but rather should remain silent until after the Tarat sequence. This is not as printed in some machzorim. It is preferable to blow the shofar from the right side if possible, rather than the left side, for the right signifies mercy and the left signifies judgment. There is an opinion that a left-handed person should blow from the left side, which is his right, similar to the practice with tefillin (see there, subsection 4). However, this is perplexing: since the blowing is for the sake of the public, one should follow the public's right side. But the Levush wrote that according to Kabbalah, it is better to blow from the left side; see there. The shofar should be held with its mouth slightly upwards, based on the verse "God has ascended with a blast." In all these matters, there is no strict requirement; however it is done, it is acceptable. If one is in doubt whether they heard the shofar blasts or not, they should blow again without a blessing, as the blessings do not impede the fulfillment of the mitzvah. On the second day, there is no need to blow again, as it is a rabbinic doubt (see there, subsection 3). This doubt is generally uncommon.

If he began to blow (the shofar) and was unable to complete it, another person may complete it based on the blessing of the first, even if several blowers were exchanged. This applies specifically when the subsequent blowers were present at the time of the blessing. If not, they must recite the blessing. Moreover, even if he recited the blessing but was totally unable to blow, his blessing is not considered in vain, and another person may blow based on the blessing of the first.

With regard to the shofar blasts that accompany the blessings during the Musaf prayer, the prayer leader (shaliach tzibur) should not blow the shofar, but rather someone else should, in order to prevent him from becoming confused in his prayers. However, if he is confident that he will not become confused and can return to his prayers, he is permitted to blow the shofar. But for the seated blasts that precede Musaf, the prayer leader is allowed to blow the shofar. It is proper that the one who blew the shofar previously should also blow during Musaf, because it is said that one who begins a mitzvah is told to complete it; unless it is difficult for him to blow, for there is no impediment in the matter. The custom is to call out each word to the blower before he blows to prevent mistakes, and this is proper. The one who calls out should be the greatest in Torah, for according to the Kabbalah, there is a great significance in this. One who takes payment to blow the shofar on Rosh Hashanah, to lead prayers, or to translate on Shabbat and holidays in places where the custom is to translate, does not see a sign of blessing from that payment, but there is no prohibition in this. The main intention of the blower and the listeners should be to fulfill the positive commandment that the Holy One, blessed be He, commanded us to blow the shofar on Rosh Hashanah. If one knows additional matters related to this according to the Zohar, fortunate is his lot, but the primary intention is as we have stated, and the general intention is considered for its own sake. (Refer to Magen Avraham, for a remedy if one cannot blow: turn the shofar around and call into it, "Vihi Noam," refer there. For the seated blasts, this should not be done, as it constitutes an interruption between the blessing and the blasts; refer to Shaarei Teshuvah).

The Rambam wrote at the beginning of the first chapter of Shofar: "The shofar that is blown, whether on Rosh Hashanah or during the Jubilee, is the horn of a ram, which is curved. All other shofars are invalid except for the ram's horn." This is his exact wording. In other words, it is the horn of a male sheep, which is a ram that has a horn. It is curved, as that is its nature. However, a female sheep does not have a horn, as it is stated in Rosh Hashanah (16a): Rabbi [Abahu] said: "Why do we blow a ram's horn? The Holy One, blessed be He, said: Blow before Me with a ram's horn so that I will remember for you the binding of Isaac, the son of Abraham, and I will consider it as if you had bound yourselves before Me." Therefore, even though it is taught at the beginning of the third chapter of Rosh Hashanah that all shofars are valid except for that of a cow, and it is later taught: "The shofar of Rosh Hashanah is from a wild goat, straight," the law is not so. Rather, it follows Rabbi Yehuda who says in the Mishnah in Rosh Hashanah: "One blows with the horns of male sheep." And in the Baraita there, it is further explained: "On Rosh Hashanah, one blows with the curved horns of male sheep." The reason "curved" is not mentioned in the Mishnah is because all ram's horns are naturally curved (as also written by the Beit Yosef). The Baraita tends to explain more. And "males" refers to rams, as it is taught at the beginning of the fifth chapter of Shabbat: "Males go out adorned," referring to rams, see there. It appears to me that in the species of sheep, the difference between males and females is considerable, as males have horns and females do not, which is not the case in all species. Therefore, rams are called simply "males." And in the Gemara there, the law is decided according to Rabbi Yehuda, as it is stated there: Rabbi Levi said: "The mitzvah of Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur is with curved [shofars], as the law follows Rabbi Yehuda," see there.

And when Rabbi Levi says "bent," it must be referring to a ram, as he rules according to Rabbi Yehuda. And when he says "bent," it is like saying "rams," as Rashi explains there. And this is his wording in Rosh Hashanah: "The more a person bends... it is better – in his prayer, his face is lowered to the ground, it is preferable..." Therefore, on Rosh Hashanah, which is for prayer and to mention the binding of Isaac – we need bent... until here is his wording. It is explicitly stated that it is of a ram, since it comes to mention the binding of Isaac. And the reason he only says "bent" – is because the horns of rams are generally bent. (According to what I have written, it makes sense why in the Mishnah, Rabbi Yehuda only mentions males, and in the Baraita, he mentions bent males, and Rabbi Levi only mentions bent ones, and Rabbi [Abahu] (Abuha) only mentions a ram – because it is all one, as the ram's horn is bent and is not found in females. Therefore, sometimes he uses this term, and sometimes that term. And this is a great support for the opinion of the Rambam, and examine and you will find it easy.)

And behold, according to the opinion of the Rambam, Rashi, Tosafot, the Sefer Mitzvot Gadol (SeMaG), and the Hagahot Maimoni also ruled similarly. Behold, Rashi, since he wrote about using a curved shofar and also mentioned the binding of Isaac, it is clear that it is specifically from a ram. And the Tosafot (16a, s.v. "B'Shofar") wrote, and this is their language: "But we hold according to Rabbi Yehuda that we blow with curved ram's horns, as we concluded there in the Gemara"; thus their language. And similarly, the SeMaG wrote in Mitzvah 42, and this is his language: "We learned in the first chapter of Rosh Hashanah: Rabbi [Abbahu] said: Why do we blow with a ram's horn... even though we learned that all shofars are valid except for that of a cow? Rabbi [Abbahu] holds like Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Levi, who believe that the mitzvah of the shofar on Rosh Hashanah is with curved ram's horns, meaning 'rams', which we translate as 'dikhrin', and so is the law"; thus his language. And similarly, the author of the Hagahot Maimoni wrote in section 2, and this is his language: "Like Rabbi Yehuda, etc., and Rabbi Levi said, etc., and Rabbi [Abbahu] said, and not like the Mishnah, etc." And so he ruled in the Sefer HaMitzvot. And so he ruled in the Sefer Yeraim, etc.; thus his language. And according to this, I am very puzzled by our Rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, who did not bring the opinion of the Rambam at all. And it seems that because they saw that the Tur brought the opinion of the Rambam and wrote that everyone opposed it, see there – therefore, they did not bring his opinion. But in truth, even though the Ra'avad, the Rosh, the Ran, and the Tur ruled not according to him, as will be explained, nevertheless, since Rashi, Tosafot, the SeMaG, the Hagahot Maimoni, and the Yeraim ruled like the Rambam, that no shofar is valid except that of a ram and it must be curved – it is obvious that we must be concerned with their words, especially regarding a Torah prohibition not to render any other type of shofar valid. And so all of Israel has practiced. (See Taz, what he wants to say in the intention of the Rambam. And all his words are puzzling, and a mistake came from his sanctity, to switch aleph with a hiriq for aleph with a kamatz. And already the Chacham Tzvi, the Pri Megadim, and the GriB have refuted him. And the essence of his grammatical explanations have no understanding. And the foundation that a ram's horn is curved, and also the Beit Yosef mentioned this. With this, all the grammatical points are clear, as I have written. And be precise and you will find it easy.)

And the Rosh in the third chapter wrote in the name of the Ramban, that there are three categories regarding shofars: all shofars, even if not from a ram, are valid post facto, whether straight or curved, except for that from a cow, because it is a horn and not a shofar. Ideally, the mitzvah is with curved ones, and the optimal mitzvah is with one from a ram to remember the binding of Isaac. The Rosh, the Ran, and the Tur agreed with his words. And so wrote the Raavad, see there. For these Rabbis hold that the halacha follows the anonymous Mishna, that all shofars are valid except for that from a cow, and like the second Mishna which states that the shofar of Rosh Hashanah is a straight one from an ibex. However, in this the halacha follows Rabbi Yehuda: that for the mitzvah it is curved, as stated by Rabbi Levi, and optimally from a ram, as stated by Rabbi Abbahu. And the words of Rabbi Levi and Rabbi Abbahu are not essential, but Rabbi Levi's is for the mitzvah, and Rabbi Abbahu's is for the optimal mitzvah.

And this is the language of our Rabbi the Beit Yosef in Section 1: The shofar of Rosh Hashanah—its mitzvah is [fulfilled] with a ram's horn and it should be curved. However, after the fact, all shofars are valid, whether straight or curved. But there is a greater mitzvah with a curved [shofar] than with a straight one. A cow's horn is invalid in all cases. Likewise, the horns of most wild animals, which are a single bone and have no internal hollow, are invalid. Thus far is his language, and it is necessary to say that this is its explanation: The preferred mitzvah is a ram's horn and it should be curved, but after the fact, all are valid. A curved [shofar] is more of a mitzvah than straight, as it is only a preferred mitzvah, as I have written (and so wrote the Taz in Subsection 1). And it is also possible to say the opposite, that he holds that a ram's horn is more of a mitzvah than a curved one, because regarding a ram's horn, everyone agrees it is better to remember the binding of Isaac. However, regarding curved [shofars], the first Tanna disagrees with Rabbi Yehuda, and holds that only a straight [shofar] is valid. And even though the law is not like that, in any case, in the end, it can be said that it is only a preferred mitzvah. To exclude [the case of] a ram's horn, everyone agrees. And the measure of his words is this: The shofar of Rosh Hashanah—its mitzvah is with a ram's horn and it should be curved, meaning: this is the preferred mitzvah in all aspects. But after the fact, all are valid. And do not say that initially there is no strictness except with a ram's horn, because there is no disagreement about this, to this he says: And there is a greater mitzvah with curved ones than with straight ones, meaning: that even in this there is a beautification of the mitzvah. And we have already written that the opinion of the Rambam, Rashi, Tosafot, SeMaG, Hagahot Maimoniot, and Yerei'im is that even after the fact, only a ram's horn and it should be curved is valid. And even if the ram was slaughtered or became blemished, it is valid, because it is a pure species.

Our teacher, the Rema, wrote: "Similarly, a shofar from an impure animal is invalid." These are his exact words. This means that even according to those authorities who hold that a shofar from any species is valid, nevertheless, from an impure animal, it is invalid. For only a pure animal is suitable for the service of Heaven, as we say in Shabbat (28b) regarding the work of the Tabernacle, see there. This means that any commandment that involves an animal must involve a pure animal. This is in contrast to cases where the commandment does not require an animal, such as the walls of a sukkah, where wood and stone are also valid. It is obvious that it is permissible to use even an impure animal as a wall, as stated in Sukkah (23a) that it is permitted to use an elephant as a wall for a sukkah, see there, because it is no worse than wood and stone. And know that even though it explicitly states in the Mishnah in Niddah (51b) that an impure animal does not have horns, see there, and if so, this law does not apply — this is not universally accepted, and the Sages dispute this Mishnah, as stated in Chullin (59a). Furthermore, the Rambam explains there that it refers to a wild animal, but in the case of a domesticated animal, even an impure one can have horns (see Ba’al HaGolah, Magen Avraham, and Eliyah Rabbah).

A stolen or robbed shofar, if one blew it – he has fulfilled [the obligation], even if the owners have not despaired of its return, for there is no theft concerning sound. For even regarding sacred items, we say that sound, sight, and smell do not constitute misappropriation. And even though there is still a prohibition, as it is mentioned in Pesachim (26a), certainly it is forbidden initially. And one should not recite a blessing over it (Magen Avraham, subsection 4), for how can one bless over a stolen item? Nevertheless, the positive commandment of the shofar – he has fulfilled. And it is permissible to take a friend’s shofar without his knowledge and blow it, for it is certainly pleasing to him that a mitzvah be performed with his property, in something that incurs no loss. And as I have written in Siman 11 regarding a tallit, see there. And one should not ask: why does a lulav on the first day need to be one's own, and one cannot fulfill the obligation with another's [lulav]? Because it is written (Leviticus 23:40): "And you shall take for yourselves" – from your own, as I will write in Siman 658. If so, we should also require one's own shofar, for it is also written regarding the shofar (Numbers 29:1): "It shall be a day of blowing for you"? However, it is not similar, for there "for you" is written regarding "and you shall take", implying "and you shall take from your own", but here it pertains to "a day of blowing". And so it is stated in the Jerusalem Talmud at the beginning of "The Stolen Lulav" (Jerusalem Talmud, Sukkah, Chapter 3, Halacha 1), see there. (And see Beit Yosef, and Taz subsection 2. And this resolves the Raavad's objection to the Rambam in the first chapter of this law, see there. And be precise and you will find it easy.) (And in the Hagahot Ashri, a stolen shofar is invalid based on the Jerusalem Talmud. But the early authorities explained this concerning the lulav, and this is the main opinion, for regarding the lulav the language of "shaved" applies. See there at the end of the third chapter, and be precise and you will find it easy.)

It is stated in the Gemara (Rosh Hashanah 28a) that one should not initially blow a shofar that comes from a burnt offering or peace offering. However, if one did blow such a shofar, he has fulfilled his obligation because commandments were not given for benefit. This means that any commandment that does not involve physical enjoyment, but rather the fulfillment of the commandment itself, is not considered deriving benefit from consecrated property, because commandments were not given for benefit. But if not for this reasoning, one would not fulfill the obligation with them. And although sound itself does not constitute misuse of consecrated property, this applies to merely hearing the sound of consecrated property. However, taking a consecrated item and blowing it – one immediately commits misuse by taking it because there is misuse of consecrated property, even in an item that is not diminished, as is taught in the Mishnah at the beginning of the fifth chapter of Me'ilah. And even though there must be a benefit equivalent to a perutah (small coin), as taught there, it can be said that even here, though commandments were not given for benefit, nonetheless, everyone would give a perutah to fulfill the commandment. (This interpretation is necessary, for otherwise, how could Rabbi Yochanan say that there was misuse? See there, and examine and you will find clarity.)

It is forbidden to blow a shofar that was used for idol worship, such as one that was bowed to, or one that is an accessory of idol worship, as it is considered repulsive to use for a mitzvah. However, if one blows it, they have fulfilled their obligation. This is not considered as deriving benefit, since mitzvot were not given for enjoyment, as I have written. This applies when the shofar belongs to a non-Jew, as it can be nullified, and therefore even before it is nullified, one fulfills their obligation. But when it belongs to a Jew, it cannot be nullified, as I have written in Yoreh De'ah 146, and it needs to be burned. A shofar needs to have a length that allows it to be held in the hand and seen on both sides, as will be explained later, with the required length being four thumb-widths. Since it needs to be burned, it is considered as if it is already burned, and its measure is fragmented. However, for a non-Jew's shofar, even before nullification, since it can be nullified, we do not say its measure is fragmented. But this is only if the Jew did not intend to acquire the shofar. If they did intend to acquire it, it becomes the property of the Jew and cannot be nullified. Even though the shofar has a non-Jewish owner, and thus what benefit is there in the Jew wanting to acquire it, since the non-Jew does not transfer ownership? Indeed, some say that only a shofar that is ownerless becomes the property of the Jew when they intend to acquire it, not a non-Jew's shofar (Bach) – this is not the case, as proven in many places. The reason is that since the Jew intended to steal it, they are accountable for it, and hence it is considered as belonging to the Jew in this regard (Taz, subsection 3, and Magen Avraham, subsection 5, as well as Beit Yosef wrote). Additionally, there is a simple reason here, as we must be referring to before nullification, as after nullification, it becomes completely permissible. But we do not consider it as fragmented because the non-Jew can nullify it. Since the Jew intended to acquire it, they will not hand it over to the non-Jew, and how will it be nullified? Thus, its measure is considered fragmented.

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote in paragraph 3 that there are those who are stringent, saying that even with a non-Jew's [item] one does not fulfill [the mitzvah], unless it was nullified before Yom Tov; thus are his words. The explanation of the matter is: Rabbeinu Tam holds that the reason one fulfills [the mitzvah] with a non-Jew's [item] is only after nullification, as explained in Tosafot Chullin (89a). But before nullification, since it requires burning, its measure is considered as though it is ground down. Consequently, it must be nullified before Yom Tov. Otherwise, since it was rejected at the beginning of the day, it does not return and become fit [for use]. This is unlike what will be explained in Siman 676 regarding the myrtle, that if its berries outnumber its leaves, it is invalid, but if one plucks them, it becomes valid. And it is effective even if one plucks them on Yom Tov; see there. This is because one has the ability to rectify it, and it is not considered rejected. But here, one does not have the ability to nullify it (Magen Avraham, subsection 6). And even though we hold in Yoreh De'ah Siman 28 that there is no rejection concerning commandments, see there. However, in Sukkah (33a) we say that this is a doubtful law. And since it is a doubt, it follows that one does not fulfill [the mitzvah], as it is considered as though it was seen and then rejected, and it does not return and become fit, as is proven in several places. For before it was processed, it was fit for a shofar, and when it was processed, it was rejected from being a shofar, and when they nullified it, it returned and became fit. (See Magen Avraham there, and according to what I have written, it is well explained. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

A shofar that was used as an offering to idols, even if it belonged to a non-Jew, one does not fulfill their obligation by blowing it, because it can never be nullified, as is written in Yoreh De'ah, section 146. Similarly, a shofar from a city that was led astray, one does not fulfill their obligation with it because it is considered as if it has no measure (Rosh Hashanah 28a). It appears to me that a shofar of idols is only prohibited if one bowed to the shofar. But if one bowed to the ram, the shofar is not prohibited, for living beings are not prohibited, as written in Yoreh De'ah, section 145. Additionally, it appears to me that when we said it needs nullification before the holiday, it applies even on the night of the holiday; since it is before the time of blowing, it is considered as if it is before the holiday.

One who is forbidden by a vow to benefit from a shofar, such as if he said, "The benefit of this shofar is forbidden to me" – he is permitted to hear the blasts when another person blows this shofar, because this is not considered a benefit, as commandments were not given for enjoyment. However, he should not blow it himself initially, because some people derive pleasure when they blow. Nevertheless, if there is no one else to blow – he may blow it himself, as this is not considered enjoyment at all, as stated in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 241 (Magen Avraham, Subsection 7). However, initially it is better for someone else to blow. This is when he said, "The benefit of this shofar is forbidden to me." But if he said, "This shofar is forbidden to me for its blowing" – he is forbidden to blow it himself, and also to hear it blown by others for the purpose of a commandment, and certainly for a non-commandment blowing. This is not similar to one who swears not to blow a shofar, for such a person is flogged and blows, because an oath does not apply to a commandment. But vows do apply to commandments, as stated in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 215, where the reason is explained. Although a vow does not apply to something that has no substance, and blowing a shofar has no substance, this is when he said, "The blowing of this shofar is forbidden to me" or "blowings" in general. But if he said, "This shofar is forbidden to me for its blowing" – since the shofar itself has substance. This distinction is explained in Siman 213, see there.

All sounds are valid for the shofar. Therefore, if its sound is very thick or very thin, or very dry – it is valid. However, it seems to me that all this is specifically when the sound is loud, but if the sound is a whisper – one has not fulfilled their obligation, even if someone next to them hears it. For a whisper is not considered a sound at all, and we require "to hear the sound of the shofar." Similarly, the essence of the term "teruah" is a loud sound, like "he shall shout and also roar." Therefore, it is true that all sounds are valid for the shofar; however, in any case, a sound is required (so it seems in my humble opinion).

The Rambam wrote in the first chapter, law 5: The minimum size of the shofar is such that one can hold it in his hand and it can be seen extending to both sides. If it is cracked along its length, it is invalid. If it is cracked across its width, if the remaining part is of the minimum size, it is valid, as if the place of the crack had been removed. If it has a hole, if it was sealed with something not of its kind, it is invalid. If it was sealed with something of its kind, if the majority of it remains intact and the sealed holes do not obstruct the sound, it is valid. This is the end of his words. And what he wrote "so that one can hold it in his hand and it can be seen extending to both sides" does not mean that it is measured according to the person blowing it, which would differ if the blower has a thick hand or a thin hand. It has already been explained in the Gemara Niddah (26b) that we go according to an average person, and its size is a tefach, which is four thumb-widths. Some require a "laughing" tefach (Tur in the name of R' Yitzchak Gaon), as in this size it can be seen extending to both sides. But the Tur and Shulchan Aruch did not require this, rather that a precise tefach is valid. For in this too it can be seen extending to both sides, as the blower holds it with four fingers, which do not amount to four thumb-widths, and thus something is left on this side and something on that side (Ran in the third chapter). And the reason it must be seen extending to both sides is so that people will not say that he is blowing into his hand (Rosh, third chapter, sign 6).

And this which is written "if it is cracked lengthwise, it is invalid" – he did not explain how much of the length must be cracked, whether entirely or partially. And there are different opinions on this: some say that even the smallest amount – it is invalid, because when the crack is lengthwise – it continues to expand due to the force of the blowing, until it becomes entirely cracked, which is worse than a hole, and worse than a crack across its width, and we view it as if it is entirely cracked (there in the name of some authorities). And it is obvious that even according to this opinion, in any case, some length is required, and it must be cracked through the entire thickness of the wall to the hollow, for if not – it is no worse than a hole. And there is no difference in a lengthwise crack whether it impedes the blowing due to the crack or does not impede; even if it does not impede – it is invalid, because the reason is that it stands to become entirely cracked. And it seems to me that according to this view, the invalidity is only rabbinic, for from the Torah there is no reason. For it is impossible to say that anything that stands to crack is considered as already cracked, like we say in general: anything that stands to be redeemed is considered as already redeemed; for even in that we do not hold this way. And it is Rabbi Shimon who holds this throughout the Talmud, and the Rabbis disagree with him, as we wrote similarly in Yoreh De'ah, section 33, paragraph 6, regarding an irregular adhesion, see there. Rather, the invalidity is rabbinic, for perhaps it will become entirely cracked during the blowing and he will not notice.

Now, the Rosh agreed with this opinion, and therefore the Tur also wrote similarly. And this is the language of the Tur: If it is cracked lengthwise, even slightly, it is invalid. And this applies only if it is not glued, but if it is glued, it is valid. And this is when it is glued with its own kind. And the Ramban wrote that sealing with glue is not considered its own kind, unless it is heated with fire until it melts and joins its edges one to another. And the Rosh wrote that glue is considered its own kind, and it is not considered a different kind unless the hole is sealed with another piece. But when it is joined with glue, it returns to how it was. And the glue is not noticeable between the cracks. Thus far is his language. And in any case, even according to the Rosh who permits with glue because it is not noticeable, if it is joined with something noticeable that is of another kind, it is invalid.

And our teacher, the Beit Yosef, ruled differently in Section 8, and this is his language: If it is cracked lengthwise, it is invalid. Some say that even if it is only a small amount, it is invalid unless it is tightly bound with a string or with glue. Until here is his language. And behold, this is not considered its own kind. And indeed, the Ran disagrees with the Rosh, and this is the language of the Ran: According to the commentators who say that any small amount of a crack invalidates it, if it is tightly bound with a string or with glue, it is valid because the string holds it together so that it does not split. And this is also the opinion of the Ra'avad in his discourse, etc.; until here is his language. Nevertheless, in my humble opinion, the Rosh and the Ran do not disagree. For the Kolbo wrote about this that it is specifically when the measure for the blowing remains, from the place of the binding and upwards towards the mouth; until here is his language. And this is what our teacher the Rema also wrote in this language: And the measure for the blowing remains, etc.; until here is his language. And according to this, I say that in such a case, even the Rosh and the Tur would agree with this. And what they wrote that it needs to be of its own kind – this is when the measure does not remain. And the reason is simple, for when the measure for the blowing does not remain up to its end, it can be said that it is invalid from the Torah, because it is considered as if it is separated. Therefore, it needs to be attached specifically with its own kind. But when the measure for the blowing remains, surely its invalidity is only rabbinic, for the reason we have written, and therefore binding with a string or glue suffices, as this removes the concern that it might split entirely. (And this is the depth of the Rema's intention, but he was brief. Be precise and you will find it easy.)(And this resolves the difficulty of the Magen Avraham in sub-section 11, and the Taz in sub-section 12.)

However, from the language of the Rambam (Chapter 1, Halacha 5) it implies that it is specifically when it is cracked entirely along its length that it is invalid. This is also evident from the language of Rashi, see there, who wrote "it is cracked entirely." Similarly, our Rabbis, the Ba'alei Tosafot, wrote there (27b, s.v. "nis'dak") that along its length it is not invalid unless it is cracked along its entire length from its top to its bottom. Thus are their words. Also, if the Rambam had held that it is invalid even if cracked in part or in most of it, he would have explained, and it is clear that his intention is like Rashi and Tosafot, that it is specifically when it is cracked entirely. The reason is that it becomes like two shofars. Therefore, even joining it with its own kind does not help, just as it does not help with two shofars, for the Merciful One said "a shofar," not two or three shofars (Gemara).

Some say that if the majority of it is cracked, it is invalid (Magid Mishneh in the name of commentators). This is what Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote there: And some say specifically if the majority, but if it is bonded—it is valid, even if bonded with glue. And there is one who says it is not valid unless it bonded by itself, by heating it in fire until it melts, and then joining its ends together. And if it is entirely cracked, even from one side—it is invalid, even if heated in fire and its cracks joined together. Up to here is his language, and the reason is simple: As long as a minority of it is connected, even a tiny amount—it is not considered as two separate shofarot, and therefore bonding helps. This is not the case if it is entirely cracked. The Magid Mishneh wrote there that even for the majority, bonding does not help, see there. The poskim (decisors of Jewish law) disagreed with him. It is clear that even if it is entirely cracked—it is not called cracked unless it is cracked all the way to the hollow. But if the crack does not pass through the entire wall—it is valid without any repair, and this is found in several shofarot. And all this is when it is cracked lengthwise.

And if it is cracked across its width, the Gemara states that if there remains a measure sufficient for a valid sounding, it is kosher, but if not, it is invalid. Rashi explains that "across its width" means the entire circumference, see there. However, the Rosh and the Tur write that even if the majority of the circumference is cracked, it is invalid, and thus, if it is cracked halfway, it is also invalid, since it is impossible to be precise with a small amount. Furthermore, with a Torah prohibition, half and half is considered as the majority, if the majority is stringent. And even for leniency, there are those who consider it as the majority, as explained in Chullin (Chullin 28b), although we do not hold this way. For stringency, everyone agrees that it is considered the majority. And we also hold that it is impossible to be precise (there), and this is the law. Here too, it must be until the hollow, and therefore, even if it does not prevent the sounding and is only in a minority, it is completely kosher without any correction. For in its width, it does not entirely crack due to the strength of the sounding as it does in its length, because the sound travels and tears lengthwise and not widthwise.

And this is the language of our teacher, the Beit Yosef, in paragraph 9: If it is cracked widthwise in a small portion - it is kosher; in a large portion - it is invalid, unless there remains from the crack toward its mouth the measure of a blast, which is four thumb-widths. And if there remains such a measure - it is kosher, even if it hinders the blast. And there are those who permit it if there remains even not toward its mouth. Until here is his language, and the reason is simple: since there remains enough for a blast - we do not need the additional parts at all. And it appears to me that for the "those who permit" it if there remains even not toward its mouth - we require in any case that it does not hinder the blast, for if not so, since he is blowing in the upper part, it is not in its usual manner of blowing. And therefore our teacher the Beit Yosef wrote the opinion of the "those who permit" after "even if it hinders" etc., meaning: in such a case we certainly require that it does not hinder the blast. But the main ruling is according to the first opinion, as this is the opinion of most of the decisors (see Beit Yosef). And know that the thumb-widths are measured by the width of the thumb in its middle (Magen Avraham, subsection 18).

If a hole is made in the shofar, that is, a hole in the chamber and not a crack, we have already written in Section 14 that the Rambam wrote that if it is sealed not with its own kind, it is invalid. However, if it is sealed with its own kind, if most of it remains intact and the sealed holes do not hinder the sound, it is valid. See there. Clearly, he only permits it under three conditions: the seal must be with its own kind specifically, and if it is not with its own kind, it is invalid even if it is a minor part, and even if it does not hinder the sound. Most of it must remain intact, and if most of it is punctured, it is invalid in all cases. The sealed holes must not hinder the sound. However, if they do hinder the sound in any case, it is invalid. The explanation of "hindering the sound" means that the sound becomes weaker after sealing compared to how it was before being punctured (Maggid Mishneh). But if the sound changed before sealing, we do not worry about it, and it neither adds nor detracts. The main issue depends on the change after sealing (Kesef Mishneh), and this is the opinion of the Rif in the third chapter, see there, and the Geonim (Tur).

However, the opinion of the Tosafot and the Rosh (Chapter 3, Section 5) is: If one sealed it with its own kind, and the majority remained, even if it impedes the sound so that it does not return to its original state – it is valid. If one sealed it not with its own kind, if it impedes the sound so that it does not return to its original state as it was whole – it is invalid, even if the majority remained, and even if its sound now is like it was when it was punctured – it is invalid, because it did not return to how it was before it was punctured (Tur). However, if it did not impede the sound, meaning that its sound after sealing is like its sound before the puncture, even if it was sealed not with its own kind – it is valid, since the majority remained unpunctured. And in the Jerusalem Talmud it is stated that if it was not sealed at all – it is valid, even though its sound changed from how it was, because all sounds are valid in a shofar. According to this, sealing is not necessary, unless it is impossible to blow without sealing. But as long as it is possible to blow – one should blow as it is. And even the Raavad brought this from the Jerusalem Talmud, see there. Even if the amount remaining from the puncture upwards is not enough for a proper blow (Taz, Subsection 7). And so ruled the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch, Section 7. And our master the Rema wrote about this: that when there is another shofar – one should not blow with this one, because some say one should not blow with a punctured shofar. This is his exact language, and it is a wonder: And who has the power to dispute the Jerusalem Talmud on something about which our Talmud does not argue? And the Rif and the Rambam also do not provide evidence, as they only wrote the laws that are in the Gemara. And it seems to me that their reasoning is because usually, when the puncture is large, it is impossible to blow without sealing, since the air escapes from the puncture, and the sound will not be heard. If it is a small puncture and does not impede the blow – it is obviously permissible to blow with it. Therefore, they did not bother to mention it. And in the dispute between the Rif and Rambam with the Tosafot and the Rosh – certainly one should be stringent like the Rif and Rambam, but if there is no other shofar, one can rely on the Tosafot and the Rosh and bless on it. This also seems to be the opinion of our master the Beit Yosef in Section 7, see there.

If one glued together pieces of broken shofars and made from them a shofar, it is invalid, as the Merciful One said "a shofar"—one shofar, not two or three shofars (26:1). And even though in all other cases, gluing makes it as one, like the cases of the compartments of tefillin and similar, nevertheless, you are forced to say that the Torah invalidated two shofars—even when glued. Otherwise, it would be impossible to blow it without gluing. And one cannot say that the Torah's intention is only not to blow two shofars literally at the same time, as that is impossible. And blowing one after the other—of course it is permitted, and it happens every day. Furthermore, this verse is unnecessary for that, as we know this from the prohibition of "bal tosif" (not adding to the commandments) according to the Rambam in the seventh chapter, where taking two lulavs transgresses "bal tosif," see there, and the same applies to two shofars. And according to the Raavad there, and Tosafot in Rosh Hashanah (28b), that "bal tosif" only applies with a different species, see there—in truth, there is no prohibition with two shofars. Rather, certainly the Torah warned that the shofar should not be made of two glued pieces. (And even Rabbi Yosi, who said at the beginning of the third chapter 26b: "since they are joined together, it is one," only said this regarding a cow, where its layers are naturally one, see there. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

Therefore, it is forbidden to make a shofar by joining two pieces, one on top and one on the bottom, even if the piece on top, which is near the mouth, has the required measure of a shofar. Even with a large shofar, if one attaches even a small amount from another shofar to the top or bottom, the shofar is invalid because the scripture decrees that it must be a single shofar, not two or three shofars. Therefore, if one adds anything to the shofar, whether of its own kind or not, it is invalid. If it is not of its own kind, it is obviously invalid, just like adding a different kind to a lulav invalidates it. 

One should not question how filling a hole in the shofar with its own kind is effective, as it might seem like it is becoming two shofars. This is not the case, as it only fills the hole and does not count as an addition. The proof is that according to Tosafot and the Rosh in section 23, even filling with a different kind is permissible as long as it does not change the sound. And surely a different kind is generally forbidden, but here, since it is used to fill a hole, it becomes nullified to the essence of the shofar, and the filling does not have any independent status at all.

If one reversed and blew into a shofar, he has not fulfilled his obligation, whether he reversed it in the manner one turns a garment inside out, making the inner side the outer and vice versa, or whether he left it as it is but widened the narrow end and narrowed the wide end; as it is stated, "And you shall pass the shofar" – we require that it be passed in its normal manner (Rosh Hashanah 27b), just as a ram passes it over its head while alive (Rashi). There are some who wish to permit it if reversed like a garment, since the narrow and wide ends remain in their places. However, it is explicitly stated in the Jerusalem Talmud that it is invalid, as we require that the inner side face the hollow. The Rosh in the third chapter (siman 4) cites from the Jerusalem Talmud, how do we know that one must blow from the narrow end? As it is written, "From the straits, I called" etc. Therefore, even if he did not alter the shofar but blew from the wide end, it is invalid. However, if the shofar was long and he shortened it from the top by cutting off a part – it is valid, as long as the required size of the shofar remains. Nevertheless, it seems to me that if he cut it from the bottom and removed the entire wide end – it is invalid, as we require a shofar to have a narrow and wide end, as it is in life. But if he cut a part of the wide end – it is valid, as long as there is still a wide part. Similarly, if he scraped it, whether from the inside or the outside, until it became as thin as a membrane – it is valid, as there is no required thickness for a shofar. Since he did not alter it – it is valid (and reversing is invalid even from one side).

The shofar is hollow, as is known. While it is still in the ram's horn, it is not hollow, as a bone from the head extends into the horn. This bone is not hollow, but when it is removed from the ram, the bone is pushed out, leaving it hollow. Even if the bone was not removed but was punctured while still inside, it is valid, and it is even permissible to do so initially, since a kind within its kind does not create a barrier (as per Magen Avraham, section 20), given that this is its natural formation. Nevertheless, it is more commendable to remove the bone, and this is the common custom which should not be changed. If this bone is removed from the horn, punctured, and used for blowing, it is invalid, as this is not a shofar at all. A shofar must be hollow, and this is not hollow; it merely does not create a barrier but cannot serve as the shofar itself. (In the Jerusalem Talmud, third chapter, halacha 6, there are those who would initially blow by drilling into the bone while it was still inside, as brought in the Beit Yosef.)

It is stated in the Gemara (27b): If one plated the shofar with gold at the place where the mouth rests – it is invalid. If it was plated not at the place where the mouth rests – it is valid. If it was plated with gold from the inside – it is invalid. From the outside, if its sound has changed from what it was – it is invalid, and if not – it is valid. Look there. The early authorities deduced that this "not at the place where the mouth rests" certainly refers to the outside, for if it were from the inside – it would be invalid, and if so, it refers to the outside (Tosafot and Rosh). Therefore, some explained that everything refers to the thickness of the upper part. And "at the place where the mouth rests" refers to part of the thickness towards the hollow, where the mouth is placed. And "not at the place where the mouth rests" means part of the thickness towards the outside (Ran there). And plating at the place where the mouth rests – is invalid because it constitutes a separation, as the gold interposes between the mouth and the shofar. And there is one who explained that "not at the place where the mouth rests" means from the outside, on its upper half, and we hold that in this case, even if its sound has changed slightly – it is valid, for the primary change depends on the second half, the wider part, where the main expansion of the sound occurs (Rosh in the name of Rabbeinu Yonah). And this is a significant leniency (there), and it is difficult to rely on it.

And the Rosh explained that it certainly refers to the outside, and its sound does not change because of a little coating; and if it did change, it would be invalid. And previously, we held that this is not like a shofar within a shofar, and later we held that there is a distinction between whether its sound changes or not. And this is also clarified from the words of the Rambam, that if not in the place where the mouth rests and from the outside – this is the matter. As he wrote in the first chapter, law 6: If he coated it with gold from the inside, or in the place where the mouth rests – it is invalid. If he coated it from the outside, if its sound changed, etc.; thus far his words. Thus, he did not mention not in the place where the mouth rests, because this is "from the outside." And so it is explained in the Jerusalem Talmud (third chapter, law 3), which says there: If he coated it with gold from the inside – it is invalid, from the outside – it is valid. If he coated the place where the mouth rests, or if its sound was thick because of the coating – it is invalid; thus far his words, and he did not mention not in the place where the mouth rests.

Behold, the reason for its invalidity at the place where the mouth is placed, we explained that this is due to the issue of an interposition, as it is necessary for the mouth to be attached to the shofar. Therefore, if one blows with a gap of air between his mouth and the shofar, without attaching his mouth to the shofar—it is invalid. Some have explained the reason as being that the sound comes from the gold and not from the shofar. According to this, there is no proof that it would be invalid without attaching the mouth to the shofar (see Taz, subsection 18). And one should not ask: why is it valid on the outside, since we hold in section 25 that an addition not of its kind invalidates it in any amount? For it can be said that "addition" is called when it extends the shofar in its length, and not in the coating from inside or outside. Therefore, if one placed gold on the thickness of the shofar on the wide side, meaning he added to it any amount, it is invalid. And certainly, if he added to the thickness on the narrow side, as this also involves the invalidity of an interposition between his mouth and the shofar. And we have already written that if one distanced the shofar from his mouth and blew into it—it is invalid. And the Ramban wrote that those who paint designs on the shofar with various colors are not doing well, for perhaps the sound will change because of the color. And even if the color did not spread through the entire shofar, perhaps the sound will change because of this (Tur). But it is permitted to engrave designs on the shofar itself to beautify it, for without color the sound will not change.

If one placed a shofar within another shofar and blew it, if he heard the sound of the inner shofar, he has fulfilled his obligation; but if he heard the sound of the outer shofar, he has not fulfilled his obligation (Gemara there). This means: if he heard only the sound of the inner shofar, for example, if it extends beyond the outer one on both sides, and he placed the inner one in his mouth and blew it – it is valid, because the sound comes only from the inner shofar. Even if it extends only at the top towards the mouth, and at the wider end it is equal with the outer one – it is still valid. But if the outer one protrudes – it is invalid, because the sound also comes from the outer one, which would be the sound of two shofars. Similarly, if the inner one does not extend beyond the outer one at the top – there is a concern that the sound comes from both of them, and it is invalid. Certainly, if the sound comes from the outer one and not from the inner one – it is invalid, because there is an interruption between the sound of the shofar and the shofar itself. And know that even if he heard only the sound of the inner one, we require that its sound is not altered by the outer one, because if it is altered – it is invalid, as I have written. And even according to those who permit sealing it with its own kind, if it is altered as I have written in section 25, nevertheless here it is invalid, because of the two shofars (Magen Avraham, subsection 22).

The shofar of Rosh Hashanah—one does not desecrate the festival for it. And we do not say that the positive commandment of shofar comes and overrides the prohibition of the festival. For it has already been explained in Siman 288 that the festival is both a positive and a negative commandment, and a positive commandment does not override a negative and a positive commandment. And even in a situation where the positive commandment is removed, the positive commandment of shofar does not override the negative commandment of the festival, for even a Rabbinic prohibition is not overridden by the shofar. Because the sages equated their decrees to the Torah law and upheld their decrees regarding the shofar with a passive stance, just as they upheld their decrees not to blow the shofar on Rosh Hashanah that falls on Shabbat due to a decree, as I wrote in Siman 588. And as we say in Yevamot (90b), that in a passive stance, the sages upheld their decrees in several matters such as shofar, lulav, and more. See there.

Therefore, if the shofar is at the top of a tree or across the river, and he has no other shofar except for that one, he should not climb the tree nor swim across the water to bring it. Similarly, if it is under a pile of stones, it is forbidden to move the stones to take it. One should not go beyond the Shabbat boundary to hear the sound of the shofar, and certainly, one should not bring the shofar from beyond the boundary. All the more so, one should not cut the shofar, whether by hand or with a tool. Using a tool would be a Torah prohibition because it constitutes making a utensil, and doing it by hand, which is considered an unusual manner of fixing, would be a rabbinic prohibition. The Gemara (Rosh Hashanah 33a) explains that using a knife is a Torah prohibition, while using a sickle is a rabbinic prohibition, as it is considered fixing in an unusual manner. See there.

In what case are these words said? [They are said] regarding a Jew. But regarding a non-Jew – it is permissible to do anything whose prohibition is only from the rabbis, for it is a "shvut d'shvut" (a rabbinic prohibition upon another rabbinic prohibition) in the context of a mitzvah, and it is permitted. But for a Torah prohibition, it is forbidden to tell him to do it. And even according to the words of our master, the Rema, earlier in Siman 276, that for a great need it is permitted to tell [a non-Jew to perform an act] even if it is a Torah prohibition, see there – in any case, in the context of a mitzvah where one should remain inactive, it is not permitted. Moreover, we do not hold like this according to the name, as I wrote there. Therefore, we tell a non-Jew to climb a tree and to go beyond the Shabbat boundary to bring a shofar. This is [allowed] beyond two thousand cubits and not beyond twelve mil, according to the Rif and the Rambam, who hold that the boundary of twelve mil is a Torah prohibition. It is possible that in this case we rely on most of the poskim (decisors) who hold that even this is rabbinic, and this seems to be the main opinion (and so wrote the Eliyah Rabbah, subsection 29). Know that from the plain language of the poskim it implies that even on the second day of Rosh Hashanah, when the shofar blasts are rabbinic – in any case it is permitted to tell a non-Jew to do a rabbinic prohibition for him. Since it is permitted on the first day – it is permitted on the second day as well. For in the end, it is only a "shvut d'shvut," and they did not decree in the context of a mitzvah, even if it is rabbinic. It is not worse than a loss, where they did not decree in such a manner. (And so it seems from the words of the Maharshal in his responsa, Siman 1. And I am astonished at the Eliyah Rabbah, subsection 29, who wants to question this, see there.)

And if the non-Jew himself performed a complete labor, such as making the shofar on Yom Tov – it is permitted to blow it, even though he did it for the sake of the Jew. This is not comparable to a non-Jew who performed labor for a Jew on Shabbat and Yom Tov, where it is forbidden for a Jew to benefit from it. There, there are two reasons: not to benefit from Shabbat and Yom Tov labor, and also lest he tell him to do it for him. But with the shofar, this doesn't apply, because there is no benefit, as commandments were not given for enjoyment. Also, we do not decree that one might tell him to do it for him, because we only decree this in matters that have benefit – we are concerned he might transgress for the sake of his enjoyment. But in matters that do not have benefit, just a commandment, why would he transgress for the sake of a commandment?

However, this applies when the non-Jew made the shofar from his own ram or from his own horn, as there is no prohibition of muktzeh. There is no muktzeh for a non-Jew, as I wrote in Siman 292. And even though this is also considered nolad (something that came into existence on the festival), and nolad is prohibited even for a non-Jew, as I wrote in Siman 505, in this case, one can rely on the poskim (halachic authorities) who permit nolad on a festival, as I wrote in Siman 496 (the Gra, Siman 25, and see Magen Avraham, Siman Katan 25). But if a shofar was made on the festival from a Jew’s horn – it is prohibited to blow it, because at twilight it was not fit for blowing, and since it was set aside (muktzeh) at twilight – it remains set aside for the entire day. Additionally, it is considered nolad and it is prohibited to handle it in order to blow it. (And the Gra wrote that one can rely on those who permit nolad on the festival, and this also seems to be implied by the Magen Avraham there. However, this requires further examination, as it is also muktzeh at twilight, and since it was set aside then, etc. Examine and you will find it easy.)

He can put water or vinegar or wine inside the shofar to clean it, so that it will sound better. There is no concern of "repairing a vessel" because this is merely for enhancement. However, urine is prohibited even on a weekday, due to the issue of respect. (And be aware that if it was brought from outside the Shabbat boundary, it is forbidden to carry it outside.)

The commandment is "to hear the sound of the shofar," meaning the blasts as they truly are. But if one hears merely an echo, such as when the blower stands in a pit, and the person standing on the ground outside the pit hears only an echo, even if he hears both the echo and the sound of the shofar – he has not fulfilled his obligation, because the sound is mixed, and this is not considered the "sound of the shofar." And thus it is stated in the Mishnah (Rosh Hashanah 27a): If one blows into a pit, or a cistern, or a barrel, if he hears the sound of the shofar – he has fulfilled his obligation, but if he hears the sound of an echo – he has not fulfilled his obligation. (And in Rashi on 28a, s.v. "if he hears the sound of an echo" – it is explained that if the sound of the shofar is mixed with the echo, he has not fulfilled his obligation.)

The Gemara explains: This rule applies only to those standing at the edge of the pit. But those standing inside the pit have fulfilled their obligation; see there. According to Rashi and the Rambam in the first chapter, the explanation is as follows: Those in the pit always hear the sound of the shofar, and those standing at the edge of the pit sometimes hear the pure sound of the shofar and fulfill their obligation, and sometimes hear an echo along with the shofar sound (Rashi 28a) and do not fulfill their obligation. This is the language of the Rambam at the end of the first chapter and the Shulchan Aruch, Section 1: One who blows the shofar inside a pit or a cave - those standing inside the pit or cave have fulfilled their obligation; and those standing outside: if they hear the sound of the shofar – they have fulfilled their obligation, if they hear the sound of an echo – they have not fulfilled their obligation. Similarly, one who blows into a large barrel, or something similar, if they hear the sound of the shofar – they have fulfilled their obligation, if they hear the sound of an echo – they have not fulfilled their obligation. This is the end of his words. Even one standing inside it has not fulfilled their obligation (Magen Avraham, Section 2), because in barrels the sound can be mixed even for those standing inside, unlike in pits and cisterns. Note that a "cistern" is a structure below ground. If most of it is built above ground, even though part of it is built below ground – it is considered like a house (ibid., Section 1).

And behold, the Rosh challenged this interpretation, as those who stand at the edge of the pit sometimes hear the sound of the shofar, and sometimes the sound of an echo. And these are his words: "I do not know what distinction there is 'if he heard the sound of the shofar or the sound of an echo,' etc. It is not reasonable that it should depend on human perception, etc. And if it depends on the depth of the pit and its proximity – all this requires a measure; thus far his words." Therefore, the Rosh explained that the interpretation is as follows: Those who stand at the edge of the pit – they always hear only the sound of an echo, and they have not fulfilled their obligation. And those who stand in the pit – they always hear the sound of the shofar, and they have fulfilled their obligation. (And the Gemara explains that when the Mishnah states "if he heard the sound," etc., it is not conditional, but rather the interpretation is: if they heard the sound of the shofar, such as those standing in the pit – they have fulfilled their obligation. And if they heard the sound of an echo, meaning those outside the pit – they have not fulfilled their obligation.)

The Tur also ruled this way, and this is his wording: "One who stands in a pit or a large barrel and blows [the shofar], and others outside hear it — they have not fulfilled their obligation, because they are only hearing an echo. But he himself has fulfilled his obligation," etc. This is his wording. Therefore, he established a general rule that anyone standing outside has not fulfilled their obligation, even if standing close to the pit. Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, did not bring this opinion at all, because the language of the Mishnah and the Gemara explicitly supports Rashi and the Rambam. And regarding the Rosh’s question, "What is the distinction?" — it is answered in his large book that every person can discern this, whether the sound is that of a shofar or an echo. See there. And it seems to me to add to this, that there is a clear clarification: Rashi explained that if one heard an echo along with the sound of the shofar — he has not fulfilled his obligation. See there. And what did Rashi mean by this? His intention was not that he heard an echo alone, without distinguishing at all that it was the sound of a shofar, for it is obvious that this is nothing. Rather, the echo is heard as the sound of the shofar, but not clearly. And like in the end of Gittin, when they heard that a certain woman was betrothed to a certain man, it is stated there that they did not hear the echo, but for example, there were candles burning and beds spread, etc., see there. It is clear that the term "echo" does not refer to the actual hearing, but that the matter is not clear. Similarly with the shofar, there are various types of blasts, namely the tekiah is a simple sound, the shevarim are broken sounds, and the teruah is wailing sounds. Therefore, if one hears the sound of the shofar without mixing the sounds — he hears the tekiah as a tekiah, the shevarim as shevarim, and the teruah as teruah. But if the sound is mixed, he does not hear the details clearly, but rather all as one shofar sound. According to this, every person can discern. (And regarding what the Taz questioned in subsection 1 from 28a: Sometimes he sticks out his head and mixes the sound, etc. This implies that even if he is close, the sound is mixed. See there. This is not a difficulty at all, for on the contrary, this itself teaches us that the sound is not mixed due to his proximity. And it does not mean sometimes he sticks out and we decree. It teaches us that we do not decree, but even if he sticks out — we do not concern ourselves with it. And so wrote the Knesset HaGedolah there in note 40, see there. Moreover, this is not analogous to one who stands from beginning to end outside, for here due to his movement from the pit to outside the pit — the sound is mixed. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

Just as the law is regarding one who blows the shofar in a pit and the listener is outside the pit, so too the opposite: if the blower is outside the pit and the listener is in the pit, according to the Tur, he has not fulfilled his obligation. According to the Rambam, it depends on whether he heard the sound of the shofar or an echo, as explained (Beit Yosef and Taz, subsection 3). And some say that in this case, everyone agrees he has fulfilled his obligation, because when the blowing is in the pit, the sound gets confused for those standing outside it. But when the blowing is outside the pit, the sound does not get confused, even for those standing inside the pit (Bach and Magen Avraham, subsection 4).

And know that there is a doubt regarding a pit, cistern, and barrel, whether this applies specifically when the pit is covered, and similarly the cistern and barrel, for then the sound becomes confused. But not when they are open, or even with an uncovered pit, because the sound from the depth, when it rises to the surface, can become confused. And this is also implied from the simple meaning of the Talmud and the legal decisors. And similarly, there is a doubt regarding one who blows the shofar in a house or in a synagogue, that those who hear from outside the house or synagogue in a place where the sound reaches clearly—they certainly fulfill their obligation, and this happens every day—whether this is specifically when there is an open door or window, but when it is sealed from all sides, the sound becomes confused; or perhaps the sealing of the house does not confuse the sound. And this is also implied, since the legal decisors did not mention this at all. However, it is certain that when the house is sealed, the sound will not be heard as clearly from a distance as when the door is open, obviously.

The halachic authorities have written the phrase "one who blows into a pit," but in the Mishnah it states "one who blows within a pit." It seems to imply that even for the blower himself who stands outside the pit and blows into the pit, there is a difference between hearing the sound of the shofar and hearing an echo. For although he stands close to the shofar, nevertheless, because of the depth of the pit, even he might only hear an echo. Conversely, according to the Rosh and the Tur, anyone else who hears in any manner has not fulfilled their obligation, as I have written. In any case, the blower himself can hear the sound of the shofar, even when he is outside the pit, because the shofar is in his mouth (so it seems in my humble opinion).

If he began to blow the shofar in a pit and then ascended out of the pit and completed the blowing, he has fulfilled his obligation, because all that he heard, whether inside or outside, was the sound of the shofar. However, if when he ascended from the pit, he brought his ears outside the pit before bringing the shofar outside, according to the Tur, he has not fulfilled his obligation. According to the Rambam, it needs to be distinguished: if he heard the sound of the shofar, he has fulfilled his obligation, but if he heard an echo, he has not. Based on what I wrote in the previous section, it could be that the Tur agrees with this as well. Therefore, it is advisable to bring the shofar out before the ears, for then he will certainly hear the sound of the shofar, as the shofar will be outside in an open space. Those who were standing with him in the pit, where he began to blow, have fulfilled their obligation, even though the blower ascended in the middle and completed the blowing outside the pit. For we have already written that if the listener is in the pit and the blower is outside the pit, they have fulfilled their obligation. According to the first opinion in section 5, they have not fulfilled their obligation, because it is necessary to hear the entire blowing properly, and the beginning without the end or the end without the beginning is considered nothing. However, some say that if there is the measure of a proper blowing in part of it, he has fulfilled his obligation, as will be explained. (The Magen Avraham in subsection 3 is very brief, but his intention is as we have stated. Investigate and you will find it easy.)

One who hears part of a blast that was not in the time of obligation and part of it in the time of obligation, such as if part of the blast was before dawn and the end of it during the day, or if someone was sounding the shofar casually, which does not fulfill the obligation of sounding the shofar, and one cannot say in the middle of the blast, "Have intention and sound for me for the sake of the mitzvah," and he completed the blast for the sake of the mitzvah, even if the completion was for the requisite length of a blast - he has not fulfilled his obligation, because we require it to be valid from the beginning to the end. Some say that if the length of the blast during the obligation time is sufficient, he has fulfilled his obligation. However, the primary opinion is the first one. Therefore, if one heard part of the blast as an echo and part of it as the sound of the shofar, such as if one sounded the shofar in a pit and then came out and completed the blast outside the pit, and the listener was outside the pit - he has not fulfilled his obligation. If the completion was for the requisite length of a blast, it depends on the aforementioned opinions. The primary ruling is that it is invalid, as I have written.
