People should be warned that during the sounding of the shofar, everyone should stand quietly, without commotion, without spitting or moving, and without coughing, so as not to confuse the sound of the shofar blasts, so that they do not become like mere echoes.

The time for blowing the shofar is during the day and not at night, as it is stated: "It shall be a day of blowing the shofar for you" (Megillah 20b). And even though every instance of "day" in the Torah generally refers to the entire 24-hour period, this "day" is extra, because it is written (Numbers 29:1): "In the seventh month, on the first day of the month" etc. – it should have concluded "a blowing for you" just as it is written in Emor, where it says (Leviticus 23:24): "In the seventh month, on the first day of the month" etc., "a remembrance of blowing" etc., and it does not say "a day of remembrance of blowing." Rather, we learn from this that it comes to teach: "during the day and not at night."

And according to Torah law, it is valid from dawn when it rises, for from then it is considered day. However, ideally, the Sages (there) said that one should blow [the shofar] from sunrise, for that is the main part of the day. And so it is with all matters whose mitzvah is during the day; it is taught there that ideally, it is from sunrise, but after the fact, it is valid from dawn. Its end time is until sunset, for afterwards twilight begins, and one blows without a blessing. And see what I wrote in Siman 261. If one heard part of the blast before dawn and part afterwards, he has not fulfilled his obligation, even if the part afterwards consists of the time required for a blast. There are those who disagree with this, as I wrote in the previous Siman, Section 5; see there.

The measure of the blasts will be clarified in Siman 590, and there it will be explained that one is obligated to hear nine blasts on Rosh Hashanah, which are: three teruot and six plain blasts. For each teruah, there is a plain blast before it and a plain blast after it. And we hold that even if one heard the nine blasts over nine hours of the day, he has fulfilled his obligation (34b), meaning: if one blew the plain blast before it in the first hour, the teruah in the second hour, and the plain blast after it in the third hour, and so on with all of them, he has fulfilled his obligation, for we do not require them to be consecutive, and even such a large interruption is still called "before it and after it." And even if they come from nine different individuals, provided they blew in sequence: first a plain blast, then a teruah, then a plain blast, and so on with all of them. But if it was not in sequence, he has not fulfilled his obligation.

And there are those who say that this applies specifically when there is no interruption between them with a shofar sound that is not appropriate in that sequence. That is to say, if one heard a teruah (a series of short blasts) followed by two tekiahs (long blasts) – he has not fulfilled his obligation. But if one heard a tekiah and a teruah, and then a teruah and a tekiah – the second teruah is not considered an interruption, as it is no worse than a delay. For although we hold later in Siman 590 that if the blower himself did so, he has not fulfilled his obligation, in such a case it is because he is performing an act that is not according to the law. This does not apply to the listener, for regarding the listener, it is as if this sound itself does not exist (according to Levush and Magen Avraham, subsection 3). However, there are those who disagree, saying that the listener is similar to the blower, as the main mitzvah is the hearing (according to Taz, subsection 2), and this is also implied by the Ran (Magen Avraham there).

And specifically when the nine people blew the shofar one after the other in order. But if they all blew together at the same time, they do not fulfill the obligation, because we require that the teki'ah (long blast) precede the teru'ah (short blasts), and the teru'ah precede the teki'ah that follows it, and the order of one for the second and the second for the third, and here they all came at once and it is not effective. And even though Rashi there disagrees with this, nevertheless, the halachic authorities have decided to invalidate it in this manner. However, if two or more people blew the teki'ah together, and afterwards two people blew the teru'ah, and similarly further on – they fulfill the obligation. Because even though two sounds cannot be heard simultaneously, the shofar is different since it is cherished, and they pay attention to hear the sound of the shofar.

If Reuven needed the preceding tekiah (blast), and Shimon needed the following tekiah, and they both heard one tekiah – they have fulfilled their obligation, for this tekiah counts for Reuven as the preceding and for Shimon as the following. One tekiah discharges the obligations of both, since it is all a tekiah. Even if the blower himself needed the preceding tekiah and had intention for it, nevertheless, the listener who needed the following tekiah has fulfilled his obligation. Similarly, from one sequence to another, since there is no essential difference in the tekiah itself – we do not concern ourselves with the intention of the blower, as long as he intends to discharge the listener's obligation. For if he did not intend to discharge it, it is as if nothing was done.

Rosh Hashanah that falls on Shabbat, we do not blow the shofar. And this is the language of the Rambam in the second chapter, law 6: Even though blowing the shofar is a rabbinic prohibition, and by right we should blow, let a positive commandment of the Torah come and override a rabbinic prohibition. So why do we not blow? It is a decree lest one carry it in his hand to someone who will blow for him, and he will carry it four cubits in the public domain, or carry it from one domain to another, and come to a prohibition that incurs stoning. For everyone is obligated in blowing, but not everyone is skilled in blowing. Until here is his language. And even though blowing does not override a rabbinic prohibition, as I wrote at the end of Siman 586, and how did he write that it overrides a rabbinic prohibition? This is a temporary rabbinic prohibition, such as bringing it from outside the boundary, or climbing a tree. But the act of blowing itself, which is a rabbinic prohibition, must perforce override even on Shabbat, for this rabbinic prohibition also exists on Yom Tov. And if you say that even on Yom Tov this rabbinic prohibition is not overridden, then you have nullified the mitzvah of blowing entirely, and this is impossible. But the rabbinic prohibition of carrying is not like Yom Tov, therefore they decreed on Shabbat due to this concern (Lechem Mishneh, Magen Avraham, and Taz).

Therefore, it is forbidden to move the shofar on Shabbat, as it is muktzeh (set aside). This is unless it is for a permissible use of its body or its place, such as using it to give water to a child. Otherwise, even for a permissible use of its body or its place, it is prohibited, as I have written in Siman 308. And on Yom Tov, although it is obvious that it is permitted to move it, since it is needed to blow, nevertheless, there is one aspect in which it is stricter than Shabbat. That is: it is forbidden to use it for a mundane purpose, such as to give water, since it is set aside for its mitzvah (Magen Avraham, Siman 669:5). This is not the case on Shabbat, since it is not blown, it is not set aside for its mitzvah at all. And it appears to me that even on Yom Tov, if one has two shofars, and designated one for blowing, and did not intend to blow the other – it is not set aside for its mitzvah.

And even though the prohibition against blowing the shofar on Shabbat is rabbinic due to a decree, as I have written, nevertheless, the Torah also alludes to this. In Parashat Pinchas (Numbers 29:1) it is written, "It shall be a day of blowing the shofar for you," and in Parashat Emor (Leviticus 23:24) it is written, "a remembrance of blowing the shofar," and this refers to when Rosh Hashanah falls on Shabbat, when it is only a remembrance of blowing and not a day of blowing (Gemara, beginning of the fourth chapter, 29b). There is also a deeper hint to this, as the section "An ox or sheep" in Emor was stated in the second year after the Exodus from Egypt, and this pertains to the shofar, as this section was stated after the giving of the Torah. And Pesach, when the Israelites left Egypt, fell on a Thursday, as it says in Shabbat (87b). Consequently, in the second year, Rosh Hashanah fell on Shabbat, as the third day of Pesach is Rosh Hashanah, as is known. Therefore, the Torah said, "In the seventh month, on the first day of the month, there shall be a rest day for you, a remembrance of blowing the shofar, a holy convocation," meaning that this Rosh Hashanah will fall on Shabbat, and therefore only "a remembrance of blowing" and not "a day of blowing." And there is nothing that is not hinted at in the Torah, for all the words of the sages were given by the Holy One, Blessed be He, to Moses at Sinai, and He revealed to him what the sages would innovate.

The Sages taught in the Mishnah (beginning of the fourth chapter): On a Yom Tov (festival) of Rosh Hashanah that falls on Shabbat, in the Temple they would sound the shofar, but not in the country. After the destruction of the Temple, Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai decreed that they should sound the shofar in any place where there is a court. The reason is that the court is diligent and will not come to desecrate Shabbat, and certainly in the Temple they were diligent, and there was no concern that they might carry it, etc. This all applied when there were ordained courts. But now, due to our sins, we do not have ordained courts – we do not sound the shofar anywhere in the world, even in the Land of Israel. And when the righteous Redeemer comes, then we will sound the shofar in Jerusalem, God willing. And one of our great Rabbis wanted to say that even now, when there is a great court in the world, they should sound the shofar there. But his words were not accepted. (See in Maor, Milchamot, and Magid Mishnah that the Rif holds this opinion, but even his students did not practice this; see there.)

Everyone is obligated to hear the sound of the shofar on Rosh Hashanah, except for women, slaves, minors, a deaf person, and a mentally incapacitated person. Women are exempt because it is a positive commandment that is time-bound, and slaves are likened to women: for any commandment that a woman is not obligated in, a slave is also exempt. Minors are not of age for commandments, except for a minor who has reached the age of education, for whom the father is obligated to educate in commandments. A deaf person and a mentally incapacitated person are obviously not included in the commandments, nor in the obligation of education. A deaf person is one who cannot hear and cannot speak. However, one who can hear but cannot speak is like any other person and is obligated. A tumtum (a person with indeterminate sex) and an androgynous person (one with both male and female characteristics) are obligated out of doubt, as they might be male. However, one who can speak but cannot hear is exempt because they are not capable of hearing.

Anyone who is obligated in the mitzvah of shofar can fulfill the obligation on behalf of others with their blowing, even if they have already fulfilled their own obligation, as is the rule with all blessings of the commandments, that even if one has already fulfilled their obligation, they can fulfill it for others. However, anyone who is not obligated in the mitzvah of shofar cannot fulfill it for others with their blowing, for how can they fulfill an obligation for others in something that they themselves do not need at all? This is not comparable to someone who is obligated, has already fulfilled their own obligation, and still fulfills it for others; this is due to the principle of mutual responsibility, for all of Israel are responsible for one another. But someone who is not obligated in this mitzvah is not included in the mutual responsibility for this mitzvah at all.

And therefore, a woman, a slave, a minor, a deaf-mute, and a mentally incapacitated person do not fulfill the obligation for others with their blowing (of the shofar). But one who hears but cannot speak can fulfill the obligation for others, and the others should recite the blessings. And even without the blessing, the blessing does not prevent the fulfillment of the mitzvah. However, one who speaks but cannot hear does not fulfill the obligation for others, since he himself is exempt. Indeed, the main ruling that our master the Beit Yosef introduced in Section 2, that a deaf person who speaks but does not hear is not obligated, is based on his great work where he brought this from the Kolbo and the Rashbatz, that since the essence of the mitzvah is hearing, and he cannot hear, he is exempt. Therefore, he also does not fulfill the obligation for others. See there, and I find this difficult.

In the Mishnah of Rosh Hashanah (29a), we learned: a deaf person, an insane person, and a minor do not fulfill [the obligation]. And at the beginning of Chagigah, it is taught: everyone is obligated in the pilgrimage offering, except for a deaf person, an insane person, and a minor. And in the Gemara there, it states: it teaches a deaf person similar to an insane person and a minor, etc., as it is taught: a deaf person referred to by the sages everywhere – is one who neither hears nor speaks. However, if one speaks but does not hear, or hears but does not speak, they are obligated, etc., see there. If so, this same precision exists in our Mishnah as well. And what they wrote because the primary point is hearing - this means that one should not say that each person is obligated to blow the shofar themselves, as it appears from the language "everyone is obligated in the blowing of the shofar" that we learned there in the Baraita. Rather, one fulfills the obligation even with hearing. Therefore, Rambam carefully wrote at the beginning of the second chapter: everyone is obligated to hear the sound of the shofar, see there. But certainly, the blowing is also a primary part of the commandment, and hearing is not possible without blowing. However, to say that due to the lack of hearing one would be completely exempt – such a thing should have been explained by the Mishnah and the Gemara, and it is not found in any of the poskim (decisors of Jewish law).

And even though in the Mishnah of Megillah (19b) it is stated: "Everyone is qualified to read the Megillah except for a deaf person, an imbecile, and a minor," and by necessity, its explanation is also that he speaks but does not hear, as is evident in Berachot (14a), in truth, the Tosafot there wrote as follows: "A typical deaf person is one who neither hears nor speaks; but the deaf person here speaks, since he reads the Megillah, etc."; thus are their words. And if so, there was no need to explain, for it is already explained that he speaks since he reads the Megillah. But here it needed to be explained, and the proof: Why did the Tosafot not write the same thing here as they wrote in Megillah?

And furthermore, it is difficult for me, for behold, in Berachot (14a), Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yossi disagree regarding one who reads the Shema and does not make it audible to his ears. Rabbi Yehuda holds that he has fulfilled his obligation, while Rabbi Yossi holds that he has not fulfilled his obligation, because he interprets "Shema" (hear) to mean that it must be audible to your ears. They also disagree about the Grace After Meals, see there. According to this, according to Rabbeinu the Beit Yosef, for Rabbi Yossi, a deaf person who speaks but does not hear is exempt from reading the Shema and from Grace After Meals. And we have never heard such a thing. Rather, it is certain that even according to Rabbi Yossi, the Torah only required making it audible to one's ears for someone who is able to make it audible to his ears. But someone who is unable is not exempt because of this and reads with his mouth, even though it is not audible to his ears. And here too, with the blowing of the shofar, it is the same. Therefore, in my humble opinion, this ruling requires further examination. A deaf person who speaks but does not hear is obligated to blow the shofar himself, but he should not recite the blessing, since according to Rabbeinu the Beit Yosef, he is completely exempt.

A tumtum and an androgynous person do not fulfill the obligation for men, because perhaps they are females, and a woman does not fulfill the obligation for a man. A tumtum does not fulfill the obligation even for another tumtum, because perhaps one is a female and the other is a male. However, an androgynous person does fulfill the obligation for another androgynous person, because the entire category is the same. It is obvious that they, when they blow the shofar for themselves, should not recite a blessing, because perhaps they are females. And even though it will be explained that women also recite blessings, that is because they do so with the understanding that it is optional, not obligatory. Unless they also intend it as optional if they are females. A blind person recites the blessing and fulfills the obligation for others. And although Rabbi Yehuda holds (Bava Kamma 88a) that a blind person’s obligation is only rabbinic, and a rabbinic obligation cannot fulfill a Torah obligation, we do not hold this way. The Radbaz ruled that if a person was proficient in blowing the shofar and then became blind, they should not be removed from their position. (Magen Avraham, subsection 1; and even though in section 273 the Beit Yosef brings that the R”I was concerned about this, we do not hold this way, see there.)

There are those who say that according to the opinion that an androgynous person is half male and half female, he cannot fulfill the obligation even for himself, and certainly not for another androgynous person. It is similar to someone who is half slave and half free man, as will be explained, where the slave side cannot fulfill the obligation of the free side. Here too, the female side cannot fulfill the obligation of the male side (Ra'avad in his glosses at the beginning of the second chapter). However, the Rambam, who ruled that one can fulfill the obligation for someone of the same type, as we have written, follows his view in the first chapter of the laws of forbidden relations, that an androgynous is a distinct entity. But there are those who say that even if one is half male and half female, he can fulfill the obligation for himself and for others like him. This is not comparable to someone who is half slave and half free man, which depends on human action to make him one or the other, and therefore they are considered like two bodies. But an androgynous is entirely one kind and cannot change, and therefore he fulfills the obligation for himself and for others like him (Maggid Mishneh). There are those who say that an androgynous is sometimes male and sometimes female, and if he is currently female, he cannot fulfill the obligation for someone who is currently male (Magen Avraham, section 2). This is astonishing, as no one holds this view at all, and there are many contradictions to this (and the Machatzit Hashekel and Be'er Hetev also found this astonishing).

And one who is half-slave and half-free cannot even fulfill his own obligation, much less that of others, because the slave part of him cannot fulfill the obligation for the free part of him. And even though we maintain that we force his master to make him fully free, nonetheless, as long as he has not been freed, he is considered half-slave. One should not ask why the free part of him cannot fulfill the obligation with the sounding of the shofar, since that part is the one blowing. It can be said that in every blast, there is a part that is from the slave, and one cannot fulfill the obligation with half a blast. However, when another person blows, the free part of him hears a valid blast.

Even though women are not obligated in the mitzvah of sounding the shofar, nevertheless, they may blow the shofar and recite the blessings. It has already been explained earlier in Siman 17 that women can recite blessings on all positive time-bound commandments, as we hold that women have permission to perform סמיכה (leaning on sacrifices). Similarly, after someone has already fulfilled his own obligation, he may blow the shofar for them to fulfill their obligation; however, he should not recite the blessings for them, but they should recite the blessings themselves if the one blowing has already fulfilled his own obligation. He should blow the shofar solely for their sake, and therefore, if he wishes to recite the blessings, he should either blow the shofar for them before his own prayer so that he fulfills his own obligation with this blowing, or one of the listeners should be an adult male. According to what I will write later in Siman 591, that it is not advisable to blow the shofar alone during the first three hours of the day, he should not blow the shofar before the prayer. Rather, he should either blow for them at the time they blow in the synagogue if he has another shofar, or he should intend not to fulfill his obligation with the synagogue's blowing and then blow for them after the prayer and recite the blessings for himself. If not, they should recite the blessings themselves, as I have written. (See Magen Avraham, subsection 4, where he questions whether walking constitutes an interruption; see there.)

And similarly, young children who have reached the age of education—the father must bring them to the synagogue to educate them to hear the shofar blasts. He should warn them not to cause a disturbance, and to listen to the blasts and respond "Amen" to the blessings. However, many young children should not be brought to the synagogue, as they disrupt the concentration of the listeners.

The Tur writes at the end of the previous section: Even though Shabbat is not a time for blowing the shofar, it is permitted to tell a child who has not reached the age of education to blow the shofar on Shabbat, so that he can learn to blow. But if he has reached the age of education, it is forbidden to tell him to blow. And if he blows on his own, we do not prevent him. So far his words. And likewise on Yom Tov, we do not tell a child who has reached the age of education to blow (Bach), after he has already heard the blasts.

But Maimonides writes in the second chapter, law 7, and these are his words: Children who have not reached the age of education—we do not prevent them from blowing the shofar on Shabbat that is not Yom Tov of Rosh Hashanah, so that they may learn. And an adult is permitted to engage with them to teach them on Yom Tov, whether the child has reached the age of education or not, as blowing the shofar is prohibited only due to a rabbinic decree. So far his words. This means: On an ordinary Shabbat, we do not prevent a child who has not reached the age of education from blowing the shofar. But on a Shabbat that is Rosh Hashanah, we do prevent it, so that the listeners do not think that the shofar needs to be blown on Rosh Hashanah that falls on Shabbat. This is also stated in the Jerusalem Talmud.

And similarly, if the child has reached the age of education, it is forbidden even on an ordinary Shabbat, and we do prevent him. And although we hold that if a child eats non-kosher food, the court is not commanded to stop him, as I wrote in section 343, shofar blowing is different because it is heard by many, and there is a desecration of Shabbat when he has reached the age of education.

And on Rosh Hashanah itself that falls on a weekday, we engage with them and teach them to blow, whether they have reached the age of education or not, even if they have already blown, since the time for blowing is today. The disagreement between Maimonides and the Tur depends on the version of the Talmud in Rosh Hashanah (33a), see there.

A person who is forbidden to benefit from his fellow is permitted to blow a shofar blast for him as a mitzvah, for mitzvot were not given for benefit. This applies specifically when he blows on his own to fulfill the other’s obligation, but it is forbidden to tell him, "Blow for me and fulfill my obligation," as listening to his words constitutes a benefit. Rabbi Rema wrote in Section 7: If he says, "Konam (a type of vow) his shofar blasts are upon me," in any case it is forbidden; thus are his words. It seems to me that the explanation is as follows: If he says, "Konam – what is of the shofar for his blast that he blows," this is upon me, for otherwise the blast is something intangible, and the konam does not take effect, as I have written in Siman 586; see there. Similarly, if he says, "Konam the shofar blast that so-and-so blows is upon me," it is also forbidden, for since he mentioned the shofar, it is as if he said "the shofar for his blast," which has substance, and this refers to the shofar.

One who engages in blowing the shofar for the purpose of learning has not fulfilled his obligation, since he did not intend to perform the mitzvah of blowing. Similarly, one who hears from someone who is engaged in such practice has not fulfilled his obligation, even if the listener intended to fulfill his obligation, because the one blowing was merely engaged in practice and did not intend to fulfill the mitzvah. Likewise, one who blows for the sake of a song and not for the mitzvah has not fulfilled his obligation. For we hold that mitzvot require intention, meaning that at the time of performing them, one must intend for the sake of the mitzvah, as I wrote above in Siman 60, see there. And there are those who say that even according to the opinion that mitzvot do not require intention, this applies to a mitzvah involving an action, like eating matzah, where in the end he is eating the matzah. But a mitzvah involving speech, like the recitation of Shema, or hearing, like the shofar, if done without the intention to fulfill the mitzvah, it is as if he has done nothing. This seems to be the opinion of the Rambam, who ruled in the sixth chapter of Chametz and Matzah that matzah does not require intention, and in the second chapter of Shofar ruled that intention is required (as written by the Maggid Mishneh and the Lechem Mishneh there, Halacha 5. See what I wrote in Siman 585, and above in Siman 60, and from the Talmud it appears that they are similar to each other).

Therefore, if the listener intended to fulfill his obligation, but the one blowing (the shofar) did not intend to enable him to fulfill it, even though he himself intended to fulfill his own obligation, or if the blower intended to enable him to fulfill it but the listener did not intend to fulfill it through his blowing—he has not fulfilled his obligation until both the listener and the blower intend (to fulfill the mitzvah). What are we speaking of? That the blower needs to intend to enable this person to fulfill his obligation when he blows for one or two people. But if he blows for many, like in the synagogue, he does not need to specifically intend for this person and that person, rather he should intend to enable anyone who hears to fulfill their obligation, and he should intend to fulfill his own obligation, even if he does not know them at all. And even if they are not in the synagogue but stand outside the synagogue, since the prayer leader’s intention is for everyone, for anyone who hears and intends to fulfill his obligation. Therefore, someone who was walking on the road or sitting in his house and heard the shofar blasts from the prayer leader—he has fulfilled his obligation if he intended to fulfill it, since the prayer leader intends to enable the multitude to fulfill their obligations. (See Magen Avraham, subparagraph 5, who brings a Jerusalem Talmud: Regarding one walking on the road, they only taught this about one who is passing through. But one who is standing still—there is a presumption that he intended, meaning: if he forgot whether he intended or not, since when passing there is a presumption that he did not intend, and when standing there is a presumption that he did intend, see there.)

Three "teru'ot" (blasts) are mentioned in the Torah regarding the seventh month. Two of them pertain to Rosh Hashanah: one in "Emor" (Leviticus 23:24), "In the seventh month, on the first of the month... a remembrance of blasts"; and the second in "Pinchas" (Numbers 29:1), "In the seventh month, on the first of the month... it shall be a day of blasts for you." The third pertains to the Jubilee year, in the portion "Behar" (Leviticus 25:9), where it is written: "And you shall make the shofar sound on the tenth day of the seventh month... you shall make the shofar sound..." The phrase "in the seventh month" is superfluous, as it could have written "And you shall make the shofar sound on the tenth day of the month." Rather, it comes to teach that all the blasts in the seventh month are equal (Gemara Rosh Hashanah 34a and Torat Kohanim). And from where do we derive that what is stated regarding the Jubilee applies to Rosh Hashanah, and what is stated regarding Rosh Hashanah applies to the Jubilee? It is derived from the phrase "in the seventh month," "in the seventh month" as a verbal analogy (Torat Kohanim and Gemara there).

According to this, there are three "teru'ot" (broken sounds) on Rosh Hashanah. And we have learned that one should blow the shofar on Rosh Hashanah like on Yovel (Jubilee), as it is written: "a shofar blast of teru'ah." Each "teru'ah" has a simple sound before it and a simple sound after it, as it is written: "and you shall cause a shofar blast to pass" etc., "you shall pass a shofar" etc. "Causing to pass" refers to a simple sound: a "tekiah" (unbroken sound). And the "teru'ah" is between two passings. And since there are three "teru'ot," it follows that there are three simple sounds before them and three simple sounds after them, and thus there are nine sounds in total: tekiah, teru'ah, tekiah; tekiah, teru'ah, tekiah; tekiah, teru'ah, tekiah. And this is the Torah obligation. However, what is the reason that we blow thirty sounds three times: Tashrat, Tashat, Tarat? The matter is as follows: The term "teru'ah" is a cry of brokenness, as it is written in the section of Beha'alotcha (Numbers 10:9): "When you go to war… you shall sound a teru'ah on the trumpets… and on your days of rejoicing… you shall blow the trumpets…" – thus, for rejoicing it is the term "tekiah," and for the time of war it is the term "teru'ah."

And because we are uncertain as to what exactly the "teruah" is: Is it the wailing that women do when they cry, which is continuous wailing one after another, like the "teruah" that we perform? Or is it the sighing as a person sighs repeatedly when his heart is troubled by some great distress; and these are not continuous, but rather one broken sigh after another. This is like the "shevarim" that we perform. Or perhaps it is specifically both together, a sigh and a wail, for this is the way of someone who is troubled: he first sighs and then wails, and this is the "shevarim-teruah." But the reverse—wailing first and then sighing—is not the way of people. Therefore, there is no need to perform "teruah-shevarim." And thus, for dignified people, the term "sigh" is used: "And the children of Israel sighed because of the bondage" (Exodus 2:23); "Her priests sigh" (Lamentations 1:4) — because it is not their way to raise their voices in continuous wailing. And for people of lesser stature, the term "wail" is used: "Wail, all you drinkers of wine" (Joel 1:5); "Wail like a virgin" (ibid. 8); "The sound of the wailing of shepherds" (Zechariah 11:3). (And the prophet Micah who said "Woe is me" (Micah 7:1), and similarly "I will lament and wail," concluded with "I will go stripped and naked" (ibid. 1:8), meaning: like one lacking sense. And similarly, in Joel: "Wail, you ministers of the altar" (Joel 1:13), because he previously said "Wail like a virgin" etc. And similarly in Zephaniah (1:10): "and a wailing from the second quarter," and so in many places. Examine and you will find it precise.)

Therefore, due to these uncertainties, they instituted a practice to address all the uncertainties. This means: for every "Teruah" (a specific shofar sound), we blow a "Shevarim-Teruah" together, "Shevarim" alone, and "Teruah" alone, each with a "Tekiah" (a different shofar sound) before it and after it. It turns out that instead of three sounds – Tekiah, Teruah, Tekiah – it is necessary to blow ten sounds: Tashrat (Tekiah, Shevarim-Teruah, Tekiah), Tashat (Tekiah, Shevarim, Tekiah), Tarat (Tekiah, Teruah, Tekiah). Doing this three times results in thirty sounds. The Rosh cited in the name of Rav Hai Gaon at the end of Rosh Hashanah that these are not complete uncertainties. According to Torah law, all these sounds are considered "Teruah": the Shevarim, the Teruah, and both together. However, because some of Israel would do the Shevarim, some would do the Teruah, and some would do both together, it was not appropriate for us, in a mitzvah established for generations, for these to do one way and those to do another way. Therefore, Rabbi Abahu instituted that all of Israel should follow one uniform practice (besides which, there is a significant matter in this).

There is a question regarding this matter: why do we need the first Tekiah in the sequence of Tekiah-Shevarim-Tekiah (Tashat)? Since it is due to uncertainty, then logically: if the primary sequence is Tekiah-Shevarim-Teruah-Tekiah (Tashrat), he has already fulfilled the obligation; and if the primary sequence is Tekiah-Shevarim-Tekiah (Tashat), then the last Tekiah of Tashrat should suffice for the first Tekiah of Tashat. Similarly, why do we need the first Tekiah in the sequence of Tekiah-Teruah-Tekiah (Tarat)? If the primary sequence is Tashat, he has already fulfilled the obligation; and if the primary sequence is Tarat, then the last Tekiah of Tashat should suffice for the first Tekiah of Tarat. However, in such a manner, an error might occur, as people might say there is no need for a Tekiah before the Teruah, because the masses will not understand that the reason is that the last preceding Tekiah counts for this sequence (Tosafot). Additionally, since initially he intended the Tekiah to follow the Teruah, it is not appropriate to consider it for the Tekiah before the Teruah (Rosh). Furthermore, as will be explained, the Tekiah of Tashrat is longer than that of Tashat, and that of Tashat is longer than that of Tarat. Therefore, we should not consider the Tekiah of Tashrat for Tashat, nor that of Tashat for Tarat (Taz, subsection 1). Moreover, it appears to me that since it is difficult for the Baal Tokeah (the one who blows the shofar) to blow thirty sounds in one continuous sequence, he must necessarily rest a bit, as is our custom to rest a bit between Tashrat and Tashat and between Tashat and Tarat. Hence, it is impossible to count the last preceding Tekiah for the first upcoming one due to the interruption. And even though one fulfills the obligation post facto, since even if he heard nine Tekiahs in nine different hours he has fulfilled the obligation, nevertheless, it is not ideal initially.

We learned in the Mishnah and Gemara (33b) that the length of a tekiah (a long, straight shofar blast) is the same as the length of a teruah (a series of short, staccato blasts), and the length of a teruah is equivalent to three sobs or three broken sounds. The three sobs are what we call a “teruah.” Rashi explains that these are three simple sounds of any length. Therefore, whether it is the shevarim (three broken sounds) or the teruah, they are only three each: either three sobs or three wails. The sobs are long, and the wails are short. This also seems to be the opinion of the Raavad in the third chapter, see there.

Based on this, since the length of a tekiah is the same as the length of a teruah, the tekiah of a tashat (tekiah-shevarim-tekiah) is longer than the tekiah of a tarat (tekiah-teruah-tekiah), and the tekiah of a tashrat (tekiah-shevarim-teruah-tekiah) is longer than the tekiah of a tashat. However, this is only to ensure it is not less than the required length. But one may extend the tekiah as long as desired, as it has no upper limit. Similarly, one can do more than three shevarim, and can do four, five, or more shevarim. Likewise, one can do more than three sobs, as in practice we indeed perform many tremolos in the teruah. The main concern is not to fall short of the required length.

However, according to this approach, one must be careful with the shevarim (the broken sounds of the shofar), not to extend each shever (broken sound) to the duration of three tromitin; for if so, it would cease to be considered a shever and each shever would be like a tekiah (the long, unbroken sound), and the three shevarim would be considered three tekiot, since the duration of a tekiah is the same as that of a teruah (a series of short, staccato sounds), and a teruah is only three tromitin. Some say that with shevarim, this is not a concern, for if the shevarim were to be considered a teruah, the duration of a tekiah would be the same as that of three shevarim, not three tromitin. One must only be careful not to extend each shever to the duration of three shevarim, for then it would cease to be considered a shever and would be considered a tekiah. In the case of tashrat (a sequence of tekiah-shevarim-teruah-tekiah), this is not a concern, but in the case of tashat (tekiah-shevarim-tekiah), one must be careful not to extend each shever to the duration of three shevarim and three tromitin, obviously. And Rabbeinu Chananel also explained like Rashi.

But the opinion of our rabbis, the Tosafists, and this is agreed upon by the Ramban, the Rashba, and the Maggid Mishneh, is that when it is said that the measure of a teruah is like three yevavot, the explanation is as follows: Each yevava consists of three short sounds of any length, and three yevavot are nine short sounds. Their reasoning seems to me to be that with one short sound of any length, no yevava sound is heard at all unless three tromitin are combined, as this then becomes like a wailing sound. Therefore, three yevavot are nine tromitin. Accordingly, the measure of a tekiyah is always as long as nine tromitin. Likewise, it is straightforward to extend each shevar to the measure of three tromitin, only not to extend it to nine tromitin. Therefore, the measure of the three shevarim is equivalent to the measure of the nine short tromitin. However, according to this opinion, one must be careful to extend the tekiyah of tashrat (tekiyah-shevarim-teruah-tekiyah) to the measure of eighteen tromitin, which is the measure of shevarim and teruah, as I have written. And one who did not extend the tekiyah of tashrat to this measure, and extended each shevar to the measure of three tromitin, has not fulfilled his obligation, neither according to one opinion nor the other. This is according to the first opinion in the previous section. But according to those who say otherwise, we do not concern ourselves with it, as I have written there.

In my humble opinion, the dispute among our Rabbis corresponds to a disagreement in the Jerusalem Talmud (Chapter 4, Halacha 10) regarding the Mishnah that the measure of a teruah is like three sobs. It says there: What is a teruah? Rabbi Hananiah and Rabbi Mana—one said: That trembling sound, and the other said: Three thin sounds. This is its wording, and this is its explanation: The Mishnah states that the measure of the duration of a teruah is like three sobs, but what is the nature of the teruah? Meaning, each part of the teruah, that is the sob, what is it? One said: That trembling sound, meaning: one tremor, and the measure of a teruah is like three tremors. And the other said: Three thin sounds, meaning: each sob is like three thin sounds. So it turns out that a teruah is like the duration of nine thin sounds. The Rosh and the Ran wrote that in the Jerusalem Talmud it is proven like Rashi and Rabbeinu Chananel, who say: What is a teruah? Three thin sounds. Look there. And they explain that it refers to the entire teruah. But I do not understand, for if so, when it says "that trembling sound"—does it mean the entire teruah is one tremor? This is surprising. And it seems that they had a different version in the Jerusalem Talmud. But according to our version, the dispute among our Rabbis is the same as the dispute in the Jerusalem Talmud, and its explanation is as I have written. (And "that" in the Jerusalem Talmud means "one," as in the end of the first chapter of Nazir "one." Look there, and in Bava Batra 164b.)

The words of the Rambam are perplexing, as he wrote in Chapter 3, Law 4: The measure of a teruah is like two tekiot, the measure of three shevarim is like a teruah; thus is his language. And the Ra'avad wrote that this is an error, and the commentators toiled over his words, see there. And it seems that his intention is as follows: for behold, in the Mishnah it is taught that the measure of a teki'ah is like three teruot, and it questions: but isn't it taught: the measure of a teki'ah is like a teruah? And Abaye answers: our Tanna counts the tekiot of all the blasts together, and the teruot of all the blasts together. The external Tanna counts one blast, and no more. According to Rashi and Tosafot, they do not disagree, and the measure of a teki'ah is like a teruah. But the Rambam explains that they do disagree, for the Baraita holds that the measure of a teki'ah is like one teruah, but the Mishnah that counts all the blasts together - it is as if saying: the measure of all the tekiot is like three teruot. And there are six tekiot, and consequently a teki'ah is like half a teruah, and a complete teruah is like two tekiot. And afterward, he says that the measure of three shevarim in continuation is like a teruah, for the teruah is nine short sounds, and the shevarim are three long sounds. (And it seems this is the intention of the Maggid Mishneh, see there. And the Lechem Mishneh elaborated on his intention, and remained in doubt. Also, the M"A did not find his way. And according to what I have written, it fits well. Investigate, and you will find it easy.)

And with this, it has been explained that the length of the tekiah (a type of shofar blast) depends on the teruah (another type of shofar blast) according to most authorities. Therefore, the tekiah of the sequence of Tashrat (tekiah-shevarim-teruah-tekiah) is longer than that of Tashat (tekiah-shevarim-tekiah), and Tashat is longer than Tarat (tekiah-teruah-tekiah), according to Rashi and the Ra’avad. The opinion of the Ra’avad differs; he wrote that the length of the tekiah is not dependent on the teruah at all, and the length of the tekiah is always like nine tromitin (a measure of length).

Therefore, there are three opinions regarding the length of the tekiah: according to most authorities, it depends on the teruah, and its length is as per the teruah in that sequence. In Tashrat, its length is eighteen tromitin; in Tashat, nine; and in Tarat—according to Rashi and the Ra’avad, three tromitin; according to Tosafot, Ramban, and Rashba, nine tromitin. According to Rambam, its length is like half the teruah, and according to the Ra’avad, its length is always nine tromitin.

And we are stringent according to all opinions, meaning that it is never shorter than nine tromitin, and in Tashrat, it is eighteen, as this is the opinion of the Geonim. Similarly, we always make the teruah not less than nine tromitin. Regarding the shevarim (yet another type of shofar blast), there is no dispute; everyone agrees that it is three.

Every teki'ah, or every shevarim, or every teru'ah must be performed with one breath. If not, one must go back and do it again. And regarding the "shevarim-teru'ah" of tashrat, which is due to doubt, as perhaps both are considered a teru'ah – there are also those who say that both must be done with one breath, since it is a different sound, like the shevarim of tashat and the teru'ah of tarat. And there are those who say it is not necessary, because since this is due to the doubt of whether it is a groan or a wail combined – it is not customary to wail immediately after a groan with one breath, but rather with a slight pause. As long as the pause does not exceed the time of a breath. It is proper to be stringent according to the first opinion, and this is the custom. All of this is for the initial performance. But after the fact – it does not invalidate even if the shevarim or the teru'ah were done with two breaths (Taz, small section 5). And it seems to me that for the teki'ah, it is invalid even after the fact, because it is a simple sound, and if there is a pause – it is no longer simple.

And know that there are those who say that "shevarim-teruah" not only does not need to be done in one breath, but it is forbidden to do it in one breath, and it must specifically be done in two breaths (Terumat HaDeshen, Siman 142). Based on this, our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote at the end of Section 4 that a God-fearing person should fulfill all opinions: for the seated tekiot, he should do it in one breath, and for the standing tekiot, he should do it in two breaths; thus are his words. And our teacher, the Rema, wrote: the simple custom is to do everything in two breaths, and one should not change; thus are his words. It is puzzling to say that it is forbidden in one breath (and the proof from the end of the first chapter of Chullin is not a proof at all, as the Taz wrote in subsection 6. Also, the Bach wrote that those who practice in one breath should not change, see there. And it seems to me that many of the blowers in our times do likewise, and therefore the one who prompts calls "shevarim-teruah" as one.)

The Tur wrote that if one blows a tekiah, teruah, and tekiah in one breath, it would seem that he has not fulfilled his obligation, as there is neither a beginning nor an end. However, from the Jerusalem Talmud, it does not appear so, as we find there: "If he did them in one breath, he has fulfilled his obligation"; thus is its language. And the conclusion is that he has fulfilled his obligation. But Rabbeinu Yerucham wrote in the name of the Rosh that he has not fulfilled his obligation. Likewise, we have learned in the Tosefta (Chapter 2, Halacha 12): "If he blew, made a teruah, and blew in one breath, he has not fulfilled his obligation"; see there. And behold, even if the Tosefta disagrees, it seems that the law follows the Jerusalem Talmud in a matter not mentioned in our Talmud. Also, from the Beit Yosef, Section 5, it appears so, as he wrote: "If one blew a tekiah-teruah-tekiah in one breath, he has fulfilled his obligation. And there are those who say he has not fulfilled his obligation"; thus is its language. Hence, he wrote that someone who holds that one has not fulfilled his obligation in the name of "there are those who say," and the main opinion is the first opinion, as is known from his way in the Shulchan Aruch.

If one prolonged the last teki'ah of the sequence of TaShRaT (Tekiah-Shevarim-Teruah-Tekiah) to the length of two teki'ot, intending it to count both as the final teki'ah of TaShRaT and as the initial teki'ah of TaShaT (Tekiah-Shevarim-Tekiah), it only counts as one teki'ah. This is because a single teki'ah cannot be divided to fulfill two separate obligations. Some say that it does not even count for one obligation, since the first half was intended for TaShRaT and cannot count for TaShaT, and the second half was intended for TaShaT and cannot count for TaShRaT. Consequently, TaShRaT would lack an end, and TaShaT would lack a beginning. Every teki'ah must have a distinct beginning and end; if one is missing, the obligation is not fulfilled, and one must start the teki'ah again.

However, within one sequence, such as the first TaShRaT, if one intended the final teki'ah to serve both as the teki'ah following Shevarim-Teruah and the teki'ah preceding Shevarim-Teruah, everyone agrees that it counts as one teki'ah, since they are within the same sequence (Levush). Some say that even in this case, it does not count even for one teki'ah (Magen Avraham, end of Subsection 5, see there). Nevertheless, the main ruling follows the first opinion: even between TaShRaT and TaShaT, it counts as one teki'ah, specifically as the last of TaShRaT, and another teki'ah should be blown for the beginning of TaShaT (Eliyah Rabbah, Subsection 11, in the name of the Ri"V, Tosefta, and Shevilei Leket. This is also explicitly implied in the Mishnah and Gemara. The Jerusalem Talmud cited by the Rosh and the Tur, which claims that it does not count even for one teki'ah, is questionable, as it contradicts the Mishnah. The Rosh's interpretation that it refers to the preceding teki'ah is also questionable. In truth, the Ramban writes that the Jerusalem Talmud is discussing a case of unintentional action, and the primary Jerusalem Talmud reference is in Chapter Three, Halacha 3, concerning unintentional action. The Jerusalem Talmud states that one should not compare unintentional action to the Mishnah, which discusses prolonging the second teki'ah as two, implying that even for one obligation it does not count. However, it is clear that they are not comparable, and the Jerusalem Talmud incidentally brings this up in Chapter Four, Halacha 10, regarding the Mishnah's case of prolonging the second teki'ah as two, as is the custom of the Jerusalem Talmud. This resolves the difficulty raised by the Ran in Chapter Four against the Ramban, see there. Similarly, the Pnei Moshe in Chapter Three explains this, see there. Be precise and you will find clarity.)

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote in paragraph 6: If one sounded a single blast between two sets [of shofar blasts] and stipulated that whichever set is correct, that blast would count – he has fulfilled his obligation; thus are his words. This means: What we said that a blast does not count for two sets, and according to some opinions, it does not even count for one – this is when he blew it without specification, but intended for it to count for both, as I have written. However, if he made an explicit condition, meaning that since we blow the sequences of Tashrat, Tashat, and Tarat due to doubt, as explained, and he stipulated that this blast would count for the correct sequence – according to the law, in any case, he has fulfilled his obligation, since he did not intend it for two blasts. And why did the Sages not establish this initially? Because of the reasons we explained in paragraph 5, see there. But if he stipulated – what was done is done. And this applies to blasts between sets, and it does not apply to blasts within a single set, obviously.

If one began to blow the shofar and blew a tekiah, and then needed to perform three shevarim and a teruah, but made a mistake and only performed two shevarim and then a teruah – if he immediately remembers, he should perform the third shever and then blow the teruah. This applies when he has not yet finished the teruah. But if he has finished the teruah, he must perform all three shevarim and then the teruah. However, the first tekiah is not invalidated by this interruption, as it was not interrupted by a sound unrelated to the shofar. Some disagree and hold that the first tekiah is also invalidated, requiring him to start a new tekiah, followed by shevarim and teruah. Similarly, those who believe that all the shevarim must be performed in one breath hold that even if the teruah is not completed, one must return to the beginning of the tekiah or the beginning of the shevarim according to the first opinion. This all applies to the sequence of tekiah-shevarim-teruah-tekiah (Tashrat). But in the sequence of tekiah-shevarim-tekiah (Tashat), if there was a mistake in the shevarim, or in the sequence of tekiah-teruah-tekiah (Tarat), if there was a mistake in the teruah, and one began the tekiah that follows, even if it is not completed, one must return to the beginning of the shevarim or the beginning of the teruah, according to the first opinion, as the interruption was unrelated to the teruah. According to those who disagree, one must return to the tekiah that precedes the shevarim or the teruah where the mistake occurred. If the mistake happened in the second Tashat or Tarat, one does not need to return to the first Tashat or Tarat, only to the second. If it occurred in the third, one returns to the third. Similarly, in the sequence of Tashrat, if one needs to return to the beginning, this is the case. This is what our teacher the Beit Yosef wrote in section 9: If one blew two proper Tashrats, or two proper Tashats, or two proper Tarats, and made a mistake in the third – one only needs to return to the last one blown; this is his language. The same rule applies if one made a mistake in the second – return to the second, and if the mistake was in the first, return to the beginning of the first.

The Tur writes: If one performed two Teruahs consecutively, or if he sounded a Tekiah after the Teruah without intending it as a Tekiah, thereby interrupting between the Teruah and the Tekiah; or if after sounding three Shevarim he paused and then subsequently sounded other Shevarim – some say this is not considered an interruption unless one interrupts with a Teruah between the Shevarim and the Tekiah (in Tashrat), or interrupts with Shevarim between the Tekiah and the Teruah (in Tarat). But if one sounded two Teruahs consecutively (or similarly two Shevarim), or sounded a Tekiah in the middle without intention – it is not considered an interruption that requires starting over. Rather, one completes and fulfills the obligation, and the order is not disrupted. However, the Ramban wrote that in all these cases it is considered an interruption. He brought the Tosefta as proof: If one sounded a Tekiah, then a Teruah, then another Teruah, and then another Tekiah – it is only counted as one. Meaning, the final Tekiah counts, but the first one is invalidated by the Teruah sounded in between. This is not a contradiction to what we wrote, that even if the Teruah was completed by mistake – it is not considered an interruption (as stated in the previous section according to the first opinion), because there it is in Tashrat, where the mistaken Teruah resembles the required Teruah. But in Tarat, once the Teruah is completed, any subsequent Teruah is considered an interruption; thus far his words. And Rabbeinu Beit Yosef, in Section 8, rules according to the Ramban, where he wrote that even one Shever is considered an interruption and invalidates the first Tekiah as well; thus far his words.

And there are those who say that the Ramban only disagreed if one blows the shofar for the sake of the mitzvah in the interim, but if one blows the shofar as a distraction – why should it be invalid? It should be no different than if one performed work in the interim. For it is established: if one heard nine shofar blasts over nine hours in a day – he has fulfilled his obligation. Is it possible that he sat all day without speaking in the interim, or that he did not hear any other sound from a person or animal? And this too, since he was engaged without intent – it is like another sound, and even though he diverted his intention – he has fulfilled his obligation (Ran there). Therefore, it seems appropriate to be lenient in this matter, since there are those who dispute this entire law, as the Tur wrote (Magen Avraham, small section 10). And according to the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, it can be said that it is not similar to the nine hours in a day, where what he heard has no relevance to the shofar, but here, where the blowing is done in order – it is an interruption even if done without intent. (And the distinction we wrote in the previous section between Tashrat and Tashat and Tarat – is only when one blows the teruah within the shevarim, it is in Tashrat akin to what he needs to blow. But in a teruah before the shevarim, or two shevarim one after the other – even in Tashrat it is invalid, as Magen Avraham wrote in small section 11, see there.)

And that which we have said, that two Teruot, or two Shevarim one after the other, invalidate – this is when the first one was blown properly. But if one began to blow, and it did not come out properly – he must return and blow that sound again, for the first one is not counted by itself, and it is all considered one sound, as the Tur wrote, see there (ibid.). And if he is standing in Tashat (Tekiah-Shevarim-Tekiah) and remembers that he made a mistake in Tashrat (Tekiah-Shevarim-Teruah-Tekiah) – he completes the sequence, and then blows Tashrat once (ibid., subsection 12). And there is no concern about the interruption in the sequence of Tashrat, and also about preceding Tashat – for each one is a matter by itself. And know that in all these laws – there is no difference between the seated blows and the blows in the order of the blessings, for in all that requires returning to the beginning – also in the seated blows one must return. And we do not rely on the blows in the order of the blessings, since he has blessed on the seated blows. However, for the blows after the prayer, there is no need to be meticulous (ibid.).

We have already explained in Siman 576 that one must blow the shofar from the narrow end, and not from the wide end. And your mnemonic is: "From the straits I called upon God." And no supplication should be said in the middle of the shofar blasts, between the sets of Tashrat, Tashat, and Tarat. After the blasts, the blower recites the verse "Happy is the people who know the sound of the shofar," and the congregation responds after him, and they say "Happy...," "They shall praise...," and then they return the Torah scroll to its place and pray the Musaf prayer.

And the Rambam wrote in the third chapter of Hilchot Teshuva, law 4: Even though the blowing of the shofar on Rosh Hashanah is a decree of the verse, there is a hint in it, as if to say: "Awaken, you sleepers, from your sleep, and arise, you slumberers, from your slumber. Examine your deeds, and return in repentance, and remember your Creator." Those who forget the truth amidst the vanities of time, and spend all year in vanity and emptiness, which neither benefit nor save – look to your souls, improve your ways and your deeds. Let each one of you abandon his evil ways and his thoughts that are not good.

The Musaf prayer on Rosh Hashanah is different from all the other Musaf prayers of the year, as all other Musaf prayers consist of seven blessings, while the Musaf on Rosh Hashanah has nine blessings. This is because the blessings of Malchuyot (Kingship), Zichronot (Remembrances), and Shofarot (Shofar blasts) are added. And if you ask: if so, aren't there ten blessings? It is not so, as the sanctity of the day is included with Malchuyot (Rosh Hashanah 32b). These nine blessings on Rosh Hashanah correspond to the nine mentions that Chana mentioned in her prayer (Berachot 29a), as Sarah, Rachel, and Chana were remembered on Rosh Hashanah. There is a hint in the Torah to mention Malchuyot, Zichronot, and Shofarot on Rosh Hashanah, as it is stated (Leviticus 23:24): "a memorial of blowing of horns, a holy convocation" – "a memorial" – these are Zichronot, "blowing of horns" – these are Shofarot, "a holy convocation" – this is the sanctity of the day, "who sanctifies Israel and the Day of Remembrance." We learn Malchuyot from what is written (ibid. 22): "I am the Lord your God… and in the seventh month…", and this is kingship (Rosh Hashanah 32b). And furthermore, it is written (Numbers 10:10): "and they shall be for you as a memorial before your God, I am the Lord your God". Why does it say "I am the Lord your God"? This serves as a general rule: wherever it says "memorials" – there shall be Malchuyot with them (ibid.). And the Holy One, blessed be He, said: Say before Me Malchuyot, Zichronot, and Shofarot on Rosh Hashanah. Malchuyot – so that you will proclaim My kingship over you, Zichronot – so that your remembrance will rise before Me for good. And with what? With the Shofar (Rosh Hashanah 16a).

It is established for us above in Siman 124 that for all prayers, the chazzan (cantor) only fulfills the obligation for someone who is not proficient in prayer. But one who can pray by himself—the chazzan does not fulfill his obligation. This applies to the prayers of the entire year. However, for the prayers of Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, it is ruled at the end of Rosh Hashanah that just as the chazzan fulfills the obligation for one who is not proficient, so too does he fulfill the obligation for one who is proficient, because there are many blessings and they are very long. But this requires a condition: that one listens to the chazzan from beginning to end and does not interrupt with speech at all. Since this is difficult for a person, our practice is that each individual prays the entire Musaf prayer silently from beginning to end. The chazzan also prays silently, and afterward, the chazzan repeats the prayer as throughout the year. Another reason: according to Rashi and Tosafot, the chazzan only fulfills the obligation for one who is proficient on Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur if he was coerced and could not pray (Magen Avraham). One should not ask: what lengthiness is there on Yom Kippur? It can be said that it includes confession and "Al Chet." However, according to this, it should also apply to Shacharit and Mincha, but it is possible that they do not include sacrifices, thus it is not lengthy (see Rashi and Tosafot at the end of Rosh Hashanah). It seems more likely that this refers to Yom Kippur of the Jubilee year.

And know that the Rosh and the Tur brought from the responsa of the Geonim that the congregation never prayed the Mussaf of Rosh Hashanah with anything but seven blessings. And the prayer leader would only pray with nine blessings. And so wrote Rav Sherira and Rav Hai Gaon, and so was the custom in the two yeshivot in Babylonia. But the Ritz Gaiot wrote: We received from great sages, who themselves received from great sages, like Rav Shmuel HaLevi who received from our teacher Rav Chanokh, the great of the generation: The practical law is that the congregation also prays with nine blessings. And the Rosh and the Tur agreed with their words, as we do. And the Rosh was astonished at the Geonim, that since they established nine blessings on Rosh Hashanah, then those who pray seven blessings, their blessing is in vain; see there. And this is not a difficulty on the Geonim, for they explain that what we say in the blessings: on Rosh Hashanah the prayer leader also fulfills the obligation for those who are experts – is only regarding Malchuyot, Zichronot, and Shofarot. But for the seven, each one is obligated to pray for himself. And indeed the Ran of blessed memory explained so, and it also appears from the Ramban. And there is much support for this from the Jerusalem Talmud, see there. And if so, this was the original enactment, and they are not blessings in vain.

Therefore, it seems to my humble opinion that if someone remains on the road during Rosh Hashanah, and prays alone, and does not have a prayer book, and does not know the entire Mussaf service by heart – nevertheless, he is obligated to pray the first three blessings and the last three blessings, and the sanctity of the day in the middle, which includes also the Malchuyot (verses of Kingship), and to say "Because of our sins" with the sacrifices, if he knows this by heart. Because, according to the Geonim and the Jerusalem Talmud, this was the initial enactment – it has not been nullified even now, when there is no other choice. And although this seems to me, in practice one should deliberate on this, as perhaps the enactment was only when afterwards he would hear it from the prayer leader. And even though he is not worse than the people in the fields, if so, he should rely on the prayer leader for the entire prayer. Nevertheless, logic dictates that for everything he can pray by himself – he is obligated to pray, since in the time of the Geonim they prayed this way.

The Sephardim do not have the custom to silently recite the additional offerings, except on Shabbat and Rosh Chodesh, where they are accustomed, and will not make mistakes. But not on Yom Tov, nor on Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, because they are not proficient in them and might err. They fulfill their obligation with what they say, "As it is written in Your Torah, through Moses Your servant, by Your glorious mouth." But the custom of Ashkenaz is not like this, and we say all the additional offerings. If one does not know it by heart, he should pray from the siddur. And this is the simple custom, and it should not be changed. According to Rabbeinu Tam in Tosafot at the end of Rosh Hashanah, it is an obligation on each individual to mention the additional offerings, see there. But the offerings of the additional prayer of Rosh Chodesh are not mentioned explicitly, because it is written (Psalms 81:4) "At the concealed time for our festival," meaning the month should be concealed. We mention it indirectly by saying "the offerings of this memorial day," as Rosh Chodesh is also called a memorial day. And we also say "and the two goats for atonement, one for Rosh Hashanah and one for Rosh Chodesh." At the end of the offerings, we say "besides the burnt offering of the month and its meal offering, and the continual burnt offering and its meal offering, and their libations," etc. And on the second day, we say the same, although we count Rosh Chodesh from the first day, since from the days of Ezra onward we have not found Elul to be extended. In any case, perhaps with the coming of the redeemer, they will make it extended, and they will count from the second day. Therefore, the text should not be changed from the first day to the second day. Just as on every Rosh Chodesh when it is two days, we say the additional prayer and its offerings on the first day, similarly, even if we count from the second day, there is no concern, although it is not entirely similar, as is clear.

And know that the custom of Ashkenazim is not to blow the shofar during the silent Amidah, and the great authorities agreed with this (Magen Avraham at the beginning of Siman 592 and Knesset HaGedolah). However, the Sephardic custom is to blow the shofar even during the silent Amidah. This means that the one blowing the shofar has the shofar placed before him, and when all the people reach the end of the Malchuyot blessings, they wait until the shofar blower also reaches that point, and he blows without a prompter, for it is forbidden to interrupt. The same applies at the end of the Zichronot and at the end of the Shofarot. The congregation should be careful that if the shofar blower makes a mistake, it is forbidden to interrupt and rebuke him; they should leave it as is, for they have already fulfilled the obligation of the shofar blasts. The blasts that accompany the blessings are not indispensable. At most, after the prayer, they can tell him that he made a mistake, and he should blow again in the part where he erred, for the sequence is not crucial, as I wrote in the previous Siman. (I learned this from the words of the Rashba, cited by the Magen Avraham in Siman Katan 2, see there.)

The Sages taught in the Mishnah (Rosh Hashanah 32a): One must not recite fewer than ten verses of Kingship, ten verses of Remembrances, and ten verses of Shofars. And the Gemara explains: Corresponding to the ten times it is written (Psalms 150) "Praise God in His sanctuary," where it says "Praise Him with the blast of the shofar…" and "Hallelujah" is not counted, nor is "Let every soul praise God." And corresponding to the Ten Commandments that were given with the sound of a shofar, and corresponding to the ten sayings with which the world was created. And the world was created on Rosh Hashanah, when humankind was created, which is the purpose of creation. As we say in "You remember": "This day is the beginning of Your works," etc. And it seems to me that the verses of Kingship correspond to the sayings of the creation of the world, for the purpose of creation is to accept the yoke of His kingdom, blessed be He. And the verses of Remembrances correspond to the Ten Commandments, for by the merit of the Torah our remembrance will rise for good. And the verses of Shofars correspond to "Praise," as it is written there "Praise Him with the blast of the shofar."

These ten verses – we recite three from the Torah, three from the Writings, three from the Prophets, and conclude with one from the Torah. The reason we recite from the Writings before the Prophets, even though the Prophets are of a higher status than the Writings, which are only of divine inspiration, is because the verses from the Writings are from Psalms, which were said by David, and he preceded the later Prophets from whom the verses are taken (Levush). Additionally, since we ascend in holiness, it is necessary to begin with the Torah, then the Writings, and then the Prophets, to ascend in holiness (Ran). It is permissible to add to the ten verses. Even though, as they allude to the praises, the Ten Commandments, and the ten utterances, it would not seem proper to add, we find a similar case with the seven readers on Shabbat, who allude to the seven who see the king's face, and yet we add to them. So too, it is the case here (there and Mordechai).

All this is preferable and for enhancement. However, post factum, even if one only completed with verses from the Prophets, he has fulfilled his obligation (Gemara). And it seems that the same applies to verses from the Writings, for what difference does it make? Similarly, if one only said three verses in total, meaning one verse from the Torah, one from the Prophets, and one from the Writings for the Malchuyot (verses mentioning kingship), as well as for the Zichronot (verses mentioning remembrance) and Shofarot (verses mentioning the shofar) - he has fulfilled his obligation (Tur according to the Rivash). Moreover, even if one did not say any verses at all, but only stated "For the kingship is Yours" etc., "As it is written in Your Torah, and similarly in Your Holy Words, and similarly in Your Prophets" - he has fulfilled his obligation. And this applies to Zichronot and Shofarot as well. Only if he began with a verse from the Torah, he must also say a verse from the Writings and a verse from the Prophets (Tur). But if he did not begin, he has fulfilled his obligation with saying "As it is written in Your Torah." According to the Tur, one does not need to also say "and similarly in Your Holy Words" etc., because all are included in the term Torah, see there. According to the Rambam, one has not fulfilled his obligation unless he said a verse from the Torah, see there, and the poskim disagreed with him.

And the custom is to recite the verses in order, such as in the Malchuyot (verses of Kingship) from the Torah, "The Lord shall reign forever" until "He perceives no iniquity… and there was a king in Jeshurun" and so on for all of them. However, if one changed the order and recited a later verse before an earlier one, he has fulfilled his obligation, as it also implies in the Talmud. And we do not mention verses of Kingship, Remembrances, or Shofarot that involve calamity for Israel, such as "In fury poured out, I will reign over you," "He remembered that they were but flesh," "Blow the shofar in Gibeah," and similar verses. Nor do we say verses of Remembrances concerning an individual, even for good, such as "Remember us, O Lord, in the favor of Your people," "Remember me, O my God, for good."

And behold, there are those who object to the custom of concluding the verses of Shofrot with the verse "On the day of your gladness," since it only mentions trumpets and not the shofar. However, the Rosh and the Ran, of blessed memory, wrote to justify the custom, that just as a verse that mentions a teruah (a trumpet blast) without specifying a shofar is considered as if it mentions a shofar, as it is written, "And the teruah of a king is among them," and it counts for the verses of Shofar, as explained in the Talmud. Similarly here, when the verse mentions a tekiah (a type of trumpet blast), it is also considered as if it mentions a shofar. And here it is written, "And you shall sound a blast," and just because it also mentions trumpets, does that diminish its value? And so it is explicitly implied in the Yerushalmi, and therefore the custom should not be changed.

One should not say "and the binding of Isaac, for the offspring of Jacob, today mercifully remember," for even if one says "for his offspring" without specification, it is as if he said "for the offspring of Jacob," as we expound: "For in Isaac shall your seed be called"—in Isaac, and not all of Isaac. Therefore, one who says "of Jacob" changes the formula established by the Sages. And there are those who say that this does not change the formula, and on the contrary, in prayer, it is appropriate to clarify more precisely what one is praying for. Furthermore, one who vows by the seed of Isaac is prohibited from benefiting Esau's descendants, and therefore some have the custom of saying it (see Taz, subsection 3, and Magen Avraham, subsections 7 and 8). However, our custom is not to say it. And if it is because of the vow, one could say that in vows, we follow the common language usage.

Our sages of blessed memory have said that a person should not pray the Musaf prayer of Rosh Hashanah alone during the first three hours of the day, because during this time the Holy One, blessed be He, judges His world, and it is a time of wrath. Therefore, one needs the merit of the community, and the community prays Musaf after the first three hours. This is not the case with Shacharit, as everyone prays at this time, so he can also pray. Rashi explains that the concern is only with Musaf, because it includes the sections of Malchiyot (Kingship), Zichronot (Remembrances), and Shofarot (Shofars) - the judgment is commanded. But with Shacharit, there is no concern at all. He says "Aleinu" and "Reign over the entire world". The prayer leader adds "Ochila" and various piyutim (liturgical poems), each place according to its custom. (See Rashi on Avodah Zarah 4b, s.v. "Musafim", who writes as I have written. This requires further study, for if so, what is the Talmud's question: if so, why not also in the morning? See Magen Avraham, subsection 9, who elaborates. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

Afterward, the prayer leader repeats the Amidah, and the shofar is blown in accordance with the order of the blessings. Even though, according to Torah law, the shofar blasts are not directly related to the blessings and are considered a separate mitzvah, and the blessings themselves are not from the Torah; nonetheless, when the Sages instituted the blessings, they also instituted that the shofar should be blown with them, as it is taught (Rosh Hashanah 33b): "One who has recited the blessings and then a shofar became available to him, should blow, etc." The Gemara deduces: The reason is that he did not have a shofar; but if he had a shofar, he should hear them in the order of the blessings. And this applies specifically in a communal setting and not for an individual. An individual blows all the shofar blasts and then prays the Musaf. The reason appears to be that since the Torah decreed to blow three times—tekiah, teruah, tekiah—it is reasonable that in the first order, they accept the yoke of His kingship, as one blows before a king. The second is that our remembrance should come before Him, as it is written, "You shall sound the trumpets, and you shall be remembered before the Lord your God" (Numbers 10:9), and similarly, "You shall blow the trumpets, and they shall be a remembrance for you" (Numbers 10:10). The third is to proclaim the sound of the shofar as it was at the giving of the Torah, and so it will be in the future, God willing. Therefore, they instituted the order of shofar blasts with these blessings. However, such a matter is only for the community, as the merit of the community is very great, and not for an individual. Therefore, the individual does not blow in the order of the blessings, as I have written.

And the Rif and the Rambam wrote in the third chapter that this is the order of the shofar blasts: for the blessings of Malchuyot – one blows a set of Tekiah-Shevarim-Teruah-Tekiah (Tashrat), for Zichronot – a set of Tekiah-Shevarim-Tekiah (Tashat), and for Shofarot – a set of Tekiah-Teruah-Tekiah (Tarat). And similarly, the Tosafot and the Rosh wrote there that this was the custom of the early ones. They were puzzled by this, questioning how the sound of the Teruah could be changed from Malchuyot to Zichronot and from Zichronot to Shofarot? And the Rif wrote in this language: "In principle, they should blow according to the order of the blessings, just as they blew while seated. But since they have already fulfilled the obligation of the blasts, we do not burden the congregation excessively." And this is the custom throughout the world and in the two academies. Thus far his language, and similarly wrote the Tosafot and the Rosh.

However, Rabbeinu Tam instituted that they should blow a sequence of Tashrat (Tekiah, Shevarim-Teruah, Tekiah) for each set, as the change was not so significant from what was done previously, and it does not burden the congregation. Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote that in their practice, they blew Tashrat three times for Malchiyot, three times Tashat (Tekiah, Shevarim, Tekiah) for Zichronot, and three times Tarat (Tekiah, Teruah, Tekiah) for Shofarot. This is a strange and unusual custom, and it has no rationale. In his larger work, this is not mentioned at all. It seems there is some printing error here, and the intention was Tashrat, Tashat, Tarat for Malchiyot, and similarly for Zichronot and Shofarot, as we do today in most places (and so wrote the Gra"iB). Rabbeinu the Rema wrote according to the enactment of Rabbeinu Tam. However, now the prevalent practice in most places is to blow Tashrat, Tashat, Tarat for Malchiyot, and similarly for Zichronot and Shofarot, and this is the main practice according to the law.

And the reason given by our early sages is not sufficient, the reason we brought because of the burden on the congregation. After all, they are mere moments, and how much do we lengthen with "Mi Sheberach" and other matters? Therefore, it seems in my humble opinion that according to what the Rosh wrote in the name of Rav Hai Gaon at the end of Rosh Hashanah, that by Torah law, both the shevarim (broken sounds) are considered teruah (wailing sounds), as well as the teruah itself, and also the shevarim and teruah together. However, Rabbi Abahu instituted that all Israel should perform uniformly, and there is no real doubt about this. We brought this in Siman 593, paragraph 4; see there. Therefore, our early sages instituted the sequence of Tashrat for Kingship, Tashat for Remembrances, and Tarat for Shofarot, to teach us that all of these are fundamental to the law. There is no doubt at all, and however they perform, they fulfill their obligation.
