And many times we find that in order to teach the law, they did something that was better to do, only to instruct the law.

We have already written that an individual does not blow the shofar in the order of the blessings, even if he does not need to blow it himself, which would be somewhat of an interruption, but rather someone else should blow for him when he hears that he has finished the blessing. However, he is also not permitted to do so for the reason we wrote at the end of section 1. Instead, he should blow himself, or another should blow for him before he prays the Mussaf, and he does not need to blow again. It is customary that after the shofar blasts of Malchuyot, the congregation says "Hayom Harat Olam" and "Areshet Sefateinu." Even on Shabbat, they say "Hayom Harat Olam," but "Areshet" is not said on Shabbat, for how can we say "the sound of our shofar blasts" when there is no shofar blowing on Shabbat? And just as they say after Malchuyot, so too after Zichronot and after Shofarot.

The explanation of "Today the world was created" – its meaning is: that Adam, the first man, was created on Rosh Hashanah. On the twenty-fifth of Elul the creation began, and man was created on the sixth day, and on it the pregnancy of the world was completed, as man is the purpose of creation. And he sinned on that day with the Tree of Knowledge, and was judged on that day, and therefore "today all creatures of the world stand in judgment," as it is stated in the Pesikta (section 23): The Holy One, blessed be He, said to Adam, the first man: You are a sign for your children, just as you stood before Me in judgment on this day and emerged with clemency – you did not die on that day, and your life was extended until the day of the Holy One, blessed be He, which is a thousand years – so too, your children will stand before Me in judgment on this day. And afterwards we say "whether as children or as servants," for in Kiddushin (Kiddushin 36a) Rabbi Yehuda holds that when we act as children, meaning when we fulfill the will of our Father in Heaven – we are called children, and if not, we are called servants. Therefore, we plead because we do not know our status, and thus we say that in any case, whether as children or as servants, have mercy on us.

And the Rambam wrote (Chapter 3, Halacha 11) that one who blows the shofar during the sitting (i.e., the preliminary set of shofar blasts) should also blow during the order of the blessings (i.e., during the Amidah), see there. This does not mean it is necessary to do so, but it is a matter of decorum: since he began the mitzvah, why should we prevent him from completing it? However, it is not mandatory, and another person can blow the shofar. Therefore, in places where the custom is to honor all the shofar blowers, with one blowing during the sitting and another during the Musaf (the additional service), there is no concern. After all, during the daily offering (Tamid), several priests were honored with different parts (Magen Avraham, subsection 9). Thus, it is permissible to honor several shofar blowers in this manner, with one blowing for Malchuyot (kingship), another for Zichronot (remembrances), and another for Shofarot (shofar blasts). However, in the middle of the set, one should not take the shofar from the first and honor another, as this would be a slight to the first. Therefore, for the sitting blasts, one person should blow all the blasts, unless it is difficult for him to finish, as I have written in section 586, see there.

Initially, one should not interrupt with any speech unrelated to the shofar blowing and the prayers, whether between the seated shofar blasts and the standing shofar blasts, whether the blower or the congregation. However, if one spoke idle words, there is no need to repeat the blessing. This is not analogous to speaking between the donning of the tefillin of the arm and the tefillin of the head, where one must repeat the blessing, as these are two separate mitzvot, unlike here where it is one mitzvah. Additionally, one has already fulfilled the Torah obligation of shofar blasts. According to the first reason, even if one spoke between the seated shofar blasts themselves, one does not repeat the blessing, unlike the second reason. If one spoke between the blessing and the shofar blast about matters unrelated to the shofar blasts, one must repeat the blessing. Even if the conversation was related to the shofar blasts, one should not initially interrupt unless necessary, such as to give the shofar to someone, or something similar. If one spoke about another matter, even if it pertains to the prayers, one must repeat the blessing, as this is not related to the shofar blasts (Magen Avraham, subsection 5). Only between the seated shofar blasts and the standing shofar blasts, prayer-related matters are not considered an interruption, as there the interruption is not absolutely forbidden, unlike between the blessing and the shofar blast. In all of this, there is no difference between the blower and the listener (ibid.). (See Ran and Maor, who were puzzled by the prohibition of interruption between the seated and standing shofar blasts, but since the Geonim ruled thus, we should not deviate from their words.)

The sounding of the shofar does not impede the blessings, and the blessings do not impede the sounding of the shofar. For example, someone who does not have a shofar to blow should still recite [the blessings of] Malchiyot, Zichronot, and Shofarot. Similarly, someone who does not know the blessings must still blow the shofar when he has one. Even though the Sages decreed that the shofar should be blown in the order of the blessings, this is not indispensable. This law applies both on Rosh Hashanah and on Yom Kippur of the Jubilee year, which was during the time of the Temple, when they would blow the shofar and recite Malchiyot, Zichronot, and Shofarot.

However, the blessings of Rosh Hashanah and the Yom Kippur of the Jubilee year are interdependent, such that if one does not know all of them, one should not say only the ones he knows, but rather he should not say any of them. This specifically applies to Malchuyot (Kingship), Zichronot (Remembrances), and Shofarot (Shofar blasts), as all of them were instituted together. However, the other blessings are not subject to this rule. Similarly, the blessings throughout the year do not prevent one another; whichever blessings one knows, he should say (Magen Avraham).

And similarly, the blasts (of the shofar) prevent one another: If one knows how to produce a tekiah (long blast) but is unable to produce a teruah (series of short blasts), he should not even produce the tekiah. However, if one knows how to produce a tashat (combination of tekiah, shevarim, and tekiah) but does not know how to produce a tarat (combination of tekiah, teruah, and tekiah), or vice versa, he should do so. For both of them are considered teruah, according to what the Rosh wrote in the name of the Gaon, as I wrote in the previous section, and he fulfills the Torah obligation. And all the more so, the order of the blessings and the blasts do not prevent one another, and he can precede the blessings to the blasts or the blasts to the blessings. However, ideally, one should precede the blasts. But the order within the blasts themselves or within the blessings themselves is critical; if one precedes the teruah to the tekiah, he has done nothing. Similarly, if he precedes the Zichronot (remembrances) to the Malchuyot (sovereignties), or the Shofarot (shofar-related verses) to the Zichronot, he must go back and blow or bless in the correct order.

One who did not hear the shofar blasts – another person who has already blown can blow for him, as with all mitzvot, that even though he has already fulfilled the obligation, he can fulfill it for someone else. And he can also recite the blessings for him, just like with Kiddush and Havdalah. But one who did not recite the blessings of kingship, remembrances, and shofarot, or did not pray at all – his fellow cannot fulfill it for him. Specifically, only the prayer leader can fulfill it for others, because this is done publicly. But one individual cannot fulfill it for another in prayer, even if he himself also needs to pray. An individual does not become an agent for his fellow to fulfill the prayer, whether on Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, or throughout the year, unless there are ten, as the prayer leader fulfills it.

And this is what our sages of blessed memory said (Berakhot 45b): "The scribe recites the blessing, and the unlearned person fulfills his obligation" – this applies to the Grace after Meals and the blessings on commandments, but not to the prayer that was instituted to be recited silently. No individual has the authority to raise his voice and fulfill the obligation on behalf of others, until he descends before the ark (i.e., leads the prayer publicly). And thus Rav Sherira Gaon sent (Tur), and similarly, Rambam wrote in the fourth chapter of Prayer. Nevertheless, there are those who say that if one is unable to pray, his friend may fulfill his obligation with his prayer, for this applies only to one who is capable of praying himself that he cannot fulfill the obligation for another, but not to one who is incapable. One can rely on this in a pressing situation.

A person who is unable to blow the shofar himself, nor to recite the blessings himself, and has before him two options: in one place they blow the shofar but do not recite the blessings—since there is no one there who knows how to recite the blessings of Malchuyot, Zichronot, and Shofarot; and in another place they recite the blessings, but there is no shofar or no one who knows how to blow it—it is obvious that he should go to the place where they blow the shofar and not to the place where they recite the blessings. For the blowing of the shofar is a Torah obligation, whereas the blessings are rabbinic.

Not only that, but even if the sounding of the shofar is in doubt, and the blessings are certain, one should go to the place of the shofar sounding, because a doubt regarding a Torah commandment is more serious than a certainty regarding a rabbinic commandment. It is also obvious that if one can go to a place where they pray and still have enough time during the day to go to a place where the shofar is sounded, one is obligated to first go to the place of prayer, even though it is rabbinic, because afterward, an individual will no longer be able to pray on his behalf, which is not the case with the shofar, as I wrote in the previous section. It has also been explained in Siman 586 that the shofar does not override a rabbinic prohibition. Only through a non-Jew, which constitutes a double rabbinic prohibition in the context of a mitzvah, is it permitted (see Magen Avraham, subsection 2).

We are accustomed to sounding the shofar after the prayer, to complete one hundred blasts, corresponding to the one hundred cries of Sisera's mother, as mentioned by the Aruch. This is brought by the Tosafot and the Rosh in the fourth chapter of Rosh Hashanah. The Tur, in the name of Rav Amram, wrote that after the prayer, a great teruah (a specific type of shofar blast) is sounded without a preceding tekiah (another type of shofar blast) in order to confound Satan. However, we do not follow this practice.

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote that after fulfilling the obligation, one should not blow the shofar again without purpose. However, for a minor, even one who has reached the age of education, it is permissible to tell him to blow, and he may blow all day; thus are his words. And regarding the law of a minor, we have explained in Siman 589; see there. But what he wrote, that afterwards one should not blow again without purpose – the Tur did not write this in the name of Rav Hai Gaon, see there. (He brought proof from the case where, when the prayer leader finished blowing the shofar in Yavneh, no one could hear the sound of the shofar, see there. However, the Rema follows the opinion of the Tosafot, that this applies to those who did not hear the blasts, as the Taz wrote in subsection 2, see there. And see Magen Avraham subsection 2 in the name of the Ra'avan, that when there is no longer a need to blow, it is forbidden to move the shofar due to muktzeh; see there, and it requires further examination. Also, what he wrote from the first day to the second day – requires further examination. Be precise and you will find clarity.)

The Tur wrote in the name of Rav Hai Gaon that it is prohibited to fast on Rosh Hashanah, as it is written in Nehemiah (Nehemiah 8) that Ezra and Nehemiah said to all the people on Rosh Hashanah: "Go, eat of the fat, and drink of the sweet, for this day is holy to our Lord"; and it is written: "And all the people went to eat and to drink," etc. Similarly, the Mordechai writes in the first chapter of Rosh Hashanah, in the name of Rav Nachshon Gaon, that it is prohibited to fast. There are proofs from the Torah, from the tradition, from the Baraita, and from the Jerusalem Talmud. From the Torah: since it is included with all the festivals, and it is written concerning it (Leviticus 23:21) "a holy convocation"; and we expound in the Sifra and the Sifrei: sanctify it with food and drink, and clean clothing. And Rosh Hashanah is called a "festival" like all the other festivals, as it is written (Psalms 81:4): "At the concealed time for our festival." And we say: what is the festival during which the new moon is concealed? You must say this is Rosh Hashanah. And from the words of the tradition, as it is written in Ezra: "Go, eat of the fat," etc. And from the Baraita: as it was taught in the Jerusalem Talmud that on Rosh Hashanah, they blow the shofar but do not fast (in the third chapter, fourth halacha of Taanit). And from the Jerusalem Talmud in the first chapter, fourth halacha of Rosh Hashanah, which says: there is no nation like this nation, etc., they wear white, they eat and drink and rejoice, and they know that the Holy One, blessed be He, will perform a miracle for them, see there. And in Arachin (10b) we say that Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur are called "festivals," and so it is in Sotah (41a), see there. And so rules the Tur.

And this is the language of our teacher, the Beit Yosef: "They eat, drink, and rejoice. And they do not fast on Rosh Hashanah, nor on Shabbat Shuvah. However, they should not eat everything they desire, nor treat the day with lightheadedness, and the fear of God should be upon their faces." Until here is his language. And the Maharshal did not eat fish on Rosh Hashanah because he was fond of them and wanted to reduce his desire in a specific matter. And they should not wear important clothing on Rosh Hashanah as on other festivals, but rather white (Bach and Magen Avraham). And among us, it is not customary to wear white on Rosh Hashanah, only on Yom Kippur. And they also eat and drink as on other festivals. And behold, it is an explicit verse: "Eat rich foods and drink sweet beverages." And only in this matter is Rosh Hashanah different from other festivals: that they extend the prayers much until after midday (see Taz). And there are also those who do not sleep on the first day of Rosh Hashanah, based on the Jerusalem Talmud: "One who sleeps on Rosh Hashanah, his fortune sleeps." And we do not know where this Jerusalem Talmud is found. And the Ari did not concern himself with this (and said that after the shofar blasts and after midday, the judgments have already been sweetened).

In the responsa of the Terumat HaDeshen (Siman 278), it is written that there are opinions that permit fasting on Rosh Hashanah, and there are those who say it is a mitzvah to fast. See there. And although the law is not like this, as decided by the Geonim and the majority of our early and later sages, nevertheless, regarding what we wrote earlier in Siman 519 about one who swears to fast on Shabbat and Yom Tov, or vows to fast – that the oath or vow does not take effect, see there. Still, if one swears or vows to fast on Rosh Hashanah, it requires annulment, since there are opinions that there is no prohibition to fast. (And this is the intention of the Rema in Siman 597, Section 2).

It is a simple matter that a dream fast must be observed, for even on Shabbat it is permitted, all the more so on Rosh Hashanah. And our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 3: One who fasts once on Rosh Hashanah as a dream fast, if it was on the first day, must fast on both days for the rest of his life. And if it was on the second day, he need only fast on the second day for the rest of his life. These are his words, and the explanation of the matter is because there are places where it is accepted that anyone who is accustomed to fasting on Rosh Hashanah and changes his custom and does not fast will not complete his year, as is written in section 2. The reason is that since Heaven showed him that his fast is cherished above, even those who are of the opinion that one should not fast on Rosh Hashanah must nevertheless observe this practice for the rest of their life if they were once shown to fast. And he does not need to substitute a fast for his fast, as on Shabbat and Yom Tov, because there are those who hold that it is permitted and a mitzvah to fast. There is only a practical difference between the first day and the second day, for if Heaven showed him to fast on the first day, which is primary, all the more so he should also fast on the second day. But if they showed him to fast on the second day, he should not fast on the first day, as it is stricter than the second and is primary.

And one who is not concerned about this and is not fearful for his soul does not need to fast all his days. The Levush wrote that one who fasts on Rosh Hashanah should not bake or cook, but rather engage all day in prayer, supplications, and Torah study; since he does not fulfill "half for you," he should fulfill "all for God." Thus far his language. And consequently, the same applies to other Yom Tov days. There is an opinion that the fasting itself is considered "all for God" (Magen Avraham, subsection 1). Furthermore, if fasting is a delight for him, as it nullifies a decree through a dream fast, it is also considered "half for you" (ibid.). One who is fasting does not say "Aneinu" in the afternoon prayer, just as we do not say "Aneinu" on Yom Kippur, because how can he say "the day of our fast"? For these days are not called days of fasting, but days of judgment. One who is fasting should not make Kiddush during the day for someone else, since it only contains the blessing over the wine. On the night of Rosh Hashanah, it is always forbidden to fast, for a dream fast applies only to the day and not to the night. Similarly, if there is doubt whether it was a dream for which one must fast or not, he does not need to fast (ibid., subsection 4). And similarly, one who is not concerned about dreams should not fast.

There are those who say that one who fasts on Rosh Hashanah should not eat even when there is a circumcision, since in any case it is a Yom Tov (festival day), and nevertheless one fasts. Therefore, what does the circumcision add (Shaarei Teshuva in the name of Shvut Yaakov)? And this reasoning is sound. All the more so with a fast due to a bad dream, for even throughout the year, one who fasts due to a bad dream should not eat even at a meal of a mitzvah, since a fast due to a bad dream is observed even on Shabbat.

For Mincha, one says "Ashrei", "Uva LeTzion", and the seven blessings as in Maariv and Shacharit. If it falls on Shabbat, the weekly Torah portion is read. The prayer leader repeats the prayer and Kedusha, as on weekdays. Only on Yom Kippur do they also say the Kedusha of Musaf during Mincha, but not on Rosh Hashanah. Some also do not say it even on Yom Kippur, only as on weekdays. "Avinu Malkeinu" is recited, but if it falls on Shabbat, it is not said. Know that in our city, when praying Mincha on Rosh Hashanah immediately after Musaf, "Avinu Malkeinu" is not said even on weekdays, because it was already recited in Shacharit.

If it falls on Shabbat, the Tur writes in the name of Rav Amram that we say "Tzidkatcha Tzedek," because although we do not say it on any other holiday, nevertheless, on Rosh Hashanah, which is a Day of Judgment, it should be said. However, there are those who say not to say it, because in any case, it is a holiday and also Rosh Chodesh. And this is our prevalent custom. And regarding the Day of Judgment – the judgments have already been sweetened after the Musaf prayer.

The Tur wrote: "On the night of Rosh Hashanah, we pray the evening service the same way as we do on the first night. If it falls on Shabbat, the Ra'avyah wrote: I asked my teachers whether one should say 'V'Todieinu' because it includes 'the festival offering,' and Rosh Hashanah is neither a 'festival' nor a 'pilgrimage festival.' They answered me that nevertheless, we say 'V'Todieinu,' similar to how we say in the Havdalah after a festival 'between the seventh day and the six days of work,' as it is part of the order of distinctions. Here too, it is part of the order of the service." Thus ends his words.

And besides this, according to several early Geonim, Rosh Hashanah is called a "festival," as the phrase "on the day of our festival" (Psalms 81:4) refers to Rosh Hashanah, as I have written in Siman 597. Similarly, the Tur himself wrote in Siman 582 that it is called a "holiday" according to several Geonim. See there. However, the Tur did not elaborate here, since, in any case, it is necessary to say for the reason he wrote.

Know that the two festival days of Rosh Hashanah are not similar to the two festival days of other holidays, for on other holidays, only one day is observed in the Land of Israel, whereas Rosh Hashanah is observed for two days even in the Land of Israel to this day, as the Rif writes in the first chapter of Beitzah. The reason for this is that when the months were sanctified based on the sighting of the moon, all the holidays in the Land of Israel were clearly known on which day they fell, as many days had passed since the beginning of the month. However, in the Diaspora, where the messengers of the court did not reach, they would observe two days due to doubt, as they did not know on which day the new month had been established. Therefore, even though nowadays we are proficient in calculating the months, as we establish the months based on the calculations from the days of Hillel the Prince and onward, the original decree remains in place. Nevertheless, in any case, one of the days is certainly a weekday, and its initial observance was only due to doubt.

But on Rosh Hashanah, which is itself also Rosh Chodesh (the New Moon), even in Jerusalem they would often observe two days. This means: if witnesses came on the first day and testified that they saw the new moon, they would observe only the first day as holy. However, if the witnesses came at night after the first day, and certainly if they came the next day, then Rosh Chodesh and Rosh Hashanah would be established for the next day, and the first day they would also observe as holy in anticipation of the witnesses' arrival. Even if the witnesses came on the first day from the afternoon and onwards, they would still observe two days of Rosh Hashanah, as it is taught in the fourth chapter of Rosh Hashanah. Therefore, in most years, they observed two days of Rosh Hashanah in Jerusalem as well. This was not due to doubt, but because this was the established practice. Therefore, even today, two days are observed. This is what our sages meant when they said it is like one long day, meaning that both days are considered certainly holy, not one being mundane as in the case of other festivals. (There is a discussion and issue regarding this in Beitzah 5b according to Rashi, Tosafot, Rif, and Rosh. However, the halacha is as stated.)

Therefore, on Rosh Hashanah, several laws regarding muktzeh and nolad differ from other holidays. On any other holiday, an egg that was laid on one day is permitted on the next day. Similarly, milk that was milked on the first day is permitted on the second day. But on Rosh Hashanah, this is not the case, because on other holidays, one of the days is considered a weekday, whereas on Rosh Hashanah, both days are holy, and they are considered as one extended day. Except in the case of a deceased person, where leniency is applied on the second day of Rosh Hashanah out of respect for the deceased, as I wrote in Siman 526, but not for other matters. Similarly, something that was trapped or picked on the first day of Rosh Hashanah is forbidden on the second day, as I wrote in Siman 515. See there.

Based on this, a dispute arose among the early authorities regarding whether to recite "Shehecheyanu" during Kiddush and the sounding of the shofar on the second day of Rosh Hashanah. The Tur brought a responsum from Rashi of blessed memory, who wrote: "My teachers say not to recite the time blessing on the second day because it is like one long day. But I say that one should recite the time blessing, because although it is considered one long day for other matters, the main biblical festival is only one day." Most halachic authorities agreed with Rashi. However, to satisfy the opinion of the Geonim, the widespread custom in all communities is to take a new fruit during Kiddush, for in any case, one would need to recite "Shehecheyanu"; or to wear a new garment. Regarding the shofar, where a new fruit is not relevant, one should wear a new garment. All this is not strictly necessary, as the common practice is to recite "Shehecheyanu" in all cases. And although during Kiddush we place a new fruit, the one sounding the shofar does not wear a new garment and still recites "Shehecheyanu." Similarly, in Kiddush, if one does not have a new fruit, nevertheless, one recites "Shehecheyanu." So wrote our teacher the Rema. (The Beit Yosef ruled to recite "Shehecheyanu" during Kiddush, but not during the shofar blasts, except when the first day falls on Shabbat. This is puzzling: why should the shofar be different from Kiddush? See Beit Yosef, further research is required.)

On the second day, we pray as we did on the first day. We read the portion of the Binding of Isaac until the end of the section, in order to recall the merit of the Binding of Isaac. The reason it is not read on the first day is because "And the Lord visited Sarah" precedes it, as Sarah was remembered on Rosh Hashanah, which is relevant to the day's theme. Therefore, we read the Haftarah about Hannah on the first day for the same reason, as Hannah was also remembered on Rosh Hashanah. On the second day, we read the Haftarah from Jeremiah: "Thus says the Lord: The people who survived the sword found grace in the wilderness" until "Is Ephraim My dear son?", for it is written there "I will surely remember him," which corresponds to the remembrances of Rosh Hashanah. The shofar blasts are the same as on the first day. It has already been explained that Rosh Hashanah is observed for two days even in the Land of Israel. (Refer to the Taz at the end of section 600 regarding when Rosh Hashanah falls on Thursday and Friday, and the community did not have a shofar until after they had accepted the Sabbath. It was still a long day, and he ruled to blow without a blessing. The Eliyah Rabba agreed with this; see there.)

There is a positive commandment for every person to repent from their sins. The entire book of Deuteronomy, as well as all the Prophets, admonished regarding repentance. Israel will not be redeemed except through repentance. The Torah has already assured that the end of Israel will be to repent at the end of their exile, and immediately they will be redeemed, as it is stated (Deuteronomy 30:1-3): "And it shall come to pass, when all these things are come upon you… and you return to the Lord your God… and the Lord your God will return your captivity and have compassion upon you" (Rambam, Chapter Seven of the Laws of Repentance). Great is repentance, for it brings the redemption closer, as it is stated (Isaiah 59:20): "And a redeemer shall come to Zion, and unto those who turn from transgression in Jacob." What is the reason "And a redeemer shall come to Zion"? Because of "and unto those who turn from transgression in Jacob" (Yoma 86b). Great is repentance, for it reaches up to the Throne of Glory, as it is stated (Hosea 14:2): "Return, O Israel, unto the Lord your God" (ibid.). Great is repentance, for intentional sins are considered as accidental when one repents out of fear, and they are considered as merits when one repents out of love (ibid.).

A person who repents should not think that he is distanced from the ranks of the righteous because of the sins and transgressions he committed. This is not the case; rather, he is beloved and cherished before the Creator, blessed be He, as if he had never sinned at all. Furthermore, his reward is great, for he has tasted sin and separated from it for the honor of the Almighty, blessed be He. The Sages said: "In the place where penitents stand, even the completely righteous cannot stand" (Berachot 34b). This means that their level is greater than that of those who have never sinned at all, for they have tasted sin and distanced themselves from it (Rambam there). How great is the virtue of repentance! Yesterday this person was despised and abominable before the Creator, blessed be He; and now he is beloved and cherished before Him, blessed be He. Yesterday he was separated from the Lord, the God of Israel, as it is written: "Your iniquities have separated between you and your God"; he would cry out and not be answered, as it is said: "Even though you make many prayers, I will not hear." And today he is attached to the Divine Presence, as it is said (Deuteronomy 4:4): "But you who cleave" etc.; he cries out and is answered, as it is said (Isaiah 65:24): "And it shall come to pass that before they call, I will answer."

Penitents (Baal Teshuva) have the practice of being exceedingly humble and modest. If fools insult them because of their past actions, they should not be affected by this, but rather listen and rejoice. For it is a great merit for them to feel ashamed of their past deeds, and they should not respond at all. Thus, our sages of blessed memory said: "Those who are insulted and do not insult in return, who hear their disgrace and do not reply, who act out of love and rejoice in their suffering, concerning them the verse states: 'And those who love Him are like the sun rising in its might' (Shabbat 88b)." The one who shames them commits a very great sin. It is forbidden to say to a penitent: "Remember your former deeds." This is included in the prohibition of verbal oppression, as explained at the end of the chapter "HaZahav." The one who shames them needs to repent and seek forgiveness from the one they insulted.

And do not say that repentance is only for transgressions that involve action, such as immorality, theft, robbery, or forbidden foods, and the like. Rather, just as a person must repent from those, so too must he repent from bad traits that he has, and repent from anger, enmity, jealousy, hatred, mockery, the pursuit of money and honor, the pursuit of food, and the like. For all these, one must repent. And these sins are harder than those that involve action, because one is accustomed to them, and it is difficult to separate from them. And so it says, "Let the wicked forsake his way" (Isaiah 55:7), meaning the habit that he is accustomed to.

And all the more so, if God forbid, a thought of heresy or apostasy enters his mind, this is like a spiritual leprosy. And in the times preceding the Messiah – the forces of the evil inclination and Satan will be entirely present. This is what our Sages of blessed memory meant when they said: "In the footsteps of the Messiah, insolence will increase." That is to say: insolence towards Heaven. And one should consider: Who am I – a lowly, despised, and insignificant creature, of little understanding, filled with many base desires – to doubt any matter from the words of the Torah or the words of our Sages of blessed memory? I, a simpleton, cannot even comprehend the mundane conversations of the disciples of their disciples, so how could I dispute them? Therefore, he should strengthen himself in Torah, prayer, and the hymns of King David, peace be upon him. And it will be fulfilled in him: "The righteous shall live by his faith."

Maimonides writes in the first chapter of Teshuva: Every commandment in the Torah, whether positive or negative, if a person transgresses one of them, whether intentionally or unintentionally, when they repent and return from their sin, they are obligated to confess before the Blessed God. As it is stated in the section of Naso: "A man or a woman who does... and they shall confess the sin they have committed" - this is verbal confession. And this confession is a positive commandment. How does one confess? One says: "Please, O Lord! I have sinned, I have committed iniquity, I have transgressed before You, and I have done such and such. And I regret and am ashamed of my deeds, and I will never return to this matter again." This is the essence of confession, and whoever elaborates and extends on this matter is praiseworthy.

And so too, those who bring sin offerings and guilt offerings, when they bring their sacrifices for their inadvertent or intentional sins—they are not atoned for by their sacrifices until they repent and confess verbally, as it is said: "and he shall confess that he has sinned in that thing" (Leviticus 5:5). Similarly, all those liable for capital punishment by the court or liable for lashes—they are not atoned for by their death or by their lashes until they repent and confess. Likewise, one who injures his fellow or damages his property, even if he has paid what he owes him—it is not atoned for until he confesses and resolves never to do such a thing again, as it is said: "from all the sins of man" (Numbers 5:6).

And one should not wonder: why should the inadvertent sinner need to repent? Certainly, this is the case, for in Leviticus regarding the sin offerings and guilt offerings, which are for inadvertent sins, it is written several times: "and the priest shall atone for him from his sin and it shall be forgiven him" (Leviticus 4:26, 31, 35). Evidently, it is called a sin and requires forgiveness and atonement. And at the end of Parshat Shelach, it is written: "And the priest shall atone for the soul that sins inadvertently, when he sins by inadvertence before the Lord, to atone for him, and it shall be forgiven him" (Numbers 15:28). The reason is that even inadvertent sin comes from a lack of caution, unlike coercion, which does not require repentance, as Rambam wrote in his commentary on the Mishnah at the end of Yoma. See there. But an inadvertent sin is not comparable to coercion.

Additionally, it is written: The scapegoat, because it was an atonement for all of Israel, the High Priest confesses upon it for all of Israel, as it is said (Leviticus 16:21): "and confess over it all the iniquities of the children of Israel." The scapegoat atones for all sins in the Torah, whether minor or severe, whether committed intentionally or unintentionally, whether known to him or not known to him—all are atoned for by the scapegoat. This is provided that he has repented. But if he has not repented, the scapegoat only atones for minor sins. And what are minor sins and what are severe sins? Severe sins are those for which one is liable to death by the court or karet. False and vain oaths, even though they do not incur karet, are considered severe. All other negative commandments and positive commandments that do not incur karet are considered minor. Thus far is his language.

Behold, what he wrote that without doing teshuva (repentance), the scapegoat atones for light transgressions – is very puzzling. For at the end of Yoma and in Shevuot (13a), Rabbi and the Rabbis disagree. Rabbi holds that Yom Kippur atones even for those who have not repented, and the Rabbis hold that it atones only for those who have repented. And we follow the opinion of the Rabbis, that even for light transgressions, it does not atone without teshuva. And already they have questioned his words (Kesef Mishneh and Lechem Mishneh). And in the Gemara there, it questions simply: What is the case of this positive commandment? If he did not do teshuva – "the sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination," see there (and the explanation of the Lechem Mishneh on this is puzzling, see there). 

And it seems that he derived this law from the Yerushalmi there in Yoma and Shevuot, which says that for a positive commandment it atones even without teshuva. And even though it says there that for a negative commandment it does not atone without teshuva – nevertheless, the Rambam equated them in this matter, because in our Talmud – both are considered light transgressions. And even though at the end of Yoma they want to distinguish between a regular negative commandment and a negative commandment that is connected to a positive commandment, and perhaps the Yerushalmi also holds this way, nevertheless, the plain meaning of the Sugya in Shevuot is that there is no distinction. See there.

In our times when the Temple does not exist and we do not have an altar for atonement, we have only repentance. And repentance atones for all sins. Even if a person was wicked all his life and repented at the end, his wickedness is not mentioned, as it is said: "The wickedness of the wicked shall not cause him to stumble on the day he turns from his wickedness." The essence of Yom Kippur atones for those who repent. However, a person should not delay and say: I still have time to repent. For who knows, perhaps he will die tomorrow, and he will be found to have died without repentance. This is what Solomon said: "Let your garments always be white." Additionally, the primary repentance is during the days of youth, and this is what Solomon said (Ecclesiastes 12:1): "Remember your Creator in the days of your youth" – while your strengths are still strong, and you can commit sins, and you refrain because of His honor and awe, may He be blessed. This is what they said at the end of Yoma: What is the case of a true penitent? It is with the same woman, in the same period, in the same place. That is to say: when you are in all your strengths, and the sin is ready, and you refrain.

But when one repents in their old age, when their strength diminishes – this is not considered complete repentance. Nevertheless, it is still considered repentance, and such a person is called a "penitent." Even if one transgressed all their life and repented on the day of their death, and died in a state of repentance – their sins are forgiven, as it is said: "Before the sun and the light and the moon and the stars grow dark, and the clouds return after the rain" – which refers to the day of death, implying that if one repents before death, they are forgiven (there).

And what is repentance? That the sinner should abandon his sin, remove it from his thoughts, and resolve in his heart not to commit it again, as it is said: "Let the wicked forsake his way"; and he should regret the past, as it is written: "For after I turned back, I repented"; and He who knows all secrets will testify about him that he will never return to that sin again, as it is said: "And we will no more say to the work of our hands, 'You are our gods'" (Hosea, Chapter Two, also in Yalkut at the end of Hosea). And this is what the Torah says: "Before the Lord, you shall be purified," meaning: the Holy One, Blessed be He, will testify about you that you are pure. And one needs to confess verbally. And anyone who confesses but has not resolved in his heart to abandon the sin – it is as if he immerses while holding a defiling creature in his hand. As it is said: "He who confesses and forsakes [his sin] will obtain mercy," meaning: both confession and forsaking the sin are required, not just one of them.

One must specify the sin when it is a sin between a person and their fellow. However, for sins between a person and God, it is audacious to reveal them; rather, one should confess them quietly between oneself and one's Creator. And regarding what is written: "He who conceals his sins will not succeed" – this refers to sins between a person and their fellow (Gemara). And one of the ways of repentance is for the penitent to always cry out before the blessed God with weeping and supplications. And to give charity according to one's ability. And to distance oneself greatly from the matter in which one sinned. And if one can go into exile – how good, for exile atones for sin and causes one to be humble, meek, and of lowly spirit.

Yom Kippur is a time of repentance for both individuals and the community, and it is the pinnacle of forgiveness and atonement for Israel. Therefore, everyone is obligated to repent on Yom Kippur and to confess in every prayer. The order of the confessions will be explained in Siman 607. This applies to sins between a person and God. However, for sins between a person and his fellow, neither repentance nor Yom Kippur is effective until he appeases his fellow, if he only insulted him with words. And if he has stolen money from him, whether in business or in any other manner, it is not effective until he returns the stolen item and also asks for his forgiveness. This is what the Torah means when it says: "For on this day He shall atone for you... before the Lord you shall be purified." This means that Yom Kippur atones for sins before the Lord, but not for those between a person and his fellow (Mishnah there).

Not all transgressions are equal in their atonement, and there are four categories of atonement. How so? If a person transgressed a positive commandment and repented, he is forgiven immediately. About this, it is said: "Return, O backsliding children, I will heal your backslidings." If he transgressed a prohibition that does not carry the penalty of karet (excision) or death, and repented, repentance suspends the punishment, and Yom Kippur atones. Concerning this, it is said: "For on this day atonement shall be made for you" etc. If he transgressed commands that carry karet or the death penalty by the court, and repented, repentance and Yom Kippur suspend the punishment, and suffering that comes upon him completes the atonement. About this, it is said: "I will punish their transgression with the rod, and their iniquity with stripes." All these transgressions are when there is no desecration of God’s name involved. But one who desecrates God's name, even though he repented, and Yom Kippur has arrived while he remains in his repentance, and suffering has come upon him, he does not receive complete atonement until he dies. Rather, repentance, Yom Kippur, and suffering all suspend the punishment, and death atones, as it is said: "It has been revealed in my ears by the Lord of hosts: Surely this iniquity shall not be atoned for you until you die."

Desecration of God's name (Chilul Hashem) depends on the stature of the individual. The greater the person, even a minor transgression constitutes a grave desecration. As Rav said in Yoma (86a): "For instance, I, if I purchase meat from a butcher and do not immediately pay, in a place where the butcher does not usually demand immediate payment." And Rabbi Yochanan said: "For instance, I, if I walk four cubits without Torah or Tefillin." There are those who say: "For example, if his peers are embarrassed because of his reputation, or if people say: 'May God forgive him for his actions.'" Or a Torah scholar who does not conduct his business faithfully, or whose speech is not gentle with others; see there. From this, we learn that the greater the person, the greater the desecration of God's name.

And all the more so regarding the desecration of God’s name among the nations. This refers to when a Jew commits some injustice or fraud against a non-Jew, or with measures and weights—it is an immeasurable desecration of God’s name. Concerning this, the prophet Ezekiel (Ezekiel 36:17) said: "Son of man, the house of Israel dwelt upon their land, and they defiled it... Their way before Me was as the defilement of a woman in her impurity... And I scattered them among the nations... And they came among the nations, and they desecrated My holy name; in that it was said of them: 'These are the people of the Lord, and they have gone out of His land.'” This means that the Holy One, blessed be He, laments that when they were in the land of Israel and defiled it, their way before Me was like the defilement of a woman in her impurity. This means: just as when a woman is in her impurity, no one knows of it except her husband, so too the nations did not know of their defilement, only I knew. But when I exiled them among the nations, and the nations became aware of their defilement—was it not a great desecration of God's name? They say to Israel: Are you not the people of the Lord? How can you defile yourselves? You should also know that you went out from your land; therefore, Israel should not rejoice like the nations. We must sanctify the name of Heaven and the name of Israel.

And even though repentance and crying out [to God] are always good, nevertheless, during the Ten Days between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, they are especially good and are accepted immediately, as it is stated: "Seek the Lord while He may be found." Our Sages explained (Rosh Hashanah 18a) that these are the ten days between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, during which even an individual is answered immediately. Because of this, the entire House of Israel has the custom to increase in charity and good deeds, and to engage in commandments from Rosh Hashanah until Yom Kippur more than during the rest of the year. It is also customary for everyone to rise at night during these ten days and to pray in synagogues with supplications and words of exhortation until daybreak (Rambam, Hilchot Teshuvah, Chapter 3). During the Selichot prayers, they say the confession three times, except on the eve of Yom Kippur when they say it only once. They also say "Avinu Malkeinu" in the evening and morning, except on Shabbat and the eve of Yom Kippur. However, when Yom Kippur falls on Shabbat, they say "Avinu Malkeinu" during the Shacharit prayer on the eve of Yom Kippur. Even if there is a Brit Milah, during which Tachanun is not said, "Avinu Malkeinu" is still recited. On Shabbat Teshuva, they recite "Tzidkatecha" during Mincha. The day after Rosh Hashanah is a public fast, the Fast of Gedaliah. Some do not sanctify the moon until after Yom Kippur, while others, to add to the mitzvah before Yom Kippur, do sanctify it. This is also our custom. It is customary not to pronounce a curse in a court during these days, nor to administer oaths until after Yom Kippur.

The Tur brings a Yerushalmi: Rav Chiyya instructed Rav, "If you are able to eat in purity throughout the entire year, do so. If not, then eat in purity for seven days each year" (Chapter 1 of Shabbat, Halacha 3). And the Ra'avyah wrote: I have received that these seven days are those between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur. They are called "seven days" because on Rosh Hashanah in any case, one eats in purity, as one is obligated to purify oneself for the festival. Therefore, he wrote that even someone who is not careful throughout the year with the bread of a non-Jew should be careful during the Ten Days of Repentance. See there.

It appears to me, in my humble opinion, that this only applies to matters that are not prohibited by law, for in such cases it is merely an act of piety, and it is proper to be stringent during these days. However, matters that some authorities prohibit by law, but are permitted according to other opinions and thus are customarily allowed – such as consuming new grain outside the Land of Israel, or meat without a sircha (adhering lesion), and similar cases – it is not possible to act leniently during the Ten Days of Repentance. For since one refrains from eating them during these days, it is as though they have accepted the opinions of those who prohibit them. Therefore, how can they eat them afterward? (See Magen Avraham, who writes that regarding bread baked by a non-Jew, one should at least be careful to throw a splinter of wood into the oven. One should also be careful not to separate challah from a non-Jew's dough. Concerning what he writes about someone traveling, etc., see there – it requires further examination. And a woman who finds a dead child near her – she must accept repentance. And someone who sends a messenger, and the messenger is killed on the way, also – see there. From a legal perspective, there is room for skepticism, and we have explained this elsewhere. Scrutinize and you will find leniency.)

Every person should examine their actions during the Ten Days of Repentance and repent from them. A doubtful transgression is more severe than a certain transgression and requires more effort in repentance, because one regrets more when they know they have sinned than when they do not know for certain. Therefore, a provisional guilt offering is more expensive than a definite guilt offering, as explained in the Torah, Mishnah, and Gemara. Additionally, the evil inclination entices more regarding doubt than certainty, saying that there is no transgression here. Therefore, more strengthening is needed for this. And one who comes to purify themselves is assisted. With divine assistance, the laws of Rosh Hashanah are concluded.

We learn in Yoma (81b): Chiya bar Rav of Difti taught: It is written, "And you shall afflict your souls on the ninth day of the month at evening." Do we fast on the ninth? Do we not fast on the tenth? Rather, this comes to tell you that anyone who eats and drinks on the ninth, the scripture considers it as if they fasted on both the ninth and the tenth. And it seems to me that this is the explanation: the entire verse is superfluous, for at the beginning of the section it is written, "But on the tenth day of this seventh month is the Day of Atonement, a holy convocation shall it be for you, and you shall afflict your souls." Furthermore, where do we find in all Sabbaths and festivals that it says to make the Sabbath or festival on the preceding day in the evening? For on the Sabbath it is written, "Remember the Sabbath day," and the day includes also the night prior, as the night follows the day that follows it. And so it is with all festivals. And even concerning Yom Kippur itself, it is written here and in the section of Pinchas, "on the tenth day of the seventh month," and consequently, this includes the night and the day. So why here did the Torah change to write about the preceding day, that the fast begins on the evening of that day? Moreover, according to the plain meaning of this very verse itself, it is not correct, for at night the affliction is not yet noticeable, since he ate close to the evening. The main affliction is during the day.

It is not comparable to what is written in Parashat Bo: "On the first day, on the fourteenth day of the month in the evening you shall eat unleavened bread," where it is written "you shall eat" at the end, implying that you shall eat unleavened bread at night. But here it is written "and you shall afflict" before "in the evening," implying that "and you shall afflict" – immediately on the ninth day (Tosafot Berakhot 8b). Furthermore, there it is necessary to write so, because the obligation to eat matzah is only on the first night and not during the day. It teaches us that the obligation is only on the fourteenth in the evening. But here, the night and the day are equal, and on the contrary: the main affliction is during the day, as I wrote. And regarding "until the twenty-first day of the month in the evening" – it is also necessary to write so, because otherwise I would say "until but not including." But here, the entire verse is completely redundant. And also according to the language, it is not correct, as I wrote.

Therefore, our sages of blessed memory expounded that it is as if it is written (Leviticus 23:32), "And you shall afflict your souls on the ninth of the month," and also in the evening, from evening to evening, which is the following day, the tenth day. Practically speaking, it is impossible to say that this "in the evening" is a separate matter by itself, and necessarily its meaning is in the evening of the ninth. Rather, the reverse is true: "And you shall afflict yourselves on the ninth in the evening," not on the ninth. And it is considered a negative commandment derived from a positive commandment: on the ninth you shall not fast, but I will consider it for you as if you also fasted on the ninth, and "you shall afflict" will be fulfilled for both the ninth and the tenth, meaning: that for me it is counted as fasting on both the ninth and the tenth. And the interpretation of the verse is as follows: "And you shall afflict your souls on the ninth of the month in the evening," meaning: prepare yourselves so that you can fast in the evening, from evening to evening, which means that you shall eat a lot on the ninth, and you will have the strength to fast on the tenth. And for me, it is considered as fasting for two days (see Rashi).

It is from the love of the Holy One, blessed be He, for Israel that He decreed upon them to fast, and He commanded them to eat and drink beforehand so that they would have strength to fast (Beit Yosef). And concerning the fast, it is like two days of fasting. As it is stated in the Mishnah at the beginning of the fourth chapter of Ta'anit, that the members of the Ma'amad would not fast on Sunday, so that they would not go from rest and delight to exertion and fasting. See there. Therefore, the fast that comes after delight is harder for a person. And since on the eve of Yom Kippur it is a commandment to eat, drink, and delight - consequently, the distress of the fast is greater. Therefore, it is as if they fasted on both the ninth and the tenth. However, the body's strength is greater to endure the fast when one has eaten beforehand, but the distress is greater due to the sudden reversal.

Therefore, it is a mitzvah to eat and drink on the eve of Yom Kippur, and to rejoice on it. And our hearts should be certain that Yom Kippur will be beneficial and a blessing for us, and that the Holy One, blessed be He, will forgive our sins and inscribe us for a good and blessed year. And we eat fish and meat as on a Yom Tov. And it appears that the mitzvah is only during the day of the eve of Yom Kippur, and not the night before, since the reason is to be strong for fasting on Yom Kippur – this applies only during the day, and not at night. And this is explicitly implied in Rashi on Ketubot (5a, in the commentary beginning with the word "Yidcheh," see there). And one should minimize their learning on the eve of Yom Kippur in order to eat and drink (Magen Avraham).

And know that in the Rambam, in all the laws of Yom Kippur, this law that anyone who eats and drinks on the ninth [of Tishrei] etc. is not found. And it seems that his reasoning is simple: Behold, in Yoma there, the Tannaim disagree on this verse. One Tanna derives from this the extension of Yom Kippur, and so it is stated there: "And you shall afflict" etc. "on the ninth of the month" – one might think he begins and afflicts himself on the ninth? The verse states: "in the evening." If "in the evening" – one might think from when it gets dark? The verse states: "on the ninth." How so? He begins and afflicts himself while it is still day; from here we learn to add from the profane to the sacred etc. And it asks: This Tanna who derives the extension from another verse, what does he do with this verse? And it answers: For anyone who eats and drinks on the ninth, it is as if he fasted etc. And the Rambam in the first chapter of the laws of Yom Kippur, law six, wrote, and this is his language: And one needs to add from the profane to the sacred etc., as it is said: "And you shall afflict your souls on the ninth day of the month in the evening," meaning: begin to fast and afflict from the evening of the ninth, which is adjacent to it etc. Until here is his language. And since he derives this verse for the extension, consequently he does not have the derivation that anyone who eats and drinks etc., and therefore he omitted it.

But if so, why did the Rambam mention this in Hilchot Nedarim, Chapter 3, Halacha 9? This is his wording: "One who vows to fast on Sunday or Monday, etc., and it happens to be a holiday or the eve of Yom Kippur – he must fast, etc. If it falls on Chanukah or Purim – his vow is deferred, etc., since their prohibition is rabbinic – they require reinforcement." This is his wording, and it clearly implies that fasting on the eve of Yom Kippur is forbidden by Torah law, like on a holiday, and does not require reinforcement. This is also the stance taken by his commentators. (And the Kesef Mishneh is puzzled, stating that it is a complete derivation, and in his opinion, it is merely a rabbinic support. But the Lechem Mishneh wrote that it is a complete derivation, and this is also implied by the discussions in Rosh Hashanah 9a and Yoma there. This is also implied by the Maggid Mishneh in Hilchot Shvitat Asor there, see there.)

And I am very perplexed by this. For if you were to think that the Rambam believes it is forbidden by Torah law to fast on the eve of Yom Kippur, or even by rabbinic decree, and that one is obligated to eat and drink on it – how could he not mention it in its place in the laws of Yom Kippur, and instead rely on mentioning it incidentally in the laws of vows, and conversely, that one must fast? 

Therefore, it seems to me clearly, as I have written, that the Rambam dismissed this from the law, for the reasons I have stated. And what he wrote in the laws of vows that one must fast – the reason is not like on a festival, because it is a Torah obligation or something akin to a Torah obligation. It does not need strengthening, but on the contrary, because there is no commandment at all to eat, neither from the Torah nor from the Rabbis. Therefore, the vow automatically applies. 

And the reason he needed to mention this at all – is because the custom of the world is to increase in meals on the eve of Yom Kippur. As explained in the Midrash, in the story of that tailor who spent a lot of money for a fish on the eve of Yom Kippur, and it is brought in the Tur. And at the end of the fifth chapter of Chullin (83a), we also find that in the Galilee they increased in meals on the eve of Yom Kippur. And to avoid the mistake that there is at least a rabbinic commandment in this, and that the vow does not apply as on Chanukah and Purim – it teaches us that there is no complete rabbinic commandment, and the vow applies. And the Rambam is not alone in this, because I also did not find this law, that it is a commandment to eat on the eve of Yom Kippur, in the Rif and the SeMaG. And their reason is also because they brought that verse for the purpose of addition, see there.

However, the Rosh, the Tur, and the Shulchan Aruch ruled according to Chiya, that it is a mitzvah to eat on the eve of Yom Kippur. It is possible that they believe this is of Torah origin, and for the additional requirement they derive it from another verse, "selfsame," "selfsame," as they said there in Yoma. Or they hold like Rabbi Akiva in Rosh Hashanah (9a), who derives it from the Sabbatical year, see there. Or it is possible to say that they believe the main verse is for the addition, and Chiya's statement is merely an allusion (as the Kesef Mishneh wrote in Nedarim there). And from the end of the fifth chapter of Chullin, there is evidence for the Rif, Rambam, and Smag, who says there that in the Galilee they would increase meals on the eve of Yom Kippur. This implies that in other places they did not hold it to be a mitzvah. However, Tosafot wrote there that in every place they would increase meals, but they would eat poultry, see there. And similarly in Ketubot (5a), it implies that in every place they would increase the meal on the eve of Yom Kippur, as is our custom.

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote that it is forbidden to fast on this day, even a fast for a troubling dream (Ta'anit Chalom). If one vowed to fast on this day, see Siman 568. Thus far are his words. One should not be surprised and ask: Could it be more stringent than Shabbat and Yom Tov, upon which one may fast a fast for a troubling dream? For on the eve of Yom Kippur, there is a different reason: since eating on this day is considered as if one fasted, it is as if he fasted on both the ninth and tenth [of Tishrei], as we have written. Therefore, it is indeed fitting to fast [for a troubling dream] (Taz, subsection 2; and this resolves the difficulty posed by the Magen Avraham, subsection 1). Nevertheless, until the concluding meal, if he wishes, he can fast and then eat the meal of the eve of Yom Kippur. For there is no specific measure for the mitzvah of eating (Magen Avraham there), and it will also improve the dream.

If one vowed not to eat meat except on Shabbat and Yom Tov, he is permitted to eat on the eve of Yom Kippur, as it is considered a Yom Tov in common parlance. However, this applies only during the day and not at night, as there is no mitzvah at night, as I have written. There is an opinion that those who refrain from eating meat except on days when Tachanun is not recited may also eat meat at night (as cited in the name of the Shlah). And even though Tachanun is recited in the afternoon prayer preceding it, nevertheless, it is certain that this night is considered at least like days when Tachanun is not recited.

And we do not fall on our faces on the eve of Yom Kippur. Also, we do not say "Lamenatzeach Ya'ancha" and "Mizmor LeTodah," because the thanksgiving offering was not offered on the eve of Yom Kippur, as there is not enough time to consume it. Additionally, we do not say many Selichot before dawn. In some places, the custom is to increase the recitation of Selichot. However, our custom is not to do so; rather, we begin with "Lecha Hashem HaTzedakah" up to "Shomea Tefilah," and afterward, we say two Selichot, the poem "Yeratze Tzom Amecha," etc., "Shema Kolenu," and the confession once up to "HaRachaman VeHaselichot" and no more. Everything follows the custom. Regarding the recitation of "Avinu Malkeinu," there are differing opinions. Our custom is not to say it unless Yom Kippur falls on Shabbat, in which case we do not say "Avinu Malkeinu," and then we say it on the eve of Yom Kippur at Shacharit but not at Mincha, just like on the eve of Shabbat.

The custom of kaparot, where they are accustomed to slaughter a rooster for every male and a hen for every female – several great authorities were not pleased with this. The Ramban and the Rashba, of blessed memory, nullified this custom because of superstitious practices and the ways of the Amorites, as written in the Responsa of the Rashba (section 395, and see Beit Yosef). Therefore, our master the Beit Yosef wrote that this custom should be stopped.

However, several great authorities upheld the custom, and it is also found in the responsa of the Geonim. Additionally, Rashi in Shabbat (81b) cites the responsa of the Geonim, where they would perform kaparot with seeds, and on the eve of Rosh Hashanah, they would circle them around the head and say: "This is my exchange." See there. However, the Tur mentions that they would perform it with chickens and rams, and on the eve of Yom Kippur.

The words of our master, the Rema, are as follows: "There are some of the Geonim who wrote about this custom, and many of the later authorities also wrote about it, and it is practiced in all these countries. One should not change it, for it is an ancient custom. And they are accustomed to take a male rooster for a male, and for a female, they take a hen. And for a pregnant woman, they take two roosters, perhaps she will give birth to a male. And they choose white roosters, as it is said: 'Though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow.' And they are accustomed to give the kaparot to the poor, or to redeem them with money given to the poor. There are places where they are accustomed to go to the graves and to increase in charity, and all this is a good custom. It is proper to slaughter the kaparot immediately after it has been swung over the head and hands were laid on it like a sacrifice, and they throw the intestines on the roofs or in the courtyard, where the birds can take them from there." Until here are his words.

And in what matters did the great authorities question? It is in the embellishment after white ones, as this is similar to the ways of the Amorites, who would seek out a white rooster, as it is mentioned in the chapter "Before Their Festivals" (14a). Therefore, one should not seek out a white one, but if it happens to come into his possession, he may keep it (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 3, and Beit Yosef). Also, he should not take turtledoves and young pigeons that are suitable for sacrifice, so that it should not appear as a sacrifice (ibid). Furthermore, what he wrote about laying hands on it – one should not do this, as it appears like laying hands on sacrifices. And even though roosters are not suitable for sacrifice – nevertheless, it is no less than the meat for Passover, which is forbidden, so how can we do this from the outset? Therefore, one should not do this (Taz, subparagraph 3). The reason for throwing the intestines to the birds is to have mercy on the creatures, and also so that Heaven will have mercy on us. And it is written that it is good to slaughter during the watch of the night, which is a time of mercy, and they should say: "This is my exchange, this is my substitute, this is my atonement" – the initials of which are the word "חת"ך" (chet-tet-kaf), referring to "He who cuts life for every living being". The idea is that if death were decreed, Heaven forbid – this shall be my substitute. (And in my opinion, it would be more appropriate to say "this is under me", and not the term "substitute", as both remain in their sanctity, see Temurah 26b, and analyze and you will find it easy.)

All this pertains to the essence of the matter. But due to our many sins, we see a deterioration in the practice of slaughtering because of the multitude of atonements, the haste, and the pressure. The slaughterers do not pay proper attention due to fatigue and the burden, and many improperly slaughtered animals (treifot) come from their hands. Also, it is impossible to inspect the knife properly. Moreover, the hands of the slaughterer become heavy. And now, in our times, it is a mitzvah and an obligation to reduce them and not to enter the holy day with concerns about slaughtering. In previous generations, they also tried to abolish this practice, but they were not successful, as the masses are attached to it as if it were a mitzvah like the etrog, and even more so. At the very least, efforts should be made to begin the slaughtering a few days in advance and to avoid the early hours of the morning when the slaughterer's hands are heavy.

It has already been explained in Siman 572 that Yom Kippur atones only for sins between a person and God, but not for sins between a person and his fellow. If it is a matter of money, there is no atonement until he pays his fellow and asks him for forgiveness for causing him distress. If someone has stolen from the public and does not know from whom he has stolen, for example, if he sold with an inaccurate measure or with merchandise that is not his, and similar cases, he should spend it for the needs of the public. If it is not a matter of money, but he offended his fellow’s honor, cursing or insulting him and the like, he is not forgiven until he asks him for forgiveness and appeases him. He should specify the sin he committed against him. However, if his fellow would be embarrassed by this, he should not specify it, but just ask him to forgive him in general.

In truth, one is also warned about this throughout the entire year, and should not postpone it to a later time, for who knows what the day will bring? However, on the eve of Yom Kippur, it is an obligation to do so. And the one who forgives should not be cruel and refrain from forgiving immediately, as we find with our forefather Abraham, who immediately forgave Abimelech and prayed for him. And we, his descendants, should uphold his good traits. However, if one intends for the good of the person seeking forgiveness, by not forgiving him, it is permissible, as we find such an incident at the end of Yoma. But in truth, this is not common. Likewise, if someone has spread a bad name about him, he does not need to forgive, because many people know about the bad name that was spread, but do not know about the forgiveness. Nevertheless, it is a trait of piety to forgive even in this case. And if the one who insulted does everything possible, and publicly declares that the bad name he spread is false, and seeks forgiveness, it seems to me that according to the law he is required to forgive, for "your friend has a friend," and everyone will come to know that it was false (and in Yoma it is not exactly as mentioned here, see there).

And if he is not appeased the first time, he should go to him a second and third time, each time with a different type of appeasement. He should bring along friends who will request on his behalf that he forgive him. Each time, he should take with him three people. If even on the third time he does not forgive him, he is no longer obligated, for he has done what he could. However, if it is his teacher, he is obligated to go to him many times until he forgives him, even if he is not his primary teacher but merely heard words of Torah from him (Magen Avraham, section 3). He may also go many times to others if he wishes, as long as it does not bring disgrace to the Torah, which means if the one asking is not a Torah scholar. But if he is a Torah scholar, he should not go more than three times.

If the one who sinned against him has died, if it pertains to financial matters – he must pay his heirs; and if it pertains to verbal matters – he brings ten people, stands them by his grave, removes his shoes, and says: "I have sinned against the Lord, God of Israel, and against this person." The reason he needs ten people is because the Divine Presence rests wherever ten are gathered, and out of respect for the Divine Presence, the deceased surely forgives him. Even though actions cannot be performed after death – for "today is for doing them," and not tomorrow – nonetheless, when he is forgiven, he is forgiven, and he is no longer punished. However, in financial matters, this does not help, because why should he forgive him? After all, he can pay. And if he has nothing to pay – then he is automatically not guilty. If the journey is longer than three parasangs – he can send a messenger in his place (Magen Avraham, subsection 7). If he insulted him after death – he does not need to go to his grave, but should seek forgiveness in the place where he shamed him (ibid.), and it suffices to do so before three people. If he insulted someone and also shamed his ancestors – he also needs to seek forgiveness. It is customary on the eve of Yom Kippur for many people to ask each other for forgiveness, even if they have not insulted each other at all, but perhaps have offended each other's honor (this is the intention of the Rema in subsection 2). There is an ancient decree and curse not to spread slander about the dead. That is to say, even though it is stated in Berakhot (19a) that whoever speaks ill of the dead is like speaking ill of a stone, whether because they do not know or because they do not care, except in the case of a student of the sages, because the Holy One, blessed be He, demands retribution for his insult, see there – nonetheless, they decreed thus.

It is stated in Pirkei DeRabbi Eliezer (Chapter 46) that Samael, who always accuses Israel, advocates for them on Yom Kippur and says to the Holy One, blessed be He: "Master of the Universe! You have one nation that is like the ministering angels. Just as angels are barefoot, so are they. Just as angels do not have joints and stand constantly, so do the Israelites (in their prayers and confessions). Just as angels are clean, so are they. Just as angels have peace among them, so do they." And the Holy One, blessed be He, hears his testimony and atones for them, see there. From this, all of Israel have the custom to seek forgiveness so there will be peace, and they immerse in the mikvah to be clean. The Rosh at the end of Yoma (Chapter 8, Siman 24) brought in the name of Rav Saadia Gaon that one must recite a blessing on this immersion. The Rosh rejected this, and the custom is not to recite a blessing. The reason of the Gaon seems to be because it is written "before Hashem you shall be purified," and the mikvah purifies the impure, and therefore, this is also included in "you shall be purified."

The custom is to receive thirty-nine lashes with a calfskin strap. One can immerse in a mikvah and receive lashes whenever he wishes. However, since it is customary to confess during the Mincha prayer, it is good to receive the lashes and immerse before Mincha, so that the confession will be in a state of purity and after atonement. He only needs to immerse once due to a seminal emission; however, the custom is to immerse three times. If there is no mikvah or the weather is cold, he should have nine kavs of water poured over his body, which is fifteen quarts. No more than three vessels should be used, and he should start pouring the second vessel before the first one finishes, and the third before the second finishes, or all at once.

If someone has a relative who passed away between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, they are permitted to bathe and immerse in a mikvah on the eve of Yom Kippur, because Yom Kippur cancels the decree of the seven days of mourning (shiva). Although the custom is not to bathe during the thirty days of mourning, on the eve of Yom Kippur it is permitted, even two or three hours before nightfall. Other mourning practices are observed on the eve of Yom Kippur as they would be on any other day that is not a festival, except that it is a mitzvah to eat and drink on this day. One should rise from mourning as they would on any Friday or the eve of a festival (see Magen Avraham, subsection 10). We have already explained in Siman 88 that immersion for ritual impurity (keri) is effective even in drawn water, if it is in the ground and not in a vessel, and this also applies to immersion on the eve of Yom Kippur.

It has already been explained in Siman 606 that repentance requires confession, and that confession is a positive commandment from the Torah, as it is written: "They shall confess their sin" (Numbers 5:7). The primary mitzvah of confession is on Yom Kippur. During the time of the Temple, the High Priest would confess on behalf of all Israel over the scapegoat, as it is written: "He shall confess over it all the iniquities of the children of Israel" (Leviticus 16:21). Therefore, everyone is obligated to confess on Yom Kippur, in every prayer. And even though the main obligation is on Yom Kippur, the Sages said at the end of Yoma that one should confess at Mincha on the eve of Yom Kippur, before eating and drinking the seudah hamafseket (pre-fast meal). The reason: lest something untoward happen to him during the meal, causing his mind to become confused due to drunkenness, and he will be unable to confess afterward. And the Rambam in the second chapter of Hilchot Teshuvah explains: lest he choke during the meal.

Thus, we learned in a Baraita there: The Rabbis taught: The mitzvah of confession is on the eve of Yom Kippur at twilight. However, the Sages said: One should confess before eating, etc. And even if one confessed earlier, etc., one confesses again after eating and drinking, lest a sin occurred during the meal. And even though one confessed in the evening, one confesses again in the morning, etc., during Mussaf, etc., during Mincha, etc., during Ne’ilah. See there. According to many commentators, the statement that the mitzvah of confession is at twilight and that one confesses after eating refers to the evening service. But Ramban explained that this refers to a separate confession before twilight, before the evening service, so that one enters Yom Kippur at the beginning of the day having already confessed. Based on this, many pious individuals, when coming to the synagogue and the time is close to sunset, confess.

Where does one recite the confession (vidui)? An individual recites it after the prayer, before taking three steps back. The prayer leader (shaliach tzibbur) recites it within the prayer service before "Forgive us our transgressions." It appears to me that the individual should say "May the words of my mouth be acceptable" after the blessing of peace, then say the confession, and after the confession say "My God, guard my tongue from evil," etc., and "May the words of my mouth be acceptable," etc. Since the prayer has concluded, it is necessary to say "May the words of my mouth be acceptable," as this is also considered part of the prayer. After the confession, it is obvious that one must say "May the words of my mouth be acceptable" so that their confession will be accepted.

In the afternoon service of the Eve of Yom Kippur, the prayer leader does not repeat the confession but prays the Amidah as on the other days of the year, since this confession is only due to a general concern, as I have written. I do not understand the words of Rabbeinu the Beit Yosef in paragraph 5, where he writes: "In the afternoon prayer of the Eve of Yom Kippur, he does not conclude with the confession that follows it." Until here are his words. It is surprising: what conclusion is there in the prayer of an individual after the confession? He recites it after the prayer! From the Levush, it seems that its intention is not specifically about the Eve of Yom Kippur, but also about Yom Kippur itself (as the GR"A also wrote). This does not settle well with me. It appears to me that the explanation is: on Yom Kippur itself, there is no need for a conclusion after the confession, as "King who pardons and forgives," etc., has already been said. But on the Eve of Yom Kippur, when the weekday prayer is recited, one might think that a conclusion is needed. Therefore, we are informed that it is not required. We do not fall on our faces in the afternoon service, nor do we say "Avinu Malkeinu."

(It seems to me that the Beit Yosef's intention is because according to Rashi of blessed memory, one can conclude with the confession of Yom Kippur, as the Tur wrote, see there. Therefore, we are informed that in the afternoon prayer of the Eve of Yom Kippur, even according to Rashi, one should not conclude.)

The essence of confession is when one says "I have sinned." One must confess while standing and with a bowed head. According to the law, one does not need to specify their sins, and it is sufficient to say "I have sinned, I have transgressed, I have rebelled."
