Nevertheless, it is preferable to initially specify the sin, saying quietly "I did such and such," which causes one to feel more ashamed before the Holy One, blessed be He, and to repent from the depths of their heart. However, it is forbidden to specify sins out loud in public, as it is stated (Psalms 32:1), "Happy is he whose transgression is forgiven, whose sin is covered," as I wrote in section 563. This applies to a sin that is not publicly known. But a sin that is publicly known may be confessed even out loud, though it is not obligatory to do so. One may specify it quietly. The recitation of "Al Chet" (the confession prayer) in alphabetical order is not considered specifying one's sins, since it is a uniform text for all, similar to the prayer text, and it is permissible to recite it out loud.

The order of the confession in "Al Cheit" (for the sins) is: burnt offering, sin offering, variable offering, definite guilt offering, and suspensive guilt offering, as they are arranged in the portion of Vayikra. Following that: the punishment of lashes (makkat mardut), the punishment of forty lashes (actually thirty-nine, missing one). Then: death by divine intervention, and then: excision and childlessness, and then: the four types of death penalties by the court. For one must first request atonement for the lighter sins and then for the graver ones, as I have written in Siman 592.

He uses the term "atonement" for sins, "forgiveness" for iniquities, and "pardon" for transgressions. For a sin is lighter than an iniquity, as a sin is committed inadvertently, while an iniquity is committed intentionally. And an iniquity is lighter than a transgression, as a transgression is rebellious. "Atonement" is the greatest of all, as it is written: "And he shall atone for the sin of the soul" (Leviticus 4:35), which is a cleansing and washing away, like "gold-plated," and therefore it is called "Yom Kippur" (Day of Atonement), and thus it pertains to sins. "Forgiveness" is greater than "pardon." The term "forgiveness" is not found in the Bible, nor do we know its root, except in the language of the Mishnah, where it pertains to monetary claims, where one forgives and does not demand, and it pertains to iniquities. "Pardon" is the least of all, as it only implies forgiving but not entirely absolving, and therefore it pertains to rebellious acts. However, in the Torah, we find "pardon" used for iniquities: "Pardon the iniquity of this people" (Numbers 14:19). And in the Bible, we find "atonement" used for iniquities: "And He, being merciful, atoned for iniquity" (Psalms 78:38), "By this, the iniquity of Jacob shall be atoned for" (Isaiah 27:9). And in the Torah, we find "pardon" alongside "atonement": "And the priest shall atone for him... and it shall be forgiven him" (Leviticus 4:26). However, the version we have written is so, as testified about Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) who said so (Magen Avraham end of small section 3 in the name of Shelah; and in Magen Avraham there is a printing error, see there). And it also seems from the wording of "El Melech" that we say "abundant forgiveness for sins, and pardon for transgressions" – hence "pardon" is for "transgressions," and "abundant forgiveness" is like atonement. And it also seems from the wording of "and for all" in "Al Chet": "forgive us, pardon us, atone for us," as he first requests the lighter matter, etc. However, we find in the prayer "pardon" for "sin" and "forgiveness" for "transgression": "Forgive us, our Father, for we have sinned; pardon us, our King, for we have rebelled."

In the Jerusalem Talmud at the end of Yoma, it says: How does one confess? Rabbi Berechiah etc.: "I have sinned… May it be Your will to atone for all my transgressions, and pardon my iniquities, and forgive all my sins," see there. It is exactly the opposite: "atonement" for transgressions, "pardon" for iniquities, and "forgiveness" for sins. In my humble opinion, it seems that the term "atonement" does not apply to prayer at all. It is only used in the context of the altar, where the sacrifice atones, or the essence of the day atones, such as Yom Kippur. But in prayer, only the term "forgiveness" is applicable. Therefore, Moses our teacher, when dealing with the spies, requested using the term "forgiveness": "Please forgive the iniquity of this people." And the Holy One, blessed be He, responded: "I have forgiven according to your word." For us, according to the language of the Mishnah, the term "pardon" is also added. Therefore, in prayer, we say "Forgive us, our Father… pardon us, our King." Only in the penitential prayers and liturgical poems do they also use the term "atonement" for prayer. We find the term "atonement" in the Torah regarding the heifer whose neck is broken, which is also like a sacrifice. And the term "atonement" found in the Prophets, such as "By this shall Jacob's iniquity be atoned" – is not a prayer. Similarly, in Psalms: "He will atone for iniquity." But in prayer, only "forgiveness" and "pardon" are appropriate. And there is no strictness in how one says it, since we find all these terms – it indicates that there is no strictness in the language (so it appears in my humble opinion).

One must confess while standing and with a bow, similar to [the bowing in] "Modim." One should not lean on the wall. Even during the confessions recited with the prayer leader, one must stand. During all the piyyutim (liturgical poems), one may sit. However, when the prayer leader reaches "But we have sinned," one must stand (Talmud, end of Yoma). The custom is to strike the chest, indicating: "You have caused me [to sin] through thoughts of sin." Some strike the chest. The main part of the confession is "But we have sinned." Some say "But we have sinned," and some say "But we and our ancestors have sinned." Similarly, we find that David said: "We have sinned with our ancestors" (Psalms 106:6); and Daniel said: "Because of our sins and the sins of our ancestors, Jerusalem and Your people have become a disgrace" (Daniel 9:16). One should not speak during the confession (Magen Avraham). Sins confessed on the previous Yom Kippur, if one did not repeat them, one may still confess them again. On the contrary, this is praiseworthy, as it is written: "My sin is always before me" (Psalms 51:5). This applies when specifying each sin, but regarding the formula of "Al Chet" (For the sin), this does not apply at all, since it is a uniform formula for everyone, and it does not differentiate between sins committed and those not committed in different years.

The custom is to receive forty lashes after the Mincha prayer, so that one takes it to heart to repent from the sins he has committed. And earlier in the previous section, paragraph 6, we explained that it is better to receive the lashes before Mincha; see there. It is customary for the person receiving the lashes to confess during the lashes, and the one administering the lashes says "And He, the Merciful One, will forgive iniquity" three times, which consists of thirty-nine words corresponding to the thirty-nine lashes. The lashes are administered with any kind of strap, as it is only a remembrance of the lashes. He should take a calf’s strap, in the manner of "The ox knows its owner... Israel does not know." The person receiving the lashes should be inclined, neither standing nor sitting, with his face to the north and his back to the south. And know that Yom Kippur does not atone except for those who believe in its atonement and repent. But for the one who scorns it and thinks in his heart "What benefit is Yom Kippur to me?" and even if he believes but does not repent – it does not atone for him.

Maimonides wrote at the end of the first chapter that one must add from the mundane to the holy at its entrance and at its exit, as it is said: "And you shall afflict your souls on the ninth day of the month at evening," meaning: begin fasting and afflicting oneself from the evening of the ninth which is adjacent to it. And similarly, at its exit, one should delay in one's affliction a bit from the night of the eleventh which is adjacent to the tenth, as it is said (there): "From evening to evening you shall keep your Sabbath." Until here are his words. Meaning: "until evening" and including it. And it is impossible to say the entire evening, for it says "from evening to evening" – thus only from one time to the same time. Rather, the explanation is: from the evening and a little before, as is evident from "on the ninth," as I have written, and "until evening" and a little after.

It appears clearly from the words of the Rambam that there is an addition only regarding affliction, but not concerning labor. Just as on Shabbat and Yom Tov, according to the Rambam, there is no addition, since he did not mention this anywhere, so too on Yom Kippur in matters equivalent to Shabbat and Yom Tov, namely labor. Only in terms of affliction, which is unique to Yom Kippur, there is an addition of affliction; and so wrote the Maggid Mishneh. And even though in that Baraita that expounds on the addition of affliction, it also expounds on the addition of labor for Shabbat and Yom Tov, according to the Rambam, the law is not like this, because in the first chapter of Rosh Hashanah (9a) it is proven that this exposition is according to Rabbi Yishmael and not Rabbi Akiva, and the halacha follows Rabbi Akiva against Rabbi Yishmael as is known. Indeed, the addition of affliction is explained in Beitzah (30a) to be of Torah origin. And regarding Shabbat and Yom Tov, it is clarified at the beginning of Moed Katan (4a) that there is no addition; and so it is explained in the Jerusalem Talmud at the beginning of Tractate Shevi'it (brought by Tosafot in Rosh Hashanah there). And although Rabbi Akiva says there that there is an addition in the Sabbatical year, it is stated at the beginning of Moed Katan and in the Jerusalem Talmud there that the halacha is not like this, see there. (And it turns out that the main reason of the Rambam is because in Beitzah there it is proven that there is an addition in affliction, and in Moed Katan there it is proven that there is no addition in labor. And it is also clearly implied in Pesachim 54b that there is no addition in labor, see there. And know that even though there is an addition in affliction, nevertheless it does not involve karet or a prohibition, but only a positive commandment, as is proven in Yoma there. Refer to Maggid Mishneh and Lechem Mishneh who have delved into the words of the Rambam, and analyze and you will find it easy.)

However, the Rif and the Rosh ruled that there is an addition even with regard to labor, and similarly on Shabbat and Yom Tov there is an addition. This is also the opinion of the Tur, who wrote that one must cease eating before twilight, as it is derived from Scripture that one must add from the mundane to the holy, both in terms of refraining from eating and in terms of performing labor. This addition has no fixed measure, but it is before twilight, which is the duration of walking fifteen hundred cubits before nightfall – one must add a bit from the mundane to the holy. (See Taz, who explains that the Tur derives the addition from the Baraita of "Atzem" "Atzem," and therefore did not write about the addition on Shabbat and Yom Tov. This is the main point, as it is impossible to say that the Tur derives from the Baraita of "On the ninth day of the month" like the Rif, because the Tur requires eating on the eve of Yom Kippur. Moreover, it is clear there that it also applies to Shabbat and Yom Tov. And indeed, the Rif holds there is an addition on Shabbat and Yom Tov, and many of the Rishonim agree with this. Analyze and you will find it easy.)

The Rosh at the end of Yoma and the Ran at the beginning of the fourth chapter of Beitzah wrote that this additional time (Tosefet) must necessarily have a certain measure, and not just an undefined moment. For if this were not the case, one would anyway need to separate oneself a little earlier, because it is impossible to be precise, and a doubt concerning a Torah prohibition is treated stringently. Rather, it is certain that this additional time has a measure, only we do not know its exact measure. Therefore, all of Israel is careful to cease their eating and drinking while the sun is clearly visible on the earth, and not right before sunset. Regarding this measure, it is stated in Beitzah (30a): "These women who eat and drink until it becomes dark, and we do not protest against them, for it is better that they be unwitting sinners rather than intentional sinners." The intention is not literally "until it becomes dark," Heaven forbid to say such a thing, for even during twilight one must protest against them. Rather, the intention is concerning the additional time, which is while the sun is still shining, and they will not listen to us. It is explained there that this concerns the additional time, because in their light-minded thinking, it is impossible that it would be forbidden to eat while the sun is still shining, and they will not accept from us if we tell them that the additional time of Yom Kippur is from the Torah.

And this is when he knows for certain that they will not accept [the rebuke] from him (Magen Avraham). But if there is a doubt whether they will accept it – he must protest. And when he sees that they will not obey – he should no longer protest. And our teacher the Rema wrote that the same law applies to any matter of prohibition; we say: it is better that they should be inadvertent sinners and not intentional sinners. And specifically when it is not explicitly stated in the Torah, even though it is a Torah prohibition. But if it is explicitly stated in the Torah – one protests against them. And if he knows that his words will not be heeded – he should not say it publicly to rebuke them more than once, but should not increase the rebukes, since he knows they will not listen to him. But with an individual – he is obligated to rebuke him until he strikes or curses him. So far his words. And his words require explanation: for the beginning of his words are about inadvertent sinners, and the end of his words are about intentional sinners (since this is from the Nimukei Yosef at the end of the sixth chapter of Yevamot, and there it deals with intentional sinners regarding rebuke, see there).

And it appears to me that the explanation is as follows: When there are people who are mistaken in a law and think that something is permitted, if it is certain that they will not accept [the correction] from him—he should remain silent, and it is better that they be unintentional sinners rather than intentional sinners. However, if there is a doubt that perhaps they will listen—he is obligated to inform them that this matter is prohibited and to protest against them. The righteous were also punished at the time of the destruction for not protesting. And the attribute of judgment said before the Holy One, blessed be He: "If before You it is revealed that they will not listen to them, is it revealed before them?" (Shabbat 55a; see Taz, subsection 2).

There is no distinction in this matter between a Torah prohibition and a Rabbinic prohibition. Even with a Rabbinic prohibition, if there is a doubt that perhaps they will listen—he is obligated to inform them and protest against them. And if he informs them and protests, and they do not listen—he should remain silent, and it is better that they be unintentional sinners. This applies to a matter that is not explicitly stated in the Torah. But in a matter that is explicitly stated in the Torah, even if he knows for certain that they will not listen—or if he protested once and they did not listen, since they are unintentional sinners, as they do not intend to transgress intentionally but are mistaken in thinking that this matter is permitted, and this matter is explicitly stated in the Torah—he is obligated to speak and rebuke them multiple times and show them that this is explicitly prohibited in the Torah. And it is likely that they will heed him, since they are unintentional sinners. However, after he has protested several times and achieved nothing—he should remain silent.

And all this applies to those who sin unintentionally. But if they transgress intentionally – and in this case, it is not relevant to inform them that it is forbidden, since they already know and are willfully transgressing – it is stated in the Gemara at the end of the sixth chapter of Yevamot (65b): Just as it is a mitzvah to say something that will be heeded, so it is a mitzvah not to say something that will not be heeded. And one said that it is an obligation not to say it, as it is written: "Do not rebuke a scoffer, lest he hate you." The Nimukei Yosef raised an objection: Isn’t there a mitzvah of "You shall surely rebuke," whose primary application is for intentional transgressions? And he answered that certainly one is obligated to rebuke them once, and perhaps they will listen. And even if it is clear to him that they will not listen, nevertheless, to prevent them from having an excuse, one is obligated to rebuke them publicly once, but no more. Accordingly, what is stated there that it is a "mitzvah" not to say, or "obligation" – this applies to more than once, and this is in public. But to an individual, it is written "You shall surely rebuke" even a hundred times, as I wrote above in Siman 156: until he strikes or curses him, according to the opinions we explained there. And for a private transgression, he should rebuke him privately, and for a public transgression, he should rebuke him immediately, so that the Name of Heaven is not desecrated (Magen Avraham, subsection 3). And know that all this applies to a believing Jew, but whose inclination has overpowered him to sin, and in this case, rebuke is relevant. But those who deny the words of our Sages of blessed memory – in these cases, rebuke is not applicable, for they are heretics and apostates, and one should not argue with them. (And if not for the words of the Nimukei Yosef and the Rema, I would have said that the passage in Yevamot refers to these individuals.)

If he interrupted his meal while it was still daylight, he can resume eating as long as he has not yet accepted the fast upon himself. Even if he accepted the fast before "plag hamincha" (an hour and a quarter before sunset), it is of no consequence. This is specifically when he accepted it as a fast for Yom Kippur. However, if he accepted upon himself not to eat anymore, it is no different than the rest of the year, and he must uphold his vow, as I have written in Siman 562 (and this is the intent of Magen Avraham in Subsection 4). An acceptance in the heart is not considered an acceptance. Some are concerned that it is considered an acceptance, which is an extra stringency. Nevertheless, there are those who practice this way (see Magen Avraham there). It is good to practice that before sunset, everyone should say: "I hereby accept upon myself the positive commandment of the fast of Yom Kippur, as You have commanded us in Your holy Torah, through Moses Your servant. And I hereby accept upon myself the five afflictions, as Your holy ones have instructed us." Consequently, if one practices this way, his previous intention is of no consequence.

On the eve of Yom Kippur, one should only eat foods that are easy to digest. Therefore, one eats poultry at the pre-fast meal, so that one will not be overly full and haughty when praying. Similarly, one should not eat foods that warm the body, to avoid seminal emissions. One should also avoid dairy products that increase seed. Some have the custom to eat them in the morning, but among us, this is not the practice. The caution regarding light foods applies only to the pre-fast meal, not to the morning meal, as the fullness will dissipate by night. One should also avoid foods that increase phlegm and saliva, such as sesame seeds and similar items; they are also regurgitated and are not suitable for eating on the eve of this holy day.

The Tur brings the words of the Geonim, who prohibited insulating hot food on the eve of Yom Kippur for the end of Yom Kippur. The Tur was astonished by them. Similarly, our teacher the Beit Yosef in his great book: What prohibition is there in preparing from weekday to weekday? And if it is because it stands on the stove on Yom Kippur – what of it? After all, it also stands on the stove on Shabbat. Therefore, our teacher the Beit Yosef wrote: It is permissible to insulate hot food on the eve of Yom Kippur for the end of Yom Kippur; thus far his words. That is to say: there is no reason for the prohibition.

Nevertheless, since the matter was decreed by the Geonim, they refrained from doing so. And this is what our master, the Rema, wrote: "And some say that one should not insulate on Yom Kippur, and this is the custom in these regions." Thus far his words. And some say the reason is because on every Friday, it is not proper to do work after midday except for the honor of Shabbat, and so it is on the eve of Yom Kippur. And since this is for a weekday, it is not appropriate (Bach). And some say it is so that one's soul will be distressed (see Taz). And there are those who wrote that since on Yom Kippur the dish heats up, this is considered preparation for a weekday (see Magen Avraham). And this reason holds no reason. And perhaps it is so that the household members will not smell the aroma of the dishes in the usual manner of insulation, and due to the desire for the aroma, they may come to experience a ravenous hunger.

It is stated in Shabbat (119a): What is the meaning of "and the Holy of the Lord…" (Isaiah 58:13)? This refers to Yom Kippur, which has neither eating nor drinking. The Torah said, "Honor it with clean garments." In other words, previously it is written, "And you shall call the Sabbath a delight, the Holy of the Lord honored," and if you think it refers only to the Sabbath, it should have said "the Holy of the Lord…" before the other things. Rather, it is certain that they are two separate matters. In other words, on the Sabbath, which you can delight in with eating and drinking, you shall call it "a delight." And "the Holy of the Lord…" refers to Yom Kippur, which has only the holiness of the Lord and not physical delight – you should honor it in other ways that you can. Therefore, you should honor it with clean garments. Thus, clean clothes are worn on Yom Kippur.

And this is what our teacher, the Rema, wrote in section 4: There are those who wrote that it is customary to wear clean white clothes on Yom Kippur, similar to the ministering angels. And so, it is customary to wear the kittel, which is white and clean. It is also a garment for the dead, and through this, a person’s heart is broken and humbled. Thus far his words. In other words, the main reason is because it is white and clean, and it is a garment of honor. Additionally, another reason: since it is customary to bury the dead in it, wearing it will remind one of the day of death, which will aid in repentance. (See Taz, section 3, who holds that these are two reasons, and in my humble opinion, it appears as I have written.) Therefore, a mourner should not wear a kittel, because one should not adorn oneself during the days of mourning. Women do not wear the kittel, but in any case, it is customary for them to wear white clothes. And know that even one who wears sackcloth as an act of repentance is forbidden to wear it on Yom Kippur (Magen Avraham, section 5). Our teacher, the Rema, also wrote that there are those who say that one should set the tables on Yom Kippur as on Shabbat; thus far his words. In other words: although there is no eating on Yom Kippur, nevertheless, this too is part of honoring the day. Therefore, one should also set the beds. And similarly, the house should be clean like on Shabbat and Yom Tov.

And since we have seen that the Torah is particular about honoring the holy day in whatever way we can, and it is written, "Honor the Lord with lights…" (Isaiah 24), and the Targum explains: "with lanterns," meaning with the lights of lanterns, and it is customary to honor the king with great lights — therefore, all of Israel has the custom to increase the number of candles in honor of this holy day, both in synagogues and in one's home in all rooms. And they light in synagogues and study halls, and in dark alleyways, and for the sick, so that there will be abundant and available light everywhere, even though there is not much movement in these places on Yom Kippur.

In a room where a man and his wife sleep, it is taught in Pesachim (53a): "In a place where they have the custom to light, they light; and in a place where they do not have the custom to light, they do not light." This means that there are places where the custom is not to light there, so that she should not be seen. For if she is seen, we are concerned about impropriety. And there are places where, to the contrary, for this reason they light, because it is forbidden to have marital relations in the light of a candle. Regarding this it is said: "And your people are all righteous" – whether they say to light or not to light, they have the same intention.

Some say that one should not recite a blessing over lighting a candle on Yom Kippur, as on Shabbat the primary reason for the blessing is due to the meal. Others say that one should recite a blessing, as the primary purpose of the candle is for peace in the home. Our custom is to bless "Who has sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us to light the candle of Yom Kippur." If Yom Kippur falls on Shabbat, it is obvious that one is obligated to light, and the blessing recited is "to light the candle of Shabbat and Yom Kippur." Women recite "Shehecheyanu" as they do on all festivals. Regarding the room where a man and his wife sleep, it depends on the custom. If there is a candle in the house, one must light in the room where they sleep, even in a place where the custom is not to light, because if he sees her by the candle in the house, there is a concern that it may lead to intimacy, as there is no distinction in his room. Therefore, at the very least, it is good to create a distinction. It appears to me that this is the case if he sees her in his room by the candle in the house.

It is customary that every person, whether great or small, has a candle made for them as a good sign. Nowadays, however, a candle is only made for a married man, and not for a woman. Additionally, a memorial candle ("Ner Neshama") is made for one's deceased father or mother, or for one of them who has passed away. This is proper, and some of the sages have written this. This is a rectification for the soul, as the soul is called a "candle" as it is written, "The candle of the Lord is the soul of man." Also, the deceased require atonement, as stated in the Sifrei. Know that some people, if their candle goes out on Yom Kippur, become distressed and consider it a bad omen. In truth, this is nothing. However, for those who are concerned about this – it is better to mix their candle among other candles so that they do not know which one is theirs. It is not fitting for the holy people to follow omens, rather, "You shall be wholehearted with the Lord, your God."

If these candles go out, it is forbidden to tell a non-Jew to relight them, for instructing a non-Jew is considered a rabbinic prohibition on Yom Kippur just as it is on Shabbat. Even to say "repeat" is forbidden, and it is better not to recite a liturgical poem than to instruct through a non-Jew. However, nowadays, due to the abundance of candles and to prevent any mishap, God forbid, a non-Jew is appointed before Yom Kippur and comes at any time to attend to the candles on his own initiative. It is forbidden to tell him to gather the wax. The custom is that if one's candle goes out on Yom Kippur, they should relight it after Yom Kippur and not extinguish it again, but let it burn completely. Also, one should resolve that on every subsequent Yom Kippur, neither he nor anyone else will extinguish his candle. This is found in customs and is considered a mystical matter. It appears that the strictness applies only to the candle made for the living. It is customary to make thick wicks for Yom Kippur candles to increase their light. Rabbi Yosef Karo wrote in section 3 that it is customary to spread fine clothes in the synagogue; see there. We are not familiar with this custom, except that a white curtain is hung for Yom Kippur.

It is well known that all prohibitions that are forbidden on Yom Kippur are forbidden both by day and by night. And what are the things that are forbidden on Yom Kippur? Five things: eating and drinking, washing, anointing, wearing leather shoes, and marital relations. And one is only liable for karet (spiritual excision) for eating and drinking. However, according to many poskim (halachic authorities), all of them are prohibited by Torah law.

And this is also the opinion of the Rambam in the first chapter, law 4, where he wrote: There is a positive commandment on Yom Kippur, and it is to abstain from eating and drinking, as it is stated, "You shall afflict your souls." From tradition, we learned what kind of affliction is for the soul: this is fasting. And anyone who fasts on it fulfills a positive commandment, and anyone who eats or drinks on it nullifies a positive commandment and transgresses a negative commandment, and is liable for karet, as it is stated, "For any soul that shall not be afflicted on that very day, shall be cut off from its people." And since the scripture imposes karet on one who does not afflict themselves, we learn that we are warned against eating and drinking on it. And anyone who eats or drinks on it unintentionally is liable to bring a fixed sin offering. Thus far his words. And this that he wrote, "and since it imposes karet, we learn that we are warned," is because it is a settled law that the scripture does not impose a punishment unless it has already issued a warning.

He further wrote: And so we learned from tradition that it is forbidden to bathe, anoint oneself, wear sandals, or engage in marital relations [on Yom Kippur]. It is a mitzvah to abstain from all these as one abstains from eating and drinking, as it says: "Shabbat Shabbaton" – "Shabbat" regarding eating, and "Shabbaton" regarding these matters. One is not liable for karet (excision) or a sin offering except for eating and drinking. But if one bathed, anointed, wore sandals, or engaged in marital relations – he is given lashes of rebellion. So far is his wording. Therefore, it is clear that he holds that all these afflictions are from the Torah. And so we learned in a Baraita (Yoma 77a): From where do we know that on Yom Kippur it is forbidden to bathe, wear sandals, and engage in marital relations? The Torah states: "Shabbaton" – a cessation. However, they do not incur a prohibition or karet, only a positive commandment, which is to abstain from these things.

However, the Rosh wrote that all of these are of rabbinic origin, and the verses cited are merely supportive references. And the proof: for indeed they were lenient in several matters, as will be explained. And if it were of Torah origin, how could they be lenient? But according to Maimonides, this is not a question, for there are several matters that the Torah entrusted to the sages, such as work on Chol HaMoed for those who hold it is of Torah origin, but the Torah entrusted it to the sages. There is a practical difference in the law between these two opinions: if some doubt arises, according to Maimonides, the doubt leads to stringency, and according to the Rosh, the doubt leads to leniency. And it seems to me that most opinions hold that it is of Torah origin, like Maimonides (see Ran, Maggid Mishneh, and Kesef Mishneh).

And it is a positive commandment to cease from work on Yom Kippur, as it is stated: "It shall be a Sabbath of complete rest for you." Anyone who performs work on this day nullifies a positive commandment and transgresses a negative commandment, as it is stated: "On the tenth of the seventh month... you shall do no work." What is the penalty for performing work on this day? If he does so intentionally and willfully, he is liable for karet (spiritual excision). If he does so unintentionally, he is liable to bring a fixed sin-offering.

Any labor for which one is liable to receive the death penalty by stoning for willful transgression on Shabbat incurs the penalty of karet (excision) on Yom Kippur. Any labor for which one is liable to bring a sin-offering for unwitting transgression on Shabbat incurs the same liability on Yom Kippur. Any rabbinically prohibited activity (shevut) that is forbidden on Shabbat is also forbidden on Yom Kippur. Any act that incurs lashes of rebellion (malkot mardut) on Shabbat incurs the same on Yom Kippur. Any item that is forbidden to carry (muktzeh) on Shabbat is also forbidden to carry on Yom Kippur. However, food and drink, even though they are not suitable for Yom Kippur, are not considered muktzeh since they are suitable for children. Similarly, all eating and drinking utensils are not muktzeh. Anything that is forbidden to do on Shabbat is forbidden to do on Yom Kippur. The general principle is that there is no difference between Shabbat and Yom Kippur regarding forbidden labor except that on Shabbat, willful transgression incurs stoning, whereas on Yom Kippur it incurs karet. Consequently, this also affects liability: the principle of "he is liable for the greater penalty" applies. On Shabbat, one is exempt from monetary compensation, whereas on Yom Kippur, one is liable, as the penalty of karet does not exempt one from making restitution, as I have written in Choshen Mishpat, sections 351 and 424. Although there is an opinion in the Gemara that there is no requirement for eruv and carrying on Yom Kippur, we do not rule this way. Therefore, on Yom Kippur, it is necessary to have an eruv for courtyards and shared alleyways, just as on Shabbat, as the Rif wrote in the first chapter of Beitzah.

And there is a question regarding the opinion that on Shabbat, "the prohibition of kindling is singled out as a prohibition": From where do we derive the prohibition of kindling on Yom Kippur from the verse "You shall not kindle"? However, this is not difficult, for it is also included in "You shall not do any work." But if so, Shabbat is more lenient than Yom Kippur, for on Shabbat it is a prohibition, and on Yom Kippur it is punishable by karet (excision). We must say that we derive it through a fortiori reasoning from Shabbat, where it is punishable by stoning and is only a prohibition – Yom Kippur, which is punishable by karet, is not all the more so? However, the halacha is that also on Shabbat, the kindling is singled out to divide (the prohibitions), and one is liable to stoning on Shabbat. Similarly, regarding the resting of a servant, the resting of an animal, and leading a burden – Yom Kippur is equal to Shabbat, for the Torah did not differentiate between them.

Except for one thing, the Sages said regarding something that is not a complete prohibition: they permitted it on Yom Kippur but not on Shabbat, as Maimonides wrote there. And this is his wording: "It is permitted to clean vegetables on Yom Kippur from Mincha time and onwards." And what is this cleaning? It is to remove the spoiled leaves, cut the remainder, and prepare it for eating. Similarly, it is permitted to crack walnuts and break pomegranates from Mincha time and onwards, because of mental anguish. But if Yom Kippur falls on Shabbat, it is forbidden to clean vegetables, crack walnuts, and break pomegranates all day. And the people in Shinar and the West have already practiced not doing any of these on the fast day, treating it like Shabbat in every respect. This is the end of his wording. 

The explanation of the matter: There is no labor involved here, only mere effort. On Shabbat, it is forbidden to exert oneself for weekday purposes, but on Yom Kippur, they permitted it because of mental anguish, meaning they would see and be distressed. This is not like selecting food from waste, as all of it is food. Nevertheless, the custom now is to forbid it. Similarly, in the Gemara (Shabbat 114b), they began to disrespectfully clean even before Mincha, and it was forbidden. Because of this, it became customary for children to play with nuts, and one should not prevent them, even before Mincha. This custom developed from the law of cracking nuts mentioned. Now, we do not see this custom, and one should prevent children from doing so. If a fire breaks out on Yom Kippur, it is permitted to save one meal for the night. The primary laws of fire on Shabbat are also explained in Siman 334, see there.

Even though in all of the Torah, the measure for eating is an olive's bulk, nevertheless, on Yom Kippur, the tradition is that the measure is a date’s bulk, which is slightly less than an egg's bulk. The reason for this is that on Yom Kippur, the term "eating" is not written, but rather "for any soul that is not afflicted," meaning that when one is hungry, their mind becomes settled. The tradition from the laws given to Moses at Sinai is that this measure is a large date’s bulk. This measure is the same for everyone, whether for a dwarf or Og, king of Bashan, and whether for simple foods or rich foods. However, for a dwarf, their mind becomes much more settled with this measure, and for Og, king of Bashan, it becomes settled only a little. Similarly, with rich foods, the mind becomes much more settled with this measure, and with simple foods, it becomes settled only a little (Gemara Yoma 82b).

All types of food combine with one another to complete the required measure. If one ate a little of this and a little of that, they combine to incur the penalty of karet (spiritual excision). However, if one ate half the measure and drank half the measure, they do not combine, as this does not satisfy one's mind. Nevertheless, liquids that come to enhance the food, making it better to eat, such as vegetables with their sauce or meat with salt—even if it melts and becomes liquid—do combine, as any enhancement of food is considered food. Similarly, meat fried in oil and the like combine. If it had the required measure and then dried out in the sun or by fire and decreased from the required measure, or vice versa, if it did not have the required measure and was in a moist place and then gained the required measure, we follow the current measure. This rule is explained in Yoreh De'ah, Chapter 85, regarding all prohibitions. There, it is also explained that what is between the teeth does not combine, but what is between the gums does combine, along with other laws. See there for further details.

This measure applies even if one did not eat it all at once but with interruptions, eating a little and then stopping, eating again and stopping, until the required measure is completed – they combine. This is similar to all prohibitions regarding foods, where if the time from the beginning to the end is not more than the time it takes to eat a "pras" (half a loaf) – they combine. But if there was a delay – they do not combine. And this is a law given to Moses at Sinai. Even though in all other measures it is an olive's bulk, which is much less than a date's bulk, nevertheless regarding interruptions – they are the same. And it is established that if it takes longer than the measure of a "pras" – it does not settle the soul.

The measure of "eating a portion" (k'dei achilat pras), whether on Yom Kippur or regarding all prohibitions – according to Rashi, is the equivalent of four eggs, and according to the Rambam, it is three heaping eggs, meaning: fully and generously filled, not precisely measured. Regarding the law: for Torah prohibitions, we follow the stringent opinion, and for Rabbinic prohibitions, we follow the lenient opinion. These measures are relevant only for the liability of karet (spiritual excision) and a sacrificial offering. However, a general prohibition – is forbidden by Torah law even in any amount, as half a measure is forbidden by Torah law, both on Yom Kippur and for other prohibitions.

One who eats on Yom Kippur in a state of gluttony (i.e., beyond satiation) is exempt. For example, if on the eve of Yom Kippur, close to nightfall, he ate a lot and was full and satisfied; and then after nightfall, he ate, and it was gluttonous eating, which is harmful to the body—he is exempt from karet (spiritual excision), as it is stated: "who will not afflict themselves," and on the contrary, with this eating he is afflicted, as it harms his body. And this refers to eating coarse foods, like bread and the like. But if he ate spiced foods, or types of fruits and the like, which are customarily eaten after being full—he is liable for karet. As people say: "There is always room for dessert." However, this too is only when he ate to the point of satisfaction. But if he did not eat so much that he is disgusted by the food, in such a case he is exempt from all foods, because his soul is disgusted by any kind of food. And this matter cannot be explained by a precise measure, but rather is according to what he feels within himself. However, with drinking—he is liable, as on the contrary: when the stomach is full—the desire for drinking is even greater.

The pleasure of eating and drinking is forbidden on Yom Kippur, even if it does not enter one's stomach. For example, if one eats, chews, and spits it out, since the palate still derives pleasure from it. And although it is impossible to obligate one with karet (spiritual excision) for this, nevertheless it is forbidden by Torah law, since it provides some degree of mental satisfaction. This applies to all prohibitions. Even things that are not fit for eating, such as aromatic woods or sweet wood—it is forbidden to taste and spit them out. However, it is permissible to smell all types of fragrances on Yom Kippur. And even if we say that in all prohibitions, fragrance is significant and forbidden, nevertheless on Yom Kippur it is only prohibited if the body derives pleasure from it, excluding fragrance which the body does not benefit from at all, only the soul. Therefore, it is not forbidden on Yom Kippur. On the contrary, it is a mitzvah to smell fragrances on Yom Kippur in order to complete the one hundred blessings. This excludes other prohibitions, where the soul should not benefit from a prohibition, and therefore fragrance is forbidden if fragrance is significant.

If one ate foods that are not fit for human consumption, even if one ate a lot of them, one is exempt from karet (spiritual excision), but they are given lashes of rebellion. Therefore, if one ate reeds, one is exempt, because they are not food for humans. If one ate grape shoots that sprouted before Rosh Hashanah, one is exempt, because they are just wood. However, if they sprouted after Rosh Hashanah, they are still soft on Yom Kippur, and therefore, one who eats them on Yom Kippur is liable for karet. If one ate dry peppers and dry ginger, one is exempt, because they are not fit for eating. But if one ate them when they are moist, one is liable, because then they are fit for eating. Similarly, if one ate salt or spices, one is exempt, because they are not food. If one ate food that has spoiled and is not fit for human consumption, even though it is still fit for a dog, one is exempt from karet. There is no distinction on Yom Kippur between eating prohibited and permitted items: if the food is fit for eating, one is liable for karet, and if not, one is exempt. One cannot say that eating a prohibited item on Yom Kippur does not incur the prohibition of Yom Kippur, because that is not the case. Not only if the other prohibition is a simple prohibition (issur lav), where the severe prohibition of Yom Kippur applies to it, but even if it is a severe prohibition like forbidden fat or blood, still Yom Kippur is an inclusive prohibition that includes all foods. An inclusive prohibition applies, and we do not say that one prohibition does not apply to another. This matter is explained in Rambam, Chapter 6 of Shegagot, Law 4; see there. It is also explained there that one who eats and drinks on Yom Kippur inadvertently, in one lapse, is only liable for one sin offering. But one who eats and does work is liable for two sin offerings. It is also explained there in Chapter 3 that those liable for sin offerings and guilt offerings who passed Yom Kippur must bring them after Yom Kippur. But those liable for conditional guilt offerings who passed Yom Kippur are exempt; see there.

The measurement for drinking on Yom Kippur is also not like other prohibitions, for the reason explained. Because on Yom Kippur, the measurement is the amount needed to restore one's soul, but it is the opposite of eating: For eating, the measurement on Yom Kippur is more than the measurement for all other prohibitions, where for all other prohibitions it is an olive's bulk (kezayit) and on Yom Kippur it is a date's bulk (kakotevet). And for drinking, it is the opposite: For all other prohibitions, the measurement for drinking is a quarter-log (revi'it), but on Yom Kippur the measurement is a mouthful, which for an average person is less than a quarter-log. And the "mouthful" that we mentioned means anything that, if moved to one side of the mouth, it would appear as a full mouthful. And we measure for each individual according to his own mouthful. And in this as well, it is not like eating, where for all people there is one measurement, but not so with drinking. And all of this is a law given to Moses at Sinai, because for each person, his own mouthful settles his mind, and all liquids combine together to complete the measurement of a mouthful.

However, regarding delays, there is a disagreement. According to Rashi and Tosafot, the amount of time is the same as the time it takes to eat a piece of bread, just as with eating. This is explicitly clarified in Keritot (13a). However, Rambam in the second chapter, fourth halachah, wrote: If one drank a little and then drank a little more, if the time from the beginning of the first drink to the end of the last drink equals the time it takes to drink a revi'it (a quarter-log), they combine to form the required measure. If not, they do not combine. This is his exact wording, and he ruled the same way for all prohibitions in the fourteenth chapter, nineteenth halachah of Forbidden Foods. The sages of the generations have already questioned him. We have explained his words in Yoreh De'ah, section 85; see there. The primary ruling follows the first opinion, as this is the view of most authorities.

And also with liquids, if one drank liquids that are not fit for drinking – he is exempt from Karet. Therefore, if one drank brine, or fish oil, or raw vinegar that is so strong that it bubbles when it falls on the ground – he is exempt from Karet, but we administer disciplinary lashes. However, if one drank vinegar diluted with water to the measure of a mouthful – he is liable. It seems to me that one who drinks oil on Yom Kippur is exempt from Karet, because it is harmful to him, as it is stated at the beginning of the chapter "How to Bless," see there.

All these measurements are for the obligation of karet. But regarding the prohibition, even the smallest amount of drinking is forbidden by Torah law, just like with eating, where half a measure is forbidden by Torah law. However, with the saliva in one's mouth, swallowing is not applicable, as there is no substance in it. Otherwise, one would have to spit all day without stopping. Our teacher, the Rema, wrote that it is permissible on Yom Kippur to touch food and drink and to give them to children, and we are not concerned that one might eat or drink by touching them; thus far is his language. And it is not similar to chametz on Pesach, as the awe of Yom Kippur is upon him. Furthermore, on Pesach one is not abstaining from eating and drinking, and we are concerned that he might eat or drink the chametz as well, which is not the case on Yom Kippur, where he abstains completely – there is no concern in this. And so it seems in Yoma (14a), see there (see Magen Avraham, subsection 6).

It is forbidden to wash on Yom Kippur, even a single limb, whether with hot water or cold water. Even to dip one's finger in water, not in the manner of washing, is prohibited, as this also provides some degree of pleasure. Even if one's hands, face, or body are covered in sweat, it is prohibited (Taz, subsection 1), as removing the sweat is also considered a form of pleasure. However, if one's hands, feet, or other parts of their body are dirty with mud or excrement, it is permitted to wash the dirty area (Magen Avraham, subsection 1), as this is not for pleasure, but to remove the dirt. Care should be taken that the water does not reach the clean parts of the body. Similarly, if blood is dripping from one's nose, it is permitted to wash the nose and mustache that are dirty with blood for this reason. If blood is oozing from one's teeth, it is forbidden to take water into the mouth and rinse, but one should wipe it with a cloth.

And since only washing for pleasure is forbidden, therefore our sages of blessed memory (Tosafot 77b, s.v. "Mishum") said that it is permissible to wash one’s hands in the morning on Yom Kippur when one rises from bed. For there is nothing dirtier than this, and one is forbidden to touch his mouth, his ear, his nose, or his eyes, as we say in Shabbat (108a). This is not for the pleasure of washing, but to remove the evil spirit that rests on the hands before the morning washing. Therefore, one should not intend to derive pleasure from it, even though it happens incidentally, and it is considered as if it is unavoidable and unintentional, which is permitted. This is in contrast to if one intends to derive pleasure, even though it is unavoidable – it is forbidden. And one should be careful to wash only up to the end of his knuckles, for the evil spirit only rests there, and no further. (See Pesachim 25b, and this is the intention of the Rama in section 2. Study it carefully and you will find it easy.)

If he urinated and rubbed with his hand, or touched his covered flesh, and certainly if he relieved himself and wiped – it is obvious that he is permitted to wash up to the end of his knuckles, or more if he also touched the area, since his hands are dirty, and this is no less than mud or excrement. However, if he urinated without rubbing or touching – he does not need to wash, as he can recite the blessing "Asher Yatzar" even without washing. Nevertheless, if he wants to pray, even if he did not touch – he is allowed to wash up to the end of his knuckles, because for prayer it is necessary to wash his hands, even without touching. However, some say that even for the blessing "Asher Yatzar" – he needs to wash even without touching. Therefore, to avoid dispute – it is good that he should rub or touch, and then wash (Beit Yosef and Magen Avraham, and Taz subsection 2). And this is the main ruling, that even without rubbing – he may wash his hands for the blessing "Asher Yatzar." And all this is at night after prayer. But during the day – he certainly needs to wash in any case, since all day one prays (ibid).

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote in Paragraph 3: Similarly, a Kohen who ascends to the platform (to bless the congregation) must wash his hands, even though they are already pure, because any washing that is not intended for pleasure is permitted. Therefore, even if he comes from the road and his feet are dirty, he is permitted to wash them. Thus are his words. And with regard to his dirty feet, it is explained in the Jerusalem Talmud that this is for healing purposes, and it is permitted.

However, regarding the washing of hands for the Priestly Blessing, it is true that the Tosafot in Sotah (39a) hold that even if he washed his hands in the morning, he must wash them again before going to the platform. But Maimonides, in Chapter Fifteen of Prayer, did not require washing unless his hands are impure. However, if he washed his hands in the morning, he does not need to wash them again. And so testified the son of Maimonides that this was their practice (Kesef Mishneh there).

If so, for those who hold that all the afflictions (of Yom Kippur) are from the Torah, how can one enter into a doubt of a Torah prohibition on this holy day? Perhaps this is why our teacher the Rema was careful to say "not intending for pleasure," meaning: if he does not intend it for pleasure, and even if we assume that it is possible without washing, it is considered possible but not intended, and we rely on those who permit in such a case in Pesachim (25b), see there. And so the simple custom is to wash their hands, but it still requires further examination.

The Tur wrote in the name of a Gaon: Someone who is fastidious and needs to wash his face with water, and his mind is not settled all day until he washes – he may wash on Yom Kippur. Similarly, R. Yitzchak Gaon wrote: If there is dirt on his face or on his eyes – he may remove it with water. And even any person may soak a cloth in water on the eve of Yom Kippur, wring it out until the water is removed, and the next day he may wipe it over his eyes, even though some moisture remains in it. Thus are his words.

Based on this, our master the Beit Yosef wrote in section 4: "One who is fastidious, and his mind is not settled until he rinses his face with water – it is permitted." Thus far his words. And our master the Rema wrote: "And the custom is to be stringent. And even regarding washing the eyes, which is somewhat medicinal – the custom is to be stringent. And it is forbidden to rinse one's mouth on Yom Kippur." Thus far his words. 

The main issue is perplexing: how can the sage permit a fastidious person to rinse his face with water, when it is obvious that this is for pleasure? Furthermore, what is the meaning of what the Tur said, "And so wrote R. Yitzchak Giat: if there is dirt on his face," etc.? What comparison is there? Certainly, if there is dirt, it is permitted, as this is not for pleasure, as explained. It must be said that our master the Beit Yosef holds that the reason of the sage is that for a fastidious person, this is not for pleasure, and for him, it is like dirt, and so he explained in his great book. But how forced is this explanation! Therefore, our master the Rema ruled to be stringent. 

There are those who say that the sage's intent is also when there is dirt on his face (Bach). But this cannot be said, for if so, the main permission is missing from his words. Moreover, we do not need the sage's words for this. Furthermore, if so, even one who is not fastidious, such as with mud and filth, it is permitted for everyone, as I wrote. Furthermore, if so, R. Yitzchak Giat disagrees with the sage, for R. Yitzchak Giat permits it for everyone. Moreover, what is this language of "rinse"? 

In conclusion: the words of the sage and the Tur require great investigation.

According to my humble opinion, it seems there is another intention in their words. Behold, the Rosh, after bringing the words of the Gemara (78b) that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi had a cloth which he would soak in water on the eve of Yom Kippur and make it like a dry cloth and the next day he would pass it over his eyes, wrote: "The Gaon said: One who seeks to wipe his face on Yom Kippur – if he is delicate and his mind is not settled all year until he wipes with water, and certainly on Yom Kippur when he needs to purify and wipe himself, let him wipe. But for all other people it is forbidden, etc." This is his language. And this is its explanation: The Gemara only permitted with dry cloths to pass over his eyes. But the Gaon permits a delicate person to also wipe his face with dry cloths since every day he is accustomed to water – we permit him to wipe with dry cloths. This is also the words of the Tur that a delicate person who needs water on his face – he can wipe his face on Yom Kippur with dry cloths. And the Ritz Giath permitted even with water for dirt on his face, and for all people. The level of dirt with water and a delicate person with wiping with dry cloths – they are equal. And afterward he wrote that to pass over his eyes with dry cloths is permitted even for all people. And certainly, these laws are clear in their reasoning, and so should be instructed.

And regarding what the Tur wrote that one can soak a cloth on the eve of Yom Kippur and wring it out, and the next day pass it over his eyes – so it is in the Gemara there. And the Rambam in the third chapter, law 5, wrote: "And he passes it over his face," see there. And it must be said that this was his version in the Gemara. And our teacher, the Beit Yosef, omitted this, and I do not know why. And our teacher, the Rema, in section 9 wrote that it is forbidden to soak a cloth the day before, make it like dry utensils, and use it to cool oneself on Yom Kippur. For we are concerned that it might not be wrung out well, and one may come to wring it out. These are his words. And it seems to me that this is its explanation: Even though in the Gemara they permitted in such a manner – this is when it is done only to pass over his eyes, and he wrings it out well, for even the slight moisture that will remain in the cloth will be enough to pass over his eyes. But if it is done to cool oneself – we are concerned that it might not be wrung out well, and one may come to wring it out. And even though it will remain for washing – we are not concerned, nevertheless, for a small amount of wringing – we are concerned (and there is no need for what the Magen Avraham wrote in subsection 11).

And the Rambam wrote there that a sick person may bathe in his usual manner, even though he is not in danger. This is his language: because the bathing of the sick person is not for pleasure but for the health of the body, or to wash off some dirt. But anything that is not for the health of the body, nor to remove dirt – certainly, even for a sick person, it is forbidden. And a woman who has given birth, who is frequently with blood – it is obvious that she can wash her body, both because she is like a sick person, and because it is to remove dirt. And it is clear that one who has been seized by a shiver on Yom Kippur, it is permissible to wash his face and hands and other places, and to pour water on his head to remove the shiver, for this is like a complete illness.

A fundamental principle regarding Yom Kippur is that any washing that is not for pleasure is permitted. Therefore, it is taught in the Mishnah: a king and a bride may wash their faces; a king because "Your eyes shall behold the king in his beauty" and this is not for his pleasure, and a bride for thirty days from her wedding so that she does not become unpleasant to her husband, and this is not for her pleasure. After thirty days, she is like all other women. For any matter of joy, or conversely in mourning, it extends up to thirty days and no more (and this resolves the question of the Magen Avraham, section 12). Conversely, for the sake of pleasure, it is forbidden even if it is not a complete washing, such as cooling off with moist clay if it is damp enough to wet something else. It is forbidden to cool off with vessels that contain water, and not only when they are full, where there is concern that the water might spill on the body, but even if they are not full, it is forbidden. If the vessel is made of earthenware, it is forbidden because it exudes moisture outward, and with metal vessels that do not exude, we are concerned that since they are smooth, they might slip from the hand and the water will spill on him. But with empty vessels, it is permitted to cool off, as well as with fruits, and to hold a baby next to oneself when it is cooled. Since there is no water in these, there is no concern of washing.

And similarly, even actual washing—so long as it is evident that it is not for the pleasure of washing, but rather that it is necessary for his way, such as someone who goes on Yom Kippur to the study hall, or to greet his father, or his teacher, or someone greater than him in wisdom, who are on the other side of the river, or for other mitzvah needs which require him to pass through water—he may pass and need not be concerned, for this is not washing for pleasure. He may pass through water up to his neck, both while going and returning. For if you do not permit him to return, he would not go in the first place, and he would refrain from performing the mitzvah. Our Sages, of blessed memory, required that he should not lift the hem of his cloak onto his arm, nor take his hand out from under the edge of his cloak, because that is the usual way to do it on a weekday. And we are concerned that he might come to wringing out [the garment]. Therefore, they required him not to do so as on a weekday, and through this change, he would remember that it is Yom Kippur and would not come to wringing out [the garment]. And this is when the waters are not rushing, and there is no danger in going up to his neck in the water. For if the waters are rushing, it is forbidden for a person even on a weekday to go into a depth above his waist. For when the waters are rushing, he might drown from the force of the waters, and it is forbidden for a person to put himself in a place of danger. And specifically, walking in water is permitted, but swimming is forbidden, for it is forbidden to swim on Shabbat, Yom Tov, and Yom Kippur because of a rabbinic prohibition. Similarly, using a ferry is forbidden. This is not comparable to bathing which was permitted, for this is not bathing, since it is not for pleasure. But swimming in any manner is forbidden. And this is the reason of the Bahag which the Tur brought. (And the Tur questioned: how is this different from bathing? And the Beit Yosef, the Bach, and the Taz [subsection 4] exerted effort to explain, see there. And the explanation is simple as I have written.)

And our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in paragraph 6, and this is his language: The permission to pass through water for the sake of a mitzvah applies specifically to passing through the water with one's body itself. But to pass through in a small boat – there is one who prohibits it. Thus far his language. And he wrote "there is one who prohibits" because the prohibition was written by the Tur in the name of the Ba'al Halachot Gedolot (BHG), and he questioned it, wondering how it differs from bathing. However, according to what we have written, this is not a valid comparison, and according to all opinions, it is forbidden. And also the Tur only wondered about the BHG's ruling; he did not disagree with him in practice. (And so wrote the Bach, and look there where he wrote as we have, and not as the Taz wrote in his name, look there. And this also resolves the question of the Magen Avraham, paragraph 8, look there.)

And similarly, one who goes to guard his fruits—it is permitted to pass through water while going, but not while returning, because in this case, it is not applicable to permit the end for the sake of the beginning. If he does not want to go, we have no objection. However, while going, it is permitted, for this is not considered pleasurable bathing, and it was permitted for him due to the potential financial loss, since there is no prohibition in this. And in any situation where it is permitted to pass through water, even if there is a way to go around on dry land, it is permitted to pass through water, because minimizing walking is preferable.

The Tur and Shulchan Aruch wrote in Section 7: A rabbi is forbidden to cross water to visit his student; thus is their wording. The Rambam did not mention this law at all. And in the Gemara (Avodah Zarah 2b), this was questioned and not resolved. Some are puzzled as this is a rabbinic doubt, so why do we rule stringently (Taz, subsection 6)? It seems to me that if we scrutinize what the Talmud is questioning, since it is not for pleasure – it should be permitted? Rather, the matter is like this: Certainly, a student going to greet his rabbi – his intention is for a mitzvah. Similarly, one going to guard his fruits – his intention is to guard his property, and there is no bathing for pleasure. But a rabbi visiting a student, which he is not obligated to do, perhaps his intention is for pleasure. And even though for the holy ones like the Amoraim – certainly their intentions are for the sake of Heaven, in other generations we cannot rely on this. Therefore, the Tur and Shulchan Aruch prohibited it. The Rambam avoided this issue because it cannot be stated definitively in law. Just as a rabbi visiting a student is prohibited, so too a friend visiting a friend. However, if it is known that it is necessary to ask a halachic question pertinent to the moment – it is certainly permitted, as it is clear to all that his intention is not for pleasure (see Beit Yosef, Taz, and the Gra).

One who experiences a seminal emission during Yom Kippur: If it is still moist, he wipes it with a cloth, and that suffices. If it has dried on the body or has dirtied him, he washes only the soiled areas. It is forbidden to wash his body or immerse, even if he is usually meticulous about immersing after a seminal emission during the rest of the year. Instead, he cleanses himself and prays. If his garment is not clean: if it is moist, he wipes it with anything, and if it has dried, he changes to another garment. In this time, a woman is forbidden to immerse on Yom Kippur when her time has arrived, as we hold that immersion at its due time is not a commandment, and she should immerse at night after Yom Kippur. A woman who wears white garments is permitted to wash a little between her thighs. A mohel, when he sucks (the wound), is forbidden to rinse his mouth with water.

Anointing is completely forbidden. This means anointing the body or head with any substance is prohibited, even part of the body, even a single limb, or even part of a limb. However, if one is ill, even if the illness is not life-threatening, and needs anointing for healing purposes – it is permitted, just as bathing is permitted for healing, as I wrote in the previous section. Similarly, someone who has sores on their head – this is considered an illness, and it is permitted to anoint in the usual manner, without concern. But if one is not ill, and does not have sores – it is forbidden even to remove dirt. In this respect, anointing is stricter than bathing. It is also clarified in the Jerusalem Talmud that anointing to remove dirt is forbidden because anointing is more pleasurable than bathing. In any case, there is pleasure involved, but in truth, even for bathing, not all types of dirt are permitted, only when one is soiled with mud or excrement. Nonetheless, even in such a case, anointing is forbidden. (See Magen Avraham, subsection 1, and the explanation of the author of Macha Shekel, see there. Analyze carefully and you will find it easy.)

Wearing sandals is considered an "affliction" when one does not wear them. Therefore, it is forbidden on Yom Kippur, as it is written: "Restrain your foot from being barefoot"; and it is also stated: "And David went up by the ascent of the Mount of Olives, weeping as he went up, and his head was covered, and he was barefoot"; and in Isaiah (20:2) it is written: "Remove the shoe from your foot" to afflict oneself, see there. There are three opinions on this matter: [1] The opinion of the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch, section 2, which states that any footwear made of leather is forbidden, and any that is not made of leather is permitted. They wrote, and this is their language: It is forbidden to wear a shoe or sandal made of leather, even a prosthetic foot or similar, even if made of wood and covered with leather - it is forbidden. But those made of reed, or straw, or cloth, or other materials - are permitted, even to go out with them into the public domain. This is their language. And it does not mean that these materials are permitted even if covered with leather, as might superficially seem from the language, for it is certainly forbidden. Rather, because in the case of wood we find in the Gemara (Yevamot 103a) that it can be covered with leather, they wrote thus, but in reality, there is no distinction. This is the opinion of the Rif and the Rosh.

[2] However, according to Rashi's opinion, a wooden shoe is forbidden. This also appears to be the view of the Tosafot in the discussion in Yoma (78b), for Rava concludes there regarding the Mishnah about the amputee going out with his wooden leg, that on Yom Kippur, everyone agrees it is called a "shoe" and it is forbidden to go out with it. See there. But a shoe made of reed, cork, straw, cloth, and other materials is permitted. [3] The opinion of the Ba'al HaMaor is that according to Rava's conclusion, all types are forbidden when made in the manner of a shoe. However, this opinion was refuted by the Ramban, see there. But the opinion of Rashi and Tosafot is clearly proven in the discussion there. In truth, the discussions in Shabbat (66b) and Yevamot there contradict the discussion in Yoma, for it is clearly proven there that according to the Rabbis, the amputee's wooden leg is not called a "shoe." One must say, as the Ramban wrote there, that in Yoma it is only according to Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yose, and not according to the Rabbis, and the halacha follows the Rabbis. See there. Therefore, the Rif did not mention this at all. Similarly, in the Jerusalem Talmud (Taanit Chapter 1, Halacha 6) it says: "It was taught: One may go out with slippers; and it was taught: One may not go out." This refers to cloth slippers and leather slippers, respectively. See there. Therefore, even though in the Tosefta at the beginning of the fourth chapter it is taught that even cloth slippers are forbidden, this was not taken into account as it is against the Bavli and Yerushalmi. However, regarding wooden shoes, there is no proof from the Yerushalmi to permit them. In the Yerushalmi, Chapter 12 of Yevamot (Halacha 2), there is a dispute regarding the matter of chalitzah, whether a wooden shoe is called a "shoe." See there.

In the words of the Rambam, Chapter 3, Law 7, there is room for examination. The commentators have assumed that he follows the view of the Rif and the Rosh, that anything not made of leather is permitted, even if made of wood. However, in my humble opinion, this does not seem to be the intent of his language, as he wrote: "It is forbidden to wear a shoe or sandal, even on one foot. But it is permitted to go out with a sandal made of cork or reed, and similar materials. And a person may wrap a cloth around his feet and go out with it, because the hardness of the ground reaches his feet, and he feels that he is barefoot." This is his language. Thus, he requires that the foot feels its bareness, and with wood, it is obvious that this is not felt, and it is forbidden. It seems to me that the reason is not because a wooden shoe is called a "shoe," for regarding the laws of halitzah (divorce by shoe removal), he himself ruled in Chapter 4 of Yibbum (Law 18) that a wooden shoe is invalid. Rather, it seems to me that the reason is: since the reason for Yom Kippur is affliction, therefore anything that does not cause affliction, and one does not feel that he is walking barefoot, is forbidden. With all the other materials like cork, reed, and cloth, the foot feels because they are soft. But not so with wood. Therefore, in my humble opinion, it appears that one should not go out with a wooden shoe on Yom Kippur, as this is the opinion of Rashi, Tosafot, and the Rambam.

And know that among us, we walk in kalsin on Yom Kippur because they are not made of leather. They are a type of rubber, and they are also soft, so the foot feels the hardness of the ground, as is known. All the more so it is permissible to walk in slippers which are made of simple wool, and they are very soft. However, some of them are thick and very hard, to the extent that the foot does not feel the hardness of the ground. According to what I have written from the words of the Rambam, it is not proper to walk in them on Yom Kippur, especially when they are covered with leather (and so wrote the Peri Megadim, brought in Shaarei Teshuva, Siman 594). Rabbi Rema wrote that it is permissible to stand on leather cushions and pillows, but nevertheless, one who is stringent will be blessed. These are his words. 

Seemingly, there is no reason for this stringency, and it is permissible from the outset since it is not considered a shoe (Magen Avraham, section 4, in the name of Radbaz). However, according to the Rambam, this is understandable, as the Torah is particular that the foot feels the hardness of the ground, as I have written. (See the Bach, who wrote that some people walked barefoot. It seems they were concerned with the opinion of the Maor, who concluded that even cloth is forbidden. There is a semblance of proof from the Baal Halachot Gedolot, brought by the Tur, that initially, one should not do so. However, in truth, the opinion of the Maor is a singular opinion against all our Rabbis, against the Jerusalem Talmud, and against the discussions in Shabbat and Yevamot. And from the Baal Halachot Gedolot there is no proof, as he was speaking in the ordinary way of the matter. And see Magen Avraham, section 2, that people walk to the synagogue barefoot before sundown. I do not know what the stringency in this is. Some walk in shoes and remove them in the synagogue before sundown. And for what he wrote in section 3, that standing on cushions during the Amidah prayer is considered arrogance, see there. This is only when they are at least a handbreadth high, and not when they are close to the ground. Be precise and you will find clarity.)

A midwife (or a woman who has given birth) throughout the thirty days [after childbirth], and a sick person even if there is no danger – are permitted to wear sandals, for to them the cold is very difficult, and they could be endangered. Likewise, someone who has a wound on their feet. If they have a wound on one foot – they may wear a shoe on that foot, but it is forbidden on the other foot. And it is permitted for anyone to wear a sandal due to scorpions or similar creatures, to prevent being bitten, if there are scorpions or biting creatures present. However, due to mere discomfort, such as in places where the streets are paved with stones and it is difficult to walk barefoot – it is forbidden to wear a shoe. For indeed, in such a case, we are commanded to afflict ourselves by not wearing sandals.

And our teacher the Rema wrote: If it is raining, and one wishes to go from his house to the synagogue or vice versa, and he is delicate (an istanis) – he is allowed to wear his shoes until he reaches his place. So far his words. But if he is not delicate – it is forbidden. And the delicate person should leave his shoes in a concealed place in the synagogue. There are those who object to those who are lenient in going out in the rain, arguing that not every person can claim to be delicate (Magen Avraham, sub-paragraph 5). In my humble opinion, in our country when the weather is cold – this is considered a danger, and it is certainly permitted. And it is obvious that when there is mud and mire, it is permitted to wear shoes (Taz, sub-paragraph 3). There are those who require switching the left shoe to the right foot and the right shoe to the left foot, or wearing a shoe without a heel (Magen Avraham, sub-paragraph 6). This is not the custom, for we do not have shoes without heels. And switching the left to the right – it is impossible for us to walk according to our shoes.

Yom Kippur is prohibited in marital relations, and this is also included in "you shall afflict yourselves," for abstaining from marital relations is called "affliction." And in the Gemara (Yoma 77b), this is derived from a verse, see there. And even in a place where immersion for seminal emission is not practiced, marital relations are prohibited (Tur), meaning: do not say that the prohibition is due to the immersion that follows, because of the prohibition of bathing; rather, the marital relations themselves are prohibited. Therefore, a person should keep away from his wife the entire day as with a menstruant. This means: he should not sleep with her in the same bed, and he should not touch her at night. However, during the day there is no concern, of course (Taz). But some prohibit even during the day (Magen Avraham), though it seems that the custom is not so. And he should not engage in much conversation with her (ibid.).

We learn at the end of Yoma (88a): The school of Rabbi Yishmael taught: One who experiences a nocturnal emission on Yom Kippur should worry throughout the entire year. But if the year passes and nothing bad happens to him, it is assured that he is destined for the World to Come. And this is the language of the Tur: He should worry, etc. — because it shows that his fast was not accepted, and they satisfied their need through him, like a servant who mixes a cup for his master and then spills the jug in front of him. But if the year passes and nothing bad happens to him, it is assured that he is destined for the World to Come, because he certainly has merits that protected him. This is the end of his language. Rashi and Tosafot wrote: And a sign of this is "He will see offspring, he will prolong his days," and so the Tur wrote. (And I heard, based on what is written in Shabbat 105b: "All the days of the elders that they prolonged their days," etc. — they prolonged days, but not years. And the question is raised: But what about "so that your days may be multiplied"? And it is answered: A blessing is different, see there. And this is that if a year does not pass for him — he will see offspring, prolong his days, but not years. And if the year passes for him — it is a blessing, and he will prolong both days and years.)

Children are permitted to eat and drink, and also to bathe and anoint themselves when they need to. Except for wearing sandals, which it is appropriate to train them in, because there is not much concern for this, as often even without Yom Kippur they do not wear sandals. So why shouldn't they be trained in this on this holy day? But eating and drinking are necessary for them, and bathing and anointing depend on their habits. Among us, children are not accustomed to this, and therefore it seems appropriate to train them in it as well. The time for training will be explained in section 4.

Eating and drinking – an adult is permitted to feed and give drink to children, and we do not decree that he might come to eat himself, as we do with chametz on Passover and a nazirite with wine. For it is not similar, because in those cases, all foods are eaten, and therefore we are concerned that he might also eat this. This is not the case on Yom Kippur, especially since the fear of judgment is upon him. There is someone who wishes to be stringent in this matter, but this is not the main opinion (see Beit Yosef). However, if the boy and girl do not need to be fed – prepare their food for them, and they will eat on their own. This is not because of a prohibition, but because of the exertion, and why should one do something himself that is not necessary?
