However, washing and anointing—an Israelite should not do them himself for the infant, because when he washes and anoints the infant, he also derives some personal benefit. Therefore, he should tell a non-Jew to wash and anoint the infant. There is an opinion that even an Israelite himself is permitted to wash and anoint them (Bach), as this is not considered personal benefit. Another opinion distinguishes between hot and cold water: with cold water, where the prohibition is only due to affliction, and since it is permitted for infants, he may do it himself. But with hot water, which is also forbidden on Shabbat, he should not do it himself, only through a non-Jew (Magen Avraham, Small Section 1). However, in the Gemara (78a) it is explained that even with hot water, it is permitted, see there (Eliyahu Rabbah). There is a difference between Shabbat and Yom Tov (ibid.). Nonetheless, practically speaking, there is no difference now, as our infants are not accustomed to washing and anointing, and it is forbidden (Levush and Magen Avraham).

And even though we feed the young children, nonetheless we train them for fasting by hours. For example, if a child is accustomed to eating at two hours into the day, we feed him at three hours. If he is accustomed to eating at the third hour, we feed him at the fourth hour. Because delaying by an hour does not pose any health concern, as sometimes, even without this practice, they naturally extend by about an hour. And according to the child's strength, we increase the fasting by hours. This applies to girls as well. And the training begins from nine years old and above, but not earlier, as training does not apply to a very young child.

And this is the language of the Tur: A healthy child – we train him to fast for hours at the age of ten and eleven, and at the age of twelve and thirteen, he completes the fast by rabbinic decree, and at the age of fourteen, he completes the fast by Torah law. And a sick child (meaning: one who is not strong enough to endure the fast) – we train him to fast for hours at the age of eleven and twelve, and at the age of thirteen, he completes the fast by rabbinic decree, and at the age of fourteen, he completes the fast by Torah law. And a girl, who is considered mature a year earlier than a boy – if she is healthy, we train her to fast for hours at the age of nine and ten, and at the age of eleven and twelve, she completes the fast by rabbinic decree, and at the age of thirteen, she completes the fast by Torah law. And if she is sick – we train her to fast for hours at the age of ten and eleven, and she completes the fast by rabbinic decree at the age of twelve, and by Torah law at the age of thirteen. And just as we train them in eating, so too we train them in washing and anointing. Thus ends his language.

However, Maimonides writes at the end of the second chapter: A minor who is nine or ten years old is trained to fast for a few hours, etc. An eleven-year-old, whether male or female, fasts and completes the fast by rabbinic decree in order to train them in the commandments. A girl who is twelve years and one day old, and a boy who is thirteen years and one day old who have brought forth two pubic hairs are considered adults for all commandments and complete the fast by Torah law. However, if they have not brought forth two pubic hairs, they are still considered minors and only complete the fast by rabbinic decree. A minor who is less than nine years old is not made to fast on Yom Kippur, lest it endanger their health. So far his words. And even if they wish to be stringent upon themselves, they are not allowed to do so, as those under nine years old could be endangered. Their dispute depends on the Talmudic discussion.

Some of our rabbis believe that rabbinically – there is no need for any completion [of fasting]. They ruled according to Rabbi Yochanan in the Talmud (Yoma 82a) who says this, see there. And this is the custom of the world. And our master, the Rema, wrote that one can rely on this for a youth who is weak and not strong enough to fast. This is his language. And now, most children are studying, and they are weak and frail (Bach, and Magen Avraham at the end of section 2). However, the training for hours [of fasting] – we still practice this even now, as there is no disagreement on this. And know that a boy of thirteen years and one day, or a girl of twelve years and one day, if we do not know if they have brought two hairs – they are required to fast by Torah law. For anyone who reaches the age of years – there is a presumption that they have brought the signs. And even if we do not currently see the signs – we are concerned that perhaps they fell out, as a doubt regarding a Torah law is to be ruled stringently. And even if he is soft and weak, and even if he becomes thirteen on Yom Kippur, unless we know clearly that he has not yet brought hairs. And if he is certainly mature, but they say he will not endure the fast and will become ill – they should ask doctors, and his law is like all the sick people that will be explained in section 618. And there is no difference in this between a boy and a girl.

Pregnant and nursing women fast and complete the Yom Kippur fast like other people. Even on Tisha B'Av, the law is the same, as I have written in Siman 554, because there is no danger to them when they fast, unless they are already ill, in which case their law is like all the ill, which will be explained in the next Siman. However, a pregnant woman who smells the aroma of food, and the fetus smells it, and she craves it, and if she does not eat, both are in danger (Rashi 82a). And how do we know this is the case? For example, if her face changes, even if she does not say "I need it." Or if she says "I need it," even if her face does not change (Magen Avraham, subsection 1). For any other healthy person who says "I need it," if their face does not change, it is not possible to believe them without a doctor (there). And it is also clear that when it reaches such a stage, their face will change. However, the pregnant woman is believed even without a change in her face, because this is common in pregnant women.

A pregnant woman who has a craving, as I have written – they whisper to her ear that today is Yom Kippur. If her mind is calmed and she says that her craving has been removed, as we find such stories in the Gemara there – it is better. If her mind is not calmed – they feed her until her mind is settled. They feed her less than the prohibited amount at a time, as will be explained in the next Siman regarding a sick person. However, if according to observation it is not sufficient for her, and she is compelled to eat a lot at once to remove the craving – they feed her a lot.

And so too, any person who smells the aroma of good food and their face changes, this is [a sign of] bulmus, and they could be in danger if they are not given some of the food – they are also given less than the prohibited amount, as it is assumed this will suffice for them. If it is not enough – they are given as much as they need. More will be explained on this in the next section. And know that sometimes a pregnant woman’s mind is calmed by tasting even a small amount. Therefore, they first dip something in the sauce and place it in her mouth. If her mind is settled – all is well. If not – they return and give her from the sauce. If this too is not enough – they give her from the food itself (see Magen Avraham, sub-paragraph 2).

A woman who has given birth within three days, even if she is healthy and says she does not need to eat, is forbidden to fast, for the sages have determined that she would be endangered by fasting. However, feed her less than the measure. From the third to the seventh day, their conditions are not uniform: some can endure the fast without any harm to their bodies, and some cannot. Therefore, it depends on her: if she says, "I need to eat," then feed her. If she says, "I do not need," then let her fast. Ask her, and she will respond "yes" or "no." In our times, it is known that they will always say they do not need, and this cannot be relied upon. Therefore, if there is a doctor, consult the doctor. If not, let knowledgeable women say. If there is doubt, feed her less than the measure, for in cases of doubt concerning life, we are lenient. From the seventh day onward, she is like a sick person who is not in danger, and her law is like other illnesses that will be explained. (What the author of Kessef Mishnah wrote in Chapter "Mephanin" to reject the words of the Tur and Shulchan Aruch based on the Rosh there is not at all difficult. This is not comparable, for with eating, only she knows. But the needs of a woman who has given birth, they know. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

These days are not counted from moment to moment. For example, if she gave birth on the seventh of Tishrei in the evening, we do not feed her on Yom Kippur unless she says, "I need [to eat]." Even though three days have not completed for her until the evening of Yom Kippur, nevertheless, since Yom Kippur is the fourth day from her giving birth, her status is like that after three days. For all natural matters follow this course.

Know that in the Mishnah (Yoma 83a), the Gemara, and the poskim (decisors of Jewish law) it is explained that the eating of a sick person on Yom Kippur depends on the doctors and the sick person himself. As we have learned in the Mishnah there: A sick person – they feed him based on the opinion of experts. If there are no experts there – they feed him based on his own opinion. And what is the law when there is no doctor, and the sick person does not say anything, as is the case in most illnesses? And we know that the sick person will always say to be strict, and we should not rely on his words. It would seem to say that all the laws that will be explained apply to illnesses where we do not know if there is danger or not. But in the case of a dangerous illness – there is neither a question nor opinions, and it is obvious that we do not let him fast, for there is no greater danger than this!

And what is considered a danger when there is no doctor? It seems that when he is bedridden and cannot get out of bed – he is considered a sick person with danger. Similarly, if he is one of those with tuberculosis, which they call "sohatka" or "dar" – it is considered a danger. And even if there is doubt among us – a doubt regarding the saving of a life also overrides Shabbat and Yom Kippur.

Indeed, from the words of the Rambam in the second chapter, law 8, it does not seem so, for he wrote: "A sick person who is in danger who requests to eat on Yom Kippur, even though expert doctors say he does not need to – we feed him, etc." Thus far his words. Behold, even in a case of danger, it requires the statement of the sick person that he needs to eat. However, one could say that this applies when the doctors say he does not need to. But when there are no doctors present, we do not need his statement that he needs; rather, we feed him regardless. And this appears to be the primary ruling in practice.

And one should not wonder that if he is in danger, how can the doctor say he does not need [to eat]? This is not difficult at all, for there are several illnesses that do not require eating, and the lack of eating will not harm them. However, this depends on the wisdom of the doctor who understands the illness and understands that this illness does not require eating and drinking. But in general, when there is no doctor before us, if there is danger – we feed and give him to drink as on any other day, but in less than the required quantity if it suffices for him, as will be explained later. And there are illnesses for which the entire treatment is through abundant eating, like those with tuberculosis which is called suhatek'a, or diabetes, for these, less than the required quantity will not suffice, and they need to be given a lot as they desire, for that is their treatment.

And this is the language of the Tur: A sick person who needs to eat, if there is an expert doctor who says: if he is not given [food], it is possible that the illness will become more severe, and he will be in danger – they feed him based on his word. And the doctor does not need to say "perhaps he will die." And if there is no doctor there – they feed him based on his own word, for since he has been informed that it is Yom Kippur, and he asks to eat – there is no need to scrutinize him further, etc. Thus far is his language. And he was precise in saying "a sick person who needs to eat" to indicate that he is not speaking exclusively about a dangerously ill person, as per the words of the Rambam, but even if he is not in danger, and he says he needs to eat – they feed him (Bach). For there are illnesses where the sick person can walk in the marketplace, and with these, certainly, in general, they do not feed him, unless the doctor says he needs [food], or he himself says he needs [food]. But with dangerous illnesses, such as an illness where the person is confined to bed – no statement is needed, rather, even generally, they feed him, as we have written.

And furthermore, we learn from his words that it is not necessary for the doctor to say that if the patient does not eat, he will die. Rather, even if the doctor says that the illness will worsen, and consequently he could be endangered by this, we feed him. Not only that, but even if the doctor does not say this definitively, but merely that it is possible that the illness will worsen, we still feed him. For there is a great principle: When it comes to matters of life and death, we are lenient, and it is forbidden to be stringent in this matter. And a sick person who needs to eat and does not want to – we feed him against his will. We rebuke him, as he is obligated by the Torah to eat, and if he does not eat and dies – it is considered as if he has committed suicide, and he has no share in the World to Come. Likewise, there is no difference between a Jewish doctor and a non-Jewish doctor regarding the laws that will be explained, nor is there a difference between a male doctor and a female doctor.

And if he (the patient) says that he needs (to eat), even if one hundred expert doctors say that he does not need (to eat) – we listen to the patient, for "the heart knows the bitterness of its soul." And even if they say that the food will harm him – we listen to the patient (Magen Avraham, section 3, in the name of Radbaz). And even though it is mentioned above in Siman 328 that when the patient says he needs a particular remedy, and the doctor says it will harm him, we listen to the doctor – this is because in matters of medication, the doctor is certainly more knowledgeable. But in the matter of eating – the patient certainly knows more about himself when he says he needs (to eat) (Acharonim). But this is perplexing, for it appears that even not on Yom Kippur, if the patient requests to eat, and the doctor says that the food will harm him – we do not give it to him. And this is the practice every day. For it is also within the doctor's expertise to understand that the food will harm him. And many times we see that the patient requests something that will harm him, and we do not give it to him based on the doctor's instruction. And because it is now Yom Kippur, should it be different?! This is surprising. And it makes sense that when the doctor says he (the patient) does not need (to eat), meaning: that he will live without it – we listen to the patient due to the doubt, since even according to the doctor, the food will not harm him. But when he says that the food will harm him – how can we feed him, even not on Yom Kippur, and all the more so on Yom Kippur? This requires great examination.

It seems to me, in my humble opinion, that the authorities who stated this ruling were not referring to a bedridden patient. For with such a patient, it is obvious that we heed the physician when he says that eating will harm him. This is true even for a regular patient. It is only when the physician says that the food will neither harm nor help, and the patient claims he will be harmed if he does not eat, that our sages stated we should listen to the patient. But not when the physician says that eating will harm him. The statements of the authorities apply to those with ailments who go about in the marketplace, but have a severe pain in the heart, head, or intestines, such as tuberculosis or similar conditions. In these cases, the person himself is more familiar with his own nature than the physician who examines him periodically. The physicians do not have clear laws regarding those with such ailments, as is known. In these cases, we listen to the patient even when the physician says that eating will harm him, because the patient with the ailment is more familiar with his own nature than the physician.

If the sick person says that he does not need to eat, and the doctor says he does need to eat – we listen to the doctor and feed him. The Rambam adds to this by saying: Provided that the doctor is an expert, see there. And I do not know what he means to teach us – for any doctor in this matter is considered an expert, as the Rambam himself initially said: This is a sick person, etc., who asked to eat, even though the expert doctors say, etc., see there. And behold, in the laws that follow regarding doctors against doctors – this condition is not specified, as a general doctor is considered an expert. (And the Maggid Mishneh wrote that he mentioned "expert" because in the Mishnah "experts" are also mentioned, see there. And I am puzzled: for the Rambam also mentioned this earlier, as I have written.)

It appears to me that an important principle is conveyed here. Behold, in the Jerusalem Talmud (Chapter Eight, Halacha 4), it is stated regarding this Mishnah: "A sick person says, 'I can fast,' and a doctor says, 'I do not know'—Rabbi Eleazar in the name of Rabbi Yochanan says: It becomes a matter of doubt concerning life-threatening danger, and in such cases, we are lenient." See there. However, our Talmud does not hold this view, as it maintains that we only listen to the doctor when he says it is necessary, and not in cases of doubt. This is because our Talmud holds that the statement of the sick person carries weight, as he knows his own condition. It is only when the doctor says the opposite that we necessarily attribute it to a loss of reason, as stated in the Gemara. In other words, the sick person is not in his right mind. But when the doctor is uncertain, the sick person's statement is considered definite, and the doctor's doubt does not override his certainty. The Jerusalem Talmud holds that the sick person's statement is insignificant, and therefore, even the doctor's uncertainty constitutes a matter of doubt concerning life-threatening danger. According to the Jerusalem Talmud, even if the doctor is not very knowledgeable, if he says "it is necessary," it still constitutes a doubt concerning life-threatening danger, as his lack of expertise is not worse than the uncertainty of an expert. However, according to our Talmud, this only applies to an expert. Therefore, Maimonides carefully stated: "And he should be an expert doctor," to exclude the view of the Jerusalem Talmud. This is the opinion of Maimonides.

However, the Ramban, the Ran, and the Maggid Mishneh brought this Jerusalem Talmud and ruled accordingly. Similarly, our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 5: If the patient says he does not need [to eat] and the doctor is uncertain – we feed him. But if the doctor says he does not need [to eat] and the patient says, "I don't know" – we do not feed him. This is his exact wording. For the patient's "I don't know" is certainly of no consequence, for how should he know? And now, regarding the law, even though we explained that the Rambam does not hold this way, nevertheless, the law follows the Jerusalem Talmud, since these authorities ruled accordingly, and in cases of doubt regarding life-threatening situations, we are lenient. Therefore, according to what we explained regarding a doctor who is not an expert, when he says "necessary" – it is as if an expert says "I don't know." Therefore, when he says "necessary" – it applies even if he is not an expert. (And the Beit Yosef in section 1 who wrote "expert" – it seems that he does not hold this way. Practically, it seems to me in my humble opinion to be lenient in cases of doubt regarding life-threatening situations. Be precise and you will find leniency.)

If one doctor says that it is necessary [to feed him], and another says that it is not necessary – we feed him, because a doubt about life is judged leniently. The same applies if there are two against two, or three against three. Even if those who say it is not necessary are more expert – we do not consider their opinion, and we feed him. There are those who hold that when the opinions are equal, we follow the more expert ones, even to be stringent (Ran, see Beit Yosef). However, this does not seem to be the opinion of the poskim (decisors), as it is clear that we should follow the more expert opinion leniently, not stringently. This is the opinion of the Ramban, as brought by the Tur, see there (see Magen Avraham, subsection 4, and it seems there is a textual error there). And see in section 13.

And if the sick person, along with one doctor, say that he does not need [to eat on Yom Kippur], and one doctor says that he does need [to eat]; or if the sick person says nothing, but one doctor says that he needs [to eat], and two say that he does not need [to eat] – we do not feed him, for one against two is not considered. However, some say that if the single doctor is exceedingly wise, we follow his words to be lenient, even against many (Magen Avraham, subsection 5 in the name of the Ramban, and Taz, subsection 5). And one should be lenient in cases of doubt regarding the saving of a life.

If two people say "he needs [to eat]" – even if one hundred say he does not need [to eat], and even if the sick person is among those who say he does not need [to eat] – we feed him, because two are considered as one hundred. And since two people say "he needs [to eat]" – nothing can override their words. Similarly, if the sick person, along with one doctor, says he needs [to eat], even if one hundred say he does not need [to eat] – we feed him. We do not say that in such a case, the words of the sick person are meaningless because he is influenced by the doctor. We do not say this. A doctor who says he does not recognize the illness at all – is considered like any other person, and his words mean nothing; they neither add nor detract. This is not comparable to a case of doubt by a doctor, which was explained as when a doctor recognizes the illness but is unsure whether the patient can endure the fast or not. But when he does not recognize the illness – he is not considered a doctor in this context. However, if the patient has weakened greatly, to the extent that most people around him see him as in danger if he does not eat – we feed him. All the more so if the patient is bedridden, he does not need the opinions of others, and he is certainly considered a dangerously ill person, as I have written.

However, the Rambam wrote there: Some doctors say "necessary," and some say "not necessary" – we follow the majority, or the experts, etc. And if the doctors are divided, and they are all experts, and those who say "not necessary" are equal in number to those who say "necessary" – we feed him. Thus far his words, and we learn from his words that there is no difference between a group of two or fewer than two, and there is no difference for him between leniency and stringency, but we always follow the majority or expertise. This means that if they are equal in wisdom – we follow the majority, and if they are equal in number – we follow the more expert. And if on one side there is a majority, and the minority has more experts – it appears that it is considered as half and half, and we go leniently. But the Tur and Shulchan Aruch ruled as I wrote previously. And regarding the law, it is a great principle: whether in a doubt of law, or in a dispute among the decisors – we go leniently in matters of saving a life. (However, it seems to me that in our times, there are doctors called "Feldshers," who do not have government certification to give treatments, and doctors called "Doctors," who do have government certification – the words of the Feldsher are nothing against the words of the Doctor. And perhaps we consider his words leniently if he is an expert in his city, for a doubt in matters of life should be treated leniently.)

The Tur and Shulchan Aruch wrote in Section 7: When feeding a pregnant woman or a sick person, they should be fed little by little to avoid reaching the [prohibited] amount. Therefore, they should be fed about two-thirds of a medium egg, or slightly more, and wait the time it takes to eat four eggs, but not less than the time it takes to eat three eggs. Then they should eat a little more. And so on perpetually, so that they do not eat the amount of a date within the time it takes to eat a "pras" (half a loaf). Regarding drinking, as explained in section 612, where it is measured according to each person's mouthful capacity, the patient’s mouthful capacity should be assessed, and they should drink slightly less than this amount, and wait between each drink the time it takes to eat four or three eggs, but not less than the time it takes to drink a " revi'it" (a quarter of a log). This is according to the opinion of Rambam, as I wrote there, and then they should drink again. And so on perpetually. And we are accustomed to give a measure to the inquirer for both eating and drinking, and we measure the time for "eating a pras" as six or seven minutes.

It is clear that all this applies when this amount suffices for the patient. But if it has been assessed that he needs a lot at once, or the patient himself says so, or there is doubt whether this amount will suffice for him – he is given all that he needs to eat and drink without precise measures. And it is almost known to us that for those bedridden with illness, and similarly for a woman who has given birth – these measures will generally suffice. But for those with tuberculosis, which they call sochatka or dar – their treatment requires eating a lot, and no precise measures are taken with them. 

The Rambam and the Rif did not write this law at all, because it is not found in the Talmud concerning Yom Kippur. Rather, it is in Keritot (13a) concerning a pregnant woman who smelled something forbidden, that she is fed less than the prohibited measure. And from this, the Rosh, the Tur, and the Shulchan Aruch also derived it for the sick. But the Rif and the Rambam hold that this applies only to a pregnant woman who smelled, and for her, the eating is not the main concern, unlike a patient. And regarding a pregnant woman, the Rambam wrote this law in chapter fourteen of Forbidden Foods, law fourteen, see there. And the custom follows the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch. (And we do not follow what the Magen Avraham wrote in subsection 8 in the name of the Bach.)

And one who is seized by bulmus, which is an illness that comes from hunger, and its sign is that his eyes become dim and he cannot see — we feed him until his eyes brighten. And if there is no permissible food available — we feed him forbidden food. And if there are two types of forbidden foods — we feed him the lesser prohibition first. This is explained by the Rambam in Chapter Fourteen, Halacha 16 of Forbidden Foods. And we have explained this in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 85. And if he needs meat, whether we feed him nevelah (carcass) or shechutah (properly slaughtered) — this is explained above in Siman 328.

A sick person who ate on Yom Kippur and has reached a state of mind where he can recite a blessing – must mention Yom Kippur in the Grace After Meals. This means he should say "Ya'aleh V'Yavo" as in the prayer, and he should say it in the "Boneh Yerushalayim" blessing as on any festival. If it falls on Shabbat, he says "Retzei V'hachalitzenu." However, the great later authorities have many doubts about this ruling, for it is not the day that causes the eating, but rather his illness caused it. So why should he mention Yom Kippur in the Grace After Meals (Taz, and Magen Avraham Section 10)? And I do not know how the sick conduct themselves in this matter. However, Kiddush is certainly not required (ibid.).

On the night of Yom Kippur, it is customary that before praying, we grant permission to all transgressors. This is so that we can pray together with them in unity. As we say in Menachot (27a), during the acceptance of a fast and prayers, it is necessary for both the good and the bad to be together in unity, as it is stated: "And His band set upon the earth." And in Keritot (6b) we say: Any fast that does not include the sinners of Israel is not a fast. For indeed, the Chelbana (galbanum) has a bad smell, yet the Torah includes it among the ingredients of the incense.

And how do they permit them? The greatest among the community joins with two others, so that they are considered as the emissaries of the entire community. The greatest says: "In the assembly above and the assembly below, with the consent of the Omnipresent and with the consent of the congregation, we permit to pray with transgressors." This means that the assemblies agree to combine the consent of the Omnipresent with the consent of the congregation to permit them. In some places, the prayer leader says this, and he does not need to join with two others, for he is already the emissary of the community.

Afterward, the prayer leader stands and says "Kol Nidrei" with a melody three times. We have already explained at the end of Yoreh De'ah, section 211, that this does not actually effect anything. Not only in the case of vows and oaths made to others, since one does not swear according to his own intention but according to the intention of the one administering the oath. And certainly in the case of oaths made to the king or government, they cannot be annulled at all. But even in the case of oaths and vows that pertain only to oneself, such as if one vows or swears not to eat meat or to fast, and the like – this is only effective for future vows: any vow that one makes will be null, and he will forget this at the time of making the vow. Since now it is a fixed formula, forgetfulness does not apply to it, and it is only a prayer like all other prayers. It hints that our prayer will be accepted, as explained in the words of the Zohar printed in the machzorim before "Kol Nidrei." The entire prayer is referred to as the "Kol Nidrei" prayer.

According to the opinions of the ancients, the intention is regarding vows from the past, that perhaps they violated them so they would not be punished. Therefore, we immediately say, "And it shall be forgiven to the entire congregation of the children of Israel," as is evident from the language "that I vowed and that I swore," which refers to the past. They used to recite, "from the previous Yom Kippur until this Yom Kippur." Rabbeinu Tam had a difficulty with this: What benefit is there in annulling what has already been violated? Therefore, he explained that it refers to the future: if one vows, it will be nullified. He corrected the wording to "from this Yom Kippur until the coming Yom Kippur." According to this, one would need to say "if I vow and if I swear" in a language referring to the future. And we, who say "that I vowed and that I swore, from this Yom Kippur until the coming Yom Kippur," are creating a contradiction. Therefore, some say quietly, "from the previous Yom Kippur until this Yom Kippur, and from this Yom Kippur until the coming Yom Kippur." And both refer to the past and the future (see Magen Avraham, Taz, and Levush).

And they say it three times, as we find in several matters, such as the reaping of the omer: "This sickle, this sickle, this sickle" (Menachot 65b). Then they say "and it shall be forgiven" three times as well, for the same reason. Also, "And the Lord said, 'I have forgiven according to your word'" three times. The main intention is to serve as a good sign that the Holy One, blessed be He, will forgive our sins. Afterwards, the prayer leader recites the blessing of "Shehecheyanu," as on every festival. According to the law, everyone fulfills their obligation with the prayer leader's blessing when he intends to fulfill it for them and they intend to fulfill it, and they respond "Amen." However, because there are some who do not intend to fulfill their obligation, and some who do not hear the blessing from the prayer leader, the custom is that each person recites the blessing quietly to themselves and finishes before the prayer leader, so they can respond "Amen" to the prayer leader's blessing. Although "Shehecheyanu" is said on every festival, on Yom Kippur it is impossible because it is forbidden to drink it. Giving it to a child is not proper because it would habituate them to something that is established every year, and they might come to do so regularly. This is different from the cup of the circumcision blessing, which is occasional and not regular.

It is customary for everyone to wrap themselves in their tallitot before nightfall and to recite the blessing "to wrap oneself in tzitzit". The "Kol Nidrei" prayer is recited before nightfall, because one may not annul vows on a festival. All the more so if Yom Kippur falls on Shabbat, in which case it is necessary to begin much earlier, as "Psalm for the Sabbath day" must be recited before nightfall. They then wait for Maariv until it becomes dark. It is customary to take out two or three Torah scrolls, which stand around the prayer leader during the recitation of "Kol Nidrei". Some recite the verse "Light is sown for the righteous, and gladness for the upright in heart," in which there are profound matters that cannot be fully explained. The prayer leader raises his voice each time he says the "Kol Nidrei," and the congregation recites it softly along with the prayer leader. The verse "And it shall be forgiven" is first recited three times by the prayer leader, and then by the congregation. After that, the prayer leader says "Please forgive the iniquity of this people..." and when he reaches "And the Lord said, 'I have forgiven according to your word,'" the congregation shouts it three times. The prayer leader then repeats it three times, and recites the Shehecheyanu blessing. No one should deviate from the customary prayers, hymns, and melodies, and one who does so is at a disadvantage.

On the night of Yom Kippur, and on the following morning during Shacharit, we say "Blessed be the name of His glorious kingdom forever and ever" aloud. Throughout the rest of the year, we say it quietly because it is a significant and awe-inspiring praise that the angels recite, and we are not worthy to say it aloud. But now, on Yom Kippur, when we are like angels, we are permitted to say it aloud. It is stated in the Midrash on Parashat Va'etchanan: When Moses ascended to the heavens, he heard the ministering angels praising the Holy One, blessed be He, saying: "Blessed be the name of His glorious kingdom forever and ever." He brought it down to Israel, etc. And our sages of blessed memory alluded to this in the Gemara in Pesachim (56a), see there.

If Yom Kippur falls on Shabbat, we say "Vayechulu" and the blessing "Magen Avot" as on all Shabbats, and conclude with "Mekadesh HaShabbat." We do not mention Yom Kippur in this blessing, as it was not instituted for Yom Kippur. "Avinu Malkeinu" is not recited on Shabbat. However, other piyutim (liturgical poems) and confessions are recited on Shabbat as they are on weekdays, as well as the Thirteen Attributes of Mercy, since it is a day of forgiveness and atonement. This is done only to distinguish that it is Shabbat. "Avinu Malkeinu" has already been recited throughout the Ten Days of Repentance, and it will also be recited during Ne'ilah, hence it is not recited on Ma'ariv and Shacharit on Shabbat.

There are some who stand on their feet all day and all night during the prayers. For those who are weak, it is not possible to do so. Also, the custom to stand when the Ark is opened is difficult for those who are weak, and they can sit. And those who stand all night will not be able to pray during the day, and it should not be done. There are those who customarily sleep in the synagogue and recite songs and praises all night. It is good to sleep far from the Ark, or if the Ark is elevated, to lie down below it. One who does not want to recite songs and praises should not sleep there. Some have the custom to recite "Shir HaYichud" and "Ana'im Zemirot" after Maariv. Cantors who pray all day should not stay awake all night, for they will lose their voice if they do not sleep. Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 4: "One should place one person to the right of the prayer leader and one to his left"; thus are his words. For even on a public fast day, they do so, as I wrote in section 566. And just as with Moses, "Aaron and Hur supported his hands, one on this side and one on that side." All the more so on Yom Kippur. However, our custom is not so; rather, we stand only until "Barechu" and no longer. One may say the reason is: since there is no public fast day outside of the Land [of Israel], as I wrote there, therefore we do not do so even on Yom Kippur.

The translation of the passage:

On Yom Kippur during Shacharit – we pray as usual. It is customary to recite "Shir Hayichud" for that day, "An'im Zemirot," and the Song of the Day – before the prayer. The blessing "Who has provided me with all my needs" is not said. The Rosh, the Ran, and the Tur in Siman 613 disagree with this, see there. Each person can do as he wishes. From the Rambam, it seems that this blessing is not recited. The piyyutim – all follow the custom. What astonishes me: the Rosh at the end of Yoma and the Tur in this Siman brought in the name of the Geonim to say "Vaya'avor" five times during Shacharit. Some say thirteen times corresponding to the thirteen attributes. Some say seven times, and in Musaf seven times, and similarly in Mincha, see there. And we do not mention it even once. There are customs without any basis – and people are careful with them, but this one from the Geonim involving the mention of the thirteen attributes – and they are not careful with it. (And this all arose from the elongation of the melodies, until there is no time left to say Selichot. And the recitation of the thirteen attributes is impossible without saying Selichot. The great Geonim have already cried out against the cantors, but we do not have the power to protest, and may God forgive us.)

The Tur and Shulchan Aruch wrote that it is proper to shorten the poems in the morning service, in order to pray the Musaf prayer before the seventh hour, so that the time for the Mincha prayer does not arrive and they would need to pray it first, as I wrote in Siman 286. The Tur wrote that the Rosh, when he saw that the congregation was prolonging the morning service, would pray Musaf individually, see there. And we are careful about this from the outset. But in retrospect, there is no concern, because many disagree about this, as I wrote there. Especially since there are those who say that this is only because of eating, since it is forbidden to eat once the time for Mincha arrives, as I wrote there, and this does not pertain on Yom Kippur. (And the Magen Avraham brought that the Maharil, when the morning service was delayed, did not say "Avinu Malkeinu".)

On Yom Kippur, six people are called to the Torah. On a festival, five are called, and since Yom Kippur is of higher status, as all labor is forbidden and it is punishable by karet, one more is called. On Shabbat, where the prohibition is punishable by stoning, seven are called, one more than on Yom Kippur (Megillah 22b). Additionally, we find that when Ezra read the Torah on the first day of the seventh month, six stood to his right and six to his left, as explained in Nehemiah (8), and corresponding to this, they instituted six readers (ibid 23a). And even though this was on Rosh Hashanah, nevertheless, since there all of Israel performed great repentance, as explained there, and Yom Kippur is the primary day of repentance, they therefore instituted the same number. (And six symbolizes completeness: the four directions, above and below. Also, repentance is the foundation of the world.)

If Yom Kippur falls on Shabbat, seven people are called up to the Torah, and additional aliyot (call-ups) can be added as on any Shabbat. The Torah reading is "Acharei Mot..." which includes the entire service of Yom Kippur, and the mention of the death of Aaron's sons aids in the atonement of Israel, as the death of the righteous atones. It is appropriate for every person to feel sorrow and shed tears over their death, and anyone who does so can hope that their own children will not die during their lifetime, and their sins will be forgiven (Magen Avraham citing the Zohar and the Ari). The Maftir (additional reading) is "U'Vaasor" from Parashat Pinchas. The Haftarah (prophetic reading) is from Isaiah (57) "And he will say, 'Clear the way, clear the way...'" until "for the mouth of the Lord has spoken," which warns about repentance. Some have written that the Maftir does not conclude with "King who forgives and pardons..." but rather "King over all the earth..." (Levush and Magen Avraham). However, this is not our custom; rather, we conclude as in the prayer, and it is printed this way in the Machzorim (prayer books for the High Holidays). (Some say that additional aliyot beyond seven are not added on Shabbat.)

Circumcision on Yom Kippur – The circumcision is performed between "Yotzer" and Mussaf, after the Torah reading. Following the circumcision, "Ashrei" is recited so that there is something on which to say Kaddish before Mussaf. However, the custom is to perform the circumcision after "Ashrei," and it seems the reason is because the circumcision is done after the Torah scroll is placed back in the ark. Why should the Torah scroll be delayed? Therefore, "Ashrei" is recited as on all Sabbaths and festivals, where "Ashrei" is said before the Torah is returned to the ark. But if the circumcision is indeed performed before the Torah is returned, then "Ashrei" should certainly be recited afterward. If the circumcision is performed outside the synagogue, it is not done until after the Torah scroll is returned. In any case, Kaddish is recited, as many people say several psalms before Mussaf, as well as prayers. The blessing for the circumcision is recited without a cup [of wine], since there is no one to drink it. Some say the blessing is recited over a cup and given to a child, similar to Tisha B'Av, because since it is incidental, there is no concern it will lead to a habitual practice. Others say that on Yom Kippur, one should be strict and not give it to any child, and they fulfill the requirement by giving a little to the mouth of the circumcised infant. (See Magen Avraham at the end of subsection 3, who advises giving the infant a little to drink, in addition to what is given with a finger during the recitation of "By your blood, live." I am puzzled: is a newborn infant even capable of drinking a little? And the Rema wrote that the custom is to fulfill the requirement with the circumcised infant. Nowadays, I believe they give to another child, following the opinion of the author of Minhagim, because otherwise it would be disrespectful to the cup.)

In the Musaf service, the prayer leader recites the order of the Temple service. It is customary to fall on one's face when saying "and the priests…", and similarly, during "Aleinu" one falls. Also, on Rosh Hashanah, the custom is to fall during "Aleinu". However, the prayer leader is forbidden to move from his place to fall on his face, because it is prohibited to move from his place in the middle of the prayer. Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote that one should protest against those who do so. Nevertheless, our custom is that even the prayer leader falls, and they prepare themselves in a way that they do not need to move from their place, and others lift him. During "Aleinu," it is not appropriate for the prayer leader to fall.

It is customary to pledge charity on behalf of the deceased on Yom Kippur. And they mention their souls, for the deceased also have atonement on Yom Kippur. And they ascend to the platform during the Musaf service. The order of confession is: "I have sinned, I have transgressed, I have rebelled." During the service, one first says "Please, Hashem" and then "Please, in the name of Hashem." However, when saying "Before Hashem you shall be purified" – it is said with His name as in Adonai, like all the names. (And in the order of the service of "Amits Koah" there are several things that need correction. See Neshamat Adam, and this is not the place to elaborate.)

We do not recite "Ein Kamocha" (There is none like our God) on Yom Kippur after Musaf. On every Sabbath and festival, it is recited corresponding to the eighteen blessings of the weekday Amidah. However, on Yom Kippur, many praises, such as "Ahallelcha," have already been recited aloud in the piyutim (liturgical poems). Nevertheless, it would be appropriate to say "Pitum ha-Ketoret" (the Incense Offering) (Magen Avraham, Section 1). In any case, this is also unnecessary for one who is accustomed to reciting the passage of the Tamid Offering and the Incense Offering before Mincha, as this will also cover the incense recited after Musaf. According to our master, the Beit Yosef, we do recite "Ashrei" and "Uva L'Tzion" before Mincha, as we do throughout the year, except for the verse "Va'ani Tefilati" (And I, my prayer) which is not said, even when Yom Kippur falls on Shabbat. On all Shabbats, we recite it based on the Midrash that Israel is not preoccupied with eating, and thus we say "Va'ani Tefilati..." On Yom Kippur, this is not relevant. However, our master, the Rema, wrote that we do not recite "Ashrei" and "Uva L'Tzion" before Mincha, but rather before Ne'ilah. This is also our simple custom, to expedite the Mincha prayer. Additionally, it is appropriate to say "Ashrei" and "Uva L'Tzion" in the final prayer of the day.

Before the prayer, we take out a Torah scroll and three men read from "Acharei Mot" about the forbidden relationships, so that one will reflect and repent if he has any sin in this matter. It also hints that the Holy One, blessed be He, should not reveal our nakedness from our sins (Taz). The third reader is the maftir, as in every public fast. We read from Jonah, because it contains the repentance of the people of Nineveh. Additionally, from Jonah, it is clear that it is impossible to flee from God. We conclude with the verses "Who is a God like You," which includes the thirteen attributes of mercy. The reader also blesses before and after, and concludes with "Shield of David." We do not say "for the Torah and for the service," because the service is already completed. Moreover, this is to ensure that it is like other public fasts.

If Yom Kippur falls on Shabbat, the prayers also mention Shabbat, and the conclusion is according to Shabbat (see Taz, subsection 5). The Tur and Beit Yosef believe that in the Maftir, we also say "Al HaTorah" and mention Shabbat when it coincides with Shabbat. However, our custom is entirely different; we do not say "Al HaTorah" in the Maftir, as I have written. Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote that if it falls on Shabbat, we say "Tzidkatecha" and "Avinu Malkeinu." But Rabbeinu Rema wrote that we do not say either "Tzidkatecha" or "Avinu Malkeinu" on Shabbat. Even on a weekday, when it is close to sunset, we do not say "Avinu Malkeinu" in order to hasten the Ne'ilah prayer. We do not perform the priestly blessing during Mincha on Yom Kippur. However, if a Kohen ascended to the platform, he indeed performs the blessing, and we do not remove him because on Yom Kippur it is appropriate to perform the blessing during Mincha, since we are fasting. The Ba'al Halachot Gedolot rules this way, but we do not practice thus, as I have written in Siman 129. Therefore, after the fact, there is no concern. Nevertheless, the prayer leader says "Barechenu" and "Sim Shalom."

Before the Ne'ilah prayer, we say "Ashrei," "Uva L'Tzion," and Kaddish. Those who recite this before Mincha should only say "Ashrei" so that there will be something over which to recite Kaddish. The essence of the Ne'ilah prayer is that on every full public fast day, an additional prayer is added after Mincha, which is called the Ne'ilah prayer, as explained in the fourth chapter of Taanit (26b). However, outside the Land of Israel, we do not have a full public fast day, as I have written in the laws of fasting, and the only time we have the Ne'ilah prayer is on Yom Kippur. As the Rambam writes in the first chapter of the laws of prayer, law 7, and this is his wording: "And they also instituted a prayer after the Mincha prayer on a fast day, close to sunset, to add supplication and request because of the fast. And this is called the Ne'ilah prayer, meaning: the gates of heaven are locked with the setting of the sun, as it is not prayed except near sunset. Thus, the daily prayers are three... and on Yom Kippur, five." This is the end of his wording.

And in the Jerusalem Talmud, the fourth chapter of Berachot (Halacha 1), it states: From where do we derive Ne'ilah? Rabbi Levi said: "Even if you pray more and more" - from here we learn that anyone who increases prayer is answered... And this is referring to communal prayer... When is Ne'ilah? Rav said: At the closing of the gates of heaven. Rabbi Yochanan said: At the closing of the gates of the Temple. Meaning: The closing of the gates of heaven is at the beginning of the night, and the closing of the gates of the Temple is during the day, close to dusk. And the Jerusalem Talmud brings proof for Rabbi Yochanan, see there. Additionally, since Rav and Rabbi Yochanan - the law follows Rabbi Yochanan. If so, why did Rambam rule according to Rav? And conversely, it is not understood: since he ruled the closing of the gates of heaven, how did he rule it close to sunset?

However, in the Jerusalem Talmud there, it questions Rav himself, who would pray Ne'ilah when the sun was at the treetops. And it answers that Rav would prolong his prayer, and he would finish it at the closing of the gates of heaven, see there. Thus, it is explicit that the conclusion should be at the beginning of the night. And since the Rambam wrote that we pray close to sunset, therefore, even for us who do not prolong the prayer — in any case, the conclusion will be at the beginning of the night. And the fact that he ruled like Rav against Rabbi Yochanan is because it is proven in our Talmud that the Ne'ilah prayer concludes at night. Therefore, the Ne'ilah prayer exempts the evening prayer, like Rav. And similarly, the Rif ruled like Rav, as the Ran wrote at the end of Yoma. And even though in the Jerusalem Talmud it does not rule like Rav in this, and also the Rosh at the end of Yoma ruled not like Rav, nevertheless, the Rif and the Rambam rule like Rav. However, the Rif wrote that in any case the custom is to pray Maariv separately, see there. But fundamentally, the law follows Rav.

However, the Rambam himself in the third chapter of Tefillah, at the end of Halacha 5, wrote the following: "And the time for the Ne'ilah prayer is so that it is completed close to sunset." Thus is his language. According to this, it is explained that also in the first chapter his intention is at the end of the prayer, that it should be close to sunset. If so, this is according to Rabbi Yochanan, that it is the closing of the Temple gates. How then did he write "the closing of the heavenly gates"?

One cannot say that the Rambam holds that the closing of the heavenly gates occurs before the closing of the Temple gates (as the Taz suggested in subsection 1), because it is explicitly stated in the Jerusalem Talmud the opposite. See there. Therefore, it seems that the Rambam holds that even close to sunset is called "the closing of the heavenly gates," and the "closing of the Temple gates" happens much earlier. This is also the opinion of our teacher, the Beit Yosef, in subsection 1, who wrote: "The time for the Ne'ilah prayer is when the sun is at the tops of the trees, so that it is completed close to sunset. The prayer leader must shorten the supplications and verses in the middle of the prayer. He should also not extend each word of the Ne'ilah prayer as he does in other prayers, in order to finish before sunset." Thus is his language.

(And the Magen Avraham in subsection 1 wrote that this means the end of sunset, the appearance of the stars. See there. His words are perplexing, for he elaborated and was precise to say before sunset. If according to the words of the Magen Avraham, why did he not write in the language of the Tur? See there.)

The Tur wrote: Its time is close to sunset, when the sun is at the top of the trees. One must be careful not to delay praying it into the night, but rather close to sunset, such that one finishes with the appearance of the stars. These are his words, and this is exactly like Rav. However, it is difficult, for the Rosh ruled according to Rabbi Yochanan at the end of Yoma. Additionally, the sun at the top of the trees is earlier than close to sunset. And there is clear proof of this, as the Jerusalem Talmud says about Rav that because he would extend his prayer significantly, he would begin to pray when the sun was at the top of the trees, and he would finish at the beginning of the night. We learn from this that for other people, this much time is not necessary. And if so, why did the Tur write that one should finish it at the appearance of the stars? Why do we need to begin when the sun is at the top of the trees?

Therefore, it appears in my humble opinion that this is what he meant: Its time is close to sunset, when the sun is at the top of the trees, meaning: one should begin when the sun is at the top of the trees and finish close to sunset. However, one should be careful in any case not to delay praying it into the night. At the very most, one should begin close to sunset and finish by the appearance of the stars. (And regarding the words of the Rosh, one should understand as the Bach wrote: that although he brings the words of the Rambam who ruled according to Rabbi Yochanan, nevertheless, the Rosh ruled according to the Rif. See there. And the words of the Magen Avraham and the Taz are puzzling. And the Taz questioned: Why did the Rema not bring the words of the Tur? See there. And the Rema did well, for the words of the Tur are not properly settled, as I have written. Study and you will find clarity.)

In truth, amongst us, at the time of the silent prayer of the congregation, the sun is always still above the horizon. And regarding the chazzan (prayer leader) extending the prayer until nightfall—there is no concern about this. On the contrary, it is even better, so that the people do not rush to pray Ma'ariv (the evening prayer), since the extension of Yom Kippur is a Torah obligation. Therefore, on the contrary, it is better not to finish before nightfall. And if because of the verse "The sun shall set and disappear," which needs to be said before sunset (as per the Magen Avraham)—there is also no concern if it is said before the appearance of the stars (as per the Eliyahu Rabbah).

In the Ne'ilah prayer, we say "seal us" instead of "inscribe us." If Yom Kippur falls on Shabbat, we mention Shabbat in the Ne'ilah prayer because this day requires the Ne'ilah prayer, making it like all other prayers where Shabbat must be mentioned. However, in the confession that follows the prayer, we do not mention Shabbat. This applies to the silent confession recited after the prayer. But the prayer leader, who recites it within the prayer, does mention Shabbat in the confession. Nevertheless, if he did not mention Shabbat in the confession, he is not required to repeat it. However, in the main prayer, if Shabbat is not mentioned, he must repeat it, as with other prayers. Some also mention Shabbat in the silent confession in the "You have distinguished" passage, and this is printed in prayer books and machzorim, and this is our custom. In the Kedusha, we say "Keter" or "Na'aritzcha" and "Adir Adireinu." According to the law, the priests (Kohanim) should raise their hands and bless the people during Ne'ilah, but the custom in these regions is not to do so. This is appropriate because it usually ends at night, and the priestly blessing is not done at night. We say "Avinu Malkeinu" even if Yom Kippur falls on Shabbat, and we say "seal us" instead of "inscribe us."

And after completing the prayer, we say "Shema Yisrael" out loud, as well as "Baruch Shem Kevod Malchuto Le'olam Va'ed" three times, and "Hashem Hu HaElohim" seven times, to indicate that nature, which is under the influence of time, surrounded by seven days and the seven celestial bodies – all is Hashem and His providence, may He be blessed. If He were to remove His providence even for a moment, the world would revert to chaos. This is to counter the beliefs of heretics. We blow a series of sounds (Tashrat), and in our custom, we blow a single teki'ah. This is a good sign, heralding that the Holy One, blessed be He, has accepted our prayer. We say "Next year in Jerusalem." Even if it is not fully night, but rather twilight, there is no concern in blowing, as it is not a prohibited labor (Tur and Magen Avraham section 4). Some blow after the full Kaddish, and some blow before, and such is our custom. Know that earlier, they were accustomed to spread dry grasses on the floor of the synagogue and the study hall. However, because it raises much dust and was harmful to health, this practice was discontinued. Especially since we do not have stone floors, there is no concern in this.

One prays the evening prayer (Ma'ariv) and recites Havdalah in the blessing of "Chonen HaDa'at." We do not follow the opinion that the Ne'ilah prayer exempts one from the evening prayer. Even those who hold this view in theory — nonetheless, we have accepted upon ourselves to pray the evening prayer separately, as the Rif writes at the end of Yoma, see there. One must also add from the mundane to the holy at its departure, meaning that one should wait a little even after the appearance of the stars. Therefore, on Yom Kippur, one should not hasten to pray Ma'ariv as one does on other fast days. After Ma'ariv, Havdalah is recited in the synagogue over a cup (of wine) to fulfill the obligation for those who do not recite Havdalah at home. There are those who do not recite Havdalah in the synagogue, but this is not a correct practice (Magen Avraham). One does not bless over spices even when Yom Kippur falls on Shabbat because on all Shabbatot, one smells them due to the extra soul that benefits from the Shabbat delicacies, and on Yom Kippur, this is not applicable. However, many great authorities have ruled that if Yom Kippur falls on Shabbat, one does bless over the spices, and this is the widespread custom, and it should not be changed (Magen Avraham section 1, and see Taz section 2).

One must make Havdalah over a candle on the night following Yom Kippur, just as one does on the night following Shabbat. However, the reasons are not the same: on the night following Shabbat, the reason is that fire was created then, as stated in Pesachim (54a). But for Yom Kippur, this reason does not apply; rather, it is because lighting a fire was prohibited all night and all day, and now it is permitted, similar to a blessing over enjoyment. There is a significant difference between Shabbat and Yom Kippur: on the night following Shabbat, one blesses over a new flame that has just been created, like fire produced from wood or stones, as I wrote in Siman 298. This is because its initial creation was on the night following Shabbat, and this fire is also its initial creation. This is not the case on the night following Yom Kippur, as the reason is that we refrained from using fire – therefore, one must bless over a fire that was refrained from use on Yom Kippur, meaning it was lit before Yom Kippur. Similarly, if it was lit permissibly on Yom Kippur, such as for a sick person or a woman in childbirth – one also blesses over it, because in any case, this fire refrained from prohibited work. But over a new fire, one does not bless, as it bears no resemblance to Yom Kippur, since it was not in existence – it does not make sense to say it refrained from prohibited work. Even if Yom Kippur falls on Shabbat – in any case, one needs a fire that refrained from work, to demonstrate the inherent sanctity of the day, as in all other years.

And so, we bless on a light that was kindled from a pre-existing light, because its source is from a pre-existing light. But on a light that was kindled from a new light, we do not bless. And there are those who say that on this we do bless, and this is what our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 4, and this is his language: "And we do not bless on the light that was just now brought out... and there are those who say that we bless on it from the first time and onwards." Until here is his language. Because this is not its original creation. However, it is still puzzling, for is it not yet a pre-existing light? And the Levush wrote that this too is called a pre-existing light, see there, and his words are wondrous to me (and also the Gra did not include this), and see in section 6.

And similarly, if a Jew lit a candle from a non-Jew's candle, one does not recite a blessing over it, for this light has not rested from forbidden labor. And even though the non-Jew is not subject to the prohibition – nevertheless, the very light itself was kindled on Yom Kippur. This is not similar to the candle of a sick person or a woman in childbirth, where it was obligatory to light according to the Torah, due to the necessity of saving a life. And it is also not similar to a light kindled from a new light according to those who say so, since in any case it was not kindled on Yom Kippur (and this answers the question of the Magen Avraham, section 4). And even though on Motzei Shabbat one recites a blessing in such a manner – this is because one blesses over the addition, which is considered like new light. But not on Motzei Yom Kippur, for one does not bless over new light, because on Yom Kippur one only blesses over light that rested or what was kindled from it, for the addition is considered like the main part. And some say further that one does not bless over candles that stood in the synagogue all of Yom Kippur, because they were not made to illuminate, but for honor. However, one blesses over the light kindled from them. But there are those who disagree and say that one does bless over the synagogue candle, since it is light that rested.

And so is the simple custom: If one has at home a candle that was lit from before Yom Kippur, one blesses over it. If he does not have one at home, he blesses over the synagogue candle, or a candle that was lit from it. And many are accustomed to light a candle from the synagogue candle, bring it home, and bless over it. And our teacher, the Rema, wrote in paragraph He: Some say to make Havdalah over the synagogue candle. And some say not to make Havdalah over it, but rather to light another candle from it. And the proper practice is to make Havdalah over both together, meaning to light one candle from the synagogue candle, and not make Havdalah over the synagogue candle alone. Thus far his words. And if it is not possible with both, it is better to make Havdalah on another candle alone, or from the synagogue candle alone (Magen Avraham, small paragraph Zayin). But the custom of the world is to bless over the synagogue candle alone, and it can be said the reason is: that among us, the synagogue candles are also made to provide light.

One might question whether, if one does not have a candle that was lit on Shabbat, nor a candle lit from it, one is completely exempt from the blessing over the light of the fire? Or is this only the case when one can obtain a light that was lit on Shabbat, but not when one cannot obtain it? On Yom Kippur that falls on Shabbat, it is obvious that one recites the blessing over a new light, for it is no less than any other Saturday night. But when it falls on a weekday, there is a question. From the language of the poskim (decisors of Jewish law), it seems clear that one does not recite the blessing. Nevertheless, it seems to me, in my humble opinion, that in this case one can rely on the opinion of those who say in section 3 that when a new light is kindled, one can recite the blessing. Their intention is that in such a situation, one does not need to be concerned about a light that was lit on Shabbat itself, since it is impossible to obtain it. It suffices that one does not recite the blessing over a completely new light, but over a light kindled from it, and this is considered as if it were a light kindled from a light that was lit on Shabbat in a pressing situation.

One eats, drinks, and rejoices on the night after Yom Kippur. Regarding this, it is said: "Go, eat your bread in joy, for God has already accepted your deeds." It is considered somewhat like a holiday. We do not say Tachanun or "Tzidkatecha Tzedek" between Yom Kippur and Sukkot, and all these days are considered days of joy. Those who are meticulous begin immediately to prepare the Sukkah on the night after Yom Kippur, to start the mitzvah right away, fulfilling the verse "They go from strength to strength." And if someone has nothing to do, he should study a bit from Tractate Sukkah or the laws of the Sukkah, and the next day, after Yom Kippur, he should start building the Sukkah immediately. A mitzvah that comes to your hand, do not let it become leavened (i.e., do not delay). The custom is to pray the Shacharit morning prayer early, at dawn, on the day after Yom Kippur, so that there is no opportunity for the Satan to accuse. If someone fasts a "dream fast" on the night after Yom Kippur, he does not need to fast another fast in atonement for fasting. Even though one does not fast on those days, still, fasting in atonement for fasting is only necessary on Shabbat and Yom Tov.

And the reason we do not observe two days of Yom Kippur, like we do with the two days of other holidays in the diaspora, is because we are knowledgeable about the fixing of the calendar. Even when the sanctification of the month was based on the sighting of the moon, we have not found, from the time of Ezra onward, that the month of Elul was extended. Therefore, there is no doubt for us as to which day is Yom Kippur. And we only observe two days of holidays due to the custom of our ancestors, but with Yom Kippur, we have never had the custom to fast for two days because of the danger involved. As it is stated in the Jerusalem Talmud, the first chapter of Tractate Challah: "There they were concerned about fasting for two days. Rav Chisda said: 'Why do you put yourselves in potential danger?' The father of Shmuel fasted for two days and one of his intestines burst, and he died." See there. Nevertheless, there were some of the pious of earlier generations who practiced this way. And whoever has practiced this once needs a release from the vow. However, we have neither heard nor seen anyone who practices this. With the help of Heaven, the laws of Yom Kippur are concluded.

It is a positive commandment from the Torah to dwell in a sukkah for seven days, from the fifteenth of the month of Tishrei until after the twenty-first day of Tishrei, as it is written in the section of Emor (Leviticus 23:34): "On the fifteenth day of this seventh month is the Festival of Sukkot, seven days for the Lord... You shall dwell in sukkot for seven days; every native in Israel shall dwell in sukkot, so that your generations shall know that I made the children of Israel dwell in sukkot when I brought them out of the land of Egypt" (Leviticus 23:42-43).

It is taught in a Baraita (Sukkah 11b): "For I made the children of Israel dwell in booths" – these were clouds of glory, according to Rabbi Eliezer. Rabbi Akiva says: They actually made booths for themselves. According to Rabbi Eliezer, it is certainly appropriate to commemorate this great event, that He surrounded them with clouds of glory. And as they confessed upon their return from exile in Nehemiah (9), they said: "Even though they made for themselves a molten calf... in Your manifold mercies You did not forsake them in the wilderness, the pillar of cloud did not depart from them... and the pillar of fire by night..." For in the clouds of glory there was a true revelation of divinity, as Moses our teacher said in the context of the spies: "As You are seen eye to eye, O Lord, and Your cloud stands over them, and in a pillar of cloud You go before them by day, and in a pillar of fire by night" (Numbers 14:14). But according to Rabbi Akiva, who says the reference is to actual booths – what is significant about this, that the Torah would say "so that your generations will know that I made the children of Israel dwell in booths"? (And Rabbi Akiva holds that a booth is not analogous to the clouds of glory. It is impossible to make clouds of glory, and we do not derive what is possible from what is impossible. And Rabbi Eliezer holds: We do derive. And they follow their respective opinions in Menachot (82a) regarding the tithe in the Passover of Egypt, see there.)

And this is the matter: For this reason, we were commanded to make sukkot (booths) similar to the sukkot they made in the desert, so that through the commandment of the sukkah, the great virtue of Israel in the desert would be revealed and publicized. They were traveling with the burden of men, women, and children, myriad upon myriad, in a place where it is not in human nature to be. As the scripture testifies: "It is not a place of seed." And so the prophet said to Israel: "Was I a wilderness to Israel, or a land of thick darkness?" – meaning: In the desert, I prepared everything for them, and they lacked nothing. And as Moses our teacher said in the portion of Devarim: "He knows your walking through this great desert, these forty years, the Lord your God has been with you; you have lacked nothing." It turns out that the essence of this commandment is the remembrance of the great journey in the desert, where not only was it not a place of seed, but they did not even have permanent houses, only mere sukkot. Therefore, we were commanded to make sukkot similar to them, so that we remember our great virtue from the providence of God upon us after the exodus from Egypt.

And this is the language of the Tur: The Torah linked the commandment of Sukkah to the Exodus from Egypt, as it did with many other commandments, because it is something we saw with our own eyes and heard with our own ears, and no one can deny it. It serves as a testimony to the truth of the existence of the Creator, may He be exalted, who created everything by His will, and who has the power, authority, and ability over the heavens and the earth to do with them as He wishes, just as He did with us when He brought us out of the land of Egypt with signs and wonders. The sukkot refer to the clouds of His glory, which surrounded them to protect them from heat and sun. He commanded us to make sukkot so that we would remember His wonders and His awe-inspiring deeds. And although we left Egypt in the month of Nisan, He did not command us to make a sukkah at that time, because it is the summer season, and everyone makes a sukkah for shade, and it would not be evident that this is for the commandment of the Creator, may He be blessed. Therefore, He commanded us to make it in the seventh month, which is the rainy season, and everyone usually leaves their sukkah and returns home. But we leave our homes to sit in the sukkah, and through this, it is evident to all that the commandment of the King is upon us to do so. Thus far his words. And this is a correct reasoning according to the plain meaning.

And furthermore, a valid reason can be given for why the mitzvah (commandment) is in Tishrei (the seventh month) and not in Nisan (the first month), because He, blessed be He, wanted to show that even though we sin, nonetheless His providence has not departed from us, and we sit in His shade and take refuge under His wings. Just as after the giving of the Torah, they made the Golden Calf, and despite this, the Holy One, blessed be He, was appeased with the second tablets, and this was on Yom Kippur; and after Yom Kippur, He commanded us to make the Tabernacle so that His presence would dwell among us, as it is written: "And I will dwell among the children of Israel"; and He did not remove the clouds of glory from them, as it is written in Nehemiah, which we brought in section 2. Similarly, the Holy One, blessed be He, did for us with this mitzvah for generations, that even though we sin throughout the year, nonetheless on Yom Kippur, He atones for our sins when we repent. A sign of this is that immediately after Yom Kippur, He commanded us to make a sukkah, so that we would sit in the shade of the Holy One, blessed be He, as it is written: "In His shade I delighted and sat" – this refers to the mitzvah of sukkah, "and His fruit was sweet to my taste" – this refers to the mitzvah of the etrog (citron), as our sages of blessed memory said in Midrash Chazit. This demonstrates that after all the sins, He, blessed be He, is with us in love and watches over us to save us from all trouble and harm, and He seats us in His holy and pure shade, and He, blessed be He, shelters us (and therefore "sukkah" in gematria equals the names of God: YHVH and Adonai). One should intend, while sitting in the sukkah, that the Holy One, blessed be He, commanded us to sit in the sukkah as a remembrance of the Exodus from Egypt (Magen Avraham and Bach). This means that even though in all mitzvot, even for those who hold that mitzvot require intention, it is sufficient to intend to fulfill the mitzvah, nonetheless, for the sukkah, the Torah was particular: "So that your generations may know that I made the children of Israel dwell in sukkot when I brought them out of the land of Egypt," and the intention is that at the time of fulfilling the mitzvah, we should know and intend for the reason of the mitzvah, which is a remembrance of the Exodus from Egypt (Machatzit HaShekel). And we have already written in the previous section that it is a mitzvah to prepare and make the sukkah immediately after Yom Kippur, for a mitzvah that comes to your hand, do not delay it, and the diligent precede in performing mitzvot.

A sukkah must be under the open sky. If it is under something else, it is invalid, as it is taught (Sukkah 9b): "You shall dwell in booths"—not in a booth under another booth, not in a booth under a tree, and not in a booth inside a house. The interpretation is because it is written "in booths" without a vav, implying one booth and not two coverings. It is obvious that the one booth must be properly covered, meaning with something detached that does not receive impurity, as will be explained in Siman 629. And its shade must be greater than its sunlight, meaning there must be enough covering so that the shade of the covering is more than the sunlight between them, as will be explained in Siman 631. The law of a sukkah under a sukkah will be explained in Siman 628. The law of a sukkah inside a house does not need further explanation; it is invalid in all cases. However, regarding a sukkah under a tree, there are many details and opinions from our early rabbis, as will be explained with Divine assistance.

Rashi and Tosafot's opinion there is that if the tree's shade is greater than its sunlight, the sukkah is invalid in any case: even if the sukkah’s shade is greater than its sunlight, and even if the sukkah preceded the tree. However, if the tree’s sunlight is greater than its shade, and the sukkah’s shade is greater than its sunlight, it is valid in any case, since this is not considered a sukkah under a tree because the tree does not have the definition of a sukkah. This applies when the sukkah’s shade is greater than its sunlight by itself, not through the combination of the tree. But if the sukkah itself has more sunlight than shade, but together with the tree both would have more shade than sunlight, then if one lowers the tree branches while they are still connected to the tree and mixes them with the valid sukkah covering, and the valid covering is greater than the invalid covering, the invalid is nullified by the valid majority. For from the Torah, anything is nullified by a majority, and the sukkah is valid. But if one does not lower them and they stand by themselves without being mixed, they cannot be nullified by the majority, because anything that stands by itself is not nullified. Thus, there is no valid sukkah here. The Tur brought this view, and this is the first opinion in the Shulchan Aruch, Section 1, see there.

There is a question here: Is it permissible to mix a prohibition from the outset? Behold, if this was done before Sukkot, it is not applicable to call it a prohibition. And even during Sukkot itself, this is not analogous to prohibitions, for it is not a food item but merely a mitzvah, and mitzvot were not given for enjoyment. In this specific case, the Torah permitted fulfilling the obligation of Sukkah with it, and in this specific case, one does not fulfill the obligation with it. It turns out that it is not a prohibition at the time of the mixture, for is one obligated to sit specifically in this Sukkah? Surely one can sit in another. And afterward, when it is mixed, it is permissible to sit in it. Moreover, this is the oral law given to Moses at Sinai, that any Sukkah covering with a majority of valid and a minority of invalid [materials] is permissible to sit in such a Sukkah, and it was permitted to do so. And if one asks: If so, why do we need a majority of valid [materials]? For we maintain to state later in Siman 631 that even equal parts are permissible, as an opening equal to standing is permissible. However, the Ran of blessed memory explained that the matter is as follows: Certainly, an opening equal to standing, when not mixed, is permissible, but when mixed, the importance of the permit is nullified due to the mixture. A majority is needed to consider it significant. And even though the invalid [material] is mixed and its importance is nullified, we seek the importance of the valid [material]. And when it is mixed, its significance is nullified.

One might ask: On the contrary, we required it to be lowered and mixed, and if this was not done, it is invalid. So how can we say that for this very reason it lost its significance? Moreover, a great question arises: Why indeed do we require it to be lowered and mixed? After all, invalid and valid roofing, even if each stands by itself, is valid, as explained in Siman 631 concerning metal spits, where if there is a gap between them equivalent to their width, it is valid. There, the spit stands by itself, and the valid roofing stands by itself.
