However, the matter is thus: Certainly, mixing is not required, and this is how the law was stated, but this is when the invalid material is not completely separated from the valid material, rather they lie together as in Siman 631. But this is not the case with a tree above the roofing, which constitutes another layer of roofing, resulting in roofing under roofing. Therefore, we must necessarily lower it and mix it, for otherwise, it remains as the tree itself, having no connection to the valid roofing. Therefore, mixing is necessary. According to this, the question we raised is not difficult at all: How can one initially nullify a prohibition? On the contrary, here nullification is not needed, and the nullification itself does not cause the permit. Rather, it weakens the force of the permit, for we require the majority. The need for nullification is for a different reason, as I have written. This is not similar to other prohibitions, where the nullification causes the main permit (this seems clear in my humble opinion). And further explanation will be provided in Siman 22. (The Choshen Mishpat rejected what the Rema wrote to be explained in section 6, and according to what I have written, it fits well.)

And furthermore, the Rosh brought a method in the name of the Ra'avan and Ra'avyah, and similarly the Ran wrote according to this method, and it is as follows: Regarding what we said according to the opinion of Rashi and Tosafot, that when there is valid roofing (s'chach) whose shade is greater than its sunlight, and in the case of the tree, its sunlight is greater than its shade – it is valid in every aspect – this is not so. And it means that in this manner it is only valid if the s'chach of the tree is opposite the air between the valid s'chach, for then the validity of the sukkah is through the valid s'chach, in that its shade is greater than its sunlight. But if the s'chach of the tree is opposite the valid s'chach, since the shade of the tree stands above – it nullifies the shade of the valid s'chach below it, as it covers it. Consequently, the primary shade of the sukkah is from the invalid part, and there is no difference whether the tree preceded or the sukkah preceded. And it is not valid when the branches of the tree are opposite the valid s'chach, unless even if the valid s'chach opposite the tree were removed – there would still remain, by this validity alone, its shade greater than its sunlight. And this opinion was also brought by the Tur, and the Shulchan Aruch in the second opinion, see there.

Moreover, according to this opinion, our teacher, the Rema, wrote, and this is his language: "However, if one lowers the branches downward and mixes them with the schach (roofing material for the sukkah) so that they are not distinguishable, they are nullified, and the sukkah is valid. Similarly, if one places invalid schach on top of valid schach, or vice versa, it is called mixing, and it is valid." Until here is his language. This means that actual mixing is not required, as I wrote in section 4. His main intention is that in the law of lowering, this opinion does not differ from the previous opinion. And there are those who wrote that this is specifically when the sukkah's shade is greater even without the tree, and the tree does not join with it, for this is not a complete nullification because it can be removed (Magen Avraham, subsection 4). And these words are puzzling, for it is explicitly proven in the Rosh, Tur, and Shulchan Aruch that in this matter, this opinion does not differ from the previous one. And our teacher, the Rema, precisely said that they were mixed. And this is clearly proven in the Gemara, Rashi, Tosafot, Rosh, and Ran that lowering is considered actual mixing. And also, what he wrote that they are not distinguishable, meaning: they are not distinguishable by themselves, but are placed together—this has no relevance to any mixtures of prohibition within permissibility, as I wrote in section 4. (Also, the Pri Megadim remains in need of investigation on the Magen Avraham, and the Chamad Moshe rejected his words at length, see there. And his words in subsection 2 were not clarified to me at all. And also the Machatzit Hashekel found it difficult, see there. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

And there is another opinion that is not brought in the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, and that is that what we have said, that when the shade of the tree is more than its sunlight, it is invalid in any case, this is only when the tree preceded the sukkah covering. But if the valid sukkah covering preceded the tree, and its shade is more than its sunlight, then the tree that comes afterward does not invalidate it, even if the shade of the tree is also more than its sunlight. And this is the opinion of the Geonim, and the opinion of Rabbeinu Tam regarding the Mishnah that states one spread a sheet over it because of the sun (Sukkah 10a), as Tosafot and the Rosh wrote in their name that the sheet that comes after the valid sukkah covering does not invalidate it, unless the valid covering does not have more shade than sunlight. But when it has more shade than sunlight, then the sheet does not invalidate it, even though the sheet also has more shade than sunlight. And the same rule applies to a tree, that as long as the valid covering precedes, the invalidation does not invalidate it. And it seems to me that even according to this opinion, in any case, a sukkah inside a house, even if the sukkah preceded, is invalid, because there is another invalidation there: that "sukkah" the Merciful One said, and not the house one lives in all year (Rashi Sukkah 14a, s.v. "the dispute"). And also from the derivation of "in sukkahs" - and not under the house.

And it is puzzling regarding the Tur, that here he did not bring this view. On the contrary, he explicitly wrote that there is no difference whether the tree preceded or the sukkah preceded. And later, at the end of Siman 629, regarding the law of spreading a sheet over it, he wrote according to this view; see there. And our teacher, the Beit Yosef, already questioned this in his great book, and he wrote that necessarily the Tur distinguishes between a sheet and a tree, but did not write the distinction; see there. However, the distinction is simple for two reasons: Certainly, even if a tree is invalid in all cases, nevertheless, regarding a sheet, when the valid schach preceded, the sheet is like a sukkah decoration, since it is made to protect from the sun (Bach and Maharil). Additionally, one can distinguish: Even if there is a difference as to which came first, it is only when the valid and invalid are close to each other, like the sheet and the schach. And here, we are discussing where the tree is higher than the schach, and it is a scriptural decree "in booths you shall dwell" – and not in a booth under a tree (Maharsha there, and see Pnei Yehoshua there, that we do not require a height of ten handbreadths).

And the Rambam, of blessed memory, has a completely different approach to this, and this is also the opinion of the Rif, of blessed memory. That is: according to all the opinions that have been explained, if one lowers the branches and mixes them with the valid s'chach, and the valid s'chach is predominant, it is valid, as has been explained. And this is the explanation of what the Gemara said there about "shachbatan," meaning: he lowered them, even if they are still connected to the tree. And the Rambam, in his commentary on the Mishnah, explains "shachbatan" to mean that he cut them from the tree, and then they are nullified by the majority. But if he did not cut them, it is invalid in every situation. 

And behold, Rashi, of blessed memory, brought this explanation and completely rejected it, saying: regardless, if he cut them, they are valid by themselves. Moreover, it is explicitly taught in another Mishnah there (11a) that if he cut them, it is valid, meaning that they themselves are valid s'chach. And the Rambam explains that to validate them by themselves, one needs to shake them due to "you shall make and not from the already made," as will be explained, and this is the cutting mentioned in the Mishnah. But "shachbatan" refers to a situation where he did not shake them, and they were not validated by themselves. Rather, the benefit is that they are nullified by the majority of valid s'chach (Beit Yosef). This is also his opinion in his great work, Chapter Five, Law 12, and this is also the approach of the Rif, of blessed memory. But otherwise, it is invalid in every situation. 

And the Ba’al HaMaor explains "shachbatan" as a term for the beating of the willow, meaning: when he beat the branches to remove their leaves, indicating his intention that they should not be combined with the valid s'chach, then they do not invalidate. But otherwise, it is invalid in every situation. These two opinions are also not brought in the Tur and Shulchan Aruch. Nevertheless, for the sake of the law, each one must be concerned with the words of these Rabbis. (And the Magid Mishneh explained that according to the Rif and the Rambam, the interpretation of "shachbatan" is that he separated them from each other, and when they are mixed, it is invalid, see there. But from the commentary on the Mishnah, it is clearly proven like the words of the Beit Yosef, and this will be further explained. And the Rashba in his novellae wrote like the Maor, see there.)

If one cuts down a tree to make it suitable, with the intention that it itself will be used for the sukkah covering, it is valid. However, this is only if one shakes it, meaning: that one lifts each branch individually and places it for the purpose of providing shade, then lifts another and places it similarly, and so forth for all. If one does not do this, it is invalid because of "you shall make" and not from something that is already made. In other words, anything that is made in an invalid state remains invalid even if the invalidating factor is later corrected. For example, here the invalidity was because it was attached, and one corrected it by cutting it from the tree. Nevertheless, if no action is taken on the sukkah covering itself afterward, it remains made in an invalid state. This principle applies to several commandments. Specifically, when the invalidity is in the substance of the sukkah covering, a new action is required, such as when it is attached or similar cases. However, if the invalidity is due to an external factor to the sukkah covering, such as making a sukkah inside a house or under a tree, and then the house is dismantled or the tree is cut down, no further action is needed on the sukkah covering itself. This is not considered "you shall make" from something already made, since the sukkah itself was made validly, and removing the external invalidity makes it valid. According to this, in our constructed sukkot where we open the roof for the sukkah, if the sukkah covering was placed while the roof was still covered over it, the sukkah covering is not invalidated. One can open the roof and it becomes valid. Nevertheless, ideally, we try to open the roof at the time when we place the sukkah covering. Some are stringent even after the fact (Bach), and see further in section 25.

And know that Rashi, of blessed memory, wrote according to his method that when the tree provides more shade than sun, and the sukkah provides more shade than sun, it is valid. From here we learn that it is permissible to use the reeds of the roof, which are called "latias," even though they are close to each other within less than three handbreadths, as long as their sun is more than their shade. Thus are his words. Meaning, the "latias" built on the roof are invalid as s'chach because they are considered a structure. However, this is like a tree whose sun is more than its shade. And when the s'chach provides more shade than sun, it is valid. And according to this, for the second opinion that it is only valid with a tree if it is opposite the air between the s'chach, or if even upon removing the s'chach that is opposite the tree, it would still provide more shade than sun, then in the case of these "latias," if the s'chach opposite the "latias" is removed and it remains with more sun than shade, it is invalid. And indeed, the Tur wrote thus according to this opinion, as will be explained with Heaven's help.

And this is the language of the Tur, after the words of the Ra'avyah and the Ra'avan who hold this opinion: "Because of this, there are those who are stringent not to make a sukkah inside a house under the roof, even if the tiles have been removed, since the thin beams upon which the tiles rest still remain, even though there is a large space of air between the beams greater than the size of the beams." That is the end of his language. Because all the covering opposite them is invalid, and perhaps when they are removed from the calculation of the covering, there will be more sun than shade. But I do not understand this, since if the air is greater than the beams, it follows that even without this, there would be more shade than sun. And it is possible that although the air is greater than the beams, nevertheless, there are also gaps in the covering of the sukkah, and perhaps in the aggregate, there will be more sun than shade.

And it is further written that our teacher, Rabbi Yechiel, used to practice, when making his sukkah inside the house under the roof, that he would remove the tiles and erect sticks from the sukkah covering to the roof in order to join the two coverings together, so that they would be as one covering. Thus far his words. This means that even according to this opinion, when the branches are lowered, it is valid, and since he erects the sticks, it is as if he lowered them. It follows that the intention is in such a way that the individual tiles are not distinguishable, as it has been explained that they need to be mixed together (Bach, and the Beit Yosef was puzzled by this).

And the Tur himself completely disagrees with this, stating that no correction is needed at all. This is his language: "It appears to me that it is permitted, for even according to the one who invalidates because he did not mix them, this is specifically when there is more shade than sunlight, and nevertheless, there is air between the valid roofing (as I have written). Therefore, when we consider the valid roofing opposite the tree as if it does not exist, it combines with the air there, and the sunlight exceeds the shade. But in a sukkah that is entirely covered, and there is no air at all, even if we consider the valid roofing as if it does not exist, there will still be more shade than sunlight, and it is permitted." And the Baal Ha'itur also permits it for a different reason, saying: "Since he removed the tiles, the remaining wood does not have the status of invalid roofing. As it is taught (Sukkah 15a): 'A roof that does not have plaster, one shakes or removes one from between them.' Until here is his language. And his proof is either from shaking, and here, having removed the tiles, it is like shaking the boards themselves (Beit Yosef); or from removing one from between them, and he holds that the rest are also rendered valid by this removal. And here too, by removing the tiles, the boards are also validated (Bach and Maharlach). And the first opinion holds that shaking is needed for each thing by itself, and by removing one from between them, only that place is validated. And this is proven in the Gemara there. If so, there is no proof from this. (And the Baal Ha'itur holds that in the Gemara it is only according to Rabbi Meir, and not according to Rabbi Yehudah, as the Bach wrote, see there. Examine and you will find it easy.)

However, in practice, our master the Beit Yosef ruled this way in paragraph 3, and this is his wording: "One who makes a sukkah inside a house, under a roof from which the tiles have been removed, even though the thin wooden planks that the tiles rest on remain – it is valid." Thus far his wording. And it seems to me clearly, in my humble opinion, that our master the Beit Yosef agreed to this ruling based on the reasoning of the Tur: since even if the lattes (thin wooden planks) are removed – there will still be more shade than sun. And if so, the removal of the lattes is not necessary for the removal of the tiles as per the words of the Itur. And there are those who understood his intent to mean that the reason is due to the removal of the tiles. Therefore, if previously there were lattes without a roof – they have the status of invalid schach (roof covering of a sukkah) (Magen Avraham, small section 6). And in my humble opinion, even with the removal of the tiles, it would be considered invalid schach, for perhaps the law follows the first opinion, as I wrote. However, the permission is that even if it is invalid schach – there will still be more shade than sun without the place of the lattes, according to the Tur's opinion as I wrote. (And regarding his objection to the Bach, who required there to be more than three handbreadths between the lattes – surely this is correct, for we do not say "lavud" (the halachic principle that gaps less than three handbreadths are considered closed) to be stringent. However, the main intent of the Bach is not to rely on the Itur's permission, see there. But the permission of the Tur is straightforward and clear, and only in this manner does the Beit Yosef permit. And the Taz in small section 3 elaborated to refute, and innovated that the prohibition of the lattes is due to the issue of two roofs, see there. And his words are puzzling, for what relevance is there to the issue of two roofs with thin wooden planks? And his words were already refuted by the author of Chemed Moshe, see there. Be precise and you will find clarity.)

And know that all the laws that were explained regarding a sukkah under a tree, according to the methods that were explained – all of this originates from the Mishnah which states that one who makes a sukkah under a tree, it is as if he made it inside the house. The Gemara clarifies that this applies when the tree's shade is greater, for then in any case it is invalid. However, when the tree’s sunlight is greater and one lowered it down – it is valid. The explanation of "lowered": According to Rashi, Tosafot, the Rosh, and the Tur – the intention is that one lowered the branches down and mixed them with the s’chach (roofing). According to the Rambam, the explanation is that he cut them off. According to the Maor, the explanation is when he shook the leaves off the branches. The Rashba, in his commentary, agreed with this and wrote that this is also how the Geonim explained it. There are those who wanted to say that the Rambam’s intention is also like the Maor (Pnei Moshe on the Jerusalem Talmud there), but it does not appear so. And also our teacher, the Beit Yosef, in his great book and in Kesef Mishneh did not explain it thus, but as I have written. (And the Maggid Mishneh explains the Rambam like Rashi and Tosafot, which is not understood at all. And see Lechem Mishneh. Be precise and you will find ease.)

And behold, we have further learned in the Mishnah (Sukkah 11:1): If one raised a vine or a gourd over the sukkah and covered it with schach (the roofing material for the sukkah) – it is invalid. But if there was much schach more than them, or if he cut them – it is valid. And the Gemara brought this Mishnah in the context of under a tree, and it also explained that when is it valid if there was much schach more than them? Specifically when he shook them. According to Rashi, Tosafot, and the Rosh, shaking, and according to the Rambam, cutting, and according to the Me'or and the Rashba, shaking the leaves. One should not challenge the Rambam with the question: does it not state "or if he cut them" – implying that beforehand the intention was without cutting. And indeed, they challenged him thus. However, he, of blessed memory, explained in his commentary on the Mishnah that the explanation is as follows: that "or if he cut them" explained there in the Gemara requires also shaking, for otherwise, it is invalid due to "make and not from what is made." And if so, the beginning refers to cutting without shaking. And this "or if he cut them" refers to with shaking. And it is possible to explain the matter, that behold, without shaking, the cutting is not so noticeable, obviously. And this is what it means by "or if he cut them," meaning that the cutting is noticeable, which is through shaking.

And there is a great question in this: since the two Mishnayot are essentially the same matter, why do we need both? Indeed, according to the opinion of Rabbeinu Tam and the Geonim which we brought in section 7, this works out well, as the Rashba and Ran wrote, that Rabbeinu Tam derived from this a distinction between when the tree preceded the covering, where we require the conditions that have been explained, and when the covering preceded the tree, where even if the tree's shade is greater than its sunlight, it is still valid. This is why the Mishnah precisely states: "if one stretched a vine over it... and covered it" – indicating that the vine came first. But if the covering came first, it is valid. And in such a case, this Mishnah about the tree also refers to when the tree came first. Thus, it teaches us something significant that we wouldn't have known so clearly from the first Mishnah. The Rashba and Ran refuted his words, see there. And as the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch ruled, there is no difference whether the tree preceded or the covering preceded, as explained. But if so, it is difficult: why do we need both? Indeed, the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch did not bring this Mishnah of stretching a vine over it at all, because it contains no novelty. And it is difficult: why do we need both?

Here is the translation of the provided passage:

And behold, in the Gemara (9b) on the Mishnah of "under the tree," as it establishes "when they are bound," it questions: "Isn't this also taught in the case of 'he raised [the vine] etc.'?" And it answers: "What might you have thought? That this applies only after the fact, but not ideally? It comes to teach us [that it applies ideally as well]." Meaning: from the Mishnah of "he raised [the vine]" we only hear that it applies after the fact. But from the Mishnah of "under the tree," we know it even ideally; see there in Rashi. According to this, it might seem that for this reason, we need two Mishnayot. But it is impossible to say so. For since it first taught us that it is also permitted ideally, all the more so after the fact. And it is difficult to say that we learned this from the redundancy of the Mishnah, for that is not the way of the Mishnayot. Furthermore, if so, how do we know to be precise in Rabbeinu Tam's ruling? Perhaps it only applies ideally and after the fact? Rather, certainly there is some new law in this.

Therefore, it seems to me in my humble opinion that, on the contrary, the majority of our sages understand this Mishnah to teach us that there is no difference whether the tree preceded the roofing or the roofing preceded the tree, contrary to the words of Rabbeinu Tam, of blessed memory. For behold, the Rashba and the Ran explained the Mishnah which states: "If one spread a vine or a gourd over it and thatched on top of it" – it is as if it says "or thatched on top of it." Meaning, if one spread it on top of the roofing, where the roofing came first, or thatched on top of it, where the tree came first, it is all the same, see there. And this is what this Mishnah innovates. For the previous Mishnah, which states "One who makes his sukkah under a tree," clearly implies that the tree came first. And so that you do not say that if the sukkah came first it is valid in every case, it teaches us that it is not so, and that the law is the same in all cases.

And behold, the Rambam there wrote two mishnayot, and this is his language: "One who makes his sukkah under a tree, it is as if he made it inside the house. If he raised [the branches of] the tree and its twigs and covered [the sukkah] on top of them, and afterward cut them, if the valid covering was more than them – it is kosher. And if the covering that was initially valid was not more than them – he needs to shake them after cutting them, so that it is made for the sake of the sukkah. If he mixed something that can be used for covering with something that cannot be used for covering, and covered with both, even though the valid part is more than the invalid part – it is invalid. If he covered with this separately and with that separately, side by side... and in one place there is not a width of three handbreadths of covering – it is invalid." End of his language.

According to the Rambam, both Mishnayot (teachings) are necessary. In the first Mishnah, it teaches us that under the tree, the sukkah is invalid in any case, even if the sukkah's shade is greater than its sunlight, and the tree's sunlight is greater, since the branches were not cut down. And this, which is explained in the Gemara as when they are pressed down, which for the Rambam means they are cut down, does not refer to the Mishnah but to the statement of Rava there (and what the Gemara questions about having already learned 'if he spread' – also refers to Rava, as Rashi writes). The second Mishnah teaches us that when the branches are cut down and the sukkah covering is more than them, it is valid, but if they themselves are still not valid, because of "you shall make" and not from what is made. And if the covering is not more, it needs to be shaken to make them themselves valid. And then it says: He mixed something that can be used for covering, etc. This law is not mentioned anywhere in the Gemara, but the Rambam himself came to explain how we said that even if the tree's sunlight is greater and the sukkah's shade is greater, it is invalid when not cut down? And we have established that when there is an equal amount of open space and standing space, it is permitted, and at most when something can come in and out, as will be explained. If so, why is it invalid here? To this, the Rambam answers that this is when the valid part is by itself and the invalid part is by itself, not when they are mixed together, meaning both are under each other. And the reason for the matter seems to me: This law was said to Moses at Sinai also regarding partitions. Just as in partitions, the standing part is by itself and the open part is by itself, so too with the covering. Only when they are cut down and not shaken, where the invalidity is only because of "you shall make" and not from what is made, in this they were lenient to follow the majority (and in this all the words of the Rambam are explained and justified).

From everything that has been explained, we learn that a mixture of invalid sukkah covering (s'chach) with valid sukkah covering is not comparable to all other mixtures of prohibition with permissibility. For in those cases, the more it is mixed and not recognizable, the better it is for nullification, whereas with s'chach, it is exactly the opposite. According to the Rambam, it is entirely invalid when they are mixed together, as I have written. And even according to other commentators, who explain "beating" as lowering and nullifying, it is still worse than without the mixture, for when there is a gap as large as what stands, in a mixture, we require a majority, as I have written in section 3 in the name of the Ran, not like the words of those who say here the matter of nullification. It has also been explained that there is no difference whether the invalid is placed on the valid, or the valid on the invalid, as in the Mishnah of a sukkah under a tree where the invalid is on the valid, and in the Mishnah of one who spreads, where the valid is on the invalid, and they have one and the same law. And this is according to the words of our teacher the Rema, which we brought in section 6, and not like the words of those who rejected his words (and maybe this is the reason for the second Mishnah).

Rabbeinu the Rema writes at the end of this chapter: It is also permissible to make a sukkah under roofs that are made to open and close. And it is permissible to close them because of the rain and to open them again. And even on Yom Tov, it is permissible to close and open them if they have hinges that allow them to open and close, and there is no issue of building and demolishing a tent on Yom Tov, nor of "you shall make" and not from what is made. However, one should be careful not to sit under them when they are closed, as then the sukkah is invalid. Thus far are his words. And the reason is that any roof that opens by means of hinges is considered merely as a door. And it appears to me that even according to the opinion of Rabbeinu Tam and the Geonim, which we mentioned in section 4, that any time the valid skhakh (roof covering of the sukkah) precedes the invalidation, the invalidation does not invalidate it even if its shade is more than its sunlight. And here, if they placed the skhakh while the roof was open as usual, then the valid skhakh preceded. Nevertheless, when the roof is closed, it is invalid, as this is like a sukkah inside a house, which is invalid because of the scriptural decree "You shall dwell in sukkot" and not in a house of all the days of the year, and not because of invalid skhakh over valid skhakh alone.

Now, we have already written in section 10 that anything which is not in the s’chach itself is not subject to the principle of "ta'aseh v'lo min ha'asuy" (you shall make it, and not from what is made). Therefore, it is permissible to place the s’chach even when the roof is not open. See there. 

However, there is an opinion that even here, one must specifically place the s’chach when the roof is open, because only when the roof is completely removed afterwards is this considered an actual action, and not when it is merely opened, as this is not considered an action. This opinion does not differentiate between when the invalidity is in the s’chach itself or not in the s’chach, as is the opinion of our teacher, the Rema. Rather, in all cases, the principle of "ta'aseh v'lo min ha'asuy" applies. However, by completely removing the roof, it is now considered a complete action to render it valid. And it cannot be said that this is not from what is made in the case of invalidity because this is not a past action, but now it is a complete action. This is not the case with merely opening the roof. Therefore, one must be careful to only place the s’chach when the roof is open, and this is the custom and should not be changed. If one placed the s’chach when the roof was closed, one should reopen it and shake all the s’chach, which means to lift it and place it again.

Some leading authorities have stated that when the roof of the sukkah is opened, as is customary among us, the open roof should not be positioned in the middle of the s'chach (thatched covering), but rather on the side. Their reasoning is based on the Talmudic statement (Sukkah 14b): "If one turns the boards on their sides, it is invalid." This means that a board that is four handbreadths wide, even if turned on its side, is still forbidden to use as s'chach due to the rabbinic decree against using roofing materials. As I will explain at the end of Siman 629, if so, here the entire width of the open roof standing on its side is considered as if it is placed on the roof (as brought in the Pri Megadim, cited in Shaarei Teshuvah). However, this is not the customary practice, and the reasoning is not correct, for the entire prohibition is due to the decree against using roofing materials, as will be explained there. Since the person is engaged in nullifying the roof, and thus opens it, the decree against using roofing materials does not apply. This is not the case when one uses them as s'chach, where the decree applies. (There is evidence for this from the Talmudic statement (Sukkah 15a): "They disagree regarding nullifying the roof." According to Rabbi Yehudah in the opinion of Beit Hillel, since it is nullified, there is no longer a need for the decree, as Rashi explains. All the more so in this case where one raises it and places it on its side so that only the valid s'chach remains, there is no reason for a decree even according to those who disagree. Certainly, the law follows Rabbi Yehudah in the opinion of Beit Hillel. Examine this and you will find it clear.)

Just as the sukkah must be under the open sky, as I wrote in the previous section, so too must the person who sits and sleeps in the sukkah be under the air of the sukkah and not under another air that interrupts between the sukkah and the person. Therefore, the Sages taught in the Mishnah (beginning of the second chapter): One who sleeps under a bed in the sukkah has not fulfilled his obligation. And we establish in the Gemara that this is when the bed is ten tefachim high, as it is considered a significant tent on its own, and one who sleeps under the tent of the bed is not under the tent of the sukkah. But when it is not ten tefachim high, we do not worry about it because it is not considered a significant tent. And even though it is considered a tent for many things even if it is less than ten tefachim high when it is one tefach wide, such as for impurity and similar matters, and an ordinary bed is one tefach wide or more – nevertheless, this is not considered a complete tent to nullify the tent of the sukkah, except if it is ten tefachim high, as it is explicitly stated in the Talmud (beginning of the second chapter). And although in the Jerusalem Talmud it clearly implies that even if it is not ten tefachim high, nevertheless, in our Talmud, it is not so.

And know that there are some of the early authorities who said that this is only rabbinic, but from the Torah law — he has fulfilled his obligation, for the covering of the bed does not nullify the covering of the sukkah (Baal HaMaor). However, this is not the opinion of the Rif and the Rosh, who wrote that it is like a sukkah within a sukkah. So too wrote the Rambam. And certainly, their intention is not that this is exactly the law of a sukkah within a sukkah, for a sukkah within a sukkah is derived from a verse. Rather, their intention is that the invalidity under the bed is from the Torah law, similar to the invalidity of a sukkah within a sukkah. And so wrote the Ramban in Milchamot, see there (and see Taz, subsection 1, and Bach).

And one who sleeps on a bed under a canopy, which are curtains spread around the bed and also attached above like a roof, if it is not ten handbreadths high, even though it has a roof that is one handbreadth wide, or if it does not have a roof that is one handbreadth wide, even though it is ten handbreadths high – it is not considered a separate tent and does not create a separation between the sukkah and the person. But when it is ten handbreadths high and the roof is one handbreadth wide, it is considered a tent like the bed and creates a separation, and one who sleeps under it has not fulfilled his obligation from the Torah. The general rule of a tent is that it should not be less than a handbreadth wide, and for it to be considered a significant tent, it must be ten handbreadths high. And why did we not specify the bed in terms of a width of one handbreadth? Because there is no bed less than a handbreadth wide.

And know that even though the roof does not have a width of a tefach, if it gradually widens until it reaches a width of a tefach within less than three handbreadths close to the roof at a height, it is considered as if the roof has a width of a tefach. For anything less than three handbreadths is considered as lavud (connected). But if it is more than three, or exactly three, we do not consider it. And the walls of the canopy that we mentioned are ten handbreadths high—this is only when they reach the ground within less than three handbreadths, which is considered lavud. But if they are three handbreadths high from the ground, it seems to me that it is not considered a tent, for it is not better than a partition. (This seems to be my humble opinion. And the words of the Magen Avraham in subsection 1 have no resolution, as the Pri Megadim wrote. And from the Bach it implies that it should not be higher than a tefach from the ground, see there. And the Chemed Moshe disagrees about less than three close to the roof being a tefach, see there. But this is not the main point, rather as I wrote. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

The wood poles that extend from the four corners of the bed, which are fixed to the bed, and upon which they spread a sheet like a canopy, and are called in the language of the Mishnah (Sukkah 10a) "kinof" – it is forbidden to sleep under it, even if it is not ten handbreadths high, because it is fixed (as stated in the Gemara there). It is considered a tent that nullifies the tent of the sukkah. However, if the poles do not extend from the four corners of the bed, but rather there is one pole in the middle of the bed at its head, and one pole in the middle of the bed at its foot, and a sheet is spread over them, and it is called in the language of the Gemara "naklitein"; that is, they place rods from one to the other, and they do not have a width of a handbreadth at the top, and the sheet that is spread over the rods is not ten handbreadths above the ground – it is permitted to sleep under it. But when it is ten handbreadths high – it is forbidden, even if it does not have a width of a handbreadth. It is not comparable to a canopy, which is not fixed, even though the bed itself is certainly fixed. And with all this, we require two conditions: a height of ten handbreadths and a width of a handbreadth. It is not comparable, for the bed is not made as a tent for what is beneath it, but rather to sleep upon it. This is not the case with these, which are made as a tent for what is beneath them.

Based on this, it is explained that there are three types of curtains: a canopy (kilah), supports (naklitin), and a mosquito net (kinofet). A canopy, which is not fixed, is only forbidden under two conditions: if it has a roof of a handbreadth, and if it is ten handbreadths high. Supports are more fixed than a canopy, and therefore, even if they do not have a roof of a handbreadth, if they are ten handbreadths high, it is forbidden to sleep under them. A mosquito net, which is fixed and has a roof, even if it is not ten handbreadths high, it is forbidden to sleep under it (Ran, first chapter). This is also explicitly stated in the Gemara (11a). However, the Rif and the Rambam permitted even supports, even if they are ten handbreadths high, because they do not have a roof of a handbreadth. The commentators have already labored over their words, as this goes against the Talmudic discussion. They also permitted a mosquito net if it is not ten handbreadths high. All of this is against the Talmudic discussion and requires great examination. (See Maggid Mishneh there, who wrote that this Talmudic discussion was dismissed from the law. Also see Lechem Mishneh there, Chapter 5, Laws 23 and 24).

It is permissible to hang decorated curtains and decorated sheets in the sukkah for decoration, whether around the walls or under the s’chach, even though they are invalid for use as s’chach. It is permissible to sit under them. They are not considered an intervening tent, since they are there for decoration—they are nullified in relation to the s’chach, provided they are within four handbreadths of the s’chach. However, if they are more than four handbreadths away, they are not nullified in relation to the s’chach, as I will write in siman 632. Therefore, if one spreads a sheet under the s’chach for decoration, if it is within four handbreadths of the roof, it is valid. If it is more than four handbreadths from the roof, it is invalid. If it is not for decoration, even if it is within four handbreadths, it is invalid. Therefore, one must be careful not to place any decoration under the s’chach except within four handbreadths of the s’chach, even with something that does not pose a concern of an intervening tent, so that no one will hang something that does pose such a concern. The Maharil was careful about this, though many are not careful, since according to the law it is permissible (Taz, small section 5).

It is a scriptural decree that a sukkah under another sukkah, even though the upper one is valid, nevertheless the lower one is invalid because it is a sukkah under a sukkah. As it is written, "You shall dwell in sukkot," and it is written "in sukkot" without a vav, to tell you: you shall dwell in one sukkah, and not in a sukkah under another sukkah. Therefore, in the case of a sukkah under another sukkah: the upper one is valid, and the lower one is invalid. And we do not say: just as the upper one invalidates the lower one, so too the lower one should invalidate the upper one because it is a sukkah on top of another sukkah. It is not so, for the Torah invalidates a sukkah under another sukkah, not a sukkah on top of another sukkah. And the reason for this matter: the main part of the sukkah is the sekhakh (roof covering), and the Torah invalidates two roof coverings, not two grounds. And the lower sekhakh to the upper one is considered like the ground, since one treads upon it.

It is obvious that when does the upper sukkah invalidate the lower one? When it is properly covered, its shade is greater than its sunlight; and it has walls, and it has the dimensions of a sukkah. For if not – it is not a sukkah, to invalidate the lower because of a sukkah beneath a sukkah. Additionally, the Sages said (10a) that the lower one must be able to support the cushions and blankets of the upper one. For if not, what kind of sukkah is the upper one, since it is not suitable for use? However, even if it cannot support them comfortably, but only with difficulty – it still invalidates, because a sukkah is a temporary dwelling, and regarding a temporary dwelling, even use with difficulty is considered use. Likewise, the upper one must be at least ten handbreadths above the lower one, for less than this, it does not have the status of a sukkah, since it is not suitable for use at all.

And if there are not ten handbreadths between them, or if the upper one cannot hold cushions and pillows – the lower one is valid, if it is covered properly, with more shade than sun. Even if the upper covering is above twenty cubits, which disqualifies a sukkah, as I will write in section 733. And even though it is explained in section 726 that if there is invalid covering above the valid covering – it invalidates the sukkah, this is when the invalidity is in the covering itself. But here, the covering is valid, only it stands above the place where it is valid – it is not considered as truly invalid covering that would invalidate the lower sukkah because of invalid covering. However, this is only when the lower sukkah does not need the upper one for its validity. But when it needs it, for example, if by itself it has more sun than shade, and only with the addition of the upper one does it have more shade than sun – then certainly the upper one must also be within twenty cubits.

One who makes his sukkah on top of a wagon or on top of a ship, even though it is a temporary structure, nevertheless the sukkah is valid, because a sukkah is meant to be a temporary dwelling. However, we require in any case that it be able to withstand a typical land wind. Because if not, it is nothing, for the wind will come and uproot it. But if it can withstand a typical land wind, even though it cannot withstand a typical sea wind, because at sea the wind is stronger, and a typical sea wind is not common on land, nevertheless the sukkah is valid even if the ship is moving on the sea, because a typical sea wind does not blow at all times.

One who makes his sukkah on the back of a camel, or on the top of a tree, where in both cases it is forbidden to make use of them on Yom Tov, nevertheless the sukkah is valid. However, one may not go up to it on Yom Tov. For the prohibition of using animals and things attached [to the ground] is rabbinic, and from the Torah's perspective, it is a valid sukkah: even if we say that a sukkah must be fit for all seven days, and even if the sukkah itself stands on the ground, but the branches of the schach (roofing) are supported by the tree – it is forbidden, as a decree lest one place his belongings on the schach. Therefore, in a place where it is not customary to use the schach – it is permitted in such a manner (Magen Avraham, subsection 6). And if not all of the sukkah is on the tree, but part of it is supported by the tree and part by another object, if it is such that if the tree is removed it would still remain standing and not fall – one may go up to it on Yom Tov. And if not – one may not go up to it on Yom Tov.

The covering (s'chach) must be made from something that does not receive impurity and grows from the ground, such as wood, leaves, branches, straw, and stubble. We learn this from what is written: "The festival of Sukkot you shall make... from your threshing floor and from your winepress." This means the waste from the threshing floor, which is straw and stubble, and the waste from the winepress, which is vine branches. "From your threshing floor" – but not the threshing floor itself, "from your winepress" – but not the winepress itself, because the grain and the grapes receive impurity. Similarly, we find in Nehemiah (8) when they returned from exile and made Sukkot, it is written: "Go out to the mountain and bring olive branches, and oil tree branches, and myrtle branches, and palm branches... to make Sukkot as it is written" (Gemara 12a).

And know that there is a doubt in our northern regions, where it often snows during the festival of Sukkot, and a lot of snow falls on the Sukkah's covering (s'chach), whether the Sukkah becomes invalid because of this or not? I have seen someone write that it remains valid, because snow does not form a barrier against impurity (Ohalot, Chapter 4, Mishnah 5), and therefore it is not considered a roof over the Sukkah (Be'er Heitev and Sha'arei Teshuvah on Siman 626, Se'if 1). And I say that there is no proof from this, for even seeds and vegetables attached to the ground are mentioned there as not forming a barrier, yet they certainly invalidate the Sukkah. The reason snow does not form a barrier is because it does not last. But at the time, it certainly nullifies the s'chach. However, one might say it does not invalidate for another reason, as snow does not receive impurity, as stated in Niddah (17a). And the Mordechai in the sixth chapter of Chullin writes in the name of a Gaon that one covers with snow, as it is written: "For He says to the snow, 'Be on the earth,'" see there – thus it is like growing from the earth and does not receive impurity. However, our teacher the Beit Yosef in Tur Yoreh De'ah, at the end of Siman 28, rejects this, see there. Therefore, it seems to me that when the snow accumulates on the s'chach, one should not recite the blessing "to dwell in the Sukkah."

Animals, even though regarding tithing they are referred to as products of the ground, as we say at the beginning of "B'chol Ma'arvin" – nevertheless, their growth is not from the ground, since they do not sprout from the ground. Therefore, we do not cover with their hides, even when they do not yet receive impurity, such as when they have not yet been processed. Similarly, we do not cover with earth, and with all types of metals that are mined from the ground, but their growth is not from the ground.

In the case of ordinary wood that is not fashioned into utensils, one may use them for sechach (roofing material for a sukkah). However, when they are made into utensils, they become susceptible to impurity. As for simple wooden vessels, some of them are susceptible to impurity by rabbinic decree and cannot be used for sechach, whereas those that are not susceptible to impurity even by rabbinic decree can be used for sechach. This means that those which only serve human use, like a ladder or a hanger, are completely pure. However, those that serve both humans and vessels, such as a table or a baker's board, are susceptible to impurity, as Rambam writes in Chapter Four of Hilchot Keilim, and as our teachers the Tosafists explain in Sukkah (5a). It appears that those which are susceptible to impurity by rabbinic decree are invalid by rabbinic law and not by Torah law. The practical difference regarding a doubt in this matter is that one would be lenient in cases of doubt, following the principle of leniency in rabbinic doubts.

According to this, it appears that one may use wooden vessels that can hold more than forty se'ah for schach, as they do not become impure. Likewise, all those mentioned in the twenty-fourth chapter of Keilim with three measurements, where the last measurement is completely pure—if they are made of wood or cloth, they may be used for schach. However, vessels that have broken in a manner that purifies them from their impurity cannot be used for schach, since they originated from something that can become impure. This is also stated in the Gemara (16a): if one uses worn-out vessels, which refers to rags smaller than three by three [fingerbreadths], which do not become impure, it is invalid because they come from something that can become impure. Consequently, the same applies to all vessels. The Rambam, at the beginning of the fifth chapter, wrote that the reason is that one might use fragments that are not yet purified; see there. According to this, the invalidation is rabbinic. It seems to me that if one deliberately purifies it for the sake of schach, it is permitted to use it for schach. There is proof from what will be explained in section 23, where an act (which contradicts this rule) is effective, and according to what I have written, it makes sense.

This is what we have learned in the Mishnah (Sukkah 15a): If one roofs his sukkah with skewers or with the boards of a bed, if there is a gap between them equivalent to their size, it is valid. The skewers and the boards themselves are invalid, for the skewers are made of metal, and all metal is invalid for roofing, and the boards of the bed are pieces of the bed. The Mishnah informs us that whether it is an invalidation from the Torah or an invalidation from the Rabbis, they are equal. And even though the Gemara establishes it with a long board and two legs, which themselves can contract impurity – this is according to the attempt to reject the law that roofing with worn-out utensils is invalid. Refer there. But in truth, this is not necessary, and therefore Rambam, of blessed memory, did not mention them. (And the Tur Orach Chaim 629 and the Shulchan Aruch in section 2 that mentioned skewers and bed boards – they used the language of the Mishnah, and the skewers are made of metal. And what the Beit Yosef questioned, that if so, it mentioned it unnecessarily, as iron is invalid in any case, and the Taz in section 2 also wrote this, and the Bach struggled with this – I do not understand the difficulty. The Mishnah informs us of the law that iron is invalid, and the Tur uses the language of the Mishnah. And it seems to me that this is the intention of the Magen Avraham in section 1. Therefore, the Beit Yosef's question remains unresolved, refer there. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

There is a wooden case that is connected to iron arrows, and there are cases that are hollow and the arrows are placed inside them, and there are those that are not hollow, and the arrows are inserted into the receptacle of the arrow. These are valid for use as sukkah covering, as long as the arrows have not been inserted into the receptacle. But once they have been inserted – they become invalid, even if they are later removed, because once they have been connected to the arrow – they have received impurity, and therefore they remain invalid forever, like worn-out utensils that we have mentioned. And those that are hollow, since they have a receptacle – they are impure, and one may not use them as sukkah covering. (And the Tosafot on Yevamot 12b, in the commentary beginning with "in the holes," wrote that it is somewhat surprising: since it is made to be filled, it should be considered unfinished wooden utensils that are pure, like the handle of a knife before the iron is placed. So far their words. But I have not merited to understand, for how do our Rabbis know that the handle of a knife does not become impure? And it is explained in the Rambam in the fifth chapter of Utensils that if only the form of the utensil is completed, even if it is not finished – it is impure. And it is explicitly stated in the Mishnah at the end of the twelfth chapter of Utensils that all unfinished wooden utensils are impure, except those of the ash tree, meaning: when they are not completely finished. And similarly in Chullin 25a where it counts unfinished wooden utensils that are deficient in the body of the utensil, see there. This needs investigation.)

Any vessel that was not made to contain, such as a gutter, as well as a natural receptacle, like hollow reeds and the like, and are not intended to contain – are pure, and one may use them for covering (Magen Avraham §2). If one covers with flax that has not been combed or beaten – it is valid, for it is simply wood. But if it has been combed and beaten – it is invalid, for although it still does not receive impurity, it is close to being spun, which would make it susceptible to impurity, and the Rabbis decreed upon it (Taz §6). The Rambam wrote that the reason is because its form has changed – it is considered as if it is no longer grown from the ground. According to this, also cotton and hemp, if combed and beaten – one may not cover with them (Bach and Magen Avraham §3). There are those who wrote the reason is because they are suitable to be placed in pillows and cushions (there in the name of the Ran). Therefore, also the refuse that falls from flax – one may not cover with them for this reason (there).

If one covers the sukkah with linen ropes, it is invalid. Even though ropes do not accept impurity, nevertheless, since they do not retain their natural form, they are considered as not growing from the ground (Maggid Mishneh). However, those made of reed or palm fibers are valid, as these have not changed their form. This is from the Jerusalem Talmud. Mats that are fit for lying upon – it is obvious that one does not use them for covering the sukkah, as they can become impure with the impurity of treading. But those that are not fit for lying upon – one may use them for covering.

This is the language of the Rambam there, Halacha 6: A mat of reeds, or a mat of bulrushes, or a small mat made of rushes – its default purpose is for lying down, therefore one may not use it for roofing a sukkah, unless it was made specifically for roofing. But a large mat – its default purpose is for roofing, therefore one may use it for roofing a sukkah, unless it was made for lying down. And if it has a rim – even if it is large, one may not use it for roofing, because it is considered a vessel. And even if its rim is removed – one may not use it for roofing, because it is considered as broken vessels. Up to here is his language. And the rim, even if it is very small, as long as it surrounds [the mat] – it is considered suitable for holding (Kesef Mishneh from Rashi at the end of the first chapter, see there).

The Raavad, of blessed memory, ruled that if it is made in a braided and woven manner – even if it is small, it can be used for schach, because it is not suitable for lying upon. The Rambam does not differentiate in this matter. This is also the opinion of the Tur, who wrote: Whether it is woven and smooth and suitable for lying upon, or whether it is made in a chain-like manner, which is not smooth and not so suitable for lying upon. If it is small – it is generally meant for lying upon, etc. Thus are his words. Their reasoning is that even something made in a braided and woven manner can be used for lying upon in a pressing situation, as is evident from his wording, where he wrote that it is not so suitable for lying upon – this clearly implies that in a pressing situation one can lie upon it. However, if it is truly not suitable for lying upon at all – it is obvious that they also agree that even if it is small, it can be used for schach.

And what is called "made it for reclining," "made it for roofing"? The Rosh explained that it depends on the custom of the place, as Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote in paragraph 6, that most of the people in the city make it for roofing or reclining, and it does not depend on the individual himself. However, this is certainly the case where there is no known custom – it depends on his intention, whether his intention was for reclining or for roofing. And generally, there is a difference between a small and a large one, and between one that has a wall and one that does not have a wall. But if he made it for roofing – it is explicit that even if it has a wall, it can be used for roofing. (See Taz, subsection 7, and it is not an objection, see there.)

There are those who have written that in these places, mats are generally made for lying upon (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 5). However, among us, this is not the case, as all mats are made for wrapping merchandise. Yet, by law, it appears that they are considered for lying upon since they are made to receive merchandise, and thus function as a receptacle. Even though they are currently flat, when they are used to wrap merchandise, they are made into a receptacle. Nevertheless, they are ultimately made to receive items. Therefore, it is clear that one should not use them for sukkah roofing. Even old mats that have been torn are considered like worn-out vessels. Hence, it is invalid to use mats for sukkah roofing.

Rabbeinu Rema wrote: In a place where the custom is to fix mats on roofs, like a ceiling, one should not use them for sukkah roofing. This is his language, meaning even large ones that are not meant for lying upon, since they are made for a ceiling, we decree that one might come to sit under the ceiling of the house. Consequently, the same rule applies among us, where thin planks are made into ceilings called 'gantes' or 'shindlen', it is forbidden to use them for sukkah roofing, lest one comes to sit under the house ceiling (Taz, subparagraph 7). Therefore, we have never heard of anyone using thin wood or boards for sukkah roofing, since they are used to make roofs. And although by Torah law they are fit, nevertheless, they should not be used due to the decree concerning a ceiling, meaning one might come to sit under the house ceiling. (However, if one is in a remote place where it is impossible to use other materials, one should use thin planks and not neglect the mitzvah of sukkah, since by law they are fit. See paragraph 32.)

In our region, some people use woven reeds, called palofeskes, for the roofing of the sukkah, and it is obvious that they are fit for use. However, there are some of them that are used to make the walls and bottoms of wagons, and they are invalid for roofing, since they are made for sitting and become impure by treading. Therefore, one must warn against using these woven materials from the wagons for the roofing of the sukkah. They are invalid according to Torah law. Even those made specifically for the wagons are invalid for roofing, like the small mats that were explained. And even if they are generally made for the wagons, they are invalid, like the mats. One must be very careful about this because in our region, most of the wagons are made from this material.

The author of Terumat HaDeshen (Siman 90) wrote: It appears that it is permissible to use even all of the sukkah's covering with our ladders, as they are not invalid covering: even though they are vessels, they do not receive impurity, since they do not have a receptacle, etc. For it is taught in Torat Kohanim: a ladder and a hanger, even though one ascends and descends with them, they do not become impure through treading. And the reason is explained that they are not made for the benefit of treading, but only for ascending and descending. And so it is stated in Tosafot, etc. Thus far is his wording.

In the responsa of the Rashba (Part I, Siman 195), it is written: "You asked about a movable ladder, if it is permissible to use it for s'chach (roofing for a sukkah) etc. Answer: This ladder, if it is made to be moved like a sack, and its legs are perforated to receive the ends of the rungs – it appears that it is susceptible to impurity, for a receptacle that is made to be filled is considered a receptacle, etc. And the ladder mentioned in Torat Kohanim, etc., and similarly in the Tosefta, etc., that are pure – it appears that they do not have a receptacle, but rather their rungs are fixed upon their legs. Thus far his language. According to this, he does not disagree with the Terumat HaDeshen, for the Terumat HaDeshen is discussing when it does not have a receptacle, or like our standard ladders, where the carving in the legs is hollow from side to side, and this is not considered a receptacle. And even if it were considered a receptacle according to the Rambam in the second chapter of Keilim – it would not be considered a receptacle. The Rashba disagrees with him. And behold, Rashi in Sanhedrin (68a) also holds like the Rambam, and the Tosafot in Sukkah (12b) hold like the Rashba. See there. However, in any case, our ladders that are perforated from side to side – certainly according to all opinions it is permissible to use them for s'chach (and so it appears from the Magen Avraham, Siman Katan 8)."

According to this, I am puzzled by our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, in section 7, who wrote: "There is uncertainty whether it is permitted to place a ladder on the roof to use it for s'chach (roofing material for a sukkah). Therefore, one should not use it for s'chach. Even placing it on the s'chach to support it is forbidden. The same applies to any vessel that can become ritually impure, such as a bench or chair, which can become impure through treading." This is their language, and I do not understand the source of the doubt: if the ladder is a receptacle, it is certainly invalid for s'chach. If it has holes from side to side, or if the rungs are on the sides, it is certainly valid for s'chach. The commentators on the Shulchan Aruch (Taz section 9 and Magen Avraham section 8) wrote that the doubt arises with a ladder that is not a receptacle, but perhaps the Rabbis did not differentiate and prohibited all ladders. This is perplexing: is it possible to decree prohibitions based on our own reasoning? Furthermore, later in section 18 of the Shulchan Aruch, it is explained that it is permitted to use boards less than four handbreadths wide, even if they are smoothed and similar to vessels, and we do not decree against them because of vessels. Certainly, we do not decree against a ladder because of another ladder (the Magen Avraham himself hints at this, as written in Machatzit Hashekel). Moreover, on Yom Tov, there are ladders that are forbidden to move and those that are permitted to move, as I wrote in Siman 518, and we do not decree against one ladder because of another. Why then should we decree here? (However, in the name of the prohibition is rabbinic.)

However, in truth, it appears from their words that they are not discussing the law of roofing with ladders at all. Rather, they are referring to a ladder that is prohibited for roofing because it has a receptacle, and regarding roofing on top of it due to the issue of supporting with an object that can become impure. The point of doubt is because most authorities have rejected this issue of supporting with an object that can become impure. The authors of the Shulchan Aruch themselves ruled in this very siman, in section 8, that it is permitted to connect the beams with iron nails. And similarly, later in the end of siman 630, they ruled that it is permitted to support with an object that can become impure. However, here, it is more forbidden because there the supports are on the side and not so noticeable. This is not the case here, where the support is along the entire length of the roofing, below or above to hold it, and it is as if it is an essential part of the roofing. And so it is with any vessel that can become impure. The commentators of the Shulchan Aruch (Taz section 10 and Magen Avraham section 9) wrote that the doubt is because the ladder itself is the roofing, and it is four handbreadths wide, and four handbreadths of invalid roofing invalidates in the middle, as they wrote in siman 630. And they themselves rejected this, since this is only when there is no valid sukkah left, as explained there (Taz there). Furthermore, between each rung there is much air. And there are those who say the reason is because of supporting with an object that can become impure. And what was permitted later – that is only after the fact, but initially it is forbidden (Magen Avraham there). And it is surprising: because later it also refers to initially. But in any case, in my humble opinion, the law seems to be that with our ladders that are carved from side to side – it is permitted to roof with them, and all the more so to place them on the roofing or under the roofing. And those rungs that are placed in stables, in which they put food for the horses and animals, called zalab – it is obvious that they are receptacles and can become impure, and it is forbidden to roof with them. (And I did not understand the view of the Taz, who first wrote that the ladder itself is the roofing, and then in section 11 wrote because of supporting, and because of observers who might come to make them the body of the roofing, see there. This is a new decree that we have not heard of. The clear understanding is as I have written. Examine and find it easy.)

And if it is permitted to use an object that is susceptible to impurity: Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, ruled in Section 8 that it is permitted, and this is his language: "To connect the poles of the sukkah with an iron nail or to tie it with worn-out garments that are susceptible to impurity — there is no concern." This is his language, and he ruled similarly at the end of Section 630; see there, as this is the opinion of most authorities. Similarly, in the Jerusalem Talmud, Chapter Two, this matter is completely dismissed, as there is no prohibition to use an object that is susceptible to impurity. Similarly, the Rosh wrote and elaborated on this. This is the opinion of most of our rabbis. (Except for the Ran, who ruled it is prohibited due to a decree that people might say: just as it is permitted to support [the sukkah] with them, so too, it is permitted to use them as the roofing. The Bach elaborated that it is a Biblical prohibition and brought proof from Rashi. I find this surprising: Even if it were so, Rashi did not rule according to Rabbi Yose. Similarly, it appears from the responsa of the Rashba, Section 195, who ruled that a ladder does not invalidate the roofing. And what the Bach wrote, that he follows the approach of Rabbeinu Tam, who differentiates between before placing valid roofing and invalid roofing, see there – his words are puzzling: For the Rashba explicitly rejected Rabbeinu Tam's approach in his novellae on the Mishnah that discusses one who draped a vine over it, as I wrote in Section 626. And since even according to the Ran it is only a rabbinical prohibition, and most authorities and the Jerusalem Talmud do not hold this way, why should we be stringent? Moreover, there are many difficulties with this approach, and they had to force themselves into strained interpretations, as the Beit Yosef and the Bach themselves wrote. And since this is also the conclusion of our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch and the later authorities — we should not be stringent about this.)

All types of food that are fit for human consumption receive impurity and cannot be used as sukkah covering. However, animal feed does not receive impurity. This is how we derive it in Torat Kohanim: "Of all the food… it will become impure" – food that is specifically for humans, excluding animal feed. Therefore, straw and stubble, although they are fit for animal consumption, can be used as sukkah covering. They are the primary materials for sukkah covering, as we derive from the verse "from your threshing floor and from your winepress."

There is a question: since all foods before being wetted do not receive impurity, then it should be permitted to use foods that have not been wetted as sukkah covering? The answer is: since they only lack impurity due to a secondary reason, it cannot be said that they do not receive impurity, for they do receive impurity through water and a creeping creature. Moreover, how can one use such materials for covering, and after an hour rain will fall and render them completely invalid? Rather, it is certain that their disqualification is from the Torah, just like any item that receives impurity.

Branches of a fig tree with figs on them, and grapevine branches with grapes on them: if the waste is greater than the food, one may use them for schach (roofing for a sukkah), but if not, one may not use them (Baraita 13b). One should not question the Rambam, who ruled in Chapter 5, Law 13: If one mixed something that can be used for schach with something that cannot be used for schach, even though the permissible material is greater than the forbidden material, it is invalid, as I wrote in Siman 626. How then do we follow the majority here? One can say that what the Rambam wrote there applies when each item is separate and then they were combined to be used for schach, for the reason we wrote there. However, if they were together from the start, the minority is nullified by the majority, as it is throughout the Torah. Proof is from the verse "from your threshing floor and from your winepress," for surely in the waste of the threshing floor there are some edible grains, and similarly in the waste of the winepress? Rather, it is certain that we follow the majority in such a manner.

We hold that there is a concept of "yad" (handle) for impurity, meaning: if the food requires a handle outside of the food itself, the handle has the same status as the food and can also receive impurity. We derive this from a verse at the beginning of the chapter "The Hide and the Broth" (Chullin 118). Therefore, if one harvests grain for food, and the food requires the stalks to be able to hold the food, the handle has the status of food and can receive impurity. There needs to be enough waste material to nullify both the food and the handle. The handle cannot be more than three handbreadths for grain and all harvested items, as stated in the first chapter of Uktzin. It is clarified there that the handle of dates is four handbreadths, and for clusters of grapes, there is no measure for the handle. Some say that we should enact decrees for these as for those (Magen Avraham, subsection 12). I do not understand why we need to make decrees from our own reasoning. This is also explicitly evident from the responsa of the Rosh, section 24.

And when does it have a handle? When it was cut for food. But if it was cut for roofing – it does not have a handle, because it was not cut for the sake of food. And on the contrary, the handle combines with the rest to nullify the food by majority, as I have written. And if it was cut for food, and one changed their mind to use it for roofing – we maintain that regarding impurity, a change of thought does not remove the impurity unless an action is taken. Therefore, an action must be taken to make it evident to all that it is for roofing and not for eating. For example, one should thresh them to remove the grain. Consequently, it does not need a handle. And our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, wrote in section 11: One may use for roofing the plant called “pigon” which is called in Arabic “shomer,” and it is animal feed, and people do not eat it except for medicinal purposes. So far his words. And we do not know what this is, but from their words we learn that even though people eat it for medicinal purposes – it is not considered food at all. For people also take bitter things for medicine, but does that make them considered food?

Later in Siman 632, it will be explained that invalid schach (roofing material for a sukkah) invalidates the sukkah with four tefachim (handbreadths). Air is more stringent than this, as it invalidates the sukkah with three tefachim. The sages have said that if one covers part of the sukkah with vegetables that dry quickly within the seven days of the festival and fall, leaving air space, and they are invalid for schach because they are susceptible to impurity, their status is not like that of invalid schach which requires four tefachim to invalidate the sukkah, but rather they are considered as air space and invalidate with three tefachim. If their nature is not to dry within the seven days of the festival, their status is like that of invalid schach and they invalidate only with four tefachim, even if they will dry out after the festival. And when do we judge them as if they are dry immediately, even when they are still moist, and not just when they begin to dry out a bit? Rather, anything that tends to dry within the seven days of the festival is immediately judged as air and invalidates, whether in the middle of the sukkah or at the sides, with three tefachim. Also, valid schach that will not last all seven days is invalid. (And this is the intention of the Rema in section 12, for if not, what is he teaching us? The author’s intention is also the same, as I have written. Be precise and you will find it easy.) And further explanations will be provided in Siman 630, section 3; refer there.

Anything connected to the ground is invalid as s’chach (roofing for the sukkah), as it is written: "When you gather from your threshing floor and your winepress" – when you gather them from the ground and detach them, and not when they are still connected to the ground. Something that was detached and then reattached is valid as s’chach (Beit Yosef and Bach, end of Siman 626 in the name of Terumat HaDeshen). And even though for the matter of slaughtering it is considered as if it is connected, as I wrote in Yoreh De’ah Siman 6, nevertheless, since for the matter of the preparation of seeds and gentiles it is considered as detached, as it is stated in Chullin (16a), regarding the sukkah it is also considered as detached (and so wrote the Magen Avraham in this Siman, subsection 11).

There are things that the Sages prohibited for use as sukkah covering (schach) initially, even though they are fit for use as schach, but they have a bad smell. There are types of grasses that are not suitable for consumption and do not become impure, but they have a bad odor, and we are concerned that one will not be able to sit in the sukkah because of the bad smell. Similarly, there are branches from which the leaves constantly fall, even though they still provide more shade than sunlight, but people cannot tolerate the falling leaves, and we are concerned that one might leave the sukkah. All this applies initially. However, if it was already done – it is valid. Similarly, anything that is valid by Torah law, but the Sages decreed against it – certainly, initially, one should not sit in it, but if one does sit – he has fulfilled the mitzvah of sukkah. And know: this that one should not sit when the leaves are falling – this is when they fall by themselves. But if they only fall when the wind blows them – there is no problem. (See Tosafot Sukkah 3a s.v. "d'amar," and Berakhot 11a s.v. "tani." This is only according to Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel. Indeed, from there, there is proof for one who examines it well. Be precise and you will find it easy.) (And similarly, proof from Magen Avraham, section 22.)

And behold, with reeds—it is permitted to use them for roofing [a sukkah]. Nevertheless, the Rabbis prohibited roofing with a bundle of reeds, which means that there are twenty-five reeds in one tied bundle. The reason for this is that all roofing of a sukkah, even though it does not require that it be placed specifically for the commandment of the sukkah, still requires that the intention be for providing shade, to sit under it and protect from the sun, as will be explained in Siman 635. However, if one placed them to dry or for merchandise, and afterward wants to fulfill the commandment of sukkah with them—it is invalid according to the Torah, and it requires a new act of making. Therefore, the Sages said that a bundle of reeds is customarily placed on the roof to dry, and afterward one might decide to use it for a sukkah, and it is invalid because of "you shall make" and not from something that was made invalidly. Therefore, they prohibited even placing the bundle for the purpose of the commandment of sukkah, due to a decree lest one place it to dry, and afterward sit in it for the purpose of the commandment of sukkah.

And so said the Sages (12a, and in the Jerusalem Talmud there) that any bundle which is less than twenty-five reeds – one may use it for sechach (roofing of the sukkah), because it is not customary to dry them in a bundle of less than twenty-five reeds. But if it has twenty-five reeds – it is forbidden to use it for sechach. And this is specifically when the bundle is tied at both ends, such that it is easy to carry it, or tied in the middle. But if it is tied at one of the two ends – it is not considered a bundle, and it is permitted to use it for sechach, because it is not fit to be carried in such a way that they may fall. And likewise: this is specifically when the reeds are completely separate from one another. But if twenty-five reeds or more come from one stalk, and at the other end they separate from each other, and they are bound there – it is not called a bundle, since their base is one. However, if he bound even one more reed with them, and bound them – they are all called a bundle because of that one reed. The reason it is not called a bundle is because binding one thing is not considered binding. Therefore, when there is another reed with them – it is indeed considered binding. And also any bundle whose tying is not for a long time, but for a short period, in order to sell them by number, and immediately when the buyer purchases them he unties the binding – it is not called a bundle, and one may use it for sechach. For there is no decree to dry them, as it is not customary to dry such reeds on the roof.

Any bundle that was gathered to be dried, and afterwards one wants to use it for the purpose of sukkah covering (schach) – it does not suffice to merely untie it from its binding. Since it is invalid by Torah law due to the principle of "you shall make, and not from that which is made" – this is not considered making by merely untying it. Rather, one must untie it and then shake each and every stalk individually. However, if one placed the bundle for the purpose of sukkah covering, which by Torah law is valid, but the Rabbis decreed otherwise as previously explained – then merely untying it is sufficient.
