One may use boards for the sukkah covering (s'chach) if they are not four handbreadths wide. According to Torah law, this is permitted, but the Sages decreed against it because otherwise, one might say: "What difference is there between these and the ceilings of a house?" This would invalidate the sukkah according to Torah law, for the Torah commanded to make a sukkah, not a house that is used all year round. However, they only decreed against boards that are four handbreadths wide because the typical width of house ceilings is not less than four handbreadths. Even if one places them on their sides, so there is no width of four handbreadths, nonetheless, such a board is invalid for s'chach in any manner that one places it, and it becomes like iron spits. But if they are not four handbreadths wide, one may use them for s'chach even if they are smooth, planed, and shaped so that they are fit for use and resemble utensils; nevertheless, they may be used for s'chach.

And the reason for this matter: since they grow from the ground, and they do not contract impurity as is the law with simple wooden vessels. And even though simple wooden vessels that are suitable for use receive impurity by rabbinic decree and are also invalid for use as sukkah covering as I have written, this applies to very broad ones, like tables and baker's boards, which are used for complete uses. But those less than four [handbreadths wide], which are not suitable for complete use, only for light use, do not receive impurity. And also the impurity of medras (impurity from being sat or stepped on) does not apply to boards that were not made for medras, nor designated for sitting or use. For if they are designated for sitting, they are invalid by Torah law. And if they are designated for use, they are invalid by rabbinic decree. Even though they are only for light use, nevertheless, they were designated for use, and they are like simple broad wooden vessels that receive impurity by rabbinic decree. (See Taz, subsection 20, that even intention does not suffice for medras, but rather an action, to fix it in a place where it is needed, see there. And I am astonished: are boards not suitable for sitting without any adjustment, and are they worse than palm branches on Shabbat 50a, see there. And consequently, it suffices to contract impurity with mere thought, and it is not relevant to all that he brought. And there in Shabbat 49b it is clearly implied that boards are generally for use, see there. Analyze and you will find light.)

Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote in Section 18, regarding wooden boards, that it is customary not to use boards at all for roofing [a sukkah]. Thus are his words. And this custom is based on the essential law, for nowadays it is customary to build houses with boards less than four or three [handbreadths wide]. Therefore, it is obvious that there is a decree concerning roofs. Hence, we have never heard in our days to roof with boards, even short ones, as I wrote in Section 13. Likewise, with "latos" and any type of wood. Therefore, those who roof with small, decorated boards – the sages do not approve of them. All the more so, one should not roof with shingles. However, in a place where it is impossible to obtain other roofing material, it is necessary to roof with boards less than four handbreadths wide. But one should not fix them with nails, for in such a manner it is a complete house, and invalid according to Torah law. (See Magen Avraham, Subsection 22, and Eliyah Rabbah, Subsection 15, in the name of Agudah, who ruled as I have written).

The Sages taught in the Mishnah (10:1): If one spreads a sheet over it because of the sun, or beneath it because of falling leaves – it is invalid. And it is stated in the Gemara that specifically for falling leaves it is invalid, but if it is for decoration – it is valid. Rashi and Rambam explain it straightforwardly. However, Tosafot and the Rosh write that if the sheet is to prevent the sun from shining on it, or to prevent leaves and twigs from falling – it is no worse than for decoration, since his intention is not for roofing. And here it is discussing a case where without the sheet, the sun would dry out the roofing, and its sunlight would be more than its shade. And similarly, beneath it because of falling leaves. Without the sheet, the leaves would fall, and it would result in more sunlight than shade. And since the sheet helps make the sukkah valid – therefore it is invalid. But for decoration – it is valid, since without the sheet, its shade would still be more than its sunlight.

According to Rashi and Rambam, if the reason is to beautify the sukkah, there is another reason: because the beauty of the sukkah within four tefachim (handbreadths) close to the s'chach (roofing) is nullified to the sukkah and is not considered a separate entity, as I wrote at the end of Siman 627. But if it is to protect from the sun or falling leaves, it is considered an interruption, and he is not sitting in the shade of the sukkah. Tosafot and the Rosh hold that these too are for beautification, and nullified to the sukkah. According to their opinion, all of this refers to within four tefachim close to the s'chach, because if not, in any case it is invalid. This is also true according to Rashi and Rambam.

The view of the Geonim is that if the valid s'chach precedes the sheet, the sheet does not invalidate it, similar to their opinion regarding a sukkah under a tree in Siman 626. The Rosh, although he disagrees with them there, teaches here that if it is to protect from the sun or falling leaves, it is considered for beautification, and not because the s'chach precedes. According to this, even if the sheet came first, it is valid, just like for beautification, as there is certainly no difference. Also according to the Geonim, even if the sheet is four tefachim away from the s'chach, it is valid if the s'chach precedes, but according to the Rosh, this is not the case. (This seems to be my humble opinion on this matter, and it resolves well the question of the Beit Yosef on the Tur regarding a tree, see there.)

Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, in section 19, brought two interpretations. The Tur only brought the words of the Tosafot and the Rosh. Afterwards, they wrote as follows: "However, one should not do this initially, unless it is evident to everyone that the intention is to provide protection, or if one is immersed in water, then it is clear to everyone that he is not spreading it there except to dry." This is their wording. And to provide protection, it must be evident to all, such as when the sun reaches the place where he is sitting. Even if it is not during a meal, he should not spread it when there is no clear indication. During a meal, even if there is a clear indication, it is not proper (Magen Avraham, subsection 125), as one can tolerate such a brief period. However, if rain is dripping into the sukkah and it is impossible to eat there, and he is able to spread a sheet, it is better to spread a sheet than to eat outside of the sukkah. Nevertheless, he should not recite the blessing "to dwell in the sukkah," for two reasons: Firstly, because he is exempt according to the law. Secondly, because since the sheet acts as an interruption, he is not sitting under the shade of the sukkah according to Rashi and the Rambam, as this is like being in the sun and rain.

All the disqualifications apply only to the sechach (roof covering), and not to the walls of the sukkah, as the walls can be made of any material. Similarly, regarding the amount of sunlight versus shade – it is valid for the walls. In the glosses of the Rosh (Chapter 1, Siman 24), it is found in these words: According to the Jerusalem Talmud, one must be careful not to make walls from something that can become ritually impure or that does not grow from the ground. Thus are his words. Similarly, it is found in the Or Zarua (Siman 289), and these are his words: Jerusalem Talmud: Rabbi Levi in the name of Rabbi Chama: It is written, "And you shall cover the Ark with the cover" – from here we learn that the wall is called 'sechach', from here we learn that walls should be made from something that does not become ritually impure. According to this, we must explain that which is taught in the Mishnah (12a): bundles of straw... and all are valid for walls – this is specifically concerning bundles of straw, etc., that are valid from the Torah, etc. According to this, it would be necessary to be careful not to make the walls from something that can become ritually impure, and does not grow from the ground. Thus are his words. Aside from the fact that this is not found in any halachic authority, and on the contrary, they all explicitly write the opposite, I am further puzzled: the Mishnah explicitly states (24b): One who makes his sukkah among the trees, and the trees are the walls for it – it is valid. And behold, something attached (to the ground) is invalid from the Torah, as is proven from the Mishnah about a sukkah under a tree! And this requires great examination. Concerning the Jerusalem Talmud, there is no difficulty, as will be explained with the help of Heaven.

Now, before us is the version in the Jerusalem Talmud (Chapter 1, Halacha 6): From here, we learn that one can make walls from something that can become ritually impure. Certainly, this version is perplexing, and the commentators have struggled to explain it, and there is no rationale in their words. Certainly, the primary version is with something that cannot become ritually impure, as the Or Zarua stated. Nevertheless, it is not difficult at all, for in our Talmud (7b) it is taught: The Rabbis taught: "Its shade should be from the roofing, not from the walls." Rabbi Yoshiya says: "Even from the walls." What is Rabbi Yoshiya's reasoning? Because it is written: "And you shall screen the Ark with the curtain" – the curtain is a partition, and the Merciful One called it a covering, hence we require a partition like the roofing. And the Rabbis? That is for bending it slightly. And the law follows the Rabbis. Thus, it turns out that the Jerusalem Talmud follows Rabbi Yoshiya, who derives it from this verse, and the Rabbis disagree with him. And the Mishnayot follow the Rabbis. And Rabbi Yoshiya is a Tanna and argues. (And I learned this from the words of the Gra, see there.)

Nevertheless, one should not make the walls from something that has a bad smell or from something that dries out within seven days and would not have the measure required for a partition. This is the ruling of our teacher, the Rema, in Section 1. Regarding something with a bad smell, this is certainly correct. However, concerning something that dries out within seven days, I am puzzled: in the Gemara (27b), Rabbi Eliezer and the Rabbis disagree. Rabbi Eliezer derives from the verse "You shall make the festival of Sukkot for seven days" that one should make a sukkah that is fit for seven days. The Rabbis, on the other hand, say the opposite: make the sukkah during the festival. If so, according to the Rabbis, whose opinion we follow, a sukkah does not need to be fit for seven days. This is also the ruling of all the legal decisors, as I will write in Section 637. Similarly, one may question what was explained in the previous section, Section 24, that s'chach (roofing material) that dries out within seven days is invalid. This is only according to Rabbi Eliezer's opinion, while we follow the Rabbis.

However, the opposite is difficult for me, from the case where Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda (23a) disagree about making a sukkah on the back of an animal. Rabbi Meir deems it valid, and Rabbi Yehuda deems it invalid. And it says: What is Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning? The verse states: "You shall make the festival of Sukkot for seven days" – a sukkah that is fit for seven days is called a sukkah, a sukkah that is not fit for seven days is not called a sukkah. And according to Rabbi Meir, this too is fit from the Torah, etc., see there. If so, both Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda hold that we need a sukkah that is fit for seven days. Do they then hold like Rabbi Eliezer and not like the Rabbis? And what forced the Gemara to say that even according to Rabbi Meir this is so? Furthermore, if so, we should rule according to Rabbi Eliezer, since Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yehuda, and the anonymous opinion of the Gemara hold this way.

Therefore, it appears to me in my humble opinion that in this matter, everyone agrees that it is necessary for the seven days of the festival to be fulfilled, even without the derivation of "seven days" – make a sukkah that is fit for seven days. Since it is written "You shall dwell in booths for seven days" – it follows that the simple meaning of the verse is that it is necessary for it to be fit for seven days. If not, it is not a sukkah at all. Rabbi Eliezer and the Sages only disagree about making a sukkah during the intermediate days of the festival, for Rabbi Eliezer derives from "The festival of booths you shall make for seven days" – make a sukkah that is fit for seven days, meaning: when you make a sukkah, make it so that you will have it for seven days, and therefore, during the intermediate days of the festival, one does not make a sukkah. But the Sages derive the opposite, that you should make a sukkah for all seven days, and one does make a sukkah during the intermediate days of the festival. In this, the halacha follows the Sages. However, when building it before the festival – it is obvious that it needs to be fit for seven days. And you should know that this is so, for many Tannaim hold that a sukkah must be a permanent dwelling, and if one does not build it as a permanent dwelling, it is invalid. And we hold that it must be a temporary dwelling. Nevertheless, our temporary dwelling is not inferior to their permanent one, for our temporary dwelling lasts seven days. Therefore, in any case, it is necessary for it to be fit for this temporariness just as for those Tannaim who require permanence.

It is clear that it is forbidden to make the walls [of the sukkah] from wood of an Asherah (a tree worshipped as an idol), and certainly the roofing (schach). And it is not only concerning the Asherah of Moses’ time, which is considered as if it were ground down and its measure nullified (Sukkah 31b, "with the lulav"), and a sukkah requires a specific measure. Rather, even if it is an Asherah of idol worshippers—it is forbidden to derive benefit from it. And even though mitzvot were not given for benefit, nevertheless, it is forbidden from the outset, just like with a shofar in Siman 586. Moreover, in a sukkah, the body actually derives benefit from sitting in the sukkah. Nevertheless, if one sat in such a sukkah—it can be argued that he has fulfilled the obligation, and even though it is a mitzvah that comes through a transgression, which is only a rabbinic prohibition as the Tosafot wrote in Sukkah (9a s.v. "that one"), and also perhaps because the transgression is not the cause of the mitzvah—it is not called a mitzvah that comes through a transgression (there 30a s.v. "because"). And one of the great authorities extensively investigated this (Nodah B'Yehudah, second section, Siman 133).

The Tur wrote: There are those who are particular, when making a wall from reeds, to set them up in the way they grow. As we say regarding the lulav, that one only fulfills the obligation with it in the way it grows. But this is not necessary, since the walls are valid if made of any material. Thus are his words, and similarly, Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote in section 1 that it is not necessary to set up the wood in the way it grows.

And the explanation of the matter is: Even though we say in the Tractate Sukkah (45b) that all mitzvot are only fulfilled with them in the way they grow, as it is stated: "standing acacia wood," and if so, when making the sukkah walls and wood, they should also be set up in the way they grow, because is not a sukkah included in all mitzvot? And this is the reasoning of those who are particular. But the Tur dismisses this, saying that this applies to a mitzvah that specifically needs to be made of wood, like the walls of the Tabernacle and the lulav. But a sukkah, which is valid if made of any material, even stones and metals – the way they grow does not apply to it. (And the s'chach is in the way they grow because they lie down. And "not in the way they grow" is called when the top is below and the bottom is above. And see section 29).

The walls of the sukkah – a law given to Moses at Sinai, like all partitions (Rashi, Sukkah 6b, s.v. "halakha"): Two walls according to their proper measure, and the third even a handbreadth. And this is derived from verses, as it is written: "in sukkot," "in sukkot," "in sukkot" – twice written in deficient spelling, and once in full spelling, which makes four. Exclude one for its own sake, as it is not for derivation but for its meaning (there, s.v. "legufei") – leaving three. And the halakha comes and reduces the third, establishing it with a handbreadth (Gemara there). Meaning: this was said to Moses at Sinai, that the third suffices with a handbreadth. And it is stated in the Gemara there that this handbreadth must be a "small handbreadth," meaning: slightly more than a handbreadth. And it is placed less than three handbreadths close to the wall, and it is considered as a wall of four, which is most of the wall of the sukkah, whose measure is seven handbreadths, as will be explained. And Rava added that a form of a doorway is also required, as will be explained. And from where do we know all these, since the halakha only mentions a handbreadth? And the Rosh wrote that Rava received this from his teachers, see there. And still, it needs to be understood where his teachers got this from? And if we say that this is only rabbinic, it is difficult to say so, for the handbreadth is certainly from the Torah. And even though in the Jerusalem Talmud at the beginning of Sukkah it says that the handbreadth is rabbinic, and from the Torah there are only two partitions, see there – nonetheless, in our Talmud in Niddah (26b) it is explicitly stated that the handbreadth is from the Torah, see there. And necessarily it is so, according to what they said that the halakha comes and reduces the third, and establishes it with a handbreadth. And from the Torah, there are three partitions, as explained in the Gemara. (And so wrote Tosafot 7b s.v. "sikkach," that the handbreadth is from the Torah, see there.)

And further, we need to understand: In the beginning of the Mishnah in Sukkah, it is taught that a Sukkah without three walls is invalid. But does a Sukkah truly have three walls? There are only two walls, and a handbreadth of the third wall does not qualify to be called a wall, obviously. And it appears to me, in my humble opinion, that the explanation of the teaching is as follows: Since a Sukkah is, in any case, a dwelling, albeit a temporary dwelling, it is still certain that the Torah requires one to sit in a place that has the status of a dwelling. Similar to the Sukkot in which Israel encamped in the desert. And since, according to the Torah, a private domain does not exist without three partitions, and with less than that it is considered a public domain, it is unreasonable to think that the Torah would designate such a place as a house. Therefore, it must have three partitions. However, the Torah only commanded two walls and a handbreadth, so how can we state the opposite? Hence, our Sages said that there are always three partitions. And it is this that is taught in the Mishnah "three walls." Nevertheless, regarding a Sukkah, it is only two walls and a handbreadth, as we will explain with Divine assistance.

The Ran of blessed memory has already written in the first chapter that even though a "tzurat hapetach" (form of an entrance) is considered a complete partition regarding Shabbat and Kilayim (forbidden mixtures) – nevertheless, regarding Sukkah it is not considered a partition. And proof of this is that they required a "tzurat hapetach" for the third partition. If this "tzurat hapetach" were effective for the other two partitions, it would not diminish the requirement for the third partition. Therefore, it is certain that a "tzurat hapetach" is not considered a partition for a Sukkah. There are several differences between the laws of Shabbat and the laws of Sukkah (as brought by the Rosh from the Jerusalem Talmud). And thus, the law comes that the third partition of a Sukkah is not like the other two partitions, but a complete partition of one handbreadth, and the rest is not a complete partition of a Sukkah but only a "tzurat hapetach". And it turns out that it is considered a private domain. This is why the Mishnah says: three walls. Nevertheless, regarding Sukkah, it is only two complete walls, and the third is just one handbreadth, aside from the "tzurat hapetach". (And one should not ask: if so, why did Rava say regarding two walls according to the law, etc. And similarly regarding Shabbat: "since it is a wall, etc.", why does he need the principle of "since"? For even regarding Shabbat alone, there are three partitions. But in truth, the version in the Rosh is "Rabbah", as written by the K"N and the P"Y, and they do not hold of the concept of "tzurat hapetach". Therefore, the Rif omitted it, as the Rosh wrote. Additionally, even without this, the principle of "since" is needed in several matters, as the Ran wrote regarding a breach being greater than what stands, and regarding the protrusion extending from the Sukkah, as will be explained. And pay attention and you will find it easy.)

The walls of the sukkah, if two are adjacent to each other in the shape of a "dalet" (like the Hebrew letter "ד"): one to the east and one to the south or north – make a wall that is slightly wider than a handbreadth, and place it less than three handbreadths away from one of the existing walls, so that it is considered connected (as if it were one continuous wall). This results in a partition of four handbreadths, which is the majority required for a valid sukkah. Additionally, place another beam at the end of this handbreadth-width wall, at the corner aligned with the second wall. Create a "tzurat hapetach" (a doorway frame) by placing a beam above, on top of the vertical beam and the handbreadth-width wall – and it will be kosher. It is not necessary for the beam on top to touch the vertical beams, as I wrote in Siman 362, since for a "tzurat hapetach" (doorway frame) the top beam does not need to touch the side beams. Rather, they need to be aligned with the top beam and be ten handbreadths high. See there.

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote in section 2 that if the tefach (handbreadth) and the wall reach the s'chach (roofing) - there is no need for a beam above them. And the custom of making the shape of the entrance round - is for decoration only. Thus far his language. And it is a printing error, and it should be said: that if the beam and the wall, etc. And the wall means the tefach (according to Eliyahu Rabbah), because the s'chach serves as the beam above them. And it is true that in the Jerusalem Talmud it is stated that one needs to make the beam above them for the purpose of the shape of the entrance, see there. However, when one roofs for the purpose of a sukkah - it automatically serves this purpose (see there). Additionally, in the Jerusalem Talmud Eruvin it is said that even if it was not made for that purpose - it is permitted (see there. But in our version in Eruvin chapter 1 halacha 9, it is the same as in Sukkah chapter 1 end of halacha 1, like the Magen Avraham).

If two of the walls are opposite each other and there is an open space between them, a tefach (handbreadth) does not help, because we require that the three walls be connected together. Rather, in such a case, we need for the third wall to be a valid wall of a sukkah, seven tefachim; and also through the principle of lavud, one should make a wall slightly more than four tefachim and place it within less than three tefachim of one of the walls. And since there is the measure of a sukkah, we do not worry even if it is far from the second wall. There is no need for the connection of the walls in this manner, as the s'chach (roof covering) connects them. There are those who are uncertain about this (Magen Avraham, subsection 3), but there is no doubt in this matter (Eliyahu Rabbah). If this were not the case, the poskim (decisors of Jewish law) would not have overlooked it. This is also explained by the language of the Gemara (7a), see there.

Some say that even in this case, a "tzurat hapetach" (form of a doorway) is required, which means placing a rod from the beam to the other wall. This is the opinion of the Rambam at the beginning of the fourth chapter; see there. And some say that in this case, a "tzurat hapetach" is not needed, as is explained by the language of Rashi and Tosafot there, that only for a handbreadth a "tzurat hapetach" is required; see there. In my humble opinion, it would seem that if the fourth wall is not more than three handbreadths away from the other wall, and it is considered as if it is a complete wall, a "tzurat hapetach" is not required even according to the first opinion, for they are like three complete partitions. And if a wall of seven handbreadths is made, it certainly does not require a "tzurat hapetach," even if it is distant from the other wall, for regarding the measure of a sukkah, they are three complete partitions. All the more so, a complete wall does not require a "tzurat hapetach." Those who customarily make a "tzurat hapetach" even with three complete partitions do so only for beautification purposes. But according to the law of partitions, it is not necessary.

And know that the Tur wrote that when there is a "tzurat hapetach" (form of a doorway), it is permitted to carry within it even on Shabbat. Just as it is considered a partition regarding a sukkah, so too it is considered a partition regarding Shabbat. This is his language. Meaning: even though rabbinically, three partitions are not effective for Shabbat without a side-post or cross-beam, nevertheless, on the Shabbat of Sukkot it is permitted due to the principle of "migu" (since). However, our Rabbi the Beit Yosef did not bring this in the Shulchan Aruch. His opinion seems to be that since the Rif and the Rambam omitted this statement, it implies that they did not agree with it. (See Beit Yosef. And in truth, there is no proof, for they explained in the Gemara regarding a Biblical matter, and as we hold, saying that a "tzurat hapetach" is not required Biblically, but rabbinically they agree. And the reason they did not write this is because it is not their practice to explain a law that is not in the Gemara, and regarding the law, they agree. And why should we say they disagree with the Tur on a rabbinic matter? Delve and you will find clarity.)

Some say that in the case where two walls are opposite each other and there is a gap between them, a wall of seven handbreadths is required. This means a wall larger than four handbreadths that can be positioned less than three handbreadths away from one of the existing walls. This applies when the walls are placed in an open area, such as a public domain or a plain, where there are no other walls opposite them. However, when two walls are placed opposite each other in a courtyard that has a surrounding wall, even if the surrounding wall is far from these walls, it is still considered as a third wall. In such a case, it suffices to have a partition more than one handbreadth wide, placed less than three handbreadths away from one of the existing walls (Beit Yosef). There are those who disagree with this, holding that it makes no difference since the surrounding wall is far from these walls (Magen Avraham, subsection 4). It is proper to be stringent according to the second opinion, as it seems to be the primary one, unless the walls are close to the courtyard wall, less than three handbreadths away, in which case nothing additional is needed.

And know that our teachers, the Tosafists (Sukkah 16b s.v. "bepachot"), raised a difficulty regarding this: It has been explained that a sukkah with two walls opposite each other requires a partition more than four handbreadths wide, and it must be placed within less than three handbreadths of one of the walls. Why do we need a partition more than four handbreadths wide? One could place a partition of two handbreadths close to the wall, leave a gap of less than three handbreadths, and then place another partition of slightly more than two handbreadths, creating a wall of seven handbreadths in total. Moreover, this is not even necessary, as one could make a partition of half a handbreadth and a bit more, place it within less than three handbreadths of the wall, and then place another such partition within less than three handbreadths of the first partition, totaling seven handbreadths. One cannot argue that the airspace on either side would nullify the standing partition, for any gap of less than three handbreadths is considered as joined (lavud). And with lavud, we do not say that the airspaces nullify the standing partition, as this is a law given to Moses at Sinai.

And they answered: Because it is said in the first chapter of Eruvin (16b) that any partition that is not made of both vertical and horizontal elements is not considered a partition. Therefore, a fourth side is specifically required, see there. This is not understood, as that is not the law, as explained there (Maharsha and Maharam). However, their intention is to say it qualifies universally, see there. This interpretation is strained. Rather, their intention is that in a sukkah that has only two complete walls, and a third wall of one handbreadth or four handbreadths – everyone agrees that we require complete partitions, and sticks less than a handbreadth or four handbreadths do not suffice (Magen Avraham). Certainly, this is true, for if it were not so, why would the law state a third wall of one handbreadth? Could one not erect sticks of something less than three handbreadths? Rather, it is certainly as the law stated that specifically one handbreadth is required, and here too specifically four handbreadths. And this is not surprising, for the form of a doorway is also not permitted in a sukkah except for the third wall, and not for all the walls, even though on Shabbat and in forbidden mixtures it is permitted for all the walls, as I wrote in paragraph 10. And here too, it is the same, see paragraph 20.

Regarding the matter of a breach being greater than the standing part – the laws of Sukkah are more lenient than those of Shabbat. For on Shabbat, if the majority of the partitions are breached without the form of a doorway, the partitions are nullified, as I wrote in Siman 362. However, regarding a Sukkah, even if there are breaches without the form of a doorway and the breach is greater than the standing part, the Sukkah is still valid. This is a halacha transmitted to Moses at Sinai, provided that the doorway is not wider than ten cubits, unless it has the form of a doorway, similar to Shabbat. With the form of a doorway, it is permitted even if it exceeds ten cubits. According to the Rambam, even the form of a doorway does not help if it exceeds ten cubits, unless the standing part is greater than the breach. We have already explained this in Siman 362, section 29, and most of the poskim disagree with him, see there. The poskim agree that the leniency of a breach being greater than the standing part in a Sukkah applies in general. However, with only two walls, there must be more standing part than breach (as the Maggid Mishneh, Bet Yosef, Taz, and Magen Avraham in section 6 state). There is a doubt whether the continuation under the form of a doorway is considered standing, since regarding Shabbat and kilayim it is considered a complete partition. Or perhaps, since regarding a Sukkah it is not considered a partition with only two walls, as I have written, it is not considered sealed. This latter view seems to be the main one.

Even when openings are permitted in two of the walls without the form of a doorway, nevertheless, the openings should not be made in the two corners but rather in one of them, because we require that the two walls be connected to each other, as explained. And although without the partitions themselves the majority being open was not permitted, nevertheless, with each reed being less than three [handbreadths apart] – it is permitted, because "lavud" is considered as connected (Taz, subsection 6). However, according to what I wrote in subsection 18, this only helps when there are four partitions, and not with two as they should be and a third of a handbreadth. This is not implied by Rashi (7a, s.v. "dofen"; see there). In any case, this is not a contradiction to subsection 18, because a handbreadth or four handbreadths of partition is certainly required, and with them alone, "lavud" does not help. For thus the law was stated that a partition of a handbreadth or four is required, but aside from that, "lavud" is effective.

Nowadays, the custom is to make complete partitions, because not everyone is knowledgeable in the laws of partitions. And one who does not have the means for four partitions – it is preferable to make three complete partitions rather than two complete ones and partial ones for the other two, for perhaps they will not be according to the law. One must also take care that the partitions are close to the covering itself. However, if it is impossible to make three complete partitions, it is necessary to make them according to the laws that have been explained. Also, the permissible distance between the covering and the partition will be explained with the help of Heaven.

It has already been explained that a "tzurat hapetach" (form of a doorway) without walls does not suffice for a sukkah except for the third wall. All the more so if one inserts four posts into the ground and places s'chach (roofing) on them, this is nothing. Even if one inserts four posts at the edge of the roof and the house's walls are visible on the roof, meaning that the roof does not extend beyond the walls below, like in our "capes" where the roof extends, if so, this is not a novelty; but even if it does not extend and one might say "extend the walls upward" — nevertheless, walls created by the principle of "extend the walls upward" are not permitted for a sukkah. Certainly, if the posts are placed in the middle of the roof, where "extend the walls upward" does not apply — it is obvious that this is invalid. And some say that at the edge of the roof with visible walls, we say "extend the walls upward," and the sukkah is valid. In this matter, the early authorities disagreed based on the versions in the Gemara (4b), and consequently, one should be stringent with a Torah prohibition.

The Gemara states (Sukkah 7a): "If one places a sukkah covering over a courtyard that has a side post, it is valid." Rashi, as well as the Rambam and the Rosh, explain that this refers to a thoroughfare (mavoi) that is open on both ends (mavoi mefulash), and we hold that a side post (lechi) serves as a partition. If one throws an object into a thoroughfare that has a side post from a public domain, he is liable. Although rabbinically, it is forbidden to carry even in a space enclosed by three complete partitions unless there is a side post on the fourth side, nonetheless, since from a Torah perspective, the side post renders it a private domain on Shabbat, therefore on Shabbat during Sukkot, the sukkah is valid as well. This is because, since the side post serves as a partition for Shabbat from a Torah perspective, it also serves as a partition for the sukkah. Therefore, even though for a sukkah, when there are two partitions opposite each other, a third partition of four handbreadths is required, and even when the two partitions form an L-shape (like the letter "dalet"), a third partition of one handbreadth and a bit more is required, nonetheless on Shabbat during Sukkot, one fulfills the requirement even with a minimal side post.

The Tosafists wrote that this refers to a closed courtyard with a side post, where carrying is permitted. But in an open thoroughfare, where carrying is forbidden, it does not help for the sukkah. And if you ask: if so, the sukkah is valid regardless? It is not so, such as where the sukkah covering was placed next to the side post and does not extend until the third wall. Thus, regarding the sukkah, there are only two walls and a side post. However, due to "migo" (since it serves as a partition for Shabbat), it is valid on Shabbat during Sukkot. (According to the Rif, it always is valid, and they were puzzled by this. See there.)

They also said there: If one placed schach (the covering of a sukkah) on top of the enclosures around wells, it is valid. These enclosures are four partitions, each one cubit by one cubit, and they permitted it for pilgrims, as explained in the second chapter of Eruvin (20b). Therefore, if they made a sukkah there, it is valid for the Sabbath within the festival, because of the principle that since it is effective for the Sabbath, it is also effective for the sukkah. And even though this was only permitted for pilgrims, and according to Tosafot, we do not permit this in an open area based on partitions that are only rabbinic, as I have written – this is because in that case, it was not permitted at all by rabbinic law. But here, it has been permitted for pilgrims in any case. And know that our teacher, the Rema, wrote about these two laws in section 7, and this is his language: “One should not permit except in a place where the side-posts and enclosures are permitted for the Sabbath, for then the principle of 'since' applies.” This is his language, and it seems to me that his intention is that for side-posts, they are only permitted in a closed alleyway, according to Tosafot, and for enclosures, they are only permitted in a place where the enclosures around wells are permitted, such as in the Land of Israel and not outside of it, as stated in Eruvin (21a) and in the Rambam, chapter seventeen of Shabbat. And the Levush omitted this gloss, see there. (And the Magen Avraham in small section 10 explained: when the side-post is standing next to the alleyway, and the enclosures are in the field, see there. And this requires investigation: what is the novelty, it is obvious?! Additionally: its source is from the Ran, and the Ran follows the approach of Tosafot that wherever there is no permission to carry, the principle of 'since' does not apply. See there.)

It is further stated in the Gemara (18a): If one places a sukkah covering over a portico that has posts— it is valid. If it does not have posts— it is invalid. According to Rashi’s interpretation, this is the explanation: Every courtyard is in front of the houses, and the houses are built on both sides of the courtyard. A portico is made in front of the houses along the entire length of the courtyard, and it is a roof without walls, which is wider than four cubits. Therefore, one who makes a sukkah covering in the airspace of the courtyard and supports the covering on the edge of the portico’s roof—the walls of the house do not count for the sukkah. Since they are more than four cubits away, we do not say "bent wall," as will be explained in Siman 632. However, if the portico has posts, meaning columns, less than three handbreadths apart along the edge of the roof—they are considered as three walls. For anything less than three handbreadths is considered as "joined." We do not hold that "joined" does not help for all walls. And even according to what we wrote in section 18, that with two walls and a handbreadth "joined" does not help—in any case, with three walls it does help. Here, the posts are on all three sides. But if it does not have posts—it is invalid, even though one might say that the edge of the portico’s roof descends and seals, making it as if there are walls—we do not say this. Because the edge of the roof only helps for the space under the portico, for which the edge was made, and not to be considered a wall for the space outside the portico (Gemara 19a). (See Magen Avraham, section 17, and in my humble opinion, it is not so. Be precise and you will find the light.)

The Tosafot, the Rosh, and the Tur explained that it has two complete walls in the shape of an "L," either east and south or east and north, and the third wall rests against the portico, with the s'chach (roof covering) touching the edge of the portico. If there are posts less than three handbreadths apart from each other – it is valid, meaning: even if these posts do not have a handbreadth in one of them. If not – it is invalid, and we do not say that the edge of the roof descends and seals, for the reason explained according to Rashi. According to both Rashi and Tosafot, when there are doorposts it is valid, even if these doorposts are visible from the outside and not from the inside, or from the inside and not from the outside – they are valid. This matter and its explanation were clarified earlier in Siman 663, see there. The Tosafot and the Rosh questioned: How is it possible to validate the visible from the outside and level from the inside? For it is obvious that the wall of the sukkah must be visible within the sukkah. The Rosh answered that it speaks of a case where there is also the form of a doorway, as I wrote earlier that the form of a doorway is also necessary. If so, it is sufficient from the Torah with just the form of the doorway. Therefore, the doorposts suffice when visible from the outside and level from the inside.

(There is a difference between Rashi and Tosafot regarding the place where we say the edge of the roof descends. For example, if one made the sukkah under the portico, where the walls are made within it, according to Rashi, we say the edge of the roof descends on all three sides, and according to Tosafot, only on one side, as written at the beginning of the chapter "All Roofs." From the Tur, it seems that with a beam of a handbreadth width, we say the edge of the roof descends, see there. It is surprising that in Siman 661 it is explained that with less than four handbreadths, we do not say the edge of the roof descends. The Bach explained that since only a wall of a handbreadth is needed according to Tosafot – a handbreadth suffices, see there. He also wrote that when visible from the inside, the form of a doorway is not needed when there are many doorposts. The Magen Avraham in subsection 12 disagrees with him and also wrote that we require an edge of the roof of four handbreadths. The Maharshal wants to say that even under the portico, we do not say the edge of the roof descends for the sake of the sukkah, and the Maharshal, the Bach, and the Magen Avraham disagreed with him, stating that we only do not say the edge of the roof descends outside of the portico. See there.)

The Rambam in Chapter 4, Halacha 8 has a different approach to this matter. He wrote: If one places the roof covering on top of a colonnade that has side posts, whether the posts are visible from the inside and not from the outside, or visible from the outside and not from the inside – it is valid. If it does not have side posts – it is invalid because it is like a sukkah made in the manner of an alleyway. For it only has the two sides of the colonnade, and the middle of the colonnade does not have a wall, and the opposite side does not have side posts. End of his words. The Maggid Mishneh explained that this means: the colonnade has two walls opposite each other, and the roof covering is placed next to the walls, and it has two side posts on the third side at its beginning and end – therefore we say the edge of the roof descends and seals. But if it does not have side posts – we do not say the edge of the roof descends and seals. (And the reason he does not explain with many side posts in the manner of 'lavud', but rather with the principle of the edge of the roof descending and sealing, seems to be because if so, how would it help if it is visible from the outside and flush from the inside, as per the question of Tosafot and the Rosh. But according to the reason of the edge of the roof descending and sealing, it works out well.)

Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, in paragraph 8 brought only the language of the Rambam. And our teacher, the Rema, wrote about it: "All this is the language of the Rambam. But others disagree, and therefore one should not make a sukkah in this manner." Up to here is his language, meaning: According to Rashi, Tosafot, the Rosh, and the Tur, the permissibility of the posts is due to the principle of "lavud" and not the principle of "pi tikrah" (Taz, subsection 9). And even though according to the Rambam, where the sukkah is inside the portico, certainly according to these authorities we also say "pi tikrah" as I wrote – nevertheless, here for another reason we do not say "pi tikrah," as I wrote at the end of section 661: that we only say "pi tikrah" in the case of two walls forming an "L" shape, and not when they are opposite each other. (And this is the intention of the Magen Avraham in subsection 12, and according to this, one should not be lenient even after the fact. And the Taz wrote in the name of the Levush to be lenient after the fact, and he did not mention at all what is at the end of section 661. Therefore, one should not be lenient even after the fact.)

Whoever wishes to open up his roof to the east or south, or in a similar manner, and to place roofing there next to the walls, and at one end there is a beam that is four handbreadths wide – we say that the edge of the roof descends and closes off, and it constitutes a third wall. There is one who requires also two posts under the beam, so that it forms a doorway frame (Taz there). I do not know why, according to a complete edge of the roof, a doorway frame is needed. (And perhaps he holds like the Maharshal in section 26, but others have already disputed his opinion, see there.) And know that the Maharil wrote: when they make the sukkah from boards, and after Sukkot they dismantle it, and in the next Sukkot they reassemble it, and so every year – they should mark the boards "A", "B", "C", so as not to change their arrangement from year to year. As it is stated in the Jerusalem Talmud: "And you shall set up the Tabernacle according to its plan". Is there a plan for the boards? Rather, a board that merited to be placed in the north – should always be placed in the north. This is the end of his words, and according to what I wrote in section 7, it is not necessary. Nevertheless, it is appropriate to do so, and this is the custom.

The height of the sukkah needs to be ten tefachim, like all partitions, since a partition cannot be less than ten tefachim. It is not necessary for the walls to reach the schach, as will be explained in Siman 633. Therefore, one can make a wall of seven tefachim and a bit more, and place them within less than three tefachim from the ground. And it is valid even if the roof is much higher, as long as it is aligned with the schach. Even if it is not perfectly aligned—as long as it is within three tefachim from the schach—it is valid, as it is considered as if it is connected (lavud). This applies to a tall sukkah. But if the sukkah is only ten tefachim high, one can make a wall of four tefachim and two small bits, placing it within less than three tefachim from the schach and within less than three tefachim from the ground, and it is valid. This is when there is no other partition. But when there is, the partitions should be made properly. Any time the walls are more than three tefachim from the ground, it is invalid, as it is considered a partition that kids can break through. But within less than three tefachim, we say lavud. All these laws are Halacha l'Moshe mi'Sinai (law given to Moses at Sinai).

One who makes his sukkah among the trees and does not support it on the tree – for if he did, it would be prohibited to enter it on a festival day – but supports it on pillars, with the trees merely serving as walls (i.e., the branches of the trees), and we hold that any partition that cannot withstand a common wind is not a valid partition – what should he do? He should tie the branches together and secure them so that the wind does not constantly move them. Even if it is in a place where the wind does not reach, it is invalid if the wind might move them, because it is not considered a partition if a common wind can move it. However, if most of the wall consists of strong and sturdy branches that the wind cannot move, it is valid. Alternatively, he can fill the spaces between the branches with straw and stubble, so they do not move when tied.

Therefore, one should not make the partitions of the sukkah from linen sheets or thin mats that the wind moves. And even though they are tied with pegs, we are concerned that they might become detached and he won't notice, making it a partition that cannot withstand a common wind (Tur). Nevertheless, after the fact, if he tied them, they are valid. And there is an opinion that one partition can be made even initially (Taz, subsection 11), and one can rely on this in a time of need. For someone who wants to make all the partitions from sheets, it is good to weave reeds into the partitions less than three handbreadths apart, so that the reeds themselves serve as a partition by the principle of lavud. (What the Magen Avraham wrote in subsection 17, that lavud does not help with three partitions, requires investigation. And it is explicitly proven from Rashi 18a, starting with "sikhakh," regarding a portico with partitions, that we say lavud with three partitions. And the main point is as I wrote in subsection 25, that with two partitions we do not say lavud, nor with three, see there. Analyze and you will find it easy.)

If someone is missing one wall to make the sukkah kosher, he can use living animals, setting up the animal as a wall. Even an impure animal is valid for the wall of a sukkah. And even though some forbid a shofar made from an impure animal, as I wrote in Siman 586, in this case of the sukkah wall we do not care, since inanimate objects and plants are also valid, the impure animal is not worse than them, as I wrote there. It is obvious that the animal needs to be ten handbreadths high, and the space between its legs must be less than three handbreadths from the ground. If not, it is necessary to fill the gap between the legs. And the animal must be high enough that even if it dies, it will still be ten handbreadths high, or it should be positioned in a way that it won't fall if it dies. There is an opinion that we do not worry about it dying, but this does not seem to be the case according to the Gemara (23a). This is specifically when the animal is tied, so it cannot move from that spot. But if it is not tied, it is not considered a wall, since it can run away, making it like a wall that cannot stand in a normal wind. Even though there is a concern that the tied animal might break free, as long as it hasn't, it is considered a wall, and we are not concerned it might break free. This is similar to the case of sheets where, for one wall, we do not worry about this, as I wrote.

In the previous section 362 it was explained that a person can also be used for a partition. However, on Shabbat and Yom Tov, one should not position him as a partition unless he is unaware, so that it does not appear like building, see there. Therefore, similarly regarding the wall of a sukkah, one can make his friend into a wall for the sukkah on Chol Hamoed, even if the friend knows he is being positioned as a wall. But on Yom Tov, it is forbidden to position him if he knows he is being used as a partition, and it is only permitted if he does not know, as explained there. Even on Yom Tov, the prohibition when he knows is only for the three walls upon which the validity of the sukkah depends. For the fourth wall, it is permitted since it is not necessary. With a person, we do not worry that he might leave, like an animal, since he has understanding. However, on Yom Tov when he does not know, there is a concern that he might leave. Nevertheless, as we explained there, with a person, this concern does not exist, see there. Be aware that the animal we permitted for a partition is only on Chol Hamoed and not on Yom Tov. Even though we made a distinction with a person between knowing and not knowing, and an animal does not know, it is still forbidden because it is like wood and stone since it lacks understanding, and it is considered as making a partition on Yom Tov (Magen Avraham, subsection 19, and Eliyahu Rabbah).

If one supports his sukkah on the legs of a bed, meaning: the bed is entirely enclosed by walls up to the bed on all sides, and he places the bed and roofs it on the tops of its sides, which are called the legs of the bed; and it is known that the mattress of the bed is in the middle of the height, and in such a way that if we measure from the mattress to the roofing there are not ten handbreadths, but only from the roofing to the ground there are ten handbreadths, and the roofing rests on the bed itself – it is invalid, because this sukkah has no permanence. That is to say, since there are not ten handbreadths from the mattress to the roofing. But when there are ten handbreadths – it is valid. There are those who wish to invalidate it due to the reason of supporting with something that is susceptible to impurity. However, this is not so, for it has already been explained in section 629, paragraph 19 that most authorities are not concerned with this, see there.

And this is when the sukkah is supported by the bed, such that if the bed were removed, the s'chach (covering) would fall. But if the s'chach is supported by four pillars, and only the walls of the sukkah are the walls of the bed, as I have written – the sukkah is not invalidated by the fact that there are not ten handbreadths from the bed to the s'chach, since there are ten handbreadths from the s'chach to the ground. The bed does not reduce the airspace, because even if the bed were removed, the s'chach would not fall, and then there would be a height of ten handbreadths. And if one asks: if the bed is removed, there will be no walls left for the sukkah. However, this is not relevant, because regarding the walls, we consider the walls of the bed as the walls of the sukkah, but not regarding the reduction of airspace. This is similar to placing a table or a high chair in the sukkah, such that there would not be ten handbreadths from their tops to the s'chach – would the sukkah be invalid because of this? Here too, it is the same concerning the validity of the sukkah, even though it is impossible to remove the bed because the walls would be missing for the sukkah. Regarding the validity of the sukkah, we consider it like other movable objects, which do not invalidate the sukkah by reducing its airspace. Some are concerned about not placing anything that can become impure as a support, and therefore refrain from fixing wooden slats in the s'chach of the sukkah, and this is correct. Nevertheless, after the fact, it is not invalid, because most of our Rabbis were not concerned with the reason of supporting with something that can become impure. And so it is in the Jerusalem Talmud. (Some have asked, according to what I have written that we say the edge of the roof descends and seals: if so, in every sukkah, we should say the edge of the roof descends and seals? However, this is not a question, because since the law of two walls and a third of a handbreadth has been stated – it is as if it is explicitly stated that we do not say the edge of the roof. Be precise and you will find it light.)

It is a law given to Moses at Sinai that the roofing (s'chach) of a sukkah must have more shade than sunlight. This is not similar to the concept of breaches in walls, where an equal amount of breaches and standing walls is permissible. With sunlight and shade, it is not the same. Therefore, if the roofing and the gaps above it are equal, the sukkah is invalid because this indicates that below, there is more sunlight than shade. This is known from the science of vision, that sunlight entering a window spreads out more than the width of the window itself, because light has a spreading property (Rambam in his commentary on the Mishnah, Chapter Two). Hence, since there must be more shade than sunlight, it is necessary that the roofing above is much more than the gaps. This is the view of Rashi (Sukkah 22b), the Rosh, as well as the Rif and the Rambam in Chapter Five, and this is also what the Tur wrote. This is the opinion of most of our rabbis.

Rabbeinu Tam, Rabbeinu Eliezer of Metz, and the Maor have a different approach to this matter. Their view is that the law regarding sun and shade was not stated independently, but rather is included in the principle of gaps and standing parts of partitions, and similarly, gaps and standing parts of the schach (roofing of the sukkah): if there is schach and airspace above, it is considered as gaps and standing parts, and it is permitted, and we do not measure the sun and shade. However, when we stand below and it appears to us that the schach is like airspace, it is invalid, because the airspace appears to shorten in the visual perception of the eye at a distance more than the schach. Therefore, if below it appears that the gaps are equal to the standing parts, it is a sign that the gaps outweigh the standing parts. This is also the case with partitions, when viewed from a distance. (And the Tur cites in the name of the Itur that he also permits in such a manner, but he writes that if above they are equal, it is a sign that below the shade outweighs the sun, see there. This requires further examination, as it goes against sensory perception.)

And the law is certainly according to the majority of the authorities. Nevertheless, the approach of Rabbeinu Tam is correct: if we look from the bottom upwards, not only if they appear equal is it invalid, but even if the covering (schach) appears slightly more – it is also invalid according to the approach of Rashi, because the air space diminishes in appearance. Therefore, even if it appears slightly more – nevertheless, they are equal, and when they are equal, it is invalid, because below the sunlight is more than the shade, as I have written. Therefore, from below it is necessary that the schach appears much more than the air (Bach). The general rule is: when we measure from above – the schach needs to be more than the air by a proper measure, so that below the shade will be more than the sunlight. All the more so, when we measure by eye from below upwards, it needs to be even more. And if we measure from below – the shade needs to be more than the sunlight.

And if the majority of the sukkah's covering provides more shade than sun by a small amount, and in the minority section, the sun is more prevalent than the shade by a small amount – it is valid, and one may even sit under the minority section, since overall, the shade is greater by a small margin. Just as with partitions regarding breaches and standing sections, we follow the overall measurement, as I wrote in Siman 362, so too regarding sun and shade. However, if in the majority section, the shade is only greater by a small amount – it is invalid, because in that case, the shade and sun are considered equal (Perisha). Similarly, if in the minority section, the shade is much greater, and in the majority section, the sun is slightly more prevalent, even though overall the shade is greater – it is invalid, because in any case, in the majority section, the sun is more prevalent (there in the name of the Riva). And even if in the majority section it is equal – it is obviously invalid.

Some of our rabbis are uncertain: Perhaps when we follow the majority, as I mentioned, it applies only to a small sukkah. However, in a large sukkah, where within the span of seven handbreadths, which is the measure of a sukkah, there is more sunlight than shade—perhaps it is forbidden to sit there, even though in total the shade is greater (Ran there). And even though regarding the partitions of Shabbat, it is clear that we follow the total, even in a very large area, that is because there is no measure for partitions. But within the span of a sukkah, perhaps each measure is considered as an individual sukkah. Based on this, our teacher the Rema wrote in section 2 that some are stringent if the sukkah is large and there is an area of seven by seven handbreadths where sunlight is greater, even though when combined with the whole sukkah, the shade is greater. These are his words. And from the general consensus of the poskim (decisors) it is clearly evident that this is also the case with a large sukkah. This is also clearly evident from the language of the Talmud (19a: Rabba bar bar Chana said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: the need is only for a sukkah where the majority is shaded, etc. Rabbi Oshaya said: the need is only for invalid schach less than three handbreadths in a small sukkah, etc., see there. And if you think that Rabba bar bar Chana in the name of Rabbi Yochanan is also referring to a small sukkah, as the Ran says, he would have also said "in a small sukkah," as Rabbi Oshaya did. This requires much analysis; examine and you will find it clear).

The manner of constructing the sukkah covering should be light, so that the stars of the sun are visible from within it, and also the stars of the night and the stars of the sun are sparks of the sun. However, post facto, even if it is as thick as a house, and even the stars of the sun are not visible from within it, it is valid. The Tur wrote that Rabbeinu Tam ruled that if rain cannot descend into it, it is invalid. The Rosh did not bring this, see there. And the reasoning of Rabbeinu Tam is from what we say at the beginning of Taanit that rain is a sign of a curse on the Festival. And they also said that one leaves the sukkah when it rains. And if it is permissible to cover it in a way that rain does not descend, it is not a sign of a curse, and one would not leave the sukkah. And the reasoning of the Rosh seems to me to be that we learned: one covers with boards that are less than four handbreadths wide. And it is obvious that when we cover with them, rain does not descend. And it cannot be said that one should distance one board from another; from where do we say this? Rather, certainly, most coverings are from things through which rain descends, as it is written in Nehemiah (8): "Go out to the mountain and bring olive branches," etc., and like our coverings. And about such it is taught that it is a sign of a curse, and one leaves the sukkah. But if someone covers with a valid covering material, and rain does not descend, it is valid. And it further seems to me in the reasoning of the Rosh, for it is written: "And a sukkah shall be for shade in the daytime from the heat, and for a refuge and for a covert from storm and from rain." And from this verse, it is derived at the beginning of Sukkah that above twenty cubits is invalid, see there. And according to Rabbeinu Tam, one must say that it is a refuge from the storm, and rain always drips (see Bach, and it needs investigation). And some of the great ones were concerned with the words of Rabbeinu Tam and invalidate when rain cannot descend (Levush and Bach, and see Magen Avraham). And our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, did not mention this at all. And it seems to my humble opinion that in a time of need, one may simply rely on the opinion of the Rosh to validate when rain does not descend into it.

The roofing, even if its covering is very thin, with much air space, as long as there are not three handbreadths in one place, which would invalidate it, as I will write in the next section; if overall its shade is more than its sunlight – it is valid. This means: this is the definition of roofing, and it does not depend on thickness or thinness. Likewise, if the covering was not evenly straight but disordered, meaning that some of the roofing is higher and some is lower, and this is so throughout the entire roofing – it is valid, provided that one part is not higher than another by three handbreadths, for then they are like two separate roofs. And sometimes even with a separation of three handbreadths it is permitted, such as if there is a continuous handbreadth in the higher part or more, and there is a place directly below it with a length of a handbreadth – we say "Chavot Rami," meaning: we consider it as if it is lowered from above and placed below. This is a law given to Moses at Sinai, that with a length of a handbreadth we say "Chavot Rami," and not with less than a handbreadth. And we see it as if it descended down and touched the edge of that which is below. Therefore, it needs to be aligned with the edge of that below, and there should be a free space of a handbreadth there.

And know: Even though when some of them are higher than three handbreadths, it is inevitable that the sunlight will be abundant there because it will enter from the side, nevertheless, since if we lower them, their shade will be abundant, and also now when the sun is in the middle of the sky and the shadow strikes beneath it, their shade will also be abundant. Therefore, we are not concerned about this. And even though there are those who disagree, as explained in the Tur, nevertheless, all the poskim (decisors) agree with this, as the Tur wrote, see there.

Reeds that extend behind the sukkah, such as when reeds protrude from the sukkah covering behind the middle wall, and they have the valid dimensions for a sukkah, and their shade is more than their sunlight; and this area has three walls, such as when the middle wall is not at the edge of the side walls but extends into them – it is valid. The novelty here, as written by the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch in Section 6, is that even though the middle wall was not made for this area, but for the main sukkah that is inside – it is still valid. This is their language. At first glance, this is not understood, for is it necessary to make the walls with specific intent for the sukkah? After all, even if the covering was made not for the sake of the sukkah, it is valid, as I wrote in Siman 635, and all the more so for the walls. However, their main intention is: Since the middle wall was not made for this area, there is room to say that the covering outside the wall was also not placed for the sake of providing shade, and in such a manner, it would be invalid, as explained there. But they inform us that this is not so. (I learned this from the words of the Perisha, see there. And according to the version of Tosafot 19a, beginning with "Le-barei" – it fits smoothly, see there.)

And similarly, the reeds that protrude from the sukkah covering towards the fourth open side, and one wall extends with them—it is permissible to sit under this covering, even if there is no wall opposite it. And not only if the second short wall is merely seven handbreadths, the measure of a sukkah, for it is obvious that every valid sukkah is thus: two walls according to the law, and the third a handbreadth. And it is permissible to use the entire wall even not opposite the handbreadth. Similarly, if one made the wall seven handbreadths, the measure of a valid sukkah, it is permissible to use beyond it. But even if one made the short wall much more than seven handbreadths, yet did not extend it to the long wall opposite it, one might say that this person did not extend the wall for the sake of validating the sukkah, for if so, why would he extend it more than seven handbreadths? Rather, it is certain that his intention was not to use more than the length of the short wall, and this part of the long wall extending with the covering has no relation to this sukkah, and it is like a separate sukkah. If so, it has only one wall, yet it is still valid, for it is always considered one sukkah. He did not want to extend the short wall further, and not for the reason of nullifying this part.

One might question whether this applies specifically when the entire sukkah was constructed continuously in one go. However, if initially, the walls were made equal and the s'chach extended beyond the sukkah, and then afterward, one wall was extended under the s'chach, making it like a separate sukkah, would this not be considered a valid sukkah? Or perhaps, even in such a case, since it is adjacent to the sukkah, it becomes as one sukkah and is valid. And so it appears to me, in my humble opinion, to be the main point. (All these laws are not found in the Rif, and I do not know why. Perhaps because the situation is uncommon.)

It has already been explained that it is a law given to Moses at Sinai that if the open space is equal to the standing space, it is permitted. Therefore, even though regarding sun and shade the ruling is not the same according to most authorities, as I have written, nevertheless regarding invalid and valid schach (roofing for a sukkah), this is indeed the case. Nonetheless, the Sages said (Sukkah 15b): Since it is impossible to be precise, it is necessary for the valid schach to slightly exceed the invalid schach. Therefore, if one roofed part of the sukkah with iron spits, which are invalid for schach, and none of them are four handbreadths wide, and he also did not place the short spits of four handbreadths in one place, for if there were four handbreadths of invalid schach in width, it would invalidate the entire sukkah, as I will write in the next section; but rather they are not four in one place, and between each spit he left open space equal to the width of the spit, and he placed valid schach there – it is still invalid, because it is impossible to be precise so that all the open space is filled with valid schach, and it turns out that the invalid schach is more. Therefore, it is necessary to have a bit more valid schach than the spits. Or if the spits were placed lengthwise, he should place the valid schach crosswise, or vice versa, for in this manner it is unavoidable that all the open space will be filled with valid schach. This means that in such a case, he places the edges of the valid schach on the invalid schach, for if not, they would fall, and thus all the open space is filled. (Such as when the valid schach has no other support except on the invalid schach from lengthwise to crosswise or vice versa. Examine this and you will find it easy to understand.)

And that which we said that there should not be four handbreadths (tefachim) in one place – this applies to a large sukkah. But in a small sukkah, which only has seven handbreadths by seven handbreadths – there should not be three handbreadths of invalid roofing (s'chach pasul) in one place, but rather less than three, as will be explained in the next section.

It has already been explained in Siman 629, Section 30, that according to Torah law, one may cover the sukkah even with planks that are four handbreadths wide. However, rabbinically it is forbidden, due to the decree regarding roofs. This means that one might say, "What difference does it make whether I sit under [the sukkah] or under the roof of my house?" But with planks less than four handbreadths wide, one may cover the sukkah, because roofs of houses are not made with planks less than four handbreadths wide. And for this reason, in our times, when roofs are made with planks less than four handbreadths wide, it is not permitted to cover the sukkah with planks at all. See there.

And it is stated in the Mishnah and Gemara (Sukkah 15b) that a house roofed with planks that have no overlay, meaning clay and pebbles, but are merely laid as they are, and now one wants to render them fit for a sukkah, and the planks are four handbreadths wide — and if one initially intended to use them for roofing it would be forbidden, as I have written. However, since it was initially a roof, and now one wishes to nullify its status as a roof and make it suitable for a sukkah, the sages permitted it in one of two ways: either remove all the nails and lift each plank and place them for the sake of the mitzvah of sukkah, or remove one plank from between these planks, meaning one plank between every two planks in the entire sukkah, and place valid sukkah covering in its place, and the entire sukkah will be valid for the reason that will be explained.

And the reason for this matter is that this sukkah is invalid due to "you shall make [the sukkah], and not [use] something that was already made" in its state of invalidity. Therefore, when one lifts each board and then replaces it, it constitutes a new act of making for the purpose of the sukkah. Similarly, if one removes one out of every two boards and covers the space with valid schach (sukkah covering), it is obvious that this constitutes a new act of making. And since one performs an act on each board between the two boards, it is as if he performed an act on the entire length of the sukkah (Bach). This follows the opinion of the Rosh, the Tur, and the Shulchan Aruch, section 9. However, from Rashi (Sukkah 15a, s.v. "Rabbi Meir") it is understood that not the entire length of the sukkah becomes valid through this, but only those between the boards, while the boards themselves remain in their state of invalidity. See there. And if you ask: there still remains the decree of a ceiling, since they are four handbreadths wide. However, in this context, they did not decree, because when we see that this person is knowledgeable about "you shall make, and not [use] something that was already made," and he makes a correction to validate it, how can we decree about him that he might sit under the ceiling of his house? Therefore, it is better than one who initially comes to cover [the sukkah] with boards that are four handbreadths wide.

But the Rambam wrote in Chapter 5, Halacha 8: A roof that does not have a coating... – this is invalid, for it was not made for the sake of the sukkah, but for the sake of a house. Therefore, if one shakes the boards and loosens the nails for the sake of the sukkah – it is valid, provided that no board is four handbreadths wide. Similarly, if one removes one from between them and places valid roofing material for the sake of the sukkah in its place – it is valid. So far his language. And it appears clearly that the Rambam holds the opposite: when the invalidity is also because of "ta'aseh v'lo min ha'asuy" (it must be made and not just happen) – it is more stringent. And it is obvious that boards four handbreadths wide are invalid, but even those that are not four – the Talmud invalidates them because they had an invalid status due to "ta'aseh v'lo min ha'asuy." But we do not hold this way. And this is the novelty he informs us: that even when the roofing material had the invalidity of "ta'aseh v'lo min ha'asuy" – nonetheless, shaking or removing one from between them helps. (And the Gemara there explains: they argue regarding the nullification of the roof, and this is its explanation: it is always when they are not four handbreadths, but one holds that in this invalidity shaking does not help, and one holds that it does. And this is the law. And the Magen Avraham, in subparagraph 8, wanted to explain that only shaking does not help with four, because of the appearance. But if one removes etc. – it is permitted even with four, as there is no concern for appearance, see there. And I am astonished: for according to the Rambam, the explanation of the argument about the nullification of the roof must be whether this nullifies it or not, and what relevance does appearance have? And this is also proven in the Magid Mishneh, the Beit Yosef, and the Bach, that all agree. And this is also the opinion of the Rif, as the Ran wrote, see there. Also, the Chomat Moshe objected to the Magen Avraham, see there, and see Taz, subparagraph 9. Examine and you will find clarity.)

A sukkah without a roof, such as when the tops of the walls are joined together like a beehive, or when the top of the wall of the sukkah is leaned against a wall and stands at an angle, is invalid because a sukkah must have a roof. The slants of tents are not considered as tents. However, if it has a roof even one handbreadth wide, or if it is less than three handbreadths from the roof and it is one handbreadth wide, and a handbreadth is considered a tent for several matters—therefore, it is called a tent, and it is valid, and the slant is considered as the roof of the sukkah. If it is made of materials suitable for sechach (roofing), it is permissible to sleep under the entire slant. Similarly, if it is leaned against a wall at an angle, and the wall is raised one handbreadth from the ground, and an upright structure of one handbreadth is made, with the slant resting on this structure, this handbreadth makes it as if it has a roof. According to Rashi, even if the handbreadth is air, this handbreadth makes it like a tent, as this handbreadth is considered a wall, and the entire slant is like a roof. It is clear that it must be ten handbreadths high, seven by seven, which is the measure of a valid sukkah. This is considered as a wall, and the rest above as a roof. Therefore, there must be valid sechach there. The ten handbreadths are measured vertically and not diagonally. It seems that even above the height of ten handbreadths, there must be seven handbreadths, as there is no valid sechach less than this measure. There are those who disagree with this, but the main opinion is as I have written (see Beit Yosef).

We hold that invalid schach (roofing material) invalidates the entire sukkah if it is in the middle by four handbreadths, and from the side by four cubits. And airspace invalidates the entire sukkah, whether in the middle or from the side, by three handbreadths. And the explanation of the matter is: When there is a sukkah with three walls, and the fourth side is open, and the invalid schach or airspace starts from the beginning of the middle wall and extends across the entire sukkah to the open side, dividing the sukkah into two parts, each part only remains with two walls. Therefore, when the interruption is less than three handbreadths, it is considered as if it is closed (lavud) and is not significant. But three handbreadths of airspace divides it into two, invalidating it completely. Invalid schach only divides at four handbreadths, as that is a significant measure. But less than four handbreadths is not considered significant enough to divide it. The reason airspace divides at three handbreadths is because the division is clearly noticeable. Therefore, when it goes beyond lavud, it divides. But invalid schach, where the division is not noticeable, only divides in a significant measure of four handbreadths.

Air that invalidates (a sukkah) with three handbreadths – invalidates whether it is in the middle of the sukkah or at the side. But invalid roofing (s'chach) – it only invalidates with four handbreadths if it is in the middle. However, at the side – it does not invalidate until four cubits, because we say: "bent wall." Meaning, we view this continuation of the invalid roofing placed on the roof as if it is part of the wall, except that the wall is bent onto the roof.
