And this is not from logical reasoning, but rather a law given to Moses at Sinai, that we say for invalid roofing at the side "bent wall" up to a span of four cubits. And for air, it is impossible to say this, as there is nothing to extend the wall to.

This is what we have explained regarding the concept of a "bent wall," that we consider the invalid sukkah covering as if it were part of the wall, bent and curved. This is how Rashi (17a) explained it, and similarly, Rambam wrote at the end of Halacha 14 in the fifth chapter, and this is his wording: "We see it as if the wall is bent, and we consider this invalid sukkah covering as part of the wall – and it is kosher. And this matter is a law given to Moses at Sinai." Until here is his wording. But if so, we need to understand: since we consider it part of the wall, then the valid sukkah covering is far from the wall? However, it seems to me, in my humble opinion, that the matter is as follows: The halacha was stated in this way – that we consider the invalid sukkah covering as if it were part of the wall and bent, and afterward, we consider it as if the wall bent and extends to reach the valid sukkah covering. And evidence for this is from the case of the bench, which will be explained in the next section, when the sukkah is higher than twenty cubits, and a bench was built within it to reduce the height. And we say in the Gemara (4a) that if there is less than four cubits from the edge of the bench to the wall – it is kosher due to the concept of a bent wall. And there, it is necessarily considered as if the wall is bent and reaches the bench, as Rambam wrote in Chapter 4, Halacha 14, and this is his wording: "He built a bench in the middle... less than four cubits – it is kosher, and it is as if the partition touches the bench..." Until here is his wording, which clearly supports our view. (And what Rashi there rejected this interpretation – it is not that this alone, but both are needed. And also with the bench, we can say the same, see there. And be precise and you will find it easy.)

There are those who say that we only apply the principle of a bent wall (dofen akuma) to partitions that reach the roofing. But if the partitions do not reach the roofing, we do not apply the principle of a bent wall (Ran and Kesef Mishnah there). The reason appears to be that wherever there is an interruption of air, even at a height, there is no place for the partition to be joined, and how can we say that the invalid roofing is considered part of the partition and bent? It does not extend to the partition on the side because of the intervening air. However, the Tur wrote that we do apply the principle of a bent wall even if the partition is only ten handbreadths high, and the roof is much higher, for we see the partition as if it extends upward, and then we say it is a bent wall. This is his language. Meaning, that we see it as if the partition extends upward. And if one asks: if so, should we also say a bent wall in the case of air? It is not so, for it is specifically with the upper air spaces of the partitions above the valid sukkah area where we can say so, and not with the air on the roof, which is the main area of the valid sukkah. As for the practical law, one should be stringent. (And so wrote the Bach, and the Magen Avraham in subsection 1. The Taz in subsection 1 elaborated in questioning the stringent view. According to what I have written, it is clear. Study and you will find it easy.)

And know: Regarding invalid schach (roofing material) that is less than four handbreadths – it is permitted to sleep under it, as it is considered nullified in relation to the entire sukkah. But at the side, where it invalidates at four cubits, and is valid at less – one should not sleep under it if it is four handbreadths wide, as it is considered a significant space. And with airspace, even less than three handbreadths, which does not invalidate the sukkah – nevertheless, one should not sleep under it, even though less than three handbreadths also contributes to the validity of the sukkah, as will be explained. Nonetheless, one should not sleep under it if it spans the entire sukkah, as it is very noticeable; or even if it does not span the entire sukkah, but it has a length such that a person can sleep under it with their head and most of their body. But otherwise – it is permitted, as there is no sukkah that does not have some holes. However, when there is a significant length of airspace – one should not sleep under it, nor eat or sit under it. And it is not comparable to invalid schach, because it is very noticeable.

And this distinction we made between airspace and invalid roofing, and between the middle and the sides – this all applies to a large sukkah. But in a small sukkah, which only has the minimum size of a sukkah of seven handbreadths – there is no difference between airspace and invalid roofing, or between the middle and the sides. Rather, in all cases, less than three handbreadths is valid and joins to make the sukkah valid, and one may sleep under it, as it is considered as if it is sealed. And three handbreadths invalidates it. The reason is simple: since it is small, it is impossible to have invalid roofing up to the measure of four handbreadths. For if so, most of it would be invalid, and it is necessary to reduce it to the measure of lavud. And anything that exceeds the rule of lavud is invalid in every matter and in every place.

A bent wall, as stated in the law concerning four cubits, applies whether it is in one wall or in all the walls. Therefore, if the roof of a house is breached in the middle, and one places valid schach (roof covering for Sukkah) in the breached area, and there remains from the ceiling around between the valid schach to the walls less than four cubits, it is kosher. However, one should not sleep under it as long as there are four handbreadths. If in one place there are four handbreadths, and in another place less – it is permitted to sleep in the area with less.

This is what has been explained: invalid roofing (s'chach pasul) disqualifies the sukkah in the middle if it measures four handbreadths, and an air gap disqualifies it if it measures three handbreadths. This is as I have written, that the sukkah only has three walls. One starts from the middle wall and moves across the entire sukkah until reaching the open side. In such a case, the invalid roofing or air gap separates the valid roofing on either side, leaving only two walls on each side. However, if one starts from the side wall and moves to the opposite wall, if there remains valid roofing next to the middle wall sufficient for a valid sukkah, which is seven handbreadths, the sukkah is valid since it has three walls. As for the side beyond the entrance, if the interruption is due to an air gap of three handbreadths, it is invalid in any case, as I have written. But if the interruption is due to invalid roofing of four handbreadths, and there remains sufficient valid roofing for a sukkah next to the entrance, if the valid roofing from the side reaches the middle wall within the measure of a curved wall (less than four cubits), the entire sukkah is valid. The inner side has three walls, and the outer side is made valid by the curved wall, as we consider the middle wall to be as if it stands next to the outer side. One cannot say that since the wall is removed from there, how is the inner side valid? For in truth, the wall is not removed, but is considered as if it stands there, and thus the entire sukkah is valid (Tur). It is obvious that if the third wall is only seven handbreadths and there are four handbreadths of invalid roofing after the seven handbreadths towards the open wall, only the inner side is valid. But the outer side has only two walls (ibid), the long wall and the middle wall, and it is invalid.

All of this is when the airspace or invalid roofing runs across the entire sukkah. But if in the middle of the sukkah there is an airspace of three [handbreadths] by three [handbreadths], or invalid roofing of four [handbreadths] by four [handbreadths], and on the sides the valid roofing is connected to each other, if there is from the airspace or invalid roofing to the valid sukkah until the middle wall – everything is valid. That which is on the sides is certainly valid, as it is connected to the measure of a valid sukkah. And also that which extends from the sides to the entrance is connected. And even the valid roofing that is after the invalid roofing or after the airspace towards the entrance, which is connected only through the sides – nevertheless, it is ultimately connected to the valid sukkah. It is no worse than the extension of the sukkah, which is considered like a sukkah as I wrote in the previous chapter. Only under the airspace or under the invalid roofing itself is it invalid to sleep there, as I wrote. And indeed, even if there is not from the airspace or the invalid roofing to the valid sukkah until the middle wall – we also do not hold it against it, as the entire sukkah combines together to the measure of a valid sukkah, since they are connected from the sides.

If there is invalid roofing (s'chach) less than four handbreadths, and next to it an open space less than three handbreadths – they do not combine to invalidate the sukkah. Therefore, if there is an open space of three handbreadths – it can be reduced by placing invalid s'chach, and it is valid. This applies specifically to a large sukkah. However, in a small sukkah that is only seven by seven handbreadths – they combine to invalidate. This is not due to combination, but because of the lack of the required measurement. If there are two handbreadths of invalid s'chach, then an open space less than three handbreadths, and then another two handbreadths of invalid s'chach – the Rosh, of blessed memory, is uncertain whether the two invalid sections combine to invalidate the sukkah. Do we say: Since the open space interrupts between them – they do not combine? Or perhaps: Since the open space is not seven handbreadths – they do combine. And it is not because of the principle of lavud, for we do not apply lavud to be stringent. If we applied lavud to be stringent – it would suffice with one handbreadth of invalid s'chach here, and one handbreadth there, with two handbreadths of open space in between, and through lavud it would become four handbreadths of invalid s'chach. Rather, it is certain that we do not apply lavud to be stringent. And even according to the one who holds that we apply lavud to be stringent – it is only when both are adjacent to each other, but not that the open space combines (see Magen Avraham, subsection 5, and earlier in Siman 382, subsection 9). However, the doubt here is that since it is not a significant space – it is not considered an interruption, and it is as if they are connected, making it four handbreadths of invalid s'chach. And we follow the stringent view, because this is a doubt concerning a Torah law.

It is stated in the Gemara (14b) that the rule that invalid roofing (s'chach) invalidates the sukkah with four handbreadths, applies even if the entire four handbreadths are not within the sukkah. For example, if one placed invalid roofing near the breached wall of the sukkah, it is impossible to apply the rule of a bent wall since there is no wall there. If three handbreadths extend into the sukkah and one handbreadth extends outside the sukkah, it is considered like invalid roofing extending from the sukkah and is treated as part of the sukkah. The three handbreadths are counted as invalid roofing, and it is forbidden to sleep under it because the handbreadth outside is considered as if it is inside. If it is a small sukkah, the entire sukkah is invalidated, as it is like a small sukkah with four handbreadths of invalid roofing, which invalidates the entire sukkah, as explained. Therefore, even if it is not by the breached side but by the wall side, where one could invoke the rule of a bent wall, nonetheless in a small sukkah, the measurement is lacking (Maharshal there).

According to this, one must be careful with our constructed sukkahs, where there is some building up to the point where the roof opens, which is considered invalid schach. It is true that it is less than four handbreadths, but in most cases, some parts extend outside the wall, outside the sukkah, and together it will be four handbreadths. Therefore, it is forbidden to sleep under it. There is an opinion that since there is a wall between them, they do not combine with each other. Therefore, if there are not four handbreadths of invalid schach within the sukkah, it is permitted to sleep under it (Magen Avraham, at the end of subsection 1). One should be stringent according to the first opinion. (Also, the Chemed Moshe disagrees with the Magen Avraham. The Pri Megadim is also uncertain about this and tends to be stringent; see there.)

And know that when we say that a bent wall up to four cubits is valid, this is in a horizontal plane. But with a sloped roof, even if its slope extends four cubits or more, if it does not extend four cubits in a horizontal plane, we still say it is a bent wall (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 2). Regarding what we say about a small sukkah of seven handbreadths, that any gap of three handbreadths invalidates the sukkah: it is not specifically seven handbreadths, but rather any sukkah less than ten handbreadths where a gap of three handbreadths would invalidate it, because seven handbreadths, the measure of a sukkah, would not remain (ibid., subparagraph 3). (And what the Magen Avraham wrote in subparagraph 2, that if the roof is bent upwards, sloping, and there are not four cubits in a horizontal plane, and only at its lower slope is there a beam within three handbreadths, if it combines to make four cubits, we do not say it is a bent wall – in any case, since on the side of the height it is three handbreadths away, we must say "lower and attach." However, we do not say this stringently, see there. And this is according to his view in Siman 492, where we say "attach" stringently, as I wrote in subparagraph 10. But for those who say we do not say "attach" stringently, even without lowering, we do not say "attach." Similarly, the Ran wrote in the dispute between Rav Acha and Ravina, that we do not say "attach" and a bent wall together, see there and in Mahatzit HaShekel, subparagraph 2.)

We learned at the beginning of Tractate Sukkah: A sukkah that is taller than twenty cubits is invalid. For a sukkah is meant to be a temporary dwelling, and up to twenty cubits, a person can make his dwelling a temporary one if he wishes. But above twenty cubits, it is impossible to make it a temporary dwelling because of its height. And the Torah is particular that the sukkah should be able to be a temporary dwelling (as explained by Rava there, and this is the ruling of the Rif, see there). There is no difference between a small sukkah and a large sukkah, and whether the walls reach the roof covering or not – in all these cases, it is invalid if it is above twenty cubits. (Because according to the other Amoraim there is a distinction, as explained in the Gemara, but according to Rava there is no distinction.)

Do not err in thinking that since the Torah commanded that a sukkah be a temporary dwelling, it cannot be made strong; this is not so. It can even be made with iron walls. Rather, the Torah said that it should be fit to be made temporary (Talmud). There is a question: Indeed, although this is certainly true, perhaps there is still more beauty in making it temporary, like the sukkahs made for the festival of Sukkot, and then dismantling them, rather than making them in permanent houses by removing the roofs, as we do with permanent sukkahs in houses? 

It appears that there is no concern at all, and there is no greater beauty in one over the other. The main aspect of "temporary" refers to the covering (schach) and not to the walls. However, it is still not possible to make walls in such a way that it is impossible to make them temporary at all. (And even though it somewhat seems from the language of Rava there, who says: up to twenty cubits... if it is made as a permanent dwelling, it is also valid, etc., and it implies "valid" post facto. This is not so, as he states this in reference to above twenty cubits, which is invalid even post facto. This is also explained in Tosafot, in the commentary beginning with "because," see there. Analyze and you will find clarity.)

Each cubit is six precise handbreadths, which corresponds to the wider ones being less by half a finger per cubit. And what we said above about being invalid if it is above twenty cubits, the intention is regarding the space, meaning: that the space should not be more than twenty cubits. But the roofing can be above twenty cubits. And so it is stated at the beginning of Eruvin, see there.

If it was higher than twenty cubits, and the twigs descend into the space within twenty cubits, if their shade is greater than their sunlight – it is valid. This is how it is stated in the Gemara (4a). The Rosh explains that "the twigs descend into the space within twenty cubits" means that they reach the interior space of twenty cubits, see there. That is to say, we maintain that the interior space of the sukkah should not be more than twenty cubits, but the roofing can be above twenty cubits. However, in this case, the interior space is more than twenty cubits, and only the twigs, that is, the branches and leaves that extend down, cover the space that is more than twenty cubits. And we require that these twigs themselves have more shade than sunlight. If not, it is as if they do not exist, since they are not part of the main roofing. For the main roofing, we would not require that at the end of the twenty cubits their shade is greater than their sunlight, as there is no reason for this except because they are twigs.

Some say that for this reason, since the protrusions are not an essential part of the sukkah covering, they must be within twenty [cubits] precisely, and their shade must exceed their sunlight. If they were above twenty [cubits], even if their shade exceeds their sunlight, we consider them as if they do not exist (Kesef Mishneh, Maharan; see there). This is also evident from the language of the Rambam in the fourth chapter; see there. However, the Tur wrote: and the protrusions descend to twenty [cubits]; see there. And this is in the language of the Rosh; see there. And Rabbeinu Beit Yosef in paragraph 2 concludes it ambiguously. (See Magen Avraham, subsection 2, who assumes that the words of the Rosh and the Ran are the same. But this is not so; see Machatzit Hashekel and Pri Megadim.)

A sukkah whose interior space is more than twenty cubits high, and one hangs beautiful objects under the s'chach (the roofing material), thereby reducing the interior space—it does not help, since this is not part of the s'chach. This is not comparable to adding leafy branches. Even though they are valid for s'chach, since they were hung for decoration and not for providing shade, they are not considered part of the s'chach and do not reduce the interior space that exceeds twenty cubits. Similarly, if one wants to reduce the interior space by raising the ground, such as by placing cushions or other objects on the ground to reduce the interior space—it does not count as reducing the space, since they are not nullified to the ground, even if one explicitly nullifies them. However, if one reduces the space with a large amount of straw placed on the ground and explicitly nullifies it, it is considered a reduction. All the more so if one places dirt and explicitly nullifies it forever—it is considered a reduction. But if one does not explicitly nullify it, even dirt is not considered a reduction. Even though it is known that it will not be removed, if it is not explicitly nullified, it is not considered a reduction, and certainly not straw. It seems to me that the same rule applies if one places wood on the ground, like a floor, and explicitly nullifies it—it is considered a reduction. Perhaps flooring is generally considered as if it were explicitly nullified. However, with all other objects, it does not help even if explicitly nullified, since they are not typically nullified. His intent is nullified against common practice, even if he genuinely wants to nullify them. Reducing the space on a holiday is not allowed, as this is considered building.

If the sukkah was higher than twenty cubits, and he built a platform against the middle wall across its entire length, and since it is a permanent structure, it certainly reduces the height, and if it has the dimensions of a sukkah, seven by seven handbreadths, it renders the entire sukkah valid. The rest of the sukkah is considered like the canes that extend behind the sukkah, which are considered part of the sukkah. And even though in that case the roofing is valid, whereas here the roofing above twenty cubits is invalid, nevertheless, this is not called invalid roofing, since it is valid, except that its height disqualifies it from being a valid sukkah. There is an opinion that holds that in this case, only the platform is valid, not the whole sukkah (Ran and Rabbi Yeshaya in the Tur). The Tur and Shulchan Aruch rule according to the first opinion, which is also the view of most authorities.

If one builds a platform on the side, meaning against one of the side walls, if there is more than four cubits from the edge of the platform to the other wall, it is completely invalid because the platform only has two walls. We do not say regarding the platform "extend and raise the partition," since these are not recognizable partitions, and they do not resemble the walls of the house. However, if it is less than four cubits, it is valid specifically on the platform, because we say "curved wall," and we view the covering as if it bends down to the edge of the platform at its border. But the rest cannot be validated as before, like the case of reeds extending behind the sukkah, since we remove the covering from there and place them opposite the platform. And even though this is only a conceptual view, how is it different from the previously explained law regarding invalid covering that interrupts in the middle of the sukkah? Even though regarding the outer side we view as if the middle wall stands here, nevertheless the inner side is also valid. This is not the same, because there the inner side is completely valid, and only regarding the outer side do we say "view." But here, outside the platform, it is invalid, and since we also lower it here regarding the platform, how do we make it valid for the platform? (And the Magen Avraham, section 6, elaborates on this; see there. And according to what I have written, it is straightforward. Also, what he questioned from the end of Siman 631 – I do not understand, because there we do not have "view," so what similarity is there? Be precise and you will find it easy.)

And if he built the platform in the middle, if there is less than four cubits from it to the wall on each side, it is valid on the platform. For it has already been explained in the previous section that we say 'curved wall,' even from four directions, and even if the platform is higher than ten [handbreadths], we do not say it is a separate domain, but it is nullified to the sukkah. But if there are four cubits between it and the wall, it is invalid. And we do not say 'extend and raise the partition,' even if it is ten high, as it is considered a domain by itself – in any case, it is not similar to the partitions of the house, as I have written, and we do not say 'extend and raise the partition.' And even if it is within four cubits to two walls, it does not help, for it only has two partitions, unless it is within four cubits to three partitions.

A sukkah has a specified measure for its height, both above and below. Above: as explained, it should not be higher than twenty cubits. Below: it should not be less than ten handbreadths, because anything less than ten handbreadths is not suitable even for a temporary dwelling and is considered merely a chicken coop, not fit for human habitation. Therefore, a sukkah whose interior height is less than ten handbreadths is invalid. Even if it is ten handbreadths high, if the covering (schach) is above ten handbreadths but the branches (that form the schach) hang down into the ten handbreadths, it is also invalid, even if they provide more shade than sunlight, because the invalidation is not due to the schach itself but because there is not ten handbreadths of usable space left, making it unfit for human habitation. Nevertheless, if decorations are hung there for the beautification of the sukkah, it is valid, even if they hang down into the ten handbreadths. Similarly, anything that is not considered part of a tent is permitted, since a tent is defined as ten handbreadths. This applies to the accessories of the sukkah, unlike the branches which constitute the roof of the sukkah and reduce the space of the sukkah's tent.

If the sukkah was less than ten handbreadths high, and one dug out the ground across the entire sukkah, thereby completing the height to ten handbreadths, it is valid. It is not necessary to shake the covering (s'chach) and place it again because of the principle "you shall make and not from what is made," since the covering is already valid. The lack of sufficient height in the walls does not invalidate the covering. To what is this similar? To someone who constructs a sukkah, first placing the covering and afterward making the walls. Should it be invalid because of this? Here, too, it is the same. However, there are those who invalidate it, and this will be explained in Siman 635.

If one did not carve the ground across the entire sukkah, but only carved out an area sufficient for the minimum requirement of seven by seven [handbreadths], if there is a gap of three handbreadths between the carved area and the wall, the sukkah is invalid, because the walls are too far from the valid sukkah area. We do not apply the principle of "bent wall" in this case, which is only said about complete walls that are invalid due to their distance from the schach (roof covering); in such cases, we say "bent wall." But we do not use the concept of "bent wall" to create a wall where there is no wall at all. However, if the gap is less than three handbreadths, the sukkah is valid because anything less than three handbreadths is considered as if it is connected (lavud). The Tur writes that the valid area is only under the carved space, not beyond it. This is not similar to the case of a platform, where we consider the excess as if they are sticks extending out, because in this case, it is not suitable for use at all. And it is not similar to the case at the end of section 631 in a sloped sukkah, where it is permitted to sleep even in the sloped area that does not have ten handbreadths, because there the wall is a complete wall, but due to the slope, it is shortened in one place, and it is all considered one wall. But here, where the wall stands, it is not considered a wall at all, so how can we validate it? (And this answers the question of the Magen Avraham, subsection 8, and so wrote the Chemed Moshe.) It is obvious that just as carving the ground to complete the required measure is effective, similarly if the schach is very thick, and one removes from the schach below until it completes ten handbreadths, it is effective like carving (there). (See Pri Megadim, subsection 9, who is uncertain about a pit that is ten handbreadths deep, and one places four poles on its edge and covers them with schach: do we say "extend and raise" because the partitions are recognizable from the inside? Or do we require them to be recognizable from the outside? See there. In my humble opinion, it is obvious that it is invalid. For in such a case at the edge of the roof, many also invalidate, as I wrote in section 630. And even those who validate, only validate walls that are on the ground. And proof: in the middle of the roof, according to everyone, it is invalid. And in a house, the partitions are recognizable. Therefore, we certainly require them to be recognizable outside, visible to all. Examine this and you will find it clear.)

Even though any house that does not measure four cubits by four cubits is not considered a house at all for any purpose—whether for a mezuzah, a parapet, leprosy, houses of walled cities, exemption from military service, or for placing an eruv, and it is not sufficient for division (Sukkah 3a), and it is not immersed for tithes and vows (Tosafot there in the name of the Jerusalem Talmud), and it is not considered the entrance of her father's house for a betrothed maiden (ibid.), because people do not live in it (Gemara there); nevertheless, regarding a sukkah, which is a temporary dwelling, tradition has come that seven handbreadths by seven handbreadths is sufficient, so that a person's head and most of his body can fit inside, along with a small table of one handbreadth by one handbreadth, and he fulfills his obligation with it.

Even though it is not suitable for a person to sleep in it lying down as usual, nevertheless, one can sleep in it sitting, leaning against the wall. And specifically, it must be seven by seven [handbreadths]. But if the length is less than seven and the width is much more than seven, or vice versa, even though in total it would be more than this measure, it is still not valid; for any dimension where the length or width is less than this measure, a person cannot sit in it properly (Taz and Magen Avraham). This is not like the opinion of those who wish to validate it if it is long and narrow. Even though for a mezuzah and other matters such a configuration is valid, that applies to an area of four cubits by four cubits, which has ample space, and not to seven by seven [handbreadths]. Regarding the size of the sukkah, there is no maximum measure. Even though for height there is a limit of twenty cubits, nevertheless, for length and width there is no maximum measure for a sukkah.

And if it is round, it is necessary to encircle it with a string of twenty-nine and two-fifths handbreadths, for in this way, according to the measurement calculation, it will have the equivalent of a square of seven by seven handbreadths. And even if it is a very large sukkah, but in one place there is a corner that does not have seven by seven handbreadths, it is forbidden to sit there; because since the place is narrow and not suitable for sitting, it is not considered part of the sukkah (Magen Avraham). There is proof for this from the Gemara regarding the cubicles of Queen Helena at the beginning of Tractate Sukkah, see there. And these seven handbreadths by seven handbreadths must be completely empty, except for the small table upon which one eats. And even if one places clothes to beautify it, and they reduce it from seven by seven handbreadths, it is invalid, because there will not remain enough space to sit. And it is not similar to the height of ten [handbreadths] mentioned in the previous section, where the width and length are as required.

Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote: If someone was with his head and most of his body in the sukkah, but his table was outside the sukkah, and he ate— it is as if he did not eat in the sukkah, even if it is a large sukkah. This is a decree lest he be drawn after his table. So far his language. And he ruled like the Rif and the Rambam in the sixth chapter, law 8, that just as the measure of a sukkah must be enough for his head, most of his body, and his table, so too in a large sukkah, one should not sit at the entrance and eat from a table that is outside the sukkah. But the Rosh, the Tur, and many of the Geonim ruled that in this case there is no prohibition, as the Tur wrote.

We should carefully examine the language of our teacher, the Beit Yosef, who wrote: "as if he did not eat in the sukkah." From a Torah perspective, he certainly fulfills the obligation, since this is only a rabbinic decree lest one follows after his table! Indeed, the language of Maimonides, who wrote: "If one’s head and most of his body were in the sukkah, but his table was outside the sukkah, and he ate – this is forbidden, and it is as if he did not eat in the sukkah... this is a decree, etc." up to here is his language. He elaborated intentionally, and this is its explanation: This is rabbinically forbidden, and they were strict with him as if he did not eat in the sukkah. But from a Torah perspective, he certainly fulfills the obligation. However, our teacher the Beit Yosef explicitly wrote "as if he did not eat in the sukkah" – implying that this is also from a Torah perspective, which is impossible. It appears that the matter is as follows: Certainly, this is only rabbinic, but the rabbis made it so that even from a Torah perspective, he does not fulfill the obligation, because the error is close at hand. They were compelled to this from the language of the Mishnah (Sukkah 28a), which states about this that one who does so has never fulfilled the mitzvah of sukkah in his life. This is what Maimonides says: "this is forbidden," meaning rabbinically, and they made it as if he did not eat from a Torah perspective. And our teacher the Beit Yosef also intended this, but he shortened his words (and so wrote the Tosafot in Berakhot 11a and at the beginning of Sukkah). And if part of the table is in the sukkah and part of it is outside the sukkah – it is permitted (Magen Avraham).

It is not necessary to construct the sukkah for the sake of the mitzvah, i.e., specifically for the purpose of the mitzvah of sukkah. And that which is written: "The festival of Sukkot, seven days for Hashem" – the intention is not to make it for the sake of the mitzvah, but rather that it is forbidden all seven days as if it were sacred, and this will be explained in Siman 638. Similarly, that which is written: "The festival of Sukkot you shall make for yourself for seven days" – this means that one is permitted to make a sukkah during the intermediate days of the festival, and this will be explained in Siman 637. And that which is written "for yourself" – the intention is not "for yourself" = "for the sake of the mitzvah," as we expound regarding tzitzit: "You shall make fringes for yourself" – "for your own obligation" (Menachot 42b). Rather, here the intention is to exclude a stolen sukkah, and this will be explained in Siman 637. For the implication of "for yourself" is "it should be yours," similar to "for yourselves" regarding the lulav. However, in the case of tzitzit, there is another verse: "and they shall make for themselves fringes," "for themselves" – from their own, not stolen. Therefore, we expound "for yourself" – for your own obligation, which is not the case with the sukkah (Sukkah 9a).

Nevertheless, even though we do not require a sukkah to be made with specific intent ("for its own sake"), not all sukkahs are valid. This is true even if the sukkah covering (schach) is made from materials suitable for covering, the walls are constructed according to the law, and the shade provided by the sukkah is greater than the sunlight. Specifically, we require that the sukkah be made for the purpose of providing shade, to hide from heat and sun, as it is written: "And a sukkah shall be for shade by day from the heat." 

But if the sukkah was made on its own (without human intention), it is invalid because it was not made for the purpose of providing shade. Similarly, if it was made to store items or for a grain warehouse, and the like, it is not considered a sukkah, because it was not made to hide oneself in the shade from the heat. 

Even if it was made to hide oneself, but was constructed to live in it all year round, it is considered a regular house for the entire year. The Torah states: "You shall dwell in sukkahs," not in a house where one lives all year long. Therefore, it is only valid if it was made as a temporary dwelling for the purpose of shade, to hide oneself occasionally from the heat of the sun, the rain, and the cold. Then it has the status of a sukkah, and one can fulfill the mitzvah of dwelling in a sukkah even if it was not made specifically for the mitzvah (see Bach and Magen Avraham).

Thus the sages taught: A sukkah of "Ganvach" is valid, a sukkah of "Rakbash" is valid. And this is its explanation: A sukkah made by a non-Jew or a woman to provide shade, as well as a sukkah made for animals to shelter them from the intense heat of the sun, and similarly a sukkah of Kutim who travel with flocks, and similarly a sukkah of shepherds, a sukkah of guards of dried figs left in the field to dry, and similarly a sukkah of city watchmen, and similarly a sukkah of fruit guards – all these are valid, because they are made for shade, as they make a sukkah to shelter themselves from the heat of the sun. (The Kutim mentioned are the Samaritans found in II Kings 17, who did not follow the Jewish religion. The novelty in all these cases is that, even though they were certainly not made for the sake of the mitzvah, they are nonetheless valid, since they were made for shade.)

And since it has been clarified that a sukkah made on its own is invalid, therefore: if someone has a pile full of grain, with straw on top, and he digs inside the pile, removing from it until there remain walls as required by law, and the straw serves as the covering – nevertheless, it is invalid, because the covering was not made for the purpose of shade. And if you say: let this digging be considered as making? It is not so, for this is the principle of "you shall make and not from what is already made," since he did no act to make it a covering. Specifically, this is when no space was left there at all. But if at the beginning of making the pile he left below, near the ground, a space of one handbreadth in height, spanning the area of seven handbreadths by seven handbreadths, and this space remained open, and he piled on top of it – the entire pile is considered like a roof, since it has a space of one handbreadth, which is for the purpose of a sukkah or for shade. And if he later dug into it and completed it to ten handbreadths – it is valid, since this is not considered "from what is already made," as it was made for the purpose of a sukkah or for shade. It is not only if he dug from below and left the handbreadth as it was, but even if he dug from above and did not reach the handbreadth – nevertheless, it is valid, because the entire pile has the name of a covering, only that it later became thin. This applies to a small pile. But if it is a large pile, and he left a space of one handbreadth spanning seven handbreadths, and afterwards he dug – the entire pile is not valid, only this area of seven handbreadths is valid. But the rest of the pile is invalid. It does not become like the reeds behind the sukkah, since there is neither a sukkah nor a wall here, only the name of a tent in general. And since the rest of the pile is invalid, therefore, if he dug the pile from both sides of the seven handbreadths, more than four cubits to each side – there is an interruption of more than four cubits of invalid covering between the area of the seven handbreadths and the walls. And it is not possible to say a bent wall for more than four cubits, and consequently, the seven handbreadths are also invalidated.

Rabbeinu the Rema wrote that one should not put up the roofing before making the walls. If one makes a handbreadth near the roofing, it is permissible to put up the roofing before making the rest of the walls, as in the case of one who hollows out a heap of grain. So far his words. And certainly, this is only a caution, for what invalidation is there in making the roof before the walls? This is not similar to hollowing out a heap of grain, where there is no name of a roof at all. But here, it is a complete roof. Some have invalidated it even after the fact (Levush and Taz), and they bring proof because a roof without walls is not called a tent. See there. And I am astonished: for regarding impurity, a roof without walls is considered a tent, with explicit proof from the Mishnah about one who hangs walls from top to bottom. See there in Rashi. Some have rejected this proof, but it is not clear. Nevertheless, there are those who are concerned about this opinion. (And the Bach and Magen Avraham permit it, see there.)

It is taught (Sukkah 9a): An old sukkah—Beit Hillel deems it valid. And what is an old sukkah? Any sukkah that was made thirty days before the festival. However, if it was made for the sake of the festival, even from the beginning of the year, it is valid. That is to say, anyone who makes it thirty days before the festival is presumably not making it for the festival. Nevertheless, it is valid because we do not require a sukkah to be made for its specific purpose, as I wrote in the previous section. And this is what this Mishnah teaches us: that we do not need a sukkah to be made for its specific purpose. And in the Jerusalem Talmud, it says that in any case, one must add something new to it for the sake of the mitzvah of the sukkah: either an additional handbreadth or something small over the entire sukkah. And if it was made for the sake of the festival, there is no need to add anything new, even if it was made from the beginning of the year. (See Chayei Adam, who wrote that if it was made for the sake of the festival for the following year, one must add something new. His words are puzzling.)

And certainly, the requirement to innovate something in it is not from the Torah. And even Rabbinically, it is not an absolute necessity, but rather an enhancement (Ran, Rivash, and Magen Avraham). The proof is that this is not mentioned in the Gemara. Additionally, in the context of Sukkot, the Ganevach and Rakbash mentioned in the previous section do not mention this. Nevertheless, for the most preferred observance of the mitzvah, it is clear that one should also innovate something in the name: either a handbreadth by a handbreadth in one place, or a slight amount across the whole. The innovation is simply to raise the schach slightly by this measure, and then to place it back for the purpose of the mitzvah of Sukkah (Taz and Magen Avraham).

A potter who has two huts, one inside the other, and makes his pots in the inner one and sells them in the outer one – the inner one cannot be used to fulfill the mitzvah of Sukkah, because it is his dwelling place all year round, and it is not apparent that he is dwelling there for the sake of the mitzvah. As I have written, one cannot fulfill the mitzvah of Sukkah with his house that he lives in all year. The outer one, however, can be used to fulfill the mitzvah, since he does not dwell there all year.

One who did not make a sukkah before the festival, whether unintentionally or intentionally, may make his sukkah during the festival days, even at the end of the festival days. And we do not require a sukkah for all the festival days. And that which is written: "The Festival of Sukkot you shall make for yourself for seven days" – on the contrary, its explanation is that for all seven days you can make yourself a sukkah (Talmud Sukkah 27b). Therefore, a person is permitted to leave his sukkah in the middle of the festival and sit in another one, even in several sukkahs (there), for each day is a separate commandment. Therefore, a child who becomes of age during the festival days is obligated in the sukkah for the remaining days. Similarly, a convert who converts in the middle of the festival is obligated in the sukkah for the remaining days (there).

One fulfills the obligation with a borrowed sukkah, and likewise one fulfills the obligation with a partnership sukkah, but one does not fulfill the obligation with a stolen sukkah. The reason for this is: even though it is written, "The festival of Sukkot you shall make for yourself," and it should have said "for yourself" and not for a partnership, "for yourself" and not borrowed, like by the lulav where it is written "you shall take for yourselves," and we derive this; but since it is written, "Every native in Israel shall dwell in sukkot," and it is written "in sukkot" (in an incomplete form), which implies that all of Israel could dwell in one sukkah. Consequently, it would not reach each person a value of a perutah. Therefore, we infer from this that one fulfills the obligation with a partnership and a borrowed sukkah, because it is necessarily like a borrowed one. However, the term "for yourself" excludes a stolen one. (Talmud there).

The Tur wrote in the name of Rashi that a stolen sukkah is only found when someone steals a sukkah that is made on the deck of a ship or on a wagon. For if someone forcefully took his friend's sukkah and expelled him from it, we hold that land cannot be stolen. And if he stole wood and used it for schach (roofing), he only owes the value of the wood, even if he did not change anything about it, and he fulfills his obligation with it after the fact. Ba'al Ha'itur wrote that if he stole wood and used it for schach and does not want to pay for it, it is considered stolen. This is his language: The sages decreed for the sake of penitents that if someone stole wood and used it for schach, he does not need to return the wood itself, but rather the value of the wood. Therefore, according to Rashi, even if he did not pay, there is no remaining debt on him, but the wood belongs to him, and it is not considered stolen. However, according to Ba'al Ha'itur, if he did not pay, the wood returns to the one from whom it was stolen, and it turns out that the sukkah is stolen. But a sukkah that is on a ship or a movable wagon - the sages did not decree on this, and according to everyone, it is considered stolen, and he is obligated to return it (and the Magen Avraham ruled according to Ba'al Ha'itur).

And the same law applies if Reuven built a sukkah on Shimon's land without his knowledge, and Shimon forcibly removed Reuven from his sukkah, took it over, and sat in it – he does not fulfill his obligation, because Reuven only has movable property, i.e., the wood, which can be stolen and needs to be returned, as there is no remedy for the repentant in this case. This is not comparable to someone who steals wood and uses it to cover his sukkah, where the thief only owes the value of the wood because he exerted effort in covering the sukkah. But here, the thief did not exert any effort and did not incur any expenses, and he is obligated to return the wood itself, making it so that he is sitting in a stolen sukkah. However, if Reuven built it with Shimon's knowledge, where Shimon lent him the land for the seven days of the festival, and Shimon then forcibly removed him and sat in it – he fulfills his obligation, because for all seven days the land is considered as belonging to Reuven, and what is attached to the land is considered like the land itself and cannot be stolen, and it is considered as borrowed. There are those who wish to say that even with his knowledge, it is not included in this rule, because land cannot be stolen (Magen Avraham, Siman 7). But the main opinion is the first one (as written by the Bach and the Gra).

All this applies after the fact. However, initially, a person should not sit in another’s sukkah without their knowledge, unless it is known that the owner would not object. Generally, it is assumed that people are pleased for others to perform a mitzvah with their property (Taz). But if the owner does object, or if the owner is present and presumably would object to someone else sitting there at that time, one should not sit there without permission. All the more so, it is forbidden to construct a sukkah on another’s land without their knowledge. Similarly, on communal land, one should not build a sukkah since no one has the authority to grant permission. However, it is customary to build sukkahs in the courtyards of synagogues, as it is assumed that the public is pleased for Jews to fulfill the mitzvah of sukkah there. Nevertheless, in a public thoroughfare, one should not build a sukkah, but if one does, the sukkah is valid, and one may recite the blessing over it. (The words of the Magen Avraham in sub-section 3 are not conclusive; see there.) Similarly, if a man's wife gives permission for another to sit in her husband's sukkah or to build a sukkah in their yard, this is allowed as it is assumed this is also the husband's will. However, if permission is given by the son or another member of the household, it is not valid and does not help. Possibly, in a pressing situation, their permission might also be valid, as it is assumed that the owners are pleased for others to perform a mitzvah in their sukkah or to build a sukkah on their land. Likewise, Jews should be careful not to cut the s’chach (roofing material) themselves if they do not have permission to cut s’chach for their sukkah. Since any stolen item may not be used to construct a sukkah initially, they should rather purchase it from a non-Jew, as the act of purchase constitutes a change of ownership, and it comes into their possession lawfully.

It is written: "On the fifteenth day of this seventh month is the Festival of Sukkot, seven days for the Lord." The word "Sukkot" seems redundant, since we already know it refers to Sukkot, as it is written later: "You shall dwell in booths..." It should have written "a festival of seven days," and I would know it refers to Sukkot (Baḥ). Rather, it comes to teach a lesson: the term "festival" (Chag) implies a celebration, which is the festival offering. Just as the divine name is invoked upon the festival offering, which is forbidden to benefit from until after the burning of its fats and limbs, so too the divine name is invoked upon the sukkah. This is what it means by "for the Lord," indicating that the sukkah should be holy for all seven days of the festival, and it is forbidden to derive benefit from it (Sukkah 9a). It is prohibited to take even a splinter from it to clean one's teeth.

According to Maimonides at the end of the sixth chapter, both the roof covering (s'chach) and the walls (d'fanos) are included in this prohibition. Similarly, the Tosafot explicitly write in Beitzah (30b). And the Rosh in Sukkah there wrote that the prohibition applies only to the s'chach and not to the walls. Most of the poskim agree with Maimonides and Tosafot, that just as the s'chach is from the Torah, so too the walls of the sukkah according to halachah—two as required and the third a handbreadth—are from the Torah. And so ruled our master, the Beit Yosef. (The Taz in subsection 1 elaborates that Maimonides' intention regarding the walls is not from the Torah, but due to the reason of muktzeh, see there. And the Tosafot in Beitzah there explicitly wrote that the walls are also from the Torah. And so the Rosh and the Tur understood Maimonides' view, and this is the opinion of most of the poskim. There is a practical difference in law, as I will write with Heaven's help.)

Based on this, the prohibition of deriving benefit from a sukkah is from the Torah. And even though in Shabbat (45a) it is explained that the prohibition is due to the principle of muktzeh, this applies when it has fallen. But as long as it stands, the prohibition is from the Torah (Tosafot there). Similarly, from the Torah, the prohibition is only for what is necessary for the preparation of the sukkah, but due to muktzeh, even what is more than needed for the preparation of the sukkah is forbidden (there in the name of Rabbeinu Tam). The Tur also wrote, and this is his language: "The wood of the sukkah, as long as the sukkah exists, is forbidden by the Torah. If it falls, it is forbidden by rabbinic decree. And Rabbeinu Tam explained that even while it exists, the prohibition is not from the Torah except for what is necessary for the preparation of the sukkah. The rest is only forbidden by rabbinic decree. And in the walls, there is no prohibition at all." But the Rambam wrote that even the wood of the walls is forbidden, and this was not clear to my master, my father, of blessed memory. This is his language. And we have already written that most of the authorities hold like the Rambam.

And certainly there is a distinction between whether the prohibition is from the Torah or from the Rabbis. For if it is from the Rabbis, then when a minor or a non-Jew takes from it – we do not need to be concerned with this. But if it is sanctified from the Torah like consecrated items – it is obvious that we must ensure that it is not desecrated by others. There is another distinction, for if the prohibition is from the Torah – no condition can be of any use. But if it is from the Rabbis due to the reason of muktzeh – sometimes a condition can be of use, as will be explained. Additionally, there is a distinction that if it is due to muktzeh from the Rabbis – it is permitted for the sake of a sick person who is not in danger as I wrote in section 328, and for the sake of human dignity as I wrote in section 312, and for indirect handling as I wrote in section 311. This is not the case if it is sanctified from the Torah – it is not permitted in all these instances, as is obvious.

Even on the eighth day, it is forbidden because since it was prohibited the entire seventh day, it was considered muktzeh during the twilight period (bein hashmashot) between the seventh and eighth days. And since it was set aside (muktzeh) during the twilight period, it remains set aside for the entire eighth day. Why don't we say that an egg laid on the first day of Yom Tov, which is forbidden on the second day of Yom Tov, is because it was muktzeh during the twilight period and should remain muktzeh for the entire day? This principle is only applied to muktzeh due to a mitzvah, such as the case of the sukkah and etrog, or muktzeh due to prohibition, like a candle burning on the eve of Shabbat during the twilight period, and not to ordinary muktzeh (see Tosafot Beitzah 30b, s.v. "ad").

If after having made the required dimensions for a kosher sukkah he added another wall, it is not prohibited, as this is considered like a mundane wall. And if it falls, it is permitted to move it, as it was not sanctified at all. Even while it stands, it is permitted during Chol HaMoed. But on Yom Tov, it is forbidden due to [the prohibition of] dismantling. However, if he made all four walls together, all of them are prohibited and set aside (muktzeh), even if they fall, since you do not know which one was for the purpose of making the sukkah kosher and which one was not. Therefore, the sanctity and muktzeh status apply to all of them. It appears to me that this applies to walls. But if he added to the schach (roof covering) even after achieving the required dimensions, in any case, he has sanctified it for schach, since it is placed on the previous schach. This is not the case for a wall that he built afterward, since it stands by itself (and similarly, it implies this in Beitzah 30b, see there).

And Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote that even if the sukkah fell apart, the materials are still prohibited, and a stipulation does not help. But the wood that is adjacent to the sukkah is permitted. Refer to above in Siman 668, Section 8. Until here is his language. Meaning: Later on, regarding the construction of the sukkah, it will be explained that a stipulation helps if one says: "I do not separate from them the entire twilight period." And this is what he says that a stipulation does not help with the walls – because one is forced to separate from them due to the prohibition of dismantling a tent. But the wood that is adjacent to the sukkah, meaning that he placed more than necessary for the qualification – is permitted if they fell due to a stipulation. But if they did not fall, they are prohibited due to muktzeh, as I wrote in Siman 668, that even the excess over the required amount for the sukkah is prohibited by rabbinic decree due to muktzeh. Similarly, if he placed wood or sacks on the walls of the sukkah to thicken them – they are prohibited if the sukkah did not fall, but if it fell, they are permitted if he made a stipulation before twilight. (The Taz, Section 2, is amazed that it contradicts there. And according to what I wrote, the explanation is the same here. And this also seems to be the opinion of the Magen Avraham, Section 1.)

Since the reason that a condition does not work for walls is due to the prohibition of dismantling a structure, as I have written, therefore, if it is in a manner where there is no issue of dismantling a structure, as I have written in Siman 618, a condition helps when it falls. Similarly, if it was built during Chol HaMoed, where there is no prohibition of dismantling a structure, a condition also helps. However, this is only in situations not prohibited by Torah law. But in matters that are prohibited by Torah law, no condition helps, even if it falls (Magen Avraham in the name of the Ran, see there).

And all of this only applies to a sukkah in which one has already sat once, for it has been sanctified. But if one designated it as a sukkah and did not sit in it – it is not prohibited when it falls, or in cases where there is no dismantling of a tent, or during Chol HaMoed even without a condition; for designation is not significant. And the same applies to a sukkah in which one sat the previous year; if one does not sit in it now – its sanctity is nullified, and it is as if one never sat in it at all. And a new action is required for its sanctity to take effect (there, subsection 2). And if one sat in it, even if it was not made for the sake of a sukkah, and even if nothing new was added to it, nevertheless, if one sat in it once for the sake of the mitzvah of sukkah – it becomes sanctified (there). But designation is not significant. And even though we derive the sukkah from the festival offering, and the sukkah has intrinsic sanctity like the festival offering, and concerning intrinsic sanctity we hold that designation is significant as above in Siman 42 – but in truth it is not exactly like the festival offering, and it is considered as items used for a mitzvah in this regard, that designation is not significant (Magen Avraham, and Taz subsection 3).

All decorations hung in the sukkah for the sake of adornment, if they are food or drink, it is forbidden to derive benefit from them all eight days, even if they fall, because they have been set aside for the mitzvah. And on Yom Tov and Shabbat, it is forbidden to move them, as they are muktzeh. Even one who does not hold by muktzeh agrees with muktzeh for the sake of a mitzvah, as even Rabbi Shimon agrees with this. If it is known that children will eat them, it is better not to hang them, or one should make a condition as will be explained. And if the sukkah decorations are objects, they should not be moved on Shabbat and Yom Tov, and one should not use them on Chol HaMoed for personal use. If one used myrtle branches that have a pleasant fragrance for roofing, or hung etrogim for sukkah decorations, or other fruits that have a pleasant fragrance, in any case, it is permitted to smell them, as they were not set aside from their fragrance. They were set aside from use, but not from their fragrance. However, one must be careful not to move them on Shabbat and Yom Tov due to the reason of muktzeh, as I have written. There are those who forbid smelling myrtle branches because, unlike the etrog which is suitable for eating (about which we say it was set aside from eating, but not from smelling), myrtle branches are solely for fragrance, so when they are set aside, they are set aside from their fragrance. This will be explained further in Siman 668 with Heaven's help.

Building a sukkah with these conditions is effective, and that is if one says on the eve of the festival, during the day: I do not separate from them for the entire twilight period. Meaning: I do not designate them for the mitzvah. And it is better to say: for the entire twilight period of all the days of the festival. However, in general, when one says: for the entire twilight period – it also means for all the days of the festival. And he may use them whenever he wants, for he did not designate them, and the sanctity of the sukkah and its mitzvah did not apply to them, and they are not considered sukkah decorations. And this is specifically when he said it in this manner. But if he said: I conditionally intend to eat them when they fall – this is nothing, for it is as if he says: the sanctity applies to them now, and when they fall – the sanctity will be removed. And this is impossible. However, if he said: I conditionally intend to eat them whenever I want – it is effective, as this includes the twilight period, and consequently, the sanctity does not apply to them. And there are those who believe that this wording is not effective (Ran there), but the Tur and Shulchan Aruch ruled that it is effective, and this is the ruling we follow. Nonetheless, it is better to satisfy all opinions, and to say in the wording: I do not separate from them for the entire twilight period. And there are those who believe that the condition is only effective after they have fallen, which is not the main opinion, as written by the Tur and Shulchan Aruch. Nevertheless, it is proper to be stringent, as this is the opinion of Tosafot in Shabbat (45a) according to one explanation, and the Baal Halachot Gedolot according to what the Tur wrote, see there.

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote: Some of the later authorities wrote that in these times we do not customarily make conditions (stipulations), because we are not proficient in the laws of stipulations. And this is the custom concerning decorations that are hung on the s’chach (roof covering). But decorations placed on the walls, such as painted sheets, are customarily moved because of the rain, even without a stipulation, because some say that there is no prohibition even on the walls themselves, all the more so on decorations. Nevertheless, it is good to make a stipulation regarding them. Thus far his words, and it is a great wonder: for there is no one who holds that there is no prohibition on the walls themselves (Taz, subparagraph 8). And also what he wrote, "all the more so on decorations," as it is clearly implied in the Gemara that there is a prohibition on Sukkah decorations (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 9). Rather, one can say a leniency, since it is the custom to use them, it is presumably based on the custom (Taz, ibid.). And one should make loops in the Sukkah decorations, so as not to untie a knot. And one should not hang shaatnez (a forbidden mixture of wool and linen) in the Sukkah, unless they are higher than a man's height. And those who engrave the verse "You shall dwell in booths" on fruits are not doing well. And everyone should be careful after Sukkot not to trample on the s’chach, and all the more so not to use them for a disgraceful purpose. Rather, one should place them in a corner and burn them bit by bit. And do not take this matter lightly, for the Name of Heaven has been invoked upon them (see Magen Avraham).

How is the mitzvah of dwelling in the sukkah fulfilled? By eating, drinking, sleeping, and spending time in the sukkah. Likewise, when one speaks with a friend, he should speak with him in the sukkah, for it is his home for all the days of Sukkot, as it is stated: "You shall dwell in sukkot for seven days." This means that all your dwelling during these days should be in the sukkah and not in the house. And from where do we know that these seven days include even the nights? We learn this from the seven days of the inauguration (of the Tabernacle), as it is written, "And at the entrance of the Tent of Meeting you shall dwell day and night for seven days." Just as there it included days and nights, so too here it includes days and nights (Sukkah 43b), and so it is in Torat Kohanim.

And this is what our sages of blessed memory said (Sukkah 26a): "You shall dwell" in a manner similar to the way you live, just as one lives in his house all year long—the Torah obligates him to leave his house and dwell here in the sukkah, with his beds, utensils, and bedding (Rashi). And for all seven days, a person makes his sukkah his permanent dwelling and his house temporary. If he has beautiful utensils and fine bedding, he should bring them into the sukkah. Similarly, all drinking vessels should be brought into the sukkah, such as flasks, cups, bottles, and glass pitchers. But eating utensils should not be brought into the sukkah. And thus it is said in the Gemara (Sukkah 29a): Drinking vessels should be in the sukkah, and eating vessels should be outside the sukkah. Rashi explained: The bowls, after they have been used for eating, need to be taken out. And this is also what the Tur wrote. But the Tosafot wrote that some explain this as referring to pots and kneading basins, and the reason is that we require it to be similar to the way one lives, and these items are not usually kept in a dwelling place but have a house of their own. And similarly, the Ba'al HaMaor explained: such as pots, spits, and bread ovens, and baking houses. This is his language. And so is the custom of the world not to bring earthenware vessels into the sukkah, like pots and the like, because these belong in the cooking house, and it is a disgrace to the sukkah. But as for bowls after eating, people are not careful. And it seems that people hold the explanation of the Tosafot and the Ba'al HaMaor as the main one (see Magen Avraham, subparagraph 3).

Our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, wrote following the explanation of Rashi and the Tur, and here are their words: "But eating utensils after eating, such as pots and bowls – outside the sukkah. The lamp – in the sukkah, but if the sukkah is small, place it outside the sukkah." This is their language. And now the custom is that pots are not brought into the sukkah even before eating, and bowls are not taken out even after eating. Nevertheless, one should be cautious about this, so that immediately after eating, the bowls and platters are taken out of the sukkah (Magen Avraham, subsection 3). However, if one brought eating utensils and earthenware vessels into the sukkah, the sukkah is not invalidated by this (ibid.). And the jug used for drawing water should not be brought into the sukkah (ibid.), as well as vessels used for storing flour, kneading troughs, and vessels for spices and pepper – these should be outside the sukkah (ibid.). Similarly, the vessel used for storing a lot of salt, from which small amounts are taken to put on the table. Also, one should be careful not to bring an earthenware lamp into the sukkah. The reason for not bringing any lamp into a small sukkah is obvious, so that the sukkah does not catch fire. There is no specific measure for this, but it is according to estimation.

One should not perform any disgraceful acts in the sukkah, so that the mitzvot are not disgraced in his eyes. Therefore, at night, one should not urinate into a vessel in the sukkah. Similarly, for washing hands, it is better to do so outside the sukkah. However, for the morning washing of hands, which is done right by the bed, it is necessary to wash them in the sukkah, and immediately afterward, remove the vessel from the sukkah. Similarly, placing shoes in the sukkah is not respectful. Only at night, when removing his shoes, is it necessary to place them on the ground next to his bed, but other shoes should not be brought into the sukkah. The etrog and lulav, however, should be kept in the sukkah, even if the lulav is in a vessel with water. Also, clothes that one removes, if they are not folded, should not be left in the sukkah. And his walking stick, if it is not a respectable stick, should not be placed in the sukkah. The general rule is: anything that one would not leave in his nice room at home, he should not leave in the sukkah. It is impossible to detail every specific case. (See Taz, Section 4, which states that this does not include the use of the bed.)

They eat, drink, and sleep in the sukkah all seven days, both by day and by night. One should not sleep outside the sukkah, even a brief nap. And even though casual eating is permitted, with sleep there is no such thing as casual. Thus, our sages of blessed memory said (Sukkah 26a): "There is no fixed measure for sleep." This means that sometimes a person who wants to sleep and dozes off for a little while has considered it a fixed sleep. But casual eating and drinking are permitted. And one who is stringent with himself and does not want to drink even water outside the sukkah is praiseworthy. We do not say that this appears as arrogance, for we find among the Tannaim that some acted this way and some acted differently, as explained there in the Mishnah. This teaches us that a person can act in this matter as he wishes. We do not say that one who eats casually outside the sukkah is not meticulous in the mitzvah, nor do we say that one who does not eat outside the sukkah is showing off. Rather, one does as he wishes, and another does as he wishes.

And what is considered a temporary eating? Bread up to the size of an egg, and an egg is included. And the Rambam in the sixth chapter wrote: A temporary eating is the size of an egg, or a little more or less. And his reasoning: This is the implication in the Gemara there, which says as much as a student tastes and then goes to the lecture, and certainly he does not measure precisely but approximately the size of an egg, or a little more or less. And the Rambam wrote: It is permissible to drink water and eat fruits outside the sukkah. So far his words. And he did not mention wine, because in the Gemara there only water and fruits are mentioned, and it is not his way to bring something that is not mentioned in the Gemara.

The Tur wrote that Rabbi Meir of Rothenburg was stringent even with fruits, not to eat them outside the sukkah. And Rabbeinu Peretz would say that fruits do not require a sukkah, but other things such as meat, cheese, and the like require a sukkah. And the Rambam wrote: It is permissible to drink water and eat fruits outside the sukkah. And one who is stringent not to drink even water outside the sukkah—blessing will come upon him. And my master and father, the Rosh, of blessed memory, wrote that even if you say that fruits and cheese require a sukkah, this is specifically for someone who establishes a meal over them. But one who eats them casually certainly does not require a sukkah. And drinking wine is also casual. However, since it is not customary to establish a meal over them, even one who does establish his meal over them is not considered fixed, as it is not more significant than casual eating of bread, which does not require a sukkah. But a cooked dish made from the five species of grain—one who establishes a meal over it is considered fixed and requires a sukkah. So far his words, and his words need explanation.

And the matter is as follows: In the Mishnah of Sukkah there, only fruit and water are mentioned as not requiring a sukkah, and no distinction is made between regular and temporary eating. However, in Yoma (79b), the Talmud discusses whether fruit eaten regularly requires a sukkah or not. The conclusion of Rava is that it does not require a sukkah. An objection is raised against him based on the statement of Rabbi, who said that we ate figs and grapes as a temporary meal outside the sukkah. Temporary – yes; regular – no? And the Talmud resolves: We ate them in a manner of temporary eating, meaning: we ate them regularly, but their eating was like temporary. And it is known that the law follows Rava, as he is later, and he is a great authority in the Talmud. However, Rabbi Meir of Rothenburg was concerned with the opinion of Rav Zevid, who resolves there not like Rava, and according to him, it is prohibited to eat fruit as a regular meal outside the sukkah. And Rabbi Rabbeinu Peretz disagrees with him, for it is obvious that the halacha follows Rava, and a sukkah is not required for fruit even if eaten regularly. He brought support from Maimonides, who holds this way, as he writes regarding temporary bread "the size of an egg," and for fruit, he writes it generally. From this, we learn that even regularly – a sukkah is not required for fruit. There is no doubt about this at all, and so is the law. (See Milchamot, which states that it is not necessary according to Rava's conclusion. The decisors did not agree with him on this.)

However, regarding meat and cheese, it is a different matter. For it is evident from the Talmud in Yoma that types of delicacies, when eaten as a fixed meal, require a sukkah (since it refers to a fixed meal of fruit, examine and you will find it clear). Tosafot and the Rosh in Sukkah there explain that "types of delicacies" refer to meat and fish, and other items that are eaten with bread, see there. Therefore, if one eats meat and cheese, which are eaten with bread, as a fixed meal, Rabbi Peretz agrees that it requires a sukkah. The Rosh of blessed memory disagrees with this for another reason, which is: both Rabbi Meir of Rothenburg, who is stringent about fruit, and Rabbi Peretz, who is stringent about meat and cheese, obviously only meant for a fixed meal, as we have explained, since for a casual meal there is no doubt that it does not require a sukkah. Therefore, since it is not customary to establish a meal on meat and cheese without bread, it follows that it is always considered a casual meal and does not require a sukkah. Drinking wine is always considered a casual act, and therefore it is also permitted to drink wine outside the sukkah. In the time of the Gemara, it was customary to establish meals on these items, but this is not the case for us. Now, "types of delicacies" also include food made from the five species of grain, as is evident from the Tosefta in Berakhot (chapter four), where it is taught: if they brought before him types of delicacies, he blesses "Borei Minei Mezonot" (in our text it reads "Borei Minei Kisnin," see there). And if one establishes a meal on it, it is considered a fixed meal and requires a sukkah. But with cheese and meat, it is not customary to establish a meal. According to this, all items other than bread and food made from the five species of grain can be eaten outside the sukkah, whether as a fixed meal or a casual meal. Establishing a meal with bread is more than the size of an egg, and establishing a meal with food made from the five species of grain in a cooked dish is not dependent on this measure, but rather on whether it is eaten casually or as a fixed meal.

Our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch in Section 2, ruled according to the Rosh and the Tur that aside from bread and a cooked dish from the five species, nothing else establishes a fixed meal. However, some of the great authorities have questioned this. There is an opinion that this applies only when one is alone, but when in a group, there is a fixed meal for drinking, whether wine or other beverages (Bach and Magen Avraham, sub-section 5). However, according to our custom, one does not recite the blessing "to sit in the sukkah" except during a meal (ibid.), and similarly for meat, cheese, and other items (ibid.). But with fruits, which is explicitly stated in the Gemara that there is no fixed meal for fruits, one certainly does not need a sukkah. There is an opinion that is stringent even when alone, if one eats and drinks in a fixed manner all items except fruits and water (Levush). However, in a fixed group, one should certainly be stringent in practice, as this is the leaning opinion. Additionally, perhaps the Tur and Shulchan Aruch only referred to an individual and not to a group. (There are those who are stringent even with fruits, but this does not seem correct. Delve into it and you will find it light.)

And behold, it has already been explained that sleeping [in the sukkah] is stricter than eating [in the sukkah], for even a temporary sleep is forbidden. Nowadays, however, people are lenient regarding sleeping [in the sukkah]. Our master, the Rema, has already addressed this in section 2, and this is his wording: "And regarding the current custom to be lenient with sleeping, where only those meticulous in mitzvot sleep in the sukkah – some say it is because of the cold, since there is discomfort in sleeping in cold places. It seems to me that it is because the mitzvah of sukkah is for a man and his household, a man and his wife, in the way he lives all year round. And in a place where he cannot sleep with his wife, as he does not have a separate sukkah – he is exempt. And it is good to be stringent and be there with his wife, as he lives all year round, if it is possible for him to have a separate sukkah." So far his words. And one should not ask: How can he fulfill [the mitzvah] at all in a place that is not suitable for being together? For it will be explained in the next section that a sukkah that is not suitable for sleeping is not a valid sukkah even for eating. This is not a question, for "not suitable for sleeping" means a place where a person cannot sleep at all, as will be explained there, not a place suitable for sleeping but where, due to another reason, he cannot sleep there (and this is the intention of the Magen Avraham at the end of subsection 8). A clear proof of this: the measure of a sukkah is seven handbreadths by seven handbreadths, and it is obvious that it is not suitable for two people, and even for one person, sleeping is difficult, as is clear. However, since in a pinch he can squeeze in and nap – he has fulfilled [the obligation]. All the more so in such a case.

However, this primary reason is very perplexing. For in the Gemara (Sukkah 28b), Rava does not hold the principle of "you shall dwell" similar to how you live in regard to a man and his wife at all. And it is Abaye who says this, but we hold according to Rava. For other matters, Rava does use this interpretation of "you shall dwell" similar to how you live, as we have learned many things from this. And even Abaye, who said that he thought to say this, teaches us that it does not apply in this matter, see there. (And what the Magen Avraham wrote there, that even with all this, one who is distressed is not relevant to this. And whenever he needs to, he should leave the sukkah.) And indeed, in the beginning of Arakhin regarding Kohanim, it truly says this, that even though they cannot be with their wives, in any manner that they can fulfill it – they should fulfill it. As Rashi explains there, and this is his language: it teaches us that even though it is not possible for them to fulfill it as they live, in the manner that it is possible for them – they are obligated. Until here are his words. Furthermore, the law given to Moses at Sinai states that the sukkah should be seven by seven, and surely it is not possible to be with one's wife there. (And also the proof of the Magen Avraham from the fact that all of Israel dwell in one sukkah, which certainly is not fit for this – is a clear proof. And in Arakhin there is also another version, for this version is difficult to explain the conclusion, see there. Be precise and you will find ease.)

Therefore, it seems to me in my humble opinion that the primary reason is the first one: due to cold.
